# Loci Communes Theologici


## 1 Prolegomena


### Chapter I. Prolegomena Concerning the Author of this little book

That the author of the little book which we have in hand is that Great Philip Melanchthon, the Phoenix of our Germany, a man most learned in every respect, and one who has deserved most excellently of the whole of literature, the very title indicates. Although, however, the nature of our time and our undertaking does not at all permit us to weave here the complete history of his life and the things done by him: yet one thing occurs which we neither wish to wrap in silence, nor can or ought to, while maintaining the reason of our office and duty,

Since in the previous century, and indeed already from the very beginning of the Evangelical Reformation undertaken by Luther, the Sacramentarian sect had moved a war without truce against the purer Church concerning the Eucharistic matter: and had indeed fought for many good years with great, but vain, effort: it happened that in the progress of time, and especially around A.D. 1554 and subsequent years, it came forth onto the stage of the Church with a changed appearance, as it were: that is, not by open war any longer, selling its tenets under the name and authority of Carlstadt, Zwingli, Oecolampadius, and others of that sort: but attempting its fortune through tunnels: namely, appealing not obscurely to the very authority of Philip Melanchthon: and seeking patronage for its error especially under his doctrine.

Hence John Calvin, in his second defense opposed to Westphal, while Philip Melanchthon was still alive, did not hesitate to burst out into these words: Concerning the sense of the Augsburg Confession, because Westphal is not a suitable judge, to whom shall I appeal rather than to the author himself (Philip Melanchthon)? Who, if he declares with a little word that I deviate from his mind, I shall immediately desist. The case of Luther is different, in whose words I have always frankly professed what I desire; so far am I from having bound myself.

And in his last admonition against the same Westphal: If I am found to have rashly abused the name of Philip, I refuse no marks of ignominy. I confirm only what I said, and indeed a hundred times if there be need, that Philip can no more be torn from me than from my own bowels in this Sacramentarian cause.

Hence the Wittenberg Crypto-Calvinists, soon after the death of the Blessed Luther, about to foist the Sacramentarian poison upon the Saxon Churches, sought a defense for their cause under the one Philippic Body of Doctrine.

Thus therefore it happened, that concerning the faith, confession, and constancy of Philip, a quarrel and contention between

theologians arose: while some indeed affirmed that he stood simply on the side of the Calvinists: others on the contrary maintained that he held a sort of middle opinion between the doctrine of Luther and Calvin: others finally contended that he remained entirely, and indeed always until his very last breath, addicted to Lutheran purity.

Concerning which controversy, what ought to be thought, so that it may be more correctly established, I am pleased to show a little more accurately: provided that we have observed, as if in passing, that Orthodox Doctors are whipped beyond all merit, when they are named Philippomastiges and Sycophants, who rage against great men, long since deceased, because of their profession of the truth. Certainly, if it had depended on us, the faith and Confession of Philip would never have been called into doubt, even in the smallest part. But since the Adversaries themselves have attempted, and today still attempt, to strike at the throat of the purer Lutheran doctrine through his side, we certainly could not and ought not to have approved of those wicked attempts by remaining silent, unless we had wished to betray the truth itself. Therefore, let them blame themselves, not us, if anything less than honorable redounds to the person and doctrine of Philip from this dispute.

But as for the matter itself, it is asked, what ought to be thought, in such a variety of opinions, concerning the faith and Confession of Philip? It is commonly said: Distinguish the times, and the Scriptures will agree: we can use this same thing in this place: Distinguish the times, and the truth will be clear. But with this distinction of times more accurately established: a different Philip will certainly emerge at the time of the writing and publication of the Augsburg Confession: and a different one in subsequent times.

Philip was therefore a pure and Orthodox, and clearly faithful defender of Luther against the Sacramentarians, in the year 1529, in the Marburg Colloquy, explaining his mind in these words: I, Philip, have decreed and decided that I never wish to consent with Zwingli: for I know that Zwingli and his associates do not write correctly about the Sacrament. In that same year, from the Diet of Speyer, he wrote to Oecolampadius: When I have weighed everything that seems most firm on both sides; I will say with all respect to you, I do not however go into your opinion. For I find no firm reason that satisfies a conscience departing from the literal meaning of the words.

And a little later: Therefore, if your opinion about the Lord's Supper pleased me, I would simply profess that you contend that the body of the absent Christ is represented, as in a tragedy. I see that promises exist concerning Christ: I will be with you until the end of the age, and similar ones: Where there is no need to tear the divinity away from the humanity. Therefore I feel that this Sacrament is a testimony of the true presence. Since this is so, I feel that in that Supper there is a communion of the present Body: Since the literal meaning of the words conflicts with no article of faith, there is no sufficiently great cause why we should abandon it. And this opinion concerning the presence of the body agrees with other scriptures that speak of the true presence of Christ among us. For that is an opinion unworthy of Christians, that Christ occupies a certain part of Heaven in such a way that he sits in it as if enclosed in a prison.

Philip professed the same purity in the following year, '30, and indeed in those very Augsburg Diets, manfully with Luther, thus formulating the Tenth Article concerning the Lord's Supper against the Sacramentarians: Concerning the Lord's Supper, they teach that the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat in the Lord's Supper: and they disapprove of those who teach otherwise. In order to assert this purity more evidently, in the same year he opposed the Sacramentarians with a booklet in which he collected the testimonies of the Fathers concerning the Lord's Supper, where in the preface to Friedrich Myconius he writes thus: To some we seem very dull, because in the words of the Gospel, This is my body; we do not see a Metaphor, nor do we understand that we are freed from infinite questions by the benefit of one Metaphor. It seems to be madness to hold tenaciously to the most absurd opinion of all, when a metaphor offers another most convenient one. Here they will also find fault with my judgment, because I did not detect hyperboles and allegories in these testimonies. But I am not ignorant of these 'wise drugs,' as the Poet calls them, with which others medicate these sentences. But what could not be evaded by this art? I have proposed these sentences of the Fathers naked, without glosses, so that I might leave the judgment to the candid Reader, whether they speak of a Corporal presence, or of efficacy alone. I indeed maintain that they expressly assert that the Body of the Lord is truly present in the Lord's Supper.

And a little later, having brought forward the passage of Augustine from Epistle 57 to Dardanus, he adds these for the sake of explanation: Nor could anyone persuade me that Augustine in this place so binds the Body of Christ to one place, that it cannot be elsewhere. For what can be brought forward, besides the judgment of human reason, why we should include Christ in one place in this passage?

And a little later: Nor do I find any sufficiently firm reason why we should depart from this opinion (of Luther). It may be that another opinion flatters an idle mind, which is more agreeable to human judgment, especially when thus instructed and adorned with learnedly conceived arguments. But what will happen in temptation, when the conscience will dispute, what cause it had for dissenting from the opinion received in the Church? Then those words: This is my body, will be thunderbolts. What will a terrified mind oppose to these? With what scriptures, with what voice of God will it fortify itself, and persuade itself that a Metaphor necessarily had to be interpreted here.

And again: I therefore follow the opinion of the ancient Church, which affirms that the Body of Christ is present in the Supper, and I judge that this has the testimony of scripture. For I do not find a firm reason why, by the name of Body in the words of the Supper, it is necessary to understand only a sign of an absent Body.

In the same year, or certainly in the one immediately following, in a letter to Martin Gorlitius, Pastor of Brunswick, he likewise candidly opened his mind, writing thus: As far as the Zwinglian faction is concerned, I bid you be of good cheer. I have acknowledged in the presence of those who heard the leaders of that sect how they have no Christian doctrine, but merely philosophize in a childish manner; therefore they will not be able to endure. For every plant which is not of God shall be rooted up. Although they have disputed for a full six hundred years, they bring forward nothing except this saying: The flesh profiteth nothing. This they have recently twisted to refer to the Flesh of Christ. You have seen what I have gathered concerning this matter, from which you can know my opinion: (he understands the booklet concerning the opinions of the Fathers) I would rather die than affirm this, which they affirm, that the body of Christ cannot be in more than one place. Therefore, you should constantly argue against them publicly and privately, when there is opportunity. You should also blame this in them, that they say nothing about the use of the Sacraments; there is no mention of justifying faith in all the books of the Zwinglians. When they name Faith, they do not understand that which believes in the remission of sins, which believes that we are received into grace, heard, and defended by God, but they understand a historical one. But Christians ought to know the use and exercise of faith.

In the same year 1530, the same Philip and Brentius wrote to Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, and having brought forward the most serious reasons, they dissuaded him, while maintaining the purity of Religion, from the possibility that the Zwinglians could in any way be received into society and brotherhood. Where, among other things, they also have this: As far as brotherhood is concerned, perhaps brothers who are entangled in some error can be tolerated, just as the Savior Christ himself bore with his erring disciples. But those who not only introduce monstrous doctrines into the Church, but also defend them, are not to be acknowledged as brothers. For one must in no way assent to impious and uncertain dogmas. Wherefore, what is discussed at length in that very writing which has been returned to us concerning the toleration of the weak, is to be understood only of those who do not attempt to defend uncertain dogmas: For indeed, the divine Paul received the Galatians into brotherhood; but concerning those who defended errors, he said: I would that they were even cut off who unsettle you, etc.

Latin:

Autorem libelli, quem præ manibus habemus, esse Magnum illum Philippum Melanchthonem, Germaniæ nostræ Phœnicem, Virum undiquaque doctissimum, deque re literaria universa præclarissimè meritum, vel ipse titulus indicat. Quanquam verò integram vitæ rerumque ab ipso gestarum historiam, hoc loco ut pertexamus, Temporis & instituti nostri ratio minimè permittit: Unum tamen occurrit, quod silentio involvere neque volumus: neque etiam salvâ officij & muneris nostri ratione, possumus aut debemus,

Cum superiore seculo proximo, & quidem jam inde à primo fermè Reformationis Evangelicæ per Lutherum susceptæ, exordio, Gens Sacramentaria ἄσπονδον planè bellum puriori Ecclesiæ de negotio Eucharistico movisset: & verò annis benè multis, magno quidem, sed irrito conatu pugnasset: factum, ut progressu temporis, & potissimùm circa A. D. 54. & subsequentes, mutato quasi habitu in proscenium Ecclesiæ prodiret: hoc est, non aperto amplius Marte, sub nomine & autoritate Carolostadij, Zwinglij, Oecolampadij, & id genus aliorum sua venditaret placita: sed per cuniculos fortunam tentaret: ad ipsam nimirum Philippi Melanchthonis autoritatem haud obscurè provocans: & sub hujus potissimum doctrina, errori patrocinium quærens.

Hinc Johannes Calvinus, in secunda defensione opposita Westphalo, vivente adhuc Philippo Melanchthone, in hæc verba erumpere, non dubitavit: De sensu Confessionis Augustana, quia idoneus judex non est Vvestphalus, ad quem potiùs, quàm ad autorem ipsum (Philippum Melanchthonem) provocabo: Qui si verbulo declaret, me à sua mente deflectere, protinus desistam, Lutheri alia est ratio, in cujus verbu, quid ego desiderem, semper ingenuè professus sum: tantùm abest, ut me obstrinxerim.

Et in admonitione ultima contra eundem Westphalum: Si Philippi nomine temerè abusus comperiar, nullas ignominiæ notas recuso. Salum quod dixi, & quidem centies, si opus sit, confirmo, non magis à me Philippum, quàm à proprijs visceribus, in hac causa Sacramentaria, posse divelli.

Hinc Crypto-Calvinistæ Witebergenses, mox post obitum B. Lutheri virus Sacramentarium Ecclesijs Saxonicis obtrusuri, sub uno Corpore Doctrinæ Philippico, causæ præsidium quærebant.

Sic ergò factum, ut de Philippi fide, Confessione & Constantia, rixa & contentio inter

Theologos oriretur: alijs quidem à Calvinianorum parte ipsum simpliciter stetisse affirmátibus: alijs contrà mediam quasi quandam sententiam inter Lutheri & Calvini doctrinam ipsum tenuisse, statuentibus: alijs denique totum ipsum, & quidem semper ad extremum usque halitum, Lutheranæ puritati mansisse addictum, pugnantibus.

De qua satè controversia quid sit sentiendũ, ut rectius constet, libet paulò accuratius ostendere: dum modò illud quasi ἐν παρόδῳ observaverimus, pręter omne meritum Orthodoxos flagellari Doctores, dum Philippomastiges, & Sycophantæ nominantur, qui in viros summos, jam-pridem vitâ functos, ob veritatis professionem rabiosè invehantur. Certè si per nos stetisset, nunquam fides & Confessio Philippi, vel ex parte minimâ in dubium esset vocata. Sed cùm per ipsius latus ipsi Adversarij jugulum purioris doctrinæ Lutheranæ petere conati sint, hodieƣ; petant: haud profectò improbos istos conatus silendo approbare vel potuimus vel debuimus etiam, nisi ipsam veritatem prodere voluissemus. Sibi ergò, non nobis imputent, si quid minƣ honorificum ad Philippi personam & doctrinam ex hac disputatione redundat.

Cæterùm ad rem ipsam quod attinet, Quæritur, quid in tanta varietate sententiarum, de Philippi fide & Confessione sit sentiendum? Vulgò dici consuevit: Distingue tempora, & concordabunt Scripturæ: idem hoc loco usurpare possumus: Distingue tempora, & patebit veritas. Distinctione autem hâc temporum accuratiùs institutâ: alius certè prodibit Philippus tempore conscriptæ & editæ Confessionis Augustanæ: alius verò temporibus subsequentibus.

Purus ergò & Orthodoxus, ac fidus planè Lutheri ὑπερασπίστης adversus Sacramentarios fuit Philippus, Anno 1529. in Colloquio Marpurgensi, his verbis mentem suam explicans: Ego Philippus decrevi & statui, me nunquam consentire velle cum Zvvingliano: Scio enim Zvvinglium & Socios ejus, non rectè de Sacramento scribere. Quo eodem anno ex Comitijs Spirensibus ad Oecolampadium scripsit: Cum omnia, quæ in utraque parte firmissima videntur, expendi; dicam pace tua, non tamen eo in tuam sententiam. Nullam enim firmam rationem invenio, quæ conscientiæ discedenti à verborum proprietate satisfaciat.

Et paulò pòst: Itaq̃, si mihi vestra sententia de Cœna Domini placeret, simpliciter profiterer, vos absentis Christi Corpus, tanquam in tragœdia, repræsentari contenditis. Ego de Christo video extare promissiones: Ero vobiscum usque ad consummationem sœculi, & similes: Vbi nihil opus est divellere ab humanitate divinitatem. Proinde sentio, hoc Sacramentum veræ præsentiæ testimonium esse. Quod cum ita sit, sentio in illa Cœna præsentis Corporis κοινωνίαν esse: Cum proprietas verborum cum nullo articulo fidei pugnet, nulla satis magna causa est, cur eam deseramus. Et hæc sententia de præsentia corporis, convenit alijs cum scripturis, quæ de vera præsentia Christi apud nos loquuntur. Nam illa est indigna Christianis opinio, quod Christus ita quandam Cæli partem occuparit, ut in ea, tanquam inclusus carceri, sedeat.

Eandem puritatem Anno subsequente 30. & quidem in ipsis illis Comitijs Augustanis masculè cum Luthero professus est Philippus, sic adversus Sacramentarios Articulum Decimum de Cœna Domini informans: De Cœna Domini docent, quod Corpus & Sanguis Christi verè adsint, & distribuantur vescentibus in Cœna Domini: & improbant secus docentes. Quam puritatem ut evidentius assereret, eodem anno Sacramentarijs opposuit libellum, in quo collegit testimonia Patrum de Cœna Domini, ubi in præfatione ad Fridericum Myconium sic scribit: Quibusdam valdè hebetes videmur, quod in verbis Evangelij, Hoc est Corpus meum; non videamus Metaphoram, nec intelligamus nos ab infinitis quæstionibus unius Metaphoræ beneficio liberari. Videtur insania esse, sententiam omnium longè absurdissimam mordicùs tenere, cùm aliam commodissimam offerat metaphora. Hic desiderabunt in me judicium etiam, quòd in his testimonijs hyperbolas & allegorias non deprehenderim. Ego verò non ignoro hæc σοφὰ Φάρμακα; ut Poëta vocat, quibus medicantur has sententias alij. Verùm quid non poterit eludi hâc arte. Ego has sententias Patrum sine glossematis nudas proposui, ut judicium candido Lectori relinquerem, utrum de Corporali præsentia loquantur, an de sola efficacia. Ego quidem statuo, eas ῥητῶς asseverare, quod Corpus Domini verè adsit in Cœna Dominica.

Et paulò pòst allato Augustini loco ex Epistola 57. ad Dardanum hæc explicationis causâ subjungit: Neq́; quisquam mihi persuaserit, Augustinum hoc loco sic alligare Corpus Christi ad unum locum, ut alibi esse non possit. Quid enim afferri potest, præter humanæ rationis judicium, cur hoc loco includamus Christum in unum locum?

Et paulò pòst: Neque ego ullam satis firmam rationem invenio, cur ab hac sententia (Lutheri) discedamus. Fieri potest, ut alia sententia blandiatur animo otioso, quæ est magis cōsentanea humano judicio, præsertim sic instructa & ornata argumentis eruditè cogitatis. Sed quid fiet in tentatione, cùm disputabit conscientia, quam habuerit causam dissentiendi à recepta sententia in Ecclesia? Tunc ista verba: Hoc est Corpus meum, fulmina erunt. Quid his opponet mens perterrefacta? Quibus scripturis, quâ Dei voce muniet se, ac sibi persuadebit, necessariò fuisse hîc interpretandam Metaphoram.

Et rursus: Ego itaque sequor veteris Ecclesiæ sententiam, quæ affirmat, adesse Corpus Christi in Cœna, ac judico hanc habere scripturæ testimonium. Non enim invenio firmam rationem, cur nomine Corporis in verbis Cœnæ oporteat tantum absentis Corporis fignum intelligi.

Eodem anno, vel certè subsequente statim proximo, in Epistola ad Martinum Gorlitium, Pastorem Brunswicensem mentem suam itidem candidè aperuit, sic scribens: Quantum attinet ad factionem Zvvinglij, jubeo te bono animo esse. Ego agnovi coràm auditis ante signanis illius sectæ, quàm nullam habeant Christianam doctrinam, tantùm pueriliter philosophantur: ideò non poterunt durare. Omnis enim plantatio, quæ non est ex Deo, eradicabitur. Cum totis sexcentis annis disputaverint, nihil afferunt præter hanc vocem; Caro non prodest quicquam. Hanc nuper torquent ad Christi Carnem. Vidisti, quid ego collegerim de hac re, unde meã sententiam cognoscere potes: (intelligit libellum de sententijs Patrum) Ego mori malim,quàm hoc affirmare, quod illi affirmant, Christi corpus non posse nisi in uno loco esse. Ideò constanter arguas eos publicè & privatim,cum erit occasio. Vituperes hoc quoq́; in eis,quod de usu Sacramentorum nihil dicunt,nulla est mentio fidei justificantis in omnibus Zwinglianorum libris. Cum nominant Fidem,non intelligunt illam,quæ credit remissionem peccatorum,quæ credit nos recipi in gratiam, exaudiri & defendi à Deo, sed intelligunt historicam. Vsum autê & exercitium fideiChristianos nosse oportet.

Eodem anno 1530. idem Philippus & Brentius scripserunt ad Philippum Landgravium Hassiæ, & gravissimis in medium adductis rationibus dissuaserunt, salvâ puritate Religionis, Zvvinglianos in societatem & fraternitatem, minimè posse recipi. Ubi inter reliqua sic etiam habent: Quod ad fraternitatem attinet,fortassis fratres,qui aliquo errore impliciti sunt, tolerari possunt, ut & ipse Servator Christus discipulos errantes ferebat. At qui doctrinas prodigiosas non modo introducunt in Ecclesiam, sed etiam defendunt, pro fratribus agnoscendi non sunt.Nullo enim modo impijs& incertis dogmatibus assentiendum est. Quare quæ in ipso scripto, quod nobis redditum est, de tolerandis infirmis prolixè agitantur,de ijs demum intelligêda sunt, qui incerta dogmata non conantur defendere : Etenim Divus quidem Paulus Galatas in fraternitatem suscepit:de ijs autem, qui errores defendebant, dixit : Vtinam & abscindantur,qui vos labefactant &c.


### Chapter I. Prolegomena Concerning the Author of this little book (continued)

And at the end of that letter: If the reasons by which Zwingli is moved satisfied consciences in such a way that they could rely upon them in the Judgment of God, we would easily approve of his allegories: But it is certain that consciences cannot rest in these arguments.

For the response of the Landgrave, by which he attempted to extenuate the error of the Zwinglians, see Defense II of Dr. Johannes Pappus against Sturm, p. 25. Similarly, the other response of Philip and Brentius to the letters of the Landgrave, page 27.

In the following year, 31, with the consent of Luther and the Protestants, he caused the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, which was indeed written at the Diet itself but not received by the Emperor, to be published in print together with the Confession.

But so far is it from the case that Philip at that time made a divorce from the Doctrine of Luther by even a hair's breadth, that he rather not only repeats the words of the Confession nakedly, but asserts through a clear declaration that the body and blood of Christ are substantially present and dispensed in the Supper: nay, he even confirms that not only the Roman Church affirms the corporal presence, but that the Greek Church formerly thought and now thinks the same.

And that Philip persevered constantly in this truly Orthodox and genuinely Lutheran opinion up to the year 1535 is clearly evident from the fact that not even the Calvinists themselves can produce any testimony from the writings of Philip published thus far by which they could clearly prove the contrary.

And thus far Philip has shown himself to be an entirely faithful assistant and colleague to our blessed Luther, so that it could truly be said of them: Their labors were divided, but their mind was one: Luther fed the sheep with his mouth, Melanchthon the bees with the flower; or that of the Italian poet:

To will and to nill was the same for both, and their mind was associated in a happy age, and rich in sacred things, Concord.

Moreover, the use of what has been said so far can and ought to be twofold, yet both are refutatory; the former is to be opposed to the Crypto-Calvinists, who today, while magnificently extolling that golden Concord of Luther and Philip, seek this one thing, but quite insidiously, that under the cloak of Philip they may hide the Calvinist dogma and tacitly introduce it into the Church of God, just as if it were the dogma of Luther himself, for the reason that Luther and Philip are in no way to be torn apart. Their mouths must therefore be shut by showing how far that Concord extends and how long it lasted. The latter refutatory use concerns the manifest Calvinists, who shamelessly and mendaciously boast that Philip always stood on their side. For the contrary is clearly evident from those things which we have proposed thus far.

Moreover, how Philip, using his own counsel and perhaps more from an innate softness and timidity of spirit than from deliberate malice, gradually and increasingly fell away from the purity and ὀρθοδοξία of true Lutheranism, and began to conspire with the Zwinglians, the very safety of the Church demands that we show in good faith.

And to begin from the year 1536, in which occurred that famous Act of Concord between B. Luther and Martin Bucer: or what is the same, between the Saxon and Swabian Churches: there indeed Philip, no less than Pomeranus, Justus Jonas, Cruciger, and others, wished to appear to stand entirely on the side of Luther against the stratagems of the Sacramentarians: But before that meeting, what deceit he was already fostering in his mind, he revealed not obscurely in a letter written to Joachim Camerarius, in these words: Yesterday I returned home for the first time from the Hessians, whither ὁ μακεδών (thus he names Philip, Landgrave of Hesse) had called me and Bucer, so that I might bring the opinions of our side, and he those of his own, περὶ τῆς διαλλαγῆς in that well-known cause, that is, concerning Concord in the Supper of the Lord. Do not ask for MY opinion NOW: FOR I HAVE BEEN A MESSENGER OF ANOTHER'S, although I will certainly not conceal what I think when I have heard what our people reply.

In the year 1537, the same Philip subscribed to the Schmalkaldic Articles, in which a certain brief epitome of the Augsburg Confession was contained: but yet, in the immediately following year, '38, he did not hesitate to write to Veit Dietrich, a preacher at Nuremberg: I, so that I might not recede too far from the Ancients, placed in the usage a sacramental presence, and said: given these things (bread and wine), Christ is truly present and is efficacious. To this confession, surely, no Sacramentarian would not subscribe with the most ready mind, believing with Philip that the Person of Christ is present to the Sacraments, and that He dispenses His body and blood to be partaken of spiritually through faith. For that this was Philip's intention is clearly evident from the subsequent words of the same letter: Nor did I add an inclusion or such a conjunction by which the body would be affixed τῷ ἄρτῳ: or soldered or mixed. That these words are opposed to the corporal presence of the body and blood of Christ, as well as to oral manducation, one must be a fool not to see.

Furthermore, in subsequent years, he agitated in his mind plans for changing the purity of the Augsburg Confession; which, a little later, around the year 41, he brought to a sufficiently unhappy realization, having so enormously corrupted and depraved the Tenth Article concerning the Lord's Supper, that any of the Sacramentarians could find a completely safe hiding place under that mask: while, of course, he craftily expunged these two words (adsint & distribuantur) and even that whole ἀνευϑετικὴν clause (Et improbant secùs docentes), which was expressly opposed to the error of the Sacramentarians.

And although the illustrious Elector of Saxony, John Frederick, through Chancellor Dr. Pontanus, took care to rebuke Philip most severely for the sake of this change undertaken by private daring: and indeed Luther himself vehemently reproved him on this account, saying, 'Who, Philip, commissioned you to do this?' Nay, Philip himself also, in the year 41, at the Colloquy of Regensburg instituted with the Pontificals, at the insistence of the Protestant Estates, publicly and solemnly disavowed this change undertaken by his own daring and judgment, and in the tenth Article restored and reintegrated those things which he had previously expunged: nevertheless, he did not hide that he was more favorable to the dogma of the Calvinists. Whence, in the immediately following year 42, in a certain Epistle prefixed to the third volume of his works, he did not hesitate to expunge with a single stroke that unanimous consensus of Orthodox Antiquity, which he himself had previously collected in a special little book in the year 30 concerning the true and real presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper, and had opposed to the Sacramentarian sect, writing: 'There are also recent opinions collected περὶ δείπνε κυριακ̄, some of which in those authors who are cited are supposititious: I would prefer that these and certain similar things had been omitted.'

In the year 1545, the Tigurines took care to have the writings of Zwingli published in one volume. When Blessed Luther had decided to oppose his Minor and final Confession to these, Philip, taking this indignantly, having written an epistle to the Tigurines, especially to Bullinger, complained vehemently about this undertaking of Luther, in these words: 'Perhaps before these letters of mine are delivered to you, you will receive a most atrocious writing of Luther, in which he renews the war περὶ δείπνε κυριακ̄. He has never conducted this cause with greater force: I cease, therefore, to hope for the peace of the Churches.'

Observing this inconstancy of Philip and his clandestine collusion with the Sacramentarians, Blessed Luther was so far from descending into Philip's opinion and becoming more favorable to the Sacramentarians (as Peucer and Pezelius lie) that he rather openly professed that he would publicly sharpen his pen against him as well as the rest of the Sacramentarians. Concerning which matter, the most pious Elector, having been made certain, sent Chancellor Dr. Pontanus the Elder here to Wittenberg with this mandate: 'We have received from the report of certain men that Dr. Martin is now entirely occupied in preparing some writing against the Sacramentarians: which we understand from his own mouth to be with his Clement will and singular approval.' As for Philip, however, whom we hear is to be specifically censured in that booklet, we clemently desire that the Lord Doctor, following our counsel, which certainly proceeded from the best spirit, should summon him privately to himself and paternally admonish him: if that is done, we are clemently persuaded that he will entirely give place to admonition and instruction. But if, beyond all our hope and expectation, he leaves no place for exhortation, then the Lord Doctor will be able to enter upon those measures which he has already instituted, and others also which he shall judge convenient and useful.' An ἀντίγραφον of which Electoral mandate still exists today in the Saxon Archives.

And although Blessed Luther satisfied the most clement will of the Elector, he was nevertheless unable to fully explore Philip's opinion. Concerning which matter, Chancellor Pontanus wrote again to the Elector in this manner: 'Illustrious Elector, most Clement Lord, Dr. Martin said that he was not entirely without fear, nor could he sufficiently know what Philip's mind and opinion is concerning the Sacrament. For he said that it is named by him as nothing other than a bare ceremony, and that it has been a long time since he has seen him using the Holy Supper of the Lord. Afterwards also, when he had been at Kassel, most of the arguments brought forward by him were such that he gathered not obscurely that he leans toward the opinion of the Zwinglians, etc.' See the Refutation of the Peucerian booklet published by our Theological College, page 44, of the second edition.

And a little later the same Pontanus adds: 'I, from the conversations held with me by your Highness at Lochau, reported to the Lord Doctor what seemed to your Highness concerning Philip's opinion: namely, that he is lying low until a more convenient occasion offers itself, which he hopes for and expects especially once the Lord Doctor has been taken from the living. And indeed I fear that it is not entirely for nothing that your Highness thinks so.'

Moreover, Philip, noticing that the Elector's inclemency was prepared for him unless he proved himself ἐμόψηφον καὶ ὁμόσπονδον to Luther, in that same year 45, confirms to both the Elector and Luther in many ways that he utterly abhors the opinion and fraternity of the Sacramentarians. Whom, in the end, he dissuades with many reasons and arguments from receiving the Helvetians into the league of the allies of the Augsburg Confession, and also from permitting the books of the Zwinglians to be imported into that Electorate.

In this way, indeed, although outwardly Philip seemed to be entirely one of us, he nevertheless did not cease to cherish a δυςμενεία in his heart, writing to Calvin and complaining most grievously that he was being severely tormented on account of Luther’s Confession and was placed in great danger. And indeed, while Luther was still alive, Philip could the less be convinced of defection to the Sacramentarians because, in his writings published up to that time, he had so tempered his style that he completely covered and concealed the opinion which he cherished in his heart. But after the blessed Luther ceased to be among the living in the year '46, he began to speak and write a little more freely, yet in such a way that even Calvin himself desired greater clarity and candor from him in publishing his Confession, as is evident from his own letter 170, written to Melanchthon.

But whatever the case may be, it is nevertheless manifest that he himself afterwards established no other manducation of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Holy Supper than a spiritual one, which is by faith alone. And indeed he inserted this Sacramentarian opinion into the very Saxon Confessions themselves, without any of the theologians or politicians noticing. For thus the Confession of the Saxon Churches, which was to be offered to the Council of Trent, was drafted in the year '51: Men are taught that in the use of the Sacrament, the Body and Blood of Christ are truly exhibited to those who receive, that is, that Christ testifies that He is in them, and makes them members of Himself, and that He has washed them with His Blood.

This very thing is detected in the Agenda of Mecklenburg, where to the question (What is distributed and received in the Lord's Supper) the answer is given thus from the information of Philip: the true Body and true Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ: for our Lord Jesus Christ instituted this reception so that He might testify that He truly and essentially wishes to be with us and in us, and to dwell in those who are converted, to communicate His benefits to them, and to be efficacious in them, as John 15 says: Abide in me, and I in you.

He repeated this same affectation in the Colloquy of Worms in the year '57, saying thus: He is present substantially, so that by the communion of His body and blood He may make us members of His body, and testify that He applies His benefits to us, and wishes to be efficacious in us, and wishes to save and vivify our miserable mass, inserted into Himself. This very formula of the Confession Philip subsequently also always retained and used in all assemblies, synods, and colloquies, in almost the same words. And although in the Colloquy of Worms itself Johannes Brentius, intending to recall Philip to the right path, asked him most earnestly that he would at least read through and examine more accurately just four pages in Luther's book, That the words of the Supper still stand firm; and even from that learn what it is to sit at the right hand of God: yet, frustrated in his hope, he received this answer from Philip: These things are already known to me, but know this, that I by no means consent to this doctrine of Luther: nor will I speak with you further about this matter.

In the year 1560, Albert Hardenberg, a most bitter Calvinist, was at Bremen, to whom the remaining ministers of the Church, who were Orthodox, were opposing themselves. What did Philip do here? He was, of course, inciting Hardenberg against his colleagues, writing to him thus: I am an encourager to you that, if they call you into a contest (namely Heshusius, Mörlin, and others), you should also demand that it be granted to you to summon Peter Martyr, myself, and certain other friends. If the Senate of Bremen and your college permit a theatrical disputation to be instituted, many wise men will judge that they are acting imprudently, etc. Fare well. The day before the Kalends of March, 1560.

At the same time, Philip was called into council by the Elector Palatine Frederick as to how the controversy concerning the Lord's Supper, which had arisen between Dr. Heshusius, an Orthodox, and Wilhelm Klebitius, might be quieted: he gave this answer, that both of the dissenters should be cast out from their place and offices: and that it should not be granted that controversies be agitated, but that thought should be given to one certain form which all would use thereafter. And indeed to prescribe that form, he cited the Apostle saying: The bread which we break is the κοινωνία of the body of Christ: where the word κοινωνία is to be explained in such a way that the bread is that by which association with the body of Christ is effected in the use of the Sacrament.

By this one piece of advice, Philip moved the excellent Elector to incline toward the side of the Calvinists, and, having ejected the Lutheran Doctors, to substitute Calvinists. The very words of Philip sound thus: Therefore I praise the plan that silence is imposed and commanded upon the quarrelsome church ministers on both sides, so that no division or schism might follow in the tender and weak church. And I wish that the wranglers from both sides were away from there.

Secondly, where the quarrelsome ones are removed, it would be good that the other church ministers agreed upon a unanimous, certain form of speaking. And in this dispute it would be for the best that one kept the words of Paul, namely: The bread which we break is the fellowship of the body; and it should be taught often and much about the fruit and benefit of the Lord's Supper, so that people might be enticed to the love of this pledge and to constant use. And the little word (fellowship) should be well explained. The Apostle does not say that the nature of the bread is transformed or changed, as the Papists speak of it, and he does not say, as those at Bremen do, that the bread is the essential body of Christ, and he also does not say, as Heshusius does, that the bread is the true body of Christ, but that it is the fellowship, that is, so much is said: It is that by which the society and fellowship with the body of Christ happens, in the right use, and does not proceed without faithful contemplation, as when mice gnaw the bread, etc.

Nor did he hold a sounder opinion in the writings or commentaries published by him, but rather he manifestly testified that he was addicted to the Calvinists. Certainly, in his commentary on the 10th chapter of the first epistle to the Corinthians, he was not afraid to interpret the word κοινωνία in the Calvinist sense: κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος, he says, is that external visible thing by which the blood of the Lord is exhibited to us: so the bread which we break is that external visible thing by which we are made partners and members of the body of Christ; just as it is said: THE GOSPEL IS THE POWER OF GOD, that is, that thing or instrument by which God is efficacious.

And more clearly in chapter 11 of the same first [epistle] to the Corinthians. When Luke and Paul say: This cup is the New Testament, it is a metonymy, as if I were to say: The fasces are the Roman empire.

Hence was born that excellent definition of the Lord's Supper, which Philip prescribed for those to be ordained in his Examination; and which, like a buskin, fits both the Calvinist dogma and our own, concerning which [I shall speak] in its proper place expressly, but it sounds thus: The Supper of the Lord is the communication of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, as it was instituted in the words of the Gospel, in which reception the Son of God is truly and substantially present, and testifies that He applies His benefits to believers, and Himself assumed human nature for our sake, so that he might also make us, inserted into himself by faith, his own members, and that we have been washed by his blood, etc. But here we plant our feet, and from the documents already proposed, even if unwilling, we gather that Philip suffered something human, and that from the year 1535, at first indeed secretly, but afterwards a little more openly, he made a secession from the doctrine of Luther.

Latin:

Et sub finem illius Epistolæ: Si rationes,quibus Zvvinglius movetur,conscientijs ita satisfacerent, ut in Judicio Dei ijs niti possint,facilè nos allegorias ipsius approbaremus: Certum autèm est,non posse acquiescere conscientias istis argumentis.

Responsum Landgravij, quo Zvvinglianorum errorem extenuare conatus est, vide Defens. II. D. Johannis Pappi contra Sturmium: p. 25. Similiter alterum responsum Philippi & Brentij ad literas Landgravij pag. 27.

Anno subsequente 31. consensu Lutheri & Protestantium, Apologiam Confessionis Augustanæ in ipsis quidem Comitijs conscriptam: sed ab Imperatore non receptam, typis publicis unâ cum Confessione describi curavit.

Tantùm autem abest,ut tùm Philippus vel latum unguem à Doctrina Lutheri divortium fecerit, ut potius non nudè tantùm verba Confessionis repetat, sed per luculentam declarationem asserat, corpus & sanguinem Christi substantialiter in Cœna adesse & dispensari: quin etiam confirmet,non Romanam tantùm Ecclesiam affirmare corporalem præsentiam: sed idem olim sensisse & nunc sentire Græcam Ecclesiam.

Et in hac quidem Sententiâ verè Orthodoxâ ac γνησίως Lutherana ad annum usq; 1535. constanter perseverasse Philippum, vel inde liquidò constat, quod nec ipsi quidem Calviniani vix ullum ex scriptis Philippi hactenus in lucem editis, testimonium proferre possunt, quo diversum liquidò evincere queant.

Et sic hactenus Philippus fidum omninò παραστάτην & Collegam se B. Luthero nostro præstitit: ut verè de illis dici potuerit: Divisæ his operæ, sed mens fuit uniça: pavit ore Lutherus oves,floreMelanchthon apes;vel illudPoetæ Italici:

Velle ac nolle ambobus idem, fociataq̃, læto Mens ævo, ac sacris dives Concordia rebus.

Cæterum usus hactenus dictorum potest & debet esse geminus, uterq̃ tamen ἐλεγκτικὸς; Prior quidem Cripto-Calvinianis opponendus, qui hodie magnificè extollentes auream illam Concordiam Lutheri & Philippi, id unicè sed satis insidiosè quærunt, ut sub pallio Philippi, dogma Calvinianum occultent, & tacitè in Ecclesiam Dei invehant, haud secus, ac si ipsissimi Lutheri dogma esset, proptereà quod Lutherus & Philippus nullatenus sint divellendi. His ergò os obturari debet, ostendendo, quo usq̃ Concordia illa se extendat, & quamdiu ea duraverit. Posterior usus ἐλεγκτικὸς manifestos Calvinianos respicit, qui Philippũ semper à suis stetisse partibus, impudenter & mendaciter gloriantur. Diversum enim ex ijs, quæ hactenus proposuimus, luculenter patet.

Cæterùm, quomodo Philippus suo usus consilio & magis fortassè ex innata animi mollitie ac timiditate, quàm destinata malitia pedetentim magis magisq̃ à puritate & ὀρθοδοξία verè Lutherana defecerit, & cum Zvvinglianis conspirare cœperit, vel ipsa salus Ecclesiæ flagitat, ut bona fide ostendamus.

Et ut ab anno 1536. ordiamur, in quem incidit celebris illa Actio Concordiæ inter B. Lutherum & Martinum Bucerum: vel quod idem est, inter Ecclesias Saxonicas & Svevicas: ibi profectò Philippus, haud minus atque Pomeranus, Justus Jonas, Crucigerus atque alij, totus à partibus Lutheri adversus Sacramentariorum strophas stare videri volebat: Sed ante conventum istum, quid ὕπουλον jam tùm sub animo foveret, haud obscurè in literis ad Joachimum Camerarium scriptis prodidit, his verbis: Heri primùm domum reversus sum ex Cattis, quò me & Bucerum vocarat ὁ μακεδών (ita nominat Philippum Landgravium Hassiæ) ut ego nostrorum, ille suorum sententias adferret, περὶ τῆς διαλλαγῆς in illa pervulgata causa, id est, de Concordia in Cæna Domini. MEAM sententiam noli NVNC requirere: FVI ENIM NVNCIVS ALIENÆ, etsi profectò non dissimulabo, quid sentiam, ubi audiero, quid respondeant nostri.

Anno 1537. Articulis Schmalkaldicis, quibus brevis quædam quasi Epitome Confessionis Augustanæ comprehendebatur, subscripsit idem Philippus: sed tamen mox sequente Anno 38. ad Vitum Theodorum Concionatorem Noribergensem scribere non dubitavit, Ego, ne longius recederem à Veteribus, posui in usu sacramentalem præsentiam, & dixi: datis his rebus (pane & vino) Christum verè adesse & efficacem esse. Cui sanè Confessioni nullus non Sacramentariorum promptissimo animo subseribit, cum Philippo credens, Personam Christi adesse Sacramentis, & spiritualiter per fidem participandum corpus & sanguinem suum dispensare. Hanc enim fuisse mentem Philippo, ex subsequentibus ejusdem Epistolæ verbis liquidò patet: Nec addidi inclusionem aut conjunctionem talem, quâ affigeretur, τῷ ἄρτῳ τὸ σῶμα: aut ferruminaretur aut misceretur. Quæ sanè verba opponi corporali præsentiæ corporis & sanguinis Christi: ut & manducationi orali, bardum esse oporteat, qui non videat.

Accedit quòd annis subsequentibus de mutanda puritate Augustanæ Confessionis, consilia jam modò apud animum agitavit: quę etiam paulò pòst circa An. 41. in actum satis infehcem perduxit, ita enormiter corrupto ac depravato Articulo Decimo de Cœna Domini, ut quisque Sacramentariorum, tutum omninò latibulum sub cothurno isto figere possit: dum nimirùm duo hæc vocabula (adsint & distribuantur) quin & totam illam clausulam ἀνευϑετικὴν (Et improbant secùs docentes) quæ Sacramentariorum errori ex professo erat opposita, subdolè expunxit.

Et quanquam inclytus Saxoniæ Elector Johannes Fridericus per Cancellarium D. Pontanum, mutationis hujus privato ausu susceptæ gratiâ severissimè objurgari curavit Philippum: quin & Lutherus ipsum hoc nomine vehementer reprehendit, Quis, inquiens, tibi hoc mandavit, Philippe? Imò ipse quoque Philippus Anno 41. in Colloquio Ratisponæ cnm Pontificijs instituto, ad instantiam Ordinum Protestantium publicè ac solenniter mutationem hanc à se proprio ausu ac arbitrio susceptam exautoravit, inq; decimo Articulo restituit ac redintegravit ea, quæ prius expunxerat: Interim tamen Calvinianorum dogmati æquiorem se esse, haud dissimulavit. Unde Anno statim subsequente 42. in quadam Epistola, Tomo tertio operum præfixa, unanimem illum consensum Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, quem de vera ac reali præsentia corporis & Sanguinis Christi in Sacra Cœna, peculiari quodam libello Anno 30. prius ipsemet collegerat, & genti Sacramentariæ opposuerat, unâ liturâ expungere non dubitavit, scribens: Sunt & sententiæ recentes collectæ περὶ δείπνε κυριακ̄, quarum aliquæ in illis autoribus, qui citantur, sunt supposititiæ: Hæc & similia quædam mallem omissa esse.

Anno 1545. Tigurini scripta Zvvinglij in unum volumen congesta, typis publicari curabant. Quibus cum B. Lutherus Minorem ac ultimam suam Confessionem opponere constituisset, Philippus indignè hoc ferens, scriptâ epistolâ ad Tigurinos, cumprimis ad Bullingerum vehementer de hoc Lutheri instituto conquestus est, his verbis: Fortassis priusquàm hæ meæ literæ ad te perferentur accipies atrocissimum Lutheri scriptum, in quo bellum περὶ δείπνε κυριακ̄ instaurat. Nunquam majore impetu hanc causam egit: Desino igitur sperare Ecclesiarum pacem.

Quam Philippi inconstantiam & clanculariam cum Sacramentarijs collusionem animadvertens B. Lutherus, usque adeò non in Philippi descendit sententiam, & Sacramentarijs æquior est factus (uti Peucerus & Pezelius mentiuntur) ut potius apertè profiteretur, se stylum quoque publicè tàm adversus ipsum, quam reliquos Sacramentarios stricturũ. Qua de re certior factus pijssimς Elector, Cancellarium D. Pontanum Seniorem cum hoc mandato, hûc Witebergam ablegavit: Certorum hominum relatu accepimus, Doct. Martinum totum jam in eo esse, ut scriptum aliquod contra Sacramentarios adornet: id quod Clementi voluntate, & singulari approbatione de ipso intelligimus. Ad Philippum verò quod attinet, quem nominatim in eo libello taxatum iri audimus, clementer cupimus, ut Dominus Doctor, consilium nostrum, optimo certè animo profectum, secutus, privatim ipsum ad se accersitum, paternè admoneat: id si fiat, locum ipsum admonitioni atq; institutioni omninò daturum esse, clementer persuasum habemus. Si verò præter omnem nostram spem & expectationem, nullum adhortationi locum relinquat, tum Dominus Doctor, & eas, quas jam instituit, & alias etiam, quas commodas atq; utiles judicarit, rationes inire poterit. Cujus Electoralis mandati ἀντίγραφον, in Archivis Saxonicis hodieq; extat.

Et quanquam B. Lutherus clementissimæ voluntati Electoris satisfecit, haud tamen plenè Philippi sententiam explorare potuit. Qua de re rursum Cancellarius Pontanus ad Electorem scripsit in hunc modum: Inclyte Elector, Domine Clementissime, Ajebat D. Martinus, se non prorsus absq; metu esse, neq; satis scire posse, quænam Philippi de Sacramento sit mens atq; sententia. Non enim aliter quàm nudam ceremoniam illud ab ipso nominari, & diu jam esse, ex quo ipsum Sacræ Domini Cœnæ utentem conspexerit. Postea etiam cum Cassellis fuisset, pleraq; ab ipso in medium allata esse argumenta, ex quibus ipsum in sententiam Zvvinglianorum propendere, non obscurè collegerit &c. Vide Refut. libelli Peuceriani à Collegio nostro Theologico in lucem editam, pag. 44. Edit. secundæ.

Et paulò post subjicit idem Pontanus: Ego ex vestræ Celsitudinis Luchoviæ ad me habitis sermonibus, Domino Doctori referebam, quid Celsitudini vestræ de Philippi sententia videretur: ipsum videlicet latitare, donec commodior sese offerat occasio, quam præcipuè Domino Doctore è vivis sublato speret, atq; expectet. Et sanè metuo, non prorsus de nihilo esse, quod Celsitudo V. cogitat.

Cæterùm Philippus animadvertens Electoris inclementiam sibi paratam esse, nisi Luthero se ἐμόψηφον καὶ ὁμόσπονδον probaret: eodem ann. 45. & Electori & Luthero multis confirmat, se à Sacramentariorum opinione, & fraternitate penitùs abhorrere. Quem in fine multis rationibus atque argumentis dissuadet Electori, ne Helveticos in fœdus sociorum Confessionis Augustanæ recipiat, neque etiam Zvvinglianorum libros in Electoratum istum importari permittat.

Quo sanè pacto etsi foris videbatur Philippus totus noster esse: interim tamen δυςλον in animo fovere minimè desiit: scribens ad Calvinum, & gravissimè conquerens, se ob Lutheri Confessionem graviter cruciari, inq; magno periculo esse constitutum. Et sanè tantò minùs Philippus vivente adhuc Luthero, Defectionis ad Sacramentarios convinci poterat, quòd hactenus suis in scriptis publicè editis, Stylum ita attemperavit, ut sententiam, quam in corde fovebat, omninò tegeret & occultaret. Postquam verò B. Lutherus An. 46. in vivis esse desiit, ibi paulò quidem liberius, loqui & scribere cœpit, sed ita tamen, ut vel Calvinus ipse, majorem in ipso perspicuitatem & candorem in edenda Confessione desideraret: uti patet ex Epistola ipsius 170. ad Melanchthonem scripta.

Sed quicquid sit, manifestum tamen est, ipsum postmodùm nullam aliam manducationem Corporis & Sanguinis Christi in S. Cœna statuisse, quàm Spiritualem, quæ sit sola fide. Et quidem hanc Sacramentariam sententiam in ipsas etiam Confessiones Saxonicas, nemine vel Theologorum vel Politicorum animadvertente, insarsit. Sic enim Confessio Saxonicarum Ecclesiarum, quæ Synodo Tridentinæ erat offerenda, Anno 51. informabatur: Docentur homines in usu Sacramenti, verè exhiberi sumentibus Corpus & Sanguinem Christi, hoc est, Christum testari, quòd sit in eis, & faciat eos sibi membra, & quod abluerit eos Sanguine suo.

Quod ipsum deprehenditur in Agenda Mechelburgensis, ubi ad Quæstionem (Quid in Cœna Domini distribuitur & accipitur) sic ex informatione Philippi respondetur: verum Corpus & verus Sanguis Domini nostri Jesu Christi: Dominus enim noster Jesus Christus, hanc sumtionem instituit, ut testetur, quod verè & essentialiter nobiscum & in nobis esse, & in conversis habitare, illis beneficia sua communicare, & in illis efficax esse velit, ut inquit Joh. 15. Manete in me, & ego in vobis.

Quem cothurnum repetijt in Colloquio VVormatiensi Anno 57. sic inquiens: adest substantialiter, ut communione sui corporis & sanguinis nos membra faciat sui corporis, & testetur, se nobis applicare sua beneficia, & velle se in nobis efficacem esse, & nostram miseram massam, sibi insertam, velle servare & vivificare. Quam ipsam Confessionis formulam deinceps quoque Philippus in omnibus conventibus, Synodis ac Colloquijs, ijsdem fermè verbis semper retinuit & usurpevit. Et quanquam in ipso Colloquio VVormatiensi Johannes Brentius Philippum in viam revocaturus, maximoperè rogavit, ut vel quatuor tantùm pagellas in libro Lutheri, Quod verba Cœnæ adhuc firma stent; perlegeret, & accuratius evolveret: & vel inde addisceret, Quid sit, sedere ad dextram DEI: tamen spe frustratus, illud responsi accepit à Philippo: Jamantè mihi nota sunt isthæc, sed hoc scito, me in doctrinam hanc Lutheri minimè consentire: neque etiam tecum de hoc negotio amplius collocuturum.

Anno 1560. erat Bremæ Albertus Hardenbergius, Calvinista acerrimus, cui reliqui Ecclesiæ Ministri Orthodoxi sese opponebant. Quid hîc Philippus? Hardenbergium nimirùm adversus Collegas incitabat, sic scribens ad ipsú: Tibi hortator sum, ut si te in certamen vocabunt (Heshusius scilicet Mörlinus & alij) postules tibi quoq; concedi, ut accersas Petrum Martyrem, Me, & alios quosdam amicos. Si Senatus Bremensis & Collegium vestrum permittunt, institui theatricam disputationem, multi sapientes judicabunt, eos imprudenter facere, &c. Benè vale. prid. Cal. Mart. 1560.

Eodem tempore in Consilium adhibitus ab Electore Palatino Friderico Philippus, Quonam pacto controversia de Cœna Domini inter D. Heshusium Orthodoxum, & Wilhelmum Klebitium orta, sopiri posset: hoc dedit responsi, loco & muneribus suis ejiciendos esse utrosque dissidentes: neque concedendum esse, ut controversię agitentur, sed de una quadam, certa formâ, quâ deinceps omnes uterentur, cogitandum esse. Illam verò formam præscribere Apostolum dicentem: Panis, quem frangimus, est κοινωνία corporis Christi: ubi vocabulum κοινωνίας ita sit declarandum, ut panis sit hoc, quo fiat consociatio cum corpore Christi in usu Sacramenti.

Quo uno Consilio Philippus optimum Electorem permovit, ut ad partes Calvinianorum inclinaret, & ejectis Lutheranis Doctoribus Calvinianos substitueret. Verba ipsa Philippi sic sonant: Darumb so lobe ich das fürnemen/ das beyderseits den zänckischen Kirchendienern/das still schweigen aufferleget vnnd befohlen/ damit in der zarten vnd schwachen Kirchen kein trennung oder spaltung erfolgete. Vnd wüntsche/daß die Hadderer von beyden seiten von dannen weren.

Zum andern/ wo die Zänckische hinweg gethan/were gut/ daß die andern Kirchendiener sich einer einhelligen/gewissen Form zu reden/ vergliechen. Vnnd in diesem Streit were es zum besten/ daß man die Wort Pauli behielte/ Nemlich/ das Brodt/ das wir brechen/ ist die Gemeinschafft des Leibes/ Vnnd solte von dem Frucht vnd Nuz des Herrn Nachtmahl/ offt vnd viel gelehret werden/ damit die Menschen gereitzet werden/zur liebe dieses Pfandes/vnd stetem gebrauch. Vnd das Wörtlein (Gemeinschafft)solte man wol erkleren.DerApostel sagt nicht/daß sich die Natur des Brodts verwandele/oder verendere/ wie die Papisten davon reden/ vnd saget nicht/wie die zu Bremen/daß das Brodt seye der wesentliche Leib Christi/vnd sagt auch nicht/ wie Heshusius,daß das Brodt sey der warhafftige Leib Christi/Sondern daß es sey die Gemeinschafft/ das ist so viel geredet/ Es ist das/ mit welchem die Gesellschafft vnnd Gemeinschafft mit dem Leib Christi geschicht/in dem rechten gebrauch/ vnd nicht ohne gleubige betrachtung zugehet/als wann die Mäuse das Brodt nagen/ zc.

Neque saniorem tenuit sententiam in scriptis sive Commentarijs abs se editis, quin Calvinianis se addictum esse, manifestè testatus est. Certè in Commentario in 10. caput prioris ad Corinthios, vocem κοινωνίας sensu Calviniano interpretari haud fuit veritus: κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος, inquiens, est illa res externa visibilis, quâ sanguis Domini nobis exhibetur: sic panis,quem frangimus, est illa res externa visibilis,quâ efficimur socij & membra corporis Christi; sicut dicitur: EVANGELIUM EST POTENTIA DEI, id est,illa res seu instrumentum, quo Deus est efficax.

Et clariùs in caput 11. ejusdem prioris ad Corinth. Cum Lucas & Paulus dicunt: Hic Calix est Novum Testamentum,μετωνυμία est, ut si dicam: Fasces sunt imperium Romanum.

Hinc nata egregia illa definitio Cœnæ Dominicæ, quam in Examine suo Ordinandis præscripsit Philippus: quæque Cothurni instar tàm Calviniano, quàm nostro dogmati,competit, de qua suo loco ex professo, ea verò sic sonat: Cœna Domini est communicatio corporis & sanguinis Domini nostri Jesu Christi, sicut in verbis Evangelij instituta est, in qua sumtione Filius Dei verè & substantialiter adest, & testatur, se applicare credentibus sua beneficia, & se assumsisse humanam naturam propter nos, ut nos quoq; sibi insertos fide membra sua faciat, & nos ablutos esse sanguine suo &c. Sed hîc pedem figimus, & ex documentis jam propositis, vel inviti colligimus, Philippum humani quid passum, & à doctrina Lutheri, jam inde ab Anno 35. supra sesquimillesimum, initiò quidem clanculùm, postmodum verò paulò apertiùs secessionein fecisse.


### On the Authority of the Philippian Writings

In what place the writings of Philip can and ought to be held in the Church of GOD has been inquired into and disputed in previous years, and is inquired into today. But the handle and occasion for this question were provided most of all by those crafty counsels by which the Wittenberg Crypto-Calvinists—Pezelius, Widebramus, Cruciger, Mollerus, Stoffelius, and the theologian Christianus Sagittarius, together with Cracovius the jurist and Caspar Peucer, physician and philosopher—around the year of Christ 1571 and some subsequent years, attempted to suppress the pure doctrine of B. Luther and to shake it from the hands, eyes, and minds of men, and to introduce the Sacramentarian virus tacitly into this very Academy, and indeed into the whole Electorate; for since they did not dare to attack the Catechism and the writings of Luther in open warfare, they thought that the matter should be approached through remarkable πανεργίαν [craftiness] and a clearly cunning art.

And at the beginning, indeed, they always had the name of Luther on their lips, and they referred their hearers to his Catechism as if it were the sacrosanct and infallible Cynosure of heavenly doctrine, and they boasted in magnificent words that they were clearly ὁμοψήφες καὶ ὁμοσπόνδες [of one mind and one covenant] with Luther: so that you would have sworn that those men were the sharpest and most faithful ὐπερασπιστὰς [defenders] or champions of the genuinely Lutheran doctrine.

With the minds of men thus demented, in the second place they proclaimed with splendid words the unanimous consent of Luther and Philip, repeatedly emphasizing that: 'We will not suffer these two men to be separated from us: Philip was the heart and soul of Luther, who knows the one, knows both.' And this was the chief foundation of the whole subsequent structure of Simony. For if they had candidly explained to their hearers (as they ought to have done) how Philip had defected from the doctrine of Luther, then they certainly would never have obtained what the outcome later demonstrated they had astutely sought.

Thirdly, this foundation being laid, which was sufficiently plausible, they further attempted to persuade men that the writings of Luther were too prolix, written in German, and, because of various occupations, published in a confused and ἀμεθόδως [methodless] manner, and that they could neither be proposed to students of theology with profit, nor even be purchased by all pastors or ministers of the Church because of the magnitude of the price. For which reason they did not want those truly golden booklets of B. Luther, published expressly on the matter of the Eucharist against the Sacramentarians, to be printed separately any further, but rather to be gathered into volumes and hidden, as it were, among the rest of Luther's

writings. And lest anyone should notice the deceit, they boasted of the faithful care and effort which they were expending for the benefit of the Church of GOD in that they were collecting the writings of Luther as an incomparable treasure and storing them in libraries.

Fourthly, lest the youth and others be overwhelmed by the excessive prolixity of the writings of Luther, they persuaded the people that Philip had reduced into brief compendia and synopses and epitomes all those things which Luther had explained more diffusely; and that Luther had written nothing in the vast ocean of his books which was not contained, fully, solidly, and methodically explained, in those most limpid rivulets of the Examination and Commonplaces of Philip.

Fifthly, they laboriously commended to both students of theology and ministers of the Church the Corpus Doctrinae, as something that had been collected with great fidelity from the writings of Luther and contained most fully the entire doctrine of Luther, so that whoever made that familiar to himself would not greatly need the reading of the writings of Luther.

From this very body they concocted the Wittenberg Catechism, and they craftily foisted it upon schools both illustrious and others throughout that Electorate; likewise, they took care to have their Stereoma (Grundfest) and the Dresden Consensus described in public print; and thus, under the name and authority of the Philippic Corpus Doctrinae, they proposed to their hearers (with almost no one noticing) a certain synopsis of the entire Calvinian doctrine.

So that both the name and the writings of Philip might be rendered more commendable, but the books of Luther might be removed more and more from the memory of men, they instituted annual πανηγύρεις [festivals] and funeral orations concerning the merits and labors of Philip; but concerning Luther, they fostered the deepest silence.

Finally, if any of the more sensible people had produced the books of Luther that were elenchtic and opposed to the error of the Sacramentarians, and had shown the dissonance of the Philippic doctrine, then those Cadmean brothers would immediately shout that there was need of great judgment in reading the books of Luther, because in his didactic writings he indeed always remained sufficiently consistent with himself, but in his polemical ones, he was often carried away by the fervor of disputation and the impulse of his passions, and overstepped the limits of moderation and ὀρθοδοξίας [orthodoxy]. Wherefore they said it was most advisable that those polemical books of Luther be examined and judged according to the writings of Philip, and especially according to the Philippic Corpus Doctrinae. With these foundations thus sufficiently and impudently laid, while almost no one in these regions even noticed, they were incrusting Calvinism; and they were foisting the Philippic Corpus Doctrinae upon the Church of GOD, as the norm and form according to which all other dogmas and questions ought to be judged: so that whoever felt differently was accused of defection from the common teacher Philip, and consequently from Luther himself, and was held suspect in the name of schism, or even heresy. Which unhappy persuasion even today has so occupied minds throughout Denmark, Holstein, the March, Pomerania, Silesia, Lusatia, Noricum, and here and there elsewhere, that whoever dares to struggle against the writings of Philip is arraigned for the crime of divine lese-majesty, and appears worthy of any punishment whatsoever. But it was brought about by the singular goodness of GOD, that through the labor and care both of the renowned Elector of Saxony, Augustus, a Prince of most blessed memory, and of the Saxon and Swabian Theologians, especially those of Tübingen, the remarkable πανουργία (craftiness) and treacherous cunning of those men was detected, once detected was suppressed, and once suppressed was condemned: and at the same time, it was shown in what place the Philippic Corpus of Doctrine can and ought to be held in the Church of GOD. A twofold decision of this question, however, was given: one general, the other special. That protestation of the Electors, Princes, and estates of the Empire, who in the preface prefixed to the Book of Concord set forth their opinion concerning the writings of Philipp and others in this way, shows the general one: Nor do we judge that by the publication of the Book of Concord, other useful writings of Lord Philipp Melanchthon, nor of Brentius, Urbanus Rhegius, Pomeranus, and the like, are to be repudiated and condemned, insofar as they agree in all things with that norm which is expressed in the Book of Concord. But that norm, (the Book of Concord defining it again) looks to the Prophetic and Apostolic writings in the place of foundation and Judge: And because the remaining Symbolic books of our Churches, such as the three Ecumenical Creeds, the Augsburg Confession, that first and least varied one: the Smalcald Articles: both of Luther's Catechisms: and the Book of Concord, agree with this norm: this general decision has most rightly defined that all other writings, and thus those of Philipp as well, must be tested and judged by these books also, as by the voice of a witness.

Now, however, regarding the special definition of this question; if the Philippic Corpus of Doctrine is tested a little more accurately both against Holy Scripture, as Judge, and against the Symbolic books, as the voice of a witness: it will be clearer than the midday sun that it cannot be acknowledged or held as a norm and form of sounder doctrine, while preserving the purity of religion: which it will be worth the effort to demonstrate a little more fully for the sake of those to whom this Corpus of Doctrine might at some time be foisted upon as a certain Orthodox Symbol.

In the beginning, therefore, in that Corpus, there presents itself that Changed or spurious Confession, which can more truly be called Wittenbergian than Augustan: for it was written here at Wittenberg within private walls by Philipp alone, it never saw Augsburg, it was likewise never approved by the calculation of the Emperor and the Orders of the Empire, it servilely flatters the Roman Pontiff, it opens the gates as if to two parents to Calvinism: it establishes Synergism: it confuses the Gospel with the Law; and finally, like a buskin, it provides a sufficiently safe hiding place for various heretics.

Then, however, and specifically, seven can be given, and indeed easily, primary Articles of faith, in which the Philippic Corpus of Doctrine most dangerously departs from the ὑποτυπώ- σει ὑγιαινόντων λόγων (pattern of sound words), and thus from the purity of Christian doctrine.

The first Article is concerning Free Will, regarding which it manifestly subscribes to the Synergists: which is proven in many ways. For first, the fifth Article of the Changed Confession bends its style thus: When we console ourselves with the promise or the Gospel, and raise ourselves up by faith, the Holy Spirit is given to us at the same time. For the Holy Spirit is given and is effective through the Word

of GOD and through the Sacraments. When we hear the Gospel, think, or handle the Sacraments, and console ourselves by faith, the Holy Spirit is effective at the same time. Now who is of such dull judgment that he does not see that this is Synergistic delirium. For if the Holy Spirit is given to us only then, when we first raise and console ourselves by faith: then certainly some cooperation or at least some preparation for our conversion, out of the freedom of the will, must be left to us: which fights diametrically against the word of GOD and the Symbolic books.

Then this very thing is evident from Article XVIII of the same Changed Confession, which in the Corpus of Doctrine holds thus: Spiritual Justice is effected in us when we are helped by the Holy Spirit: furthermore, we conceive the Holy Spirit when we assent to the Word of GOD, so that we may console ourselves by faith in terrors. And in the Antithesis of the same Article: (Human nature) cannot effect interior motions, such as true fear, true trust, patience, chastity, unless the Holy Spirit governs and helps our hearts. Thus far Philipp.

Now if the Holy Spirit is not the sole and only efficient and operating cause of Conversion: but only a co-helper: then certainly some faculty will remain in human powers to apply itself to Conversion: which manifestly fights against Holy Scripture and the prototype of the Augsburg Confession. For that first Confession holds thus: Man does not have the power without the Holy Spirit to effect the justice of GOD, or spiritual justice, because the animal man does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of GOD, but this is done in hearts when the Holy Spirit is conceived through the word. And in the Antithesis: Man cannot effect interior motions, such as fear of GOD, trust toward God, chastity, patience, etc.

Thirdly, the same Synergistic error, and indeed one deliberately encrusted into our German Confession, is detected in the Apology, Article XVIII, where we read thus in the German body: Free Will and reason in spiritual matters can do NOTHING ALONE. And a little later in §. three: The Holy Spirit works faith and fear of God. Where a twofold remarkable depravation has been committed. For the first and least varied exemplar of the German Apology, in the first paragraph, does not have the exclusive particle ALONE: but the words sound thus: We affirm that Free Will and Reason in spiritual matters can do NOTHING. Then in §. three: That to be regenerated and to have another heart and other motions effected within, the Holy Spirit ALONE works that.

Fourthly, the same is evident from the fact that Philipp, after the death of Blessed Luther, encrusted into his Commonplaces in the Article concerning Free Will a definition of Erasmus that is entirely Synergistic, which Luther had rejected with great zeal: Free Will is the faculty of applying oneself to grace, that is, it hears the promise, and tries to assent, and casts away sin against conscience.

Fifthly, in the same place Philip writes thus according to the opinion of the Synergists: Since the Promise is universal, and there are not contradictory wills in God, it is necessary that the cause of some distinction be IN US, why Saul is cast away, David is received, that is, it is necessary that there be some dissimilar action in these two.

Finally, he betrayed this very error in the examination of those to be ordained: where he discourses thus on the Article concerning Free Will: These causes concur in Conversion: The Word of GOD: The Holy Spirit, whom the Father and Son send, that He may kindle our hearts: and our will assenting and not resisting the Word of GOD.

Latin:

QUo loco in Ecclesia DEI Scripta Philippi haberi possint ac debeant, superioribus annis quæsitum ac disputatum fuit, hodieque quæritur. Ansam verò & occasionem Quæstioni huic vel maximè præbuerunt, callida illa consilia, quibus Crypto-Calvinistæ Witebergenses, Pezelius, Widebramus, Cruciger, Mollerus, Stoffelius, Christianus Sagittarius Theologi unà cű Cracovio JCto, & Casparo Peucero, Medico & Philosopho, circa Annum Christi 1571. & aliquot subsequentes puram B. Lutheri doctrinam opprimere, èque manibus, oculis & animis homi num excutere, virus contrâ Sacramentarium in hanc ipsam Academiam, imò totum Electoratű tacitè invehere conati sunt, cum enim aperto Marte, Catechismum & scripta Lutheri oppugnare non auderent, per insignem πανεργίαν, & artem planè veteratoriam, rem aggrediendam sibi esse putarunt.

Ac initiò quidem nomen Lutheri semper in ore ferebant, ad ejusdem Catechismum, tanquam Sacrosanctam ac infallibilem Cynosuram cœlestis doctrinæ Auditores remittebant, seque Luthero planè ὁμοψήφες καὶ ὁμοσπόνδες esse magnificis verbis gloriabantur: ita ut jurasses, homines istos, esse acerrimos & fidelissimos doctrinæ γνησίως Lutheranæ ὐπερασπιστὰς sive propugnatores.

Animis hominum ita dementatis secundo loco splendidis verbis deprædicabant unanimem consensum Lutheri & Philippi: subindè ingeminantes illud: Non patemur nobis duos istos viros separari: Philippus cor & anima Lutheri fuit, qui unum novit, utrumq; novit. Et hoc erat totius subsequentis structuræ Simoniæ fundamentum præcipuum. Nam si (uti debuissent) Auditoribus suis candidè explicassent, quo pacto Philippus à doctrina Lutheri defecisset: tum sanè nunquam obtinuissent, quod astutè ipsos quæsivisse, exitus postmodùm demonstravit.

Tertiò, jacto hoc fundamento satis plausibili, persuadere porrò hominibus conabantur: Lutheri scripta nimis esse prolixa, germanicè scripta, & propter varias occupationes confusè καὶ ἀμεθόδως edita, neque illa vel studiosis Theologiæ cum fructu proponi, vel etiàm ab omnibus pastoribus sive Ecclesiæ ministris, propter precij magnitudinem comparari posse. Quam ob causam opuscula illa verè aurea B. Lutheri, de negocio Eucharistio contra Sacramentarios ex professo edita, seorsim ampliùs excudi nolebant: sed potiùs in Tomos redigi, ac inter reliqua Lutheri

Scripta quasi abscondi curabant. Et ne quis dolum animadverteret, gloriabantur de fideli cura atque operâ, quam in commodum Ecclesiae DEI impenderent in eo, quod scripta Lutheri, tanquam incomparabilem Thesaurum colligerent, inque Bibliothecas reponerent.

Quartò, Ne juventus & alij nimia Scriptorum Lutheri prolixitate obruerentur, persuadebant populo, Philippum in brevia Compendia & Synopses atque Epitomas omnia ea retulisse, quae fusiùs Lutherus explicasset: neque quicquam Lutherum in amplissimo suorum librorum Oceano scripsisse, quod non in limpidissimis illis rivulis Examinis & locorum Communium Philippi plenè, solidè & methodicè explicatum contineretur.

Quintò, Operosè commendabant tùm studiosis Theologiae, tùm Ministris Ecclesiȩ, Corpus doctrinae, ut quod ex Lutheri scriptis magna fide sit collectum, & plenissimè contineat universam doctrinam Lutheri: ut qui istud sibi familiare reddiderit, haud magnopere indigeat lectione Scriptorum Lutheri.

Ex hoc ipso corpore concinnabant Catechesin Witebergensem, eamque Scholis tàm illustribus, tàm alijs per Electoratum istum subdolè obtrudebant: typis item publicis describi curabant Stereoma suum (Grundfest) & consensum Dresdensẽ: & sic Synopsin quandam universae Doctrinae Calvinianae sub nomine & autoritate Corporis doctrinae Philippici suis auditoribus (nemine fermè animadvertente) proponebant.

Ut & nomen & scripta Philippi redderentur Commendatiora: Lutheri autem libri magis magisqué ex memoria hominum eximerentur: an niversarias instituebant πανηγύρεις & parentationes, de meritis & laboribus Philippi: de Luthero autem altissimum fovebant silentium.

Tandem si cordatiorum aliquis libros Lutheri elenchticos Sacramentariorum errori oppositos, produxisset, & doctrinae Philippeae dissonantiam ostendisset: tùm fratres isti Cadmei subinde clamitabant, Magno judicio opus esse in legendis libris Lutheri, propterea quod in scriptis didacticis ipse quidem sibi semper satis constiterit: sed in Polemicis saepius fervore disputationis, & affectuum impetu abreptus, limites moderationis & ὀρθοδοξίας transilierit. Quare Consultissimum esse dicebant, ut libri illi Polemici Lutheri secundum scripta Philippi, & cumprimis secundùm Corpus doctrinae Philippicum examinetur & dijudicentur. His ita satis improbè jactis fundamentis, nemine fermè in his quidem regionibus animadvertente incrustabant Calvinismum: & Corpus Doctrinae Philippicum Ecclesiae DEI obtrudebant, ceu normam ac formam, secundum quam omnia alia dogmata & Quaestiones dijudicari debeant: ita ut qui diversum sentiret, is defectionis à com̃uni Praeceptore Philippo, & consequenter à Luthero ipso argueretur, & Schismatis, imò hereseos nomine suspectus haberetur. Quae infelix persuasio hodieque plurimotú animos per Daniam, Holsatiam, Marchiam, Pomeraniam, Silesiam, Lusatiam, Noricum, & passim alibi ita occupavit, ut qui Philippi scriptis reluctari ausit, is criminis laesae Majestatis divinae reg peragatur, & quovis supplicio dignus videatur. Sed singulari DEI factum bonitate, ut operâ ac curâ tùm inclyti Electoris Saxoniæ Augusti beatissimæ recordationis Principis, tùm Theologorum Saxonicorum & Svevicorum, Tubingensium cumprimis, insignis istorum hominum πανουργία, & veretoria calliditas detegeretur, detecta reprimeretur, repressa damnaretur: & simul, Quo loco in Ecclesia DEI Corpus Doctrinæ Philippicum haberi possit ac debeat, ostenderetur. Gemina autem hujus quæstionis decisio data est: Una generalis, Altera specialis. Generalem monstrat protestatio illa Electorum, Principum ac statuum Imperij, qui in præfatione Libro Concordiæ præfixa sententiam suam de Scriptis Philippi & aliorum sic informarunt: Neǵ; etiam publicatione libri Concordiæ, alia scripta utilia Domini Philippi Melanchthonis, neǵ; Brentij, Vrbani Regij, Pomerani & similium repudianda ac damnanda esse judicamus, quatenus cum ea norma, quæ Concordiæ libro expressa est, per omnia consentiunt. Norma verò illa, (definiente iterum Libro Concordiæ) fundamenti & Judicis loco respicit scripta Prophetica & Apostolica: Et quia cum hac norma congruunt reliqui libelli Ecclesiarum nostrarum Symbolici, ut tria Symbola Oecumenica, Augustana Cõfessio, prima illa minimeque variata: Articuli Schmalcaldici: uterque Catechismus Lutheri: & Liber Concordiæ: utique ad hos quoque libros, tanquam ad vocem testis reliqua scripta omnia, & sic Philippi quoque exigenda ac dijudicanda esse, generalis hæc decisio rectissimè definivit.

Jam verò, quoad specialem Quæstionis hujus definitionem; si Corpus doctrinæ Philippicum & ad Scripturam Sacram, tanquam Judicis, & ad libellos Symbolicos, tanquam testis vocem paulò accuratiùs exigatur: Sole meridiano clariùs patebit, non posse illud pro norma ac forma sanioris doctrinæ, salvâ religionis puritate, agnosci aut haberi: id quod propter eos, quibus aliquando Corpus hoc Doctrinæ, tanquam Symbolum quoddam Orthodoxum obtrudetur, paulò fusiùs demonstrare operæ precium fuerit.

Initiò igitur in Corpore illo sese offert Mutata sive spuria illa Confessio, quæ Witebergensis veriùs, quàm Augustana appellari potest: quippè quæ hic Witebergæ intra privatos parietes à solo Philippo scripta, Augustam vidit nunquam, quæ item Imperatoris & Ordinum Imperij calculo approbata nunquam, quæ Pontifici Romano serviliter adulatur, quæ Calvinismo portas quasi biparentes aperit: quæ Synergismum stabilit: quæ Evangelium cum Lege confundit; quæ deniq; cothurni instar varijs hæreticis tutum satis præbet latibulum.

Deinde verò ac in specie septem dari possunt, & quidem facilè primarij Articuli fidei, in quibus Corpus doctrinæ Philippicum ab ὑποτυπώσει ὑγιαινόντων λόγων, & sic à puritate doctrinæ Christianæ, periculosissimè deficit.

Articulus primus est de libero Arbitrio, circa quem Synergistis manifestè illud subscribit: id quod multipliciter probatur.
