Primùm enim Articulus quintus mutatæ Confessionis sic stylum inflectit: Cum consolamur nos promissione seu Evangelio, & erigimus nos fide, simul nobis datur Spiritus Sanctus. Nam Spiritus Sanctus datur & est efficax per Verbũ

DEI & per Sacramenta. Cum Evangelium audimus, cogitamus, aut Sacramenta tractamus, & fide nos consolamur, simul est efficax Spiritus Sanctus. Jam quis ita hebetis est judicij, qui non videat Synergisticum hoc esse delirium. Quod si enim Spiritus Sanctus tum demum nobis datur, quando nos ipsos prius fide erigimus & consolamur: utique cooperatio vel saltem præparatio aliqua ad conversionem nostri, ex libertate arbitrij, nobis sit relicta, necesse est: id quod cum verbo DEI & libellis Symbolicis e diametro pugnat.

Deinde patet hoc ipsum ex Articulo XVIII. ejusdem Confessionis mutatæ, qui in Corpore Doctrinæ sic habet: Efficitur spiritualis Justitia in nobis, cum adjuvamur a Spiritu Sancto: porro Spiritum Sanctum concipimus, cum Verbo DEI assentimur, ut nos fide in terroribus consolemur. Et in Antithesi ejusdem Articuli: Interiores motus, ut verum timorem, veram fiduciam, patientiam, castitatem, non potest (humana natura) efficere, nisi Spiritus S. gubernet & adjuvet corda nostra. Hactenus Philippus.

Jam si Spiritus Sanctus non est solus & unus, causa illa efficiens & operans Conversionis: sed tantum coadjuvans: utiq; viribus humanis aliqua supererit facultas applicandi se ad Conversionem: id quod cum Scriptura Sacra, & prototypo Confessionis Augustanæ manifestè pugnat. Sic enim habet prima illa Confessio: Homo non habet vim sine Spiritu Sancto, efficiendæ justitiæ DEI, sive justitiæ spiritualis, quia animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus DEI, sed hæc fit in cordibus, cum per verbum Spiritus Sanctus concipitur. Et in Antithesi: Homo non potest interiores motus efficere, ut timorem DEI, fiduciam erga Deum, castitatem, patientiam, &c.

Tertiò, idem error Synergisticus, & quide de industria Confessioni nostræ Germanicæ incrustatus deprehenditur in Apolog. Art. XVIII. ubi sic in corpore Germanico legimus: Liberum Arbitriū & ratio in spiritualibus nihil SOLA potest. Et paulo post §. tertio: Fidem & timorem Dei operatur Spiritus Sanctus. Ubi gemina insignis depravatio est commissa. Nam exemplat primum minimeq; variatum Apologiæ Germanicæ, in primo paragrapho, particulam exclusivam SOLA non habet: sed sic sonant verba: Affirmamus Liberum Arbitrium & Rationem in spiritualibus NIHIL posse. Deinde in §. tertio: Regenerari & intus aliud cor, aliosq; motus effici, illud operatur SOLVS Spiritus Sanctus.

Quartò, idē patet exinde, quòd Philippus post obitum B. Lutheri in locis suis communibus Articulo de Libero Arbitrio incrustavit Definitionem Erasmi prorsus Synergisticam, quam Lutherus magno zelo rejecerat: Liberum Arbitrium est facultas applicandi se ad gratiam, hoc est, audit promissionem, & assentiri conatur, & abijcit peccatum contra conscientiam.

Quintò, ibidem Philippus ex sententia Synergistarum sic scribit: Cum Promissio sit universalis, nec sint in Deo contradictoriæ voluntates, necesse est IN NOBIS esse, aliquam discriminis causam, Cur Saul abijciatur, David recipiatur, id est, necesse est aliquam esse actionem dissimilem in his duobus.

Tandem hunc ipsum errorem prodidit in examine Ordinandorum: ubi Art. de Libero Arbitrio sic differit: Concurrunt in Conversione hæ causæ: Verbum DEI: Spiritus Sanctus, quem Pater & Filius mittunt, ut accendat corda nostra: & nostra voluntas assentiens & non repugnans verbo DEI.


### On the Authority of the Philippian Writings: The Second Article, in which the Philippic Corpus Doctrinae most dangerously deviates from the purity of sound words and the analogy of…

THE SECOND ARTICLE, in which the Philippic Corpus Doctrinae most dangerously deviates from the purity of sound words and the analogy of faith, is concerning LAW and GOSPEL.

Soon after the death of the blessed Luther, the Antinomians argued with great effort that the use of the Law in the Church is null: but that the Gospel alone is to be proposed, inasmuch as it not only comforts terrified consciences, but also reproves sins. A dispute therefore arose. Whether the Gospel, insofar as it is contradistinguished from the Law, is a preaching of repentance and reproves sins? Luther and all the Orthodox fought most constantly for the Negative according to the mind of the Scriptures. The Antinomians for the Affirmative. Philip, therefore, did not so much reject or disapprove of their opinion in his corpus, that he has everywhere interspersed this Antinomian error. As in Article 4 of the altered Confession: Since all men propagated in a natural way have sin, and cannot satisfy the Law of GOD, the Gospel reproves, and shows us Christ the mediator, and thus teaches us concerning the remission of sins.

Item Article 5 of the same altered Confession: Therefore Christ instituted the ministry of teaching the Gospel, which preaches repentance and the remission of sins.

Item Article 20, section on Faith. The Gospel reproves sins, and requires repentance, and at the same time offers the remission of sins on account of Christ.

And indeed, that Philip understood the doctrine of the Gospel in these passages properly and specifically, and insofar as it is opposed to the Law of GOD or the Decalogue ἀντιδιῃρημένως, is evident from the fact that in the German repetition of the Augsburg Confession, under the title concerning repentance and conversion to GOD, he wrote thus: Diss erschrecken wird denn erwecket/wenn die Hertzen empfinden/ dass sie von wegen der Sünden/vnd verachtung des Sohns Gottes/ durch das Evangelium gestrafft werden/wie Johan. 16. geschrieben stehet: Der Heilige Geist wird die Welt straffen vmb die Sünde/daß sie nicht gleuben an mich/ Darnach werden auch die andere Sünde/durch das Gesetz der Zehen Gebot Gottes gestrafft/ wie Paulus spricht: Durch das Gesetz wird die Sünde erkandt. Which sentiment the Latin edition has somewhat more concisely as follows: Fiunt autem hi veri dolores, cum arguitur peccatum (ut in Evangelio ostenditur) contemtus Filij DEI. The Spirit will reprove the world of sin, because they do not believe in me, John 16. And by the voice of the moral law OTHER SINS are reproved: as Paul says in Romans 3, through the law is the knowledge of sin.

This is most clearly evident from the definitions of the terms, where the Gospel, opposed to the Law and thus taken specifically, is defined as the preaching of repentance.

Latin:

SECUNDUS ARTICULUS, in quo à puritate sanorum verborum, & analogia fidei periculosissimè aberrat Corpus Doctrinæ Philippicum, est de LEGE & EVANGELIO.

Mox post obitum B. Lutheri, magno conatu Antinomi disputarunt, Legis usum in Ecclesianullum esse: sed Evangelium solùm esse proponendum, quippè quòd non solùm consoletur perterrefactas conscientias, sed & arguat peccata. Disputatio ergò orta fuit. An Evangelium, quatenus Legi ἀντιδιῃρημένως contradistinguitur, sit Concio pœnitentiæ & arguat peccata? Lutherus & Orthodoxi quiq; secundum mentem Scripturarum pro Negativa constantissimè pugnarunt. Antinomi pro Affirmativa. Horum ergò sententiam Philippus in corpore suo usq; adeò non rejecit aut improbavit, ut passim errorem istum Antinomicum incrustraverit. Ut Artic. 4. mutatæ Confessionis: Cum omnes homines naturali modo propagati, habeant peccatum, nec possint Legi DEI satisfacere, Evangelium arguit, & ostendit nobis mediatorem Christum, & sic docet nos de remissione peccatorum.

Item Art. 5. ejusdem mutatæ Confessionis: Itaq; instituit Christus ministerium docendi Evangelij, quod prædicat pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum.

Item Art. 20. §. de Fide. Evangelium arguit peccata, & requirit pœnitentiam, & simul offert remissionem peccatorem propter Christum.

Et sanè Philippum doctrinam Evangelij in his locis propriè ac specificè, & quatenùs Legi DEI sive Decalogo ἀντιδιῃρημένως opponitur, intellexisse, vel indè patet, quòd in repetitione Germanica Confessionis Augustanæ, tit. de pœnit. & Conversione ad DEUM, sic scripsit: Diss erschrecken wird denn erwecket/wenn die Hertzen empfinden/ dass sie von wegen der Sünden/vnd verachtung des Sohns Gottes/ durch das Evangelium gestrafft werden/wie Johan. 16. geschrieben stehet: Der Heilige Geist wird die Welt straffen vmb die Sünde/daß sie nicht gleuben an mich/ Darnach werden auch die andere Sünde/durch das Gesetz der Zehen Gebot Gottes gestrafft/ wie Paulus spricht: Durch das Gesetz wird die Sünde erkandt. Quam sententiam latina editio paulò contractius sic habet: Fiunt autem hi veri dolores, cum arguitur peccatum (ut in Evangelio ostenditur) contemtus Filij DEI. Spiritus arguet mundum de peccato, quod non credunt in me Johan. 16. Et voce legis moralis arguuntur ALIA PECCATA: ut inquit Paulus Rom. 3. per legem cognitio peccati.

Patet hec ipsum luculentissimè ex definitionibus appellationum, ubi Evangelium Legi oppositum, & sic specificè sumtum definitur prædicatio pœnitentiæ.


### On the Authority of the Philippian Writings: The Third Article, concerning which the Corpus Doctrinae holds a heterodoxy, is concerning Good Works, to which it indeed ascribes that…

THE THIRD ARTICLE, concerning which the Corpus Doctrinae holds a heterodoxy, is concerning Good Works, to which it indeed ascribes that they preserve the grace of God and Faith. Hence in the Loci Communes, Article on Good Works, Question 4, among the remaining causes for which good works are to be done, he also recounts this: That through good works Faith is retained.

Item in Repetit. Germanica Confessionis Augustanæ tit. de Nova Obed. Therefore it is God’s earnest will, since we have received forgiveness of sins, and are in God’s grace, and are God’s dwellings, and sealed with the Holy Spirit, and have eternal salvation, that we do not cast away this great grace and goodness, but KEEP it in ourselves with constant calling upon God, and with earnest struggle.

THE FOURTH ARTICLE is concerning Adiaphora, where the first and least-varied Confession in Article XVIII of the German Apology held as follows: In these Augsburg Diets we have shown more than enough that for the sake of charity we would not unwillingly observe CERTAIN adiaphora with others: Here the changed Confession omits this particle, CERTAIN, and strokes the Papists, as if they wished to observe all Adiaphora of our Church indefinitely. By which means that collusion of Philipp and others with the Papists at the time of the Interimistic συῤῥάξεως could seek a disguise and pretext under the Augsburg Confession, had not this deceit and depravation been detected.

THE FIFTH ARTICLE is concerning the Sacraments in general: where Philipp in his Commonplaces, in the Question concerning the Number of the Sacraments, writes thus: It pleases me greatly that Ordination, as they call it, should also be added, that is, the Calling to the ministry of the Gospel, and the public approval of that calling. Which opinion is certainly erroneous. For God did not add the promise of grace to Ordination: which nevertheless ought to be annexed to individual Sacraments. Furthermore, if all those things which enjoy the command of God, and which are to be treated with reverence, were to obtain the name and definition of a Sacrament: innumerable Sacraments would emerge.

THE SIXTH ARTICLE is concerning the Supper of the Lord; concerning which at the beginning the Corpus Doctrinae exhibits the tenth Article of the changed Confession, such as provides a most safe hiding place for the Calvinists: while, namely, not only have those two words, originally expressly opposed to the Sacramentarian Spirit (are present and are distributed), been craftily expunged, but also the Antithesis condemning the dogma of the Sacramentarians has been entirely omitted.

Which same depravation happens also to the Apology in this Article: where that spurious edition omits at the beginning the words (are present and are exhibited). Secondly, the entire citation of the ancient Greek Canon: thirdly, the Orthodox explanation of the Apostolic saying: the bread, which we bless, is the κοινωνία of the body of Christ.

Which same thing is evident from the Examination of those to be ordained, into which such a definition of the Lord's Supper has been inserted, which, as we have also warned above, like a buskin can be accommodated as much to the dogma of the Calvinists as to our doctrine: as we shall show in its own place in the exposition itself.

THE SEVENTH and last Article, concerning whose ὀρθοδοξίαν the Philippic Corpus Doctrinae errs, is concerning the Real communication of Idioms in the Person of Christ. Which Philipp in his Refutation of Servetus calls a physical confusion of natures, and plainly rejects it: and therefore in all his writings he passes over it with dry foot

Latin:

ARTICULUS TERTIUS, circa quem ἑτεροδοξίαν tenet corpus Doctrinæ, est de Bonis Operibus, quibus nimirùm adscribit, ut quod gratiam Dei & Fidem conservent. Hinc in Locis Communibus Artic. de Bonis Operibus Quæst. 4. inter reliquas causas, propter quas facienda sint bona opera, recenset etiam hanc: Quòd per bona opera retineatur Fides.

Item in Repetit. Germanica Confessionis Augustanæ tit. de Nova Obed. Darumb ist Gottes ernstlicher Wille/so wir Vergebung der Sünden empfangen haben / vnd seyn in Gottes Gnaden/ vnd Gottes Wohnungen / vnnd versiegelt mit dem Heiligen Geist / vnd haben ewige Seligkeit / Das wir diese grosse Gnade vnnd Güte/ nicht ausstossen/ sondern mit steter anruffung Gottes/vnnd mit ernstlichem Streit in vns BEHALTEN.

ARTICULUS QUARTUS est de Adiaphoris, ubi Confessio prima miniméq; variata Articulo XVIII. Apologiæ Germanicæ sic habuit: In his Comitijs Augustanis satis superq; ostendimus, nos propter charitatem haud gravatim QUÆDAM adiaphora observaturos esse cum alijs: Hîc mutata Confessio, particulam hanc, QUÆDAM, omittit, & Pontificijs palpum facit, ac si indefinitè omnia Adiaphora nostræ Ecclesiæ observare velint. Quo pacto collusio illa Philippi & aliorum cum Pontificijs tempore συῤῥάξεως Interimisticæ, fucum & prætextum quærere posset, sub Augustana Confessione, nisi dolus & depravatio isthæc fuisset deprehensa.

QUINTUS ARTICULUS est de Sacramentis in genere: ubi Philippus in locis communibus, Quæstione de Numero Sacramentorum, sic scribit: Mihi maximè placet etiam addi Ordinationem, ut vocant, id est, Vocationem ad ministerium Evangelij, & publicam ejus vocationis approbationem. Quæ sanè opinio est erronea. Neque enim Deus promissionem gratiæ ad Ordinationem addidit: quæ tamen singulis Sacramentis debet esse annexa. Deinde, si singula illa, quæ gaudemt mandato Dei, quæque cum reverentia tractanda sunt, Sacramenti nomen & definitionem sortirentur: innumera prodirent Sacramenta.

SEXTUS ARTICULUS est de Cœna Domini; circa quem initiò Corpus Doctrinæ exhibet Articulum decimum mutatæ Confessionis talem, qui Calvinianis latibulum tutissimum præbet: dum nimirùm non modò subdolè expuncta sunt duo isthæc vocabula, Spiritui Sacramentario primìtùs ex professo opposita (Adsint & distribuantur) sed & Antithesis damnans Sacramentariorum dogma, penitùs est omissa.

Quæ ipsa depravatio evenit etiam Apologiæ in hoc Articulo: ubi spuria illa editio, omittit initio vocabula (Adsint & exhibeantur) Deinde integram citationem antiqui Græci Canonis: tertiò Orthodoxam explicationem dicti Apostolici: panis, cui benedicimus, est κοινωνία corporis Christi.

Quòd ipsum patet ex Ordinandorum Examine, cui talis inserta est definitio Cœnæ Dominicæ, quæ, uti suprà etiam admonuimus, cothurni instar cùm Calvinianorum dogmati, quàm nostræ doctrinæ accommodari potest: uti suo loco in ipsâ diexodo ostendemus.

SEPTIMUS & postremus Articulus, circa cujus ὀρθοδοξίαν errat Corpus Doctrinæ Philippicum, est de Reali communicatione Idiomatum in Persona Christi. Quam Philippus in Refutatione Serveti nominat physicam naturarum confusionem, eamq; planè rejicit: ac proinde in omnibus suis scriptis sicco planè pede


### Third Prolegomenon Chapter

has passed. Since these things are truly so, we infallibly conclude that the Corpus doctrinae of Philipp in churches that are truly reformed and genuinely Lutheran can and should in no way be held as the norm of doctrine, but that it stands in need of clear correction in very many articles. We are truly grieved, and God knows we are grieved from the heart, that such a man, who has deserved so excellently of the whole world of letters, is being snatched away from our churches; and we are so far from deriving any pleasure from his fall that we would rather redeem such a loss with our own blood, not to mention covering his sad fall with perpetual silence, were it not that partly the preposterous boastings of our adversaries, and partly the designs and arts of the Crypto-Calvinists, by which they strive to foist Calvinism upon the purer churches under the venerable name of Philipp, and consequently the very salvation of the Church, were compelling us, even against our will, to confess that which, without prejudice to the truth, can in no way be denied. Nor is there any reason for anyone to rave against us on this account, as if we were attacking Philipp savagely and acting hostily like hyenas against the ashes of the blessed dead: as if we were stripping Philipp of all authority: as if we were removing his monuments from the schools by evil arts: and finally, as if we were adjudging him to the eternal flames of the underworld: just as a certain Johannes Sturmius in part 3 of the Antipappus quartus, page 201, some years ago, and then quite recently a certain babbler in the neighborhood (Rollenhagen), wished to adorn us with such flowers and emblems, with these verses added to the likeness of Luther and Philipp: The Fates, O LUTHER, gave you the sword of the brave ELIJAH: The Fates, O PHILIPP, gave you the mantle of the prophet ELISHA; With as much zeal as you yourself cover the errors of your Master, with so much zeal do your descendants desire to strip you; These are the ways of Ham, and the fate of Ham shall follow them. G. R. But these are calumnies born of a preposterous love for Philipp, or rather, born of pure malice. For it grieves these men that that crafty cunning, or those arts and frauds, have been detected by which they have hitherto, with almost no one noticing, wickedly imposed upon the churches of God in many places, while they wished to appear Orthodox, because they would repeatedly harp on Philipp and his writings: and yet under this specious pretext they were attempting to encrust Calvinism. After it was therefore shown by the grace of God to the Church of God what kind of person Philipp was in the matter of the Holy Supper: and in what place and number his writings ought to be held in the Church of God; the nerve of these clandestine arts and deceits has certainly been cut and disrupted. Furthermore, if that is to rage against the ashes of the dead, what, I ask, must be thought of it when words are spoken in a public sermon about David's adultery, about Solomon's idolatry, about Moses' doubting, about Aaron's making of the calf, about the sins of Adam and Eve and other saints? When Paul himself complains in heavy words to the Galatians about Peter's fall? Indeed, when these very idle men chatter quite frequently about the flaws and errors of Luther? Therefore, we oppose to such Aristarchuses that saying of Solomon: Proverbs 27:5-6. Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Better are the wounds of a friend than the deceitful kisses of an enemy. Thirdly, the collection of these censors is clearly ridiculous and childish: The errors of Philipp are noted: Therefore all his books are to be cast out of the churches and schools. Which collection certainly possesses no more strength than if someone were to infer thus: Scripture testifies that King Solomon was an idolater: Therefore Scripture itself implies that Solomon's books, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs, are to be rejected. Or: Very many of the Fathers noted grave lapses and errors in Origen: Therefore they determined that Origen's books were to be entirely eliminated. Even a boy understands that the fallacy of the vicious consequent and of non-cause as cause is being committed.

We therefore read and value the writings and books of Philipp, but we read them with judgment: so that according to the precept of the Apostle in 1 Thessalonians 5:21, we may retain what is good; reject what is false and erroneous: and according to the counsel of the Book of Concord, we may weigh them by the norm and form of sounder doctrine.

Finally, as regards the person of Philipp and his death, it is certainly not for us to pass judgment on him. He was a servant of Christ: to this his own Lord he both stood and fell. And although we can neither praise nor ought to praise in him the defection from the purity of heavenly doctrine: we do not doubt, however, that toward the end of his life, having performed serious repentance, he both sought and obtained forgiveness for this sin also from Christ the Savior.

Latin:

præterijt. Quæ cum ita revera sefe habeant, infallibiliter concludimus, Corpus doctrinæ Philippi in Ecclesiis, verè reformatis ac γνησίως Lutheranis, pro norma Doctrinæ haberi nulla ratione vel posse vel debere: sed luculenta correctione plurimis in Articulis indigere. Dolemus profectò, & quod Dʊs novit, ex animo dolemus, tantum virum, deque re literariâ universâ præclarissimè meritum, nostris Ecclesiis eripi: & tantum abest, nos ex ipsius lapsu quicquam voluntatis percipere, ut mallemus vel sanguine nostro tantam jacturam redimere, nedum tristem ejus lapsum perpetuo involvere silentio, nisi partim Adversariorum præposteræ gloriationes, partim verò Crypto-Calvinistarum consilia & artes, quibus sub venerando Philippi nomine Calvinismum purioribus Ecclesiis obtrudere satagunt, & per consequens ipsa Ecclesiæ salus, nos etiam invitos impelleret ad fatendum id, quod salva veritate negari nulla ratione potest. Neque est, ut quisquam hoc nomine in nos debacchetur, ac si immaniter in Philippum invehamur, inq; beatè mortui cineres hostiliter hyænarum instar sæviamus: omni autoritate Philippum spoliemus: malis artibus monumenta ejus è Scholis removeamus:æternis deniq; inferorum flammis ipsum adjudicemus: Quemadmodum hujusmodi flosculis & Emblematis tũ superioribus annis Iohannes Sturmius parte 3. Antipappi quarti pag. 201. tum nuper admodum spermologus quidam in vicinia (Rollenhagen) nos exornare voluit: his ad effigiem Lutheri & Philippi adscriptis versibus: Fata, LVTHERE, dabant ensem tibi fortis ELIÆ: Fata, PHILIPPE, dabant vestem tibi Vatis ELISÆ; Hâc quanto studio tegis ipse errata Magistri, Tanto te studio cupiunt nudare Nepotes; Sunt mores Chami, Chami quoq; fata sequentur. G. R. Verùm calumniæ hæ sunt ex præpostero amore Philippi, imò potius ex mera malicia profectæ. Dolet enim istis hominibus veteratoriam illam calliditatem, sive artes & fraudes illas esse detectas, quibus hactenus, nemini fermè animadvertente, multis in locis Ecclesiæ Dʊi nequiter imposuerunt, dum nimirum Orthodoxi videri volebant, eò quod Philippum, & ejus scripta subindè creparent: & tamen sub hoc specioso prætextu Calvinismum incrustare conabantur. Postquam ergò per Dʊi gratiam ostensum est Ecclesiæ Dʊi qualis in negotio S. Cœnæ fuerit Philippus: quo etiam loco numeroq; scripta ipsius in Ecclesia Dʊi haberi debeant; utiq; nervus etiam clandestinis hisce artibus atque dolis est incisus & disruptus. Deinde si istud est in demortuorũ cineres sævire, quid quæso sentiendum erit de eo, cùm de Davidis adulterio, de Salomonis Idololatria, de Moysis dubitatione, de Aaronis μοσχοποιία, de Adami, & Evæ, aliorũmq; Sanctorum delictis, pro publica con cione verba fiunt: Cum de Petri lapsu Paulus ipse ad Galatas gravibus verbis conqueritur? Imò cùm hi ipsi malè feriati homines de Lutheri nævis & erratis frequenter admodum garriunt? Proinde illud Salomonis hujusmodi Aristarchis opponimus: Proverb. 27, 5, & 6. Melior est manifesta increpatio, quàm amor absconditus. Meliora sunt vulnera diligētis, quàm fraudulenta oscula osoris. Tertiò ridicula & puerilis planè est istorum Censorum collectio: Errores Philippi notantur: Ergò omnes ejus libri ex Ecclesijs & Schölis ejiciuntur. Quæ sanè collectio haud plus virium obtinet, quàm si quis ita inferret: Scriptura testatur Regem Salomonem fuisse Idololatram: Ergo Scriptura ipsa, Salomonis libros, Proverbia, Ecclesiasten & Canticum canticorum, rejiciendos esse innuit. Vel: Patrum plurimi in Origene graves lapsus & errores notarunt: Ergo statuerunt Origenis libros esse prorsus eliminandos. Fallaciam vitiosi consequentis & non causæ ut causæ committi, vel puer intelligit.

Legimus proindè & magnifacimus Scripta & libros Philippi, sed cum judicio legimus: ut secundum præceptum Apostoli 1. Thess. 5. 21. quod bonum est retineamus; quod falsum & erroneum rejiciamus: & secundum consilium Libri Concordiæ, ad normam & formam sanioris doctrinæ ea appendamus.

Tandem quoad personam Philippi, ejus‐ demque obitum, nostrum sanè non est, de eo ferre judicium. Christi servus fuit: Huic suo Domino & stetit & cecidit. Et quanquam defectionem à puritate doctrinæ cœlestis, in ipso laudare neque possumus, neq; debemus: haud tamen dubitamus, quin sub finem vitæ seriâ actâ pœnitentiâ hujus etiam peccati veniam à Christo Servatore & petierit, & impetrârit.


### Third Prolegomenon Chapter: The Third Chapter of the Prolegomena. Concerning the various editions of the Philippic Loci Communes

THE THIRD CHAPTER OF THE PROLEGOMENA. Concerning the various editions of the Philippic Loci Communes.

Various editions of the Philippic Loci Communes are available: differing from one another greatly, not only in printing, but also in their very composition and in the variety of the questions explained. The first edition saw the light in the year 1521, printed here in Wittenberg under this title: Loci Communes rerum Theologicarum seu Hypotyposes Theologicae, with a preface to Tilemann Pletener.

It would be desirable, however, that copies of this first edition were still extant today. Or at least that Peucer, the compiler of Philipp's writings, had inserted that work into the Philippic Tomes: so that, partly, the progress and increments of the newly reformed Church could be more correctly observed, and partly, a more certain judgment could be formed concerning the doctrine of Philipp.

In this first edition, hardly anything occurs that dissents from the analogy of faith: if you except that one thing, that at that time Philipp thought that all things simply happen necessarily. For on leaf B. iiij. b., in the Article on Free Will, he writes thus: If you refer it to predestination, human will has no liberty either in external or in internal works, but all things happen according to divine destination. In the following year, 1522, as also in the year 1523, those same Hypotyposes were again brought to light, but with some improvement and revision by the Author himself, where, however, that error was already just noted, was not only not removed, but rather confirmed. For thus in the Article on Free Will, page 9 of the Strasbourg edition: Finally, divine predestination takes away liberty from man. For all things happen according to divine predestination, both external works and internal thoughts in all creatures. And page 10: since the matter of Free Will had to be dealt with in the very first place, how could I conceal the judgment of Scripture concerning predestination, when Scripture takes away liberty from our will through the necessity of predestination? And on the reverse side of the same page: Divine predestination therefore removes all liberty of our will.

Thirdly, in the year [15]25, the same Theological Hypotyposes, or Commonplaces, appeared again, revised by the Author, to which were added the themes of the same Philip concerning double justice, and concerning corporal and spiritual government: Where, however, the same original error is found in the Article on Free Will.

Moreover, it must be well observed that that excellent judgment or eulogy, which our blessed Luther bestowed upon Philip's Commonplaces, is to be understood as applying primarily to these editions which we have already noted, writing thus in the preface to the booklet on the Bondage of the Will against Erasmus of Rotterdam: It seems superfluous to answer the arguments of that man of yours, which were previously refuted by me so many times, and indeed trampled upon and utterly worn out by Philip Melanchthon's invincible booklet on Theological Commonplaces, which in my judgment is worthy not only of immortality, but also of an Ecclesiastical Canon.

Which judgment of Luther, since it was published in the year [15]25, is wrongly and in very bad faith applied today by the Calvinists to those Philippic commonplaces which appeared later, and were changed with great danger especially after the death of blessed Luther: with the insertion and addition of those things which most manifestly conflict with the simplicity and purity of that first edition, as was shown in the preceding second chapter, and will be most faithfully demonstrated in the exposition itself.

Eight years later, namely in 1533, another edition of the Commonplaces appeared, and indeed one more augmented and enriched, with this title: Theological Commonplaces recently collected and revised by Philip Melanchthon, with a preface to Henry VIII, King of England (who, although initially he was a most intense enemy of Luther's doctrine, yet on the occasion of the divorce of his first wife, and the joining of another, Anne Boleyn, he later defected from the Papal Religion to Lutheranism.) In this edition also, most things are quite tolerable, and not at all disapproved of by blessed Luther while he was still alive: and indeed the error concerning fatal necessity was corrected and removed.

Finally, in the year [15]45, which preceded Luther's death by one year, a new edition of the Commonplaces appeared, clearly twice, or even three times as large as those previous ones: namely, that which was inserted into the first volume of Philip's works, as well as into the Body of Doctrine. Although there are not wanting those who, from the preface prefixed to this edition, conclude that it should be referred to the year [15]43. But whatever the case may be, that can certainly be denied by no reason, that this edition is filled with many errors, as we showed in the immediately preceding chapter: and it will be shown more fully in the exposition itself: So much so, that it is not probable that this last edition was read by Luther, much less approved. For Philip himself, in his Epistle to Karlowitz in the following year, 1548, did not hesitate to confess expressly that he had defected from Luther in many chapters of Christian doctrine, and especially in the Article concerning Free Will, to Erasmus: saying, "I grant many things spontaneously and liberally, about which others (namely Luther and his colleagues) have fought most fiercely." This very fact was also observed by Papist writers, such as Stanislaus Hosius in his book *de Vita, Sectis, & dogmatis hæreticorum*, page 373, under the subheading *Melanchthonis*; and Wilhelmus Lindanus in his *Panoplia*, page 132; likewise the Louvain School, and the apostate Jacobus Rabus in his *Ἀληθευτικῳ*, and many others. This latest edition is today in everyone’s hands, and therefore it will also be the one proposed for us henceforth in our explanation, using the method which the fourth and final chapter of the *προλεγομένων* will now set forth.

Latin:

TERTIUM PROLEGOMENΩN CAPUT. De variis editionibus Locorum Communium Philippicorum.

VAriæ prostant editiones Locorum Communium Philippicorum: non impressione saltem, sed ipsa quoque compositione, & Quæstionum explicatarum varietate, plurimùm à se invicem discrepantes. Prima editio vidit lucem Anno 1521. hîc Witebergæ impressa hoc titulo: Loci Communes rerum Theologicarũ seu Hypotyposes Theologicæ, cum præfatione ad Tilemannum Pletenerum.

Optandum autem esset, ut primæ hujus Editionis Exemplaria hodieque extarent. Vel saltem Peucerus, scriptorum Philippicorum Compilator, scriptum istud Tomis Philippicis inseruisset: ut partim profectus atque incrementa Ecclesiæ recens reformatæ, rectius conspici, partim de doctrinâ Philippi certius judi‐ cium informari posset.

In prima hac editione vix quicquam occurrit, quod cum analogia fidei dissentiat: si unum illud excipias, quòd tùm temporis Philippus censuit, Omnia simpliciter necessariò evenire. Nam lit. B. iiij. b. in Articulo de Libero arbitrio sic scribit: Si ad prædestinationem referas, humanam voluntatem, nec in externis, nec in internis operibus ulla est libertas,sed eveniunt omnia juxta destinationem divinam. Anno subsequenti proximo 22. ut & Anno 23. denuò in lucem prodierunt eædé Hypotyposes, sed cũ aliquâ ἐπιδόσει & recogni‐ tione ipsius Autoris, ubi tamé σφάλμα illud jāmodò notatum, non modò non sublatum, sed magis confirmatum fuit. Sic enim in Artic. de Libero Arbitrio pag. 9. editionis Argentinensis. Postremò Libertatem homini adimit divina Prædestinatio. Eveniunt enim omnia juxta divinam prædestinationem, cùm externa opera, tùm internæ cogitationes in omnibus creaturis. Et pag. 10. cum de Libero Arbitrio omninò primo loco agendum esset, qui potui dissimulare sententiam Scripturæ de prædestinatione, quando voluntati nostræ Libertatẽ per prædestinationis necessitatem adimit Scriptura. Et versa facie ejusdem paginæ: Tollit itaque omnem libertatem voluntatis nostræ prædestinatio divina.

Tertiò prodierunt Anno 25. eædem denuò Hypotyposes Theologicæ, sive Loci cōmuncs recogniti ab Autore, quibus adjecta sút themata ejusdem Philippi de duplici justitia, Regimineque corporali & spirituali: Ubi tamen pristinus idem error in Articulo de Libero Arbitrio reperitur.

Cæterùm probè observandum est, de his potissimùm editionibus, quas jam notavimus, accipiendum esse egregium illud sive judicium sive elogium, quod B. Lutherus noster Locis Communibus Philippi perhibuit, sic scribens in præfat. libelli de Servo Arbitrio contra Erasmum Roterodamum: Supervacaneum videtur respondere argumentis istius tuis, antea à me quoque toties confutatis, conculcatis verò & prorsus protritis, per Philipp: Melanthonis de locis Theologicis invictũ libellum, meo judicio, non solum immortalitate, sed Canone quoque Ecclesiastico dignum.

Quod sanè Lutheri judicium, cum Anno 25. sit proditum: perperàm illud ac fide pessima accommodatur hodiè à Calvinianis ad eos locos Philippicos, qui postmodùm in lucẽ prodierunt, & maximè post obitum B. Lutheri magno cum periculo sunt mutati: insertis & adjectis ijs, quæ cum simplicitate & puritatæ primæ istius editionis manifestissimè pugnant uti cap. præcedente secundo est ostensum, & in ipsa diexodo fidelissimè demonstrabitur.

Octennio pòst nempè. 1533. prodijt alia, & quidem auctior ac locupletior Locorum communium editio, cum hoc titulo: Loci Communes Theologici recens collecti & recogniti à Philippo Melanthchone, cum præfatione ad Henricum VIII. Regem Angliæ (qui etsi initiò doctrinæ Lutheri hostis erat infensissimus: occasione tamen divortij prioris conjugis, & conjunctionis alterius Annæ Polemiæ, à Pontificia Religione, ad Lutheranismum postea descivit.) In hac etiam ditione satis tolerabilia sunt pleraque, & B. Luthero adhuc superstiti minimè improbata: quin & error de fatali necessitate correctus & sublatus.

Tandem anno, 45. qui Lutheri mortem uno antecessit anno prodijt nova planè Locorum editio, prioribus illis duplo, imò triplo auctior: ea nimirum, quæ Tomo primo operum Philippi, ut & corporiDoctrinæ est inserta. Quanquã nō desunt, qui ex præfatione Editioni huic præ fixa colligant, ad annũ 43. eam referendam esse. Sed quicquid sit, illud certè negari nulla ratione potest, multis erroribusEditionem hanc refertam esse, uti præcedente capite proximo ostendimus: & in ipsa diexodo fusius ostẽ detur: Ita quidem, ut probabile non sit, postremam obcut hanc Editionem à Luthero lectam, multò minus approbatam esse. Siquidem ipse Philippus in Epistola ad Carolovvitzium, anno subsequente 1548. disertè fateri non dubitavit, se à Luthero in multis capitibus doctrinæ Christianæ, & cumprimis in Articulo de Libero Arbitrio, ad Erasmum defecisse: Multa, inquiens, spontè & liberaliter ego largior, de quibus acerrimè pugnaverunt alij (Lutherus nimirum & collega) Quod ipsum observarunt etiam Scriptores Pontificij, ut Stanislaus Hosius in libro de Vita, Sectis, & dogmatis hæreticorum. pag. 373. subtitulo Melanchthonis. Et Wilhelmus Lindanus in Panoplia pag. 132. Schola item Lovaniensis, & Apostata Iacobus Rabus in suo Ἀληθευτικῳ & alij complures. Hæc editio postrema hodiè in omnium versatur manibus, ac proinde ea etiam nobis deinceps in explicando erit proposita: eâ usuris methodo, quam quartum ac postremum προλεγομένων caput jam expediet.


### Third Prolegomenon Chapter: The Fourth and Final Chapter of the Prolegomena, Concerning the Method of the future treatment

THE FOURTH AND FINAL CHAPTER OF THE PROLEGOMENA, Concerning the Method of the future treatment.

SO THAT it may be clear not only to the listeners what they should expect for themselves from the future treatment, but also to me, within what boundaries and limits I ought to contain myself; the following Method will be proposed to us most precisely. First, we will resolve the Philippic treatment of individual commonplaces into their certain parts or Questions. Then, we will weave through the treatment of individual Questions, enclosed in certain propositions, in order: but in such a way that we propose the reasons and arguments which our Author uses, syllogistically: and wherever his treatment might seem to be lacking, we will compensate for the defect from elsewhere: at the same time also, we will weigh those things which occur that are either stated inconveniently or less than orthodoxly, against the analogy of faith and the balance of heavenly truth. Thirdly, we will add controversial Questions in certain Articles omitted by the Author, and about which there is most controversy today: so that our treatment does not appear too disjointed. Finally, we will append a certain brief historical notation, by whom, in what place and time, on what occasion, and finally with what arguments, the heavenly purity was contradicted in individual places: with the addition of a brief but sufficient refutation of the principal sophisms by which it was most fought against by them, and is accustomed to be fought against today.

Latin:

QVARTVM ET POSTREMVM CAPVT PROLEGOMENΩN, De Methodo futuræ tractationis.

VT non Auditoribus modò constare possit, quid ex futura tractatione sibi polliceri debeant: sed & mihi, intra quos quasi cancellos atque crepidines continere me debeam; subsequens Methodus nobis exactissimè erit proposita. Primùm singulorum locorum Tractationem Philippicam in certas suas partes sive Quæstiones resolvemus. Deinde singularum Quæstionum pertractationem certis propositionibus inclusam ordine pertexemus: sed ita, ut rationes atque argumenta, quibus Autor noster utitur, Syllogisticè proponamus: & sicubi fortè tractatio ipsius deficere videbitur, aliundè defectum compensemus: simul etiam, quæ vel incommodè, vel minus Orthodoxè dicta occurrent, ad analogiam fidei, & trutinam cœlestis veritatis appendamus. Tertiò, Quæstiones Controversas in quibusdam Articulis ab Autore prætermissas, & de quibus hodiè potissimùm controvertitur adjiciemus: ne Tractatio nostra nimis hiulca appareat. Tandem subjiciemus brevem quandam notationem historicam, à quibus, quo loco ac tempore, qua occasione, quibus deniq; argumentis in singulis locis cœlesti puritati sit contradictum: adjecta brevi, sed sufficienti refutatione præcipuorum Sophismatum, quibus ab ipsis maximè pugnatum fuit, hodiéque pugnari solet.


## 2 On Holy Scripture and Unwritten Traditions

IN THE NAME OF THE MOST HOLY AND UNDIVIDED TRINITY, God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, Amen.

As we are about to explain the CONTROVERSY concerning Holy Scripture, or the revealed word of God, against the Romanists, under the auspices of the most holy and undivided Trinity, it seems that, before all else, this one argument at this very time must be set forth by way of a preface, so that we may demonstrate in few words the horrible foulness and atrocity of the errors which the Jesuit race tenaciously holds and defends regarding this article of Christian doctrine. For if one may know the lion by his claw, certainly it should be permitted to discern the spirit of that Society even from this one Jesuit dogma. And although there are many other things which quite openly argue the remarkable distrust of these men, and their seared, as it is called, conscience in the matter of religion, this one nevertheless easily takes the first place, because they do not fear to violate most foully the majesty of Holy Scripture, which is to be dreaded even by the angels themselves. For when they understand that the βδελύγματα or abominations of their Roman synagogue will collapse and fall of their own accord if even one battering ram of the Scriptures is brought against them, they prefer to struggle with extreme fortune, and, with matters now desperate and lost, to attempt the final resort, that is, to inflict violence and wicked hands upon the divine books themselves.

Irenaeus, a most ancient writer, judges that this is a characteristic of heretics, that when they are refuted from the scriptures, they immediately turn to an accusation of the scriptures themselves, as if they were not correctly held, nor were of authority, because they were spoken in various ways, and because the truth cannot be found from them by those who do not know tradition: for it was not handed down through letters, but through the living voice, book 3, chapter 2.

And this indeed is that singular cunning of the ancient Dragon, the Devil, by which he strives to drive the unwary away from the scriptures, that is, from the certain rule of truth, into the dangerous byways of human traditions. For since he can neither remove the scriptures nor openly detract from the authority of the Apostles, he attacks the doctrine contained in the Holy Scriptures as if through tunnels, and accuses them of obscurity, imperfection, and uselessness. That this is not new or unusual for the race of Romanists, those remarkable eulogies or emblems, by which they illustrate the Holy Scriptures, make it not obscurely testified. Andradius the Spaniard, that great defender of the Council of Trent, designated the Scriptures as a flexible nose: Melchior Canus, a dead judge:

Stephanus Paletz, an inanimate thing which does not speak for itself: Latomus, obscure and ambiguous: Florobellus, mute and speechless: Petrus Sotus, a thing of little or no moment, with which the Holy Spirit has nothing to do: likewise the killing letter, committed not to the hearts or minds of men, but to membranes and tablets. Canisius, imperfect, mutilated, maimed, which does not contain all things pertaining to salvation, faith, and the morals of living piously: likewise a waxen nose, not providing any certain and immovable meaning, but one which can be bent into any interpretation whatsoever: others, a matter of litigation, cobbler's ink, the riddles of the Sphinx, the principles of Protagoras, the leaves of the Sibyl, a Lesbian rule, a leaden rule, and one flexible in all directions, a dead letter. And Brentius is a witness in his prolegomena that in his time in certain monasteries, and especially in a convent of nuns, this riddle or byword was customary: that to one asking, In what thing did the Lutheran religion consist? the answer would be: In tattered rags, thus falsely implying that Holy Scripture is merely a paper thing, as if made from worn-out and tattered rags. And so that nothing is lacking in impiety, Hosius, in book 3 on the authority of the scriptures, did not blush to excuse, and even to defend, that blasphemous pronouncement of another Papist: that the Holy Scriptures, unless they borrow their authority from the Church, would be worth no more than Aesop's fables.

Abbot Urspergensis in his paralipomena, page 494, reports that a certain Papist Doctor, otherwise a man of great authority, openly proclaimed in a sermon held at Speyer: It is safer to depart from Scripture and the Gospel than from the ceremonies of the Church. Although today the leaders of the Jesuits, Bellarmine, Gregorius de Valentia, and others, abstain from those horrible blasphemies: indeed, they seem to value Holy Scripture more: yet in this, both the old and the more recent Papist Doctors, each and all, agree: 1. that the authority of Holy Scripture depends entirely upon the Church. 2. that the authority of the Church is greater than that of the Scriptures. 3. that the Scriptures cannot be the measure and norm of faith and of the controversies of the Christian religion. 4. that finally (as Pighius was not ashamed to write) the writings of the Apostles do not preside over faith and religion, but rather are subject to them.

Hence in the recent Colloquy of Ratisbon, these emblems were heard: From Scripture alone not even one controversy can be defined: and from Holy Scripture alone, no heresy, of whatever heretic it may be, could ever be, or can even now be, sufficiently refuted. Likewise, there are many

Latin:

IN NOMINE SACRO-SANCTÆ AC INDIVIDUÆ TRINITATIS, DEI PATRIS, FILII & Spiritus Sancti, Amen.

CONTROVERSIAM de Sacra scriptura:sive verbo Dei revelato, adversus Romanenses, sub auspicijs sacrosanctæ & individuæ Trinitatis nobis explicaturis,prę reliquis,vel unū illud, hoc quidem tempore, προλεγομένων loco præmittendum videtur argumentum, ut nimirum errorum, quos gens Jesuvvitica, circa hunc doctrinæ Christianæ Articulum, mordicus tenet ac defendit, horrendam, tùm fœditatem, tùm atrocitatem paucis demonstremus. Nam si ex ungue Leonem, certè vel ex hoc uno dogmate Jesuvvitico, Spiritum istius Societatis dignoscere fas fuerit. Etsi verò multa sunt alia, quæ insignem istorum hominum diffidentiam, & cauteriatam, quod dicitur, Conscientiam, in puncto Religionis satis apertè arguunt: illud tamen primas facile obtinet, quod Scripturæ sacræ Majestatem, ipsis etiam Angelis tremendam, fœdissimè violare haud verentur. Etenim cum Romanæ suæ Synagogæ βδελύγματα sive abominationes, vel uno Scripturarum admoto ariete, ultrò labascere & concidere intelligant, malunt extrema fortunâ confligere, & rebus jam desperatis ac perditis,ultima tentare, hoc est, ipsis divinis codicibus, vim manusque sceleratas inferre.

Jrenæus scriptor antiquissimus, Hæreticorum hoc esse proprium censet, ut cum ex scripturis arguuntur, mox in accusationem ipsarum scripturarum convertantur, quasi non rectè habeant, neque sint ex autoritate, quòd variè sint dictæ, quodque non possit ex his inveniri Veritas ab ijs, qui nesciant traditionem: Non enim per literas traditam illam, sed per vivam vocem, libr. 3. cap. 2.

Et hæc quidem singularis est illa antiqui Draconis Diaboli astutia, qua à scripturis,hoc est, à certa Veritatis regula, in periculosa traditionum humanarum devia, incautos impellere studet. Cùm enim neque scripturas tollere,neque Apostolorū autoritati apertè derogare possit; canculum doctrinam scripturis sacris comprehensam, veluti per cuniculos oppugnat, & obscuritatis,imperfectionis,inutilitatis eas insimulat. Novum hoc aut insolens genti Romanensium haud esse,egregia certè illa elogia sive Emblemata,quibus scripturas Sacras illustrant, haud obscurè testatum faciunt. Andradius Hispanus, Hyperaspistes ille Concilij Tridentini, Scripturas indigitavit nasum flexibilem: Melchior Canus, judicem mortuum:

Stephanus Paletz, rem inanimatam, quæ per se non loquatur: Latomus, obscuram & ambiguam:Florobellus, mutam & eliuguem: Petrus Sotus,rem parvi aut nullius momenti, cui cum Spiritu sancto nihil sit negotij:Literam item occidentem,non hominum cordibus aut animis,sed membranis & tabulis mandatam. Canisius imperfectam, mutilam,mancam,quæ non contineat omnia ad salutem, fidem & mores piè vivendi pertinentia:item nasum cereum,non præbentem certam aliquam & immotam sententiam,sed quæ in quamvis interpretationem flecti queat:Alij materiam litis, atramentum sutorium, Sphigis ænigmata, Protagoræ principia, folia Sibyllæ,regulam Lesbiam, regulam plumbeam, & in omnes partes flexibilem,literam mortuam. Et testis est Brentius in prolegomenis, suo tempore in quibusdam Cœnobijs, & præsertim in conventu puellarum Monialium usitatum fuisse, hoc sive ænigma sive diverbium: ut interroganti; Qua in re sita esset Religio Lutherana? responderetur: In laceris panniculis,sic falsè innuendo, Scripturam Sacrā esse rem tantùm chartaceam, quippe ex detritis & laceris panniculis confectam. Et ne quid impietati desit, Hosius lib. 3.de autoritate scripturarum, blasphemum illud alius cujusdam Pontificij pronunciatum non modò excusare, sed & defendere haud erubuit; Scripturas sacras,ni si ab Ecclesia suam mutuentur autoritatem, haud plus valituras, quàm fabulæ valeant Aesopicæ,

Abbas Ursperg.in paralipomenis pag. 494. refert, quendam Doctorem Pontificium, aliâs magnæ autoritatas Virum,pro concione Spiræ habita propalàm proclamasse, Tutiús esse à scriptura & Evangelio discedere, quàm ab Ecclesiæ Ceremonijs. Quanquam verò hodiè Iesuitarum Antesignani, Bellarminus, Gregorius de Valentia, & alij ab horrendis istis blasphemijs abstinere: imò scripturam sacram pluris facere videntur: in eo tamen & Veteres & recentiores Doctores Pontificij singuli & universi consentiunt,1. quòd scripturæ sacræ autoritas tantùm pendeat ab Ecclesia. 2. quòd major Ecclesia, quam scripturæ sit autoritas. 3. quòd Scripturæ non poßint esse mensura ac norma fidei & Controversiarum Religionis Christianæ. 4. quod denique (uti Pigkius scribere non exhorruit) Apostolorum scripta non præsint fidei ac Religioni,sed potius subsint.

Hinc in Colloquio nupero Ratisbonensi, hæc audita fuêre Emblemata: Ex sola scriptura ne una quidem Controversia potest definiri: & ex sola scriptura sacra, nulla unquàm hæresis, cujuscunque tandem hæretici, aut potuit, aut etiamnum potest sufficienter refutari. Item, Multa sunt-


### Comparison of the Pontiffs with the ancient heretics, who erred concerning scripture

dogmas of faith, and necessary for salvation, which nevertheless are neither contained in Scripture, nor can be deduced from it by any other evident consequence.

Item, the fountain and source of all heresies, and the Babylonian confusion, is if anyone wishes to establish that nothing is to be believed in the cause of religion, and nothing done in worship, which is not either expressly contained in the sacred letters, or cannot be deduced from them by good consequence.

Item, neither Scripture itself, as it is the Word of God, nor the Holy Spirit, as He speaks through it, is the judge of controversies.

Item: Unwritten traditions are of the same authority, and are equally the divine Word, as is the written Word.

These and other things of this kind show clearly enough what the Jesuit society thinks in the innermost recess of their hearts about sacred Scripture, and how much they hold it in contempt.

Moreover, we shall not consider this error to be trivial, nor that our dispute in this matter with the Papists is about goat’s wool; but besides the fact that the very principles and foundation of the Christian religion are at stake, and consequently we are fighting for hearth and home, this point especially comes under consideration, and indeed more accurate consideration, that never since the beginnings of the Church of the New Testament has there existed any heresy which has so boldly attacked, impugned, and rejected the authority of the Scriptures of both Testaments in their entirety, except for this one Jesuitical heresy. And so that this may not seem to anyone too harsh, or indeed less consistent with the truth, it is our pleasure to demonstrate it clearly by a brief antithesis or comparison of this Papist doctrine with the ancient heresies that ever erred concerning Scripture.

And at the beginning, indeed, the Sadducees contended that, besides the Mosaic books and the divine laws contained in those books, no other authority of the Scriptures or tradition of men was to be received, as Epiphanius testifies. Thus, therefore, they, having rejected and reprobated the remaining books of the Old Testament, nevertheless granted the Mosaic Scripture the highest and plenary authority for deciding controversial dogmas. Whence the Savior also wished to refute their error concerning the resurrection of the dead from Moses, Matthew 12:32.

Following these were the Simonians, Basilidians, Carpocratians, Valentinians or Gnostics, Ptolemaeites, Heracleonites, Cainites, Archontics, Cerdonians, Marcionites, Apelleians, Severians, Artemonites, and today the Anabaptists, who each and all rejected the Old Testament, either in whole or in part, contending that it was created for the Jews alone by the evil god of the Jews, and was augmented by his followers with fabricated narratives, and that it is in no part consistent with the Christian faith, but is contrary to the Evangelical doctrine: as Epiphanius reports in the heresy of these people, and Augustine in the Catalogue of Heresies to Quodvultdeus: and Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 22. Whose error, indeed, although it is sufficiently impious and deservedly to be marked with the crime of heresy, the Jesuit dogma is more atrocious in this: that they diminish, undermine, and abolish the authority not only of the Old Testament, like the heretics already enumerated, but of the entire sacred Scripture, as much as lies in them. As for the New Testament, the Ebionites, having spurned the remaining Gospels, used only that which was according to Matthew, as Irenaeus reports in book 1, chapter 26. The Cerdonians and Marcion received only the Gospel of Luke, and some Epistles of Paul, as Tertullian reports in De praescriptione at the end. The Severians exploded the Epistles of Paul and the Acts of the Apostles, as Eusebius testifies in book 4, chapter 27. The Valentinians admitted only the Gospel of John, as Irenaeus testifies in book 3, chapter 11. The Marcionites repudiated both Epistles of Paul to Timothy, as also those which were written to Titus and to the Hebrews, as Epiphanius has it in heresy 42. Thus other heretics gnawed away at other particles of the New Testament: but no one can be found who has simply attacked the authority of the whole Scripture, except the Papists. For although the Manichaeans thought quite abjectly about the Scripture of both Testaments: nevertheless, they asserted that the divinity of the Son of God could be sufficiently refuted against the Ebionites from the New Testament, as Augustine reports in book 33 against Faustus, chapter 3.

Similarly, although the Schwenkfeldians also despise all the scriptures and affect them with many reproaches, yet that heresy partly nourishes a small family, and partly indeed collapses from its own futility. Moreover, that error of the Papists has long since fixed its seat in the very Church of God, and indeed so firmly that it seems it can hardly be eradicated before the last day. For which reason alone it ought to appear all the more atrocious.

And although Johannes Pistorius and the Jesuits have not rarely challenged our people to a colloquy, and indeed to be instituted under the condition that it be disputed from Holy Scripture alone, yet it is gathered most evidently from the Acts of the recent Ratisbon Colloquy alone that this protestation was contrary to the fact. For the same thing happened to them in this regard which Tertullian left written about the heretics of his own time in his book On Prescription Against Heretics: They either do not receive the Scriptures at all, or if they do receive some, they invert them by additions and subtractions for the dispute of their own institution; or they do not receive them entire, and if they do receive them to some extent entire, they nevertheless contend that diverse expositions can be given. With these things thus established, even a blind man could see what a horrendous dogma the Jesuit race fosters concerning the Article of Holy Scripture. For since it is confessed among them that scripture divinely revealed, and comprised in the Prophetic and Apostolic books, is an immediate, infallible, everlasting, in itself valid, primary principle, consisting not from elsewhere but from itself, plain and perspicuous: certainly it must necessarily follow from the Papist dogma that faith and the Christian Religion are built not upon divine, but upon human principles: not upon divine, but upon human authority. Whence what certainty and πληροφορία of faith, or on the contrary what Babylonian confusion, or certainly perpetual doubt concerning the true sense of scripture and the Articles of faith may arise, he can easily judge who only understands this, that of Principles, as of any science, so also of our Theology, there must be an undoubted certainty and immovable truth; which whether the Church, that is, the Pontiff with a Council, or rather Scripture explaining itself by Scripture, can provide, we shall demonstrate in its proper place in the Treatise itself.

Now this must be weighed in this place, since one should not dispute against one who denies principles: for as Basil the Great wrote on Psalm 115, the principles of all disciplines about which one is to dispute must be undisputed and conceded by both sides: Is it in the Christian interest to descend into a dispute with the Papists who deny the principles of the Christian Religion? Many Orthodox Theologians have certainly held the negative of this question, establishing that all labor is spent in vain, and that, as the saying goes, one wastes effort and oil, if one descends into the arena of dispute with those who simply deny the principles from which they could be convicted of error.

And indeed, if the goal that ought to be proposed for such colloquies and disputes looked only to the Jesuit race, that is, those sworn enemies of the Scriptures: we would not unwillingly grant that one should entirely concede to the Negative, since from their side clearly no fruit can be hoped for: Nay, the Devil rather rages so much the more vehemently in them against the Scriptures, the more strongly he perceives himself to be pressed by them.

However, just as Christ the Savior instituted colloquies with the Scribes and Sadducees, however unfruitful they were on their part: from which, nevertheless, great use redounded to the remaining Auditors: So today we judge that one must descend into the arena of dispute with the Jesuits, so that utility may accrue not indeed to them, but to others from it, and partly those who are held ensnared by Papist darkness through imprudence and simplicity may be led to the light of Evangelical truth: and partly that our own may be more and more confirmed in the same truth. It is added that, according to the admonition of St. Peter, 1 Pet. 3:15, we must be ready to respond even to the Jesuit Adversaries themselves, when they ask of us a reason for the hope that is in us.

Looking to both of which ends at this time, we shall, with God's help, institute a methodical treatment of those controversies, but only the principal ones, which exist between our Churches and the Jesuit race: in which we shall follow this method above all. At the beginning, we shall distribute each controversy into certain general Questions, so that it may be more exactly established what the subject of our dispute will be. Then, however, we shall treat the individual general Questions separately in order: but in such a way that we always comprehend the purer doctrine in certain theses or propositions, as it were, and confirm them, and once confirmed, assert them against Jesuitical tricks. Finally, we shall reduce the doctrines of the Adversaries into certain hypotheses likewise taken from their own books and disputes, and we shall logically and Theologically refute the Sophisms by which they strive to confirm them.

Latin:

dogmata fidei, & ad salutem necessaria, quæ tamen neque in Scriptura continentur, neque inde per ullam aliam evidentem consequentiam deduci possunt.

Item, Fons & scaturigo omnium hæresewn, & confusioins Babylonica est, Si quis statuere velit, Nihil in causa Religionis esse credendum, & in cultu faciendum, quod non vel expressè contineatur in sacris literis, vel per bonam consequentiam indè deduci queat.

Item, Neque scriptura ipsa, ut est Verbum Dei, neque Spiritus sanctus, ut per eam loquitur, est judex controversiarum.

Item : Traditiones non scriptæ ejusdem sunt autoritatis, & æquè Verbum divinum, atque est Verbum scriptum.

Hæc & id genus alia satis luculenter ostendunt, quid in intimo recessu cordium de scriptura sacra sentiat societas Iesuvvitica, & quàm habeant illam despectui.

Cæterùm non existimabimus vel levem esse istum errorem, vel litem hac in parte nobis esse cum Pontificijs tanquàm de lana Caprina: sed præterquàm quod de ipsis principijs ac fundamento Religionis Christianæ agitur, ac proinde pro aris ac focis pugnatur: illud potissimum sub considerationem & quidem accuratiorem venit, quod nulla unquam jam indè à primordijs Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti, extitit hæresis, quæ autoritatem Scripturarum utriusquè Testamenti ex toto ita audacter vellicaverit, impugnaverit, reprobaverit, præter hanc unam Iesuvviticam. Quod ne cuipiam videri possit durius, aut verò minus consentaneum, placet idipsum per brevem antithesin sive comparationem doctrinæ hujus Pontificiæ, cum veteribus hæresibus, quæ unquàm circa scripturam aberrarunt, ad oculum demonstrare.

Ac initiò quidem Sadducæi, præter libros Mosaicos, ac divinas leges, libris illis comprehensas, nullam aliam scripturarum autoritatem, aut hominum traditionem recipiendam esse contendebant, teste Epiphanio. Sic ergò isti rejectis ac reprobatis reliquis Veteris Testamēti libris, Mosaicæ tamen scripturæ autoritatem summam ac plenariam decidendi dogmata controversa largiebantur. Unde Servator quoque ipsorum errorem de Resurrectione mortuorum ex Mose refutare voluit Matth. 12. 32.

Hos insecuti Simoniani, Basilidiani, Carpocratiani, Valentiniani sive Gnostici, Ptolemeitæ, Heracleonitæ, Cajani, Archontici, Cerdoniani, Marcionitæ, Apelleiani, Severiani, Artemonitæ, & hodiè Anabaptistæ, qui singuli & universi Vetus Testamentum, vel ex toto, vel ex parte abjecerunt, contendentes, illud pro solis Judæis à malo Judæorum Deo conditum, & à sectatoribus ejus, confictis narrationibus auctum, Christianæ verò fidei nulla ex parte congruum, sed doctrinæ Evangelicæ contrarium esse: uti referunt Epiphanius in istorum hæresi, & Augustinus in Catalogo hæreseum ad Quod vult Deum: & Iræneus libr. 1. cap. 22. Quorum sanè error licet satis sit impius, & meritò hæresews crimine notandus: in eo tamen atrocius est Jesuvviticum dogma, quòd non Veteris tantùm Testamenti, sicut jam enumerati hæretici, sed totius Scripturæ sacræ autoritatem, quantum in ipsis, imminuunt, labefactant, tollunt. Quoad Novum Testamentum Ebionitæ reliquis Evangelijs spretis, solo eo, quod secundum Matthæum erat, utebantur, sic referente Irenæo l.1.cap. 26. Cerdoniani & Marcion solum Evangelium Lucæ recipiebant, & aliquot Epistolas Pauli, uti refert Tertullianus de præscript. in fine. Severiani Epistolas Pauli & Acta Apostolorum explodebant, teste Eusebio lib. 4. cap. 27. Valentiniani solum Evangelium Johannis admittebant, uti testatur Irenæus lib. 3. cap. 11. Marcionitæ repudiabant utramque epistolam Pauli, ad Timotheum, ut & eas, quæ ad Titum, & ad Hebreos scriptæ sunt, uti habet Epiphanius hæres. 42. Sic alij hæretici alias particulas Novi Testamēti arrodebant: nullus verò, qui simpliciter totius scripturæ authoritatem vellicaverit, dari potest, præter Pontificios. Nam etsi Manichæi de scriptura utriusque Testamenti satis abjectè sentiebant: tamen divinitatem Filij Dei cōtra Ebionitas satis sufficienter ex Novo Testamento refutari posse asserebant, uti refert Augustinus lib. 33. contra Faustum cap. 3.

Consimiliter etsi Schvvenckfeldiani quoque scripturas omnes contemnunt, multisq; probris afficiunt: tamen hæresis ista partim exiguam alit familiam, partim verò propria futilitate concidit. Cæterùm error iste Pontificiorum sedem in ipsa Ecclesia Dei jam pridem fixit, & quidem usque adeò firmam, ut ante diem novissimum vix eradicari posse videatur. Quo vel uno nomine tantò etiam atrocior ille videri debet.

Et quanquam Johannes Pistorius & Jesuvitæ haud rarò provocaverint nostros ad colloquium, & quidem sub ea conditione instituendū, ut ex sola Scriptura sacra disputaretur, tamen protestationem hanc contrariam fuisse facto, vel ex solis Actu nuperi Colloquij Ratisbonensis evidētissimè colligitur. Nam idem hac in parte illis usu venit, quod de sui temporis hæreticis Tertullianus scriptum reliquit, in lib. de præscript. adversus hæreses. Scripturas vel planè non recipiunt, vel si quas recipiūt, adjectionibus & detractionibus ad disputationem instituti sui invertūt: vel non recipiunt integras, & si aliquatenus integras, nihilominus diversas expositiones dari posse contendunt. Quibus ita constitutis, vel cæcus viderit, quàm horrendum dogma gens Jesuvitica circa Articulum de scriptura sacra foveat. Nam cùm illud apud eos in confesso sit, scripturam divinitus revelatam, & libris Propheticis & Apostolicis comprehensam, esse immediatum, infallibile, sempiternum, per se ratum, primum, non aliundè, sed ex se constans principiū, planum ac perspicuum: certè ex dogmate Pontificio illud sequatur necesse est, fidē ac Religionem Christianam nō divinis, sed humanis principijs: non divinæ, sed humanæ autoritati esse superstructam. Unde quænam certitudo ac πληροφορία fidei, quæ contrà confusioBabylonica, vel certè perpetua dubitatio de vero scripturæ & Articulorum fidei sensu oboriatur, facilè judicare potest, qui illud modò intelligit, quòd Principiorum, uti cujuslibet scientiæ, ita nostræ etiam Theologiæ debeat esse indubia certitudo & immota veritas, Quam nùm Ecclesia, hoc est, Pontifex cum Concilio, an verò Scriptura per Scripturam seipsam explicans, præstare possit, suo loco in ipsa Tractatione demonstrabimus.

Nunc illud hoc loco expendendum venit, cùm adversus negantem principia non sit disputandum: siquidem ut Basilius Magnus super Psalm. 115. scripsit, omnium disciplinarum, de quibus disputandum est, principia oportet esse utring; indiscussa & concessa: Utrùm è re Christiana sit, cum Pontificijs negantibus principia Religionis Christianæ in disputationem descendere? Hujus sanè quæstionis Negativam multi Orthodoxi Theologi tenuerunt, statuentes frustra omnem laborem insumi, ac operam, quod dicitur, & oleum perdi, si cum ijs in arenam disputationis descendatur, qui principia, ex quibus erroris convinci queant, simpliciter negant.

Et profectò, si scopus, qui hujusmodi colloquiis ac disputationibus debet esse propositus, solam gentem Jesuvviticam, hoc est, juratos illos Scripturarum hostes spectaret: haud inviti largiremur, in Negantem penitus concedendum esse, siquidem ex horum parte fructus planè nullus sperari potest: Quin Diabolus potiùs tantò vehementius in istis adversus Scripturas excandescit, quantò fortiùs ex illis se premi animadvertit.

Cæterùm, quemadmodum Christus Servator, cū Scribis, & Sadducæis colloquia instituit, quantumvis ex istorum parte infrugifera: ex quibus tamen ad reliquos Auditores usus magnus redundavit: Ita hodieque cum Jesuvvitis in arenam disputationis descendendum esse arbitramur, ut non quidem ad ipsos, sed ad alios indè utilitas aliqua accedat, & partim illi, qui per imprudentiam & simplicitatem tenebris Pontificijs irretiti tenentur, ad lucem veritatis Evangelicæ perducantur: partim verò nostri in eadem veritate magis magisque confirmentur. Accedit quòd secundum admonitionem D. Petri 1. cap. 3. 15. ipsis etiam Adversarijs Jesuvvitis, petentibus â nobis rationem illius spei, quæ in nobis est, ad respondendum parati esse debemus.

Ad quem utrumque finem nos quoque hoc tempore respicientes, Methodicam earum controversiarum, sed præcipuarum tantùm, quæ nostris Ecclesijs cum gente Jesuvvitica, intercedunt, pertractationem σὺν θεῷ instituemus: in quà hanc potissimum sequemur Methodum. Initiò quamlibet controversiam, in certas quasdam generales Quæstiones distribuemus, ut sic exactiùs constare possit, qua de re futura nobis sit disputatio. Deinde verò singulas Quæstiones generales seorsim ordine pertractabimus: sed ita, ut semper puriorem doctrinam certis quasi thesibus sive propositionibus comprehendamus, easdemque confirmemus, confirmatas contra strophās Jesuvviticas asseramus. Tandem Adversariorum doctrinas in certas itidem hypotheses ex ipsorummet libris & disputationibus petitas redigemus, & Sophismata, quibus illas confirmare annituntur, logicè & Theologicè refutabimus.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed

ALthough the things that come into controversy between us and the Jesuits concerning the Sacred Scriptures are almost infinite: we judge, however, that those individual and universal things can not inconveniently be recalled to seven general Questions: the first of which indeed asks about the Canon of the Scriptures: Whence and when was that Canon established, and which Books of the Scriptures are to be held as Canonical? The second, concerning the authority of the Scriptures: Is their authority greater than that of the Church? The third, concerning the various editions of Sacred Scripture, namely Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, Greek, Latin, German: and what authority does each possess? And is it of use that Sacred Scripture be translated into the vernacular language of each people, so that it can be read by all, even the Laity? The fourth, concerning the perspicuity, ease, and difficulty of the Scriptures: are they so open in themselves that they can be understood by all? The fifth, concerning the interpretation of the Scriptures: and what depends on this, concerning the judge of controversies. Namely, whether the true sense of the Scriptures is to be sought from the scriptures alone, or whether the infallible spirit of interpretation resides with the Roman Pontiff with a Council? The sixth, concerning the perfection of the Scriptures: Is the whole doctrine necessary, whether concerning faith or morals, expressly contained in them? The seventh and last, concerning human Traditions, which the Jesuits call the unwritten WORD OF GOD.

Latin:

ETsi infinita fermè sunt, quæ inter nos & Jesuvitas, de Scripturis Sacris in Controversiam veniunt: haud tamen incommodè ad Quæstiones septem generales, singula & universa illa revocari posse, judicamus: quarum prima quidem quærit de Canone Scripturarum: Vnde & quando constitutus sit Canon ille, & Quinam Libri Scripturarum pro Canonicis sint habendi? Altera, de autoritate Scripturarum: Num earum major, quàm Ecclesiæ sit autoritas? Tertia, de varijs editionibus Scripturæ Sacræ, nempè Hebræa, Chaldaica, Syriaca, Græca, Latina, Germanica: & quam autoritatem singulæ obtineant? & an ex usu sit, ut Scriptura Sacra in linguam cuique populo vernaculam transferatur, quô ab omnibus etiam Laicis legi possit? Quarta, de Scripturarum perspicuitate, facilitate & difficultate: an per se ita sint apertæ, ut ab omnibus intelligi possint? Quinta, de interpretatione Scripturarum: & quæ ab hac dependet, de judice controversiarum. An videlicet Verus sensus Scripturarum ex solis scripturis sit petendus, an verò Spiritus interpretationis infallibilis sit penes Pontificem Romanum cum Concilio? Sexta, de perfectione Scripturarum: An in his exprefsè contineatur tota doctrina neceffaria, sive de fide, sive de moribus? Septima & postrema, de Traditionibus humanis, quas Jesuitæ nominant Verbum DEI non scriptum.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Question I

ORTHODOX PROPOSITION I.

Scripture is called Canonical because it is the most exact rule or standard of the Christian faith and of the morals of living piously: according to which all other writings and dogmas, whether of the faithful or of the unfaithful, are to be judged: but it itself can neither be nor ought to be judged by any other rule.

CONFIRMATION.

The truth of this thesis is evident partly from the scriptures themselves, partly from the testimony of Orthodox Antiquity. From the scriptures indeed partly by reason of the Etymology: partly by reason of the end. As regards the etymon. Ps. 19, 5. Rom. 10, 18. Scripture is called Canon: Their Canon, or Rule of the Apostles, has gone out into all the earth. For although the Greek interpreter rendered it φθόγγον sound, which interpretation Paul also, being then customary, in the cited 10th chapter of the Romans, wished to retain: in the Hebrew however it is, קַו from the root קָוָה he waited, he leaned upon, he expected: so that this word properly signifies the expectation with which we diligently persevere in any matter. Now because architects in constructing buildings always lean upon a rule, and observe it most exactly: therefore the Hebrew word קָנֶה signifies a Canon, and is thus adapted by metaphor to Scripture, so that just as architects adjust their structures to a canon or rule, so the building up of the spiritual Church ought to be done according to the infallible Canon of Scripture. Looking to which, St. Augustine skillfully infers in book 2, chapter 6, of his work on the baptism of the Donatists: Let us not bring deceitful scales, where we weigh what we want and how we want, saying according to our own whim: This is heavy, this is light: but let us bring the divine scale from the holy Scriptures, as if from the Lord's treasuries, and on it weigh what is heavier, or rather, let us not weigh, but recognize what has been weighed by the Lord. Furthermore, regarding the end which this word or appellation concerns, it is certainly that primary one which we can name dijudicatorium, or judicial. This end God himself wished to intimate, while he refers us uniquely to the Law and to the Testimony, with this threat added, that if we do not feel and speak according to this norm or rule, we shall not see the morning light, Isa. 8:20. To which also pertains that of the Apostle: Whoever τῷ κανόνι τούτῳ στοιχήσουσι, shall walk according to this Canon, peace be upon them and mercy, Gal. 6:16. And Phil. 3:16: Let us remain in the same rule. This very primary and principal end was acknowledged also by venerable Antiquity, as Augustine, who in book 2 against Cresconius the Grammarian, chapter 31, has it thus: Not without cause, with such wholesome vigilance, has the Ecclesiastical Canon been established, to which certain books of the Prophets and Apostles belong: which we dare not judge at all, and according to which we judge the rest of the books, whether of the faithful or of the infidels. And ch. 32. I am not bound by the authority of this letter, because I do not hold the letters of Cyprian as Canonical, but I consider them from the Canonical ones, and what in them agrees with the authority of the divine Scriptures, I accept with his praise. But what does not agree, I reject with his peace. To which sentiment Chrysostom also writes in Homily 13 on 2 Corinthians. With which authorities that definition of a Canon that exists in Varinus agrees excellently, that indeed a κανὼν is a measure or infallible rule admitting no addition or subtraction at all. For that such is the nature of these canonical scriptures, that they need no addition or subtraction for their perfection, will be most clearly evident from this whole disputation.

II. ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

The constitution of the Canon has God himself as its author, who nevertheless did not constitute it immediately, but mediately, namely through the Church, yet not just any church, but only that which existed in those times when the Canonical writers lived in the flesh, not only near, but also clearly contemporary and σύγχρονος.

CONFIRMATION.

The truth of this proposition is spontaneously evident. For in the beginning, since it is placed beyond controversy that Scripture, as it is that which it is in itself, namely heavenly truth, has it only from God, its author, it will certainly also be manifest that that which is Canonical Scripture has that primarily from God alone: for by whose will, command, and revelation those books began to be held as Canonical, which

God himself wished to be Canonical and to be made known to the assembly of the faithful, so that it might be established beyond doubt not only concerning the Author, but also the Canonical authority of those books. To which end Moses himself is read to have handed over his book to the Priests, and to have deposited it at the side of the ark of the covenant, Deut. 31:26. And lest anyone could plead ignorance of the Law, he commanded that Kings should have with them an exemplar described from the Mosaic αὐτογράφῳ, and then judge controversies of both Religion and others from it, Deut. 17:18. By a like reason, the authority of the Canonical books of the N.T. was confirmed even in the times of the Apostles themselves, as Augustine testifies in book 11 against Manichaeus, chapter 5. Indeed, so that canonical faith was applied to the Gospel of Matthew, because it was held as such a Canonical writing at that time when Matthew himself lived in the flesh. Thus regarding the remaining Evangelists, although they were not eyewitnesses of the things done by Christ, because their Gospels were nevertheless approved by the Apostles themselves while they were still living in the flesh: there is certainly no doubt but that they were divinely stirred to write, and deservedly merit Canonical authority. For which end the Apostle Paul is also read to have confirmed his Epistles with a certain sign, lest perhaps some supposititious one be foisted upon the Church. 2 Thess. 3:17. My greeting with the hand of Paul, which is the sign in every epistle: Thus I write. Whence it is clearly evident: first, that as soon as the Prophets in the O.T., and the Apostles and Evangelists in the New, ceased to write and had finished their lives, so immediately the plenary constitution of the Canon began: so that the subsequent Church did not finally make any book Canonical which had not been such before: but merely commended, preserved, and propagated to posterity those that were already Canonical in themselves by its own testimony. Thence arises a clear distinction between the testimony of the primitive Church and the testimony of the present Church. For we do not believe the present Church, unless its testimony agrees entirely with the testimony of the primitive Church: but we believe the primitive Church, because it partly heard the Apostles themselves teaching, and partly had their own autographs at hand: just as Tertullian indeed affirms in his work on prescription, that in his own time those autographs still existed in the Apostolic Churches. To which sentiment St. Augustine writes in book 10 against Manichaeus, chapter 5. The excellence of the Canonical authority of the O. and N. Testament is distinct from the books of later writers, which, confirmed in the times of the Apostles, is established as if in a certain sublime seat, to which every faithful and pious intellect should be subject. And in book 1 of the consensus of the Evangelists, c. 1. Other men, who have attempted to write something concerning the acts of the Lord or the Apostles, were not such, even in their own times, that the Church should have confidence in them, and that they should be received into the Canonical authority of the sacred books. And not only because they were not such that, when they narrated, one ought to believe them; but also, because they falsely inserted into their writings certain things which the Catholic and apostolic rule of faith, and sound doctrine, condemns.

III. ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.
