The Canonical books of both Testaments, being θεόπνευστοι, and ἀναπόδεικτοι for the adjudication of Ecclesiastical dogmas

Latin:

PROPOSITIO I. ORTHODOXA.

SCriptura dicitur Canonica, quia exactissima est regula sive trutina fidei Christianæ, & morum piè vivendi: secundum quam omnia reliqua sive fidelium sive infidelium scripta ac dogmata sunt dijudicanda: ipsa verò per aliam aliquam regulam judicari nec potest nec debet.

CONFIRMATIO.

THesis hujus veritas patet partim ex scripturis ipsis, partim ex testimonio Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis. Ex scripturis quidem partim ratione Etymi: partim ratione finis. Quoad etymon. Ps. 19, 5. Rom. 10, 18. Scriptura Cano appellatur: In omnē terrā exivit Canon, sive Regula Apostolorum. Etsi n. Græcus interpres reddidit φθόγγον Sonum, Quam interpretationem Paulus quoque, quippe tum usitatam, citato capite 10. Romanorum; retinere voluit: In Hebræo tamen est, קַו à radice קָוָה expectavit, incubuit, præstolatus est: ita ut hæc vox propriè significet expectationem, quâ diligenter in re quapiam perseveramus. Jam quia architecti in extruendis ædificijs, regulæ semper incumbunt, eamq́; exactissimè observant : ideo vox Hebræa קָנֶה Canonem significat, & sic per Metaphoram ad Scripturam accommodatur, ut quemadmodum Architecti suas structuras ad Canonem sive regulam exigunt, ita secundum infallibilem Scripturæ Canonem, Spiritualis Ecclesiæ ædificatio fieri debeat. Quò respiciens D. Augustinus scitè infert. l. 2. c. 6. de baptismo Donatistarum: Afferamus non stateras dolosas, ubi appendamus quod volumus, & quomodo volumus, pro arbitrio nostro dicentes : Hoc grave, hoc leve est: sed afferamus divinam stateram de Scripturis sanctis, tanquam de thesauris Dominicis, & in illa quid sit gravius, appendamus, imò non appendamus, sed a Domino appensa recognoscamus. Porrò quoad finem, quem vox sive appellatio hæc concernit, primarius certè est ille, quem διακριτικὸν, dijudicatorium nominare possumus. Quem finem DEUS ipse innuere voluit, dum ad Legem & ad Testimonium ejus unicè nos remittit, addita hac comminatione, quòd si non sentiamus, & loquamur juxta normam aut regulam hanc, non visuri simus lucem matutinam, Esa 8, 20. Quò pertinet etiam illud Apostoli: Quicunq́; τῷ κανόνι τούτῳ στοιχήσουσι, secundum hunc Canonem incedent, pax super eos & misericordia Gal. 6, 16. Et Philip. 3, 16. In eadem maneamus regula. Quem ipsum finem primarium & principalem agnovit veneranda etiam Antiquitas, ut August. qui libro 2. contra Cresconium Grammaticum cap. 31. sic habet: Non sine causa, tàm salubri vigilantia, Canon Ecclesiasticus est constitutus, ad quem certi Prophetarum & Apostolorum libri pertineant: quos omninò judicare non audeamus, & secundum quos, de cæteris libris, vel fidelium, vel infidelium judicamus. Et c. 32. Ego hujus Epistolæ autoritate non teneor, quia literas Cypriani, non ut Canonicas habeo, sed eas ex Canonicis considero, & quod in eis divinarum Scripturarum autoritati convenit, cum laude ejus accipio. Quòd autem non congruit, cum pace ejus respuo. Quam in sententiam scribit etiam Chrysost. Homilia 13. in 2. ad Cor. Quibus autoritatibus præclarè convenit definitio illa Canonis, quæ extat apud Varinū, quod nimirùm κανὼν sit μέτρον ἀδιάψευστον πᾶσαν προσθεσιν κὶ ἀφαίρεσιν μηδαμῶς ἐπιδεχόμενον, hoc est, Mensura vel Regula infallibilis, nullam omninò additionem aut detractionem admittens. Nam talem esse harum scriptura Canonica, ut ad sui perfectionem nullâ vel appositione, vel detractione indigeat, ex tota hac disputatione dilucidissimè patebit

II. PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

COnstitutio Canonis autorem habet ipsum Deum, qui tamen non immediatè, sed mediatè illum constituit, nempe per Ecclesiam, non tamen quamlibet, sed eam tantùm, quæ fuit illis temporibus, quibus Canonici Scriptores in carne vixerunt, non modò vicina, sed & propria planè ac σύγχρονος.

CONFIRMATIO.

PRopositionis hujus veritas ultrò patet. Initiò enim cum extra controversiam sit positum, Scripturam, ut id fit, quod in se ipsa est, nempe cœlestis veritas, non habere nisi ex Deo, ipsius autore, utiq; & illud erit manifestum, quod Scriptura est Canonica, illud principaliter à DEO solo habere: quippè cujus voluntate, mandato & revelatione cœpti sunt haberi pro Canonicis illi libri, quos

Deus ipse Canonicos esse & coetui fidelium innotescere voluit, ut non tantùm de Autore, sed & Canonica autoritate illorum librorum indubitatò constaret. Quem in finem Moses ipse librum suum Sacerdotibus tradidisse, & in latere arcae foederis deposuisse legitur. Deut. 31, 26. Et ne quisquam ignorantiam Legis praetexere posset, mandavit, ut Reges subinde exemplar ex αὐτογράφῳ Mosaico descriptum penes se haberent, & tùm Religionis, tùm alias controversias inde dijudicaret, Deut. 17, 18. Pari ratione autoritas Canonicôrum librorum N T. ipsis etiam Apostolorum temporibus confirmata est, teste Augustino lib. 11. contra Manich. cap. 5. Ita quidem, ut Matthaei Evangelio fides canonica fuerit adhibita, quia pro tali scripto Canonico habitum illud est, eo tempore, quo Matthaeus ipse in carne vixit. Sic quoad reliquos Evangelistas, etsi illi non fuerunt αὐτόπται rerum à Christo gestarum, quia tamen ipsorum Evangelia ab ipsis Apostolis adhuc in carne viventibus, approbata fuerunt: utique dubium est nullum, quin ipsi divinitùs ad scribendum sint excitati, & Canonicam autoritatem jure mereantur. Quo fine legitur etiam Apostolus Paulus, certo quodam signo suas confirmasse Epistolas, ne fortè supposititia aliqua Ecclesiae obtruderetur. 2. Thess. 3, 17. Salutatio mea manu Pauli, quod est signũ in omni epistola: Ita scribo. Unde luculenter patet: primum, quod quamprimum in V. T. Prophetae: in Novo Apostoli & Evangelistae scribere cessarunt, & vitâ functi sunt, tam statim Canonis cõstitutio plenaria coeperit: ita ut Ecclesia subsequens, non ullum demum librum fecerit Canonicum, qui antea talis non fuerat: sed jam ante ex se Canonicos, suo tantum testimonio commendarit, conservarit, & ad posteros propagarit. Deinde luculentum hinc oritur discrimen inter testificationem Ecclesiae primitivae & inter testificationem praesentis Ecclesiae. Nam praesenti Ecclesiae non credimus, nisi ejus testimonium cum testificatione primitivae Ecclesiae ex asse cogruat: Primitivae autem Ecclesiae credimus, quòd partim ipsos Apostolos docentes audivit, partim ipsorum αὐτόγραφα ad manus habuit: quemadmodum sane Tertullianus de praescriptione affirmat, suo adhuc tempore illa αὐτόγραφα in Ecclesiis Apostolicis extitisse. Quam in sententiam D. Augustinus scribit lib. 10. contra Manich. cap. 5. Distincta est à posteriorum libris, excellentia Canonicae autoritatis V. & N. Testamenti, quae Apostolorum confirmata temporibus, tanquam in sede quadam sublimiter constituta est, cui inserviat omnis fidelis & pius intellectus. Et libro 1. de consensu Evangelist. c. 1. Caeteri homines, qui de Domini vel Apostolorum actibus aliqua scribere conati sunt, non tales vel suis temporibus extiterunt, ut eis fidem haberet Ecclesia, atq; in autoritatem Canonicam sacrorum librorum reciperentur. Nec solùm quia illi non tales erant, quibus narrantibus credi oporteret; sed etiam, quia scriptis suis quaedam fallaciter indiderunt, quae Catholica atq; apostolica regula fidei, & sana doctrina condemnat.

III. PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

Libri Canonici utriusque Testamenti, quippe θεόπνευστοι, & ἀναπόδεικτοι ad dijudicationem dogmatum Ecclesiasticorum


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Of Canonical and Apocryphal books

to be confirmed: but the Apocrypha are read in the Church only for the edification of the people.

CONFIRMATION.

The reason for this proposition is: 1. Because everything contained in the Canonical books conforms to the analogy of faith, inasmuch as they were written by those whose minds the Holy Spirit so illuminated, and whose hands in writing He so governed, that they could nowhere stray from the Truth, never deflect from certainty, and nowhere hallucinate in writing, as Augustine speaks in book 2 of the Consensus of the Evangelists, chapter 11. And in Epistle 19 to Jerome: I have learned to defer this honor and fear only to those books of the scriptures which are now called Canonical, so that I most firmly believe that no author of them has erred in anything in his writing.

And although in the time of Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles, various writings existed, of which mention is made partly in the sacred code itself, and partly in other monuments of the ancients; yet those were not such as the Church of the faithful ought to have used as divinely inspired for the instruction of piety and religion: being destitute of this testimony, that they proceeded from such authors who could not err in writing, as the Apostles could. Nor does it stand against this assertion that the scripture itself testifies that the Apostles also sometimes lapsed, as is evident concerning Peter from chapter 2, verse 11 of the epistle to the Galatians. For in this question it is not asked whether this gift of the Holy Spirit was so perennial and continuous in those Canonical writers that in any place and time, and indeed in common conversation or the course of their whole life, they could in no way slip or hallucinate. For if this were established, certainly the Apostles would be removed from the common census of men, and it would be believed that they were entirely ἀναμάρτητοι (sinless), which Paul manifestly denies of himself in Romans 6:15 and

following. And the example of Peter proves the contrary, concerning Evangelical Liberty, in the point of external conversation, not lightly hallucinating. But that which is disputed in this place is: Could the Apostles and the remaining Canonical writers err when their mind and tongue were the pen of the Holy Spirit Himself? Where indeed we hold the negative in all respects, relying on the twofold promise singularly given to them, concerning the Holy Spirit who would lead them into all truth, and would suggest to them what they ought to speak and write: Matthew 10:19, John 16:13. For as Augustine rightly infers, if the Apostles are conceded to have lapsed even once, they were not led into all truth: and if even one falsehood is found in any sacred book, the certainty of the whole book perishes, Epistle 8.

But as for the Apocryphal Books, Jerome rightly defined that they are indeed read in the Churches, but not for confirming the authority of Ecclesiastical dogmas, but only for the edification of the people: nor are they received among the Canonical scriptures, for those reasons which the fifth proposition will explain.

Latin:

confirmandam: Apocryphi verò tantùm ad ædificationem plebis leguntur in Ecclesia.

CONFIRMATIO.

RAtio hujus propositionis est: 1. Quia ad analogiam fidei omnia quadrant, quæ in libris Canonicis continentur, quippè scripti ab iis, quorum mentes sic illuminavit, manus verò in scribendo ita gubernavit Spiritus Sanctus, ut à Veritate nullibi aberrare, à certitudine nunquam deflectere, in scribendo nuspiam hallucinari potuerint, uti loquitur Augustinus lib. 2. de consensu Evangelist. cap. 11. Et Epistola 19. ad Hieron. Ego solus ijs scripturarum libris, qui jam Canonici appellantur, hunc honorem timoremq̃ deferre didici, ut nullum eorum autorem scribendo aliquid errasse firmissimè credam.

Et quanquàm tempore Mosis, Prophetarum & Apostolorum, varia scripta extiterunt, quorum partim in ipso sacro codice, partim in alijs Veterum monumentis fit mentio; tamen talia illa non fuerunt, quibus tanquàm divinitùs inspiratis Ecclesia fidelium ad institutionem pietatis, religionemque uti debuit: quippe destituta hoc testimonio, quòd profecta sint ab ejusmodi autoribus, qui in scribendo errare non potuerunt, ut Apostoli. Neq; assertioni huic obstat, quòd Apostolos etiam interdum lapsos esse, ipsa scriptura testatur, uti constat de Petro ex cap. 2. 11. epistolæ ad Galatas. Nam hac in quæstione non illud quæritur, Num Donum hoc Spiritus Sancti, in Scriptoribus illis Canonicis ita fuerit perenne ac continuum, ut quovis loco ac tempore, & quidem in communi conversatione, sive totius vitæ discursu, nullatenus labi aut hallucinari possent. Nam hoc si statueretur, certè Apostoli ex communi hominum censu eximerentur, & crederetur fuisse prorsus ἀναμάρτητοι, id quod de se manifestè negat Paulus Rom. 6. 15. &

seqq. Et diversum probat exemplum Petri, circa Libertatem Evangelicam, in puncto externæ conversationis, haud leviter hallucinantis. Sed illud hoc loco controvertitur, An errare potuerint Apostoli, & reliqui Scriptores Canonici, quando mens & lingua eorum fuit calamus ipsius Spiritus Sancti? Ubi sanè negativam per omnia tenemus, geminâ freti promissione ipsis singulariter data, de Spiritu Sancto introducturo ipsos in omnem veritatem, & suggesturo ipsis, quid loqui ac scribere debeant: Matth. 10, 19. Joh. 16, 13. Nam ut Augustinus rectè infert, si semel lapsi concedantur Apostoli, non in omnem veritatem inducti fuerunt: Et si in sacro quovis libro una saltem reperitur falsitas, totius libri certitudo interit, Epistola. 8.

Cæterùm quoad Libros Apocryphos, rectè definivit Hieronymus, eos legi quidem in Ecclesiis, verum non ad autoritatem Ecclesiasticorum dogmatum confirmandam, sed tantùm ad ædificationem plebis: neque inter Canonicas scripturas eos recipi, ijs de causis, quas propositio quinta expediet.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: IV. Orthodox Proposition

IV. ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

The primitive Church, performing the office not of a judge, but of a witness, testified that the Canonical books of the Old Testament are as many as are contained in the Hebrew codex: and by the universal consent of all Churches, they were received and approved without any contradiction, and indeed were cited here and there by Christ and the Apostles, and even from that source they attained a clearly heavenly and divine authority.

CONFIRMATION.

That great consensus of Antiquity confirms this thesis, which exists in Eusebius, book 4, chapter 26; Origen, book 6, chapter 18, likewise upon the first Psalm; Cyprian in his exposition of the Creed; Epiphanius in his book on measures and weights. Likewise, Vol. 1, book 1, heresy 8; Jerome in his Prologus Galeatus; Athanasius in his Synopsis; Nazianzen on the genuine books. But especially worthy of note is that Melito, Bishop of Sardis, who wrote freely to Antoninus on behalf of the Christian dogma, having traveled to the East for this reason, that he might know with certainty about the order and number of the books, he, writing to his brother Onesimus in Eusebius, book 4 of Church History, chapter 25, testifies that he had diligently inquired into the Canonical books of the Old Testament: but had found none others besides those which are found in the codex of the Hebrews even today. And although this Melito, in the enumeration of the Canonical books, also mentions Wisdom: yet it is evident from the rest of Antiquity, which appeals to Melito, that by the book of Wisdom he did not understand that which is named among the Apocryphal writings, and is ascribed by Jerome and others to Philo: but the Proverbs of Solomon, which are contained in the Hebrew codex.

Furthermore, in the first Volume of the Councils, in the Council of Laodicea, which was celebrated around the year of Christ 364, Canon 59, such a decision was made: It is not fitting for private individuals to recite composed and common psalms in the Church, nor to read books that are outside the Canon, except for the Canonical ones alone of the Old and New Testament. And what ought to be read and received into authority are these: The five books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, four books of Kings: two books of Chronicles: the book of Ezra: 150 Psalms: the Proverbs of Solomon: Ecclesiastes: the Song of Songs: Job: Esther: the twelve minor Prophets: the four major ones. And what need is there of many words? Since Christ himself defines the Canonical Scripture of the O.T. by Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets; understanding by the Prophets both the former and the latter, and the Major and the Minor, Luke 24:44. Therefore Augustine rightly infers, Sermon 129 de Tempore: If anyone shall have received or venerated any other Scriptures besides those which the Catholic Church has received or has believed ought to be held in authority, let him be anathema.

At this point the Jesuit race clamors, crying out that it is unworthy to neglect the authority of the Ecclesiastical Fathers and to flee to the Hebrews or Jews, men who are reprobate and cast off, and to stand by their testimony, in defining the Canon of the Scriptures of the Old Testament. But the answer is easy. For at the beginning we willingly admit the testimony of the Ecclesiastical Fathers, but not of just anyone, much less of those who are more recent and are not at all alien to Papal dogmas; but only of those who are known to have been as close as possible to the age of the Apostles. Furthermore, regarding the Jews, the Jesuit argument clearly does not hold. For the certainty of the Canon of the Old Testament does not depend upon their rejection, but rather upon that singular love of GOD with which He has pursued that people. Concerning which matter David says, Ps. 147, 19, & 20: He declares His Word to Jacob, His statutes and His judgments to Israel: He has not done so for any nation: and His judgments He has not manifested to them. Thus, regarding the rejection of the Jews, it is so far from being able to render the Canon suspect to us that it rather confirms it in a wonderful way. Concerning which matter let the Jesuits hear Augustine speaking thus, Epist. 3 to Volusianus: The Jewish nation, rejected on account of infidelity, has been extirpated from its seats and is scattered everywhere throughout the world, so that it may everywhere carry the Holy books, and so that the testimony of the prophecy, by which Christ and the Church were foretold, might not be thought to have been fabricated by us for the occasion, but might be brought forth by the very adversaries themselves, among whom it was also predicted that they would not believe.

And in the exposition of Psalm 56: Therefore the Jews still exist, so that they may carry our books to their own confusion. For when we wish to show that Christ was prophesied, we bring forth these writings to the pagans (infidels). And lest those who are hard to the faith should perchance say that we Christians composed them, and along with the Gospel which we preach, invented the Prophets through whom what we preach would seem to have been foretold, we convince them from this, that all those writings in which Christ was prophesied are among the Jews. We bring forth, therefore, the codices from the enemy Jews, so that we may confound the enemy pagans or infidels. In what disgrace, therefore, are the Jews? The Jew carries the codex from which the Christian believes: our librarians have been made, just as servants are accustomed to carry the codices after their masters: so that by carrying them, they may fail, and by reading them, these may profit. But if the Jesuits say that the Hebrew books were falsified by the Jews: we ask that they show whether that falsification was done before Christ was sent in the flesh, or after. Certainly not before: because, as Origen argues evidently in the eighth volume of his explanations of Isaiah, the Lord and the Apostles, who argue other crimes in the Scribes and Pharisees, would never have been silent about this crime, which was the greatest. Not after the advent of the Savior, because then the preachings of Christ and the Apostles would no longer have corresponded to the prophecies of the Prophets concerning Christ and his doctrine. Now, indeed, because even today a most beautiful consensus is perceived between the Old and New Testament: surely from that alone the vanity of the Jesuitical quibbling is abundantly clear.

Moreover, before we leave this point, it should be observed that the Biblical books are not distinguished by the ancient Fathers in the same way. Most, with the Blessed Jerome, observe that distinction which this proposition of ours has, by which Biblical books are distinguished into Canonical and Apocryphal. But Eusebius, lib. 3, cap. 3 & 25 of his Ecclesiastical History, establishes three orders of sacred books: in the first of which he places ἀναμφιλέκτως ἐνδιαθήκꙋς ἠ ὀμολογꙋμένας γραφὰς, which are, namely, those that without any contradiction, and by the consensus of all, belong to

the Testament of GOD. He makes a second order of τῶν ἀντιλεγομένων, γνωρίμων, δ᾽ ἀν ὅμως τοῖς πολλοῖς, of those which are indeed contradicted, yet are known to many: into which number he refers the Epistle of James, the second of Peter, the two later ones of John: the Epistle of Jude, and the Apocalypse of John. He makes a third order of τῶν νόθων, the adulterine: such as are the Acts of Paul, the Apocalypse of Peter, the Book of Hermes or the Shepherd: the Book of Enoch, and other supposititious writings of that kind. Thus, even though St. Augustine makes only two orders of books, Canonical and Apocryphal: it is nevertheless certain that under the Canonical he includes not only those which are truly such, and which have always been accepted by all Churches: but also those about which there has sometimes been doubt: So indeed, that under Apocryphal he only comprehends those spurious or supposititious books which Eusebius rejected into the third order. Thus, therefore, for St. Augustine the Canonical Books are the same as the Biblical, taking the term or word Canonical loosely. Whence, however, the Jesuits very poorly conclude that Augustine indifferently held even those which we designate as Apocryphal to be truly and genuinely Canonical. For in book 2, cap. 8 of De Doctrina Christiana, he puts those about which there was sometimes doubt far after the others, about which there was never doubt; and thus, although speaking loosely he refers the books of the Maccabees and the remaining Apocrypha among the Canonical, insofar as, namely, documents of virtues and rules of piety can be sought from them: yet in lib. 2 against the second Epistle of Gaudentius, cap. 23, he warns that this Scripture must be read SOBERLY, which he would never affirm of books that are truly Canonical. What of the fact that Cardinal Cajetan himself writes that the Apocryphal books were called Canonical by certain Councils and by Augustine, because a rule of morals, not of doctrine, could be sought from them: at the end of his Commentary on the history of the Old Testament. Moreover, concerning the Apocrypha so called in the Augustinian sense: that is, concerning the spurious and supposititious ones, Augustine has this in lib. 15 de Civ. Dei cap. 23: Let us omit the fables of those scriptures which are called Apocryphal, because their hidden origin was not clear to the Fathers, from whom the authority of the true scriptures has come down to us by a most certain and well-known succession. For in these Apocrypha, even if some truth is found: yet on account of many falsehoods, their authority is not Canonical. With these things observed, no repugnance now arises between Augustine and Jerome. For Jerome, whom we also follow, considers only the Biblical books, and distinguishes them into Canonical and Apocryphal, taking the term (Canonical) strictly and more properly. Augustine, however, besides the Biblical books, considers also those which do not exist in the Biblical volume, but by the consensus of all are supposititious and adulterine, in respect and comparison to which Augustine wished to name all Biblical books Canonical, taking this term loosely, insofar as it is opposed to the supposititious and adulterine. Where, however, Augustine himself would establish a clear distinction even among these very Biblical and Canonical books, it has already been shown from his own books, so that our proposition stands entirely unmoved, thus most evidently concluding with D. Jerome: The Church does not know the Apocrypha: therefore one must return to the Hebrews: whence also the Lord speaks, and the disciples take their examples: pref. in lib. Paralip.

Latin:

IV. PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

ECclesia primitiva non judicis, sed testis officio fungens, libros Canonicos Veteris Testamenti esse, testificata est, quotquot in Hebræo codice continentur: & universali omnium Ecclesiarum consensu, citra omnem contradictionem recepti & approbati, quin & à Christo & Apostolis passim allegati, & vel inde cælestem ac divinam planè autoritatem sunt consecuti.

CONFIRMATIO.

COnfirmat hanc thesin magnus ille Antiquitatis consensus, qui extat apud Eusebium libr. 4. cap. 26. Origenem libr. 6. cap. 18. item super Psalmum primum: Cyprianum in expositione Symboli; Epiphanium in libro de mensura & ponderibus. Item Tom. 1. lib. 1. hær. 8. Hieronymum in prologo Galeato: Athanasium in synopsi: Nazianzenum de libris genuinis. Comprimis autem observationem meretur, quòd Melito Sardensis Episcopus, qui pro Christiano dogmate ad Antoninum liberè scripsit, hac de causa in Orientem profectus, ut de ordine & numero librorum certò cognosceret, is apud Eusebium lib. 4. hist. eccles. cap. 25. ad fratrem Onesimum scribens: Veteris Testamenti libros Canonicos diligenter se inquisivisse testatur: nullos autem reperisse alios, præter eos, qui in codice Hebræorum hodieque inveniuntur. Et quanquam Melito iste, in enumeratione librorú Canonicorum Sapientiæ etiam meminit: tamen constat ex reliqua Antiquitate, quæ ad Melitonem provocat, ipsum sub Sapientiæ libro, non intellexisse illum, qui inter scripta Apocrypha nominatur, & ab Hieronymo ac alijs Philoni adscribitur: sed proverbia Salomonis, quæ codice Hebræo continentur.

Præterea Tomo primo Conciliorum, in Concilio Laodicensi, quod celebratum est circa An. Chr. 364. Canone 59. talis facta est decisio: Non oportet ab idiotis Psalmos compositos & vulgares in Ecclesia dici, neq; libros, qui sunt extra Canonem, legere, nisi solos Canonicos Veteris & Novi Testamenti. Quæ autem oporteat legi, & in autoritatem recipi, hæc sunt: Libri quinq; Mosis, Josua, Judicium, Ruth, Regum libri quatuor: Paralipomenon libri duo: Esdræ liber: Psalmi 150. proverbia Salomonis: Ecclesiastes: Canticum Canticorum: Job: Esther: Duodecim Prophetæ minores: Quatuor majores. Et quid multis opus? cùm Christus ipse Scripturam Canonicam V. T. definiat per Mosen, Psalmos & Prophetas; Prophetas intelligens, & priores & posteriores, & Majores & Minores Lucæ 24, 44. Proinde rectè Augustinus Serm. 129. de Tempore, infert: Si quis alio quas Scripturas, præter eas, quas Catholica Ecclesia receperit vel in Autoritate habendas esse crediderit, vel fuerit veneratus, anathema sit.

Obstrepit hoc loco gens Jesuvvitica indignum esse clamitans, neglecta Patrum Ecclesiasticorum autoritate ad Hebræos sive Judæos, homines reprobos & abjectos confugere, & ipsorum stare testimonio, in definiendo scripturarum Veteris Testamenti Canone. Sed facilis est responsio. Nam initio Patrum Ecclesiasticorum testimonium ultrò admittimus, sed non quorumvis, multò minus eorum, qui recentiores, & à dogmatibus Pontificijs haud sunt alieni; Verùm eorum tantùm, quos constat Apostolorum ætati fuisse quàm maximè vicinos. Deinde quoad Judæos, ratio Jesuvitica planè non militat. Neque enim ex eorum abjectione: sed potius ex singulari illo D E I amore, quo populum istum prosecutus est, certitudo canonis Veteris Testamenti dependet. Qua de re David Ps. 147, 19, & 20. Qui annunciat Verbum suum Jacob: Justitias & Judicia sua Israel: Non fecit taliter ulli nationi: & judicia sua non manifestavit eis. Sic quoad Judæorum abjectionem, ea usque adeò non Canonem suspectum nobis reddere potest, ut eum potius mirificè confirmet. Qua de re Jesuitvitæ audiant Augustinum sic loquentem, Epist. 3. ad Volusianum: Reproba per infidelitatem gens Judæorum à sedibus extirpata, per mundum usquequaq́; dispergitur, ut ubiq́; portet codices Sanctos, ac si prophetiæ testimonium, qua Christus & Ecclesia prænunciata est, ne ad tempus à nobis confictum existimaretur, ab ipsis adversariis proferatur, ubi etiam ipsos prædictum est non fuisse credituros.

Et in enarratione Psalmi 56. Propterea adhuc Judæi sunt, ut libros nostros portent in confusionem suam. Quando enim volumus ostendere Christum prophetatum, proferimus paganis (infidelibus) literas istas. Et ne forti illi duri ad fidem dicant, nos Christianos illas composuisse, & cum Evangelio, quod prædicamus, Prophetas finxisse, per quos prædictum videretur, quod prædicamus, hinc eos convincimus, quòd omnes illæ literæ, quibus Christus prophetatus est, apud Judæos sunt. Proferimus ergò codices ab inimicis Judæis, ut confundamus inimicos paganos sive infideles. In quali ergò opprobrio sunt Judæi? Codicem portat Judæus unde credat Christianus: Librarij nostri facti sunt, quemadmodum servi solent post dominos, ferre codices: ut illi portando, deficiant, isti legendo, proficiant. Quod si dixerint Jesuvitæ, Hebraicos libros à judæis esse falsatos: petimus ut ostendant, num ante Christum in carnem missum, an post, falsatio illa facta. Non certè ante: quia, uti Origenes in octavo volumine explanationum Esaiæ evidenter arguit. Nunquam Dominus & Apostoli, qui cætera crimina arguunt in Scribis & Pharisæis, de hoc crimine, quod erat maximum, reticuissent. Non post adventum Salvatoris, quia jam Christi & Apostolorum conciones non amplius responderent Vaticinijs Prophetarum de Christo & doctrinâ ejus. Jam verò, quia hodieque inter Vetus & Novum Testamentum pulcerrimus perspicitur consensus: utique vel inde de Esavviticæ argutationis vanitate, abundè liquet.

Cæterùm priusquàm hinc abeamus, observandum illud fuerit, à veteribus Patribus libros Biblicos non eodem modo distingui. Plerique cum B. Hieronymo eam observant distinctionem, quam propositio hæc nostra habet, quâ libri Biblici distinguuntur in Canonicos & Apocryphos. Verùm Eusebius lib. 3. cap. 3. & 25. histor. Eccl. tres constituit sacrorum librorum ordines: in quorum primo ponit ἀναμφιλέκτως ἐνδιαθήκꙋς ἠ ὀμολογꙋμένας γραφὰς, quæ scilicet sine ulla contradictione, omniumque consensu ad

Testamentum DEI pertinent. Secundum ordinem facit τῶν ἀντιλεγομένων, γνωρίμων, δ᾽ ἀν ὅμως τοῖς πολλοῖς, eorum, quibus contradicitur quidem, noti tamen sunt multis: Quem in numerum refert Epistolam Iacobi, posteriorem Petri,duas posteriores Iohannis: Epistolam Iudæ, & Apocalypsin Iohannis. Tertium ordinem facit τῶν νόθων adulterinorum: quales sunt, Acta Pauli, Apocalypsis Petri, Liber Hermetis sive pastoris: Liber Henochi, & alia id genus scripta supposititia. Sic, etsi D. Augustin. duos tantùm facit Librorum ordines Canonicos & Apocryphos: constat tamen ipsum sub Canonicis, non eos modò complecti, qui revera tales sunt, quique & semper & ab omnibus Ecclesiis sunt accepti: sed etiam eos, de quibus aliquando dubitatum est: Ita quidem, ut sub Apocryphis tantùm comprehendat nothos illos sive supposititios libros, quos Eusebius in tertium ordinem rejecit. Sic ergo D. Augustino Libri Canonici ijdem sunt, qui Biblici, laxè sumto termino sive vocabalo Canonici. Unde tamen pessimè inde colligunt Jesuvviticæ: Augustinum pro verè ac γνησίως Canonicis indifferenter habuisse etiam eos, quos nos Apocryphos indigitamus. Nam libro 2. cap. 8. de Doctrina Christiana, eos, de quibus aliquando dubitatum est, reliquis, de quibus nunquam dubitatum, longè postponit; atque ita licèt laxè loquendo libros Macchabæorum, & reliquos Apocryphos refert inter Canonicos, quatenus nimirùm documenta virtutum & pietatis regulæ inde peti possunt: tamen lib. 2. contra secundam Epistolam Gaudentij cap. 23. monet istam Scripturam SOBRIE legendam esse, quod de libris verè Canonicis nunquam affirmaret. Quid? quod ipse Cajetanus Cardinalis, libros Apocryphos à quibusdam Concilijs atq; Augustino Canonicos dictos esse scribit, quia morū ex ijs, nō doctrinæ regula peti potuit: in fine Comment. in hist. Veteris Testamenti. Cæterùm de Apocryphis sensu Augustiniano sic dictis: hoc est, de nothis & supposititiis, sic habet Aug. lib. 15. de Civ. Dei cap. 23. Omittamus earum scripturarum fabulas, quæ Apocryphæ nominantur, eò quòd occulta eorum origo non claruit Patribus, à quibus usq; ad nos autoritas verarum scripturarum certissima & notissima successione pervenit. In his enim Apocryphis etsi invenitur aliqua veritas: tamen propter multa falsa, non est Canonica earum autoritas. Quibus observatis nihil jam repugnantiæ oritur inter Augustinum & Hieronymum. Hieronymus enim, quem & nos sequimur, libros tantùm Biblicos considerat, eosque dispescit in Canonicos & Apocryphos: Vocabulo (Canonicum) strictè magisque propriè sumto. Augustinus verò præter libros Biblicos considerat eos etiam, qui in volumine Biblico non extant; sed omnium consensu sunt supposititij & adulterini, quorum respectu & comparatione, Augustinus omnes libros Biblicos voluit nominare Canonicos, laxè sumto hoc vocabulo, quatenus nimirum illud supposititio & adulterino opponitur. Ubi tamen inter hos ipsos Biblicos & Canonicos Augustinum ipsum, luculentum discrimen constitueret, jam ex ipsius libris ostensum fuit, ita ut immotâ planè subsistat propositio nostra, sic cum D. Hieronymo evidentissimè colligens: Apocrypha nescit Ecclesia: Ad Hebræos igitur revertendum est: Unde & Dominus loquitur, & discipuli exempla præsumunt: præfat. in lib. Paralip.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: V. Orthodox Proposition

V. ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

The Apocryphal books of the Old Testament are those which, first, were not even held as authentic in the Jewish Church; second, which lack the testimony of Christ and the Apostles; and third, finally, which are destitute of the Catholic consensus of the primitive Church, which is required for the definition of canonical books.

CONFIRMATION.

The Council of Laodicea truly judged so in Canon 59, removing from the Canon of the Scriptures all those books which our churches hold as Apocryphal. Cyprian, or whoever he was who wrote the exposition of the Creed, judged so in these words: It must be known that there are also other books which were called by the ancients not Canonical, but Ecclesiastical, such as the Wisdom which is called Solomon's, and the other Wisdom which is called Sirach: of the same order is also the little book of Tobit and Judith, and the books of the Maccabees.

Cyril of Jerusalem judged so in his Catecheses, contending most sharply that only those which the Hebrews receive are to be respected and read by all Christians: as being the only ones which the Apostles and the Bishops of the Old Church, who were much wiser than we, handed down to the Church: μηδὲ δὲ [τὰ] ἀπόκρυφα μηδὲν ἔχε κοινὸν, and have nothing to do with the Apocrypha.

Athanasius judged so in his Synopsis at the beginning: besides the Canonical ones, there are still other books of the same Old Testament, not Canonical, which are read only to the Catechumens.

Jerome judged so in his preface to the books of Solomon: just as, he says, the Church indeed reads Tobit, Judith, and the books of the Maccabees, but does not receive them among the Canonical Scriptures: so also it reads these two volumes, Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas.

And in the Prologus Galeatus: Whatever is outside those books which we translated from Hebrew into Latin, let us know that it must be placed among the Apocrypha. We therefore refer to the Catalogue of the Apocryphal books of the Old Testament the third and fourth book of Ezra: the book of Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit, Baruch, the books of the Maccabees, and the fragments from the history of Daniel and Esther. Concerning all of which books [see] in the prologue to the first book on the Sacraments, chapter 7.

Hugh of Saint Victor writes in this manner: There are besides in the Old Testament other books, which are indeed read, but are not written in the body of the text or in the Canon of authority: such as the book of Tobit, and Judith, and the Maccabees, and that which is inscribed the book of the Wisdom of Solomon, and Ecclesiasticus.

And St. Jerome warns very diligently that the weak should either abstain entirely from the reading of those books, or read them soberly: Beware, he says, of all Apocrypha: And if at any time they wish to read them, not for the truth of dogmas, but for the reverence of the signs, let them know that they are not by those whose titles they bear, that many faulty things are mixed into them, and that it is a matter of great prudence to seek gold in the mud. From the Institution of a daughter to Laeta.

Latin:

V. PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

LIbri Apocryphi Veteris Testamenti sunt, tùm, qui ne quidem in Judaica Ecclesia pro Authenticis fuerunt habiti: tùm quibus deest Christi & Apostolorum testimonium: tùm denique, qui primitivæ Ecclesiæ Catholico consensu, ad Canonicorum librorum definitionem requisito, destituuntur.

CONFIRMATIO.

SIc sanè censuit Concilium Laodicenum Canone 59. illos libros omnes, quos nostræ Ecclesiæ pro Apocryphis habent, à Canone Scripturarum removens. Sic censuit Cyprianus, sive quisquis ille fuit, qui Symboli expositionem scripsit hisce verbis: Sciendum est, quòd & alij libri sunt, qui non Canonici, sed Ecclesiastici à majoribus appellati sunt, ut est Sapientia, quæ dicitur Salomonis, & alia Sapientia, quæ dicitur Sirach: ejusdem ordinis est & libellus Tobiæ & Judith, & Macchabæorum libri.

Sic censuit Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus κατηχίδ. eos tantùm, quos Hebræi recipiunt, ab omnibus Christianis suspiciendos & legendos esse, acerrimè contendens: ut quos solos Apostoli & Veteris Ecclesiæ Episcopi, qui nobis multò erant sapientiores, Ecclesiæ tradiderunt: μηδὲ δὲ [τὰ] ἀπόκρυφα μηδὲν ἔχε κοινὸν, cum Apocryphis autem nihil tibi rei sit.

Sic censuit Athanasius in Synopsi in principio: præter Canonicos sunt adhuc alij ejusdem Veteris Testamenti libri, non Canonici, qui Catechumenis tantùm leguntur.

Sic censuit Hieronymus in præfat. in libros Salomonis: sicut, inquiens: Tobiam, Judith & Macchabæorum libros legit quidem Ecclesia, sed eos inter Canonicas Scripturas non recipit : ita & hæc duo volumina, Sapientiam & Ecclesiasticum legit ad ædificationem plebis, non ad autoritatem Ecclesiasticorum dogmatum confirmandam.

Et in prologo Galeato: Quicquid est extra illos libros, quos de Hebræo vertimus in latinum, inter Apocrypha ponendum esse sciamus. Referimus proinde in Catalogum librorum Apocryphorum Veteris Testamenti librum tertium & quartum Esdræ: Librum Sapientiæ, Siracidem, Judith, Tobiam, Baruch, libros Macchabæorum, Fragmenta ex historia Danielis & Esther. De quibus libris omnibus in prologo I. libri de Sacram. cap. 7.

Hugo de sancto victore hunc in modum scribit: Sunt præterea in Veteri Testamento alij libri, qui leguntur quidem, sed in corpore textus, vel in Canone authoritatis non scribuntur: ut est, Liber Tobiæ, & Judith & Macchabæorum, & qui inscribitur liber Sapientiæ Salomonis, & Ecclesiasticus.

Et D. Hieronymus diligenter admodum monet, ut infirmi à lectione istorum librorum vel planè abstineant, vel eos sobriè legant: Caveant, inquiens, omnia Apocrypha: Et si quando ea, non ad dogmatum veritatem,sed ad signorum reverentiam legere voluerint, sciant non eorum esse, quorum titulis prænotantur, multaƣ his admixta esse vitiosa, & grandis esse prudentiæ, aurum in luto quærere. De Instit. filiæ ad Lætam.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: VI. Orthodox Proposition

VI. ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

The books of the N. Testament, as many as exist in the Greek codex, are not entirely of the same authority: For some have always had testimony from the Catholic Church that they were written by the Apostles themselves: but concerning some there was doubt: Which for this reason alone were also named Apocryphal by some.

CONFIRMATION.

Since soon after the age of the Apostles, heretics brought forth various writings under the names of the Apostles, by which they attempted to convince others of their errors, such as the Gospel of Peter, Thomas, Matthias; likewise the Acts of Peter, Paul, John: And indeed they foisted upon the Church the writings of others, as if seen, read, and approved by the Apostles: such as the Gospel of Nicodemus, and also the Book of Hermes or the Shepherd: and this so plausibly that some even of the Orthodox Fathers sought foundations from these supposititious books for the confirmation of Ecclesiastical dogmas: it came about that, the deceit having been noticed, at first indeed the Holy Fathers, since on account of frequent persecutions free councils could not be convened, sought certain and indubitable documents from the authority and testimony of the most ancient Church; by which it could be confirmed, Which books were written by the Apostles themselves; Which, however, were supposititious: But then in the progress of time, and with some firmer peace established, the Church through councils defined which books of the New Testament were to be held as Apostolic and Canonical without any doubt.

Thus therefore at the beginning the Fathers, as Eusebius lib. 4. cap. 26. and book 6. cap. 18. Cypr. in exp. Symboli, Hilar. preface in Psalms. Epiph. Tom. 1. l. 1. heresy 8. and book on measures and weights. Hieronym. in Epistle to Paulinus on sacred books, and preface in books of Kings. Finally the Laodicean Council 1. Can. 59. ὁμοθυμαδὸν defined: that all and each of those books, which even today are contained in the Greek volume, a comparison having been made to those supposititious books which the Heretics brought forth, are to be held as Canonical:

First general question

Furthermore indeed, if these very books, which are contained in the Greek codex, are compared with one another; Eusebius is a witness (lib. 3. hist. Eccl. cap. 22.) that not all of them obtain equal authority in the Church, because it has always been doubted by some in the Church whether they were written by those Apostles whose names they bear. The words of Eusebius in the place cited just now contain: Let us (2. Order.) agree. In the first place is to be placed that fourfold scripture of the Evangelists; which the Acts of the Apostles follow: After these are to be subjoined the Epistles of Paul: to those is to be subjoined that which is said to be prior to John: similarly also that which is authentic of Peter. After these let there be ordered, IF IT SHALL HAVE SEEMED GOOD, the Apocalypse of John, concerning which we shall explain in its own place what is to be thought. And these writings indeed are held as indubitable. But those which are contradicted, (11. Order.) although these are known to many: the Epistle which is attributed to (III. Order.) James: the Epistle of Jude: the posterior of Peter: the second and third of John, whether they are of the Evangelist, or of some other of the same name. But among the adulterated are considered others of Paul, and the book called the Shepherd, the Apocalypse of Peter: the Epistle of Barnabas: as also the Apocalypse of John, if it seems so, which some reject, as they are called: but others adjudge them to certain and indubitable scriptures: the Gospel according to the Hebrews, the Gospels of Peter, Thomas, Matthias. Also, the Acts of Andrew, John and others: of which no writer of ecclesiastical succession anywhere or at any time deigned to make mention in his commentaries. Furthermore, the character of the phrase varies from the Apostolic custom, and the very sentiment, and the purpose of those things which are brought forward in them, differ greatly from the truth of right doctrine, and they clearly convince that they are the figments of heretical men. Wherefore they are not only to be placed among the adulterated, but are to be shunned as absurd and impious by all. Thus far the words of Eusebius, in which it deserves to be noted most of all, that Eusebius himself concerning the books of the second order, that is, concerning those which are contained indeed in the Greek codex, but have suffered some contradiction, expressly affirms that they are known to many, and are read by many Ecclesiastical writers. For from this a clear distinction can and ought to be made between the Apocryphal books of the Old, and the Apocryphal books of the New Testament, such indeed that the Apocrypha of the New Testament obtain a far greater authority than the Apocrypha of the Old Testament, and an authority indeed that is valid even in the adjudication of Ecclesiastical dogmas. (11. So that we can, nay indeed we ought, to name them authentic rather than Apocryphal. But there pertain to this class, by the consensus of all writers both ancient and modern, the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James: the Posterior of Peter: the second and third of John: the Epistle of Jude: the Apocalypse of John. Concerning which there will be a future disputation for us below, item by item, against the sophistries of the Juvvitarians, if it shall have been shown first what they themselves hold concerning this first question.

That the Scripture of the New Testament was commanded to be written by the Holy Spirit is proved against Bellarmine and in the explanation of the saying 2

Tim. 3 by Salom. Gesner, published M. 3. b. Q. 2. Vit. page 594. Although Bellarmine (lib. 4. cap. 3. de Verbo non scripto) denies that any of the Catholics taught that God had ordained that the New Testament should not be written: yet he soon contradicts himself, which is evident from his three most absurd hypotheses, of which the first denies that GOD commanded the Apostles to write: The second affirms that no necessity demanded that the N.T. should be written: The third asserts that the New Testament ought to have been written primarily in hearts, not in books. We confirm the contrary to these reasons.

I. All scripture is θεόπνευστος (God-breathed): But already at that time there existed most of the Epistles of Paul: Item certain Gospels &c. And concerning these writings the same is to be determined. Where it is to be observed that the Apostle does not say that all writing is θεόπνευστα (God-breathed): but that every writing is θεόπνευστος: so that he may show that not only the things written, but the very writing itself considered in itself is θεόπνευστον, that is, undertaken by the command of GOD.

II. The Apostles had not learned the knowledge of letters and the faculty of writing either in childhood or in more adult age, as they were for the most part engaged in manual craft: and in those times the studies of letters and languages were not except among the Scribes and Priests. But the Holy Spirit instructed the Apostles at the feast of Pentecost with the knowledge of letters, together with the knowledge of languages. (They had been unlettered:) Thus Bellarmine objects: Whatever is not proposed and enjoined by word of mouth, that cannot properly be called a precept: it shines that it is inspired by God himself.

Yet, that the Apostles should write, was nowhere enjoined upon them by living voice. E. nor, on account of speaking, was this enjoined upon them. Response to the major premise, and I deny it as false: For even that which is inspired can be shown to be able to be called a precept properly so called, from that natural knowledge of the law impressed upon the Ethnic peoples. Which the blessed Apostle expressly names the ἔργον τοῦ νόμου γραπτόν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις: and that it is a precept properly speaking, no sane man doubts. Whence the Apostle says Rom. 2. 15., the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things of the law: these not having the law, are a law unto themselves. And how could they be accused of transgression (Rom. 2.) if this inspired knowledge had not been a law for them, a precept properly so called. For where there is no law, there is no transgression. Rom. 4. 15. The same must altogether be maintained concerning that internal incitation of GOD by which they were impelled to write.

III. Confirmation: The Apostles, about to write the Epistle (A. 15.), say, It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. But concerning similar things the judgment is the same. Therefore.

IV. (Matth. 28.) Christ commands, to make disciples and to teach all nations: which is done both by word of mouth and by writings. And by writings indeed for this reason, because it would have been impossible otherwise for all nations everywhere to be instructed by the Apostles.

V. In the Apocalypse this command is found many times, Write, Apoc. 1. 11. Apoc. 2. 3. 13. 14. Hear the voice saying, Write. (Obj. h)

Obj. He commands only to write certain visions. Resp. That is indeed denied: For that John is commanded to write also the doctrine of the Gospel and the precepts of morals, is evident even from this, that the Epistles written to the seven Churches of Asia contain not so much visions as dogmas: as that he praises the Ephesian Church for good works, for labor, for patience, for purity of doctrine: for the hatred of the heresy of the Nicolaitans, etc. Furthermore, what is written there is written for all Christians, therefore John says, He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches. 3. He writes of perseverance, and of eternal beatitude Apoc. 2. & 3. 14. Blessed are the dead etc. 19, 9. Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper etc.

Obj. 2. But these do not contain the entire doctrine of the Gospel. Resp. Be it so, what then: The judgment is the same concerning similar things, 2. let him show the reason why these ought to have been written, but those not.

II. Hypothesis. Bellarmine. The Scripture of the New Testament was not necessary.

Resp. Nay, it was 1. By necessity of command, of which it has already been spoken. 2. By necessity of the propagation of the Evangelical doctrine. 3. By necessity of refuting heretics. 4. By necessity of beating back Jewish superstition and Ethnic impiety. 5. By necessity of planting piety: and working perfection, that the man of GOD may be perfectly instructed etc. 2 Tim. 3. 16. What causes impelled Matthew, what Mark, what Luke, and so on, see S. G. in the explanation of the saying 2 Tim. 3. lit. N. 6. 7.

III. Hypothesis. Bellarmine. The New Testament ought to have been written chiefly in the heart. In place of proof he brings forward Jerem. 31. concerning which see the Bible in quarto. Only the form of the argument is to be noted in this place, which is such: The doctrine of the New Testament ought to be inscribed in the hearts: Therefore it ought not to be written, or consigned to letters. If the major proposition be added: that will be discovered to be manifestly false. The Old Testament certainly ought to be written in the heart. Deut. 6, 6. & 7. but that this ought to be consigned to letters, Bellarmine himself confesses in this place, lib. 4. c. 4.

Latin:

VI. PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

LIbri N. Testamenti, quotquot quidem in Græco codice extant, non planè sunt ejusdem autoritatis: QuƊ dam enim semper à Catholica Ecclesia habuerunt testimonium, quòd sint ab Apostolis ipsis conscripti: de quibusdam verò fuit dubitatum: Qui hanc solam etiam ob causam ab aliquibus Apocryphi sunt nominati.

CONFIRMATIO.

Cùm mox post Apostolorum ætatem hæretici sub Apostolorum nominibus, varia proferrent scripta, quibus erroribus suis fidem facere conabantur, ut Evangelium Petri, Thomæ, Matthiæ; Item Acta Petri, Pauli, Johannis: Quin & aliorum scripta, tanquam ab Apostolis visa, lecta, approbata, Ecclesię obtruderent: ut Evangelium Nicodemi, Librum item Hermetis sive pastoris: idque ita plausibiliter, ut nonnulli etiam Patrum Orthodoxorum, ex supposititijs istis libris fundamenta pro confirmatione dogmatum Ecclesiasticorum peterent: factum est, ut dolo animadverso, initiò quidem S. Patres, cùm propter crebras persecutiones concilia libera cogi haud possent, ex autoritate ac testimonio antiquissimæ Ecclesiæ certa ac indubitata peterent documenta; quibus confirmari posset, Quinam Libri ab Apostolis ipsis conscripti; Qui verò essent supposititij: Deinde verò progressu temporis, & pace aliqua firmiore constitutâ, Ecclesia per concilia definiret, quinam libri Novi Testamenti citra omnem dubitationem, pro Apostolicis & Canonicis essent habendi.

Sic ergo initiò Patres, ut Eusebius lib. 4. cap. 26. & libro 6. cap. 18. Cypr. in exp. Symboli, Hilar. præfat. in Psalmos. Epiph. Tom. 1. l. 1. hæres. 8. & libro de mensuris & ponderibus. Hieronym. in Epist. ad Paulinum de libris sacris, & præfat. in libros Regum. Concilium denique Laodicense 1. Can. 59. ὁμοθυμαδὸν definiverunt: omnes ac singulos illos libros, qui hodieque in Græco volumine continentur, comparatione facta ad libros illos supposititios, quos Hæretici proferebant, pro Canonicis esse habendos:

Quaestio prima generalis

Deinde verò, si hi ipsi libri, qui in Graeco codice continentur, ad se mutuò conferantur; testis est Eusebius lib. 3. hist. Eccl. cap. 22. non parem auctoritatem omnes illos in Ecclesia obtinere, propterea quòd de quibusdam in Ecclesia semper dubitatum fuerit, an sint ab illis Apostolis conscripti, quorum nomina prae se ferunt Verba Eusebii loco proximè citato fichabent: Conue(2. Ordo.) nigamus. Priore loco ponenda est illa quadriguga Evangelistarum scriptura; quam Apostolorum acta sequuntur: Post haec subjungenda sunt Epistolae Pauli: illae subjiciatur, quae prior Johanni esse fertur: similiter & quae Petri est authentica. Post has ordinetur, Si VISUM FUERIT, Apocalypsis Johannis, de qua quid sentiat ur fuo loco exponemus. Et haec quidem scripta pro indubitatis habentur. Quibus verò contradicitur, (11. Ordo.) tametsi multis fine cognita sunt haec: Epistola quae Jo(III. Ordo.) cobo tribuitur: Epistola Judae: posterior Petri: altera & (De Apocalypsi Nota.) tertia Johannis, sive illae Evangelistae, sive alterius cujusdam ejusdem nominis. Inter adulterina verò censentur alia Pauli, & liber, dictus Pastor, Apocalypsis Petri: Epistola Barnabae: ut & Apocalypsis Johannis, si videtur, quam nonnulli, sic dictis, reprobant: alij verò certis & indubitatis scripturis adjudicant: Evangelium ad Hebraeos, Evangelia Petri, Thome, Matthiae. Item, Acta Andreae, Johannis & aliorum: quorum nullam ubique vel aliquem Ecclesiasticae successionis scriptor mentionem in commentariis suis facere dignatus est. Porrò & phraseos character à consuetudine Apostolica variat, & ipsa sententia, & propositum eorum, quae in illis adferuntur, plurimùm à veritate rectae doctrinae discrepant, & quod haereticorum virorum sint figmenta, perspicuè convincant. Quapropter non inter adulterina modò ponenda, sed tanquam omnium absurda & impia averfanda sunt. Hactenus verba Eusebii, in quibus observationem vel maximè meretur, quòd ipse Eusebius de libris secundi ordinis, hoc est, de ijs, qui in Graeco quidem codice continentur, sed contradictionem aliquam passi sunt, disertè affirmat, quòd multis sint cognita, & à multis Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis legantur. Hinc enim luculentum confici potest & debet discrimen inter libros Apocryphos Veteris, & Apocryphos Novi Testamenti, tale nimirum, quòd Apocryphi Novi Testamenti longè majorem auctoritatem, quàm Apocryphi Veteris Testamenti obtineant, & auctoritatem quidem in dijudicatione etiam dogmatum Ecclesiasticorum valentem. (11. Ita ut rectius authenticos, quàm Apocryphos nominare eos possimus, imò verò debeamus. Pertinent autem ad hanc classem, omnium tùm veterum, tùm recentiorum Scriptorum consensu, Epistola ad Hebraeos Epistola Jacobi: Posterior Petri: secunda & tertia Johannis: Epistola Judae: Apocalypsis Johannis. De quibus sigillatim infra adversus Juvvitarum strophas nobis futura disputatio, si prius, quam sententiam ipsi circa primam hanc quaestionem teneant, ostensum fuerit.

Scripturam Novi Testamenti à Spiritu Sancto scribi jussam esse, probatur adversus Bellarminum & in explicatione dicti 2. Tim. 3. à Salom. Gesnero editi M. 3. b. Q. 2. Vit. pag.

594. Etsi Bellarminus lib. 4. cap. 3. de Verbo non scripto, negat ullum Catholicorum docuisse, Deum constituisse, ut Novum Testamentum non scriberetur: tamen mox sibi ipsi contradicit, id quod patet ex tribus ipsius absurdissimis hypothesibus, quarum prima negat, DEUM mandasse Apostolus, ut scriberent: Altera affirmat, nullam necessitatem exigisse, ut N. T. scriberetur: Tertia afferit, Novum Testamentum praecipuè in cordibus, non in libris scribi debuisse. Nos contrarium his rationibus confirmamus.

I. Omnis scriptura est θεόπνευστος: At jam tum extiterunt pleraque Epistolae Pauli: Item quaedam Evangelia &c. E de his scriptis idem est statuendum. Ubi observandum, quod Apostolus non dicit πάντα γραφὴν sunt θεόπνευστα: sed πᾶσα γραφὴ ἐστὶ θεόπνευστος: ut lic ostendat, non modò res scriptas, sed ipsam scriptionem in se consideratam esse θεόπνευστον, hoc est, jussu DEI susceptam.

II. Notitiam literarum & scribendi facultatem neque in pueritia, neque in adultiore aetate addidicerant Apostoli, ut qui plerique arte manuaria tractabant: & illis temporibus literarum & linguarum studia non erant nisi penes Scribas & Sacerdotes. Sed Spiritus Sanctus Apostolos in festo Pentecostes, notitia literarum, unà cum linguarum notitia instruxit. (Fuerant ἀγράμματοι:) Sic objicit Bellarm: Quicquid non viva voce propositum & injunctum est, illud propriè non potest dici praeceptum: lucet à Deo ipso sit inspiratum.

Atqui, ut Apostoli scriberent, nusquam viva voce ipsis est injunctum. E. neque propter loquendo, hoc ipsis est injunctum. Resp. ad majorem, eamque ut falsam nego: Nam & illud quod inspiratum est, dici posse propriè praeceptum, comprobari potest ex naturali illa notitia legis, Ethnicis impressa. Quam D. Apostolus expressè nominat ἔργον τοῦ νόμου γραπτόν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις: & quàm praeceptum esse propriè loquendo, nemo sanus dubitat. Unde Apostolus Rom. 2. 15. dicit, Gentes, quae non habent legem, natura faciunt ea, quae legis sunt: ista legem non habentes, sibipsis sunt lex. Et quomodo transgres- (Rom. 2.) sionis infimulari potuissent, si inspirata haec notitia, non ipsis fuisset lex praeceptum propriè dictum. Ubi enim nulla est lex, ibi nulla est praevaricatio. Rom. 4. 15. Idem omninò est statuendum de interna illa DEI incitatione, qua ad scribendum sunt impulsi.

Differentia non est in praeceptis, sed in modo revelationis. III. Confirmatio: Apostoli scripturi Epistolam A. 15. dicunt, Sic Visum est Spiritui S. & nobis. De fimilibus autem idem est judicium. E.

IV. Matth. 28. jubet Christus, μαθητεύειν & διδάσκειν omnes gentes: id quod fit tùm viva voce, cum scriptis. Et scriptis quidem ideò, quia impossibile aliàs fuisset, omnes ubique gentes ab Apostolis erudiri.

V. In Apocalypsi multoties reperitur hoc mandatum, Scribe, Apoc. 1. 11. Apoc. 2. 3. 13. 14. Audi vocem dicentem, Scribe. (Obj. h)

Obj. Iubet tantùm scribere quasdam visiones. Resp. Id verò negatur: Nam Iohannem juberi scribere etiam doctrinam Evangelij & præcepta morum, vel inde constat, quod Epistolæ ad septem Ecclesias Asiæ perscriptæ nõ tàm visiones, quàm dogmata continent: ut quod Ephesinam Ecclesiam collaudat à bonis operibus, à labore, à patientia, à puritate doctrinæ: ab odio hærefeως Nicolaitarum &c. Deinde, quæ ibi scribuntur, omnibus Christianis sunt scripta, ideò dicit Johannes, Qui habet aurem, audiat, quid Spiritus dicat Ecclesiis. 3. scribit de perseverantia, deq; æterna beatitudine Apoc. 2. & 3. 14. Beati mortui &c. 19, 9. Beati qui ad cœnam nuptiarum &c.

Obj. 2. At ista non continent universam doctrinam Evangelij. Resp. Esto, Quid tùm: De similibus idem est judicium, 2. ostendat causam, cur hæc scribi, illa verò non scribi debuerint.

II. Hypoth. Bellarmin. Non fuit necessaria Scriptura Novi Testamenti.

Resp. Imò fuit 1. Necessitate mandati, de quà jam dictũ. 2. Necessitate propagationis doctrinæ Evangelicæ. 3. Necessitate hæreticorum refutandorum. 4. Necessitate Judaicæ superstitionis & Ethnicæ impietatis retundendæ. 5. Necessitate plantandæ pietatis: & operandæ perfectionis, ut homo DEI sit perfectè instructus &c. 2. Tim. 3. 16. Quæ causæ Matthæum, Quæ Marcum, Quæ Lucam, & sic deinceps impulerit, vide S. G. in explic. dicti 2. Tim. 3. lit. N. 6. 7.

III. Hypoth. Bell. Novum Testamentum præcipuè in cor scribi debuit. Probationis loco adducit Jerem. 31. de quo vide Biblia in quarto. Forma tantùm argumenti hoc loco notanda venit, quæ talis est: Doctrina Novi Testamenti inscribi debuit in corda: Ergo non scribi debuit, vel consignari literis. Si major propositio addatur: illa deprehendetur esse manifesta falsa. Vetus certè Testamentum debuit scribi in cor. Deut. 6, 6. & 7. sed hoc literis consignari debuisse, h. l. fatetur ipse Bellarminus l. 4. c. 4.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Second Part, the First General Questions continued

PROPOSITION I. JESUITICAL.

The Roman Church alone and its Pontiff, having neglected and disregarded the consensus of Antiquity, can judge which book ought to be held as Canonical, and which not: nay, from a non-Canonical it can make a Canonical one: and vice versa, from a Canonical, a non-Canonical one.

Ἔκθεσις ἐλεγκτικὴ.

Thus thinks Stapleton, lib. 9 of doctrinal principles, concerning the authority of the Church, cap. 14, at the end of the fifth controversy, writing: It is in the power of the Church of this time, to refer some other book, not yet received into the Canon, yet written in the time of the Apostles, and

never hitherto reprobated by the judgment of the Church; for example's sake the book of the Shepherd of Hermas, and the Apostolic constitutions edited by Clement, into the number of sacred and certainly canonical books. Therefore, it will not matter much what the Old and first Church thought about this or that book, provided the Roman Pontiff has deemed it to be received.

Thus thinks Adam Tanner, page 203 of the Compendious Relation, writing: Concerning Scripture itself, setting aside the authority of the Church without tradition, it cannot be known that it is Canonical.

Thus Melchior Canus, book 2, chapter 7: It pertains to the Supreme Pontiff to define which book is Canonical.

Thus another certain Papal writer, Melchior Zanger, Provost of Ehingen, in his Simplicianus, page 6, gave his opinion, writing: Although in the times of St. Augustine, Jerome, and certain others, it was not so clearly established concerning these aforementioned books (the Apocrypha), since nothing certain had yet been defined about them by the Church: we shall not therefore allow them to be exiled now from the Canon of sacred books; as if, indeed, that which was once doubted or disputed in ancient and imperfect centuries must necessarily be doubted or disputed forever? As if, indeed, the Church cannot progress? It progresses, to be sure, in virtues and in goodness: just as it does in knowledge and doctrine. Whence it happens that we now know many things which were either doubted or entirely unknown to the first Fathers.

Furthermore, the stupendous vanity of this proposition is self-evident. For first, it is vain and false: that the Church can make any non-Canonical book Canonical. For we have demonstrated above in Orthodox Proposition 2 that this absolute power does not belong to the Church, to be able to confer Canonical authority upon Biblical books; and it will be demonstrated more fully below in general Question 2.

Next, it is vain and false that the judgment of the more recent Roman Church concerning Canonical books should be preferred to the testimony and judgment of the most ancient primitive Church. For if it is true, as Bellarmine wrote in book 1 of the Word of God, chapter 20, that in defining the Canons of the Apostles one must stand by the authority of Pope Zephyrinus, because on account of his antiquity he knew better how many the Canons of the Apostles were than any of those who came later: Certainly we can affirm much more rightly concerning the most ancient and first successors of the Apostles, that they knew better what were the Canonical and Apostolic scriptures than any of those who came later, whether Popes, or Ecclesiastical writers, or Councils. Since indeed those more recent ones could not have known this except from the report and testimony of their predecessors. From whom, as soon as those who come later depart, and establish something different, the matter itself, as they say, immediately cries out that, having abandoned these, the more ancient and earlier ones are to be heard more.

Thirdly, it is vain and false, nay blasphemous, that it cannot be established concerning Scripture that it is CANONICAL, except from the authority and tradition of the Church. For in this question it is not only disputed whether the Gospel of Matthew is Matthew's, or whether the Epistle of Paul to the Romans is the Apostle Paul's, where we ourselves readily grant that it is established for us from the testimony of the primitive Church, which, according to Tertullian's witness, itself had the autographs of the Apostles and Evangelists, and therefore it could testify indubitably in this regard. But the controversy between us and the Jesuits is primarily about this: from where does Scripture have it that it is holy and Canonical, that is, that it deserves faith that is entirely indubitable, both regarding the judgment of Ecclesiastical dogmas and regarding the instruction of life and morals? To which question we answer candidly, first, that Scripture has this

I. from itself, inasmuch as it is divinely inspired, 2 Tim. 3:16, and written by those who, moved by the Holy Spirit, spoke and wrote, 2 Pet. 1:21.

II. Furthermore, we are certain of this very Canonical authority of Scripture, not only from the testimony of the primitive Church, but from those internal criteria: such as the miracles by which it was confirmed; the constancy of the martyrs in enduring exquisite tortures for the doctrine contained in these books; likewise the prophecies concerning the greatest matters, to be fulfilled after many centuries, and their illustrious outcome; as well as other testimonies of this kind, both very numerous and most irrefragable. And although, convinced by the external testimony of the primitive Church, we neither can nor ought to deny that the Canonical Books are Canonical, yet we only then attain a certain and saving πληροφορίαν (full assurance) when the same Spirit, by whom those books were written and published, testifies in our minds concerning their Canonical authority through those internal criteria. Whoever lacks this internal testimony, however many thousands of times he may hear the Church, will nevertheless always fluctuate, uncertain and doubtful within himself.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO I. JESUWITICA.

SOla Ecclesia Romana ejusdemque Pontifex neglecto & posthabito Antiquitatis consensu, potest judicare, qui liber haberi debeat pro Canonico, qui non: imò ex non Canonico potest facere Canonicum: & vice versa, ex Canonico, non Canonicum.

Ἔκθεσις ἐλεγκτικὴ.

SIc censet Stapletonus lib. 9. principiorum doctrinalium, de Ecclesiæ autoritate, cap. 14. in fine quintæ controversiæ, scribens: Est penes Ecclesiam hujus temporis, librum aliquem alium, nondum in Canonem receptum, Apostolorum tamen tempore conscriptum, &

nunquam hactenus Ecclesiæ judicio reprobatum; exempli causâ librum Hermæ pastoris, & constitutiones Apostolicas à Clemente editas, in numerum librorum sacrorum & certè canonicorum referre. Itaq́, non magnapere intererit, quid Vetus & prima Ecclesia, de hoc aut illo libro senserit, modò Pontifex Romanus recipiendum existimaverit.

Sic censet Adamus Tannerus pag. 203. Relationis Compendiarie, scribens: De ipsâ scriptura, sepositâ autoritate Ecclesiæ sine traditione, constare non potest, quod sit Canonica.

Sic Melchior Canus, lib. 2. cap. 7. Ad summum Pontificem pertinet definire, quinam liber sit Canonicus.

Sic alius quidam Scriptor Pontificius Melchior Zangerus, Præpositus Ehingensis, in suo Simpliciano pag. 6. censuit, scribens: Licet D. Augustini, Hieronymi, aliorumq́; quorundam temporibus, de his præmemoratis libris (Apocryphis) non adeò liquidò constiterit, cum ab Ecclesia nihil certi adhuc de illis definitum fuerit: non ideò nos eos nunc à Canone sacrorum librorum exulare patiemur: quasi verò, de quo semel priscis & imperfectis seculis fuerit dubitatum aut controversum dubitetur aut controvertatur perpetuò, necessò sit? Quasi verò Ecclesia non proficere possit? Proficit nimirum, ut in virtutibus & in bonitate: ita in scientia & doctrina. Quo fit, ut multa nunc sciamus, quæ à primis Patribus aut dubitata, aut prorsus ignorata fuerunt.

Cæterùm propositionis hujus stupenda vanitas ultrò patet, Primum enim vanum falsumq́; est: Ecclesiam posse librum aliquem non-Canonicum, facere Canonicum. Quod enim hæc absoluta potestas Ecclesiæ non competat, ut autoritatem Canonicam, libris Biblicis conciliare possit, supra Propos. 2. Orth. demonstravimus: & infra Quæst. 2. generali, ampliùs demonstrabitur.

Deinde, vanum falsumque est, recentioris Ecclesiæ Romanæ judicium de libris Canonicis proferendum esse testificationi ac judicio antiquissimæ primitivæ Ecclesiæ. Quòd si enim verum est, quod scripsit Bellarm. libr. 1. de Verbo DEI cap. 20. in definiendis Apostolorum Canonibus, ideò standum esse, autoritate Zephirini Pontificis, quod propter antiquitatem melius ipse noverit, quot essent Apostolorum Canones, quàm ulli posteriorum: Certè multò nos rectius de vetustissimis, & primis quibusq; Apostolorum successoribus affirmare possumus, melius eos novisse, quæ essent Canonicæ & Apostolicæ scripturæ, quàm ullos posteriorum sive Pontificum, sive Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum, sive Conciliorum. Siquidem recentiores isti scire hoc non potuerunt, nisi ex relatu & testimonio antecessorum. A quo quàm primùm posteriores recedunt, diversumque statuunt tàm statim res ipsa, quod aiunt, clamat, his relictis, antiquiores & priores magis audiendos esse.

Tertiò, vanum falsumq́; est, imò blasphemum, Non constare posse de Scriptura, quod sit CANONICA, nisi ex autoritate & traditione Ecclesiæ. Neq; enim in hac quæstione de eo tantũ controvertitur, utrum Evangelium Matthæi, sit Matthæi: an Epistola Pauli ad Romanos sit Pauli Apostoli, ubi nos ipsi ultrò largimur, de eo nobis constare ex testimonio Ecclesiæ primitivæ, quæ Tertulliano teste, ipsa habuit Apostolorum & Evangelistarum αὐτόγραφα, ac proinde indubitato hac in parte testari potuit. Sed de eo inter nos & Jesuvitas potissimum controvertitur, unde nam habeat Scriptura, ut sit sancta & Canonica, hoc est, ut fidem prorsus indubiam mereatur, tum circa dijudicationem dogmatum Ecclesiasticorum, tum circa informationem vitæ morumq́;? Ad quam quæstionem ingenuè respondemus, primum, habere hoc Scripturam

I. ex se ipsa, quippè quæ divinitus est inspirata. 2. Tim. 3, 16. & conscripta ab ijs, qui à Spiritu Sancto impulsi locuti sunt & scripserunt. 2. Petr. 1, 21.

II. Deinde de hac ipsa Canonica Scripturæ autoritate nobis constat, non modò ex testimonio Ecclesiæ primitivæ: sed ex internis illis κριτηρίοις: qualia sunt miracula, quibus ea confirmata est: Constantia martyrum in perferendis exquisitis supplicijs pro doctrina hisce libris comprehensa: Vaticinia item de rebus longè maximis, post multa secula complendis, eorundemq́; illustris eventus: ut & id genus alia testimonia tum plurima, tum maximè irrefragabilia. Et quanquam externo Ecclesiæ primitivæ testimonio convicti, negare neque possumus, neque debemus, Libros Canonicos esse Canonicos: tamen tum demum certam & salutarem πληροφορίαν assequimur, quando idem Spiritus, quo libri illi scripti atque editi sunt, in mentibus nostris per interna illa κριτήρια, de illorum autoritate Canonica testatur. Qui interno hoc testimonio caret, quantumvis Ecclesiam millies audiat, incertus tamen semper apud se dubiusque fluctuabit.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: II. Jesuit Proposition

II. JESUIT PROPOSITION.

The individual and entire books of both Testaments, as many as are found in the Latin Vulgate edition, are to be held as Canonical and read in the Church, not only for the instruction of morals, but also for the confirmation of faith and doctrine.

Ἔκθεσις (Exposition).

Thus the Council of Trent judged, Session 4. For after it had also included in the number or class of the Canonical books of the Old Testament the book of Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Baruch, and both books of Maccabees—which books we hold to be Apocryphal—it finally made such a Decree: If anyone does not accept these books as holy and Canonical, entire with all their parts, as they have been accustomed to be read in the Catholic (namely, Roman) Church and are held in the old Latin Vulgate edition, let him be anathema.

Thus Innocent I, Roman Pontiff, judged in Epistle 3 to Exuperius, the last chapter, not only attributing Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus to Solomon:

ted and the book of Judith, and both of the Maccabees referring to the Canon.

Thus the Pontiff with his clergy judged, in the Instruction of the Council of Florence to the Armenians, which exists in the Sum of the Councils of Bartholomew Carnuza, page 284, in these words: The Church holds, receives, and venerates as Canonical all the books which are contained in the common editions, except the third and fourth of Esdras.

Robert Bellarmine also judges thus, lib. 1, de Verbo Dei, c. 4, naming as Apocryphal only those which the Church has always held partly as dreams and fables, and partly as supposititious and spurious: such as the third and fourth of Esdras, the third and fourth of the Maccabees, the one hundred and fifty-first Psalm: the Appendix to the book of Job: and finally the book of Hermes, which is inscribed The Shepherd. But the remaining books of the Old Testament, which we designate as Apocryphal, the Jesuit adds to that order of books which, although they did not always have an equally certain and explored authority, are nevertheless truly Prophetic and Apostolic, and obtain Canonical authority.

But the vanity of this proposition also is spontaneously evident. For first, it rests upon that false hypothesis that it is placed within the power of the Church to endow with Canonical authority even that book which has always been held by the primitive Church as Apocryphal: as was shown in the preceding, nearest proposition.

Then the Council of Trent directs its anathema not primarily against the Lutherans, but rather against those upon whose authority the Lutherans rely most heavily: namely, against the Orthodox Fathers, who have always been held and acknowledged by all as Catholics, such as Cyprian, Athanasius, Jerome, Eusebius, and others, who it is certain did not receive certain books of the Old Testament as Canonical: as we demonstrated in the 4th and 5th propositions of the Orthodox. Whence the not only tyranny of that conventicle against the Church, but also its stupendous impiety, shines forth not obscurely. Augustine refuted the ancient heretics, especially the Manichaeans, who repudiated the Canonical books, by this argument above all, that they rejected with vain fury those books which the Church acknowledged as divine when they were first written, and subsequently preserved perpetually as Canonical. lib. 28, against Faustus the Manichaean, cap. 2. Which method of refutation clearly collapses if the tyranny and caprice of the more recent Pontifical Church is to prevail.

But the Jesuit race clamors in this place, and with great effort objects to the Council of Carthage III, because it names those books which we hold as Apocryphal not only Canonical, but even divine.

But the Jesuits shamefully beg the question at the start: For this very thing is in question, and therefore it cannot sustain the nerve of proof: Namely, whether either the Carthaginian, or any other Council whatsoever, has the power to endow with Canonical authority any book about which the older Orthodox Fathers doubted for so long?

Then it is committed in this objection, a shameful ignorance is exposed: while the Jesuits falsely persuade themselves that the judgment of the later universal Church is sufficient for the canonical authority of the latter, however much it may be contrary to the preceding, more ancient Church.

Thirdly, this argument sins by the fallacy of equivocation. For the Council of Carthage names all the books of the Old Testament canonical for the same reason that we showed above in the fourth Orthodox proposition that Augustine, who was present at that Council, also designated them as such: namely, by making a comparison to those books which Augustine calls adulterous, lying, and fabulous in chapter 25 of his Questions on Numbers.

Yet this usage of the word 'canonical' neither can nor ought to prejudice those Fathers who, discussing this question more properly, judged that not only those fabulous and supposititious books which are apocryphal to Augustine, but also those books which are otherwise joined to the sacred Bibles, must be distinguished from the canonical and held as apocryphal, as is especially evident from Jerome, who, after he had listed those which are held by us in the Canon, immediately adds: so that we may know that whatever is outside of these must be placed among the Apocrypha.

Finally, the Third Council of Carthage is found not without cause to be wanting in faith in the adjudication of this question. For first, it was not ecumenical or universal, but particular or provincial, of a few bishops in Africa.

Then, although we not unwillingly grant to the Jesuits that the Council of Carthage was subsequently approved by the Council of Constantinople, yet not even in this way do they obtain what they want, but rather they entangle themselves in strange ways. For it is certain that in the same Council the canons of the Council of Laodicea were also approved, to which we rightly appeal. Now, the Synod of Carthage affirms that these books are canonical, but the Council of Laodicea not only denies that they are canonical, but even forbids them to be read in the Church at all. Again, the same Council of Constantinople approved the Canons of the Apostles, as they are held at least now, in which the three books of the Maccabees are placed among the canonical, although the Synod of Carthage acknowledges only two, and the books of Wisdom, Judith, and Tobias are entirely omitted in that same Canon. Let the Jesuits see, therefore, whether they can safely trust this Council of Constantinople, since it proposes to us three mutually contradictory canons. Nor is there any room for an escape, as the Jesuits might perhaps object, that in the older canon fewer books are approved, and in the more recent one more, because it was only then that it pleased the Church to bring forth its judgment on the rest. For why, I ask, do the Synods of Laodicea and Carthage omit the third book of Maccabees, once it had been placed in the Canon, if these agree among themselves and all are true? What of the fact that the Doctors who lived even after the Council of Constantinople, neither few nor contemptible, do not acknowledge these books, nor do they allow themselves to be bound by the authority of this Council? John of Damascus certainly enumerates no more than twenty-two books of the Old Testament, namely those which are in the Hebrew Canon: he indeed praises the Book of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, but he does not place them among the canonical. This same opinion is also held by Hugh of St. Victor, whose words we recited above in the 5th Orthodox proposition, as also by the other Hugh, Cardinal of Carrensis, who, writing about the Apocrypha, says: The Church receives such books not for the proof of faith, but for the instruction of morals.
