Nicholas of Lyra held the same view, writing thus at the beginning of his commentaries on the Apocryphal books: After I have written, with God's help, on the canonical books of Holy Scripture, I intend, trusting in the same help, to write on others which are not of the Canon, namely the Book of Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobias, and the Books of Maccabees: for the authority of these is considered less suitable for proving those things which come into contention. They are therefore mere trifles when they shout that these books were struck from the Canon of the Scriptures by Luther and his followers, because most of the dogmas of the Papists can be confirmed from them, as the Jesuit Campian writes in the tenth of his ten reasons. For the contrary was demonstrated both just now and above in the 4th and 5th Orthodox propositions from Origen, Eusebius book 5, chapter 25, from Cyril, from the Synopsis of Athanasius, from Nazianzen, Rufinus or Cyprian, Jerome, Epiphanius, and very many others. What of the fact that from this very exception, the desperate malice of the Jesuit cause is openly revealed? For because they understand that they can in no way establish the principles of their faith from the canonical books, the wretches soon flee to the apocryphal books, whose faith in the Church has been and will be forever ambiguous.

But since in this controversy about the canonical books the Jesuit race accuses the blessed Luther and our churches today of various and indeed most atrocious crimes and errors, it will be worth the effort to respond to those principal accusations, briefly indeed, but as the matter stands.

Latin:

II. PROPOSITIO JESUWITICA.

Libri singuli atque universi utriusq; Testamenti, quotquot quidem in vulgata latina editione reperiuntur; pro Canonicis sunt habendi, inque Ecclesia legendi, non modò ad morum institutionem, sed ad fidei etiam & doctrinæ confirmationem.

Ἔκθεσις.

Sic censuit Concilium Tridentinum Sess. 4. Postquam enim illud in numerum sive classem librorum Canonicorum Veteris Testamenti retulit etiam librum Tobiæ, Judith, Sapientiæ, Ecclesiasticam, Baruch, utrumq́; Macchabæorum: quos libros, nos pro Apocryphis habemus: tale tandem fecit Decretum: Si quis libros hos integros, cum omnibus suis partibus, prout in Ecclesia Catholica (Romana scilicet) legi consueverunt, & in veteri vulgata latina editione habentur, pro sacris & Canonicis non susceperit, Anathema sit.

Sic censuit Innocentius I. Pontifex Romanus in Epistola 3. ad Exuperium cap. ult. non modò Sapientiam & Ecclesiasticum attribuens Salomoni:

ted & librum Judith, ac utrumque Macchabæorum referens in Canonem.

Sic censuit Pontifex cum suo clero, in Instructione Concilij Florentini ad Armenios, quæ extat in summa Conciliorum Bartholomæi Carnuzæ pag. 284. his verbis: Omnes, qui in vulgatis habentur editionibus, libros, excepto tertio & quarto Esdræ, pro Canonicis habet, suscipit & veneratur Ecclesia.

Sic censet etiam Robertus Bellarminus lib. 1. de Verbo Dei c. 4. Apocryphos nominans eos tantùm, quos partim pro somnijs & fabulis, partim verò pro supposititijs & nothis semper habuit Ecclesia: ut tertium & quartum Esdræ, tertium & quartum Macchabæorum, Psalmum centesimum quinquagesimum primum: Appendicem libri Job: librum denique Hermetis, qui inscribitur Pastor. Cæterùm libros reliquos Veteris Testamenti, quos nos Apocryphos indigitamus, illi ordini librorum Jesuvvita accenset, qui, etsi non semper æquè certam ac exploratam habuerunt autoritatem, verè tamen sunt Prophetici & Apostolici, & Canonīcam autoritatem obtinent.

Sed hujus quoque propositionis vanitas ultrò patet. Primùm enim ea nititur falsâ illâ hypothesi, quòd in Ecclesiæ potestate sit positum, donare Canonica autoritate illum etiam librum, qui à primitiva Ecclesia pro Apocrypho semper est habitus: Vti ostensum præcedente propositione proximâ.

Deinde Anathema suum stringit Concilium Tridentinum non præcipuè in Lutheranos, sed in eos potiùs, quorum autoritate Lutherani vel maximè nituntur: nempè in Patres Orthodoxos, qui semper & ab omnibus pro Catholicis sunt habiti & agniti, ut Cyprianum, Athanasium, Hieronymum, Eusebium, & alios, quos constat certos quosdam libros Veteris Testamenti, pro Canonicis non recepisse: uti propositione 4. & 5. Orthodoxæ demonstravimus. Unde conciliabuli istius, non solùm Tyrannis in Ecclesiam, sed & stupenda impietas, haud obscurè elucet, Veteres certè hæreticos, Manichæos præsertim, qui libros Canonicos repudiarunt, hoc potissimùm argumento Augustinus refutavit, quòd nimirùm illos libros inani furore abjiciant, quos Ecclesia initiò scriptos pro divinis agnovit, & deinceps perpetuò tanquàm Canonicos conservavit. lib. 28. contra Faustum Manich. cap. 2. Quæ refutandi ratio planè corruit, si recentioris Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ Tyrannis & libido, obtinere debeat.

Sed obstrepit hoc loco gens Jesuvvitica, & magno conatu objicit Concilium Carthaginense III. quòd libros illos, quos nos pro Apocryphis habemus, non modò Canonicos, sed etiam divinos nominat.

Verùm turpiter initiò petunt principium Jesuvvitæ: Hoc ipsum enim in quæstione est, ac proinde probationis nervum sustinere non potest: An videlicet vel Carthaginense, vel quodcunque aliud Concilium potestatem habeat librum aliquem, de quo vetustiores Orthodoxi Patres tàm diu dubitarunt, Canonica autoritate donare?

Deinde committitur in hac objectione, turpis ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꝢ: dum falsò sibi persuadent Jesuvitæ, sufficere ad Canonicam autoritatem posterioris Ecclesiæ universalis judicium, quantumvis id præcedenti antiquiori Ecclesiæ sit contrarium.

Tertiò peccat hoc argumentum sophismate παρὰ τὴν ὁμωνυμίαν. Eadem enim ratione Concilium Carthaginense, libros omnes Veteris Testamenti nominat Canonicos, quâ Augustinum etiam, qui Concilio isti interfuit, eos ita indigitasse, suprà propositione quarta Orthodoxa ostendimus: facta nimirùm comparatione ad eos libros, quos Augustinus nominat adulterinos, mendaces & fabulosos cap. 25. Quæstionum super Numeros.

Quæ tamen usurpatio vocabuli Canonici neque potest, neque debet præjudicare illis Patribus, qui magis propriè hanc Quæstionem ventilantes, non fabulosos tantùm illos, ac supposititios, qui Augustino sunt Apocryphi; sed & eos libros, qui aliàs sacris Biblijs conjuncti sunt, à Canonicis distinguendos & pro Apocryphis habendos esse judicarunt, uti cumprimis patet ex Hieronymo, qui postquàm recensuisset eos, qui in Canone à nobis habentur, statim subjicit: ut scire valeamus; quicquid extra hos est, inter Apocrypha esse ponendum.

Tandem Concilium Carthaginense III. non sine causa in dijudicatione hujus Quæstionis fide laborare deprehenditur. Primùm enim fuit illud non Oecumenicum sive universale; sed μερικὸν sive provinciale, paucorum in Africa Episcoporum.

Deinde, etsi Jesuvitis haud invitè largimur, fuisse Concilium Carthaginense postmodum à Concilio Constantinopolitano approbatum: tamen ne sic quidem obtinent quod volunt, quin miris potius modis semetipsos implicant. Constat enim in eodem Concilio approbatos etiam esse Canones Concilij Laodicensis, ad quod nos meritò provocamus. Jam verò Carthaginensis Synodus affirmat, libros hos esse Canonicos: Laodicensis autem non modò negat eos esse Canonicos, sed omninò etiam in Ecclesia legi prohibet. Rursus idem Constantinopolitanum Concilium Canones Apostolorum, ut nunc quidem habentur, probavit, in quibus tres Macchabæorum libri, in Canonicis ponuntur, cum tamen Carthaginensis Synodus duos tantùm agnoscat, & sapientiæ, Judith, atqꝫ Tobiæ libri eodem in Canone omninò prætermittantur. Viderint ergò Jesuvitæ, num Concilio huic Constantinopolitano tutò credere possint, cum tres sibi invicem contradictoriè oppositos Canones nobis proponat. Neque effugij locus patet, ut fortè oggerant Jesuvitæ, in antiquiore Canone pauciores: in recentiore plures libros proptereà approbari, quia tùm demùm Ecclesiæ placuerit, de reliquis suum proferre judicium. Cur enim, obsecro, Laodicensis & Carthaginensis Synodi Macchabæorum tertium omittunt, semel in Canonem relatum, si ista inter se consentiunt, & vera sunt omnia? Quid? quod post Constantinopolitanum quoq; Concilium qui vixerunt Doctores, neque pauci, neque contemnendi, hos tamen libros non agnoscunt, neque hujus Concilij autoritate se constringi patiuntur. Johannes certe Damascenus non plures, quàm viginti duos Veteris Testamenti libros enumerat, eos videlicet, qui sunt in Canone Hebræo: Librum Sapientiæ & Ecclesiasticum laudat quidem, sed inter Canonicos non reponit. Quam ipsam sententiam tenet etiam Hugo de S. Victore, cujus verba suprà propos. 5. Orth. recitavimus: ut & alter Hugo Cardinalis Carrensis, de Apocryphis scribens, Tales libros recipit Ecclesia non ad probationem fidei: sed ad morum instructionem. Idem censuit Nicolaus Lyranus, sic scribens sub initium commentariorum in libros Apocryphos: Postquàm auxiliante Deo scripsi super libros sacræ scripturæ Canonicos, ejusdem confisus auxilio super alios intendo scribere, qui non sunt de Canone, scilicet Liber Sapientiæ, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobias & Libri Macchabæorum: Horum enim autoritas ad probandum ea, quæ in contentionem veniunt, minùs idonea reputatur. Meræ proindè nugæ sunt, cum à Luthero & ejus asseclis, libros istos à Canone scripturarum dispunctos esse, vociferantur: eò quòd Pontificiorum dogmata pleraque ex ijs confirmari queant, uti scribit Campianus Jesuita in decodo decem rationum. Diversum enim & jam modo, & suprà propositione 4. & 5. Orth. ex Origene, Eusebio lib. 5. cap. 25. ex Cyrillo, ex Synopsi Athanasij, ex Nazianzeno, Ruffino sive Cypriano, Hieronymo, Epiphanio, & alijs quamplurimis demonstratum fuit. Quid? quod ex hac ipsa exceptione, causæ Jesuiticæ desperata malignitas ultrò patet. Quia enim fidei suæ principia è libris Canonicis stabilire se haud posse, intelligunt, mox ad libros Apocryphos miseri confugiunt, quorum in Ecclesia & fuit & erit imposterum perpetuò ambigua fides.

Cæterùm cum in hac Controversia de libris Canonicis B. Lutherum nostrasque Ecclesias hodie variorum & quidem atrocissimorum criminum ac errorum accuset gens Jesuitica: operæ pretium fuerit, ad præcipuas illas accusationes, breviter quidem, sed quod res est, respondere.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: I. The Jesuit accusation

I. The Jesuit accusation.

In the beginning, however, Robert Bellarmine, in book 1 of 'On the Word of God', chapter 5, accuses the blessed Luther, because in his Table Talk, under the title 'On the Patriarchs and Prophets', he affirms that he does not believe that everything in the history of Job happened as it is narrated in the book of Job: And again, under the title 'On the books of the Old and New Testament', that the book of Job is as it were the argument of a fable, for the purpose of proposing an example of patience.

But in order to respond more accurately to this accusation, which is indeed sufficiently grave and insulting to a canonical book, it must first be observed what is to be determined concerning that volume of Luther's table talks, and that without prejudice to anyone. We, however, think that they themselves That our adversaries will easily concede to us that many excellent things, and things most worthy of reading, are contained in that volume, which not even they themselves, however much they may desire it, would dare to criticize. But then, that those things which were properly Luther's Table Talk to his intimates could always be accurately observed and recorded, is by no means consistent with the truth: a fact that anyone will easily grant who considers what a variety of conversation is accustomed to be in even the most modest—I do not say more formal banquets—but daily lunches and dinners. Then we challenge the Jesuits themselves: would they permit all their own table talk to be recorded and published without their knowledge? Nay, if this were to happen, and something ambiguous or abhorrent to their own public Confession were to occur, would they not constantly appeal to the writings and doctrine publicly set forth by themselves, and would they not wish for those private conversations to be judged not by their public Confession or doctrine, but rather for their public Confession or doctrine to be judged by those private conversations? Why, therefore, should our Luther not enjoy the same right, that judgment concerning his doctrine should be rendered from the writings published by himself? For far be it from us to establish that that volume of Luther's Table Talk holds the same authority among us as his other writings. But to respond in the second place to the accusation itself, Luther's words regarding the first charge are as follows: I think that Job lived in the time of Solomon, and I hold his book to be a true history; but that all things happened and were done in this way, I do not believe. I think, however, that some good, pious, and learned man reduced these things into this order, the book itself having been written in the time of Solomon. For at that time many prudent and holy men delighted in the writing of histories. When these words of Luther are observed more accurately, it becomes plain that a manifold crime of falsehood is committed by the Jesuit. For first, he maliciously omits that Luther acknowledges the Book of Job as a true history. Then, the Jesuit maliciously adapts to the narration and truth of the events themselves what Luther intends to be understood concerning the commemoration of Job's disputation with his friends: for no logic of consequence holds: Luther maintains that those discourses were not held in the same order in which they were written down, but that the summary of them was reduced into a certain order by someone else; therefore, Luther doubted the truth of the matter itself, and consequently maintained that Job never lived among men, nor that his book should be held among the Canonical scriptures.

Thirdly, when Luther in another place warns that the transformation of the events truly performed in the history of Job is such that it can be compared with the plot of some fable: the Jesuit perverts this, claiming that Luther maintained that the Book of Job is the plot of a fable; it is truly something else and far different: that something can, because of some similarity, be compared with the plot of a comedy or fable; and that it is something else to be a fable or comedy. The former does not remove the truth of the matter and history, as the latter does. But that Luther maintained that the history of Job could be compared with the plot of some comedy, that was done both because of the distinct turns of the speaking characters, and also because of the diverse acts of the history itself which it contains, and finally because of that happy catastrophe which the history of Job finally contains.

Finally, that Luther maintained that the history of Job was reduced into that order in which it exists today by some pious person in the time of Solomon: the compiler of the table talk understood this most viciously, as if Luther maintained that Job himself lived in the time of Solomon: although he himself, in a marginal gloss to the first chapter of Job, testifies in express words that he accedes to that opinion which maintains that Job was Jobab, king of Edom, Gen. 36:33, namely near Arabia Felix, because the Sabeans rush upon him.

Latin:

I. Ἔγκλημα Jesuiticum.

INitiò autem Robertus Bellarminus libr. 1. de Verbo Dei cap. 5. accusat B. Lutherum, quòd in convivialibus sermonibus, Titulo de Patriarchis & Prophetis affirmatit, de historia Jobi se non credere, omnia ita esse gesta, ut in libro Jobi narrantur: Et rursum tit. de libris Veteris & Novi Testamenti, Librum Job esse veluti fabulæ argumentum, ad proponendum patientiæ exemplum.

Sed ut ad hoc ἔγκλημα satis profectò grave, & in librum Canonicum contumeliosum, accuratiùs respondeamus, initiò sub observationem venit, quid de volumine illo sermonum convivialium Lutheri sit statuendum, idque sine cujusdam præjudicio. Existimamus autem ipsos Adversarios facilè nobis concessuros, multa præclara maximeque lectu digna illo volumine contineri, quæ, ne ipsi quidem, ut cupiant maximè, ausint reprehendere. Deinde verò, quinam propriè fuerint Sermones Lutheri in mensa ad familiares, illos semper accuratè observari & excipi posse, vero minimè est consentaneum: id quòd facilè largietur, qui, quæ in modestissimis etiam, non dico convivijs solennioribus, sed prandijs atque cœnis quotidianis, sermonum soleat esse varietas, animadvertit. Tùm ad ipsos Jesuuvitas provocamus, utrum permissuri sint, ut ipsis insciis omnes eorum sermones conviviales excipiantur & publicentur: Quin imò, si hoc fieret, & aliquid ambiguum, aut ab ipsorum publica Confessione abhorrens, occurreret: an non ad scripta & doctrinam à seipsis publicè propositam, constanter provocarent: neque ex Sermonibus convivialibus, Confessionem sive doctrinam suam publicam: sed potiùs ex hac, sermones illos privatos, vellent dijudicari. Quidni proindè eodem jure gauderet Lutherus noster, ut ex scriptis à seipso publicatis, de doctrinâ ipsius judicium feratur. Nam ut volumen illud Sermonum convivialium Lutheri, eandem apud nos autoritatem, cum reliquis ipsius scriptis, obtineat, absit ut statuamus. Sed ut secundo loco ad ipsam accusationem respondeamus, verba Lutheri, quoad prius ἔγκλημα, sic habent: Existimo Jobum tempore Salomonis vixisse, & librum ejus statuo veram historiam esse: sed quod omnia sic acciderint & gesta sint, non credo. Existimo autem bonum quendam, pium & doctum virum, in hunc ea ordinem redegisse, ipsumķ librum Salomonis tempore scriptum. Illo enim tempore multi prudentes & sancti viri, delectati sunt scriptione historiarum. His verbis Lutheri accuratiùs observatis, multiplex crimen falsi, à Jesuuvita committi planum evadit. Primùm enim malitiosè omittit, quòd Lutherus Librum Jobi pro vera historia agnoscit. Deinde, quæ de commemoratione disputationis Jobi cum amicis intelligi vult Lutherus, ea ad ipsam rerum gestarum narrationem ac veritatem malitiosè Jesuuvita accommodat: Neque enim ulla militat ratio Consequentiæ: Lutherus statuit, non eodem ordine, quo conscripti sunt, sermones illos esse habitos, sed summam illorum ab alio quodam in certum ordinem esse redactam; Ergò Lutherus dubitavit de ipsa rei veritate, & per consequens statuit Jobum nunquàm vixisse inter homines, neque librum ejus in Canonicis scripturis esse habendum.

Tertiò, Quando Lutherus in altero loco admonet, eam esse rerum verè gestarum in historia Jobi admirabilem conversionem, ut cum argumento aliquo fabulæ comparati possit: Illud Jesuuvita sic depravat, statuisse Lutherum, Librium Jobi esse Fabulæ argumentum; Aliud profectò & longè diversum est: posse aliquid, propter aliquam similitudinem, comparari cum argumento quopiam Comœdiæ sive fabulæ; Aliud verò esse Fabulam sive Comœdiam. Prius illud, rei & historiæ veritatem non tollit, quemadmodum hoc posterius. Quòd verò Lutherus statuit, historiam Jobi posse comparari cum argumento alicujus Comœdiæ, factum illud est tùm propter personarum colloquentium distinctas vices: tùm etiam propter ipsius historiæ diversos actus, quos continet: tùm deniq; propter lætam illam Catastrophen, quàm tandem historia Jobi continet.

Tandem, quòd Lutherus statuit, historiam Jobi in illum ordinem, quo hodiè extat, à pio quodam, Salomonis tempore, redactum esse: illud compilator convivialium sermonum eò vitiosissimè intellexit, quasi statuerit Lutherus, ipsum Jobum tempore Salomonis vixisse: cum tamen ipsemet, in Glossa marginali ad primum caput Jobi disertis verbis testetur, se ad eam accedere sententiam, quæ Jobum statuit fuisse Jobab regem Edom Gen. 36, 33. scilicet juxta Arabiam fœlicem, quia irruunt in eum Sabæi.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: II. The Jesuitical charge

II. The Jesuitical charge.

The same Bellarmine accuses Luther in the place cited above, because in his table talk, under the title 'On the books of the Old and New Testament,' he said that the most holy author of the book which is inscribed Ecclesiastes seemed to him to be riding without boots and spurs, only in slippers, just as he himself was accustomed to do when he was still in the monastery.

But we respond at the beginning that Luther's correct and undoubted judgment can, nay must, be sought not from that volume of table talk, which Luther never saw, much less approved, but rather from the commentary on the same book of Ecclesiastes published by Luther himself: where indeed, even from the preface alone to the said Commentary, it is most evidently clear how holily and piously he felt about that book, and judged it to be a divine book, to be worn out by everyone's hands. Therefore, again, an enormous error was committed by the compiler of Luther's table talk, who affirms that those things which the Jesuit cites were said by Luther at the time when he was publishing his commentary on Ecclesiastes. For it is not to be thought that Luther wished to contradict at home those things which he had publicly proposed. And indeed it is evident from the consideration of that whole passage, that the Compiler, whoever he may have been, without judgment snatched up whatever was brought forth by Luther, and two diverse judgments of Luther, of which one was concerning the book of Ecclesiastes, the other concerning the book of Ecclesiasticus, or Sirach, badly and beyond and against the mind of Luther, accommodated to one book of Ecclesiastes: when it ought to have been accommodated to the book of Ecclesiasticus: Where indeed the thing itself speaks, that in that book is by no means detected that zeal or ardor of the Spirit of God, which is in the remaining Canonical Scriptures. What, that the Compiler himself writes, that Luther understood that simile concerning riding without boots and spurs, of that book which, in the time of the Maccabees, was collected from the library of Ptolemy Euergetes. Now indeed, that it is not the Ecclesiastes of Solomon, but Ecclesiasticus or the Siracide that is that book, the thing itself speaks. And if the Jesuit dares to deny this, we set before him as a witness Sixtus The Sienese, who in book 1 of the Bibliotheca sancta, section 2, page 26, has it thus: The grandson of Jesus, the son of Sirach, flourished while Ptolemy Euergetes was reigning, king of Egypt, in the year three thousand seven hundred from the creation of the world.

III. A Jesuit accusation.

Thirdly, Bellarmine in book 1 on the Word of God, chapter 6, the fourteenth heresy, Edmund Campion in the Ten Reasons, Duræus in his confutation of Whitaker, pages 33 and 36, and many other Jesuits accuse Luther of the heresy of the Valentinians, because he maintained that that false opinion should be abolished, that there are four Gospels: likewise that the Gospel of John is the unique, beautiful, true, and principal Gospel, and is to be preferred far and wide to the other three: so much so that even the epistles of Paul and Peter ought to be preferred far above those three Gospels, of Matthew, Mark, and Luke.

(1) I answer first, that the Jesuits are shamefully using sophistry, ignoring the point of the refutation. For Luther does not mean in his preface to the New Testament that only one historical narrative about Christ is to be admitted, and the remaining three are to be abolished, as the Jesuits slander; but he meant this: that those four narratives or histories of the four Evangelists are one single and clearly identical Gospel in terms of subject matter and purpose. Now, however, these two things differ greatly: There is only one Evangelist; and there is only one Gospel. The former Luther never and nowhere affirmed; but the latter, by the calculation of all who think correctly, Luther truly and entirely said and maintained. For as Chrysostom also writes in chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Galatians, κἂν μύριοι γράφωσιν ἐυαγγέλια, τάδε ἀυ- τὰ γράφωσιν ἓν ἔςι τὰ πολλὰ, that is: Although a thousand men write Gospels, if they write the same things, the many are one.

(2) Next, this objection fails through the sophistry of confusing the relative with the absolute. For what blessed Luther wrote relatively and by comparison, the Jesuits take absolutely. Now, in what way and respect Luther called the Gospel of John one, true, beautiful, and principal Gospel, his own words clearly show, which are as follows: In the Gospel of John and the epistles of Paul, you will not find many deeds or miracles of Christ described, but you will see excellently depicted that which is the head of the Gospel and of piety: How faith in Christ overturns and overcomes sin, death, and hell, and in their place bestows righteousness, life, and eternal salvation. For if one had to do without either the works or the words of Christ, I would by all means prefer to be ignorant of the deeds of Christ than to be deprived of his words or sermons. For the works of Christ do not profit me much, but his words give life: just as he himself said. Since, therefore, John described the deeds of Christ more briefly, but his sermons copiously in his Gospel; while the remaining Evangelists, on the contrary, explained the history of the deeds of Christ more abundantly, but do not recount his sermons as much, it should not be doubted that the Gospel of John, which among the remaining three has occupied the citadel, as it were, in delivering the saving doctrines of Christ, is to be held in the first place. In the same manner also, the epistles of Paul and Peter are to be preferred to the three remaining

Evangelists, whom they similarly excel. Thus far Luther, who is the least of all doing what the Jesuits infer, as if he wishes the first three Gospels to be abrogated: But by a comparison instituted only between the four Gospels among themselves, as also between the first three Gospels and the epistles of Paul, he shows which books excel the others regarding the principal goal which our faith has proposed to itself; and which books are to be studied especially by the pious, as those which contain and propose the foundation of our faith most of all.

Latin:

II. Ἔγκλημα Jesuvviticum.

IDem Bellarminus accusat loco jam supra citato Lutherum, quod in convivialibus sermonibus tit. de libris Veteris & Novi Testamenti, dixerit, sanctissimum illum autorem libri, qui Ecclesiastes inscribitur, sibi videri ocreis & calcaribus destitutum equitare tantùm in soccis, quemadmodum ipse soleret, cum adhuc esset in cœnobio.

Sed respondemus initiò, Lutheri judicium rectum & indubitatum non ex volumine illo sermonum convivialium, quod Lutherus nunquam vidit, nedum approbavit; sed ex commentario potiùs in eundem librum Ecclesiastem ab ipso Luthero editum peti posse, imò debere: Ubi sanè vel ex sola præfatione in dictum Commentarium evidentissimè patet, quàm sanctè & piè de illo libro senserit, & tanquàm librum divinum, omnium manibus terendum esse judicaverit. Proinde rursus à compilatore sermonum convivialium Lutheri enorme σφάλμα est commissum, quod affirmat, illa, quæ Jesuvvita citat, à Luthero dicta esse tùm cùm commentarium suum in Ecclesiasten ederet. Neque enim existimandum est, Lutherum ijs, quæ publicè proposuerat, domi controtradicere voluisse. Et profectò constat ex consideratione totius illius loci, Compilatorem, quisquis tandem fuerit, sine judicio quævis à Luthero prolata arripuisse, & diversa duo Lutheri judicia, quorum unum erat de libro Ecclesiasta, alterum de libro Ecclesiastici, sive Syrach, malè & præter ac contra mentem Lutheri, ad unum librum Ecclesiastæ accommodasse: cùm ad librum Ecclesiastici accommodari debuerit: Ubi sanè res ipsa loquitur, in illo libro minimè dedeprehendi eum zelum aut ardorem Spiritus Dei, qui est in reliquis Scripturis Canonicis. Quid, quod ipse Compilator scribit, Lutherum similitudinem illam de equitatione sine ocreis & calcaribus, de eo libro intellexisse, qui Macchabæorum tempore, ex bibliotheca Ptolomæi Evergetæ collectus sit. Jam verò non Ecclesiasten Salomonis, sed Ecclesiasticum sive Syracidem esse librum illum, res ipsa loquitur. Et si negare hoc ausit Jesuvvita, testem ipsi sistimus Sixtum Senensem qui libro 1. Bibliothecæ sanctæ, sectione 2. pag. 26. sic habet: Claruit Syracides nepos ille Jesu, regnante Ptolemæo Evergete, rege Ægypti, anno ab orbe condito ter millesimo septingentesimo.

III. ἔγκλημα Jesuvviticum.

TErtiò Bellarminus lib. 1. de Verbo DEI cap. 6. hæresi decima quarta, Edmundus Campianus in decem Rationum. Duræus in confutatione Whitakeri pag. 33. & 36. & plerique Jesuvvitæ alij accusant Lutherum hæreseως Valentinianorum, eò quòd statuerit abolendam esse illam falsam opinionem, quòd sint quatuor Evangelia : item Johannis Evangelium esse unicum, pulchrum, verum ac principale Evangelium, alijsq; tribus longè ac latè præferendum: adeò ut etiam Pauli ac Petri epistolæ longè præferri debeant tribus illis Evangelijs, Matthæi, Marci, & Lucæ.

(1) Respondeo primùm, Jesuvvitas turpiter Sophisticari περὶ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε. Neque enim hoc vult Lutherus in præfatione in Nov. Testámentum, unam tantummodo narrationem historicam de Christo esse admittendam, & reliquas tres esse abolendas, uti Jesuvvitæ criminantur: sed hoc voluit, quatuor illas narrationes sive historias quatuor Evangelistarum, unum solummodò planeque idem esse Evangelium ratione argumenti & finis. Jam verò plurimùm differunt ista duo: Unus tantùm est Evangelista: Et unum tantùm est Evangelium: prius illud nunquam & nuspiam affirmavit Lutherus: posterius verò omnium rectè sententium calculo, verè omninò dixit & statuit Lutherus. Nam ut Chrysostomus etiam scribit in cap. 1. Epistolæ ad Galatas, κἂν μύριοι γράφωσιν ἐυαγγέλια, τάδε ἀυτὰ γράφωσιν ἓν ἔςι τὰ πολλὰ id est, Quanquam mille homines scribunt Evangelia, si tamen eadem scribant, unum multa sunt.

(2) Deinde fallit hæc objectio Sophisticatione περὶ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Quod enim B. Lutherus πῆ τὶ & comparatè scripsit, illud Jesuvvitæ ἁπλῶς accipiunt. Jam verò quo pacto ac respectu Lutherus Evangelium Johannis nominaverit unum, verum, pulchrum, præcipuum Evangelium, ipsiusmet verba luculenter ostendunt, quæ sic habent: In Evangelio Johannis, & Epistolis Pauli, non multa facta sive miracula Christi descripta invenies, verùm egregiè depictum videbis id, quod caput est Evangelij & pietatis: Quomodo fides in Christum, peccatum, mortem atq; inferos evertat ac superet, proq; his justitiam, vitam atq; salutem æternam largiatur. Nam si alterutro carendum esset, vel operibus, vel verbis Christi, nodis omnibus mallem ignorare Christi facta, quàm ejus verbis sive concionibus privari. Non enim multùm Christi opera mihi prosunt, sed verba ejus dant vitam: quemadmodum & ipse dixit. Cum igitur Iohannes Christi facta brevius; Conciones verò ejus copiosè suo Evangelio descripserit: reliqui verò Evangelistæ contrà, uberius historiam factorum Christi explicarint, sermones verò ejus non ita multos recenseant, dubitari non debet, quin Johannis Evangelium, quod inter reliqua tria, tanquam arcem occupavit, salutaribus Christi doctrinis tradendis, primo loco sit habendum. Ad eundem etiam modum, Epistolæ Pauli & Petri tribus reliquis Evange-

listis, quos similiter excellunt, sunt præponendæ. Hactenus Lutherus, qui minimè omnium hoc agit, quod Jesuvvitæ colligunt, quasi prima tria Evangelia velit abrogata: Sed comparatione tantùm inter quatuor Evangelia ad se invicẽ, sut & inter tria prima Evangelia & Epistolas Pauli institutâ, ostendit qui nam libri reliquis antecellant, quoad principalem scopum, quem fides nostra sibi habet propositum : quique libri à pijs potissimùm sint evolvendi, ut qui fundamentum fidei nostræ vel maximè contineant & proponant.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: IV. A Jesuit accusation

IV. A Jesuit accusation.

Edmund Campion in his letter to the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge, as also in his first Reason: Duræus in his Confutation of Whitaker: Francis Coster in his Enchiridion, page 64, and many others accuse Luther because he blasphemously called the Epistle of James swollen, dry, contentious, straw-like, and not worthy of an Apostolic spirit. But at the beginning, the Jesuits commit the crime of falsehood. For it is nowhere evident from his own writings that the Epistle of James was marked by Luther with these insulting epithets. Then again, the adversaries use sophistry with the fallacy of confusing the relative with the absolute: For if Luther's words in the preface to the New Testament, published in the year '25, are examined, it will be clear that these things are said by Luther only by way of comparison, namely, that this epistle, when compared with those of Paul to the Romans, Galatians, Ephesians, and also with the first epistle of Peter, is straw-like. But when he no longer considers the Epistle of James comparatively, but in itself, certainly in the same preface Luther confesses that, considered simply, it is good and useful: saying, this epistle, although rejected by the ancients, I nevertheless praise and hold as useful and convenient, if only for this reason, that it brings forward nothing of human doctrine and strongly urges the law of God. But to give my own opinion about it, yet without prejudice, I think it is not by any Apostle. Luther immediately adds some reasons for this opinion of his.

Thirdly, if this charge is indeed such, the adversaries ought to have imputed it not to Luther in the preface already cited, but to the Fathers: Eusebius certainly calls it spurious, saying: It must be known that the Epistle which is attributed to James is spurious ἰςέον ὡς νοθεύεται: since not many of the ancients have made mention of it. Jerome in his Catalogue asserts that the Epistle of James was published by some other person under his name. Erasmus in the preface to Volume 4 of Jerome writes thus: The ancients affirmed that the Epistle of James was published by some other person under his name, although little by little in the progress of time it obtained a certain authority. Following in whose footsteps Dr. Luther, in his booklet on the Babylonian Captivity, writes thus: I omit that many very probably assert that this Epistle is not of the Apostle James, nor worthy of an apostolic spirit. Nor does it stand in the way that Eusebius writes that the Epistles of James and Jude were publicly received in very many churches, δεδημοσιευμένας. for not whatever is publicly received in certain Churches is immediately also Canonical: Then, if received in very many Churches: Therefore not in all. Thirdly, it is not in the power of later Churches to endow any book with Canonical authority, concerning which the Apostolic Church, and the primitive one which followed it, was in the greatest doubt. Fourthly, the same Eusebius in book 3, chapter 3, affirms concerning the book of Hermes also, that it was publicly received and read in certain eastern Churches: But not even the Jesuits themselves attribute Canonical authority to it on that account: Indeed, Eusebius himself in book 3, chapter 25, rejects it among the spurious and supposititious.

Latin:

IV. ἔγκλημα Jesuvviticum.

EDmundus Campianus in Epistola ad Academias Oxoniensem & Cantabrigiensem : ut & Ratione primâ: Duræus in Confutatione VVhitakeri: Franciscus Costerus in Enchiridio pag. 64. & plures alij accusant Lutherum, quod blasphemê latis Epistolam Jacobi nominaverit tumidam, aridam, contentiosam, stramineam, nec Apostolico spiritu dignam. Verùm initio crimen falsi committunt Jesuvvitæ. Nam his contumeliosis Epithetis Epistolam Jacobi à Luthero esse notatam, nuspiam ex ipsius scriptis patet. Deinde rursus sophisticantur Adversarij fallacia περὶ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: Si enim Lutheri verba pæfatione super Nov. Testament. Anno 25. edita, inspiciantur, patebit ista à Luthero tantùm per comparationem dici, quòd videlicet collata hæc Epistola cum Paulinis illis ad Romanos, Galatas, Ephesios, itemque cum priore Petri epistola, sit straminea. Quando vero Epistolam Jacobi non comparatè amplius, sed in se considerat, certè in eadem præfatione fatetur Lutherus, eam simpliciter consideratam, bonam atq; utilem esse: Epistolam hanc, inquiens, quamvis rejectam à veteribus, tamen laudo, & pro utili ac commoda habeo, vel ob hanc causam, quòd planè nihil humanæ doctrinæ afferat, & legem Dei fortiter urgeat. Verùm ut meam de illa sententiam feram, extra tamen præjudicium existimo, nullius Apostoli esse. Cujus suæ sententiæ aliquot rationes mox subjicit Lutherus.

Tertiò, crimen hoc si modò tale est, non Luthero in præfat. jam citata, sed Patribus imputare debebant Adversarij: Eusebius certè adulterinam eam nominat: Sciendum, inquiens, eam Epistolam, quæ Jacobo affingitur, esse adulterinam ἰςέον ὡς νοθεύεται: quandoquidem non multi Veteres ejus meminerunt. Hieronymus in Catalogo, Epistolam Jacobi ab alio quodam sub ej9 nomine editam esse asserit. Erasmus præfat. Tom. 4. in Hier. sic scribit: Jacobi Epistolam Veteres ab alio quopiam illius nomine editam affirmabant, licèt paulatim progressu temporis obtinuerit autoritatem quandam. Quorum vestigia secutus D. Lutherus, in libello de captivitate Babylonica sic scribit: Omitto quod hanc Epistolam non esse Apostoli Jacobi, nec Apostolico spiritu dignam, multi valdè probabiliter asserant. Neq; obstat quod Euseb. scribit, Jacobi & Judæ Epistolas in plurimis Ecclesijs publicè receptas esse, δεδημοσιευμένας. enim non quicquid in quibusdam Ecclesiis publicè recipitur, statim etiam est Canonicum: Deinde, si in plurimis Ecclesiis recepta: Ergò non in omnibus. Tertiò, non in potestate posteriorum Ecclesiarum situm est, Canonica autoritate ullum aliquem donare librum, de quo Ecclesia Apostolica, & hanc secuta primitiva vel maximè dubitavit. Quartò, idem Eusebius lib. 3. cap. 3. de libro etiam Hermetis affirmat, quòd in quibusdam orientalibus Ecclesiis fuerit publicè receptus & lectus: Sed neque ipsi Jesuuitæ, propterea Canonicam autoritatem illi tribuunt: Quin ipse Eusebius libr. 3. cap. 25. inter nothos & supposititios eum rejicit.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Question II Proposition I. Positive

On the Authority of Canonical Scripture.

PROPOSITION I. Positive.

The Canonical books of both Testaments have their own authority, and that supreme, and clearly ἀνυπεύθυνον, as if exempt from laws, superior to all demonstration, not from the Church, but from themselves: as much in relation to us, as in respect to themselves.

Exposition.

This proposition is two-fold: such that the first member defines negatively that the authority of Scripture does not depend upon the Church: which is proved by the following arguments.

I. Every foundation is prior to its building, and every Measure is prior to that which is measured: But Holy Scripture is the foundation of the Church, and the measure of all Ecclesiastical doctrine.

Therefore Holy Scripture is prior to the Church: and consequently, it cannot finally borrow its true and infallible authority from the judgment and public testimony of the Church, which, with respect to the antiquity of Scripture, is many centuries later.

The evidence of the major proposition shines forth so clearly from common notion, that in all disciplines, that Aristotelian axiom has long since found a place: πᾶν τ' μέτρον τῷ μετρητῷ πρότερον ὀξί: Every measure is prior to that which is measured.

The minor proposition is written. For the divine Apostle, a witness greater than any exception, infers thus: Eph. 2:20 and 21. You have been built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure grows into a holy temple in the Lord,

And in 1 Cor. 3:10. According to the grace of GOD, which is given to me, as a skilled Architect I have laid the foundation: But no one can lay another foundation, besides that which is laid, JESUS CHRIST.

Relying on the evidence of these testimonies, for the unshakeable certainty of our consequence we infer in two ways: First, the Word of God is the foundation of the Church: Therefore the Word is prior and more ancient than the Church itself. Then, all authority of the Church rests upon the Word of God. Therefore the authority of the Word of God or Holy Scripture does not depend upon the Church: But rather the authority of the latter depends solely upon Scripture.

II. Argument. Just as Christ stands in relation to authority, as far as we are concerned: so also does Canonical Scripture stand: But indeed Christ has authority both in respect of himself and in respect of us, not from the testimony of any man, or of the Church or of a Council, but from himself. Therefore the condition of Canonical Scripture is the same.

The connection of the major premise is clear. 1. Because Holy Scripture is nothing other than the voice of Christ the Savior himself. 2. Because Holy Canonical Scripture is just as much the foundation of the Church as Christ is, Eph. 2:20 & 21, 1 Cor. 3:10. For these two foundations are not ἀντιφατικῶς or contradictorily opposed to one another: but they are συνάλληλα or subordinate: for Holy Scripture is the foundation of the Church, insofar as it is the voice of Christ the Savior, its primary Author: And conversely, Christ is not the foundation of the Church except through Scripture. For through this alone is Christ made known to the Church: in such a way, indeed, that Christ is the foundation of the Church, properly and of himself, as he who alone is that cornerstone, or the head and soul of the Church: but Scripture as the Instrument, which Christ alone uses in assembling the structure of the Church. The evidence of the minor premise is clear from that Aphorism of the Savior, John 5:34. I do not receive testimony from man: which is of the same value as if Christ had said: I excel in my authority so completely in every way that, to acquire authority, I am in no need at all of the testimony of any man. Nor does that fact stand in the way, that we read that John the Baptist bore testimony to Christ, that he is the Messiah. For by this reasoning he did not impart to Christ an authority which he had lacked before: but only commended Christ, who from himself and through himself sufficiently declared that he was the Messiah. If the Jesuits would admit this same thing concerning the Church, namely that it does not impart authority to the Church, as far as we are concerned, but merely declares by its testimony what kind and how great an authority Holy Scripture obtains, both in respect of us and in respect of itself from itself, and in itself: then a great and perhaps not the least part of this controversy would be removed. For from this, no more could be inferred than this: Just as Christ was able to demonstrate from himself that he was the Messiah: so Holy Scripture can from itself convince us that it is the Word of God. And again: Just as Christ did not receive authority from the testimony of John: So Canonical Scripture is commended by the Church, not so that it may receive any authority from it, but only so that it may become better known to men. And it especially deserves observation, that Christ in the same chapter v. 36 says: I have a greater testimony than that of John was: Where among those other greater testimonies he expressly also mentions, The testimony of Scripture. Whence I conclude thus: If the testimony of Scripture concerning Christ was more certain and evident than the testimony of John: then certainly the authority of that same Scripture will also be more certain and evident than the authority of the Church. But the former is true. Therefore also the latter. The reason for the consequence is this, That even the Jesuits themselves do not yet dare to affirm that the judgment and testimony of the Church is more certain and evident than the judgment of John the Baptist. Now, however, Christ subordinates his testimony to the judgment of Scripture, Therefore.

III. Argument: What was the reason for the unwritten word, in the Church of the Patriarchs of the Old Testament, with respect to Authority as regards us: the same is today the reason for the written word. And yet the unwritten word then obtained its far greatest authority, even as regards us, not from the authority of the Church, but from itself. Therefore neither today will the written word borrow its authority, as regards us, from the Church. The Adversaries will hardly deny the major premise, unless perhaps they wish to trifle, that the authority of the divine word as regards us was one thing in the old [Testament]: but is another now in the New Testament. To whom, however, although they affirm this, we will not believe, until they have given it demonstrated evidently.

As regards the reason for the minor premise, it is manifest that the authority of the divine word at that time was not even built upon the testimony or supreme judgment of the Patriarchs: but that it had it in itself, as if imprinted, and showed to all from itself the most certain arguments of its divinity. For as for the fact that some of the Jesuits object, that the elders or prelates of that Church commended the word of GOD to men by their own voice, and thus procured authority for it among men: that is indeed altogether vain and trifling. For it is asked, by whose Church's persuasion those very Patriarchs received the word of GOD, and believed it to be endowed with divine authority? While the Adversaries cannot explain this to eternity, they must confess that those Patriarchs and prelates of that most ancient Church did not derive the clearly divine authority of the divine word from the testimony of anyone, whether Church or Council: but rather that the word of GOD itself testified clearly from itself concerning its own authority. If they answer that there was no need for the judgment of the Church because God spoke ἀμέσως (immediately) with the Patriarchs: we certainly accept the answer, and from there we evidently infer against the Adversaries, that neither today is there need for such a public judgment of the Church to procure authority for the Scriptures, because God speaks with us today, although not ἀμέσως (immediately): yet mediately, not indeed through the Church, but through the θεοπνεύστους (God-breathed) Scriptures: and the Holy Spirit testifies today in us concerning the divine authority of the scriptures: according to that of John 1 Epistle chapter 5, 6. It is the Spirit that testifies, that is, that the Prophetic and Apostolic doctrine is the truth.

Nor do the Adversaries profit anything when they wish to derive a reason for some disparity from the fact that then in the ancient Church the Word of God was not committed to letters: For 1. this writing is an Accident, and changes nothing at all of the Substance and authority of the divine word. 2. If for that reason the Word of God needs the judgment of the Church, as regards us: because it is now committed to letters: it would follow that it is today of less authority than it was formerly: which is enormously absurd: since it simply fights against the dignity and excellence of the New Testament. 3. The Jesuit argument is inverted in this manner: If then when the Word of GOD was not yet written, it did not have its authority as regards us from the Church: much less will it have it today, after it has now been committed to letters. The reason for the consequence is this: Because that which is not written seems to stand in much greater need of some extrinsic testimony or judgment: since it is more easily exposed to both oblivion and contempt than that which, produced in letters, is always exposed to the eyes and senses of all, and can be read, weighed, and judged by all.

IV. Argument can be such. If the Church is born from the word of GOD, or Holy Scripture, as from an incorruptible seed, it cannot be otherwise than that the Word of GOD is prior to the Church, and consequently the authority of Holy Scripture precedes the Church and all its judgment. But the former is true. Therefore this latter is also established.

The connection of the major premise shines with its own light. For that the seed is prior to that which is born from it, no one unless a blockhead would deny: And again: That the seed has its goodness from the fruit born from it, no one unless a fool would affirm. Now before the Church begins to exist, its seed or foundation must necessarily precede: unless through a notable ἄῤῥωσίαν τῆς διανοίας (sickness of the mind) one wishes to feign that the fruit is prior to its seed, or which is the same, that the building is prior to its foundation: or that the building gives τὸ εἶναι (the being) to its foundation, so that it may indeed be a foundation: Or that the fruit gives to its seed, so that it may be such as it ought to be. Who does not see that all these things are more absurd than the most absurd?

The truth of the minor proposition, against Stapleton's insipid exception, by which he trifles that Scripture is posterior to the Church as regards our acceptance, can be demonstrated in many ways. For first, the original foundation of the Church after the fall of the first-formed did not become known to men except through the word of promise, concerning the seed that would crush the head of the serpent. Gen. 3, 15. Next, the procreative cause of all the faithful, and thus of the whole true Church of Christ, is none other than the word of GOD alone: so indeed that judgment ought to be made from this concerning the quality of the Church: but not from the Church concerning the approval of the word: by the power of that Apostolic Aphorism 1 Pet. 1. 23. You have been regenerated not from corruptible seed, but incorruptible through the Word of the living GOD, and remaining forever. Thirdly, this very thing is clear from the consequent Absurdity. For unless they are willing to concede that Holy Scripture is prior to the Church, even as regards our approval: they must necessarily concede that that Church, by whose judgment concerning the Holy Scriptures one must stand, must be sought outside the scriptures, and consequently is not the Church of Christ, but I know not whose other synagogue, whether of man or of the Devil. For if the Church is the sheepfold of Christ: If also the sheep hear and follow the voice of their shepherd: But Christ does not address his sheep outside of scripture: It follows necessarily that Scripture is both prior to the Church and superior, so that it may be recognized as the Church of Christ.

4. Fourthly: The Church is nothing other than a gathering of the faithful: But faith is born from the word heard: Therefore the Word of GOD, or Holy Scripture, is not only a mark, but also an efficient cause, or constitutive principle of the Church: so that it has its τὸ εἶναι [being] from Scripture alone.

The fifth and final argument is provided by the consensus of Orthodox antiquity. For thus Ambrose, book 1 de fide to Gratian, chapter 5: Do not, Arian, estimate divine things from our sayings or writings: but believe divine things where you do not find human ones: Divine things, therefore, are proven by themselves, they are believed by themselves.

Thus Bede on Psalm 8: The writings of the divine books are the foundation both of the universal Church and of individual churches, by which they themselves are strengthened and sustained, like a building from its foundation.

Augustine in Genesis ad lit: The authority of scripture is greater than all the capacity of human genius can comprehend: truly we ought to confess the inviolable authority of the sacred letters. And let these things said concerning the former member of our proposition, and that a negative one, suffice.

The latter, affirmative part of the proposition asserts that Holy Scripture has supreme authority from itself, both with respect to itself and with respect to us. The truth of the assertion is first most evidently apparent from those four arguments which we have just now treated.

1. For if Scripture does not borrow its authority from the Church with respect to us: then it is necessary that it has it from itself. For a third [option] cannot be given.

2. Then the truth of this assertion is apparent from those singular privileges, or ἀξιώμασι [axioms], which Holy Scripture enjoys, and which it keeps peculiar to itself: such as that 1. It has as its author GOD himself, the Holy Spirit, by whose instinct it was written. 2 Tim. 3:16, 2 Pet. 1:21. Then, that the same Holy Spirit, in recording Scripture, used the ministry of Prophets and Apostles: namely, those men whom GOD adorned with divine testimonies, that they could not err in writing, as Augustine speaks, Epist. 19 to Jerome.

3. Thirdly, that the nature of the things which the Holy Scriptures hand down is clearly divine and heavenly.

4. Finally, that Christ and the Apostles, and indeed the entire Orthodox Church, in refuting heresies, has always appealed to Holy Scripture alone, as an infallible and supreme judge: as will be expressly shown in the fifth question. Let a single passage of Augustine suffice in this place, which exists in book 2 de Baptismo contra Donatistas, c. 3: It is proper to holy Canonical Scripture that whatever is written in it is

true and right: but the letters of Bishops, such as those of Cyprian, and the Councils themselves, not only those which are held in individual provinces: but even plenary and general ones, often have that which is to be corrected. From which passage of Augustine I conclude against the Jesuits thus: All the words of Holy Scripture are always words of truth: On the contrary, the words of the Church and of Councils are often words of Error. By as much, therefore, as undoubted truth excels uncertain and fallible assertions: by so much is the authority of Scripture greater and more excellent than the authority of the Church. Furthermore, beyond merit, the Jesuits in this place scourge our Churches, as if they were derogating from all authority of the Church whatsoever. For first, no reason of consequence holds: According to the Lutherans, the authority of Scripture is greater than that of the Church, even with respect to us. Therefore, the Lutherans derogate from all authority of the Church whatsoever. For from the negation of one degree to the negation of another, the inference is faulty. Furthermore, how august an authority we grant to the Church is evident from the fact that we assign to it many excellent duties regarding Scripture, while it bears witness to the Scriptures or Canonical books: while it distinguishes supposititious and adulterine writings from true and genuine Prophetic and Apostolic scriptures: while it interprets the sacred Scriptures, and from the collation of more obscure passages with clearer ones, investigates and proposes their true and genuine sense: while finally, with great care and diligence, it strives to disseminate and propagate the purer sense of the scriptures far and wide. These certainly sufficiently ample duties of the Church are so far from being extenuated by us in words, or plainly denied, that we hold it most firmly persuaded that the entire hinge and sum of our salvation turns upon this dignity of the Church: although we believe that it by no means follows from this, as the Jesuits ignorantly infer, that the authority of the Church is greater than that of the Scriptures.

By the same reasoning, this proposition of ours does not obstruct the lights of the Holy Fathers, who certainly themselves wished their writings to be read on no other condition than that they be measured against the rule of the written Word, and only then approved if they agreed with it. And indeed, the voices of Cyprian, Augustine, Jerome, Chrysostom, and others cannot be unknown in this matter, by which they testify that they submit themselves and all their works to the judgment of the written Word: and this so clearly that Gratian, the compiler of Canon Law, did not hesitate to refer that classic passage of Augustine, from Epistle 19 to Jerome, and from book 2, chapter 3, on Baptism against the Donatists, into the Pontifical Law itself, as is evident from distinction 9, Canons 5 and 8. I have learned to defer this honor and fear only to those books of the scriptures which are now called Canonical, that I most firmly believe that no author of them erred in writing anything: but I read others in such a way that, however much they may excel in holiness and doctrine, I do not think it true because they thought so; but because they were able to persuade me through other authors, or canonical or probable reasons, that they do not deviate from the truth. From Epistle 19 to Jerome.

Item, book 2, chapter 3, on Baptism against the Donatists. Who does not know that the Holy Canonical Scripture, both of the Old and New Testament, is contained within its own certain limits, and is so preferred to all subsequent letters of bishops that it is impossible to doubt or dispute concerning it, whether whatever is established to have been written in it is true or right: but that the letters of bishops, which have been written or are written after the Canon was confirmed, may be reproved by the discourse of anyone perhaps wiser and more expert in that matter, and by the more weighty authority and the learning of other bishops, and by Councils, if anything in them has perhaps deviated from the truth.

Latin:

De Scripturæ Canonicæ Autoritate.

PROPOSITIO I. θετικὴ.

Libri Canonici utriusque Testamenti, suam habent autoritatem, eámque summam, ac planè ἀνυπεύθυνον, quasi legib9 solutam, omni demonstratione superiorem non ab Ecclesia, sed ex seipsis: tàm quoad nos, quàm respectu sui.

Ἔκθεσις.

Propositio hæc est bimembris: ita ut prius membrum negatè definiat, Autoritatem Scripturæ non pendere ab Ecclesia: id quod sequentibus probatur argumentis.

I. Omne fundamentum prius est suo ædificio, & omnis Mensura prior est suo mensurato: Atqui Scriptura Sacra est fundamentum Ecclesiæ, & mensura omnis doctrinæ Ecclesiasticæ.

Ergò Scriptura Sacra prior est Ecclesia: & per consequens, autoritatem suam veram ac infallibilem, no demùm mutuæri potest ab Ecclesiæ judicio ac testimonio publico, quod respectu antiquitatis Scripturæ, multis seculis est posterius.

Majoris propositionis evidentia è communi notione usque adeò perspicuè elucet, ut in omnibus disciplinis, jampridem Aristotelicum illud axioma locum invenerit: πᾶν τ' μέτρον τῷ μετρητῷ πρότερον ὀξί: Omnis mensura mensurato prior est.

Minor propositio est ἔγ[..]φ@. Divus enim Apostolus, testis omni exceptione major, sic infert: Ephes. 2, 20. & 21. Superstructi estis super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, ipso summo angulari lapide existente Jesu Christo, in quo omnis structura crescit in templum sanctum Domino,

Et in 1. Cor. 3, 10. Secundùm gratiam DEI, quæ data est mihi, ut peritus Architectus fundamenmentum posui: Fundamentum autem aliud nemo potest ponere, præter id, quod positum est, JESUS CHRISTVS.

Quorum testimoniorum evidentiâ freti, pro consequentiæ nostræ immota certitudine dupliciter inferimus: Primò, Verbum Dei est fundamentum Ecclesiæ: Ergò Verbum prius & antiquius est ipsa Ecclesiâ. Deinde, omnis Ecclesiæ autoritas innititur Verbo DEI. Ergò Verbi DEI sive Scripturæ Sacræ autoritas non pendet ab Ecclesiâ: Sed hujus potius autoritas, dependet unicè à Scriptura.

II. Argumentum. Quemadmodum se habet Christus ratione autoritatis, quoad nos: ita se quoque habet Scriptura Canonica: Atqui verò Christus tùm respectu sui, tùm respectu nostri autoritatem habet, non ex cujusquam hominis, sive Ecclesiæ aut Concilij testimonio, sed ex seipso. Ergò eadem est conditio Scripturæ Casonicæ.

Majoris connexum patet. 1. Quia Scriptura sacra nihil est aliud, quàm vox ipsius Christi Servatoris. 2. Quia Scriptura Sacra Canonica æquè est fundamentum Ecclesiæ, atq; est Christus Ephes 2, 20. & 21. 1. Cor. 3, 10. Neque enim duo hæc fundamenta ἀντιφατικῶς sive contradictoriè sibi invicem sunt opposita: sed sunt συνάλληλα sive subordinata: Scriptura enim sacra est fundamentum Ecclesiæ, quatenus ea est vox Christi Servatoris, Autoris ejus primarij: Et vice versa, Christus non est fundamentum Ecclesiæ, nisi per Scripturam. Per hanc enim solam Christus innotescit Ecclesiæ: ita quidem, ut Christus sit fundamentum Ecclesiæ, propriè & per se, ut qui solus est lapis ille angularis, sive caput & anima Ecclesiæ: Scriptura verò tanquam Organum, quo solo Christus in coagmentanda Ecclesiæ structura utitur. Minoris evidentia liquet ex Aphorismo illo Servatoris, Johan. 5, 34. Ego ab homine testimonium non accipio: qui ejusdem est valoris, ac si dixisset Christus: Ego meâ autoritate ita undiquaque excello, ut ad comparandam autoritatem, nullius prorsus hominis testimonio indigeam. Neque obstat illud, quòd Johannem Baptistam legimus Christo perhibuisse Testimonium, quòd sit Messias. Neque enim hac ratione Autoritatem ipse Christo, quâ antè destitutus fuerit, impertijt: sed tantùm Christum, qui ex se & per se satis declarabat, Messiam se esse, commendavit. Quod ipsum, si admitterent Jesuwaitæ de Ecclesia, nempè hanc non impertire autoritatem Ecclesiæ, quò ad nos, sed suo duntaxat testimonio declarare, qualem & quantam autoritatem Scriptura Sacra, tàm respectu nostri, quàm respectu sui ex se, & in seipsa obtineat: tùm magna & fortè non postrema pars hujus controversiæ esset sublata. Hinc enim non plus posset inferri, quàm istud: Quemadmodum Christus ex se potuit demonstrare, se esse Messiam: sic Scriptura Sacra ex se nobis fidem facere potest, se esse Verbum DEI. Et rursus: Quemadmodum CHRISTVS ex testimonio Johannis non autoritatem accepit: Ita Scriptura Canonica commendatur ab Ecclesia, non ut aliquam autoritatem inde accipiat, sed tantùm ut hominibus magis innotescat. Et observationem vel maximè meretur, quòd Christus eodem capite v. 36. ait: Ego habeo majus testimonium, quàm fuit Johannes illud: Ubi inter reliqua illa majora testimonia expressè etiam refert, Testimonium Scripturæ. Unde sic colligo: Si Scripturæ testimonium de Christo certius & evidentiùs fuit, testimonio Johannis: utíq; ejusdem etiam Scripturæ autoritas certior erit ac evidentior, autoritate Ecclesiæ. At prius verum. Ergò & posterius. Ratio consecutionis est hæc, Quod vel ipsi Jesuitæ nondum affirmare audent, judicium ac testimonium Ecclesiæ certius esse ac evidentius judicio Johannis Baptistæ. Jam verò hujus testimonium Christus postponit judicio scripturæ, Ergò.

III. Argumentum: Quæ fuit ratio verbi non scripti, in Ecclesia Patriarcharū Veteris Testamenti, respectu Autoritatis quoad nos: eadē hodie est ratio verbi scripti, Atqui verbum non scriptū suā tùm obtinebat autoritatem longè maximam, etiam quoad nos, non ex autoritate Ecclesiæ, sed ex se ipso. Ergò neq; hodie verbum scriptum suam mutuabitur autoritatem, quoad nos ab Ecclesia, Majorem vix negabunt Adversarij, nisi Fortè nugari velint, aliam fuisse autoritatem verbi divini quoad nos in veteri: aliam verò jā esse in Novo Testamento. Quibus tamen hoc licèt affirmantibus, prius non credemus, quàm evidenter illud demonstratum dederunt.

Quoad rationem Minoris, manifestum est, verbi divini autoritatem tum temporis, ne quidem Patriarcharum testimonio aut summo judicio fuisse superstructam: sed habuisse illud in se, quasi impressa, omnibusq; ex se ostendisse divinitatis suæ certissima argumenta. Nam quòd nonnulli ex Jesuitis oggerunt, Majores sive præsules illius Ecclesiæ, sua voce hominib9 commendasse verbum DEI, & sic autoritatem ei apud homines conciliaffe: id verò omninò vanum & nugatorium est. Quæritur enim, cujusnam Ecclesiæ suasu, illi ipsi Patriarchæ verbum DEI susceperint, & divinâ illud autoritate præditum esse, crediderint? Hoc dum explicare in æternum non possunt Adversarij, fateantur necesse est, Patriarchas illos & Antistites Ecclesiæ illius antiquissimæ, verbi divini autoritatem planè divinam, non ex ullius sive Ecclesiæ, sive Concitij testimonio addidicisse: sed ipsum potiùs verbum DEI ex se de autoritate sua luculenter testatum esse. Si responderint, non opus fuisse Ecclesiæ judicio, quia Deus ἀμέσως cum Patriarchis locutus fuerit: acceptamus utíq; responsionem, & inde evidenter contra Adversarios inferimus, neq; hodiè ad conciliandam Scripturis autoritatem opus esse tali publico Ecclesiæ judicio, propterea quod Deus hodieq; nobiscum loquitur, licèt non ἀμέσως: tamen mediatè, non quidem per Ecclesiam, sed per Scripturas θεοπνεύστης: & Spiritus Sanctus hodieq; testatur in nobis, de divina scripturarum autoritate: secundum illud Johannis 1. Epistola cap. 5, 6. Spiritus est, qui testatur Spiritum, hoc est, doctrinam Propheticam & Apostolicam esse veritatem.

Neque etiam quicquam proficiunt Adversarij, quando disparitatis alicujus rationem exinde eruere volunt, quòd tum in antiqua Ecclesia Verbum Dei non fuerit literis consignatum: Nam l. scriptio hæc estAccidentis, &Substantiam autoritatemq́; verbi divini nihil quicquam mutat. 2. Si ideò Verbum Dei indiget Ecclesiæ judicio, quoad nos : quia literis jam consignatum est: consequens fuerit, illud hodie minoris esse autoritatis, quam olim fuerit : id quod enormiter est absurdum: cum dignitate atq́; excellentia Novi Testamenti simpliciter pugnat. 3. Invertitur argumentum Jesuvviticum in hunc modum : Si tunc cum nondum scriptum esset Verbum DEI, autoritatem suam quoad nos, non habuit ab Ecclesiâ : multò minùs hodie habebit, postquam literis jam consignatum est. Ratio consecutionis est hæc : Quia quod scriptum non est, illud multò magis indigere videtur extrinseco aliquo testimonio sive judicio : siquidem facilius & oblivioni & contemtui est obnoxium, quàm illud, quod literis proditum, omnium oculis & sensibus semper est expositum, & ab omnibus legi, expendi ac judicari potest.

IV. Argumentum tale esse potest. Si Ecclesia ex verbo DEI, sive Scriptura Sacra, tanquam semine incorruptibili nascitur, fieri aliter non potest, quin Verbum DEI prius sit Ecclesiâ, & per consequens Scripturæ Sacræ autoritas præcedat Ecclesiam, omneq́; ejus judicium. Atqui prius illud verum. Ratum ergò & hoc posterius.

Connexum Majoris suâ luce lucet. Semen enim priùs esse eo, quod inde enascitur, nemo nisi bardus negaverit: Et rursus: Semen suam habere bonitatem ex fructu enascente, nemo nisi stultus affirmaverit. Jam antequam existere Ecclesia incipiat, semen aut fundamentum ejus præcedat necesse est : nisi per insignem ἄῤῥωσίαν τῆς διανοίας fingere quis velit, fructum priorem esse suo semine, vel quòd idem est, ædificium prius esse suo fundamento : vel ædificium suo fundamento dare τὸ εἶναι, ut nimirum sit fundamentum: Aut fructum dare suo semini, ut tale sit, quale esse debet. Quæ omnia absurdissimis absurdiora esse, quis non videt?

Minoris propositionis veritas, adversus infulsam Stapletoni exceptionem, quâ nugatur, Scripturam posteriorem esse Ecclesiâ, quoad acceptationem nostram, multipliciter demonstrari potest. Primùm enim fundatio originalis Ecclesiæ post lapsum protoplastorum, hominibus non innotuit, nisi per verbum promissionis, de semine contrituro caput serpentis. Gen. 3, 15. Deinde, omnium fidelium, & sic totius veræ Ecclesiæ Christi causa procreans non est alia, præter solum verbum DEI : ita quidem, ut ex hoc de Ecclesiæ qualitate : non verò ex Ecclesia de verbi approbatione fieri debeat judicium: vi Aphorismi illi9 Apostolici 1. Pet. 1. 23. Regeniti estis non ex semine corruptibili, sed incorruptibili per Verbū DEI vivi, & manentis in secula. Tertiò, patet hoc ipsum ex consequente Absurdo. Nisi enim Scripturam Sacram Ecclesiâ priorem esse concedere velint, etiam quoad approbationem nostram : concedant necesse est, Ecclesiam illam, cujus judicio de Scripturis Sacris sit standum, extra scripturas quærendam, ac proinde non Christi Ecclesiam, sed, nescio, cujus alterius sive hominis sive Diaboli Synagogam esse. Nam si Ecclesia est ovile Christi: Si etiam oves audiunt & sequuntur vocem pastoris sui: Christus autem extra scripturam oves suas non alloquitur: Sequitur necessario, Scripturam & priorem esse Ecclesiâ, & præstare, ut pro Ecclesia Christi agnoscatur.

4. Quartò: Ecclesia nihil est aliud, quàm cœtus fidelium: Fides verò nascitur ex audito verbo: Ergò Verbum DEI, sive Scriptura Sacra non modò est nota, sed etiam causa efficiens, sive principium constitutivum Ecclesiæ: ita ut suum τὸ εἶναι non nisi ex sola Scriptura habeat.

Quintum & postremum argumentum suppeditat Orthodoxæ antiquitatis Consensus. Sic enim Ambrosius lib. 1. de fide ad Gratianum cap. 5. Noli Ariane ex nostris dictis vel scriptis æstimare divina: sed divina crede, ubi humana non invenis: Divina ergò ex se probantur, ex se creduntur.

Sic Beda in Psalm. 8. Scripta divinorum librorum sunt fundamentum & universalis Ecclesiæ, & singularum Ecclesiarum, quibus ipsa roborantur & sustentantur, velut ædificium à fundamento.

Augustinus in Genesi ad lit: Major est scripturæ autoritas, quàm omnis humani ingenij capacitas comprehendere potest: profectò inviolabilem sacrarum literarum autoritatem confiteri debemus. Et hæc quidem de priore propositionis nostræ membro, eoq́; negativo, dicta sufficiant.

Posterior propositionis pars Affirmativa, Scripturam Sacram ex seipsa autoritatem summam habere asserit, tùm respectu sumptius, tùm respectu nostri. Assertionis veritas primùm evidentissimè patet ex quatuor illis argumentis, quæ jam modò pertractavimus.

1. Si enim non ab Ecclesia mutuatur autoritatem suam Scriptura quoad nos: utique ex seipsa illam habeat necesse est. Tertium enim dari nequit.

2. Deinde patet assertionis hujus veritas, ex singularibus illis privilegijs, sive ἀξιώμασι, quibus Scriptura Sacra gaudet, quæq́; sibi servat peculiaria: ut quòd 1. Autorem habet ipsum DEUM Spiritum Sanctum, cujo instinctu ea conscripta est. 2. Tim. 3, 16. 2. Pet. 1, 21. Deindè, quòd idem Spiritus Sanctus in consignanda Scriptura, usus est Prophetarum & Apostolorum ministerio: eorum nimirum hominum, quos DEUS divinis testimonijs ornavit, quòd in scribendo errare non possint, uti loquitur Augustinus Epist. 19. ad Hieron

3. Tertiò, quòd rerum, quas tradunt Scripturæ Sacræ, natura planè divina ac cœlestis est.

4. Tandem, Quod Christus & Apostoli, atque adeò universa Ecclesia Orthodoxa in refellendis hæresibus, ad solam Scripturam Sacram, tanquam judicem infallibilem ac supremum, semper provocavit: uti quæstione quinta ex professo ostendetur. Sufficiat hoc loco unicus locus Augustini, qui extat lib. 2. de Baptismo contra Donatistas, c. 3. Proprium est Scripturæ sanctæ Canonicæ, ut quicquid in ea scribitur, sit

staverum & rectum: Episcoporum autem literæ, ut Cypriani, & ipsa Concilia non modò, quæ per singulas fiunt provincias: sed etiam plenaria atque generalia, habent sæpenumerò, quòd corrigatur. Ex quo loco Augustini contra Jesuvvitas sic colligo: Omnia verba Scripturæ Sacræ semper sunt verba veritatis: Contrà verò verba Ecclesiæ & Conciliorum, sæpenumerò sunt verba Erroris. Quantum ergò indubia veritas præstat incertis & fallibilibus assertionibus: tantò major & excellentior est Scripturæ autoritas, præ autoritate Ecclesiæ. Cæterùm præter meritum Jesuvvitæ hoc loco nostras flagellant Ecclesias, ac si omnem prorsus Ecclesiæ autoritatem derōgent. Primùm enim nulla militat ratio consequentiæ: Secundum Lutheranos major est Scripturæ, quàm Ecclesiæ autoritas etiam quoad nos. Ergò Lutherani omnem prorsus autoritatem Ecclesiæ derogant. Nam ex negatione unius gradus ad negationem alterius, vitiosa est collectio, Deinde, quam augustam Ecclesiæ autoritatem largiamur, vel inde patet, quòd multa præclara erga Scripturam officia, ipsi assignamus, dum nimirum ea testimonium fert de scripturis sive libris Canonicis: dum scripta supposititia & adulterina à veris ac genuinis scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis discernit: dum Scripturas sacras interpretatur, & ex collatione locorum obscuriorum cum dilucidioribus, verum ac germanum earum sensum investigat ac proponit: dum deniq; magna cura atq; diligentia puriorem scripturarum sensum longè lateq; disseminare ac propagare studet. Hæc certè satis ampla Ecclesiæ munera tantum abest, ut vel verbis extenuemus, vel planè negem9; ut in hac Ecclesiæ dignitate omnem salutis nostræ cardinem atq; summam versari, habeamus persuasissimum: licet indè minimè illud sequi credamus, quod Jesuvvitæ inscitè inferunt, Majorem videlicet Ecclesiæ, quàm scripturarum esse autoritatem.

Pari ratione neq; Sanctorum Patrum luminibus, nostra hæc propositio obstruit, qui certè ipsi non aliâ conditione sua legi scripta voluerunt, quàm ut ad regulam Verbi scripti exigerentur, & tum demum probarentur, si cum illa consentirent. Et profectò haud ignota esse possunt hac de re Cypriani, Augustini, Hieronymi, Chrysostomi & aliorum voces, quibus se suaque omnia Verbi scripti judicio submittere attestantur: idq; adeò dilucidè, ut Gratianus etiam, Compilator Juris Canonici, locum illum classicum Augustini, ex Epistola 19. ad Hieronymum, & ex l 2 c. 3. de Baptismo adversus Donatistas, in ipsum Jus Pontificium referre non dubitaverit, uti patet ex dist. 9. Can. 5. & 8. Ego solis eis scripturarum libris, qui jam Canonici appellantur, didici hunc honorem, timoremq; deferre, ut nullum eorum autorem in scribendo aliquid errasse firmissimè credam: Alios autem ita lego, ut quantalibet sanctitate doctrinaque polleant; non ideò verum putem, quia ipsi ita senserunt; sed quia mihi per alios autores, vel Canonicas, vel probabiles rationes, quòd à vero non abhorreant, persuadere potuerunt. Ex Epistola 19. ad Hieronymum.

Item lib. 2. cap. 3 de Baptis. adversus Donatistas. Quis nesciat Sanctam Scripturam Canonicam tàm Veteris, quàm Novi Testamenti certis suis terminis contineri eamǫ, omnibus posterioribus Episcoporum literis ita præponi, ut de illa omninò dubitari & disceptari non possit, utrum verum, vel utrum rectum sit, quicquid in ea scriptum esse constiterit: Episcoporum autem literas, quæ post confirmatum Canonem vel scriptæ sunt, vel scribuntur, & per sermonem fortè sapientiorem cujuslibet in ea re peritioris, & per aliorum episcoporum graviorem autoritatem, doctiorumquè prudentiam, & per Concilia licere reprehendi, si quid in eis fortè à veritate deviatum est.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Second Part of the Second Question, Antithetical

In defining the controversy concerning the authority of the Scriptures, the Roman or Papal Church is not sufficiently consistent with itself, but departs into diverse opinions. This is evident, first, from the fact that 1. The parties of the Council of Trent wished to define nothing at all concerning this Question: 2. That the Jesuit Bellarmine, even while expressly disputing in four entire books concerning the written and unwritten Word of God, nevertheless left this Question untouched; convinced, without doubt, by the testimony of his own conscience that the blasphemies impudently cast by Romanists against the authority of the Scriptures could be defended by no reasoning.

Furthermore, the same thing is evident from the fact that those among the Papists who have taken this Question upon themselves to treat do not hold one and the same opinion: a fact which the following two Jesuitical propositions will sufficiently and evidently establish.

JESUITICAL PROPOSITION I.

Holy Scripture is indeed of the highest authority in itself: but as regards us, it borrows it from the Church.

Ἔκθεσις.

The more recent Jesuit monks almost all hold this proposition. For thus Thomas Stapleton argues in book 9 of his Doctrinal Principles: The question is not whether Scripture is holy and divine in itself, but whence it is established to us that it is such. And after a few words: All things are worthy of reverence in themselves, but not as regards us, in such a way that they would be held in honor by themselves.

For thus Bellarmine thinks, writing in book 2 of Councils, chapter 12: Catholics do not subject Holy Scripture to the Church and Councils, but prefer it to them: nor is there any controversy in this. But if Catholics sometimes say that Scripture depends on the Church or on a Council, they do not mean as regards authority and in itself: but as regards explanation, and as regards us.

The first author of this distinction is Cochlaeus; who in his Reply against Bullinger, chapter 2, writes this opinion: The Scriptures are firm, clear, perfect, and most worthy of faith in themselves, as being the work of GOD: but as regards us, however, it needs the approval and commendation of the Church, on account of the depravity of our mind and the weakness of our intellect.

But it will be worth the effort for us to weigh more accurately what is to be determined concerning that distinction.

For it is so insidiously and plausibly concocted that it has basely imposed upon many learned men who are very far from the Jesuitical heresy.

But at the beginning, it comes under consideration what the Jesuits understand by Scripture taken in and by itself. This is evident enough from the other member of the distinction: while, namely, they oppose Scripture considered in itself to Scripture as regards us, and as regards explanation. The sense therefore emerges as follows: that Holy Scripture, considered in and by itself, has no explanation with respect to us, or no certain sense: but that this must be sought from the Church and Councils. Where it immediately shines forth of its own accord that the Jesuits establish that Holy Scripture, with respect to us and with respect to a certain opinion or explanation, is a dead letter, and devoid of any certain opinion in itself, just as the Anabaptists even today dream. And this is that remarkable authority which this fine society bestows upon the Holy Scriptures, and does not hesitate to call supreme. Where anyone not completely stupid easily understands that these men are presenting mere deceptions and tricks to the more incautious, so that while they strip the Holy Scriptures of all authority whatsoever, they still wish to appear to grant them supreme authority: which is the first ψεῦδος (falsehood) of this distinction.

Next, let the Jesuits explain whether the Church has derived that explanation of Scripture, as regards us, by which one must simply stand, from the Scriptures themselves or not: if it has derived it, then Scripture itself will already have its own certain explanation in itself, even as regards us: since the Church and a Council is nothing other than a society of men professing the faith of CHRIST. If it has not derived it from the Scriptures: then the Church has certainly erred, not to say lied, while it gave to Scripture that explanation or opinion which it did not have in itself, or does not have, and which cannot be elicited from it. Therefore, this Jesuitical distinction is destitute of a correct and legitimate ἀντιδιαιρέσει (division), or contradiction of opposite members, which is nevertheless necessarily required in every true division or distinction.

Thirdly, it is false and impious that Holy Scripture borrows its authority and explanation from the Church, AS REGARDS US. For although we perhaps do not unwillingly grant that infidels, and those not yet illuminated by the spirit of GOD, can to some extent learn from the voice and interpretation of the Church what the opinion of the Scriptures is: nevertheless, it is not about them that inquiry or dispute is made in this controversy: but the question is about the faithful, that is, about those who are engrafted into the Church through baptism, and gifted and illuminated with the Holy Spirit and true faith: whether indeed these need to borrow the sense and explanation of Scripture as to us from the Church, or whether they can indeed draw it out, and that a far most certain one, from the Scriptures themselves considered in themselves, where indeed we certainly maintain this latter against the Jesuits again and again. For those faithful ones are children of GOD, and are led by the Spirit of GOD: Rom. 8, 14 and 15. They are those in whose hearts Christ dwells through faith, Eph. 3, 17.
