They are those whom the Holy Spirit illuminates and leads through meditation on the Word into all truth. John 14, 16. 15, 26. 16, 13. They are those who, as the Apostle testifies, are the Epistle of Christ, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living GOD, not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of flesh of the heart: 2 Cor. 3, 3. Finally, they are those who believe the Scriptures, not because of the testimony of the Church, but because of the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit: Who is present to the Word of GOD heard, read, and pondered by the faithful, and persuades them that this is the mind and meaning of GOD speaking in the Scriptures, so that now a man may rest uniquely in the Word of GOD with full πληροφορίᾳ (full assurance). To which opinion Alphonsus de Castro wrote not inappropriately in book 1 against heresies, chapter 8: We have this from the Church, that we may know what is Divine Scripture (namely, in respect of attestation). But when it has been established to us that it is Divine Scripture, it now has from ITSELF that we are bound to believe it in all things.

4. Fourthly: If the explanation of Scripture, and thus its authority as far as we are concerned, depends upon the Church or a Council, then it will certainly depend upon men. But this is false. For with St. Peter as witness, the interpretation of Scripture is not of human interpretation, but depends upon the same Spirit of GOD by whom it was both dictated and revealed to men, 2 Pet. 1, 20 and 21. For as the jurists say, it belongs to him to interpret the law whose right it is to establish it.

But Holy Scripture is a Law established, given, and proceeding from GOD himself, 2 Tim. 3, 16. Therefore, it will also be the right of GOD himself, and indeed of him alone, to explain and interpret the same law: which GOD performs through Scripture itself in such a way that what is obscure in one place appears clearly and perspicuously explained in another, as Augustine says somewhere. And the Jesuits commit a huge sacrilege, who splendidly lie that this gift of interpretation has been granted to the Pope alone with a Council, or even deciding something without a Council. The testimonies which we proposed a little earlier concerning the state of the faithful certainly demonstrate the opposite. But more on this question below, where we will expressly dispute concerning the gift of the interpretation of Scripture. Let it suffice in this place to have demonstrated the vanity of the Jesuitical distinction a little more accurately. But it is pleasing to overwhelm the same with some evident contradictions and absurdities.

First, therefore: If the authority of Scripture, as regards explanation and as far as we are concerned, depends upon the judgment of the Church or a Council, it will follow that before any public judgment of the Church—which is much more recent with respect to the antiquity of Scripture—Holy Scripture possessed no authority as far as the pious and faithful are concerned. But this latter is impious and absurd. Therefore, the former is as well. On the contrary, however, if Scripture had divine authority, as it certainly had among all the pious and true worshippers of GOD before it was approved by any public judgment of the Church, then it must necessarily possess divine authority from itself, and indeed as far as we are concerned. The reason for this consequence is this: Because Scripture could not have obtained divine authority among the pious before the public judgment of the Church by any other means than that it showed and proved its divine majesty FROM ITSELF.

Next, the term Authority is a term πρός τι (relative), and it relates to others, since nothing can be said to have authority that has authority with no one. Now, if before the public judgment of the Church, Holy Scripture had supreme authority and indeed IN ITSELF, as the Jesuits themselves admit, it follows ἐξ ἀνάγκης (of necessity) that it had authority as far as we are concerned, and indeed without the judgment of the Church. Or if the Jesuits do not wish to grant this, they must necessarily admit that before the public judgment of the Church, Scripture had absolutely no authority IN ITSELF. Thus, therefore, the former consequence convicts the Adversaries of a shameful contradiction, while this latter convicts them of a shameful absurdity.

Thirdly, if the Church imparts authority to Scripture by its own judgment, as far as we are concerned, certainly it will form that judgment of its own either from the Scriptures themselves, or from certain secret and internal revelations of the Holy Spirit, or finally from the authority of men. But this last is openly absurd; that middle way, however, is Anabaptistic: for those internal revelations either agree with the written word or they differ. If they agree, then that judgment will depend no more on internal revelations than on the dictation of Scripture itself; and consequently, Scripture will have its authority, even as far as we are concerned, from itself. If they differ, then we rightly reject them; it remains, therefore, that that judgment of the Church depends entirely upon Scripture itself, and consequently that this [Scripture] testifies of its own divine certainty and majesty, even as far as we are concerned, from itself and through itself.

Fourthly, if the public judgment of the Church imparts divine authority to the holy Scriptures, as far as we are concerned: then certainly Scripture will not, conversely, impart authority to the Church, as far as we are concerned: but this latter is false and impious by the confession of the Jesuits themselves. For when they are asked about the authority of the Church, they bring forward many promises from the scriptures by which they establish the same. Therefore, that former point will also be false, namely that the authority of Scripture, as far as we are concerned, depends upon the public judgment of the Church.

Fifthly: If the authority of the Church, as far as we are concerned, depends upon Scripture: then Scripture already judges of the Church from itself, and indeed as far as we are concerned.

But let these suffice: the other Jesuitical proposition will now set forth more and weightier absurdities.

Latin:

IN definienda controversia, de Scripturarum autoritate, Ecclesia Romana sive Pontificia sibi satis non constat: sed in diversas abit sententias. Patet hoc Primùm indè, 1. Quòd Concilij Tridentini partes nihil quicquam de hac Quæstione definire voluerunt: 2. Quòd Jesuvvita Bellarminus, ex professo etiam libris integris quatuor de Verbo Dei scripto & non scripto disputans, hanc tamen Quæstionem intactam reliquit; propriæ sine dubio conscientiæ testimonio convictus, blasphemias à Romanensibus contra Scripturarum autoritatem impudenter projectas, nullâ ratione defendi posse.

Deindè verò patet idipsum inde etiam, quòd qui ex Pontificijs hanc sibi Quæstionem tractandam sumserunt, non unam eandemque tenent sententiam: id quod sequentes duæ propositiones Jesuiticæ satis evidenter astruent.

PROPOSITIO I. JESUVVITICA.

SCriptura sacra in se quidem summæ est autoritatis: sed quoad nos, mutuatur eam ab Ecclesia.

Ἔκθεσις.

PRopositionem istam recentiores Monachi Jesuvvitæ, plerique omnes tenent. Sic enim Thomas Stapletonus lib. 9. principiorum doctrinalium differit: Non quæritur, utrum Scriptura in se sacra ac divina sit, sed undè nobis constet, eam talem esse. Et post pauca: Omni reverentiâ scriptura digna sunt in se, non autem quoad nos, in tanto honore per se haberentur.

Sic enim censet Bellarminus lib. 2. de Conciliis cap. 12. scribens: Catholici scripturam sacram non subjiciunt, sed anteponunt Ecclesiæ & Concilijs: neque in hoc ulla Controversia est. Quòd si interdum Catholici dicunt, Scripturam pendere ab Ecclesia, sive à Concilio, non intelligunt, quoad autoritatem & secundum se: sed quoad explicationem, & quoad nos.

distinctionis primus autor esse, Cochlæus; qui in Replica contra Bullingerum, cap. 2.11 hanc scribit sententiam: Scripturæ ex se firmæ claræ, perfectæ, fideque dignissimæ sunt, utpote DEI opus: sed quoad nos tamen, approbatione ac commendatione Ecclesiæ indiget, propter mentis nostræ pravitatem, & intellectus nostri imbecillitatem.

Cæterùm quid de distinctione ista sit statuendum, accuratiùs ut expendamus, operæ fuerit pretium.

Nam usque adeò insidiosè & plausibiliter ea est conficta, ut multis viris doctis, & ab hæresi Jesuuvitica multùm abhorrentibus, turpiter ea imposuerit.

Initiò autem sub considerationem venit, quidnam Jesuuvitæ per Scripturam in & per se acceptam, intelligant. Patet verò hoc satis evidenter, ex altero distinctionis membro: dum nimirùm Scripturæ per se consideratæ opponunt Scripturam quoad nos, & quoad explicationem. Sensus ergò emergit iste: Scripturam sacram in se & per se consideratam, nullam respectu nostri habere explicationem sive nullum certum sensum: sed hunc petendum esse ab Ecclesia & Concilijs. Ubi statim ultrò elucet, statuere Jesuuvitas, Scripturam Sacram respectu nostri, & respectu certæ sententiæ sive explicationis esse mortuam literam, omnisque certæ sententiæ per se expertem, uti Anabaptistæ etiam hodie somniant, Et hæc est egregia illa autoritas, quam bella isthæc societas Scripturis sacris impertit, & summam appellare haud dubitat. Ubi quisque non planè stupidus, facilè intelligit, meros fucos ac præstigias incautioribus objicere istos homines, ut dum Scripturas sacras omni prorsus autoritate exuunt, summam tamen ijsdem concedere videri velint: id quod primum est distinctionis hujus ψεῦδος.

Deindè edisserant Jesuuvitæ, Num Ecclesia explicationem illam Scripturæ, quoad nos, quâ simpliciter standum sit, desumpserit ex scripturis ipsis, an non: si desumsit, utique Scriptura ipsa suam jam habebit explicationem certam in se ipsa etiam quo ad nos: Siquidem Ecclesia & Concilium nihil est aliud, quàm societas hominum fidem CHRISTI profitentium. Si non desumsit ex scripturis: tùm erravit utique Ecclesia, ne dicam, mentita est; dum eam scripturæ dedit explicationem, sive sententiam, quam tamen ipsa in se non habuit, aut habet, quæq; inde elici non potest. Si ergò distinctio isthæc Jesuuvitica destituitur rectâ & legitimâ ἀντιδιαιρέσει, sive contradictione membrorum oppositorum, quæ tamen in omni vera, sive divisione, sive distinctione necessariò requiritur.

Tertiò falsum & impium est Scripturam Sacrã mutuari suam autoritatem & explicationem ab Ecclesia, QUOAD NOS. Etsi enim illud fortè haud inviti largimur, Infideles, & spiritu DEI nondum illuminatos, aliquatenùs ex voce & interpretatione Ecclesiæ addiscere posse, Quænam sit Scripturarum sententia: tamen de istis hac in Controversia non quæritur aut disputatur: sed de fidelibus est Quæstio, hoc est, de illis, qui Ecclesiæ per baptismum sunt inserti, & Spiritu Sancto, veraque fide donati & illuminati: An nimirùm isti sensum & explicationem scripturæ Quoad nos, ab Ecclesia mutuari necesse habeant, an verò ex ipsis scripturis in se consideratis illam & quidem longè certissimam eruere possint, ubi sanè posteriùs hoc contra Jesuvvitas iterum atque iterum affirmamus. Sunt enim fideles isti filij DEI, & ducuntur Spiritu DEI: Rom. 8, 14. & 15. Sunt illi, in quorum cordibus Christus habitat per fidem, Eph. 3, 17. Sunt illi, quos Spiritus Sanctus illuminat, & ducit per meditationem verbi, in omnem veritatem. Johan. 14, 16. 15, 26. 16, 13. Sunt illi, qui teste Apostolo sunt Epistola Christi non atramento scripta, sed Spiritu DEI vivi, non in tabulis lapideis, sed in tabulis cordis carnalibus: 2. Cor. 3, 3. Sunt denique illi, qui Scripturis credunt, non propter testimonium Ecclesiæ, sed propter testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum: Qui ad Verbum DEI à fidelibus auditum, lectum, pensitatum adest, & persuadet, hanc DEI in scripturis loquentis esse mentem ac sententiam, ut jam homo plenâ πληροφορίᾳ in Verbo DEI unicè acquiescat. Quam in sententiam haud incommodè scripsit Alphonsus de Castro lib. 1. contra hæreses cap. 8. Hoc ex Ecclesia habemus, ut sciamus, quæ sit Scriptura Divina (nempè respectu testificationis) At cùm Scripturam divinam esse, nobis constiterit, jam ex SEIPSA habet, ut ei per omnia credere teneamur.

4. Quartò: Si explicatio Scripturæ, & sic ejusdem Autoritas quoad nos, pendet ab Ecclesia, aut Concilio: utique pendebit ab hominibus. At hoc falsum. Nam D. Petro teste, Scripturæ interpretatio non est humanæ interpretationis: sed pendet ab eodem DEI spiritu, à quo illa & dictata & revelata est hominibus 2. Pet. 1, 20, & 21. Nam ut Jurisconsulti loquuntur, illius est interpretari legem, cujus est & condere.

Atqui Scriptura sacra est Lex à DEO ipso condita, data, profecta, 2. Tim. 3, 16. Ergò ipsius etiam & quidem solius DEI erit, eandem legem explicare ac interpretari: id quod ita per Scripturam ipsam præstat DEUS, ut quod in uno loco obscurum est, id in alio appareat dilucidè & perspicuè expositum, ut alicubi loquitur Augustinus. Et ingens sacrilegium committunt Jesuvvitæ, qui donum hoc interpretationis soli Pontifici cum Concilio, vel etiam sine Concilio aliquid decernenti, concessum esse, splendidè mentiuntur. Diversum certè ea demonstrant testimonia, quæ paulò antè de fidelium statu proposuimus. Sed de hac Quæstione infra copiosiùs, ubi de dono interpretationis Scripturæ ex professo disputabimus. Sufficiat hoc loco vanitatem distinctionis Jesuvviticæ paulò accuratiùs demonstrasse. Sed placet eandem aliquot evidentibus tùm contradictionibus, tùm absurditatibus obruere.

Primùm igitur: Si autoritas scripturæ, quoad explicationem, & quoad nos, dependet ab Ecclesiæ sive Concilij judicio: Consequens fuerit, antè publicum aliquod Ecclesiæ judicium, quippè quod respectu antiquitatis Scripturæ multò est recentius, Scripturam Sacram quoad pios & fideles, nihil autoritatis obtinuisse. At posterius hoc impium & absurdum. Ergò & prius. Contrà verò, si Scriptura divinam autoritatem habuit, uti certè habuit apud pios omnes & veros DEI cultores, antequàm publico aliquo Ecclesiæ judicio est approbata: tùm ex se autoritatem divinam, & quidem Quoad nos, obtineat necesse est. Ratio consecutionis est hæc: Quia non alia ratione: Scriptura divinam autoritatem apud pios ante publicum Ecclesiæ judicium, consequi potuit, nisi quod EX SE divinam suam majestatem ostendit atque probavit.

Deindè, vocabulum Autoritatis est vocabulum πρός τι, & habet se relatè ad alios, siquidem autoritatem habere, nihil dici potest, quòd apud neminem autoritatem habet. Jam si ante publicum Ecclesiæ judicium, Scriptura Sacra autoritatem summam & quidem IN SE habuit, uti fatentur ipsi Jesuvvitæ, sequitur ἐξ ἀνάγκης, habuisse autoritatem Quoad nos, & quidem sine Ecclesiæ judicio. Aut si hoc largiri nolint Jesuvvitæ, fateantur necesse est, Scripturam ante publicum Ecclesiæ judicium planè nullam IN SE autoritatem habuisse. Sic ergò prius illud consequens turpis contradictionis: posterius verò hoc pudendæ absurditatis convincit Adversarios.

Tertiò, Si Ecclesia suo judicio impertit Scripturæ autoritatem, quoad nos: certè judicium illud suum vel ex ipsis Scripturis, vel ex arcanis quibusdam & internis revelationibus Spiritus Sancti: vel denique ex hominum autoritate informabit. At verò hoc postremum palàm est absurdum: Intermedium autem illud est Anabaptisticum: Nam revelationes illæ internæ, aut cum verbo scripto congruunt, aut discrepant. Si congruunt: tùm judicium illud non magis ex internis revelationibus, quàm ex ipsius Scripturæ dictamine pendebit: & per consequens, Autoritatem suam Scriptura etiam Quoad nos, ex seipsa habebit. Si discrepant: tùm meritò eas respuimus: Relinquitur ergò, judicium illud Ecclesiæ in solidum pendere ab ipsa Scripturâ, ac proindè hanc ex seipsa & per seipsam de divina sua certitudine & majestate, etiam Quoad nos, testari.

Quartò, si Ecclesiæ judicium publicum Scripturis sacris impertit autoritatem divinam, Quoad nos: tùm utique non è contrà Scriptura autoritatem impertiet Ecclesiæ, quoad nos: At verò posterius hoc ipsorum Jesuvvitarum confessione est falsum & impium. Nam hi rogati de Ecclesiæ autoritate, multas ex scripturis proferunt promissiones, quibus eandem astruant. Ergò falsum erit etiam prius illud, nempè Scripturæ autoritatem quoad nos, pendere ex Judicio publico Ecclesiæ.

Quintò: Si Ecclesiæ autoritas Quoad nos, pendet à Scriptura: utique Scriptura jam ex seipsa judicat de Ecclesia, & quidem Quoad nos.

Sed sufficiant isthæc: plura & graviora absurda altera propositio Jesuvvitica jam expediet.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Proposition II. Jesuitical

PROPOSITION II. JESUITICAL.

Holy Scripture was not given so that it might be a Canon or rule of faith: nor was it even inscribed by the finger of God: much less does it contain in itself anything of divinity which could indeed constrain us to believe those things: but the Church is the internal scripture, inscribed by the Spirit of God in the hearts of those who, through continuous successions, have propagated the faith from the Apostles down to us: and therefore the Church, being better known and more ancient than the Scriptures, imparts all authority to them.

Both the ancient and the more recent Papist writers have long since made this thesis their own. Eck certainly, in his Enchiridion, response 3 to the objections of the heretics, writes expressly: The Church is more ancient than the Scriptures, and scripture is not authentic except by the authority of the Church.

Thus Albert Pighius, in book 1 of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 2, did not shrink from writing in a more than blasphemous style: The writings of the Apostles were not given to the Church so that they might preside over our faith and religion, but rather so that they might be subject to it. For the Church has an authority not only not inferior, nor even merely equal, but in a certain way superior to the authority of scripture. For all the authority of the Scriptures which we now possess depends necessarily upon the authority of the Church. And lest by chance you might conclude that only those older Papist Doctors thought this way, it must be observed that Francis Coster the Jesuit increases this impiety in many ways, in his Enchiridion of Controversies, approved by the Jesuits of Cologne, Mainz, and Trier, writing thus on pages 43, 44, 45: Christ did not wish his Church to depend on paper writings, nor to commit his Mysteries to membranes (which Moses had once done in large part for a carnal people), but when he established a spiritual Church, informed by his Holy Spirit, he used a more sublime character, writing with the finger of GOD in the heart of the Church. This scripture, moreover, is the consensus of the Catholic Church, and the concordant doctrine of all Christians who are throughout the world: not only of these, but also of those who have propagated the faith from the Apostles down to us through continuous successions. The excellence of this (internal) scripture surpasses in many parts the scriptures which the Apostles left us on membranes. 1. Because it is inscribed by the finger of GOD: these by the pens of the Apostles. 2. Because it is more ancient, namely given with the Church: these are later, because it is established that for twelve whole years the Church existed without Apostolic writings. 3. Because these (Apostolic scriptures) needed the confirmation of that former one. 4. Because these (Apostolic scriptures) are a dead letter, written with ink on membrane or paper, which if anyone wishes to truncate, or twist, or corrupt with perverse expositions, he feels nothing. But that one, since it is written by the Spirit of the living GOD in the living hearts of the Church, does not allow itself to be truncated and twisted, but remains like itself in all things. 5. These do not contain all the mysteries of religion explicitly, as they were not given for the purpose of prescribing to us an exact formula, absolute in all respects, of faith, administration, Sacraments, and other things necessary in the Christian Republic: but were written by some on a certain occasion, either to refute Jews and heretics, or to remove certain abuses, or to console the faithful, and sent to some Churches. But that one (namely the scripture of the Church), which the Holy Spirit has deigned to imprint in hearts, has all truth in itself, embraces all the mysteries of faith, and every reason for the Christian religion, and dissolves all doubts which can arise concerning matters of faith, etc. From which it follows that this scripture (namely the internal one of the Church) is the interpreter of all scriptures, the judge of all opinions, the expeller of all errors, from whose judgment it is not permitted for anyone to appeal to another Judge: Indeed, whose judgment all judges are bound to inspect and follow.

Andradius also encrusted this same impiety in book 2 of his defense of the Council of Trent, in these words: For there is nothing of divinity in the very books in which the sacred mysteries are written down, which might bind us by any religion to believe what is contained in them: But the Church, which teaches that those codices are sacred and commends the faith and piety of the ancient Fathers, has such force and amplitude that no one can oppose them without the most serious mark of impiety.

Moreover, the foulness of this proposition is too foul to be sufficiently exaggerated in words. That is, without a doubt, the scope and the end set before these Jesuits, especially Costerus and Andradius, that by cashiering the Holy Scriptures, they may lead us to that internal word written in the living hearts of the Church, that is, to the decrees of the Tridentine conventicle, to the Canons of the Councils, to the traditions of the Church, to the Responses of the Roman Pontiffs, and thus assert for the Roman Pontiffs a clearly irrefragable power and license to touch upon anything whatsoever. Where, at the beginning, but as if ἐν παρόδῳ, it should be observed that these crasser Jesuits do not at all agree with the Canon Law: Gratian, certainly the compiler of this Pontifical Law, comparing the authority of the Scriptures and the Church to one another in Dist. 9. Can. 5. wished to presuppose as a foundation that classic passage of St. Augustine, taken from Epist. 19 to Jerome, which reads as follows: I have learned to defer this honor and fear only to those books of the Scriptures which are now called Canonical, so that I most firmly believe that none of their authors has erred in writing anything: But I read others in such a way that, however much they may excel in holiness and doctrine, I do not think it true because they thought so: but because they were able to persuade me, through other authors, or through Canonical or probable reasons, that it does not deviate from the truth. Thus far the Canon Law from Augustine; how it agrees with the more recent Jesuits, let them see to it themselves. But it is pleasing to examine the stupendous abomination of this proposition also a little more accurately.

And first, indeed, it is a pseudograph: that Holy Scripture was not given to be a Canon or rule of faith and of the Christian Religion. The foulness of which we shall expressly refute below in Question 6, which will be about the perfection of the Scriptures. Let that one Apostolic Aphorism suffice in this place, 2 Tim. 3:16, where Paul affirms that Scripture is useful, not (as Bellarmine contends) for admonition only, but for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction: and indeed not partially, but totally: so that, of course, the man of GOD may be PERFECT, perfectly instructed for every good work. Then, if Scripture is such as is claimed by the Jesuits in this place, by what face, I ask, can they call it Canonical? For if it is Canonical: it must certainly be a Rule. Again, if it is a Rule; it must certainly be perfect and adequate to our faith. For what is not such, can indeed hardly be called a rule. But concerning this Question, more fully below in Question 6, which will be about the perfection of the Scriptures.

The other falsehood is: that Holy Scripture was not written by the finger of GOD: nor did GOD wish His Church to depend upon paper writings: much less to commit His Mysteries to parchments. The execrable foulness of this abomination also is manifest in many ways. 1. The Apostle expressly affirms that Scripture is θεόπνευστον, 2 Tim. 3:16. Therefore Scripture has GOD Himself as its primary author. Then: Although GOD did not immediately consign the Scripture: but wished to use the pen and ministry of the Prophets and Apostles: nothing nevertheless departs from the authority of the Scripture on that account. For it is GOD, and indeed GOD alone, who inspired the Prophets and Apostles, not only with what they should speak, but also what they should write: and He used their mouth, tongues, hands, and pen. Therefore, even in this respect, Scripture, insofar as it is such, was written by GOD Himself. For the Prophets and Apostles were only Instruments. And let the Adversaries explain, I ask, Where and when did GOD immediately write His Word into the hearts of the Church? Certainly, ever since the fall of the first-formed, GOD has used the ministry of the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles in planting and gathering the Church: who, by the command of GOD, subsequently consigned to letters that very word which they announced by word of mouth, so that from it the Church might thereafter be gathered in these lands.

And what, I pray, is this madness, nay blasphemy, to affirm that Christ did not wish His Church to be bound to the paper writings of the Apostles? For what, I ask, does the Apostle mean otherwise, Eph. 2:20, asserting that the Church is built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, than that the Church is bound to the Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture, whether comprised in papers or parchments? For it is very frivolous and trifling that the Jesuits object that the Apostle is not speaking of Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture: but of doctrine, that is, their living preaching. As if, indeed, the preaching of the Prophets and Apostles were not the same as their Scripture. What of the fact that the words of the Apostle clearly confirm that the Scripture itself, insofar as it is Scripture, is more correctly understood by the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles. For it is manifest that Paul joins the Prophets with the Apostles: Now, who would be so foolish as to affirm that in the time of Paul the Prophets preached by word of mouth, when it is established that they had long since yielded to fate. Yet the Apostle asserts that the Church is built upon the foundation of these as well. Why, therefore, there can be no doubt for anyone that not their living preaching, but Scripture must be understood. Finally, it would be very absurd to establish that the Church is founded upon that preaching of the Prophets and Apostles which lasted for a short time, and ceased and stopped many centuries ago.

The third abomination of the Jesuitical proposition is: that the Holy Scriptures contain nothing of divinity in themselves which could indeed constrain us to believe them. Some Jesuits submit this reason: Because, forsooth, Scripture cannot speak. But the foulness of this abomination also is manifest of itself. 1. For GOD Himself is the author of the Scriptures, and the individual words are the individual utterances of GOD; therefore, unless it be asserted that GOD Himself has nothing of divinity in Himself: it certainly cannot be affirmed that the Scriptures are destitute of that divinity which could constrain us to believe them.

Then, GOD speaks to us in the Scriptures, as if face to face through His Holy Spirit, who so moves our hearts through the Scriptures that this word of GOD, read in the Scriptures, is sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Heb. 4:12.

Thirdly, Holy Scripture acts as a principle: a fact which the Jesuits themselves are forced to admit, even if unwillingly, when asked, whence does the Church have it that it cannot err? They recur to the promises of Scripture given to the Church, as if to first principles: Thus, when asked, where is the Roman Pontificate founded with its authority? They recur to the Scriptures, bringing forward that passage in Matt. 16:18, Thou art Peter, and upon &c., and that in Luke 22:38, Behold, here are two swords. Thus they themselves imply that the Scriptures act as a principle. Now if in other sciences, principles are indemonstrable, being indeed most certain in themselves: then certainly the principles of the Scriptures, whose author is not any man, but the Holy Spirit, will contain that divinity in themselves, so that they deserve faith of themselves, and constrain us to believe.

Fourthly, Luke in the preface of his Gospel overturns this Jesuitical collation from the foundation, writing: It seemed good to me, having traced all things from the beginning and having followed them in order, to write to you, most excellent Theophilus, that you might know the certain and not at all doubtful truth, τὴν ἀσφάλειαν [the security], that is, an unshaken firmness. Whence I conclude thus: If it was therefore necessary that those things which Theophilus had previously learned from instruction (περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων) be committed to writing, so that he might attain the certain and infallible truth of them: then Scripture, insofar as it is Scripture, will already have in itself that divinity by which it can constrain us to believe the truth. But the former is true, as Luke attests: Therefore the latter is also established. The reason for the connection is this: For unless Scripture, as Scripture, could have constrained Theophilus to believe: 1. there would have been no need for that writing. 2. The Evangelist's reasoning would be clearly impertinent: Since both of these are absurd, it follows that the connection of the Major premise is firm. Furthermore, if this use of Scripture had a place in Theophilus, who nevertheless heard the Apostles themselves teaching: How much more does Scripture today exercise that use with respect to us, indeed with respect to the Church itself: namely, that it is not constrained to believe divine mysteries except by the power of the Scriptures themselves.

And what need is there of many words, when Lord Paul commends the Scriptures alone to his Timothy most especially under this title, that they can be like all Teachers: in this illustrious subject Aphorism: These can make you wise unto salvation through faith, which is in CHRIST. 2 Tim. 3:15.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO II. JESUVVITICA.

SCriptura sacra non est data, ut esset Canon aut regula fidei: nequè etiam digito Dei est exarata: nedum quicquam in se divinitatis continet, quod quidem ad credendum illis nos constringere possit: Ecclesia verò est scriptura interna, Spiritu Dei exarata in cordibus eorum, qui per continuas successiones, ab Apostolis ad nos usq; fidem propagarunt: ac proindè Ecclesia Scripturis notior & antiquior, omnē illis autoritatē impertit.

THesin hanc tùm Veteres tùm Recentiores Scriptores Pontificij jampridem suam fecerunt. Eccius certè in Enchiridio resp. 3. ad object. hæreticorum disertè scribit: Ecclesia est Scripturis antiquior, & scriptura non est authentica, nisi Ecclesiæ autoritate.

Sic Albertus Pighius l. 1. hierarchiæ Eccl. c. 2. stylo plusquàm blasphemo scribere non exhorruit: Scripta Apostolorum non fuerunt data Ecclesiæ, ut præessent fidei religioniq; nostræ, sed ut subessent potiùs. Non enim solùm non inferiorem, non etiam tantùm parem, sed & quodammodò superiorem autoritatem, autoritate scripturæ habet Ecclesia, Nam omnis, quæ nunc apud nos est Scripturarum autoritas, ab Ecclesiæ autoritate dependet necessariò. Et ne fortè vetustiores tantùm illos Doctores Pontificios sic sensisse statuamẽ, observandum, quòd est Franciscus Costerus Jesuvvita impietatem hanc multis modis auget, in Enchiridio Controversiarum, à Coloniensibus, Moguntinensibus & Trevirensibus Jesuvvitis approbato, sic scribens p. 43. 44. 45 Christus Ecclesiam suàm neq; à Chartaceis scriptis pendēre, nec membranis Mysteria sua committere voluit (quod Moyses olim magna ex parte fecerat carnali populó) sed cùm spiritualem constitueret Ecclesiam, suo spiritu sancto informatam, usus est sublimiori charactere, scribens digito DEI in corde Ecclesiæ. Est autem scriptura hæc, Ecclesiæ Catholicæ consensus, & cōcors Christianorum omnium, qui sunt per orbem terrarum doctrina: non horum modò, sed & eorum qui per continuas successiones ab Apostolis ad nos usq; fidem propagarunt. Hujus (internæ) scripturæ præstantia multis partibus superat scripturas, quas nobis in membranis Apostoli reliquerunt. 1. Quod illa sit exarata digito DEI: hæ calamis Apostolorum. 2. Quod illa sit antiquior, nempe cum Ecclesia data: hæ posteriores, quia constat totis duodecim annis sine scriptis Apostolicis Ecclesiam fuisse. 3. quòd hæ (scripturæ Apostolicæ) prioris illius indigu‐ erint confirmatione. 4. quod istæ (scripturæ ApostoIicæ) sint litera mortua, scripta atramento in membrana, vel charta, quam si quis vel truncare velit, vel torquere, vel pravis expositionibus corrumpere, nihil sentiat. Illa verò cùm scripta sit Spiritu DEI vivi in cordibus vivis Ecclesiæ, truncari & torqueri se non sinit, sed sui per omnia similis perseverat. 5. Istæ non omnia continent religionis mysteria explicitè, utpotè non ob id datæ, ut formulam exactam, & omnibus numeris absolutam nobis præscribant fidei, administrationis, Sacramentorum, aliorumque in Repub. Christiana necessariorum: sed occasione quadam, vel ad Judæos & hæreticos confutandos, vel ad abusus quosdam tollendos, vel ad fideles consolandos, à quibusdam scriptæ, & nonnullis Ecclesijs missæ. Illa autem (Ecclesiæ scil. scriptura) quam Spiritus Sanctus in cordibꝫ imprimere dignatus est, omnem veritatem in se habet, omnia fidei mysteria, omnemque rationem Christianæ religionis complectitur, & dubia omnia, quæ de fidei negotijs exoriri possunt, dissolvit &c. Ex quo sequitur, hanc scripturam (internam videlicet Ecclesiæ) esse omnium scripturarum interpretem, omnium opinionum Judicem, omnium errorum expultricem, à cujus judicio ad alium Judicem non liceat cuiquam provocare: Imò cujus judiciū judices omnes inspicere & sequi teneantur.

Quam eandem impietatem incrustavit etiam Andradius lib. 2. defensionis Concilij Tridentini: his verbis: Neque enim in ipsis libris, quibus Sacra mysteria conscripta sunt, quicquam inest divinitatis, quæ nos ad credendum, quæ illis continentur, religione aliquâ constringat: Sed Ecclesiæ, quæ Codices, illos sacros esse docet, & antiquorum Patrum fidem & pietatem commendat, tanta est vis & amplitudo, ut illis nemo sine gravissima impietatis nota, possit repugnare.

Cæterùm fœdior est propositionis hujus fœditas, quàm ut verbis satis exaggerari queat. Ille nimirum scopus, hic finis Jesuvvitis istis est præfixus, Costero præsertim & Andradio, ut exautoratis scripturis sacris, ad internum illud verbum, scriptum in cordibus vivis Ecclesiæ, hoc est, ad Tridentini conciliabuli decreta, ad Canones Conciliorum, ad traditiones Ecclesiæ, ad Responsa Pontificum Romanorum nos deducat, & sic Pontificibus Romanis ex quolibet contingendi potestatem atq; licentiam planè irrefragabilem asserant. Ubi initiò, sed tanquam ἐν παρόδῳ illud observandum fuerit, Jesuvvitis istis crassioribus cum Jure Canonico nullatenus convenire: Gratianus certè Juris istius Pontificij Cōpilator, scripturarum & Ecclesiæ autoritatem ad se mutuò comparans Dist. 9. Can. 5. classicum illum locum D. Augustini, desumtum ex Epist. 19. ad Hieronymum, fundamenti instar præsupponere voluit, qui sic habet: Ego solis eis scripturarum libris, qui jam Canonici appellantur, didici hunc honorem timoremq́; deferre, ut nullum eorum autorem in scribendo aliquid errasse, firmissimè credam: Alios autem ita lego, ut quantâlibet sanctitate, doctrinâq; polleant, non ideò verum putem, quia ipsi ita senserunt: sed quia mihi per alios autores, vel Canonicas vel probabiles rationes, quod à vero non abhorreat, persuadere potuerunt. Hactenus Jus Canonicum ex Augustino, cum quo, quomodo recentioribus Jesuvitis conveniat, ipsi viderint. Sed placet hujus etiam propositionis stupendam abominationem paulò accuratiùs excutere.

Ac primùm quidem ψευδογράφημα est: Scripturam sacram non esse datam, ut esset Canon sive regula fidei, & Religionis Christianæ. Cujus fœditatem infra Quæst. 6. quæ erit de perfectione Scripturarum, ex professo refutabimus. Sufficiat hoc loco unus ille Aphorismus Apostolicus, 2. Tim. 3, 16. ubi Paulus Scripturam utilem esse affirmat, non (uti Bellarminus contendit) ad commonitionem tantùm, sed ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem:& quidem non partialiter, sed totaliter: ut nimirum homo DEI sit PERFECTUS, ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus. Deindè, si talis est scriptura, qualis à Jesuvitis esse hoc loco perhibetur, quâ, quæso, fronte Canonicam illam appellitare possunt. Nam Canonica si est: Regula utique sit necesse est. Rursum Regula si est; utique perfecta, & fidei nostræ adæquata ea sit necesse est. Quæ enim talis non estne regula, quidem dici potest. Sed de hac Quæstione infrà fusiùs Quæst. 6. quæ erit de perfectione scripturarum.

Alterum ψεῦδος est: Scripturam sacram non esse digito DEI exaratam: neque DEUM voluisse Ecclesiam suam à chartaceis scriptis pendêre: multò minùs membranis Mysteria sua committere. Patet hujus quoque abominationis execranda fœditas multipliciter. 1. D. Apostolus disertè affirmat, Scripturam esse θεόπνευστον, 2. Tim. 3, 16. Ergò Scriptura primum autorem habet ipsum DEUM. Deindè: Etsi DEUS non immediatè consignavit scripturam:sed Prophetarum & Apostolorum uti voluit calamo & ministerio: nihil tamen propterea decedit autoritati scripturæ. DEUS enim est, & DEUS quidem solus, qui Prophetis & Apostolis inspiravit, non modò quæ loquerentur, sed & quæ scriberent: atque illorum ore lingvis, manibus, calamo usus est. Ergò vel hoc respectu, Scriptura etiam, quatenus talis, à DEO ipso est exarata. Prophetæ enim ac Apostoli tantùm fuerunt Organa. Et edisserant, quæso, Adversarij, Ubinam & quando DEUS Verbum suum immediatè scripserit in corda Ecclesiæ? Certè jam indè post lapsum protoplastorum DEUS in plantanda & colligenda Ecclesia usus est ministerio Patriarcharũ, Prophetarum & Apostolorum: qui illud ipsum verbum, quod viva voce annunciarunt, postmodum jussu DEI literis consignarunt, ut ex eo subindè in terris hisce colligeretur Ecclesia.

Et quæ, obsecro, hæc est vesania, imò blasphemia, affirmare, Christum noluisse Ecclesiam suam alligatam ad scripta chartacea Apostolorum? Quid enim, quæso, sibi vult aliud Apostol9, Eph. 2, 20. asserens, Ecclesiam esse superstructam super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, quam Ecclesiam esse alligatam ad Scripturam Propheticam & Apostolicam, sive chartis, sive membranis comprehensam? Nam perquàm frivolum ac nugatorium est, quòd Jesuvitæ excipiunt, D. Apostolum non loqui de Scriptura Prophetica & Apostolicæ: sed de doctrinâ, hoc est, viva eorum prædicatione. Quasi verò prædicatio Prophetarum & Apostolorum eadem non fuerit cum eorundem Scriptura. Quid, quòd verba Apostoli luculenter confirmant: per fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum rectiùs ipsam Scripturam, quatenus Scriptura est, intelligi. Manifestum enim est, quod Paulus Prophetas cum Apostolis conjungit: Jam verò quis ita bardus foret, ut affirmaret, tempore Pauli Prophetas vivâ voce prædicasse, cùm illos jam pridem fatis concessisse constet. Atqui Apostolus super horum etiam fundamentum, Ecclesiam superstructam esse asserit. Quin ergò non viva horum prædicatio, sed Scriptura intelligi debeat, nemini potest esse dubium. Tandem perquàm absurdum foret, statuere, Ecclesiam fundatam esse super eam prædicationem Prophetarum & Apostolorum, quæ brevi tempore duravit, & multis abhinc seculis desiit ac cessavit.

Tertium propositionis Jesuuviticæ βδέλυγμα est: Scripturas sacras nihil in se continere divinitatis, quod quidem ad credendum illis nos possit constringere. Rationem subjiciunt Jesuvvitæ nonnulli istam: Quia nimirum Scriptura loqui non potest. Sed hujus etiam abominationis fœditas ultrò patet. 1. enim DEUS ipse autor est scripturarum, & singula verba singula DEI sunt eloquia, proinde nisi DEUS ipse nihil in se divinitatis habere asseratur: affirmari utique haud potest, scripturas divinitate eâ destitui, quæ nos ad credendum eis constringere possit.

Deindè, loquitur DEUS in Scripturis nobiscum, quasi ore ad os per Spiritum suum Sanctum, qui per Scripturas corda nostra ita movet, ut verbum hoc DEI in Scripturis lectum, sit quovis gladio ancipiti penetrantius, pertingens usque ad divisionem animæ simul ac spiritus, compagumque & medullarum, & dijudicans cogitationes & conceptiones cordis. Hebr. 4, 12.

Tertiò, Scriptura sacra habet se instar principij: id quod vel inviti fateri coguntur ipsi Jesuvvitæ, dum interrogati, unde habeat Ecclesia, quod errare non possit? Recurrunt ad Scripturæ promissiones Ecclesiæ datas, tanquam ad prima principia: Sic rogati, ubinam Pontificatus Romanus, cum ejus autoritate sit fundatus? Recurrunt ad Scripturas proferentes illud Matth. 16, 18. Tu es Petrus, & super &c. & illud Luc. 22, 38. Ecce duo gladij hîc. Sic ipsi innuentes, Scripturas habere se instar principij. Jam si in reliquis scientijs, principia sunt ἀναπόδεικτα quippè ex se certissima: multò certè magis Scripturarum principia, quorum autor non est homo aliquis, sed Spiritus Sanctus, illud divinitatis in se continebunt, ut fidem ex se mereantur, & ad credendum nos constringant.

Quartò, Lucas in proœmio sui Evangelij Jesuvviticam hanc collationem funditùs evertit, scribens: Visum est mihi omnia altiùs repetita, penitiúsque consecuto ordine, de eis ad te scribere, præstantissime Theophile, ut ἵνα ἐπιγνῶς agnoscas earum rerum, de quibus informatus es, certam minimeque dubiam veritatem, τὴν ἀσφάλειαν, id est, non labefcentem firmitatem. Unde sic colligo: Si ideò necessarium fuit scripto consignari ea, quæ antea Theophilus ex informatione (περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων) didicerat, ut certam ac infallibilem istorum veritatem consequeretur: utique scriptura quatenus Scriptura, jam in se habebit illud divinitatis, quò nos ad credendum veritati constringere possit. At prius est verum, sic attestante Luca: Ratum Ergò & posterius. Ratio connexi est hæc: Nisi enim Scriptura, ut Scriptura, Theophilum ad credendum constringere potuisset: 1. non opus fuiffet illâ scriptione. 2. Ratio Evangelistæ planè esset impertinens: Quod utrumque cum absurdum sit, sequitur connexum Majoris esse firmum. Porrò, si hic usus Scripturæ locum habuit in Theophilo, qui ipsos tamen Apostolos docentes audivit: Quantò magis Scriptura hodiè usum istum exercet respectu nostri, imò respectu ipsius Ecclesiæ: ut videlicet non nisi vi ipsarum Scripturarum ad credendum divinis mysteriis ea constringatur.

Et quid multis opus est, cum D. Paulus Timotheo suo solas scripturas hoc nomine potissimùm commendet, quòd hæ instar omnium Magistrorum esse possint: illustri hoc subjecto Aphorismo: Hæ possunt te sapientem reddere ad salutem per fidem, quæ est in CHRISTO. 2. Tim. 3, 15.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Fourth falsehood is: That the Church is an internal Scripture inscribed by the Spirit of God upon the living hearts of the Church

THE FOURTH falsehood is: That the Church is an internal Scripture inscribed by the Spirit of GOD upon the living hearts of the Church.

But the vanity of this assertion is also easily detected. And first, indeed, it is a sophism of a vicious definition of the Church, and therefore a begging of the question: for by the Church the Jesuits understand the Pope with a Council: and they imagine that the Holy Spirit is so inspired into him by some secret breath that, even without the aid of the Scriptures, he is skilled in the mind and will of GOD, and consequently in the true and genuine understanding of the Scriptures. We ask for and expect an evident proof of all these things from Coster and his associates again and again. If they provide it, then at last we will labor over a response. Furthermore, that theological axiom is not more widely bruited than it is true: one and the same is the Scripture, both that which is committed to letters and that which is inscribed by the Holy Spirit upon the hearts of the faithful: so that it is a crime to wish to imagine two specifically different Scriptures. For the Scriptures sound in our ears and hearts, whether they are read, or preached, or pondered in any other way. For toward the conversion of hearts and faith, the Scriptures are not effective unless the internal power and operation of the Holy Spirit has been added. Now, indeed, whatever the Holy Spirit reveals to the Church and the faithful, He does not reveal it except through Scripture, and that indeed, either read or heard. And therefore, if the Holy Spirit speaks and teaches something through the Church, it is certainly not believed by us to be true because of some internal, I know not what, peculiar writing made in the living hearts of the Church: but because of some other more certain judgment, namely, because of the testimony of the Scriptures, with which we observe that the voice of the Church agrees. Thirdly, if the Jesuit Coster imagines in his brain some other immediate writing or revelation made to the Church and indeed beyond the Scriptures: come, let him produce at least one evident and firm testimony of this matter. For we shall soon see what the value is of those testimonies which he himself brings forward. To us it is certainly a persuasion that, just as miracles, so also immediate revelations outside the Scriptures have long since ceased: so that it is schismatic, fanatical, and furious to either boast of or seek after revelations in these centuries outside of Scripture. Finally, if one must absolutely take refuge in some internal writing, certainly not the Church, but Scripture itself will claim such for itself with the firmest right. For does the Church speak internally with us, just as the Holy Spirit speaks internally with us through Scripture? By no means: but the Church has only an external ministry, nor can it penetrate beyond the ears: and if it penetrates to the heart, then this happens from the power of the Holy Spirit, which He exerts through the Scriptures; for Scripture is always the medium and instrument which the Holy Spirit uses to renew our minds and to excite faith: since Scripture is always the word of GOD, and therefore also always true and apt as an instrument for producing faith and renewing our minds. The voice of the Church, however, insofar as it produces the opinion and testimony of the Church, is not the word of GOD in itself, nor is it necessarily true what it defines or pronounces of itself, and therefore it is in no way effective in itself for procuring the salvation of men. For whatever power the Church has for our regeneration or information, all of it consists not in the external and proper testimony of the Church, but in the authority of the Divine word, of which the Church is not the master, but the minister of its dispensation. With these things being so, it becomes plain that it is not some internal revelation, or peculiar writing, outside the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures: but rather these, and indeed these alone by the power of the Holy Spirit, that inform and teach the Church every truth: so that even if the Church were to be silent, yet this Scripture, being in itself the word of GOD, asserts the truth and speaks that which otherwise the Church is accustomed to provide through the scriptures or external ministry. It pleases me to illustrate this very thing more vigorously with some example. For let us ask Coster, Whence does he know and believe that a promise was made to Adam concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the head of the serpent? If he wishes to deal candidly with us, he must answer that he knows and believes that because of the assent of the Pope with a Council.

But I continue by asking: Whence does this present Church, that is, the Pontiff with the Council, know that to be true which was promulgated so many centuries ago: For the Roman Church was not then present to GOD who was making the promise: Therefore it is necessary that he answer again: either that this was revealed to the Church by GOD immediately through some internal writing outside the Scriptures: or because he himself sees that this cannot be defended or proven by any probable reason at least: it is necessary that he confess: that the authority of the Scripture provides that the Church knows and believes this. Whence it follows that not the testimony of the Church, or revelation outside the Scriptures, but the Scripture itself, consigned to letters, is the primary cause of our faith and knowledge.

The FIFTH falsehood is that the Church is better known than the Scriptures. That this is a vain figment is easily evident: For if you look not at the external bodies of men, but at the true nature of the Church itself, you will surely find the Scripture to be much better known and more illustrious than the Church: For if, as all Logicians and Theologians attest, we then finally know a thing when we have its proximate cause known and perceived: then we must necessarily know the Scripture before the Church, because the Scripture, as the proximate cause, creates and effects the Church. Furthermore, it is manifest that the only legitimate and safe doctrine of faith is that which is consonant with the Scriptures: Therefore the Scripture itself must necessarily be better known than the expositions of the Church or of any other Doctors, since all the expositions of all men must be reduced to and examined by the Scriptures as if by first principles. Finally, I distinguish between confused and distinct knowledge, and between the Church simply so called and the true Church. For although perhaps it is not denied that, according to some confused knowledge, it becomes known to us that there is some Church before it is established what Scripture is: yet in the order of nature, and according to distinct knowledge, Scripture is prior and better known than the true Church. For it is only from the Scriptures that a judgment can and ought to be made concerning the quality of the Church: as from a principle concerning its principled.

Latin:

QUARTUM ψεῦδος est: Ecclesiam esse Scripturam internam Spiritu DEI exaratam vivis cordibus Ecclesiæ.

Sed & hujus assertionis vanitas facilè deprehenditur. Ac primum quidem Sophisma est vitiosæ definitionis Ecclesiæ, ac proinde petitionis principij: per Ecclesiam enim intelligunt Jesuitæ Pontificem cum Concilio: & huic fingunt ita arcano quodam afflatu inspiratum esse Spiritum Sanctum, ut etiam sine Scripturarum adminiculo calleat mentem & voluntatem DEI, ac consequenter verum ac genuinum Scripturarum intellectum. Quorum omnium probationem evidentem ex Costero & socijs etiam atque etiam rogamus & expectamus. Quàm si dederunt, tum demùm de responsione laborabimus. Deindè non magis πολυθρύλλητον, quàm verum est illud axioma Theologicum: una eademque est Scriptura, tùm quæ literis est consignata, tùm quæ cordibus fidelium à Spiritu Sancto inscribitur: ita ut nefas sit, duas specie differentes Scripturas velle imaginari. Scripturæ enim in auribus & cordibus nostris sonant, sive legantur, sive prædicentur, sive quovis alio modo pensitentur. Nam ad cordium conversionem & fidem, Scripturæ non sunt efficaces, nisi interna Spiritus Sancti vis & operatio accesserit. Jam verò, quicquid Ecclesiæ & fidelibus revelat Spiritus Sanctus, illud non revelat, nisi per Scripturam, & eam quidem, vel lectam, vel auditam. Ac proindè, si Spiritus Sanctus aliquid per Ecclesiam loquitur & docet, non certè propter internam, nescio quàm peculiarem Scriptiònem factam in vivis cordibus Ecclesiæ, illud à nobis verum esse creditur: sed ob aliud quoddam certius judicium, nempe propter Scripturarum testimonium, cum quo vocem illam Ecclesiæ congruere animadvertimus. Tertiò, si aliquam aliam immediatam Scriptionem aut revelationem, Ecclesiæ factam & quidem præter Scripturas in cerebro suo fingat Jesuvvita Costerus: age, depromat hujus rei unicum saltem evidens & firmum testimonium. Nam cujus valoris ea sint testimonia, quæ ipse in medium profert, mox videbimus. Nobis certè est persuasissimũ, quemadmodum miracula, sic revelationes immediatas extra Scripturas jam pridem cessasse: ita ut schismaticum, fanaticum & furiosum sit, revelationes his seculis extra scripturam aut jactare, aut captare. Tandem, si ad internam quandam scriptionem omninò sit confugiendum, certè non Ecclesia, sed Scriptura ipsa talem sibi jure firmissimo arrogabit. Num enim Ecclesia internè loquitur nobiscum, quemadmodum Spiritus Sanctus internè nobiscum loquitur per Scripturam? Minimè verò: sed Ecclesiæ non nisi externum ministerium est, neque ultra aures penetrare potest: & si ad cor penetrat, tùm fit hoc ex virtute Spiritus Sancti, quam per Scripturas exerit, Scriptura enim semper est medium atque organum, quo Spiritus Sanctus utitur ad renovandas mentes nostras, & excitandam fidem: quandoquidem Scriptura semper est verbum DEI, ideoque etiam verum semper & aptum fidei procreandæ, nostrisque renovandis mentibus organum. Vox autem Ecclesiæ, quatenus Ecclesiæ sententiam ac testimonium prodit, non est verbum DEI per se, neque necessariò verum, quod ipsa ex se definit aut pronunciat, ac proindè ad salutem hominum procurandam nullo modo per se efficax. Quamcunque enim Ecclesia vim habet ad nostri sive regenerationem, sive informationem, ea omnis non in externo Ecclesiæ proprioque testimonio, sed in verbi Divini, cujus dispensandi Ecclesia non domina, sed ministra est autoritate consistit. Quibus ita se habentibus, palàm fit, non internam aliquam revelationem, sive peculiarem scripturam, extra Scripturas Propheticas & Apostolicas: sed has potius, & quidem solas virtute Spiritus Sancti, Ecclesiam informare & docere omnem veritatem: ita, ut si vel maximè taceat Ecclesia, tamen Scriptura hæc quippe per se verbum DEI, veritatem asserat & loquatur id, quod aliàs Ecclesia per scripturas, sive externum ministerium præstare solet. Placet exemplo aliquo hoc ipsum illustrare nervosius. Quæramus enim ex Costero, Unde sciat & credat Adamo factam esse promissionem de semine mulieris contrituro caput serpentis? Si candidè nobiscum agere velit, respondeat necesse est, se illud scire & credere propter assensum Pontificis cum Concilio.

Sed rogando pergo: Unde præsens hæc Ecclesia, hoc est, Pontifex cum Concilio sciat, verum esse id, quod usque adeò multis retrò seculis promulgatum fuit: Neque enim affuit tum Romana Ecclesia promittenti DEO: Rursum ergo respondeat necesse est: vel esse hoc per internam quandam scriptionem extra Scripturas Ecclesiæ à DEO immediatè revelatum: vel quia prius istud ipsemet videt, nulla saltem probabili ratione defendi aut comprobari posse: fateatur necesse est: Scripturæ autoritatem præstare, ut hoc sciat & credat Ecclesia. Unde consequens, non testimonium Ecclesiæ, aut revelationem extra Scripturas, sed Scripturam ipsam, literis consignatam, esse primariam nostræ fidei scientiæque causam.

QVINTVM ψεῦδος est, Ecclesiam esse notiorem Scripturis. Vanum & hoc figmentum esse, facilè patet: Nam si non in externa hominum corpora, sed in ipsam Ecclesiæ veram naturam inspicias, scripturam profectò multò notiorem atque illustriorem Ecclesiâ deprehendes: Si enim attestantibus omnibus Logicis & Theologis, tùm demùm rem cognoscimus, quando causam ejus proximam habemus cognitam & perspectam: utique Scripturam prius etiam noscamus necesse est, quàm Ecclesiam, proptereà, quod Scriptura tanquàm causa proxima procreat atque efficit Ecclesiam. Deinde manifestum est eam solam esse legitimam & tutam fidei doctrinam, quæ Scripturis est consentanea: Ergò Scriptura ipsa notior sit necesse est, tùm Ecclesiæ, tùm quorumvis aliorum Doctorum expositionibus, quandoquidem omnes omnium expositiones ad Scripturas tanquam ad prima principia redigendæ atque examinandæ sunt. Tandem distingvo inter notitiam confusam & discretam, & inter Ecclesiam simpliciter sic dictam & Ecclesiam veram. Etsi enim fortè non negatur, secundum confusam aliquam notitiâ, prius nobis innotescere, esse aliquam Ecclesiam, quàm constet, quid sit scriptura: Naturæ tamen ordine, & secundum discretam notitiam prior est & notior Scriptura, quàm sit Ecclesia vera. Nam ex scripturis demum de Ecclesiæ qualitate fieri potest & debet Judicium: tanquam ex principio de suo principiato.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Sixth and last falsehood is: That the Church is older than the Scriptures, and therefore all authority of the Scriptures necessarily…

The SIXTH and last falsehood is: That the Church is older than the Scriptures, and therefore all authority of the Scriptures necessarily depends upon the Church.

But a base Sophistry of the Accident is committed: For the holy Scripture has its substance and its Accident. The substance is the very word of GOD revealed and handed down through the Prophets and Apostles. The Accident, however, is the writing itself on papers or membranes. Now if you look at this Accident, we do not unwillingly grant that there was a time when the word of GOD was not yet consigned to letters, and in this respect the Church is older than the Scripture, insofar as it is called Scripture. However, this Accident does not prove that which the Jesuits deservedly ought to have proven: namely, that the Church exceeds the scriptures in authority because the scripture was only related to letters after the Church was already collected. For that this consequence is false is evident from the fact that in this question the controversy is not about the Accident, but about the substance, which that Accident cannot weaken or render more contemptible. For although this Accident, namely this writing, also has its own dignity, insofar as it was itself inspired by the Holy Spirit and in a way dictated verbatim: so that no iota was inscribed by the Prophets and Apostles in those books which is not θεόπνευστον: yet the antiquity and authority, about which there is the greatest controversy between us and our Adversaries, considers primarily the substance itself of the scripture: which, considered in this way, that is, accepted as the word of GOD, is necessarily prior and older than the Church, since the latter obtains its τὸ εἶναι solely from the former. Furthermore, the Jesuitical proposition proceeds from that false hypothesis: As if everything that is prior and older in time is also prior in dignity, or more excellent than that which is later in time. The vanity of which hypothesis our people have hitherto evidently refuted by the example of John the Baptist, who, although prior in time to Christ, it is certain was not therefore more excellent in authority. Likewise by the example of the Levitical Sacrifices, which, by reason of time, were older than the sacrifice of CHRIST, yet it is certain they were not likewise more excellent in value, efficacy, and authority. With these things thus established, I finally conclude against the Jesuits as follows. Just as the word of GOD, before it was consigned to letters, had authority from itself, being indeed brought forth by GOD himself, and not by the Church: So after it was produced in the monuments of letters, it equally has its authority from itself, being indeed divinely inspired, and it did not have to beg for precarious authority from the Church: but it was in itself and from itself, always is today, and will perpetually be αὐτόπιστον: But the Jesuits willingly grant that former point concerning the word not yet written. Therefore, it is necessary that they concede this latter point concerning the word already written. The connection of the Major premise is thence sufficiently evident: That just as there is one and the same GOD: so there is one and the same word, always like itself, both by reason of the efficient cause, and by reason of the matter, and by reason of the end and effect.

But before we depart from here, it will be worth the effort to respond to the principal arguments by which the Adversaries attempt to convince others of their proposition. The first place is easily taken by that classic passage, Matthew 16:18. Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it: And v. 19. I will give to thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: Whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth, shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth, shall be loosed in heaven. For from these words the Jesuits conclude: That supreme authority and infallible judgment over the scriptures themselves has been granted to Peter and all his successors, the Roman Pontiffs. But, passing over those things which have been said by others on this passage sufficiently learnedly and vigorously, it pleases me to note only the principal Sophisms in order.

And at the beginning, indeed, a shameful Ignoratio Elenchi occurs regarding the word Rock, which in the Jesuit sense does not signify the person of Peter, but the confession already issued by Peter, or rather Christ the Savior himself, who in 1 Cor. 10:4 is expressly named the Rock, and in 1 Pet. 2:7 & 8 the cornerstone. And that the Church is built upon this rock or cornerstone, the Apostle testifies in Eph. 2:21. It would therefore be sacrilege to assign to the person of Peter that honor which Christ claims for himself alone.

Next, the adversaries use sophistry when they wish these two words (Peter & Rock) to be synonyms, for this manifestly conflicts with the very τῷ ῥητῷ of Christ's words and the different termination of the same. For thus says Christ, 'You are Peter, and upon this rock,' etc. Where, indeed, even a boy understands that there are two distinct statements, the former of which looks to Peter; the latter to his confession already issued, in this sense: Not in vain did I bestow upon you the name of Peter, seeing that you have issued such a firm monument of your faith that the Church, leaning upon this faith of yours, can easily withstand the assault of the gates of hell.

Thirdly, in the sacred scriptures it is no less a ψευδογράφημα to affirm that the Church is built upon the foundation of either Peter or any other man, than it is to say that faith itself must be fixed upon a man.

Fourthly, the words of Christ can by no means apply to Peter alone. For if they did apply, they would apply either by reason of his person, or by reason of his faith, or by reason of his ministry. But not by reason of his person, because man, as man, cannot be the foundation of the Church: Not by reason of his faith, because this does not personally belong to Peter alone: For Peter did not believe alone that Christ is the Son of God, but all the remaining Apostles, indeed every single believer, who in respect of faith can not ineptly be called Peters, seeing that, as Peter testifies in chapter 2, verse 5, they are living stones, built into the sacred edifice of the Church, which is the house of the living GOD. Finally, not by reason of his Ministry: For thus this Pontifical dignity would likewise apply to the remaining Apostles, who were called by Christ to the ministry just as immediately as Peter: nay, not only to these, but also to all faithful ministers of the Church, as they differ from Peter in no other way than that they were constituted for the Church to teach the Gospel mediately, while he was constituted immediately: which is a matter of accident: Otherwise, in building the same spiritual edifice of the Church, by the authority of the same Christ, and by the same preaching, they contribute their efforts to the same faith: so that by reason of ministry no evident ground of diversity can be given between them and Peter. Therefore, we conclude most firmly that by these words no Pontifical dignity whatsoever was granted to Peter alone.

Fifthly, it is a notable error that the Jesuits dream that in the words of Christ, by the keys, one must understand a mere and mixed authority over the scriptures, or an infallible and clearly ἀνυπεύθυνον judgment over the scriptures: For the keys, which were given to Peter, were granted to all legitimate Ministers of the Church, to whom, however, the Romanists themselves deny that this authority over the Scriptures was granted.

Sixthly, that authority of the keys was committed not only to Peter, but also to the remaining Apostles: Matt. 28:18, John 20:22 & 23.

But what need is there of many words, when the Gloss of the Pontifical Law in c. considerandum, distinct. 40, and Panormitanus in de Electione c. significasti, openly confess in these words: 'I will give you the keys,' etc., that the Pontificate of the Church was not conferred upon Peter: and consequently that no supreme Right or authority over the scriptures was given to him.

The Jesuits derive another argument from 1 Tim. 3:15. Where the Apostle calls the Church the pillar and ground of the truth. From which they conclude that the authority of Scripture depends upon the voice or testimony of the Church. But a shameful sophistry of a faulty consequent is committed. For although we do not deny that the Church sustains divine truth, so that it may not perish entirely among men: Since whatever divine truth there is in the world, it all resides in the Church, while the remaining part of men, who live outside the bosom of the Church, clearly do not see the truth. Yet it does not follow from that that the voice of the Church is greater than the Scriptures themselves: or: whatever the Church judges concerning the sacred Scriptures, that is immediately true and infallible. For first, whatever truth the Church has, it does not have it from itself, but from Scripture itself. Next, it does not have it by reason of any praetorian authority or power over the Scriptures: but only by reason of testimony, insofar as it testifies by its voice that this is the divine truth which Holy Scripture reveals clearly enough from itself. From which soon another sophism ἀπὸ τὸ πῆκαι ἁπλῶς emerges. Thirdly, it is one thing to retain and support the truth like a pillar, and to protect it from ruin, as far as testimony is concerned: which belongs not only to this or that Church, but to all Christians. But it is another thing to define and sanction the truth by one's own judgment, or to be unable to err in any matter that pertains to faith. The former we willingly grant to the Church with the Apostle: but the latter, not so. From which arises a third sophism of many questions: to which adheres a fourth, which is a begging of the question, for it is necessary that they first prove that the Apostle in this place assigns to the Church some praetorian and judicial power over the scriptures: before they strive to convince us of their delusion or rather impiety. That we do not believe this to have been the mind of the Apostle is prevented by the fact that he nowhere constitutes the Church as the foundation of Scripture: but vice versa: the Scriptures as the foundation of the Church, Eph. 2:21.

The Jesuit Costerus borrows the third testimony of Scripture from 1 John 2:20 and 27. You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things. The anointing which you have received from him abides in you: and you have no need that anyone should teach you: but the same anointing teaches you about all things, which is true and not a lie: and just as it has taught you, you will abide in him.

Whence the Jesuit gathers that it has been inspired into the Church immediately by the Holy Spirit what it ought to determine concerning the understanding of the Scriptures. Moreover, besides the sophistry of the ignorance of refutation, the Jesuit likewise betrays remarkable ignorance and malice. Ignorance, indeed, because he does not know what and of what kind this anointing is, of which John makes mention. Malice, however, because he restricts this gift of anointing to his own Church alone, that is, to the Pope with a Council. For it is evident even from this that John is not dealing with some secret inspiration made to the Pope outside the scriptures, but with the illumination of the Holy Spirit, and indeed one common to all the faithful equally, because he addresses not only the clergy, much less the Roman Pope, who at that time did not exist in the nature of things, but all the faithful, saying: You have an anointing from that Holy One: and the anointing which you have received remains in you. In which same sense the Apostle, also addressing the Corinthians, says: He who anointed us is God: And so that he may expressly establish both the definition of this anointing and its generality with respect to all the faithful, he immediately adds: Who also has sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts. Whence, against the Jesuit, we gather most evidently thus: Whoever are sealed unto eternal life by having received the earnest of the Spirit, they are anointed, with the anointing remaining in them. But the former applies to all the faithful equally. Therefore, the latter does as well. Both of the premises are clear from John and Paul, as has already been shown. Therefore, the truth of the conclusion will also remain unmoved. Now, if this anointing applies to all the faithful, then that supreme right over the holy scriptures will certainly also apply to all, provided that that anointing, as the Jesuits wish, denotes some such authority. And indeed, since the adversaries themselves easily understand that this is absurd and false, it becomes clear that the collection which they attempt to construct from that anointing for the sake of establishing the authority of the Church over the scriptures is erroneous. Pious antiquity was certainly ignorant of this Jesuitical collection, as is clear from Augustine, who interprets the words of the Apostle thus, in Tractate 3 on the Epistle of John: The anointing teaches you all things: What then shall we do, brothers, who teach you, if his anointing teaches us about all things? See a great mystery, brothers, the sound of our words strikes the ears: the Master is within. As far as I am concerned, I have spoken to all: but those to whom that anointing does not speak within, whom the Holy Spirit does not teach within, return untaught. External teachings are certain aids and admonitions: he who teaches hearts has his chair in heaven. Thus far Augustine, who interprets this anointing as the illumination of the Holy Spirit, common to all the faithful, and says that this anointing proceeds not from man, not even from him whose chair may be in Rome or in these lands: but in heaven, that is, from the Holy Spirit, effectively exercising this anointing in the heart of every pious person. Thus, therefore, collapses that entire structure which, out of ignorance of the refutation, Costerus wished to build with vain labor for the sake of establishing that supreme authority of the Church.

The adversaries seek the fourth and final foundation of their proof from chapter 5 of Augustine's Tractate against the Epistle of Manichaeus, where he writes thus about himself: I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved me. To which argument others respond in different ways, and most seize upon the fact that Augustine spoke thus about himself while he was still a Manichaean: which we leave to its own place. We, however, maintain that it can be most solidly answered to this objection from a consideration of the occasion by which Augustine was moved to burst forth into these words. And it is as follows: The Manichaeans were contending that that Epistle of Manichaeus, containing almost all their dogmas, was to be accepted and held in the same place as the Epistles of Paul. Here, therefore, Augustine replies that he could not accept the Epistle of Manichaeus in the same way as the Epistles of the Apostles, because for the receiving of these he had the testimony and recommendation of the Catholic Church, namely that those Epistles were written by the Apostles themselves: but concerning the Epistle of Manichaeus, he had nothing except the testimony of the Manichaeans. Therefore, if we thoroughly weigh Augustine's mind, he by no means makes the Church the judge of Scripture or of the canonical books, much less does he assign to it praetorian power over the scriptures: but he only permits it to bear testimony concerning them: and he opposes that very testimony of the Church, nay, prefers it to the testimony which the Manichaeans were bearing about the Epistle of Manichaeus. Which praise we today also willingly grant to the Church: but that its authority is thereby asserted to be superior to the Scriptures, that we utterly deny. For just as a witness does not have the power of approving or disapproving, according to his own whim and judgment, those things which he has seen or heard: but is compelled simply to narrate faithfully those things in whose doing he was present: so the Church does not have praetorian or judicial power over the Scriptures: but is bound only to bear faithful testimony concerning the Holy or Canonical Scriptures, namely that they were signed by those who could not err in writing: and that they contain heavenly truth in themselves, as above: Question 1, proposition 2, Orthodox; and proposition 1, Jesuitical.

Latin:

SEXTUM & postremum ψεῦδος est: Ecclesiam esse antiquiorem Scripturis, ac proindè omnem Scripturarum autoritatem dependere necessariò ab Ecclesia.

Sed turpis Sophisticatio Accidentis committitur: Scriptura enim sacra suam habet substantiam, suumq; Accidens. Substantia est, ipsum verbum DEI revelatum & per Prophetas & Apostolos traditum. Accidens verò est, ipsa Scriptio in chartas sive membranas. Jam si Accidens hoc spectes, haud inviti largimur, fuisse tempus, quando verbum DEI nondum fuit literis consignatum, & hoc respectu Ecclesiâ antiquiorem esse Scripturâ, quatenùs dicitur Scriptura, Cæterùm hoc Accidens non probat id, quod meritò probare debebant Jesuvvitæ: ideò videli cet Ecclesia autoritate superare scripturas, quia post Ecclesiam jam collectam scriptura demum in literas sit relata. Falsum enim hoc esse consequens, vel inde constat, quod in quæstione hac non controvertitur de Accidente, sed de substantia, quam Accidens illud labefactare aut contemptiorem reddere non potest. Etsi enim Accidens hoc, nempe scriptio isthæc suam quoque habet dignitatem, quatenùs videlicet & ipsa a Spiritu Sancto fuit inspirata, & quodammodo verbatim dictata: ita ut nullum Jota a Prophetis & Apostolis in istis libris sit exaratum, quod non sit θεόπνευστον: Antiquitas tamen & autoritas, de qua maximè inter nos & Adversarios controvertitur, præcipuè considerat ipsam substantiam scripturæ: quæ hoc modo considerata, hoc est, pro verbo DEI accepta, necessariò prior est & antiquior Ecclesia, siquidem hæc ex illa suum τὸ εἶναι unicè obtinet. Deinde procedit Jesuvitica propositio ex falsa ista hypothesi: Quasi omne, quod tempore prius est & antiquius, sit etiam prius dignitate, sive præstantius eo, quod est tempore posterius. Cujus hypothesews vanitatem evidenter nostri hactenus refutârunt, Exemplo Johannis Baptistæ, quem Christo quidem tempore priorem, non tamen propterea autoritate præstantiorem fuisse, constat. Item Exemplo Sacrificiorum Leviticorum, quæ ratione temporis, sacrificio CHRISTI antiquiora, non tamen itidem valore, efficacia & autoritate præstantiora fuisse constat. Quibus ita constitutis, sic tandem contra Jesuvitas colligo. Quemadmodum verbum DEI, antequam literis est consignatum, ex se autoritatem habuit, quippè a DEO ipso prolatum, non verò ab Ecclesia: Ita postquam proditum illud est literarum monumentis, æque suam ex se autoritatem, quippe divinitùs inspiratum, habet, non verò precariam demùm ab Ecclesia autoritatem emendicare necesse habuit: sed ipsum in se & ex se, fuit semper hodieque est & perpetuò erit αὐτόπιστον: Sed prius illud de verbo nondum scripto ultrò largiuntur Jesuvitæ. Posterius ergò hoc de verbo jam scripto concedant necesse est. Connexum Majoris inde satis evidenter patet: Quod sicut unus & idem est DEUS: ita unum idemque est verbum, sibique semper simile, tùm ratione causæ efficientis, tùm ratione materiæ, tùm ratione finis & effectus.

Cæterùm priusquam hinc abeamus, operæ pretium fuerit ad præcipua respondere argumenta, quibus Adversarii propositioni suæ fidem facere conantur. Primum autem facilè locum fortitur illud Classicum, Matth. 16, 18. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc, petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam; & portæ inferorum non prævalebunt adversus eam: Et v. 19. Tibi dabo claves regni Cælorum: Quicquid ligaveris in terra, erit ligatum in cœlis: & quicquid solveris in terra, erit solutum in cœlis. Ex his enim verbis colligunt Jesuvitæ: Petro & omnibus ejus successoribus, Pontificibus Romanis, autoritatem summam, atq; judicium infallibile in ipsas scripturas esse concessum. Sed ut prætermissis illis, quæ ab alijs in hunc locum satis eruditè & nervosè dicta sunt, placet præcipua tantùm Sophismata ordine annotare.

Ac initiò quidem turpis occurrit Ignoratio Elenchi in vocabulo Petræ, quæ non in sensu Jesuvitico personam Petri, sed confessionem jam à Petro editam, imò potiùs ipsum Christum Servatorem significat, qui 1. Cor. 10, 4. Petra, 2. Pet. 2. 7. & 8. Lapis angularis expressè nominatur. Et huic petræ sive lapidi angulari superstructam esse Ecclesiam, testatur Apostolus. Ephes. 2, 21. Sacrilegium proindè fuerit, Personæ Petri illum assignare honorem, quem Christus sibi soli vendicat.

Deindè Sophisticantur Adversarij, quando duo hæc vocabula (Petrus & Petra) volunt esse Synonyma, pugnat enim hoc manifestè cum ipso τῷ ῥητῷ verborum Christi, & diversa eorundem terminatione. Sic enim Christus, Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram &c. Ubi profectò duas distinctas enunciationes esse, etiam puer intelligit, quarum prior respicit Petrum; posterior ejusdem confessionem jam editam hoc sensu: Non frustra Petri appellationem tibi indidi, quippè, qui usque adeò firmum fidei tuæ monumentum edidisti, ut Ecclesia huic fidei tuæ innixa, portarum infernalium impetum facilè sustinere possit.

Tertiò, in scripturis sacris haud levius ψευδογράφημα est, affirmare Ecclesiam esse superstructam super fundamentum sive Petri, sive cujusquam alterius hominis; quàm fidem ipsam in hominem figendam esse.

Quartò, verba Christi soli Petro competere nulla ratione possunt. Si enim competerent, tùm vel ratione personæ, vel ratione fidei, vel ratione ministerij competerent. Non autem ratione personæ, quia homo, ut homo, fundamentum Ecclesiæ esse nequit: Non ratione fidei, quia hæc soli Petro personaliter haud convenit: Neque enim solus Petrus credidit, Christum esse Filium Dei, sed reliqui Apostoli omnes, imò singuli atque universi fideles, qui respectu fidei haud ineptè Petri nominari possunt, quippè, qui teste Petro 1. cap. 2, 5 vivi sunt lapides, extructi in sacro Ecclesiæ ædificio, quæ est domus DEI viventis. Non denique ratione Ministerij: Sic enim dignitas hæc Pontificialis itidem competeret reliquis Apostolis, qui æquè ac Petrus à Christo immediatè ad ministerium sunt vocati: quin non his modò, sed & omnibus fidelibus Ecclesiæ ministris, ut qui à Petro non alia ratione differunt, quàm quòd hi mediatè, ille verò immediatè Ecclesiæ ad docendum Evangelium fuit constitutus: id quod Accidentis est: Aliàs in eodem Ecclesiæ Spirituali ædificio extruendo, ejusdem Christi autoritate, eâdem prædicatione in eandem fidem operas suas conferunt: ut ratione ministerij inter hos & Petrum ulla evidens diversitatis ratio dari non possit.
