Proindè firmissimè colligimus, soli Petro his verbis nihil quicquam dignitatis Pontificalis esse concessum.

Quintò, insignis error est, quòd Jesuvitæ somniant, in verbis Christi per claves intelligi debere, merum ac mixtum imperium in scripturas, sive Judicium infallibile & planè ἀνυπεύθυνον in scripturas: Claves enim, quæ datæ sunt Petro, omnibꝫ legitimis Ecclesiæ Ministris sunt concessæ, quibus tamen imperium illud in Scripturas concessum esse, ipsi negant Romanenses.

Sextò, Autoritas ista clavium non Petro tantùm, sed & reliquis Apostolis fuit commissa: Matth. 28, 18. Johan. 20, 22. & 23.

Sed quid multis opus est, cum Glossa Juris Pontificij in c. considerandum, distinct. 40. & Panormitanus de Electione c. significasti, apertè fateantur his verbis: Tibi dabo claves &c. Petro non esse collatum Pontificatum Ecclesiæ: & per consequens neque datum ipsi esse summum aliquod Jus, aut imperium in scripturas.

Alterum argumentum desumunt Jesuvitæ ex 1. Tim. 3, 5. Ubi D. Apostolus Ecclesiam nominat columnam & stabilimentum veritatis. Undè colligunt Autoritatem Scripturæ pendere ex voce sive testimonio Ecclesiæ. Sed turpis committitur Sophisticatio vitiosi consequentis. Etsi enim non imus inficias, quòd Ecclesia veritatem divinam sustentet, ne videlicet prorsus inter homines intercidat: Siquidem quicquid in mundo divinæ veritatis est, id totum in Ecclesia conversatur, cum reliqua pars hominum, qui extra gremium Ecclesiæ versantur, veritatem planè non videat. Non tamen indè sequitur, vocem Ecclesiæ majorem esse Scripturis ipsis: aut: quicquid Ecclesia de Scripturis sacris judicat, id statim verum esse & infallibile. Primùm enim quicquid veritatis habet Ecclesia: illud ex se non habet, sed ex Scriptura ipsa. Deindè non habet illam ratione prætoriæ alicujus autoritatis, sive potestatis in Scripturas: sed tantùm ratione testimonij, quatenùs videlicet sua voce testatur, eam esse: divinam veritatem, quam Scriptura Sacra ex se ipsa satis luculenter prodit. Undè mox alterum Sophisma ἀπὸ τὸ πῆκαι ἁπλῶς emergit. Tertiò, longè aliud est, veritatem retinere, & suffulcire instar columnæ, atque à ruina tueri, quoad testimonium: id quod non huic, vel illi tantùm Ecclesiæ, sed omnibus Christianis competit. Aliud verò est, ex proprio arbitrio definire ac sancire veritatem, vel in nulla re, quæ ad fidem spectat, posse errare, Prius quidem illud Ecclesiæ cum Apostolo libenter largimur: Posterius verò hoc non item. Undè tertium Sophisma plurium quæstionum oritur: cui adhæret Quartum, Quod est petitionis principij, prius enim probent necesse est, Apostolum hoc loco prætoriam quandam, & judicialem in scripturas potestatem Ecclesiæ assignare: quàm ut indè suo delirio vel impietati potiùs fidem facere studeant. Quô minus nos hanc mentem Apostolo fuisse credamus, obstat, quòd ipse nuspiam Ecclesiam constituit fundamentum Scripturæ: sed vice versa: Scripturas fundamentum Ecclesiæ, Ephes. 2, 21.

Tertium Scripturæ Testimonium mutuatur Jesuvvita Costerus ex 1. Johan. 2, 20. & 27. Vos Unctionem habetis à Sancto profectam, & nostis omnia. Unctio quam accepistis ab eo, manet in vobis: nec necesse habetis, ut quisquam doceat vos: Verùm eadem Unctio docet vos de omnibus, quæ & verax est, & non mendax: & sicut docuit vos manebitis in eo.

Unde colligit Jesuvvita, Ecclesiæ immediatè à Spiritu Sancto esse inspiratum, quid de Scripturarum intellectu statuere debeat. Cæterùm præter Sophisticationem παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχη, insignem pariter inscitiam & malitiam prodit Jesuvvita. Inscitiam quidem, quod nescit, Quæ & qualis hæc sit unctio, cujus Johannes meminit. Malitiam verò, quod donum hoc unctionis, ad solam suam Ecclesiam, hoc est, Põtificem cum Concilio restringit. Neque enim de arcana aliqua inspiratione extra scripturas Pontifici facta: sed de illuminatione Spiritus Sancti, & quidem omnibus fidelibus ex æquo communi agere Johannem, vel indè patet, quòd non solos Clericos, nedum Pontificem Romanum, qui tùm in rerum natura non erat, sed omnes fideles, alloquens, Vos, inquit, Unctionem habetis à Sancto illo: & Unctio, quam vos accepistis, manet in vobis. Quo eodem sensu Apostolus etiam Corinthios compellans: Qui unxit nos inquit, Deus est: Et ut unctionis hujus tùm definitionem, tùm generalitatem respectu omnium fidelium disertè astruat, statim subjicit: Qui etiam obsignavit nos, deditquè arrhabonem Spiritus in cordibus nostris. Unde adversus Jesuvvitam sic evidentissimè colligimus: Quicunquè accepto Spiritus arrhabone ad vitam æternam obsignantur, illi sunt uncti, unctione in ipsis permanente. At prius illud omnibus fidelibus ex æquo competit. Ergò & hoc posterius. Utraque præmissarum patet ex Johanne & Paulo, uti jam ostensum Constabit Ergò Conclusioni sua etiam immota veritas. Jam si fidelibus omnibus unctio isthæc competit:utique omnibus etiam competet summum illud jus in scripturas sanctas: dummodò unctio illa, prout Jesuvvitæ volunt, talem aliquam autoritatem denotet. Ac verò cùm absurdum falsumque hoc esse, ipsi facilè intelligant Adversarij, palàm fit erroneam esse collectionem, quàm pro stabilienda autoritate Ecclesiæ supra scripturas ex Unctione ista extruere conantur. Ignoravit sanè collectionem istam Jesuvviticam pia Antiquitas: uti patet ex Augustino, qui verba Apostoli sic interpretatur, Tractatu 3. in epistolam Johannis: Unctio vos docet omnia: Quid ergò nos faciamus fratres, qui docemus vos, si unctio ejus docet nos de omnibus: Videte magnum mysterium fratres, Sonus Verborum nostrorum aures percutit: Magister intus est, Quantum ad me attinet, omnibus locutus sum: sed quibus Unctio illa intus non loquitur, quos Spiritus Sanctus intus non docet, indocti redeunt. Magisteria forinsecus adjutoria quædam sunt, & admonitiones: Cathedram in Cœlo habet, qui corda docet. Hactenus Augustinus, qui Unctionem istam, de illuminatione SpiritusSancti, omnibus fidelibus communem interpretatur, & Unctionem hanc promanare dicit non ab homine, non ab eo etiam, cujus Cathedram sit Romæ, vel in terris hisce: sed in cœlo, hoc est, à Spiritu Sancto, in cujusvis pij corde efficaciter hanc unctionem exercente. Sic ergò corruit structura illa universa, quàm ex Ignoratione Elenchi, Costerus pro astruenda summa illa Ecclesiæ autoritate, irrito labore ædificare voluit.

Quartum & postremum probationis Fundamentum petunt Adversarij ex cap. 5. Tractatus Augustini contra Epistolam Fundamenti, ubi de se sic scribit: Ego Evangelio non crederem, nisi me Catholicæ Ecclesiæ commoveret Autoritas. Ad quod sanè argumentum alij aliter respondent, & plerique illud arripiunt, Quod Augustinus de se, adhuc Manichæo, sic locutus sit : id quod suo nos loco relinquimus: Statuimus autem solidissimè ad objectum istud responderi posse, ex consideratione τῆς ἀφορμῆς, quâ motus Augustinus in hæc verba proruperit. Ea autem sic habet: Contendebant Manichæi, Epistolam illam Fundamenti, continentem penè omnia ipsorum dogmata, pari accipiendam habendamquè esse loco, quo Epistolæ Pauli. Hic ergò respondet Augustinus, se haud posse eâdem ratione accipere Epistolam Fundamenti, quâ Epistolas Apostolorum, propterea quòd de his recipiendis testimonium haberet & commendationem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, quod videlicet Epistolæ illæ ab ipsis Apostolis essent scriptæ: De Epistola verò Fundamenti, nihil præter Manichæorum haberet testimonium. Proindè si penitùs Augustini mentem expendamus, nequaquam ille Ecclesiam facit Judicem Scripturæ sive librorum Canonicorum, ne dum prætoriam ei potestatem in scripturas assignat: Sed Testimonium tantummodò de his ferre permittit: & id ipsum Testimonium Ecclesiæ opponit, imò anteponit Testimonio, quod de Epistola Fundamenti ferebant Manichæi. Quod elogium nos hodieq; Ecclesiæ ultrò largimur: sed ut indè superior asseratur ejus autoritas Scripturis: id verò pernegamus. Quemadmodum enim testis non habet potestatē probandi vel improbādi, pro suo lubitu ac arbitrio, ea quæ vidit aut audivit: sed simpliciter ea narrare fideliter cogitur, quibꝫ agendis interfuit: Ita Ecclesia non habet potestatem prætoriam sive judiciariam in Scripturas: sed fidelitèr tantùm testimonium ferre tenetur de Scripturis Sacris sive Canonicis, quòd nimirùm ab ijs sint cōsignatæ, quæ in scribendo errare non potuerunt: quodque cœlestem veritatem in se contineant, uti supra: Quæst. 1. propositione 2. Orthodoxa; & proposit. 1. Jesuitica.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Question III. General. Concerning the various editions of the Biblical books, and their authority

QUESTION III. GENERAL. Concerning the various editions of the Biblical books, and their authority.

There are two main points which come into controversy regarding the proposed Question. For in the beginning, since various and very many editions of the Biblical books are available today, it is not without reason asked: Which one of them all is authentic, and deserves credence above all the rest? Then, indeed, this also is disputed: Whether it is for the benefit of the Church and the Christian religion that Holy Scripture be translated into the language vernacular to each nation or people, so that it may be read and known not only by the more learned, but also by the laity. Concerning both of which questions, since the Jesuit order greatly disagrees with us, it is our pleasure at the beginning to comprehend the thesis of our Churches in a few propositions.

I. PROPOSITION. Thetic.

The Hebrew edition of the Old, and the Greek of the New Testament, is the sincere and authentic Scripture of God: Nay, the fountain to which, in all doubts concerning the interpretation of the Scriptures, as also in the adjudication of controversies, one must always and solely have recourse.

CONFIRMATION.

The truth of the proposition is evident even from this, that Moses and the Prophets of the Old Testament consigned their books and writings in no other than the Hebrew, which is indeed the most ancient; but the Evangelists and Apostles consigned the books and writings of the New Testament in no other than the Greek language; that the Hebrew language is certainly the most ancient of all, and that not only our first parents, but also their long posterity until the confusion of languages, which occurred in the year of the world 1790, used this language alone, Moses himself testifies quite clearly. Gen. 11, 1. He says, The whole earth was of the same lip, and the words were the same. Where that is very emphatic which Moses subjoins in v. 7 and 9: that at the building of Babel, the lip of the whole earth was first confused, that is, then first it began to be divided and various and manifold, which before had been simple, undivided, and unique: Which Mosaic passage Chrysostom also explains, homily 30 on Genesis. It is evident from this, he says, that before the construction of the tower of Babel, there was one natural language for all men, and all mortals used the same speech. The judgment of Philastrius, Bishop of Brescia, is therefore rash, who in the Catalogue of Heresies, chapter 106, rejects this opinion of ours and of Chrysostom, although suppressing his name, as heretical, asserting: that it must be firmly believed that even before the building of Babel, for many centuries, there were many varieties of speech and languages. For that which Moses says: that the earth was of one lip, was said because, although there were many kinds of languages, everyone nevertheless understood one another, and there was one language and the same speech for all, not according to the same use of words, but according to the same understanding of meanings. But the Mosaic text is too clear to be overturned in any way by this weak cavil of Philastrius: so that Alphonsus de Castro, in book 9 against heresies, rightly branded Philastrius with the crime of heresy in this part. Nor can it stand against this assertion that Moses writes in the preceding chapter, 10, 5, that the seven sons of Japheth divided the islands of the nations in their regions, each according to their languages and families. For the thing itself speaks that Moses used a certain anticipation here: For the Holy Spirit, who spoke through Moses, does not disagree with Himself, much less can or should He be accused of any contradiction. And the Holy Scriptures are not infrequently accustomed to commemorate certain things by anticipation in such a way that, according to the surface of the letter, it seems to have happened before it actually occurred. Which very thing Augustine also observed in book 16 of the City OF GOD, chapter 4, writing: Although these nations are reported in chapter 10 of Genesis to have been in their own languages: yet Moses returns to that time when there was one language for all, and from there he now explains what happened so that the diversity of languages was born. And this is the first member of our confirmation.

Furthermore, after the confusion of tongues, there is no one from all of Antiquity who has doubted even in the slightest that Moses and the Prophets used only the Hebrew idiom in composing their writings, as witnessed by St. Jerome in epistle 142. Therefore, we rightly acknowledge the Hebrew edition of the Old Testament as the mother and fountain of all the rest, and with Canon Law, citing St. Augustine, we declare: Just as the reliability of the books of the Old Scripture is to be examined from the Hebrew volumes, so the truth of the New books requires the standard of the Greek language. dist. 9. c. ut veterum. Nor is it an obstacle that we read that certain things were written in the Chaldean idiom, partly in the prophecy of Daniel, and partly in the book of Ezra. For 1. the state of the Jewish people, who had then been led away into the Babylonian captivity, required the use of the Chaldean language, as it was familiar to everyone there, by a kind of right of its own. 2. There are very few things that bear a Chaldean style, so that Jerome rightly determined that they are not of such importance that we should not maintain that the whole Old Testament was written in Hebrew. Finally, since those very things written in Chaldean were inserted into the Prophetic books and have always earned canonical authority by the consent of the whole Catholic Church, he would be reasoning quite viciously and ὠδῆστο μη ἐπόμενον who would contend that any other language could be preferred to Hebrew in the Old, or Greek in the New Testament, by reason of faith and authority: a thing which modern Jesuits do quite ἀπαιδεύτως, preferring the Latin Vulgate in all ways to both Hebrew and Greek, as we shall show a little later.

III. But a more difficult question arises here: namely, whether that Hebrew Scripture which was composed by Moses and the Prophets has reached us, or whether it perished at the time of the Babylonian captivity and the burning of the Jerusalem Temple, and was only later restored by Ezra the priest. And indeed it is read in the 4th book of Ezra, ch. 4, 23, and ch. 14, 21 and 44, that the volume of the law had clearly perished, so that not even one copy remained for any of the Jews: and that Ezra, inspired by the divine Spirit, dictated for forty whole days to five men, who took down with the greatest speed what was said by him, and in this way the entire scripture, which had clearly perished, was recovered. To confirm this narrative, some enlist the Epistle of Basil to Chilo as support. But our blessed Luther rightly determines from Jerome that this fourth book of Ezra, as well as the third, contains many falsehoods, indeed, entirely old-wives' tales. For it would perhaps not be very difficult to demonstrate that this narrative, too, is nothing other than a Jewish fable.

Latin:

QUÆSTIO III. GENERALIS. De Varijs editionibus librorum Biblicorum, earundemquè autoritate.

DUo potissimùm sunt capita, quæ circa propositam Quæstionem in controversiam veniunt. Initiò enim cùm variæ eæque benè multæ hodiè prostent librorum Biblicorum editiones: haud immeritò quæritur; Quænam ex illis omnibus sit Authentica, & fidem præ reliquis omnibus mereatur? Deinde verò & illud controvertitur; Num ex usu sit Ecclesiæ & Religionis Christianæ, ut scriptura Sacra, in lingvam, cuique genti sive populo vernaculam, transferatur; ut sic non à doctioribus modò, sed & à Laicis legi & cognosci possit. De qua utraque Quæstione cum gens Jesuitica plurimium à nobis dissentiat, placet initiò nostrarum Ecclesiarum θέσιν paucis quibus dam complecti propositionibus.

I. PROPOSITIO. θετικὴ.

HEbræa Veteris; & Græca Novi Testamenti editio, est sincera & avthentica Dei scriptura: Imò fons, ad quem in omnibus dubijs Scripturarum interpretationibus; ut & controversiarum dijudicationibus, semper & unicè est recurrendum.

CONFIRMATIO.

PRopositionis veritas vel inde patet, quòd Moses & Prophetæ Veteris Testamenti, nullâ aliâ quàm Hebræa, quippe antiquissimâ: Evangelistæ verò & Apostoli, Novi Testamenti libro s & scripta, non nisi Græcâ lingvâ consignâruut; Hebræã certè lingvam omnium esse antiquissi mam, & non primos modò parentes nostros: sed & longam eorum posteritatem ad confusionem usq; lingvarum, quæ incidit in A. M. 1790. hac solâ lingvâ usam fuisse, Moyses ipse satis luculenter testatur. Gen. 11, 1. Fuit, inquiens, Universa terra ejusdem labij, & verba erant eadē. Ubi valdè emphaticum est illud, quòd Moses v. 7. & 9. subjicit: In ædificatione Babel, primùm confusum esse labium universæ terræ, hoc est, tunc primò divisum & varium multiplexq; esse cœpisse, quòd antè simplex indivifum & unicum fuerat: Quem locum Mosaicum Chrysostom9 etiam explicans, homilia 30. in Genesin. Constat hinc, inquit, ante extructionem turris Babel, unam fuisse omnium hominũ naturalem lingvam, eâdemq; loquelâ omnes mortales usõs. Temerariũ proindè est Judicium Philastrij Episcopi Brixiensis, qui in Catalogo hæreseœn cap. 106. nostram hanc & Chrysostomi sententiam, suppresso licet ipsius nomine, tanquam hæreticam reprobat, asserens: firmiter esse credendum, quòd etiam ante ædificationem Babel, multis seculis, plures fuerint sermonum ac lingvarum varietates. Nã quòd Moses dicit: terrã fuisse labij unius, ideo dictũ est, quia licèt plura essent genera lingvarũ, omnes tamen se invicem intelligebant, eratq; omnib9 lingva una & sermo idem, non secundum eundem vocabulorum usum, sed secundum eandem sensuum intelligentiam. Cæterùm dilucidior est textus Mosaicus, quàm ut elumbi hac cavillatione Philastrij ullatenus everti queat: Ita ut rectè Alphonsus de Castro lib 9 adversus hæreses, Philastrium hac in parte hæreseœs crimine notaverit. Neq; etiam assertioni huic obstare potest, quòd Moses cap præcedente 10, 5. scribit, Septem filios Japheti divisisse Insulas gentium, in regionibus suis, singulas secundum lingvas & cognationes suas. Nam anticipatione quadam hic usum esse Mosen, res ipsa loquitur: Neque enim Spiritus Sanctus, qui per Mosen locutus est, à seipso dissentit, multò minus contradictionis alicujus insimulari vel potest, vel debet. Et Scripturæ Sacræ haud infrequenter per anticipationẽ ita quædam commemorare folent, ut secundum superficiem literæ, antè videatur evenisse, quàm revera contigerunt. Quod ipsum observavit etiam Augustinus lib. 16. de Civit. DEI, cap. 4. scribens: Cùm in suis lingvis istæ gentes cap. 10. Geneseos fuisse referantur: redit tamen ad illud tempus Moses, quando una lingva omnium fuit, & indè jam exponit, quid acciderit, ut lingvarum diversitas nasceretur. Et hoc primum est confirmationis nostræ membrum.

Deindè verò post confusionem lingvarum, Mosen & Prophetas in exarandis suis scriptis non nisi Hebræo idiomate, usos fuisse, nemo est ex universa Antiquitate, qui vel tantillum dubitaverit, teste B. Hieronymo epistola 142. Proindè Hebræam editionem Veteris Testamenti, tanquam matrem & fontem reliquarum omnium, meritò agnoscimus, & cum Jure Canonico ex D. Augustino pronunciamus: Quemadmodum veterum Scripturæ librorum fides ex Hebræis voluminibus examinanda est: Ita Novorum librorum veritas, Græci sermonis normam desiderat. dist. 9. c. ut veterum. Neq; obstat, quòd partim in Prophetia Danielis, partim in libro Esdræ quædam Chaldaico idiomate scripta legimus. Nam 1. status populi Judaici, qui in captivitatem Babylonicam, tùm erat abductus, usum lingvæ Chaldaicæ, quippe omnibus ibi familiarem, suo quodam quasi jure requirebat. 2. pauca admodum sunt, quæ stylum Chaldaicum præ se ferunt, ut rectè statuerit Hieronymo, non tanti ea esse momenti, quô minùs totum Testamentum Vetus, Hebraicè scriptum statuamus. Tandem cùm illa ipsa Chaldaicè exarata libris Propheticis sint inserta, & Canonicam autoritatem totius Catholicæ Ecclesiæ consensu semper promeruerint: vitiosè omninò, & ὠδῆστο μη ἐπόμενον colligeret, qui ullam lingvam aliam, vel Hebrææ in Veteri, vel Græcæ in Novo Testamento, ratione fidei & autoritatis, præferri posse contenderet: id quod ἀπαιδεύτως planè faciunt moderni Jesuitæ, latinam vulgatam, utriq; & Hebrææ & Græcæ modis omnibus præferentes, uti paulò pòst ostendemus.

III. Cæterùm difficilior hîc oritur Quæstio: An nimirùm Scriptura illa Hebræa, quæ à Mose & Prophetis est condita, ad nos usq; pervenerit, an verò tempore captivitatis Babylonicæ, & incendij Templi Hierosolymitani perierit: ac postmodùm demùm ab Esdra Sacerdote reparata fuerit. Et sanè legitur in lib. 4. Esdræ c. 4, 23, & c. 14, 21. & 44. quòd volumen legis planè perierit, ita ut nemini Judæorum, vel unum Exemplar manserit reliquum: quodq; Esdras divino Spiritu afflatus, totis quadraginta dieb. dictasse quinq; viris, qui summa celeritate, quæ ab eo dicebantur, exceperint, atq; hoc modo universam scripturam, quæ planè perierat, esse recuperatam. Cui narrationi confirmandæ nonnulli in subsidium adsciscunt Epistolam Basilii ad Chilonem. Verùm rectè B. Lutherus noster ex Hieronymo statuit, Quartum istum librum Esdræ, ut & tertium, plurima falsa, imò somnia prorsus anilia continere. Nam hanc quoq; narrationem, nihil aliud esse, quàm Judaicam fabulam, fortè haud ita difficile fuerit demonstratu.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Question III. General First: for in that whole multitude of the Jews led away into Babylon, that not even one, whether pious man or…

For in the first place, that in that whole multitude of Jews carried off to Babylon there was not even one pious person or prophet who preserved a copy of the divine law is clearly inconsistent with the truth. For who would dare to affirm this of the prophets Ezekiel and Daniel, whom it is acknowledged even in the captivity itself instructed the Jewish people from the volume of the law, nay, that the people themselves from the daily recitation and meditation of the law instructed themselves regarding the true worship of the true GOD: and that as much as was permitted they served their GOD according to the prescription of the law, is easily evident from the prophets who prophesied at that time. For the Babylonians are nowhere read to have raged against the Sacred books, or even against the Jewish worship itself. Furthermore, Nehemiah testifies in chapter 8, 2, that Ezra the priest brought the book of the law which the Lord had given to Israel, and read it before the whole multitude that had returned from Babylon from morning until midday. Thirdly, if Ezra had dictated the books of the law anew, he certainly would have done so, not in the purely Hebrew language, but in Chaldean, or at least in a mixed one: such as he used in writing his own book. Now, however, no one will deny that the books of Moses were written in the purely Hebrew language. Fourthly, regarding the authority of Basil, that passage is certainly either entirely supposititious, or at the very least highly depraved. As an argument for this matter, there is the fact that this Fourth Book of Ezra never existed in Hebrew or in Greek, as witnessed by St. Jerome in his preface to the 3rd and 4th books of Ezra, but only in Latin. Now, however, Basil was not skilled in the Latin language. How, therefore, could he read this book of Ezra, not to mention understand it? Finally, if Ezra undertook any care regarding the books of the Old Testament, he is certainly not to be thought to have undertaken any other than that which concerns the τάξιν or order of the books themselves: so that he reduced them into a more convenient order. Where perhaps we may also grant that which some report, that Ezra discovered new and more prompt Hebrew letters for writing: namely those which we call cursive, and which the Jews use to this day: a fact which nevertheless detracts nothing at all from the authority of the Hebrew codex. And therefore we conclude that the Biblical books of the Old Testament remained safe even during the Babylonian captivity: and that they are the very same as those which we use today with the Jews. For as to what Sixtus of Siena mentions in book 2 of his Bibliotheca concerning I know not what peculiar Pentateuch of Ezra, written by Ezra's own hand, without any vowel points, on a certain oblong parchment, and which is preserved in the Dominican monastery at Bologna, we leave that to its own place: especially since the leaders of the Jesuits wish to appear not to disagree with us on this point.

IV. It is further asked, whether the Hebrew edition which we have is complete, or whether it is corrupt? Robert Bellarmine, in book 2, chapter 2, on the written word of God, is vehemently angry with us because, out of hatred for the Latin Vulgate edition, we attribute too much to the Hebrew edition, as if everything ought to be examined and corrected according to it, as if it were the purest fountain. But he undertakes to prove in two ways that this is not the purest fountain: first, indeed, by certain examples or testimonies in which he thinks this fountain flows turbid. Then, however, he contends that certain things are clearly not in the Hebrew text which nevertheless are lacking neither in the version of the 70 interpreters nor in Jerome's translation.

Regarding the first argument, the Jesuit brings forward the passage Isaiah 9:6. Where in the Hebrew it is יִקְרָא in an active sense: although most people explain it in the passive sense יֻקְרָא (he shall be called); but these do not differ from each other at all, and have the same meaning: he shall call his name, namely either the eternal Father, or everyone who is going to call him by his name, or he shall be called. Furthermore, no corruption of the Hebrew fountains can be inferred from this: since the letters of this word, considered in themselves, admit both the active and passive meaning according to the different position of the vowel points. It is certain, however, that the use of those vowel points is more recent, and does not pertain to the very substance of the Hebrew language: and therefore, from the change of points which occurs in different Hebrew copies, it is viciously concluded that there is a change or corruption of the Hebrew text itself.

Sixtus of Siena himself admits in book 2 of his Bibliotheca that the vowel points were finally discovered by the Rabbis of the city of Tiberias in the year 436 from the last devastation of the temple, that is, in the year of Christ 476. We answer this same thing to the other passage which the Jesuit objects to us from chapter 23:6: For although in the Hebrew it is read in the singular number, they shall call him וְקָרְאוֹ, and it is usually explained by the plural וְיִקְרְאוּ they shall call him: nevertheless, this Enallage of numbers is customary among the Hebrews, so that there is no need to change the fountain itself on account of it. Thirdly, Psalm 22:17 is certainly read in the usual copies כָּאֲרִי Caari, which is 'as a lion': and yet it is explained by כָּרוּ Karu, which is 'they dug': yet Galatinus and others are witnesses that in many copies כָּרוּ Caru is read. What of the fact that those very people who follow the former reading nevertheless admit that it is not to be accepted in its ordinary meaning: just as the Chaldean Paraphrast joins both interpretations, as if the Psalm were saying: they dug or struck my feet and hands, just as a lion is accustomed to strike with its teeth.

Fourthly, Psalm 19:5 indeed reads קַוָּם, that is, their line or plumb line: and yet the Apostle in Romans 10:18 follows the exposition of the LXX Interpreters, Φθόγγος αὐτῶν, their sound, as if they had read קוֹלָם. Of which kind, indeed, very many things can be observed in the translation of the LXX Interpreters: But the Jesuit himself meets this entire objection at the end of this second chapter, expressly asserting that errors of this kind, if indeed they are errors, are not of such moment that the integrity of the Hebrew Scriptures should be found wanting in those things which pertain to faith and good morals: and for the most part the entire discrepancy of various readings lies in certain expressions, which change the sense either little or not at all. As for the latter argument of the Jesuits, it is so far from hindering our cause that we can much more rightly retort it upon the Adversary himself by inversion, indeed in such a way that we deny that those things which are contained in the LXX version or in Jerome's translation are of such a kind that they must necessarily be received. Because, namely, they are missing in the Hebrew edition: and we firmly assert that the Scriptures nevertheless retain their authority and integrity, even if those things are omitted. And let these things said concerning the Hebrew edition of the Old Testament and its authority suffice. Now, to say something about the Greek edition of the New Testament, we are most firmly persuaded that the books of the New Testament were written in the Greek language alone. For although we do not unwillingly believe that the Gospel of Matthew also existed in Hebrew in the time of Jerome, because the Fathers unanimously admit it, and we know that it was reprinted in previous years by the labor and care of Sebastian Münster; yet that Matthew the Evangelist himself is not the author of that edition is clear from this: 1. That the Fathers themselves write that it was translated by someone else from the Greek into the Hebrew language, and some assign it to James the Apostle, others to John. 2. That the Jews, in the time of Christ, when Matthew wrote his Gospel, spoke not Hebrew, but Syriac. Thus, therefore, Matthew, if he had wished to gratify the Jews, would have written his Gospel in Syriac rather than in Greek. What kind of Syriac Gospel of Matthew, however, certainly existed, is a matter of clearly doubtful opinion among the ancient Fathers. 3. Since Christ wished the Gospel in the New Testament to be made known not only to the Jews, but to the whole world, it is certainly most consistent with the truth that it was written by Matthew, as by the rest of the Apostles, not in the Hebrew or Syriac language, known to very few peoples, but rather in the Greek idiom, which the Jews even then understood.

We affirm the same thing also concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews, whose archetype learned men conjecture was consigned to the Greek language, from the fact that the Hebrew copy which is circulated does not attain the emphasis of the things which are most clearly expressed in the Greek.

Latin:

Primùm enim in universa illa Judæorum in Babylonem abductorum multitudine, ne unum quidem vel pium, vel prophetam fuisse, qui exemplar legis divinæ asservarit, planè à vero est absonum. Quis enim hoc affirmare ausit de Ezechiele & Daniele Prophetis, quos sanè in ipsa quoq; captivitate, ex volumine legis populum Judaicum informasse, in confesso est, imò populum ipsum ex quotidiana recitatione & meditatione legis seipsum quoad Verum veri DEI cultum informasse: & quantum licuit DEO suo secundum præscriptum legis servijsse, ex Prophetis, qui tùm vaticinati sunt, facilè liquet. Neq; enim Babylonij in libros Sacros, vel etiam in cultum ipsum Judaicum sævijsse, uspiam leguntur. Deindè testatur Nehemias cap. 8, 2. Esdram Sacerdotem attulisse librum legis : quam dederat Dominus Israeli, & coram universa multitudine, quæ ex Babylone reversa erat, legisse illum à mane usq; ad meridiem. Tertiò, si Esdras libros legis de novo dictasset, certè fecisset id, non linguâ purè Hebraicâ, sed Chaldaicâ, vel certè mixtâ: quali in suo libro exarando; usus est. Jam verò libros Mosis, lingvâ purè Hebræâ scriptos esse, nemo negaverit. Quartò, quoad autoritatem Basilij, sanè locus iste, vel omninò est supposititius, vel certè summè depravatus, Cujus rei argumento potest esse, quod liber iste Quartus Esdræ, neq; Hebraicè; neq; Græcè unquam extitit, teste D. Hieronymo præfatione in lib. 3. & 4. Esdræ: sed tantum latinè. Jam verò Basilius lingvam latinam non calluit. Quomodo ergò librum hunc Esdræ legere, ne dicam intelligere potuit? Tandem, si ullam circa libros Veteris Testamenti curam suscepit Esdras, haud certè aliam suscepisse censendus est, quàm quæ ipsorum librorum τάξιν sive ordinem respicit: ita ut in ordinem convenientiorem eos redegerit. Ubi fortè illud etiam largiri possumus, quod nonnulli referunt, Esdram novas, ac ad scribendum promtiores literas Hebræas reperisse: eas nimirùm, quas currentes appellamus, & quibus hodieq; Judæi utuntur: id quod tamen autoritati Hebræi codicis nihil quicquam derogat. Ac proindè concludimus, libros Biblicos Veteris Testamenti, etiam durante captivitate Babylonicâ salvos mansisse: ac illos ipsos, planè eosdem esse cum ijs, quibus nos hodie cum Judæis utimur. Nam quæ Sixtus Senensis libro 2. Bibliothecæ commemorat, de nescio quo peculiari quodam Esdræ Pentateucho, ipsius Esdræ manu, absq; ullis punctis vocalib9, in oblongam quandam membranam exarato: quiq; in cœnobio prædicatorum Bononiensi asservetur, suo nos loco relinquimus: præsertim cum Jesuvvitarum Antesignani hac in parte à nobis haud dissentire videri velint.

IV. Quæritur porrò, An editio Hebraica, quam nos habemus, sit integra, an verò corrupta? Robertus Bellarminus lib. 2. cap. 2. de verbo Dei scripto vehementer nobis succenset, quod odio editionis latinæ vulgatæ, nimium tribuamus editioni Hebraicæ, quasi ad eam, tanquàm ad fontem purissimum omnia examinari & emendari debeant. Non autem esse hunc fontem purissimum, dupliciter probandum sumit: primùm quidem Exemplis aliquot sive Testimonijs, in quibus hunc fontem turbidum fluere existimat. Deindè verò quædam in Hebræo textu planè non haberi contendit, quæ tamen neq; in versione 70. interpretum, neq; in Hieronymi translatione desint.

Quoad prius argumentum, profert Jesuvvita locum Efa. 9, 6. Ubi in Hebræo est יִקְרָא activa significatione: cum tamen pleriq; exponant significatione passiva יֻקְרָא (vocabitur) verùm nihil ista inter se differunt, eandemq; significationem habent: vocabit nomen ejus, videlicet vel æternus Pater, vel unusquisq;, qui nomine eum suo appellaturus est, vel vocabitur. Deindè nulla hinc corruptio fontium Hebræorum inferri potest: siquidem literæ verbi hujus in se consideratæ, pro diversa positione punctorum vocalium, utramque, significationem Activam & Passivam admittunt. Constat autem usum punctorum istorum vocalium esse recentiorem, & ad ipsam substantiam Lingvæ Hebrææ haud pertinere: ac proindè ex mutatione punctorum, quæ in diversis Exemplaribus Hebræis occurrit, vitiosè colligitur ad mutationem aut corruptionem ipsius textus Hebræi.

Fatetur ipse Sixtus Senensis lib. 2. Bibliothecæ, puncta vocalia demum reperta esse à Rabbinis urbis Tiberiadis anno ab ultima templi devastatione 436. hoc est, Anno Christi 476. Respondemus hoc ipsum ad alterum locum, quem ex cap. 23, 6. nobis objicit Esavvita: Etsi enim in Hebræo, numero singulari legitur, vocabunt eum וְקָרְאוֹ, & usitatè exponitur per plurale וְיִקְרְאוּ vocabunt eum: tamen usitata hæc est numerorum Enallage apud Hebræos, ut ipsum propterea fontem nihil necesse sit mutare. Tertiò, Pf. 22, 17. legitur sanè in usitatis exemplaribus כָּאֲרִי Caari, quod est tanquam Leo: & tamen exponitur per כָּרוּ Karu, quod est foderunt: testis tamen est Galatinus, & alij, quod in multis exemplaribus כָּרוּ Caru legatur. Quid? quòd illi ipsi, qui priorem lectionem sequuntur, tamen fatentur, eam non esse accipiendam in ordinaria significatione: quemadmodum & Chaldæus Paraphrastes, utramq; interpretationem conjungit, quasi dicat Psalmus: foderunt sive percusserunt pedes manusq; meas, sicut Leo dentibus suis solet percutere.

Quartò, Psalm. 19, 5. legitur quidem קַוָּם, id est, linea sive perpendiculum eorum: & tamen Apostolus Rom. 10, 18. LXX. Interpretum sequitur expositionem, Φθόγγος αὐτῶν, Sonus eorum, quasi ipsi legissent קוֹלָם. Cujus sanè generis, quamplurima observari possunt in translatione LXX. Interpretum: Verùm huic objectioni universæ occurrit ipse Jesuvvita, in fine capitis hujus secundi, disertè asserens, non tanti momenti esse ejusmodi errores, si tamen errores sunt, ut in ijs, quæ ad fidẽ & bonos mores pertinent, Scripturæ Hebrææ integritas desideretur: & plerumq; totam discrepantiam variarum letionum in dictionibus quibusdam positam esse, qua sensum aut parum, aut nihil mutant. Quoad posterius Jesuitæ argumentum, usque adeo illud causæ nostræ nihil officit, ut rectissimè potiùs id in ipsum Adversarium per inversionem retorquere possimus, ita quidem, ut ea, quæ in versione LXX, aut in Hieronymi translatione habentur: ideò negemus ejus generis esse, ut necessariò recipi debeant. Quia videlicet in Hebræâ editione desiderantur: & constanter asseramus, nihilominus Scripturis suam & autoritatem & integritatem constare, si vel maximè illa omittantur. Et hæc quidem de Editione Hebræâ Veteris Testamenti, ejusdemque autoritate, dicta sufficiant. Nunc ut de Editione Græcâ Novi Testamenti aliquid dicamus, initiò non nisi Græco Sermone libros Novi Testamenti conscriptos esse, habemus persuasissimum. Etsi enim Evangelium Matthæi Hebraicè quoque scriptum, tempore Hieronymi extitisse haud inviti credimus, propterea quod & Patres illud unanimiter fatentur: & superioribus etiam annis operâ ac curâ Sebastiani Munsteri illud recusum esse novimus: tamen ipsum Matthæum Evangelistam autorem illius editionis haud esse, vel inde patet, 1. Quod Patres ipsi ab alio quodam ex Græco in Hebræum sermonem translatum illud esse scribunt, & alij Jacobo Apostolo, alij Johanni assignant. 2. Quod Judæi; tempore Christi, quo Matthæus suum scripsit Evangelium, non Hebraicè, sed Syriacè loquebantur. Sic ergò Matthæus, si Judæis gratificari voluisset, Syriacè potiùs, quàm Græcè suum conscripsisset Evangelium. Quale tamen Syriacum Evangelium Matthæi, utrum certò extiterit, dubia planè apud antiquos Patres est sententia. 3. Cum Christus Evangelium in Novo Testamento non solis Judæis, sed toti mundo innotescere voluerit, veritati certè maximè est consenta neum, non vel Hebræo; vel Syriaco, paucis admodum populis cognito: sed Græco potiùs idiomate, quod Judæi etiam tum callebant, uti à reliquis Apostolis, sic à Matthæo quoque Evangelium conscriptum esse.

Quod ipsum affirmamus etiam de Epistolâ ad Hebræos, cujus Archetypum, Græco sermone consignatum esse, vel inde viri docti conjiciunt, quod exemplar Hebræum, quod circumfertur, emphasin rerum, quæ in Græco dilucidissimè sunt expressæ, haud assequitur.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Proposition II. Affirmative

PROPOSITION II. Affirmative.

Holy Scripture ought to be translated into the languages vernacular to every people, so that it may be read by all Christians, as much the unlearned as the learned, as much by the Laity as by the Clergy.

The truth of the proposition can be demonstrated by several arguments: The first is as follows: If GOD himself exhorts each and every Christian to read and understand Scripture, then it is necessary that Scripture itself first be translated into the language vernacular to every people. But the former is true: Therefore the latter is also established.

The nerve of the hypothetical connection in the major proposition is self-evident. For how could Holy Scripture, written in Latin or Greek or Hebrew, I do not say be understood, but even just be read by those who know only the German, or Italian, or French language?

Many testimonies of the Scriptures build up the evidence of the minor: Certainly Deut. 31:10, Moses diligently commends the Scripture to be read by the people. And David indiscriminately declares all those blessed who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, Ps. 1:1, Ps. 119:1, 2, and following. Thus Isaiah refers all men to Scripture, saying, To the law and to the testimony: If they do not speak according to this word, they will not see the morning dawn, Isa. 8:20. Abraham sends the brothers of the rich glutton back to Moses and the Prophets, Luke 16:29. Thus CHRIST sends the promiscuous crowd of Jews to Scripture, saying, John 5:39, Search the scriptures. For these are they which testify of me. Col. 4:16, Paul wishes that the Epistle written to the Colossians be read also by the Laodiceans: and conversely that which was written to the Laodiceans be read by the Colossians: namely, the former to Timothy. 2 Pet. 1:19, 20, and 21. We have a more sure prophetic word: to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. And what else do the inscriptions and openings of almost all the Apostolic Epistles mean, than that the knowledge and understanding of Holy Scripture pertains to all Christians? For although the gift of interpreting the Scriptures does not belong to the Laity in the same way and degree as it does to the Doctors of the Church: it is nevertheless certain from these testimonies that the Laity, searching in true piety and faithful meditation in the Scriptures, can test the spirits, and can distinguish false prophets from true and sound doctors: Just as we read in Acts 17:11 concerning the Bereans, that they searched the Scriptures to see whether those things which were said by Paul were consistent with them. For which end the Apostle also exhorts his Thessalonians, that they prove all things, and hold fast that which is good. 1 Thess. 5:21. And Christ indifferently [exhorts] all, that they beware of false teachers, Matt. 7:15, and John, that they test the spirits, whether they are of God, 1 John 4:1. All of which things, indeed, that they cannot be performed except from the assiduous reading and meditation of the Scriptures, is more certain than that it needs proof.

II. If the Apostles, dispersed into the whole world by the order and command of Christ, announced the Gospel to individual peoples in a known language, and one familiar to each people: certainly even now the doctrine of the Gospel [ought] to be interpreted and written down in all languages not only lawful, but exceedingly useful and necessary. But the antecedent is most manifest: therefore, it is necessary that the consequent be of the same evidence. The hypothetical connection is clear in itself. For 1., what reason and necessity prevailed in the times of the Apostles, that the doctrine of the Gospel should be proposed to any peoples whatsoever in a known and familiar dialect: the same today prevails. Namely, the conversion of all peoples to the kingdom of Christ prevails today. Namely, the conversion or gathering of all peoples to the kingdom of Christ. One will hardly deny the evidence of the minor premise, unless he be ignorant that the Apostles were for that reason sent by Christ into the whole world: and for that reason also, in that first Pentecost, were instructed with the New Testament gift of various languages, so that they might indeed announce the Word to all nations in a known language. Nor is the condition of all Christians today worse than that of those to whom the Apostles themselves announced the Gospel. For there is no respect of persons with GOD. Rom. 2, 11. III. Argument: If the Jews of the Old Testament were bound to read the books of Moses and the Prophets in a language familiar to them, daily in private and in public, and indeed by the command of GOD: then surely the same will be lawful and granted to the Christians of the New Testament. But the former is true: therefore the latter is also established. The reason for the hypothetical connection is this: 1. that the same command of GOD obliges Christians no less to the reading of Scripture than it obliged the Jews: unless perhaps the Jesuits wish to affirm that that command was only of the ceremonial law, and therefore concerned only the Jews: both of which, being manifestly impious and blasphemous, falls of its own accord: especially since Christ the Savior wished to confirm that very command through this new constitution, as it were, John 5, 39. Search the Scriptures. 2. Because the Christians of the New Testament are not only not in a worse condition, but in a better condition than were the Jews of the Old Testament: according to that saying in Luke 10, 23. Blessed are the eyes which see the things that you see: For I say to you, that many prophets and kings &c. 3. Because the knowledge of heavenly mysteries is equally necessary to these as it was once to the Jews: For there is no respect of persons with God, Rom. 2, 11. Nor is God the God of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles: Since there is one God, who shall justify the circumcision (the Jews) by faith, and the uncircumcision (the Gentiles) through faith. Rom. 3, 29. & 30. IV. Argument. If, even by the opinion of the Jesuits themselves, the Church deserves no reproach because it took care for the Holy Scripture to be translated into the Greek and Latin language: certainly it will not deserve reproach today if it takes care for the same to be translated into other languages vernacular to other peoples. But the antecedent is placed beyond all doubt; therefore, it is necessary that the consequent be of immovable certainty. The reason for the hypothetical connection appears clearly enough, because the Jesuits themselves can demonstrate by no probable reason at least, that Scripture ought to have been translated only into those two languages, namely Greek and Latin, and not likewise into other languages as well. For the reasons they are accustomed to bring forward for those two languages, they necessarily militate likewise for the use of all other languages. That they object that other versions are faulty is too weak and trifling. For 1. in judging versions, one must not stand by the opinion of the Jesuits: but judgment must be sought from a collation with the sources themselves. If this is instituted a little more accurately, it is irrefragably established that other versions, and especially the German version of B. Luther, approach incomparably closer to the sources than either the Greek or Latin ever could. 2. Then let the adversaries remember that those very two versions, which they esteem so highly, are so constituted that much is desired in them. Jerome certainly in his commentaries very often disapproves of the Greek version of the LXX interpreters, not only as corrupted by scribes, but also as faulty in itself. Thus, that the Latin Vulgate is faulty and imperfect to the point of being a prodigy is evident even from the fact that the Jesuits themselves, by order of the Roman Pontiff, undertook its emendation a few years ago: having published a booklet, the title of which is: Roman correction in the Latin Bibles of the Vulgate Edition, recognized by order of Sixtus V. P. M., the more notable places, observed by Franciscus Lucas Brugensis, Antwerp, from the Plantin press, A.D. 1603. But concerning this matter, in the second part, we shall have to deal professedly.

V. We seek the argument from the unanimous consent of orthodox Antiquity, which in this whole Question stands on our side. Chrysostom, Homily 29 on Genesis: I beseech you, that you diligently listen to the reading of the divine scriptures: and not only when you come here, but also take the Bibles into your hands at home, and receive with great zeal the utility placed in them. For much profit is born from thence. For first, the mind is reformed by reading: then the soul assumes wings and is elevated, is illuminated by the rays of the Sun of Justice: through it, that time is freed from the allurements of unclean thoughts, enjoying much quiet and tranquility. Moreover, what that sensible food does to increase the strength of the body, reading does for the soul. For it is spiritual nourishment, and makes the soul strong and more constant, not permitting it to be captured by absurd thoughts. Augustine in the Sermon on the meditation of the law of GOD: The reading of the Holy Scriptures is no small foreknowledge of divine Blessedness: for in these, as if in a certain mirror, a man can consider himself, what sort he is, or whither he tends. Assiduous reading purifies all things, brings on the fear of hell, and incites the heart of the reader to heavenly joys. He who wishes to be always with God ought frequently to pray and to read. For when we pray, we ourselves speak with God: but when we read, GOD speaks with us. Jerome to the virgin Demetrias: Read the divine scriptures more often, nay, let sacred reading never be laid down from your hands, through the Scriptures alone you can clearly understand the will of GOD.

And lest by chance a Jesuit might object that sayings of this kind are to be understood only of those who, having left this world, have hidden themselves in monasteries: that distinguished passage of Chrysostom, which exists in Homily 3 on …Lazarus, deserves the greatest observation. Let no one say to me: I am attached to forensic causes: I conduct public business, I exercise a craft, I support a wife and children, I take care of a household, I am a worldly man, it is not mine to read the Scriptures, but of those who have said farewell to the world, who have occupied the summits of mountains, who continually lead a life of that kind. What does a man say? Is it not your business to unfold the Scriptures, since you are distracted by countless cares? Nay, it is yours more than theirs. For they do not need the protection of the Scriptures as much as you do, tossed about in the midst of the waves of business. For those who have fixed their little huts in the desert are free from the forum and forensic business, nor do they have dealings with anyone: but in that quiet tranquility, sitting as if in a harbor, they enjoy things that are exceedingly safe. We, on the contrary, fluctuating as if in the middle of the sea, and bound by countless sins, whether we wish it or not, always have need of the perpetual and constant solace of the Scriptures, etc.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO II. θετικὴ.

SCriptura sacra in lingvas, cuilibet populo vernaculas, transferri debet, ut ab omnibus Christianis, tàm indoctis, quàm doctis, tàm à Laicis, quàm Clericis, legi possit.

PRopositionis veritas aliquot argumentis demonstrari potest: Primum sic habet: Si DEUS ipse singulos ac universos Christianos, ad legendam atquè intelligendam Scripturam exhortatur: utique Scriptura priùs ipsa in lingvā cuilibet populo vernaculam transferatur, necesse est. At prius verum: Ratum ergò & posterius.

Connexi hypothetici nervus in Majore propositione per se patet. Quomodo enim Scriptura sacra Latinè aut Græcè, aut Hebraicè exarata, non dico, intelligi: sed vel legi tantùm queat ab ijs, qui Germanicam tantùm, vel Italicam? aut Gallicam modò lingvam callent?

Minoris evidentiam astruunt plurima Scripturarum testimonia: certè Deut. 31, 10. Scripturam populo legendam Moses diligenter commendat. Et David indifferenter quosvis beatos prædicat, qui meditantur in lege Domini die ac nocte, Ps. 1. 1. Psal 119, 1. 2. & seqq. Sic Esaias omnes homines ad Scripturam ablegat, Ad legē, inquiens, & ad Testimonium: Quod si non fecerint secundum hæc, non videbunt auroram matutinam, Jes 8, 20. Abraham remittit fratres divitis Epulonis ad Mosen & Prophetas, Luc. 16, 29. Sic CHRISTUS promiscuam Judæorum turbam ablegat ad Scripturam, inquiens, Joh. 5, 39. Scrutamini scripturas. Hæ enim sunt quæ testificantur de me. Col. 4, 16. vult Paulus, ut Epistola ad Colofsenses scripta, legatur etiam à Laodicensibus: & vicissim ea, quæ scripta est Laodiceâ, legatur à Colossensibus: nempe prior ad Timotheum. 2. Pet. 1, 19. 20. & 21. Habemus firmiorem sermonem propheticum: cui rectè facitis, attendentes, tanquam lucernæ lucenti in loco caliginoso, usque dùm dies illucescat, & exoriatur lucifer in cordibus vestris. Et quid si volunt aliud, singularum fermè Epistolarum Apostolicarum inscriptiones atque exordia, quàm ad quoslibet Christianos Scripturæ sacrę cognitionem atque intelligentiam pertinere? Nam licèt donum interpretandi Scripturas, Laicis non eo modo atque gradu competat, quo Doctoribus Ecclesiæ: cóstat tamen ex testimoniis istis, posse Laicos, in vera pietate ac fideli meditatione in Scripturis scrutantes, probare Spiritus, posse dignoscere Pseudoprophetas à veris & sanis doctoribus: Quemadmodum legimus Act. 17, 11. de Berrhoensibus, quod scrutati fuerint in Scripturis, utrū ea, quæ à Paulo dicebantur, illis essent consona. Quo fine Apostolus etiam suos hortatur Thefsalonicenses, ut omnia probent, quod bonū est, retineant. 1. Thess. 5, 21. Et Christus indifferenter omnes, ut sibi caveant à falsis doctoribus Matth. 7, 15. & Johannes, ut Spiritus probent, num ex Deo sint, 1. Joh. 4, 1. Quæ sanè omnia, non nisi ex assiduâ lectione ac meditatione Scripturarum præstari posse, certius est, quàm ut probatione indigeat.

II. Si Apostoli dispersi in universum terrarum orbē jussu ac mandato Christi, singulis populis annūciarunt Evangelium lingvâ cognitâ, & cuivis populo familiari:utique etiamnū omnibus etiā lingvis do ctrina Evangelij interpretari & conscribere nō modò licitum, sed perquàm utile ac necessarium fuerit. Atqui Antecedens est manifestissimum: Ejusdem ergò evidentiæ Consequens sit, necesse est. Connexum hypotheticum per se liquet. 1. enim, Quæ ratio ac necessitas temporibus Apostolorum militavit, ut Evangelij doctrina, quibuslibet populis cognita ac familiari dialecto proponeretur: eadem hodieque militat. nempè omnium populorum ad regnum Christi conversio sive aggregatio. Minoris evidentiam vix negabit, nisi qui ignoraverit, Apostolos ideò à Christo ablegatos esse in universum orbem: ideò etiam in primâ illâ pentecoste Novi Testamenti dono variarum lingvarum instructos fuisse, ut videlicet omnibus gentibus lingvâ cognitâ Verbum annunciare possint. Neque deterior hodie est omnium Christianorum conditio, quàm quæ fuit eorum, quibus ipsi Apostoli Evangelium annunciarunt. Non enim apud DEUM acceptio est personarum Rom. 2, 11. III. Argumentum: Si Judæi Veteris Testamenti libros Mosis & Prophetarum lingvâ sibi familiari, quotidie privatim & publicè, & quidem mandato DEI legere debuerunt: utique Christianis Novi Testamenti idem erit licitum & concessum, At prius verum: Ratum ergò & posterius. Ratio connexi Hypothetici militat isthæc. 1. quod idem Mandatum DEI Christianos haud minùs obligat ad lectionem Scripturæ, quàm Judæos obligavit: nisi fortè Jesuvvitæ affirmare velint, mandatu illud fuisse legis tantùm ceremonialis, & ad solos proindè Judæos spectasse: Quod utrumque, quippe manifestè impium & blasphemum suâ sponte corruit: præsertim, cum Christus Servator illud ipsum mandatum per hanc novellam quasi constitutionem confirmare voluerit, Joh. 5, 39. Scrutamini Scripturas. 2. Quia Christiani Novi Testamenti non modò non deterioris, sed melioris sunt conditionis, quàm fuerunt Judæi Veteris Testamenti: juxta illud Luc. 10. 23. Beati Oculi, qui vident quæ vos videtis: Dico n. vobis, quòd multi prophetæ & reges &c. 3. Quia cognitio mysteriorum cœlestium, his æquè est necessaria, atque olim Judæis olim fuit: Non enim est acceptio personarum apud Deum, Rom. 2, 11. Neque Deus Judæorum tantùm DEUS est, sed & Gentiũ: Siquidem unus DEUS est, qui justificabit circumcisionem (Judæos) ex fide, & præputium (Gentes) per fidem. Rom. 3, 29. & 30. IV. Argumentum. Si ex ipsorum etiam Jesuvvitarum sententiâ, reprehensionem minimè meretur Ecclesia, quod Scripturam Sacram in lingvam Græcam & Latinam transferri curavit: certè neque hodie reprehensionem merebitur: si in alias lingvas alijs populis vernaculas eandem transferri curet. At Antecedens extra omnem dubitationis aleam est positum, Immotæ igitur certitudinis Consequens etiam sit, necesse est. Connexi Hypothetici ratio satis evidenter patet, quòd Jesuvvitæ ipsi, nulla probabili saltem ratione demonstrare possunt, quòd Scriptura tantùm in duas illas, Græcam videlicet & Latinam, non verò itidem in alias etiam lingvas verti debuerit. Nam quas causas pro duabus illis lingvis proferre solent, eæ pro reliquarum lingvarum omnium usu itidem necesfariò militant. Quòd objiciunt, verfiones reliquas efse vitiofas, nimis dilutum & nugatoriũ eft. Nam 1. in dijudicandis verfionibus non standum est Jesuvvitarum sententia: sed ex collatione cum ipsis fontibus peti debet judiciũ. Quæ si paulò accuratiùs instituatur, irrefragabiliter constat, alias versiones, & cumprimis Germanicam B. Lutheri, incomparabiliter propiùs ad fontes accedere, quam vel Græca vel Latina unquam accedere possit. 2. Deinde meminerint Adversarii, illas ipsas versiones duas, quas tantopere illi suspiciunt ita esse comparatas, ut plurimum in ipsis desideretur. Hieronymus certè in commentarijs suis, versionem Græcam LXX. interpretum sæpissimè improbat, non modò ut corruptam à librarijs, sed etiam ut in se vitiosam, Sic Latinam vulgatam ad prodigium usque mendosam & imperfećtam esse, vel inde patet, quod ipsi Jesuvvitæ jussu Pontificis Romani, ante paucos annos ejus emendationem susceperunt: publicato libello, cui titulus est: Romanæ correctionis in latinis Bibliis Editionis vulgatæ, jussu Sixti V. P. M. recognitis, loca insigniora, observata à Francisco Luca Brugensi Antuerpiæ ex officinâ Plantinianâ A. 1603. Sed hac de re, parte jam secundâ, ex professo nobis agendum erit.

V. Argumentum petimus ex unanimi consensu orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, quæ hac in Quæstione totâ à nostris stat partibus. Chrysostomus Homil. 29. in Genesin: Obsecro, ut divinæ scripturæ lećtionē diligenter auscultetis: nec solùm, cũ buc venitis, sed & domi Biblia in manus sumite, & utilitatē in illis positam magno studio suscipite. Inde n. multũ lucri nascitur. Primum n. lećtione lingvareformatur: Deinde anima pennas assumit & elevatur, Jubareƣ, Solis Justitiæ illustratur: perƣ, tempus illud ab immundarũ cogitationũ illecebris liberatur, multâ quiete & tranquillitate fruens. Insuper quod adaugendas vires corpori sensibilis ille cibus facit, id animæ lećtio præstat. Spirituale n alimentũ est, & fortem reddit animam & constantiore, non permittens ut ab absurdis cogitationib. capiatur. Augustinus in Sermone de meditatione legis DEI: Sacrarum Scripturarũ lećtio, non parva est præcognitio divinæ Beatitudinis: In his n. quasi in quodâ speculo, homo seipsũ considerare potest, qualis sit, vel quò tendat. Lećtio assidua purificat omnia, timorē incurit gehennæ, ad gaudia superna cor instigat legētis. Qui vult cũ Deo semper esse, frequenter debet orare & legere. Nã cũ oramus, ipsi cũ Deo loquimur: cũm verò legimus, DEUS nobis cũ loquitur. Hieronym9 ad Demetriam virginem: Divinas scripturas sæpius lege, imò nunquam de manibus tuis sacra lećtio deponatur, per solas Scripturas potes planè intelligere voluntatem DEI.

Et ne fortè hujusmodi dićta, de ijs tantummodò intelligēda esse, objiciat Jesuvvita, qui relićto mundo isto, in monasteria sese abdiderunt: observationem vel maximè meretur, insignis ille locus Chrysostomi, qui extat Homilia 3. de Lazaro. Ne quis mihi dixerit: Ego forensib9 causis affixus sum: publica gero negotia, artificiũ exerceo, uxorē alo & liberos, familiæ curâ gero, mundanus homo sum, non est meũ legere Scripturas,sed eorũ, qui valedixerunt mundo, qui montiũ verticesoccuparunt, qui vitã ejusmodi cotinēter agūt. Quid ait homo? Non est tui negotij Scripturas evolvere, quoniam innumeris curis distraheris? Imò tuum magis est, quàm illorum. Neque enim illi perindè Scripturarum egent præsidio, atque vos in medijs negotiorum undis jactati. Nam qui in deserto fixêre tuguriola, sunt à foro, forensibusque negotijs liberi, neque cum quoquam habent commercium: sed in illa quieta tranquillitate, velut in portu sedentes, rebus vehementer tutis fruuntur. Nos contra velut in medio mari fluctuantes, innumerisque, velimus, nolimus, peccatis obstricti, semper opus habemus perpetuo jugiq́; Scripturarum solatio &c.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Second Part of Question III, General, Etc

PROPOSITION I. JESUITICAL.

The Latin Vulgate edition is to be preferred not only to all other Latin editions, but even to the Hebrew text of the Old Testament and the Greek text of the New Testament: and in public readings, disputations, preachings, or expositions it is to be held as Authentic: and is to be rejected by no one under any pretext.

ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστικὴ.

There are two main heads which come into controversy today regarding the Latin Vulgate edition: the former of which concerns its Author; the latter, its Authority.

Regarding the first member; although before the rise of the new Jesuitical sect, there was no disagreement among the Papists other than that the entire Latin Vulgate edition was St. Jerome's: to which, in order to assert greater authority, they always painted a Cardinal's hat on the frontispiece of old editions: Now, however, the new Jesuitical society brings forward a new opinion as well: namely, that not the entire Latin Vulgate edition, but only certain parts of it are St. Jerome's: but the rest are of another, older interpreter, whose name, however, they do not dare to express: just as the Jesuit Bellarmine thinks in book 2, On the Word of God, chapter 9. Although this assertion seems to obtain some semblance of truth: yet it is so uncertain that those very parts which the Jesuit assigns to Jerome are Jerome's, that far stronger reasons fight for the negative. For the Jesuit contends that all the Biblical books, except the Psalter, and also except the books of Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, and Maccabees, have Jerome as their author. Now, however, anyone even moderately skilled in the Hebrew language, from a collation of the Hebrew text and the Vulgate version, easily perceives that even regarding the remaining biblical books, that interpreter, whoever he may be, has fallen most shamefully in many places, and has rendered many things very obscurely: a thing which it would be a sin even to think of regarding St. Jerome, as he was not only most skilled in the holy language, but also a most severe critic of that faulty version. And lest this assertion of ours seem too insolent to our adversaries, it pleases us to demonstrate its truth to the eye with a few examples. Gen. 1:2, the Latin Vulgate has: The Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters: Criticizing which version, Jerome shows that it should have been translated from the Hebrew, The Spirit of the Lord was brooding over the waters, or was warming the waters, like a bird. In chapter 3:15 of Genesis it is read in the Hebrew, He, that is, the Messiah, shall crush the head of the Serpent: But the interpreter ignorantly rendered the Masculine by the Feminine: She, that is, Mary, shall crush the head of the Serpent. Thus in chapter 4:1, in the Hebrew it is: I have acquired a man, the Lord Jehovah himself. But the Latin interpreter wrongly rendered it, I have possessed a man through GOD: thus impiously twisting the words of Eve into a foreign sense. The Old [version] in Ecclesiastes reads in chapter 2:3, I thought in my heart to withdraw my flesh from Wine: Jerome writes in his commentaries that it should be translated thus: I considered in my heart, to draw my flesh with Wine: signifying that he wished to live delicately and sumptuously. Thus in chapter 9:1. The Old [version] has: Man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred: But Jerome renders it thus: And indeed man is not knowing of charity, and indeed of hatred. Which very errors, and indeed not lighter ones, occur in the remaining books of the Old Testament: nay, not only in these, but also in the books of the New Testament, as when in chapter 5:9 of the epistle to the Galatians, the Vulgate has: A little leaven leavens the whole lump: There Jerome, in book 3 of his commentary on this Epistle, sharply criticizes the author of this version, who should have translated it, a little bit of leaven: for the reason that 'a little' is a matter of virtue and praise. Thus the same Jerome warns. 2 Cor. 1:22 and Eph. 1:13. That the interpreter most faultily rendered the word αρραβων by 'pledge', for the reason that a pledge is given for borrowed money: but an earnest is given for a future purchase, as a kind of testimony and obligation. Who, therefore, would dare to affirm that that Vulgate version, either in whole or in part, is Jerome's, when there is almost no book in which he himself does not find things to be desired regarding the version: as Pagninus truly wrote in his entirety to Pope Clement VII, in the preface to his Bibles, that he was of the opinion that that Vulgate version was not Jerome's: and that he wished that it were still extant today, as that concerning which Jerome himself testified in these words: Certainly I will say confidently, and I will cite many witnesses of this work, that I have changed nothing at all in my judgment concerning the Hebrew truth: If therefore my edition has anywhere differed from the ancients, ask any of the Hebrews, and you will clearly see that I am being torn apart in vain by rivals, who prefer to seem to despise excellent things rather than to learn. Therefore the vanity of the former member of the Jesuitical assertion is clear of its own accord. But what does it matter to waste time on those things at greater length? Since from what has already been said, a judgment can easily be made concerning the first member of the Jesuitical assertion: and from the subsequent ones the same will be more manifest.

The later head, therefore, of the Jesuitical proposition is concerning the Authority of the Latin Vulgate Edition: concerning which the Council of Trent defined thus: Furthermore, the same holy Synod, considering that no small utility can accrue to the Church of God if it becomes known from all the Latin editions of the sacred books which are circulated, which one is to be held as Authentic; it decrees and declares that this very old and Vulgate edition, which has been approved in the Church itself by the long use of so many centuries, be held as Authentic in public readings, disputations, preachings, and expositions: and that no one dare or presume to reject it under any pretext. Where, at the beginning, the stupendous rashness and ἀκρισια of the Roman Pontiffs comes under admiration. For when Erasmus of Rotterdam had published his lucubrations on the New Testament, and had shown that the Latin Vulgate not only labored under innumerable errors, but had also prepared a clearly new version from the Greek language: there Leo X, of pious memory, approved it as most absolute, and signified not obscurely that he was greatly delighted by it and, furthermore, that it was praised by the calculation of others as well. Now if Leo X judged correctly: then his successors, and namely the Roman Pontiffs Paul III, Julius III, and Pius IV in the Council of Trent, decreed wrongly, because, dissenting from Leo, they defined only that old one to be Authentic. Furthermore, why did the Louvain College so greatly praise the Latin version of Benedictus Arias Montanus, and approve it as a most necessary work: if there was no fault in the Latin Vulgate? But by what counsel those later ones departed from Leo, there would be no need for an Oedipus as a diviner. For when they noticed that B. Luther was unwilling to descend into the arena of disputation with the Pontificals unless they convinced him of their dogmas from the Canonical Scriptures themselves, and indeed clearly perceived that the patronage of most errors could be sought from the Latin Vulgate: therefore they preferred to pronounce even this most vicious version as Authentic, rather than to profess ingenuously that they were utterly destitute of all authority of Scripture in the defense of their dogmas. Whence, for example, intending to prove the adoration of the virgin Mary, they brought forward the vicious version of the Vulgate, Gen. 3:15, 'She shall crush the head of the serpent.' Thus, intending to assert the powers of Free Will in spiritual matters, they appealed to the truncated version, Gen. 8:21, 'The sense and thought of the human heart are prone to evil from youth.' Where in the Hebrew it is read: 'Every figment of the thoughts of his (man's) heart is ONLY evil, every day': so that, where the Vulgate 1. omits the particle 'Only', then for the act it puts δύναμιν, namely that it is prone to evil. Where it is one thing to be prone to evil: but another thing to be only evil; the former still leaves some goodness to man in spiritual matters: but the latter simply denies the same. Thus, intending to confirm the Invocation of Saints, they fled to the Latin Vulgate, which has in Gen. 48:16: 'And let my name be invoked upon them (Ephraim and Manasseh), and the names of my fathers, Abraham and Isaac': When in the Hebrew it is read, as interpreted by Vatablus: 'And let the name of my fathers be called in them': Thus, intending to assert the Justice of one's own merits, they called into aid that of the Vulgate version, Heb. 13:16. Do not forget beneficence and communion: For with such sacrifices GOD is well-pleased: When in the Greek it is: εὐαρεστῆ- ται ὁ Θεὸς: GOD is delighted with such sacrifices. Thus, therefore, in the place that is mentioned, the Fathers of the Council of Trent were wise, because they decreed that the Latin Vulgate should be rejected under no pretext in expositions, readings, and disputations. For from this they can borrow the greatest protection for their errors. Moreover, since not only God in the Old, but also in the New Testament has most severely commanded that nothing at all be added to or taken away from His Word, much less that it be changed or corrupted: and since it is clearer than the midday sun, both from the examples already brought forward and from infinite other examples, that both are done in the Latin Vulgate: we shall have acted most correctly if, having paid no heed to that brute thunderbolt of the Council of Trent, we have not applied faith to the Vulgate edition before we have discovered that it agrees in every respect with the fountains themselves.

It is pleasing, however, to weigh in a few words by what arguments our adversaries strive to reconcile the authority of their Vulgate edition. The FIRST is Bellarmine's, taken from the long use of so many centuries, by which in the Latin Church this Vulgate edition has been approved in every way. The Council of Trent also appeals to this very argument. But this argument proceeds initially from a false hypothesis, and therefore begs the question. For it is just as uncertain and false that what the Latin Church has approved for many centuries must immediately be held as authentic, as it can be uncertain and false that the Latin Vulgate edition is authentic. For this very thing is being sought: whether the Church, either the Latin or any other, ought to have been content with one Vulgate edition, while meanwhile neglecting and setting aside the Hebrew and Greek sources. Augustine certainly, who easily obtained the leading place in the Latin Church, informs his opinion on this matter far differently, in book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 12, in these words: Men of the Latin tongue have need of two other languages for the knowledge of the divine scriptures, namely Hebrew and Greek, so that one may recur to the preceding exemplars if the infinite variety of Latin interpreters has brought any doubt: for it is uncertain which of the interpreters has followed the truth, unless the exemplars of the preceding language are read. And chapter 15: There is no doubt that if anything in the Latin varieties of the books of the New Testament wavers, it ought to yield to the Greek.

Then the Jesuitical argumentation proceeds from a part. For a collection is made from the Latin Church, which is only particular, to the whole Catholic Church. But now the error of a particular Church can neither and ought not to prejudice the whole Catholic Church: even if it were placed beyond all doubt that the Latin Church had always held the Vulgate Edition as Authentic: Although we have already learned otherwise from Augustine. In place of a second argument, Bellarmine appeals to the consensus of Augustine and very many other Doctors of the Latin Church, who approved the Latin Vulgate with unanimous suffrage. But not even in this way does the Jesuit profit in the slightest. For it cannot be denied that those very Ancients whom he cites, and among them even Augustine, were unskilled in the Hebrew language, so that they could not even judge accurately how well the individual Latin versions, both in words and in whole sentences, depart from the Hebrew truth itself. Furthermore, Augustine praises the Latin version, whether that which they called the Itala, or any other, κατὰ τὶ [in a certain respect], but not ἁπλῶς [absolutely], and therefore there is more in the Consequent than there was in the Antecedent. κατὰ τὶ indeed, insofar as much convenience and benefit accrued to the Latin Church from that version, such as it was: Meanwhile, however, he preferred the Hebrew and Greek to all those versions; and he wished all others to be amended and evaluated as if from these fountains. Finally, the Jesuit again collects from a part in this manner: Augustine, Isidore, Anselm, Bernard, and certain others praised the Latin version, Therefore all the Doctors of the Latin Church held that Latin one to be Authentic. For why, I ask, does he not appeal to that chief light of the Latin Church, namely St. Jerome, who was most skilled in the Hebrew language? Who, it is clearly evident, wished his own Latin version to be tested against the Hebrew fountains, both from other places and indeed from his own preface to the Pentateuch, where he addresses his rivals thus: Why are you tormented by envy? Why do you stir up the minds of the unskilled against me? If anywhere in the translation I seem to you to err, ask the Hebrews, consult the masters of different cities. But furthermore, and in the third place, the Jesuits object: If one must stand by the Hebrew edition, there will be no end to contentions, because the ambiguity of Hebrew words is so great that even those most skilled in that language contend over their certain meaning. Therefore, it is most advisable that we submit ourselves to the judgment of the Church, which, as a true arbiter and judge, can pronounce upon whose interpretation of the meaning one should acquiesce. For example, Gen. 36:24: This is Ana, who found הַיֵּמִים Hajemim in the wilderness, when he was feeding the donkeys of his father: Likewise Gen. 30:14: Reuben went out in the time of wheat harvest into the field, and found דּוּדָאִים Dudaim and brought them to Leah: Where other interpreters have translated that former word Jemim as hot waters, others as mules, others as wild asses: But the latter word Dudaim others rendered as mandrakes, others as lilies, others as violets: others as fruit of a choice flavor and

taste, ripe at the time of wheat harvest. But this knot too can be easily untied. For first, a fallacy of τῆς πλεονεξίας [excess] is committed, that is, more is inferred in the Consequent than can be built from the Antecedent. For that Antecedent only proves that there are words found in the Hebrew which, because of a certain kinship and similarity, admit multiple meanings. But the Consequent infers, Therefore there will be no end to contentions in the doctrine of faith if one must stand by the Hebrew edition. How sophistical this collection is, even a boy understands. For neither are the Christian faith and Religion in peril, even if grammarians contend about these and other words of that kind, and the dispute is still under judgment as to which meaning is most to be embraced. Nor, when some circumstance of history is difficult, is the Religion itself and the substance of the Articles of faith immediately to be judged as difficult. What of the fact that, for the most part, those multiple meanings of a single word produce not contradictory, but related meanings that harmonize beautifully with the subject matter? Whence the Spaniard Benedict Arias Montanus, in the preface prefixed to the Hebrew Bibles, elegantly responds to the Jesuitical objection in this manner: When some ambiguous word, which signifies two things, is used in that primordial language, we persuade ourselves that the Holy Spirit did not use it without some choice, and that each meaning demands its own interpretation, and for this reason we believe those words were proposed to us so that we might interpret them in both directions. Then a fallacy of ὡς πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον [non sequitur] is committed. For one should not therefore flee to the judgment of the Church if a controversy arises concerning the proper meaning of some word, but rather to grammarians and those most skilled in this language, since every craftsman is to be trusted in his own craft. Finally, this Jesuitical collection is clearly ἀσύστατον [inconsistent]: For either the Church will settle such controversies by a certain praetorian and absolute power, or from certain principles and reasons: for a third option cannot be given. But now, such a praetorian and absolute power neither belongs to the Church, nor can it satisfy the minds of those who doubt. It remains, therefore, that even if one must recur to the judgment of the Church, it still cannot pronounce upon the certainty or uncertainty of any Version except from its own principles, that is, from the fountains themselves; which is the very thing we also assert.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO I. JESUVITICA.

LAtina vulgata editio, non modò omnibus alijs editionibus Latinis; verùm etiam Hebraico Veteris, & Græco Novi Testamenti textui anteponenda: inque publicis lectionibus, disputationibus, prædicationibus, aut expositionibus pro Authentica est habenda:& à nemine quovis prætextu rejicienda.

ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστικὴ.

DUo potissimùm sunt capita, quæ de vulgatâ latinâ editione in Controversiam hodiè veniunt: quorum prius ejus Autorem; posterius Autoritatem respicit.

Quoad prius membrum; etsi ante exortum novæ sectæ Jesuvviticæ, nihil inter Pontificios magistritum erat, quàm totam vulgatam editionem Latinam, esse B. Hieronymi: cui etiam ut majorem assererent autoritatem, semper in frontispicio veterum editionum, Cardinalitium pileum appinxerunt: Nunc tamen nova societas Jesuvvitica, novam etiam sententiam in medium profert: nempè non totam vulgatam editionem Latinam, sed ejus tantummodò partes quasdam esse B. Hieronymi: reliquas verò alterius antiquioris interpretis, cujus tamen nomen exprimere non audent: quemadmodum censet Jesuvvita Bellarminus lib. 2. de Verbo Dei, cap. 9. Quanquam verò assertio isthæc verisimilitudinis aliquid obtinere videtur: usque tamen adeò incertum est, illas ipsas partes, quas Jesuvvita Hieronymo assignat, esse Hieronymi: ut pro negativa longè firmiores militent rationes. Contendit enim Jesuvvita, omnes libros Biblicos, excepto Psalterio, exceptis item libro Sapientiæ, Ecclesiastici & Macchabæorū, autorem habere Hieronymum. Jam verò vel mediocriter saltem lingvæ Hebrææ peritus, ex collatione textus Hebræi, & versionis vulgatæ, facilè deprehendit, etiamquoad reliquos libros biblicos in multis turpissimè lapsum esse Interpretem illum, quisquis tandem sit, multa etiam obscurissimè reddidisse: id quod de B. Hieronymo, quippe non modò lingvæ sanctæ peritissimo, sed & vitiosæ istius versionis censore severissimo, vel cogitare nefas fuerit.
