Et ne nimis insolens videatur Adversariis nostra hæc assertio, placet, paucis exemplis ad oculum demonstrare ejus veritatem. Gen. 1, 2. habet vulgata latina: Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas: Quam versionem reprehendens Hieronymus ostendit, ex Hebræo vertendum fuisse, Spiritus Domini incubabat aquis, sive fovebat aquas, instar avis. Capite 3, 15. Geneseos legitur in Hebræo, Ipse, hoc est, Messias, conteret caput Serpentis: Sed interpres Masculinum per Fœmininum inscitè reddidit: Ipsa, hoc est, Maria conteres caput Serpentis. Sic cap. 4, 1. in Hebræo est: Acquisivi virum ipsum Dominum Jehovah. Sed latinus Interpres perperam reddidit, Possedi hominem per DEUM: sic verba Hevæ in alienum sensum impiè detorquens. Vetus in Ecclesiaste legit cap. 2, 3. Cogitavi in corde meo abstrahere à Vino carnem meam: Hieronymus in commentariis sic vertendum esse scribit: Consideravi in corde meo, ut traherem in Vino carnem meam: significans velle se delicatè & lautè vivere. Sic cap. 9, 1. Vetus habet: Nescit homo, utrum amore an odio dignus sit: Hieronymus verò sic reddit: Et quidem charitatem, & quidem odium non est cognoscens homo. Quæ ipsa σφάλματα, & quidem haud leviora occurrunt in reliquis libris Veteris Testamenti: quin non in his solùm, sed & in libris Novi Testamenti, ut cum cap. 5, 9. epistolæ ad Galatas, vulgata habet: Modicum fermentum fermentat totam massam: Ibi Hieronymus lib. 3. commentarij in hanc Epistolam acriter reprehendit versionis hujus autorem, qui vertere debuerit, paululum fermenti: propterea quod Modicum sit virtutis & laudis. Sic monet idem Hieronymus. 2. Cor. 1, 22. & Eph. 1, 13. Vitiosissimè interpretem vocem αρραβων reddidisse per pignus, propterea quòd pignus pro mutua pecunia opponatur: Arnhabo verò futuræ emptioni, quasi testimonium quoddam & obligamentu detur. Quis proinde affirmare ausit, versionem illam vulgatam, vel ex toto, vel ex parte esse Hieronymi, cű nullus fermè sit liber, in quo non ipsemet, quoad versionem quædam desideret: ut verè omninò ad Clementem VII. P. M. scripserit Pagninus, in præfatione suorum Bibliorum, in ea se opinione esse, versionem illam vulgatam non esse Hieronymi: seq; optare, illam hodieq; esse superstitem, ut de qua ipse Hieronymus his verbis sit testatus: Certè confidenter dicam, & multos hujus operis testes citabo, me nihil duntaxat sententia de Hebraica veritate mutasse: Sicubi igitur mea editio à veteribus discrepârit, interroga quemlibet Hebræorum, & liquidò pervidebis, me ab æmulis frustra lacerari, qui malunt videri contemnere præclara, quàm discere. Proindè prioris membri assertionis Jesuvviticæ vanitas ultrò liquet. Sed quid attinet tempus in istis terere prolixius? cùm ex jam dictis, de assertionis Jesuvviticæ membro primo facilè fieri possit judicium: & ex subsequentibus idem futurum sit manifestius.

Posterius ergò propositionis Jesuvviticæ caput est de Autoritate vulgatæ latinæ Editionis: de qua Concilium Tridentinum sic definivit: Insuper eadem sacrosancta Synodus considerans nõ parùm utilitatis accedere posse Ecclesiæ Dei, si ex omnibus latinis editionibus, quæ circum feruntur sacrorum librorum, quænam pro Authentica habenda sit, innotefcat; statuit & declarat, ut hæc ipsa vetus & vulgata editio, quæ longo tot seculorum usu in ipsâ Ecclesia probata est, in publicis lectionibus, disputationibus, prædicationibus & expositionibus pro Authentica habeatur: & ut nemo illam rejicere quovis prætextu audeat vel præsumat. Ubi initiò sub admirationem venit stupenda Pontificum Romanorum temeritas & ἀκρισια. Cũ enim Erasmus Roterodamus, lucubrationes suas, in Novum Testamentum edidisset, & Latinam vulgatam non modò innumeris mendis laborare ostendisset: sed & planè novam è Græco sermone versionem adornasset: ibi illam Leo X. p. m. tanquam absolutissimam probavit, seq; eâ valde delectari & prætereà aliorum etiam Calculo eam laudari, haud obscurè significavit. Jam si Leo X. rectè censuit: utique successores ipsius, & nominatim Paulus III. Julius III & Pius IIII. Pontifices Romani in Concilio Tridentino malè decreverunt, quod à Leone dissentientes solam illam veterem definiverunt esse Authenticam. Porrò cur Collegium Lavanieuse versionem latinam Benedicti Ariæ Montani tantoperè collaudavit, & tanquam opus maximè necessarium approbavit: si vulgatæ latinæ nihil inerat vitij? Quo autem consilio posteriores isti à Leone defecerint, Oedipo divinatore opꝰ haud fuerit. Cùm enim animadverterent, B. Lutherum cum Pontificijs in arenam disputationis descendere haud velle, nisi suis dogmatibus ex ipsis Scripturis Canonicis fidem facerent, & verò probè perspicerent, ex vulgatâ latinâ, plerorumque errorum patrocinium peti posse: ideò maluerunt etiam vitiosißimam hanc versionẽ pronunciare Authenticam, quàm ingenuè profiteri, se, in defensione suorum dogmatum omni prorfus Scripturæ autoritate destitui. Unde exempli gratiâ, probaturi adorationem virginis Mariæ, protulerunt vitiosam versionem vulgatæ, Gen. 3, 15. Ipsa conteret caput serpentis. Sic Liberi Arbitrij vires in rebus spiritualibus asserturi, provocarunt ad truncatam versionem, Gen. 8, 21. Sensus & cogitatio cordis humani, ad malum prona sunt, ab adolescentia. Ubi in Hebræo legitur: Omne figmentum cogitationum cordis ejus (hominis) DUNTAXAT malum est, omni die: ita ut, ubi vulgata 1. omittit particulam Duntaxat, Deinde pro actu ponit δύναμιν, nempè quod prona sit ad malum. Ubi longe aliud est, pronum esse ad malum: aliud verò, tantùm malam esse, prius illud aliquam adhuc homini bonitatem in spiritualibus relinquit: posterius verò hoc eandem simpliciter negat. Sic Invocationem Sanctorum confirmaturi confugerunt ad vulgatam latinam, quæ Gen. 48, 16. habet: Et invocetur super eos (Ephraim & Manasse) nomen meum, nomina quoque patrum meorum, Abraham & Isaac: Cum in Hebræo legatur, Interprete. Vatablo: Et vocetur in eis nomen patrum meorum: Sic Justitiam propriorum meritorum asserturi, in subsidium vocarunt illud versionis vulgatæ, Hebr. 13, 16. Beneficentiæ & communionis nolite oblivisci: Talibus enim hostiis promeretur DEUS: Cùm in Græco sit: εὐαρεστῆται ὁ Θεὸς: Talibus hostijs delectatur DEUS. Sic ergò in loco, quod dicitur, sapuerunt Paterculi Concilij Tridentini, quòd latinam vulgatam nullo prætextu in expositionibus, lectionibus, disputationibus rejiciendam esse decreverunt. Hinc enim maximum errorum suorum præsidium mutuati possunt. Cæterùm cùm non modò Deus in Veteri, sed & in Novo Testamento severissimè præceperit, ut nihil quicquam Verbo suo vel addatur, vel adimatur, nedum mutetur aut corrumpatur: utrumq́; verò in vulgatâ Latinâ factitari, tum ex jam allatis, tùm ex infinitis alijs exemplis, Sole meridiano clarius constet: rectissimè fecerimus, si nihil morati brutum illud Concilij Tridentini fulmen, non priùs vulgatæ editioni fidem adhibuerimus, quàm ad fontes ipsos eam ex asse congruere, deprehenderimus.

Placet autem paucis expendere, quibusnam argumentis Adversarij vulgatæ suæ editionis Autoritatem conciliare studeant. PRIMUM est Bellarmini, desumptum à longo tot seculorum usu, quo in latina Ecclesia, Editio hæc vulgata sit omnibus modis approbata. Ad quod ipsum Argumentum Concilium etiam Tridentinum provocat. Cæterùm procedit hoc argumentum initiò ex falsa hypothesi, ac proindè petit principium. Tàm enim incertum ac falsum est, illud statim pro Authentico esse habendum, quod latina Ecclesia multis seculis approbavit, quàm incertum falsumque esse potest, Editionem vulgatam latinam esse authenticam. Hoc ipsum enim quæritur, Utrum Ecclesia sive latina, sive quævis alia, contenta esse debuerit unâ editione vulgatâ, neglectis interim & posthabitis fontibus Hebraic & Græcis. Augustinus certè, qui in latina Ecclesia locum facilè principem obtinuit, longè aliter suam hac de re informat sententiam, lib: 2. de doctr. Christiana cap. 12. his verbis: Latina linguæ homines, duabus alijs ad scripturarum divinarum cognitionem opus habent, Hebræâ scilicet & Græcâ, ut ad Exemplaria præcedentia recurratur, si quam dubitationem attulerit Latinorum interpretum infinita varietas: Quis enim interpretum vera secutus sit, nisi Exemplaria linguæ præcedentis legantur, incertum est. Et cap: 15. Libros Novi Testamenti si quid in latinis varietatibus titubat, Græcis cedere oportere, non est dubium.

Deindè ex parte procedit Argumentatio Jesuvvitica. Fit enim collectio à latina Ecclesia, quæ tantùm particularis est, ad totam Catholicam Ecclesiam. Jam autem error particularis Ecclesiæ, neque potest neque debet præjudicare toti Ecclesiæ Catholicæ : si vel maximè extra omne dubium esset positum, quod Latina Ecclesia, vulgatam Editionem semper pro Authentica habuerit : Quanquam diversum jam ex Augustino cognovimus. Secundi Argumenti loco Bellarminus provocat ad consensum Augustini & plurimorum aliorum latinæ Ecclesiæ Doctorum, qui vulgatam latinam unanimi suffragio approbârunt. Verùm ne sic quidem Jesuvvita tantillum proficit. Negari enim non potest, illos ipsos Veteres, quos citat, & in his etiam Augustinum lingvæ Hebrææ imperitos fuisse, sic ut ne judicare quidem exactè potuerint, quàm probè ab ipsa Hebraicâ veritate singulæ versiones latinæ, quâ voces, quâ sententias integras absint. Deindè, laudat Augustinus versionem latinam sive illam, quam Italam vocarunt, sive aliam quamcunque κατὰ τὶ, non verò ἁπλῶς, ac proindè plus est in Consequente, quàm fuit in Antecedente. κατὰ τὶ quidem, quatenus ex illa versione quali quali, multum tamen commodi ac emolumenti ad Ecclesiam latinam accessit : Interim tamen illis versionibus omnibus Hebræam & Græcam præposuit: atq; ex his tanquam fontibus, omnes alias emendari æstimarique voluit. Tandem, rursus ex parte colligit Jesuvvita, in hunc modum: Augustinus, Isidorus, Anshelmo, Bernhardus, & alij quidam laudarunt versionem latinam, Ergo omnes Doctores Ecclesiæ latinæ habuerunt latinam illam pro Authentica. Cur n. obsecro ad præcipuum illud lumen Ecclesiæ latinæ nempè D. Hieronymum non provocat lingvæ Hebrææ peritissimum ? Quem sanè suam quoque versionem latinam, ad fontes Hebræos exigi voluisse, liquidò constat, tū ex locis alijs, tùm verò ex præfatione ipsius in Pentateuchum, ubi suos æmulos sic alloquitur : Quid livore torqueris? quid imperitorum animos contra me concitas ? Sicubi in translatione tibi videor errare, interroga Hebræos, diversarum urbium Magistros consule. Sed porrò & tertio loco oggerunt Jesuvvitæ : Si Hebræa editione standum sit, nullum fore contionum finem, propterea quod tanta sit vocum Hebræarum ambiguitas ut vel istiq lingvæ peritissimi, de certa significatione digladientur. Proindè consultissimum esse, ut Ecclesiæ judicio nos submittamus, quæ tanquam verus arbiter & judex pronunciare possit, cujus interpretis sententiæ acquiescendum sit. Exempli gratia, Genes. 36, 24. Iste est Ana, qui invenit הַיֵּמִים Hajemim in solitudine, cū pasceret asinas patris sui: Item Gen. 30, 14. Egressus Ruben tempore messis triticeæ in argum, reperit דּוּדָאִים Dudaim & attulit eas ad Leah: Ubi priorē illam vocem Jemim alij interpretes verterunt aquas calidas, alij mulos, alij onagros: Posteriorem verò vocem Dudaimalij reddiderunt mandragoras, alij lilia, alij violas: alij fructum selecti saporis &

gustus tempore messis triticeae maturo. Sed & iste nodus facilè dissecari potest. Primùm enim committitur Sophisma τῆς πλεονεξίας, hoc est, plus infertur in Consequente, quàm ex Antecedenti potest extrui. Antecedens enim illud tantùm probat, reperiri voces in Hebræo, quæ propter quandam cognationem & similitudinem, plures significationes admittunt. Consequens autem infert, Ergò nullum fore contentionum finem in doctrina fidei, si Hebræa standum sit editione. Quæ collectio quàm sit sophistica, vel puer intelligit. Neque enim fides & Religio Christiana periclitantur, etiamsi de istis & id genus alijs vocabulis certent Grammatici, & adhuc sub judice lis sit, quænam significatio maximè sit amplectenda. Neque etiam, ubi circumstantia aliqua historiæ laborat, statim ipsa quoque Religio, & Articulorum fidei substantia laborare censenda est. Quid? quod plerumŃ; plures illæ significationes unius vocis non contradictorias, sed cognatas, & ad subjectam materiam pulcrè congruentes pariunt sententias. Unde Hispanus Benedictus Ariæ Montanus, in præfatione Biblijs Hebræis præfixa, objectioni Jesuviticæ hunc in modum eleganter respondet: Cum vox aliqua ambigua, quæ duo significat, in primæva illa lingva usurpatur, eâ Spiritum Sanctum sine delectu aliquo usum non esse, nobis persuademus, & utramque significationem suam interpretationem postulare, & hac de causa eas voces, nobis, ut in utramque partem eas interpretemur, propositas esse credimus. Deindè committitur Sophisma ὡς πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Neque enim propterea ad Ecclesiæ judicium est confugiendum: si de vocis alicujus significatione propria oriatur Controversia, sed potiùs ad Grammaticos & lingvæ hujus peritissimos, siquidem omni artifici in sua arte est credendum. Tandem ἀσύστατον planè est collectio isthæc Esavvitica: Aut enim Ecclesia dirimet controversias hujusmodi, ex prætoria quadam & absoluta potestate: aut ex certis principijs atq; rationibus: Tertium enim dari non potest. Jam verò potestas talis prætoria & absoluta, neque Ecclesiæ comperit, neque etiam dubitantium animis potest satisfacere. Relinquitur Ergò, si vel maximè ad Ecclesiæ judicium recurrendum sit, tamen illam de Versionis alicujus certitudine aut incertitudine, non pronunciare posse, nisi ex proprijs principijs, hoc est, ex ipsis fontibus; Quod ipsum & nos asserimus.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Jesuitical Proposition II

JESUITICAL PROPOSITION II.

It is not expedient that Biblical books be translated into the vernacular language for every people: For those who wish religion to be safe must entirely forbid the laity from the reading of sacred literature. For to them it is not only not useful: but in many ways pernicious.

Ἕκθεσις ἄνασκευαστική.

The Jesuit theologians of Cologne set forth this thesis in almost the same words in their censure on page 21, writing thus: The reading of Holy Scripture is not only not useful, but in many ways pernicious to the Church: And that we may speak more boldly, no heresy has ever been found which has not taken occasion from the Scriptures. Johannes Molanus of Louvain supports them in Tract 3 of Practical Theology, ch. 27, Conclusion 2, writing thus: We deny that the study of the Scriptures is required of them (the laity), nay, we healthfully say that they are to be kept from the reading of the Scriptures, and that it suffices for them to moderate the course of their lives according to the prescription of the Pastors and Doctors of the Church. Whence Sanders, book 7, On the Visible Monarchy, determined that it is heretical to affirm that the Scriptures must necessarily be translated into common languages. And Tanner, pp. 264 and 265 of the Compendious Relation. The Church does not act badly, he says, while it does not indiscriminately permit the reading of the Bibles in the common language to all the laity: For it is not fitting that Holy Scripture should be published everywhere in any common language, so that it may be read by all, because of many and most grave causes: which, however, he does not express. This very thing the Roman Church repeats in the Catechetical work of Canisius, page 301. Thus the Jesuit Ledesma, in his book on Divine Scriptures not to be read everywhere in any language, page 147, writes: It is expedient that there be one Latin version, which all may receive, and follow as approved by the Church. The Jesuit Bellarmine indeed complains, book 2, On the Word of God, ch. 15, that the Roman Church is falsely slandered by Chemnitz and others, because they prohibit common translations of the Bibles: but he himself is found to be inconsistent and mendacious. For although Pius IV, in the index of prohibited books, Rule 4 seems to grant the reading of Biblical books: yet soon by a manifest Restriction, he adapts this concession only to those who can use it (that reading) usefully and with fruit: that is, to those who have obtained permission from the ordinary. Now, however, they never obtain this permission, unless those who have first subjected themselves in all things to the Roman Pontiff and his decrees, in whose number that one easily obtains the first place: That it is not to be determined concerning the Christian religion from the sacred letters alone. Thus, therefore, the Roman Church grants the reading of the Bibles only to those of whom it is already certainly established that they are not much moved by the authority of the Bibles. Therefore, no injury is done to the Papists when they are accused because they do not want the Scriptures to be translated everywhere into common languages. For it matters so much whether they are not translated at all, or, having been translated, are not granted to be read by those for whom they were translated.

Furthermore, the arguments with which the Jesuits are commonly accustomed to fight are these principal ones:

The first of the Jesuit Bellarmine is such: The Lord himself honored only the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin language with the title of his cross, John 19:20. Therefore we ought to be content with these three languages also. But I answer that a shameful sophistry is committed παρὰ τὸ ἑπόμενον (by the consequent), which will become more manifest if the entire Syllogism is formed. For the major will emerge as such: In whatever languages Christ the Savior wished his cross to be inscribed: those only, and not more, are to be used both in the version and in the reading of the scriptures. But Christ truly wished his cross to be inscribed only in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages. Therefore. Who does not see that the major, as the κρινόμενον (the point in question), stands in need of clear proof? And while the adversaries do not bring it forth, it is evident that they weave their argument from false presuppositions. For if they should bark ever so much that Christ honored those three languages only with the title of his cross so that he might establish their perpetual use concerning the Holy Scriptures: again it becomes manifest that they are begging the question and are sophistical under the fallacy τοῦ μὴ αἰτίου ὡς αἰτίου (of the non-cause as a cause). For let them demonstrate that that title of the cross was formed in only those three languages for this very reason, that it might be hinted that the Scriptures were not to be translated into any other languages: but let them demonstrate this from the Holy Scriptures themselves. Certainly, that this cause is frivolous and nugatory is evident even from the fact that the Holy Spirit himself did not wish to be content with the use of those three languages, but so that the preaching of the Gospel might be disseminated in any languages whatsoever throughout the whole world, he instructed the Apostles with the gift and knowledge of various, nay, of all languages. Now, what the reason for preaching is, that the same is also for writing, hardly anyone would deny, unless he wished to feign that the Holy Spirit indeed wished that the Gospel concerning CHRIST should be taught in various languages, but not written: which would be prodigiously absurd.

The other Jesuit argument is as follows: The Apostles wrote only in Hebrew & Greek, and perhaps also in Latin. Therefore, it is not permitted either to translate Holy Scripture into more or other languages, or to read it when translated.

But I respond: The argument fails παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον, καὶ τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ αἰτήσκενον: whence a childish inconsistency, nay, a garrulity, is easily detected. For if the complete syllogism is formed: the major proposition will emerge as follows: In those languages in which the Apostles wrote the Gospel: in those only is one to be used in the reading of the Scriptures. Which proposition, indeed, the Jesuits are neither able to confirm by any apodictic reasoning, nor can we admit it, as it is something that manifestly begs the question. For this very thing is sought, whether one is to use only those languages in the reading of the Bibles which the Apostles used in writing.

Then, this major proposition collapses by its own absurdity and futility. For if the Scripture ought to be read only in those languages in which the Biblical books were written by their authors, and ought not to be translated into other languages: it will follow that the books of Moses and the Prophets ought not to have been poured into the Greek language: much less into the Latin, which it is certain that not even the Apostles themselves used in writing. For the fact that Bellarmine narrates that his Mark wrote his Gospel in Latin must be considered clearly an old wives' tale. Finally, I invert the Jesuit argument in this manner: If the Apostles announced the Gospel in all the languages of all the peoples to whom they arrived: it will certainly be lawful to have their doctrine also written in all languages. For the same Gospel, as Irenaeus says in book 3, chapter 1, which the Apostles preached, they later by the will of GOD handed down to us in the Scriptures, to be the foundation and pillar of our faith. But how can the Gospel, proposed in an unknown language, be the foundation and pillar of our faith?

The third argument is such: The universal Church has always used only these three languages, namely Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, in reading and explaining the Scriptures: Nor does any ancient writer mention any other translation. Therefore, it is evident from this alone that in the first four hundred years, during which the Church flourished most, the Sacred Scriptures were read in none but those three languages, let alone translated into any other vulgar one.

But I respond 1. that the fallacy of the accident is committed: For the fact that it came about through the diffusion of those three languages that their use prevailed in the Church over others, that is a matter of accident: and it does not sustain the strength of an apodictic proof. Next, the argument fails by taking that which is not a cause as a cause. For no firm reason militates that the Scripture was therefore translated into no vulgar languages, because no ancient writer mentioned any other translation. For the Jesuits ought to have remembered that the entire ecclesiastical history of all peoples has not come down to us: which, if it were indeed extant, there is no doubt that the contrary could be clearly proven from it.

Finally, the argument labors under a manifest falsehood. For Sixtus of Siena himself, in book 4 of the Holy Library, page 334, commemorates that in the year of Christ 370, Ulphilas, Bishop of the Goths, first invented letters for the Goths; and first converted all the divine Scriptures from Greek into the Gothic language. The same thing is reported about the same Ulphilas by Socrates in book 4 of his ecclesiastical history, chapter 27. Whom Socrates does not at all reproach for this, which he would certainly have done if the Scripture ought not to have been translated into vulgar languages. What of the fact that St. Jerome translated the holy Bibles not only into Latin, but also into the Dalmatian language, as he himself testifies in his letter to Sophronius? And he himself flourished around the year of the Lord 400.

They formulate the fourth argument thus: Moses himself, in Deuteronomy 31:9 and 26, handed over the tablets of the divine law enclosed in the ark of the covenant to be guarded by the Levites, and established that the reading of the Scripture was not common to all but lawful only to the Priests, and consequently, that it was not to be translated into any languages whatsoever.

I respond that the Jesuits repeat the same warmed-over cabbage, or sophistry, in this place, and that the fallacy of taking that which is not a cause as a cause and of the non-sequitur is committed. For Moses wanted the Law to be enclosed and kept in the ark, not so that it would not be read by the common people: for he had expressly commanded them in chapter 6, 6 and following, that they should meditate daily on the law of the Lord, both at home and abroad, both by night and by day: and that they should inscribe the words of the law not only on their hearts, but also on the doorposts and gates of their houses. But this was done by Moses so that the Volume of the Law might be saved from destruction, and be kept in eternal memory, as a testimony against the Israelite people, as the text has in verse 26. Nor does it stand in the way that Moses, ibid. verse 10, commands that the volume of the law be read before the whole people only in the seventh year, namely the Jubilee. For this is not to be taken as if the Law of the Lord were supposed to remain as if hidden from the people for all the rest of the time: For GOD wanted the Levites to be daily teachers for this reason, that they might instruct the people in the true sense of the law, whose precepts they were constantly reading, hearing, and meditating upon: But that in this seventh year the explanation of the Law ought to be proposed with greater solemnity than was accustomed to be done otherwise, because of the occasion which the timing provided: Since at that time the people had leisure from agriculture and other labors of that kind, to which they were otherwise devoted: and therefore they could so much more conveniently be free for the reading and listening to the divine Law.

And what, I ask, is this childish method of arguing? The law was required to be solemnly proposed and explained to the people every seventh year. Therefore, it was not lawful for anyone at any other time either to meditate upon the law of the Lord or to keep a copy of it in his own home. By the same sophistry they can argue thus: On every seventh day, by virtue of the third commandment of the Decalogue, GOD is to be worshipped, invoked, and celebrated. Therefore, on the remaining days this is not permitted. Which argument is certainly to be referred to those things which Aristotle calls κολάσεως δεόμ̄εα (things needing correction).

Finally, the Jesuits rise up against us with this horned dilemma: If it is lawful to translate the Bibles into vernacular languages, it will be lawful either for the sake of the teachers or for the sake of the learners. Not for the sake of the teachers, since they, if not the sources themselves, at least are skilled in the Latin language and understand it. Not for the sake of the learners, because they can progress more correctly from the instruction of Doctors than from the reading of Bibles. But this whole dilemma is woven from false presuppositions. For first, it is false that it belongs only to those who are trained in the original languages to teach. For although the public duty of teaching properly belongs to these, nevertheless any layman by divine right not only can, but even ought to, sustain those parts of teaching even within private walls, according to that passage in Colossians 3:16: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, TEACHING and admonishing one another. Then it is false that it is the duty of learners only to listen to teachers: As if, indeed, it had not been said to them just as much as to the teachers, Search the Scriptures, John 5:39, and prove all things, hold fast that which is good, 1 Thessalonians 5:21.

Item, test the spirits, whether they are from God. 1 John 4:1. Certainly the Bereans are commended on this account by the Holy Spirit, Acts 17:11, because they searched the Scriptures to see whether those things which were said by Paul and Silas were so. But how could they search the Scriptures if they were destitute of a version known to them? And what are the laity to do if a doctor is infected with some heresy? Must they then also simply hang upon the mouth of the teacher? Finally, the Jesuits ought to remember that precept of the logicians: a dilemma is only good when it is constructed from immediate contraries. Now, however, that the duty of learners is immediately, and thus contradictorily, opposed to the reading and meditation of the Scriptures, which is instituted by any pious person, no one but a madman would affirm. Let the adversaries see, therefore, how they can defend, I will not say the matter, but only the form of this dilemma.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO II. JESUVVITICA.

Non expedit, ut libri Biblici in lingvam cuilibet populo vernaculam transferantur: Qui n. salvam volunt esse religionem, omninò debent Laicis interdicere in universum lectione sacrarum literarum. His enim non modò non utilis ea est: sed multis modis perniciosa.

Ἕκθεσις ἄνασκευαστική.

THesin hanc ijsdem penè verbis prodiderunt Jesuvitá Colonienfes in censura sua pag. 21. sic scribentes: Lectio Sacræ Scripturæ nõ tantùm non est utilis, sed multis modis perniciosa Ecclesiæ: Et ut audentius dicamus, nulla unquàm reperta est hæresis, quæ non ex Scripturis occasionem acceperit. Quibus suffragatur Johannes Molanus Lovaniensis Tract. 3. Theol. practicæ c. 27. Conclus. 2. sic scribens: Negamus ab eis(Laicis) requiri studium Scripturarum, imò salubriter dicimus, eos à Lectione Scripturarum arceri, eisquè sufficere, ut ex præscripto Pastorum & Doctorum Ecclesiæ, vitæ cursum moderentur. Unde Sanders lib. 7. de Visibili Monarchia, Hæreticum esse, statuit, affirmare, Scripturas necessariò debere in vulgares linguas converti. Et Tannerus p. 264. & 265. Relationis Compendiarie. Non malè, inquit, facit Ecclesia, dum non indifferenter omnibus Laicis lectionem Bibliorum in lingua vulgari permittit: Conveniens enim non est, ut sacra Scriptura quavis lingua vulgari ità passim edatur, ut ab omnibus legatur, propter multas & gravissimas causas: quas tamen non exprimit. Quod ipsum Ecclesia Romana repetit in opere Catechetico Canisij pag. 301. Sic Jesuvvita Ledesima lib. de divinis Scripturis, quavis passim lingva non legendis pag. 147. scribit: Expedit unam esse latinam versionem, quam omnes recipiant, & ab Ecclesia approbatam sequantur. Conqueritur quidem Jesuvvita Bellarminus lib. 2. de Verbo Dei cap. 15. à Chemnitio, & alijs falsò infamulari Ecclesiam Romanam, quod vulgares Bibliorum translationes prohibeant: sed ipsemet varius ac mendax deprehenditur. Etsi n. Pius IV. in indice librorum prohibitoru. Regula 4. cõcedere videtur lectionẽ librorum Biblicorũ: tamen mox per Restrictionem manifestam, concessionem hanc ad eos tantùm accommodat, qui utiliter & cum fructu eà (lectione) uti possunt: hoc est, ad eos, qui facultatem ab ordinario obtinuerint. Jam verò facultatem hanc nunquam obtinent, nisi qui se prius Romano Pontifici, ejusquè placitis, per omnia subjecerint, in quorum numero illud primas facilè obtinet: Non esse ex solis sacris literis de religione Christiana statuendum. Sic ergò lectionem Bibliorum ijs tantùm concedit Romana Ecclesia, de quibus jam certò constat, eos Bibliorum autoritate non multùm moveri. Nulla proinde Pontificijs fit injuria, cùm accusantur, quod nolint passim verti Scripturas in lingvas vulgares. Tantum enim interest, aut planè non verti, aut jam versas, non concedi legendas ijs, propter quos versæ sunt.

Cæterùm argumenta quibus communiter Jesuvitæ pugnare solent, sunt isthæc præcipua:

Primum Jesuvitæ Bellarmini tale est: Dominus ipse titulo crucis suæ honoravit tantùm linguam Hebraicam, Græcam, Latinam Johan. 19, 20. Ergò tribus etiam istis lingvis debemus esse contenti. Sed respondeo, turpem committi Sophisticationem παρὰ τὸ ἑπόμενον, quæ manifestior fiet, si integer formetur Syllogismus. Major enim talis emerget: Quibus lingvis Christus Servator crucem suam insigniri voluit: ea tantùm, & non plures tùm in versione, tùm in lectione scripturarum, usurpandæ sunt. At verò Christus Hebræâ tantùm, Græcâ & Latinâ lingvis crucem suam insigniri voluit. E. Jã Majorem tanquam κρινόμενον probatione luculentâ indigere quis non videt? quam dum Adversarij non proferunt, patet, ex falsis præsuppositis ipsos nectere argumentum. Nam si vel maximè ogganniant, ideò Christum tres tantùm istas lingvas titulo crucis suæ honorasse, ut earum usum circa Scripturas Sacras perpetuum astrueret: rursum manifestum fit, eos petere principium, & Sophisticari sub Elencho τοῦ μὴ αἰτίου ὡς αἰτίου. Demonstrent enim ob hanc ipsam causam, titulum illum crucis, tribus tantùm istis lingvis informatum fuisse, ut in nullas alias lingvas Scripturas vertendas esse, innueretur: sed demonstrent hoc ex ipsis Scripturis Sacris. Certè frivolam esse & nugatoriam hanc causam vel inde patet, quòd ipse Spiritus Sanctus, noluit esse contentus trium illarum lingvarum usu, sed ut prædicatio Evangelij in quibusvis lingvis per universum terrarum orbem disseminaretur, instruxit Apostolos variarum, imò omnium lingvarum dono ac notitiâ. Jam quæ ratio est prædicationis, eandem Scriptionis etiam esse, vix iverit inficias, nisi qui fingere voluerit, Spiritum Sanctum voluisse quidem, ut in varijs lingvis doceretur, non verò scriberetur Evangelium de CHRISTO: id quod prodigiosè esset absurdum.

Alterum argumentum Jesuviticum tale est: Apostoli non scripserunt, nisi Hebraicè & Græcè, & fortassis etiam latinè. Ergò in plures aut alias lingvas non licet Scripturam sacram vel transferre vel translatam legere.

Sed Respondeo: Fallit argumentum παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον, καὶ τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ αἰτήσκενον: Unde puerilis ἀσυστασία, imò ἀδολεσχία facilè deprehenditur. Quòd si enim integer formetur Syllogismus: major propositio emerget talis: Quibus lingvis Apostoli conscripserunt Evangelium: illis tantùm in lectione Scripturarum est utendum. Quam sanè propositionem neque Jesuvitæ ulla ratione aliquâ apodictica confirmare valent, neque nos eam, ut quæ manifestè petit principium, admittere possumus. Hoc ipsum enim quæritur, an illis tantùm lingvis in lectione Bibliorum sit utendum, quibus Apostoli in scribendo usi sunt.

Deindè, Major hæc propositio propriâ suâ absurditate & futilitate concidit. Si enim ijs tantummodò lingvis, quibus libri Biblici à suis Autoribus scripti sunt, Scriptura legi, neque in alias lingvas transferri debet: sequetur, neque libros Mosis, & Prophetarum in Graecam lingvam transfundi debuisse: multò minùs in latinam, quâ ne ipsos quidem Apostolos in scribendo usos fuisse constat. Nam quòd Bellarminus Marcum suum Evangelium latinè conscripsisse narrat, anilis planè fabula censeri debet. Tandem inverto argumentum Jesuvviticum in hunc modum: Si Apostoli omnibus lingvis omnium populorum, ad quos pervenerunt, annunciaverunt Evangelium: licebit utique doctrinam etiam ipsorũ omnibus in lingvis scriptam habere. Idem enim Evangelium, ut Irenaeus ait lib. 3. cap. 1. quod praeconiaverunt Apostoli, postea per DEI voluntatem in Scripturis nobis tradiderunt, fundamentum & columnam fidei nostrae futurum. Quomodo autem potest Evangelium ignotâ lingva propositum, esse fundamentum & columna nostrae fidei?

Tertium Argumentum tale est: Ecclesia universalis semper his tantùm tribus lingvis, nempe Hebra, á Graecá, Latiná, in legendis & explicandis Scripturis usa est: Neq; ullus antiquus Scriptor meminit alicujus alterius translationis. Ergò vel indè constat primis quadringentis annis, quibus Ecclesia maximè floruit, Scripturas Sacras non nisi in lingvis istis tribus esse lectas, nedum in vulgarem ullam aliam transfusas.

Sed respondeo 1. committi fallaciam τů συμβεβηκότως: Nam quòd trium illarum lingvarum diffusione factum est, ut prae caeteris earum usus obtineret in Ecclesia, illud Accidentis est: neque nervum probationis Apodicticae sustinet. Deinde fallit argumentum ὧσπερ το μη αἴτιον εἱς αἴτιον. Neq; enim ulla militat firma ratio, ideò in nullas lingvas vulgares, transfusam esse Scripturam, quia nullus antiquus Scriptor ullius alterius translationis meminerit. Meminisse enim debebant Jesuvvitae, non omnium populorum historiam Ecclesiasticam integram ad nos pervenisse: Quæ sanè si extaret, nullum est dubium, quin diversú luculéter ex ea comprobari possit.

Tandem laborat argumentum manifestò ψευδει. Nam ipse quoq; Sixtus Senensis lib. 4 Bibl. sanctae, pag 334. commemorat Anno Christi 370. Ulphilam Gothorum Episcopum, primum Gothorum literas invenisse; primumq; omnes divinas Scripturas è Greco in Gothicam lingvam convertisse. Quod ipsum de eodem Ulphila refert etiam Socrates lib. 4. hist. eccl. cap. 27. Quem etiam hoc nomine Socrates minimè reprehendit, id quod facturus omninò fuisset, si in lingvas vulgares Scriptura verti non debuisset. Quid? quòd D. Hieronymus, sacra Biblia non solummodò in Latinam, sed in Dalmaticam quoque lingvam transtulit, uti ipsemet testatur in Epistola ad Sophroniu. Floruit a. ipse circa An. D. 400.

Quartum argumentum sic informant: Moses ipse Deut. 31, 9. & 26. tabulas legis divinae arcae foederis inclusas custodiendas tradidit Levitis, & lectionem Scripturae non omnibus communem sed Solis Sacerdotibus licitam esse, & per Consequens, nō in quasvis lingvas eam vertendam esse, statuit.

Respondeo, eandem crambem, sive Sophisticationem & hoc loco repetere Jesuitas & committi Sophisma τὸ μὴ αἰτιὸ ὡς αἰτίκ & ὠδῷ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Moses enim Legem includi & asservari voluit in arca, non ut ea à plebe non legeretur: Huic enim cap. 6, 6 & seqq. expressè mandaverat, ut quotidiè meditaretur in lege Domini, tùm domi, tùm foris, tùm noctu, tùm interdiu: inscriberetq; verba legis non modò cordibus, sed & liminibus & ostijs domuū suarū. Sed ideò hoc à Mose factum, ut Volumen Legis ab interitu vindicaretur, & asservaretur in memoriam sempiternam, in testimonium contra populum Israeliticum, uti habet textus v. 26. Neque obstat, Moses ibid. v. 10. jubet, volumen legis septimo demùm anno, Jubilæo nimirum, coram toto populo legatur. Hoc enim non ita accipiendum est, ac si omni reliquo tempore Lex Domini à populo abscondita quasi manere debuisset: Ideò enim DEUS Levitas quotidianos Doctores esse voluit, ut populum de vero sensu legis, cujus præcepta subinde legebant, audiebant, meditabantur, erudirent: Verùm quòd anno hoc septimo majori cum solennitate, quàm aliàs fieri consueverat, Legis explicatio proponi deberet, propter occasionem, quā temporis ratio subministrabat: Siquidem tum populus ocium habebat ab agricultura, & id genus alijs laboribus, quibus aliàs erant dediti: ac proinde tantò commodiò lectioni & auscultationi Legis divinæ vacare poterat.

Et quæ obsecro, puerilis hæc est argumentandi ratio. Lex septimo quovis anno solenniter populo proponi & explicari debuit. E. nemini fas erat reliquo tempore, vel legem Domini meditari; vel ejus Exemplum domi suæ asservare. Pari Sophistica sic argumentari possunt: Die quovis septimo, vi tertij præcepti Decalogi, DEUS est colendus, invocandus, celebrandus. Ergò reliquis diebus hoc non licet. Quod sanè argumentum inter ea referendum est, quæ Aristoteles nominat κολάσεως δεόμ̄εα.

Tandem, Jesuitæ hoc cornuto Dilemmate adversum nos insurgunt: Si licet Biblia in linguas vernaculas transfundere, licebit id, aut propter docentes: aut propter discentes. Non propter docentes: siquidem hi, si non fontes ipsos, saltem linguam latinam callent, eamq; intelligunt. Non propter discentes: Quia hi rectius ex institutione Doctorum, quàm ex lectione Bibliorum proficere possunt. Cæterùm totum hoc Dilemma ex falsis contextum est præsuppositis. Primùm enim falsum est, Eorum tantùm esse docere, qui in lingvis Originalibus sunt exercitati. Etsi enim his publicum docendi munus propriè competit: quivis tamen Laicus jure divino partes istas docendi intra privatos etiam parietes sustinere non modò potest, sed etiam debet: juxta illud Coloss. 3, 16. Verbum Christi habitet in vobis abundanter in omni scientia, DOCENTES & commonefacientes vos ipsos. Deinde falsum est, Discentium officium esse, tantùm audire Docentes: Quasi verò non his æquè ac docentibus dictum sit, Scrutamini Scripturas. Johann. 5, 39. & omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete 1. Thessal. 5, 21.

Item, probate Spiritus, num ex Deo sint. 1. Joh. 4, 1. certè Berrhoënses hoc nomine à Spiritu Sancto commendantur, Act. 17, 11. quod scrutati sint in Scripturis, utrum ita se haberent, quæ dicebantur à Paulo & Sila. Quomodo verò Scripturas poterunt scrutari, si versione ipsis cognitâ destituantur? Et quid faciendum Laicis, si Doctor hæresi aliquâ sit infectus? Annè & tùm ab ore docentis simpliciter pendere ipsos necessum fuerit? Tandem meminisse debebant Jesuvvitæ præcepti illius Logicorum: Dilemma tùm demùm bonum esse, quando conficitur ex contrarijs immediatis. Jam verò discentium officium immediatè, & sic contradictoriè esse oppositum lectioni & meditationi Scripturarum, quæ à quolibet pio instituitur, nemo nisi planè amens affirmaverit. Viderint proindè Adversarij quomodo, non dicam materiam, sed tantùm formam hujus Dilemmatis tueri possint.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Question IV. General. On the perspicuity of Holy Scripture

In treating this question, the state of the controversy, which exists today between our churches and the Jesuit faction, comes under more accurate consideration at the beginning. But it is not, as the adversaries falsely assume, that the question is: Is Holy Scripture so perspicuous and easy that it can be understood by anyone, even those who are not illuminated by the Holy Spirit? For we ourselves hold and defend the negative of this question. Nor is it a matter of controversy whether there are some things in the Scriptures that are obscure and difficult to understand. This we also readily admit. But the controversy is about this: Is Holy Scripture, where it deals with the business of our faith and salvation, so perspicuous and easy that it can be understood by those who have received the first fruits of the Holy Spirit and have been illuminated by faith in Christ? Or is it so obscure that it cannot be understood even by them, unless they follow the guidance or explanation of the Church and the judgment or interpretation of the Roman Pontiff? We simply deny the latter part of this question, while strenuously fighting for the affirmative of the former part. Therefore, the proposition of our churches will be as follows.

Canonical Holy Scripture, in matters concerning our faith and salvation, is so perspicuous and clear that it can be understood by a pious and faithful man, even without the testimony of the Church.

CONFIRMATION.

Scripture itself shows the primary argument of our confirmation. For what else do these words of David mean, Ps. 119

34. Give me understanding, and I will search thy law: And verse 18. Reveal my eyes, and I will consider the wondrous things of thy law. And verse 135. Make thy face to shine upon thy servant, and teach me thy justifications.

What, I ask, do these testimonies mean, other than that those who have received the first fruits of the Holy Spirit and have been gifted with faith are able to search the law of the Lord and his wondrous things, and are able to meditate and learn the justifications of the Lord from the Scriptures? And that they have no need to suspend their assent until they have perceived the certain meaning of Scripture from either the Pope or some Council?

Furthermore, what will the Romanists answer to David, because in Ps. 119:105 he calls the Word of the Lord a lamp to his feet and a light to his paths? Because he calls the commandment of the Lord clear, enlightening the eyes, Ps. 19:9? Because Christ himself asserts that he does not speak in proverbs, but announces openly about his Father, John 16:25? Because the same, in his most ardent prayer, expressly professes: Father, I have manifested thy name to men, John 17:6? Because the Apostle declares that his Timothy has known the sacred letters from childhood, which can make him learned unto salvation, 2 Tim. 3:15? Because finally Peter himself, calling us away from all human tradition, says: We have a more firm prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star arises in your hearts, 2 Pet. 1:19. Now if these praises belong to the prophetic books of the Old Testament, they can certainly be applied much more to the whole of Scripture, as it now consists of the prophetic and apostolic books.

Moreover, Bellarmine responds with two points in this place. 1. That in all those passages the subject is not the entire Scriptures, but only the Lord's commandments. Then, that the subject is indeed all the Scriptures, but the scriptures are called clear, and likewise a light and a lamp, not because they are easily understood, but because when they have been understood, they illuminate the mind. But both responses are feeble: nay, the former is clearly trifling. For the cited testimonies prove by the very letter that the subject is the entire Scriptures. And the Jesuit ought to have remembered that the Hebrew word Thorah, in the Psalms and the Prophets, does not denote only the Law properly so called, namely the Decalogue, but the entire doctrine of the Church, as much of the Gospel as of the Law. Which the Jesuit himself also acknowledged in this very chapter, writing thus: David by the name of Law does not understand only those ten commandments, but all the divine Scriptures. Therefore, a liar ought to have a good memory.

The second response is so constructed that it entangles the Jesuit more than it explains him. For none of us has ever denied that the Holy Scriptures are obscure to man in himself, and appear as foolishness. Now, indeed, that which the Jesuit confesses, that the Scriptures are clear to those whom the Holy Spirit has illuminated with faith: certainly he confesses, even unwittingly, that which we assert. For who would be so prodigiously absurd as to contend that the Scriptures illuminate the mind, even when not yet understood? But here is Rhodes, here is the leap: whether the Scriptures themselves provide their own understanding to believers and those desirous of learning, or indeed there is need of some other light arriving from the outside, which might be introduced into Scripture either by the Pope or by a Council. Here therefore the Jesuit would have to leap, and show that the testimonies of Scripture produced do not evidently demonstrate our thesis or affirmative. While he does not perform this, nor indeed can he perform it, we conclude from that, that the Scriptures, by the power of the testimonies already produced, are so clear and lucid to believers, that he who desires human authority in this place is no less foolish than one who would wish to illuminate the meridian sun with a lit candle.

Another argument, by which we confirm our thesis: we borrow from the mutual proper affection of Scripture, which acts as a principle. Indeed, there is in all sciences and disciplines this condition of principles, that they are αὐτόπισα, ἀναπόδεικτα, which require no external proofs, but from which, as being γνωριμωτέροις (more known), all other things are proven. Now, if there is anything in the whole nature of things so certain and illustrious that it needs no proof, is self-evident, and shines by its own light, such is primarily the Holy Scripture, as it is most truly and is called the principle of all principles, nay, the rule of the remaining principles.

But in this place the Jesuit Stapleton clamors in this manner. Just as the principles and axioms of the sciences are demonstrated by the demonstration of the Masters, who affect them with their voice, so that those principles are believed by us to be true, so the Scriptures are demonstrated by the Church, so that they are accepted by us, and are believed to be what they are.

Moreover, this similitude wanders clearly off the mark and lacks a true refutation. For the question in this place is not about such men who, just like novices of the schools, have perceived no taste of the sciences or principles, that is, who have not yet received the first fruits of the Holy Spirit: but the question is about those who are already gifted with faith in Christ. Can they not seek and draw the understanding of the Scriptures, as divine principles, except from the information of the Church? Where indeed we hold the negative in all respects, and we confirm the same from this very similitude of Stapleton, by a kind of inversion, as follows: Just as those who have perceived the knowledge of the sciences and arts believe in their principles, not because of the testimony of the teachers, but because of the open and necessary truth of the axioms themselves, which those principles have in themselves and bring forth from themselves. Thus, even if the Church initially commends Scripture to novices and those not yet illuminated, and leads them by this commendation of hers to recognize the Scriptures: yet after the Holy Spirit has illuminated our minds from these very Scriptures, then indeed we believe the Scriptures, not because of the judgment or testimony of the Church: but because we now perceive those principles to be most known, most certain, and most firm in themselves, even with the Church being silent.

Nor, however, is the office of the Church or the ecclesiastical ministry abolished by this pact: but both can stand together. For just as the axioms of the sciences, although known by themselves, do not exclude the industry of the professor, who deduces conclusions from the principles and teaches the art: so the Scriptures, although they are perspicuous by themselves to believers, yet do not exclude the office of the Church or of theologians, by whom they are explained and accommodated to the various uses of men: although we do not believe the Scriptures because of the consent of the Church, or even because of the authority of theologians, but because they themselves are such in themselves that they oblige us to believe. Thus therefore, to encompass the whole matter in a few words, we do not deny that the Scriptures can be demonstrated a posteriori, and that the consent of the Church helps us much, because of the slowness and fluctuation of our mind: but that Scripture itself needs this testimony of the Church for its understanding among believers and those illuminated by faith, that is indeed what we are fighting against the Jesuits in this place.

The third and final argument of proof is provided by venerable Antiquity, which in this Question also stands on our side.

For thus Epiphanius, in heresy 76, book 3, volume 1, against the Anomoeans: All things are clear in divine Scripture to those who wish to approach the divine Word with reasoning, and have not conceived a diabolical operation within themselves, and are not attempting to cast themselves into the abyss of death.

Hilary, book 2, on the Trinity: What is there that remains obscure in the Scriptures? In the Word of God all things are full and perfect, as from one who is full and perfect.

Chrysostom, Homily 3 on Lazarus, Volume II, Column 1354: It is impossible that you should be ignorant of all things equally, since the grace of the Spirit has so dispensed and tempered them, that publicans, fishermen, tentmakers, shepherds, unlearned men, and the illiterate might be saved through these books.

Augustine, book 2, on Christian doctrine, chapter 6: The Holy Spirit has so magnificently and wholesomely modified the sacred Scriptures that He might meet hunger in the open passages, but in the more obscure ones might remove disdain. For almost nothing is extracted from those obscurities which is not found stated most plainly elsewhere.

In order for Bellarmine to be able to snatch this passage of Augustine from us, he urges at the beginning the particle 'almost' (fere): for there are many things in the Scriptures that are most obscure, which nevertheless are not explained in the whole of Scripture. But the Jesuit fights without an adversary in this place. For we ourselves willingly grant that in Ezekiel, in the Apocalypse, and in the oracles of the remaining prophets, many prophecies are contained which are by far the most obscure, and cannot be understood before their fulfillment. But this is what is asked: are those very obscure things so constituted that without them, either the doctrine of the Gospel and of our salvation, or those things which pertain to life and morals, cannot be fully or plainly understood and known from the remaining Scriptures alone? If he demonstrates this, then at last he will have refuted this passage of Augustine.

But then the Jesuit adds, that this very thing is very difficult, namely, to find where that which is said most obscurely in one place is said plainly. But he commits the fallacy of accident. For the negligence of readers cannot or ought not to prejudice the clarity of the Scriptures. It is indeed difficult, that is, for those who treat the Scriptures negligently and perfunctorily. But it is easy for those who, according to the command of Christ, search the Scriptures, and meditate in the law of the Lord day and night: just as it is read concerning the Berrhoeans, that they received the Word with all eagerness, searching daily whether these things were so.

Lactantius, book 6, on true worship, ch. 21. Can GOD, the artificer of both mind and tongue, not speak clearly? Nay, rather, the highest providence wished those things which are divine to be free from deceit: so that all might understand what He Himself was speaking to all.

Chrysostom. What need is there of a Preacher? This necessity has been created by our negligence. For why is there need of a sermon? All things are clear and plain from the divine Scriptures, whatever things are necessary are manifest.

Latin:

IN hac pertractandâ Quæstione initiò Status Controversiæ, qui nostris hodiè Ecclesijs cum gente Jesuvviticâ intercedit, sub accuratiorem considerationem venit. Non autem, uti falsò autumant Adversarij, illud in Quæstionem venit, An Scriptura sacra ita sit perspicua & facilis, ut à quibusvis, etiam illis, qui à Spiritu Sancto nõ sunt illuminati, intelligi possit? Hujus enim Quæstionis negativam, nos ipsi tenemus ac defendim̃. Neque de eo etiam controvertitur, An aliqua in Scripturis sint obscura & difficilia intellectu? Quod ipsum itidem ultrò fatemur. Verùm de eo controvertitur, An Scriptura sacra, ubi agit de negotio fidei & salutis nostræ, ita sit perspicua & facilis, ut ab ijs, qui primitias Spiritus Sancti acceperunt, & per fidem in Christum illuminati sunt, intelligi possit? An verò ea ita sit obscura, ut ab his etiam intelligi non possit, nisi sequatur ductum sive explicationem Ecclesiæ, & sententiam sive interpretationem Pontificis Romani? Cujus sanè Quæstionis posterius membrum, Nos simpliciter negamus, pro affirmativâ prioris membri, strenuè pugnantes: Proinde Ecclesiarum nostrarum propositio talis erit.

SCriptura sacra Canonica, in rebus fidem ac salutem nostram concernentibus, usque adeò est perspicua & clara, ut ab homine pio ac fideli, etiam sine testimonio Ecclesiæ, intelligi possit.

CONFIRMATIO.

ARgumentum Confirmationis nostræ primarium monstrat Scriptura ipsa. Quid enim sibi volunt aliud verba hæc Davidis Ps. 119.

34. Da mihi intellectum, & scrutabor legem tuam: Et vers. 18. Revela oculos meos, & considerabo mirabilia de lege tua. Et vers. 135. Faciem tuam illumina super servum tuum, & doce me justificationes tuas.

Quid inquam, hæc Testimonia aliud sibi volunt, quàm eos, qui primitias Spiritus Sancti acceperunt, & fide donati sunt, posse scrutari legé Domini, & mirabilia ejus, posse meditari & discere ex Scripturis justificationes DOMINI? neque opus habere, ut eò usque assensum suum suspendant, donec vel à Pontifice, vel à Concilio aliquo, certum Scripturæ sensum perceperint?

Porrò, quid respondebunt Romanenses Davidi, quòd Pf. 119, 105. Verbum DOMINI nominat Lucernam pedibus suis, & lumen semitis suis. Quòd præceptum DOMINI appellat lucidum, illuminans oculos, Psal. 19, 9. Quòd Christus ipse asserit, se non per proverbia loqui, sed palàm de Patre suo annunciare, Joh. 16, 25. Quòd idem in ardentissimâ suâ precatione, disertè profitetur: Pater manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus, Joh. 17, 6. Quòd D. Apostolus Timotheum suum à pueris sacras literas novisse prædicat, quæ ipsum eruditum reddere possint ad salutem. 2. Tim. 3, 15. Quòd ipse denique Petrus, ab omni humana traditione nos avocans, Habemus, inquit, firmiorem sermonem Propheticum, cui rectè facitis attendentes, tanquam lucernæ in loco caliginoso, donec dies illucescat, & exoriatur Lucifer in cordibus vestris. 2. Pet. 1, 19. Jam si elogia isthæc competunt libris Propheticis Veteris Testamenti, multò certè magis ad totam Scripturam, uti nunc ex libris Propheticis & Apostolicis constat, accommodari poterunt.

Cæterùm duo hoc loco respondet Bellarminus. 1. In locis istis omnibus non agi de universis Scripturis, sed tantùm de præceptis Dominicis. Deinde, agi quidem de Scripturis omnibus, sed scripturas dici dilucidas, item lucem & lucernam, non quòd facilè intelligantur, sed quòd intellectæ cum fuerint, mentem illustrent. Verùm elumbis utraque est responsio: Imò prior planè nugatoria. Nam de universis Scripturis agere citata testimonia, vel ipsa litera evincit. Et meminisse debebat Jesuvvita. Vocem Hebræam Thorah, in Psalmis, & Prophetis, non notare tantùm Legem propriè sic dictam, nempe Decalogum: sed universam doctrinam Ecclesiæ, tàm Evangelii, quàm Legem. Quod ipsum agnovit ipse quoq; Jesuvvita, hoc ipso capite sic scribens: David nomine Legis non intelligit decem illa præcepta solum, sed omnes divinas Scripturas. Mendacem proinde oportebat esse memorem.

Altera Responsio ita est comparata, ut Jesuvvitam magis implicet, quàm explicet. Scripturas enim Sacras homini per se obscuras esse, & stultitiam videri, nemo nostrûm negavit unquam. Jam verò, quod Jesuvvita fatetur, Scripturas esse dilucidas ijs, quos Spiritus Sanctus fide illuminavit: Certè illud ipsum vel inscius fatetur, quod nos asserimus. Quis enim ita prodigiosè absurdus foret, ut contenderet, Scripturas mentem illustrare, etiam nondum intellectas? Cæterùm hîc Rhodus, hîc saltus est: Utrum Scripturæ ipsæ sui intellectum præbeant credentibus, & discendi cupidis, an verò alià quapiam extrinfecus accedente luce opus sit, quæ vel à Pontifice, vel à Concilio in Scripturam inferatur, Hîc ergò saltandum esset Jesuuvitæ, & ostendendum, producta Scripturarum testimonia, nostram thesin sive affirmativam non evidenter demonstrare. Quod dum non præstat, neque etiam præstare potest, colligimus nos inde, Scripturas vi testimoniorum jam productorum, usq; adeò credentibus esse claras & dilucidas, ut qui humanam autoritatem hoc loco desiderat, haud minùs ineptiat, ac qui Solem meridianum accensâ candelâ illustrare velit.

Alterum Argumentum, quo Thesin nostram confirmamus: mutuamur à mutuâ propriâ Scripturæ affectione, quæ se habet instar principij. Est verò in omnibus scientijs atq;, disciplinis, ea Principiorum conditio, ut sint αὐτόπισα, ἀναπόδεικτα, quæ probationes externas nullas requirunt, sed ex quibus tanquam γνωριμωτέροις notioribus cætera omnia probantur. Jam verò, si quicquam est in universâ rerum naturâ, tàm certum & illustre, ut probatione nullâ indigeat, per se liqueat, suâq; luce luceat; talis inprimis Scriptura sacra est, ut quæ principium principiorum omnium, imò regula reliquorum principiorum verissimè est ac dicitur.

Obstrepit verò hoc loco Jesuitavita Stapletonus in hunc modum. Quemadmodum scientiarum principia & axiomata demonstrantur demonstratione Magistrorum, qui sua voce afficiunt, ut principia illa, à nobis vera esse credantur, sic Scripturæ per Ecclesiam demonstrantur, ut à nobis acceptentur, & ea esse credantur, quæ sunt.

Cæterùm similitudo isthæc planè extra oleas vagatur, & vero caret elencho. Neque enim de ejusmodi hominibus hoc loco est quæstio, qui haud sec9 ac Tyrones Scholarum nullum scientiarum aut principiorum gustum perceperunt, hoc est, qui Spiritus Sancti primitias nondum acceperunt: Sed de illis est quæstio, qui fide in Christum jam sunt donati. An isti Scripturarum, tanquàm divinorum principiorum intelligentiâ nõ nisi ex informatione Ecclesiæ petere ac haurire possint? Ubi sanè Negativam per omnia tenemus, eandemque ex hac ipsa similitudine Stapletoni, per quandam quasi inversionem sic confirmamus: Quemadmodum illi, qui Scientiarum atque artium notitiam perceperunt, credũt Principijs illarum, non propter testimonium Præceptorum, sed propter ipsorum axiomatum, apertam ac necessariam veritatem: quam principia illa in se habent, & ex se proferunt. Sic etsi Ecclesia initiò Tyronibus, & nondum illuminatis, commendat Scripturam, illosq; sua hac commendatione ad Scripturas agnoscẽdas adducit: tamen postquam Spiritus Sanctus ex his ipsis Scripturis, mentes nostras illuminavit, tùm sanè credimus Scripturis, non propter judicium aut testimonium Ecclesiæ: sed quia jam Principia illa in se notissima, certissima atque firmissima esse deprehendim9, etiam tacente Ecclesia.

Neque tamen propterea officium Ecclesiæ, vel Ministerium Ecclesiasticum hoc pacto tollitur: sed utrumq; simul stare potest. Quemadmodum enim Scientiarum axiomata, quamvis per se nota, Professoris tamen industriam non excludunt, qui ex principijs conclusiones deducat, ártemq́; tradat : Ita Scripturæ, etsi per se sunt perspicuæ credentibus: tamen neque Ecclesiæ aut Theologorum officium excludunt, à quibus illæ exponantur,& ad varios hominum usus accommodentur : Quanquam Scripturis non propter consensum Ecclesiæ, vel etiam propter Theologorum autoritatem credimus, sed quia ipsæ in se sunt tales, ut nos ad credendum obligent. Sic ergò, ut paucis rem omnem complectamur, non negamus, Scripturas à posteriori demonstrari posse, & Ecclesiæ consensum nos multùm juvare, propter mentis nostræ tarditatem, & fluctuationem : Sed ut Scriptura ipsa hoc testimonio Ecclesiæ ad sui intelligentiam apud credentes,& per fidem illuminatos, indigeat, id verò est, quod hoc loco adversus Jesuvvitas pugnamus.

Tertium ac postremum probationis argumentum subministrat veneranda Antiquitas, quæ in hac etiam Quæstione â nostris stat partibus.

Sic enim Epiphanius hæresi 76. lib. 3. Tom. 1. contra Anomæos. Omnia clara sunt in divina Scriptura his, qui ratiocinatione Sermonem divinum adire volunt, & non Diabolicam operationem in seipsis conceperunt, ac seipsos in barathrum mortis præcipitare conantur.

Hilarius lib. 2. de Trinit. Quid est, quod in Scripturis reliquum sit aut obscurum? In Verbo DEI plena sunt omnia & perfecta, ut à pleno & perfecto.

Chrystost. Homil. 3. de Lazaro Tom. II. Col. 1354. Fieri non potest, ut omnia ex æquo ignores,siquidem ita Spiritus gratia dispensavit illa, temperavitq́; quo Publicani, piscatores, tabernaculorum Opifices, Pastores, Idiotæ, illiterati, per hos libros salvi fierent.

Augustinus lib. 2. de doctr. Christi c. 6. Spiritus Sanctus Scripturas sacras ita magnificè & salubriter modificavit, ut locis apertis fami occurreret: obscurioribus autem fastidia detergeret. Nihil enim ferè de illis obscuritatibus eruitur, quod non planissimè alibi dictum reperiatur.

Quem locum Augustini ut nobis eripere queat Bellarminus, urget initiò particulam illá FERE : nam multa in Scripturis esse obscurissima, quæ tamen in tota Scriptura non explicentur. Verùm sine Adversario hoc loco dimicat Jesuvvita. Nam nos ipsi ultrò largimur, in Ezechiele, in Apocalypsi, inque reliquorum Prophetarum Oraculis, multa contineri vaticinia, quæ longè sint obscurissima, neque ante complementum intelligi possunt : Cæterùm hoc quæritur, an illa ipsa obscura ita sint comparata, ut absque ijs, vel doctrina Evangelij & salutis nostræ, vel quæ ad vitam & mores attinent, non plenè aut planè ex solis Scripturis reliquis intelligi & cognosci possint? Hoc si demonstraverit, tùm demùm locum istum Augustini eliserit.

Deinde verò addit Jesuvvita, Hoc ipsum valdè difficile esse, invenire nimirum id, quod uno loco obscurissimè dicitur, ubinam apertè dicatur. Sed Accidentis Sophisma committit. Nam negligentia lectorum non potest aut debet præjudicare claritati Scripturarũ. Difficile quidé est, id est, illis, qui negligéter & perfunctoriè tractãt Scripturas. Facilè verò illis, qui secundum mandatum Christi, scrutantur Scripturas, & in lege Domini meditantur die ac nocte: quemadmodum de Berrhoensibus legitur, quod susceperint Verbum cum omni aviditate, quotidiè scrutantes, utrum hæc ita se haberent.

Lactantius lib. 6. de vero cultu. c. 21. Num DEUS & mentis & linguæ artifex disertè loqui non potest? Imò verò summa providentia carere fuco voluit ea, quæ divina sunt: ut omnes intelligerent, quæ ipse omnibus loquebatur.

Chrysoft. Quid opus est Concionatore? per nostram negligentiam necessitas ista facta est. Quamobrem namq́; concione opus est? Omnia clara sunt & plana ex Scripturis divinis, quæcunq́; necessaria sunt, manifesta sunt.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Second Part of the Fourth General Question

Holy Scripture is obscure, and in those things which it contains and proposes, it does not offer any certain, perspicuous, and immovable meaning: until the voice and authority of the Church approaches.

Ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστικὴ.

The Jesuit Cologne theologians brought forth this thesis on page 117 of the Censura, and they subject it to Article 1 of the same Censura thus. All and singular things which are comprised in Scripture are wrapped in such obscurities that not even the most learned can gather a certain knowledge from thence, unless they borrow it from elsewhere; namely, from the praetorian interpretation of the Prelates of the Church. Canisius supports them in his Catechetical work, p. 44. The Jesuit Costerus, page 50 of the Enchiridion, fixing an obelisk to the Cologne Censura, says: It is not to be denied that many things in the sacred letters are perspicuous: but that all are of such a kind that they can be understood by anyone without labor, even those places which contain the dogmas of faith, conflicts with experience. Where Costerus says what is partly true, namely that many things in the Scriptures are obscure and difficult to understand: Which very thing we also readily grant, especially concerning certain Prophetic oracles: but he assumes what is partly false, namely that the dogmas of faith, that is, those things which concern our faith and salvation, are obscure, and cannot be understood by the faithful without the interpretation of the Church. Likewise, Robert Bellarmine, Stapleton, and others subscribe entirely to the Cologne Censura, relying chiefly on the following two arguments.

First: St. Peter, 2 ch. 16, asserts that in the Epistles of Paul there are some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable pervert. Therefore, Holy Scripture is obscure, and stands in need of interpretation.

I respond 1. that a manifold sophistication of several questions is being committed, for first it is not asked, Whether Scripture stands in need of interpretation? Which very thing we readily confess. Then, neither is this in controversy, Whether many things in the Scriptures are obscure: Which we have likewise never denied. Then, neither is that being disputed: Whether Scripture is so clear and manifest that it can be understood by anyone immediately. Where we firmly hold the negative ourselves. Therefore, when the Jesuit, both in this and in the remaining arguments, infers that: Therefore Holy Scripture stands in need of interpretation: then indeed they fight without an adversary: But how they conclude thus: Some things in the sacred letters, nay very many, are obscure: Therefore the whole of Holy Scripture is obscure, and cannot by itself provide an interpretation, but it is necessary that it borrow it from the Church: then indeed they infer more in the Consequent than is in the Antecedent. This very fallacy of the consequent emerges of its own accord in this first argument. For he does not say to St. Peter, 'In which all things are difficult to understand,' but 'in which some things, or not a few, are difficult to understand.' But just as it is not permitted to infer the whole from a part, so this inference is also most vicious: 'Some things in the Epistles of Paul are difficult to understand; therefore, the Epistles of Paul are obscure in all respects.' Or: 'Some things in the Scriptures are obscure; therefore, the whole Scripture is obscure.' Thirdly, there occurs the fallacy 'secundum quid et simpliciter.' For St. Peter, as the Jesuit trifles, does not say absolutely that some things in the Pauline Epistles are difficult to understand; but rather he clearly restricts that difficulty of understanding, showing that those things are difficult because they are depraved or distorted by the unlearned and unstable (στρεβλοῦσι), clearly implying that those things are not difficult in themselves, but only become such from that depravation of the unlearned: where the fallacy of the accident is simultaneously involved.

Finally, there also emerges the fallacy 'ignoratio elenchi.' For St. Peter is not dealing directly with the Pauline Epistles, but with certain matters of which Peter himself had made mention a little before: such as the end of the age, the conflagration of this universe, the new heaven and the new earth; about which mockers and other unlearned and unstable persons have invented many false things. Wherefore St. Peter also shapes his style so that he does not say 'in which' (namely, epistles), but 'in which' (namely, the topics about which I have just spoken to you), so that the construction coheres thus: 'as our brother Paul according to the wisdom given to him wrote to you, as in almost all his epistles speaking of these things: in which (namely, things) are some things difficult to understand,' etc.

The second argument: If clear and perspicuous testimonies existed in the Scriptures concerning all articles of faith and all sacraments, all controversies would be finished. But this latter is false: therefore the former is also false.

I reply that, in the first place, the fallacy of equivocation is committed in the word 'finished.' For if that is said to be finished which is defined, decided, and explained, whether it is acknowledged as such or not, certainly in the Holy Scriptures all controversies are defined, and no question can be raised to which an answer cannot be given from the authority of the Holy Scriptures. But if that is said to be 'finished' which is removed, and which

no longer exists, then there is absolutely no reason for the Consequence to fight. For such is the arrogance of petulant minds, and the perversity of the Devil himself, that they do not allow themselves to be satisfied even by the clearest testimonies; and they would sooner deny that the Sun shines at midday than allow themselves to be satisfied by the Scriptures. Whence immediately another Sophistry arises, τῶ μὴ αἰτίω ὡς αἰτίω. For Controversies about Articles of faith exist and remain, not because clear and perspicuous testimonies regarding their vanity do not exist in the Scriptures: but because they either will not, or cannot, understand them, however perspicuous they may be, because by the just judgment of GOD, GOD has blinded the eyes of those people. Finally, we turn this argument much more rightly against the Romanists themselves. For if their interpretation is so clear and perspicuous: Whence, I ask, do so many Controversies arise, not only between us and them, but also among themselves? Thus, therefore, they must necessarily acknowledge the futility of the Consequence.

The third and final argument: Both the things that are said in the Scriptures are most obscure, and the manner in which they are said. Therefore, the Scriptures themselves are most obscure.

I respond: The argument fails by the Sophism ἀπὸ τῶ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: καὶ ἀπὸ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς. For even if the Scripture is obscure in some way and in a certain respect, the whole Scripture should not immediately be argued to be simply obscure. We confess, indeed, that some things, especially in the Prophets, are so obscure that it is more possible to divine what the Prophets meant than to know it: which is especially true in those visions that are about future things, the fulfillments of which we do not yet see. Furthermore, we also willingly confess that the Scriptures are obscure with respect to our intellect not yet illuminated: but if anyone wishes to conclude from that to the obscurity of the Scriptures themselves, he sins enormously by the fallacy of the Accident. For this very obscurity, whatever and however great it may be, is not from the Scripture itself. For indeed GOD did not offer those very visions to the Prophets so that they would not be understood by them, nor by the people: But that obscurity is from and in us ourselves, while we are of such obtuse judgment that we cannot perceive the things far removed which were shown to the Prophets through those visions: and thus, by Accident, they appear most obscure to us. For just as the rest of the Word of GOD cannot be perceived by those who are without the Spirit of GOD (1 Cor. 2:14), however perspicuous it may be in itself: whence afterwards it is most manifest to those illuminated by faith: So Prophetic visions and Oracles about future things cannot be perceived without the Prophetic Spirit: nevertheless, the Prophetic Scriptures themselves remain perspicuous in themselves. For as soon as our intellect is illuminated by the Scripture itself, by the power of the Holy Spirit, so that we understand those visions: then indeed they no longer appear to us as prophecy about future things; but as a most clear history. For example, the visions and prophecies of Isaiah 7:14 and 9:6 concerning the Nativity of the Messiah, and likewise the prophecy concerning the four Monarchies (Dan. 2:37 and 7:17), and other things of that kind, were seen as most obscure before they were fulfilled: but to us today they are most perspicuous: because that Accident, namely the dullness and stupidity of our intellect, has been removed: so that the immoveable perspicuity of the Scriptures in themselves remains, however much they may seem obscure to us. But regarding the Manner of speaking, the Jesuit raises six difficulties, which are, however, of such a kind that a remedy for them is abundantly prepared from the Scriptures themselves. For first, although at first glance and according to the surface of the letter many ἐναντιοφανῆ, which seem contrary, occur, yet from the considered circumstances of individual passages, every contradiction expires of its own accord. Then, if any words and sentences seem ambiguous at first sight: yet from a diligent comparison of the Antecedents and Consequents, every ambiguity is easily removed. Thirdly, if even a sentence sometimes seems most imperfect: yet either what is missing is easily understood: or it can be easily supplied from what follows or precedes. Fourthly, if even some things in histories are commemorated in preposterous order: yet nothing departs from the perspicuity of the Scripture, such as we have defined above with respect to the Articles of faith. Fifthly, the Idioms of the Hebrew language are both rare and are explained by other perspicuous phrases elsewhere in the Scriptures. Finally, the Tropes and figures that occur in the Scriptures do not make the sense of the Scripture more obscure, but rather illustrate it wonderfully. In which part we fearlessly appeal to the judgment of all Doctors, both profane and ecclesiastical.

Latin:

Scriptura sacra est obscura, inque illis, quæ continet & proponit, non præbet certam aliquam, perspicuam & immotam sententiam: donec accedat vox & autoritas Ecclesiæ.

Ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστικὴ.

THesin hanc prodiderunt Jesuvvitæ Colonienses pag. 117. Censuræ & Articulo 1. ejusdem Censuræ sic subjiciunt. Omnia & singula, quæ in Scriptura comprehensa sunt, tantis involuta sunt obscuritatibus, ut ne doctissimi quidem certam cognitionem inde colligere possint, nisi illam aliunde mutuentur; ex prætoria scilicet Prælatorum Ecclesiæ interpretatione. Quibus suffragatur Canisius in opere Catechistico P. 44. Jesuvvita Costerus pag 50. Enchiridij Colonienfium Censuræ obeliscum figens, Multa, inquit, in sacris literis esse perspicua, negandum non est: Omnia autem esse hujusmodi, ut sine labore à quovis intelligi possint, etiam illaloca, quæ dogmata fidei continent, cum experientia pugnat. Ubi Costerus partim verum dicit, nempè multa in Scripturis esse obscura & intellectu difficilia: Quod ipsum & nos, præsertim de quibusdam oraculis Propheticis ultrò largimur: partim verò falsum assumit, nempe dogmata fidei, hoc est, ea, quæ fidem & salutem nostram concernunt, esse obscura, neque sine interpretatione Ecclesiæ à fidelibus intelligi posse. Rob. item Bellarminus, Stapletonus & alij Coloniensiu Censuræ omninò subscribunt, sequentib9 duob9 potissimùm freti argumentis.

Primùm: D. Petrus 2. cap 3, 16. asserit, In Epistolis Pauli esse quædam intellectu difficilia, quæ indocti & instabiles depravant. Ergò Scriptura Sacra est obscura, & interpretatione indiget.

Respondeo 1. multiplicem committi Sophisticationem plurium Quæstionum, primùm e-nim nō quæritur, Utrum Scriptura interpretatione ne indigeat? Quod ipsum nos ultrò fatemur. Deinde neque hoc in Controversia est, An multa in Scripturis sint obscura: Quod itidem nunquam negavimus. Tum neque illud disceptatur: An Scriptura ita sit clara & manifesta, ut à quovis statim intelligi possit. Ubi Negativam ipsi firmiter tenemo. Proindè quando Jesuuvita tùm in hoc, tùm in reliquis argumentis, illud inferunt: Ergò Scriptura Sacra interpretatione indiget: tùm profectò sine Adversario pugnant: Quomodo verò sic colligunt: Quædam in sacris literis, imò plurima sunt obscura: Ergò Scriptura sacra tota est obscura, & ipsa per se interpretationem subministrare non potest, sed ut ab Ecclesia eam mutuetur, necesse est: tùm profectò plus inferunt in Consequente, quam est in Antecedente. Quæ ipsa πλεονεξία Consequentis in primo hoc argumento ultrò emergit. Non enim dicit D. Petro, In quibus omnia sunt intellectu difficilia: sed in quibus quædam, sive nonnulla sunt intellectu difficilia: Quemadmodum verò ex parte non licet colligere totum, ita vitiosissima etiam hæc est Collectio: Quædam in Epistolis Pauli sunt intellectu difficilia. Ergò Epistolæ Pauli per omnia sunt obscuræ: Vel: Quædam in scripturis sunt obscuræ: Ergò tota Scriptura est obscura. Tertiò occurrit Sophisticatio παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς Non enim D. Petrus, uti Jesuvvita nugatur, absolutè dicit, in Epistolis Paulinis quædam esse difficilia intellectu: sed potiùs difficultatem illam intelligendi manifestò restringit, ostendens, propterea illa esse difficilia, quia ab indoctis & instabilibus depravantur sive detorquentur: (ςρεβλῦσι (sic perspicuè innuens, illa per se difficilia non esse, sed ex depravatione demùm illâ indoctorum talia evadere: ubi Sophisticatio Accidentis simul involvitur.

Tandem emergit etiam Sophisticatio παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε. Neque enim D. Petrus directè agit de Epistolis Paulinis: sed de quibusdam rebus, quarum ipse Petrus paulò ante mentionem fecerat: ut de fine seculi, de conflagratione hujus universi, de novo cœlo & nova terra: de quibus ἐμπαῖκται, & alij ἀμαθεῖς & ἀςήρικτοι multa falsa sunt commenti. Quare D. Petrus stylum etiam sic informat, ut non dicat ἐν ἆις scilicet ἐπιςολαῖς: sed ἐν οἷς, scilicet capitibus, de quibus jam ad vos verba feci: ut sic cohæreat constructio: sicut frater noster Paulus pro sibi data sapientia scripsit vobis, ut in omnibus ferè epistolis loquens de istis rebus: in quibus (scilicet rebus) sunt nonnulla difficilia intellectu &c.

Alterum Argumentum: Si de omnibus Articulis fidei, omnibusq́, Sacramentis, clara & perspicua in Scripturis extarent testimonia, Omnes Controversiæ essent finitæ. At posterius hoc falsum: Falsum ergò & prius.
