Respondeo initiò committi Sophisticationem παρὰ τὴν ὁμωνυμίαν, in Verbo (Finitæ) si enim finitum esse id dicatur, quod est definitum & decisum explicatumq́;, sive agnoscatur pro tali, sive non agnoscatur: certè sacris in literis omnes Controversiæ sunt definitæ, neque ulla potest moveri quæstio, ad quam ex S. literarum autoritate non possit responderi. Sin autem Finitæ dicatur id, quod sublatu est, quodq́;

ampliùs non extat, tum nulla prorsus militat Consequentiæ ratio. Ea enim est tùm petulantium ingeniorum arrogantia, tùm ipsius Diaboli perversitas, ut ne clarissimis quidem testimonijs satisfieri sibi patiantur; & citiùs Solem in meridie lucere negent, quàm ex Scripturis sibi satisfieri patiantur. Unde statim altera Sophisticatio τῶ μὴ αἰτίω ὡς αἰτίω oritur. Sunt enim & manent Controversiæ de Articulis fidei, non quòd clara & perspicua testimonia in Scripturis de earum vanitate non extent: sed quod intelligere ea, quantumvis perspicua, vel nolunt, vel non possunt, propterea quòd justo DEI judicio DEUS oculos istorum excæcavit. Tandem longè rectiùs argumentum istud in ipsos Romanenses detorquemus. Si enim tam clara & perspicua est ipsorum interpretatio: Unde quæso tot Controversiæ, non modò inter nos & ipsos: Sed & ipsorum mutuæ oriuntur? Sic ergò futilitatem Consequentiæ ipsi agnoscant, necesse est.

Tertium & postremum argumentum: Et res, quæ dicuntur in Scripturis obscurissimæ sunt, & modus, quo dicuntur. Ipsa igitur Scripturæ sunt obscurissimæ.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate ἀπὸ τῶ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: καὶ ἀπὸ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς. Neque enim si aliquo modo, & secundum quid Scriptura obscura est, tota statim Scriptura simpliciter obscuritatis arguenda fuerit.. Fatemur sanè, nonnulla in Prophetis præsertim ita esse obscura, ut quid sibi voluerint Prophetæ, divinare magis, quàm scire liceat: id quod imprimis verum est, in ijs visionibus, quæ sunt de rebus futuris, quorum complementa nondum videmus. Deindè & illud libenter fatemur, Scripturas respectu intellectῥ nostri nondum illuminati esse obscuras: sed si quis indè ad ipsarum Scripturarum obscuritatem, colligere velit, enormiter peccat ex fallaciâ Accidentis. Hæc enim ipsa obscuritas, qualis & quanta ea unquam esse potest, non est à Scripturà ipsâ. Siquidem DEUS illas ipsas visiones non obtulit Prophetis, ut eas ab ipsis, ut & à populo, non intelligerentur: Sed obscuritas illa ab & in nobis ipsis est, dum ita obtusi sumus judicij, ut res procul dissitas, quæ per illas visiones Prophetis ostendebantur, intueri nequeamus: ac sic ex Accidenti nobis illæ apparent obscurissimæ. Quemadmodum enim reliquum DEI Verbum non potest percipi ab illis, qui sunt sine Spiritu DEI 1. Cor. 2, 14. quantumvis etiam illud in se est perspicuum: Unde postmodum illud fide illuminatis, est manifestissimum: Ita visiones Propheticæ & Oracula de rebus futuris, non possunt percipi sine Spiritu Prophetico: nihilominus ipsis Scripturis Propheticis in se, perspicuis manentibus. Nam simulac intellectus noster ex ipsâ Scripturâ, virtute Spiritus Sancti illuminatur, ut visiones illas intelligamus: tum sanè non ampliùs, ut Prophetia de rebus futuris; sed ut historia longè clarissima, nobis apparent, Exempli gratia visiones & vaticinia Esā. 7, 14, & 9, 6. de Nativitate Messiæ, Vaticinium item de quatuor Monarchijs. Dan. 2, 37. & 7, 17. & id genus alia priusquam complerentur, visa fuerunt obscurissima: Nobis autem hodiè maximè perspicua: propterea quod Accidens illud, nempe hebetudo & stupiditas intellectus nostri, est sublatum: ita ut Scripturis quibusvis sua in se constet immota perspicuitas, quantumvis etiam ea nobis videantur obscuræ. Cæterùm quoad Modum dicendi, sex difficultates Jesuvvita movet, quæ tamen sunt ejusmodi, ut ex Scripturis ipsis, remedium illis abundè sit paratum. Primùm enim etsi primo aspectu, & secundum superficiem literæ multæ ἐναντιοφανῆ, quæ videntur contraria, occurrunt, tamen ex consideratis singulorum locorum circumstantiis, omnis contrarietas ultrò expirat. Deinde, si quæ verba & sententiæ primâ specie videntur ambiguæ: tamen ex diligenti comparatione Antecedentium & Consequentium, omnis ambiguitas facilè tollitur. Tertiò, si vel maximè interdum sententia aliqua videatur imperfecta: tamen vel facilè id quod deest, intelligitur: vel ex subsequentibus aut antecedentibus facilè suppleri potest. Quartò, si vel maximè quædam in historijs, ordine præpostero commemorantur: nihil tamen indè decedit perspicuitati Scripturæ, qualem quidem nos respectu Articulorum fidei, supra definivimus. Quintò, Idiotifmi lingvæ Hebrææ & rariores sunt & alijs perspicuis phrasibus, alibi in Scripturis explicantur. Tandem Tropi & figuræ, quæ in Scripturis occurrunt, usque adeò sensum Scripturæ non reddunt obscuriorem, ut potiùs illum mirificè illustrent. Quâ in parte ad omnium Doctorum, tùm prophanorum, tùm Ecclesiasticorum judicium, intrepidè provocamus.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: On the Interpretation of the Scriptures: and the judge of the same

THAT we may expedite this controversial classification without offense, we must first attend to the state of the controversy. First, however, the question is not, Is the gift of interpreting the Scriptures common to all who profess the faith of Christ? For we ourselves also hold and defend the negative: and we freely confess that this gift is not of all indiscriminately, but only of those who are so divinely illuminated by the Holy Spirit that they are able to investigate the emphasis of individual phrases and words, partly from a knowledge of the original languages, and partly from a diligent collation of the Scriptures. Hence the Apostle, 1 Cor. 12:10, To one is given by the Spirit the gift of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.

Furthermore, neither is this in controversy: Is the interpretation of Scripture to be left to the judgment and discretion of each individual? For in this point also we urge the negative most strongly, not being ignorant that Scripture is not of ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, 2 Pet. 1:20. But the hinge of the whole controversy turns chiefly upon this: Whose is it to interpret the Scriptures, and to point out their true and genuine sense? Now, since for the most part between dissenting parties, the controversy arises not so much about the word as about the meaning of the word: therefore the Romanists insist that the interpretation and meaning of Scripture must be sought not from this or that individual man, but from the Church. For they contend, as Bellarmine testifies, lib. 3. de Verbo DEI cap. 3. that the Spirit of Interpretation is certainly found in the Church, that is, in a Council of Bishops confirmed by the supreme Pastor of the whole Church, or in the supreme Pastor, with the Council of other Pastors.

The meaning of these words is this: that Scripture is not to be interpreted otherwise than as the Councils have interpreted it, not indeed all of them, but only those which have been confirmed by the supreme Pastor of the Church, namely the Roman Pontiff: so that the plain and categorical sense of this Jesuitical assertion emerges as follows: The interpretation of Scripture rests with the one Roman Pontiff, without whose approval or confirmation not even the interpretation of Councils is valid. Since we simply deny this assertion, there arises at last this true and legitimate state of the controversy: Whether the interpretation of the Scriptures must necessarily be sought from the Roman Pontiff and his Council: Or whether Scripture is sufficient unto itself for its own interpretation, and its true and proper sense can and ought to be sought by the Doctors of the Church, as interpreters of the sacred letters, even without consulting the Roman Pontiff? Our Churches hold and defend the latter member of this question, the former having been denied.

But before we confirm our thesis, it will not be ill-advised to premise a few things concerning the senses of the Scriptures: so that both the opinion of the Papists on this matter, and the sense about which we are chiefly disputing with the Jesuits, may be more clearly established. The sense of divine Scripture is commonly said to be twofold; one Literal or historical, which the very narrative of the event and the series of words, under the common and customary signification of the terms, whether proper or metaphorical, the letter itself represents. The other Mystical or Spiritual, which is more secret, and lies as it were hidden in things: Hence two kinds of interpretation are also commonly established: one Historical or Literal; the other Mystical and Spiritual. But in the progress of time, to this latter, namely the Mystical, others were superadded. And indeed that first Origen Adamantius introduced a triple mode of interpreting the Scriptures: Historical, Moral, and Mystical: Homil. 5 in Levit: of which he named the Historical the Literal, or the letter that kills: but the Mystical the spiritual, or the spirit that gives life. And although he sometimes acknowledged the Historical sense, and did not wish for Allegories to be sought, since the Letter also edifies: yet in the very treatment of the Scriptures, he for the most part neglected the Historical sense: and by prodigious Allegories, he overturned the true and simple meaning of the Scriptures: and introduced into the Church dogmas conflicting with the analogy of Faith: and by this reason alone exposed Scripture to be mocked by Porphyry and Julian, and others of that kind who are enemies of the Gospel. Therefore, Orthodox antiquity rightly and prudently opposed itself to this immoderate zeal for Allegories: and admonished that one certain sense of the Scriptures, which the very propriety of the Speech exhibits in individual places, should be retained. Whence was born that Rule, which that most ancient Church in Epiphanius lib. 2. Tom. 1. Hæresi 61. opposed to the Apostolic or Apotactic heretics: πάντα τὰ θεῖα ῥήματα οὐκ ἀλληγορίας δεῖται, ἀλλ' ὡς ἔχει: θεωρίας δὲ δεῖται καὶ αἰσθήσεως, εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ἑκάστης ὑποθέσεως τὴν δύναμιν: that is, All divine sayings do not have need of allegory, but (are to be accepted) as they stand: but they have need of speculation (that is, assiduous reading and collation of the Scriptures) and sense (that is, the spiritual experience of the pious) for knowing the force and faculty of each proposed argument.

After Origen, and indeed in later centuries, the Monks and Scholastic Doctors invented four kinds of interpreting the Scriptures: Literal, which, however, imitating Origen in this part, they neglected almost everywhere: Tropological: Allegorical: Anagogical. They called it Tropology, when they transferred history, or any saying of Scripture, to the doctrine of morals. Which kind they would have more correctly called ἠθικὸν, since by τροπολογίαν something far other and different is understood by the Learned, especially by Rhetoricians. But they indicated Allegory, when some saying already exposed concerning morals through τροπολογίαν, was explained concerning the militant Church, or even concerning Christ the Savior. Finally Anagogy, or rather ἀναγωγὴν, when that same saying of Scripture was referred to the Church even in the triumphant heavens, or to the mystery of the most holy Trinity. As for example, the word Jerusalem, wherever it occurred in the Scriptures, they initially accepted according to the letter, concerning the City of Jerusalem, the metropolis of Judea: then Tropologically, concerning any well-constituted Republic: 3. Allegorically concerning this Church militant in this life. 4. Anagogically concerning the eternal beatitude of the Elect.

Moreover, since every discourse which does not have one and simple meaning teaches nothing certain, it is evident even from this that this scrupulous and manifold method of interpreting is clearly vain and useless: especially since not even the figures which occur here and there in the sacred writings produce any new sense, but are to be referred to that which agrees with the others simply stated: Furthermore, a new sense of Scripture should by no means arise from tropology, but individual examples should be recalled to their own kinds and, as it were, to the sources of the precepts. What is more, allegory and anagoge (which the Scholastics have most ineptly separated, since the rationale of both is the same, and the ancients also did not distinguish anagoge from allegory) neither introduce any new sense into the words of Scripture, nor can they have a place in just any passages of Scripture, as certainly not in precepts, not in promises of grace, not in articles of faith, but only in certain deeds or historical events and ceremonies: where, however, the literal sense is also by no means to be neglected, but [is to be held] like a foundation

must always be placed beneath allegories: in such a way, indeed, that allegories can neither be adapted to prove dogmas of such a kind that are not proposed elsewhere simply and without figures: but only to those which can be proven from other certain passages: nor can they produce proofs that are firm in themselves: but like pictures they only render more illustrious that which they are employed to explain, as Thomas also admits from the Scholastics in Part 1 of the Summa, question 1, article 10.

With these things thus explained, it is spontaneously clear, 1. what is to be determined concerning those various senses of the Scriptures about which the Romanists rhetoricate splendidly, namely, that to wish to urge all those four in interpreting individual sayings of the Scriptures is sheer insanity. 2. concerning which sense of Scripture, or kind of interpretation, the dispute and controversy is for us with the Papists, namely, the Literal, since it is most needed partly for the confirmation of faith, partly for the instruction of those things which must be both believed and done by us, and partly, finally, for the solid refutation of those who contradict the truth. Therefore, what our Churches think about this, the following θετικὰς (thetic) Propositions will demonstrate.

Latin:

UT sine offensione clasficam hanc Controversiam expediamus, initiò attendendus venit status Controversiæ. Primò autem non quæritur, An Donum interpretandi Scripturas commune sit omnibus, fidem Christi profitentibus? Negativam enim ipsi quoq; tenemus ac defendimus: ac ultrò fatemur Donum hoc non esse omnium quorumcunq́;: sed eorum tantùm, qui divinitùs ita sunt Spiritu Sancto illustrati, ut singularum & Phrasewn, & verborum emphasin, partim ex cognitione lingvarum originalium, partim ex diligenti collatione Scripturarum investigare queant. Hinc Apostolus 1. Cor. 12, 10. Uni per Spiritum datur donum lingvarum, alii interpretatio lingvarum.

Deinde neque hoc in Controversiâ est: An interpretatio Scripturæ uniuscujusque judicio & arbitrio sit relinquenda? Nam & hoc loco Negativam vel maximè urgemus, haud ignorantes, Scripturam non esse ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως 2. Petr 1, 20. In eo autem cardo totius Controversiæ potissimùm vertitur, Cujusnam sit interpretari Scripturas, & sensum earundem verum ac genuinum monstrare? Jam cum plerumq; inter partes dissidentes, non tam de dicto, quam de Sententia dicti, existat Controversia: Ideo Romanenses interpretationem & sententiam Scripturæ, non ab hoc vel illo homine individuo: sed ab Ecclesia requirendam esse dictitant. Contendunt enim, teste Bellarmino, lib. 3. de Verbo DEI cap. 3. Spiritum Interpretationis certo inveniri in Ecclesia, hoc est, in Cōcilio Episcoporum confirmato a summo Ecclesiæ totius Pastore, sive in summo Pastore, cum Concilio aliorum Pastorum.

Quorum verborum hæc est sententia, Non aliter interpretandam esse Scripturam, quam sicut Concilia eam interpretata sunt, non quidem omnia, sed ea demum, quæ a summo Ecclesiæ Pastore, Pontifice nimirum Romano, sint confirmata: ita ut assertionis hujus Jesuvviticæ sensus planus ac categoricus emergat iste: Scripturæ Interpretatio est penes unum Pontificem Romanum, sine cujus approbatione, sive confirmatione, nec Conciliorum quidem valeat interpretatio. Quam assertionem cum nos simpliciter negemus, oritur tandem verus & legitimus status Controversiæ iste: An Scripturarum Interpretatio, necessario a Pontifice Romano ejusq; Concilio sit petenda: An vero Scriptura sibi ipsi ad sui interpretationem sufficiat, ejusque verus ac propriq sensus a Doctoribus Ecclesiæ, tanquam sacrarum literarum interpretibus; etiam inconsulto Romano Pontifice, ex solis Scripturis peti possit ac debeat? Cujus sane Quæstionis membru posteri9, priore negato, nostræ tenent ac defendunt Ecclesiæ.

Priusquam vero thesin nostram confirmemus, haud inconsultum fuerit, pauca quædam præmittere de sensibus Scripturarum: ut tum Pontificiorum hac de re sententia, tum de quo potissimum sensu nobis cum Jesuvvitis sit disputatio, liquidius constet. Sensus Scripturæ divinæ vulgo gemin9 esse dicitur; Unus Literalis sive historicus, quem ipsa rei gestæ narratio ac series verborū, sub communi & usitata vocum, sive propria, sive metaphorica significatione, ipsa litera repræsentat. Alter Mysticus sive Spiritualis, qui secretior est, & in reb9 latet quasi absconditus: Hinc duo etiam interpretationis genera vulgo constituuntur: Historicum unum sive Literale; alteru Mysticum & Spirituale. Cæterum progressu temporis, posteriori huic, nempe Mystico, alia fuerunt superaddita. Et primus quidem Origenes ille Adamantius triplicē interpretandi Scripturas modū introduxit: Historicum, Moralem & Mysticum: Homil. 5 in Levit: e quibus Historicū quidem nominavit Literalem, sive literam occidentem: Mysticum vero spiritualem, sive spiritum vivificantem. Et quanquam Historicus illum sensum interdum agnovit, neq; quæri voluit Allegorias, cum Litera etiam ædificet: in ipsa tamen Scripturaru tractatione, Historicum sensum plerumque neglexit: & prodigiosis Allegoriis, veram ac simplicem Scripturarum sententiam evertit: & dogmata cum Fidei analogia pugnantia in Ecclesiam invexit: & vel hac sola ratione Porphyrio ac Juliano, ac id gen9 aliis Evangelii hostibus, Scripturam ridedam exposuit. Proinde recte ac prudenter immodico huic Allegoriarum studio, vetustas Orthodoxa sese opposuit: & de uno certo Scripturaru sensu, quem ipsa Sermonis proprietas singulis locis exhibet, retinendo admonuit. Unde nata est Regula illa, quam Ecclesia illa antiquissima apud Epiphanium lib. 2. Tom. 1. Hæresi 61. opposuit hæreticis Apostolicis, sive Apotacticis: πάντα τὰ θεῖα ῥήματα οὐκ ἀλληγορίας δεῖται, ἀλλ' ὡς ἔχει: θεωρίας δὲ δεῖται καὶ αἰσθήσεως, εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ἑκάστης ὑποθέσεως τὴν δύναμιν: hoc est, Omnia divina dicta non opus habent Allegoriâ, sed prout se habent (accipienda sunt) op9 autem habent speculatione (hoc est, assiduâ lectione & collatione Scripturarum) & sensu (hoc est, experientiâ spirituali piorum) ad cognoscendam uniuscujusq; propositi argumenti vim atq; facultatē.

Post Origenem, & quidem seculis posterioribus Monarchi & Doctores Scholastici, quatuor confinxerunt interpretandi Scripturas genera: Literale, quod tamen imitati hac in parte Origenem, fermè ubique negligebant: Tropologicum: Allegoricum: Anagogicum. Tropologiam nominabánt, cum historiam, aut quodcunque Scripturæ dictum ad doctrinam de moribus transferebant. Quod sanè genus rectiùs ἠθικὸν appellassent, cum per τροπολογίαν longè aliud ac diversum à Doctis, præsertim à Rhetoribus intelligatur. Allegoriam verò indigitabant, quando dictum aliquod de moribus per τροπολογίαν jam erat expositum, de Ecclesiâ militante, aut etiam de Christo Servatore explicabatur. Anagogiam denique, vel potiùs ἀναγωγὴν, quando illud ipsum dictum Scripturæ ad Ecclesiam etiam in cœlis triumphantem, vel ad sacrosanctæ Trinitatis mysterium, referebatur. Ut Exempli gratiâ, vocem Jerosolyma, ubicunque in Scripturis occurrebat, initiò accipiebant secundum literam, de Urbe Hierosolymitanâ, Judææ metropoli: deinde Tropologicè, de quavis Repub. benè constitutâ: 3. Allegoricè de Ecclesiâ hac in vitâ militante. 4. Anagogicè de æternâ beatitudine Electorum.

Cæterùm cùm omnis Oratio, quæ non habet unam & simplicem sententiam, nihil certi doceat: vel indè patet, frustraneam planè & inutilem esse scrupulosam istam ac multiplicem interpretandi rationem: præsertim cùm ne quidem Figuræ quę in sacris passim occurrunt, novum aliquem sensum pariant: sed ad eum, qui cum cæteris simpliciter prolatis consentit, referendæ sint: Quin etiam ex Tropologiâ novus sensus Scripturæ minimè oriatur: sed exempla singularia, ad sua genera & quasi fontes præceptorum revocanda sint. Quid, quòd Allegoria etiam & Anagoge (quas ineptissimè Scholastici divulserunt, cùm par sit utriusque ratio, & Veteres quoque Anagogen ab Allegoriâ non distinxerint) nequè ullum novum senfum dictis Scripturæ inferant: neque etiam in quibusvis Scripturæ locis, uti certè non in præceptis, non in promissionibus gratiæ, non in articulis fidei: sed tantùm in quibusdam factis, sive rebus gestis ac ceremoniis locum obtinere possint: Ubi tamen Literalis etiam sensus minimè negligendus: sed fundamenti instar

Allegorijs semper substernendus: ita quidem, ut Allegoriæ neque ad ejusmodi probanda dogmata accommodari possint, quæ alibi simpliciter, & sine figuris proposita non sunt: sed ad ea dūtaxat, quæ ex alijs certis locis probari possunt: neq; etiam firmas per se probationes pariant: sed instar picturarum tantúm illustrius reddant id, ad quod explicandum adhibentur, uti ex Scholasticis etiam fatetur Thomas 1. parte Summæ, quæst. 1. art. 10.

Quibus ita explicatis ultró patet, 1. quid de varijs illis Scripturarum sensibus, de quibus Romanenses splendidé rhetoricantur, sit statuendum, nempè, in singulis Scripturarum dictis interpretádis omnes illos quatuor urgere velle, meram esse insaniam. 2. de quonam Scripturæ sensu, sive interpretationis genere, lis & Cōtroversia nobis sit cum Pontificiis, nempè de Literali, quippe quo partim ad fidei confirmationem, partim ad earum rerum, quæ nobis sunt & credendæ & faciendæ, instructionem, partim deniq; ad eorum, qui veritati contradicunt, solidam refutationem, maximè opus est. De hoc igitur quid nostræ sentiant Ecclesiæ, sequentes Propositiones θετικὰς demonstrabunt.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Proposition I. Thetic

PROPOSITION I. Thetic.

The literal sense of Scripture alone is genuine, and provides firm, valid, and effective arguments, both regarding διδασκαλίαν (teaching) and regarding ἔλεγχον (refutation).

CONFIRMATION.

The truth of this thesis is placed so far beyond the hazard of doubt that Bellarmine himself, driven by the force of truth, admits in book 3 of On the Word of God, chapter 3: It is agreed on both sides that effective arguments ought to be sought from the literal sense alone: for it is certain that the sense which is gathered immediately from the words is the sense of the Holy Spirit. But mystical and spiritual senses are various; although they may edify when they are not against faith or good morals, yet it is not always certain whether they were intended by the Holy Spirit. Andradius also acknowledged this same thing in book 2 of his Defense of the Council of Trent, saying, the literal sense alone supplies arguments to confirm the dogmas of religion. Whence we infer the following Corollaries.

I. If firm and effective arguments can be sought from the literal sense alone, both for refutation and for teaching: it is evident that the remaining mystical senses are not proper and genuine. The reason for the connection is this: For whatever is not proper and genuine, that can possess no force either for confirming or for refuting: as is abundantly clear also from the precepts of the Logicians.

II. If the remaining Mystical senses are proper and genuine, it is necessary that they be literal, and that they do not dissent even a hair's breadth from this literal sense. The reason is clear from the premises. For by the concession of the Jesuits themselves, only the literal sense is proper and genuine.

III. If the interpretation of any passage of Scripture is found to fight with the literal sense, it can be an evident argument that it is erroneous: such as that of the Romanists: Peter feed my sheep: Therefore Peter was constituted by Christ as supreme pontiff and general Bishop of the Catholic Church in this passage: Likewise Psalm 91:13, you shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the Lion and the Dragon: Therefore the Roman Pontiff has the right and supreme Empire even over the Roman Emperors themselves: just as Alexander III, at Venice at the temple of Mark, trampling with his feet upon the neck of the most excellent Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa, did not blush to cloak this unspeakable crime with those words of the Psalm.

Such is the interpretation of a certain Papal writer: All things are subject to the feet of the Pope, according to Ps. 8. Sheep, that is, the souls of the faithful. Oxen, that is, the Jews; the beasts of the field, that is, the Gentiles: the birds of the air, that is, the blessed in heaven: and the fish of the sea, that is, the souls of the departed.

IV. And lastly. If the literal sense alone is proper and genuine: it follows that this alone is intended by the Holy Spirit: and therefore the remaining mystical senses do not have the Holy Spirit as their author: but are of human, and therefore doubtful and uncertain, interpretation or exegesis.

Furthermore, in order that the nature and, as it were, the proper affection of this very literal sense or interpretation may be rightly established: certain observations must be noted:

I. The literal sense is not only that which the propriety of the words themselves immediately presents: as when Christ says in John 3:16, 'For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life': where the individual words, according to the propriety they possess, immediately produce the literal sense, which is very true. But that is also the literal sense which results from topical and figurative words or sentences: where figurative speech is not to be explained as the words themselves sound according to their surface and propriety: for thus Herod, speaking properly, would have been a fox: thus the right hand offending us, speaking properly, would have to be cut off: thus the right eye offending us, speaking properly, would have to be plucked out: thus the pious, speaking properly, ought to walk upon asps and basilisks, and trample upon lions and dragons: all of which, how absurd they are, anyone easily understands: but in figurative propositions of this kind, not so much the words and their proper signification, as the thing which is expressed through those words according to a certain similarity, is to be regarded. Once that is regarded, the literal sense emerges, even from the figurative words or sentences themselves.

II. Observation: if ever allegories insinuated by the Holy Spirit Himself occur in the Scriptures: it is least of all permitted to conclude from that that there are various senses of Scripture, or that various explanations of one passage can be given: but in these places also, a single literal and historical sense prevails: from which, however, various things can be gathered and accommodated to other matters. For example;

Latin:

PROPOSITIO I. θετικὴ.

SOlus Scripturæ sensus literalis, est genuinus, & firma, valida ac efficacia argumenta, tùm quoad διδασκαλίαν, tùm quoad ἔλεγχον subministrat.

CONFIRMATIO.

THesews hujus veritas usque adeò extra dubitationis aleam est posita, ut ipse quoque Bellarminus, vi veritatis adactus, fateatur lib. 3. de Verbo DEI cap. 3. Convenire ex utraq́ parte, ex solo literali sensu peti debere argumenta efficacia: nã eum sensum, qui ex verbis immediatè colligitur, certum est, Sensum esse Spiritus Sancti. At sensus mystici & spirituales varij sunt, licet ædificent, quãdo non sunt contra fidem, aut bonos mores: tamen non semper constat, an sint à Spiritu Sancto intenti. Quod ipsum agnovit etiam Andradius lib. 2. Defensionis Tridentini Concilij Sensus, inquiens, literalis solùm suppeditat argumenta ad religionis dogmata confirmanda. Unde sequentia Corollaria inferimus.

I. Si ex solo literali sensu firma & efficacia argumēta quâ ἔλεγχον, quâ διδασκαλίαν peti possunt: Constat reliquos sensus mysticos non esse proprios ac genuinos. Ratio Connexi est hæc: Quicquid enim proprium ac genuinum non est: illud neq; vel ad confirmandum, vel ad refutandum vim obtinere potest: uti ex Logicorum etiam præceptis abundè liquet.

II. Si reliqui sensꝰ Mystici sunt proprij & genuini, oportet ut sint literales, & ab hoc sensu literali ne latum quidem ungvem dissentiant. Ratio constat ex præmissis. Nam ipsorū Jesuvvitarum concessione solus sensꝰ literalis est proprius & genuinus.

III. Si interpretatio loci alicujus Scripturae cum literali sensu pugnare deprehenditur, evidenti argumento esse potest, eam esse erroneam: qualis est illa Romanensium: Petre pasce oves meas: Ergo Petrus a Christo, summus pontifex, & generalis Episcopo Catholicae Ecclesiae hoc loco est constitutus: Item Psalm. 91. 13. super aspidem & basiliscum ambulabis, & conculcabis Leonem & Draconem: Ergo Pontifex Romanus jus ac Imperium summum habet, in ipsos etiam Imperatores Romanos: quemadmodum Alexander III. Venetiis ad templum Marci pedibus conculcans collu optimi Imperatoris Friderici I. Barbarossae, verbis istis Psalmi, infandum hoc facinus palliare haud erubuit.

Talis est interpretatio cujusdam Scriptoris Pontificij: Omnia sunt subjecta pedibus Papa, juxta Ps. 8. Oves, id est, fideliu animae. Boves id est, Judaei; pecora campi, id est, Ethnici: volucres caeli, id est, Beati caelestes: & pisces maris, id est, animae defunctorum.

IV. ac postremum. Si solus sensu literalis est proprius ac genuinus: sequitur, hunc etiam solum a Spiritu Sancto intendi: ac proinde reliquos sensus mysticos, non autorem habere Spiritum Sanctum: sed humanae, ac proinde dubiae & incertae esse Epiluseos sive interpretationis.

Caeterum, ut hujus ipsius Literalis sensus sive interpretationis Natura, & propria quasi affectio rite constituatur: certae quaedam notandae veniunt observationes:

I. Sensus Literalis non tantum ille est, quem ipsa Verborum proprietas immediate pre se fert: ut quando Christus inquit Joh. 3. 16. Sic DEUS dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis, qui credit in ipsum, non pereat sed habeat vitam aeternam: Ubi singula verba, secundum proprietatem quam habent, immediate pariunt sensum literalem, longe verissimu. Sed & ille est sensus literalis, qui ex verbis sive sententiis Topicis ac figuratis resultat: ubi oratio figurata, non sic exponenda est, prout verba ipsa secundum superficiem & proprietatem verborum, immediate sonant: Sic enim Herodes proprie loquendo, fuisset vulpes: Sic manus dextra nos offendens, proprie loquendo esset abscindenda: Sic oculus dexter nos offendens, proprie loquendo esset eruendus: Sic pii proprie loquendo ambulare deberent super aspides, & basilicos, & conculcare Leones & Dracones: Quae omnia quam sint absurda, facile quivis intelligit: Sed in hujusmodi figuratis propositionibus, non tam vocabula, eorundemq; propria significatio, quam res, quae per vocabula illa secundum quandam similitudinem exprimitur, est spectanda. Qua spectata, sensus emergit literalis, ex ipsis etiam figuratis sive vocabulis, sive sententis.

II. Observatio: sicubi in Scripturis occurrunt Allegoriae ab ipso Spiritu Sancto insinuatae: minime omnium licet inde colligere, varios esse Scripturae sensus, aut varias dari posse unius loci explicationes: sed in his quoque locis, unicus sensus literalis & historicus obtinet: ex quo tamen varia colligi, & ad alia accommodari possunt. Exempli gratia;


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Five rules to be observed in the interpretation of Scripture

That history concerning Sarah and Hagar, the two wives of Abraham, contains one historical and literal sense. Although indeed the Apostle in Galatians 4:24 adapts it to the distinction between Law and Gospel, he does not for that reason remove the historical or literal sense, or superinduce some new sense; but from that very literal sense, he elicits by a certain similarity that which seemed to be suitable to his purpose. This very observation ought to have use when Types are adapted to antitypes: where two different senses cannot or ought not to be given, but only one, namely the Literal and Historical, which nevertheless can afterwards be adapted δευτέρως, through and because of a certain analogy, to other things either to be proved or illustrated. Where, however, this also is to be well noted: that the Literal sense, and its true and correct adaptation in such typical histories, is to be sought partly from the words themselves, partly from the thing itself which was done, and finally partly from the Type. Which members, considered separately, produce an imperfect sense; but when joined and weighed together, they produce a full and perfect one. For example: Joseph, son of the Patriarch Jacob, was sold to the Ishmaelites by his brother Judah (Gen 37:28), where the historical sense, as the letter lies, is to be retained. Now if one wishes to adapt that history typically to Christ betrayed by the disciple Judas, it emerges; but with the literal sense remaining safe, through a certain similarity or Type, the history of Joseph is adapted to the history of Christ, with those three members observed; so that it is clearly absurd to wish to invent various senses of Scripture from it, since there are only various adaptations or applications of one literal or historical sense. III. And the final Observation. Just as in the adaptation of a Type to an Antitype only one literal or historical sense remains, and yet it can be adapted to various things: so when we construct Ethical precepts from sacred histories, or refer a sign to the thing signified, there always remains one literal sense, which nevertheless is either adapted for our information, or referred to the thing signified through the explanation of a similarity.

II. ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

The true and legitimate method of interpreting the Scriptures consists chiefly in this, that Scripture be explained by Scripture, according to the analogy of faith.

CONFIRMATION.

The truth of the assertion is evident, even from that one Petrine Aphorism: No prophecy or interpretation of Scripture is of ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, of one's own explanation. For we have a more firm prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, 2 Pet. 1:20, 21. To which the Apostle agrees in Rom. 12:6, saying, let prophecy be κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν τῆς πίστεως, according to the analogy of faith. The evidence of which places is such that Gratian himself inserted into the Canon Law a Canon in every way in agreement with our assertion, which holds as follows: When the Law of God is read, it should not be read and taught according to one's own power of wit or understanding. For there are many words in the divine Scriptures which can be drawn to that sense which each person may spontaneously presume for himself: but it is not fitting. For you ought not to seek a sense from the outside that is foreign and extraneous, or in any way confirm it by the authority of the Scriptures: But to take the sense of the truth from the Scriptures themselves. Distinct. 37, can. 14, Relatum est. And indeed no other method of interpreting the Scriptures, either more certain or more safe, can be given besides this one of which we have spoken: For if we follow Scripture itself as its own interpreter, we follow indeed not the leading and dictation of any man, but of the Holy Spirit; which is clearly contained in Scripture itself, which, as a most competent Judge, holds out light and a torch to us as to what the Holy Spirit intends in any given place.

Furthermore, in order that this very comparison of the Scriptures may be rightly instituted, and, as the Apostle speaks, that spiritual things may be compared with spiritual, so that one may nowhere sin against the analogy of faith, five Rules in particular come to be observed by a good Interpreter.

I. Regula: In the interpretation of any place, it must be very diligently perceived what end and scope each place has proposed for itself: and therefore a meaning is not to be brought into the Scriptures from our own wit, but rather to be brought out from them. We have as the author of this rule the Blessed Hilary, who in book 1 de Trinitate holds as follows: The best interpreter is he who expects the understanding of what is said from the words themselves rather than imposes it, and brings it back rather than brings it in, and does not force that to seem to be contained in the words which he had presumed to understand before the reading.

II. Regula: The words of any place should be accurately weighed, and from them the true literal and native meaning should be elicited, which is done the more easily the more accurately the whole συνάφεια or coherence of any place, and what both precedes and follows, is considered.

III. Regula: If any passage occurs that is more obscure, then an interpretation must be sought from another related and clearer one. For, as Augustine writes excellently, the Holy Spirit has modified the holy Scriptures so magnificently and wholesomely that He might meet hunger with the more open passages, but brush away disdain with the more obscure ones. For almost nothing is extracted from those obscurities that may not be found stated most plainly elsewhere. Lib. 2. de doct. Christi. cap. 6. To this Ambrose also agrees, whose words are most worthy of note for blunting the impiety of the Adversaries, who persuade that in the interpretation of more obscure passages one must have recourse solely to the Church, that is, to the Pontiff with a Council. Thus, however, he says in Serm. 8. in Pf. 118: There is much obscurity in the Prophetic scriptures, but if with a certain hand of your mind you knock at the door of the Scriptures, and those what is hidden, you should examine diligently. Little by little you should begin to collect the reasoning of what is said: and it will be opened to you NOT BY ANOTHER, but BY THE WORD OF GOD. Which rule, undoubtedly taught by his own experience, Ambrose prescribed, who, snatched from the tribunal while still a catechumen, was called to the dignity of the Episcopate: when as yet there existed no commentaries of either Jerome or Augustine: and perhaps he neither had nor understood the commentaries of the Greeks: And yet, in the interpretation of the Scriptures, he was most happily engaged in the observation of this rule.

IV. Rule: If any passage seems to conflict with the analogy of faith: then one must have recourse to other more manifest passages dealing with that very question, and indeed especially to those in which the seat of each subject is proper, and where that subject matter is treated expressly: so that thus from the collation of those passages an interpretation may be made: and attention may be paid to what the analogy of faith can bear: Since it is necessary that Scripture be consistent with itself everywhere: and nothing more should be established as conflicting in it than that the Holy Spirit himself cannot contradict himself. For example: When in Daniel, James, and elsewhere such passages occur, they seem to ascribe our justification and salvation to the merits of good works: then one must immediately have recourse to those passages which expressly teach the doctrine of justification: such as the Epistles of Paul, to the Romans, Galatians, Ephesians: where from the collation you will discover that the analogy of faith does not permit those passages of Daniel and James to be explained for the sake of establishing the righteousness of one's own merits. Then, if you observe the circumstances of those passages, if the antecedents and consequents, if finally the whole structure of those passages, it will become plain that they are directed either to impious persons and those sinning enormously against the law of charity, or that they deal with the effects of justifying faith: or finally that they show by what external signs a man, already justified through faith, can and ought to be probably recognized and judged.

Fifth and lastly. The most necessary aids for the interpretation of the Scriptures are 1. The humanities: and among these especially Dialectic, which is τρόπος παιδείας, and as Augustine writes in book 1 against Cresconius, chapter 20, and book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 21, it is of the greatest value for penetrating and resolving all kinds of questions that are in the holy writings. Then indeed the knowledge of languages: Hebrew and Greek above all: as they are, as it were, the wrappings of Scripture. For as Augustine again has it in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 14: If anything is held to be so different that both cannot be true, the truth of the events must be sought from that language from which what we have was translated. And book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 11. Men of the Latin language have need of two others for the knowledge of the divine Scriptures: namely Hebrew and Greek, so that one may have recourse to the preceding exemplars, if the infinite variety of Latin interpreters has brought any doubt.

With these things thus established concerning the interpretation of the Scriptures according to our opinion: it has become plain: That the gift of interpreting the Scriptures is not of all people whatsoever: but only of those who are divinely illuminated by the Holy Spirit in such a way that they understand Scripture and can refute erroneous opinions. It is therefore a trifling and pure lie, as Bellarmine writes: that we teach that in interpreting Scripture everyone ought to follow his own spirit. For we ourselves freely admit that the Spirit of interpreting the Scriptures is not granted to all indiscriminately and promiscuously. But, whether for that reason that Spirit is so bound to the Church, that is, to the Pope and the Council, that whatever it establishes or defines must be accepted without any doubt as an oracle of the Holy Spirit: that, indeed, both the two following propositions and the other part of this analytical question will expressly show.

Latin:

Historia illa de Sara & Hagar, duabus uxoribus Abrahæ, unum sensum historicum & literalem continet. Quanquam verò Apostolus Gal 4,24. eam accommodat ad discrimen Legis & Evangelii : non tamen ideò tollit sensum historicum sive literalem : aut novum aliquem sensum superinducit : Sed ex illo ipso sensu literali, elicit per quandam similitudinem id, quod instituto suo videbatur esse accommodum. Quæ ipsa observatio usum habere debet, quando Typi ad antitypos accommodantur : ubi non duo diversi sensus dari possunt aut debent : sed unus tantùm, nempè Literalis & Historicus : qui tamen postea δευτέρως, per & propter quandam ἀναλογίαν, ad alia vel probanda, vel illustranda accommodari potest. Ubi tamen & illud probè notandum est : Sensum Literalem, ejusdemq́; veram ac rectam accommodationem, in hujusmo dihistoriis typicis, partim ex verbis ipsis, partim ex re ipsâ, quæ gesta fuit : partim deniq; ex Typo petendam esse. Quæ membra seorsim considerata, imperfectum : simul verò juncta ac expensa, plenum perfectumq́; sensum pariunt. Exempli gratiâ: Josephus filius Patriarchæ Jacobi venditus fuit Ismaelitis, à fratre Judâ : Gen 37,28. ubi historicus sensus prout Litera jacet, est retinend9. Jam si ad Christum à discipulo Judâ proditum, historiam illam typicè accommodare emergit: sed salvo manentem literali sensu, per quandam similitudinem aut Typum, historia Josephi, ad historiam Christi, observatis tribus illis membris, accommodatur : ita ut absurdum planè sit, varios inde Scripturæ sensus velle comminisci, cùm varię tantùm sint accommodationes sive applicationes, unius sensus literalis sive historici. III. Et postrema Observatio. Quemadmodum in accommodatione Typi ad Antitypum unus tantùm manet sensus literalis sive historicus : & tamen ille ad varia accommodari potest : Ita quando ex historiis sacris, præcepta Ethica extruimus : vel signum ad signatum referimus : semper manet unus sensus literalis, qui tamen vel ad nostri informationem accommodatur, vel per similitudinis explicationem ad signatum refertur.

II. PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

VEra ac legitima interpretandi Scripturas ratio in eo præcipuè consistit, ut Scriptura per Scripturam, secundum analogiam fidei explicetur.

CONFIRMATIO.

PAtet assertionis veritas, vel ex uno illo Aphorismo Petrino : Nulla Scripturæ Prophetia sive interpretatio est ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως propriæ explicationis. Habemus enim firmiorẽ sermonem Propheticum, cui dum attenditis, tanquam lucernæ lucenti in loco caliginoso rectè facitis, 2. Pet. 1, 20. 21. Cui suffragatur Apostolus Rom. 12. 6. Prophetia inquiens, sit κτ' τὴν ἀναλογίαν τῆς πίσεως. Quorum locorum tanta est evidentia, ut ipse quoq; Gratianus Canonem nostræ assertioni per omnia ὁμόψηφον, Juri Canonico inseruerit, qui sic habet: Lex Dei cum legitur, non secundum propriam ingenii virtutem, vel intelligentiam legatur & doceatur. Sunt enim multa verba in Scripturis divinis, quæ possunt trahi ad eum sensum, quem sibi unusquisq; spontè præsumserit: sed non oportet. Non enim sensum extrinsecus alienum & extraneum debetis quærere, aut quoquo modo illum Scripturarum autoritate confirmare: Sed ex ipsis Scripturis sensum capere veritatis. Distinct. 37. can. 14. Relatum est. Et profectò nulla alia vel certior, vel tutior interpretandi Scripturas ratio dari potest, præter hanc, de quâ diximus: Nam si scripturam ipsam sui ipsius interpretem sequamur: sequimur utiq; non hominis alicuj9, sed Spiritus Sancti ductum & dictamen; quod in ipsa Scriptura perspicuè continetur, quæ tanquam Judex maximè competens lucem nobis & facem præfert, quid quovis in loco Spiritus Sanctus intendat.

Cæterùm, ut hæc ipsa Scripturarum collatio ritè instituatur, & ut Apostolus loquitur, spiritualia cum spiritualibus ita comparentur, ut nuspiam in ἀναλογίαν fidei peccetur, quinq; potissimùm Regulæ, Bono Interpreti subindè observandæ veniunt.

I. Regula: In cujuslibet Loci interpretatione diligenter admodum perspiciendum, quem finem ac scopum sibi quisq; locus habeat propositum: ac proinde non ex nostro ingenio inferenda est in Scripturas sententia: sed inde potiùs efferenda. Regulę hujus autorem habemus B. Hilarium, qui libro 1. de Trinit. sic habet: Optimus interpres est, qui dictorum intelligentiam ex Dictis potiùs expectet, quàm imponat: & retulerit magis, quàm attulerit: neq; cogat id videri dictis contineri, quod ante lectionem præsumserit intelligendum.

II. Regula: Verba cujuslibet loci, accuratè expendantur, ex iisque vera literalis ac nativa sententia eruatur, id quod tantò fit faciliùs, quantò accuratius tota cujuslibet loci συνάφεια sive cohærentia, quidq; & antecedat & consequatur, consideratur.

III. Regula: Si locus aliquis occurrat obscurior, tùm ex alio cognato & manifestiore petenda est interpretatio. Nam, ut Augustinus præclarè scribit, Spiritus Sanctus Scripturas sanctas ita magnificè ac salubriter modificavit: ut locis apertioribus fami occurreret; Obscurioribus autem fastidia detergeret. Nihil enim ferè ex obscuritatibus illis eruitur, quod non alibi planissimè dictum reperiatur. Lib. 2. de doct. Christi. cap. 6. Cui astipulatur etiam Ambrosius, cujus verba ad retundendam Adversariorum impietatem, suadentium in interpretatione locorum obscuriorum ad Ecclesia, hoc est, Pontificê cum Concilio unicè recurrendum esse, notatu sunt dignissima. Sic autem ille Serm. 8. in Pf. 118. Multa obscuritas est in scripturis Propheticis, sed si manu quâdã mentis tuæ Scripturarũ januam pulses, & ea quae occulta sunt, diligenter examines. paulatim incipias rationem colligere dictorum: & aperietur tibi NON AB ALIO, sed A DEI VERBO. Quam regulam haud dubiè propriâ experientiâ edoctus praescripsit Ambrosius qui raptus de tribunali Catechumenus adhuc ad Episcopatus dignitatem vocatus est: cùm nondum extarent, vel Hieronymi, vel Augustini Commentarij: & fortè Graecorum etiam Commentaria nec haberet nec intelligeret: Et tamen Interpretatione Scripturarum, Regulae hujus observatione felicissimè versatus est.

IV. Regula: Si locus aliquis pugnare videatur cum analogiâ fidei: tùm recurrendum est ad alia loca manifestiora, de illâ ipsâ Quaestione agentia, & quidem praecipuè ad ea, in quibus sedes cujusq; materiae est propria, & ubi ex professo materia illa tractatur: ut sic ex collatione eorum locorum fiat interpretatio: & quid analogia fidei ferre possit, attendatur: Siquidem Scriptura sibi ipsi undiquaque consciens sit, oportet: & nihilo magis quicquam in eâ pugnant statuatur quàm Spiritus ipse Sanctus sibi nequit contradicere. Exempli gratia: Cùm in Daniele, Jacobo & alibi occurrunt ejusmodi loca, meritis bonorum operum videntur adscribere justificationem nostram & salutem: tùm statim recurrendum ad ea loca, quae ex professo Justificationis Doctrinam tradunt: ut ad Epistolas Pauli, ad Romanos, Galatas, Ephesios: ubi ex collatione deprehendes, Analogiam fidei haud permittere, ut pro justitiâ propriâ meritorum stabiliendâ, loca illa Danielis, & Jacobi explicentur. Deinde, si locorum illorum circumstantias, si antecedentia & consequentia, si denique totam locorum illorum compagem observes, planum evadet ea vel ad personas impias & circa Legem charitatis enormiter peccantes esse directa, vel agere de effectibus fidei justificantis: vel denique ostendere, ex quibus signis externis, Homo jam per fidem justificatus, probabiliter agnosci judicariq; possit & debeat.

Quintò & postremò. Adminicula interpretationis Scripturarum maximè necessaria, sunt 1. Artes humaniores: atque inter has cumprimis Dialectica, quae est τρόπος παιδείας, & ut Augustinus scribit lib. 1. contra Gresconium cap. 20. & lib. 2. de doct. Christ. cap. 21. ad omnia genera quaestionum, quae in literis sanctis sunt, penetranda & dissolvenda plurimùm valet. Deinde verò lingvarum cognitio: Hebraeae cumprimis & Graecae: ut quae sunt quasi involucra Scripturae. Nam ut Augustinus rursus habet lib. 15. de civit. DEI cap. 14. Si quid ita habetur diversum, ut verum esse utrumq, non possit, verum gestarum fides ab eâ lingvâ repetenda est, ex quâ interpretatum est, quod habemus. Et lib. 2. de doctrinâ Christ. cap. 11. Latina lingva homines, duabus aliis ad Scripturarum divinarum cognitionem opus habent: Hebraeâ scilicet & Graecâ, ut ad Exemplaria praecedentia recurratur, siquam dubitationem attulerit Latinorum interpretum infinita varietas.

Quibus de interpretatione Scripturarum ex nostrâ sententiâ ita constitutis: planum evastit dit: Donum interpretandi Scripturas non esse omnium quorumcunque: sed eorum tantùm, qui divinitùs ita sunt Spiritu Sancto illustrati, ut Scripturam intelligant, & erroneas opiniones refutare queant. Nugatorium proindè ac putum mendacium est, Bellarminus scribit: Docere nos, in interpretandâ Scripturâ quemq́; suum sequi debere Spiritum. Nam nos ipsi non indifferenter & promiscuè omnibus Spiritum interpretandi Scripturas concessum esse ultrò fatemur. Cæterùm, nùm propterea Spiritus iste ita ad Ecclesiam, hoc est, ad Pontificem & Concilium sit alligatus, ut quicquid ea statuit aut definit, illud tanquàm Oraculum Spiritus Sancti, sine ullâ dubitatione sit acceptandum: Id verò tùm subsequentes propositiones duæ: tùm pars altera Quæstionis hujus ἀνλυτικὴ ex professo ostendet.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: III. Orthodox Proposition

III. ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

The interpretation of Scripture, which the Apostle calls Prophetic in 1 Cor. 12:10, is a gift of the Holy Spirit, indeed proper to the Church: yet not bound either to certain men or to any certain seat or succession of men.

CONFIRMATION.

This thesis is two-membered: For in the beginning it asserts that the supreme right and supreme authority of interpreting the Scriptures resides with the Holy Spirit alone, speaking through the Scriptures. But the persuasion by which the Holy Spirit renders us most certain of the true and genuine sense of Scripture is twofold: One is internal, by reason of which the Holy Spirit illuminates each of the faithful, so that he may hold the mind and sense of Scripture with great πληροφορίᾳ, and not doubt it in any way: even if the testimony and authority of the Church does not at all approach. The other is external persuasion, which looks especially to those who are not yet illuminated by the Holy Spirit: but are finally to be informed about the dogmas of the Christian religion. With respect to these certainly, the Holy Spirit himself uses the ministry of Doctors and the Church, yet in such a way that even these do not invent the sense of Scripture from their own genius: but explain Scripture through Scripture: in the way that was shown in the immediately preceding thesis.

The latter part of our thesis is that the gift of interpreting the Scriptures is indeed proper to the Church, but yet neither incommunicable nor altogether inseparable; so indeed that it sometimes pertains even to the members of a false Church, and in the true Church itself this gift does not always flourish equally: nor is the Holy Spirit so bound, either to a place or to certain persons, that He does not breathe where He wills, but rather works with a most free will: and He frequently imparts this gift even to private believers, according to that 1 Cor. 2:15: The spiritual man judges all things. This thesis standing, we infer that, not only with respect to internal but also with respect to external persuasion, the supreme judgment and authority of interpreting the Scriptures cannot be attributed to the Church: But this right belongs both to Scripture, which explains itself, and to the Holy Spirit, who not only speaks with us through the Scriptures, but also confirms and seals their true sense by a certain internal power: so that, if anything is to be granted to the Church in this regard, beyond the mere ministerial voice, which both Scripture itself and the Holy Spirit are accustomed to use as an instrument, nothing more at all is to be conceded to it. It is our pleasure, however, to demonstrate the immovable certainty of this very assertion with certain firm arguments.

Let the first be such: To whom alone it belongs to work faith in the hearts of men, with him also alone rests the supreme right and supreme authority of interpreting the Scriptures.

But it is the proper office of the Holy Spirit alone, insofar as He speaks through the Scriptures, to work faith in the hearts of men.

Therefore, with the Holy Spirit alone, insofar as He speaks through Scripture, also rests the supreme right and supreme authority of interpreting Scripture: and consequently, this right can neither be, nor ought to be, ascribed to the Church.

The connection of the major premise is evident from this: Because faith relates to the sense of Scripture as a relative to its correlate. For if faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word (Rom. 10:17), it would certainly follow that faith looks to the true and genuine sense of Scripture as the object which is proposed to be believed in the Scriptures. Now, if faith is conceived by man through the power of the Holy Spirit, then, when the same Spirit opens and confirms the true sense of Scripture through Scripture itself, the evidence of the major proposition will certainly stand: that the supreme right of interpreting the Scriptures rests with him alone with whom rests the power of working faith.

The adversaries will hardly deny the minor proposition, unless they wish to foist upon the Church of God some new and hitherto entirely unheard-of paradox; namely, that it is the proper office of the Church to work faith in the hearts of men. The Scholastics indeed, as do most Jesuits, distinguish between infused and acquired faith: in such a way that infused faith is saving and is infused by the Holy Spirit alone through the hearing of the Word. But acquired faith is that which depends on the authority of the Church, but does not suffice for the full assurance of faith. Bellarmine himself admits this in Book 1, On Grace and Free Will, chapter 6, p. 539 C, writing thus: The seed from which we are regenerated is the Word of God, 1 Pet. 1:23: Being born again not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the Word of the living God. And James 1:18: He begat us with the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of His creatures. But the Word properly begets faith in us, and that a living one, which works through love. From which words of the Jesuit we thus evidently gather: If the Word of God, or Holy Scripture, PROPERLY begets faith in us, then certainly this cannot be properly ascribed to the Church: and consequently, neither will the supreme right of interpreting the Scriptures belong to it.

A second argument can be as follows: Whatever our Faith is ultimately resolved into—that is, that in which, as in a first principle, Faith uniquely rests and relies—it is necessary that that same thing should possess the supreme right and supreme Authority to interpret the Scriptures. Now, however, our Faith is not ultimately resolved into the authority and opinion of the Church, that is, of the Pope and Councils; since it neither can nor ought to rest in that. But the voice of the Holy Spirit alone, speaking through the Scriptures, is that first principle in which alone Faith can rest firmly and without hesitation. For example: We do not believe that the world was created by GOD, that Christ died for us, or that He made satisfaction to GOD the Father for the sins of the whole world, because the Church testifies that this is true, but because the Holy Spirit Himself reveals and confirms these things in the Scriptures.

Therefore, that supreme right and supreme authority of interpreting the Scriptures will not rest with the Church, but with the Holy Spirit alone speaking through the Scriptures.

The connection of the major premise is readily apparent: For whatever acts as a first principle that is indemonstrable, that also possesses by its authority what is clearly unaccountable. Furthermore, such a first principle is the cause of the conclusion, that is, it ensures that what is inferred from it is necessarily true: therefore, it is necessary that our faith also be ultimately resolved into it.

Third Argument: If the Holy Spirit alone is the author of the Scriptures, then certainly He alone will also have the supreme right of interpreting them. But the former is true. Therefore, the latter is also true.

The connection of the Major premise is evident from this, 1. Because it belongs to him who establishes a Law, also to interpret it. 2. Because the Scriptures ought not to be understood in any other sense, or by any other Spirit, than that in which they were written. Furthermore, the Jesuits rise up at this point, and accuse us of I know not what ἀσυλλογισίας, because we prove that which, even on their own side, is placed beyond controversy. For it is not doubted that the Holy Spirit is required as the supreme interpreter. But that the point in question is this: Who indeed possesses that Holy Spirit, and through whom he speaks. Which insistence of the adversaries, although it seems to carry with it some appearance of probability, yet when weighed a little more accurately, reveals a remarkable lust for sophistry: for first, when asked with whom that Holy Spirit resides, and through whom he speaks in such a way that it is in no wise permitted to doubt any longer, they are accustomed to name the Roman Pontiff; whether he pronounces it alone or with a council. Where at the beginning they beg the question: and in a matter of the greatest seriousness they trifle too scurrilously. Then, however, they commit a manifest ψεῦδος (falsehood). For it is so far from being true that the Roman Pope has the Holy Spirit so enslaved to himself, as it were, that he cannot err: that the Apostle rather testifies that the Holy Spirit resides in every believer who interprets the Scriptures correctly: saying, The spiritual man judges all things 1 Cor. 2, 15. To which pertains the fact that, although not all are endowed with the Gift of interpretation, which Moses once wished to be the case Num. 11, 29. Nevertheless, the Apostle wishes the judgment concerning the interpretation of Scripture to be common to all: Which certainly necessarily presupposes the presence of the Holy Spirit, and indeed this special presence, which can judge concerning the true sense of Scripture: and which the Roman Pontiff through horrible sacrilege claims for himself alone. Of this kind is that which Paul exhorts the Thessalonians, that they should prove all things, and hold fast that which is good. 1 Thess. 5, 21. that they should not quench the Spirit, nor despise prophesyings. Ibid. verses 19 and 20: Which likewise John warns all believers, that they should not believe every spirit: but rather test the spirits, whether they are of GOD? 1 John 4, 1. Which finally the same John repeats from chapter 54, 13 of Isaiah: That all believers will be ϑεοδιδάκτυς (taught by God): but taught only through the Spirit of GOD, John 6, 45.

The fourth and final argument is provided by Orthodox Antiquity: since its testimonies can be sought from the writings of our people, and especially from the Protocol of the Colloquy of Ratisbon: we, having already passed over those, will be content with the opinion of one or another Scholastic Doctor.

Thus Gerson, part 1, on the examination of doctrines. The first Truth would stand, that some simple person, not authorized, might be so excellently learned in the sacred letters, that in a doctrinal case, more credence should be given to his assertion than to the Pope's declaration. For it is certain that more credence should be given to the Gospel than to the Pope. If, therefore, such a learned person (a layman) teaches some truth contained in the Gospel, where even the Pope might not know it, or might voluntarily err; it is clear whose judgment should be preferred. And after a few words: Such a learned person (a layman) ought, in a case, if and while a general Council were being held, at which he himself were present, to oppose it, if he felt the greater part were declining to the opposite of the Gospel either through malice or ignorance.

Panormitanus the Canonist supports Gerson in C. significasti, on Election. In matters concerning the faith, even the statement of one private individual is to be preferred to the statement of the Pope: If he were moved by better authorities of the Old and New Testament than the other. The same. More credence is to be given to even a simple layman bringing forward Scripture, than to a whole Council together, speaking without Scripture.

Latin:

III. PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

INterpretatio Scripturæ, quam Apostolus nominat Propheticā 1. Cor. 12, 10. est donum Spiritus Sancti, Ecclesiæ quidem proprium: non tamen vel ad certos homines, vel ad certam aliquam sive sedem, sive successionē hominum alligatum.

CONFIRMATIO.

THesis hæc est bimembris: Initiò enim asserit, Summum jus summamq́; autoritatem interpretandi Scripturas, esse penes solum Spiritum Sanctum, per Scripturas loquentem. Gemina verò est persuasio, quâ Spiritus Sanctus de vero ac genuino Scripturæ sensu nos reddit certissimos: Una interna, ratione cujus Spiritus Sanctus quemlibet fidelium illuminat, ut magnâ cùm πληροφορίᾳ teneat mentem ac sensum Scripturæ, neque ullatenus de eo dubitet: si vel maximè Ecclesiæ testimonium & autoritas non accedat. Altera est Externa persuasio, quæ illos potissimum spectat, qui Spiritu Sancto nondum sunt illuminati: sed demùm de dogmatibus Religionis Christianæ sunt informandi. Horum certè respectu, ipse Spiritus Sanctus utitur ministerio Doctorum & Ecclesię, ita tamen, ut & hi Scripturæ sensum non ex suo ingenio comminiscantur: sed Scripturam per Scripturam explicent: eo modo, quo thesi præcedente proximâ fuit ostensum.

Posterius membrum thesews nostræ est, Donum interpretandi Scripturas esse quidem Ecclesiæ proprium: sed tamē neq́; incōmunicabile, neq́; prorsus inseparabile: Ita quidem, ut falsæ etiam Ecclesiæ membris illud interdum competat: & in ipsâ sæpius verâ Ecclesiâ Donum hoc non semper pariter floreat: neque etiam Spiritus Sanctus non ita sit, vel ad locum, vel ad personas certas alligatus, ut non spiret ubi vult, quin potiùs operetur voluntate liberrimâ: & donum hoc fidelibus etiam privatis frequenter impertiat, secundum illud 1. Cor. 2, 15. Spiritualis homo omnia dijudicat. Quâ thesi stante, inferimus, non modò respectu internæ, sed & respectu externæ persuasionis, Ecclesiæ non posse tribui summum judicium atque autoritatem interpretandi Scripturas: Sed hoc jus competere tùm Scripturæ, quæ semetipsam explicat, tùm Spiritui sancto, qui non tantùm per Scripturas nobiscum loquitur: sed & verum earundem sensum internâ quadam virtute confirmat & obsignat: ita ut, si hac in parte aliquid Ecclesiæ sit largiendum, præter solam vocem ministerialem, quâ tanquam Organo, tùm Scriptura ipsa, tùm Spiritus Sanctus uti solet, nihil quicquam amplius ipsi sit concedendum. Placet autem hujus ipsius assertionis immotam certitudinem, firmis quibusdam demonstrare argumentis.

Primum tale esto: Cujus solius est operari fidem in cordibus hominum, penes illum etiam solum est summum jus, summaque autoritas interpretandi Scripturas.

Atqui solius Spiritus Sancti, quatenus per Scripturas loquitur, proprium munus est, operari fidem in cordibus hominum.

Ergò penes solum etiam Spiritum Sanctum, quatenus per Scripturam loquitur, est summum jus summaque autoritas interpretandi Scripturam: ac per consequens Ecclesiæ hoc jus adscribi nec potest, nec debet.

Majoris connexum patet indè: Quia Fides habet se ad sensum Scripturæ, tanquam Relatum ad suum correlatum. Si enim Fides est ex auditu: Auditus autem per verbum, Rom. 10, 17. utique consectaneum fuerit, Fidem respicere verum & genuinum Scripturæ sensum, tanquam Objectum, quod credendum in Scripturis proponitur. Jam: Si Fides virtute Spiritus Sancti ab homine concipitur, tùm, quando verum Scripturæ sensum per ipsam Scripturam, idem Spiritus aperit & confirmat: stabit utiq; Majoris propositionis evidentia: penes illum solum esse summum jus interpretandi Scripturas, penes quem est vis operandi fidem.

Minorem propositionem vix negabunt Adversarii, nisi novum quoddam, & antehac prorsus inauditum paradoxum Ecclesiæ DEI obtrudere velint; nempè Ecclesiæ proprium munus esse, operari fidem in cordibus hominum. Scholastici sanè, ut & plerique Jesuitæ distingvunt inter Fidem Infusam & Acquisitam: ita quidem, ut, infusa fides sit salutifera, & à solo Spiritu Sancto per auditum Verbi infundatur. Acquisita verò sit, quæ ab Ecclesiæ autoritate dependet, sed ad πληροφορίαν fidei non sufficiat. Fatetur hoc Bellarminus ipse lib. 1. de Gratia & Libero Arbitrio, cap. 6. p. 539. C. sic scribens: Semen ex quo regeneramur, est Verbum DEI, 1. Pet. 1, 23. Renati nõ ex semine corruptibili, sed ex incorruptibili, per Verbum DEI vivi. Et Jacobi 5, 18. Genuit nos Verbo veritatis, ut simus initium aliquod Creaturae ejus. Verbum autem propriè Fidem in nobis gignit, eamq́; vivam, quae per dilectionem operatur. Ex quibus verbis Jesuvitae sic evidenter colligimus: Si Verbum DEI, sive Scriptura Sacra, PROPRIE Fidem in nobis gignit: utique Ecclesia hoc adscribi non poterit propriè: ac proindè neque summum jus interpretandi Scripturas ei conveniet.

Alterum argumentum tale esse potest: In quodcunq; Fides nostra postremò resolvitur: hoc est, in quo tanquàm primo principio, Fides unicè acquiescit & innititur: illud summum etiam jus summamq́; Autoritatem interpretandi Scripturas obtineat, necesse est. Jam verò in autoritatem ac sententiam Ecclesiae, hoc est, Pontificis & Conciliorum Fides nostra postremò non resolvitur: Siquidem in eâ acquiescere nec potest nec debet: Sed solius Spiritus Sancti per Scripturas loquentis vox, est primum illud principium, in quo solo firmiter & sine dubitatione Fides acquiescere potest. Exempli gratiâ: Non ideò credimus Mundum à DEO conditum: Christum pro nobis mortuum: satisfecisse DEO Patri pro peccatis totius mundi. Quia Ecclesia hoc verum esse testatur: Sed quia ipse Spiritus Sanctus in Scripturis isthac revelat & comprobat.

Ergò summum etiam illud jus summamq́; autoritas interpretandi Scripturas, non erit penes Ecclesiam, sed penes solum Spiritum sanctum per Scripturas loquentem.

Connexum Majoris ultrò liquet: Quicquid enim se habet instar primi Principii ἀναποδείκτꙋ: illud etiam autoritate obtinet planè ἀνυπεύθυνον. Porrò ejusmodi primum principium est causa Conclusionis, hoc est, praestat, ut necessariò verum sit, quod ex eo infertur: Ergò in illud etiam Fides nostra postremò resolvatur, necesse est.

Tertium Argumentum: Si solus Spiritus sanctus est autor Scripturarum, utiq́; solus etiam ipse habebit summum jus interpretandi easdem. At prius verum. Ritum ergò & posterius.

Connexum Majoris patet inde, 1. Quia cujus est condere Legem, illius etiam est illam interpretari. 2. Quia Scripturae non debent alio intelligi sensu, sive Spiritu; quàm quo scriptae fuerunt. Caeterùm insurgunt hoc loco Jesuvvitae, & nescio cujus ἀσυλλογισίας nos insimulant, propterea quòd probemus id, quod ex ipsorum etiam parte extra Controversiam sit positum. Neque enim dubitari, Spiritum Sanctum requiri tanquam summum interpretem. Verùm illud in Quaestione esse positum: Quisnam habeat Spiritum illum Sanctum, & per quem ille loquatur. Quae sanè Adversariorum instantia, etsi probabilitatis aliquid prae se ferre videtur: paulò tamen accuratiùs expensa, insignem sophisticandi libidinem prodit: Primùm enim rogati, penes quem sit Spiritus ille Sanctus, & per quemnam ille ita loquatur, ut nullatenùs ampliùs dubitare liceat: subindè nominare solent Pontificem Romanum; sive solus, sive cum concilio pronunciet. Ubi initiò petunt principium: & in re maximè feria nimis scurriliter nugantur. Deindè verò manifestum ψεῦδος committunt. Nam usque adeò falsum est, quòd Papa Romanus ita Spiritum Sanctum mancipatum quasi sibi habeat, ut errare non possit : ut potiùs in quolibet fideli, Scripturas rectè interpretante, Spiritum Sanctum residere, Apostolus testetur: Spiritualis, inquiens homo omnia dijudicat 1. Cor. 2, 15. Quò pertinet illud, quòd quamvis Dono interpretationis non sunt instructi omnes, quod tamen esse optabat olim Moses. Num. 11, 29. Judicium tamen de Interpretatione Scripturæ, D. Apostolus vult esse commune omnium: Idquod certè Spiritus Sancti, præsentiam & quidem hanc specialem, quæ de vero Scripturæ sensu judicare possit: & quam Pontifex Romanus per horrendum Sacrilegium sibi soli vendicat, necessariò præsupponit. Hujus generis est, quod Paulus Thessalonicenses hortatur, ut omnia probent, quod bonum est, teneant. 1. Thess 5. 21. ut ne Spiritum sextingvant, neque Prophetias spernant. Ibid. vers. 19. & 20: Quod item Johannes fideles quosvis monet, ut ne omni Spiritui credant: sed potiùs probent Spiritus, num ex DEO sint? 1. Johan. 4, 1. Quod denique idem Johannes ex capite 54, 13. Jesaiæ repetit: Omnes fideles fore ϑεοδιδάκτυς, doctos à DEO: doctos autem non nisi per Spiritum DEI, Joh. 6, 45.

Quartum ac postremum argumentum subministrat Orthodoxa Antiquitas: cujus testimonia cùm ex nostrorum Scriptis, & præsertim ex Protocollo Colloquii Ratisbonensis peti possint: nos illis jam prætermissis, unius aut alterius Scholastici Doctoris sententiâ contenti erimus.

Sic Gerson, part. 1. de examinatione doctrinarum. Prima Veritas staret, quòd aliquis sim plex, non autorizatus, esset tam excellenter in sacris literis eruditus, quòd plus esset credendum in casu doctrinali, hujus assertioni, quàm Papæ declarationi. Constat enim plus esse credendum Evangelio, quàm Papæ. Si doceat igitur talis eruditus (Laicus) veritatem aliquam in Evangelio contineri, ubi & Papa nesciret, vel ultrò erraret; patet, cujus præferendum sit judicium. Et post pauca: Talis eruditus (Laicus) deberet in casu, si & dum celebraretur generale Concilium, cui & ipse præsens esset, illi se opponere, si sentiret majorem partem ad oppositum Evangelii vel malitiâ vel ignorantiâ declinare.

Gersoni suffragatur Panormitanus Canonista in C. significasti, de Electione. In concernentibus fidem, etiam dictum unius privati præferendum est dicto Papæ: Si ille moveretur melioribus autoritatibus Veteris & Novi Testamenti, quàm iste. Idem. Plus credendum est vel simplici Laico Scripturam proferenti, quàm toti simul Concilio, loquenti sine Scriptura.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: IV. Orthodox Proposition

IV. ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

Holy Scripture alone and by itself is the infallible Judge of all Controversies which have ever arisen or can arise concerning the heads of the Christian Religion: Inasmuch as it is nothing else than the voice of the supreme Judge, the Holy Spirit, whom it is fitting for all to acknowledge, fear, and venerate.

CONFIRMATION.

Logicians teach that there is a certain Genus of Homonyms, which Aristotle in book 2 of On Coming-to-be and Passing-away calls κῂ τὸ πρότερον καὶ ὕστερον (the prior and the posterior). But otherwise they are called Homonyms signifying πρὸς ἓν ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς (in relation to one from one). In these significations, there is a certain Principal one, and in respect to which the rest are understood to exist. Although the same Philosopher in book 7 of the Metaphysics does not think that this Genus of words should be called either Homonym or Synonym, for the reason that in these neither One nor Many are signified simply: but certain Many, by referring those very things to a certain πρὸς ἓν (one) principal thing.

Into the census and number of those words must also be referred the word (Judge) which we are accustomed to use in this dispute: indeed in such a way that it is accommodated to many things, now in the supreme, now in the secondary, now in the lowest signification; which nevertheless are referred to one principal thing. For in the supreme and principal signification we establish that the Judge of all Controversies, which have ever arisen or can arise, is only GOD the Holy Spirit, by whose breath and impulse the holy men of GOD spoke and wrote, as Peter has it 2 Pet. 1, 21 and the Apostle Paul 2 Tim. 3, 16. All Scripture is divinely inspired. Now indeed, in so far as this very GOD the Holy Spirit utters a decisive judgment not otherwise than ἐμμέσως, mediately, namely through the written Word: to that extent now, but in a secondary sense, this Word of GOD is and is called the Judge of Controversies: In which sense the Apostle in the place already cited from 2 Tim. 3, 16, affirms that all Scripture inspired by God is useful also πρὸς ἔλεγχόν, for reproof or refutation, namely of all heresies. This very thing is evidently confirmed by that saying of the Savior in John 12, 48: He who rejects me and does not receive my words has one who JUDGES him: the WORD which I have spoken, that will judge him on the last day. And this is the very thing concerning which we are warned by GOD himself, while we are referred solely to the Law and to the Testimony of his, with this threat added, That if we do not think and speak according to this Law, we shall not see the morning light. Isa. 8, 20. To which pertains that clearly illustrious Aphorism of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 4, 12.

The Word of GOD is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and reaches even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow, and JUDGES the thoughts and intentions of the heart, κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων, καὶ ἐννοιῶν καρδίας. Furthermore, Christ and the Apostles, both in their sermons and in their disputations with heretics, always appealed to the scriptures: demonstrating by their own example that true Theological πρᾶξιν which ought to be used in judging Controversies, so that, namely, all spirits, that is, both the Doctors themselves and any doctrines whatsoever, and individual Controversies, may be examined, tested, and judged as if by a Lydian stone from the Canonical Books and Scriptures.

Moreover, since the judgment of Scripture concerning individual Controversial Questions is not immediately obvious to everyone: therefore the Holy Spirit uses the ministry of the Church, that is, of the faithful, who, endowed with the gift of Interpretation, can draw out that judgment, as if hidden in Scripture. These faithful themselves are placed in such a distinction that some are public, others private.

We call those Doctors and Ministers of the Church public, to whom the public duty of Teaching has been legitimately entrusted and assigned. It is certainly the proper duty and office of these, not only to propose sound doctrine: but also to judge the dogmas of others.

But we name as a private Judge any Christian believer to whom the salvation of his own soul is a concern. For it was said to these also by Christ: Beware of false prophets Matth. 7, 15. And it was enjoined by Paul and John that they should test all things, hold fast to what is good: and not believe every spirit: But test the spirits, whether they are from GOD. 1. Thess. 5, 21. 1. Joh. 4, 1. Moreover, since the power of these private individuals, and of those public ones, is not immense: that is, since neither any praetorian authority, nor an absolute or indeterminate Arbitrium has been granted to them: But they can not only err in judging, but do in fact err very often: therefore only a determined and limited Judgment belongs to them, insofar as it agrees precisely with the norm of sacred Scripture: and consequently the voice and title of Judge is attributed to them only in the lowest degree: while one supreme Judge remains in the meantime, the Holy Spirit, speaking in and through the Scriptures.

The very gravity of this Question demands that we confirm this thesis or assertion of ours with firm arguments. Therefore, let this be the first:

To whomever alone all the marks, κριτήρια, and requirements that are most strictly demanded of a Supreme and infallible Judge belong: to him also this Right and title properly and uniquely belongs. But the marks, κριτήρια, and requirements, etc., belong to the Holy Spirit alone. Therefore, the right and title of Supreme and infallible Judge belongs to Him alone.

The certainty of the major premise is placed beyond Controversy even among the Adversaries themselves.

The evidence of the minor premise is clear from a full and sufficient enumeration of those requirements which are most necessary for the supreme and infallible Judge of dogmas and interpretations, the first of which is that he cannot err in judging: and consequently the litigating parties can rest in his sentence and judgment without any hesitation. 2. That it is not permitted for anyone to appeal from his sentence. 3. That he himself is not a party to the litigants or the Controversy. 4. That he is not led by any partiality, and is most alien to all respect of persons (πρωσωποληψίᾳ). 5. That by his authority he can compel transgressors to justice and right, so that they stand by the sentence or decision, as the Jesuit Tanner speaks in the Colloquy of Ratisbon: Protocoll. p. 273.

Now, these κριτήρια belong neither to the Church, nor to the Pope, nor to the Fathers, nor to Councils, nor to any mortal: But they belong to the Holy Spirit alone: as will be demonstrated to the eye below in the second, affirmative part. Therefore, the title and designation of supreme and infallible Judge belongs to Him alone.

The second argument can be such: Whose voice and authority as Judge, individual and universal heresies are suppressed and refuted: he must certainly be the supreme and infallible Judge.
