But indeed, individual and universal heresies in the Church in past times were repressed only by the voice and authority of the Holy Spirit, pronouncing a definitive sentence through the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, etc.

The major proposition, in turn, among the Jesuits themselves is certain and indubitable.

I prove the minor, 1. indeed by the example of the heresy of the Ebionites, blaspheming that Christ is not true GOD, nor existed before Mary. Which heresy, indeed, was most sufficiently refuted and overturned by the Gospel of John alone, without any other presupposed authority, and without any other traditions. Then, the truth of the major is established by the authority of the most ancient Fathers, who teach with the highest consensus that, from the scriptures alone, as the voice of the Holy Spirit, both heresies are to be condemned and all controversies concerning Religion are to be defined. Where it is highly memorable that the Emperor Constantine exhorted the Fathers of the Nicene Council that, since the Evangelical and Apostolic books, and the oracles of the ancient Prophets, teach us clearly what we ought to think about divine matters, ἐκ τῶν θεοπνεύσων λόγων, that is, from the divinely inspired words, they should take the explanation of those things which are called into question. Theodoret, book 1, chapter 6. Thus Augustine, Epist. 163, prescribing the form of a legitimate disputation, advises this primarily, that the Canonical Books be at hand: For thus the matter can be brought to the end of the inquiry. And in book 2, chapter 33, de nupt. & Conc., he writes thus: These controversies require a judge: let Christ therefore judge: let the Apostle Paul judge with Him, because Christ also speaks in the Apostle himself.

Then I prove the minor premise with examples and practice, always used in the Catholic Church. For Ecclesiastical history is a witness that that rule of the Emperor Constantine was observed, not only in that Nicene Council against Arius: but that the same thereafter also prevailed in all pious councils gathered against any heretics whatsoever. For the Jerusalem Synod refuted the Pseudo-apostles: the Nicene, Arius: the Constantinopolitan, Macedonius and Eunomius: the Ephesian, Nestorius: the Chalcedonian, Eutyches, by the Scriptures alone: so that Augustine wrote no less truly than brilliantly: Let us not bring deceitful scales, where we may weigh what we wish, according to our own will, saying: This is heavy, this is light: but let us bring the divine scale from the holy Scriptures, as from the Lord's Treasuries, and on it, let us weigh what is heavier. Which sentiment Gratian cites in Canon Law, Causa 24, quest. 1, Can. 21.

The third argument is as follows: In the doctrine of faith, both in explaining it and in refuting it against heresies, the example of Christ and the Apostles must be uniquely imitated.

And yet both Christ and the Apostles, in the doctrine of faith, both in explaining it and in refuting it against heresies, used only the testimonies of the holy Scriptures. Therefore, this example of theirs should be imitated today most of all.

The major premise is self-evident: For whom should we follow either more rightly or more safely than Christ, of whom it is written: Hear him: Likewise: He who follows me does not walk in darkness: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Moreover, that the theological actions of the Apostles are to be uniquely imitated by us, both in teaching and in refutation: even that Pauline precept confirms, 1 Cor. 11:1, Be imitators of me, just as I am of Christ.

Hardly anyone will deny the minor premise, unless he is ignorant that Christ, in his disputes with the Pharisees, repeatedly called them back to Scripture: Have you not read in Moses? Is it not written in your law? How do you read? etc.

The fourth argument, taken from the recent Ratisbon Colloquy, is as follows: In matters of faith, religion, and worship, that alone is not only to be acknowledged as the norm, but also most rightly sustains the role of judge, which suffers neither addition nor subtraction.

And yet the written Word of God alone suffers neither addition nor subtraction in matters of faith, religion, and worship.

Therefore, the written Word of God alone is not only to be acknowledged as the norm, but also most rightly sustains the role of judge.

The adversaries themselves concede the major premise. But the minor, which they deny, is confirmed by all those testimonies by which GOD most severely prohibited that anything be either added to or subtracted from His Word, Deut. 4:2, and chap. 5:32, and chap. 12:32, Prov. 30:6, Ezek. 20:18. Moreover, it is clearly frivolous and trifling what the Jesuits object, that this prohibition concerned only the people and private persons. For such a distinction based on persons is nowhere found in the Scriptures, but since it speaks indefinitely and universally, it is most rightly concluded that all men of all orders and times, and therefore not only the people, but also the Magistrate and the Priests: not only private, but also public persons, are bound by this prohibition.

Nor does it infringe upon the firmness of this argument of ours that, in the passage of time, many books were added to the law of Moses, both in the Old and in the New Testament. For it is not to be thought that on account of this any new worship or new dogma of faith and religion was added to them. Since in those additions, the prior dogmas concerning the Messiah and the promise of the Seed of the woman, already published long ago, are partly repeated, partly illustrated, and partly more fully confirmed, and that not by the will and pleasure of men, but of GOD himself, who would not have been bound to those precepts in the least, even if He had added some new worship or new dogma. Thus, even if in the New Testament certain forms of worship, such as the Levitical, were abrogated: yet it does not follow that any subtraction against the will of GOD occurred to the written Word of GOD. For GOD himself did not wish those Levitical forms of worship, being typical, to be perpetual: but he wished them to endure only until Christ himself, whom they foreshadowed, should be exhibited.

The fifth argument, taken from the same Colloquy, can be formulated thus: If GOD so refers the Jews to the Law and to the Testimony, that is, to the Written Word, that he simultaneously declares that those who have not spoken according to this Word will not see the morning light: it follows ἐξ ἀνάγκης (of necessity) that the Written Word is the sole Norm in matters pertaining to faith and Religion: and consequently that it is the infallible Judge of controversies of the Christian Religion. But the former is true, from Isaiah chapter 8, verse 20. Therefore the latter is also true.

The connection of the major premise is evident from this, that according to the LAW is nothing else than ACCORDING TO THE NORM of this Law. Now because in all matters of faith and religion and worship, GOD wills that only the Law and the Testimony be heeded, and indeed under an added grave threat: it would certainly follow that there was no cause of religion, nor could one have been given, in which they were not bound to the Law and to the Testimony. And therefore it is most false that there were certain causes which ought to have been judged OUTSIDE the Law and OUTSIDE the written testimony, as the Jesuits contend.

Nor is the exception of the trifling adversaries worth a farthing, that according to the Law is not the same as expressed in the Law. For every decision which had to be made according to the Law, even if it was not expressed in the Law in so many words, was nevertheless so founded in it that it could be deduced and confirmed from the Law itself.

The sixth argument of our theologians was as follows: If all constitutions and reformations of religious exercises pleasing to God, instituted in the time of the Old Testament, were undertaken from the written Word of God ALONE, or according to that ALONE: then that written Word was certainly the unique, total, most perfect, and most exact norm of religion and faith: and consequently also the Judge of controversies of the Christian religion.

But the former is true, therefore the latter.

The major premise having been conceded by the adversaries themselves: our theologians confirm the minor by an induction of examples and an enumeration of the exercises and reformations which pious kings undertook, such as David, 1 Chron. 16:40, where he commanded the priests to offer burnt offerings according to all that is written in the law of the Lord: likewise Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 17:9 and 10; Hezekiah, 2 Chron. 30:5 and 31:2; Josiah, 2 Chron. 34:21 and 2 Kings 22:13; Zerubbabel, Nehemiah, Joshua the priest, and Ezra the scribe, Ezra 2:2, Neh. 8. Now since the conclusion rests upon a legitimate induction, and no dissimilar example is found in the sacred writings: the conclusion will certainly retain its invincible certainty and truth, which the Jesuits will not infringe upon until they have shaken it by the instance of a contrary example: a thing which, however, they have not been able to perform thus far, nor will they ever perform. The collection of this argument is indeed so evident that the Jesuits find nothing to object, except for that childish quibble: That, forsooth, it is one thing to institute a reformation from the written Word alone, but another to look to the written Word alone in a reformation already instituted. This objection would possess some appearance of truth if the Jesuits could demonstrate that the said kings and princes, in the reformations they instituted, undertook or ordained even the least thing apart from and beyond the written Word of God, which directly concerns the very worship of God or the dogmas of faith. While they cannot show this, the vanity of this distinction collapses of its own accord. Furthermore, these two phrases, when weighed more accurately, clearly coincide and yield the same sense. For he who institutes a reformation FROM the written Word of God ALONE, and ACCORDING to that alone: he certainly looks to nothing else in the undertaking and directing of that very reformation of his than to the written Word of God alone. For if it were otherwise, then it could not be said that the reformation was instituted from the written Word of God ALONE. And again, if those pious reformers had looked to another norm: then they would certainly not have undertaken their reformations from the written Word of God ALONE, and according to that ALONE.

But a certain one of the Jesuits (Tanner) clamors that Queen Esther and Mordecai instituted the feast of Purim or Lots; that Christ himself sanctioned the feast of Dedication, John 10:22, formerly instituted by the Maccabees, 1 Maccab. 4. Yet no commandment for any of these is found in divine writ. Therefore, even by this one instance given, this whole argument collapses.

I reply that a fallacy of ignorance of the refutation (παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχου) is being committed. For the question and controversy is about those things which concern divine worship and the dogmas of faith: whether in these one must stand precisely by the written Word of God alone: which we constantly affirm. Now, however, the adversary objects in the place of an instance the sanction of those feasts, which concerned the worship of God not at all, but were of most free observance, for the reason that they were neither instituted by God's command, nor instituted under any necessity. Such feasts it is indeed permitted for the Church to institute for pious causes: and it is fitting to observe them once instituted, lest occasion be given for schism. Where, however, one must always distinguish most accurately between the thanksgiving which is rendered to God on days of such feasts, and the circumstance of time: the former is of divine precept, and consequently of necessity; the latter, however, is free and clearly indifferent (ἀδιάφορον).

The seventh and final argument, which was proposed in the third place by our side in the Colloquy, was as follows:

He who reproves and punishes all those who depart from the written Word of GOD with whatever intention, and turns aside either to the right or to the left: by this very fact he clearly testifies that the written Word ought to be the sole Norm, and consequently also the sole Judge, to which all worship ought to be conformed, and every religion or dogma ought to be examined and judged. But God in the Old Testament reproved and punished all those who departed from his written Word with whatever intention, and turned aside either to the right or to the left, and by this fact repeated so many times, GOD clearly testified that the written Word ought to be the sole Norm and judge of religion and worship.

Regarding the major proposition of this argument, in order to press the adversaries more strongly, this should be noted: that not only those were reproved and punished by GOD who turned aside from the Law by TRANSGRESSING it with an act openly contrary: but also those who departed from the written Word, in any way, and with whatever intention, so that outside of that Word they attempted or innovated something in matters of faith and worship, in whatever guise or manner that might be done.

The evidence of the minor is proved by an induction of the examples of Jeroboam, 1 Kings 12:28; Gideon, Judges 8:27; the mother of Micah, Judges 17:3; Saul, 1 Samuel 13:9, 11, 13, and chapter 15:19, 22, etc.

Latin:

IV. PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

SCriptura Sacra sola atq; una, est Judex infallibilis omnium Controversiarum, quæ circa capita Religionis Christianæ, vel unquam sunt obortæ, vel oboriri possunt: Quatenus videlicet ea nihil est, aliud quàm vox supremi Judicis Spiritus Sancti, quem omnes agnoscere, timere ac venerari, cōvenit.

CONFIRMATIO.

TRadunt Logici esse Genus quoddam Homonymorum, quod Aristoteles lib. 2. de Ortu & Interitu, κῂ τὸ πρότερον καὶ ὕστερον appellat. Aliàs verò πρὸς ἓν ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς significantia Homonyma dicuntur. In his significatis, quoddam est Principale, & respectu cujus reliqua esse intelliguntur. Quanquam idem Philosophus lib. 7 Metaphysicorum, Genus istud vocabulorum non censet appellandum esse vel Homonymum, vel Synonymum, propterea, quòd in his neque Unum, neque Multa simpliciter significentur: sed Multa quædam, πρὸς ἓν principale quoddam illa ipsa referendo.

In censum numerumq; istorum vocabulorum referendum etiam est vocabulum (Judicis) quo in hac disputatione uti solemus : ita quidem, ut jam in suprema, jam in secundaria, jam in infima significatione multis accommodetur; quæ tamen ad unum principale referuntur. In suprema enim & principali significatione Judicem omnium Controversiarum, quæ unquam vel ortæ sunt, vel oriri possunt, statuimus esse solum DEUM Spiritum Sanctum, cujus afflatu ac impulsu locuti sunt & scripserunt Sancti DEI homines, uti habet Petrus 2. Pet. 1. 21 & D. Paulus 2. Tim. 3, 16. Omnis Scriptura divinitùs est inspirata. Jam verò, quatenùs hic ipse DEUS Spiritus Sanctus, non nisi ἐμμέσως, Mediatè, nempé per Verbum scriptum sententiam decisivam profert: eatenùs jam, sed in secundaria significatione Verbum hoc DEI, est & dicitur Judex Cōtroversiarum: Quo sensu Apostolus loco jam citato ex 2 Tim. 3, 16. affirmat, Omnem Scripturam divinitùs inspiratam, esse utile etiam πρὸς ἔλεγχόν, redargutionem sive refutationē, nempe omnium hærefeων. Quod ipsum evidenter confirmat illud Servatoris Johan. 12, 48. Qui rejicit me: nec accipit Verba mea, habet qui JVDICET ipsum: SERMO quem locut 9 sum, ille judicabit eum in novissimo die. Et hoc ipsum est, de quo â DEO ipso monemur, dum ad Legem & ad Testimonium ej9 unicè remittimur, additâ hac comminatione, Quod si non sentiamus & loquamur juxta Legem hanc, non visuri simus lucem matutinam. Jes. 8, 20. Quo pertinet illustris planè Aphorismus ille Epistolæ ad Hæbræos cap. 4, 12.

Vivum est Verbum DEI & efficax, & penetrantius quovis gladio ancipiti, ac pertingit usq; ad divisione animae simul ac spiritus, cōpagumq́; & medullarum, & DIiUDICAT cogitationes & conceptiones cordis, κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων, καὶ ἐννοιῶν καρδίας. Præterea Christus & Apostoli tùm in concionibus, tùm disputationibus suis cum hæreticis ad scripturas semper provocarunt : suo exemplo veram illam πρᾶξιν Theologicam commonstrantes, quâ utendum sit in dijudicandis Controversiis, ut nimirum ex Libris & Scripturis Canonicis Spiritus omnes, hoc est, tùm Doctores ipsi, tùm doctrinæ quælibet, singulǽque Controversiæ, tanquam ad Lydium lapidem examinentur, probentur, dijudicentur.

Cæterùm cùm Judicium Scripturæ de singulis Quæstionibus Controversis, non cuivis statim sit obvium: ideò Spiritus Sanctus utitur ministerio Ecclesiæ, hoc est, fidelium, qui dono Interpretationis præditi, Judicium illud, in Scriptura quasi reconditum, eruere possunt. Sūt verò hi ipsi fideles in eo discrimine positi, ut alii sint publici, alii privati.

Publicos appellamus illos Doctores & Ministros Ecclesiæ, quibus Docendi munus publicum legitimè est concreditum ac demandatum. Horum certè proprium munus atque officium est, non modò sanam proponere doctrinam: sed & aliorum dogmata dijudicare.

Privatum verò Judicem nominamus quemlibet Christianum fidelem, cui animæ suæ salus curę est. Nam & his à Christo dictum : Cavete à Pseudoprophetis Matth. 7, 15. à Paulo verò & Johanne injunctum, ut omnia probent, Quod bonum est, teneant: neq; cuilibet spiritui credant: Sed probent spiritus, num ex DEO sint. 1. Thess. 5, 21. 1. Joh. 4, 1. Cæterum, cùm neque privatorum istorum, neque publicorum illorum immensa sit potestas: hoc est, neque prætoria aliqua autoritas, neque absolutum aut indeterminatum illis concessum sit Arbitrium: Sed judicando errare non modò possint, verùm etiam errent sæpissimè: ideò determinatum tantùm ac limitatum Judicium ipsis competit, quatenus nimirum illud cum norma Scripturæ sacræ ex amussi congruit: ac proindè Judicis etiam vox atq; appellatio in infimo gradu illis tribuitur: uno interim supremo manente Judice, Spiritu Sancto, in & per Scripturas loquente.

Efflagitat autem ipsa Quæstionis hujus gravitas, ut hanc ipsam thesin sive assertionem nostram firmis confirmemus argumentis. Primum proinde esto istud:

Cuicunque soli conveniunt omnes notæ, κριτήρια atque requisita, quæ à Supremo & infallibili Judice vel maximè exiguntur: illi etiam hoc Jus atque elogium propriè ac unicè competit. Atqui soli Spiritui Sancto conveniunt notæ, κριτήρια atq; requisita illa &c. Ergò huic etiam soli jus atque elogium Judicis Supremi atq́; infallibilis competit.

Majoris certitudo extra Controversiam apud ipsos etiam Adversarios est posita.

Minoris autem evidentia patet ex plena ac sufficienti enumeratione eorum requisitorum, quæ summo ac infallibili dogmatum & interpretationum Judici maximè sunt necessaria, quorum 1. est, ut errare judicando non possit : ac proinde in illius sententiâ ac judicio citra omnem hæsitationem partes litigantes acquiescere possint. 2. Ut ab illius sententiâ nemini provocare liceat. 3. Ut non ipsemet sit pars litigantium sive Controversiæ. 4. Ut nullo partium studio ducatur, & ab omni πρωσωποληψίᾳ sit alienissimus. 5. Ut sua autoritate compellere possit transgressores ad jus & fas, ut sententiæ, sive decisioni stent, quemadmodum Jesuvvita Tannerus loquitur in Colloquio Ratisbonensi : Protocoll. p. 273.

Jam verò κριτήρια isthæc neque Ecclesiæ, neque Pontifici, neque Patribus, neque Conciliis neque ulli mortalium : Sed soli Spiritui Sancto conveniunt: ut infrà parte altera ἀνθετικῇ ad oculum demonstrabitur. Ergò huic etiam soli supremi ac infallibilis Judicis appellatio atque elogium competit.

Secundum Argumentum tale esse potest : Cujus Judicis voce atq; autoritate, singulæ atq; universæ hæreses sunt oppressæ & refutatæ : ille pro ectò summus atq; infallibilis Judex sit, necesse est. Atqui verò singulæ universæ in Ecclesiâ hæreses anteactis temporibus, non nisi voce & autoritate Spiritus Sancti, per Scripturas Sacras sententiam definitivam pronunciantis fuerunt repressæ. Ergò &c.

Major propositio rursus apud ipsos Jesuvvitas est certa ac indubia.

Minorem probo, 1. quidem exemplo hæreseωs Ebionitarum, blasphemantium, Christum non esse verum DEUM, neq; ante Mariam extitisse. Quæ sanè hæresis solo Evangelio Johannis sufficientissimè est refutata & eversa, sine ulla aliâ præsuppositâ autoritate, & sine ullis traditionibus aliis. Deindè constat Majoris veritas autoritate antiquissimorum Patrum, qui summâ consensione docent, ex scripturis solis, tanquam voce Spiritus Sancti, & hæreses damnandas, & omnes de Religione Controversias definiendas esse. Ubi perquàm memorabile est, quod Constantinus Imp. Patres Niceni Concilii hortatus est, ut, cum Evangelici atq; Apostolici libri, & Veterum Prophetarum oracula, nos perspicuè doceant, quid de divinis sentire oporteat. ἐκ τῶν θεοπνεύσων λόγων, hoc est, ex divinitus inspiratis sermonibus, sumant explicationem eorum, quæ in Quæstionem vocantur. Theodoretius lib. 1. cap. 6. Sic Augustinus Epist. 163. Legitimæ disputationis formam præscribens, id imprimis monet, ut Codices Canonici præstò sint: Ita enim rem posse ad inquisitionis terminum perduci. Et lib. 2. cap. 33. de nupt. & Conc. sic scribit : Istæ Controversiæ Judicem requirunt : Judicet ergò Christus : Judicet cum illo & Apostolus Paulus, quia & in Apostolo ipso loquitur Christus.

Tum probo Minorem Exemplis & praxi, semper in Ecclesia Catholicâ usitatâ. Nam testis est historia Ecclesiastica, Regulam illam Constantini Imp. observatam fuisse, non modò in Concilio illo Niceno contra Arium: sed eandem deinceps etiam valuisse in omnibus piis conciliis, adversis quosvis hæreticos congregatis. Nam & Hierosolymitana Synodus Pseudoapostolos: Nicena Arium: Constantinopolitana Macedonium atque Eunomium: Ephesina Nestorium: Chalcedonensis Eutychetem, solis Scripturis refutavit: ut non minus verè quam præclarè scripserit Augustinus: Non afferamus stateres dolosas, ubi appendamus, quod volumus, quo arbitrio nostro, dicentes: Hoc grave est, hoc leve est: sed afferamus divinam stateram de Scripturis sacris, tanquam de Thesawris Dominicis, & in illa, quid sit gravius, appendamus. Quam sententiam in jure Canonico citat Gratianus Causa 24. quæst. 1. Can. 21.

Tertium argumentum sic habet: In fidei doctrina tum explicanda, tùm adversus hæreses refutanda, Christi & Apostolorum Exemplum unicè imitandum fuerit.

Atqui & Christus, & Apostoli in doctrinâ fidei tùm explicanda, tùm adversus hæreses refutanda, solis sacrarum Scripturarum testimoniis sunt usi. Ergò hoc ipsorum exemplum hodieq́ vel maximè fuerit imitandum.

Major est ἀυτόπιστος: Quem enim vel rectius, vel tutius sequamur, quàm Christum, de quo scriptum est: Hunc audite: Item: Qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris: Ego sum via, veritas & vita. Apostolorum autem πράξεων Theologicam nobis unicè esse imitandam, quâ διδασκαλίαν, quâ ἔλεγχον: vel illud præceptum Paulinum confirmat, 1. Cor. 11, 1. Imitatores mei estote, sicuti ego Christi.

Minorem vix negabit quisquam, nisi qui ignorat Christum suis in disputationibus cum Pharisæis, subindè ad Scripturam eos revocasse: An non legistis in Mose? Nonne scriptum est in lege vestra? Quomodo legis? &c.

Quartum Argumentum ex Colloquio nupero Ratisbonensi desumtum, tale est: In rebus fidei, Religionis & cultuum, id tantùm non modò pro norma est agnoscendum, sed & judicis partes rectis simè sustinet, quod nec additionem, nec detractionem patitur.

Atqui solum DEI Verbum scriptum, nec additionem, neque detractionem in rebus fidei, Religi onis & cultuum patitur.

Ergò solum DEI Verbum scriptum, non modò pro Norma est agnoscendum, sed & judicis partes rectissimè sustinet.

Majorem concedunt ipsi Adversarii. Minorem autem, quam negant, confirmant universa illa testimonia, quibus severissimè DEUS prohibuit, ne quid Verbo suo vel addatur, vel detrahatur, Deut. 4, 2. & cap. 5, 32. & cap. 12, 32. Prov. 30, 6. Ezech. 20, 18. Frivolum autem & nugatorium planè est, quod Jesuitæ oggerunt, prohibiprohibibitionem istam tantùm populum & personas privatas spectasse. Nam talis distinctio ratione personarum in Scripturis nuspiam invenitur, sed cùm indefinitè ac universaliter illa loquatur, utique omnes etiam omnium ordinum ac temporum homines, ac proindè non populum modò, sed & Magistratum atq; Sacerdotes: non privatas tantúm, sed & publicas personas, hac prohibitione obligari, rectissimè colligitur.

Neque etiam argumenti hujus nostri firmitatem infringit, quod progressu temporis ad legem Mosis accesserunt plurimi libri tùm in Veteri, tùm in Novo Testamento. Neque enim propterea ipsis dogmatis fidei atque Religionis novum aliquem cultum, sive novum dogma accessisse existimandum est. Siquidem in additamentis illis priora tantùm dogmata de Messia, & promissione Seminis mulieris jam pridem edita, partim repetuntur, partim illustrantur, partim fusiùs confirmantur, idque non hominum, sed ipsius DEI voluntate ac arbitrio, qui ad præcepta illa minimè fuisset alligatus, si vel maximè novum aliquem cultum, novumque dogma addidisset. Sic etsi in Novo Testamento quidam cultus, utpote Levitici, sunt abrogati: non tamen ideo Verbo DEI scripto detractio aliqua contra DEI voluntatem accidit. Siquidem DEUS ipse cultus illos Leviticos, quippe typicos, noluit esse perpetuos: sed eò usque durare voluit, donec Christus ipse, quem adumbrarunt, esset exhibitus.

Quintum argumentum ex eodem Colloquio petitum, sic informari potest: Si DEUS Judæos ita remittit ad Legem & ad Testimonium, hoc est, ad Verbum Scriptum, ut simul enunciet, non visuros lucem matutinam, qui non dixerint juxta Verbum hoc: sequitur ἐξ ἀνάγκης, Verbum Scriptum esse Normam unicam, in rebus ad fidem & Religionem pertinentibus: ac per consequens infallibilem esse Judicem Controversiarum Religionis Christianæ. At verum prius, ex cap. 8, 20. Jesaiæ. Verum Ergò & posterius.

Connexum Majoris vel indè evidenter patet, quod juxta LEGEM, nihil est aliud, quàm JUXTA NORMAM hujus Legis. Jam quia in omnibus rebus fidei & Religionis & cultus, vult DEUS tantùm attendi Legem & Testimonium, & quidem sub addita gravi comminatione: Consequens utique fuerit, nullam fuisse, vel etiam dari potuisse causam religionis, in qua non ad Legem & ad Testimonium fuerint alligati. Ac proinde falsissimum esse, quòd causæ quædam fuerint, quæ EXTRA Legem & EXTRA testimonium scriptum, dijudicari debuerint, uti Jesuitæ contendunt.

Neque unius est teruntii Exceptio Adversariorum nugantium, JUXTA Legem non idem esse, quod expressum in Lege. Omnis enim decisio, quæ juxta Legem fieri debebat etsi non totidem verbis, in Lege expressa erat: in eâ tamen sic extabat fundata, ut ex ipsamet Lege deduci & confirmari possit.

Sextum Argumentum nostrorum Theologorum fuit tale: Si omnes Exercitiorum Religionis constitutiones & reformationes DEO placentes, tempore Veteris Testamenti institutæ, ex SOLO Verbo Dei scripto, vel secundum illud SOLUM fuerunt susceptæ: fuit utiq; Verbum illud scriptum unica, totalis, perfectissima & exactissima norma Religionis & fidei: ac proinde Judex etiam Controversiarum Religionis Christianæ.

At verò prius Verum, Ergò & posterius.

Majore ab ipsis Adversariis concessâ: Minorem nostrates Theologi confirmant inductione Exemplorum, & enumeratione exercitiorum & reformationum, quas susceperunt pii Reges, ut Davidis 1. Par. 16, 40. Ubi præcepit Sacerdotibus, ut offerrent holocautomata Juxta omnia, quæ in lege Domini scripta sunt: Item Josaphati. 2. Paral. 17, 9. & 10 Ezechiæ 2. Par. 30, 5. & 31, 2. Josiæ. 2. Par. 34, 21. & 2. Reg. 22, 13. Zorobabelis, Nehemiæ, Josuæ Sacerdotis, & Esdræ legisperiti, Esdræ 2, 2. Nehem. 8. Jam quia conclusio nititur legitimâ inductione, neque aliud dissimile exemplum in sacris reperitur: utique constabit Conclusioni sua invicta certitudo & veritas: quam haud prius infringent Jesuvvitæ, quàm per instantiam contrarii Exempli illam labefactarint: id quod tamen hactenus præstare non potuerunt, neque unquam præstabunt. Est verò argumenti hujus Collectio usque adeò evidens, ut, quod Jesuvvitæ obvertant, non inveniant, præter puerile illud cavillum, Quod nimirum, Aliud sit ex solo Verbo scripto Reformationem instituere: Aliud verò in institutâ Reformatione ad solum Verbum scriptum respicere. Quod objectum speciem aliquam Veri obtineret tùm, si Jesuvvitæ demonstrare possent, dictos Reges ac Principes in institutis Reformationibus vel minimum citra & præter Verbum DEI scriptum suscepisse aut ordinasse, quod quidem ipsum cultum DEI, sive dogmata fidei directè respiciat. Quod dum monstrare non possunt, ultrò corruit distinctionis huj9 vanitas. Deinde, duæ istæ phrases accuratiùs expensæ, planè concidunt, eundemque sensum pariunt. Qui enim EX SOLO Verbo DEI scripto, & SECUNDUM illud Solum, Reformationem instituit: is utiq; in illa ipsa sua Reformatione suscipienda & dirigenda, ad nihil aliud, quàm ad solum scriptum DEI Verbum respicit. Nam si secus esset, tùm non dici posset, Ex SOLO Verbo DEI scripto, Reformationem esse institutam. Et rursus, si ad aliam Normam pii illi Reformatores respexissent: utique jam non ex SOLO Verbo DEI scripto, & secundum illud SOLUM, Reformationes suas suscepissent.

Sed obstrepit quidam ex Jesuvvitis (Tannerus) Reginam Esther, & Mardochæum instituisse festum Purim sive Sortium: Christum ipsum sanxisse festum Encæniorum Joh. 10, 22. olim à Macchabæis institutum 1. Macchab. 4. Quorum tamen nullum præceptum in divinis habeatur. Ergò vel unâ data hac instantiâ, corruere totum hoc argumentum.

Respondeo committi Sophisma παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε. Quæstio enim est & Controversia de illis rebus, quæ cultum divinum & dogmata fidei concernunt: An in istis solo Dei Verbo scripto præcisè sit standum: id quod constanter affirmamus. Jam verò Adversarius illorum festorum sanctionem Instantiæ loco obvertit, quæ cultum DEI nihil quicquam attinebant, sed liberrimæ erant observationis, propterea, quòd neque DEI mandato erant instituta, neque sub aliqua necessitate instituta. Qualia fanè Festa ob causas pias instituere licet Ecclesiæ: & sic instituta observare convenit, ne Schismati detur occasio. Ubi tamen semper accuratissimè distingvendum inter gratiarum actionem, quæ diebus hujusmodi festis, DEO persolvuntur, & inter circumstantiam temporis: Illud præcepti divini est, ac proindè necessitatis: Hoc verò liberum & planè ἀδιάφορον.

Septimum & postremum argumentum, quod in Colloquio à nostris tertio loco proponebatur, tale erat:

Qui reprehendit & punit eos omnes, qui à scripto DEI Verbo quacunq; intentione recedunt, & vel ad dextram, vel ad sinistram deflectunt: Is hoc ipso facto perspicuè testatur, Scriptum Verbum debere esse unicã Normam, & per Consequens etiam unicum Judicem, ad quem cultus omnis conformari, & Religio sive dogma quodvis exigi, dijudicariq́; debeat. Atqui Deus in Veteri Testamento reprehendit & punivit eos omnes, qui à scripto suo Verbo quacunq́; intentione recesserunt, & vel ad dextram vel ad sinistram deflexerunt, & hoc facto toties iterato, perspicuè DEUS testatus est, Scriptum Verbum esse debere unicam Normam ac judicem Religionis & cultuum.

Argumenti hujus Major propositio, ut fortius premat Adversarios, illud monendum fuerit: Non eos solùm esse reprehensos à DEO & punitos, qui à Lege deflexerunt TRANSGREDIENDO illam facto palàm contrario: Sed & eos, qui à Verbo scripto, quocunque modo, & quacunque tandem intentione sic recesserunt, ut extra Verbum illud, aliquid in rebus fidei & cultus attentarent, aut innovarent, quacunque etiam specie aut ratione illud fieret.

Minoris evidentia probatur Inductione exemplorum Jeroboami, 1. Reg. 12, 28. Gedeonis. Judic. 8, 27. Matris Michæ. Judic. 17, 3. Saulis 1. Sam. 13, 9, 11, 13. & cap. 15, 19, 22. &c.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Second Part Antithetical. Proposition I

PROPOSITION I. JESUITICAL.

The interpretation of Scripture, or the Spirit of interpreting the Scriptures, although it is often granted to many private men: yet it is certainly and infallibly found in the Church:

that is, in a Council of Bishops, confirmed by the supreme pastor of the whole Church: or in the supreme Pastor, with a Council of other pastors.

Ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστική

Bellarmino set forth this proposition in exactly the same words in book 3 of his work on the Written Word of God, chapter 3, page 172 D, the meaning of which is this: that Scripture is not to be interpreted otherwise than as Councils have interpreted it, yet not all of them, but only those which have been confirmed by the Roman Pontiff, whom he himself names the supreme Pastor of the Church: or, as the Jesuit explains himself a little more openly shortly after, that the interpretation of Scripture rests with the Roman Pontiff alone, without whose approval or confirmation not even the interpretation of Councils would be valid. The Jesuit Costerus sets this same thing forth at great length in his Enchiridion, pages 133, 134. The Jesuit admits, however, that this opinion is held in the Council of Trent, session 4. Decree 2, which is as follows: Furthermore, to restrain petulant minds, the same holy Synod decrees that no one, relying on his own prudence in matters of faith and morals pertaining to the edification of Christian doctrine, twisting the Holy Scripture to his own senses, should dare to interpret the Holy Scripture itself against that sense which holy mother Church has held and holds, whose it is to judge of the true sense and interpretation of the holy Scriptures, or even against the unanimous consent of the Fathers, even if such interpretations were never at any time to be published. Let those who contravene this be declared by the Ordinaries and punished with the penalties established by Law. So far the words of the Tridentine Decree, whose authority among the Romanists was so great that they claimed for their Church, that is, for the Roman Pontiff, the interpretation of Scripture as a kind of royal prerogative and no small part of their competent Law: so much so that if anyone had an interpretation of the Roman Church concerning some passage of Scripture, even if he neither knows nor understands whether or how it agrees with the words of Scripture, he nevertheless has the very Word of GOD: just as Cardinal Hosius was not ashamed to write in his book on the express Word of GOD. The Jesuit Thyræus of Mainz, in chapter 15 of the third part of his disputation on Ecclesiastical power, did not shudder to establish this detestable impiety not long ago, writing: Holy Scripture does not have this power, that we should seek a definition and opinion from it itself. Scripture was not always in the Catholic Church: and yet there was always the faculty of deciding what is to be thought concerning controversies of faith.

But it will be necessary to examine more accurately with what impostures in part, and with what abominations in part, this first Jesuitical proposition is burdened. And at the beginning, that notable fraud, deceit, and cunning which the Fathers of the Council of Trent concealed under that Decree, and which the Jesuits are accustomed to conceal even today, comes under consideration. For first, when they write and decree: That no one should rely on his own prudence: that no one in matters of faith and morals pertaining to the edification of Christian doctrine should twist the Holy Scripture to his own senses: that no one should interpret Scripture against that sense which holy mother Church has held and holds, whose it is to judge of the true sense and interpretation of the Holy Scriptures: this limitation should be added: If the Church has not erred in judging. When, I say, they amplify these things with magnificent words, they strive to burden our Churches with notable injury and suspicion. For because we teach that the Word of GOD must be followed, and that it is lawful for any believer to bring an interpretation to the touchstone of the Scriptures, they try to persuade the simpler folk that we, by this reasoning, permit everyone to be wise in his own eyes, to rely on his own prudence, and, as Bellarmino speaks, that everyone should follow his own Spirit in the interpretation of the Scriptures: a thing which has never entered our minds, neither in fever nor in sleep. Wherefore, from this alone, a judgment can be made concerning the candor of our Adversaries.

The second part of the observation is that the Romanists speak too indefinitely and ambiguously when they assert that it rests with the Church to judge of the true sense and interpretation of the Scriptures. For, not to urge in this place that which we said in the thesis, that by the command of GOD it belongs not only to the Church but to all believers to judge of the interpretation of the Scriptures: this is especially to be noted in this place, that since the Church is twofold: the True and the false or that of the malignant: they speak indiscriminately, and do not clearly explain which Church they mean. For if they mean the True one, we certainly subscribe to their opinion willingly, in the sense in which it was said above in the thesis. But we define this to be that which hears only the voice of its Pastor, Christ: and does not deflect even a hair's breadth from His Word: according to that in John 10:5 and 27: My sheep hear my voice, they do not hear the voice of a stranger, but flee from him. And John 8:31: If you remain in my Word, and my Word remains in you, you will truly be my Disciples, and you will know the Truth. Now, however, because it is confessed that by the true and Catholic Church they understand only the Pontiff and the prelates of the Roman Synagogue, as those to whom the sense of Scripture is known and perfect through the revelation of the Holy Spirit: we affirm that they are clearly trifling and playing too craftily in a very serious matter: for it is necessary first that they prove that the Pontiff with his clergy is the True and Catholic Church, before they demonstrate that this or that sense of Scripture has been revealed by the Holy Spirit to the Pontiff and the Council.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO I. JESUVVITICA.

INterpretatio Scripturæ, sive Spiritꝰ interpretãdi Scripturas, etsi multis privatis hominibus sæpè conceditur: certò tamen & infallibiliter invenitur in Ecclesia:

hoc est, in Cōcilio Episcoporum, confirmato à summoEcclesiæ totius pastore: sive in summo Pastore, cum Concilio aliorum pastore.

Ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστική

PRopositionem hanc, iisdem planè verbis prodidit Bellarminus lib. 3. de Verbo Dei scripto. cap. 3. pag. 172. D. quorum hæc est sententia, Non aliter esse Scripturam interpretandam, quàm sicut Concilia eam interpretata sunt, nec tamen omnia, sed ea tantùm, quæ à Pontifice Romano, quem ipse summum Ecclesiæ Pastorem nominat, sunt confirmata: vel ut apertiùs paulò pòst semetipsum explicat Jesuvvita, Scripturæ interpretationem penes unum Pontificem Romanum esse, sine cujus approbatione sive confirmatione, nec Conciliorum quidem valeat interpretatio. Quod ipsum prolixè admodum proponit Jesuvvita Costerus in Enchirid. pag. 133. 134. Fatetur autem Jesuvvita, haberi hanc sententiam in Concilio Tridentino. sess. 4. Decreto 2. quod sic habet: Præterea ad coercenda petulantia ingenia decernit eadem Sactosancta (scilicet) Synodus, ut nemo suæ prudentiæ innixus in rebus fidei & morum, ad ædificationem doctrinæ Christianæ pertinentium, Sacram Scripturam ad suos sensus contorquens, contra eum sensum, quem tenuit, & tenet sancta mater Ecclesia, cujus est judicare de vero sensu & interpretatione Scripturarum sanctarum, aut etiam contra unanimem consensum Patrum, ipsam Scripturam sacram interpretari audeat: etiamsi hujusmodi interpretationes nullo unquam tempore in lucem edendæ forent. Qui contravenerint, per Ordinarios declarentur, & pœnis à Jure statutis puniantur. Hactenus Verba Decreti Tridentini, cujus tanta apud Romanenses fuit autoritas, ut suæ Ecclesiæ, hoc est, Pontifici Romano, tanquam Regale quoddam, & partem Juris competentis non postremam, vendicarent Scripturæ interpretationem: ita quidem, ut si quis haberet Romanæ Ecclesiæ de loco aliquo Scripturæ interpretationem, etiamsi nec sciat, nec intelligat, an aut quomodo cum Scripturæ verbis conveniat, eum tamen habere ipsissimum Verbum DEI: sicuti Hosium Cardinalem scribere non puduit, in libro de expresso DEI Verbo. Cujus detestandam impietatem haud ita pridem stabilire non exhorruit, Jesuvvita Thyræus Moguntinus. Cap. 15. partis tertiæ disputationis de potestate Ecclesiastica, scribens: Sacra Scriptura hanc potestatem non habet, ut ab ipsa definitionem & sententiam petamus. Non fuit semper in Ecclesia Catholica, Scriptura: & tamen fuit semper, de fidei controversiis quid sit sentiendum, facultas statuendi.

Cæterùm, quibus partim imposturis, partim abominationibus laboret propositio hæc prima Jesuvvitica, accuratiùs dispiciendum fuerit. Ac initiò quidem sub Considerationem venit, insignis illa fraus, dolus atque astutia, quam Patres Concilii Tridentini, sub Decreto isto occultarunt, & quam hodieque Jesuvitæ occultare solent. Primùm enim, quando scribunt & decernunt: Ut nemo suæ prudentiæ innitatur: ut nemo in rebus fidei & morum ad ædificationem doctrinæ Christianæ pertinentium, sacram Scripturam ad suos sensus contorqueat: ut nemo interpretetur scripturam contra eum sensum, quem tenuit & tenet sancta mater Ecclesia, cujus est judicare, de vero sensu & interpretatione Scripturarum Sacrarum: modò hæc addatur limitatio: Si Ecclesia in judicando non erraverit. Quando, inquam, magnificis verbis isthæc amplificant, insigni injuriâ ac suspicione prægravare student nostras Ecclesias. Quia enim docemus, Sequendum esse Verbum DEI, & cuilibet fideli fas esse, exigere interpretationem ad trutinam Scripturarum: illi persuadere conantur simplicioribus, nos hac ratione permittere, ut quisque apud semetipsum sapiat, prudentiæ suæ innitatur, & ut Bellarminus loquitur, In interpretatione Scripturarum quisque suum Spiritum sequatur: id quod nobis neque per febrim, neq; per somnum unquam in mentem venit. Quare vel inde de candore Adversariorum poterit fieri judicium.

Alterum observationis membrum est, quod Romanenses nimis indefinitè & ambiguè loquuntur, quando asserunt, penes Ecclesiam esse, judicare de vero sensu & interpretatione Scripturarum. Nam ut hoc loco non urgeamus id, de quo in thesi diximus, quod ex mandato DEI, non soli Ecclesiæ, sed omnibus fidelibus competat judicare de interpretatione Scripturarum: illud vel maximè hoc loco notandum, quòd cùm duplex sit Ecclesia: Vera & falsa sive malignantium: illi indistinctè loquuntur, & quamnàm Ecclesiam intelligant, haud disertè explicant. Nam si Veram intelligunt: nos certè ultrò sententiæ ipsorum subscribimus, eo sensu quo supra est dictum in thesi. Hanc autem definimus esse eam, quæ audit solummodò vocem Pastoris sui Christi: & ab ejus Verbo ne latum quidem pilum deflectit: secundum illud Joh. 10, 5. & 27. Oves meæ vocem meam audiunt, Alieni vocem non audiunt, sed fugiunt ab eo. Et Joh. 8, 31. Si manseritis in Sermone meo, & Sermo meus manserit in vobis: verè Discipuli mei eritis, & cognoscetis Veritatem. Jam verò, quia in Confesso est per Ecclesiam veram & Catholicam ipsos intelligere tantùm Pontificem & prælatos Romanæ Synagogæ, ut quibus sensus Scripturæ ex revelatione Spiritus Sancti sit cognitus & perfectus: nos manifestè ipsos nugari & in re admodum seriâ nimis veteratoriè ludere affirmamus: priús enim necesse est, probent: Pontificem cum suo clero, esse Veram ac Catholicam Ecclesiam, quàm demonstrent hunc vel illum Scripturæ sensum à Spiritu Sancto Pontifici & Concilio esse revelatum.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Reasons, why the Pope cannot be Judge of Controversies of Faith

Then it is permitted to inquire of the Jesuits, When the Roman Church interprets Scripture, by what means was it itself taught this very sense? From the Scriptures themselves, or from some Spirit without the Scriptures? If from the Scriptures alone, then it is necessary that they admit with us that the scriptures must be interpreted from the Scriptures alone: But if from the Spirit without the Scriptures, what else do they do than approve and defend the enthusiasms of the Anabaptists? Finally, that which that conventicle feigns, that the Church has such and so great authority that it can decide concerning the Scriptures and their sense according to its own pleasure and will: that betrays the abomination of the Roman Church too manifestly. For since, as the Apostle testifies, the Church is constituted on no other foundation than that of the Apostles and Prophets, of which Christ himself is the lowest cornerstone: it certainly ought to rely on this foundation alone, and build and place upon it every interpretation of Scripture. Therefore, when the Romanists suspend the sense of Scripture from the will and Decrees of the Church, what else do they do than impiously subject the Holy Spirit to the judgments of men? By which one means alone they see that they can easily prove all their dogmas, however impious and blasphemous. For if you say that they are contrary to the Scriptures, they immediately object that they have been sanctioned and approved by the Church: Just as Gregorius de Valentia, in his Treatise on the Mass, page 95, did not shudder to write: The chalice cannot be given to the laity according to Christ's Institution because of the contrary disposition of the Church. Thus, therefore, by these wicked deceits, they craftily delude both GOD and men.

But, that we may press Bellarmine more strongly, the question in this place comes chiefly to this: Can or ought the sense of Scripture to be tied to the interpretation of one man: just as the Romanists are accustomed to tie it today? For although he seems to require also the authority and consent of Councils: because, however, he himself immediately adds that Councils are not to be believed until they have been approved by the Pontiff: it remains, certainly, even from his own side, beyond doubt that the right of interpreting the Scriptures rests with the Pontiff alone. We, indeed, descend entirely into the Negative, relying on the following reasons.

For first, that we should seek and expect the interpretation of Scripture from a manifest and, as it were, sworn enemy of Scripture, who is as suited for this matter as an Ass is to the Lyre: would be clearly inconvenient. Which reason is indeed of the greater evidence, because Stapleton himself, in book 10, chapter 11 of his Doctrinal Principles, includes it among those cautions which are to be observed concerning an interpreter of Scripture.

Then, what assurance of faith can there be, if we must necessarily stand by the interpretation of him whom we have most firmly persuaded ourselves is that very great Antichrist? Therefore, the Jesuits are not only unjust, but they also manifestly betray their own diffidence when, in Colloquies and elsewhere, they expressly admit that they cannot prove their cause to us unless they refer everything to the judgment and interpretation of the Roman Pontiff, whom they know will pronounce nothing against them. Thirdly, the interpretation of one man can not only be suspect, but also in many ways erroneous, nay even heretical: Such are most of the interpretations of the Roman Pontiffs: as, Take, Eat, that is, you priests, celebrate private Masses: Drink of this all of you, that is, be only holy sacrificers, because I am holy; Therefore it is a sin for a Minister of the Word to take a wife in marriage: Do not give what is holy to dogs: Therefore the laity are to be kept away from the reading of Scripture: etc.

Fourthly, no one can safely acquiesce in the Pontiff's interpretation, because he did not shudder to write openly that the meaning of Scripture is mutable, various, unstable, and flexible according to the changes of times. For thus Nicolaus Cusanus, a Cardinal of the Roman Church, did not shudder to write to the Bohemians. Understand that the Scriptures are adapted to the time, and variously understood, so that at one time they are explained according to the current universal rite: when the rite is changed, the meaning is changed again. It is no wonder if the practice of the Church interprets Scripture in one way at one time, and in another way at another time.

Finally, that we may not go further, it is clearly false and absurd that the Gift of interpretation is so tied to the Roman Pontiff that one must simply stand by his judgment. The Apostle himself denies this, saying, To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom: to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit: To another prophecy (that is, the interpretation of Scripture), to another the discerning of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the Interpretation of languages: But one and the same Spirit works all these things, dividing to each as he wills. 1 Cor. 12, 8. and following. And the Savior himself, John 3, 8. The Spirit, he says, blows where he wills. Moreover, what we have now said about the Roman Pontiff: that must also be accepted concerning the Fathers and any Councils whatsoever. For as regards the Fathers, they themselves ingenuously admit that they are subject to error, both concerning themselves and others, as is to be seen in Augustine, who in book 2 to Vincent. he writes thus: I cannot deny, nor ought I, that in my greater works, as in so many of my little works, there are many things which can be blamed with just judgment and no rashness. A proof of this matter can be the books of Retractations written by the man himself. And memorable is the confession of St. Basil, writing thus of himself: We do not deny that we are subject to infinite errors, since we are men and live in the flesh. Irenaeus approved the error of the Chiliasts. Tertullian the heresy of Montanus, which is also condemned in him. Cyprian decreed that those baptized by heretics must be rebaptized. Jerome disapproved of second marriages, comparing them to fornication.

Moreover, they have diverse interpretations of the Scriptures: as Augustine interpreted the sixth chapter of John concerning sacramental eating, and from thence wished necessarily to prove that infants also ought to be admitted to the Holy Supper: which interpretation other of the Fathers disapproved; and they accepted that chapter concerning spiritual eating, which is done by faith, even outside the use of the Lord's Supper. Therefore, it is very rash that Bellarmine, together with the Council of Trent, refers us regarding the present question to the unanimous consent of the Fathers: For there is not found such great concord among the Fathers and writers of all ages that their unanimous consent can be demonstrated without any doubt: which not even the Fathers themselves attributed to their own writings: as can be seen in Distinction 9, Canon 10 of the Decree of Canon Law: Where Augustine speaks thus: We ought not to hold the disputations of any persons whatsoever, even though they be Catholic and praiseworthy men, as Canonical Scriptures, so that it is not permitted to us, without prejudice to the honor which is owed to those men, to disapprove and reject something in their writings, if by chance we find that they have thought otherwise than the truth holds, with divine assistance, either understood by others or by us. Such am I in the writings of others, as I wish readers to be in mine.

And although the Roman Church judges certain of the Fathers to be so worthy of a Canon that they decree it a sin to appeal from their authority: yet this very Canonization is null and void ipso facto: For as legal experts rightly define: No one can transfer more right to another than he himself possesses.

Furthermore, what a stupendous vertigo this is, that one must believe the Fathers, who disagree among themselves, more than the Scriptures, which agree with themselves most beautifully and most correctly everywhere?

But what need is there of many words? Since the Apostle permits not to certain specific Doctors of the Church, but to all Ministers and Doctors of the Church, that they should judge concerning every interpretation of the Scriptures from the very Word of God: Let the prophets (he says, meaning interpreters) speak two or three, and let the others judge: and if anything be revealed to another that sitteth by, let the first hold his peace. 1 Cor. 14:29 & 30.

Thus, as regards Councils, neither can we grant to them an infallible authority for interpreting the Scriptures. For that these also can err, and have erred most frequently in interpreting the Scriptures, is better known than to require laborious proof. An example of which matter can be that most holy Council of Nicaea, where three hundred and eighteen Bishops did not hesitate to yield to the appeal of Paphnutius alone. Whence Augustine himself also replied to Maximinus, the Bishop of the Arians, who was appealing to a Council: Neither ought you to produce the Council of Nicaea, nor I the Council of Ariminum, as if to prejudice the matter.

Moreover, by what arguments the Adversaries strive to confirm this proposition: it will have to be seen in the digression of the following second proposition, which has a great connection with this first one.

Latin:

Deindè percontari licet ex Jesuvvitis, Quando Ecclesia Romana interpretatur Scripturam, quonam pacto hunc ipsum sensum ipsa edocta fuerit? ex ipsisne Scripturis, an ex aliquo sine Scripturis Spiritu? Si ex solis Scripturis, tùm nobiscum fateantur necesse est, ex solis Scripturis interpretandas esse scripturas: Sin ex Spiritu sine Scripturis, quid aliud faciunt, quàm quòd Anabaptistarum Enthusiasmos approbant ac defendunt? Tandem, quod fingit conciliabulum illud, Ecclesiam habere talem ac tantam autoritatem ut pro suo libitu ac arbitrio, de Scripturis earundemque sensu statuere possit: id abominationem Ecclesiae Romanae nimis manifestè prodit. Nam cùm, teste Apostolo, Ecclesia non nisi in Apostolorum & Prophetarum fundamento sit constituta, cujus ipse Christus est lapis imus angularis: hoc utique solo fundamento ea niti, atque in eo omnem Scripturae interpretationem aedificare ac collocare debet. Proinde quando sensum Scripturae ab Ecclesiae arbitrio atque Decretis suspendunt Romanenses, Quid faciunt aliud, quàm quòd Spiritum Sanctum hominum Judiciis impiè subjiciunt? Quo vel uno pacto omnia sua dogmata, quantumvis impia & balsphema, probare se posse facilè vident. Nam si Scripturis ea adversari dicas mox illi oggerunt, ab Ecclesia esse illa sancita & approbata: Quemadmodum Gregorius de Valentia, Tractatu de Missa pag. 95. scribere non exhorruit: Laicis calix dari non potest juxta Christi Institutionem propter contrariam Ecclesiae dispositionem. Sic ergo nefandis istis praestigiis, & DEO & hominibus veteratoriè illudunt.

Verùm, ut fortius premamus Bellarminum, sub quaestionem hoc loco praecipuè venit, An sensus Scripturae possit aut debeat, ad unius hominis interpretationem alligari: quemadmodum hodiè Romanenses eum alligare solent? Etsi enim Conciliorum etiam autoritatem & consensum requirere videtur: quia tamen ipsemet statim subjungit, Conciliis haud prius credendum esse, quàm à Pontifice approbata fuerint? manet utiq; ex ipsius etiam parte indubium, penes solum Pontificem esse jus interpretandi Scripturas. Nos sanè in Negantem, sequentibus freti rationibus, omninò descendimus.

Primùm enim, ut à manifesto & quasi jurato Scripturae hoste, praecipuè hanc ad rem tàm apto, quàm est Asinus ad Lyram, Scripturae interpretationem petamus & expectemus: planè inconveniens fuerit. Quae sanè ratio eò majoris est evidentiae, quòd ipse Stapletonus lib. 10. cap. 11. Principiorum Doctrinalium, eam refert inter cautiones illas, quae circa Interpretem Scripturae sint observandae.

Deinde, Quae poterit esse πληροφορία fidei, si interpretatione illius standum nobis sit necessariò, quem ipsissimum esse Antichristum illum magnum, habemus persuasissimum. Proinde non modò iniqui sunt Jesuvvitae, sed & manifestè suam diffidentiam produnt, quando in Colloquiis & aliàs disertè fatentur, se non posse suam causam nobis probare, nisi ad Pontificis Romani Judicium & interpretationem omnia referant, quem contra se nihil quicquam pronunciaturum, noverunt. Tertio, Unius Hominis interpretatio non modò potest esse suspecta, sed & multis modis erronea, imò hæretica: Quales sunt pleræq; interpretationes Pontificum Romanorum: ut, Accipite, Comedite, hoc est, vos Sacerdotes, Missas privatas celebrate: Bibite ex hoc omnes, id est, Soli sacrificuli Sancti estote, quia ego Sanctus sum; Ergò nefas Ministro Verbi uxorem in matrimonium ducere: Nolite dare sanctum canibus: Ergò Laici à Scripturæ lectione arcendi sunt: &c.

Quartò, In Pontificis interpretatione, nemo tutò acquiefcere potest, quia palàm scribere non exhorruit, Scripturæ sententiam esse mutabilem, variam, instabilem, & secundum temporum mutationes esse flexibilem. Sic enim Nicolaus Cusanus, Ecclesiæ Romanæ Cardinalis ad Bohemos scribere non exhorruit. Intellige, Scripturas esse ad tempus adaptatas, & variè intellectas, ita ut uno tempore secundum currentem universalem ritum exponantur: mutato ritu, iterum sententia mutetur. Non mirum, si praxis Ecclesiæ uno tempore interpretetur Scripturam uno modo, & alio tempore, alio modo.

Tandem, ne longiùs abeamus falsum planè & absurdum est, Donum interpretationis ita ad Pontificem Romanum esse alligatum, ut simpliciter ipsius standum sit Judicio. Negat hoc ipse Apostolus, Alii, inquiens, datur per Spiritum, sermo sapientiæ: alii autem sermo scientiæ secundum eundem Spiritum: Alii prophetia (hoc est, interpretatio Scripturæ) alii discretio Spirituũ, alii genera lingvarum, alii Interpretatio Sermonum: Hæc autem operatur unus atq; idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult. 1. Cor. 12, 8. & seqq. Et Servator ipse Johan. 3, 8. Spiritus, inquit, spirat ubi vult. Cæterùm, quod de Pontifice Romano jam diximus: illud de Patribus quoque & Conciliis quibusvis accipi debet. Nam quoad Patres, Errori illos esse obnoxios, ipsi tùm de se tùm de aliis ingenuè fatentur, uti videre est apud Augustinum, qui libro 2. ad Vincent. sic scribit: Negare non possum, nec debeo, ficuti in ipsis Majoribq; ita multa esse in tàm multis opusculis meis, quæ possunt justo judicio & nullà temeritate culpari. Cujus rei documento esse possunt Retractationum libri ab ipsomet conscripti. Et memorabilis est D. Basilii confessio, sic de se scribentis: Non negamus nos infinitis erroribus subjectos esse, cum homines simus & in carne vivamus. Irenæy Chiliastarum errorem probavit. Tertullianus Montani hæresin, quæ & in ipso est damnata. Cyprianus ab hæreticis baptizatos rebaptizandos statuit. Hieronymus secundas nuptias improbavit, fornicationi conferens.

Quin diversas habent Scripturarum interpretationes: ut Augustinus caput Sextum Johannis interpretatus est de Sacramentali manducatione, & inde necessariò voluit evincere, Infantes quoq; ad Sacram Cœnam admittendos esse: Quam interpretationem alii ex Patribus improbarunt: & caput illud acceperunt, de Spirituali manducatione, quæ fit fide, etiam extra usum Cœnæ Dominicæ. Proinde perquàm temerarium est, quód Bellarminus unà cùm Concilio Tridentino, nos circa præsentem quæstionem remittit ad unanimem consensum Patrum : Neque enim in Patribus & Scriptoribus omnium seculorum tanta reperitur concordia, ut sine ullâ dubitatione unanimis ipsorum consensus possit demonstrari : quem ne ipsi quidem Patres suis scriptis tribuerunt : uti videre est Dist. 9. Can. 10. Decreti Juris Canonici: Ubi Augustinus sic loquitur: Neque quorumlibet disputationes, quamvis Catholicorum & Laudatorum hominum, velut Scripturas Canonicas habere debemus, ut nobis non liceat salva honorificentia, quæ illis debetur hominibus, aliquid in eorum scriptis improbare atque respuere, si fortè invenerimus, quod aliter senserint, quàm veritas habet, divino adjutorio, vel ab aliis intellecta, vel à nobis. Talis ego sum in scriptis aliorum, quales volo esse intellectores meorum.

Et quanquam Ecclesia Romana quosdam ex Patribus ita Canone dignos judicat, ut ab eorum autoritate provocare nefas esse statuant: tamen hæc ipsa Canonizatio ipso facto nulla est: Nam uti rectè Juris consulti definiunt. Nemo potest plus in alium transferre Juris, quam ipse habet.

Deinde quæ hæc stupenda est vertigo, magis credendum esse Patribus invicem dissentientibus: quàm Scripturis secum pulcherrimè & ubique rectissimè convenientibus?

Sed quid multis opus? Cúm Apostolus non certis quibusdam Ecclesiæ Doctoribus, sed omnibus Ministris ac Doctoribus Ecclesiæ permittat, ut de omni Scripturarum interpretatione ex ipso DEI Verbo judicent : Prophetæ (interpretes inquiens) duo aut tres loquantur, & alii dijudicent: siquè alii patefactum fuerit assidenti, prior taceat. 1. Cor. 14, 29. & 30.

Sic Quoad Concilia neque his infallibilem interpretandi Scripturas autoritatem largiri possumus. Nam & hæc errare posse, & errasse sæpissimè in interpretandis Scripturis, notius est, quàm ut operosa probatione indigeat, Cujus rei Exemplo esse potest, vel sanctissimum illud Concilium Nicenum, ubi unius Paphnutii provocationi, trecenti octodecim Episcopi cedere non dubitarunt. Unde ipse quoque Augustinus Maximino Arianorum Episcopo ad Concilium provocanti, respondit. Neque ego Nicenum, neque tu Ariminense Concilium, tanquam præjudicaturus, proferre debes.

Cæterùm, quibus argumentis propositionem hanc confirmare studeant Adversarii: videndum fuerit in diexodo subsequentis propositionis secundæ, quæ cum prima hac magnam cognitionem habet.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Jesuitical Proposition II Sacred Scripture is not the Judge of all controversies of faith and the Christian Religion: But this duty pertains to the Roman Pontiff… A…

JESUITICAL PROPOSITION II.

Sacred Scripture is not the Judge of all controversies of faith and the Christian Religion: But this duty pertains to the Roman Pontiff, whose definition, proposed to the whole Church with authority, is infallible in deciding controversial Questions of Religion, whether he defines with a Council or without a Council.

A refutatory exposition.

The Bavarian Jesuits proposed this thesis in exactly the same words at the Colloquy of Ratisbon, as is evident from the protocol on page 168, for which thesis the way had already been paved long ago at the Colloquy of Worms, celebrated in the year 1557, where this blasphemous utterance of the Romanists was first heard publicly: that Holy Scripture is not the voice of the Judge, but the subject matter of the dispute; nay, that it is a mute letter which requires the living voice of the Church: or, as Albert Pighius blasphemed, that Scripture is like the leaden rule of a certain Lesbian building: for just as that can be adapted to every shape, so Scripture can be adapted to every error, because it easily allows itself to be bent, led, and even drawn into a different meaning. In which sense the Cologne Jesuits also did not shrink from writing, on page 117. Censures: Holy Scripture, in those very dogmas or precepts which it contains and proposes, is like a nose of wax, not providing any certain and immovable meaning, but can be bent into any interpretation whatsoever. And on the preceding page, 21: No heresy has ever been found which did not take its occasion from the Scriptures. And these were those famous postulates which the adversaries did not so much prove as demand to be believed, and upon which they subsequently built this proposition of theirs. It is, in fact, partly a negative part, denying that Holy Scripture is the supreme and infallible judge of controversies; and partly an affirmative one, asserting that this right and this judicial authority belong solely to the Roman Pontiff. Regarding the former negative opinion, the Bavarian interlocutors testified that they held it so tenaciously that Gretser did not hesitate to burst forth into these detestable words: 'The Highest is here in the sight of Holy Scripture and the Holy Spirit; let Him therefore pronounce judgment, if He is the judge, and say, "You, Jacob Gretser, think wrongly, you have lost your case: You, Jacob Heilbrunner, have won," then I will immediately cross over to your bench: Let Him be present, let Him be present, let Him be present, and condemn me.' And a little later: 'Holy Scripture and the Holy Spirit cannot pronounce judgment so that the other party may evidently know that it has won its case: Now therefore let the Holy Spirit be present, now let Him judge, now let Him condemn me: Even now the Holy Spirit cannot pronounce a condemnatory judgment through this book, so that it may be evidently clear what His judgment is: Therefore He CANNOT be the Judge: Now, I am here: let Him say: "You err, Jacob Gretser."

Regarding the latter affirmative opinion, the Jesuits commonly embrace it today, although they are receding somewhat timidly from the opinion of their predecessors, which was indeed entirely approved in the Roman Church before this. For it is certain that before the Council of Constance and the Council of Basel, the authority of Councils was always greater than that of the Popes in judging Controversies. Whence Alphonsus de Castro also, book 1 against heresies, chapter 4, writes that the Council alone has this supreme authority, for the reason that the Council alone is the representative Church. And chapter 8, he expressly affirms that the Apostolic See holds the place next after the general Council in defining: But that it does not only comprise the Supreme Pope, but also that Council which the Pope uses, and by which he is assisted in defining: that is, the College of Cardinals. Making a divorce from this opinion, those new-fangled sycophants assign the supreme right and supreme Judicial authority to the Roman Pope alone, whether he defines with a Council or without a Council. Bellarmine himself confesses this very thing: For although in book 3, chapter 3, concerning the written Word of GOD, he joins a Council to the Pope: yet he immediately adds that that Council must be confirmed by the supreme pastor of the whole Church, that is, the Roman Pope.

Moreover, we have abundantly shown above in the second positive proposition by what arguments that former part of this Jesuitical proposition, namely the Negative, can and ought to be refuted. Therefore, only these two things remain to be settled. 1. That we may show that the supreme judgment of settling Controversies cannot reside with the Roman Pope alone: whether he defines with a Council or without a Council. Then that we may respond to the principal arguments of the Adversaries Logically and Theologically.

Regarding that first point, we simply Deny that an infallible judgment concerning Controversies resides with the Roman Pope alone: and that one must stand by his definition without any exception.

For first, the Supreme Judge of interpretations and Controversies must be such that he cannot err in judging.

But now the Roman Pope can not only err in judging, but has also erred, and always errs most gravely. Therefore.

The major premise shines by its own light. For how can the sentence of him be infallible who is liable to most grave errors in judging.

The minor premise is evident even from this: Every heretic errs: The Roman Popes are heretics. Therefore. I prove the assumption 1. By induction of examples. Pope Anastasius stood by the opinion of the Nestorians, as witnessed by Platina in the life of Anastasius. Pope Achatius was a heretic, and for that reason excommunicated by Gelasius: as the Canon Law testifies, cause 24, Question 1, chapter Achatius. Pope Liberius fostered the Arian heresy, and felt the same as the heretics in all matters, as Platina confirms; Innocent I felt that the Sacrament of the Eucharist was necessary for infants for salvation, which the fathers of Trent define to be heretical: Honorius was a Monothelite, and for that reason condemned by name in the Council of Constantinople: Nor can any Roman Pope be given today who is immune from heresy or error. Therefore. Then I prove it from the very head of pontifical doctrine, which directly impinges upon the foundation of the Christian faith, as in the Article of Justification and others.

II. Furthermore, in a supreme and infallible judge it is also required that he himself not be a party to the Controversy. But now the Roman Pope is that very person whom all the Orthodox accuse of idolatry and false dogmas: Therefore, judgment in his own cause is not permitted to him, not even by Pontifical Law itself: as is evident from cause 4, Question 2, chapter 3, §. Nullus. No one is understood to be a suitable witness in his own affair. And Question 4, chapter Nullus. Let no one ever presume to be accuser and judge and witness at the same time, since in every judgment it is necessary that four persons always be present, that is, chosen judges, suitable accusers, appropriate defenders, legitimate witnesses.

Thirdly, an appeal from the supreme and infallible Judge has no place. But an appeal has been made from the Roman Pontiff to another judge very often, and it is permitted to appeal today. Therefore, he cannot be the supreme and infallible judge himself.

The major premise is evident from the very concession of the adversaries, as they themselves urge such a judge, by whose sentence and judgment it is necessary for the parties simply to abide; as witnessed by Gretser, page 292 and following.

The minor premise is evident in two ways. 1. By example: For an appeal has been made from the judgment of the Pope to the judgment of others quite often: a fact which the adversaries cannot deny, even if they wished to most strongly. An example of this matter is found in Donatus, who appealed from Miltiades, the Roman Bishop, to another judge: and that by the permission of the Church.

Then it is evident by Right: for if it is permitted for the Papists to appeal from the Scriptures to the Fathers: from these to Councils: and finally from Councils to the Pontiff: why is it not permitted for us with a better right to appeal from the Pontiff, as a man, to GOD, that is, to the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scriptures? For nothing militates that could despoil us of that right, especially since the appeal is made by us to a Judge superior to every exception.

Fourthly: If in bodily causes, much more in a spiritual cause must the supreme Judge be chosen as one who is said to be influenced by no partiality for the parties, but is most alien to all προσωποληψίᾳ (respect of persons). Now, indeed, because the Roman Pontiff favors the Jesuits, as the pillars of the Antichristian Kingdom, and therefore is less fair or suitable for rendering judgment between us and them, it can be a matter of doubt to no one. For which reason the Donatists also formerly did not wish to admit the Roman Pontiff as a judge in adjudicating the controversy: Whether one who is baptized is to be rebaptized? Concerning which matter a very illustrious passage exists in Optatus of Milevis, most worthy of mention, book 5, which reads as follows: Judges of this controversy must be sought. Christians from either side cannot be given, because truth is hindered by partisanship. A judge must be sought from outside. If a pagan, he cannot know Christian secrets. If a Jew, he is an enemy of Christian baptism. and on earth no judgment can be found concerning this matter.

Must the Judge be sought from heaven? But why do we knock at heaven, when we have him here in the Gospel?

Fifth, such a supreme judge is required who has coercive power, that is, who by his own authority can compel transgressors to justice and right, so that they stand by the sentence or decision: as even the Jesuit Tanner himself judges: as is evident from the Colloquy of Ratisbon, p. 273. But the Pope does not have such coercive power, by which he can compel the parties to obedience. Therefore.

The adversaries will hardly deny the minor premise, which contains the matter to be judged, unless by some crafty trickery they wish to understand by that coercive power some external force or tyranny, by which one rages with arms and punishments against those who refuse to kiss the dogmas of the Antichrist. That the Roman Pope has for some centuries now exercised such power more than tyrannically, and even by this means has sufficiently fulfilled the mark of the Antichrist, is testified to by the blood of those martyrs who have been most cruelly slaughtered throughout Italy, France, Belgium, and Spain, because they constantly contradicted the pontifical idolatry. However, this coercive power is entirely irrelevant to the present business. For because faith is not a gift of men, but of GOD, it can in no way be struck into the minds of men by human force or external coercion. But just as GOD alone searches the innermost recesses of human hearts, so he is also the sole moderator of minds and wills, according to that passage in Deut. 29:4: The Lord has not given you a heart to understand, and eyes to see, and ears that can hear. And Jerem. 31:33: I the Lord will give my law in their inward parts, and write it in their heart. For which reason GOD is read to have opened the heart of Lydia the purple-seller, that she might attend to those things which were spoken by Paul. Acts 16:14. Wherefore it is necessary that that internal coercion, which consists in the impulse and bending of the souls themselves, be understood in this place: since the Roman Pontiff is destitute of this, he certainly will not be able to be the chief judge; but he is forced, even against his will, to yield this right to GOD the Holy Spirit alone.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO II. JESUVVITICA.

SAcra Scriptura non est Judex omnium controversiarum fidei & Religionis Christianæ: Sed hoc munus pertinet ad Pontificem Romanum, cujus definitio toti Ecclesiæ cum autoritate proposita, in controversis Quæstionibus Religionis decidendis, infallibilis est, sive cum Concilio, sive absque Concilio definiat.

ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστικὴ.

THesin hanc iisdem planè verbis proposuerunt Jesuitæ Bavarici in Colloquio Ratisbonensi, ut patet ex protocollo pag. 168 cui thesi via jam olim strata fuit in Colloquio VVormatiensi, Anno 57. supra sesquimillesimum celebrato, ubi blasphema hæc vox Romanensium primitùs publicè audita fuit, Scripturam Sacram non vocem Judicis, sed materiam litis esse: imò esse literam mutam, quæ vivam Ecclesiæ vocem desideret: vel ut Albertus Pighius blasphemavit, Scripturam esse veluti Lesbiæ cujusdam ædificationis plumbeam regulam: Sicut enim hæc omni figuræ: ita Scripturam omni errori posse accommodari, quia flecti, duci, & in diversam etiam sententiam trahi se facilè patiatur. Quo sensu Jesuitæ etiam Colonienses scribere non exhorruerunt, pag. 117. Censuræ: Sacra Scriptura in illis ipsis sive dogmatibus, sive præceptis, quæ continet & proponit, est veluti nasus cereus, non præbens certam aliquam & immotam sententiam, sed in quamvis interpretationem flecti potest. Et p. præced. 21. Nulla unquam reperta est hæresis quæ non ex scripturis occasionem acceperit. Et hæc fuerunt præclara illa αἰτήματα, quæ non tàm probarunt, quàm credi postularunt Adversarii, & quibus ipsi postmodùm, propositionem hanc suam substruxerunt. Est verò ea parti negativa, negans Scripturam Sacram esse judicem summum ac infallibilem Controversiarum: partim affirmata, afferens hoc jus & autoritatem hanc Judiciariam soli competere Pontifici Romano. Quoad priorem negativam sententiam, illam usque adeò mordicus tenere se, testati sunt Bavarici collocutores, ut Gretserus in detestantes hasce voces erumpere non dubitaverit: Summus hîc in conspectu sacræ Scripturæ & Spiritus Sancti: pronunciet ergò sententiam, si judex est, & dicat, Tu, Jacobe Gretsere, malè sentis, cecidisti causa tua: Tu, Jacobe Heilbrunnere, vicisti, tunc ego statim transibo ad vestrum scamnum: Adsit, Adsit, Adsit, & condemnet me. Et Paulò pòst: Non potest Scriptura sacra & Spiritus Sanctus dicere sententiam, ut altera pars evidenter sciat, se causam obtinuisse: Jam ergò adsit Spiritus Sanctus, jam judicet, jam condemnet me: Jam jam non potest Spiritus Sanctus dicere sententiam condemnatoriam per hunc librum, ita ut evidenter constet, qua sit ejus sententia: Ergò NON POTEST esse Judex: Jam, adsum: dicat: Erras Jacobe Gretsere.

Quoad posteriorem sententiam affirmativam, communiter eam hodiè amplectuntur Jesuvitæ, licet timidiufculè à prædecessorum suorum sententiâ, & quidem antehâc in Ecclesia Romanâ omninò approbata, manifestè recedentes. Constat enim ante Constantiense ac Basiliense Concilium, Majorem semper fuisse Conciliorum, quàm Pontificiis autoritatem in dijudicandis Controversiis. Unde Alphonsus etiam de Castro, lib. 1. contra hæreses cap. 4. Solū Concilium hanc summā autoritatē habere scribit, proptereà, quod Concilium solum sit repræsentativa Ecclesia. Et cap. 8. disertè affirmat, Sedem Apostolicam proximum post Concilium generale in definiendo locum habere: Eam verò non tantùm comprehendere Pontificem Summum, sed & Concilium illud, quo Pontifex utitur, & quo in definiendo adjuvatur: hoc est, Collegium Cardinalium. Ab hac sententiâ divortium facientes novelli isti Gnathones sedes Apostolicæ summum jus, summamq; autoritatem Judiciariam soli adsignant Pontifici Romano, sive cum Concilio, sive fine Concilio definiat. Quod ipsum fatetur Bellarminus: Nam etsi lib. 3. c. 3. de Verbo DEI scripto, Pontifici adjungit Concilium: tamen statim subjicit, Concilium illud debere esse confirmatum à summo Ecclesiæ totius pastore, hoc est, Pontifice Romano.

Cæterùm, quibus argumentis prior illa pars propositionis hujus Jesuvviticæ, Negativa nimirum, refutari possit ac debeat, suprà propositione secundâ θετικῇ abunde ostendimus. Proinde duo tantùm isthæc expediunda restant. 1. Ut ostendamus, penes solùm Pontificem Romanum judicium summum dirimendi Controversias esse non posse: sive cùm Concilio, sive sine Concilio definiat. Deindè ut ad præcipua argumenta Adversariorum Logicè & Theologicè respondeamus.

Quoad prius illud, simpliciter Negamus penes solùm Pontificem Romanum esse judicium infallibile de Controversiis: & hujus definitione sine ullâ exceptione esse standum.

Primùm enim, Summus interpretationum & Controversiarum Judex esse debet talis, ut errare judicando non possit.

Jam verò Pontifex Romanus non modò judicando errare potest, sed & erravit, semperq; errat gravissimè. Ergò.

Major suâ luce lucet. Quomodo enim illius sententia possit esse infallibilis, qui erroribus in judicando gravissimis est obnoxius.

Minor vel inde patet: Omnis hæreticus errat: Pontifices Romani sunt hæretici. Ergò. Assumptionem probo 1. Inductione exemplorum. Papa Anastasius stetit à sententiâ Nestorianorum, teste Platina in vitâ Anastasii. Papa Achati9 fuit hæreticus, & ob id à Gelasio excommunicat9: uti testatur Jus Canonicum causa 24. Quæst. 1. cap. Achatius. Papa Liberi9 Arianam hæresin fovit, & cum hæreticis in omnibus rebus sensit, sic cōfirmante Platina, Innocentius I. Eucharistiæ Sacramentum infantibus ad salutem necessarium esse sensit, quod Tridentini patres hæreticum esse definiunt: Honorius fuit Monotheleta, & ob id nominatim in Concilio Constantinopolitano damnatus: Neque hodiè dare potest ullus Pontifex Romanus, qui ab hæresi aut errore sit immunis. Ergò. Deindè probo ex ipso capite doctrinæ pontificiæ, quod in fundamentum fidei Christianæ, ut in Articulo Justificationis & aliis directè impingit.

II. Deinde, in summo & infallibili judice requiritur etiam, ut non ipsemet sit pars Controversiæ. Jam verò Pontifex Romanus est is ipse, quem idololatriæ falsorumq́; dogmatum rerum peragunt omnes Orthodoxi: Ergò in propriâ causâ judicium ipsi, ne quidem ab ipso Jure Pontificio permittitur: uti patet ex causâ 4. Quæst. 2. cap. 3. §. Nullus. Nullus idoneus testis in re suâ intelligitur. Et Quæst. 4. cap. Nullus.
