Nullus unquàm præsumat accusator simul esse & judex, & testis, quoniam in omni judicio quatuor personas necesse est semper adesse, hoc est, Judices electos, accusatores idoneos : defensores congruos : testes legitimos.

Tertiò, A summo & infallibili Judice Provocatio, locum non habet. Atqui à Pontifice Romano ad alium Judicem provocatum est sæpissimè, hodieq; licet provocare. Ergò summus ac infallibilis judex ipse esse non potest.

Major patet ipsâ concessione Adversariorum, ut qui ipsi talem urgent judicem, cuj9 sententiâ ac judicio partes simpliciter stare necesse habeant; teste Gretsero pag. 292. & seqq.

Minor patet dupliciter. 1. Exemplo : Provocatum enim fuit, à Papæ judicio ad aliorum judicium sæpiusculè: id quod negare non possunt Adversarij, si maximè velint. Cujus rei exemplum habetur in Donato, qui provocavit à Meltiade Episcopo Romano ad alium judicem: idque permissu Ecclesiæ.

Deinde patet Jure: si enim Pontificijs licitum est provocare à Scripturis ad Patres: ab his ad Concilia : à Concilijs deniq; ad Pontificem: Quidnî potiore jure nobis licet provocare à Pontifice, tanquam homine ad DEUM, hoc est, ad Spiritum Sanctum in Scripturis loquentem? Neque enim quicquam militat, quod nos jure isto spoliare possit, præsertim cum ad Judicem omni exceptione superiorem à nobis fiat provocatio.

Quartò: Si in causis corporalibus, multò magis in causâ spirituali Judex summus eligendus fuerit is, qui nullo partium studio dicitur, sed ab omni προσωποληψίᾳ est alienissimus. Jam verò, quia Pontifex Romanus Jesuvvitis, tanquam Regni Antichristiani columnis, faveat, ac proindè ad ferendum judicium inter nos & ipsos minùs sit vel æquus vel idoneus, nemini potest esse dubium. Quam ob causam donatistæ etiam olim Romanum Pontificem noluerunt admittere Judicem, in dijudicandâ Controversiâ: An baptizatus sit rebaptizandus? Quâ de re illustris admodum extat locus apud Optatum Milevitanum, memoratu dignissimus lib. 5. qui sic habet: Quærendi sunt huj9 controversiæ Judices. Christiani de utraq; parte dari nõ possunt, quia studiis veritas impeditur. De foris quærend9 est Judex. Si pagano, nõ potest nosse Christiana secreta. Si Judæ9 inimic9 est Christiani baptismatis. & in terris de hac re nullũ poterit reperiri judicium.

De cœlo quærendus est Judex? sed quid pulsamus cœlum, cùm habeamus hic in Evangelio?

Quintò, talis supremus judex requiritur, qui potestatem habeat coactivam, hoc est, qui sua autoritate compellere possit transgressores ad jus & fas, ut stent sententiæ sive decisioni: sic censente ipso etiam Jesuvvita Tannero: uti patet ex Coll. Ratisp. p. 273. Atqui Papa talem potestatem coactivam non habet, quâ ad obedientiam partes compellere possit. Ergò.

Minorem, quæ continet τὸ κρινόμενον, vix negabunt adversarij, nisi veteratoriâ quâdam πανουργίᾳ, per potestatem illam coactivam intelligere velint, externam aliquam vim sive Tyrannidem, quâ armis atque supplicijs sævitur in eos, qui Antichristi dogmata exosculari detrectant. Qualem sanè potestatem aliquot jam seculis Papam Romanum plusquàm Tyrannicè exercuisse, & vel hoc pacto se Antichristi notam sufficienter explevisse, testatur sangvis illorum Martyrum, qui per Italiam, Galliam, Belgiam, Hispaniam, crudelissimè trucidati sunt: eò quòd pontificiæ Idololamaniæ, constanter contradixerunt. Cæterum absona prorsus à præsenti negotio hæc est potestas coactiva. Quia enim Fides non hominum, sed DEI donum est, utique vi etiam humana incuti, aut coactione externa animis hominum inferi, nullo modo potest. Solus autem DEUS uti cordium humanorum intimos scrutatur recessus: Ita animorum etiam atque voluntatum solus est moderator, secundum illud Deut. 29, 4. Non dedit vobis Dominus cor intelligens, & oculos videntes, & aures quæ possint audire. Et Jerem. 31, 33. Ego Dominus dabo legem meam in visceribus eorum, & in corde eorum scribam eam. Qua ratione DEUS legitur aperuisse cor mulieri Lydiæ purpurinæ, ut intenderet his, quæ dicebantur à Paulo. Act. 16, 14. Quare interna illa coactio, quæ ipsarum animarum impulsu atque flexione constat, hoc loco intelligatur necesse est: Quâ cùm destituatur Romanus Pontifex, certè neque ἀρχιδικαστὴς esse poterit: sed hoc jus Soli DEO Spiritui Sancto cedat, vel invitus cogitur.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Jesuitical Proposition II Sacred Scripture is not the Judge of all controversies of faith and the Christian Religion: But this duty pertains to the Roman Pontiff… A…

Sixth: If the Roman Pontiff is the supreme and infallible Judge of controversies, it will certainly be permitted to appeal to him in any doubtful question. But the latter is false: Therefore the former will also be false.

The major proposition being conceded even by the adversaries themselves.

We confirm the minor premise with those reasons by which the sixth Synod of Carthage evidently demonstrated that appeals to the Roman See are not to be granted.

For first, GOD, out of his fatherly benevolence toward the Church, has bestowed upon every ecclesiastical assembly so many gifts of the Holy Spirit that they can rightly discuss and settle controversies that have arisen. Nor is the Holy Spirit, as the Jesuits rave, so affixed either to the boards of the Chair or to the chest of the Roman Pontiff's heart, that he has him as if enslaved. The Holy Scripture is witness that the grace of the Holy Spirit is not only promised, but also undoubtedly conferred, to any pious and faithful mind, to any congregation of the faithful, imploring divine aid: Matt. 10:19 and ch. 18:20, Luke 11:13. Nor can either the Chair itself or the succession to the Chair claim any prerogative for itself in this regard: Zedekiah certainly succeeded David; Caiaphas succeeded Aaron; and an idol has often stood in the temple of GOD: Thus, if the Roman Pope succeeded the Apostle Peter—a matter which is nevertheless not undeservedly doubted. He succeeded indeed in the place, but not in piety and doctrine.

Then, in more serious and difficult matters, a challenge is granted to the Metropolitan Church, or even to the entire Synod of any province, so that there is no need for an appeal to the Roman Pope.

Third, it would be not only of great arrogance, but also of audacity and tyranny, if some one Pope should boast that the justice of cognition and examination was inspired in him alone, but denied to innumerable priests legitimately gathered in a Synod.

Finally, it is impossible, on account of the distance of the place and the magnitude of the expenses, that an appeal should be made to an overseas Judge.

Seventh. If the Roman Pontiff is the supreme and infallible Judge of all Controversies, and cannot err in judging when he pronounces from the Chair: To what purpose, I pray, was there need for the Romanists themselves to expend so much labor, expense, and time in unrolling the books of the Fathers, in gathering Councils, in reading even the Scriptures, and finally in pouring out prayers? For that which can be done by fewer means ought not to be done by more. What? That the Pontiff himself has consulted very poorly for his own Church as well, when he could have provided the true interpretation of the whole Scripture for so many centuries now, and could have removed all false ἐξηγήσεις (exegeses), of which infinite numbers have existed among the Pontifical Doctors themselves, as Bellarmine himself admits, and exist to this day: yet hitherto he has been unwilling to confer this benefit upon his Church. And what, I pray, is the reason that the Pontiff, more solicitous about secular than ecclesiastical government, has neither taught the people publicly hitherto, nor issued those Oracles from his Chair, nor published Commentaries on Scripture, so that some fruit from this supreme and infallible judgment of his might have redounded to the Church? Finally, this Jesuitical Assertion is destitute of all authority of the Scriptures. For we are not commanded by even a single testimony to defer to any one man the infallible authority of defining Controversies: It is also destitute of the applause of Orthodox Antiquity, whose testimonies may be seen in the Protocol of the Ratisbon Colloquy, page 206 and following. With these things thus established, we conclude invincibly that a supreme and infallible Judgment does not belong to the Roman Pontiff by any pact or Right, which will become more manifest if we examine the principal Arguments of the Adversaries a little more accurately.

BUT they first take their argument from the Old Testament, arguing thus: If Moses, as prince and head of the Jewish Church, answered all doubts arising concerning the Law of GOD, and did not send men to some revealing Spirit: And, if Moses reserved to himself doubts concerning religion: it follows from this that today, too, there must be one common tribunal, from which all may seek the interpretation of the divine law, and to which all may simply acquiesce.

But the former is true: Therefore the latter also.

I reply to the major premise, and I simply deny its consequence based on the Rule of Logicians: The consequence is not valid when there is a dissimilarity in the Examples: Which is certainly found to be very great in this argument. For Moses was not only a Judge, but also a Prophet, extraordinarily and quite immediately called by GOD himself, and commended to the Jewish people with such praises that it was certain he could not err in judging. Now, however, the Roman Pontiff enjoys not only no extraordinary and immediate calling, but not even an ordinary or legitimately mediated one: Indeed, even if he did enjoy such a mediated one in the highest degree, this would still be in many ways inferior to that extraordinary and immediate one. Therefore, contrary to the precepts of the Logicians, the Jesuit also argues most viciously affirmatively from the Major to the Minor.

It is added that the Roman Pontiff is so destitute of that testimony, that he cannot err, that it is established that his predecessors were involved in various horrible heresies: and that he himself, who presides today, is not undeservedly accused not only of heresy, but also of base ἀποστασίας and defection, according to that 2 Thess. 2, 3.

Then, the argument fails by the sophistry παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For Moses did not have such a supreme tribunal that, even with the authority of the divine Scriptures set aside, it was permitted for him to pronounce whatever he wished: For he himself in all chapters, and in almost all verses, most diligently inculcates: that the Lord spoke each thing to him: Thus, therefore, Moses pronounced nothing other than what GOD himself had revealed to him. In which part the authority of the Roman Pontiff again clearly fails and expires.

Thirdly, the argument fails by the sophism παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον: For although we do not deny that in individual churches there ought to be some who interpret the Scriptures for the people: it is nevertheless most viciously inferred from that: Therefore the same is necessary in the whole Catholic or universal Church, namely that all interpretations should finally be referred to the judgment of one man. For if this were valid, it could be proven by the same reason or logic that Moses was the supreme political Judge in the Jewish Republic, to whom alone the decision of all lawsuits belonged. Therefore, today also, all Christians ought to have one supreme political head; and that very one, indeed, not from the number of politicians, but of ecclesiastics: Since the Romanists themselves, out of ignorance of Scripture, contend that Moses was the supreme Priest, which, however, we do not grant them in the least. For Moses was for some time a Priest, until he anointed and initiated his brother Aaron: But it is nowhere written that he performed the Priesthood further after that.

The other argument taken from Deut. ch. 17. 8. & following is such: The Israelites are commanded in doubtful questions to come to the Priest of the Levitical kind, and to the Judge who shall be at that time, and to seek from them, who shall indicate to them the truth of the judgment: and to follow their sentence and not to decline to the right, nor to the left. Therefore, today also, those who are in doubt ought not to be sent to their own Spirit: but to a living judge, that is, the supreme Priest.

I reply. 1. This argument reeks of calumny. For we do not establish that everyone in doubts is to be sent to their own private Spirit, as the Jesuit trifles: but to the holy Scripture and its author and supreme and infallible interpreter, GOD the Holy Spirit. Then, this argument is destitute of a true refutation, which might prove that which was most to be proven. For the Jesuit, intending to prove that there ought to be one supreme Judge of Controversies, brings forth such a passage which does not define one, but several: namely, the Priest of the Levitical kind, and the Judge. And the response of the Jesuit, contending that by the name of Judge is not understood a political judge, but the Prince of Priests, is clearly cold and weak, as if he were saying: Ascend to the Council of Priests, and their prince, or the supreme Priest. That force is being brought to the text is evident even from the fact that in verse 12 the distinctive particle is expressly read in this way: He who does not wish to obey the Priest, or the Judge וְאֶל: Just as Cyprian also cites this passage, Epistle 69. Then, not even by the Priest of the Levitical kind is one alone, namely the supreme Pontiff, understood: But collectively, Whichever Priest of the Levitical kind: which is evident from the tenth verse, where it is read in the plural and thus collectively: And they shall teach you: not in the singular: And he shall teach you.

Furthermore, it is false what the Jesuit infers, if we understand by the name of Judge a political Prince, that distinct offices are denoted: so that the definitive sentence is attributed to the Priest: but the execution against the contumacious to the Judge. For not only is the execution attributed to the Judge, but the definitive sentence itself: For thus the text holds: By the decree of the Judge he shall die.

The third fallacy of the Jesuit argument is τοῦ διὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: for that Priest of the Levitical line, and the Judge, had to judge not without the written Word of GOD, from their own brain, but only from the prescription of the Law: For thus the text sounds: And you shall do all that they shall teach you according to the word of the law which they shall teach you: וְשָׁמַרְתָּ לַעֲשׂוֹת כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר יוֹרוּךָ עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה אֲשֶׁר יוֹרוּךָ: that is, if you render word for word: And you shall keep by doing according to all that they shall teach you, upon the mouth of the law which they shall teach you. But now the Roman Pontiff draws out interpretations not from the written Word, but from his own ingenuity.

Nor is there any reason for the Jesuit to object that these words are not of a condition, but of a promise: because GOD wishes to render the people secure, namely that the high priest cannot but judge according to the law.

For if this were true, it would follow that no high priest of the Jews could have erred in any judgment according to this promise; indeed, it would also follow that not even the political judges of the Jewish people could have erred in any judgment: for that political causes are also being dealt with in this place, even these words of the text prove: between cause and cause: between leprosy and leprosy. Now, however, how absurd this is, it is a wonder if the adversaries themselves do not recognize and confess it.

The fourth fallacy is ὡς ἀπὸ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For no reason permits one to connect an argument from one nation, and that one enclosed by the very narrow borders of Judea or Palestine, to the whole Catholic Church dispersed throughout the entire world, or to the whole human race. The Jews were commanded to consult the high priest, and to acquiesce in his response given from the law: Therefore all men, even those who have never heard of the Pontiff, must approach the Roman Pontiff, and acknowledge him as their judge. To this is added that the high priest of the Jews was a type not of the Roman Pontiff, but of Christ, to whom, the priesthood having been transferred, that right also passed.

The third argument, which seems to be of some moment, is such: Holy Scripture receives various senses, nor can it itself say which is the true one. Therefore Holy Scripture cannot be the supreme judge of controversies.

I respond: and I deny the antecedent, which is most false, consisting of a double lie. The first is: that Scripture receives various senses. The falsity of this assertion is most evidently apparent from those things which we said above, just from the beginning of this fifth controversy, concerning the various senses of Scripture. For Scripture does not admit various senses because various senses are brought into it: but the sense of Scripture is one, simple, and perpetual. The second lie is: that Scripture cannot speak, or say, which is the true sense. Which very lie Gretser repeated again and again in the recent colloquy. Which blasphemy surely redounds not so much upon Scripture as upon GOD himself. For GOD speaks to us in the Scriptures, as if mouth to mouth: for this reason the Savior commands it to be searched, because it testifies of him. John 5:39. Hence Scripture itself is said to speak and say. John 7:42. Does not Scripture say? Rom. 4:3. For what does Scripture say? And ch. 9:17. Scripture says to Pharaoh. Gal. 4:30. But what does Scripture say? And elsewhere passim. And why, I beseech you, is this Scripture called the Word of GOD, if GOD does not speak to us in it? Therefore, just as he who reads the letters of a friend easily perceives his mind and opinion, even if the letters themselves do not emit an articulated voice: so also Holy Scripture is the Epistle of GOD, sent to the human race, in which he proposes his mind and will to us quite clearly.

Fourthly, they also bring forward this argument from the place of comparisons: In every well-constituted Republic, the Law and the Judge are distinct things, and the Law indeed teaches what is to be done: but the Judge interprets the Law, and directs men according to it. Therefore the reason ought to be the same in the Church.

But I reply, and I deny, that the reason for the Law and forensic judges is exactly the same as that for Scripture and its interpreter. For a forensic judge can change something in his decree according to the variety of circumstances, and remit something from the strict law on account of some probable cause: but concerning holy Scripture and its interpretation, we have express commands that we neither add anything, nor take anything away: nor turn aside either to the right hand or to the left, Apoc. 22, 18. Deut. 17, 11.

Then I reply ex abundanti, even if it were granted in the highest degree that the reason is equal in both cases: yet when the question is about the meaning of the Law, certainly it is not permitted even for a forensic judge to interpret the Law against itself: but he is bound to declare the meaning of the Law from its very words. In which respect a political judge is not above, but below the Law, and thus the Jesuits cut their own throats with this comparison. For if Scripture is Law, as it certainly is: then by the force of this comparison it is necessary that the judge pronounce things consistent with the Law, and subject himself to the Law.

Fifthly, they clamor thus: If the Word of GOD were sufficient for the refutation of heresies, those four Ecumenical Councils (Nicene, Constantinopolitan, Ephesian, Chalcedonian) would never have used the authority of the Church. But they did use it, as is evident from the acts of those very Councils. Therefore.

I reply: this argument sins first by Ignoratio Elenchi. For we have never even in a fever dreamed that the authority of the Church is absolutely nothing, which certainly, as was shown above, in its own way and respect, it is confessed that it sustains the role of a judge in refuting heresies. But this is what is disputed, Whether the Word of GOD needs the authority of the Church for a supplement: Likewise, Whether the Church, even with the Scriptures set aside and neglected, can define Controversies at its own pleasure. Where we maintain the negative in both cases. And indeed if they wish to fight for the affirmative from that argument, a manifest begging of the question emerges, and a Sophistication of the non sequitur. For this very thing is what is sought, and must be proved by the Adversaries: Whether Scripture is therefore insufficient for the refutation of heresies, because both the Fathers and the Councils added also the consent of the Church to the testimonies of holy Scripture? For that these things are subordinate, and therefore do not mutually exclude each other, but can stand together in different degrees and respects, has already been demonstrated several times.

Sixthly, they rise up thus: GOD established a certain order of judging in his Church through men: therefore he himself is not the supreme Judge of Truth: but he has delegated the power of judging to others, namely to the Roman Pontiff. I answer. The argument fails, 1. by the fallacy τꭣ̃ μὴ ἀιτίꭣ ὡς ἀιτίꭣ [of the non-cause as cause]. For GOD did not therefore establish a certain order of judging in the Church through men, so that they might define matters of doubt from their own brain and judgment, but so that they might be bound to the Law and to the Testimony, and might not deviate from it even by a hair's breadth. 2. It fails by the fallacy ὠπꭣ̃ τꭣ̃ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς [of the particular and the absolute]: For men are not primary judges: but rather ministers of the supreme Judge, whose voice sounding in the Scriptures, as soon as they neglect, they immediately bring forth not a right, but a false judgment: as the Prophet speaks. Finally, it fails by the fallacy ὠπꭣ̃ τꭣ̃ μὴ ἑπόμενον [of the non-consequent]. For no reason of consequence holds: GOD established a certain order of judging in the Church through men: Therefore He abdicated Himself of this right of judging: and delegated the parts of supreme judgment to the Roman Pontiff, or to the Church. Subordinate things, as has been said just a little before, do not conflict. The primary cause subordinates to itself secondary and intermediate causes, which it uses without any prejudice to itself, or any diminution of its own right, as ministers and servants: as if bound and obligated to the prescription of its own law.

Seventhly: If one must contend only with the testimonies of Scripture, disputes can never be finished with the obstinate.

I answer. The error arises from the fallacy ὠπꭣ̃ τꭣ̃ μὴ ἑπόμενον [of the non-consequent]. For it does not follow, the obstinacy of heretics cannot be so repressed by the testimonies of the Scriptures that they confess themselves to be defeated: Therefore controversies cannot be finished by the testimonies of the Scriptures alone. For this consequence is denied, because there is a twofold finishing of controversies or disputes: One, which regards the heresies or errors themselves: The other, which looks to the obstinacy of the heretics or erring persons. Now, indeed, if that former finishing of controversies could not subsist before this latter also followed in actual fact, and heretics publicly confessed themselves to be defeated: then no controversy was ever perfectly defined: nay, not even Christ Himself and the Apostles rightly and perfectly settled controversies with the Scribes and Pharisees. Therefore the falsity of this argument is evident even from this, that from the negation of this latter kind, a collection is most viciously instituted to the negation of that former kind as well. For the perfect decision of controversies does not consist in the compliance of heretics: but in the demonstration of the errors themselves, sought from none but the sacred Scriptures. Which duty Scripture performs most sufficiently, whether heretics acquiesce or not.

And here we plant our foot, and desiring the refutation of other Jesuitical arguments as well, we refer partly to the protocol of the recent Ratisbon Colloquy: and partly to the books of our own theologians published expressly on this matter: especially since from these things which have been disputed thus far, the rest can be judged most easily.

Latin:

Sextò: Si Pontifex Romanus summus est & infallibilis controversiarum Judex, utique licebit ad ipsum in quavis quæstione dubia appellare. Atqui falsum hoc posterius: Falsum igitur erit & prius.

Majore propositione ab ipsis etiam Adversarijs concessâ.

Minorem confirmamus illis rationibus, quibus Carthaginensis Synodus sexta evidenter demonstravit, appellationes ad Romanam Sedem non esse concedendas.

Primùm enim DEUS pro sua in Ecclesiam paterna benevolentia unicuique Ecclesiastico cœtui tantùm donorum Spiritus Sancti largitus est, ut possint obortas Controversias rectè disceptare & componere. Neque enim, uti Jesuvvitæ delirant, Spiritus Sanctus ita affixus est vel asseribus Cathedræ, vel scrinio pectoris Pontificis Romani, ut eum ipse quasi mancipatum habeat. Testis est Scriptura Sacra, Spiritus Sancti gratiam non tantùm promitti, sed & indubitatò conferri, cuilibet animo pio ac fideli, cuilibet congregationi fidelium, divinam opem implorantium: Matth. 10, 19. & cap. 18, 20. Luc. 11, 13. Neque quicquam prærogativæ hac in parte sibi vendicare potest, vel Cathedra ipsa, vel successio in Cathedram: Davidi profectò successit Zedechias: Aaroni successit Caiphas: & idolum sæpè stetit in templo DEI: Sic si Apostolo Petro successit Papa Romanus: de quo tamen haud immeritò dubitatur. Successit sanè in loco, sed non in pietate & Doctrina.

Deindè in gravioribus & difficilioribus negotijs concessa est provocatio ad Metropolitanam Ecclesiam, vel etiam ad integram Synodum cujuscunque provinciæ, ut appellatione ad Romanam Papam non sit opus.

Tertiò, non magnæ modò esset arrogantiæ, sed etiam audaciæ & Tyrannidis, si unus aliquis Papa jactitet, sibi soli cognitionis & Examinis inspiratam esse justitiam: innumerabilibus autem in Synodo legitimè congregatis Sacerdotibus eandem denegatam.

Tandem impossibile est, propter loci distantiam, & sumtuum amplitudinem, ut ad transmarinum Judicem appelletur.

Septimò. Si Pontifex Romanus est summus & infallibilis omnium Controversiarum Judex: neque judicando errare potest, quando è Cathedra pronunciat: Quorsum, obsecro, opus erat, ipsos Romanenses, in Patrum libris evolvendis, Concilijs congregandis, in Scripturis etiam legendis, in fundendis denique precibus, tantum laboris, sumtus, temporis insumere? per plura enim fieri non debet, quod fieri potest per pauciora. Quid? quòd ipse Pontifex pessimè consuluit suæ quoque Ecclesiæ, cum tot jam seculis veram totius Scripturæ, interpretationem tradere, & omnes falsas ἐξηγήσεις, quarum infinitæ inter ipsos Doctores Pontificios, ipso Bellarmino fatente, extiterunt, hodiequè existunt, tollere potuisset: hactenus tamen hoc beneficij in suam Ecclesiam conferre noluit. Et quæ, obsecro, causa est, quod Pontifex, de Regimine magis seculari, quàm Ecclesiastico sollicitus, neque populum publicè hactenus docuit, neque Oracula illa, ex Cathedra sua edidit, neque Commentarios in Scripturam publicavit, ut aliquis ex summo hoc ipsius & infallibili Judicio fructus ad Ecclesiam redundare potuisset? Tandem destituitur Assertio hæc Jesuvvitica omni Scripturarum autoritate. Neq; enim vel unico testimonio jubemur uni cuipiam homini deferre infallibilem autoritatem definiendi Controversias: Destituitur etiam applausu Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, cujus testimonia videre licet in Protocollo Colloquij Ratisbonensis, pag. 206. & seqq. Quibus ita constitutis invictè concludimus, Pontifici Romano Judicium summum ac infallibile, nullo pacto aut Jure competere, id quod evadet manifestiùs, si paulò accuratiùs Argumenta Adversariorum præcipua examinaverimus.

PRIMUM autem desumunt ipsi ex Veteri Testamento sic arguentes: Si Moses tanquam princeps & caput Ecclesiæ Judaicæ ad omnia dubia circa Legem DEI exorta respondit, nec homines remisit ad Spiritum aliquem revelantem: Et, si Moses sibi reservavit dubia circa religionem: sequenter indè, hodieq́, unum esse debere commune tribunal, à quo omnes petant divinæ legis interpretationem, & cui omnes simpliciter acquiescant.

Sed prius verum: Ergò & posterius.

Respondeo ad Majorem, ejusque consecutionem simpliciter nego ex Regula Logicorum: Non valet Consequentia, quando dissimilitudo est in Exemplis: Quæ certè in hoc argumento maxima deprehenditur. Moses enim non modò Judex, sed & Propheta fuit, extraordinariè, & prorsus immediatè ab ipso DEO vocatus, & ejusmodi elogiis commendatus populo Iudaico, ut constaret ipsum in judicando errare non posse. Jam verò Pontifex Romanus non modò non extraordinariâ & immediatâ, sed ne quidem ordinariâ, sive legitimè mediatâ vocatione gaudet: Quin si vel maximè tali mediatâ gauderet, tamen multis modis hæc esset inferior illâ extraordinariâ ac immediatâ. Proindè contra præcepta Logicorum etiam vitiosissimè argumentatur Jesuuvita affirmativè à Majore ad Minus.

Accedit, quòd Pontifex Romanus usque adeò testimonio illo destituitur, quòd errare nõ possit, ut tùm prædecessores ipsius, varijs horrendis hæresibus implicitos fuisse constet: tùm ille ipse, qui hodie præsidet, non hæreseos tantùm, sed & turpis ἀποστασίας & defectionis haud immeritò insimuletur, secundum illud 2.Theß. 2, 3.

Deindè, fallit argumentum Sophisticatione παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Moses enim non tale summum habuit tribunal, ut posthabitâ etiam divinarum Scripturarum autoritate, pronunciare ipsi licet quod vellet: Nam ipsemet omnibus in capitibus, & fermè versibus omnibus diligentissimè inculcat: Dominum singula ad se locutum esse: Sic ergò nihil aliud pronunciavit Moses, quàm quod DEUS ipse ei revelaverat. Qua in parte rursus Pontificis Romani autoritas planè deficit & expirat.

Tertiò fallit argumentum Sophismate παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον: Etsi enim non negamus, in singulis Ecclesiis aliquos esse oportere, qui Scripturas populo interpretentur: vitiosissimè tamen indè colligitur: Ergò in tota Catholica sive universali Ecclesia idem est necessarium, ut videlicet omnes interpretationes, ad unius tandem arbitrium referantur. Si enim hoc valeret, eadem ratione sive logicâ evinci posset, Moses in Repub. Judaicâ summus fuit Judex politicus, ad quem unum decisio omnium litium pertinebat. Ergò hodiequè Omnes Christiani unum supremum politicum caput habere debent; & id ipsum quidem non ex politicorum, sed Ecclesiasticorum numero: Siquidem ipsi Romanenses ex ignorantia Scripturæ contendunt, Mosen summum fuisse Sacerdotem, id quod tamen ipsis minimè largimur. Fuit enim Moses aliquandiu Sacerdos, donec Aaronem fratrem inungeret & initiaret: Sed postea Sacerdotio eum ulteriùs functum esse nuspiam scriptum est.

Alterum Argumentum petitum ex Deut. cap. 17. 8. & seqq. tale est: Israelitæ jubentur in quæstionibus dubijs venire ad Sacerdotem Levitici generis, & ad Judicem qui fuerit illo tempore, & quærere ab eis, qui indicabunt ipsis judicij veritatem: & horum sequi sententiam neq́; declinare ad dextrã, neq; ad sinistram. Ergò hodieq́; dubitantes non remitti debent ad Spiritum suum: sed ad judicem vivum, hoc est, summum Sacerdotem.

Respondeo. 1. Argumentum hoc calumniam resipit. Nequè enim statuimus, quemq́; esse in dubijs remittendum ad suum privatum Spiritum, uti nugatur Jesuvvita: sed ad Scripturam sacram ejusq́; autorem ac interpretem summũ & infallibilem DEUM Spiritum Sanctum. Deindè destituitur hoc argumentum vero elencho, qui probet id, quod probandum maximè erat. Nam Jesuvvita probaturus unum debere esse summum Judicem Controversiarum, profert locum talem, qui non unum definit, sed plures: nempè Sacerdotem Levitici generis, & Iudicem. Et frigida ac elumbis planè est responsio Jesuvvitæ contendentis, Judicis nomine non intelligi Judicem politicum: sed Principem Sacerdotum, quasi diceret: Ascende ad Concilium Sacerdotum, & eorum principem, sive summũ Sacerdotem. Vim inferri textui, vel indè patet, quòd versu 12. expressè legitur particula distinctiva hoc modo: Qui non vult obedire Sacerdoti, aut Judici וְאֶל: Quemadmodum etiam Cyprianus hunc locum citat, Epistola 69. Deindè ne quidem per Sacerdotem Levitici generis, unus tantummodò, nempè summus Pontifex intelligitur: Sed collectivè, Quicunq́; Sacerdos Levitici generis: id quod patet ex versu decimo, ubi in plurali & sic collectivè legitur: Et docuerint te: non in singulari: Et docuerit te.

Porrò falsum est, quod Jesuvvita infert, si intelligamus nomine Iudicis politicum Principem, notari distincta officia: ita ut Sacerdoti tribuatur sententia Definitiva: Judici autem executio in contumaces. Non enim tantùm executio Judici tribuitur, sed ipsa sententia definitiva: Sic enim habet Textus: Ex Decreto Judicis morietur.

Tertium Sophisma argumenti Jesuvvitici est τοῦ διὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: Sacerdos enim ille Levitici generis, & Judex non sine scripto DEI Verbo, ex proprio cerebro, sed tantùm ex Legis præscripto Iudicare debuerunt: Sic enim sonat textus: Et facies omnia, quæ docebunt te juxta sermonem legis, quam docebunt te: וְשָׁמַרְתָּ לַעֲשׂוֹת כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר יוֹרוּךָ עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה אֲשֶׁר יוֹרוּךָ: hoc est, Si verbum verbo reddas: & custodies faciendo juxta omnia, quæ docebunt te, Super os legis, quam docebunt te. Jam verò Romanus Pontifex non ex scripto Verbo, sed ex ingenio suo interpretationes depromit.

Neque est ut excipiat Jesuuvita, Haec verba non conditionis, sed promissionis esse: quia DEUS velit securum reddere populum, quòd videlicet summus sacerdos, non possit non judicare secundum legem.

Hoc enim verum si esset, sequeretur, nullum Judæorum summum Pontificem, ullo in judicio, secundum hanc promissionem errare potuisse, imò sequeretur & illud, ne Iudices quidem politicos populi Iudaici, ullo in Iudicio errare potuisse: Nam de politicis etiam causis hoc loco agi, vel hæc verba textus evincunt, inter causam & causam: inter lepram & lepram. Jam verò, quàm absurdum hoc sit, mirum, nî ipsi agnoscant & fateantur Adversarij.

Quartum Sophisma est ὡς ἀπὸ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Nam ab una gente, eâque angustis admodum Iudææ sive palæstinæ terminis inclusâ, ad totam Catholicam Ecclesiam per universum terrarum orbem dispersam, sive ad totum genus humanum, nectere argumentum, nulla ratio permittit. Judæi jussi sunt summum Sacerdotem consulere, atque in ejus responso ex lege reddito acquiescere: Ergò omnes homines, etiam qui nunquam de Pontifice audiverunt, debent adire Romanum Pontificem, atque illum pro suo Judice agnoscere. Huc accedit, quod Iudæorum summus Pontifex, non Pontificis Romani, sed Christi typus fuit, ad quem translato Sacerdotio Ius etiam illud transijt.

Tertium argumentum, quod videtur alicujus esse momenti, tale est: Scriptura sacra varios sensus recipit, nec potest ipsa dicere, quis sit verus. Ergò Scriptura sacra non potest esse summus Iudex Controversiarum.

Respondeo: & Nego Antecedens, quod est falsissimum, gemino constans mendacio. Prius est: Scripturam varios sensus recipere. Falsitas assertionis hujus evidentissimè patet ex ijs, quæ suprà mox ab initiò Quintæ hujus Controversiæ, de varijs Scripturæ sensibus diximus. Non enim Scriptura propterea varios sensus admittit, quia varij in eam sensus inferuntur: sed unus, simplex, & perpetuus est Scripturæ sensus. Posterius mendacium est: Scripturam non posse loqui, aut dicere, quis si verus sensus. Quod ipsum mendacium in Colloquio nupero, subindè repetijt Gretserus. Quæ sanè blasphemia non tàm in Scripturam, quàm in DEUM ipsum redundat. Loquitur enim DEUS nobis in Scripturis, quasi ore ad os: Hanc propterea jubet scrutari Servator, quia ipsa testetur de ipso. Ioh. 5, 39. Hinc Scriptura ipsa loqui ac dicere perhibetur. Johan. 7, 42. Nonne Scriptura dicit. Rom. 4, 3. Quid enim dicit Scriptura. Et cap. 9, 17. Dicit Scriptura Pharaoni. Gal. 4, 30. Sed quid dicit Scriptura: Et passim alibi. Et cur, obsecro, Scriptura hæc dicitur Verbum DEI, si non DEUS in eo nobis loquitur. Proindè quemadmodum qui Literas amici legit, mentem ejus atque sententiam facilè percipit, etiamsi ipsæ literæ vocem articulatam non emittant: Ita etiam Scriptura Sacra DEI est Epistola, missa ad genus humanum, in qua mentem suam atq; voluntatem satis perspicuè nobis proponit.

Quartò proferunt & istud argumentum ex loco comparatorum: In omni Repub. benè constituta Lex & Judex distinctæ res sunt, & Lex quidem docet, quid agendum: Judex autem Legem interpretatur, & secundum eam homines dirigit. Ergò par debet esse ratio in Ecclesia.

Sed Respondeo, & nego, eandem planè esse rationem Legis, Judicumque forensium: Et Scripturæ, ejusque interpretis. Forensis enim Judex pro varietate circumstantiarum mutare aliquid in suo decreto potest, & de summo jure aliquid remittere, propter probabilem aliquam causam: De sacrâ verò Scripturâ ejusque interpretatione, expressa habemus mandata, ut neqs addamus aliquid, neq; auferamus aliquid: neq; declinemus vel ad dextram, vel ad sinistram, Apoc. 22, 18. Deut. 17, 11.

Deinde respondeo ἐκ περιουσίας, si vel maximè concedatur, parem utrobique esse rationem: quando tamen de sententia Legis est quæstio, certè ne forensi quidem Iudici licet Legem contra seipsam interpretari: sed Legis sententiam ex ipsis ejus verbis tenetur declarare. Quo respectu Judex politicus non est supra, sed infra Legem, atque ita seipsos Jesuitæ hac similitudine jugulant. Si enim Scriptura Lex est, uti certè est: utique vi similitudinis hujus Iudex consentanea Legi pronunciet, seq; ipsum Legi subjiciat, oportet.

Quintò sic obstrepunt: Si Verbum DEI ad hærefeωn refutationem sufficeret, quatuor illa Oecumenica Concilia (Nicenum, Constantinopolitanũ, Ephesinũ, Chalcedonense) Ecclesiæ autoritate, nunquam fuissent usa. Atqui usa sunt, uti patet ex ipsis Conciliorum illorum actis. Ergò.

Respondeo: peccat hoc argumentum primùm Ignoratione Elenchi. Neque enim unquam vel per febrim somniavimus, Ecclesiæ autoritatem planè nullam esse, quam utique, uti supra ostensum, suo modo ac respectu, Iudicis partes in refutandis hæresibus sustinere, in confesso est. Sed hoc controvertitur, An Verbum DEI Ecclesiæ autoritate indigeat ad supplementum: Item, An Ecclesia etiam posthabitis & neglectis Scripturis possit pro arbitrio definire Controversias. Ubi negativam utrobique tuemur. Et sanè si pro affirmativa ex argumento isto pugnare velint, manifesta emergit petitio principij, & Sophisticatio πᾶς τὸ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Hoc ipsum enim quæritur, & ab Adversarijs probandum est: An ideò Scriptura non sufficiat ad hærefeωn refutationẽ, quia & Patres & Concilia ad Scripturæ sacræ testimonia, adjunxerunt etiam Ecclesiæ consensum? Subordinata enim hæc esse, ac proinde se mutuò non excludere, sed diversis gradibus ac respectibus simul stare posse, jam aliquoties demonstratum.

Sextò sic insurgunt: DEUS certum judicandi ordinem in Ecclesia sua constituit per homines: ipse igitur non est summus Iudex Veritatis: sed alij Iudicandi potestatem delegavit, nempe Pontifici Romano. Respondeo. Fallit argumentum 1. Sophismate τꭣ̃ μὴ ἀιτίꭣ ὡς ἀιτίꭣ. Neque enim DEUS ideò certùm judicandi ordinem in Ecclesia constituit per homines, ut illi definirent de dubijs ex suo cerebro & arbitrio, sed ut alligati essent ad Legem & ad Testimònium, neque ab eo vel latum pilum deflecterent. 2. fallit Sophismate ὠπꭣ̃ τꭣ̃ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: Non enim homines sunt judices primarij: sed potiùs supremi Judicis ministri, cujus vocem in Scripturis sonantem, quamprimùm negligunt, mox non rectum, sed falsum ferunt judicium: uti Propheta loquitur. Tandem fallit Sophismate ὠπꭣ̃ τꭣ̃ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Nulla enim militat ratio Consequentiæ: DEUS in Ecclesia constituit certum judicandi ordinem per homines: Ergò ipse addicavit se hoc Judicandi jure: & partes supremi Judicij delegavit Pontifici Romano, vel Ecclesiæ. Subordinata, uti jam paulò ante dictum, non pugnant. Primaria causa sibi subordinat causas secundas & intermedias, quibus sine ullo vel sui præjudicio, vel ulla sui juris diminutione utitur tanquam ministris & famulis: ad præscriptum legis suæ quasi devinctis & obligatis.

Septimò: Si solis pugnandum sit Scripturæ testimonijs, nunquam lites cum protervis finiri possunt.

Respondeo. Error oritur ὠπꭣ̃ τꭣ̃ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Non enim sequitur, Scripturarum testimonijs non potest ita protervia hæreticorum reprimi, ut fateantur se victos esse: Ergò solis Scripturarum testimonijs non possunt finiri Controversiæ. Negatur enim hæc Consequentia, Qua gemina est Controversiarum sive litium finitio: Una, quæ respicit ipsas hæreses sive errores: Altera, quæ spectat proterviam hæreticorum sive errantium. Jam verò si prior illa finitio Controversiarum, non priùs posset subsistere, quàm posterior etiam hæc ipso actu subsequeretur, & hæretici publicè faterentur se victos esse: tum nulla unquam controversia, perfectè definita fuit: imò nec Christus ipse & Apostoli ritè ac perfectè diremisse Controversias cum Scribis & Pharisæis. Proinde falsitas argumenti hujus vel inde elucet, quod ex posterioris hujusmodi negatione, vitiosissimè instituitur collectio ad negationem prioris etiam illius modi. Perfecta enim Controversiarum decisio non consistit in hæreticorum obsequio: sed in demonstratione ipsorum errorum, non nisi ex Scripturis sacris petita. Quo suo officio sufficientissimè fungitur Scriptura, sive hæretici acquiescant, sive non.

Et hîc pedem figimus, & aliorum etiam argumentorum Jesuvviticorum refutationem desiderantes, partim ad protocollum Colloquij Ratisponensis proximi: partim verò ad libellos nostratium Theologorum hac de re ex professo editos, ablegamus: præsertim cum ex his, quæ hactenus disputata sunt, de reliquis facillimè possit judicari.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: On the Perfection of the Scriptures

Sacred Scripture is perfect, and in all respects so absolute, that it contains all things which pertain to salvation, faith, and the morals of living piously.

CONFIRMATION.

Faith entirely indubitable is given to this assertion by many testimonies of the Scriptures, which are indeed good, such as these: John 5:39. Search the Scriptures: For you think you have eternal life in them: and these are they which testify of me.

John 20:31. These are written, that you might believe that Jesus is the Christ the Son of GOD, and that believing you might have life through his name.

Rom. 15:4. Whatsoever things were written, were written for our learning, that through patience and comfort of the Scriptures, we might have hope.

1 John 1:4 & 5. These things we write to you, that your joy may be FULL: And this is the announcement, which we have heard from him, and announce to you. Furthermore, this Word, which both Paul, and John, and the remaining Apostles heard from CHRIST, and announced by living voice, was clearly the same as that which they afterwards committed to writing. The same John clearly testifies. 1. c. 2, 7. I write no new commandment to you, but the old commandment, which you had from the beginning: The old commandment, moreover, is the Word, which you have heard.

Psalm 19:8. The law of GOD is perfect, converting the soul, Gal. 1:8. Even if we or an Angel from Heaven should preach the Gospel to you beyond that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema.

But that one Apostolic passage, which exists in 2 Tim. 3:14, 15, 16, & 17, can be worth all others, in which we also deservedly plant our foot against the Jesuits in this dispute: For it reads thus: But you continue in those things which you have learned, and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you have learned them: and that from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures (γράμματα), which are able to make you wise (σοφίσαι) unto salvation, through the faith which is in Christ Jesus. For all Scripture is divinely inspired and useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction, which is in righteousness: that the man of GOD may be perfect (ἄρτιος), perfectly instructed (ἐξηρτισμένος) for every good work.

Since this Apostolic testimony, indeed, comprises in a certain brief compendium all things which can and ought to be said concerning the perfection and sufficiency of the Scriptures: it is my pleasure to demonstrate this very thing in order, part by part. In the beginning, therefore, the subject of this proposition comes under consideration, which is ALL SCRIPTURE: That this, under its scope and complexity, comprises not only the books of the Old Testament, but also the writings of the New Testament, as many as existed at the time this Epistle was written: this will have to be demonstrated a little later in the dissolution of a certain Jesuit objection. That which must be considered chiefly concerning the notation of the subject is: Is the universal particle (ALL) to be taken collectively concerning the whole body of Canonical books which existed at that time, or indeed distributively, or separately, concerning individual books, individual chapters, periods, and sentences? The Jesuit race, and especially Stapleton and Bellarmine, defend this latter opinion: But wrongly. For although we do not deny that no Biblical writing, nay, no chapter, and thus no period and no sentence, is found in the Canonical Scriptures which cannot, γενικῶς in its own way and respect, be referred both to διδασκαλίαν and to the remaining ends noted by the Apostle: yet we do not undeservedly deny that the Apostle is acting in this place generally, concerning any doctrine, any refutation, correction, or instruction. For the very words themselves, and the whole context of the Apostolic passage, clearly evince that the Apostle is speaking κατ’ έξοχήν, or definitely concerning such doctrine, refutation, correction, and instruction, from which the man of GOD may emerge perfect and perfectly instructed for every good work: indeed, in such a way that he may be skilled in the refutation not of one or another heresy or error, but of all; that he may hold the doctrine not of one or another, but of all Articles of faith; that, finally, he may know the correction of all vices and the instruction of all virtues, not by half, but in full: a thing which not one or another book, but the whole System of the Canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testament provides. Therefore, we most firmly conclude that the Apostolic Aphorism is to be taken concerning the whole body of the Canonical books of both Testaments: and consequently, we interpret the universal particle (πᾶσα, all) most correctly not distributively, concerning the parts of Canonical Scripture, but collectively, concerning the whole body: a thing which will be demonstrated more evidently below with examples. Just as this particle also sounds the same elsewhere as 'the whole' or 'the entire': as Colossians 2:9, πᾶν πλήρωμα, the whole fullness, etc.

The other member, which deserves consideration in the Apostolic Aphorism, respects that Predicate which is enunciated concerning the Subject, namely, concerning the whole Scripture, that it is, to be sure, not only by reason of its origin or efficient cause, but also in respect of its efficacy and virtue, θεόπνευstos, divinely inspired. Whence the first argument of confirmation immediately emerges of its own accord, and it is such: As is the cause, so is the effect: But indeed

The efficient cause of Holy Scripture is by far the most perfect of all, which is GOD: Therefore, it is necessary that Scripture itself, as an effect, should also be most perfect.

But the Jesuit race clamors that, at the time of the Apostle Paul, the books of the New Testament did not yet exist: therefore, this Apostolic Elogium also cannot be accommodated to the books of the New Testament.

But I respond that, in the beginning, a παραλογισμὸν τẽ μὴ ἐπομένε is committed: For it does not follow: The books of the New Testament did not exist then. Therefore, the Apostle did not understand this Elogium of his to refer to them. For when the Apostle names πᾶσαν γραφlώ, ALL Scripture, which is divinely inspired: either he certainly includes by this mark of Universality all books which were already consigned by the inspiration of GOD, and which could be consigned in the progress of time by the same instinct: or the Consequent would be that the books of the New Testament are not θεοπνεύςες: For whatever is excluded from the complexity of the subject is also excluded from the complexity of the predicate. Or if they are θεοπνεύςες, they are nevertheless not of the same authority and perfection as the θεοπνεύςες books of the Old Testament are. Since both of these are absurd, nay, blasphemous against GOD himself, the first and supreme Author of the books of the New Testament: it remains that the former is true, that the Apostle wished to extend the mark of universality to all θεοπνεύςες books, not so much those which already existed at the time of the Apostle, as those which could be added to the Canon of the Old Testament in the New Testament by the authority and instinct of GOD. Next, a manifest ψεῦδος is committed in this argument. For it is false, and simply conflicts with more accurate Chronology, that at the time of the Apostle, when he himself wrote this latter Epistle to Timothy, no books of the New Testament existed. Irenaeus indeed reports in book 3, chapter 1, that Matthew published his Gospel in the year in which Paul was founding the Roman Church: which falls in the year of Christ 54, the 20th from His Ascension. Although Eusebius, in book 3, chapter 21, refers the publication of the Gospel of Matthew to the year of Christ 41. Thus the same Eusebius is a witness in book 3, chapters 4 and 21, that the Gospel of Luke was published, written in the Greek language, in the year of Christ 52. But the Gospel of Mark in the year of Christ 61, according to the same Eusebius in book 2, chapter 15. Finally, the Acts of the Apostles in the year of Christ 63. Now, it is agreed by the consensus of all historians that the latter Epistle to Timothy was written by the Apostle last of all: and indeed in the year of Christ 68, in that very year in which he himself was again presented to Nero at Rome: as he himself testifies in chapter 4:23. In which same year he was also affected by martyrdom, as Eusebius testifies in book 2, chapter 25. Whence it is evinced that the remaining Epistles of Paul, each and every one, already existed when he wrote this latter one to Timothy: and therefore that the Apostle, even in this Aphorism of his, wished to note not so much the books of the Old, as the writings of the New Testament, as θεοπνευστα. The Apostle himself, in Chapter 1, verse 13 of this latter epistle, gives entirely undoubted assurance to this assertion, in that he sends Timothy to those writings which he has already received: Hold, he says, the form of sound words which you have heard FROM ME, keep that excellent deposit. Therefore, the argument of Bellarmine is ridiculous, inferring thus: Paul testifies that Timothy knew the sacred letters from infancy: But at the time of Timothy's infancy, only the Old Testament existed. Therefore, the Apostle, also adding, ALL Scripture is divinely inspired, etc., is understood by the note of universality to comprehend only the books of the Old Testament. For, to say nothing of the ἀσυλλογισίᾳ (non-syllogism) of four terms, which is confused by the confusion of infantile age with the subsequent more mature age, who, I ask, would think that Timothy had completely neglected the writings of the Evangelists and the Apostle Paul? The contrary is proven by that which Timothy, Acts 16, 3. joined himself as a companion to Paul, and in the cities proposed those dogmas which had been defined by the Apostles at the Council of Jerusalem. And also that he confirmed the Second Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, to the Philippians, Colossians, both to the Thessalonians, and that which was written to Philemon, with his own autograph: as is evident from the beginnings of those Epistles. Who, therefore, would not wonder at, or rather detest, the insanity of the Jesuit, asserting that Timothy had clearly neither seen nor read any writings of the New Testament.

The third member of the observation is taken by that final cause, for which it is divinely inspired and committed to writing; but this is twofold; one closer, the other more remote. The Apostle defines the closer one, asserting that All Scripture is divinely inspired and ὠφέλιμον (useful) for doctrine with respect to sound doctrine: for ἔλεγχον (refutation) of false doctrine: for the correction of vices: and finally for instruction, which is done for righteousness. Whence it pleases me to argue thus again: The most perfect end, absolute in all respects, depends upon a cause likewise perfect and absolute in all respects. But this fourfold end or use already enumerated is most perfect and absolute in all respects.

Therefore, it is necessary that Scripture itself, from which as from a cause this end depends, be most perfect and absolute in all respects.

The major premise shines by its own light. For an imperfect cause never achieves a most perfect end.

The minor premise is established even by the concession of the Adversaries themselves. For besides the four ends already enumerated, nothing can be given or shown that pertains to a full and perfect instruction regarding Religion and morals. Since the entire duty of the Ecclesiastical office is completed in διδασκαλίᾳ (teaching), ἐλέγχῳ (refutation), ἐπανoρθώσει (correction), παιδείᾳ (instruction), as much regarding dogmatics as regarding governance or practical matters.

Therefore, the truth of the Conclusion remains unmoved. The latter, more remote final cause is expressed by the Apostle in these words: that the man of GOD may be perfect, thoroughly equipped for every good work. Where by the man of GOD, he principally denotes the ministers of the Church, whose proper task and office it is to Teach, refute, correct, instruct: but consequently, any faithful man. Moreover, against these two ends, Bellarmine clamors in this sentiment, lib. 4. cap. 10. p. 241. That (it is useful) never signifies, it is sufficient: for whether you say, Scripture is useful for this, or it has this use, or it is referred and ordered to this, or anything else similar: you will never signify that it alone is sufficient. Just as also, he who says, food is useful for nourishing a man, indeed says that food is instituted for this, that it may nourish, but he does not say that food alone is sufficient; For if natural heat is lacking, or some instrument of the body necessary for nutrition, food will not nourish. Thus, the Apostle does not say that Scripture alone is sufficient for teaching, refuting, etc., and therefore for perfecting and equipping a man: but yet that it is profitable and helpful for all these things. I answer 1. The Jesuit wanders off the path, and fights without an adversary: For who of us has ever argued thus: Scripture is useful: Therefore it is sufficient. But rather, from the induction of all parts of most absolute and most sufficient utility, we conclude to the most absolute perfection of the Scriptures themselves. For because no other utility that contributes to this perfection can be given outside the Scriptures: it is rightly inferred that Scripture contains in itself that utility which is joined with most absolute perfection. And because logicians teach that universal affirmative propositions are most correctly converted per accidens, with the quality retained but the quantity changed: therefore, although we do not deny that Not every useful thing is sufficient: yet since it is established that every sufficient thing is useful, by the force of conversion per Accidens, A certain useful thing will be sufficient. And that Holy Scripture is such a useful thing, from the induction of those four parts which are uniquely required for the sufficiency and perfection of the Scriptures, we have demonstrated most evidently a little before. Stapleton attempts to evade this response with such an instance: All perfect and holy men do good works: yet not everyone who does good works is holy and perfect. I answer 1. This argument does not strike us, since we teach that a universal affirmative in a contingent matter is not to be converted simply, but per accidens. Furthermore, it is also false in itself that this proposition is not converted: for since truly good works are not done except by faith: and faith is not without holiness and perfection before GOD: therefore these are necessarily joined, and consequently a universal in a perpetual and necessary matter, with the same quantity retained, is converted. Therefore the Jesuit speaks falsely, arguing that we infer the sufficiency and perfection of Scripture from its bare and simple utility. And it deserves observation that the Apostle himself, before he explains the utility of Scripture through those four parts, asserts the perfection and sufficiency of Scripture so generally that it might seem a wonder if an Adversary dared even to mutter against it.

For the Apostle says that the Scriptures are able to σοφίσαι a man unto salvation, that is, to make him wise. But where there is wisdom, and indeed wisdom unto salvation, there must necessarily be the most absolute perfection of that knowledge which is indeed necessary unto salvation: unless perhaps, by an unheard-of absurdity, one might wish to affirm that Wisdom can coexist with an imperfection of knowledge.

Thirdly, we elicit the perfection of the Scriptures from the fact that the Apostle affirms that the Scriptures cause the man of GOD to be ἄρτιος, perfect, and ἐξηρτισμένος, perfectly instructed for every good work. For whatever instructs a man PERFECTLY for EVERY good work, that must necessarily also be sufficient.

Finally, the distinguished man Dr. Sal. Gesner, in his book on this saying, argues thus: Something is said to be useful in two ways: one, by itself and necessarily: the other, by accident and contingently. By itself, indeed, when it is considered as useful, relatively or πρός τι, and that to which the subject is useful is expressly attached to the subject. Now, when a correlate is attached to the subject which pertains to the το ἗ιναι and the essence and definition of the subject, and which is the specific difference of the subject: there it is predicated καθ' αυτό, by itself, and constitutes a necessary predication, indeed a definition constant in genus and specific difference, taken from its proper πάθει. And this happens in all true and essential definitions of instruments and organs: For whenever anything is defined as an organ, it is necessary to employ the word useful, apt, prepared for this or that: as the eye is an organic member of the body, useful or apt for seeing: the hand is an organ useful for grasping, the foot for walking; the stomach for directing food and drink, etc. And thus consequently also in inanimate (ἀψύχοις) instruments made by art, as: a pen is an instrument useful for writing, a saw for sawing, a knife for cutting, etc. Here, therefore, I ask, what force does the word (useful, apt, suitable) have? Is it that of an assisting cause, as the adversaries contend? By no means: but it signifies exactly the same as sufficient and perfect, because it attaches to the subject a specific difference, taken from its proper use, and from its natural, inherent habit and power, which gives being to the thing and perfects the thing. For if the assigned difference were not sufficient, it would be poorly assigned: but if it is well assigned, then it is certainly also sufficient, as it is that which gives being to the thing and confers upon it the τὸ εὖ καὶ αὐτάρκως εἶναι without any defect. For when I say, the stomach is an internal organ of the body given by nature to an animal, so that it is useful for digesting food, it is the same as if I say that the stomach is sufficient for it to digest food. Nor does the cavil have any place here, that natural heat and the integrity of all the viscera are required for digestion. For the ventricle is not defined outside the animal, which is no longer a ventricle, but an inanimate (ἄψυχον) and empty pouch. And the same is to be established concerning the eye, hand, foot, etc. Where likewise the cavil does not stand, that one hand is not sufficient, one eye, etc., is not sufficient. For we are not defining a hand, eye, ear, foot, etc., in the individual, but the species, which is in each individual. The definitions of the arts, etc., pertain here. See Gesner, tr. D. 2, in the explanation of this Apostolic saying.

But when, through that Relate (useful or suitable), some fortuitous or more remote thing is attached to the subject, which is not contained in its essence and definition: then it signifies only an assisting and concurrent cause. As for example in the instances which Stapleton brings forward: Bread is useful for nourishing the body, not primarily and immediately by itself. For primarily and by itself, bread is only useful for providing the principal part of dry food, as a material cause, to which, from the blessing of GOD and the heat of the stomach, it afterwards happens δευτέρως and ἑπομένως that it becomes suitable nourishment for the body. Thus, rain is useful for generating herbs, not by itself, not primarily and immediately, but secondarily. For by itself and immediately, rain is useful for irrigating the earth, Isa. 55. When that is done, then by the operation of GOD, with the heat of the sun and the fertility of the soil added, it happens to the rain that herbs are generated.

Now that Scripture is primarily and by itself useful for teaching, etc., and not by accident, is evident first because it was inspired by GOD for the purpose that it might be useful for teaching, so that it might be able to σοφίσαι, etc. Secondly, because otherwise it would be useless by itself for teaching. Finally, because nothing else can be given that is useful by itself for teaching.

Latin:

S Acra Scriptura est perfecta, omnibusque numeris ita absoluta, ut contineat omnia, quæ ad salutem, fidem & mores piè vivendi pertinent.

CONFIRMATIO.

FIdem prorsus indubiam assertioni huic faciunt, benè quidem multa Scripturarum testimonia, qualia sunt isthæc: Johan. 5, 39. Scrutamini Scripturas: Nam videmini vobis in ipsis habere vitam æternam: & hæ sunt, quæ testificantur de me.

Johan. 20, 31. Hæc sunt scripta, ut credatis Jesum esse Christum Filium DEI, & ut credentes vitam habeatis per nomen ejus.

Rom. 15, 4. Quæcunq; scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut per patientiam & consolationem Scripturarum, spem habeamus.

1. Joh. 1, 4. & 5. Hæc scribimus vobis, ut Gaudium Vestrum sit PLENUM: Et hæc est annunciatio, quam audivimus ab eo, & annunciamus vobis. Cæterum Verbum hoc, quod & Paulus, & Johannes, ac reliqui Apostoli audiverunt à CHRISTO, & vivâ voce annunciarunt, idem planè fuisse cum eo, quod postmodum literis consignarunt. Idem Johannes perspicuè testatur. 1. c. 2, 7. Non novum mandatum scribo vobis, sed mandatum vetus, quod habuistis ab initio: Mandatum autem Vetus, est Verbum, quod audivistis.

Psalm. 19, 8. Lex DEI perfecta est, convertens animam, Gal. 1, 8. Etiamsi nos aut Angelus de Cælo Evangelizet vobis præter id, quod vobis Evangelizavimus, anathema esto.

Verùm unicus ille locus Apostolicus, qui extat in 2. Tim. 3, 14. 15. 16. & 17. potest esse instar omnium, in quo etiam adversus Jesuvvitas hac in disputatione pedem meritò figimus: Sic autem ille habet: Tu verò maneto in ijs, quæ didicisti, & quæ tibi concredita sunt, sciens, à quo didiceris: & quia ab infantia Sacras Scripturas (γράμματα) nosti, quæ te possunt (σοφίσαι) sapientem reddere ad salutem, per fidem, quæ est in Christo Jesu. Omnis enim Scriptura divinitùs est inspirata & utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in justitia: ut perfectus (ἄρτιος) sit homo DEI, ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus (ἐξηρτισμένος)

Quod fanè testimonium Apostolicum, cum brevi quodam compendio comprehendat omnia, quæ de Scripturarum perfectione ac fufficientiâ dici posfunt ac debent: placet per partes ordine istud ipsum demonstrare. Initiò igitur sub considerationem venit Subjectum propositionis hujus, quod est OMNIS SCRIPTURA: Quod sub suo ambitu & complexu non libros tantùm Veteris Testamenti, sed & scripta Novi Testamenti, quotquot quidem tempore scriptæ hujus Epistolæ extiterunt, complecti: paulò pòst in dissolutione objecti cujusdã Jesuvitici, demonstrandum fuerit. Illud circa subjecti notationem præcipuè considerandum venit, An particula universalis (OMNIS) collectivè de toto corpore librorum Canonicorum, qui tunc extabant, an verò distributivè sive seorfim de singulis libris, singulisq; capitibus, periodis ac sententiis, sit accipienda? Gens Jesuvitica & Stapletonus præsertim ac Bellarminus, posteriorem hanc tuentur sententiam: Sed malè. Etsi enim non imus inficias, nullum scriptum Biblicum, imò nullum caput, átq; adeò periodum & sententiam nullam in Scripturis Canonicis reperiri; quæ non γενικῶς suo modo ac respectu, tùm ad διδασκαλίαν, tùm ad reliquos fines ab Apostolo notatos referri possit: tamen illud haud immeritò negamus, quod D. Apostolus hoc loco agat generaliter, de quavis doctrina, de quavis refutatione, correctione, institutione. Verba enim ipsa, & tota loci Apostolici συνέτεια luculenter evincit, κατ’ έξοχήν loqui Apostolum, sive definitè de tali doctrina, Refutatione, Correctione & institutione, ex quâ homo DEI evadat perfectus, & ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus: ita quidem, ut non unius, aut alterius hæreseωs sive erroris, sed omnium refutationem calleat, ut non unius aut alterius, sed omnium Articulorum fidei doctrinam teneat: ut denique; non ex semiffe, sed ex asse omnium vitiorum correctionem, omniumque virtutum institutionem noverit: id quod non unus aut alter liber; sed totum Systema Scripturæ Canonicæ Veteris & Novi Testamenti præstat. Proindè de toto corpore librorum Canonicorum utriusque Testamenti, Aphorismum Apostolicum accipiendum esse, firmissimè colligimus: & per consequens particulam universalem (πᾶσα omnis) non distributivè, de Scripturæ Canonicæ partibus, sed collectivè, de toto corpore rectissimè interpretamur: id quod infrà exemplis evidentiùs demonstrabitur. Quemadmodum & aliàs particula hæc idem sonat, ac totum sive universum: ut Coloss. 2, 9. πᾶν πλήρωμα, tota plenitudo &c.

Alterum membrum, quod Aphorismo Apostolico considerationem meretur, respicit Prædicatum illud, quod de Subjecto, nempe de tota Scriptura enunciatur, quòd nimirùm non modò ratione originis, sive causæ efficientis, sed etiam respectu efficaciæ & virtutis, sit θεόπνευstos, divinitùs inspirata. Unde primum statim confirmationis argumentum ultrò emergit, idque tale: Qualis causa, talis effectus: At verò

Scriptura sacra causa efficiens longè omnium est perfectissima, quæ est DEUS: Ergò Scripturam etiam ipsam tanquam effectum, perfectissimam esse oportet.

Sed obstrepit gens Jesuitica, tempore Apostoli Pauli, nondum extitisse libros Novi Testameti: proinde Elogium etiam istud Apostolicum ad libros Novi Testamenti accommodari haud posse.

Sed Respondeo, committi initiò παραλογισμὸν τẽ μὴ ἐπομένε: Non enim sequitur: Libri Novi Testamenti tùm non extiterunt. Ergò neque Apostolus de illis elogium istud suum intellexit. Quando enim Apostolus nominat πᾶσαν γραφlώ, OMNEM Scripturam, quæ divinitùs est inspirata: Aut certè notâ hac Universalitatis comprehendit omnes libros, qui & jam modò inspiratione DEI erant consignati: & qui progressu temporis ejusdem instinctu consignari poterant: aut Consequens fuerit, Libros Novi Testamenti non esse θεοπνεύςες: Quicquid enim excluditur à complexu subjecti, idem excluditur etiam à complexu prædicati. Vel si θεόπνευςοι, haud tamen esse ejusdem autoritas & perfectionis, cujus sint libri θεόπνευςοι Veteris Testamenti. Quod utrumque cùm sit absurdum, imò blasphemum in ipsum DEUM, librorum Novi Testamenti Autorem primum ac summum: relinquitur prius illud verum esse, Apostolum notam universalitatis extendere voluisse, ad omnes libros θεοπνεύςες, non tàm eos, qui jam tempore Apostoli extabat, quàm eos, qui Canoni Veteris Testamenti, in Novo Testamento autoritate ac instinctu DEI potuerunt adjici. Deinde committitur in hoc argumento manifestum ψεῦδος. Falsum enim est, & cum accuratiore Chronologia simpliciter pugnat, Tempore Apostoli, quo quidem ipse hanc posteriorem scripsit ad Timotheũ, nullos libros Novi Testamenti extitisse. Refert sanè Irenæus lib. 3. cap. 1. Matthæum suum edidisse Evangelium eo anno, quo Romanam Ecclesiam Paulus fundaret: id quod incidit in A. C. 54. ab Ascensione ejusdem, 20. Quanquam Eusebius lib 3. cap 21. publicationẽ Evangelij Matthæi refert ad A. C. 41. Sic testis est idem Eusebius lib. 3. cap. 4. & 21. Evangelium Lucæ editum esse, Græco sermone conscriptum, A. C. 52. Evangelium verò Marci. A. C. 61. eodem referente Eusebio lib. 2 cap 15. Acta denique Apostolorum A. C. 63. Jam verò posteriorem ad Timotheum, omnium postremam scriptam esse ab Apostolo, omnium historicorum consensu constat: & quidem A.C. 68. eo nimirùm anno, quo ipse iterum Romæ sistebatur Neroni: uti ipsemet testatur cap. 4. 23. Quo ipso anno etiam martyrio affectus est, teste Eusebio. lib. 2. cap. 25. Unde evincitur, reliquas Epistolas Pauli singulas atque universas, jam tùm extitisse, quando posteriorem hanc scripsit ad Timotheum: ac proindè Apostolum etiam Aphorismo hoc suo, non tàm libros Veteris, quàm scripta Novi Testamenti, tanquam θεόπνευςα, notare voluisse. Cui assertioni fidem planè indubiam facit, quod ipse Apostolus Cap. 1, 13. posterioris hujus, Timotheum ablegat ad ea scripta, quæ jam acceperit: Formam, inquiens, Sanorum verborum habe, quæ A ME audivisti, præclarum illud depositum servato. Ridiculum proindè est argumentum Bellarmini sic inferentis: Paulus testatur Timotheum sacras literas novisse ab infantia: At tempore Infantiæ Timothei, extabat tantùm Vetus Testamentum. Ergò Apostolus etiam subjiciens, OMNEM Scripturam, esse divinitùs inspiratam &c. notâ universalitatis tantùm comprehendi libros Veteris Testamenti. Nam ut nihil de ἀσυλλογισίᾳ quatuor terminorum dicamus, quæ ex confusione ætatis infantilis, cum subsecuta ætate maturiore confunditur, quis, quæso, existemet, Timotheum Evangelistarum & Apostoli Pauli scripta prorsus neglexisse? contrarium evincit id, quod Timotheus Act, 16, 3. Paulo comitem se adjunxit, & in civitatibus ea proposuit dogmata, quæ in Concilio Hierosolymitano ab Apostolis erant definita. Quòd item Posteriorem Pauli ad Corinthios, ad Philippenses, Colossenses, utramque ad Thessalonicenses, & eam, quæ ad Philemonem est scripta, suo Chyrographo confirmavit: uti patet ex Epistolarum illarum exordijs. Quis proinde non miretur, vel detestetur potiùs, insaniam Jesuvvitæ, asserentis, Timotheum scripta Novi Testamenti planè nulla vel vidisse, vel legisse.

Tertiū observationis membrum sortitur causa illa finalis, propter quam ea sit divinitùs inspirata, inq; literas relata; Hæc verò duplex est; una propinquior: altera remotior. Propinquioré definit Apostolus afferens, Totam Scripturam divinitùs inspiratā esse ὠφέλιμον utile ad doctrinam respectu sanæ doctrinæ: ad ἔλεγχον sive refutationē falsæ: ad correctionem vitiorum: & denique ad institutionem, quæ fit ad justiciam. Unde sic rursus libet argumentari: Finis perfectissimus, omnibusq; numeris absolutus, dependet à causa itidem perfecta omnibusq; numeris absoluta. Atqui finis sive usus iste quadruplex jam enumeratus, est perfectissimus omnibusq; numeris absolutus.

Ergò Scriptura ipsa, à quà tanquam à causa finis iste dependet, perfectissima, omnibusq; numeris absoluta sit, necesse est.

Major sua luce lucet. Causa enim imperfecta, finem perfectissimum nunquam assequitur.

Minor vel ipsorum Adversariorum concessione constat. Neque enim præter quatuor jam enumeratos fines, quicquam dari aut monstrari potest, quod quidem ad plenam ac perfectam de Religione & moribus institutionem pertineat. Siquidem universum muneris Ecclesiastici officium, absolvitur in διδασκαλίᾳ ἐλέγχῳ, ἐπανoρθώσει, παιδείᾳ, tàm quoad δογματικὰ: quam quoad κυβερνητικὰ ἤ πρακτικά.

Constat proindè Conclusioni sua immota veritas. Posterior causa finalis remotior exprimitur his verbis ab Apostolo: ut homo DEI sit perfectus, ad omne opus bonum absolutus. Ubi per hominem DEI, principaliter quidem notat ministros Ecclesiæ, quorum proprium munus ac officium est, Docere, refutare, corrigere, instituere: Consequenter autem quemlibet hominem fidelem. Cæterùm, adversus duos istos fines, obstrepit Bellarminus in hanc sententiam lib. 4. cap. 10. p. 241. Illud (utilis est) nunquam significat, sufficiens est: sive enim dicas, Scriptura utilis est ad hoc, sive hunc habet usum, sive ad hoc refertur & ordinatur, sive quidlibet aliud simile: nunquam tamen significabis eam solam sufficere. Sicut etiam, qui dicit, cibus utilis est ad nutriendum hominem, dicit quidē cibum ad hoc esse institutū, ut nutriat, sed nō dicit, sufficere solum cibum; Nam si calor naturalis deficiat, aut aliquod instrumentum corporis ad nutritionem necessarium, cibus non nutriet. Itaq; Apostolus non dicit, solam Scripturam sufficere ad docendum, arguendum &c. & proinde ad hominem perficiendum & absolvendum: sed tamen ad hæc omnia prodesse & juvare. Respondeo 1. Jesuvvitam extra oleas vagari, & sine adversario pugnare: Quis enim nostrûm unquàm ita Argumentatus est: Scriptura utilis est: Ergò sufficiens est. Quin potiùs ex inductione omnium partium absolutissimæ & sufficientissimæ utilitatis, colligimus, ad absolutissimam etiam perfectionem ipsarum Scripturarum. Quia enim alia utilitas, quæ ad perfectionem istam faciat, extra Scripturas dari non potest: rectè utique infertur, Scripturam eam in se utilitatem continere, quæ cum perfectione absolutissima sit conjuncta. Et quia Logici tradunt propositiones universales Affirmativas rectissimè converti per accidens, retenta quidem Qualitate, Quantitate autem mutata: ideò, licet haud negemus, Non omne utile esse sufficiens: tamen cùm constet, omne sufficiens esse utile, utique vi conversionis per Accidens, Quoddam utile erit sufficiens. Et tale quidem utile esse Scripturam sacram, ex inductione quatuor illarum partium, quæ ad sufficientiam & perfectionem Scripturarum unicè requiruntur, paulò antè evidentissimè demonstravimus. Eludere conatur Stapletonus hanc responsionem tali instantiâ: Omnes perfecti & sancti viri faciunt opera bona: non tamen quisquis facit bona opera, sanctus & perfectus est. Respondeo 1. Argumentum hoc nos non ferit, cùm nos universalem Affirmativam in materia ἐνδεχομένῃ non simpliciter convertendam, sed per accidens doceamus. Deindè per se quoque falsissimum, non converti istam propositionem: cùm enim opera verè bona non fiant, nisi fide: fides verò non sit absque sanctitate & perfectione coram DEO: ideò hæc necessariò conjuncta sunt, & proinde universalis in materia perpetua & necessaria, retentâ eadem quantitate, convertitur. Proinde falsum dicit Jesuvvita, arguens, Nos sufficientiam atq; perfectionem Scripturæ, ex nuda ac simplici ejus utilitate colligere. Et observationem meretur, quòd Apostolus ipse, priusquam utilitatem Scripturæ per quatuor illas partes explicat, ita generaliter perfectionem & sufficientiam Scripturæ asserit, ut mirum videri possit, si vel contra mutire ausit Adversarius.

Dicit enim Apostolus, Scripturas posse hominem ad salutem σοφίσαι, hoc est sapientem reddere. Ubi verò est sapientia, & sapientia quidem ad salutem, ibi absolutissima perfectio scientiæ illius, quæ quidem ad salutem est necessaria, sit necesse est: nisi fortè per inauditam absurditatem, Sapientiam cum imperfectione scientiæ stare posse, affirmare quis velit.

Tertiò, Scripturæ perfectionem elicimus ex eo, quòd Apostolus affirmat, Scripturas præstare, homo DEI sit ἄρτιος, perfectus, & ad omne opus bonum ἐξηρτισμένος perfectè instructus. Quicquid enim hominem PERFECTE instruit ad OMNE opus bonum, illud utiq; sufficiens etiam sit, necesse est.

Tandem Cl. vir Dn. D. Sal. Gesnerus in libro suo de hoc dicto, ita arguit: Utile aliquid esse duobus modis dicitur: uno, per se & necessariò:altero, per accidens & contingenter. Per se quidem, quando utile, relatè sive πρός τι consideratur, & subjecto expressè attexitur id, ad quod subjectum est utile. Quando jam subjecto attexitur correlatum, quod pertinet ad το ἗ιναι & essentiam ac definitionem subjecti, quodq; est specifica subjecti differentia: ibi prædicatur καθ' αυτό per se & constituit prædicationem necessariam, imò definitionem constantem genere & differentiâ specificâ, à proprio πάθει desumtâ. Atque hoc fit in omnibus instrumentorum ac organorum veris & essentialibus definitionibus: Quandocunq; enim aliquid definitur ut organon, necesse est adhiberi vocabulum utile, aptum, paratum ad hoc aut illud: ut oculus est Organicum corporis membrum, utile sive aptum ad videndum: Manus est Organum utile ad apprehendendum, pes ad ambulandum; stomachus ad dirigendum cibum potumq; &c. Et sic consequenter etiam in instrumentis ἀψύχοις & artificio confectis, ut: calamus est instrumentum utile adscribendum, serra ad secandum, culter ad scindendum &c. Hic igitur quæro, Quâ vim habeat vox (utile, aptum, idoneum?) num causæ adjuvantis, ut Adversarij contendunt? Nequaquam: sed idem planè significat, quod sufficiens & perfectum, quia attexit subjecto specificam differentiam, desumptam à proprio usu, & naturali insita habitudine ac potentia, quæ dat esse rei, atq; rem perficit. Nisi enim sufficiens esse affignata differentia, malè esset assignata: si verò benè, utiq; etiam sufficiens, utpote, quæ dat esse rei, & confert ei τὸ εὖ καὶ αὐτάρκως εἶναι sine ullo defectu. Cum n. dico, Stomachus est organũ internũ corporis naturâ datum animali, ut sit utile ad concoquendum cibum, idem est, ac si dicam, stomachum ei sufficere ad concoquendũ cibum. Neq; locum hîc habet cavillũ, quod requiratur ad concoctionẽ, calor naturalis, & integritas omnium viscerum. Non enim definitur ventriculus extra animal, qui jam non amplius ventriculus, sed ἄψυχον & inanis utriculus est. Idemq; de oculo, manu, pede &c. est statuendũ. Ubi similiter non obstat cavillus, quòd una manus non sufficiat, unus oculus &c. non sufficiat. Non enim unam in individuo, manum, oculú, aurem, pedem &c. definimus; sed speciem, quæ est in utroque individuo. Huc pertinent definitiones artium &c. Vide Gesnerum tr. D. 2. explicatione hujus dicti Apostolici.

Quando verò per Relatum illud (utile vel idoneum) attexitur subjecto quoddam fortuitum, aut longiùs remotum, quod in ejus Essentia & definitione non continetur: tùm significat causam solùm adjuvantem & concurrentem. Ut verbi gratiâ in Exemplis, quæ adducit Stapletonus: Panis est ad alendum corpus utile, non per se primò & immediatè. Nam primò & per se, Panis solummodò est utilis ad præbendam præcipuam partem alimenti aridi, tanquam causa materialis, cui ex benedictione DEI, & calore stomachi, id postea δευτέρως & ἑπομένως contingit, ut fiat idoneum nutrimentum corporis. Sic pluvia est utilis ad generandas herbas non per se, non primò & immediatè, sed secundariò. Nam per se & immediatè, pluvia utilis est ad irrigandam terram Jes. 55. Quod cùm factum est, tùm operatione DEI, accedente calore Solis, & fertilitate soli, accidit pluviæ, ut progenerentur herbæ.

Jam quòd Scriptura primò, per se sit utilis, ad docendum &c. & non per accidens, constat primò, quia ideo â DEO est inspirata, ut sit utilis ad docendum, ut possit σοφίσαι &c. Deinde, quia aliàs per se esset inutilis ad docendum. Tandem, quia nihil aliud dari potest, quod per se utile sit ad docendum.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: I. Objection of Stapleton

I. Objection of Stapleton.
