Godliness is useful for all things: yet not sufficient: because bodily exercise is useful for a little, 1 Tim. 4.

I answer. A sophism of vicious opposition. For godliness and bodily exercise are not opposed antithetically (ἀντιθετικῶς): but are compared subordinately (ὑπαλλήλως). For godliness also equally embraces that external or bodily exercise (γυμνασίαν): such as fastings, vigils, abstinence, and similar works. Now because the Apostle says that godliness is useful for all things: he certainly shows that it is also sufficient. Since nothing can be given that contributes to either eternal or temporal happiness which godliness does not embrace under its scope.

II. Stapleton's objection.

Pastors and Doctors are useful for obtaining eternal life: they are not, however, sufficient on that account: but only an assisting cause.

I answer. The ministry, when it is compared with GOD, is an assisting cause, which no one denies: but when it is compared in itself with its end and effect, it is certainly a sufficient cause in its own order.

But, cast down from this stronghold, the Jesuits betake themselves to other κρησφύγετα, by which they may be able to evade this illustrious testimony of the Apostle. Therefore, in place of a second argument, they object: that the Scriptures sufficiently instruct and perfect a man in that respect, not because they alone are sufficient: but because they contain many things expressly: and what they do not contain, they show from where they are to be sought. But I answer: In the beginning, the Jesuit is not disputing, but trifling. For the Apostle does not ascribe some, but a plenary sufficiency to Scripture: as that which can make one wise for salvation, and to instruct a man perfectly for every good work. Furthermore, if Scripture contained only some particular sufficiency, and showed from where a fuller one ought to be sought: certainly there would have been no need for the Holy Spirit to publish so many books of Scripture: but He could have been content with one or two, and Why would it not be permitted to depart from the Scriptures either to the right or to the left, if Scripture were imperfect? Finally, the Jesuit begs the question by asserting that Scripture shows from where those things which are lacking in the Scriptures themselves are to be sought? For it is necessary that he first prove this very thing, before he so boldly pronounces it as if it were an ἀπόῤῥητον (secret).

The third Jesuit argument is such: The Apostle says: ALL Scripture is useful, etc. Therefore, if the perfection and sufficiency of Scripture is evidently gathered from thence, then certainly every Biblical Book will contain this perfection: Since All Scripture signifies any sacred book whatsoever. But the latter is false. Therefore, the former is as well.

I answer. The argument proceeds from a part: and therefore concludes nothing at all: For no reason of Consequence holds in this argument: In many places of Scripture, as also in common usage of speech, the particle All is frequently taken distributively: Therefore it must be accepted thus everywhere. For this Consequence is overturned by contrary examples, in which the Universal particle, ALL, signifies not only distributively the individuals of a genus: but also collectively, the Genus of individuals, or the Whole: as Matt. 3:5, All Judea, and all the region: that is, the whole of Judea. Eph. 4:16, πᾶν τὸ σῶμα: where the Latin Vulgate itself rendered it: The whole Body. Thus Matt. 21:10, πᾶσα πόλις, the whole city. For the discourse is about one city, and not indeed about every one, or distributively about any city whatsoever. And indeed that this little word is to be understood collectively is evident even from this: because otherwise not only individual Biblical books: but also individual chapters of books: individual verses of chapters: nay, even individual words of verses, would all be useful: The reason is: Because that distributive meaning, which the Jesuits urge, can also be accommodated to individual verses, and individual words, and individual books. But because they themselves find it necessary to confess that this is false and absurd: it is truly a wonder if they do not notice the prodigious vanity of their objection.

Moreover, if the Jesuits frame their argument thus: No individual Biblical book is sufficient and perfect: Therefore neither is the whole Scripture taken together: they certainly put forward a notable futility, to be laughed at even by children: For a Consequence from a part to the whole does not hold negatively. Furthermore, Scripture is considered in two ways: either as it is some whole body, collected and joined together from all the books of both Testaments: or as it is considered and accepted separately and individually according to its individual parts. In the former way and respect, Scripture being accepted, it embraces also all the ends joined together; διδασκαλίαν, ἔλεγχον, ἐπανόρθωσιν, καὶ παιδείαν: Moreover, when Scripture is taken in the latter way and respect, regarding individual parts considered separately: we certainly grant willingly that not all these ends are intended by the Holy Spirit in individual chapters, sentences, words, or even individual books, especially the smaller and purely historical ones: but in different ones, different ends: yet all of them together concur in that entire body of Scripture: and that, sufficiently and perfectly: so that nothing at all can be added from outside Scripture to complete the sufficiency of Scripture.

Fourthly, Bellarmine rises up thus: When this Epistle was written, the Apocalypse did not yet exist, nor the Gospel of John, and perhaps something else was missing from the body of Scripture: Therefore the Apostolic Aphorism cannot be understood of the whole Canon of Scripture.

But I answer, the Jesuit's argument labors under the Sophism of Ignorance of the Refutation and a vicious definition. For the integrity and perfection of the Canon is not to be defined by the mere number of books, as great and of such a kind as it is today: But partly by the perfection of the doctrine itself, and partly by the number of those books which GOD Himself willed to complete the Canon: as for example: In the time of Moses, the volume of the Pentateuch constituted the whole Canon, concerning which GOD Himself testified that it was so perfect that it was not lawful for any mortal to add anything to it, or to take anything away. Similarly, after the Prophetic books were added in the progress of time: and indeed by divine authority: then certainly the Canon was also whole, perfect, and entire: so much so, that Abraham, placed in Paradise, would not have the brothers of the rich glutton referred to anyone but Moses and the Prophets, Luke 16. Thus, when afterwards some books of the New Testament were added, of which we showed above that Timothy also had a copy: and finally the Apocalypse, the Gospel, and the Epistles of John were added: even then the Canon of Scripture was whole, full, and entire. Since those additions of others, individually and universally, neither argue the imperfection of the Canon of the prior time, nor did they add any new doctrine to the pristine Canon: but they only explained that most ancient doctrine, already comprised in the Mosaic books, more deeply, and illustrated it more richly with various Examples and histories: and that not by the authority and will of men, but of GOD Himself: so that if the Romanists wish to gather from these additions of books the completion of their own Traditions, they commit a gross Ignorance of the Refutation. Wherefore, although there is no doubt that Timothy did not see or read all the books of the New Testament: yet because the Apostle speaks indefinitely and in general about the Canon, which both existed at that time and was of such a kind, and contained full and perfect doctrine: and indeed by the command of GOD other books were added afterwards, it is certainly proven even from this that the Apostolic Aphorism contains these books also, inasmuch as they pertain to the Canon of Scripture, within its scope.

Fifthly, the Jesuit faction objects thus: The Apostle is not dealing in this place with the written Word, but with the heard Word. Therefore, this passage is poorly applied to the written Word. They prove the antecedent from the fact that the Apostle says, Hold fast those things which you have heard from me.

I answer. The Jesuit errs in two ways. 1. By the fallacy of τὸ μὴ αἰτίς ὡς αἰτίᾳ (treating that which is not a cause as a cause). For Timothy is not to be thought to have made no progress from the reading of the Holy Scriptures, just because he learned the form of sound words from the Apostle. As if both could not stand together; nay, rather, one presupposes the other rather than excludes it; especially since the Apostle expressly mentions ἱερῶν γραμμάτων (sacred writings) SCRIPTURES.

Then the Jesuit is deceived by the fallacy of the vicious Consequent: For what, I ask, is the reason for the consequence: Timothy learned the form of sound words from Paul by the information of the living voice. Therefore, Paul delivered something else to Timothy by living voice than what he later comprehended in writing? The subsequent sixth and final Question or Controversy, about which we must dispute, will show the nature of these collections.

But let it suffice to have said these things concerning the Apostolic Aphorism. There remain, however, in the Scriptures no less evident passages, clearly demonstrating the perfection and sufficiency of Holy Scripture.

Therefore, he provides another Argument, the passage Acts 20:27. I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of GOD. Whence I argue thus:

If the Apostle declared to the Ephesians not one part or another, but all the counsel of GOD: and afterwards comprehended the same mystery of GOD in a written Epistle: It follows, 1. That the doctrine of the Apostle is perfect and absolute in all respects, both as to the information of faith and of morals. 2. That this very perfection is to be drawn from nowhere else than from Scripture itself.

But the Antecedent is true, which is evident from a comparison of the passage Acts 20:27 and Eph. 3:2, therefore the Consequent is true.

A third Argument may be borrowed from the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1:1. God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son: Whence we can infer thus.

If GOD spoke to men concerning the business of our Salvation first through the Prophets: Then through the Son revealed in the flesh, and through his ministers, the Apostles: It follows that in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles, those things which are necessary for our Salvation are perfectly contained. But the Antecedent is true, therefore the Consequent is also true.

The connection of the Major premise is evident 1. from this. Because no one knows better what is required for our salvation than GOD himself. 2. Because such is the Φιλαν- θρωπία (love for mankind) of our GOD, that He has kept nothing in secret which pertains to the business of our Salvation. 3. Because the Apostles themselves assign this perfection to the Scriptures Ἐξαρχή- δην (from the beginning): as Rom. 15:4. For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the SCRIPTURES might have hope. And John 5:46. For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me. If you do not believe his writings, how shall you believe my words?

The final Argument is supplied by the Unanimous consensus of Orthodox Antiquity, which we shall touch upon in a few words.

Augustine, book 2 of Christian Doctrine, chapter 9. In those things which are plainly set forth in Scripture, all those things are found which contain faith and the morals of living. Chrysostom, Homily 1 on Titus. The Gospel contains all things, both present and future; honor, piety, faith, he included all things together in the word of preaching. Hilary, book 12 on the Trinity. The word of GOD and true wisdom, the doctrine by which He speaks, are both perfect and absolute. Athanasius against the Gentiles. The holy and divinely inspired Scriptures are sufficient for ALL instruction of truth. Cyril, book 12 on John. Not all things which the Lord did are written down: but those things which the writers thought sufficient both for morals and for dogmas: so that, shining with right faith and works and truth, we may arrive at the kingdom of heaven through Jesus Christ.

Latin:

I. Objectio Stapletoni.

Pietas ad omnia est utilis: non tamen sufficiens: quia corporalis Exercitatio ad modicum utilis est 1. Tim. 4.

Respondeo. Sophisma vitiosæ oppositionis. Neque enim pietas & corporalis Exercitatio ἀντιθετικῶς opponuntur: sed ὑπαλλήλως comparantur. Pietas enim etiam illam externam sive corporalem γυμνασίαν æquè complectitur: ut Jejunia, Vigilias, abstinentiam & similia opera. Jam quia Apostolus dicit, Pietatem ad omnia esse utilem: utiq; illam sufficientem etiam esse ostendit. Siquidem nihil dari potest, quod quidem vel ad æternam, vel temporalem felicitatem faciat, quod Pietas sub suo ambitu non complectatur.

II. Objectio Stapletoni.

Pastores & Doctores sunt utiles ad vitam æternam consequendam: non tamen propterea sunt sufficientes: sed tantùm causa adjuvans.

Respondeo. Ministerium, quando cum DEO confertur, est causa adjuvans, quod nemo negat: Quando verò ipsum per se cum fine & effectu suo comparatur, utique est causa in suo ordine sufficiens.

Cæterùm, ab hoc dejecti præsidio Jesuitæ, ad alia se recipiunt κρησφύγετα, quibus illustre hoc testimonium Apostoli eludere queant. Ergò secundi argumenti loco objiciunt: Scripturas eo respectu sufficienter instruere & perficere hominem, non quòd ipsa sola sufficiat: sed quia multa expressè continet: & quæ non continet, ostendit, unde sint petenda. Sed Respondeo: Initiò Jesuitam non disputare, sed nugari. Neq; enim Apostolus aliquam, sed plenariam sufficientiam Scripturæ adscribit: ut quæ possit σοφίσαι ad salutem, & perfectè instruere hominem ad omne opus bonum. Deinde, si Scriptura particularem tantùm aliquam sufficientiam contineret, & ostenderet unde plenior peti debeat: non certè opus fuisset, ut Spiritus Sanctus tot libros Scripturæ ederet: sed uno aut altero potuisset esse contentus, & ablegare nos ad Traditiones Ecclesiæ non scriptas. 3. Cur non liceret à Scripturis vel ad dexteram, vel ad sinistram recedere, si Scriptura esset imperfecta? Tandem petit principium Jesuvvita afferens, Scripturam ostendere, unde sint petenda, quæ in ipsis desiderantur? priùs enim hoc ipsum probet necesse est, quàm tam audacter illud quasi ἀπόῤῥητον pronunciet.

Tertium argumentum Jesuvviticum tale est: Apostolus dicit: OMNIS Scriptura utilis est &c. Ergò si inde evidenter colligitur perfectio & sufficientia Scripturæ, utiq; quilibet Liber Biblicus hanc perfectionem continebit: Siquidem Omnis Scriptura significat quemlibet librum sacrum. Atqui posterius hoc falsum. Ergò & prius.

Respondeo. Argumentum procedere ex parte: ac proindè nihil prorsus concludere: Neque enim militat ratio ulla Consequentiæ in hoc argumento: In multis locis Scripturæ, item in communi usu loquendi frequenter particula Omnis sumitur distributivè: Ergò ubiq; sic accipienda est. Nam contrarijs exemplis Consequentia isthæc evertitur, in quibus particula Universalis, OMNIS non modò distributivè significet singula generis: sed etiam collectivè, Genus singulorum, sive Totum: ut Matth. 3, 5. Omnis Judæa, omnisq; regio: hoc est, tota Judæa. Eph. 4, 16. πᾶν τὸ σῶμα: ubi Latina ipsa vulgata reddidit; Totum Corpus. Sic Matth. 21, 10 πᾶσα πόλις tota civitas. Nam de una civitate, non verò de omni, sive distributivè de qualibet civitate, sermo est. Et sanè sic collectivè voculam hanc intelligendam esse, vel inde patet: quia aliàs non modò singuli libri Biblici: sed & singula librorum capita: singuli capitum versus: imò singula versuum verba, adhæc omnia essent utilia: Ratio est: Quia distributiva illa significatio, quam urgent Jesuvvitæ, atque ad singulos versus, verbaq; singula, atque ad singulos libros accommodari potest. Quia verò falsum & absurdum hoc esse, ipsimet fateri necesse habent: mirum profectò, si prodigiosam objectionis suæ vanitatem non animadvertant.

Cæterùm, si ita informent argumentum suum Jesuvvitæ: Non quilibet liber Biblicus sufficiens est & perfectus: Ergò neque tota Scriptura simul sumpta: certè insignem proeunt futilitatem, vel pueris ridendam: Nam à parte ad totum negativè non valet Consequentia. Deinde, dupliciter consideratur Scriptura: vel quatenq est totum aliquod corpus, ex omnibus libris utriusque Testamenti, collectum & coagmentatū: vel quatenus seorsim ac sigillatim secundum singulas partes consideratur & accipitur. Priore modo ac respectu Scriptura accepta, complectitur etiam omnes fines simul junctos; διδασκαλίαν, ἔλεγχον ἐπανόρθωσιν κὴ παιδείαν: Cæterùm quando posteriore modo ac respectu Scriptura de singulis partibus seorsim consideratis sumitur: certè ultrò largimur, non omnes hosce fines singulis capitibus, sententijs, verbis, vel etiam singulis libris, præsertim minoribus & purè historicis, â Spiritu Sancto intendi: sed in diversis diversos: qui verò omnes conjunctim, in integro illo corpore Scripturæ concurrunt: idq; cùm sufficienter & perfectè: ut nihil quicquam ad perficiendam Scripturæ sufficientiam, extra Scripturam accedere possit.

Quartò sic insurgit Bellarminus: Cum hac Epistola scriberetur, nondum extabat Apocalypsis, nec Evangelium Johannis, & fortè aliud aliquid deerat ex corpore Scripturæ: Ergò non potest Aphorismus Apostolicus intelligi de toto Canone Scripturæ.

Sed Respondeo, Laborat argumentum Jesuvvitæ Sophismate Ignorationis Elenchi & vitiosæ definitionis. Neque enim integritas & perfectio Canonis, definienda est solo librorum numero, quantus ille & qualis hodiè est: Sed partim ipsius doctrinæ perfectione, partim verò numero eorum librorum, quem DEUS ipse Canonem absolvere voluit: ut Exempli gratia: Tempore Mosis, Canonem totum constituebat Volumen pentateuchi, de quo DEUS ipse testatus est, usque adeò perfectum eum esse, ut nemini mortalium fas esset, quicquam ei vel addere, vel adimere. Consimiliter, postquam progressu temporis accesserunt libri Prophetici: & quidem autoritate divinâ: utique tum etiam Canon erat totus, perfectus, & integer: usque adeò, ut Abrahamus in Paradiso constitutus, fratres divitis epulonis, non nisi ad Mosen & Prophetas ablegare voluerit, Luc. 16. Sic quando postmodum accesserunt libri aliquot Novi Testamenti, quorum etiam copiam Timotheum habuisse, supra ostendimus: & tandem etiam accessit Apocalypsis, Evangelium & Epistolæ Johannis: etiam tùm Canon Scripturæ erat totus, plenus & integer. Siquidem accessiones istæ aliorum singulæ & universæ, neque arguunt imperfectionem prioris tempore Canonis, neque etiam novam aliquam doctrinam Canoni pristino adposuerunt: sed antiquissimam illam doctrinam, libris statim Mosaicis comprehensam, tantùm altiùs explicarunt, & varijs Exemplis atque historijs uberiùs illustrarunt: idque non hominum, sed ipsius DEI autoritate atque voluntate: ut si ex istis accessionibus librorum ad Traditionum suarum complementum colligere velint Romanenses, crassam omninò Ignorationem Elenchi committant. Quare etsi nullum est dubium, quin Timotheus non omnes libros Novi Testamenti viderit aut legerit: Quia tamen Apostolus indefinitè & in genere loquitur de Canone, qui & qualis tùm extabat, & plenam perfectamque doctrinam continebat: & vero DEI jussu postmodum alij libri accesserunt, utique vel hinc evincitur, Aphorismum Apostolicum hos etiam libros, quippe ad Canonem Scripturæ pertinentes, suo complexu continere.

Quintò sic obstrepit gens Jesuvvitica: D. Apostolus non agit hoc loco de Verbo scripto: sed de Verbo audito. Ergò malè hic locus accommodatur ad Verbum scriptum. Antecedens probat indè, quòd Apostolus dicit, Tene ea, quæ à me audisti.

Respondeo. Dupliciter fallit Jesuvvita. 1. Sophismate τὸ μὴ αἰτίς ὡς αἰτίᾳ. Neq; enim ideò Timotheus existimandus est non profecisse ex lectione S. literarum:quia nimirum formam sanorum verborum didicit ab Apostolo. Quasi non utrumque simul stare possit: imò potiùs unum alterum præsupponat potiùsquàm excludat: præsertim cúApostolus disertè meminerit ἱερῶν γραμμάτων SCRIPTURARUM sacrarum.

Deinde fallitur Jesuvvita Sophismate vitiosi Consequentis: Quæ enim, obsecro, est ratio Consequentiæ: Timotheus ex vivæ vocis informatione didicit à Paulo formam sanorum verborum. Ergò Paulus aliud aliquid vivâ voce Timotheo tradidit, quàm quod postea literis comprehendit? Quarum collectionum ostendet subsequens sexta & postrema Quæstio sive Controversia, de qua nobis erit disputandum.

Verùm de Aphorismo Apostolico hæc dixisse, sufficiat. Superfunt autem in Scripturis haud minus evidentia loca, perfectionem ac sufficientia Scripturæ sacræ evidenter demonstrantia.

Alterum proinde Argumentum subministrat, Locus Actor.20,27. Non subterfugi, quò minus annunciarem vobis omne consilium DEI. Unde sic argumentor:

Si Apostolus Ephesijs non partem unam aut alteram, sed omne consilium DEI annunciavit: & postmodum idem mysterium DEI scriptâ Epistolâ complexus est: Consequens fuerit, 1. Doctrinam Apostoli omnibus numeris esse perfectam & absolutam, tùm quâ fidei, tùm quà morum informationem. 2. Hanc ipsam perfectionem non aliunde, quàm ex ipsa Scriptura hauriendam esse.

Sed verum est Antecedens, id quod patet ex collatione loci Act.20, 27. & Eph. 3, 2. verũ E. & Consequens.

Tertium Argumentum mutuari licet ex Epistola ad Hebræos cap 1,1.Multis vicibus, multisq; modis olim DEUS locutus est Patribus in Prophetis, ultimis diebus hisce locutus est nobis in Filio: Unde sic inferre possumus.

Si DEUS per Prophetas primùm:Deinde per Filium in carne revelatum, perq; bujus ministros, Apostolos: de Salutis nostræ negotio ad homines locutus est: Consequitur, in Prophetarum etiam & Apostolorum scriptis,quæ ad Salutem nostram sunt necessaria, perfectè contineri. At verum est Antecedens,verum Ergò & Consequens.

Connexum Majoris patet 1.inde. Quia, quæ ad salutem nostram requiruntur, nemo rectiùs novit, ipso DEO, 2. Quia ea est DEI nostri Φιλανθρωπία, ut nihil in arcano retinuerit, quod quidemSalutis nostræ negotium spectet.3. Quia ipsi Apostoli Scripturis hanc perfectionem Ἐξαρχήδην adsignant: utRom.15.4. Quæ antè scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt,ut per patientiâ & Consolationem SCRIPTURARUM spem haberemus.Et. Joh.5,46. Si crederetis Mosi, crederetis etiam mihi: de me enim ille scripsit. Quod illius scriptis non creditis,quomodo verbis meis creditis?

Postremum Argumentum suppeditat Unanimis consensus Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, quem paucis delibabimus.

Augustinus lib.2.de doctr. Christ.cap.9.In his, què apertè posita sunt in Scriptura, inveniuntur illa omnia, quæ continent fidem, moresᾶ vivendi. Chrysost. Homil.1.ad Titum. Omnia Evangelium continet, & præsentia & futura, honorem, pietatẽ, fidẽ, simul omnia prædicationis verbo inclusit. Hilar. lib. 12. de Trinit. DEI sermo & vera sapientia doctrina, qua loquitur, & perfecta & absoluta sunt. Athanasius contra Gentes. Sufficiunt sanctæ ac divinitùs inspiratæ Scripturæ ad OMNEM instructionem veritatis. Cyrill.lib.12. in Joh. Non omnia quæ Dominus fecit, conscripta sunt: sed quæ scribentes tam ad mores, quàm ad dogmata putarunt sufficere: ut rectâ fide & operibus ac veritate rutilantes ad regnum cœlorum perveniamus per Jesum Christum.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Second Part the Jesuit Proposition

Holy Scripture is a mutilated, maimed, and imperfect doctrine, which does not contain all things that pertain to faith and the morals of living piously: but that defect is to be mended by the patch of traditions.

ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστικὴ (Refutatory exposition).

Thus indeed the Cologne Jesuits judged, in that ill-fated Censure of theirs, page 220. Thus Canisius judged in his Catechetical work, pages 126, 160, 161, 162. Thus the Bavarian interlocutors judged in the recent Ratisbon Colloquy, descending into this opinion: Scripture is indeed an infallible rule of religion: but it is neither the sole nor the unique one: but besides this, Traditions and the definitions of the Church and the consensus of Orthodox Doctors must necessarily be admitted. Thus Francis Coster judges, writing on page 47 of his Enchiridion: When it is asked, whether all things that pertain to faith are written, that is, expressed in the written Word of GOD? it must be said: All the mysteries of faith, and other things necessary to be believed and known, are most clearly inscribed in the heart of the Church: in the membranes of the New as well as the Old Testament, many things are lacking. Indeed, they have progressed to such a point of audacity, or rather blasphemy, that a certain Scottish Jesuit, by the name of John Hay, has not feared to write: In these last times, Scripture is not only imperfect and useless, but plainly pernicious: and therefore to be exterminated by the Church. The Jesuit Bellarmine informs his thesis and that of his accomplices thus: We assert that the whole doctrine necessary, whether concerning faith or morals, is not contained expressly in the Scriptures, and therefore, besides the written Word of GOD, the unwritten Word of GOD is also required, that is, divine and Apostolic Traditions, book 4 on the unwritten Word of GOD, chapter 3. But before we make an approach to the Refutation of the Jesuit arguments: a twofold Observation must be premised concerning this Question, Whether all necessary things are contained in the Scriptures: of which the former concerns the subject, the latter the predicate, τὸ κατηγορέμενον.

The first is as follows: There is a twofold kind of things which is handed down in the Scriptures. For some things are necessary for all to know, and pertain to the very salvation of men. These are handed down in the Scriptures so clearly and perfectly that whoever wishes to accuse them in this kind of things of either obscurity or imperfection, let him consider himself struck by that twofold Pauline thunderbolt: Gal. 1, 8. If anyone should announce another Gospel than that which has been announced to you, let him be anathema: And 2 Cor. 4, 3, & 4. If our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled in those who are perishing, in whom the GOD of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers. But some things are not necessary for salvation, nor do they even pertain to the very substance of divine worship: Such are those things which make for order and decency, so that divine worship may be performed with greater solemnity. Where we readily grant that indeed only the kind, but not the very species of rites and ceremonies, is expressed in the Scriptures: and therefore we rightly conclude that they cannot be proposed for observance under the opinion of absolute necessity, either of worship, or of righteousness, or of merit.

The latter observation concerns the predicate. For something is said to be contained in the Scriptures in two ways. For some things are contained formally and verbally at the same time, as they speak in the Schools, that is: they are contained in the sacred writings not only as to the things, but also as to the words. But some things exist there formally only, whose words, although they are not found, yet the things themselves are not lacking their foundation in the Sacred Scriptures. And these are said to be expressed in the Scriptures just as much as those. For as Nazianzen writes in book 5 on Theology (where he writes about the Holy Spirit): Those things which are gathered from the Scriptures are just as much as those which are written: Some things are not, and yet are said to be in the Scriptures: such as that GOD sits, has eyes, ears, etc. Some things are, yet are not said expressly and in so many words, such as that the Holy Spirit is GOD: Some things are neither, nor are they said: Finally, some things both are and are said. The Orthodox Church opposed this observation to the Arian fury, which exploded the term ὁμουσία, of the Trinity, and similar things, because they were not written: The Anabaptists of today, imitating them, eliminate infant baptism from the Church, since its tradition cannot be demonstrated from Scripture as written. This petulance Nazianzen most rightly calls a devotion to the letter, and affirms that it is nothing other than a cloak for wickedness. With these two observations premised, the refutation of the Jesuit arguments will be easier.

But that which Bellarmine moves in book 4 on the unwritten Word of GOD, ch. 4, easily holds the chief place. If Scripture is sufficient, then either the whole Canon taken together is sufficient: or individual books by themselves are sufficient. But neither is true. Therefore, Scripture is not sufficient and perfect. He proves the minor thus: Individual books are not sufficient by themselves: that which is placed beyond controversy on both sides: The whole Canon taken together is not sufficient, because many truly sacred and Canonical books have perished.

I answer: The first error arises from the sophism of a faulty definition: For the integrity and perfection of the Canon is not defined by the number or multitude of books: but only by the divine will, which from the very beginnings of the Church, at any time according to its own good pleasure, has constituted a certain Canon, consisting now of fewer, now of more books. Therefore, when only the five books of Moses existed, that Canon was certainly sufficient for the Church, because GOD at that time did not wish the Canon to consist of more books. Afterwards, when in the progress of time the books of the Psalms and the Prophets were added: at that time also the Canon was perfect and sufficient: and GOD willed that those things also be believed which are contained in those books. By the same reasoning, after the books of the New Testament were added, the Canon of the Old Testament was no longer sufficient: but GOD himself willed that these also be added, and held in equal place.

With these things thus presupposed, we answer to the major proposition, that at individual times, not individual books taken separately, but the whole Canon always sufficed for the doctrine and faith of the Church: and especially that today the whole system of Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture joined together suffices for us: after those things which, by the nature of the New Testament under the kingdom of Christ, had to be added, are now fully added.

Then another error is committed, of the non-cause as cause: For nothing is lost to the perfection and sufficiency of the Canon, even if some sacred books have perished. For if those books had been necessary for establishing the perfection of the Canon: GOD would have surely saved them from destruction just as much as those which exist even today. For the Holy Spirit willed that only those books be preserved for constituting the Canon of Scripture, which He knew to be necessary for confirming the doctrine of truth and for establishing the form of the Church: But the rest, which had been written either peculiarly for the use of certain churches, or served mainly for those times, He allowed to perish, both so that the Church would not be burdened by a multitude of books: and so that a limit might be set to human curiosity in investigating those things whose knowledge was to be less necessary for future centuries.

Another argument of the same Bellarmine is such. For many centuries the Church worshipped GOD without Sacred Scripture, from the tradition of the living voice alone. Therefore, after Sacred Scripture was published by the command of GOD, it will not suffice for the doctrine of faith and morals, but there will be need of traditions.

I answer. A manifold paralogism arises. The first is of indefiniteness and confusion. For the state of the controversy is not placed in this, whether GOD could, without Scripture, and could today, preserve the doctrine of faith and morals among men through Tradition: For who would be so impious, or so stupid, as to dare to deny this? But it is disputed about this, when GOD has revealed His will in the written Word, and wishes us to be simply bound to it, whether it be lawful beyond and outside

Does the written Word of GOD embrace any other unwritten traditions concerning our faith and salvation? The Jesuit tries in vain to establish the affirmative of this question from a consideration of that Adamic Church up to Moses: For, as a second fallacy, he shamefully confuses the times through a gross Ignorance of the Refutation: and at the same time begs the question. For the Jesuit ought to have proved this: Even now, after GOD himself has taken care to have his Word committed to writing, must the information of faith and morals be sought not from that written Word alone, but from human traditions? For it is not from the condition of that ancient primitive Church, but from the will of GOD, that one must determine the norm of faith and morals.

The Jesuit takes his third argument of the same kind from an enumeration of some things which cannot be unknown, and yet are not contained in the Scriptures: For first, in the Old Testament, without doubt, women no less than men had some external remedy by which they were purged from original sin. But what that was, Scripture nowhere contains.

I answer. 1. The argument proceeds from a false hypothesis, or a certain erroneous preconceived opinion of the mind. For the Jesuits dream that salvation depends upon the use of the Sacraments, as if by a work performed, and that no one can be saved without an external Sacrament or remedy. The vanity of this opinion is evident from the purer doctrine of our Churches concerning the use and Ends of the Sacraments. The cause of this gross error, however, is that they either utterly ignore, or certainly enervate, the power of justifying faith.

Then the argument fails by the fallacy of ignorance of the refutation: For it does not follow: An external remedy was ordained for boys, namely circumcision: Therefore such an external remedy was also ordained for females. For it was sufficient for them, just as for boys dying before the eighth day, to have that internal remedy by which they could be purged from Original sin: and that was twofold: For with respect to GOD it was that which exhibits, namely the promise, and that the general one made to our first parents in Paradise. Gen. 3, 15. and afterwards repeated several times to the Patriarchs. Gen. 12, 3: 18, 18. 22, 17. In thy seed, which is Christ, shall all nations be blessed: but then that special one given to Abraham and his seed, Genesis 17, 7. I will be thy GOD and the GOD of thy seed after thee. Now, however, the Seed of Abraham was not only males, but also females. With respect to men, however, the internal remedy corresponding correlatively to the former was FAITH, by which women even of the Old Testament applied to themselves that divine promise, or rather Christ, who was the sole object of that promise. By this faith, therefore, the Israelite females were purged from original sin, and were finally saved. Whence St. Peter, 1 Pet. 3, 5. 6. calls the Israelite women holy women, and establishes Sarah as the mother of the faithful: Indeed, Heb. 11, 11. they are reckoned in the Catalogue of those who are justified by faith. Which very opinion Peter Lombard held even from the Scholastic Doctors, lib. 4. dist. 1. Women are justified by faith and good works. And Thomas on 4. Sent. dist. 2 quest. 6. writes: That for infants before the giving of Circumcision, faith alone without any exterior sign sufficed for salvation: for adults, their own faith together with the sign performed by them. He understands the sign to be Sacrifices and offerings. This very thing must be answered to the instance of Bellarmine, which he raises concerning the remedy for infants who died before the eighth day. For no other remedy can be given except faith alone, which GOD kindles in them in an extraordinary way, just as in the Thief. For the Sacraments are not of such absolute necessity that GOD, in a case of necessity, cannot work faith and salvation in infants even without a Sacrament. Concerning which matter Augustine speaks rightly and elegantly, lib. 4. contra Donatistas cap. 23. Just as in the thief, because Baptism was bodily lacking through necessity, there is perfect salvation, because it was present spiritually through piety: So also then in infants, whether uncircumcised or unbaptized, faith itself is present, if through necessity that which was lacking to the thief is missing, salvation is perfected. For then it is fulfilled visibly, when the mystery of Baptism excludes it, not by contempt of religion, but by an article of necessity.

Latin:

Scriptura Sacra est doctrina mutila, manca & imperfecta, quæ non continet omnia, quæ ad fidem, moresq; piè vivendi pertinent: sed ille defectus sarciendō est,assumento traditionū.

ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστικὴ.

SIc sanè censuerunt Jesuvvitæ Colonieuses, in malè feriata illa Censura sua pag. 220. Sic censuit Canisi9 in opere suo Catechistico p. 126.160.161.162. Sic censuerunt collocutores Bavarici in Colloquio nupero Ratisbonensi, hanc in sententiam descendentes: Est quidem Scriptura Religionis norma infallibilis:Verùm nec sola nec unica:sed præter hanc necessariò admitti debent Traditiones, & Ecclesiæ definitiones, Doctorumq̃, Orthodoxorũ Consensus. Sic Franciscus Costerus censet, p. 47. Enchiridij scribens: Quãdo quæritur, Utrùm omnia, quæ ad fidem pertinent, sint scripta, id est, in Verbo DEI scripto expressa? dicendum est; Omnia fidei mysteria,cæteraq̃ creditu & scitu necessaria, in corde Ecclesiæ esse clarissimè exarata:in membranis tam novi, quàm Veteris Testamenti, multa desiderari. Quin eò usque progressi sunt audaciæ, vel potiùs blasphemiæ, ut Jesuvvita quidam Scotus, cognomento Johannes Haijus scribere non exhorruerit:His extremis temporibus non modò imperfectam & inutilem esse Scripturam, sed planè perniciosam: ac proinde ab Ecclesia exterminandam. Jesuvvita Bellarminus suam suorumque complicum thesin sic informat: Nos asserimus,non contineri expressè in Scripturis totam doctrinã necessariam, sive de fide, sive de morib9, ac proinde præter DEI Verbum scriptum, requiri etiam Verbum DEI non scriptum, id est, divinas & Apostolicas Traditiones lib. 4. de Verbo DEI non scripto cap. 3. Cæterùm priusquàm argumentorum Jesuvviticorum Refutationem accessum faciamus:Gemina præmittenda est Observatio, circa Quæstionem hanc, An omnia necessaria in Scripturis contineantur: Quarum prior subjectum:posterior τὸ κατηγορέμενον prædicatum concernit.

PRIOR talis est : Duplex est rerum Genus, quod in Scripturis traditur. Quædam enim scitu omnibus sunt necessaria, & ad salutem ipsam hominum pertinentia. Hæc usque adeò dilucidè & perfectè in Scripturis sunt tradita, ut qui hoc in rerum genere, vel obscuritatis, vel imperfectionis eas accusare velit, is gemino illo Paulino fulmine se tangi statuat : Gal. 1, 8. Si quis aliud Evangelium annunciet quàm quod vobis annunciatum est, Anathema sit: Et 2. Cor. 4, 3, & 4. Si opertum est Evangelium nostrum, in ijs, qui pereunt, opertum est, in quibus DEUS hujus seculi, excæcavit mentes infidelium. Quædam verò ad salutem non sunt necessaria, neque etiam ad ipsam substantiam cultus divini pertinent: Qualia sunt ea, quæ faciunt πρὸς τάξιν καὶ ἐυσχημοσύνην, ut majore cum solennitate cultus divinus peragatur. Ubi sanè Genus tantùm, non verò ipsam speciem rituum & ceremoniarum in Scripturis expressam esse, ultrò largimur : ac proindè neq; sub opinione absolutè necessitatis, vel cultus, vel justitiæ aut meriti, ad observandum proponi ea posse, rectè colligimus.

Posterior Observatio prædicatum respicit. Duobus enim modis aliquid in Scripturis contineri dicitur. Quædam enim formaliter & verbaliter simul, ut in Scholis loquuntur, hoc est; non modò quoad res, sed & quoad verba in sacris continentur. Quædam verò Formaliter duntaxat istic extant, quorum licèt verba non reperiantur, res tamen ipsæ in Sacris fundamento suo non destituuntur. Et hæc æquè dicuntur in Scripturis esse expressa, atq; illa. Nam ut Nazianzenus lib 5. de Theologia (ubi de Spiritu Sancto scribit) scribit: Perindè sunt ea, quæ ex Scripturis colliguntur, atq; ea, quæ scribuntur: Quædam non sunt, & tamen dicuntur esse in Scripturis : ut DEUM sedere, habere oculos, aures, &c. Quædam sunt, nec dicuntur tamen expressè, & totidem verbis, ut Spiritum Sanctum esse DEUM: Quædam verò neq; sunt, neq; dicuntur : Quædam denig; & sunt, & dicuntur. Opposuit observationem hanc Orthodoxa Ecclesia furori Ariano, qui vocabulum ὁμουσία, Trinitatis, & similia explodebat, quia non essent ἔγγραφα: Quos imitati hodie Anabaptistæ pædobaptismum ex Ecclesia eliminant, quippe cujus ex Scriptura traditio ἔγγραφω̄ demonstrari non possit. Quam petulantiam rectissimè Nazianzenus nominat Studium Literæ, & affirmat illud nihil esse aliud, quàm pallium improbitatis. Duabus istis observationibus præmissis, facilior erit Argumentorum Jesuiticorum Refutatio.

Principem autem locum facilè obtinet illud, quod movet Bellarminus lib. 4. de Verbo DEI non scripto. cap. 4. Si Scriptura est sufficiens, tum vel totus Canon simul sumtus est sufficiens: vel singuli libri per se sunt sufficientes. At neutrum. E. Scriptura non est sufficiens & perfecta. Minorem sic probat: Non singuli libri sunt per se sufficientes: id quod utrinque extra Controversiam est positum : Non totus Canon simul sumtus est sufficiens, quia multi libri verè sacri & Canonici perierunt.

Respondeo : Error primus oritur ex Sophismate vitiosæ definitionis : Nam Canonis integritas & perfectio non definitur, librorum numero aut multitudine : sed tantùm divinâ voluntate, quæ jam indè à primordijs Ecclesiæ, quovis tempore pro suo beneplacito , Canonem certum constituit, jam paucioribus, jam pluribus libris constantem. Proindè quando tantùm extiterunt quinque libri Mosis, utique fuit ille Canon sufficiens Ecclesiæ, Quia DEUS tùm temporis noluit pluribus libris constare Canonem. Postmodùm quando progressu temporis accefferunt libri Psalmorum & Prophetarum: utique illo etiam tempore Canon erat perfectus & sufficiens : voluitq; DEUS ea etiam credi, quæ illis libris continentur. Eâdem ratione, postquam Novi Testamenti libri accesserunt, non ampliùs sufficiebat Canon Veteris Testamenti : sed hos etiam adjici, parique haberi loco, DEUS ipse voluit.

His ita præsuppositis respondemus ad Majorem propositionem, singulis temporibus, non singulos libros seorsim acceptos, sed totum semper Canonem suffecisse ad doctrinam & fidem Ecclesiæ : & cumprimis nobis hodiè sufficere totum systema Scripturæ Propheticæ & Apostolicæ simul junctæ : postquàm nunc ea, quæ ex Naturâ Novi Testamenti sub regno Christi addenda fuerant, plenè sunt addita.

Deindè committitur alter error non causæ ut causæ : Non enim ideò perfectioni & sufficientiæ Canonis quicquam decedit, licèt quidam libri sacri perierint. Si enim libri illi ad perfectionem Canonis stabiliendam fuissent necessarij : utique DEUS æquè ipsos ab interitu vindicasset, atque eos, qui hodieq; extant. Eos enim libros duntaxat Spiritus Sanctus ad constituendum Scripturæ Canonem servatos voluit, quos ad confirmandam veritatis doctrinã, & Ecclesiæ formam constituendam scivit esse necessarios : Reliquos autem, qui vel in usum certarum quarundam Ecclesiarum peculiariter scripti fuerant, vel illis potissimùm temporibus serviebant, interire passus est, tùm, ne Ecclesiæ multitudine librorum gravaretur: tùm, ut curiositati humanæ modus statueretur in investigandis ijs, quorum cognitio posteris seculis minus futura erat necessaria.

Alterum argumentum ejusdem Bellarmini tale est. Multis seculis Ecclesia DEUM coluit absque Sacrâ Scripturâ, ex solâ vivæ vocis traditione. Ergò, postquàm Sacra Scriptura DEI jussu edita est, illa non sufficiet ad doctrinam fidei & morũ, sed traditionibus opus fuerit.

Respondeo. Multiplicem oriri paralogismum. Primus τῆς ἀοριστίας & confusionis. Non enim status Controversiæ in eo est positus, An DEUS sine Scriptura potuerit, hodieq; possit doctrinam fidei morumq; per Traditionem inter homines conservare: Quis enim ita vel impius, vel bardus foret, qui hoc negare ausit ? Sed de eo controvertitur, cum DEUS voluntatem suam in Verbo scripto revelaverit, & ad illud nos simpliciter velit alligatos, Anne fas sit præter & extra

Verbum DEI scriptum ullas alias amplecti traditiones non scriptas de fide & salute nostra? Cujus quæstionis affirmativam frustra stabilire conatur Jesuvvita ex consideratione Ecclesiæ illius Adamicæ ad Mosen usque: Nam quod alterum est Sophisma, per crassam Ignorationem Elenchi turpiter confundit tempora: & simul petit principium. Hoc enim probare debebat Jesuvvita, Etiam nunc, postquam DEUS ipse suum Verbum in literas referri curavit, non ex solo illo Verbo scripto, sed ex traditionibus humanis, fidei morumq; informationem petendam esse? Neque enim ex conditione antiquæ illius primævæ Ecclesiæ: sed ex voluntate DEI statuendum est de norma fidei & morum.

Tertium ejusdem argumentum desumit Jesuvvita ab enumeratione aliquot rerum, quæ ignorari non possunt, & tamen in Scripturis non continentur: Primum enim in Veteri Testamento sine dubio non minus fœminæ quàm viri remedium aliquod externum habebant, quo à peccato originali purgarentur. Quale autem illud esset, nuspiam habet Scriptura.

Respondeo. 1. Procedit argumentum ex falsa hypothesi, sive erronea quadam animi præconcepta opinione. Somniant enim Jesuvvitæ, salutem a Sacramentorum usu, tanquam ab opere operato, pendere: neque sine externo Sacramento sive remedio quempiam salvari posse. Cujus opinionis vanitas patet ex puriore Ecclesiarum nostrarum de usu ac Finibus Sacramentorum doctrina. Causa autem crassi hujus erroris est, quod vim fidei justificantis isti penitus vel ignorant, vel certe enervant.

Deinde fallit argumentum Sophismate ignorationis Elenchi: Neque enim sequitur: Pueris ordinatum fuit externum aliquod remedium, nempe circumcisio: Ergo & fœmellis tale aliquod Externum fuit ordinatum. Sufficiebat enim his æque ac pueris ante octavum diem decedentibus, internum illud remedium, quo a peccato Originali purgari poterant: idq; geminum: Respectu enim DEI erat illud exhibitivum, nempe promissio, eaq; tum generalis illa, facta primis parentibus in Paradiso. Gen. 3, 15. & postmodum Patriarchis reliquis aliquoties repetita. Gen. 12. 3: 18, 18. 22, 17. In semine tuo, qui est Christus, benedicentur omnes gentes: tum vero specialis illa, Abrahamo & semini ipsius data, Genes. 17, 7. Ero DEUS tuus & DEUS seminis tui post te. Jam vero Semen Abrahæ non tantum erant masculi, sed etiam fœminæ. Respectu vero hominum, Remedium internum prioricorrelatè respondens, erat FIDES, qua mulieres etiam Veteris Testamenti promissionem illam divinam, vel Christum potius, qui promissionis illius erat objectum unicum, sibi applicabant. Hac fide ergo fœmellæ Israeliticæ a peccato originis purgabantur, & tandem salvabantur. Unde D. Petrus 1. cap. 3, 5. 6. mulieres Israëlitas nominat sanctas mulieres, & Saram constituit matre fidelium: Quin & Hebr. 11, 11. accensentur Catalogo eorum, qui per fidem sunt justificati. Quam ipsam sententiam ex Scholasticis etiam Doctoribus tenuit Petrus Lombard. lib. 4. dist. 1. Mulieres justificatæ sunt per fidem & operationem bonam. Et Thomas super 4. Set. dist. 2 quest. 6. scribit. Quod parvulis ante datam Circumcisionem, ad salutem suffecerit sola fides sine omni exteriori signo: adultis fides propria cum signo ab eis facto. Signum autem intelligit Sacrificia & oblationes. Quod ipsum responderi debet ad instantiam Bellarmini, quàm movet de remedio pro parvulis, qui decefferunt ante octavum diem. Neque enim ullum aliud dari porest remedium præter solam fidé, quam in illis DEUS modo extraordinario accendit, sicut in Latrone. Nam Sacramenta non ita sunt de absoluta neceffitate, quin DEUS in casu neceffitatis, possit etiam sine Sacramento in infantibus operari fidem & salutem. Qua de repiè & eleganter August. lib. 4. contra Donatistas cap. 23. Sicut in latrone, quia per necessitatem Baptismus corporaliter defuit, perfecta salus est, quia per pietatem spiritualiter adfuit: Sic etiam tùm in infantibus, vel non circumcisis, vel non baptizatis fides ipsa præstò est, si per necessitatem desit, quod latroni defuit, perficitur salus. Tunc enim impletur visibiliter, cum mysteriũ Baptismi, non contemtus religionis, sed articulus necessitatis excludit.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Second Part the Jesuit Proposition (continued)

Thus, what Bellarmine objects in the third place, that many Gentiles could have been saved in the time of the Old Testament, and truly belonged to the Church: And yet nothing at all is held in Scripture concerning their Justification from original sin and other sins: and therefore the Scriptures are not perfect: that certainly lacks any true Refutation. For either those Gentiles were admitted into the Republic of the Jews, using the very same laws as they did: or they lived outside Judea, and had become proselytes merely by Profession, or Religion: such as were Naaman the Syrian, Cyrus, Darius, Nebuchadnezzar, and many others. The former were not admitted to the sacred rites of the Jews until they were circumcised, according to the prescription of the divine law which exists in Exod. 12, 48. But it was free for these latter whether they wished to be circumcised or to abstain from Circumcision. Both, however, were meanwhile Justified by faith in the Messiah of the World who was to come. And indeed Scripture is so far from keeping silent about this means of their Justification that it openly confesses that, just as there was one GOD from the very origin of the Church, so there has been one Faith of all. Eph. 4, 5.

Fourthly, the Jesuit presses the point further thus: It is necessary to know that some truly divine books exist: Which certainly can in no way be had from the Scriptures: For even if Scripture says that the books of the Prophets and Apostles are divine, nevertheless I would not certainly believe that, unless I had first believed that the Scripture which says this is divine. For we also read everywhere in the Alcoran of Mahomet that the Alcoran itself was sent from heaven by GOD, and yet we do not believe it. Therefore this dogma, so necessary, namely that there is some divine Scripture, cannot be sufficiently had from Scripture alone.

I answer 1. We leave that blasphemy taken from the comparison of the Alcoran to be defended by its author, exclaiming with the Prophet: The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan: Zech. 3:2. For who would not shudder with his whole heart hearing the assertion of Paul, when he says: That every Scripture is θεόπνευσον [God-breathed], can and ought to be believed with no greater certainty without the Tradition of the Church, than when we read in the Alcoran that the Alcoran itself was sent from Heaven by GOD.

Next, regarding the matter itself, we deny most absolutely that it cannot be had from the Scriptures, which books are truly divine. For the doctrine which is contained in the Canonical Scriptures provides a most sufficient testimony of its Divinity for itself, whether you look at its antiquity, or its sublimity, or its most beautiful and everywhere consistent harmony, or the power of its internal testimony, or the admirable efficacy of its admonitions, rebukes, and consolations, or its perpetuity and least interrupted propagation, or the dignity of its miracles, or the truth of its predictions, or the constancy of its martyrs; or finally, that fatal hatred with which the Devil and the world persecute these books. These are truly such criteria of evidence that they are contained neither in any other writings, nor does Scripture borrow them from the voice or tradition of the Church at last.

But not even thus does the Jesuitical spirit soften, but in the fifth place it urges more peevishly that: It is not enough to know that there is divine Scripture: but it is also necessary to know, Which one it is: For example: It is necessary to know that the Gospel of Mark is the true Gospel: that the Gospel of Thomas is not the true Gospel: Furthermore, it is necessary to know that this Gospel, which is now read under the name of Mark, is that true and uncorrupted one which Mark wrote. But all these things cannot be known from the Scriptures themselves. Therefore.

But I answer, the argument fails by the sophistry of multiple questions: for it is asked either about the divine majesty and certainty of the Doctrine itself, which is contained in the Canonical books: or separately about any book, whence it may be known that these or those books are truly Canonical: or finally, whence it may be certainly established that this or that book is of this or that author, whom the title itself or the inscription bears: therefore a distinct answer must also be given. And indeed, regarding the first question, it was shown a little earlier that the divine majesty and certainty of the doctrine of the Canonical books does not consist for the pious and faithful primarily from the testimony of the Church: but rather from those internal criteria which we have just recounted.

Regarding the other question, the Jesuit's argument proceeds initially from a false hypothesis: For if it were true, as the Jesuit maintains, that it is necessarily to be believed by all, and that it pertains to the Articles of the Christian faith, that one should believe not only that there are Canonical books, but also, Which are Canonical: it would certainly follow that before the constitution of the Canon, or certainly before the testimony of the Church, no one was saved regarding the Canonical books: it would also follow that today, not even a thousandth part of the believers could be saved: For how many of the faithful are there who have an exact and distinct knowledge of this question? Indeed, how many were, or are even in the Papacy itself, who have undertaken any care for this question, and today still undertake it. Concerning whom, however, that they perish, not even the Jesuits themselves would affirm. Thirdly, it would follow that there are now more Articles of faith after the constitution of the Canon of the New Testament than there were before. Since all these things are most absurd, one must most accurately distinguish between General and Special Faith: General Faith receives various objects, not only dogmatic, but also historical, which are contained in the Scriptures: And this Faith does not justify or save: For thus almost no one would be saved: For who is there who has an exact knowledge of all things which are contained in the Scriptures? What? That thus we would be justified by faith as by a certain habit, consisting of a perfect knowledge of all things which are contained in the sacred writings, which is manifestly false. Therefore, although this question: Which books are Canonical, is an object of General Faith: it is nevertheless viciously inferred from thence, That this, this question, is necessary for all to believe. Special faith is that alone which, just as it includes under its complex the whole foundation of faith, that is, the Articles of faith properly so called, so also it is said to save, only insofar as it looks to and apprehends Christ, toward whom all Articles of faith uniquely aim. Therefore, the question, Which books are Canonical, does not pertain to this faith.

Furthermore, the Jesuit's assertion is manifestly false. For regarding the Canonical books of the Old Testament, it is established concerning them from the New: where Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets enjoy the testimony of Christ the Savior himself, Luke 24:44, they enjoy the testimony of the Apostles, and especially that famous eulogy, that they are θεόπνευςοι, 2 Tim. 3:16. To which pertains that which the Apostle affirms, that the Israelite Church guarded τὰ λόγια θε̃, Rom. 3:2. What? That Moses himself deposited the Pentateuch written by him, by divine command, at the side of the ark of the covenant, with the whole people watching, Deut. 31:26, and Joshua similarly his book, Josh. 24:26. Thus we read that Ezra after the Babylonian captivity reduced the Canon of the books of the Old Testament, namely the Writings of Moses and the Prophets, into order. Let the Jesuit go now, therefore, and further if he likes, lie, that the Canonical books of the Old Testament are destitute of internal testimony that they are Canonical.

Thus regarding the books of the New Testament, they also enjoy internal testimony. For as was shown above, that Apostolic Aphorism: All Scripture is θεόπνευς, includes under its scope even the books of the New Testament, most of which had just now been brought to light. Furthermore, it is read that the Apostle marked his Epistles with a peculiar character, for the difference of other supposititious writings. 2 Thess. 2:17.

Regarding the third question, we certainly do not deny that, besides those internal testimonies which the Canonical books contain in themselves, there is some use of external testimony, which however does not regard the Canonical authority primarily, but the certainty of the Author. For so that it may be certainly established for me whether the Epistles of Paul, which exist under his name, are truly Paul's: here I certainly seek those Churches to which they were written, which, because they infallibly knew them to be Paul's, and therefore truly could also testify concerning this matter. Thus, if one asks about the authors of the remaining books of the New Testament, the same testimony would be needed from that Church which itself preserved and guarded the ἀυτόγραφα. And Eusebius is a witness in book 3, chapter 21, that John, who wrote last, saw and approved the very ἀυτόγραφα of the Evangelists Matthew, Mark, and Luke.

Furthermore, that the Jesuit adds: that it is necessary to believe that this Gospel, which is now read under the name of Mark, is that very one which Mark wrote: that certainly is not entirely free from all sophistry. For he wishes in this way to imply that that external testimony of the Church must necessarily be believed by all as an article of faith, and consequently that there can exist some unwritten tradition which constitutes an article of faith. But it was most correctly answered by our side in that very Colloquy that this testimony of the Church pertains not to the dogmas themselves, but to history, and consequently to general faith: nor can any new and peculiar dogma be forged by that testimony of the Church, and indeed such a one that it must then be added to the remaining articles of saving faith expressed in Scripture and proposed to all as necessary to be believed. The matter is illustrated by an example. In Colossians 4 it is read that the Epistle inscribed to the Colossians was transmitted through Onesimus: he, therefore, bringing the Epistle written by Paul to the Colossians, testifies that he received it from the hands of the Apostle. The question now is, whether Onesimus, by this external testimony of his being offered, adds to the Epistle to the Colossians any new dogma pertaining to special or justifying faith beyond those things which are contained in the Epistle? Where anyone who is able to judge anything at all will readily defend the negative, and will answer that no such new dogma is derived from it, but only an external testimony is offered. Therefore, one must most accurately distinguish between historical testimony and the contents of those books concerning which the testimony is made. But if that external testimony were to constitute an article of faith, then it would be an article of justifying faith that Onesimus testifies that the Epistle to the Colossians is Paul's: which is absurd. Furthermore, if testimony concerning the books were a peculiar article of faith, then it would follow that the Church, before the writing of the sacred books of the New Testament, had fewer articles of faith than afterwards, when the doctrine of the Gospel had been committed to writing: It would also follow that through the writing of the books of the New Testament the number of dogmas and articles of faith had been increased. But this latter is absurd: since one and the same Gospel remains in respect to articles and dogmas, whether it is preached by voice or committed to letters. Therefore, the former is also absurd, namely that the testimony of the Church is a peculiar article of faith.

Latin:

Sic quod tertio loco oggerit Bellarminus, Gentiles multos salvari potuisse tempore Veteris Testamenti, & verè ad Ecclesiam pertinuisse: Et tamen nihil prorsus de eorum Justificatione ab originali peccato, aliisq; peccatis in Scriptura haberi: ac proinde Scripturas non esse perfectas: id certè omni vero Elencho caret. Vel enim Gentiles illi in Rempublicam Judæorum erant asciti, ijsdem planè legibus cum ipsis utentes: vel extra Judæã vivebant, ac Professione tantùm, sive Religione facti erant proselyti: quales erant; Naaman Syrus, Cyrus, Darius, Nebucadnezar, & plures alii. Priores illi ex præscripto legis divinæ, quæ extat Exod. 12, 48. non priùs ad sacra Iudæorũ admittebantur, quàm essent circumcisi. His verò posterioribus liberum erat, sive circumcidi, sive à Circumcisione abstinere vellent. Utriq; tamen interim Iustificati fuerunt fide, in venturum Mundi Messiam. Et sanè hoc medium Iustificationis ipsorum Scriptura usq; adeò non silentio tegit: ut apertè fateatur, jam inde ab origine Ecclesiæ, uti unum DEUM; sic unam fuisse Fidem omnium Eph. 4. 5.

Quartò sic porrò instat Jesuvvita: Necesse est nosse, extare libros aliquos verè divinos: Quod certè nullo modo ex Scripturis baberi potest: Nam etsiamsi Scriptura dicat, libros Prophetarum & Apostolorum effe divinos, tamen non certò id credã, nisi priùs credidero, Scripturam quæ hoc dicit, effe divinam. Nam etiã in Alcorano Mahumeti paffim legimus, ipsum Alcoranũ de cœlo à DEO missum esse, & tamen ei non credimus. Ergò hoc dogma tam necessarium, quòd scilicet aliqua sit Scriptura divina, nõ potest sufficienter haberi ex sola Scriptura.

Respondeo 1. Nos blasphemiam illam â comparatione Alcorani desumptam autori suo defendendam relinquere, cum Prophetâ exclamantes: Increpet te DEUS Sachan: Zach.3.2. Quis enim non toto pectore exhorresceret audiens, Assertionem Pauli, quando dicit: Omnem Scripturam eff θεόπνευσον, haud majore certitudine absq; Traditione Ecclesiæ credi posse ac debere, quàm cùm in Alcorano legimus, ipsum Alcoranum à DEO de Cœlo esse missum.

Deinde, quoad rem ipsam, negamus simplicissimè ex Scripturis haberi non posse, Quinam libri sint verè divini. Nam doctrina, quæ in Scripturis Canonicis continetur, sibiipsi sufficientissimum perhibet Divinitatis Testimonium, sive ejus antiquitatem, sive sublimitatem, sive pulcherrimam & undiquaque consentientem harmoniam, sive internæ testificationis vim, sive admonitionem, objurgationum consolationum admirandam efficaciam, sive perennitatem ac minimè interruptam propagationem, sive miraculorum dignitatem, sive prædictionum veritatem, sive martyrum constantiam; sive denique fatale illud odium, quo Diabolus & mundus libros istos persequuntur, respicias. Hæc profectò ejusmodi evidentia sunt κριτήρια, ut neque in ullis scriptis alijs continentur: neque etiam ab Ecclesiæ demùm voce aut traditione ea mutuetur Scriptura.

Verùm, ne sic quidem mitescit Spiritus Jesuvviticus, sed quinto loco morosiùs urget illud: Non satis est, scire esse Scripturam divinam: sed oportet etiam scire, Quænam sit illa: Verbi gratia: Oportet scire, Evangelium Marci esse verum Evangelium: Evangelium Thomæ non esse verum Evangelium: Quin & illud scire oportet, hoc Evangeliũ, quod nunc legitur nomine Marci, esse illud verum & incorruptum, quòd scripsit Marcus. Sed hæc omnia ex Scripturis ipsis scire non possunt. Ergò.

Sed Respondeo, fallit Argumentum Sophisticatione plurium Quæstionum: vel enim quæritur, de ipsius Doctrinæ, quæ in libris Canonicis continetur, divinâ majestate & certitudine: vel seorsim de quolibet libro, unde sciri possit, Hos vel illos libros verè esse Canonicos: vel denique, unde certò constet, hunc vel illum librum, esse hujus vel illius autoris, quem titulo ipse, sive inscriptio præ se fert: Distincta proindè dari etiam debet responsio. Et quidem quoad primam Quæstionem, paulò antè ostensum, de divinâ majestate ac certitudine ipsius doctrinæ librorum Canonicorum pijs ac fidelibus non principaliter ex æterno constare Ecclesiæ testimonio: sed potiùs ex internis illis κριτηρίοις, quæ modò recensuimus.

Quoad alteram Quæstionem, procedit initiò argumentum Jesuvvitæ ex falsa hypothesi: Si enim verum esset, quòd Jesuvvita autumat, Necessariò omnibus credendum esse, & ad Articulos fidei Christianæ pertinere, ut quis credat, non tantùm esse Canonicos libros, sed etiã, Qui sint Canonici: sequeretur profectò ante Constitutionem Canonis, vel certè ante testificationem Ecclesiæ, de libris Canonicis neminem salvatum esse: sequeretur etiam hodiè, ne millesimum quidem credentium salvari posse: Quotus enim quisque est fidelium, qui quæstionis hujus exactam ac discretam habeat notitiam? Imò quotus quisque fuit, aut est in ipso Papatu, qui quæstionis hujus curam aliquam susceperit, hodieq́; suscipiat. De quibus tamen, quòd pereant, ne ipsi quidem Jesuvvitæ affirmaverint. Tertò sequeretur, plures jam esse Articulos fidei post constitutionem Canonis Novi Testamenti, quàm antè fuerint. Quæ omnia cùm sint absurdissima, accuratissimè distingvendum fuerit inter Fidem Generalem & Specialem: Generalis Fides varia recipit objecta, non modò dogmatica, sed & historica, quæ in Scripturis continentur: Et hæc Fides non justificat aut salvat: Sic enim nemo fermè salvaretur: Quis enim est, qui omnium rerum, quæ in Scripturis continentur, exactam habeat notitiam? Quid? quòd sic justificaremur fide tanquam habitu quodam, constante perfectâ notitiâ omnium rerum, quæ in sacris continentur, id quod manifestè falsum. Proindè etsi Quæstio hæc: Quinam Libri sint Canonici, est objectum Fidei Generalis: vitiosè tamen indè infertur, Quod hæc, hæc Quæstio, omnibus creditu sit necessaria. Fides specialis est illa sola, quæ uti sub suo complexu totum fundamentum fidei, hoc est, Articulos fidei propriè sic dictos comprehendit, ita etiam salvare dicitur, non nisi quatenus Christum ad quem omnes Articuli fidei unicè collimant, respicit & apprehendit. Proinde ad hanc fidem, Quæstio, Quinam libri sint Canonici, non pertinet.

Deinde verò Jesuvvitæ assertio, manifestè falsa est. Nam quoad libros Canonicos Veteris Testamenti, de ipsis constat ex Novo: ubi Moses, Psalmi & Prophetæ gaudent testimonio ipsius Christi Servatoris, Luc. 24, 44. gaudent testimonio Apostolorum, & cumprimis præclaro illo elogio, quòd sint θεόπνευςοι, 2. Tim. 3, 16. Quò pertinet illud, quod Apostolus affirmat, Ecclesiã Israeliticam custodivisse τὰ λόγια θε̃ Rom. 3, 2. Quid? quòd Moses ipse Pentateuchum â se conscriptum, mandato divino ad latus arcæ fœderis, spectante universo populo, reposuit. Deut. 31. 26 & Josua similiter suum librum Jos. 24, 26. Sic legimus Esdram post captivitatem Babylonicam, Canonem librorum Veteris Testamenti, Scripta nimirùm Mosis & Prophetarum, in ordinem redegisse. Eat ergò nunc Jesuvvita, & porrò si lubet, mentiatur, Libros Canonicos Veteris Testamenti destitui interno testimonio, quòd sint Canonici.

Sic quoad libros Novi Testamenti, gaudent & isti interno Testimonio. Nam uti supra ostensum, Aphorismus ille Apostolicus: Omnis Scriptura est θεόπνευς , sub suo ambitu comprehendit libros etiam Novi Testamenti, quorum plerique jam modò in lucem erant editi. Deinde legitur Apostolus suas Epistolas peculiari charactere notasse, ad differentiam aliorum scriptorum supposititiorum. 2. Theß. 2, 17.

Quoad Tertiam Quæstionem, non sanè negamus, præter interna illa testimonia, quæ libri Canonici in se continent, usum aliquem esse externæ testificationis, quæ tamen non autoritatẽ Canonicam primò, sed certitudinem Authoris respicit. Nam ut mihi certò constare possit, utrum Epistolæ Pauli, quæ sub ipsius nomine extant, sint reverà Pauli: hîc sanè quæro Ecclesias illas, ad quas illæ sunt scriptæ, quæ, quia infallibiliter sciverunt eas esse Pauli, ideoque verè etiam hac de re testari potuerunt. Sic si de reliquorum scriptorum Novi Testamenti autoribus quæratur, iidem testificatione opus fuerit illius Ecclesiæ, quæ ipsa ἀυτόγραφα asservavit, & custodivit. Et testis est Eusebius lib. 3. cap. 21. Johannem, qui postremo loco scripsit, vidisse & approbasse ipsa ἀυτόγραφα Evangelistarum Matthæi, Marci & Lucæ.

Cæterum, quòd Jesuvvita subjicit: Oportere credere, hoc Evangelium, quod nunc nomine Marci legitur, esse illud ipsum, quod scripsit Marcus: id sanè non planè omni Sophisticatione caret. Vult enim hoc pacto innuere, externam illam Testificationem Ecclesiæ tanquam Articulum fidei necessario esse credendam omnibus, ac proindè dari posse Traditionem aliquam non scriptam; quæ constituat Articulum fidei. Sed rectissimè à nostris in ipso etiam Colloquio responsum fuit, Testificationem hanc Ecclesiæ, non ad ipsa per se dogmata: sed ad historiam, ac proinde ad Fidem generalem pertinere: neque posse per Testimonium illud Ecclesiæ, novum aliquod & peculiare procudi dogma, & quidem tale, quod deindè reliquis Articulis fidei salvificæ in Scripturâ expressis, & ad credendum omnibus necessario propositis affuendum sit. Exemplo res illustratur. Coloff. 4. legitur, Epistolam ad Colossenses inscriptam, transmissam esse per Onesimum: ille ergò afferens Colossensibus Epistolam à Paulo scriptam, testatur se illam accepisse, ex Apostoli manibus. Quæritur jam, utrum Onesimus hoc externo suo testimonio perhibito, Epistolæ ad Colossenses novum aliquod dogma pertinens ad fidem specialem sive justificantem, adjiciat iis, quæ in Epistola continentur? Ubi qui modò aliquid judicare potest, ultrò negativam tuebitur, & respondebit, non tale novum dogma inde confici, sed tantùm externum testimonium perhiberi. Proinde accuratissimè est distingvendum inter testificationem historicam, & inter contenta in iis libris, de quibus fit testificatio. Quod si testificatio illa externa constituat Articulum fidei, tùm Articulus fidei justificantis erit, quòd Onesimus testatur Epistolam ad Colossenses, esse Pauli: id quod absurdum. Porrò si Testificatio de libris esset peculiaris articulus fidei, tùm sequeretur Ecclesiam ante scriptionem sacrorum librorum Novi Testamenti, pauciores habuisse articulos fidei, quàm postea, cùm doctrina Evangelii in literas relata esset: Sequeretur etiam, per scriptionem librorum Novi Testamenti auctum fuisse numerum dogmatum & fidei Articulorum Atqui hoc posterius est absurdum: Siquidem unum idemque prorsus Evangelium, manet ratione Articulorum & dogmatum, sive prædicetur voce, sive literis mandetur. Absurdum Ergò & prius illud, nempè quod testificatio Ecclesiæ sit peculiaris articulus fidei.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Second Part the Jesuit Proposition (continued)

Thirdly: If the testimony of the primitive Church concerning the sacred books of the New Testament constitutes a peculiar article of faith: it will follow that the testimony of the Jewish Synagogue concerning the books of the Old Testament (which Paul attributes to it in Rom. 3 and

9.) likewise constitutes a peculiar article. But this latter is absurd. Therefore, the former is too.

But the Jesuit Tanner objects against the given answer concerning Onesimus: that the argument is not valid because the condition and authority of some particular person in the Church is not equal to that of the whole Church, or of the highest heads in the Church, so that what the former cannot do, the latter cannot do either. For this exception fails through ignorance of the point at issue. For the question is not, Does the testimony of the whole primitive Church have more authority than the testimony of a private individual, namely Onesimus? But this is asked: Can that which is not of itself a dogma or article of faith be turned and changed into an article of faith by any testimony coming from without (whether it be that of Onesimus, or of the Church, or of many, or of few, or of a private, or of a public person)? We say that a dogma of faith must by its own nature, and by an inherent quality, be so constituted that it obtains the definition of a dogma or article of faith even without any adventitious external testimony. For if it does not have in itself the force of a dogma, it can no more be turned into an article of faith through the testimony of the Church than it could through the testimony of Onesimus, or of any private person. For example, that Tobias had a dog with him on his journey, because it does not have in itself the nature of an ecclesiastical dogma or article of faith: it can never be changed into an article of faith, even if not only private persons, but also the whole Church, nay, even the whole world besides, should bear witness to it.

Nor does the Adversary blunt this weapon when he adds: Certainly Onesimus wrote no Canonical book, nor could he write one. Therefore neither did the Apostles write, nor could they write. For he ought to have argued not from Onesimus to the Apostles, but to the Church: then he would have seen that here too the Church and Onesimus walk with equal step, and that it is no more permitted to the Church, even if universal (except for the immediately called and illuminated Prophets and Apostles), to write Canonical books than it is permitted to Onesimus.

Furthermore, and indeed in the sixth place, the Jesuit clamors that it cannot be known from the Scriptures which books are sacred and Canonical, but that this is established from tradition: and he endeavors to confirm this by the testimony of Serapion, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Basil, etc.

I answer. The Jesuit is proving that which is placed beyond controversy even on our part. For we ourselves do not deny that some place must be granted to the tradition, or rather the testimony, of the Church concerning the Canonical books: but such a place as fulfills not that of a judge, but only that of a witness.

Thus Serapion, in book 6 of his history, chapter 11, according to Eusebius, expressly confesses that he had read through that book which was brought forward under the name of Peter. Therefore he took his argument from the book itself, by which he might distinguish that supposititious one from the genuinely Petrine book.

Thus Clement of Alexandria was as close as possible to the age of the Apostles, as witnessed by Eusebius, book 6, chapter 12. Therefore he could bear witness. For he lived under the reign of Commodus, A.D. 183, and was a disciple of Pantaenus, whom he also subsequently succeeded.

Thus Origen speaks of nothing else than the tradition of the Apostles and the testimony of the Church, which was in the age of the Apostles: For so his own words sound, in Eusebius, book 6, chapter 24. In the tradition concerning the four Gospels I have received, which alone are received in the whole Church which is under heaven. We answer the same thing concerning the testimony of Basil also.

Seventhly, the Jesuit thus makes a disturbance: If this tradition, which books are Canonical, could reach us: why could not others also reach us by the same way?

It is answered: The consequence from possibility to actuality is not valid. 2. Not even the Papists themselves derive their traditions by the same way, namely by the unanimous testimony, and indeed of the most ancient and Apostolic Church: Which very thing they cannot perform for all eternity.

Of the same kind is this cavil: The tradition of the Church, which books are Canonical, is either the Word of GOD, or it is not: If not: Therefore we do not have faith. For faith relies on the Word of GOD. If it is: Why then do they cry out that there is no Word of GOD, unless it is written.

It is answered by a distinction between historical and saving faith: Historical faith relies not only on divine testimony, but also on human. But saving faith is only from hearing the Word of GOD; Rom. 10, nor does it rely on this foundation, that it may know, Which book is Canonical, integral, uncorrupted: Which is not? For the Devil also knows and believes this very thing, etc. James 2.

But the Jesuit proceeds in enumerating those things which are necessary to be believed for salvation, which nevertheless are not contained in the Scriptures. For it must be believed, he says, that the Blessed Mary was always a virgin, against the error of Helvidius, which thing is nevertheless not expressed in the sacred writings.

I answer: The error arises from a confusion of several questions, one is: Whether it is established from the Scriptures that Mary was an uncorrupted virgin before birth and in birth? Another is: Whether it can likewise be demonstrated from the Scriptures that Mary remained a virgin after birth? The third, finally and lastly: Whether the knowledge of either of the preceding questions constitutes an Article of faith, and indeed one necessary for salvation.

The truth of the first question is most clearly established from the Scriptures alone: Isaiah certainly, chapter 7, 14, says: Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a Son. Therefore she remained a virgin in conception and birth: Otherwise she would have borne as a wife, not a virgin, as Epiphanius rightly gathers, book 1, Tom. 2, heresy 28, Jerem. 31, 22. The Lord has created a New thing upon the earth, a Woman shall encompass a Man. If the Prophet were speaking of natural conception, he would not have said: The Lord will create a New thing upon the earth. Then, as often as Scripture calls Christ the Seed of the woman: It is certain that nothing else is demonstrated, than that he himself was conceived and born without male seed, according to the flesh. Thirdly, if Mary had conceived and borne by means of male seed, there would have been no need for that peculiar overshadowing of the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High. Luke 1, 35. Finally, she herself bears witness to her own virginity, Luke 1, 34, saying to the Archangel Gabriel: How shall this be: Since I do not know a man.

The second question: Whether Mary remained a Virgin after childbirth, is likewise most evidently established from the Scriptures. For in Matthew 1:25, concerning Joseph, Mary's

spouse, it is read thus: He knew her not, until she had brought forth her firstborn Son: that is, never: For the force of this proposition is the same as that of Gen. 8:7: Neither did the raven return, until the earth was dried: that is, it never returned. Likewise that promise of Christ in Matt. 28:20: I am with you, even unto the consummation of the age. And that of Psalm 110:1: The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool. Which very thing pious Antiquity also established by unanimous consent. Whence was born that rule of Nazianzen, Orat. 2 on the Son: The particle 'until', or 'unto', is not altogether placed for the distinction of future time: But it does indeed posit 'how long': but the time that follows from it, it does not altogether deny. Then this very thing is clear from the Scriptures, and indeed from the place already cited before, Luke 1:35, concerning the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, and the power of the Most High.
