For because Mary's body was peculiarly deputed by GOD for such a work, than which no other work could be named either holier or more divine in its majesty: certainly every pious person easily understands that it is utterly abhorrent to this very majesty of the conception and birth of the Son of GOD, that that virginal body, which had been the habitation of the Holy Spirit and the temple of the Son of GOD, per modum quendam μονότροπον καὶ ἐξαίρετον, as Justinian speaks, should afterwards be set forth as having been exposed to the work of conjugal concupiscence.

As regards the third and last question: I maintain that the preceding two questions are not of the same condition. For the former, if it does not constitute an article of faith by itself, is nevertheless certainly a part of that supreme Article by which we believe that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary. And indeed, whoever dares to deny this, he strikes against the analogy, nay, against the very foundation of faith: and makes a loss of it. For unless I certainly believe that Christ was born of a true virgin, and one remaining such in the very birth, faith truly totters as to whether Christ is that promised Messiah of the World who was to be born of a virgin. But, as regards the latter question, Whether Mary also remained a Virgin after childbirth: I maintain that it pertains to general faith, and is to be believed for a reason consistently drawn from the Scriptures: but not to justifying or special faith: since the virginity of Mary after childbirth does not necessarily pertain to the article concerning the Incarnation and birth of Christ. Which is the reason that Basil, in his Homily on the Nativity of Christ, maintains that one should not scrupulously litigate about this question.

But Bellarmine brings forward still more things which he believes are indeed necessary to be believed, but are not contained in the Scriptures: such as that Easter in the New Testament is to be celebrated on a Sunday: Because the ancient Church held the Quartodecimans to be heretics.

But I answer, and I simply deny the subsumption, that the festival of Easter, considered in itself, either by reason of the ceremonies or by reason of the time, constitutes any Article of faith necessary to be believed. For I distinguish between the Resurrection of the Lord, which comes to be considered at Easter: and the time in which this consideration ought to be solemnly made. The very Resurrection of Christ itself is not only an Article, but the basis and foundation of all the remaining Articles, 1 Cor. 15.

Latin:

Tertiò: Si Testificatio Ecclesiæ primitivæ delibris sacris Novi Testamenti peculiarem constituit articulum fidei: Sequetur, quòd etiam Testificatio Synagogæ Judaicæ, de libris Veteris Testamenti (quam ei tribuit Paulus Rom. 3. &

9.) itidem constituat peculiarem Articulum. Atqui posterius hoc ab surdum. Ergò & prius.

Excipit verò Jesuvvita Tannerus adversus datam responsionem de Onesimo: Non valere argumentum quia non par sit Conditio & autoritas particularis alicujus in Ecclesia personæ, & totius Ecclesiæ, sive summorum in Ecclesia capitum, ut quod ille non potest, neque isti possint. Fallit enim hæc exceptio Ignoratione Elenchi. Non enim quæstio est, An plus autoritatis habeat Testimonium totius Ecclesiæ primitivæ, testimonio privati, videlicet Onesimi: Sed hoc quæritur, An, Quod ex sese dogma sive Articulus fidei non est, possit ullo testimonio forinsecus accedente (sive id sit Onesimi, sive Ecclesiæ, sive multorum, sive paucorum, sive privatæ, sive publicæ personæ) verti & mutari in articulum fidei? Dicimus E. Dogma fidei oportere sua naturâ, & insitâ quadam affectione sic comparatum esse, ut etiam sine adventitio externo testimonio fortiatur definitionem dogmatis sive articuli fidei. Si enim non in sese habet vim dogmatis, tàm non verti poterit in articulum fidei, per testimonium Ecclesiæ, quàm nec per testificationem Onesimi, aut cujusvis privatæ personæ. Exempli gratiâ, quòd Tobias fecum canem habuerit in itinere suo, quia non in se habet naturam dogmatis Ecclesiastici, sive articuli fidei: nunquam mutari potest in fidei articulum, si de eo non modò personæ privatæ, sed etiam tota Ecclesia, imò totus insuper mundus testimonium ferat.

Neque hoc telum elidit Adversarius, cum addit: Certè Onesimus nullum librum Canonicum scripsit, nec scribere potuit. Ergò nec Apostoli scripserunt, nec scribere potuerunt. Argumentari enim debebat ab Onesimo non ad Apostolos: Sed ad Ecclesiam: tunc vidisset hîc quoq; pari passu ambulare Ecclesiam & Onesimum, & Ecclesiæ licèt universali (præter immediatè vocatos & illuminatos Prophetas & Apostolos) tàm non licere scribere libros Canonicos, quàm nec Onesimo liceat

Porrò & quidem sexto loco obstrepit Jesuvvita, è Scripturis sciri non posse, quinam libri sint sacri & Canonici: sed constare illud ex traditione: idque confirmare studet testimonio Serapionis: Clementis Alex. Origenis, Basilii & c.

Respondeo. Probare id Jesuvvitam quod ex nostra etiam parte extra Controversiam est positum. Nam traditioni vel potiùs testificationi Ecclesiæ de libris Canonicis locum aliquem concedendum esse, ne ipsi quidem negamus: sed talem locum, qui non judicis, sed testis tantummodò suppleat.

Sic Serapion lib. 6. hist. cap. 11. apud Eusebium disertè fatetur, se Librum illum, qui sub Petri nomine proferebatur, perlegisse. Ergò ex ipso libro argumentum sumpsit, quo discerneret supposititium illum, à libro γνησίως Petrino.

Sic Clemens Alexandrinus fuit ætati Apostolorum quàm proximè vicinus, teste Eusebio lib. 6. cap. 12. Ergò testari potuit. Vixit enim sub imperio Commodi A.C. 183. & fuit Pantæni discipulus, cui etiam postmodum successit.

Sic Origenes de nulla alia, quàm de Apostolorum traditione, & testificatione Ecclesiæ, quæ Apostolorum fuit ætate, loquitur: Sic enim sonant ipsius verba, apud Eusebium lib. 6. c. 24. In traditione de quatuor Evangeliis accepi, quæ sola, in universa, quæ sub cælo est, Ecclesiâ recipiũtur. Quod ipsum de Basilii etiam testimonio respondemus.

Septimò sic tumultuatur Jesuvvita: Si hæc traditio, qui libri sint Canonici, ad nos pervenire potuit: cur non per eandem viam potuerunt etiam aliæ pervenire?

Respondetur enim: A posse ad inesse non valet Consequentia. 2. Ne ipsi quidem Pontificii suas traditiones per eandem viam deducunt, nempè per testificationem unanimem, & quidé antiquissimæ & Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ: Quod ipsum in omnem æternitatem præstare non possunt.

Ejusdem generis est, & hæc est cavillatio: Traditio Ecclesiæ, qui libri sint Canonici, vel est Verbum DEI, vel non est: Si non: Igitur non habemus fidem. Fides enim Verbo DEI nititur. Si est: Cur ergò clamant, nullum esse Verbum DEI, nisi scriptum.

Respondetur enim per distinctionem Fidei historicæ & salvificæ: Historica fides nititur non tantùm testimonio divino, sed etiam humano. Salvifica autem fides tantùm est ex auditu Verbi DEI; Rom. 10 neque nititur hoc fundamento, ut sciat, Qui liber sit Canonicus, integer, incorruptus: Qui non? Nam & hoc ipsum novit & credit Diabolus &c. Jacob. 2.

Sed pergit Jesuvvita in enumerandis illis, quæ creditu ad salutem sint necessaria, quæ tamen in Scripturis non contineantur. Credendum enim est, inquit, B. Mariam semper fuisse virginem, contra errorem Helvidii, id quod tamen in sacris non sit expressum.

Respondeo: Error oritur ex confusione plurium Quæstionum, una est: An ex Scripturis constet, quòd Maria ante partum & in partu fuerit virgo incorrupta? Altera est: An itidem ex Scripturis demonstrari possit, quòd Maria post partum virgo manserit? Tertia denique ac postrema. An præcedentis utriusq; quæstionis notitia constituat Articulum fidei, & quidem ad salutem necessarium.

Primæ Quæstionis veritas ex solis Scripturis dilucidissimè constat: Iesaias certè cap. 7, 14. Ecce, inquit, Virgo concipiet & pariet Filium. Ergò in conceptu & partu mansit virgo: Alioquin non virgo, sed uxor peperisset, ut rectè colligit Epiphanius lib. 1. Tom. 2. hær. 28, Jerem. 31, 22. Dominus creavit Novum super terram, Fæmina circundabit Virum. Si de naturali conceptione ageret Propheta, non dixisset: Dominus creabit Novum super terram. Deindè, quoties Scriptura Christum nominat Semen mulieris: Certum est, nihil demonstrari aliud, quàm ipsum sine virili semine conceptum & natum esse, secundum carnem. Tertiò, si mediante virili semine Maria concepisset & peperisset, nihil opus fuisset, peculiari illâ obumbratione Spiritus Sancti & virtute Altissimi. Luc. 1, 35. Tandem ipsamet Virginitati suæ perhibet Testimonium, Luc. 1, 34. dicens ad Gabrielem Archangelum: Quomodo fiet istud: Siquidem virum non cognosco.

Altera Quæstio: An Maria post partum manserit Virgo, itidem ex Scripturis evidentissimè constat. Matthæi enim 1, 25. de Josepho Mariæ

Sponso sic legitur: Non cognovit eam, donec peperit Filium suum primogenitum: hoc est, nunquam: Eadem enim vis est propositionis hujus, quæ est illius Gen. 8, 7. Neq; rediit corvus, donec siccaretur terra: hoc est, nunquam rediit. Item illius promissionis Christi Matth. 28, 20. Ego sum vobiscum, usq; ad Consummationem seculi. Et illius Psal. 110, 1. Dixit Dominus Domino meo, sede à dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos ad Scabellum pedum tuorum. Quod ipsum etiam unanimi consensu statuit pia Antiquitas. Unde nata est regula illa Nazianzeni Orat. 2. de Filio; Particula Donec, vel usq;, non omninò ponitur ad distinctionem futuri temporis: Sed ponit illa quidem, Quousque: verum Tempus, quod ab eo sequitur, non omninò inficiatur. Deinde patet hoc ipsum ex Scripturis & quidem loco jam ante citato Luc. 1, 35. de obumbratione Spiritus Sancti, & virtute altissimi. Quia enim Mariæ corpus peculiariter à DEO ad tale opus deputatum fuit, quo non aliud opus vel sanctius, vel majestate suâ diviniùs nominari queat: certè quisque pius facilè intelligit, ab hac ipsa majestate conceptionis & nativitatis Filii DEI, penitùs abhorrere, ut Virgineum illud corpus, quòd Spiritus Sancti habitaculum, & Filii DEI templum, per modum quendam μονότροπον καὶ ἐξαίρετον, ut Justinian9 loquitur, fuerat, postea concupiscentiæ conjugalis operi statuatur fuisse expositum.

Tertiam & postremam quæstionem quod attinet: statuo præcedentes duas quæstiones non cujusdem esse conditionis. Prior enim, si non articulum fidei per se constituit, tamen certè pars est Articuli illius summi, quo credimus, Christum natum esse ex Maria Virgine. Et sanè qui hoc negare ausit, is impingit in analogiam, imò in ipsum fundamentum fidei: ejusque jacturam facit. Nisi enim certò credam, Christum natum esse ex vera virgine, & tali quidem in ipso partu permanente, labascit profectè fides, An Christus sit promissus ille Mundi Messias, qui ex virgine nascendus erat. Cæterùm, quoad posteriorem Quæstionem. An Maria post partum etiam manserit Virgo: statuo pertinere illam ad Fidem generalem, & credi eam, ob rationem è Scripturis consentaneè depromptam: non verò ad fidem justificantem sive specialem: siquidem ad articulum de Incarnatione & nativitate Christi, non necessariò pertinet Virginitas Mariæ post partum. Quæ causa est, quòd Basilius Homil. de Nativitate Christi: statuit, haud scrupulosè hac de Quæstione esse litigandum.

Sed plura adhuc profert Bellarminus, quæ creditu quidem sint necessaria: in Scripturis autem non contineantur: ut quod Pascha in Novo Testamento sit celebrandū die Dominico: Quia ab Ecclesiâ âtiquâ hæretici sunt habitati Quartadecimani.

Sed Respondeo, & nego simpliciter subsumtionem, quòd Festivitas paschæ in se, vel ratione ceremoniarum, vel ratione temporis considerata, constituat aliquem Articulum fidei, creditu necessarium. Distingvo enim inter Resurrectionem Domini, quæ in paschate consideranda venit: & inter tempus, quo hæc consideratio solenniter fieri debeat. Resurrectio sanè ipsa Christi non modò est, Articulus, sed Articulorum reliquorum omnium basis ac fundamentum 1. Cor. 15.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Second Part the Jesuit Proposition (continued)

However, knowledge of this does not become clear to us from any unwritten tradition, but most clearly from the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures. Furthermore, the time for celebrating the Paschal solemnity is most correctly referred to among the Adiaphora, according to that passage in Colossians 2:16: 'Let no one judge you in food or in drink, or in part of a feast day.' Therefore, this circumstance also contributes nothing to our faith and salvation. Nor is he a heretic who might determine otherwise: just as, indeed, the Asians are read to have been reproached by no one on this account, because according to ancient custom, derived from the Apostles themselves, they celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, whether it was the Lord's Day or another: as Polycrates writes in his letter to Victor. Just as the Nicene Council also did not make a decree so that henceforth Easter would be celebrated by all Christians everywhere on one day, and indeed on the Lord's Day: as if this matter were necessary for faith and salvation, and to be observed under some absolute necessity: but because it wished, out of Christian liberty, to remove by this agreement that dissension which existed between the Western and Eastern Churches regarding this matter. For it is unseemly that there should be any difference in such great holiness, and it is more honorable to adhere to the same opinion, as that Decree held, according to Socrates, book 1, chapter 6, and Theodoret, book 1, chapter 10. As for the Quartodecimans, they are not read to have been accused of heresy properly so called: but only of schism, because they departed from that order sanctioned by the Church: as witnessed by Epiphanius, heresy 50. The Quartodecimans have everything as the Church does: but they err in that they do not attend to the consequences and the doctrine of the RITES.

Furthermore, the Jesuit clamors thus: It is necessary to believe against the Anabaptists that the baptism of infants is valid: but neither the Catholics prove this from the Scriptures alone, nor can the Lutherans prove it in any way.

But I respond. 1. Regarding the so-called Catholics, we cannot be held responsible for their fault: for if they searched the Scriptures at the command of Christ, perhaps it would not be difficult for them to demonstrate infant baptism most evidently from the Scriptures themselves. Then, indeed, regarding the Lutherans, the Jesuit says what is so false that nothing fights more against the Anabaptists than that the baptism of children can be evidently demonstrated from the Scriptures alone: which they also prove in reality in the Exegesis of the Article on Baptism. For 1. Christ commands to baptize all nations: Matthew 28:19. And yet infants constitute easily the most significant part of these. Therefore.

2. No one can be made a participant of the kingdom of heaven unless he has been regenerated from water and the Spirit: John 3. Therefore, this means of arriving at salvation cannot or ought not to be denied even to infants: especially since Christ himself commands infants to come to him, Mark 10:14, and wishes that none of them perish, Matthew 18:14. But they would certainly perish if they were not washed from the guilt of sins by the washing of water, Ephesians 5:16, and if they did not put on Christ through baptism, Galatians 3:27, and were not grafted into him, Romans 8, and were not buried into his death through baptism, Romans 6:3.

3. The Apostles are read to have baptized entire families: Why then not also infants?

Nor does it stand in the way that many of the Fathers call the baptism of infants a Tradition. For they understood a tradition not as unwritten and finally devised by the Pope: but as written, namely received from the Apostles themselves, and founded in the Scriptures. To which opinion Augustine writes: The Church received from the Apostles the tradition to give baptism even to infants: for they knew, to whom the secrets of the mysteries were entrusted, that there are in all people the genuine stains of sin, which ought to be abolished through water and the Holy Spirit, John 3.

Furthermore, what Bellarmine adds in this place concerning the actual faith of infants, and brings forward arguments for the negative, do not belong to this place.

Let these few things suffice by the way. I. Without faith it is impossible to please GOD, Rom. 14, 33. Hebr. 11, 6. But infants please GOD, so much so that the Savior promises the kingdom of heaven to them, Mark 10, 14. Therefore. II. Infants are regenerated through baptism, and are adopted into the children of GOD, John 3, 5. Titus 3, 5. And yet Regeneration cannot exist without faith: For by faith alone are hearts purified, Acts 15, 9. John 1, 12. Therefore. III. Infants regenerated through baptism are saved: For where there is Regeneration, there is Faith: where there is Faith, there is Salvation: And conversely: Where there is Salvation, there is Faith. John 3, 5. Mark 16, 16. IV. Without faith no one can come to Christ, John 6, 37. & 40. But infants are not only commanded to come, but are received with fatherly benevolence. Mark 10, 14. Therefore. V. Circumcision was nothing else than a seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4, 11. Baptism has succeeded into the place and effect of circumcision. Coloss. 2, 11, & 12. Therefore. VI. Christ, Matt. 18, 6, expressly testifies that infants believe. Therefore.

[NB. The distinguished theologian Dr. Salomon Gesner argues excellently concerning habitual and actual faith, against the Jesuits, in his explanation of the saying 2 Tim. 3. X. 1. b. & following.]

Eleventhly, the Jesuit argues thus: Luther believed that Purgatory existed, and yet he asserts that it cannot be proven from the Holy Scriptures. But I answer briefly: 1. We accept with both hands, as they say, that Bellarmine in this place does not at all deny that Purgatory cannot be proven from the sacred writings. 2. As regards Luther, it certainly could not have been unknown to Bellarmine that Luther wrote those things around the beginning of his struggles: and later retracted them: so that nothing can be inferred from that to the prejudice of Luther's doctrine.

Finally, the Jesuit also brings forward this: All the heretics of this time believe that there is no Word of GOD except what is written: But this is certainly nowhere found in the whole Scripture. Therefore.

I answer that the argument labors under a manifest falsehood. For it is simply false that this very thing is not expressly contained in Scripture. For what else does that command, so often repeated, about adding nothing to and taking nothing from the Word of GOD mean, other than that besides these very Scriptures no other Word of GOD is to be sought or hoped for by us? Deut. 4, 2. & chap. 12, last. Whatever I command you, do only this, neither add anything, nor take away. Whence we evidently conclude thus: If it was not permitted to the Jews, as it was not permitted, to add anything to the books of Moses, therefore it will be much less lawful for us to add anything to the Canon of Scripture, already augmented and confirmed by so many books. The Jesuit insists that these precepts do not help us, because Moses does not say that nothing is to be added to the written Word, but to the Word which he spoke. But this argument lacks any refutation, and proceeds from a false hypothesis, as if the condition of the Word which GOD spoke through Moses were one thing, and the condition of the Word already written were another, regarding that precept. Certainly, since Moses did not speak one Word and leave another written, but rather consigned to letters that very Word which he had announced to the Jews by living voice, by the command of GOD (Exod. 17:14; Deut. 31:24), the vanity of this objection is clearly evident even from that. What of the fact that those precepts principally concern the Moral law, which no one would deny was written twice by the finger of GOD himself? Add that the same precept is repeated and expressly accommodated to the book of the written Word in Rev. 22:18 & 19. Where it is manifest in itself that that precept refers not only to the visions of that book, but also to the Articles of faith which are contained in that book. I testify to everyone hearing the words of the Prophecy of this book: If anyone adds to these, GOD will add upon him the plagues written in this book: And if anyone diminishes from the words of the book of this Prophecy, GOD will take away his part from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from those things which are written in this book. See more Objections and Instances in Tom. VI. of the Jesuits: Page 482 & following up to page 506. Also, page 175, 184, 193 & following.

As if in place of a conclusion, to the arguments discussed thus far, one may also add that which the Jesuits bring forward from Tertullian and exaggerate in many ways. For he has it thus in his book De praescriptione haereticorum, chapter 5: 'One must not appeal to the Scriptures, nor should the contest be established in those things in which there is either no victory, or an uncertain one, or one that is little certain.' But a notable fallacy is committed here, a paralogism of taking what is said in a specific context as if it were said simply and universally. For Tertullian does not speak simply and universally, as if in settling controversies of the Christian Religion one must not appeal to the Scriptures simply. For we shall show a little later that he himself maintains the opposite. But he speaks in a qualified sense, namely, with respect to those heretics who simply strip away all authority of Scripture, that is, who, as Tertullian himself reports, partly do not accept all the Scriptures, partly pervert those which they do accept with their own additions and subtractions, and partly accuse the Apostles, their authors, of not having known all things, and consequently of not having handed down all things perfectly in them, but that these things must be supplemented by unwritten Traditions. If, therefore, a dispute is to be instituted with these people concerning books that are truly Canonical, Tertullian rightly maintains that it is altogether in vain to refute them from the Scriptures, since they reject all its authority; but he judges that they are to be convinced rather by the testimony of the Church. He understands, however, the testimony not of just any church, but only of that Church which was contemporary with the times of the Apostles.

Another error arises from the sophistry of the non sequitur. For the consequence does not hold: 'That this book is believed to be the work of this or that author is known by the testimony of the Church; therefore, no article of faith can be sufficiently demonstrated from the Scriptures.' For one must accurately distinguish between those things which inform general and historical faith, and those things which directly concern saving Faith, or the articles of faith. The certainty of the former can be sought from the testimony of the Church; but that of the latter from the Scriptures alone. This is evident from Tertullian himself, who elsewhere, and indeed when placed outside of that state of affairs, writes thus in his book De Resurrectione, chapter 3: 'Take away from the heretics what they hold in common with the Heathens, so that they may base their questions on the SCRIPTURES ALONE, and they will not be able to stand.' Whence the same Tertullian again refutes the heretics who deny that the Apostles knew all things, in express words, from nothing but Scripture, citing the testimonies of Matthew chapter 10:27. & 25:24. Also John 16. Where Christ promises that the Paraclete will lead the Apostles into all truth: as can be seen in chapters 9, 13, & 14 of the book De praescriptione haereticorum.

Latin:

Hujus autem notitia nobis non ex traditione aliquâ non scriptâ, sed ex Scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis, luculentissimè elucescit. Cæterùm Tempus celebrandi solennitatem Paschalem rectissimè refertur inter Adiaphora, juxta illud Coloss 2, 16. Nemo vos judicet in cibo aut potu, aut in parte diei festi. Quare nihil etiam hæc circumstantia facit, ad fidem & salutem nostram. Neq; etiam hæreticus est, qui diversum statueret: Quemadmodum sanè hoc nomine Asiatici à nemine ideò reprehensi leguntur, quòd ex antiquâ consuetudine, ab ipsis Apostolis deducta, decimâ quartâ Lunâ, sive dies esset Dominicus, sive alius, pascha celebrarunt: uti scribit Polycrates in suâ ad victorem Epistolâ. Quemadmodum etiam Concilium Nicenum non ideò decretum fecit, ut deinceps ab omnibus Christianis ubique Pascha uno die, & quidem Dominico celebraretur: quasi hæc res ad fidem & salutem esset neceffaria: & sub absolutâ quadam necessitate observanda: Sed quia ex libertate Christiana voluit hoc pacto dissidium illud, quod Ecclesiæ Occidentali cum Orientali super hac re intercedebat, tollere. Indecorum enim est, aliquam esse in tantâ sanctitate differentiam, & honestius eidem adhærere sententiæ, ut habuit Decretum illud, referente Socrate lib. 1. cap. 6. & Theodoreto lib. 1. cap. 10. Quoad Quartadecimanos illi nõ leguntur hæreseos propriè sic dictæ fuisse insimulatos: Sed tantum Schismatis, eò quòd ab ordine illo ab Ecclesia sancito, discederent: teste Epiphanio hæres. 50. Quartadecimani omnia habent ut Ecclesia: Aberrant autem eò, quod Consequentia & doctrinæ RITUUM non attendunt.

Porrò sic obstrepit Jesuvvita: Credere oporter contra Anabaptistas, baptismum parvulorum esse ratum: id autem ex solis scripturis nec Catholici probant, nec Lutherani ullo modo probare possunt.

Sed Respondeo. 1. Quoad Catholicos falsò sic dictos, nos ipsorum culpam præstare non posse: Si enim ad mandatum Christi Scripturas scrutarentur, fortè non difficile ipsis foret, pædobaptismum ex ipsis Scripturis evidentissimè demonstrare. Deindè verò quoad Lutheranos, usque adeò falsum dicit Jesuvvita, ut nihil magis contra Anabaptistas illi pugnẽt, quàm ex Solis scripturis puerorum Baptismum evidenter demonstrari posse: id quod illi etiam reipsâ præstant in diexodo Articuli de Baptismo. Nam 1. Christus omnes gentes jubet baptizare: Matth. 28, 19. Atqui harum partem facilè potissimam constituunt Infantes. Ergò.

2. Regni cœlorum nemo potest reddi particeps, nisi qui regeneratus fuerit ex aquâ & Spiritu: Johan. 3. Ergò ne quidem Infantibus hoc medium perveniendi ad salutem denegari potest aut debet: præsertim cum Christus ipse jubeat infantes ad se venire. Marci 10, 14. & istorum neminem perire velit: Matth. 18, 14. Perirent autem utiq;, nisi lavacro aquæ à peccatorum reatu abluerentur Eph. 5, 16. & nisi per baptismum Christum induerent, Gal. 3, 27. eique infererentur, Rom. 8. & in mortem ejus per baptismum sepelirentur Rom. 6, 3.

3. Apostoli leguntur integras familias baptizasse: Quid ni ergò & Infantes?

Neque obstat, quòd Patrum plurimi, Baptismum parvulorum nominant Traditionem. Intellexerunt enim Traditionem non ἄγραφον, & à Pontifice demùm excogitatam: sed ἔγγραφον, ab ipsis nimirum Apostolis acceptam, & in Scripturis fundatam. Quam in sententiam scribit Augustinus: Ecclesia ab Apostolis accepit traditionem, etiam parvulis dare Baptismum: Sciebant enim illi, quibus arcana mysteriorum commendata fuerunt, quòd sint in omnibus genuinæ sordes peccati, Quas per aquam & Spiritum Sanctum aboleri oporteret Johan. 3.

Quæ porrò hoc loco annectit Bellarminus de Fide actuali infantum, & pro negativâ profert argumenta, non sunt hujus loci.

Pauca hæc obiter sufficiant I. Sine fide impossibile est placere DEO, Rom. 14, 33. Hebr. 11, 6. Infantes autem DEO placent, adeò, ut regnum cælorum Servator illis spondeat, Marci 10, 14. E. II. Infantes per baptismum regenerantur, inq́ue filios DEI adoptantur, Joh. 3, 5. Tit. 3, 5. Atqui Regeneratio sine fide stare nequit: Solâ enim fide purgantur corda, Act. 15, 9. Joh. 1, 12. Ergò. III. Infantes regenerati per baptismum salvantur: Ubi enim Regeneratio, ibi Fides: ubi Fides, ibi Salus: Et vice versâ: Ubi Salus, ibi Fides. Joh. 3, 5. Marci 16, 16. IV. Sine fide nemo potest venire ad Christum, Joh. 6, 37. & 40. Infantes autem non modò jubentur venire, sed paternâ benevolentiâ excipiuntur. Marc. 10, 14. Ergò. V. Circumcisio nihil fuit aliud, quàm signaculum Justitiæ fidei, Rom. 4, 11. Baptismus successit in locum & effectum circumcisionis. Coloss. 2, 11, & 12. Ergò. VI. Christus Matth. 18, 6. disertè testatur, Infantes credere. Ergò.

[NB. Egregiè disputat de fide habituali & actuali, contra Jesuvvitas Cl. Theologus D. Salom. Gesnerus in explicatione dicti 2. Tim. 3. X. 1. b. & seqq.]

Undecimò, sic arguit Jesuvvita: Lutherus credidit Purgatorium esse, & tamen asserit, id non posse probari ex S. Literis. Sed paucis respondeo 1. nos utrâque, quod ajunt, manu acceptare, quod Bellarminus hoc loco minimè inficiatur, Purgatorium ex sacris probari non posse. 2. Quoad Lutherum, haud certè ignotum esse potuit Bellarmino, ista circa principium certaminum suorum Lutherum scripsisse: & postea retractasse: ut inde nihil in præjudicium doctrinæ Lutheri inferri possit.

Tandem profert Jesuvvita & istud: Credunt omnes hæretici hujus temporis, nullum esse Verbum DEI, nisi scriptum: At hoc certè nuspiam in tota Scriptura invenitur. Ergò.

Respondeo, laborare argumentum manifesto ψεῦδει. Nam simpliciter falsum est, hoc ipsum expressè non contineri in Scriptura. Quid enim sibi vult aliud præceptū illud toties iteratum, de nihil addendo & detrahendo de Verbo DEI, quàm præter has ipsas Scripturas nullum aliud Verbum DEI à nobis quærendum & sperandum esse? Deut. 4, 2. & cap. 12, ult. Quicquid præcipio tibi, hoc tantùm facito, neq; addas quicquā, neq; minuas. Unde evidenter sic colligimus: Si Judæis non licuit, uti non licuit, quicquam addere ad libros Mosis: Ergò multò minùs nobis licebit aliquid addere ad Canonem Scripturæ, tot jam libris auctum confirmatumque. Instat Jesuvita, Præcepta isthæc nihil nos juvare, propterea quòd Moses non dicat, nihil addendum esse verbo scripto: sed Verbo quod locutus sit. Verùm caret hoc argumentum omni ἐλέγχῳ: & ex falsa procedit hypothesi, quasi alia sit conditio Verbi, quod DEUS per Mosen est locutus, alia verò Verbi jam scripti conditio, quoad præceptum illud. Certè cùm non aliud Verbum locutus sit Moses, aliud verò scriptum reliquerit Moses: sed illud ipsum Verbum, quod vivâ voce Judæis annunciaverat, postmodum jussu DEI, literis consignarit, Exod. 17, 14. Deut. 31, 24. vel inde vanitas instantiæ hujus liquidò patet. Quid quòd præcepta illa principaliter legem Moralem concernunt, quàm certè ipsius DEI digito bis scriptam fuisse, nemo negaverit. Adde, quòd idem præceptum repetitur & ad librum Verbi scripti expressè accommodatur Apoc. 22, 18 & 19. Ubi non tantùm de visionib9 illius libri, sed & de Articulis fidei, qui in libro illo continentur, præceptum illud sonare, per se manifestum est. Contestor omni, audienti Verba Prophetiæ libri hujus: Siquis apposuerit ad hæc, apponet DEUS super illum plagas scriptas in libro isto: Et si quis diminuerit, de verbis libri Prophetiæ hujus, auferet DEUS partem ejus de libro vitæ, & de civitate Sancta, & de his, quæ scripta sunt in libro isto. Plures Objectiones & Instantias Vide Tom. VI. Jesuvit: Pag 4. 82. & seqq. usq; ad pag. 506. Item, pag. 175. 184. 193. & seqq.

Potest coronidis quasi loco, argumentis hactenus discussis, adjici etiam illud, quod Jesuvvitæ ex Tertulliano proferunt & multis exaggerant. Sic enim ille habet lib. de præscript. adv. hær. cap. 5. Non ad Scripturas provocandum est: nec in his constituendum certamen, in quib9 aut nulla aut incerta victoria est, aut parum certa. Sed infignis committitur παραλογισμὸς παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Neq; enim simpliciter ac universaliter loquitur Tertullianus, ac si in Controversiis Religionis Christianæ dirimendis, ad Scripturas simpliciter non sit provocandum. Diversum enim ipsum statuere, paulò pòst ostendemus. Sed κατὰ τι loquitur, nempè, respectu illorum hæreticorum, qui simpliciter omnem Scripturæ autoritatem adimunt, hoc est, qui referente ipso Tertulliano, partim non omnes Scripturas recipiunt, partim verò quas recipiunt, suis additionibus & detractionibus pervertunt, partim earum autores Apostolos non omnia scivisse, ac proinde non omnia perfectè in illis tradidisse, sed ea ex Traditionibus non scriptis supplenda esse, criminantur. Quod si ergò cum his de libris verè Canonicis instituenda sit disputatio, rectè omninò statuit Tertullianus, frustrà ex Scripturis illos redargui, siquidem omnem ejus autoritatem respuunt: Sed ex Testimonio potiùs Ecclesiæ, convincendos illos esse, judicat. Intelligit autem non cujusvis, sed illius tantùm Ecclesiæ testimonium, quæ temporibus Apostolorum fuit σύγχρονος.

Alter error oritur ex Sophisticatione παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Non enim valet consequétia: Quod hic liber creditur esse hujus vel illius autoris, parum tet Testimonio Ecclesiæ: Ergò nullus Articulus fidei & Scripturis sufficienter demonstrari potest. Nam accuratè distinguendum inter ea, quę fidem generalem & historicam informant: & inter ea, quæ Fidem salvificam, sive articulos fidei directè concernunt. Illorum certitudo peti potest ex testimonio Ecclesiæ; Horum verò ex solis Scripturis. Patet hoc ipsius Tertulliani, qui alibi, & quidem extra istum statum positus, sic scribit libro de Resurrectione cap. 3. Aufer hæreticis, quæ cum Ethnicis sapiunt: ut de SCRIPTURIS SOLIS quæstiones suas sistant, & stare non poterunt. Unde ipse iterum Tertullianus, hæreticos, negantes omnia Apostolos scivisse, disertis verbis refutat, non nisi ex Scriptura, citatis testimoniis Matthæi cap. 10, 27. & 25, 24. Item Johan. 16. Ubi Christus promittit, Paracletum inducturum Apostolos in omnem veritatem: uti videre est cap. 9, 13. & 14 libri de præscript. adver. hær.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Question VII and the final general concerning Traditions

Traditions, which the Romanists commonly, but quite ignorantly, call the unwritten Word of GOD, and sell as Apostolic, are neither to be rejected simply, nor are they to be approved.

CONFIRMATION.

The word tradition, or paradosis, is homonymous and common, and taken generally it denotes any doctrine whatsoever, whether it consists of bare words or of writing: and it is taken now in a good sense, now in a bad one: and is attributed now to truth, now to falsehood. Whence Tertullian rightly distinguished them into Apostolic and Apostatic. And indeed that there are Apostolic Traditions is evident even from that saying of the Apostle in 2 Thess. 2:15: 'Stand fast, brethren, and hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by our Word or by our Epistle.' Furthermore, in order that these may be more accurately distinguished from the supposititious and spurious constitutions which are circulated under the name of the Apostles, the written Word of GOD alone will be the rule of judgment by far the most exact of all. And indeed, under the name of Apostolic Traditions, we willingly admit many constitutions.

I. For 1. That the books of Moses and the Prophets constitute the Canon of the Old Testament is an Apostolic Tradition: since they confirmed it by their own authority.

II. The Apostolic doctrine itself is Tradition, first indeed promulgated by word of mouth, afterwards committed to writing.

III. Apostolic Tradition is that these very books, which we acknowledge as Apostolic, are genuinely Apostolic: inasmuch as that ancient Church received them from the Apostles themselves.

IV. Apostolic Tradition is that constitution of the Creed, which if we believe Rufinus, the Apostles gathered together before their dispersion into the whole world, and commended to the Churches.

V. Apostolic Tradition is the ordination of Bishops and Deacons with the laying on of hands, the Presbytery, the Excommunication of those who sin stubbornly and contumaciously, the collection of alms, Psalmody, the Lord's day, and if there are any traditions similar to these, which are partly indicated not obscurely in the Apostolic writings themselves, and partly were proposed and prescribed more broadly to the Churches by the Apostles themselves by word of mouth.

VI. In place of Apostolic traditions, we also willingly admit certain other rites, ordained by the Apostles themselves to be observed in public ecclesiastical assemblies. Which, however, were not proposed under absolute necessity, so as to be for all times, places, and persons, nor indeed much less under the opinion of worship or merit: but only to serve certain times, places, persons, and as the Apostle says, for order and decency. Hence it happened that, with the cessation of that condition of time and persons, those rites and constitutions also fell into disuse, nay, clearly expired. In which respect we today also have and retain many Traditions, relying on that liberty into which we have been asserted through Christ: so far are we from rejecting all traditions in general.

Therefore, the controversy between us and the Romanists does not properly concern the Apostolic ones already enumerated, nor other Traditions legitimately ordained by the Church: but concerns those primarily which the Romanists, under the name of the Apostles, foist upon the Churches, not so much regarding morals and ecclesiastical ceremonies as regarding the very dogmas of faith, and indeed under the opinion of necessity, worship, and merit: when yet in the writings of the Apostles, not only is there clearly nothing about them, but something clearly different is contained.

Traditions of this kind, according to the opinion of the Romanists, are: The oblation of the Mass: The anointing of Chrism: The invocation of Saints, Prayers for the dead, The primacy of the Roman Bishop, The consecration of water in Baptism, the whole Sacrament of Confirmation, of Order, of Matrimony, of Penance, of extreme Unction, the merits of works, the necessity of satisfaction, the Enumeration of sins to be made to a Priest. To which Canisius adds in chapter 5, concerning the precepts of the Church, the worship of images, appointed fasts, Lent, all things which are performed in the office of the Mass, prayers, and oblations for the dead: because these are of such a kind that they cannot be defended by the Scriptures, and others. The Jesuit Bellarmine, for his own liberty, adds also the Signing of the Cross, the Turning to the East when we pray, the Triple immersion of the one being baptized, the Renunciation of Satan. All of which he contends must be observed under absolute necessity, as Apostolic dogmas. Therefore, it is about these and other traditions of this kind that the controversy properly exists in this place, concerning which what should be thought, the other positive proposition will now explain.

The Traditions which the Romanists today foist upon the Church of GOD, concerning the dogmas of faith, apart from and beyond the Word of GOD, under the name of the Apostles, as necessarily to be observed and believed, are neither Apostolic: nor are they necessary to be observed and believed: but are to be held as false, impious, and blasphemous.

Latin:

TRaditiones, quas Romanenses vulgò, sed satis inscitè nominant Verbum DEI non scriptum: & pro Apostolicis venditant; neque simpliciter omnes sunt rejiciendæ, neque etiam approbandæ.

CONFIRMATIO.

TRaditionis sive παραδόσεως vocabulum est ὁμώνυμον atque commune, ac generaliter sumtum quamlibet notat doctrinam, sive nudis verbis, sive scripto constantem: & jam in partem bonam, jam in malam accipitur: Jamve ritati, jam mendacio tribuitur. Unde Tertullianus rectè eas dispescuit in Apostolicas & Apostaticas. Et sanè Apostolicas esse Traditiones vel ex dicto illo Apostoli 2. Thess. 2, 15. ita patet: State fratres, & tenete traditiones, quas didicistis, sive per Sermonem, sive per Epistolam nostram. Cæterùm, ut hæ à supposititiis & spuriis constitutionibus, quæ sub Apostolorum nomine circumferuntur, accuratiùs discernantur, solum Verbum DEI scriptum, dijudicationis erit Regula longè omnium exactissima. Et quidem sub Apostolicarum Traditionum nomine multas constitutiones libenter admittimus.

I. Nam 1. Libros Mosis & Prophetarum constituere Canonem Veteris Testamenti, Traditio est Apostolica: Siquidem suâ hi autoritate illum confirmarunt.

II. Ipsa doctrina Apostolica, est Traditio primùm quidem vivâ voce promulgata, postmodùm literis consignata.

III. Traditio Apostolica est, quod hi ipsi libri, quos pro Apostolicis agnoscimus γνησίως sint Apostolici: quippe, quos Ecclesia illa antiqua ab ipsis Apostolis accepit.

IV. Traditio Apostolica est constitutio illa Symboli, quod si Ruffino credimus, Apostoli ante dispersionem in universum terrarum orbem congeslerunt, & Ecclesiis commendarunt.

V. Traditio Apostolica est Episcoporum & Diaconorum ordinatio cu manuum impositione, Prœfbyterium, Excommunicatio præfractè ac contumaciter peccantium, Eleemosynarum collectio, Psalmodia, dies Dominica, & si quæ his sunt similes traditiones, quæ partim haud obscurè in scriptis ipsis Apostolicis indigitantur, partim verò ab ipsis Apostolis vivâ voce Ecclesiis latiùs propositæ sunt & præscriptæ.

VI. Apostolicarum traditionum loco libenter etiam admittimus alios quosdam ritus, in publicis congressibus Ecclesiasticis ad observandum ab ipsis Apostolis ordinatos. Qui tamen neq; sub absolutâ necessitate proponebantur, ut omnium essent temporum, locorum, personarum, neque & quidem multò minùs sub opinione cultus aut meriti: sed tantùm ut inservirent certis temporibus, locis, personis, & ut Apostolus loquitur τῇ τάξει καὶ ἀσχημοσύνῃ. Unde factum, ut cessante illa temporis & personarum conditione, illi etiam ritus & constitutiones in desuetudinem abierint, imò planè expirarint. Quo respectu nos hodieque multas habemus & retinemus Traditiones, freti libertate illâ, in quam per Christum sumus asserti: tantum abest, ut omnes in universum traditiones rejiciamus.

Proindè neque de Apostolicis jam enumeratis, neq; de aliis Traditionibus legitimo modo ab Ecclesia ordinatis, nobis propriè cum Romanensibus intercedit Controversia: sed de illis potissimùm, quas non càm de moribus & ceremoniis Ecclesiasticis, quàm de ipsis dogmatibus fidei, sub Apostolorum nomine, Ecclesiis obtrudunt Romanenses, & quidem sub opinione necessitatis, cultus & meriti: Cum tamen in Apostolorum scriptis, de illis non modò planè nihil, sed diversum planè contineatur.

Traditiones verò istiusmodi ex sententia Romanensium sunt: Oblatio Missæ: Unctio Chrismatis: Invocatio Sanctorum, Orationes pro defunctis, Primatus Episcopi Romani, Consecratio aquæ in Baptismo, totum Sacramentum Confirmationis, Ordinis, Matrimonii, Pœnitentiæ, Unctionis extremæ, merita operum, necessitas satisfactionis, Enumeratio peccatorum facienda Sacerdoti. Quibus addit Canisius cap. 5. de præceptis Ecclesiæ, cultum imaginum, statuta jejunia, quadragesimam, omnia quæ in Missæ officio peraguntur, precationes, & oblationes pro defunctis: propterea quòd ista ejusmodi sunt, ut Scripturis defendi nequeant, & alia. Jesuvvita Bellarminus pro libertate sua adjicit etiam Signationem Crucis, Conversionem ad Orien. tem, quando precamur, Trinam immersionem baptizandi, Renunciationem Satbanæ. Quæ omnia sub absolutâ necessitate, tanquam Apostolica dogmata, observari debere contendit. De his ergò & id genus aliis Traditionibus propriè hoc loco controvertitur, de quibus quid sit sentiendum, altera propositio θετικὴ jam expediet.

TRaditiones, quas de dogmatibus fidei, citra & præter Verbum DEI, sub Apostolorum nomine, necessariò observandas credendasque Ecclesiæ DEI hodie Romanenses obtrudunt, neque sunt Apostolicæ: neque etiam observatu credituque necessariæ: sed pro falsis, impiis, blasphemis habendæ.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Confirmation

CONFIRMATION.

The truth of this proposition can be confirmed by many most evident arguments. The first is such: Whatever assertion is built upon uncertain foundations and conjectures not even probable in appearance, but rather manifestly false: that is without all doubt erroneous. But such is the assertion of the Papists concerning Apostolic Traditions. Therefore.

For the minor premise, containing the matter in question, is manifoldly evident. 1. It is uncertain that the Apostles defined anything concerning such matters as the Romanists today commend to the Churches under the authority of Apostolic Traditions. For although many prattle that books of Apostolic Traditions once existed among Ignatius and Clement: yet they cannot produce a witness worthy of belief for this matter. For 1. regarding Ignatius, we shall show below that it is not without reason to doubt those epistles which are produced. 2. That Clement of Alexandria wrote many erroneous things, most ecclesiastical writers, both ancient and modern, testify besides Eusebius; in book 1 of the Stromata he says: The laborer who is sent into the harvest of the Lord has a double agriculture, written and unwritten. Likewise, that Christ taught for only one year, who yet taught for three whole years and more. Likewise, that the Gentiles were saved through Philosophy. Likewise book 2. Stromata: he lays the foundations of the Nestorian heresy. Likewise, that no one before Christ was saved. Book 3. That Christ neither truly hungered nor truly thirsted: but only seemed to hunger and thirst. Book 6. That Christ and the Apostles converted many in the underworld to the faith by the preaching of the Gospel, etc. See Witteb. page 667. 3. Granting that such books existed: Because, however, they have perished, who, I ask, will convince us that this or that dogma was contained in those Apostolic Traditions. 4. Because GOD allowed those books, if indeed they ever existed, to perish: certainly from that very fact it is evident that they would have been neither useful nor necessary to the Church of GOD.

Then, the truth of the minor premise is evident from the fact that a great diversity presents itself between those traditions, of which we do not deny there was some use in the times of the Apostles, and those which the Jesuits urge today. For example; the Jesuit Lenten fast δὶς διὰ πα-

differs from the Fast of the Apostles, which was not bound to certain foods, or certain days, much less to an opinion of worship and merit: so much so that the Apostle does not want the Colossians to be judged either in food, or drink, or in a part of a feast day. And although Epiphanius against Aetius affirms that it is an Apostolic Constitution to receive nothing in the Fast except bread, salt, and water: nevertheless Socrates is a witness in the Tripartite history that this is false, and not Apostolic. Whence Augustine, Epist. 86, did not hesitate to write: Although in the Evangelical and Apostolic writings I see that a fast is commanded: yet on which days one ought not to fast, and on which one ought, I do not find defined by the command of the Lord or the Apostles. And the thing itself speaks, that most of the Epistles of Ignatius are spurious and adulterated. For it is read in the Epistle to the Philadelphians that Ignatius defends this opinion: Whoever shall have fasted on the Lord's Day or the Sabbath, except for one Sabbath of Easter, he is a murderer of Christ.

Which assertion, indeed, is not only destitute of the Apostolic Spirit, but even lacks all reason: but it also manifestly fights with the practice of the Roman Church, in which it was customary to fast on the Sabbath, as Augustine is a witness in the already cited Epist. 86. Therefore we conclude that not the Apostles, but rather the heretic Montanus, is the author of the Jesuitical Lenten Fast. For Eusebius reports concerning this in book 5 of the Ecclesiastical History, ch. 16, that he was the first to impose laws of fasts, and professed that he ordained new ceremonies by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, just as Apollonius the Apostolic man is a witness.

In place of a second example, and indeed one that can stand for all, is that Jesuitical Tradition concerning the celibacy of priests; which so far from admitting the Apostles as authors, rather manifestly rejects them. For the Apostle expressly condemned this Tradition, naming it doctrines of demons, of those speaking lies in hypocrisy, forbidding marriages and foods, 1 Tim. 4:2 and 3. And lest by chance the Apostle might seem to wish to bind priests by another and different law, namely celibacy, he himself indeed in 1 Cor. 7:9 prescribes this authentic rule to all indefinitely who do not have the gift of continence: It is better to marry than to burn. Moreover, he clearly shows by his own example that the same is permitted to priests, saying, Do I not also have the power to lead about a sister, a wife? 1 Cor. 9:5.

Universal history provides a third proof of the minor premise, which clearly testifies that most of the Traditions which the Roman Church designates as Apostolic were devised long after the times of the Apostles. An example can be that single Canon of the Mass, which, by the admission of the Romanists themselves, was hardly finished after the passage of several centuries, if indeed it is finished. How, therefore, can the Papal Mass with all its parts be an Apostolic Tradition?

Fourthly and lastly, the certainty of the minor premise is evident from that Apostolic caution which the Lord Paul prescribed to the Thessalonians, warning them to be circumspect, and not to allow themselves to be moved from their mind, either by spirit, that is, Enthusiasms, or by word, or by letter as if written by the Apostles, 2 Thess. 2:2. And that authentic rule prescribed to the same Thessalonians in ch. 3:4 is worthy of note: If anyone does not listen to our word by letter, note him: and do not even have commerce with him. Now if, while the Apostles themselves were still surviving, there were not lacking those who did not hesitate to cloak the sacrosanct authority of the Apostles with their own dreams: what, I ask, shall we think has been done by heretics and the Antichrist, now that they have fulfilled their fate, and especially in these last times? Eusebius is a witness in book 3 of the Ecclesiastical History, last chapter. Papias, however much he was very close to the times of the Apostles, indeed a most studious hearer of the same disciples: yet he was drawn into the horrendous errors of the Chiliasts, especially because he believed that he could profit more from the living voice than from written books.

A second argument of confirmation can be formed thus: Whatever diminishes and undermines the Apostolic Doctrine and its authority, that is beyond controversy to be rejected.

But the traditions of the Romanists do this. Therefore.

The minor premise is confirmed thence: 1. If the Apostles omitted anything in their Scriptures which indeed pertains to the business of salvation and divine worship: that fact is necessary, either because they were ignorant of those things which they did not write: or if they knew them, that they did not wish to reveal them to men by writing. But that is manifestly false: since the Apostles are those who were led into all truth, they are those whose mouth and pen was the mouth and pen of the Holy Spirit himself. This, however, would brand the Apostles with a mark of envy and malice. Far be it, therefore, that we should conclude that even a jot was omitted by the Apostles which is indeed necessary to be known for salvation.

2. The truth of the minor premise is evident from this more clearly, if we argue thus from the opinion of the Jesuits: The Apostles did not comprehend everything in their writings: Now indeed, those things which were thus omitted, are either necessary for salvation, or they are not. If they are necessary: then certainly the Apostles will be to be branded with the crime of poorly administered duty of their office, as those who did not in good faith fulfill the duty of the embassy entrusted to them. Moreover, the Apostle Paul is to be accused of a lie, who expressly affirms that the holy scriptures, and the God-breathed writing, can make a man wise; that is, make him wise, or what is the same, perfectly instruct him for salvation. If they are not necessary; why, I ask, are they now thrust upon the Church by the Jesuits as necessary?

3. It was never ordained for the Apostles to enact laws concerning feast days, or to prescribe certain days of fasting, or to promulgate precepts concerning other rites: but to introduce true faith and holy piety, as the Tripartite History says. Whence Paul exhorts the faithful, that they do not suffer the yoke of servitude and of those ceremonial burdens to be cast upon them again, Gal. 5,1.

Finally, the Apostles taught all things, and did not shrink from announcing the whole counsel of GOD: and that not only by living voice, but as Irenaeus speaks in book 3, chapter 1, the same Gospel which they preached at the beginning, they afterwards by the will of GOD delivered to us in the scriptures, to be the foundation and pillar of our faith. Nor in this part do we delay over Clement of Alexandria, who in book 1 of the Stromata, disputing at length concerning unwritten Traditions, affirms that Christ and the Apostles delivered many secrets, just as the Philosophers, to their more secret disciples: nor did they reveal to many things which were not for many, because he knew that τὰ ἀποῤῥητα were suitable for few. For what Clement says, that is diametrically opposed to those testimonies of scripture, which above concerning the perfection of the Scriptures we have produced: nor does it confirm that even in appearance with probability. The third argument of confirmation is supplied by those clear testimonies of the Scriptures, which in the cause of faith and salvation send us away to Scripture alone, having neglected human traditions: Such as are: Matt. 15, 9. In vain they worship me teaching doctrines, the commandment of men. Gal. 1, 8. And if we or an Angel from heaven should announce to you another Gospel, besides that which we have announced to you, let him be anathema. Where it is worth noting, that the Apostle did not say Against that, but besides that, which &c: For by this particle he wished to note, not only those who scatter some dogma contrary to the Gospel: but also those who decree that things which have been omitted by the Apostles must be supplied by human traditions, are to be marked with an Anathema. In which sense the particle (besides) is also equivalent to the particle, Against. John 20. last. These are written, that you may believe, that Jesus is the Christ the son of GOD, and that believing, you may have life in his name. Weighing which words, Augustine in tract 49 on John, says, Those things were chosen to be written, which seemed sufficient for the salvation of believers: And book 1 on the consensus of the Evangelists, last chapter. Whatever Christ wished us to read concerning his deeds and words, this he commanded the Apostles to write, as if by his own hands. And Cyril book 12 on John, last chapter. Not all things, which the LORD DID, have been written down: but those which the writers thought sufficient, both for morals, and for dogmas. Isa. 8, 20. To the Law and to the Testimony: if they do not speak according to this word, they will not see the morning dawn. By which Aphorism, although we do not deny that the impiety of the Jews is taxed, who having abandoned the express Word of GOD, consulted soothsayers and pythonesses, or even the dead themselves, when calamities were pressing: yet we most rightly conclude from thence, that in any similar doubts whatsoever, according to this Prophetic Oracle, nothing but the Law and the Testimony, that is, the written Word of GOD, is to be followed. For the judgment is the same concerning similar things. And although the Prophet did not add an Exclusive, that only the Law, and only the Testimony is to be heard: yet the immediately annexed imprecation or commination, contains the force of an Exclusive most evidently. For if he, who does not consult the Law and the Testimony, is adjudged to eternal darkness: certainly from the contrary sense, he who wishes to be illuminated by the Light of celestial truth, has a necessity to consult nothing but the Law and the Testimony. 1 Cor. 4, 6. These things, however, brothers, I have figuratively applied to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to think beyond what is written. 2 Tim. 3:14, 15. But you, remain in those things which you have learned and which have been entrusted to you: knowing from whom you have learned them; and that from infancy you have known the sacred scriptures, which are able to make you wise unto salvation, through the faith which is in Christ Jesus. Which single passage provides several arguments for confirmation, most especially to be opposed to the Jesuitical sect: indeed in such a way that in order. The fourth argument of our thesis may be as follows: In which doctrine alone the faithful must remain, with all other doctrines or traditions excluded, by whatever name they may come: that doctrine, being most perfect, stands in need of no unwritten word for a supplement.

Latin:

CONFIRMATIO.

PRopositionis hujus veritas, multis evidentissimis argumentis confirmari potest. Primum tale est: Quæcunque assertio incertis fundamentis & conjecturis ne quidem in speciem probabilibus, quin manifestè falsis superstruitur: ea citra omnem dubitationem est erronea. Sed talis est assertio Pontificiorum de Traditionibus Apostolicis. Ergò.

Minor quippe κερινόμενον continens, multipliciter patet. 1. Incertum est, Apostolos de ejusmodi rebus, quas sub Traditionum Apostolicarum autoritate hodie Romanenses Ecclesiæ commendant, quicquam definivisse. Etsi enim apud Ignatium & Clementem libros Traditionum Apostolicarum olim extitisse multi garriunt: fide tamen dignum hujus rei testem proferre haud possunt. Nam 1. quoad Ignatium haud immeritò de illis, quæ proferuntur epistolis, dubitari, infra ostendemus. 2. Clementem Alexandrinum multa scripsisse erronea, testantur præter Eusebium Scriptores plerique Ecclesiastici, tùm Veteres, tùm recentiores, l. 1. Stromat. ait: Operarium, qui mittitur in messem Domini habere duplicem agriculturam, ἔγγραφον & ἄγραφον. Item, Christus per unum tantùm annum docuisse, qui tamen per triennium integrum & amplius docuit. Item, Gentes per Philosophiam servatas fuisse. Item lib. 2. Stromat: ponit fundamenta hærefeos Nestorianæ. Item, neminem ante Christum servatum fuisse. l. 3. Christum nec verè esuriisse, nec verè sitiisse: sed visum tantùm esse esurire ac sitire. lib. 6. Christum & Apostolos multos apud inferos prædicatione Evangelii ad fidem convertisse. &c. Vide VVitteb. pag. 667. 3. Esto tales libri extiterint: Quia tamen illi interierunt, Quis, obsecro, fidem nobis faciet, hoc vel illud dogma in Traditionibus illis Apostolicis fuisse comprehensum. 4. Quia DEUS libros illos, si modò aliquando extiterunt, interiere passus est: certè vel inde patet, ipsos Ecclesiæ DEI neq; utiles, neque necessarios fuisse futuros.

Deindè, patet minoris Veritas exindè, Quòd magna se offert diversitas earum Traditionum; quarum Apostolorum temporibus usum aliquem fuisse, non imus inficias, & earum, quas Jesuvvitæ hodiè urgent. Exempli gratiâ; Jejunium Quadragesimale Jesuvviticum δὶς διὰ πα-

σῶν distat, à Jejunio Apostolorum, quod neque ad certos cibos, aut certos dies, nedum ad opinionem cultus & meriti erat alligatum: usque adeò, ut Apostolus nolit Colossenses judicari aut in cibo, aut potu, aut in parte diei festi. Et quanquam Epiphanius contra, Aetium affirmat, Constitutionis Apostolicæ esse, in Jejunio nihil præter panem, salem & aquam accipere: tamen testis est Socrates in historia Tripartita, falsum hoc esse, & non Apostolicum. Unde Augustinus Epist. 86. scribere non dubitavit: Etsi in Evangelicis & Apostolicis literis video præceptum esse Jejunium: tamen quibus diebg non oporteat jejunare, & quibus oporteat, præcepto Domini, vel Apostolorum non invenio definitum. Et res ipsa loquitur, plerasq́; Epistolas Ignatii esse spurias & adulterinas Legitur enim in Epistola ad Philadelphos Ignatium hanc tueri sententiam: Quicunq; Dominicam aut Sabbatu jejunaverit præter unū Sabbatu Paschæ, ipse est Christi interfector.

Quæ sanè assertio, non modò Spiritu Apostolico destituitur, imò ratione omni caret: sed & manifestè pugnat cum praxi Ecclesiæ Romanæ, in quâ Sabbato jejunari consuevisse, testis est Augustinus Epist. jam citata 86. Proindè non Apostolos, sed Montanum potiùs hæreticum, Quadragesimalis Jejunii Jesuvvitici, autorem esse statuimg. De hoc enim refert Eusebius l. 5. hist. Eccl. c. 16. quod primus jejuniorum leges imposuerit, & se Spiritus Sancti inspiratione novas ceremonias ordinare professus sit, sicut Apollonius vir Apostolicus testis est.

Secundi Exempli loco, & quidem instar omnium esse potest, Traditio illa Jesuvvitica de cœlibatu Sacerdotum; quæ usque adeò Apostolos autores non admittit, ut potiùs manifestè eos respuat. Disertè enim Apostolus Traditionem hanc damnavit, nominans doctrinas dæmoniorum, in hypocrisi mendacium loquentium prohibentium nuptias & cibos 1. Tim. 4, 2, & 3. Et ne fortè Sacerdotes alia ac diversa lege, nēpè cœlibatus, constringere velle videatur Apostolus ipse sanè in 1. Cor. 7, 9. omnibus indefinitè, continentiæ donum non habentibus, hanc præscribit Authenticam: Melius est nubere, quàm uri. Quin suo exemplo idem Sacerdotibus licere, luculenter ostendit, Annon, inquiens, ego quoq́; potestatem habeo sororem uxorem circumducendi, 1. Cor. 9, 5.

Tertiam Minoris probationem suppeditat Universalis historia, quæ luculenter testatur, plerasq́; Traditiones, quas Romana Ecclesia Apostolicas indigitat, longè post Apostolorum demùm tempora excogitatas esse. Exemplo potest esse vel unicus ille canon Missaticus, qui ipsis fatentibus Romanensibus, aliquot sæculorum decursu vix tandem absolutus fuit, si modò est absolutus. Qui ergò Missa Pontificia cum omnibus suis partibus, queat esse Traditio Apostolica?

Quartò & postremò patet, Minoris certitudo ex cautione illâ Apostolicâ, quam D. Paulus Thessalonicensibus præscripsit, monens, ut sint circumpspecti, neq; à mente dimoveri se patiantur, vel per spiritum, hoc est, Enthusiasmos, vel per sermonem, vel per Epistolam tanquàm ab Apostolis scriptam, 2. Thess. 2, 2. Et observatu digna est Authentica illa iisdem Thessalonicensib9 præscipta, 2. c. 3, 4. Si quis non auscultat nostro per Epistolam sermoni, hunc notate: & ne quidem commercium habete cum eo. Jam si ipsis adhuc Apostolis superstitibus, non defuerunt, qui sacrosanctam Apostolorum autoritatem suis somniis prætexere non dubitarunt: quid quæso non ipsis jam fato functis, & postremis præsertim his temporibus, per hæreticos & Antichristum factitatum esse, existimabimus? Testis est Eusebius lib. 3. hist. Eccl c.ult. Papiam, quantumvis Apostolorum temporibus, quàm proximè vicinum, imò eorundem discipulorum studiosissimum ἀκροατὴν: in horrendos tamen Chiliastarum cumprimis errores protractum esse, eò quod crederet, plus se ex vivâ voce, quàm libris scriptis proficere posse.

Alterum confirmationis argumentum sic informari potest: Quicquid Apostolicam Doctrinam ejusq́; autoritatem imminuit & labefactat, illud extra controversiam est rejiciendum.

Atqui traditiones Romanensium hoc faciût.Ergo.

Minor confirmatur indè 1. Si aliquid in Scripturis suis prætermiserunt Apostoli, quod quidem ad negotium salutis & cultus divini pertineat: factum illud necesse est, vel, quod ignorarent ea, quæ non scripserunt: vel si noverunt, quòd nollent ea hominibus per scriptum patefacere. Atqui illud manifestè est falsum: siquidem Apostoli sunt illi, qui inducti fuerunt in omnem veritatem, sunt illi, quorum os & calamus fuit os & Calamus ipsius Spiritus Sancti. Hoc v. invidiæ & malignitatis notam inureret Apostolis. Absit proindè, ut vel γρὺ ab Apostolis prætermissum esse statuamus, quod quidem ad salutem scitu sit necessarium.

2. Constat Minoris veritas indè luculentiùs, si ex sententia Jesuvvitarum sic arguamus: Apostoli non omnia suis scriptis comprehenderunt: Jam verò illa, quæ sic prætermissa sunt, vel ad salutem sunt necessaria, vel non sunt. Si sunt necessaria: tùm certè Apostoli ἀξιοπιστείας malè administrati muneris crimine notandi erunt, ut qui non bonâ fide legationis demandatæ munere sint defuncti. Quin Apostolus Paulus mendacii arguendus, qui disertè affirmat ἱερᾳ γράμματα, sacras literas, & γραφὴν θεόπνευςον, posse hominem σοφίσαι; hoc est, sapientem reddere, vel quo idem est, perfectè instruere ad salutem.Si non sunt necessaria; Cur, obsecro à Jesuvvitis, jam ut necessaria obtruduntur Ecclesiæ?

3. Nunquàm constitutum fuit Apostolis, leges ferre de diebus festis, aut certos præscribere Jejuniorum dies, vel de aliis ritibꝫ præcepta promulgare: sed veram fidem & sanctâ pietatem inducere, ut loquitur Historia Tripartita. Unde Paulus hortatur fideles, ut ne patiantur sibi denuò jugum servitutis & onerũ illorũ ceremonialiu, injici, Gal. 5,1.

Tandem, Apostoli omnia docuerunt, & non subterfugerunt, quò minus annunciarent omne consilium DEI: idq; non vivâ tantùm voce, sed ut Irenæus loquitur lib. 3. cap 1. idem Evangelium, quòd initiò prædicaverunt, postmodum per DEI voluntatem in scripturis nobis tradiderunt, fundamentum & columnam fidei nostræ futuram. Neq; hac in parte moramur Clementem Alexandrinum, qui libro 1 Stromatum, de Traditionibꝫ nõ scriptis prolixè disputans, affirmat, Christum & Apostolos multa secreta, sicut Philosophos, secretioribꝫ suis discipulis tradidisse: neq́; revelasse multis, quæ nõ fuerint multorũ, quia sciebat paucis cõvenire τὰ ἀποῤῥητα. Nã quod dicit Clemens, illud è diametro adversatur iis scripturę Testimoniis, quę suprà de perfectione Scripturarum produximus: neque etiam vel in speciem probabiliter illud confirmat. Tertium confirmationis argumentum suppeditant perspicua illa Scripturarum testimonia, quæ nos in causa fidei & salutis ad solam Scripturam sacram, neglectis Traditionibus humanis ablegant: Qualia sunt: Matth. 15, 9. Frustra me colunt docentes doctrinas, mandato hominum. Gal. 1, 8. Et si nos aut Angelus de cœlo aliud Evangelium annunciaverit vobis, præter id, quod annuciavimus vobis, sit anathema. Ubi observationem meretur, quòd Apostolus non dixit Contra id, sed præter id, quod &c: Hâc enim particula notare voluit, non illos modò, qui dogma aliquod Evangelio contrarium spargunt: sed & eos, qui statuunt Traditionibus humanis supplenda esse, quę ab Apostolis sint prætermissa, Anathemate notandos esse. Quo sensu particula etiam (præter) æquipollet particulæ, Contra. Joh. 20. ult. Hæc scripta sunt, ut credatis, quòd Jesus est Christus filius DEI, & ut credentes, vitam habeatis in nomine ejus. Quæ verba expendens Augustinus tractatu 49. in Joh. Electa sunt, inquit, quæ scriberentur, quæ saluti credentium sufficere videbantur: Et l. 1. de consensu Evangelist. cap. ult. Quicquid Christus de suis factis & dictis nos legere voluit, hoc scribendum Apostolis, tanquam manibus suis imperavit. Et Cyrillus l. 12. in Joh. cap. ult. Non omnia, quæ DOMINUS FECIT, conscripta sunt: sed quæ scribentes, tàm ad mores, quàm ad dogmata putarunt sufficere. Ies. 8, 20. Ad Legem & ad Testimonium: si non dixerint secundum verbum hoc, nō videbunt aurorā matutinam. Quo Aphorismo etsi non negamus taxari Judæorum impietatem, qui relicto expresso DEI Verbo, ariolos & pythonissas, quin mortuos ipsos, ingruentibus calamitatibus consulebant: rectissimè tamen indè concludimus, in similibus quibusque dubiis, secundum Oraculum hoc Propheticum, non nisi Legem & Testimonium, hoc est, Verbum DEI scriptum, esse sequendum. De similibus enim idem est judicium. Et quanquam Propheta non adjecit Exclusivam, solam Legem, & solum Testimonium esse audiendum: tamen immediatè annexa imprecatio sive comminatio, vim Exclusivæ evidentissimè continet. Si enim ille, qui non consulit Legem & Testimonium, æternis tenebris est adjudicatus: utique è contrario sensu, qui Luce veritatis cœlestis illuminari velit, non nisi Legem & Testimonium consulat, necesse habet. 1. Cor. 4, 6. Hæc autem fratres, figurâ quadã transtuli ad meipsum & Apollo, propter vos, ut in nobis discatis, non sapere supra id, quod scriptum est. 2. Tim. 3, 14, 15. Tu verò mane in his, quæ didicisti & credita sunt tibi: Sciens à quo didiceris: & quia ab infantia sacras literas nosti, quæ te possunt sapientem reddere ad salutem, per fidem, quæ est in Christo Jesu. Qui unicus locus plura suppeditat confirmationis argumenta, genti Jesuvviticæ vel maximè opponenda: ita quidem ut ordine. Quartum θέσεως nostræ argumentum, tale esse possit: In quâ sola doctrina fidelibus manendum est, seclusis omnibus aliis sive doctrinis, sive Traditionib9, quocunq; veniat nomine: ea doctrina, quippe perfectissima, nullo indiget verbo nō scripto, in supplemētū,


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Confirmation (continued)

But in the sacred Prophetic and Apostolic scripture alone, just as it has been consigned to letters, all believers must remain, with all other things excluded, whether doctrines, or Traditions.

Therefore Sacred Scripture needs no unwritten word, for a supplement.

The truth of the minor premise is evident from the example of Timothy, whom Paul warns to remain in those things, which from infancy he had learned from the sacred letters. Therefore while he must remain in these: certainly those things must be fled and avoided, which are brought forward in any way short of and besides the authority of the S. letters. 2 Timothy ought to avoid all heterodoxy, and WHATEVER opposes sound doctrine, which is according to the Gospel of the glory of the blessed GOD, 1 Tim. 1, 10. and 11. But that is the proper affection as it were of Pontifical Traditions, that they lead us away from the Scriptures, and obscure and diminish the glory of the Gospel. Therefore. 3. Timothy ought to avoid those, who not content with sound doctrine comprised in the Word of GOD, according to their own concupiscence heap up for themselves Teachers according to the itching of ears, and turn away ears from the truth to fables of human traditions. 2 Tim. 4, 3. and 4. But that Pontifical Traditions are of this kind and condition: is evident even from this, that the Apostle himself divides those fables of human traditions into two main kinds as it were, of which the former concerns the prohibition of marriages, the latter abstinence from certain foods: not obscurely hinting, that from these, the same judgment must be passed entirely on the remaining swamp of human traditions. 1 Tim. 4, 3.

Fourthly the same Apostle chap. 6, 3. If anyone, he says, teaches otherwise, and does not acquiesce in the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the doctrine which is according to piety, he is puffed up, knowing nothing &c. But the doctrine of the Romanists concerning Traditions is of this kind. Therefore. 5. and lastly the same Apostle asserts, that Sacred Scripture, which Timothy had learned from infancy, can make him wise unto salvation through faith, 2 Tim. 3, 15. Therefore it is most evidently gathered from this, that there is no need for any other knowledge or Tradition, either for Timothy, or for any other believers whatsoever.

The same Apostolic passage supplies a fifth argument; and it is such:

If sacred Scripture alone is the Canon and measure, according to which alone all heterodoxies ought to be examined, and judged: certainly it will need no other Traditions for a supplement. But the former is true. Therefore the latter also. The connection of the Major premise is evident most clearly from this, that the Apostle orders Timothy to judge all heterodoxies, to convince those who contradict, not either from his own brain, or from the specious pretext of human traditions: But he shows at the same time according to which Canon that ought to be done solely, ordering him to remain in that, which he had learned from the sacred letters: 2 Tim. 3, 16.

The sixth argument of our confirmation can be as follows: If the Gospel preached by the Apostles, and afterwards indeed committed to letters or writing by the inspiration of God himself (2 Tim. 3:16), renders a man perfect before the tribunal of God, then certainly there would be no need for any unwritten word of God to attain this perfection. But the former is true; therefore, the latter is also true. The minor premise is established from chapter 1, 26, and the following verses of the Epistle to the Colossians, where the Apostle discourses thus concerning the effect of the Gospel: The mystery which has been hidden from ages and generations, is now made manifest to his Saints, to whom GOD willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory, whom we preach, admonishing every man, and teaching in all wisdom, that we may present every man PERFECT in Christ Jesus. From which passage we now infer the seventh argument, and it is this: If Holy Scripture is divinely inspired for this reason, that through it the man of GOD may be perfect in Christ; either it alone will accomplish this end, or it will not alone. If it cannot accomplish this alone, let the Jesuits explain the reason why the Apostle dared to pronounce that Scripture, divinely inspired, accomplishes this virtue and end most perfectly: Let them also show what, on the part of GOD and the Apostles as amanuenses, could be desired in addition? Certainly, if GOD willed us to be bound to this word of His alone, if He most severely prohibited every addition and subtraction, if through the Apostles He revealed to us His whole counsel concerning our salvation: then He has attested that this Scripture alone contains the highest perfection both in itself and in relation to us. But the former is true, Deut. 4, 2: 12, 32. Isa. 8, 20. Acts 20, 27, etc. Therefore the latter is established. Now if Scripture alone accomplishes this end most perfectly: certainly there will be no need to assume further human traditions. The force of this consequence, and indeed concerning Holy Scripture, insofar as it is such, is irrefragably confirmed by that of the Apostle in 1 Tim. 3, 14: These things I WRITE, that you may know how you ought to behave in the house of GOD. And chapter 4, 13: Until I come, attend to reading. And 2 Tim. 1: Hold fast the form of sound words, which you have heard from me. The eighth and final argument is supplied by the consensus of Orthodox Antiquity. For although we cannot deny that there are found even among the Fathers not a few who, bearing a certain appearance of good intention, have kissed human παραδόσεις (traditions) more than is right: whence also in that ancient Church of the fathers, that infinite abundance and variety of human rites and observances was born: so that little by little, the Apostolic simplicity expired more and more: yet there are very few who have opposed those human traditions to the Word of GOD, or at least equaled them: and finally, far fewer who have decreed that they must be observed under the opinion of absolute necessity, or worship, or merit: so that St. Augustine did not hesitate to promulgate this general axiom: The whole of this class of things, he says, has free observances. And before him Tertullian in the book De Corona Militis, Therefore let us ask, he says, whether an unwritten tradition ought also to be received? We clearly deny that it should be received, if no examples prejudice other observances, which without the instrument of any Scripture, we claim from that time by the title of tradition alone. And in the book De Resurrectione Carnis: Take away from heretics what they think in common with the Heathens, so that they may base their questions on the Scriptures alone, and they will not be able to stand. And in the book De Praescriptione Haereticorum: We have no need of curiosity after Christ Jesus, nor of inquiry after the Gospel; when we believe, we desire to believe nothing

beyond; for this we believe first, that there is nothing which we ought to believe beyond the Gospel. And against Hermogenes: Let Hermogenes teach that it is written: If it is not written, let him fear that woe destined for those who add or subtract.

Moreover, the Canon Law, Dist. 8, Can. 9, cites this sentence from the Epistle of Cyprian to Caecilius: If Christ alone is to be heard, we ought not to attend to what anyone before us thought should be done: But what Christ, who is before all, did first. For one ought not to follow the custom of man, but the truth of GOD: Since GOD speaks through the Prophet Isaiah and says, In vain they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men.

See more testimonies of Antiquity in Tom. 1, page 495, 613, Tom. IV, page 415, Tom. VI, page 313.

The ninth argument can be taken from those four inconveniences which certainly arise from the observance of unwritten traditions.

I. For it is impossible that in such great perversity and negligence of men, unwritten traditions could have remained uncorrupted.

Bellarmine replies that the providence of GOD, upon which the care of the Church rests, can no less preserve traditions than it preserves the Church.

But I respond, thus there would have been no need at all for Scripture, if it had pleased divine providence to preserve the Church through unwritten Traditions. 2. The reason for the preservation of the Church and of Traditions is different: for the Church has express promises concerning its own preservation: Traditions do not.

II. The observance of unwritten Traditions would overturn that proper and adequate end of holy Scripture, which is, that it be a certain rule and norm of faith and morals.

Bellarmino retorts, asserting that holy Scripture is not the norm and rule of faith: but is only a certain reminder, useful for preserving and fostering the doctrine received from preaching, that is, to unfold these trifles: that the voice of the Roman Pontiff is the infallible rule and norm of faith: but that he himself, to attest his benevolence toward the scriptures, does indeed employ the scriptures: not so that he may be informed from them what or how he ought to pronounce: since he could perform this even without the scriptures: but only so that he may be amicably and humbly reminded by them.

Since we refuted this calumny above in Question 5, it is not relevant to deal with it at greater length in this place.

This one thing should be observed in this place, that this opinion of Bellarmino overturns itself with the most absurd contradictions.

I. All faith is from hearing, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. 10, 17. But hearing is through the Word of GOD: Therefore Faith regards no other adequate object, except the Word of GOD alone, whether read, or written, or preached.

Now if our Faith is from the hearing of the Pontiff, it is necessary that he preach the Word, either his own, or GOD'S. If his own, then it is false what the Apostle said, that Faith is from the hearing of the Word of GOD: But if he preaches the Word of GOD, certainly this Word will no longer be a mere reminder, but a most exact Rule and norm, according to which the Pope himself also ought to measure his own definitions.

II. If the Roman Pope can discern true dogmas from false ones without the Word of God, it is necessary that he do so by some extraordinary instinct of the Holy Spirit. For otherwise the Pope, being a man, differs in no way from other men, so that what the Apostle says is true of him as well as of others: 1 Cor. 2:14. The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. Now if the Pope has that from an instinct or extraordinary inspiration of the Holy Spirit: either that inspiration will agree entirely with the written Word, or it will be diametrically opposed to it: If it agrees, then it is not extraordinary: since it agrees plainly with the ordinary means, namely with the Scriptures: and thus whatever the Romanists prattle about this extraordinary inspiration is false and fabricated.
