For there is no need for the extraordinary where the ordinary suffices: But if that inspiration disagrees: then it is most certain that not the Holy Spirit, but the Devil is its author. Nor is there any reason for the Jesuit to take refuge in the gift of understanding and interpretation of the Scriptures. For even so he will be held constrained. For that understanding and interpretation of Scripture will either agree entirely with the remaining passages of the Scriptures, in which that understanding is most plainly contained: and thus the Pope will not have it from some extraordinary inspiration: But if it disagrees: then we reject it simply as heretical. But if the Jesuit objects that the Holy Spirit inspires the true sense of Scripture into the Pope without reading or meditation on the Scriptures: and therefore that for this very reason that inspiration is most rightly called extraordinary: and that Scripture is indeed only a certain reminder with respect to the Pope: then we answer in one word that the Jesuit is trifling in a matter too serious: and that it must be proven by him what he says, before he himself may infer anything against us from false presuppositions or we allow ourselves to be constrained by his preconceived opinions.

III. The Danger. If any dogmas were to be received which cannot be proven by any testimony of Scripture, an infinite license would be opened for introducing any dogmas whatsoever into the Church.

Bellarmino replies: By this means the Scriptures themselves must also be rejected, because many false books were also adorned with the title of Canonical books. But there is a very great difference in the examples: For true books can be distinguished from false ones much more easily than traditions from traditions. For the Sacred books themselves, to pass over other reasons in silence for now, by their perpetual consensus bear most true testimony to one another, and by the same consensus refute even supposititious books. Traditions, however, are so various and discordant that a certain judgment can in no way be taken from them.

IV. It is characteristic of heretics to hide their dogmas and to say that Christ and the Apostles preached some things openly to all, and some things secretly to only a few. Which reasoning, since the Jesuit can refute with no argument, he attempts to elude with a vain cavil: Heretics, he says, are in this respect the Apes of the Catholics, and received this method of hiding certain dogmas from the Catholics: Which he thinks Christ himself insinuated when he said in Matt. 10:27, What you have heard in the ear, preach upon the housetops: namely, if there should be need. As if indeed there were no need, or as if the Apostles had not been called for this very purpose, that they might preach in season and out of season what they heard from the Lord. Just as Theophylact also explains this passage: What I have said to you alone, he says, teach with the greatest freedom and with a great straining of the voice, so that all may hear you.

Latin:

Atqui in sola scriptura sacra Prophetica & Apostolica, prout quidem literis ea est consignata, fidelibus quibusq; manendum est, seclusis omnibus aliis sive doctrinis, sive Traditionibus.

Ergo Scriptura Sacra, nullo indiget verbo non scripto, in supplementum.

Minoris veritas, patet exemplo Timothei, quem Paulus monet manere in iis, quæ ab infantia ex sacris literis didicerat. Ergò dum manendum ipsi in his : utique fugienda & vitanda erunt, quæ citra & præter S. literarum autoritatem, quoquo modo proferuntur. 2. Timotheus vitare debet omnem ἑτεροδιδασκαλίαν, & QuicQUID sanæ doctrinæ adversatur, quæ est secundum Evangelium gloriæ beati DEI, 1. Tim. 1, 10. & 11. Atqui Traditionum Pontificiarum ea est propria quasi affectio, ut à Scripturis nos abducant, & gloriam Evangelii obscurent ac imminuant. Ergo. 3. Timotheus vitare debet eos, qui non contenti sanâ doctrinâ Verbo DEI comprehensâ secundum propriam concupiscentiam sibi coacervant Doctores juxta pruritum aurium, & avertunt aures à veritate ad fabulas traditionum humanarum. 2. Tim. 4, 3. & 4. Atqui hujus generis ac conditionis esse Traditiones Pontificias : vel indè patet, quòd ipse Apostolus fabellas illas Traditionum humanarum, in duo quasi genera summa dispescit, quorum prius concernit prohibitionem nuptiarum, posterius abstinentiam à certis cibis: haud obscurè innuens, ex his, de reliquâ traditionum humanarum lernâ, idem omninò ferendum esse judicium. 1. Tim. 4, 3.

Quartò idem Apostolus cap. 6, 3. Si quis, inquit, aliud docet, & non acquiescit sanis sermonibus Domini nostri Jesu Christi, & quæ est secundum pietatem doctrinæ, is inflatus est, nihil sciens &c. Atqui hujus generis est doctrina Romanensium de Traditionibus. Ergo. 5. & postremò idem Apostolus asserit, Sacram Scripturam, quam ab infantia Timotheus didicerit, posse ipsum σοφίσαι, sapientem reddere ad salutem per fidem, 2. Tim. 3, 15. Ergo non ullâ aliâ γνώσει sive Traditione tùm Timotheo, tùm quibusvis aliis fidelibus opus esse, vel indè evidentissimè colligitur.

Quintum argumentum idem locus Apostolicus suppeditat; idque tale:

Si sola Scriptura sacra est Canon & mensura, secundum quam solam omnes ἑτεροδιδασκαλίαι examinari, dijudicariq; debent : utiq; nullis Traditionib. aliis in supplementum indigebit. At prius verum. E. & posterius. Connexum Majoris, patet evidentissimè ex eo, quod Apostolus jubet Timotheum omnes ἑτεροδιδασκαλίας dijudicare, τὺς ἀντιλέγοντας convincere, non vel ex proprio cerebro, vel ex traditionum humanarum specioso prætextu: Sed simul secundum quem Canonem unicè illud fieri debeat, ostendit, jubens ipsum manere in eo, quod ἐξ ἱερῶν γραμμάτων didicerat: 2. Tim 3, 16.

Sextum Argumentum confirmationis nostræ tale esse potest : Si Evangelium ab Apostolis prædicatum, postmodum verò ipsius Dei instinctu in literas sive scripturam relatum. 2. Tim. 3, 16. reddit hominem coram tribunali Dei perfectum: utiq; ullo aliquo verbo Dei non scripto, ad hanc consequèdam perfectionē opus haud fuerit. At prius verum; Ergò & posterius. Minor constat ex cap. 1, 26. & seqq. Epistolæ ad Colossenses, Ubi de Effectu Evangelii sic Concionatur Apostolus: Mysterium quod absconditum fuit à seculis & generationibus, nunc est manifestatum Sanctis ejus, quibus DEUS voluit notas facere divitias gloriæ mysterii hujus in gentibus, quod est Christus in vobis, spes gloriæ, quem nos prædicamus, adhortantes omnem hominem, & Docentes in omni sapientia, ut sistamus omnem hominem in Christo Jesu PERFECTUM. Ex quo loco jam Septimum inferimus argumentum, idą; tale: Si Scriptura sacra ideò divinitùs est inspirata, ut per eam Homo DEI sit perfectus in Christo; aut ipsa sola hunc finem præstabit, aut non sola. Si non sola præstare hoc potest, causam edisserant Jesuitæ, cur Apostolus ausus fuerit pronunciare, Scripturam divinitùs inspiratam, virtutem & finem istum perfectissimè præstare: Monstrent etiam, quid ex parte DEI & Apostolorum, tanquam amanuensium insuper desiderari queat? Certè si DEUS nos ad solum hoc verbum suum voluit alligatos, si omnem additionem & detractionem severissimè prohibuit, si per Apostolos Omne suum consilium de salute nostra nobis revelavit: utią; solam hanc Scripturam perfectionem summam tùm in se, tùm ratione nostri continere attestatus est. At prius illud verum, Deut. 4, 2: 12, 32. Jes. 8, 20. Actor. 20, 27. &c. Ratum ergò & Posterius. Jam si sola Scriptura finem istum perfectissimè præstat: certè ulteriore assumendo traditionum humanarum opus haud fuerit. Cujus consecutionis vim, & quidem de Scriptura sacra, quatenus talis, irrefragabiliter confirmat illud Apostoli 1. Tim. 3, 14. Hæc ideò SCRIBO, ut scias, quomodo debeas in domo DEI versari. Et cap. 4, 13. Donec venio, attende Lectioni. Et 2. Tim. 1. Retine formam sanorum verborum, quæ à me didicisti. Octavum & postremum argumentum subministrat Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis consensus. Nam etsi inficias ire haud possumus, reperiri etiam inter Patres haud paucos, qui humanas παραδόσεις, speciem aliquam bonæ intentionis præ se ferentes, plus æquo sunt exosculati: Undè etiam in antiqua illa patrum Ecclesia, nata est infinita illa rituum & observationum humanarum copia atque varietas: ita ut pedetentim, magis magisque simplicitas Apostolica expiraverit: paucissimi tamen sunt, qui Traditiones illas humanas vel Verbo DEI opposuerint; vel saltem æquârint: multò deniquè pauciores, qui sub opinione absolutæ necessitatis, vel cultus, aut meriti, illas observandas esse statuerint: ita ut D. Augustinus generale hoc axioma promulgare non dubitaverit: Totum, inquiens, hoc genus rerum liberas habet observationes. Et ante hunc Tertullianus in libro de Corona Militis, Ergò quæramus, inquit, an & Traditio non scripta recipi debeat? planè negamus recipiendam, si nulla exempla præjudicent aliarum observationum, quas sine ullius Scripturæ instrumento, solius traditionis titulo exindè vindicemus. Et libro de Resur. Carnis. Aufer hæreticis, quæ cũ Ethnicis sapiūt, ut de Scripturis solis quæstiones suas sistant, & stare non poterunt. Et l. de præscript. hær. Nobis curiositate opus non est post Christũ Jesum, nec inquisitione post Evangeliũ cum credimǫ, nihil desideramǫ

ultra credere: hoc enim primum credimus, non esse, quod ultra Evangelium credere debeamus. Et advers. Hermog. Doceat, Hermogenes, Scriptum esse: Si non est scriptum: timeat væ illud, adjicientibus aut detrahentibus destinatum.

Quin jus etiam Canonicum Dist. 8. Can. 9. ex Epistola Cypriani ad Cæcilium hanc citat. sententiam: Si solus Christus audiendus est, non debemus attendere, quid aliquis ante nos faciendum putaverit: Sed quid, qui ante omnes est Christus, prior fecerit. Neque enim hominis consuetudinem sequi oportet, sed DEI veritatem: Cum per Esaiam Prophetam DEUS loquatur, & dicat, sine causa colunt me, docentes mandata & doctrinas hominum.

Vide plura Testimonia Antiquitatis Tom. 1. Es. pag. 495, 613, Tom. IV. pag. 415. Tom. VI. p. 313.

Nonum argumentum desumi potest ex quatuor illis Incommodis, quæ ex observatione Traditionum non scriptarum certò oboriuntur.

I. Enim, Impossibile est, ut in tanta hominum perversitate & negligentia Traditiones non scriptæ mansissent incorruptæ.

Regerit Bellarminus, DEI providentiam, cui incumbat cura Ecclesiæ, haud minus conservare posse Traditiones, atq́; conservat Ecclesiam.

Sed Respondeo, Sic nullâ planè opus fuisset Scripturâ, si providentiæ divinæ placuisset, Ecclesiam per Traditiones non scriptas conservare. 2. Dispar est ratio conservationis Ecclesiæ & Traditionum: Ecclesia enim de sui conservatione expressas habet promissiones: Traditiones non item.

II. Traditionum non scriptarum observatio everteret finem illum proprium & adæquatum Scripturæ sacræ, quæ est, ut sit certa regula & norma fidei & morum.

Regerit Bellarminus asserens, scripturam sacram non esse normam & regulam fidei: sed esse tantùm quoddam commonitorium, utile ad conservandam ac fovendam doctrinam ex prædicatione acceptam, hoc est, ut tricas istas evolvamus: Vocem Pontificis Romani esse regulam infallibilem & normam fidei: ipsum verò ad contestandam suam erga scripturas benevolentiam, adhibere quidem scripturas: non ut ex illis informetur, quid aut quomodo pronunciare debeat: siquidem & absque scripturis hoc præstare possit: sed tantùm, ut ex iis amicè & humiliter commoneatur.

Quam Calumniam cùm supra Quæst. 5. refutaverimus, nihil attinet hoc loco prolixiùs de ea agere.

Unum istud hoc loco observandum fuerit, quod sententia hæc Bellarmini absurdissimis contradictionibus semetipsum evertit.

I. Fides omnis est ex auditu, teste Apostolo, Rom. 10, 7. Auditus autem per Verbum DEI: Ergò Fides nullum aliud objectum adæquatum respicit, præter solum Verbum DEI, sive lectum, sive scriptum, sive prædicatum.

Jam si Fides nostra est ex auditu Pontificis, necesse est, ut ille prædicet Verbum, vel suum, vel DEI. Si suum, tùm falsum est, quòd Apostolus dixit, Fidem esse ex auditu Verbi DEI: Sin DEI Verbum prædicat, utiq́; Verbum hoc non ampliùs erit nudum commonitorium, sed exactissima Regula & norma, secundum quam ipse quoque Pontifex suas definitiones exigere debeat.

II. Si Pontifex Romanus sine Verbo DEI, vera dogmata à falsis discernere potest, necessum est, ut id faciat extraordinario quodam Spiritus Sancti instinctu. Nam aliàs Pontifex, quippè homo, à reliquis hominibus nihil quicquam differt, ut tàm de ipso, quàm de aliis verum sit illud Apostoli: 1. Cor. 2. 14. Animalis homo non percipit, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Jam si ex instinctu sive inspiratione extraordinariâ Spiritus Sancti illud habet Pontifex: vel inspiratio illa ex asse conveniet cum Verbo scripto, vel è diametro repugnabit: Si convenit, tùm extraordinaria non est: Siquidem cum ordinario medio, nempè cum Scripturis planè convenit: & sic falsum ac commentitium est, quicquid de extraordinariâ hac inspiratione garriunt Romanenses. Extraordinario enim opus non est: ubi ordinarium sufficit: Sin discrepat illa inspiratio: tùm non Spiritum Sanctum, sed Diabolum ejus autorem esse, certissimum est. Neque est ut ad donum intelligentiæ & interpretationis Scripturarum confugiat Jesuvvita. Nam & sic constrictus tenebitur. Nam illa intelligentia & interpretatio Scripturæ, vel ex asse conveniet cum reliquis Scripturarum locis, in quibus intelligentia illa planissimè continetur: & sic non ex quadam extraordinariâ inspiratione Pontifex eam habebit: Sin discrepabit: tùm simpliciter eam ut hæreticam rejicimus. Sin excipiat Jesuvvita, Spiritum Sanctum inspirare Pontifici verum Scripturæ sensum sine Scripturarum lectione aut meditatione: ac proindè vel hoc pacto inspirationem illam rectissimè dici extraordinariam: Scripturam verò commonitorium tantùm quoddam esse respectu Pontificis: tùm uno verbo respondemus, nugari Jesuvvitam in re nimis seriâ: & priùs probandum ipsi esse, quod dicit, quàm ut vel ipse ex falsis præsuppositis quicquam adversum nos inferat vel nos ipsius præconceptis opinionibus constringi patiamur.

III. Periculum. Si recipienda essent aliqua dogmata, quæ nullo Scripturæ testimonio probari possunt, infinita aperiretur licentia, quævis dogmata in Ecclesiam introducendi.

Regerit Bellarminus: Hoc pacto ipsas quoq; Scripturas rejiciendas esse, quia multi etiam falsi libri, ornati fuerint titulo librorum Canonicorum. Sed maxima diversitas est in Exemplis: Libri enim veri à falsis multò faciliùs possunt dignosci, quàm traditiones à traditionibus. Ipsi enim libri Sacri, ut alias nunc rationes silentio involvam, perpetuo suo consensu, verissimum sibi mutuò perhibent testimonium, eodemque consensu supposititios etiam libros refellunt. Traditiones autem ita variæ & discordes sunt, ut ex ipsis judicium certum nullo modo possit sumi.

IV. Hæreticorum proprium est, abscondere sua dogmata & dicere, Christum atq; Apostolos quædam palàm omnibq prædicasse, quædam quibusdam occultè tantùm. Quam sanè rationem, cum infringere nullo argumento Jesuvvita possit, inani cavillo illam eludere conatur: Hæretici, inquiens, hac in parte Simiæ sunt Catholicorum, & à Catholicis hanc occultandi quædam dogmata rationem acceperunt: Quod ipsum Christum insinuasse putat, quando dixit Matth. 10, 27. Quod in aurem audistis, prædicate super tecta: nimirùm, Si opus fuerit. Quasi verò non opus sit, aut quasi non ad hoc ipsum vocati fuerint Apostoli, ut opportunè & importunè, quod audiverunt à Domino, prædicarent. Quemadmodum & Theophilactus hunc locum explicat: Quæ, inquiens, vobis soliùm dixi, summa cum libertate, magnaq́; vocis contentione docete, ut omnes vos exaudiant.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: The Second Part, Antithetical Proposition I. Jesuitical

THE SECOND PART, ANTITHETICAL.

PROPOSITION I. JESUITICAL.

The Word of God is twofold, from which the way of attaining blessedness and happiness is known: Written, and unwritten, or uttered by voice, which is far older than the former.

ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστικὴ.

The Jesuit theologians of Dillingen put forth this proposition in the very same words, in their disputation concerning the Authority of the Church, in the sixth thesis: and they judged it to be so certain that they did not hesitate to affirm that those who dare to deny it are plucking out one of the eyes of the Word of GOD. This opinion is held commonly by the Jesuits today, to such an extent that Bellarmine has not feared to designate human Traditions as the unwritten Word of GOD. This partition, however, seems to have been taken from the Schools of the Jurisconsults. For just as civil law consists either of what is written or what is not written: and consequently one is ἔγγραφον (written), the other ἄγραφον (unwritten): and this unwritten law indeed is placed either in the custom of ancestors, or in adjudicated matters, or in the interpretation of Jurisconsults: So the Jesuits, estimating the Church from the quality of political terms, invent two species or forms of the Word of GOD: so that indeed one is the Word of GOD, consigned to the writings of the Prophets and Apostles: but the other is entirely placed in the judgment of the Church or of men, and transmitted without writing by ancestors, that is, by the Pontiff, the Fathers, and Councils to posterity, and is transmitted today.

However, so that we may proceed with an unoffending foot in explaining this Question: we establish at the beginning that it must not be denied that there is some word of God that is not written, but uttered by living voice: Such was that which was delivered partly to the Patriarchs at the beginning, before the writing of the books of Moses: partly to the Jewish people through the Prophets, and finally partly by Christ and the Apostles, before it was consigned to letters.

Latin:

PARS ALTERA ἀντιθετικὴ.

PROPOSITIO I. JESUVVITICA.

DUplex est Dei Verbum, ex quo via consequendi beatitudinem & felicitatem cognoscitur: Scriptum, & non scriptum, sive voce prolatum, quod illo longè antiquius.

ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστικὴ.

PRopositionem hanc totidem verbis prodiderunt Jesuvvitæ Dilligenses, in disputatione de Autoritate Ecclesiæ, Thesi sexta: eamque ita certam esse judicarunt, ut affirmare haud dubitarent, eos, qui negare eam ausint, alterum DEI Verbo oculum eruere. Quam sententiam hodiè communiter tenent Jesuvvitæ, adeò ut Bellarminus Traditiones humanas Verbum DEI non scriptum indigitare haud sit veritus. Videtur autem partitio isthæc petita ex Scholis Jureconsultorum. Quemadmodum enim Jus civile constat aut scripto, aut sine scripto: ac proindè aliud est ἔγγραφον, aliud ἄγραφον: & hoc quidem jus non scriptum, vel in more majorum est positum, vel in rebus judicatis, vel in JCtorum interpretatione: Sic Jesuvvitæ Ecclesiam ex terminorum politicorum qualitate æstimantes, duas DEI Verbi species sive formas comminiscuntur: ut quidem unum sit DEI Verbum, Prophetarum & Apostolorum literis consignatum: alterum verò totum sit in Ecclesiæ sive hominum arbitrio positum, & sine scripto à majoribus, hoc est, Pontifice, Patribus, Conciliis ad posteritatem transmissum, hodieque transmittatur.

Cæterùm, ut inoffenso pede in hac Quæstione explicanda versemur: initiò haud negandum esse statuimus, esse aliquod Dei verbum non scriptum, sed vivâ voce prolatum: Quale fuit illud, quod partim Patriarchis initiò, ante scriptionem librorū Mosis: partim populo Judaico per Prophetas, partim deniq; à Christo & Apostolis fuit traditū, priusquã literis illud consignaretur.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Second Part of the Seventh Question

But we assert that this unwritten Word of God is one and the same clearly with the written Word of God, and that the whole difference consists only in the mode of handing down or promulgating. Concerning both this Word of God sounds that of the Apostle 2 Thess. 2:15: Stand fast, brethren, and hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word or by our Epistle. For if the Apostles had afterwards written other and diverse, or even contrary things to those which they handed down by living voice, certainly they would have to be held not as Apostles, but as Apostates. Therefore, this is not what the question turns upon: Whether any unwritten Word of God can be given? But this is what is controverted: Whether, after the Word of God was committed to letters and commended to the Church, there is any other unwritten Word of God to be received with equal or even greater authority than the written Word. Where the Romanists, fighting for the affirmative, cherish that ὕπυλον, by which they understand by the unwritten Word of God the Traditions which they call Apostolic: and they prefer them in all ways to the written Word of God: so that no dogma so absurd or erroneous can be devised by them that they do not hope it can defend itself under that honorable cloak of Apostolic Traditions. It pleases me, however, to overwhelm this fictitious distinction with some absurdities.

I. Therefore, either that unwritten word is in all things analogous to the written Word of God, or it is heterogeneous. If it is analogous, then this distinction is consistent: since the unwritten and written Word will now be one and the same in species and number, and an accident does not constitute an essential difference. But if it is heterogeneous and foreign, it certainly cannot be assigned to the Apostles: whom it is confessed both taught and wrote the same things.

II. That unwritten word either exists written nowhere, or it exists. If the former: who, I pray, will be able to affirm what that unwritten word is? If the latter: therefore it is ridiculously called unwritten, that which nevertheless exists written. If the Jesuits object: that it is called unwritten because it is not contained in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles: we accept indeed what they say: And from thence we invincibly infer that the dogmas of this unwritten word are contained neither materially nor formally in the sacred Scriptures: and consequently are not the Word of God.

III. If the written Word is the very Word of God: if this very Word of God teaches one truth of one God: if no other Gospel, besides that which the Apostles preached, ought to be acknowledged: If, finally, these same Apostles wrote no other Gospel than what they preached: it would follow that, given another unwritten word, and that indeed of the same authority as the written, another Word of God is also given: nay, another God, another truth, another Gospel. But this latter is no less blasphemous than it is absurd. Therefore, that Jesuitical assertion concerning the unwritten Word of God will be of the same character.

The reason for the consequence is most evidently clear even from this. Either this unwritten Word of God is the same as the written: or it is another: If the same: it certainly does not constitute any peculiar species of the Word of God: If another: it certainly will not be true: since truth cannot be more than one.

Latin:

Verùm, hoc Verbum DEI non scriptum, unum idemque planè esse cum Verbo DEI scripto, & differentiam omnem, tantùm in modo Tradendi sive promulgandi consistere, afferimus. De utroque hoc Verbo DEI sonat illud Apostoli 2. Thess. 2, 15. State fratres & tenete traditiones, quas didicistis, sive per sermonem, sive per Epistolam nostram. Quod si enim alia ac diversa, vel etiam contraria iis, quæ vivâ voce tradiderunt, postmodum scripsissent Apostoli: certè non pro Apostolis, sed pro Apostatis habendi essent. Proindè non hoc in quæstione versatur, An dari possit ullum aliquod Verbum Dei non scriptum? sed illud controvertitur: An postquam Verbum DEI literis consignatum, & Ecclesiæ commendatum fuit, sit ne aliud quodpiam DEI Verbum non scriptum, pari vel majori etiam cum Verbo scripto autoritate recipiendum. Ubi Romanenses pro affirmativa pugnantes illud ὕπυλον fovent, quod per Verbum DEI non scriptum intelligunt Traditiones, quas vocant, Apostolicas: easque Verbo DEI scripto modis omnibus anteponunt: ita ut nullum tàm absurdum aut erroneum dogma ab iis excogitari queat, quod nó sub honorifico isto, Traditionum Apostolicarum pallio, defendere se posse sperent. Placet autem Discrimen istud commentitium nonnullis absurditatibus obruere.

I. Igitur, Aut verbum illud non scriptum, est Verbo DEI scripto per omnia ἀνάλογον: vel est ἑτερογενὲς. Si est, ἀνάλογον, tùm convenit hæc distinctio: siquidem unum jam idemq; erit specie ac numero, Verbum non scriptum & Scriptum, neque Accidens discrimen constituit Essentiale. Si verò est ἑτερογενὲς & peregrinum, non certè Apostolis illud assignari poterit: quos eadem & docuisse, & scripsisse, in confesso est.

II. Verbum illud non scriptum aut planè nullibi extat scriptum, aut extat. Si prius illud: ecquis obsecro, affirmare poterit, quodnam sit illud verbum non scriptum: Sin hoc: Ergò ridiculè dicitur non Scriptum id, quod tamen scriptum extat. Sin obverterint Jesuitæ: Non-scriptum iccircò appellari, quòd in Prophetarum & Apostolorum scriptis minimè contineatur: acceptamus utique, quod dicunt: Et indè invictè inferimus, Dogmata verbi hujus non scripti, neque materialiter, neque formaliter in Scripturis sacris contineri: ac per consequens Verbum DEI non esse.

III. Si Verbum scriptum est ipsissimum Verbum DEI: si hoc ipsum Verbum DEI, unam unius DEI veritatem docet: si nullum aliud Evangelium, præter id, quod Apostoli prædicarunt, agnosci debet: Si deniquè hi ipsi Apostoli, nullum aliud Evangelium scripserunt; quàm quòd prædicarunt: consequens fuerit, dato verbo alio Non-scripto, & eo quidem ejusdem autoritatis cum Scripto, aliud etiam dari DEI Verbum: imò alium DEUM, aliam veritatem, aliud Evangelium. Sed posterius hoc haud minus est blasphemum, quàm absurdum. Ejusdem igitur notæ erit assertio illa Jesuitica de Verbo DEI non-scripto.

Ratio consecutionis evidentissimè patet vel inde. Aut Verbum hoc DEI non-scriptum est idem cum Scripto: aut aliud: Si idem: non utique peculiarem aliquam Speciem Verbi DEI constituit: Sin aliud: utique verum non erit: Siquidem plus uno verum esse nequit.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Proposition II. Jesuitical

PROPOSITION II. JESUITICAL.

THOSE things which are proposed under the title and pretext of Traditions, although they cannot be proved from the Scriptures, nevertheless have equal authority, and are to be believed with the same faith as those which have manifest testimonies in the Scriptures. For after so many Councils it is no longer to be disputed about Traditions, but simply to be believed, without any proof, that they are truly Apostolic, even if they manifestly fight with Scripture.

Refutatory Exposition

The Cologne Jesuits published this proposition in the very same words in their Censure p. 230. And Canisius in his Catechetical work p. 124, 126, following the authority and definition of the Council of Trent, which in Sess. 4, Decree 1, decreed that Traditions are to be received and venerated with an equal affection of piety and reverence as the books of the Old and New Testament. Which Decree, when a certain Bishop had signified in the same Council that it displeased him, he was soon driven from the Council by the Papal legates. Wishing to cloak the impiety of this dogma, Hosius from book 1 of Plato's Laws, says: This one most excellent law will be, which commands that no one of the younger men dare to inquire whether the laws are rightly or wrongly established: but with one mouth and one voice of all, as if placed by the Gods, it commands that it be conceded, nor in any way allowed that anything be thought otherwise by the younger men: but if an old man has devised anything, he ought to report it to the princes and his equals, with no young man listening. Subscribing to this, brother Petrus à Soto, a Spanish Dominican, wished to insert this as if it were Authentic into his Catholic Confession: Since those things which pertain to the integrity of our dogmas are not in Scripture, it is necessary that they be of Apostolic Tradition. Petrus Thyraeus, a Jesuit of Mainz, in Disp. on Sacramental Confession thesis 352 and 353, defends the same impiety. Divine institution, he says, is not only expressed in sacred letters: but also by the Tradition of the elders. But whether it reaches us by writing, or by the Tradition of others, it has and ought to have the same force. Nor does this Institution have its authority from letters, but the letter from the institution. Jesuit Gretser p. 39 protocol, Traditions, he says, are the divine Word, but not written: and they are of the same authority as the written. And Tanner, page 355: There are certain Articles pertaining to faith or the worship of religion, necessarily to be accepted by all, which nevertheless do not exist openly in Scripture, nor can they be evidently deduced from it, setting aside the authority of the Church. Bellarmine confesses in book 4, chapters 4 and 5, concerning the unwritten Word of God, that the Scriptures without traditions were neither entirely necessary nor sufficient: Indeed, so that he may seem to be dealing with a very serious matter, he proposes five Rules by which it must be investigated which are the true and genuine Traditions of the Apostles. Which rules, indeed, since they seem to support the foundation of this whole dispute on the part of the Jesuits, it is pleasing to examine them a little more accurately by the scales of truth.

The first Rule sounds thus: When the universal Church embraces something as a dogma of faith, which is not found in the divine scriptures, it is necessary to say that it is held from the tradition of the Apostles. Because the universal Church cannot err: but whatever it believes to be of faith, without doubt is of faith: But nothing is of faith, except what GOD has revealed through the Prophets or Apostles.

But I answer, this Rule shamefully begs the question at the beginning. For this very thing is in Question, whether the universal Church embraces something as a dogma of faith, which is either not contained at all in the Sacred scriptures, or cannot be evidently deduced from them. For what he brings forward concerning the perpetual virginity of Mary, and concerning the number of the Canonical books, is frivolous and trifling: as has been abundantly shown above in the dispute concerning the Perfection of the Scriptures. Therefore, although I willingly concede that the universal or Catholic Church never errs in its entirety or all at once: for thus the whole would fail: I nevertheless deny in the meantime that the universal or Catholic Church has ever embraced any dogma of faith which is neither found in the divine scriptures nor can be deduced from them. For we have it most clearly perceived that the Roman Church is not Catholic, but particular, and therefore can err. We therefore correct this first Rule, substituting this orthodox one: Whatever is not found in the divine scriptures, nor is evidently deduced from them, that neither has the universal Church ever acknowledged as a dogma of faith, nor can it be called an Apostolic Tradition concerning faith. Furthermore, this first rule cannot hold place even among the Papists themselves, unless they wish to reject and abrogate very many Traditions which they undoubtedly hold as Apostolic. For example: It is an Apostolic tradition among the Romanists that the Epistle of James is of the Apostle James himself, and is Canonical: But the universal Church never believed this; rather, the most ancient Church consistently protested, as witnessed by Eusebius in book 2, chapter 23, and St. Jerome. Therefore, by the force of this first Rule, that Tradition is no longer to be held as Apostolic.

The second Rule of the Jesuit is such: When the universal Church observes something which no one could establish except GOD, which nevertheless is nowhere found written, it is necessary to say that it was handed down by Christ himself and his Apostles. The reason: Because the universal Church can no more err in acting than in believing.

I answer, this Rule sins 1. by begging the question: For it is asked whether the universal Church ever observed any such thing, and indeed one necessary to the faith and worship of Religion, which is nowhere found in the Scriptures: which we most simply deny: For just as the Church in matters of faith is bound to the Law and to the Testimony, Is. 8:20, so also in deeds it ought to follow only the Law of GOD: Whatever I command you, this only do, Deut. 12:32. What the Jesuit brings forward to the contrary concerning the Baptism of infants, and also concerning the rebaptizing of those who have been baptized by heretics: these are too diluted: as was likewise shown in the previous dispute. This rule proceeds from that false hypothesis, as if it were placed in the power of the Church to ordain or institute something concerning faith and the worship of Religion, which nevertheless has nowhere been handed down by GOD in the Scriptures: which is manifestly false: Since in such matters, one must stand most firmly not on the consent of the Church, but on the will of GOD alone: lest that be objected to the Church which the Apostle objects to the Jews, Rom. 10:2, I bear them witness that they have a zeal for GOD, but not according to knowledge.

The third rule of the Jesuit is thus: What the universal Church has observed in all past centuries and times, that is Apostolic: even if it is of such a kind that it could have been instituted by the Church.

I answer 1. by a distinction: Either this Rule speaks of matters of faith and divine worship: and then it labors under that double Sophistry which we just noted in the refutation of the preceding Rule: or it deals with matters that are merely indifferent, pertaining only to order and decorum, and then it is true in a qualified sense, but not absolutely. For it is established that the Genus of such things is noted in the writings of the Apostles: so that such indifferent matters ought to be referred not so much to certain unwritten Traditions as to the Apostolic Scripture itself. Furthermore, this Rule, taken in the Jesuitical sense, labors under manifest falsity, as it implies that there can be given Traditions which, although they are not found in the Scriptures, have nevertheless been observed by the universal Church as necessary in every past century. For such they have not been able to show to this very day. The Jesuit indeed appeals to the Tradition concerning the Lenten Fast: But he shamefully binds himself. For if that Fast has always been observed by the universal Church, the Papist writers have lied, and especially Platina, who refers its first institution to Pope Telesphorus, and indeed to the year of Christ 100. Furthermore, if the Lenten fast enjoys Apostolic authority, we ask the Jesuits to show us, both in those Canons which circulate under the title of the Apostles and in the monuments of the ancient Fathers, not merely the word for fasting—which is more ἔγγραφον and is contained in the Scriptures themselves—but to show us in them that entire doctrine and practice concerning the observance of Lent which is in use today among the Papists: such as the necessity of abstaining from meats, yet the free power of eating the most select fish; let them show us also where it was granted to the Pope to indulge the license of eating meat during the time of Lent to those who redeem themselves and their own by the intervention of a certain sum of money; let them show us where a penalty was established by the Apostles against those who do not observe this fast holily in every respect. Moreover, since they cannot demonstrate these things, it remains that a completely varied and diverse Use of Fasting obtained in the Catholic Church: One Apostolic, defined throughout the Scriptures: The other Apostolic, peculiar to the Roman Synagogue. Therefore, since a varied and diverse observation of Fasting can be demonstrated in the Catholic Church, we conclude from this very third Rule that this rite is not Apostolic. Nor does it help the Jesuit even in the slightest that he traces this very Lenten Fast, ascending as it were by degrees, from Bernard, all the way to Ignatius, and Clement of Rome, and indeed to the very Canons of the Apostles. For, not to mention that this Induction is imperfect, since it consists of an insufficient enumeration of both the Fathers and those most ancient Churches, whose practice testifies to something far different, as can be seen from the Catalogue of witnesses of the truth: I urge that point above all, that the writings from which the Jesuit confirms his opinion are clearly supposititious and adulterated. For regarding the Epistles of Ignatius, it is not without reason doubted whether all are legitimate. Eusebius certainly, in book 3, chapter 35, as also Jerome in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, recognize no more than seven epistles of Ignatius, whereas today twelve printed ones exist; so that those last five, to the Virgin Mary, to the Tarsians, to Hero, to the Antiochians, to the Philippians, must necessarily be adulterated and forged. Indeed, if we weigh the matter in an equal balance, perhaps one could doubt concerning each and every one of those epistles, whether they recognize Ignatius as the author in all respects. Jerome certainly, in his third Dialogue against the Pelagians, brings forward a certain testimony from an Epistle of Ignatius concerning the Apostles, which nevertheless is found in none of those twelve. Thus Theodoret, in his third Dialogue against heretics, cites a notable passage from the Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, which however is missing in that epistle today. What of the fact that Sixtus of Siena himself passed over these Epistles with, as they say, a dry foot, tacitly implying that they are not at all certain and genuine? See more in Withack, disp. on Sacred Scripture, in octavo, page 651. As for Clement of Rome, we certainly do not care at all for him as the patron of all heretics, as Epiphanius testifies in heresy 30. And it ought to seem strange that the Jesuit dares to appeal to the books of the constitutions of this Clement, which he nevertheless knows were eliminated from the Church by the Sixth Synod in Trullo, celebrated in the year of Christ 681, by an express decree. And indeed, that they were rejected by Gratian in the Decrees, Dist. 15, among the Apocryphal writings.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO II. JESUVVITICA.

EA, quæ sub titulo & prætextu Traditionum proponuntur, licet ex Scripturis probari non possint, habent tamen parem autoritatem, eademque fide sunt credenda sicut illa, quæ manifesta habent in scripturis testimonia, Neque enim post tot Concilia disputandum ampliùs est de Traditionibus, sed simpliciter credendum, sine ulla probatione, quòd sint verè Apostolicæ, licet manifestè pugnent cum Scriptura.

Ἔκθεσις ἀνασκευαστική

PRopositionem hanc iisdem omninò verbis prodiderunt Jesuvvitæ Colonienses in Censura p. 230. Et Canisius in opere Catechetico p. 124. 126. secuti autoritatem ac definitionem Concilii Tridentini, quod Sess. 4. Decret. 1. Traditiones, pari pietatis affectu & reverentiâ cumVeteris Noviq; Testamenti libris, suscipiendas venerandas q; esse, decrevit. Quod Decretum, cùm in eodem Concilio sibi displicere significasset Episcopus quidam, mox per legatos Pontificios è Concilio pulsus fuit. Impietatem dogmatis hujus palliaturus Hosius ex libro 1. Platonis de Legibus, Una hæc, inquit, præclarissima lex erit, qua jubeat, ne quis juniorum quærere audeat, rectène an secus leges se habeant: sed uno omnium ore, unaq́; voce, tanquam à Diis posita, concedi præcipiat, nec ullo modo aliter pati quicquam à Junioribus cogitari: Senem autem, si quid excogitarit, principibus & æqualibus, nemine juvenum audiente, debere referre. Huic subscribés, frater Petrus à Soto Dominicanus Hispanus hanc quasi Authenticam Confessioni suæ Catholicæ inserere voluit: Cum ea, quæ ad integritatem nostrorum dogmatum pertinent, in Scriptura non sint, necesse est; ea Apostolica esse Traditionis. Petrus Thyræ9 Jesuvvita Moguntinus, in Disp.de Sacramentali Confessione thef. 352. & 353. eandem impietatem defendit. Divina, inquiens, institutio non solùm sacris literis est expressa: sed & Traditione majorum. Sive autem scripto ad nos eaperveniat, sive aliorum Traditione, eandẽ & habet & habere debet vim. Neque Institutio hæc ex literis, sed litera ex institutione suam habent autoritatem. Jesuvvita Gretserus p. 39protocolli, Traditiones, inquit, sunt Verbum divinum, sed non scriptum: & sunt ejusdem autoritatis, ac scriptum. Et Tannerus pag. 355. Sunt Articuli quidam ad fidem seu cultum religionis spectantes, necessariò ab omnibus accipiendi, qui tamen in scripturâ apertè non extant, nec ex ea evidenter deduci possunt sepositâ autoritate Ecclesiæ. Bellarminus fatetur l. 4. c. 4. & 5. de Verbo Dei non-scripto, Scripturas sine traditionibus nec omninò necessarias, nec sufficientes fuisse: Quin, ut rem admodum seriam agere videatur, quinq; proponit Regulas, quib9 indagandum sit, quæ sint veræ ac germanæ Apostolorum Traditiones. Quæ sanè regulæ, cùm fundamentum totius hujus disputationis ex parte Jesuvvitarum sustinere videantur: placet eas ad veritatis trutinam paulò accuratiùs exigere.

Prima Regula sic sonat: Quando universa Ecclesia aliquid tanquàm dogma fidei amplectitur, quod non invenitur in divinis literis, necesse est dicere, ex Apostolorum traditione id haberi. Quia Ecclesia universa errare non potest: sed quicquid ea credit esse de fide, sine dubio est de fide: At nihil est de fide, nisi quod DEUS per Prophetas aut Apostolos revelavit.

Sed Respondeo, Regulam hanc turpiter initiò petere principium. Hoc ipsum enim in Quæstione est, an universa Ecclesia aliquid tanquàm fidei dogma amplectatur, quod vel omninò in Sacris literis non contineatur, vel evidenter indè deduci non queat. Frivolum enim & nugatorium est, quod de perpetua Mariæ virginitate, deque numero librorum Canonicorum profert: uti suprà in disputatione de Scripturarum Perfectione abundè est ostensum. Proindè etsi libenter concedo, universam sive Catholicam Ecclesiam nunquam totam sive simul errare: sic enim tota deficeret: nego tamen interim, universam sive Catholicam Ecclesiam, unquam ullum fidei dogma essu amplexam, quod in divinis literis neque inveniatur, nequè indè deduci queat. Romanam enim Ecclesiam, non Catholicam, sed particularem esse, ac proindè errare posse, habemus perspectissimum. Corrigimus proindè primam hanc Regulam, substituentes istam Orthodoxam: Quicquid in divinis literis non invenitur, neque evidenter indè deducitur, id neque universa Ecclesia unquam pro dogmate fidei agnovit, neque etiam Traditio Apostolica fidem concernens, dici potest. Deindè prima hæc regula locum apud ipsos etiam Pontificios obtinere nequit, nisi plurimas Traditiones, quas ipsi indubitatò pro Apostolicis habent, rejicere & abrogare velint. Exempli gratiâ: Traditio apud Romanenses Apostolica est, Epistolam Jacobi esse ipsius Apostoli Jacobi, & esse Canonicam: Atqui nunquam universa Ecclesia hoc credidit, quin antiquissima Ecclesia constanter reclamavit, teste Eusebio lib. 2. cap. 23. & D. Hieronymo. Ergò vi hujus primæ Regulæ, Traditio illa non amplius pro Apostolicâ est habenda.

Secunda Regula Jesuvvitæ talis est: Quando universa Ecclesia aliquid servat, quod nemo constituere potuit nisi DEUS, quod tamen nusquàm invenitur scriptum, necesse est dicere, ab ipso Christo & Apostolis ejus esse traditum. Ratio: Quia Ecclesia universa non magis in operando, quàm in credendo errare potest.

Respondeo, peccat Regula isthæc 1. petitione principii: Quæritur enim, an tale aliquid unquam universa Ecclesia servarit, & quidem ad fidem & cultum Religionis necessarium, quod nuspiam in Scripturis inveniatur: id quod nos simplicissimè negamus: Nam uti Ecclesia in rebus fidei alligata est ad Legem & ad Testimonium, Es. 8, 20. ita in factis etiam solam DEI Legẽ sequi debet: Quicquid ego Tibi præcipio, hoc tantum facito, Deut. 12, 32. Quæ in contrarium profert Jesuvvita de Baptismo parvulorum, item de rebaptizandis iis, qui ab hæreticis sunt baptizati: nimis diluta sunt: uti superiore disputatione proximâ itidem ostensum. 2. Procedit hæc regula ex falsa illa hypothesi, ac si in potestate Ecclesiæ esset positum, ordinare sive instituere aliquid circa fidem & cultum Religionis, quod tamen à DEO in Scripturis nuspiam sit traditum: id quod manifestè est falsum: Siquidem in hujusmodi reb9, non consensu Ecclesiæ: sed solius DEI voluntate firmissimè est standum: ne illud Ecclesiæ objici queat, quod Judæis objicit Apostolus, Rom. 10, 2. Testimonium perhibeo illis, quod æmulationem DEI habeant, ἀλλ᾿ ὀυκἀτ᾿ ἐπίγνωσιν.

Tertia regula Jesuvvitæ sic habet: Quod universa Ecclesia observavit omnib9 retrò seculis & temporibus, illud est Apostolicum: etsi sit ejusmodi, ut ab Ecclesia, institui potuisset.

Respondeo 1. per distinctionem: Vel n. Regula isthæc de reb. fidei & cultus divini loquitur: & tùm gemina illa Sophisticatione laborat, quam modò in præcedẽtis Regulæ refutatione notavimus: vel agit de rebus merè adiaphoris ad ordinem tantùm & decorum spectantib9, & tum vera est κ[..]τὶ, non verò ἁπλῶς. Nam Genus rerum istarum in scriptis Apostolorum notari constat: ut non tàm ad Traditiones quasdam nõ scriptas: quàm ad ipsam Scripturam Apostolicam hujusmodi adiaphora referri debeãt. Deindè Regula isthæc sensu Jesuvvitico accepta, manifestâ falsitate laborat, ut quæ innuit, dari posse Traditiones, quæ licèt in Scripturis non inveniantur, tamen singulis retrò seculis ab universa Ecclesia tanquàm necessariæ sint observatæ. Tales enim in hunc usq; diem monstrare nõ potuerunt. Provocat quidem Jesuvvita ad Traditionem de Jejunio Quadragesimali: Sed semetipsum turpiter cõstringit. Si n. Jejunium istud ab universa Ecclesia semper est observatum, mentiti sunt Scriptores Pontificii, & cumprimis Platina, qui ejus institutionem primam refert ad Thelesphorum Pontificẽ, & quidem ad A. C. 100. Deindè si Quadragesimale jejunium Apostolicâ autoritate gaudet: rogam9 Jesuvvitas, ut tùm in Canonibus illis, qui sub Apostolorum titulo circumferũtur, tùm in antiquorum Patrum monumentis nobis monstrent, non vocabulum tantùm Jejunii: Quod magis est ἔγγραϕον, & in Scripturis ipsis continetur: sed ut monstrent nobis in illis, universam illam de observatione Quadragesimæ Doctrinam & praxin, quæ hodiè apud Pontificios in usu est: ut necessitatem abstinendi à carnibus: liberam autem potestatem vescendi piscib9 selectissimis: monstrẽt item, ubi Pontifici concessum indulgendi licentiam vescendi carnibus, tempore quadragesimæ iis, qui ab hac necessitate se suosq; intervẽtu certæ pecuniæ redimunt: monstrent, ubinam ab Apostolis constituta sit pœna in eos, qui Jejunium istud non ex omni parte sanctè observant. Cæterùm, cum isthæc monstrare non possint, relinquitur varium omninò & diversum in Ecclesiâ Catholicâ Usum Jejunii obtinuisse: Unum Apostolicum in Scripturis passim definitum: Alterum Apostolicum, Romanæ Synagogæ proprium. Proindè cum varia & diversa observatio Jejunii in Ecclesia Catholica mostrari possit: colligimus ex hac ipsa Regulâ tertiâ, ritum istum Apostolicum non esse. Neque vel tantillum juvat Jesuvyiram, quòd hoc ipsum Jejunium Quadragesimale per gradus quasi ascendens, à Bernhardo, usque ad Ignatium, & Clementem Romanum, atque adeò ad ipsos Canones Apostolorum deducit. Nam ut nihil dicam de eo, quòd Imperfecta est hæc Inductio, quippe constans insufficiente enumeratione & Patrum, & Ecclesiarum illarum antiquissimarum, quarum praxis longè aliud testatur, uti ex Catalogo testium veritatis videre est: illud potissimum jam urgeo, quod scripta, ex quibus suam Jesuvvita confirmat sententiam, producit planè supposititia & Adulterina. Nam de Epistolis Ignatii, num omnes sint legitimæ, haud haud immeritò dubitatur. Eusebius certè lib. 3. cap. 35. ut & Hieronymus in Catalogo Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum, non nisi septem Ignatii epistolas agnoscunt, cum hodiè duodecim impressæ extent; ut quinque illas postremas ad Mariam Virginem, ad Tharsenses, ad Heronem, ad Antiochenos, ad Philippenses, adulterinas & confictas esse, necesse sit. Quin si rem æqua lance ponderemus, fortè de singulis ac universis illis epistolis subdubitari posset, an Ignatium autorem per omnia agnoscerent. Hieronymus certè Dialogo tertio contra Pelagianos, profert quoddam testimonium ex Epistola Ignatii, de Apostolis, quod tamen in nullâ illarum duodecim reperitur. Sic Theodoretus Dialogo tertio contra hæreticos insignem locum refert, ex Epistola Ignatii ad Smyrnenses, qui tamen hodiè in illa epistola desideratur. Quid? quòd ipse Sixtus Senensis Epistolas hasce sicco, quod ajunt, pede præteriit, tacitè innuens, illas haud unde quaque esse certas & genuinas. Vide plura apud VVithack. disp. de Scriptur. Sacr. in octav. pag. 651. Quoad Clementem Romanum, illum certè tanquam hæreticorum omnium patronum, teste Epiphanio hæresi 30. nihil quicquàm moramur. Et mirum videri debet quòd ad libros constitutionum Clementis hujus provocare audet Jesuvvita, quos tamen novit à Synodo Sexta in Trullo, A. C. 681. celebrata, expresso decreto, ex Ecclesia fuisse eliminatos. Quin & à Gratiano in Decretis. Dist. 15. inter scripta Apocrypha rejectos esse.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Proposition II. Jesuitical (continued)

As for the Canons of the Apostles, even the Papists themselves are forced to concede that they are not theirs, as is evident from dist. 16 in Gratian, where in the very first chapter it is read thus: The Canons, which are called the Apostles', because neither the Apostolic see received them, nor did the holy fathers give their assent to them, for the reason that they are known to have been composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles, although useful things may be found in them: yet it is established that their deeds are removed from Canonical and Apostolic authority, and are reckoned among the Apocrypha. What of the fact that the Roman Church does not even agree with itself to this day on the number of those Canons: with some counting sixty, others 70, others again 50, others 85. Thus, therefore, the Lenten Fast enjoys an excellent foundation, namely not Apostolic, but Apocryphal, or rather Apostatic. As for the other example concerning the Minor Orders, as Apostolic Traditions, the Apostle himself is certainly the author that there ought to be orders of ministers in the Church, 1 Cor. 12:28, Eph. 4:11. Moreover, the manner of both initiating and of the offices, which the Roman Church embraces today, is unknown not only to Scripture, but also to purer Antiquity. Certainly St. Ambrose, in chapter 4 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, clearly omits the Acolytes and Ostiaries, who are counted among the minor orders today, and thus, almost in mid-course, this succession of minor orders is found to be interrupted.

The fourth rule of the Jesuit is this: When all the Doctors of the Church teach by common consensus that something descends from Apostolic tradition, whether gathered in a general Council, or writing separately in books, that is to be believed to be an Apostolic tradition. The reason is: Because if all the Doctors of the Church, when they agree on some opinion, could err, the whole Church would err: since it is bound to follow its Doctors, and does follow them.

I answer: 1. The Rule fails through a manifold Ignorance of the Refutation. For it is a false refutation that those Traditions are to be recognized as Apostolic which the common consensus of the Doctors of the Church affirms to descend from the Apostles. Certainly, the common consensus of the Apostles was at one time that Christ's kingdom would be earthly or worldly. Therefore, will that unanimous consensus give assurance to this opinion? Then, that refutation is much weaker which the Jesuit contends, that that consensus of the Doctors of the Church is to be restricted both to a general Council and to all who write. For we do not maintain that either that [Council] or these [writers] can be so absolved from error that one must stand by their decision simply and absolutely. And what dogma, I ask, however absurd and erroneous, could not be defended by the Romanists if this rule were to prevail? For even the single Council of Trent could suffice to establish the entire pontifical idolomania. Whence a manifest begging of the question emerges. For it is no less in question whether the Doctors gathered in a general Council can create [traditions], than whether one must stand by their judgment concerning Traditions? Wherefore we do not care for the example of the Second Council of Nicaea, as one which defined, against both the Scriptures and the Canons of the Fourth Council of Constantinople, that Images are to be worshipped. Thirdly, that fallacy is also to be noted, that the Jesuit dreams that that consensus is sufficient if a few Fathers of great name assert something, with the others not contradicting: For 1. Who, I ask, will be those Fathers of great name? Are they those whom Bellarmine knows to be more favorable to the Traditions of the Papists? Not so: But rather those who subject their own opinions both to the Holy Scriptures and examine them according to their rule. 2. That unanimous consensus is most viciously defined by the testimony of one or another, or even of several Fathers: but it ought to be defined by the consensus of all ages, right from the times of the Apostles, an equable and in no way failing consensus. For if a certain tradition was in use in the time of Basil, but the same was not in use in the time of Irenaeus or Cyprian, it is certainly most viciously concluded: This tradition was in use in Basil's time: and Irenaeus and Cyprian do not contradict it: Therefore it proceeded from the Apostles. For Irenaeus and Cyprian do not fail to contradict it because they approve of those traditions by their silence, but because, since they were not in use, there was no dispute about their observance either. It is therefore more correctly concluded, when we gather that those more recent traditions are not Apostolic, because those who were most contemporary (σύγχρονοι) to the Apostles made no mention of them at all. Nor is it even enough for the Fathers to mention something in general, such as the rite of renunciation in Baptism, or Lent: but it is required above all that express evidence of these and other ceremonies of that kind, which Basil or someone else mentions, be shown from the most ancient writers who were either entirely contemporary (σύγχρονοι) to the Apostles, or certainly very close to them. Finally, that refutation (ἔλεγχος) is also vicious, that it is necessary for the whole Church to err if all the Doctors of the Church err. For the Catholic Church is defined not by the Doctors alone, but by the inclusion of all the faithful, even the laity. Where it never happens that the Doctors and the laity, or all the faithful, err together in the foundation. For thus the whole Church would perish: which cannot happen.

The fifth and last rule of the Jesuit sounds thus: That is without doubt to be believed to descend from Apostolic tradition, which is held as such in those churches where there is an integral and continued succession from the Apostles.

I answer, that this rule overturns itself. For 1. The Jesuit himself immediately in the following requires as an essential part of ordinary succession that it cannot be shown that any of those bishops introduced a new doctrine. But if we test the Roman bishops and pontiffs by this mark, it will be evident to the eye that that ordinary succession, of which the Roman Church boasts so magnificently, was not only interrupted some centuries ago, but has plainly perished. Anastasius II, Liberius, Felix II publicly fostered the Arian heresy. Leo X believed in neither heaven nor hell; he denied the resurrection of the flesh and the immortality of the soul; finally, he held the Gospel concerning Christ as a fable, saying to Cardinal Bembo: How much has the fable about Christ profited us and our company? Julius III vomited forth horrible blasphemies against God: and what crime and wickedness have the others not committed? Then, what can this be, an integral and uncorrupted succession, which sometimes had four, sometimes three, and very often two pontiffs at the same time, each enjoying an ordinary election? Which likewise was often interrupted ipso facto for a year and more? Which abdicated three popes at once, and elected a new fourth, as was done in the Council of Constance? Indeed, which left Rome and migrated to the Gauls? Finally, I now allow the true definition of ordinary succession to lie hidden, which consists not in the succession and propagation of places and persons, but of faith and doctrine.

These five rules having been thus discussed, it must be seen with what further arguments the Jesuit rises against us. And at the beginning, he gathers quite a few testimonies of the Scriptures, which he himself wishes to be understood concerning that kind of tradition which cannot be proved from the Scriptures: such as John 16:12, 'I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.' II. John 21:25, 'And there are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they were written one by one, I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that should be written.' III. 1 Cor. 11:2, 'I praise you, that you are mindful of me in all things, and keep my precepts as I delivered them to you.' IV. 2 Thess. 2:15, 'Hold the traditions which you have received, whether by word or by our epistle.' V. 1 Tim. 6:20, 'Keep that which is committed to thy trust.' and 2 Tim. 1:13, 'Hold the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me. Keep the good thing committed to thy trust.' and chapter 2:2. The things that you have heard from me through many witnesses, these commit to faithful men, who shall be fit to teach others also. VI. And lastly, in the 2nd and 3rd Epistles of John: Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink.

Moreover, since the responses of our theologians to these sayings are everywhere obvious, it would hardly be worth the effort to repeat them at length. Therefore, we shall be content with certain few hypotheses which can be observed in responding. And in the first saying, an ignorance of the refutation (ἄγνοια ἐλέγχου) is committed. For there is no nerve in the argument: I have many things to say to you; therefore those many things are these very traditions which the Roman churches foist upon us. St. Augustine, bearing this argumentation indignantly, affirms that it is characteristic of heretics that they attempt to color the boldness of their own inventions with these words of Christ. Tertullian therefore more correctly infers (de praescript. adv. haeret.): He had indeed said to Christ at some time: I have many things yet to say, etc. But yet adding: When that Spirit of truth shall come, he will lead you into all truth: he shows that they were ignorant of nothing, whom he had promised would attain all truth through the Spirit of truth: And he certainly fulfilled the promise, with the descent of the Holy Spirit proving it in the Acts of the Apostles. Christ therefore did not promise that he would teach new dogmas, but that the same things which he had previously delivered were to be demonstrated as needing to be insinuated more deeply and profoundly.

In the second testimony, a childish non-sequitur of multiple terms is committed. For the saying of Christ refers to miracles and deeds: but Jesuvvita adapts this to the dogmas and sayings of Christ in this way: Not all of Christ's signs or miracles are written: Therefore, neither are all dogmas of faith written. 2. If those traditions of the Romanists were to be understood by those 'many other things': it would follow that they are infinite and could not be contained by the whole world: and consequently that it is in vain that any part of them is thrust upon us to be embraced.

Latin:

Quoad Canones Apostolorum, ipsos eorum non esse, vel ipsi Pontificii concedere coguntur, uti patet ex dist. 16. apud Gratianum, ubi capitulo statim primo sic legitur: Canones, qui dicuntur Apostolorum, quia eosdem nec sedes Apostolica recepit, nec sancti patres illis assensum præbuerunt pro eo, quòd ab hæreticis, sub nomine Apostoloru compositi dignoscuntur, quamvis in eis utilia inveniatur: tamē ab autoritate Canonica atq́; Apostolica, eorū gesta constat esse remota, atq́; inter Apocrypha deputata. Quid? Quod in numero eorum Canonum Romana Ecclesia nec in hunc usque diem sibi constat: Aliis Sexaginta: Aliis 70: aliis rursum 50: aliis 85. numerantibus. Sic ergò Jejunium Quadragesimale egregio gaudet fundamento, nempè non Apostolico, sed Apocrypho, vel potius Apostatico: Quoad alterum exemplum de Ordinibus Minoribus, tanquam Traditionibus Apostolicis, certè ipse Apostolus autor est, Ministrorum in Ecclesia ordines esse debere 1. Cor. 12, 28. Eph. 4, 11. Cæterum, eam & initiandi & officiorum rationem, quam Ecclesia Romana hodiè amplectitur, ignorat non modò Scriptura, fed & purior Antiquitas. Certè D. Ambrosius in cap. 4. Epistolæ ad Eph. Acoluthos & Ostiarios, qui hodiè inter minores ordines recensentur, planè omittit, atque ita in medio fermè cursu, ista successio minorum ordinum interrupta deprehenditur.

Quarta Jesuvvitæ regula hæc est: Cùm omnes Doctores Ecclesiæ communi censu docent, aliquid ex Apostolica traditione descendere, sive in Concilio generali congregati, sive scribentes seorsim in libris, illud credendum est Apostolicam esse traditionem. Ratio est: Quia si omnes Doctores Ecclesiæ, cum in aliquâ sententiâ conveniunt, errare possunt: tota Ecclesia erraret: quippe quæ Doctores suos sequi tenetur, & sequitur.

Respondeo: 1. Fallit Regula multiplici Ignoratione Elenchi. Nam falsus ἔλεγχος, illas Traditiones pro Apostolicis agnoscendas esse, quas communis Doctorum Ecclesiæ consensus affirmat ab Apostolis descendere. Certè communis consensus Apostolorum aliquando erat, Christi regnum fore terrenum aut mundanum. Ergonè opinioni huic unanimis ille consensus fidem faciet? Deindè multò infirmior ille est ἔλεγχος, quòd contendit Jesuvvita, consensum illum Doctorum EcccIesiæ restringendum esse, tum ad generale Concilium: tùm ad omnes scribentes. Neque enim vel illud, vel hos ab errore ita absolvi posse statuimus, ut eorum decisione simpliciter & absolutè sit standum. Et quodnàm obsecro dogma, quantumvis absurdum & erroneum à Romanensibus defendi non queat, si hæc regula militare debeat. Nam vel unicum Concilium Tridentinum, universæ idolomaniæ pontificiæ astruendæ sufficere posset. Unde manifesta emergit petitio principii. Non enim minùs quæritur, utrum Doctores in Concilio generali congregati creare possint, quàm utrùm eorum judicio de Traditionibus sit standum? Quare Exemplum Niceni Concilii Secundi non moramur: ut quod & contra Scripturas, & contra Canones Concilii Constantinopolitani Quarti definivit, Imagines esse colendas. Tertiò, notandus venit & ille παρελεγχος, quòd sominat Jesuvvita, illum consensum sufficere, si aliquot Patres magni nominis aliquid asserant, cæteris non contradicentibus: Nam 1. Quinam, obsecro, erunt Patres illi magni nominis? Num illi, quos Traditionibus Pontificii, æquiores novit esse Bellarminus? Haud ita: Sed illi potiùs, qui sua placita & Scripturis Sanctis subjiciunt, & ad earum normam ea exigunt. 2. Consensus ille unanimis vitiosissimè definitur, unius aut alterius, vel etiam plurium Patrum testimonio: Sed definiri debet omnium ætatum, jam indè ab Apostolorum temporibus, æquabili & nullatenus deficiente consensu. Nam si traditio quædam in usu fuit tempore Basilii: eadem verò in usu non fuit tempore Irenæi aut Cypriani: vitiosissimè sanè concluditur: Hæc Traditio Basilii tempore in usu fuit: neque Irenæus & Cyprianus contradicunt: Ergò ab Apostolis ea est profecta. Neque enim Irenæus & Cyprianus ideo non contradicunt, quod silentio suo probent illas Traditiones: sed quia, cùm in usu non fuerint, de illarum etiam observatione non fuerit disceptatum. Rectiùs proindè concluditur, quando Traditiones illas recentiores non esse Apostolicas indè colligimus, quia illi, qui Apostolis quàm maximè fuerunt σύγχρονοι, nullam prorsus earum fecerunt mentionem. Neque satis etiam est, Patres in genere alicujus rei meminisse, veluti Ritus abrenunciationis in Baptismo, aut Quadragesimæ: sed illud cumprimis requiritur, ut istarum & id genus aliarum Ceremoniarum, quarum Basilius, aut aliquis alius meminit, expressa monstrentur documenta, ex antiquissimis Scriptoribus, qui Apostolis fuerunt vel omninò σύγχρονοι, vel certè quàm proximè vicini. Tandem vitiosus est & ille ἔλεγχος, quod necesse sit totam Ecclesiam errare, si omnes Doctores Ecclesiæ errent. Nam Catholica Ecclesia non solo Doctorum: sed omnium fidelium, etiam Laicorum complexu definitur. Ubi nunquam contingit, Doctores simul, & Laicos, sive fideles omnes errare in fundamento. Sic enim tota interiret Ecclesia: id quod fieri nequit.

Quinta & Postrema regula Jesuuvitæ sic sonat: Id sine dubio credendum est, ex Apostolica traditione descendere, quod pro tali habetur in illis Ecclesiis, ubi est integra & continuata successio ab Apostolis.

Respondeo, Regulam istam seipsam evertere. Nam 1. Jesuuvita ipse statim in subsequentibus ad Ordinariam successionem tanquam partem essentialem requirit, ut non possit ostendi, quod ullus eorum Episcoporum introduxerit novam doctrinam. Ad hanc autem notam si Episcopos & Pontifices Romanos exigamus: ad oculum patebit, Ordinariam illam successionē, de qua Romana Ecclesia adeò magnificè gloriatur, non modò ante aliquot secula interruptam fuisse, sed planè interiisse, Anastasius 11. Liberius, Felix 11. hæresin Arianam publicè foverunt. Leo. X. neque cœlum, neque Infernum credidit: Resurrectionem Carnis & Immortalitatem Animæ negavit: Evangelium deniq; de Christo pro Fabula habuit: dicens ad Bembum Cardinalem: Quantum nobis ac nostro cœtui profuit fabula de Christo? Julius III. blasphemias horredas in DEUM evomuit: & quod non scelus atque flagitium designarunt reliqui? Deindè, quæ hæc possit esse integra & incorrupta successio, quæ interdū quatuor, interdum tres, sæpissimè duos Pontifices simul habuit, singulos de ordinaria Electione gaudentes: Quæ itidem sæpiùs ad annum unum & plures ipso facto interrupta fuit? quæ tres Papas simul abdicavit, & novum quartum elegit, uti in Concilio Constantiensi factum? imò quæ relictâ Româ in Gallias transmigravit: Tandem latere jam patior veram successionis Ordinariæ definitionem, quæ non in locorum & personarum: sed fidei & doctrinæ successione & propagatione consistit.

Regulis istis quinque ita discussis, videndum, quibus porrò argumentis adversum nos insurgat Jesuvvita, Ac initiò quidem congerit benè multa Scripturarum testimonia, quæ ipse de eo Traditionum genere vult intelligi, quod ex Scripturis probari non potest: Qualia sunt Joh. 16,22. Multa habeo vobis dicere: sed jam non potestis portare. II. Joh. 21, 25. Sunt & alia multa quæ fecit Jesus, quæ si scribantur per singula, nec ipsum arbitror mundum capere posse eos, qui scribendi sunt, libros. III. 1. Cor. 11, 2. Laudo vos, quod per omnia mei memores estis, & sicut tradidi vobis præcepta mea tenetis. IV. 2. Thess. 2, 15. Tenete traditiones quas accepistis, sive per sermonem sive per Epistolam nostram. V. 1. Tim. 6, 20. Custodi depositum. & 2. Tim. 1, 13. Formam habe sanorum verborum, quæ à me audisti. Bonum depositum custodi. & cap. 2, 2. Quæ audisti à me per multos testes, hæc commenda fidelibus hominibus, qui idonei erunt & alios docere. VI. Et postremù, 2. & 3. Epistolis Johannis: Multa habēs scribere vobis, nolui per chartā & atramenti.

Cæterùm cùm nostrorū Theologorum responsiones ad hęc dicta passim sint obviæ, haud operæ pretiū fuerit altius eas repetere. Proindè paucis quibusdam hypothesibus contenti erimus, quæ in Respondēdo observari queant. Et in primo quidem dicto committitur ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꙋ. Nullus enim nervus inest argumento: Multa habeo vobis dicere: Ergò illa multa sunt hæ ipsæ Traditiones, quas obtrudunt Ecclesiæ Romanenses. Quam argumentationē indignè ferens D. Augustinus, hæreticorum proprium esse affirmat, ut his verbis Christi audacias figmentorū suorū colorare conentur. Rectiùs proindè Tertullianus sic infert (de præscript. adv hæret.) Dixerat quidē Christo aliquando: Multa habeo adhuc &c. Sed tamen adjiciens: Cùm venerit Spiritus ille veritatis, ille vos inducet in omnē veritatē: ostendit illos nihil ignorasse, quos omnem veritatem consecuturos per Spiritum veritatis repromiserat: Et utiqꝫ implevit repromissū probantibus, actibus Apostolorū descensum Spiritꝰ Sancti. Nō ergò pollicitꝰ est Christus nova se dogmata docturum, sed eadem, quæ antea tradiderat, altiùs atqꝫ profundiùs demonstrat insinuanda.

In secundo testimonio puerilis committitur ἀσυλλογισία plurium terminorum. Nam dictum Christi sonat de miraculis & factis: Jesuvvita verò id accommodat ad dogmata & dicta Christi hoc modo: Non omnia Christi signa sive miracula sunt scripta: Ergò neque omnia dogmata fidei sunt scripta. 2. Si Traditiones ille Romanésium per illa Multa alia, essent intelligendæ: sequeretur, eas infinitas esse nec à toto mundo eas capi posse: ac proindè frustra particulam earū aliquam nobis amplexandam obtrudi.


### On Holy Scripture or the Word of God Revealed: Proposition II. Jesuitical (continued)

The third testimony Chrysostom and Ambrose understand concerning ecclesiastical rites: others concerning doctrine as well as rites: But in either way the Papists achieve nothing. They have not yet proven that those things were not subsequently committed to writing by the Apostle. Chrysostom indeed in Homily 26 on the first to the Corinthians judges far otherwise: saying, When he had already admonished them of these things face to face, and perhaps some had obeyed, but others not at all: therefore through the Epistle again like a good physician he corrects the sin by washing it away with his speech. But what that thing is, which he admonished face to face, is manifest from those things which he committed to writing in his letters.

The fourth deals either with doctrine or with rites: If with doctrine, then those traditions either agree with those things which the Apostle wrote, or they disagree. If they agree: it would be frivolous to fabricate new and dissenting ones: If they disagree: then they are not Apostolic. If the Romanists understand those traditions to be about rites and ceremonies, let them show them to us, and let them make us as certain of them as we are certain of the Epistles. And the perpetual sophistry of the non sequitur in the Jesuit argument is to be noted. The Apostle commands to hold the traditions which the Thessalonians had received by word: Therefore the Apostle delivered other things than he wrote. Or: Therefore those traditions are these very ones which the Romanists peddle.

In the fifth the same sophistry of the non sequitur occurs: Then the ignorance of the refutation. For by the deposit and by the pattern of sound words the Apostle does not understand that patchwork or farrago of human traditions, for which the Romanists contend: but the Holy Scripture itself which Timothy had learned from infancy. 2 Tim 3, 15.

The sixth and final argument labors under the same inconsistency and futility. For what reason of consequence is there: John informed one or another friend by word of mouth: Therefore he taught other and different things from those which he had written before: Or: Therefore he taught those things which today the Romanists attempt to foist upon the Churches under the cloak of Apostolic Traditions.

These things having been thus premised, the Jesuit institutes a transition to the second part of the Proof, which is as it were supplementary. For he flees first to the Decretal Epistles of certain Popes: partly to the authority of three Councils, the first and second Nicene, and the eighth general Constantinopolitan: and finally partly to the Fathers. To which we respond briefly as follows. As regards the Decretal Epistles of the Popes, we cannot be bound by them in this matter, for the reason that in them sounds not the voice of a judge, but of a party. What? That it is established that those very ones are supposititious: which fact Cardinal Nicholas Cusanus acknowledged from Papist writers in book 3 of the Catholic Concordance, chapter 2, saying, in my judgment, those things concerning Constantine are apocryphal, and perhaps also some other long and great writings attributed to the holy Popes Clement and Anacletus. If anyone were to read those writings diligently, and apply their times to their writings: and from thence had use and memory of the works of all the Fathers who were up to Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose: and also of the acts of the Councils, where authentic writings are alleged: he would find this, that in all those writings there is no mention of those aforementioned Epistles, and also the Epistles themselves, when applied to the time of those Saints, betray themselves. Erasmus acknowledged this very thing, determining that those Epistles are unworthy of the name of Popes: and he finds wanting in them both the diction, and the genius, and the erudition. Nor should it seem a wonder that various opinions about Traditions had already crept into that ancient Church, since the mystery of iniquity had begun to work while the Apostles were still living. 2 Thess. 2, 2 and 7.

As regards the authority of Councils and Fathers, we respond at the beginning in general that it does not bind us except in a certain respect and conditionally, insofar as their sayings are consonant with the Scriptures: For we repudiate dissenting ones with the same ease with which they can be foisted upon us. Furthermore, specifically regarding those three Councils to which the Jesuit appeals in this place, I respond: The latter two, namely the second Nicene and the eighth Constantinopolitan, have long since made shipwreck of the faith, in that they established new, impious dogmas, unknown to both the Scriptures and the primitive Church, and much less approved: such as the veneration of images: with such a Canon promulgated: Whoever does not from the heart teach the Christian people the veneration of the holy and honorable images of all the Saints who have pleased God from the beginning, let him be Anathema. Thus the eighth Constantinopolitan defined that secular princes are not to be admitted to Councils or Synods: that the Metropolitan has supreme jurisdiction over the other Bishops: that no one ought to even hiss against the Roman Bishop: and other absurd and impious things of that kind, so that the legates of the Greeks complained not without cause of the fraudulence of the Pope, Adrian, which he exercised in that Council. Furthermore, as regards the first Nicene Council, although it perhaps cannot be entirely exempted from every error: yet the Jesuit writes falsely that it borrowed the word homoousios from Tradition: For Theodoret clearly testifies to the contrary, asserting, The Arians were condemned in the Council from the appellations of Holy Scripture piously considered, book 1 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 8.

Finally, as regards the Fathers: their authority certainly does not suffice to confirm that patchwork of human traditions. For it is established, and can or ought to be denied by no reason, that these very men were miserably deceived in this matter: and that they dragged others after them into the same error. Tertullian certainly followed the heretic Montanus in many things, who cloaked his figments under the pretext of the Paraclete. Cyprian the Martyr also followed him, and erred with his whole African Council concerning the rebaptizing of heretics. Likewise Epiphanius and Clement of Alexandria are too numerous in describing and praising Traditions. Damascenus [concerning] the tradition of venerating images. Furthermore, that some Fathers, such as Irenaeus and others, appeal to Traditions and Apostolic Churches; they certainly do not understand such Traditions as cannot be confirmed by any testimony of the Scriptures: But they accept the etymon of Tradition generally, for the doctrine of the Apostles and the principal parts of Christian doctrine, which are comprised in the Apostolic Creed (which Irenaeus frequently designates as the Tradition of the Apostles). Thirdly, the causes are to be noted for which the Fathers were accustomed to appeal to Traditions. The principal one, however, is: Because they had business with such heretics who did not receive the Scriptures, or if they did receive them, they did not receive them entire, or they were slandering them, whence Tertullian: This heresy does not receive certain scriptures, and if it receives any, it inverts them by additions and subtractions for the sake of the argument of its own institution, and if it receives them, it does not receive them entire. Therefore, they appealed to the Traditions of the Church, not, however, just any, but those which they knew to agree entirely with the written doctrine of the Apostles; according to that saying of Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 3: Let all things be in agreement with the scriptures. And Cyprian, Epistle to Pompeianus: If it is either commanded in the Gospel, or contained in the Apostles' Epistles and Acts, let it be observed as a Holy Tradition. And Basil, Epistle 80: Custom is to be rejected, and one must stand by the judgment of the doctrine inspired by GOD: therefore, among whomsoever dogmas consonant with the divine oracles are found, to them let the judgment be entirely awarded. Fourthly, the Fathers understand by the name of Traditions those rites and ordinances which can either be gathered from the writings of the Apostles, or are instituted by the Church by free observation for the sake of order and decorum. Concerning which we today do not move a dispute with the Papists. Finally, in the monuments of the Holy Fathers, not everything is to be embraced immediately; for it is certain that there are many supposititious books, which ought to be cautiously distinguished from the genuine ones. For example: many things are brought forward under the name of Clement of Rome, which, however, Eusebius, book 3 of his history, chapter 38, testifies to be forged and adulterated, as does Nicephorus, book 3, chapter 18. Thus, today, five books of Hegesippus are circulated, which, however, even the Romanists themselves cannot deny are not his. Thus, that Dionysius, to whom the Romanists appeal from time to time, is not that Areopagite, but a certain Pseudo-Dionysius. Thus, the books of Clement of Alexandria, which he designates by the title of Stromata, are either corrupted, or certainly do not deserve the faith and authority otherwise owed to the Fathers, because they contain many fabulous things, as even Eusebius himself testifies. Which same thing must be established concerning many books of Origen, which Jerome did not hesitate to call poisoned. Thus, that most sharp censor of the Fathers, Erasmus, observed that there are many supposititious things in the writings of Basil. That the same thing has happened to the monuments of others also through the fraudulence of heretics, hardly anyone would deny, unless he were completely a stranger to Ecclesiastical history.

But to return to the Jesuit, in the last place he rises up against us with four arguments in book 4, chapter 8.

And indeed, first, he objects to us the custom of the heretics, who by common consent rejected the Traditions of all ages. But the Jesuit plays the Sophist, while he mixes false things with true, and pours out mists, so that the state of the controversy might not be more correctly known in this place.
