For the heretics did not reject Traditions alone, nor even all Traditions; nor did they reject Traditions primarily; but primarily and above all they rejected the Authority of the sacred Scripture; and to this they opposed those Traditions which they were circulating: against which, as they were also urging their own Traditions, the Orthodox rightly opposed the Traditions received from the Fathers; as can be seen especially in Tertullian.

Secondly, the Jesuit derives his argument from the customs of all Nations, from the practice of profane republics, from the example of certain Philosophers, who are accustomed to rely most heavily upon Traditions. But I reply that this method of arguing is completely frivolous and trifling: indeed, it is such that it could be more correctly inverted and twisted back upon the Adversary. For because the Jews did not allow themselves to be ruled and bound by the written Word of God alone; but wished to insist upon the Traditions of the Fathers; and indeed for this very reason they shamefully strayed from the true worship of God, indeed were for that reason rebuked by the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles, because, having abandoned the Word of God, they persistently insist upon the precepts of the fathers, certainly even from that it is irrefragably proven that one must by no means stand by Traditions that fight against the written word of God. What anarchy and confusion it breeds in Republics if subjects, having neglected written laws, are ruled now by this, now by that Tradition, the thing itself and Experience speak. For which reason Emperors also wished judgments to be restricted to certain laws and constitutions, which it would be free or lawful for no one to change or bend at their own discretion. In which part the Canon Law also opposes the Jesuit more than it supports him. For distinct. 8. c. Veritate; Item c. Si consuetudinem: Item, c. Qui contemta, not only prohibits custom from being preferred to reason and truth, because reason and truth always exclude custom; but it also confirms that very thing by the authority of Christ, Cyprian, and Augustine. As for the philosophers, since their science relies on human principles, it is certainly left free for them also to appeal likewise to the traditions of men. But from human principles to divine, the consequence is not valid.

He takes his third argument from the dignity and privilege of the Church, the loss of which it would suffer if all things were written, and heretics, Pagans, and Jews knew nothing of the mysteries of our faith. But this argument fails by the Sophism of the non-cause as a cause. For nothing at all is lost from the dignity and privilege of the Church, even if heretics, pagans, and Jews have some knowledge of the mysteries of the faith. For such people perceive only the bark of them, that is, only a bare historical knowledge, however they may; but they never reach the very core, that is, the spiritual sense and knowledge, which is proper to justifying faith; as it is and remains solely in the possession of the Church as a royal right and a certain privilege. Whence Irenaeus also rightly calls the Church a rich Repository, because of the doctrine contained in the sacred writings; which has been entrusted to it to be guarded.

The Jesuit borrows the fourth and final argument from the dignity of many mysteries, the holiness of which is so great that it is better to wrap them in silence than to explain them in the scriptures, so that they may be read by all. But the Savior himself infringes upon this rule as impious, Matt. 10, 27: What I tell you in the dark, speak in the light, and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops; and the Apostle, Acts 20, 27, asserting that he had announced the whole counsel of God to the Ephesian Church, without making any distinction among the hearers. Furthermore, the argument is inverted: If it was not useful for those mysteries to be explained in the scriptures, so that they could not be read by all, then certainly they will be much less to be explained by the living voice; since the living

Latin:

Tertium Testimonium Chrysostomus & Ambrosius de ritibus Ecclesiasticis intelligunt: Alii de de doctrinâ simul & ritibus: Sed utrovis modo nihil proficiunt Pontificii. Nondum. probarūt, ea non fuisse postea consignata ab Apostolo. Chrysostomo sanè Homil. 26. in priorē ad Gorinth. longè aliter judicat: Cum inquiens horum jam coràm admonuisset, & fortassè alij quidā paruerāt, alij verò minimè: propterea per Epistolam iterùm tanquam bonꝫ Medicus oratione sua abluens peccatum corrigit. Quid autē illud sit, quod coràm admonuit, ex his, quæ jaliteris consignavit manifestū est.

Quartum agit vel de doctrina, vel de ritibus: Si de doctrina, tum παραδόσεις illæ vel consentiunt cum ijs, quæ Apostolus scripsit, vel dissentiunt. Si consentiunt: frivolum fuerit, novas & dissentientes confingere: Si dissentiunt: tùm nō sunt Apostolicæ. Si de ritibus, atq; ceremonijs traditiones istas intelligunt Romanenses, monstrent nobis eas, & tam certos nos de ijs faciant, atque certi sumus de Epistolis. Et notanda perpetua Sophisticatio ὠπὸ τὸ μὴ ἐπόμενον in argumento Jesuvvitico. Apostolus jubet tenere traditiones, quas per Sermonem acceperint Thessalonicenses: Ergò Apostolus alia tradidit, quàm scripsit. Vel: Ergò Traditiones illæ sunt hæ ipsæ, quas Romanenses venditant.

In Quinto eadem occurrit Sophisticatio ὠπὸ τὸ μὴ ἐπόμενον: Deinde ἄγνοια ἐλέγχε. Per depositum enim & per ὑποτύπωσιν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων non intelligit Apostolus centonem sive farragine illam traditionum humanarum, pro qua digladiantur Romanenses: sed ipsam Scripturā S. quā ab infātia didicerat Timotheꝫ. 2 Tim 3, 15.

Sextum & postremum argumentum eâdem ἀσυςασίᾳ ac futilitate laborat. Quæ enim ratio est consequentiæ: Johannes unum aut alterum amicum viva voce informavit: Ergò docuit alia ac diversa ab ijs, quæ ante scripserat: Vel: E. docuit ea, quæ hodie sub Traditionum Apostolicarum pallio Romanenses Ecclesiæ obtrudere conantur.

His ita præmissis, transitum instituit Jesuvvita ad alterum Probationis, quod est quasi ascitiū. Confugit enim primò ad quorundam Pontificum Decretales Epistolas: partim ad autoritatem trium Conciliorum Niceni I. & II. & Constantinopolitani Octavi generalis: partim deniquè ad Patres. Ad quæ breviter sic respondemus. Quoad Decretales Epistolas Pontificum, eas hac in parte nos non posse constringere, propterea, quod in ijs sonat non vox judicis, sed partis. Quid? quod illas ipsas suppositias esse constat: id quod ex Pontificijs scriptorib. agnovit Nicolaus Cusanus Cardinalis lib. 3. de ConcordiaCatholica. cap. 2. inquiens, meo judicio, illa de Constantino Apocrypha, sunt etiā fortassè quædā alia, longa & magna scripta, Sanctis Clementi & Anaclet to Papæ attributa. Si quis illas Scripturas diligēter perlegeret, & eorum tempora ad eorum Scripturas applicaret: ac de indè opusculis omnium Patrum, qui usque ad Augustinum, Hieronymum & Ambrosium fuerunt: ac etiam de gestis Conciliorum, ubi authentica scripta allegantur, usum & memoriam haberet: hoc inveniret, quia nec in illis omnibus Scripturis, de illis præfatis Epistolis mētio habetur, & etiam ipsæ Epistolæ applicatæ ad tempus eorum Sanctorū seipsas produnt. Agnovit hoc ipsum Erasmus, statuens Epistolas illas indignas esse nomine Pontificum: inquè illis & dictionem, & ingenium & eruditionem desiderat. Neque mirum videri debet, jam in antiqua illa Ecclesia opiniones varias de Traditionibus irrepsisse, cùm viventibus adhuc Apostolis mysterium hoc iniquitatis cœperit operari. 2. Thess. 2,2. & 7.

Quoad Conciliorum & Patrũ autoritatem initiò in genere respondemus, eam non nisi κατά τι & δοτικῶς nos constringere, quatenus nimirũ eorum dicta consona sunt Scripturis: Dissentientia enim eâdem facilitate repudiamus, quâ illa nobis obtrudi possunt. Cæterùm, in specie ad tria illa Concilia, ad quæ hoc loco provocat Jesuvvita, respondeo: Posteriora duo Nicenum nimirum II. & Constantinopolitanum VIII. Jam pridem jacturam fidei fecisse, eò quod nova impia, & tùm Scripturis, tùm primæ Ecclesiæ incognita, multò minùs approbata dogmata stabiliverunt: ut Imaginum venerationem: tali promulgato Canone: Qui ex animo Christianum populum non docent venerationem sanctarum & honorabilium imaginum omnium Sanctorum, qui ab initio Deo placuerunt, sit Anathema. Sic definivit Constantinopolitanum VIII Principes seculares non esse admittendos ad Concilia vel Synodos: Metropolitano competere summam jurisdictionem in cæteros Episcopos: Neminem debere vel biscere adversus Episcopum Romanum: & id genus alia absurda & impia, ita ut Græcorum legati haud injuriâ conquesti sint de fraudulentia Pontificis, Adriani, quam in illo Concilio exercuerit. Cæterùm quoad Concilium Nicenum I. etsi illud fortè non planè ab omni errore eximi potest: tamen falsum scribit Jesuvvita, quod vocem ὁμοούσιος mutuatum illud sit ex Traditione: Diversum n. luculenter testatur Theodorētus asserens, Ex appellationibus Scripturæ Sacræ pie consideratis damnati sunt in Concilio Ariani lib. 1. hist. Eccl. cap. 8.

Tandè Quoad Patres: non certè sufficit ad confirmandũ centonẽ illũ Traditionũ humanarum eorú autoritas. Constat n. & negari nulla ratione vel potest vel debet, hos ipsos hac in parte miserè fuisse deceptos: & alios postmodù in eundé secũ errorẽ abripuisse. Tertullian. g certè in multis secutus est Montanũ hæreticũ, qui sub prætextu Paracleti sua figmenta palliavit. Hunc etiam secutus Cyprianus Martyr, erravit cum toto suo Africano Concilio de rebaptizandis hæreticis Epiphanius item, Clemens Alexandrinus, in describendis & collaudandis Traditionibus nimis multi sunt. Damascenꝰ traditionem de venerandisimaginibus. Deindè quòd nonnulli Patres, ut Irenæus & alij, ad Traditiones & Ecclesias Apostolicas provocant; non certè intelligunt ejusmodi Traditiones, quæ nullo Scripturarũ testimonio confirmari queant: Sed generaliter accipiunt Traditionis ἔτυμον, pro doctrina Apostolorum ac præcipuis doctrinæ Christianæ partibus, quæ in Symbolo Apostolico (quod Irenæꝰ frequenter Traditionem Apostolorum indigitat) sunt comprehensæ. Tertiò notandæ sunt causæ, propter quas Patres ad Traditiones provocare sunt soliti, Præcipua autem est, Quia illis negotium fuit cum ejusmodi hæreticis, qui Scripturas non recipiebant, aut si recipiebant, non tamen integras, aut calumniabantur eas, Unde Tertullianus: Ista hæresis non recipit quasdam scripturas, & si quas recipit, adjectionibus & detractionibus ad disputationem sui instituti invertit, & si recipit, non recipit integras. Proindè provocarunt ad Traditiones Ecclesiæ non tamen quasvis, sed eas, quas noverat cu doctrinâ scriptâ Apostolorum ex asse convenire; secundum illud Irenæi, l. 3. cap. 3 Omnia sint σύμφωνα ταῖς γραφαῖς. Et Cypriani Epist. ad Pompejanum: Si aut in Evangelio præcipitur, aut in Apostolorum Epistolis & Actibus continetur; observetur id ut Sancta Traditio. Et Basilij Epist. 80. Rejicienda est consuetudo, & standum arbitratu inspiratæ à DEO doctrinæ: Apud quoscunq́;, ergò inveniuntur dogmata divinis oraculis consona, illis omninò adjudicetur sententia. Quartò Patres intelligunt Traditionum nomine ritus & ordinationes eas, quæ vel ex scriptis Apostolorum colligi possunt, vel libera observatione ad ordinem & decorum ab Ecclesia instituuntur. De quibus neque nos hodiè litem movemus Pontificijs. Tandem in monumentis Sanctorum Patrum, non statim omnia sunt amplexanda; Constat enim multos esse libros supposititios, qui à genuinis cautè discerni debent. Exempli gratia: multa proferuntur sub nomine Clementis Romani, quæ tamen conficta & fucata esse, testis est Eusebius lib. 3. hist. cap. 38. ut & Nicephorus lib. 3. cap. 18. Sic hodiè circumferuntur quinque libri Egesippi, quos tamen ejus non esse, vel ipsi Romanenses diffiteri non possunt. Sic Dionysius ille, ad quem subindè provocant Romanenses, non est Areopagita ille, sed Pseudo Dionysius quidam. Sic libri Clementis Alexandrini, quos Stromatum titulo indigitat, vel sunt corrupti, vel certè fidem autoritatemque Patribus aliàs debitam non merentur, propterea quod multa fabulosa continent, teste ipso etiam Eusebio. Quod ipsum de multis etiam libris Origenis est statuendum, quos Hieronymus venenatos appellitare non dubitavit. Sic in scriptis Basilij multa esse supposititia, acerrimus ille Patrum censor Erasmus observavit. Quod ipsum aliorum etiam monumentis hæreticoru fraudulentia accidisse, vix negaverit, nisi qui in historia Ecclesiastica hospes planè fuerit.

Sed ut ad Jesuvvitam redeamus, ultimo loco quatuor adversum nos insurgit rationibus lib. 4. cap. 8.

Ac I. quidem Hæreticorum nobis objicit consuetudinem, qui communi consensu rejecerint omnium ætatum Traditiones. Sed Sophistam agit Jesuvvita, dum falsa permiscet veris, & nebulas offundit, ne status controversiæ hoc loco rectiùs cognosci queat. Neque enim Hæretici Traditiones solas, neque etiam Traditiones omnes; neque Traditiones imprimis rejecerunt; sed primariò & potissimùm Autoritatem rejecerunt Scripturæ sacræ; & huic opposuerunt eas, quas circumferebant Traditiones: Quibus etiam suas Traditiones urgentibus, Orthodoxi rectè opposuerunt Traditiones à Patribus acceptas; uti cumprimis videre est apud Tertullianum.

Alterâ rationem deducit Jesuvvita à moribus omnium Gentium, à consuetudine prophanarum rerumpublicarum, ab exemplo quorundam Philosophorum, qui Traditionibus vel maximè niti soleant. Sed respondeo, hanc argumentandi rationem planè esse frivolam & nugatoriam: imò talem omninò quæ rectiùs inverti, & in Adversarium detorqueri possit. Etenim quia Judæi non solo Verbo Dei scripto, se regi & constringi sunt passi; sed Traditionibus Patrum insistere voluerunt; & verò hanc ipsam ob causam à vero Dei cultu turpiter aberrarunt, imò ideò à Prophetis, Christo & Apostolis objurgati sunt, quòd relicto Verbo Dei, patrum præceptis pertinaciter insistant, certè vel indè irrefragabiliter evincitur, Traditionibus cum scripto Dei verbo pugnantibus, minimè esse standū In Rebuspublicis quam ἀναρχίαν & confusionem pariat, si subditi neglectis legibus scriptis, nunc hujus, nunc illius Traditionibus regantur, res ipsa & Experientia loquitur. Quam ob causam Imperatores etiam Judicia voluerunt esse adstricta ad certas leges atque constitutiones, quas nemini pro arbitratu vel mutare vel inflectere esset liberum aut licitum. Qua in parte Jus etiam Canonicum Jesuvvitæ magis adversatur, quàm patrocinatur. Nam distinct. 8. c. Veritate; Item c. Si consuetudinem: Item, c. Qui contemta, non tantùm prohibet consuetudinem rationi & veritati præponendam, quod consuetudinem ratio & veritas semper excludat; sed autoritate etiam Christi, Cypriani & Augustini illud ipsum confirmat. Quoad Philosophos, cum eorum scientia humanis nitatur principiis, liberum utiq; ipsis etiam relinquitur, ad Traditiones hominum itidem provocare. Sed à principijs humanis ad divina non valet consequentia.

Tertiam rationem sumit à dignitate & privilegio Ecclesiæ, cujus jacturam ea patiatur, si omnia scripta sint, & nihil minus sciant hæretici, Pagani & Judæi de mysteriis fidei nostræ. Sed fallit hæc ratio Sophismate τὸ μὴ ἀιτίε ὡς ἀιτίε. Neque enim quicquàm indè decedit dignitati & privilegio Ecclesiæ, si vel maximè hæretici, pagani & Judæi mysteriorum fidei aliquam habeant notitiam. Nam tales corticem tantùm eorum, hoc est, nudam tantùm notitiam historicam, utcunque percipiunt; ad ipsum verò nucleum, hoc est, sensum & notitiam spiritualem, quæ est fidei Justificantis propria, nunquam pertingunt; ut quæ penes solam est & manet Ecclesiam tanquam regale ac privilegium quoddam. Undè Ireneus etiam rectè Ecclesiam appellat Repositorium dives, ob doctrinam in sacris comprehensum; quæ ei custodienda est concredita.

Quartam & postremam rationem mutuatur Jesuvvita à dignitate multorum mysteriorum; quorum tanta sit sanctitas, ut præstet silentio ea involvere, quàm in scripturis explicari, ut ab omnibus legi queant. Verùm Regulam hanc tanquàm impiam infringit ipse Salvator, Matth. 10, 27. Quod dico vobis in tenebris, dicite vos in luce, & quod in os auditis, prædicate super tectis; Et Apostolus Actor. 20, 27. asserens, sed Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ, nullo habito delectu inter Auditores, annuncialle omne consilium Dei. Deindè invertitur ratio: Si ideò inscripturis mysteria illa explicari non fuit utile, ut ne ab omnibus legi possent; multò certè minus viva voce erunt explicanda; siquidem vivam


## 3 On God, One and Triune

many more understand the voice than know how to read Scripture. Thirdly, who has ever even heard it said that Papal Traditions are of greater and more sublime knowledge than the Holy Scriptures, when it is certain that they are for the most part old wives' tales: so much so that they are not unknown even to the Heathens and Jews themselves, that they might seem to have been taken almost entirely from the superstitions of the Heathens, the synagogues of the Jews, and the schools of the Heretics.

The Fifth Reason, which many Jesuits argue today, can also be added in place of a corollary, who ask very solicitously: Since we receive the Tradition concerning the Canonical books from the Church, how does it happen that we do not receive other traditions of the same? But the answer is at hand, that this is done because the reason for each is very different. For as regards the Tradition of the Church concerning the Canonical Books, we have faith in it for this reason: 1. Because it proceeds from that most ancient Church, which partly received the tradition from the Apostles themselves, and partly was able to distinguish most correctly the genuine books from the spurious and supposititious. 2. Because that very testimony of the Church agrees entirely with those internal κριτηρίοις or Testimonies, which Scripture itself bears concerning itself regarding its own Canonical authority. Since the Papal Traditions are entirely destitute of these κριτηρίοις or marks, we certainly can and ought not to receive them with equal faith: and that the most merciful Heavenly Father may paternally deliver us and all posterity, if there is to be any, from their yoke, we simple ones venerate Him with our whole heart. To Whom on this account be glory and Adoration for ages never to be ended. Amen.

FIRST TOPIC CONCERNING GOD ONE AND TRIUNE.

The Philippean treatment of this first topic is completed in three main parts: the first of which deals with the Knowledge of GOD, whence and of what kind it can be obtained by man in this life, partly from the light of nature, and partly from the revealed word of GOD. The second proposes the definition of GOD from the sacred writings, and compares it with the description of Plato. The third, finally and lastly, explains the same definition more fully by an explanation of each of its members: and especially discusses quite accurately the unity of the divine Essence and the Trinity of persons in it.

This treatment therefore consists of a continuous thesis: unless perhaps that which the Author institutes several times, a comparison of the purer doctrine concerning GOD with the knowledge of Philosophers, Turks, and other Gentiles, might seem able to supply the place of an antithesis. However, the same treatment is deficient in that it makes absolutely no mention of the Tritheists, nor of the ancient and recent Sabellians, nor finally of other heretics who wickedly defile the mystery of the Trinity. Our Author seems to have had a sufficiently pregnant reason for this defect. For because the blasphemies of those ancient heretics had long since been driven from the Church of GOD by the care and zeal of both the Fathers and the Councils: it could seem better and more prudent to bury the wicked impiety of those men in perpetual silence, than by speaking of them, to inject some scruple of doubt into the minds of the pious.

But since in this our age, more recent Antitrinitarians are attempting with great zeal and effort to bring the very same blasphemies back onto the stage of the Church throughout Poland, Transylvania, and other places, and by the same public writings and newly devised Sophistries, are attempting to convince or at least to deceive, I think I shall be doing something worth the effort if I do not so much uncover the blasphemies of these madmen, as refute them, though briefly, from the Word of GOD.

Therefore, regarding this Article, we establish two chapters for our future treatment: the FIRST will be positive, explaining the purer doctrine of our Churches concerning GOD One and Triune in certain propositions, following the thread of the Philippean treatment: the LATTER, however, will be antithetical, refuting the blasphemies and Sophisms of both ancient and recent heretics.

Latin:

vocem multô plures intelligunt, quàm Scripturam legere norint. Tertiò quis unquam vel fando audivit, Traditiones Pontificias majoris atque sublimioris esse scientiæ, quàm sacræ sint literæ: cùm constet eas maximam partem aniles esse nugas: usque adeò ipsis Ethnicis ac Judæis, non ignotas, ut penè omnes è superstitionibus Ethnicorum, Judæorum Synagogis, Hæreticorum Scholis petitæ videri possint.

Potest Corollarij loco Quinta Ratio, quam plerique Jesuvvitæ hodiè arguunt, etiam adjici, Qui solicitè admodum quærunt: Cùm Traditionem de libris Canonicis ab Ecclesia recipiamus, qui fiat, quòd non alias ejusdem Traditiones recipiamus? Sed in promtu est Responsio, ideò hoc fieri, quia diversissima utriusque est ratio. Nam quoad Traditionem Ecclesiæ de Libris Canonicis, ideô fidem illi habemus. 1 Quia proficiscitur ab antiquissima illa Ecclesia, quæ partim ab ipsis Apostolis traditionem accepit, partim verò genuinos libros à Spuris & supposititijs rectissimè discernere poterat. 2. Quia illa ipsa testificatio Ecclesiæ ex asse concordat cum internis illis κριτηρίοις sive Testimonijs, quæ de Canonica sua autoritate Scriptura ipsa de se perhibet. Quibus sanè κριτηρίοις sive notis cùm Traditiones Pontificiæ ex toto destituantur, certè pari fide recipere eas nec possumus nec debemus: utque ab earum jugo nos Clementissimus Pater cœlestis, omnemque, si quæ futura est, posteritatem paternè asserat, simplices ipsum toto pectore veneramur. Cui hoc nomine sit gloria & Adoratio seculis nunquàm finiendis Amen.

LOCUS PRIMUS DE DEO UNO ET TRINO.

TRibus potissimùm partibus, primi hujus loci Tractatio Philippea absolvitur: quarum prima agit de Notitia DEI, undè & qualis homini hac in vita ea obtingere possit, partim ex lumine naturæ, partim verò ex revelato DEI verbo. Secunda definitionem DEI ex sacris proponit, & cum descriptione Platonis comparat. Tertia denique & postrema eandem definitionem κατʼ ἐπεξήγησιν singulorum ejus membrorum fusiùs explicat: & cumprimis de unitate Essentiæ divinæ ac personarum in ea Trinitate satis accuratè differit.

Constat proindè Tractatio isthæc perpetua θέσει: nisi fortè ἀντιθέσεως vicem supplerê posse videatur illud, quòd Autor aliquoties purioris de DEO Doctrinæ collationem cum Philosophorum, Turcarum ac reliquorum Gentilium notitiâ, instituit. Deficit autem eadem Tractatio in eo, quòd tùm Tritheitarũ, tùm Sabellianorum Veterum & recentiorum, tùm deniquè aliorum hæreticorum, mysterium Trinitatis nefariò conspurcantium, mentionem facit prorsus nullam. Cujus defectus causam videtur Autor noster habuisse satis prægnantem. Quia enim veterum illorum hæreticorum blasphemiæ curâ ac studio tùm Patrum, tùm Conciliorum, ex Ecclefia DEI jampridem erant profligatae: satiùs profectò & consultiùs videri poterat, nefandas hominũ illorum impietatis perpetuo involvere silentio, quàm verba de ijs faciendo, aliquem piorum animis dubitationis scrupulum injicere.

Caeterùm cùm nostro hoc seculo easdem planè blasphemias, magno studio ac conatu, recentiores Antitrinitarij per Poloniam, Transsylvaniam & loca alia in proscenium Ecclesiae revocare, ijsdemque publicis scriptis, & novis conquisitis Sophisticationibus, fidem vel saltem fucum facere conentur: operae pretium me facturum arbitror, si maleferiatorum istorum hominum blasphemias non tàm detegam, quàm ex Verbo DEI, sed breviter, refutem.

Proindè futurae Tractationis nostrae, quoad istum Articulum, duo constituimus capita, PRIUS erit θετικὸν puriorem Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctrinam de DEO Uno & Trino certis propositionibus comprehensam, secundum filum Tractationis Philippeae expediens: POSTERIUS verò erit ἀντιθετικὸν tùm veterum, tùm recentiorum haereticorum blasphemias & Sophismata refellens.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition

QUESTION I. CONCERNING THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOD.

PROPOSITION I.

Nothing more excellent and useful than the knowledge of GOD can befall man, not only in this life, but also in the next.

CONFIRMATION.

Our Author confirms the certainty of this first proposition with a double kind of argument. The FORMER, taken from the end of the created and redeemed human race, can be formulated thus.

For the sake of which the human race was initially created and subsequently redeemed, that must be most excellent.

But the human race was initially created, and subsequently redeemed, for this reason: that it might acknowledge and celebrate GOD.

Therefore, this very knowledge of GOD must be of the highest dignity and excellence.

The Author does not laboriously confirm the assumption, as it is sufficiently manifest in itself, but is content with a bare assertion. Therefore, he says, the human race was created, and subsequently redeemed, so that it might be the image and temple of GOD, celebrating GOD. For GOD wishes to be acknowledged and celebrated, where he deserves observation; Melanchthon is acting in this place not concerning any knowledge of GOD, but concerning that special knowledge which proceeds from true faith, and is always conjoined with the right invocation and celebration of GOD. Moreover, that illustrious Aphorism of Christ, John 17:3, can serve in place of a plenary proof: This is eternal life, that they may know you the only true GOD, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

Latin:

QUAESTIO I. DE NOTITIA DEI.

PROPOSITIO. I.

DEI notitiâ nihil praestantius & utilius, non in hâc modò, sed & in alterâ vitâ homini obtingere potest.

CONFIRMATIO.

DUplici argumentorum genere primae hujus propositionis certitudinem confirmat Autor noster. PRIUS desumtum à fine creati & redemti generis humani, sic informari potest.

Cujus gratiâ Genus humanum initiò est conditum ac deindè redemtum, illud praestantissimum sit oportet.

Atqui ideò genus humanum initiò est conditum, & deindè redemtum, ut Deũ agnosceret & celebraret.

Ergò haec ipsa DEI notitia summae dignitatis & praestantiae sit oportet.

Assumtionem tanquàm per se satis manifestam, haud operosè confirmat Autor: sed nuda assertione contentus. Ideò, inquit, conditum est genus humanum, ac deinceps ideò redemtum est, ut sit imago & templum DEI, DEUM celebrans. Vult enim DEUS agnosci & celebrari, ubi observationem meretur, agere hoc loco Melanchthonem non de quavis notitia DEI, sed de speciali illa, quae ex vera fide proficiscitur, & cum recta DEI invocatione & celebratione semper est conjuncta. Potest autem plenariae probationis loco esse illustris ille Aphorismus Christi, Johan. 17, 3. Haec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum DEUM, & quem misisti, Jesum Christum.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Propositio II. Knowledge of God is either natural, depending on the light of nature: Or it is revealed, obtained from the Word of God alone…

The Author derives the latter argument from a comparison of the knowledge of GOD with all other things, whether works or habits, which can indeed fall to man: and such a thing can be as follows.

Not only in the state of integrity: but also after Adam and Eve were received into grace: there could be no other work of man, either greater or better, than the true recognition of GOD.

Therefore, it is necessary that its excellence be the greatest.

The Author confirms the antecedent from Psalm 118:17, 'I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the Lord.' And Psalm 149:1, 'His praise in the assembly of the saints.' To this proof we add that the whole sum of human wisdom, which ought indeed to be considered true and solid wisdom, consists of these two parts: the knowledge of GOD, and the knowledge of ourselves. Now, that this latter depends upon the former, no one can doubt: for no one can rightly know himself unless he immediately turns his senses toward GOD, in whom he lives and moves. And since 'every good gift descends from the Father of lights,' James 1:17, surely even by this means, from the consideration of the good things bestowed upon us, as if from rivulets, we are led and instigated to the knowledge of the source itself.

PROPOSITION II.

The knowledge of GOD is of one kind, natural, depending upon the light of nature: but another kind is revealed, coming to us from the Word of GOD alone by the power and operation of the Holy Spirit.

CONFIRMATION.

About to treat of Natural Knowledge, we establish two species of it: One ἔμφυτον, Inborn, which is implanted in the minds of all men, and consists of those natural notions which the Greeks call κοινὰς ἐννοίας, and which concerns the distinction between honorable and base things. The other ἐπίκτητον, acquired, which is gathered from the principles of νοημάτων or demonstrations: namely, when from the certain and fixed order of nature, from the admirable structure of man and other creatures, from the perennial and uniform motion of the celestial bodies, from the perpetuity of rivers, from the perpetual terrors of conscience, from the revolutions or periods of Empires and kingdoms, from the preservation of all created things, and from other νοήμασι of this kind, the human mind gathers that there is some supreme and eternal Deity, from whom all other things, as from a first principle, solely depend.

Both of these species of natural knowledge, our author not only confirms in express words: saying, 'It is impressed upon human minds that there is a GOD, and that He commands obedience, according to the distinction between honorable and base things, and regularly punishes atrocious crimes with atrocious punishments': but also the Holy Spirit

in the Scriptures quite expressly asserts. Paul certainly, Rom. 1:19 & 20, says, 'τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, That which can be known of GOD, is manifest to the Gentiles: for GOD has manifested it to them: for the invisible things of Him, from the creation of the world, are perceived by the things that are made, namely His eternal power and divinity, to the end that they might be without excuse.' And Rom. 2:15, 'The work of the law is written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another.' This very thing is also clearly evident from the fact that the Apostles, when about to speak to Gentiles not yet converted, for the most part derive arguments from this natural knowledge by which to convince them of impiety: as we have already learned from Paul's Epistle to the Romans. He used this same kind of argument in Acts 14:15 & 16. In past generations He allowed the nations to walk in their own ways: yet He did not leave Himself without witness, doing good from heaven, giving rains and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness. Thus Acts 17:24 and following, in the sermon delivered to the Athenians, he uses arguments taken from this natural knowledge: saying, 'GOD is not worshipped with men's hands, as though He needed anything, seeing He gives to all life and breath and all things, and has made of one blood all mankind to dwell on all the face of the earth, etc.' Therefore, those who either plainly deny these natural knowledges of GOD, or at least contend that they are false, seem to suffer from a deficiency of Reason and Judgment.

However, lest we happen to seem to extend this natural knowledge too widely, it is our pleasure to investigate its nature and condition a little more accurately. Therefore, at the beginning, we restrict that γνωσιν of God to the question of the 'that', whether God exists? Where indeed we affirm that the existence of GOD is impressed by nature upon all nations. For no nation, says M. Tullius, is so barbarous, no race so savage, that this persuasion does not reside in it, that GOD exists. And in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods: that GOD exists is innate and as it were engraved in all, and there is no race of men, neither so untamed, nor so wild, which does not know, even if it is ignorant of what kind of GOD it is fitting to have, that one must be had. And indeed, as Lactantius in book 3 of the Institutes, chapter 10, argues excellently, although in other parts of life most of the Gentiles seem to differ very little from beasts: yet they retain a certain perpetual seed of religion, so deeply has that common presumption occupied the minds of all, so tenaciously does it cling to the vitals of all. Furthermore, since from the very beginning of the world there has been no region, no city, and finally no house, which has either wished or even been able to be without religion: in this there is a certain tacit confession that a sense of divinity is inscribed on the hearts of all. Indeed, even Idolatry is a sufficiently illustrious argument for this knowledge: for although man does not willingly cast himself below the rest of the creatures, he nevertheless preferred to worship either wood or stone than to be thought to have no GOD. Whence was born that aphorism of the Apostle Paul, Rom. 1:21: The Gentiles knew GOD; but they did not glorify Him as God. Nor does it stand in the way of this assertion; that not only M. Tullius reports concerning Diagoras of Melos, who was surnamed the atheist, and concerning Theodorus the Cyrenaic, that they simply denied that there is any GOD: but David also writes in Psalm 14:1: The fool has said in his heart, There is no GOD. For this is to be understood rather of an affection or wish. Because the worm of conscience, sharper than any cautery, bites such impious men inwardly from time to time: therefore they wish that there were absolutely no GOD, whom nevertheless they know and feel to exist, even against their will and desire.

Furthermore, we restrict that τὸ γνωστὸν [that which is known] of the Gentiles also to the question τὸ τί ἐστι [what it is], but only in some part. For the Apostle himself does not extend it further than partly to that knowledge alone which can be drawn from the consideration of visible creatures: and partly to those attributes in GOD, the power of which is especially seen in the governance of created things: such as eternal divinity, justice, power, and goodness. Finally, if one asks about the will of GOD, whether men have some knowledge of this too from the light of nature: we answer again with the Apostle, that the τὸ δικαίωμα θεῶ [the righteous judgment of God] becomes known to them from it, namely that will of GOD which regards the precepts of the second table, and is divinely implanted in the minds of men, which philosophers are accustomed to call the Law of Nature, jurists the Law of Nations, and in the schools it is commonly called κοινὰς ἐννοίας, common notions, of the just and the good, or, as our author speaks, the distinction between honorable and base things. A twofold ἐνέργεια or operation of this knowledge was detected even among the Gentiles themselves: One, that one must live honestly: that no one should be harmed: but that each should be given his due: The other: that those who do otherwise are worthy of hatred and death.

And thus far this natural knowledge of GOD, considered so absolutely and in itself, is quite excellent and illustrious, and provides a clear distinction between man and brute animals. However, if it is considered relatively or comparatively to the revealed knowledge of GOD, of which we shall treat in proposition 3, it fails completely and becomes useless; indeed, left to itself, it displeases God, since it is destitute of faith: and it is ignorant of all those things which cannot be known and learned except from the revealed word concerning the Essence and will of GOD, concerning the mystery of our Redemption, and concerning the remaining articles of the Christian faith.

But it is asked at this point: Are these natural notions, considered in themselves, false: just as today there are said to be some who do not hesitate to affirm that, when a man not yet reborn, or a Gentile philosopher, says from the principles of this natural knowledge, THERE IS A GOD, that GOD is eternal, that He is omnipotent, that He is the cause of good in nature, that GOD wills what is just and good: then each and every one of these pronouncements is false: because they are the concepts and notions of a man not yet reborn. We certainly cannot, nor should we, approve of their opinion, moved by many other very serious reasons, but especially by this one, that the Apostle in Romans 1:18 expressly affirms that the Gentiles held down the TRUTH OF GOD in unrighteousness. Where the Apostle himself explains sufficiently what he wishes to be noted by the term Truth, when in the verse immediately following, 19, he defines that truth by the γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ [that which is known of God] taken from visible creatures. Therefore, the TRUTH OF GOD in this place does not denote that attribute of GOD by which God Himself is truthful, or rather the very truth itself: For no mortal can hold this down in unrighteousness. For just as the unbelief of men cannot make void the Faith of GOD: so neither can the unrighteousness of men undermine the Truth of GOD. For GOD is true: but every man a liar. Rom. 3:3 and 4. But in this place, THE TRUTH OF GOD signifies that knowledge of the divine essence and will, such as we demonstrated a little earlier falls to the lot of Gentiles and men not yet reborn. Whence we infer two infallible conclusions: one: that that τὸ γνωστὸν θεῒ [that which is known of God], or those concepts about GOD known by nature and deduced from the principles of reason, are true in themselves and by their own nature: For unless this is granted, it must necessarily be false what the Apostle just affirmed, that the Gentiles hold down the TRUTH OF GOD in unrighteousness. The other: that in this question one must most diligently distinguish between those natural notions and their use or practice. For because the Apostle complains that that Truth of GOD is held down in unrighteousness, that is, that some force is applied to those natural notions about GOD: he most clearly demonstrates that those notions in the mind are indeed good and true in themselves: but as soon as men, carried away by the depraved desires of the will, do and follow something other and different than what they have impressed upon their minds: then immediately that truth is suppressed in the soul, and GOD, though acknowledged, is in a way denied and treated with contumely. If those who today maintain that these natural notions are false in and of themselves observed this distinction more accurately, perhaps the entire controversy would be removed.

But it is asked further at this point, Is there any use for this γνωστὸν [that which is known], or these natural notions about GOD, and what is it? To which question the Apostle answers, Rom. 1:20, saying, The invisible things of GOD, namely both His eternal divinity and power, are perceived from the creation of the world, εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυ- τοὺς ἀναπολογήτους, to the end that they might be without excuse. For because they did not glorify Him as GOD, whom they acknowledged, nor gave thanks: but changed His glory into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things: therefore this very natural knowledge will take away from them every excuse, which might indeed somewhat cover and mitigate the sum of their impiety. Where, however, it is certain that it is not the proper, but only the eventual or accidental use that is noted by the Apostle. For GOD did not impress these natural notions upon the minds of men to this end, that they might have no excuse for their impiety, but rather that they might use them rightly for the true worship of God. Moreover, the proper use of these natural notions is that man, by the guidance and persuasion of nature, should rule his τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν [desiring faculty], and perform those things which are required for maintaining civil society and for preserving discipline and public honesty.

These things having been thus explained, that old opinion of certain Scholastics and Monks is deservedly exploded from the Schools and Churches of Christians, who most ineptly compared the mind of man with a rasa tabula,

Latin:

Posterius argumentum desumit Autor ex comparatione Notitiæ DEI cum reliquis omnibus sive operibus, sive habitibus, qui quidem in hominem cadere possunt: idque tale esse potest.

Non modò in statu integritatis: sed & postquam in gratiam recepti sunt Adam, & HEva: nullum aliud vel majus, vel melius opus hominis esse potuit, quàm vera DEI agnitio.

Ergò maxima ejus sit præstantia, necesse est.

Antecedens confirmat Autor, ex Psalmo 118, 17. Non moriar, sed vivam, & opera Domini enarrabo. Et Psalm. 149, 1. Laus ejus in Ecclesia Sanctorum. Cui probationi addimus illud, quòd tota Sapientiæ humanæ summa, quæ quidem vera ac solida sapientia censeri debeat, duabus his partibus constat: Notitiâ DEI, & notitiâ nostri. Jam verò posterior hæc, quin ab illa priore dependeat, nemini potest esse dubium: Neque enim rectè semetipsum quis noverit, nisi ad DEUM, in quo vivit & movetur, sensus suos protinus convertat. Et cùm Omne donum bonum descendat à patre luminum, Jacob. 1, 17. utique vel hoc pacto, à bonorum in nos collatorum consideratione, tanquam à rivulis, ad notitiam ipsi9 fontis deducimur, & instigamur.

PROPOSITIO II.

NOtitia DEI, alia est naturalis ex lumine naturæ dependens: Alia verò est patefacta, ex solo Verbo DEI nobis virtute & operatione Spiritus Sancti obtingens.

CONFIRMATIO.

DE Notatione Naturali acturi, duas ejus constituimus species: Unam ἔμφυτον, Ingenitam, quæ omnium hominum mentibus est insita, & constat naturalibus illis notionibus, quas Græci κοινὰς ἐννοίας appellant, & circa discrimen honestorum & turpium versatur. Alteram ἐπίκτητον, acquisitam, quæ ex νοημάτων sive demonstrationum principiis colligitur: quando nimirùm ex certo ac fixo naturæ ordine, ex admiranda hominis, aliarumque creaturarum fabrica, ex perenni & æquabili motu corporum cœlestium, ex perennitate fluminum, ex perpetuis conscientiæ terroribus, ex conversionibus sive periodis Imperiorum ac regnorum, ex conservatione rerum creatarum omnium, & ex alijs id genus νοήμασι, mens humana colligit, esse Numen aliquod supremum atque æternum, à quo reliqua omnia tanquàm à primo principio, unicé dependeant.

Utramq; hanc Notitiæ naturalis speciem, non modò autor noster disertis verbis confirmat: Impressum est, inquiens, humanis mentibus esse DEUM, & præcipere obedientiam, juxta discrime honestoru & turpiū, & regulariter punire atrocia scelera atrocibus supplicijs: sed & Spiritus Sanct9

in Scripturis fatis expresse astruit. Paulus certe Rom. 1, 19. & 20. το γνωστον του θεου, inquit, Quod de DEO cognosci potest, manifestum est gentilibus: DEUS enim illis manifestavit: Invisibilia enim ipsius, a creatura mundi per res conditas intellecta, perspiciuntur, aterna scilicet ej9 tum potentia, tum divinitas, ad hoc, ut sint inexcusabiles. Et Rom. 2, 15. Opus legis scriptum est in cordibus ipsorum, attestante ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese invicem accusantibus, vel etiam excusantibus. Quod ipsum vel inde etiam luculenter patet, quod Apostoli verba facturi ad gentiles nondum conversos plerunq; ex naturali hac notitia, desumferunt argumenta, quibus ipsos impietatis convincerent: uti jam ex Pauli Epistola ad Romanos cognovimus. Quo ipso argumenti genere usus est Act. 14, 15, & 16. In præteritis quidē generationibus dimisit gentes ingredi in viis suis: sed nō sine testimonio reliquit semetipsum, benefaciens de cælo, dans pluvias & tempora fructifera, implens cibo & latitia corda nostra. Sic Act. 17, 24. & seqq. in concione ad Athenienses habita, argumentis utitur ex naturali hac notitia petitis: DEUS, inquiens, non manibus hominum colitur, indigens aliquo, cu ipse det omnibus vitam & inspirationem, & omnia, fecitq; ex uno omne genus humanum inhabitare super universam faciem terræ &c: Proinde Rationis & Judicii deliquium pati videntur, qui Notitias istas naturales de DEO, vel plane negant, vel faltem falsas illas esse, contendunt.

Cæterum, ne forte nimis late notitiam hanc naturalem extendere videamur: placet ejus naturam & affectionem paulo accuratius investigare. Initio igitur γνωσιν istud του θεου restringimus ad Quæstionem του οτι, An sit Deus? Ubi sane DEUM esse, omnibus gentib9 natura impressum esse, affirmamus. Nulla enim natio, inquit M. Tullius, tam est barbara, nulla gens tam efferata, cui non insideat hæc persuasio, DEUM esse. Et lib. 2. de Nat. Deor. DEUM esse, omnibus innatu & quasi insculptum est, & nulla de hominibus gens est, neq; tam immansueta, neque tam fera, quæ non, etiamsi ignoret, qualem DEUM habere deceat, tamen habendum sciat. Et sane, uti Lactantius lib 3. Instit. cap. 10. præclare disputat, licet in alijs vitæ partibus plurimi gentilium, minimum a beluis differre videantur: quoddam tamen perpetuo religionis semen retinere, adeo penitus omnium animos occupavit, adeo tenaciter omnium visceribus inhæret, communis ista præsumtio. Præterea cum jam inde a prima mundi origine, nulla regio, nulla urbs, nulla deniq; domus fuerit, quæ religione carere vel voluerit, vel etiam potuerit: In eo tacita quædam confessio est, inscriptum esse omnium cordib9, divinitatis sensum. Quin & Idololatria, Notitiæ hujus satis illustre argumentum est: etsi enim Homo infra reliquas creaturas haud libenter sese abjiciat: maluit tamen vel lignum vel lapidem colere, quam ut nullum putaretur habere DEUM. Unde natus est Aphorismus ille Apostolo Paulo, Rom. 1, 21. Gentiles cognoverunt DEUM; sed nō, ut DEum, glorificaverunt. Neque obstat assertioni huic; quod non modo M. Tullius de Diagora Melio, qui cognomento vocabatur αθεος: & de Theodoro Cyrenaico refert, simpliciter negasse ipsos, esse aliquem DEUM: sed & David Psal. 14, 1. scribit: Dixit impius in corde suo, Non est DEUS. Nam de affectu potiùs sive voto hoc intelligendum est. Quia enim hujusmodi impios subindè intùs mordet conscientiæ vermis, quovis cauterio acrior: ideò optant prorsus non esse DEUM, quem tamen esse vel inviti ac nolentes sciunt & sentiunt.

Deindè τὸ γνωστὸν istud Gentilium restringimus etiàm ad Quæstionem τὸ τί ἐστι, sed tantùm ex parte aliqua. Nam Apostolus ipse illud non latiùs extendit, quàm partim ad eam tantùm notitiam, quæ hauriri potest ex consideratione Creaturarum visibilium: partim verò ad ea in DEO attributa, quorum vis in gubernatione rerum conditarum præcipuè conspicitur: qualia sunt æterna divinitas, justitia, potentia & bonitas. Tandem si de voluntate DEI quæratur, an hujus quoque notitiam aliquam ex lumine naturæ habeant homines: respondemus rursum cum Apostolo, τὸ δικαίωμα θεῶ ipsis indè innotescere, eam nimirum DEI voluntatem, quæ secundæ tabulæ præcepta respicit, & hominum animis divinitùs est insita, quam Philosophi, Jus Naturæ, Jureconsulti Jus gentium, In Scholis autem vulgò κοινὰς ἐννοίας, communes notiones, de æquo & bono, sive, uti Autor noster loquitur, discrimen honestorum & turpium appellitare solent. Cujus notitiæ gemina apud ipsos etiam gentiles deprehensa fuit ἐνέργεια sive operatio: Una, Honestè esse vivendum: neminem lædendum: sed jus suum cuique tribuendum: Altera: Secus facientes odio & morte dignos esse.

Et hactenùs quidem naturalis hæc DEI notitia, sic absolutè & in se considerata, admodum præstans & illustris est, ac luculentum præstat discrimen inter hominem & bruta animantia. Cæterùm, si Relatè sive comparatè ad notitiam DEI patefactam, de qua proposit. 3. agemus, consideretur, prorsus deficit & inutilis evadit, imò sibi soli relicta, Deo displicet, quippè quæ fide destituitur: & ignorat ea omnia, quæ non nisi ex verbo revelato de Essentia & voluntate DEI, de Redemptionis nostræ mysterio, deque reliquis Christianæ fidei articulis sciri & addisci possunt.

Quæritur autem hoc loco: Anne notitiæ istæ naturales, in se consideratæ, sint falsæ: quemadmodum hodiè nonnulli esse dicuntur, qui affirmare non dubitent, Quando homo nondum renatus, vel Philosophus gentilis ex principijs naturalis hujus notitiæ dicit, ESSE DEUM, esse DEUM æternum, esse omnipotentē, esse causam boni in naturâ, velle DEUM id quod æquum est ac bonum: tùm falsa esse pronunciata hæc singula & universa: propterea, quòd sint conceptus & notiones hominis nondum renati. Horum certè sententiam approbare nequimus, neq; debemus, tùm multis aliis gravissimis, tùm hâc potissimùm moti ratione, quòd Apostolus Roman. 1, 18. disertè affirmat, Gentiles VERITATEM DEI in injustitia detinuisse. Ubi quid Veritatis termino notatum velit Apostolus, ipsemet satis explicat, quando versu statim subsequente 19. Veritatem istam definit per γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ ex visibilibus creaturis desumtum. Veritas proindè DEI hoc loco non notat attributum illud DEI, quo Deus ipse est verax, imò ipsissima veritas: Hanc enim nemo mortalium in injustitia detinere potest. Quemadmodum enim incredulitas hominum Fidem DEI evacuare nequit: ita neque hominum injustitia, Veritatem DEI labefactare potest. Est enim DEUS verax: Omnis verò homo mendax. Rom. 3, 3. & 4. Sed significat hoc loco VERITAS DEI notitiam illam essentiæ & voluntatis divinæ, qualem in Gentiles, & homines nondum renatos cadere, paulò antè demonstravimus. Unde duo infallibilia inferimus πορίσματα: unum: τὸ γνωστὸν illud θεῒ, sive conceptus illos de DEO natura notos, & ex principijs rationis deductos, ex se & suâ naturâ veros esse: Nisi enim hoc concedatur, falsum fit necesse est, quod Apostolus modò affirmavit, Gentiles detinere VERITATEM DEI in injustitia. Alterum: inter Notiones illas naturales, & inter earundem usum sive praxin diligentissimè hac in Quæstione esse distingvendum. Quia enim Apostolus conqueritur, Veritatem illam DEI in injustitia detineri, hoc est, notitijs illis naturalibus de DEO, vim aliquam inferri: utiq; luculētissimè demonstrat, notitias illas in mente per se quidem esse bonas & veras: sed quamprimùm pravis cupiditatibus voluntatis abrepti homines, aliud ac diversum agunt & sequuntur, quàm quod menti ipsorum habent impressum: tùm statim veritatem illam in animo opprimi, & DEUM agnitum quodammodo negari, ac contumeliâ affici. Quam distinctionem si accuratiùs observarent illi, qui notiones istas naturales, in se & per se falsas esse hodie autumant, fortè omnis controversia esset sublata.

Sed quæritur porrò hoc loco, Num & quis sit usus γνωςοῦ hujus, sive notitiarum istarum de DEO naturalium? Ad quam Quæstionem respondet Apostolus, Rom. 1, 20. Invisibilia DEI, inquiens, nempè æterna ejus tùm divinitas, tùm potentia, ex creatura mundi, perspiciuntur, εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυτοὺς ἀναπολογήτους, ad hoc, ut sint inexcusabiles. Quia enim DEUM, quem agnoverunt, non ut DEū glorificarunt, aut gratias egerunt: sed mutarunt gloriam ejus ad similitudinem imaginariam corruptibilis hominis, & volucrum, & quadrupedum, & serpentium, & reptilium: ideò hæc ipsa naturalis notitia omnē ipsis excusationē præripiet, quæ quidem summā ipsorum impietatē nonnihil tegere ac mitigare possit. Ubi tamen non proprium: sed eventuale tantùm, sive accidentariū usū ab Apostolo notari, certum est. Neq; n. in hunc finē DEUS naturales istas notitias hominū mentibus imprefsit, ut impietatis nullam haberent excusationé, ut illis potiùs ad verum Dei cultū, rectè uterentur. Cæterùm proprius usus naturalium istarum notitiarum est, ut homo naturæ ductu & suasu regat τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν, & præstet ea, quæ ad civilem tuendam societatem, & conservandam disciplinam ac honestatem publicā requiruntur.

Quibus ita explicatis, meritò ex Scholis & Ecclesijs Christianorum exploditur Vet9 illa Scholasticorū quorundā & Monachorū opinio, qui nimis ineptè mentē hominis compararunt cū rasa tabula,


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition III. Not the natural knowledge of GOD, but that alone which is prepared from the Word of GOD, by the power and operation of the…

to which nothing is inscribed, yet all things can be inscribed. By which way, indeed, they foolishly deny the γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, which the Apostle affirms is imprinted on men by nature, and they leave hardly any distinction between man and brute animals: nay, they quite clearly accuse GOD himself of injustice in condemning the Gentiles.

We also reject the error of Zwingli and his associates, who in the Exposition of the Christian Faith to the King of France did not shudder to write that the Gentiles were saved by that light of nature: having undoubtedly borrowed the handle for this error from the doctrine of the ancient Scholastics, who assigned such great power to that natural knowledge that they contended that the Gentiles could have been saved by the Law of Nature, and that very many had been saved: as is evident from book 3 of the Orthodox Explanations of Andrade, p. 292.

PROPOSITION III.

Not natural knowledge of GOD, but only that which is prepared from the Word of GOD, by the power and operation of the Holy Spirit, can lead us into a saving recognition of GOD.

CONFIRMATION.

The truth of this proposition is evident partly from clear testimonies of the Scriptures, and partly from certain reasons or arguments. And indeed, regarding the Reasons, our Author infers most correctly. Although it is imprinted on human minds that God exists, yet minds are tormented by horrible doubt. For that natural knowledge is languid and, shaken by perpetual waves of doubt, cannot provide assent. It is then also maimed and imperfect, as one that has only a small particle of the law known and perceived, namely that which concerns the precepts of the second table. Finally, it is destitute of faith in CHRIST. Wherefore, however great the Light of nature may be, it can open the way to the fellowship of eternal life to no one: But that knowledge is required which the Word of GOD shows, in which alone GOD has most fully revealed himself in respect of his essence and his will: to which revelation GOD also simply wills that his Church be bound:

This is what our Author now confirms in the second place from clear testimonies of the Scriptures: as from 1 Cor. 1:21, it pleased GOD through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. Thus CHRIST leads us to the revealed God. For when Philip asked that the Father be shown to him, He rebukes him severely, and calls him back from that speculation, and says: He who sees me, sees the Father, John 14:9. To this pertain those illustrious statements John 1:18: No one has ever seen GOD: the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him. Matt. 11:27: No one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son has willed to reveal him. Matt. 3:17 and ch. 17:5: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, Hear him. Moreover, this revealed knowledge of GOD ensures that our recognition and invocation of GOD differs greatly from that which falls even to the heathens. For first, in respect of essence, they indeed invoke GOD the creator of heaven and earth: but they are ignorant that this same GOD is one in Essence, but three in persons: and therefore, when they invoke GOD without CHRIST and the Holy Spirit, they invoke not the true GOD, but rather an idol. Then, in respect of the will of GOD, while they are ignorant that GOD the Father does not wish to be honored or invoked except in the Son: and consequently, while they do not honor the Son, they are not to be considered to honor the Father, as Christ himself testifies in John 5:23. Furthermore, what and of what kind this revealed knowledge is, the following Questions will expressly show.

Latin:

cui nihil sit inscriptum, inscribi tamen omnia possint. Quo sanè pacto γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, quod Apostolus naturâ hominibus impressum esse affirmat, stolidè negant, & vix quicquam discriminis inter hominem & bruta animantia relinquunt: quin ipsum DEUM injustitiæ in damnandis gentilibus, haud obscurè infimulant.

Rejicimus etiam Zvvinglij & sociorum errorem, qui in expof. fidei Christ. ad Regem Galliæ: Gentiles per lumen istud naturæ salvatos esse, scribere non exhorruit: mutuatus sine dubio erroris istius ansam, ex doctrina Veterum Scholasticorum, qui notitiæ isti naturali tantam vim adsignarunt, ut Lege Naturæ Gentiles salvari potuisse, plurimosq́; salvatos esse contenderent: uti patet ex lib. 3. Orth. explic. Andradij p. 292.

PROPOSITIO III.

NOn notitia DEI naturalis, sed sola illa, quæ ex Verbo DEI, virtute & operatione Spiritus Sancti, paratur, in salutarem DEI agnitionem nos perducere potest.

CONFIRMATIO.

PAtet propositionis hujus veritas partim ex perspicuis Scripturarum testimonijs, partim verò ex certis rationibus sive argumentis. Et quidem quoad Rationes, rectissimè infert Autor noster. Quanquam Deum esse, impressum est mentibus humanis tamen horrendâ dubitatione cruciantur animi. Est enim notitia illa naturalis, Languida & perpetuis dubitationum fluctibus concussa, assensum præstare nequit. Est deinde etiam manca & imperfecta, ut quæ aliquam duntaxat legis particulam habet cognitam & perspectam, eam videlicet, quæ secundæ tabulæ præcepta concernit. Destituitur deniq; fide in CHRISTUM. Quare quanta quanta etiam sit Lux naturæ: ad æternæ tamen vitæ consortium aditum nemini patefacere potest: Sed ea requiritur notitia, quam Verbum DEI monstrat, in quo solo DEUS seipsum ratione essentiæ & voluntatis suæ plenissimè patefecit: ad quam etiam patefactionem DEUS Ecclesiam suam simpliciter vult alligatam:

Id quod secundo jam loco ex perspicuis Scripturarum testimoniis Autor noster confirmat: ut ex 1. Cor. 1, 21. placuit DEO per stultitiam prædicationis, salvos facere credentes. Sic CHRISTUS deducit nos ad patefactum Deum. Nam cùm peteret Philippus monstrari Patrem, graviter objurgat eum, & ab illa speculatione revocat, ac inquit: Qui videt me, videt Patrē, Joh. 14, 9. Quò pertinent illustres illæ sententiæ Joh. 1, 18. DEUM nemo vidit unquam: Filius, qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit. Matth. 11, 27. Nemo novit Patrem, nisi Filius, & cui voluit Filius revelare. Matth. 3, 17. & cap. 17. 5. Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacitum est, Hunc audite. Præstat autē patefacta hæc DEI notitia, ut nostra DEI agnitio & invocatio, plurimùm differat, ab ea, quæ in Ethnicos etiam cadit. Nam primùm ratione essentiæ, invocant illi quidem DEUM conditorem cæli & terræ: sed quod idem ille DEUS sit unus in Essentia, trinus autem in personis, ignorant: ac proindè, quando DEUM sine CHRISTO & Spiritu Sancto invocant, non verum DEUM, sed idolum potiùs invocant. Deindè ratione voluntatis DEI, dum videlicet ignorant, DEUM Patrem nolle honorari aut invocari, nisi in Filio: ac per consequens, dum Filium non honorant, neque Patrem honorare censendi sunt, sic ipso attestante Christo Johan. 5, 23. Cæterùm, quæ & qualis sit notitia hæc patefacta, subsequentes Quæstiones ex professo ostendent.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Question II. On the Definition of God

We most rightly begin, with our author, the treatment of the Article concerning GOD with the question τί ἐστι, What is GOD: not delaying in this part for the Laws of Method, which not ineptly advise in their own place that the question εἰ ἐστι, Whether there is a God, ought to have prior consideration. For first, just as Solon, that most wise legislator, when asked why he had enacted no law concerning parricides, is said to have replied: Because I thought there would be none such, and lest by enacting a law I should provide an occasion for thinking about such a crime: So we also judge that this question is unworthy of a special treatment, lest even from that, material for doubting concerning GOD be supplied to anyone.

Furthermore, from the preceding matters which we have discussed concerning natural notions, it is sufficiently clear that a detailed examination of this question would be entirely superfluous. For, as M. Tullius also testifies in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods, that GOD exists is innate in all, and as it were inscribed, and there is no race of men, neither so untamed nor so savage, which does not know that a GOD must be had, even if it is ignorant of what kind of GOD it is fitting to have.

Diogenes Laërtius indeed reports in book 2, in the life of Aristippus, that Theodorus the Cyrenaic philosopher was the first to deny God, whom many other philosophers later followed as companions in the same impiety; yet that this action of theirs was feigned and simulated rather than true and serious can be seen even from those things which both Aristotle in his Metaphysics and M. Tullius in his books On the Nature of the Gods argue quite learnedly against them. For the knowledge of GOD adhered more deeply in their minds than an affected impiety of the mouth could eradicate its sense. But if, however, anyone desires to know the reasons from which men, even regarding the revealed Word of GOD, can infer that GOD exists, we find the following to be assigned primarily by the philosophers themselves.

1. The very admirable and most beautiful structure of man, adorned with such countless testimonies of GOD that there is nothing so minute in him that does not argue for GOD and divine care and providence.

2. The sense of conscience: which, in the case of heinous crimes, trembles at the fear of the divine Deity and dreads the punishments destined from heaven.

3. The beauty, order, effects, propagation, conservation, and duration of all things in the world. Just as Tullius, following Aristotle, treats this kind of argument most excellently.

4. The distinction and conservation of species, which multiply themselves at fixed turns and times.

5. The wonderful preservation of kingdoms, empires, and human society: which no reason permits you to ascribe to chance or fortune.

6. Grave and atrocious punishments, which are very often divinely inflicted upon those against whom, on account of committed crimes, the political magistrate does not legitimately take action.

7. The order and connection of causes, which in the nature of things does not proceed to infinity: but it is necessary at last to arrive at some supreme Being, who rules and governs all things: just as Thomas treats this argument quite prolixly, besides Aristotle in his Physics (book 2.7. & 8. Phys.) and Metaphysics (book 2.10. & 12.), in part 1 of the Summa, question 12, article 12.

8. Prodigies, signs, and other meteors of that kind, which (as Cicero speaks in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods) terrify minds, and by which not rarely entire cities, regions, and provinces are overturned.

These indeed, and similar reasons of that kind, are of such evidence that they impel and convince the mind of a man, not entirely hardened and blinded by the Devil, to conclude that there is a Numen or some GOD: a thing which is confessed among us, so that we are accustomed to seek arguments from it even against those who, as the Apostle speaks, confess GOD with their mouth indeed, but deny him with their deeds, 2 Tim. 3:5, having followed in this part the footsteps of the Ecclesiastical Fathers, especially Tertullian in his little book On the Testimony of the Soul, and Eusebius in his books on the Preparation for the Gospel. Atrocious, therefore, is the calumny of Gabriel Prateolus, who in book 1 of his Heresiology, heresy 77, from the Dubitantius of Willem Lindanus, did not shudder to write that Lutherans or Evangelicals, after they deserted the Catholic (namely, the Pseudo-Roman) Church, for the most part eventually slide into that atheism, so that they believe there is no GOD: For from Catholics, he writes, we see Lutherans made, from Lutherans Zwinglians, from Zwinglians Schwenckfeldians, and then soon atheists or Epicureans. The astounding vanity of which calumny we deservedly leave to be avenged by GOD, the most just avenger of crimes: and we answer with the Apostle, if by chance they have been made atheists from Lutherans, denying GOD: They went out from us, but they were not of us: for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us: but they went out from us, that it might be made manifest that not all are of us, 1 John 2:19.

But it is asked in this place, whether those philosophical reasons can also suffice for a man when, in more grave temptations, the Devil strives to instill seeds of doubt about GOD into the minds of men: especially from that very dissimilar lot and condition of the pious and the impious in this life: and likewise from the perpetual affliction by which the Church of GOD is pressed in these lands, and all but completely oppressed.

We answer that they can indeed do something: but they do not suffice to avert those more grave temptations. Asaph can be an example in Psalm 73, who, established in such a paroxysm, said, I labored to know this: namely, by the strength and sharpness of my reason: but with labor clearly in vain, until I entered into the Sanctuary of GOD, that is, I consulted the revealed Word of GOD, which alone can raise up the hesitating, recall them to the way, and fully confirm them. The Church of GOD, therefore, setting aside those philosophical reasons, has truly apodictic arguments by which it convinces that GOD exists, not at least probably, but necessarily.

1. THE FIRST is the Word of GOD itself, which is ἀναπόδεικτον καὶ ἀυτόπιστον (indemonstrable and self-evident), which expressly testifies that GOD exists.

2. The manifold revelations and apparitions of GOD.

3. Miracles, which clearly argue for divine power and might: as, that the Sun stood still in the time of Joshua: That likewise the Sun went back ten degrees in the time of King Hezekiah: That the waves of the Red Sea and the Jordan, divided, provided a dry and silent passage for the Israelites: Likewise, the resurrection of the dead: The miraculous and immediate healing of the blind, the deaf, and the mute.

4. Prophecies concerning future things, and their most exact fulfillment: which, as they are simply repugnant to natural causes, so they admit no author but GOD.

5. Evangelical promises, concerning the free remission of sins through and on account of Christ: concerning eternal life and glory.

To which can be added other foundations, which we shall assign below in the Article concerning the providence of GOD (σὺν Θεῷ). These things concerning the Question εἰ ἔστι, Whether GOD exists, having been premised in this manner, as it were ὥς παρασκευαστικῶς καὶ ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, we make an approach to the Question τὸ τί, What GOD is: Which it pleases us to propose, having been comprised in certain propositions.

Latin:

REctissimè cum autore nostro, Tractationem Articuli de DEO auspicamur à Quæstione τί ἐστι, Quid sit DEUS: nihil morati hac in parte Leges Methodi, quæ Quæstionis εἰ ἐστι, An sit Deus, priorem curam habendam esse, suo quidem loco haud ineptè monent. Primùm enim quemadmodum Solon Sapientissimus ille legislator, interrogatus, Cur legem de parricidiis nullam tulisset, respondisse fertur: Quoniam nullos tales futuros existimabam, & ne legem ferendo, de tali flagitio cogitandi ansam præberem: Ita quæstionem etiam istam peculiari tractatione indignam censemus: ne vel indè alicui dubitandi, de DEO materia subministretur.

Deindè ex superioribus, quæ de notitiis naturalibus disputavimus; satis liquidò constat, Quæstionis hujus diexodon prorsus fore supervacaneam. Nam teste etiam M. Tullio lib. 2. de Nat. Deorum, DEUM esse omnibus innatum, & quasi insculptum est, & nulla de hominibus gens est, neque tàm immansveta, neq; tàm fera, quæ non etiamsi ignoret, qualem DEUM habere deceat, tamen habendum sciat.

Refert quidé Diogenes Laërtius libro 2. in Aristippo, Theodorum Cirenacum Philosophū primùm negasse Deum, quem postmodùm plures alij indecuti sint Philosophi, ejusdem Impietatis socij: fictam tamen magis atq; simulatam, quàm verā atq; seriam hanc ipsorum actionem fuisse, vel ex ijs videre est, quæ tùm Aristoteles in Metaphysicis, tùm M. Tullius in libris de Natura Deorum, adversus illos, satis eruditè disputant. Profundiùs enim ipsorum mentibus inhærebat Notitia DEI, quàm ut sensum ejus eradicare potuerit affectata oris impietas. Quod si tamen aliquis rationes cognoscere aveat, ex quibus homines etiam circa Verbum DEI revelatum, DEUM esse colligere possint: sequentes potissimùm ab ipsis Philosophis assignari deprehendimus.

1. Ipsa hominis admiranda & pulcherrima fabrica, usq; adeò innumeris Testimonijs DEI ornata ut nihil tamén minutum in eo sit, quod non DEUM, divinamq; curam ac providentiam arguat.

2. Sensus Conscientiæ: quæ in tetris facinoribus, metu divini Numinis trepidat, pœnasq; cœlitùs destinatas exhorrescit.

3. Pulchritudo, ordo, effectus, propagatio, conservatio & duratio rerum omnium in mundo. Quemadmodum præclarè omninò hoc argumenti genus, pertractat Tullius ex Aristotele.

4. Distinctio & conservatio specierum, quæ statis vicibus atque temporibus sese multiplicant.

5. Miranda Conservatio regnorum, Imperiorum, & Societatis humanæ: quam ut Casui aut Fortunæ adscribas, nulla ratio permittit.

6. Graves & atroces pœnæ, quæ divinitùs sæpissimè infliguntur ijs, in quos ob commissa scelera, Magistratus Politicus non legitimè animadvertit.

7. Ordo & nexus causarum, qui in rerum Natura non procedit in infinitum: Sed necesse est tandem ad aliquod Ens summum devenire, quod regat & gubernet omnia: Quemadmodum hoc argumentum præter Aristotelem in Physicis (lib 2.7. & 8. Phys.) & Metaphysicis (lib. 2.10. & 12.) prolixè admodum pertractat Thomas part. 1. summæ quæst. 12. art 12.

8. Prodigia, signa, aliaq́; id genus Meteora, quæ (uti Cicero loquitur lib. 2 de Nat. Deorum) animos terrent, & quibus haud rarò integræ civitates, regiones, & provinciæ evertuntur.

Quæ sanè, & id genus consimiles rationes, illius sunt evidentiæ, ut animum hominis, non prorsus â Diabolo induratum & excæcatum, impellant & convincant, ut statuat, esse Numen sive DEUM aliquem: id quod apud nos in confesso est, ut vel indè argumenta soleamus petere adversus eos, qui, ut Apostolus loquitur, ore quidem confitentur DEUM, factis autem negant, 2. Tim. 3, 5. secuti hac in parte vestigia Patrum Ecclesiasticorum, Tertulliani cumprimis, in libello de Testimonio Animæ, & Eusebij in libris de præparatione Evangelica. Atrox proindè est calumnia Gabrielis Prateoli, qui lib. 1. hæreseologiæ, hæresi 77 ex Dubitantio Guilelmi Lindani scribere non exhorruit, Lutheranos sive Evangelicos postquam Catholicam (Pseudo-Romanam nimirùm) deseruerunt Ecclesiam, ad Atheismum istum plerumq́; tandem prolabi, ut credant nullum esse DEUM: Ex Catholicis enim, scribit ille, fieri videmus Lutheranos ex Lutheranis Zvvinglianos: ex Zwinglianis Svvenckfeldianos, tùm mox Atheos sive Epicuræos. Cujus calumniæ stupendam vanitatem meritò DEO justissimo scelerum Vindici, ulciscendam relinquimus: & cum Apostolo respondemus, si fortè ex Lutheranis facti sunt Athei, negantes DEUM: Egressi sunt è nobis: Sed non erant ex nobis: nam si fuissent ex nobis permã sissent utiq́; nobiscum: sed egressi sunt ex nobis, ut patefieret, non omnes esse ex nobis 1. Joh. 2, 19.

Quæritur autem hoc loco, Num rationes istæ Philosophicæ homini etiam sufficere possint, quando in tentationibus gravioribus, Diabolus semina dubitationum de DEO, animis hominum instillare studet: præsertim ex dissimillima illa forte atq́; conditione piorum & impiorum hac in vita: ex perpetua item afflictione quâ Ecclesia DEI hisce in terris premitur, ac tantùm non planè opprimitur.

Respondemus, posse quidem eas aliquid: sed non sufficere ad avertendas tentationes illas graviores. Exemplo potest esse Asaphus Psalmo 73. qui in tali paroxismo constituto, laborabam, inquit, ut cognoscerem hoc: nempè ex vi & acumine rationis meæ: sed labore planè irrito, donec intrarem in Sanctuarium DEI, hoc est, consulerem Verbum DEI patefactum, quod unum hæsitantes erigere, in viam revocare & plenè confirmare potest. Ecclesiæ proindè DEI, missis Philosophicis illis rationibus, verè Apodictica habet argumenta, quibus DEUM esse, non probabiliter saltem, sed necessariò convincit.

1. PRIMUM est, ipsum Verbum DEI ἀναπόδεικτον καὶ ἀυτόπιστον, quod DEUM esse expressè attestatur.

2. Multiplices patefactiones & apparitiones DEI.

3. Miracula, quæ divinam vim ac potentiam luculenter arguunt: ut, quòd Sol stetit tempore Josuæ: Quòd item Sol retrocessit decem gradibus, tempore regis Hiskiæ: Quòd undæ maris rubri & Jordanis, divisæ, siccum tacumq́; præbuerunt Israëlitis transitum: Item, Resuscitatio mortuorum: Miraculosa & immediata sanatio cæcorum, surdorum, mutorum.

4. Vaticinia de rebus futuris, eorumq́; exactissimum complementum: quæ uti causis naturalibus simpliciter repugnant: ita non nisi autorem DEUM admittunt.

5. Promissiones Evangelicæ, de gratuita peccatorum Remissione per & propter Christum: de æterna vita & gloria.

Quibus addi possunt fundamenta alia, quæ infrà in Articulo de providentia DEI assignabimus (σὺν Θεῷ.) His de Quæstione εἰ ἔστι, An sit DEUS, hunc in modum, tanquam ὥς παρασκευαστικῶς καὶ ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, præmissis; ad Quæstionem τὸ τί, Quid sit DEUS, accessum facimus: Quam certis comprehensam propositionibus proponere placet.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition I What GOD is by reason of essence, can by no reason, either from the Light of Nature, or from Philosophical principles or reasons, not even……

PROPOSITION I.

What GOD is by reason of essence, can by no reason, either from the Light of Nature, or from Philosophical principles or reasons, not even from the smallest particle, be learned or known.

Ἔκθεσις.

This Thesis of ours considers the Knowledge of GOD, not that general and confused one, which both from creation and from the wonderful government of created things, gathers to some extent ἀΐδιον δύναμιν Θεῦ, Rom 1, 20, but the special and distinct one, which defines what GOD is, or, if it be lawful to speak so, What sort He is, by reason of essence, from the Word of GOD alone revealed. Where all Philosophy and human reason is clearly silent: to such an extent that if it arrogates to itself any knowledge in this part: it immediately leaps over the limits of its profession. Concerning which opinion Thomas rightly pronounced altogether in part one, question 32. He derogates from faith in two ways, who strives to prove the Unity of the divine Essence and the Trinity of persons by natural reason: 1. Because Faith is concerning invisible things, which surpass human reason. 2. because by this reason he exposes the Christian faith itself to mockery. Some today object with the authority of Plato and Mercury Trismegistus, of whom the former in his second Epistle to Dion makes mention of the first, second, and third principle or GOD: but the latter in the Pimander, in the first section, discourses eloquently concerning Mind, Word, and Spirit. And indeed, relying on the authority of these, some presume that the Articles of faith can be derived to some extent from Philosophical principles: indeed, they proceed so far that they do not fear to write that Theology and the Metaphysics of Aristotle are subordinate sciences. But in many ways this collection of theirs is found to be vain.

For first, what Mercury Trismegistus and Plato handed down concerning the threefold Principle, they did not construct from Metaphysical doctrine, nor from other Philosophical principles: but they had it partly from the very reading of Moses and the Prophets: and partly from the instruction of those who lived in the times of the Prophets, and from their sermons perceived something concerning that Mystery of the Trinity. Marsilius Ficinus the Florentine reports from Augustine: At the time when Moses was in Egypt, there flourished Atlas the Astrologer, brother of Prometheus the Physicist, and maternal grandfather of Mercury, whose grandson was Mercury Trismegistus: so called because he was not only a supreme Philosopher, but also an Egyptian Priest and a Great King. Now, that the Religion of the Egyptians was as it were mixed and fused from Gentile and Jewish sources, is most clearly evident both from other writers and indeed also from the little book of Iamblichus on the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians. Thus historians record of Plato that he set out from Italy to Egypt, so that there he might not only hear the Gymnosophists, but also read the books of Moses. Thus, therefore, what those Philosophers drew from the Mosaic and Prophetic doctrine, and that violently twisted to the magisterium of human reason, is most ineptly ascribed to Philosophical Principles. But then, those very things which they meditated concerning the threefold principle or GOD, fight diametrically against the doctrine of the Holy Spirit. For they established three separate GODS, such as are three Individuals of the same species: but they did not acknowledge one in number, and the same essence of the Three ὑποστάσεων: Which is most clearly evident especially from Mercury's Pimander. For which reason Cyril, in book 1 against Julian, most rightly writes that they invented a composition and division in the divine persons: Whence afterwards the heresies of the Manichaeans and Arians sprouted. So far, therefore, is it from the case that these speculations of the Philosophers support those excessive preachers of Metaphysics even in the slightest: that they rather scatter the seeds of the foulest heresies, and are contradictorily opposed to our most sacred Theology. But to pass over the Philosophers and move on to the Scholastic Doctors, neither did these always enter upon the truth with a straight foot regarding the proposed question. The Master of Sentences, book 1, dist. 3, ch. 6, argues at length, How the trace of the Trinity appears in Creatures, and he urges certain similarities produced from Augustine in such a way that he writes eloquently that a clear and manifest knowledge of so great a mystery can be sought from them:

clearly sufficient. Although we do not deny that Augustine, in those entire fifteen books which he wrote on the Trinity, and especially from the sixth book up to the last, recites various images of the Trinity: yet we simply deny that it was done by him for this end which Lombard assigns, namely, that he might show that the Philosophers saw the truth of the Trinity as if through a shadow and from afar: even though they failed in the contemplation of it. For first, Augustine himself, in book 15 on the Trinity, ch. 7, expressly confesses that those similarities or images are most dissimilar from the Trinity itself: and in ch. 13 he says that it is sought altogether in vain, images of an incomprehensible thing in created things. Then, Augustine nowhere affirms that the images brought forward can impart any knowledge of the Trinity to Gentiles or Ethnic Philosophers: but he intended their use to be only among those who have already learned this doctrine from the Word of GOD: so that this mystery might become known to them all the more clearly: as is evident from book 15 on the Trinity, ch. 3. Now, however, Lombard draws a very poor conclusion from the pious and faithful to the unfaithful or Gentiles. These things being thus established, we conclude with Thomas against the Master, that it is impossible to arrive at the knowledge of the divine Essence through natural reason. Which assertion is supported by that of the Savior, Matt. 11:27: No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him.
