And John 1:18: No one has ever seen GOD; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him. And it is worth noting what Plato betrayed concerning such images or similarities, namely, that they have the greatest power for deceiving: writing thus in the Phaedrus: Δεῖ ἄρα τὸν μέλλοντα ἀπατήσειν μὲν ἄλλον, ἀυτὸν δὲ μὴ ἀπατήσεσθαι, τὴν ὁμοιότητα τῶν ὄντων, καὶ ἀνομοιότητα ἀκριβῶς διδέναι. Δῆλον γδ ὡς τὸ πάθος τῆς ἀπάτης, δι ὁμοιοτήτων τινῶν εἰσεῤῥύη: that is: It is necessary, therefore, that he who wishes to deceive another, but not be deceived himself, should perfectly know and discern the similarity and dissimilarity of all things. For it is certain that error and deception flow into minds especially through similarities. See the Response of Schegkius to the booklet of the Anonymous interpreter, etc., page 34.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO I.

Quid sit DEUS ratione essentiæ, nullâ ratione, vel ex Lumine Naturæ, vel ex principijs sive rationibus Philosophicis, ne quidem ex minimâ particulâ, disci aut cognosci potest.

Ἔκθεσις.

COnsiderat Thesis hæc nostra, Notitiam DEI, non generalem & confusam illam, quæ tùm ex creatione, tùm ex miranda gubernatione rerum conditarum, aliquatenùs colligit ἀΐδιον δύναμιν Θεῦ, Rom 1, 20. sed specialem & discretam, quæ quid sit DEUS, vel, ut si ita loqui fas sit, Qualis ipse sit, ratione essentiæ, ex solo Verbo DEI revelato definit. Ubi omnis Philosophia & ratio humana planè conticescit: usque adeò ut si quicquam scientiæ hac in parte sibi ea arroget: statim limites suæ professionis transiliat. Quam in sententiam rectè omninò pronunciavit Thomas parte prima quæst. 32. Dupliciter fidei derogat, qui Unitatem Essentiæ divinæ & Trinitatem personarum, naturali ratione probare nititur: 1. Quia Fides est de invisibilibus, quæ rationem humanam superant. 2. quia hac ratione exponit ludibrio ipsam fidem Christianam. Objiciunt hodie nonnulli autoritatem Platonis & Mercurij Trismegisti, quorum ille Epistola 2 ad Dionem primi, secundi, & tertij principij sive DEI meminerit: Hic vero in Pimandro, sectione prima, de Mente, Verbo & spiritu diserte disputet. Et sane horum autoritate freti aliqui, Articulos fidei ex principijs Philosophicis aliquatenus erui posse autumant: imo eo usque progrediuntur, ut Theologiam & Metaphysicam Aristotelis, scientias esse subordinatas, scribere haud vereantur. Verum multis modis hæc ipsorum collectio, vana deprehenditur.

Primum enim quæ Mercurius Trismegistus & Plato de trino Principio tradiderunt, neq; ex doctrina Metaphysica, neque ex alijs principijs Philosophicis extruxerunt: sed partim ex ipsa lectione Mosis & Prophetarum: partim ex eorum institutione habuerunt, qui temporibus Prophetarum vixerunt, ex eorundemque concionibus aliquid de Mysterio isto Trinitatis perceperunt. Refert Marsilius Ficinus Florentinus ex Augustino. Eo tempore, quo Moses in Ægypto versatus est, floruisse Atlantem Astrologum, Promethei Physici fratrem, ac avum maternum Mercurij, cujus nepos fuerit Mercurius Trismegistus: ideo sic dictus, quia non Philosophus modo summus, sed & Sacerdos Ægyptius, & Rex Maximus extiterit. Jam vero Religionem Ægyptiorum ex gentilitia & Judaica mixtam & conflatam quasi fuisse, tum ex alijs Scriptoribus, tum vero etiam ex libello Jamblichi de Mysterijs Ægyptiorum, Chaldæorum & Assyriorum, liquidissime constat. Sic de Platone commemorant historici, quod ex Italia in Ægyptum profectus sit, ut ibi non modo Gymnosophistas audiret, sed & libros Mosis legeret. Sic ergo, quod Philosophi isti ex doctrina Mosaica & Prophetarum, eaq; ad humanæ rationis magisterium violenter detorta, hauserunt, ineptissime Principijs Philosophicis adscribitur. Deinde vero illa ipsa, quæ de trino principio sive DEO meditati sunt, cum doctrina Spiritus Sancti e diametro pugnant. Constituerunt enim tres DEOS separatos, qualia sunt tria ejusdem speciei Individua:non autem unam numero, & eandem Trium ὑποστάσεων essentiam agnoverunt: Id quod ex Mercurij cumprimis Pimandro liquidissime patet. Quam ob causam rectissime Cyrillus lib. 1. contra Julianum, Συνθεσιν & διασιν in personis divinis illos finxisse scribit: Unde postmodum Manichæorum & Arianorum hæreses pullularunt. Tantum ergo abest, ut hæ Philosophorum speculationes nimijs illis Metaphysicæ prædicatoribus vel tantillum patrocinentur: ut potius teterrimarum hæreseon semina spargant, & sacratissimæ nostræ Theologiæ contradictorie sint oppositæ. Sed ut missis Philosophis ad Doctores Scholasticos transeam9, neq; hi semper circa propositum ζήτημα recto pede ad veritatem sunt ingressi. Magister sententiarum lib 1.dist. 3. c. 6. prolixe disputat, Quomodo in Creaturis appareat Trinitatis vestigium, & productas quasdam ex Augustino similitudines ita urget, ut ex illis præclaram & perspicuam tanti mysterij notitiam peti posse, diserte scribat:

planè sufficientem. Etsi verò non diffitemur Augustinum totis illis libris quindecim, quos de Trinitate scripsit, cumprimis verò à libro Sexto usq́; ad ultimum varias Trinitatis imagines recitare: simpliciter tamen negamus, hoc fine ab eo id factum esse, quem Lombardus assignat, nempè ut ostenderet, Philosophos quasi per umbram, & de longinquo vidisse veritatem Trinitatis: licet in ejus contuitu defecerint. Primùm enim ipse Augustinus lib. 15. de Trinitat. cap. 7. disertè fatetur, Similitudines sive imagines illas, ab ipsâ Trinitate esse dißimilimas: & cap. 13. frustrà omninò quæri ait, incomprehensibilis rei imagines in rebus creatis. Deindè allatas imagines gentilibus aut Philosophis Ethnicis, aliquid cognitionis de Trinitate impertire posse, nuspiam affirmat Augustinus: sed earum usum aliquem apud eos tantùm esse voluit, qui jam modò ex Verbo DEI doctrinam istam didicerunt: ut tantò dilucidius hoc mysterium ipsis innotesceret: uti patet ex lib. 15 de Trin. cap. 3. Jam verò à pijs & fidelibus ad infideles sive Gentiles pessimè colligit Lombardus. Quibus ita constitutis, concludimus cum Thoma contra Magistrum, Impossibile esse per rationem naturalem ad notitiam divinæ Essentiæ pervenire. Cui assertioni suffragatur illud Servatoris Matth. 11, 27. Nemo novit Filium nisi Pater, & nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius, & cui voluerit Filius revelare. & Joh. 1, 18. DEUM nemo vidit unquam, unigenitus Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit. Et notationem meretur, quod Plato de ejusmodi imaginibus sive similitudinibus prodidit, maximam nimirùm ad decipiendum vim eas habere: Sic scribens in Phædro: Δεῖ ἄρα τὸν μέλλοντα ἀπατήσειν μὲν ἄλλον, ἀυτὸν δὲ μὴ ἀπατήσεσθαι, τὴν ὁμοιότητα τῶν ὄντων, καὶ ἀνομοιότητα ἀκριβῶς διδέναι. Δῆλον γδ ὡς τὸ πάθος τῆς ἀπάτης, δι ὁμοιοτήτων τινῶν εἰσεῤῥύη: hoc est: Oportet imagò, ut is, qui velit alium decipere, ipse autem non decipi, similitudinem & dissimilitudinem omnium rerum, agnoscat perfectè & discernat. Constat enim, quod error & deceptio, præsertim in animos influat per similitudines. Vide Responsum Schegkii ad libellum Anonymi interpretis &c. pag. 34.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition II

PROPOSITION II.

GOD is a spiritual, intelligent, eternal, truthful, good, pure, just, merciful, most free essence of immense power and wisdom: the eternal Father, who begat his Son, his image, from eternity, and the Son, the co-eternal image of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son.

Ἔκθεσις.

WHETHER God can be defined has been doubted not only by Gentile philosophers, but also by Christians, and indeed even by certain theologians, with most descending into the negative. The principal causes of doubting were these: 1. Q-

I. Every definition is of finite things, or as Athanasius speaks in his treatise on Definitions, every definition is of boundaries. But GOD is infinite. Therefore, he does not fall under a definition.

II. Nothing infinite falls under the categories. Therefore, neither does GOD. Now, whatever is in the class of Transcendentals: no reason can be found for a more sublime Genus of it, and indeed such a Genus, which is predicated univocally and equally of the species subject to it.

III. Of whatever thing a certain Genus cannot be predicated: of the same, much less can a genuine and proper difference be predicated: that is, a Definition cannot be given of it. But a certain Genus cannot be predicated of GOD. Therefore, neither can genuine differences and properties be predicated, and indeed much less so: and consequently, no definition of GOD can be given.

However, to speak candidly what seems to us to be the case, these and other similar arguments are not of such weight and moment among us that we should allow ourselves to be imposed upon by Logicians in this matter. We readily grant that for them, while they keep themselves within the bounds of their Science, it is absolutely impossible to define GOD. But since, as Aristotle defines it, every definition is λόγος, ὁ τὸ ἦν εἶναι δηλῶν: a speech which explains what a thing is: we are most firmly persuaded that a definition of GOD can certainly be given. For unless this is conceded, it would follow that it cannot be certain to us in this life what GOD is, which would be prodigiously absurd. Now, this very thing can be known from no other source than the definition of GOD. They object: If a Definition of GOD can be given, then surely his logical Genus can be given. But the consequence is denied. For because it is established from logical doctrine that the Genus of any definition must be sought from that Category to which the Defined thing itself, or the subject to be defined, belongs: and since they themselves admit that GOD cannot be referred to any category: then surely it is elicited from that only that GOD cannot be logically defined: which we again readily concede to them. But whether, on that account, no certain and perfect definition of GOD, revealed from the Word of GOD, can be given: that we certainly neither wish nor are able to grant them. For definitions are not only of things that are ζητητῶν, or those which are subject to Categories: but also of those that are πισῶν, namely, those things which are of Faith. Where the true and proper Genus must be sought also from that Science to which the Subject uniquely belongs: so that Logic can arrogate to itself no more right in this matter than it has over GOD himself. Such a perfect Definition is that Philippean one which our second proposition recites, with perfection understood as that which can be obtained by us in this life from the revealed Word of GOD and which can suffice for salvation. It consists, however, of Genus and specific Difference. The word Essence holds the place of the Genus. Where, however, it is not at all necessary that this Genus be predicated univocally both of GOD and of other species subject to it. For this method of predication is proper only to a logical Genus: and it clearly expires in the mysteries of faith: in which a Genus is given that pertains properly and primarily to only one subject. But if by chance this seems to anyone absurd and to imply an opposition in the adjective: I answer. This is an absurdity of Reason only: not, however, of Faith. All other things which follow the Genus sustain the role of the specific Difference: so that we do not fear to name this Definition Essential. Regarding the Genus, namely the word Essence, two things especially come to be noted concerning it: 1. That GOD himself produced this Genus of the definition of GOD, Exod. 3, 14. For to Moses asking who GOD was, and what his name was, GOD replied: I am who I am: And you shall say to the sons of Israel: HE WHO IS, has sent me to you. Whence that most holy name, communicable to no Creature, JEHOVAH, took its origin, and began to be in use among the faithful: which was previously clearly unknown to them, as GOD himself attests in Exod. 6, 3. I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, as God Almighty: and by my name Jehovah I was not known to them. Next, that also deserves observation, that the word Essence, when it is predicated of GOD, obtains a far different meaning than it is accustomed to have otherwise. For in common and daily usage of speaking, the word Essence is something common to all substances, not existing by itself, but understood only by thought or conception. However, when it is predicated of GOD, it denotes the divine Essence truly existing and communicable to no Creature: so indeed that this word is predicated properly of GOD alone: but of men and other creatures, only analogically and consequently. For GOD alone exists properly, by himself and from himself; but all other created things, even if they do subsist, yet they do not exist from themselves, but by the power and virtue of GOD, who sustains them, lest they perish and be reduced to nothing: so that they ought to be named sustained things rather than existing things. In which respect the Holy Fathers most rightly named GOD ὑπερέσιον, that is, existing in a way that differs in its whole kind from the remaining creatures. Likewise ἀνέσιον, namely with respect to that existence in which creatures participate. Although the word Essence, thus taken of GOD, is absolutely incommunicable with regard to creatures: yet it is meanwhile communicable to the remaining persons of the divinity; but in such a way that, as D. Augustine rightly admonishes, it is not predicated of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as a Genus of species; or as a species of individuals; or as a whole of parts; but in some other ineffable and incomprehensible way; which is proper to the unity of essence in the Trinity.

The rest, which are placed in this Philippean Definition, since they occur explained everywhere in most Methodical books, and since our Author also treats them quite prolixly, we omit by design in this place. But before I depart from here, some more abstruse questions must be explained. For first it is asked in this place: Can any composition be given in GOD? But it is answered simply in the Negative. For 1. Every composition is either of parts of quantity: or it is of universals and particulars, or finally it is of a subject and Accidents. But none of these falls into GOD. Therefore.

For in the first place there is no diversity of parts in GOD, and consequently neither of matter and

Latin:

PROPOSITIO II.

DEUS est essentia Spiritualis, intelligens, æterna, verax, bona, pura, justa, misericors, liberrima, immensæ potentiæ & sapientiæ: Pater æternus, qui Filium imaginem suam ab æterno genuit, & Filius imago Patris coæterna, & Spiritus Sanctus procedens à Patre & Filio.

Ἔκθεσις.

AN Deus definiri possit, non à Philosophis modò gentilibus: sed & à Christianis, imò à quibus dam etiam Theologis dubitatum fuit: in negantem plerisq́; descendentibus. Causæ dubitandi præcipuæ erant hæ: 1. Q-

I. Omnis definitio est rerum finitarum, vel ut Athanafius tractatu de Definitionibus loquitur, Omnis definitio est finitionum. Atqui DEUS est infinitus. Ergò sub definitionem non cadit.

II. Nullum infinitum cadit sub prædicamenta. Ergò nec DEUS. Jam quicquid est in classe Transcendentium: de eo Genus sublimius inveniri nulla ratione potest, & quidem tale Genus, quod de subjectis sibi speciebus συνωνύμως & ex æquo prædicetur.

III. De quocunq́ Genus certum prædicari non potest: de eodem multò minùs genuina differentia & propria prædicari possunt: hoc est, de eo Definitio dari nequit. Atqui de DEO Genus certum prædicari non potest. Ergò nec, & quidem multò minùs genuinæ differentiæ & propria prædicari possunt: & per Consequens DEI definitio dari nulla potest.

Cæterùm, ut ingenuè quod nobis videtur, dicamus, rationes istæ & consimiles aliæ apud nos non tanti sunt ponderis & momenti, ut à Logicis hac in parte nobis imponi patiamur. Ipsis quidem intra terminos suæ Scientiæ sese continentibus, impossibile prorsus esse, Definire DEUM, ultrò largimur. Verùm cum definiente Aristotele, Omnis definitio sit λόγος, ὁ τὸ ἦν εἶναι δηλῶν: Oratio, quæ quid res sit explicat: Certè DEI definitionem dari posse, habemus persuasissimum. Nisi enim hoc concedatur: Consequens fuerit, Nobis hac in vita constare non posse, Quid sit DEUS, id quod prodigiosè absurdum fuerit. Jam verò hoc ipsum non aliundè, quàm ex definitione DEI, innotescere potest. Objiciunt illi: Si dari potest DEI Definitio: Utiq́, dari poterit Genus ipsius logicum. Sed negatur consequentia. Quia enim ex doctrina Logica constat, cujuslibet definitionis Genus, ex ea Categoria petendū esse, ad quam pertinet ipsum Definitum, sive subjectum definiendum: Jam verò ipsimet fatentur ad nullū prædicamentum DEUM referri posse: utiq́, illud indè tantùm elicitur, DEUM Logicè definiri non posse: id quod ipsis iterum facilè concedimus. Num verò proptereà nulla certa, & ex Verbo DEI patefacto, perfecta DEI definitio dari queat: illud sanè ipsis largiri nec volumus nec possumus. Definitiones enim non tantùm sunt rerum ζητητῶν, sive earum, quæ Categorijs subsunt: sed & τῶν πισῶν, earum nimirùm rerum, quæ sunt Fidei. Ubi Genus verum ac proprium ex ea etiam Scientia petendum est, ad quam Subjectum unicè pertinet: ut haud plus Juris hac in parte sibi arrogare possit Logica, quàm in DEUM ipsum habet. Talis perfecta Definitio est Philippea illa, quam propositio nostra secunda recitat, perfectione ea intellecta, quæ ex Verbo DEI revelato nobis hac in vita obtingere, & ad salutem sufficere potest. Constat verò ea Genere & Differentia specifica. Genus locum obtinet vocabulum Essentiæ. Ubi tamen haud necessum est, ut Genus istud συνωνύμως tùm de DEO, tùm de alijs sibi subjectis Speciebus, prædicetur. Nam hæc prædicandi ratio, duntaxat Logici Generis est propria: & in mysterijs fidei planè expirat: In quibus datur Genus, uni tantùm subjecto propriè & πρώτως competens. Quod si fortè hoc absurdum cuipiam, & oppositum rein adjecto implicare videatur: Respondeo. Absurdum hoc tantùm Rationis esse: non autem Fidei. Differentia specifica vicem sustinent cætera omnia, quæ Genus subsequuntur: ita ut Definitionem hanc Essentialem nominare haud vereamur. Quoad Genus, nempè vocabulum Essentiæ duo potissimùm circa illud notanda veniunt: 1. Genus hoc definitionis DEI, ipsum DEUM de se prodidisse, Exod. 3, 14. Mosi enim roganti, quis esset DEUS, & Quodnam ipsi nomen, Respondit DEUS: Ego sum qui sum: Et dices filiis Israel: QUI EST, misit me ad vos. Unde sanctissimum illud, nulliq; Creaturæ communicabile nomen JEHOVAH originem sumpsit, & apud fideles in usu esse cœpit: quod priùs illis erat planè incognitum, sic attestante DEO ipso Exod. 6, 3. Ego apparui Abraham, Isaac & Jacob, Beel, Schaddai, in DEO omnipotente: & in nomine Jehovah non sum cognitu' illis. Deinde & illud observationem meretur, quod vox Essentia, quando de DEO prædicatur, longè aliam significationem sortiatur, quàm alioqui obtinere solet. Nã in communi & quotidiano usu loquendi, vox Essentia, est quiddam omnibus substantiis κοινό- τητὸν per se non existens, sed νοήσει tantùm sive cogitatione intellectum. Cœterùm de DEO, quando prædicatur, ibi notat divinam Essentiam reverà existentem & nulli Creaturæ communicabilem: ita quidem ut vox hæc de solo DEO propriè prædicetur: de hominibus verò & creaturis alijs, analogicè tantùm & ἑπομένως. Solus enim DEUS propriè, per se & ex seipso existit; Cætera verò creata omnia, etsi subsistunt etiam, tamen non ex se existunt, sed potestate atque virtute DEI, qui ea sustentat, ne intereant & in nihilum redigantur: ita ut sustentata potiùs, quàm existentia nominari debeant. Quo respectu Sancti Patres rectissimè DEUM nominarunt ὑπερέσιον, hoc est, existentem ratione quadam toto genere à reliquis creaturis distante. Item ἀνέσιον, respectu nimirùm illius existentiæ, quâ creaturæ participant. Quanquam verò Essentiæ vox sic de DEO accepta, prorsus incommunicabilis est, quoad creaturas: interim tamen communicabilis est reliquis personis divinitatis; sed ita, ut, quemadmodum rectè admonet D. Augustinus, non prædicetur de Patre, Filio, & Spiritu Sancto, tanquam Genus de Speciebus; Vel ut species de individuis; vel ut totum de partibus; sed alio quodam ineffabili & incomprehensibili modo; qui unitatis essentiæ Trinitate, est proprius.

Cœtera, quæ in Definitione hâc Philippea ponuntur, cùm in plerisq; libellis Methodicis passim explicata occurrant, quin Autor etiam noster satis prolixè ea pertractet, studio hoc loco prætermittimus. Priusquam verò hinc abeam9, abstrusiores nonnullæ quæstiones explicandæ veniunt. Primùm enim quæritur hoc loco: An ulla in DEO dari possit compositio? Sed respondetur simpliciter Negativè. Nam 1. Omnis compositio vel est partium quantitatis: vel est universaliũ & particularium, vel deniq; est subjecti Accidentium. Sed nulla harum in DEUM cadit. Ergò.

Primùm enim in DEO non est partium diversitas, & per Consequens nequè materiæ &


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Whether Accidents fall into GOD

form combination or union: since this pertains only to corporeal creatures. But GOD is Spirit. Therefore, that first mode of composition does not fit Him. Furthermore, in GOD all things are of singularity: as Isaiah 42:8 expressly protests that He does not communicate His nature or essence with anyone: saying, I am Jehovah: This is my name: and my glory I will not give to another. Therefore, the conjunction of Universal and particular Nature finds no place in GOD. Finally, the composition of Essence and Accidents likewise does not fall into GOD. For those things which in Angels are concreated Qualities: or in us are mutable qualities and accidents: those in GOD are essential: as will be shown presently in the third and final Question. Therefore, II. The argument of our Negative can be such: Every composite is posterior to its component parts: and has a cause composing it prior to itself. But God, being eternal, can have nothing prior to Himself: and consequently not even a cause, upon which He might depend. III. In every composition there is Act and potency. But potency does not fall into GOD, being that He is perpetual Act, that is, most pure and most simple. Therefore, it is necessary that He be entirely devoid of composition.

Furthermore, it is asked at this point, Whether GOD is the same as Essence: and Whether in GOD Being and Essence are the same: Likewise, Whether in GOD Essence and Existence differ? The Scholastic Doctors, and especially Thomas in part 1, art. 3, Question 3, teaches that a twofold sense can be given to this Question: For either, he says, by Essence is understood a quiddity in the abstract: and then the sense is, Whether Deity is distinguished from its concrete, which is GOD: or by essence is understood the common Nature in the concrete, when indeed that is compared to its individual: and then the sense is; Whether this GOD adds something over and above GOD.

But there is no need for this subtlety of the Scholastics. For it is clear from those things which we have hitherto disputed concerning the Essence of GOD, what can and ought to be answered to this Question, in whatever way it is finally accepted or formulated. For although in all other creatures, Essence is one thing, and Being is another; since these two differ as Abstract and concrete: likewise in Creatures Essence is one thing, and Existence is another: In GOD, however, that diversity entirely expires. Because GOD is most pure act, most simple, and entirely devoid of all composition: certainly in Him also, Essence is the same as Being: Essence is also the same as Existence, so that it is not permitted to think of any discrepancy whatsoever. Concerning which matter Thomas disputes not ineptly in the place already cited. A certain conclusion, he says, is that GOD is not distinguished from His nature or Essence. For in the concept of GOD, it is essentially included that He is this GOD: Since singularity is the ultimate perfection; therefore it is necessarily included in the essential concept of GOD. Hence it is that there cannot be multiple divine Essences: For that which is Essentially This singular, cannot be multiplied: Indeed, not only in reality are GOD and this GOD not distinguished: But neither according to concept. For unless this GOD is conceived, GOD is not conceived. This is Thomas.

Finally, it is asked at this point, Whether Accidents fall into GOD? or which is the same, Whether those Attributes, which our Definition assigns to GOD, are predicated of GOD as Accidents?

To this Question our Author rightly answers Negatively: Let us know, he says, that these mighty works, which we attribute to GOD, are not in Him Accidents, as in man or Angel, Wisdom, Justice, Goodness are accidents and mutable things: But just as the power of GOD is not to be discerned from Essence, nor is it another thing: So there are not other things, the Wisdom, Truth, Justice, Goodness of GOD: but they are the essence itself, which is a living quiddity subsisting through itself, intelligent, eternal, Omnipotent, good, just.

Thus far Philip, whose decision constitutes a clear distinction, not only between the habits of mighty works, which are predicated both of GOD and of men: but also between a most diverse manner of predicating. In created things, the habits of mighty works differ primarily from the Essence of the subject. For an Angel is one thing by reason of Essence; another is the perfection already concreated to him: A man is one thing, by reason of subject or his Nature: but another is the goodness, justice, etc., which is in him. But in GOD, Essence and those mighty works are a most simple quiddity, the same, and are mutually convertible with one another. Furthermore, in creatures those mighty works are either separable from their Subjects, or at least suffer intension and remission, that is, more and less, in the same. In GOD, however, the habits of those mighty works are neither separable from the divine Essence: nor did they finally accrue to the same Essence already existing; nor do they in any way admit of change according to more and less in God.

Finally, the habits of virtues are predicated of creatures only paronymously, that is, concretely: but of GOD, not only are the paronyms of these virtues predicated in concrete expressions: but the abstract species themselves are also predicated: so that it is equally permissible to say, GOD is goodness itself, Justice, Truth, &c., just as it is permissible to say, GOD is good, Just, truthful. Therefore, these virtues are deservedly said to be essential in GOD: and are most correctly predicated of Him substantially.

But concerning the resolution of this Question, that also must be most diligently observed, which we read has been observed even by some Scholastics: namely, that it is one thing for something to inhere in GOD accidentally: but another thing for something to be predicated of GOD accidentally: or which is the same thing: that a distinction must be made between a predicamental Accident and a predicable one. For a predicable Accident does not immediately imply a predicamental Accident: especially in those predicables which are said by extrinsic denomination: since an extrinsic denomination posits nothing in the thing, nor is it predicated of it through any change of the thing itself, but through the change of another thing constituted outside the thing: therefore it neither presupposes Composition, nor requires potency in the thing denominated: as a predicamental accident does. For example: The Creation of this universe is predicated of GOD: where something is predicated of GOD accidentally: although meanwhile the very force and power by which God created heaven and earth is not Accidental in GOD, but simply Essential. Thus, He is said by Moses to be seen, by the faithful to be loved, by the pious to be adored: where accidents are predicated of GOD; yet meanwhile no accident inheres in Him: as Augustine excellently argues in book 5 of the Trinity, chapter 10. And as the Scholastics infer: Real accidents are denied of GOD: but not accidental predicates.

Latin:

formæ combinatio sive unio : siquidem hæc tantùm Creaturis corporeis competit. Atqui DEUS est Spiritus. E. primus ille compositionis modus in ipsum non quadrat. Deindè, in DEO omnia sunt singularitatis: ut disertè protestetur Jes. 42. 8. se naturâ aut essentiam suâ cum nemine communicare: Ego, inquiens, Jehovah sum: Hoc nomen meum: & gloriā meā alteri non dabo. Ergò Naturæ Universalis & particularis conjunctio; locum in DEO non invenit. Tandé compositio Essentiæ & Accidentium in DEUM itidé non cadit. Quæ n. in Angelis sunt Qualitates concreatæ: vel in nobis sunt qualitates mutabiles & accidētia: ea in DEO sunt essētialia: ut mox ostendetur Quæst: tertia & postrema. E. II. Argumentū nostræ Negativæ tale esse potest: Omne compositū posteriꝰ est partibꝰ suis cōponentibꝰ: & habet causam componentē seipso priorē. Atqui Deus, quippè æternus, nihil seipso priꝰ habere potest: ac per consequens nec causā quidē, à qua dependeat. III. In omni compositione Actus est & potentia. Atqui potentia non cadit in DEUM, quippè qui est Actus perpetuus, iod; purissimus & simplicissimus. Ergò compositionis planè expers sit, necesse est.

Porrò quæritur hoc loco, An idem sit DEUS, quod Essentia: & An in DEO idem sit Esse & Essentia: Item, An in DEO differant Essentia & Existentia? Doctores Scholastici, & cumprimis Thomas part. 1. art. 3. Quæst. 3. tradit, geminum dari posse sensum Quæstionis hujus: Vel enim, inquit, per Essentiam accipitur quidduas in abstracto: & tunc est sensus, Num Deitas distinguatur, à suo concreto, quod est DEUS: vel per essentiam intelligitur Natura communis in concreto, quando nimirùm illa cōparatur ad suum individuum: & tunc sensus est; Utrum hic DEUS addat aliquid supra DEUM.

Verùm subtilitate hac Scholasticorum minimè est opus. Patet enim ex ijs, quæ hactenus de Essentia DEI disputavimus, quid ad Quæstionem hanc responderi possit & debeat, quocunque tandem modo ea accipiatur, vel informetur. Etsi enim in creaturis reliquis omnibus, aliud est Essentia, aliud Ens; quippè quæ duo differunt ut Abstractum & concretum : aliud item in Creaturis est Essentia, aliud verò Existentia : In DEO tamen diversitas ista planè expirat. Quia enim DEUS est actus purissimus, simplicissimus, omnisque compositionis planè expers : utique in ipso etiam, idem est Essentia, quod Ens : idem etiam est Essentia, quod Existentia, ut nihil quicquam discrepantiæ vel cogitare fas sit. Qua de re haud ineptè disputat Thomas loco jā citato. Certa, inquiens, est conclusio, DEUM non distingvi à sua natura sive Essentia. Nam in conceptu DEI, essentialiter includitur, quod sit hic DEUS: Siquidem singularitas est ultima perfectio; ideò necessariò includitur in conceptu essentiali DEI. Hinc est, quod plures Essentiæ divinæ esse non possunt: Nā id quod est Essentialiter Hoc singulare, non potest plurificari : Imò, non tantùm reipsa DEUS, & hic DEUS non distingvuntur : Sed neque secundum conceptum. Nisi enim concipiatur hic DEUS, non concipitur DEUS. Hæc Thomas.

Tandem quæritur hoc loco, An in DEUM cadant Accidentia? vel quod idem est, An Attributa illa, quæ Definitio nostra DEO assignat, prædicentur de DEO, ut Accidentia?

Ad quã Quæstioné rectè respondet Autor noster Negativè: Sciamus, inquiens, has virtutes, quas DEO tribuimq, in ipso nō esse Accidentia, ut in homine seu Angelo, Sapientia, Justitia, Bonitas sunt accidentia & res mutabiles: Sed sicut potētia DEI nō discernēda est ab Essentia, nec aliud est: Sic nō sint aliæ res, Sapientia, Veritas, Justitia, Bōitas DEI: sed sunt ipsa essentia, quæ est quiddã vivum per se subsistens, intelligens, æternum, Omnipotens, bonum, justum.

Hactenus Philippus, cujus decisio luculentum constituit discrimen, non modò inter habitus virtutum, qui prædicantur & de DEO, & de hominibus: sed etiã inter diversissimã prædicandi rationē. In rebus creatis virtutū habitus primū differunt ab Essentia subjecti. Aliud n. est Angelus ratione Essentiæ; aliud concreata já ipsi perfectio: Aliud homo, ratione subjecti sive Naturæ suæ: aliud verò, quæ ipsi inest bonitas, justitia &c. Cæterù in DEO Essentia & virtutes illæ, sunt quiddã simplicissimum ταυτό, & inter se mutuò convertuntur. Deindè in creaturis virtutes illæ vel à Subjectis suis sunt separabiles, vel intensionem saltē ac remissioné, hoc est, magis & min9, in ijsdem patiuntur. In DEO verò virtutū istarū habitus, neq; sunt separabiles ab Essentia divina: neq; Essentiæ eidem priùs existenti demum accesserunt; neque mutationem secundum magis & minus ullo modo in Deo admittunt.

Tandem virtutum habitus prædicantur de creaturis παρωνύμως tantùm, hoc est, Concretive: De DEO verò, non παρώνυμα tantum virtutum istarum, in concretis locutionibus: sed ipsæ etiam abstractæ species prædicantur: ut æquè liceat dicere, DEUS est ipsissima bonitas, Justitia, Veritas, &c. atque dicere licitum est, DEUS est bonus, Justus, verax. Essentiales proindè in DEO virtutes istę meritò esse dicuntur: deque eo substantialiter rectissimè prædicantur.

Est verò circa Quæstionis hujus enodationem, & illud diligentissimè observandū, quòd à nonnullis etiam Scholasticis observatum fuisse, legimus: nempe, Aliud esse, aliquid accidentaliter inhærere DEO: aliud verò, aliquid accidentaliter prædicari de DEO: vel quod idem est: distingvendum esse inter Accidens predicamentale & prædicabile. Nam prædicabile Accidens, non statim subinfert Accidens prædicamentale: in illis præfertim prædicabilibus: quæ dicuntur per denominationem extrinsecam: Siquidem denominatio extrinseca nihil ponit in re, neque prędicatur de ea, per aliquam ipsius mutationem, sed per mutationem alterius extra rem constituti: ideò neque præsupponit Compositionem, neq; requirit potentiam in re denominata: quemadmodum accidens prædicamentale. Exempli gratiâ: De DEO prædicatur Creatio hujus universi: ubi aliquid accidentaliter de DEO prædicatur: licet interim ipsa vis atque potentia, quâ Deus creavit cœlum & terram, in DEO non sit Accidentalis, sed simpliciter Essentialis. Sic DEO dicitur à Mose visus, à fidelibus amatus, à piis adoratus: ubi accidentia prædicantur de DEO; nulla tamen interim accidente ipsi inhærente: uti præclarè disputat August. lib. 5. de Trin. c. 10. Et uti Scholastici inferunt: Negatur de DEO accidentia realia: sed non prædicata accidentalia.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition I. God is one, by a singular and most absolute unity: which is the Unity of Number and Essence

Moreover, human reason objects two things in particular at this point: 1. If the virtues in GOD are something most simple, ταυτό, one and the same with the very Essence of GOD: It would follow that those individual attributes of the virtues, which are predicated of GOD, are συνώνυμα: and consequently, that the Justice of GOD is the Mercy of GOD: that the truth of GOD is the eternity of GOD, and so vice versa. But the latter is absurd. Therefore, the former is as well.

But it is most correctly answered that a fallacy of definition is being committed. For synonyms, as the Philosopher defines them, are those things which not only signify one and the same thing, but which also denote it according to one definition: συνώνυμα λέγεται, ὧν τότε ὄνομα κοινὸν καὶ ὁ κατὰ τὔνομα λόγος τῆς ὐσίας ὁ αὐτὸς. And as Damascene has it in chapter 32 of his Dialectics: Synonyms are those which agree with one another both in word and in definition. Now, however much those attributes of GOD, namely Goodness, Justice, Omnipotence, etc., denote one thing in GOD, namely the Essence: they do not, however, denote it under one definition or rationale: but under a diverse and manifold one, which even our intellect apprehends not by one, but by a manifold notion.

The other thing which is objected at this point is a philosophical axiom: Whatever is an Accident in one thing cannot be a substance in another. Therefore, the habits of the virtues, which are Accidental in Angels and men, can be Essential in GOD. But the argument fails by the fallacy of Ignoratio Elenchi, and ὡς δέ τό πη καὶ ἁπλῶς. For that cannot be a Substance in one thing which is an Accident in another, specifically when univocal predication has a place, that is, when both the name is common and the definition is also the same. Now, however, as was shown a little earlier, the attributes of those virtues are not predicated univocally of GOD and men: since the habits of those virtues are predicated of Angels and men only παρωνύμως: but of GOD they are predicated not only παρωνύμως, but also abstractively, so that the Essence of GOD is most simply convertible with the attributes themselves.

THE THIRD AND FINAL QUESTION,

Concerning the Unity of the divine Essence: and the Trinity of Persons.

PROPOSITION I.

GOD is one, with a singular and most absolute unity: which is the Unity of Number and Essence.

Ἔκθεσις.

Concerning this proposition, Philosophy also claims something for itself as a science. For it is accustomed to demonstrate by reasons drawn from nature that one first and highest principle of all things must be granted: among which that argument of Aristotle holds not the least place, by which, from the manifold motion of things, so that there may not be a progression to infinity, he necessarily establishes that there is only one first mover, by which all other things are moved. Related to this is that other argument, which the same Philosopher produced toward the end of the second book of the Metaphysics: showing that whatever is the cause for other things to exist, that in any given genus is the first, one, and highest. A good many arguments of this kind have been collected by Damascene in book 1 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 5; Augustine in his work On Faith to Peter; Justin the Philosopher and Martyr; Lactantius, and many others; and they have opposed them to the multitude of Gentile gods. Moreover, however firm those arguments drawn from reason may appear: they prove nothing more than that GOD is ONE: but in the meantime, that in which the whole mystery of this Article consists, namely that that ONE is at the same time, and indeed without any contradiction, Trine: they have not at all explained, nor could they even have done so. Therefore, having left this imperfect kind of proof to the Philosophers, we judge that other one to be more suitable for Christians, which the Holy Spirit has revealed in the sacred scriptures.

Now, Holy Scripture confirms the Unity of the divine essence in three ways in particular: 1. By simple affirmation; when it affirms that GOD is one: as in Deut. 6:4, Hear, O Israel, the Lord our GOD, the LORD is one. Eph. 4:6, There is one GOD, and Father of All. 1 Tim. 2:5, There is ONE GOD, one Mediator between GOD and men, etc. 1 John 5:7, There are three that bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit: and these three are one.

Then by simple negation, when he expressly denies that there are many Gods. And finally by exclusive enunciation, when he asserts that there is no one, and no other, besides one GOD: as Deut. 4, 35. Know that the Lord is GOD, and there is no other besides him. Deut. 32, 39. See that I am alone, and there is no other GOD besides me. Isa. 44, 6. Thus says the Lord: I am the first and the last, and besides me there is no GOD. Isa. 45, 5, 6, and 7. I am GOD, and no other. And v. 21. Is it not I the Lord: and there is no other GOD besides me. A just GOD and a savior there is none besides me. And v. 22. I am GOD and there is no other. 1 Cor. 8, 4. We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other GOD, except one: For although there are those who are called Gods, whether in heaven or on earth, just as there are many Gods and many Lords: Yet to us there is one GOD.

With these foundations of proofs thus laid, it is immediately accustomed to be asked, In what manner, or in what respect, is GOD said to be one? A question which indeed would be entirely unnecessary among the pious and faithful, as those who acquiesce with simple faith in the foundations of Scripture; were it not that partly the tricks of heretics, and partly the snares of the Devil, require a more accurate explanation of it. But it can be most correctly resolved, if by ἄρσιν or the removal of those modes of Unity which to this mystery do not are appropriate, so that one may finally arrive at the true mode of unity.

And in the beginning, indeed, certain things are said to be one in species. But this Unity does not apply to GOD: for those things which are One in this way are many in number, and at least are said to be One in a νόητῇ species: the cause of which Multitude philosophers say is matter. Wherefore, if the three persons of the Divinity were posited to be some One thing, by logical species, namely on account of the concretion of some matter: it would follow that there are three Gods in number: which is absurd; since everything material is mutable and finite: Furthermore, for this reason also, the persons of the Divinity cannot be one species; because the definition of GOD the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. But of those things whose species is one, their definition also ought to be one.

Next, certain things are said to be One in Genus. Which mode of Unity itself is also alien to this mystery. For those things which are One in Genus are not One in species and Definition on account of contrary differences. Whence it would follow, if GOD were One in this way, that the Father is GOD by one species and Essence; and the Son by another; and finally the Holy Spirit by another. Furthermore, those things which are One in Genus cannot have the same difference of perfection: just as indeed a Horse and a man are in a certain way One in Genus: but as regards the difference of perfection, they differ from each other as much as τὸ λογικὸν differs from the brute or ἀλόγῳ. But far be it that we should even imagine such a difference of perfection between the three persons of the Divinity. Therefore, neither can this mode of Unity, which is of Genus, have a place in this mystery.

There is also this, that these two species of Unity, of which we have already treated, since by them is signified νόημα καθόλε, that is, the Universal species, are by no means substance, or any part of the substance of things: but are merely certain substantial Reasons, which are certain Logical Accidents of our Mind, and not things subsisting by themselves.

Thirdly, certain things are said to be One by subject, or τῷ πάθει, that is, by affection. In which manner, if GOD were posited to be one; he would certainly be mutable: just as Sabellius and Servetus blasphemed that GOD is one τῷ πάθει, that is, by various dispensations.

Fourthly, those Modes of Unity are abhorrent from this mystery, according to which something is said to be One either by definition; or by that reason by which something is continuous. For as regards the former: not one, but another and clearly different definition of the Father is given, another of the Son, another of the Holy Spirit. But the latter mode of Unity is Accidental, and has mixed potentiality, which always argues an imperfection of the subject. Whence the continuous, however much it may be one in act: can nevertheless be divided, and is Many δυνάμει: Which far be it that we should even think of regarding the Unity of the divine Essence.

Fifthly: nor is that Mode of Unity sufficient in all respects, which is defined by the unity of will, consent, and concord. For although there is the highest and perpetual Consent and Concord between the three persons of the Divinity: yet the Unity of the divine Essence cannot be sufficiently demonstrated from it.

It remains, therefore, that we say GOD is One in NUMBER, and as some most simple and most absolute τό δέ τι, that is, as one singular Thing; or One Essence. Whence in the Schools of the Theologians this Term has long since obtained a place, that GOD should be said to be one in NUMBER and ESSENCE.

Latin:

Caeterùm duo potissimùm humana ratio hoc loco objicit: 1. Si virtutes in DEO sunt cum ipsa Essentia DEI quiddam simplicissimum ταυτό, unum & idem: Consequens fuerit, Singula illa virtutum attributa, quae de DEO enunciantur, esse συνώνυμα: ac per Consequens, Justitiam DEI, esse Misericordiam DEI: veritatem DEI esse aeternitatem DEI, & sic vice versa. At posterius hoc absurdum. Ergò & prius illud.

Sed rectissi nè respondetur, committi Sophisma definitionis. Nam Synonyma, definiente Philosopho, ea sunt, quae non modò rem unam eandemque significant, sed quae etiam secundum unam rationem notant: συνώνυμα λέγεται, ὧν τότε ὄνομα κοινὸν καὶ ὁ κατὰ τὔνομα λόγος τῆς ὐσίας ὁ αὐτὸς. Et ut Damascenus habet cap. 32. Dialecticae: Synonyma sunt, quae & voce & definitione inter se conveniunt. Jam verò quantumvis attributa illa DEI, nempe Bonitas, Justitia, Omnipotentia &c. Unam in DEO rem, nempe Essentiam notant: non tamen eam notant sub unâ ratione sive definitione: sed diversâ & multiplice, quam Intellectus etiam noster, non unâ, sed multiplice notione apprehendit.

Alterum, quod hoc loco objicitur, est axioma Philosophicum: Quicquid in uno est Accidens, id in alio non potest esse substantia. Ergò virtutum habitus, qui in Angelis, & hominibus sunt Ac cidentales, in DEO Essentiales esse possunt. Sed fallit Argumentum Sophismate Ignorationis Elenchi, & ὡς δέ τό πη καὶ ἁπλῶς. Tùm enim in uno non potest esse Substantia, quod in alio est Accidens, quando nimirùm praedicatio univoca locum habet, hoc est, quando & nomen est commune, & ratio etiam est eadem. Jam verò, uti paulò antè ostensum, attributa istarum virtutum de DEO & hominibus non praedicantur univocè: Siquidem de Angelis & hominibus virtutum istarum habitus, tantùm παρωνύμως praedicantur: de DEO verò non παρωνύμως tantùm, sed & abstractivè, ita ut Essentia DEI, cum ipsis attributis simplicissimè convertatur.

TERTIA ET POSTREMA QUAESTIO,

De Unitate Essentiae divinae: ac Personarum Trinitate.

PROPOSITIO I.

DEUS est unus, unitate singulari & absolutissima: quae est Unitas Numeri & Essentiae.

Ἔκθεσις.

CIrca hanc propositionem, Philosophia etiam Scientiae sibi aliquid vendicat. Unum enim primum & summum rerum omnium principium dandum esse, rationibus ex natura petitis, ea demonstrare solet: inter quas minimè postremum locum obtinet argumentum illud Aristotelis, quo ex multiplici motu rerum ne in infinitum progressio fiat, necessariò statuit, unum tantùm primum movens esse, à quo cætera omnia moveantur, Cui cognatum est illud alterum, quod idem Philosophus sub finem secundi Metaphysicorum prodidit: ostendens, Quicquid rebus aliis est causa: ut sint, id in quolibet genere esse primum, unum & summum. Cujus generis argumenta benè multa collegerunt Damascenus lib. 1. Orth fid c. 5. Augustinus de Fide ad Petrum: Justinus Philosophus & Martyr: Lactantius & alij complures: eaque multitudini DEOrum Gentilium opposuerunt. Cæterùm ut ut firma appareant argumenta ista ex ratione petita: nihil tamen magis probant, quàm DEUM UNUM esse: at interim id, in quo Articuli hujus mysterium omne consistit, nempè UNUM illud simul, & quidem sine ulla contradictione esse Trinum: minimè expeditum dederunt vel etiam dare potuerunt. Proindè Imperfecto hoc probationis genere Philosophis relicto, illud alterum Christianis magis convenire arbitramur, quod Spiritus Sanctus in sacris revelavit.

Tribus autem potissimùm modis Unitatem essentiæ divinæ Scriptura Sacra confirmat: 1. Simplici affirmatione; quando DEUM unum esse affirmat: ut Deut. 6, 4 Audi Israel Dominus DEUS noster, DEUS unus est. Eph. 4, 6. Unus est DEUS, & Pater Omnium. 1. Tim. 2, 5. UNUS est DEUS, Unus Mediator DEI & hominum &c. 1. Johan. 5, 7. Tres sunt qui testificantur in cœlo, Pater, Verbum, & Spiritus Sanctus: & hi tres unum sunt.

Deindè Simplici negatione, quando multos esse DEos disertè negat. Et tandem exclusivâ enunciatione, quando nullus, & non alius, præter unum DEUM esse asserit: ut Devt. 4, 35. Scias, quod Dominus est DEUS, & non est alius præter eum. Deut. 32, 39. Videte, quod ego sim solus, & non sit alius DEUS præter me Jes. 44, 6. Hæc dicit Dominus: Ego sum primus & novißimus, & præter me non est DEUS Jes. 45, 5. 6. & 7. Ego DEUS, & non alius. Et v. 21. Numquid non ego Dominus: & non est ultrà DEUS absque me. DEUS justus & salvans non est præter me. Et v. 22. Ego DEUS & non est alius. 1. Cor. 8, 4. Scimus, quod nihil est idolum in mundo, & quod nullus est alius DEUS, nisi unus: Nam etsi sunt qui dicantur Dij, sive in cœlo, sive in terra, sicuti sunt Dij multi & Domini multi: Nobis tamen unus est DEUS.

Hïs probationũ fundamentis ita jactis, statim quæri solet, Quanam ratione, sive quo respectu, DEUS unus esse dicatur? Quâ sanè Quæstione nihil prorsus opus esset apud pios & fideles, ut qui simplici fide in fundamentis Scripturæ acquiescunt; nisi partim hæreticorum strophæ, partim Diaboli insidiæ, accuratiorem ejus diexodon requirerent. Rectissimè autem ea expediri potest, si per ăρσιν sive remotionem eorum Unitatis modorum, qui huic mysterio non competunt, ad verùm tandem unitatis modum perveniatur.

Ac initiò quidem quædam dicuntur specie esse unum. Cæterùm hæc Unitas DEO non competit: Nam quæ hoc modo Unum sunt, ea numero multa sunt, & saltem specie νόητῇ Unum esse dicuntur: cujus Multitudinis causam esse materiam, Philosophi dicunt. Quare si tres personæ Divinitatis statuantur Unum quid esse, specie Logîcâ, nimirùm propter concretionem materiæ cujusdam: Consequens foret, numero tres Deos esse: id quod absurdum; cum omne materiatum, sit mutabile & finitum: Porrò hanc etiam ob causam personæ Divinitatis non possunt esse unam species; quia alia est definitio DEI Patris, alia Filij, alia Spiritus Sancti. Quorum autem species est una, eorum quoque definitio una esse debet.

Deinde, Quædam dicuntur esse Unum Genere. Qui & ipse Modus Unitatis ab hoc mysterio est alienus. Nam quæ Genere sunt Unum, ea propter Contrarias differentias, specie & Definitione non sunt Unum. Unde sequeretur, si hoc modo DEUS esset Unus, tùm alia specie atque Essentiâ Divinitatis, Patrem esse DEUM: & aliâ Filium: aliâ denique Spiritum Sanctum. Porrò, quæ Genere sunt Unum, ea non possunt habere eande perfectionis differentiam: quemadmodum sanè Equus & homo Genere quoddam sunt Unum: sed quoad differentiam perfectionis tantùm à se mutuò discrepant, quantum τὸ λογικὸν distat à bruto sive ἀλόγῳ. Absit autem, ut talem perfectionis differentiam inter tres personas Divinitatis, vel saltem imaginemur. Proindè neque iste Unitatis modus, qui Generis est, in mysterio isto locum habere potest.

Accedit & illud, quòd hæ duæ Unitatis species, de quibus jam actum, quippe quibus significatur νόημα καθόλε, hoc est, species Universalis, nequaquam sunt substantia, aut pars aliqua substantiæ rerum: sed duntaxat sunt Rationes quædam substantiales, quæ Mentis nostræ sunt quædam Logica Accidentia, & non res quædam seipsis subsistentes.

Tertiò, quædam dicuntur esse Unum subjecto, sive τῷ πάθει, id est, affectione. Quo pacto, si DEUS unus esse statueretur; utique mutabilis esset: quemadmodum Sabellius & Servetus DEUM τῷ πάθει, hoc est, varijs dispensationibus unum esse, blasphemarunt.

Quartò, abhorrent ab hoc mysterio illi Unitatis Modi, secundùm quos aliquid dicitur esse Unum vel definitione; vel ea ratione, quâ aliquid est continuum. Nam quoad priorem: non una, sed alia & planè diversa datur definitio Patris, alia Filij, alia Spiritus Sancti. Posterior verò modus Unitatis Accidentalis est, & admixtam habet potentiam, quæ imperfectionem subjecti semper arguit. Unde continuum, quantunvis sit unum actu: potest tamen dividi, & est Multum δυνάμει: Quod absit, ut de Unitate Essentiæ divinæ vel saltem cogitemus.

Quintò: neq; ille Modus Unitatis per omnia sufficit, quid definitur per unitatem voluntaris, consensus & concordiæ. Etsi enim summus & perpetuus est Consensus, & Concordia inter tres personas Divinitatis: Unitas tamen Essentiæ divinæ indè sufficienter demonstrari nequit.

Relinquitur proindè, ut DEUM dicamus Unum NUMERO, & ut simplicissimum aliquod absolutissimumq; τό δέ τι, hoc est, ut Res una singularis; sive Essentia Una. Undè in Scholis Theologorum Terminus iste locum jampridem obtinuit, ut DEUS diceretur esse unus NUMERO & ESSENTIA.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition II. in one divine Essence, three distinct Persons are, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit

IN one divine Essence, there are three distinct Persons, FATHER, SON, AND HOLY SPIRIT.

Ἔκθεσις.

Here at last unfolds that ineffable Mystery, inscrutable to any sharpness of human reason: but to be grasped only by the embrace of faith: That, namely, in the one most absolute and most simple essence of GOD, there must nevertheless be believed a Multitude, or Number, namely the Sacrosanct and adorable Trinity. This Multitude, however, as our Author rightly admonishes, is not to be defined by reason of the divine Essence? For so many gods would have to be posited: But with respect to the ὑποστάσεις or Persons: because, namely, the divine Essence is one in Number: In this, however, there are three distinct ὑποστάσεις or Persons; FATHER, SON, AND HOLY SPIRIT: so that according to the Athanasian Creed, Unity in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity is to be venerated. Many, and indeed most intricate, Questions are moved in this place, to the treatment of which, however, we deservedly premise as a kind of foundation the oracles of the Holy Scriptures, by which this Mystery can be confirmed.

The first kind of proof, taken from the Old Testament, is found to be built upon four principal Observations or Rules.

The first Observation considers that notable revelation of all three Persons in the Creation of this universe. For in the Beginning GOD (the first person) created Heaven and Earth: but he created by speaking, that is, through that Word of his, not προφορικὸν, but ὁμοούσιον, John 1, 3. where the second person of the Trinity is expressed: And the Spirit of the Lord (the third person) was moving over the waters. David understood this Mystery, who, alluding to this history of Creation, says, BY THE WORD OF THE LORD were the heavens established, and BY THE SPIRIT of his mouth, all their host.

II. The word Elohim, which is of plural Number, when it is predicated of GOD in the scriptures, does not always, according to the propriety of Grammar, take to itself a plural verb: but sometimes, and indeed more often, a singular Verb: By which reason also that both unity and plurality in GOD are noted, is evidently demonstrated: as Gen. 1, 1. Elohim barah, Gods created heaven and earth. To which pertains also, that not only is God read to speak of himself in the plural many times: as Gen. 1, 26. Let us make man in our image. Gen. 2, 18. Let us make a helper for man. Gen. 3, 22. Behold Adam is become as one of us. Gen. 11, 7. Come, let us descend, and confound their language. Isa. 6, 8. I heard the voice of the LORD saying, whom shall I send, and who will go, FOR US &c. But also Jehovah is found to make words of Jehovah: as Gen. 19, 24. Jehovah rained from Jehovah fire and brimstone upon Sodom. Ps. 110, 1. The LORD said to my LORD, &c.

Nor does it stand in the way, that in Hebrew the word Jehovah is not placed twice. For by the word Adonai, that no other than the true Jehovah or GOD ought to be understood, the immediately annexed ἐπεξήγησις proves: Sit at my right hand. For to none of the Angels, much less to any man, was it said, Sit at my right hand: but to the incarnate Son of GOD alone. Heb. 1, 13.

III. Observation. When in the sacred writings one sentence is repeated three times concerning GOD, it could be a clear Testimony of the Trinity: as Num. 6, 24. in that solemn blessing of the people: Isa. 6, 3. Holy, Holy, Holy Lord GOD of Hosts. Ps. 67, 7. Isa. 33, 22.

IV. And the last Observation is sought from the most holy, and only Essential name of GOD, Jehovah, which since it is attributed in the Scriptures not only to the Father, but also to the Son and the Holy Spirit, it certainly ought to be an infallible indication of this Mystery; as Jer. 26, 6. and 33, 16. Behold the days come, saith Jehovah: and I will raise up unto David a righteous branch: And this is the name, which they shall call him, Jehovah, our Righteousness. Where it is certain that the name Jehovah is assigned not only to the Father, but also to the Son. Thus the Holy Spirit, who professes that he will speak through the Prophets, nay truly did speak, as is evident from Acts 1, 16. Eph. 3, 5. 2 Pet. 1, 21. is expressly named Jehovah and GOD. Num. 12, 2. Luke 1, 35.

And these indeed were those arguments, from which the Patriarchs, Prophets, and the faithful under the Old Testament, could elicit and confirm the Unity of the divine Essence, and in it the Trinity of persons, although somewhat more obscurely. But to us in the New Testament this Mystery is expressed so clearly and perspicuously, that he who wishes to foster any ignorance or doubt in this part, he may seem, nay indeed ought to seem, to bind his own eyes with the spell of impiety by his own will. Our author is content with a twofold means of proof, sought indeed from the New Testament, not counting, namely, but weighing the moments of the arguments. THE FORMER is taken from that solemn revelation of all three Persons, made in the Baptism of Christ: Where the voice of the Father concerning the Son was heard from the heavens: The Son himself was baptized in the Jordan: But the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a Dove Matt. 3, 16. Luke 3, 22.

Johan. 1, 32. & seqq. A further point was requested from the institution of our Baptism, which the command of Christ most strictly enjoined to be conferred in the Name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, Matth. 28, 19.

There can be added in place of a third proof, those testimonies of the Scriptures, which partly distinguish the Father from the Son as the begetter from the begotten, Ps. 2, 7. as the sender from the sent, John 8, 16. likewise the Father and the Son from the Holy Spirit clearly. John 14. throughout almost the whole, and chap. 15, 26. but partly assert and confirm the Trinity of persons αὐτολεξεὶ: Such as that golden one, 1 John 5, 7. THERE ARE THREE, that bear Testimony in Heaven: THE FATHER, THE WORD and THE HOLY SPIRIT, and these THREE ARE ONE.

Latin:

IN una divina Essentia, tres distinctæ sunt Personæ, PATER, FILIUS, ET SPIRITUS SANCTUS.

Ἔκθεσις.

HIc demùm sese pandit ineffabile illud Mysterium, nulli rationis humanæ acumini perscrutabile: sed solius fidei amplexu capiendum: Quod nimirùm in unicâ absolutissimâ simplicissimâque DEI essentiâ, nihilo minus Multitudo, sive Numerus, Sacrosancta videlicet & adoranda Trinitas, credi debet. Est verò Multitudo hæc, uti rectè admonet Autor noster, non ratione Essentiæ divinæ? Sic enim multi Dij statuendi forent: Sed ὑποστάσεων sive Personarum respectu definienda: quod nimirum una Numero sit Essentia divina: In hac verò tres sint distinctæ ὑποστάσεις sive Personæ; PATER, FILIUS, ET SPIRITUS SANCTUS: ita ut secundum Symbolum Athanasij, Unitas in Trinitate, & Trinitas in Unitate sit veneranda. Moventur hoc loco multæ, & quidem intricatissimæ Quæstiones, quarum tamen Tractationi, meritò Fundamenti quasi loco præmittimus Sacrarum Scripturarum oracula, quibus Mysterium istud confirmari potest.

Primum autem probationis Genus ex Veteri Testamento petitum quatuor potissimùm Observationibus sive Regulis superstructum esse deprehenditur.

Prima Observatio considerat insigné illam revelationem omnium trium Personarũ in Creatione hujus universi. In Principio enim DEUS (prima persona) creavit Cœlum & Terram: sed creavit dicendo, hoc est, per Verbum illud suum, non προφορικὸν, sed ὁμοούσιον, Johan. 1, 3. ubi secunda Trinitatis persona exprimitur: Et Spiritus Domini (tertia persona) ferebatur super aquis, Intellexit hoc Mysterium David, qui ad hanc Creationis historiam alludens, VERBO, inquit, DOMINI cæli firmati sunt, & SPIRITU oris ejus, omnis exercitus eorum.

II. Vox Elohim, quæ pluralis Numeri est, ubi in sacris de DEO prædicatur, non semper secundum proprietatem Grammaticæ, sibi adsciscit verbum plurale: sed interdum & quidem sæpius, Verbum singulare: Qua ratione & Unitatem & pluralitatem in DEO notari, evidenter demonstratur: ut Gen. 1, 1. Elohim barah, Dij creavit cælum & terram. Quò pertinet etiam, quòd non modò Deus de se in plurali multoties loqui legitur: ut Gen. 1, 26. Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram. Gen. 2, 18. Faciamus homini adjutorium. Gen. 3, 22. Ecce Adam quasi unus ex nobis, factus est. Gen. 11, 7. Venite, descendamus, & confundamus lingvam ipsorum. Jesi. 6, 8. Audivi vocem DOMINI dicentis, quem mittam, & quis ibit, NOBIS &c. Verùm etiam Jehovah de Jehovah verba facere deprehenditur: ut Gen. 19, 24. Jehovah pluit à Jehovah ignem & sulphur super Sodomam. Psal. 110, 1. Dixit DOMINUS DOMINO meo, &c.

Neque obstat, quod in Hebræo non bis ponitur vox Jehovah. Nam per vocem Adonai, nullum alium, quàm verum Jehovah sive DEUM intelligi debere, evincit annexa statim ἐπεξήγησις: Sede à dextris meis. Nulli enim Angelorum, multò minus hominum cuipiam dictum est, Sede à dexteris meis: sed soli Filio DEI incarnato. Heb. 1, 13.

III. Observatio. Quando in sacris una sententia ter de DEO repetitur, Trinitatis luculentum potuit esse Testimonium: ut Num. 6, 24. in solenni illa benedictione populi: Esa. 6, 3. Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus DEUS Zebaoth. Psalm. 67, 7. Esa. 33, 22.

IV. & postrema Observatio petitur ex sanctissimo, solique DEO Essentiali nomine Jehovah, quod cùm in Scripturis non modò Patri, sed & Filio ac Spiritui Sancto tribuatur, utique Mysterij hujus indicium minimè fallibile esse debuit; ut Jerem. 26, 6. & 33, 16. Ecce dies venient, dicit Jehovah: & suscitabo Davidi germen justum: Et hoc est nomen, quod vocabunt eum, Jehovah, Justitia nostra. Ubi non modò patri, sed & Filio nomen Jehovah adsignari certum est. Sic Spiritus Sanctus, qui per Prophetas se locuturum profitetur, imò verè locut9 est, uti patet ex Actor 1, 16. Eph. 3, 5. 2. Pet. 1, 21. expressè nominatur Jehovah & DEUS. Num. 12, 2. Luc. 1, 35.

Et hæc quidem erant ea argumenta, ex quibus Patriarchæ Prophetæ, & fideles sub Veteri Testamento, Unitatem Essentiæ divinæ, & in ea Trinitatem personarum, licet paulò obscuriùs elicere & confirmare potuerunt. Nobis verò in Novo Test. usq; adeò clarè & perspicuè Mysteriu hoc est expressum, ut qui vel ignorantiæ vel dubitationis aliquid hac in parte fovere velit, is propriâ voluntate oculos sibi impietatis fascino perstringere, videri possit, imò verò debeat. Autor noster gemino probationis medio, ex Novo quidem Testamento petito, est contentus, non videlicet numerans, sed ponderans argumentorum momenta. PRIUS desumtum est à solenni illa revelatione omnium triũ Personarum, in Baptismo Christi facta: Ubi Patris vox de Filio è cœlis audita: Filius ipse in Jordane baptizatus fuit: Spiritus autem Sanctus in specie Columbæ apparuit Matt. 3, 16. Luc. 3, 22.

Johan. 1, 32. & seqq. POSTERIUS petitum est ex institutione Baptismi nostri, quem in Nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus Sancti conferendum esse, mandatum Christi severissimè præcepit, Matth. 28, 19.

Addi possunt tertiæ probationis loco, illa Scripturarum testimonia, quæ partim Patrem à Filio ut gignentem à genito, Psal. 2, 7. ut mittentem à misso, Johan. 8, 16. Patrem item & Filium à Spiritu Sancto dilucidè distingvunt. Joh. 14. per totum ferè, & cap. 15, 26. partim verò Trinitatem personarum αὐτολεξεὶ asserunt & confirmant: Quale est aureolum illud, 1. Joh. 5, 7. TRES sunt, qui Testimonium dant in Cælo: PATER, VERBUM & SPIRITUS SANCTUS, & hi TRES UNUM SUNT.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition III. A Person is an individual, intelligent, incommunicable substance, not sustained in or by another

A Person is an individual, intelligent, incommunicable Substance, not sustained in or by another.

Exposition.

What the Orthodox Church wishes to be noted by the term PERSON, has been debated in various ways long ago. Peter Lombard lib. 1. distinct. 25. lit. B. A person, he says, is said in relation to itself, and it is the same to GOD, to be a person, as to Be, just as it is the same for him to be, as it is for GOD to be: whence it is manifestly gathered, that we preach the divine Essence, saying: The Father is a Person, the Son is a person, the Holy Spirit is a person, that is, the divine Essence: and altogether one and the same thing is signified by the name of person, that is, the divine Essence, when it is said, The Father is a person, the Son is a person, as is signified by the name of GOD, when it is said, The Father is GOD, the Son is GOD. So also the same thing is signified, when it is said, GOD, is GOD, and GOD is a person. Thus far Lombard: Whose opinion is found to be vicious and erroneous in many ways. 1. For if the word "person" signifies the same thing as the word "Essence," it would follow that, just as there are three persons, really distinct, so also three Essences must be conceded, likewise really distinct: and consequently, that not one, but three Gods must be confessed: which is impious and blasphemous. 2. From this of Lombard it would also follow that, just as GOD is one by reason of Essence, so also He would be one by reason of person: and consequently only one person: which, by a detestable blasphemy, recalls the heresy of the Sabellians from the pit: and simply overturns the mystery of the Trinity. 3. If these two propositions, GOD is GOD, and GOD is person, signify one and the same thing, it follows that there is one and the same reason for both propositions, with respect to predication. But this latter is false. For that proposition, GOD is GOD, is an identical predication: and merely ἐξηγητική: for the same thing is enunciated of itself.

Latin:

PErsona est Substantia individua, intelligens, incommunicabilis, non sustentata in vel ab alio.

Έκθεσις.

QUidnam PERSONÆ termino Ecclesia Orthodoxa notatum velit, variæ jam olim disceptatum fuit. Petrus Lombardus lib. 1. distinct. 25. lit. B. Persona, inquit, ad se dicitur, & idē est DEO, esse personam, quod Esse, sicut idem est ei esse, quod DEUM esse: unde manifestè colligitur, quod Essentiam divinam predicamus, dicentes: Pater est Persona, Filius est persona, Spiritus Sanctus est persona, id est, Essentia divina: & omninò unum & idem significatur nomine personæ, id est, Essentia divina, cùm dicitur, Pater est persona, Filius est persona, quòd significatur nomine DEI, cùm dicitur, Pater est DEUS, Filius est DEUS. Ita etiam idem significatur, cùm dicitur, DEUS, est DEUS, & DEUS est persona. Hactenus Lombardus: Cujus sententia multis modis vitiosa & erronea deprehenditur. 1. enim, si vox personæ idem significat, quod vox Essentiæ, consequens fuerit, quemadmodū tres sunt personæ, realiter distinctæ, sic tres etiam concedendas esse Essentias, istidem realiter distinctas: & per consequens, nō Unum, sed tres Deos confitendos esse: id quod impium & blasphemum. 2. Ex hac Lombardi sequeretur etiam illud, ut quemadmodum DEUS est unus ratione Essentiæ, sic etiam sit unus ratione personæ: & per consequens una tantùm persona: id quod per detestandam blasphemiā Sabellianorum hæresin ab orco revocat: & Trinitatis mysterium simpliciter evertit. 3. Si duæ hæ propositiones, DEUS est DEUS, & DEUS est persona, unum idemque significant, sequitur, unam eandemq; utriusque propositionis esse rationē, respectu prædicationis. Atqui hoc posterius falsum. Illa enim propositio, DEUS est DEUS, est identica prædicatio: & duntaxat ἐξηγητική: idem enim de seipso enunciatur.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Why the Fathers used the term Persona

This proposition, however, 'God is a person,' is not an identical predication: but it enunciates concerning GOD, or the divine Essence, that it admits and receives the definition of person, and the ὑπάρξεως ἴδιον καὶ χαρακτηριστικὸν τρόπον. Whence this difference is immediately detected between those two propositions: that the former, which is identical, is true and understood concerning the whole divine Essence in general. This latter, however, concerns the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit individually: but not the whole Essence itself, as if it were a single person. Wherefore in the former, the word (God) is something undistributed; but in the latter, it is distributed, so that the sense is, either the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, who is God, is a person: but the Trinity or Deity itself is not one person. And although to be GOD, and to be a person, do not differ in reality: meanwhile, however, the notation of person expresses the τρόπον ὑπάρξεως, as Justin speaks, or as Basil has it, it designates a different δήλωσιν ὑπάρξεως in the individual persons of the Trinity: as will be shown more fully a little later.

The ancient heretics, and especially the Sabellians, objected at this point with this argument: To every question, by which one asks περὶ τοῦ τί, it is always answered by that which is the essence of the thing itself. But, when it is asked, What is the Father: What is the Son: What is the Holy Spirit, it is always answered, That he is a person. Therefore the word Person and Essence will denote one and the same thing.

But it is most correctly answered that a fallacy παρὰ τὸ ἑπόμενον is committed. For it does not immediately follow that, because the things which are and are called Persons are a certain essence, therefore the word Person denotes this very essence. For even if the term Person includes at the same time the essence of the thing itself: since the definition of Person adds nothing real to the divine essence—otherwise person and Essence would differ in reality, which is false—even if, I say, the term Person includes the Essence of the thing itself; yet it includes it only in one certain ὑφισταμένῳ, or, as the Scholastics speak, in a certain suppositum, existing in its own special mode and manner, distinct from the remaining persons: so that it is indeed permitted to say: The Father is God: but not absolutely, but relatively, namely, God begetting. Thus the Son is God, namely, God begotten: Thus the Holy Spirit is God, namely, proceeding from the Father and the Son. In which respect, certainly, the word Person does not now properly denote the Essence of the thing which is a person: but rather its Relation or characteristic property. Therefore, even if it is customary to answer the question, What is the Father, What is the Son, What is the Holy Spirit, by saying, He is a Person: yet, as the heretics viciously established, the Essence considered simply is not expressed by the word person: but that Relation which is in the Essence is expressed. Where the response to the question fits most perfectly. For when it is asked, What is the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, it is not asked what the THING is, but what the Relation is: where it is most correctly answered even by the Relation, That he is a Person. Therefore, so that the definition of Person may be established more correctly, it will be necessary to distinguish altogether accurately between the words Essence and Person, or οὐσίας and ὑποστάσεως: lest from the confusion of these words, we seem to deny either the unity of the Essence or the plurality of the persons. The ancient Greek Theologians called οὐσίαν or Essence that which is common in the Most Holy Trinity: that is, according to the interpretation of Basil the Great, the community of Nature, or divine Essence, which is predicated commonly and equally of all three persons. But they called Person or ὑπόστασιν that which is proper to each person, in that very community or unity of the divine Essence: and which really distinguishes each Person from the remaining Persons of the Trinity. Whence not ineptly some have written that the word οὐσίας describes generally and commonly the nature and perfection of God itself: but that the word ὑποστάσεως denotes a certain singular and as it were individual thing: endowed indeed with the divine nature: yet distinguished from another individual by some property, or as Thomas writes in part 1, question 39, article 3; The form signified by the name Person is not Essence or Nature, but Personality: Because the word for Nature or Essence does not essentially include the Individuating principles: which, however, the word and signification of person does include.

Moreover, that the Latin Fathers wished to render the word ὑποστάσεως by the word Person, when yet that perhaps seems to denote substance more correctly, was done to avoid the various snares of the heretics, which they constructed in this dispute under the equivocation of words against the purer doctrine. For since the word ὑπόστασις sometimes sounds the same as substance, the heretics, and especially Sabellius, argued that just as there is one divine Essence or substance, so there is also only one person; therefore, so that the Latin Church might avoid the danger of that ambiguity, and assert the difference of the hypostases or persons more clearly: it therefore wished to render the Greek term ὑποστάσεως as Persons. Which manner of speaking the Greek Church also began to observe in the progress of time, so that for three ὑποστάσεσι, it might name three πρόσωπα. And although there are not lacking Theologians who suppose that this signification of the word ὑποστάσεως has its origin only from the use of Christian Liberty, and does not rest upon any express testimony of Scripture, because the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1, 2, takes the word ὑποστάσεως for the word οὐσίας, when it affirms that the Son is ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆς ὑποστάσεως τῦ πατρὸς, the brightness of the glory and the character of the substance of the Father, as the Latin Version has it: yet, with all respect to them, not a slight error seems to be committed in this part. For the Son cannot be called the express essence of the Father, since it is rather one and the same, and indeed simple, essence of both: but it is asserted truly and according to the mind of Scripture: Whatever the Father has that is proper (that is, to beget), that is expressed in the Son, Who, because He is Begotten, is therefore the character of the person (but not of the Essence) of the Father. Although elsewhere and outside the discussion of these terms it is also truly said that, on account of the unity and community of the Essence, the Father is also seen, from him who sees the Son John 14, 9. And indeed this interpretation of the present passage both clearly distinguishes the three ὑποστάσεις against Sabellius, and at the same time confirms the τὸ ὁμοούσιον against the Arians.

Furthermore, even if it were granted in the highest degree that the Catholic Church, using the right of Liberty, had devised entirely new terms to use in explaining that mystery—as indeed it cannot be denied regarding the word ὀυσίας, ὁμοουσίȣ, Trinity, and others of that kind—nothing nevertheless is lost to our cause, nor is any support added to the impiety of heretics. For as St. Augustine rightly admonishes in book 7 of De Trinitate, chapter 4: It is wickedness if anyone disapproves of terms which explain nothing other than what is handed down as expressed in the sacred writings. And, as Cyril infers, although the terms may not exist in Scripture, the things themselves, which are understood and signified by these terms, are held to be expressed in Scripture. For we do not announce anything else or different by these terms, but that very thing which we understand even without words: since we cannot think of one GOD without being surrounded by the radiance of the Three, and we cannot speak of the Three without being suddenly caught up to the One, as Augustine speaks in book 5 of De Trinitate, chapter 9, and Nazianzen.

Furthermore, it is asked in this place, whether the three persons of the Divinity might not more conveniently be called three ἄτομα or Individuals? And indeed there are not lacking even among Orthodox Theologians those who in this Article establish that ὑφισάμενον, ὑπόστασιν, πρόσωπον and ἄτομον, subsistent, subsistence, person and Individual are synonyms. There are others who stubbornly resist this opinion. But perhaps all this discrepancy can be removed without such great difficulty. For if we look at the proper, and as they speak in the Schools, formal definition of these terms, it cannot be denied that some difference exists between them; so that (as regards the present question) Durandus wrote truly in book 2 Sent. dist. 3. quest. 2. and 10. l. 3. dist. 1. quest. 1. N. 17. Every person is a suppositum (or subsistence) and every suppositum is an Individual: but not every Individual is a suppositum, nor is every suppositum a person: For any singular nature, in whatever genus it may be, can be called individual: but it is not called a suppositum unless it is a singular nature in the category of Substance: and not just any such nature: but only a complete person is so called, and that only in an intellectual nature: as in the divine, Father, Son and Holy Spirit: in the Angelic nature, Michael, Gabriel, Raphael: in the human, Peter, Paul, John. Wherefore singular irrational animals, such as Bucephalus, Pyrois and Aëthon can be called ἄτομα καὶ ὑφιστάμενα: but they cannot be called πρόσωπα. Looking to this, the ancient Ecclesiastical Writers are nowhere (so far as I know) read to have named the three persons τρία ἄτομα or individuals. However, when we use the term Individuals not formally, but analogically, and by it express something noted as καθ᾽ ἕκαστον, really distinguished by its characteristic properties: then indeed, Person, Individual and suppositum seem to be equivalent, and to stand for one and the same thing. Although it is more prudent that, having dismissed the κενοφωνίαις, we speak with Scripture and the Orthodox Church as far as it can be done.

The use of those things which we have discussed so far regarding the term Person and Essence can be very great, both in dissolving the many twists and sophisms of heretics, especially the Anti-Trinitarians, and also in refuting that apparent contradiction which seems to be implied when we predicate One and Three of God. For if a diversity of Subject is shown, that is, if it is shown that God is and is called One by reason of Essence, but Three by reason of Person: and that Person and Essence are not entirely One and the same: then all appearance of Contradiction vanishes entirely. Furthermore, if it is demonstrated that the Divine essence in itself is entirely ἀμέριστον, indivisible: but by reason of characteristic properties the same is divisible into three ὑποστάσεις: then again all Contradiction expires. Just as Augustine illustrates this with the example of the Soul, which by reason of Essence is One, and entirely ἀμέριστος, yet in the meantime admits a plurality and division with respect to δυνάμεων and distinct faculties, without any contradiction.

These things having been premised, it will now be easier to investigate what definition of Person can be given and admitted in this mystery. In creatures, a Person is defined as a certain singular thing, which has the whole and perfect substance of the same species: and which subsists by itself, distinguished or separated from the remaining Individuals of the same nature, not by essence, but by number. However, since according to this definition each person has its own essence, different from another person: so that besides the name and appellation it has nothing in common with the other: In the present Mystery of the Trinity, however, not every person has its own Essence distinct from the remaining persons: But all three persons participate in One Essence only, without any composition or division: and therefore the Fathers investigated another definition of Person, congruent to this mystery, with great solicitude.
