And indeed the first, Boethius, a Christian philosopher and martyr, understanding from the decree of the Council of Chalcedon that there is only one Person in Christ, but meanwhile two Natures, gave this definition: A person is an individual substance of a rational nature. Which definition, in the progress of time, was made more correct and refined by the study and effort of the Holy Fathers: while initially, for 'rational nature', was substituted 'intelligent substance': then indeed, lest the word 'substance' be taken for the word 'essence', and thus person be confused with essence, therefore the word 'incommunicable' was added, to distinguish it from essence, which is communicable to all three persons: and finally, since it was established from the Article concerning the Person of Christ that human nature is indeed an individual, intelligent, incommunicable substance, but meanwhile is not a person, because it does not subsist by itself, but is sustained by the λόγῳ: therefore, in the definition of a person, this limitation was also added: 'not sustained in another'. Whence at length that perfect, and, as they say, formal definition of a person emerged, consistent with this mystery: which our author also proposed in part: A person is an individual, intelligent, incommunicable substance, not sustained in another.

Latin:

Hæc autem propositio, Deus est persona, non est identica prædicatio: sed enunciat de DEO, sive divina Essentia, quod personæ rationem, & ὑπάρξεως ἴδιον καὶ χαρακτηριστικὸν τρόπον admittat & suscipiat. Unde statim inter duas illas propositiones hoc discriminis deprehenditur: quod prior illa, quæ est identica, de tota divina Essentia in universum vera est & intelligitur. Hæc autem posterior, de Patre, Filio & Spiritu Sancto sigillatim: non autem de tota ipsa Essentia, quasi sit unica persona. Quare in priore illa vox (Deus) est quiddam non distributu; in posteriore verò, est distributum, ut sit sensus, vel Pater, vel Filius, vel Spiritus Sanctus, qui Deus est, est persona: non autem ipsa Trinitas aut Deitas est una persona. Et quanquam DEUM esse, & personam esse, realiter non differunt: interim tamen personæ notatio exprimit τρόπον ὑπάρξεως, uti Justinus loquitur, vel uti Basilius habet, δήλωσιν ὑπάρξεως designat in singulis personis Trinitatis, diversam: uti paulò pòst ostendetur fusiùs.

Objecerunt Veteres hæretici hoc loco, & cumprimis Sabelliani, hoc argumentum: Ad omnem Quæstionem, quâ quæritur περὶ τοῦ τί, semper per id respondetur, quod est ipsius rei essentia. Atqui, quando quæritur, Quid sit Pater: Quid sit Filius: Quid sit Spiritus Sanctus, semper respondetur, Quòd sit persona. Ergò Persona & Essentiæ vox, Unum idemq; notabunt.

Sed rectissimè respondetur, committi Sophisma παρὰ τὸ ἑπόμενον. Neq; enim statim est consequens, Res eæ, quæ sunt & dicuntur Personæ, sunt essentia quædam: Ergò Personæ vox notat hanc ipsam essentiam. Nam etsi Personæ termino comprehenditur simul ipsa rei essentia: Siquidem Personæ ratio, nihil reale addit ad divinam essentiam: aliàs persona & Essentia realiter differrent: id quod falsum: etsi, inqua, Personæ terminus comprehendit simul ipsam rei Essentiam; tamen eam comprehendit, non nisi in uno quodam certo ὑφισταμένῳ, sive, uti Scholastici loqunntur, in certo quodam supposito, suo speciali modo & ratione, à reliquis personis distinctâ, exintentem: ut dicere quidem liceat: Pater est Deus: sed non absolutè, verùm relatè, nempè Deus gignens. Sic Filius est Deus, nempè Deus genitus: Sic Spiritus Sanctus est Deus, nempe procedens à Patre & Filio, Quo sanè respectu non jam Persona propriè notat rei, quæ persona est, Essentiam: sed ejus potiùs Relationem sive proprietatem characteristicam. Proinde si vel maximè ad Quæstionem, Quid est Pater, Quid est Filius, Quid est Spiritus Sanctus, responderi solet, Est Persona: non tamen, uti hæretici vitiosè statuerunt, per vocabulum personæ exprimitur Essentia simpliciter considerata: sed exprimitur Relatio illa, quæ est in Essentia. Ubi Responsio ad Quæstionem maximè quadrat. Quando enim quæritur, Quid est Pater, aut Filius, aut Spiritus Sanctus, non quæritur, quid REI, sed quid Relationis sit: ubi rectissimè respondetur etiam per Relationem, Quod sit Persona. Proindè, ut Personæ definitio rectiùs constituatur, accuratè omninò inter vocabula Essentiæ & Personæ sive οὐσίας & ὑποστάσεως distinguendum fuerit: ne ex confusione istorum vocabulorum, vel unitatem Essentiæ, vel pluritatem personarum inficiari videamur. Veteres Græci Theologi, οὐσίαν sive Essentiam nominarunt id, quod in Sacrosanctâ Trinitate est commune: hoc est, interprete Basilio Magno, Naturæ, sive Essentiæ divinæ communitatem, quæ de omnibus tribus personis communiter & æqualiter prædicatur. Personam verò sive ὑπόστασιν nominarunt id, quod unicuique personæ proprium est, in illâ ipsâ Essentiæ divinæ communitate sive unitate: & quod quamlibet Personam, à reliquis Personis Trinitatis, realiter distingvit. Undè haud ineptè nonnulli scripserunt, vocabulum οὐσίας generatim atque communiter describere ipsam Dei naturam atque perfectionem: ὑποστάσεως verò vocabulum notare singulare quoddam ac velut individuum: naturâ quidem divinâ præditum: proprietate tamen aliqua, ab alio individuo distinctum, vel ut Thomas parte 1. quæst. 39. art. 3. scribit; Forma significata per nomen Persona, non est Essentia vel Natura, sed Personalitas: Quia Naturæ sive Essentiæ vox, non includit essentialiter principia Individuantia: quæ tamen vox & significatio personæ includit.

Cæterùm, quòd Latini Patres vocabulum ὑποστάσεως per vocem Personæ reddere voluerunt, cum tamen illud fortassis rectiùs substantiam notare videatur, factum est, ad evitandum varias insidias hæreticorum, quas hac in disputatione sub æquivocatione vocabulorum, puriori doctrinæ struxerunt. Cùm enim vox ὑπόστασις interdum idem sonet atque substantia, hæretici, & cumprimis Sabellius pugnarunt, quemadmodum una sit Essentia sive substantia divina, sic unam etiam tantùm esse personam; proindè ut Ecclesia Latina istius ambiguitatis periculum evitaret, & discrimen hypostaseon sive personarum luculentiùs assereret: ideoque terminum Græcum ὑποστάσεως, Personarum reddere voluit. Quam loquendi rationem progressu temporis Græca quoque Ecclesia observare cœpit, ut pro trib. ὑποστάσεσι, tria nominaret πρόσωπα. Et quanquam non desunt Theologi, qui autumant hanc significationem vocabuli ὑποστάσεως duntaxat originem habere ex usu Libertatis Christianæ, neque eam niti expresso aliquo Scripturæ testimonio, propterea quòd Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 1, 2. voce ὑποστάσεως pro vocabulo οὐσίας accipiat, quando affirmat, Filium esse ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆς ὑποστάσεως τῦ πατρὸς, splendorem gloriæ & characterem substantiæ Patris, uti Latina habet Versio: tamen, quod bona istorum pace dixerim, haud levis hac in parte error committi videtur. Neque enim Filius potest dici expressa essentia Patris, cùm potiùs una eademq́; sit, & quidem simplex utriusque essentia: sed verè & secundum mentem Scripturæ hoc asseritur: Quicquid habet Pater proprium (hoc est gignere) id in Filio est expressum, Qui, quia est Genitus, ideò character est personæ (non verò Essentiæ) Patris. Quanquam aliàs & extra disputationem de istis vocabulis verè etiam dicitur, propter unitatem & communitatem Essentiæ videri etiam Patrem, ab eo, qui videat Filium Joh. 14, 9. Et sanè hæc interpretatio præsentis loci tùm tres ὑποστάσεις adversus Sabellium apertè distingvit, tùm simul τὸ ὁμοούσιον adversus Arianos confirmat.

Præterea si vel maximè concederetur, Ecclesiâ Catholicâ jure Libertatis usam, nova planè excogitasse vocabula, quibus in explicando isto mysterio uteretur:quemadmodum sanè de voce ὀυσίας, ὁμοουσίȣ, Trinitatis, & id genus alijs illud negari non potest: nihil tamen propterea vel nostræ causæ decedit, vel hæreticorum impietati accedit præsidij. Nam uti rectè D. Augustinus admonet lib. 7. de Trin. cap. 4. Improbitas est, si quis vocabula improbet, quæ non aliud explicant, quàm quod sacris expressum traditur. Et, ut Cyrillus infert, licet vocabula nõ extent in Scriptura, res tamen ipsæ, quæ vocabulis istis intelliguntur & significantur, in Scriptura expressæ habentur. Neque enim aliud aut diversum vocabulis iftis enunciamus: sed illud ipsum quod etiam fine verbis intelligimus: Siquidem non possumus unum cogitare DEUM, quin Trinum fulgore circumfundamur: & nõ possumus Trinum dicere, quin subitò ad unum rapiamur, uti loquuntur Augustinus lib. 5. de Trin. cap. 9. & Nazianzenus.

Porrò quæritur hoc loco, An non tres personæ Divinitatis commodiùs dici possint tria ἄτομα sive Individua? Et sanè non desunt ex Orthodoxis etiam Theologis, qui in hoc Articulo Synonyma esse statuunt ὑφισάμενον, ὑπόστασιν, πρόσωπον καὶ ἄτομον, subsistens, subsistentiam, personam & Individuum. Sunt contrà qui sententiæ huic mordicùs repugnant. Sed fortè haud ita magno negotio omnis isthæc discrepantia tolli potest. Nam si propriam, & uti in Scholis loquuntur, formalem vocabulorum istorum definitionem spectemus, haud negari poterit, discriminis aliquid eis invicem intercedere:ita ut (quoad præsentem quæstionem) verè scripserit Durandus in lib. 2 Sent. dist. 3. quæst. 2. & 10. l. 3. dist. 1. quæst. 1. N. 17. Omnis persona est suppositũ (seu subsistentia) & omne suppositum est Individuum: sed non omne Individuum est suppositum nec omne suppositum est persona: Nam quælibet natura singularis, in quocunq; genere sit, potest dici individua: Suppositum autem non dicitur, nisi natura singularis in prædicamento Substantiæ: nec quæcunque talis: sed solùm completa persona dicitur, idque in natura intellectuali solùm: velut in divinis, Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus: in Angelica natura, Michael, Gabriel, Raphael: in humana, Petrus, Paulus, Johannes. Quamobrem animalia irrationalia singularia, ut Bucephalus, Pyrois & Aëthon ἄτομα καὶ ὑφιστάμενα dici possunt: πρόσωπα verò dici non possunt. Hunc respicientes Veteres Scriptores Ecclesiastici nusquam (quod sciam) leguntur tres personas nominasse τρία ἄτομα sive individua. Cæterùm, quando non formaliter, sed analogicè Individuorum termino utimur, & eo exprimimus aliquid καθ᾽ ἕκαστον suis proprietatibus characteristicis realiter distinctum, notamus: tùm sanè, Persona, Individuum & suppositum æquipollere, & pro uno eodemque supponere videntur. Quanquam consultius est, ut missis κενοφωνίαις cum Scriptura & Ecclesia Orthodoxa, quoad ejus fieri potest, loquamur.

Usus autem eorum, quæ hactenùs de vocabulo Personæ & Essentiæ disputavimus, maximus esse potest, tùm in dissolvendis hæreticorum, AntiTrinitariorum cumprimis, strophis & Sophismatis quàmplurimis: tùm verò etiam in refellenda φαινομένη illa contradictione, quæ implicari videtur, quando Unum & Trinum de Deo prædicamus. Nam si diversitas Subjecti mõstretur, hoc est, ostendatur, Deum Unũ esse ac dici ratione Essentiæ, Trinum autem ratione Personæ: Personam verò & Essentiam non planè Unum & idem esse: tùm omnis Contradictionis apparentia prorsus evanescit. Porrò si demonstretur, Divinam essentiam in se planè esse ἀμέριστον individuam: sed ratione proprietatum characteristicarum eandem in tres ὑποστάσεις esse dividuam: tùm rursus omnis Contradictio expirat. Quemadmodum exemplo Animæ hoc illustrat Augustinus, quæ ratione Essentiæ est Una, & planè ἀμέριστος, interim tamen respectu δυνάμεων & facultatum distinctarum pluralitatem & divisionem admittit, sine ulla contradictione.

His ita præmissis, faciliùs jam erit investigare, Quænam Personæ definitio, hoc in mysterio dari & admitti possit. In creaturis definitur Persona, quod sit quoddam singulare, quod totam quidem & perfectam ejusdem speciei substantiam habet: quodque à reliquis ejusdem naturæ Individuis, non essentiâ, sed numero discretum seu distinctũ per se subsistit. Cæterùm cùm secundum hanc definitionem unaquæq; persona suam propriam, & ab alia persona differenté essentiam ita habeat: ut præter nomen & appellationem nihil commune cum altera habeat: In præsenti autem Trinitatis Mysterio, non quælibet persona propriamEssentiamà reliquis personis distinctam habeat: Sed omnes tres personæ Unâ tantùm Essentiâ sine ulla vel compositione, vel divisione participent: ideoque Patres aliam Personæ definitionem, huic mysterio congruentem admodùm sollicitè investigarunt. Et primus quidem Boëthius Philosophus Christianus & Martyr, intelligens ex decreto Cõcilii Chalcedonensis, in Christo Unam tantùm esse Personam, at duas interim Naturas, hanc Definitionem dedit: Persona est Naturæ rationabilis individua substantia. Quæ definitio progressu temporis studio & opera S. Patrum correctior & limatior facta est: dum initiò pro Natura Rationabili, substitutum est, Substantia intelligens: deindè verò, ne vox Substantiæ accipiatur pro voce Essentiæ, & sic persona cum essentia confunderetur, ideò adjecta fuit vox Incommunicabilis, ad differentiam Essentiæ, quæ est omnibus tribus personis Communicabilis: ac deniq; cùm constaret ex Articulo de Persona Christi, Humanam Naturam esse quidem Substantiam individuam intelligentem, incommunicabilem: Sed interim non esse personam, propterea, quòd perse non subsistat: sed à λόγῳ sustentatur: ideò in definitione personæ addita fuit & hæc limitatio, Non sustentata in alio. Unde tandem ea perfecta, &, uti loquuntur, Formalis prodijt Definitio personæ, huic mysterio congruens: quã etiam autor noster ex parte proposuit: Persona est substantia individua, intelligens, incommunicabilis, non sustentata in alio.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition IV. In the divine οὐσίᾳ καὶ ὑπόστασις (essence and hypostasis), that is, Essence and person differ by λόγῳ (word/reason) or…

Which definition is certainly able to easily sustain the censure of any Doctors: yet not a few Theologians are found, and those by no means ignoble, who, having neglected it, prefer to define Persons in the Divinity through the differences of the producers and the produced in one and the same divine essence. Whose opinion, although we do not wish to mark with a black coal: that, however, is of deeper inquiry, Whether a Person in the divine is the same as what that Difference of the producers and the produced is: or what comes to the same thing: Whether a person and a personal or characteristic property are plainly one and the same, and are mutually convertible with each other. But although it is extremely difficult to define anything certain about this Question, and perhaps that ancient saying can be apprehended more safely: It is not clear: Since whether you answer affirmatively or negatively, the matter is not without danger: For in this place expires every affection of Difference, not only Real, but also rational: Which, however, both have a place elsewhere in this Mystery, as we shall show below. But if, however, something must be answered, we think it sufficient that which Justin Martyr and Philosopher handed down, namely that a Person differs from its personal or characteristic property, in the way in which subsistence is accustomed to differ from the Mode of subsistence; or as ὑπαρξις from τρόπω τῆς ὑπαρξεως. And indeed, if only νόησις, or some place is left for a concept of the mind in this Mystery, a pious mind easily conceives and understands that Filiation itself is one thing, but the Son is another: Thus that divine spiration, by reason of which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, is one thing: but the Holy Spirit is another: That behaves as a cause: But this as an Effect of personation: if only it be lawful to use such words in this Mystery. Damascene certainly in book 1 of the Orthodox faith, chapter 9, sometimes names the Generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit τρόπυς ὑπάρξεως, nay he names τὸ ἀγέννητον Ingenitum a τρόπον ὑπάρξεως, from which at last comes ὑπαρξις or ὑπόστασις, but whatever it may be, we establish that one must philosophize here with complete sobriety.

PROPOSITION IV.

IN the divine ὐσία καὶ ὑπόσασις, or Essence and person differ τῷ λόγῳ or by Reason: but the three persons themselves differ from each other Really.

Ἔκθεσις.

Although the Mystery of the Trinity is entirely ἀῥῥητον and inscrutable: yet those various Disputations, instituted long ago against heretics, have caused it to be explained subsequently more clearly and more lucidly: By words indeed used for this matter from Philosophy, yet by no means accepted in a Philosophical sense. Which very thing is also discovered to have happened in this place: Since the terms of Rational and Real Distinction, accepted in the manner of Philosophers, are less suitable here.

For 1. In Philosophical matters, those things which differ really, they also differ Essentially. For a Real distinction could not be said, unless the things which it distinguishes differed among themselves by diverse natures. But neither does a person differ from the Essence: nor do persons differ from each other mutually in the divine, essentially. For in both cases, with the unity of the divine Essence denied, a plurality of Gods would be established. Therefore neither is a Person distinguished from the Essence, nor persons from each other, Really. Then, Those things which differ in Philosophical matters really, they are separable. But this affection also has no place in the present Mystery, because of that most simple unity of Essence of which I spoke: Therefore neither is there a Real difference. Then: Those things which differ really, they differ also by their very subjects. But the condition of subjects, just as of Adjuncts, is entirely abhorrent from this mystery of the Trinity. Therefore. By equal reason the Distinction also Rational, philosophically accepted, must be excluded from this mystery. For those things which differ only by λόγῳ or Reason, they are also diverse only by words, but not in truth: But the persons of the Trinity are not, as Sabellius blasphemed, diverse only by words, but in truth. For the Person of the Father can never be the person of either the Son or the Holy Spirit: and vice versa. Therefore neither can they differ by Reason. It remains therefore, both by Scholastic Doctors long ago, and hitherto by our own Theologians, that those Philosophical Terms have been accepted in a far different sense: so indeed that to differ Really, for them in this Mystery, was nothing, and today is nothing, other than to differ not imaginarily, not in word only, but in Truth. But a Rational discrimination involves at least some Respect, by reason of which one differs from another: although meanwhile by reason of the Thing they are the same.

With these things thus presupposed, it will now be more clearly evident, first, Whether οὐσία and ὑπόσασις, or essence and person: and how they differ. And indeed that some Difference intervenes between them, is evident even from this, that the οὐσία or divine Essence is Communicable to the Three persons; and indeed to each not in part, but in whole ἀδιαιρέτως: But persons behave themselves mutually toward each other plainly incommunicably. Whence it will be prompt to conclude that one definition or account of Essence, but another of Person, can be given: and consequently that they are not plainly one and the same. But, whatever the discrimination may be, it certainly must not be established as Essential: since the divine Essence is equally Communicable to each person: nor also as Real: since in GOD, Nature or Essence, and Person, do not differ in reality: or what is the same, to be GOD, and to be the Father. For it is predicated of each person of the Trinity that He is GOD. What is more, the individual persons taken together are nothing other than that one divine Essence; and this, outside of those persons, can neither be conceived nor ought to be conceived even in thought. It follows, therefore, that Essence and Person differ from one another only by way of logic or Reason, for the reason is that the definition of Essence is one thing—namely, communicable—while that of Person is another—namely, incommunicable.

Latin:

Quæ sanè definitio est Doctorum quorumvis censuram facilè sustinere possit : reperiuntur tamen haud pauci Theologi, ijsque minimè ignobiles, qui eâ neglectâ, malunt, Personas in Divinitate definire per producentium & productorum in unâ atque eadem divinâ essentiâ differentias. Quorum sententiam etsi atro carbone minimè notatam volumus: illud tamen altioris est indaginis, An Persona in divinis idem sit, quod est Differentia illa producentium & productorum : vel quod eodem recidit : An persona & proprietas personalis sive characteristica sint planè unum & idem, & inter se mutuò convertantur. Etsi verò perquàm difficile est, certi aliquid de hac Quæstione definire, & fortè tutiùs apprehendi potest illud antiquum: Non liquet : Siquidem sive affirmativè, sive negativè respondeas, res non caret periculo : Expirat enim hoc loco omnis omninò non modò Realis, sed & rationalis Differentiæ affectio: Quæ tamen utraque aliàs hoc in Mysterio locum habet, uti infrà ostendemus. Quod si tamen aliquid sit respondendum, sufficere arbitramur illud, quod Justinus Martyr & Philosophus prodidit, differre nimirum Personam à proprietate sua personali sive characteristica, eo modo, quo differre solet subsistentia à Modo subsistentiæ; vel quò ὑπαρξις à τρόπω τῆς ὑπαρξεως. Et profectò, si modò νόησις, sive mentis conceptui hoc in Mysterio locus aliquis relinquitur, mens pia facilè concipit & intelligit, aliud esse Filiationem ipsam, aliud verò Filium : Sic aliud esse divinam spirationem, ratione cujus Spiritus Sanctus procedit à Patre & Filio : aliud verò Spiritum Sanctum : Illud habere se tanquam causam : Hoc verò ut Effectum personationis: si modo hujusmodi vocabulis hoc in Mysterio uti fas sit. Damascenus certè lib. 1. Orth. fidei cap. 9. aliquoties Generationem Filij & processionem Spiritus Sancti nominet τρόπυς ὑπάρξεως, quin τὸ ἀγέννητον Ingenitum nominat τρόπον ὑπάρξεως, ex quo demùm fiat ὑπαρξις sive ὑπόστασις, sed quicquid sit sobriè omninò hîc philosophandum esse statuimus.

PROPOSITIO IV.

IN divinis ὐσία καὶ ὑπόσασις, sive Essentia & persona differunt τῷ λόγῳ sive Ratione: ipsæ verò tres personæ à se mutuò differunt Realiter.

Ἔκθεσις.

QUanquam Mysterium Trinitatis est prorsus ἀῥῥητον & imperscrutabile : effecêre tamen variæ illæ Disputationes, adversus hæreticos jam olim institutæ, ut subindè clariùs ac dilucidiùs illud explicaretur : Vocabulis quidem hanc ad rem ex Philosophia usurpatis, minimè tamen sensu Philosophico acceptis. quod ipsum etiam hoc loco usu venisse deprehenditur : Siquidem termini Distinctionis Rationalis & Realis, more Philosophorum accepti, minus huc quadrant.

Nam 1. In Philosophicis, quæ realiter differunt, ea differunt etiam Effentialiter. Realis enim distinctio dici non posset, nisi res, quas distingvit, distarent inter se naturis diversis. Atqui neq;, persona ab Essentia: neque persona inter se mutuò in divinis, differunt essentialiter. Utrobique enim negatâ Essentiæ divinæ unitate, pluralitas Drum statueretur. Ergò nec Realiter vel Persona ab Essentia, vel personæ à se invicem distingvntur. Deinde, Quæ differunt in Philosophicis realiter, ea sunt separabilia. Atqui & hæc affectio locum non habet in præsenti Mysterio, propter simplicissimam illam, de qua dixi, Essentiæ unitatem: Ergò neque Realis differentia. Tùm: Quæ realiter differunt, ipsis etiam subjectis differunt. Atqui ab hoc mysterio Trinitatis, uti Adjunctarum sic subjectorum etiam conditio, prorsus abhorret. Ergò. Pari ratione Distinctio etiam Rationalis philosophicè accepta ab hoc mysterio est secludēda. Quæ enim tantùm λόγω sive Ratione differunt, ea etiam vocabulis tantùm, non autem reverâ sunt diversa: Atqui personæ Trinitatis non uti Sabellius blasphemavit, vocabulis tantûm, sed revera diversæ sunt. Persona enim Patris nunquam potest esse persona vel Filij vel Spiritus Sancti: & viceversâ. Ergò neque Ratione differre possunt. Relinquitur proindè tùm à Scholasticis Doctoribus jam olim, tùm hactenus à nostratibus Theologis, Terminos istos Philosophicos longè ab alio sensu esse acceptus: ita quidem ut Realiter differre, ipsis hoc in Mysterio nihil fuerit, hodieque sit aliud, quàm non imaginariè, non verbotenus, sed Revera differre. Rationale verò discrimen involvat saltem Respectum aliquem, ratione ejus unum ab altero differat: licet interim ratione Rei idem sint.

His ita præsuppositis luculentiùs jam patebit, initiò, Num οὐσία & ὑπόσασις, sive essentia & persona: ac quomodo differant. Et profectò Differentiæ aliquid ipsis invicem intercedere, vel indè patet, quod οὐσία sive Essentia divina, Tribus personis; & quidem singulis non ex parte, sed ex toto ἀδιαιρέτως est Communicabilis: Personæ autem invicem ad se mutuò habent se planè incommunicabiliter. Undè aliam Essentiæ, aliam verò Personæ rationem sive definitionem dari posse: & per consequens non planè unum idemque esse, promptum erit colligere. Cæterùm, quicquid sit discriminis, illud certè neque Essentiale: siquidem Efsentia divina singulis personis ex æquo est Communicabilis: neque etiam Reale constitui debet: siquidem in DEO non differunt reipsa, Natura sive Essentia, & Persona: vel quod idem est, DEUM esse, & Patrem esse. Prædicatur enim de qualibet persona Trinitatis, quod sit DE9. Quid? quòd singulæ personæ simul sumtæ, nihil sunt aliud, quàm unica illa divina Essentia: & hæc extra personas illas, ne quidem cogitando concipi vel potest vel debet. Relinquitur proindè Essentiam & Personam à se invicem differre, tantùm λόγω sive Ratione: propterea quòd alia est Ratio Essentiæ: nempè communicabilis: alia verò personæ: nempè incommunicabilis.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Question III

Yet no distraction, or pulling apart or separation of Nature and Person follows at all. This can be illustrated in this way: God and the Father are said to differ τῷ λόγῳ or by reason: Because although they are One ὀυσίᾳ: meanwhile, however, one thing is predicated of the Father, insofar as he is Father, namely λόγῳ ἀκοινωνήτῳ, which is to beget: but another thing is predicated of the same, insofar as he is God: namely λόγος κοινωνητος, which is, to be of the divine essence. Whence the ancients most correctly said that a Person in divine matters is constituted from a communicable Nature; and an incommunicable difference.

Moreover, the case is clearly different when it is no longer a question of person and Essence: but three persons are compared to one another, and it is asked what distinction exists between them. That they differ is evident even from the fact that the relation of the Father does not belong to the Son: and again the Relation of the Son cannot belong to the Father, nor to the Holy Spirit: and vice versa. Indeed, even the Number Three itself, which is predicated of the Persons, expresses the mark of some Difference quite clearly. For far be it that we should approve in this matter the opinion of Lombard, who asserts that numerical names and words posit nothing when they are used of GOD and the divine persons: but only remove their contrary signification: that is, they only ensure that besides the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, no other or contrary one is understood. lib. 1. Sent. dist. 24. c. 5. Just as indeed not a few even of the Scholastics have fixed an obelisk against the Master in this matter: whence that quatrain was born.

To posit nothing, but only to remove, is the Master's view on names that denote numbers in the Deity. But that matter, little praised thereafter by our Masters, is today of no value.

The occasion for this error seems to have been provided by that Disputation which was then being agitated concerning countable words: Since, namely, God was predicated as One: but the divine Persons were established as three, it was asked whether by the Ternary something Real was added to GOD, besides the divine Essence itself: so that either God himself, or the individual persons, are something συνθετον, that is, composed of different things or beings? When this question was answered in the negative: it was immediately asked further: Why then are these words (ONE and THREE) used of GOD. Here, when Lombard was stuck, he replied that by these words only contrary significations are removed from GOD: but that nothing is posited or affirmed about him. But this response not only did not dissolve the knot, but rather heaped error upon error. For this assertion not only completely removes that difference of the persons among themselves (of which we shall speak presently): But it also fights against all reason and Antiquity. Certainly, when we name three men, or three animals: we do not only remove something: but we posit at the same time τρία ὑφιστάμενα or three beings: so that our mind thinks not so much of negation as of position. St. Basil in his book on the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius, chapter 18, teaches that the use of these numerical words in divine matters is such that the three persons are understood to exist in the Divinity in reality, not only in the thought of the mind, while nevertheless the Essence remains one in number, and not multiple or diverse. And in the preceding chapter, 17, he says: Ἀριθμὸς σημεῖον γνωριστικὸν τẽ πλήθες τῶν ὑποκειμένων παρ' ἡμῶν ἐφαρμόζεται: Number is applied by us for the sake of explaining the multitude of existing things.

It is added that this opinion of Lombard manifestly confirms the heresy of the Sabellians, who established that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same ὑπόστασιν, which is only called by various names for different effects. To oppose this impiety, Orthodox Antiquity established that the divine essence is to be asserted as one in number, in such a way that at the same time in that one and undivided Essence, both the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit constitute a proper ὑπόστασιν or person, distinct from the other person: and in this way those three persons differ greatly from one another. Where, however, one must proceed cautiously in defining the mode of this difference. For at the beginning, the mode of Essential difference must be removed: since these three persons communicate in one and the same nature of Divinity: so that God is not three, but is one in number and is said to be so. Then, neither should the distinction be established as merely Rational. For thus again some support would accrue to the Sabellian heresy. For those things which differ only by reason are not diverse in reality, but only in words. Which, far be it from us to think regarding the three persons of the Divinity. For in this way, the Person of the Father would not be one, the Son's another, the Holy Spirit's another: But only one, which is enunciated by these three words: which is impious and blasphemous to think.

It remains, therefore, that the Three Persons of the Divinity differ from one another Really, that is, not only in name, not only imaginarily: but in truth, indeed most really: so that the personal property of the Father is never, for all eternity, the personal property of the Son or the Holy Spirit, and vice versa: but each person has its own definition: as the following propositions will show more fully.

Latin:

Undètamen nulla prorsus distractio, sive divulsio aut separatio Naturæ & Personæ sequitur. Id quod hunc in modum illustrari potest: Deus & Pater dicuntur differre τῷ λόγῳ sive ratione: Quia licet Unum sint ὀυσίᾳ: interim tamen aliud prædicatur de Patre, quatenusPater, nempè λόγῳ ἀκοινωνήτῳ, qui est Gignere: aliud verò prædicatur de eodem, quatenus Deus est: nempè λόγος κοινωνητος, qui est, esse essentiæ divinæ. Undè rectissimè veteres dixerunt, Personam in divinis constitui ex Natura communicabili; & differentiâ incommunicabili.

Cæterùm, diversa planè est ratio, quando non ampliùs persona & Essentia: sed personæ tres ad se mutuò conferuntur, & quid discriminis illis invicem intercedat, quæritur. Differre autem eas vel indè constat, quod relatio Patris, non competit Filio: & rursum Relatio Filij, neque Patri, neque Spiritui Sancto convenire potest:& vice versâ. Quin imò vel ipse Numerus Ternarius, qui de Personis prædicatur, Differentiæ alicujus notam satis luculenter exprimit. Absit enim, ut hac in parte probemus Lombardi sentetiam asserentis, Nomina & vocabula numeralia nihil ponere, cùm de DEO divinisq́; personis usurpantur: sed duntaxat contrariam sibi significationem removere: hoc est, præstare tantùm, ut præter Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum, nullus alius aut contrarius intelligatur. lib. 1. Sent.dist.24.c.5. Quemadmodum sanè haud pauci etiam ex Scholasticis, Magistro hac in parte obeliscum fixerunt: undè natum illud τετράςιχον.

Ponere nil, imò tantùm removere Magistro Nomina, quæ numeros in Deitate notant. Sed res ista parùm deinceps laudata Magistris A nostris, hodiè, nullius est pretij.

Errori autem huic occasionem præbuisse videtur Disputatio illa, quæ tùm de vocabulis numerabilibus agitabatur: Cum n. Deus prædicaretur Unus: Personæ autem divinæ statuerentur tres, quæsitum fuit, utrum per Ternarium aliquid Reale DEO, præter ipsam divinam Essentiam, adderetur: ita ut, vel Deus ipse, vel singulæ personæ sint quippiam συνθετον, hoc est, ex diversis rebus sive entibus compositum? Ad quod ζήτημα cum Negatè responderetur: statim ulterius quæsitum fuit? Cur ergò vocabula ista (UNUS & TRES) de DEO usurpantur. Hic cùm Lombardo aqua hæreret, respondit, vocib9 istis contrarias tantùm significationes à DEO removeri: non autem quicquam de eodem poni, aut affirmari. Verùm hoc responso non modò non nodum dissolvit, sed magis errorem errore cumulavit. Hæc enim assertio non modo differentiam illam personarum inter se mutuò (de qua mox dicemus) prorsus tollit: Sed & cum omni ratione & Antiquitate pugnat. Certè quando tres homines, aut tria animalia nominamus : non tantùm removemus quidpiam : sed ponimus simul τρία ὑφιστάμενα sive τρία ὄντα: ut mens nostra non tam de ἀποστερήσει, quàm de θέσει cogitet. D. Basilius libro de Spiritu Sancto ad Amphilochium cap. 18. Numeralium istorum vocabulorum usum in divinis eum esse tradit, ut tres personæ reipsâ, non tantùm animi cogitatione in Divinitate esse intelligantur, eâdem nihilominus ac unâ numero, non autem multiplici, aut diversa Essentiâ existente. Et præced. cap. 17. Ἀριθμὸς inquit, σημεῖον γνωριστικὸν τẽ πλήθες τῶν ὑποκειμένων παρ' ἡμῶν ἐφαρμόζεται : Numerus rerum existentium multitudinis explicandæ gratiâ à nobis accommodatur.

Accedit, quod sententia hæc Lombardi Sabellianorum hæresin manifestè confirmat, qui statuerunt, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum, unam & eandem esse ὑπόστασιν, quæ tantùm variis nominibus, pro diversis effectis appelletur. Cui impietati ut obviam irent, Antiquitas Orthodoxa, ita unam numero divinam essentiam asserendam esse statuit, ut simul in una illa & indivisa Essentia, & Pater & Filius & Spiritus Sanctus, propriam & ab alterâ persona distinctam ὑπόστασιν sive personam constituat: & vel hoc pacto tres illæ personæ plurimùm à se mutuò differant. Ubi tamen in definiendo differentiæ hujus modo cautè progrediendum est. Nam initiò removeri debet Modus differentiæ Essentialis: Siquidem tres hæ personæ, unâ eademque Divinitatis naturâ communicant: ut non tres, sed unus numero sit & dicatur esse Deus. Deindè neque Discrimen constitui debet tantùm Rationale. Sic enim rursus hæresi Sabellianæ patrocinii aliquid accederet. Quæ enim ratione tantùm differunt, ea non reipsâ, sed vocabulis duntaxat diversa sunt. Quod absit, ut de tribus personis Divinitatis saltem cogitemus. Hoc enim pacto non alia esset Persona Patris, alia Filij, alia Spiritus Sancti: Sed una duntaxat, quæ tribus hisce vocabulis enuncietur: id quod cogitatu impium ac blasphemum.

Relinquitur ergò Tres Personas Divinitatis à se mutuò differre Realiter, hoc est, non nominetenus tantùm, non imaginariè solùm: sed reverà, imò realissimè: ita quidem, ut proprietas personalis patris, nunquàm in omnem æternitatem, sit aut fiat proprietas personalis Filij aut Spiritus Sancti, & vice versa: sed quælibet persona propriam definitionem habeat: uti propositiones sequentes fusiùs ostendent.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition V

The order of the persons of the most holy and undivided Trinity does not depend either on time, or on dignity, or on the order of nature, or on composition, but only on the mode, or τάξις, that is, the order of production.

Exposition.

In the refutation of the Sabellian heresy, among other things, it also began to be asked: Can a certain order of persons be given in the divine? And what is the foundation of that very order? Or, because of the unity of the divine essence, is it right to place or name this or that person indiscriminately, whether in the first, intermediate, or last place? But the Orthodox Church, having most rightly applied this question to the touchstone of the Word of God, has defined that a certain and altogether immutable order of persons must be established in the divine. But it has determined that the foundation of this order is by no means to be taken from time, as if by reason of time the Father were prior to the Son, and again the Father and the Son were in time prior to the Holy Spirit. For the unity of the divine essence does not permit this at all: for if the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are that one eternal God, as they certainly are, then it is necessary that they themselves also be coessential, just as they are coeternal, among themselves. Furthermore, because the individual persons are of the same majesty and omnipotence, the Church has most rightly denied that either the Father is prior to the Son, or the Father and the Son are prior to the Holy Spirit in dignity. By the same reasoning, it has not approved that manner of speaking whereby the producing persons are said to be prior to the produced by the order of nature. For because nature and essence are equivalent in the divine, in this way the producing persons would be established as prior to the produced by essence itself, which is impious and blasphemous. Moreover, there exists no foundation in all of Scripture from which that mode of priority or order, which is of nature, can be elicited. Thus that mode of priority which is of composition clearly expires in this place, since neither into the divine essence nor into the persons of the Trinity can any composition, which argues the imperfection of matter, fall, as was shown above.

It is added that the distinction of the post-predicament of PRIOR is applied either not at all or certainly most improperly to declare the order of the persons of the Trinity. For speaking properly, God and the persons of the Trinity can be referred neither to the class of ante-predicaments, nor to that of predicaments, nor to that of post-predicaments. Therefore, the Church has most rightly pronounced that the cause or foundation of this order depends on the order of production, which is revealed in the sacred writings. For because the generation of the Son pertains to the Father, the Father will certainly constitute the first person, and the Son the second; and again, because not the Father alone, but the Father and the Son together by breathing forth produce the Holy Spirit, the Spirit will certainly constitute the third person by reason of this production. That this very τάξις or order of the producing and the produced must be holily observed is clearly evident even by the example of Christ, who is read to have confirmed this very order of persons in the formula of baptism to be conferred in the name of the most holy Trinity, Matthew 28:19.

But it is disputed in this place, since the order of persons depends on the order of the producing, how many modes can and ought to be given by which the divine persons are constituted: whether only those three already designated, namely, to beget, to be begotten, to proceed; or whether there are more?

Most Scholastics, and among these especially Thomas in part 1, question 28, article 4, assigns four modes of production: namely, 1. Paternity, 2. Filiation, 3. Spiration, 4. Procession. Indeed, in the subsequent article 32, article 3, he adds one more mode: saying there are five notions in the divine: 1. Innascibility, 2. Paternity, 3. Filiation, 4. Common Spiration, 5. Procession. By 'notion,' however, the Scholastics understand nothing else in this place than the proper way of knowing a divine person, as Cajetan defines in article 2. Scotus, that he may be more liberal than the others, adds a sixth notion, namely, inspirability in the Son: saying, just as in the Father innascibility, which is the negation of procession, is a certain note distinct from paternity and spiration, so inspirability is a certain notion in the Son, distinct from filiation and spiration. Which signifies the negation of passive spiration, just as innascibility in the Father signifies every negation of passive procession. Scotus in 1, d. 28, q. 1, art. 3.

Moreover, all this contradiction or difficulty is most easily removed by a more accurate distinction of the hypostatic properties which are inherent in the individual persons. For there are other personal properties that are relative, constituting the person himself, which indeed have a relation to another person and constitute the order of those producing and those produced: such properties are only three: To beget, To be begotten, To proceed: or, Paternity, Filiation, Procession. For as regards Spiration, that is certainly not the property of one person only: but is common to the Father and the Son, who by a certain common act produce the eternal Spirit by spirating. Wherefore this common spiration can and ought to be called the χαρακτηρισμός of neither the Father nor the Son, but rather of both with respect to the third person. Furthermore, there are other personal properties which are not relative-constituting, that is, they do not have a relation to another person with respect to production: for they do not define the person as to what he is by reason of production, but only as to what he is in himself and from himself, that is, insofar as he obtains something distinct from another person. As for example, Innascibility is indeed a personal property of the Father: but not insofar as he relates relatively to producing the Son: but only insofar as he is viewed from himself and in himself: and insofar as he has this peculiarity, that he is produced by no one else, but rather is the fountain, principality, and Origin of the Godhead personally.

Latin:

ORdo personarum Sacrosanctæ & Individuæ Trinitatis, non dependet vel à tempore:vel à dignitate:vel ab ordine Naturæ : vel à compositione:sed tantùm à modo, sive τάξει, hocest, ordine productionis.

Ἔκθεσις.

IN refutatione hæreseos Sabellianæ, inter reliqua etiam quæri cœptum est : An certus personarum Ordo in divinis dari possit : & Quodnam illius ipsius Ordinis sit Fundamentum? An verò propter Unitatem Essentiæ divinæ, fas sit promiscuè vel hanc vel illam personam, sive primo, sive intermedio, sive postremo loco ponere aut nominare? Rectissimè autem Orthodoxa Ecclesia, Quæstione hac ad trutinam verbi DEI adhibitâ, definivit, certum omninò & planè immutabilem ordine Personarum in divinis constituendum esse. Cæterùm ordinis hujus fundamentum minimè omnium statuit desumendum esse à Tempore : ac si ratione temporis Pater prior esset Filio: & rursum Pater & Filius tempore essent priores Spiritu Sancto. Hoc enim Essentiæ divinæ unitas minimè permittit : Nam si Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus, unus sunt DEUS ille æternus, uti certè sunt: utique ipsi quoque inter se, uti ὁμοόσιοι coëssentiales, sic etiam συναΐδιοι sint, necesse est. Deindè, Quia personæ singulæ ejusdem sunt Majestatis & Omnipotentiæ, rectissimè Ecclesia negavit, vel Patrem Filio, vel Patrem & Filium Spiritu Sancto priores esse Dignitate. Pari ratione neque illam loquendi rationem approbavit, ut Personæ producentes dicerentur priores esse productis, Ordine Naturæ. Quia enim Natura & essentia in divinis æquipollent, utique hoc pacto personæ producentes statuerentur priores esse productis, ipsâ essentiâ : id quod impium & blasphemum : Quid: quòd nullum in universa Scriptura fundamentum extat, ex quo modus iste prioritatis sive ordinis, qui Naturæ est, possit elici. Sic modus ille prioritatis, qui est συνθέσεως hoc loco planè expirat: Siquidem neque in Essentiam divinam, neque in personas Trinitatis, ulla compositio, quæ materiæ imperfectionem arguit, cadere potest, uti supra ostensum.

Accedit, quod distinctio postpædicamenti PRIUS, vel planè non, vel certè improprijssimè ad declarandum ordinem personarum Trinitatis accommodatur. Propriè enim loquendo Deus & personæ Trinitatis neque ad Anteprædicamentorum, neque in Prædicamentorũ, neque in Postprædicamentorum classem referri possunt. Rectissimè proindè Ordinis hujus causam sive Fundamentum ab ordine productionis, qui in sacris revelatus est, dependere, Ecclesia pronunciavit. Quia enim Patri competit Generatio Filij; utique Pater primam, Filius secundam personam constituet: Et rursus; quia non solus Pater: sed Pater & Filius simul spirando producunt Spiritum Sanctum: utique Spiritus ratione productionis hujus tertiam personam constituet. Quam ipsam τάξιν sive ordinem producentium & productorum sanctè observandum esse, vel Christi Exemplo liquidò patet, qui in formula Baptismi in nomine Sacro sanctæ Trinitatis conferendi, hunc ipsum personarum ordinem confirmasse legitur, Matth. 28, 19.

Cæterùm controvertitur hoc loco, cum Ordo Personarum dependeat ab ordine producentium, Quotnam dari possint & debeant Modi, per quos personæ divinæ constituantur: An tantùm tres illi, jam designati, nempè Gignere, Gigni, Procedere: An verò plures?

Scholastici pleriq;, & inter hos cumprimis Thomas part. 1. Quæst. 28. art. 4. Quatuor productionis modos assignat: nempè 1. Paternitatem, 2 Filiationem 3. Spirationem, 4. Processionem. Quin subseq. 32. art. 3. unum adhuc modum superaddit: Quinque, inquiens, sunt notiones in divinis: 1. Innascībilitas, 2. Paternitas. 3. Filiatio, 4. Communis Spiratio. 5. Processio. Per Notionem autem nihil intelligunt Scholastici hoc loco aliud, quàm propriam rationem cognoscendi divinam personam, uti definit Cajetanus art. 2. Scotus, ut liberalior sit reliquis, sextam addit notionem, nempè inspirabilitatem in Filio: Sicut, inquiens, in patre innascibilitas, quæ est negatio processionis, est quædam nota distincta, à Paternitate & Spiratione: Ita inspirabilitas est quædam notio in Filio, distincta à Filiatione & Spiratione. Quæ significat negationem Spirationis passivæ, sicut innascibilitas in patre significat omnem negationem processionis passivæ. Scot. in 1. d. 28. q. 1. art 3.

Cæterùm omnis isthæc sive contrarietas sive difficultas facillimè tollitur, per accuratiorem distinctionem proprietatum hypostaticarum, quæ singulis personis insunt. Aliæ enim sunt proprietates personales Relativæ, personam ipsam constituentes, quæ nimirum Relationem ad aliam personam habent, & ordinem producentium & productorum constituunt: Quales proprietates sunt tantùm tres: Gignere, Gigni, Procedere: sive, Paternitas, Filiatio, Processio. Nam quoad Spirationem, illa certè non est Unius tantùm personæ proprietas: sed communis Patri & Filio, qui uno quodam communi actu, æternum Spiritum spirando producunt. Quare communis etiam hæc spiratio, neq; Patris, neq; Filij, sed potiùs utriusq; χαρακτηρισμός respectu tertiæ personæ dici potest & debet. Deindè verò aliæ sunt proprietates personales, quæ non sunt Relativæ constituentes, hoc est, non relationem habent ad alteram personá respectu productionis: neq; enim personam, qualis ratione productionis sit, sed tantùm qualis in se, & ex se sit, hoc est, quatenù aliquid ab altera persona distinctũ obtineat, definiunt. Ut exempli gratia, Innascibilitas est quidem proprietas personalis Patris: sed non quatenus ille Relativè se habeat ad producendum Filium: sed tantùm quatenus ex sese & perse spectatur: & quatenù hoc peculiare habet, ut à nemine alio sit productș, sed potiù est fons, principatus & Origo Divinitatis personaliter.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition VI. Phil. page 310. The eternal Father is a person not born, but who begat the Son from eternity into the image of Himself

The same must be established regarding the passive inspirability of the Son, about which Scotus discourses. For this belongs to the Son, not insofar as he relates relatively to producing the Holy Spirit: but only insofar as he obtains this, which is distinct and peculiar from the Holy Spirit, that he was produced not by breathing, but by begetting. Therefore, although the properties of this second kind, by reason of their signification, have a certain general relation to the remaining persons: yet they do not have that Relation which is constitutive of personality: just as the three properties enumerated above have such a Relation. It is added that innascibility and common spiration are understood not obscurely under the remaining three relative constitutive personal properties. For because it is the personal property of the Son alone to be Begotten: it follows spontaneously that this property cannot be predicated of the Father: But that innascibility belongs to him. For otherwise the Father would not constitute a proper person distinct from the Son: if he obtained the same personal property as the Son: Similarly, because it is the personal property of the Holy Spirit alone to proceed from the Father and the Son: certainly the common spiration of the Father and the Son is spontaneously presupposed. These things having been discussed in this way, it is prompt to conclude that that scrupulous disputation of both the Scholastics and others concerning the Number of notions in the persons is not needed at all.

PROPOSITION VI.

The eternal Father is a person not born, but who from eternity begat the Son, the image of himself: and together with the Son breathes the consubstantial Holy Spirit.

Ἔκθεσις.

Various things are accustomed to be moved concerning this proposition, which deserve a more accurate explanation altogether. For first it is asked, Whether the first person of the Divinity is named Father because he has his Origin from No one: or whether another cause for this denomination can be given? Although indeed the Scholastics torture themselves wonderfully concerning this Question: yet they implicate the matter itself more than they explain it: as is especially evident from book 1 of the Sentences of Lombard, distinction 29. But the most convenient answer will be for us to say that the Father is called the first person not from such a property by which he is distinguished from only one hypostasis: Such as being ἀγέννητον, which also belongs to the Holy Spirit, Who is himself also Unbegotten: Such as also the property of Breathing the Holy Spirit, Which the Son also performs: But that the denomination is made from the power and faculty of a father, which is, To beget a Son consubstantial to himself. Which property belongs neither to the Son nor to the Holy Spirit.

Then it is asked, In what respect the Father is called Unbegotten, or as our author speaks, a person not born. Augustine, book 5 on the Trinity, chapters 6 and 7, and many others who followed him, distinguish very solicitously between these two, to be Unbegotten and to be not begotten, as if they were words of different signification and notion. But the matter having been weighed a little more deeply, it is evident that that distinction betrays a play of human wit more than anything of solidity. The Greek Theologians, certainly, otherwise most exercised in this argument, and vexed by the Eunomians and other heretics especially because of this single word Ἀγεννήτου, never and nowhere distinguished between τὸ ἀγέννητον and μὴ γεννητον: as is evident from Epiphanius in the heresy of the Eunomians and Aëtians.

Damascene, expressly discussing this term, writes that a distinction must be made between τὸ ἀγέννητον with a double nu and τὸ ἀγένητον with a single nu. Because ἀγέννητον simply excludes every thought of emanation, and thus properly belongs to the Father alone; but τὸ ἀγένητον only removes that thought of emanation which occurs in the manner of created things: and in this respect τὸ ἀγένητον with a single nu would belong to all three persons, lib. 1. Orth. fid. cap. 9. But having bid farewell to these subtleties, since they seem to explain the matter less solidly and sufficiently, we determine that it should rather be observed that the word Ingenitus (Unbegotten) is not accepted by the Latin Fathers in one and the same sense. Augustine in his books on the Trinity takes τὸ Ingenitum for that which is devoid of all production, and is clearly not from any other. And in this sense he rightly affirms that the Father alone is Ingenitus, lib. 15. de Trin. c. 26. And in this respect he also rightly denies in his book to Orosius that the Holy Spirit can be called Ingenitus. Jerome, however, and others who followed him, call him Ingenitus simply who is not begotten: that is, who, although he is produced by another, is not produced by way of Generation. In which sense they thought that not only the Father, but also the Holy Spirit could be called Ingenitus. We, to settle this controversy in a few words, determine that it must be answered simply that the Father is called Ingenitus both privatively and negatively. Privatively, because he is not produced in the manner of the Son through Generation: Negatively, because the person of the Father is not produced by any other mode of production, whatever may be imagined: as Thomas also, not inconveniently, defined this dispute from the Scholastics, part 1, Quest. 38, Art. 4. Thirdly, it is asked, when God the Father begat the Son, does the Nature or Divine essence beget? This question seemed very difficult to explain, not only to the Scholastics, but also to certain more recent Doctors. Robert Bellarmine, in the preface which he chose to prefix to the second General controversy, which is about Christ, disapproves of and rejects the affirmative of this question as erroneous in Johannes Wigandus, writing thus: Wigandus, in his book against the new Arians, approves and defends Luther's opinion: that the Essence in the divine [nature] begets and is begotten: From which opinion, however, whether Wigandus likes it or not, it follows that the nature of the Father is one, and the nature of the Son is another, since nothing can beget itself, and nothing can be generated by itself. But this was first moved

The question confirmed and later augmented by the Master of the Sentences, book 1, dist. 5, c. 5, and following, is this controversy around A. D. 1190, as is evident from the acts of the Roman Synod, c. 2, under Innocent III, and from the Decretals of Gregory IX, cap. Firmiter, and cap. Damnamus, tit. de Trinitate. But however that may be, among the Scholastic Doctors themselves who have commented on the Master of the Sentences, no slight discrepancy is detected. For although Thomas, part 1, Quest. 29, art. 5, likewise William of Ockham, lib. 1, dist. 5, Quest. 1, and also John Durandus, John Scotus, and many others have defined that the Divine Essence neither generates nor is generated: there are nevertheless others who have cried out against them with full mouth: such as Richard of Villanova, who (erring on the side of ὑπερβολῆς) affirmed that the Divine essence generates and is generated, even insofar as it is viewed by itself and nakedly, outside of ὑπόστασιν. Following him, Joachim the Abbot of Fiore wrote expressly against this passage of Lombard: for which reason he was condemned by Innocent III in the Lateran Council. Basil, lib. 1, against Eunomius, testifies that this axiom of theology has always been held as indubitable: τὸ τὸν θεὸν μήτε παρ' ἑαυτῦ, μήτε παρ' ἑτέρꙋ γενέσθαι, that GOD is neither begotten by himself nor by another: which we are most persuaded Basil understood concerning the Divine Essence considered absolutely and by itself. Thus, therefore, this question was fought over no less dangerously than curiously.

But as for what can and ought to be answered to him in an orthodox manner, it pleases me to begin by making it clear with the words of Luther, whom Bellarmine lashes without merit. He says this, however, in Vol. 1, Jena, page 572, edition of the year 1556, in the Disputation on the Mystery of the Holy Trinity, held in the year 1544, thesis 15 and following: The Master of the Sentences did not teach quite correctly that the divine essence neither generates nor is generated: but he is correctly rebuked by Joachim the Abbot, because he asserted a Quaternity in the Divine. Nor does the chapter Firmiter, de Trinitate, do anything, proving the Master and condemning the Abbot. For since the Master could not deny from Augustine that Substance is generated from substance, wisdom from wisdom: he could in no way deny Essence from Essence, and whatever can be said so similarly about the true GOD, except that all other things are suspect which that abomination, standing in the holy place, has determined. The Master fears, it seems, that two or three Essences might be spoken of if one were born of another. But he ought similarly to have feared that two or three Gods might be made if one were generated from another. We concede that Essence in a creature is not spoken of relatively (to use Augustine's word) but only absolutely. But when he saw Substance, Wisdom, Nature, and the like in the divine accepted relatively by Augustine and Hilary, there was no reason why he should deny that Essence is spoken of relatively, and move such great disturbances over one word. Whence also to the Cardinal of Cambrai, most learned among the Scholastics, this determination did not unjustly displease greatly. Thus far Luther, whose decision rests chiefly on two arguments. The former is taken from the absurd consequence: For if we posit that the divine essence neither generates nor is generated: it follows that that Essence, which neither generates nor is generated, is something different from the Essence of the Father who generates, and from the Essence of the Son who is generated: and consequently that a Quaternity must be posited in the divine: namely, those Three persons which we confess: and then that divine Essence, neither generating nor generated. The latter argument is taken from that most useful distinction by which the divine Nature or Essence is accepted either absolutely or relatively. Absolutely, indeed, insofar as it is common to all three persons: but relatively, insofar as it is determined in some certain person. Therefore, even if the divine Essence neither generates nor is generated insofar as it is accepted absolutely: yet it is piously and orthodoxly posited that the divine Essence generates and is generated insofar as it is accepted relatively. For just as in the Article concerning the person of Christ the divine Essence or GOD is said to be Incarnate, not insofar as that Essence is common to all three persons: for thus the Whole Trinity would be incarnate: but insofar as the word of the divine Essence or God is referred relatively or determinately to the person of the Son. Thus in the present Question, the act of begetting falls not upon the essence considered absolutely, but upon the Essence of the Father. Whence it is now easy to gather what ought to be answered to the Reason of the Master, asserting, If Essence generates Essence, or is generated by Essence, there will be more Essences in the Divine in number, namely, the Generated and the Generating. For the paralogism of the vicious consequence is most manifest: which can be demonstrated to the eye even by this single objection: For just as more Gods are not posited, although according to the Decree of the Council of Nicaea, we truly believe GOD true from GOD true: so neither are more Essences in number constituted, although we believe that the divine Essence, not indeed ἁπλῶς, but accepted relatively, both generates and is generated. The reason is: Because the generating Essence and the generated Essence in the divine are not distinguished from each other by number: which is falsely presupposed by the Master: But the Essence is and remains One in Number: which insofar as it generates, constitutes the Person of the Father who generates: but insofar as it is generated, it constitutes the person of the Son who is generated. And although in creatures these things cannot be perceived by thought: if, however, we wish the Mystery itself of the Unity of the divine Essence in the Trinity of persons to be preserved: this must be posited entirely, that the Son has not only the person or personal property: but the essence itself also from the eternal Father, yet without any beginning of time.

From this it is also clear what may be answered to Bellarmine’s little argument, by which he rises up against Luther’s opinion: It is indeed true, this Jesuit axiom: Nothing can beget itself, and nothing can be generated by itself: But it is true only of those things which differ not only in persons, or ὑποστάσεσι: but also in essence itself. Now, however, because in divine matters the begetting Essence does not differ in number from the begotten Essence, just as it does not differ from the proceeding person: although by reason of characteristic properties they do in reality differ from one another in number: this argument concludes nothing at all: because, the fallacy of four terms having been demonstrated, it spontaneously collapses and expires.

These things having been thus discussed, it becomes manifest. 1. In what sense this Rule has deserved belief in the Schools of the Theologians: The divine Essence neither begets, nor is begotten: then, however, what is to be thought concerning those four propositions. 1. The Essence begets the Essence: 2. The Essence begets the person. 3. The person begets the Essence: 4. The person begets the person. For it is asked, which of these is true, which is false? It is answered, that the first, if the word Essence is taken absolutely, as also the second and third, are to be rejected as impious and erroneous: but that only the fourth and last is true: yet not so simply, as if a person begat a person outside the essence: which would constitute a Quaternity in the divine: But with this declaration, that a person begets a Person within one and the same most simple Essence of the Divinity: Whence it happens, that in the diversity of persons, the communication of the Essence nevertheless has a place.

Finally, it is also clear from this what can and ought to be answered to those classic objections which have been opposed to the purity of this doctrine by heretics. Such as: I. If GOD is begotten of GOD: then there are many Gods: But the former is true according to our assertion: Therefore the latter must also be conceded. II. The begetting God is not the begotten God. But the begetting GOD is GOD essentially. Therefore the begotten God is not GOD essentially. III. The begetter and the begotten can never be one and the same. Now, however, according to our assertion, the Essence in GOD the Father is the begetting Essence: In the Son, however, it is the Begotten Essence. Therefore the Essence of the Father and of the Son is not the same.

For in these and similar arguments is committed the fallacy σόφισμα παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: which is clearly evident from those things which have been discussed thus far. For the word GOD sometimes denotes ὀσίας absolutely, sometimes denotes ὑπόστασιν relatively. When therefore it is asserted by us that GOD is begotten of GOD, we do not wish the Essence of GOD, taken absolutely, to be denoted by the word GOD: But we denote limitatively or determinately τὸ εἶναι ὑποστατικον. In which same sense the word GOD is also taken in the major proposition of the second argument. For the begetting GOD is the begotten God ὑποστατικῶς, or considered relatively with respect to the person: Essentially, however, the Father and the Son are One GOD. Thus the Major proposition of the Third argument is indeed true with respect to the persons: but most false with respect to the Essence. Now, because in the Minor a manifest consideration of the diversity of persons is instituted: the Conclusion is certainly inferred most viciously from a confusion of the Absolute and the Relative.

Latin:

Quod ipsum de inspirabilitate passiva filij, de qua Scotus disserit, est statuendum. Competit enim hæc Filio, non quatenus ille Relativè se habet ad producendum Spiritum Sanctum: sed tantùm quatenus hoc à Spiritu Sancto distinctum & peculiare obtinet, quod non spirando, sed gignendo sit productus. Proindè etsi secundi hujus generis proprietates, ratione significationis suæ, generalis quandam relationem ad reliquas personas habent: tamen non habent eam Relationem, quæ est constitutiva personalitatis: quemadmodum talem Relationem habent tres suprà enumeratæ proprietates. Accedit quòd innascibilitas & communis spiratio sub reliquis tribus proprietatibus personalibus relativis constituentibus haud obscurè intelliguntur. Quia enim Solius Filij proprietas personalis est, Genitum esse: utique ultrò consequitur, hoc proprium de Patre non posse prædicari: Sed innascibilitatem ipsi competere. Alioqui enim non propriam ac à Filio distinctam personam Pater constitueret: si eandem cum Filio proprietatem personalem obtineret: Consimiliter, quia Solius Spiritus Sancti proprietas personalis est, procedere à Patre & Filio: certè ultrò præsupponitur communis spiratio Patris & Filij. Quibus ita discussis, scrupulosâ illâ tùm Scholasticorum, tùm aliorum disputatione de Numero notionum in personis, minimè opus esse, promptum est colligere.

PROPOSITIO VI.

PAter æternus est persona non nata, sed quæ genuit ab æterno Filium imaginem sui: & unà cum Filio spirat Spiritum Sanctum consubstantialem.

Ἔκθεσις.

VAria circa hanc propositionem moveri solent, quæ accuratiorem explicationem omninò merentur. Primùm enim quæritur, Num prima persona Divinitatis ideò nominetur Pater, quia ea à Nemine Originem habet: vel an alia hujus denominationis causa dari possit? Quàquam verò circa Quæstionem istam mirè se tor quent Scholastici: rem tamen ipsam magis implicant quàm explicant: uti cùmprimis patet ex lib. 1. Sentent. Lombardi dist 29. Commodissima autem responsio fuerit, ut dicamus, Patrem dici primam personam non à tali proprio, quo distingvatur ab una duntaxat hypostasi: Quale est ἀγέννητον esse, quod etiam Spiritui Sancto competit, Qui & ipse est Ingenitus: Quale item proprium est Spirare Spiritum Sanctum, Quod ipsum præstat etiam Filius: Sed fieri denominationem, à vi & facultate patriâ, quæ est, Gignere Filium sibi consubstantialem. Quæ proprietas neque Filio competit neque Spiritui Sancto.

Deindè quæritur, Quo respectu Pater dicatur Ingenit9, sive uti autor noster loquitur, Persona nõ nata. Augustinus lib. 5. de Trin. cap 6. & 7. cumque secuti plures alij sollicitè admodum distingvũt inter hæc duo, Ingenitum esse & non genitum esse, Quasi sint diversæ significationis & notionis vocabula. Verùm paulò altiùs re expensa, patet lusum magis ingenij humani, quàm aliquid soliditatis distinctionem illam prodere. Græci certè Theologi, aliàs in hoc argumento exercitatissimi, & ab Eunomianis, alijsque hæreticis maximè propter unicam hanc vocem Ἀγεννήτυ vexati, nunquàm & nuspiam inter τὸ ἀγέννητον & μὴ γεννητον distinxerunt: uti patet ex Epipha nio in hæresi Eunomianorum & Aëtianorum.

Damasceenus de voce hac ex professo disputans, distingvendum esse, scribit, inter τὸ ἀγέννητον per duplex v: & inter τὸ ἀγένητον per simplex v. propterea quod ἀγέννητον omnem emanationis cogitationem simpliciter excludat, & ita propriè Soli Patri conveniat: τὸ ἀγένητον autem tantùm removeat eam emanationis cogitationem, qua fiat in modũ rerum creatarum: & hoc respectu τὰ ἀγένητον per simplex, v. omnibus tribus personis competeret, lib. 1. Orth fid. cap 9. Sed subtilitatibus istis valere jussis, quippè quæ minùs solidè ac sufficienter rem explicare videntur, id potiùs observandum esse statuimus, vocem Ingeniti, non uno eodemque sensu à Patribus Latinis accipi. Augustinus in suis de Trinitate libris sumit τὸ Ingenitum pro eo quod omnis productionis expers, planè non est de alio aliquo. Et hoc sensu rectè affirmat, Solum Patrem esse Ingenitum lib. 15. de Trin. c. 26. & hoc respectu rectè etiam negat in libro ad Orosium, Spiritum Sanctum dici posse Ingenitum. Hieronymus verò, & eum secuti alij, Ingenitum simpliciter vocant eum, qui non est Genit9: hoc est, qui, licèt producatur ab alio: non tamen per modum Generationis producitur. Quo sensu non Patrem modò, sed & Spiritum Sanctum dici posse Ingenitum existimarunt. Nos ut paucis controversiam hanc expediamus, simpliciter respondendum esse statuimus, Patré dici Ingenitum & privatitè & negativè. Privativè, Quia non in modum Filij per Generationem est productus: Negativè: Quia nullo alio productionis modo, quicunque etiam fingatur, patris persona est producta: uti ex Scholasticis quoq;, haud incommodè, disputationem hanc definivit To mas part. 1 Quæst. 38. Art. 4. Tertiò quæritur, cum Deus Pater genuerit Filium, An Natura sive essentia Divina gignat? Difficilis perquàm explicatu visa fuit hæc Quæstio, non modò Scholasticis, sed & recentioribus quibusdam Doctoribus. Robertus Bellarminus in præfatione, quam secundæ controversiæ Generali, quæ est de Christo, præfigere voluit, Affirmativam Quæstionis hujus, tanquam erroneam improbat ac rejicit in Johanne Vvigando, sic scribens: Vvigandus in libro contra novos Arianos, Lutheri sententiam approbat ac defendit; Essentiam in divinis generare & generari: Ex qua tamen sententia, velit nolit Wigandus, efficitur, aliã Patris, aliam Filij esse naturam, cum nihil possit seipsum gignere, nihil à seipso generari possit. Mota autem primum fuit hæc

Quæstio à Magistro sententiarum lib. 1. dist. 5. c. 5. & seqq. confirmata posteà & aucta est hæc controversia circa A. D. 1190. uti patet ex actis Romanæ Synodi, c. 2. sub Innocentio. III. & ex Decretalibus Gregorij IX. cap. Firmiter, & cap. Damnamus, tit. de Trinitate. Sed quicquid sit, inter ipsos tamen Doctores Scholasticos, qui in Magistrum Sent. commentati sunt, haud levis deprehenditur discrepantia. Etsi n. Thomas part. 1. Quæst. 29. art 5. Ité Wilhelmus Occam. lib. 1. dist. 5. Quæst. 1. Johannes etiam Durandus, Johannes Scotus, & plerique alij definiverunt, Divinam Essentiam neque generare, neque generari: Sunt tamen alij, qui istis pleno ore reclamarunt: ut Richardus de villanova, qui, (ex parte ὑπερβολῆς peccans) affirmavit, Divinam essentiam generare & generari, etiam, quatenùs per se, & nudè spectatur, extra ὑπόστασιν. Quem secutus Joachimus Abbas Florentinus, ex professo contra hunc locum Lombardi scripsit: Qua de causa ab Innocentio III. in Concilio Lateranensi damnatus fuit. Basilius lib. 1. contra Eunomium testatur, semper pro indubitato habitum fuisse hoc Theologiæ axioma: τὸ τὸν θεὸν μήτε παρ' ἑαυτῦ, μήτε παρ' ἑτέρꙋ γενέσθαι, DEUM neque à se, neque ab alio gigni: id quod Basilium de divinâ Essentiâ absolutè, & per se consideratâ, intellexisse, habemus persuasissimum. Sic ergò de hac quæstione non minus periculosè, quàm curiosè pugnatum fuit.

Cæterùm, quid ad eum responderi orthodoxè possit ac debeat, placet initiò verbis Lutheri, quem Bellarminus præter meritum flagellat, expeditum facere. Sic autem ille Tom. 1. Jenensi pag. 572. edit. anni 1556. Disputatione de Mysterio S. Trinitatis, anno 1544. habita: thesi 15. & seqq. Magister sententiarum non satis rectè docuit, essentiam divinam nec generare, nec generari: sed rectè à Joachimo Abbate reprehenditur, quod in Divinis Quaternitatem asseruerit. Nec quicquam facit cap. Firmiter, de Trinitate, probans Magistrum & damnans Abbatem. Cumenim negare ex Augustino non potuit Magister, Substantiam de substantia, sapientiam de sapientia generari: nullo modo potuit negare Essentiam de Essentia, & quicquid de DEO vero, tam simile dici potest, præterquàm, quòd omnia alia suspecta sunt, quæ ista abominatio, stans in loco sancto determinavit. Metuit, ut videtur, Magister, ne duæ vel tres Essentiæ dicerentur, si una de alia nasceretur. At similiter illi metuendū fuit, ne duo vel tres Dij fierent, si unus de alio generaretur. Concedimus Essentiam in creatura, non dici relativè (ut Augustini verbo utar) sed absolutè tantùm. Sed cum Substantiam, Sapientiam, Naturam & similia in divinis apud Augustinum & Hilarium accipi relativè videret, non erat, cur Essentiam negaret relativè dici, & ob unum vocabulum tantas turbas moveret. Undè & Cardinali Cameracensi doctissimo inter Scholasticos, ista determinatio nõ injuriâ valdè displicuit. Hactenus Lutherus, cujus decisio duobꝫ potissimùm argumentis nititur. Prius desumptum ab absurdo consequente: Si enim statuamus, Essentiam divinam nec generare, nec generari: Sequitur Essentiam illam, quæ nec generat, nec generata est, diversi aliquid esse ab Essentia Patris generantis, & ab Essentia Filij generati: & per consequens Quaternitatem in divinis statuendam esse: nempè Tres illas, quas confitemur, personas: & deindè Essentiam illam divinam, nec generantem, nec generatam. Posterius argumentum est petitum ex utilissima illa distinctione, quâ Natura sive Essentia divina vel absolutè, vel Relativè accipitur. Absolutè quidem, prout ea communis est omnibus tribus personis: Relativè verò, quatenus ea in certa aliquâ persona determinatur. Proindè etsi Essentia divina neque generat, neque generatur, quatenus absolutè accipitur: tamen piè & orthodoxè statuitur Essentia divina generare & generari, quatenus relatè accipitur. Quemadmodum enim in Articulo de persona Christi Essentia divina sive DEUS dicitur Incarnatus, non quatenùs Essentia illa communis est, omnibus tribus personis: Sic enim Tota Trinitas esset incarnata: sed quatenùs Essentiæ divinæ sive Dei vocabulum relatè sive determinatè ad personam Filij refertur. Sic in præsenti Quæstione, Gignendi actio, non in essentiam absolutè consideratam, sed in Essentiam Patris cadit. Undè promptum jam est colligere, quid responderi debeat ad Rationem Magistri, asserentis, Si Essentia Essentiam generat, aut ab Essentia generatur, plures erunt in Divinis Essentia numero, Generata videlicet & Generans. Nam paralogismus vitiosi consequentis est manifestissimus: id quod vel unicâ hâc ἐνστάσει ad oculum demonstrari potest: Quemadmodum enim non plures Dij statuuntur, licet secundum Decretum Concilij Nicœni, verè credamus DEUM verum de DEO vero: Sic neque plures numero Essentiæ constituuntur, licet credamus, Essentiam divinam nō quidem ἁπλῶς, sed relatè acceptam & generare & generari. Ratio est: Quia Essentia generans, & Essentia generata in divinis, non distingvuntur inter se numero: id quod à Magistro falsò præsupponitur: Sed Una Numero est & manet Essentia: quæ quatenus generat, constituit Personam patris generantis: quatenus verò genita est, constituit personam Filij geniti. Et quanquam in creaturis ista percipi cogitatione non possunt: si tamen ipsum Mysterium Unitatis Essentiæ divinæ in Trinitate personarum salvum esse volumus: hoc omninò statuendum fuerit, Filium, non modò personam sive personalem proprietatem: sed ipsam quoque essentiam ab æterno patre, sine ullo tamen temporis principio, habere.

Patet hinc etiam, quid ad Bellarmini ratiunculam, quâ adversus Lutheri sententiam insurgit, responderi possit: Verum quidem est axioma hoc Jesuvviticum: Nihil seipsum potest gignere, & nihil à seipso potest generari: Sed verum est tantùm de ijs, quæ non modò personis, sive ὑποστάσεσι: sed ipsâ etiam essentiâ differunt. Jam verò, quia in divinis Essentia generans, ab Essentia gignente Numero non differt, quemadmodum nec à procedente persona: licet ratione proprietatum characteristicarum numero à se invicem reverâ distent: nihil utiq; Ratio isthæc concludit: quia monstrato Paralogismo quatuor Terminorum, ultrò illa concidit & expirat.

His ita discussis, manifestum evadit. 1. Quo sensu in Scholis Theologorum fidem meruerit hæc Regula: Essentia divina nec generat, nec generatur: deindè verò, Quid sentiendum sit de quatuor istis propositionibus. 1. Essentia generat Essentiam: 2. Essentia generat personam. 3. Persona generat Essentiam: 4 Persona generat personam. Quæritur enim, quænam vera, quæ falsa sit? Respondetur, primam, si vox Essentia absolutè accipiatur, ut & secundam ac tertiam esse rejiciendas, ut impias & erroneas: solam autem quartam & postremam veram esse: sed tamen non ita simpliciter, ac si persona personam generaret extra essentiam: id quod Quaternitatem in divinis constitueret: Sed cum hac declaratione, ut persona generet Personam intra unam & eandem simplicissimam Divinitatis Essentiam: Undè fit, ut in diversitate personarum, locum tamen habeat Essentiæ communicatio.

Tandem patet etiam hinc, quid responderi possit & debeat, ad classicas illas objectiones, quæ puritati hujus doctrinæ, ab hæreticis sunt oppositæ. Ut: I. Si DEUS gignitur de DEO: tùm sunt plures Dij: At prius secundum nostram assertionem verum: Ergò concedendum etiam posterius. II. Gignens Deus non est genitus Deus. At Gignens DEUS est DEUS essentialiter. Ergò Deus genitus non est DEUS essentialiter. III. Gignens & genitum nunquam possunt esse unum & idem. Jam verò secundum nostram assertionem, Essentia in DEO Patre est Essentia gignens: In Filio autem est Essentia Genita. Ergò non eadem est Essentia Patris ac Filij.

In his enim & similibus argumentis committitur σόφισμα παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: id quod ex ijs, quæ hactenus disputata sunt, liquidò patet. Vocabulum enim DEI aliàs absolutè ὀσίας, aliàs relatè ὑπόστασιν notat. Quando igitur à nobis asseritur, DEUM de DEO esse genitum, vocabulo DEI non notatam volumus Essentiam DEI, absolutè sumtam: Sed limitatè sive determinatè notamus τὸ εἶναι ὑποστατικον. Quo eodem sensu accipitur etiam vox DEI in majore propositione secundi argumenti. Nam gignens DEUS, est genitus Deus ὑποστατικῶς, sive relatè quoad personam consideratus: Essentialiter tamen Pater & Filius Unus sunt DEUS. Sic Major etiam propositio argumenti Tertij, vera est quidem respectu personarum: falsissima verò respectu Essentiæ. Jam Quia in Minore manifesta instituitur consideratio diversitatis personarum: utique Conclusio ex confusione Absoluti & Relati infertur vitiosissima.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition VII

The Son is the second person of the Trinity, begotten from the Father from eternity: and together with the Father, by one certain common act, producing the Holy Spirit: of the same divine essence and Majesty as the Father: but in the fullness of time, assuming a true and entire human nature into the singularity of his person, for us men and for our salvation, he was made flesh.

ἔκθεσις.

Our Author disputes in this place at the beginning concerning those four words by which the second person of the Divinity is distinguished in the Scriptures: while they name him 1. λόγον, the Word, John 1, 1. 2. εἰκόνα θεῦ, the Image of GOD, Col. 1, 15. 3. ἀπάυγα- σμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆν ὑποστάσεως τῦ πατρὸς : The brightness of the glory and the character of the subsistence of the Father: Heb. 1, 3. Fourthly and lastly the Son of GOD, Ps. 2, 7. Matt. 14, 33. and ch. 16, 16. Concerning which words, since the Author discourses accurately enough, we do not wish to do what is already done. One thing, however, occurs, which Philip wished to assert in this place concerning the mode of the Generation of the Son: writing thus: The Son is called image and λόγος: He is therefore an Image begotten by the thought of the Father: Which, that it may be explained in some way, let us take examples from our own mind.
