The human mind by thinking soon paints an image of the thing thought of: but we do not transfuse our Essence into those images, and those thoughts are sudden and vanishing actions: But the eternal Father, beholding himself, begets a thought of himself, which is his image, not vanishing, but subsisting, with the essence communicated to it. And a little later the same Philip adds that the Son of GOD is called λόγον, not only because all things were created by the word of power Gen. 1, 3. and following, Ps. 33, 6. because also by the virtue of that same Word all things are preserved and subsist, Heb. 1, 3. because finally in the last times GOD has spoken to us through the Son, and the Son brought forth the Word of Salvation from the bosom of the Father, John 1, 19. But also, Because the Son was begotten by the Father by thought. Which assertion of Philip gave handle and occasion to that controversy which was moved in these regions: Whether indeed the Father begat the Son by thinking: some strenuously fighting for the affirmative, others for the negative; neither perhaps sufficiently attaining the mind of Philip. Those who defended the negative were accustomed to say that they were moved by these reasons in particular.

1. Because this mode of generation is destitute of all authority from the Holy Scriptures.

2. Because it is plainly ἄῥῥητῶ ineffable, as St. Basil truly wrote: The generation of the Son is to be honored entirely with silence: do not say when, nor ask how? Because the answer is impossible.

3. Because no one among the orthodox fathers dared to describe the eternal generation of the Son in this manner: with whom, however, there otherwise existed a very great controversy expressly with the Arians and other heretics concerning the divinity of the Son and his eternal generation.

4. Because the same fathers simply did not want the mode of this generation to be investigated; just as many testimonies to this effect have been collected by Dr. Wigand,

Latin:

Filius est secunda Trinitatis persona, à Patre ab æterno genita: & unâ cū Patre, uno quodā communi actu, producens Spiritum Sanctum: ejusdem cū Patre divinæ essentiæ & Majestatis : in plenitudine verò temporis, veram ac integram naturam humanam, in singularitatem personæ suæ, propter nos homines & propter nostram salutem, assumens, caro facta est.

ἔκθεσις.

DIsputat hoc loco Autor noster initiò, de quatuor illis vocabulis, quibus secunda persona Divinitatis, in Scripturis insignitur : dùm eam nominant 1. λόγον, Verbum, Joh. 1, 1. 2. εἰκόνα θεῦ, Imaginem DEI, Coloß. 1, 15. 3. ἀπάυγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆν ὑποστάσεως τῦ πατρὸς : Splendorem gloriæ & characterem subsistentiæ Patris : Heb. 1, 3. Quartò & postremò Filium DEI, Psal 2, 7. Matth. 14, 33. & cap. 16, 16. De quibus vocabulis cùm satis accuratè disserat Autor, nolumus actum agere. Unum autem occurrit, quod de modo Generationis Filij, Philippus hoc loco asseverare voluit : sic scribens : Filius dicitur imago & λόγος : Est igitur Imago cogitatione Patris genita: Quod ut aliquo modo explicari poßit, à nostrâ mente exempla capiamus. Mens humana cogitando mox pingit imaginem rei cogitatæ : sed nos non transfundimus nostram Essentiam, in illas imagines, suntque cogitationes illæ subitæ & evanescentes actiones : At pater æternus sese intuens, gignit cogitationem sui, quæ est imago ipsius, non evanescens, sed subsistens, communicatâ ipsi essentiâ. Et paulò pòst subjungit idem Philippus, Filium DEI dici λόγον, non ideò tantùm, quia verbo potentiæ creatæ sunt omnia Gen. 1, 3. & seqq. Psal 33, 6. quia etiam ejusdem Verbi virtute omnia conservantur & subsistunt, Heb. 1, 3. quia denique novißimis temporibus per Filium locutus nobis est DEUS, & Verbum Salutis Filius ex sinu Patris protulit, Joh. 1, 19. Sed &, Quia Filius cogitatione à Patre est generatus. Quæ assertio Philippéa ansam & occasionem præbuit controversiæ illi, quæ in hisce regionibus mota fuit : An nimirùm Pater cogitando genuerit Filium : nonnullis pro affirmativâ, alijs pro negativâ strenuè pugnantibus ; neutris fortasse mentem Philippi satis assequentibus. Qui Negantem tuebantur, his potissimùm rationibus se moveri dictitabant.

1. Quia Modus iste Generationis omni destituitur Sacrarum literarum autoritate.

2. Quia ille planè est ἄῥῥητῶ ineffabilis, ut verè scripserit D. Basilius : Generatio Filij prorsus silentio honoranda est : nec dicas quando : nec quæras, quomodo? Quia impoßibilis est responsio.

3. Quia ex Orthodoxis patribus nemo ausus fuit, hunc in modum describere æternam Generationem Filij: quibus tamen alioqui de Divinitate Filij, ejusdemque æterna generatione, cum Arianis, alijsque hæreticis, ex professo intercessit controversia longè maxima.

4. Quia ijdem patres simpliciter noluerunt investigari modum Generationis hujus; quemadmodum hanc in sententiam Testimonia plurima collecta sunt à Doct. Vvigando,


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Whether the Father is the cause and Principle of the Son, and the Son the caused and Principle of the Father

in the booklet on the Generation of the Son, page 4, edition of the year 1590.

5. Because the Affirmative [position] seems to bring back, as it were by a right of return, into the proscenium of the Church those foul heresies, long since rejected and condemned by the Orthodox Church in the Valentinians, Basilidians, Samosatenians, Servetians, Osiandrians, and others of that kind, both heretical and schismatic. For the Valentinians, as Augustine testifies in his work on heresies to Quodvultdeus, contended that the λόγον or Word proceeded from Intellect and Truth; but the Basilidians asserted that ἐνθύμησιν, that is, thought, produced the λόγον, as Irenaeus testifies in book 2, chapters 48 and 49. The Servetians, denying the ὑπόστασιν of the Son subsisting in the divine Essence, maintained that that Generation which the Sacred Scriptures proclaim concerning the Son is nothing other than the thought of GOD; the Samosatenians feigned that the Son of GOD is a λόγον προφορικὸν and ἀνυπόστατον: like a thought conceived by the mind and vanishing again. Thus that Andreas Osiander the Elder, the disturber of the Prussian Churches, used to cavil: If the thought of the Father contemplating himself constitutes a certain peculiar ὑπόστασιν, then certainly the Son also and the Holy Spirit, by thinking of themselves, will produce peculiar ὑποστάσεις: or the two persons will be entirely destitute of the substantial faculty of thought: which is blasphemous. Nor would it be right to say that the thought of the Father is better or nobler than the thought of either the Son or the Holy Spirit. Since in this way the ὁμοούσια of the persons would be entirely taken away. Therefore, lest a handle and occasion be provided for these and other similar heresies of that kind, Philip’s opinion on the Generation of the λόγος should be simply rejected.

6. And finally: because this Assertion of Philip seems to be a dream of human and foolish reason, which in the mysteries of faith cannot and ought not to be believed without the loss of salvation. Others, contradicting these, strenuously denied [this] in favor of the Affirmative, relying primarily on the authority of the Holy Fathers, some of whom, and perhaps not the least, are read to have defined this mode of the Generation of the Son.

In which part they brought forward that statement of Basil in his Sermon on chapter 1 of John: Why is the Son called λόγος? So that it may be shown that he proceeds from the mind. Why, he says, is he called the Word? Because he was begotten without motion. Why, finally, the Word? Because the figure of their generation shows the generator in itself, drawing no part from thence, just as our word, which bears the image of our entire thought. To this they also accommodated that statement of Nazianzen: The Son is called λόγος, because he is related to the Father as a word is to the mind.

But so that we may at last disclose what we think about this Controversy, we believe it can be resolved by a distinction. For either Philip and his associates wanted to define the Mode of this eternal generation and express it, as it were, to the life; or they merely wanted to delineate it παρεγγυτῶς and, as it were, with a crude Minerva, by a certain similarity: namely, so that a matter removed from the apprehension and intellect of all might at least be shadowed forth by some example: if the Son is said to be related to the Father in the same way as a word, or speech, or even a thought is related to our mind.

For just as our minds, by thinking, form images of things, and our speech is an image and character of the thoughts of the mind: so the eternal Father, knowing himself and thinking by a certain essential act, begets an entire image of himself, in which he himself shines forth entirely, as Basil holds.

If Philip intended his assertion to be understood in this latter sense, we certainly cannot or ought not to disapprove of it so simply; especially since we know that both Augustine and the great Luther, our own, used similarities of this kind. Although, meanwhile, we willingly admit that neither this nor any other similarity can express this Mystery of the Generation of the Son, and that this similarity also must be used very cautiously and soberly.

But if it can be proven that Philip used this similarity in the former sense—which, however, we are most persuaded can hardly be done—then certainly we do not allow ourselves to be moved by his authority either; but we reject it by all means, relying on the same reasons which we said were used by those who opposed Philip quite rigidly in this part.

Moreover, on the occasion of this Controversy concerning the Generation of the Son, that other [question], as it were subordinate to the former, began to be moved: Whether, namely, with respect to this Generation, the Father can be called the Cause and Principle of the Son, and the Son the caused and principled? And although this Question may seem superfluous, because those terms taken from philosophical sciences are entirely alien to this mystery of the Trinity, meanwhile, however, both ancient and more recent heresies seem to demand some explanation of this Question by a certain right of their own. And indeed it is evident from the Homily of Basil on the first chapter of John, as also from the Dialogue of Damascene against the Manichaeans, that the Greek and Latin Fathers did not undertake the care of this Question in a perfunctory manner: For at the beginning, among the various meanings of the word ἀρχῆς or Principle, they distinguished very solicitously; when they showed that it is predicated in different ways, whether concerning place, or Time, or order, or cause, or finally other things. But then, as for the decision of this Question itself, the Greeks did not hesitate to name the Father αἰτίαν καὶ ἄναρχον; but the Son ἔναρχον, indeed αἰτιατὸν, that is, Initiated and Caused. The Latins, however, being more cautious than the Greeks in this regard, never wished to use those terms so simply, but always with a clear declaration: namely, to establish that the Son could be called Caused and Principiate, but only in that sense in which the Son is believed to be from the Father: not, clearly, by reason of time, nor of creation, nor of essence, nor of inferior power, but only by way and respect of comparison, relation, and ὑπάρξεως: that is, not essentially, but only personally. And although this declaration is in complete agreement with the analogy of Faith, it would nevertheless be more prudent to abstain entirely from such forms of speech, for the reason that neither is their proper meaning suitable to this Mystery, nor

even that τὸ ἄναρχον καὶ αἰτιατὸν, that is, principled or caused, does not in any way attain that personal difference by which the Father is distinguished from the Son: nay, it seems to provide the Arians, who impugn the τὸ ὁμοούσιον of the Son, an occasion for caviling at our doctrine: so that not undeservedly some of the Latin Fathers abhorred the term (principled), and today the sounder theologians most rightly abhor it: although in the meantime they do not deny that the Father, with respect to the production of the other persons, is most rightly called ἀρχὴν or principle. Where, however, a new scruple again moved many, not a small one, that Johannine passage chap. 8, 25, where Christ, being asked who he was, answered, The Principle. Whence not a few heretics have gathered that not only the Father, but also the Son can be called the Principle, and thus two principles must be established. Which knot indeed St. Augustine, book 5, On the Trinity, chap. 13, determined could be dissected in this manner: The Father is spoken of relatively, and the same is spoken of relatively as Principle, and if by chance anything else: But he is spoken of as Father in relation to the Son: but as Principle in relation to all things that are from him. Likewise, the Son is spoken of relatively, and he is also spoken of relatively as Word and Image: and in all these terms he is referred to the Father. But the Father is called none of these. The Son is also called Principle. For when it was said to him, Who are you? He answered, The Principle, who also speak to you: But is he the principle of the Father? For he wished to show himself to be the Creator, when he said that he was the Principle, just as the Father is the principle of the creature, because all things are from him. For he is also called Creator in relation to the creature, just as Lord in relation to a servant. And therefore when we say both the Father is a principle, and the Son is a principle, we do not say there are two principles of the creature: Because both the Father and the Son together are one Principle to the creature, just as one Creator, just as one God.

Thus far Augustine: whose decision, although it is most true in its own place, yet does not seem to touch the scope of Christ's response. For in the beginning in the Greek, it is not read that Christ answered, I am the Principle: but τὴν ἀρχὴν, ὅ, τι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν. Where the Latin Vulgate viciously rendered these words thus: The Principle, Because I also speak to you: Since no certain sense, and one suitable to the proposed question, is found to be in this interpretation. But then if you look at the entire context of the text, it will clearly appear that that Greek τὴν ἀρχὴν sounds the same in this place as ἐξ ἀρχῆς: and must be construed through a certain transposition with the verb λαλῶ, in this sense: I am he whom I told you from the beginning: He had, however, said that he was the Son of God the Father, verse 18. Where not only must the verb εἰμὶ be repeated from the common, but also that ὅ, τι must be taken not as a conjunction, but in the place of a relative pronoun or postpositive article.

These things having been thus far dispatched, it seems that only this one thing remains in this proposition, that we see upon what foundations the eternal divinity of the Son can be demonstrated, and corroborated against the furies of the Arians. Although it is not our intention to repeat in this place those things which have been excellently disputed on this theme partly by our Author, and partly by others: it pleases us, however, as if in a synopsis or some table, to record for the sake of memory only those foundations whose use in disputes against the Arians could be the greatest.

A double class of such proofs can most rightly be established: indeed in such a way that the former contains names denoting divinity: but the latter contains attributes partly, and partly works, immediately competent to divinity alone.

The names of the former class, therefore, denoting the divinity of the Son, are: EL, Elohim, Adonai, and especially that tetragrammaton Jehovah. Although it cannot be denied that those first three names are not rarely assigned even to men, either because of the amplitude of the office which they hold, or because of the benefits which they confer upon others, which are clearly divine: yet a diligent comparison of the places of Scripture most evidently demonstrates that the Son of God claims these names for himself in a far more sublime way, and one communicable to no human being. Whence the Savior himself determined that he is to be judged not only nominally, as men are: but properly and truly to be God, not from the name alone, but from the testimony of things and deeds. John 10, 24 and 25. The words are thus: The Jews therefore surrounded him, and said to him, How long do you hold our soul in suspense? if you are the Christ, tell us plainly. Jesus answered them: I told you, and you do not believe: The works which I do in the name of my Father, these bear witness of me. Thus Psalm 110, 1. The Son of David is named Adonai, not in that common sense in which this name is attributed even to men: but in a sense entirely peculiar, and simply incommunicable to creatures. For that by Adonai, the true Jehovah and God by nature is to be understood, the immediately added epexegesis proves: Sit at my right hand: For to none of the angels, much less to any mere man, has it been said, Sit at my right hand: But only to the incarnate Son of God, Heb. 1, 13. Now if a comparison of this very place be instituted with that disputation of Christ which is described, Matt. 22, 43, it will irrefragably appear that the name Adonai is attributed to the Son of God by a certain excellence. For Christ, intending to confirm his divinity, convinces the Pharisees with this argument, that David names Christ or the Messiah not only his Son, but also his Lord: that is, not a mere man, but also true God: He said, he says, The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand. That the adversaries of Christ felt the force of this argument is witnessed by the Evangelist: so that they did not even dare to mutter against it.

The same must be determined concerning other places of Scripture also, in which the Son of God is named either EL or Adonai. Where the very circumstance of the place always proves that the discourse is about such a one who is called God not only nominally, or only by adoption: but who is truly and essentially God, as Isaiah 7, 14. Where Christ is named Immanuel, God with us: Likewise Isaiah 9, 6. Where he is called EL Gibbor, the strong God.

But lest we should seem to contend against the Arians with arguments sought from too far afield, we rightly urge this point, that the name Jehovah, that classic name which, even by the admission of the Jews themselves, belongs properly to GOD alone, is many times attributed in the Scriptures to the Son of GOD: as in Jerem. 33, 16. This is his name (the Branch of David) which they shall call him Jehovah Zidkenu, Jehovah our righteousness. Thus in the New Testament the same appellation occurs very frequently reductively. For John 12:41, the glory of Christ is said to be that which in Isaiah 6:1 is asserted to have been the glory of Jehovah. Thus Paul, 1 Cor. 10:9, testifies that Christ was he who in Num. 14:22 is named Jehovah of which kind can be gathered from methodical booklets. But if from the New Testament such passages are to be brought forward which expressly name the Son of God God, certainly even that one which is contained in chapter 1 of John, immediately from the beginning and in some subsequent verses, can be worth all of them. For as our author also will observe, he provides the weight of such proofs that it cannot be refuted by any sophistry. Samosatenus indeed, Photinus, Servetus, and others have impiously and wickedly contended that λόγον does not signify a person, but just as in a man we do not say that a man's thought or his speech is a person, but a quality or a passing motion: so in John it is to be understood that λόγον is not a person, but the thought or purpose of the Father, which is the Father himself, just as we say the mind or goodness of the Father is the Father himself. But the whole context of the Johannine passage refutes that impiety in many ways. For first, John affirms of this λόγῳ that it is, that it was, and indeed in the beginning. Therefore it is necessary that λόγῳ denotes not a motion or a passing quality of thought in God, but a person, or a personal subsistence. The reason for the consequence is that τὸ εἶναι is never proper to words or vanishing thoughts: since they are said to be made rather than to be.

Then John affirms that this λόγῳ or Word created all things, that without it nothing was made, by which also this Word was made flesh. But such works cannot by any reason be attributed to a passing thought or a vanishing word, as if it were a non-entity. Therefore it is necessary that λόγῳ in this place denotes a proper and indeed the second person of the Divinity. The consequence follows. Again, if λόγῳ were only a thought, which is the Father himself, it would follow that the Father was incarnate: which is impious and absurd.

Thirdly: John explicitly predicates of this λόγῳ that it is God, where our author rightly admonishes that the Greek article proves that λόγον must be placed in the position of the subject, and God in the position of the predicate.

Finally, lest any ambiguity be established in the appellation of God: and perhaps the word God be taken only nominally regarding the dignity of some office, or in another respect: and not most properly regarding the divine essence: John protests again, marking this God λόγῳ with such attributes which cannot belong to any but the true and essential God: such as are: 1. to have been with God from eternity. 2. To create all things that exist created. 3. To be the true Light and life. 4. To save those who believe in him. 5. To have been before John, and yet to have been made only after John. 6. To receive from his fullness grace for grace: and other attributes of this kind, which are fitting only to God.

The latter class of arguments solidly demonstrating the divinity of the Son can be dispatched by this general syllogism.

To whomever the attributes and works proper to God alone belong primarily, truly, and really: he must be God, and indeed not by grace, but by essence. But such works and attributes belong to the Son of God primarily, truly, and really. Therefore.

Scripture most clearly confirms the minor, which assigns to the Son of God, first, eternity (John 1:1, 1 John 1:1, John 8:58, Isa. 9:6, Mic. 5:2, Rev. 1:17); second, the worship of adoration (Phil. 2:10, Rev. 5:12 & 13); third, the work of creation and the conservation of all things (John 1:3, Col. 1:16, Heb. 1:3); fourth, omniscience (Mark 2:8, John 2:25, Rev. 2:23); fifth, salvation, and other plainly divine works of that kind: concerning which it will be very useful and necessary to consult the methodical booklets of our theologians.

Latin:

libello de Generatione Filij pag. 4. Edit. Anni 1590.

5. Quia Affirmativa videtur postliminiò quasi in proscenium Ecclesiæ revocare, tetras illas hæreses, jampridem in Valentinianis, Basilidianis, Samosatenianis, Servetianis, Osiandristis, & id genus alijs tùm hæreticis, tùm Schismaticis ab Orthodoxa Ecclesia rejectis & damnatis. Valentiniani enim, teste Augustino de hæresibus ad Quodvult DEUM, contendebant, λόγον sive verbum proceflisse, de Intellectu & Veritate, Basilidiani verò asserebant ἐνθύμησιν, hoc est, cogitationem produxisse λόγον, teste Irenæo lib. 2. cap. 48. & 49. Servetiani negantes ὑπόστασιν Filij in divina Essentia subsistentem statuerbant Generationem illã, quam Sacræ literæ de Filio prædicent, nihil esse aliud, quàm cogitationem DEI, Samosateniani fingebant, Filium DEI esse λόγον προφορικὸν & ἀνυπόσατον: instar cogitationis à mente conceptæ: & rursum evanescentis. Sic Andreas Osiander Senior ille, turbator Ecclesiarum prutenicarum, subinde cavillabatur: Sicogitatio Patris semetipsum intuentis, constituit peculiarem quandam ὑπόσασιν: utique vel Filius etiam & Spiritus Sanctus, cogitando semetipsos, producent peculiares ὑποσάσεις: vel duæ personæ cogitationis facultate substantiali prorsus destituentur: id quod blasphemum. Neque fas fuerit dicere, cogitationem Patris, meliorem nobilioremvé esse cogitatione vel Filij, vel Spiritus Sancti. Siquidem hoc pacto ὁμοούσια personarum prorsus tolleretur. Proindè ne ansa & occasio præbeatur istis & id genus alijs consimilibus hæresibus, sententia Philippi de Generatione τῶ λόγα simpliciter rejicienda fuerit.

6. Et postremò: quia Assertio hæc Philippi videtur esse somnium humanæ & stolidæ rationis: cui in mysterijs fidei, sine jacturâ salutis credi nec potest nec debet. His contradicentes alij, pro Affirmativâ strenuè negabant, freti potissimùm autoritate Sanctorum Patrum, quorum aliqui & fortè minimè postremi, modum istum Generationis Filij definivisse leguntur.

Quâ in parte illud Basilij Serm. super cap. 1. Johannis, proferebant: Cur Filius dicitur λόγος? ut ostendatur, quod ex mente procedit. Cur, inquit, dicitur verbum? Quoniam sine motu genitum est. Cur denique verbum? Quoniam figura generatio eorum in se monstrat generantem nullam indè partẽ deducens, quemadmodum ferè verbum nostrum, quod totius nostræ cogitationis imaginem refert. Huc accommodabant etiam illud Nazianzeni: Filius dicitur λόγος, quia ita se habet ad Patrem, sicut verbum ad mentem.

Sed ut vel tandem, quid nobis de hac Controversia videatur, aperimus: distinctione eam tolli posse arbitramur. Aut enim Philippus & Socij, æternæ generationis hujus Modum definire, & ad vivum quasi exprimere: aut duntaxat παρεγγυτῶς & rudi quasi Minerva, per quandam similitudinem eum delineare voluerunt: nempe ut res ab omnium apprehensione & intellectu remota, saltem exemplo aliquo adumbretur: si ita se Filius ad Patrem habere dicatur: quemadmodum se habet verbum, aut sermo, vel etiam cogitatio ad mentem nostram.

Quemadmodum enim nostræ mentes cogitando formant imagines rerum, & noster sermo est imago & character cogitationum mentis: ita æternus Pater sese agnoscens, & essentiali quodam actu cogitans, gignat integram sui imaginem, in quâ ipse integrè luceat, uti habet Basilius.

Si posteriore hoc sensu Philippus assertionem suam voluit intellectam, haud certè ita simpliciter eam improbare vel possumus vel debemus: præsertim cùm hujusmodi similitudinibus & Augustinum & Megalandrum Lutherum, nostrum usos esse, sciamus. Quanquam interim libenter fatemur, neque hanc, neque ullam aliam similitudinem Mysterium hoc Generationis Filij exprimere posse: & cautè admodum atque sobriè hac etiam similitudine utendum esse.

Sin verò priore sensu similitudine hac Philippus usus esse probari queat: id quod tamen vix fieri posse, habemus persuasissimum: tùm certè nos quoque ipsius autoritate moveri minimè patimur: sed eam modis omnibus reprobamus: ijsdem freti rationibus, quibus eos usos fuisse diximus, qui Philippo sese hac in parte satis rigidè opposuerunt.

Cæterùm, occasione Controversiæ istius de Generatione Filij, moveri cœpta est & altera illa, priori quasi subordinata. An nimirùm respectu Generationis hujus Pater dici queat Causa & Principium Filij: Filius verò causatum & principiatum? Etsi verò hæc Quæstio videri queat supervacanea, propterea quòd termini istiex scientijs philosophicis petiti, ab hoc mysterio Trinitatis prorsus sunt alieni: Interim tamen tùm Veteres, tùm recentiores hæreses, aliquam hujus Quæstionis explicationem suo quodam jure postulare videntur. Et sanè constat ex Homilia Basilij ad primũ caput Johannis ut & ex Dialogo Damasceni contra Manichæos, Patres Græcos & Latinos Quæstionis hujus curam minimè perfunctoriam suscepisse: Nam initiò inter varia significata vocabuli ἀρχῆς sive Principij sollicitè admodũ distinxerunt: dú vel de loco, vel de Tempore, vel de ordine, vel de causa, vel deniq; alijs de rebus diversimodè illud prædicari, ostenderunt. Deindè verò quoad ipsam Quæstionis hujus decisionem, non dubitarunt Græci Patrem nominare αἰτίαν καὶ ἄναρχον: Filium verò ἔναρχον, imò αἰτιατὸν, hoc est, Initiatum & Causatum. Latini verò Græcis hac in parte cautiores, nunquàm ita simpliciter, sed semper cum luculenta declaratione Terminis istis uti voluerunt: ut nimirum statuerent, Filium dici posse Causatum & Principiatum, sed eo tantùm sensu, quo Filius à Patre esse creditur: non videlicet temporis, non creationis, non essentiæ, non potestatis inferioris ratione: sed tantùm comparationis, relationis & ὑπάρξεως modo atque respectu: hoc est, non essentialiter, sed tantùm personaliter. Etsi verò declaratio hæc cum analogiâ Fidei omninò consentit: Consultius tamen fuerit, ab ejusmodi loquendi formulis penitùs abstinere: propterea quòd neque propria eorũ affectio Mysterio huic convenit: neq;

etiam illud τὸ ἄναρχον καὶ αἰτιατὸν, hoc est, principiatum sive causatum, differentiã illam personalem, quâ Pater distat à Filio, ullâ ratione assequitur: quin Arianis τὸ ὁμοούσιον Filij impugnantibus, occasionem cavillandi nostram doctrinam subministrare videtur: ut haud immeritò aliqui ex Latinis Patribus à Termino (principiatum) abhorruerint, hodieque Saniores Theologi rectissimè abhorreant: licèt interim haud negent, Patrem respectu productionis reliquarum personarum rectissimè dici ἀρχὴν sive principium. Ubi tamen novum rursus scrupulum, multis haud exiguum movit, locus ille Johanniticus cap. 8, 25. ubi Christus Interrogatus, Quis esset, Respondit, Principium. Undè non Patrem modò, sed & Filium Principium dici posse, & sic duo principia constituenda esse, hæreticorum haud pauci, collegerunt. Quem sanè nodum D. Augustinus lib. 5. de Trinitate, cap. 13. hunc in modum dissecari posse statuit: Dicitur Relativè Pater, idemque Relativè dicitur Principium, & si quid fortè aliud: Sed Pater ad Filium dicitur: Principium verò ad omnia quæ ab ipso sunt. Item, Relativè dicitur Filius, Relativè dicitur & Verbum & Imago: & in omnibus his vocabulis ad Patrem refertur. Nihil autem horum Pater dicitur. Dicitur Filius etiam Principium. Cum enim diceretur ei, Tu quis es? Respondit, Principium, Qui & loquor vobis: Sed numquid Patris principium est? Creatorẽ se quippe ostendere voluit, cum se dixit esse Principium, sicut & Pater principium est creaturæ, eò quòd ab ipso sunt omnia. Nam & Creator dicitur ad creaturam, sicut Dominus ad servum. Et ideò cum dicimus & Patrem principium, & Filium principium, non duo principia creaturæ dicimus: Quia & Pater & Filius simul ad creaturam unum Principium est, sicut unus Creator, sicut unus Deus.

Hactenus Augustinus: cujus decisio, etsi suo loco est verissima: Scopum tamen Responsionis Christi nondum tangere videtur. Nam initiò in Græco, non legitur respondisse Christus, Ego sum Principium: sed τὴν ἀρχὴν, ὅ, τι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν. Ubi latina vulgata vitiosè hæc verba sic reddidit: Principium, Quia & loquor vobis: Siquidem Interpretationi huic nullus certus, & propositæ Quæstioni conveniens sensus inesse deprehenditur. Deindè verò si textus συνέπειαν integram spectes, liquidò patebit, Græcum illud τὴν ἀρχὴν idem sonare hoc loco, quod ἐξ ἀρχῆς: & per quandam trajectionem construendum esse cum verbo λαλῶ, hoc sensu: Sum is quem ab initio vobis dixi: Dixerat autem esse se Filium DEI Patris, vers. 18. Ubi non modò ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ repetendum est verbum εἰμὶ: sed & illud ὅ, τι non conjunctionis, sed provocabuli sive Articuli postpositivi loco habendum.

His hactenus ita expeditis, unicum illud hac in propositione restare videtur, ut quibusnam fundamentis æterna Filij Divinitas demõstrari, & adversus Arianorum furores corroborari possit, videamus. Quamquam verò nostri non est instituti, hoc loco repetere ea, quæ partim ab Autore nostro, partim verò ab alijs egregiè de hoc themate sunt disputata: placet tamen tanquam in συνόψει sive tabella quapiam, memoriæ causa consignare ea tantùm fundamenta, quorum usus in disputationibus contra Arianos vel maximus esse queat.

Rectissimè autem gemina classis ejusmodi probationum constitui potest: ita quidem, ut prior Nomina, divinitatem notantia: posterior verò Attributa partim, partim opera soli divinitati immediatè competentia, contineat.

Prioris igitur classis nomina, Divinitatem Filij notantia, sunt. EL, Elohim, Adonai, & cumprimis illud tetragrammaton Jehovah. Quanquam verò negari non potest, tria illa priora nomina, haud rarò, vel propter muneris, quod gerunt, amplitudinem, vel propter beneficia, quæ in alios conferunt, planè divina, hominibus etiam adsignari: Longè tamen sublimiore, & nemini hominum communicabili ratione, Filium DEI hæc sibi nomina vendicare, diligens locorum Scripturæ collatio evidentissimè demonstrat. Undè Servator ipse non nuncupativè tantùm, uti homines: sed propriè & reverà se DEũ esse, non ex solo nomine, sed ex rerum factorumquè testimonio judicandum esse statuit. Joh. 10, 24. & 25. Verba sic habent: Circumdederunt ergò eum Judæi, & dicebant ei, Quousq́, animam nostram suspendis? si tu es Christus, dic nobis palàm. Respondit eis Jesus: Dixi vobis, & non creditis: Opera, quæ ego facio in nomine Patris mei, hæc testimonium perhibent de me. Sic Psal. 110, 1. Filius Davidis nominatur Adonai, non communi illo sensu, quo hominibus etiam hoc nomen tribuitur: sed prorsus peculiari, & creaturis simpliciter incommunicabili. Nam per Adonai, verum Jehovah, & naturâ DEUM intelligendum esse, evincit adjecta statim ἐπεξήγησις: Sede à dextris meis: Nulli enim Angelorum, multò minùs, nudo cuipiam homini, dictum est, Sede à dextris meis: Sed soli Filio DEI incarnato, Hebr. 1, 13. Jam si hujus ipsius loci collatio instituatur, cum disputatione illa Christi, quæ describitur, Matth. 22, 43. irrefragabiliter patebit, Nomen Adonai Filio DEI κατʼ ἐξοχὴν quandam tribui. Nam Christus divinitatem suam confirmaturus hoc argumento convincit Pharisæos, quòd David Christum sive Messiam non modò Filium, sed & Dominum suum: hoc est, non nudum hominẽ, sed & verum DEUM nominat: Dixit, inquiens, Dominus Domino meo sede à Dextris meis. Cujus argumenti vim tantam Adversarios Christi sensisse, testis est Evangelista: ut contra id ne hiscerequidem ausi sint.

Quod ipsum statuendum est de alijs etiã Scripturæ locis, in quibus Filius DEI vel EL vel Adonaj nominatur. Ubi semper ipsa loci περίστασις evincit, de tali sermonem esse, qui non nuncupativè tantùm DEUS appelletur, vel adoptivè tantùm: sed qui reverâ & essentialiter DEUS sit, ut Esaiæ 7, 14. Ubi Christus nominatur, Immanuel, DEUS nobiscum: Item Esaiæ 9. 6. Ubi EL Gibbor, DEUS fortis appellatur.

Sed ne longiùs petitis argumentis adversus Arianos militare videamur, meritò urgemus illud, quòd Filio DEI, Clasficum illud, & ex ipsorum etiam Judæorum concessione, Soli DEO propriè conveniens nomen Jehovah in Scripturis multoties tribuitur: ut Jerem. 33, 16. Hoc est nomen ejus (Germinis Davidis) quod vocabũt eum Jehovah Zidkenu, Jehovah justitia nostra. Sic in Novo Testamento eadem appellatio Reductivè sæpissimè occurrit. Nam Job. 12, 41. Gloria Christi ea esse dicitur, quæ Ies. 6, 1. Gloria Jehovæ fuisse asseritur. Sic Paulus 1. Cor. 10, 9. testatur Christum fuisse illum, qui Num. 14, 22. Jehovah nominatur, & à Judæis tentatus esse perhibetur. Cujus generis exempla plurima ex libellis Methodicis colligere licet. Quod si ex Novo Testamento, ejusmodi loca sint proferenda, quæ Filium DEI expressè DEUM nominant, certè vel unus ille, qui cap. 1. Johannis mox ab initio & aliquot subsequentibus versibus continetur, instar omnium esse potest. Nam uti noster etiam Autor observabit, ejusmodi probationum momenta ille subministrat, ut nulla Sophisticatione elidi queat. Samosatenus quidem, Photinus, Servetus & alii impiè & sceleratè contenderunt, λόγον non significare personam, sed sicut in homine, cogitationem hominis aut Sermonem ejus non dicimus esse personam, sed qualitatem aut motum transeuntem : Ita in Johanne intelligi λόγον non esse personã, sed cogitationem seu propositum Patris, quod sit ipse Pater, sicut dicimus mentem aut bonitatem Patris esse ipsum Patrem. Verùm tota loci Johannitici περίστασις impietatem istam multis modis refellit. Primùm enim de λόγῳ isto affirmat Johannes quòd sit quòd fuerit, & quidem in principio. Ergò λόγῳ non motû aut qualitatem cogitationis in DEO transeuntem, sed personam, sive subsistens personale, notet, necesse est. Ratio consecutionis est, τὸ εἶναι nunquam est proprium verborum sive cogitationum evanescentium: quippè quæ fieri magis, quàm esse dicuntur.

Deindè affirmat Johannes, quòd λόγῳ sive Verbum hoc omnia condiderit, quòd sine eo factum sit nihil, quo etiam Verbum hoc factum sit caro. Atqui cogitationi transeunti, sive verbo evanescenti, tanquam non-enti, talia opera tribui nulla ratione possunt. Ergò λόγῳ hoc loco propriam & quidem secundam personam Divinitatis notet, necessarium est Consequens. Rursum si λόγῳ tantùm esset cogitatio, quæ est ipse Pater, sequeretur, Patrem esse incarnatum : id quod impium & absurdum.

Tertiò : De λόγῳ isto disertè prædicat Johannes; quod sit DEUS, ubi rectè admonet Autor noster, Græcum Articulum evincere, λόγον collocandum esse loco subjecti, DEUM, loco prædicati.

Tandem, Ne ambiguitas aliqua in appellatione DEI constituatur : & fortè nuncupativè tantùm de officii alicujus dignitate, aut alio respectu : non verò propriissimè de divina Essentia, vox DEI accipiatur : reclamat rursum Johannes, ejusmodi attributis DEUM istum λόγον insigniens, quæ non nisi verò & essentiali DEO competere possunt : Qualia sunt: apud DEUM fuisse ab æterno : 2. Creare universa quæ existunt creata. 3. esse Lucem & vitam veram. 4. Credentes in se salvare. 5. ante Johannem fuisse, & tamen post Johannem demùm factum esse. 6. ex plenitudine ejus accipere gratiam pro gratiâ : & quæ hujus generis attributa sunt alia, non nisi DEO convenientia.

Posterior classis argumentorum Divinitatem Filii solide demonstrantium, generali hoc Syllogismo expediri potest.

Cuicunq; attributa & opera Soli DEO propria, primo, vere ac realiter competunt: ille DEUS sit, necesse est, & quidem non per gratiam: sed per essentiam. Atqui Filio DEI hujusmodi opera & attributa primo, vere ac realiter competunt. E.

Minorem luculentissime confirmat Scriptura, quæ primo, Æternitatem Joh. 1, 1. 1. Joh. 1, 1. Joh. 8, 58. Esa 9, 6. Mich 5, 2. Apoc. 1, 17. secundo, Adorationis cultum Phil. 2, 10. Apocal. 5, 12. & 13. Tertio, opus creationis, & conservationis rerum omnium Joh. 1, 3. Col. 1, 16. Hebr. 1, 3. Quarto, Omniscientiam Marc. 2, 8. Joh. 2, 25. Apoc. 2, 23. Quinto, Salvationem, & id genus alia plane divina opera Filio Dei adsignat: de quibus libellos nostratium Theologorum Methodicos consulere, utile perquam & necessarium fuerit.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition VIII

The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, proceeding from the Father and the Son, or as from one essential source, in an ineffable manner from eternity.

Exposition.

The heresy of the Macedonians has caused not only our author, but also most theologians, to prefix to the disputation concerning the Holy Spirit an accurate explanation of the manifold power or meaning of the word SPIRIT. Lest we seem to do what has already been done, having omitted those things which can be sought from methodical textbooks, we shall gather the whole matter into a few points by a certain brief schema.

The word Spirit, therefore, is polysemous: and it is predicated either of God or of creatures. Taken of GOD, it denotes either essentially all three persons of the Trinity, which by reason of their Essence are Spirit: according to that in John 4:24, GOD is Spirit: or effectively it denotes the virtue and power, indeed more often the wrath and fury of GOD, Exod. 15:8, 'In the Spirit of thy fury the waters were gathered together' (by which, clearly, the Egyptians were suffocated in the desert): Psalm 18:16, 'At thy rebuke and the inspiration of the Spirit of thy wrath the foundations of the world were revealed': or finally, personally, it denotes as it were separately the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity: that common and coessential breath of the Father and the Son.

1. Taken of creatures, the word Spirit is predicated either of angels, and those both good, Heb. 1:14, Psalm 104:4, and evil: Luke 11:24 and 26, 1 Sam. 18:10, or

2. is predicated of wind: Ecclesiastes 11:4, 'As thou knowest not what is the way of the Spirit: so thou knowest not the works of GOD,' John 3:8, 'The Spirit bloweth where it listeth.'

3. Or it is predicated of any spiritual thing or nature,

tual, or animate, as well brute as intelligent: as Ecclesiastes 3:21. Who knoweth the spirit of the sons of Adam that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beasts that goeth downward? Acts 7:59. Lord Jesus, receive my spirit: or it is predicated of the inclination, or motion or impulse of the human mind, as well evil as good Psalm 76:13. 2 Chronicles 21:16 and chapter 36:22. Proverbs 17:22 etc. or finally by the name of Spirit are noted the gifts of the Holy Spirit conferred upon the pious and faithful 2 Kings 2:9. I pray that a double portion of thy Spirit may be in me Exodus 31:2. I have filled him (Bezalel) with the Spirit of GOD in all work etc. Numbers 11:17. I will take of thy Spirit, and will give unto them, that they may bear the burden of the people with thee. John 7:39. This he said of the Spirit, which they that believed were to receive etc.

But to return to the Holy Spirit, that is, the third person of the Trinity: we believe that he is true and Essential GOD, moved by the authority of the scriptures, which expressly name him GOD: as Acts 5:3 and 4. Ananias is said to have lied, not to man, but to GOD and indeed to the Holy Spirit. 1 Corinthians 6:19. Believers are held to be temples of the Holy Spirit, who 1 Corinthians 3:16 2 Corinthians 6:16 are called temples of GOD. But concerning this kind of proof, as also concerning that other later one, which is derived partly from attributes, partly from works, which are congruent to GOD alone, let both our Author be seen, and Chemnitius in his Loci, and the Methodical booklets of others.

We proceed rather to the treatment of those Questions which are wont to be moved concerning that characteristic difference of the Holy Spirit. And in the beginning indeed, as a presupposed postulate (ἄιτημα προϋπόθετον), we assume that the Holy Spirit constitutes a proper and peculiar person, distinct from the Father and the Son, or a hypostasis (ὑπόςασιν) or subsistent (ὑφισάμενον): that which, besides that classic testimony 1 John 5:7, There are three that bear witness in Heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit: and these three are one: and the Institution of our Baptism clearly argues, since it ought to be conferred not only in the name of the Father, and of the Son: but also in the Name of the Holy Spirit. Matthew 28:19. and that solemn manifestation of the Holy Spirit, which occurred at the Baptism of Christ, clearly demonstrates, Matthew 3:16. And our Author very skillfully urges those words of Christ John 14:16, I will send you another Comforter. For if the Holy Spirit did not constitute a proper person: but signified a created agitation: he would certainly not be a Teacher, but a doctrine: he would not be Another from the Father and the Son hearing and receiving. It is added that a certain and peculiar personal difference is assigned to the Holy Spirit in the scriptures: so that it is prompt to conclude even from thence that the Holy Spirit constitutes a proper person.

But concerning this very personal property, it was already long ago variously debated: and even now today it is fought against quite vehemently by more recent Anti-Trinitarians. For it is asked in the beginning, whether to proceed (τὸ ἐκπορεύεσθαι) so belongs to the Holy Spirit that it constitutes his personal difference: and whether that cannot be attributed to the Son, or to other things. Damascenus indeed, book 1, On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 9, established that one must distinguish so solicitously between to be born (τὸ γεννᾶσθαι) and to proceed (ἐκπορεύεσθαι), or between that which is born and that which proceeds (τὸ γεννώμενον καὶ ἐκπορευόμενον), that the former is assigned only to the Son: but the latter only to the Holy Spirit. Whence most of the more recent writers are also wont to distinguish, to go out (τὸ ἐξελθεῖν) and to proceed (τὸ ἐκπορεύειν): so that they show that the former is predicated in the Scriptures of the Son: but the latter only of the Holy Spirit. But the thing itself and the usage of the Greek language seem not to confirm the truth of those distinctions in all respects. In the Scriptures, certainly, the word to proceed (ἐκπορεύεσθαι) is also predicated of other things: as Matthew 15:11, That which proceedeth out of the mouth, this defileth the man (τὸ ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκ τοῦ στόματος, τοῦτο κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον): And it cannot be denied that the Greek words to go out (ἐξῆλθεν) and to proceed (ἐκπορεύεσθαι), as all Lexicographers attest, are of the same general signification. Hence it happened that not only the Scholastics, but some of the Latin Fathers, were not at all averse to this phrase: The Son proceeds from the Father: as can be seen in Augustine, Question 10 to Orosius, who has it thus: No one is a Son, unless of two, a Father and a Mother. Which God forbid, that we should suspect such a thing between GOD the Father and the Son: Because neither does the son of man proceed at the same time from the Father and from the Mother, Because when he proceeds from the Father, then he does not proceed from the Mother: and when he proceeds from the Mother into this light, then he does not proceed from the Father. This very formula of speaking was also held by the Scholastics, as is evident from Thomas, part 1, question 27, Articles 1 and 2. Furthermore, when the word to go out (ἐξελθεῖν) is predicated of the Son in the Scriptures, then it ought to be referred rather to the office, in respect of which he was sent by the Father, than to that secret mode of production which consists in generating: so that it is sufficiently clear even from thence that it is not so conveniently to compare to go out (ἐξελθεῖν) and to proceed (ἐκπορεύεσθαι) with one another, since the former denotes an office, the latter a characteristic property of a person. Therefore, in deciding this controversy, it seems hardly advisable that we should stick to words, and think that apodictic arguments should be derived from a certain proper affection of the words to go out (ἐξελθεῖν) and to proceed (ἐκπορεύεσθαι): for they will hardly be able to sustain the attack of the Adversaries. What then? The whole momentum, of course, consists in the thing itself, and in the mode of production, which is one and different in the Father in respect of the Son: and another and different in the Father and the Son in respect of the Holy Spirit. And although the sharpness of human reason can in no way attain the manner of either production: since that is a work ad intra, not ad extra; nor does it happen, as in created things, either from imperfect to perfect, or by some local motion, or by the production of some exterior effect: but in a manner altogether ineffable and incomprehensible: yet if we consult the Scriptures themselves, the diversity of that manner regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit will appear more than sufficiently. The Scholastic Doctors commonly teach that the procession of the Son from the Father is by way of intellect, which reflects the likeness of the thing understood: but that the procession of the Holy Spirit is by way of will, which loves and embraces the thing understood.

Basilius and Nazianzenus also seem to have held this very opinion, while they expressly wrote that to be born is from the mind or thought: but to proceed is from the will. Although, indeed, we can neither prove nor ought to prove this assertion in all respects, because in GOD the intellect and the will do not differ as they do in a rational creature; where every action of the intellect is internal, and terminates in the will itself: for the intellect rests only when the will approaches, in which it may entirely acquiesce: meanwhile, however, the scripture itself being witness, the mode of production in the Son and the Holy Spirit differs from one another, not only by reason of order, but also in respect of the thing itself. By reason of order indeed, insofar as the Son is produced from the Father alone, but the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son together. But by reason of the thing, insofar as the Son is produced from the Father alone by begetting; Psalm 2:7, I have said, You are my Son: I have this day begotten you. But the Holy Spirit is produced not from the Father alone, but from the Father and the Son together by spiration: Whence he is named: The Spirit of the mouth of Jehovah, Psalm 33:6. The Spirit of the lips of the Messiah, Isaiah 11:4. The Spirit of the mouth of Christ, 2 Thess. 2:8. These foundations having been well weighed, the assertion of the Orthodox remains undoubted and clearly irrefragable, that just as the characteristic property of the Son according to Scripture is τὸ γεννητὸν, to be begotten: so according to the same, the personal property of the Holy Spirit is τὸ ἐκπορευτὸν, to proceed. It is further asked in this place, Whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, or indeed from the Father and the Son together and equally? And certainly that he proceeds from the Father is placed beyond the hazard of controversy: For Christ himself attests to this, John 15:26, saying, When the Paraclete shall come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.

But whether he also proceeds from the Son was doubted by certain Greeks, because that is not contained in the scriptures literally or word for word. But it was rightly answered by the Latins: It is vain to seek from scripture formal words by which some thing is proven, when it can be manifestly gathered from the same: as Cardinal Toletus sometimes answered, annot. 23, to the cited chapter of John. That the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son can be most solidly gathered and demonstrated from the scriptures, both ancient and recent theologians have shown at length. For first, by what right would the Holy Spirit be sent by the Son equally as by the Father, unless he also proceeded equally from the same. For this temporal Mission presupposes that eternal procession from the Son: since no other reason of right or power of this sending of the Spirit can be assigned, than that which depends upon the procession. Now, however, Christ also sends the Holy Spirit, John 14:26 and chapter 15:26. Therefore.

Then, whatever is the cause for which the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Father, it is necessary that it be also the very same cause for which the same Spirit is also named the Spirit of the Son. Now he is called the Spirit of the Father because of that eternal spiration by which the Father breathes the Holy Spirit consubstantial to himself. Therefore, because of the same common spiration, it is necessary that he also be called the Spirit of the Son. Nor can any reason for a difference be assigned. And the exception of the Greeks is too ἀσύστατος (unstable), saying that the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son because he is of the same Essence as the Son. For by this reasoning the Son could also be called the son of the Holy Spirit, because the Essence is equally common between the Son and the Spirit as it is between the Father and the Son: which would be prodigiously absurd. But the Holy Spirit is expressly called the Spirit of the Son in the scriptures, Rom. 8:9, Gal. 4:6, Isa. 11:4. The Messiah shall slay the Wicked with the Spirit of his lips: Which the Apostle, 2 Thess. 2:8, interprets concerning the Antichrist: Whom, he says, the Lord shall consume with the Spirit of his mouth, and shall abolish with the Brightness of his coming. Whence Augustine also, lib. de fide ad Petrum cap. 11, most rightly concludes, that it is in no way to be doubted, but most firmly to be held, that the same Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The same Augustine gathers this very thing in place of a third argument from that insufflation by which Christ communicated the Holy Spirit to the Apostles, John 20:22. For what else, says Augustine, did this insufflation declare, except that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son: For if he did not proceed from him, breathing upon his disciples, he would not have said, Receive the Holy Spirit.

And that we may not go further, the same Augustine again, lib. 15 de Trin. cap. 26, shows a far most firm argument from the fact that it is read written in John 16:13: The Holy Spirit shall not speak from himself, but whatever he shall hear, he shall speak: He shall receive of Mine, and shall announce it to you. Hence he infers very skillfully: Therefore the Holy Spirit receives not from the Father alone, but also from the Son: But if receiving from the Father, he is deservedly said to proceed from the same: and receiving from both; yet he cannot be said to be begotten by both: For thus two Begotten, and in the Divinity two Sons would be constituted: therefore it is to be believed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. This reason of Augustine is wonderfully confirmed by the fact that no other mode by which the Holy Spirit is said to receive from the Father can be given than that Essential communion through procession. And as to how this can also obtain a place by reason of the Son, from whom the Holy Spirit is said to receive no less than from the Father, there can be given absolutely no reason for a difference.

Finally, the Scholastic Doctors have fought not unsuccessfully against the Greeks with this argument also: If the Holy Spirit does not proceed equally from the Son as from the Father, then the Son is not really distinguished from the Holy Spirit: or what is the same, no relation of the Son to the Spirit can be given; and vice versa of the latter to the Son. But this is absurd: since the most absolute perfection of the Trinity requires even most especially that all Persons be related to each other by certain relations, and thus each to each. Furthermore, the hypostatic relation between the Son having been removed

& the Holy Spirit, there remains a certain kind of gap or διάστημα between the hypostasis of the Son & of the Spirit, or any personal connection: a thing which both that most absolute perfection of the Trinity, and the mutual respect of the persons toward one another, by no means admits. But let these things suffice, for this time: Whoever desires more, let him consult Chemnitz, Hunnius, & others, who dispute expressly on this matter. We shall respond below in the Antithesis to the arguments of the Greeks.

Latin:

SPiritus Sanctus est tertia perssona Trinitatis à Patre & Filio, vel ut ex uno fonte essentiali, ineffabili modo ab æterno procedens.

Ἔκθεσις.

FEcit Macedonianorum hæresis, ut non modo Autor noster, sed & plerique Theologi, Disputationi de Spiritu Sancto, præmittant accuratam explicationem multiplicis potestatis sive significationis vocabuli SPIRITUS. Nos ne actum agere videamur, missis illis, quæ ex libellis Methodicis peti possunt, brevi quodamSchematismo rem universam in pauca colligemus.

Vocabulum ergo Spiritus est πολύσημον: & prædicatur vel de Deo, vel de creaturis. De DEO acceptú, vel essentialiter notat omnes tres personas Trinitatis, quæ ratione Essentiæ sunt Spiritus: secundum illud Joh. 4, 24. DEUS est Spiritus: vel Effectivè notat virtutem & potentiam, imò sæpius iram & furorem DEI, Exod. 15, 8. In Spiritu furoris tui congregatæ sunt aquæ (quibus videlicet Ægyptii in deserto sunt suffocati:) Psal. 18, 16. Ab increpatione tua & inspiratione Spiritus iræ tuæ revelata sunt fundamenta orbis terrarum: vel deniquè Personaliter seorsim quasi notat Spiritum Sanctum, tertiam Trinitatis personam: commune illud & coëssentiale Patris & Filii spiraculum.

1. De Creaturis acceptum vocabulum Spiritus, prædicatur vel de Angelis, iisque tam bonis Hebr. 1, 14. Psal. 104, 4. quam malis: Luc. 11, 24. & 26. 1. Sam. 18, 10. vel

2. prædicatur de Vento: Ecclesiastæ 11, 4. Quomodo ignoras, quæ sit via Spirit9: Sic nescis opera DEI Joh. 3, 8. Spiritus ubi vult, spirat.

3. Vel prædicatur de qualibet re sive natura Spirituali,

tuali, aut animata, tam bruta, quàm intelligente: ut Ecclesiastæ 3, 21. Quis novit an Spiritus filiorum Adam ascendat sursum, & Spiritus jumentorum descendat deorsum? Act. 7, 59. Domine Jesu suscipe Spiritum meum: vel prædicatur de Inclinatione, sive motu aut impetu animi humani, tàm malo, quàm bono Psalm. 76, 13. 2. Paral. 21, 16. & cap 36, 22. Proverb. 17, 22. & c. vel denique Spiritus appellatione notantur dona Spiritus Sancti in pios atque fideles collata 2. Reg. 2, 9. Obsecro, ut in me duplex sit Spiritus tuus Exod. 31, 2. Implevi eũ (Besoleel) Spiritu DEI in omni opere & c. Num. 11, 17. Auferam de Spiritu tuo, & tradam eis, ut sustentent tecum onus populi tui. Johan. 7, 39. Hoc dixit de Spiritu, quem accepturi erant credentes &c.

Cæterùm ut ad Spiritum Sanctum, hoc est, tertiam personam Trinitatis redeamus: verum & Essentialem ipsum DEUM esse, credimus, moti scripturarum autoritate, quæ expressè ipsum DEUM nominant: ut Act. 5, 3. & 4. Ananias mentitus esse dicitur, non homini, sed DEO & quidem Spiritui Sancto. 1. Cor. 6, 19. Credentes perhibentur esse templa Spiritus Sancti, qui 1. Cor. 3. 16 2. Cor. 6, 16. DEI templa appellantur. Verum & de hoc probationum genere, ut & de posteriore illo altero, quod partim ab attributis, partim ab operibus, Soli DEO congruentibus, desumitur, videatur tùm Autor noster, tùm Chemnitius in locis, tùm aliorum libelli Methodici.

Nos ad earum potiùs Quæstionum tractationem accedimus, quæ de characteristica illâ differentia Spiritus Sancti, moveri solent. Ac initiò quidem tanquam ἄιτημα προϋπόθετον sumimus, Spiritum Sanctum propriam atque peculiarem, & à Patre ac Filio distinctam personam sive ὑπόςασιν aut ὑφισάμενον constituere: id quod præter classicum illud testimonium 1. Joh. 5, 7. Tres sunt qui testimonium dant in Cælo, Pater, Verbum & Spiritus Sanctus: & hi tres unum sunt: tùm Institutio Baptismi nostri luculenter arguit, quippe qui non modò in nomine Patris, & Filii: Sed & in Nomine Spiritus Sancti conferri debet. Matth. 28, 19. tùm solennis illa manifestatio Spiritus Sancti, quæ circa Baptismum Christi, obtigit, luculenter demonstrat, Matth. 3, 16. Et scitè admodum urget Autor noster verba illa Christi Joh. 14, 16. Alium paracletum mittam vobis. Si enim Spiritus Sanctus non propriam constitueret personam: sed significaret agitationem creatam: utique non esset Doctor, sed doctrina: non esset Alius à Patre & Filio audiens & accipiens. Accedit, quod Spiritui Sancto certa quædam & peculiaris personalis differentia, in scripturis assignatur: ut vel indè promtum sit colligere, Spiritum Sanctum propriam personam constituere.

Cæterùm de hac ipsa proprietate personali, & jam olim variè controversum fuit: ac etiam num hodiè à recentioribus Anti-Trinitariis satis vehementer pugnatur. Quæritur enim initiò, utrum τὸ ἐκπορεύεσθαι, procedere, ita Spiritui Sancto conveniat, ut constituat personalem ejus differentiam: neque illud vel Filio, vel rebus aliis tribui queat. Damascenus quidem lib. 1. Orth. fid. cap. 9. inter τὸ γεννᾶσθαι & ἐκπορεύεσθαι, Nasci & procedere, sive inter τὸ γεννώμενον καὶ ἐκπορευόμενον ita sollicitè distingvendum esse statuit, ut prius illud tantùm Filio: posterius autem hoc tantùm Spiritui Sancto adsignetur. Undè plerique etiam recentiores distingvere solent, τὸ ἐξελθεῖν exigere, & inter τὸ ἐκπορεύειν procedere: ut illud quidem de Filio: hoc autem tantùm de Spiritu Sancto, in Scripturis prædicari ostendant. Sed videtur res ipsa, & usus lingvæ Græcæ distinctionum istarum veritatem non per omnia comprobare. In Scripturis certè Verbum ἐκπορεύεσθαι etiam de aliis rebus prædicatur: ut Matth. 15, 11. τὸ ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκ τοῦ στόματος, τοῦτο κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον : Quod procedit ex ore, hoc polluit hominem: Et negari non potest, verba Græca ἐξῆλθεν καὶ ἐκπορεύεσθαι, attestantibus omnibus Lexicographis, ejusdem esse generalis significationis. Hinc factum, ut non modò Scholastici, sed quidam ex Patribus Latinis, ab hac phrasi minimè abhorrerent: Filius procedit à Patre: uti videre est apud Augustinum Quæst. 10. ad Orosium, qui sic habet: Nullus Filius est, nisi duorum Patris & Matris. Quod absit, ut inter DEUM Patrem & Filium, tale quid suspicemur: Quia nec Filius hominis simul ex Patre procedit, & ex Matre, Quia cùm procedit ex Patre, tunc non procedit ex Matre: & cùm procedit ex Matre in hac luce, tunc non procedit ex Patre. Quam ipsam loquendi formulam tenuerunt etiam Scholastici, uti patet ex Thoma part. 1. quæst. 27. Artic. 1. & 2. Præterea, quando in Scripturis de Filio prædicatur verbum ἐξελθεῖν tùm illud potius ad officium, respectu cujus à Patre missus est, quàm ad arcanum illum productionis modum, qui in generando consistit, referri debet: ut vel indè satis dilucidè constet, haud ita commodè ἐξελθεῖν & ἐκπορεύεσθαι inter se mutuò conferri, cum illud officium, hoc proprietatem characteristicam personæ notet. Proindè in decidenda hac controversia vix consultum videtur, ut in vocabulis hæreamus, & ex propria quadam affectione verborum ἐξελθεῖν, ἐκπορεύεσθαι argumenta apodictica desumenda esse arbitremur: vix enim Adversariorum impetum ea sustinere poterunt. Quid igitur? Omne nimirùm momentum in re ipsa, & modo productionis consistit, qui alius est & diversus in Patre respectu Filii: alius & diversus in Patre & Filio respectu Spiritus Sancti. Et quanquam modum utriusque productionis rationis humanæ acumen nullo modo affequi potest: Siquidem ille est opus ad intra, non ad extra; neque fit, ut in rebus creatis vel ex imperfecto ad perfectum, vel motu quodam locali, vel productione effectus alicujus exterioris: sed modo prorsus ineffabili & incomprehensibili: tamen si Scripturas ipsas consulamus, Modi istius diversitas quoad Filium & Spiritum Sanctum satis superq; apparebit. Doctores Scholastici communiter tradunt, processionē Filii ex Patre esse per modum intellectus, qui rei intellectæ similitudine refert: Processionem verò Spiritus Sancti esse per modū voluntatis, quæ rē intellectā amat & āplectitur.

Quam ipsam sententiam Basilius & Nazianzenus quoque tenuisse videntur, dum expressè scripserunt, Nasci esse à mente seu cogitatione: Procedere autem à voluntate. Quanquam verò assertionem hanc per omnia probare nec possumus nec debemus, propterea quòd in DEO intellectus, & voluntas non ita differunt, uti in creatura rationali; ubi omnis intellectus actio interna, in ipsa voluntate terminatur: Siquidem tum demùm quiescit intellectus, quando accedit voluntas, in qua ille omninò acquiescat: Interim tamen scriptura ipsa teste, productionis modus in Filio & Spiritu Sancto, non modò ratione ordinis, sed & ipsius rei respectu à se invicem differt. Ratione ordinis quidem, quatenus Filius à solo Patre, Spiritus verò Sanctus, à Patre, & Filio simul est productus. Ratione rei verò, quatenus Filius à solo Patre Generando; Psal. 2, 7. Dixi, Filius meus es tu: Ego hodie genui te. Spiritus verò Sanctus non à solo Patre, sed à Patre & Filio simul spirando est productus: Unde nominatur: Spiritus oris Jehova Psal. 33, 6. Spiritus labiorum Messiæ Iesai, 4. Spiritus oris Christi, 2. Thess. 2, 8. Quibus fundamentis probè expensis, indubia & planè irrefragabilis manet Orthodoxorum assertio, quod quemadmodum Filii proprietas Characteristica secundum Scripturam est τὸ γεννητὸν, Generatum esse: ita secundum eandem Spiritus Sancti proprietas personalis sit τὸ ἐκπορευτὸν, procedere. Quæritur autem porrò hoc loco, Num Spiritus Sanctus procedat à Patre solo, an verò à Patre & Filio simul & æqualiter? Et sanè à Patre ipsum procedere, extra controversiæ aleam est positum: Hoc enim Christus ipse attestatur, Joh. 15, 26. Cum inquiens, venerit Paracletus, quem ego mittam vobis à Patre, Spiritus veritatis, qui à Patre procedit.

Cæterùm num à Filio quoque procedat, à Græcis quibusdam dubitatum fuit, propterea quòd in scripturis illud ad literam aut verbum nõ expressum continentur. Sed rectè à Latinis responsum fuit: Vanum est petere ex scriptura verba formalia, quibus aliqua res comprobetur, quando ex iisdem manifestè ea colligi potest: uti aliquando respondit Card: Tolet. annot. 23. ad citatum caput Johannis. Solidissimè autem ex scripturis processione Spiritus Sancti etiam à Filio, colligi & demonstrari posse, tum veteres tum recentiores Theologi prolixè ostenderunt. Primùm enim quo jure Spiritus Sanctus à Filio æquè atque à Patre mitteretur, nisi ab eodem etiam pariter procederet. Præsupponit enim temporalis hæc Missio, æternam illam processionem à Filio: Siquidem nulla alia potest adsignari ratio Juris sive potestatis, hujus mittendi Spiritum, quàm quæ ex processione dependet. Jam verò Christus etiam mittit Spiritum Sanctum, Joh. 14, 26. & cap. 15, 26. Ergo.

Deindè, Quæ causa est, propter quam Spiritus Sanctus dicitur Patris Spiritus, eadem etiam omninò causa sit necesse est, propter quam idem Spiritus Filii etiam Spiritus nominatur. Jam verò Patris Spiritus dicitur, propter æternam illam spirationem, qua Pater spirat Spiritum Sanctum sibi consubstantialem. Ergò ob eandem communem spirationem, Filii etiam Spiritus dicatur necesse est. Neq; enim ulla diversitatis ratio assignari potest. Et nimis ἀσύστατος est exceptio Græcorum dicentium, Spiritum Sanctum dici Sanctum etiam Filii, quia ejusdem sit cum Filio Essentiæ. Hâc enim ratione Filius etiam dici posset, Spiritus Sancti filius, quia æquè communis est Essentia inter Filium, & Spiritum, atque est inter Patrem & Filium: id quod prodigiosè fuerit absurdum. Dicitur autem SpiritusSanctus in scripturis expressè Spiritus Filii, Rom. 8, 9. Gal. 4, 6. Ies. 11, 4. Messias Spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet Impium : Quod Apostolus 2. Thess. 2, 8. de Antichristo interpretatur: Quem, inquiens, Dominus conficiet Spiritu oris sui, & abolebit Claritate Adventus sui. Undè Augustinus quoque lib. de fide ad Petrum cap. 11. rectissimè colligit, Nullatenus dubitandum, sed firmissimè tenendum esse, eundem Spiritum Sanctum, qui Patris & Filii unus est Spiritus, de Patre & Filio procedere.

Quod ipsum Tertii argumenti loco colligit idem Augustinus ex insufflatione illa, qua Christus Spiritum Sanctum communicavit Apostolis Johan. 20, 22. Quid enim aliud inquit Augustinus, declaravit insufflactio isthæc, nisi quòd etiam Spiritus Sanctus procedat de Filio: Si enim de eo non procederet, discipulis suis insufflans, non dixisset, Accipite Spiritum Sanctum.

Et ne longiùs abeamus, idem rursus Augustinus lib. 15. de Trin. cap. 26. argumentum longè firmissimum monstrat, ex eo, quòd Johan. 16, 13. scriptum legitur: Spiritus Sanctus à seipso non loquetur, sed quæcunque audierit, loquetur: Ille de Meo accipiet, & annunciabit vobis. Hinc scitè admodum ille infert: Accipit E. Spiritus Sanctus non à solo Patre, sed & à Filio: Quod si accipiens à Patre, meritò dicitur ab eodē procedere: & accipiens ab utroque; non tamen potest dici ab utroque gigni: Sic enim duo Geniti, & in Divinitate duo Filii constituerentur: utique ab utroque Spiritus Sanctus procedere, credendum est. Rationem hanc Augustini mirificè confirmat illud, quòd nullus alius modus, quo Spiritus Sanctus à Patre accipere dicitur, dari potest, quàm Essentialis illa communio per processionem. Quæ quo minus etiam ratione Filii locum obtinere queat, â quò haud minus atque à Patre, Spiritus Sanctus accipere dicitur, ratio diversitatis planè nulla dari potest.

Tandem Scholastici Doctores adversus Græcos hoc etiam argumento haud infeliciter pugnarunt: Si Spiritus Sanctus non procedit æquè à Filio atque à Patre, tùm Filius non distingvitur realiter à Spiritu Sancto: vel quod idem est, nulla dari potest relatio Filii ad Spiritum; & vice versa hujus ad Filium. Atqui hoc absurdum: siquidem absolutissima Trinitatis perfectio vel maximè requirit, ut certis quibusdam relationibus Personæ omnes ad se mutuò, adeoque singulæ ad singulas referantur. Porrò sublata relatione hypostatica inter Filium

& Spiritum Sanctum, relinquitur quidam quasi hiatus sive διάστημα quoddam inter hypostasin Filii & Spiritus, sive ullo personali nexu: id quod tùm absolutissima illa Trinitatis perfectio, tùm mutuus personarum ad se invicem respectus nullo pacto admittit. Sed sufficiant isthæc, hac quidem vice: Qui plura desiderat, consulat Chemnitium, Hunnium & alios, hac de re ex professo disputantes. Nos infra in Antithesi, ad argumenta Græcorum respondebimus.


### Chapter I. Question I. On the Knowledge of God. Proposition: Proposition IX

The three persons of the Divinity, regarding external manifestation, & in respect of works which are performed outside the divine Essence, are so distinguished that Creation is attributed to the Father: Redemption to the Son: Sanctification to the Holy Spirit.

Exegesis.

The three persons of the Divinity differ both from within and from without. The internal distinction is constituted by those internal characteristic properties or personal differences: concerning which it has been disputed thus far. The external distinction, however, is taken from external manifestation; and from those works which are performed outside the divine Essence; such as the Creation and Preservation of created things. The Redemption of the human race: The sanctification of the same: and other works of this kind. Concerning both distinctions, two Rules of St. Augustine are to be observed: the former of which, concerning works from within, holds thus: The works of the Trinity from within are divided & incommunicable: such as, To beget, To be begotten, and To proceed. For these are common to the three persons: but each of them claims one of these for itself in such a way that it never communicates it with another. According to this Rule, To beget belongs to the Father alone: To be begotten, to the Son alone: To proceed, to the Holy Spirit alone.

The latter Rule concerning works from without is such: The works of the Trinity from without are undivided & communicable. For when God works something outside His Essence in creatures: then the three persons work together and jointly. For although in this kind of work, a certain work is sometimes assigned to one person above the remaining persons: yet this is by no means to be understood exclusively, as if the remaining persons were excluded from that very work: But it is done only by reason of Order and Manifestation. Which Order Scripture itself seems to have defined, when it speaks thus: From him, through him, and in him are all things, Rom. 11:36. For example: The work of creation is indeed common to all three persons: but by reason of Order and Manifestation it is principally attributed to GOD the Father. For just as in each work, each person has manifested Himself in a peculiar way: so that work is ascribed to Him with a certain notation of Order. Now, because in the Creation of this Universe GOD the Father revealed Himself principally: In Redemption, however, the Son manifested Himself peculiarly: In Sanctification, indeed, the Holy Spirit manifested Himself most of all: certainly these works are attributed to each individually κατ' ἐξοχὴν: yet without the community being meanwhile excluded or removed, by which in those very works, all persons participate by reason of one and the same divine essence. Whence it is that Basil calls GOD the Father the προκαταρκτικὴν or primogenial cause of creation: the Son the δημιουργικὴν or Instrumental: the Holy Spirit the τελειωτικὴν or consummative. Which diversity of causes, however, denotes not any inequality of Nature: but only a certain order of the persons. And deservedly is the Sophistry of the Arians exploded in this place, who blaspheme that all things were created through the Son, as if through some created Instrument. For in divine matters the nature of a mediate or Instrumental cause is far different from what it is accustomed to be for organs or Instruments, either in Nature or in Art. For as the Father works in creating: so also the Son works: John 5. The Father indeed, as the fountain of all divine actions, obtaining the primacy in this work of Creation: but not by reason of time or power: but only in respect of order to the remaining persons of the Trinity. Blessed Luther has encompassed this whole dispute with a certain concise rule: These works, he says, from without are either considered Absolutely: When they are common to all three persons without any distinction: or Relatively: when, namely, it is considered in what order the persons act, or in what work each person has manifested Himself above the rest.

Furthermore, the Fathers have noted that in this kind of divine operations from without, the Scriptures sometimes make mention of only one person, sometimes of two, and sometimes even of all three persons: Just as the Church also not rarely does not observe the order of persons: but both in prayers and otherwise, it attributes one and the same action now to the Father, now to the Son, now to the Holy Spirit. Where, however, it is to be noted that this is done, not to confuse the distinction of persons: But partly to signify the unity of the Essence, and partly the community of the operations.

Finally, it deserves observation that in the Scriptures the word Father is accepted in two ways: Sometimes Personally: In which respect the word Father belongs incommunicably to the first person of the Divinity alone: Sometimes, however, it is accepted Essentially: in which respect the word Father belongs equally to all three persons. Thus the Son, Isa. 9:6, is called the Father of eternity: Thus Eph. 4:6, it is accommodated to all three persons: One GOD and Father of all, who is over all (Father) through all (Son) and in all (Holy Spirit).

THE LATTER CHAPTER.

Latin:

Tres personæ Divinitatis, quoad patefactionem externam, & respectu operum, quæ extra divinam Essentiam perficiuntur, ita distingvuntur, uti Patri tribuatur Creatio: Filio, Redemptio: Spiritui Sancto, Sanctificatio.

Exegesis.

Differunt tres personæ Divinitatis tùm ab intra, tùm ab Extra. Discrimen internum constituunt proprietates illæ internæ characteristicæ sive differentiæ personales: de quibus hactenus disputatum. Extrinsecum verò discrimen sumitur à patefactione externa; & ab iis operibus, quæ extra divinam Essentiam perficiuntur; qualia sunt Creatio & Conservatio rerum creatarum. Redemptio generis humani: Ejusdem sanctificatio: & quæ hujus generis opera sunt alia. De utróque discrimine observandæ sunt duæ Regulæ D. Augustini: quarum prior de operibus ad intra sic habet: Opera Trinitatis ad intra sunt divisa & incommunicabilia: qualia sunt, Gignere, Gigni, & Procedere. Hæc enim sunt communia tribus personis: sed quælibet earum unum istorum ita sibi vendicat, ut cum altera nunquam communicet. Secundum hanc Regulam, Gignere soli Patri: Gigni, soli Filio: Procedere, Soli Spiritui Sancto competit.

Posterior Regula de operibus ad extra talis est: Opera Trinitatis ad extra sunt indivisa & communicabilia. Quando enim Deus extra suam Essentiam in creaturis aliquid operatur: tunc tres personæ simul & junctim operantur. Etsi enim in hoc genere operum, uni personæ interdum opus quoddam præ reliquis personis adsignatur: minimè tamen exclusivè hoc intelligendum est, ac si reliquæ personæ ab illo ipso opere exclusæ essent: Sed fit illud tantùm ratione Ordinis & Patefactionis. Quem Ordinem ipsa Scriptura definivisse videtur, quando sic loquitur: Ex ipso, per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia, Rom. 11,36. Exempli gratia: Opus creationis commune quidem est omnibus tribus personis: sed ratione Ordinis & Patefactionis principaliter tribuitur DEO patri. Nam prout in unoquoque opere, persona quælibet peculiariter sese patefecit: ita cum certa Ordinis notatione opus illud ipsi adscribitur. Jam, quia in Creatione hujus Universi DEUS Pater præcipuè sese revelavit: In Redemtione autem peculiariter sese manifestavit Filius: In Sanctificatione verò Spiritus Sanctus sese maximè patefecit: utique singulis κατ' ἐξοχὴν opera ista Sigillatim tribuuntur: non exclusa tamen interim sive sublata communitate, quâ in illis ipsis operibus, personæ omnes, ratione unius ejusdemque essentiæ divinæ participant. Undè est, quòd Basilius DEUM patrem vocat Causam creationis προκαταρκτικὴν primogeneam: Filium δημιουργικὴν Instrumentalem: Spiritum Sanctum τελειωτικὴν consummativam. Quæ tamen causarum diversitas non aliquam Naturæ inæqualitatem: sed tantùm ordinem certum personarum notat. Et meritò exploditur hoc loco Arianorum Sophisticatio, blasphemantium, Per Filium, tanquam per Instrumentum aliquod creatum, omnia creata esse. Nam in divinis longè alia est ratio causæ mediæ sive Instrumentalis, quàm quæ esse solet organorum sive Instrumentorum, vel in Naturâ, vel in Arte. Creando enim uti Pater operatur: ita operatur etiam Filius: Joh. 5. Patre quidem ceu fonte actionum divinarum omnium, principatum obtinente in opere isto Creationis: sed non ratione temporis aut potentiæ: sed tantùm respectu ordinis ad reliquas personas Trinitatis. B. Lutherus compendiosâ quadam regulâ universam hanc disputationem est complexus: Opera isthæc, inquiens, ad extra vel considerantur Absolutè: Quando eâ sine ullo discrimine communia sunt omnibus tribus personis: vel Relatè: quando nimirùm consideratur, quo ordine agant personæ, vel in quo opere quælibet persona, præ reliquis sese patefecerit.

Annotarunt præterea Patres, In hoc genere operationum divinarum ad Extra, Scripturas interdum unius duntaxat personæ, aliquando duarum, nonnunquam etiam omnium trium personarum mentionem facere: Quemadmodum Ecclesia quoque haud rarò personarum ordinem non observat: sed tùm in precibus, tùm aliàs unam eandemque actionem modò tribuit Patri, modò Filio, modò Spiritui Sancto. Ubi tamen notandum, fieri hoc, non ad confundendum personarum discrimen: Sed partim ad Essentiæ unitatem, partim verò ad operationum communitatem significandam.

Tandem observationem meretur, quod in Scripturis vocabulum Patris bifariam accipitur: Interdum Personaliter: Quo respectu soli primæ personæ Divinitatis vox Patris competit incommunicabiliter: Interdum verò accipitur Essentialiter: quo respectu vox Patris omnibus tribus personis ex æquo competit. Sic Filius Ies. 9, 6. dicitur Pater æternitatis: Sic Eph. 4, 6. Omnib9 tribus personis accommodatur: Unus DEUS & Pater omnium, qui est super omnes (Pater) per omnes (Filius) & in omnibus (Spiritus Sanctus.)

CAPUT Po. STERIUS.


### Later Chapter. Containing the artifice, and a succinct refutation of both ancient and more recent heresies which impinge upon the mystery…

What we read that Simeon once predicted concerning CHRIST the Savior, that He would be a sign to be contradicted: that can most truly be affirmed of the Mystery of the Unity of the Divine Essence and the Trinity of Persons. For from the very beginnings of the Church of the New Testament, this Article concerning the One and Triune GOD has been set before heretics as a target, against which all of them have vied in directing their arrows.

Moreover, all those heresies, manifold not so much in number as in impiety, can most conveniently be divided into four distinct classes: the first of which contains those that either plainly denied the unity of the divine essence or otherwise foully defiled it. The second, however, sets forth those that strove to undermine, nay, utterly to overthrow, the mystery of the Trinity in various ways. The third weaves together a catalog and the blasphemies of those heresies that impugned partly the divinity and partly the generation of the Son. The fourth, finally and lastly, submits a brief notation and refutation of those who did not fear to deny the divinity of the Holy Spirit and His procession from the Son.

Latin:
