Quod de CHRISTO Servatore olim Simeonem prædixisse legimus, fore ipsum in signum cui contradicatur: illud verissimè de Mysterio Unitatis Essentiæ divinæ, & Trinitatis personarum affirmari potest. Fuit enim jam indè à primordiis ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti, Articulus iste de DEO Uno & Trino, ceu scopus hæreticis præfixus, adversus quem certatim omnes tela sua dirigent.

Possunt autem universæ illæ hæreses, non tàm numero quàm impietate multiplices, in quatuor distinctas classes commodissimè dispesci: quarum prima eas contineat, quæ unitatem essentiæ divinæ, vel planè negarunt, vel aliàs fœdè conspurcarunt. Altera verò eas expediat, quæ Trinitatis mysterium variis modis convellere, imò prorsus evertere studuerunt. Tertia earum hæreseωn Catalogum & blasphemias pertexat, quæ partim divinitatem, partim verò Generationem Filii impugnarunt. Quarta denique & postrema subjiciat brevem tùm Notationem, tùm Refutationem eorum, qui Spiritus Sancti divinitatem, & processionem à Filio, negare haud sunt veriti.


### Later Chapter. Containing the artifice, and a succinct refutation of both…: Class the First. Heresies attacking the unity of the Divine Essence

Of heresies impinging upon the unity of the Divine Essence.

To this Class the Audians may not inappropriately be referred at the beginning, who, denying that GOD is a most simple, spiritual, and incorporeal Essence, must be judged to have denied the very unity of the divine Essence at the same time. For that which is composite and corporeal cannot certainly have an Essence that is one in number within a plurality of persons. These men contended, however, that GOD is corporeal and similar to the human form. And so they assigned to Him arms, and feet, and ears, and other members of this kind, similar to ours. Whence the sect of the Anthropomorphites later took its origin. Although this heresy was indeed too gross and palpable, and expired almost of its own accord through its own futility, there have nevertheless always been those who would scatter the seeds of that impiety: and partly appealed to the Holy Scriptures, which expressly assign such corporeal members to GOD; and partly urged the fact that man was created in the image of GOD: whence they supposed that a conformity of Essence between GOD and man necessarily followed. But it was most rightly answered long ago by Damascene, lib. 1, Orthod. fid. cap. 12, that those former phrases of Scripture are to be taken not properly, but equivocally and κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν concerning GOD: so that the former argument labors under a double sophistication, both of equivocation and of the Figure of Diction. Furthermore, that Image of GOD, to which the first man was created, did not concern a confirmation of essence: but looked to that justice and holiness, and the rectitude of all the powers of both body and soul, whence the refutation of the vicious definition, and ὥς τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς, emerges of its own accord.

Next to these, those claim a place for themselves who established that there is indeed one GOD, αἰνώτατον and supreme, as Epiphanius speaks, from whom, however, other Gods originate: so that that one supreme GOD is the principle of the remaining gods, and as it were the informer, or essence-giver, as the Servetians spoke in the previous century. The Apellites, Messalians, Monarchians, and others erred in this error, as testified by Epiphanius and Augustine. But since they fought neither with testimonies of Scripture nor with reasons, but recalled into the Church of GOD, as if by a postliminy, the filth of the Platonists, already long since explored and condemned: it happened that this heresy collapsed through its own impiety.

The third place in this first Class is occupied by the Carpocratians, Gnostics, Cerdonians, Apellites, Valentinians, Marcionites, and Manichaeans, who partly approved of the polytheism of the Gentiles; but partly indeed imagined two GODS of a nature and essence entirely different, nay, contrary: one Good, the other Evil, from whom, as from first, eternal, and co-eternal principles, all things might draw their origin: good things indeed from the good GOD; but evil things from the evil GOD. To cloak this impiety of theirs, they pretended that passage of Micah 1:12, 'Evil came down from the Lord, even unto the gate of Jerusalem,' and that of Amos 3:6. 'Is there evil in a city, which the Lord hath not done?' being deceived by a very base and gross ignorance, because they did not know how to distinguish between the evil of punishment and the evil of fault; the former of which is indeed assigned to GOD in the Scriptures, as the just avenger of crimes; but the latter is not assigned in the same way, as that which received its origin in time from the fall of our first parents and the corruption of our Nature.

We assign the fourth place to the Tritheists, who, intending to avoid the heresy of the Sabellians, have fallen into the opposite hyperbole, contending that there are Three Gods, distinct and separated not only by persons, but even by the subjects or individuals themselves. The sole cause of the error was that, neglecting the word of GOD, they wished to measure and explain this mystery by the acuteness of human reason: which their own arguments clearly demonstrate, the chief of which were these.

I. Jehovah denotes the divine essence: But each of the three persons is and is called Jehovah. Therefore there are three divine Essences, or three Gods.

But the vanity of this argument is easily detected by applying that distinction which we explained above in Question 3, proposition 6: if, namely, it is shown that in the major proposition the word GOD or Jehovah is taken absolutely, as it belongs to all three persons: In the Minor, however, insofar as it is relative, and with a certain determination, it is accommodated to each person: where Jehovah begetting is the same as the Father: Jehovah begotten is the same as the Son: Jehovah proceeding is the same as the Holy Spirit: defined indeed by three persons, but only in one Essence. Whence a πλεονεξία of four terms results.

II A person is nothing other than Essence: But there are three persons: Therefore there are also three divine Essences: or, three Gods.

I answer that the major premise is not simply true. For although in the Trinity a person is not, nor can be, without the divine Essence: yet in divine matters a person is far different from an Essence. For an Essence does not define, or even constitute, a certain mode of subsisting: that which a Person performs, which causes each person, in that very one in number divine Essence, to obtain a peculiar and distinct τρόπον ὑπάρξεως, or a certain reason or mode of subsisting, from the remaining persons.

Then they also differ in this, that Essence is communicable: but a person is simply incommunicable: Whence the immovable certainty of our doctrine clearly appears: That indeed there is One divine Essence communicable to all three persons: and therefore also One GOD: But in this very divine essence three persons subsist, distinguished by their own characteristic and utterly ἀκοινωνήτοις properties.

Finally, they also rose up thus: If the Essence of the Father and the Son is one in number, it would follow that the Father, by begetting the Son, begat himself: Because he communicated the same Essence to the Son. But this latter is absurd. Therefore the former is also.

I answer, the error arises from a confusion of the communication of the Essence and the generation of the person: Which two things, however, ought to be accurately distinguished in this matter. For what is communicated is not properly begotten. For a person begets and is begotten: Generation, therefore, is not of the Essence, but of the person: that is, a person begets a person. Furthermore, communication is of the Essence, but not of the person. Therefore GOD the Father, insofar as he is GOD, communicates the Essence: but insofar as he is Father, he begets the Son: he does not, however, beget himself: for the reason that he begets not by essential power, but by personal property.

These solutions having been observed, the remaining arguments of the Tritheists can be solved and refuted without any difficulty.

Latin:

Hæreseωn impingentium in unitatem Essentiæ divinæ.

AD hanc Classem haud incommodè initiò referri possunt Audiani, qui negantes DEUM esse simplicissimam spiritualem & incorpoream Essentiam: ipsam simul unitatem Essentiæ divinæ negasse censendi sunt. Compositum enim & corporeum quod est, illud certè in pluralitate personarum, unam numero Essentiam habere nequit. Contendebant autem isti, DEUM esse corporeum, humanæque formæ similem. Itaque & brachia, & pedes, & aures, & cætera hujusmodi membra, nostris similia, ipsi assignabant. Undè postmodum Antropomorphitarum secta originem sumsit. Etsi verò hæresis isthæc nimis crassa & palpabilis fuit, suaque propria futilitate ultrò quasi expiravit: reperti tamen semper sunt, qui semina istius impietatis spargerent: & partim ad Scripturas Sacras provocarent, quæ DEO hujusmodi membra corporea expressè assignent: partim verò urgerent illud, quòd homo esset conditus ad imaginem DEI: Undè DEO & homini conformitatem Essentiæ intercedere, necessariò consequi autumabant. Sed rectissimè jam olim à Damasceno lib. 1. Orthod. fid. cap. 12. responsum fuit, priores illas phrases Scripturæ non propriè, sed æquivocè & κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν de DEO esse accipiendas: ita ut gemina Sophisticatione, tùm æquivocationis, tùm Figuræ Dictionis prius argumentum laboret. Deindè verò Imago illa DEI, ad quam primus homo erat conditus, non essentiæ confirmationem: Sed justitiam illam & Sanctitatem, omniumque virium tùm corporis, tùm animi rectitudinem respiciebat, Undè Elenchus vitiosæ definitionis, & ὥς τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς ultrò emergit.

Proximum ab his ilocum sibi vendicant illi, qui statuerunt, Unum quidem esse DEUM αἰνώτατον & summum, ut Epiphanius loquitur, à quo tamen alii Dii oriantur: ita ut Unus ille summus DEUS, sit reliquorum Deorum principium, & velut informator, sive effentiator, quemadmodum superiore seculo locuti sunt Servetiani. Hunc errorem teste Epiphanio & Augustino errarunt Apellitæ, Messaliani, Monarchitæ, & alii. Cæterùm cùm neque Scripturæ testimoniis, neq; rationibus pugnarint, sed Platonicorum sordes jampridem exploras & damnatas in Ecclesiam DEI postliminiò quasi revocarint: factum, ut hæresis isthæc propria impietate conciderit.

Tertium in Classe hac prima locum occupant, Carpocratiani, Gnostici, Cerdoniani, Apellitæ, Valentiniani, Marcionitæ, & Manichæi, qui partim Gentilium πολυθεΐαν approbarunt: partim verò duos DEOS, diversæ planè, imò contrariæ naturæ & essentiæ finxerunt, unum Bonum, alterum Malum, à quibus tanquam primis, æternis & coæternis principiis, res omnes ortum suum traherent: Bonæ quidem à DEO bono: malæ autem à DEO malo. Impietati huic suæ palliandæ prætenderunt locum illum Michææ 1, 12. Descendit malum à Domino, usque ad portas Hierusalem: & illud Amosi 3, 6. Non est malum in civitate, quod non fecerit Dominus: turpi admodum & crasfâ inscitiâ decepti, quòd haud noverunt distingvere inter malum pœnæ, & malum culpæ: quorum illud quidem in Scripturis DEO, ut justo scelerum vindici: hoc verò non itidem adsignatur: ut quod ex lapsu primorum parentum, & Naturæ nostræ corruptione in tempore originem suam accepit.

Quartum locum assignamus Tritheitis, qui Sabellianorum hæresin evitaturi, in contrariam hyperbolen sunt prolapsi, contendentes Tres esse Deos, non personis tantùm, sed ipsis etiam subjectis sive individuis distinctos atque separatos. Unica erroris causa fuit, quod neglecto DEI verbo, mysterium hoc rationis humanæ acumine metiri & explicare voluerunt: id quod argumenta ipsorum liquidò demonstrant: quorum præcipua isthæc fuerunt.

I. Jehovah denotat essentiam divinam: At quiqualibet trium personarum est & dicitur Jehovah. Ergò tres sunt Essentiæ divinæ, sive tres Dii.

Facilè autem argumenti hujus vanitas deprehenditur, adhibita distinctione illâ, quam supra Quæst. 3. prop. 6. expedivimus: Si nimirùm ostendatur, in Majore propositione vocabulum DEI sive Jehovæ sumi absolutè, prout omnibus tribus personis competit: In Minore autem quatenus relatè, & cum certa quadam determinatione ad quamlibet personam accommodatur: ubi Jehovah gignens idem est, qui Pater: Jehovah genitus idem est, qui Filius: Jehovah procedens, idem est, qui Spiritus Sanctus: tribus quidem personis, sed non nisi in una Essentia, definitis. Unde πλεονεξία quatuor terminorum resultat.

II Persona nihil est aliud, quam Essentia: Atqui tres sunt personæ: Ergo tres etiam Essentiæ divinæ: sive, tres Dii.

Respondeo, Majorem non esse simpliciter veram. Etsi enim in Trinitate persona non est, nec esse potest sine Essentia divina: longè tamen aliud in divinis est persona, aliud Essentia. Nam Essentia non definit, vel etiam constituit certum subsistendi modum: id quod præstat Persona, quæ facit, ut quælibet persona, in illa ipsa una numero Essentia divina, peculiarem & à reliquis personis distinctu τρόπον ὑπάρξεως, sive certam subsistendi rationem aut modum obtineat.

Deindè in eo etiam differunt, quòd Essentia est communicabilis: persona verò simpliciter incommunicabilis: Undè doctrinæ nostræ immota certitudo liquidò patet: Quod nimirùm Una sit Essentia divina omnibus tribus personis cummunicabilis: ac proindè Unus etiam DEUS: In hac ipsa verò divinâ essentiâ tres personæ, suis proprietatibus characteristicis & prorsus ἀκοινωνήτοις distinctæ subsistant.

Tandem & sic insurgebant: Si una est numero Essentia, Patris & Filii, consequens fuerit, Patrem gignendo Filium, seipsum genuisse: Quia eandem Essentiam Filio communicavit. Atqui posterius hoc absurdum. Ergò & prius illud.

Respondeo, Error oritur ex confusione communicationis Essentiæ, & generationis personæ: Quæ duo tamen accuratè hoc in negotio forent distingvenda. Non enim quod communicatur, propriè gignitur. Nam persona gignit & gignitur: Generatio ergò non est Essentiæ, sed personæ: hoc est, persona personam generat. Cæterùm communicatio est Essentiæ, non verò personæ. Ergò DEUS Pater quatenus DEUS est, communicat Essentiam: quatenus verò Pater est, generat Filium: non verò generat seipsum: propterea quod non potentiâ essentiali, sed proprietate personali generat.

His solutionibus observatis, reliqua Tritheitarum argumenta nullo negotio solvi & refutari possunt.


### Later Chapter. Containing the artifice, and a succinct refutation of both…: Second Class

Of those heretics who partly foully defiled the Mystery of the Trinity, and partly denied it altogether.

Those heretics who impugned the Divinity of both the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, and thus consequently the Trinity of persons in one divine Essence, could in the first place be referred to this class: But since the following two classes are to treat of them expressly, it is of no use to speak of them in this place.

Then, the blasphemy of those who did not hesitate to affirm that the Trinity is an extension of one and the same thing, like wax, could deservedly be noted in this place: just as Epiphanius reports concerning the Marcellians: who likewise blasphemed that the persons of the Trinity were as it were vessels contained in others and skins folded within themselves: which Augustine assigns to the Metangismonites in his book on heresies, chapter 58, and Philastrius in his Catalogue of heresies. Who likewise trifled that a person in the Trinity is as it were several lights of one lamp: As Augustine is witness that the Hierarchites raved in his book on heresies, chapter 47. Who finally contended that the Three persons are only three Qualities: as the Tripartite History reports concerning the Aetians, book 5, chapter 42, and Augustine in his book on heresies to Quodvultdeus. Moreover, since these and other heresies of this kind have led to no family, and were immediately repressed by the efforts of the earlier doctors of the Church: those now being passed over, we proceed to the diexodon of those heresies which have obtained some applause in the Church.

And indeed, Praxeas seems to claim the first place for himself, who contended that the three persons of the Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are not in reality distinct, but differ only in names: while in the meantime there exists only one person or ὑπόστασις which is GOD, and which presents itself to our mind under different notions. Whence the disciples and followers of this αἵρεσις were called not only Praxeans, from their author; but from the head of the error, they were also called Noetians: Nay, in the progress of time, they were also named Patripassians, because it necessarily had to be maintained by them, if there were only one person in the Divinity, that it was that very one which also suffered, was crucified, and died.

According to Augustine and Epiphanius, the Simonians, Ptolemaeans, Colarbasians, Montanists, Apollinarists, and Priscillianists also fostered the same heresy: but especially the Sabellians, under whose name the rest of the heretics already enumerated were included. The head of the Sabellian αἵρεσις was this one thing: that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same person, who is called by various names only for the diversity of works and effects: thus the distinction of persons being utterly denied and abolished: Cyprian first took it upon himself to refute this error, who wished to censure Praxeas in a special book. Athanasius, however, opposed that truly golden Creed of his to the Sabellian and partly to the Arian fury. The Sabellians, moreover, attempted to confirm their opinion from chapter 6, verse 4 of Deuteronomy: where Moses says to the Jews: Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy GOD, is one GOD. Now, indeed, if three persons, distinct and subsisting in reality, are established in one and the same divine Essence: they clamored that a πολυθεΐαν or multitude of Gods is certainly being established.

But it could be most correctly answered that the argument fails by the fallacy of the consequent. For that polytheism of the Gentiles would only then be established if three persons were determined to subsist outside the unity of the divine Essence itself. But now, since one divine Essence in number is believed, and yet in it three persons are believed who are truly distinct from one another, no multitude of gods is introduced at all: provided that the divine Essence is not separated or torn into three Essences; but each person is taught and believed to obtain its own subsistence in that one divine Essence in number.

But furthermore they insisted thus: Those things which differ in persons also differ in Essences. But this proposition was rightly denied, as it is not only most false in this mystery, but is not even simply true in natural things. Certainly Peter, Paul, and John differ in persons, or individuals; but no one was ever so absurd as to affirm that the Essence of Peter is one thing, that of Paul another, and that of John another. For although they differ in number, they do not differ in species.

Moreover, the reason that a multitude of Essence does not arise in the Divinity from the plurality of persons, neither by reason of number nor by reason of species, is that those persons do not subsist separately or apart; but each has its own existence or hypostasis, or what is the same thing, a mode of subsisting, in that one divine Essence, without any division or separation.

Furthermore, they urged that passage of John 14:9, where Christ says: 'Philip, he who sees me, sees also the Father.' From which they argued thus: If by seeing the Son the Father is seen, it follows that the person of the Father and the Son is the same. But the former is true, by the testimony of Christ himself. Therefore, this latter is also true. And from the verse immediately following, 10, they concluded thus: If Christ is in the Father, and the Father in Christ, it follows that Christ is not distinct from the Father, but one in number, and the same person of both. But the former is true; therefore.

I answer: in both arguments the fallacy of the consequent and of ignorance of the refutation is committed. For in the former saying, Christ by no means wishes an identity of his and the Father's person to be asserted; since he himself in John 5:19 openly distinguishes himself from the Father, saying: 'The Son can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father working. For whatever things the Father does, these also the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son, and shows him all things that he himself does; and he will show him greater works than these, that you may marvel.' Where, that the Father is clearly distinguished from the Son, as one from another, hardly anyone would be so dull as not to understand. The sense, therefore, is to be looked for in the words of Christ, which is this: Since no one can see the Father with external eyes, and therefore no one can be instructed about his will except through Christ, in whom he has revealed himself, according to that passage of John 1:18. 'No one has ever seen GOD; the Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.' In the latter saying, Christ notes the unity of the divine Essence; from which it is most viciously concluded to establish the unity of the person. The vanity of which collection is evident even from this, that it would follow that we also constitute one person with Christ; since in the verse immediately following, 20, the same Savior says: 'In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.' Since that is absurd, it is spontaneously evident that the mode of that unity, by which the Father is in Christ and Christ in the Father, must be defined otherwise than with respect to the unity of the person.

That heresy of Sabellius, already long ago condemned by the Church, was in the previous century, namely around A.D. 1538, as it were recalled from the underworld by Michael Servetus the Spaniard, who, having initially traveled to Africa, made the Turkish Alcoran most familiar to himself, and strove to transform the entire Christian doctrine into the Mahometan, as Palladius testifies in his catalogue of heretics. Then, having returned to Geneva in Savoy, on account of the dire and execrable blasphemies contumaciously belched forth against the Most Holy Trinity, he was condemned to the stake and suffered the punishment of his impiety in the year 1553. The primary head of his error was that there is only one person in the Divinity, which has represented itself to the human race in one way or another; so that those different modes of representation have also produced the names of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The primary argument with which he fought was this: 'Person' signifies nothing other than a habit or a distinction of office, as when we say, Roscius represents now the person of Achilles, now of Agamemnon; or, just as one and the same man represents now the person of a Consul, now of a servant, now of some other person, while one person meanwhile remains: so in divine matters one 'hypostasis' or one person is to be established, which, for different relations or offices, is called now by the name of Father, now of Son, now of Holy Spirit.

But the impiety of that argument arises from a false principle. For 'Person' in this mystery does not denote that theatrical representation of various persons, but a substance, individual, intelligent, incommunicable, not sustained by another, as was shown above in Question 3, proposition 3.

Latin:

Eorum hæreticorum, qui Trinitatis Mysterium, partim fœdè conspurcarunt, partim prorsus negârunt.

POssent primo loco ad classem istam referri illi hæretici, qui Divinitatem tum Filii Dei, tum Spiritus Sancti, & sic consequenter Trinitatem personarum, in una divina Essentia impugnarunt : Verum cum de iis, subsequentes duæ classes ex professo sint aucturæ, nihil attinet, hoc loco de illis dicere.

Deindè notari hoc loco meritò posset eorum etiam blasphemia, qui affirmare haud dubitarunt, Trinitatem esse extensionem unius ejusdemque rei, veluti ceræ : quemadmodum de Marcellianis refert Epiphanius : qui item blasphemabant, personas Trinitatis esse veluti vasa alia in aliis contenta & pelles in se implicatas: id quod Metangismonitis assignat Augustinus lib. de hærefibus cap. 58. & Philastrius in Catalogo hæreseon. Qui item nugabantur, personã in Trinitate esse, veluti unius lucernæ plura luminaria: Quemadmodum Hierarchitas delirasse, testis est Augustinus lib. de hæresibus cap. 47. Qui deniq; contendebant, Tres personas, tantum tres esse Qualitates: uti de Aëtianis refert historia Tripartita lib. 5. cap. 42. & Augustinus lib. de hæresibus ad Quodvultdeum. Cæterum cum hæ & hujus generis aliæ hæreses nullam familiam duxerint, & operâ priorum doctorum Ecclesiæ statim sint repressæ : illis jam præteritis, ad earum hæreseων diexodon accedimus, quæ in Ecclesia applausum aliquem sunt sortitæ.

Et primum quidem locum sibi vendicare videtur Praxeas, qui contendebat, tres personas Trinitatis, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum, nõ esse revera distinctas, sed nominibus tantum differre: unâ interim tantùm existente persona sive ὑποστάσει quæ DEUS sit, & menti nostræ diversis notionibus se ingerat. Unde discipuli & sectatores hujus hæreseως, non modò Praxeani, ab autore; sed ab erroris capite, Noëtiani etiam dicti sunt: Quin progressu temporis Patripassiani etiam nuncupati sunt, propterea quòd necessariò istis statuendum fuit, si una duntaxat in Divinitate esset persona, eam illam ipsam esse, quæ etiam passa, crucifixa, mortua esset.

Eandem hæresin Augustino & Epiphanio referentibus, foverunt etiam Simoniani, Ptolomæi, Colarbasii, Montanistæ, Apollinaristæ, Priscillianistæ: Cumprimis verò Sabelliani, sub quorum nomine, reliqui jam enumerati hæretici, comprehendebantur. Caput hæreseως Sabellianæ hoc unicum fuit: Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum, unam & eandem esse personam, quæ variis tantùm nominibus pro diversitate operum atque effectuum appelletur: sic discrimine personarum penitus negato & abolito: Errorem istum sibi primùm refutandum sumsit Cyprianus, qui peculiari libro Praxeam perstringere voluit. Athanasius verò Sabelliano partim, partim Ariani furori, Symbolum illud suum verè aureum opposuit. Confirmare autem suam sententiam conabantur Sabelliani, ex cap. 6. 4. Deuter: ubi Moses ad Judæos : Audi Israel, Dominus DEUS tuus, DEUS unus est. Jam verò si tres in una & eadem divina Essentia personæ, reipsa distinctæ & subsistentes constituantur: utique πολϋϑεΐαν sive multitudinem Deorum statui, clamitabant.

Sed rectissimè responderi poterat, Fallere argumentum Sophismate ῶδα τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Tum enim demùm πολυθεΐα illa Gentilium stabiliretur, si tres personæ extra ipsam Essentiæ divinæ unitatem, subsistere statuerentur. Jam verò quando una numero divina Essentia, in eâdem autem tres personæ revera à se mutuò distinctæ creduntur: nulla prorsus Deorum multitudo introducitur: siquidem non separatur Essentia divina, sive in tres Essentias discerpitur: Sed unaquæque persona in Una illa numero Essentiâ divina, propriam subsistentiam obtinere docetur & creditur.

Sed porrò sic instabant: Quæ personis differunt: differunt etiam Essentiis. Verùm rectè negata fuit hæc propositio, ut quæ non in hoc modò mysterio est falsissima: sed etiam in naturalibus non simpliciter vera est. Certè Petrus, Paulus, Johannes differút personis, sive individuis: sed nemo unquàm ita absurdus fuit, qui affirmârit, aliam esse Essentiam Petri, aliam Pauli, aliam Johannis. Etsi enim numero: non tamen specie differunt.

Cæterùm quòd in Divinitate ex pluralitate personarum non oritur Essentiæ multitudo, neque ratione numeri, neque ratione speciei: causa est, quod personæ illæ non separatim aut serorsim subsistunt: sed quælibet suam ὕπαρξιν sive ὑπόστασιν, vel quod idem est, modum subsistendi habet, in una illa divina Essentia, sine ulla vel divulsione aut separatione.

Præterea urgebant illud Joh. 14, 9. ubi Christus ait: Philippe qui videt me, videt etiam Patrem. Unde sic arguebant: Si viso Filio videtur Pater, sequitur eandem esse personam Patris & Filii: At prius verum, teste ipso Christo. Ergò verum & hoc posterius. Et ex versu statim subsequente 10. sic colligebant: Si Christus est in Patre, & Pater in Christo: Sequitur Christum non esse distinctam à Patre, sed unam numero, eademq; utriusque personam. Sed verum prius: E.

Respondeo: in utroque argumento committi σόφισμα τὸ μὴ ἑπομένε: & τῆς ἀγνοίας τοῦ ἐλέγχυ. Nam in priore dicto, Christus neutiquam identitatem suæ & Patris personæ vult affertam: siquidem ipsemet Joh: 5, 19. apertè se à Patre distingvit, inquiens: Non potest Filius à semetipso quicquam operari, nisi quod viderit Patrem operantem. Quæcunq; enim Pater facit; hæc etiam Filius pariter facit. Pater enim amat Filiu, & omnia monstrat ei, quæ ipse facit: & operahis tis majora monstrabit ei, ut vos miremini. Ubi Patrem à Filio, tanquam alium ab alio luculenter distingvi, vix quisquam ita bardus fuerit quin intelligat. Sensus ergò in verbis Christi est spectandus, qui iste est: Cùm externis oculis Patrem nemo videri queat: ideoq; de voluntate etiam ipsius erudiri posse neminem, nisi per Christum, in quo ipse se patefecerit, secundum illud Johan. 1, 18. DEUM nemo vidit unquam: Filius qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit. In posteriore dicto notat Christus Essentiæ divinæ unitatem: ex qua ad unitatem personæ stabiliendam, vitiosissimè colligitur. Cujus collectionis vanitas vel indè etiam patet, quod sic sequeretur, nos quoque cum Christo unam personam constituere: siquidem versu statim subsequente 20. idem Servator inquit: In die illo cognoscetis, me esse in Patre meo, & vos in me, & me in vobis. Quod cùm sit absurdum, ultrò patet, Unitatis illius modum, quo Pater est in Christo, & Christus in patre, aliter definiendum esse, quàm respectu Unitatis personæ.

Hæresin istam Sabellii, jam pridem ab Ecclesia damnatam, superiore seculo, nimirùm circa A. C. 1538. ab Orco quasi revocavit Michaël Servetus Hispanus, qui initiò in Africam profectus, Alcoranum Turcicum sibi reddidit familiarissimum: & universam doctrinam Christianam in Mahometicam transformare studuit: teste Palladio in catalogo hæreticorum. Deindè Genevam Sabaudiæ reversus, ob diras & execrandas blasphemias in Sacrosanctam Trinitatem contumaciter eructatas, ad rogum damnatus, suæ impietatis suppliciū sustinuit Anno 1553. Erroris caput primarium fuit, in Divinitate unam tantùm esse personam, quæ aliter atq; aliter humano generi sese repræsentaverit: ita, ut diversi illi repræsentationis modi, vocabula etiam Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti, pepererint.

Argumentum primarium quo pugnabat, erat istud: Persona nihil significat aliud quàm habitum, aut officii distinctionem, ut cum dicimus, Roscius aliàs Achillis, aliàs Agamemnonis personam repræsentat: vel, quemadmodum unus idemq; homo, jã Consulis, jam servi, jam alterius alicujus personam repræsentat: unâ interim manente personâ: Sic in divinis unum est statuendum ὑφισάμενον, sive una persona, quæ pro diversis relationibus sive officiis, nunc Patris, nunc Filii, nunc Spiritus Sancti nomine appelletur.

Sed impietas argumenti istius ex falso principio oritur. Neq; enim Persona hoc in mysterio, notat Scenicam illam variarum personarum repræsentationem: sed substantiam, individuam, intelligentem, incommunicabilem, non sustentatam ab alio: uti supra Quæst. 3. prop. 3. fuit ostensum.


### Later Chapter. Containing the artifice, and a succinct refutation of both…: Third Class

A very wide field of heretics of this third class indeed opens itself, so that if we wished to treat of each one separately, an entire volume would have to be woven by us. There were those who contended that the Son of GOD is 'nous' or a created mind, but created before all other creatures, as Augustine reports that the Basilidians and Origenists blasphemed. Again, others, and indeed the Marcionites, fought that the Son is not of the creator GOD, but the Son of some other GOD. Others, such as the Heracleonites and Bardesanists, termed the eternal generation of the Son a fable; the Nativitarians, opposing them, conceded that the Son was indeed begotten by the Father, but not from eternity; the Valentinians, Seleucians, and Colarbasians, dissenting from both, feigned that Christ was indeed begotten, but not from GOD, rather from the Aeons; and that He was not the Son of GOD by nature, but only adoptive, as it pleased the Bonosians, according to Philastrius, and the Circumcellions to rave; nay, that GOD the Father had indeed begun to beget from eternity, but finally brought forth His Son in the virgin Mary, as the Servetians blasphemed.

Moreover, those who led some sect and brought no small harm to the Church of GOD with arguments that were plausible in appearance surpassed these individuals and all others in impiety and the stubbornness of error. In this class, the Cerinthians and Ebionites easily take first place, who contended that the λόγον or Son of GOD was indeed something divine, but that He existed without substance in GOD the Father, in the very same way that a sensing or intelligent faculty is said to exist in the soul of a man. Thus, therefore, while conceding the Unity of Essence, they simply denied that the Son and the Holy Spirit constitute distinct ὑποστάσεις, for the reason that the Son and the Holy Spirit are in GOD no differently than wisdom, Justice, Mercy, and other virtues are said to exist in GOD, namely, entirely ἀνυποστάτως.

Furthermore, they blasphemed that Christ, having been illuminated by the Word of GOD, had indeed prophesied and performed divine miracles, but as a participant with other Prophets and Apostles in manner and power, albeit in a more excellent degree. Since these blasphemies were creeping far and wide, a certain necessity was laid upon John the Evangelist and Apostle to write both the Gospel and that Canonical Epistle; by both of which writings this impiety was also driven out of Asia, as Eusebius testifies in book 3, chapter 28. But the Church was not permitted to enjoy this restored purity of the Gospel for long, before both Paul of Samosata around A.D. 270 and Photinus around A.D. 345 infected Greece with the same poison; which sink of impieties and blasphemies flowed together into the one heresy of Arius, which happened around A.D. 320. For when the Fathers of the Synod of Antioch, relying on the authority of the Johannine Gospel, had solidly refuted, nay, had utterly overturned the error of Samosata, Arius, at the instigation of Satan, thought that the matter should be approached by another way. He conceded, therefore, that the λόγον was indeed ἐνυπόστατον or a certain person before the incarnation, nay, even before the creation of the world, but a created and finite person. To cast some veil over this impiety, he spun a sweet fable: that GOD, when He had decreed to create the human race and to free it from sin through Christ, before He proceeded to the creation of this visible World, had created a certain rational Spirit, and upon him, as His most noble work, had imposed the name of Son of GOD and τῆ λόγꙋ, and subsequently through him had created all other visible and invisible things; and this λόγον or created and finite Spirit he feigned to have been incarnated in time.

The Holy Fathers, however, and especially Basil, Athanasius, Theodoret, Augustine, and others, observed certain phrases or propositions which both Arius and his followers used in their disputations and sermons. It would be very useful to have observed all of these, so that from them a judgment might also be made as to whether today even some, both among the Sacramentarians and other fanatics, are reviving the same impiety, which they nevertheless wish to be most alien to themselves.

The first Arian hypothesis was this: 1. The Son of GOD or λόγꙋ is a mere creature, but adorned with gifts and virtues surpassing all human and Angelic nature.

2. The λόγον deserved to be called the Son of GOD on account of those gifts and virtues.

3. The λόγον was created ἐκ μὴ ὄντων, from non-entities; whence they were also called Exoucontii, although afterwards some from the School of the Arians affirmed that the λόγον was not created from nothing, as Augustine testifies in book 3 against Maximin, chapter 14.

4. The λόγος is not the Son of GOD by nature, but by adoption. Nor is He the Essential Word of GOD, but is called so abusively, because He was made the Word of GOD; for He was not born of GOD, but was made of GOD. Theodoret, book 1, chapter 4.

5. The Son of GOD is not ὁμοούσιος with the Father, but ἑτερούσιος, of a different nature and essence from the Father.

6. The Son of GOD is not συναΐδιος πατρὶ, nor was He always with the Father, or at the Father's side; but there was once a time when the Son was not: ἦν ποτε ὅταν οὐκ ἦν ὁ λόγος, Basil, Orat. 1, on the Son.

7. The Son of GOD has no power except that received from creation and donation. Athanasius against the Arians, Hilary on the Trinity.

8. The Son of God did not perfectly know the Father: nor did He know the secrets of the Father, except insofar as the Father reveals them to Him.

9. The Son of God does not comprehend the whole Father, nor was He in heaven with the Father when He was living among men.

10. The Son of God is not to be worshipped in the flesh, Athan. orat. 5. against the Arians.

11. The Son of God, by the freedom of His will, was prone to good and evil. Theodor. lib. 1. cap. 9.

12. The Son of God was passible and mortal in His substance. Athanas.

13. Finally, the Son of God has, by a gratuitous gift, a certain Kingdom, but not an eternal one: but one that will perish with this world. Athanas.

Arius himself briefly encompassed each of these heads of impiety in his Confession, which exists in Athanasius, and it reads thus: I believe in one eternal GOD, and His Son whom He created as GOD before the ages, and made Him a Son to Himself: And whatever the Son has, He received from GOD when He did not have it, and therefore He is not equal to the Father, nor of the same dignity: but as a Creature He is left and falls short of the glory of GOD, and He is lesser, as far as it pertains to the power of GOD: and I believe in the Holy Spirit begotten by the Son.

Moreover, this heresy spread more widely than any other, infecting not only the entire East, but also the West, so that for more than eighty years it held supremacy in the Church of GOD, as appears from the Epistle of the Council of Constantinople to Damasus. And although it was condemned while Arius was still alive, in the Nicene Synod, around A.D. 325: nevertheless, it always sprouted again in the East and Africa, until finally Mohammedanism was built from it by the Arian monk Sergius around A.D. 620.

Afterward, the pestilent heresy of the Eunomians was added, which around A.D. 358 not only confirmed the greater part of the madness of Arius, but also increased it with new paradoxes: while it indeed conceded that the Word was ἐνυπόστατον (subsistent) and the Son of GOD: but not only ἑτερούσιον (of a different substance) to the Father, but κατὰ πάντα ἀνόμοιον (in all things unlike), that is, altogether disparate not only in person, but also in Essence, power, and will. Whence they were afterward called Anomii and Anomæi.

But neither is the end of evils thus, but that most hostile enemy of the human race, the Devil, in this our century, partly through Transylvania, partly through the nearer places of Sarmatia, vomits forth the same impiety, not without huge damage to the Church, through the more recent Arians, Photinians, Eunomians, and Anti-Trinitarians, of whom the chief are: Antonius Possevinus: Christophorus Ostorodus: Sommerus: Blandrata: Socinus: Franciscus Davidis: and many others.

Now both the ancient and the more recent Arians have fought thus far against the Orthodox, partly by Reasons, partly by sayings of Scripture. It is pleasing, however, on this occasion to engage primarily with the more recent ones, and to examine their reasons by the balance of truth a little more accurately, not indeed each and every one: but only the principal ones.

The first, therefore, of the principal ones was this: When GOD the Father begat the Son, either the Son existed then, or he did not. If he existed, there was no need to beget him at last: If he did not exist: then he was not eternal: and consequently, he is neither συναϊ̈διός to the Father, nor is he even truly GOD.

But most rightly at the beginning, and indeed in general, it can be answered to this and other arguments of this kind, that which GOD himself answered in Num. 23:19: GOD is not as a man, nor as the son of man, that he should be changed, and Hosea 11:9: I am GOD: not man. For since this Mystery of the Trinity, and especially that Generation of the Son, is ὑπὲρ νῦν καὶ πᾶσαν Κατάληψιν, as Justin speaks: certainly it is evident even from this, that arguments are wrongly sought from the sharpness of Reason to overthrow this Mystery, which belongs to faith alone. Therefore, to answer the Dilemma itself, that is true in things that exist according to the course of Nature: but most false in the present Mystery. Therefore, just as Aristotle himself forbids that there be a μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος, and that sciences be not confused: so neither in this place can Philosophy prejudice those things which are of the revealed Word alone, and consequently, of faith alone. Then a Sophistry is committed παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For in causes and effects differing by Essence, and in producers and products that are not co-essential, that which is presupposed in this Dilemma has a place, namely that to beget is to produce that which did not exist before. But in producers and products that are co-essential and co-eternal, this Reason simply expires. Which even sounder Philosophy seems to have acknowledged, while it teaches that in homogeneous things, cause and effect, producer and product, differ not in time, but only by reason of Order. To which pertains that Rule of the Philosopher, which exists in book 4 of the Physics, ch. 12, T. 112: τοῖς δὲ εἶ ὄντα ἧ ἀεὶ ὄντα, οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν χρόνῳ: ὅ γὰρ πε- ριέχεται ὑπὸ τῶν χρόνῳ, ὐδὲ μετρεῖται τὸ εἶναι αὐτῶν ὑπὸ τῸ χρόνῸ: Eternal things are not in time, for the very reason that they are eternal: for neither does time encompass them, nor does it measure their reason or essence. Thus, therefore, GOD the Father also begat the Son ἀνάρχως καὶ ἀτελευτήτως, without beginning and without end, in a manner entirely incomprehensible.

The Arians urge: If the Father always and without end begets the Son, it would follow that the Generation of the Son is never perfect. For that which does not attain its end, certainly does not have its perfection either.

But I answer, that this reason has a place only in Physical generations, which are of corporeal things, which produce something from themselves, outside themselves: but that it is most false in Metaphysical Generation, which is of transcendent things and Spirits, which is evident even from the single example of the soul. Our mind, certainly, as some simple Spirit, begets reason, not indeed from itself or outside itself, but through itself and in itself, and indeed without end: so that the Philosopher rightly establishes that Reason is συναΐδιον to the Mind, lib. 1 de Anima. What, therefore, shall we establish concerning this divine generation, which takes place in the Trinity, and transcends not only Physical, but also every Metaphysical reason, by infinite degrees. Where perfection does not depend on the end of the act itself: but on the most simple perfection of the Divinity: which as it was from eternity, such as it is, both by reason of essence and by reason of personal operations: so it remains such for all eternity, and admits of no change, being simply immutable.

The third reason among the principal ones is this: If the Son was begotten from the Substance of the Father, it is necessary that the Father communicated either the whole or a part of it to the Son. But neither can be affirmed without manifest blasphemy. For if the former is granted, it would follow that the Father had completely perished: If the latter is given, the Substance of the Father would have been diminished, which nevertheless is ἀδιαίρετος: Therefore the Son was not begotten from the Substance of the Father.

I answer, that the argument is again built from false principles. For that has a place in such a Physical generation as is made from matter, or from a movable Being. Although not even in natural things is the reason of this argument true in all respects: which is clearly evident, both from the propagation of souls: and from the generation of Light from Light. Whence also some of the Fathers have very frequently used this simile, to say that the Son was begotten from the Father, just as Light is kindled from Light; not indeed to define the Mode of this generation, which is entirely ἄῤῥητος: but to show that this Generation was made without any change or diminution of the Substance of the Father. Therefore, the conclusion of this Argument also does not fit the present mystery in the least.

Finally, they are also accustomed to clamor thus: If GOD begat the λόγον, either the whole divine Essence begat, or the Person of the Father alone. If the whole Essence, then it begat either itself or another. But neither can be affirmed without absurdity. But if the Person of the Father begat, either it alone will be the True GOD, and thus the λόγος will not be such, or the λόγος will not be the Son of one True GOD.

I answer: The error arises from the fallacy of the consequent. For although we by no means deny, not

Latin:

LAtissimus sanè campus hæreticorum tertiæ hujus classis sese aperit: ita ut de singulis seorsim, si agere vellemus, integrum volumen nobis pertexendum esset. Fuerunt, qui contenderent, Filium DEI esse νῦν sive mentem creatam, sed creatam ante cæteras creaturas omnes: uti Basilidianos & Origenistas blasphemasse, refert Augustinus. Rursus alii, & quidem Marcionitæ pugnarunt, Filium non esse DEI creatoris, sed alterius cujusdam DEI Filium. Alii ut Heracleonitæ & Bardesanistæ, æternam Generationē Filii, nominarunt Fabulam: quibus sese opponentes Nativitarii, cõcesserunt, Filiū quidé à Patre genitum esse, sed non ab æterno: ab utriusq; autem dissidentes Valentiniani, Seleuciani, Colarbasii, Christum genitum quidem esse finxerunt: Verùm non ex DEO, sed ex Aeonibus: neq; naturâ Filium DEI esse, sed tantùm adoptivum, uti Bonosianis, teste Philastrio, & Circumcellionibus delirare libuit: Quin DEUM Patrem ab æterno quidem cepisse gignere, sed demùm in virgine maria genuisse Filiū suū: uti Servetiani blasphemarunt.

Cæterùm hos singulos ac universos, impietate & erroris contumaciâ superarunt ii, qui familiam aliquam duxerunt, & argumentis in speciem plausibus, Ecclesiæ DEI, haud parùm damni intulerunt. Qua in classe, primas facilè obtinent, Cerinthiani & Ebionitæ, qui contendebant, λόγον sive Filium DEI, esse quidem aliquid divinum: sed sine substantia in DEO Patre esse, eodem planè modo, quo in anima hominis dicitur esse facultas sentiens, aut intelligens. Sic ergò concessâ Essentiæ Unitate, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum proprias ὑποστάσεις constituere, simpliciter negabant, propterea quòd Filius & Spiritus Sanctus sint in DEO haud secus atque sapientia, Justitia, Misericordia & cæteræ virtutes in DEO esse dicuntur, nimirùm prorsus ἀνυποστάτως.

Porrò blasphemabant Christum Verbo DEI illuminatum, prophetasse quidem, & miracula divina edidisse: sed communicum aliis Prophetis & Apostolis modo ac virtute: gradu licet excellentiore. Quæ blasphemiæ cum longè latéque serperent, necessitas quædam Johanni Evangelistæ & Apostolo illata fuit, scribendi tùm Evangelium, tùm Canonicam illam Epistolam: Quo utroque scripto impietas etiam isthæc ex Asia profligata fuit: teste Eusebio lib. 3. cap. 28. Sed restituta hac puritate Evangelii haud diu frui licuit Ecclesiæ, quin tùm Paulus Samosatenus circa A. C. 270. tùm Photinus circa A. D. 345. eodem veneno Græciam infecerunt: quæ impietatum & blasphemiarum sentina, in unam Arii hæresin confluxit: id quod factum circa A. D. 320 cum enim Patres Synodi Antiochenæ, freti autoritate Evangelii Johannitici, Samosateni errorem solidè refutassent, imò penitùs evertissent, Arius instinctu Satanæ rem alia via aggrediendam sibi esse putavit. Concessit igitur λόγον esse quidem ἐνυπόστατον sive certam personam ante incarnationem, imò etiam ante mundi creationem: sed personam creatam & finitam, Cui impietati ut fucum aliquem faceret, suaviter fabulabatur: DEUM, cùm decrevisset condere genus humanum, idque à peccato per Christum liberare, antequam ad creationem hujus visibilis Mundi accederet, creasse Spiritum quendam rationalem, eiq́; tanquam nobilissimo suo operi, Filii DEI & τῆ λόγꙋ nomen imposuisse, & deinceps per eum creasse omnia alia visibilia & invisibilia: & hunc λόγον sive Spiritum creatum & finitum finxit in tempore incarnatum esse.

Observârunt autem S. Patres, & imprimis Basilius, Athanasius, Theodoretius, Augustinus & alii certas phrases sive propositiones, quibus tùm Arius, tùm ipsius asseclæ, in disputationibus & concionibus, utebantur: Quas omnes observasse, perquàm utile fuerit, ut indè etiam judicium fieri queat, an hodiè, etiam nonnulli, tùm ex Sacramentariis, tùm aliis fanaticis eandem impietatem reponant: quam tamen à se volunt esse alienissimam.

Prima hypothesis Ariana erat isthæc. 1. Filius DEI sive λόγꙋ est mera creatura: donis autem ac virtutibus, omnem tùm humanam, tùm Angelicam naturam superantibus exornata.

2. Λόγον propter dona ac virtutes istas, Filius DEI in Scripturis appellari meruit.

3. Λόγον creatus est ἐκ μὴ ὄντων ex non entibus: Unde etiam Exoucontii appellati sunt: quanquam postea nonnulli ex Scholâ Arianorum, λόγον non ex nihilo creatum esse affirmarunt, teste Augustino lib. 3. contra Maximin. cap. 14.

4. Λόγος non est naturâ Filius DEI, sed adoptivè. Neque est Essentiale DEI Verbum, sed abusivè sic dictum: quia factus est DEI Verbum: Non enim ex DEO natus: sed ex DEO factus est. Theodor. lib. 1. cap. 4.

5. Filius DEI non est ὁμοούσιος Patri, sed ἑτερούσιος diversæ naturæ & essentiæ à Patre.

6. Filius DEI non est συναΐδιος πατρὶ, neq; semper fuit cum Patre, aut apud Patrem: sed fuit aliquando tempus, cùm non esset Filius: ἦν ποτε ὅταν οὐκ ἦν ὁ λόγος, Basil. Orat. 1. de filio.

7. Filius DEI nullam habet potestatem, nisi ex creatione & donatione acceptam. Athanas. contra Arian. Hilar. de Trin.

8. Filius DEI non perfectè cognovit Patrem: neq; novit arcana Patris, nisi quatenus ei revelat Pater.

9. Filius DEI non capit totum Patrem, nec fuit in cælis apud Patrem, cum inter homines versaretur.

10. Filius DEI in carne non est adorandus, Athan. orat. 5. contra Arianos.

11. Filius DEI libertate voluntatis suæ in bonum & malum proclivis fuit. Theodor. lib. 1. cap. 9.

12. Filius DEI in sua substantia passibilis fuit & mortalis. Athanas.

13. Tandem, Filius DEI habet ex gratuita donatine, Regnum aliquod, verùm non æternum: Sed cum Mundo hoc interiturum. Athanas.

Singula isthæc impietatis capita ipse Arius breviter complexus est in sua Confessione, quæ extat apud Athanasium, & sic habet: Credo in unum DEUM æternum, & Filium ejus quem ante secula creavit ut DEUS, Filiumq; sibi fecit: Et quæcunq; habet Filius, ea, cùm non haberet, accepisse à DEO, atque ideò illum Patri non æqualem esse, neq; ejusdem dignitatis: sed ut Creaturam relinqui & deficere à gloria DEI, eundemq; minorem esse, quantum attinet ad potentiam DEI: credoq; in Spiritum Sanctum à Filio genitum.

Grassata est autem hæc hæresis latiùs quàm ulla alia, non Orientem modò universum, sed & Occidentem ita inficiens, ut octoginta annis ampliùs in Ecclesia DEI principatum obtinuerit, uti apparet ex Epistola Concilii Constantinopolitani ad Damasum. Et quanquam ea, vivente adhuc Ario, in Synodo Nicena, circa A. D 325. damnata fuit: tamen in Oriente & Africâ semper repullulavit, donec tandem Mahometismus indè per Sergium Monachum Arianum est extructus circa A. D. 620.

Accessit postmodum pestilens Eunomianorum hæresis, quæ circa A. D. 358 non modò furores Arii maximam partem confirmavit, sed & novis paradoxis adauxit: dum λόγον quidem concessit esse ἐνυπόστατον & Filium DEI: verùm non tantùm Patri ἑτερούσιον, sed κατὰ πάντα ἀνόμοιον per omnia dissimilem, hoc est, non modò personâ, sed & Essentiâ, potentiâ voluntate prorfus disparem. Unde postmodùm Anomii & Anomæi dicti sunt.

Sed neque sic malorum finis, quin infensifsimus ille humani generis hostis Diabolus, nostro hoc seculo partim per Transylvaniam, partim per viciniora Sarmatiæ loca, eandem impietatem, non sine ingenti Ecclesiæ damno eructat per recentiores Arianos, Photinianos, Eunomianos, & Anti-Trinitarios, quorum præcipui sunt: Antonius possevinus: Christophorus Ostorodus: Sommerus: Blandrata: Socinus: Franciscus Davidis: & alii complures.

Pugnarunt autem tùm Veteres, tum recentiores Ariani hactenùs adversus Orthodoxos, partim Rationibus, partim dictis Scripturæ. Placet autem hac vice cùm Recentioribus potissimùm congredi, eorumque rationes ad veritatis trutinam paulò accuratiùs examinare, non quidem singulas & universas: sed tantùm præcipuas.

Prima ergò ex præcipuis fuit isthæc: Cùm DEUS Pater gigneret Filium, aut tùm fuit Filius, aut non fuit. Si fuit, non opus erat ipsum demùm gignere: Si non fuit: utique non fuit æternus: & per consequens, neque Patri συναϊ̈διός, neque etiam revera DEUS est.

Rectissimè autem initiò & quidem in genere, tùm ad hoc, tùm id genus argumenta alia responderi potest, illud, quod DEUS ipse respondit Num. 23, 19. Non est DEUS quasi homo, nec ut filius hominis, ut mutetur, & Hoseæ 11, 9. DEUS ego sum: non homo. Cum enim Mysterium hoc Trinitatis, & cumprimis Generatio illa Filii sit ὑπὲρ νῦν καὶ πᾶσαν Κατάληψιν, uti Justinus loquitur: certè vel indè constat, perperam ex Rationis acumine, ad evertendum hoc Mysterium, quod solius est fidei, argumenta peti. Proindè ut ad Dilemma ipsum respondeamus, verum illud est, in rebus secundum Naturæ cursum sese habentibus: Falsissimum autem in præsenti Mysterio. Ergò, uti Aristoteles ipse prohibet, ne fiat μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος, neque scientiæ confundantur: Ita neque hoc loco, Philosophia potest præjudicare iis, quæ sunt solius Verbi revelati, & per consequens, solius fidei. Deindè committitur Sophisticatio παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Nam in causis & effectis per Essentiam differentibus, & in producentibus & productis non coëffentialibus, locum habet id, quod in Dilemmate isto præsupponitur, nempè τὸ Gignere esse producere id, quòd antea non fuit. Cæterùm in producentibus & productis coëffentialibus & coæternis, Ratio isthæc simpliciter expirat. Quod ipsum videtur sanior etiam Philosophia agnovisse, dum in homogeneis causam & effectum, producens & productum, non tempore, sed Ordinis tantùm ratione differre, docet. Quò pertinet Regula illa Philosophi, quæ extat lib. 4. Φυσ. cap 12. T. 112. τοῖς δὲ εἶ ὄντα ἧ ἀεὶ ὄντα, οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν χρόνῳ: ὅ γὰρ περιέχεται ὑπὸ τῶν χρόνῳ, ὐδὲ μετρεῖται τὸ εἶναι αὐτῶν ὑπὸ τῸ χρόνῸ: Res æternæ non sunt in tempore, hoc ipso, quòd æternæ sunt: neq; enim eas complectitur tempus, neque earum rationem sive essentiam metitur. Sic ergò DEUS Pater etiam genuit Filium ἀνάρχως καὶ ἀτελευτήτως, sine principio & sine fine, modò prorsus incomprehensibili.

Instant Ariani: Si Pater semper & sine fine generat Filium, consequens fuerit, Generationem Filii nunquam esse perfectam. Quod enim finem suum non assequitur, utique perfectionem etiam suam non habet.

Sed Respondeo, Locum habere rationem istam tantùm in generationibus Physicis, quæ sunt rerum corporearum, quę de se aliquid producunt, extra se: Falsissimam verò illam esse in Generatione Methaphysica, quæ est transcendentium, & Spirituum, id quod constat vel unico exemplo animæ. Mens certè nostra, ut Spiritus aliquis simplex gignit rationem, non quidem de se vel extra se, sed per se & in seipsa, & quidem sine fine: ita ut rectè Philosophus Rationem Menti συναΐδιον esse statuat. lib. 1. de Anima. Quid igitur statuemus de divina hac generatione, quæ in Trinitate fit, & non modò Physicam, sed etiam omnem Metaphysicam rationem, infinitis paralangis transcendit. Ubi perfectio non ex fine dependet ipsius actus: sed à simplicissima Divinitatis perfectione: quæ uti ab æterno fuit, qualis est, tum ratione essentiæ, tùm ratione personalium operationum: ita talis in omnem æternitatem manet, neque mutationis quicquam admittit, quippè simpliciter immutabilis.

Tertia ratio inter præcipuas est hæc: Si de Substantia Patris genitus est Filius, aut totam, aut partem illius, Pater Filio communicaverit, necesse est. At neutrum sine manifesta blasphemia affirmari potest. Nam concesso priore, Patrem penitus interiisse foret consequens: Dato posteriore diminuta esset Patris Substantia, quæ tamen est ἀδιαίρετος: Ergò Filius de Substantia Patris non est genitus.

Respondeo, Rursum ex falsis principiis extrui argumentum. Locum enim illud habet in tali generatione Physica, quæ fit ex materia, vel ex Ente mobili. Quanquam ne quidem in rebus naturalibus per omnia vera est argumenti hujus ratio: id quod palàm patet, tùm ex propagatione animarum: tùm ex generatione Luminis de Lumine. Undè Patrum etiam nonnulli frequenter admodum hoc simili usi sunt, ut dicerent, Filium de Patre esse genitum, quemadmodum Lumen de Lumine accenditur; non quidem ut definirent Modum generationis hujus, qui prorsus est ἄῤῥητος: sed ut ostenderent, Generationem hanc sine ulla mutatione aut diminutione Substantiæ Patris factam esse. Proindè Argumenti etiam hujus collectio, ad præsens mysterium minimè quadrat.

Tandem sic quoque obstrepere solent: Si DEUS genuit λόγον, aut tota Essentia divina genuit, aut sola Patris Persona. Si tota Essentia, tum aut seipsam, aut aliam genuit. Sed utrumque sine absurditate affirmari non potest. Sin Persona Patris genuit, vel sola ipsa erit Verus DEUS, & sic λόγος talis non erit, vel λόγος non erit unius Veri DEI Filius.

Respondeo: Error oritur ex Sophismate vitiosi consequentis. Etsi enim minimè negamus, non


### Later Chapter. Containing the artifice, and a succinct refutation of both…: Chapter I. On the Truth of the Human Nature which the Word (Λόγος) assumed

the whole divine essence, but only the person of the Father has begotten: yet that must be noted, that this person of the Father did not beget outside, but within the Essence of the Divinity. Wherefore it by no means follows, what the Adversaries infer, If the person of the Father has begotten. Therefore only the Father is the true GOD: But only this follows, that the Father alone is the only true GOD begetting. Now indeed, Because this generation was made, within the complex of the divine Essence, it follows: That just as the Father is the only true GOD begetting: So the Son also is the only true GOD begotten: and the Holy Spirit is the only true GOD proceeding from the Father and the Son. And the Adversaries clearly seek in vain some protection for their cause, in the exclusive particle ALONE or ONLY. For this does not exclude the remaining persons from the Divinity: but partly separates the remaining persons from this Act of Generation; which is proper to the Father alone: but partly excludes Idols and fictitious GODS from the participation of the Divinity.

FOURTH CLASS. Of those Heretics, who impugned both the Divinity and the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.

The Devil has at no time ceased to try to obscure, nay, to utterly overturn the article concerning the Holy Spirit through various heretics. Certainly in the age of the Apostles themselves, the Simonians maintained that the Holy Spirit was only a name of energy and power, but not of divine Essence. Following them, the Hieracites contended that the Holy Spirit was Melchizedek: Nay, that it was the Sister of Christ, as the Elcesaites blasphemed. Indeed, some progressed to such a point of impiety that they would sell themselves as the Holy Spirit, just as ecclesiastical history testifies concerning Simon and his harlot Helena, as also concerning Manichaeus and Montanus. Furthermore, the Origenists, Acacians, and Arians imagined that the Holy Spirit was not the true GOD, but only a Creature, and indeed, as it pleased the Servetians to rave, such a creature as is diffused through all creatures according to parts. But all those heresies finally flowed together, as it were, into that one heresy which the Macedonians or πνευματομάχοι began to spread publicly, and indeed not without some applause, around A.D. 360 under the Emperor Constantius. For Macedonius, Bishop of the Church of Constantinople, taught in his sermon that the Holy Spirit was lesser than the Father and the Son, and not of the same Substance as both, but a mere Creature and a force created by GOD: which by the division of the Essence is present in created things: as witnessed by Rufinus, book 1 of Ecclesiastical history, chapter 25, and Augustine in his book on heresies, chapter 52.

Although indeed the Arians also defended this very heresy at the same time; because, however, they were primarily impugning the divinity of the Son of GOD: it therefore happened that this heresy was called not Arian, but Macedonian: and the heretics themselves, followers of this sect, were named πνευματόμαχοι from the Head of the Error. And although this heresy, after it had gravely afflicted the most noble Church of Constantinople for more than thirty years, was condemned by the zeal and effort of the Emperor Theodosius the Great in the first universal Council of Constantinople, in the presence of 150 Bishops, in A.D. 381 (others say 383), yet more recent Anti-Trinitarians strive to revive it as if from the dead, contending that the Holy Spirit is nothing other than a certain power of GOD, a divine efficacy in creatures.

Certainly both the ancient and the more recent Pneumatomachi, for the defense of their error, object at the beginning those testimonies of the Scriptures which affirm that GOD created the Spirit; as Amos 4:13: Behold I am GOD creating the Spirit: where, however, it is manifest that they are playing with the base Sophistry of equivocation: since Scripture there treats not of the third person of the Trinity, but of the wind.

Then, however, they repeatedly appeal to the authority of the Nicene Council, which defined nothing at all concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit. But the answer is ready. Nothing indeed was defined in that Council concerning this matter, nay, it did not even need to be defined, because at that time the Question was not being agitated concerning the Divinity of the Holy Spirit: but only concerning the Divinity of the Son of GOD. For although the Arians also denied the Divinity of the Holy Spirit; yet they concealed this error with the greatest zeal they could: lest, namely, this error also being betrayed, they should be held clearly as Atheists, as witnessed by Basil in his Epistles. Hence, therefore, it happened that nothing at all was defined in the Nicene Council concerning the Divinity of the Holy Spirit. But in the progress of time this was sufficiently compensated for in the Council of Constantinople: where these things were added to the Nicene Creed: I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son: who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified together: πιστεύω εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, τὸ κύριον, τὸ ζωοποιὸν, τὸ ἐκ τῶ πατρὸς, καὶ τῶ ὑιῶ ἐκπορευόμενον, τὸ σὺν πατρὶ καὶ ὑιῷ συμπεσκυνόμενον, καὶ συν- δοξαζόμενον. Which part the Macedonians themselves understood to be opposed to their heresy.

But more recent Arians are accustomed to fight today with other and more numerous weapons. And at the beginning indeed they appeal to the Scriptures, which nowhere expressly name the Holy Spirit GOD. But the falsity of this assertion, which even Erasmus was not ashamed to vomit forth, is most manifestly evident from those foundations by which we demonstrated above the immovable certainty of our Affirmative: see proposition 8 of Question 3. Let that one passage suffice in this place, which exists in 1 Cor. 12. Where the Apostle expressly treats of the variety of gifts in the Church, and names the Author of them, the Holy Spirit, expressly GOD, in verse 6.

Then they object to that which the Apostle prays for his Corinthians, the communion of the Holy Spirit: which certainly would conflict with the person of the Holy Spirit, if only it were a person. But again by the Sophism of equivocation the error is concealed. For the Apostle is not dealing with the Essential communication, which has a place only within the fellowship of the most holy Trinity: but with the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit, or what is the same thing, with the communication of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. That this is not contradictorily opposed to the Person of the Holy Spirit is evident from the fact that GOD the Father himself is also said to dwell in the pious. Yet it was never even heard by report that anything should depart from his person on that account.

Thirdly, they are accustomed to argue thus: Whoever is sent, it is necessary that he be of a transitory substance. But the Holy Spirit is said to be sent from heaven. Therefore, it follows that he is of a transitory substance, and consequently a creature. But the fallacy arises from the phrase, 'to be sent': which does not signify a transition from place to place, but in the Scriptures denotes a certain presence of the Holy Spirit, joined with spiritual energy in the pious and faithful. Furthermore, this sending is to be accurately distinguished from the Procession of the Holy Spirit, since that denotes his personal difference or property, by which he is personally distinguished from the Father and the Son: whereas the mission pertains not only to the Holy Spirit, but also to the Son, by reason of operation ad extra.

Fourthly, they rise up thus: He who searches the depths of GOD is not GOD: since, he who searches has indeed a desire for some thing to be known: but he does not yet know it. But the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. 2, is said to search all things, even the depths of GOD. Therefore he is not GOD. But a gross fallacy of amphibology is again committed in the phrase, 'to search the depths of GOD': which if it is taken of man, it obtains that meaning which the adversaries assigned in the proof of the major premise: but if it is taken of GOD, then according to the propriety of the Hebrew phrase, it does not signify an affection, but rather an effect: and it denotes the most absolute knowledge of all divine mysteries. Since this is everywhere assigned to the Holy Spirit, an argument for his Divinity can be clearly drawn from that very fact. In which same sense GOD the Father is also said to search the hearts and reins. Ps. 7, 10. Jerem. 17, 10.

Finally, they heap up many testimonies of the Scriptures, which make mention only of the Father and the Son: with the Holy Spirit excluded: whence they suppose an argument can be drawn to overturn the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit. But the sophists in this place do not distinguish the doctrine of the Trinity of Persons from the doctrine of the office of the Mediator. Certainly, as often as Christ speaks of his office, so often he distinguishes himself as a sent person from the Father, the sending person: for the reason that he was sent by the Father alone: a fact which, however, neither can nor ought to prejudice the doctrine of the Trinity of persons in the slightest.

But there remains also another error concerning the Spirit

Spirit, and that by no means light, which is of the Greeks, and still endures today, concerning that eternal procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son. For the Greeks contended, and today still contend, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and not likewise from the Son. But a threefold age of the Greeks is most rightly established by certain theologians: First, Middle, and Last: so that it may be clear which Greek theologians can and ought to be accused of this error concerning the Holy Spirit. The first age lasts from Christ's passion, and especially from the time when Greece was converted to the faith of Christ, up to the times of Basil. Therefore, the Greek theologians who lived during this entire first age did not in any way disagree with the Latins on this article. The middle age extends from the century of Basil (which falls in the three hundred and seventieth year from the birth of Christ) up to the thousandth year. And around this age some of the Greeks began to dispute about the Divinity of the Holy Spirit, although still secretly and somewhat timidly, up to Macedonius, who was the first to dare to deny his Divinity publicly and pertinaciously. Although Basil fought against him most fiercely: he nevertheless used certain forms of speech which presented an ambiguous and not altogether convenient sense, and gave occasion for other errors: as when he very often used this phrase: πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ζῶν ἐκ θεῦ πατρὸς, δὶ υἱῶ: The Holy Spirit is from GOD the Father through the Son. Hence Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, who followed Basil, having seized the opportunity, is written to have been the first to deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son. But in this very middle age this opinion was not yet received and approved by all Greek theologians: much less pertinaciously defended by all.

But the last age, which succeeded the age of Basil, Theodoret, Cyril, and other luminaries of Greece, finally undertook to defend this error contumaciously, and simply denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son. To which opinion also Theophylact and many other doctors of Greece, otherwise most orthodox, conceded. And indeed this dispute finally flared up to such an extent that under the Empire of Michael the Drunkard, the Greeks openly made a secession from the Latin Church: in vain entirely to this very day, with various conditions for restoring peace and concord sought and attempted. And indeed, if the truth must be confessed, the Greeks are found in the beginning to have sinned more out of emotion, so that they might show, for instance, that they did not approve of that authority and posterity which the Roman Church was even then arrogating to itself over the Greeks, much less that they would stand by its calculation and judgment in doubtful matters and questions: although in the passage of time this error of the Greeks began to take such roots of impiety that to this very day it cannot be torn from their minds.

The arguments by which they have hitherto endeavored to put a gloss upon the error, when in places are extant, having been refuted at length in the booklets of Chemnitz and others, but especially in the Acts of the Tubingensians with the Greeks: or I draw back, and sound the retreat: humbly venerating GOD, that having rooted out the weeds of all errors, He may continue to preserve us in the truth. His word is truth. AMEN.

Latin:

totam effentiam divinam, sed solam Patris personam genuisse: tamen illud attendédum, quod hæc Patris persona non genuerit extra, sed intra Divinitatis Effentiam. Quare neutiquam sequitur, quod inferunt Adversarii, Si Patris persona genuit. Ergò solus Pater est verus DEUS: Sed illud tantùm sequitur, solum Patrem esse solum verum DEUM gignentem. Jam verò, Quia generatio hæc facta est, intra divinæ Essentię cõplexum, sequitur: Quod quemadmodum Pater est solus verus DEUS gignens: Ita Filius etiam sit solus verus DEUS genitus: & Spiritus Sanctus sit solus verus DEUS à Patre Filioque procedens. Et frustrà planè præsidium aliquod causæ quærunt Adversarii, in particula exclusivâ SOLUS sive SOLUM. Hæc enim non excludit reliquas personas à Divinitate: sed partim sejungit reliquas personas ab hoc Generationis Actu; qui solius Patris proprius est: partim verò excludit Idola & fictitios DEOS à Divinitatis participatione.

CLASSIS QUARTA. Eorum Hæreticorum, qui tùm Divinitatem, tùm processionem Spiritus Sancti à Patre & Filio impugnarunt.

Articulum de Spiritu Sancto, nullo non tempore Diabolus per varios hæreticos obscurare, imò penitùs evertere studuit. Certè ipsorum Apostolorum ætate statuebant Simoniani, Spiritum Sanctum esse tantùm nomen energiæ & virtutis, non autem Essentiæ divinæ. Hos insecuti Hierachitæ, contendebant Spiritum Sanctum esse Melchisedecum: Imò esse Sororem Christi, uti Helcesaitæ blasphemarunt. Quin eò impietatis progressi nonnulli, ut sese pro Spiritu Sancto venditarent, quemadmodum de Simone ejusque scorto Helena, ut & de Manichæo & Montano, Ecclesiastica testatur historia. Porrò Origenistæ, Acaciani & Ariani fingebant, Spiritum Sanctum non esse verum DEUM, sed tantùm Creaturam, & quidem uti Servetianis delirare libuit, ejusmodi Creaturam, quæ secundum partes, per omnes creaturas sit diffusa. Cæterùm universæ istæ hæreses, in uná tandem illam hæresin quasi confluxerũt, quam Macedoniani sive πνευματομάχοι circa A. D. 360. sub Imp. Constantio, publicè & quidem non sine aliquo applausu spargere cœperunt. Macedonius enim Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitanæ Episcopus; pro concione docebat, Spiritum Sanctum Patre & Filio minorem, nec ejusdem cum utroque Substantiæ, sed meram Creaturam esse & vim, à DEO conditam: qua per divisionem Essentiæ rebus creatis insit: teste Ruffino, lib. 1. hist. Eccl. cap. 25. & Augustino l. de hæresibus c. 52.

Quanquam verò hanc ipsam hæresin eodem tempore tuebantur etiam Ariani; quia tamen hi potissimum Filii DEI divinitatem impugnabant: ideò factum, ut hæresis isthæc non Ariana, sed Macedoniana diceretur: ipsi verò hæretici resews hujus Sectatores, ab Erroris Capite πνευματόμαχοι nominarentur. Quanquam verò hæresis isthæc postquam ea nobilissimam Ecclesiam Constantinopolitanam annis triginta ampliùs graviter afflixisset, studio & opera Theodosii Majoris Imperatoris, in prima Synodo universali Constantinopolitana, præsentibus Episcopis 150. damnata fuit A.D. 381. (alii 383.) tamen recentiores Anti-Trinitarii eandem ab inferis quasi resuscitare student, contendentes Spiritum Sanctum nihil esse aliud, quàm virtutem quandam DEI, divinam efficaciam in creaturis.

Utique tùm Veteres, tùm recentiores Pneumatomachi pro erroris patrocinio objiciunt initiò illa Scripturarum testimonia, quæ DEUM creasse Spiritum affirmant; ut Amos. 4, 13: Ecce ego DEUS creans Spiritum: ubi tamen turpi Sophisticatione æquivocationis ipsos ludere, manifestum est: cum non de tertia persona Trinitatis, sed de vento Scriptura ibi agat.

Deindè verò subindè provocant ad autoritatem Synodi Nicenæ, quæ de divinitate Spiritus Sancti nihil quicquam definiverit. Sed in promtu est responsio. Nihil quidem in Synodo illa hac de re fuisse definitum, imò ne quidem definiri debuisse, quia tùm Quæstio non agitabatur de Divinitate Spiritus Sancti: sed tantùm de Divinitate Filii DEI. Etsi enim Ariani Divinitatem Spiritus Sancti etiam negabant; tamen errorem hunc, studio quo poterant maximo, occultabant: ne videlicet hoc etiam errore prodito, planè pro Atheis haberentur, teste Basilio in Epistolis. Hinc ergò factum, ut in Nicæna Synodo nihil quicquam de Spiritus Sancti Divinitate definiretur. Cæterùm progressu temporis abundè satis hoc compensatum fuit, in Synodo Constantinopolitana: ubi Symbolo Niceno hæc adjecta fuêre: Credo in Spiritum Sanctum, Dominum & vivificantem, qui ex Patre, Filioq́; procedit: qui cum Patre & Filio simul adoratur & glorificatur: πιστεύω εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, τὸ κύριον, τὸ ζωοποιὸν, τὸ ἐκ τῶ πατρὸς, καὶ τῶ ὑιῶ ἐκπορευόμενον, τὸ σὺν πατρὶ καὶ ὑιῷ συμπεσκυνόμενον, καὶ συνδοξαζόμενον. Quam partem suæ hæresi oppositam esse, vel ipsi intellexerunt Macedoniani.

Cæterùm recentiores Ariani aliis etiam & pluribus armis hodiè pugnare solent. Ac initiò quidem provocant ad Scripturas, quæ Spiritum Sanctum nuspiam expressè DEUM nominent. Sed falsitas hujus assertionis, quam etiam Erasmum evomere non puduit, manifestissimè patet ex iis fundamentis, quibus supra Affirmativæ nostræ immotam certitudinem demonstravimo: videatur propositio 8. Quæstionis 3. Sufficiat hoc loco unus ille locus, qui extat 1. Cor. 12. Ubi de varietate donorum in Ecclesia ex professo agit Apostolus, eorundemque Autorem, Spiritum Sanctum, expressè DEUM nominat, versu 6.

Deindè objiciunt illud, quod Apostolus suis Corinthiis precatur κοινωνίαν Spiritus Sancti: id quod certè pugnaret cum personâ Spiritus Sancti, si modò esset persona. Sed rursum Sophismate æquivocationis error tegitur. Neque enim de communicatione Essentiali, quæ intra consortium sacrosanctæ Triados tantùm locum habet: sed de gratiosa Spiritus Sancti inhabitatione, vel quod idem est, de Donorum Spiritus Sancti communicatione, agit Apostolus. Hanc verò non contradictoriè esse oppositam Personæ Spiritus Sancti, vel indè patet, quod ipse quoque DEUS Pater in piis inhabitare dicitur. Unde tamen personæ ipsius aliquid decedere, nunquam vel fando auditum fuit.

Tertiò sic argutare solent: Quicunque emittitur, ille transitoriæ sit substantiæ, necesse est. Atqui Spiritus Sanctus dicitur emitti de cœlis. Ergò transitoriæ ipsum Substantiæ, & per Consequens creaturam esse, consequitur. Sed oritur fallacia ex phrasi, Emitti: quæ non transitum de loco ad locum significat, sed in Scripturis notat certam Spiritus Sancti præsentiam, conjunctam cum πνευματικῇ ἐνεργείᾳ in piis ac fidelibus. Deindè Emissio hæc accuratè est distingvenda à Processione Spiritus Sancti, quippe quæ personalem ejus differentiam sive proprietatem, quâ à Patre & Filio personaliter distingvitur, denotat: Cùm Missio non soli Spiritui Sancto, sed & Filio competat, ratione Operationis ad extra.

Quartò sic insurgunt: Qui scrutatur profunditates DEI, is DEUS non est: Siquidem, Qui scrutatur, is desiderium quidem habet alicujus rei cognoscendæ: illam verò nondum cognoscit. Atqui Spiritus Sanctus, 1. Cor. 2. dicitur, Scrutari omnia, etiam profunditates DEI. Ergò DEUS non est. Sed crassa iterùm committitur fallacia amphibologias in phrasi, Scrutari profunditates DEI: quæ si de homine accipitur, eam significationem sortitur, quam Adversarii in probatione Majoris assignarunt: Si verò de DEO sumitur, tùm secundùm proprietatem phrasis Hebrææ, non significat affectum; sed potiùs effectum: & notat absolutissimam omnium mysteriorum divinorum scientiam. Quæ cum Spiritui Sancto passim adsignetur, vel indè de Divinitate ipsius luculentum peti potest argumentum. Quo ipso sensu DEUS Pater etiam dicitur scrutari corda & renes. Psal. 7, 10. Jerem. 17, 10.

Tandem coacervant plurima Scripturarum testimonia, quæ mentionem tantùm faciunt Patris & Filii: excluso Spiritu Sancto: undè ad evertendam Spiritus Sancti ὑπόςασιν argumentum peti posse, autumant. Sed Sophistæ hoc loco non distingvunt doctrinam de Trinitate Personarum, à doctrinâ de officio Mediatoris. Certè quoties Christus de officio suo loquitur, toties se tanquam personam missam distingvit à Patre, personâ mittente: ideò quòd à solo Patre missus est: id quòd tamen doctrinæ de Trinitate personarum nihil quicquam præjudicare vel potest, vel debet.

Sed superest alius etiam error de Spiritu

Sancto, isque minimè levis, qui Græcorum est, ac etiamnùm hodiè durat, de æterna illa processione Spiritus Sancti à Patre, & à Filio. Contenderunt enim Græci, hodieque contendunt, Spiritum Sanctum à solo Patre, non item à Filio procedere. Rectissimè autem à quibusdam Theologis, Triplex Græcorum ætas constituitur: Prima, Media, & postrema: ut sic constare queat, quinam Græci Theologi erroris istius de Spiritu Sancto insimulari possint & debeant. Prima ætas, à Christo passo, & ab eo cumprimis tempore, quo Græcia ad fidem Christi conversa fuit, durat usque ad Basilii tempora. Qui igitur tota hac prima ætate vixerunt Græci Theologi, in hoc articulo à Latinis nullatenùs dissenserunt.
