Media ætas à Basilii seculo (quod in annum trecentesimum, septuagesimum à nato Christo incidit) usque ad annum millesimum se extendit. Et circa hanc ætatem ceperunt Græcorum nonnulli de Divinitate Spiritus Sancti disputare, quanquàm adhuc clanculùm & timidiusculè, usque ad Macedonium, qui primus publicè & pertinaciter illius Divinitatem negare ausus est. Adversus quem licet Basilius acerrimè pugnaret: usus tamen est quibusdam loquendi formulis, quæ sensum ambiguum, & haud usque adeò commodum præ se ferebant, & aliis erroribus ansam præbebant: ut quando sæpissimè hac phrasi utebatur: πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ζῶν ἐκ θεῦ πατρὸς, δὶ υἱῶ: Spiritus Sanctus, est ex DEO Patre per Filium. Hinc Theodoretus Cyri Episcopus, qui Basilium insecutus est, arrepta occasione primus scribitur negasse Spiritum Sanctum procedere etiam à Filio. Sed hac ipsa media ætate nondum ab omnibus Græcis Theologis recepta & approbata est hæc sententia: nedùm ab omnibus pertinaciter defensa.

Cæterùm postrema ætas, quæ Basilii, Theodoreti, Cyrilli, & aliorum Græciæ luminum ætatem excepit, contumaciter demùm errorem istum defendendum suscepit, & simpliciter negavit, Spiritum Sanctum etiam procedere à Filio. Quam in sententiam concesserunt etiam Theophylactus, & complures alii Græciæ Doctores aliàs ὀρθοδοξότατοι. Et sanè disputatio hæc ita tandem in immensum exarsit, ut sub Imperio Michaëlis Ebriosi, Græci apertè à Latina Ecclesia secessionem fecerint: Frustrà omninò in hunc usque diem, variis redintegrandæ pacis & concordiæ quæsitis & tentatis conditionibus. Et profectò, si quod res est, fatendum sit, deprehenduntur Græci initiò, magis ex affectu peccasse, ut videlicet vel hoc pacto ostenderent, se autoritatem & posteritatem illam; quam Romana Ecclesia jam tùm in Græcas sibi arrogabat, minimè approbare, nèdum in rebus & quæstionibus dubiis, illius stare calculo & judicio: Quanquam progressu temporis Error iste Græcorum, ita radices impietatis agere cœpit, ut in hunc usque diem ex animis ipsorum evelli haud queat.

Argumenta, quibus Errori fucum facere hactenus studuerunt, cum in locis Chemnitii & aliorum libellis prolixè refutata extent, cumprimis verò in Actis Tubingenfium cum Græcis: vel ego contraho, & receptui cano: DEUM fupplex venerans, ut radicitùs evulfis omnium errorum loliis, in veritate nos confervare pergat. Sermo ipfius eft veritas. AMEN.


## 4 On the Person and Two Natures of Christ

The controversy concerning the Person of Christ the Savior, not so much regarding its breadth as regarding its utility, which has redounded most greatly from it to the Church of GOD, is by far the most noble of all. For what Evagrius once pronounced concerning the ancient heretics in book 1, hist. Eccl. chap. 9, that through those who tore the Church apart, the dogmas of the right faith emerged: that can, nay, must, be most truly affirmed concerning this very controversy. Nor, however, can we meanwhile approve of the attempts and designs of those who, captured more by a zeal for contentiousness than for a love of truth, have sought in the previous century to revive the most troublesome coals of the ancient heretics, especially those of Nestorius, fanned by new bellows. In which part those first authors of the struggle, the Sacramentarians, Carlstadt, Zwingli, Oecolampadius and their accomplices, devoted diligent effort entirely: who finally dragged our Blessed Luther into this arena, even against his will. He himself had indeed wished, and had prayed with earnest groans to GOD, that that great mystery of godliness, that GOD was manifested in the flesh, might be allowed to be retained sound and uncorrupted in silence and faith, without any dissensions: But the trickery and craftiness of the adversaries toward the method of error, as our Apostle speaks in Eph. 4:14, required something far other and different. For since the adversaries could by no means resist those foundations which Luther had brought forth from the Formula of institution for the sake of asserting the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Holy Supper: they immediately changed the seat of war, and sought a retreat in the Article concerning the Person of Christ, repeatedly chanting: That it could by no means happen, nay, that it was utterly impossible, while the properties of a true and natural human body remain, for the Body of Christ to be simultaneously in Heaven and in all those places present where the Sacrament of the Eucharist is dispensed. Thus, therefore, Luther also finally found it necessary to descend to a disputation concerning the Person of Christ in the Sacramentarian struggle. And although this tragic struggle not a little delayed the course of the reborn Gospel, nay, quite dangerously obscured the beauty and ornament of the tender Lutheran Church, which had scarcely aspired from Pontifical servitude to the true liberty of the Gospel: yet for this reason its condition was more tolerable, that then, as also for many subsequent years, he had the Romanists in this Article clearly of the same opinion as himself: however much the Jesuit Busaeus may dare to deny that today in his Apologetic against Gerlach. It is certainly established that the Romanists in the third Article of the Augsburg Confession desired nothing at all at the time that Confession was presented, so that at those very Diets they publicly testified concerning their consent in these words: In the third Article there is nothing that offends, since its whole confession agrees with the Apostles' Creed and with the certain rule of faith. Which very thing Johannes Cochlaeus also expressly confessed in the following year, 1541, writing in his discussion of the Confession: Concerning this Article there is no discord between us and them, neither in the Confession nor in the Apology. Now, however, it is also established that this very third Article asserts in words that are by no means obscure that very Majesty and exaltation of the assumed Flesh of Christ, which the Jesuits today strive with such great effort to oppose, nay, to overturn from the foundations. For the words of the Latin Confession are thus: He ascended into heaven, that He might sit at the right hand of the Father, and reign perpetually, and rule over all Creatures. Now, however, since it is placed beyond controversy that no Exaltation at all could accrue to the Divinity of Christ from the Ascension: it certainly becomes clear even from that, that the Augsburg Confession and its associates, one and all, and even the Pontifical approvers, understood the particle UT (that) as concerning the exaltation and Majesty of the Human nature in Christ.

It is established, moreover, that the Romanists were clearly lynx-eyed censors and Aristarchuses of all the writings of Luther, especially the Polemical ones: but that they did not even once mark with a black coal, or even lightly disapprove of, that dogma which he had publicly proposed with great spirit against the Sacramentarians concerning the Omnipresence or Majesty of the Son of man. Finally, it is established that even the classical Pontifical writers, and among these, especially Faber Stapulensis, strenuously defended this very dogma of Luther and our churches concerning the Person of Christ.

And it is clearly trivial what the Jesuit Busaeus objects in this place, that Stapulensis was publicly contradicted, and that he was condemned by the Church for that dogma concerning the Majesty of the flesh of Christ. For although we cannot deny the former, that his doctrine suffered a certain contradiction, yet we simply deny the latter, namely that he was condemned by the Church for any error. For Sleidanus is a witness in book 5, that that contradiction proceeded not from a love of truth, but from private hatred toward Stapulensis. But then, that Francis, King of the Gauls, gave this task to certain great and learned men, that they should examine the books and writings of his, for which he had been accused. And they, having investigated and weighed all matters, bore an ample and honorable testimony of purity and innocence to him: Finally, that the same King Francis wrote to the Parisian Senate, and severely commanded, in order to absolve Stapulensis from every accusation and to restrain his adversaries: thus, therefore, the Jesuit did not hesitate to vomit forth a triple lie with one Spirit. And if he is a good man, let him demonstrate it himself, but let him demonstrate from records worthy of belief that the Roman Church ever and anywhere produced any disagreement concerning this dogma, until, under clearly unhappy auspices, at length in the Year of our Lord 1564, the Jesuit race, having entered into a Syncretism with the Calvinists, in a certain public Disputation concerning the Majesty of the Man Christ, instituted against Doctor Jacob Andreae at Ingolstadt on the Kalends of July, testified that it had made a divorce not so much from our Church as from its own Roman Church, and in this Article had crossed over to the camp of the Calvinists. Upon this being done, certain clandestine Sacramentarians in this very Academy of ours at Wittenberg were filled with such joy that seven years later, namely in the year 71, they not only reprinted that very Calvinist-Jesuit disputation here with public types, but also the Rector of the Academy, M. Erasmus Rudinger, most diligently commended it to the studious youth with a special address to the reader, as a form of sound words. For that address contains, among other things, this: Certain ones from the family of the Jesuits have studied to comprehend and explain the doctrine concerning the personal union of the two natures in Christ and the communication of idioms so briefly, clearly, distinctly, and thus rightly and well, that for the sake of the public good we have judged that it should be expressed again among us, so that these chapters may exist in the Orthodox Church before the eyes of those who are learning the doctrine of the Church, as a table, and that a formula of sound words which ought to be used may be at hand. That the Jesuits today still foster this same mutual Syncretism with the Calvinists is sufficiently clearly evident from the disputation of Robert Bellarmine, which he pursued in several books concerning Christ. Thus, therefore, we, placed as it were in the middle at this time and surrounded on both sides by the battle lines of enemies, find it necessary to fight on the right indeed with the Calvinists, but on the left with the Jesuits. For although it might perhaps seem to someone that both walls can be whitewashed with one trowel, and that the refutation of Calvinism is also the refutation of the Jesuits, yet to those weighing the writings of both more accurately, it cannot be obscure that the Jesuits have certain peculiar assertions and also certain peculiar arguments, which it will hardly be demonstrated that the Calvinists have ever used until now, as the future Treatise, with Christ himself, whose glory is at stake, graciously favoring, will show more evidently.

Regarding the Philippist Treatise of this Article, it is certain that in the earlier editions of the Loci of the years 22 and 25 there is a deep silence entirely concerning the mystery of the union of the two natures in Christ: but in the two later ones of the year 35, 41, etc., it is indeed proposed, but in such a way that it may not undeservedly seem a wonder to anyone why it is that Philip, conscious of, nay, even a not insignificant part of those struggles which were known in the Church of GOD concerning this Article, nevertheless explained it so briefly and succinctly, nay, coldly and meagerly, that he did not even once make mention of that Controversy: so far is he from having undertaken to explain for himself the doctrine concerning the hypostatic Union of the two natures in Christ, concerning the Communication of Idioms, concerning the Majesty and Exaltation of the Human Nature of Christ, and to assert it with Blessed Luther against the babblings of the Sacramentarians. If there could be room for conjectures and suspicions, we would perhaps note no other cause for the fact than that Philip, although secretly, defected from the purity of the Lutheran doctrine to the School of the Calvinists: but because of his innate timidity, he did not wish to profess openly and plainly what he felt inside in his heart. But what need is there for suspicions, when above in the general prolegomena we have demonstrated this very thing concerning Philip with firm and immovable foundations. What is more, even in this place, in that succinct brevity which he used, he nevertheless wished not obscurely to instill the seeds of Calvinist heresy into the minds of the readers. Of which kind are the following aphorisms, which it would be worth the effort to note, so that students of Theology may learn to guard themselves all the more rightly against such insidious locutions.

I. When the Apostle says: In him dwells all the fullness of the godhead bodily: It is the same as if he were to say: In others GOD dwells by his Spirit, kindling new light and new motions: But in Christ he dwells not only by the Spirit: But also, so that the human nature is united to the divine by a personal union. For as we say persons now in common usage: so the ancient Greeks said bodies.

This Philippist interpretation against the Orthodox doctrine of our Churches is vehemently urged by that weathercock Christopher Pezel, asserting that this, and no other, is the sense of the words of Paul, that the Word dwells in the assumed human Flesh, not as in Elijah and Peter: but by such a dwelling as is that by the grace of Union. How insufficient, nay, sophistical this interpretation is, and how shamefully it begs the question, we shall show in its proper place.

II. If it is objected: The divine nature does not suffer, does not die, but Christ died, which is customary, true, and necessary. The response is: Since there are two Natures in Christ, certain things proper to one nature do not prevent the other Nature from being present. With this Philippist assertion standing, it would be a consequence that those propositions, GOD redeemed the Church with his own blood: And GOD suffered, was crucified, died, etc., are merely verbal propositions: and are to be explained thus: GOD suffered, was crucified, died: that is: The human nature suffered: but this passion did not prevent the other nature, namely the divine, from being present at the same time. But concerning this Sophistication also, which introduces the Zwinglian alteration into the Church of GOD with full sails, as they say, we shall have to deal expressly below, in the first kind of the Communication of Idioms.

III. In this doctrine are delivered the Rules concerning the Communication of idioms, that is, concerning the predication of properties, which are spoken of commonly concerning both natures, but in the concrete, namely, so that the properties may be understood to be attributed to the Person. Which rule, in the third kind of Communication of idioms, looks back too manifestly upon Calvinism, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place.

How it can and ought also to be referred hither, that Definition of the Communication of Idioms proposed by Philip in his loci of the year 1535, which sounds thus: The Communication of Idioms is a figure of speech, by which a property belonging to one nature is attributed to the whole person, in the concrete.

But let it suffice to have noted these things briefly in this place: we shall examine the individual points more fully in a future exposition, which, according to the diversity of the Questions and Controversies, we can not inconveniently divide into five distinct chapters: So indeed that the first may settle the Controversy which is agitated today concerning both the Truth and the properties of the human nature which the λόγος assumed: The second, however, may inquire into the mode and Definition of the personal Union of the two Natures in Christ: The third may weave through that classic and truly noble Disputation concerning the effect of the Hypostatic Union, which consists in a true and real κοινωνία or Communication, both of the Natures to each other, and also of the Idioms themselves. The fourth may consider the State of Exinanition. The fifth, finally, the State of Exaltation, and may especially settle the Disputation concerning the Ascension and Session of Christ at the Right hand of GOD the Father. We have determined to weave through the exposition of these Chapters, with God's help, in such a way that, having passed over and neglected those things which are either sufficiently clear and perspicuous by themselves, or are everywhere obvious in Methodical textbooks, we may hold in high regard those things especially in which the Calvinists and Jesuits have been accustomed to plant their feet and seek the protection of their cause.

Latin:

COntroverfia de Perfona Chrifti Servatoris, non tam quoad ejus amplitudinem, quàm quoad utilitatem, quæ inde ad Ecclefiam DEI redundavit maxima, longè omnium eft nobiliffima. Quod enim de Veteribus olim hæreticis pronunciavit Evagrius lib. 1. hist. Eccl. cap 9. per eos, qui Ecclefiam difcerpferunt, recta fidei dogmata emerferunt: id de hac ipfa etiam controverfia, veriffimè affirmari poteft, imò debet. Neque tamen interim eorum conatus & confilia probare poffumus, qui φιλονικείας magis, quàm φιλαληθείας ftudio capti, moleftiffimos veterum hæreticorum Neftorii cumprimis carbones, novis flabellis accenfos, fuperiori feculo refufcitare ftuduerunt. Qua in parte fedulam omninò operam navarunt, primi illi autores certaminis, Sacramētarii, Carolostadius, Zvvinglius, Oecolampadius & complices: qui B. Lutherum nostrum, vel invitum etiam in hanc palæstram tandem protraxerunt. Optaverat quidem ipfe, & feriis gemitibus à DEO precatus fuerat, ut magnum illud pietatis mysterium, quòd DEUS manifestatus est in carne, liceret in silentio & fide, fine ullis diffidiis, retinere fanum & incorruptum: Sed adverfariorum κυβεία καὶ πανεργία πρὸς τὴν μεθοδίαν τῆς πλάνης, ut Apostolus noster loquitur Eph. 4, 14. longè aliud ac diverfum requirebat. Cùm enim fundamentis illis, quæ pro afferenda vera ac reali præfentia Corporis & Sangvinis Chrifti in S. Cœna, ex institutionis Formula produxerat Lutherus, refiftere Adverfarii haud poffent: ftatim mutata belli fede, in Articulo de Perfona Chrifti, receptum quæfiverunt, fubinde occinentes: Fieri nulla ratione posse, imò salvis proprietatibus veri & naturalis corporis humani, prorsus impossibile esse, ut Corpus Christi simul sit in Cælo, & in omnibus illis locis præsens, ubi Eucharistiæ Sacramentum dispensatur. Sic ergò Lutherus etiam tandem, in certamine Sacramentario, ad difputationem de Perfona Chrifti defcendere neceffe habuit. Quanquam verò tragicum hoc certamen, haud parùm curfum renafcentis Evangelii remorabatur, imò decus atque ornamentum tenellæ Ecclefiæ Lutheranæ, quæ vix ex Servitute Pontificia ad veram Evangelii libertatem adfpiraverat, fatis periculosè obfufcabat: tamen vel hoc nomine tolerabilior erat ejus conditio, quòd tùm, ut & annis subsequentibus benè multis, hoc in Articulo Romanenses sibi habuit planè ὁμοψήφους: quantumvis illud negare hodiè ausit Jesuvvita Busæus in suo Apologetico adversus Gerlachium. Constat certè Romanenses in Articulo tertio Confessionis Augustanæ, nihil quicquam tempore oblatæ illius Confessionis desiderasse, ita ut illis ipsis Comitiis, de Consensu suo his verbis publicè testati sint: In tertio Articulo nihil est, quod offendat, cum tota ejus Confessio, cum Symbolo Apostolorum, & cum certa fidei regula conveniat. Quod ipsum Anno subsequente 41. supra sesquimillesimum, Johannes Cochlæus etiam disertè fassus est, scribens in discussione Confessionis: De hoc Articulo neque in Confessione, neque in Apologia, ulla est discordia inter nos & illos. Jam verò & illud constat, Articulum istū tertium, verbis minimè obscuris asserere illam ipsam Majestatem & exaltationem assumtæ Carnis Christi, quam tanto hodiè conatu Jesuvvitæ oppugnare, imò funditùs evertere studēt. Sic enim habent verba Latinæ Confessionis: Ascendit in cælos, ut sedeat ad dexteram Patris, & regnet perpetuò, & dominetur omnibus Creaturis. Jam verò cum extra Controversiam sit positum, ex Ascensione, nihil prorsus Exaltationis Divinitati Christi obtingere potuisse: utique vel indè perspicuum evadit, Confessionem Augustanam ejusdemque socios singulos & universos, quin etiam approbatores Pontificios Particulam UT, de exaltatione & Majestate Humanæ naturæ in Christo intellexisse.

Constat insuper, Romanenses omnium scriptorum Lutheri, cumprimis Polemicorum, Lynceos planè fuisse Censores & Aristarchos: verùm ne semel quidem atro carbone notasse, vel leviter saltem improbasse dogma illud, quod de Omnipræsentia sive Majestate Filii hominis, magno Spiritu adversus Sacramentarios publicè proposuerat. Constat denique classicos etiam Scriptores pontificios, & inter hos, Fabrum cumprimis Stapulensem, hoc ipsum Lutheri & nostratium Ecclesiarum dogma, de Persona Christi strenuè propugnasse.

Et nugatorium planè est, quod Busæus Jesuvvita hoc loco objicit, Stapulensi fuisse publicè contradictum, & ob dogma istud de Majestate carnis Christi ipsum ab Ecclesia damnatum. Etsi enim prius illud negare non possumus, doctrinam ipsius Contradictionem quandam passam esse, tamen posterius hoc simpliciter negamus, quòd videlicet erroris alicujus sit ab Ecclesia damnatus. Testis enim est Sleidanus lib. 5, l. Contradictionem istam non ex amore veritatis, sed ex privato odio in Stapulensem, profectam esse. Deindè verò Regem Galliarum Franciscum, magnis quibusdam & claris doctrinâ Viris, negotium hoc dedisse, ut de libris atque Scriptis illius, quorum nomine fuisset accusatus, cognoscerent. Eos autem rebus omnibus investigatis atque perpensis, amplum & honorificum puritatis & innocentiæ testimonium ipsi perhibuisse: Tandem eundem Franciscum Regem scripsisse ad Senatum Parisiensem, & severè mandasse, ut Stapulensem ab omni accusatione absolveret, & adversarios ipsius compesceret: Sic ergò tergeminum mendacium Jesuvvita uno Spiritu evomere non dubitavit. Et si vir bonus est, demonstret ipse, sed demonstret ex tabulis fide dignis Romanam Ecclesiam publicè de hoc dogmate unquam uspiam dissensum aliquem prodidisse, donec infelicibus planè auspiciis, tandem Anno Domini 1564. gens Jesuvvitica inito cum Calvinianis Syncretismo, publicâ quadã Disputatione, de Majestate Hominis Christi, adversus Doctorem Jacobum Andreæ, Ingolstadij Calendis Julij institutâ, se non tàm à nostrâ, quàm à suâ Romanâ Ecclesia, divortium fecisse, & hoc in Articulo ad castra Calvinianorum transijsse, testata est. Quo facto clancularij quidam Sacramentarij in hac ipsâ nostrâ Witebergensi Academia, tanto perfusi sunt gaudio, ut septennio pòst, Anno nimirum 71. illã ipsam disputationem Calvino-Jesuvviticam, nõ modò typis publicis hîc recuderent: sed & Academiæ Rector M. Esramus Rudingerus, peculiari ad Lectorem προσφωνησει eam, tanquam formã sanorum verborum, studiosæ juventuti diligentissimè commendaret. Sic enim inter reliqua habet illa προσφωνησις: Quidam ex familia Esavvitarum ita breviter, disertè, distinctè, itaque rectè ac benè doctrinam de unione personali duarũ naturarum in Christo & communicatione Idiomatum comprehendere & exponere studuerunt, ut boni publici causa denuò apud nos exprimendas censuerimus: quó in Ecclesia Orthodoxa extent hæc capita, ante oculos eorum, qui discunt doctrinam Ecclesiæ, tanquam tabella: & in promptu sit formula sanorũ verborum quâ utendum est. Quem eundem mutuum Syncretismum hodieque Jesuvvitas cum Calvinianis, fovere, satis luculenter patet ex disputatione Robert Bellarmini, quam de Christo aliquot libris prosecutus est. Sic ergò nos hoc tempore in medio quasi constituti, & ex utroque latere hostium agminibus cincti, à dextra quidem cum Calvinianis, à sinistra verò cum Jesuvvitis pugnare necessum habemus. Quamvis enim cuipiam fortè videri possit, unâ fideliâ utrumque de albari posse parietem, & Calvinismi refutationem, esse etiam Jesuvvitarum refutationem: utrorumq; tamen scripta accuratius pensitantibus, obscurum esse haud potest, habere Jesuvvitas peculiares quasdam assertiones peculiaria etiam quædam argumenta: quibus Calvinianos hactenùs unquam usos fuisse, vix demonstrabitur: quemadmodum futura Tractatio, Christo ipso, cujus gloria agitur, benè annuente, evidentius ostendet.

Quoad Tractationem Philippéam Articuli hujus, constat in prioribus Locorum editionibus anni. 22. & 25. altum prorsus de mysterio Unionis duarum naturarum in Christo esse silentium: in posterioribus verò duabus Anni 35. 41. &c. eam proponi quidem: sed ita, ut haud immeritò mirum cuipiam videri possit, quid sit, quod Philippus, conscius, imò pars etiam haud postrema eorum certaminum, quæ hoc de Articulo in Ecclesia DEI nota fuêre; usque tamen adeò breviter ac succinctè, imò frigidè & jejunè eum explicârit, ut ne quidem semel Controversiæ istius mentionem fecerit: tantùm abest, ut doctrinam de Unione hypostatica duarum naturarum in Christo, de Communicatione Idiomatum, de Majestate & Exaltatione Humanæ Christi Naturæ, sibi explicandam, & cum B. Luthero, adversus Sacramentariorum Φλυαρολογήματα asserendam sumserit. Si conjecturis & suspicionibus locus esse posset, fortè haud aliam facti causam annotaremus, quàm quòd Philippus, licèt clanculum, à puritate doctrinæ Lutheranæ, ad Scholam Calvinianorum defecit: pro innata autem timiditate, quid intùs in corde sentiret, propalàm & apertè profiteri noluit. Sed quid suspicionibus opus est, cum suprà in generalibus prolegomenis, hoc ipsum de Philippo, firmis & immotis fundamentis demonstraverimus. Quid, quod etiam hoc loco, in succincta illa brevitate, qua usus est, haud obscurè tamen semina Calvinianæ hæresews, animis legentium instillare voluit. Cujus generis sequentes sunt aphorismi, quos, ut tantò rectius studiosi Theologiæ ab ejusmodi insidiosis locutionibus sibi cavere discant, annotare operæ pretium fuerit.

I. Quando Apostolus dicit: In ipso inhabitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis Corporaliter: Idem est, ac si dicat: In alijs habitat DEUS Spiritu suo, novam lucem, & novos motus accendens: Sed in Christo habitat non solùm Spiritu: Sed etiam, ut personali unione humana natura divinæ unita sit. Nam ut nos dicimus nunc usitatè personas: ita Veteres Græci dixerunt σώματα.

Quam interpretationem Philippéam adversus Orthodoxam Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctrinam, vehementer urget Ecebolus ille Christophorus Pezelius, asserens hunc, non alium esse sensum verborum Pauli, Quod λόγος habitet in humana assumta Carne, non ut in Elia & Petro: sed tali habitatione, quæ sit illa Unionis gratia. Quàm verò insufficiens, imò sophistica hæc sit interpretatio, & quàm turpiter petat principium, suo loco ostendemus.

II. Si objicitur: Naturam divinam non pati, non mori Christum autem mortuum esse, usitata, vera & necessaria. Responsio est: Cum in Christo duæ Naturæ sint, quædam propria uni naturæ non impediunt, quô minùs adsit altera Natura. Stante hac assertione Philippêa, Consequens fuerit propositiones illas, DEUS suo sanguine redemit Ecclesiam: Et DEUS passus est, crucifixus, mortuus, &c. duntaxat verbales esse propositiones: & sic explicandas: DEUS passus est, crucifixus, mortuus: hoc est: Humana natura passa est: sed hæc passio non impedivit, quô minus simul adesset altera natura, nempè divina. Sed de hac etiam Sophisticatione, quæ Cinglianam ἀλλοίωσιν plenis, quod ajunt, vel is in Ecclesiam DEI invehit, ex professo infra, in primo genere Communicationis Idiomatum nobis agendum erit.

III. Traduntur in hac doctrina Regulæ de Communicatione idiomatum, id est, de prædicatione proprietatum, quæ de utraque natura communiter, sed in concreto, dicuntur, videlicet, ut intelligantur proprietates Personæ tribui. Quæ regula in tertio genere Communicationis idiomatum, Calvinismum nimis manifestè respipit, uti suo loco demonstrabimus.

Quamò potest & debet etiam huc referri Definitio illa Communicationis Idiomatum à Philippo proposita in locis Anni 35 supra, sesquimillesimum, quæ sic sonat: Communicatio Idiomatum est figura Sermonis, quà proprietas alteri naturæ conveniens, tribuutur toti personæ, in concreto.

Verùm hæc hoc loco paucis annotasse sufficiat: Pleniùs singula examinatuti in futura diexodo, quam pro diversitate Quæstionum & Controversiarum haud in commodè in quinque distincta capita partiri possumus: Ita quidem ut primum expediat Controversiam, quæ tùm de Veritate, tùm de proprietatibus naturæ humanæ, quam λόγος affumsit, hodiè agitatur: Alterum verò inquirat modum ac Definitionem Unionis personalis duarum Naturarum in Christo: Tertium pertexat classicam illam ac verè nobilem Disputationem de effectu Unionis Hypostaticæ, qui consistit in vera ac reali, tùm Naturarum ad se invicem, tùm ipsorum etiam Idiomatum κοινωνία sive Communicatione. Quartum consideret Statum Exinanitionis. Quintum denique Statum Exaltationis, & potissimùm Disputationem de Ascensione & Sessione Christi ad Dexteram DEI Patris expediat. Quorum Capitum diexodon, ita σὺν Θεῷ pertexere constituimus, ut præteritis & neglectis ijs, quæ vel per se satis sunt clara & perspicua, vel in libellis Methodicis passim sunt obvia, pensi habeamus ea potissimùm in quibus Calviniani & Jesuitæ pedem figere, suæquè causæ præsidium quærere consueverunt.


### Chapter I. On the Truth of the Human Nature which the Word (Λόγος) assumed Proposition I

Concerning the Truth of the Human Nature which the λόγος assumed.

PROPOSITION I.

The Son of GOD, or the λόγος, in the fullness of time, united to Himself by an eternal covenant, and by uniting assumed, a true, entire, and in all things consubstantial human Nature to us, endowed with its own true and Essential properties.

Concerning the Nature and Quality of the hypostatic Union of the two Natures in CHRIST, there will be a Disputation for us in the next following Chapter. In this place, however, the Human Nature, considered in itself and by itself, must be weighed: and this on account of various heresies and corruptions, both ancient and more recent.

Of the Ancients, Marcion once blasphemed that CHRIST was not a true man: but had a feigned and phantastical body, which He took from heaven, not from the substance of the Virgin Mary: and consequently that He did not even truly suffer, was crucified, and died, but only κατ' δόκησιν καὶ φαντασίαν, putatively and by a certain illusion. Which madness the Manichaeans later recalled, as it were, from the infernal regions.

Arius, following him, contended that the flesh of Christ was plainly inanimate, πάντη ἄψυχον: so that the Divinity supplied the place of the soul.

Apollinaris succeeded, who imagined that a soul, ἀλόγῳ, was not assumed in the Incarnation. But soon, as if led by repentance, wishing to appear to have corrected his language and mind, he said that a soul was indeed assumed, which however did not have a mind: but that GOD the λόγος was assumed in the man in place of a mind.

Nor did the Valentinians of old cherish a more tolerable heresy, who, although they by no means denied that Christ had a true body, nevertheless contended that it was, by reason of its stock, origin, and substance, plainly ἑτερούσιον to our bodies: being celestial and spiritual: and that it was not born of Mary, but through Mary: for the reason that the λόγος received nothing at all from the holy Virgin: but like water through a stream or conduit, that is, through Mary, passed with his celestial body.

The Monothelites also pertain to this, who, by granting only one will and divine operation in Christ, are to be judged as having likewise granted only one nature.

Furthermore, Eutyches contended that the human nature of Christ, formed by the Holy Spirit in the womb of Mary, was, immediately after the very moment the hypostatic union was made, absorbed by the divinity, and thus reduced to nothing, so that only the divine nature remained surviving in Christ.

In the previous century, while our blessed Luther was still living, a certain Caspar Schwenckfeld, a Silesian nobleman, recalling as it were from hell ancient and long-condemned heresies, vomited forth such monstrosities regarding the human nature of Christ that the mind shudders even to recount them: among the rest, however, the following three hypotheses are not the least.

Making a divorce from these and other heresies of that kind, our Church firmly believes and decrees that the λόγος had assumed, 1. A true human Nature, which is certainly not imaginary, not similar to a specter or a phantom, but in the truth of the thing, although it does not subsist in itself and by itself, but truly in the person of the λόγος. The first attribute, therefore, which our proposition declares concerning the assumed human nature, is the TRUTH of human Nature, which is opposed to fantasy or a specter. The Savior confirms this attribute quite clearly, Luke 24:39, where, distinguishing his body from a spirit or specter, he says, Handle me, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have. It is added that the Apostle gravely attests that we are at some time to be conformed to the body of Christ, Phil. 3:21, where indeed every condition of a specter and spirit or phantom utterly expires.

Nor does that cavil of the ancient Marcionites obtain even the slightest strength: In the Old Testament the Son of GOD appeared many times not clothed in the truth of flesh, but merely dressed in a human form. Therefore, the reason for the same appearance in the New Testament will be equal. For the futility of this inference is manifest in many ways.

For 1. The argument proceeds from a particular case. 2. From a false principle: as if the reason for the Old and New Testament were the same. 3. It is inverted, by βίαιον: For this very reason, the Son of GOD did not appear in the form or species of a body, but in and under a true human body, or, as the Apostle speaks, 1 Tim. 3:16, it was necessary that GOD be manifested in the flesh because this manifestation was not of the Old, but of the New Testament. The reason for the connection is this: In the Old Testament was the time of signs, shadows, and images: but in the New Testament came the fullness of time, which required not shadows anymore, but the body itself. Col. 2:17, Hebrews 10:1. 4. And finally, that solemn description which exists in the sacred writings concerning the conception and Nativity of Christ proves the difference. Matt. 1:18, Luke 1:27, 2:6, and following.

The second attribute, which our proposition declares concerning the assumed humanity of Christ, is INTEGRITY: which includes under itself those two Essential or constituent parts: namely, body and soul: Which both parts the Orthodox Church believes and confesses that the λόγος assumed. The first attribute will explain the truth of the former part: the clear testimonies of the Scriptures confirm the certainty of the latter; Matt. 20:28, The Son of man came to give his soul. Matt. 26:38, My soul is sorrowful even unto death. Luke 23:46, Father, into thy hands I commend my Spirit. John 12:27, Now is my soul troubled. Regarding the faculties of the Soul, the matter is likewise clearly confessed. For when in Luke 2:52, Christ as a little boy is said to have increased in wisdom: certainly that faculty of the soul is noted, which is referred to the Mind and is proper to the τό ἡγεμονικόν. Thus when the Savior says, Matt. 26:39, Not what I will, but what thou wilt. And John 5:30, I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father who sent me: And John 6:38, He descended from heaven, not to do my will, but the will of him who sent me: certainly the other Faculty of the rational Soul, which is and is called the will, is expressed quite clearly.

It is added that the Body alone does not constitute a Man, but necessarily requires the presence of a Soul. Now, Christ is called Man in the Scriptures. Therefore. Furthermore, here has place that saying of Nazianzen, τὸ ἀπροσλήπτον ἀϑεράπευτον: ὁ δὲ ἥνωται τῷ θεῷ τῦτο καὶ σώζεται. Therefore, unless Christ assumed a true and rational Soul, together with a true body, certainly neither can our Soul hope for any salvation from the incarnation of the λόγος: which is absurd.

Nor is it worth even a farthing that some of the ancient heretics objected to that passage in John 1:14, The Word was made flesh, where the notation of Flesh, not of Soul, may be found. For the ambiguity of the word Flesh is known even to boys and beginners, which sometimes denotes only one part of man, namely the body, as Job 19:26, In my Flesh I shall see the Lord: Likewise Psalm 16:9, My flesh shall rest in hope. Sometimes, however, it signifies the affections, or inclinations, or depraved senses of our corrupt nature: as John 3:6, That which is born of the flesh is flesh. Matt. 16:17, Flesh and blood hath not revealed this unto thee. Sometimes it is taken synecdochically for the whole substance of man, consisting of body and soul, naturally united: as Romans 3:20, By the works of the Law shall no flesh be justified, that is, interpreting the Apostle, no man, Gal. 2:16. In which sense it is also taken in this place in John: The Word was made flesh: that is, the λόγος was made man. Whence the Son of GOD is called man: Rom. 5:15, 1 Tim. 2:5, There is one Mediator of GOD and men: The man Christ Jesus.

The third attribute, which our proposition declares concerning the assumed human nature, is ὁμουσία or consubstantiality with our human nature. For the flesh of Christ was neither created from nothing, nor formed from some celestial or sidereal matter, nor from a peculiar confluence of Elements: But it was formed, conceived, and assumed by the λόγος from the substance of the Virgin Mary, and in her very womb, by the power and operation of the Holy Spirit. That classic passage Heb. 2:14 proves this: Forasmuch as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same: and in the following verse 16, He took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham, verse 17. Whence he had to be made like UNTO US BRETHREN, where however that congenital stain of our nature, that is, sin, is always excepted: inasmuch as it does not constitute man, insofar as he is such: but is a property of the corruption of human nature. Therefore the flesh of Christ is like and clearly ὁμούσιος, consubstantial with us, but without sin Hebr. 4, 15.

This part of Christian doctrine has also suffered quite sharp contradiction, both from the ancient Valentinians, as well as the more recent Schwenkfeldians, both of whom contended that the flesh of Christ was simply ἐπꙋ́σιον [super-substantial] to our own: relying primarily on those Scriptures which partly claim that Christ descended from heaven, and partly expressly name him the Man from heaven, or the heavenly man: as John 3:13, The Son of man descended from heaven: John 6:51, I am the living bread, which descended from heaven, 1 Cor. 15:47, The first man is of the earth, earthy: The second man is from heaven, heavenly. But the matter is safe. For as regards the first two testimonies of the Scriptures, they are to be understood in a qualified sense: namely, with respect to the Unity of the Person of Christ, on account of which that which is proper to only one Nature is most truly stated of the whole person: as we shall show in the third chapter following, concerning the first kind of Communication of idioms.

Augustine himself also acknowledged the truth of this answer, in his book against Maximinus, Bishop of the Arians, chapter 24, saying: Nor let it disturb you how Christ, according to that which he is man, descended from heaven, since he was made Man from a mother who was on earth. For this was said on account of the Unity of the Person, since CHRIST is one person, GOD and Man. On account of which he also says: No one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. If, therefore, you attend to the distinction of the Substances; the Son of GOD descended from heaven: but the Son of Man was crucified. But if you attend to the unity of the person, both the Son of Man descended from heaven: and the Son of GOD was crucified. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. On account of this unity of the person, therefore, he not only said that the Son of Man descended from heaven: but he also said that he was in heaven, when he was speaking on earth.

Latin:

De Veritate Humanæ Naturæ quam λόγος affumsit.

PROPOSITIO I.

FIlius DEI, sive λόγος, in plenitudine temporis veram, integram, nobisque per omnia consubstantialem Naturam humanam, veris suis & Essentialibus proprietatibus præditam, æterno sibi fœdere univit, ac uniendo assumsit.

DE Unionis hypostaticæ duarum Naturarum in CHRISTO Naturâ & Qualitate, subsequenti Capite proximo, nobis futura Disputatio. Hoc verò loco, Natura Humana, in se & per se considerata, expendenda venit : idque propter varias hæreses & corruptelas, tùm Veteres, tùm recentiores.

Ex Veteribus olim Marcion blasphemabat, CHRISTUM non verum fuisse hominem: sed fictum & phantasticum habuisse corpus, quod è cælo, non ex Virginis Mariæ substantiâ sumserit: neque etiam consequenter reverà ipsum passum, crucifixum & mortuum esse, sed tantùm κατ' δόκησιν καὶ φαντασίαν, putative & per quandam illusionem. Quem furorem postea Manichæi ab inferis quasi revocarunt.

Hunc subsecutus Arius, Carnem Christi planè inanimatam πάντη ἄψυχον esse contendebat: ita ut Animæ vicem Divinitas suppleverit.

Successit Apollinaris, qui fingebat, Animam ἀλόγῳ in Incarnatione non esse assumptam. Sed mox quasi pœnitentia, ductus, lingvam & mentem correxisse videri volens, dicebat, Animam quidẽ assumptã, quæ tamen non haberet mentem: Sed DEUM λόγον esse pro mente in homine assumtum.

Neque tolerabiliorem hæresin ex Veteribus olim fovebant Valentiniani, qui licèt minimè negabant, Christo verum fuisse corpus, tamen contendebant, illud ratione stirpis, originis, & substantiæ planè nostris corporibus fuisse ἑτερούσιον: quippe cæleste & spirituale: neq, ex Maria, sed per Mariam illud esse natum: Propterea quod λόγος nihil quicquam acceperit de sancta Virgine: sed instar aquæ per rivum sive canalem, hoc est per Mariam cælesti suo corpore transierit.

Pertinent huc etiam Monothelitæ, qui unam tantum in Christo voluntatem & operationem divinam' nimirùm concedentes, unam itidem naturam tantùm concessisse statuendi sunt.

Porrò Eutyches contendebat, humanam Christi Naturam à Spiritu Sancto in utero Mariæ, formatam, statim post ipsum Unionis hypostaticæ factæ momentum à divinitate absorptam, & sic in nihilum redactam esse, ut sola divina natura in Christo superstes remanserit.

Superiori seculo proximo, vivente adhuc B. Luthero nostro, quidam Caspar Schwenckfeld, Nobilis Silesius, veteres & jam pridem damnatas hæreses ab orco quasi revocans, de humana Christi Natura ejusmodi τερατολογίας evomuit, quas percensere saltem exhorrescit animus: Inter reliquas autem non postremæ sunt subsequentes tres hypotheses.

Ab his & id genus alijs hæresibus divortium faciens Ecclesia nostra firmiter credit ac statuit, λόγον asfumsisfe, 1. Veram Naturam humanam, quæ nimirum non sit imaginaria, non spectro aut phantasmati similis sed in rei veritate, licet non in se, & per se, verùm in persona λόγα subsistat. Primum Ergò attributum, quod de asfumta humana natura, nostra propositio enunciat, est humanæ Naturæ VERITAS, quæ opponitur phantasiæ sive spectro. Confirmat autem hoc Attributum satis luculenter Servator, Luc. 24, 39. ubi à Spiritu sive spectro corpus suum discriminans, Palpate, inquit, & videte: Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere. Accedit, quòd Apostolus graviter attestatur, nos aliquando conformandos esse corpori Christi, Phil. 3, 21 Ubi sanè omnis spectri & Spiritus sive Phantasmatis conditio penitus expirat.

Neque vel tantillum roboris obtinet cavillum illud veterum Marcionitarum: In Veteri Testamento Filius DEI multoties apparuit non veritate carnis vestitus: sed forma duntaxat humana indutus. Ergò par erit ratio ejusdem apparitionis in Novo Testamento. Futilitas enim hujus collectionis multipliciter patet.

Nam 1. Ex particulari procedit argumentum. 2. Ex falso principio: quasi eadem sit ratio Veteris & Novi Testamenti. 3. Invertitur, per βίαιον: Ob hoc ipsum enim non in forma sive specie corporis, sed in & sub vero corpore humano Filium DEI apparere, vel, ut Apostolus loquitur, 1. Tim 3, 16. Ideò DEUM in carne manifestari oportuit quia hæc manifestatio non fuit Veteris, sed Novi Testamenti. Ratio connexi est hæc: In Veteri Testamento tempus fuit signorum, umbrarum & imaginum: In Novo autem Testamento venit plenitudo temporis, quæ non umbras ampliùs, sed ipsum corpus requirebat. Coloß. 2, 17. Hebræor. 10, 1. 4. Et postremò diversum evincit solennis illa descriptio, quæ de conceptione & Nativitate Christi, in sacris extat. Matth. 1, 18. Luc. 1, 27. 2, 6. & seqq.

Alterum attributum, quod de asfumta humanitate Christi, Propositio nostra enunciat, est INTEGRITAS: quæ sub se complectitur duas illas partes Essentiales sive susatıxàs: Corpus nimirùm atque animam: Quam utramque partem λόγον asfumsisfe, Orthodoxa credit ac confitetur Ecclesia. Prioris partis veritatem primû attributum expediet: Posterioris certitudinem confirmant perspicua Scripturarnm testimonia; Matth 20, 28. Venit Filius hominis dare animam suam. Matth. 26, 38. Tristis est anima mea ad mortem usq; Luc. 23, 46. Pater in manus tuas commendo Spiritum meum. Joh. 12, 27. Nunc anima mea turbata est. Quoad facultates Animæ, res itidem planè in Confesso est. Cùm enim Luc. 2, 53. Christus puerulus dicatur profecisse sapientia: utique ea notatur animæ facultas, quæ ad Mentem refertur & τό ήγεμονιxὸν est propria. Sic quando Servator inquit, Matth. 26, 39. Non quod ego volo, sed quod tu vis. Et Johann. 5, 30. Non quæro voluntatem meam, sed ejus, qui misit me, Patris: Et Joh. 6, 38. Descendit de cælo, non ut faciam voluntatem meam, sed ejus qui misit me: utique altera Animæ rationalis Facultas, quæ voluntas est ac dicitur, satis perspicuè exprimitur.

Accedit quod solum Corpus non constituit Hominem, sed Animæ præsentiam necessariò requirit. Jam verò Christus in Scripturis Homo nominatur. E. Porrò hîc locum habet illud Nazianzeni, τὸ ἀπροσλήπτον ἀϑεράπευτον: ὁ δὲ ἥνωται τῷ θεῷ τῦτο καὶ σώζεται. E. nisi veram & rationalem Animam, unà cùm vero corpore Christus assumserit, utique neq; Anima nostra ex incarnatione λόγε, quicquam salutis sperare potest: id quod absurdum.

Neque vel unius teruntij est, quòd veterum hæreticorum nonnulli objecerunt illud Johan. 1, 14. Verbum caro factum est, ubi Carnis non Animæ notatio inveniatur. Nota enim vel pueris & tyronibus est æquivocatio vocabuli Carnis, quæ interdum unam tantùm hominis partem, nempè corpus notat, ut Job. 19, 26. In Carne mea videbo Dominum: Item Psalm. 16, 9. Caro mea requiescet in spe. Interdum verò significat affectus, sive inclinationes aut sensus pravos, corruptæ nostræ naturæ: ut Joh. 3, 6. Quicquid natum est ex carne, caro est. Matth. 16, 17. Caro & sangvis non revelavit tibi hoc. Interdum συνεκδοχικῶς accipitur pro tota hominis substantiâ, constante ex corpore & anima, naturaliter unitis: ut Roman. 3, 20. Ex operibus Legis non justificabitur ulla caro, id est, interprete Apostolo, nullus homo, Gal. 2, 16. Quo sensu accipitur etiam hoc loco apud Johannem: Verbum caro factum est: hoc est, λόγος homo factus est. Unde Filius DEI homo appellatur: Rom. 5, 15. 1. Tim. 2, 5. Unus est Mediator DEI & hominum: Homo Jesus Christus.

Tertium attributum, quod de assumta humana natura, propositio nostra enunciat, est ὁμουσία sive consubstantialitas cum nostra natura humana. Neque enim caro Christi vel ex nihilo est creata, vel ex materia quadam cœlesti aut siderea, vel ex peculiari Elementorum confluxu condita: Sed ex substantiâ Mariæ Virginis, & in ipsius utero reverà, virtute & operatione Spiritus Sancti, formata, concepta, & à λέγῳ assumpta est. Evincit hoc classicus ille locus Heb. 2, 14. Quemadmodum pueri participes sunt carnis & sangvinis: ita ipse quoque consimiliter particeps factus est eorundem: & subsequente versu 16. Non Angelos assumsit, sed semen Abrahæ assumsit versu 17. Undè debuit NOBIS FRATRIBUS similis fieri, Ubi tamen Congenita illa Naturæ nostræ labes, hoc est, peccatum semper excipitur: quippè quod non Hominem, quatenus talis, constituit: Sed corruptionis Naturæ humanæ est proprium. Similis ergò & planè ὁμούσιος, consubstantialis nobis est caro Christi, sed absque peccato Hebr. 4, 15.

Passa est hæc quoque pars Doctrinæ Christianæ satis acrem contradictionem, tùm à Veteribus Valentinianis, tùm à recentioribus Schvvenckfeldianis, qui utrique carnem Christi nostræ simpliciter ἐπꙋ́σιον contenderunt: illis potissimùm freti Scripturis, quæ partim Christum de cælo descendisse perhibent, partim verò expressè Hominem de cælo, sive hominem cælestem nominant: ut Johan. 3, 13. Filius hominis descendit de Cælo: Johan. 6, 51. Ego sum panis vivus, qui de Cælo descendi, 1. Cor. 15, 47. Primus homo de terra, terrenus: Secundus homo de cælo, cælestis. Sed salva res est. Nam quoad duo priora Scripturarum testimonia, secundum quid ea sunt intelligenda: nempè respectu Unitatis Personæ Christi, ob quam de tota persona verissimè enunciatur id, quod unius tamen Naturæ duntaxat est proprium: uti capite subsequente tertio, de primo genere Communicationis idiomatum ostendemus.

Agnovit responsionis hujus veritatem ipse quoque Augustinus, libro contra Maximinum Arianorum Episcopum cap 24. inquiens: Nec moveat, quomodo Christus secundum id, quod homo est, descenderit de Cælo, cum de matre, quæ in terra erat, factus sit Homo. Hoc enim propter Unitatem Personæ dictum, quoniam una persona est CHRISTUS DEUS & Homo. Propter quod etiam inquit: Nemo ascendit in Cælum, nisi qui descendit de cælo, Filius Hominis, qui est in cælo. Si ergò attendas distinctionem Substantiarum; Filius DEI de cælo descendit: Filius verò Hominis crucifixus est. Verùm si unitatem personæ attendas, & Filius Hominis descendit de cælo: & Filius DEI est crucifixus. Si enim cognovissent, nunquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. Propter hanc ergò unitatem personæ, non tantùm Filium Hominis dixit descendisse de cælo: Sed etiam eum dixit esse in cælo, cum loqueretur in terra.


### Chapter I. On the Truth of the Human Nature which the Word (Λόγος) assumed Proposition I (continued)

And in Sermon 14 on the words of the Apostle: He was on earth, and he said that he was in heaven: And what is more, The Son of man in heaven, so that he might demonstrate one person in both natures. But who of us, who perceive little, or understand little, would not rather wish to distinguish thus: The Son of GOD in heaven, and the Son of Man on earth. But, lest we should divide in this way and by dividing in such a way introduce two persons: No one, he says, has ascended into heaven, but he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. Therefore the Son of Man descended from heaven: Was not the Son of Man made on earth? was not the Son of Man born of Mary? But O man, do not separate what I wish to join: It is little: Because he descended as the Son of man: For Christ descended: and the same is the Son of man, who is the Son of GOD: But also in Heaven, he who walks on earth. He was in heaven, because Christ is everywhere, and the same Christ is both the Son of GOD: and the Son of man: on account of the unity of the person, the Son of GOD is on earth: on account of the same Unity of the person, we have proved that the Son of Man is in Heaven, from these words of the Lord: The Son of Man, he says, who is in heaven.

In the third and final testimony, the error arises from a less suitable Latin version: For it is not in the Greek, The second Man from heaven, heavenly: but the words sound thus: δεύτερος ἄνθρωπῶς, ὁ κύριος ἐξ ἐρανᾶ: The second Man is the Lord from heaven. For although Christ is true Man from the virgin Mary: yet at the same time he is also the Lord from heaven, because he constitutes one person with the Son of GOD, that Lord of Lords: so that now not only the Son of GOD, but also the Son of Man, or the second man, truly is and is called the Lord from heaven, through the communication of idioms of the first Kind, concerning which more fully in its proper place.

The attribute of which, which our proposition states concerning the assumed human Nature of Christ, is the truth, integrity, and perfection of natural properties, which is indeed of the greatest importance to be correctly established in the Church. For the rule of our Blessed Luther is and remains true: If the properties are denied, the nature itself is denied. But the Properties of Human Nature are most correctly distinguished into Essential and Accidental. Essential are again subdivided into constitutive or συςατικὰς τῆς Φύσεως, as those without which human Nature cannot subsist even for a moment. Such are, to consist of a body and a rational soul, and the powers or faculties of this. And into Essential properties improperly so called, which are named by the Greeks ἰδιώματα τὰ περὶ τὴν Φύσιν, or παρεπόμενα τῇ Φύσει, that is, Accidents as it were inseparable, which follow the constitution of the Nature, or the Essence already constituted: Such are: To be circumscribed in a certain place, to be able to be seen from a certain distance, to be able to be touched, etc.

Accidental properties are those without which Human Nature indeed retains its species safe and intact: but without which, in this life at least, its Quality and Condition can hardly be correctly known. And these likewise are twofold: for they are either Natural Infirmities, which have followed the whole species of human Nature after the fall: such as, Mortality, passibility, hunger, thirst, weariness, sadness, weeping, and other infirmities of that kind. Or they are created gifts, or virtues and qualities, which are inherent in Human Nature, formally, habitually, subjectively, and successively grow until they attain the condition of a habit.

With these distinctions thus premised, it must also be answered distinctly when it is asked, Whether the λόγος assumed such a Nature as was endowed with each and all of these properties? For as regards the Essential constitutive [properties], which constitute the very species of human nature, we have already confirmed clearly and evidently in the preceding [sections] that the λόγος assumed a human nature that is true, integral, and ὁμούσιον [consubstantial] with us. From which it necessarily follows that he also assumed the essential properties of the same Nature, namely those which are properly required for the constitution of the whole. For which reason the heresy of the Monothelites was most correctly condemned, who wish there to be two wills in CHRIST, one human, the other divine: and they simply denied the two actions depending therefrom, contending that there is only one will in Christ: namely, the divine alone. By which course, indeed, denying the human will and its certain and peculiar operation, they must be judged to have denied the rational soul itself, and thus the more important Essential part, and that which constitutes Human Nature: according to that most true rule of Antiquity: Those whose operation is one and the same, their Nature and substance is also one.

But then, regarding the Essential properties improperly so called, or ἰδιώματα τῇ φύσει παρεπόμενα, we maintain that the λόγος also assumed those, but in such a way that this was not of necessity, but of most free will, as will be demonstrated shortly.

Thirdly, regarding the Accidental properties, and indeed the Natural Infirmities, we maintain this: Since the human nature of Christ is not only ἀναμάρτητος, devoid of all sin: but also personally united with the λόγος: it was certainly not subject to passions, nor to other infirmities, much less to death, by the condition of its own nature. Now, however, because the human race could not be redeemed by Christ from death and eternal damnation except through most bitter passions, infirmities, and finally death itself: therefore, in assuming human Nature, the λόγος also assumed those infirmities which drew their origin from sin: but he assumed them, not insofar as they have a respect to any guilt, but only insofar as they have the condition of punishment: nor did he assume these individually and universally, but only those which the work of redemption required to be assumed by him: and which detracted nothing from the dignity of Nature: as Lombard rightly wrote, lib. 3. dist. 15. lit. A. Scripture confirms this very thing throughout: but especially in the Old Testament, Isa. 53, 4. Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our sorrows: He was wounded for our sins, and bruised for our iniquities; In the New, however, the whole history of the life and Passion of CHRIST. Hence it is read that he truly hungered, Matt. 4, 2. thirsted, John 19, 28. was wearied, John 4, 6. wept three times, Luke 10, 41. John 11, 35. Heb. 5, 7. and underwent other infirmities of this kind: so that the opinion of the Manichaeans, who blasphemed that these things did not happen to CHRIST in reality, but were done only putatively and in appearance, ought to be called madness rather than heresy.

Regarding the Qualities or created gifts, which we likewise refer to Accidental properties: In the beginning, it is beyond controversy that the λόγος assumed a human Nature that was clearly ἀναμάρτητος, devoid of all sin or Original stain: and therefore not subject in itself to any guilt or corruption. The indication of which thing must be the least doubtful, the Formation and Conception of this human Nature, done by the Holy Spirit himself, in the womb of the Virgin, Luke 1, 35.

Then it is also certain that the λόγος assumed such a human Nature as truly grew in wisdom and Knowledge before GOD and men according to Qualities or habits, Luke 2, 53. Scholastics call these habitual gifts, or habitual Grace, which indeed has an analogy to the natures of other men: but meanwhile, by reason of excellence and dignity, it can rightly be called Supernatural, since it surpasses and transcends every other human, and indeed even Angelic Nature, in infinite ways.

Some add in this place another prerogative also, which accrued to the Human Nature of Christ, not indeed with respect to time, but in the order of Nature and our intellect, which they call the Grace of Union: Which is nothing other than that this human Nature is personally united with the λόγος: as will be said in the next following Chapter.

These things being thus dispatched, there remains that Disputation which is agitated today concerning those properties which we named ἰδιώματα παρεπόμενα τῇ φύσει, and especially concerning circumscription, or Physical locality: as concerning visibility and palpability.

For it is disputed at the beginning whether to be circumscribed by some place surrounding from without is an essential property, constituting the very τὸ εἶναι, of a true and natural human body. To which question, against the affirmative of the Calvinists, we answer simply in the Negative; relying on firm and immovable hypotheses, both Philosophical and Theological.

1. The Essence and Definition of a true and natural body is to consist of certain dimensions, that is, as the Philosopher explains, for magnitude to be long, broad, and deep: lib. 1. de caelo cap. 1. But to be circumscribed by a place surrounding from without, or, which comes to the same thing, to be in a Physical place, and to be contained by the same surrounding from without, is absolutely neither the Essence nor a property of a true body: But that happens to bodies only in this life on account of matter and passibility, or as the Philosopher speaks, lib. 2. de caelo cap. on account of θνητὴν ἀσθένειαν, on account of mortal infirmity. Whence the same Philosopher, lib. 4. Phys. cap. 1 & 5, expressly affirms that to be in a Physical place belongs only to a body that is αἰσθητῷ, sensible, and κινητῷ, mobile: that is, as he himself explains, lib. β. Metaph. cap. p. 4. To a body that is Φθαρτῷ, that is, perishable or corruptible: Which our Apostle in 1. 1 Cor. 15:44, he names σῶμα ψυχικὸν an animal body, which by the intervention of death is corrupted, and rises again, πνευματικὸν a spiritual one: as will be shown more fully presently. We conclude therefore by the force of this first hypothesis: 1. That our bodies in this life are always circumscribed in the very act by a certain place surrounding them from without: but that this does not belong to them by any essential constitutive property, but by an adherent, concreated imperfection and corruptibility. Which is the first point. Whence it is easy to gather how weak an argument is drawn from thence for the Locality of the body of Christ, no longer ψυχικῶς or φθαρτῶς, but πνευματικῶς and gloriously, nay, raised to the very throne of the Divine right hand.

Latin:

Et Serm. 14. de verbis Apostoli: In terra erat, & in cælo se esse dicebat: Et quod magis est, In Cælo Filium hominis, ut unam demonstraret in utraq; natura personam. Qui autem nostrûm, qui parùm advertimus, aut parùm sapimus, non potiùs ita vellet distingvere: Filius DEI in cælo, & Filius Hominis in terra. Sed, ne sic divideremus & ita dividendo duas personas induceremus: Nemo, inquit, ascendit in cælum, nisi qui de cælo descendit, Filius Hominis. Filius ergò Hominis descendit de cælo: Nonne Filius Hominis in terra factus est? nonne Filius Hominis ex Maria natus est? Sed ô homo, noli separare, quæ volo copulare: Parùm est: Quia Filium hominis descendit: Christus enim descendit: idemq́; Filius hominis, qui Filius est DEI: Sed & in Cælo, qui ambulat in terra. In cælo erat, quia ubiq; Christus, idemque Christus & Filius DEI: & Filius hominis: propter unitatem personæ, in terra est Filius DEI: propter eandem Unitatem personæ, esse probavimus in Cælo Filium Hominis, ex his Verbis Domini: Filius Hominis, inquit, qui est in cælo.

In tertio ac postremo testimonio error oritur ex minùs commoda versione Latina: Neque enim in Græco est, Secundus Homo de cælo, cælestis: sed sic sonant verba: δεύτερος ἄνθρωπῶς, ὁ κύριος ἐξ ἐρανᾶ: Secundus Homo est Dominus de Cælo. Etsi enim Christus Verus Homo est ex Maria virgine: simul tamen est etiam Dominus de cœlo, quia cum Filio DEI Domino illo Dominantium, unam personam constituit: ita ut jam non solus Filius DEI, sed & Filius Hominis, sive secundus homo, verè sit ac dicatur Dominus de cœlo, per communicationem idiomatum primi Generis, de qua suo loco fusiùs.

Quarum attributum, quod de assumta humana Natura Christi, propositio nostra enunciat, est proprietatum naturalium veritas, integritas & perfectio de qua sanè, ut rectè in Ecclesia constet, plurimum interest. Vera enim est & manet regula B. Lutheri nostri: Negatis proprietatibus, negantur natura ipsa. Rectissimè autem distingvuntur Proprietates Humanæ Naturæ in Essentiales & Accidentales. Essentiales rursus subdividuntur, in constitutivas sive συςατικὰς τῆς Φύσεως, uti sine quibus Natura humana ne ad momentum quidem subsistere potest. Quales sunt, Constare corpore & animâ rationali, & hujus potentiis sive facultatibus. Et in Essentiales impropriè sic dictas, quæ à Græcis nominantur ἰδιώματα τὰ περὶ τὴν Φύσιν, sive παρεπόμενα τῇ Φύσει, hoc est, Accidentia quasi inseparabilia, quæ Naturæ constitutionem, vel Essentiam jam constitutam consequuntur: Quales sunt: Certo quodam loco circumscribi, ex certa quadam distantia posse videri, posse palpari &c.

Accidentales proprietates sunt, sine quibus Humana quidem Natura suam speciem salvam ac integram retinet: sed sine quibus, hac quidem in vitâ vix ejus Qualitas & Conditio rectè cognosci queat. Et hæ itidem sunt duplices: vel enim sunt Naturales Infirmitates, quæ totam speciem humanæ Naturæ post lapsum sunt insecutæ: quales sunt, Mortalitas, passibilitas, fames, sitis, lassitudo, tristitia, fletus, & id genus infirmitates aliæ. Vel sunt dona creata, sive virtutes & qualitates, quæ Humanæ Naturæ insunt, formaliter, habitualiter, subjectivè & successivè tamdiu crescunt, donec habitus conditionem sortiantur.

His distinctionibus ita præmissis, distinctè etiam respondendum fuerit, quando quæritur, An λόγος ejusmodi Naturam assumserit, quæ singulis & universis istis proprietatibus fuerit prædita? Nam quoad Essentialis συςατικὰς, quæ ipsam Naturæ humanæ speciem constituunt, jam in præcedentibus satis liquidò & evidenter confirmavimus, λόγον assumsisse Naturam humanam veram, integram, nobisque ὁμούσιον. Undè necessariò consequitur, ipsum assumsisse etiam proprietates ejusdem Naturæ essentiales, eas nìmirùm quæ ad constitutionem totius propriè requiruntur. Quam ob causam rectissimè damnata fuit hæresis Monotheletarum, qui duas in CHRISTO esse voluntates, humanam unam, alteram divinam : duasque indè dependentes actiones, simpliciter negarunt, contendentes unam duntaxat in Christo esse voluntatem : nempè solam divinam. Quo sanè pacto, negantes voluntatem humanam, ejusdemque certam ac peculiarem operationem, ipsam quoque animam rationalem, & sic potiorem partem Essentialem, & Humanæ Naturæ constitutivam negasse, censendi sunt : secundum verissimam illam Antiquitatis regulam : Quorum una est & eadem operatio, eorum una est etiam Natura & substantia.

Deindè verò, Quoad proprietates Essentiales impropriè sic dictas, sive ἰδιώματα τῇ φύσει παρεπόμενα, statuimus, λόγον illas quoque assumpsisse, sed ita, ut non necessitatis, sed liberrimæ voluntatis istud fuerit, uti paulò demonstrabitur.

Tertiò, Quoad proprietates Accidentales, & quidem Naturales Infirmitates, sic statuimus : Cum humana Christi natura, non modò sit ἀναμάρτητος, expers omnis peccati : sed & cum λόγῳ personaliter unita : utique illam neque passionibus, neque infirmitatibus aliis, nedum morti, ex naturæ suæ conditione fuisse obnoxia. Jam verò, Quia Genus humanum per Christum à morte & æternâ damnatione, non nisi per acerbissimas passiones, infirmitates, & denique mortem ipsam redimi poterat : ideò λόγον assumendo Naturam humanam assumpsisse etiam infirmitates istas, quæ ex peccato Originem suam traxerunt : sed assumpsisse eas, non quatenus culpæ alicujus respectum, sed duntaxat quatenus pœnæ conditionem habent : neque etiam istas singulas & universas, sed eas tantummodò, quas ab ipso assumi, opus redemtionis requirebat : quæque dignitati Naturæ nihil derogabant : uti rectè scripsit Lombardus, lib. 3. dist. 15. lit. A. Confirmat autem hoc ipsum Scriptura passim : Cumprimis verò in Veteri Testamento Jes. 53, 4. Verè languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse sustinuit : Ipse vulneratus est propter peccata nostra, & attritus propter scelera nostra; In Novo autem tota historia vitæ & Passionis CHRISTI. Hinc ipsum verè esurijsse, Matth. 4, 2. sitijsse, Johan. 19, 28. defatigatum fuisse, Joh. 4, 6. ter flevisse Luc. 10, 41. Joh. 11, 35 Heb. 5, 7. & hujus generis infirmitates alias subiisse legitur : ita ut furor rectiùs, quàm hæresis dici debeat sententia illa Manichæorum, qui non reverâ isthæc CHRISTO obtigisse, sed putativè tantùm & simulatè sic gesta esse blasphemabant.

Quoad Qualitates sive dona creata, quæ itidem ad Accidentales proprietates referimus : Initio extra controversiam est, λόγου assumpsisse Naturam humanam planè ἀναμάρτητον, expertem omnis peccati sive labis Originalis: ac proindè nulli vel reatui, vel corruptioni in se obnoxiam. Cujus rei indicium minimè dubium esse debet, Formatio & Conceptio Naturæ hujus humanæ, per ipsum Spiritum Sanctum, in utero Virginis, facta Luc. 1, 35.

Deindè constat & illud, λόγον assumsisse talem Naturam humanam, quæ secundum Qualitates sive habitus verè creverit sapientiâ & Scientiâ coram DEO & hominibus Luc. 2, 53. Scholastici hæc dona vocant habitualia, sive Gratiam habitualem, quæ analogiam quidem habeat ad reliquorum hominum naturas: sed interim ratione excellentiæ & dignitatis rectè dici queat Supernaturalis, quippe omnem aliam humanam, quin imò Angelicam etiam Naturam, infinitis modis superans & transcendens.

Adjiciunt nonnulli hoc loco aliam quoque prærogativam, quæ Humanæ Naturæ Christi non quidem temporis respectu, sed ordine Naturæ & intellectus nostri, accesserit, quamque vocant Gratiam Unionis: Quæ nulla est alia, quàm quod hæc Natura humana cum λόγῳ personaliter est unita: uti Capite subsequente proximo dicetur.

His ita expeditis superest Disputatio illa, quæ de proprietatibus illis, quas nominavimus ἰδιώματα παρεπόμενα τῇ φύσει, & cumprimis de circumscriptione, sive de localitate Physica: ut de visibilitate, ac palpabilitate hodiè agitatur.

Initiò enim controvertitur, an certò quopiam forinsecùs ambiente loco circumscriptum esse, sit proprietas essentialis, constituens, ipsum τὸ εἶναι, veri & naturalis corporis humani. Ad quod ζήτημα adversus Calvinianorum affirmativam, simpliciter Negatè respondemus; firmis & immotis freti hypothesibus, tùm Philosophicis, tùm Theologicis.

1. Corporis veri ac naturalis Essentia & Definitio est, certis constare dimensionibus, hoc est ut Philosophus explicat, magnitudinem esse longã, latam, profundam: lib. 1. de cælo cap. 1. At loco forinsecùs ambiente circumscribi, vel, quod eodem recidit, Esse in loco Physico, ab eodemque forinsecus ambiente contineri, absolutè corporis veri neque Essentia, neque proprietas est: Sed accidit illud tantùm hac in vita corporibus propter materiam & passibilitatem, vel ut Philosophus loquitur, lib. 2. de cælo cap. propter θνητὴν ἀσθένειαν, propter mortalem imbecillitatem. Undè idem Philosophus lib. 4. Phys. 1. cap. 1 & 5. disertè affirmat, In loco Physico esse, competere tantùm corpori αἰσθητῷ sensili, & κινητῷ mobili: hoc est, ut ipsemet explicat lib. β. Metaph. cap. p. 4. Corpori Φθαρτῷ, hoc est, caduco sive corruptibili: Quod Apostolus noster in 1. Cor. 15, 44. nominat σῶμα ψυχικὸν corpus animale, quod mortis interventu corrumpitur, & resurgit, πνευματικὸν Spirituale: uti mox fusiùs ostendetur. Colligimus proindè vi primæ hujus hypothesews. 1. Corpora nostra hac in vitâ circumscribi semper ipso actu, Loco quodam forinsecùs ambiente: Sed hoc illis non ex proprietate constitutiva Essentiali: Sed ex adhærente concreata imperfectione & corruptibilitate competere. Quod unum est. Undè quàm infirmum indè argumentum ad Localitatem corporis Christi non ψυχικῶς ampliùs aut φθαρτῶς, sed πνευματικῶς & gloriosi, imò in ipsum thronum dexteræ Divinæ evecti, petatur, promptum est colligere.


### Chapter I. On the Truth of the Human Nature which the Word (Λόγος) assumed Proposition I (continued)

Thence from this first hypothesis it is clear, 1. That a body can be said to be circumscribed in two ways: either by a place surrounding it from without: or by the proper limits of its own finite nature: the former is accidental, and to be removed in the Resurrection of the dead: but the latter is Essential and perpetual: Since even in the Resurrection itself and eternal life, glorified bodies will not be infinite, but finite, and circumscribed by the limits of their own Essence. Therefore, in this latter sense, we willingly concede to the Calvinists that any true and natural body, nay, even the body of Christ itself, is always actually circumscribed: but in the former sense we simply deny it. Moreover, whether that circumscription, which depends upon the finitude of the Essence, removes the personal omnipresence of the Body of Christ, we shall see below in its own place, where we are to have a discussion on this matter expressly.

Thirdly, this first hypothesis also demonstrates that a distinction between Physical or corruptible bodies and glorified bodies is not to be established with respect to essential συστατικῶν properties, which as to essence always remain the same: but only with respect to those properties which in this life follow the infirmity of our nature: and are called ἰδιώματα παρεπόμενα τῇ φύσει: which do not fall upon glorified bodies. Concerning which matter, let it be permitted to hear the most acute Philosopher Jacob Scheckius in his booklet on the Person of Christ, page 52, distinguishing thus.

Since the human Nature of Christ is somewhere, it certainly exists either within or outside those corporeal heavens. We speak, however, of that glorious body absolutely, which itself also is devoid of all physical accidents, which happen to things by reason of matter and passibility: except for Quantity, which nevertheless is not physical, fencing and excluding other bodies, with which (Quantity) a glorious body must necessarily be endowed: since if it were devoid of Quantity, it would not be a body, but some incorporeal thing and a Spirit. By this reason, therefore, as a body it does not have in itself any physical spiritual thing. But yet that body will not be entirely a Spirit. But to be in a place, or to be moved from place to place by some motion, happens to bodies on account of matter and nature. Likewise, that they mutually exclude one another, and are ἀντίτυπα; that they are circumscribed by Physical places and times, of which there is nothing in the glorious and Spiritual bodies of the blessed, which like some light through a διαφανὲς, that is, a pellucid body, penetrate in a moment in the twinkling of an eye, most closely imitating the power and substance of the soul. Furthermore, these celestial things, by which these Elements are comprehended, and those which are composed of Physical Elements, are bodies, by reason of motion in a place, since each sphere is rotated with its own place and its own certain period of time. But outside those heavens there is no Physical body: Wherefore there will not be a place or time either: For so the Philosopher in book 1 of On the Heavens, chapter 9. His words are these: Δῆλον ἔν, ὅτι ὅτε τόπος, ἐδὲ κενὸν, ἐδὲ χρόνος ἐςιν ἔξω τᾶ ἐρανᾶ. Διόπερ, ἔτ' ἐν τόπω τακεῖ πέφυκεν, ὅτε χρόνος ἀυτὰ ποιεῖ γηράσκειν, ἐδ' ἐςὶν ἐδενὸς μεταβολὴ τῶν ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐξωτάτω φορὰν τεταγμένων, ἀλλ' ἀναλλοίωτα, καὶ ἀπαθῆ τὴν ἀρίσην ἔχοντα ζωὴν, καὶ τὴν ἀυταρκετάτην, διατελεῖ τὸν ἅπαντα αἰῶνα: that is, It is manifest that outside this heaven, there is neither Place, nor vacuum, nor Time. Wherefore those things which are outside the heaven are not of such a kind that they are either in a place, or grow old in time, nor is there any change of them, which are placed outside the supreme heaven, since they are unalterable, and without affection lead the best and most self-sufficient life forever. It is therefore consistent, if Physical bodies are of themselves somewhere, and are arranged by a certain order of places and times, that as ὀυσίαι devoid of matter and Physical nature, they should not of themselves be in a place somewhere, nor in time: But of themselves be without a place somewhere, where there is neither a Physical place nor time, that is, outside the complex of these natural and celestial bodies, which are contained by motions, places, and times. Thus far Scheckius, to whose decision we subscribe in all things, and in the fourth place we gather from it that the proposition of the Calvinists, which they repeatedly chant as universally true, is entirely false: namely, That every Body is in a Place.

Therefore, for the Confirmation of our opinion, and indeed in the place of the second hypothesis, we posit this Proposition: Not every true Body is actually in a Physical place. The truth of which proposition is confirmed, in the beginning, by those things which have just now been said concerning bodies partly established outside the supreme heaven, and partly freed from the mortality of this life.

Then, however, because the Philosopher expressly confesses that τὸ πᾶν or the universe, which is certainly a true Body, is nevertheless not in a place, book 4 Physics, chapter 5, text 5. Nay, he even expressly affirms that only the τὸ αἰσθητὸν and κινητὸν σῶμα, the Sensible and mobile body, is in a place, book 4 Physics, chapter 1, text 6 and chapter 5, text 47. Which body, insofar as it is γεννητὸν, is also Φθαρτὸν, caducous and corruptible, as the same Philosopher teaches in book 2 Metaphysics, chapter 4, text 12. Now because glorified bodies, as all the sounder Philosophers attest, are no longer κινητὰ, not αἰσθητὰ, not γεννητὰ: but πνευματικὰ, it is certainly clearer than the midday light, from the doctrine of the Philosophers also, that glorified bodies are not actually in a Physical place. It is added, moreover, that glorified bodies are eternal. Now indeed τὰ ἀεὶ ὄντα ᾗ ἀεὶ ὄντα ἐκ ἐςὶν ἐν χρόνῳ : ὀ γὰρ περιέχεται τῷ χρόνῳ, ἐδὲ μετρεῖται τὸ εἶναι ἀυτῶν ὑπὸ τῶ χρόνω.

Eternal things are not in time, for the very reason that they are eternal: neither does time comprehend them, nor does time measure their Essence, lib. 4. Phys. cap. 12. T. 117. Now, from the negation of Time, it is most correctly inferred to the negation of locality, even from the fact that, by the consent of all philosophers again, Time only happens to natural things on account of motion, which is an inseparable companion of locality. Therefore, once Time is denied, the very Place and physical motion are most truly denied as well. However, it deserves more accurate observation that this second Hypothesis of ours does not simply deny that every body is in a place: but it expressly expresses the Act of Locality, in this sense, That not every true body is in a place by the very act. Therefore, we by no means deny the Power: namely, that such a body, which by itself and from the condition of its Essence is not in a place, can, I say, when it wills, be and appear in a certain place. Which we by no means deny even regarding the body of Christ. Wherefore, if the Calvinists understood that proposition of theirs, Every body is in a place, while maintaining the distinction between power and act: that is, if they confessed without sophistry that it is not required for the truth of a body that it always be in a place by act: but that it is sufficient that it be so constituted by power or δυνάμει that it can be in a place: then we would willingly and readily embrace their proposition: and from that very thing we would seek the refutation of all those arguments by which they have hitherto contended that every body must necessarily be in a place by act: and cannot be nonlocal, or outside of a place, by act. Likewise, that the circumference of a containing place is a necessary correlate of the body of CHRIST, as Pezelius wrote quite ignorantly on page 36 of his Demonstration against D. Hunnius. Likewise, that being contained in a place by act regards the specific form of the body itself, namely the dimensions themselves: as Pezelius again judged quite ἀφιλοσόφως on page 22. Since it can be most well-known even to beginners in philosophy: that Location or Locability is said and denominated not from dimensions but from place: and therefore when some body is not enclosed by an externally surrounding place: it cannot even be called Located anymore. For although such a body, which is not in a place by act, retains its dimensions safe and entire: yet in respect of these it can and should be called a Quantum, not located. And again, Because a Located thing is not understood except by a certain σχέσει or relation to a Place properly so called: it follows necessarily that this relation expires and ceases as soon as the place itself (the other correlate, that is) is lacking.

Moreover, it is further asked in this place: Whether it is not proper and of the Essence of a true human body that it be SOMEWHERE. Which question, in order to be defined more correctly, must first be carefully weighed regarding the ambiguity of the phrase, To be SOMEWHERE.
