For either to be somewhere sounds the same as ἐν πᢢ εἶναι, to be in some where: and in this sense it belongs not only to all corporeal creatures, but also to Spirits, that they be ἐν πᢢ, that is, somewhere. Hence the Philosopher, lib. 4. Phys. c. 1, T. 1, says: τὰ γὰ ὄντα πάντες ὑπολαμβάνήσιν εἶναι πᾶ: τὸ δὲ μὴ ὄν, ἐδαμῦ εἶναι: all, he says, posit that Beings are somewhere: but that non-Beings are nowhere. Hence David also, speaking words about God, Psalm 139:6, says: πᾶ Where or Whither shall I flee from thy Spirit? Or, to be somewhere signifies ἐν τόπῳ εἶναι, To be in a Place: and then it is false that it is proper to every creature to be in a place. For no one will deny that the soul is a creature: but the Philosopher most correctly denies that it is in a Place, l. 1. de anima, cap. 3. T. 38. & 39., arguing against those who thought that the Soul is that which is endowed with the greatest power of moving: using this argument: Every motion is in a place: The Soul, which is the form of the body, is not in a place. Therefore its Essence is not to move itself: and, there is no motion of the Soul. Thus, Angels are beyond all controversy creatures: yet no one, either of the philosophers or theologians, would affirm that they are in a place. Therefore, a body can be somewhere, even if it is not in a place: that is, to speak philosophically: When we deny that a body is in a place, we do not take away from it an Essential property. But we deny that the body is Mobile. Nor is that objection worth even a penny: Every finite thing is in a place: Every body is finite. Therefore, Every body is in a place. For the Major proposition is true neither Theologically nor Philosophically. Not Theologically: Because it has already been proven above that glorious bodies will indeed be finite, that is, circumscribed by the limits of their Essence: but they will by no means be in a physical place: since they are πνευματικὰ and freed from the infirmities of this age. But the major proposition is Philosophically false, Because according to Aristotle that body alone is in a place which περιέχεῒαι, is contained, lib. 4. Phys. c. 5. T. 43. Likewise that which is touched by another, τὸ ἁπτόμενον T. 46. Now, it is one thing to be ἅπλεσθαι Touched, and another to be πεπέρανθαι Finite: so that it happens only by accident to a Finite thing that it is touched. Whence, from the opinion of the Philosopher, it is most correctly concluded that some body can be finite, which nevertheless is contained by no place: But enough about Locality: Now order demands that we treat of Visibility.

Latin:

Deindè ex prima hac hypothesi patet, 1. Duobus modis corpus dici posse circumscribi: vel loco forinfecùs ambiente: vel propriis naturæ suæ finitæ terminis: illam accidentariam, & in Resurrectione mortuorum tollendam: Hanc verò Essentialem & perpetuam esse: Siquidem in ipsa etiam Resurrectione & vita æterna, corpora glorificata non erunt infinita, sed finita, & Essentiæ suæ finibus circumscripta. Proindè posteriore hoc sensu corpus quodlibet verum ac naturale, quin ipsum quoque Christi corpus actu semper circumscribi, Calvinianis ultrò concedimus: priore verò sensu simpliciter negamus. Cæterûm, nùm circumscriptio illa, quæ ab Essentiæ finitate dependet, tollat personalem Corporis Christi omnipræsentiam, infra suo loco videbimus, ubi hac de re ex professo futura nobis est disputatio.

Tertiò & illud prima hæc hypothesis demonstrat, Discrimen inter corpora Physica sive corruptibilia, & inter corpora glorificata non constituendum esse respectu proprietatum essentialium συσατικῶν, quæ quoad essentiam semper manent eadem: sed duntaxat respectu earum proprietatum, quæ hac in vita naturæ nostræ infirmitatem consequuntur: & dicuntur ἰδιώματα παρεπόμενα τῇ φύσει: quæ in corpora glorificata non cadunt. Qua de re liceat audire acutissimum Philosophum Jacobum Scheckium in libello de Persona Christi pag. 52. sic differentem.

Quoniam Natura humana Christi est alicubi, utique vel intra vel extra cœlos illos corporeos cōfistet. Loquimur autem de glorioso illo corpore absolutè, quod ipsum quoque expers sit omniũ accidentium physicorum, quæ rebus causa materia & patibilitatis accidunt: exceptâ Quantitate, quæ tamē physica non sit, arcēs & excludes alia corpora, quâ(Quātitate) omninò præditum sit oportet etiam gloriosum corpus: siquidem expers Quantitatis ἀοία, non corpus, sed incorporeum quiddam & Spiritus existāt. Hac igitur ratione, quà corpus in se non habet πᾷν Physica spiritale quoddam. Sed tamen non planè Spiritus erit corpus illud. Esse autem in loco, aut motu quodam transferri de loco in locum, corporibus accidit propter materiam & naturam. Item, quod mutuò sese excludant, & sunt ἀντίτυπα; quod locis Physicis & temporibus sunt circumscripta, quorum nihil est in gloriosis beatorum, & Spiritalibus corporibus quæ tanquam lumen quoddam per διαφανὲς, hoc est pellucidum corpus, momento in ictu oculi penetrant, animæ vim & substantiam proximè imitantia. Porrò cælestia hæc, quibus comprehendŭtur Elemẽta hæc, & cōcreta ex Elemẽtis Physica sunt corpora, ratione motus in loco, cũ suo loco & sua quadā tēporis periodo quilibet orbis circumrotetur. Verùm extra cælos illos non est Physicum aliquod corpus: Quare nec locus etiam erit aut tempus: Sic enim Philosophus lib.1.de cælo cap.9. Verba ejus hæc sunt : Δῆλον ἔν, ὅτι ὅτε τόπος, ἐδὲ κενὸν, ἐδὲ χρόνος ἐςιν ἔξω τᾶ ἐρανᾶ. Διόπερ, ἔτ' ἐν τόπω τακεῖ πέφυκεν, ὅτε χρόνος ἀυτὰ ποιεῖ γηράσκειν, ἐδ' ἐςὶν ἐδενὸς μεταβολὴ τῶν ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐξωτάτω φορὰν τεταγμένων, ἀλλ' ἀναλλοίωτα, καὶ ἀπαθῆ τὴν ἀρίσην ἔχοντα ζωὴν, καὶ τὴν ἀυταρκετάτην, διατελεῖ τὸν ἅπαντα αἰῶνα: id est, Manifestum est, quod extra hoc cælum, neque fit Locus,neque vacuum, neque Tempus. Quapropter quæ sunt extra cælum, non sunt hujusmodi, ut vel in loco sint, aut in tempore consenescant, neque eorum ulla est mutatio, qua scilicet extra cælum supremū sunt collocata,cùm sint inalterabilia, & absq; affectione optimam, ac seipsâ sufficientissimam vitam in perpetuum agant. Consentaneum itaque est, si corpora Physica per se sunt alicubi, & τάξει quadâ locorum & temporum digeruntur, ut ὀυσίαι materiæ & Physicæ naturæ expertes, per se, neque sint in loco alicubi, neq; in tempore: Sed per se sint fine loco alicubi,ubi neq; locus sit Physicus,neque tempus,id est, extra complexum horum naturalium & cælestium corporum,quæ motibus, locis & temporibus continentur. Hactenus Scheckius, cujus decisioni nos per omnia subscribim9,&quarto loco ex ea colligimus falsam omninò esse propositionem Calvinianorum, quam tanquàm universaliter veram subindè occinunt : nempè, Omne Corpus esse in Loco.

Proindè pro Confirmatione nostræ sententiæ,& quidem secundæ hypothesews loco, hanc Propositionem ponimus: Non omne verum Corpus actu est in loco Physico. Cujus propositionis veritatem confirmant, initiò ea, quæ de corporibus partim extra supremum cælum constitutis, partim verò à vitæ hujus mortalitate liberatis, jam modò sunt dicta.

Deindè verò, quod Philosophus disertè fatetur, τὸ πᾶν sive universum, quod utique Corpus verum est, in loco tamen non esse, lib.4.Φυσ.c.5.T.5. Quin & illud expressè affirmat, τὸ αἰσθητὸν tantùm & κινητὸν σῶμα, Sensile tantùm & mobile corpus esse in loco, lib.4 Physic.c.1.T.6 & cap.5.T.47. Quod corpus quatenus γεννητὸν generabile est, etiam Φθαρτὸν caducum & corruptibile est, uti idem Philosophus docet lib. β. Metaph.cap.4. T. 12. Jam quia corpora glorificata attestantibus omnibus sanioribus Philosophis non ampliùs sint κινητὰ, non αἰσθητὰ, non γεννητὰ : sed πνευματικὰ, certè luce meridiana clarius, ex Philosophorum etiam doctrina liquet, corpora gloriosa actu non esse in loco Physico. Accedit insuper, quòd corpora gloriosa sunt æterna. Jam verò τὰ ἀεὶ ὄντα ᾗ ἀεὶ ὄντα ἐκ ἐςὶν ἐν χρόνῳ : ὀ γὰρ περιέχεται τῷ χρόνῳ, ἐδὲ μετρεῖται τὸ εἶναι ἀυτῶν ὑπὸ τῶ χρόνω.

Res æternæ non sunt in tempore, hoc ipso quòd æternæ sunt : neque eas comprehendit tempus, neque eorum Essentiam meritur tempus lib. 4. Phys. cap. 12. T. 117. Jam verò ex negatione Temporis, ad negationem localitatis rectissimè colligi, vel indè patet, quòd omnium rursus Philosophorum consensu, Tempus rebus naturalibus propter motum, qui localitatis individuus est comes, tantùm accidit. Proindè negato Tempore, negatur verissimè ipse etiam Locus & motus Physicus. Cæterùm observationem accuratiorem meretur, quòd secunda hæc nostra Hypothesis non simpliciter negat, omne corpus esse in loco: sed disertè Localitatis Actum exprimit, hoc sensu, Quòd non omne verum corpus, ipso actu sit in loco. Proindè minimè omniù negamus Potentiam : nempè posse etiam tale corpus, quod per se, & ex suæ Essentiæ conditione non est in loco, posse, inqua, quando velit, esse & apparere in certo loco. Quod ipsum de Christi etiam corpore minimè diffitemur. Quare si Calviniani propositionem illam suam, Omne corpus est in loco, intelligerent, Servatâ distinctione potentiæ & actus: hoc est, si sine Sophistica faterentur, non requiri ad veritatem corporis, ut semper actu sit in loco: sed satis esse, ut potentia seu δυνάμει sic comparatum sit, ut in loco esse possit: tùm nos propositionem ipsorum libenter, & ultrò amplecteremur: & vel indè peteremus refutationem omnium eorum argumentorum, quibus hactenus contenderunt, Omne corpus necessariò esse in loco actu: neque posse actu esse illocale, sive extra locum. Item loci continentis ambitum esse necessarium correlatum corporis CHRISTI, uti Pezeli9 inscitè admodum scriptitavit pag. 36. Demonstrationis contra D. Hunnium. Item actu loco contineri, respicere ipsam formam specificam corporis, nempè ipsas dimensiones : uti rursum ἀφιλοσόφως planè censuit Pezelius, pag. 22. Cùm vel tyronibus Philosophiæ possit esse notissimum : Locationem vel Locabilitatem dici & denominari non à dimensionibus sed à loco: ac proindè quando corpus aliquod à loco extrinsecus ambiente non clauditur : illud ne quidem Locatum ampliùs dici posse. Etsi enim tale corpus, quod actu in loco non est, retinet dimensiones suas salvas & integras: tamen harum respectu non locatum, sed Quantum dici potest & debet. Et rursus, Quia Locatum non nisi σχέσει sive relatione quadam ad Locum propriè sic dictum, intelligitur: consequitur necessariò, statim relationem hanc expirare & definere, quàm primùm locus ipse (alterum videlicet correllatum) deficit.

Cæterùm hoc loco porrò quæritur : An non proprium & de Essentia veri corporis humani sit, ut sit ALICUBI. Quæ quæstio, ut rectiùs definiatur, initiò probè expendenda venit, æquivocatio phrasews, ALICUBI esse. Vel enim Alicubi esse idem sonat, atque ἐν πᢢ εἶναι, in aliquo ubi esse: & hoc sensu non modò omnibus creaturis corporeis, verùm etiam Spiritibus competit, ut sint ἐν πᢢ, hoc est, alicubi. Hinc Philosophus lib. 4. Phys. c. 1, T. 1, τὰ γὰ ὄντα πάντες ὑπολαμβάνήσιν εἶναι πᾶ: τὸ δὲ μὴ ὄν, ἐδαμῦ εἶναι: omnes, inquit,statuunt, Entia esse alicubi: non Entia verò, nullibi esse. Hinc David etiam de Deo verba faciens, Psal. 139, 6. dicit: πᾶ Ubi vel Quô fugiam à Spiritu tuo? Vel, Alicubi esse, significat ἐν τόπῳ εἶναι, In Loco esse: & tùm falsum est, quòd omnis creaturæ proprium sit, in loco esse. Animam enim creaturam esse nemo negabit: at eam in Loco esse, rectissimè negat Philosophus l. 1. de anima, cap. 3. T. 38. & 39. disputans contra eos, qui existimarunt, Animam id potissimùm esse, quod maxima vi movendi sit præditum: hoc usus argumento: Omnis motus est in loco: Anima, quæ est formarei, non est in loco. Ergò Essentia ejus non est seipsum movere: &, Animæ nullus est motꝰ. Sic Angeli extra omnem controversiam sunt creaturæ: nemo tamen vel Philosophorum vel Theologorum in loco eos esse, affirmaverit. Proindè corpus alicubi esse potest, licet non sit in loco: hoc est, ut Philosophicè loquamur: Quando corpus in loco esse inficiamur, non proprietatem Essentialem ei adimimus. Sed corpus Mobile esse negamus. Neque vel unius teruntij est ἔιςασις illa, Omne finitum est in loco: Omne corpus est finitum. Ergò, Omne corpus est in loco. Nam Major propositio, neque Theologicè, neque Philosophicè vera est. Theologicè non: Quia jam supra probatum, corpora gloriosa futura quidem finita, hoc est, Essentiæ suæ terminis circumscripta: In loco autem physico minimè futura: quippè πνευματικὰ & ab infirmitatibꝰ hujus seculi liberata. Philosophicè verò falsa est major propositio, Quia secundum Aristotelem illud tantùm corpus est in loco, quod περιέχεῒαι, continetur, lib. 4. Phys. c. 5. T. 43. Item quod ab alio tangitur, τὸ ἁπτόμενον T. 46. Jam verò aliud est ἅπλεσθαι Tangi, & aliud πεπέρανθαι Finitum esse: ità ut per accidens tantùm obtingat πεπερασμένῳ Finito, ut tangatur. Undè ex Philosophi sententia rectissimè concluditur, Finitum posse esse corpus aliquod, quod tamen nullo contineatur loco: Sed de Localitate satis: Nunc de Visibilitate ut agamus, ordo flagitat.


### Chapter I. On the Truth of the Human Nature which the Word (Λόγος) assumed: On Visibility

It is also asked today concerning Visibility, whether it is an Essential property of a True Human body, that it always be visible by act, that is, that it can always be seen from a certain just distance? The Calvinists say yes: we deny it. But so that this Negative of ours may be better understood: two distinctions are especially to be observed, of which the former regards the Subject, the latter the predicate of the proposed Question.

For at the beginning a distinction must be made between a physical and corruptible body (which the Apostle calls ψυχικὸν animal, Φθαρτὸν corruptible, ἄτιμον ignoble, and ἀσθενὲς infirm) and a glorious body, called by the Apostle πνευματικὸν spiritual, ἄφθαρτον incorruptible, τίμιον glorious, δυνατὸν powerful: 1 Cor. 15:43 and 44.

That physical bodies, on account of their inherent and concreated imperfection, are always actually visible at a due distance, none of us has ever denied: But that glorified bodies are subject to the same infirmity, hardly anyone would affirm, for those reasons which we shall soon explain. Furthermore, as regards physical bodies themselves, we do not concede that this is a proper συστατικὸν (constitutive element) of the human body, that it is always actually seen by all to whom it is present. For this visibility does not enter into the definition of man, which is evident from that change which, while the substance remains the same, will befall those same bodies by reason of qualities only, so that they will be entirely free and immune from the infirmities to which they were subject in this life, both by reason of locality and with respect to visibility, and likewise by reason of food and drink: for they are endowed with spiritual gifts and properties, like unto the angelic spirits as ἰσάγγελα (equal to angels), in all those things which are not destructive of nature, that is, which do not overturn their substance. Therefore, just as glorious and πνευματικὰ (spiritual) bodies have no need of any bodily or physical place by which they might be supported, as they will be more subtle than any element: so neither will they have need to be always actually visible, that is, always seen from a due distance.

Furthermore, this very thing is evident from the example of those saints who, when Christ rose from the dead, came out of the tombs and appeared to many: Matt. 27:53. Where the Greek word ἐνεφανίσθησαν πολλοῖς (they appeared to many) deserves note, which does not signify, as Pezelius interprets, that those bodies of the saints were seen by all the citizens of Jerusalem whom they happened to meet: But it signifies that those bodies of the saints presented themselves to be seen by many, namely, by those whom they wished.

Finally, this is also evident from the example of the body of Christ, which is read in Luke 24:31 to have vanished from the sight of the disciples and to have become ἄφαντον (invisible). Whence it is infallibly concluded that it is not of the essence of a glorified body that, wherever it may be, it is always visible. For what is affirmed of the body of Christ in this place: the same must be entirely established concerning the remaining glorified bodies of the blessed: since Christ will transform our lowly body, that it may be made conformable to his glorious body. Phil. 3:21. And the interpretation of Theodore Beza is by no means to be borne, who rendered the words of the Evangelist, καὶ ἀυτὸς ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ᾽ ἀυτῶν: thus: And he was taken away from their sight. For let all who have perceived any taste of Greek literature judge whether ἄφαντον γίνεσθαι (to become invisible) is the same as to be taken away from sight, or to go out of a room while the body remains visible. The Apostle himself certainly refutes this version, who reports that Christ, in that place where he had sat down, suddenly became invisible to the eyes of the disciples, so that this appeared to them entirely new, miraculous, and unusual: which cannot be understood as a local departure from the room.

Indeed, that kind of proof also pertains to this last point, that CHRIST is read to have entered to the Apostles with the doors closed: Likewise, having left the sepulcher with the monument closed. John 20:19. Mark 16:4 & 6.

The Calvinist spirit clamors in this place, and as if it were the shield of Achilles, it turns against us that saying of the Savior, in the same chapter 24 of Luke, verse 39: See my hands and my feet: for it is I myself: handle me, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as you see me have. Hence they argue thus: Christ, intending to confirm to the disciples the reality of his glorified body, ordered them to look at and handle his flesh and bones. Therefore, visibility and palpability are essential properties of even a glorified body.

I answer. The argument fails. 1. By the fallacy of a faulty consequence. For there is no strength in the connection: Christ after the Resurrection, intending to confirm the reality of his body, presented himself to be handled and seen: Therefore, to be actually visible and palpable is an ἰδίωμα συςατικὸν (constitutive property) of a true human body, even a glorified one. For this consequence is refuted by an infallible ἔλεγχον (refutation), which can be sought from the same 24th chapter of Luke and turned back upon the adversaries in this way: Christ after the resurrection, to assert the reality of his body, partakes in the sight of the disciples of broiled fish and a piece of a honeycomb: Likewise he drinks, as Peter testifies, Acts 10:41. Therefore, to eat and to drink are συςατικὰ ἰδιώματα (constitutive properties) of the body of Christ even when glorified. Since even the adversaries themselves understand that this is absurd, whether they like it or not, they must confess that a distinction must be made entirely between a necessary and a voluntary act: or between that which Christ assumed by the condition of nature, and that which he assumed by a most free οἰκονομίᾳ (economy) or dispensation. Therefore, just as it was of the economy and most free dispensation that Christ ate and drank after the resurrection: for they will not eat or drink, or marry or be given in marriage in the kingdom of heaven, but will be as the angels of GOD, as the Savior testifies in Matt. 22:30, Rom. 14:17. So it was of the same most free dispensation that he wished to present himself to be seen and touched by the disciples.

Furthermore, the argument fails by the confusion of disparate questions. For it is one thing when it is asked, What is it that constitutes the reality of a body, and distinguishes a body from a spirit or a specter? But it is another thing when it is asked, In what manner, or by what means, did Christ confirm the reality of his body to the disciples? To the former, the Savior himself answers: A spirit hath not flesh and bones. Therefore, flesh and bones pertain to the reality of even a glorified body. To the latter, it is answered that the manner by which the Savior wished to demonstrate this very true body of his was that he presented it to the disciples primarily to be seen and touched. For as the Philosopher rightly warns in Book 1 of the Metaphysics, figure and magnitude, and any other sensible thing, are perceived more by sight and touch than by other senses. Now, if anyone should subsume in the Calvinist sense, Therefore, just as that former thing is a constitutive property of a glorious body: thus this later one also will be of the same kind and condition: he most shamefully confuses disparate things. And this consequence is to be valued no more than if someone wished to argue thus: Christ after the resurrection appeared to Mary Magdalene in the vile and abject form of a gardener therefore such infirmities are of the essence of even glorified bodies. Now since the Calvinists themselves are forced to admit that these things were of a voluntary dispensation and economy, undertaken to this end, that he might demonstrate the truth of his body and his Resurrection to his disciples: What kind of vertigo is this, to be unwilling to admit the same regarding visibility and palpability?

But neither does the Calvinist spirit rest in this way, but rather they strive to tear down in various ways the examples concerning the disappearance of Christ, and concerning the bodies of the Saints rising with Christ, brought forward by us a little earlier in place of confirmation. For first they say there is no consequence in our argument: Christ became invisible. Therefore the glorious body of Christ is not always actually visible. For it could have happened for other reasons, either because the eyes of the disciples were hindered by some object-impediment, so that they could not see Christ: just as Scripture testifies that this happened in the Ascension, where a cloud took the body of Christ from the sight of the disciples in such a way that they could no longer see it, or, that the eyes of the disciples were restrained, and only afterwards opened: verse 16 and 31. Just as also the eyes of the citizens of Jerusalem did not see the bodies of the Saints, not because they were actually invisible: But because their eyes were restrained, so that they could not see those things which otherwise, without this restraint, they could have seen entirely.

I answer: The argument fails due to vicious and manifestly false fallacies. For as regards the former reason, nowhere in this place does the Evangelist Luke mention any object-impediment, just as in the history of the Ascension mention is expressly made of an intervening cloud. Wherefore in both histories the diversity is manifest: which emerges even more clearly from the fact that in the history of the Ascension Luke does not say that Christ became invisible to them: as he testifies happened in this place at Emmaus: But that a cloud took him from their eyes.

Then this dream is overturned by the very property of the Greek phrase. For of him who is not seen only because of external obstacles placed in the way, it can never be said that he became invisible, or that he vanished, or disappeared. As regards the latter reason, it likewise limps on all sides. For first, the text in Luke does not have it that the eyes of the disciples were restrained so that they would not see Christ. For how would they not have seen him with whom they traveled, and conversed, and whom they also compelled to stay with them: But the words of the Evangelist sound thus in verse 16. But their eyes were restrained, so that they would not recognize him. This restraint, therefore, was not of the eyes of the body, in respect of sight: but of the eyes of the mind, in respect of recognition. Wherefore the subsequent opening was also not of the eyes of the body, so that they might see him with whom the disciples were conversing: but of the eyes of the mind, so that they might now recognize him, with whom they had hitherto been exchanging words, to be Christ himself. Then this Calvinist reason strangles and overturns itself. Because the text expressly admits that Christ became invisible, not when the eyes of the disciples were still restrained, but when they had already been opened: Therefore it is false and trivial that the disciples did not see Christ any longer because their eyes were restrained. Finally, what the Adversaries blather about the restraint of the eyes of the citizens of Jerusalem is a mere figment, of which one cannot see even a shadow in Matthew.

The latter distinction, which is especially to be observed regarding the present Question, looks to the predicate itself: and that in two ways: first by reason of visibility itself considered in itself: then indeed, by reason of the object, around which visibility can be considered. By reason of visibility, something is said to be visible in two ways; either potentially or actually. When therefore it is asked, Are glorious bodies visible? it must be answered by this former distinction: namely that they are of such a nature and condition that they are potentially visible: or what is the same thing, that they have in themselves that power, so that they can present themselves to be seen by others. But that they are actually seen by all to whom they are present, that is not of their nature, or of necessity: but of most free will.

As regards the object, around which the Visible can revolve, that likewise is not of one kind. For either glorified bodies are placed in the position of the object: or bodies still living in these lands. When therefore it is asked, Are glorious bodies actually visible to bodies that are likewise glorified? We answer affirmatively: and that because of the proportion which these glorified bodies and glorified eyes mutually have between themselves. But when it is asked, Are glorified bodies actually visible to those to whom they are present and with whom they converse in these lands? We answer by that former distinction: first indeed Negatively, by reason of act and necessity. Because for natural and spiritual men there is no proportion intervening: nor are natural eyes reduced to the perfection of the other life: therefore it is not of nature or of necessity that glorified bodies are actually seen by those to whom they are present in these lands. But as regards power we answer affirmatively: namely that glorified bodies can expose themselves to the sight of those to whom they are present in this life.

With these distinctions observed, first that apparent contradiction collapses, which the Adversaries object to us, repeatedly shouting that it is impossible that one and the same body be simultaneously visible and invisible. For with the distinction of act and power observed, and the diversity of objects also noted, every contradiction vanishes of its own accord.

But they further object that it cannot be confirmed by any testimony of Scripture that any glorious body is IN ITSELF visible and invisible. Then they repeatedly claim it is absurd that any body should truly be a body and yet not be actually seen by those to whom it is present. Then they contend it is clearly impossible that a body which has a certain form and figure should not be seen by all to whom it is present. But those objections suffer partly from false preconceived opinions and partly from a manifest ignorance of the Elenchus. For as regards the first argument, who among us ever said or wrote that one and the same glorious body is IN ITSELF visible and invisible? Rather, this is our meaning: a glorified body, which by reason of its nature, and thus PER SE, is visible as regards its δύναμιν (power), that same body is invisible to us in this life for the reason we have just explained. Nor is this affirmed without Scripture. For does not Scripture assert both, namely that the body of Christ could be visibly where He willed, and again become ἄφαντον (invisible), which we have just now proven quite evidently from the 24th chapter of Luke? And does not the Gospel history clearly confirm this very thing, which relates that Christ appeared to the disciples many times, but shortly thereafter vanished from their eyes in such a way that the disciples could indeed truly affirm that the Lord had been seen by them, but could not explain where He had gone? And indeed, unless Christ had been made invisible in His body, there can be no doubt that the disciples, having followed Him not only with their eyes but also with their feet, would not have allowed themselves to be torn away from His company, since they were held by an insatiable desire not only to see Him but also to hear Him. The second argument casts the snare of absurdity not upon us, but upon the adversaries themselves. For just as it is very true that everything which is seen is a body, so it is very false that every body is actually seen; or by conversion, that everything which is not actually seen, if it is present, is not a body. For simple conversion only has a place in a universal affirmative when it consists of a definition or has convertible terms. Otherwise, a universal affirmative is converted by accident, as it ought to be converted in this place in this manner: Everything which is seen is a body, and some body is seen. And let the adversaries explain to us whether the air surrounding us is a body, and if it is a body, whether it is an actually visible body. They cannot deny the former; let them deliberate well whether they wish to affirm the latter.

The third and final argument fails through the confusion of disparate questions. For it is one thing to have a certain form or figure, but it is another thing, because of that same form and figure, to be necessarily and actually visible. We simply affirm the former regarding bodies that are even glorified. For because they will not be changed into spirits, although they will be πνεύματικὰ (spiritual), but will remain true bodies, and indeed in respect of substance and essential properties, ὑσιαστικω̃ν (substantial), clearly the same as they were before in this life, they will certainly retain also their native form or figure as a property co-created with the body and inherent in its subject, whether it is seen or not seen. But the latter, or the Calvinian consequence, we simply deny: namely, that every body must therefore be actually seen by all to whom it is present because it is endowed with its native form and inherent figure. The reason for our negative is this: because visibility and invisibility is not a part of the inherent form, much less a property of the body itself, but only relates to the seeing eye and the body which is seen, so that whether it is seen or not seen, the form and figure of the glorious body remains exactly the same. Wherefore, only the δύναμις (power) of visibility follows this form, so that such a body can indeed present itself to be seen by those to whom it is present in this life, and indeed by its own most free will, although in the meantime it is always actually visible to the blessed in eternal life, as was shown more fully above.

But let it suffice to have disputed these things concerning the properties of a true body, both natural and glorious, leaving this now for the adversaries to weigh more deeply: since the body of Christ has obtained from the Resurrection a mode of existing somewhere in an illocal and invisible manner, might it not much more, from its personal union with the illocal and invisible λόγῳ (Word), and likewise from its session at the illocal and invisible right hand of GOD, have a mode, or rather truly have one, by which it is present illocally and invisibly to all creatures, and everywhere most presently reigns and dominates over all the works of the hands of GOD? And especially that it is present illocally and invisibly to the most holy Eucharist, and most presently dispenses and exhibits its own body and blood therein.

And thus far concerning the properties of the human nature in Christ. It remains that we attend to what the idioms of the divine nature are.

Latin:

QUæritur etiam hodiè de Visibilitate, an Essentialis sit proprietas Veri corporis Humani, ut semper actu sit visibile, hoc est, ut semper ex justa quadam distantia possit conspici? Calviniani ajunt: nos negamus. Sed ut de Negativâ istâ nostrâ rectiùs constet: duæ potissimùm observandæ sunt distinctiones, quarum prior Subjectum, posterior prædicatum propositæ Quæstionis respicit.

Initiò enim distingvendum est, inter corpus Physicum & corruptibile (Quod Apostolus ψυχικὸν animale, Φθαρτὸν corruptibile, ἄτιμον Ignobile, & ἀσθενὲς Infirmum vocat) & inter corpus gloriosum, Apostolo πνευματικὸν Spirituale, ἄφθαρτον incorruptibile, τίμιον, gloriosum δυνατὸν potens dictum: 1. Cor. 15. 43. & 44.

Corpora quidem Physica ob adhærentem & concreatam imperfectionem, in debita distantia semper actu visibilia esse, nemo nostrum unquam negavit: Sed corpora glorificata eidem infirmitati subjecta esse, vix quisquam affirmaverit, iis de causis, quas mox expediemus. Deindè quoad corpora etiam Physica, haud concedimus, proprium συστατικὸν hoc esse corporis humani, ut actu semper conspiciatur, ab omnibus quibus adest. Neque enim definitionem hominis, visibilitas isthæc ingreditur, id quod patet ex mutatione illa, quæ eadem manente substantia, ratione Qualitatum tantùm ijsdem corporibus obtinget, ut ab infirmitatibus, quibus tùm ratione localitatis, tùm respectu visibilitatis, ratione item cibi & potus hac in vita subjacebant, prorsus futura sint libera & immunia: quippe prædita Spiritualibus dotibus & proprietatibus, tanquam ἰσάγγελα Angelicis Spiritibus similia, in illis omnibus, quæ non sunt destructiva naturæ, hoc est, quæ illorum substantiam non evertunt. Proindè quemadmodum gloriosa & πνευματικὰ corpora, nullo corporali sive Physico loco quo fulciantur, op9 habent, ut quæ omni Elemento subtiliora erunt: ita neque opus habebunt, ut semper actu sint visibilia, hoc est, semper ex debita instantia conspiciantur.

Deindè patet hoc ipsum exemplo eorum Sanctorum, qui resurgente Christo ex mortuis, egressi sunt è Sepulchris, & apparuerunt multis: Matth. 27. 53. Ubi notationem meretur Verbum Græcum ἐνεφανίσθησαν πολλοῖς, quod non, uti Pezelius interpretatur, hoc significat, quòd corpora illa Sanctorum conspecta sint, ab omnibus civibus Hierosolymitanis, quibus obviam facta sunt: Sed hoc significat, quod corpora illa Sanctorum, sese conspicienda præbuerint multis, illis nimirùm quibus volebant.

Tandem patet hoc quoque, exemplo corporis Christi, quod Luc. 24. 31. ex conspectu discipulorum evanuisse, & ἄφαντον invisibile factum fuisse legitur. Undè infallibiliter colligitur, de Essentia corporis gloriosi non esse ut ubi ubi sit, semper sit visibile. Quod enim de corpore Christi hoc loco affirmatur: idem de reliquis beatorum corporibus gloriosis omninò statuendum est: Siquidem Christus transformabit corpus nostrum humile, ut conforme fiat corpori ejus gloriosi. Phil. 3, 21. Et minimè ferenda est interpretatio Theodori Bezæ, qui verba Evangelistæ, καὶ ἀυτὸς ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ᾽ ἀυτῶν: Sic reddidit: Et ipse ablatus est, ex eorum conspectu. Num enim ἄφαντος γίνεσθαι idem sit, quod auferri ex conspectu, vel è conclavi egredi, visibili manente corpore, judicent quotquot aliquem Græcæ literaturæ gustum perceperunt. Redarguit sanè hanc versionem ipse Apostolus, qui refert, Christum eo loco, quo assederat, subitò factum esse inconspicuum à discipulorum oculis, ita ut illis novum hoc planè, miraculosum & insolitum accideret: id quod de locali recessione ex conclavi intelligi non potest.

Pertinet verò ad hoc postremum probationis Genus & illud, quod CHRISTUS legitur claufis ostijs intrasse ad Apostolos : Item clauso monumento, è sepulchro egressus. Johan. 20, 19. Marci 16,4. & 6.

Obstrepit hoc loco Spiritus Calvinianus, & tanquam Achillis Clypeum obvertit illud Servatoris, eodem cap. 24. Lucæ, versu 39. Videte manus meas, & pedes meos : nam ego ipse sum: palpate me, & videte : nam Spiritus Carnem & ossa non habet, prout me videtis habere. Hinc sic arguunt: Christus corporis sui gloriosi veritatem confirmaturus discipulis, jußit ipsos intueri & palpare carnem & ossa sua. Ergò Visibilitas & palpabilitas sunt proprietates Essentiales corporis etiam gloriosi.

Respondeo. Fallit argumentum. 1. Sophismate vitiosi consequentis. Neque enim ullus nervus inest connexo : Christus post Resurrectionem confirmaturus corporis sui veritatem, palpandum sese visendumque præbuit : Ergò actu visibile & palpabile esse, est ἰδίωμα συςατικὸν veri corporis humani, etiam gloriosi. Refutatur enim hæc consecutio per infallibilem ἔλεγχον, quæ ex eodem cap. 24. Lucæ peti, & in Adversarios retorqueri potest hoc modo : Christus post resurrectionem, ad asserendam corporis sui veritatem concedit in conspectu discipulorum, de pisce asso & flavo apiario : Item bibit teste Petro, Act. 10, 41. Ergò manducare & bibere sunt συςατικὰ ἰδιώματα corporis Christi etiam gloriosi. Quod cùm absurdum esse intelligant vel ipsi Adversarij, nolint velint fateantur necesse est, omninò distingvendum esse, inter actum necessarium & voluntarium: sive inter id, quod ex naturæ conditione, & quod ex liberrima οἰκονομίᾳ sive dispensatione suscepit Christus. Quemadmodum ergò οἰκονομίας & liberrimæ disputationis fuit, quod Christus post resurrectionem comedit & bibit : Neque enim in regno cælorum manducabunt aut bibent, vel nubent aut nuptum dabunt, sed erunt, sicut Angeli DEI, teste Servatore Matth. 22. 30. Rom. 14, 17. Ita ejusdem liberrimæ dispensationis fuit, quod se sevisendum, contrectandumque discipulis præbere voluit.

Deindè fallit argumentum Confusione disparatarum Quæstionum. Aliud enim est, quando quæritur, Quid nam sit, quod veritatem corporis constituat, & corpus à Spiritu sive spectro discernat ? Aliud verò est, quando quæritur, Quonam modo, sive quo medio Christus veritatem corporis sui, discipulis confirmârit. Ad prius respondet ipse Servator : Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet. Ergò ad veritatem corporis etiam gloriosi pertinent caro & ossa. Ad posterius respondetur, Modum, per quem hoc ipsum verum corpus suum demonstrare voluit Servator, fuisse, quòd illud discipulis visendū potißimùm contrectandumq; præbuit. Nam uti Philosophus lib. 1. Metaph. rectè admonet, figura & magnitudo, & alia qualibet res sensibilis magis percipiuntur visu & tactu, quã alijs sensibus. Jam verò si quis subsumat sensu Calviniano, Ergò, quemadmodum prius illud est συςατικὸν ἴδιωμα corporis gloriosi: ita posterius etiam hoc ejusdem erit generis & conditionis: is disparata turpissimè confundit. Et haud pluris facienda est hæc consecutio, quàm si quis ita vellet arguere: Christus post resurrectionem apparuit Mariæ Magdalenæ in vili & abjecta forma hortulani: Item monstravit vestigia clavorum in latere & manibus: ergò ejusmodi infirmitates sunt de Essentia corporum etiam glorificatorum. Jam cùm ipsi Calviniani fateri coguntur, fuisse isthæc voluntariæ dispensationis & οἰκονομίας, hunc in finem suscepta, ut veritatem sui corporis & Resurrectionis suæ, discipulis suis commonstraret: Quæ hæc vertigo fuerit, idem de visibilitate & palpabilitate fateri nolle?

Sed neque sic quiescit Spiritus Calvinianus, quin Exempla de disparitione Christi, & de corporibus Sanctorum cum Christo resurgentium, paulò antè confirmationis loco in medium à nobis allata, variis modis convellere student. Primùm enim dicunt nullum esse consequens in argumento nostro: Christus ἄφαντος ἐγένετο. Ergò corpus Christi gloriosum non semper actu est visibile. Nam aliis de causis illud accidere potuit, vel quod per objectum quoddam impedimentum, oculi discipulorum impedirentur, quô mînus Christum viderent: quemadmodum in Ascensione id factum esse testatur Scriptura, ubi nubes corpus Christi è conspectu discipulorum ita abstulit, ut videre illud amplius non possent, vel, quod retinerentur oculi discipulorum, & postmodum demùm aperirentur: versu 16. & 31. Quemadmodum etiam oculi civium Hierosolymitanorum non videbant corpora Sanctorum, non quod actu essent invisibilia: Sed quòd oculi ipsorum retinerentur, ne ea videre possent, quæ aliàs absque hac retentione, omninò videre potuissent.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum vitiosis & manifestè falsis παραλογηοις. Nam quoad priorem rationem, nuspiam hoc loco Evangelista Lucas ullius objecti impedimenti meminit, quemadmodum in historia Ascensionis nubeculæ intervenientis expressa fit mentio. Quare in utraque historia manifesta est diversitas: quæ indè etiam emergit luculentior, quod in historia Ascensionis Lucas non dicit, Christum ἄφαντον γενόμενον ἀπ' ἀυτῶν: quemadmodum hoc loco Emaunti evenisse testatur: Sed nubem abstulisse ipsum ab oculis eorum.

Deindè evertit hoc somnium ipsa proprietas phrasis Græcæ. Nam de eo, qui tantùm propter externa obstacula interjecta, non videtur, nunquam dici potest, quòd factus sit ἄφαντος, vel quod evanuerit, sive disparuerit. Quoad posteriorem rationem, illa itidem undiquaque claudicat. Primùm enim textus apud Lucam non habet, retentos fuisse oculos discipulorum, ut ne viderent Christum. Quomodo enim non vidissent, cum quo iter fecerunt, & collocuti sunt, quem item secum manere coëgerunt: Sed sic sonant verba Evangelistæ v. 16. Oculi autem tenebantur, μὴ ἐπιγνῶναι ἀυτὸν, ne agnoscerent eum. Retentio ergò isthæc non erat oculorum corporis, ratione visus: sed oculorum mentis, respectu agnitionis. Quare subsecuta etiam adapertio non erat oculorum corporis, ut viderent eum, cum quo confabulabantur discipuli: sed oculorum mentis, ut jam agnoscerent eum, cum quo hactenus sermones contulerant, esse ipsum Christum. Deindè hæc ratio Calviniana seipsam jugulat & evertit. Quia enim textus disertè fatetur, Christum ἄφαντον factum esse, non cùm adhuc discipulorum oculi tenerentur, sed cùm jam adaperti essent: Ergò falsum & nugatorium est, ideò discipulos Christi non amplius vidisse, quia oculi ipsorum tenebantur. Tandem quod de retentione oculorum civium Hierosolymitanorum blaterant Adversarij, merum figmentum est, cujus ne umbram quidem apud Matthæum videre licet.

Posterior distinctio, quæ circa præsentem Quæstionem cumprimis observanda, respicit ipsum prædicatum: idque dupliciter: primùm ratione ipsius visibilitatis in se consideratæ: deindè verò, ratione objecti, circa quod visibilitas considerari potest. Ratione visibilitatis, duobus modis aliquid dicitur esse visibile; vel δυνάμει sive potentia: vel ἐνεργείᾳ sive actu. Quando ergò quæritur, An corpora gloriosa sint visibilia? per distinctionem hanc priorem responderi debet: nempè ejus naturæ & conditionis ea esse, ut δυνάμει sint visibilia: vel quod idem est, habere ea in se eam δύναμιν, ut aliis sese visenda præbere possint. Sed ut ipso actu conspiciantur ab omnibus, quibus adsunt, illud non vel naturæ ipsorum, vel necessitatis: sed liberrimæ voluntatis esse.

Quoad objectum, circa quod τὸ Visibile versari potest illud itidem non unius est generis. Vel enim objecti loco ponuntur corpora glorificata: vel corpora in his terris adhuc viventia. Quando E. quæritur, An corpora gloriosa, corporibus itidem gloriosis actu sint visibilia? Respondemus affirmatè: idque propter proportionem, quam corpora isthæc glorificata, & oculi glorificati inter se mutuò habent. Quando verò quæritur, An corpora glorificata ipso actu visibilia sint illis, quibus in his terris adsunt & conversantur? Respondemus per distinctionem illam priorem: primùm quidem Negativè, ratione actus & necessitatis. Quia enim hominibus ψυχικοῖς & πνευματικοῖς nulla intercedit proportio: neque oculi ψυχικοὶ ad alterius vitæ perfectionem sunt reducti: ideò non vel naturæ vel necessitatis est, ut corpora glorificata, ipso actu conspiciantur ab ijs, quibus in his terris adsunt. Cæterùm quoad δύναμιν sive potentiam respondemus affirmatè: nempè posse corpora glorificata illorum conspectui sese exponere, quibus hac in vita adsunt.

Distinctionibus istis observatis primùm corruit apparens illa contradictio, quam Adversarij nobis objiciunt, subindè clamitantes, Impossibile esse, ut unum idemque corpus simul sit visibile & invisibile. Nam observata distinctione actus & potentiæ, notatâ item diversitate objectorum omnis ἀντίφασις ultrò evanescit.

Sed obstrepunt illi porrò, nullo Scripturæ testimonio confirmari posse: Corpus aliquod gloriosum IN SE esse visibile & invisibile. Deindè absurdum esse dictitant, ut corpus aliquod reverà sit corpus: & tamen actu non videatur ab iis, quibus adest: Tum impossibile planè esse contendunt, ut corpus, quod certam habet formam & figuram, non videatur ab omnibus, quibus præsens adest. Verùm objectiones istæ, partim falsis præconceptis opinionibus: partim manifesta Ignoratione Elenchi laborant. Nam quoad primam argumentationẽ, Quis nostrûm unquá vel dixit vel scripsit, unum idemq; corpus gloriosum IN SE esse visibile & invisibile: Quin hæc potiùs nostra est mens: Corpus glorificatum, quod ratione naturæ suæ, & sic PER SE, quoad δύναμιν est visibile: idem illud corpus, Nobis hac in vita esse invisibile, eam ob causam, quam modò explicatam dedimus. Neque sine Scriptura hoc affirmatur. Annon enim utrumque Scriptura asserit, videlicet corpus Christi potuisse esse visibiliter, ubi voluit: & rursum ἄφαντον invisibile fieri: id quod ex cap. 24. Lucæ jam modò satis evidenter evincimus. Et annon hoc ipsum luculenter confirmat historia Evangelica, quæ refert, Christum multoties apparuisse discipulis: sed paulò pòst ex ipsorum oculis ita evanuisse, ut discipuli possent quidem verè affirmare, visum sibi esse Dominum: sed quò pervenisset, explicare haud possent. Et sanè, nisi invisibilis factus esset corpore suo Christus, dubium potest esse nullum, quin discipuli ipsum non oculis modò, sed & pedibus insecuti, neque abipsius consortio avelli sese passi fuissent: quippè cujus non visendi modò, sed & audiendi, infatiabili desiderio tenebantur. Altera ratio non nobis, sed ipsis Adversarijs absurditatis laqueum injicit. Quemadmodum enim longè verissimum est: Omne id quod videtur, corpus est: Ita longè falsissimum est: Omne corpus actu videtur: vel per conversionem, Omne quod non actu videtur si præsens sit, non est corpus. Nam conversio simplex locum tum demùm habet in universali Affirmativa, quando ea constat vel Definitione: vel terminos habet convertibiles. Aliàs universalis Affirmativa convertitur per Accidens: uti hoc loco converti debet in hunc modum: Omne id, quod videtur, corpus est: Et Quoddam corpus videtur. Et edisserant nobis Adversarii, An aër nos ambiens sit corpus: Et si corpus, nùm actu sit visibile corpus? Prius illud negare non possunt: posterius hoc num affirmare velint, probè deliberent.

Tertia ac postrema ratio fallit confusione disparatarum Quæstionum. Aliud enim est, habere certam formam sive figuram: Aliud verò est, propter eandem formam & figuram, necessariò & ipso actu esse visibile. Prius illud simpliciter affirmamus de corporibus etiam glorificatis. Quia enim ea non mutabuntur in Spiritus, licet futura sint πνεύματικὰ: sed vera manebunt corpora, & quidem ratione substantiæ & proprietatum Essentialium, ὑσιαστικω̃ν, planè eadem, quæ priùs in hac vita fuerunt: utique retinebunt etiam formam sive figuram nativam, tanquàm proprietatem corpori concreatam, suoq; subjecto inhærentem, sive ea videatur, sive non videatur. Cæterùm posterius hoc, sive consequens Calvinianum, simpliciter negamus: nempè quòd omne corpus ideò ipso actu debeat conspici ab omnibus, quibus adest, quia illud nativâ suâ forma & inhærente figura sit præditum. Ratio negativæ nostræ est hæc: Quia visibilitas & invisibilitas non est pars formæ inhærentis, nedum proprietas ipsius corporis: Sed tantùm relatè se habet ad oculum videntem, & corpus quod videtur, ita ut sive videatur, sive non videatur, eadem prorsus maneat forma & figura corporis gloriosi. Quare Formâ hanc tantùm δύναμις visibilitatis sequitur: ut nimirùm tale corpus possit sese conspiciendum præbere ijs, quibus præsens hac in vita adest: & quidem ex liberrima voluntate: licèt interim actu sit semper visibile beatis in vita æterna: uti suprà fusius ostensum.

Sed hæc de proprietatibus corporis veri, tùm Naturalis, tùm gloriosi disputasse sufficiat: hoc jam Adversariis altius expendendum relinquentes: Cùm corpus Christi ex Resurrectione fortitum sit modum, illocali atque invisibili ratione alicubi existendi: an non multò magis ex unione personali cum illocali atque invisibili λόγῳ, item ex sessione ad illocalem atque invisibilem dextram DEI, modum habere possit, imò verè habeat, quo illocaliter & invisibiliter omnibus Creaturis sit præsens, & ubique præsentissimè regnet & dominetur omnibus operibus manuum DEI? Cumprimis verò illocaliter & invisibiliter adsit præsens Sacrosanctæ Evcharistiæ, suumque corpus & sangvinem præsentissima in eadem dispenset & exhibeat.

Et hactenus quidem de Proprietatibus Humanæ Naturæ in Christo. Restat ut quænam Idiomata Divinæ Naturæ sint, attendamus.


### Chapter I. On the Truth of the Human Nature which the Word (Λόγος) assumed: Idioms or properties of the Divine Nature

The idioms of the divine nature are most correctly distinguished into essential and personal. The essential are simply such; for neither do παρεπόμενα τῇ Φύσει (things accompanying the nature) nor other accidents of any kind fall into the most simple divine nature or essence. But the idioms of the divine nature are those which are commonly enumerated in the definition of GOD, and which are converted with the most simple divine essence, and are one and the same thing with it.

Personal idioms are those by which the person of the λόγος (Word) is distinguished from the two remaining persons of the Trinity: such as being the Son of GOD, being begotten from eternity. After the incarnation of the λόγος (Word), it can and ought to be referred to His personal idioms that He now constitutes one composite person with the assumed humanity, consisting, that is, of two natures.

OBSERVATION.

Because the human nature of CHRIST is in itself ἀνυπόστατος (anhypostatic): but has been made ἐνυπόστατος (enhypostatic), it is asked whether in this respect it has obtained a certain property which can be called personal. Where it is most correctly answered in the negative: lest we seem to believe that it is a person. Meanwhile, however, because it is not entirely ἀνυπόστατος, but has obtained personality in the person of the λόγος (Word), some not ineptly maintain that in this respect a quasi-personal property can be attributed to the humanity: according to which the individual of the human nature in Christ, by reason of subsistence in the λόγος, differs from all other individuals of the human species. Whence it has even deserved to be called by the ancients the Person of the Nature. To this quasi-personal property can also be referred: conception by the Holy Spirit: birth from the virgin Mary: illocal subsistence in the ὑπόστασις (hypostasis) of the Word: sitting at the right hand of the power and Majesty of GOD.

Latin:

IDiomata Divinæ Naturæ rectissimè distingyuntur, in Essentialia & personalia. Essentialia simpliciter sunt talia: neque enim in simplicissimam Divinam Naturam sive Essentiam, cadunt vel παρεπόμενα τῇ Φύσει: vel alia cujuscunque Generis Accidentia. Sunt verò Essentia Divinæ Naturæ idiomata, quæ in Definitione DEI vulgò enumerantur, quæque simplicissima Divina Essentia convertuntur, & cum ea sunt quiddam ταυτό & idem.

PERSONALIA Idiomata sunt, quibus persona τῦ λόγε à duabus reliquis Trinitatis personis distingvitur: ut, Esse Filium DEI, esse Genitum ab æterno. Post Incarnationem λόγε, ad personalia ejus Idiomata referri potest & debet, quòd cum Humanitate assumta jam unum personam compositam constituit: constantem videlicet ex duabus naturis.

OBSERVATIO.

QUia Humana CHRISTI Natura per se est ἀνυπόστατος : facta autem est ἐνυπόστατος, Quæritur, num hoc respectu ea Idioma quoddam sortitum sit, quod Personale dici queat. Ubi rectissimè negatè respondetur: ne eam personam esse credere videamur. Interim tamen, quia non planè est ἀνυπόστατος, sed personalitatem in persona τοῦ λόγου fortita est, haud ineptè quidam statuunt, Hoc respectu tribui posse Humanitati Idioma Quasi personale: secundum quod Individuum Naturæ humanæ in Christo, ratione subsistentiæ in λόγῳ differt ab omnibus aliis humanæ speciei individuis. Undè à veteribus etiam Persona Naturæ dici meruit. Ad hoc Idioma Quasi Personale referri etiam potest, conceptio ex Spiritu Sancto: Nativitas ex virgine Maria: subsistentia illocalis in ὑποστάσει λόγου: Sessio ad dextram virtutis ac Majestatis DEI.


### Chapter Second


### Chapter Second: On the Union of the Two Natures in Christ

Just as in other sciences and faculties, truth is most correctly elicited from the opposition of true and false: according to that common saying: Truth shines forth more when contraries are placed next to each other: So also in the present mystery, which is otherwise entirely ἐξαίρετον (exceptional), transcending all the grasp of our intellect, we will hardly deal more correctly than if we always proceed to the investigation of truth from the consideration of opposites. Before, therefore, we propose and confirm the Orthodox Doctrine of our Churches concerning the union of the two Natures in Christ, it will be worth the effort to know more diligently the errors and tenets of both ancient and modern heretics concerning the same mystery: and this all the more, the more insidiously the Jesuitical and Calvinian faction today strives to pervert the history of ancient heresies and to convict our Churches of the same. Although indeed there were many among the ancients who horribly defiled this part of Christian doctrine: yet each and every one of them can be recalled to two classes; of which Nestorianism occupies one, and Eutychianism the other: concerning which we shall see in order.

I. NESTORIANISM.

The Jesuit Bellarmine, in book 3 on the Person of Christ, chapter 5, intending to convict our Churches of the Nestorian heresy, establishes four main heads of it.

For he writes first that Nestorius taught that the Blessed Virgin gave birth to a mere man, and one who had not only a human nature but also a human person.

Then indeed that the Blessed Mary is not the mother of GOD, but the mother of Christ.

3. That the Nativity, Passion, Resurrection and Ascension of CHRIST are to be attributed to the man alone.

Finally, that the same Nestorius contended that the Son of GOD was united to the Son of Man afterwards, in many ways, not indeed by substantially communicating οὐσίαν, but accidentally. First, according to habitation, because the Word dwelt in the man Christ, as in His own temple, according to that in John 2:19: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. And therefore they said, in chapter 7 of Isaiah, it was written cautiously: His name shall be called Emmanuel, that is, He shall not be called GOD, but GOD with us, that is, dwelling in us, according to that in John 1:14: And dwelt among us. Second, through a union of will and love, because that Son of Man was always most closely joined with the will of GOD. Third, according to operation, because the man Christ was an instrument which the Word used in those admirable works which were done by Christ. Fourth, according to participation, because the Word imparted to that man His own name and dignity, so that he might indeed be called God and the Son of GOD, and be adored by all creatures, not for his own sake, but for the sake of Him by whom he had been assumed: in the same way in which images of the Saints are sometimes called by their names, and are even honored and adored on their account.

That this was the heresy of Nestorius, the Jesuit contends, and impudently adds at the end of the cited chapter: Brentius clearly favors this heresy in his book on the Majesty of the Man Christ, where he very often repeats that the Son of GOD is in the Son of Mary.

The Calvinists describe the confession of Nestorius in their Orthodox Consensus, page 52, in these words: Nestorius, they say, confessed that GOD the Word, in that highest and inseparable conjunction, leads His own flesh to the man, as the proper temple of His indwelling, and appropriates to Himself his passion and properties. But he understood this in no other way than by a certain Relation, just as it is proper to a man to be clothed in a garment, and insofar as a man considers an injury done to the garment to be his own. On account of the garment, he says, I venerate the clothing, and on account of the hidden one, I adore the visible one, the Indivisible GOD from the visible one according to this union and conjunction of humanity to GOD the Word; in the same way, he says that the visible GOD is called GOD, on account of the communion of names, but not on account of the same dignity.

Moreover, if we weigh a little more accurately both the writings of Cyril and the acts of the Synod of Ephesus, in which Nestorius was convicted and condemned of error, it becomes manifest that both the Jesuits and the Calvinists define the heresy of Nestorius less than candidly, and corrupt the same through manifest crimes of falsehood.

And that we may treat separately of each of those four chapters which the Jesuit has proposed: It is indeed certain at the beginning that Nestorius was condemned by the Ephesian Synod for the reason that he had taught that the Blessed Virgin Mary had given birth to a mere man: But yet it is also certain that Nestorius himself was not accustomed to speak in that way. For there exists his Epistle to Cyril of Alexandria, Vol. 4 of the works of Cyril: There exist also certain testimonies taken from the books of Nestorius, toward the end of that volume, in which with great asseveration Nestorius contends that there is only one person in Christ, and that the same person is both truly GOD and truly man: writing thus among other things to Cyril: In the second chapter of your Epistle, you proclaim the distinction of the natures, according to the reason of the incarnation and the Divinity, and the conjunction of these into one person: and you confess that the GOD Word had no need of the generation which was made from a woman, nor was the divinity capable of suffering. These things are truly Orthodox, and contrary to the perverse dogmas of all heresies concerning the Lord's natures. And toward the end of the same Epistle: That the body is the temple of the divinity: and that this temple, having been made absolute and united by divine coupling, the Nature of the divinity joined to itself as its own, it is good that we confess, and worthy of the Evangelical traditions. And more clearly Nestorius himself again in a certain peculiar book in the seventeenth Quaternio, Vol. IV of the works of Cyril, Col. 300. The GOD Word was indeed before he was made man GOD, and joined to the Father: But in later times he received the form of a servant: But since he was and was called the Son before: the assumed form of a servant cannot be called Son SEPARATELY: lest we establish two Sons. But since he is joined to him who was the Son in the beginning, after he is joined to him, he cannot receive division.

From which testimonies it is most evidently clear that what the Jesuit affirms is false. That Nestorius at the beginning taught that the Blessed Virgin gave birth to a mere man, and one who had not only a human Nature, but also a human Person. For in express words Nestorius asserted one singular person in Christ, and openly testified that two distinct Natures in Christ had arrived at the conjunction of one person.

But let someone object, if Nestorius did not foster that error, why then was he condemned in the Council of Ephesus as one who established two persons in Christ? We answer with our Blessed Luther from his book on Councils and the Church, that he was condemned with the best right. For Nestorius involved a most manifest contradiction. For although he openly taught Christ as true GOD and man in one person: yet he established such a union from which neither the communication of Natures nor of Idioms would follow. And thus in the very same way in which the Calvinists and Jesuits do today, he conceded in words that the Antecedent was indeed true: that is, he confessed that two natures were united into one person: but he denied the Effect or consequent, which nevertheless necessarily followed from the Antecedent, whence Cyril above all, and the remaining Orthodox fathers of the Ephesian Council demonstrated with many arguments: that he was tearing one person in Christ into two; although he was unwilling to confess this. Let the Adversaries therefore remember that Anathema, by which the fathers of the Ephesian Synod struck the opinion of Nestorius by reason of this first chapter: that it directly touches and strikes their own doctrine as well: however much they may be unwilling to confess with Nestorius that they, by denying the real communion of both Natures and idioms, are tearing the person of Christ into two persons. But we Christians, says Luther, ought to believe such a union of two Natures, from which the idioms of each Nature are attributed to the person equally and all at once: namely, when we say, Christ is GOD and man, in one person: therefore whatever is said of Christ as Man, the same must also be affirmed of GOD: namely, Christ is dead, and Christ is GOD, Therefore GOD is dead; not a separated GOD, but GOD united with humanity. For concerning a separated GOD both are false, namely, that Christ is GOD, and that GOD is dead: Since by such a consideration GOD is not man: But if it seems admirable in the eyes of Nestorius that GOD is dead: he ought to have thought in turn that it is also admirable that GOD was made man. For in this way the immortal GOD becomes This, which can suffer, die, and has all human idioms. For what would that Man be, with whom GOD is united, if he did not have human Idioms? He would be a phantom, just as the Manichaeans and Marcionites taught. For unless GOD had died for us, but only a man, we would by no means have been redeemed, but we would all have perished together. For we are redeemed by the passion and death, not of a man only, but of the GOD-man, who as GOD-man suffered and died for us: And thus the Church is redeemed by the blood of GOD. Similarly, whatever is said of GOD, the same must also be attributed to man, namely, God is omnipotent, the Man Christ is GOD, therefore the Man Christ is omnipotent. Since GOD and Man are one person: therefore the person of Christ has the Idioms of each Nature. Thus far Luther.

As for the other chapter of the Nestorian heresy, we do not move a dispute about it with the Jesuits: For Ecclesiastical history testifies that around A.D. 430, a certain presbyter Anastasius, whom Nestorius the Bishop of Constantinople had brought with him from Antioch to Constantinople, taught in a public sermon that Mary should be called by no one θεοτόκον, Deipara, or Mother of GOD, but only χριϛοτόκον. For that she was only a Man, and that it was absolutely impossible for GOD to be generated by a Man. And when all the pious were averse to this novelty of both words and dogmas; Nestorius, who attributed more to his friend Anastasius than to the truth, undertook his patronage: bursting forth even into these words: Do not boast, Jew: You did not crucify GOD, but a man: denying likewise that the Son of GOD could be called διμηνιαῖον καὶ τριμηνιαῖον, two months old, or three months old. The sole cause of this error was this, that he posited such a union of the two natures in Christ, from which no real communication whatsoever, whether of the natures or of the properties, could flow.

The third chapter of the Nestorian heresy, according to the opinion of Bellarmine, is that Nestorius established that the Nativity, passion, death, Resurrection, and Ascension of Christ are to be attributed to the Man ALONE. In this part, the Jesuit has written the truth: since from the denial of the communication of idioms this very thing necessarily follows, just as that was shown a little earlier from Luther. However, we cannot sufficiently marvel that the Jesuit rejects and condemns this dogma in Nestorius as heretical, when in the same book 3, chapter, he condemned it among our Doctors as a Eutychian dogma, because they ascribe those Actions and passions not to the man alone, but to the whole person: so that although the Divinity itself is and remains impassible: yet the Son of GOD in the assumed flesh is said to have truly suffered.

In the Fourth chapter of the heresy, which Bellarmine attributes to Nestorius, we willingly grant certain things: but we reject others as adulterated and fabricated to the detriment of our Churches. We grant that the first three modes of Union were explained and defended by Nestorius's own followers not so much in the way they are defined by the Jesuit. But we reject the fact that he neither candidly proposes nor skillfully explains that Fourth mode of Union, which consists in the participation or communication of Natures and idioms: indeed with a cunning design, establishing that even by this pact our Churches can be dragged into suspicion of this most foul heresy because of the doctrine concerning the true and real communication of both Natures and Idioms. But this matter stands far otherwise. For since Nestorius, as the Jesuit himself admits, taught that the Son of GOD assumed not only a Nature, but a human person: he certainly asserted such a participation or communication of Names and dignities as would be merely verbal, and would accrue to the human Nature as if it were a separate person subsisting by itself. From which opinion the confession of our Churches dissents with its whole camp, as they say, establishing such a Union of two Natures in Christ (as we shall show below) that neither one nor any Nature constitutes the person separately: But both together and simultaneously constitute one person: and thus, through this Union, the participation or κοινωνία of the divine Majesty itself, not just of the name, has accrued to the assumed humanity in the very unity of the person. And indeed, let the Jesuit consider well whether it is heretical and Nestorian if, according to this dogma of ours, the Son of Man is called and adored as the Son of GOD, not by himself or for his own sake, but for the sake of him by whom he was assumed.

As for the Calvinists, it is evident from their own words that they, just as much as the Jesuits, maliciously pervert the state of the Nestorian Controversy. For they too have contended that Nestorius divided Christ through different substances and hypostases into GOD separately, and man also separately: and taught that those very different hypostases were joined not by a substantial, but by a RELATIVE union according to an equality of authority and dignity, yet in a sublime and inseparable way through assistance. But we have just shown above that Nestorius never and nowhere affirmed this in open words: But constantly denied it, and indeed perpetually complained that he was unjustly condemned by Cyril and the Council of Ephesus on this account.

With these things thus established, it is easy to see what was the proper state of the controversy between Nestorius and Cyril and the remaining Orthodox: namely, concerning the communication of the Idioms of the two Natures in the one person of Christ: Whether, namely, the Union of these most diverse natures is to be defined in such a way that what is proper to humanity can be truly and really attributed to GOD because of the unity of the person: and vice versa? Since Nestorius stubbornly denied this Effect of the Hypostatic Union, it happened that consequently the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus, and especially Cyril, accused and convicted Nestorius, because from the denial of the Real communication of idioms, there follows also the denial of the personal Union: and the heretical tearing apart of one person into two separate persons. For if Mary did not give birth to GOD, but to a mere man: If the Jews crucified only a man, not GOD, it follows necessarily that there are two Christs, one born of Mary and crucified by the Jews: and another, not born of Mary, nor crucified by the Jews.

The Calvinist and Jesuit race so studiously conceals and covers up this state of the Nestorian controversy because it sees well that one egg cannot be more like another than their doctrine is like the Nestorian heresy. Certainly, if we descend to the very beginnings, as it were, of the unhappy controversy stirred up between the Sacramentarians and our side concerning the person of Christ, it is clearer than the midday sun: This and no other was the state of the controversy: Whether those things which are proper to the Divinity are, because of the unity of the person, also communicated to the human Nature? Where our side held the affirmative, and holds it today, teaching that from the personal union it followed that the body of Christ, because of the communication of divine Majesty that has taken place, can be present simultaneously and at once not only in many places, but in all places.

The Calvinists, or Sacramentarians, and those who today follow in their footsteps, the Jesuits, have simply embraced the negative, inventing a personal union of such a kind that from it no true and real communication of either natures or properties follows in any way: so that the human nature, even in the unity of the person itself, cannot be called omnipotent, nor omniscient, nor life-giving, nor omnipresent, nor adorable: but has received only a certain intermediate power, which is greater than that of the angels, and less than the power of God.

Here let the Church of God judge whether we, or indeed the Calvinists and Jesuits, are held guilty and convicted of the Nestorian heresy: and whether it can absolve them from this heresy, that, repeatedly imitating the language of Nestorius, they cry out that they believe and confess only one person of Christ, not two Christs. For the sentence of the Council of Ephesus stands firm and immovable: Whoever denies the Real Communication of Idioms: he also denies the unity of person in CHRIST: or: The communication of both Natures and these Idioms being denied as true and real, as that which is a necessary consequence of the personal Union; the unity of person in Christ is also denied.

Latin:

QUemadmodum in reliquis scientiis atque facultatibo, ex oppositione veri & falsi, veritas rectissimè elicitur: secundum vulgatum illud: Contrariis juxta se positis veritas magis elucescat: Ita in præsenti etiam mysterio, quod alioqui est planè ἐξαίρετον, omnem ingenii nostri captum transcendens, vix rectius versabimur, quàm si ex consideratione oppositorum, ad veritatis investigationem semper progrediamur. Priusquam igitur Orthodoxam nostrarum Ecclesiarum Doctrinam, de unione duarum Naturarum in Christo proponamus & confirmemus: operæ pretium fuerit, tùm veterum, tùm recentiorum hæreticorum, de eodem mysterio errores & placita diligentiùs cognoscere: idque tantò magis, quantò insidiosiùs hodiè factio tùm Jesuvitica, tùm Calviniana historiam veterum hæreseon pervertere, & earundem nostras Ecclesias reas peragere studet. Quanquam verò plures fuerunt ex veteribus, qui hanc doctrinæ Christianæ partem horribiliter conspurcarunt: ad duas tamen classes isti singuli & universi revocari possunt; quarum Unam Nestorianismus: alteram verò Eutychianismus occupat: de quibus ordine videbimus.

I. NESTORIANISMUS.

J Esuvita Bellarminus lib 3. de Persona Christi, cap 5. nostras Ecclesias Nestorianæ hæreseos reas peracturus, quatuor potissimùm constituit ejus capita.

Primum enim Nestorium docuisse scribit, B. Virginem purum hominem peperisse, & qui non solum Naturam, sed etiam personam humanam haberet.

Deinde vero B Mariam non esse DEI genetricem, sed Christi genericem.

3. Nativitatem, Passionem, Resurrectionem & Ascensionem CHRISTI soli homini tribuendam.

Tandem contendisse eundem Nestorium, Filium DEI unitum esse postea Filio Hominis, multis modis, non quidem substantialiter communicando οὐ- σίαν, sed Accidentaliter. Primo, secundum habitationem, quia verbum habitavit in homine Christo, ut in suo templo juxta illud Joh. 2, 19. Solvite templum hoc, & in tribus diebus excitabo illud. Et propterea dicebant, cap. 7. Jesaiae caute scriptum esse: Vocabitur nomen ejus Emmanuel, id est, non vocabitur DEUS, sed, Nobiscum DEUS, id est, in nobis habitans, juxta illud Joh. 1, 14. Et habitavit in nobis. Secundo per Unionem voluntatis & dilectionis, quia Filius ille hominis conjunctissimus erat semper cum DEI voluntate. Tertio, secundum operationem, quia Christus homo erat instrumentum, quo utebatur verbum in operibus illis admirandis, quae a Christo facta sunt. Quarto, secundum participationem, quia verbum illi homini impertivit nomen & dignitatem suam, ut nimirum Deus & DEI Filius vocaretur, & ab omnibus creaturis adoraretur, non propter se, sed propter eum, a quo assumtus fuerat: eo modo, quo imagines Sanctorum, nominibus eorum interdum appellantur, & propter eos etiam honorantur & adorantur.

Hanc Nestorij haeresin fuisse contendit Jesuvvita & impudenter sub finem citati capitis subjicit: Clarissime huic haeresi favet Brentius in lib. de Majestate Hominis Christi, ubi saepissime repetit, Filium DEI esse in Filio Mariae.

Calviniani Nestorij Confessionem in consensu suo Orthodoxo, pag. 52. his verbis describunt: Fatebatur, inquiunt, Nestorius DEUM verbum in ista summa & inseparabili conjunctione ad hominem suam ducere carnem, velut proprium sua inhabitationis templum, ipsiusque passionem & proprietates sibi appropriare. Verum hoc non aliter intellexit, quam per quandam Relationem, sicut proprium est hominis, quo indutus est vestimentu, & quatenus injuriam, que vesti fit, suam esse propriam ducit homo. Propter indutum inquit, Indumentum veneror, & propter occultum, adoro visibilem, Indivisibilis a visibili DEUS secundum hanc humanitatis ad DEUM verbum unionem & conjunctionem, eodem modo DEUM visibilem vocari dicit DEUM, propter nominum communionem, non autem propter eandem dignitatem.

Caeterum, si tum scripta Cyrilli, tum acta Synodi Ephesinae, in qua Nestorius erroris convictus & damnatus est, paulo accuratius expendamus, manifestum evadit, tum Jesuvvitas, tum Calvinianos Nestorij haeresin minus candide definire, & per manifesta crimina falsi, eandem corrumpere.

Et ut seorsim de singulis illis quatuor capitib9, quæ Jesuvvita proposuit, agamus: Constat quidé initiò, Nestorium à Synodo Ephesina damnatum propterea fuisse, quod docuisset, B. Virginem Mariam, purũ hominẽ peperisse: Verum tamen & illud constat, ipsum Nestorium non ita solitum esse loqui. Extat enim Epistola ejus ad Cyrillũ Alexandrinũ, Tom. 4. operum Cyrilli: Extant & Testimonia quædam ex Nestorij libris desumta, sub finem illius Tomi, in quibus magna asseveratione Nestori9 contendit, unam tantummodò in Christo personam esse, eandemq; personam & verè DEUM & verè hominem: sic inter reliqua ad Cyrillum scribens: In secundo capite Epistolæ tuæ, Naturarũ quidem distinctionem, secundum incarnationis & Divinitatis rationem, & harum in unam personam conjunctionem prædicas: & DEUM verbum, secundâ illâ, quæ ex muliere facta est, opus non habuisse generatione, nec divinitatem passionis fuisse capacẽ, confiteris. Sunt ista verè Orthodoxa, & perversis omnium hæreseon, circa Dominicas naturas, dogmatibus contraria. Et sub finem ejusdem Epistolæ: Quòd divinitatis templum sit corpus: & quòd templum hoc, absolutum ac divina copulatione coadunatũ, Natura sibi divinitatis, velut proprium conjunxerit, bonum est, ut confiteamur, & Evangelicis traditionibus dignum. Et dilucidiùs ipse rursum Nestorius peculiari quodam libro Quaternione decima septima Tom. IIII. operum Cyrilli, Col. 300. Erat quidem DEUS Verbũ antequàm homo fieret DEUS, & patri conjunctus: Posterioribus autem temporibus formam servi accepit: Verùm cùm antea Filius & fuerit & vocatus sit: non potest assumptam servi formam SEPARATIM vocari Filius: ne duos Filios statuamus. Quoniam autem ei conjunctus est, qui in principio Filius erat postquam illi conjunctus est, non potest recipere divisionem.

Ex quibus sanè testimonijs falsum esse evidentissimè patet, quòd Jesuvvita affirmat. Nestorium initiò docuisse B. Virginem purum hominem peperisse, & qui non solum Naturam, sed & Personam humanam haberet. Disertis enim verbis Nestorius unam singularem perfonam in Christo asseruit, & apertè testatus est, quòd duæ in Christo Naturæ distinctæ, in unig personæ conjunctionem pervenerint.

Sed objiciat aliquis, si errorem istum non fovit Nestorius, Quorsum ergò in Concilio Ephesino damnatus fuit tanquam qui duas personas in Christo statucret? Respondemus eum B. Luthero nostro ex libro de Conciliis & Ecclesia, jure optimo ipsum damnatum esse. Implicabat enim Nestorius manifestissimam contradictionem.. Etsi enim Christum verum DEUM & hominem in una persona apertè docebat: ejusmodi tamen unionem statuebat, ex qua neque Naturarum, neq; Idiomatum communicatio sequeretur. Atque ita eodem planè modo, quo hodiè Calviniani & Jesuvvitæ, Antecedens quidem verum esse verbis concedebat: hoc est, duas naturas in unam personam unitas esse, fatebatur: sed Effectum sive consequens negabat, quod tamen ex Antecedente necessario sequebatur, undè Cyrillus cum primis, & reliqui Orthodoxi patres Concilij Ephesini multis argumentis demonstratè runt: ipsum unam in Christi personam in duas divellere; licèt hoc fateri nolit. Meminerint proindè Adversarij Anathema illud, quo patres Ephesinæ Synodi sententiam Nestorij ratione primi hujus capitis percusserunt: ipsorû simul doctrinam directè tangere & ferire: quantumvis etiam cum Nestorio fateri nolint, se negatâ reali tùm Naturarum tùm idiomatum κοινωνίᾳ personam Christi, in duas personas discerpere. Nos autem Christianos, inquit, Lutherus, ejusmodi unionem duarum Naturarum credere oportet, ex qua idiomata utriusꝙ, Naturæ, personæ pariter & simul omnia tribuantur: videlicet, cum dicimus, Christus est DEUS & homo, in una persona: ideo quicquid dicitur de Christo tanquam Homine, idem quoque de DEO oportet affirmare: videlicet, Christus est mortuus, & Christus est DEUS, Ergò DEUS est mortuus; non separatus DEUS, sed cum humanitate unitus DEUS. Nam de separato DEO utrumꝙ falsum est, videlicet, quod Christus DEUS sit, & quod DEUS mortuus sit: Quoniam tali consideratione DEUS non est homo: Si verò admirabile in oculis Nestorij videtur, DEUM esse mortuũ: vicissim cogitare debebat, mirabile quoque esse, quòd DEUS factus est homo. Hoc enim modo immortalis DEUS fit Hoc, quod pati, mori potest, & omnia humana idiomata habet. Quid enim esset Homo ille, cum quo DEUS unitus est, si humana Idiomata non haberet? Phantasma esset, sicut Manichæi & Marcionitæ docuerunt. Nisi enim DEUS pro nobis esset mortuus, sed homo tantùm, nequaquam redemti essemus, sed periissemus simul omnes. Passione enim & morte redemti sumus, non hominis tantùm, sed DEI hominis, qui DEUS homo pro nobis passꝫ & mortuꝫ est: Et sic DEI sangvine Ecclesia redemta est. Similiter quicquid de DEO dicitur, idem quoque homini tribuendum est, videlicet, Deus est omnipotens, Homo Christus est DEUS, ideò Homo Christus est omnipotens. Quoniam una persona sunt DEUS & Homo: ideò persona Christi, utriusꝙ Naturæ Idiomata habet. Hactenus Lutherus.

Quoad alterum caput Nestorianæ hæreseos, litem de eo Jesuvvitæ non movemus: Testatur enim historia Ecclesiastica, circa A. C. 430. Anastasium quendam presbyterum, quem Nestoriꝫ Episcopus Constantinopolitanus Antiochiâ secum Constantinopolim adduxerat, pro publica Concione docuisse, Mariam à nemine appellandam esse θεοτόκον, Deiparam, sive DEI genetricem, sed χριϛοτόκον tantùm. Fuisse enim eam Hominem tantùm, & DEUM ab Homine generari, prorsus esse impossibile. Quam & verborum & dogmatum novitatem cum omnes pij aversarentur; Nestorius, qui plus amico Anastasio quàm veritati tribueret, patrocinium illius suscepit: in hæc etiam verba erumpens: Noli gloriari Judæe: Non DEUM, sed hominem crucifixisti: negans itidem Filium DEI dici posse διμηνιαῖον καὶ τριμηνιαῖον, bimestrem, aut trimestrem appellari.
