Erroris hujus causa unica erat hæc, quod talem statuebat unionem duarum naturarum in Christo, ex qua nulla prorsus realis tùm Naturarum, tùm idiomatum Communicatio flueret.

Tertium hæreseos Nestorianæ caput, ex sententia Bellarmini est, quòd statuerit Nestorius, Nativitatem, passionem, mortem, Resurrectionem & Ascensionem Christi, SOLI Homini tribuendam esse. Qua in parte Jesuvvita verum scripsit: Siquidem ex negatione communicationis idiomatum hoc ipsum necessariò sequitur, quemadmodum illud paulò antè ex Luthero est ostensum. Mirari autem satis non possumus Jesuvvitam hoc dogma in Nestorio, tanquam hæreticum rejicere ac damnare, cùm eodem l. 3. cap. in nostris Doctoribus, tanquam Eutichianum dogma damnaverit, quòd non soli homini, sed toti personæ, Actiones & passiones illas adscribant: ita ut quamvis Divinitas ipsa sit & maneat impassibilis: Filius tamen DEI in carne assumta verè passus esse dicatur.

In Quarto hæreseos capite, quod Nestorio tribuit Bellarminus, quædam libenter largimur: nonnulla verò tanquam adulterina & in fraudem nostrarum Ecclesiarum conficta improbamus. Largimur, primos tres Unionis modos, non tàm à Nestorio, quàm ab ipsius asseclis eo modo explicatos & defensos fuisse, quo à Jesuvvita definiūtur. Improbamus verò, quòd Quartum illum Unionis modum, qui in participatione sive communicatione Naturarum & idiomatum consistat, neque candidè proponit, neque dextrè explicat: astuto sanè consilio, vel hoc pacto nostras Ecclesias ob doctrinam de vera ac reali tùm Naturarum, tùm Idiomatum communicationem, in suspicionem teterrimæ hujus hæreseos rapi posse, statuens. Sed longè aliter res hæc se habet. Cùm enim Nestorius, ipso Jesuvvita fatente, docuerit, Filium DEI, non Naturam tantum, sed personam humanam assumsisse: utique talē participationem sive communicationem Nominum ac dignitatum asseruit, quæ verbalis tantùm esset, & Naturæ humanæ, tanquam personæ separatæ & per se subsistenti, obtingeret. A qua sententia nostrarum Ecclesiarum confessio, totis, quod ajunt, castris dissidet, talem (uti infra ostendemus) Unionem duarum Naturarum in Christo statuens, ut non alterutra, vel quælibet Natura seorsim personam: Sed utraque junctim & simul unam personam constituat: & sic mediante hac Unione, assumtæ humanitati in ipsa personæ unitate, non nominis modò: sed & ipsius Majestatis divinæ participatio sive κοινωνία obvenerit. Et sanè, num hæreticum & Nestorianum sit, si secundum hoc dogma nostrum Filius Hominis, non per se aut propter se: sed propter eum, à quo assumtus est, Filius DEI vocetur & adoretur, probè dispiciat Jesuvvita.

Quoad Calvinianos, constat ex ipsorum verbis, ipsos æquè ac Jesuvvitas statum Controversiæ Nestorianæ, malitiosè pervertere. Contenderunt enim & isti, Nestorium divisisse Christum per diversas substantias & hypostases in DEUM seorsim, & hominem quoq; seorsim: & docuisse, illas ipsas diversas hypostases, non substantiali quadam, sed RELATIV A unione secundū autoritatis & dignitatis aqualitatem, sublimi tamen & inseparabili modo per assistentiam esse conjunctas. Sed jam modò supra ostendimus, Nestorium nunquam & nuspiam apertis verbis hoc affirmasse: Sed constanter negasse, imò perpetuò conquestum esse, se hoc nomine à Cyrillo & Concilio Ephesino injustè damnatum esse.

Quibus ita constitutis, facilè videre est, Quis fuerit proprius status controversiæ inter Nestorium & Cyrillum ac reliquos Orthodoxos: nempè, De communicatione Idiomatum duarum Naturarum, in una Christi persona: An videlicet Unio istarum diversissimarum naturarum ita sit definienda, ut quæ humanitatis propria sunt, DEO propter unitatem personæ, verè ac realiter tribui possint: & vice versà? Hunc Effectum Unionis Hypostaticæ cùm Nestorius pertinaciter negaret, factum, ut sic consequenter Patres Concilii Ephesini, & cumprimis Cyrillus Nestorium accusarent & convincerēt, quod ex negatione Realis communicationis idiomatum, sequatur etiam Unionis personalis negatio: & unius personæ in duas separatas personas, hæretica discerptio. Si enim Maria non DEUM peperit, sed nudum hominem: Si Judæi hominem tantùm, non DEUM crucifixerunt, sequitur necessariò, duos esse Christos, unum ex Maria natum, & à Judæis Crucifixum:alterum verô, non ex Maria natum, neque à Judæis crucifixum.

Statum istum controversiæ Nestorianæ, ideo Calviniana & Jesuvvitica gens usque adeò studiosè occultat & tegit, quia probè videt, neque ovum ovo similius esse posse, quam ipsorum sit doctrina cum hæresi Nestoriana. Certè si ad ipsa quasi primordia infelicis controversiæ, inter Sacramentarios & nostros de persona Christi motæ, descendamus, Sole meridiano clarius patet: Hunc & non alium fuisse statum controversiæ: An quæ Divinitatis propria sunt, propter personæ unitatem, etiam Naturæ humanæ sint communicata? Ubi nostri Affirmativam tenuerunt, hodieque tenent, docentes, ex unione personali illud consecutum esse, ut corpus Christi propter factam communicationem Majestatis divinæ, possit simul & semel non modò in plurimis, sed & in omnibus locis præsens adesse.

Calviniani verò sive Sacramentarii, & horum hodiè vestigiis insistentes Jesuvvitæ, Negativam simpliciter sunt amplexi, ejusmodi Unionem personalem comminiscentes, ex qua vera ac Realis vel Naturarum, vel idiomatum Communicatio nullo pacto sequatur: ita ut Humana natura neque omnipotens, neque omniscia, neque vivifica, neque omnipræsens, neque adorabilis, in ipsa etiam unitate personæ dici possit: Sed MEDIAM tantùm quandam potentiam acceperit, quæ major sit quàm Angelorum, & minor quàm DEI potentia.

Hic judicet Ecclesia DEI, num nos, an verò Calviniani & Jesuvvitæ Nestorianæ hæresews rei & convicti teneantur: & num eos ab hac hæresi absolvere possit, quòd lingvam Nestorii imitati subindè clamitant, se unam tantùm personam Christi, non duos Christos credere & confiteri. Stat enim firma & immota sententia Concilii Ephesini: Quisquis Realem Communicationem Idiomatum negat: is quoq́; unitatem personæ in CHRISTO negat: vel: Negata communicatione verâ & reali, tùm Naturarum, tùm harum Idiomatum, ut quæ Unionis personalis necessarium consequens est; unitas quoque personæ in Christo negatur.


### Chapter Second: II. Eutychianism

II. EUTYCHIANISM.

The Jesuit Bellarmine likewise establishes four heads of the Eutychian heresy: indeed in such a way that he taught, 1. That in Christ after the incarnation there was and is only one nature. Then: That one nature was made from Divinity and flesh, through the conversion of Divinity into flesh, because it is written, John 1:14, The Word was made flesh: And for one thing to become another is to be turned into it, just as when water was made wine, water was converted into wine: and now, when bread through consecration becomes the flesh of Christ, bread is converted into the flesh of Christ. Thirdly: That the Divinity of the Word was born, suffered, died, and was buried. Fourthly: That the flesh of Christ is not of the same nature as ours, nor was the Word converted into true flesh, but into a certain apparent and phantastic flesh: so that the Word rather simulated that he was born and died as a man, than that he truly was.

Moreover, one could hardly judge more correctly either of this Jesuit narrative or of the Eutychian heresy than if we hear Eutyches himself speaking: who in the Council of Chalcedon comprised his Confession in these words; as witnessed by Evagrius, book 1, chapter 9. I confess our Lord, before the divinity was joined with the humanity, to have been of two natures: but after the conjunction of these things, I affirm that only one nature existed in him: I also affirm that the body of the Lord does not consist of the same substance as our body. Nicephorus also confirms this same thing, book 18, chapter 52, saying: Eutyches, he himself also said there were two natures before the union, then united: But after the union, he opined that they had passed into one nature, and were confused, and had undergone a mixture. But since Leo the Roman and other ecclesiastical writers everywhere assert that the heresy of Eutyches was diametrically opposed to the Nestorian heresy, it must certainly be seen how that matter stands. Vigilius explains this most excellently in book 2 against Eutyches: Nestorius, looking at two natures, thought there were two persons: Eutyches, looking at one person, judged there to be one nature. And because there is in Christ both the property of Natures and the union of person; Nestorius, attending to the property of the natures, fell away from the union of the person: And Eutyches, looking at one person, failed in the property of the natures, and asserted that the divinity itself suffered. You see what a dangerous thing it is either not to believe one person in Christ, or to refuse to confess two natures. While I defend one person of Christ against Nestorius, I am thought, according to Eutyches, to deny the human nature: while I bring forward two natures against Eutyches, I am thought, according to Nestorius, to profess two persons: because he believed that two Christs and two persons were to be ascribed to two natures. Thus far Vigilius. It is certain, however, from these narratives: Just as Nestorius did not at all confess that he expressly asserted two persons, and yet he was most justly condemned on this very account: So also Eutyches, even though he complained that certain things were imputed to him unjustly, such as that he taught that the Divinity suffered: and that the flesh of Christ was apparent and phantastic: so that the Word rather simulated that he was born and died as a man, than that he truly was: yet he too was most justly both accused and condemned on this account.

For because he feigned such a Union of two Natures in Christ, from which the Idioms of the divine nature became the Idioms of the human nature itself: Therefore he was judged to have clearly annihilated and denied the human nature.

It is certain, then, that those four heads of heresy which Bellarmine designated are not to be ascribed simply to Eutyches. Eutyches held the first and second entirely. But the third, Eutyches himself complained was imputed to him unjustly: although in reality it followed from the two following heads. Eutyches openly asserted the former part of the fourth head: but he denied the latter in words: although it necessarily followed from the former.

It is certain, finally, with what effrontery and conscience both the Calvinists and the Jesuits accuse our churches of Eutychianism. Let them produce, I beseech you, a Council, a Synod, an Assembly, in which the Lutherans were legitimately heard, and convicted and condemned of this or any other heresy? Let them also demonstrate that we constitute such a Hypostatic union that leaves only one Nature in Christ. For what the Adversaries bark about in this place from the doctrine concerning the Majesty of the flesh of Christ will be subjected to censure below in chapter 3.

Latin:

II. EUTYCHIANISMUS.

EUtychianæ hæresews quatuor itidem Capita constituit Jesuvvita Bellarminus: ita quidem ut docuerit, 1. In Christo post incarnationem unam tantùm fuisse & esse naturam. Deindè: Unam esse factam naturam ex Divinitate & carne, per conversionem Divinitatis in carnem, quia scriptum est, Joh. 1, 14. Verbum caro factum est: Et unum fieri alterum, est verti in illud, sicut cùm aqua facta est vinum, aqua conversa est in vinum: & nunc, cùm panis per consecrationem fit caro Christi, panis convertitur in carnem Christi. Tertiò: Divinitatem Verbi natam, passam, mortuam, sepultam fuisse. Quartò: Christi carnem non esse ejusdem naturæ cum nostrâ, neque Verbum in veram carnem esse conversum, sed in carnem quandam apparentem & phantasticam: ita ut potiùs Verbum simulaverit se hominem natum & mortuum esse, quàm revera fuerit.

Cæterùm vix rectiùs vel de narratione ista Jesuvvitica, vel de hæresi Eutychiana judicari poterit, quàm si ipsummet Eutychen loquentem audiamus: qui in Concilio Chalcedonensi his verbis suam Confessionem complexus est; teste Evagrio lib. 1. cap. 9. Confiteor Dominum nostrum antequam divinitas cum humanitate conjungeretur, ex duabus fuisse naturis: at post harum rerum conjunctionem, unam solùm naturam in eo extitisse affirmo: Idem etiam corpus Domini non ex eadem substantia cum nostro corpore constare, affirmo. Quod ipsum confirmat etiam Nicephorus lib. 18. cap. 52. Eutyches, inquiens, duas quidem & ipse ante unionem naturas dixit, deindè unitas: Post unionem autem in unam eas naturam abiisse, confusaque esse, mixtionem subiisse, opinatus est. Verùm cum Leo Romanus, aliique passim Scriptores Ecclesiastici asserant, Eutychis hæresin, Nestorianæ hæresi è diametro fuisse oppositam, utique videndum fuerit, Quomodo & istud sese habeat. Id verò præclarissimè explicat Vigilius lib. 2. contra Eutychen: Nestorius duas intuens naturas, duas putavit esse personas: Eutyches unam respiciens personam, unam censuit esse naturam. Et quia est in Christo, & Naturarum proprietas & personæ unio; Nestorius proprietatem attendens naturarum, à personæ excidit unione: Et Eutyches unam intuens personam, à naturarum proprietate defcivit, & ipsam divinitatem asseruit passam. Vides, quanti periculi res sit, aut unam in Christo non credere personam, aut duas confiteri nolle naturas. Dùm unam contra Nestorium, Christi defendo personam, existimor secundum Eutychen, humanam negare naturam: dum contra Eutychen duas affero naturas, existimor secundum Nestorium, duas profiteri personas: quia ille duabus naturis, duos Christos duasq́; personas credidit adscribendas. Hactenus Vigilius. Constat verò ex narrationibus istis: Quemadmodum Nestorius expressè duas à se personas asseri, minimè confitebatur, & tamé hoc ipso nomine justissimè est condemnatus: Ita etiam Eutychen, etsi quædam sibi per injuriam imputari conquerebatur, ut quòd Divinitatem passam esse doceret: & carnem Christi apparentem, & phantasticam fuisse: ita ut potiùs Verbum simulavit, se hominem natum & mortuum esse, quàm revera fuerit: tamen ipsum quoque hoc nomine justissimè & accusatum & condemnatum esse.

Quia enim ejusmodi Unionem duarum in Christo Naturarum fingebat, ex qua Idiomata divinæ naturæ, facta sint Idiomata ipsius humanæ naturæ: Ideò humanam naturam planè annihilasse, & negasse, judicatus est.

Constat deindè, quatuor illa hæreseos capita, quæ Bellarminus designavit, non simpliciter Eutychi esse adscribenda. Primum quidem & Secundum Eutyches omninò tenuit. Tertium verò, ipse Eutyches sibi per injuriam imputari conquestus est: quamvis reverâ illud exprimis duobus capitibus sequeretur. Quarti capitis membrum prius apertè asserebat Eutyches: posterius verò itidem verbis negabat: licèt illud ex priore necessariò sequeretur.

Constat denique, quâ fronte & conscientia tùm Calviniani, tùm Jesuvvitæ, nostras Ecclesias Eutychianismi insimulent. Proferant, obsecro, Concilium, Synodum, Conventum, in quo Lutherani legitimè auditi, & vel hujus, vel alterius alicujus hæreseos convicti & damnati? Demonstrent etiam, Nos ejusmodi unionem Hypostaticam constituere, quæ unam tantùm in Christo Naturam relinquat. Nam quæ hoc loco Adversarii ex doctrinâ de Majestate carnis Christi ogganniunt, infrà cap. 3. censuræ subjicientur.


### Chapter Second: III. Jesuitism

III. JESUITISM

What the doctrine of the Jesuits is concerning the Hypostatic Union of the two natures in Christ, [may be learned] most correctly from their leader Bellarmine as he, in book 3 on the Incarnation, chapter 8, page 471, letter A, explains his own mind and that of his associates thus: That GOD and Man are united hypostatically is nothing else than that the human Nature does not have its own subsistence, but has been assumed by the eternal Word to the very subsistence of the Word. This Jesuitical confession is entirely stitched together and conflated from Sophistries. For he shamefully explains the same thing by itself, and says that a personal Union is nothing else than a personal Union: or that this Union is that which the Human nature does not subsist by itself, but is assumed into the subsistence of the Word. Where the point is shamefully begged. For this very thing is sought, What is that which the Human nature, which by itself is ἀνυπόςατος, is so united with the λόγῳ, that it constitutes one person with him. While the Jesuits do not explain this, it is manifest that they are foisting upon us a lame, mutilated, and imperfect Definition of this Union. Nor should this seem a wonder to anyone, since they stubbornly deny the Effect of this Union, which consists in the mutual κοινωνίᾳ of the Natures toward one another, and in the communication of their idioms: so that phrases and locutions that are clearly Nestorian, nay, worse than Nestorian, occur in great number in the writings of the Jesuits.

For is it not Nestorian, what Bellarmine in the preceding chapter 7, page 469, letter D, did not shrink from writing: Christ GOD does not receive the divine Nature from Mary, but the human, nor is he her Son, except insofar as he is Man. Thus, therefore, Mary will not be θεοτόκος: which is the very thing Nestorius felt.

Is it not Nestorian that in the preceding chapter, the fourth, the same Jesuit does not concede this proposition, This Man is GOD, otherwise than that the subject, This Man, does not stand also for the human nature of Christ, or, which is the same thing, for the whole person of Christ: but only for his Divinity. The Angel, of course, was ignorant of this permutation of supposita, saying to Mary, This your Son shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the highest: Likewise, That which shall be born of you, shall be called the Son of GOD. Luke 1, 31 and 35.

Does it not smack of Nestorianism what he asserts in the same chapter 4, page 457, letter D, that one can no more say there are two Christs, on account of the union of two natures, than it is permitted to call him who has two crafts two craftsmen: or to say that he who has several garments is several clothed persons: but one craftsman, and one clothed person: Do two crafts, therefore, or several garments, constitute one Man, just as two Natures constitute one person?

But the Jesuit proceeds, intending to confirm his own definition: In three ways, he says, can several things be united: First, Essentially, when one essence is made from several. In the second way, Accidentally, as when Accidents are joined to a subject, or when a substance is coupled to a substance: but from the coupling nothing arises except an accidental form. In the third way, substantially, as when a substance, which otherwise would exist by itself, is drawn to the being of another suppositum, and depends upon it, as a part of it. And in this third way alone has the union been made. Thus far the Jesuit. To whose assertion, as regards the first two ways, we willingly subscribe,

That, namely, this union is not to be defined by an Essential, nor by an Accidental Mode of Union. For as regards the Essential Mode, it is either hyperphysical or physical. The former has a place only in the Mystery of the Trinity, where the three persons communicate in the unity of the most simple Essence: so that it ought to be called the unity rather than the union of the three persons, for the reason that a union is of those things which at one time were not one: which are at least separable by ἐπινοίᾳ, by thought: Neither of which has a place in the Essence of the Divinity, which is most simply and eternally one. The latter mode, which is Physical, has a place when one Essence is made from several Essences, and one certain composite thing from matter and form: as from Soul and body one Man is naturally made. Which Natural mode, although it has some kinship with the Mode of the Union of the two natures in Christ: yet it is in no way similar to it. For in that Natural Union the united parts are separable. 2. Neither has its perfection in itself without the other. 3. From that composition arises some third thing, which is most different from both parts: namely, Man. All of which things clearly abhor this Mystery, as our thesis will explain a little later.

Thus as regards the Accidental Mode, although it is various and manifold, and is either made κατὰ μῖξιν, which is the union of altered mixables, as when mead is made from water and honey: or κατὰ σῶρον, by aggregation, as when one heap arises from a collection of grains: or κατὰ συνάφειαν, by contact, as stone is glued and joined to stone, iron to iron, plank to plank: or κατὰ τάξιν καὶ σχέσιν, as Mars and his Spouse, or the multitude of the faithful are said to be one. Acts 4, 22. or finally ἀξίας καὶ τιμῆς, by respect of dignity, several are said to be one thing. These modes already enumerated, both essential and accidental, Bellarmine very rightly rejects and disapproves: In which part he also has us clearly in agreement.

But in the third mode, which he names Substantial, we initially disapprove of the fact that he has taken the substantial and subsistential or personal Mode as the same: quite foolishly and unskillfully indeed. For since Essential and substantial differ from each other only as Genus and Species: if indeed Essential is as it were a certain Genus: comprehending under its scope both substantial and Accidental: How, I ask, can he call it a Substantial Mode of this union, when he himself denies, and indeed very rightly, that it can be called Essential? For this mode of the Union of the two Natures in Christ cannot by any reason be referred to the Essential, as a Species to its Genus: but it differs from it, and thus also from the Substantial Mode, in its whole genus. Whence it is clearly evident that the Jesuit names the mode of this union καταχρηστικῶς, abusively and clearly improperly, nay, falsely, as Substantial. Nor is there any reason for him to protect himself by the authority of certain ancient Ecclesiastical Writers, who it is established used the word ὑποστάσεως, through the word

of substance formerly rendered. For it cannot be denied that this inconvenient version was seized upon and adapted by certain heretics, and especially by the Sabellians, to cloak a most foul heresy. Whence this explanation was clearly rejected by later writers, and the word ὑποστάσεως was most correctly rendered by the term subsistence or person.

Furthermore, we cannot approve of the definition of this substantial mode in every respect. For Bellarmine says that a substantial union (he understands it as personal) exists when a substance, which would otherwise exist by itself, is drawn to the being of another suppositum and depends upon it as a part of it: and in this way the incarnation was effected. Nor does it square with the ὑποτύπωσιν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων (pattern of sound words) what the Jesuit asserts, that the person of the Word depends upon that other suppositum, that is, upon the human nature, as a part of it. For if he understands this by reason of the humanity of Christ, considered in itself, it would be most false, nay, most heretical, to assert that the substance or person of the Word depends upon it as a part. But if he wishes this to be understood of the whole person of Christ, and maintains that it is composed of two parts, we bid him consider only this: whether he is speaking with the Roman Church and explaining that sublime mystery of the Hypostatic union accurately enough. The Scholastic Doctors themselves certainly did not wish to concede that in the person of Christ two natures are to be considered as parts, as can be seen in Gabriel Biel, in Book 3 of the Sentences, dist. 6, Q. 2, Art. 1, Doubt 1, letter F. And although among ancient and more recent writers there are perhaps not lacking those who call the human nature a part—just as Hesychius in chapter 5 of Leviticus expressly calls it a part of the Trinity—yet it is clear to those weighing the matter more accurately that they spoke, and speak today, improperly. For first, parts as parts are predicated neither of the whole nor of each other: just as certainly a man is neither soul nor body; nor is the soul the body, nor is the body the soul. Yet the two natures in the person of Christ are most truly predicated of each other in the concrete, as: GOD is Man: Man is GOD. Furthermore, every part without the conjunction of the other principal parts is imperfect, as the body, for example, without the soul is a corpse rather than a body; and the soul separated from the body always has a certain dependence upon the body, whence it awaits the resurrection of the body. But far be it from us to posit such a thing concerning the Word, the Son of GOD, who even if He had never assumed human nature, or (if it were possible) were to lay it aside again, would nevertheless be a whole that is most absolute and most perfect. A more convenient mode of speech, therefore, will be if the person of Christ is said to consist not of two parts, but of two wholes and entireties, each most perfect in its own kind: yet so that the assumed could be perfected by the assumer above the condition of its own nature. But perhaps under this phrase the Jesuit wished to hide that clearly Nestorian dogma which the Jesuit faction today holds and strives to defend, along with certain ancient Scholastics, concerning the truth of these propositions: This Man is GOD: and This GOD is Man; contending that this Man cannot be GOD ὑπερφυτικῶς (supernaturally), because GOD and Man are two disparate species, neither of which can be the other, just as an ass cannot be a man, nor a man an ass. Wherefore they interpret this proposition, This Man is GOD, thus: The Son of GOD is GOD, who sustains the human nature: by which method every respect of the assumed Man is entirely excluded from the subject (Man), and nothing is left besides the bare name. But of these things more fully below. Let these things suffice in this place, from which the impiety of the Jesuit dogma concerning the Hypostatic union of two natures in Christ is more than sufficiently known.

Latin:

III. JESUITISMUS

QUæ sit Jesuvvitarum doctrina de Unione Hypostatica duarum Naturarum in Christo, rectissimè ex ipsorum coryphæo Bellarmino cognoscitur. Is autem lib. 3. de Incarnat. cap. 8. p. 471. lit. A. suam suorumque sociorum mentem sic explicat: Uniri hypostaticè DEUM & Hominem, nihil est aliud quàm Naturam humanam non habere propriam subsistentiam: sed assumtam esse à Verbo æterno, ad ipsam verbi subsistentiam. Confessio hæc Jesuvitica ex Sophisticationibus tota est consuta & conflata. Turpiter enim idem per seipsum explicat, & Unionem personalem dicit nihil esse aliud, quàm Unionem personalem: vel Unionem hanc esse id, quod Humana natura non per se subsistit, sed est assumta in Verbi subsistentiam. Ubi turpiter petitur principium. Hoc ipsum enim quæritur, Quod sit illud, quod Humana natura, quæ per se est ἀνυπόςατος, ita est unita cum λόγῳ, ut unam cum eo personam constituat. Quod dum Jesuvvitæ non explicant, manifestum est, mancam, mutilam & imperfectam Definitionem Unionis huj9 ipsos nobis obtrudere. Neque hoc mirum cuipiam videre debet, cùm Effectum Unionis hujus, qui in mutuâ Naturarum ad se invicem κοινωνίᾳ, earundemque idiomatum communicatione consistit, mordicus negent: ita ut Nestorianas planè, imò Nestorianis deteriores phrases & locutionem in Jesuvvitarum scriptis, magno numero occurrant.

Annon enim Nestorianum est, quod Bellarminus præcedente capite 7. pag. 469. lit. D. scribere non exhorruit: Christus DEUS non accipit à Maria Naturam divinam, sed humanam, nec est ejus Filius, nisi quatenus Homo. Sic ergo Maria non erit θεοτόκος : quod ipsum sensit Nestorius.

An non Nestorianum est, quòd cap. præced. quarto idem Jesuvvita, propositionem hanc, Hic Homo est DEUS, aliter non concedit, quàm ut subjectum Hic Homo, non supponat etiam pro humana Christi natura, vel, quod idem est, pro tota Christi persona: sed tantùm pro ejus Divinitate. Ignoravit nimirùm hanc suppositorum permutationem Angelus, dicens ad Mariam, Hic tuus Filius erit magnus, & Filius altissimi vocabitur: Item, Quod ex te nascetur, Filius DEI vocabitur. Luc. 1, 31. & 35.

Annon Nestorianismum resipit quod eodem cap. 4. p. 457. lit. D. asserit, tàm non posse duos Christos dici, propter duarum naturarum unionem, quàm non liceat eum, qui duas habet artes, vocare duos artifices: vel qui plures habeat vestes, dicere plures vestitos: sed unum artificem, & unum vestitum: Siccinè ergo duæ artes, vel plures vestes, unum constituunt Hominem, sicut duæ Naturæ unam personam?

Sed pergit Jesuvvita, suamq; definitionem confirmaturus: Tribus, inquit, modis, aliqua plura possunt uniri: Primo Essentialiter, cùm ex pluribus fit una essentia. Secundo modo Accidentaliter, ut cùm Accidentia subjecto adjungūtur, vel cum substantia substantiæ copulatur: sed ex copula non exurgit nisi forma accidentalis. Tertio modo substantialiter, ut cùm substantia, quæ alioqui per se existeret, trahitur ad esse alterius suppositi, & ab illo pendet, tanquam pars ipsius. Et hoc solo modo tertio facta est unio. Hactenus Jesuvvita. Cujus assertioni, quoad duos priores modos libéter subscribim9,

Quòd nimirùm neque Effentiali, neque Accidentali Unionis Modo, unio isthæc sit definienda. Nam quoad Modum Effentialem, ille vel hyperphysicus est, vel physicus. Prior ille tantùm in Mysterio Trinitatis locum habet, ubi tres personæ, simplicissima Essentiæ unitate communicant: ita ut unitas magis & rectiùs, quàm unio trium personarum dici debeat, propterea quòd unio est eorum, quæ aliquando unum non fuerunt: quæ saltem ἐπινοίᾳ cogitatione sunt separabilia: Quorum neutrum in Divinitatis Essentiâ simplicissimè atque æternùm una, locum habet. Posterior modus, qui Physicus est, tùm locum habet, quando ex pluribus Essentiis una fit Essentia, & ex materia & formâ unum quiddam compositum: ut ex Anima & corpore Naturaliter unus fit Homo. Qui modus Naturalis etsi aliquid cognationis habet cum Modo Unionis duarum naturarum in Christo: tamen ei undiquaque minimè est similis. Sunt enim in Unione illa Naturali partes unitæ separabiles. 2. Neutra in sese fine altera perfectionem suam habet. 3. Ex compositione ista oritur aliquod tertium, quod est à parte utraque diversissimum: nempè Homo. Quæ omnia ab hoc Mysterio planè abhorrent, uti paulò pòst, thesis nostra expediet.

Sic quoad Modum Accidentalem, etsi varius ac multiplex ille est, & vel fit κατὰ μῖξιν, quæ est τῶν μικτῶν ἀλλοιοθέντων ἕνωσις miscebilium alteratorum unio, ut cùm ex aqua & melle fit mulsum: κατὰ σῶρον aggregationem, ut quando ex collectione granorum, unus acervus oritur: vel κατὰ συνάφειαν, contactum lapis lapidi, ferrum ferro, asser afferi, conglutinatur & compingitur: vel κατὰ τάξιν καὶ σχέσιν, Martius & Conjux, vel multitudo fidelium unum esse dicuntur. Act. 4, 22. vel denique ἀξίας καὶ τιμῆς dignitatis respectu, plures unum quid esse dicuntur. Hos sanè modos jam enumeratos tùm essentiales, tùm Accidentales rectissimè rejicit & improbat Bellarminus: Quæ etiam in parte nos sibi planè habet ὁμοψήφους.

Cæterùm in modo tertio, quem Substantialem nominat, illud initiò improbamus, quod substantialem & subsistentialem sive personalê Modum pro iisdem sumsit: satis profectò & ineptè & imperitè Cum enim Essentiale & substantiale tantùm à se invicem differant, ut Genus & Species: siquidem Essentiale est quasi Genus quoddam: sub suo ambitu comprehendens & substantiale & Accidentale: Quomodo, quæso, Substantialem appellare potest unionis hujus Modum, cùm Essentialem ipsum dici nulla ratione posse, ipsemet neget, & quidem rectissimè. Neque enim modus iste Unionis duarum Naturarum in Christo ad Essentialem ulla ratione referri potest, tanquam Species ad suum Genus: sed ab eo potiùs, & sic à Substantiali etiam Modo, toto genere discrepat. Undè liquidò constat, Jesuitam Unionis hujus modum καταχρηστικῶς, abusivè & planè impropriè, imò falsò nominare Substantialem. Neque est, ut veterum quorundam Ecclesiasticorum Scriptorum autoritate se tueatur, quos constat vocabulum ὑποστάσεως, per vocem

Substantiæ olim reddidisse. Nam negari non potest, hanc incommodam versionem, à quibusdã hæreticis, & cumprinis à Sabellianis, ad palliandam teterrimam hæresin raptam & accommodatam fuisse. Undè à posterioribus hæc explicatio planè est rejecta, & vocabulum ὑποστάσεως per vocem subsistentiæ sive personæ, rectissimè redditum.

Deindè verò neque Definitionem Modi hujus substantialis per omnia probare possumus. Dicit enim Bellarminus, unionem substantialem (Personalem autem intelligit) esse, cùm substantia, quæ alioqui per se existeret, trahitur ad esse alterius suppositi, & ab illo pendet tanquàm pars ipsius: Et hoc modo facta est incarnatio. Neque enim ad ὑποτύπωσιν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων quadrat, quod asserit Jesuvvita, personam λόγου pendere à supposito illo altero, hoc est, à Natura humana, tanquam partem illius. Si enim hoc intelligat ratione Humanitatis Christi, in se consideratæ, falsissimum fuerit, imò hæreticifsimum asserere, substantiam sive personam λόγου pendere ab ea tanquam partem. Sin autem de tota persona Christi hoc velit intellectum: eamque ex duabus partibus compositam esse statuat; jubemus ipsum illud tantùm pensi habere, nùm cum Ecclesia Romana loquatur, & sublime istud mysterium unionis Hypostaticæ satis accuratè explicet. Ipsi certè Doctores Scholastici noluerunt concedere, in persona Christi duas Naturas, tanquam partes considerandas esse, uti videre est apud Gabrielem Biel in l. 3 Sent. dist. 6. Quæst. 2. Art. 1. Dubio 1. lit. F. Et quanquam ex Scriptoribus veteribus & recentioribus fortè non desunt, qui Humanam Naturam partem nominant: quemadmodum Hesichius in cap. 5. Levitici, eam expressè appellat partem Trinitatis: tamen accuratiùs rem pensitantibus, impropriè ipsos locutos esse, hodieque loqui, constat. Primùm enim partes ut partes neque de toto, neque de se invicem prædicantur: Sicut certè Homo nec anima est, nec corpus: neque anima est corpus, neque corpus est anima. Atqui duæ Naturæ in persona Christi, verissimè de se invicem in concreto prædicantur, ut: DEUS est Homo: Homo est DEUS. Deindè omnis pars fine conjunctione cæterarum partium principalium, imperfecta est, ut corpus, verbi gratia, fine anima cadaver potiùs est, quàm corpus: & anima à corpore separata, suam quandam ad corpus dependentiam semper habet: undè corporis Resurrectionem expectat. Sed absit, ut tale quid de Λόγῳ, sine Filio DEI statuamus, qui etsi humanam naturam nunquam assumsisset, aut (si fieri posset) eandem rursus deponeret, nihilo minus tamen Totum quid esset longè absolutissimum perfectissimumque. Commodior proindè erit locutio, si persona Christi dicatur constare, non duabus partibus, sed duobus totis ac integris, unoquoque in suo genere perfectissimo: Sic tamen ut assumtum, supra conditionem Naturæ suæ ab assumente perfici potuerit. Sed fortè sub hac phrasi Jesuvvita occultare voluit dogma illud planè Nestorianum, quod de veritate istarum propositionum: Hic Homo est DEUS: & Hic DEUS est Homo, cum veteribus quibusdam Scholasticis, factio Jesuvvitica hodiè tenet, ac defendere studet: contendentes, Hominem hunc non posse ὑπερφυτικῶς esse DEUM, quia DEUS & Homo sint duæ disparatæ species, quarum neutra possit esse altera, sicut nec Asinus Homo, nec Homo Asinus esse queat. Quare propositionem hanc, Hic Homo est DEUS, sic interpretantur: Filius DEI est DEUS, qui sustentat humanam naturam: Quo pacto à subjecto (Homo) omnis prorsus assumti Hominis respectus excluditur, & nihil præter nudum nomen relinquitur. Sed de his infrà fusiùs. Sufficiant hoc loco isthæc, ex quibus impietas Dogmatis Jesuvvitici de Unione Hypostatica duarum naturarum in Christo, plus satis cognoscitur.


### Chapter Second: IV. Calvinism

IV. CALVINISM.

The doctrine of the Calvinists concerning the person of Christ labors under the same manifest impiety that we have just now noted in the Jesuits. For they all commonly define the personal union solely by the sustentation of the human nature, which it receives from the Divinity of the Word; and in this sustentation they constitute the specific difference of the personal union, simply and stubbornly denying the effect of this union, namely, the mutual communion of both the natures and the idioms in Christ with each other, so much so that they do not shrink from writing that when GOD is predicated of Man, or Man of GOD, that is done only by a tropical and figurative mode of speech; because disparate things can be enunciated of each other only through a trope, which is one of ἀλλοιώσεως (alteration) or the permutation of names.

For first, regarding the union itself, Peter Martyr, Dial. p. 10, holds thus: To define the personal union of two natures in Christ, it suffices if it be said that the Deity, however immense and infinite, supports and sustains the humanity with its own hypostasis, wherever it may be. To this the Bremensians subscribe: To be sustained in God the Word is nothing other than to be united to the Word personally. Grab. against Hunnius, p. 56.

Furthermore, regarding the effect of this union, the authors of the Calvinistic consensus philosophize thus: when it is said, This Man is GOD, the subject (this Man) does not stand for the human nature, but for the hypostasis of the Son of GOD. For of these predications: Man is GOD, Son of GOD is Man, this is the sense: Man is Man: Son of GOD is GOD. Hence the Neustadian Sacramentarians, in Admonit. pp. 70 & 250, write repeatedly that GOD suffered and died really, insofar as He is man; but in name only insofar as He is GOD. Thus, that Christ is omnipotent really, insofar as He is GOD, but in name only, insofar as He is man.

This is what Beza explains more clearly, Part 1, Tractat. Theol. p. 624: If at any time these properties seem to be interchanged, as when the GOD of glory is said to be crucified, and the Son of Man to have then been in heaven, when he was with Nicodemus on earth, it is the trope ἀλλοίωσις, consisting within the words: in which, however, there is no falsehood, although in reality that which is incommunicable in the Deity is not communicated to the flesh: nor, conversely, to the Deity, that which is incommunicable in Man. But this ἀλλοίωσις or VERBAL communication of idioms arises from there, and is therefore true, because on account of the unity of the person, the whole Christ is sometimes denominated from one Nature only.

Thus, therefore, two foundations of the Calvinist doctrine are detected, regarding the present Question: the former of which is: That the Hypostatic union is the sustaining of the Human Nature, lest it be reduced to nothing: The latter, however, that the phrases of Scripture, establishing the communication of both Natures and idioms, are to be understood κατ' ἀλλοίωσιν, or according to a permutation of all things. Both are certainly so infirm, impious, and blasphemous, that they can scarcely be explained sufficiently in words. For first, regarding the sustaining, it certainly cannot be denied by any reason, because that very sustaining would apply more correctly to all other creatures than to the assumed human Nature. For unless all creatures were sustained by GOD in this way, just as they are now sustained, they would not subsist even for a moment, but would be reduced to nothing. Heb. 1. 3. Acts 17, 28. Coloss. 1, 17. 30.

Then, if to be united to the WORD personally is nothing else than to be sustained in GOD the Word: and if from this very sustaining, the flesh of Christ does not obtain a real communication of the divine Majesty: certainly such a union will never correspond in its majesty and loftiness to that great mystery of godliness, by which the Apostle exclaims with admiration that GOD was manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3. 16. nor, and indeed much less, will such a union attain the height of that secret, for the sake of which the same Apostle pronounces that all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily in Christ. But if the Adversaries object that they attribute to the Humanity, because it is united with the person of the Word, that which applies to no other man: it is nevertheless clear from what has already been said, how they explain that union with the person of the Word: namely, as a sustaining in the WORD of such a kind that the assumed Humanity receives only those gifts which some other of the Saints receives: although in a more excellent degree: meanwhile, however, it does not participate in the divine Majesty, nor indeed even in the ὑπόστασις of the Word, in such a way that the Word is truly flesh: or the Son of Mary is truly the only-begotten Son of GOD. Finally, the escape that they say the Human nature of Christ is reduced to nothing unless it is thus carried or sustained in the WORD is clearly feeble: As if the WORD could not, outside of his own ὑπόστασις, grant a peculiar subsistence to the Humanity? Reduced to these straits, the Adversaries find nowhere to turn, except that some more recent ones clamor from time to time that that specific difference of this union is sufficient, namely that the sustaining of other creatures is to be referred not to the Son alone: but equally to GOD the Father also and the Holy Spirit: and therefore it is named universal Sustaining: but the Human Nature is carried and sustained by the WORD alone, whence it ought also to be named personal sustaining. But this is nothing else than to heap absurdities upon absurdities. For it is absurd to constitute the specific difference of the Hypostatic Union in the fact that the Human nature is sustained, lest it be reduced to nothing. It is more absurd to affirm that the Human nature is sustained by the WORD ALONE, lest it perish. It is most absurd that those Sophists so confuse the Assumption of the Human Nature and its sustaining, that they dare to refer both to one principle. The Assumption of the Human Nature is indeed most correctly referred to the WORD alone: but not likewise its sustaining, as that which, according to the Scriptures, is to be ascribed to all three persons of the Trinity. Certainly, the Angel Gabriel, Luke 1, 35, in express words, attributes the creation or formation of this Human Nature not to the Son alone, but to the Father and the Holy Spirit: saying, The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee. Did the Father and the Holy Spirit, therefore, having once created that Human Nature, so desert it afterwards that they do not even sustain it any longer, lest it be reduced to nothing? This is absurd, and blasphemous even to think. And what, I pray, is the reason that Christ on the Mount of Olives, and indeed on the Cross also, prayed for help and sustaining from GOD the Father with most ardent groans: and, just about to breathe out his soul, so diligently commended his spirit to the same, if the Father is to be sequestered from the sustaining of the Human Nature of Christ? Furthermore, it would be most false that which Scripture inculcates many times, that GOD the Father raised the body of the Son from the dead? Indeed, that consolation would have been clearly superfluous, with which Christ raised himself against the terrors of death and hell: The Lord is at my right hand, that I may not be moved: therefore my heart is glad, and my tongue has exulted: Moreover, my flesh also shall rest in hope: Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell: nor wilt thou give thy Holy One to see corruption, Psalm 16, and following.

Nor is it the case that the Adversaries can say that this prayer was directed to the divine nature of the Son of GOD: For although the Son of GOD never deserted his flesh: yet Peter and Paul are witnesses above all exception that this sustaining of the flesh of Christ in the sepulcher is to be ascribed to GOD the Father also, Acts 2, 23, and following, chapter 13, 33, and following.

Let the Calvinists, therefore, see how they wish to extricate themselves from these Absurdities: Indeed, let them see how they can assert the very mystery of the Hypostatic Union as sound and entire: For if the Hypostatic union consists in the fact that the Son of GOD sustains the human Nature, lest it be reduced to nothing: Now, since GOD the Father, as also GOD the Holy Spirit, sustain the same equally as the Son: it would certainly be a necessary consequence: that not only the Son, but also the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate.

Regarding the other foundation of the Calvinist doctrine, it consists in the Zwinglian

ἀλλοιώσεις or permutation of names: concerning which B. Luther rightly writes in the Greater Confession: Beware, I say, beware diligently of the Allæosis of Zwingli: For it is the very mask of the Devil: which finally makes such a Christ: from whom I would not wish to be called a Christian: namely, that Christ henceforth is nothing else, or does nothing by his passion and whole life, than any one from the flock of the Saints. Indeed, if I believe that only Christ's human nature suffered for me, Christ would be a very slight Savior to me: but he himself would rather have need of a Savior: Indeed, it cannot be told: what evil the Devil seeks under that mask. But since below in the special exposition of the three Genera of the communication of Idioms, we are to treat of this Calvinistic abomination expressly: it does not pertain to treat of it more fully in this place.

Latin:

IV. CALVINISMUS.

DOctrina Calvinianorum de persona Christi, eâdem planè impietate laborat, quam jam modò Jesuvvitis notavimus. Communiter enim omnes, Unionem personalem definiunt, sola sustentatione Humanæ naturæ, quæ à Divinitate τοῦ λόγου finiat: atque in hac sustentatione specificam Unionis personalis differentiam constituunt, simpliciter & mordicus negantes Unionis hujus Effectum, nempè tùm Naturarum, tùm Idiomatum in Christo mutuam ad se invicem κοινωνίαν, usque adeò, ut scribere non exhorrescant, quando DEUS de Homine, vel Homo de DEO prædicatur; illud non nisi Tropica & figurata locutione fieri: propterea quòd disparata de se invicem, non nisi per Tropum, qui sit ἀλλοιώσεως sive permutationis nominum, enunciari queant.

Primùm enim quoad unionem ipsam, sic habet Petrus Martyr. Dial. pag. 10. Ad definiendam Unionem personalem duarum Naturarum in Christo sufficit, si dicatur, Deitatem, quamvis immensam & infinitam, suâ hypostasi fulcire ac sustentare humanitatem, ubicunq; illa fuerit. Cui subscribunt Bremenses: Sustentari carnem in DEO verbo nihil est aliud, quàm unitum esse verbo personaliter Grab. contra Hunnium pag. 56.

Deindè verò, quoad effectum unionis hujus, sic philosophantur autores consensus Calvinistici: cum dicitur: Iste Homo est DEUS, subjectum (iste Homo) non supponit pro natura humana: sed pro hypostasi Filii DEI. Prædicationum enim istarum: Homo est DEUS, Filius DEI est Homo, hic est sensus: Homo est Homo: Filius DEI est DEUS. Hinc Sacramentarii Neostadienses, in Admonit. pag. 70. & 250. scriptitant, DEUM passum & mortuum esse realiter, quatenus homo est; sed nominetenus quatenus DEUS est. Sic omnipotentem esse Christum realiter, quatenus DEUS est, sed nominetenus, quatenus homo.

Id quod clariùs explicat Beza, part. 1. Tractat. Theol. p. 624 Siquando proprietates istæ videntur permutari, ut cum DEUS gloriæ dicitur crucifixus, & Filius Hominis tùm fuisse in cælo, cùm esset cum Nicodemo in terris, tropus est ἀλλοίωσις, intra verba consistens:in quo tamẽ nulla est falsitas, quamvis Reipsa nec carni communicetur, quod est in Deitate incommunicabile: nec vicissim Deitati, quod incommunicabile est in Homine. Hæc autem ἀλλοίωσις sive VERBALIS ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία indè orta, & ideò vera est, quod propter unitatem personæ, Christus totus interdum, ex altera tantùm Natura denominetur.

Sic ergò Calvinianæ Doctrinæ duo deprehenduntur firmamenta, quoad præsentem Quæstionem: quorum prius est: Quod unio Hypostatica sit sustentatio Humanæ Naturæ, ne in nihilum redigatur: Posteriùs verò, quòd phrases Scripturæ, communicationem tùm Naturarum, tùm idiomatum stabilientes, sint intelligendæ κατ' ἀλλοίωσιν, sive secundum permutationem omnium. Utrumque sanè usque adeò infirmum, impium, blasphemum, ut vix verbis satis explicari possit. Primùm enim quoad sustentationẽ, certè negari nullâ ratione potest, quia illa ipsa sustentatio, omnibus aliis creaturis rectiùs conveniat, quàm assumtæ humanæ Naturæ. Nisi enim omnes creaturæ, sic à DEO sustentarentur, sicut nunc sustentantur, nec ad momentum quidem subsisterent, sed in nihilum redigerentur. Heb. 1. 3. Act. 17, 28. Coloss. 1, 17. 30.

Deindè si uniri τῷ λόγῳ personaliter, nihil est aliud, quam sustentari in DEO verbo: & si ex hac ipsa sustentatione, caro Christi realem divinæ Majestatis κοινωνίαν non sortitur: certè talis unio nunquam suâ majestate & celsitudine respõdebit magno illi pietatis mysterio, quo DEUM in carne manifestatum, cum admiratione exclamat Apostolus 1. Tim. 3. 16. neque & quidem multò minus, talis unio altitudinem assequetur istius arcani, cujus gratia idem Apostolus, Omnem plenitudinem Deitatis corporaliter in Christo inhabitare pronunciat. Sin excipiant Adversarii, se Humanitati tribuere, quòd unita sit, cum persona verbi, id quod nulli alii homini conveniat: patet tamen ex jam dictis, quomodo illam unionem cum verbi persona explicent: nempè de ejusmodi in λόγῳ sustentatione, quâ assumta Humanitas ea tantùm dona accipiat, quæ alius aliquis Sanctorum: gradu licèt excellentiore: interim verò divinâ Majestate, imò ne quidem ὑποστάσει τοῦ λόγου ita participet, ut verbum verè sit caro: vel Mariæ Filius, verè sit unigenitus DEI Filius. Tandem elumbe planè effugium est, quod dicút, Humanam Christi naturam redigi in nihilum, nisi ita gestetur aut sustentetur in λόγῳ: Quasi verò λόγος non posset extra suam ὑπόστασιν, peculiarem subsistentiam tribuere Humanitati? In has angustias redacti Adversarii, quô se vertant, non inveniunt, quàm quòd recentiores nonnulli subindè clamitant, sufficere differentiam illam specificam unionis hujus, quod nimirùm aliarum creaturarum sustentatio referenda sit non ad solum Filium: sed æqualiter ad DEUM Patrem etiam & Spiritum Sanctum: ac proindè ea nominetur universalis Sustentatio: Humana autem Natura à solo λόγῳ gestetur, & sustentetur, Undè personalis etiam sustentatio nominari debeat. Sed nihil hoc est aliud, quam absurditates absurditatibus cumulare. Absurdum enim est, differentiam specificam Unionis Hypostatica in eo constituere, quod Humana natura sustentetur, ne in nihilum redigatur. Absurdius est, affirmare, Humanam naturam a SOLO λόγῳ sustentari, ne intereat. Absurdissimum est, Sophistas istos Assumtionem Humana Natura, ejusdemque sustentationem ita confundere, ut ad unum principium, utrumque referre ausint. Assumtio quidem Humanæ Naturæ ad solum λόγον rectissimè refertur: non verò itidem ejusdem sustentatio, ut quæ omnibus tribus personis Trinitatis, secundum Scripturas, est adscribenda. Certè creationem sive formationem. Naturæ hujus Humanæ Angelus Gabriel, Luc. 1, 35. non soli Filio, sed Patris & Spiritui Sancto, disertis verbis acceptam refert: Spiritus Sanctus, inquiens, superveniet in te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Siccinè ergò Pater & Spiritus Sanctus, Naturam istam Humanam semel à se conditam, ita postmodum deseruerunt, ut ne quidem ampliùs sustentent, ne in nihilum redigatur? Absurdum hoc, & vel cogitatu blasphemum. Et quæ obsecro causa est, quòd Christus in monte Olivarum, imò in Cruce quoque à DEO Patre auxilium & sustentationem ardentissimis gemitibus precatus est: eidemque Spiritum suum jam jam animam exhalaturus, adeò diligenter commendavit, si Pater à sustentatione Humanæ Naturæ Christi est sequestrandus? Præterea falsissimum foret, quod Scriptura multoties inculcat, DEUM Patrem, corpus Filii à mortuis resuscitasse? Imò supervacanea planè fuisset illa consolatio, quâ Christus seipsum adversus terrores mortis & inferni erexit: Dominus à dextris mihi, ne commovear: propter hoc lætatum est cor meum, & exultavit lingva mea: Insuper & caro mea requiescet in spe: Quoniam non derelinquens animam meam in inferno: nec dabis Sanctum tuum videre corruptionem, Psal. 16, & seqq.

Neque est, ut ad divinam naturam Filii DEI, hanc precationem directam fuisse, dicant Adversarii: Etsi enim Filius DEI carnem suam nunquàm deseruerit: testes tamen omni exceptione majores sunt, Petrus & Paulus, sustentationem hanc carnis Christi in sepulchro, DEO Patri etiam adscribendam esse, Act 2, 23. & seqq. cap. 13, 33. & seqq.

Viderint proindè Calviniani, quo pacto ex istis Absurditatibus sese extricare velint: Imò viderint, quomodo ipsum mysterium Unionis Hypostaticæ sartum ac integrum asserere queát: Si enim unio Hypostatica consistit in eo, quòd Filius DEI Naturam humanam sustentat, ne in nihilum redigatur: Jam verò DEUS Pater, ut & DEUS Spiritus Sanctus, eandem æquè ac Filius sustentent: utiq; necessarium fuerit consequens: non solum Filium, sed & Patrem ac Spiritum Sanctum incarnatos esse.

Quoad alterum Doctrinæ Calvinianæ firmamentum, consistit illud in Zvvingliana

ἀλλοιώσεις sive permutatione nominum: de qua rectè B. Lutherus in Confessione Majore scribit: Cave tibi, cave, inquam, sedulò ab Allæosi Zvvinglii: Nam est ipsa Diaboli larva: quæ talem tandem Christum efficit: à quo ego Christianus appellari nolim: nempè ut Christus deinceps non aliud sit, aut agat suâ passione vitaque omni, quàm quivis ex Sanctorum grege. Enimverò si Christi humanam tantùm naturam pro me passum fuisse credo, leviculus Salvator Christus mihi fuerit: sed ipse potiùs Salvatore opus habeat: Imò dici non potest: quid mali Diabolus sub ista larva quærat. Sed cùm infra in speciali diexodo trium Generum communicationis Idiomatum, de hac abominatione Calvinistica ex professo simus arcturi: fusiùs hoc loco de ea agere haud attinet.


### Chapter Second: On the Hypostatic Union of the Two Natures in Christ

The Λόγος or Son of God, assumed the entire human nature into the unity of his ὑπόστασις or person inseparably, indistantly, and unconfusedly, and united it to himself, so that he not only carried and sustained it, lest it be reduced to nothing: but also truly rendered it a κοινωνὸν or participant of his Nature or divinity: Indeed in such a way, that the whole fullness of the Divinity might inhabit the assumed human nature σωματικῶς corporally.

Exposition.

There are two principal members of this proposition of ours, the FORMER of which is concerning the Natures united to one another, not indeed by reason of their Essence; but by reason of the Union. The LATTER, however, is concerning the Mode of the Union of the two Natures in CHRIST.

I. Member: concerning the united Natures.

Regarding the Natures themselves united to one another, the ASSUMED NATURE must first be weighed, concerning which our Thesis asserts that the Λόγος assumed not a Person, but a human Nature. It is therefore implied that this human Nature is not of itself an ὑπόστασις ἰδιοσύστατον, a person subsisting by itself: nor was it so formed or created in the womb of Mary, that it subsisted alone by itself at any moment of time: and to which, thus subsisting in itself and having the separate account of some Individual, the person of the Son of GOD subsequently acceded, and was united to the same. For thus two persons would immediately be established in Christ. Then it would follow that Mary was not θεοτόκον: inasmuch as she conceived, carried, and brought forth a Man subsisting by himself, and not yet united with the λόγος. Finally, it would follow that it is plainly False, what Scripture affirms, that the Virgin Mary conceived and brought forth Immanuel: Isa. 7, 14. Matth. 1, 23. Likewise that it is False, what the Angel said to Mary: Behold you will conceive in the womb, and bring forth a son, who will be called the Son of the most high. Luke 1, 31. and 32. And after a few words: That which will be born of you, will be called the Son of GOD, verse 35. It would be False, that Elizabeth names Mary the Mother of the Lord, verse 43. Finally, it would be False, that in the Apostolic Creed we confess that we believe in Jesus Christ: the only-begotten Son of GOD, conceived and born of the Virgin Mary. With these reasons indeed militating, it must be established altogether thus: that the human nature, at that very moment in which it was separated and formed from the substance of the Virgin Mary by the operation of the Holy Spirit, since it did not subsist by itself and in itself, at that very moment, I say, it was assumed by the λόγος or Son of GOD: so that what was by itself ἀνυπόστατος, might now become and forever be ἐνυπόστατος, that is, might obtain its τὸ εἶναι in the person of the Son of GOD: Indeed in such a way, that it not only did not subsist by itself in the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος, but not even in its own idioms. For although the Human Nature, even in the Union itself, always retains its Idioms, saved: yet it is never to be considered to subsist in those idioms of its own. For thus it would certainly subsist in itself, and have its own personality: which is the Nestorian delirium.

Moreover, when the Son of GOD is said to have assumed this Nature, and to have united it to himself: it is soon accustomed to be asked and disputed: Who indeed can and ought to be established as the Term of this Union, both the Term from Which; and the Term into which. And indeed regarding the Term from which, the matter is placed beyond doubt, that namely the Incarnation of the Son of GOD, or the union of the two natures, was made in the very womb of the B. Virgin Mary. But regarding the Term into Which, the opinions are discrepant. For although most agree on this, that the human nature was assumed by the person of the λόγος: yet they partly say that they abhor that phrase, by which it is asserted that the Human Nature is assumed IN, or rather INTO the very ὑπόστασις of the λόγος: partly they truly define the Term of this assumption in such a way, that they leave little discrepancy between these two phrases: Human nature is assumed into the λόγος: and Human nature is assumed into Place: so that according to the Bremensians, these two phrases differ only in reason.

Since their assertion labors under manifest absurdities: we most rightly do not establish: that Human Nature, with respect to the term INTO WHICH, was indeed assumed in the maternal womb, but not into the maternal womb, or into any place, whatever it may be called: but INTO and WITHIN a most distinct Person, or ὑπόστασις, which the λόγος obtains distinct from the persons of the Father and the Holy Spirit, and proper and singular to himself: where also the assumed Nature subsists forever.

Furthermore, the Reasons which most solidly refute that former assertion of the Bremensians are chiefly these: 1. If being in a place and subsisting in the λόγος differ only by reason: then Human Nature will be in the λόγος in the same way as it is in a place, namely Naturally: which is absurd. 2. It will follow that Human nature subsists in the hypostasis of the λόγος through physical location: because, forsooth, through such physical location it was in a certain place. 3. It will follow that we likewise have been made similar to Christ the Man by personal subsistence in the person of the λόγος, just as he himself was made similar to us by physical location. The Reason for the Consequence is, according to the opinion of the Bremensians, Because being in a place and subsisting in the λόγος are the same in reality, and differ only by reason: or they have only a bare relation to another (πρὸς ἄλλο σχέσιν). 4. It will follow that the Union itself and its mode must likewise be established as local. For if, according to the Bremensians, the personal subsistence of the Humanity in the λόγος is in reality nothing other than local existence in a place (since being in a place and subsisting in the Person of the Word differ not in reality, but only by reason), how would the Union itself not also have been local: since the Union of Natures in Christ is infallibly estimated from the mode of subsistence of the assumed Nature in the λόγος. It is evident, therefore, even from this, that the Adversaries, as much as in them lies, utterly overturn and annihilate the mystery of the Hypostatic Union: which will be shown more fully below in the Disputation concerning Omnipresence.

Regarding the other Nature, namely the Divine, it is disputed today at the beginning: Whether only the person of the λόγος, but not the Divine Nature, which the λόγος obtains as one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is incarnate: so that it may indeed be lawful to say: The whole Person of the Son of GOD is incarnate: but it is not permitted to say: The Divine Nature, and indeed the whole of it, of the Son of GOD is incarnate. And truly there were not lacking those who defended the Affirmative stubbornly: moved by the authority of the Sixth Council of Toledo, whose first Chapter holds thus: The Son alone took upon himself humanity into the singularity of his person: but not into the unity of the Divine Nature: that is, into that which is proper to the Son: not what is common to the Trinity.

Which Canon indeed caused much trouble both to the Master of the Sentences and to the remaining Scholastics, inasmuch as it seemed to contradict all Antiquity, and to deny that the Divine nature, in the person of the Son of GOD, had assumed human nature. But at length Lombard strove to extricate himself from that difficulty, asserting that that Canon must be understood and explained thus: That the Nature of humanity was not assumed into the unity of the Divine Nature, insofar as this is common to all three persons: but into the singularity of the person of the Son of GOD, where, however, the Person cannot or ought not be understood without the Divine Nature in the Son of GOD. lib. 3. Sent. dist. 5. & 6.

Which explanation indeed, although it is not entirely to be repudiated, yet deserves a more severe censure in this, that both Lombard and most other Scholastics considered the Divine Nature as something existing by itself and outside the persons themselves: which is false and plainly heretical. For the Divine Nature is so common to the whole Trinity that it is nevertheless whole in the individual persons: Nor is Person in divine matters some thing existing outside or beyond the Divine essence, to which the Essence was afterwards communicated: Nor does the Divine Essence exist outside or beyond the persons in such a way that in one and the same person, the ὑπόστασις and the essence differ really. For in either way a Quaternity would be made. Therefore, it is more rightly answered by our Theologians that that very unique, same, and most simple Divine Essence is considered in two ways: either Absolutely, insofar as it is common to the three persons: or Relatively. Just as it is whole in the individual persons, limited by its own certain personal character: in the Father begetting: in the Son Begotten: in the Holy Spirit proceeding: Now therefore, regarding the proposed Question, it is most rightly answered: Not separately the person of the λόγος alone: but the whole Divine Nature considered relatively, and limited in the person of the Son: or what is the same, the whole Divine Nature Begotten, is incarnate: although with this distinction, that the person is primarily, but consequently the Divinity of the Son is incarnate. And this is what the testimonies of the Scriptures mean, which confirm that the Word was made Flesh: Likewise, that GOD was manifested in the flesh: that the Son of GOD was born of a woman. Where certainly the Divine Nature of the λόγος, Hypostatically determined, is clearly noted and expressed: Since the Divine Nature of the λόγος, and his person, just as the person of the Word and his Divine Nature, cannot be torn away or separated.

Finally, in this place this also is asked: Whether from the reception of Human Nature the person of the λόγος has obtained a fuller or more perfect integrity? Where, by distinction, it is most rightly answered: for either it is asked concerning the person of the λόγος not yet incarnate, that is, considered in itself and simply. And then we answer Negatively.

For the λόγος is and has been from all eternity, no less a most perfect and absolute ὑπόστασις than that of the Father or the Holy Spirit. But if the question is concerning the incarnate λόγος, or Christ, consisting of two natures, then we answer affirmatively that the assumed Human Nature pertains entirely to the integrity of the person of Christ. Which person of Christ does not differ from the person of the λόγος considered in itself and simply, as if a new person had now been added: but rather that this person, which before the incarnation was simple and consisted of one nature, namely the divine, is now composite, consisting of two, indeed most diverse, but most unitively joined natures, the Divine and the Human: Hence Damascen. did not hesitate to name the person of Christ μίαν σύνθετον ὑπόστασιν, one composite person.

Finally, this question is also asked: since the ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου is infinite, is most simple, and is ὅλως ὁλότης, having absolutely no part outside of a part: but the Human Nature is finite, and circumscribed by the limits of its own nature. Does the λόγος so unite the assumed humanity to himself, that he indeed dwells entirely in the assumed flesh, but is also entirely outside the same assumed flesh? And indeed the Calvinist party began to champion the affirmative long ago, so that Pezelius, on pages 35 and 36 of his Demonstration against Dr. Hunnius, did not shrink from writing: both are true, rightly understood, that the whole λόγος is in the flesh, and that the same λόγος is whole in the bosom of the Father, and in all creatures. For because the essence of the λόγος is infinite, the whole λόγος is not in the flesh in such a way that he ceases to be whole elsewhere: since this is a property of the infinite: to be so whole in all things, that he is at the same time whole outside all things. And shortly after in the margin of the same page 36. They do not conflict with one another: that the λόγος is in the flesh through the hypostatic union: that the same is outside the flesh through the infinity of the Essence, included in no place, excluded from no place. And after a few words: But while this indwelling of the Word in the Flesh is preserved, which constitutes one person with it, he is by no means in the flesh in such a way that he is not present OUTSIDE or BEYOND IT, either to creatures, or to the Father, etc. Moreover, we judge this assertion of the Calvinists to be not so much new and dangerous as impious and heretical: which will be more clearly revealed below in Chapter 3, from the refutation of the arguments which they are accustomed to bring forward from this false hypothesis against the omnipresence of the Flesh of Christ. In this place it suffices to remember the principal reasons by which the impiety of that assertion can be demonstrated.

1. If the λόγος, with his whole hypostasis and person, is also outside the assumed nature after the union: the hypostatic union is dissolved. The reason for the consequence is this: Because the term IN WHICH of this union is the very ὑπόστασις of the λόγος, into the real κοινωνίαν of which ὑπόστασις the Human Nature, otherwise ἀνυπόστατος, arrives through this union: indeed so that the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος is also the very ὑπόστασις of the assumed Humanity. Now therefore, when according to the Calvinists this hypostasis of the λόγος is constituted outside the assumed flesh: the union itself is certainly now torn apart and dissolved: since the ὑπόστασις of the λόγος will now be outside the flesh: that is, outside that of which it is the ὑπόστασις: which is absurd and Nestorian.

2. If the λόγος, through and because of the infinity of his Essence, is outside the assumed humanity, and indeed whole (for he has no part outside of a part): he will certainly also be outside the same, through and because of the infinity of his person. The reason for the connection is: Because the Essence and the person of the λόγος do not differ in reality at all. Now if the λόγος is outside the flesh through and because of the infinity of his person, the whole mystery of the personal union of the two natures in Christ collapses.

3. If the infinity of the Essence of the λόγος prevents the Human Nature from being able to be capable of his whole self: the infinity of the Person will certainly also prevent the Human Nature from being able to be capable of his whole self: And consequently the λόγος is neither whole: nor according to a part, which he has absolutely none of: and thus he is not incarnate at all.

4. If after the incarnation the λόγος, through and because of the infinity of his person, is also whole outside the flesh, the Articles of Faith will be false, which testify that the Son of GOD himself was conceived in the Virgin Mary, and born of her, suffered, was crucified, etc. Or it must be imagined that, in the respect in which the λόγος was whole in the flesh, he was also whole conceived, born, etc. But in the respect in which he was whole outside the flesh, he was not whole incarnate, which is again and again heretical, and blasphemous even to think.

Finally, this Calvinist assertion undermines and overturns itself with infinite absurdities. For if the whole λόγος is also outside the assumed flesh: he will certainly operate wholly outside the same: he will be worshipped wholly outside the same: he will be present wholly outside the same to his Church: he will be wholly outside the same in the bosom of the Father; the whole fullness of the Godhead of the Son will dwell outside the same: And, to say everything in one word: If the whole λόγος is also outside the flesh: then the flesh itself will also be outside the whole λόγος. A pious mind easily understands that all these things are more absurd than the most absurd.

Nor is there any reason for the adversaries to argue from the example of creatures, in which it is established that GOD is whole, in such a way that he is also whole outside them. For the reason for the assumed Nature and the remaining creatures is very different. For these are not ὑποστατικῶς united with the λόγος: these do not constitute one person with the λόγος: these obtain their τὸ εἶναι outside the person of the Son of GOD: these, finally, are never admitted or assumed into the κοινωνίαν of the divine Nature for eternity. Wherefore, although they are in GOD as regards their sustenance: yet by reason of their existence they are outside the ὑπόστασιν of GOD: and conversely, GOD is in them in such a way that he is also whole outside them.

We correct this error, however, by showing that it arises from a false, preconceived hypothesis. For the adversaries imagine and dream of such an infinity, both of the Essence and of the person of the λόγος, which, through a certain extension of οὐσία, exceeds the flesh of Christ, which is indeed finite: Such an infinity, however, cannot fall into the most simple and most absolute Essence of GOD, since it is simply devoid of all extension, excess, or expansion. Now because the whole, however infinite, ὑπόστασις and divine Essence of the λόγος is, I say, wholly incarnate: he is certainly not outside this flesh of his, which he assumed, nor can he be while this personal union is preserved: not indeed that the λόγος is compressed into a narrow space through the Incarnation: such compression does not fall into the most simple ὑπόστασις of the λόγος: but rather that the λόγος [has] this flesh of his, [as] his own ὑπό-

of deification, and consequently of his very Omnipresence, he rendered [it] a sharer or participant: and that concerning every expansion or extension: since it reigns only in Locality: as will be shown below in chapter 3.

Latin:

Λόγος sive Filius Dei, Humanam naturam integram, in unitatem suæ ὑποστάσεως sive personæ inseparabiliter, indistanter, & inconfusè assumsit, sibique univit, ut non modò eam gestaret ac sustentaret, ne in nihilum redigeretur: sed & Naturæ sive divinitatis suæ revera redderet κοινωνὸν sive participem: Ita quidem, ut tota plenitudo Divinitatis, in assumta natura humana, inhabitaret σωματικῶς corporaliter.

Ἔκθεσις.

DUo potissimùm propositionis hujus nostræ sunt membra, quorum PRIUS est de Naturis invicem unitis, non quidem ratione suæ Essentiæ; sed ratione Unionis. POSTERIUS verò est de Modo Unionis duarum Naturarum in CHRISTO.

I. Membrum: de Naturis unitis.

QUoad Naturas ipsas invicem unitas initiò expendenda venit NATURA ASSUMPTA, de qua Thesis nostra asserit, quod Λόγος assumserit non Personam, sed Naturam humanam. Innuitur proindè, Humanam hanc Naturam per se non esse ὑπόςασιν ἰδιοσύςατον, personam per se subsistentem: neque etiam in utero Mariæ ita formatam aut conditam fuisse, ut seorsim ullo temporis momento sola subsisteret: & cui, hoc modo in seipsa subsistenti, atque Individui alicujus separatam rationem habenti, persona Filii DEI postmodum accesserit, eidemque unita fuerit. Sic enim duæ statim in Christo personæ statuerétur. Deindè sequeretur, Mariam non fuisse θεοτόκον: quippe quæHominem per se subsistentem, & nondum cum λόγῳ unitum, in utero cõceperit, gestarit & enixa sit. Tandé sequeretur, Falsum planè esse, quod Scriptura affirmat, Mariam Virginem Jmmanuelem concepisse & peperiisse: Jes. 7, 14. Matth. 1, 23. Falsum item esse, quod Angelus dixit ad Mariam: Ecce concipies in utero, & paries filium, qui Filius altissimi vocabitur. Luc. 1, 31. & 32. Et post pauca: Quod ex te nascetur, Filius DEI vocabitur, versu. 35. Falsum esset, quod Elizabeth Mariam nominat Matrem Domini, versu. 43. Falsum denique foret, quod in Symbolo Apostolico credere nos confitemur in Jesum Christum: Filium DEI unigenitum, conceptum & natum ex Maria Virgine. Quibus sanè rationibus militantibus, sic omninò statuendum fuerit: Naturam humanam, eo ipso momento, quo operatione Spiritus Sancti, ex substantia Mariæ Virginis segregrata & formata fuit, cùm per se & in seipsa non subsisteret, illo ipso inquam, momento, à λόγῳ sive Filio DEI assumtam esse: ita ut quæ per se esset ἀνυπόςατος, jam fieret & in perpetuum esset ἐνυπόςατος, hoc est, suum τὸ εἶναι, in persona Filii DEI obtineret: Ita quidem, ut non modò non per se in ipsa ὑποσάσει τꙋ λόγꙋ, sed nec in suis idiomatis subsisteret. Etsi enim Humana Natura in ipsa etiam Unione, sua Idiomata, salva perpetuò retinet: tamen nunquam in suis illis idiomatis subsistere censenda est. Sic enim in seipsa certè subsisteret, propriamque personalitatem haberet: id quod Nestorianum est delirium.

Cæterùm cum Filius DEI hanc Naturam assumsisse, sibique univisse dicitur: mox quæri & controverti solet: Quis nam Unionis hujus constitui possit & debeat, tùm Terminus ex Quo: tùm Terminus in quem. Et quidem quoad Terminum ex quo, res extra dubium est posita, quod nimirùm Incarnatio Filii DEI, sive unio duarũ naturarum, facta sit in ipso utero B. Virginis Mariæ. Verùm quoad Terminum in Quem, discrepantes sunt sententiæ. Etsi enim plerique in eo conveniunt, Naturam humanam assumtam esse à persona λόγꙋ: tamen partim abhorrere se dicunt ab ea phrasi, quâ asseritur, HumanaNatura esse assumta, IN imò INTRA ipsam ὑπόςασιν τꙋ λόγꙋ: partim verè assumtionis hujus Terminum ita definiunt, ut parum discrepantiæ relinquant inter duas hasce phrases: Humana natura assumta est in λόγον: & Humana natura assumta est in Locum: adeò ut secundum Bremenses, duæ hæ phrases tantùm ratione differant.

Quorum assertio cum manifestis absurditatibus laboret: rectissime non statuimus: Humanam Naturam respectu termini IN QUEM, assumtam quidem esse in utero materno, sed non in uterum maternum, sive in locum aliquem, quicunque etiam nominetur: sed IN imo INTRA diversissimam Personam, sive ὑπόστασιν, quam λόγος a Patris & Spiritus Sancti personis distinctam, sibique propriam ac singularem obtinet: ubi etiam assumta Natura in perpetuum subsistit.

Caeterum Rationes, quae priorem illam Bremensium assertionem solidissime refutant, praecipuae sunt hae: 1. Si in loco esse & in λόγῳ, subsistere, sola ratione differunt: tum Natura humana eodem modo erit in λόγῳ, quo in loco, nempe Naturaliter: id quod absurdum. 2. Consequetur, Humanam naturam per locationem physicam subsistere in hypostasi τοῦ λόγου: quia nimirum per talem Physicam locationem fuit in certo quodam loco. 3. Sequetur, nos itidem similes esse factos Christo Homini personali subsistentia in persona λόγου, atque ipse similis nobis factus est locatione Physica. Ratio Consequentiae est, ex sententia Bremensium, Quia in loco esse, & in λόγῳ subsistere, Re idem sunt, & sola ratione differunt: vel nudam tantum πρὸς ἄλλο σχέσιν habent. 4. Unionem ipsam ejusdemque modum constituendum esse itidem localem consequetur. Si enim secundu Bremenses, personalis subsistentia Humanitatis in λόγῳ, reipsa nihil aliud est, quam localis existentia in loco (siquidem in Loco esse, & in Persona Verbi subsistere, non reipsa, sed sola ratione differunt) Quomodo non ipsa etiam Unio localis fuerit: Cum Unio Naturarum in Christo, ex modo subsistentiae assumtae Naturae in λόγῳ infallibiliter aestimetur. Constat ergo vel inde Adversarios quantum in ipsis, Unionis Hypostaticae mysterium prorsus evertere & annihilare: id quod infra in Disputatione de Omnipraesentia fusius ostenderur.

Quoad alteram Naturam Divinam nimirum, controvertitur hodie initio: An persona tantum λόγου, non autem Natura divina, quam cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto λόγος unam obtinet, sit incarnata: ita ut dicere quidem fas sit, Persona tota Filii DEI est incarnata: non autem liceat dicere: Natura divina & quidem tota Filii DEI est incarnata. Et profecto non defuerunt, qui Affirmativam mordicus defenderent: moti autoritate Concilii Toletani VI. cujus Caput primum sic habet: Solus Filius suscepit humanitatem in singularitatem personae suae: non autem in unitatem divinae Naturae: hoc est, in id, quod proprium est Filii: non quod commune est Trinitati.

Qui sane Canon tum Magistro Sententiarum, tum reliquis Scholasticis plurimum negotii exhibuit, quippe qui universae Antiquitati videbatur contradicere, & negare Divinam naturam, in persona Filii DEI, assumsisse humanam naturam. Sed tandem Lombardus ex ista difficultate sese extricare studuit, asserens, Canonem istu ita intelligendum & explicandum esse: Humani Naturam no esse assumtam in unitatem Naturae divinae, quatenus nimirum haec omnibus tribus personis est communis: sed in singularitate personae Filii DEI, ubi tamen Persona non sine Natura divina in Filio DEI, intelligi possit aut debeat. lib. 3. Sent. dist. 5. & 6.

Quæ sanè explicatio, etsi non omninò est repudianda, in eo tamen censuram severiorem meretur, quod tùm Lombardus, tùm plerique alii Scholastici, considerârunt divinam Naturam, tanquam aliud per se, & extra ipsas personas existens: id quod falsum ac hæreticum planè est. Nam Natura divina ita communis est toti Trinitati, ut tamen tota sit in singulis personis: Neque in divinis Persona est res aliqua, extra vel præter divinam essentiam existens, cui postea Essentia communicata sit: Neque Essentia divina extra vel præter personas existit tali modo, ut in una & eadem persona, ὑπόστασις & essentia realiter differant. Utroque enim modo fieret Quaternitas. Proindè à nostratibus Theologis rectius respondetur, illam ipsam unicam eandem & simplicissimam divinam Essentiam dupliciter considerari: vel Absolutè, quatenus communis est tribus personis: vel Relatè. Sicut tota est in singulis personis, certo suo personali charactere limitata: in Patre generans: in Filio Genita: in Spiritu Sancto procedens: Jam ergò quoad propositam Quæstionem, rectissimè respondetur: Non seorsim solam personam λόγου: sed totam Naturam divinam relatè consideratam, & in persona Filii limitatam: vel quod idem est, Totā Naturam Divinam Genitam, esse incarnatam: licèt sub hoc discrimine, quòd persona πρώτως Consequenter autem Divinitas Filii est incarnata. Et hoc ipsum sibi volunt Scripturarum testimonia, quæ confirmant, Verbum factum esse Carnem: Item, DEUM esse manifestatum in carne: Filium DEI natum ex muliere.
