Ubi certè Natura divina λόγου, Hypostaticè determinata, difertè notatur & exprimitur: Siquidem Natura divina λόγου, ab ejusdem persona, sicut & persona Verbi ab ejusdem Natura divina, divelli aut separari non possunt.

Tandem hoc loco & illud quæritur: An ex acceptione Humanæ Naturæ persona τοῦ λόγου pleniorem perfectioremvè integritatem sit sortita? Ubi per distinctionem rectissimè respondetur: vel enim quæritur de persona λόγου nondum incarnati, hoc est, in se & simpliciter considerati. Et tùm Negativè respondemus.

Est enim & fuit λόγος jam indè ab omni æternitate, haud minus perfectissima absolutissimaque ὑπόστασις, quàm Patris aut Spiritus Sancti. Sin verò quæritur de λόγῳ incarnato, sive de Christo, constante ex duabus naturis, tùm affirmativè respondemus, quod nimirùm Humana Natura assumta, ad integritatem personæ Christi omninò pertineat. Quæ persona Christi non in eo differt à persona τοῦ λόγου in se & simpliciter considerati, ac si jam nova persona accesserit: sed quòd ea persona, quæ ante incarnationem simplex erat, & ex una constabat Natura, divinâ nimirùm, jam est composita, ex duabus, diversissimis quidem, sed unitissimè junctis Naturis, Divinâ & Humanâ constat: Hinc Damascen. personam Christi μίαν σύνθετον ὑπόστασιν, unam compositam personam nominare non dubitavit.

Tandem & illud quæritur, cùm ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου sit infinita, sit simplicissima, & ὅλως ὁλότης, partem extra partem planè nullam habens: Humana Natura autem sit finita, & naturæ suæ finibus circumscripta. Num λόγος ita sibi univerit assumtam humanitatem, ut totus quidem habitet in carne assumta. Totus autem etiam sit extra eandem carnem assumtam? Et sanè Gens Calviniana Affirmativam jam pridem propugnare cœpit, ita ut Pezelius pag. 35. & 36. suæ Demonstrationis adversus D. Hunnium scribere non exhorruerit: utrumque, verum est, dextrè intellectum, & quòd totus λόγος in carne sit, & quòd idem λόγος Totus sit in sinu Patris, & in creaturis omnibus. Nam quia essentia τοῦ λόγου infinita est, non ita est in carne λόγος totus, ut alibi totus esse desinat: Cum infiniti sit hæc proprietas: Sic totū esse in omnibus, ut simul totum sit extra omnia. Et mox in margine ejusdem paginæ 36. Non pugnant inter se: λόγον esse in carne per Unionem hypostaticam: eundem esse extra carnem per infirmitatem Essentiæ, nullo loco inclusam, nullo loco exclusam. Et pòst pauca: At salvâ hac inhabitatione Verbi in Carne, quæ cum ea personam unam constituit, neutiquam sic in carne est, ut EXTRA seu PRÆTER EAM, non sit præsens, aut Creaturis, aut Patri, &c. Cæterùm non tàm novam ac periculosam, quàm impiam ac hæreticam statuimus hanc esse Calvinianorum Assertionem: id quòd dilucidiùs infra Cap. 3. patebit, ex refutatione argumentorum, quæ ex falsa hac hypothesi, adversus Omnipræsentiam Carnis Christi, proferre solent. Hoc loco meminisse sufficiat præcipuas rationes, quibus Assertionis istius impietas demonstrari potest.

1. Si λόγος tota hypostasi & persona sua post Unionem etiam est extra naturam assumtam: solvitur Unio Hypostatica. Ratio consecutionis est hæc: Quia Unionis hujus Termino IN QUEM, est ipsa τοῦ λόγου ὑπόστασις, in cujus ὑποστάσεως realem κοινωνίαν Natura Humana, aliàs ἀνυπόστατος, per unionem hanc pervenit: ita quidem, ut ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου, sit ipsa etiam assumtæ Humanitatis ὑπόστασις. Jam ergò quando secundum Calvinianos, hypostasis hæc λόγου, extra carnem assumtam constituitur: utique Unio ipsa jam distrahitur ac dissolvitur: Siquidem ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου jam erit extra carnem: hoc est, extra id, cujus est ὑπόστασις: id quod absurdum & Nestorianum.

2. Si λόγος, per & propter infinitatem Essentiæ, extra humanitatem assumtam, & quidem Totus (nam partem extra partem nullam habet) est: utique extra eandem etiam erit, per & propter infinitatem personæ. Ratio connexi est: Quia Essentia & persona λόγου, neutiquam realiter differunt. Jam si λόγος per & propter Infinitatem personæ est extra carnem, corruit totum mysterium Unionis personalis duarum naturarum in Christo.

3. Si Infinitas Essentiæ τοῦ λόγου obstat, quo minùs Humana natura possit ejus totius capax esse: obstabit utique Infinitas etiam Personæ, quò minùs Humana Natura ejus totius capax effe queat: Et per consequens λόγος neque totus: neque secundum partem, quam nullam prorsus habet: atque sic prorsus non est incarnatus.

4. Si post incarnationem λόγος, per & propter infinitatem suæ personæ, est etiam totus extra carnem, falsi erunt Articuli Fidei, qui attestantur, ipsum Filium DEI, conceptum esse in Maria Virgine, ex eademque natum, passum, crucifixum, &c. Vel fingendum, Eo respectu, quo totus fuit in carne λόγος, totum etiam fuisse conceptum, natum &c. Quo verò extra carnem fuit totus, totum etiam non fuisse incarnatum, id quod iterum atque iterum hæreticum, & vel cogitatu blasphemum fuerit.

Tandem assertio hæc Calviniana seipsam infinitis absurditatibus subruit & evertit. Si enim totus λόγος est etiam extra carnem assumtam: utique extra eandem totus operabitur: extra eandem totus adorabitur: Extra eandem totus aderit suæ Ecclesiæ: extra eandem totus erit in sinu Patris; extra eandem tota plenitudo Deitatis Filii habitabit: Et, ut uno verbo dicam omnia: Si totus λόγος est etiam extra carnem: utique ipsa quoque caro erit extra totum λόγον. Quæ omnia absurdissimis absurdiora esse, mens pia facilè intelligit.

Neque est, ut ab exemplo creaturarum argumententur Adversarii, in quibus ita DEUM totum esse constat, ut sit etiam totus extra eas. Nam diversissima ratio est assumtæ Naturæ & reliquarum creaturarum. Hæ enim non sunt ὑποστατικῶς unitæ cum λόγῳ: hæ non unam cum λόγῳ personam constituunt: hæ suum τὸ εἶναι extra personam Filii DEI obtinent: hæ denique in κοινωνίαν Naturæ divinæ in æternum nunquam admittuntur, aut assumuntur. Quare licèt quoad sustentationem in DEO sint: tamen ratione suæ existentiæ sunt extra DEI ὑπόστασιν: & vicissim sic DEUS sit in illis, ut etiam totus extra illas sit.

Corrigimus autem errorem istum, ostendentes oriri eum ex falsa præconcepta hypothesi. Talem enim fingunt & somniant Adversarii Infinitatem, tùm Essentiæ tùm personæ λόγου, quæ per quandam οὐσίας extensionem, carnem Christi quippè finitam, excedat: Qualis tamen infinitas in simplicissimam absolutissimamque DEI Essentiam cadere non potest, quippè quæ omnis sive Extensionis sive Excessionis, sive Expansionis simpliciter est expers. Jam quia tota quantumvis infinita ὑπόστασις & Essentia divina τοῦ λόγου, Tota inquam est incarnata: utique extra carnem hanc suam, quam assumsit, non est, nec salvâ hac Unione personali esse potest: non quidem, quod λόγος per Incarnationem in angustum coarctetur: Qualis coarctatio etiam in simplicissimam λόγου ὑπόστασιν, non cadit: sed potiùs quòd λόγος carnem hanc suam, propriæ suæ ὑπο-

ξεώσεως, & consequenter ipsius etiam Omnipræsentiæ, reddidit κοινωνὸν sive participem: idquè circa omnem expansionem sive extensionem: quippè quæ in Localitate tantùm regnat: uti infra cap. 3. ostendetur.


### Chapter Second: On the Mode of the Union

On the Mode of the Union of the two Natures in Christ.

The third member of our proposition is the other, concerning the Mode of the Union of the two Natures in Christ: What this is, is sufficiently clearly evident from those things which we have just now said. Various modes of Union are indeed recounted both by Philosophers and by Theologians, especially by Damascenus in book 3, chapter 3: just as we also refuted the principal false modes above in the refutation of the Jesuitical [doctrine]: so that it is of no use to deal with them at greater length in this place. Having therefore rejected and reprobated each and every Mode of Union that can indeed be spoken or thought of, we admit only that one which is and is called Hypostatic or personal: not indeed in this sense, as if person were united to person: for thus not one, but two Christs would emerge, which is what conflicts with the Christian faith: but neither in that sense, as if neither Nature had the character of a person, but only from the concurrence of two natures simply, one person began to be: For in this way the Whole Trinity would be established as incarnate itself: nay, Christ himself would also be established as something different from his natures: and as a kind of third thing: But in this one true and Orthodox sense: That the Second Person of the Trinity, namely the λόγος, assumed the human nature, destitute of its own personality, into the most intimate embrace and subsistence of his ὑπόστασις or person: and communicated his own πρόσωπότητα to it, so that this ὑπόστασις of the λόγος is at the same time the ὑπόστασις of the assumed Human nature, in which it also subsists forever.

Although indeed this phrase has long since obtained both among the Ancients and more recent Theologians, that it should be said that the Union of the Natures was made in the Person: yet some have very viciously inferred from that, that the Union was made in a certain third thing, different from either Nature. For then at last would this inference be valid, If the divine Nature, and the person of the λόγος, differed Really, or τῷ εἶναι. Since this can in no way be conceded without prejudice to the Christian Religion, whatever some dream and invent about the Medium or bond of this Union is frivolous and nonsensical.

The Scholastic Doctors dispute in this place, Whether this Hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ is the greatest of all Unions, either by reason of the mode of union or by reason of nobility: Where they depart into completely different opinions: Durandus indeed defending the Negative in book 1, distinction 3, but Bonaventura in 3, distinction 6, article 2, questions 1 and 3, with others defending the Affirmative:

with some walking as it were a middle path and contending that this Union is not the greatest in respect of those things which are united, that is, in respect of the humanity and the Word: But in respect of that in which they are united: Likewise, If the divine and human Nature are taken, insofar as they are joined in one suppositum absolutely: then the Hypostatic union is the greatest of all created unions: but not nobler than the union of the divine persons: as both others, and especially Suarez, disputes at very great length in Disputation 1, Section 2. But these and other such disputations of the Scholastics are clearly useless and idle: such as Whether, with personality abstracted by the intellect, a nature can assume a Nature? Whether the Human Nature assumed by the λόγος was abstracted from all individuals? and similar ones: clearly unworthy of more accurate meditation: That study should rather be approved and imitated, which orthodox Antiquity placed in explaining the Form of this Union. For although this Mystery is truly ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ νοῦν καὶ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν: as Justinus speaks: yet the Fathers established certain marks, from the observation of which one may arrive at a richer understanding of it.

At the beginning, indeed, they said that two Natures in Christ are united ἀδιαιρέτως καὶ ἀδιαλύτως, indivisibly and indissolubly: implying that the λόγος retains the human nature once assumed, united to himself by an everlasting covenant for all eternity. Scripture confirms this very thing, which asserts that that same Body of Christ, which on the Mount of Olives ascended visibly to the heavens, will return on the last day, visible to our eyes: Acts 1:11, John 19:37, Heb. 9:28. They shall look on him whom they pierced: which likewise attests that Christ, in that very flesh of his, now also appears in the presence of GOD for us, Heb. 9:24. Indeed, that he will one day render our most vile bodies conformed to his glorious body: Phil. 3, last verse.

Then they said that the Natures are united ἀδιαςάτως, indistantly. The truth of this assertion is evident from the very proper Term of the Hypostatic Union. For since this Union was made in the very ὑπόςασις of the Son of GOD: or which is the same thing, since the Human Nature assumed is in the illocal ὑπόςασις of the Son of GOD, to which no spatial διαςήματα can reach: certainly no physical place, no spatial διαςήματα, or intervals, can separate these Natures, once united ὑποτατικῶς, from one another.

Thirdly, they said that the Natures are united ἀχωρίτως, inseparably. This note has some kinship with the preceding one, and it means this: Not some part, but the whole ὑπόςασις of the λόγος, or, as the Apostle speaks, the whole fullness of the Godhead of the Son of GOD, is so united to the assumed humanity that no separation or absence of the assuming Nature from the assumed can be admitted at all: but that this Union is immediately dissolved, or rather, two ὑπόςάσεις are imagined or persons, as soon as it is established that the assumed nature is absent somewhere from the one assuming.

Fourthly, they said that the Natures were united ἀτρέπτως καὶ ἀσυγχύτως, inconvertibly and inconfusedly: for neither Nature was changed into the other, but each remained what it was: since the Exaltation of the assumed Nature does not destroy the truth of the flesh, but perfects it; it does not take away, but exalts it. Finally, they attempted to explain by various similitudes that this Union not only could not happen, but could not even be conceived, without a true and real communication: and that, indeed, all the more close and excellent, the more sublime and close this very Union is, the more noble and excellent the natures themselves are: and finally, the more lofty and divine the very end of this Union is. Although indeed concerning those similitudes, each and all, that saying of Justin the Philosopher and Martyr can be truly applied: ἁρμόδιον τόγε τὸ παράδειγμα κῆ τί γεν, ἀλλὰ μὴ παντελὲς: The example is indeed conformable, but only in part and in a certain respect, not however in whole: yet we willingly concede that they have great use in the present dispute, provided they are rightly accommodated. Concerning which matter, both the writings of other theologians and especially the most learned booklet of Doctor Chemnitz can and ought to be read with great profit: Chapter 6, for me page 35 and following.

Moreover, from these marks it can be most correctly established concerning the specific Difference, which will indeed clearly show what that is which evidently distinguishes the degree, or mode, of this Union from all other modes of presence by which GOD is said to be present to creatures: namely,

1. that the λόγος is not only present to the human Nature according to universal presence, or general action, by which He is essentially present to all creatures, sustains, preserves, rules, and governs them:

2. nor also only according to indwelling and sanctification, by which He is not only essentially present to the Saints and dwells within them: But also imparts His grace to the same: In which sense Lord Peter affirms that the Saints are made partakers of the divine nature:

3. nor also only according to that heavenly mode of presence by which He is present to the Angels and the Blessed in heaven in eternal life:

4. but according to the PERSONAL presence, by which not the Father, not the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone, or the λόγος, has so assumed the human nature into the unity and κοινωνίαν ὑποστάσεως, or of His Person: that the two natures, thus personally united, have become one ὑποστατικὸν thing, and have coalesced into one ὑφιστάμενον: which is and is called CHRIST: indeed so that now, when CHRIST is named, neither should GOD alone be thought of, nor should Man alone be conceived in the mind: but in GOD, Man: and in Man and with Man, GOD, that is, the θεάνθρωπος, must always be thought of.

With these things observed at the beginning, that accusation is found to be vain and false, by which our adversaries scourge our churches, as if they taught that to be united hypostatically is nothing other than for divine attributes or properties to be communicated to the humanity of Christ.

For it has already been shown that the specific difference of this union is not the communication of idioms itself, but that singular and clearly unique mode of union by which the divine and human natures, personally and inseparably united, constitute one person, in the way that has been explained; although meanwhile the communication of idioms necessarily follows from this union, as will soon be demonstrated, as an effect from which one may judge more correctly concerning the union itself.

Thence it is also clear what must be answered to that other reproach by which the Jesuit Bellarmine lashes us, namely that we maintain that the hypostatic union was brought about not per se, but per accidens. For we do not remember that any such thing was ever said or written by our people, nor can the adversary himself produce any witness. For we know by the grace of God that those things which behave according to nature, or naturally, are contained within the distinction of essence and accident. Now since the hypostatic union, as also the subsequent communication, does not behave according to the order of nature, therefore it will be neither essential nor accidental, but of its own proper genus: that is, personal. Where, however, it can neither be nor ought to be simply rejected that the Scholastic Doctors themselves, in this very matter, established a third thing between these two, per se and per accidens, and named it 'quasi per accidens' and contingently. Whence not ineptly Gabriel, dist. 6, Quest. 2, notable 4, in book 3 of the Sentences: Although the human nature is adventitious to the person of the Word, it is nevertheless not accidental to the Word itself. For it is not the same thing to be contingently and to be accidentally: because to be man happens to the Word contingently, yet not accidentally: because the humanity did not befall the Word as an accident to its subject. Hence Orthodox writers also, among whom is that most acute Schekius, have not at all abhorred this term, 'quasi per accidens,' in explaining this mystery personally.

Finally, the same Bellarmine cries out quite impudently that it is plain from our doctrine that we maintain such a union of two natures in Christ as exists between a principal agent and an instrument. Where the Jesuit without doubt understands such an instrument as Nestorius once imagined, namely a separated one, just as tools are distinct from the persons of the craftsmen. But he will never prove that any such thing was ever said or written by our people. But if he censures that which we teach, that the Word exerts his operations through the human nature as through an instrument, then he maliciously and by a manifest crime of falsehood perverts our opinion. For we do not understand an instrument that is either inanimate or inactive, and least of all a separated one, but such a one as no similar example can be given for, neither in heaven nor on earth: which is, of course, personally united with the Word, and concurs effectively to the perfecting of the same result, not only by working that which is proper to nature: but also that which it has truly and really received from the communicated divine power and majesty, so that it can also perform divine actions, such as: to justify, to give life, to recall from the dead, to save, and others of that kind, as we shall show in the proper place. Agent and the Instrument.

These things being thus dispatched, we finally subjoin such a Definition of the Hypostatic Union, that it is a singular and admirable work of the whole Trinity, by which the Λόγος or Son of GOD, by the power of the Holy Spirit and the overshadowing of the Most High, did not assume a person, but a human nature consisting of a body and a rational soul, from the B. Virgin Mary, into the unity of his ὑπόστασις, and so inseparably, unconfusedly, and indistantly united it to himself, that by communicating his whole self to it, as to a ὑπόστασις, as to properties, he not only constituted one thing subsisting with it, which is and is called CHRIST: But also in, with, and through it, anointed with the infinite fullness of his Divinity, and everywhere most present to himself, both in the time of his Exinanition, the work of Redemption: and after the laying aside of the form of a servant, he exercised and perfected all the works of his Divinity and omnipotence in heaven and on earth.

Latin:

De Modo Unionis duarum Naturarum in Christo.

ALterum propositionis nostræ tertium membrum est, de Modo Unionis duarum Naturarum in Christo: Qui qualis sit, vel ex iis, quæ jam modò diximus, satis luculenter patet. Varii quidem Unionis modi tùm à Philosophis, tùm à Theologis, cumprimis à Damasceno lib. 3. cap. 3. percensentur: quemadmodum suprà etiam in refutatione Jesuiticissími præcipuos falsos modos refutavimus: ut hoc loco pluribus de iis agere nihil quicquam attineat. Rejectis proindè & reprobatis Modis Unionis singulis & universis, qui quidem dici aut excogitari possunt, solum illum admittimus qui Hypostaticus sive personalis est ac dicitur: non hoc quidem sensu, quasi personæ persona sit unita: sic enim non unus, sed duo prodirent Christi, id quod cum fide Christiana pugnat: sed neque eo etiam sensu, quasi neutra Natura personæ rationem habuerit, sed demùm ex concursu duarum simpliciter Naturarum, una persona esse cœperit: Hoc enim pacto Tota Trinitas statueretur ipse incarnata: quin ipse quoque Christus statueretur esse quiddam diversum à suis naturis: & quoddam quasi tertium: Sed hoc unico vero ac Orthodoxo sensu: Quod Secunda Trinitatis Persona, nempè λόγος Naturam humanam, propriâ personalitate destitutam, intra arctissimum ὑποστάσεως sive personæ suæ complexum & subsistentiam assumsit: eidemque suam πρόσωπότητα communicavit, ut ὑπόστασις hæc λόγου, simul sit ὑπόστασις assumtæ naturæ Humanæ, in qua etiam in perpetuum ea subsistat.

Quanquam verò tùm apud Veteres, tùm recentiores Theologos hæc Phrasis jam pridem obtinuit, ut diceretur, Unio Naturarum facta esse in Persona: tamen vitiosissimè indè nonnulli collegerunt, Unionem factam esse in tertio quodam, ab utraque Natura diverso. Tùm demùm enim valeret hæc collectio, Si Natura divina, & persona τοῦ λόγου, Realiter, sive τῷ εἶναι differrent. Quod cùm concedi nullo pacto salvâ Religione Christiana queat: frivolum & nugatorium est, quicquid nonnulli de Medio sive vinculo Unionis hujus somniant & fabulantur.

Disputant hoc loco Doctores Scholastici, An unio hæc Hypostatica duarum naturarum in Christo sit maxima omniũ Unionũ, vel ratione modi unionis vel ratione nobilitatis: Ubi in diversas planè sententias abeunt: Durando quidé Negativam defendente in l. 1. d. 3. Bonaventura autem in 3. d. 6. art. 2. q. 1. & 3. cum aliis Affirmativam propugnãte:

nonnullis mediâ quasi viâ incedentibus & contendētib9, Unionem hanc non esse maximam respectu eorum, quæ uniuntur, id est, respectu humanitatis & Verbi: Sed respectu ejus, in quo uniuntur: Item, Si Natura divina & humana fumantur, quatenns conjunguntur in uno supposito absolutè: tùm upionem Hypostaticam esse omnium unionum creatarum maximam: sed non nobiliorem unione divinarum personarum: uti tùm alii, tùm cumprimis Suarez prolixè admodum disputat Disp.1.Sect.2. Sed inutilis planè & ociosa hæc & id genus aliæ Scholasticorum sunt disputationes: ut An abstractâ personalitate per intellectum natura possit assumere Naturam? An Natura humana à λόγῳ assumta, fuerit abstracta ab omnibus individuis? & consimiles: indignæ planè accuratiore meditatione: Illud potiùs studium probandum & imitandum fuerit, quod orthodoxa Antiquitas, in explicanda Forma Unionis hujus posuit. Etsi enim Mysterium hoc verè est ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ νοῦν καὶ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν: ut Justinus loquitur: certas tamen notas constituerunt Patres, ex quarum observatione ad uberiorem ejus intelligentiam perveniri queat.

Acinitio quidem dixerunt, Naturas duas in Christo unitas esse ἀδιαιρέτως καὶ ἀδιαλύτως Indivisè & insolubiliter: innuentes λόγον semel assumtam naturam humanam, sempiterno sibi fœdere unitam in omnem æternitatem retinere. Confirmat hoc ipsum Scriptura, quæ asserit illudipsum Corpus Christi, quod in monte Oliveti, ascendit ad cœlos visibiliter, in novissimo die rediturum, oculis nostris adspectabile: Act. 1, 11. Joh. 19, 37. Heb. 9, 28. Videbunt in quem transfixerunt: quæ itidem attestatur, Christum in illa ipsa carne sua,nunc etiam apparere vultui DEI pro nobis Hebr. 9, 24. Imò ipsum nostra vilissima corpora aliquando redditurum conformia glorioso suo corpori: Phil.3. ult.

Deindè dixerunt, Naturas unitas esse ἀδιαsάτως indistanter. Cujus assertionis veritas patet ex ipso Unionis Hypostaticæ Termino proprio. Cùm enim Unio hæc facta sit in ipsa ὑποτάσει Filii DEI: vel quod idem est, cùm Humana Natura assumta, sit in illocalem ὑπόςασιν Filii DEI, ad quam nulla locorum διαςήματα possunt pertingere: utique nullus etiam locus Physicus, nulla locorum διαςήματα, sive intervalla Naturas hasce semel ὑποτατικῶς unitas, à se invicem dirimere possunt.

Tertiò dixerunt, Naturas unitas esse ἀχωρίςως inseparabiliter. Quæ nota cum præcedente cognationem aliquam habet, & hoc sibi vult, Non partem aliquam, sed totam ὑπόςασιν τῶ λόγω, sive, ut Apostolus loquitur, totam plenitudinem Divinitatis Filii DEI, ita unitam esse assumtæ humanitati, ut nulla prorfus vel separatio vel absentia Naturæ assumentis ab assumta, admitti possit: sed statim Unionem hanc solvi, imò duas fingi ὑποςάσεις five personas, quamprimùm assumta natura, ab assumente absens alicubi esse, statuitur.

Quartò dixerunt Naturas unitas esse ἀτρέπτως καὶ ἀσυγχύτως inconvertibiliter & inconfusè: Neutra enim Natura in alteram mutata est: sed mansit quælibet quod erat: Siquidem Assumtæ Naturæ Exaltatio, veritatem carnis non interficit, sed perficit, non tollit, sed extollit. Tandem variis similitudinibus explicare conati sunt, Unionem hanc non modò non fieri, sed ne cogitari quidem potuisse, sine verâ ac reali communicatione: & eâ quidem tantò arctiore & præstantiore, quantò hæc ipsa Unio est sublimior & arctior, quantò naturæ ipsæ sunt nobiliores & præstantiores: quantò denique finis ipse Unionis hujus est excelsior ac divinior. Quanquam verò de similitudinibus illis singulis ac universis verè usurpari potest illud Justini Philosophi & Martyris: ἁρμόδιον τόγε τὸ παράδειγμα κῆ τί γεν, ἀλλὰ μὴ παντελὲς: Conforme quidem est exemplum, sed ex parte tantùm & secundum quid, non autem ex toto: magnum tamen earum usum in præsenti disputatione esse, libenter concedimus: dummodò ritè accommodentur. Quâ de re tum aliorum Theologorum scripta, tum imprimis eruditissimus libellus Doctoris Chemnitii, magno cum fructu legi potest & debet: Cap. 6. mihi pag. 35. & seqq.

Potest autem ex notis istis rectissimè statui de Differentia specifica, quæ quidem dilucidè ostendet, Quidnam sit illud, Quod Unionis hujus gradum, sive modum, à reliquis omnibus præsentiæ modis, quibus DEUS præsens Creaturis adesse dicitur, evidenter discernat: nimirùm

1. quod λόγος Naturæ humanæ non tantùm adsit secundum universalem præsentiam, sive actionem generalem, quâ omnibus creaturis adest essentialiter, eas sustentat, conservat, regit ac gubernat:

2. neque etiam tantùm secundum inhabitationem & sanctificationem, quâ Sanctis non modò essentialiter adest, & inhabitat: Sed & iisdem suam gratiam impertit: Quo sensu D. Petrus affirmat, Sanctos reddi participes divinæ naturæ:

3. neque etiam tantùm secundum cœlestem illum præsentiæ modum, quo Angelis & Beatis cœlitibus in vitâ æternâ adest:

4. sed secundum præsentiæ PERSONALEM, quo non Pater, non Spiritus Sanctus, sed solus Filius, sive λόγος naturam humanam in unitatem & κοινωνίαν ὑποστάσεως sive Personæ suæ ita assumsit: ut duæ naturæ sic personaliter unitæ, factæ sint unum quiddam ὑποστατικὸν, & in unum coaluerint ὑφιστάμενον: quod est ac dicitur CHRISTUS: ita quidem ut jam CHRISTO nominato, neque DEUS tantùm cogitari, neque Homo solùm animo concipi debeat: sed in DEO, Homo: & in Homine ac cum Homine, DEUS, id est, θεάνθρωπος semper cogitandus sit.

Quibus observatis initiò vana & falsa deprehenditur accusatio illa, quâ Adversarii nostras flagellant Ecclesias, ac si docerent, Uniri Hypostaticè nihil esse aliud, quàm communicari attributa sive proprietates divinas, humanitati Christi.

Jam enim ostensum est, Differentiam specificam Unionis hujus non esse ipsam Communicationem Idiomatum: sed singularem illum & planè μονότροπον Unionis Modum, quo divina & humana naturæ, personaliter & inseparabiliter unitæ, unam constituunt personam; eo modo, quo explicatum est: licèt interim Communicatio Idiomatum ex Unione hac necessariò consequatur, uti mox demonstrabitur: tanquam Effectus, ex quo de ipsa Unione rectiùs judicari possit.

Deindè patet hinc etiam quid respondendum sit ad illud alterum Convitium, quo Jesuvvita Bellarminus nos perstringit, quòd nimirùm statuamus, unionem Hypostaticam factam esse, non per se, sed per Accidens. Nam tale quid à nostris vel dictum, vel scriptum esse non meminimus: neque Adversarius ipse etiam testem aliquem producere potest. Novimus enim per DEI gratiam, Essentiæ & Accidentis discrimine ea contineri, quæ secundum naturam, sive naturaliter se habent. Jam cùm Unio Hypostatica, ut & subsequens Communicatio, se secundum naturæ ordinem non habeat: ideò neque Essentialis, neque Accidentalis ea erit: sed sui proprii generis: hoc est, Personalis. Ubi tamen simpliciter repudiari nec potest, nec debet, quod ipsi etiam Doctores Scholastici, inter hæc duo, Per se, & per Accidens, in hac ipsâ materiâ, tertium aliquod constituerunt, idque nominarunt Quasi per Accidens & contingenter. Undè haud ineptè Gabriel dist. 6. Quæst. 2 notabili 4. in l. 3. Sent: Licèt humana natura sit adventitia personæ Verbi, non tamen est accidentalis ipsi verbo. Non enim est idem, Contingenter & Accidentaliter esse: Quia esse Hominem, contingenter evenit verbo: non tamen Accidentaliter: Quia Humanitas non obtigit Verbo, tanquam Accidens suo subjecto. Hinc Orthodoxi etiam Scriptores, inter quos est & acutissimus ille Schekius ab hoc termino, Quasi per accidens, Personaliter, in hoc explicando Mysterio minimè abhorruerunt.

Tandem idem Bellarminus satis impudenter clamitat, ex doctrina nostra planum esse, Nos talem statuere unionem duarum Naturarum in Christo: qualis est inter agens principale & inter instrumentum. Ubi Jesuvvita sine dubio tale instrumentum intelligit, quale finxit olim Nestorius, nempè separatum, quemadmodum artificium Instrumenta à personis artificum sunt distincta. Sed tale quid à nostris unquam vel dictum vel scriptum fuisse, in æternum non probabit. Sin illud sugillat, quod docemus, λόγον per Humanam naturam tanquam per Instrumentum exserere suas operationes: tùm malitiosè & per manifestum crimen falsi nostram pervertit sententiam. Neque enim vel ἄψυχον, vel ἄπρακτον, minimè omnium separatum intelligimus instrumentum: sed tale, cujus Exemplum simile, nequè in cœlo, neque in terra dari possit: quod nimirùm personaliter cum λόγῳ sit unitum: & ad idem perficiendum ἀποτέλεσμα efficaciter concurrat, non tantùm operando id, quod naturæ proprium est: sed & id, quod ex communicatâ virtute & majestate divinâ verè ac realiter accepit, ut divinas etiam actiones edere possit, quales sunt: Justificare, vivificare, ex mortuis revocare, salvare, & id genus aliæ, uti solo loco ostendemus. Quare mendacium luculentum sit oportet, quicquid hoc loco, de Agente principali, & Instrumento garrit Jesuvita.

His ita expeditis talem tandem Unionis Hypostaticæ Definitionem subjungimus, quòd ea sit Singulare ac admirandum opus totius Trinitatis, quo Λόγος sive Filius DEI virtute Spiritus Sancti, & obumbratione altissimi non personam, sed naturam humanam corpore & animâ rationali constantem, ex B. Virgine Maria, in unitatem suæ ὑποστάσεως affumtam, inseparabiliter inconfusè & indistanter sibi ita univit, ut totum sese ei, quâ ὑπόστασιν, quâ idiomata, communicando, non modò unum cum ea ὑφιστάμενον constitueret, quod est ac dicitur CHRISTUS: Sed & in, cum, & per eam, infinitâ Divinitatis suæ plenitudine inun&tam, ac ubique sibi præsentissimam, tùm tempore Exinanitionis, opus Redẽtionis: tùm post depositam servi Formam, omnia Divinitatis ac omnipotentiæ suæ opera in cælo & in terra exerceret ac perficeret.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ

The tighter and more divine the Union of the two Natures in Christ is, the more sublime and excellent must be the κοινωνία or communication that intervenes between them. For no mode of union can be given, whether in divine or natural things, which does not import some certain respect of κοινωνία or communication: so that they are insane with reason who dare to despoil that highest mode of Hypostatic Union of its native Effect, and to deny every real or true κοινωνία which intervenes between the united natures. Certainly, it is placed beyond controversy for both sides that Union is something πρός τι, or a Relative: since it is a conjunction not of one, but of more, or at the very least of two. Now where there is a Relative, there the consideration of the Foundation and the Term altogether deserves a place: and indeed not without its certain correlate. For just as a Relation arises when the affection of the Foundation is referred to its term: so when by a certain ἀντιςροφή or reciprocation, the σχέσις or habit of the Term is referred to its foundation, a correlation immediately emerges.

Nothing prevents us from adapting this very consideration of Relatives, although logical, to the present mystery. For in it is discovered such a Union, which arises from two natures: But it terminates in a person: Whence immediately arises that Relation which is the Union of two Natures into one person: where the Foundation is the twin Nature: but the Term is one person. With this Relation thus standing, immediately by Reciprocation, from the consideration of the Term, that is, the person, to the Foundation, that is, the two Natures, arises a correlation, which is nothing else than a mutual communication or affection, by which the two natures participate with one another. For just as the Person is the principle in which the two Natures meet: and become one personal thing: So if by a certain reflection, as it were, you turn yourself from this principle to the united natures, it cannot happen otherwise than that that very principle should become common not to one or the other separately, but to both Natures: in which, indeed, their union is terminated: Wherefore it is evident from this alone that they are clearly foolish who dare to deny the closest κοινωνία or Communication of the Natures: when nevertheless they wish to appear to believe in the union of two natures into one person. Certainly, as long as it is and remains true that Union and Communion cohere as Correlates, so that neither can be defined without the other: so long will it also remain true that this union of the two natures in Christ cannot subsist unless the communication itself is also granted: so indeed that, although Union and Communication are not one and the same, yet they behave as prior and posterior, by reason of Order: or, as Cause and consequent effect. But lest we seem to fight with philosophical subtleties rather than with the Scriptures, it pleases us to demonstrate the truth of this our assertion to the eye, by producing those authorities of Scripture which can easily sustain every attack of the Adversaries. But to those weighing the Scriptures more accurately, it cannot be obscure that from this hypostatic Union a twin Effect arises, or a double communication: of which one is and is called of the Natures: the other, however, of the Idioms. Of both of which we shall treat separately, if we first observe that: the word κοινωνία, which has its foundation in the sacred writings, and indeed in Heb 2:14, sustains some ambiguity among the Fathers: and is sometimes taken for the Hypostatic Union itself: but sometimes for the Effect of the Union, namely the Communication of Natures and Idioms. We, having set aside the former sense in this disputation, embrace the latter: but in such a way that we rightly abhor the futility of that consequence when the Adversaries repeatedly clamor: The Fathers called the union itself communication, Therefore they denied that communication for which we are fighting. For the writings of our own attest sufficiently that they felt and believed both.

OF

Latin:

QUô arctior ac divinior est duarum in Christo Naturarum Unio: eò sublimior etiam & præstantior κοινωνία sive communicatio illis invicem intercedat, necesse est. Neque enim ullus dari potest modus Unionis, sive in divinis, sive in naturalibus: qui non certum aliquem κοινωνίας sive communicationis respectum importet: adeò ut cum ratione insaniant, qui summum illum Unionis Hypostaticæ modum, suo nativo Effectu spoliare, ac omnem realem sive veram κοινωνίαν, quæ naturis unitis invicem intercedat, negare audent. Certè extra controversiam utrique est positum, Unionem esse quiddam πρός τι, sive Relatum: Siquidem non unius, sed plurium, vel ad minimum duorum ea est conjunctio. Jam ubi Relatum est, ibi Fundamenti & Termini consideratio locum omninò meretur: & quidem non sine suo certo correlato. Sicut enim Relatio tùm oritur, quando affectio Fundamenti refertur ad suum terminum: ita quando per quandam ἀντιςροφήν sive reciprocationem, σχέσις sive habitudo Termini refertur ad fundamentum suum, statim emergit correlatio.

Hanc ipsam, Logicam licèt Relatorum considerationem, ut ad præsens mysterium accommodēmus, nihil prohibet. Nam in eo deprehenditur talis Unio, quæ à duabus naturis oritur: Sed definit in personam: Undè statim ea oritur Relatio, quæ est duarum Naturarum in unam personam Unio: ubi Fundamentum est, Natura gemina: Terminus verò est una persona. Quâ Relatione sic stante statim per Reciprocationem, ex consideratione Termini, hoc est, personæ, ad Fundamentum, hoc est, duas Naturas, oritur correlatio, quæ nihil est aliud, quàm mutua sive communicatio, sive affectio, quâ duæ naturæ invicem participant. Quemadmodum enim Persona principium est, in quo duæ Naturæ conveniunt: & unum quiddam personale fiunt: Ita si per quandam quasi reflexionem, ab hoc principio, ad naturas unitas te convertas, fieri aliter nequit, quin illud ipsum principium non uni aut alterutri seorsim, sed utrique Naturæ commune evadat: in quo nimirùm earum unio terminatur: Quare velindè constat, insulsos planè esse qui negare audent arctissimam Naturarum κοινωνίαν sive Communicationem: cum tamen Unionem duarum naturarum in unam personam credere, videri velint. Certè quamdiu verum est & manet, Unionem & Communionem cohærere tanquàm Correlata ita ut neutrum sine altero definiri queat: tamdiu verum etiam manebit, Unionem hanc duarum naturarum in Christo subsistere non posse, nisi concedatur ipsa etiam communicatio: ita quidem, ut licèt Unio & Communicatio non sint unum & idem, tamen sese habeant ut prius & posterius, ratione Ordinis: vel, ut Causa & effectus consequens. Verùm ne argutiis magis philosophicis, quàm Scripturis pugnare videamur, placet hujus ipsius assertionis nostræ veritatem ad oculum demonstrare, illis in medium productis Scripturæ autoritatibus, quæ omnem Adversariorum impetum facilè sustinere queant. Accuratiùs autem Scripturas pensitantibus non obscurum esse potest, Ex Unione hac hypostatica, geminum oriri Effectum, sive duplicem communicationem: quarum una est & dicitur Naturarum: altera verò Idiomatum. De qua utraque seorsim agemus, si illud prius observaverimus: vocabulum κοινωνίας, quod fundamentum suum habet in sacris, & quidem Hebr 2,14. apud Patres æquivocationem aliquam sustinere: & interdum accipi pro ipsa Unione Hypostatica: interdum verò de Unionis Effectu, nempè Communicatione Naturarum & Idiomatum. Nos priore sensu in hac disputatione seposito: posteriorem amplectimur: sed ita: ut futilitatem illius consequentiæ meritò abominemur, quando Adversarii subindè obstrepunt: Patres communicationem nominarunt ipsam unionem, Ergò negarunt communicationem eam, pro qua nos pugnamus. Utrumque enim illos sensisse & credidisse, nostrorum Scripta fusè satis attestantur.

I. DE


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: I. On the Communication of Natures

The Word, by assuming human nature, not only was made a participant of flesh and blood himself, but also so really communicated himself to the assumed flesh that it may most truly be said: This Man is GOD: and GOD is Man: Likewise, the Son of Mary is the Son of the most high GOD: and the Son of the most high GOD is the Son of Mary.

Exposition.

The foundations of this proposition may be sufficiently clearly sought from the sacred writings. Where, in the beginning, that Johannine passage occurs, chapter 1, 14: The Word was made flesh. For this phrase obtains a peculiar emphasis: WAS MADE: as one which points out as if with an index finger what the Word was made, namely, flesh: 2. into what, or within what, term this assumed flesh arrived: namely, into the very hypostasis of the Word. Whence, that this most intimate communion of natures arises, there would hardly be anyone so dull as not to understand. Hence Athanasius in his Creed confesses that the Word was made flesh, not by the conversion of the Deity into flesh, but by the assumption of Humanity INTO GOD: showing that the hypostasis of the Word is that divine term into which the assumed flesh was raised through the Union.

Then the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 2, 14, confirms this very thing. Saying, Just as children have participated in flesh and blood, similarly, he himself also was made a participant of the same. From which passage one may argue thus.

If the Son of God, by assuming human nature, was truly and really made a participant of flesh and blood: then conversely, the assumed nature itself also was rendered a participant and sharer, that is, a participant of the assuming Word himself. But the former is true, as the present Apostolic passage teaches: Therefore the latter will also be established. I prove the connection of the major premise thus: If the assumed Human nature, through union with the Word, did not arrive into the communion of the hypostasis of the Word—which is what the Adversaries wish—it would follow that neither the Nativity from the Virgin, nor the obedience rendered to the Law, nor the passion, nor the death of the human nature would pertain in any way to the Word: But that the Word, through a mere presence, without any real communion of the natures with one another, adheres to the assumed human nature: But this latter is false, impious, and blasphemous. For Scripture manifestly testifies that not a mere man, but the Word himself,

the Word himself, the Son of God himself, the Lord of glory himself, the Prince of life himself, was born of a woman, subject to the law, crucified, and killed. Luke 1:32, Galatians 4:4 and 5, Acts 3:15, 1 Corinthians 2:8, Romans 8:32, Galatians 2:20. Therefore, that former point will also be of the same character.

Thirdly, those locutions which occur in the Scriptures demonstrate the immovable certainty of our assertion: as when either GOD is predicated of the assumed Man: The Branch of David is Jehovah: Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15. The Son of Man is the Son of God, Matthew 16:16. The Son of David is the Lord of David, Matthew 22:40. The Son of Mary is the Son of the Most High, Luke 1:32. The Second Man is the Lord from heaven, 1 Corinthians 15:47. Or, when the assumed Man is predicated of the assuming God: as The Word is Flesh, that is, true man, John 1:14. The Son of GOD is that man who came after John, John 1:30 and 34. The Son of GOD is the son of Joseph of Nazareth, John 1:45 and 50, etc. Finally, the unanimous consensus of Orthodox Antiquity obtains a force of proof that is by no means to be despised: which in this part fights so much on our side that, because of this most intimate communion of natures with one another, it does not hesitate to call the personal union a mixing and a blending, not indeed understanding that physical and corruptive one, which is nothing other than the union of altered things that can be mixed, but this singular and clearly hyperphysical one, by which two most diverse natures concur into one hypostasis, and, as Epiphanius speaks in the Ancoratus, are mixed into one thing. Although in the progress of time, and indeed after the Eutychian controversy was stirred up, the Church not inappropriately abstained from this formula of speaking. But it pleases us to hear from that orthodox Antiquity only Athanasius and Basil, those two lights of Greece, of whom the former in his epistle to Epictetus says: The human nature was made an accession from the communication and union of the Word to it: The latter, however, in his Sermon on the Holy Nativity, says: The Lord's own human flesh was made a participant of the Deity. More clearly, Damascenus, Orat. 3 on Images: The Creator lowered himself, that he might honor my nature and make it a participant and sharer of the divine nature.

And it deserves observation that Samosatenus was for this reason also convicted and condemned of error and heresy, because he denied this mutual and most intimate communion of natures with one another, positing that the two natures were altogether incommunicable to one another.

That same thing is meant by that perichoresis, very celebrated in the writings of the Fathers, by which they established that the natures in Christ, without any conversion, permeate and pass through one another, that is, as it were, migrate into and permeate one another.

Moreover, this is as it were the proper affection of that Communication of Natures, that it admits not abstractive, but only concretive forms of speech: namely, that the concrete of one Nature is correctly predicated of the concrete of another nature; indeed in such a way that it is most truly said: This Man is GOD: and GOD is Man: but it is not permitted to say in the abstract: This Humanity is Divinity: or Divinity is Humanity.

The reason for the affirmation is 1. Because neither nature is changed into the other, therefore neither can be predicated of the other in the abstract. Furthermore. Because the concrete stands for the person, that is, it has the notation of a person, which consists of two natures. Wherefore whether you name GOD or Man, the other is always correctly predicated of him in the concrete: Because that one person is always understood, who is Christ.

Moreover, a question is raised at this point concerning both the quality and the truth of those propositions, This Man is GOD, and GOD is Man, and the cause of the same. Certainly, our adversaries will perhaps also admit with us that they are neither essential nor accidental, for the reason that the Union itself is neither essential nor accidental. However, there are some who contend that the predications are identical, such as Bellarmine, writing that this proposition, The Son of GOD is the Son of Mary, is to be understood thus: The Man, who is united to the Son of GOD, is the Son of Mary, as we showed above in chapter 2 in our Jesuitism. But in this way it will be false, what Scripture affirms, that the Word was made flesh, that is, that the ὑπόστασις of the Word was made the ὑπόστασις of the flesh: Thus it will be false: that the Son of GOD is the seed of David: indeed, thus it will be false, that there is one person of both natures: but two persons will necessarily have to be posited: one which is the Son of GOD, the other, the Son of Mary, who communicates nothing in ὑπόστασις with the Son of GOD.

Furthermore, there are others, and especially the Calvinists, who contend that the predications of those propositions are figurative: so that, namely, through the τρόπον ἀντιδόσεως one nature is predicated of the other: because the notation of the first act is put for the signification of the second act: so that God is said to be Man: that is, to have Man united to Himself and to sustain him. But our blessed Luther rightly affirms that this is said most heretically, because by this means, the whole mystery of the Union of the two natures into one ὑπόστασις is simply undermined and overturned, as we have already shown concerning the identical predication. Therefore, having rejected all these false modes entirely, we maintain that the predications of those propositions are clearly unusual and singular: yet true and real, indeed most real: Where, however, some most viciously define the cause of this truth or reality as the Communication of Idioms. For it is most evident even from the mere sound of the words that no mention of any idiom at all is made in those propositions. It is therefore more correctly affirmed that the truth or reality of those predications depends solely upon the closest κοινωνίᾳ or Communication of the Natures to one another, by which it comes about that the λόγος is the ὑπόστασις not only of His own divine, but also of the assumed human nature: and thus this assumed nature does not subsist in itself, but has the λόγος Himself as its ὑπόστασις: so that now truly and really, This man, who has no other ὑπόστασις than that of the Son of GOD Himself, is and is called the Son of GOD: and vice versa: the Son of GOD, since He no longer has His ὑπόστασις separately: but has really communicated with the assumed human nature: truly is and is called the Son of Mary. With these things thus explained, it is plain that the explanation of those predications, which the compilers of the Calvinistic consensus foist upon the Church of GOD in this manner, is clearly heretical: The Man Christ is GOD: namely, not as Man, but as GOD: or, Christ GOD is Man: namely not as God, but as Man: or Christ is the Son of GOD, as GOD, not as Man. For 1. by this means that κοινωνία of the Natures, of which we are treating, is denied, and consequently the Union itself. Furthermore, the question here is not about the natures considered in themselves, from whence, or in respect of which Nature, Christ is the Son of GOD, or the Son of Man: but it concerns the whole person, insofar as it is indeed one ὑπόστασις, but meanwhile consists of two natures: Where whether you say the Son of Man, or the Son of GOD, you have not named a nature, but one and the same person, who is not separately GOD, and separately Man: but is and is called at once and in one ὑφισταμένῳ, both God, and Man, and the Son of GOD, and the Son of Man. From which, however, no confusion of the Natures follows: for communication simply removes all confusion or equalization. For because communication takes place at the very least between two, it is necessary that that which communicates itself be one thing: and that to which the communication is made be another. Add that this κοινωνία is not essential: but personal: as was shown a little before.

The Calvinist spirit clamors at this point, and accuses us of some novelty, because we maintain that the Communication of the Natures is one thing, and the Union of the natures is another: When yet this Communication is the Union itself, as Pezelius writes: page 90 of his Demonstration. But he who has weighed a little more accurately by what reason we teach that that κοινωνία follows from the Union of the Natures, as an effect, will easily pronounce us free from this accusation. The matter stands thus: Since the divine Nature is not communicated to the humanity primarily and immediately (for thus the whole Trinity would be incarnate) but consequently and secondarily, namely under the person of the λόγος: so that through the mediation of this person, the divine Nature itself (inasmuch as it differs from the person of the λόγος by reason only, but not in reality) is also united and communicated to the flesh: therefore we call the Person or ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου the immediate term of that assumption: And hence we place the specific difference of the Union primarily in such a Communication of the PERSON of the λόγος with the human nature. Which communication is nothing else than the Union itself. Now, however, since the Deity, or the divine nature of the λόγος, does not differ in reality from the λόγος himself: therefore the Communication of the Person, or the Union, necessarily implies also the Communication of the divine Nature, or of the Divinity, yet without any confusion of the Natures. Whence it is clearer than the midday light that this Communication of the Natures is something distinct from the Union itself: so indeed that, this Communication of the divine nature of the λόγος being denied, as regards the assumed flesh, let the Communication of his very person be immediately denied: and consequently the Union itself: for the reason that the divine Nature and the ὑπόςασις of the λόγꞣ do not really differ. Hence Scripture, speaking of Christ as Man, makes mention expressly in this matter not only of the λόγꞣ as a person, but also of the very Deity communicated: as when the Apostle affirms that in Christ dwells all the fullness of the Deity according to the flesh. Hence JESUS of Nazareth, because of this κοινωνία of Natures, is GOD. Which would be false, if the assumed flesh had no real κοινωνία with the λόγꞣ along with the eternal Deity of the Word.

But furthermore, the Adversaries are in an uproar here: If this Man is truly and really GOD: Therefore the Humanity is absorbed into the divinity: which thing manifestly confirms the Eutychian heresy. Which argument, indeed, must be weighed the more diligently, the more certainly they are accustomed to seek the protection of their error in it. At the beginning, however, they deceive under the sophism of equivocation, which they craftily conceal in the phrase 'really to be': while this signifies nothing else to them than a certain Physical effusion of the Divinity into the assumed flesh: through which it has been made equal to the divine Nature in all things: Which opinion, indeed, has never entered the minds of our people. For they understand by the word 'really' nothing else than that which is in truth, which is not merely verbal, feigned, or fictitious.

Next, the word GOD is considered either absolutely or relatively with respect to some certain suppositum, or person: Taken absolutely, it denotes all three persons of the Trinity, of which one in number and essence is the Divinity. Taken relatively, the word GOD denotes a certain person of the Trinity: just as in the present Question it denotes the person or ὑπόςασις of the λόγꞣ: as that which does not really differ from its Deity: and it denotes this ὑπόςασις indeed, either before the Incarnation or after the incarnation. Now, therefore, the Question arises, Whether and in what respect can the human Nature be called GOD? Where we indeed hold the affirmative, but with a double limitation. For first, because the human Nature of Christ is not a person: but a Nature, lacking its own personality: therefore it cannot be predicated of it absolutely that it is GOD: lest it be thought to be absorbed into the Divinity, as the Eutychians and Schwenkfeldians rave: or be considered to constitute its own person and thus add a Fourth person to the Trinity: as Nestorius blasphemed. But then, because after the Incarnation the λόγꞣ, his Person consists of two Natures: certainly the word GOD applies also to this Person, who is both GOD and Man, although in a most diverse respect. For in that this Person is GOD, this appellation applies to him Essentially: but in that he is man, it applies to him personally, namely by the grace of the Union, by reason of which he really arrives at the Fellowship of the Divinity. For although the assumed humanity has not been converted into the Nature of the Deity: whereby it happens that not even Nature is predicated of Nature abstractly: yet insofar as it is assumed within the very ὑπόςασις of the λόγꞣ, it has certainly been made a participant of the Divinity of the Word personally: unless perhaps someone wishes to separate and tear apart the person and the divine Nature of the Word. For which reason many of the Orthodox Fathers did not hesitate to name the Human Nature (but in a sound sense) ἀποθεωθεῖσαν, deified: likewise ὁμόθεον.

Although, indeed, to avoid the suspicion of both Eutychianism and Schwenkfeldianism, we willingly abstain from such abstract locutions: yet when the word CHRIST is placed in the position of the subject with this added determination, 'according to the Humanity': then we do not hesitate to assert, Christ according to the Humanity is also God, not indeed Essentially: but Personally, in the manner already explained. Which very thing can be demonstrated most evidently from the Scriptures.

For what else does the Epistle to the Hebrews ch. 1, 4 & 5 mean, when it affirms that Christ has been made so much better than the Angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they? than that it indicates quite clearly, just as the λόγος was from eternity the Son of GOD, as GOD: so by assuming human nature, he has inherited that same name of Son of GOD in a new way, according to his human nature.

And that we may press the Adversaries more closely, we like to argue thus:

Either Christ according to his assumed Humanity is clearly to be excluded from the denomination of Son of GOD: or he is to be admitted entirely into the fellowship of this name.

But the former would be impious and blasphemous even to think: For thus Christ according to his assumed Humanity would be of a worse lot and condition than we, who are named Sons of GOD in the Scriptures; John 1, 12. Rom. 8, 16. The Spirit bears witness to our spirit, that we are Sons of GOD. Therefore the latter must be established entirely.

Now, indeed, if Christ according to his humanity is the Son of GOD, he will be such either by Essence: or by adoption: or by a singular mode, common or communicable to no Creature.

And yet it is confessed on both sides that in the first way the name of Son of GOD does not belong to Christ according to His Humanity. Nor does it belong in the second way, which is that of Adoption: for this way, as Scripture testifies, belongs only to those who are reborn through water and the Spirit, John 3:5, who are born of GOD through faith, John 1:12, and who, finally, are led by the Spirit of GOD, that is, who walk according to the spirit in newness of life, Rom. 8:14.

It remains, therefore, that the name belongs to Christ according to His assumed humanity in a way that is clearly singular and communicable to no other creature: namely, by the personal κοινωνίᾳ of the Son of GOD Himself, who communicated His whole self to this humanity, as has been demonstrated thus far.

Latin:

ΛΌγος affumendo naturam humanam, non modò ipse particeps est factus Carnis & Sangvinis: sed & se totum affumtæ carni ita realiter communicavit, ut verissimè dici queat: Hic Homo est DEUS: & DEUS est Homo: Item, Filius Mariæ est Filius DEI altissimi: & Filius DEI altissimi est Filius Mariæ.

Ἔκθεσις.

Fundamenta Propositionis hujus satis perspicua ex sacris petere licet. Ubi initiò occurrit illud Johanniticum, cap. 1, 14. Verbum Caro factum est. Emphasin enim peculiarem obtinet phrasis hæc: FACTUM est: ut quæ ceu digito indice monstrat Quid λόγος factus sit, nempè caro: 2. in quem sive intra quem Terminum, affumta hæc caro pervenerit: nempè in ipsam ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου. Unde arctissimam hanc Naturum κοινωνίαν oboriri, vix quisquam ita bardus fuerit, quin intelligat. Hinc Athanasius in Symbolo suo confitetur, Verbum carnem esse factum non conversione Deitatis in carnem, sed affumtione Humanitatis IN DEUM: ostendens, ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου, esse divinum illum terminum, in quem per Unionem evecta sit affumta caro.

Deindè confirmat hoc ipsum Epistola ad Hebræos, cap. 2, 14. Quemadmodum, inquiens, pueri communicaverunt Carni & Sangvini: Similiter, ipse quoque particeps factus est eorundem. Ex quo loco sic argumentari licet.

Si Filius DEI affumendo naturam humanam, verè ac realiter particeps est factus carnis & sangvinis: utique è converso, ipsa quoque affumta natura, reddita est μέτοχος καὶ κοινωνός, hoc est, particeps ipsius affumentis λόγου. At prius verum, sic docente præsenti loco Apostolico: Ratum igitur erit & posterius. Connexum Majoris sic probo: Si affumta natura Humana, per unionem cum λόγῳ, in κοινωνίαν ὑποστάσεως τοῦ λόγου non pervenit: id quod volunt Adversarii: Consequens fuerit, neque Nativitatem ex Virgine, neque obedientiam Legi præstitam, neque passionem, neque mortem humanæ naturæ quicquam ad λόγον pertinere: Sed λόγον per nudam tantùm παράστασιν, sine ulla reali naturarum ad se invicem κοινωνίᾳ, affumtæ naturæ humanæ adhærere: Sed posterius hoc falsum impium & blasphemum. Manifestè enim Scriptura testatur, non nudum hominem: sed ipsum

λόγον, ipsum Filium Dei, ipsum Dominum gloriæ, ipsum principem vitæ, ex muliere natum, legi subjectum, crucifixum & interfectum esse. Luc. 1, 32. Galat. 4, 4. & 5. Actor. 3, 15. 1. Cor. 2, 8. Rom. 8, 32. Gal. 2, 20. Ejusdem ergò notæ erit etiam illud prius.

Tertiò demonstrant assertionis nostræ immotâ certitudinem eæ locutiones, quæ in Sacris occurrunt: ut quando vel DEUS prædicatur de asfumto Homine: Germen Davidis est Jehovah: Jerem. 23, 5. & 33, 15. Filius Hominis est Filius Dei, Matth. 16, 16. Filius Davidis est Dominus Davidis, Matth. 22, 40. Filius Mariæ est Filius Altissimi Luc. 1, 32. Secundus Homo est Dominus de cœlo 1. Cor. 15, 47. Vel, Quando Homo asfumtus prædicatur de asfumente Deo: ut Verbum est Caro, hoc est, verus homo. Joh. 1, 14. Filius DEI est vir ille, qui post Johannem venit, Joh. 1, 30. & 34. Filius DEI est Filius Joseph à Nazareth, Joh 1, 45. & 50. & c. Tandem probationis vim minimè contemnendam obtinet unanimis consensus Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis: quę usque adeò hac in parte à nostris militat partibus, ut propter hanc arctiffimam Naturarum ad se invicem κοινωνίαν, haud dubitet Unionem personalem nominare μίξιν & σύγκρασιν, Mixtionem: non Physicam quidem illam & corruptivam intelligens, quæ nihil est aliud, quàm miscibilium alteratorum unio, sed singularem hanc & planè hyperphysicam, quâ duæ diversissimæ naturæ in unam hypostasin concurrūt, & ut Epiphanius in Ancorato loquitur, in unum quid miscentur. Quanquam progressu temporis, & quidem post motam controversiam Eutychianam haud incommodè ab hac loquendi formulâ Ecclesia abstinuit. Sed placet ex orthodoxa illa Antiquitate Athanasium tantum & Basilium duo illa Græciæ audire lumina quorum ille in epistola ad Epictetū: Magis, inquit, Humana natura facta est accessio ἐκ τῆς τοῦ λόγου πρὸς αὐτὸν κοινωνίας τε καὶ ἑνώσεως : hoc est, ex communicatione & Unione Verbi ad naturam humanam: Hic verò Sermone in Sanctam Natipitatem: Humana, inquit, Domini caro ipsa particeps facta est Deitatis. Dilucidiùs Damascenus Orat. 3. de Imag. Creator sese demisit, ut Naturam meam cohonestaret, & divina Naturæ κοινωνὸν participem faceret.

Et observationem meretur quod Samofatenus ideò quoque erroris & hærefeos convictus & damnatus est, quòd mutuam hanc & arctiffimam Naturarum ad se invicem κοινωνίαν negavit, statuens tὰς δύο Φύσεις παντάπασιν ἀκοινωνήτους πρὸς ἑαυτὰς : Duas naturas simpliciter ad se invicem incommunicabiles.

Quod ipsum sibi vult περιχώρησις illa, Patrum Scriptis percelebrata, quâ statuerunt, Naturas in Christo sine ulla conversione περιχωρεῖν ἐν ἀλλήλαις, id est, in se mutuò quasi immigrare & permeare.

Cæterùm Communicationis istius Naturarum, hæc est propria quasi affectio, ut non abstractivas, sed concretivas tantùm locutiones admittat: nempè ut unius Naturæ concretum recte praedicetur, de concreto alterius naturae; ita quidem, ut verissime dicatur: Hic Homo est DEUS: & DEUS est Homo: non vero in abstracto liceat dicere, Humanitas haec est Divinitas: vel Divinitas est Humanitas.

Ratio arrfirmati est 1. Quia neutra natura in alteram est mutata, ergo neutra etiam de altera in abstracto praedicari potest. Deinde. Quia Concretum supponit pro persona, hoc est, notationem habet personae, quae ex duabus constat naturis. Quare sive DEUM, sive Hominem nomines, de eo semper alterum inconcreto recte praedicatur: Quia semper Una illa persona intelligitur, quae est Christus.

Caeterum movetur hoc loco Quaestio, de propositionum istarum, Hic Homo est DEUS, & DEUS est Homo, tum Qualitate, tum Veritate, ejusdemque causa. Certe nec Essentiales, nec Accidentales eas esse, forte nobiscum etiam fatebuntur Adversarii, propterea quod Unio ipsa nec est Essentialis, nec Accidentalis. Caeterum sunt nonnulli, qui Identicas esse praedicationes contendunt, ut Bellarminus, scribens propositionem hanc, Filius DEI est Filius Mariae, sic accicipiendam esse: Homo, qui est unitus Filio DEI, est Filius Mariae, uti supra cap. 2. in Jesuitismo ostendimus. Verum sic falsum erit, quod Scriptura affirmat, Verbum factum esse carnem, hoc est, ὑπόστασιν Verbi, factam esse carnis ὑπόστασιν: Sic falsum erit: Filium DEI esse germen Davidis: imo sic falsum erit, Unam utriusque naturae esse personam: sed duae necessario statuendae erunt personae: una quae sit Filius DEI, Altera, Filius Mariae, qui cum Filio DEI ὑποστάσει nihil communicat.

Sunt porro alii, & cumprimis Calviniani, qui contendunt, Propositionum istarum praedicationes esse figuratas: ut nimirum per τρόπον ἀντιδόσεως una natura de altera praedicetur: propterea quod primi actus notatio, ponatur pro significatione actus secundi: ita ut Deus dicatur esse Homo: id est, Hominem sibi habere unitum & sustentare. Sed recte B. Lutherus noster haereticissime hoc dici affirmat, propterea quod hoc pacto, totum mysterium Unionis duarum naturarum in Unam ὑπόστασιν simpliciter subruatur & evertatur, uti de praedicatione Identica jam ostendimus. Proinde falsis istis modis omnibus prorsus rejectis, statuimus, predicationes istarum propositionum esse plane inusitatas ac singulares: veras tamen & reales, imo realissimas: Ubi tamen veritatis sive realitatis hujus causam, vitiosissime nonnulli definiunt esse Communicationem Idiomatum. Nam vel ex solo Verborum sono evidentissime patet, nullam prorsus ullius Idiomatis mentionem in propositionibus illis fieri. Rectius proinde affirmatur, veritatem sive realitatem istarum praedicationum unice dependere ab arctissima Naturarum ad se invicem κοινωνίᾳ sive Communicatione, quippe qua fit, ut λόγος, non tantum sua divina, sed & assumta natura humana sit ὑπόστασις: & sic assumta haec natura, non subsistat in se, sed ipsum λόγον habeat pro ὑποστάσει: ut jam vere ac realiter, Hic homo, qui non aliam, quam ipsius Filii DEI habet ὑπόστασιν, Filius DEI sit & dicatur: & vice versa: Filius DEI, quin suam ὑπόστασιν non amplius seorsim habet: sed cum assumta humana natura, realiter communicavit: vere sit & dicatur, Filius Mariae. Quibus sic expeditis, planum sit, haeretica plane esse praedicationum istarum explicationem, quam Copilatores consensus Calvinistici in hunc modum Ecclesiae DEI obtrudunt: Homo Christus est DEUS: nempe, non qua Homo, sed qua DEUS: vel, Christus DEUS est Homo: nempe non qua Deus, sed qua Homo: vel Christus est Filius DEI, qua DEUS, non qua Homo. Nam 1. hoc pacto negatur illa, de qua agimus, Naturarum κοινωνία, & per consequens ipsa Unio. Deinde non quaeritur hic de naturis in se consideratis, unde, vel cujus Naturae respectu, Christus sit DEI filius, vel Hominis filius: sed agitur de tota persona, prout ea una quidem est ὑπόστασις, sed interim duabus constat naturis: Ubi sive Filium Hominis, sive Filium DEI dicas, non jam naturam, sed personam unam eandemque nominasti, quae est non seorsim DEUS, & seorsim Homo: sed simul & in uno ὑφισταμένῳ, & Deus, & Homo, & DEI filius, & Hominis Filius est & dicitur. Unde tamen nulla Naturarum sequitur confusio: Communicatio enim confusionem sive exaequationem omne simpliciter tollit. Quia enim communicatio fit ad minimum inter duo, utique aliud sit necesse est, ID, quod se communicat: aliud vero id, cui fit communicatio. Adde, quod haec κοινωνία non essentialis est: sed Personalis: uti paulo ante ostensum.

Obstrepit hoc loco Spiritus Calvinianus, & novitatis alicujus nos insimulat, eo quod statuamus, Aliud esse Naturarum Communicationem, Aliud vero Unionem naturarum: Cum tamen Comunicatio haec sit ipsa Unio, uti scribit Pezelius: pag. 90. Demonstrationis suae. Sed ab hac accusatione liberos nos facile pronunciabit, qui paulo accuratius expenderit, Quanam ratione, κοινωνίαν illam, ex Unione Naturarum, ceu Effectum, consequi doceamus. Res vero sic habet: Cum Natura divina primo & immediate non sit communicata humanitati (sic enim tota Trinitas esset incarnata) sed consequenter & secundario, nempe sub persona λόγου: ita ut haec persona mediante, ipsa quoque Natura divina (quippe quae ratione tantum, non autem reipsa differt a persona λόγου) unita & communicata sit carni: ideo Persona sive ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου, immediatum terminum assumtionis istius dicimus: Et proinde differentiam specificam Unionis, primo ponimo in tali Communicatione PERSONAE τοῦ λόγου cum humana natura. Quae communicatio, nihil est aliud, quam ipsa Unio. Jam vero, quoniam Deitas, sive natura divina τοῦ λόγου, a' λογω, ipso realiter non differt: ideo Personae Communicatio, sive Unio, necessario importat etiam Naturae divinae, sive Divinitatis Communicationem, sine ulla tamen Naturarum confusione. Unde luce meridiana clarius patescit, Communicationem hanc Naturarum esse distinctum quid ab ipsa Unione: ita quidem ut negata hac naturae divinae τοῦ λόγου Communicatione, quoad asfumtam carnem, statim ipsius etiam personæ negetur Communicatio: & consequenter ipsa Unio: propterea quòd Natura divina & ὑπόςασις τ῏ λόγꞣ realiter non differunt. Hinc Scriptura, de Christo, quâ Homo, verba faciens, non tantùm λόγꞣ ut personæ: sed & ipsius Deitatis communicatæ expressè meminit, in hoc negotio: ut quando Apostolus affirmat In Christo secundum carnem habitare omnem plenitudinem Deitatis. Hinc JESUS Nazarenus, propter hanc Naturarum κοινωνίαν, DEUS est. Quod falsum esset, si cum æterna Deitate Verbi, caro assumta, nullum haberet realem κοινωνίαν cum λόγῳ.

Sed porrò tumultuantur hîc Adversarii: Si hic Homo verè ac realiter est DEUS: Ergò Humanitas est absorpta in divinitatem: id quod Eutychianam hæresin manifestè confirmat. Quod sanè argumentum tantò diligentiùs expendendum fuerit, quatò certiùs erroris sui præsidium in eo quærere solent. Initiò autem sub sophismate æquivocationis fallunt, quam in phrasi Realiter esse, subdolè occultant: dum hæc nihil illis significat aliud, quàm Physicam quandam effusionem Divinitatis in assumtam carnem: per quam ea divinæ Naturæ per omnia exæquata sit: Quæ sanè sententia nostris nunquàm in mentem venit. Intelligunt enim illi per vocem Realiter nihil aliud, quàm quod revera est, quod non est verbale tantùm, simulatum aut fictitium.

Deindè vox DEI vel consideratur absolutè vel relatè respectu certi alicujus suppositi, sive personæ: Absolutè accepta notat omnes tres personas Trinitatis, quarum una numero & essentiâ est Divinitas. Relatè accepta vox DEI, notat certam quandam Trinitatis personam: quemadmodum in præsenti Quæstione notat personam sive ὑπόςασιν λόγꞣ: ut quæ à sua Deitate realiter non differt: & notat quidem hanc ὑπόςασιν, vel ante Incarnationem vel post incarnationem. Jam ergò oritur Quæstio, An & quo respectu Natura humana DEUS dici possit? Ubi Affirmativam quidem tenemus, sed cum duplici limitatione. Primùm enim, quia Natura humana Christi non est persona: sed Natura, propria personalitate carens: ideò de ea absolutè etiam prædicari non potest, quod sit DEUS: ne vel putetur in Divinitatem abforpta, ut Eutychiani & Schvvenkfeldiani delirant: vel existimetur propriam personam constituere & sic Quartam superaddere Trinitati personam: uti Nestorius blasphemavit. Deindè verò, quia post Incarnationem λόγꞣ, Persona ipsius ex duabus Naturis constat: utique vox DEI competit huic etiam Personæ, quæ & DEUS & Homo est, licet diversissimo respectu. Quâ enim Persona hæc DEUS est, competit ei hæc appellatio Essentialiter: Quâ verò homo est, competit ei personaliter, nempè ex Unionis gratia, ratione cujus in Consortium Divinitatis realiter pervenit. Etsi enim in Deitatis Naturam non est conversa assumta humanitas: quô fit, ut etiam non Natura de Natura abstractivè prædicetur: tamen quatenus assumta est intra ipsam ὑπόςασιν τ῏ λόγꞣ, certè personaliter particeps facta est Divinitatis τοῦ λόγου: nisi fortè quis personam & Naturam Divinam λόγου dirimere ac divellere velit. Quam ob causam Patrum Orthodoxorum plurimi, non dubitarunt Naturam Humanam (sed sano sensu) nominare ἀποθεωθεῖσαν deificatam: item ὁμόθεον.

Quanquam verò ad evitandam suspicionem tùm Eutychianismi, tùm Schvvenkfedianismi, nos ab ejusmodi locutionibus abstractivis libenter abstinemus: quando tamen subjecti loco ponitur vox CHRISTI cum adjecta hac determinatione, secundum Humanitatem: tùm non dubitamus asseverare, Christus secundum Humanitatem etiam est Deus, non quidem Essentialiter: sed Personaliter, modò jam explicato. Quod ipsum ex Scripturis evidentissimè demonstrari potest.

Quid enim sibi vult aliud Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 1, 4. & 5. quando affirmat, Christum tantò meliorem Angelis effectum esse, quantò excellentius nomen præ illis κεκληρονόμηκε hæreditariò fortitus est? quàm quòd satis perspicuè innuit, quemadmodum λόγος ab æterno fuit Filius DEI, quâ DEUS: sic humanam naturam affumendo, nova quadam ratione, idem illud nomen Filii DEI, juxta humanam naturam fortitum esse.

Et ut pressiùs urgeamus Adversarios, sic libet argumēti:

Aut Christus juxta affumtam Humanitatem, planè est excludendus à denominatione Filii DEI: aut omninò intromittendus in consortium hujus nominis.

Sed prius illud vel cogitatu impium & blasphe mũ fuerit: Sic enim Christus juxta affumtam Humanitatē deterioris esset sortis atq; conditionis, quàm nos, qui in Scripturis Filii DEI nominamur: Job. 1, 12. Rom. 8. 16. Spiritus testimonium reddit Spiritui nostro, quòd sumus Filli DEI. Ergò posterius hoc omninò statuendum.

Jam verò si Christus secundum humanitatem est Filius DEI, aut talis erit per Essentiam: aut per adoptionem: aut per modum singularem, nullique Creaturæ communem aut communicabilem.

Atqui primo modo Christo secundùm Humanitatem, nomen Filii DEI non competere, utrinq; in confesso est. Non etiam secundo modo, qui Adoptionis est: Hic enim modus illis tantùm teste Scripturâ competit, qui per aquam & spiritū renati sunt, Ioh. 3, 5. qui ex DEOper fidem nati sunt, Job. 1, 12. qui deniq; ducuntur Spiritu DEI, hoc est, secundum spiritum, in novitate vitæ ambulant Rom. 8, 14.

Relinquitur ergò Christo secundum affumtam humanitatem, nomen hoc singulari planè, nulliquè alii Creaturæ Communicabili ratione competere: nempè personali κοινωνίᾳ ipsius Filii DEI, qui se totum humanitati huic sua communicavit, uti hactenus demonstratum.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: Whether Union and Communication are the same

In this part of Christian doctrine also, the Sacramentarians or Calvinists have made a divorce from our Churches: whose confession concerning the Communication of Properties is this:

We believe that the Divinity has communicated to the humanity this highest dignity, that it is the flesh of the coeternal Son: that it has received many excellent and illustrious gifts: even more sublime than the gifts and mighty works of the Angels themselves: which indeed can fall into a created nature, in the most excellent degree: that is, as Sadeel interprets, which the essence of human nature can bear. We believe also, that the divinity has communicated to the humanity the fellowship of the office of Mediator between God and men, the honor of Head of the Church, of governor and Judge of the whole World, the fellowship of worship and adoration of the one with the λόγῳ. Admonit. Neostad. p. 65. Sadeel de verit. nat. hum. Beza.

But what the mode of this very communication may be, the authors, in the Staffurt book page 458, explain more clearly, in these words: We believe and ingenuously confess, that the Communication of idioms has not been made in the Natures, but in the person of whom the Natures themselves, and their properties and operations, but in the Concrete, can be truly and properly enunciated. As when it is said, The man Christ is omnipotent: The man Christ is with us, all days, even unto the consummation of the age: That is true through the Communication of Idioms.

But this confession is clearly Sophistical, and so composed partly of true, partly of false principles: that a more accurate explanation is altogether necessary.

For first, it is clearly Sophistical that they say, that the highest dignity has been communicated to the assumed flesh, which the essence of Human nature can bear. For this can be understood in two ways: Either that those communicated dignities do not destroy the assumed nature: or that only finite and created gifts, which have a certain analogy to the finite essence of human nature, have been communicated to it. Perhaps in both senses, the Adversaries accept their assertion. We, while agreeing with the former in all respects, simply reject and disapprove of the latter. For our Orthodox proposition will shortly demonstrate irrefragably that not only finite and created gifts, but the infinite and uncreated Divine Majesty itself, nay, the whole fullness of the divinity, has been truly and really communicated to the assumed humanity.

Then they clearly try to impose upon us craftily: while they indeed use words sufficiently convenient, which if they were not brought forward by others whose sense is known, could be tolerated: as Augustine spoke somewhere about the heretics of his own time. But soon they betray themselves like mice, while by the following declaration, they take away with one hand what they seemed to have given with the other: expressly writing: that the human nature contributes to the government and administration of the office of Mediator only as much as it can contribute from its own powers: But that with respect to the personal Union, and the subsequent Exaltation, it can perform anything beyond its natural powers, and beyond those finite, created and habitual gifts: that they most simply deny. Whence they have that saying of Cassian in their mouths: It is of no less error to add improper things to Christ, than to derogate from his own.

Thirdly, that the communication has not been made in the Natures, but in the person, is partly true, partly false. For as regards the first two kinds of Communication of Idioms, we easily grant this: but not so concerning the Third: where the divine Majesty is so communicated not to the whole person, but to the assumed Nature: that now it is true in the abstract: The flesh of Christ is life-giving.

Fourthly, this very assertion of the Calvinists is too ambiguous. For if they deny that the communication was made in the natures in this sense and respect, that indeed the Idioms of the λόγος, not outside the person, but in the unity of the person, have been communicated to the assumed Humanity: then we do not oppose it at all. But if they mean this, as they certainly do mean and contend, that it can indeed be said of the person, The man Christ is omnipotent, The man Christ is omniscient, omnipresent etc. But that this omnipotence, omniscience, and Omnipresence, has by no means been truly and really communicated to the human Nature, not even insofar as it subsists in the person of the λόγος: then we simply repudiate that dogma as contrary to both the scriptures and the orthodox Antiquity.

Finally, it is clear from what has already been said, that the Calvinists believe and confess nothing but a verbal communication of idioms: in this sense indeed, that the Humanity of Christ is indeed said to be omnipotent, omniscient etc. But is not, Because it cannot naturally be such.
