Hence in express words, they explain the κοινωνίαν of idioms through the word PERMUTATION, so that the communication is only a permutation, not a true or Real Commutation: as can be seen in the Calvinistic consensus, page 52 for me. But by this pact, we shall soon demonstrate that the Hypostatic Union itself of the two natures in Christ is utterly removed and denied, if we first show what the opinion of the Jesuits is concerning this chapter of Christian Doctrine.

Thus, however, Bellarmine, book 3 on the Incarnation, chapter 9, page 478. Catholic doctrine teaches two things. First: That from the Hypostatic Union many created and infused gifts have followed into the humanity of Christ: such as most excellent grace, greatest wisdom, singular power and other things of that kind, which however are not attributes of the Deity, except through a certain participation, just as we also participate in the attributes of GOD through created qualities, although less perfectly than the humanity of Christ participates in them. Nor does the communication of Idioms consist in these: for that communication is mutual: but the communication of these gifts is not mutual, for nothing has accrued to the Deity.

Secondly, from the Hypostatic union follows the communication of Idioms: which communication indeed is not real with respect to the natures themselves, as if the Divinity itself were made passible: and the Humanity were really made omnipotent, as the Lutherans will have it: nor is it purely verbal, as Beza wishes in his book against Brentius: and Peter Martyr in his Dialogue on the two natures: But it is indeed real, but with respect to the Hypostasis, or the person

And after a few words: Therefore we rightly say: GOD is born of a Virgin, suffered, died, etc. because GOD can be taken for any divine suppositum, and therefore for the suppositum of the second person, which is at once divine and human. Which suppositum is truly and really God, is truly and really Man: and therefore is truly and really born of a Virgin, suffered, died, etc. by the same reasoning we rightly say, Christ the man is omnipotent, eternal, everywhere, etc. because Man in the concrete stands for the human suppositum. But in Christ the divine and human suppositum is one: and since it is divine, consequently it is omnipotent, eternal, and everywhere, etc.

In order to examine this Jesuitical Confession more accurately, we first remove those things which, being truly said by him, easily deserve our consent: such as that he confesses that some Communication of Idioms follows from the Hypostatic Union: Item, that this Communication is not purely Verbal: Although the thing itself speaks, that neither of these do the Jesuits sincerely believe and confess: which is sufficiently clear from the Jesuitical Confession itself. For if the Communication of Idioms follows from the Hypostatic Union: and it is truly real with respect to the natures: then it is necessary that the Communication of Idioms itself be true and real with respect to the natures. For such as the Union is, such also is the Communication. Then, since between that which is verbal and that which is real there is no third: and everything that is, is either said to be, or is, either verbal or real, then whoever denies that this Communication is purely verbal, it is necessary that he concede it to be Real: and vice versa, whoever denies it to be Real, he tacitly asserts and confesses it to be verbal.

Thirdly, the Jesuit's Sophistry is purely frivolous, by which he hopes to emerge from these difficulties, when he invents a sort of third thing, saying that the real Communication of Idioms is one thing with respect to the natures themselves: but another with respect to the hypostasis, or the person of each nature. For the very same fallacy is hidden in this place, which we noted a little earlier, and indeed in the fourth place, in the opinion of the Calvinists.

Fourthly, that he himself establishes a Verbal Communication, however much he may dare to deny this in words, is clearly demonstrated by the Examples produced by him. For since the suppositum or person of Christ consists of two natures, that is, is both GOD and Man: he therefore contends that all propositions are true with respect to the person, but not all true and real with respect to the natures. For example, he thinks this proposition, GOD is born of a Virgin, must be interpreted with respect to the suppositum in such a way that it is enunciated of the whole person: but is only true insofar as this person is Man: so that its sense is purely the same as, Man is born of a Virgin. Thus, Christ the Man is omnipotent: that is, the Person of Christ is omnipotent, insofar as he is GOD, not insofar as he is Man. By which way, indeed, it is as certain and undoubted that the Jesuit believes not in a real, but only a verbal Communication, nay, absolutely none at all, as it is certain and undoubted that they strip the assumed humanity of all divine Majesty whatsoever: as will appear from their own objections in its proper place.

Fifthly, it is false and purely heterodox that the Jesuit writes: That many created and infused gifts have followed into the humanity from the Hypostatic Union. For such gifts are proper to human nature, habitually and subjectively inhering in it: according to which our own bodies (the distinction of degrees being nevertheless preserved) will one day be made conformable to his own glorious body. Phil. 3. last. And indeed in this part most of the Old Scholastics dissent from him, as also Alexander Pesantius argues from the more recent ones. 1. on the third part of Thomas, Question 7. Art. 3. page 801. and following.

Finally, it is a very enormous pseudographēma that Bellarmine writes, that in this proposition, GOD is born of a Virgin, the word GOD can be taken for any divine suppositum: as if this same statement could be understood of the Father, and of the Holy Spirit. Certainly, the Christian Religion maintains that the word GOD, in this proposition, is not to be taken essentially for any divine suppositum: but personally for the Son alone. But so that, leaving aside the tricks and Sophistries of the Adversaries, we may propose the Orthodox doctrine of our Churches: we like to premise this general proposition at the beginning.

Latin:

IN hac quoque parte Doctrinæ Christianæ, divortium à nostris Ecclesiis fecerunt Sacramentarii sive Calviniani: quorum hæc est de Communicatione Idiomatum Confessio:

Credimus Divinitatem communicasse humanitati hanc summam dignitatem, quòd est caro filii coæterni: quòd accepit multa eximia & illustria dona: ipsorum etiam Angelorum donis ac Virtutibus sublimiora: quæ nimirum in Creatam naturam cadere possunt, in gradu excelsissimo: hoc est, interprete Sadeele, quæ humanæ naturæ essentia ferre potest. Credimus etiam, quòd divinitas communicavit humanitati societatem officii Mediatoris inter Deum & homines, honorem Capitis Ecclesiæ, gubernatoris & Judicis totius Mundi, societatem cultus & adrationis unius cum λόγῳ. Admonit. Neostad. p. 65. Sadeel de verit. nat. hum. Beza.

Sed quis modus sit hujus ipsius communicationis, autores, libri Staffurtensis pag. 458. dilucidiùs explicant, his verbis: Credimus & ingenuè confitemur, Communicationem idiomatum non factam esse in Naturis, sed in persona de qua Naturæ ipsæ, earumque proprietates & operationes, sed in Concreto, verè & propriè enunciari possunt. Ut quando dicitur, Homo Christus est omnipotens: Homo Christus est nobiscum, omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi: Verum illud est per Communicationem Idiomatum.

Sed Sophistica planè hæc est confessio, & ita partim ex veris, partim ex falsis principiis, conflata: ut accuratiore enodatione omninò opus sit.

Primùm enim Sophisticum planè est, quòd dicunt, Assumtæ carni eam communicatam esse dignitatem summam, quæ Humanæ naturæ efsentia ferre queat. Duobus enim modis hoc intelligi potest: Vel quòd dignitates illæ communicatæ assumtam naturam non destruant: vel quòd finita tantùm & creata dona, quæ ad finitam naturæ humanæ essentiam analogiam quandam habeant, eidem sint communicata. Utroque fortè sensu, Adversarii assertionem suam accipiunt. Nos quoad priorem per omnia consentientes, posteriorem simpliciter rejicimus & improbamus. Neque enim finita tantùm & creata dona, sed ipsam infinitam atque in creatam Majestatem divinam, imò omnem plenitudinem divinitatis assumtæ humanitati, verè ac realiter communicatam esse, paulò pòst Orthodoxa nostra propositio irrefragabiliter demonstrabit.

Deindè veteratoriè planè nobis imponere student: dùm verbis quidem utuntur satis commodis, quæ si non ab aliis, quorum sensus notus est, proferrentur, tolerari possent: ut alicubi de sui temporis hæreticis locutus est Augustinus. Sed mox seipsos soricum instar produnt, dùm subjecta declaratione, alterâ manu eripiunt, quod una dedisse videbantur: expressè scribentes: ad gubernationem & administrationem officii Mediatoris tantùm conferre humanam naturam, quantum è propriis possit conferre viribus: Quod autem respectu Unionis personalis, & subsecutæ Exaltatiois, ultra vires suas naturales, & ultra finita illa, creata atque habitualia dona aliquid præstare possit: id verò simplicissimè negant. Undè subindè illud Cassiani in ore habent: Non minoris erroris est, Christo impropria addere, quàm propria derogare.

Tertiò, Communicationem non in Naturis, sed in persona factam esse, partim verum, partim falsum est. Nam quoad duo prima genera Communicationis Idiomatum, facilè hoc largimur: de Tertio autem non item: ubi non toti personæ, sed Naturæ assumtæ ita communicata est divina Majestas: ut jam in abstracto verum sit: Caro Christi est vivifica.

Quartò, hæc ipsa assertio Calvinianorum nimis ambigua est. Si enim hoc sensu ac respectu, negant communicationem factam esse in naturis quòd nimirùm Idiomata τοῦ λόγου, non extra personam, sed in unitate personæ, communicata sint assumtæ Humanitati: tùm minimè repugnamus. Sin hoc volunt, uti certè volunt & contendunt, de persona quidem dici posse, Homo Christus est omnipotens, Homo Christus est omniscius, omnipresens &c. Verùm omnipotentiam hanc, omniscientiam, & Omnipræsentiam, neutiquàm humanæ Naturæ verè ac realiter communicatam esse, ne, quidem, quatenus ea in persona λόγου subsistit: tùm dogma istud & scripturis & orthodoxæ Antiquitati adversum, simpliciter repudiamus.

Tandem liquet ex jam dictis, Calvinianos non nisi verbalem communicationem idiomatum credere & confiteri: hoc nimirùm sensu, ut Humanitas Christi dicatur quidem omnipotens, omniscia &c. Sed non sit, Quia Naturaliter talis esse non potest. Hinc disertis verbis, idiomatum κοινωνίαν, per vocabulum PERMUTATIONIS explicant, ut communicatio sit permutatio tantùm, non vera aut Realis Commutatio: uti videre est in consensu Calvinistico, mihi pag 52. Hoc autem pacto, ipsam Unionem Hypostaticam duarum naturarum in Christo prorsus tolli & negari, mox demonstrabimus, si priùs ostenderimus, quænam Jesuvvitarum, de hoc Doctrinæ Christianæ capite sit sententia.

Sic autem Bellarminus, lib. 3. de Incarnatione cap. 9. p. 478. Catholica doctrina duo docet. Primò: Ex Unione Hypostatica consecuta esse in Christi humanitatem multa dona creata & infusa: ut gratiam excellentissimam, sapientiam maximam, potentiam singularem & alia id genus, quæ tamen non sunt attributa Deitatis, nisi per participationem quandam, quomodo etiá nos participamus DEI attributa per creatas qualitates, licet minùs perfectè, quàm Christi humanitas ea participet. Neque in his consistit communicatio Idiomatum: nam illa communicatio est mutua: Horum autem donorum communicatio non est mutua, nihil enim Deitati accessit.

Secundò, ex unione Hypostatica sequitur communicatio Idiomatum: quæ quidem communicatio non est realis respectu ipsarum naturarum, quasi ipsa Divinitas facta sit passibilis: & Humanitas realiter facta sit omnipotens, ut volunt Lutherani: neque est planè verbalis, ut vult Beza in lib. contra Brentium: & Petrus Martyr in Dialogo de duabus naturis: Sed est realis quidem, sed respectu Hypostasis, sive personae utriusque naturae: non autem respectu ipsarum naturarum.

Et post pauca: Itaque rectè dicimus: DEUS est natus ex Virgine, passus, mortuus &c. quia DEUS accipi potest, pro quolibet supposito divino, & proindè pro supposito secundae personae, quod est simul divinum & humanum. Quod suppositum verè & realiter Deus est, verè & realiter Homo est: & proindè verè & realiter natum est ex Virgine, passum, mortuum &c. pari ratione rectè dicimus, Christus homo est omnipotens, aeternus ubique &c. quia Homo in Concreto stat pro supposito humano. In Christo autem suppositum divinum & humanum unum est: & cùm sit divinum, consequenter est omnipotens, aeternum & ubique & c.

Hanc Jesuiticae Confessionem ut accuratiùs evolvamus, initiò removemus ea, quae verè ab ipso dicta, nostrum consensum facilè merentur: ut, quòd fatetur, ex Unione Hypostatica sequi aliquam Communicationem Idiomatum: Item, Communicationem hanc non planè esse Verbalem: Quanquam res ipsa loquitur, neutrum istorum Jesuvitas sincerè credere & confiteri: id quod ex ipsa Jesuiticae Confessione satis liquidò patet. Nam si Communicatio Idiomatum ex Unione Hypostatica sequitur: ea verò respectu naturarum verè est realis: utique ipsa etiam Communicatio Idiomatum respectu naturarum vera ac realis sit necesse est. Qualis enim est Unio, talis etiam est Communicatio. Deindè cum inter id, quod est verbale, & id, quod est reale, nullum sit tertium: & omne, quod est, aut dicitur, vel verbale sit, vel reale, utique qui negat Communicationem hanc planè verbalem esse, is eam Realem esse concedat necesse est: & vice versa, Qui Realem negat, is verbalem vel tacitè asserit & confitetur.

Tertiò frivola planè est Sophisticatio Jesuvitae, quà ex istis difficultatibus se emersurum sperat, cum tertium quasi quiddam comminiscitur, Realem, inquiens, Communicationem Idiomatum aliam esse respectu ipsarum naturarum: aliam verò respectu hypostaseos, sive personae utriusq; naturae. Nam eadem planè fallacia hoc loco occultatur, quam paulò antè & quarto quidem loco in Calvinianorum sententia notavimus.

Quartò Verbalem ipsum Communicationem, quantumvis hoc verbis negare ausit, statuere, liquidò demonstrant Exempla ab ipso producta. Cùm enim suppositum sive persona Christi ex duabus constet naturis, hoc est, & DEUS sit & Homo: ideoque contendit, omnes propositiones veras esse respectu personae, non autem omnes veras ac reales respectu naturarum. Exempli gratia, Propositionem hanc, DEUS est natus ex Virgine, sic respectu suppositi interpretandam effe censet, ut de tota quidem persona enuncietur: sed vera tantùm sit, quatenus hæc persona Homo est: ut idem planè ejus sit sensus, Homo est natus ex Virgine. Sic Christus Homo est omnipotens: hoc est, Persona Christi est omnipotens, quatenus DEUS, non quatenus Homo est. Quo sanè pacto non realem, sed verbalem tantùm Communicationem, imò prorsus nullam Jesuuvitas credere, tàm certum est, quam certum & indubitatum est ipsos assumtam humanitatem omni prorsus Majestate divina spoliare: ut ex ipsorum objectionibus suo loco patebit.

Quintò falsum & ἐτερόδοξον planè est, quòd Jesuuvita scribit: Ex Unione Hypostatica consecuta esse in humanitatem multa creata & infusa dona. Nam ejusmodi dona propria sunt humanæ naturæ, habitualiter & subjectivè ipsi inhærentia: secundum quæ, nostra etiam corpora (servatâ tamen distinctione graduum) aliquando conformia reddentur corpori ipsius glorioso. Phil. 3. ult. Et sanè hac in parte ab ipso dissentiunt plerique Veteres Scholastici, ut & ex recentioribus Alexander Pesantius disputat. 1. in partem tertiam Thomæ, Quæst. 7. Art. 3. pag. 801. & seqq.

Tandem enorme admodum ψευδογράφημα est, quod scribit Bellarminus, in hac propositione, DEUS est natus ex Virgine, vocem DEUS pro quovis supposito divino accipi posse: quasi & de Patre, & de Spiritu Sancto, hæc eadem sententia intelligi queat. Certè Vocem DEUS, in hac propositione, non essentialiter pro quovis supposito divino: sed personaliter pro solo Filio accipiendam esse Religio Christiana statuit. Sed ut missis Adversariorum præstigiis & Sophisticationibus, Orthodoxam nostrarum Ecclesiarum doctrinam proponamus: initiò generalem hanc propositionem libet præmittere.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: General Proposition I. Orthodox

General PROPOSITION.

I. ORTHODOX.

The Son of God or the Word, by assuming human Nature, both appropriated to himself the Idioms of the same Nature: and indeed rendered the same not only a koinōnon or participant of his hypostasis: but also anointed it with the infinite fullness of his Divinity.

Exposition.

In disputing about the Communication of Idioms, we understand by Idioms nothing else than those differences of natures by which, as if by certain marks and characters, the Natures are distinguished and discerned from one another. For because in Christ there has been made no conversion or ταυτότης of natures: but they are and remain most diverse for eternity: therefore whatever occurs in either this or that nature, by which one is distinguished or differs from the other: that is called a property, or difference, ἰδίωμα in Greek.

Similarly, we do not take the word κοινωνία (Communication) transitively, as it is accustomed to be taken elsewhere: so that to communicate is nothing other than to make some thing common to another or to many by the definition of a Property or Accident: but intransitively or correlatively, so that to communicate in this place is nothing other than to admit something into fellowship and society, and so to join it to oneself, that it has communion or fellowship with it, always in that degree and respect which the Union of the United things themselves imports. Now, however, that some Communication of Idioms in the Natures of Christ has truly and really occurred through and because of the Personal Union: can be demonstrated invincibly to the eye. Let this be the first argument:

I. Whatever comes under the Union in the assumption of Human Nature: that also comes under κοινωνία or communion. But it is not naked natures, but those furnished with their own properties, that came under the Union, at the very first moment of the Union. Therefore, the properties of the Natures themselves also came under κοινωνία or Communion.

The certainty of the major premise is clearly evident, first from those reasons by which we proved above that this union of the two natures in Christ was not made without the closest κοινωνία of the united things with one another. Then, because the ὑπόστασις of the Word is ἀμέριστος, having no part outside of part: and thus it could not be that one thing was united with the Humanity, while another was communicated: but it is necessary that that very thing which is united, is also communicated. Now as regards the minor premise, the matter is likewise sufficiently plain. For no nature is naked, but is endowed with its own Idioms: if it were deprived of which, it would no longer be a Nature: For Φύσις ἀνιδίω- τος, πάντως καὶ ἀνύπαρκτος: A nature lacking properties also lacks existence. Furthermore, the divine nature with the Word is something most simple, the same; since the divine Idioms, not as in humans, admit the condition of accidents or Qualities; but are most simply converted with the divine Essence itself. Wherefore it could by no means happen that the ὑπόστασις of the Word was truly communicated to the assumed humanity: while the Communication of the divine Idioms themselves did not at the same time truly and really accrue to the same humanity.

II. The argument resulting from this former one is as follows: If a true and real Communication of Idioms does not arise from the Hypostatic Union: then the Union of the two natures in Christ itself will no longer be able to subsist. But this latter is heretical, nay, blasphemous: Therefore, the former will also be of the same kind.

The connection of the major premise is most firmly established from this: The Person of the Word, and his Idioms, are so one ἀδιαιρέτως, that whoever denies that the Idioms of the Word have been really communicated to the human nature, (as the Adversaries certainly deny expressly) he by this very fact openly denies that the ὑπόστασις or person of the Word (which is most simply one thing with the Idioms of the Word) has been really communicated to the assumed nature, and consequently, that it is not personally united to it either.

III. The lowest degree of Union is where the united things communicate nothing to each other, as when two boards are glued together. Which combination is more correctly called παράθεσις than ἕνωσις.

But as Scripture defines, the personal Union not only surpasses all individual and universal modes of Union, which indeed occur in natural things, by infinite parasangs: but also transcends in its whole genus those by which both the three persons are united to each other, and indeed by which GOD is said to be present to created things: so that from two most diverse natures, one ὑποκείμενον has been made.

Why, therefore, is it not necessary that not some naked παράθεσις or παράστασις of Natures, but the closest κοινωνία or communication, both of the Natures to each other and of the properties, arises from this Union? And indeed, if we are rendered κοινωνοὶ θείας φύσεως, partakers of the divine nature, through faith and because of the gracious presence and indwelling of GOD, as Peter testifies in chapter 1, verse 4. How much more incomparably has the human nature of Christ become a partaker of the divine Majesty of the Word: as one which assumed it into its own ὑπόστασις, not merely through a gracious presence by itself, but through a personal Union.

IV. Holy Scripture describes the mystery of the personal union in such a way that it expressly defines also the effect or consequence of it, namely this real κοινωνίαν of the attributes, of which we are speaking.

Therefore it would be a sign of proven impiety to either deny or tear down this same effect in any way.

The antecedent is evident from the first chapter of John, verse 14. Where the union itself is described at the beginning: The Word was made flesh: But soon the effect of the union is subjoined: And we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. Where the particle 'as it were' points out, as with an index finger, that this glory is to be understood as the glory of the human nature communicated from the union: and not indeed as the eternal glory of the Son of God: for he is not 'as it were' the only begotten: but by nature the only begotten Son of God the Father. Which very thing Hilary also observed from antiquity in book 3 of the Trinity, saying: The Son was made flesh, so that the flesh might begin to be that to God the Father which the Word was: so that that which was of time might receive the glory of that brightness which was without time, so that the flesh might be transferred into the power of God.

With these things thus established, the explanation of that controversy which is agitated concerning the quality of the communication of attributes will now be easier. For it is evident from both sides that it is neither essential nor accidental, because the union itself is not such. For although some of the orthodox have by no means shrunk from the word effusion in this very matter, yet this was not done in the Eutychian or physical sense, as if the properties of the divine nature had been so poured into the human, that it possessed them in itself, and by itself, as if separated from the Divinity: but in a metaphorical sense, most customary to the scriptures themselves, signifying by this that the human nature was anointed with the infinite fullness of the Divinity of the Word, not by measure, but without measure: in a manner not Physical, but Hyperphysical. Which Metaphorical signification reveals itself also in those places of scripture which declare that the gifts of the Holy Spirit have been poured out upon the faithful. Joel 2. Zach. 12.

As regards verbal Communication, it is most clearly evident that it in no part reaches the sublimity of this mystery, but is a fabrication of Samosatenus from the same principle. For here too that customary rule of the Theologians holds: As is the Union, so also is the Communication: Therefore, if a verbal communication is established, it is necessary that a verbal union also be granted. But now, what is verbal: is not true: Nay, it is plainly not. For if it were true, it would no longer be Verbal, but Real. For a word or logical symbol of a thing is not the thing itself, or a part, or an Idiom of the thing: But it is a mark of a concept in the mind, which, if it does not correspond to the thing which is outside the intellect, is certainly more correctly called false than verbal. It is evident from this what must be determined concerning the Philippean Definition, by which he defines the Communication of Idioms through a figure of Speech, or a mode of speaking, etc.

It remains therefore, with all those false modes removed, that such a Mode of communication must be established which follows the Nature and Quality of its principle, that is, of the personal Union. Just as therefore the Union itself is neither Essential, nor Accidental, nor merely Logical or verbal: But personal, true and real: So the communication of idioms is also most correctly called Personal, true and real.

However, this Real Communication differs as much as possible from the Physical effusion of properties. For although the Natures in Christ are said to communicate their properties: yet each Nature retains its own Idioms within its own essence: so that the properties of one nature are never in the other, as a certain form, or habit in a subject: For in this way the absurdity of Effusion and confusion would be rightly objected to us. But this communication is such that it follows the condition of its Foundation: namely: that, just as the Word made its own hypostasis common to the assumed nature, not verbally, but really: So the human nature subsisting in the person of the Word, possesses all divine things, and has them in common in the Word: likewise it participates in all human things for a common use and effect. Therefore, since we establish that the idioms of the Natures are not really common to themselves among each other, but to the Person: that is, that the natures with their properties are in themselves and among themselves incommunicable: yet we establish that they communicate among each other in one common person: a Physical or Eutychian confusion or Effusion is altogether vainly objected to us. With these things observed, it is immediately evident of its own accord that it is altogether foolishly gathered by the Adversaries from the Real communication, which we establish, that there is a Physical effusion. For Real and Physical are not opposites, that is, reciprocal in each of their parts: so that whatever is real, that is also immediately Physical: But they are only convertible, reciprocal in one part only: so that while every Physical thing is indeed real: it is not vice versa, that every real thing is Physical, and thus Real extends far more widely than Physical. For the sake of example, in the article of the Trinity, the three persons differ really: but not Essentially: since they are one in Essence. Thus the Human and divine Natures are united really: but not Essentially. Whence the Communication also flowing from thence is Real, although it is not Essential. Therefore the same Term Real or Really in this dispute sounds the same to us as True: and thus it is opposed to fictitious, or verbal, which consists only in a bare title or name: so that it is truly that which is, not having the name by imagination only: Truly and really, or in the very act, not imaginarily, or according to the name only, it pertains to the thing of which it is predicated. But the question is asked in this place: If the communication of idioms is to be granted; is it so reciprocal with respect to the natures: that just as the divine nature communicated its idioms to the assumed humanity: so in turn has the Humanity communicated its idioms to the Divinity of the Word? We answer that one must diligently distinguish between the Thing and the Mode of the thing. For as regards the thing itself, that is, the Real Communication of idioms, we grant that it is reciprocal: insofar as those things which are proper to humanity are enunciated of the divine nature just as truly and really: as those things which are proper to the Divinity are enunciated of the humanity. And here that saying of Damascenus has place: This mode is of alternation, and of the alternate attribution of each nature, rendering to the other in turn what is proper to each, because of the identity of the hypostasis, and their mutual immanence and indwelling. But as regards the Mode of the thing, we deny that the mode of this Reciprocation is equal and the same. For the properties of the Human Nature are indeed truly and really enunciated of GOD, but only in the concrete, and not in the abstract, of the divinity itself. On the contrary, however, the idioms of the Divine nature are truly enunciated not only of the Man Christ, in the concrete: but also of the humanity in the abstract. Whence a clearly different mode of this Reciprocal communication emerges. The cause of this diversity, however, is that the Natures themselves are most diverse: one is assuming: the other is assumed: One in itself most absolute, and most perfect: the other such that it could be raised to a higher degree of dignity. Now therefore it is for the Assumer to give: it is for the Assumed to receive: Again, it is for the Assumer to appropriate to itself those things which are proper to the assumed nature: if indeed it wishes to constitute one hypostasis with the assumed nature: but not vice versa, the Assumed Nature is to communicate its own properties: for since that which subsists in the ὑποστάσει τοῦ λόγου [hypostasis of the Word] obtains all that from the grace of the Union, it is so far from being able to communicate anything to that hypostasis, which is entirely immutable, either regarding exaltation or regarding humiliation. From which foundation different kinds of communication of properties also follow, as we shall soon show.

Orthodox Antiquity acknowledged this very thing, not denying the reciprocity of the communication, but denying the mode of that same reciprocity or ἀντιδόσεως [exchange]. Hence Damascene says: 'The divine nature itself, indeed, handed over its own glorifications to the flesh, while it itself remains impassible and immune to the passions of the flesh.' The same, book 3, chapter 3: ὁ λόγος τὰ ἀνθρώπινα οἰκειῶται [The Word appropriates human things]: The Word attributes to himself, and makes peculiar to himself, those things which are human; for those things which are of his own holy flesh are his. Hence Cyril, book 1, On the Right Faith to the Queens: 'The Word, having a PROPER BODY, is for this reason said to have been born carnally, for he made the birth of his own Flesh proper to himself.' The same, Chapter 11, On the Incarnation. Of the Only-Begotten: The Word, through whom all things are, infused himself into that which he was not, so that the Nature of Man also, shining by union with the dignities of the divine Majesty, which was raised up more beyond nature than it cast down the immutable God below Nature. At this point, both the Calvinist and the Jesuit spirit become tumultuous, and they impugn not so much the thing as the mode of the thing: that is, not so much the communication as the Mode of the communication, with various contrived and thought-out arguments, the chief of which we shall examine in this place: namely, those which seem to militate generally against the communication of properties.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO Generalis.

I. ORTHODOXA.

FIlius Dei sive λόγος assumendo Naturam humanam, tùm ejusdem Naturæ Idiomata sibi ipsi appropriavit: tùm verò eandem non modò ὑποστάσεως suæ reddidit κοινωνὸν sive participem: sed & infinitâ Divinitatis suæ plenitudine inunxit.

Ἔκθεσις.

DE Communicatione Idiomatum disputaturi, per Idiomata nihil intelligimus aliud, quàm differentias illas naturarum, quibus tanquam notis & characteribus quibusdam, Naturæ à se invicem discernuntur & dignoscuntur. Quia enim in Christo non est facta naturarum conversio aliqua sive ταυτότης: sed illæ sunt manentque in æternum diversissimæ : ideò quicquid vel in hac vel in illa natura occurrit, quo una ab altera distet sive differat : illud proprietas, sive differentia, Græcis ἰδίωμα appellatur.

Consimiliter Vocabulum κοινωνίας Communicationis non accipimus transitivè, prout alias sumi consuevit : ita ut Communicare nihil sit aliud, quàm rem aliquam alteri vel multis per definitionem Proprii aut Accidentis communem facere : sed intransitivè sive correlativè, ut Communicare hoc loco nihil sit aliud, quàm in consortium & societatem aliquid admittere, & ita sibi illud adjungere, ut communionem sive consortium cum eo habeat, eo semper gradu & respectu, quem rerum Unitarum Unio ipsa importat. Jam verò aliquam Communicationem Idiomatum in Naturis Christi per & propter Unionem Personalem, verè ac realiter obtigisse: ad oculum invictè demonstrari potest. Argumentum primum hoc esto :

I. Quicquid in assumtione Humanæ Naturæ sub Unionem venit : illud venit etiam sub κοινωνίαν sive communionem. Atqui non naturæ nudæ sed proprietatibus suis instructæ, venerunt sub Unionem, in ipso statim primo Unionis momento. Ergò ipsæ quoque proprietates Naturarum sub κοινωνίαν sive Communionem venerunt.

Majoris certitudo liquidò patet, primùm ex iis rationibus, quibus suprà evicimus, Unionem hanc duarum naturarum in Christo non factam esse, sine arctissimâ unitorum ad se invicem κοινωνίᾳ. Deindè, Quia ὑπόστασις λόγε est ἀμέριστος, partem extra partem nullam habens : usique non aliud cum Humanitate uniri : aliud verò communicari potuit: sed illud ipsum quod unitum est, communicatum etiam sit, necesse est. Jam quoad minorem, res itidem satis est plana. Natura enim quælibet nuda non est, sed suis prædita Idiomatis : quibus si destitueretur, Natura ampliùs non esset : Nam Φύσις ἀνιδίωτος, πάντως καὶ ἀνύπαρκτος : Natura carens proprietatibus, caret etiam existentiâ. Deindè divina natura τꭣ λόγꭣ cum suis Idiomatis est quiddam simplicissimum ταυτὸ, Siquidem Idiomata divina, non ut in hominibus, accidentium aut Qualitatum conditionem admittunt; sed cum ipsa Essentia divina simplicissimè convertuntur. Quare fieri nullâ ratione potuit, ut ὑπόστασις λόγε verè communicaretur assumtæ humanitati: ipsorum autem divinorum Idiomatum Communicatio non simul verè ac realiter, eidem humanitati obtingeret.

II. Argumentum ex priore hoc resultans tale est : Si vera & realis Idiomatum Communicatio, ex Unione Hypostatica non oritur : neque ipsa Unio duarum naturarum in Christo, ampliùs subsistere poterit. Sed posterius hoc hæreticum, imò blasphemum est : Ergò ejusdem generis erit etiam prius illud.

Connexum Majoris vel indè firmissimè constat : Persona τꭣ λόγε, & ejus Idiomata, sic unum sunt ἀδιαιρέτως, ut qui λόγου Idiomata, humanæ naturæ realiter communicata esse, negaverit, (uti, certè διαῤῥήδην negant Adversarii) is hoc ipso palàm neget, neque λόγου, ὑπόστασιν sive personam (quæ cum λόγου Idiomatis simplicissimè Unum quid est) assumtæ naturæ realiter communicatam, & per consequens, neque ei personaliter unitam esse.

III. Infimus Unionis gradus est, ubi unita nihil sibi mutuò communicant, ut quãdo duo asseres conglutinantur. Quæ combinatio rectiùs παράθεσις quàm ἕνωσις dicitur.

Atqui definiente Scriptura, Unio personalis non modò singulos ac Universos Unionis modos, qui quidem in naturalibus occurrunt, infinitis parasangis altius superat: sed & eos, quibus tùm tres personæ invicem sunt unitæ, tùm verò DEUS rebus creatis adesse dicitur, toto genere transcendit: ita ut ex duabus diversissimis naturis, unum factum sit ὑποκείμενον.

Quin igitur non nuda aliqua Naturarum sive παράθεσις, sive παράστασις: sed arctissima tum Naturarum ad se invicem, tùm proprietatum κοινωνία sive communicatio, ex Unione hac oriatur necesse est. Et sanè, si nos per fidem, & propter gratiosam præsentiam ac inhabitationem DEI reddimur κοινωνοὶ θείας φύσεως, participes divinæ naturæ, teste Petro 2. cap. 1, 4. Quantò incomparabiliter magis humana Christi natura, particeps evasit divinæ Majestatis τꭣ λόγου: ut qui non per se gratiosam tantùm præsentiam: sed per personalem Unionem, eam intra υπόστασιν suam assumsit.

IV. Scriptura Sacra Mysterium Unionis personalis ita describit, ut expressè Effectum etiam sive Consequens illius, nempè realem hanc, de qua agimus, Idiomatum κοινωνίαν, definiat.

Ergò de testandæ Impietatis fuerit, eundem effectum ullo pacto vel negare, vel convellere.

Antecedens patet ex primo cap Johannis versu 14. Ubi Unio ipsa initiò describitur: Verbum caro factum est: Sed mox subjungitur Effectus Unionis: Et vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti à Patre, plenum gratiâ & veritate. Ubi particula Quasi, ceu digito indice monstrat, Gloriam hanc de gloria humanæ naturæ ex Unione communicatâ: non verò de æterna gloria Filii DEI intelligendam esse: ut qui non est Quasi unigenitus: sed Naturâ Filius DEI Patris Unigenitus. Quod ipsum ex Antiquitate observavit etiam Hilarius lib. 3. de Trin. Filius, inquiens, Caro factus est, ut hoc Deo Patri caro inciperet esse, quod Verbum: ut id, quod de Tempore erat, Gloriam ejus claritatis, quæ sine tempore erat, acciperet, ut in DEI virtutem caro transferretur.

His ita constitutis, facilior jam erit explicatio illius Controversiæ, quæ de Qualitate Communicationis Idiomatum agitatur. Nam neque Essentialem neque Accidentalem eam esse, utrinque vel indè constat, quia ipsa etiam Unio talis non est. Etsi enim nonnulli Orthodoxorum à vocabulo Effusionis, in hac ipsa materia, minimè abhorruerunt: non tamen factum id est, sensu Eutychiano sive Physico, ac si divinæ naturæ proprietates, in humanam ita efsent effusæ, ut eas in se, & per se, tanquam separatas à Divinitate possideret: sed sensu Methaphorico, scripturis ipsis usitatissimo, hoc significantes, humanam naturam infinitâ plenitudine Divinitatis τᾶ λόγε, non ad mensuram, sed citra mensuram esse inunctam: modo non Physico, sed Hyperphysico. Quæ Metaphorica significatio sese in illis quoque scripturæ locis prodit, quæ Spiritus Sancti dona super fideles effusa esse, perhibent. Joel. 2. Zach. 12.

Quoad verbalem Communicationem, nulla ex parte ad mysterii hujus sublimitatem eam pertingere: sed Samosateni figmentum esse ex eodem principio, liquidissimè constat. Nam & hîc valet usitata illa Theologorum regula: Qualis Unio, talis etiam est Communicatio: Ergò, si verbalis communicatio statuitur, verbalis etiam unio concedatur, necesse est. Jam verò verbale quod est: verum non est: Imò planè non est. Verum enim si esset, non ampliùs Verbale, sed Reale esset. Nam verbum sive Symbolum rei Logicum, non est res ipsa, aut pars, sive Idioma rei: Sed est nota conceptus in mente, qui, si rei, quæ est extra intellectum, non respondet, certè rectiùs appellatur fals9, quàm verbalis. Patet hinc, quid de Definitione Philippéa, quâ Communicationem Idiomatum definit per figuram Sermonis, sive modum loquendi &c. sit statuendum.

Relinquitur proindè, remotis falsis istis modis omnibus, talem constituendum esse communicationis Modum, qui Naturam & Qualitatem principii sui, hoc est, Unionis personalis sequatur. Quemadmodum igitur Unio ipsa neque est Essentialis, neque Accidentalis neque Logica tantùm aut verbalis: Sed personalis, vera ac realis: Ita communicatio etiam idiomatum rectissimè Personalis, vera ac realis dicitur.

Differt autem Realis hæc Communicatio, quàm plurimùm à Physicâ proprietatum effusione. Etsi enim Naturæ in Christo proprietatibus communicare dicuntur: Naturæ tamen quævis Idiomata sua intra οὐσίαν suam retinet: ita ut nunquam unius naturæ proprietates sint in altera, tanquam forma quædam, aut habitus in subjecto: Hoc enim pacto Effusionis & confusionis absurditas rectè nobis objiceretur. Sed ita se habet ista communicatio, ut Fundamenti sui conditionem sequatur: nempè: ut, quemadmodum λόγ☿ assumtæ naturæ, suam ὑπόστασιν communem fecit, non verbotenus, sed realiter: Ita humana natura in persona τᾶ λόγε subsistens, omnia divina possideat, & communia in λόγῳ habet: divina itidem humanis omnibus ad communem usum & effectum participet. Proindè cum Naturarum idiomata non sibiipsis inter se invicem, sed Personæ statuamus realiter esse communia: hoc est, naturas cum suis proprietatibus per se & inter se incommunicabiles: in una tamen communi persona communicare invicem statuamus: frustrà omninò Physica nobis sive Eutychiana objicitur sive confusio sive Effusio. Quibus observatis, illud ultrò statim liquet, bardè omninò ex Reali communicatione, quam nos statuimus, ab Adversariis colligi Physicam effusionem. Neque enim Reale & Physicum, sunt ἀντίστροφα, hoc est, utraque sui parte reciproca: ita ut quicquid reale est, illud etiam statim sit Physicum: Sed ἀναστρέφοντα duntaxat sunt, ex una tantùm parte reciproca: ut Omne quidem Physicum sit reale: sed non vice versa, Omne reale sit Physicum, & sic Reale longè latiùs patet Physico. Exempli loco in articulo Trinitatis tres personæ differunt realiter: non autem Essentialiter: siquidem Essentiâ unum sunt. Sic Humana & divina Naturæ unitæ sunt realiter: non autem Essentialiter. Undè Communicatio etiam indè fluens, Realis est, licèt Essentialis non sit. Idem ergò nobis Terminus Reale sive Realiter hac in disputatione idem sonat, quod Verum: & sic opponitur fictitio, sive verbali, quod nudo tantùm constat titulo sive nomine: ita ut ὄντως τῷ ὄντι, ὀ κτ' φαντασίαν μόνον τ' ὀνομα ἔχον: Verè ac realiter, sive actu ipso, non imaginariè, sive secundum nomen tantùm competat rei, de qua prædicatur. Quæritur autem hoc loco: Si concedenda communicatio idiomatum; an respectu naturarum ita ea sit reciproca: ut quemadmodum divina natura sua idiomata communicavit assumtæ humanitati: ita vicissim Humanitas communicaverit Divinitati λόγῳ sua idiomata? Respondemus, diligenter distingvendum esse inter Rem & Modum rei. Nam quoad rem ipsam, hoc est, Realem Communicationem idiomatum, concedimus eam esse reciprocam: quatenus nimirùm de divina natura æque verè ac realiter enunciantur ea, quæ humanitatis sunt propria: atq; de humanitate enunciantur, quæ Divinitatis sunt propria. Atque hîc locum habet illud Damasceni: Modus iste est alternationis, alternatæq; attributionis utriusq; naturæ, alterutri propria vicissim reddentis, propter hypostaseως identitatem, & ipsarum invicem immanentiam ac incesssionem. Cæterùm Quoad Modum rei, negamus parem esse eundemq; Reciprocationis hujus modum. Nam Humanæ Naturæ proprietates verè quidem ac realiter de DEO, sed in concreto tantùm, non autem in abstracto, de ipsa divinitate enunciantur. Contrà verò Divinæ naturæ idiomata, non tantùm de Homine Christo, in concreto: sed & de humanitate in abstracto verè enunciantur. Undè diversus planè Reciprocæ communicationis hujus modus emergit. Causa autem diversitatis hujus est, quòd Naturæ ipsæ sunt diversissimæ: una est assumens: altera assumta: Una in se absolutissima, & perfectissima: altera talis, ut in altiorem dignitatis gradum evehi protuerit. Jam ergò Assumentis est dare: Assumti est accipere: Rursus Assumentis est, appropriare sibiipsi ea, quæ assumtæ naturæ sunt propria: si modò unam cum assumta natura ὑπόστασιν constituere velit: non verò vice versa, Assumtæ Naturæ est communicare sua Idiomata assumendi Naturæ: quippè quæ, quod subsistit in ὑποστάσει τοῦ λόγου: illud omne obtinet ex gratia Unionis: tantùm abest, ut ὑποστάσει illi, quippè prors9 immutabili, quicquam vel quoad exaltationé, vel quoad humiliationem communicare possit. Ex quo fundamento diversa etiam communicationis idiomatum genera consequuntur: uti mox ostendemus.

Agnovit hoc ipsum Orthodoxa Antiquitas, Reciprocationem communicationis nó negans: negans, autem ejusdem reciprocationis sive ἀντιδόσεως modum. Hinc Damascenus, ipsa quidem, inquit, (divina natura) proprias glorificationes carni tradidit: cum ipsa maneat impassibilis, & immunis passionum carnis. Idem lib. 3. cap. 3. ὁ λόγος τὰ ἀνθρώπινα οἰκειῶται: Verbum, quæ humana sunt, sibi attribuit, ac peculiaria facit: Nam ipsius sunt ea, quæ sanctæ ipsius carnis sunt. Hinc Cyrillus lib. 1. de recta fide ad Reginas: Verbum PROPRIUM habens CORPUS, propter hoc dicitur natum carnaliter: quæ suæ Carnis nativitatem sibi propriam fecit. Idem Cap. 11. de incarnat. Unigeniti: Verbum, per quod omnia, in id quod non erat, se immisit, ut & Hominis Natura, id quod non erat, divinæ Majestatis dignitatibus per adunationem nitescens, quæ sublevata est magis ultra naturam, quàm dejecit infra Naturam invertibilem DEUM. Tumultuatur hoc loco Spiritus tùm Calvinianus tùm Jesuvviticus, & non tàm rem, quàm modum rei: hoc est, non tàm communicationem, quàm Modum communicationis impugnat variis conquisitis, & excogitatis argumentis, quorum præcipua hoc loco examinabimus: ea nimirùm, quæ generatim adversus communicationem propriorum militare videntur.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: Refutation of the Principal Arguments by which the Calvinist brothers endeavor to overthrow and overthrow the Communication of Idioms in…

THE FIRST is such: The principle of contraries is the same: But the distinction of Natures and properties is Essential: Therefore the communication of the same must also be such. I answer: 1. The major proposition is true κατά τι [in a certain respect], not ἁπλῶς [simply]: it is true, indeed, of those contraries which are also immediately contrary. But we simply deny that the distinction and communication of Natures and properties behave like equal contraries, because such contraries overturn one another. So that in this way, not only would the Real communication, but the very real Union itself, collapse entirely. Since in the Union, the distinction of Natures is also essential and remains: whence, however, the Union itself is not, nor is it called, essential, but personal and real. The argument therefore proceeds from a false hypothesis: as if the Mode of communication must be exactly the same as that of the distinction of natures itself. The falsity of this hypothesis is evident even from the fact that while the Natures in the person of Christ differ Essentially, the Union itself is not therefore Essential. Furthermore, the Distinction and the communication of Natures and their properties are viciously opposed to one another. For κοινωνία [communion] does not depend on the difference of Natures and properties, but depends on the union itself: so that this Rule is true: As is the union, so is the Communication: But this one is false: As is the distinction of Natures and properties, so is their communication. Thus, therefore, this first argument labors under a perpetual Ignorance of the Refutation.

THE SECOND: A property is that which is not communicated to another subject: Therefore the attributes of the Deity are not communicated to another subject, such as humanity.

I answer: 1. The whole argument is conceded if understood concerning Physical and Essential communication, which so transfuses the properties of one nature into another nature that they now inhere in it subjectively. For in this way, we ourselves also simply deny that the properties of Natures are communicated to one another. Furthermore, if this argument is opposed to the Real communication for which we are fighting, we answer first that the argument fails by the Sophism of equivocation. For something is said to be communicated in two ways, as the Philosopher himself teaches in book 4, Topics, chapter 3: either κατὰ μέθεξιν [by participation], or according to the participation of a definition: as when it is established that a property of the union of a thing is so communicated to another that it is constituted as its subject, and the property thus communicated now exists by definition in the subject to which the communication has been made. In which way, indeed, we readily concede that no property can be communicated, for thus a property would depart from its own subject, and a property would no longer be a property: which would imply a contradiction. Wherefore we willingly admit the major proposition understood in this sense. But then, there is another κοινωνητὸν [communicable thing], which occurs by a certain συνδυασιν [combination] or coupling. In which way, hardly anyone would deny that properties can be communicated; just as, indeed, in this way Fire communicates its own properties, to burn and to shine, to iron, not κατὰ μέθεξιν [by participation] or definition, but by κοινωνίαν [communion] or συνδυασμὸν [combination] or coupling. Wherefore the major proposition is not universally true. Since a property is incommunicable not in every way, but only in that way which is peculiar to the property itself, and in a certain way convertible with it: namely, when it is said to be so communicated from one Nature that it exists in another as in a subject, and is attributed to the same of itself by the nature of the subject. In which way, indeed, we simply deny that properties are communicated in the Natures of Christ. Meanwhile, however, a property is and is called communicable in another way, if, namely, the communicated properties do not exist in the thing to which the communication has been made as in a subject, nor are they said to exist in it of themselves by the nature of the subject, but remain properties of their own subject, yet communicate themselves to another Nature in their own way, by means of the most intimate bond of Union. An example of this thing is to be seen in soul and body, where all animal and vital powers and operations are truly and really communicated to the animated body: yet they never depart from their subject, nor are they attributed to the body from the nature of the subject.

THIRD. Whatever is not the subject of the essential properties of GOD, the essential properties of God cannot be predicated of it really and truly. For if an attribute is predicated of any thing affirmatively, and the antecedent is in no way the subject of the attribute, a fiction is being put forward.

Therefore, if the human nature is not the subject of the essential properties of GOD, then certainly those cannot be predicated of it truly and really; and consequently, there is no real communication of idioms.

I answer. A distinction must be made between a logical and a physical subject. For the antecedent is true concerning a logical subject. For in this way, if we were to deny that the human nature of Christ is the logical subject of those predications which arise from the communication of idioms, then at last the communication of idioms would collapse. But if the adversaries understand their antecedent concerning a physical subject, so that to whatever the essential properties of GOD do not subjectively inhere, they cannot be truly and really predicated of it, then that is far most false. And we oppose to it a clearly contrary axiom, and it is this: The essential properties of GOD are predicated of NO THING which is their physical subject. For neither are his essential properties predicated of GOD himself in this way, namely subjectively: since neither is the Divinity their physical subject, nor do these inhere subjectively in the Divinity; but they are with the very essence of GOD a most simple thing, ταὐτό. Furthermore, it is not even philosophically true that nothing can be attributed to any thing, or truly and really predicated of it, unless that thing becomes the subject of the attribute. For the body does not become the subject of the faculties or powers of the soul; nor do the actions and operations of the soul become ἰδιώματα or properties of the body; but the soul, retaining its powers and its ἰδιώματα within itself, exercises its ἐνεργείας through the body. So also the λόγος is compelled by no necessity to communicate its ἰδιώματα subjectively to the humanity; but retaining them within itself, it makes the humanity a participant in divine glory, virtue, and majesty, while THROUGH IT it performs the works of its omnipotence.

FOURTH. If a real communication of idioms is to be granted, then it must also be granted that the properties of one nature are not only predicated of the other, but also in reality inhere in the other nature. For unless they inhere in the other nature in reality, then they are no longer predicated of it really, but only verbally.

I answer. The adversaries play at first under the sophism of equivocation in the word 'real' or 'really,' which they take for 'physical' and 'essential,' and thus they fight only against a figment of their own brain. To us, however, 'real' is nothing other than that which is true, not fictitious, not imaginary, not merely verbal or titular. But such a real communication does not any more provide that the properties of one nature inhere in the other nature in reality, that is, subjectively, than the most real union itself provides that the two natures should be confused or equalized with one another. Furthermore, there is also an equivocation in the phrase 'to inhere in reality,' which either signifies the same as 'subjectively'—and then we deny that the properties of one nature inhere in the other in reality; for thus a physical communication would be established—or it sounds the same as 'in truth,' not merely in name. And then we concede that the properties of the divinity, through the communication, inhere in the humanity in truth, that is, personally; so that just as the divine nature is essentially omnipotent, so the human nature is personally and indeed in truth omnipotent, while meanwhile the omnipotence remains one, and indeed proper to the Divinity in the fourth mode. In which sense the Apostle affirms that the whole fullness of the Divinity dwells in the assumed humanity σωματικῶς, Colossians 2.

Finally, the argument fails by the sophism of disparate questions. For it is one thing when it is asked whether the properties of one nature are truly and really predicated of the other. It is another thing whether that which is proper to one nature inheres in the other nature in reality, that is, subjectively. Since these two questions are not equipollent, but differ greatly, the adversaries conclude most viciously from the affirmation of one to the affirmation of the other; because they beg the question most shamefully, falsely persuading themselves that the humanity of Christ cannot truly and really become a participant in divine properties unless they inhere in it subjectively. Which hypothesis would only then have a place if the human nature subsisted outside the λόγος; for thus the divine idioms could not be communicated to it unless they were poured out from the λόγος into the humanity existing outside the person of the λόγος. But now, because it is assumed WITHIN that very hypostasis of the Son, within which his idioms remain, hence the flesh of the Lord could arrive at a real participation of the properties remaining within the hypostasis, just as it arrived at the κοινωνία of his very ὑπόστασις. As for what pertains to the properties of the human nature, no one of us has ever affirmed that they are predicated of the Deity or that they inhere in the Deity in reality.

FIFTH. The eternal Father communicated all his attributes to the Son most perfectly; and yet the hypostatic union of the Father and the Son does not follow from that. Therefore, similarly, from the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ, a real communication of idioms does not follow.

I reply. The argument fails, 1. by a manifest dissimilarity in the Example. For the Father and the Son are the same, that is, they are one GOD essentially, but not personally: whereas the Divine and human Natures in Christ are one ὑφιστάμενον, that is, one person: not essentially, but personally. Furthermore, the Father and the Son are equal in essence in the Godhead: but in the person of Christ, the two natures are most diverse in essence, namely the one human, the other divine: of which the latter is αὐτοτελής and most perfect in itself: but the former could be perfected and exalted.

Then I invert the argument in this manner: Just as the Son, insofar as He is one in Essence with the Father, shares in all the Essential properties of the Father: So also the Human nature, insofar as it constitutes one Personal [entity] with the λόγῳ, shares indeed in the ὑποστάσει & Divinity of the λόγῳ personally.

Thirdly: Just as the hypostatic union of the Father and the Son does not follow from the coessential union of the Father and the Son, so the essential union, and consequently the essential communication, does not follow from the personal union of the two natures in Christ; so that in both cases the rule is most true: As is the union, so also is the communication; and conversely: As is the communication, so also is the union.

Finally, the Jesuit antecedent, as far as the first part is concerned, is manifestly false and unworthy of a Christian man. For who would tolerate this proposition: The eternal Father communicated to the Son all His attributes? For regarding the personal attributes, such as being Unbegotten and Begetting, which are in the Father, this is most false. For these two attributes remain so exclusively proper to the Father that the Son does not participate in them for eternity. And indeed, the Jesuit position is not far from the heresy of Sabellius, who once maintained that the three persons of the Divinity, just as they are one in essence, are also one thing in person, and are distinguished only by mere appellations.

SIXTH. Divine idioms are generally common to the whole Trinity: Therefore, if there is a real communication of idioms, it is a necessary consequence of the Incarnation: it would follow that the whole Trinity is incarnate: Since this is absurd, it is clearly evident that a real communication is not a necessary consequence of the Incarnation.

I answer: Divine idioms may be considered in two ways: either absolutely or γενικῶς, insofar as they are common to all three persons of the Godhead; or relatively, or ὑποστατικῶς, insofar as those idioms are determined in the one singular ὑποστάσει of the Son of GOD. In the former manner and respect, if divine idioms were established to be communicated to the assumed humanity, then it would follow that all the persons were incarnate. But now, because divine idioms are said to be communicated through and on account of the Hypostatic Union, not insofar as they are considered absolutely, but insofar as they are considered relatively and determinately in the person of the Son, the incarnation of the whole Trinity cannot therefore be elicited from it. For just as it cannot be denied that the divine Nature, considered relatively in the Son, is truly incarnate, without the incarnation of the remaining persons: so also the properties of that divine Nature, when considered in such a relative manner, can truly be communicated: however much they may meanwhile be absolutely common to the whole Trinity. And again: Just as it is truly permissible to affirm that the divine Nature, as begotten, is united to humanity: so also it is truly permissible to affirm: That the properties of the same begotten divine nature have been communicated to the same humanity: or: That the begotten Omnipotence, the begotten Omniscience, etc., has been communicated to the Flesh of Christ.

SEPTIMUM: The communicated property is either the essence of GOD, or some person. If it is the essence of GOD: it follows that eternity, infinity, and spirituality, which are the very essence of GOD, belong really to the humanity: and thus the person of the Father, the person of the Son, and the person of the Holy Spirit belong to the humanity, which is abominable. But if the communicated property is the person of the Word itself, it follows that the human nature bears within itself a person, and consequently the Person of the Son of GOD. For whatever really communicates a substance to someone, that thing really has and bears the substance within itself. But the Human nature does not bear the Person of the Son of GOD: rather, the whole person of the Son of GOD bears and sustains the Human Nature. Therefore they do not dare to assert that the communicated property is the person of the Son of God himself. Since, therefore, the communicated property is neither the Es-

I reply: A twofold fallacy is committed παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For first, although we willingly confess and concede that the divine properties which have been communicated to the assumed Humanity are the very divine essence of the Son, nay, the very λόγος or Son of GOD himself: it does not therefore immediately follow: Therefore eternity, infinity, and spirituality, which are the very Essence of GOD, and thus of the person of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, belong really to the Humanity. For two things prove the vanity of this consequence. 1. That the Essence of GOD considered absolutely is sophistically confused with the essence of GOD taken relatively: and from the latter to the former, by a fallacy of four terms, the argumentation is ineptly made. Certainly, if it were permitted to argue thus, not only from the Communication, but even from the Union itself, this absurd consequence could be elicited: and that in this manner: The divine Essence of the Son is common to all three persons. But the Essence of the Son is communicated or united to the assumed Humanity. Therefore, all three persons are united to the Humanity. Since the Adversaries themselves see here that in the Major premise the term Essence is taken Absolutely, but in the Minor Relativel: and consequently that there are four terms in the argument: what, the devil, a blindness this must be, to be unwilling to see and acknowledge that very thing with respect to the Communication? The other reason, which refutes the vanity of the consequence, is that a distinction must be made between the Essential properties of the λόγος, insofar as they are considered within the most simple ἐσία of the Deity λόγῳ, where they are something ταυτὸ: and insofar as they proceed outwards, and exert themselves with respect to the assumed Humanity, or other creatures. Where certainly it cannot by any reason be denied that they admit of a distinction: so that although the whole fullness of the Godhead has been assumed by the Humanity, it is nevertheless not right to name it eternal, infinite, or Spirit in the same way; and yet it is right to name it omnipotent, omniscient, and life-giving.

The reason for the diversity is, because although these properties are something most simple and identical within the 8σίαν λόγε: yet they do not act equally ad extra, and with respect to the Humanity: as will be expressly shown below in the digression of the Third Genus of the Communication of Idioms.

Another sophistication of the vicious consequent lies in the fact that it concludes: If the communicated property is the person of the Word itself: Therefore the human nature carries the Word for the reason that whatever communicates a substance really to someone: that (to whom the communication has been made) really has in itself and carries that substance which communicated. The vanity of this rule or axiom is clearly evident even from this single instance: 1. The eternal Father truly and really communicates his essence to the Son: Therefore does the Son carry and sustain the Essence of the Father? This is false and abominable. 2. A distinction must be made between Physical communication, from which follows that which the adversary infers: and true and real communication, which leaves both Natures and the properties of the Natures safe, sound, and intact. With that former one we have no business: Therefore neither can the Consequent apply to us.

Latin:

PRIMUM tale est: Contrariorum eadem est ratio: Sed distinctio Naturarum & proprietatum est Essentialis: Ergò earundem etiam communicatio talis sit necesse est. Respondeo. 1. Major propositio vera est κατά τι, non ἁπλῶς: vera nimirùm de iis contrariis, quæ & immediatè sunt contraria. Jam verò distinctionem & communicationem Naturarum ac proprietatum habere se, ut pariter contraria, simpliciter negamus: propterea quòd talia contraria se mutuò evertunt. Ita ut hoc pacto non modò Realis communicatio: sed & ipsa realis Unio prorsus corrueret. Siquidem in Unione etiam Essentialis est & manet Naturarum distinctio: Undè tamen Unio ipsa non est aut dicitur Essentialis, sed personalis ac realis. Procedit Ergò argumentum ex falsa hypothesi: Quasi idem planè Modus communicationis esse debeat, qui est ipsius distinctionis naturarum. Falsitas hujus hypostaseos vel indè patet, quòd Naturæ quidem in persona Christi Essentialiter differant: non tamen propterea Unio ipsa est Essentialis. Deindè verò vitiosè sibi mutuò opponuntur Distinctio & communicatio Naturarum earumque idiomatum. Neque enim κοινωνία dependet à differentiâ Naturarum & proprietatum: sed dependet ab ipsa unione: ita ut hæc Regula vera sit: Qualis est unio, talis est Communicatio: Falsa autem isthæc: Qualis distinctio Naturarum & proprietatum: talis etiam earundem communicatio. Sic ergò perpetuâ Ignoratione Elenchi, argumentum hoc primum laborat.

ALTERUM: proprium est, quod alteri subjecto non communicatur: Ergò attributa Deitatis alteri subjecto, ut humanitati, non communicantur.

Respondeo. 1. Concedi totum argumentum de communicatione Physica & Essentiali intellectum: quæ unius naturæ proprietates, in alteram naturam ita transfundit, ut ei subjectivè jam inhæreant. Hoc enim modo proprietates Naturarum invicem communicari simpliciter ipsi quoque negamus. Deindè verò si communicationi Reali, pro qua nos pugnamus, argumentum hoc opponatur, respondemus initiò, fallere argumentum Sophismate æquivocationis. Nam communicari aliquid duobus modis dicitur, docente ipso etiam Philosopho lib. 4. Top. cap. 3. vel κατὰ μέθεξιν, sive secundum participationem definitionis: ut quando statuitur, proprium Unionis rei, ita alteri communicari, ut ejus subjectum constituatur: & proprium sic communicatum jam definitione insit subjecto, cui facta est communicatio. Quo sanè pacto nullum proprium communicari posse, ultrò concedimus, sic enim proprium suum egrederetur subjectum, & proprium non ampliùs esset proprium: id quod ἀντίφασιν implicaret. Quare hoc sensu intellectam Majorem propositionem libenter admittimus. Deindè verò Aliud est κοινωνητὸν sive communicabile, quod fit quandã συνδυασιν sive copulationem. Quo pacto propria communicari posse, vix quisquam iverit inficias; quemadmodum sanè hoc pacto Ignis suæ propria, urere & lucere communicat ferro non κτ' μέθεξιν sive definitionem: sed per κοινωνίαν sive συνδυασμὸν sive copulationem. Quare Major propositio non universaliter vera est. Siquidem proprietas incommunicabilis est non omni modo, sed eo tantùm, qui proprietatis ipsius est peculiaris, & cum eâdé quodammodo convertibilis: Quando nimirùm unius Naturæ sic communicari dicitur, ut insit alteri, tanquam subjecto, & eidem ex natura subjecti per se tribuatur. Quo sanè modo propria in Naturis Christi communicari, simpliciter negamus. Interim verò alio modo proprietas est & dicitur communicabilis, si nimirùm communicata idiomata non insint rei, cui facta communicatio, tanquam subjecto: neque dicantur ei etiam inesse, per se naturæ subjecti: sed propria sui subjecti permanentia: alteri tamen Naturæ suo quodam modo se communicant, mediante Unionis arctissimè vinculo. Cujus rei exemplum in anima & corpore videre est, ubi potentiae & operationes animales, vitalesque omnes Corpori animato verè ac realiter communicantur: nunquam tamen egrediuntur subjectum suum, neque corpori ex natura subjecti attribuuntur.

TERTIUM. Quicquid non est subjectum Essentialium DEI proprietatum, de eo realiter & verè Essentiales Dei proprietates prædicari nequeunt. Nam si attributum de quapiam re prædicatur affirmativè: & Antecedens nullo modo est subjectum attributi, figmentum profertur.

Ergo si humana natura non est subjectum Essentialium DEI proprietatum: utique de ea verè & realiter illæ prædicari non possunt: & per consequens, Nulla est realis Idiomatum Communicatio.

Respondeo. Distingvendum esse inter Subjectum Logicum & Physicum. Antecedens enim verum est de Subjecto Logico. Hoc enim pacto si negaremus, Humanam naturam Christi non esse Subjectum Logicum earum prædicationum, quæ ex Communicatione Idiomatum oriuntur: tùm demùm corrueret Communicatio Idiomatum, Sin Adversarii Antecedens suum intelligant de subjecto Physico, ita ut, cuicunque non subjectivè insunt Essentiales DEI proprietates, de eo etiam verè ac realiter prædicari nequeant: tùm illud longè est falsissimum. Et opponimus ei contrarium planè axioma: idque tale: Essentiales DEI proprietates, de RE NULLA prædicantur, quæ sit illarum Subjectum Physicum. Nam neque de DEO ipso, essentiales ejus proprietates hoc modo, nempè Subjectivè, prædicantur: Siquidem neque Divinita est earum Subjectum Physicum, neque hæ Subjectivè inhærent Divinitati: sed sunt cum ipsa DEI essentia quiddam simplicissimum ταυτὸ. Deindè ne quidem Philosophicè verum est, quòd nihil possit alicui rei tribui, vel de ea verè ac realiter prædicari, nisi res ea fiat attributi subjectum. Non enim corpus fit sub jectum facultatum sive potentiarum animæ: nec actiones & operationes animæ fiunt ἰδιώματα vel proprietates corporis: sed anima vires suas, suaque ἰδιώματα intra se retinens, per corpus suas exercet ἐνεργείας. Ita etiam λόγος nulla necessitate cogitur, ut subjectivè sua ἰδιώματα humanitati communicet: sed ea intra se retinens, humanitatem divinæ gloriæ, virtutis & majestatis participem facit: dum PER EAM omnipotentiæ suæ opera perficit.

QUARTUM. Si Realis Idiomatum Communicatio concedenda: tùm concedendum etiã propria unius naturæ non modò prædicari de alterâ: sed & reipsâ alteri naturæ inesse: Nisi enim alteri Naturæ reipsâ insint: tùm non realiter ampliùs, sed verbaliter duntaxat de ea prædicantur.

Respondeo. Ludunt initiò Adversarii sub Sophismate Aequivocationis in vocabulo, Reale vel Realiter: quòd ipsi pro Physico & Essentiali accipiunt: & sic contra proprium cerebri figmentum tantùm pugnant. Nobis autem Reale nihil est aliud, quàm quod verum est, non fictitium, non imaginarium, non verbale aut titulare tantùm. Talis autem realis Communicatio haud magis præstat, ut unius naturæ propria alteri Naturæ reipsa, hoc est, Subjectivè insint: atque Unio ipsa realissima præstet, ut duæ naturæ invicem confunderentur vel exæquarentur. Deindè æquivocatio etiam est in phrasi Reipsa inesse: Quæ vel idem significat, quod Subjectivè: & tùm negatur à nobis, propria Unius naturæ, Reipsa inesse alteri: Sic enim Physica statueretur Communicatio, vel idem sonat ac revera, non nominetenus tantùm: Et tùm concedimus, propria divinitatis per Communicationem revera, hoc est, personaliter inesse humanitati: ut quemadmodum divina natura Essentialiter: Sic Humana natura personaliter & quidem reverà sit Omnipotens: unâ interim manente Omnipotentiâ, & quidem Divinitati in quarto modo propria. Quo sensu Apostolus affirmat, totam plenitudinem Divinitatis habitare in assumta humanitate σωματικῶς Coloss. 2.

Tandem fallit argumentum Sophismate disparatarum Quæstionum. Aliud enim est, quando quæritur, An propria Unius naturæ verè ac realiter prædicentur de altera. Aliud est, An id quod unius naturæ proprium est, alteri naturæ reipsa, hoc est, subjectivè insit. Quæ duæ Quæstiones cùm non sint æquipollentes, sed plurimùm differant, vitiosissimè utique colligunt Adversarii, ex unius affirmatione, ad affirmationem alterius: Quia principium turpissimè petunt, falsò sibi persuadentes, Humanitatem Christi non posse verè ac realiter participem evadere divinarum proprietatum, nisi Subjectivè ei insint. Quæ hypothesis tùm demùm locum haberet, si Humana natura extra λόγον subsisteret: ita namque communicari ei non possent divina Idiomata, nisi è λόγω in humanitatem, extra personam λόγꙋ existentem, foràs effunderentur. Jam verò, quia assumta est, INTRA ipsam illam hypostasin Filii, intra quam manent idiomata ipsius: hinc adeò caro Domini, uti in κοινωνίαν ipsius ὑποστάσεως, sic & in proprietatum intra hypostasin manentium realem participationem pervenire potuit. Quod attinet propria humanæ naturæ, ea vel de Deitate prædicari, vel Deitati reipsa inesse, nemo nostrûm unquam affirmavit.

QUINTUM. Pater æternus communicavit Filio omnia sua attributa perfectissimè: & tamen non sequitur indè Unio Hypostatica Patris & Filii: Ergò consimiliter ex Unione Hypostatica duarum naturarum in Christo, non sequitur realis Communicatio Idiomatum.

Respondeo. Fallit argumentum 1. manifesta dissimilitudine in Exemplo. Pater enim & Filius idem sunt, hoc est, unus sunt DEUS essentialiter, non verò personaliter: Divina autem & humana Naturæ in Christo unum sunt ὑφιστάμενον, hoc est, una persona: non essentialiter, sed personaliter. Deindè Pater & Filius in divinitate sunt essentiâ pares: At in persona Christi, duæ naturæ, Essentiâ sunt diversissimæ, Humana nimirùm una: altera divina: quarum hæc αὐτοτελής in seipsa est perfectissima: illa verò perfici & exaltari potuit.

Deindè inverto argumentum in hunc modum: Quemadmodum Filius, quatenus unus est Essentiâ cum Patre, communicat omnibus Essentialibus proprietatibus patris: Ita Humana quoque natura, quatenus cum λόγῳ unum constituit Personale, communicat utique de ὑποστάσει & Divinitate λόγῳ personaliter.

Tertiò: Quemadmodum ex unione coëssentiali Patris & Filii, non sequitur unio Hypostatica Patris & Filii: ita ex Unione personali duarum naturarum in Christo, non sequitur unio Essentialis, ac per consequens, neque Communicatio Essentialis: ita ut utrobique verissima sit regula: Qualis est Unio, talis est etiam Communicatio: & vice versa: Qualis Communicatio, talis est & Unio.

Tandem Antecedens Jesuiticum, quoad prius membrum, est manifestè falsum: & homine Christiano indignum. Quis enim ferret hanc propositionem: Pater æternus communicavit Filio omnia sua attributa. Nam de attributis Personalibus, qualia sunt in Patre, Ingenitum esse, & Generare, falsissimum hoc est. Manent enim hæc duo attributa ita Patri in solidum propria: ut de iis Filius, in æternum non participet. Et sanè ab hæresi Sabellii parùm abest Jesuitica, qui olim statuit, tres personas Divinitatis uti Essentiâ, sic personâ etiam unum quid esse: & nudis tantùm appellationibus distingvi.

SEXTUM. Idiomata divina γενικῶς sunt communia toti Trinitati: Ergò si realis Idiomatum Communicatio, necessarium est consequens Incarnationis: sequetur totam Trinitatem esse incarnatam: Quòd cum sit absurdum, patet utique Realem Communicationem non esse incarnationis necessarium consequens.

Respondeo: Idiomata divina duobus modis considerari: vel absolutè sive γενικῶς, quatenus Communia sunt omnibus tribus personis Divinitatis: vel Relatè, sive ὑποστατικῶς, quatenus idiomata illa determinantur in una singulari ὑποστάσει Filii DEI. Priore modo ac respectu Idiomata divina, si statuerentur esse communicata assumtæ humanitati: tùm demùm sequeretur Incarnatio omnium personarum. Jam verò, quia Idiomata divina non quatenus absolutè, sed quatenus relatè & determinatè in persona Filii considerantur, dicuntur communicari per & propter Unionem Hypostaticam: non utique totius Trinitatis Incarnatio indè elici potest. Quemadmodum enim negari potest Naturam divinam, relatè in Filio consideratam, verè esse incarnatam, sine incarnatione reliquarum personarum: Ita verè etiam illius Naturæ divinæ Idiomata sic relatè considerata possunt communicari: quantumvis interim absolutè communia sint toti Trinitati. Et rursum: Quemadmodum verè licet affirmare, Naturam divinam genitam esse unitam humanitati: ita verè etiam licet affirmare: Ejusdem naturæ divinæ genitæ idiomata eidem humanitati esse communicata: vel: Omnipotentia genita, Omniscientia genita &c. Carni Christi est communicata.

SEPTIMUM: Communicata proprietas, vel DEI essentia est, vel persona aliqua. Si DEI essentia est: sequitur, realiter æternitatem, infinitatē, Spiritualitatem, quæ sunt ipsa DEI essentia: & ita personam Patris, personam Filii, personam Spiritus Sancti, humanitati competere, quod abominabile est. Si verò communicata proprietas est ipsa persona verbi, sequitur, humanam naturam in se personam, & per consequens Personam Filii DEI gestare. Nam quicquid alicui substantiam realiter communicat, id substantiam realiter in se habet & gestat. At Humana natura non gestat Personam Filii DEI: sed tota Filii DEI persona gestat & sustentat Humanam Naturam. Ergò non audent asserere, communicatam proprietatem esse ipsam personam Filii Dei. Cum igitur communicata proprietas neque Essentia DEI sit, neque persona: Sequitur dogma illud de reali communicatione Essentialium DEI proprietatum, esse merum figmentum.

Respondeo: Geminam committi Sophisticationem παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Primùm enim etsi ultrò fatemur & concedimus, divinas proprietates, quæ Humanitati assumtæ sunt communicatæ, esse ipsam divinam essentiam Filii, imò ipsissimum λόγον sive Filium DEI: non tamen statim sequitur: Ergò æternitas, infinitas, Spiritualitas, quæ sunt ipsa Essentia DEI, & ita persona Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti, realiter Humanitati competit. Vanitatem enim huj9 Consequentiæ duo evincunt. 1. Quod Essentia DEI absolutè considerata, sophisticè confunditur cum essentia DEI relatè accepta: & ex hac ad illam, ἀπολλογισίας quatuor terminorum, ineptè fit argumentatio. Certè si sic liceret arguere, non ex Communicatione tantùm, sed ex ipsa etiam Unione absurdum istud consequens elici posset: idque in hunc modum: Essentia Filii divina, communis est omnibus tribus personis. Atqui Essentia Filii est communicata sive unita assumtæ Humanitati. Ergò, omnes tres personæ sunt unitæ Humanitati. Hic cum ipsi Adversarii videant, in Majore accipi vocabulum Essentiæ Absolutè: in Minore verò Relatè: ac proindè quatuor terminos esse in argumento: Quæ, malum, hæc cæcitas fuerit, nolle id ipsum, respectu Communicationis, videre & agnoscere? Altera ratio, quæ vanitatem consecutionis redarguit, est, quod distingvendum est inter proprietates λόγꙋ Essentiales, quatenus illæ intra simplicissimam ἐσίαν Deitatis λόγꙋ considerantur, ubī sunt quiddam ταυτὸ: & quatenus illæ foràs progrediuntur, & respectu assumtæ Humanitatis, vel aliarum creaturarum se exerunt. Ubi certè distinctionem eas admittere negari nulla ratione potest: ita ut licèt tota plenitudo Deitatis Humanitati sit assumta: non tamen fas sit, eam æquè nominare æternam, infinitam, Spiritum: atque licet nominare omnipotentem, omnisciam, vivificam.

Ratio diversitatis est, Quia etsi proprietates hæ, intra 8σίαν λόγε sunt quiddam simplicissimum ταυτό: tamen ad extra, & respectu Humanitatis non pariter agunt: uti infra in diexodo Generis Tertii Communicationis Idiomatum ex professo ostendetur.

Altera Sophisticatio vitiosi consequentis latet in eo, quod colligit: Si Communicata proprietas est ipsa persona Verbi: Ergo humana natura gestat Verbum propterea, quòd quicquid alicui substantiam realiter communicat: id (cui facta est Communicatio) realiter in se habet & gestat eam substantiam, quæ communicavit. Vanitas hujus Regulæ sive axiomatis vel ex solâ hac instantiâ liquidò patet: 1. Pater æternus verè ac realiter Communicat Filio suam essentiam: Ergone Filius gestat & sustentat Essentiam Patris? Falsum hoc & abominale. 2. Distingvendum inter Communicationem Physicam, ex qua sequitur id, quod infert Adversarius: & inter veram ac realem communicationem, quæ & Naturas & Naturarum proprietates, salvas, sartas, tectas relinquit.
