Cum priore illa nihil nobis commercii: Ergo neque Consequens in nos quadrare potest.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: On the Three Kinds of Idiomatic Communication, in General

Although very clear traces of the doctrine concerning the Communication of Idioms, with respect to the different degrees or genera, exist in the Scriptures: and it was not entirely unknown to purer antiquity: yet its more accurate elucidation is owed especially to our century. For before the conflicts of Nestorius and Eutyches were stirred up, there could scarcely be found, either from the Greek or the Latin Church, those who had undertaken a more accurate care of this question. But afterwards, from the refutation of Nestorius and Paul of Samosata in particular, this part of Christian doctrine was made a little more refined: so much so, that the Greek theologians in particular, especially Cyril, Gregory of Nyssa, Damascenus, and others, asserted the Communication of Idioms, both with respect to the Person and with respect to the human Nature and its Exaltation, in express words, and defended it manfully against the heretics of that time. But not even then was there such light and perspicuity of this doctrine as shines upon us today by the benefit of GOD. Whence most Scholastic Doctors acknowledged only one genus of the Communication of Idioms: such indeed as seems to agree with our first one. It happened, however, around A.D. 1551, that Philip Melanchthon, stirred by the Stancarus controversy, undertook some care and thought as to how, indeed, the locutions about Christ and his two natures, which occur in the Scriptures, could be rightly distinguished and distributed into certain, as it were, seats and domiciles. Stancarus contended, among other things, that our Christ is Mediator only according to his human nature: likewise, that the divine nature is to be excluded entirely from the office of Mediation and Priesthood, for the reason that the death and the entire passion of Christ is to be referred only to the human nature: just as he wrote expressly in a booklet against the Tigurines. Here, therefore, Philip, noticing that in the Scriptures the passion, crucifixion, and death of Christ are attributed not to his humanity alone: but to the whole person: and expressly and word-for-word to the Son of GOD himself: most rightly determined that such propositions are to be explained through the Communication of Idioms, and indeed that which we define in the first genus.

Although, to speak frankly as the matter is, Philip explained this First genus less sufficiently through this rule: Since there are two natures in Christ, certain things proper to one nature do not prevent the other nature from being present. For Stancarus did not deny this very thing, as one who least of all wished to appear to tear apart the person, writing expressly to the Tigurines, F. 8, likewise in his writing on the Exclusive particle, 'Only': I exclude the divine nature from the office of Priesthood and Mediation of Christ, but not from his person: For in this proposition: Christ is Mediator according to human nature ONLY, but not according to the divine: this exclusive ONLY does not exclude the divine nature from the Person of Christ, but from his office of Mediation. Least of all, therefore, did Stancarus deny that the divine nature was present to the Humanity in the very passion and death: but he denied this, that the passion pertained in any way to the Son of GOD. That, therefore, should have been shown, how, because of the unity of the person, it could by no means happen that a naked man should suffer and die: and that through the Communication of Idioms of the first genus. But whatever the case may be, the first stone was nevertheless laid in this place by Philip for the doctrine concerning the different genera of predications about Christ.

In the progress of time, our purer theologians, in the conflict concerning the divine Majesty communicated to the assumed flesh of Christ, began to elaborate more and more the doctrine concerning the communication of Idioms, especially of those things which are considered in the third genus by reason of humanity: and that, as it were, gradually. For first they noticed that Scripture makes mention of a certain divine glory and majesty which was given to Christ, and indeed in time. Then they gathered from the analogy of Faith, the most certain teacher of truth, that the office of Mediation and Redemption is attributed to the whole Christ according to both natures in the sacred writings. Finally, they also saw that, while saving the analogy of faith, nothing could have been given to Christ according to the divine Nature in time: as that which is from eternity and remains most absolute and most perfect, devoid of all change: but rather that the Holy Spirit in the scriptures attributes to the Humanity of Christ, divine Majesty, under the abstractive locutions. By observing these three notations, three Genera were finally established and elaborated. And in the beginning, indeed, Brentius and Heshusius devoted effort in this part that was entirely useful to the church of GOD: until at last that incomparable Theologian Martin Chemnitz distinguished the propositions more accurately, and recalled them to those three genera, which are observed by the Orthodox even today. But since the generality of κοινωνίας or Communication offended some, especially since it seemed to square less properly with the second Genus: therefore Chemnitz himself, for the sake of greater clarity, distinguished those three genera in such a way that he named the first the Communication of Idioms: the second the Communication of operations: the third the Communication of Majesty. The foundation, however, upon which these three genera are built, is shown by those diverse phrases or locutions which are enunciated in the Scriptures now concerning the whole person, now concerning the natures.

For in the beginning occur phrases which prove that the Son of GOD, by assuming human nature, at the same time so appropriated its Idioms to himself that now it is not right to enunciate those things which are proper to humanity abstractively concerning human nature alone: but they must be attributed concretively to the whole person: as when it is read in Acts 20:28 that GOD redeemed the Church with his own blood. Hence, therefore, the first Genus of the Communication of Idioms arises.

Then the Scriptures testify that Christ produces the ἀποτέλεσμα of Mediation, or Redemption, not according to one or the other, whether divine or human, but according to both; not a double or distinct one, but one: as in Galatians 4, Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. Hence, therefore, the Second Genus was born: with respect to operations.

Finally, Scripture demonstrates in clear words that the idioms of Divine Majesty have been truly communicated to Human nature: so that even in the abstract, although not outside the Union, it is right to say, The flesh of Christ is life-giving, John 6:51. Hence, therefore, the Third Genus proceeded: which is, the Communication of Majesty.

There are indeed and are found today Theologians who are by no means ignoble, and those Orthodox, who do not hesitate to add a Fourth Genus, which belongs to those propositions when the Idioms of both Natures are enunciated concerning the whole person of Christ: as in John 8:56, Christ is, before Abraham was made. 1 Cor. 10:9, Christ was tempted by the Jews in the desert. Matt. 22:42, Christ is from the Seed of David. But since these propositions and similar ones do not enunciate the idioms of one nature concerning the other nature either in the concrete or in the abstract through any Communication: But predicate of the whole person that which, with respect to one nature, is rightly attributed to the whole person: therefore in these propositions, speaking properly, there does not seem to be a Communication of Idioms. For in order for this to be able to have a place, it is necessary that in the Subject, in place of Christ, there be placed such a word that has respect to that nature whose idiom is not alien to what the predicate enunciates. Therefore, just as he allows them to abound in their own sense, so we, following the book of Christian Concord, acknowledge only three Genera: those, indeed, about which we shall soon treat separately.

Thirdly, it is also disputed at this point: In what order should those three genera of Communication be placed? For there are those who reject that which we place in the second position into the third: and conversely count the Third in the second position. But perhaps this controversy will not be of great moment. For those who are the Authors of this innovation, they consider only the order of nature: and because they see that it cannot be denied that the Communication of operations necessarily presupposes, as an efficient cause, the Communication of Majesty, by which the flesh of Christ concurs to perform those ἀποτελέσματα of Mediation, not only by its own, but also by clearly divine working: therefore they wish to place the cause before the Effect, that is, the Third Genus before the Second. From which, however, no discrepancy arises in the doctrine itself. We shall follow the footsteps used hitherto, and we shall treat the three genera of Communication in the order in which we see them placed in the Symbolic books of our Churches.

Finally, it is also asked at this point concerning the true use of the words Concrete and Abstract, the usage of which, first introduced by the Scholastics, began to be most frequent in this dispute. And indeed, in the beginning, having dismissed those equivocations by which these words are accepted in one way or another in Philosophy: having also repudiated that signification by which the Natures in Christ are considered as separated from each other outside the Union: by CONCRETE we understand nothing else than the person of CHRIST himself, the whole subsisting in two Natures: but by ABSTRACT we denote the natures themselves in Christ, distinctly indeed: but not dividedly or separately, that is, outside the Union, but always considered in union.

Furthermore, since the Adversaries lay snares for purer doctrine under these terms, it will have been highly necessary to keep the following rules in view from time to time.

I. In the first kind of Communication of Idioms, only concrete expressions have a place: Because in it, attention is not paid to what dignity accrued to that nature which could be exalted from the Union: but only to how those things which are proper to one nature are truly and really predicated of the other: But in the Concrete, that is, by reason of the unity of the person: In the third kind, however, abstract expressions also obtain a place: Because in it, consideration is given to what exaltation and Majesty befell the Humanity of Christ from the Union, As: The flesh of Christ is life-giving: The blood of Christ cleanses us from all sin: The body of the flesh of Christ has redeemed and given life to us. John 6. 1 John 1. Colossians 1.

II. In the writings of the Fathers, Concretes for Abstracts and Abstracts for Concretes are found quite frequently placed: especially before the stirred-up controversies of Nestorius and Eutyches. As when they used abstractive terms where there had been need for concretive ones: As when Athanasius says: That flesh was suspended on the cross, but not he himself. Where he certainly notes the Nature viciously: when he ought to have named the person: for the reason that actions and passions are not of Natures, but of the whole person. And vice versa, when they were about to speak of Natures, they used concrete terms where abstract ones were to be used: as Athanasius, Tom. 1, in the exposition of the faith: The Son of God assumed our Man, whom he delivered to passion, and in him rose again.

III. Abstracts are never predicated of each other: Because the Union was made ἀσυγχύτως (without confusion): and in that very Union, the Natures without any confusion, as also the properties of the natures, are and remain distinct. Therefore it is not lawful to say: Humanity is Divinity: or the contrary: or Humanity is omnipotence itself, etc.

IV. Concretes can be predicated of each other, and of the ὑποστάσει (hypostasis) subsisting in two Natures: as: GOD is Man: Man is GOD: the Son of Mary is the Son of the Highest: and the contrary, the foundations of which predication we assigned above, where we dealt expressly with the Communication of Natures.

V. Abstracts cannot be predicated of Concretes: nor concretes of Abstracts: as, it cannot be said: Christ is Humanity: or, Humanity is Christ: or, Christ is Divinity, or, Divinity is Christ: for the same reasons which we noted above.

VI. Although those things which are proper to the Divine are predicated of the Human nature in the Abstract: as when I say, The flesh of Christ is life-giving: The Humanity of Christ is omnipotent: the Sense nevertheless is always Concretive as the Scholastics speak: and it is shown: not what the Human nature has received of itself, outside the person, but what it has received by the grace of the Union within the person.

VII. Finally, concerning the use of the terms Concrete and Abstract, the κυβεία (trickery) or tergiversation of the Adversaries is especially to be noted. For when it is asked: With respect to which Nature is the person of Christ exalted? They never answer directly, but repeatedly clamor that they are speaking in the Concrete. But when it is asked: With respect to which Nature is Christ begotten from eternity? He answers in the abstract according to the divine. Likewise if it is asked: With respect to which nature was Christ conceived of the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered, crucified, died, buried, rose again, ascended into heaven.

They always answer in the Abstract, with respect to the Human Nature. But when I proceed in the Articles of faith and ask, According to which nature did Christ sit down at the right hand of the Power and Omnipotence of God, so that he might now most presently rule over all Creatures in heaven and on earth? Here they seek hiding places, and clamor that this is to be understood of the concrete, that is, of the person. But who would not understand even from this, that the Calvinists are so held constrained in their conscience, that, distrusting their own cause, they prefer to hide under the shameful confusion of Concrete and Abstract, rather than candidly profess what they feel in their heart.

Nor do they profit even in the slightest, when, asked about the Exaltation of Christ, they answer that it is enough that the concrete or person be named, without the added determination of the Human Nature: for the reason that, if the Human Nature is expressed, the Abstract is immediately confused with the Concrete. For if they establish in their heart that this axiom is true, why, I ask, when asked about the preceding Articles of the Creed, as also about the immediately following one, which is about the Return to judgment, do they always answer in the Abstract, that those are true, indeed of the person, but with respect to the Human Nature? Then what, I ask, will they answer to the Holy Spirit, who in the Abstract, concerning the Blood, flesh, and body of the flesh of Christ, enunciates those things which do not properly belong except to the divinity? Shall he perhaps also be considered to confuse the Concrete with the Abstract? Shall perhaps the whole Orthodox Antiquity also be established to have confused the Concrete with the Abstract, and the latter with the former: as often as it confesses the flesh of Christ to be life-giving? The Council of Ephesus: as often as it asserts that the flesh of Christ has all power in heaven and on earth: as Athanasius: as often as it affirms that the assumed flesh possesses the Glory of the λόγυ (Word) himself: as Hilary lib. 9 de Trin. Chrysostom on chapter 2 to the Hebrews. Damascene lib. 2. cap. 22. l. 3. c. 21. Augustine Serm. 58 on chapter 14 of John, and many others. Which indeed, since it would be absurd even to think, it is sufficiently clear, both what a monster the Adversaries nourish under these terms: and also, how they can and ought to be dragged from their hiding places and convicted of error.

But the Adversaries object in this place that of Justin the Philosopher and Martyr, who in the book on the exposition of the faith prescribes this rule: When you hear contrary voices about the Son, distribute those things which are said, placed among themselves: If anything divine, ascribe it to the divine nature: If anything humble and human, imputing it to the human nature. Thus you will avoid the dissonance of the voices, with each nature receiving what is proper to itself. And that of Nazianzen: Orat. 2 on the Son, page 149. This is what provides heretics with the occasion for erring, namely the mutual attribution of terms, which are predicated of one Christ. Hence the Adversaries argue: Therefore it is not permitted to use abstractive locutions, so that you might say: The Humanity of Christ is Omnipotent, omniscient, etc.

But by a gross confusion of disparate Questions, and a shameful Ignorance of the Elenchus, the Adversaries deceive both themselves and others. For it is one thing to speak of Natures, insofar as they are considered from themselves and their properties even in the Union itself. Where certainly according to the rules of the Fathers, entirely Divine things only to the divine nature: but humble things only are to be ascribed to Human Nature: a fact which we ourselves willingly confess and concede. But it is another thing to speak of the assumed Nature, insofar as it is no longer considered from the property of its own Nature: but attention is paid to what it has received from the Union with the λόγῳ. Where indeed, even in the abstract, the Rules prescribed by the Fathers do not deny that divine idioms can or ought to be truly and really predicated of the Human nature or flesh of Christ: and even if they were to deny it most strongly: they would certainly not be contradicting us, but the Holy Spirit, whose language and style we uniquely imitate in this regard. Nor does a confusion of either the Natures or the properties themselves follow from this manner of speaking: as our Adversaries ignorantly infer, as we shall expressly show in the third Genus of the Communication of Idioms.

Latin:

ETsi doctrinæ de Communicatione Idiomatum, respectu diversorum graduum, sive generum, clarissima in Scripturis extant vestigia: eaque puriori antiquitati non planè fuit ignota: ejus tamen accuratior enodatio, nostro comprimis debetur seculo. Nam ante mota certamina Nestorii & Eutychis, vix dari poterunt vel ex Græca, vel ex Latina Ecclesia, qui accuratiorem quæstionis hujus curam susceperint. Deindè verò ex refutatione Nestorii comprimis & Pauli Samosateni, paulò limatior facta est pars hæc doctrinæ Christianæ: ita quidem, ut Græci comprimis Theologi, Cyrillus potissimùm, Gregorius Nyssenius, Damascenus & alii, Communicationem Idiomatum, tùm respectu Personæ, tùm respectu Naturæ humanæ, ejusdemque Exaltationis, disertis verbis assererent, & masculè adversus hæreticos illius temporis, propugnarent. Verùm neque tùm ea fuit doctrinæ hujus lux & perspicuitas, qualis DEI beneficio nobis hodiè affulget. Undè Doctores Scholastici plerique Unum tantùm agnoverunt Communicationis Idiomatum genus: tale nimirùm quod cum primo nostro congruere videtur. Factum autem est, circa A. D. 1551. ut Philippus Melanchthon, Stancari controversiâ excitatus, curam aliquam cogitationemque susciperet, quo nimirùm pacto locutiones de Christo, & duabus ejus naturis, quæ in Scripturis occurrunt, ritè distingvi, & in certas quasi sedes atque domicilia distribui possent. Contendebat inter reliqua Stancarus, Christum nostrum esse Mediatorem, tantùm secundum humanam naturam: item, ab officio Mediationis & Sacerdotii, divinam naturam prorsus excludendam esse, eò quòd mors & universa passio Christi tantùm ad humanam naturam sit referenda: quemadmodum expressè scripsit, in libello contra Tigurinos. Hic ergò Philippus animadvertens in Scripturis passionem, crucifixionem & mortem Christi non soli ejus humanitati: sed toti personæ: & disertè ac ἀυτολέξει ipsi Filio DEI tribui: rectissimè statuit, ejusmodi propositiones explicandas esse per Communicationem Idiomatum, & eam quidem, quam nos in primo genere definimus.

Quanquam ut ingenuè dicamus quod res est, minus sufficienter Primum hoc genus explicavit Philippus per hanc regulam: Cùm in Christo duæ sint naturæ, quædam propria uni naturæ non impediunt, quò minùs adsit altera natura. Nam hoc ipsum non negavit Stancarus, ut qui personam minimè omnium divellere videri volebat, disertè scribens ad Tigurinos, F. 8. item in scripto, de particula Exclusiva, Tantùm: Excludo naturam divinam ab officio Sacerdotii & Mediationis Christi, sed non à persona ejus: In hac enim propositione: Christus est Mediator secundum humanam naturam TANTUM, non autem secundum divinam: hæc exclusiva TANTUM, non excludit divinam naturam à Persona Christi, sed ab officio Mediationis ejus. Minimè omnium Ergo negavit Stancarus, divinam naturam adfuisse Humanitati in ipsa passione & morte: sed hoc negavit, passionem nihil quicquam pertinere ad Filium DEI. Illud ergò ostendendum fuerat, quomodo propter unitatem personæ, fieri nullâ ratione potuerit, ut nudus homo pateretur & moreretur: idque per Communicationem Idiomatum primi generis. Sed quicquid sit, primus tamen lapis quasi hoc loco à Philippo positus est doctrinæ de diversis prædicationum de Christo generibus.

Progressu temporis puriores nostrates Theologi, in certamine de Majestate divina, assumtæ carni Christi communicatâ, magis magisque doctrinam de communicatione Idiomatum, eorum comprimis, quæ in tertio genere ratione humanitatis considerantur, elaborare cæperunt: idque gradatim quasi. Primùm enim animadverterunt, Scripturam meminisse gloriæ & majestatis cujusdam divinæ, quæ Christo, & quidem in tempore sit data.. Deindè collegerunt ex analogia Fidei, certissima veritatis magistra, toti Christo secundum utramque naturam in sacris tribui Mediationis & Redemtionis officium. Tandem viderunt etiam salva analogia fidei, Christo secundum divinam Naturam nihil in tempore dari potuisse: ut quæ ab æterno est & manet absolutissima & perfectissima, omnis mutationis expers: quin potiùs Spiritum S.in scripturis tribuere Humanitati Christi, divinam Majestatem, sub abstractivis locutionibus. Tribus istis notationiobservatis tria tandem Genera constituta & elaborata fuerunt. Acinitiò quidem hac in parte utilem omninò ecclesiæ DEI operam navarunt Brentius & Heshusius: donec tandem incomporabilis ille Theologus Martinus Chemnitius, accuratiùs propositiones distinxit, & ad tria illa genera revocavit, quæ hodieq́; ab Orthodoxis observantur. Cæterùm cum generalitas κοινωνίας sive Communicationis nonnullos offenderet, præsertim cum ad secundum Genus minùs propriè ea quadrare videretur: ideoque ipse Chemnitius uberioris diluciditatis gratia, tria illa genera ita distinxit, ut primum nominaret Communicationem Idiomatum: Secundum Communicationem operationum: Tertium Communicationem Majestatis. Fundamentum autem, cui tria isthæc genera sunt superstructa, monstrant diversæ illæ phrases sive locutiones, quæ in Sacris jam de tota persona, jam de naturis enunciantur.

Initiò enim occurrunt phrases, quæ evincunt, Filium DEI assumendo naturam humanam, simul ejus Idiomata sibiipsi ita appropriafse, ut jam ea quæ humanitatis sunt propria, non abstractivè de sola humana natura fas sit enunciare: sed concretivè toti personæ sint tribuenda: ut quando Act. 20, 28. DEUS proprio sangvine redemisse Ecclesiam legitur. Hinc ergo primum Genus Communicationis Idiomatum oritur.

Deindè Scripturæ testantur, Christum non secundum alterutram, sive divinam, sive humanam, sed secundum utramque; non geminum aut distinctum, sed unum producere ἀποτέλεσμα Mediationis, sive Redemtionis: ut Galat. 4, Christus nos redemit à maledictione legis. Hinc ergo Secundum Genus natum est: respectu operationum.

Tandem Scriptura perspicuis verbis demonstrat Humanæ naturæ verè esse communicata Divinæ Majestatis idiomata: ita ut in abstracto etiam, licet non extra Unionem, fas sit dicere, Caro Christi est vivifica Joh. 6, 51. Hinc ergò Tertium prodiit Genus: quod est, Communicatio Majestatis.

Sunt quidem & reperiuntur hodiè Theologi minimè ignobiles, iique Orthodoxi, qui Quartum Genus adjicere haud dubitant, quod earum sit propositionum, quando de tota persona Christi, utriusque Naturæ Idiomata enunciantur: ut Joh. 8, 56. Christus est, antequam Abraham fieret. 1. Cor. 10.9. Christus tentatus est à Judæis in deserto. Matth. 22, 42. Christus est ex Semine David. Cæterùm cum propositiones hæ & consimiles: non per Communicationem aliquam, uni9 naturæ idiomata de altera natura vel in concreto vel in abstracto enuncient: Sed de tota persona prædicent id, quod respectu unius naturæ, toti personæ rectè tribuitur: ideòque in his propositionibus propriè loquendo non videtur esse Communicatio Idiomatum. Nam ut hæc locum obtinere possit, necessum est, ut in Subjecto, loco Christi, ponatur talis vox, quæ respectum habeat ad eam naturam, cujus idioma alien non est, quod prædicatum enunciat. Proindè uti illos suo sensu libenter abundare patitur: ita nos secuti librum Christianæ Concordiæ, tria tantùm Genera agnoscimus: ea nimirùm, de quibus mox seorsim agemus.

Tertiò controvertitur etiam hoc loco. Quo ordine tria illa Communicationis genera collocari debeant? Sunt enim qui illud, quod nos secundo loco ponimus, in tertium rejiciunt: & vicissim Tertium, secundo loco numerant. Sed fortè non magni momenti hæc erit controversia. Qui enim novationis istius sunt Autores, illi Ordinem tantùm naturæ considerant: & quia vident, negari, non posse, Communicationem operationum, necessariò præsupponere tanquam causam efficientem, Communicationem Majestatis, quâ Caro Christi ad efficienda illa ἀποτελέσματα Mediationis, non sua tantùm, sed etiam divina planè operando concurrit: ideòque causam Effectui hoc est, Tertium Genus Secundo præmittere volunt. Undè tamen in doctrina ipsa, nulla oritur discrepantia. Nos usitata hactenus vestigia sequemur, & tria Communicationis genera, eo ordine pertractabimus, quo in libellis Ecclesiarum nostrarum Symbolicis, posita ea esse, videmus.

Tandem quæritur etiam hoc loco de vero usu vocabulorum Concreti & Abstracti, quorum usurpatio à Scholasticis primùm introducta, hac in disputatione cœpit esse frequentissima. Et quidem initiò missis illis æquivocationibus, quibus vocabula isthæc in Philosophia aliter atque aliter accipiuntur: repudiatâ etiam eâ significatione, quâ Naturæ in Christo, extra Unionem à se invicem separatæ considerantur: per CONCRETVM nihil intelligimus aliud, quàm ipsam personam CHRISTI totam subsistentem in duabus Naturis: per ABSTRACTUM verò notamus ipsas naturas in Christo, distinctè quidem: sed non divisè aut separatè, hoc est, extra Unionem, verùm semper in unione consideratas.

Deindè verò cùm sub istis vocabulis puriori doctrinæ insidias struant Adversarii, sequentes regulas subindè inconspectu habere perquam fuerit necessarium.

I. In primo genere Communicationis Idiomatum, concretivæ tantùm locutiones locum habent: Quia in eo non attenditur, quid dignitatis ex Unione ad eam naturam accesserit, quæ exaltari potuit: sed tantùm, quomodo ea, quæ unius naturæ sunt propria, de altera verè & realiter prædicentur: Sed in Concreto, hoc est, ratione unitatis personæ: In tertio autem genere Abstractivæ etiam locutiones locum obtinent: Quia in eo consideratur, quid exaltationis & Majestatis, Humanitati Christi, ex Unione obtigerit, Ut: Caro Christi est vivifica: Sangvis Christi emundat nos ab omni peccato: Corpus carnis Christi redemit & vivificavit nos. Johan. 6. 1. Joh. 1. Coloss. 1.

II. In Patrum scriptis, frequenter admodum Concreta pro Abstractis : & Abstracta pro Concretis posita reperiuntur : potissimùm ante mota certamina Nestorii & Eutychis. Ut quando vocabulis Abstractivis usi sunt, ubi Concretivis opus fuerat : Ut cùm Athanasius dicit : Illa caro suspensa est in cruce : non verò ipse . Ubi sanè vitiosè Naturam notat : cùm personam nominare debuisset : propterea quòd actiones & passiones non sunt Naturarum : sed totius personæ. Et vice versa, quando de Naturis verba facturi vocabulis concretis usi sunt, ubi Abstractis utendum erat : ut Athanas. Tom. 1. in expos. fid. Filius Dei nostrum assumsit Hominem, quem passioni tradidit, & in eo resurrexit.

III. Abstracta nunquam de se invicem prædicantur : Quia Unio facta est ἀσυγχύτως : & in ipsa Unione, Naturæ sine ulla confusione, ut & naturarum proprietates sunt & manent distinctæ. Non ergò dicere fas est : Humanitas est Divinitas : aut contra : vel Humanitas est ipsa omnipotentia &c.

IV. Concreta de se invicem, & de ὑποστάσει in duabus Naturis subsistente, prædicari possunt : ut : DEUS est Homo : Homo est DEUS : Filius Mariæ est Filius Altissimi : & contra, cujus prædicationis Fundamenta supra assignavimus, ubi de Communicatione Naturarum ex professo egimus.

V. Abstracta non possunt prædicari de Concretis: neque concreta de Abstractis : ut, non dici potest : Christus est Humanitas : vel, Humanitas est Christus : vel, Christus est Divinitas, aut, Divinitas est Christus : iisdem de causis, quas supra notavimus.

VI. Etsi de Humana natura in Abstracto prædicantur ea, quæ Divinæ sunt propria : ut quando dico, Caro Christi est vivifica : Humanitas Christi est omnipotens : Sensus tamen semper est Concretivus ut Scholastici loquuntur : & ostenditur : non quid Humana natura ex se, extra personam sed quid ex Unionis gratia intra personam acceperit.

VII. Tandem circa usum vocabulorum Concreti & Abstracti, cùmprimis notanda est Adversariorum κυβεία sive tergiversatio. Quando enim quæritur : Cujus Naturæ respectu persona Christi sit exaltata? Nunquam directè respondent, sed subindè obstrepunt, se in Concreto loqui. Quando autem quæritur : Cujus Naturæ respectu Christus ab æterno sit genitus? Respondet in abstracto secundum divinam. Item si quæritur : Cujus naturæ respectu Christus sit conceptus è Spiritu Sancto, natus ex Maria Virgine, passus, crucifixus, mortuus, sepultus, resurrexerit, ascenderit ad cælos.

Semper respondent in Abstracto, respectu Humanæ Naturæ. Sed quando in Articulis fidei pergo & quæro, Secundum quam naturam Christus consedit ad dextram Virtutis & Omnipotentiæ Dei, ut jam præsentissimè dominaretur omnibus Creaturis in cælo & in terra? Hîc latebras quærunt, & de concreto, hoc est, de persona hoc intelligendum esse clamitant. Quis verò non vel indè satis intelligeret, Calvinianos ita teneri constrictos in sua conscientia, ut causæ suæ diffisi malint latitare sub turpi confusione Concreti & Abstracti, quàm candidè profiteri, quid sentiant in corde suo.

Neque vel tantillum proficiunt, quando de Exaltatione Christi interrogati, respondent, satis esse, ut concretum sive persona nominetur, sine abjecta determinatione Humanæ Naturæ: propterea quòd, si Natura humana exprimatur, statim confundatur Abstractum cum Concreto. Hoc axioma enim si verum esse, in corde suo statuunt, cur ipsimet, obsecro, de præcedentibus Articulis Symboli, ut & de immediatè subsequenti, qui est, de Reditu ad judicium, quæsiti, semper in Abstracto respondent, veros illos esse, de persona quidem, sed respectu Humanæ Naturæ. Deindè quid, obsecro, respondebunt Spiritui Sancto, qui in Abstracto, de Sangvine, carne, corpore carnis Christi, ea enunciat, quæ non nisi divinitati propriè competunt? Num fortè & ipse Concretum cum Abstracto confundere censendus fuerit? Num fortè tota etiam Orthodoxa Antiquitas Concretum cum Abstracto, & hoc cum illo confundere statuenda fuerit: quoties fatetur carnem Christi esse vivificam. Concilium Ephesinum: quoties asserit, carnem Christi omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra habere: ut Athanasius: quoties affirmat carnem assumtam possidere ipsius λόγυ Gloriam: ut Hilarius lib. 9. de Trin. Chrysostomus super cap. 2. ad Hebr. Damasc. lib. 2. cap. 22. l. 3. c. 21. Augustinus Serm. 58. super cap. 14. Joh. & alii complures. Quod sanè cùm vel cogitatu absurdum fuerit, satis luculenter patet, tùm quid monstri sub istis vocabulis alant Adversarii: tùm verò etiam, quomodo è latibulis protrahi, & erroris convinci possint ac debeant.

Sed objiciunt hoc loco Adversarii illud Justini Philosophi & Martyris, qui in libro de expos. fidei hanc præscribit regulam: Cùm de Filio contrarias voces audieris, illa, quæ dicuntur inter se collocata, distribue: Si quid divinum, divinæ naturæ adscribas: Si quid humile & humanum, humanæ naturæ imputans . Sic vocum dissonantiam vimbis, unaquaque naturâ, quod sibi proprium est, recipiente. Et illud Nazianzen: Orat. 2. de Filio. pag. 149. Hoc est, quod hæreticis præbet errandi occasionem, nempè mutua vocabulorum attributio, quæ de uno Christo prædicantur. Hinc arguunt Adversarii: Ergò non licet abstractivis uti locutionibus, ut dicas: Humanitas Christi est Omnipotens, omnifcia &c.

Verùm crassa confusione disparatarum Quæstionum, & turpi Ignoratione Elenchi, tùm seipsos, tùm alios dicipiunt Adversarii. Aliud enim est loqui de Naturis, quatenus ex se & suis proprietatibus in ipsa etiam Unione considerantur. Ubi certè secundum regulas Patrum, Omninò Divina tantùm divinæ naturæ : Humilia verò tantùm Humanæ Naturæ sunt adscribenda: id quod nos ipsi ultrò fatemur & concedimus. Aliud verò est loqui de Natura assumta, quatenus ea non ampliùs ex proprietate suæ Naturæ consideratur: sed quid ea ex Unione cum λόγῳ acceperit, attenditur. Ubi sanè in abstracto etiam de Humana natura sive carne Christi, divina idiomata verè ac realiter enunciari posse aut debere, Regulæ à Patribus præscriptæ non negant: & si vel maximè negarent: non certè nobis, sed Spiritui Sancto contradicerent, cujus lingvam & Stylum nos hac in parte, unicè imitamur. Neque ex hac loquendi ratione, sequitur vel Naturarum, vel ipsarum proprietatum confusio: uti inscitè inferunt Adversarii, uti in tertio Genere Communicationis Idiomatum ex professo ostendemus.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: The First Genus of the Communication of Idioms

In defining the first Genus of the Communication of Idioms, our own theologians also do not seem to agree in all respects. For some describe it thus: The first Genus is that by which the property of one nature in Christ is predicated of the other in the Concrete. Others, however, do so a little differently in this manner: The first Genus is when that which is proper to one nature is attributed, not to that nature alone whose property it is, separately, but to the whole person, who is GOD and Man at the same time: and again, by a distinctive particle, it is shown according to which nature that belongs to the person. That diversity was produced by different locutions about Christ which were less distinctly related to this first Genus by some. For those who embrace the latter definition look primarily to those propositions which have the express word CHRIST in the place of the Subject: as

Joh. 8, 56. Christ is, before Abraham was made.

Eph. 3, 9. GOD created all things through Christ.

1. Cor. 10, 9. Christ was tempted in the desert.

Actor. 2, 30. Christ is from the loins of David.

Rom. 9, 5. Christ is from the Fathers.

1. Pet. 3, 18. Christ was put to death and made alive.

Which individual and universal propositions indeed define the whole person of Christ in the Subject, which, although it is one in number, consists of two distinct natures: hence it comes about that the Idioms of both Natures are predicated of this very person of Christ: and those things which are proper to one Nature are attributed, not to the other Nature separately, but to the whole person, who is GOD and man at the same time: with respect to one Nature indeed through the Communication of Idioms: but by reason of the other through the property of the Nature: so indeed, that now divine Idioms, now human, are predicated of this whole person.

Moreover, those who hold that former definition seem to have observed the Nature of the Communication of Idioms more properly, and to have looked to those locutions of Scripture which show that the λόγον or Son of God so appropriated the human nature to himself, along with its Idioms, that now the Idioms of one Nature are predicated of the other in the Concrete. Such as are:

Acts 20:28. GOD redeemed the Church with his own Blood: where not the Redemption itself, which pertains to the second Genus, is viewed: but the Mode, namely that it was so accomplished that not some mere Man, but GOD himself shed his blood.

Rom. 1, 3. The Son of GOD born of the seed of David. Gal. 4, 4. The Son of GOD made of a woman. 1 Tim. 3, 16. GOD was manifest in the flesh. 1 John 1, 1. The Word of life handled with hands, and seen with eyes. Gal. 2, 20. The Son of GOD gave himself for me. Ps. 45, 8. GOD is anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows.

Heb. 1, 3. The Son who is χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ πατρὸς, καὶ ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, was made so much better than the angels, as he hath by inheritance obtained a more excellent name than they.

In these propositions, therefore, not as in the former, the word Christ is placed in the position of the subject, expressing both natures: But the word Son of GOD, which has respect to the other nature, but in the concrete. Whence it is also most rightly established by these men, that the property of one nature is predicated of the other in this genus: but only in the concrete: never in the abstract, to avoid the error of Eutyches, which he admitted in confounding the two natures.

The foundation of this first Genus is manifest. For since there is one and the same ὑπόστασις of both natures: certainly when the unity of this ὑπόστασις is supposed, it is evident that the properties of one nature are rightly attributed to the other, in the concrete, that is, in respect of this one person: and thus divine things to man, and human things to GOD.

Thus therefore 1. in this Genus every predication is concretive. Then it is ἀντίστροφος or reciprocal: so that I can truly say: The Son of GOD is dead: as the Son of Mary is immortal. Finally, the explanation of these phrases is always done κατ᾽ ἄλλο: so that by a distinctive particle, whether it be added in express words or not, it is shown according to the property of which nature something is predicated of the other nature in the concrete. Just as Scripture itself sometimes has used such a declaration: as Rom. 1, 3. The Son of GOD is of the seed of David κατὰ σάρκα.

Moreover, the controversy in this place concerns the quality of those propositions: whether they are true and real, or indeed only verbal: when it is said: The Son of God was born, suffered, was crucified, died, was buried, etc. We, in this part, making a divorce from the camps of the Jesuits and the Calvinists, believe and confess that they are not verbal or logical, but real, indeed most real: not, to be sure, only in that sense which Philip noted in this place, that the nativity, passion, death, and other attributes of that kind of human nature did not prevent the other nature, namely the divine, from being present: but in a far different and truer sense, which itself, however, has nothing in common with Eutychian impiety. For although the divine nature is entirely immutable and ἀπαθὴς (impassible): and therefore according to this the Son of God cannot be said to have been born or to have suffered: yet he suffered in his own flesh. For this flesh is not the flesh of some mere man: but because the Son of God so assumed it into his own ὑπόστασιν (hypostasis), that what would be ἀνυπόστατος (anhypostatic) by itself, might now subsist in his own hypostasis, and be the proper flesh of the Son of God himself: certainly, this flesh suffering, the Son of God himself suffered in this his flesh as truly and really as if, which is ἀδύνατον (impossible), he had suffered in his very divinity itself: Nor do we admit in this place that explanation which certain secret Sacramentarians, who call themselves disciples of Philip, are accustomed to rattle off, saying: God so suffered, that the humanity ALONE is understood to have suffered. For besides the fact that this sophistry admits only a verbal predication with respect to the λόγος (Word): it also at the same time strangles and constricts itself with a shameful contraction. For if the humanity alone has suffered: it follows that not the person any longer, but only the nature has suffered: since the humanity alone constitutes not a person, but merely a nature. And what a hollow mockery of words this will be: God has suffered; that is: The humanity alone has suffered. For although it may be granted that it is the property of the humanity alone to suffer and die: because, however, this flesh is not its own flesh, like the flesh of some other man or individual: but is the flesh of God himself: therefore it necessarily follows that not the humanity alone: but the person himself, and thus the Son of God himself, has suffered in this his flesh. Where, although the divinity itself did not suffer: it was not, however, for that reason entirely idle in the accomplishing of this work: but as our LUTHER piously speaks, it also played its parts in the passion, not only by sustaining the flesh, lest it succumb to such a great burden, but furthermore by bestowing price and weight upon the passion, so that it might be a most perfect λύτρον (ransom) for the reconciliation of the whole human race. For if the human nature had suffered, void of Deity, or not personally united with the Deity: this passion would have profited nothing for reconciling men to God. Since, however, the whole Christ suffers and dies according to his flesh, in which all the fullness of the Divinity dwells σωματικῶς (bodily): hence this passion certainly profits and suffices for that arduous work of the redemption of the world.

With these things observed, that contradiction also collapses, which the adversaries frequently object to us in this place, that we maintain that not the humanity alone has suffered, and nevertheless affirm that the Son of God has suffered according to the humanity alone. For these two phrases are not of one and the same kind and condition, as the adversaries falsely dream. For we have already shown that the former, The humanity alone has suffered, is not ours, but heretical and Nestorian. The latter phrase, however: It is the property of the humanity alone to be passible: is ours, and is also most true. Yet it is not permitted to infer from it: Therefore the humanity alone has suffered: For just as to be passible designates a property by which Christ's humanity, remaining in the union itself naturally distinct from the λόγος (Word), is signified: so conversely, when it is asked: What is that which suffers and dies? Does the passible and mortal nature alone suffer and die? or rather the person, with whom the passible and mortal nature has been made personally one ὑφισάμενον (subsistent thing)? there the whole Scripture cries out: By no means does the human nature alone suffer: but the λόγος (Word) suffers, the Son of God suffers, the Lord of glory suffers, the author and prince of life suffers: but in this his passible and mortal nature. But in this place the arguments of our blessed Luther are to be well observed, with which he fought strongly against the Zwinglian ἀλλοίωσιν (alteration) in explaining the phrases of this first kind. For Zwingli contended that those phrases, The Son of God was born, suffered, was crucified, etc., were to be understood κατ' ἀλλοίωσιν (by alteration), or ἀντίδοσιν τῶν ὀνομάτων (exchange of names), that is, according to a permutation of names, in this way: The Son of God has suffered: that is, the man, who is united with the Son of God, has suffered. But those arguments are as follows:

I. If, according to the mind of Zwingli, not the Son of God himself in his own flesh, but the human nature alone, has suffered for me: Christ will have been a very slight Savior for me: but rather he himself will have need of a Savior.

II. With the Zwinglian ἀλλοίωσιν (alteration) standing, the person of Christ is dissolved, and reduced into two persons. For if actions and passions are separated, so that they are attributed to the natures separately, the unity of the person soon expires: so that two persons emerge, of which one has suffered, the other has not suffered. Now, however, operations and passions are not of the natures; but of the person only.

III. The Zwinglian ἀλλοίωσις (alteration) takes away from the midst all the faith and salvation of all Christians. For he who has been redeemed by a bare humanity has not yet truly been redeemed, nor will he ever be redeemed. For if a bare or sole humanity could have accomplished this, what need would there have been for the Son of God to be incarnate?

IV. The natures are so personally united that they communicate most closely among themselves: so that what is proper to the humanity, Scripture attributes to the Divinity in the concrete, because of the personal union, and vice versa. While the Zwinglian ἀλλοίωσις (alteration) denies this, it certainly denies the personal union itself.

V. And finally: There is a communication in the person of Christ not only of properties, but also of all actions, operations, and passions. For because the natures are personally united, it follows from this that whatever GOD the λόγος does, the Man Christ is said to have done: And whatever the Son of Mary suffered, the Son of GOD is said to have suffered. For it is the person that acts and suffers. Hence this phrase is true: This Man born of Mary is the Creator of Heaven and Earth. For he was made that very thing in the unity of the person: namely, GOD, who created heaven and earth. Thus far Luther, whose arguments can, and indeed ought to, be most rightly opposed to our modern adversaries, both Jesuit and Calvinist.

But they complain about the inconsistency of our theologians, who in this part disagree among themselves: while some contend that only concrete phrases have a place in this genus, so that it is permissible to say: The Son of GOD has suffered, in the concrete: but others do not shrink from abstract phrases as well, saying that the Divinity itself has suffered. But we respond that either this has been said by none of our side: or if it was said, it was understood by them in a sounder sense than it is taken by the adversaries: in such a way, indeed, that they would say the Divinity was made a participant of the passion IN ITS OWN WAY: and in that very way which was mentioned a little earlier: namely, not only by sustaining the flesh: but also by bestowing price and weight upon the passion, as has been said. Then it is to be noted that some of our side did indeed write that the Deity suffered: but not so nakedly and simply as the adversaries cavil: but with that clear determination, The Deity suffers Impassibly. By this adverb they certainly meant to note that passibility does not penetrate into the Deity itself in any way: meanwhile, however, that which is most excellent in this passion is credited to the Deity, namely that this passion might suffice and be profitable for the redemption of the World. Thirdly, let the adversaries themselves direct their dispute on this account against the Holy Spirit, who affirms not only in the concrete that the λόγος who is eternal life was seen by the Apostles: but in the Abstract, that LIFE itself was manifested and seen. Which phrase is not to be understood abstractly outside the person: but has a concrete sense: namely, that the λόγος himself was manifested and seen in the flesh. But if now some of our side have written in this very Concrete sense that the Divinity has suffered: certainly no good man would hold this against them as a fault. In which sense Vigilius long ago did not hesitate to assert that the Deity was nailed to the cross in the passion: but in such a way that it nevertheless remained indivisible and impenetrable.

Latin:

IN definiendo primo Genere Communicationis Idiomatum, haud per omnia nostrates etiam Theologi consentire videntur. Alii enim sic illud scribunt: Primum Genus est quo unius naturæ proprietas in Christo, prædicatur de altera in Concreto. Alii verò paulò aliter in hunc modum: Primum Genus est, quando id, quod uni naturæ proprium est, non soli ei naturæ, cujus proprium est, seorsim, sed toti personæ, quæ DEUS simul & Homo est, tribuitur: & rursum per distinctivam particulam ostenditur secundum quam naturam id personæ competat. Diversitatem istam peperère diversæ locutiones de Christo quæ à quibusdam minùs distinctè ad hoc primum Genus sunt relatæ. Nam qui posteriorem definitionem amplexantur, illi ad eas propositiones præcipuè respiciunt, quæ Subjecti loco habent expressam vocem CHRISTI: ut

Joh. 8, 56. Christus est, antequam Abraham fieret.

Eph. 3, 9. DEUS per Christum omnia creavit.

1. Cor. 10, 9. Christus in deserto tentatus est.

Actor. 2, 30. Christus est ex lumbis Davidis.

Rom. 9, 5. Christus est ex Patribus.

1. Pet. 3, 18. Christus mortificatus est & vivificatus.

Quæ sanè propositiones singulæ & Universæ, totam Christi personam in Subjecto definiunt, quæ cum numero una sit, constet verò ex duabus distinctis naturis: hinc adeò fit, ut de hac ipsa persona Christi, utriusque Naturæ Idiomata prædicentur: & ea, quæ Uni Naturæ propria sunt, non alteri Naturæ seorsim: sed toti personæ, quæ simul DEUS & homo est, attribuantur: alterius quidem Naturæ respectu per Communicationem Idiomatum: alterius verò ratione per Naturæ proprietatem: ita quidem, ut jam divina Idiomata, jam humana, de tota hac persona enuncientur.

Caeterùm qui priorem illam definitionem tenent, magis propriè Naturam Communicationis Idiomatum observasse, & ad eas locutiones Scripturae respexisse videntur, quae ostendunt, λόγον sive Filium Dei humanam naturam, unà cum ejus Idiomatis, ita sibi appropriasse, ut jam Unius Naturae Idiomata praedicentur de altera in Concreto. Quales sunt:

Actor. 20, 28. DEUS suo Sangvine redemit Ecclesiam: ubi non Redemptio ipsa, quae ad secundum Genus pertinet: sed Modus spectatur, quòd nimirùm ea ita peracta sit, ut non nudus aliquis Homo, sed DEUS ipse sangvinem suum effuderit.

Rom. 1, 3. Filius DEI natus ex semine David. Gal. 4, 4. Filius DEI factus ex muliere. 1. Tim. 3, 16. DEUS manifestatus est in carne. 1. Joh. 1, 1. Verbum vitae manibus contrectatum, & oculis conspectum. Gal. 2, 20. Filius DEI tradidit semetipsum pro me. Psal. 45, 8. DEUS unctus est oleo laetitiae prae consortibus.

Heb. 1, 3. Filius qui est χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τῦ πατρὸς, καὶ ἀπαύγασμα της δόξης ἀυτῦ, tantò melior Angelis factus est, quantò excellentius nomen prae illis sortitus est.

In his ergò propositionibus, non ut in superioribus, subjecti loco ponitur vox Christi, utramque naturam exprimens: Sed vox Filii DEI, quae ad alteram naturam, verùm in Concreto, respectum habet. Undè rectissimè etiam ab his statuitur, quòd unius naturae proprietas, praedicetur de altera in hoc genere: sed tantùm in Concreto: nunquàm in abstracto, ad vitandum Eutychis errorem, quem in confundendis duabus naturis ille admisit.

Fundamentum primi istius Generis est manifestum. Cùm enim una & eadem sit ὑπόστασις utriusque naturae: utique quando supponitur ὑποστάσεως hujus Unitas, statim proprietates unius naturae, de altera, in Concreto, hoc est, respectu hujus unius personae, praedicari: & sic divina homini, humana DEO rectè tribui constat.

Sic ergo 1. in hoc Genere omnis praedicatio est Concretiva. Deindè est ἀντίστροφος sive reciproca: ut verè dicere queam: Filius DEI est mortuus: quàm Filius Mariae est immortalis. Tandem explicatio istarum phrasewn semper fit κατ᾽ ἄλλο: ita ut per particulam distinctivā, sive ea expressis verbis adjecta sit, sive non sit, ostendatur, secundum cujus naturae proprietatem aliquid de altera natura in Concreto praedicetur. Quemadmodum scriptura ipsa interdum tali declaratione usa est: ut Rom. 1, 3. Filius DEI est ex semine David κτ̄ σάρκα.

Cæterùm controvertitur hoc loco de Qualitate istarum propositionum: Utrum veræ ac reales, an verò verbales tantùm sint: quando dicitur: Filius DEI est natus, passus, crucifixus, mortuus, sepultus &c. Nos hac in parte à Jesuiticarum & Calvinianorum Castris divortium facientes, non verbales sive Logicas, sed reales, imò realissimas eas esse, credimus & confitemur: non eo quidem tantùm sensu, quem Philippus hoc loco annotavit, quòd nativitas, passio, mors, & id genus alia attributa humanæ naturæ, non impediverint, quò minùs altera etiam Natura, nempè divina adfuerit: Sed longè alio & veriore, qui ipse tamen cum Eutychianâ Impietate nihil habeat commercii. Etsi enim Divina natura, prorsus est immutabilis & ἀπαθὴς: ac proindè secundum hanc Filius DEI neque natus, neque passus esse, dici potest: passus tamen est, in propriâ suâ carne. Neque enim hæc caro est nudi alicujus hominis caro: sed quia Filius DEI eam ita assumsit intra suam ὑπόστασιν, ut, quæ per se esset ἀνυπόστατος, jam in sua hypostasi subsisteret, & esset ipsius Filii DEI propria caro: utique patiente hac carne, tàm verè ac realiter ipse Filius DEI in carne hac sua passus est, ac si, quod ἀδύνατον est, in ipsissima divinitate sua passus esset: Neque admittimus hoc loco explicationem illam, quàm Clancularii quidam Sacramentarii, qui se Philippi discipulos nominant, subindè crepare solent, dicentes: Sic DEUS est passus, ut SOLA Humanitas intelligatur esse passa. Nam præterquàm quòd verbalem tantùm prædicationem respectu λόγε hæc Sophisticatio admittit: simul etiam turpi contractione seiipsam jugulat & constringit. Nam si sola Humanitas est passa: sequitur non personam ampliùs, sed tantùm Naturam passam esse: Siquidem Humanitas sola, non personam, sed Naturam duntaxat constituit. Et quæ hæc erit inanis verborum ludificatio: DEUS est passus; hoc est: Sola Humanitas est passa. Nam licet concedatur Solius Humanitatis proprium esse Pati & mori: Quia tamen hæc caro, non est suipsius caro, sicut caro alterius alicujus Hominis aut Individui: sed est ipsius DEI caro: idcircò non solam Humanitatem: sed personam ipsam, & sic ipsum Filium DEI in carne hac sua passum esse, necessariò sequitur. Ubi licet Divinitas ipsa non est passa: non tamen propterea in hoc etiam opere efficiendo, planè fuit ociosa: sed ut LUTHERUS noster piè loquitur, in passione suas quoque egit partes, non tantùm sustentando carnem, ne tantæ moli succumberet, sed insuper precium & pondus largiendo passioni, ut pro totius humani generis reconciliatione perfectissimum esset λύτρον. Si enim passa esset humana natura, Deitate vacua, seu cum Deitate personaliter non unita: nihil profuisset hæc passio ad reconciliandum DEO homines. Quoniam autem patitur ac moritur totus Christus juxta carnem suam, in qua omnis plenitudo Divinitatis habitat σωματικῶς: hinc utique prodest & sufficit passio hæc, ad arduum illud opus Redemtionis mundi.

Quibus observatis corruit etiam illa contradictio, quam nobis hoc loco Adversarii frequenter objiciunt, quòd statuamus, non solam Humanitatem esse passam, ac nihilominus affirmemus, Filium DEI passum esse secundum solam Humanitatem. Neque enim duæ hæ phrases unius ejusdemque sunt generis & conditionis, uti falsò somniant Adversarii. Priorem enim illam, Sola Humanitas est passa, non nostram, sed hæreticam & Nestorianam esse, jam ostendimus. Posterior verò phrasis: Solius Humanitatis proprium est, ut sit passibilis: nostra est, verissima etiam est. Neque tamen ex ea licet inferre: Ergò Sola Humanitas est passa: Sicut enim passibilem esse, proprietatem designat, quâ Christi Humanitas, in ipsa Unione manens à λόγῳ naturaliter distincta, & significatur: Sic vicissim, cum quæritur: Quid sit illud, quod patitur ac moritur? Num sola passibilis & mortalis Natura patiatur atque moriatur? an verò persona, cùm quâ passibilis & mortalis Natura personaliter unum factum est ὑφισάμενον? ibi tota Scriptura clamat: Minimè omnium solam humanam Naturam pati: sed pati λόγον, pati Filium DEI, pati Dominum gloriæ, pati autorem & principem vitæ: sed in Naturâ hac suâ passibili & mortali. Sunt verò hoc loco probè observanda argumenta B. Lutheri nostri, quibus adversum Zvvinglianam ἀλλοίωσιν in explicandis phrasibus primi hujus generis fortiter pugnavit. Contendebat enim Zvvinglius, phrases istas, Filius DEI est natus, passus crucifixus &c; intelligendas esse κατ' ἀλλοίωσιν, sive ἀντίδοσιν τῶν ὀνομάτων, hoc est, secundum permutationem nominum, hoc modo: Filius DEI est passus: hoc est, Homo, qui est unisus cum Filio DEI, est passus. Argumenta autem illa sic habent:

I. Si secundum mentem Zvvinglii non ipse Filius DEI in propria sua carne, sed sola humana natura, pro me est passa: leviculus Salvator mihi Christus fuerit: sed ipse potiùs Salvatore opus habebit.

II. Stante Zvvingliana ἀλλοιώσει, persona Christi solvitur, & in duas personas redigitur. Nam si actiones & passiones segregantur, ut naturis seorsim tribuantur, mox Unitas personæ expirat: ut duæ emergùnt personæ, quarum una passa, altera non passa est. Jam verò operationes & passiones non sunt Naturarum; sed personæ tantùm.

III. Zvvingliana ἀλλοίωσις omnem omnium Christianorum fidem & salutem è medio tollit. Qui enim à nudâ humanitate redemtus est: nondum sanè redemtus est, neque unquàm redimetur. Si enim nuda aut sola Humanitas hoc præstare potuisset, quid opus fuisset, Filium DEI incarnari?

IV. Naturæ sic personaliter unitæ sunt, ut arctissimè inter se communicent: ita, ut quod proprium est Humanitatis, Scriptura Divinitati in concreto tribuat, propter Unionem personalem, & vice versa. Quod dum negat Zvvingliana ἀλλοίωσις, utique negat ipsam Unionem personalem.

V. Et postremum: Non proprietatum tantùm, in persona Christi est communicatio: sed & actionum, operationum, atque passionum omnium. Quia enim personaliter unitæ sunt naturæ, hinc adeò fit, ut quicquid facit DEUS λόγος, dicatur fecisse Homo Christus: Et quicquid passus Filius Mariæ, passus dicatur Filius DEI. Persona enim est, quæ operatur & patitur. Hinc vera est hæc phrasis: Hic Homo ex Maria natus, est Creator Cæli & Terræ. Factus enim est idipsum in unitate personæ: nempè DEUS, qui cælum & terram condidit. Hactenus Lutherus, cujus argumenta modernis etiam nostris Adversariis, Jesuiticis & Calvinianis rectissimè opponi possunt imò debent.

Sed conqueruntur illi de inconstantia nostrorum Theologorum, qui hac in parte à se mutuò dissensent: dum alii contendunt, phrases duntaxat concretivas, hoc in genere locum habere: ut dicere fas sit: Filius DEI est passus, in concreto: alii verò non abhorreant à phrasibus etiam abstractivis, dicentes, ipsam Divinitatem esse passam. Sed respondemus, vel hoc à nemine nostratium dictum esse: vel si dictum, saniore sensu ab iis hoc intellectum esse, quàm ab Adversariis accipiatur: ita quidem ut dicerent, Divinitatem SUO MODO passionis facta esse participem: & eo quidem modo, quo paulò antè dictum est: nempè non tantùm sustentando carnem: sed & passioni precium, ac pondus largiendo, uti dictum. Deindè notandum, quòd quidam ex nostris, scripserunt quidem Deitatem passam esse: non autem ita nudè & simpliciter: uti Adversarii cavillantur: sed cum luculenta ista determinatione, Deitas patitur Impassibiliter. Quo Adverbio notatum sanè voluerunt, in ipsam Deitatem nullo pacto penetrare passibilitatem: interim tamen id, quòd in hac passione præstantissimum est, Deitate acceptum ferri, ut videlicet passio hæc sufficeret & prodesset ad redemtionem Mundi. Tertiò litem hoc nomine intendant Adversarii ipsi, Spiritui Sancto, qui affirmat, non modò in concreto, λόγον qui est vita æterna, conspectum esse ab Apostolis: sed in Abstracto, ipsam VITAM manifestatam & visam esse. Quæ phrasis non abstractivè extra personam est intelligenda: sed concretivum habet sensum: nempè λόγον ipsum manifestatum & visum esse in carne. Quod si jam nonnulli ex nostratibus, hoc ipso sensu Concretivo, scripserunt, Divinitatem esse passam: nemò certè bonus, vitio hoc ipsis verterit. Quo sensu jam olim Vigilius etiam asserere non dubitavit, Deitatem clavis confixam esse in passione: sed ita, ut nihilominus indivisibilis atque impenetra bilis manserit.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: Second Kind of the Communication of Idioms

CONCERNING this Second Genus of Communication, some doubt whether, speaking properly,

it can be called a Communication of Idioms? And indeed to many it seems that it cannot: and that for two reasons primarily: 1. Because the Examples or propositions pertaining to this genus do not predicate divine idioms of human ones: nor human ones of the Divinity: but attribute to the whole person those effects of the office of Christ. 2. Because, speaking properly, a Communication of Idioms, which is between two, then has a place when one is said to have something in common from the other. But be that as it may, in this respect this Genus cannot be called a Communication of Idioms: yet there can be given another respect, by reason of which this appellation cannot be denied to this Genus: namely, that in which one obtains such a communion with the other, that neither of the United ones acts separately, but always with the communication of the other. Which very thing indeed happens even in this second Genus, which is occupied primarily with the office and operations of the Messiah. For in these, whatever is done or acted, it is not said that one nature, whether divine or human, has done it: but the whole person, by the power of both natures: with each nature indeed acting and performing what is proper to itself: But yet that with the communication of the other nature. Whence by the Greeks this Genus is also called κοινοποιία or κοινοποίησις, because, namely, in it the power of both natures concurs commonly to any work of the office, merit, or benefit of Christ the Savior.

With these things thus premised, it will be easier to determine concerning the Definition of this Genus: that it is, namely, a true and real communication of the natural and proper operations of both Natures in Christ, for producing one effect of Redemption: Where the person does not act or operate in, or with one, or through one Nature only: But in, with, through, and according to both Natures: Or as the Council of Chalcedon speaks: Where one nature operates, with the communication of the other, that which is proper to each. Hence our Christ is Mediator, Redeemer, King, high Priest, head, Doctor, Pastor, etc., not according to one nature only, whether divine or human: but according to both. Hence it is that Scripture, dealing with the work of Mediation, sometimes uses such phrases as point the finger to the divine Nature: as Jer. 23:6, Jehovah our righteousness:

Acts 20:28. God acquired the Church with his own blood: Rom. 5:10. We were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. Gal. 4:4. The Son of God freed us from the curse of the law. 1 John 3:8. The Son of GOD dissolved the works of the Devil. 2. Meanwhile, however, it notes the Human Nature of Christ: as Gen. 3:15. The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the Serpent. Luke 9:56. The Son of Man came to save souls. 1 Tim. 2:5. There is one Mediator of GOD and men, the Man Jesus Christ. 3. Finally, it sometimes assigns these ἀποτελέσματα (effects) to the whole person, as in Gal. 3:13: Christ became a curse for us, he redeemed us from the curse of the law. Eph. 2:5: Christ gave himself for us as an offering and a sacrifice to GOD, for a sweet-smelling savor. These statements, indeed, would not be true if the propositions of that first kind were to be accepted according to Osiander as concerning only the divinity, or the enunciations of the latter kind according to Stancarus as concerning only the humanity. But the propositions of this third kind clearly demonstrate that both, however much they may point a finger at one or the other nature, are nevertheless to be understood concerning the whole person of Christ, in respect of both natures.

From this observation, Theological Rules most worthy of note have been born.

I. Actions and passions belong not to the natures, but to the person: yet with the properties of the natures remaining intact.

II. To the division of operations follows also the division of the person: since it is not the nature that acts or suffers, but the person. For unless the operation of the whole person were required, there would have been no need at all for the union of two natures into one person.

III. To produce one effect or ἀποτέλεσμα (effect), either nature always acts with the communication of the other, with each one indeed acting what is proper to itself: yet with the power and faculty of the other nature concurring. For example: The divine nature acts those things which are proper to divinity: but to perfect the ἀποτέλεσμα (effect) of Redemption, it uses the operations proper to humanity: Thus the Human likewise acts those things which are proper to itself: but not these alone: but also those things which exceed the powers and faculties of humanity, by the power of communicated divine wisdom and power: as will be demonstrated presently in the third Kind.

The Calvinist Spirit is in an uproar at this point, and objects to us a Confusion of the Second and the subsequent third Kind, because we maintain that the Human nature concurs to perfect the ἀποτελέσματα (effects) of Mediation, not only according to natural powers and properties, but also according to those things which it received from the Communication of divine Majesty. But the Consequence is rightly denied: For these two Kinds are not immediately confused when it is asserted that this second kind presupposes the ὑπερύψωσιν (exaltation) of Christ's Human nature, which is comprised in the third kind: but it is only shown whence the human nature has it that, beyond and above its natural powers, it can also perform divine works. But what and of what sort that ὑπερύψωσιν (exaltation) is, is explained not in this second, but in the subsequent third Kind.

Then they object to that Rule of the Council of Chalcedon: Each nature acts, with the communication of the other, that which is proper to each. Which they understand in this way: that in perfecting such ἀποτελέσματα (effects), the divine Nature acts divine things: but the Human truly only acts also what it can perform from its own natural properties, namely Human things.

I answer: The argument fails by a manifest ψεύδει (falsehood) or Crime of falsity: and that in two ways:

1. Because they attach a meaning to this Rule that is entirely false and foreign: which they manifestly mutilate, as if those words which are expressed in the Rule were not of a certain emphasis: That each nature indeed acts that which is proper to each: But with the Communication of the other. 2. Because they understand these very words only of a bare παραστάσει (assistance), by which the two natures in perfecting those ἀποτελέσματα (effects) are only mutually present to each other without any real κοινωνίᾳ (communion) of operations. From both of which inventions, the Chalcedonian Rule abhors in every way: establishing that each nature so acts that which is proper to each, that nevertheless a most true communion intervenes between them: so that the divine nature indeed participates in human operations in its own way: but the Human truly communicates with divine operations in such a way that, beyond natural things, it also performs divine things: and that by the grace of Union. Whence the Fathers were accustomed to call the divine Action of Christ Humanized: the Human truly Deified: and finally the ἀποτέλεσμα (effect) or the Effect itself, θεανδρικὸν, that is, God-manly.

And indeed, since the Adversaries manifestly betray the impiety of their Dogma in this very Objection, we shall demonstrate with firm and immovable reasons that the Human nature, in perfecting those operations of Mediation, beyond and above natural powers, also performs and perfects divine things.

I. It is established beyond controversy that the divine actions of the office of Christ are: to crush the head of the Serpent, to redeem the human race, to expiate the sins of the whole world, to satisfy infinite divine justice, to vivify, rule, and preserve the universal Church, to feed and save it, etc.

And yet Holy Scripture expressly assigns those actions also to Christ, according to his assumed humanity, when it affirms in the abstract: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the Serpent. Gen. 3, 15. In the seed of Abraham shall all nations be blessed: Gen. 12, 3. 18, 18. 22, 18. The Son of Man came to save that which was lost. Luke 9, 56. The Branch of David is Jehovah, our righteousness. Jerem. 23, 5. 33, 15. The flesh of Christ is life-giving, John 6, 51 & 53. The body of the flesh of Christ reconciles us to God the Father, Coloss. 1, 22. The blood of Christ cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1, 7. Heb. 9, 14, etc.

Therefore, that the human nature of Christ, in accomplishing these ἀποτελέσμασι (effects), produces and performs also divine actions beyond and above its natural faculties, out of the communicated wisdom and power of the λόγου (Word): no pious person has certainly ever doubted.

II. In order for the work of mediation to be integral and perfect, it consists not only of merit or the acquisition of salvation, but also of its efficacy and application.

Now if merit alone, and not likewise the efficacy and application of salvation, were to be assigned to Christ according to his human nature also: it would follow that the execution of the office, which consists in the application of acquired merit, pertains in no way to Christ according to his human nature: and consequently that he is clearly idle in conferring life according to the same.

Since this is manifestly absurd and contrary to the scriptures, which indeed assert that the very flesh of Christ is life-giving: it would certainly be false that, in perfecting and consummating this work of Mediation, the human nature provides only a natural action.

III. That miracles, performed by Christ even in the state of Humiliation, argue for his divine majesty and power, no one can doubt.

And yet these very miracles must be ascribed to Christ even according to his human nature. Therefore.

I prove the minor premise in two ways: 1. By the clear assertion of the Scriptures themselves, which affirm that Christ at the wedding in Cana of Galilee made a beginning of signs, and manifested his glory, John 2:11. Moses, indeed, the Prophets and Apostles, when performing miracles, are nowhere read to have manifested THEIR OWN glory, but another's. Hence Peter, about to heal the lame man, does not say: I say to you, Arise and walk: But he frames his speech thus: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth arise and walk: Acts 3:6. And when the Apostles were asked by the Scribes and Pharisees: By what power, or in what name have you done this? They answer clearly: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth does this man stand before you whole. Acts 4:7 and 10. Moreover, John narrates that this miracle done at the wedding was performed not by the λόγος alone, or by the divine nature of Christ, but by Christ, insofar as he is Christ, that is, anointed, and indeed so that he might manifest HIS glory, that very glory, namely, which he had indeed received through the Union, but which he concealed hidden under the form of a servant. 2. By the very illustrious example of the woman with the issue of blood, in whose healing Christ asserts that power had gone out FROM HIM: Luke 8:46. Now, indeed, according to his Deity, Christ could not have felt this: as it is entirely devoid of such a sensation as is expressed here. Therefore, in his holy Humanity he felt this, namely that such power had gone out from him: insofar as the power, existing as proper to the Deity, but dwelling personally in the flesh in all its fullness, exercised itself through the same flesh in the healing of the woman. On which matter Cyril is very excellent: Because the woman understood what the flesh of the Holy of Holies was, therefore she also approached. She herself indeed does not dare to touch his Flesh: for she had not yet been cleansed: nor had she apprehended those things which are perfect: but she touched the hem of the garment by which the holy Flesh was covered, and by a faithful touch drew POWER FROM THE FLESH, by which she might sanctify herself from uncleanness. Cyril, lib. 4, in Levit.

IV. Acts 10:38, Peter says: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with Power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the Devil: Because GOD was with him.

according to his human nature, this anointing happened to him, is a necessary and infallible consequence.

Where it also deserves observation that Peter says: Because GOD was with him, thus manifestly implying that GOD the λόγος, personally united to the humanity, performed prodigies not only by his essential divine Omnipotence, but through the assumed humanity, exercised that very omnipotence of his: not in that manner by which he did so through the Apostles: but in a far more sublime way, insofar as he anointed it with the infinite fullness of his Spirit, that is, he admitted it into a real κοινωνία of omnipotent power, by which it might perform those miracles which it could never have performed by natural power, so that this Human nature in performing these miracles was not a dead, inanimate or ἄπρακτον instrument: but most highly a σύνεργον and efficacious one: and the λόγος employed this very flesh of his for the efficacious operation of miracles: with the divine power working on both sides: but in a different respect: As regards the λόγος, originally and essentially: As regards the assumed flesh, personally and ἑπομένως, that is, from the hypostatic Union, and the real κοινωνία of Idioms consequent to this.

V. And the Orthodox Antiquity shows the final argument, whose testimonies one may read in the Appendix of the Book of Concord. Let one Cyril suffice in this place, who in his book on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten has it thus: The Only-Begotten makes the divine operations of his Majesty common with his flesh, so that he can also make the dead alive, and heal the infirm.

And in chapter 6 of Isaiah: Just as a coal is indeed wood by nature, but is entirely full of fire in every part, and possesses its power and efficacy; in the same way, our Lord Jesus Christ himself can deservedly be understood: for the λόγος became flesh and dwelt among us. But although he was a man seen as similar to us by reason of the dispensation, yet all the fullness of the Divinity dwelt in him, I mean in the manner of union. Hence also in HIS OWN FLESH HE IS SEEN TO HAVE THE MOST DIVINE POWER OF WORKING. For by touching the bier he raised the widow's dead son, and when he had spat, having anointed the eyes with clay, he restored sight to the blind.

With these things thus established, the execrable blasphemy of Lambert Daneau is to be condemned, who in his epistle to the Tübingen brethren, pp. 19 and 20, and likewise in his Examination of Chemnitz's booklet on the two natures in Christ, pages 118 and 156, did not shudder to write that the human nature of Christ did no more in performing miracles than the rod of Moses did in the miracles performed before Pharaoh. Likewise, that that voice of Christ raising Lazarus and saying, 'Lazarus, come forth,' was merely a bare sound, which contributed nothing to the life of Lazarus. Whence it is manifest that he and his associates attribute nothing at all to the assumed humanity in miracles beyond that external ministry and voice (which the Apostles also could provide), and restrict the testimonies of the Fathers to this external ministry alone, by which the flesh of Christ accommodated his voice or touch, contrary to the very mind and opinion of the Fathers themselves.

For although Athanasius says that miracles were performed by the MINISTRY OF THE BODY, he does not understand such a ministry as the Calvinists describe, but a ministry that concurs most effectively even with the divine operation itself. He wished, however, to name it a ministry in order to show that the power of performing miracles is originally proper to the λόγῳ, and thus that the principality of Christ’s miracles resides with the Deity, but that it belongs to Christ, as He is Man, in a less principal way and by virtue of the union. In which sense the same Athanasius also most correctly wrote that the resuscitation of Lazarus was designed not by humanity, but DIVINELY, namely by reason of the Origin or principality of the miracles. Meanwhile, however, that he by no means denied that the Human Nature of Christ was equipped and endowed with the power of performing miracles by virtue of the Union, is evident even from what he writes in the Gospel concerning the Most Holy Mother of God: This Man, whom we call carried by the λόγῳ, this very one GOD the Father, by the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, with the Son working together at the same time, anointed with the Holy Spirit, granting him all efficacy, and girded him about with the power of the Most High, so that he might be able to withstand every assault of the adversarial power, and thereafter work healing among the people.

And in the fifth Dialogue against the Apollinarists: As the soul in the body: So GOD the λόγος united to man brought forth miracles, not separated from the nature assumed: but it pleased Him, IN IT, WITH IT & through IT, to exert His divine power.

And it is clearly foolish that some of the Calvinists dare in this place to distinguish between omnipotent ἐνεργείας and apotelesmata (ἐνέργημα): as if the flesh of Christ effectively concurred toward the accomplishment of the latter, but not of the former. For who would be so dull as to dare to deny that miracles are omnipotent ἐνεργείας? Are we to believe, then, that restoring sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, the use of speech to the mute, healing the lepers, nay, even curing those who were absent by a mere word, and indeed recalling the dead to life, and other stupendous works of this kind, will be human, and not divine ἐνέργειαι? But, of course, this is what the Sophists intend by this distinction: that while these miracles arise from divine power, in their execution there is absolutely no difference between Christ, as regards His humanity, and the Apostles, so that just as an external ministry is left to the latter, so too is it left to Him. It is rightly doubted whether anything more impious, or more intolerable to hear, has ever been said or written in the Church of GOD. And to what end this impiety will eventually come is sufficiently testified by the defection of Neuser and other Calvinists to the camps of the Mahometans, who have openly taught with the Turks that Christ, as a man, performed His mighty works and miracles in no other way than the rest of the Prophets and Apostles.

Latin:

DE Secundo hoc Genere Communicationis dubitant nonnulli, An propriè loquendo

Communicatio Idiomatum dici possit? Et sanè multis videtur, quòd non : idque duabus potissimùm de causis : 1. Quòd Exempla sive propositiones ad hoc genus pertinentes, neque divina idiomata de humana : neque humana de Divinitate enunciant : sed toti personæ tribuunt ἀποτελέσματα illa officii Christi. 2. Quia propriè loquendo, Communicatio Idiomatum, quæ est inter duo, tùm locum habet, quando unum ex altero Commune quiddam habere dicitur.
