We therefore correct the gross error of the Calvinists in this way: Since the divine Majesty, communicated to the humanity, is defined not only by a bare communion; but also by an ἐνέργειαν (energy), as a second act: insofar as the Word exerts the operations of his Divinity in, with, and through his humanity: therefore it is that the divine idioms, while remaining within the essence of the Word a most simple and altogether indivisible thing, nevertheless act distinctly: and thus also obtain distinct predications: so indeed that whatever idioms exert their own certain energies through the humanity: such as omnipotence, omniscience, and others: they are said to be communicated immediately; and therefore the humanity can also be most rightly denominated by them. But those which exert no energy, just as those more abstruse idioms, eternity, spirituality, immateriality, immensity, etc. exert none at all: those are also said to be communicated to the flesh of Christ not immediately but only mediately: namely, by means of the energetic idioms. Which is the reason that the humanity cannot be said to be eternal, immaterial, uncreated, in the same way as it can most rightly be said to be omnipotent, omniscient, etc. But the adversaries, not content with this answer, mutter that it is plainly absurd if it be posited that there are certain idioms in God that are idle and inactive: because God is perpetual act. But I answer that this would be absurd only if we were to posit that those more abstruse idioms, even within the most simple essence of the Divinity, were idle and inactive: which, however, never entered our minds. For we firmly believe and posit that, considered in this way, they are in the highest degree energetic: so that in respect of his eternity, God himself is said to be eternal: by reason of his spirituality, he is said to be Spirit, etc.

However, these very Idioms are otherwise when they are considered either according to the assumed Nature or with respect to creatures externally: as those which do not immediately exert themselves in secondary act: although in the meantime they operate and perform mediately, as the Omnipotence communicated to the Son of Man is eternal, is immense, is immaterial, uncreated, Spiritual omnipotence, Dan. 7, 14. And that we may more strongly urge our Adversaries, let them explain to us, whether Omnipotence in GOD was idle from all eternity, until it exerted itself in secondary act in the creation of this universe: I do not think they will answer affirmatively. Therefore, let them pass the same judgment concerning Eternity and the other more abstruse idioms, about which there is controversy in this place.

But not even thus do the Adversaries acquiesce, but they press by asking: Why does the λόγος indeed exert his Omnipotence and Omniscience through the assumed Humanity, but not likewise his eternity, spirituality, etc., when nevertheless these idioms are to each other a certain purest act.

I answer that in this place one must most diligently distinguish between the primary act of the divine Idioms and the secondary act. The primary act is of absolute necessity, and is so constituted that it admits no distinction of idioms in GOD at all: but is and remains one certain purest and simplest act. The secondary act, however, is of most free will, and admits a distinction of idioms by reason of predication. For example: That GOD is Omnipotent, or rather more truly Omnipotence itself, that is of absolute necessity. For unless he were such, he would not be GOD. Now, insofar as he is God, he is indeed the purest and simplest act, admitting no distinction of Idioms within his Essence at all: so that as soon as you name GOD, you have immediately named Omnipotence, Eternity, and the other divine Idioms, each and all.

However, when God as it were proceeds outwardly, and exerts the same Omnipotence in secondary act either in the creation of this universe or in other works: that is of most free will. Where it is not immediately necessary that, although GOD is the purest act, he must therefore immediately exert also some ἐνέργεια of eternity when he exerts his Omnipotence. These things being so, we again correct the error of the Calvinists, establishing that the divine idioms and their ἐνέργειαι must be so distinguished that the idioms themselves, remaining within the οὐσία of the Deity, are a certain purest and simplest act, and are and remain invariant: but the secondary act of the Idioms, which is considered externally, can most freely be both exerted and withdrawn. Now since Scripture clearly affirms that the λόγος communicated all the fullness of his Divinity to the Human Nature in such a way that he indeed exerts Omnipotence, Omniscience, the power of vivifying, and other things of that kind, but does not likewise immediately exert any act of eternity, immateriality, or spirituality through it: Therefore most rightly

following the Scriptures, we name the Human Nature omnipotent, omniscient, vivifying, etc., but not likewise eternal, uncreated, etc.

THE FOURTH argument among the principal ones is this: If the Human nature of Christ truly and really received all the fullness of Divinity through communication: It will follow that a twofold omnipotence must be established in Christ, and consequently a twofold Divinity as well. But the Ubiquitarians concede the former: Therefore it is necessary that they concede the latter as well.

I answer: The argument fails by the fallacy παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For it does not follow that there is a twofold Omnipotence, although CHRIST is said to be Omnipotent essentially according to his divine Nature, and personally according to his Human nature: but the Omnipotence remains one in number: and consequently the Divinity also remains one. The reason is: Because that determination PERSONALLY does not define a peculiar species of divine Omnipotence: just as the same term in the Question concerning Personal Union does not make a proper person out of the Human Nature: but only shows the mode and the cause on account of which the Human nature in CHRIST participates truly and really in the Essential Omnipotence: namely, not from the property of its own nature, not through a certain Essential Communication or Deification, but only on account of the personal Union with the Λόγος. Therefore, this Term is taken in a far different sense than elsewhere, where I affirm concerning any person of the Trinity that he is Omnipotent not only essentially, but also personally. For thus I wish it to be noted that any person is omnipotent both by the power of his own divine Essence and by the property of his person. Which respect has no place in the Question concerning the Human nature: but only that which has just been defined, by reason of communication.

Then the Argument proceeds from a false hypothesis, which defines Real Communication through a Physical effusion of Divinity into the Humanity. Which delirium was evidently discussed and refuted above in the general objections. For that one Omnipotence in number is not so communicated to the Humanity of CHRIST that that Omnipotent virtue of the Deity is poured out extra Λόγον into another Subject, but that the Λόγος, assuming the humanity into himself and rendering it a participant in the real κοινωνία of his ὑπόστασις, simultaneously renders it a participant in the real κοινωνία of his Omnipotence (which is one thing with the ὑπόστασις without division). Whence an infinite difference arises, so that Omnipotence is attributed to the Deity in a mode and manner of a whole genus more sublime than to the Humanity. Whence also that other thing follows, that it is most viciously inferred from that that there is a twofold Divinity. For God is not, nor can he be, except that which is Omnipotent by Essence or by property of Nature, or rather is Omnipotence itself: Neither of which can or ought to be affirmed of the Human Nature, as has been shown several times hitherto.

Latin:

Alterum argumentum tale est : Si Humana Christi natura verè ac realiter possidet Omnem plenitudinem Deitatis; utique ea deificata, & Naturæ divinæ exæquata sit, necesse est.

Atqui prius illud ex sententiâ Ubiquitariorum verum est.

Ergò posterius etiam hoc concedant necesse est.

Majoris connexum sic probant: Proprietates essentiales in simplicissima Jehovæ Essentia non disparantur: aliàs Jehovæ Essentia in multas diversas partes divideretur. Ergò Omnipotentem esse, Omniscium esse, vel omnem Divinitatis plenitudinem habere, idem est, ac esse DEUM Essentialiter.

RESPONDEO. Committi Sophisticationem παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Major enim propositio procedit ex Hypothesi, quæ non simpliciter, sed tantùm secundum quid vera est. Ea verò talis est: Quicquid habet sive possidet omnem plenitudinem Deitatis; illud deificatum est, vel, Deus est.

Hæc Hypothesis vera tantùm de eo, qui per Naturæ suæ proprietatem ita possidet omnem plenitudinem Divinitatis, ut essentialiter sit omnipotens, omniscius, &c. vel ut sit Naturaliter ipsa Omnipotentia, Omniscientia &c. Falsa verò est de eo, qui non est ipsissima plenitudo Deitatis per Essentiam neque Naturaliter est ipsa Omnipotentia, Omniscientia &c. Sed tantùm ex virtute & Unione alterius Naturæ participat Omnipotentiam. Ratio affirmati est: Quia DEUM esse, & non ex se per Essentiam, sed κατ᾽ ἄλλο, per participationem & gratiam habere omnipotentiam, se mutuò excludunt. Jam ergò, Quia secundum Nostram doctrinam, Humana Christi Natura, non ex se, non per essentiam, est ipsa Deitatis plenitudo: sed κατ᾽ ἄλλο, respectu Unionis, & ex participationis tione quadam in tempore reddita est κοινωνὸς sive particeps plenitudinis hujus Divinitatis: manifestum est, commentum illud exequationis Naturarum, aut Definitionis jure nobis imputari non posse.

Neque Majoris propositionis Confirmatio hoc loco, ullâ ex parte militat. Non enim quæritur, utrum proprietates Essentiales, in simplicissima Divinitatis Essentia dispareantur? hoc est, utrum separari possint, & utrum Essentialiter ac subjectis discrepent: Quod ipsum nos quoque constanter negamus: Sed hoc quæritur, utrum divinitatis propria, Humanitati, sine ejusdem abolitione, aut naturarum exæquatione, in Persona Filii DEI, reverà, suo tamen modo communicari possint? Ubi nos Affirmatè respondemus iis freti fundamentis, quæ supra ex scripturis desumsimus. Adversarii verò Negatè respondent. Quæ tamen ipsorum Negatio necessariò involvit abnegationem ipsius etiam unionis duarum Naturarum. Quomodo enim, quæso, ipsarum naturarum veram κοινωνίαν crediderit, qui quod Naturis ipsis minus est, communicari posse negat. Et ut fortiùs premamus Adversarios, edisserant nobis, Annon infinitæ & immensæ, imò verè divinæ virtutis sit, homines ex mortuis in vitam revocare, dæmonia cum autoritate profligare, morbos quoslibet vel verbo profligare? Affirmatè nimirùm respondebunt, & rectè quidem. Jam verò virtutum istarum communicatio, sine ullâ proprietatum Essentialium, in simplicissima divina Essentia, disparatione sive separatione, obtingere potuit, imò verò obtigit Patriarchis, Prophetis, Apostolis: quibus tamen Divinitas non unita fuit ὑποστατικῶς, sed tantùm adfuit παραστατικῶς καὶ ἐνέργειαν τῆς χάριτος, per gratiosam præsentiam. Quæ ergò stupenda hæc fuerit absurditas, Christi humanitatem, cui Spiritus Sanctus non ad mensuram datus, & in qua omnis plenitudo Divinitatis habitat corporaliter: à vera ac reali κοινωνίᾳ divinæ virtutis & omnipotentiæ excludere, quæ tamen unum cum λόγῳ ὑφιστάμενον constituit: id quod nulli Sanctorum unquam obtigit, aut obtinget.

Instant Adversarii; & objiciunt illud Damasceni, τὰ παρὰ φύσιν sunt Φθαρτικὰ τῶν κατὰ φύσιν: hoc est, ea quæ sunt præter naturam, sunt destructiva eorum, quæ sunt secundum naturam.

Ergò si supernaturalia illa ac divina sunt Humanitati realiter communicata: utique destructiva erunt ipsius Naturæ: & per consequens, concessareali communicatione divinæ Majestatis ac Omnipotentiæ abolitio humanæ Naturæ itidem concedatur, necesse est.

Respondeo. Fallit argumentum Sophifmate Ignorationis Elenchi. Neq; enim ea, quæ supra Naturam humanam sunt: Sed quæ Naturæ ἐναντίως sunt opposita, quæque simul in eodem Subjecto naturali, citra ejus corruptionem consistere non possunt, Naturam humanam destruunt:

Qualia sunt ἀντιφυσικὰ Damasceno καὶ παρὰ φύσιν καὶ dicta: ut morbus & sanitas: Lux & tenebræ: Vita & mors. Verùm longè alia ac diversa est conditio infinitorum illorum, divinæ Majestatis propriorum donorum, quæ Humanæ Christi Naturæ ex gratia Unionis accesserunt. Neque enim hæc sunt παρὰ φύσιν, uti Damascenus loquitur, sive ἀντιφυσικά: sed ὑπὲρ φύσιν, Naturam non destruentia, sed perficientia. Certè modo hyperphysico & planè miraculoso Sol stetit, ferrum natavit, ignis non adussit, sterilis concepit, virgo peperit: neque tamen ulla subjecti abolitio est subsecuta. Quomodo ergò Exaltatio Humanæ Naturæ eandem aboleret aut destrueret, quamvis etiam consuetum Naturæ ordinem, & humanæ sortis conditionem superare videatur. Nam ut rectè Augustinus alicubi dicit: Cum Christus carni suæ gloriam dedit, Naturam non abstulit: Et ut Gerson subjicit: Gloria Humanitatem non tollit, sed extollit: non interficit, sed perficit.

Deindè locum haberet hæc Objectio, si statueremus ita idiomata divina, sive omnem plenitudinem Divinitatis effusam esse in Humanam Naturam, ut subjectivè jam ipsi inhæreat. Quo sanè pacto Naturæ humanæ abolitio, necessariò sequeretur. Verùm cùm prius illud ex nostra doctrina non sequatur, neque posterius hoc indè elici posse, constat.

TERTIUM argumentum, quo omnem plenitudinem Divinitatis Humanitati Christi communicatam impugnant Adversarii, est istud:

Si universa plenitudo Divinitatis Humanitati Christi est communicata: ac exindè Omnipotens, Omniscia, Adorabilis &c. ea dici potest: utique eandem ob causam poterit etiam dici ea Æterna, increata, spiritualis. Atqui hoc posterius absurdum. Ergò & illud prius.

Connexum Majoris probant indè: Quia Idiomata divina sunt unum quid simplicissimè, neque ullo pacto distrahi possunt: Ita ut uno Idiomate communicato, necessariò communicetur etiam alterum.

Respondeo 1. Generaliter, Quoad nos ceu firmissimam fidei anchoram tenere, non quasdam proprietates divinas τοῦ λόγου, Humanitati Christi esse communicatas: quasdam verò non: sed totam plenitudinem Divinitatis: uti Apostolus loquitur. Cùm enim Humana Natura Christi, pervenerit in κοινωνίαν ὑποστάσεως τοῦ λόγου: quidni pervenisset etiam in totius Divinitatis τοῦ λόγου, & sic singulorum ac univerforum ejus idiomatum realissimam κοινωνίαν? Siquidem ὑπόστασις & Divinitas τοῦ λόγου, ejusdemque idiomata realiter non differunt. Deindè verò quoad connexum Majoris respondeo fallere illud Sophismate τοῦ μὴ ἑπομένου.

Deindè verò in specie, quoad argumentum ipsum. Neque enim militat ratio consequentiæ: Idiomata Divinitatis sunt simplicissimum quiddam ταυτὸ. Ergò si ob realem illorum κοινωνίαν fas est dicere: Humana Natura est Omnipotens: utig, licebit etiam dicere: Humana Natura est æterna, spiritualis, increata &c. Ratio enim diversitatis dari potest longè evidentissima. Nam licèt idiomata divina intra simplicissimam Deitatis ὀύσιαν, absque ulla distractione sint unum quid simplicissimè: quando tamen consideratione vel alterius Naturæ in Unione, vel extra Unionem aliarum Creaturarum respectu, in operatione ad Extra pensitantur: tùm profectò illa ipsa divina Idiomata, quantumvis Essentialiter unum quid sint, distinctionem quandam fortiuntur: neque parem per omnia prædicandi sive enunciandi modum aut rationem admittunt. Exempli gratia: Æternitas & Omnipotentia DEI intra divinam Essentiam sunt quiddam simplicissimum ταυτὸ: Interim tamen non licet dicere, DEUS æternitate suâ condidit Mundum: sed suâ Omnipotentiâ. Sic Misericordia & justitia DEI, intra Divinitatis essentiam sunt quiddam simplicissimum ταυτὸ: sed tamen ad Extra disparem prædicandi rationem fortiuntur: ut non Justitia, sed Misericordia DEI nos salvare: non Misericordia, sed justitia DEI impios damnare dicatur. Corrigimus proindè crassum Calvinistarum errorem in hunc modum: Cum Majestas divina, communicata Humanitati, non per solam ac nudam κοινωνίαν definiatur; sed & per ἐνέργειαν, tanquam actum secundum: quatenus nimirùm λόγος Divinitatis suæ operationes, in, cum, & per Humanitatem suam exerit: Ideò sit, ut Idiomata divina, intra λόγε quidem Essentiam, simplicissimum aliquid & prorsus ἀδιαιρετόντι permanentia, distinctè tamen agant: & sic distinctas etiam sortiantur prædicationes: ita quidem, ut quæcunque Idiomata certas suas ἐνεργείας, per Humanitatem exerunt: ut Omnipotentia, Omniscientia & alia:ea immediatè dicantur esse communicata; ac proindè Humanitas etiam ab iis rectissimè denominari queat. Quæ verò nullam ἐνέργειαν exerunt, quemadmodum sanè abstrusiora illa idiomata, æternitas, Spiritualitas, immaterialitas, immensitas, &c. nullam prorsus exerunt: illa etiam non immediatè sed mediatè tantùm dicuntur carni Christi communicata: mediantibus nimirum Idiomatis ἐνεργητικοι̃ς. Quæ causa est, quod Humanitas non æquè dici potest æterna, immateriata, increata: atque rectissimè dici potest Omnipotentia, Omniscia &c. Sed responsione hac non contenti Adversarii, mussitant, Absurdum planè esse, si statuantur, in DEO Idiomata quædam esse ociosa, & ἀνέργητα: propterea quod DEUS sit perpetuus actus. Sed respondeo, tùm demùm Absurdum hoc fore, si statueremus Idiomata illa abstrusiora, etiam intra simplicissimam Divinitatis ὀύσιαν, esse ociosa & ἀνέργητα: id quod tamen nobis nunquàm in mentem venit. Firmiter enim credimus & statuimus, ea hoc modo considerata, vel maximè esse ἐνέργητικὰ: ita ut respectu Æternitatis suæ, DEUS ipse dicatur æternus: ratione spiritualitatis, dicatur Spiritus &c.

Cæterùm secus habent hæc ipsa Idiomata, quando vel secundum Naturam assumtam, vel respectu creaturarum ad extra considerantur: ut quæ actu secundo immediatè se non exerunt: licèt interim mediatè operentur, & præstent, ut Omnipotentia Filio Hominis communicata, sit æterna, sit immensa, sit immateriata, increata, Spiritualis omnipotentia, Dan. 7, 14. Et ut fortiùs urgemus Adversarios, edisserant nobis, Num Omnipotentia in DEO jam indè ab omni æternitate fuerit ociosa, usque dum actu secundo sese exeruit, in creatione hujus universi: haud opinor affirmatè respondebunt. Idem ergò judicium ferant de Æternitate, & reliquis abstrufioribus idiomatis, de quibus hoc loco controvertitur.

Verùm ne sic quidem acquiescunt Adversarij, sed quærendo instant: Cur λόγος per assumtam Humanitatem exerat quidem suam Omnipotentiam, Omniscientiam: non verò itidem æternitatem, spiritualitatem &c. cum tamen idiomata isthæc ad se mutuò sint actus quidam purissimus.

Respondeo, diligentissimè hoc loco esse distinguendum inter actum primum Idiomatum divinorum, & actum secundum. Actus primus est absolutæ necessitatis, & ita comparatus, ut nullam prorsus idiomatum in DEO distinctionem admittat: sed sit maneatq́; unus quidam actus purissimus simplicissimusq́;. Actus verò secundus est liberrimæ voluntatis, & distinctionem idiomatum ratione prædicationis admittit. Exempli gratia: Quòd DEUS est Omnipotens imò veriùs Omnipotentia ipsa, illud absolutæ est necessitatis. Nisi enim talis esset, DEUS non esset. Jam quâtenus Deus est, utique est actus purissimus & simplicissimus, nullam prorsus intra suam Essentiam Idiomatum distinctionem admittens: ita ut quamprimùm DEUM nominas, statim Omnipotentiam, Æternitatem, & reliqua Idiomata divina singula & universa nominaveris.

Cæterùm quando Deus foràs quasi progreditur, & eandem Omnipotentiam actu secundo vel in creatione hujus universi, vel in aliis operibus exerit: illud liberrimæ est voluntatis. Ubi non statim necessarium est, ut licèt DEUS sit actus purissimus, tamen statim exerat etiam aliquam æternitatis ἐνέργειαν, quando Omnipotentiam suam exercet. Quibus ita habentibus, corrigimus iterùm errorem Calvinianorum, statuentes, idiomata divina, & eorundem ἐνεργείας ita distinguendas esse, ut idiomata ipsa, intra Deitatis ὐσίαν permanentia, sint actus quidam purissimus simplicissimusq́;, & sint maneantq́; invariata: Idiomatum verò actus secundus, qui ad extra confideratur, possit liberrimè & exerceri & retrahi. Jam cum Scriptura dilucidè affirmet, λόγον omnem plenitudinem Divinitatis suæ, Humanæ Naturæ ita communicasse, ut Omnipotentiam quidem, Omniscientiam, vim vivificandi, & id genus alia: non verò itidem ullam æternitatis, immaterialitatis, spiritualitatis actum, immediatè per eandem exerat: Ideò rectissimè

Scripturas secuti, Humanam Naturam nominamus omnipotentem, omnisciam, vivificam &c. non verò itidem æternam, increatam &c.

QUARTUM argumentum ex præcipuis est istud: Si Humana Christi natura per communicationem, verè ac realiter accepit omnem plenitudinem Divinitatis: Consequetur geminam in Christo constituendam esse omnipotentiam, & per consequens geminam etiam Divinitatem. At prius concedunt Ubiquitarij: Posterius Ergò hoc itidem concedant necesse est.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Neque enim ideò gemina fit Omnipotentia, licèt CHRISTUS secundum divinam Naturam essentialiter: secundum Humanam personaliter dicatur Omnipotens: sed una numero manet Omnipotentia: & per consequens una etiam Divinitas. Ratio est: Quia determinatio illa PERSONALITER non definit peculiarem speciem Omnipotentiæ divinæ: quemadmodum etiam idem terminus in Quæstione de Unione Personali, non facit ex Natura humana propriam personam: sed ostendit tantùm modum & causam propter quam Humana natura in CHRISTO, de Essentiali Omnipotentia verè ac realiter participat: nempè non ex naturæ suæ proprietate, non per Essentialem quandam Communicationem, sive Deificationem, sed tantùm propter personalem Unionem cum Λόγῳ. Proinde Terminus iste, longè alio sensu accipitur, quàm aliàs, ubi de qualibet persona Trinitatis affirmo, quòd sit Omnipotens non modò essentialiter, sed & personaliter. Nam sic illud notatum volo, quòd quælibet personâ tùm ex vi propriæ suæ divinæ Essentiæ, tùm ex personæ proprietate sit omnipotens. Qui respectus in Quæstione de Humana natura, locum non habet: sed ille tantùm, qui modò est definitus, ratione communicationis.

Deindè procedit Argumentum ex falsa hypothesi, quæ Realem Communicationem definit per Physicam Divinitatis effusionem in Humanitatem. Quod delirium supra in generalibus objectionibus evidenter est discussum & refutatum. Neque enim una illa numero Omnipotentia, sic Humanitati CHRISTI communicatur, ut Omnipotens illa virtus Deitatis extra Λόγον in aliud Subjectum effundatur, sed ut Λόγος humanitatem intra sese assumens, & suæ ὑποστάσεως reali κοινωνίᾳ participem reddens, simul suæ Omnipotentiæ (quæ cum ὑποστάσει est unum quid citra divisionem) reali κοινωνίᾳ participem reddat. Undè infinitum oritur discrimen, ita ut modo & ratione toto genere sublimiore, Omnipotentia Deitati quàm Humanitati tribuatur. Undè alterum etiam illud sequitur, vitiosissimè geminam indè colligi Divinitatem. Neque enim Deus est aut esse potest, nisi quòd per Essentiam, sive ex proprietate Naturæ est Omnipotens, imò Omnipotentia ipsa: Quorum neutrum de Humana Natura affirmari potest aut debet, uti hactenus aliquoties ostensum.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: Refutation of Calvin’s Arguments

The fifth argument, directed against the response already given, deserves a more accurate explanation: but it is formulated by some in this way:

Whatever dogma confirms the Arian heresy in many ways: that is without doubt heretical. But the doctrine concerning the real communication of divine Majesty into the assumed Humanity does that. Therefore.

They confirm the minor premise with several reasons: The first is such: If at any time the Orthodox wish to confirm the Divinity of the Son against the Arians who deny the same, from this foundation, that divine properties are attributed in the Scriptures: they can immediately clamor in the same way that is answered by the Ubiquitarians: that there is no reason for the consequence in the argument, because the Human Nature of Christ likewise really possesses divine idioms: nor yet is He on that account that true God Jehovah.

The second proof is as follows: If by chance someone should answer the objection of the Arians, that the Human Nature in Christ possesses the idioms of divine Majesty through real communication: but the Son of GOD possesses them by property of Nature: they will answer that the Son of GOD is not GOD by nature, but is called GOD only on account of a divine office.

Finally: If anyone wishes to confirm the divinity of the Son of God from essential divine properties: because these belong to no creature: they will answer him, if this is true, why then do we teach that those essential divine properties belong to the Human Nature of Christ, which is certainly a creature.

I answer: The argument fails by a perpetual sophistry of a faulty consequence. For as regards the first proof, its extreme vanity is detected even from this, that it can be demonstrated to the Arians before their eyes from the Scriptures themselves, that the Son of God is Omnipotent, Omniscient, Omnipresent, not by grace of Union, or by any other gratuitous communication: But by essence, and by the property of His Nature: that which can belong to the only true Jehovah, but to no other creature, and not even to the assumed Humanity for eternity.

As regards the second proof, it relies on mere conjectures: For what if they did not answer as the proof holds? But be it so, let them answer in this way: yet this instance of the Arians can be repelled without any trouble: by bringing into the middle those testimonies which demonstrate that the Son is GOD not by reason of any divine office: but by reason of Essence, and is ὁμοόσιον to the Father: as has been most clearly shown by our people hitherto against the Arians.

Finally in the third proof, the instance of the Arians would then at last obtain a place, if we were to posit that the Human nature of Christ is Omnipotent, Omniscient, Omnipresent in the same way: as the Divinity Itself is believed to be such: namely by Nature and the properties of Nature: that which, however, never even in a fever came into our mind. And indeed if our Doctrine concerning the real Communication of Majesty to the Humanity of Christ savored of Arianism: certainly Christ Himself must have been an Arian, who did not hesitate to ascribe a life-giving power to His own Flesh, John 6. Thus those two hundred Fathers of the Council of Ephesus would have been Arians, who likewise assigned the power of giving life to the Flesh of Christ. Thus finally the whole Orthodox Antiquity would have to be accused of the Arian heresy, to whom this rule was clearly ἀυτόπιστος καὶ ἀναπόδεικτος: Whatever Christ has as GOD BY NATURE: that He received as Man, BY GRACE. But let the Calvinists see how they themselves can repel the Arian heresy, as long as they accept and interpret the sayings of the Scriptures, which testify that divine Majesty and Omnipotence were communicated to Christ in time, concerning His Divinity. Where that saying of Leo, Epist. 23, is rightly sung to them: Let the adversaries of the truth say, when the Omnipotent Father, or according to which Nature He raised His Son above all things, or to which Substance He subjected all things? For by Deity, they had always been subject as to the creator. If power was added to this, if the exalted sublimity was less than the one promoting it, nor did it have the riches of that nature whose bounty it needed: But Arius drags one who thinks such things into his own society. We certainly repel the impiety of the Arians most powerfully even from the doctrine of the real Communication of divine Idioms in the Person of Christ alone. For unless the Human Nature, when it was personally united with the true, eternal, natural and only-begotten Son of GOD: it could never have been made a participant of divine Majesty and Omnipotence. For what one does not have, one cannot transfer to another. It is pleasing to declare the matter by an example: Just as it is a necessary and infallible consequence: if someone concludes thus: The body of this Man lives, feels, moves, acts: Therefore it is necessary that it has a living soul in itself: So it follows irrefragably also: The Human nature of Christ from the union with the λόγῳ, has been made a participant or κοινωνὸς of divine Majesty and Omnipotence: Therefore it is necessary that the λόγος Himself, with whom it is united, and from whom it received that Majesty, be the true, eternal and essential God. Let the Calvinists go now, and chatter further, if they like, that Arianism is established by our dogma concerning the real Communication of Idioms.

Latin:

QVINTVM argumentum, adversus jam datam responfionem directum, accuratiorem enodationem meretur : id verò sic à quibusdam informatur :

Quodcunque dogma Arianam hæresin multipliciter confirmat : illud sine dubio est hæreticum. Sed id facit Doctrina de reali Communicatione divinæ Majestatis in affumtam Humanitatem. Ergò.

Minorem aliquot rationibus confirmant : Prima talis est : Si quando Orthodoxi Divinitatem Filij, contra Arianos eandem abnegantes, ex hoc fundamento confirmare velint, quòd in Scripturis divinæ proprietates attribuantur : statim illi eodem modo, quo ab Ubiquitarijs respondetur, obstrepere possunt : Nullam esse rationem consequentiæ in argumento, eò quòd Humana Christi Natura itidem realiter habeat divina idiomata : nequè tamen propterea sit Deus ille verus Jehovah.

Secunda probatio sic habet: Si fortè Arianorum objecto quis respondeat, Humanam Naturam in Christo habere divinæ Majestatis Idiomata, per realem communicationem : Filium autem DEI, habere ea ex Naturæ proprietate: respondebunt illi, Filium DEI non naturâ esse DEUM, sed tantùm propter divinum officium DEUM appellari.

Tandem : Si quis divinitatem Filij Dei ex proprietatibus divinis essentialibus confirmare velit : eò quòd hæ nulli creaturæ competant : respondebunt illi, si hoc verum, quorsum ergò nos doceamus, essentiales illas divinas proprietates competere Humanæ Naturæ Christi, quæ certè creatura sit.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum perpetua Sophisticatione vitiosi consequentis. Nam quoad primam probationem, extrema ejus vanitas vel indè deprehenditur, quòd Arianis ad oculum ex Scripturis ipsis demonstrari potest, Filium Dei esse Omnipotentem, Omniscium, Omnipræsentem, non ex gratia Unionis, vel ex alia quapiâ gratuita communicatione : Sed per essentiam, & per Naturæ suæ proprietatem : id quod soli vero Jehovæ, nulli autem alii creaturæ, & ne quidem affumtæ Humanitati in æternum competere potest.

Quoad alteram probationem, meris conjecturis ea nititur : Quid si enim non ita responderent, uti habet probatio. Sed esto, respondeant hoc modo : nullo tamen negotio hæc Arianorum instantia retundi potest : in medium productis ijs testimoniis, quæ Filium non ratione alicujus divini officij : sed ratione Essentiæ DEUM, Patriq; ὁμοόσιον esse, demonstrant : uti à nostratibus hactenus contra Arianos præclarissimè est ostensum.

Tandem in tertia probatione, Instantia Arianorum tùm demùm locum obtineret, si statueremus, Humanam Christi naturam eodem modo esse Omnipotentem, Omnisciam, Omnipræsentem : quo Divinitas ipsa talis esse creditur : nempè per Naturam & Naturæ proprietates : id quod tamen ne quidem per febrim unquam nobis in mentem venit. Et sanè si Arianismum resiperet nostra Doctrina de reali Cómunicatione Majestatis Humanitati Christi: certè Christus ipse Arianus fuerit, necesse est, ut: qui Carni suae vivificam virtutem adscribere non dubitavit, Johan. 6. Sic Ariani fuissent ducenti illi Patres Concilii Ephesini, qui itidem Carni Christi vivificandi potentiam adsignarunt. Sic denique tota Orthodoxa Antiquitas Arianae haereseos insimulanda foret, cui regula isthaec planè fuit ἀυτόπιστος καὶ ἀναπόδεικτος: Quicquid habet Christus ut DEUS PER NATURAM: id accepit ut Homo, PER GRATIAM. Viderint autem Calviniani, quo pacto ipsi Arianam haeresin propulsare queant, quamdiu quidem Scripturarum dicta, quae Christo in tempore divinam Majestatem & Omnipotentiam communicatam esse testantur: de Divinitate ipsius accipiunt & interpretantur. Ubi rectè ipsis occinitur illud Leonis Epist. 23. Dicant Adversarii veritatis, quando Omnipotens Pater, vel secundum quam Naturam Filium suum super omnia evexerit, vel cui Substantiae cuncta subjecerit? Deitate enim, ut creatori semper subjecta fuerant. Huic si addita potestas, si exaltata sublimitas minor erat provehente, nec habebat divitias ejus natura, cujus indiguit largitate: Sed talia sentientem in suam societatem Arius rapit. Nos certè Arianorum impietatem vel ex sola doctrina de reali Communicatione divinorum Idiomatum in Persona Christi, potentissimè refellimus. Nisi enim Humana Natura, cùm vero, aeterno, naturali & unigenito DEI Filio, personaliter esset unita: nunquã potuisset reddi particeps divinae Majestatis & Omnipotentiae. Nam quod quis non habet, in alium transferre non potest. Exemplo libet rem declarare: Quemadmodum necessariu & infallibile est consequens: si quis ita colligat: Corpus hujus Hominis vivit, sentit, movetur, operatur: Ergò animam viventem in se habeat necesse est: Sic irrefragibiliter consequitur etiam: Humana Christi natura ex unione cum λόγῳ, particeps sive κοινωνὸς est reddita divinae Majestatis & Omnipotentiae: Ergò λόγος ipse, cum quo ipsa est unita, & à quo Majestatem istam accepit, verus, aeternus & essentialis Deus sit, necesse est. Eant nunc Calviniani, & nostro dogmate de reali Communicatione Idiomatum, Arianismum stabiliri porrò, si lubet, garriant.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: IV. Argument κατασκευαστικὸν, sought from Omniscience, communicated to the Flesh of Christ

IV. ARGUMENT κατασκευαστικὸν, sought from Omniscience, communicated to the Flesh of Christ.

It is placed beyond controversy, that OMNISCIENCE is a divine idiom, and cannot be referred to the class of finite or created gifts. But Omniscience has been truly and really communicated to Christ according to the assumed Human Nature. Why therefore is it not a necessary consequence that the gifts communicated to the Humanity of Christ are not created or finite, but clearly divine and uncreated, and proper to the Divinity alone. That Apostolic aphorism confirms the minor premise, Colossians 2:3. In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Although this passage is indeed rendered by certain interpreters thus: That all our wisdom and knowledge consists in the recognition of Christ: according to that saying of the Apostle: I did not judge myself to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. 1 Cor. 2:2. It is certain, however, that the majesty of omniscience, which is hidden in Christ, is noted at the same time. Furthermore, that this passage is to be understood concerning Christ with respect to his assumed humanity: First, it is evident from that prophecy of Isaiah, who, speaking of the root of Jesse, namely of the Messiah, according to his human nature, with respect to which he is called the root of Jesse, says: The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might: the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord, Isa. 11:1.

Then John is a witness that this very Spirit of knowledge and wisdom was given to Christ by the Father without measure. John 3:34.

Finally, the Apostle in the passage already cited points out, as if with a finger, according to which nature the majesty of omniscience fell to Christ: saying, In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, ἀπόκρυφοι. Now, indeed, the ἀπόκρυφον or hidden thing does not befit the Deity: since in it omniscience is not hidden; but by essence it is omniscience itself. Therefore, it is one thing for a thing to be said to be hidden: but it is another thing for that in which it is hidden: which can only be true of Christ with respect to his human nature. The disciples confirm this very thing, saying, We know that you know all things: so much so that John affirms that Christ had no need that anyone should testify about man: because he himself knew what was in man. John 2:25, 16:30. And John 6:64, καρδιογνωσία, the scrutiny of human hearts themselves, is attributed to Christ: For thus John says: Jesus knew who they were that did not believe, and who it was that would betray him. Thus Peter, John 21:17: Lord, you know that I love you. Thus it is read in Mark 2:8, that Christ knew by his spirit what the scribes were thinking within their hearts. Thus Christ, John 16:19, knew that the disciples wanted to ask him about what that 'little while' was. Thus the Epistle to the Hebrews testifies that Christ, according to that nature, hears the inner groans, vows, and sighs of those who are tempted, and seek his help: according to which he himself was also tempted, Heb. 2:18.

Indeed, that which Scripture affirms depends upon this communicated omniscience, that the Father has given to the Son the power to execute judgment, inasmuch as the Son is man. For the Son of Man could never exercise that universal judgment over the living and the dead, unless he were truly omniscient, indeed καρδιογνώστης: since in this judgment not only words and deeds, but also the hidden things of darkness 1 Cor. 4:5.

Indeed, the most abstruse thoughts of hearts will have to be judged: so much so that even internal concupiscences, however much they may never have erupted into action, will be about to come under the censure of this judge.

But it would be ridiculous, or rather more truly impious, to maintain with the Calvinists that these things already enumerated pertain to Christ in this respect, namely that he knows all things by the Logos, and searches the hearts and reins of men, but that in exercising such energies, and also in refuting the internal thoughts of the scribes and Pharisees, he wished to use a human voice, and will at some time use it in the final judgment, although he himself is ignorant of those things which were not obvious to the senses, but lay hidden in the hearts of men: and which he did not know before he had learned them from the revelation of the Logos. Thus, indeed, these men leave no more to Christ according to his assumed humanity than to the prophets, to whom, existing outside the hypostasis of the Logos, many arcane and abstruse things were revealed. But away with this stupendous impiety: for such prophetic revelation dissolves and destroys the mystery of the union. Thus it should rather be maintained according to the Scriptures: that Christ, according to his assumed human nature, knows all things, knows the hearts and reins and innermost thoughts: with such a degree of manifestation, which differs in its entire kind from all other species of divine revelations; and which consists in this, that the human nature, assumed within the very innermost complex of the hypostasis of the Logos, which does not really differ from his omniscience, beholding with most perfect vision the Logos personally inhabiting it, beholds at the same time, knows, and understands all things, I say, by the knowledge of vision.

In which sense also he is said to have truly and really arrived at the communion of the infinite omniscience of the Logos: so indeed, that just as the Logos, beholding himself, is omniscient essentially and by nature: so the human nature, beholding not itself, but the Logos united to it, becomes omniscient personally from the union with the omniscient Logos. And the entire orthodox antiquity abhors this crafty sophistication: from which let Cyril suffice, who in book 10 of the Thesaurus, chapter 2, has it thus: If therefore he says that the power of judging has been given to him, not for any other reason, but because he was made man: it is clear that he did not receive it as Logos and God, but as man. To receive all things, therefore, must be attributed to him as man, which he has naturally as God.

But this omniscience must be distinguished from that habitual knowledge which formally and subjectively resides in the soul of Christ: and by reason of which Christ truly, not feignedly, grew before God and men, as Luke has in chapter 2:40. For this habitual knowledge is finite and created, according to which the elect also in eternal life, will be conformed to the body of CHRIST, the difference of degrees being nevertheless preserved. Phil. 3, 21. That communicated Omniscience, however, is infinite, and proper to the Divinity.

But it is asked at this point: How could that habitual knowledge in the humanity of CHRIST have grown, since the Omniscience, which was truly and really communicated to him at the very first moment of conception, excludes all ignorance whatsoever?

But it is most rightly answered 1. from the distinct consideration of the different States of CHRIST: of Exinanition and Exaltation. For if Christ had wished to fully use and exercise the communicated Omniscience already from his childhood: then certainly the accretion, or rather the augmentation, of that habitual knowledge could not have stood.

Furthermore, if today in the State of Exaltation, both knowledges, both that habitual one and this one proper to the divine Majesty, can stand together in one Subject of Christ: Why then could not each, even in the State of Exinanition, have produced its functions without the impediment of the other? For these two knowledges are not contradictorily opposed to each other: but they are subaltern: so that one does not destroy the other any more than the personal Union overturns the properties of the human nature. With these things observed, it is spontaneously evident that, in the state of Exinanition, Christ grew in a twofold manner: First indeed according to that habitual knowledge. Luke 2, 40. but then truly according to the communicated Omniscience, not indeed that the wisdom of the λόγος itself grew: For this, being indeed invariable, cannot grow: but that the little boy Jesus, by reason of the usurpation or second Act, grew IN that wisdom of the λόγος. In which sense it is read in John 2, 11, that Christ made the beginning of signs, and manifested his glory. For although he was anointed with the infinite fullness of the Omniscience of the λόγος at the very first point of conception: yet in the time of Humiliation he did not fully exercise it: But only when he willed, he willed the rays of it to be seen to some extent in the performing of miracles.

The Calvinists clamor at this point: Whatever is variable by reason of the first act and the second act: That cannot be called a divine Idiom: Since divine Idioms are a certain most pure and most simple act.

But according to the doctrine of the Ubiquitarians, the Omniscience communicated to the Flesh of Christ is variable by reason of the first act and the second act.

That this Omniscience, therefore, is not a divine idiom: but only a finite and created knowledge: can be a doubt to no one.

I answer: The argument fails by the fallacy πῆ, τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς, for the Major proposition is not ἁπλῶς true, but only κατά τι. For divine Idioms do not admit the distinction of the first and second act, insofar as they are considered within the most simple ὐσία of GOD. In which way and respect, certainly, Omniscience in GOD is a certain perpetual and invariable act, always most similar to itself, receiving neither more nor less, neither growing nor failing. Otherwise, the Major proposition is false, insofar as divine Idioms are no longer considered within the most simple ὐσία of the Deity: but insofar as they are weighed in operations ad extra, either with respect to the assumed humanity or with respect to other Creatures. Where certainly it cannot be denied that they admit the distinction into the first and second Act, unless perhaps someone through stupendous absurdity dares to affirm that no second act at all belongs to the most simple and immutable Act. For did not GOD exercise the ἐνέργεια of his power by a second act in the creation of this universe? Did not GOD exercise the ἐνέργεια of his justice by a second act in damning the fallen Angels? Did not he exercise the second act of his Mercy in redeeming the human race, through the Son? In which individual and universal ἐνέργειαι the second Act is certainly really distinct from the first act: otherwise GOD would have created the World from eternity: would have damned the Angels from eternity: would have sent the Son from eternity: which conflicts with Scripture, which testifies that these things happened in Time.

Similarly with regard to the Minor, Omniscience is considered by us according to the distinction of the first Act and the second Act, not insofar as it remains an invariable act within the most simple ὐσία of the Deity of the Λόγος: but insofar as it now produces its ἐνεργείας through the assumed humanity. Which ἐνεργείαι, since they are not, like the first act, of absolute necessity: but of most free will: they could certainly now be exercised, now retracted, and suspended for a time. Insofar, therefore, as the Omniscience of the λόγος exercised and manifested itself more and more in the human soul of CHRIST: to that extent it is also said to have grown by a second act.

Latin:

IV. ARGUMENTUM κατασκευαστικὸν, petitum ab Omniscientia, Carni Christi communicata.

Extra controversiam est positum, OMNISCIENTIAM, esse idioma Divinum, neque in classem donorum finitorum aut creatorum referri posse. Atqui Christo secundum assumtam Humana Natura verè ac realiter communicata est Omniscientia. Quin Ergò non creata aut finita, sed divina planè & increata, soliusq́; Divinitatis propria, dona, Humanitati Christi Communicata sint, necessarium est consequens. Minorem confirmat Aphorismus ille Apostolicus, Coloss. 2, 3. In Christo omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ sunt reconditi. Qui sanè locus etsi à quibusdam interpretibus sic redditur: Quod in agnitione Christi consistat omnis nostra sapientia & scientia: secundum illud Apostoli: Non indicavi me scire aliquid inter vos, nisi Jesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum. 1. Cor. 2, 2. Certum tamen est, notari simul Omniscientiæ Majestatem, quæ in Christo sit abscondita. Cæterùm respectu assumtæ humanitatis locum istum intelligendum esse de Christo: Primùm constat ex Vaticinio illo Esaiæ, qui de radice Isai, nempè de Messia, secundum humanam naturam, respectu cujus radix Jesse nominatur, verba faciens, Requiescet, inquit super eum Spiritus Domini, Spiritus sapientiæ & intellectus, Spiritus Consilij & fortitudinis: Spiritus scientiæ & timoris Domini, Jes. 11, 1.

Deindè testis est Johannes, hunc ipsum Spiritum scientiæ & sapientiæ datum esse Christo à Patre non ad mensuram. Joh. 3, 34.

Tandem Apostolus loco jam citato, ceu digito indice monstrat, secundum quam Naturam Majestas Omniscientiæ Christo obtigerit: In ipso, inquiens, Omnes thesauri Sapientiæ & Scientiæ sunt reconditi, ἀπόκρυφοι. Jam verò τὸ ἀπόκρυφον sive absconditum, Deitati non quadrat: quippe in qua non est recondita Omniscientia; sed per Essentiam est ipsissima Omniscientia. Aliud proindè est res quæ dicitur esse recondita: Aliud verò est id, in quo ea est recondita: Id quod de Christo non nisi respectu humanæ naturæ verum esse potest. Confirmant hoc ipsum discipuli, Scimus, inquiunt, quod scias omnia: adeò ut Johannes affirmet, Christum non opus habuisse, ut quisquam testaretur de Homine: proptereà quod ipse sciret, quid esset in homine. Joh. 2, 25. 16, 30. Et Johann. 6, 64. tribuitur Christo καρδιογνωσία ipsorum cordiũ humanorum scrutinium: Sic enim Johannnes: Noverat Jesus, qui essent non credentes, & quis proditurus esset illum. Sic Petrus Johan. 21, 17. Domine tu nosti, quòd te diligam. Sic Marci 2, 8. legitur, Christus spiritu suo cognovisse, quid Scribæ intra pectora sua cogitarent. Sic Christus Johan. 16, 19. cognovit, quòd discipuli vellent ex seipso percontari, quid esset Modicum illud. Sic Epistola ad Hebræos testatur, Christum secundum eam naturam exaudire intimos gemitus, vota & suspiria eorum qui tentantur, & opem ipsius experunt: secundum quam & ipse tentatus fuit, Heb. 2, 18.

Dependet verò ab hac Communicatâ Omniscientiâ etiam illud, quod Scriptura affirmat, Patrem tradidisse Filio potestatem Judicij faciendi, Quatenus Filius Homo est. Neque enim Filius Hominis unquam Judicium illud universale in vivos & mortuos exercere posset, nisi esset reverà Omniscius, imò καρδιογνώστης: Siquidem in hoc judicio non tantùm dicta & facta, sed & occulta tenebrarum 1. Corinth. 4, 5.

Imò abstrusissimæ cordium cogitationes judicandæ erunt: adeò ut internæ etiam concupiscentiæ, quantumvis in actum nunquam eruperint, sub judicis hujus censuram sint venturæ.

Ridiculum autem, imò veriùs impium fuerit, cum Calvinianis statuere, CHRISTO hæc jam enumerata hoc respectu competere, quod videlicet λόγῳ omnia sciat, corda renesque hominum scrutetur, sed in exercendis ejusmodi ἐνεργείαις, item in refutandis internis Scribarum & Pharisæorum cogitationibus humanâ voce uti voluerit, & aliquando in novissimo judicio usurus sit, licèt ipsa sit inscia eorum, quæ non sensibus erant obvia, sed in cordibus hominum latebant abscondita: quæque non priùs ea cognoverit, quam ex revelatione λόγε didicisset. Sic nimirùm plus non relinquunt isti homines CHRISTO secundum assumtam humanitatem, quàm Prophetis, quibus extra λόγε ὑπόςασιν existentibus, plurima arcana & abstrusa fuerunt revelata. Facessat autem hæc stupenda impietas: Nam talis Prophetica revelatio mysterium Unionis solvit & dirimit. Sic potiùs secundum Scripturas statuendum fuerit: CHRISTUM secundum assumtam humanam naturam omnia scire, corda renesque & intimas cogitationes nosse: tali patefactionis gradu, qui à reliquis omnibus Revelationum divinarum speciebus toto genere discrepet: quique in eo consistat, quòd Humana natura, intra ipsum intimum ὑποςάσεως τẽ λόγε, quæ à sua omniscentia realiter non differt, complexum assumta, perfectissima visione intuens λόγον personaliter inhabitantem, intuetur simul, scit ac novit omnia, notitiâ inquam visionis.

Quo etiam sensu dicitur pervenisse verè ac realiter in κοινωνίαν infinitæ Omniscientiæ tẽ λόγε: Ita quidem, ut quemadmodum λόγος seipsum intuens omniscius est Essentialiter, & per naturam: Ita Humana Natura non seipsam, sed unitum sibi λόγον intuens omnscia fit personaliter ex unione cum Omniscio λόγῳ. Et abhorret à Veteratoria hac Sophisticatione tota Antiquitas Orthodoxa: ex qua unus sufficiat Cyrillus, qui lib 10. Thesauri, cap. 2. sic habet: Si ergò judicandi potestatem datam sibi esse ait, non alia quadam de causa, sed quia factus est Homo: perspicuum est, quod non ut λόγῳ & DEUS ipse accepit, sed ut Homo. Accipere igitur omnia, ipsi ut HOMINI attribuendum, quæ ut DEUS naturaliter habet.

Distingvenda verò est hæc Omniscientia, à Scientia illa habituali, quæ Animæ Christi formaliter & subjective inest: & ratione cujus verè, non simulate Christus creavit coram DEO & hominibus, uti habet Lucas cap. 2, 40. Hæc enim habitualis scientia est finita & creata, secundùm quam Electi etiam in vita æterna, corpori CHRISTI conformabuntur, servatâ tamen graduum differentia. Phil. 3, 21. Illa verò communicata Omniscientia, est infinita, & Divinitatis propria.

Quæritur autem hoc loco: Quomodo habitualis illa scientia in CHRISTI humanitate crescere potuerit, cùm Omniscientia, quæ ipsi in primo conceptionis momento, verè ac realiter communicata est, omnem prorsus ignorantiam excludat?

Sed rectissimè respondetur 1. ex distincta consideratione diversorum Statuum CHRISTI: Exinanitionis, & Exaltationis. Nam si Christus jam indè à pueris communicatam Omniscientiam plenè usurpare atque exercere voluisset: utique stare non potuisset accretio, vel potiùs augmentum habitualis illius scientiæ.

Deindè si hodiè in Statu Exaltationis, utraq; scientia, tùm habitualis illa, tùm hæc divinæ Majestatis propria in uno Subjecto Christi simul stare possunt: Quidnî etiam tùm in Statu Exinanitionis, quælibet sine alterius impedimento, suas functiones edere potuisset? Neque enim duæ hæ scientiæ contradictoriè sibi sunt oppositæ: sed sunt subalternæ: ut haud magis una alteram destruat: atque personalis Unio, naturæ humanæ proprietates evertit. Quibus observatis, ultrò patet, in statu Exinanitionis, Christum duplici ratione crevisse: Primùm quidem secundum scientiam illam habitualem. Luc. 2, 40. deindè verò secundum Communicatam Omniscientiam, non quidem quod ipsa τοῦ λόγου sapientia creverit: Hæc enim quippè invariabilis, crescere non potest: sed quòd puerulus Jesus, ratione usurpationis sive Actus secundi IN illa sapientia τοῦ λόγου creverit. Quo sensu Johann. 2, 11. legitur, Christus initium fecisse signorum, & manifestasse suam gloriam. Nam etsi in primo statim conceptionis puncto, infinitâ Omniscientiæ τοῦ λόγου plenitudine inunctus erat: tempore tamen Humiliationis plenè eam non exeruit: Sed tantùm quando voluit, radios illius, in miraculis edendis, aliquatenus conspici voluit.

Obstrepunt hoc loco Calviniani: Quicquid ratione actus primi & actus secundi variabile est: Illud non potest dici Idioma divinum: Siquidem Idiomata divina sunt actus quidam purissimus & simplicissimus.

Atqui ex doctrina Ubiquitariorum, Omniscientia Carni Christi communicata, variabilis est ratione actus primi & actus secundi.

Quin igitur Omniscientia hæc, non sit idioma divinum: sed finita tantùm & creata scientia: nemini potest esse dubium.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate πῆ, τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς, Major enim propositio non ἁπλῶς vera est, sed tantùm κατά τι. Idiomata enim divina distinctionem actus primi & secundi, non admittunt, quatenus nimirùm secundum quid, intra ipsam simplicissimam DEI ὐσίαν considerantur. Quo sanè modo ac respectu, Omniscientia in DEO est perpetuus quidam & invariabilis actus, sibi semper simillimus, neque magis aut minus recipiens, neque crescens, neque deficiens. Cæterùm falsa est Major propositio, quatenus Idiomata divina non ampliùs undè intra simplicissimam Deitatis ὐσίαν considerantur: sed quatenus vel respectu assumtæ humanitatis vel respectu, aliarum Creaturarum, in operationibus ad extra pensitantur. Ubi sanè illa distinctionem in Actum primum & secundum admittere, negari non potest, nisi fortè quis per stupendam absurditatem affirmare ausit, Actui simplicissimo & immutabili, nullum prorsus actum secundum competere. Annon enim DEUS actu secundo potentiæ suæ ἐνέργειαν exeruit in creatione hujus universi? Annon DEUS actu secundo justitiæ suæ ἐνέργειαν exeruit, in damnandis lapsis Angelis? Annon Misericordiæ suæ actum secundum exeruit in redimendo genere humano, per Filium? In quibus ἐνέργείαις singulis & universis Actus certè secundus ab actu primo realiter est distinctus: aliàs DEUS ab æterno condidisset Mundum: ab æterno damnasset Angelos: ab æterno Filium misisset: id quod cum Scriptura pugnat, quæ in Tempore isthæc evenisse testatur.

Consimiliter quoad Minorem, consideratur Omniscientia à nobis secundum distinctionem Actus primi & Actus secundi, non quatenus intra simplicissimam Deitatis τῦ Λόγω ὐσίαν manet actus invariabilis: sed quatenus jam per assumtam humanitatem suas edit ἐνεργείας. Quæ ἐνεργείαι cum non, uti actus primus, absolutæ sint necessitatis: sed liberrimæ voluntatis: utique jam exeri, jam retrahi, & ad tempus suspendi potuerunt. Quatenus ergò Omniscientia τῦ λόγε, magis magîsq; in humana CHRISTI anima se exeruit, & manifestavit: eatenus etiam actu secundo crevisse dicitur.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: The Other argument of the Calvinists is such

THE OTHER argument of the Calvinists is such:

Omniscience is neither an Essential property, nor an Accident of the Flesh, nor is it even either a Genus or a Species: nor, finally, is it the flesh itself.

Therefore, omniscience does not inhere in the human nature, nor can it be said that it is really omniscient.

I answer, the antecedent is fallacious παρὰ τὸ ἐλλιπὲς τῆς διαιρέσεως, by an insufficient enumeration of the predications concerning CHRIST. For we indeed willingly concede that omniscience is predicated of the flesh of Christ, by none of those modes which

The antecedent mentions: yet the falsity of this predication can by no means be elicited or demonstrated from it. For thus countless other propositions would be false: such as: The Word was made flesh: The Son of Mary is the Son of the Highest: GOD was manifested in the flesh: The Son of GOD born of a woman: The flesh of Christ is life-giving: The Eucharistic bread is the κοινωνία of the Body of Christ: the blessed cup is the κοινωνία of the blood of Christ: and others of that kind. Indeed, none of these propositions can be referred to those modes of predication which the antecedent assigns. Therefore, the adversaries themselves must necessarily confess that they are arguing from an insufficient enumeration. For besides the indicated modes, there remains that which results from the personal union, and is and is called personal.

The third of the principal ones is as follows: It smacks of the Arian heresy if anyone maintains that something is really attributed to the flesh of Christ which, however, is neither a relation and mode of subsistence, nor something essential in the divine, nor something physical. But those who contend that omniscience is really communicated to the flesh of Christ maintain this latter point. Therefore, this opinion of theirs smacks of the Arian heresy, and consequently, as heretical, is to be rejected.

I answer. 1. The major proposition labors under a manifest ψευδολεφήματι (false assumption). For it attributes to the Arians an error of such a kind that it is not without reason doubted whether they ever fostered it; because no traces of it can be detected among the Fathers and ecclesiastical historians.

Then, as regards the minor, it labors at the beginning under a manifest crime of falsehood. For who among our people has said or written that the omniscience which was communicated to the flesh of Christ is not an essential idiom of the λόγῳ? Furthermore, who would have been so foolish or rash as to dare to conclude from our doctrine thus: The communicated omniscience is not essential to the flesh of Christ: Therefore, neither is it essential to the λόγῳ? As if, indeed, there were not one and the same omniscience that remains: although it is considered differently in the λόγῳ, and differently in the assumed humanity? In the λόγῳ essentially and by nature: but in the humanity of Christ personally, and by the grace of the union.

Then this very minor proposition labors under the sophism of a faulty consequent. For it does not follow: If the COMMUNICATION of omniscience, which was made to the flesh of Christ, is REAL: it is necessary that it be either a relation or a τρόπ@ ὑπάρξεως (mode of existence) in the divine: or that it be an essential or physical communication. For the communication follows the nature of the union: so that, as the union is, such also is the communication. Now, however, the union itself is neither a relation or a τρόπ@ ὑπάρξεως in the divine; nor is it essential or physical: but yet it is hypostatic and real. Therefore, the communication itself is also established to be of the same kind. It is, however, to be observed in this place, that not every relation is denied simply, but only that which the present objection urges: such as is between the three persons of the Divinity. Nevertheless, we demonstrated soon after the beginning of this chapter that the communication belongs to the class of those things which are called πρός τι (relative): showing that the foundation of this relation is the ὑπόστασιν of the λόγῳ. For this is what communicates: and that the term is the assumed humanity, as that in which this communication terminates.

The fourth is such: That to which a thing expressed by an abstract term does not subjectively inhere, of that not even the concrete can be truly said.

But omniscience does not subjectively inhere in the soul of Christ. Therefore, it cannot even be said of it in the concrete that it is omniscient.

I answer. The argument fails at the beginning with the sophism of equivocation. For the phrase TO INHERE IN SOMETHING is taken in two ways: either of subjective and habitual inherence, such as is that of habits, virtues, and vices in creatures: or of any true and real attribution. Now, therefore, with respect to the former meaning, the major proposition is true: but with respect to the latter, it is far most false. For in the present mystery, the concrete of a thing, which is expressed by an abstract term, can truly and really inhere in something, that is, can truly and really be predicated of something, although it does not subjectively inhere in it. Omniscience certainly does not subjectively inhere in the Deity itself either: therefore, let no one affirm that omniscience cannot be predicated of the Divinity: the antecedent is true, because the Divinity with omniscience itself is something the same and convertible: 2. If omniscience inhered in the Divinity as in a subject, then it would also be something distinct from it: namely, in the way in which accidents differ from their subjects in reality and by definition. Thus, the proposition by which we assert that the human nature of Christ is omniscient is most true and most real: not indeed by reason of any subjective inherence: but with respect to the personal inhabitation of the whole fullness of the Divinity in this assumed humanity of Christ: which brings it about that the λόγῳ with the entire fullness of the Divinity inheres, that is, interpreting the Apostle, INHABITS in the assumed flesh: not as in a physical subject: but as in its own temple. Thus, therefore, the rule is found to be most false: That nothing can inhere in something, unless it inheres subjectively.

In the fifth place, they bring forward that passage of Mark 13:32. Of that day and hour, no one knows, not even the angels who are in heaven: nor the Son himself, but the Father: and indeed as Matthew has it, chapter 24:36. The Father ALONE. Now, however, this ignorance of the Last Day cannot be ascribed to the Son according to his divine nature. Therefore, it must belong to him according to his human nature, and consequently, the κοινωνία of omniscience must expire.

I answer. 1. It is not without reason that it is doubted concerning those words of Mark, asserting that not even the Son knows the day of the last judgment: whether Mark himself is the author of them? St. Augustine certainly expressly reports that the Arians interpolated in Mark name of the Son, so that by this insertion they might impugn the Divinity of the Son of GOD. Thus Jerome, in his Commentary on chapter 24 of Matthew, reports that these words (nor the Son) are found in very few Greek copies. Ambrose, in book 5, chapter 8 of his work On the Faith, agrees with this, asserting that those words were interpolated by heretics. And quite probably from the fact that Mark reads as an abbreviator of Matthew: yet in him those words are not read.

Nor is it an objection that the exclusive particle 'Alone' is found in Matthew. For the rule of antiquity, which is truly self-evident, must be referred to here: When in those things which properly pertain to the Deity considered absolutely, something is either affirmed or denied in the Scriptures concerning one person, whether of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, and an exclusive particle is found added: then that exclusive is not opposed to the remaining persons, but is accommodated to excluding those things only which are outside the unity. Thus in this place in Matthew, the exclusive particle 'Alone' excludes only creatures, but does not seclude either the Holy Spirit or the Son from this knowledge. For as Cyril rightly infers in book 9 of the Thesaurus, chapter 4: If the Holy Spirit is not ignorant of the last day, as one who searches even the depths of GOD (1 Cor. 2), how, I ask, will the Son be ignorant of the same, who is nevertheless the giver and bestower of the Spirit who knows all things? But whatever the case may be, even if these words have Mark himself as their author: yet, as Cyril again holds in the place already cited, they are to be understood concerning the Son, not according to his Deity, but according to his assumed humanity, and that indeed either in the state of humiliation or considered with respect to natural properties. In which sense our blessed Luther wrote most correctly in his Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord: Some bring forward an untimely narrative here, saying: The Son does not know, that is, he did not want to know. What need is there for these inventions? CHRIST was true man: Therefore, like any other pure but holy man, he did not think, say, will, or understand all things at every time.

Furthermore, insofar as Christ is considered according to his humanity, as it now is in the state of glory and divine majesty: to that extent this ignorance certainly can neither be, nor ought to be, referred to his humanity; for in it all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, as was demonstrated more fully above.

Moreover, we plant our foot here, and from the arguments of our adversaries refuted thus far, we elicit that they are with very good reason accused of that most foul and long-since condemned heresy of the Agnoetae: concerning which heresy Nicephorus writes in book 18, chapter 50: These taught that GOD the Word indeed knew all things, but that his humanity, according to the subsistence united to him, was ignorant of very many things: that he was indeed ignorant of the hour of the last judgment, etc. Which heresy one may call a certain stream of the Arian dogma.

Danaeus indeed clamors, and in his treatise on heresies, under this very heresy, he writes that the Agnoetae taught that the divine nature of Christ was ignorant of certain things, such as the hour of judgment, and he cites Nicephorus as a witness to this assertion. But Danaeus admits a shameful crime of falsehood, as the words of Nicephorus already recited clearly prove. Therefore, they will never free themselves from the crime of this heresy until they cease to impugn the omniscience communicated to the humanity of Christ.

We rightly oppose to the impiety of both those ancients and these recent ones the unanimous consent of Orthodox Antiquity, which entirely fights on our side.

Epiphanius, book 2, Tom. 2, against heresies: HUMANITY is united to the Divinity, and in itself KNOWS MOST PERFECTLY, as being united to GOD.

Damascenus, book 3, 22: The SOUL of the Lord, united according to hypostasis to GOD the Word, has KNOWLEDGE OF ALL THINGS.

Latin:

ALTERUM Calvinianorum argumentum tale est:

Omniscientia neque est Essentialis proprietas, neque Accidens Carnis, neque etiam est vel Genus vel Species: nec denique est caro ipsa.

Ergò Omniscientia humanæ naturæ non inest, neque dici potest, quòd ea realiter sit omniscia.

Respondeo, Antecedens fallit παρὰ τὸ ἐλλιπὲς τῆς διαιρέσεως, insufficienti enumeratione prædicationum de CHRISTO. Nam libenter quidem concedimus, Omniscientia de carne Christi prædicari, nullo eorum modorum, quos

Antecedens commemorat : neutiquam tamen prædicationis hujus falsitas indè elici aut demonstrari potest. Sic enim falsæ forent innumeræ propositiones aliæ : ut : Verbum Caro factum est : Filius Mariæ est Filius Altißimi : DEUS manifestatus est in Carne : Filius DEI natus ex muliere : Caro Christi est vivifica : Panis Eucharisticus est κοινωνία Corporis Christi : calix benedictus est κοινωνία sangvinis Christi : & id genus aliæ. Siquidem nulla istarum propositionum, ad eos prædicationis modos referri potest, quas Antecedens adsignat. Fateantur Ergò ipsi Adversarij necesse est, se ex insufficiente enumeratione argumentari. Relinquitur enim præter indicatos modos ille, qui ex Unione personali resultat, & personalis est & dicitur.

TERTIUM è præcipuis sic habet : Arianam hæresin resipit, si quis statuat, Carni Christi aliquid realiter tribui, quod ipsum tamen, neque sit relatio & modus subsistendi : neque aliquid Essentiale in divinis; neq́; aliquid physicum. At posterius hoc statuunt ij, qui contendunt Omniscientiam realiter Carni Christi esse communicatam. Ergò hæc ipsorum sententia Arianam hæresin resipit, & per consequens, ceu hæretica est repudianda.

Respondeo. 1. Major propositio laborat : manifesto ψευδολεφήματι. Affingit enim ea Arianis ejusmodi errorem, quem utrum aliquando foverint, haud immeritò dubitatur : proptereà quòd ejus vestigia apud Patres, & historicos Ecclesiasticos nulla deprehendere licet.

Deindè quoad Minorem, laborat ea initiò manifesto crimine falsi. Quis enim ex nostratibus dixit aut scripsit, Omniscientiam, quæ carni Christi communicata est, non esse Essentiale Idioma τꭣ̃ λόγꭣ? Quis porrò ita vecors aut temerarius fuerit, qui ex nostra doctrina sic colligere ausit : Omniscientia communicata non est carni Christi essentialis : Ergò neque λόγῳ est essentialis? Quasi verò non una numero sit maneatq́; Omniscientia : licet aliter in λόγῳ, aliter in assumta humanitate consideretur ? in λόγῳ Essentialiter & per Naturam : in Humanitate autem Christi personaliter, & per Unionis gratiam.

Deindè hæc ipsa Minor propositio laborat Sophismate vitiosi consequentis. Neq́; enim sequitur : Si Omniscientiæ COMMUNICATIO, quæ facta est Carni Christi, est REALIS: necesse est, ut ea sit vel Relatio aut τρόπ@ ὑπάρξεως in divinis: vel sit Essentialis aut Physica communicatio. Nam Communicatio sequitur Naturam unionis : ut, Qualis est unio, talis etiam sit Communicatio. Jam verò unio ipsa neque est Relatio aut τρόπ@ ὑπάρξεως in divinis; neque est Essentialis aut Physica : Sed tamen est Hypostatica & Realis. Ergò ipsa quoque Communicatio ejusdem generis esse statuitur. Est verò observandum hoc loco, negari non simpliciter omnem Relationem, sed eam tantùm, quam præsens objectio urget : qualis est inter tres Divinitatis personas. Nihilominus communicationem pertinere ad classem eorum, quæ dicuntur πρός τι, mox sub initium hujus capitis demonstravimus: ostendentes, Relationis hujus Fundamentum esse ὑπόστασιν τꭣ λόγꭣ. Hæc enim est, quæ communicat: Terminum esse assumtam Humanitatem, ut in qua communicatio hæc definit.

QUARTUM tale est: Cui non subjectivè inest res quæ effertur voce Abstracti, de eo ne quidem Concretum verè dici potest.

Atqui Omniscientia non inest subjectivè Animæ Christi. Ergò ne quidem in Concreto de ea dici potest, quod sit omniscia.

Respondeo. Fallit Argumentum initiò Sophismate Æquivocationis. Nam phrasis INESSE ALICUI duobus modis accipitur: Vel de subjectiva & habituali inhærentia, qualis est habituum, virtutum & vitiorum in creaturis: vel de quavis attributione vera ac reali. Jam ergò respectu prioris significati vera est Major propositio: respectu verò posterioris, longè est falsissima. Nam in præsenti mysterio, Concretum rei, quæ voce Abstractivâ effertur, verè ac realiter alicui inesse potest, hoc est, verè ac realiter de aliquo prædicari, licet subjectivè ei non insit. Omniscientia certè ipsi quoque Deitati non inest subjectivè: Ergò ne quis affirmaverit, Omniscientiam de Divinitate prædicari non posse: Antecedens verum est, quia Divinitas cum ipsa Omniscientia est quiddam ταυτὸ & convertibile: 2. Si Omniscientia inesset Divinitati tanquam subjecto, tùm esset etiam aliquid ab eadem distinctum: eò nimirùm modo, quo accidentia à suis subjectis reipsa & definitione differunt. Sic propositio, quâ afferimus, Humanam Christi naturam esse Omnisciam, est verissima & realissima: non quidem ratione subjectivæ alicujus inhæsionis: sed respectu personalis Inhabitationis totius plenitudinis Divinitatis in hac assumta Humanitate Christi: Quæ præstat, ut λόγꭣ cum universa plenitudine Divinitatis insit, hoc est, interprete Apostolo, INHABITET in assumta carne: non tanquam in subjecto physico: sed tanquam in proprio suo templo. Sic ergò falsissima deprehenditur Regula: Quod nihil possit alicui inesse, nisi quod subjectivè insit.

Quinto loco proferunt illud Marci 13, 32. De die illo ac hora, nemo scit, ne Angeli quidem, qui in cælo sunt: nec ipse Filius, sed Pater: & quidem ut Matthæus habet, cap. 24, 36. SOLUS Pater Jam verò hæc Ignorantia diei Novissimi, non potest adscribi Filio secundùm divinam naturam. Ergò secundum humanam hæc ipsi competat, & per consequens, Omniscientiæ κοινωνία expiret, necesse est.

Respondeo. 1. Haud immeritò dubitari de verbis illis Marci, asserentibus, ne quidem Filium scire diem novissimi judicij: nùm ipsum Marcum autorem habeat? D. Augustinus certè exprefsè refert, Arianos apud Marcum interpolasse nomen Filij, ut hac insertione impugnarent Divinitatem Filij DEI. Sic Hieronymus Commentario in cap 24. Matthæi, refert, hæc verba (neque Filius) in perpaucis Exemplaribus Græcis haberi. Quibus adstipulatur Ambrosius lib. de Fide 5. cap. 8. Verba illa ab hæreticis interposita esse, afferens. Et sanè rem ita se habere, satis probabiliter vel indè colligi potest, quòd Marcus abbreviatorem Matthæi legit: apud quem tamen verba illa non leguntur.

Neque obstat, quod apud Matthæum habetur particula exclusiva Solus. Huc enim referenda est Antiquitatis Regula verè αὐτόπιστος: Quando in ijs, quæ Deitati absolutè consideratæ, propriè competunt, quippiam de una persona, sive Patris, sive Filij, sive Spiritus Sancti, in Scripturis vel affirmatur, vel negatur, & exclusiva particula adjecta reperitur: tùm ea exclusiva, non personis reliquis opponitur: sed ijs duntaxat, quæ extra unitatem sunt, excludendis accommodetur. Sic hoc loco apud Matthæum particula exclusiva Solus, tantùm Creaturas: non verò vel Spiritum Sanctum vel Filium ab hac notitia secludit. Nam ut rectè Cyrillus lib. 9. thesauri cap. 4. infert: Si Spiritus Sanctus diem novissimum non ignorat, ut qui scrutatur etiam profunditates DEI 1. Cor. 2. Quomodo, quæso, Filius ignorabit eundem, qui tamen est dator & largitor, omnia scientis Spiritus? Sed quicquid sit, licet hæc verba ipsum Marcum autorem habeant: tamen uti rursum Cyrillus loco jam citato habet: de Filio ea sunt intelligenda, non secundum Deitatem, sed secundum assumtam humanitatem, & eam quidem vel in statu Exinanitionis: vel respectu naturalium proprietatum consideratam. Quo sensu Beatus Lutherus noster in Concione de Natali Domini rectissimè scripsit: Intempestivam narrationem quidam hîc adferunt, dicentes: Filius nescit, id est, noluit nescire: Quid opus est istis commentis? CHRISTUS verus homo fuit: Quare ut alius purus, sed sanctus homo, non quolibet tempore cogitavit, dixit, voluit, intellexit omnia.

Cæterùm quatenus Christus secundum Humanitatem, prout ea jam est in statu Gloriæ & Majestatis divinæ, consideratur: eatenus certè hæc ignorantia ad humanitatem ipsius referri nec potest, nec debet: quippè in qua omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ sunt absconditi: uti suprà fusius demonstratum.

Cæterùm pedem hîc figimus, & ex Adversariorum argumentis hactenus refutatis, illud elicimus, ipsos jure optimo, teterrimæ illius & jampridem damnatæ hærefeos Agnoëtarum, insimulari: de qua hæresi sic Nicephorus lib. 18. cap. 50. Docuerunt hi, DEUM quidem Verbum omnia nosse: humanitatem verò secundum subsistentiam ei unitatem permulta ignorasse:nescire sanè horam novissimi Judicij &c. Quam hæresin liceat rivum quendam Ariani dogmatis dicere.

Obstrepit quidem Danæus, & in tractatu de hæresibus sub hac ipsa hæresi, Agnoëtas docuisse, scribit, Divinâ Christi naturam quadam ignorasse, veluti horam judicij, & hujus assertionis testem citat Nicephorum. Sed turpe falsi crimen admittit Danaeus: uti verba Nicephori jam recitata luculenter evincunt. Prius ergò haereseos hujus crimine se nunquàm liberabunt, quam Omniscientiam Humanitati Christi communicatam impugnare desierint.

Opponimus autem meritò tùm veterum illorum, tùm recentiorum istorum impietati unanimem consensum Orthodoxae Antiquitatis, quae tota à nostris militat partibus.

Epiphan. lib. 2. Tom. 2. contra haereses: HVMANITAS unita est Divinitati, & in ipsa PERFECTISSIMA NOVIT, utpote DEO unita.

Damascenus lib. 3, 22. ANIMA Domini, secundum hypostasin unita DEO verbo, OMNIVM NOTITIAM habet.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: V. a constructive Argument taken from the power of vivifying

V. A constructive ARGUMENT taken from the power of vivifying.

It is placed beyond controversy that the POWER OF VIVIFYING is not something created or finite, but an idiom proper to the Divinity.

And yet Christ, according to his assumed humanity, is so anointed with the infinite fullness of the Divinity that his flesh also has truly and really received the power of vivifying.

Therefore, that Christ, according to his assumed humanity, received not created or finite gifts, but the infinite divine Majesty itself truly and really, ought likewise to be placed beyond controversy.

They confirm the minor premise with those words of the Savior, John 6:53 and following: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life: for MY FLESH is TRULY food: and my BLOOD is truly drink.

To this also pertains that passage of the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 10, 19: We have liberty to enter into the sanctuary by the blood of Christ and a living way THROUGH his FLESH: ὁδὸν ζῶσαν διὰ σαρκὸς αὐτῶ.

Hence were born for the Fathers those excellent aphorisms concerning the flesh of Christ: such as: The FLESH of the Lord is a VIVIFYING Spirit, because it was conceived from the vivifying Spirit, Athanas. de nat. hum. cont. Apoll.

THE BODY OF CHRIST IS FULL of the power of the Word, by which ALL THINGS LIVE and exist. Cyrill. l. 3. in Johann. c. 37.

THE FLESH OF CHRIST HAS BEEN MADE WHOLLY VIVIFYING, since it is joined with the vivifying Word: The same, l. 4. in Johan. cap. 23.

Although the Nature of the Flesh, as it is flesh, cannot vivify, it nevertheless does this because IT HAS RECEIVED THE WHOLE OPERATION OF THE WORD, Ibid.

The BODY of the Lord, by the virtue of the joined Word, is sanctified, and becomes so ACTIVE for mystical blessing, that

MAY BE ABLE TO IMPART HIS SANCTIFICATION TO US. The same, book 11, on John, ch. 22.

Moreover, the power of RESUSCITATING THE DEAD must also be referred to this Vivifying power: concerning which the Apostle in 1 Cor. 15, 21. Just as through Man death: So THROUGH MAN THE RESURRECTION of the dead. And in verse 45. The first man Adam was made into a living soul. But the last Adam into a LIFE-GIVING SPIRIT. Where in both Apostolic aphorisms, the Divinity of Christ can neither be, nor ought to be, understood: 1. Because the Apostolic antithesis between Man and Man does not admit this. For if the Divinity were understood, this sense would emerge, which is far most inept: Just as through Man death: so through the Son of GOD the resurrection of the dead. As if indeed the Son of GOD, insofar as he is such, would constitute the later Adam, who would be opposed to the former Adam. 2. Because, without prejudice to the analogy of faith, the Divinity of the Son cannot be said to have been MADE into a life-giving Spirit: Since it is from eternity Essentially the very life itself: Therefore, that this is to be understood of the Soul of Christ is a necessary consequence.

We have in this part, again, the Orthodox Antiquity supporting us: and especially Cyril, who in his book on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten, ch. 7, expressly writes: The Only-Begotten Son of GOD makes the operations of his divine Majesty common as if with his own flesh, so that HE MAY BE ABLE also TO GIVE LIFE TO THE DEAD.
