And on chapter 6 of Isaiah: The λόγος was made Flesh, and dwelt among us, but although he was Man, he was seen by us as similar by reason of the dispensation: yet all the fullness of the Divinity dwelt in him, in the manner, I say, of union. Hence also IN HIS FLESH HE IS SEEN TO HAVE A PLAINLY MOST DIVINE POWER OF OPERATING: For having touched the bier, HE RESUSCITATED the widow's dead Son: And, when he had spat on the ground and anointed the eyes, he RESTORED sight to the blind.

But that we may return to the confirmation of our Doctrine, the flesh of Christ is said to be life-giving in two ways especially: first MERITORIOUSLY, Insofar as it was delivered unto death for the life of the world, according to that John 6, 51. The bread which I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world. Then, however, EFFECTIVELY & ἐνεργητικῶς (energetically): insofar as the flesh of Christ exerted its life-giving force not only most clearly in miracles, when it restored the sick of every kind to their former health: nay, the dead themselves to life: and at some time on the last day will effect the universal Resurrection of all the dead by the power of his voice: But also, and indeed principally, insofar as it effectively & ἐνεργητικῶς (energetically) bestows and applies eternal life to believers through the ministry of the Word and Sacraments: partly by exciting faith in men, by which they apprehend the merit of Christ, partly by illuminating, renewing, sanctifying, preserving in good: and finally saving eternally. For which end he also really dispenses this very flesh of his, as the food of life, in the Sacrament of the Supper.

Moreover, this life-giving force is in the flesh of Christ, not from itself, nor from the property of nature Formally, habitually, or subjectively: But through and on account of the Union with the λόγος: who, by assuming it into his ὑπόστασις (hypostasis), at the same time also assumed it into the κοινωνίαν (communion) of this life-giving power: so that through this flesh life was acquired for the whole World: and yet every work of vivification is most effectively performed in men.

Moreover, this part of the Christian Religion is a thorn in the eyes of the Calvinists, who although they boast in words that they also grant a life-giving power to the flesh of Christ: yet in the thing itself and in fact they deny it. For they do not understand it in that way, other than that the Son of GOD, having suffered in the flesh, merited life for us in it: meanwhile, however, simply denying that the flesh of Christ, from the Union with the λόγος, has a true and real κοινωνίαν (communion) with the Essential life-giving power of the λόγος: since it is simply incommunicable: which is clearly evident from their own arguments by which they impugn our thesis in this part also: The chief of which it is pleasing to refute in a few words.

THE FIRST is such: The life-giving force, which is attributed to the flesh of CHRIST in the Scriptures, is not an Essential idiom of the λόγος, but only a θεανδρικὸν (theandric) attribute, in which divine things are to be ascribed to the divine, and human things to the human Nature. Therefore, it is most viciously inferred from there that a True and real communication of the divine Majesty of the λόγος has been made to the flesh of Christ.

I answer. 1. The argument fails by a base begging of the question. For in the Antecedent it is assumed as confessed, that which we nevertheless most simply deny, relying on those foundations of the Scriptures which have just now been proposed. Then it implicates and overturns itself with most base absurdities: For if the flesh of Christ, from the Union with the λόγος, does not arrive at a real κοινωνίαν (communion) of the very Essential life-giving power of the λόγος: then certainly it does not arrive also at a real κοινωνίαν (communion) of the very ὑπόστασις (hypostasis) of the λόγος: and consequently it is not personally United with the λόγος: which is absurd and prodigiously false. The reason for the consequence is this, far most invincible: because the ὑπόστασις (hypostasis) of the λόγος and his life-giving force do not differ in anything really: so that it is absolutely impossible that the One could have been United or communicated to the Humanity without the other.

Furthermore, it will not even be true any longer what the Adversaries otherwise wish to appear to concede concerning the θεανδρικῇ action. For as long as they contend in those θεανδρικoῖς attributes that only human, but not divine, ἐνεργήματα are to be ascribed to the human nature, for so long do they deny that the human nature of CHRIST is life-giving, even by reason of merit.

This being posited, it is manifest that nothing else remains but an empty play on words: whatever they may otherwise prattle about theandric actions, and however splendidly they may discourse about the vivifying virtue which, by reason of merit, is congruent to the flesh of Christ. The reason for the consequence is likewise impregnable: Because to merit eternal life for the whole world is not a human action, but simply and solely divine. For neither do the torments of the passions and death constitute or complete this merit; otherwise, a mere man could have redeemed the human race.

Finally, if it is true, as they assert in this place, that a vivifying power does not belong to the human nature, it must necessarily be false and plainly contradictory that which they otherwise contend with full mouth: that we do not receive the body of Christ from the unworthy in the use of the Supper because the impious are not vivified: which would altogether be the case if they were to become participants by eating of the body of Christ, inasmuch as it is only vivifying.

THE SECOND they formulate thus: In what manner the flesh of Christ applied and conferred eternal life to believers in the Old Testament, in the same manner it will confer and apply the same to the faithful in the New Testament. Since there is one and the same reason for both justification and vivification in both cases, Acts 15. But in the Old Testament, the flesh of Christ was vivifying solely by merit and future death, not by a virtue inherent in the flesh: Therefore, in the same manner, it can and ought to be said today that the flesh of Christ is vivifying.

I answer 1. The argument fails by a change in the state of the controversy. For the fight between us and the adversaries is not whether the flesh of Christ ought to be called vivifying through and because of the inherence of a vivifying virtue, but whether the flesh of Christ, from the union, has been made a participant of the vivifying virtue of the Word personally, without the effusion of that virtue into the assumed flesh. Where we hold the affirmative: to which, if the adversaries wish to oppose this argument of theirs, I answer that a fallacy is committed, namely, a fallacy of equivocation (παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς). For it is true in a certain respect that the flesh of Christ confers and applies life to the faithful today in the same manner as it once conferred and applied it to the fathers of the Old Testament: namely, in respect of the merit of Christ applied through faith, insofar as they believed that the Seed of the woman was their own righteousness, Jer. 33:16, that is, that the Son of God, about to assume human nature, would crush the head of the Serpent, Gen. 3:15. That he would blot out sins and bring everlasting righteousness, Daniel 9:24. In this respect and thus far, the decision of the Council of Jerusalem is most true, Acts 15:11: We believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as the fathers were saved, who were no more able to bear the yoke of the law than we.

Latin:

V. ARGUMENTUM κατασκευασικὸν â vivificandi virtute desumtum.

EXtra Controversiam est positum, VIM VIVIFICANDI, non creatum aliquod aut finitum, sed Idioma esse Divinitatis proprium.

Atqui Christus secundum assumtam humanitatem ita inunctus est infinitâ Divinitatis plenitudine, ut caro etiam ipsius vivificandi virtutem verè ac realiter acceperit.

Ergò Christum secundum assumtam humanitatem non creata aut finita dona, sed ipsam infinitam Majestatem divinam verè ac realiter accepisse, itidem extra Controversiam debet esse positum.

Minorem confirmant verba illa Servatoris, Joh. 6, 53. & seqq. Nisi manducaveritis carnem Filij Hominis, & biberitis ejus sangvinem non habebitis vitam in vobis: Qui manducat meam carnem, & bibit meum sangvinem, habet vitam æternam: CARO enim MEA VERE est cibus: & SANGV IS meus verè est potus.

Quò pertinet etiam illud Epistolæ ad Hebræos c. 10, 19. Habemus libertatem ingrediendi in sacrarium per sangvinem Christi & vivam viam PER CARNEM ejus: ὁδὸν ζῶσαν διὰ σαρκὸς αὐτῶ.

Hinc nati sunt Patribus egregij illi Aphorimi de carne Christi: ut: CARO Domini est Spiritus VIVIFICANS, quia ex Spiritu vivificante concepta est, Athanas. de nat. hum. cont. Apoll.

CORPUS CHRISTI PLENUM est potestate verbi, quâ UNIVERSA VIVUNT & sunt. Cyrill. l. 3. in Johann. c. 37.

CARO CHRISTI TOTA effecta est VIVIFICA, quoniam cum vivificante Verbo conjuncta est: Idem l. 4. in Johan. cap. 23.

Etsi Natura Carnis, ut caro est, vivificare nequit, facit tamen hoc, quia TOTAM VERBI OPERATIONEM SUSCEPIT, Ibid.

CORPUS Domini, virtute conjuncti Verbi sanctificatur, & ad benedictionem mysticam adeò ACTIVUM fit, ut

POSSIT SANCTIFICATIONEM SUAM NOBIS IMMITTERE. Idem lib. 11. in Joh. c. 22.

Referenda est autem ad hanc Vivificandi virtutem etiam potentia RESUSCITANDI MORTUOS: de qua Apostolus in 1. Cor. 15, 21. Quemadmodum per Hominem mors: Ita PER HOMINEM RESURRECTIO mortuorum. Et versu 45. Factus est primus homo Adam in animam viventem. Postremus autem Adam in SPIRITUM VIVIFICANTEM. Ubi in utroque Aphorismo Apostolico, Divinitas Christi intelligi nec potest, nec debet: 1. Quia antithesis Apostolica inter Hominem & Hominem hoc non admittit. Si enim Divinitas intelligeretur, sensus iste prodiret longè ineptissimus: Sicut per Hominem mors: ita per Filium DEI resurrectio mortuorum. Quasi verò Filius DEI, quatenus talis, posteriorem Adamum constitueret, qui priori Adamo opponeretur. 2. Quia salva analogia fide, Divinitas Filij non potest dici FACTA esse in Spiritum vivificantem: Quippè quæ ab æterno Essentialiter est ipsissima vita: Ergò de Anima Christi istud intelligatur, necessarium est consequens.

Habemus hac in parte rursum nobis suffragantem Orthodoxam Antiquitatem: & cumprimis Cyrillum, qui lib. de Incarnat. Unigeniti, cap. 7. disertè scribit: Unigenitus DEI Filius communes facit tanquàm cum sua carne divinæ suæ Majestatis operationes, ut POSSIT etiam VIVIFICARE MORTUOS.

Et in caput 6. Jesaiæ: λόγος Caro factus est, & commoratus est inter nos, verùm quamvis esset Homo, visus nobis similis ratione dispensationis: tamen omnis plenitudo Divinitatis in eo habitavit, modo inquam adunationis. Hinc & IN CARNE SUA PLANE DIVINISSIMAM OPERANDI VIRTUTEM habere cernitur: Tacto siquidem loculo, MORTUUM viduæ Filium RESUSCITAVIT: Et, cum inspuisset luto inunctis oculis, cæcis visum RESTITUIT.

Sed ut ad Doctrinæ nostræ confirmationem redeamus, dicitur caro Christi vivifica esse, duobus potissimum modis: primùm MERITORIE, Quatenus ea pro mundi vita, ceu victima in mortem est tradita: secundum illud Joh. 6, 51. Panis quem ego dabo, caro mea est, pro mundi vita. Deindè verò EFFECTIVE & ἐνεργητικῶς: quatenus caro Christi, vim vivificam non in miraculis tantùm præclarissimè exeruit, quando omnis generis infirmos pristinæ sanitati: imò mortuos ipsos vitæ restituit: & aliquando in die novissimo vi vocis suæ universalem mortuorum omnium Resurrectionem efficiet: Verùm etiam, & quidem principaliter, quatenus vitam æternam, efficaciter & ἐνεργητικῶς per ministerium Verbi & Sacramentorum, credentibus largitur & applicat: partim excitando in hominibus fidem, qua apprehendant meritum Christi, partim illuminando, renovando, sanctificando, in bono conservando: & tandem æternùm salvando. Quo fine etiam in Sacramento Cœnæ, hanc ipsam carnem suam, tanquam cibum vitæ realiter dispensat.

Cæterùm vis hæc vivifica inest carni Christi, non ex sese, neque ex proprietate naturæ Formaliter, habitualiter, aut subjectivè: Sed per & propter Unionem cum λόγῳ: qui eam in suam ὑπόστασιν assumendo, simul etiam in κοινωνίαν vivificæ hujus virtutis assumsit: ita ut per hanc carnem tùm vita toti Mundo sit acquisita: tùm verò omne vivificationis opus in hominibus efficacissimè perficiatur.

Cæterùm & hæc pars Religionis Christianæ, sudes est in oculis Calvinianorum, qui etsi verbis gloriantur, se quoque carni Christi vivificam concedere virtutem: re tamen ipsa & facto illud negant. Neque enim illa ratione hoc intelligunt, quàm quòd Filius DEI in carne passus, vitam in ea nobis promeruerit: interim verò simpliciter negantes carnem Christi ex Unione cum λόγῳ, veram ac realem habere κοινωνίαν cum Essentiali virtute vivifica τοῦ λόγου: quippè quæ simpliciter sit incommunicabilis: id quod ex ipsorum argumentis quibus thesin nostram hac etiam in parte impugnant, liquidò patet: Quorum etiam præcipua paucis libet refellere.

PRIMUM tale est: Vis vivifica, quæ in Scripturis carni CHRISTI attribuitur, non est idioma Essentiale λόγου, sed tantùm attributum θεανδρικὸν, in quo divina divinæ; Humana humanæ Naturæ sunt adscribenda. Ergò vitiosissimè indè colligitur, Majestatis divinæ τοῦ λόγου, Veram ac realem communicationem factam esse carni Christi.

Respondeo. 1. Fallit argumentum turpi petitione principij. Nam in Antecedente sumitur pro confesso, id quod tamen nos simplicissimè negamus, freti illis Scripturarum fundamentis, quæ jam modò proposita sunt. Deindè semetipsum turpissimis absurditatibus implicat & evertit: Nam si caro Christi ex Unione cum λόγῳ non pervenit in realem κοινωνίαν ipsius Essentialis vivificæ virtutis τοῦ λόγου: utiq; non pervenit etiam in realem κοινωνίαν ipsius ὑποστάσεως τοῦ λόγου: & per consequens cum λόγῳ personaliter non est Unita: id quod absurdum & prodigiosè falsum. Ratio consecutionis est hæc longè invictissima: quia ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου & vis ipsius vivifica, nihil quicquam realiter differunt: ita ut impossibile prorsus sit, Unum sine altero Humanitati Uniri aut communicari potuisse.

Deindè nè quidem verum ampliùs erit id quod aliàs de actione θεανδρικῇ concedere videri volunt Adversarii. Quamdiu enim pugnant in attributis illis θεανδρικoῖς, Naturæ humanæ tantùm Humana, non autem divina ἐνεργήματα esse adscribenda: tamdiu Humanam CHRISTI naturam negant esse vivificam etiam ratione meriti,

Quo posito, nihil aliud quam inanem verborum lusum relinqui manifestum: quicquid etiam alias de theandricis actionibus garriant, & quam splendide etiam disserant de virtute vivifica, quæ carni Christi ratione meriti congruat. Ratio consecutionis est hæc itidem inexpugnabilis: Quia Mereri vitam æternam universo mundo, non est Humana actio: sed simpliciter & solum Divina. Neque enim passionum cruciatus, & Mors, meritum hoc constituunt aut absolvunt: alioqui purus Homo Genus Humanum redimere potuisset.

Tandem si verum est, quod hoc loco asserunt, Humanæ Naturæ vim vivificam non competere: falsum sit & contradictorium plane necesse est: quod alias pleno ore contendunt, ideo ab indignis in usu cœnæ non sumus Corpus Christi, quia non vivificentur impij: Quod omnino futurum sit, si corporis Christi, quippe quod sit tantum vivificum, maducando fierent participes.

SECUNDUM sic informant: Quo pacto in Veteri Testamento caro Christi credentibus vitam æternam applicavit & contulit: eodem pacto in Novo etiam Testamento eandem Fidelibus conferet & applicabit. Siquidem una eademque est uti Justificationis, ita Vivificationis utrobique ratio Act. 15. Atqui in Veteri Testamento caro Christi fuit vivifica solo merito & morte futura, non virtute carni inhærente: Ergo eodem pacto hodieque dici potest & debet caro Christi esse vivifica.

Respondeo 1. Fallit argumentum mutatione Status controversiæ. Neque enim pugnatur inter nos & Adversarios. An caro Christi dici debeat vivifica, per & propter inhæsionem virtutis vivificæ: sed Num caro Christi ex Unione particeps sit facta virtutis vivificæ τοῦ λόγου personaliter? sine effusione virtutis illius in assumtam carnem. Ubi nos affirmativam tenemus: cui si velint oppositum suum hoc argumentum Adversarij, Respondeo; committi Sophisma παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Secundum quid enim verum est, quod eodem hodie pacto fidelibus vitam conferat & applicet caro Christi, quo olim contulit & applicavit Patribus Veteris Testamenti: nempe respectu meriti Christi per Fidem applicati: quatenus videlicet crediderunt, Semen mulieris esse suam ipsorum justitiam Jerem. 33, 16. hoc est, Filium DEI Naturam humanam assumturum caput Serpenti contriturum Gen. 3, 15. Peccata deleturum, & sempiternam justitiam allaturum Daniel. 9, 24. Hoc respectu & hactenus verissima est decisio concilii Hierosolymitani Act. 15, 11. Credimus salvari nos per gratiam Domini Jesu Christi, quemadmodum & Patres salvati sunt, qui legis jugum, æque ac nos, portare non potuerunt.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: V. a constructive Argument taken from the power of vivifying (continued)

However, the argument is false if it is taken absolutely (ἁπλῶς), not only concerning the merit of Christ and its application through faith, but also concerning the mode of application. For here, because of the diversity of the Old and New Testaments, it is not one and the same, because in the Old Testament the flesh of Christ was not yet in the nature of things, and therefore this flesh did not concur effectively (ἐνεργητικῶς) for the application of the merit of Christ; but the Son of God, only by his divinity, applied to believers the merit of the whole person of Christ, which was at some time to be performed according to both natures. But now, after the Son of God in the New Testament assumed his own flesh and in it paid the price of redemption, he certainly confers and applies life to believers not by his divinity alone, but simultaneously in, through, and with his humanity, as was demonstrated a little earlier from the Scriptures.

THE THIRD sounds thus: If there had been a divine and infinite vivifying power in the flesh of Christ, surely it could not have been overcome and killed by any finite power. But the flesh of Christ was killed. Therefore, it follows that that power of life was not infinite and divine.

I answer: The argument fails by the fallacy of ignoring the refutation (παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχου). For the major proposition is indeed devoid of a true refutation. For the connection of the major would only proceed if the full exercise of the communicated infinite vivifying virtue and death or killing were mutually opposed to each other. For thus it could not have happened that the flesh of Christ, fully exercising that vivifying virtue, could be killed. But now, because there intervened the most profound state of emptying, which brought it about that the real communication of the vivifying virtue did not indeed cease, but only that the Word did not exercise himself and his life through his flesh, but by an evacuation of use or exercise, rested in it; therefore, it could be overcome and killed by death. Although, speaking properly and indeed according to the Scriptures, the flesh of Christ was not overcome, since he did not undergo death unwillingly or against his will, but spontaneously and most freely. For thus he himself says: I lay down my life, that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I have the power to lay down my life and to take it up again, John 10:17-18. And again: The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many, Matthew 20:28.

Furthermore, if the major proposition is examined a little more accurately, it becomes most manifest that it savors not obscurely of Nestorianism itself. For if at the time of the passion and death of Christ there was no divine and infinite vivifying power in his flesh, then certainly neither was the hypostasis of the Word in it, and consequently, in the passion and death, the hypostatic union was dissolved; which is impious and blasphemous. The reason for the connection is: Because the vivifying power and the hypostasis of the Word do not really differ, but are something the same. Let the adversaries, therefore, at last grow wise and weigh whither this lust of theirs for arguing will eventually lead; namely, that they might invent and profess two Christs with Nestorius. But if they firmly and from the heart believe that the union was not dissolved in death, it is a wonder if, even without us saying anything, they themselves do not perceive the stupendous futility of the major proposition. question recognize and detest. For if the communion of the λόγος itself, and of the same infinite and divine ὑποστάσεως, by which, as Cyril speaks, the λόγος HIMSELF, who is LIFE itself, communicated himself to the flesh, did not prevent Christ from being able to die in the flesh: If all that fullness of the Divinity, inhabiting in this flesh as in its own temple, did not hinder the death of the flesh of Christ: then certainly the communicated vivifying power did not hinder it either: especially since he did not exert it, as was shown above.

Finally, let the Adversaries explain, if this infinite and truly divine vivifying power was not truly and really in the flesh of Christ at the time of his death: How can it be that through this death of the flesh of Christ, our death is swallowed up into victory, and eternal life is restored to us? If by chance they answer that these things could happen because the λόγος was and remained in the flesh of Christ even when dead: we certainly accept this, and retort it upon them, even if they are unwilling to confess that the infinite and divine vivifying virtue was and remained in the flesh of Christ, however dead it may have been.

The fourth is such: In that in which all the powers of life were extinguished: in it life could not exist: and consequently, it cannot vivify others, by an inherent power.

But all the powers of life were extinguished in the killed and buried flesh of Christ.

Therefore, in the killed and buried flesh of Christ, there was no life, and consequently, it could not vivify others by an inherent power.

I answer 1. The major proposition falls into the same sophistications, impieties, and blasphemies: which, having been noted in the Refutation of the previous argument, we shall most rightly apply here.

The minor labors partly under equivocation, partly under calumny. Under equivocation, indeed, insofar as it does not distinguish between the natural life of the flesh of Christ, which was truly extinguished in death according to all its powers, while the soul was truly separated from the flesh of Christ: and that divine vivifying power, which it received really from the personal Union with the λόγος, and retained most present to itself even in death: and which could no more be extinguished by death than the hypostatic Union itself could be dissolved: although it did not exert it in the second act: as was shown a little earlier. But the minor labors under calumny, insofar as it pretends that we posit that the flesh of Christ vivifies by some inherent power: which is a rotten and foul fiction we have already worn out several times: clearly unworthy of being refuted at greater length.

THE FIFTH is formed thus: We are vivified by his power and virtue, by whose operation the dead human Nature of Christ was vivified and recalled to life.

But the buried flesh of Christ was vivified and recalled to life by the power of the Deity alone: Rom. 1, 4. 1 Pet. 3, 11. Rom. 8, 11.

Therefore we are recalled to life by the power of the Deity alone.

I answer that both of the premises are far from the truth. For as regards the major proposition; Scripture expressly ascribes the vivification or resurrection of our bodies not to the divinity alone, excluding the humanity: but to the whole Christ, GOD and Man. As: John 5, 28. The hour is coming in which all who are in the graves will hear the voice of the Son of Man, and will come forth. 1 Cor. 15, 22. As in Adam all die: so in CHRIST (the word CHRIST denotes both natures) all shall be vivified. Rev. 1, 18. I am the first and the last, and the living: and I WAS DEAD and behold I am living, for ever and ever, and I have the keys of death and of hell.

As for the minor, it is deceived by the sophism παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For it is true in this sense, that the dead flesh of Christ was recalled to life by that power which is proper to the Deity alone: but which was truly communicated to the flesh from the union with the λόγος. But it is most false if it is taken in such a way that that vivifying power, by which the flesh of Christ was recalled to life, is so proper to the Divinity of the λόγος that this flesh never attained to its κοινωνίαν through and because of the Union. For we have clearly demonstrated the contrary from the Scriptures thus far. And indeed, as regards the resuscitation of the flesh of Christ: Although this flesh, because of the intervention of the deepest Exinanition, did not raise itself: yet it would not be right to remove the whole Human Nature from this work on that account. For 1. the λόγος raised the flesh from the dead by that power and potency which the flesh of Christ indeed had really communicated to itself: but yet, by reason of use, did not exert.

Then the Soul of Christ, for the vivification of its own body, certainly concurs by the power of the communicated vivifying virtue: according to that in John 2:19, Destroy this temple (meaning his own body) and in three days I will raise it up. John 10:18, I have power not only to lay down, but also to take up my soul again. Nor does it stand against this assertion that in Romans 6:4 and Ephesians 1, Christ is said to have been raised from the dead by the glory of the Father. For according to the rule of Augustine: The works of the Trinity to the outside are undivided. Therefore Christ rose from the dead, partly by the power common to the whole Trinity, but partly by his own power.

THE SIXTH [argument] Oecolampadius drew from the Scriptures: It is written, John 6:63, The flesh profiteth nothing: it is the Spirit that vivifieth, therefore the flesh of Christ is not vivifying.

I answer with Beza, who in this part differs from his fellow-partisans, Epist. 5: If you understand these words of Christ simply and without distinction concerning his own flesh, you are refuted by the testimony of Christ himself, who inculcates the partaking of his flesh so many times in this very sixth chapter: And why, I pray, did the Son of God assume useless flesh? which nevertheless was given for the life of the world. John 6:51.

Wherefore, as our B. Luther rightly gathers, Christ does not understand his own flesh: But that sense and those carnal thoughts of the Capernaites, which they had conceived concerning the gross and carnal eating of the flesh of Christ. Thus by Spirit, the Savior denotes not his divinity, but the spiritual sense or understanding of his words. And indeed, if this license be permitted to the Adversaries, that, wherever flesh is found placed absolutely in the scriptures, they may immediately institute a collection to the flesh of Christ, what will prevent them from eventually asserting, with the Valentinians and Manichaeans, that not even true flesh and blood of human nature was assumed by Christ? Of which sort, says Luther, is that which Zwingli writes: If CHRIST'S flesh is eaten, it is necessary that it be converted into flesh: For whatever is born of flesh, is flesh. May the LORD rebuke you, Satan.

See more objections, and their refutation, part 1. Apolog. in the Book of Concord: page 9. b. up to page 18.

Latin:

Cæterum falsum est argumentum, si ἁπλῶς, non tantum de merito Christi, ejusdemque per Fidem applicatione: sed & de Modo applicationis accipiatur. Hic enim pro diversitate Veteris & Novi Testamenti non uninus idemque est, Quia enim in Veteri caro Christi nondum erat in rerum natura, ideoque etiam caro hæc ad applicationem meriti Christi ἐνεργητικῶς non concurrebat: sed Filius DEI tantum Divinitate sua, Meritum totius personæ Christi, quod aliquando secundum utramque naturam præstandum erat, credentibus applicabat. Jam vero postquam Filium DEI in Novo Testamento carnem suam affumsit, inque ea etiam pretium Redemtionis persolvit: utique non sola sua divinitate, sed simul in, per & cum humanitate sua, vitam credentibus confert & applicat: uti paulo ante ex Scripturis demonstratum.

TERTIUM sic sonat: Si in Christi carne fuisset divina & infinita Vivificandi vis, profecto, non potuisset ea ab ulla finita potentia superari & occidi. Atqui caro Christi fuit occisa. Ergo sequitur, Eam vitæ vim non fuisse infinitam & divinam.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχου. Major enim propositio vero ἐλέγχῳ destituitur. Tum enim demum procederet Majoris Connexum, si plena usurpatio communicatæ infinitæ virtutis vivificæ: & Mors sive occisio, sibi mutuo opponerentur. Sic enim fieri non potuisset, ut Caro Christi, plene virtutem illam vivificam exerens, occideretur. Jam vero, quia intervenit exinanitionis status longe profundissimus, qui præstitit, ut non quidem defineret realis communicatio virtutis vivificæ: sed tantu, ut λόγος se suamque vita per carne sua non exerceret: sed evacuatione usus sive usurpationis, in illa quiesceret: ideo a morte superari & occidi potuit: Quanquam proprie loquendo, & quidem secundum Scripturas, caro Christi non fuit superata: siquidem non nolens aut invita mortem obijt: sed sponte & liberrime: Sic enim ipsemet: Ego depono animam meam, ut eam rursus assumam: Nemo tollit eam a me: sed Ego habeo potestatem ponendi animam meam, & resumendi eam. Joh. 10, 17, 18. Et rursum: Filius hominis non venit, ut sibi ministretur, sed ut ministret, & det animam suam in redemtionem pro multis, Matth. 20, 28.

Præterea si paulo accuratius Major propositio examinetur, manifestissimum evadit, ipsam Nestorianismum haud obscure sapere. Si enim tempore passionis & mortis Christi in carne ipsius, non fuit divina & infinita vivificandi vis: utique neque ὑπόστασις λόγου in ea fuit: & per consequens, in passione & morte, soluta fuit Unio Hypostatica: id quod impium & blasphemum. Ratio connexi est: Quia vis vivifica & ὑπόστασις λόγου, realiter non differunt: sed sunt quiddam ταυτὸ. Sapiant Ergo vel tandem Adversarii, & expendant, quorsum tandem hæc ipsorum argumentandi libido evasura sit: nempe ut duos Christos cum Nestorio fingant & profiteantur. Sin vero firmiter & ex animo credunt, Unionem in morte solutam non fuisse: mirum est, ni vel nobis tacentibus, ipsimet stupendam futilitatem Majoris propositionis stionis agnoscant & detestentur. Nam si ipsius λόγω, ejusdemque infinitæ & divinæ ὑποστάσεως κοινωνία realis, quâ, ut Cyrillus loquitur, SEIPSUM λόγος, qui est ipsissima VITA, carni communicavit, non obstitit, quô minus carne mori potuerit Christus: Si omnis illa plenitudo Divinitatis, in carne hac, tanquam in proprio suo templo inhabitans, non impedivit mortem carnis Christi: utique nec communicata vis vivifica eam impedivit: præsertim cùm eam non exereret, uti supra ostensum.

Tandem edisserant Adversarij, Si infinita hæc & verè divina vis vivifica, in carne Christi, tempore mortis ejus, non verè ac realiter fuit: Quî fieri poterit, ut per Mortem hanc carnis Christi, nostra Mors in victoriam absorbeterur, & vita æterna nobis restitueretur. Si fortè responderint, Hæc ideò fieri potuisse, quia in carne Christi etiam mortuâ Λόγος fuerit & manserit: nos sanè hoc acceptamus, & in ipsos retorquemus, vel nolentes ipsos confiteri infinitam & divinam virtutem vivificam in carne Christi, quantumvis mortuâ, fuisse & mansisse.

Quartum tale est: In quo extinctæ fuerunt omnes vires vitæ: in eo vita esse non potuit: & per consequens, id alios vivificare non potest, vi inhærente.

Atqui omnes vires vitæ in carne Christi occisa & sepulta extinctæ fuerunt.

Ergò in carne Christi occisa & sepulta, non fuit vita, & per consequens, alios virtute inhærente vivificare non potuit.

Respondeo 1. Major propositio in easdem Sophisticationes, impietates & blasphemias incurrit: quas in præcedentis argumenti Refutatione notatas, hûc rectissimè accommodabimus.

Minor partim æquivocatione, partim calumniâ laborat. Aequivocatione quidem, quatenus non distingvit inter vitam Naturalem carnis Christi, quæ in morte secundum omnes vires verè fuit extincta; dùm anima verè separata fuit à carne Christi: & inter divinam illam vim vivificam, quam ex personali Unione cum λόγω realiter accepit, & in ipsa morte sibi præsentissimam retinuit: quæque per mortem haud magis extingvi, atque Unio ipsa hypostatica dissolvi potuit: licet actu secundo eam non exereret: uti paulò antè est ostensum. Calumniâ verò laborat Minor, quatenus nos statuere fingit, carnem Christi vivificare credentes, vi quadam inhærente: Quod putridum & putidum commentum jam aliquoties protrivimus: Indignum planè quod prolixiùs refutetur.

QVINTVM sic informatur: Nos ejus vi & virtute vivificamur, cujus operatione, mortua Christi humana Natura, vivificata fuit, & in vitam revocata.

Atqui caro Christi sepulta, sola Deitatis virtute fuit vivificata, & in vitam revocata: Rom. 1, 4. 1. Pet. 3, 11. Rom. 8, 11.

Ergò sola Deitatis virtute in vitam revocamur.

Respondeo, utramque præmissarum longè esse falsissimam. Nam quoad Majorem propositionem; Scriptura vivificationem sive resuscitationem corporum nostrorum: non soli divinitati, exclusa humanitate: sed toti Christo DEO & Homini disertè adscribit. ut: Joh. 5, 28. Venit hora, in qua omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem Filij Hominis, & prodibunt. 1. Cor. 15, 22. Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur: Ita in CHRISTO (vox autem CHRISTI utramque naturam notat) omnes vivificabuntur. Apoc. 1, 18. Ego sum primus & novissimus, & vivus: & FVI MORTUUS & ecce sum vivens, in secula seculorum, & habeo claves mortis & inferni.

Quod Minorem, fallit ea Sophismate παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Vera enim ea est, hoc sensu, quòd caro Christi mortua, in vitam sit revocata, eâ virtute, quæ soli Deitati propria est: carni autem ex unione cum λόγῳ verè communicata est. Falsissima verò est, si sic ea accipiatur, quòd virtus illa vivifica, quâ caro Christi in vitam revocata est, ita sit propria Divinitati λόγꙋ, ut caro hæc in ejus κοινωνίαν, per & propter Unionem nunquam pervenerit. Diversum enim hactenus ex Scripturis liquidò demonstravimus. Et sanè quoad resuscitationem carnis Christi: Etsi caro hæc, propter interventum profundissimæ Exinanitionis, seipsum non suscitavit: tamen non propterea totam Humanam Naturam ab opere hoc removere fas fuerit. Nam 1. λόγꙋ suscitavit carnem ex mortuis ea virtute atque potentia, quam, caro Christi realiter sibi communicatam habebat quidem: sed tamen ratione usus, non exercebat.

Deinde Anima Christi, ad sui corporis vivificationem, utique vi communicatæ virtutis vivificæ concurrit: secundum illud Joh. 2, 19. Destruite templum hoc (corpus suum intelligens) & ego triduo illud excitabo. Joh. 10, 18. Ego habeo potestatem non modò ponendi, sed & resumendi animam meam. Neque assertioni huic obstat, quod Rom. 6, 4. & Eph. 1. Christus dicitur excitatus à mortuis per gloriam Patris. Nam secundum regulam Augustini: Opera Trinitatis ad extra sunt indivisa. Resurrexit Ergò Christus à mortuis, partim virtute communi toti Trinitati, partim verò virtute propria.

SEXTUM ex Scripturis depromsit Oecolampadius: Scriptum est, Joh 6, 63. Caro non prodest quicquam: Spiritus est, qui vivificat, Ergò caro Christi non est vivifica.

Respondeo cum Beza, qui hac in parte à suis gregalibus differint, Epist. 5. Si simpliciter & sine distinctione verba hæc Christi, de carne ipsius intelligas, convelleris ipsius Christi testimonio, qui carnis suæ perceptionem, toties hoc ipso capite sexto inculcat: Et cur obsecro inutilem carnem Filius Dei affumsit? quæ tamen data est pro mundi vita. Joh. 6, 51.

Quare, ut rectè colligit B. Lutherus noster, non suam carnem intelligit Christus: Sed sensum illum & cogitationes Capernaitarum carnales, quas de crassa & carnali manducatione carnis Christi conceperant. Sic per Spiritum, non divinitatem suam, sed spiritualem verborum suorum sensum, sive intellectum notat Servator. Et profectò, si hæc licentia Adversarijs permittatur, ut, ubi caro absolutè in scripturis posita reperiatur, statim ad carnem Christi collectionem instituant, Quid obstabit, quô minus tandem cum Valentinianis & Manichæis, ne veram quidem carnem ac Sangvinem humanæ Naturæ à Christo assumpta esse asserant? Cujus farinæ, inquit Lutherus, est illud, quod Zvvinglius scribit: Si CHRISTI caro manducatur, in carnem eam converti necesse est: Quicquid enim ex carne natum est, caro est. Increpet te DOMINUS, Satan.

Vide plures objectiones, earumque refutationem part. 1. Apolog. in lib. Concordiæ: pag. 9. b. usq; ad pag. 18.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: VI. a constructive Argument, taken from the worship of Adoration

VI. A constructive ARGUMENT, taken from the worship of Adoration.

It is placed beyond controversy that the worship of religious Adoration is an idiom properly belonging to the Divinity.

But this very worship belongs to Christ, not only as he is GOD, but also as he is man.

That therefore not only finite and created gifts, but truly divine ἀξιώματα (dignities) really accrued to Christ according to his human Nature, from the union with the λόγῳ (Word), is an infallible consequence.

The assumption, since it contains the τὸ κρινόμενον (matter in judgment), I wish to confirm with firm and immovable arguments.

The FIRST is taken from the authority of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which assert that the worship of Adoration ought to be paid to the Messiah who was to be born, both by men and by Angels: as Ps. 72, 11. All kings shall adore him: All nations shall serve him: And Ps. 97, 8. Adore him all ye Angels: which the Epistle to the Hebrews ch. 1, 6 accommodates to Christ even according to his assumed humanity. Isaiah 45, 23. Every knee shall bow to me: Which the Apostle explains concerning the Son of Man, Phil. 2, 10. Daniel 7, 14. To the Son of MAN such power is given, that all nations, peoples, tribes, and tongues may serve him.

The SECOND argument is shown by the Scripture of the New Testament, in which at the beginning that Apostolic Aphorism offers itself, Phil. 2, 10. Therefore the Father exalted him (namely Christ humbled) to the highest sublimity, and gave him a name which is above every name, that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. Moreover, many things prove that this Aphorism cannot be understood concerning Christ according to his divinity: For 1. This exaltation accrued to Christ according to that nature according to which he had previously humbled himself even unto death. 2. The same is confirmed by the Greek word ἐχαρίσατο. He gave, or gave out of Grace. For it would have been heretical to establish that an Adorable name could be given or granted out of grace to the Divinity of Christ only in time and as if in reward for his preceding humiliation. Finally, the Name Jesus, in which every knee is to be bowed, is a name not of the divine Nature alone: but of the whole person.

The THIRD argument of proof is supplied by the Examples of those who, in the Evangelical history, adored CHRIST, even as he is Man: and religiously bowed their knees before the Humanity of Christ: as: Matt. 2, 11. The Magi from the East falling on their knees adored the Child Jesus. Matt. 17, 14. The father of the Lunatic falls at the feet of Christ, and directs his prayers even to his humanity. John 9, 38. The man born blind falling down adores Christ. What of the fact that in express words they said to Christ, even as he is the Son of David, and the Son of Man, and also as he is that Lamb that was slain: As: Matt. 20, 30. and Luke 18, 38. The blind man cries out: Jesus SON OF DAVID have mercy on me. Matt. 15, 22. The Canaanite woman: Have mercy on me O Lord, SON OF DAVID. Matt. 21, 19. The citizens of Jerusalem sing Hosanna to the Son of David. Luke 17, 13. The ten Lepers: Jesus MASTER have mercy on us. Acts 7, 56. and 59. Stephen the protomartyr commends his Spirit to the Son of MAN, whom he saw standing at the right hand of GOD. Apocal. 5, 12. and following. Worthy is the LAMB, who was SLAIN, to receive power and glory etc. I heard all saying, to him who sits on the Throne, and to the LAMB, be blessing and honor.

The fourth argument of proof, and indeed by far the most evident, is supplied by the very union of the two Natures in Christ. For because the flesh of Christ constitutes one person with the λόγῳ: certainly this whole person ought also to be worshipped with one Adoration, unless you wish to tear the divinity, the λόγον, away from the assumed Humanity, and invoke it separately: which would be a Nestorian βδέλυγμα.

The fifth argument results from the consideration of the Office of Mediation or Redemption, which Christ executed according to both Natures: as was demonstrated above in the second Genus of the Communication of Idioms. Hence it is permitted to argue thus.

The Mediator between GOD and Men is to be invoked. But Christ is the Mediator between GOD and Men, not only as GOD, but also as Man. Therefore Christ is also to be invoked, not only as GOD, but also as Man.

The major premise is firm in itself: Since he is to be invoked from whom our life, Redemption, and Salvation uniquely depend: and in whom we believe according to that of the Apostle, Rom. 10, 14. How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? The Apostle confirms the minor premise 1 Tim. 2, 5. There is one GOD: One Mediator of GOD and men, the MAN Jesus Christ. He confirms it with the Epistle to the Hebrews, asserting that Christ is our High Priest, according to that nature also, according to which he was tempted: Heb. 2, 18. 4, 15. Finally, the Savior himself confirms it, asserting that his flesh also truly gives us life, John 6, 53. and following.

The SIXTH and final argument is provided by the unanimous consensus of Orthodox Antiquity: and especially Canon VIII of the Council of Ephesus: If anyone dares to say that the Man who was assumed is to be co-worshipped with the GOD Word, and co-glorified, and co-called GOD, as one with another: (For the syllable CON, added above, forces one to understand this) and does not rather worship Immanuel with one supplication, and pay him one glorification, according to that the Word was made flesh, let him be Anathema.

Athanas. Orat. 5. against the Arians: Those who do not wish to worship the λόγον made flesh show themselves ungrateful to his Humanity. But those who tear the λόγον away from his flesh believe in no redemption of sin or destruction of death at all. For where, I ask, will these wicked men find that flesh separately by itself, which our Savior Jesus Christ assumed: so that they dare to say: We do not worship the Lord with the flesh: but we separate the body, and serve the Lord alone with worship.

Cyril Dial. 6. Every knee is bent to him: But he received this according to his Humanity.

Chrysost. Homil. 24. on 1 Cor. 10. This body of Christ lying in the manger, the Magi worshipped: And the Barbarians coming from afar, with fear and much trembling προσεκύνησαν worshipped.

The same, above on chapter 2 of Hebrews. Truly it is great and admirable, and full of astonishment, that our FLESH sits on high, and is worshipped by Angels and Archangels, by Cherubim and Seraphim. Often revolving this in my mind, I suffer an excess, and meditate on the greater part of the human race.

These things having been thus settled, we most firmly conclude that Christ, whole according to both natures, is most rightly established as the object of religious adoration: not indeed that this worship can or ought to be paid to the Human nature of Christ by itself, in itself, and without respect to the Union, much less separately, or abstracted from the Divinity by the λόγῳ: but always considered in the Union.

But this part of Christian Doctrine is also so constituted that it must necessarily suffer sharp contradiction from the Calvinists: although some are found to depart into clearly different opinions:

For some, a little more timid, indeed profess in express words that they grant religious adoration to the flesh of Christ: but not because of a real κοινωνίαν of divine Majesty: but only by and because of the grace of the Union.

But others, among whom Lambertus Danaeus easily holds the first place, expressly write and contend that the Worship of adoration must be directed ONLY to the divine nature of Christ in such a way that, although he who united the flesh to himself is worshipped: yet the Flesh itself cannot be the object of Adoration: nor can or ought this Adoration be referred to it, however much it is united to the λόγῳ and remains in this union, through a real κοινωνίαν of that honor. Danaeus in Exam. Chemnit. p. 415. and following.

But both opinions are found to be in many ways impious and blasphemous.

And those former ones indeed slay themselves with the foul sword of contradiction. For if religious Adoration does not pertain to the flesh of Christ because of a real κοινωνίαν of divine Majesty: it will not pertain to the same either, by or because of the grace of the Union.

The reason for the consequence is this. 1. The cult of adoration belongs properly to the divine Majesty alone: so entirely, that whatever is adorable must be endowed with divine Majesty: and conversely: whatever is not endowed with divine Majesty, that neither is nor can be called adorable. Now, according to the opinion of these men, the divine Majesty does not really belong to the assumed flesh. Therefore, neither can the cult of adoration pertain to it: according to their own opinion: however much they may dare to deny this in words.

2. Reason: Whatever is adorable must be omnipotent and omniscient: that is, it must be both able to help, and it is necessary that it have the prayers, sighs, and groans of hearts, even the most hidden, known and perceived. And yet these very Calvinists deny this majesty of divine omniscience to the flesh of Christ. With what face, therefore, do they dare to affirm that the cult of religious adoration belongs to the flesh of Christ.

These latter are manifestly blasphemous, and they can, nay must, be most solidly refuted by those arguments with which we asserted our doctrine a little while ago, invincibly. On this occasion, it pleases me to beat back their blasphemy with a single, and sufficiently illustrious, example. John 9:36. Christ asks that man born blind, but now healed, whether he believes in the Son of God? There the blind man immediately replies, Who, I pray, Lord, is that Son of God, that I may believe in him? Then the Savior: He is the one whom you have seen, and who speaks with you. Thereupon the blind man immediately says: I believe, Lord, and falling down he worshipped him.

Let them now explain to us, what was that object in which that blind man both believed, and which he worshipped.

If they should answer that it was Christ, but according to his Divinity alone: then the text most manifestly refutes them, showing that the blind man believed in him, and also worshipped him, whom he saw, and with whom he spoke: so that even from this it can be most invincibly gathered that the object of faith and invocation is the Son of God, not only according to the invisible divine Nature: but also according to that Nature, which could be seen, heard, and touched before the eyes: namely, according to the Human Nature.

Latin:

VI. ARGUMENTUM κατασκευασικὸν, à cultu Adorationis petitum.

EXtra controversiam est positum, cultum religiosæ Adorationis, esse idioma Divinitati propriè competens.

Atqui hic ipse cultus competit Christo, non tantùm quâ DEUS, sed & quâ homo est.

Quin igitur non finita tantùm & creata dona, sed verè divina ἀξιώματα Christo secundum humanam Naturam, ex unione cum λόγῳ realiter obtigerint, infallibile est consequens.

Assumtionem, quippè quæ τὸ κρινόμενον continet, firmis & immotis argumentis confirmare libet.

PRIMUM desumitur ab autoritate Scripturarum Vet. Test. quæ Messiæ nascituro, cultum Adorationis, tùm ab hominibus, tùm ab Angelis dependi debere, asserunt: ut Psal. 72, 11. Adorabunt eum omnes reges: Omnes gentes servient ei: Et Ps. 97, 8. Adorate eum omnes Angeli: id quod ad Christum etiam secundum assumtam humanitatem accommodat Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 1, 6. Esaiæ 45, 23. Mihi curvabitur omne genu: Quod de Filio Hominis explicat Apostolus Phil. 2, 10. Daniel. 7, 14. Filio HOMINIS data est talis potestas, ut omnes gentes, populi, tribus, linguæ serviant ipsi.

SECUNDUM argumentum monstratScriptura Novi Testamenti, in quo initiò sese offert Aphorismus ille Apostolicus, Phil. 2, 10. Propterea exaltavit eum pater (nempè Christum humiliatum) in summam sublimitatem, & donavit ipsi nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu se flecteret omne genu cælestium, terrestrium & inferorum. Cæterùm Aphorismum istum, non posse de Christo secundum divinitatem intelligi, plurima evincunt: Nam 1. Exaltatio hæc obtigit Christo secundum eam naturam, secundùm quam priùs sefe humiliaverat usque ad mortem. 2. Idem confirmat vox Græca ἐχαρίσατο. Donavit, vel ex Gratia dedit Divinitati enim Christi in tempore demùm & quasi in premium antegressæ humiliationis, donari aut ex gratia dari potuisse nomen Adorabile, [hæreticum fuerit statuere]. Tandem Nomen Jesus, in quo omne genu flectendum, est nomen non solius Naturæ divinæ: sed totius personæ.

TERTIUM probationis argumentum subministrant Exempla eorum, qui in historia Evangelica, CHRISTUM, etiam quâ Homo est, adorarunt:& coram Humanitate Christi genua religiosè flexerunt: ut: Matth. 2, 11. Magi ex Oriente procidentes in genua adoraverunt Puerum Jesum. Matth. 17, 14. Pater Lunatici procumbit ad pedes Christi, suasq; preces ad ipsius etiam humanitatem dirigit. Joh. 9, 38. Cæcus natus procidens adorat Christum. Quid quòd disertis verbis ad Christum, etiam quâ Filius Davidis, & Filius Hominis, item quâ Agnus ille occisus est, dixerunt: Ut: Matth. 20, 30. & Luc. 18, 38. Clamat cæcus: Jesu FILI DAVID miserere mei. Matth. 15, 22. Mulier Cananæa: Miserere mei Domine, FILI DAVID. Matth. 21, 19. Hosianna Filio David concinunt cives Hierosolymitani. Luc. 17, 13. Decem Leprosi: Jesu PRÆCEPTOR miserere nostri. Actor. 7, 56. & 59. Stephanus protomartyr commendat Spiritum suum Filio HOMINIS, quem vidit stantem à dextris DEI. Apocal. 5, 12. & seqq. Dignus est AGNUS, qui OCCISUS est, accipere virtutem & gloriam &c. Audivi omnes dicentes, sedenti in Throno, & AGNO, sit benedictio & honor.

QUARTUM probationis argumentum, & quidem longè evidentissimum suppeditat ipsa unio duarum Naturarum in Christo. Quia enim caro Christi cum λόγῳ unam personam constituit: utiq; una etiam Adoratione tota hæc persona coli debet, nisi divinitatem, λόγον ab Humanitate assumta divellere, & seorsim invocare velis: id quod Nestorianum foret βδέλυγμα.

QUINTUM argumentum resultat ex consideratione Officii Mediationis sive Redemptionis, quod Christus secundum utramq; Naturam executus est: uti supra in secundo Genere Communicationis Idiomatum, demonstratum fuit. Hinc sic argumentari licet.

Mediator inter DEUM & Homines est Invocandus. Atqui Christus est Mediator inter DEUM & Homines, non tantùm quà DEUS, sed & quâ Homo. Ergò Christus etiam non tantùm quâ DEUS, sed & quâ Homo, est invocandus.

Major per se firma est: Siquidem invocandus est is, à quo vita, Redemptio & Salus nostra unicè dependet: & in quem credimus, juxtà illud Apostoli, Rom. 10, 14. Quomodo invocabunt, in quem non crediderunt? Minorem confirmat Apostolus 1. Tim. 2, 5. Unus est DEUS: Unus est Mediator DEI & hominum HOMO Jesus Christus. Confirmat Epistola ad Hebræos asserens, Christum esse Pontificem nostrum, secundum eam etiam naturam, secundum quam tentatus est: Hebr 2, 18. 4. 15. Confirmat denique ipse Servator, asserens suam quoque carnem nos verè vivificare Joh. 6, 53. & seqq.

SEXTUM & postremum argumentum subministrat unanimis consensus Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis: & cumprimis Canon VIII. Concilii Ephesini: Si quis audet dicere, assumtum Hominem coadorandum DEO verbo, & conglorificandum, & connuncupandum DEUM, tanquam alterum cum altero: (Nam, CON, syllaba superadjecta hæc cogit intelligi) ac non potiùs una supplicatione veneratur Immanuelem, unamque ei glorificationem dependet, juxta quod Verbum caro factum, s, Anathema sit

Athanas. Orat. 5. contra Arianos: Qui λόγον carnem factum adorare nolunt: ingratos se exhibent ejus Humanitati. Qui verò distrahunt λόγον à sua carne, nullam omninò Redemtionē peccati, aut devastationem mortis credunt. Ubi enim, quæso, nefarii isti homines seorsim per se invenient illam carnem, quam Salvator noster Jesus Christus assumsit: ut audeant dicere: Non adoramus Dominum cum carne: sed disjungimus corpus, & soli Domino cultu inservimus.

Cyrilli Dial. 6. Curvatur ei omne genu: Accepit autem hoc secundum Humanitatem.

Chrysost. Homil. 24. in 1. Cor. 10. Hoc corpus Christi in præsepi jacens, Magi venerati sunt: Et à longè venientes Barbari, cum timore & tremore multo προσεκύνησαν adoraverunt.

Idem supra cap. 2. Hebr. Revera magnum est & admirabile, & stupore plenum, CARNEM nostram sursum sedere, & adorari ab Angelis & Archangelis, à Cherubin & Seraphin. Hoc sapè in mente mecum versans excessum patior, & majore de genere humano meditor.

His ita expeditis, firmissimè concludimus, Christum totum secundum utramque naturā, religiosæ adorationis objectum rectissimè constitui: non quidem quòd Humanæ Christi naturæ per se, in se, & sine respectu Unionis, multò minùs seorsim possit, aut à Divinitate τῶ λόγω abstractæ: sed semper in Unione consideratæ, cultus iste dependi possit aut debeat.

Est verò hæc etiam Doctrinæ Christianæ pars ita comparata, ut à Calvinianis acrem contradictionem pati necesse habeat: quanquàm nonnulli in diversas planè sententias abire deprehendantur:

Quidam enim paulò timidiores, disertis verbis quidem profitentur, se religiosam adorationem concedere carni Christi: verùm non propter realem divinæ Majestatis κοινωνίαν: sed tantùm per & propter Unionis gratiam.

Alii verò, inter quos Lambertus Danaeus primas facilè obtinet, expressè scribunt & contendunt, Cultum adorationis ita SOLUM ad divinam Christi naturam dirigendum esse, ut licet adoretur is, qui carnem sibi univit : Caro ipsa tamen Adorationis objectum esse nequeat : neque ad eam, quantumvis unitam λόγῳ & in unione hac manentem, Adoratio haec per realem honoris istius κοινωνίαν referri possit aut debeat. Danaeus in Exam. Chemnit. p. 415. & seqq.

Verùm utrumque sententia multis modis impia & blasphema deprehenditur.

Et priores quidem illi semetipsos turpi contradictionis gladio jugulant. Si enim ad carnem Christi religiosa Adoratio non pertinet, propter realem Majestatis divinae κοινωνίαν: neque ad eandem etiam pertinebit, per aut propter Unionis gratiam.

Ratio Consequentiae est haec. 1. Cultus Adorationis non nisi Soli divinae Majestati propriè competit: ita in solidum, ut quicquid adorabile est, illud divina Majestate praeditum sit oportet: & vice versa: quicquid divina Majestate non est praeditu, illud nec Adorabile sit aut dici queat. Jam ex sententia istorum, Majestas divina assumtae carni realiter non competit. Ergò neque Adorationis cultus ad eam pertinere potest: ex eorundem opinione: quantumvis etiam verbis id negare ausint.

2. Ratio: Quicquid Adorabile est, illud omnipotens & omnifcium sit oportet: hoc est, & juvare potens sit, & preces, suspiria & gemitus cordium etiam abstrusissimos, cognitos, perspectosque habeat, necesse est. Atqui hi ipsi Calviniani Majestatem hanc divinae Omniscientiae carni Christi derogant. Qua ergò fronte affirmare audent, carni Christi competere cultum Adoratione religiosa.

Posteriores hi manifestè sunt blasphemi, & argumentis illis, quibus nostram doctrinam paulò antè, invictè asseruimus, solidissimè refutari possunt, imò debent. Hac vice, unico, eoque satis illustri exemplo istorum blasphemiam retundere placet. Johannis 9, 36. Christus quaerit ex caeco illo nato, sed jam sanato, Num credat in Filium DEI? ibi statim excipit Caecus, Quis quaeso Domine est ille Filius DEI, ut credam in eum? Tum Servator: Ille est, quem VIDISTI, & QUI LOQUITUR TECUM. Ibi statim Caecus: Credo, inquit, DOMINE, & procidens adoravit eum.

Edisserant jam nobis, Quodnam fuerit objectum illud, in quod caecus iste & crediderit, & quod adoraverit.

Si respondeat, CHRISTUM fuisse, sed secundum solam Divinitatem: tùm textus manifestissimè ipsum redarguit, ostendens in illum credidisse caecum, eum etiam adorasse, Quem VIDIT, & cum QUO LOCUTUS est: ita ut vel indè invictissimè colligi possit, Objectum fidei & invocationis, esse Filium DEI, non tantùm secundum invisibilem divinam Naturam: sed & secundum eam Naturam, quæ coràm oculis videri, audiri, & palpari poterat: nimirùm secundum Humanam Naturam.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: VII. And the final constructive argument taken from the communicated Majesty of Omnipresence

VII. And the final constructive argument taken from the communicated Majesty of Omnipresence.

It is placed beyond controversy that Omnipresence is not to be referred to the class of finite or created gifts, but to the Idioms proper to the Divine Majesty: according to that word of Jer. 23:23 & 24. Do I not fill heaven and earth, says JEHOVAH. And Isa. 66:1. Thus says JEHOVAH, heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. But that this very Majesty of Omnipresence has been truly and really communicated to the flesh of Christ, both Holy Scripture most evidently asserts, and the Orthodox Church has always believed. Therefore, from this it is most clearly evident that not finite or created gifts, however sublime, but the very divine Majesty of the Word has been truly and really communicated to the flesh of Christ from the Union with the Word. We demonstrate the minor premise, which is the stake in the eyes of those who Calvinize either in whole or in part, by the following arguments, invincibly.

THE FIRST ARGUMENT taken from the Union itself is as follows:

Whatever is assumed not into some place, but into the very illocal hypostasis of the Word, to which no intervals of places can reach at all: nay, in which every thought of all places utterly expires: that thing is by this very assumption lifted above all locality. But the flesh of Christ, through the Union with the Word, has been assumed into, nay, within the illocal hypostasis of the Word. Therefore, it is necessary that the flesh of Christ also be lifted above all locality. The connection of the major premise is infallibly clear: 1. Because this Union was made from two natures inseparably: but now the Natures would certainly be separated if one were established to be in a certain place, and the other to be everywhere present. 2. Because these two Natures are united in Christ, not only inseparably, but also indivisibly: that is: Because the Word is and is called wholly incarnate, not insofar as He sustains the humanity existing in this or that place, as the Adversaries dream: but insofar as He assumes it within Himself: and without any interval, above all locality whatsoever, by an intimate and most secret Union of this or the other age, He has it most present to Himself everywhere, existing nowhere outside of it, nowhere distant from it, nowhere separated by any interval, whether of place or of any other thing, so that one Nature of this person cannot be Omnipresent, while the other is present in only one place. For thus the non-conjunction of the Natures would necessarily follow. Finally: If the flesh of Christ were not Omnipresent with the Word, it would follow that the Word is a Man somewhere, namely there where He has the flesh present to Himself: but that He is not a Man somewhere else, but is present in the remaining places only according to His divine Nature, where He does not have the flesh present to Himself.

One would hardly deny the minor premise, unless he dared to affirm: 1. That the Human Nature is not personally united with the Word: 2. That the same nature has its existence elsewhere than in the sole illocal hypostasis of the Word. Both of which would be prodigiously absurd, nay, extremely impious.

Therefore, the conclusion will also have its unmoved certainty and truth: namely, that the flesh of CHRIST is most present everywhere to the Word who assumes it. Furthermore, that this very Omnipresence may be vindicated, right at the threshold of this disputation, from those crass thoughts and absurdities which might come into anyone's mind, two hypotheses will be especially needed.

I. The Human nature of Christ has been made a real participant in the Majesty of Omnipresence, without any expansion of itself. The reason is: Because expansion only follows the condition of Locality: since the flesh of Christ is free from this, it certainly cannot be subject to expansion. That this may be explained and understood more skillfully, it must be held: that created things are not present to GOD according to the spaces of places, as they are distinguished in these lands by their intervals and distances. For hence an Expansive Omnipresence would have to be established in GOD Himself. But thus, both all things are present to GOD, and GOD Himself is most present to all things: insofar as He, transcending and surpassing all places by His infinite divine Majesty, has and beholds all things as most present to Himself, outside and above the nature of place, in a manner clearly hyperphysical and divine: So that before GOD there is no greater breadth of the whole world than of a single palm or finger. Now therefore, since the flesh of Christ has been assumed within that most infinite hypostasis of the eternal Word: it will certainly be present to all creatures, not through any locality, or diffusion from one place into another, from a second place into a third, from a third into a fourth, and so on: but in that divine manner which transcends every place: so that there is no need for it to be extended from one place into another: because in this hypostasis of the Word, in which this flesh solely subsists, and outside of which it cannot even be thought of: no place or locality reigns: but rather all places relate themselves to the infinite hypostasis of the Word as a most minute point. With these things thus observed, that fiction about crass ubiquity, by reason of which the flesh of Christ is in all pears, apples, cheeses, beer glasses, etc., falls of its own accord, and vanishes like the lightest smoke.

II. Hypothesis: Every Nature in Christ, as much Divine as Human, even in the Union itself, obtains a twofold respect: one NATURAL, the other PERSONAL. Thus the λόγος according to the natural respect can be considered even in the Union itself: as when it is said to be begotten from the Father from eternity: Likewise, with the same eternal Father, to breathe forth one Spirit, ὁμούσιον καὶ συναῖδιον to Himself and the Father. For these things belong to the λόγος not by respect of the union, but by respect of eternal existence in the Divinity. Furthermore, the same λόγος is considered according to the personal respect, when it is attended to that He constitutes one ἑφιςάμενον with the assumed humanity: that He has appropriated to Himself the same Human Nature, with all actions and passions κατ᾽ ἰδιοποίιαν, as Cyril speaks.

Regarding the Human Nature, about which there is the greatest controversy, it likewise can be considered in the Union itself, first indeed, according to the natural respect: when it is attended to what it can do and has in itself, and from the property of its Nature: By which respect Christ is said to have been made like us, His brothers. Then, however, the PERSONAL respect of the same Human Nature is instituted when it is no longer weighed what it is distinctly and by itself, even if in the Union: but what it has obtained, peculiar and plainly divine, from the Union with the λόγος.

For the diversity of these two respects, the flesh of Christ also obtains a twofold mode by which it can be somewhere. For according to the Natural respect, the flesh of Christ can be locally in some certain place, or in some πῧ: Just as in the state of Exinanition according to this mode, it truly progressed from place to place: Likewise, born in one place, suffered, crucified, died, buried. Now, however, according to the mode of glorified bodies, it is in some heavenly πῧ. And this Natural mode of being somewhere belongs to the flesh of Christ even in the Union, because it retains the properties of its Nature safe forever: But not by respect of the Union with the λόγος: For it does not have from the union that it is or can be in a certain place: but it has this from the property of its nature or Essence. Therefore, by respect of the Union with the λόγος, the flesh of Christ obtains another mode of being somewhere, namely PERSONAL, by which, existing in the ὑποςάσει of the λόγος, it is simultaneously outside and above every condition of place and locality, most present everywhere to the λόγος.

These two distinct respects are indeed not contradictorily opposed to each other, as the Calvinists maintain: but subordinately (ὑπαλλήλως) subordinated: because the causes themselves, from which these respects arise, are not contradictory: but subordinated. For if they were contradictory, then the Human nature would neither have retained its properties in the Union: or if it had retained these intact, it could not have been united with the λόγος. For which reason, neither does Local presence in one place take away the illocal ὕπαρξιν or existence outside and above every place: nor does this illocal ὕπαρξις destroy that Local condition, or stand in the way of Christ being able to subject Himself to the other conditions of this world in the state of exinanition, nay, truly subjecting Himself by most free will: so that He could be born, suffer, be crucified, and die in one place: nor finally does this illocal ὕπαρξις of the flesh of Christ in the λόγος hinder anything, so that it could not, according to the condition of human Nature, even in the state of Glory and Exaltation, appear visibly in a certain π̄̄: as was shown more fully above in chapter 1.

Some fear that the flesh of Christ might be placed outside the Union according to this Natural and Local respect: But that fear is plainly vain: For just as the divine Nature of the λόγος is not placed outside the Union, but remains in the Union, although eternal Nativity from the Father, and eternal Spiration of the Holy Spirit with the Father, are attributed to it, and indeed not by respect of the Union, but rather of its eternal existence and divinity: So also the flesh of Christ is not placed outside the Union, even if it is shown what mode and reason of existing somewhere it can have, and indeed not from the union, but yet in the union, and indeed from the property of its nature: and had in the state of Exinanition.

Similarly, just as this twofold respect of the Divinity does not make a twofold Divinity: but one and the same λόγος remains: although it is considered differently by respect of the Union, and differently without the intuition of the Union: So the Humanity or flesh of Christ does not therefore become twofold, because it is considered differently by respect of its Nature: and differently by respect of the Union with the λόγος.

The use of this second hypothesis can certainly be greatest in refuting those arguments of the Calvinists: when they repeatedly clamor: The flesh of Christ was born in one place, not everywhere: suffered, was crucified, died, buried in one place, etc. Therefore the flesh of Christ does not have from the union that it is everywhere: Or if it truly has this, then it will follow that it was born, suffered, etc., everywhere, which would be prodigiously absurd. For the consequence is most rightly denied, because arguments of this kind always proceed from the affirmation of that Natural respect of the flesh of Christ, to the negation of the same Personal existence in the ὑποστάσει of the λόγος: As if these two respects were contradictorily opposed. Therefore it must be shown that the Human nature of Christ, even when it was born and suffered, etc., in one place: was simultaneously, without any contradiction, both in a place, and in the λόγος, by those different respects which have …now been explained. In a place indeed locally from the condition of its Nature: but in the λόγος not naturally, but Personally, and in a mode of Union that is plainly divine. In the former mode, namely the natural, He was truly born, suffered, crucified, died, and buried in one place: likewise truly and not feignedly progressed from place to place: In the latter mode, outside every reason of place

Latin:

VII. Et Postremum Argumentum κατασκευασικὸν à communicata Omnipræsentia Majestate desumtum.

EXtra Controversiam est positum, Omnipræsentiam non adclassem finitorum aut creatorum donorum, sed ad Idiomata Divinæ Majestatis propria, referendam esse: secundum illud Jerem. 23, 23, & 24. Annon Cœlum & terram ego impleo, dicit JEHOVAH. Et Esa. 66, 1. Hæc dicit JEHOVAH, cœlum sedes mea, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum. Atqui hanc ipsam Omnipræsentia Majestatem carni Christi, verè ac realiter communicatam esse, tùm Scriptura Sacra evidentissimè adstruit, tùm Ecclesia Orthodoxa semper credidit. Ergò hinc vel liquidissimè constat, carni Christi ex Unione cum λογῳ non finita aut creata dona, quantumvis sublimia, sed ipsàm divinam τꭢ λόγꭢ Majestatem verè ac realiter communicatam esse. Minorem, quæ sudes est in oculis eorum qui vel ex toto, vel ex parte Calvinizant, omnium, sequentibus argumentis invictè demonstramus.

PRIMUM ARGUMENtum ab ipsa Unione petitum, tale est:

QUicquid non in locum aliquem, sed in ipsam illocalem ὑπόςασιν λόγꭢ, ad quam nulla prorsus locorum διαςηματα pertingere possunt: imò in qua omnis cogitatio locorum omnium penitùs expirat, est assumtum: illud hac ipsa assumtione evectum est supra omnem localitatem. Atqui caro Christi per Unionem cum λόγῳ assumta est in, imò intra illocalem ὑπόςασιν λόγꭢ. Ergò caro etiam Christi supra omnem localitatem evecta sit, necesse est. Majoris connexum infallibiliter patet: 1. Quia Unio hæc facta est ex duabus naturis inseparabiliter: Jam autem separarentur utique Naturæ, si una statueretur esse in certo loco, altera ubique præsens. 2. Quia Naturæ hæ duæ unitæ sunt in Christo, non modò inseparabiliter, sed & ἀδιαςάτως indistranter: hoc est: Quia Λόγος est & dicitur totus incarnatus, non, quatenus humanitatem in hoc vel illo loco existentem sustentat, uti Adversarii somniant: sed quatenus eam intra se assumit: & citra omnem διάςασιν, supra omnem omninò localitatem, vel hujus vel alterius seculi intima secretissimaque Unione, sibi ubique præsentissimam habet, extra eam nullibi existēs, nullibi ab ea distans, nullibi per ullum διάςημα, sive loci, sive ullius alterius rei sejunctus, utiq; non potest una hujus personæ Natura esse Omnipræsens, altera verò in uno tantùm loco præsens, Sic enim Naturarum Ἀζευξις necessariò sequeretur. Tandem: Si caro Christi non esset cum λόγῳ Omnipræsens, sequeretur, λόγον alicubi esse Hominem, ibi nimirùm, ubi sibi præsentem habet carnem: alicubi autem non esse Hominem, sed secundum solam divinam Naturam in reliquis locis adesse, ubi carnem sibi non habet præsentem.

Minorem vix negaverit, nisi qui affirmare ausit. Humanam Naturam cum λόγῳ non esse unitam personaliter : 2. Eandem naturam alibi habere suam existentiam, quàm in sola illocali ὑποστάσει τοῦ λόγου. Quod utrumque prodigiosè absurdum, imò extremè impium fuerit.

Constabit proindè conclusioni sua etiam immota certitudo & veritas: nempè, carnem CHRISTI assumenti λόγῳ, ubique locorum esse præsentissimam. Cæterùm hæc ipsa Omnipræsentia mox in limine disputationis hujus, à crassis illis cogitationibus & absurditatibus, quæ in mentem alicui venire queant, vendicetur, duabus potissimùm hypothesibus opus fuerit.

I. Humana natura Christi realiter particeps est facta Majestatis Omnipræsentiæ, citra omnem sui expansionem. Ratio est: Quia expansio tantùm sequitur Localitatis conditionem: à quâ cum caro Christi sit libera, utique nec expansioni subjacere poterit, Quod ut dexterius explicetur & intelligâtur, tenendum; res creatas DEO non esse præsentes, secundum locorum spacia, prout ea hisce in terris, suis ἀδιαστήμασιν ac intervallis sunt distincta. Hinc enim in ipso DEO Expansiva Omnipræsentia statuenda esset. Verùm sic tùm res omnes DEO siunt præsentes, tùm DEUS ipse rebus omnibus adest præsentissimus: quatenus ipse infinitâ suâ Majestate divinâ omnia loca transcendens ac supergrediens, omnia sibi habet & intuetur præsentissima, extrà & supra loci rationem, modo planè hyperphysico & divino: Ita ut coram DEO haud major sit latitudo totius orbis terrarum, quàm vel unius palmæ aut digiti. Jam ergò cùm caro Christi, intra illam æterni λόγου infinitissimam ὑπόστασιν assumta sit : utique non per localitatem aliquam, aut diffusionem de loco uno in alterum, de loco secundo in tertium, de tertio in quartum, & sic deinceps, omnibus creaturis erit præsens : sed divino illo modo, qui locum omnem transcendit: ut ei opus non sit, de uno loco extendi in alium: proptereà quòd in hac ὑποστάσει τοῦ λόγου, in qua caro hæc unicè subsistit, & extra quam ne cogitari quidem potest: nullus vel locus vel localitas regnat: sed potiùs loca ad unum omnia habent sese ad infinitam τοῦ λόγου ὑπόστασιν, veluti punctulum minutissimum. Quibus ita observatis, commentum illud de crassa ubiquitate, ratione cujus caro Christi, sit in omnibus pyris, pomis, caseis, vitris cerevisiariis &c. sponte sua corruit, & ceu levissimus fumus evanescit.

II. Hypothesis: Quælibet Natura in Christo, tam Divina, quàm Humana, in ipsa etiam Unione, duplicem obtinet respectum: Unum NATURALEM, alterum PERSONALEM. Sic λόγῶ̅ secundum naturalem respectum in ipsa etiam Unione considerari potest: ut cùm dicitur, ab æterno gigni à Patre: Item cum eodem æterno Patre, spirare unum Spiritum, sibi Patrique ὁμούσιον καὶ συναῖδιον. Hæc enim λόγῳ competunt non respectu unionis: sed respectu æternæ existentiæ in Divinitate. Porrò idem λόγο̅ς̃ secundum respectum personalem consideratur, quando attenditur, quod ille unum ἑφιςάμενον cum assumta humanitate constituat: quod eandem Naturam Humanam, cum omnibus actionibus & passionibus κατ᾽ ἰδιοποίιαν, ut Cyrillus loquitur, sibi appropriaverit.

Quoad Hamanam Naturam, de qua potissimùm controvertitur, ea itidem in ipsa Unione considerari potest, primùm quidem, secundum respectum naturalem: quando attenditur, quid ea in se, & ex Naturæ suæ proprietate possit & habeat: Quo respectu nobis fratribus suis similis factus esse Christus dicitur. Deindè verò PERSONALIS ejusdem Humanæ Naturæ respectus instituitur tùm, quando non amplius expenditur, quid ea distinctè & per se, licet in Unione: sed quid ex Unione cum λόγῳ, peculiare, planequè divinum sit sortita.

Pro diversitate duorum istorum respectuum, caro Christi geminum etiam obtinet modum, quo alicubi esse possit. Nam secundum Naturalem respectum potest caro Christi localiter in loco aliquo certo, vel in aliquo πῧ esse: Quemadmodum in statu Exinanitionis secundum hunc modum, verè de loco in locum est progressa: Item, uno in loco nata, passa, crufixa, mortua, sepulta. Jam verò secundum modum corporum clarificatorum est in cœlesti aliquo πῧ. Et competit iste modus Naturalis alicubi essendi, carni Christi etiam in Unione, quia proprietates Naturæ suæ retinet salvas in perpetuum: Sed non respectu Unionis cum λόγῳ: Nam ex unione non habet, ut sit vel possit esse in certo quodam loco: sed habet hoc ex naturæ sive Essentiæ suæ proprietate. Proindè respectu Unionis cum λόγῳ alium sortitur modum caro Christi essendi alicubi, nempè PERSONALEM, quo in ὑποςάσει τῶ̅ λόγῳ existens, simul extra & supra omnem loci & localitatis conditionem, ubique τῷ λόγῳ adest præsentissima.

Sunt verò duo isti distincti respectus, non contradictoriè sibi oppositi, uti Calviniani autumant: sed ὑπαλλήλως subordinati: propterea quod ipsæ quoque causæ, ex quibus respectus isti oriuntur, non sunt contradictoriæ: sed subordinatæ. Contradictoriæ enim si essent, tùm Humana natura, neque in Unione suas retinuisset proprietates: vel si has retinuisset integras, cum λόγῳ uniri non potuisset. Qua de causa, neque Localis etiam præsentia in uno loco, tollit illocalem ὕπαρξιν sive existentiam extra & supra omnem locum: neque illocalis hæc ὕπαρξις destruit Localem illam conditionem, vel obstat, quin cæteris etiam mundi hujus conditionibus Christus instatu exinanitionis, sese subjicere potuerit, imò liberrima volūtate revera subjecerit: ita ut uno in loco nasci, pati, crucifigi, mori posset: neque tandem hæc illocalis ὕπαρξις carnis Christi in λόγῳ quicquam impedit, quô minus secundum Naturæ humanæ conditionem, etiam in statu Gloriæ & Exaltationis, in certo quodam π̄̄ visibiliter apparere possit: uti fusius supra cap. 1. ostensum.

Metuunt nonnulli, ut non secundum Naturalem istum & Localem respectum collocetur caro Christi extra Unionem: Sed vanus planè est metus iste: Quemadmodum enim divina Natura τῦ λόγᾳ, non extra Unionem collocatur, sed in Unione manet, licet ei æterna Nativitas à Patre, & æterna Spiratio Spiritus Sancti cum Patre, tribuatur, & quidem non Unionis, sed potiùs æternæ suæ existentiæ & divinitatis respectu: Ita caro etiam Christi non ponitur extra Unionem, sive maximè ostendatur, qualem existendi alicubi modum & rationem, & quidem non ex unione, sed tamen in unione, & quidem ex proprietate suæ naturæ habere possit: & in statu Exinanitionis habuerit.

Consimiliter, quemadmodum geminus iste respectus Divinitatis, non geminam efficit Divinitatem: sed unus idemque manet λόγος: licèt aliter consideretur respectu Unionis, aliter citra Unionis intuitum: Ita Humanitas etiam sive caro Christi non ideò evadit gemina, quia aliter consideratur respectu Naturæ suæ: aliter respectu Unionis cum λόγῳ.

Secundæ hujus hypothesews usus certè maximus esse potest in refutandis illis argumentis Calvinianorum: quando subindè obstrepunt: Caro Christi uno in loco nata est, non ubique: uno in loco passa, crucifixa, mortua, sepulta, &c. Ergò caro Christi ex unione non habet, ut sit ubique: Vel si hoc revera habet, tùm sequetur, eam ubique natam, passam &c. id quod prodigiosè absurdum fuerit. Rectissimè enim negatur consequentia, proptereà quòd argumenta ejusmodi semper procedunt ex affirmatione Naturalis illius respectus carnis Christi, ad negationem ejusdem Personalis existentiæ ὑποστάσει λόγᾳ: Quasi verò duo isti respectus contradictoriè essent oppositi. Proindè ostendendum, Humanam Christi naturam etiam tùm, quando uno in loco nata & passa &c. est: simul sine ulla contradictione fuisse & in loco, & in λόγῳ, diversis iis respectibus, qui jam sunt explicati. In loco quidem ex Naturæ suæ conditione localiter: in λόγῳ autem non naturaliter, sed Personaliter, & modo Unionis planè divino. Priore modo, nempè naturali, uno in loco verè natus, passus, crucifixus, mortuus & sepultus est: de loco item in locum verè & non simulatè progressus: Posteriore modo, extra omnem loci rationem man-


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: VII. And the final constructive argument taken from the communicated Majesty of Omnipresence (continued)
