let it be most presentially united to the Word everywhere: although then, on account of the intervention of the most profound Self-Emptying, it was not actively applied to the governance of creatures.

To this first argument of ours, drawn from the mystery of the union, the Adversaries oppose themselves with the greatest effort: so that, if they cannot utterly overturn it, they may at least in some way weaken it.

And at the BEGINNING, indeed, they object against us the non-syllogism of four terms, if we say: that the hypostasis of the Word is illocal: but that the flesh subsists in the hypostasis of the Word. Therefore, that the flesh of Christ is illocal: whereas the argument, if it ought to conclude correctly, should be formed thus: the hypostasis of the Word is illocal: the flesh of Christ is the very hypostasis of the Word. Therefore. Where, however, the Minor proposition is immediately detected to be most false. Although, indeed, our argument proceeded in a far different form and one truly Syllogistic, so that the fallacy of four terms cannot be demonstrated: yet if it be proposed even in the highest degree according to the Calvinian form: nevertheless the conclusion will be true: Because the substance of the middle term remains the same. Since in the Minor as well as in the Major proposition one and the same Question is agitated, namely, concerning the presence of Christ: For in the Major it is asked concerning the presence of the Word: or of the hypostasis of the Word: In the Minor, however, concerning the presence of the assumed flesh, where, namely, it is and subsists from the union with the Word. Whence it is manifestly evident, without any distinction of terms, that the middle term is only slightly inflected. And if the Adversaries so greatly disapprove of this method of arguing, how does it happen that they themselves repeatedly rise up against us with the same Logic, shouting: Heaven is distant from the Sacrament of the Supper by infinite spaces, or intervals. But the flesh of Christ is in heaven. Therefore, the flesh of Christ is absent from the Sacrament of the Supper by infinite spaces or intervals.

THE OTHER argument of the Adversaries is such: If the flesh on account of the union is outside of place, because the Word himself is outside of place: then by reciprocation, and indeed on account of the same union, the Deity of the Word will be in a certain place, because the flesh itself is naturally in a place: But this latter is absurd. Therefore, the former is also.

I answer: The argument fails by the sophism of a faulty consequence: which arises from that fictitious reciprocation which the Adversaries falsely imagine for themselves in this question. For the reason is most different in both cases: which emerges from this, that in the Union the Human nature did not assume the Word INTO ITSELF, or in, or within its own hypostasis, which of itself has none: But that the Word transferred and assumed the Human nature into his own hypostasis. Wherefore, although the Word was truly made flesh: yet one may by no means imagine any translation of the Word into a local and earthly state: as if he himself, moved from the illocal state of his divinity, had submerged himself through some immigration into the Humanity and its local state.

But he was made flesh in such a way that, by assuming the Humanity into himself and his own hypostasis, he at the same time truly transferred and exalted it from the state of locality, above and outside all places. Therefore, the diversity of the Assumer and the Assumed being observed, the vanity of this argument is spontaneously revealed.

THE THIRD argument is as follows: If the flesh of Christ is therefore outside of place, because it is assumed into the illocal hypostasis of the Word: it will follow, for the same reason, that this flesh is also from eternity, is exempt from time, and thus not incarnated in time, is incorporeal, is spiritual, is devoid of composition, etc. Since such is the hypostasis of the Word: But this latter is false and absurd. Therefore, the former is also.

I answer: The argument fails by the confusion of most disparate Questions, and by the non-syllogism of four terms. For if the whole Syllogism is formed, it will become plain that the Major proposition deals with the Essence itself: what, namely, the Word is by reason of his Essence: but the Minor deals not with the Essence: but with the presence of the flesh, where it subsists, and obtains its being. For such will be the Syllogism: The hypostasis of the Word by reason of its essence is eternal, is Spirit, is devoid of all composition, is begotten of the Father from eternity. But the Human Nature is assumed into this hypostasis of the Word. Therefore, the Human Nature is also such. Where the fallacy of four terms may be detected without any effort from the distraction of the middle term. Furthermore, as regards our argument, it is manifest that in both of the premises it is dealt only with presence: and not with the Essence of the Natures itself. Therefore, as our argument concludes most correctly: So the objection of the Adversaries collapses by its own futility.

Let it be permitted to illustrate this with an example: When I argue thus: Wittenberg is the eye or light of Germany: But Peter is in Wittenberg: Therefore, Peter is the light of Germany. Here even a Boy easily detects the non-syllogism of four terms, and the confusion of two Questions, of which one deals with the Nature itself, and as it were the Essence of Wittenberg: the other with the presence of Peter. But when I argue thus: Wittenberg is outside of Leipzig. Peter is in Wittenberg. Therefore, Peter is outside of Leipzig: here the argument proceeds: Since in both of the premises it is asked concerning presence.

But they further insist: That their own certainty remains unmoved by their argument, for the reason that the Omnipresence of the Word is nothing other than his Essence itself. Therefore, the argument proceeds most correctly, since in both of the premises it is dealt with presence.

I answer: This argument also fails through the sophistication of multiple questions. For it is one thing when Omnipresence is considered in itself, as an Idiom proper to the Divine Essence: but it is another when it is weighed with respect to creatures, insofar as the λόγος is said to be present to them outside of place or locality.

In that former way I willingly grant that the Omnipresence is most simply converted with the Essence of the λόγῳ, and that it is something ταυτὸ: but in the latter way, in this respect, I simply deny it. For to be present to all creatures outside of place does not pertain to the Essence simply, but to the presence of the Essence. I prove this very thing by a twofold reason: 1. Before the creation of this Universe, GOD by His Essence was not present to any creatures outside of place, because there were none then. Therefore, to be present to creatures outside of place does not pertain to the Essence simply: For if it did pertain, then it would follow that the Essence of GOD was imperfect before the creation: Inasmuch as it was destitute of presence outside of place, with regard to creatures: which is impious and blasphemous. Furthermore, the divine presence of the Essence to creatures truly admits a variety and difference of modes and degrees: for it is present to creatures in one way by reason of general conservation: it is present in another way to believers, κατ' ἐνέργειαν τῆς χάριτος: it is present in another way to the Damned: it is present in another way to the blessed in eternal life: and finally, it is present in another way to the assumed humanity. But indeed such variety and difference does not fall into the Essence of GOD itself, inasmuch as it is simply invariable. Most rightly, therefore, a distinction is made between the Essence of the λόγῳ and the presence of the same outside of place to creatures: so that by reason of the ἐσίας or Essence, the λόγῳ is said to be what it is TO ITSELF: but by reason of presence outside of place, it is said to be present not to itself, but to others.

The Adversaries frame the FOURTH point thus: If the Hypostatic union provides that the flesh of Christ is outside of place, it will certainly also provide that it is outside of Time. But this latter point would be absurd even to think of: inasmuch as by this arrangement the flesh of Christ was neither born in time, nor suffered, was crucified, or died in time. Therefore, that former point also would be likewise absurd even to think of.

I REPLY by a distinction from that second hypothesis, which we noted a little earlier: that, namely, one must distinguish between the Natural and the Personal respect of the flesh of Christ: which are so related to each other that as soon as an inference is made from the affirmation of the personal respect to the negation of the Natural respect, or vice versa, a base Sophistry of a most vicious consequence is committed. For those two respects can stand together without any contradiction: namely, that the Human Nature, even though through the Union it was raised into the ὑπόστασιν of the λόγῳ, so as to be absolute from place: and thus it itself also was made a κοινωνὸς of this Majesty Personally: yet the λόγῳ in the state of Exinanition willed that this flesh of His, just as it was subject to the remaining infirmities and conditions of this World, so also to Time (while that Majesty meanwhile remained safe, by which in the person of the λόγῳ it subsists outside of place, and so outside of Time) and therefore it could be conceived, born, suffer, be crucified, die, etc., in time. Moreover, the Adversaries betray either stupidity or malice, because even in the state of Exaltation and sitting at the right hand of GOD they do not wish to grant to the flesh of Christ that axiom, which nevertheless the Saints and Blessed in eternal life will most really enjoy. For because in this age, Time happens to natural things only on account of that φυσικὸν motion, about which the Philosophers dispute: but in eternal life that motion will cease entirely: inasmuch as its condition is so ordered that eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what GOD has prepared for those who love Him: 1 Cor. 2, 9. Certainly in that eternal life also the Elect will be without Time. Now, since the flesh of Christ is not only assumed into eternal life, but is furthermore raised to the very right hand of divine Majesty: What, I ask, would this prodigious impiety be, to wish to subject it still to Time.

The FIFTH is such: The union of two natures in Christ is not such an immanence as is that of the three persons of the divinity: where on account of the infinity of one and the same Essence, the hypostasis of one person is always where the hypostasis of the other person is also. Therefore, from the Union with the λόγῳ it does not follow that where the ὑπόστασις of the λόγῳ is, there also is the assumed flesh: The reason for the consequence is that the flesh of Christ is not of the same infinity as the ὑπόστασις of the λόγῳ.

I REPLY: The argument fails παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχου: And that in many ways. For first, the cause and foundation of the Omnipresence of the flesh of Christ is not the Infinity of the Essence of the λόγῳ, insofar as it is considered in itself: but the sole cause is the Assumption of this flesh of Christ into this infinite ὑπόστασις of the λόγῳ. Therefore, whatever the Adversaries prattle about the Infinity of the Essence, as the foundation of Omnipresence, with regard to the assumed flesh, collapses. For because the whole ὑπόστασις of the λόγῳ, however infinite it is, is incarnate, so that it is a sin to imagine that some part of this ὑπόστασις is incarnate, and another part is not incarnate: inasmuch as it has clearly no part outside of a part: therefore the ὑπόστασις of the λόγῳ also, with this Union remaining, neither is nor can be outside of this assumed flesh: and by force of consequence, where the ὑπόστασις of the λόγῳ is, however infinite, there this assumed flesh must also be: unless one wishes to dissolve the Union. Furthermore, the Essence as well as the Person of the λόγῳ is neither infinite, nor is it said to be infinite, in the Calvinistic sense, through some infinite and immense expansion of ὀσίας, by which it exceeds the flesh of Christ in infinite ways: but it is and is said to be infinite in such a way that it is always whole, where it is. Wherefore, most viciously, the assumed flesh of Christ, which by reason of quantity and magnitude, from the condition of its Nature, is finite, is compared to this infinity of the Essence and Person of the λόγῳ by a certain opposition. For this opposition does not occur in equal degrees and terms: to say nothing now of the fact that the union itself is entirely overturned if this mystery must be defined and estimated according to the condition of human Nature.

Finally, we invert the argument in this way: If the Father is nowhere and never outside the Son, on account of the unity of the infinite divine Essence: So the λόγῳ is also nowhere and never PERSONALLY outside its assumed flesh, on account of the Unity and identity of the infinite person.

SIXTH. The ubiquity of the flesh of Christ is either absolutely necessary for the personal union, or it is not. If it is absolutely necessary, it follows that the human nature, being local, palpable, and circumscribed, is not really united to the Son of God according to a SUPERNATURAL respect, and is excluded from the personal union: because the Ubiquitarians write publicly that, according to a natural respect, the human nature remains finite and retains a finite quantity, according to the natural condition of which it is in one place only, at one and the same time, and not everywhere. But if the ubiquity of the flesh of Christ is in no way necessary for the union, then the supernatural respect of the human nature is in no way necessary.

I ANSWER: The argument fails through ignorance of the refutation. For as regards the major proposition, it can be understood either concerning the constitution of the union itself, or concerning the consequent effect. If concerning the constitution of the union: we ourselves readily grant that the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ does not constitute the hypostatic union: and in this sense the argument is effective. But if concerning the consequent effect, then it is plain that the natures could not be personally united unless the assumed flesh were raised into the illocal ὑπόστασις itself. Which effect the first member of the disjunction does not remove. For a double humanity does not follow from that—one local, palpable, circumscribed; the other illocal, impalpable, uncircumscribed—but the humanity remains one in number, yet considered under different respects, as has been shown hitherto. The latter member of the disjunction likewise collapses of itself. For although the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ is not necessary for the union as a constitutive part, it is nevertheless necessary for the effect which results from this union.

SEVENTH. Whatever is not in the essence of human nature can in no way be in humanity. But an illocal respect is not in the essence of human nature. Therefore, an illocal respect can in no way be in humanity.

I answer, the argument fails through the fallacy of equivocation, which lurks in the major. For it can be understood either concerning such attributes as pertain to the very τὸ εἶναι (being) of human nature, in which sense we ourselves readily grant that an illocal respect is not in the essence of human nature, as the minor proposition correctly subsumes. Or it can also be understood concerning that mode of inherence by which accidents exist in a subject; then we do not concede that an illocal respect is in the essence of human nature even in that way, and in this manner we again concede the minor. Or finally, it can be taken to mean that nothing can be in the essence of human nature unless it is also of its essence; then we deny the major most simply. For something can be in the essence of human nature, although it is not of the essence, nor a part of the essence, nor finally does it inhere in it subjectively: as for example: the Son of God himself, and all the fullness of his divinity, dwells in the assumed human nature, Col. 2:9. Yet none of these three modes can be referred to this inhabitation. Now because an illocal respect results from the habitation of all the fullness of the divinity of the λόγος in the assumed flesh, it is certainly said to be truly and really in the human nature: but in a certain peculiar mode, which is proper and peculiar to this inhabitation of the λόγος in humanity.

EIGHTH. That nature is united with the λόγος which, while preserving the essential property of soul and body, concurs into the person of the λόγος. But an illocal and omnipresent humanity has no local and circumscribed essence. Therefore, an illocal and omnipresent humanity is not united with the λόγος.

I answer, the argument fails through a shameful ignorance of the refutation. For the author of this argument imagines that the flesh of Christ is rendered infinite and uncircumscribed by reason of quantity because of its omnipresence. If that were posited by us, it would certainly follow that such a humanity, infinite and uncircumscribed by reason of quantity, could not have been united with the λόγος. But the matter is far otherwise. Since the flesh of Christ, by reason of the essential property of soul and body, remains finite and circumscribed by the limits of its nature forever, it is nevertheless not circumscribed by any place externally surrounding it while in the ὑποστάσει τꭣ͂ λόγꭣ and at the right hand of God. Where, because a very different respect applies on each side, both are truly affirmed of the flesh of Christ without contradiction.

NINTH. In the death of Christ, the body lay lifeless in the sepulcher; the soul, however, was definitively outside the body elsewhere; and yet the hypostatic union was not dissolved. Therefore: the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ does not necessarily follow from the union.

I answer: The argument fails ὥςτε τὴν ἀγνοιαν ἐλέγχꭣ: and ὥςτε τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For it does not follow: The body of Christ was in the sepulchre circumscriptively: and the Soul was definitively elsewhere outside the body. Therefore the λόγꭣ also was then outside the body, that is, it did not have that most present to itself everywhere. For although the Natural Union of body and Soul was truly dissolved in the death of Christ: nevertheless the Personal Union remained indissoluble: so that although the body was in the sepulchre, and the Soul in Paradise: yet nevertheless the λόγꭣ, beyond the consideration of both Sepulchre and Paradise, outside and short of the place contemplated, held both most unitively present within itself, through an inhabitation and immanence nowhere disjoined. The reason for the assertion is: Because the Personal Existence of Body and Soul is not referred to the place of either the sepulchre or Paradise: but to the ὑπόστασιν of the λόγꭣ, which is the one term of their subsistence, just as it is of their assumption. Which personal existence, the Natural existence of the body in the Sepulchre, and of the Soul in Paradise, does not take away.

Latin:

sit τῷ λόγῳ ubique præsentissimè unita: licet tùm propter interventum profundissimæ Exinanitionis gubernationi creaturarum ἐνεργητικῶς non adhiberetur.

Primo huic argumento nostro, à mysterio unionis petito, maximo conatu sese opponunt Adversarii: ut, si non penitùs evertere, saltem aliquo modo labefactare illud queant.

Ac INITIO quidem ἀσυλλογισίαν quatuor terminorum nobis objiciunt, si dicamus: λόγο ὑπόστασιν esse illocalem: carnem autem subsistere ὑποστάσει τꙋ λόγꙋ. Ergò carnem Christi esse illocalem: cum potiùs argumentum, si rectè concludere debeat, sic informandum sit: λόγο ὑπόστασις illocalis: caro Christi est ipsa ὑπόστασις τꙋ λόγꙋ. Ergò. Ubi tamen statim Minor propositio deprehendatur esse falsissima. Quanquam verò argumentum nostrum longè aliâ formâ & quidem verè Syllogisticâ prodiit, ut πλεονεξία quatuor terminorum demonstrari non queat: tamen si vel maximè secundum formam Calvinianam illud proponatur: nihilominùs vera erit conclusio: Quia eadem manet medii termini substantia. Siquidem tàm in Minore, quàm in Majore propositione una eadémque agitatur Quæstio nempè de præsentia Christi: In Majore enim quæriturde præsentia λόγꙋ: sive ὑποστάσεως τꙋ λόγꙋ: In Minore verò, de præsentia affumtæ carnis, ubi nimirùm illa sit & subsistat ex unione cum λόγῳ. Undè manifestè patet, sine ulla terminorum distinctione, Medium terminum tantùm nonnihil inflecti. Et si hanc argumentandi rationem usque adeò improbant Adversarii, quî fit, quòd subindè eadem Logicâ subindè adversum nos insurgunt, clamitantes: Cælum infinitis spatiis, sive intervallis distat à Sacramento Cœnæ. Atqui caro Christi est in cælo. Ergò caro Christi infinitis spatiis sive intervallis abest à Sacramento Cœnæ.

ALTERUM argumentum Adversariorum tale est: Si caro propter unionem est extra locum, quia λόγꙋ ipse est extra locum: utique per reciprocationem, & quidem propter eandem unionem Deitas verbi erit in certo loco, quia caro ipsa naturaliter est in loco: At posterius hoc absurdum. Ergò & prius.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate vitiosi consequentis: quod oritur ex fictitia illa reciprocatione, quam Adversarii sibi hac in quæstione falsò imaginantur. Diversissima enim est utrobique ratio: quæ indè emergit, quod in Unione non Humana natura assumsit λόγον IN SE, vel in, sive intra suam ὑπόστασιν, quam per se nullam habet: Sed quòd λόγꙋ Humanam naturam in suam transtulit & assumsit hypostasin. Quare etsi λόγꙋ revera factus est caro: nequaquam tamen translationem aliquam τꙋ λόγꙋ in statum localem ac terrenum, ideò fingere licet: quasi ipse è statu illocali divinitatis suæ emotus, per immigrationem quandam, in Humanitatem, & statum ejus localem se demerserit.

Sed ita caro factus est, quòd Humanitatem intra se suamque ὑπόστασιν assumendo, simul eam è localitatis statu, supra & extra loca omnia verè transtulit & evexit. Observata proindè diversitate Assumentis & Assumenti, vanitas Argumenti hujus ultrò patescit.

TERTIUM argumentum sic habet: Si caro Christi ideò est extra locum, quia assumta est in illocalem ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου: sequetur, eandem ob causam, carnem hanc etiam esse ab æterno, esse exemtam à tempore, & sic non in tempore incarnatam, esse incorpoream, esse spiritualem, esse compositionis expertem &c. Siquidem talis est ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου: Atqui posterius hoc falsum & absurdum. Ergò & prius.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum confusione disparatissimarum Quæstionum, & ἀσυλλογισίᾳ quatuor terminorum. Nam si integer formetur Syllogismus, planum fiet, Majorem propositionem agere de ipsa Essentia: quid nimirùm sit λόγος ratione suæ Essentiæ: Minorem verò agere non de Essentia: sed de præsentia carnis, ubinam subsistat, & suum τὸ εἶναι obtineat. Talis enim erit Syllogismus: ὑπόστασις λόγου ratione ὀυσίας suæ est æterna, est Spiritus, est compositionis omnis expers, est à Patre ab æterno genitus. Atqui Humana Natura est assumta in hanc ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου. Ergò & Humana Natura talis est. Ubi πλεονεξίαν quatuor terminorum nullo negotio ex distractione medii termini licet deprehendere. Cæterùm quoad nostrum argumentum, manifestum est, in utraque præmissarum agi tantùm de præsentia: non autem de ipsa Naturarum Essentia. Ergò uti nostrum argumentum rectissimè concludit: Ita Adversariorum ἔνστασις sua futilitate propria concidit.

Exemplo liceat hoc illustrare: Quando sic argumentor: VViteberga est oculus sive lumen Germaniæ: Atqui Petrus est VVitebergæ: Ergò Petrus est lumen Germaniæ. Hic vel Puer ἀσυλλογισίαν quatuor terminorum, & confusionem duarum Quæstionum, quarum una de ipsa Natura, & quasi Essentia VVitebergæ: altera de præsentia Petri agit, facilè deprehendit. Quando verò sic argumentor: VViteberga est extra Lipsiam. Petrus est VVitebergæ. Ergò Petrus est extra Lipsiam: hic procedit argumentum: Siquidem in utraque præmissarum quæritur de præsentia.

Sed porrò instant: Constare argumento suo immotam suam certitudinem, propterea, quòd τοῦ λόγου Omnipræsentia nihil aliud sit, quàm ipsa ejus Essentia. Rectissimè proindè argumentum procedere, siquidem in utraque præmissarum agatur de præsentia.

Respondeo: Fallit hoc etiam argumentum Sophisticatione plurium quæstionum. Aliud enim est, quando Omnipræsentia in se consideratur, ut Idioma Divinæ Essentiæ proprium: Aliud verò quando ea respectu creaturarum expenditur, quatenus λόγος extra locum sive localitatem illis adesse dicitur.

Illo priore modo libenter largior, Omnipræsentiam cum Essentia τꭣ̃ λόγꭣ simpliciffimè converti, & esse quiddam ταυτὸ: Posteriore verò hoc respectu simpliciter nego. Nam extra locum sive localitatem adesse omnibus creaturis, non pertinet ad Essentiam simpliciter, sed ad Essentiæ præsentiam. Probo hoc ipsum geminâ ratione: 1. Ante creationem hujus Universi, DEUS suâ Essentiâ nullis creaturis extra locum adfuit, quia nullæ tùm erant. Ergò adesse Creaturis extra locum, ad Essentiam simpliciter non pertinet: Nam si pertineret: tùm sequeretur, Essentiam DEI fuisse ante creationem imperfectam: Siquidem destituebatur præsentia extra locum, quoad creaturas: id quod impium & blasphemum. Deindè præsentia divina Essentiæ ad creaturas, varietatem & differentiam modorum atque graduum reverà suscipit: aliter enim adest creaturis ratione generalis conservationis: aliter adest credentibus, κατ' ἐνέργειαν τῆς χάριτος: aliter adest Damnatis: aliter adest beatis in vita æterna: aliter denique etiam assumtæ humanitati. Atqui verò talis varietas & differentia in ipsam Essentiam DEI, quippè simpliciter invariabilem, non cadit. Rectissimè proindè inter Essentiam λόγꭣ, & præsentiam ejusdem extra locum ad creaturas sic distingvitur: ut λόγꭣ Ratione ἐσίας sive Essentiæ dicatur, SIBI IPSI esse, quod est: Ratione verò præsentiæ extra locum, non sibi, sed aliis adesse.

QUARTUM sic informant Adversarii: Si unio Hypostatica præstat, ut caro Christi sit extra locum præstabit utique etiam, ut sit extra Tempus. Hoc posterius autem vel cogitatu absurdum fuerit: siquidem hoc pacto caro Christi neque in tempore nata, neque in tempore passa, crucifixa aut mortua est. Ergò prius etiam illud itidem vel cogitatu absurdum fuerit.

RESPONDEO per distinctionem ex hypothesi illa secunda, quam paulò antè notavimus: quòd nimirùm distingvendum sit, inter respectum carnis Christi Naturalem. & Personalem: qui ad se mutuò ita se habent, ut quàm primùm ex affirmatione respectus personalis, ad negationem respectus Naturalis, vel vice versa, sit collectio, turpis committatur Sophisticatio vitiosissimi consequentis. Possunt enim duo illi respectus, sine ulla contradictione simul stare: ut videlicet, Humana Natura, etsi per Unionem evecta est in ὑπόστασιν τꭣ̃ λόγꭣ, uti à loco: sic à tempore absolutam: & sic ipsa quoque hujus Majestatis Personaliter facta est κοινωνὸς: tamen λόγꭣ in statu Exinanitionis Carnem hanc suam, uti reliquis Mundi hujus infirmitatibus & conditionibus, ita Tempori etiam, subjectam voluerit (salva interim permanente ea Majestate, qua in persona λόγꭣ, uti extra locum, sic extra Tempus subsistit) ac proindè in tempore concipi, nasci, pati, crucifigi, mori &c. potuerit. Cæterùm stupendam sive cæcitatem, sive malitiam produnt Adversarii, quod instatu etiam Exaltationis & sessionis ad dexteram DEI carni Christi concedere nolunt illud axioma, quo tamen Sancti & Beati in vita æterna realissimè perfruentur. Quia enim hoc in seculo; rebus naturalibus accidit Tempus tantùm propter motum φυσικὸν illum, de quo disputant Philosophi: in Vita verò æterna motus ille prorsus cessabit: quippè cujus conditio sic comparata est, ut oculus non viderit, auris non audierit, nec in cor hominis descenderit, quid DEUS præparaverit diligentibus se: 1. Cor. 2, 9. Utique in Vita etiam illa æterna Electi futuri sunt sine Tempore. Jam verò cùm caro Christi non modò sit assumta in vitam æternam, sed insuper evecta in ipsam dexteram Majestatis divinæ: Quæ obsecro, prodigiosa hæc fuerit impietas, eam Tempori adhuc velle subjicere.

QUINTUM tale est: Unio duarum naturarum in Christo, non est talis immanentia, qualis est trium personarum divinitatis: ubi propter infinitatem unius ejusdemque Essentiæ semper unius personæ hypostasis est, ubi est & alterius personæ hypostasis. Ergò ex Unione cum λόγῳ non sequitur, ut ubi est ὑπόστασις τꙋ λόγꙋ, ibi etiam sit assumta caro: Ratio consequentiæ, qui caro Christi non est ejusdem infinitatis cum ὑποστάσει λόγꙋ.

RESPONDEO: Fallit argumentum παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχꙋ: Idque multipliciter. Primùm enim Omnipræsentia carnis Christi causa ac fundamentum non est, Infinitas Essentiæ τꙋ λόγꙋ, quatenus ea in se consideratur: sed causa unica est, Assumtio carnis hujus Christi in hanc infinitam ὑπόστασιν τꙋ λόγꙋ. Corruit proindè, quicquid de Infinitate Essentiæ, tanquam Omnipræsentia fundamento, quoad assumtam carnem, garriunt Adversarii. Quia enim tota ὑπόστασις λόγꙋ, quantumvis infinita est incarnata, ut nefas sit fingere, partem aliquam hujus ὑποστάσεως esse incarnatam, partem aliam non esse incarnatam: siquidem ea partem extra partem planè nullam habet: ideò ὑπόστασις etiam λόγꙋ, salva hac Unione extra carnem hanc assumtam, nec est, nec esse potest: & vi consequentiæ, ubi est ὑπόστασις τꙋ λόγꙋ, quantumvis infinita: ibi caro etiam hæc assumta sit, necesse est: nisi Unionem dirimere quis velit. Deindè Essentia ut & Persona τꙋ λόγꙋ, neque est, neque dicitur infinita sensu Calvinistico, per infinitam quandam & immensam ὀσίας expansionem, quâ carnem Christi infinitis modis excedat: sed ita est ac dicitur infinita, ut semper tota sit, ubi est. Quare vitiosissimè ad hanc infinitatem Essentiæ & Personæ τꙋ λόγꙋ, per oppositionem quandam comparatur assumta caro Christi, quæ ratione quantitatis & magnitudinis, ex Naturæ suæ conditione, est finita. Nam oppositio hæc non fit in æqualibus gradibus ac terminis: ut nihil jam dicam de eo, quod ipsa unio prorsus evertitur, si mysterium hoc secundum conditionem Naturæ humanæ definiri & æstimari debeat.

Tandem invertimus argumentum in hunc modum: Si Pater nusquam & nunquàm est extra Filium, propter unitatem infinitæ Essentiæ divinæ: Sic λόγος nusquam etiam & nunquam est PERSONALITER extra assumtam suam carnem, propter Unitatem & identitatem infinitæ personæ.

SEXTUM. Ubiquitas carnis Christi, vel est ad Unionem personalem omninò necessaria, vel non est. Si est omninò necessaria, sequitur humanam naturam localem, palpabilem & circumscriptam, secundum respectum SUPERNATURALEM, Filio DEI non esse realiter unitam, & ex Unione personali exclusam: quia publicè scribunt Ubiquitarii, juxta respectum Naturalem, humanam naturam finitam manere, & finitam quantitatem retinere, juxta cujus conditionem naturalem, uno tantùm in loco, simul & semel, non ubique est. Sin Ubiquitas carnis Christi, nullo modo est ad Unionem necessaria, tunc etiam respectus supernaturalis humanæ Naturæ, nullo modo est necessarius.

RESPONDEO: Fallit argumentum Ignoratione Elenchi. Nam quoad Majorem propositionem, intelligi illa potest vel de constitutione ipsius Unionis; vel de Effectu consequente. Si de constitutione Unionis: ipsi ultrò largimur, Omnipræsentiam carnis Christi, non constituere Unionem Hypostaticam: Et hoc sensu militat argumentum. Sin de Effectu consequente, tùm planum est, Naturas personaliter uniri non potuisse, nisi caro assumta eveheretur in ipsam illocalem ὑπόστασιν. Quem etiam Effectum prius membrum disjunctivæ non tollit. Neque enim gemina indè sequitur Humanitas, una localis, palpabilis, circumscripta: altera illocalis, inpalpabilis, incircumscripta: sed una numero manet Humanitas, diversis autem respectibus considerata: uti hactenus fuit ostensum. Posteriùs membrum disjunctivæ itidem per se corruit. Etsi enim Omnipræsentia carnis Christi, ad unionem non est necessaria, tanquam pars constitutiva: est tamen necessaria ad Effectum, qui ex Unione hac resultat.

SEPTIMUM. Quicquid non est in Essentia humanæ naturæ, id nullo modo in humanitate esse potest. Atqui illocalis respectus non est in essentia naturæ humanæ. Ergò illocalis respectus nullo modo in humanitate potest.

Respondeo, Fallit argumentum Sophismate æquivocationis, quæ in Majore latitat. Vel enim ea intelligi potest, de ejusmodi attributis, qui ad ipsum τὸ εἶναι Naturæ humanæ pertinet, Quo sanè sensu ipsi ultrò largimur, illocalem respectum non esse in Essentia Naturæ humanæ, uti rectè subsumit Minor propositio. Vel intelligi etiam ea potest, de eo modo inhæsionis, quo Accidentia insunt Subjecto: tùm ne sic quidem illocalem respectum in Essentia Naturæ humanæ esse, concedimus: Et hoc pacto rursum Minorem concedimus. Vel denique sic ea accipi potest, quod nihil possit esse in Essentia Naturæ humanæ: nisi quòd etiam sit de ejus Essentia: tùm Majorem simplicissimè negamus. Potest enim aliquid esse, in Essentia Naturæ humanæ, licèt non sit de Essentia, neque etiam pars Essentiæ, neque denique ei inhæreat subjectivè: ut Exempli gratia: ipse Filius DEI, & omnis plenitudo Divinitatis ejus, habitat in assumta Natura humana, Col. 2, 9. Neque tamen trium istorum modorum aliquis ad hanc inhabitationem referri potest. Jam quia ex habitatione omnis plenitudinis Divinitatis τꭣ͂ λόγꭣ in assumta carne, resultat respectus illocalis, utique in humana Natura ille verè ac realiter inesse dicitur: sed modo quopiam peculiari, qui est inhabitationis hujus τꭣ͂ λόγꭣ in Humanitate, proprius ac peculiaris.

OCTAVVM. Ea Natura unita est cum λόγῳ, quæ servatâ Essentiali Animæ & Corporis proprietate, concurrit in personam λόγꭣ. Atqui illocalis & ubique præsens humanitas, nullam Essentiam localem & circumscriptam habet. Ergò illocalis & ubique præsens Humanitas non unita est cùm λόγῳ.

Respondeo, Fallit argumentum turpi ignorantiâ Elenchi. Fingit enim autor hujus argumenti, carnem Christi ex Omnipræsentia reddi ratione quantitatis infinitatâ & incircumscriptam. Quod si à nobis statueretur, sequeretur utique, talem infinitam & ratione Quantitatis incircumscriptam Humanitatem, non potuisse uniri cum λόγῳ. Cæterùm longè secus se habet. Siquidem caro Christi ratione proprietatis Essentialis Animæ & Corporis, finita & naturæ suæ terminis circumscripta manens in æternum: nihilominùs tamen in ὑποστάσει τꭣ͂ λόγꭣ, & in dextra DEI, nullo loco forinsecùs ambiente circumscribitur. Ubi quia diversissimus respectus utrinque militat, utrumque etiam verè, & sine contradictione de carne Christi affirmatur.

NONVM. In Morte Christi, corpus jacebat exanime in sepulchro: Anima verò erat definitivè extra corpus alibi: & tamen non solvebatur Unio Hypostatica. Ergò: Ex unione non sequitur necessariò Omnipræsentia carnis Christi.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum ὥςτε τὴν ἀγνοιαν ἐλέγχꭣ: & ὥςτε τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Neque enim sequitur: Corpus Christi fuit in sepulchro circumscriptivè: & Anima fuit definitivè alibi extra corpus. Ergò λόγꭣ quoque tùm fuit extra corpus, hoc est, non ubique sibi habuit illud præsentissimum. Etsi enim Naturalis Unio corporis & Animæ, in morte Christi verè soluta fuit: tamen Personalis Unio mansit indissoluta: ita ut licèt corpus esset in sepulchro, & Anima in Paradiso: tamen nihilominus λόγꭣ, utrumque extra Sepulchri & Paradisi considerationem, extra & citra locum intuitum, intra se unitissimè præsens habuit, per inhabitationem & immanentiam nullibi disiunctam. Ratio assertionis est: Quia Personalis Existentia Corporis & Animæ non fertur ad locum vel sepulchri, vel Paradisi: sed ad ὑπόστασιν λόγꭣ, quæ una, uti assumtionis: sic & subsistenttiæ illorum est terminus. Quam personalem existentiam, non tollit Naturalis existentia corporis in Sepulchro, & Animæ in Paradiso.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: The Second Argument Constructive argument for the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ

THE SECOND ARGUMENT.

Constructive argument for the omnipresence of the flesh of CHRIST.

The second argument, by which we demonstrate our doctrine concerning the omnipresence of the flesh of CHRIST, is provided by clear testimonies of the Scriptures: such as these.

Matt. 18:20. Where two or three are gathered: there am I in the midst of them.

Matt. 28:20. Behold I AM with you always, even unto the end of the world.

Eph. 1:22. GOD the Father appointed him head over all things, which is his body, namely the fullness of him who fills all in all.

Eph. 4:10. He ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill ALL THINGS.

From these and similar sayings we infer a threefold argument:

THE FIRST is such: If Christ is with us always even unto the end of the world, and is in the midst of those who are gathered in his name, only according to his divine nature, and not also according to his human nature: certainly all that consolation which we can derive from the presence of the humanity of Christ perishes. For he was made like us his brothers according to his human nature for this reason: and was tempted in all things just as we are, so that according to the same nature he might be able to sympathize with us and succor us. Heb. 2:18.

THE SECOND can be formulated thus: According to the same nature by which Christ was raised from the dead: indeed, according to which he himself is proportional to the faithful under the analogy of head and members by reason of substance: according to that same nature he also attained to fill all things in all, that is, to work present in all things.

But the former statement is true of Christ only according to his assumed humanity.

Therefore it is necessary that the latter also be true in the same way according to the same humanity: so that, namely, according to this he attained to work all things in all: and that not absent, but present: since the word 'to fill,' used concerning the kingdom of Christ, never and nowhere denotes such an operation as excludes the presence of the Operator: but always includes and joins both. There is added also that reason, that it would be clearly absurd to posit that the head is absent from its body: for thus the faithful would constitute no longer a true and living body, but a completely headless monster: which is absurd. Now, indeed, that Christ is the head of his body, that is, of the Church, also according to his human nature: is evident from the fact that only according to this his Humanity is he proportional under the relation of head and members. Far be it, therefore, that we should posit that Christ the Man is absent from the body of the Church.

A third [argument] can be such: If Christ ascended above all heavens, that he might fill all things: it follows that he attained this by his ascension: that he might most presently and most powerfully reign and rule over all creatures. But Christ according to his human nature ascended above all heavens, that he might fill all things. Therefore Christ according to the same human nature attained that he might most presently and most powerfully reign and rule over all creatures. The connection of the major premise from the scriptures is sufficiently plain. For to fill all things is nothing else than to be present most presently everywhere in places, and to rule most powerfully: according to that Jerem. 23, 23. Do not I fill heaven and earth, saith the LORD. Wisd. 1, 7. The Spirit of the LORD filleth the world. The context of the Apostolic passage proves this very thing: For the notation of places, higher and lower, which the Apostle opposes to one another by reason of descent and ascent: necessarily implies also the filling of those places, which followed upon that descent and ascent. The minor premise likewise is most evidently clear. 1. Because to attribute an ascension to Christ according to his Divine nature, and indeed a local ascension, would be plainly absurd and impious, abominable even to the Calvinists themselves. 2. If, arguing from the Calvinist hypothesis, I say thus: Christ ascending according to his human nature above all heavens attained that he might fill all things according to his divinity: it will follow that his Humanity by this ascension finally obtained Omnipresence for his Deity: which is prodigiously blasphemous: because the Divinity never does not fill all things through the infinity of its Essence and is immutably Omnipresent. The adversaries clamor, and object two things especially: 1. That the Apostolic aphorism must be restricted only to the Church, which Christ has filled with his various gifts: therefore the Apostle himself also immediately makes mention of the enrichment of the Church. 2. If the words of the Apostle are referred even to the kingly office of Christ, yet it is not correctly gathered thence that the flesh of Christ is Omnipresent: since it is one thing for Christ according to his humanity to have received dominion over all creatures: but another thing for his humanity to be everywhere by its own Essence. I ANSWER. The prior objection proceeds from the affirmation of a part to the negation of the whole. Where a childish hallucination and non-sequitur is detected, to be restrained by clubs rather than words. For who would endure this method of concluding: Christ filled his Church with gifts. Therefore the filling of all things is only to be restricted to the Church. For 1. the universal particle ALL refutes this collection: Which universality can neither be, nor ought to be, confined by the limits of the Church alone. 2. The express notation of higher and lower places: Where certainly the predicate will be of the same breadth as the subject: so that as far and wide as the scope of the higher and lower places extends: so far and wide the filling of all things itself also extends. Whence in chapter 1 to the Eph. the Apostle names it the filling of all in all. 3. The same Apostle in the same chapter 1 of Eph. defines this filling of all by the subjection of all, and the dominion of the universe: which again cannot be circumscribed by the narrow limits of the Church. Therefore, when the Apostle introduces the mention of the Church and its enrichment, he intended to describe only some species of that divine Majesty, to which Christ, ascending to the heavens, was exalted in respect of plenary usurpation. For a certain part and, as it were, a certain fruit of this divine Majesty is the gathering, enrichment, and governance of the Church. Now, indeed, from the position of one part, the Consequence to the negation of the remaining parts is not valid. What? That they do not even sincerely grant this part of divine Majesty to the humanity of Christ: since they contend that that most divine action, the effusion of the Holy Spirit and the bestowal of gifts, pertains solely to the divine nature: where the human nature has not operated more than it could have operated from the property of its nature. Which stupendous obstinacy, however, is most rightly refuted if the absurdity emerging from it is set before their eyes: Namely, 1. that in this way Christ according to his humanity ascended and descended, so that according to his divinity he could exercise those actions: 2. that thus that Petrine statement is false: Exalted by the right hand of GOD, he poured out this, which you see and hear, Acts 2:33.

The latter Instance is entirely destitute of every ἐλέγχῳ: Whence the Sophistry of the vicious Consequent arises. For what, I ask, is the force of the consequence in this argument: It is one thing that Christ according to his humanity received authority over all creatures: it is another thing that the same, according to the same, is everywhere. Therefore, from the Apostolic Aphorism, the Omnipresence of the flesh of Christ is not correctly inferred. For many things argue the stupendous vanity of this collection. 1. The Apostle confirms both in distinct words: namely, that all things are subject to Christ according to the flesh: and that Christ according to the flesh therefore descended into the lowest parts of the earth, and ascended far above all heavens, that he might fill all things. 2. Authority over all created things necessarily presupposes Omnipresence: so that from the former, one is most rightly concluded to the latter in this manner: If to the assumed and exalted Man Christ, sitting at the right hand of God, all things are subject: and nothing is omitted which is not subject to him: it would be clearly impious to wish to exempt places and the διαστήματα of places from this Subjection of all things, as if these were not subject to him, but rather had this power, that they could hinder and delay the presence of the reigning Christ in these lands and elsewhere. But to Christ according to his humanity, sitting at the right hand of GOD, all things are subject: and NOTHING is omitted which is not subject to him. Heb. 2:8. Therefore. 3. If Christ, according to the opinion of the Adversaries, is absent according to his humanity by the distances of places from those Creatures over whose administration he presides: certainly it will now be established that he himself reigns not from the unlocated throne of the right hand of GOD: but rather from that most remote place or UBI, in which alone the Calvinists dream he dwells according to his natural property. But this is absurd and impious. Therefore that is too. 4. If the λόγος alone, present to all Creatures, administers the dominion of this universe through an absent Humanity: it will follow that the λόγος and those Creatures are more present to each other than the λόγος and the Humanity are present to those creatures to whom the λόγος is present without his Humanity. But this also would be most absurd, indeed clearly Nestorian. Therefore that is too. 5. If the flesh of Christ, being absent, administers authority over all creatures, it will certainly administer it, no longer according to the condition of the kingdom of GOD, nor according to the mode of the right hand of GOD: but after the manner, condition, and lot of the earthly kings of this age: But this also would be impious: since in this way Christ according to his humanity would be dislodged from the throne of the right hand of GOD, into which he has been placed, with all things subject to him that can be named, not only in this age, but also in the future. Therefore it is impious, and the former is necessarily so. But what need is there of many words, when the Adversaries do not even believe that, namely, that the Humanity of Christ, although absent, powerfully dominates all creatures. For this very thing is the work of the uncreated and infinite divine power alone, which they simply deny him.

Latin:

ALTERUM ARGUMENTUM.

Κατασκευαστικὸν pro Omnipræsentia carnis CHRISTI.

ALterum argumentum, quo Doctrinam nostram de Omnipræsentia carnis CHRISTI, demonstramus, subministrant perspicua Scripturarum testimonia: qualia sunt.

Matth. 18, 20. Ubi duo vel tres congregati: ibi sum in medio eorum.

Matth. 28, 20. Ecce EGO SUM vobiscum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi.

Eph. 1, 22. DEUS Pater constituit ipsum caput Ecclesiæ, super omnia, quæ est corpus ipsius, nempè complementum ejus, qui omnia in omnibus adimplet.

Eph. 4, 10. Ascendit supra omnes cælos, ut OMNIA impleret.

Ex his & similibus dictis tergeminum inferimus argumentum:

PRIMUM tale est: Si Christus secundum divinam tantùm, non autem secundum humanam etiam naturam, est nobiscum omnibus diebus usq; ad consummationem seculi, & est in medio eorum qui in nomine ipsius sunt congregati: certè perit omnis illa consolatio, quam ex præsentia humanitatis Christi capere possumus. Hic enim ideò secundum humanam naturam nobis fratribus suis similis factus: inque omnibus, quemadmodum nos, tentatus est, ut secundum eandem naturam nobis compati & succurrere posset. Hebr. 2. 18.

ALTERUM sic informari potest: Secundum quam naturam Christus à mortuis resuscitatus est: imò secundum quam ipse ad fideles, sub analogia capitis & membrorum ratione substantiæ est proportionabilis: juxta illam etiam adeptus est, ut omnia in omnibus adimpleret, hoc est, ut præsens omnia in omnibus operaretur.

Atqui prius illud de Christo secundum assumtam humanitatem tantùm verum est.

Ergò posterius etiam hoc itidem secundum eandem humanitatem verum sit, necesse est: ut nimirùm juxta hanc adeptus sit, ut omnia in omnibus operaretur: idque non absens, sed præsens: Siquidem implendi vox, de regno Christi usurpata, nunquam & nuspiam talem operationem notat, quæ Operantis præsentiam excludat: sed semper utramque includit & conjungit. Accedit & illa ratio, quod absurdum planè foret, statuere, caput abesse à suo corpore: Sic enim fideles non verum ampliùs ac vivum corpus, sed monstrum prorsus ἀκέφαλον constituerent: quod absurdum. Jam verò Christum secundum humanam etiam naturam esse caput sui corporis, hoc est, Ecclesiæ: vel indè constat, quòd tantùm secundum hanc Humanitatem suam, sub ratione capitis & membrorum est proportionabilis. Absit proindè ut Christum Hominem à corpore Ecclesiæ abesse, statuamus.

TERTIUM tale esse potest: Si Christus ascēdit supra omnes cælos, ut impleret omnia: sequitur, ipsum ascensu suo hoc esse consecutū: ut præsentisse simè & potentissimè regnaret & dominaretur omnibus creaturis. Atqui Christus secundum humanam naturam ascendit supra cælos omnes, ut impleret omnia. Ergò Christus secundum eandem humanam naturam consecutus est, ut præsentissimè & potentissimè regnaret ac dominaretur omnibus creaturis. Connexum Majoris ex scripturis satis planum est. Nam implere omnia, nihil est aliud, quàm ubique locorum præsentissimè adesse, & potentissimè dominari: secundum illud Jerem. 23, 23. Nonne DEUS ego cælum & terram impleo. Sap. 1, 7. Spiritus DOMINI replet orbem terrarum. Quod ipsum evincit περίστασις loci Apostolici: Nam notatio locorum, superiorum & inferiorum, quæ ratione descensus & ascensus sibi invicem opponit Apostolus: necessariò istorum etiam locorum impletionem, quæ descensum & ascensum istu insecuta est, subinfert. Minor itidem evidentissimè patet. 1. Quia ascensionem Christo secundum Divinam naturam, & quidem localem ascensionem tribuere, planè absonum & impium foret, ipsis etiam Calvinianis abominabile. 2. Si ex hypothesi Calviniana arguendo sic inquam: Christus secundum humanam naturam ascendens supra omnes cælos consecutus est, ut secundum divinam impleret omnia: sequetur Humanitatem suo hoc ascensu impetrasse demùm Deitati Omnipræsentiam: id quod prodigiosè blasphemum: propterea quòd Divinitatis nunquam non per infinitatem Essentiæ omnia implet & immutabiliter est Omnipræsens. Obstrepunt Adversarii, & duo potissimùm obvertunt: 1. Aphorismum Apostolicum restringendum esse tantùm ad Ecclesiam, quam Christus variis suis donis impleverit: ideò ipsum quoque Apostolum statim mentionem facere locupletationis Ecclesiæ. 2. Si vel maximè ad regium Christi officium verba Apostoli referantur, non tamen rectè indè colligi carnis Christi Omnipræsentiam: siquidem aliud sit, Christum secundum humanitatem imperium in omnes creaturas accepisse: aliud verò humanitatem Essentia sua esse ubique. RESPONDEO. Prior instantia procedit ex affirmatione patris, ad negationem totius. Ubi puerilis hallucinatio & ἀσυλλογισία deprehenditur, fustibus magis quàm verbis coercenda. Quis enim ferret hanc concludendi rationem: Christus Ecclesiam suam implevit donis. Ergò Impletio omnium, tantùm ad Ecclesiam est restringenda. Nam 1. redarguit hanc collectionem particula Universalis OMNIA: Quæ Universalitas solius Ecclesiæ terminis coarctari nec potest, nec debet. 2. Expressa notatio locorum superiorum & inferiorum: Ubi certè ejusdem latitudinis erit prædicatum, cujus est subjectum: ita ut quàm longè latéque se extendit ambitus locorum superiorum & inferiorum: tàm longè latéque se extendat ipsa quoque impletio omnium. Undè cap 1. ad Eph. Apostolus eam nominat Impletionem omnium in omnibus. 3. Idem Apostolus eodem cap. 1. Eph. hanc impletionem omnium definit, per Subjectionem omnium, & Dominium Universorum: id quod rursum angustis Ecclesiæ terminis circumscribi non potest. Proindè quando Apostolus mentionem subjicit Ecclesiæ & ejus locupletationis: speciem tantùm aliquam divinæ illius Majestatis, ad quam Christus ascendens ad cælos plenariæ usurpationis respectu evectus est, describere voluit. Hujus enim divinæ Majestatis, pars quædam & quasi fructus quidam est Ecclesiæ collectio, locupletatio & gubernatio. Jam verò ab unius partis positione, ad reliquarum partium negationem non valet Consequentia. Quid? Quòd ne quidem hanc partem Majestatis divinæ, sincerè largiuntur humanitati Christi: siquidem divinissimam illam actionem, effusionem Spiritus Sancti, & collationem donorum ad solam divinam naturam pertinere contendunt: ubi humana natura plus non operata sit, quàm ex proprietate naturæ suæ operari potuerit. Quæ tamen stupenda pervicacia rectissimè retunditur, si absurdum indè emergens ob oculos illis constituatur: Quod nimirùm, 1. hoc pacto Christus secundum humanitatem ascenderit & descenderit, ut secundum divinitatem posset actiones istaserercere: 2. quòd sic falsum sit Petrinum illud: Dextera DEI exaltatus, effudit hoc, quod videtis & auditis Act. 2, 33.

Posterior Instantia prorsus omni destituitur ἐλέγχῳ: Undè Sophisticatio vitiosi Consequentis oritur. Quæ enim, obsecro, militat ratio consequentiæ in hoc argumento: Aliud est, Christum secundum humanitatem accepisse imperium in omnes creaturas: aliud verò eundem secundum eandem esse ubique. Ergò ex Aphorismo Apostolico Omnipræsentia carnis Christi non rectè colligitur. Nam stupendam vanitatem istius collectionis plurima arguunt. 1. Apostolus utramque difertis verbis confirmat: nempè Christo secundum carnem subjecta esse omnia: & Christum secundum carnem ideò descendisse in infimas partes terræ, & ascendisse longè supra omnes cælos, ut omnia impleret. 2. Imperium in omnes res creatas præsupponit necessariò Omnipræsentiam: ita ut ex illo ad hanc rectissimè concludatur in hunc modum: Si assumto & exaltato Homini Christo, sedenti in dextera Dei, omnia sunt subjecta: & nihil omissum, quod ei non sit subjectum: impium planè fuerit, ab hac Subjectione omnium eximere velle loca, & locorum διαστήματα, quasi hæc ipsi subjecta non sint, sed potiùs hanc vim habeant, ut regnantis Christi præsentiam in his terris & alibi impedire & remorari queant. Atqui Christo secundum humanitatem, sedenti in dextera DEI omnia sunt subjecta: & NIHIL omissum, quod ei nõ sit subjectũ. Hebr. 2, 8. Ergò. 3. Si Christus ex sententia Adversariorum, secundum humanitatem abest locorum distantiis, à Creaturis illis, quibus administrandis præsidet: certè jam statuetur ipse regnare non illocati throno dexteræ DEI: sed potiùs ex remotissimo illo loco sive UBI, in quo solo juxta naturalem suam proprietatem illum commorari somniant Calviniani. Atqui hoc absurdum & impium. Ergò & illud. 4. Si λόγος tantùm præsens Creaturis omnibus per absentem Humanitatem administrat dominium hujus universi: sequetur λόγον & Creaturas illas sibi invicem præsentiores esse, quàm sit λόγος & Humanitas apud illas creaturas, quibus λόγος sine sua Humanitate adest præsens. Sed & hoc absurdissimum, imò planè Nestorianum foret. Ergò & illud. 5. Sic caro Christi absens administrat imperium super omnes creaturas, administrabit utiq́; illud, non jam ampliùs juxta conditionem regni DEI, neque juxta modum dexteræ DEI: sed ex more, conditione & sorte terrenorum regum hujus seculi: Atqui hoc quoque impium fuerit: siquidem hoc pacto deturbaretur Christus secundum humanitatem, ex solio sive throno dexteræ DEI, in quem collocatus est, subjectis ipsi omnibus, quæ nominari possunt non in hoc modò, sed & in futuro seculo. Ergò impium sit, & prius illud, necesse est. Sed quid multis opus, cum ne quidem illud credant Adversarii, nempè Humanitatem Christi, licet absentem, potenter dominari omnibus creaturis. Nam hoc ipsum est opus solius increatæ infinitæque potentiæ divinæ, quam ipsi simpliciter derogant.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: III. Argument Constructive [argument] for the Omnipresence of Christ even according to his assumed humanity

III. ARGUMENT.

Constructive [argument] for the Omnipresence of CHRIST even according to his assumed humanity.

The third and final argument is subsidiary, taken from the consensus both of Orthodox Antiquity and also of the Scholastic Doctors, from whom the modern Jesuits have made a secession. Regarding the Fathers, the Appendix of the Book of Christian Concord can and ought to be consulted: We are content with one or two. Cyril on John 12, book [12], chapter 32. Passing through individuals partibly, the only-begotten, sanctifying their soul and body through his flesh, is in all things impartibly and integrally: since he is one EVERYWHERE, in no way divided. Theophylact on Eph. 4. For this reason, therefore, he effects all these things, that he may fill all things with his dominion and operation: And that IN THE FLESH, since he already filled all things before with his Divinity. Oecumenius on chapter 4 of Eph. He ascended above all heavens, that he might fill all things: For indeed, he formerly filled all things with his naked divinity also, And having been incarnated, that he might fill all things WITH FLESH, μετὰ σαρκὸς, he descended and ascended. Chrysostom, Homily on John the Baptist: Do you seek Jesus? He is not here. Where is he? In heaven? He is beyond the heavens: on earth? He is beyond the earth: Wherever he wills, he is; wherever he is, he is whole; wherever he is, and wherever he shall be: you yourself, who seek him, are in him whom you seek. Regarding the Scholastics, not even they abhorred this doctrine, so that Hugo on 1 Cor. 10 expressly asserts that the body of Christ can be simultaneously and at once in several places, that it has from the personal union. Gabriel, book 4, dist. 10. The body of Christ is not circumscriptively in the Sacrament, but only as in a place, namely definitively. And after a few words: In the same way, by which the The intellectual soul is in the flesh, as in a place, taking place broadly, not only the unique body of Christ: but also any other body through divine power, can be in several different places uncircumscriptively and definitively, in the manner of a spirit, nay even if it wills, circumscriptively and commensurably.

Durandus of Saint-Pourçain later repeated this same thing from Gabriel, lib. 4, dist. 11, quest. 1. Petrus Aquilanus, by the nickname Scotellus, l. 4, Sent. dist. 10, quest. 1. Christ, he says, is in the Eucharist by such power, which does not require for its action that they have LOCAL BEING: but purely spiritual active powers are of this kind, namely intellect and will, which abstract from place.

Among more recent authors, Johannes Stapulensis, on John 14, writes thus: Wherever Christ is, he is incarnate: But he is not incarnate without a body. And it is a great faith to know that Christ is corporally where he is sacramentally: But it is greater to know that he is absolutely EVERYWHERE corporally: For this is to know without a mode: That is with a mode: But faith which is without a mode is greater than that which has a mode.

The same author in Chapter 12 of the first to the Corinthians: You are members of Christ in part, that is, a part of the members of Christ, but not all the members of Christ. For the faithful Corinthians were not the whole body of Christ, nay, not even Europe, nor Asia, nor Africa is capable of the fullness of Christ, I say of the body of Christ, to which our bodies are united in a spiritual way, and so to speak, are incorporated, which fills heaven and earth: For he is wherever the Word is: for the Word was made flesh. Wherefore the Word is nowhere without the flesh, nor that flesh without the Word. See that a corporal imagination does not deceive you, multiplying places, extending spaces. Neither is a multiplication of places nor an extension of spaces understood here, but a fullness without place, above every place, below every place, outside and inside every place, without space, above and below every space. And the body of Christ, according to that spiritual mode which is without a mode, is comparable to nothing, proportional to nothing, but according to the corporal mode, in which he was seen on earth, it is both comparable and proportional. This, from the assumed infirmity, admits both mode and comparison: but that, from the assuming nature, avoids mode, comparison, and every proportion. Reason does not attain this by just imagination: nor remaining rationally in itself: But it speaks and fashions absurdities on both sides: but escaping outside itself, through a power infused by a superior mind, where neither places, nor spaces, nor number, nor multitude, nor time are thought of, it truly perceives and speaks.

What? That from the Jesuit society itself, Gregorius de Valentia, in a writing published against Dr. Jacob Andreae, expressly grants several modes of being somewhere to the body of Christ, when on page 40 he writes thus: Those who are more learned see by what reason it is defended that the true body can be in several places without contradiction, by the same reason it can be defended that it can be in all places without contradiction through the absolute power of GOD.

These testimonies are certainly not produced to the end that we might build the foundations of our doctrine upon the writings of the Fathers and Scholastics: but only to show that both Orthodox Antiquity and the Scholastic Doctors even under the Papacy itself granted not just one mode of being somewhere, but several to the flesh of Christ: and utterly abhorred that dogma by which it is established that the body of Christ cannot be anywhere except locally.

Latin:

III. ARGUMENTUM.

Κατασκευατικὸν Omnipræsentiæ CHRISTI etiam secundum assumptam humanitatem.

TErtium & postremum argumentum est subsidiarium, petitum à consensu tùm Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis: tùm Scholasticorum etiam Doctorum, à quibus moderni Jesuvvitæ secessionem fecerunt. Quoad Patres, consuli potest & debet Appendix libri Christianæ Concordiæ: Nos uno atque altero contenti sumus. Cyrillus in Johan. 12. lib. cap. 32. In singulos partibiliter transiens unigenitus, & animam atque corpus eorum, per carnem suam sanctificans, impartibiliter atque integrè in omnibus est: cum unus UBIQUE sit, nullo modo divisus. Theophyl. ad Eph. 4. Ob hanc igitur causam hæc omnia efficit, ut omnia impleat dominatione operationeque: Idque IN CARNE, quandoquidem Divinitate jam ante cuncta compleret. Oecumenius ad cap. 4. Eph. Ascendit super omnes cælos, ut impleret omnia: Etenim nuda quoque divinitate olim implebat omnia: Et incarnatus, ut omnia CUM CARNE, μετὰ σαρκὸς, impleret, descendit & ascendit. Chrysost. Homil. de Johanne Baptista: Jesum quæritis? Non est hîc. Ubi est? in cælo? ultra cælos est: in terra? ultra terram est: Ubicunq; voluerit, est, ubicunq; est, totus est, ubicunq; est, & ubicunq; fuerit: tu ipse, qui illum quæris, in ipso es, quem quæris. Quoad Scholasticos, ne illi quidem ab hac doctrina abhorruerunt, ita ut Hugo in 1. Cor. 10. disertè asserat, Quòd corpus Christi potest esse simul & semel in pluribꝫ locis, id habet ex unione personali. Gabriel libro 4. dist. 10. Corpus Christi non est circumscriptivè in Sacramento, sed tantùm ut in loco definitivè scilicet. Et post pauca: Eodem modo, quo anima intellectiva est in Carne, tanquam in loco, capiendo locum largè, non solùm unicum Christi Corpus: sed & aliud quodlibet Corpus per divinam potentiam, incircumscriptivè & definitivè potest esse in pluribus diversis locis, ad modum Spiritus, imò etiam si velit, circumscriptivè, & commensurabiliter.

Quod ipsum ex Gabriele repetiit postmodùm Durandus de Sancto Portiano, lib. 4. dist. 11. quæst. 1. Petrus Aquilanus cognomento Scotellus l. 4. Sent. dist. 10. quæst. 1. Christus, inquit, ætitur in Eucharistia tali potentia, quæ non requirit ad suam actionem, ut habeant ESSE LOCALITER: sed potentiæ activæ merè spirituales sunt hujusmodi, scilicet Intellectus & voluntas, quæ abstrahunt à loco.

Ex recentioribus Johannes Stapulensis, super 14. Johannis, sic scribit: Ubicunque Christus est, incarnatus est: Incarnatus autem sine corpore non est. Et magna est Fides, cognoscere Christum corporaliter esse, ubi sacramentaliter est: Sed major est, cognoscere eum absolutè esse UBIQUE corporaliter: Nam hoc est sine modo cognoscere: Illud cum modo: Fides autem quæ est absque modo, major est, quàm quæ modum habet.

Idem in Cap. 12. prioris ad Corinth. Vos estis membra Christi ex parte, id est, pars membrorum Christi, non autem omnia membra Christi. Non enim Corinthii fideles, erant totum Corpus Christi, imò nec Europa, neq́; Asia, neq́; Aphrica capax est plenitudinis Christi, Corporis inquam Christi, cui corpora nostra spirituali modo uniūtur, & ut sic dicam, concorporantur, Quod cælum implet & terram: Est enim ubicunque Verbum est: nam Verbum Caro factum est. Quare Verbum nusquam est sine Carne, neque Caro illa sine Verbo. Videte, ne corporalis imaginatio vos ludat, loca multiplicans, spatia distendens. Neq́; hic locorum multiplicatio, neque spatiorum distensio intelligitur, sed plenitudo sine loco, supra locum omnem, infra locum omnem extra & intra locum omnem, sine spacio, supra & infra omne spacium. Et Corpus Christi super spirituali illo modo qui sine modo est, nulli comparabile, nulli proportionabile, sed corporali modo, quo in terra visus est, & comparabile, & proportionabile. Hoc ex assumta infirmitate, & modum & comparationem admittens: illud autem ex assumente Natura, modum, comparationem, omnẽq́; proportionem diffugiens. Id ratio imaginatione justa nō attingit: neq́; rationaliter in seipsa manens: Verùm absurda utrinque loquitur & effingit: sed extra se evadens supernaturaliter superiore mente infusa virtute, ubi neque loca, neque spacia, neque numerus, neq́; multitudo, neque tempus cogitantur, verè sentit & loquitur.

Quid? quòd ex ipsa societate Jesuvvitica Gregorius de Valentia, in scripto adversus D. Jacobum Andreæ edito, plures essendi alicubi modos corpori Christi expressè largitur, quando pag. 40. sic scribit: Vident qui doctiores sunt, quá ratione verum Corpus in pluribus locis, sine repugnantia esse posse defenditur, eadem ratione defendi posse, quod sine repugnantia esse possit in omnibus locis per absolutam DEI potentiam.

Quæ sanè testimonia non eo fine producuntur, quasi Patrum & Scholasticorum scriptis, doctrinæ nostræ fundamenta superstruamus: sed tantùm ut ostendamus, tùm Orthodoxam Antiquitatē, tùm sub ipso etiam Papatu Doctores Scholasticos, non unum tantùm Essendi alicubi modum, sed plures carni Christi concessisse: & ab eo dogmate prorsus abhorruisse, quo statuiter corpus Christi non nisi Localiter posse esse alicubi.


### Chapter III. on the Effect of the Hypostatic Union of the two Natures in Christ: On the State of Christ's Exinanition

ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

Although CHRIST, according to the assumed humanity, was truly and really anointed in the first moment of his conception with the entire fullness of Divine Majesty: so that even then the whole fullness of the Godhead dwelt in it bodily: yet, so that he might accomplish the work of Redemption, and be able to suffer and die: he therefore most freely emptied himself of the plenary use of that same divine Majesty according to the same humanity.

Exposition.

The Apostle lays the foundation of this thesis in Phil. 2:6 & 7. Christ Jesus, when he was in the form of GOD, did not think it robbery to be equal with GOD: but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in fashion as a man: He humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death: even the death of the cross.

Moreover, immediately at the threshold of this Question a controversy arises: according to which nature this Apostolic passage concerning Christ can and ought to be understood?

And indeed the Calvinists, who interpret that passage concerning Christ according to his divine nature, declare that they are moved by these reasons.

For first, they say, the Apostle is dealing with Christ according to that nature according to which he was equal to God: then concerning him who was found in the likeness of men, that is, concerning the λόγος, insofar as he is incarnate. Finally, they produce Athanasius, Basil, and other Fathers, who explain the form of a servant as the human nature: in this sense, that the λόγος humbled himself by assuming human nature.

But these reasons and similar ones are not of such weight or moment that they can deserve to convince.

For as regards the first Reason, a gross Sophistry is committed, τὸ μὴ ἐπομλύκ. For no argument holds: the Apostle in the place of the Subject names the person who was equal to GOD: Therefore the Emptying must be referred to the divine nature of Christ, according to which he is equal to the Father. For 1. the Apostle does not treat of the λόγῳ absolute in itself, considered by reason of divinity alone: but he treats of the λόγῳ incarnate, that is, of CHRIST, as the text expressly places the word Christ. This CHRIST therefore, who was equal to GOD the Father according to his divine nature: emptied himself, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death: But he emptied himself according to that nature which could suffer and die. For this Emptying does not pertain to the humanity by itself, or considered separately: but to the whole person; so that now not a naked Man, but the λόγος who was equal to GOD, emptied himself according to his own flesh. Then the futility of the first argument is evident also from this, that if, in the Calvinian sense, all those things which are predicated in the Scriptures concerning the λόγῳ were to be referred to his divinity alone: it would follow that the λόγον according to his divine nature was born of a woman: that according to his divine nature he suffered, was crucified, and died: Because Scripture affirms Gal. 4, 4. that GOD sent HIS SON made of a woman. Likewise. Rom. 1, 3. that he was born of the seed of David: Likewise. that the LORD OF GLORY was crucified: that GOD shed HIS OWN BLOOD: that the AUTHOR AND PRINCE OF LIFE was killed: 1. Cor. 2, 8. Acts 20. 28. Acts 3, 15. The error of the first argument is therefore corrected in this manner, that we establish: That the Emptying pertains to the person of Christ, or the λόγον incarnate: but according to that nature which is capable of Emptying: Which cannot be understood of the divine, unless one makes a secession to the camp of the Arians. THE SECOND REASON labors under a gross Ignorance of the Refutation. For the Apostle does not mean this: that the λόγον by assuming human flesh, that is, the form of a Servant, was made Man, and in this respect, the λόγον emptied himself. For the Notation of the Subject, of which the Apostle treats, opposes this Interpretation. For in the place of the Subject is not placed the word λόγος, or the Son of GOD considered absolutely: But the Word CHRIST, who is the same as the λόγος incarnate. The Sense therefore cannot be that Christ, who was already both GOD and MAN, assumed the Form of a Servant, that is, the Human Nature. Then, what is to be understood by the Form of a Servant, the immediately added ἐπεξήγησις sufficiently shows, where the Apostle defines this Form of a Servant by ὁμοίωμα καὶ σχῆμα ἀνθρώπινον, by likeness and human habit: Which notation does not regard the Essence of the human Nature: but the quality and condition of his conversation: namely, the servile one, to which the Human nature of Christ had spontaneously subjected itself. Finally, although it is a stupendous condescension that the λόγος assumed our human Nature,

& in this respect it can not inappropriately be said that the λόγον humbled himself, while for our sake he was made man: yet this is not what is properly sought between us and our Adversaries: but rather that, what is the genuine scope, and what is the proper intention of the words of the Apostle in this place. But if those things are considered more carefully, it is manifest that he does not treat of such a submission, which in its own way might also befit the Divinity: but of an Emptying, or, as the force of the Greek word declares, such an Evacuation: which cannot be attributed to the immutable Deity, as it cannot evacuate itself to death, since it does not change: Malach. 3, 6.

THE THIRD Reason does not strike us in the least: For although Athanasius, Basil, and several others of the Fathers, explained the Form of a Servant as the Human Nature: indeed, in their own sense, but less skillfully, accepted this whole Apostolic passage concerning the Incarnation of the λόγε: yet it is certain that they never and nowhere seized upon this to impugn the Majesty of the assumed Humanity. Therefore, no one of the Orthodox wished to move a dispute against them on account of this hallucination. Furthermore, it is certain that there are not lacking among the Fathers those who, having more accurately weighed the words of the Apostle, stand entirely on our side. Let a single Jerome suffice in this place, who discourses thus upon this passage to the Philippians: Because the ASSUMED MAN deigned to humble himself: the Divinity, which CANNOT BE HUMBLED, exalted him who had been humbled: But also to him was given a name which he did not have before. HENCE THIS PASSAGE IS MORE RIGHTLY TO BE UNDERSTOOD ACCORDING TO THE HUMAN NATURE, than the divine.

These things having been thus discussed, it remains that the present Apostolic passage is most rightly accepted and expounded by us concerning the emptying of CHRIST according to his human nature, according to which in the second act, he did not fully exert that divine Majesty, by which he was in the form of GOD, and which in the first point of conception, from the Union with the λόγῳ had really fallen to his lot: except for certain miraculous actions, from which, as if from rays, a judgment could be made of the indwelling Sun of divine majesty.

But the reasons and foundations, besides those already enumerated, are these:

1. The Form of a Servant in this place does not denote the human nature: but only its ὁμοίωμα καὶ σχῆμα, namely the Servile condition, or humiliation even unto the death of the cross, the Apostle himself being the interpreter. But such a Form of a Servant does not fall upon Christ according to his divine Nature. Therefore it is necessary that it be accepted according to his human nature.

2. With the ὑπερυψώσει or Exaltation of Christ succeeding, this Form of a Servant ceased: which is evident from the Apostolic opposition, by which the Form of a Servant and the ὑπερύψωσις are mutually opposed to each other, and it is asserted that the latter succeeded into the place of the former. But neither concerning the divine, nor even the Human Nature, can such a thing be said or thought, without prejudice to the analogy of faith, indeed without prejudice to the hypostatic union. Therefore it is necessary that the Form of a Servant be accepted not concerning the Essence of the human Nature, but concerning its servile condition.

§. Christ emptied himself according to that Nature according to which he was ἐν μορφῇ θεῢ, in the form of GOD. And yet Christ is in the form of GOD not according to his divine, but according to his Human Nature. For according to his divine Nature Christ is the very μορφὴ θεῢ, being indeed ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης τῢ πατρος, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως ἀυτῢ Heb. 1, 3. But it is one thing to be the very μορφὴν θεῢ: and another thing to be in μορφῇ θεῢ: the former pertains to the most absolute perfection of the Divine Essence or Nature: the latter, however, to that real κοινωνίαν of the two Natures in Christ, by which the assumed Humanity of Christ so enters into the society of the divine Nature of the λόγος, that it constitutes one person with it, and has been made σύνθρονος θεῢ. 4. These words can be understood only of the human Nature of Christ: He did not think it robbery to be equal with GOD. For robbery is that which one does not have as his own or as one, but has either snatched away from another by force, or has obtained in any other way, so that he may be able to show off another's glory or power as his own. CHRIST therefore, by reason of his humanity, did not exalt his own power, which he had, nor did he even act proudly because he was one person with him who was equal to GOD: nor did he boast as a robbery that he could by his own power conquer death and the Devil: but rather, although being GOD in the flesh, he bore humility and contempt, as a man of sorrows, Is. 53, 3. and thus, as it were, concealed the fact that he was GOD. And I ask the Adversaries to explain: In what way could the Son of GOD show off his own robbery? For robbery is nothing with respect to himself. But the λόγος is his very own Deity, far most absolute and most perfect: being GOD ἀυτοφυὴς, not by spoliation, but by nature. 5. The Greek word ἐκένωσε, He emptied, demonstrates the same thing. For κένωσις does not fall upon the Divine Nature: as was shown a little before. Finally, the Scope and intention of the Apostle proves this very thing wonderfully. For, intending to commend the zeal of humiliation to the Philippians, he wished to use the Example of Christ in this manner: If the incarnate λόγος, that is, Jesus Christ, lowered himself to such a degree that, when he had the infinite fullness of divinity dwelling in his flesh: and could most gloriously demonstrate it and show it off by a plenary usurpation: yet for our sake he spontaneously and freely abdicated this usurpation of divine Majesty: nay, he allowed himself to be snatched away to the most ignominious death of the cross: certainly it will much more behoove you, Philippians, to conform your life and morals in true humility to this Example of Christ. This orthodox doctrine concerning the State of the Exinanition of Christ is a thorn in the eyes and hearts of the Calvinists: therefore they rise up against it with great effort. They formulate their first argument thus: If Christ according to his human Nature did not in the second act exercise the Communicated Majesty: then he was not everywhere with the λόγος. Or if he was nevertheless everywhere, this Exinanition of the Human Nature collapses: and thus in both ways the doctrine of the Ubiquitarians labors. I ANSWER. The argument fails through a gross Ignorance of the Elenchus, and through the Sophism of a faulty consequence. For it does not follow: In the State of Exinanition Christ according to his human

Nature, did not in the second act exercise the Communicated Majesty: Therefore he was not then present everywhere with the λόγος? For the first personal act of the Omnipresence of the flesh of Christ is confused with the second personal act. The first personal act is that the flesh of Christ so constitutes one ὑφισάμενον with the λόγος, that it is present everywhere most presently, ἀδιαστάτως καὶ ἀχωρίστως, indistanter and inseparably with the λόγος. But the second act of the Omnipresence of the flesh of Christ is that it is not only personally present everywhere with the λόγος: but also at the same time most powerfully administers Dominion over all creatures in heaven and on earth. Now, therefore, from the State of Exinanition, the evacuation not of the first Personal act of Omnipresence, as regards the flesh of Christ: but only of the second, is most correctly inferred. Therefore, even in the deepest state of Exinanition, the flesh of Christ was nowhere distant from the λόγος even by a hair's breadth: but had the λόγος everywhere with all the fullness of his Deity dwelling within it.
