But, as regards the second personal act of Omnipresence, the flesh of Christ emptied itself by a plenary usurpation of it, in so far as it was not present to Creatures ἐνεργητικῶς: but withdrew its dominion over them: until, having laid aside the form of a Servant, it began to exercise the divine Majesty most fully. Thus, therefore, both the Omnipresence and the Exinanition of the flesh of Christ do not destroy each other, but can stand together without Contradiction.

THE OTHER Argument, which seems to be of some weight, is as follows.

The Use or Second act of Majesty is either the Word itself, or the effect of the Word: Since between Cause and Effect there is no Essential medium.

Now if the Use of Majesty is the Word itself: then it follows that by the use the evacuation, the Word itself has been evacuated, and consequently, that the personal Union itself has been dissolved: which is to be detested and abhorred.

But if the use of Majesty is an effect of the Word; it follows that the Majesty, as a created gift, has habitually inhered in the human nature, and afterwards has been evacuated, which is something the Ubiquitarians cannot concede.

If, therefore, the Use of Majesty is neither the Word itself, nor an Effect of the Word, it follows that the evacuation or exinanition has no place at all in the human nature: and consequently, that the essential properties of the Word do not belong to the human nature, except by the grace of Union or of the communication of Idioms in the Concrete: but not in the abstract.

I RESPOND, The argument fails, partly through mere petitio principii, and partly through perpetual sophistications ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐλλι- πὲς & τοῦ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For in the Major premise, an ἐλλιπὲς of division or an insufficient enumeration is immediately detected. For a third [option] can be shown, such that the use of the communicated Majesty is either the Word Himself: or the Effect of the Word, or the consequence and operation of the personal Union of the two natures in Christ. This being established, that logical axiom militates not at all. Between cause and effect, there is no essential medium. Since we ourselves [distinguish] between the personal Union, which is the true and sole cause of the Communication

Of the idioms, and between its effect, namely the communication of Majesty, we posit no essential medium. Therefore, since from our doctrine neither follows, that is, the use of Majesty, by our own concession, is neither the Word itself, nor the effect of the Word: but a third thing can be given, which is neither the Word itself simply, nor also simply the effect of the Word: certainly the entire structure of the rather prolix subsumption collapses.

For as regards the first member of the disjunctive, none of us ever said or wrote that the communicated Majesty itself, considered in itself, was emptied in the State of Humiliation. For Christ always retained that, even as Man, as invariable: since it is nothing else than the very fullness of the Divinity τῶ λόγω, with which the flesh of Christ is personally united: so that if the Majesty itself, considered in itself, were posited as emptied, the Union itself would immediately be dissolved. Wherefore from this it also manifestly appears that the consequent of this first member is clearly vicious, which concludes thus: If the use of Majesty is emptied, therefore the Word itself is emptied, and consequently, the personal Union is dissolved. For the Consequence is denied, Because the Majesty itself and the use of Majesty differ, as the first act and the second act: so that although the divine Majesty itself is nothing else than the Word itself: yet this is falsely referred to the use of this Majesty, by reason of the assumed flesh: which could be withdrawn and exercised most freely: although meanwhile the Majesty itself, or the Word, remains invariable in itself. And to this pertains that common rule: The abdication of the second act does not take away the first act.

As regards the later member of the disjunctive, the subsumption likewise labors under the sophistry παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For what reason, I ask, supports the consequence: If the use of Majesty is an effect of the Word: does it follow that Majesty, as a created gift, habitually inhered in the human nature, and was afterwards emptied?

We rather invert the argument in this manner: If the use of Majesty is an effect of the Word: it follows that the Majesty itself, from which this operation of the Word evidently emanates, is not a created gift. The reason for the consequence is this: Because the Word does not exert its divine ἐνεργείας through created gifts or created qualities. For thus an opposite in the adjunct would be posited: because the ἐνέργεια of the divine Majesty and a created quality mutually exclude each other by reason of one and the same ἀποτελεσματος. Wherefore it is necessary that this divine Majesty, which is the sole cause of such ἐνεργειῶν or ἀποτελεσματῶν, is the proper and essential, uncreated and infinite Majesty of the λόγος itself. Whence that other point about habitual inhesion also immediately collapses of its own accord. For they differ greatly, indeed in their whole genus, to inhere habitually, and to inhabit personally, and to exert and work its ἐνεργείας effectively in, with, and through the assumed flesh. And from this it now follows that Christ could indeed, by reason of the assumed Flesh, for some time empty the use, or second act, of this communicated Majesty, because it did not habitually inhere in this flesh as in a subject.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

ETsi CHRISTUS secundum assumtam Humanitatem in primo Conceptionis momento universa pleninitudine Divinæ Majestatis, verè ac realiter inunctus erat: ita ut jam tùm πᾶν πλήρωμα θεότητος in ea inhabitaret σωματικῶς: tamen, ut opus Redemtionis perficere, pati & mori posset: ideò liberrimè usum ejusdem divinæ Majestatis plenarium secundum eandem Humanitatem evacuavit.

Ἔκθεσις.

FUndamentum theseos hujus ponit Apostolus Phil. 2, 6. & 7. Christus Jesus cum in forma DEI esset, non rapinam arbitratus est, esse æqualem DEO: sed semetipsum exinanivit, Formam Servi accipiens, in similitudinem hominum factus, & habitu inventꝫ est, ut homo: Humiliavit semetipsum, factus obediens usq; ad mortem: mortem autē crucis.

Cæterùm statim in limine hujus Quæstionis oritur Controversia: secundum quam naturam locus iste Apostolicus de Christo accepti possit ac debeat?

Et sanè Calviniani, qui de Christo secundum divinam naturam, illum interpretantur, his se rationibus moveri dictitant.

Primùm enim, ajunt, de Christo secundum eam Naturam agere Apostolum, secundum quam DEO æqualis erat: Deindè de eo, qui in similitudine hominum inventus est, hoc est, de λόγῳ, quatenus incarnatus est. Tandem producunt Athanasium, Basilium, & alios Patres, qui Formam servi de Humana natura exponunt: hoc sensu, quòd λόγος se humiliârit assumendo Humanam Naturam.

Verùm rationes hæ & consimiles non tanti sunt ponderis aut momenti, ut fidem mereri possint.

Nam quoad primam Rationem craffa committitur Sophisticatio τὸ μὴ ἐπομλύκ. Neque enim ulla militat ratio: Apostolus Subjecti loco nominat personam, quæ DEO æqualis erat: Ergò Exinanitio referenda est ad divinam Christi naturam, secundum quam Patri æqualis est. Nam 1. non agit Apostolus de λόγῳ absoluto in se ratione solius divinitatis considerato: sed agit de λόγῳ incarnato, hoc est, de CHRISTO, uti textus expressè vocabulum Christi ponit. Hic CHRISTUS ergò, qui æqualis erat DEO Patri secundum divinam naturam: exinanivit seipsum obediens factus Patri ad mortem usq́; : Exinanivit autem se secundum eam naturam, quæ pati & mori potuit. Neque enim Exinanitio hæc ad humanitatem per se, aut seorsim consideratam: sed ad totam personam pertinet; ut jam non nudus Homo, sed λόγος qui æqualis erat DEO, se exinaniverit secundum propriam suam carnem. Deindè patet futilitas argumenti primi vel indè etiam, quòd, si sensu Calviniano, omnia ea, quæ in Scripturis de λόγῳ prædicantur, ad solam etiam ipsius divinitatem referenda essent: sequeretur, λόγον secundum divinam naturam natum esse ex muliere: secundum divinam naturam, passum, crucifixum, mortuum esse: Quia scriptura affirmat Gal. 4, 4. DEUM misisse FILIUM SUUM factum ex muliere. Item. Rom. 1, 3. genitum esse ex semine David: Item. DOMINUM GLORIÆ crucifixum: DEUM SUUM SANGVINEM effudisse: AUTOREM ET PRINCIPEM VITÆ interfectum esse: 1. Cor. 2, 8. Act. 20. 28. Act. 3, 15. Corrigitur proindè error primi argumenti in hunc modum, ut statuamus: Exinanitionem pertinere ad personam Christi, sive λόγον incarnatum: sed secundum eam naturam, quæ Exinanitionis capax est: Id quod de divinâ intelligi non potest, nisi ad castra Arianorum fiat secessio. SECUNDA RATIO laborat crassâ Ignoratione Elenchi. Non enim hoc vult Apostolus: λόγον assumendo carnem humanam, hoc est, Servi formam, factum esse Hominem, & hoc respectu, λόγον semetipsum exinanivisse. Repugnat enim huic Interpretationi Notatio Subjecti, de quo agit Apostolus. Subjecti enim loco non ponitur vox λόγος, sive Filii DEI absolutè considerati: Sed Vocabulum CHRISTI, qui idem est ac λόγος incarnatus. Sensus Ergò esse nequit, quòd Christus qui jam modò DEUS & HOMO erat, assumserit Formam Servi, hoc est, Humanam Naturam. Deindè, quid per Formam Servi sit intelligendum, satis ostendit mox adjecta ἐπεξήγησις, ubi Apostolus Formam hanc Servi definit per ὁμοίωμα καὶ σχῆμα ἀνθρώπινον, per similitudinem & habitum humanum: Quæ notatio non Naturæ humanæ Essentiam: sed conversationis qualitatem ac conditionem respicit: Servilem nempè, cui se Humana Christi natura spontè subjecerat. Tandem etsi stupenda dignatio est, quod λόγος humanam nostram Naturam assumsit,

& hoc respectu haud incommodè dici potest, λόγον se humiliaffe, dùm nostri causâ homo factus est: tamen non hoc propriè inter nos & Adversarios quæritur: sed illud potiùs, quis sit scopus genuinus, & quæ propria intentio verborum Apostoli hoc loco. Illa autem si pensiculatiùs considerentur, manifestum est, non de tali submissione agere, quæ suo modo etiam Divinitati conveniat: sed de Exinanitione, vel, ut vis græci verbi declarat, Evacuatione tali: quæ Deitati immutabili tribui nequit, ut quæ seipsam evacuare ad mortem non potest, cum non mutetur: Malach. 3, 6.

TERTIA Ratio nos minimè ferit: Etsi enim Athanasius, Basilius, & complures alii ex Patribus, Formam Servi, de Humanâ Naturâ expofuerunt: imò totum istum locum Apostolicum de Incarnatione λόγε, suo quodam sensu, sed minùs dextrè acceperunt: nunquam tamen & nuspiam ipsos hoc ad impugnandam Majestatem assumtæ Humanitatis, rapuisse constat. Proindè litem etiam propter hanc hallucinationem ipsis nemo Orthodoxorum movere voluit. Deindè constat non deesse ex Patribus, qui accuratiùs expensis verbis Apostoli, à nostris omninò stant partibus. Sufficiat hoc loco unicus Hieronymus, qui super hunc locum ad Philippenses sic disserit: Quia se ASSUMPTUS HOMO humiliare dignatus est: Divinitas, quæ HUMILIARI NON POTEST, eum, qui humiliatus fuerat, exaltavit: Sed & illi donatum est nomen quod antea non habuit. UNDE RECTIUS HIC LOCUS SECUNDUM HUMANAM NATURAM intelligendus est, quàm divinam.

His ita discussis, relinquitur rectissimè à nobis præsentem locum Apostolicum accipi & exponi, de exinanitione CHRISTI secundum humanam naturam, secundum quam actu secundo, non plenariè exeruit divinam illam Majestatem, quâ erat in forma DEI, quæque in primo puncto conceptionis, ex Unione cum λόγῳ realiter ipsi obtigerat: exceptis miraculosis quibusdam actionibus, ex quibus tanquam radiis, de inhabitante Sole majestatis divinæ judicium fieri poterat.

Rationes verò & fundamenta, præter jam enumerata, sunt isthæc:

1. Forma Servi hoc loco non notat humanam naturam: sed ejus tantùm ὁμοίωμα καὶ σχῆμα, nempè Servilem conditionem, sive humiliationem usq; ad mortem crucis, interprete ipso Apostolo. Atqui talis Forma Servi in Christum secundum divinam Naturam non cadit. Ergò secundum humanam naturam ea accipiatur, necesse est,

2. Succedente ὑπερυψώσει sive Exaltatione Christi, desiit Forma hæc Servi: id quod patet ex oppositione Apostolicâ, quâ sibi mutuò opponuntur Forma Servi ὑπερύψωσις, & hæc in illius locum successisse asseritur. Atquineque de divina, neque de Humana etiam Natura, tale quid, salvâ analogiâ fidei, imò salvâ unione hypostaticâ dici aut cogitari potest. Ergò Forma Servi non de Naturæ humanæ Essentia, sed de servili ejus conditione accipiatur, necesse est.

§. Christus secundum eam Naturam se exinanivit, secundum quam erat ἐν μορφῇ θεῢ, in forma DEI. Atqui non secundum divinam, sed secundum Humanam Naturam Christus est in forma DEI. Nam secundum divinam Naturam Christus est ipsissima μορφὴ θεῢ, quippè ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης τῢ πατρος, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως ἀυτῢ Heb. 1, 3. Aliud autem est, Esse ipsam μορφὴν θεῢ : aliud verò, esse in μορφῇ θεῢ: illud pertinet ad absolutissimam perfectionem Essentiae sive Naturae Divinae: Hoc verò ad realem illam κοινωνίαν duarum Naturarū in Christo, quâ assumta Humanitas Christi ita pervenit in societatem divinæ Naturæ λόγυ, ut cum ea unam personam constituat, & σύνθρονος θεῢ facta sit. 4. Non nisi de humana Christi Natura intelligi possunt hæc verba: Non arbitratus est rapinam, ut esset æqualis DEO. Rapina enim est, quod quis non ut proprium sive unum habet, sed vel alii per vim eripuit, vel quovis alio modo sortitus est, ut alienam gloriam sive potentiam tanquàm suam ostentare queat. CHRISTUS ergo ratione humanitatis suæ non extulit potentiam suam, quam habuit, neque etiam superbivit, quod unum personale esset cum eo, qui æqualis erat DEO : neque ceu rapinam jactitavit, quod posset visua mortem & Diabolum vincere : sed potiùs, quamvis DEUS existens in carne, humilitatem & despectum tulit, tanquam vir dolorum, Es. 53, 3. & sic se DEUM esse, quasi dissimulavit. Et edisserant quæso Adversarii. Quonam pacto Filius DEI sui ipsius rapinam ostentare potuerit? Rapina enim nihil est, respectu sui. Λόγος autem est ipsissima sua Deitas longè absolutissima perfectissimaque: non exspolio, sed natura existens DEUS ἀυτοφυὴς. 5. Idem demonstrat verbum Græcum ἐκένωσε Evacuavit. Neque enim κένωσις cadit in Divinam Naturam : uti paulò antè est ostensum. Tandem Scopus & intentio Apostoli hoc ipsum mirificè comprobat. Nam studium humiliationis commendaturus Philippensibus, uti voluit Exemplo Christi in hunc modum : Si λόγος incarnatus, hoc est, Jesus Christus eò usque se demisit, ut, cùm infinitam plenitudinem divinitati, in carne sua inhabitantem haberet : eamque gloriosissimè demonstrare & plenariusurpatione ostentare posset: tamen nostri causâ hanc usurpatione Majestatis divinæ sese spontè ac liberè abdicavit : imò ad ignominosissimam mortem crucis se rapi passus est : certè multò magis vos Philippenses decebit, ad Exemplum hoc Christi, vitam moresque in vera humilitate conformare. Orthodoxa hæc de Statu Exinanitionis Christi doctrina, sudes est in oculis & cordibus Calvinistarum : proindè adversus eam magno conatu insurgunt. Primùm argumentum sic informant: Si Christus secundum humanam Naturam actu secundo non exeruit Communicatam Majestatem: utique non fuit cum λόγῳ ubique. Vel si fuit nihilo minus ubique, corruit hæc Exinanitio Humanæ Naturæ: & sic utroq́; modo laborat Ubiquitariorum doctrina. RESPONDEO. Fallit argumentum crassa Ignoratione Elenchi, & Sophismate vitiosi consequentis. Non enim sequitur: In Statu Exinanitionis Christus secundum humanam

Naturam, actu secundo non exeruit Communicatam Majestatem: Ergò tùm non fuit ubique cum λόγῳ præsens? Nam confunditur actus primus personalis Omnipræsentiæ carnis Christi, cum actu secundo personali. Actus primus personalis est, quòd caro Christi ita cùm λόγῳ unû constituit ὑφισάμενον, ut ἀδιαστάτως καὶ ἀχωρίστως indistanter & inseparabiliter λόγῳ, ubique adsit præsentissima. Actus verò secundus Omnipræsentiæ carnis Christi est, quòd ea non modò cum λόγῳ ubique personaliter præsens est: sed & simul potentissimè administrat Dominium super omnes creaturas in cœlo & in terra. Jam ergò ex Statu Exinanitionis non primi actus Personalis Omnipræsentiæ, quoad carnem Christi: sed secundi tantum evacuatio rectissimè colligitur. Proindè in profundissimo etiam Exinanitionis statu, nusquàm caro Christi vel latum pilum à λόγῳ distabat: sed λόγον ubique cum omni plenitudine Deitatis suæ in se habitantem habuit. Verùm, quoad secundum actum personalem Omnipræsentiæ, caro Christi sese plenaria ejus usurpatione evacuavit, quatenus ἐνεργητικῶς Creaturis non adfuit: sed dominium in eas retraxit: usque dùm deposita Servi formâ, plenissimè Majestatem divinam exercere cœpit. Sic ergò & Omnipræsentia & Exinanitio carnis Christi, se mutuò non tollunt, sed sine Contradictione simul stare possunt.

ALTERUM Argumentum, quòd alicujus videtur esse ponderis sic habet.

Usus sive actus Secundus Majestatis, aut est ipsum Verbum, aut Verbi effectus: Siquidem inter Causam & Effectum nullum est Essentiale medium.

Jam si Usus Majestatis, est ipsam Verbum: tunc sequitur, usu evacuatio, ipsum Verbum evacuatum esse, & per consequens, ipsam Unionem personalem dissolutam esse: quod detestandum & abominandum est.

Sin usus Majestatis est Verbi effectus; sequitur, Majestatem tanquam creatum donum, habitualiter humanæ naturæ inhæsisse, & postea esse evacuatam, id quod concedere non possunt Ubiquitarii.

Si Ergò Usus Majestatis neque ipsum Verbum, neque Verbi Effectus est, sequitur evacuationem sive exinanitionem, nequaquam in humana natura locum habere: & per consequens, Verbi essentiales proprietates humanæ naturæ non competere, nisi per gratiam Unionis seu communicationis Idiomatum in Concreto: non autem in abstracto.

RESPONDEO, Fallit argumentum, partim meris principii petitionibus, partim verò perpetuis Sophisticationibus ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐλλιπὲς & τοῦ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Nam in Majore statim ἐλλιπὲς διαιρέσεως sive insufficiens enumeratio deprehenditur. Tertium enim monstrari potest, ita ut usus communicatæ Majestatis sit vel Verbum ipsum: vel Verbi Effectus, vel Unionis personalis duarum in Christo naturarum consequens & operatio. Quo stante, nihil quicquam militat axioma illud Logicum. Inter causam & effectum, nullum est essentiale medium. Siquidem nos ipsi inter personalem Unionem, quæ est vera ac unica causa Communicationis

Idiomatum, & inter ejus Effectum, nempè communicationem Majestatis, nullum Essentiale medium statuimus. Proindè cùm ex nostra Doctrina neutrum sequatur, hoc est, Usus Majestatis, nostra etiam concessione, neque sit Verbum ipsum, neque Verbi Effectus: sed dari possit tertium, quod neque Verbum ipsum sit simpliciter, neque etiam simpliciter Verbi effectus: utique corruit universa structura subsumtionis satis prolixæ.

Nam quoad prius membrum disjunctivæ, nemo nostrûm unquàm vel dixit, vel scripsit, Majestatem communicatam ipsam in se consideratam in Statu Exinanitionis esse evacuatam. Nam illam Christus semper invariabilem etiam ut Homo, tùm retinuit: quippè quæ nihil est aliud, quàm ipsa Divinitatis τῶ λόγω plenitudo, cum qua caro Christi personaliter unita est: ita ut si Majestas ipsa in se considerata evacuata statueretur, ipsa statim Unio solveretur. Quare hinc etiam manifestè patet, vitiosum planè esse consequens prioris hujus membri, quod sic colligit: Si usus Majestatis est evacuatus, Ergò Verbi ipsum est evacuatum, & per consequens, Unio personalis dissoluta. Negatur enim Consequentia, Quia Majestas ipsa & Majestatis usus differunt, ut Actus primus & Actus secundus: ita ut licèt Majestas ipsa divina, nihil sit aliud, quàm Verbum ipsum: tamen falsò hoc referatur ad Majestatis hujus usum, ratione assumtæ carnis: qui retrahi & exerceri potuit liberrimè: licèt interim Majestate ipsa, sive Verbo in se manente invariabili. Et huc pertinet vulgata illa regula: Abdicatio actus secundi, non tollit Actum primum.

Quoad posterius membrum Disjunctivæ subsumti itidem laborat Sophisticatione παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Quæ enim, obsecro, militat ratio consequentiæ: Si usus Majestatis est Verbi Effectus: sequitur, Majestatem tanquam creatum donum, habitualiter humanæ naturæ inhæsisse, & postea esse evacuatam?

Nos invertimus potiùs argumentum in hunc modum: Si usus Majestatis est Verbi Effectus: sequitur, Majestatem ipsam, quâ videlicet hæc Verbi operatio emanat, non esse creatum donum. Ratio Consequentiæ est hæc: Quia Verbum divinas suas ἐνεργείας non exerit per creata dona sive creatas Qualitates. Sic enim Oppositum in adjecto statueretur: proptereà quòd divinæ Majestatis ἐνέργεια, & creata Qualitas, se mutuò ratione unius ejusdem ἀποτελεσματος, excludunt. Quare Majestatem hanc divinam, quæ ejusmodi ἐνεργειῶν sive ἀποτελεσματῶν unica causa est, ipsius λόγε propriam ac essentialem, increatam ac infinitam Majestatem esse, necesse est. Undè illud etiam alterum de habituali inhæsione statim sua sponte coincidit. Plurimùm enim, imò toto genere differunt, Habitualiter inhærere, & personaliter inhabitare, suasque ἐνεργείας, in, cum & per assumtam carnem efficaciter exerere & operari. Et hinc jam sequitur, potuisse utique Christum ratione assumtæ Carnis, aliquandiu evacuare usum, sive actum secundum communicatæ hujus Majectis, Quia ea non habitualiter in carne hac, tanquam in subjecto inhærebat.


### Chapter V. & the Last. On the State of Exaltation. Orthodox Proposition

ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

The Exaltation of CHRIST is that State by which, having laid aside the form of a Servant, CHRIST, in himself, with respect to the assumed Flesh, having become more excellent, began to enjoy so plenarily that majesty and glory which he had indeed received from the very first moment of the incarnation, but had only rarely used during the time of humiliation; that, having been made and declared Lord of all things, he might most presently and most powerfully administer the dominion not only of the Church, but also of heaven and earth.

Ἔκθεσις.

About to dispute concerning this Exaltation of the human Nature in Christ, we first diligently distinguish the Hypostatic Union itself, and the Exaltation, which is sought in this place. For although the Human nature of Christ, hypostatically united τῷ λόγῳ, was indeed at the very first moment of the Incarnation most highly raised into the very ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου: so that a greater sublimity could not have been obtained by it: and in this respect it may deservedly be said to be exalted: yet because that Servile State intervened, and the abdication of plenary use for a time, joined with the deepest Humiliation: therefore Scripture itself did not wish to designate that raising with the word Exaltation until Christ, having finished the work of our redemption, returned victor from the dead: and having made an ascension to the heavens, sat at the right hand of GOD the Almighty Father. Which Exaltation, however, is not the acquisition of some new Majesty: but only the plenary use of that divine Majesty already communicated long ago: so that these two Exaltations differ from each other, as χρῆσις differs from κτήσει. For in the very Union itself, the Flesh of Christ was so exalted to the right hand of the divine Majesty, that if you look at the κτῆσιν, it could not have been raised more sublimely to the pinnacle of divine Majesty: but after it had now from the resurrection sat down at the right hand of GOD the Father, and began to exercise the communicated divine Majesty most fully and most powerfully: there at last that pristine κτῆσις (possession) is to be judged to have erupted into χρῆσις (use), and thus to have been manifested. With these things standing thus, it is piously and rightly believed that Christ was exalted twice according to the assumed flesh: once at the first point of conception: then in the ascension to the heavens after the resurrection from the dead. There he is believed to have obtained the κτῆσις, that is, the right and possession of divine Majesty: here, however, the χρῆσις, or full usurpation of the same, and one never again to be abdicated by any moment of eternity, so that this Exaltation depends upon the Union as χρῆσις upon κτῆσις. Nor does it stand in the way that scripture describes this Exaltation as the fruit and Effect of the preceding passion. For it did not intend to note the cause, but the manner of the thing in this way: so that it pleased GOD to introduce the Son into his glory through those passions: just as the pious also are compelled to enter into the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations. Where not the cause of this entry: but only the manner is expressed. And it is concerning this later Exaltation that it is properly disputed in this place.

There are, however, clear testimonies of the Scriptures which evidently confirm this State of Exaltation.

These two are classic: The first Eph. 1, 20. & 21. The Father raised Christ from the dead, and set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality and power, and might and dominion, and every name that is named not only in this age, but also in the future.

The latter, Phil. 2, 9. & 10. Therefore GOD exalted him, and gave him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth: and every tongue should confess that Christ is Lord in the glory of GOD the Father.

If the weight of these testimonies is observed more accurately, it will be easy to know: 1. That this Exaltation does not regard finite or created gifts as its object, but the very infinite fullness of divine Majesty. 2. To whom this very Exaltation has happened.

Certainly, that it must be referred to Christ, and thus to his person, is not ambiguous: since both Apostolic Aphorisms have the word CHRIST placed in the position of the subject. But with respect to which nature CHRIST is thus exalted, that does not seem so plain to all. We judge that defining the Exaltation of Christ with respect to his Divinity is entirely at odds with pious truth. For, to use the words of Cyril, To whom Humility is appropriate, he is also said to be exalted conveniently. But Christ was humbled according to his human Nature: therefore he is understood to be exalted also. Furthermore, the word Exaltation cannot be attributed to Divinity. For, as Cyril speaks again in the same place, The Son of GOD is always most high, as GOD. Then the Greek word ἐχαρίσατο (he gave) clearly proves this very thing: For we are nothing removed from Arianism, if

we judge that something was given to Christ in time with respect to his Divinity. Therefore, according to the nature of the flesh, he was exalted, crowned, and obtained a name of better dignity, he who according to the nature of the Word never needed these things at any time, as Vigilius piously spoke: lib. 5. against Eutyches. Which very thing orthodox Antiquity felt most firmly: from which let it be permitted to hear one Athanasius, who writes most excellently in Orat. 2. against the Arians: That it is said, He exalted him: does not signify that the substance of the Word was exalted: For he was and always is equal to GOD: but it regards his humanity. Nor were these things said before, than when, when the Word had already been made Flesh, so that it might be made plain that that (He humbled) and that (He exalted) were said concerning man. For whose it is to be humble, his it will also be to be exalted: And if this word (He humbled) was written because of the assumption of Flesh: it is clear and manifest that that (He exalted) was used because of the same Flesh. Many today offend against this purer doctrine. For there are those who restrict this glory of exaltation to that office alone, which Christ performs in the Church. Those who reduce this Exaltation only to the office of Mediator do not differ much from their opinion. But both are refuted most vigorously if any discrepancy between the office of Mediation and Exaltation is weighed more accurately. For although we do not entirely separate Mediation from exaltation: meanwhile, however, we maintain that these two are not one and the same. First, it is certainly established that the parts of the office of Mediation are momentary, and durable for a time: so that the Apostle expressly asserts that this kingdom will have an end at some time, and is to be handed over to the Father, then when the whole Church is transferred to blessed tranquility. 1. Cor. 15, 24. But the power of Exaltation is eternal, Dan. 7, 27. Luc. 1, 33. Eph. 1, 21. Then these two offices differ in Latitude or Amplitude of object. For the office of Mediation regards only the Redemption of the human race, and its application to the pious and faithful. But the power or glory of Exaltation regards all the works of GOD, so that even the Demons themselves are subject to him. Then they differ in the manner of administration. For the office of Mediation is performed by mercy and grace. But the Majesty of Exaltation is administered also by justice and judgment. Finally, Christ did not need the office of Mediation by reason of himself: but we needed it: Thus he himself is not perfected by it: but we are, and are rendered more blessed: and therefore this office could be entrusted to him in time even by reason of his Divinity, without any change of his Deity. But the Holy Spirit describes the glory and office of Exaltation in such a way that Christ himself was MADE more excellent thereby, and indeed in time. Hebr. 1, 4. But since the glory of this Exaltation shines forth most of all from the Ascension of Christ to the heavens and his sitting at the right hand of GOD the Father; it is pleasing to treat of each separately.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

EXalatio CHRISTI est Status ille, quo depositâ Servi formâ CHRISTUS in se ipso, respectu assumtæ Carnis, præstantior factus, eâ majestate atque gloriâ, quam à primo statim incarnationis momento acceperat quidem:sed exinanitionis tempore non nisi rarò usurpaverat; sic plenariè frui cœpit, ut Dominus rerum omnium, factus declaratusque, præsentissimè potentissimeque non Ecclesiæ tantùm, sed & cœli terræquè dominium administraret.

Ἔκθεσις.

DE hac Exaltatione humanæ Naturæ in Christo disputaturi, initiò Unionem ipsam Hypostaticam, & Exaltationem, de qua hoc loco quæritur, diligenter distingvimus. Etsi enim Humana Christi natura τῷ λόγῳ hypostaticè unita, primo quidem statim Incarnationis momento summè evecta est in ipsam nimirùm ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου: ita ut hac sublimitate major ipsi obtingere haud potuerit: & hoc respectu exaltata ipsa meritò dici queat: Quia tamen intervenit Status ille Servilis, & usurpationis plenariæ ad tempus abdicatio, cum profundissima Exinanitione conjuncta: ideò Scriptura ipsa Evectionem illam haud prius Exaltationis vocabulo insignire voluit: quàm Christus consummato redemtionis nostræ opere, victor ex mortuis rediit: & ascensione ad cœlos facta, ad dexteram DEI Patris Omnipotentis consedit. Quæ tamen Exaltatio non est novæ alicujus Majestatis acquisitio:sed plenaria tantùm communicatæ jampridem illius Majestatis divinæ usurpatio: ita ut duæ hæ Exaltationes differant à se mutuò, ut χρῆσις differt à κτήσει. Nam in ipsa statim Unione Caro Christi sic ad dexteram Majestatis divinæ exaltata est, ut si κτῆσιν spectes, sublimiùs ad divinæ Majestatis fastigium evehi haud potuerit: postquam verò jam à resurrectione consedit ad dexteram DEI Patris, & communicatam Majestatem divinam plenissimè ac potentissimè exercere cœpit: ibi demùm pristina illa κτῆσις, in χρῆσιν erupisse, & sic manifestata esse, censenda est. Quibus sic stantibus piè rectéque Christus secundum assumtam carnem bis exaltatus esse: semel in primo conceptionis puncto: deindè in ascensione ad cœlos post resurrectionem ex mortuis. Ibi κτῆσιν, hoc est, Majestatis divinæ jus ac possessionem: hîc verò ejusdem χρῆσιν, sive usurpationem plenariam, & nullo æternitatis momento ampliùs abdicandam, adeptus esse creditur, ita ut Exaltatio hæc ab Unione dependeat tanquàm Χρῆσις â κτήσει. Neque obstat, quòd scriptura hanc Exaltationem tanquam fructum & Effectum passionis antegressæ describit. Neque enim causam, sed modum rei hoc pacto notare voluit: ita ut placuerit DEO per passiones istas introducere Filium in gloriam suam: quemadmodum pii etiam per multas tribulationes ingredi coguntur in regnum cœlorum. Ubi non causa ingressus hujus: sed modus tantùm exprimitur. Et de posteriore hac Exaltatione propriè hoc loco controvertitur.

Sunt autem perspicua Scripturarum testimonia, quæ Statum istum Exaltationis evidenter confirmant.

Classica sunt hæc duo: Priùs Eph. 1, 20. & 21. Pater suscitavit Christum à mortuis, & constituit ipsum ad dexteram suam in cœlestibus, supra omnem principatum & potestatem, & virtutem & dominationem, & omne nomen, quod nominatur non solùm in hoc seculo, sed & in futuro.

Posterius, Phil. 2, 9. & 10. Propterea exaltavit ipsum DEUS, & donavit illi nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, cœlestium, terrestrium, & inferorum: & omnis lingva confiteatur, quod Christus sit Dominus in gloria DEI Patris.

Quorum testimoniorum momenta si accuratiùs observentur, promptum fuerit cognoscere: 1. Exaltationem hanc objecti loco non finita aut creata dona, sed ipsam infinitam divinæ Majestatis plenitudinem respicere. 2. Cuinam hæc ipsa Exaltatio obtigerit.

Certè ad Christum, & sic ad personam referri illam debere, non est ambiguum: cum uterque Aphorismus Apostolicus, subjecti loco habeat positum vocabulum CHRISTI. Cæterùm cujus naturæ respectu, CHRISTUS sit sic exaltatus, illud non ita planum videtur omnibus. Nos Divinitatis respectu Exaltationem Christi definiendam esse, à pia veritate prorsus dissentaneum esse, arbitramur. Nam ut Cyrilli verbis utamur, Cui Humilitas congruit, hic exaltari quoque dicitur convenienter. Atqui secundum humanam Naturam Christus humiliatus est: ipsa ergò exaltata quoque esse intelligitur. Porrò Exaltationis vox Divinitati tribui nequit. Nam uti rursum Cyrillus ibidem loquitur, Filius DEI semper est altissimus, ut DEUS. Tùm verbum græcum ἐχαρίσατο Donavit, hoc ipsum luculenter evincit: Nihil enim ab Arianismo absumus, si

Christo respectu Divinitatis aliquid in tempore donatum esse, arbitramur. Proindè secundum carnis naturam exaltatus, coronatus, melioris dignitatis nomen adeptus est, qui secundum naturam Verbi horum nullo eguit aliquando, ut Virgilius piè locutus est: lib. 5. contra Eutychen. Quod ipsum orthodoxa Antiquitas firmitsimè sensit: ex qua liceat unum audire Athanasium, qui Orat. 2. contra Arianos, sic præclarissimè scribit: Quòd dicitur, Exaltavit eum: non substantiam Verbi exaltatam significat: Fuit enim & semper est æqualis DEO: sed humanitatem ejus spectat. Neque ista priùs dicta fuêre, quàm cùm, cùm jam Verbum Caro esset factum, ut palàm fieret illud (Humiliavit) & illud (Exaltavit) de homine dictum essê. Cujus enim est humilem esse, ejus quoque fuerit exaltari: Et si ob assumptionem Carnis Verbum hoc (Humiliavit) est scriptum: clarum manifestumq; est, propter eandem Carnem illud (Exaltavit) usurpatum esse. Contra puriorem istam doctrinam à multis hodiè delinquitur. Sunt enim, qui gloriam istam exaltationis ad illud duntaxat officium restringunt, quo Christus in Ecclesia fungitur. A quorum sententia haud multùm distant, qui Exaltationem hanc ad officium Mediatoris tantùm redigunt. Sed utrique nervosissimè refutantur, si quid discrepantiæ Mediationis officio & Exaltationi intercedat, accuratiùs expendatur. Etsi enim Mediationem ab exaltatione non omninò sejungimus: Interim tamen duo isthæc unum idemque esse pergamus. Primùm certè constat Mediationis officii partes, esse momentaneas, & ad tempus durabiles: ita ut Apostolus disertè asserat, hoc regnum aliquando finem habiturum, & Patri tradendum esse, tùm quando universa Ecclesia ad beatam tranquillitatem transferetur. 1. Cor. 15, 24. Atqui potestas Exaltationis est æterna, Dan. 7, 27. Luc. 1, 33. Eph. 1, 21. Deindè differunt hæc duo officia Latitudine sive Amplitudine objecti. Officium enim Mediationis respicit tantùm Redemtionem generis humani, ejusque ad pios & fideles applicationem. At potestas sive gloria Exaltationis respicit omnia opera DEI, ita ut ipsi quoque Dæmones ipsi subjaceant. Tùm differunt modo administrationis. Officium enim Mediationis peragitur misericordia & gratia. Majestas autem Exaltationis, administratur etiam justitia & judicio. Tandem Officio Mediationis Christus ratione sui non indiguit: sed nos indiguimus: Sic non ipse: sed nos indè perficimur, & beatiores reddimur: ideoque hoc officium etiam ratione Divinitatis in tempore ei demandari potuit, sine ulla Deitatis ipsius immutatione, Atqui Exaltationis gloriam & officium ita describit Spiritus Sanctus, ut Christus ipse indè præstantior sit FACTUS & quidem in tempore. Hebr. 1, 4. Cæterùm cùmExaltationis hujus gloria, ex Ascensione Christi ad cœlos ejusdemque sessione ad dextram DEI Patris, vel maximè elucescat; placet de utramque seorsim agere.


### Chapter V. & the Last. On the State of Exaltation. Orthodox Proposition: I. On the Ascension of Christ to Heaven

ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

CHRIST, after he had spent forty days with his disciples since his resurrection, while they were looking on, truly and not feignedly with his body from the lower place of the Mount of Olives, through τοπικὴν μετάστασιν or local translation, was gradually lifted up more and more, until a cloud received him, and having been withdrawn from the sight of the disciples, carried him into heaven: where he sat down at the right hand of the infinite Omnipotence of GOD the Father.

Ἔκθεσις (Exposition).

The history of the Ascension, described in Mark 16:19 and Acts 1:9 et seqq., confirms the truth of this proposition: which we are so far from transmuting into an allegory, or interpreting as some empty spectacle or imaginary play, or even as a disappearance, that we rather take its individual and universal parts κτ᾽ ῥητὸν (according to the letter): and we understand this Ascension as a true and real ascent, a true change of place, and a local lifting up of the body of Christ.

There are, however, two things especially that come under consideration regarding this Ascension of CHRIST. The first, indeed, is what difference exists between the Ascension of Christ and that of other Saints into heaven. The second, however, is how that Heaven, to which Christ ascended, is to be defined.

Regarding the first member, the Ascension of Christ differs from the ascension of other Saints, such as Enoch and Elijah, in three ways especially.

For first, CHRIST by his own virtue and power—both that which he received according to the flesh from the Union as truly divine, and that which is proper to the Divinity—lifted his body to the heavens: Enoch and Elijah, however, were translated into heaven not by their own, but by a clearly alien virtue: Hence John 20:17 says: I ascend to my Father and your Father, etc.

Then, from the Ascension to the heavens, Enoch, Elijah, and other Saints were lifted up to eternal life and that glory which they have in common with all the blessed and elect, though with a difference of degrees maintained. But Christ the Savior, ascending to heaven, arrived not only at that glory according to the flesh which is proper to eternal life and celestial blessedness, but at that which is comparable to the glory of the Saints by no degrees and in no ways, being in its whole kind greater, more sublime, and more divine, which is evident from his session at the right hand of the Omnipotence of GOD: as will be demonstrated a little later.

Finally, the Saints ascended into heaven in such a way that they completely removed all their presence from these lands: 2 Kings 2:16 et seqq. Christ, however, was lifted up into Heaven with his body in such a way that he is nevertheless truly and most presently present in these lands, both to the faithful and to all creatures, in that same body of his: not indeed by a local or visible presence, but by an illocal and invisible one: according to the manner of his session at the right hand of GOD, by whose virtue, even after the Ascension, he was present and working with the Apostles as they preached everywhere, Mark 16:24, and works with them today: according to that most sweet promise of the Savior himself: Behold I AM with you all days even to the consummation of the age, Matt. 28:20. Likewise, Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them, Matt. 18:20. Indeed, by whose virtue he also rules, as man and Son of David, in the midst of his enemies, Psalm 110:2. he walks in the midst of the golden lampstands, even as the Son of Man, Rev. 2:1.

The Apostle embraced these individual and universal things with very significant words and phrases, Ephesians 4:9 and 10. Saying, Now that he ascended, what is it, but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth? He that descended is the same also that ascended up above all heavens, that he might FILL ALL THINGS: that is, that he might rule everywhere most presently. That this passage is understood by Adversaries of CHRIST according to his divine nature too absurdly is evident from the fact that it would follow: that Christ therefore ascended and descended according to his divine Nature, so that according to his divine Nature he might fill all things and rule everywhere most presently: which would be prodigiously both absurd and blasphemous.

The latter part of this treatise is concerning Heaven, into which Christ ascended: What that may be, and how it can and ought to be defined? There are found some among the Scholastics who define Heaven as a higher, most ample, round place, surrounding the primum mobile, while it itself remains immobile, which is the domicile or house of the Father, and the seat of the blessed spirits, of angels and of men: Which Heaven they named Empyrean, in which dances and leaps and other ludic actions of that kind are sometimes to be instituted by the blessed inhabitants of heaven. This opinion was embraced from the Ancients by Rosetus, Bernardinus, and from the more recent ones, Johannes Keisersbergius. But these gross imaginations concerning Heaven are clearly unworthy to be refuted more copiously, as they collapse by their own subtlety.

Then, however, the Jesuits, not much abhorring from that gross delirium of the Scholastics, while they establish that this Heaven is corporeal, for so Bellarmine [states] in book 3 of the Incarnation of the Word, chapter 12.

Catholics believe that Christ ascended into a true corporeal heaven, whether he remains within that heaven itself, or remains above and outside all heavens, in such a way that he touches with his feet the convex surface of the highest heaven. But these profane imaginations are refuted without any difficulty. For if Christ ascended into a certain corporeal heaven in such a way that he nevertheless remains within heaven, it would be false that Scripture affirms that CHRIST ascended above all heavens (Eph. 4, 10), that he penetrated the heavens (Heb. 4, 14), and was made higher than the heavens (Heb. 7, 26). And again, if he remains above and outside all heavens, it would be most absurd to affirm that the heaven into which Christ ascended is a corporeal heaven: as if, indeed, outside and above all heavens there could be any corporeal heaven, which is something that conflicts even with sounder philosophy.

But however absurd this opinion may be, the Jesuit nevertheless tries to defend it, saying: CHRIST ascended to that heaven where the seat of GOD is; but that heaven is corporeal. Therefore, Christ ascended to a corporeal heaven, and is in a corporeal heaven. He confirms the minor premise thus: Those things which are mutually opposed to one another must be of the same nature. But Scripture in many places opposes heaven to earth, taking the word 'earth' in its proper signification: as in Psalm 115, 16: 'The heaven of heaven is for the Lord, but the earth he has given to the children of men.' Isaiah 66, 1: 'Heaven is my seat, the earth is the footstool of my feet,' etc. Therefore, the heaven which is opposed to the earth must be taken in the same way, for a corporeal heaven.

I answer that the major premise is simply false. For not only is it not necessary that those things which are mutually opposed to one another be of the same nature, but on the contrary, those things which are of different natures are opposed to each other. Therefore, from the produced testimonies of Scripture, by the force of opposition it necessarily follows that the heaven which is the throne of GOD is not of the same nature as the earth, but of a very different one, because heaven is opposed to earth. Furthermore, if according to the Jesuit hypothesis the heaven which is the throne of GOD is corporeal, then the throne of GOD itself will certainly be corporeal; and indeed, he who sits on this throne will be a corporeal GOD. All these things are absurd, impious, and blasphemous. And rightly did St. Augustine once respond to these crude and old-womanish imaginations: If the heaven which is the throne of GOD is corporeal, and if we have understood the corporeal heaven which we see with our eyes to be the dwelling of GOD, the dwelling of GOD will pass away, because heaven and earth will pass away. But before GOD made heaven and earth, where did He dwell? GOD dwelt in Himself; GOD dwelt with Himself; and GOD is with Himself.

Thirdly. The Calvinists take 'Heaven' to mean a certain finite and distinct dwelling above the starry region, by which the body of CHRIST is so received that it has occupied a certain space and circumference of place in it, by which it is so circumscribed and contained that, while it is encompassed by it, it cannot be elsewhere, either in heaven or on earth; indeed, outside of which it is in no way anywhere; from which it also follows that his body is distant from us by as great an interval of places as Heaven is distant from the earth; so that, on account of this very ascension into the heavens, his true and substantial body cannot be present in the Holy Supper; much less should it be believed that Christ, through His Humanity, is present in any way to the whole Church or to all other creatures. The Calvinists do not only hold this opinion, as Calvin in the Formula of Confession, p. 25, and Beza, Vol. 1, Theological Tracts, p. 658, Question 15, and likewise Bullinger and others. But our author Philip also, in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 3, wished not obscurely to insinuate this, writing thus: 'He ascended into the heavens; he ascended, that is, by a bodily and physical location: Into Heaven, that is, into a heavenly place, wherever it is, because here allegories are not to be feigned.' Likewise, 'He ascended into the heavens, where the Word made flesh did not sit before: that is, WHERE THE BODY HAD NOT PREVIOUSLY HAD A BODILY LOCATION.' Which words surely argue clearly that Philip, by the Ascension into the heavens and the subsequent session at the right hand of GOD, understood a bodily location, and thus not obscurely criticized the opinion of Luther, who explained the heavens not at all by a Place, but by the Heavenly Kingdom, and the session at the right hand of GOD the Father not by a bodily location, but by divine Majesty and Omnipotence.

However, this opinion labors under the same absurdities which we have already noted in the dogma of the Jesuits. For this heaven, as it has now been defined, will certainly perish on the last day (Ps. 102, 27), nor will any account of it be held among the elect, because THEY WILL NOT REMEMBER the former heavens and the former earth (Isa. 65, 17; 2 Pet. 3, 13).

2. If the Heaven to which Christ ascended is a corporeal place, above all visible heavens, it will follow, as often as GOD is said in the Scriptures to look down upon the children of men (Psalm 14), that He beholds men far removed from a most distant corporeal heaven: that He sends down His help through the primum mobile, through the Sphere of the fixed stars, and the remaining lower orbs? That GOD, also, about to descend from heaven to the children of men, lowers Himself from that highest corporeal Heaven, until at last He comes through all the orbs of the planets, and the air, down to the earth. Who does not see that these things are more absurd than the most absurd? Certainly, since GOD is not far from each one of us (Acts 17, 27). Since GOD is not from afar, but is a GOD who is near; since He is near to all who call upon Him in truth: it is certain that GOD, and outside of which He can never and nowhere be, is most viciously defined by some highest, and indeed corporeal, place. Since GOD is not deprived of this heaven of His, to which Christ also ascended and in which He sat down at the right hand of GOD, even in the lowest earth: But as from eternity before the creation of heaven and earth, He was in this His heaven, so in the same He immutably always is and remains, whether He is present to us in these lands, or to the Elect in eternal life, or to other creatures.

Finally, no condition of place or physical locality falls upon the glorified bodies of the Elect, so much so that it is not even essential in a ψυχικῷ or animal body: as we have shown professedly above in Chapter 1. What, therefore, was this stupendous audacity, to include the Body of Christ—which is not only glorious from the Resurrection, but is also anointed with the infinite fullness of divine Majesty—in some corporeal Heaven, such that it must necessarily be circumscribed by a physical place? Jacob Faber Stapulensis judged much more correctly, writing on Chapter 12 of the first to the Corinthians: 'One must take care that a corporeal imagination does not play here, multiplying places, extending spaces: for here neither the multiplication of places nor the extension of spaces is understood: but fullness without place, above every place, outside and inside every place, without space, above and below every space, outside and inside every space.'

But however impious and absurd this opinion of the Calvinists concerning Heaven may be, they nevertheless do not fear to undertake its defense. And at the beginning, there are those who strive to infringe upon our first argument by saying that not this corporeal Heaven, but only the remaining heavens will perish. But I respond that this is nothing other than heaping absurdities upon absurdities. For from this it would follow that, with the other Heavens or Orbs, both individual and universal, perishing—which were enclosed round about by this Heaven to which Christ ascended, and by a corporeal heaven indeed—a vacuum or void would be left within the circuit of that Heaven: which is by far the most absurd thing, both in our Theology and in Philosophy.

Then they very ignorantly urge those testimonies of the Scriptures in which Heaven is named a mansion, likewise a house, indeed a place. For that the heavenly Kingdom or blessed life is named thus figuratively and metaphorically is more manifest than to require laborious proof. And Scripture uses such words taken from the condition of our age and the likeness of earthly kingdoms, because 'Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man, what the condition of the other life will be.' 1 Cor. 2:9.

Thirdly, they also strive to strike us with this horned Syllogism: 'No one betakes himself to where he is already actually present with his body: No one also departs from where he remains with his body. Therefore, if Christ truly ascended into heaven with his body: he certainly was not there before, and thus Ubiquity collapses: or if he was there before, the Ascension itself collapses.'

Therefore it would be safest to establish that Christ ascended with his body to where he was not before: and thus departed from these lands in such a way that he remains in a certain place of Heaven until the last day.

I respond. The argument fails through the confusion of disparate modes of presence, of which one is Natural: the other Personal: which two Modes, being subordinate, can stand together, nor do they mutually overturn each other: as was shown more fully above. Therefore, it is to be referred to natural presence that the body of Christ was lifted upward by local translation, in such a way that, by this reason, it as it were emptied and left behind one lower place after another: and ascended upward on high by a solid and real change of places. Which local change and condition did not prevent it from being simultaneously in Heaven in the hypostasis of the λόγῳ: Just as Christ himself explicitly attests, John 3:13: 'No one has ascended into Heaven, except he who descended from heaven, the SON OF MAN, who is in Heaven.' Again, that Christ, having been translated into heaven with his body, nonetheless remains invisibly in these lands, that happens on account of the personal subsistence in the λόγῳ, who, being most present everywhere in Heaven and on earth, has nothing more present to himself than this very flesh of his, in that the Union is simply ἀδιάsατῶ, conveniently excluding every distance of natures and absence from one another. It is added that the ultimate terminus of the Ascension of the Flesh of Christ was not some physical Place by which it would be circumscribed: but the very right hand of GOD, included by no place, excluded by no place, as will be demonstrated presently: so that, although according to the condition of Nature the Body of Christ is Naturally in some certain πῷ: nevertheless, from the Union and session at the right hand of GOD, it is most present everywhere Personally.

Finally, as the shield of Achilles, they turn against us that passage Acts 3:21: ὃν δεῖ τὸν ὐρανὸν δέξαź: Which they translate thus: 'Whom it behooves to be taken by heaven.'

I respond. The crime of falsity is committed in the vicious Latin version. For Scripture itself demonstrates most sufficiently that the Greek words are not to be understood passively, but actively. For if Christ ascended into Heaven for this reason, that he might be taken or contained by Heaven, how, I ask, could it be said that he penetrated the heavens themselves, how that he was made higher than the heavens themselves, how that he was exalted from this ascension above everything that is named not only in this age, but also in the future one, Heb. 7:26, Eph. 1:21? How, finally, would it be true that all things are subject to him according to that nature according to which he ascended, so that nothing is omitted which is not subject to him, Heb. 2:8? For if All things are subject to him: why not even Heaven itself. Therefore, having repudiated the passive signification of the verb δέξαź, we most rightly urge the active, moved moreover by Apostolic authority, who explains this phrase, "it behooves Heaven to receive Christ," by this equipollent one, "it behooves Christ to reign &c," 1. Cor. 15, 25. Whence Peter describes this effect of the reception of Heaven thus: Christ has gone into Heaven, with Angels, authorities, and powers being made subject to him. 1. Petr. 3, 22. If to these: Why not with Heaven itself also being made subject? Finally, Calvin himself, expounding this passage, willingly confessed that from the word δέξαź, since it is middle and ambiguous, nothing certain can be concluded in this controversy. Although Beza in his Greater annotations persuades that the passive interpretation of this verb must be retained: in the place, which is called, Wise: For thus he himself writes: a certain text can be had, which ought to be opposed to those who teach that the true Body of Christ is present and consumed in the Supper.

Such a manifest depravation of Scripture is that asylum of the Sacramentarians, to which they retreat in this lost cause of theirs. A manner of disputing which we certainly do not envy them; meanwhile committing the judgment concerning it to others, nay, to the whole Church of CHRIST.

Those false opinions concerning Heaven, to which Christ ascended, being rejected and condemned, we finally establish that this Heaven is most rightly defined, both by heavenly condition, state, glory, and blessedness; and also by that divine, infinite, and uncreated majesty and inaccessible light, in which GOD dwells, exposed to no physical places or any other earthly conditions: which will now appear more clearly from the Session at the right hand of the Father.

Latin:

PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

CHRISTUS postquàm à resurrectione sua quadraginta dies conversatus est cum discipulis suis, intuentibus his, verè & non simulate corpore suo ex inferiore loco Oliveti per τοπικὴν μετάστασιν sive localem translationem, paulatim sursum magis magisque evectus est, donec nubes ipsum excepit, & è conspectu discipulorum subductum, in cœlum transtulit: ubi consedit ad dextram infinitæ Omnipotentiæ DEI Patris.

Ἔκθεσις.

PRopositionis hujus veritatem confirmat historia Ascensionis, Marci 16, 19. & Act. 1, 9. & seqq. descripta: quam tantum abest, ut in Allegoriam transmutemus: vel per inane quoddam spectaculum, sive lusum imaginarium: vel etiam per disparitionem interpretemur: ut potiùs singula & universa ejus membra κτ᾽ ῥητὸν accipiamus: & Ascensionem hanc, de vero ac reali ascensu, veraque loci mutatione, & locali corporis Christi subvectione intelligamus.

Duo autem potissimùm sunt, quæ circa Ascensionem hanc CHRISTI sub considerationem veniunt, Primum quidem, quid discriminis intercedat Ascensioni Christi, & aliorum Sanctorum in cœlum. Alterum verò, Quomodo Cœlum illud, ad quod Christus afcendit, sit definiendum.

Quoad prius membrum, Ascensio Christi ab ascensione aliorum Sanctorum, ut Henochi & Eliæ, tribus potissimùm modis differt.

Primùm enim CHRISTUS propriâ virtute potentiâque tam eâ, quam secundum carnem ex Unione verè divinam accepit, quàm eâ, quæ Divinitatis est propria, corpus suum ad cœlos evexit: Henoch verò & Elias non propriâ, sed alienâ planè virtute in cœlum sunt translati: Hinc Johan. 20, 17. dicit. Ascendo ad Patrem meum & Patrem vestrum &c.

Deindè ex Ascensione ad cœlos, Henoch, Elias & alii Sancti, ad vitam æternam & eam gloriam sunt evecti, quam cum beatis & electis omnibus, servatâ tamen graduum differentiâ communem habent. At Christus Servator ascendens ad cœlum, non ad eam tantùm gloriam secundum carnem pervenit, quæ vitæ æternæ & beatitudinis cœlestis est propria, sed ad eam, quæ nullis gradibus, nullísque modis ad Sanctorum gloriam est comparabilis, toto quippè genere major, sublimior ac divinior, id quod ex sessione à dextris Omnipotentiæ DEI elucet: uti paulò pòst demonstrabitur.

Tandem Sancti ita in cœlum ascenderunt, ut omnem sui præsentiam in terris hisce prorsus sustulerint: 2. Reg. 2, 16. & seqq. Christus autem ita in Cœlum evectus est suo corpore, ut nihilominus eodem suo corpore reverà in terris hisce tùm fidelibus, tùm universis creaturis præsentissimè adsit: non quidem locali aut visibili præsentia, sed, illocali ac in visibili: secundum modum sessionis ad dextram DEI, cujus virtute post Ascensionem etiam, Apostolis ubique prædicantibus præsens cooperabatur. Marci 16, 24. hodieque cooperatur : secundum promissionem illam dulcissimam ipsius Servatoris: Ecce E G O sum vobiscum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem sæculi, Matth. 28, 20. Item, Ubi duo aut tres congregati sunt in nomine meo, ibi sum in medio eorum Matth. 18, 20. Imò cujus virtute, dominatur etiam quà homo & Filius Davidis in medio inimicorum suorum, Psal. 110, 2. ambulat in medio candelabrorum aureorum, etiam, quà Filius Hominis Apoc. 2, 1.

Quæ singula atque universa significantibus admodùm verbis atque phrasibus complexus est Apostolus, Ephes. 4, 9. & 10. Quod, inquiens, ascendit, quid est, nisi quod & descendit primùm in infimas partes terræ? Qui descendit ipse est, qui & ascendit supra omnes cælos, ut O M N I A I M P L E R E T: hoc est, ubique præsentissimè dominaretur. Quem sanè locum de CHRISTO secundum divinam naturam nimis absurdè ab Adversariis intelligi, vel indè patet, quod sic sequeretur: Christum ideò secundum divinam Naturam ascendisse & descendisse, ut secundum divinam Naturam impleret omnia, & ubique dominaretur præsentissimè: id quod prodigiosè & absurdum & blasphemum foret.

Posterius Tractationis hujus membrum est, de Cœlo, in quod Christus adscendit, Quidnam illud sit, & quomodo definiri possit ac debeat? Reperiuntur ex Scholasticis nonnulli, qui Cœlum definiunt loco supero, amplissimo, rotundo, ambiente primum mobile, ipso verò permanente immobili, quod sit domicilium sive domus Patris, & sedes Spirituum beatorum, Angelorum & hominum: Quod Cœlum nominarunt Empyreum, in quo à beatis cœlitibus aliquando instituendæ sint choreæ & saltationes, aliæque id genus actiones ludicræ. Quam sententiam ex Veteribus amplexi sunt Rosetus, Bernardinus, & ex recentioribus, Johannes Keisersbergius. Sed crassæ hæ imaginationes de Cœlo, indignæ planè sunt, ut refutentur copiosiùs, qui propria sutilitate concidunt.

Deindè verò Jesuvvitæ, haud multùm à crasso isto Scholasticorum delirio abhorrentes, dùm Cœlum istud statuunt esse corporeum, Sic enim Bellarminus lib. 3. de Incarnat. verbi cap. 12.

Catholici credunt, Christum in verum cœlum corporeum adscendisse sive maneat intra ipsum cœlum, sive maneat supra & extra omnes cœlos, ita ut pedibus tangat convexum summi cœli. Sed & hæ prophanæ imaginationes nullo negotio refelluntur. Si enim Christus ita in cœlum quoddam corporeum adscendit, ut tamen maneat intra cœlum: falsum fuerit, quod Scriptura affirmat, CHRISTVM adscendisse supra omnes cœlos. Eph. 40, 10. penetrasse cœlos, Hebr. 4, 14. Cœlis excelsiorem factum, Hebr. 7, 26. Et rursum, si manet supra & extra omnes cœlos, absurdissimum fuerit affirmare, cœlum in quod Christus adscendit, esse cœlum corporeum: Quasi verò extra & supra omnes cœlos, corporeum aliquod cœlum esse possit: id quod cum saniore etiam Philosophia pugnat.

Sed quantumvis absurda hæc sit sententia, eam tamen defendere conatur Jesuvvita: CHRISTVS, inquiens, ad illud cœlum adscendit, ubi est sedes DEI: illud autem cœlum corporeum est. Ergò ad corporeum cœlum Christus adscendit, & in corporeo cœlo est. Minorem sic confirmat: Ea quæ sibi mutuò opponuntur, ejusdem naturæ esse oportet. Atqui Scriptura multis in locis cœlum terræ opponit, vocabulo terræ in propriâ significatione accepto: ut Psal. 115, 16. Cœlum cœli Domino, terram autem dedit filijs hominum. Jes. 66, 1. Cœlum mihi sedes, terra scabellum pedum meorum &c. Ergò cœlum, quod terræ opponitur, eodem modo accipiendum est, pro cœlo corporeo.

Respondeo, Majorem simpliciter esse falsam. Non enim modò non necesse est, ut ea, quæ sibi mutuò opponuntur, ejusdem planè sint naturæ: Sed contra potiùs ea, quæ diversarum sunt naturarum, inter se opponuntur. Proindè ex productis Scripturarum testimoniis, vi oppositionis necessariò sequitur, Cœlum quod est thronus DEI, non ejusdem cum terra esse naturæ, sed longè diversissimæ: eò quòd cœlum Terræ opponitur. Prætereà si ex hypothesi Jesuvvitica, Cœlum quod est thronus DEI, est corporeum: utique ipse etiam thronus DEI erit corporeus: quin & ille ipse, qui sedet in throno hoc DEUS corporeus erit. Absurda, impia & blasphema omnia. Et rectè D. Augustinus aliquando, erassis istis & anilibus imaginationibus respondit: Si cœlum quod est thronus DEI, est corporeum: & si cœlum corporeum, quod oculis videmus, intellexerimus esse habitationem DEI, transitura est habitatio DEI, quia cœlum & terra transibunt. Sed antequam faceret DEUS cœlum & terram, ubi habitabat? in se habitabat DEUS: apud se habitabat DEUS: & apud se est DEUS.

Tertiò. Calviniani Cœlum accipiunt pro finito quodam ac distincto domicilio supra regionem sideream, quo corpus CHRISTI sic exceptum sit, ut certum quoddam loci spacium atque ambitum in eo occupaverit, quo sic circumscriptum contineatur, ut dùm isto ambitur, alibi vel in cœlo vel in terra esse non possit: Imò extra quem sit nullo modo uspiam: quò etiam fiat, ut tanto locorum intervallo distet à nobis corpus ejus, quanto Cœlum abest à terrâ: ita ut propter hunc ipsum adscensum in cœlos, corpus ejus verum ac substantiale, præsens esse in S. Cœna nequeat: multò minùs per Humanitatem suam, Christus toti Ecclesiæ, aut creaturis reliquis universis quoquo modo adesse credi debeat. Quam sententiam non manifesti tàntùm Calviniani tenent: ut: Calvinus in Formula Confeßionis p. 25. & Beza, Vol. 1. tractat. Theol. p. 658. Quæst. 15. Bulling. item & alij. Sed autor etiam noster Philippus in Commentar. super Epist. ad Coloss. cap. 3, haud obscurè incrustare voluit: sic scribens: Adscendit ad cœlos: adscendit scilicet, corporali & Physicâ locatione: In Cœlum, id est, in locum cœlestem, ubicunque est quia hic non sunt fingenda Allegoriæ. Item, Ascendit ad Cœlos, ubi Verbum Caro factum anteà non sedebat: id est; UBI CORPUS ANTEA NON HABUERAT CORPORALEM LOCATIONEM. Quæ sanè verba luculenter arguunt, Philippum per Ascensionem ad Cœlos, & subsequentem sessionem: ad dexteram DEI, intellexisse corporalem locationem: & sic haud obscurè reprehendisse sententiam Lutheri, qui cœlos nequaquàm per Locum, sed per Regnum Cœleste: & sessionem ad dexteram DEI Patris, non per corporalem locationem: sed per divinam Majestatem & Omnipotentiam constanter explicavit.

Laborat autem hæc sententia ijsdem initiò absurditatibus, quas jam in Jesuvvitarum dogmate notavimus. Cœlum enim istud, quemadmodum jam definitum est, interibit utique in novissimo die Pf. 102, 27. nequè ejus habebitur ratio apud electos, quia NON RECORDABUNTUR priorum cœlorum, & prioris terræ Jef. 65, 17. 2. Pet. 3, 13.

2. Si Cœlum ad quod Christus adscendit, est locus corporeus, supra omnes cœlos aspectabiles: sequetur, quoties DEUS in Scripturis dicitur prospicere super filios hominum, Psalm. 14. quod è longissimè remoto cœlo corporeo, homines procul dissitos intueatur: quod auxilium suum demittat per primum mobile, per Sphæram stellarum fixarum, & reliquos orbes inferiores? quòd DEUS etiam itidem descensurus de cœlo ad filios hominum, ex altissimo illo Cœlo corporeo se demittat, donec tandem per omnes orbes planetarum, & aërem, in terram usque veniat. Absurdissimis absurdiora hæc esse, quis non videt? Certè cum DEUS non sit procul ab unoquoque nostrûm Act. 17, 27. Cùm non sit DEUS è longinquo, sed DEUS qui propè est: Cùm propè sit omnibus invocantibus eum in veritate: Utiq; Cœlum etiam, in quo semper est DEUS, & extra quod nunquam & nusquam esse potest, vitiosissimè per locum aliquem altissimum, & quidem corporeum definiri constat. Siquidem DEUS ne in infimâ quidem terrâ, Cœlo isto suo, ad quod Christus etiam adscendit, & in quo consedit ad dexteram DEI, destituitur: Sed uti ab æterno ante creationem coeli & terræ, fuit in cœlo hoc suo, sic in eodem immutabiliter semper est & manet, sive nobis in his terris, sive Electis in Vita æterna, sive aliis creaturis adfit.

Tandem nulla Loci vel Localitatis Physicæ conditio cadit in corpora Electorum glorificata, usque adeò, ut ne quidem in corpore ψυχικῷ sive animali ea sit essentialis: uti supra Cap. 1. ex professo ostendimus. Quæ ergò hæc stupenda fuerit protervia, Corpus Christi, quod non modò ex Resurrectione gloriosum est: sed & insuper infinitâ divinæ Majestatis plenitudine inunctum, corporei alicui Cœlo ita includere, ut loco physico semper circumscribi necesse habeat. Multò rectiùs censuit Jacobus Faber Stapulensis, super Caput 12. prioris ad Corinth. scribens: Videndum est, ne corporalis imaginatio hîc ludat, loca multiplicans, spacia distendens: Hîc enim neque locorum multiplicatio, neque spaciorum distensio intelligitur: sed plenitudo sine loco, supra locum omnem, extra & intra locum omnem, sine spacio, supra & infra omne spacium, extra & intra omne spacium.

Sed quantumvis impia & absurda hæc de Cœlo Calvinianorum sit sententia: ejus tamen patrocinium suscipere non verentur. Et initiò sunt, qui primam rationem nostram sic infringere student, ut dicant, non Cœlum hoc corporeum, sed reliquos tantùm cælos perituros. Sed respondeo, hoc nihil esse aliud, quàm absurditates absurditatibus cumulare. Hinc enim sequeretur, ut pereuntibus cæteris Cœlis sive Orbibus singulis ac universis, qui circumcirca claudebantur Cœlo hoc ad quod Christus adscendit, & corporeo quidem cœlo, ut relinquatur intra ejus Cœli ambitum, vacuum sive inane: id quod tàm in Theologia nostra, quàm in Philosophia longè est absurdissimum.

Deindè inscitè admòdum urgent illa Scripturarum testimonia, in quibus Cœlum nominatur, mansio, item domus, imò locus. Nam Regnum cœleste sive vitam beatam figuratè & Metaphoricè sic nominari, manifestiùs est, quàm ut operosâ probatione indigeat. Et utitur Scriptura ejusmodi vocabulis à nostri seculi conditione, & regnorum terrenorum similitudine petitis, quia Oculus non vidit, auris non audit, neque in cor hominis ascendit, quæ sit futura alterius vitæ conditio. 1. Cor. 2, 9.

Tertiò etiã Cornuto hoc Syllogismo nos ferire satagũt: Nemo se cõfert eò, ubi antea reipsa præsens est suo corpore: Nemo etiã indè discedit, ubi corpore suo manet. Ergò si corpore suo Christus verè adscendit in cælum: utique prius ibi non fuit, & sic corruit Ubiquitas: vel si antea ibi fuit, corruit ipsa Ascensio.

Proindè tutissimum fuerit statuere, Christum corpore suo adscendisse, ubi antea non fuit: & ita è terris hinc discessisse, ut in certo Cœli loco maneat, ad diem usq; novissimum.

Respondeo. Fallit argumentum confusione disparatorum præsentiæ modorum, quorum unus est Naturalis: Alter Personalis: Qui duo Modi, quippè subordinati simul stare possunt, neque se mutuò evertunt: uti supra fusiùs ostensum. Ad naturalem ergò præsentiam refertur ferendum est, quòd corpus Christi locali translatione sursum elatum fuit, ita, ut hac ratione locum inferiorem unum post alterum quasi evacuaret, & relinqueret: ac solidâ realique locorum mutatione sursum in altum adscenderet. Quæ localis mutatio ac conditio, non obstitit, quò minùs in hypostasi τῶ λόγῳ simul esset in Cœlo: Quemadmodum Christus ipse disertè attestatur, Joh. 3, 13. Nemo adscendit in Cœlum, nisi qui descendit de cœlo, FILIVS HOMINIS, qui est in Cœlo. Rursum, quòd Christus corpore suo in cœlum translatus, nihilominùs manet in his terris invisibiliter, illud fit propter personalem subsistentiam in λόγῳ, qui in Cœlo & in terris ubique præsentissimus, nihil sibi præsentiùs habet, quàm hanc ipsam suam carnem, eò quòd simpliciter ἀδιάsατῶ est Unio, omnem distantiam naturarum, & absentiam à se invicem commodè secludens. Accedit, quòd Ascensionis Carnis Christi terminus ultimus non fuit Locus aliquis physicus, quo ea circumscriberetur: sed ipsissima dextera DEI, loco nulli inclusa, à loco nullo exclusa, uti mox demonstrabitur: ita, ut, licèt secundum Naturæ conditionem sit in aliquo certo πῷ Corpus Christi Naturaliter: tamen ex Unione & sessione ad dexteram DEI, sit ubique præsentissimum Personaliter.

Tandem ceu Achillis clypeum obvertunt illud Act. 3, 21. ὃν δεῖ τὸν ὐρανὸν δέξαź: Quod ipsi sic vertunt: Quem oportet cœlo capi.

Respondeo. Crimen falsi committi in vitiosa versione Latina. Neque enim passivè, sed activè verba Græca intelligenda esse, Scriptura ipsa sufficientissimè demonstrat. Si enim ascendit ideò Christus in Cœlum, ut à Cœlo capiatur sive contineatur, quomodo, quæso, cœlos ipsos penetrasse, quomodo cœlis ipsis Excelsior factus esse, quomodo ex hac ascensione exaltatus, supra omne, quod non solum in hoc, sed & in futuro seculo nominatur, dici posset, Heb. 7, 26. Eph. 1, 21. Quomodo denique verum esset, quod ei secundum eam naturam, secundum quam adscendit, subjecta sint omnia, ita, ut nihil omissum, quod ipsi non sit subjectum, Hebr. 2, 8. Si enim Omnia ipsi sunt subjecta: cur non ipsum etiam Cœlum. Proindè repudiatâ passivâ significatione verbi δέξαź, Activam rectisimè urgemus, moti insuper autoritate Apostolicâ, qui phrasin hanc, oportet Christum Cœlum recipere, per hanc æquipollentem, Oportet Christum regnare &c, 1. Cor. 15, 25. explicat. Undè Petrus Effectum istum receptionis Cœli sic describit: Christus profectus est in Cœlum, subjectis sibi Angelis, potestatibus & virtutibus. 1. Petr. 3, 22. Si his: Cur non ipso etiam Cœlo subjecto? Tandem Calvinus ipse exponens hunc locum, ultrò fassus est, è verbo δέξαź, cùm medium & ambiguum sit, nihil certi in hac controversia concludi posse. Quanquam Beza in annotationibus Majoribus passivam verbi hujus interpretationem retinendam esse svadet: in loco, quod dicitur, Sapiens: Sic enim scribit ipse: potest haberi certus textus, qui opponi debet ijs, qui docent, verum Christi Corpus in Cœna adesse & sumi.

Sic manifesta Scripturæ depravatio est asylum illud Sacramentariorum, ad quod in perdita hac sua causa, se recipiunt. Quod sanè disputandi genus nos illis non invidemus: alijs interim, imò toti Ecclesiæ CHRISTI judicium de eo committentes.

Falsis istis sententijs de Cœlo, ad quod Christus adscendit, rejectis & damnatis, statuimus tandem, Cœlum istud definiri rectissimè, tùm cœlesti conditione, statu, gloriâ & beatitudine: tùm divinâ etiam illâ, infinitâ, & increatâ majestate atque luce inaccessâ, in quâ DEUS habitat, nullis locis Physicis, aut quibusvis aliis terrenis conditionibus expositâ: id quod ex Sessione ad dexteram Patris, jam patebit luculentiùs.


### Chapter V. & the Last. On the State of Exaltation. Orthodox Proposition: II. on the Session of Christ at the right hand of God the Father Orthodox Proposition

II. ON THE SESSION OF CHRIST at the right hand of GOD the Father.

ORTHODOX PROPOSITION.

CHRIST the Savior, according to his human nature ascending to the heavens, sat down at the right hand of infinite virtue, Majesty, and divine Omnipotence, included in no place, and excluded by none: so that according to this very humanity of his, he might be most present everywhere to his Church, and might most powerfully rule over all Creatures in heaven and on earth.

Ἔκθεσις.

Clear testimonies of the Scriptures give assurance to this proposition, which at the beginning of the Ascension of CHRIST to the Heavens establish the final goal, the Session at the right hand of GOD the Father: Mark 16:19. And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into Heaven, and sits at the right hand of GOD. Eph. 1:20. The Father raised Christ from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places. Heb. 1:13. To which of the Angels did he say: Sit at my right hand. Heb. 10:12. CHRIST sits forever at the right hand of GOD.

But then, they explain clearly enough what this very right hand of GOD is, at which CHRIST sat down, when they name it the right hand of GOD in the heavenly places, above every principality and power, etc. Eph. 1:21. The right hand of the virtue of GOD. Luke 22:29. The right hand of Majesty in the highest. Heb. 1:3. as:

Eph. 1:21. He set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in the future. Luke 22:29. From this the SON OF MAN will be sitting at the right hand of the virtue of GOD. Heb. 1:3. He sat down at the right hand of Majesty in the highest. Heb. 8:1. We have a high Priest, who sat down at the right hand of the Throne of Majesty in the Heavens. Hence the Savior himself, Matt. 25:31, affirms that he, in the final judgment, will sit upon the throne of his Majesty. From the Old Testament, neither fewer nor obscure [testimonies] can be given: as: Exod. 15:6. Thy right hand, O Lord, is magnified in strength: thy right hand has struck the enemies. Ps. 44:4. They did not possess the land by their sword, and their arm did not save them: but thy right hand and thy arm. Ps. 77:11. The right hand of GOD changes all things. Ps. 98:1 & 2. Sing to the LORD a new song, because he has done wonderful things: His right hand and his holy arm have saved him. Ps. 118:16. The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly: The right hand of the Lord is exalted: The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly. Ps. 139:10. If I take the wings of the dawn, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, behold there thy hand will lead me, and thy right hand will hold me. Isa. 48:13. My hand has founded the earth, and my right hand has measured the heavens with a span.

Such is the clarity and evidence of these testimonies, that the Adversaries seem to blind their own eyes with the fascination of impiety, who dare to define the Right hand of GOD, at which Christ sat down, as a certain created and finite place of happiness. Certainly, any created place, whatever it may be, is far too base to be worthy of this dignity, that it should be called the Right hand of GOD, the Right hand of virtue, of majesty, and of divine omnipotence in the highest.

And how, I ask, would the Right hand of GOD signify either a place or anything corporeal, since GOD is a Spirit, in whom, speaking properly, there is neither right nor left.

We, moved by the authority of the Scriptures, invincibly conclude that by the name of the divine Right Hand nothing else is understood in the sacred writings than the very empire, powers, and dominion of the omnipotent GOD, included in no place, but excluded by none, nay rather most powerfully present in all things: the appellation being taken from human affairs. For just as any man has almost all the force and momentum of his strength in his right hand, by which he also accomplishes all things: so through anthropopathy the right hand of GOD denotes His Omnipotence governing all things.

By which same figurative manner of speaking, the word To sit is not taken concerning any bodily position, but signifies the same as to reign, as the Apostle interprets in 1 Cor. 15:25. And to reign indeed, not from any interval of places: but most presently everywhere. For since to sit infallibly includes the presence of the one reigning: it would follow that this sitting extends itself as far and wide as the Right Hand of GOD itself diffuses: otherwise it would not sit everywhere at the right hand of God: but only in the heavens, or in some other certain place: which is manifestly false. For although Scripture assigns this Session of CHRIST in the highest, in the heavens, in the heavenly places: yet it intended to denote nothing less than that which the Adversaries dream: namely that this Session is to be restricted to a certain place of Heaven: but by these phrases it partly intended to distinguish the kingdom of Christ at the right hand of GOD from the earthly habit and form of the kingdoms of this world: inasmuch as Christ now is, lives, and rules in a certain heavenly, invisible, and incorruptible kingdom, at the very right hand of GOD the Father: but partly it intended to define in this Session the divine majesty itself, which fell to CHRIST: so that just as GOD himself is said to be in heaven, to look down from heaven, to send help from his high throne, to hear from on high: so Christ sits at the right hand of GOD the Father in the highest, in heaven, in the heavenly places, that is, according to his divine majesty and power, most present everywhere: Which explanation of ours is also held from Antiquity by Chrysostom, Vol. 4, Homily 2, on chapter 1 to the Hebrews, writing: In the right hand of Majesty, in the highest, what is it? Is GOD included in a place? Far be it: but just as, when he said, in the right hand, he did not attribute a human figure of a body to GOD, but showed a likeness of the honor which the Son has equal with the Father: so, when he says in the Highest, he DOES NOT INCLUDE him IN A PLACE, but shows him to be higher than all, and more eminent than all.

Likewise Vol. 3 in the sermon on the Passion, Homily on the Cross: When I shall have said that GOD is sitting in the highest, believe that GOD is present EVERYWHERE.

Nor does the Apostle oppose this doctrine of ours, who in Eph. 2:6 affirms that the Faithful will sit together with Christ in the heavenly places: For it is answered that there is an evident diversity of phrase in both cases.
