For the Apostle indeed affirms that the faithful will sit together with Christ in the heavenly places: but he does not say that they will sit together at the right hand of GOD in the heavenly places. Therefore that sitting of the faithful in the heavenly places denotes nothing other than the society and communion of the same eternal life and blessedness. But now, because Christ not only sits in the heavenly places: but also sits at the right hand of the power and majesty of GOD in the highest: certainly a peculiar, and indeed such a glory is defined by this session, which is comparable to none of either angels or men. Heb. 1:13. but transcends all the glory of the saints and the blessed by an infinitely vast interval, indeed by a whole genus more sublimely. Such glory it is, to govern and administer all creatures, to be Lord over the works of the hands of GOD, Psalm 8, to rule in the midst of his enemies Psalm 110, to exercise all power conferred upon him in heaven and on earth Matt. 28. To fill all things Eph.

4. Indeed to fill all things in all things. Eph. 1. To sit in the midst of the throne of God. Apoc. 7.

Which same Response ought to be given to other places of Scripture also, by which the Adversaries strive to enervate this Session of the Son of Man. For although Scripture affirms that the souls of the just are in the hand of God: yet they cannot therefore be said to Sit at the right hand of God. For there is a clear distinction between these two phrases: Inasmuch as to be in the hand of God is nothing other than to be under the protection and grace of God: As that immediately subjoined epexegesis clearly confirms: And the torment of the wicked shall not touch them. Wis. 3:1. and soon v. 3. but they are in peace. Which glory is surely far inferior than to be able to be compared to the Session of Christ at the right hand of the Father. Thus, although in Matt. 25:23 the Sheep are said to be placed at the right hand of the Son of Man: yet they are not said to be about to sit together at the very right hand of God the Father. Where again there is a clear distinction between the right hand of the Son of Man, and the Right Hand of God the Father: of which the former denotes eternal blessedness: but the latter divine empire over all creatures.

Thus, although Augustine in his book on the Christian Combat, chapter 25, and other Fathers following him affirm that the Church in the other life will be at the very right hand of God: yet they do not speak with Scripture: and without doubt they intended to denote nothing other than that the Church will be in eternal blessedness, free and immune from all adversities, under the protection and custody of the omnipotent divine right hand itself: so that this phrase, To be at the right hand of God, is predicated of the Church more passively than actively.

Thus when in the Apocalypse the Son of God says: To him that overcometh, I will grant to sit with me in my throne: he clearly mentions there not one, but a double throne: of which the one is eternal beatitude, or the heaven of the blessed: which is called the Throne of Christ, with a certain respect to the faithful; for whom by his merit he acquired this throne of glory and eternal beatitude: And in this respect the faithful are said to sit with Christ, in his throne. But the other throne is the throne of God the Father, namely his infinite and omnipotent right hand: at which besides the Son of Man no one will be placed: just as neither does the Son of God in this place say that he will grant to those who have overcome that they should sit with him in the throne of the Father, or at the right hand of the Father, but in my throne: and this throne of his, he expressly distinguishes from the throne of the Father, in which he himself sits: To him that overcometh, saying, I will grant to sit with me in my throne: as I also overcame, and sat with my father, in his throne. Whence also the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1, 13. To which of the angels said he at any time: sit at my right hand.

These things being thus established, we now invincibly gather from this Session of Christ at the right hand of God the Father, that Christ, not only according to his divine, but also according to his assumed human nature: is most present and most powerfully rules, not only over the Church, but over all creatures whatsoever in heaven and on earth.

Whence we argue thus: If Christ according to the assumed humanity sits at the whole right hand (for he is simply a̓́ue- e̓́ρίs καὶ a̓́πληστος) of infinite divine virtue and majesty, and indeed outside and beyond all locality: just as through locality he is also nowhere distant from the right hand of GOD but is everywhere most present with it and rules most powerfully. But the former is true: Therefore also the latter. The connection of the major premise is clearly evident even from this, Because locality cannot anywhere separate or disjoin from the right hand of GOD that which transcends all locality whatsoever at the right hand of GOD: Now indeed the Humanity of Christ at the right hand of GOD transcends all locality, as has already been shown before. The truth of the minor premise is likewise clearly evident from the preceding: where it was shown 1. That this session fell to Christ according to his human Nature: 2. That to sit at the right hand of GOD is nothing else than to rule most presentially over all creatures with infinite virtue and power. The conclusion will therefore also have its own immovable certainty. Nor does the Apostolic Creed stand in the way of this Demonstration, in which we profess to believe that Christ indeed sat down at the Right hand of GOD the Father in the heavens, but that he himself will also return from thence, to judge the living and the dead. For the particle THENCE cannot or ought not to be referred to the right hand of GOD: For thus it would follow that Christ, when he shall appear for judgment, would be about to desert the right hand of GOD: which is prodigiously absurd: Since Christ himself affirms that he, then appearing in the clouds, will sit at the right hand of the power of GOD Luke 22. That he will sit on the throne of his Majesty: Matth. 19, 25. Therefore this particle ought not to be referred to the right hand of GOD, but to Heaven, to which Christ ascended: As the Apostle himself explains Phil. 3. Our conversation is in heaven, FROM WHENCE, or FROM WHERE we expect Christ. From this Heaven therefore Christ will visibly return to judgment: who invisibly fills heaven and earth. For a visible return does not take away or subvert the invisible Omnipresence of Christ, even as he is Man, by which he fills all things at the right hand of Majesty, and walks in the midst of the Churches dispersed in this world. Concerning which sentiment Ambrose excellently says: Although you are everywhere and standing in the midst of us you are not discerned by us: yet there will be a time when all flesh shall behold you returning.

Latin:

II. DE SESSIONE CHRISTI ad dextram DEI Patris.

PROPOSITIO ORTHODOXA.

CHRISTUS Servator secundum humanam naturam adscendens ad cœlos, consedit ad dextram infinitæ virtutis, Majestatis ac Omnipotentiæ divinæ nulli loco inclusam, à nullo etiam exclusam: ut sic secundum hanc ipsam humanitatem suam, ubiq; præsentissimè tùm suæ adesset Ecclesiæ, tùm omnibus Creaturis in cœlo & in terrâ potentissimè dominaretur.

Ἔκθεσις.

FIdem propositioni huic faciunt perspicua Scripturarum testimonia, quæ initiò Ascensionis CHRISTI ad Cœlos terminum ultimum constituunt, Sessionem ad dextram DEI Patris: Marc, 16, 19. Et Dominus Jesus, postquàm locutus est eis, assumptus est in Cœlum, & sedet à dextris DEI. Eph. 1, 20. Pater suscitavit Christum à mortuis, & constituit ipsum ad dexteram suam in cœlestibus. Heb. 1, 13. Ad quem Angelorum dixit: Sede à dextris meis. Heb. 10, 12. CHRISTUS in sempiternum sedet ad dexteram DEI.

Deindè verò, quid sit hæc ipsa dextera DEI, ad quam consedit CHRISTUS, satis luculenter explicant: dùm eam nominant dexteram DEI in cœlestibus, supra omnem principatum & potestatem &c. Eph. 1, 21. Dexteram virtutis DEI. Luc. 22, 29. Dexteram Majestatis in altissimis Hebr. 1, 3. ut:

Eph. 1, 21. Constituit ipsum ad dexteram suam in coelestibus, supra omnem principatum, & potestatem, & virtutem, & dominationem, & omne nomen, quod nominatur non solùm in hoc seculo, sed & in futuro. Luc. 22, 29. Ex hoc erit FILIUS HOMINIS sedens à dexteris virtutis DEI. Hebr. 1, 3. Consedit ad dexteram Majestatis in altissimis. Hebr. 8, 1. Habemus summum Pontificem, qui consedit ad dexteram Throni Majestatis in Coelis. Hinc Servator ipse Matth. 25, 31. affirmat, se in judicio novissimo, sessurum super thronum Majestatis suae. Ex Veteri Testamento dari possunt neque pauciora, neque obscura: ut: Exod. 15, 6. Dextera tua Domine magnificata est in fortitudine: dextera tua percussit inimicos. Psal. 44, 4. Non in gladio suo possederunt terram & brachium eorum non salvavit eos: sed dextera tua & brachium tuum. Psal. 77, 11. Dextera DEI mutat omnia. Psal. 98, 1. & 2. Cantate DOMINO Canticum novum, quia mirabilia fecit: Salvavit eum dextera ejus, & brachium sanctum ejus. Psal. 118, 16. Dextera Domini fecit virtutem: Dextera Domini est excelsa: Dextera Domini fecit virtutem. Psal. 139, 10. Si sumsero pennas aurorae, & mansero in extremis maris, ecce illic manus tua deducet me, & apprehendet me dextera tua. Jes. 48, 13. Manus mea fundavit terram, & dextera mea palmo mensa est coelos.

Quorum sanè testimoniorum ea est diluciditas & evidentia, ut impietatis fascino sibi ipsi oculos perstringere videantur Adversarij, qui Dexteram DEI, ad quam Christus consedit, per locum quendam felicitatis creatum & finitum definire audent. Locus certè creatus quisque, qualis qualis ille sit, longè vilior est, quàm cui dignitas isthaec competat, ut vocetur Dextetera DEI, Dextera virtutis, majestatis, & omnipotentiae divinae in altissimis.

Et qui, quaeso, Dextera DEI vel locum, vel corporale aliquid significaret, cùm DEUS sit Spiritus, apud quem propriè loquendo, nec dextrum est, nec sinistrum.

Nos moti Scripturarum autoritate, invictè colligimus, Dexterae divinae nomine nihil in sacris intelligi aliud, quàm ipsum DEI omnipotentis imperium, potestates & dominium, loco nulli inclusum, sed à nullo exclusum, quin potiùs rebus omnibus potentissimè praesens: sumptâ appellatione à rebus humanis. Sicut enim homo quispiam omnem penè vim, atque momentum roboris sui habet in manu dexterâ, quâ etiam perficit omnia: sic per ἀνθρωποπάθειαν dextera DEI notat Omnipotentiam ejus omnia gubernantem.

Quâ ipsâ figuratâ loquendi ratione, verbum Sedere non accipitur de situ aliquo corporeo, sed idem sonat ac regnare, interprete Apostolo 1. Cor. 15, 25. & regnare quidem, non ex aliquo locorum intervallo : sed ubiq; præsentissimè. Cùm enim Sedere infallibiliter præsentiam regnantis includat: Consequens fuerit, hoc sedere tam longè lateq; se extendere, quàm longè lateq; se diffundit ipsa Dextera DEI : alioqui no ubiq; sederet ad Dexteram Dei : sed in cœlis tantùm, vel in alio quodam certo loco : id quod manifestè est falsum. Etsi enim Scriptura Sessionem hanc CHRISTI adsignat in excelsis, in cœlis, in cœlestibus : tamen nihil minus notatum voluit, quàm id quod somniant Adversarij: nempè Sessionem hanc ad certum quendam Cœli locum restringendam esse: sed phrasibus istis partim regnum Christi ad dexteram DEI distingvere voluit à terreno habitu & formâ regnorum hujus mundi : siquidem Christus jam sit, vivat ac dominetur in Cœlesti quodam invisibili, incorruptibilique regno, ad ipsam DEI Patris dexteram : partim verò ipsam majestatem divinam, quæ CHRISTO obtigit, in Sessione hac definire voluit : ut quemadmodum DEUS ipse dicitur esse in cœlo, prospicere de cœlo, auxilium mittere de excelso suo throno, exaudire in alto : ita Christus sedeat ad dexteram DEI Patris in excelsis, in cœlo, in cœlestibus, hoc est secundum divinam majestatem ac potentiam, ubiq; præsentissimam : Quam explicationem nostram ex Antiquitate tenet etiam Chrysostomus, Tom. 4. Homil. 2. in cap. 1. ad Hebr. scribens : In dexterâ Majestatis, in excelsis, quid est ? nùm DEUM loco includi? Absit : sed sicut, cùm dixit, in dexterâ, non figuram humanam corporis DEO tribuit, sed similitudinem monstravit honoris, quem Filius æqualem habet cum Patre : ità, cùm dicit in Excelsis non eum LOCO INCLUDIT, sed ostendit omnibus altiorem, & omnibus eminentirem esse.

Item Tom. 3. in serm. de Passione, Homilia de Cruce : Quando dixero DEUM sedentem in excelsis, UBIQUE eum credite DEUM esse præsentem.

Neque doctrinæ huic nostræ adversatur Apostolus, qui Eph. 2, 6. affirmat, Fideles consessuros cum Christo in cœlestibus: Respondetur enim evidentem utrobique esse diversitatem phrasews. Nam Apostolus affirmat quidem, quòd fideles consessuri sint cum Christo in cœlestibus : sed non dicit, quòd consessuri sint ad dexteram DEI in cœlestibus. Proindè sessio illa fidelium in cœlestibus, nihil notat aliud, quàm societatem & communionem ejusdem æternæ vitæ ac beatitudinis. Jam verò quia Christus non tantùm sedet in cœlestibus : sed sedet etiam ad dexteram virtutis & majestatis DEI in excelsis : utique peculiaris, & talis quidem gloria hâc sessione definitur, quæ nulli vel Angelorum vel hominum est comparabilis. Hebr. 1, 13. sed omnem Sanctorum ac beatorum gloriam infinito prorsus intervallo, imò toto genere sublimiùs transcendit. Qualis gloria est, gubernare & administrare omnes creaturas, esse Dominum super opera manuum DEI, Psalm. 8. dominari in medio inimicorum Psalm. 110. exercere collatam sibi omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terrâ Matth. 28. Implere omnia Eph.

4. Imò omnia in omnibus implere. Eph. 1. Sedere in medio throno Dei. Apoc. 7.

Quæ ipsa Responsio dari debet ad alia etiam Scripturarum loca, quibus Adversarii Sessionem hanc Filij Hominis enervare student. Etsi enim Scriptura affirmat, Justorum animas esse in manu Dei: non tamen proptereà dici possunt Sedere ad dexteram Dei. Nam inter duas istas phrases luculentum est discrimen : Siquidem in manu Dei esse, nihil est aliud, quàm esse sub protectione & gratiâ Dei : Quemadmodum illud statim immediatè subjuncta ἐπεξήγησις dilucidè confirmat : Et non tanget illos tormentum mali. Sap. 3, 1. & mox v. 3. illi autem sunt in pace. Quæ sanè gloria longè inferior est, quàm ut ad Sessionem Christi ad dexteram Patris comparari queat. Sic etsi Matth. 25, 23. Oves dicuntur collocandæ à dextris Filij Hominis: Non tamen dicuntur consessuræ in ipsâ dexterâ Dei Patris. Ubi rursus luculentum est discrimen inter dextram Filij Hominis, & inter Dextram Dei Patris: quarum illa æternam notat beatitudinem : Hæc verò divinum imperium super omnes creaturas.

Sic licèt Augustinus lib. de Agone Christiano, cap. 25. alijque ipsum secuti Patres affirment, Ecclesiam in alterâ vitâ fore in ipsâ dexterâ Dei: tamen cum Scripturâ non loquuntur : & procul dubio nihil voluerunt notatum aliud, quàm Ecclesiam fore in æternâ beatitudine liberam ac immunem ab omnibus adversitatibus, sub tutelâ ac custodiâ ipsius omnipotentis dextræ divinæ: ita ut phrasis hæc, Esse in dextrâ Dei, passivè magis, quàm activè de Ecclesiâ prædicetur.

Sic cùm in Apocalypsi dicit Filius Dei : Qui vicerit, dabo ei sedere in throno meo: perspicuè ibi non unius, sed duplicis throni meminit: quorum alter est æterna beatitudo, sive cœlum beatorum : quod Thronus Christi dicitur, respectu quodam ad fideles; quibus suo merito hunc thronum gloriæ & beatitudinis æternæ acquisivit: Et hoc respectu dicuntur fideles sedere cum Christo, in throno ejus. Alter autem thronus est Dei Patris thronus, nempè infinita & omnipotens ejus dextera : ad quem præter Filium Hominis nemo collocabitur : quemadmodum neq; Filius Dei hoc loco dicit, se daturum illis, qui vicerint, ut sedeant secum in throno Patris, vel in dexterâ Patris, sed in meo throno: & hunc suum thronum, expressè distingvit à throno Patris, in quo ipse sedeat: Qui vicerit, inquiens, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo: sicut & ego vici, & sedi cum patre meo, in throno ejus. Undè Epistola etiam ad Hebr. cap. 1, 13. Cui Angelorum dixit unquam : sede à dextris meis.

Quibus ita constitutis, invictè jam ex Sessione hac Christi ad dexteram Dei Patris colligimus, Christum non secundum divinam tantùm, sed & secundum assumtam humanam naturam: non Ecclesiæ modò, sed omnibus omninò creaturis in cœlo ac in terrâ, semper præsentissimè adesse, ac potentissimè dominari.

Undè sic argumentamur: Si Christus secundum assumtam humanitatem sedet ad totam dextram (est enim simpliciter a̓́uee̓́ρίs καὶ a̓́πληστος) infinitae virtutis ac majestatis divinae, & quidem extra & citra omnem localitatem: utiǵ per localitatem etiam nusquam à dexterà DEI distat sed ubiq́ cum ea praesentissimè adest & dominatur potentissimè. Atqui prius est verum: Ergò & posterius. Connexum Majoris liquidò patet vel indè, Quia localitas non potest ullibi à dexterà DEI separare aut sejungere id, quod omnem omninò localitatem in dexterà DEI transcendit: Jam verò Humanitas Christi in dexterà DEI omnem localitatem transcendit, uti jam antè ostensum. Minoris veritas itidem luculenter patet ex praecedentibus: ubi ostensum 1. Christo hanc sessionem obtigisse secundum humanam Naturam: 2. Sedere ad dexteram DEI nihil esse aliud, quàm infinitâ cum virtute & potentiâ praesentissimè omnibus creaturis dominari. Constabit igitur conclusioni sua etiam immota certitudo. Neq; obstat huic Demonstrationi Symbolum Apostolicum, in quo credere nos profitemur, Christum consedisse quidem ad Dexteram DEI Patris in coelis, sed indè etiam ipsum rediturum, ad judicandum vivos & mortuos. Neque enim particula INDE ad dextram DEI referri potest aut debet: Sic enim sequeretur, Christum tùm cùm apparebit ad judicium, deserturum esse dextram DEI: id quod prodigiosè absurdum: Siquidem Christus ipse affirmat, se tum apparentem in nubibus, sessurum à dexteris virtutis DEI Luc. 22. Sessurum esse in throno Majestatis suae: Matth. 19, 25. Proindè particula haec non debet referri ad dexteram DEI, sed ad Coelum, ad quod Christus adscendit: Sic explicante ipse Apostolo Phil. 3. Conversatio nostra in coelo est, EX QUO, vel UNDE expectamus Christum. Ex hoc ergò Coelo visibiliter redibit Christus ad judicium: qui invisibiliter implet coelum & terram. Neque enim visibilis reditus, tollit aut intervertit invisibibilem Christi, etiam quâ Homo est, Omnipræsentiam, quâ in dexterâ Majestatis implet omnia, & ambulat in medio Ecclesiarum hoc in mundo dispersarum. Quam in sententiam præclarè Ambrosius: Licèt ubiq́ sis & stans in medio nostrûm non cernaris à nobis: erit tamen tempus, quando universa caro te aspiciet revertentem.


## 5 On Creation

Our Author, being about to treat of Creation, weighs not so much the formation itself of created things, as their admirable preservation. Whence also the whole Philippean treatment, if you except that single question, Whether God created all things out of nothing? pertains properly to the Article concerning the eternal providence of GOD: which nevertheless the Schools of Theologians today wish to be distinct and separated from the Article of Creation: partly on account of the breadth, by which the doctrine concerning the Providence of GOD extends far more widely than the rest: and partly indeed on account of the gravity of the matter itself, by which it transcends the Article of Creation in infinite ways. Therefore we also, following the custom of the Theological Schools, departing in some measure from the footsteps of our Author, separate the Topic concerning Creation from that other, which is concerning Providence, both in number and in treatment: intending to weigh it separately in this place.

Moreover, since this Article of Creation itself also extends quite widely here, with respect to those questions which are moved today concerning created things in particular not so much by Theologians as by Philosophers: we certainly, lest we seem to μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος, intending to use a certain compendium, will recall to the anvil of treatment only those questions which pertain properly to our most sacred Theological science: and without the consideration of which, all the remaining disputes of the Physicists concerning the Heaven, Stars, World, Elements, and other created things of that kind, ought deservedly to seem maimed, mutilated, and imperfect.

But we have established the proper seat of this matter in the Mosaic description, and indeed in the first chapter of Genesis: where the Holy Spirit with singular counsel described the history of Creation so fully and perfectly: that he can deservedly be considered impious who thinks that the faith of the Church, regarding that Article, ought to be informed from the philosophy of the Gentiles. Therefore we, following the footsteps of the Holy Spirit, will include the future treatment in certain questions: namely, those which both occur in Moses, and were moved by the ancient Doctors of the Church: and finally are agitated in various ways by more recent Theologians. And in rightly treating these, we will observe that order which Moses himself seems to prescribe for the ἑξαήμερον.

Latin:

DE Creatione Autor noster acturus, non tam ipsam rerum creatarum efformationem, quàm admirandam earum conservationem expendit. Undè tota etiam Philippea tractatio, si unicam illam quæstionem excipias, An Deus ex nihilo omnia condiderit? ad Articulum de æternâ DEI providentiâ, propriè pertinet: quem tamen hodiè Scholæ Theologorum à Creationis Articulo distinctum & sejunctum esse volunt: partim propter amplitudinem, quâ præ reliquis doctrina de Providentiâ DEI, patet longè latissimè: partim verò propter materiæ ipsius gravitatem, quâ Articulum Creationis infinitis modis altiùs transcendit. Proindè nos quoque secuti morem Scholarum Theologicarum, nonnulli à vestigijs Authoris nostri deflectentes; tùm numero, tùm tractatione Locum de Creatione, ab illo altero, qui est de Providentiâ, sejungimus: seorsim ipsum hoc loco expensuri.

Cæterùm cùm hîc ipse quoque Creationis Articulus satis latè pateat, respectu earum quæstionum, quæ de rebus creatis in specie non tàm à Theologis, quàm Philosophis hodiè moventur: nos utique, ne videamur μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος, compendio quodam usuri, eas tantùm, sub tractationis incudem revocabimus quæstiones, quæ ad sacratissimam scientiam nostram Theologicam propriè pertinent: & sine quarum consideratione, reliquæ universæ Physicorum de Cœlo, Stellis, Mundo, Elementis, & id genus rebus creatis aliis disputationes, meritò mancæ, mutilæ & imperfectæ videri debent.

Sedem verò materiæ hujus propriam constituimus in descriptione Mosaicâ, & quidem capite primo Geneseos: ubi Spiritus Sanctus singulari consilio Creationis historiam ita plenè & perfectè descripsit: ut impius meritò censeri possit, qui ex Gentilium Philosophiâ, fidem Ecclesiæ, quoad istum Articulum, informandam esse arbitretur. Proindè nos secuti vestigia Spiritus Sancti, futuram tractationem, certis quæstionibus includemus: ijs nimirùm, quæ tùm in Mose occurrunt, tùm ab antiquis Ecclesiæ Doctoribus motæ fuerunt: tùm denique à recentioribus Theologis diversimodè agitantur. Et in his quidem ritè pertractandis, eum observabimus ordinem, quem ipsum Moses ἑξαήμερον præscribere videtur.


### Question I. When was this Universe created?

The necessity for treating this question was brought about by that dispute which was moved and agitated concerning the Eternity of the World, not so much by reason of the end, as by reason of the beginning, not only by Philosophers, but also by certain Fathers. For there were not lacking among the ancient Doctors of the Church those who expounded that Mosaic (IN THE BEGINNING) not concerning the beginning of time, but concerning the ἀρχῇ ἀνάρχῳ, that is, concerning a beginning without a beginning: and even by this means established the eternity of the World, even unwittingly. Whose opinion, although it has been repressed by the zeal and work of other Fathers, and especially of Ambrose: and banished from the Church of GOD; yet in the school of the Gentile philosophers (whom Augustine frequently calls Pagans) the opinion of Aristotle prevailed, who in book 1 of On the Heavens, chapter 12, strove to construct and confirm the eternity of the World, both by reason of its end and by reason of its beginning: having sought arguments especially, partly from the incorruptibility of the movable thing, that is, the heaven; partly from the eternity of the prime mover, and of motion itself, in this manner:

1. The heaven is not subject to alteration: Therefore it is ἄφθαρτον incorruptible, and consequently eternal.

2. Given the mover, the movable thing is also given: But GOD himself is the first mover and the highest mover. Therefore, because He is eternal, the movable thing will certainly also have an ὁμόχρονον καὶ συναΐδιον, such as can be given besides the world.

3. The most perfect cause can never be idle: But GOD is by far the most perfect cause of all. Therefore, He was not idle from eternity, but was most occupied in governing and preserving a World coeternal with Himself.

4. Before every motion there must be a movable thing and another motion: For a movable thing cannot exist except through motion. Therefore, in a movable thing there is given a progression to infinity: which is eternity.

Of which reasons, indeed, the evidence is such that if one must judge concerning either the beginning or the end of the World from Philosophical principles, they easily deserve place and assent among all learned men. But when they are accommodated through μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος to the Theology of Moses, or indeed of the Holy Spirit Himself, then certainly they are found to labor under perpetual παρελέγχοις.

The first reason, therefore, is true only concerning natural things, insofar as they behave naturally: Where without alteration no generation or corruption can take place. By which method, indeed, the heaven, being devoid of alteration, could neither be generated, nor corrupted, nor perish. But because the World began to exist not by natural generation, but by supernatural power, and indeed by Creation: and therefore it will not perish by natural corruption: But will be reduced to nothing by the supernatural power of GOD: the Philosopher's first reason does not apply in this place. We answer the same to the second and third reasons: as they are true only of those things which act naturally: But they are false concerning the motion of Creation, since it depends not on the laws of nature, but solely on the principle of will in GOD. There is added a gross Sophistry in the fourth reason παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For it does not follow: GOD was not idle from eternity: Therefore He preserved and governed a World coeternal with Himself: As if, indeed, GOD would have lived idly, unless He had had a World coeternal with Himself, about which He might be occupied.

By which method, indeed, GOD is imagined to have needed the World, as if it were His throne and dwelling place: and that quite impiously and blasphemously. For since GOD is sufficient unto Himself, and as the most perfect act, is content with Himself, full of all good things, indeed the most absolute good itself: He certainly lived in supreme happiness, determining at some time to create the World, and from it to gather a Church, by which He might be eternally praised and celebrated. But if by chance anyone is unwilling to be content with that answer: we give him that which exists in the tripartite history: where to someone asking what GOD did from eternity, whether He was idle, it is answered: That He was not at all idle, but for curious people of this kind, and those searching into high things, He fashioned hell.

Regarding the fourth and last reason, it is indeed true that, in a nature already established, a movable subject is always prior to motion: But in Creation neither motion nor the movable thing began to exist through another natural motion: But this motion was created by GOD out of nothing along with the movable thing itself. Therefore, neither motion nor the movable thing had anything prior in nature, by the force of which they could have participated in the right of eternity.

Let Moses, therefore, correct Aristotle, who clearly affirms that GOD created the heaven and the earth IN THE BEGINNING, as in a measure of action, which was in an instant. For GOD, by creating the heaven and the earth, simultaneously created the beginning of time, the measure of creation itself: so that He produced at once the measure and the measured action: and thus the action was measured by that very beginning of time, which was simultaneously produced. Therefore, because by the testimony of Moses the World has a beginning of time, it cannot be eternal.

Moreover, both clear testimonies of the Scriptures and by far the most evident reasons confirm this very interpretation.

From the Scriptures first occur those things which distinguish heaven and earth, as the two principal parts of the world, from the remaining created things, in such a way that they assert that those were created by GOD before these: where hardly any sane person will deny that a certain notation of Time is involved. : Such are these two, Ps. 102:26. In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth. And Prov. 8:22. The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything.

Then the Apostle expressly defines this beginning of time, as often as he distinguishes eternity and the laid foundations of the world from one another: as when he affirms, Eph. 1:4, that we were chosen in CHRIST before the foundations of the world were laid; and as the Greek words sound more emphatically, πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. When likewise he asserts, 2 Tim. 1:9: That grace was given to us in CHRIST, πρὸ χρόνων αἰονίων, before secular times: that is, before the series of years which have flowed from the beginning of time.

Latin:

QUæstioni huic pertractandæ necessitatem attulit disputatio illa, quæ de Æternitate Mundi, non tàm ratione finis, quàm ratione principij, non à Philosophis modò, sed & à quibusdam Patribus mota & agitata fuit. Non enim defuerunt ex antiquis Doctoribus Ecclesiæ, qui Mosaicum illud (IN PRINCIPIO) non de initio temporis, sed de ἀρχῇ ἀνάρχῳ, hoc est, de principio sine principio exposuerunt: & vel hoc pacto æternitatem Mundi, etiam inscij statuerunt. Quorum opinio licèt aliorum Patrum, & cumprimis Ambrosij studio atque opera sit repressa: & ex Ecclesiâ DEI profligata; in Philosophorum tamen Gentilium (quos Augustinus frequenter Paganos nominat) Schola obtinuit Aristotelis Sententia, qui lib 1 de cœlo cap 12. Mundi æternitatem tum ratione finis, tum ratione principij astrucre & confirmare studuit: petitis potissimum argumentis, partim ab incorruptibilitate rei mobilis, hoc est cœli; partim ab æternitate primi motoris, & ipsius motus, in hunc modum:

1. Cœlum non subjacet alterationi: Ergo est ἄφθαρτον incorruptibile, & per consequens æternum.

2. Posito motore, ponitur etiam mobile: Atqui DEUS ipse est movens primum & motor summus. Ergo quia hic est æternus, utique mobile etiam habebit ὁμόχρονον καὶ συναΐδιον, quale præter mundum dari mundum potest.

3. Causa perfectissima nunquam potest esse ociosa: Atqui DEUS est causa longè omnium perfectissima. Ergò ab æterno non fuit ociosus, sed in Mundo sibi coæterno gubernando & conservando fuit occupatissimus.

4. Ante omnem motum oportet esse res mobilis & alius motus: Nam res mobilis esse non potest, nisi per motum. Ergò in mobili datur progressio in infinitum: quod est eternitas.

Quarum sane rationum ea est evidentia, ut si vel de initio, vel de fine Mundi, ex principijs Philosophicis judicandum sit, apud omnes literatos locum facilè & assensum mereantur. Cæterum quando per μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος ad Theologiam Mosis, imò ipsius Spiritus Sancti accommodantur: tum certè perpetuis παρελέγχοις laborare deprehenduntur.

Prima igitur ratio, vera tantùm est de rebus naturalibus, quatenus naturaliter se habent: Ubi sine alteratione nulla vel generatio vel corruptio fieri potest. Quo sane pacto cœlum, quippe alterationis expers, neque generari, neque corrumpi aut interire posset. Verùm quia non naturali generatione: sed supernaturali virtute, & quidem Creatione, Mundus existere cœpit: & proindè neque naturali corruptione interibit: Sed supernaturali virtute DEI in nihilum redigetur: utique prima Philosophi ratio, hoc loco non militat. Quod ipsum ad secundam & tertiam rationes respondemus: ut quæ de ijs tantùm veræ sunt, quæ agunt naturaliter: Falsæ autem de motu Creationis, quippè qui non à legibus naturæ, sed à principio voluntatis in DEO unicè dependet. Accedit crassa Sophisticatio in ratione quartâ παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Neque enim sequitur: DEUS non ab æterno fuit ociosus: Ergò Mundum sibi coæternum conservavit & gubernavit: Quasi verò DEUS vixisset ociosus, nisi Mundum, circa quem occupatus esset, habuisset sibi coæternum.

Quo sanè pacto DEUS fingitur indiguisse Mundo, tanquàm throno & habitaculo suo: idque satis impiè & blasphemè. Cùm enim DEUS sibi ipsi sit sufficiens, & tanquàm actus perfectissimus, seipso contentus sit, plenus bonorum omnium, imò ipsum bonum absolutissimum: utique vixit in summâ felicitate, constituens aliquando creare Mundum, & ex eo colligere Ecclesiam, à quâ æternùm laudetur & celebretur. Quòd si fortè quis responsione ista contentus esse nolit: illi damus eam, quæ extat in historiâ tripartitâ: ubi cuidam interroganti, quid DEUS ab æterno egerit, an ociosus fuerit, respondetur: Ipsum minimè fuisse ociosum, sed curiosis hujusmodi, & alta scrutantibus fabricasse infernum.

Quoad quartam & postremam rationem, verum quidem est, in naturâ jam conditâ, semper subjectum mobile, prius esse motu: Verùm in Creatione neque motus, neque mobile cœpit esse per alium motum naturalem: Sed motus hic cum reipsâ mobili à DEO creatus est ex nihilo. Ergò neque motus, neque mobile quicquam in naturâ prius habuerunt, cujus vi æternitatis jure participare potuerint.

Corrigat proindè Aristotelem Moses, qui liquidò affirmat, DEUM creasse cælum & terram IN PRINCIPIO, tanquam in mensurâ actionis, quæ fuit in instanti. DEUS enim creando cœlum & terram, simul concreavit temporis initium, mensuram ipsius creationis: ita ut unà effecerit mensuram & mensuratam actionem: atq; sic actio mensurata sit illo ipso temporis initio, quod simul effectum est. Ergò quia teste Mose, temporis initium habet Mundus, utique æternus esse nequit.

Confirmant autem hanc ipsam interpretationem, tùm perspicua Scripturarum testimonia: tùm rationes longè evidentissimæ.

Ex Scripturis primùm occurrunt ea, quæ cœlum & terram, tanquam duas principes mundi partes ita distinguunt à reliquis creatis, ut ante has illa à DEO creata esse asserant: ubi Temporis certam notationem involvi, vix quisquam sanus inficiabitur. : Qualia sunt duo isthæc, Psal. 102, 26. Initio tu Domine terram fundasti. Et Proverb. 8, 22. Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quicquam faceret.

Deindè principium hoc temporis, disertè definit Apostolus, quoties æternitatem, & jacta mundi fundamenta à se invicem distingvit: ut quando Eph. 1, 4. affirmat, Nos electos esse in CHRISTO, ante jacta mundi fundamenta; & ut Græca verba ἐμφατικωτέρως sonant, πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. Quando item 2. Tim. 1, 9. asserit: Gratiam nobis datam esse in CHRISTO, πρὸ χρόνων αἰονίων, ante tempora secularia: hoc est, ante annorum seriem, qui ab initio temporis fluxerunt.


### Question the Second

Finally, when in the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1, 2, He says that GOD promised the hope of eternal life before secular times, but manifested it in His own times. Where it is better known than to require laborious proof that the times αἰώνια or secular are to be understood as those which have flowed and must be numbered from the moment and point of time when this Universe began.

The reasons which fight for our interpretation can be given as these primarily.

I. Whatever has an end, it is necessary that it also had a beginning. But the World will have an end, as the Scriptures attest. Therefore, it is necessary that it also had a beginning.

The connection of the major premise will stand firm and immovable for as long as the contrary has not been proven by some evident example. For although these things are not ἀντιστρέφοντα, that is, reciprocal in both their parts, such that whatever once had a beginning will also have an end—since the contrary is evident from the example of the Angels and our souls—yet they are so ἀναστρέφοντα in only one of their parts that it is true καθ’ ὅλου & κτ’ παντὸς: Whatever will one day have an end, that also once began.

II. Reason: Eternity with respect to the negation of a beginning is Essential to GOD, that is, it is so simply convertible with the essence of GOD that whatever is eternal in this way, that must be GOD: according to that Apocalyptic passage, chapter 1, 8: I am the α & ω, the beginning and the end, says the Lord GOD, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the almighty. Therefore, if the World is co-eternal with GOD, it is necessary that it also be GOD: which is prodigiously absurd and blasphemous.

III. Reason. GOD Himself defined certain epochs of years: such as that of fifty years, solemn for the Jubilee. Now, unless a beginning of years is granted, according to the measure of time, no beginning of any epoch or chronology will be granted either. For no calculation of years falls into an eternity defined by the negation of a beginning: since before GOD a thousand years are as one day, which passed yesterday, Psalm 90, 4.

Some object to that in John 1, 1: In the Beginning was the Word: Scripture, they say, must be explained by Scripture. But now, in John, this phrase: In the beginning was the Word, either denotes a beginning ἀναρχον, that is, absolute eternity: or a beginning ἔναρχον, namely of Time: If the former: it would follow that the World was created in a beginning ἀναρχον: and thus is eternal: If the latter: it will follow that the λόγος or Son of GOD began in a beginning ἔναρχον, that is, in Time: and thus is not συναΐδιον to the Father, and consequently not GOD.

But it is most rightly answered that a gross Sophistication is committed παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς

λέξεως. For neither should an equivalence of phrases or words be posited between John and Moses: since the very sound of the letters, not to mention the words, evidently demonstrates that they differ δὶς διὰ πασῶν. For Moses says: In the beginning GOD created the heaven and the earth: but John does not say: In the beginning GOD created the λόγος: but in the beginning WAS the Word. Therefore, as much as that which is finally to be created differs from that which already just now is or exists: so much do these two phrases also differ from each other: so that the Mosaic phrase clearly establishes the beginning of created things: but the Johannine phrase establishes the eternity of the Son of GOD: and proves that the λόγος or Son of GOD, in the beginning, when time itself together with things, and things together with time, began to be, WAS: and thus indeed before that beginning of time, where the eternity of the λόγος is defined, it is sufficiently clear by itself. For whatever was before the beginning of time and the creation of things, it is necessary that it be eternal, and consequently God: because before the beginning of time and created things, there was absolutely nothing except the eternal GOD alone. Therefore, that fictitious distinction between a beginning ἄναρχον and ἔναρχον collapses: For we concede entirely that in both places, both in Moses and in John, only a beginning ἔναρχον, which is of Time, is noted: nevertheless, the eternity of the λόγος stands: which is most rightly established not from the words, In the beginning: but from the existential verb WAS: in the same sense exactly as the Son of GOD Himself, about to assert His own eternity, uses this equivalent: Proverbs 8, 22: The Lord possessed me in the Beginning of His ways, before He made anything. Hence it is that Basil, against the Eunomians, vehemently urges the quadruple repetition of the Greek substantive verb, ἦν, was, which John used, saying: In the beginning WAS the Word: And the Word WAS with GOD: and the Word WAS GOD: this WAS in the beginning with GOD: And from there he constructs such an axiom: τέταρτον εἶπε τὸ ἦν, καὶ κατεργήσεις αὐτῶν τὸ οὐκ ἦν: He said WAS four times, and you will solve these things, That it was not.

Latin:

Quando denique in Epistolâ ad Tit. cap. 1, 2. DEUM dicit promisisse spem vitæ æternæ, antè tempora secularia, patefecisse autem suis temporibus. Ubi tempora αἱώνια sive secularia, de illis esse intelligenda, quæ ex momento & puncto temporis, quo hoc Universum cœpit, fluxerunt & dinumerari debent, notiùs est, quàm ut operosâ probatione indigeat.

Rationes, quæ pro nostrâ militant interpretatione, dari possunt hæ potissìmùm.

I. Quicquid habet finem: principium etiam habuerit, necesse est. Atqui Mundus habebit finem, attestantibus Scripturis. Ergò principium etiam habuerit, necesse est.

Majoris connexum tamdiu stabit firmum & immotum, donec evidenti aliquo exemplo contrarium probatum fuerit. Etsi enim non ἀντισρέφοντα sunt isthæc, hoc est, utraq; sui parte reciproca, ut quicquid principium aliquando habuit, illud finem etiam sit habiturum: Siquidem exemplo Angelorum & animarum nostrarum diversum patet: tamen ex alterâ tantùm sui parte ita sunt ἀναστρέφοντα, ut καθ’ ὅλε & κτ’ παντὸς verum sit, Quicquid finem aliquando habebit; illud etiam aliquando cœpit.

II. Ratio: Æternitas respectu negationis principij est DEO Essentialis, hoc est, cum DEI essentiâ ita simplicisimè convertitur, ut quicquid hoc modo æternum est, illud DEUS sit: Secundum illud Apocalypticum cap. 1, 8. Ego sum α & ω, principium & finis, dicit Dominus DEUS, qui est, quierat, & qui venturus est, omnipotens. Ergò si Mundus DEO est coæternus, DEUS & ipse sit, necesse est: id quod prodigiosè absurdum & blasphemum.

III. Ratio. DEUS ipse certas annorum Epochas definivit: qualis est illa annorum quinquaginta, Jubilæo solennis. Jam nisi detur principium annorum, juxta mensuram temporis, nullum etiam dabitur ullius Epochæ sive Chronologiæ principium. Neque enim in æternitatem negatione principij definitam, ulla cadit annorum supputatio: Siquidem coram DEO sunt mille anni, tanquam unus dies, qui heri præterijt, Psalm. 90, 4.

Objiciunt nonnulli istud Joh. 1, 1. In Principio erat verbum: Scriptura, inquiunt, per Scripturam est explicanda. Jam verò apud Johannem phrasis hæc: In principio erat verbum, vel notat principium ἀναρχον, hoc est, absolutam æternitatem: vel principium ἔναρχον, Temporis nimirùm: Si illud: Consequens fuerit, Mundum conditum esse in principio ἀνάρχω: & sic esse æternum: Sin hoc: sequetur λόγον sive Filium DEI cœpisse in principio ἐνάρχω, hoc est, in Tempore: & sic Patri non συναΐδιον, & per consequens neœ, DEUM esse.

Sed rectissimè respondetur, crassam committi Sophisticationem παρὰ τὸ σχήμα τῆς

λέξεως. Neq; enim apud Johannem & Mosen phraseōn sive verborum æquipollentia statui debet: quin δις διὰ πασῶν ea differre, ipse literarum, ne dum verborum sonus, evidenter demonstrat. Moses enim dicit: In principio creavit DEUS cœlum & terram: Johannes autem non dicit: In principio creavit DEUS λόγον: sed in principio ERAT verbum. Proindè quantum distat id, quod demùm creandum ab eo, quod jam modò est sive existit: tantùm à se invicem duæ etiam hæ phrases distant: ita ut Mosaica principium rerum creatarum: Johannitica autem æternitatem Filij DEI luculenter astruat: & evincat, λόγον sive Filium DEI, in principio, quo tempus ipsum unà cum rebus, & res cum tempore esse inciperent, FUISSE: & sic quidem ante illud temporis principium, ubi æternitatem λόγε definisi, per se satis liquet. Quicquid enim ante principium temporis, rerumque creationem fuit, illud æternum, & consequenter Deus sit, necesse est: proptereà quod ante principium temporis & rerum creatarum, nihil prorsus fuit, præter solum æternum DEUM. Corruit proindè fictitium illud discrimen inter principium ἄναρχον & ἔναρχον: Nam utrobiq; tùm apud Mosen, tùm apud Johannem, tantùm principium ἔναρχον, quod est Temporis, notari, omninò concedimus: nihilo tamen minùs stante æternitate λόγε: quæ non ex verbis, In principio: sed ex verbo ὑπαρκτικῷ ERAT, rectissimè astruitur: eodem planè sensu, quo ipse Filius DEI, æternitatem suam asserturus, æquipollente hâc utitur: Proverb. 8, 22. Dominus possedit me, in Initio viarum suarum, antequàm quicquam faceret. Hinc est, quod Basilius adversus Eunomianos, vehementer urget quaternam repetitionem verbi substantivi Græci, ἦν, erat, quâ Johannes usus sit, dicens: In principio ERAT verbum: Et verbum ERAT apud DEUM: & DEUS ERAT verbum: hoc ERAT in principio apud DEUM: Et indè tale extruit axioma: τέταρτον εἶπε τὸ ἦν, καὶ κατεργήσεις αὐτῶν τὸ οὐκ ἦν: Quater dixit, ERAT, & tu solves isthæc, Quod non ERAT.


### Question II. From what matter did God create heaven and earth?

From what matter did GOD create heaven and earth?

That GOD is one in Essence, but three in persons, the author and creator of this universe, we take for granted in this place: nor do we disapprove of the opinion of both ancient and modern theologians, who confirm this very thing from the Hebrew phrase, where Moses, contrary to the rules of grammarians, joined a singular verb with a noun of plural number, saying, בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים Bereschith Barah Elohim. In the beginning created Gods.

Latin:

Ex quâ materiâ DEUS creaverit cœlum & terram?

DEUM unum Essentiâ: trinum verò personis, esse autorem & creatorem hujus universi, hoc loco pro confesso sumimus: neque improbamus tùm veterum, tùm recentiorum Theologorum sententiam, qui hoc ipsum ex phrasi Hebræâ confirmant, ubi Moses præter regulas Grammaticorum, Verbum singulare, junxit cum nomine pluralis numeri, dicens, בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים Bereschith Barah Elohim. In principio creavit Dij.


### Question III. How chiefly and immediately from Nothing are they produced?

For neither does God the Father alone, to the exclusion of the other two persons, claim for himself this work of creation, although he is the προκαταρκτικὴ [prokatarktike] cause, and as it were the fountain from which all things flow: nay, Scripture testifies concerning the Son, John 1:3, that all things were made through him: and Heb. 1:2, that GOD created the ages through the Son: and concerning the Holy Spirit, that he brooded over the waters, that is, rendered them fit for producing other creatures. Gen. 1:2. Nay, that by the Spirit of the mouth of GOD all the host of heaven was created. Ps. 33:6. Ps. 104:30. These things, I say, each and all in this place, not troubling ourselves with the trifles of Calvin and others, we presuppose: and we judge that the matter from which this Universe was produced must be examined more deeply.

But our blessed Luther rightly, in his Commentary on Genesis, reproves Nicolaus Lyra, who thought it necessary to have knowledge of the opinion of the Philosophers concerning matter, because the understanding of the operation of the six days depends upon it. For neither did Aristotle know what kind of matter that rude or indigestible mass was, which Moses names Tohu Vabohu: the Latin rendered it: Void and empty.

But that this question may be rightly resolved, it should be observed that there is absolutely no discrepancy among Theologians, some of whom maintain that created things were produced out of NOTHING, while others maintain they were produced out of some pre-existing thing. For with this one distinction applied, all discrepancy is removed, so that you may say some things were created immediately, but others mediately out of nothing. For those former ones, following Moses, mean this: that the heaven, the earth, and the Abyss, that is, the matter of those things which are in heaven, in earth, and in the sea, were created immediately out of nothing. But these latter ones attend to the fact that GOD subsequently digested that rude and unformed matter, and from it created the rest: which things themselves, however, can also be said to have been created mediately or ἑπομένως [hepomenos] out of nothing, namely by means of that rude matter, which itself also first proceeded out of nothing by the power of GOD. And in this respect it is true what is read written in the book of Wisdom ch. 11:18. The hand of GOD created the world from unformed matter.

But that (under the distinction already explained) all things were created out of nothing, Scripture testifies quite clearly, bringing forward: 1. That all things were made by the LORD speaking, and that the Universe was created by his commanding, Gen. 1, which the Apostle rendered thus, Rom. 4:17: GOD called τὰ μὴ ὄντα, ὡς ὄντα [the things that are not, as things that are]. Whence in Psalm 148:5: He spoke, and they were made: he commanded, and they were created: And the Epistle to the Hebrews 11:3: By faith we understand that the ages were adapted by the WORD of GOD, ἐκ τῶν μὴ φαινομένων τὰ βλεπόμενα γεγονέναι [so that things which are seen were made from things which do not appear], so that from invisible things visible things might be made: And Prov. 8:24: When the abysses were nothing, I was already born, says Wisdom. Nor that this was ever doubted among the people of GOD is evident even from that admonition of the Mother of the Maccabees, who addresses her youngest son, now about to be subjected to martyrdom, thus: My Son, look upon heaven and earth, and all that are in them, and understand that GOD made them out of nothing, and the race of men. 2 Macc. 7:28. Then the same is confirmed by Scripture, as often as it uses the Hebrew word בָּרָא Barah, that is, to create, in describing the creation of this universe. For although we willingly grant to Pererius and others that this word is accommodated in the Scriptures in a transferred or Metaphorical sense, by a certain similarity, to other productions also: as Ps. 51:12: Create in me, O GOD, a new heart: Although also the work of creation is not always expressed by the word of creating, but sometimes also by the word of making and similar ones: as Ps. 124, last verse. Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth: nevertheless, in its proper signification, he is Creator who makes something out of nothing: and to create, properly, is to make something out of nothing, as Lombard judged against Pererius, lib. 1, dist. 2. Which is the reason that this word of Creating is nowhere in the sacred writings attributed to man or to other creatures: But to GOD alone, and to him indeed either in respect of the works of creation, or in respect of other operations, which nevertheless have a certain kinship or similarity with Creation itself: Such are preternatural operations: The Incarnation of the Son of GOD, of which Jer. 31:22: GOD will create a new thing upon the earth: A woman shall encompass a man: Likewise the Renovation and Sanctification of man: of which David, Ps. 51:12: Create in me, O GOD, a new heart: And St. Paul, Eph. 2:10: We are his workmanship, created in CHRIST unto good works.

Latin:

Neque enim solus DEus Pater, exclusis reliquis duabus personis, hoc opus creationis sibi vendicat, licet causa sit προκαταρκτικὴ, & quasi fons, ex quo omnia: quin de Filio Scriptura perhibet, Joh. 1, 3. Omnia per ipsum facta esse: & Hebr. 1, 2. DEUM per Filium secula condidisse: de Spiritu Sancto verò, ipsum fovisse aquas, hoc est, idoneas reddidisse ad alias producendas creaturas. Gen. 1, 2. Imò Spiritu oris DEI omnem exercitum Cœli creatum esse. Psal. 33, 6. Psalm. 104, 30. Hæc, inquam singula atque universa hoc loco, nihil morari Calvini & aliorum nugas, præsupponimus: & de Materiâ, ex quâ productum sit hoc Universum, altiùs dispiciendum esse judicamus.

Rectè autem B. Lutherus noster in Commentario super Genesin, reprehendit Nicolaum Lyram, qui putavit necessarium esse cognitionem sententiæ Philosophorum de materiâ, propterea, quod ex eâ dependeat intellectus operationis sex dierum. Neque enim Aristoteles scivit qualis materia fuerit rudis illa sive indigesta moles, quam Moses nominat, Tohu Vabohu: Latinus reddidit: Inane & vacuum.

Cæterùm ut hæc quæstio ritè expediatur, observandum fuerit, nullam prorsus discrepantiam esse inter Theologos, quorum alij res creatas, ex NIHILO: alij verò ex præexistente quapiam, productas esse, statuunt. Nam unâ hac adhibitâ distinctione, omnis discrepantia tollitur, ut dicas quædam immediatè: quædam verò mediatè ex nihilo creata esse. Priores enim illi, Mosen secuti hoc volunt, Immediatè ex nihilo esse creata, cœlum, terram, Abyssum, hoc est, materiam eorum, quæ in cœlo, in terrâ, & in mari sunt. Posteriores verò hi attendunt illud, quod DEus rudem, illam & informem materiam postmodùm digessit, & ex eâ reliqua creavit: Quæ tamen ipsa quoq;, mediatè sive ἑπομένως, ex nihilo creata dici possunt, mediante nimirùm rudi illa materia, quæ & ipsa πρώτως virtute DEI ex nihilo prodijt. Et hoc respectu verum est, quod scriptum legitur in libro Sapientiæ cap. 11, 18. Manus DEI creavit orbem terrarum ex informi materiâ.

Cæterùm quòd (sub discrimine jam explicato) ex nihilo creata sint omnia, satis perspicuè testatur Scriptura, afferens. 1. Dicente DOMINO facta esse omnia, & mandante ipso, creata esse Universa Gen. 1. id quod Apostolus sic reddidit Rom. 4, 17. DEUS vocavit τὰ μὴ ὄντα, ὡς ὄντα. Undè Psalmo 148, 5. Ipse dixit, & facta sunt: ipse mandavit & creata sunt: Et Epistola ad Hebr. 11, 3. Fide intelligimus adaptata esse secula VERBO DEI, ἐκ τῶν μὴ φαινομένων τὰ βλεπόμενα γεγονέναι, ut ex invisibilibus visibilia fierent: Et Proverb. 8, 24. Cùm nihil essent abyssi, Ego jam genita eram, inquit Sapientia. Neq; in populo DEI, hæc de re aliquando dubitatum fuisse, constat vel ex illâ admonitione Matris Macchabææ, quæ filium natu minimum, jam martyrio subjiciendum, sic affatur: Mî Fili, aspice cœlum & terram, & omnia quæ in eis sunt & intelligas, quod ex nihilo fecit illa DEUS & hominum genus. 2. Macchab. 7, 28. Deindè idem confirmat Scriptura, quoties in describendâ creatione hujus universi utitur verbo Hebræo בָּרָא Barah, hoc est, creare. Etsi enim Pererio & aliis libenter largimur, verbum hoc sensu translatitio sive Metaphorico, per quandam similitudinem ad alias etiam produčtiones in Scripturis accommodari: ut Ps. 51, 12. Crea in me DEUS cor novum: Etsi etiam opus creationis, non semper verbo creandi, sed interdum etiam faciendi vocabulo & similibus exprimitur: ut Ps. 124, ult. Adjutorium nostrum in nomine Domini, qui fecit cœlum & terram: tamen propriâ in significatione Creator est, qui de nihilo facit aliquid: Et creare, proprie est facere aliquid de nihilo, uti contra Pererium censuit Lombardus lib. 1. dist. 2. Quæ causa est, quod hoc verbum Creandi, nuspiam in sacris vel homini vel aliis creaturis tribuitur: Sed Soli DEO, & huic quidem vel respectu operum creationis, vel respectu aliarum operationum, quæ tamen cognationem quandam aut similitudinem habent cum ipsâ Creatione: Quales operationes præternaturales sunt: Incarnatio Filij DEI, de quâ Jer. 31, 22. Creabit DEUS novam quiddam super terram: Fœmina circumdabit virum: Item Renovatio & Sanctificatio hominis: de quâ David, Psal. 51, 12. Crea in me DEUS cor novum: Et D. Paulus, Eph. 2, 10. Ipsius sumus creatura, creati in CHRISTO ad opera bona.


### Question III. How chiefly and immediately from Nothing are they produced?: Question III. What things were produced first and immediately out of Nothing?

QUESTION III. What things were produced first and immediately out of NOTHING?

Moses enumerates three: Heaven: Earth: The Abyss. But what should be understood by each of these is not clearly agreed upon among the Doctors.

There are those who think that Moses, in affirming, In the beginning GOD created Heaven and earth: and indeed before the first day, did not intend to define θετικῶς [positively] a certain work, but only to express the counsel of GOD, namely that He Himself had determined to create heaven and earth, and all things that are in them: which He subsequently brought into act in detail through those six days of creation. In this opinion were Augustine, Chrysostom and others: whom, however, Basil rightly contradicted: since the opinion of these men manifestly conflicts with the words of Moses: as one who affirms θετικῶς [positively]. 1. That GOD created heaven and earth in the beginning. 2. That the earth was void and empty: so that the creation of that matter is expressly defined here, from which thereafter individual things were fashioned through the six days of creation, just as they exist today.

There are others who by Heaven understand the Angels: but by earth the earthly matter of our bodies: In this opinion were Augustine, book 12 of the Confessions, chapter 7, the Master of the Sentences, book 2, distinction 12. But this opinion fails in many ways. For first, no necessity compels us to seize upon an allegorical and figurative sense in place of the literal sense of the words of Moses: especially since it is agreed that Moses, in his description of the creation, intended to convey not a mystical, but a historical sense. 2. That by Heaven a certain invisible creature, and not indeed a visible one, is to be understood, has not yet been proven. 3. Since Moses afterwards on the sixth day expressly defines the matter from which man was created, it is not likely that he intended to define the same matter twice, and indeed in a less suitable order. Finally, since Moses immediately subjoins in what manner GOD afterwards distinguished and fashioned the Heaven and the earth into those bodies which even today are visible to our sight: we certainly bid farewell to this allegorical interpretation.

In the third place, we also simply reject the trifles of the Scholastics concerning the Empyrean heaven, which, because it is distinct from the remaining heavens, has been noted in this place by Moses, for those reasons which we have just noted.

These and other inconveniences of this kind being removed from our opinions, we determine that by the appellation of Heaven and earth we are not to understand those parts of the universe as they subsequently turned out, or as they are now seen by the eyes, fashioned by an admirable and stupendous workmanship: but a formless, rude, and in some way confused mass, which GOD afterwards distinguished and fashioned according to a certain plan, in such a way indeed that under the name of Heaven comes the entire celestial body, embracing all the spheres: perfect indeed and complete in respect of substance and magnitude: but yet without light, without motion, and without the distinction of the stars, etc., which only afterwards were added. This opinion is confirmed by 1. The subsequent words of Moses in which he affirms that the Earth was void and empty, and darkness was upon the face of it. Void indeed, both in respect of form and figure, which afterwards were added: and also because that mass, mixed with waters and immersed, could not be seen. It was indeed empty, because it was still uncultivated, sterile, and destitute of inhabitants, both men and animals. In this sense Jeremiah, chapter 4, verse 7, threatens that the earth will be empty and void: where Thohu vabohu is taken for devastation and solitude, by reason of which the earth is to be so devastated that neither men, nor beasts, nor anything safe and unharmed is to be found.

Furthermore, the truth of our opinion is also evident from the fact that, according to the Mosaic description, on the third day the Earth is commanded to appear, not to be made. Therefore, by the name of Earth in verse 1 of Chapter 1 of Genesis, one must understand the very element of earth, which was afterwards on the third day distinguished and separated from the waters. Whence David also rightly sings in Ps. 102:26, In the beginning, O Lord, You founded the earth. And indeed, unless it is established that the earth was created in the beginning, insofar as it is considered by reason of its substance, it does not appear from Moses when it was finally created. For the fact that some raise objections concerning the third day is too weak; since Moses does not say that the earth was created on that third day, but that GOD said that the dry land, or earth, should appear from the waters. With these points thus established, we deservedly reject the opinion of those who understand by "Heaven and earth" created in the beginning that prime Matter, about which physicists and metaphysicians dispute with sufficient scrupulosity and anxiety, and from which all bodies, and especially heaven and earth, were subsequently produced: which is a certain meager thing, comprehensible by thought and mind, and lacking every form: As if, indeed, Moses had wished to inculcate to his Hebrews that altercation concerning prime Matter, which not even the most acute philosophers can sufficiently explain. As if also heaven, earth, and the Abyss had lacked every form and mass: that which diametrically conflicts with the text of Moses. Finally, as regards the Abyss, it was nothing other than an immense force of waters, under which the earth itself, still formless and rude, was enclosed and lay hidden: and which, being subsequently gathered into one, was called the Sea. It is called the Abyss, because that chasm of waters lacked a bottom: as Basil rightly judges in Homily 2 of the Hexaemeron. Moreover, upon that abyss there was darkness, not indeed created by GOD, as the Manichaeans raved, establishing darkness as a certain eternal principle or deity: as Epiphanius testifies: For every creation is of substances: but darkness ought rather to be called a privative accident than something positive: but because it followed that rude and undigested mass of its own accord: so that those shadows were nothing else than the defect and absence of that light, which afterwards, at the word of GOD, shone forth, according to that of the Apostle, 2 Cor. 4:6, GOD commanded light to shine out of darkness.

Latin:

QUÆSTIO III. Quænam πρώτως & immediatè ex NIHILO sint producta?

TRia enumerat Moses: Cœlum: Terram: Abyssum. Sed quid per singula isthæc intelligi debeat, non planè inter Doctores convenit.

Sunt qui existimant Mosen affirmantem, In principio DEO creasse Cœlum & terram: & quidem ante diem primum, noluisse θετικῶς certum quoddam opus definire, sed tantùm consilium DEI exprimere, quòd nimirùm ipse constituerit cœlum & terram, & omnia, quæ in ijs sunt, creare: id quod postmòdum per sex illos dies creationis, particulatim in actum deduxerit. Quâ in sententiâ fuerunt Augustinus, Chrysostomus & alij: quibus tamen rectè contradixit Basilius: Siquidem cum verbis Mosis, manifestè opinio istorum pugnat: ut qui θετικῶς affirmat. 1. DEUM creasse cœlum & terram in principio. 2. Terram fuisse inanem & vacuam: ita ut disertè hîc definiatur creatio illius materiæ, ex quâ deinceps singula per sex creationis dies ita sunt elaborata, prout hodiéque existunt.

Sunt alii, qui per Cœlum intelligunt Angelos: per terram verò materiam terrenam corporum nostrorum: Quâ in sententiâ fuerunt Augustinus lib. 12. Confessionum, cap. 7. Magister tent. lib. 2. dist 12. Verùm multis modis deficit hæc opinio. Primùm enim nulla necessitas cogit, ut pro literali sensu verborum Mosis, arripiamus allegoricum & figuratum: præsertim cùm constet, Mosen in descriptione creationis non mysticum, sed historicum sensum tradere voluisse. 2. Per Cœlum invisibilem quandam creaturam, non verò adspectabilem intelligendam esse, nondum probatum est. 3. Cùm Moses postmodùm sexto die materiam ex quâ homo creatus expresse definiat, non est verisimile, ipsum bis eandem materiam, & quidem ordine minùs congruo definire voluisse. Tandem cùm Moses statim subjiciat quo pacto DEUS Cœlum & terram postmodum distinxerit & elaborarit, in ea corpora, quæ hodiéque visui nostro sunt adspectabilia: utíq; allegoricæ huic interpretationi nuncium remittimus.

Tertio loco Scholasticorum etiam nugas, de cœlo Empyreo, quod, quippè à reliquis cœlis distinctum, hoc loco per Mosen, fuerit notatum, simpliciter rejicimus: ijs de causis, quas modò annotavimus.

His & id genus alijs incommodis opinionibus remotis, statuimus Cœli & terræ appellatione non intelligendas quidem esse partes istas universi, quales postea evaserunt, aut nunc visuntur oculis admirando & stupendo opificio elaboratæ: sed informem, rudem & inconfusam quodammodò massam, quam DEUS postmodum certâ ratione distinxit & elaboravit, ita quidem, ut Cœli nomine veniat universum corpus cœleste, cunctos orbes complectens: perfectum quidem & integrum ratione substantiæ & magnitudinis: sed tamen sine luce, sine motu & distinctione siderum &c. quæ posteà demùm accesserunt. Confirmant hanc sententiam 1. Verba Mosis subsequentia quibus affirmat Terram fuisse inanem & vacuam, & tenebras supra faciem ejus. Inanem quidem, tùm ratione formæ & figuræ, quæ postmodùm accessit: tùm quòd moles illa aquis permixta, & immersa videri non poterat. Vacuam verò, quòd adhuc erat inculta, sterilis, & cultoribus tùm hominibus, tùm animalibus destituta. Quo sensu Jeremias cap. 4, 7. comminatur terram fore vacuam & inanem: Ubi Thohu vabohu accipitur pro vastatione & solitudine: ratione cujus terra ita sit vastanda, ut nec homines, nec jumenta, nec quicquam salvum & incolume reperiatur.

Deindè patet Sententiæ nostræ veritas ex eo etiam, quòd secundum descriptionem Mosaicam, tertio die jubetur Terra apparere, non fieri. Terræ proindè nomine in versu 1. Capitis 1. Geneseos, intelligendum venit ipsum terræ Elementum, quod postmodùm tertio die ab aquis distinctum & separatum fuit. Undè David etiam Pf. 102, 26. rectè canit, Initio Domine terram fundasti. Et sanè nisi in principio statuatur creata esse terra, quatenus ratione substantiæ consideratur, non apparet ex Mose, quando illa tandem creata sit. Nam quòd de tertio die nonnulli obstrepunt, nimis dilutum est: Siquidem Moses non dicit, die illo tertio creatam esse terram: sed DEUM dixisse, ut appareret ex aquis arida, sive terra. Quibus ita constitutis meritò explodimus eorum opinionem qui per Cœlum & terram in principio creata intelligunt Materiam illam primam, de quâ Physici & Metaphysici satis scrupulosè & anxiè disputans, & ex quâ omnia corpora, & cumprimis cœlum & terra postmodùm sint producta: quæq; sit exilis quædam res, cogitatione & animo comprehensibilis: omnique formâ carens: Quasi verò Moses suis Hebræis inculcare voluerit altercationem illam de Materiâ primâ, quam ne quidem acutissimi Philosophi satis explicare possunt. Quasi etiam cœlum, terra & Abyffus omni formâ & mole caruerint: id quod cum textu Mofis è diametro pugnat. Tandem Quoad Abyffum, nihil ea fuit aliud, quàm immensa vis aquarum, sub quâ, terra ipsa informis adhuc & rudis concludebatur & latebat: quæque postmodùm in unum collecta, Mare appellabatur. Dicitur autem Abyssus, quia vorago illa aquarum fundo carebat: uti rectè censet Basilius Homil. 2. Hexa-emeri. Super abyssum autem istam erant tenebræ, non quidem à DEO creatæ, quemadmodum delirabant Manichæi, tenebras constituentes æternum quoddam principium sive numen: teste Epiphanio: Omnis enim creatio substantiarum est: Tenebræ verò accidens potiùs privativum, quã positivum quid dici debent: sed quod rudem illam ac indigestam molem suâ sponte subsequebantur: ita ut tenebræ istæ nihil fuerint aliud, quàm defectus & absentia illius luminis, quod postmodùm dicente DEO, illuxit, secundum illud Apostoli, 2. Cor. 4, 6. DEUS jussit ex tenebris lucem illucescere.


### Question IV. Whether besides earth and water, the other two Elements, Fire and Air, were created by God?

Concerning the air, most people maintain that there is no doubt that it was produced by GOD, either immediately from nothing or mediately from water. For since the earth, together with the waters floating upon it, was exhaling, that vast space by which the heaven and the earth were separated from one another was certainly filled with air on the second and third day; which the birds created on the fifth day enjoyed, both for the purpose of respiration and for flight. Which opinion of some, as I by no means reject, so I simply condemn the opinion of the Hebrews, as well as that of Peter Martyr, who in this part Judaizes with Calvin, who maintain that by the Spirit of the Lord, which was moving over the waters, the element of air is to be understood. For that effect, which Moses assigns to the Spirit, and indeed to the Spirit of the Lord in this place, can by no reasoning be attributed to the air. Neither air nor wind possesses such power that it can support a watery mass by motion, and by brooding over it so cherish it that it might be rendered fit for producing creatures whose species did not previously exist.

And what will those fanatics answer to David, who expressly refers the words of Moses to the Holy Spirit, saying: By the Spirit of the mouth of Jehovah, the whole heavenly host was established. Psal. 33.

We are less concerned about the Element of Fire, since there is no lack of most distinguished Theologians and Philosophers who vehemently doubt whether there is any Element of Fire above the air. We do not, however, make this dispute our own, asserting that if any such thing exists, it was certainly created together with the heaven and the earth: since nothing can deserve the name of a creature which was not created by GOD. Basil indeed maintains that the Element of Fire was created together with the earth: and he attempts to prove this from the fact that there are signs of fire latent in the earth, such as the eruptions of flames and fires, as from Mount Etna and other places, and the eruptions of many waters boiling with fiery heat. Yet it is most rightly doubted whether this opinion can stand, especially since those fiery eruptions from the earth do not at all correspond to the purity of the element of fire, nor to its place, which the philosophers establish.

Latin:

DE Aëre statuunt plerique, dubium esse nullum, quin à DEO sive immediatè ex nihilo; sive mediatè ex aquâ sit productus. Cùm enim Terra unà cum aquis supernatantibus exhalaret, utique die secundo & tertio ingens illud spatium, quo Cœlum & terra à se invicem dissidebant, aëre repletum fuit; quo volucres quinto die creati, tùm quoad respirationem, tùm quoad volatum fruebantur. Quam sanè quorundã sententiam, uti minimè rejicimo: ita simpliciter damnamus tùm Hebræorum, tùm Petri Martyris hac in parte cum Calvino Judaizantis opinionem: statuentium, per Spiritum Domini, qui ferebatur super aquis, intelligendum esse Elementum Aëris. Effectus enim ille, quem Moses Spiritui, & Spiritui quidé Domini hoc loco assignat, aëri tribui nullâ ratione potest. Neq; enim vel aër vel ventus eam habet vim, ut possit motando sustentare molem aqueam, & incubando ita eam fovere, ut producendis creaturis, quarũ species prius non extabant, redderetur habilis.

Et quid respondebunt fanatici isti Davidi, qui verba Mosis, disertè ad Spiritum Sanctum refert: Spiritu, inquiens: oris Jehova, conditus est universus exercitus cœlestis. Psal. 33.

De Elemento Ignis minùs laboramus, cùm non desint præclarissimi tùm Theologi, tùm Philosophi, qui, nùm sit aliquod Elementum Ignis supra aërem, vehementer dubitant. Quam tamen litem, nostram non facimus: asserentes, si tale aliquod extat, illud utique unà cum cœlo & terrâ creatum esse: cum nihil creaturæ nomen mereri possit, quod à DEO non est creatum. Basilius quidem statuit Elementum Ignis unà cum terrâ esse creatum: idque indè probare conatur, quod ignis latentis in terrâ indicia sint, eructationes flammarum & ignium, velut ex monte Aetnâ, alijsque locis, & complurium aquarum igneo calore ferventium eruptiones. Quæ tamen sententia, ut subsistere queat, rectissimè dubitatur: præsertim cùm eruptiones illæ igneæ ex terrâ, neque ad puritatem Elementi ignis: neque etiam ad ejus locum, quem constituunt Philosophi, minimè quadrent.


### Question Six

Were the angelic spirits created together with the heaven and the earth in the beginning?

Two things are asked here: 1. Why did Moses make no mention at all of the creation of the Angels? 2. On what day or when were they created by GOD?

To the former Question, Chrysostom answers that this was done because Moses had a rude and simple people, who did not understand what a spiritual and incorporeal nature was. He therefore wished to explain only the origin of this corporeal and visible world. Although we do not disapprove of this answer, we nevertheless think it must be added, as Athanasius and Theodoret also noted, that this was done primarily to prevent idolatry, to which the Hebrew people were very prone and inclined.

In resolving the latter Question, there are almost more opinions than interpreters. For although most Doctors of the Church agree on this, that the Angels did not exist from eternity, but were truly created from nothing by GOD at some time in time: which Scripture itself also confirms, Psal. 104, 4. Who makest the Angels spirits, and thy ministers a flaming fire. And Coloss. 1, 16. In him were all things created, in heaven and in earth, visible and invisible, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers: yet they disagree most on this, namely, on what day or when the Angels were created by GOD.

1. For some have maintained that the Angels were created by GOD many ages before this world. Their opinion is refuted even by this, that with the creation of this world, Time itself began: but before the beginning of Time, mere and simple eternity reigned. Therefore, if the Angels existed before the creation of this World, they were certainly from eternity: If from eternity, they would certainly be GOD: since besides the one and only GOD, nothing by reason of a beginning is, or was, or will ever be eternal. And the reasoning is clearly childish: Angels excel this world in dignity. Therefore they were created before this World. For the vanity of the consequence is most clearly evident from the single example of the creation of man. It is certainly established that Man was created by GOD in the last place: yet no one would say that he is therefore inferior in dignity to the other creatures.

2. Others have maintained that Moses, saying: In the Beginning GOD created heaven and earth: by the name of heaven, understood the Angels. Their opinion is easily overturned by those reasons by which we showed above that by heaven must be understood the celestial body itself, with its orbs, however undigested it may still be. And unless this is maintained, the creation of heaven can certainly no longer be proved from Moses: to say nothing now of the fact that Scripture, when speaking of creation throughout, takes the name of heaven properly and literally.

3. Others think that the Angels were created with that Light of the first day, because they are compared to Light in the Scriptures. And indeed, it is probably conjectured that they were created on the very first day, either with this Light, or with the heaven, their dwelling place, or immediately after it, from Job chapter 38, 7, where God asserts that He was praised by the morning stars and the sons of GOD when He laid the bases or foundations of the earth: which Moses testifies was done on the first day of creation. Now, that by stars cannot be understood the stars of heaven or the constellations, is evident from the fact that these were created only on the fourth day: as D. Augustine rightly concludes, lib. 11 de civ. DEI cap. 9.

4. Others opine that the Angels were created on the second day: and that some fell immediately: therefore Moses in the description of that day did not add: God saw that it was good, etc. But this conjecture is too light to deserve credence among the learned. For in this way, neither could God have said at the creation of Man: And God saw all things that He had made: and they were very good. Gen. 1, 31. If indeed we believe Irenaeus, on that very day on which Man was created, he fell into sin. More probable, therefore, is the opinion of those who, when they see that eulogy of Goodness found twice in the description of the third day, conclude from that that the sentences were transposed through the carelessness of the scribes: so that what pertained to the second day was cast over to the third. Which perhaps was the reason that the 70 Interpreters, and those who follow them, read that eulogy of Goodness added in the description of the second day.

5. Finally, there are others who relegate the creation of the Angels to the third day: because the heaven, their dwelling place, was only then adorned and completed on this very day.

We judge it to be of sounder judgment that, because Scripture has been silent on this matter, we should also willingly remain ignorant of what we can neither know nor ought to know: meanwhile, however, we offer two points: 1. that the third opinion seems to us most probable, for the reasons assigned, 2. that it is certain that the Angels were created before Man. For because the Devil laid snares for the human fall through the Serpent: it is clear that he had already fallen into sin, and thus existed before man. Likewise, because the evil Angels were cast out from the fellowship of the good Angels through the ἀποστασίαν (apostasy) by which they fell away from God, it is gathered quite evidently that the good Angels also existed even then.

Latin:

Nùm Spiritus Angelici unà cum cœlo & terrâ, in principio sint conditi?

DUo hoc loco quæruntur: 1. Cur Moses creationis Angelorum nullam prorsus fecerit mentionem? 2. Quo die vel quando illi à DEO creati sint.

Ad priorem Quæstionem respondet Chrysostomus, ideò hoc factum esse, quia Moses populum habeat rudem & simplicem, qui quid Spiritualis & incorporea natura esset, non intelligebat. Volebat proindè corporei tantùm & aspectabilis hujus mundi originem explicare. Quam responsionem etsi non improbamus: tamen illud addendum esse arbitramur, quod Athanasius etiam & Theodoreto animadverterunt, factum hoc præcipuè esse, ad præcavendâ Idololatriâ, ad quam populus Hebræus admodùm pronus & proclivis erat.

In posteriore Quæstione enodanda, plures fermè sunt sententiæ, quàm interpretes. Etsi enim plerique Doctores Ecclesiæ in eo conveniant, Angelos non ab æterno extitisse, sed aliquando in tempore reverà ex nihilo à DEO creatos esse: id quod Scriptura ipsa etiam confirmat, Psal. 104, 4. Qui facis Angelos Spiritus, & Ministros tuos ignem flammæ. Et. Coloss. 1, 16. In ipso condita sunt universa, in cælis & in terrâ, visibilia & invisibilia, throni, dominationes, principatus, potestates: in eo tamen maximè dissentiunt, Quo nimirùm die, vel quando Angeli à DEO sint creati.

I. Enim nonnulli statuerunt, multis ante hunc mundum seculis Angelos à DEO conditos esse. Quorum opinionem vel istud refutat, quod cum creatione hujus mundi, cepit ipsum Tempus: Ante initium verò Temporis, mera & simplex regnavit æternitas. Ergò si Angeli ante creationem hujus Mundi extiterunt, utíq; ab æterno fuerunt: Si ab æterno, utíq; DEUS erunt: Siquidem præter unum & solum DEUM, nihil ratione principij, vel est, vel fuit, vel erit unquàm æternum. Et puerilis planè est ratiocinatio: Angeli dignitate præstant hoc mundo. Ergò ante hunc Mundum sunt creati. Vanitas enim consequentiæ, vel unico sub exemplo creationis hominis liquidissimè patet. Constat certè Hominem postremo loco à DEO esse conditum: neque tamen reliquis creaturis ipsum ideò dignitate inferiorem, quis dixerit.

2. Alii statuerunt, Mosen dicentem: In Principio creavit DEUS cælum & terram: nomine cæli, intellexisse Angelos. Quorum opinio ijs rationibus facilè evertitur, quibus supra ostendimus, per cælum intelligendum esse ipsum corpus cæleste, cum suis orbibus, quantumvis adhuc indigestum.
