Et nisi hoc statuatur, ex Mose certè creatio cæli probari ampliùs non poterit: ut nihil nunc dicam, quòd Scriptura passim de creatione verba faciens, cæli nomen propriè & literaliter accipit.

3. Alij existimant Angelos cum Luce illâ primæ diei esse conditos, proptereà quòd Luci in Scripturis comparantur. Et sanè primo ipso die, vel cum Luce hac, vel cum cælo, domicilio ipsorum, vel statim post illud, ipsos creatos esse, probabiliter conjicitur, ex cap 38,7. Jobi, ubi Deus asserit, se ab astris matutinis & filijs DEI laudatum fuisse, cum bases sive fundamenta terræ poneret: id quod primo creationis die factum esse, Moses testatur. Jam verò per astra non intelligi posse sidera cæli sive stellas, vel indè patet, quod hæ quarto demùm die sunt creatæ: uti rectè colligit D. Augustinus lib. 11. de civ. DEI cap. 9.

4. Alij opinantur secundo die creatos esse Angelos: & statim aliquos prolapsos: ideò Mosen in descriptione illius diei non addidisse: Vidit DEUS quod esset bonum &c. Sed levior hæc est conjectura, quàm ut apud literatos fidem mereatur. Hoc enim pacto neque DEUS in creatione Hominis dicere potuisset. Et vidit DEUS cuncta quæ fecerat: & erant valdè bona. Gen. 1, 31. Siquidem si Irenæo credimus, illo ipso die, quo conditus erat Homo, in peccatum prolapsus est. Probabilior proindè eorum est sententia, qui, cum videant in descriptione tertij diei bis elogium illud Bonitatis reperi, indè colligunt, Scribarum incuria transpositas esse sententias: ita ut quod ad secundum diem pertinebat, ad tertium sit rejectum. Quæ fortè causa fuit, quod 70. Interpretes, & qui eos sequuntur, elogium illud Bonitatis in secundi diei descriptione adjectum legunt.

5. Sunt denique alij, qui Angelorum creationem ad diem tertium rejiciunt: proptereà quod cælum, domicilium eorum, hoc ipso die demùm exornatum & absolutum fuerit.

Nos Sanioris judicij esse arbitramur illud, ut quia Scriptura hâc de re tacuit, nos libenter etiam nesciamus, quod scire neque possumus neque debemus: duo tamen interim afferentes: 1. maximè probabilem nobis videri tertiam sententiam, ob causas assignatas, 2. Certum esse, Angelos ante Hominem creatos esse. Quia enim Diabolus per Serpentem lapsui humano insidias struxit: utique ipsum jam modò in peccata prolapsum, & sic ante hominem extitisse, liquet. Sic quia mali Angeli per ἀποστασίαν, quâ à Deo defecerunt, exsturbati sunt è consortio bonorum Angelorum, utique & bonos Angelos jam tùm extitisse, satis evidenter colligitur.


### Question Six: On the orders of the Angels

That nine orders or Choirs of Angels were once established is evident both from the Master of the Sentences and from other writers: and indeed in this series: that in the beginning Angels: 2. Archangels: 3. Principalities: 4. Powers: 5. Virtues: 6. Dominations: 7. Thrones: 8. Cherubim: 9. Seraphim are placed.

They distinguished these nine orders into three classes or hierarchies: of which they named the first ἐπαρχίαν (eparchy), as if supreme: and in this they placed the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones. They named the second μεσαρχίαν (mesarchy): in which are the Dominations, Principalities, and Powers. They named the third and lowest ὑπαρχίαν (hyparchy), which the Virtues, Archangels, and Angels occupy. And again they handed down these reasons for the individual appellations: that the Seraphim are called as if burning and ardent in the illumination of contemplation: but the Cherubim are named a multitude of knowledge: the Thrones are those Angels in whom the rectitude of the divine judgment and will of GOD shines forth: the Dominations are those who show the legitimate formula of ruling and empires: the Principalities, from whom comes the notion of leading and governing: the Powers, from whom come the modes of just and legitimate coercion: the Angels, who provide those strengths which are required in action and execution: which same things the Archangels and Virtues also perform, but in distinct degrees.

Although these things were indeed proposed long ago, and are proposed even today by some, under the name and authority of Dionysius the Areopagite, who is said to have been a disciple of the Apostle Paul, and is read to have observed that preternatural Eclipse in Egypt at the time of the passion of CHRIST: yet even older writers have most correctly observed that those books of the Celestial Hierarchy, from which those Orders of Angels are taken, are not by this Dionysius: but by some other person, whoever he may eventually have been: a fact which even more recent writers, Laurentius Valla, Erasmus of Rotterdam, Gaza, and others, have observed: showing that some confuse three Dionysii: 1. The Areopagite. 2. The Doctor of the Gauls. 3. The disciple of Hierotheus.

Moreover, since today Papist writers, and among them especially Bellarmine in book 4 of On the Word of God, chapter 7, and indeed Sixtus of Siena in book 2 of his Library, page 68, hold these fables in high regard, and contend with many arguments that Dionysius the Areopagite wrote, among other things, two books, one on the Celestial or Angelic hierarchy: the other on the Ecclesiastical or Priestly hierarchy: it will not be irrelevant to refute this assertion of theirs, and consequently this whole figment about the three Angelic hierarchies, with firm reasons.

And in the beginning, neither Eusebius nor Jerome make any mention of these books: who nevertheless searched for the books of the ancients most diligently, so much so that they did not neglect even any letter written by any eminent man: Why, therefore, should we think this was done regarding books of such great and arduous importance, if indeed any had been written by Dionysius the Areopagite concerning these hierarchies?

Next, no ancient author mentions these books. Therefore, they are not of that antiquity which Dionysius the Areopagite is.

Thirdly, the subject matter itself reveals that those books are not by that Dionysius, an Apostolic man. Saint Paul certainly, 2 Cor. 12:4, says that the celestial state, and what depends upon it, is ἄῤῥητα (ineffable): nay, that it is a sin for a man to speak of them. Far be it, therefore, that we should conclude that this Dionysius progressed to such a degree of audacity and rashness that he would write and explain those things which the Apostle established as ineffable and clearly unknown to men. Saint Irenaeus certainly inveighs with great zeal against these audacious men, book 2, chapter 55. They say nothing sound, he says, they rave, one ought not to believe them and abandon Moses and the Prophets. Let them tell us what the nature of invisible things is, let them recount the number of the Angels, and the order of the Archangels, let them demonstrate the sacraments of the thrones, let them teach the diversities of dominations, principalities, powers, and virtues: but they have nothing to say. And Augustine, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 58. Let those who can say what the orders of Angels are, if only they can prove what they say.

Fourthly, the author of that book concerning the Ecclesiastical hierarchy argues, and argues indeed in a style not Apostolic, nay not even Theological, but sufficiently inflated and affected, about temples, about altars, about sacred places, about the Choir, about Catechumens standing outside the doors of the temple, about Monks in chapter 6. Now, however, that none of these things existed in those times when Dionysius the Areopagite and Paul the Apostle were alive is better known than to require any proof. For in that century Christians were compelled by the cruelty of tyrants to meet in hidden and secret places, and there to perform their sacred rites.

Fifthly, that Pseudo-Dionysius, in chapter 4 of The Divine Names, cites a certain sentiment from the Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, ὁ ἐμὸς ἔρως ἐσταύρωται: My love has been crucified. Now Ignatius, as witnessed by Eusebius in his Chronicle and book 3 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 36, wrote that Epistle to the Romans during the reign of Trajan; but Dionysius the Areopagite was killed during the reign of Domitian. But what need is there of many words, when even those fictitious orders of Angels themselves are built upon no certain foundation? For although we have learned from chapter 1, verse 16 of the Epistle to the Colossians that there are certain specific orders among the Angels, yet what that difference is and what kind it is, Scripture being silent, none of us dares to define: He alone knows them who created them in such a way. Of the same vanity is that distinction of Proclus, who established three triads of Angels, the first of which he calls νοητὺς μόνον, only intelligible, which can be perceived by the mind; the second, νοητὺς καὶ νοερὰς, intelligible and intellectual; the third, νοερὰς μόνον, only intellectual. This distinction was fabricated primarily to the end that they might be able to cast some veil over the fables which the ancient philosophers and Scholastic Doctors tried with great effort to foist upon the Church of God concerning the intelligences that move the celestial spheres; so that it may seem a wonder that the most acute Scaliger allowed himself to be imposed upon in this matter, to the point of undertaking the defense of those fables, in Exercise 359 to Cardan.

Latin:

NOvem Angelorum ordines sive Choros olim constitutos fuisse, tùm ex Magistro sententiarum, tùm ex alijs Scriptoribus patet: & hac quidem serie: ut initiò Angeli: 2. Archangeli: 3. Principatus: 4. Potestates: 5. Virtutes. 6. Dominationes. 7. Throni. 8. Cherubim. 9. Seraphim collocentur.

Hos novem ordines in tres sive classes, sive hierarchias distinxerunt: quarum Primam nominarunt ἐπαρχίαν, quasi supremam: & in hanc collocarunt Seraphim, Cherubim & Thronos. Alteram nominarunt μεσαρχίαν: in quâ sint, Dominationes, Principatus & Potestates. Tertiam & infimam nominarunt ὑπαρχίαν, quam occupent, Virtutes, Archangeli & Angeli. Et rursum singularum appellationum rationes tradiderunt istas: ut Seraphim dicantur quasi incendentes & ardentes in illustratione contemplationis: Cherubim verò nominentur multitudo scientiæ: Throni sint illi Angeli, apud quos reluceat divini judicij & voluntatis DEI rectitudo: Dominationes sint, qui monstrent legitimam formulam dominandi & imperiorum: Principatus, ex quibus ducendi & regendi notio: Potestates, ex quibus modi coactionis justæ & legitimæ: Angeli, qui eas præstent vires, quæ in actione & executione requiruntur: Quod ipsum etiam Archangeli & Virtutes, sed distinctis gradibus expediant.

Quanquam verò isthæc & jam olim fuerunt proposita, & à nonnullis hodiéque proponuntur, sub nomine & autoritate Dionysij Areopagitæ, qui Pauli Apostoli discipulus fuisse perhibetur, & Eclipsin illam præternaturalem tempore passionis CHRISTI, in Aegypto observasse legitur: tamen rectissimè observarunt antiquiores etiam Scriptores, libros illos Hierarchiæ cœlestis, ex quibus Ordines isti Angelorum sunt depromti, non esse hujus Dionysij: sed alius alicujus, quisque ille tandem fuerit: id quod ex recentioribus observarunt etiam Laurentius Valla, Erasmus Roterodamus, Gaza & alij: ostendentes tres confundi a nonnullis Dionysios, 1. Areopagitam. 2. Doctorem Gallorum 3. Hirothei discipulum.

Cæterum, cum hodie Scriptores Pontificij, & inter hos cumprimis Bellarminus lib. 4. de Verbo Dei, cap. 7. quin & Sixtus Senensis lib. 2. Bibliothecæ pag. 68. fabulas istas magnifaciant, & multis contendant, Dionysium Areopagitam inter reliqua duos scripsisse libros, Unum de Cœlesti sive Angelica hierarchia: Alterum de Ecclesiastica sive Sacerdotali hierarchia: non abs re fuerit, firmis rationibus hanc ipsorum assertionem, & consequenter totum hoc figmentum de tribus hierarchijs Angelicis, prorsus retundere.

Acinitio quidem neque Eusebius, neq; Hieronymus faciunt aliquam mentionem horum librorum: qui tamen diligentissime veterum libros conquisiverunt, adeo, ut ne quidem ullam Epistolam, ab eximio quopiam viro scriptam neglexerint: Qui E. hoc factum fuisse putaremus, de libris tanti & tam ardui momenti: si modo ullus aliquis a Dionysio Areopagita de hierarchiis istis scriptus fuisset?

Deinde, Nullus antiquorum autorum, librorum istorum meminit. Ergo non illius antiquitatis sunt, cujus est Dionysius Areopagita.

Tertio, ipsum argumentum prodit libros illos non esse Dionysij illius, viri Apostolici. Divus certe Paulus, 2. Cor. 12, 4. Statum cœlestem, & quæ ab eo dependent, dicit esse ἄῤῥητα: imo nefas esse homini, ea loqui. Absit E. statuamus, Dionysium istum eo audaciæ & temeritatis esse progressum, ut scriberet & explicaret ea, quæ Apostolus ineffabilia esse, & plane incognita hominibus statuit. D. certe Irenæus, magno zelo in audaculos istos invehitur, lib. 2. cap. 55. Nihil, inquiens, sanum dicunt, delirant, non oportet ijs credere, & Mosen ac Prophetas relinquere. Dicant nobis, quæ sit invisibilium natura, enarrent numerum Angelorum, & ordinem Archangelorum, demonstrent thronorum Sacramenta, doceant diversitates dominationum, principatuum, potestatum atq; virtutum: sed non habent dicere. Et Augustinus, in Enchirid. ad Laurent. cap. 58. Dicant qui possunt, qui sint Angelorum ordines, si modo probare possunt, quod dicunt.

Quarto, Disputat autor libri illius de hierarchia Ecclesiastica, & disputat quidem Stylo non Apostolico, imo ne quidem Theologico, sed satis inflato & affectato, de templis, de altaribus, de locis sacris, de Choro, de Catechumenis extra fores templi stantibus, de Monachis cap. 6. Jam vero nihil horum fuisse illis quidem temporibus, quibus Dionysius Areopagita, & Paulus Apostolus in vivis fuere, notius est, quam ut ulla probatione indigeat. Coacti enim fuerunt illo seculo Christiani propter tyrannorum crudelitatem convenire in locis abditis atque occultis, ibique sua sacra peragere.

Quintò Pseudo-Dionysius ille cap. 4. de divinis nominibus citat sententiam quandam ex Epistolâ Ignatij ad Romanos, ὁ ἐμὸς ἔρως ἐσταύρωται: Amor meus crucifixus est. Jam Ignatius teste Eusebio in Chronico, & lib. 3. hist. Eccl. c. 36. Imperante Trajano scripsit illam Epistolam ad Romanos; Dionysius verò Areopagita, regnante Domitiano occisus fuit. Sed quid multis opus, cùm vel ipsi ordines isti fictitij Angelorum, nulli fundamento certo sint superstructi. Etsi enim ex cap. 1, 16. Epistolæ ad Coloss. didicimus, inter Angelos esse certos quosdam ordines: tamen quæ & qualis sit illa differentia, Scripturâ tacente, nemo nostrûm definire audet: Solus ille eas novit, qui ita creavit. Ejusdem vanitatis est illa quoque distinctio Procli, qui tres Angelorum triades constituit, quarum primam vocat νοητὺς μόνον tantùm intelligibiles, quæ mente percipi possint: alteram νοητὺς καὶ νοερὰς intelligibiles & intellectuales: tertiam, νοερὰς μόνον tantùm intellectuales. Quæ distinctio conficta est eum potissimùm in finem, ut fucum aliquem facere queant fabellis, quas magno conatu Ecclesiæ DEI obtrudere conati fuerunt veteres Philosophi & Scholastici Doctores, de intelligentiis motricibus orbium cœlestium: ita ut mirum videri possit, passum esse acutissimum Scaligerum hac in parte sibi imponi, ut fabellarum illarum patrocinium susceperit, Exerc. 359. ad Cardanum.


### Question Six: Are the Angels those intelligences, the movers of the celestial spheres?

There would certainly be no need for this Question if the mind of man kept itself within the limits of piety and the boundaries of the Holy Scriptures. But, alas, such an insatiable itch for disputing has seized this age of ours that, provided you can assert something with any color of probability, you dare to undertake its defense, however much you may be destitute of the authority of sacred principles. This very thing has happened to us today regarding the Question of the office of the Angels. Where certain disputants, not content with that knowledge which can be sought from indubitable sacred principles, break through the very barriers of the heavens and, walking on air, contend that such offices have been assigned to the Angels by God, about which it is most rightly doubted: Did such a thing ever enter the mind of God, the Creator of this universe? Such as is that claim that the Angels, whom they call Intelligences, move the celestial spheres by the command of God. Concerning which matter Scaliger (and I say this with all respect to such a great man) discourses and pronounces quite boldly, in this manner, as if sitting before a tribunal, in Exercise 359, Section 8: There are three offices of the intelligences: The first is primary, to attend; the second is to be sent to certain mysteries and ministries; the third is to move the spheres. We must now deal with this. What we read in the 12th book of divine science (Metaphysics) has often been repeated by us, as the matter required: that the Intelligence moving the first sphere accomplishes this by the sole intellection of itself. Which is the greatest principle of all for many conclusions. For it understands that it was created by God to do this. Wherefore, not only does consequent love and consent follow upon that intellection, but also action: so that that mass of the Heaven is agitated in a gyre. Which thing would be the most difficult of all difficult things, were it not that we have this most certain fact: that all things were made by the sole command of God: just as if that vertigo were stirred up by the command of the Intelligence. To this most profound contemplation we add: that the second intelligence does not rest in its own intellection, but also understands the primary mover. Wherefore, just as the first moves itself by understanding itself, so that it also turns others that are inferior, so the inferior, by understanding the first, wishes its own sphere to revolve simultaneously with the motion of the first sphere. Thus far Scaliger: Whose entire disputation rests upon two hypotheses that are by far the most uncertain. The former is: that the Angels are so disposed by God into three, as it were, orders or classes, that a certain office, incommunicable with the remaining orders, has been assigned to each order.

But the latter is: that the intelligences of the third order were created by God for the purpose of moving the spheres. As for the former hypothesis, it has just now been demonstrated that it is drawn from those puddles of the Pseudo-Dionysius and the dreams of the Scholastics, and is destitute of all authority of the Scriptures; nay, it is not obscurely repugnant to them, and therefore collapses by its own vanity. By which means, indeed, the primary foundation of the entire subsequent structure concerning the intelligences that move the celestial spheres also vanishes of its own accord. Holy Scripture is certainly so ignorant of those three orders of intelligences and their distinct and incommunicable offices that it ascribes the first two indiscriminately to each and every one; but concerning the third office, it does not know even a jot. It would be worth the effort to demonstrate this in a few words. Therefore, regarding the first office of the intelligences or Angels, which Scaliger names (to attend), Scripture certainly attributes that not to the Intelligences of the first order, but indiscriminately to each and every Angel: 1 Kings 22:19, 'I saw the Lord sitting upon His throne, and ALL the host of heaven attending Him on His right and on His left.' Thus Daniel 7:10, 'Thousands of thousands ministered to Him, and ten thousand times ten thousand attended Him.' Where Pererius himself, otherwise a most fierce champion of the Intelligences, concedes that a finite number is put for an infinite one, and thus for the entire multitude of the celestial host. Thus Matthew 25:31, 'The Son of Man will come in His majesty, and all the Angels with Him.' Where that deserves accurate observation, that this Advent of the Son of Man, as witnessed by the Apostle, 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and 17, will take place from Heaven: so that, while the motion of the Heaven is still preserved, all the Angels will nevertheless be present with Christ, and thus also those who are feigned to move both the primum mobile and the remaining inferior Spheres. Whence it follows that either those Angels, the motors of the spheres, would then be simultaneously and at once in many and most distant places: namely in that πῶ of his, in which they move the spheres: and at the same time in the clouds of heaven, that is, in this lower region of the air with Christ: or it will follow that other thing, that the Angels who are the movers of the spheres, at the time when they shall be present with Christ coming to judgment, will cease to move the spheres: and thus Heaven, before the consummation of the age, will be deprived of its motion: Which, since both are manifestly absurd: certainly even from that it is most evidently apparent, not only that this distinction of Angels: but also the dogma built upon this concerning the intelligent movers of the celestial spheres, is vain, fabricated, nay even superstitious, which is manifestly false and absurd: or consequently that this distinction of Angels is fabricated: which is also sufficiently evidently demonstrated even from that.

Concerning the second class of Angels, and their certain office, which Scaliger defines by a mission to certain mysteries and ministries, Scripture likewise hands down something clearly different. For this first affirms indefinitely and thus universally. That all Angels are ministering spirits, sent forth for the ministry of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation, Heb. 1, 14: Then it assigns the revelation of divine mysteries, not to a certain order of Angels, but to the whole celestial host, as Luke 2, 13. And suddenly there was with the Angel πλῆθος στρατιᾶς ὐρανίε, a multitude of the heavenly host. Finally, it expressly asserts that those who are sent into the ministry of men, nevertheless stand before GOD, and behold Him: so that even for this reason alone, the distinction of these two orders expires: as Matt. 18, 10. See that you do not despise one of these little ones: For I say to you, that their Angels always in heaven see the face of my Father, who is in heaven. Thus the Angel Gabriel is sent to Zacharias the Priest, to bring him the message concerning his Son John the Baptist: and yet this very Gabriel confesses that he stands before GOD. Therefore the order of those who stand before GOD, and of those who are sent, is the same, namely Angels. Luke 1, 19. And that which Pererius, intending to extricate himself from this labyrinth, invents—a double order of Angels standing before GOD—is clearly diluted and inconsistent: One of those who stand before GOD, and at the same time are also sent, concerning whom the testimonies of Scripture already brought forward are to be understood: The other of those who only stand before GOD, and immediately see all things in the Word, and from thence draw knowledge of all things that are to be done: and are not sent to the earth to execute ministries. For 1. what Pererius says; he does not prove, for we do not dwell on Pseudo-Dionysius. 2. He accuses Scaliger of ignorance, who was unaware of the subdivision of the first order. 3. This assertion conflicts with that statement of Raphael,

Tobias 12, 15, which affirms that only seven Angels stand before GOD. If this is true, how then could Pererius, and those who follow him, refer to the first order of those Angels who only stand before GOD, the Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, and Dominations. For since each of these is of the plural number, they certainly comprise more under themselves. But indeed that number seven of Raphael does not grant more to each, nay not even two: for thus the number seven would grow into eight. Therefore those things which are fabricated today concerning these certain orders are clearly ἀσύςατα (inconsistent): Nay, even that which is found in the book of Tobias concerning the seven Angels standing before GOD is false: inasmuch as it is taken from the ancient fables of the Jews: and manifestly conflicts with Daniel, who saw thousands of thousands ministering to GOD, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand standing before him. Dan 7, 10. The third order, which Scaliger assigns to those who move the celestial spheres, today comes primarily into dispute: and it involves that later hypothesis, upon which we said above that the fiction concerning Intelligences was built. Concerning which, in order to explain our mind candidly, we wish this to be premised at the beginning, that if only the patrons of the Intelligences did not assert these two things: 1. That the Angels themselves are those Intelligences about which they dispute. 2. That the Angels move the spheres by the command of GOD: and were created by GOD for this office: then we would willingly permit them to philosophize pleasantly, and to dispute and contend about I know not what Intelligences, no less than about Platonic ideas, or about the snow of Anaxagoras: as much and as long as they wish, by a certain play of wit. Now indeed, since these things are proposed as an Article of Faith: it must certainly be seen whether that Article of Faith has even a single foundation in the Scriptures. For the philosophical reasons by which Aristotle in book 8 of the Physics, chap. 6, text 52, and in book 12 of the Metaphysics, chap. 8, text 43, Plato in book 1 of the Laws, and other philosophers elsewhere are accustomed to fight for these Intelligences, do not strike our cause any more than those which, ignorant of the Scriptures, they have devised for the eternity of motion and of the World from the light of Nature. Moreover, if it is true what Thomas writes: Opusc. 10 art. 3, and opusc. 11 art. 2, and de potentia, Quest. 6, art. 3, that it is a sentence of Faith that separate substances or Angels move the celestial bodies: If it is true that the Jesuits of the Coimbra college assert that a foundation for this dogma can be given from the Scriptures: If finally it is true what Scaliger asserts, that he holds it as most certain that the Intelligences move the spheres by the command of GOD alone: likewise that they were created by GOD for this: then it would certainly be shameful that the purer theologians have not been able to unearth the foundations of this Faith from the Sacred Scriptures even to this very day. Therefore we rise up against them thus: Whatever is of faith, whatever is also known to be done by the command of GOD, it is necessary that it be confirmed by the Word of GOD, either explicitly or implicitly. But that the Angels are those Intelligences, the movers of the celestial spheres, can be asserted neither explicitly nor implicitly from the Word of GOD. Therefore, we also conclude invincibly that it can neither be of Faith, nor held as most certain: that the Angels are those Intelligences, and that they move the celestial spheres by the command of GOD: or that they were created by GOD for this.

We are not bound to confirm the Assumption: since the burden of proof lies not upon the one who denies, but upon the one who affirms: not only does reason suggest this, but all sacred and profane laws likewise persuade it. But lest we appear to be overly difficult, a thing which ought to be most foreign to every Disputant: we evidently demonstrate the certainty of the minor

Latin:

HAud profectò Quæstione istâ opus foret, si intra limites pietatis, & Sacrarum Scripturarum crepidines mens hominis sese contineret: Sed tantum proh dolor insatiabile disputandi κακόηθες, nostram hanc cepit ætatem, ut, dummodò aliquid quocunque colore probabiliter asserere queas, illius patrocinium suscipere ausis, quantû vis etiam sacrorum principiorum autoritate destituaris. Hoc ipsum usu venit nobis hodiè circa Quæstionem de officio Angelorum. Ubi Disputatores quidam non cotenti eâ notitiâ, quæ ex indubitatis principijs sacris peti possunt: ipsa cœlorum claustra perrumpunt, & ἀεροβατῦντες, ejusmodi officia Angelis à DEO assignata esse contendunt, de quibus rectissimè dubitatur, An DEO Conditori hujus universi, tale quid unquam in mentem venerit? Quale est & illud, quòd Angeli, quos illi nominant Intelligetias, ex mandato DEI moveant orbes cœlestes. Quâ de re sic Scaliger(id quod tanti viri bonâ pace dixerim) satis audacter, hunc in modum, tanquam pro tribunali sedens, disserit & pronunciat Exercit. 359, Sect. 8. Tria sunt officia intelligentiarum: Primum est primariũ, assistere: Alterum est, aliarum mitti ad cert a & mysteria & ministeria: Tertium est, movere orbes. De hoc nunc agendum est. Quod legimus in 12. divinæ sciẽ- tiæ(Metaphysicæ)sæpè est à nobis, exigente re ita, repetitum: Primi orbis motricem Intelligentiam sola sui ipsius intellectione id præstare. Quod est omnium maximum principium plurimarum conclusionum. Intelligit enim se à DEO creatam, ut id agat. Quare ad eam Intellectionem non solùm accedit consequens amor, & consensus, verùm etiam opera: ita ut moles illa Cæli gyro agitetur Quæ res omniũ difficillimarum esset difficillima, nisi haberemus illud compertißimum: Solo DEI jussu facta omnia: Ita quasi jussu Intelligentiæ vertiginem cieri illam. Huic tam profundæ contemplationi addimus nos. Non acquiescere secundam intelligentiam intellectioni suæ: sed intelligere etiam motricem primam. Quare quemadmodũ prima sese intelligendo movet ita suum, ut alios quoq; torqueat inferiores: sic inferior intelligendo primam, vult orbem suum cum primi orbis motu simul versari. Hactenus Scaliger : Cujus universa disputatio duabus nititur hypothesibus longè incertissimis, Prior est: Angelos in tres quasi ordines, sive classes, ita esse dispositos à DEO, ut cuilibet ordini certum, & cum reliquis ordinibus incommunicabile, sit assignatum officium.

Posterior verò: Intelligentias tertij ordinis à DEO ideò esse creatas, ut moveant orbes. Quoad priorem hypothesin, jam modò demonstratum est, eam ex lacunis illis Pseudo-Dionysianis, & Scholasticorum somniis esse petitam: omnique Scripturarum autoritate destitui: imò eidé haud obscurè repugnare: ac proindè propriâ vanitate concidere. Quo sanè pacto primarium etiam fundamentum subsequentib9 universæ structuræ de intelligentijs motricibus orbiũ cælestiũ, ultrò evanescit. Scriptura certè Sacra usq; adeò tres istos intelligentiarum ordines, & distincta ac incommunicabilia eorundé officia ignorat, ut duo priora promiscuè singulis adscribat: de tertio verò officio, ne γρῦ quidem noverit. id quod paucis demonstrare operæ pretiũ fuerit. Quoad primum ergò intelligentiarũ sive Angelorum officiũ, quod Scaliger nominat (assistere) illud certè, non primi ordinis Intelligentijs sed indifferenter singulis & universis Angelis Scriptura tribuit: 1. Reg. 22, 19. Vidi Dominum sedentẽ super Solium suum, & OMNEM exercitũ cæli assistentem ei à dextris & à Sinistris. Sic Daniel 7, 10. Millia millium ministrabant ei, & decies millies centena millia assistebant ei. Ubi numerum finitum poni pro infinito, & sic pro universâ multitudine cœlestis militiæ, concedit ipse Pererius, aliàs Intelligentiarum propugnator açerrimus. Sic Matt. 25, 31. Veniet filius hominis in majestate suâ, & omnes Angeli cum eo. Ubi illud accuratam observationem meretur, quòd Adventus iste Filij Hominis, teste Apostolo, 1. Theß. 4, 16. & 17. fiet de Cœlo: ita ut motu Cœli adhuc salvo: omnes tamen Angeli adfuturi sint Christo, & sic illi quoque, qui tùm primum mobile, tùm reliquas inferiores Sphæras movere finguntur. Undè Consequens, vel Angelos istos motores orbium tùm simul & semel in pluribus ac dissitissimis locis futuros: nempe in illo suo πῶ, in quo orbes movent: & simul in nubibus cæli, hoc est, in inferiore hac aeris regione cum Christo: vel illud alterum consequetur, Angelos motrices orbium, tum cum Christo adventanti ad judicium aderunt, cessaturos movere orbes: & sic Cœlum ante consummationem seculi, motu suo cariturum: Quod utrumque cum manifeste absurdum sit: utique vel inde evidentissime patet, non modò distinctionem istam Angelorum: sed & huic superstructum dogma de intelligentiis motricibus orbium cœlestium, esse vanum, commentitium, imò superstitiosum, id quod manifeste falsum & absurdum: vel consequenter distinctionem istam Angelorum esse commentitiam: id quod etiam vel inde satis evidenter est demonstratum.

De secunda classe Angelorum, eorumque certo officio, Quod Scaliger definit per missionem ad certa mysteria & ministeria, itidem scriptura diversum planè tradit. Hæc enim primò indefinitè & sic universaliter affirmat. Omnes Angelos esse Spiritus administratorios, emissos ad ministerium eorum, qui hæreditatem salutis percipient, Hebr. 1, 14: Deindè revelationem mysteriorum divinorum, non certo Angelorum ordini, sed universæ militiæ cœlesti assignat, ut Luc 2, 13. Et facta est subitò cum Angelo πλῆθος στρατιᾶς ὐρανίε, multitudo cælestis militiæ. Tandem expressè asserit, eos qui emissi sunt in ministerium hominum, nihilominus assistere DEO, ipsumque intueri: ut vel hac sola ratione, duorum istorum ordinum distinctio expiret: ut Matth. 18, 10. Videte, ne contemnatis unum ex his pusillis: Dico enim vobis, quod Angeli EORUM semper in cælis vident faciem Patris mei, qui in cælis est. Sic Angelus Gabriel mittitur ad Zachariam Sacerdotem, ut ipsi ferat nuncium de Filio Johanne Baptistâ: & tamen fatetur hic ipse Gabriel, se astare ante DEUM. Ergò idem est ordo assistentium DEO, & eorum qui emittuntur, Angelorum. Luc. 1, 19. Et dilutum planè est ac desultorium, quod Pererius ex isto labyrintho se extricaturus, geminum confingit ordinem, assistentium DEO Angelorum: Unum eorum, qui assistant DEO, & simul etiam emittantur, de quibus intelligenda sint allata jam in medium scripturæ testimonia: Alterum eorum, qui tantùm assistant DEO, & proximè omnia videant in verbo, & indè notitiam omnium, quæ agenda sunt, hauriant: nec mittantur in terras ad exequenda ministeria. Nam 1. quod dicit Pererius; non probat, Pseudo-Dionysium enim non moramur. 2. Inscitiæ insimulat Scaligerum, qui primi ordinis subdivisionem ignoravit. 3. Pugnat hæc assertio, cum effato illo Raphaëlis,

Tobiæ 12, 15. qui affirmat septem duntaxat Angelos assistere coram DEO. Hoc si verum, quomodo jam Pererius, & qui ipsum sequuntur, ad ordinem primum eorum Angelorum, qui tantùm assistunt DEO, referre potuerunt, Seraphim, Cherubim, Thronos & Dominationes. Nam cum singuli isti pluralis sint numeri, utique plures etiam subse complectuntur. At verò septenarius iste Raphaëlis, non largitur singulis plures, imò ne quidem duos: sic enim Septenarius in Octonarium excresceret. Ergo ἀσύςατα planè sunt, quæ de ordinibus istis certis hodiéque confinguntur: Imò falsum est & illud, quod in libro Tobiæ de septem Angelis astantibus coram DEO, reperitur: quippè quod desumtum est ex antiquis fabulis Judæorũ: & manifestè repugnat Danieli, qui vidit millia milliu ministrare DEO, & millies centena millia ei assistere. Dan 7. 10. Tertius ordo, quem Scaliger assignat illis, qui movent orbes cœlestes, hodiè potissimùm in disputationem venit: & involvit posteriorem illam hypothesin, cui figmentum de Intelligendis superstructum esse, supra diximus. De quâ ut mentem nostram candidè explicemus, initiò istud præmissum volumus, si modò duo isthæc non assererent Patroni Intelligentiarum: 1. Angelos ipsos esse Intelligentias illas, de quibus disputant. 2. Angelos jussu DEI movere orbes: & ad hoc officium à DEO creatos esse: tùm nos libenter permissuros ipsos svaviter Philosophari, & de intelligentiis, nescio quibus, haud minùs atquè de ideis Platonicis, vel de nive Anaxagoræ: per lusum quemdam ingenii, disputare & digladiari, quantum & quousque velint. Jam verò, cùm tanquam Articulus Fidei isthæc proponantur: videndum utique est, nùm Articulus iste Fidei, vel unicum saltem in Scripturis fundamentum habeat. Nam rationes Philosophicas, quibus Aristoteles lib. 8. Physic. cap. 6. textu. 52. & libro. 12. Metaphys. cap. 8. textu 43. Plato l. 1. de legibus, & alii Philosophi alibi pugnare solent pro istis Intelligentiis, nostram causam haud magis feriunt, atquè illæ, quas pro æternitate motus, atque Mundi ex Naturæ lumine, ignari scripturarum excogitarunt. Cæterùm si verum est, quod Thomas scribit: Opusc. 10 art. 3. & opusc. 11. art. 2. & de potentia, Quæst. 6. art. 3. Fidei sententiam esse, quòd substantiæ separatæ sive Angeli moveant corpora cœlestia: Si verum est, quòd Jesuvvitæ collegii Conimbricensis asserunt, ex Scripturis dari posse dogmatis hujus fundamentum: Si verum denique est, quod Scaliger asserit, compertissimum se habere, solo DEI jussu intelligentias movere orbes: item ad hoc ipsos à DEO creatos esse: tùm utique turpe fuerit, puriores Theologos istio Fidei fundamenta, ex Sacris ne in hunc usque diem eruere potuisse. Proindè adversum istos sic insurgimus: Quicquid est fidei, quicquid etiam compertum est, jussu DEI fieri, illud DEI Verbo, vel explicitè, vel implicitè sit confirmatum, necesse est. Atqui Angelos esset intelligentias illas, motrices orbium cœlestium, neque explicitè, neque implicitè ex Verbo DEI astrui potest Ergò, invictè etiam concludimus, neque Fidei esse, neque compertissimum haberi posse: Angelos esse Intelligēntias illas, & jussu DEI movere orbes cœlestes: vel ad hoc à DEO creatos esse.

Assumtionem confirmare non tenemur: Siquidem non neganti, sed affirmanti incumbit probatio: non ratione tantùm sic innuente: sed & omnibus legibus sacris & prophanis sic svadentibus. Sed ne δυςχεραίνειν videamur, id quod ab omni Disputatore debet esse alienissimum: Mi-


### Question Six: Offices of Angels from sacred letters

premise in this way: Whatever the sacred scriptures define concerning the Angels, both in respect of their Essence and in respect of their office, and that either explicitly in express words or implicitly through a certain χρεία or species of fact, from which something certain can be gathered concerning their essence as well as their office: That alone ought to be held as an article of Faith, as a command and mandate of GOD, and thus as discovered and indubitable.

But the sacred scriptures, both explicitly and implicitly, define the Angels in respect of their Essence to be finite and simple Spirits created by GOD in the beginning in His own image in the highest perfection, wisdom, justice, and Holiness: Gen. 1, 31. Psal. 104, 4. John 8, 44. He stood not in the truth, etc. Hebr. 1, 14.

Therefore, concerning the Essence of the Angels, nothing else can or ought to be established and affirmed under the heading of faith.

Thus the same Sacred scriptures, likewise partly explicitly and partly implicitly, assign only the following offices to the Angels.

1. Standing in the sight of GOD, they celebrate this their creator and Lord with eternal praises, sounding that Angelic τρισάγιον: Holy, Holy, Holy, God of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory Isa. 6, 3. Psal. 103, 20.

2. They minister to GOD in revealing and announcing the works of GOD: which is evident from chapters 1 and 2 of Luke: as also from the Old Testament, in the history of Abraham, Jacob, and others.

3, They keep watch for the salvation of pious men: but they destroy and ruin the impious by the command of GOD: Hebr. 1, 14. Psalm. 34, 8. The Angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him: Psal. 91, 11. He has commanded his Angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your ways. Thus Exod. 12, 23. & 27. One Angel, in one night, destroys all the firstborn of all Egypt. Thus 2 Sam. 24, 15. One Angel among the people of David, in one three-day period, killed seventy thousand men. Thus 2 Kings 19, 35. In the camp of the Assyrians, one Angel, in one night, slaughtered one hundred and eighty-five thousand men.

4. They carry the souls of the pious, separated from the body by death, into Abraham's bosom. Luke 16, 22.

5. They are delighted by the happy success of the Evangelical preaching, and the repentance of sinners. 1 Pet. 1, 12. The Angels desire or long to look into those things which have been announced to you by those who have preached the gospel to you. Luke 15, 7. I say that there will be greater joy in Heaven, before the Angels, over one sinner who is repenting than over ninety-nine just persons who do not need repentance.

6. And finally they will accompany the Son of Man, who is to return to judge the living and the dead, Matth. 25, 31. 1 Thess. 4, 16.

Nor can any other office be extracted from the sacred writings in any way whatsoever, which has indeed been attributed to the Angels by God, or ever anywhere been undertaken or performed by them.

We conclude therefore: that only that which has already been deduced from the sacred writings concerning the Essence and office of the Angels is to be held as an article of Faith, as a command and mandate of GOD: and thus as certain and indubitable: and therefore, since not even a jot exists concerning that office which consists in moving the celestial spheres, that also is to be held as a dream and fable of the Platonists and Scholastics and to be laughed at.

Pererius acknowledged the solidity of this argument of ours, lib. 2. of the Commentaries on Genesis, Quest. 5. page 216 of the edition in quarto format of the year 1594, at Lyons, writing thus: That the Heavens are not moved by themselves, but by Angels, I cannot gather so easily and evidently from the sacred scriptures as it is confirmed by the consensus of very many and very great Philosophers and Theologians. For that the celestial spheres are moved and ruled by divine reason and power, and not by their own force, but are driven in a circle by Angels, whom the Platonic Philosophers called GODS, was the concordant opinion of the Platonists, Peripatetics, and Stoics. Thus far Pererius, from whose words we infer three corollaries: 1. since the thesis concerning Intelligences cannot be gathered from the sacred scriptures, it is false what Thomas wrote: that it is a sentence of Faith that Angels move the celestial bodies. 2. The first foundations of the dogma concerning Intelligences are not owed to the Holy Spirit or the sacred scriptures: but to the Platonic, Peripatetic, and Stoic Philosophers. 3. That this very dogma, before the times of those Philosophers who too much admired the dreams of the Scholastics and Platonists, was completely unheard of in the Churches and Schools of Christians: which fact alone ought to warn Christians of the vanity of this dogma.

And let this indeed be the first foundation, by which we thoroughly crush and overturn the dream concerning the motive Intelligences of the celestial spheres.

The SECOND follows, taken from the dissonance of those very Philosophers who were either the first inventors or the defenders of this dream.

The Rabbis of the Jews hold the first place, as is evident from their Talmud, where Rabbi Moses, with the Jewish Synagogue concurring, assigned a double mover to each celestial sphere: namely, an Intelligence and an informing soul.

The Gentile Philosophers afterwards kissed these fables, and for the most part agreed on this, that besides GOD some other mover must be assigned to the spheres: But who that may be, and how he relates to that motion, they have departed into such diverse and even plainly contrary opinions, that not even to this day has anything certain been defined among Philosophers on this matter.

For some have feigned that only one mover should be assigned to the spheres, namely an intelligence, and indeed an assisting one: Others have contended that the spheres are moved by an Intelligence from right to left: but by the form of the sphere itself are moved from left to right. Others established that the Intelligence is in reality the form of its sphere: so that it imparts to it not only motion, but also dimension, figure, rarity and density, and other perfections congruent to the celestial nature: Others denied this very thing, establishing that Intelligences are in themselves something coherent and complete in their own species: Others, having entered upon a middle path, philosophized that although an Intelligence is not properly and simply to be called the form of its sphere: it can nevertheless be called its form by a certain likeness: and with greater right than other external movers are called the forms of the bodies which are moved by them: as the Jesuits of the Coimbra College sweetly dream, in lib. 2. de Caelo, cap. 5. Quest. 5. art. 4.

Again, concerning the motive power, many have well established among the Intelligences that the faculty by which Intelligences move the celestial spheres differs not at all from their intellect and will: others, however, contradicting these, have asserted that these things differ greatly from one another: The Coimbrans pronounce both opinions probable, but the latter nevertheless more probable, in book 2 de caelo, chapter 5, Question 8, article 2.

What? That not even Aristotle, the prince of Peripatetic philosophers, has disciples supporting him in this part. Aristotle teaches in book 12 Metaphysics, chapter 8, text 47 and following, that an Intelligence is so commensurate with its sphere regarding motive power that it cannot move another, higher one. The Coimbrans argue against Aristotle on this account: but in such a way that, hesitating greatly, they finally deny their own [position], concluding in this manner: That if anyone should contend that GOD applied Intelligences to individual spheres with such a proportion of power that each one moves only as much as it is able, and thus the sphere cannot be moved by any higher one, we say that this, although it could have happened, is nevertheless not proven by any reason such that we should think it was done. Coll. Conimbr. in book 2 de Caelo, c. 5, quest. 8, art. 2. If this is to refute, I for my part will have refuted the entire Jesuit fantasy concerning the intelligences with this one response alone, by saying: It could indeed have happened that God created such motive Intelligences of the celestial spheres: but it is not proven by any reason such that we should think it was done.

Aristotle taught: the astrologers of that age taught the very same thing, that there are no more than forty-seven or fifty-five Intelligences. The Coimbrans protest, and argue from Thomas that a much greater number must be granted. But neither these nor those prove what they say; indeed, they cannot even do so.

And thus the fighting goes on inside and outside the walls of Troy: so that it is evident enough, even from these perpetual contradictions, that the dogma concerning the Intelligences is built upon such foundations as hold together and subsist no more than a rope woven from grains of sand, where Irenaeus speaks somewhere.

The Holy Scriptures provide the third argument of the Refutation, which so assign the motion of the celestial spheres to GOD alone that they simply exclude all other creatures, individual and universal, both celestial and terrestrial, from it.

Nehem. 9, 6. You yourself, O Lord, you alone have made Heaven and the Heaven of Heavens, and all their host: the earth, and all things that are in it: the seas and all things that are in them: and YOU GIVE LIFE TO ALL these things, and the host of Heaven adores you.

Ecclesiasticus 24, 5 and following. I came out of the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature. I make it arise in the Heavens that an unfailing light may rise: I dwell in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud: I ALONE go around the circuit of the Heaven, and penetrate the depth of the abyss.

Isa. 48, 13. My right hand has measured the Heavens with a span: I will call them, and they shall stand together.

Jer. 33, 25. If I have not set my covenant between day and night, and the laws of heaven and earth, I will cast off the seed of Jacob, and David my Servant, etc.

Job 38, 12. Have you, says GOD, commanded the morning since your birth, and shown the dawn its place?

And v. 18. & 19. Have you considered the breadth of the earth? Tell me, if you know all, in what way (WAY denotes the motion of the Spheres of the Sun and Moon) Light dwells and what is the place of darkness: that you may LEAD each one to its boundaries? v. 32. Do you bring forth Lucifer in his time, and make the evening rise over the sons of the earth? Do you know the order of Heaven?

Latin:

noris certitudinem hoc pacto evidenter demonstramus: Quicquid sacra litera de Angelis, tùm ratione Essentiæ, tùm ratione officii definiunt, idque vel explicitè disertis verbis: vel implicitè per certam quandam χρείαν sive speciem facti, ex quâ de ipsorũ tùm essentiâ, tùm officio, certi quid colligi potest: Illud tantùm pro articulo Fidei, pro jussu & mandato DEI, & sic pro comperto ac indubitato haberi debet.

Atqui sacræ literæ, tùm explicitè, tùm implicitè Angelos ratione Essentiæ definiunt, esse Spiritus finitos & simplices à DEO initio creatos ad imaginem ipsius in summâ perfectione, sapientiâ, justitiâ & Sanctitate: Gen. 1, 31. Psal. 104, 4. Job. 8, 44. In veritate non stetit, &c. Hebr. 1, 14.

Ergò de Essentiâ Angelorum, nihil aliud sub ratione fidei, statui & affirmari potest, aut debet.

Sic eædem Sacræ literæ, itidem partim explicitè, partim implicitè, tantùm sequentia officia Angelis adsignant.

1. Astantes in conspectu DEI, hunc suum conditorem & Dominum æternis laudibus concelebrant, τρισάγιον illud Angelicum personantes: Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, Deus Sebaoth, plena est omnis terra gloriâ ejus Esa. 6, 3. Psal. 103, 20.

2. Ministrant DEO in revelandis & annunciandis operibus DEI: id quod patet ex capp 1. & 2. Lucæ: ut & ex Veteri Testamento, in historiâ Abrahami, Jacobi, & aliorum.

3, Pro piorum hominum salute excubias agunt: Impios verò DEI jussu perdunt ac destruunt: Hebr. 1, 14. Psalm. 34, 8. Castrametatur Angelus Domini, circa timentes illum: Psal. 91, 11. Angelis suis mandavit de te, ut custodiant te in omnibus viis tuis. Sic Exod. 12, 23. & 27. Unus Angelus, una nocte perdit omnes primogenitos totius Ægypti. Sic 2. Sam. 24, 15. Ung Angelus in populo Davidis, uno triduo, necavit septuaginta millia virorum. Sic 2 Reg. 19, 35 In Castris Assyriorum, unus Angelus, unâ nocte trucidavit, centum octoginta quinq́ millia virorũ.

4. Piorum animas, per mortem separatas à corpore, deportant in sinum Abrahæ. Luc. 16, 22.

5. Delectantur felici successu prædicationis Evangelicæ, & peccatorum pœnitentiâ. 1. Pet. 1, 12. Gestiunt sive desiderant Angeli introspicere in ea, quæ vobis annunciata sunt per eos qui evangelizarunt vobis. Luc. 15, 7. Dico quod majus futurum sit gaudium in Cœlo, coram Angelis, super uno peccatore, pœnitentiam agente quàm super nonaginta novem justis, pœnitentiâ non indigentibus.

6. Et postremò comitabuntur Filium Hominis, rediturum ad judicandum vivos & mortuos, Matth. 25, 31. 1 Thess. 4, 16.

Neque ullum aliud officium ex sacris quovis modo erui potest, quod quidem, vel Angelis à Deo attributum: vel unquam uspiam ab illis susceptum aut expeditum fuerit.

Concludimus proindè: illud tantùm, quod jam de Essentiâ & officio Angelorum ex sacris est deductum, pro articulo Fidei, pro jussu & mandato DEI: & sic pro comperto ac indubitato habendum esse: ac proindè cum de officio illo, quod in movendis orbibus cœlestibus confistit, ne γρῦ quidem extet: illud etiam pro somnio & fabellâ Platonicorum & Scholasticorum habendum & irridendum esse.

Agnovit soliditatem argumentationis hujus nostræ, Pererius, lib. 2. Commentariorum in Genesin, Quæst. 5. pag. 216. Editionis in quartâ formâ Anni 1594. Lugduni, sic scribens: Non à se moveri Cælos, sed ab Angelis, non tàm facilè atq; evidenter ex sacris literis possum colligere, quàm ex plurimorum & maximorum Philosophorum atq; Theologorum consensu firmatum. Etenim orbes cælestes, divinâ ratione potêtiâq; cieri ac regi, nec suâ vi, sed ab Angelis, quos Philosophi Platonici DEOS appellabant, in orbem perpetuò agi, concors fuit Platonicorum & Peripateticorum, Stoicorunique sententia. Hactenus Pererius, ex cujus verbis tria inferimus πορίσματα: 1. cùm thesis de Intelligentiis ex sacris literis non possit colligi, falsum esse, quod Thomas scripsit: Fidei sententiam esse, Angelos movere corpora cælestia. 2. Prima fundamenta dogmatis de Intelligentiis, non deberi Spiritui Sancto, aut scripturis sacris: sed Platonicis, Peripateticis & Stoicis Philosophis. 3. Dogma hoc ipsum ante tempora illorum Philosophorum, qui Scholasticorum & Platonicorum somnia, nimiùm sunt admirati, in Ecclesiis & Scholis Christianorum prorsus inauditum fuisse: id quod vel unicum, Christianos de vanitate hujus dogmatis admonere debeat.

Et hoc quidem primum sit fundamentum, quo somnium de Intelligentiis motricibus orbium cælestium penitùs elidimus & evertimus.

Sequitur ALTERUM, petitum à dissonantiâ illorum ipsorum Philosophorum, qui somnii hujus vel primi inventores, vel propugnatores fuerunt.

Primas autem obtinêt Rabbini Judæorum, uti patet ex ipsorum Thalmud, ubi Rabbi Moses, suffragante Synagogâ Judaicâ, singulis orbibus cælestibus, duplicem assignavit motorem: nempè Intelligentiam & animam informantem.

Horum fabellas Gentiles postmodum Philosophi exosculati, in eo plerumque convenerunt, præter DEUM assignandum esse orbibus alium quempiam motorem: Sed quis ille sit, & quomodo ad motum istum sese habeat, usque adeò in diversas imò planè contrarias abierunt sententias, ut ne quidem in hunc usq; diem certi quid inter Philosophos hac de re sit definitum.

Finxerunt enim nonnulli, unum duntaxat motorem orbibus assignandū esse, nempè intelligentiam, & quidem assistentem: Alii contenderunt, orbes moveri ab Intelligentiâ à dexterâ ad sinistram: à formâ verò ipsius orbis moveri à sinistrâ ad dexteram. Alii statuerunt Intelligentiam esse reverà formam sui orbis: ita ut ei non solùm motum, sed etiam dimêsionem, figuram, raritatem & densitatem cæterasq́; perfectiones cælesti naturæ congruentes impetiat: Alii hoc ipsum negarunt, statuentes Intelligentias esse per se quiddam cohærens & completum in suâ specie: Alii mediâ viâ ingressi Philosophati sunt, licèt Intelligentia non propriè ac simpliciter dicenda sit forma sui orbis: posse tamen similitudine quadam formam illius dici: ac majori jure, quàm cæteri externi motores dicuntur formæ corporum, quæ ab eis moventur: uti fvaviter somniant Jesuvvitæ Collegii Conimbricensis, in lib. 2. de Cælo, cap. 5. Quæst. 5. art. 4.

Rursus de vi motrice, in Intelligentiis benè multi statuerunt, Facultatem, quâ Intelligentiæ movent Sphæras cælestes, nihil prorsus differre ab earum intellectu & voluntate: alii verò his contradicentes, plurimùm à se mutuò differre isthæc asseruerunt: Conimbricenses utramque sententiam probabilem, sed posteriorem tamen probabiliorem esse, pronunciant, in l. 2. de cælo cap. 5. Quæst. 8. art. 2.

Quid? quòd ne quidem Philosophorum Peripateticorum princeps Aristoteles, sibi suffragantes hâc in parte habet discipulos. Docet Aristoteles l. 12. Metaphys. cap. 8 text. 47. & seqq. Intelligentiam quoad virtutem motivam ita suo orbi commensuratam esse, ut alium superiorem movere non possit. Erroris hoc nomine arguunt Aristotelem Conimbricenses: sed ita, ut valdè hæsitanter tandem suam negantem, in hunc modum concludant: Quòd, si quis contendat applicuisse DEUM singulis sphæris Intelligentias, eâ proportione virtutis, ut unaquæq; tantùm moveat, quantum valet, & sic à nullâ possit orbem sub altiorem moveri, dicimus id quidem, etsi fieri potuerit, nullâ tamen ratione convinci, ut factum putemus. Coll. Conimbr. in l. 2. de Cælo c. 5. quæst. 8. art 2. Hoc si refutare est, equidem vel unâ hac responsione refutavero universam Jesuvitarum phantasiam de intelligentiis, dicendo: Fieri quidem potuisse ut Deus tales Intelligentias motrices orbium cælestium, crearet : sed nullâ ratione convinci, ut factum putemus.

Docuit Aristoteles: docuerunt id ipsum Astrologi illius seculi, Intelligentias plures non esse, quàm quadraginta septem, aut quinquaginta quinque. Reclamant Conimbricenses, & multò majorem numerum dandum esse, ex Thomâ arguunt. Sed neque hi, neque illi quod dicunt, probant, imò ne possunt quidem.

Et sic Iliacos intra muros pugnatur & extra: ut vel ex perpetuis istis contradictionibus satis evidenter pateat, ejusmodi fundamentis superstructum esse dogma de Intelligentiis, quæ haud magis cohæreant & subsistant, atque funiculus ex arenulis contextus, ubi alicubi Irenæus loquitur.

Tertium Refutationis argumentum Sacræ literæ suppeditant, quæ motum orbium cælestium, ita soli DEO adsignant, ut reliquas creaturas singulas & universas, tàm cælestes, quàm terrestres, simpliciter indè excludant.

Nehem. 9, 6. Tu ipse Domine, tu solus fecisti Cælum & Cælum Cælorum, & omnem exercitum eorum: terram, & universa, quæ in eâ sunt: maria & omnia, quæ in eis sunt: & TU VIVIFICAS OMNIA hæc, & exercitus Cæli te adorat.

Ecclesiastici 24, 5. & seqq. Ex ore altissimi prodii primogenita ante omnem creaturam. Ego facio in Cælis, ut oriatur lumen indeficiens: Ego in altissimis habito thronus meus in columnâ nubis: Ego SOLA gyrum Cæli circumeo, & profundum abyssi penetro.

Jes. 48, 13. Dextera mea palmo mensa est Cælos: Ego vocabo eos, & stabunt simul.

Jerem. 34, 25. Si pactum meum inter diem ac noctem: & leges cælo & terræ non posui: projiciam semen Jacob, & David Servi mei & c.

Job. 38, 12. Nunquid tu, inquit DEUS, post ortum tuum præcepisti diluculo, & ostendisti auroræ locum suum?

Et v. 18. & 19. Nunquid considerasti latitudinem terræ? Indica mihi, si nosti omnia, in qua via (VIA motum Sphærarum Solis & Lunæ notat) Lux habitet & tenebrarum quis locus sit: ut DUCAS unüquodq; ad terminos suos? v. 32. Numquid producis Luciferum in tempore suo, & vesperū super filios terræ consurgere facis? Nunquid nosti ordinem Cæli?


### Question Six: Offices of Angels from sacred letters (continued)

What? That Scripture expressly affirms that such power is implanted in the solar body by GOD, that now, without any other impeller, by its own proper motion and by the sole power implanted by God, it maintains and completes its motion and course, and thus moves itself. Ps. 19, 6. The sun as a Bridegroom coming out of his chamber, rejoices as a strong man to run his race: his going forth is from the end of the Heavens, and his revolution over the ends of them. Now if this is true of one Sphere: why not also of the rest: For of similar things the judgment is the same.

These and other testimonies of the Scriptures of this kind, the Coimbricenses attempt to elude by some futile and feeble little distinction devised by them: Government, they say, imports two things, namely, the knowledge or internal direction of things to be done, and the external execution. If we speak of the former, GOD governs all things immediately and by Himself: If of the latter: He administers many things through creatures, to whom He has willed to impart this honor and dignity. Therefore the places of the Scriptures ought to be understood concerning government according to the former consideration. Then God is also said to have set no one else over the administration of the world, because He Himself also concurs in the external government of things, since nothing can be effected without His concurrence. Thus far the Coimbricenses, Commentaries on book 2 of Aristotle on the Heavens, chap. 5, Quest. 5, Art. 3.

But this is nothing else than childishly to βαττολογεῖν [babble] and to beg the question. Be it so, that GOD administers by some manner of execution through other creatures: will it therefore be permissible to conclude: Therefore He moves the celestial orbs through Angels. Who does not understand the πλεονεξίαν [excess/fallacy] of the consequent? Certainly, as regards that mediate government, which they call external execution, we would never admit it either, unless it partly fell under our eyes, or fell under the senses: and partly rested upon clear testimonies of the Scriptures and irrefragable reasons. As for example, that GOD uses the ministry of Angels in defending the pious, Scripture testifies, Ps. 91, 11. He has given charge to His Angels concerning you, that they may keep you in all your ways. Likewise in the promulgation of the law: Gal. 3, 19. The law ordained through Angels in the hand of a Mediator: That likewise GOD sometimes also uses the work of the pious and Saints, in ruling, informing, and converting His people, Scripture is likewise a witness: Ps. 77, 21. You led Your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron. 2 Cor. 5, 20. We perform the office of ambassadors for Christ, as though GOD were exhorting through us.

These and other things of this kind we willingly admit, and with respect to these works, we freely grant both the distinction brought forward and the other exception subjoined by the Coimbricenses.

Moreover, since it neither falls under the senses, nor is it supported by the oracles of the Scriptures, but rather is diametrically opposed to them, nor can it be demonstrated by evident reasons that Angels or Intelligences move the celestial spheres: we simply deny to them that latter species of Government, as far as the motion of the Heaven is concerned: and we respond that the distinction brought forward in this place fails entirely. By this very means, the other exception of the Coimbrans also collapses: for that will only then be valid when they have first provided proof that GOD concurs with the Angels in moving the celestial spheres, which is the sole and primary κρινόμενον of this Disputation.

But it remains that we weigh in the balance of truth the principal reasons with which the Assertors of Intelligences are accustomed to fight.

And at the beginning, indeed, Pererius and the Coimbrans bring forward that passage of Job 9:13: 'Under whom they bow, who carry the sphere': that is, the Angels, who by their motion carry around the celestial world. Comment. in l. 2. de cælo c. 1. quæst. 5. Art. 3.

But who would not exclaim here, 'Friends, hold your laughter!' For do those tender and most free Angelic Spirits labor so under the mass of the celestial spheres that they must even be bent like porters? Truly, in this way, the condition of the celestial spheres themselves would be better and more perfect than that of the Angels. But to respond to the matter itself, a notable crime of falsehood is committed in the Latin version, which dissonates from the Hebrew sources διὼ διὰ πασῶν. For thus we read in the Hebrew: 'Under him they bowed themselves, the helpers of pride,' or 'those relying on pride' עֹזְרֵי רַהַב Ozerei Rahab. That is: The proud helpers, or even the most powerful tyrants in this age, who although they may seem to carry the heaven on their own shoulders, yet at last will be compelled to be humbled before him: And as our blessed Luther renders it from the Hebrew: 'Vnter Jhm müssen sich beugen die Stoltzen Herren.' But what has this to do with the Angels? nay, what has it to do with those fictitious Intelligences, the movers of the celestial spheres?

The second argument sounds thus: Heaven is a simple body, and in all its parts uniform according to substance: Therefore it cannot move itself: For neither can a part be distinctly marked in it which moves, and another part which is moved. Perer. Commentar. in Genesin. lib. 2. Quæst. 5 p. 216. & Coimbrans in the place just cited.

I respond that the argument labors under the fallacy ὡς τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For that is true, not καθ' ὅλε, concerning every motion, but only concerning that which pertains to natural things by the condition of their nature and according to physical rules: where indeed it is necessary that one part be marked which moves, and another which is moved. But it is false concerning that motion, or faculty, which accrued to the heaven from creation; and by the virtue of the Most High was once implanted in it, and is preserved until the end of the world. Therefore, this argument does not fight for the Intelligences any more than the arguments produced above in Question 1 from the opinion of Aristotle for the eternity of the World, and taken from the consideration of physical motion. For that which moves the Heaven itself by its own virtue, and by that implanted in the Heaven at the beginning of creation: that does not depend on the conditions and rules of physical motion: but on the sole will and virtue of God, which most freely effects and preserves the principles, ends, mutations or motions of things, and rest or cessation: and sometimes even changes and withdraws them, as is most clearly evident from the history of Joshua, where the Sun and Moon stood still for the space of an entire day: Josh. 10:13; Ecclesiasticus 43:5. Likewise from the history of King Hezekiah, where the Sun went back ten degrees, 2 Kings 20:11. Wherefore that argument, and indeed the primary one of the Adversaries, commits a gross Ignoratio Elenchi through a μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος.

The third argument is thus formulated (by Pererius) in the place cited a little earlier. If the Heavens are not moved by Angels, truly no Philosophical way and reason is left by which it can be known and proved that Angels exist.

Which argument the Coimbrans propose with slightly changed words in this manner: unless the celestial spheres were moved by Intelligences, not only would the connection of sensible and intelligible things, or of the corporeal and incorporeal world, not stand: but neither would any way at all be left for Philosophers to investigate minds separated from the concretion of matter. For this reason led them most of all to the knowledge of them. For when they observed the laws, order, and constancy of the celestial motions, and saw that this could not happen except by some intellective power devoid of body, they determined that Intelligences must be granted, by which such motions were effected. Commentar. in l. 2. de cælo. cap. 5. quæst. 5. Art. 3.

I respond that this argument overturns itself with most shameful vanities and absurdities. For 1. If, according to that of the Apostle, evils are not to be done that good may come, Rom. 3:8, then certainly false principles are not to be fabricated so that the truth of some matter or Question may be asserted. 2. The assigned reason is inverted: For if, apart from the doctrine of Intelligences, no Philosophical way and reason is left by which it can be known and proved that Angels exist, therefore it is evident from that very fact that such knowledge must be obtained from a more sublime science, namely the revealed Word of God, and consequently that Angels are not the proper object of Philosophical Doctrine. 3. That ἀσύστατον, that one arrives at the knowledge of Angels through the doctrine of Intelligences, is false: since the contrary is rather true. For the Rabbis of the Jews knew and believed that Angels exist: and that from Moses and the Prophets. This knowledge also trickled down to the Gentiles, and thus consequently to the Schools of the Platonists. But since they were destitute of a distinct knowledge of the Angels, being indeed ignorant of the Scriptures, it came about that they began to dispute concerning the nature and office of those heavenly minds, and that, too, from philosophical principles. When this and that other thing were added, that they saw the Heaven observing its own certain motion, they immediately argued thus, with Augustine also as a witness, lib. de cogitatione veræ vitæ, cap. 6. That which is moved, is either moved by itself, or from elsewhere: But everything that has motion from itself, is sensible: But such is not the celestial body. Therefore it has motion from elsewhere: If from elsewhere: nothing can surely be given besides angelic minds. Therefore it is necessary that these move the Heaven. Thus, therefore, that confused notion of τȣ εἰ ἔςι, That there are Angels, which Gentiles even philosophers drew either from the schools of the Rabbis, or from the reading of the books of Moses and the Prophets, gave a handle and occasion to the doctrine concerning the intelligences moving the celestial spheres: but not vice versa. Finally, the reason of the consequence is denied, which clearly has no force in the argument of the Coimbricenses: which sounds thus: the laws, order, and constancy of celestial motions cannot be produced except by some intellectual power, devoid of body. Therefore, intelligences must be granted, by which such motions might be effected: which are none other than Angels. For this collection labors under the fallacy πρὸς τὸ ἐλλιπὲς διαιρέσεως. For the prosyllogistic collection ought to have been formed thus: The laws, order, and constancy of celestial motions argue for some incorporeal mover. Therefore, it is necessary that either GOD himself, or Angels, or some power implanted in the spheres by GOD in the first creation, effects that motion. Now, nothing of such a kind is asserted concerning Angels in the Scriptures. Therefore, it was not safe to assert this either. It remains, therefore, that either GOD himself, or that implanted power moves the spheres: Which, since both are most clearly evident from the testimonies of Scripture produced above in great number: and since in the first creation a certain moving power was implanted in individual creatures, both sensible and insensible: Whence the Savior also mentions the powers of the heavens several times, Matt. 24, 29. Luke 21, 26. it would surely be consistent with piety to refer the laws, order, and constancy of celestial motions to GOD: as one who works even today, and just as he once founded individual things, so he also preserves and sustains them with tireless effort. In which way, just as it is by no means denied that there are Angels: so the providence of GOD concerning created things, according to the sense of Scripture, is most rightly asserted.

Finally, Pererius reveals a stupendous ignorance, etc., toward the end of this disputation, arguing against us from the tripod of the Jesuits: If the Heaven were moved by its own power from itself, then it would have a natural propensity toward its own motion: Wherefore it could not be deprived of it, except miraculously and violently, and then it would lack a certain perfection naturally convenient and due to it.

Which argumentation indeed not obscurely argues that the Jesuits scarcely believe the World will ever perish: whether the Heaven is moved by itself or by Intelligences. For the same reason militates no less against the Intelligences, which are surely likewise carried by natural propensity toward their own motion: for they would not have determined that the Heaven moves them unwilling or compelled.

Then the reasoning of Pererius is clearly null. For because we have been taught by the word of GOD, and we believe,

that this World will pass away preternaturally, and thus truly miraculously and violently: it will surely also lack that perfection which it now possesses from the first creation: nay, clearly this Heaven and this earth will no longer be, Apoc.

Finally, this reasoning proceeds from a false hypothesis, which is presupposed, that the Heaven and earth are not to perish at some time according to substance: but only to be changed at some time according to qualities: that which manifestly fights with Scripture: as we shall demonstrate expressly in its own place. We leave this one thing to be weighed and deliberated by the Jesuits in place of a conclusion: Since according to their opinion the Heaven is to remain on the last day according to substance, whole and intact, whether they think that even then the Angels will be attached to their spheres, and will effect their motion for all eternity: or whether they believe that they are to be freed from that work: and who then is to perform that motion.

Latin:

Quid? quod Scriptura disertè affirmat, corpori solari à DEO eam vim esse insitam, ut jam sine alio aliquo impulsore proprio motu solâ virtute Dei insita, motum & cursum suum teneat & perficiat, & sic seipsum moveat. Psal. 19, 6. Sol tanquam Sponsus ègrediens de thalamo suo, gaudet ut potens ad currendam viam suam: ab extremo Cœlorum egressio ejus, & revolutio ejus super extrema eorum. Jam si hoc de unâ Sphærâ verum est: quid ni etiam de reliquis: De similibus enim idem est judicium.

Hæc & id genus alia Scripturarum testimonia, eludere conantur Conimbricenses, futili quapiam & elumbi excogitatâ distinctiunculâ: Gubernatio, inquiētes, duo importat, videlicet cognitionem sive internam directionem rerum faciendarum, & externam executionem. Si de priori loquamur, DEUS immediatè ac per se gubernat omnia: Si de posteriori: multa per creaturas administrat, quibus hunc honorem dignitatemq; impertire voluit. Loca ergò Scripturarum, de gubernatione secundum priorem considerationem intelligi debent. Deindè Deus etiam dicitur, neminem alium mundi administrationi præfecisse, quia ipse ad externam rerum gubernationem etiam cōcurrit, cùm nihil absq; illius concursu effici queat. Hactenus Conimbricenses, Commentar. in lib. 2. Arist. de Cœlo. cap. 5. Quæst. 5. Art. 3.

Sed nihil hoc est aliud, quàm pueriliter βαττολογεῖν & petere principium. Esto, administret DEUS nonnullâ ratione executionis, per creaturas alias: numquid propterea colligere licebit. Ergò per Angelos movet orbes cœlestes. Quis non πλεονεξίαν consequentis intelligit? Sanè quoad mediatam illam gubernationem, quam isti externam executionem nominant, nunquàm nos eam quoque admitteremus, nisi partim in oculos illa incurreret, aut sub sensus caderet: partim verò perspicuis Scripturarum testimoniis, & rationibus irrefragabilibus niteretur. Ut exempli gratia, quod DEUS Angelorum ministerio utatur in defendendis piis, testatur Scriptura, Psal. 91, 11. Angelis suis mandavit de te, ut custodiant te in omnibus tuis viis. Item in promulgandâ lege: Gal. 3, 19. Lex ordinata per Angelos in manu Mediatoris: Quod item DEUS interdum etiam piorum & Sanctorum operâ utatur, in regendo, informando & convertendo populo suo, Scriptura item testis est: Psal. 77, 21. Deduxisti sicut oves populum tuum in manu Mosi & Aaron. 2. Cor. 5, 20. pro Christo legatione fungimur, tanquam DEO exhortante per nos.

Hæc & id genus alia libenter admittimus, & respectu operum istorum, tùm allatam distinctiunculam, tùm subjunctam exceptionem alteram Conimbricensium, ultrò largimur.

Cæterùm, cùm neque sub sensus cadat, neque Scripturarum oraculis astruatur, quin potiùs iisdem è diametro repugnet, neque etiam evidentibus rationibus demonstrari possit, Angelos sive Intelligentias movere orbes cœlestes: utique posteriorem etiam illam Gubernationis speciem, quoad motum Cœli, simpliciter ipsis negamus: ac proindè allatam distinctiunculam hoc loco prorsus deficere, respondemus. Quo ipso pacto corruit altera etiam exceptio Conimbricensium: Tùm demùm enim illa militabit, quando prius probatum dederint, DEUM in movendis orbibus cœlestibus, unà cum Angelis concurrere, id quod unicum & primarium est Disputationis hujus κρινόμενον.

Sed superest, ut præcipuas rationes, quibus Intelligentiarum Assertores pugnare solent, ad trutinam veritatis appendamus.

Ac initiò quidem proferunt Pererius & Conimbricenses, illud Jobi 9, 13. Sub quo curvantur, qui portant orbem: id est, Angeli, qui suo motu cœlestem mundum circumvehunt. Comment. in l. 2. de cælo c. 1. quæst. 5. Art. 3.

Quis verò non hîc exclamet, risum teneatis amici! Siccinè enim tenelli illi & liberrimi Spiritus Angelici sub mole orbium cœlestium ita laborant, ut tanquam bajuli curvari etiam necesse habeant? Sanè hoc pacto melior & perfectior ipsorum orbium cœlestium, quàm Angelorum foret conditio. Sed ad rem ipsam ut respondeamus, insigne crimen falsi committitur in versione Latinâ, quæ à fontibus Hebræis διὼ διὰ πασῶν dissonat. Sic enim in Hebræo legimus: sub eo incurvaverunt se, adjutores superbiæ, sive freti superbia עֹזְרֵי רַהַב Ozerei Rahab. hoc est: Adjutores superbi, vel Tyranni etiam hoc in seculo potentissimi, qui licèt sibi humeris suis cœlum portare videantur, tamen tandem cogentur coram eo humiliari: Et ut B. Lutherus noster ex Hebræo reddit: Vnter Jhm müssen sich beugen die Stoltzen Herren. Sed quid hoc ad Angelos? imò quid ad fictitias illas Intelligentias orbium cœlestium motrices?

Alterum argumentum sic sonat: Cælum est corpus simplex, & in omnibus partibus suis secundum substantiam uniforme: Ergò non potest seipsum movere: Nequè enim potest in ipso distinctè signari pars, quæ moveat, & altera pars quæ moveatur. Perer. Commentar. in Genesin. lib. 2. Quæst. 5 p. 216. & Conimbricenses loco jam proximè citato.

Respondeo argumentum laborare Sophismate ὡς τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Verum enim illud est, non καθ' ὅλε, de omni motu, sed tantùm de eo, qui rebus naturalibus ex conditione naturæ suæ, & secundum regulas physicas competit: ubi sanè necesse est, ut signetur pars una, quæ moveat: & altera quæ moveatur. Falsum verò est de eo motu, sive facultate, quæ ex creatione cœlo obtigit; & virtute altissimi ipsi semel est insita, & conservatur ad finem usque mundi. Proindè haud magis militat hoc argumentum pro Intelligentiis, atque militant argumenta supra Quæstione 1. ex sententiâ Aristotelis pro æternitate Mundi producta, & ex consideratione motûs physici petita. Nam quod virtute propriâ, & in principio creationis Cœlo insita, seipsum Cœlum movet: illud non dependet à conditionibus & regulis motus physici: sed à solâ Dei voluntate & virtute, quæ principia, fines, mutationes sive motus rerum, & quietem sive cessationem, liberrimè efficit, conservat: & interdum etiam immutat, & retrahit, uti ex historiâ Josuæ, ubi Sol & Luna per integrum diei spacium constituerunt: Josu. 10, 13. Ecclesiastici 43, 5. Item ex historiâ regis Ezechiæ, ubi Sol decem gradibus retrocessit 2. Reg. 20, 11. liquidissimè patet. Quare argumentum istud, & quidem primarium Adversariorum, per μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος craffam committit Ignorationem Elenchi.

Tertium argumentum sic informat (Pererius) loco paulò antè citato. Si Cœli non moventur ab Angelis, nulla profectò relinquitur via & ratio Philosophica, qua cognosci & probari queant, Angelos esse.

Quod argumentum Conimbricenses paululùm mutatis verbis in hunc modum proponunt, nisi ab Intelligentiis moverentur orbes cælestes, non solùm connexio rerum sensibilium & intelligibilium, sive mundi corporei & incorporei non constaret: sed neq́;, ulla ferè via, ad investigandas mentes à materia concretione sejunctas Philosophis relinqueretur. Hæc enim eos potissimùm ratio ad illarum cognitionem duxit. Nam cùm motuum cælestium leges, ordinem & constantiam observarent, idq́; non nisi ab aliquâ intellectrice vi corporis experte, fieri posse viderent, statuerunt dandas esse intelligentias, à quibus ejusmodi motus efficerentur. Commentar. in l. 2. de cælo. cap. 5. quæst. 5. Art. 3.

Respondeo, turpissimis vanitatibus & absurditatibus semetipsum evertere hoc argumentum. Nam 1. Si secundum illud Apostoli, non sunt facienda mala, ut eveniant bona Rom. 3, 8. utique falsa etiam non sunt confingenda principia, ut rei sive Quæstionis alicujus veritas asseratur. 2. Invertitur ratio assignata: Si enim citra doctrinam de Intelligentiis, nulla relinquitur via & ratio philosophica, quâ cognosci & probari queat Angelos esse. Ergò vel indè constat, ex sublimiori scientiâ, nempè Verbo Dei revelato, notitiam istam comparandam esse & per consequens, Angelos Doctrinæ Philosophicæ objectum proprium non esse. 3. ἀσύστατον &c istud, Ex doctrinâ de Intelligentiis, perventum tandem esse ad Angelorum notitiam: cùm contrarium potiùs verùm sit. Nam Angelos esse, noverunt & crediderunt, Judæorum Rabbini: idque ex Mose & Prophetis. Hæc notitia dimanavit etiam ad Gentiles, & sic consequenter ad Scholas Platonicorum. Jam verò cùm discretâ Angelorum notitiâ, quippè ignari Scripturarum, destituti fuerint: factum est, ut de mentium illarum cælestium naturâ & officio cœperint disputare: & quidem ex principiis Philosophicis. Hic cum accederet & illud alterum, quod viderent Coelum certum suum observare motum, statim sic arguebant, Augustino etiam teste, lib. de cogitatione veræ vitæ, cap. 6.
