Quod movetur, aut à seipso movetur, aut aliundè: Sed omne quod motum à se habet, est sensibile: Sed tale non est corpus cæleste. Ergò motum habet aliundè: Si aliundè: nihil poterit utique dari præter mentes Angelicas. Ergò hæ moveant Cœlum necesse est. Sic ergò confusa illla notitia τȣ εἰ ἔςι, Quòd sint Angeli, quam vel Rabbinorum Scholis, vel ex lectione librorum Mosis & Prophetarum, Gentiles etiam Philosophi hauserunt, ansam & occasionem præbuit doctrinæ de Intelligentiis motricibus orbium cœlestium: non verò vice versâ. Tandem negatur ratio consequentiæ, quæ planè nulla militat, in argumento Conimbricensium: quod sic sonat: motuum cælestium leges, ordo & constantia, non nisi ab aliquâ Intellectrice vi, corporis experte, fieri potest. Ergò dandæ sunt intelligentiæ, à quibus ejusmodi motus efficerentur: quæ non sunt nisi Angeli. Nam laborat hæc collectio Sophismate πρὸς τὸ ἐλλιπὲς διαιρέσεως. Sic enim informari debebat collectio prosyllogistica: Motuum cælestium leges, ordo, constantia, arguunt incorporeum aliquod movens. Ergò vel DEUS ipse vel Angeli, vel vis quædã in primâ creatione orbibus à DEO insita motum istum efficiat, necesse est. Jam de Angelis tale nihil in Scripturis asseritur. Ergò neque hoc asserere, tutum fuit. Relinquitur proindè, ut vel DEUS ipse, vel vis illa insita moveat orbes: Quod utrumq́; cùm ex Scripturæ testimoniis suprà magno numero productis, liquidissimè pateat: & in primâ creatione singulis creaturis tàm sensibilibus, quàm insensibilibus, vis movens certa insita sit: Undè Servator etiam cœlorum virtutum aliquoties meminit Matth. 24, 29. Luc. 21, 26. utique motuum etiam cœlestium leges, ordinem & constantiam, ad DEUM referre, pietati fuerit consentaneum: ut qui hodiéque operatur, & prout semel singula condidit, ita etiam indefesso studio ea conservat & sustentat. Quo pacto uti Angelos esse minimè negatur: ita providentia DEI circa res creatas, secundum Scripturæ sensum, rectissimè astruitur.

Tandem stupendam inscitiam prodit Pererius, &c sub finem disputationis hujus, ex Jesuvvitarum tripode adversum nos arguens: Si Cœlum suâ vi moveretur à se ipso, tùm haberet naturalem propensionem ad suum motum: Quapropter non posset eo privari, nisi miraculosè & violentè, & tunc careret perfectione quadam naturaliter sibi convenienti ac debitâ.

Quæ sanè argumentatio haud obscurè arguit, Jesuitas vix credere Mundum aliquando interiturum: sive à seipso, sive ab Intelligentiis moveatur Cœlum. Nam eadem ratio militat haud minus contra Intelligentias, quæ utique naturali propensione itidem feruntur ad suum motum: neque enim invitas aut coactas Cœlum eas movere statuerint.

Deindè ratio Pererii planè nulla est. Quia enim verbo DEI edocti sumus, & credimus,

Mundum hunc transiturum præternaturaliter, & sic verè miraculosè & violentè: utique carebit etiam eâ perfectione, quàm ex primâ creatione nunc possidet: imò planè non ampliùs erit Cœlum istud, & terra isthæc, Apoc.

Tandem procedit hæc ratio ex falsâ hypothesi, quæ præsupponitur, Cœlum & terram non secundum substantiam aliquando interitura: sed tantùm secundum qualitates aliquando immutanda esse: id quod cum scripturâ manifestè pugnat: uti suo loco ex professo demonstrabimus. Unicum istud coronidis loco Jesuvvitis expendendum & deliberandum relinquimus: Cùm ex ipsorum sententiâ Cœlum in die novissimo secundum substantiam sit mansurum, integrum & sartum, an existiment, etiam tùm Angelos suis orbibus affessuros, & in omnem æternitatem motum illorum effecturos: an verò ab isto opere illos liberandos esse credant? & quis tùm motum istum perfecturus sit.


### Question VIII. What was that Light, created on the first day?

What kind was that Light, created on the first day?

Concerning this question, both ancient and more recent Theologians depart into clearly diverse opinions.

Among the ancients, Augustine interprets this Light as the spiritual, invisible, angelic nature, lib. 11. de Civitat. DEI capp. 7. & 9. Likewise lib. 1. de Genes. ad lit. cap. 3. & lib. 12. Confess. capp. 9. & 26. Following in whose footsteps Peter Lombard, l. 2. Sent. dist. 13. Beata and others, converted the words of Moses into mere allegories, establishing that by the name of Heaven, which was created in the beginning, the Angelic Nature is denoted by Moses: but by the name of Light created on the first day, the confirmation and consummation of the Angels in grace is insinuated: finally, by the division of light and darkness, the segregation of evil Angels from the company of the good is indicated. But our B. Luther rightly responds: that this is not to interpret the Scriptures: but rather to play with untimely allegories, for Moses narrates History, not allegories. Then Moses wrote for unrefined men, so that they might have open testimonies concerning the Creation: Therefore such absurd things are not to be brought in here.

The opinion of those who maintain that that Light was corporeal and visible is therefore more probable: and that for the following reasons:

I. Before the Creation of this Light there was darkness upon the face of the deep, so that it might be dispelled, this Light was created on the first day. Now indeed, once the second act is posited, the first act is certainly posited: that is, once the illumination of that unrefined and indigestible mass is posited, the luminous body itself is certainly posited: Which cannot be given as anything other than this light created on the first day. The reason is: Because the Sun and Moon were created only on the fourth day.

Latin:

Qualis fuerit Lux illa, primo die condita?

CIrca hanc quæstionem in diversas planè abeunt sententias, tùm Veteres, tùm recentiores Theologi.

Ex Veteribus Augustinus Lucem hanc interpretatur de spirituali invisibili Angelicâ naturâ lib. 11. de Civitat. DEI capp. 7. & 9. Item lib. 1. de Genes. ad lit. cap. 3. & lib. 12. Confess. capp. 9. & 26. Cujus vestigia secuti Petrus Lombardus l. 2. Sent. dist. 13. Beata & alii, verba Mosis in meras allegorias converterunt, statuentes, Nomine Cœli, quod in principio creatum est, notari à Mose Naturã Angelicam: Nomine autem Lucis primo die conditæ, insinuari confirmationem & Cõsummationẽ Angelorum in gratiâ: per divisionem deniquè lucis & tenebrarum, indicari segregationem malorum Angelorũ à bonorum consortio. Sed rectè respõdet B. Lutherus noster: hoc non esse interpretari Scripturas: sed potiùs ludere intempestivis allegoriis, Moses enim Historiam narrat, non allegorias. Deindè Moses scripsit hominibus rudibus, ut haberent testimonia aperta de Creatione: Igitur tàm absurda huc non sunt afferenda.

Probabilior proindè eorum est sententia, qui statuunt, Lucem illam fuisse corpoream & visibilem: idque propter sequentes rationes:

I. Ante Creationem Lucis hujus fuerunt tenebræ super faciem abyssi, quæ ut depellerentur, Lux hæc primo die fuit condita. Jam verò posito actu secundo, ponitur utique actus primus: hoc est, positâ illuminatione rudis illius & indigestæ molis, ponitur utique ipsum corpus luminosum: Quod dari non potest aliud, præter lucem hanc primo die conditam. Ratio est: Quia Sol & Luna, quarto demùm die sunt creata.


### Question Concerning the first-born Light

II. Before the creation of the Sun and Moon, three natural days preceded. Therefore, it is necessary that this Light created on the first day was a luminous and visible body, inasmuch as it had the power of shining like a luminous cloud, and moved from east to west in the space of twenty-four hours, during this first three-day period, it constituted a sufficiently evident distinction of night and day.

III. Thus, according to the mind of Augustine, this Light created on the first day should be taken allegorically: certainly, for the same reason, the remaining words which Moses uses would also have to be twisted to a mystical and allegorical sense; such as: Darkness, day, evening, morning: and others of that kind, which if they are transferred from their proper and literal signification to a figurative and allegorical one, the entire history of creation is immediately overturned.

A fourth reason can also be added, taken from the very nature of the thing: For because a certain fiery force was altogether necessary for the heating and fertilization of that watery matter, or matter mixed with waters: it is gathered quite probably that this Light was created on the first day for this reason, so that it might be a kind of source and spring of vivifying heat approaching from the outside. Whence it is again most rightly inferred that it was something visible and σωματικον.

II. There are others among the ancients who thought that this Light created on the first day was nothing other than the Element of Fire: Just as Damascenus touches upon their opinion in book 2, Orth. fid. chap. 7. But Johannes Clichrovæus rightly warns that this opinion is less sound or consistent with the truth: and this first for this reason. That primogenial Light distinguished day and night by its motion from east to west: so that as it rose, the whole hemisphere of the celestial machine was illuminated: as it set, darkness or night arose. But the Element of fire always surrounds the whole earth, water, and air: yet it does not illuminate the whole world: For thus either night would no longer exist: or the world would be deprived of the Element of Fire at night. Since both of these are prodigiously absurd, it follows that the Element of Fire is not that primogenial Light. Then this primogenial Light was collected on the fourth day and distinguished into the solar body. But who, unless delirious and insane, will think that the Element of Fire passed into the substance of the sun, as the same commentator on Damascenus rightly gathers.

But another Question was also raised in this place, and is raised today: Whether, namely, this Light created on the first day was a certain substance ἀυτοσύσιτος, or indeed a certain Accident, whether ενυπόστατον, or ἀνυπόστατον? And Basil indeed, in his sixth Homily on Genesis, teaches that this primogenial Light was Light in itself, and immaterial: but that on the fourth day the body of the Sun was made, as a vehicle of this light: that is, he posits that this Light was an Accident entirely ἀνυπόστατον, that is, supported by no substance. Which absurd opinion the Jesuit Bellarmine does not fear to twist to establish the dogma of Pontifical Transubstantiation, concerning the accidents of Bread substantially changed into the body of Christ. But he himself rightly protests

Pererius, dissenting from Bellarmine in this part, in these words: If Basil felt that the light created by God on the first day was an accident separated from all matter: he surely introduces a very great miracle: Now, indeed, in the first creation, institution, and disposition of things, to have recourse to miracles, especially when there is no need for them, neither pleases Augustine, nor is it approved by me. To which reason we add the following two as well. The former is: Whatever Moses commemorates as having been created in the first chapter are substances, not accidents: for these are rather concreated with substances than created.

The latter is this: A second act cannot exist without a first act, in the whole universe of things: Now, indeed, if it be posited that that primogenial Light was a mere accident and indeed separated from all substance: it will follow that the second act, namely the illumination of the celestial hemisphere, was without a first act, that is, without a luminous body: which is prodigiously absurd.

But a greater difficulty arises here now: For if the primogenial Light was not an Accident: it must have been a Substance; If a substance, then it would either still endure today: and thus two luminous bodies would have to be posited, and indeed ones constituting the day: which is absurd: or after the first three-day period, the Sun having been created, that substance was abolished: Which itself seems no less absurd, nay, impious: Inasmuch as by this arrangement GOD would be posited to have created such a work, which was soon to be destroyed: which conflicts diametrically with His infinite wisdom.

Let the moderns extricate themselves from this difficulty; they seek various escape routes. For some maintain that that primordial Light is rightly called a substance, insofar as it is opposed to darkness: that is, insofar as it is a real positive entity, it is opposed to privation: others imagine that this Light was the solar body itself, and indeed created on the first day: so that in the description of the fourth day Moses does not finally express the creation of the solar body and the stars: but only of the fixed stars and thus by a certain ανακεφαλαιωσιν or recapitulation makes mention of the principal Planets, created on the first day. But neither opinion can be simply admitted. For the former, although it contains nothing false, yet does not solve the knot of the proposed question. The latter labors under a manifest absurdity. For it imagines that GOD made at the same time the primum mobile and the seven orbits of the planets, leaving the intermediate space entirely empty, in which on the following day the firmament, or eighth Heaven, was to be formed: It imagines that the Sun could have been moved by the motion of the primum mobile with such a great empty interval interposed between the first Heaven and the orbits of the planets: as if indeed the motion of the primum mobile could have reached the orbit of the Sun through such a great vacuum as is all that space which the eighth Sphere occupies: Finally, it imagines through a shameful begging of the question that Moses on the fourth day only repeats the creation of the Sun and planets made on the first day: When nevertheless the evidence of the text clearly demonstrates that the principal work of the fourth day was the creation of the Sun and Moon, with GOD saying: Let there be lights in the firmament of the Heaven, and let them divide the day and the night Gen. 1, 14.

Having rejected those false opinions, we finally conclude with our blessed Luther that that primordial light was an inherent quality of some lucid or luminous body, like diffused air: yet determined by its own extremities in such a way that it did not illuminate the whole globe at one time, but by its motion illuminated the parts of the universe in turns. Because this lucid body was still mixed with the waters, this very light was indeed more confused and obscure, until finally on the fourth day, that very body by the power of GOD was forced and collected into one part of the heaven, which is now the Sun, and afterwards provided a greater and more illustrious brightness to the world. With this opinion standing, every difficulty completely expires. For thus that primordial light is rightly denied to have been a mere accident: then it is established that it was a substance, and indeed a durable substance, but yet rougher and more imperfect: which, when it was later made perfect and consummated on the fourth day into the solar body: certainly not two, but only one solar body is now constituted: and indeed without the abolition of that primordial light.

Latin:

II. Ante Creationem Solis & Lunæ, tres dies naturales præcesferunt. Ergò Lux hæc primo die condita, corpus luminosum ac visibile fuerit, necesse est, quippè quod lucidæ nubis instar, vim lucendi habuit, & ab ortu in occasum viginti quatuor horarum spacio mota, primo hoc triduo, discrimen noctis & diei, satis evidens constituit.

III. Sic secundum mentem Augustini, Lux hæc primo die condita, allegoricè esset accipienda: certè eâdem ratione ad mysticum & allegoricum sensum detorquenda etiam essent reliqua vocabula, quibus Moses utitur; qualia sunt: Tenebræ, dies, vespera, mane: & id genus alia, quæ si à propriâ & literali significatione ad figuratam & allegoricam transferantur, statim universa creationis historia evertitur.

Addi potest quarta etiam ratio, ab ipsâ rei naturâ petita: Quia enim vis quædam ignea, ad materiæ illius aqueæ, sive aquis permixtæ calefactionem & fœcundationem omninò erat necessaria: ut que Lucem hanc ideò primo die conditam fuisse, satis probabiliter colligitur, ut esset vivifici caloris extrinsecus accedentis fons quasi quidam & scaturigo. Undè rursus visibile & sωματικον quiddam illam fuisse, rectissœ infertut.

II. Sunt ex veteribus alii, qui Lucem istam primo die conditam existimarunt nihil esse aliud, quàm Elementum Ignis: Quemadmodum istorum sententiam perstringit Damascenus lib. 2. Orth. fid. cap. 7. Sed rectè admonet Johannes Clichrovæus, minùs sanam aut veritati consentaneam hanc esse sententiam: idƉue primùm propter hanc causam. Lux illa primogenea motu suo ab ortu in occasum distingvebat diem ac noctem: ita ut eâ oriente, illuminaretur totum cœlestis machinæ hemisphærium: eâdem occidente, orirentur tenebræ sive nox. Atqui Elementum ignis nunquam non totam terram, aquam & aërem circumdat: neque tamen totum orbem illuminat: Sic enim vel nox non ampliùs esset: vel Elemento Ignis noctu orbis destitueretur. Quod utrumque cùm prodigiosè absurdum sit, sequitur Elementum Ignis non esse lucem illam primogeneam. Deinde Lux hæc primogenea, die quartocollecta est & distincta in corpus solare. Sed quis, nisi delirus & amens, arbitrabitur Ignis Elementum transiisse in solis substantiam, uti rectè colligit idem commentator Damasceni.

Sed & alia Quæstio hoc loco mota fuit, hodiéque movetur: An nimirùm Lux hæc primo die condita fuerit substantia quædam ἀυτοσύσιτος, an verò Accidens quoddam, sive ενυπόστατον, sive ἀνυπόστατον? Et Basilius quidem Homiliâ sexta in Genesin, tradit, Lucem hanc primogeneam fuisse Lucem per se, & immaterialem: quarto autem die factum esse corpus Solis, tanquam lucis hujus vehiculũ: hoc est, statuit, Lucem hanc fuisse Accidens prorsƐ ἀνυπόσατον, hoc est, à nulla sustentatũ substãtiâ. Quâ absurdam sententiam Jesuvvita Bellarminus ad stabiliendũ dogma Transsubstãtiationis Põtificiæ, de accidētib. Panis substãtialiter mutati in corpus Christi detorquere non veretur. Sed rectè reclamat ipse

Pererius hac in parte a Bellarmino dissentiens his verbis: Si Basilius sensit, lucem a Deo primo die creatam, esse accidens ab omni materia separatum: maximum profecto inducit miraculum: Jam vero in prima rerum creatione, institutione & dispositione ad miracula confugere, praesertim cum illis minime sit opus, nec placet Augustino, nec mihi probatur. Cui rationi adjungimus sequentes etiam duas. Prior est: Quaecunque cap. primo Moses condita esse commemorat, substantiae sunt, non accidentia: haec enim substantiis concreata potius sunt, quam creata.

Posterior est isthaec: Actus secundus, sine actu primo dari non potest, in tota rerum universitate: Jam vero si statuatur Lux illa primogenea merum fuisse accidens & quidem ab omni substantia separatum: sequetur, Actum secundum, nempe illuminationem coelestis haemisphaerii, fuisse sine actu primo, hoc est, sine luminoso corpore: id quod prodigiose est absurdum.

Sed major hic jam oritur difficultas: Si enim Lux primogenea non fuit Accidens: Substantia fuerit necesse est; Si substantia, utique illa, vel etiamnum hodie durabit: & sic duo erunt constituenda corpora, lucida, & quidem diem constituentia: id quod absurdum: vel post primum triduum, condito Sole, substantia illa fuit abolita: Quod ipsum haud minus absurdum, imo impium videtur: Siquidem hoc pacto DEUS statueretur condidisse tale opus, quod mox destruendum fuerat: id quod cum infinita ipsius sapientia e diametro pugnat.

Ex hac difficultate, sese extricent recentiores, varia quaerunt effugia. Nonnulli enim statuunt, Lucem illam primogeneam recte dici substantiam, quatenus nimirum tenebris ea opponitur: hoc est, quatenus ens reale positivum, opponitur privationi: alii fingunt, Lucem hanc fuisse ipsum corpus solare, & quidem primo die conditum: ita ut in descriptione diei quarti Moses non demum exprimat creationem corporis solaris & astrorum: sed tantum stellarum fixarum & sic per quandam ανακεφαλαιωσιν sive recapitulationem mentionem faciat praecipuoru Planetarum, primo die conditorum. Sed neutra opinio simpliciter admitti potest. Prior enim etsi falsi nihil continet: Quaestionis tamen propositae nodum nondum solvit. Posterior manifesta absurditate laborat. Fingit enim DEUM fecisse simul primum mobile, & septem orbes planetarum, relicto intermedio spacio penitus vacuo, in quo postero die formandum erat firmamentum, sive octavum Coelum: Fingit, Solem tanto intervallo vacuo potuisse inter primum Coelum & orbes planetarum interjecto, motu primi mobilis cieri: quasi vero motus primi mobilis potuerit per tantum vacuum, quantum est omne illud spacium, quod occupat octava Sphaera, pertingere ad orbem Solis: Fingit denique per turpem petitionem principii, Mosen die quarto tantum repetere creationem Solis & planetarum primo die factam: Cum tamen textus evidentia perspicue demonstret, praecipuum diei quarti opus fuisse Solis & Lunae creationem, dicente DEO: Fiant luminaria, in firmamento Coeli, & dividant diem ac noctem Gen. 1, 14.

Rejectis falsis istis sententiis, statuimus tandem cum B. Luthero nostro, Lucem illam primogeneam fuisse insitam qualitatem corporis alicuj9 lucidi sive luminosi, instar aëris diffusi: suis tamen extremitatibus sic determinati, ut non unâ vice totum illustraret globum: sed motu suo partes universi per vices illustraret. Quod corpus lucidum quia aquis adhuc erat permixtum, utique hæc ipsa etiam Lux fuit confusior & obscurior, donec tandem die quarto, illud ipsum corpus virtute DEI, in unam cæli partem, quæ nunc est Sol, fuit coactum & collectum & majorem postmodùm illustrioremque mundo fulgorem præstitit. Quâ stante sententiâ difficultas omnis penitùs expirat. Sic enim Lux illa primogenea rectè negatur merum fuisse accidens: Deindè statuitur fuisse Substantia & substantia quidem durabilis, sed rudior tamen & imperfectior: quæ cum die postmodùm quarto fit perfecta & consummata in corpus solare: Utique non duo jam, sed unum tantùm corpus solare constituitur: & quidem sine Lucis illius primogeneæ abolitione.


### Question IX. What is to be understood by the Firmament, which Moses testifies was created on the second day of creation?

What is to be understood by the Firmament, which Moses testifies was created on the second day of creation?

Lambert Daneau in the second treatise of his Christian Physics, chapter 4, Benedict Pererius, p. 93, and many others, understand by the Firmament created on the second day only that tract which distinguishes the waters from the waters, and separates this whole elementary region from the ethereal by its intervention: which place is considered by philosophers to be proper to the air. But two things especially convict this opinion of error. 1. That this aerial region which surrounds us did not emerge before the waters were separated from the dry land: which was done only on the third day. 2. That in this very firmament, created on the second day, the Sun and Moon and the whole host of stars were placed: which cannot be accepted regarding the aerial tract.

More probably, therefore, we understand by the Firmament both the eighth sphere, commonly called the Firmament, and the whole system and globe of celestial bodies and all the spheres: which is enclosed by the supreme or outermost of the primum mobile and the lowest lunar orbit: and to which the adornment of the stars was added on the fourth day.

Moreover, this Firmament is called by the Hebrews Rakia רקיע, that is, expansion or extension, a metaphor taken from the very mode of formation. For GOD, about to make the heaven, made an expansion of the as it were folded matter, and just as the extension of a curtain or tapestry is made in some palace, or of a tent in a camp: so GOD drew out and expanded that matter, by which the whole machine of the world might be surrounded and encompassed.

The word Firmament corresponds properly not to a Hebrew, but rather to a Greek term, which the 70 Interpreters used. For in Greek it is called στερέωμα, a firmament or consolidation, or even a firm interval: not indeed with respect to matter, or even immobility, as will be demonstrated shortly: but only by reason of the use which this Firmament provides us. For since the upper part of that rough and undigested mass, created on the first day, was entirely occupied by waters like a certain Chaos and aqueous abyss; GOD, having made a distermination of the waters, placed this heaven in the place of an interval as a medium, so that it might both sustain the upper waters and distinguish them from the lower. Concerning which matter, Augustine says thus in book 2, On Genesis literally, chapter 10. Nor does the name of Firmament compel us to think that the heaven stands still: for one may understand the Firmament not because of station, but because of firmness, or the untransgressible boundary of the upper and lower waters.

Moreover, regarding the matter from which this Firmament was created, the opinions are clearly divergent. Aristotle, so as not to say absolutely nothing, contends that the heaven is a certain simple body, entirely devoid of the primary qualities which are in the Elements and other corporeal things. To certain ancient Theologians, even water, which is mentioned, is a sticking point: whence Chrysostom also, in homily 4 on Genesis, writes that whether the heaven is congealed water, or a certain rolled-up air, or some other substance, cannot easily be asserted by anyone. But if we examine more accurately the Mosaic description, and partly the names divinely bestowed upon those celestial bodies, such as are found in Moses, רקיע & שמים Rakia & Schamaim, we shall pronounce without hesitation that the matter was indeed aqueous. This very thing Peter also clearly testifies, 2 Peter 3:5, saying: This escapes them, that the heaven and the earth existed long ago out of water and through water by the word of GOD. But however much the heaven was made from fluid matter, GOD nevertheless so strengthened it that it is more solid than any bronze or adamant: a fact which is evident even from this, that by the most destructive and most rapid rotation of so many years, it is neither broken, nor worn away, nor weakened. Whence Job also, chapter 37:18, asserts that the heavens were cast as if from the most solid bronze. Regarding which matter Bede speaks quite elegantly in his Hexaemeron: It is certain, he says, that the starry heaven is a firmament in the midst of the waters, nor does anything prevent it from being believed to have been made from waters: For we know what great firmness, what transparency and purity a crystal stone has, which it is certain was produced from the congealing of waters: what prevents us from believing that the same disposer of natures solidified the substance of the waters into the firmament of heaven?

Latin:

Quid per Firmamentum, quod Secundo creationis die conditum esse, Moses testatur, sit intelligendum?

LAmbertus Danæus tractatu secundo Physicæ Christianæ cap. 4. Benedictus Pererius p. 93. & complures alii, per Firmamentum secundo die conditum, intelligunt illum tantùm tractum, qui distingvit aquas ab aquis, & totam hanc elementarem regionem, ab æthereâ interventu suo dispescit: Qui locus aëris esse proprius, à Philosophis censetur. Verùm sententiam hanc duo potissimùm erroris convincunt. 1. Quòd aërea ista regio, quæ nos ambit, non priùs emersit, quàm aquæ ab aridâ separatæ fuerunt: id quod factum die demùm tertio. 2. Quod in hoc ipso firmamento, secundo die condito, Sol & Luna, & universus astrorum exercitus, fuit collocatus: id quod de tractu aëreo non potest accipi.

Verisimilius proindè per Firmamentum intelligimus, tùm sphæram octavam, vulgò aliàs Firmamentum dictum: tùm universum corporum cœlestium, omniúmque Sphærarum Systema & globum: qui Supremo sive extimo primi mobilis, & infimo orbe Lunari clauditur: & cui die quarto stellarum ornatus accessit.

Dicitur autem Firmamentum hoc Hebræis Rakia רקיע, hoc est, expansio sive extensio. metaphora sumta, ab ipso formationis modo. Nam cœlum facturus DEUS, materiæ quasi complicatæ expansionem fecit, & quemadmodum aulæi sive tapetis in palatio aliquo, vel tentorii in castris fit extensio: Ita DEUS diduxit & expandit materiam istam, quâ tota mundi machina circumdata ambiretur.

Firmamenti vox non Hebræo, sed Græco magis vocabulo, quo 70. Interpretes usi sunt, propriè respondet. Græcis enim στερέωμα dicitur firmamentum sive consolidatio, vel etiam firmum interstitium: non quidem respectu materiæ, vel etiam immobilitatis: ut mox demonstrabitur: sed tantùm ratione usus, quem Firmamentum istud nobis præbet. Cùm enim pars superior molis illius rudis & indigestæ, primoq; die conditæ, ab aquis tota occupata esset quasi Chaos quoddam, & abyssus aquea; DEUS aquarum disterminatione factâ, cœlum hoc interstitii loco posuit intermedium, ut aquas superiores tùm sustineret, tùm ab inferioribus discerneret. Quâ de re sic Augustinus l. 2. super Genesin ad lit. c. 10. Nec nomen Firmamenti cogit, ut stare cœlum putemus: Firmamentum enim non propter stationem, sed propter firmitatem, sive intransgressibilem terminum superiorum & inferiorum aquarum, intelligere licet.

Cæterùm quoad materiam, ex quâ Firmamentum hoc est conditum, discrepantes planè sunt sententiæ. Aristoteles, ne planè nihil dicat, contendit, cœlum esse corpus quoddam simplex, primarum qualitatum, quæ in Elementis & aliis rebus corporeis sunt, planè expers. Priscis quibusdam Theologis etiam aqua, quod dicitur hæret: Undè Chrystomus etiam bomil. 4. in Genesin, sitnè cœlum aqua concreta, an aër quidâ cōvolutus, aut alia quædam substantia, à nemine facilè afferi posse, scribit. Cæterùm si partim descriptionem Mosaicam, partim nomina, cœlestibus istis corporibus divinitùs indita, qualia sunt apud Mosen רקיע & שמים Rakia & Schamaim accuratiùs expendamus, Aqueam sanè fuisse materiam haud hæsitanter pronunciabimus. Quod ipsum luculenter testatur etiam Petrus, 2. cap. 3, 5. Illud, inquiens, ipsos latet, quod cœlum & terra jam olim ex aquâ & per aquam DEI verbo extiterunt. Sed quatumvis ex materiâ fluidâ factum est cœlum: ita tamen illud firmavit DEUS, ut quovis ære ac adamante sit solidius: id quod vel indè patet, quòd tot annorum perniciosissimâ rapidissimâque rotatione, nec frangitur, nec atteritur, nec labefactatur. Undè Jobus etiam, cap. 37, 18. Cœlos tanquam ære solidissimo fusos esse, afferit. Quâ de re satis eleganter Beda in suo Hexaemero: In medio, inquiens, aquarum firmamentum esse constat sidereum cœlum, neq; aliquid prohibet, ut de aquis factum esse credatur: Qui enim Chrystallini lapidis quanta firmitas, quæ perspicuitas ac puritas sit, novimus, quem de aquarum concretione certum est procreatum: quid obstat credi, quod idem dispositor naturarum in firmamentum cœli solidarit aquarum substantiam?


### Question X. Are there waters above the Heaven or firmament, and what is their use?

Are there waters above the Heaven or firmament, and what is their use?

Pererius, in book 1 of his Commentaries on Genesis in the explanation of the work of the second day, simply denies that there are, or can be, any true and natural waters above any celestial sphere: It is in no way credible, he says, that there is true and natural water above the heaven:

For since water is a body heavier and coarser, and more ignoble than air, it would certainly be against the natural order of things, and against the good arrangement of the universe, that such a great force of waters, certainly far greater than all terrestrial waters, should be placed not only above the air, but even above the eight celestial spheres. For both reason teaches and experience confirms that the natural place of water is below the air, and immediately above the earth: for we see that water does not rest in the air, and that those things which are generated in the high air from clouds are immediately precipitated downward by their own inclination and weight: wherefore if water were above the heaven, it could not be denied that it is there against its nature and violently: but nothing violent is perpetual. Thus far Pererius; whom the leaders of the Calvinists, having followed, likewise depart into a negative opinion. But the words of Moses are clearer, etc., as Augustine speaks, the authority of Scripture is greater than all the capacity of human genius, book 2 of Genesis literally, ch. 4.

Therefore, having complied with Basil, relegating such arguments of the Jesuits and Calvinists as similar to dreams and old wives' tales: let us understand τὸ ὕδωρ in Moses as true and natural water: led not so much by the propriety of the Greek and Hebrew word, as moved by the agreement of the remaining Scriptures: Moses certainly shapes his style in such a way that no heterogeneity of superior and inferior waters can be admitted at all: for thus he says in ch. 1, 7. And GOD divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament. Therefore, there was one and the same mass and substance of all those waters: which the evidence of the Mosaic text simply denies to have been changed by GOD in that division, in respect to the superior waters.

Furthermore, the same Moses in Gen. 7, 11 and ch. 8, 3, dealing with the flood, expressly writes that then by the command and power of GOD the windows of heaven were opened, which contained those superior waters: a thing which could by no means have happened unless the waters were true and natural above the heaven, as Epiphanius rightly argued against Origen. David supports Moses, who does not hesitate to assert that GOD covered the highest heaven with waters, Ps. 104, 3. Nay, he also calls them into a fellowship of divine praise, together with the other creatures: Praise GOD, he says, ye heavens of heavens: and the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord, Psalm 148, 4. Which same thing the companions of Daniel are also read to have done in their hymn, Daniel 3, 60. Bless the Lord, all ye waters that are above the heavens: Praise and exalt him above all for ever.

Then the argument of Pererius also sins by the omission of the division. For it does not follow that those waters are not above the heaven by physical motion and mode. Therefore it is necessary that they be there anti-physically, that is, against nature and violently: for a third mode is given, which is supernatural, and does not depend on the condition of nature or of created things: but depends solely on the power and will of the Creator: who, as Ambrose piously writes, commands nature, and does not obey its possibility. Of the same futility is the other argument of the Jesuit: which sounds thus: If nature, as Aristotle often uses, does nothing in vain: how much less would GOD, the whole of nature and the wisest craftsman, have placed such a great force of waters above the heaven in vain. For no reason of consequence holds in this argument: It is not certainly established to us what the use of those superior waters is: Therefore, if there are such waters, it is necessary that they were created by GOD in vain. For although we cannot sufficiently explain what the nature and use of those waters is: yet our ignorance can neither prejudice, nor ought it to prejudice, the truth of things in any way. Indeed, some of the ancient philosophers imagined that by the humidity and coldness of those waters, the heat of the celestial stars is mitigated and tempered, lest they be ignited and burn up on account of their most pernicious rotation.

But Aristotle himself also rightly exploded that error, demonstrating that the stars are not hot and fiery, and therefore do not need such refrigeration at all. Furthermore, since the heaven is not subject to elemental qualities: nor can it receive them: it certainly does not contract heat and warmth either from the fire subjected to it, or from the Sun and Stars, so that a conflagration might threaten it. Therefore, let that general knowledge, which Daniel and David expressed, suffice for us, so that we may know that those superior waters serve for the amplification of divine glory: which also sufficiently and more than sufficiently displayed their use in that universal flood.

It is evident, however, from these things which have been said, that Pererius denies not only without any cause and probable reason that true and natural waters are above the firmament: but also that the error of John Calvin is too gross, who in his Commentary on that Mosaic passage, and on Psalm 148, contends that the waters above the heaven should be understood as rains superior to the air. The Hebrew word מִעַל Meal argues the falsity of this assertion, which in Moses and David signifies not below, but above the Firmament.

Furthermore, although the air may elsewhere come under the name of heaven, Matt. 6:26, yet since David, Psalm 148:4, expressly names the heavens of heavens, and asserts that the waters above are these: they certainly cannot be explained or understood as the air. What? Because rains do not stand above the air, but depend from the lowest and turbulent region of the air? Nor is it likely that David, in the passage just cited, would mix rain with the most noble bodies of heaven, when a little later he joins hail and snow to the earth and turbulent elements.

Furthermore, the vanity of the dogma of those who have interpreted these superior waters allegorically as good angelic minds, and the inferior ones as evil angels, is also evident from this. For this is nothing other than to corrupt a true historical narrative, and to involve the clear sense of the Scriptures in obscure enigmas.

Finally, the opinion of those also collapses who maintain that the supercelestial waters constitute a certain peculiar and, in order, a ninth heaven, which some, with respect to matter and external form, have been accustomed to call Crystalline. For the error of this opinion is detected even from this, that thus between this Crystalline heaven and between the Firmament itself no difference would be left: since as well this, as that, was produced from the waters. What? that beyond the firmament no other heaven at all is visible to us: nay, to the knowledge of it by no aid of the senses, by no sagacity of intellect, by the consensus of all Philosophers and Astronomers, has it hitherto been possible to arrive: so that it is more rightly denied than affirmed.

But this dispute provided an opening and occasion for that Question, which was agitated among the Fathers also concerning the Number of the Heavens. There were those who established more heavens: There were others who denied this very thing: of whose number was also Chrysostom, Homily 4 on Genesis, asserting that it is against Scripture if more heavens are posited, for that which Scripture calls the heavens of heavens, he affirms is done only for the sake of dignity. We willingly permit this question to be discussed by Philosophers and Astronomers: meanwhile approving in all things the opinion of the sounder Theologians. For these, from the sense of the Scriptures, posit indeed only one heaven: but one which it is right to distinguish into certain regions: so indeed that we may name one Elementary and Physical: by reason of which Scripture makes mention of the birds of the heaven, of the rains from Heaven, etc. The other, however, ethereal: or also Mathematical, which provides a seat for the stars and constellations: The third, finally, hyperphysical, which is the seat and receptacle of blessed minds: to which St. Paul testifies he was caught up, 2 Cor. 12:7. Concerning which last Heaven they think too carnally, nay childishly, who define it by physical places or other infirmities of this world: as was expressly demonstrated in the preceding article concerning the person of Christ.

Latin:

An sint aqua supra Cœlum sive firmamentum, & quis earum usus?

PErerius lib. 1. Commentariorum in Genesin in explicatione operis secundæ diei, simpliciter negat, supra ullum orbem cœlestem, ullas vel esse, vel esse posse veras ac naturales aquas: Nullo, inquiens, modo est credibile, veram & naturalem aquam esse supra cælum:

Etenim cum aqua sit corpus gravius & crassius, & ignobilius aëre, esset profectò contra naturalem rerum ordinem, & contra bonam universi dispositionem, tantam vim aquarum, certè longè majorem omnibus aquis terrestribus, non modò super aërem, sed etiam super octo caelestes orbes esse locatam. Nam & ratio docet & experientia confirmat, naturalem aquae locum esse infra aërem, & proximè supra terram: Cernimus enim aquam non quiescere in aere, & quae in sublimi aëre generantur è nubibus, statim suopte nutu & pondere deorsum præcipitari: Quare si aqua esset supra cœlum, negari non posset, eam illic esse contra naturam suam ac violentè: atqui nullum violentum est perpetuum. Hactenus Pererius; quem secuti Calvinianorum Antefignani, in negantem itidem abeunt sententiam. Sed apertiora sunt verba Mosis, &c, ut Augustinus loquitur, major est Scripturae autoritas, quàm omnis ingenii humani capacitas, lib. 2. de Genesi ad lit. c. 4.

Basilio ergò obsecuti, tales rationes Jesuvitarum & Calvinianorum, ut somniis similes, & aniles fabulas relegantes: τὸ ὕδωρ apud Mosen, de verâ ac naturali aquâ intelligamus: non tantùm verbi Græci & Hebræi proprietate ducti, quàm reliquarum Scripturarum συμφωνίᾳ moti: Moses certè ita stylum informat, ut nulla prorsus aquarum superiorum & inferiorum ἑτερογένεια admitti possit: Sic enim ille cap. 1, 7. Et divisit DEUS aquas, quae erant sub firmamento, ab aquis quæ sunt supra firmamentum. Una ergò eademque aquarum istarum omnium erat massa atque substantia: quam respectu aquarum superiorum, à DEO, in divisione illâ mutatam fuisse, evidentia textus Mosaici simpliciter negat.

Porrò idem Moses Gen. 7, 11. cap. 8, 3. agens de diluvio disertè scribit, tùm jussu & virtute DEI apertas fuisse cataractas cœli, quæ superiores illas aquas continebant: id quod nullâ ratione fieri potuisset, nisi Aquæ veræ & naturales essent supra cœlum, uti rectè adversus Origenem disputavit Epiphanius. Mosi suffragatur David, qui asserere non dubitat, DEUM supremum cœlum texisse aquis, Ps. 104, 3. quin societatem quoque laudis divinæ, unà cum cæteris creaturis eas vocat: Laudate DEUM, inquiens, cœli cœlorum: & aquæ quæ super cœlos sunt, laudent nomen Domini, Psal. 148, 4. Quod ipsum quoque socii Danielis in hymno suo fecisse leguntur Daniel. 3, 60. Benedicite Domino aquæ omnes, quæ supra cœlos sunt: Laudate & superexaltate eum in secula.

Deindè Ratio Pererii peccat etiam παρὰ τὸ ἐλλιπὲς τῆς διαιρέσεως. Neque enim sequitur, Aquæ illæ non sunt motu & modo physico supra cœlum. Ergò necessum est, ut ibi sint ἀντιφυσικῶς, hoc est, contra Naturam & violentè: datur enim modus tertius, qui est ὑπερφυσικὸς, & non ex conditione naturæ, sive rerum creatarum: sed à virtute & voluntate Creatoris unicè dependet: qui, ut Ambrof. piè scribit, Naturæ imperat, non ejusdem possibilitati obtemperat. Ejusdem futilitatis est & altera Jesuvitæ ratio: quæ sic sonat: Si natura, ut sæpè usurpat Aristoteles, nihil facit frustrà: quantò minus DEUS, omnis natura & sapientissimus opifex, frustrà tantam aquarum vim posuisset super cælum. Neque enim ulla militat ratio consequentiæ in hoc argumento: Non certò nobis constat, quis sit aquarum illarum superiorum usus: Ergò si sunt tales aquæ, frustrà à DEO conditæ sint, necesse est. Quamvis enim, quæ sit aquarum istarum natura & usus, explicare sufficienter non possumus: nostra tamen ignorantia rerum veritati nihil quicquam præjudicare vel potest, vel etiam debet. Finxerunt quidem nonnulli ex veteribus Philosophis, aquarum istarum humiditate & frigiditate, mitigari ac temperari ardorem siderum cœlestium, ne videlicet ob perniciosissimam rotationem accensa conflagrent.

Sed rectè errorem istum explosit ipse quoque Aristoteles, demonstrans, Sidera non esse calida & ignea, ac proindè tali refrigeratione minimè indigere. Deindè cùm cœlum non sit obnoxium qualitatibus Elementaribus: nec eas recipere possit: haud profectò vel ab igne ei subjecto, vel à Sole & Astris æstum & calorem contrahat, ut ei conflagratio immineat. Generalis proindè illa notitia, quam Daniel & David expsesserunt, nobis sufficiat, ut sciamus Aquas illas superiores, amplificationi gloriæ divinæ inservire: quæ illarum etiam usum in universali illo diluvio satis superque exeruit.

Patet verò ex his quæ dicta sunt, non modò præter omnem causam atque rationem probabilem negare Pererium: Aquas veras ac naturales esse supra firmamentum: sed & crassum nimis esse errorem Johannis Calvini, qui in suo ad locum istum Mosaïcum, & ad Psalmum 148. Commentario, contendit, quòd aquæ supra cœlum de pluviis aëre superiorib9 accipi debeant. Falsitatem assertionis hujus arguit vox Hebræa מִעַל Meal, apud Mosen & Davidem, non infra, sed supra Firmamentum significat.

Deindè licèt cœli nomine alibi aër veniat, Matth. 6, 26. cùm tamen David Psalm. 148, 4. disertè nominet cælos cælorum, & his aquas superiores esse asserat: utiq; de aëre exponi aut intelligi illæ nequeunt. Quid? quod pluviæ non supra aërem eminent, sed ex infimâ & turbulentâ aëris regione dependent? Neque verisimile est, Davidem loco jam citato, pluviam nobilissimis cœli corporibus commiscere, cùm paulò pòst grandinem & nivem, terræ ac turbulentis elementis adjungat.

Porrò vanitas etiam illorum dogmatis hinc patescit, qui superiores hasce aquas, allegoricè interpretati sunt de bonis mentibus Angelicis: Inferiores verò de Angelis malis. Hoc enim nihil aliud est, quàm veram narrationem historicam corrumpere, & Scripturarum sensum perspicuum, obscuris ænigmatibus involvere.

Tandem eorum etiam opinio corruit, qui statuunt, aquas supracœlestes constituere peculiare quoddam, & ordine nonum cœlum, quod aliqui respectu materiæ & Formæ externæ Crystallinum appellare consueverunt. Error enimhujus sententiae vel indè deprehenditur, quod fic inter cælum hoc Crystallinum, & inter Firmamentum ipsum nullum relinqueretur diferimen: Siquidem tam hoc, quam illud ex aquis est productum. Quid? quod ultra firmamentum nullum prorsus cælum aliud, nobis est aspectabile: imò ad ejus notitiam nullo sensuum adminiculo, nullâ Ingenii sagacitate, omnium Philosophorum, & Astronomorum consensu, hactenus perveniri potuit: ut rectiùs illud negetur, quam affirmetur.

Præbuit autem hæc disputatio ansam & occasionem Quæstioni illi, quæ de Numero Cælorum inter Patres etiam agitata fuit. Fuerunt qui plures Cælos constituerunt: Fuerunt alii, qui hoc ipsum negarunt: è quorum numero fuit etiam Chrysostomus, Homil. 4. in Genesin asserens, contra Scripturam esse, si plures Cæli statuantur, Nam quod Scriptura Cælos Cælorum nominat, id dignitatis tantùm causâ fieri affirmat. Nos quæstionem istam Philosophis & Astronomis discutiendam libenter permittimus: interim saniorum Theologorum sententiam per omnia approbantes. Hi enim ex sensu Scripturarum, unum quidem duntaxat cælum statuunt: sed quod in certas regiones distingvere fas sit: ita quidem ut Unam nominare queamus Elementarem & Physicam: ratione cujus Scriptura meminit avium cæli, pluviarum de Cælo &c. Alteram verò ætheream: vel etiam Mathematicam, quæ astris & sideribus sedem præbet: Tertiam denique hyperphysicam, quæ sedes est, & receptaculum beatarum mentium: ad quam D. Paulus se raptum fuisse testatur, 2. Cor. 12, 7. De quo postremo Cælo nimis carnaliter, imò pueriliter sapiunt, qui illud locis physicis, aut aliis mundi hujus infirmitatibus definiunt: uti articulo præcedente de personâ Christi ex professo fuit demonstratum.


### Question XI. What are the proper offices of the stars or sidereal bodies?

A threefold use of the stars or constellations is chiefly defined by Moses. The first can be named Phōstikos and consists in this, that the stars shine and illuminate the earth: and that by mutual turns: the Sun indeed by day: but the Moon and the Stars by night, by diffusing their radiance through the sphere. From which office depends also that which is that the Stars heat. Concerning which both offices it is easily agreed among Theologians. For we do not think those Questions pertain to the forum of Theologians: Whether the stars are by nature fiery, and are truly and properly hot: Whether they are hot either formally, or effectively, or virtually: and what other questions of this kind there are, which we willingly leave to be judged by Physicists: Meanwhile, we place it beyond controversy with David and Ecclesiasticus that the stars, and among these the Sun especially, not only shine, but also heat with their light: For so he says in Psalm 19:6 and 7. The sun as a Bridegroom proceeds from his chamber, exulting as a giant to run his course, his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit even to the extremity of the heaven: and there is no one who hides himself from his heat. So indeed that one in chapter 43:3 and 4. The sun in the meridian burns the earth, and in the sight of its heat, who shall be able to sustain it? The sun burning the mountains, breathing out fiery rays, and shining brightly, blinds the eyes with its rays.

The second use can be called diachōrismos, and consists in separating and distinguishing. For the stars were founded, and especially the Sun and Moon, to distinguish day and night: the Sun indeed by its rising beginning the day; by its setting ending the same, for all peoples: but the Moon by illuminating the night. For although before the creation of the Sun and Moon, there was day and evening; yet both were inarticulate, confused, and not at all distinguished by degrees, hours, and parts: that which was finally effected by the arrival of the Sun and Moon. Then, however, the Stars distinguish the times: and that chiefly in a threefold way: First indeed, regarding the stated solemnities, such as were among the Hebrews, the feasts of the Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, Atonement: which the Jews observed from the motion of the Moon, just as today also the Passover is celebrated at the revolution of the Moon: Likewise the Calends, Ides, Nones are constituted. Then, however, regarding the proclaimed and constituted times of things to be done; both Economic and Political. Hence certain times are observed in Leasings and Hirings, in Huntings, fowlings, and other things of that kind. Finally, regarding the four changes and vicissitudes of the year: such as are Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter, which the Sun, running through the Zodiac, effects through the solstices and equinoxes, for the use of those things which arise from the earth. For from these four changes of the year, the beginnings and causes of all things which are produced on land and sea are derived; while the approach and recession of the Sun temper the cold and heat.

The third and last office of the stars can be called sēmantikon: For, as Moses testifies, the stars were also founded for this reason: that they might be FOR SIGNS. But what is denoted by the term sign in this place is variously disputed. For there are those who by Signs understand the images themselves of the stars or constellations: Who hallucinate in this, that they do not notice that Moses in this place is not dealing with the stars considered in themselves and by reason of themselves, but chiefly with their use and effect. There are finally others who think that by the term sign are denoted those supernatural and miraculous signs which have occurred in the Sun and other stars at various times. Whose opinion fails in this, that they think Moses was concerned about those supernatural things, whom nevertheless it is certain did not wish to define in the description of the Stars their hyperphysical, but their natural effect: yet so that he did not entirely exclude a supernatural mode of signifying.

Furthermore, there are those who refer the function of 'signing,' which belongs to the stars, only to those changes and vicissitudes of the seasons, of clear weather, rains, winds, etc. Although their opinion is not to be condemned, it is nevertheless deficient, and does not explain the thing itself sufficiently, as will be clear a little later. Finally, there are those who, by the term 'signing,' have thought that judicial or divinatory astrology is confirmed, from which certain and infallible predictions can be sought concerning the future events of things, concerning the fortunes of men as individuals: concerning longevity, and death, indeed the manner of death, of this or that King, Prince, or any other man in particular: concerning the future fate of this or that region, province, city, town, house, etc., likewise in particular. We maintain that their opinion is not only manifestly repugnant to the words of Moses, but is also diametrically opposed to the Word of GOD, the analogy of Faith, and Experience. But lest we seem to determine something too harshly against the most noble science of Astronomy; and perhaps be forced to hear that common saying from some: 'Art has no enemy except the ignorant': before all else, the State of the Controversy must be rightly informed. For it does not come into controversy: Whether there is some influence of the stars upon these inferior or sublunary things? Whether they are causes, not indeed total, but mediate and particular, of those things which are done and carried out in the elementary region and inferior bodies in the ordinary and ἀπαραβάτῳ (inviolable) manner of nature? Whether, likewise, Eclipses and notable conjunctions of the planets portend something in general? Whether, finally, changes of weather can be predicted from the position of the stars? For these individual and universal things, as we have never denied on our part, nor do we even now deny: so we wish them to be placed outside of controversy. Therefore, only this comes into controversy: Whether those things which are βυλητικὰ καὶ πραιρετικὰ (deliberative and elective), that is, which depend entirely upon the free Will of man and his Election, are so subject to the stars that the actions, counsels, pursuits, morals, life, fortune, and finally the death and manner of death of men can be predicted from the position of the stars or the erection of a horoscope: or also, whether the stars can or ought to be called the causes, whether particular or universal, of all these things? Regarding this state of the controversy, we hold simply to the negative: while those who, whether out of some curiosity or hope of gain, even today attempt to predict from the position of the heavens and the Stars what will happen to each person, and by what fate each was born, fight for the affirmative.

Furthermore, it pleases me to demonstrate this negative of ours with a few reasons.

The FIRST is supplied by the very words of Moses, who, beyond the effects and uses already enumerated above, attributes nothing more to the Stars than that they are for signs, that is, that they ought to perform the function and office of 'signing.' Now, however, signs and causes of things are δὶς διὰ πασῶν (entirely) distant from each other: for the causes of things, by their own power and operation, naturally produce effects: but signs are only indicators of those Effects which are already near at hand, and either have just now been produced, or will be produced shortly. Therefore, Moses established the Stars not as causes, but only as signs of those things which naturally depend upon the Stars: as will be demonstrated more fully below.

II. Reason: GOD himself has so reserved the knowledge of predicting the future, and especially what will happen in particular to any man as an individual, what will happen specifically to this or that region and province, to His own divine Majesty entirely, that He wishes an infallible argument of His Divinity to be taken from it. Hence Isaiah 41:21 and following, about to assert His Divinity against the vanity of idols or the gods of the Gentiles, asks whether any example of foreknowledge belongs to them. And because He alone and uniquely can claim for Himself this power of predicting the future: therefore, insulting them, He says: We will confess that He is the true GOD; from whom such things are done, v. 23. Which argument of GOD Himself would certainly waver, indeed would collapse, if the δύναμις (power) of foreknowing and predicting what will happen after many years to this or that man as an individual: to this or that King or Prince in particular: to this or that Region, city, or house specifically, were to fall to men or to any human art or science.

By the same reasoning, that rather long dissertation of Daniel, Dan. 2, 21. et seqq., in which he demonstrates with many arguments that the future outcomes of events, and especially the changes and periods of kingdoms and empires, are known and understood by no mortal, but by GOD alone, would utterly collapse if astrological divinations and predictions concerning the fortunes of men, and concerning the certain and fixed periods of kingdoms and empires, and indeed of Republics, were either true or could in any way subsist.

III. REASON: GOD himself not only mocks that judicial astrology in particular, but also threatens its practitioners with eternal destruction: by the example of the Chaldeans, who had pronounced his fate to the King of Babylon from the position of the stars: 'You have failed,' he says, 'in the multitude of your counsels: let the augurs of the heavens stand and save you, who contemplated the stars and calculated the months, so that they might announce to you from them the things to come: Behold, they have become as stubble, the fire has burned them, they shall not deliver their soul from the hand of the flame.' Isa. 47, 13. and 14.

IV. REASON: The birth of the two brothers Jacob and Esau, who, as Paul has it in Romans 9, 10, were indeed conceived from one intercourse, but later brought into the light, confuses and tramples upon the vanity of judicial astrology (to speak with Blessed Luther): they differed completely not only in the form and habit of their body, but also in their pursuits and morals. Concerning this matter, St. Augustine discourses excellently in this manner: 'Twins from one intercourse are of different natures. Let the astrologers, therefore, say, why, when there has been one conception, at one point in time, under the same disposition of the heavens and stars, and yet no difference can be noted for each individual: Why, I ask, has there been such great diversity in those twins? Here they find absolutely nothing, and they easily notice, if they wish, that those answers which they sell to the miserable are brought forth not by any exposition of art, but by fortuitous suspicion.

Latin:

TRiplex potissimùm usus astrorum sive siderum à Mose definitur. Primus nominari potest Φωστικός & in eo consistit, ut sidera luceant, & illuminent terram: idque mutuis vicibus: Sol quidem interdiu: Luna verò & Stellæ noctu jubar suum per orbem diffundendo. A quo officio dependet illud etiam, quòd Sidera calefaciunt. De quo utroque officio inter Theologos facilè convenit. Neq; enim ad forum Theologorum arbitramur pertinere Quæstiones illas: An astra sint natura ignea, & sint verè ac propriè calida: An vel formaliter, vel effectivè sive virtualiter sint calida: & quæ sunt hujus generis aliæ, quas Physicis dijudicandas libenter relinquimus: Interim astra, & inter hæc Solem cumprimis non lucere tantùm, sed & luce suâ calefacere, cum Davide & Ecclesiastico extra Controversiam ponimus: Sic enim ille Psal. 19, 6. & 7. Sol tanquam Sponsus procedit de thalamo suo, exultans ut gigas ad currendum viam suam, à summo cælo egressio ejus, & circuitus ejus usq́ue ad extremitatem cæli: nec est, qui se abscondat à calore ejus. Sic verò iste cap. 43, 3, & 4. Sol in meridiano exurit terram, & in conspectu ardoris ejus, quis poterit sustinere? Sol exurens montes, radios igneos exufflans, & refulgens, radiis suis occæcat oculos.

Alter usus dici potest διαχωρισμὸς, & consistit in separando & distingvendo. Condita enim sunt astra, & cumprimis Sol ac Luna, ut diem ac noctem distingvant: Sol quidem ortu suo diem inchoando; occasu suo eandem finiendo, omnibus populis: Luna verò noctem illuminando. Etsi enim ante Solis & Lunæ creationem, dies erat & vespera; tamen utrumque inarticulatum, confusum minimeque gradibus, horis & partibus distinctum erat: id quod Solis & Lunæ accessu demùm est effectum. Deindè verò Astra distingvunt tempora: idque tripliciter potissimùm: Primùm quidem, quoad staias solennitates, quales apud Hebræos fuerunt, Paschatis, Pentecostes, Tabernaculorum, Expiationis feriæ: quas ex motu Lunæ observabant Judæi, quemadmodum hodieque ad Lunæ revolutionem Pascha celebratur: Item Calenda, Idus, Nonæ, constituuntur. Deindè verò, quoad rerum agendarum indicta & constituta tempora; tùm Oeconomica, tùm Politica. Hinc certa tempora observantur in Locationibus & Conductionibus, in Venationibus, aucupiis, & id genus rebus aliis. Tandem quoad quatuor anni mutationes & vicissitudines: quales sunt, Ver, Æstas, Autumnus, Hyems, quas per solstitia & æquinoctia, Sol per Zodiacum currens, efficit, ad usum eorum, quæ è terrâ oriuntur. Nam ex his quatuor anni mutationibus, omnium, quæ terrâ marique gignuntur, initia atque causæ ducuntur; dùm Solis accessus recessusque frigus caloremque temperant.

Tertium & postremum siderum officium dici potest σημαντικὸν: Nam, teste Mose ideò etiam sunt condita astra: ut essent IN SIGNA. Cæterùm quidnam Signi termino notetur hoc loco, variè disceptatur. Sunt enim, qui per Signa intelligant ipsas astrorum sive siderum imagines: Qui in eo hallucinantur, quòd non animadvertunt, Mosen hoc loco non de astris in se & ratione sui consideratis, sed de eorum usu atque effectu potissimùm agere. Sunt denique alii, qui signi termino notari autumnant, Signa ista supernaturalia, & miraculosa, quæ in Sole & reliquis astris, variis temporibus evenerunt. Quorum opinio in eo deficit, quòd Mosen existimant de supernaturalibus illis fuisse sollicitum, quem tamen constat in descriptione Siderum non hyperphysicum, sed naturalem eorum effectum definire voluisse: ita tamen, ut supernaturalem signandi modum non prorsus excluserit.

Porrò sunt, qui signandi munus, quod astris competit, referunt tantùm ad mutationes & vicissitudines illas tẽpostatum, serenitatis, pluviarum, ventorum &c. Quorum sententia licèt non sit improbanda; in defectu tamen peccat, & em ipsam minimè sufficienter explicat, uti paulò pòst patebit. Sunt deniq; qui signandi termino confirmari existimarunt, Astrologiam illam Judiciariam, sive divinatricem, ex quâ certæ & infallibiles peti queant prædictiones, de futuris rerum eventibus, de fortunis hominum in Individuo: de longævitate, & morte, imò mortis genere, hujus vel illius Regis, Principis, aut alius alicujus hominis in specie: de futurâ forte hujus vel illius regionis, provinciæ, civitatis, oppidi, domûs &c. itidem in specie. Quorum sanè sententiam, non modò verbis Mosis manifestè repugnare; sed & Verbo DEI, analogiæ Fidei, & Experientiæ è diametro oppositam esse, statuimus. Cæterùm ne duriùs aliquid in nobilissimam Astronomiæ scientiam statuere videamur; & fortè à nonnullis illud vulgatum audire cogamur: Ars non habet osorem, nisi ignorantem: ante omnia Status Controversiæ ritè informandus fuerit. Non autem in controversiam venit, An Astrorum in hæc inferiora sive sublunaria quædam sit influentia? An sint causæ, non quidem totalis, sed mediatæ & particularis eorum, quæ in Elementari regione & corporibus inferioribus, modo naturæ ordinario atq; ἀπαραβάτῳ fiunt & geruntur? An item Ecclipses, & insignes planetarum conjunctiones in genere aliquid ominētur? An deniq; ex positu siderum mutationes tempestatum prædici queant? Hæc enim singula & universa, uti ex nostrâ parte nunquam negavimus, vel etiamnùm negamus: ita extra controversiam posita esse volumus. Illud proindè tantùm in controversiam venit: An ea, quæ sunt βυλητικὰ καὶ πραιρεtικὰ, hoc est, quæ à Voluntate hominis libera, ejusdemq; Electione in solidum dependent, ita astris sint subjecta, ut hominum actiones, consilia, studia, mores, vita, fortuna, mors deniq; & mortis genus ex astrorumpositu, sive erectione horoscopi prædici queant: vel etiam, An astra istarum rerum omnium causæ sive particularis, sive universalis dici possint aut debeant? Circa statum istum controversiæ Negativam nos simpliciter tenemus: pro affirmativâ interim pugnantibus illis, qui sive ex curiositate quapiam, sive spe lucri alicuj9 hodieque, ex cœli & Stellarum situ prædicere conantur, quid cuique eventurum, & quo quisque fato natus sit.

Cæterùm Negativam hanc nostram paucis quibusdam rationibus demonstrare placet.

PRIMAM suppeditant ipsa verba Mosis, qui præter effectus atque usus, jam suprà enumeratos, Astris plus non tribuit, quàm quod sint in signa, hoc est, signandi munere atque officio fungi debeant. Jam verò signa & causæ rerum δὶς διὰ πασῶν à se mutuò distant: Causæ enim rerum, suâ virtute atque operatione, naturaliter effectus producunt: Signa verò tantùm sunt indices eorum Effectuum, qui jam in propinquo sunt, & vel jam modò sunt producti, vel brevi producentur. Ergò Moses Astra non causas, sed signa tantùm constituit earum rerum; quæ ab Astris naturaliter dependent: uti fusiùs infrà demonstrabitur.

II. Ratio: DEUS ipse scientiam prædicendi futura, & cumprimis, quid in specie cuilibet homini sive individuo, quid Sigillatim huic vel illi regioni atqué provinciæ eventurum sit, ita divinæ suæ Majestati in solidum reservavit, ut indè Divinitatis suæ argumentum infallibile velit desumi. Hinc Jes. 41, 21. & seqq. Divinitatem suam, contra vanitatem idolorum, sive Deorum gentilium asserturus, quærit, An Exemplum aliquod præscientiæ illis competat. Et quia hanc virtutem prædicendi futura, sibi soli & uni vendicare possit: ideò insultans quasi dicit: Fatebimur verum esse DEUM; à quo talia fiant v. 23. Quæ sanè DEI ipsius argumentatio modis omnibus vacillaret, imò corrueret, si in homines, vel in ullam humanam artem sive scientiam caderet δύναμις præsciendi ac prædicendi, quid post annos benè multos huic vel illi homini in Individuo: huic vel illi Regi aut Principi in specie: huic vel illi Regioni, civitati, aut domui sigillatim sit eventurum.

Pari ratione benè longa illa Danielis dissertatio, Dan. 2, 21. & seqq. quâ nemini mortalium, sed soli DEO futuros rerum eventus, & cumprimis regnorum & iniperiorum mutationes atqué periodos cognitas perspectasque esse, multis argumentis demonstrat: penitùs concideret, si divinationes & prædictiones Astrologicæ de fortunis hominum, dequè certis ac fixis regnorum & imperiorum, quin & Rerumpublicarum periodis, vel veræ essent, vel quovis modo subsistere possent.

III. RATIO: DEUS ipse in specie Astrologiam istam judiciariam non modò ridet: sed & ejus cultoribus æternum exitium comminatur: exemplo Chaldæorum, qui Regi Babylonico, suam ex astrorum positu sortem pronunciaverant: Defecisti, inquiens, in multitudine consiliorum tuorum: stent & salvent te augures cœli, qui contemplabantur sidera, & supputabant menses, ut ex eis tibi annuciarent futura: Ecce facti sunt quasi stipula, ignis combussit eos, non liberabunt animam suam de manu flammæ. Jes. 47, 13. & 14.

IV. RATIO: Vanitatem Astrologiæ judiciariæ (ut cum B. Luthero loquar) confundit & conculcat, Nativitas duorum fratrum Jacobi & Esavi, qui uti habet Paulus Romanorum 9, 10. ex uno quidem concubitu erant concepti, sed postmodùm in lucem editi: non modò corporis formâ atque habitu: sed etiam studiis ac moribus planè dissidebant. Quâ de re D. Augustinus hunc in modum præclarè disserit: Gemelli ex uno concubitu diversarum sunt naturarum. Dicant ergòGenethliaci, cur, cùm una fuerit conceptio, sub uno temporis puncto, sub eadem dispositione cœli & siderum, neq; diversa singulis annotari possit: Cùr inquam tanta in illis geminis fuerit diversitas? Hic prorsus non inveniunt, & facilè animadvertunt, si volunt responsa illa, quæ miseris venditant, nullâ artis expositione, sed fortuitâ suspicione proferri.


### Question XI. What are the proper offices of the stars or sidereal bodies? (continued)

But some astrologers today object, claiming that it is not the point of conception in those twins, but the different moments of birth, the different horoscope that must be heeded: for from this, they say, that diversity of the brothers has arisen. But our people have rightly answered thus far with Gregory: Since Jacob, coming out of the womb, was holding the heel of his former brother with his hand, the former could never have perfectly come out unless the subsequent one had begun: and although the mother was pregnant with both at one time and the same moment, there was nevertheless not one equality of life for both. Nor is it for them to object further: that the power of the constellation is in the stroke of the moment. For by this pact they themselves cut their own vines, as the saying goes, and betray the vanity of their art. For if the power of the constellation is in the stroke of the moment: and yet every birth entails some delay and often of many hours: it would certainly follow: either that as many fates of the born infant must be established as the time of birth itself contains points: or that nothing certain can be predicted from the point of birth. I pass over now the fact that, the astrological hypothesis standing, it would be absolutely necessary that the astrologer have the individual degrees of that hour in which someone is born most diligently noted and described. For if you err in the fewest moments or points, the great variation of the heavens and stars certainly takes away all certainty of prediction. What of the fact that ordinary clocks very rarely agree with the motion of the Sun? Therefore, if anything true were to be elicited from the very point of birth, certainly an astrolabe rather than a clock should be inspected and followed.

Finally, even if it must be judged from the point of birth: the astrologers nevertheless cannot demonstrate what the cause is that at one and the same article of time, in one and the same womb, infants of different sexes, male and female, are conceived: and at the same moment both are brought into the light: when yet the diversity of sex far exceeds all other individual and universal qualities of a human? Since they cannot assign the cause of this variety, it is at least most evidently gathered from this that it is not the power and influence of the stars which they themselves attribute to them.

V. REASON: Judges 20, 21. and 25. in two battles forty thousand Israelites are killed by the Benjamites. Therefore, either the horoscope of all these was one, or it was different. But that it was not one, the diversity of age as well as other qualities evidently argues. Therefore it was different: If different, then that which they say, that this kind of death awaited them individually from the condition of the horoscope, collapses. For where there is a diversity of horoscope: there, as of life, so also of death, diversity reigns: as the astrologers themselves teach.

Sixthly and lastly, almost all Antiquity supports our negative: as well as the consensus of Blessed Luther and most Orthodox Theologians. Certainly in the most ancient Councils, such as Aquileia, Toledo, Braga, Art. 9. and 10. and many others, nay even by pious Emperors in Civil Law, most severe mandates and decrees have been published against this Judicial Astrology: so much so that it is reprobated and condemned no differently than the magical art: and both many other most famous men, and in particular that Aquilas of Pontus, otherwise a not ignoble Doctor of the Church, was for this reason alone driven and ejected from the Church, because he was studiously occupied with the observations of nativities and other astrological divinations: as testified by Epiphanius in his book on Weights and Measures.

Moreover, the astrologers seem to have reasons for themselves by which they might, if not confirm their cause entirely, at least palliate it. And at the beginning, indeed, some clamor that they use the stars only as inferior and proximate causes, through which GOD produces various events of things. But I answer that this cavil is too cold and weak. For they have not yet given proof of that which is in controversy, namely that GOD through the stars, as secondary causes, bends and rules the wills and fortunes of men: and that the events of human affairs behave according to the position of the stars. We have already demonstrated the opposite above by the example of the twins Jacob and Esau, where the right of primogeniture, according to the order of nature, belonged indeed to Esau, but afterwards yielded to Jacob, not through the influence of the stars but by the providence of GOD so disposing: who even by this pact testified that our eyes ought to be intent and fixed upon His will alone and not deflected to any other causes. Thus 1 Sam. 10, 6. Samuel says to Saul, king of Israel: The Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you shall be changed into another man: If into another: then the power and influence of the stars, even with respect to secondary causes, expires entirely. But the judgment is the same concerning similar cases: and the promise concerning the increase of the gifts of the Holy Spirit was made not only to Saul, but to all the pious: with this or that constitution of the heavens and stars neither contributing anything, nor even hindering.

Nor is it for Astrologers to object with Ptolemy that the significations of the stars, as well as their predictions, are not the edicts of Praetors, but that both are subject to the command of GOD: or, as others speak quite barbarously, that the stars indeed incline, but do not necessitate. For that too is a vain κρησφύγετον. For all adverse things, which are predicted from the position of the stars, either depend upon their influence, or they do not: If they do not depend: all Astrological prediction is vain with respect to those adversities. If they do depend: Therefore our crimes and our shameful deeds will no longer be the causes of those calamities, but the stars: From whose condition those evils would have come to pass, even if we had been most pious. Here no escape is left for the Genethliacs. than that they heap absurdities upon absurdities, and finally say openly: that the stars are not only the cause of the evils and calamities which press upon us, but also of the sins themselves: A thing which, in the case of the Manichaeans and other heretics, has long since been most rightly condemned as impious and heretical.

Then I invert the argument in this way: If GOD changes, or rather clearly removes, the power of the stars, so that they cannot do what they would otherwise do by their own nature, then surely GOD did not intend those powers of the stars (if indeed there are any regarding the pursuits, wills, and fortunes of men) to be fixed and constant. Once this is posited and granted, it follows that predictions derived from them are not only doubtful, but most uncertain, nay, most false.

But our Chaldeans do not rest even then, but break into the Scriptures, and like the shield of Ajax, they turn against us that saying of the Savior, Luke 21:25, Matthew 25:29: There shall be signs in the sun, moon, and stars. But those disputants would have need of hellebore to purge their heads. For it would be a wonder if they themselves did not acknowledge a gross, and indeed double, ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχου: For first, the Savior is not speaking of ordinary or natural signs, but of those that are entirely miraculous and extraordinary, which, because of their novelty, could easily warn anyone of the wrath of GOD and of some singular change. Now, the consequence from the extraordinary to the ordinary is not valid.

Furthermore, those signs are not established by Christ as prognostications of the overthrow of this or that kingdom, or of the fortune or misfortune of this or that man, but of the consummation of the age; and indeed not for a distinct, but only for a confused knowledge, as far as we are concerned.

Furthermore, they object with that passage in Matthew 2:2, where the Magi from the East were able to know from the appearance of the miraculous star that the Messiah of the world was born. But the same fallacy of ignoring the point (ignoratio elenchi) is committed in this argument as well. For 1. one may not argue from the extraordinary and miraculous to that which is ordinary and behaves naturally. Then, a fallacy of 'not a cause as a cause' is simultaneously involved. For the fact that they understood from the appearance of that miraculous star that the Messiah had now been brought into the light is not to be ascribed to astrological principles, but partly to the peculiar motion of the Holy Spirit, and partly to the sermons of Daniel, from which they had learned the time when the Messiah was to be brought into the light. Daniel 9:24. Thus, therefore, the new and miraculous appearance of that star did not finally instill knowledge about Christ into the Magi, but only warned them that the time prefixed by Daniel, when the Messiah was to be brought into the light, had now been fulfilled in actual fact.

Fourthly, they celebrate a triumph before the victory when they urge those passages in Isaiah 13:10 and Ezekiel 32:7 and 8, where GOD seems to assign the overthrow of the kingdom of the Medes and Egyptians to signs that had appeared in the sun and stars. For 1. they again confuse the extraordinary with the ordinary. 2. They fall into the fallacy of the figure of speech. For those figurative phrases which occur in the Prophets denote nothing other than that there would be extreme misery and unhappiness when those kingdoms were devastated. By the same metaphorical kind of expression, the Holy Spirit denotes the atrocity of evils by an earthquake, Isaiah 24:18 and 19. Just as by the darkening of the sun and moon, and by an earthquake, He expresses the majesty of the mission of the Holy Spirit, when yet none of these things happened, as Luke testifies, Acts 2.

Finally, they take refuge in experience, the mistress of fools, which proves that the event has very often corresponded to those predictions. But this experience is first most rightly refuted by contrary experience, which even the astrologers themselves cannot deny. Then, the argument fails by the fallacy of 'not a cause': For a prediction is not immediately proven by GOD, nor does it rest on certain foundations, just because the subsequent event corresponds to it. That pythoness in 1 Samuel 28:16, or rather the Devil himself appearing in the form of Samuel, predicted true things to Saul: Shall it therefore be lawful to consult magicians and exorcists, or even Satan himself? Shall it therefore be right to affirm that they possess a certain and infallible knowledge of divining and predicting future things? Not so, because with Scripture as our teacher, we rather maintain that GOD, in His just judgment, for the punishment and hardening of the impious, often permits that to happen to them which either Satan or his instruments have predicted, according to that saying of Solomon, Proverbs 10:24. Regarding which matter, GOD Himself prescribed a general, as it were, authentic rule in Deuteronomy 13:1: If any prophet shall arise in your midst, and that finally comes to pass, and he wishes to lead you away from the worship of the true GOD and His commandments, you shall not listen to the words of that prophet: For the LORD your GOD is testing you, to make it plain whether you love Him or not, with all your heart and with all your soul. And in 2 Thessalonians 2:10 and 11: Because they did not receive the love of the truth, GOD sends them a working of error, that they may believe a lie.

These things having been thus explained, it remains finally that we make plain of what things the stars ought to be established as signs.
