In the beginning, however, the Holy Scripture wills the sun and stars to be infallible signs of divine providence and of that covenant which GOD has made with the Church: Jeremiah 31:35 and 36: Thus says the LORD, who gives the sun for light by day, the order of the moon and stars for light by night: If these laws shall fail before me, then the seed of Israel shall also fail, so that it shall not be a nation before me for all days, etc. Furthermore, the stars also perform physical roles of signifying, in announcing storms, rains, and fair weather: in the felling of trees, the sowing of seeds, the gathering of crops, the preparing and applying of medicines, and other things of that kind.

Finally, the stars also obtain a political function of signifying, in the instituting of the actions of this life: for they serve sailors on the sea, and travelers making journeys through the pathless solitudes of Arabia.

To these roles of signifying, if anyone adds a fourth function, and that indeed a preternatural one, of which Christ discourses in Luke 21:25, and of which there are examples in the history of Joshua, Chapter 10:13, and King Hezekiah, Isaiah 38:8.

Latin:

Sed excipiunt hodiè nonnulli Astrologi, dictitantes, nó conceptionis punctum in gemellis istis, sed diversa momenta nativitatis, diversum horoscopum attendendum esse: Hinc enim diversitatem illam fratrum obortam esse. Sed rectè nostri hactenus responderunt cum Gregorio: Cùm Jacob de utero egrediens, prioris fratris plantam teneret manu, prior perfectè nunquam egredi potuit, nisi subsequens inchoasset: & cum uno tempore, eodemque momento utrumque mater fuerit, non tamen una utriusque vitæ æqualitas fuit. Neque est ut porrò excipiant: Virtutem Constellationis in ictupuncti esse. Hoc enim pacto ipsimet propria, quod dicitur, vineta cædunt, & artis suæ vanitatem produnt. Si enim constellationis virtus est in ictu puncti: jam verò omnis nativitas moram aliquam & sæpiùs multarum horarum ferat: utique consequens fuerit: vel tot fata infantis progeniti constituenda esse: quot puncta ipsum Nativitatis tempus in se continet: vel nihil certi ex Nativitatis puncto prædici posse. Mitto jam illud, quòd stante hypothesi Astrologicâ, necessum omninò foret, ut singulos illius horæ gradus, in quâ quis natus est, diligentissimè notatos atque descriptos haberet Genethliacus. Nam si in paucissimis momentis sive punctis aberres, magna certè cœli & Astrorum variatio omnem certitudinem prædictionis tollit. Quid? quod horologia consueta rarissimè cum motu Solis congruunt. Ergò si ex ipso nativitatis puncto veri quid eliciendum esset, certè astrolabium potiùs, quàm horologium inspiciendum & sequendum esset.

Tandem si vel maximè judicandum sit, ex nativitatis puncto: illud tamen demonstrare nequeunt Genethliaci, Quæ causa sit, quòd uno eodemque temporis articulo, in uno eodemque utero concipiuntur diversi sexus infantes, mas & fœmina: eodemque momento uterque in lucem editur: cùm tamen Sexûs diversitas, reliquas qualitates hominis singulas & universas, longissimè superet? Cujus varietatis causam cùm assignare nequeant, utique vel indè evidentissimè colligitur, non eam esse astrorum vim atque influentiam, quam ipsi istis affingunt.

V. RATIO: Judicum 20, 21. & 25. duobus præliis à Benjamitis ceduntur quadraginta millia Israelitarum. Aut ergò omnium istorum unus fuit horoscopus, aut diversus. Atqui unum non fuisse, tùm ætatis, tùm aliarum qualitatum diversitas, evidenter arguit. Ergò fuit diversus: Si diversus, corruit utique, quod illi dicunt, ex horoscopi conditione hoc genus mortis illos singulos mansisse. Nam ubi horoscopi diverfitas: ibi, uti vitæ, ita etiam mortis regnat diversitas: sic ipsis docentibus Gene hliacis.

Sextò & postremò Negativæ nostræ suffragatur universa penè Antiquitas : nec non B. Lutheri & plerorumque Orthodoxorum Theologorum consensus. Certè in antiquissimis Conciliis, ut Aquileiensi, Toletano, Bracarensi. Art. 9. & 10. & multis aliis, quin à piis etiam Imperatoribus in Jure Civili, severissima mandata & decreta, contra Astrologiam hanc Judiciariam sunt publicata : adeò, ut haud secus, quàm ars magica, reprobata & damnata : & tum plures alii Viri Clarissimi, tum in specie Aquilas ille Ponticus, Ecclesiæ alioqui Doctor minimè ignobilis, hanc solam ob causam, ex Ecclesiâ pulsus & ejectus fuerit, quod nativitatum observationibus, cæterisque divinationibus astrologicis studiosè vacaret: teste Epiphanio in libro de Mensuris & ponderibus.

Cæterùm habere sibi videntur Genethliaci rationes, quibus causam suam, si non ex asse confirmare, saltem palliare queant. Ac initiò quidem nonnulli obstrepunt, se uti astris tantùm ut causis inferioribus & proximis, per quas DEUS varios rerum eventus producat. Sed Respondeo, nimis frigidam & elumbem hanc esse cavillationem. Nondum enim probatum dederunt id, quod est in Controversiâ, nempè DEUM per astra, tanquam causas secundas inflectere & regere voluntates, & fortunas hominum: & secundum astrorum positum se habere rerum humanarum eventus. Diversum nos jam suprà demonstravimus Exemplo gemellorum Jacobi & Esavi, ubi jus primogenituræ, secundum naturæ ordinem competebat quidem Esavo, sed postmodum cessit Jacobo, non per astrorum influentiam sed DEI sic ferente providentiâ: qui vel hoc pacto testatus est, nostros oculos in solam ipsius voluntatem intentos infixosque esse debere neque ad ullas causas alias deflectendos. Sic 1. Sam. 10, 6. dicit Samuel ad Saulem regem Iraelis: Spiritus Domini insiliet in te, & mutaberis in virum alium: Si in alium: utique astrorum vis atque influentia, etiam respectum causarum secundarum, penitùs jam expirat. Atqui de similibus idem est Judicium: & non soli Sauli, sed omnibus piis facta est promissio de augmento donorum Spiritus Sancti: nihil vel conferente, vel etiam obstante hâc vel illâ cœli astrorumque constitutione.

Neque est, ut excipiant Astrologi cum Ptolomæo: Astrorum significationes ut & prædictiones non esse Prætorum edicta: sed utrasq; DEI imperio esse subjectas: vel, ut alii satis barbarè loquuntur: Astra inclinare quidem, non autē necessitare. Nam istud quoq; inane est κρησφύγετον. Nam res adversæ omnes, quæ ex astrorum posito prædicuntur, aut ex ipsorum influentiâ dependent, aut non dependent: Si non dependent: Vana est omnis prædictio Astrologica, adversitatum istarum respectu. Si dependent: Ergò non ampliùs scelera, non flagitia nostra erunt illarum calamitatum causæ, sed astra: Ex quorum conditione eventura fuissent mala illa, si vel maximè pii fuissemus. Hic effugium nullum Genethliacis est relictum, quàm ut abfurda abfurdis cumulent, & vel tandem apertè dicant : Astra non tantùm esse causam malorum & calamitatum, quæ nos premunt : sed & ipsorum peccatorum : Id quod in Manichæis & aliis hæreticis, jampridem ut impium est hæreticum, rectissimè est damnatum.

Deindè inverto argumentum in hunc modum : Si DEUS immutat, imò planè tollit Astrorum vim : ut agere non possint, quæ aliàs ex naturâ suâ agerent : utique DEUS noluit vires illas siderum (si modò aliquæ sunt in studia & voluntates ac fortunas hominum) esse fixas ac constantes : Quo posito & concesso, sequitur prædictiones indè petitas, non modò dubias, sed longè incertissimas, imò falsissimas esse.

Sed neque sic quiescunt Chaldæi nostri, quin in Scripturas irrumpunt, & ceu Ajacis clypeum obvertunt illud Servatoris, Luc. 21, 25. Matth. 25, 29. Erunt Signa in Sole, Lunâ & Stellis. Verùm helleboro opus haberent Disputatores isti, quo caput expurgarent. Mirum enim ni ipsimet crassam, & quidem geminam agnoscunt ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε: Nam primò nó de usitatis sive naturalibus signis, sed prorsus miraculosis & extraordinariis agit Servator : quæ propter novitatem suam facilè quemvis de irâ DEI, & singulari quapiam mutatione admonere queant. Jam verò ab extraordinario ad ordinarium non valet consequentia.

Deinde signa illa non constituuntur à Christo prognostica eversionis hujus vel illius regni : hujus vel illius hominis fortunæ, aut infortunii : Sed consummationis seculi: & quidem non quoad discretam : sed tantùm confusam notitiam, ratione nostri.

Porrò objiciunt illud Matth. 2, 2. Ubi Magi ex Oriente, ex apparitione Stellæ miraculosæ in specie scire potuerunt, Messiam mundi esse natum. Verùm idem Sophisma ignorationis Elenchi in hoc etiam argumento committitur. Nam 1. ab extraordinario & miraculoso non licet argumentari, ad Ordinarium, & Naturaliter se habens. Deindè involvitur simul Sophisticatio non causæ ut causæ. Quod enim ex apparitione miraculosæ illius Stellæ, intellexerunt jam Messiam in lucem esse editum : id non adscribendum est principiis Astrologicis : sed partim peculiari motui Spiritus Sancti : partim verò Concionibus Danielis, ex quibus tempus didicerant, quo Messias in lucem erat edendus. Daniel. 9, 24. Sic ergò nova & miraculosa illius Stellæ apparitio non demùm notitiam de Christo instillavit Magis: sed tantùm admonuit eos, jam impletum esse tempus illud à Daniele præfixum, quo Messias in lucem ipso actu jam sit editus.

Quartò triumphum, sed ante victoriam agunt, quando urgent loca illa Jes. 13, 10. & Ezech. 32, 7. & 8. ubi DEUS eversionem regni Medorum & Ægyptiorum, videtur assignare Signis, quæ in Sole & Sideribus apparuerant. Nam 1. rursus extraordinaria cum Ordinariis confundunt. 2. Fallunt Sophismate Figuræ dictionis. Nam Phrases illæ figuratæ, quæ apud Prophetas occurrunt, nihil denotant aliud, quàm summam tùm fore miseriam & infelicitatem, quando regna illa devastabuntur. Quo eodem Metaphorico locutionis genere, per terræmotum, notat Spiritus Sanctus malorum atrocitatem. Jes. 24, 18. & 19. Quemadmodum per obscurationem Solis & Lunæ, & per terræmotum, exprimit majestatem missionis Spiritus Sancti: cum tamen nihil horum evenerit, teste Luca. Act. 2.

Tandem ad experientiam stultorum magistram confugiunt, quæ eventum sæpissimè prædictionibus istis respondisse, comprobat. Verùm Experientia hæc primùm per contrariam Experientiam rectissimè refutatur, quam ne ipsi quidem negare possunt Genethliaci. Deindè fallit argumentum sophismate non causæ : Neque enim ipsa statim prædictio vel DEO probatur, vel certis nititur fundamentis, quando eventus subsequens respondet. Pythonissa illa 1. Sam. 28, 16. Imò ipse potiùs Diabolus sub formâ Samuelis apparens, vera prædixit Sauli: Ergonè licebit ideò Magos & Exorcistas, imò ipsum Satanam consulere? Ergonè fas erit affirmare, certam ac infallibilem divinandi ac prædicendi futura scientiam illos callere: Haud ita, quia Scripturâ magistra sic potiùs statuimus, DEUM multòties justo judicio in pœnam & indurationem impiorum, permittere, ut ipsis eveniat id, quod vel Satanas, vel ipsius Organa prædixerunt: Secundum illud Salomonis Proverb. 10, 24. Cujus rei generalem quasi Authenticam præscripsit DEUS ipse Deut. 13, 1. Si quis Propheta surrexerit in medio tui, idq; tandem evenerit, eog; vos velit à cultu veri DEI, & præceptis ipsius adducere, non audies verba prophetæ illius : Quia tentat vos Dominus DEUS vester, ut palàm fiat, an diligatis eum, an non, in toto corde, & in totâ animâ vestrâ. Et in 2. Thess. 2, 10. & 11. Eò quòd charitatem veritatis non receperunt, mittit illis DEUS efficaciam erroris, ut credant mendacio.

His ita expeditis reliquum tandem est, ut quarum rerum signa constitui debeant astra, planum faciamus. Initiò autem Scriptura Sacra Solem & Astra vult esse infallibilia Signa divinæ providentiæ, & fœderis illius, quod DEUS cum Ecclesiâ pepegit: Jerem. 31, 35. & 36. Hæc dicit DOMINUS, qui dat Solem in lumine diei, ordinem Lunæ & Stellarum in lumine noctis : Si defecerint leges istæ coram me: tunc & semen Israel deficiet, ut non sit gens coram me cunctis diebus, &c. Deindè Physicas etiam signandi partes astra gerunt, in tempestatibus, pluviis & serenitatibus nunciandis : in cædendis lignis: spargendis seminibus, colligendis frugibus, parandis & adhibendis medicamentis, & rebus id genus aliis.

Tandem Politicum etiam signandi munus Astra obtinent, in Instituendis vitæ hujus actionibus : Serviunt enim nautis in mari : viatoribus per invias Arabiæ solitudines itinera facientibus.

His signandi partibus, si quis quartum officium, & id quidem præternaturale, de quo Christus Luc. 21, 25. differit: & cujus exempla in historiâ Josuæ Cap. 10, 13. Regis Ezechiæ Jes. 38, 8.


## 6 On Providence

Likewise of the Israelites Exod. 10, 22; and elsewhere it is permitted to read, if one wishes to add, we certainly do not object. And this is what Moses said: They shall be for Signs: nor can the office of signing be extended more widely or ought to be.

But let someone ask at this point, Do we therefore deny to the Stars any power of acting simply upon these inferior things? To which we respond, that no one, unless extremely stupid, denies that they have some power and efficacy upon these inferior things, and all elemental things, and thus even upon human bodies, insofar as they are subject to the Nature and condition of the Elements. For which reason we affirm without hesitation that Physiological and Astronomical Sciences have great use in common life: provided they contain themselves within just limits and boundaries. But as soon as they go beyond them, as when the condition of human morals and fortune, the outcome of our actions and counsels, is asserted to depend upon the stars: or it is feigned that inclinations to sin flow from a certain position of the stars: or it is said that the changes of kingdoms and empires can be predicted from the stars: then we judge that that μετάβασιν is joined with a foul profanation of the most noble art of Astronomy, indeed with a horrendous impiety: for the causes and reasons already noted above.

THEOLOGICAL TREATMENT of the Article, which is On PROVIDENCE.

Latin:

Item Israelitarum Exod. 10, 22; & alibi legere licet, addere velit, haud sanè repugnamus. Et hoc est, quod Moses dixit: Erunt in Signa: neq; signandi officium latiùs extendi potest aut deber.

Sed quærat hoc loco aliquis, Annè igitur Astris omnem simpliciter vim agendi in hæc inferiora negemus? Ubi respondemus, quin vim & efficaciam aliquam in hæc inferiora, & elementaria omnia habeant, & sic in corpora etiam humana, quatenùs nimirùm Naturæ & conditioni Elementorum subjacent: neminem nisi extremè stupidum negare. Quâ de causâ Scientiæ Physiologicæ & Astronomicæ magnum in vitâ communi usum esse, haud hæsitanter affirmamus: modò intra justas metas atqve crepidines se contineant. Quamprimùm verò eas egrediuntur, ut quando morum & fortunæ humanæ conditionem: actionum & consiliorum nostrorum eventus, ab astris pendere asseritur: vel inclinationes ad peccandum ex certo astrorum positu influere, fingitur: vel regnorum atquè imperiorum mutationes ex astris prædici posse, dicitur: tùm μετάβασιν illam cum fœdâ nobilissimæ artis Astronomicæ prophanatione, imò cum horrendâ impietate conjunctam esse arbitramur: ob causas & rationes jam suprà annotatas.

TRACTATIO THEOLOGICA Articuli, qui est De PROVIDENTIA.


### Plan of the Ensuing Treatment

Both the breadth of this Article and that singular Affinity which it has with many others have caused the rationale and Method of its Treatment to vary greatly among interpreters and Theologian Doctors. For there are not lacking, and indeed among the classical ones not the least, who under the breadth of this Article include also those Topics of the Christian Religion which expressly deal with the cause of sin, with Necessity and Contingency, and finally with Predestination, or the Election of believers to eternal life. Our Author, making a divorce from these, moved by a certain plan of his own, joined this Topic on Providence with the Article of Creation: but that one, which is on the Cause of sin, with the Article on Contingency: and thus joined, he dispatched them with one and the same thread of Treatment. We, departing from both, will follow the footsteps of those Theologians who, prudently avoiding the danger of confusion and obscurity, have been accustomed to assign to each Article a peculiar place and seat in the sanctuary of our Theology: and this the more willingly, the further those Articles are found to differ in the diversity of Questions and Controversies, or what is the same, of objects.

Therefore, about to explain the Article on the Providence of GOD at this time, we will first examine what and what kind of Treatment the Philippean one is. It proceeds indeed from ἀπαί ἄρσιν to ήσιν, that is, from antithesis to purer doctrine and opinion: Yet so that the entire Treatment consists chiefly of three members. For in the beginning the Author shows what precipices of errors, concerning this Article, are to be diligently avoided: namely, of the Stoics, who feigned that GOD is bound to secondary causes, and that nothing can happen otherwise than as secondary causes will carry it: of the Epicureans, likewise, who contended that all things are rolled and confused by chance: And finally also of those who, out of some human infirmity, dream that although GOD once founded the machine of this universe: He nevertheless subsequently departed from this Work of His, so that it might be carried by some guidance or will of its own: No differently than a carpenter, having once built a house or a ship, subsequently leaves it to the care of the inhabitants and sailors. The second member of the Philippean Treatment shows what path, as it were a Royal and military road, is to be held between these extremes and crossroads: And this partly from the Scriptures, partly from reasons and examples. The third and last member depicts in few words the πράξεων or use of this Article: which is most rightly established as threefold. For first, it illustrates the glory of GOD, as one who not only created all things, but even now preserves and governs each one. Then it informs our judgments, so that we may rightly judge and thus pronounce concerning those things which happen and are done, indeed even concerning the very works of GOD, so that the glory of GOD may shine forth and be amplified everywhere. Finally, it sets a limit to the perversity, partly to the stubbornness, of those who attribute such an absolute necessity to human affairs and events from the providence of GOD, that they either completely reject and despise legitimate means: or, like brute beasts, rush rashly into any dangers whatsoever. If anyone wishes to add a Fourth to this threefold use, he will not err in the least: namely, that which is entirely placed in consoling. For unless the mind of men, amidst the furies of the Devil and amidst so many dangers and chances of this world, were to raise and sustain itself by the consideration of divine providence: it certainly could not happen otherwise than that it would be swallowed up by the whirlpool of either despair or security.

And such indeed is the Philippic Treatise: the thread of which we shall be able to follow not inconveniently: but in such a way that we may treat more fully those things which have come into controversy concerning that Article in the years immediately preceding. We shall therefore include its entire diexodos in these four Questions. The first will investigate, Whether there is any providence of GOD concerning things created by Him. The second, however, how far this very Providence of GOD extends itself: The third, How it relates to those things about which it is concerned: or what is the same thing. What is the Form of the Providence of GOD, or what is its mode. The fourth and last: How Prescience, Providence, and Predestination of GOD relate to one another.

Latin:

FEcit Articuli hujus tùm amplitudo, tùm singularis illa, quæ cum multis alijs ipsi intercedit, Affinitas, ut Tractationis ejus ratio atqve Methodus, apud interpretes & Doctores Theologos, quàm plurimùm variet. Haud enim desunt, & quidem inter clasficos minimè postremi, qui sub Articuli hujus latitudine, illos etiam Religionis Christianæ Locos comprehendunt, qui de causâ peccati, de Necessitate & Contingentiâ, de Prædestinatione deniq;, sive Electione credentium ad vitam æternam, ex professo agunt. Autor noster ab his divortium faciens, suo quodam certo consilio motus, Locum istum de Providentiâ cum Creationis Articulo: illum verò, qui est de Causâ peccati, cum Articulo de Contingentiâ conjunxit: & sic conjunctos, uno eodemquè Tractationis filo expedijt. Nos ab utrisquè discedentes, eorum Theologorum sequemur vestigia, qui confusionis & obscuritatis periculum prudenter admodum declinantes, cuilibet Articulo peculiarem locum atquè sedem in Theologiæ nostræ sacrario assignare consveverunt: idq; tantò lubentiùs, quantò longiùs Articuli isti, Quæstionum & Controversiarum, vel quod idem est, objectorum diversitate dissidere deprehenduntur.

Articulum proindè de DEI Providentiâ, hâc vice explicaturi, initiò quæ & qualis Tractatio sit Philippéa, dispiciemus. Procedit verò ex ἀπαί ἄρσιν ad ήσιν, ab antithefi nimirùm, ad puriorem doctrinam atq; sententiam: Ita tamen, ut universa Tractatio tribus potissimùm constet membris. Initiò enim Autor ostendit, quænam errorum præcipitia, circa hunc Articulum, sedulò sint vitanda: Stoicorum nimirùm, qui fingebant, DEUM alligatum esse causis secundis, nec quicquam aliter posse fieri, quam ut causæ secundæ ferent: Epicureorum, item, qui omnia casu volvi & confundi contendebant: Et tandem eorum etiam, qui ex infirmitate quapiam humana somniant, licèt aliquando DEUS condiderit hujus universi machinam: Ipsum tamen ab isto Opificio suo postmodùm discessisse, ut illud suo quopiam ductu sive arbitrio feratur: Haud secùs, atq; faber lignarius, domum aut navim quandam à se semel extructam, postmodùm incolarum & nautarum curæ relinquit. Alterum Tractationis Philippéę membrum monstrat, quænam inter extrema ista & quasi bivia; Regia & militaris via semita sit tenenda: Idq; partim ex Scripturis, partim ex rationibus & exemplis. Tertium & postremum membrum πράξεων sive usum Articuli hujus paucis depingit: qui triplex rectissimè constituitur. Primùm enim illustrat ille DEI gloriam, ut qui non modò omnia creaverit, sed etiamnum singula conservet & gubernet. Deindè informat judicia nostra, ut de his quæ fiunt, & geruntur, imò etiam de ipsis DEI operibus rectè judicare, & sic pronunciare possimus, ut passim elucescat & amplificetur gloria DEI. Tandem eorum partim proterviæ, partim pervicaciæ modum statuit, qui talem ex providentiæ DEI, rebus & eventibus humanis absolutam necessitatem affingunt, ut vel media legitima prorsus rejiciant & aspernentur: vel brutorum instar, in quævis pericula temerè ruant. Triplici isti usui, si quis addere velit Quartum, is minimè erraverit: eum nimirùm, qui in consolando totus est positus. Nisi enim mens hominum inter furores Diaboli, & inter tot pericula & casus hujus mundi, consideratione divinæ providentiæ sese erigeret & sustentaret: fieri certè non aliter posset, quàm ut vel desperationis vel securitatis gurgite abforberetur.

Et talis quidem Philippéa est Tractatio: Cujus filum haud incommodè sequi poterimus: sed ita, ut quæ proximis superioribus annis, de Articulo isto in controversiam venerunt, pleniùs pertractemus. Totam proindè ejus diexodon Quatuor istis Quæstionibus includemus. Prima investigabit, Nùm aliqua DEI sit providentia circa res ab ipso conditas. Altera verò, quousq́; hæc ipsa DEI Providentia se extendat: Tertia, Quomodo ea sese habeat, ad eas res, circa quas versatur: vel quod idem est. Quænam sit Providentiæ DEI Forma, quivè modus. Quarta & postrema: Quomodo ad se mutuò habeant Præscientia, Providentia, & Prædestinatio DEI.


### Question I. Is there a Providence of God?

The word Providence, both among profane and ecclesiastical writers, takes on a certain ambiguity: so that sometimes it sounds the same as πρόγνωσις, prescience: and that less properly, as in Acts 2:31. David foreseeing spoke of the Resurrection of CHRIST. προϊδὼν ἐλάλησε περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Sometimes, however, and indeed according to the propriety of the Latin language, it denotes the faculty of looking out for others regarding those things which are necessary: indeed, even the care and looking-after itself. In which latter signification it is taken in this place. Moreover, we judge such providence, that is, the paternal care of created things, to belong to GOD, to be a principle of the Christian Religion so immovable that whoever dares to deny this, he cannot even believe that there is a GOD: according to that of Psalm 14:1. The fool has said in his heart, there is no GOD. Whose stupendous blindness, as we leave it to be punished by divine vengeance: so we determine that a fuller assertion of this very Question must be given for the sake of the pious. For it happens not rarely that, from the wondrous ordering of divine judgments, or what is the same thing, from that confusion which seems to dominate in human affairs: some cloud of doubt arises even in the minds of the pious, whether indeed GOD has human affairs in His care and heart, and whether all things happen and come to pass with GOD thus governing and disposing? To dispel which we shall have to contend with a twofold weight of arguments, primarily.

THE FIRST is unwritten, drawn from the oracles of the Scriptures, which expressly assign to God the care of human things and actions. Psalm 36:7. You save men and beasts, O LORD. Wisdom 6:8. GOD made the small and the great, and He has equal care for all. Thus chapter 11:13. There is no other GOD but you, who has care for all: and since you are just, you dispose all things justly. And the preceding chapter 11:26. How could anything remain, unless you willed it: or be preserved, unless it had been called by you? And chapter 14:3. Your Providence, O Father, governs all things. A full commentary on which matter one may read through the whole of Psalm 104, and through three entire chapters of Job, namely 38, 39, 40, where from the wondrous preservation of this world, and of all things that are in it, the Providence of GOD is wondrously established. In the New Testament, that sermon of Paul, held in Athens in the middle of the Areopagus, stands out above all regarding this very argument, Acts 17:24. & following, thus differing among other things: GOD who made the world and all things that are in it, since He is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by hands, nor is He worshipped by human hands, needing anything, since He Himself gives to all life, and breath, and all things, and made from one every human race, to inhabit upon the whole face of the earth, defining the appointed times, the boundaries of their habitation, to seek GOD, if perhaps they might find Him, although He is not far from each one of us: For in Him we live, and move, and are, etc. where that which Paul calls the Providence of GOD deserves observation: the dominion of heaven and earth: Likewise vivification, and indeed even determination. For by these words is expressed not some cold or superficial care, but such a care entirely as rules and governs all our acts and the end of our life according to the good pleasure of His will. Which is the reason that Scripture sometimes calls this providence of GOD also an ordering, as Psalm 119:91. By your ordering, O Lord, heaven and earth persevere even to this day. Likewise Government and administration. Wisdom 12:18. With great reverence He governs them. And chapter 14:3. Your providence, O Father, governs all things: Likewise Preservation and Sustenance. Wisdom 11:26. Colossians 1:17. Hebrews 1:3. Indeed even Care: 1 Peter 5:7. Cast all your anxiety upon Him, for He has care for you.

To this former argument succeeds another, drawn from the consideration of worldly things: which, having been treated more fully by our Author, can be dispatched by a kind of Compendium, if all things and everything that are in the world, and that happen and are done, are recalled to nine main heads of things.

The first is the perpetual Order and effect of Nature: such as is observed in the fixed and perennial motion of the celestial orbs: in the fecundity of the earth: in the perpetuity of rivers: in the generation of distinct species and other things of that kind, which show that Nature and its order did not come into existence by chance or fortuitously: but began from and are preserved by a certain divine mind.

II. The condition of the human understanding mind. For a brute thing can never be the cause of an intelligent nature, and of its powers or faculties. But neither do these have their being from themselves. Therefore, that they are from a supreme cause, namely from GOD, and are governed by Him, cannot be doubted.

III. The distinction between honorable and base things: That this should draw its origin either from chance or from some matter is entirely impossible: Therefore it is necessary that it depends upon the will and providence of GOD.

IV. Natural notions, which even after the fall, although a little more obscurely, convince the mind of man that there is some divine Deity, ruling and governing all things.

V. The terrors of conscience in the wicked, which are wont to arise in their minds on account of committed crimes, even if they fear no human judgments at all. Therefore it is necessary that the providence of GOD instills such judgments into the minds of men, which approve things rightly done: and disapprove things done otherwise. VI. The wonderful preservation of political society, and especially of the Church, amidst so many furies of the world and the Devil; which could not be preserved by human laws or forces, unless the care and providence of GOD were added, which so represses the assaults of tyrants and other enemies, that the finger of GOD is recognized even by the enemies themselves. VII. The series of efficient causes, not proceeding to infinity. Therefore, there is given one first cause, from which all the rest depend. Which reasoning physicists also acknowledge: for if there were a progression to infinity, there would be no order of causes, nor would they necessarily cohere: as our Author rightly admonishes. VIII. The most useful ends of all things: which likewise depend not on chance or fortune, nor on the corrupted will of man: but solely on the disposition of GOD. IX. Presages and indications of future events: as also the prophecies of the Prophets, which did not obtain their fulfillment from the demands of nature, or from the counsel and will of men: but only from the will and ordination of GOD. The force of all and each of which reasons is truly such, that they demonstrate not so much that there is a GOD, as that the world was established in the beginning by His Empire, and all its parts are even now administered at every time.

Latin:

PRovidentiæ vox tùm apud Prophanos, tùm Ecclesiasticos Scriptores, æquivocationem aliquam sortitur: ita ut interdùm idem sonet, quod πρόγνωσις præscientia: idq́; minùs propriè ut Act. 2,31. David providens locutus est de Resurrectione CHRISTI. προϊδὼν ἐλάλησε περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Interdum verò, & quidem secundum proprietatem lingvæ latinæ, notet facultatem prospiciendi alijs, de ijs, quæ sunt necessaria: imò ipsam quoq; curam atq; prospectionem. Quâ in postremâ significatione, hoc loco sumitur. Talem autem providentiam, hoc est, curam paternam rerum creatarum DEO competere, usq́; adeò immotum Religionis Christianæ principium esse arbitramur: ut istud negari qui ausit, is ne quidem DEUM esse, credere possit: juxta illud Psalmi 14, 1. Dixit Impius in corde suo, non est DEUS. Quorum stupendam cæcitatem, uti divinæ ultioni vindicandam relinquimus: Sic in gratiam piorum hujus ipsius Quæstionis pleniorem assertionem dandam esse, statuimus. Haud rarò enim fieri solet, ut ex mirâ judiciorum divinorum ordinatione, vel quod idem est, ex confusione illâ, quæ in rebus humanis dominari videtur: dubitationis aliqua nebula oboriatur in piorum etiam animis, An nimirùm DEUS res humanas curæ sibi cordiq́; habeat, & an omnia fiant & eveniant DEO sic gubernante, & disponente? Quam ut dispellere queamus duplici potissimùm argumentorum pondere, militandum fuerit.

PRIMUM est ἄγραφος, ex Scripturarum oraculis petitum, quæ Deo curam rerum & actionum humanarum disertè adsignant. Psal. 36, 7. Homines & jumenta servas DOMINE. Sap. 6, 8. Pusillum & magnum fecit DEUS & æqualiter cura illi est de omnibus. Sic cap. 11, 13. Non est DEUS alius, quàm tu, cui cura est de omnibus: & cùm sis justus, justè omnia disponis. Et præced. cap. 11, 26. Quomodo posset aliquid permanere; nisi tu velles: vel conservari, nisi à te vocatum esset? Et cap. 14, 3. Tua Pater Providentia omnia gubernat. Cujus rei integrum quasi Commentariū legere licet, per totum Psalmum 104. & per tria integra capita Jobi, nempè 38. 39. 40. ubi ex mirandâ conservatione mundi hujus, & rerum, quæ in eo sunt omnium, DEI Providentia mirificè adstruitur. In Novo Testamento, eminet cumprimis concio illa Pauli, Athenis in medio Areopagi, de hoc ipso argumento habita, Act. 17, 24. & seqq. sic inter reliqua differens: DEUS qui fecit mundum & omnia quæ in eo sunt, hic cæli & terræ cùm sit Dominus, non in manufactis templis habitat, nec manib9 humanis colitur, indigens aliquo, cùm ipse det omnibus vitam, & inspirationem & omnia, fecitq́; ex uno omne genus humanum, inhabitare super universam faciem terræ, definiens statuta tempora, terminos habitationis eorum, quærere DEUM, si fortè inveniant eum, quamvis non longè sit ab unoquoq́; nostrûm: In ipso enim vivimus, movemur, & sumus &c. ubi observationem meretur illud, quòd Paulus DEI Providentiam nominat, dominium cæli & terræ: Item vivificationem, quin etiam determinationem. His enim vocabulis non frigida aliqua aut superficiaria, sed talis omninò cura exprimitur, quæ omnes nostros actus, vitæq; nostræ terminum regat & gubernet pro beneplacito voluntatis suæ. Quæ causa est quòd Scriptura providentiam hanc DEI interdum nominat etiam ordinationem, ut Psalm. 119, 91. Ordinatione tuâ Domine cælum & terra perseverant usq́; in hodiernum diem. Item Gubernationem & administrationem. Sap. 12, 18. Cùm magnâ reverentiâ gubernat eos. Et cap. 14, 3. Tua Pater providentia omnia gubernat: Item Conservationem & Sustentationem. Sap 11, 26. Coloß. 1, 17. Hebr. 1, 3. Quin etiam Curam: 1. Pet. 5, 7. Omnem sollicitudinem vestram projicite in eum, quoniam ipsi est cura de vobis.

Priori huic argumento succedit alterum, à consideratione rerum mundanarum petitum: quod ab Autore nostro fusiùs pertractatum, Compendio quasi quodam expediri potest, si ad novem summa rerum capita, revocentur singula & universa, quæ in mundo sunt, fiunt & geruntur.

Primum est, Ordo & effectus Naturæ perpetuus: Qualis conspicitur in fixo & perenni motu orbium Cælestium: in fœcunditate terræ: in perennitate fluminum: In generatione distinctarum specierum & id genus rebus alijs, quæ ostendunt, Naturam ejusq́; ordinem non casu aut fortuitò extitisse: sed à divinâ quadam mente cœpisse & conservari.

II. Mentis humanæ intelligentis conditio. Res enim bruta nunquàm potest esse causa naturæ intelligentis, ejusdemq́; potentiarum sive facultatum. Sed neq́; hæ habent suum esse à sese. Quin E. à supremâ causâ nempè à DEO sint & regantur, dubium esse nequit.

III. Discrimen honestorum & turpium: Quod vel à casu, vel à materiâ quapiam, ortum suum trahat, prorsus impossibile: Ergò à DEI nutu atq́; providentiâ dependeat, necesse est.

IV. Notitiæ naturales, quæ etiam post lapsum, licet paulò obscuriùs animum hominis convincunt, esse Numen aliquod divinum, omnia regens & gubernans.

V. Terrores conscientiæ in sceleratis, qui ob commissa flagitia in eorum animis oboriri solent, si vel maximè nulla humana judicia metuant. Ergò necessum est, DEI providentiam ejusmodi judicia instillare animis hominum, quæ rectè facta probent: & improbent secus facta. VI. Societatis Politicæ & cumprimis Ecclesiæ, inter tot furores mundi ac Diaboli miranda conservatio; quæ non humanis sive legibus, sive viribus conservari posset, nisi DEI accederet cura atœ; providentia, quæ Tyrannorum, aliorumœ; hostium insultus ita reprimit, ut digitus DEI ab ipsis etiam hostibus agnoscatur. VII. Series causarum efficientium, non in Infinitum procedens. Ergò datur una prima causa, à quâ reliquæ omnes dependeant. Quam rationem Physici etiam agnoscunt: Si enim esset progressus in infinitum nullus esset ordo causarũ, neœ, hæ necessario cohærerent: uti rectè Autor noster admonet. VIII. Fines utilissimi rerum omnium: qui itidem non à casu aut fortunâ, neque à corruptâ hominis voluntate: sed à DEI dispositione unicè dependent. IX. Futurorum eventuum præsagia & indicia: ut & Prophetarum Vaticinia, quæ non vel ex naturæ postu, vel ex consilio & voluntate hominum: sed tantùm & DEI arbitrio ex ordinatione, suum complementum sunt sortita. Quarum sanè rationum omnium & singularum ea est vis, ut demonstrent, non tàm illud quòd sit DEUS, quàm quòd ipsius Imperio mundus in principio constitutus sit, & omnes ejus partes ita etiamnum omni tempore administrentur.


### Question I. Is there a Providence of God?: The impiety of the Epicureans

The school of the Epicureans declared war on this former doctrine concerning the providence of GOD, so called from Epicurus the Athenian philosopher, who not only denied the immortality of souls and established the highest good of man in pleasure: but also, denying every care and providence of GOD over human affairs, maintained that all things come to be from a blind confluence of atoms, and thus are merely fortuitous: so that just as atoms fluttering in the sun are whirled about without a certain order: so that one and the same atom, which now held the highest place, is soon carried down to the middle: from this to the lowest: and from this again to the highest, if chance has so brought it about: So created things, individual and universal, wander without a certain order: and produce their effects, not as GOD wills and governs, or as efficient causes move: but only as Chance and Fortune have brought it about. Those who, although they are Christians by profession, nevertheless openly testify by the external corruption of their life and morals that they clearly feel in their heart that which David in Psalm 94:7 revealed from the opinion of the impious: The Lord does not see, nor does the GOD of Jacob understand: Come, let us speak iniquity, and work injustice, who is there who sees? But David himself most rightly refutes the impiety and madness of these people in this manner, in the very next verse following: Understand, you senseless ones among the people, and you fools, be wise at last: He who plants the ear, shall He not hear? He who forms the eye, shall He not see? He who corrects the nations, shall He not rebuke? But GOD will render to them their iniquity: and in their malice our Lord GOD will destroy them, He will destroy them. v. 23. Isaiah supports David, who lashes out at this kind of senseless person and Epicurean in this manner, chapter 29, 15 and 16. Woe to you who are deep in heart, to hide counsel from the Lord, whose works are in darkness, and they say, Who sees us? and who knows us? This thought of yours is perverse, just as if clay should think against the potter, and the work should say to its maker, You did not make me: and the thing formed should say to its former: You do not understand.

But to return to the school of the Epicureans, they have tried to cloak their thesis, however impious it may be, by bringing forward those arguments with which even today some idle men do not fear to wage war against the providence of GOD.

Lactantius recites the first and chief argument of Epicurus in his book on the anger of GOD, chapter 13. If there is a providence of GOD, it will be concerned equally with evils as with goods. Now if it is concerned with evils, surely GOD either wishes to remove those evils and cannot: or He can and does not wish to: or He neither can nor wishes to: or He both wishes and can. But if He wishes and cannot, He will be powerless, which does not befall GOD: If He can and does not wish to, He seems to be envious: which is equally alien to GOD: If He neither wishes nor can: He will be both envious and powerless: and therefore not GOD, which is impious: If finally He wishes and can: Why then does He not remove them? And because He does not remove them: Why is providence attributed to Him?

But I answer that this whole system of impiety suffers from the fallacy of a faulty consequence. For as regards the first member of the dilemma, although we willingly concede that the providence of GOD is concerned as much with evils as with goods: it does not immediately follow: Therefore, it will be concerned with both in one and the same way: so that just as GOD not only wills but also works good in us: so He must not only not will evils, but also remove them entirely from the midst. For there are different modes and degrees, in respect of which the providence of GOD is said to be concerned with the objects of things: as will be shown expressly in Question 3. Now therefore as regards the second member of the dilemma, namely the division itself: an insufficient enumeration of the modes immediately occurs in it, in respect of which the providence of GOD is most truly concerned with evils and sins. For neither does that mode, which Epicurus defines, and which consists in removing evils, befit divine providence. For if God were to drag man away from sinning as if by the neck, and were to beat back and overthrow the depraved desires of him even against his will and resisting: certainly this would be nothing else than to destroy man entirely, and to take away from him every faculty of acting. Because since GOD created man free in the beginning, and implanted in him the will and faculty for both good and evil: Ecclesiasticus 15:14, and indeed through the sin of Origin, the will for good perished entirely, but the will for evil remained surviving: certainly if GOD were now to take this will away from man, He would be compelled to take away from him Reason itself. For as Damascenus rightly infers in book 3, chapter 27: Reason is not without will: nor is will without Reason: But will is introduced together with reason. But if Epicurus should object, that it nevertheless pertains to divine providence to call back the depraved will of man from sins: We answer that the providence of GOD does this most of all, and that in various ways: 1. by prohibiting. 2. by detesting. 3. by threatening. 4. by determining their sins to a good end. 5. by punishing. Since the providence of GOD is concerned with sins in all these ways: It is certainly evident even from this that GOD both does not will sins, and removes them, in this life indeed in the ways which have now been shown: but in the other life by casting them into the unquenchable fire of hell.

THE SECOND argument of the Epicureans sounds thus: Whatever is repugnant to GOD, that is not governed by GOD. Sins, likewise Devils, and impious men are repugnant to GOD. Therefore they are not governed by GOD.

I answer that the major premise suffers from the fallacy παρὰ τὸ πὴ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For whatever is repugnant to GOD, that is not governed by GOD, namely κατὰ τι, or in a certain respect, insofar as it is repugnant to GOD and has the nature of sin: namely by the providence of GOD effecting, or willing, or assisting, or ordering that repugnance. Furthermore, if the major premise is taken concerning government or determination to a good end, then it is simply false. For however much sin may be repugnant to GOD, yet it is governed by GOD, insofar as it is directed and ordered to a good end: as will be shown more fully and clearly in the next article.

THE THIRD is as follows: Providence excludes Chance and Fortune. But these cannot be denied: not only by Philosophers: But even by the authority of the Holy Spirit himself testifying thus, Ecclesiastes 9:11 Time and Chance happen to all, Therefore the providence of GOD itself falls.

I answer: It commits the same fallacy that was noted in the preceding argument. For the major proposition is true in a certain respect. For the providence of GOD excludes Chance and Fortune, κατὰ τι, if indeed you look at the same order of causes, namely the universal one: for just as nothing can be withdrawn from the ordination of this universal cause: so all particular causes are so concluded under its ordination, that it is impossible for any effect of causes to escape its ordination. But the major proposition is false if it is taken to another order of cause. For the providence of GOD does not exclude Chance and Fortune, or the Fortuitous: if you consider the particular order of cause. For something can deflect the order of a particular cause, through the concurrence and ἐμπόδισμα or obstacle of some other particular cause. For example: The power of fire is hindered in wood covered with ice: which is most rightly said to be casual and Fortuitous, but only with respect to this particular cause: not likewise with respect to the universal cause: for the order of which nothing at all of all things can escape, so that not even a hair falls from our head without the will of the heavenly Father. For the sake of greater clarity, it is pleasing to illustrate the matter with an example, and indeed one taken from chapter 19, 4. and following of Deuteronomy: Two men fall to felling trees: But the iron of the axe slips from the handle, and striking the head of the other, kills him. This slaughter is pronounced to be fortuitous by God himself, Num. 35:33, if indeed you look at this particular cause, because it is evident that no hatred, enmity, or ill-will had passed between those two. For which reason the Law concerning Cities of Refuge was also promulgated by God: Deut. 19:2 and following. Meanwhile, however, by reason of divine providence, as the universal cause, it is so far from being able to be said that this deed is fortuitous, that the Holy Spirit rather expressly testifies that this slain man was delivered by God himself into the hands of the slayer: Exod. 21:13.

In the allegation of the saying of Ecclesiastes, a Sophistry of Figure of Diction is committed, or rather of vicious interpretation. For in the Hebrew it is not read, Chance and Fortune: but occasion and success: By which words Solomon wished to intimate that the events and successes of all things are not placed in the power of men: but that occasion and success prevail in all things, that is, an event divinely ordered and defined.

The fourth argument is such: The confusion of all things and extreme ἀταξία exclude the providence of God: for they cannot stand together, unless we wish to establish God as the Author of confusion, which is impious to think.

Now indeed in created and worldly things, not so much those which depend on the will and choice of men, as those which depend on natural causes, extreme confusion and ἀταξία dominate: which can be confirmed by examples of Tempests, winds, likewise homicides, fires, and the tumultuous movement of most things, Therefore the providence of God cannot stand.

I answer, From that common axiom of the Logicians: Subordinated things do not fight, nor do they mutually exclude each other. When therefore Epicurean Philosophers, on account of the confusion and ἀταξία of worldly things, deny the Providence of God: they certainly most ignorantly make Contradictories out of subordinated things, and thus commit a shameful Sophistry of not the cause as the cause. For the Providence of God can neither be excluded nor ought it to be from those things which are seen to be done and happen confusedly in this world through a certain ἀταξία: Since in the governing, directing, and determining to certain ends of those very confused and inordinate things, the providence of God is most effective. There is added another Sophistry of Begging the question. For it has not been proven that those things which seem so to us are in reality inordinate and confused. For the event always demonstrates that all those things were most ordered, since they were governed by the most wise counsel of God in such a way that from them, the order of divine justice, wisdom, goodness, and power shines forth most clearly. For the reason of divine Order and Providence behaves in entirely different ways: so that it orders some things in justice: others in mercy, some in wisdom. If any ἀνομαλία seems to us to be in these, it is certainly better to put a finger to the mouth: and with the Apostle to exclaim: O the depth of the Knowledge and Wisdom, how incomprehensible are his judgments? Rom. 11:33, than to subject them to the scrutiny of our reason. Furthermore, if anything happens which seems to fight with the goodness of God, remember that it can correspond to the justice and wisdom of God: and vice versa.

Furthermore, God very often executes His providence in this world in such a way that the causes of those things which happen are simply hidden from us. If, therefore, in the acts of divine providence, the affection of mercy or the severity of justice does not always shine forth, nevertheless, God's providence itself should not for that reason be attacked with impious barking; but with minds composed to patience and piety, the outcome should be commended to God: for He at length most often demonstrates clearly that God had established most just causes even for those actions which seemed to us to be joined with some enormous disorder or lawlessness. Scripture shows sufficiently illustrious examples of this matter in the selling of Joseph, in the affliction of Job, in the betrayal and crucifixion of Christ the Savior: where, although extreme disorder and confusion seemed to rule, Scripture itself is nevertheless a witness that what was done then was what the hand and counsel of God decreed, Acts 2:23, ch. 24:28. The judgments of our blind reason can neither prejudice nor ought to prejudice divine providence.

They formulate the FIFTH [argument] thus: Whatever is in God, that is eternal: But indeed Providence is not something eternal in God: Since Providence is said to be of created things, which are certainly not eternal, therefore there is no Providence in God.

I answer that in this argument the first act is most shamefully confused with the second act: or, which is the same thing, the very principle of Order with its execution. Therefore, in God, Providence is something eternal: since this Providence is nothing other than, partly, that essential love, care, and favor by which He determined to preserve His creatures and pursue the good; and partly, that essential Justice by which He decreed from eternity to punish devils, sin, and the impious. Now, however, the second act, or the very execution of this divine goodness and justice, which happens in time, does not remove God Himself and His providence from this eternity: but considers Him remaining in eternity, insofar as He exerts His providence in time, now in this work, now in that: otherwise, God could not even be called omnipotent: since the creation of this universe was not accomplished from eternity, but finally in time. Most correctly, therefore, a distinction is made between the attributes of God insofar as they are essential and eternal, and insofar as they exert themselves in time.

The SIXTH and final argument is not so much of the Epicureans as of certain sounder philosophers, who, as Plutarch testifies, argued thus: If human affairs are dispensed by God's solicitude, why do the wicked enjoy the indulgence of Fortune? Conversely, why do the upright experience her as a stepmother? What is more, since Scripture testifies that this disparity of lot and fortune between the pious and the impious has variously exercised even the pious and faithful, so that they have often erupted into the saddest groans and complaints: as is evident from the example of Job, ch. 21:7 and following; of David, Ps. 37:1 and following; of Asaph, Ps. 73:1 and following; of Jeremiah, who expostulates with God over this matter, saying: You are indeed just, O LORD, but I will speak just things to you: Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Is it well with all who deal treacherously and act wickedly? etc., Jer. 12 and following. But all these collections suffer from the fallacy of the non-cause and an insufficient enumeration of the causes for which God in this life affects the impious with goods, but assiduously exercises the pious with hardships and calamities. The consideration of which causes demonstrates most evidently that it is so far from the case that God's providence should be denied because of that diversity of lot between the pious and the impious, that from that very diversity it can be most clearly established and confirmed.

For first, GOD by this arrangement most evidently demonstrates the certainty of the coming judgment: which St. Paul hints at in 2 Thess. 1:6 and 7: It is just, he says, before GOD to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled, rest with us, in the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven.

Then, God affects the unworthy with His benefits, so that He may declare His kindness toward them also, according to that saying of the Savior in Matt. 5:44 and 45: Love your enemies, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes His sun to rise on the good and the evil, and rains on the just and the unjust.

Thirdly, GOD by this arrangement strives to entice the impious to repentance: according to that saying of the Apostle in Rom. 2:4: Or do you despise the riches of His goodness, and patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that the kindness of GOD calls you to repentance?

Finally, the impious, while they wickedly abuse the goodness of GOD, heap up for themselves the just wrath and vengeance of GOD: as the Apostle teaches again in Rom. 2:5: because of your hardness and impenitent heart you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of GOD. Therefore, even if it should happen that in this world it is not always well with the pious and ill with the evil, there will nevertheless be a time at last when the pious will exclaim from Psalm 58:12: Now surely there is a fruit for the just: now surely GOD is judging in the earth.

But enough and more than enough about the impiety of the Epicureans, from which those seem not to differ much who say that God indeed created this world, but on the seventh day rested from His works in such a way that He keeps a perpetual Sabbath, so that He leaves this world to its own motion, namely, that motion which GOD Himself implanted in it at the first creation. The vanity of whom, being unworthy of a more prolix refutation, we judge should be beaten back with the words of Augustine, who in book 4 of De Genesi ad litteram, ch. 12, discourses thus: GOD rested on the seventh day from creating new works or kinds of creatures: not so that on that seventh day His power ceased from the governance of created things: otherwise they would immediately fall away. For the power of the Creator, and the virtue of the omnipotent and all-sustaining [One], is the cause of subsistence for every creature; which virtue, if it were ever to cease from governing those things which have been created, their form would cease at the same time, and every nature would collapse. For it is not as the structure of buildings, which, when someone has built them and departs, subsist even while he ceases and is absent: so the world could stand for the blink of an eye if GOD were to withdraw from it the governance of Himself. Hence also what the Lord says: My Father even until now he works, he shows a certain continuation of his work, by which he contains and administers the whole creation. For it is one thing (NOW) and another (UNTIL NOW) from that, namely, from which he might create all things, he has worked continuously without cessation and intermission, as it is written Wis. 8:1. It reaches from end to end mightily, and disposes all things sweetly.

Latin:

PUriori huic de DEI Providentiâ Doctrinæ bellum indixit Epicuræorum Schola, sic dicta ab Epicuro Atheniensi Philosopho, qui non modò animarum immortalitate negata, summum hominis bonum in voluptate constituit: sed & omnem DEI de rebus humanis curam & providentiam negans, statuit, ex cæco atomorum confluxu fieri omnia, & sic merè fortuita esse: ita ut quemadmodum atomi in Sole volitantes, sine ordine certo volvuntur: ut unus idemœ; atom9, qui nunc supremum obtinebat locum, mox deferatur ad medium: ex hoc ad infimum: & ex hoc rursus ad supremum, siquidem casus ita tulerit: Ita res quoœ; creatæ, singulæ & universæ, sine certo ordine vagentur: & effectus suos producant, non prout DEUS velit & gubernet, vel prout causæ efficientes movent:sed tantùm prout Casus & Fortuna tulerit. Impietatem hanc & verbis & factis haud obscurè stabilire etiam conantur illi, qui licet professione sint Christiani, externa tamen vitæ morumœ; consceleratione apertè testantur, se illud planè in corde suo sentire, quod David Psalm. 94, 7. Ex sententiâ impiorum prodidit: Non videt Dominus, nequè intelligit DEUS Jacob: Agite loquamur Iniquitatem, & operemur Injustitiam, Quis est, qui videat? Rectissimè autem ipse David stupendam istorum & impietatem & dementiam in hunc modum refutat, versu statim subsequente proximo: Intelligite insipientes in populo, & stulti aliquando sapite: Qui plantat aurē an non audiet? Qui fingit oculū, an non videbit? Qui corripit gentes, an non arguet? Sed reddet illis DEUS iniquitatē ipsorum: & in malitiâ eorū disperdet eos, disperdet illos Domin9 DEUS noster. v. 23. Davidi suffragatur Jesaias, qui hoc genus insipientium & Epicuræorum hunc in modum perstringit, cap. 29, 15. & 16. Væ, qui profundi estis corde, ut à Domino abscondatis consilium, quorum sunt in tenebris opera, & dicunt Quis videt nos? & quis novit nos? Perversa est hæc vestra cogitatio, perindè ac si lutum contra figulum cogitet, & dicat opus factori suo, Non fecisti me: & figmentum dicat fictori suo: Non intelligis.

Sed ut ad Epicuræorum Scholam redeamus, thesin illi suam quantumvis impiam, palliare conati sunt, illis in medium allatis rationibus, quibus hodieque nonnulli malè feriati homines, adversus DEI providentiam militare non verentur.

Primam & præcipuam Epicuri rationem recitat Lactantius lib. de irâ DEI cap. 13. Si est Providentia DEI, æquè versabitur illa circa mala, ac circa bona. Jam si circa mala versatur, utiq; DEUS aut vult mala illa tollere, & non potest: aut potest, & non vult: aut neq; potest, neq; vult: aut & vult & potest. Quod si vult, & non potest, impotens erit, id quod in DEUM non cadit: Si potest & non vult, invidus esse videtur: quod æq; à DEO est alienum: Si neq; vult, neq; potest: & invidus & in potens erit: ideoq; ne DEUS, id quod impium: Si deniq; vult & potest: Cur igitur non tollit? & quia non tollit: Cur ei providentia tribuitur?

Sed respondeo totum istud impietatis systema, laborare Sophismate vitiosi consequentis. Nam quoad primum Dilemmatis membrum, etsi libenter concedimus, Providentiam DEI versari tàm circa mala, quàm circa bona: non tamen statim est consequens: Ergò, uno eodemq; modo circa utraq; versabitur: ita ut quemadmodum DEUS bona non modò vult, sed & operatur in nobis: sic mala non modò non velle, sed & prorsus ea è medio tollere debeat. Diversi enim sunt modi & gradus, quorum respectu Providentia DEI circa res objectas versari dicitur: uti Quæstione 3. ex professo ostendetur. Jam ergò quoad secundum Dilemmatis membrum, ipsam nimirùm διαίρεσιν, divisionem: statim in eâ occurrit insufficiens enumeratio modorum, respectu quorum DEI providentia circa mala & peccata verissimè versatur. Neque enim modus ille, quem Epicurus definit, quíque in tollendis malis consistit, divinæ providentiæ competit. Si enim Deus obtorto quasi collo, hominem à peccando abstraheret, & ipsius etiam inviti & reluctantis pravas cupiditates retundere & profligare deberet: certè nihil hoc foret aliud, quàm hominem prorsus destruere, & omnem facultatem agendi ipsi adimere. Quia enim DEUS hominem initiò condidit liberum, eiq; voluntatem atq; facultatem tàm ad bonum, quàm ad malum indidit: Ecclesiastici 15. 14. & verò per peccatum Originis, voluntas ad bonum penitùs interijt, voluntas verò ad malum mansit superstes: certè si hanc jam voluntatem DEUS homini adimeret, ipsam etiam Rationem ipsi adimeret cogeretur. Nam uti rectè Damascenus infere l. 3. c. 27. Ratio non est absq; voluntate: neq; voluntas absq; Ratione: Sed unà cum ratione inducitur voluntas. Sin objiciat Epicurus, illud tamen competere divinæ providentiæ, ut pravam hominis voluntatem à peccatis avocet: Respondemus, id vel maximè agere DEI providentiam, idq; varijs modis: 1. prohibendo. 2. detestando 3. comminando. 4. determinando ipsorum peccata ad bonum finem. 5. puniendo. Quibus modis omnibus cùm circa peccata DEI providentia versetur_: Constat utiq; vel indè DEUM, & nolle peccata, & tollere ea, hâc quidem in vitâ ijs modis, quibus jam ostensum: in alterâ verò projiciendo ea in ignem inferni inextingvibilem.

ALTERUM Epicuræorum argumentum sic sonat: Quicquid repugnat DEO, id non gubernatur à DEO. Peccata, item Diaboli, & homines impij repugnant DEO. Ergò non gubernantur à DEO.

Respondeo, Majorem laborare Sophismate παρὰ τὸ πὴ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Quicquid enim repugnat DEO, id non gubernatur à DEO, κατὰ τι nimirùm, sive secundum quid, quatenùs repugnat DEO, & peccati rationem habet: videlicet providentiâ DEI efficiente, vel volente, vel adjuvante, vel ordinante illam repugnantiam. Deindè si de gubernatione sive determinatione ad bonum finem accipiatur Major, tùm simpliciter falsa est. Peccatum enim quantumvis repugnet DEO, tamen illud gubernatur à DEO, quatenus ad bonum finem dirigitur & ordinatur: uti Articulo sequente proximo ostendetur fusiùs & luculentiùs.

TERTIUM sic habet: Providentia excludit Casum & Fortunam. Atqui hæc negari non possunt: non Philosophorum tantùm: Sed ipsius etiam Spiritus Sancti sic attestante autoritate, Ecclesiastæ 9, 11 Tempus & Casus vaient in omnibus, Ergò cadit ipsa DEI providentia.

Respondeo: Idem committit Sophisma_, quod in præcedente argumento notatum est. Secundum quid enim vera est Major Propositio. Providentia enim DEI excludit Casum & Fortunam, κατὰ τι, si nimirùm eundem causæ ordinem, universalem videlicet, respicias: quemadmodum enim à causæ hujus universalis ordinatione subtrahi nihil potest: ita sub ejus etiam ordinatione causæ particulares omnes ita concluduntur, ut impossibile sit, ullum Effectum causarum, illius ordinationem effugere_. Falsa verò est major propositio, si ad alium causæ ordinem ea rapiatur_. Neq; enim providentia DEI excludit Casum & Fortunam, sive Fortuitum: si particularem causæ ordinem consideres. Nam ordinem causæ particularis inflectere aliquid potest, per concurrentiam & ἐμπόδισμα sive obstaculum alterius cujusdam causæ particularis. Exempli gratia: Vis ignis impeditur in ligno, glacie obducto: id quod casuale & Fortuitum esse rectissimè dicitur, sed tantùm respectu causæ hujus particularis: non item respectu causæ universalis: quippè cujus ordinem nihil quicquam rerum omnium effugere potest, adeò ut nè capillus quidem de capite nostro decidat, sine voluntate Patris cœlestis. Majoris perspicuitatis gratiâ placet rem exemplo illustrari, & quidem petito ex cap. 19, 4. & seqq. Deuteronomij: Duo quidam cadunt ligna: Sed alteriq ferrū securis manubrio elapsū, capitiq alterius inflictũ, occidit illũ. Cædes hæc fortuita esse, ab ipso Deo pronunciatur, Num. 35, 33. si nimirùm causam hanc particularem spectes, quòd nihil odij, inimicitiæ aut simultatis duobus istis intercessisse constat. Quò nomine etiam Lex de Asylis à Deo est promulgata: Deut. 19, 2. & seq. Interim tamen ratione providentiæ divinæ, tanquam causæ universalis tantum abest, ut fortuitum esse factũ istud dici queat, ut Spiritus Sanctus potiùs disertè attestetur, Occisum istum ab ipso Deo traditum esse in manus occisoris: Exod. 21, 13.

In allegatione dicti Ecclesiastæ committitur Sophisticatio Figuræ Dictionis, vel potiùs vitiosæ interpretationis. In Hebræo enim non legitur, Casus & Fortuna: sed occasio & successus: Quibus vocabulis Salomon innuere voluit, rerum omnium eventus & successus, non in potestate hominum esse positos: sed in omnibus valere occasionem & successum, hoc est, eventum divinitùs ordinatum & definitum.

Quartum argumentum tale est: Confusio rerum omnium & extrema ἀταξία excludunt Dei providentiam: quippè quæ simul stare non possunt, nisi Deum confusionis Autorem statuere velimus, id quod cogitatu impium.

Jam verò in rebus creatis & mundanis, non tàm ijs, quæ à voluntate & electione hominũ, quàm quæ à causis naturalibus dependent, extrema dominatur confusio & ἀταξία: id quod exemplis Tempestatum, ventorum, item homicidiorum, incendiorum, & tumultuario plerarũq́; rerum motu, confirmari potest, Non igitur stare potest Dei providentia.

Respondeo, Ex vulgato illo Logicorum axiomate: Subordinata non pugnant, nequè se mutuò excludunt. Quando ergò Epicurei Philosophi propter confusionem & ἀταξίαν rerum mundanarum, inficiantur Dei Providentiam: certè nimis inscitè ex subordinatis faciunt Contradictoria, & sic committunt turpem Sophisticationem non causæ ut causæ. Neqú; enim Providentia Dei excludi vel potest vel debet ab ijs, quæ per ἀταξίαν quandam hoc in mundo confusè geri fieriq́; videntur: Siquidem in illis ipsis confusis atq́; inordinatis gubernandis, dirigendis, & ad certos fines determinandis, vel maximè est efficax Dei providentia. Accedit altera Sophisticatio Petitionis principij. Neqú; enim probatum est, Ea quæ nobis sic videntur, reverà esse inordinata & confusa. Nam eventus semper demonstrat illa omnia vel maximè fuisse ordinata, quippè quæ sapientissimo Dei consilio ita fuerunt gubernata, ut ex eis, ordo justitiæ, sapientiæ, bonitatis & potentiæ divinæ clarissimè eluceat. Habet enim se Ordinis & Providentiæ divinæ ratio, diversimodè prorsus: ita ut quædam ordinet in justitiâ: alia in misericordiâ, nonnulla in sapientiâ. His si ἀνομαλία aliqua nobis videatur inesse, certè præstat digitum ori admovere: & cum Apostolo exclamare: O profunditatem Scientiæ & Sapientiæ, quàm incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus? Rom. 11, 33. quàm ad rationis nostræ scrutinium ea exigere. Deindè si quid eveniat, quod cum bonitate Dei pugnare videatur, memineris illud congruere posse ad justitiam & sapientiam Dei: ac vice versâ.

Porrò Deus providentiam suam hoc in mundo sic exequitur sæpissimè, ut eorum, quæ accidunt causæ, nos simpliciter lateant. Quòd si ergò in divinæ providentiæ actibus non semper eluceat vel misericordiæ affectus: vel justitiæ severitas: non tamen propterea impio latratu ipsa Dei providentia fuerit impetenda: sed ad patientiam & pietatem animis compositis, exitus Deo commendandus: Hic enim tandem plerumq́; luculenter demonstrat, Deo causas constituisse justissimas, earum etiam actionum, quæ nobis videbantur cum enormi aliquâ ἀταξίᾳ sive ἀνομίᾳ esse conjuncta. Cujus rei exempla satis illustria Scriptura monstrat in venditione Josephi: in afflictione Jobis, in traditione & crucifixione Christi Servatoris: ubi licet extrema videretur dominari ἀταξία & confusio: Scriptura tamen ipsa testis est, factum tunc esse id, quod manus & consilium Dei decreverunt, Act. 2, 23. Cap. 24. 28. Haud proindè cœcæ nostræ rationis judicia præjudicare vel possunt, vel etiam debent divinæ providentiæ.

QUINTUM sic informant: Quicquid in Deo est, illud æternum est: At verò Providentia non est aliquid æternum in Deo: Siquidem Providentia dicitur esse rerum creatarum, quæ utiquè non sunt æternæ, Ergò in Deo non est Providentia.

Respondeo, hoc in argumento turpissimè confundi Actum primum cum actu secundo: vel quod idem est, ipsam Ordinis rationem, cum ejusdem executione. In Deo Ergò Providentia est quiddam æternum: Siquidem Providentia hæc nihil est aliud, quàm partim essentialis ille amor, cura & favor, quo Creaturas suas conservare, & bonos prosequi constituit: partim verò essentialis illa Justitia, quâ Diabolos, peccatum & impios punire, ab æterno decrevit. Jam verò Actus secundus, sive Executio ipsa hujus tùm bonitatis, tùm justitiæ divinæ, quæ fit in tempore, non Deum ipsum, ejusdemq́; providentiam, æternitate hac eximit: sed in æternitate permanentem, considerat, quatenus in tempore nunc in hoc, nunc in illo opere suam providentiam exerit: Aliàs ne quidem Deus omnipotens dici posset: Siquidem creatio hujus universi, non ab æterno, sed in tempore demùm peracta est. Rectissimè Ergò inter Dei attributa, quatenus sunt Essentialia & æterna: & quatenùs in tempore se exerunt, distingvitur.

SEXTUM & postremum argumentum, non tam Epicureorum, quàm saniorum quorundam Philosophorum est, qui teste Plutarcho sic inferebant: Si Dei sollicitudine dispensantur res humanæ, cur Improbi Fortunæ indulgentia fruuntur: Contra verò probi eandem experiuntur novercam? Quid? quòd Scriptura teste pios etiam & fideles variè exercuit hæc fortis & fortunæ piorum ac impiorum disparitas, ita ut sæpius in tristissimos gemitus atquè querelas eruperint: uti patet exemplo Jobis: cap. 21, 7. & seqq. Davidis. Ps. 37, 1. & seqq. Asaphi, Psal. 73, 1. & seqq. Jeremiæ, qui cum Deo super hâc re quasi expostulat, Judistus quidem es DOMINE, inquiens: sed justa loquar ad te: Quare via Impiorum prosperatur: benè est omnibus, qui prævaricantur & iniq́; agunt? &c. Jer. 12. & seqq. Sed laborant singulæ hæ collectiones Sophismate non causæ: & insuffiscienti enumeratione causarum, propter quas Deus hâc in vitâ impios bonis afficit, pios verò ærumnis & calamitatibus assiduè exercet. Quarum causarum consideratio evidentissimè demonstrat, tantùm abesse, ut propter diversitatem istam fortis piorum & impiorum, neganda sit DEI providentia, ut ex illâ ipsâ potius diversitate luculentissimè astrui & confirmari queat.

Nam primò DEUS hoc pacto, venturi judicij certitudiné evidentissimè demonstrat: id quod D. Paulus innuit 2. Thess. 1, 6. & 7. Justum est, inquiens, apud DEUM retribuere tribulationem ijs, qui vos tribulant: & vobis qui tribulamini, requiem nobiscum, in revelatione Domini Jesu de cælo.

Deindè Beneficijs suis Deus indignos afficit, ut suam benignitatem erga ipsos quoq́; declaret, secundùm illud Servatoris Matt 5, 44. & 45. Diligite inimicos vestros, ut sitis filij Patris vestri, qui in cælis est, qui Solem suum oriri facit, super bonos & malos, & pluit super justos & injustos.

Tertiò DEUS hoc pacto impios ad pœnitentiam allicere studet: secundùm illud Apostoli Rom. 2, 4. An divitias bonitatis ejus, & patientiæ, & longanimitatis contemnis, ignorans, quod DEI benignitas ad pœnitentiam te vocat?

Tandem Impij, dùm nefariè abutuntur bonitate DEI, accumulant sibi justam DEI iram & vindictam: sic iterùm docente Apostolo, Rom. 2, 5. propter duritiem tuam, & cor impœnitens thesaurizas tibi iram in die iræ, & revelationis justi judicij DEI. Proindè si vel maximè hoc in mundo, non semper pijs benè, malis malè fit: erit tamen aliquando tempus, quo pij ex Psalmo 58, 12. exclamabunt: Nunc utiq́; est fructus justo: nunc utiq́; DEUS est judicans in terrâ.

Sed de Epicureorum impietate plus satis, à quâ haud multùm abhorrere videntur ij, qui autant, Deum creasse quidé hunc mundum, sed die septimo ita quievisse ab operibus suis, ut perpetuum agat Sabbatum, ut Mundum hunc proprio suo motui relinquat, illi nimirùm motui, quem DEUS ipse ei in primâ creatione indiderit. Quorum sanè vanitatem, quippè prolixiore refutatione indignam, verbis Augustini retundendam esse arbitramur, qui lib. 4. de Genesi ad lit. cap. 12. sic disserit: Requievit DEUS die septimo, à condendis novis operibus, seu generibus creaturarum: non ut ipso septimo die potentia ejus, à rerum creatarum gubernatione cessaret: alioqui continuò dilaberentur. Creatoris namq́; potentia, atq́; omnipotentis & omnitenentis virtus causa subsistendi est, omni Creaturæ, quæ virtus ab eis, quæ creata sunt, regendis si aliquando cessaret, simul & eorum cessaret species, omniq́; natura concideret. Neq́; enim sicut structura ædium cum fabricaverit quis & discedit, ipso tamen cessante & absente, subsistunt: Ita mundus vel ictu oculi stare poterit, si ei DEUS regimen sui subtraxerit. Proindè & quod Dominus ait: Pater meus usq́; nunc operatur, continuationem quandam operis ejus, qua universam creatura continet atq; administrat, ostendit. Aliud enim est (NUNC) & aliud (USQUE NUNC) ex illo scilicet, quo cuncta conderet, operato est continuo sine cessatione & intermissione, sicut scriptum est Sap.8,1. Pertingit a fine usq; ad finem fortiter, & disponit omnia suaviter.


### Question I. Is there a Providence of God?: Evils are subject to divine providence generally, but not specially?

How far does the Providence of GOD extend itself?

What the breadth of divine Providence is, and how widely its objects extend, is not one and the same opinion of all. We, taught by the oracles of the Scriptures, believe and establish that all things which are in this world, which happen and are carried out, are contained within the scope of Divine Providence: as much the evil as the good: as much the base and abject as the great and excellent. Scripture gives assurance to this assertion in two ways: First, indeed, by subjecting all things universally to the providence of GOD: then truly by referring even the lightest and most abject things, that is, those about which it could not undeservedly be doubted whether GOD took any care of them, to the government of GOD.

The classic testimonies of the former kind are these: Col. 1:17. All things through him, and in him συνέστηκε consist, that is, they are preserved and sustained in their system, order, and vigor. Heb. 1:3. The Son of GOD carries ALL THINGS by the word of his power. Wis. 11:26. How could anything remain, unless you willed it, and how could anything not sustained by you subsist? Wis. 14:3. Your Providence, Father, governs ALL THINGS.

One may see the passages of the latter kind in Psalm 104, where David refers to the scope of the Providence of GOD not only the heaven, earth, clouds, winds, Angels, the abyss, mountains, springs, rivers, and other more noble creatures of that kind: but also birds, beasts of burden, sparrows, storks, and their nests and little homes, rabbits, likewise, hedgehogs, darkness, lion cubs, reptiles, small animals, and other more abject creatures of this kind: concerning each and every one of which David pronounces this epiphonema: You have made all these in wisdom: The earth is filled with your possession: All expect from you, that you may give them food in time: when you give, they will gather: when you open your hand, all are satisfied with good things: when you turn away your face, they will be troubled: if you take away their Spirit, they fail, and return to their dust, verse 24 seqq. Psalm 148 confirms the same quite clearly, which, because of the fatherly providence of GOD, invites into the society of divine praise not only the Sun, Moon, Stars, men: but also Dragons, fire, hail, snow, ice, whirlwinds of storms, trees, beasts, all cattle, serpents, birds, and other things of that kind, in our calculation, sufficiently abject and despised. v. 7. and seqq. Thus David Ps. 146:9 asserts that even the young of ravens are

scope or Scope.

a care to GOD. And the book of Wisdom ch. 6:8 and ch. 12:13 clearly asserts that GOD has made the small and the great, and has equal care for all. Indeed, even lots, which are otherwise thought to be fortuitous, pertain under the scope of divine providence. Proverbs 16:33. Lots are cast into the lap: but they are directed by the Lord.

Furthermore, a witness greater than any exception is the Savior himself, who subjects not only living creatures but also the hairs of our heads, a thing certainly by far the most abject, to divine providence: Matt. 6:26. Behold the birds of the air, for they do not sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns: and your heavenly Father feeds them. And v. 29 and 30. If GOD so clothes and adorns the grass of the field, which is cast into the oven tomorrow, that Solomon in all his glory was not compared with it: how much more you, etc. And Matt. 10:29. Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing: and one of them shall not fall upon the earth without the will of your Father, but even the hairs of your head are numbered.

But the question is raised at this point concerning the evils that reign in the human race, whether they too depend upon the providence of GOD? To which question it is most correctly answered: Since one kind of evil is the evil of punishment, and another is the evil of fault, both are subject to divine providence, but in a very different respect. And indeed the evil of punishment, insofar as GOD, as a just Judge, sends it in vengeance for preceding crimes and wicked deeds, according to that passage in Amos 3:6: Is there evil in a city, which the Lord has not done? And Lamentations of Jeremiah, chapter 3, 37 and 38: Who is he that said that something should come to pass, when the Lord commanded it not? Out of the mouth of the Most High shall not proceed both evil and good.

Furthermore, regarding the evil of fault, the Providence of GOD is concerned with this as well, but not under the aspect of any cause whatsoever, but partly by reason of permission, and partly in respect of determination, as will be expressly shown in the following article concerning the cause of sin.

Moreover, this point merits observation regarding this question: that theologians are accustomed to call this providence, which extends so widely, the general action of GOD, or by this term they distinguish it from that special action of GOD, when, namely, at times GOD, as a most free agent, does not observe the order of his work, but either for the sake of the pious or for the punishment of the impious, changes something in secondary causes. Examples of which matter may be read in the history of the Israelites, of Joshua, of Hezekiah, of the companions of Daniel, Exod. 10:22, Jos. 10:13, Isa. 38:8, Dan. 3:23 and following.

Then also this must be observed, that although the providence of GOD takes care of all things and creatures, even the most abject, yet it exerts itself especially in the governance of the human race, governing the individual actions of men, but most of all providing and supplying those things which make for the preservation of the Church and the eternal salvation of men. Which is the reason that theologians also establish distinct degrees of the providence of GOD, and distinguish it into General and Special. Concerning the General, these testimonies of Scripture treat primarily:

Job 34:21. The eyes of GOD are upon the ways of men, and He considers all their steps.

Jeremiah 10:23. I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself: nor is it in man to walk and direct his steps.

Proverbs 20:24. Who of men can understand his own way? The steps of a man are directed by the Lord.

But concerning that special providence by which GOD embraces the pious and faithful with peculiar favor, Scripture also treats quite clearly: As

1 Timothy 4:10. CHRIST is the Savior of all men, but especially of the faithful.

Psalm 32:13. GOD indeed sees all the children of men; but in verse 18 He adds: Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear Him, and upon those who hope in His mercy: that He may deliver their souls from death.

Latin:

Quousq; DEI Providentia se extendat?

QUÆ sit Providentiæ divinæ latitudo, & quam late ejusdem objecta pateant, non una eademq; omnium est sententia. Nos Scripturarum oraculis edocti credimus & statuimus, Divinæ Providentiæ ambitu contineri in universum omnia, quæ hoc in mundo sunt, fiunt & geruntur: tam mala, quam bona: tam vilia & abjecta, quam magna & eximia. Fidem assertioni huic facit Scriptura dupliciter: Primum quidem universaliter omnia DEI providentiæ subjiciens: deinde vero levissima quoq; & abjectissima, hoc est, ea ad DEI gubernationem referens: de quibus haud immerito dubitari poterat, an DEUS istorum curam aliquam ageret.
