Prioris generis testimonia classica sunt hæc: Col. 1, 17. Omnia per ipsum, & in ipso συνέστηκε consistunt, hoc est, in suo systemate, ordine & vigore conservantur & sustentantur. Hebr. 1, 3. Filius DEI portat OMNIA verbo potentiæ suæ. Sap. 11, 26. Quomodo posset aliquid permanere, nisi tu velles, & quomodo aliquid a te non sustentatum, subsisteret. Sap. 14, 3. Tua, Pater, Providentia OMNIA gubernat.

Posterioris generis loca videre licet Psalmo 104. ubi David sub complexum Providentiæ DEI refert, non modo cœlum, terram, nubes, ventos, Angelos, abyssum, montes, fontes, fluvios, & id geno creaturas alias nobiliores: sed & volucres, jumenta, passeres, ciconias, earundemq; nidos, & domunculas, cuniculos, item, erinaceos, tenebras, catulos leonum, reptilia, animalia pusilla, & hujus generis abjectiores Creaturas alias: de quibus singulis & universis Epiphonema istud pronunciat David: Omnia isthæc in sapientia fecisti: Impleta est terra, possessione tua: Omnia a te expectant, ut des illis escam in tempore: dante te, colligent: aperiente te manu tuam, omnia satiantur bonis: avertente te faciem, turbabuntur: si aufers Spiritum eorum deficiunt, & in pulverem suum revertuntur, versu 24 seqq. Confirmat idem satis luculenter Psalmus 148. qui ob paternam DEI providentiam, in societatem laudis divinæ invitat, non modo Solem, Lunam, Stellas, homines: sed & Dracones, ignem, grandinem, nivem, glaciem, procellarum turbines, ligna, bestias, universa pecora, serpentes, volucres, & id genus res alias, nostro quide calculo, satis abjectas & contemtas. v. 7. & seqq. Sic David Psal. 146, 9. pullos etiam corvorum DEO

dine sive Ambitu.

curæ esse, asserit. Et liber Sapientiæ c. 6, 8. & c. 12, 13. Pusillum & magnum fecisse, & de omnibus æqualiter curam habere DEUM, liquidò asserit. Quin sub ambitum providentiæ divinæ pertinent etiam, sortes quæ aliàs putantur esse fortuitæ. Proverb. 16, 33. Sortes mittuntur in sinum: sed à Domino diriguntur.

Testis porrò omni exceptione major est, ipse Servator, qui non modò viva animantia: sed & capillos capitum nostrorum, rem certè longè abjectissimam, divinæ providentiæ subjicit: Matth. 6, 26. Intuemini volatilia Cæli, quoniam non serunt neŕ, metunt neŕ, congregant in horrea: & Pater vester cœlestis pascit illa. Et v. 29. & 30. Si DEUS fœnum agri, quod cras in clibanum projicitur, sic vestit & exornat, ut Salomon in omni suâ gloriâ cum eo non fuerit comparandus: quantò magis vos. &c. Et Matth. 10, 29. Nonne duo passeres asse veneunt: & unus ex illis, non cadet super terram sine voluntate Patris vestri, vestri autem etiam capilli capitis sunt numerati.

Sed quæritur hoc loco de Malis, quæ in genere humano regnant, An & illa à DEI providentiâ dependeant? Ad quam quæstionem rectissimè respondetur: Cùm aliud malum sit, malum pœnæ: aliud verò malum culpæ: utrumŕ; divinæ providentiæ subjacere: sed diversissimo respectu. Et malum quidem pœnæ, quatenus DEUS in vindictam præcedentium scelerum & flagitiorum, ut justus Judex illud immittit: Secundum illud Amos 3, 6. Non est malum in civitate, quod non fecit Dominus. Et Threnorum Jerem. cap. 3, 37. & 38. Qui est iste, qui dixit ut fieret aliquid Domino non jubente: Ex ore Altissimi non egredientur nec mala, nec bona.

Cæterùm quoad malum culpæ, versatur circa hoc quoŕ; DEI Providentia, sed non sub ratione ullius alicujus causæ: sed partim ratione permissionis: partim respectu determinationis: uti articulo subsequente de causâ peccati, ex professo ostendetur.

Observationem autem circa hanc quæstionem illud 1. meretur, Quod Providentiam hanc sic latè patente, Theologi appellare solent, Actionem DEI generalem, vel hoc termino eam distingventes, contra actionem illam DEI Specialem, quando nimirùm interdum DEUS, tanquã agens liberrimum, ordinem operis sui non servat, sed vel in gratiam piorum, vel in pœnam impiorum, in causis secundis aliquid immutat. Cujus rei exempla legere licet in historiâ Israëlitarum, Josuæ, Ezechia, Sociorum Danielis, Exod. 10, 22. Jos. 10, 13. Jes 38, 8 Dan. 3, 23 & seqq.

Deindè & illud observandum est, quod licèt DEI providentia rerum & creaturarum omnium etiam abjectissimarum curam agat: tamen in humani generis gubernatione præcipuè sese ea exerat: singulas hominum actiones gubernans: maximè autem omnium ea, quæ ad conservationem Ecclesiæ & salutem æternam hominum faciunt, providens & subministrans. Quæ causa est, quòd distinctos etiam gradus providentiæ DEI constituunt Theologi: & eam distingvunt in Generalem & Specialem. De Generali hæc potissimùm agunt Scripturæ testimonia:

Jobi 34, 21. Oculi DEI super vias hominum, & omnes gressus eorum considerat.

Jerem. 10, 23. Scio Domine, quod non est hominis via ejus: nec viri est, ut ambulet & dirigat gressus suos.

Prov. 20, 24. Quis hominum intelligere potest viam suam. A Domino diriguntur gressus viri.

De speciali verò providentiâ, quâ DEUS pios & fideles peculiari favore complectitur, satis etiam perspicuè agit Scriptura: Ut

1. Tim. 4, 10. CHRISTUS est Servator, omnium hominum: maximè autem fidelium.

Psal. 32, 13. Videt quidem DEUS omnes filios hominum; sed v. 18. subjicit: Ecce oculi Domini super timentes eum, & in eis, qui sperant super misericordiâ ejus: ut eruat à morte animas eorum.


### Question I. Is there a Providence of God?: Antithesis

Antithesis.

The Jews wickedly corrupted this part of Christian doctrine at the beginning, who, although they maintained that individual and universal things, both lower and higher, are subject to Divine providence, nevertheless contended that only the species of these, but not the individuals, are a care to GOD, with the exception only of those individuals of men in whom GOD wished some peculiar sign of His love to shine forth: as Rabbi Moses teaches, in the treatise on the direction of the perplexed, chapter 136.

Following this, certain philosophers, as witnessed by Augustine in book 5 of 'On Genesis according to the literal sense', chapter 2, did not hesitate to write: That only the sublime and celestial things are subject to divine providence: but that this lowest part of the earth and the nearer air, in which winds and clouds arise, is agitated rather by accidents and fortuitous motions: with the exception only of the species, which are incorruptible and eternal: but that human affairs are subject even to the command and disposition of men: so that just as GOD governs heaven and celestial things, so Emperors and Monarchs of this age govern the earth and terrestrial things: according to that impious utterance of a certain court flatterer: You, Caesar, have a divided empire with Jove. Nor did the Peripatetics, Platonists, Astrologers, and Stoics produce anything sounder than these: which is clearer than the midday light from their own writings and disputations.

The Peripatetics certainly assert clearly that GOD is indeed the maker of all things, but that He has committed and, as it were, sub-delegated their governance to secondary causes.

The Platonists invent a threefold Providence: The first is Universal, by which GOD disposes and rules individual things; the second is singular, which is effective through I know not what Genii, or inferior GODS, who are the guardians of individual species; the third is occupied chiefly with man, which is committed to demons, that is, to good Angels and genii.

The Astrologers write that celestial things are ruled by GOD, but mediately, namely through Intelligences; but that sublunary things are governed and disposed by the powers, influences, and constellations of the stars: the vanity of which, however, was sufficiently and more than sufficiently demonstrated in the previous article, which was about creation, Question 6 and 10.

The Stoics, from a perpetual chain of causes and a certain implicit series which is preserved in nature, constructed a certain Fate, by whose force and impulse all things happen necessarily and immutably, and cannot happen otherwise: the reasons and arguments for which the following third Question will expressly treat.

But not only did Gentile philosophers corrupt this head of Christian doctrine, but even within the very bosom of the Christian Church are found those who, although they readily grant that this whole universe and all things that are in it, both lower and higher, are subject to divine providence, yet they imagine its action to be mixed and confused, and only mediate; contending that to created things their own powers have been given by GOD, natural ones indeed to brutes and inanimate things, but rational ones and those proper to the will to men and Angels, by whose guidance both are directed, while in the meantime they deny to GOD any act of particular and immediate dispensation whatsoever. There are others who maintain that only pious men, and only their good actions, are subject to divine providence.

Finally, there are those who judge it clearly unworthy of divine Providence if it is established that it is occupied with minute and abject things. For example, if the majesty of GOD is brought down to this, that He knows at every single moment how many gnats are born, or how many die, how great is the multitude of fleas and flies, how many fish swim in the waters? Just as Jerome was of this opinion in his commentary on chapter 1 of the Prophet Habakkuk, where he also immediately adds these things: We are not such foolish flatterers of GOD that, while we drag His Providence down to the lowest things, we are injurious to ourselves by saying that the same Providence is for irrational and rational beings.

We, certainly departing from the opinion of Jerome in this part, relying on the protection of those Scriptures which prove that things as small as they are great are a care to GOD, subscribe in all things to St. Augustine, who argues so excellently on Ps. 148: Let your charity attend: Who disposed the limbs of the gnat and the flea so that they have their order, have their life, have their motion? Consider one small, most minute little beast, whichever you wish: if you consider the order of its limbs, and the animation of life by which it is moved, so that it flees death for its own sake, loves life, seeks pleasures, avoids annoyances, exercises diverse senses, flourishes in motion congruent to itself. Who gave the sting to the gnat, with which it sucks blood? How thin is the tube with which it sips? Who disposed these things? Who made these things? Do you tremble at the smallest things? Praise the great. Therefore, hold this, my brothers, let no one shake you from the faith and from sound doctrine. He who made the Angel in Heaven, He Himself made the worm on earth: but the Angel in heaven for a heavenly habitation, the worm on earth for a terrestrial habitation. Did He make the Angel to crawl in the mud, and the worm in heaven?

He distributed the inhabitants into their seats, He gave incorruption to incorrupt seats, and corruptible things to corruptible places. Attend to the whole, praise the whole. Thus far Augustine.

However, no matter how much those enumerated thus far, both Gentiles and Christians, may seem to differ in their opinions, they agree in kind, namely, that they individually deny that GOD has universal care and providence over all things: a fact which their own arguments, with which they strive to cloak their error, clearly demonstrate. It is permitted to weigh their principal arguments on the scales of truth and to examine them a little more accurately.

THE FIRST they take from those words which exist in chapter 22, 12 of Job: Do you think that GOD is higher than the Heaven, and exalted above the top of the stars? v. 14. The clouds are His hiding place, and He does not consider our affairs: but He walks about in the circuit of heaven.

But I reply that a most gross ignorance of the Elenchus is committed, and at the same time a Sophistication of the Figure of speech. For those things which are proposed in Job under the form of an interrogation, and indeed in this sense: Do you think that God neglects these lower things, and especially men, or does not penetrate into the hidden things of hearts, because He Himself dwells in the heights? Those things are accepted in that argument assertively and θετικῶς (positively): which method of arguing should be restrained by clubs rather than refuted by reasons.

THE SECOND is such: Those things which obscure and diminish His divine Majesty are not to be attributed to GOD. But this happens when Providence is assigned to GOD concerning these lower things, and likewise concerning minute and abject things. Therefore, it is not concerned with these things.

I reply that the minor premise is simply false. For since we must stand not by the judgment of our own reason, but by the teaching of Scripture in mysteries of faith of this kind: and indeed Scripture expressly asserts that GOD takes care of minute things as well as sublime ones: we certainly conclude most correctly from that very fact that nothing at all is detracted from the divine Majesty, even if He should take the greatest care of those things which seem vile and contemptible to us. What is more? The traces of the immense goodness of GOD, and of His infinite Wisdom and Omniscience, shine forth more clearly from that fact. For GOD is to be esteemed the more merciful and exalted, the more abject and small are the things upon which He bestows His care. If to know the number of the sand, to know the number and individuals of the stars, of fish, and of other animals however minute; certainly this is proper not to human, but only to divine knowledge, and never falls to man: just as indeed Archimedes lost his pains and oil, striving to know and investigate the number of the sand. So far, therefore, is it from the case that anything is detracted from divine perfection by this, that it is rather wonderfully established by it. But the reason why nothing is detracted from His most pure Essence is this: Because GOD does not communicate with their nature and impurity: just as the Sun is not defiled, even though it strikes mud, filth, and other foul and dirty places with its rays, or just as a Mirror also represents the most abject things without contagion to itself: so GOD, much less, contracts any impurity or blemish from the governance of even the vilest things.

THE THIRD argument Pliny moves in this manner: It is the providence of a wise man to avert and prohibit defects and vices.

But almost nothing happens more frequently in this world than that various defects of Nature are seen, such as monsters, prodigies, and other things of that kind, which fight against the laws of nature. Therefore, these things happen either because GOD cannot prevent them: or because it is to be judged that this is absurd, that they happen because GOD does not take care of them.

I reply: The fallacy of the non-cause as cause is committed. For the reason or cause for denying providence is most viciously sought from the errors or defects of nature. Where it is most correctly answered: Subordinated things do not fight. For concerning those very things which seem to us to be errors of Nature, divine Providence is most especially occupied: so that from them it is permitted to see sufficiently evident signs of divine Justice, Wisdom, Goodness, and Omnipotence: to say nothing now of the wondrous judgments of GOD, which are for the most part hidden under such prodigies and monsters. Furthermore, a begging of the question is also committed in the argument. For those things which seem so to us are not immediately to be held as errors and defects of nature. For there is no doubt that the causes of many things are so abstruse and hidden that they cannot be explained or investigated even by the most acute Physicists.

But some insist and ask, whether the Wisdom of divine Providence does not labor precisely because it permits very many poisonous things of the kind, both of plants and of animals, to be generated daily and to be harmful, which it would be profitable to remove and abolish entirely: such as, from the genus of plants, aconite, celery, and other poisonous plants and roots; and from the genus of animals, worms, serpents, crocodiles, flies, and others of that kind, which seem to bring more harm than benefit to the human race.

Latin:

Αντίθεσις.

PArtem hanc doctrinæ Christianæ nefariè initiò corruperunt Judæi, qui licèt res singulas atq; universas, tàm inferas, quam superas, Divinæ providentiæ subjacere statuerent: istarum tamen species duntaxat, non autem Individua DEo curæ esse contenderunt, exceptis eorum duntaxat hominum Individuis, in quibus DEUS peculiare aliquod sui amoris signum elucere voluit: sic docente Rabbi Moyse, tractatu de directione perplexorum, cap. 136.

Hoc secuti Philosophi quidam, teste Augustino lib. 5. de Genesi ad lit. cap. 2. scribere non dubitarunt: Sublimia tantùm & cœlestia divinæ providentiæ esse subjecta: Hanc autem imam terræ, & aëris vicinioris partem, in qua venti nubesq́ consurgunt, casibus potiùs & fortuitis motibus agitari: exceptis duntaxat speciebus, quæ sint incorruptibiles & æternæ: Humana verò hominum etiam imperio & dispositioni subjacere: ita, ut quemadmodú DEUS cœlum & cœlestia: sic Imperatores & Monarchæ hujus seculi, terram & terrestria gubernent: juxta impium illud cujusdam assentatoris Aulici effatum: Divisum imperium, cum Jove, Cæsar habes. Neq; his saniora prodiderunt Peripatetici, Platonici, Astrologi, Stoici: id quod ex ipsorum scriptis ac disputationibus luce meridianâ clariùs patet.

Peripatetici certè disertè asserunt, DEUM esse quidem opificem omnium: sed eorum gubernationem causis secundis commisisse & quasi subdelegasse.

Platonici triplicem confingunt Providentiam: Primam Universalem, quâ DEUS singula disponat & regat: Alteram singularem, quæ per alios nescio quos Genios, sive DEOS inferiores, sit efficax, qui præsides sint singularum specierum: Tertiam occupari præcipuè circa hominem, quæ dæmonibus, hoc est, bonis Angelis & genijs sit commissa.

Astrologi à DEO cœlestia, sed mediatè, nempè per Intelligentias regi: Sublunaria verò, astrorum viribus, influentijs & constellationibus gubernari & disponi scriptitant: Quorum tamen vanitas superiore articulo proximo, qui fuit de creatione, Quæst. 6. & 10. satis superq; est demonstrata.

Stoici ex perpetuo causarum nexu, & implicitâ quâdam serie, quæ in naturâ conservatur, extruxerunt Fatum quoddam, cujus vi atq; impulsu omnia necessario ac immutabiliter fiant: neq; aliter fieri possunt: Quorum rationes atq; argumenta subsequens Quæstio tertia ex professo pertractabit.

Sed non Gentiles modò Philosophi caput hoc doctrinæ Christianæ variè corruperunt, quin in ipso quoq; Ecclesiæ Christianæ gremio reperiuntur, qui licèt totum hoc universum & omnia quæ in eo sunt, tàm infera, quàm supera divinæ providentię subjacere facilè largiuntur: actum tamen ejus mixtum & confusum, nec nisi mediatum comminiscuntur: contendentes rebus creatis, vires suas à DEO inditas esse, Naturales quidem brutis & inanimatis: Rationales verò & voluntatis proprias hominibus & Angelis: quarum ductu utræq; dirigantur, DEO interim dispensationis particularis atq; immediatæ actum prorsus omnem negantes. Sunt alij qui pios duntaxat homines, eorumq; bonas tantùm actiones, divinæ providentiæ subjacere, dictitant.

Sunt deniq;, qui divinâ Providentiâ planè indignum Judicant, si ea statuatur, circa res minutas & abjectas esse occupata. Exempli gratiâ, Si DEI majestas ad hoc deducatur, ut sciat per momenta singula, quot culices nascantur, quotvè moriantur, quanta pulicum & muscarum sit multitudo, quot pisces natent in aquis? quemadmodum hâc in sententiâ fuit Hieronymus in suo commentario ad cap. 1. Prophetæ Habacuc: ubi & isthæc statim subjicit: Non simus tàm fatui adulatores DEI, ut dum Providentiam ejus ad ima detrudimus, in nos ipsos injuriosi simus eandem irrationabilium & rationabilium Providentiam esse dicentes.

Nos sanè à sententiâ Hieronymi hâc in parte discedentes, freti earum Scripturarum præsidio, quæ tàm pusilla, quàm magna DEO curæ esse comprobant, D. Augustino per omnia subscribimus, qui super Ps. 148. sic egregiè disputat: Attendat charitas vestra: Quis disposuit membra pulicis & culicis ut habeant ordinē suum, habeant vitam suam, habeant motum suum? Unam bestiolã brevem, minutissimam considera, quam volueris: si consideres ordinem membrorum ipsius, & animationem vitæ, quâ movetur, ut pro se fugat mortem, amet vitã: appetat voluptates: devitet molestias:exerat sensus diversos: vigeat in motu sibi congruo. Quis dedit aculeum culici, quo sangvinem sugat? Quam tenuis fistula est, quâ sorbet? Quis disposuit ista? Quis fecit ista? Expavescis in minimis? Lauda magnum. Hoc itaq;, tenete fratres mei, nemo vos de fide excutiat, & de sanâ doctrinâ. Qui fecit in Cælo Angelū, ipse fecit in terrâ Vermiculū: sed Angelum in cælo pro habitatione cælesti, Vermiculum in terrâ, pro habitatione terrestri. Nunquid Angelum fecit repere in cœno, & vermiculum in cœlo?

Distribuit sedibus habitatores, incorruptionem incorruptis sedibus dedit, corruptibilia in locis corruptibilibus. Totum attende, totum lauda. Hactenus Augustinus.

Cæterùm quantumvis sententijs discrepare videantur hactenus enumerati tùm Gentiles, tùm Christiani: in genere tamen conveniunt, quòd nimirùm singuli DEO, Universalem rerum omnium curam atque providentiam negant: id quod ipsorum etiam argumenta, quibus errorem palliare, student, liquidò commonstrant. Eorum præcipua ad trutinam veritatis appendere, & paulò accuratiùs examinare licet.

PRIMUM desumunt ex verbis illis, quæ extant cap. 22, 12. Jobi: An cogitas quòd DEUS excelsior Cælo sit, & super stellarum verticem exaltatus? v. 14. Nubes latibulum ejus, neq́; nostra considerat: sed in circuitu cæli obambulat.

Sed respondeo crassissimam committi ignorationem Elenchi, & simul Sophisticationem Figuræ dictionis. Quæ enim apud Jobum sub Formâ Interrogationis, & quidem hoc sensu proponuntur: Annè putas Deum ideò inferiora hæc, & cumprimis homines negligere, aut in abscondita cordium non penetrare, Quia in excelsis ipse habitat? Illa in argumento isto assertivè & θετικῶς accipiuntur: Quæ argumentandi ratio fustibus magis coërcenda, quàm rationibus refutanda est.

ALTERUM tale est: Non sunt DEO tribuenda ea quæ divinam ejus Majestatem obscurant & imminuunt. Atqui hoc fit, quando DEO assignatur Providentia circa hæc inferiora, item circa res minutas & abjectas. Ergò circa hasce res ea non versatur.

Respondeo, Minorem simpliciter esse falsam. Quia enim non nostræ rationis judicio, sed Scripturæ magisterio standum est, in hujusmodi fidei mysterijs: & verò Scriptura disertè asserit, DEUM tàm rerum minutarum, quàm sublimium curam gerere: utiq́; vel indè rectissimè colligimus, nihil prorsus derogari divinæ Majestati, si vel maximè ea curet, quæ vilia & contemta nobis videntur. Quid? quòd indè immensæ bonitatis DEI, ejusdemque infinitæ Sapientiæ & Omniscientiæ vestigia clariùs elucescunt. Tantò enim DEUS æstimandus est clementior & excelsior, quantò abjectiora & minora sunt, quibus ipse curam suam impen dit. Si scire arenæ numerum, nosse Stellarum, piscium, aliorumque animalia quantumvis minutorum numerum & Individua; certè non humanæ, sed solius divinæ scientiæ est proprium, & in hominem nunquam cadit: quemadmodum sanè Archimedes operam & oleum perdidit, arenæ numerum scire & investigare studens. Tantùm ergò abest, ut divinæ perfectioni hinc aliquid decedat, ut mirificè potiùs indè ea astruatur. Quòd verò nihil indè decedat purissimæ ipsius Essentiæ, ratio est hæc, Quia DEUS non communicat illorum naturæ & impuritati: haud secus ac Sol non inquinatur, quamvis suis radijs feriat lutum, fordes, aliaque loca foeda & sordida, aut quemadmodum Speculum etiam repraesentat abjectissimas res sine sui contagione: Sic DEUS multo minus ex gubernatione rerum etiam vilissimarum quicquam impuritatis aut labeculae contrahit.

TERTIUM argumentum Plinius movet in hunc modum: Sapientis Providentia est avertere & prohibere defectus & vitia.

Atqui nihil ferme frequentius hoc in mundo evenit, quam ut conspiciantur varij defectus Naturae, ut monstra, prodigia, & id genus alia, quae cum legibus naturae pugnant. Ergo isthæc sic eveniunt, vel quia DEUS ea non potest impedire: vel quia hoc absurdum, ideo evenire censenda sunt; quia DEUS istorum curam non agit.

Respondeo: Committi Sophisma τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον. Nam ex erratis sive defectibus naturae vitiosissime petitur ratio sive causa negandae providentiae. Ubi rectissime respondetur: Subordinata non pugnant. Nam circa illas ipsas res, quae nobis errata Naturae videntur, Providentia divina vel maxime est occupata: ita ut ex illis divinae Justitiae, Sapientiae, Bonitatis & Omnipotentiae signa satis evidentia conspicari liceat: ut nihil jam dicamus de mirandis DEI judicijs, quae plerumq; sub ejusmodi prodigijs & monstris occultantur. Deinde committitur in argumento etiam petitio principij. Neq; enim pro erratis & defectibus naturae statim sunt habenda, quae nobis ita videntur. Dubium enim est nullum, quin multarum rerum ita abstrusae & occultae sint causae, ut ab acutissimis etiam Physicis explicari investigarive nequeant.

Sed instant nonnulli ac quaerunt, Annon Providentiae divinae Sapientia ideo vel maxime laboret, quod ea permittit, plurima venenata ex genere, tum plantarum, tum animalium: atq; noxia indies generari, quae prodesfet prorsus tolli & aboleri: qualia sunt ex Genere plantarum, Aconitum, Apium & alia venenata tum plantae tum radices: Ex genere vero animalium, vermes, serpentes crocodili, muscae: & id genus alia, quae humano generi plus damni quam commodi adferre videntur.


### Question I. Is there a Providence of God?: Antithesis (continued)

To untie this knot, interpreters certainly depart into diverse opinions. Some indeed declare that these things are permitted by GOD as a punishment for sin. Others assert that in these very things, nothing is simply and in itself evil, but that the force of evil and poison comes to them by accident, namely, with respect to illegitimate use. These answers, although they are not to be rejected, do not yet fully solve the proposed question. Therefore, it may also be added that error arises from an insufficient enumeration of the degrees of goodness. For the logic of the consequence does not hold if someone should conclude thus: 'There is no use for this or that plant, root, or animal in common life; therefore, there is no use for them at all, and consequently, it would be better for them to be removed and abolished entirely.' For the consequence is very rightly denied: since there are many degrees of goodness and modes that can be given. For that which in the common use of things is not useful to man: that in medicine can have a use that is far most excellent. Furthermore, there is no doubt that the powers and faculties of all things are not yet known and perceived by men: whence it is that those things which sometimes seem to us harmful and useless out of ignorance: these provide others with uses most salutary and necessary to the human race.

Some are accustomed to frame the FOURTH argument in this way: Whatever things happen by necessity do not have need of providence. But very many things happen by necessity: such as Eclipses, the Rising and Setting of the Sun and Moon: the changes of the four seasons of the year: the Generation and Corruption of natural things. Therefore these and other things of this kind do not have need of singular providence.

I answer, The argument proceeds from a most false hypothesis, which will never find a place in the Schools of Christians. For it is imagined that God has so implanted in natural things their own powers and faculty of acting, that now by their own motion, of themselves, without the help and care of God, they fulfill their course and actions from the sole necessity of nature.

But the contrary has been most clearly demonstrated from the Scriptures above in the thesis of this Question: namely, that nothing, absolutely nothing from the whole universe of created things can be given; which is not enlivened and moved, preserved and directed by the secret and efficacious inspiration of divine providence. This correction therefore being applied, the nerve of the proposed argument expires, as one savoring of mere Heathenism: and laboring under a shameful begging of the question.

Some today move a FIFTH argument from the sacred Scriptures, in this manner: Scripture testifies that GOD sends many away according to their own desires, that they may go in their own inventions Acts 14, 15. Ps. 81, 13. The same testifies that GOD left Man in the hand of his own counsel, Ecclesiasticus 15, 14. The same testifies finally, that GOD has no care for oxen 1 Cor. 9, 9. Therefore not all things are subject to divine Providence.

I answer. The argument fails by the Sophistication of taking that which is not a cause as a cause. For in all those actions, with which the produced testimonies of the Scriptures deal, the Providence of God is so far from being excluded, that it rather shines forth from them wonderfully. For as regards the first testimony of Scripture, God does not so permit certain ones to go according to their own desires, as if He had no further thought of them at all: but rather He permits them to go in their own inventions in such a way that, as a just judge, in vengeance for their preceding unconquerable stubbornness, He withdraws His grace from them, so that He may bridle their wicked desires, restrain them, direct them to certain ends and those subservient to His glory, and finally punish them eternally. Just as we are to have a discussion expressly about the reprobate and the hardened in the following Article.

The other saying is not to be taken indefinitely concerning all men, but only concerning our first parents, still constituted in the state of integrity: to whom God before the fall granted both the use of reason and the freedom of the will, by which they could most freely incline themselves as much to good as to evil. In which part the condition of Man differed greatly from naturally acting things. For these always act in the same way: but Man was indeed created in the beginning in such a way that he was left in the hands of his own counsel, that is, that he might act voluntarily by deliberating and choosing. Where, however, the providence of GOD must in no way be excluded, but rather included in all ways: and indeed as much before as after the fall. For before the fall God disposed from eternity by what remedy He might wish to restore the fall of man through His Son. Eph. 1, 4. nay, by promulgating the precept concerning the forbidden tree: likewise by denouncing the punishment established for the transgression of this precept: nay, by preserving the very faculty of the will: He certainly exercised the energy of His providence quite evidently. But after the fall, GOD not only preserves for Man the use of Reason and some freedom of the will in natural and moral matters, but also inclines his will to good, and finally regenerates him through the Word and Sacraments. In which individual and universal actions, the Providence of GOD is surely found to be most efficacious.

In the allegation of the third saying of Scripture, a gross Ignorance of the Refutation is committed. For it is not to be understood absolutely, but comparatively, namely, a comparison having been made of oxen to Men. Therefore not the literal sense, but the meaning of this place should be looked at. For the literal sense is broken by the very coherence of the text, which cites from Deut. 25, 4 that command of God which is most instructive: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. But the meaning of this saying is twofold, and indeed both are placed in comparing. The former is: That God does not have as much care for oxen as for men: namely, according to the diversity of degrees. Otherwise God preserves both beasts and men: Ps. 36, 7. so that He does not neglect even sparrows and the young of ravens Matt. 6, 29. Ps. 146, 9. The latter meaning is: That there is indeed care from God for oxen: but not primarily on account of the oxen themselves: But on account of man, for whose sake all brute animals were created: secondarily meanwhile on account of the brutes themselves also. Therefore, the Apostolic negation is simple, and obtains a limited and conditional sense, and that a twofold one, as has now been demonstrated.

THE SIXTH argument is brought forward by some in this manner: Given the Universal Providence of GOD, and that too occupied as much with evil actions as with good: it seems hardly possible to provide a reason by which GOD can be asserted to be immune from the cause of sin. For although GOD is not the cause of sin in such a respect as if He either commands, or impels, or in any way entices man to sin: much less does He approve of it: yet in so far as at least His Providence seems to labor therein, insofar as he is accustomed to use the evil wills of men, and thus their sins, to produce those effects which he had long since decreed to bring into act. Therefore it would be better to deny the universal providence of GOD than, by asserting it, to impute any blame of sin to GOD. I answer. 1. This argument overturns itself: for if God neither commands sin, nor in any way impels or entices man to it, much less approves of it: certainly he must be immune from all blame of sin. Furthermore, the argument fails by a double fallacy: partly of non-cause as cause, and partly of a vicious consequence. For although all human actions, as well evil as good, are subject to Divine Providence: yet the act of governance itself is far different. For he effects, aids, approves, and rewards good ones. But he hates, detests, disapproves, and punishes evil ones. And although he sustains sinful Nature, and provides motion to men: Since both the impious and the pious are in him, live and move: Yet because the force of sin is not in that motion or natural act, insofar as it is considered in itself, and depends solely on the power of GOD: But in the adhering vice and deformity, which is from the depravity of the human will: certainly the cause of sin can in no way be ascribed to GOD. Furthermore, that a good outcome very often emerges from evil actions, that is not to be imputed to the evil actions themselves: But to an external and alien cause, namely divine wisdom and goodness, which knows how to elicit good from evil, and which, as Augustine speaks somewhere, would not permit evil to be done, unless it could produce a good end from it: even against the counsel and purpose of the impious. In which part that common rule has place: Not the outcome, but the will measures the deeds of men.

SEVENTH argument: If all things depend on the providence of GOD: the action and effect of all secondary causes collapses. But this latter assertion would be utterly absurd. Therefore, neither can the former stand. I answer: The argument fails by the fallacy of a vicious consequence: for subordinated things do not conflict: And the order of secondary causes does not so much take away the providence of GOD, as it rather establishes it. For this is, as it were, the proper office of divine Providence, to effect that created things each exercise that motion, and produce those actions or effects, which they can exercise and produce from the powers themselves implanted in them by GOD. Whence Augustine rightly writes, lib. 7. de Civit. Dei cap. 30. GOD so administers all things which he has created, that he also allows them to exercise and perform their own proper motions. Which David expresses more emphatically in Psalm 119:91, saying, By your ordinance all things PERSEVERE until this day, for they serve you: gravely implying that secondary causes are not taken away, but asserted: not abolished, but only ordered, through the providence of GOD; so that they may be held in that place which their own designation warns they should be held.

But some insist: If the Providence of GOD orders secondary causes. Therefore, just as secondary causes are, so also the Providence of GOD itself is compelled to act as the first cause. Or as some philosophers argue: With secondary causes placed in act; such an effect follows as is the very disposition of the secondary causes: but with them not placed in act: the effect does not follow: Therefore it is indeed necessary for the first cause to concur in every action of secondary causes: but in essentially ordered causes, the second acting, the first must also necessarily act: nor can the first act anything without the seconds: nor otherwise than according to the nature and disposition of the seconds.

I answer: The argument fails by the fallacy of non-cause as cause. For although GOD acts through secondary causes, and in producing certain effects, uses their ministry: yet he does not do that through, or because of, some necessary and immutable connection of secondary causes with the first: but from his most free will: so that secondary causes are not only subject to the first cause, which is the cause of causes: But GOD also, without, and indeed very often against their disposition and order, produces most notable effects: as a most free agent: nay, not rarely he produces from secondary causes placed in act a different effect than their own nature and disposition would bear: as from the history of Abraham and Sarah, at last in old age, against the disposition of secondary causes and the powers of those generating: Gen. 21:1 and 2. Likewise Elijah, at whose prayers, clouds disposed for rain could not, however, emit water, 1. Kings 18:44, clearly appears.

EIGHTH argument. If all human actions, as well good as bad, and vice versa, depend on the providence of GOD: certainly no place will any longer be left for the liberty of the human will, or for human deliberations and counsels. But this latter is absurd. Therefore the former cannot stand.

I answer: The argument fails by the same sophistry of non-cause as the one immediately preceding. For here too that Rule of the Logicians has place: Subordinated things do not conflict: Much less are they opposed to each other contradictorily, but can stand together without contradiction. For just as GOD by his providence so governs secondary causes that he permits them also to exercise their own proper motions: So he also governs and rules the will of man, that yet in natural and moral things, he leaves it some liberty of acting, namely that which man has still retained, though greatly weakened after the fall. Concerning which liberty of acting itself, the Providence of GOD also effectively concurs: first indeed by preserving the human nature created by him: then indeed by aiding and perfecting the counsels, deliberations, and actions of men, the good ones indeed: but so directing the evil ones, that they may obtain an outcome, congruent to His will alone. Then because the will of man not rarely proposes to itself those things which differ from the divine: it happens that sometimes GOD hinders the effect entirely, either immediately or mediately: while the motion of the human will is indeed acting most freely: But obtaining a different effect than that which it had proposed to itself. Thus Paul confesses that he had proposed to himself to visit the Romans, the Thessalonians, likewise to preach the Gospel in Phrygia and Galatia, and thence to go into Bithynia: but that he was always hindered by GOD. Rom. 1, 13. 1 Thess. 2, 18. Acts 16, 6 & 7. Hence we shall most rightly have established the measure of all our counsels and actions, the will of GOD: thus taught by CHRIST, Matt. 6, 10. Thy will be done as in heaven and on earth: Likewise by James chap. 4, 15. If the Lord will, and if we shall have lived, we shall do this or that,

Latin:

Hunc sane nodum ut solvant Interpretes, in diversas abeunt sententias. Alij quidem in poenam peccati a DEO isthaec permitti dictitant. Alij in his ipsis rebus, nihil simpliciter, & in sese esse malum afferunt: sed mali & veneni vim ipsis ex accidente obtingere, nempe respectu usus illegitimi. Quae sane responsiones, etsi non sunt rejiciendae, nondum tamen Quaestionem propositam plene solvunt. Addi proinde potest & illud, Ex insufficienti enumeratione graduum bonitatis errorem oboriri. Neque enim militat consequentiae ratio, si quis ita colligat: Hujus vel illius plantae, radicis, animalis, nullus est usus in vita communi. Ergo nullus plane eorum est usus: & per consequens, praestaret prorsus ea tolli & aboleri. Negatur enim rectissime consequentia: Siquidem plures bonitatis gradus & modi dari posfunt. Nam quod in communi rerum usu non prodest homini : illud in medicinâ usum habere potest longè præstantisfimum. Deindè dubium nullum est, quin nondum rerum omnium vires & facultates hominibus sint cognitæ atq; perspectæ: undè sit, ut quæ nobis interdum ex ignorantiâ videntur noxia atqūe inutilia: ea alios præbeant usus, humano generi maximè salutares & necessarios.

QUARTUM argumentum sic informare solent nonnulli : Quæcunq̄, ex necessitate eveniunt, providentiâ opus non habent. Atqui quam plurima ex necessitate eveniunt: ut Eclipses, Ortus & Occasus Solis & Lunæ: mutationes quatuor anni temporum : Generatio & Corruptio rerum naturalium. Ergò hæc & id genus alia non opus habent singulari providentiâ.

Respondeo, Procedit argumentum ex falsissimâ hypothesi, quæ in Christianorum Scholis locum nunquam fortietur. Fingitur enim Deus, rebus naturalibus, sic indidisse proprias vires & facultatem agendi, ut jam proprio motu, per se, sine Dei auxilio & curâ, ex solâ necessitate naturæ cursum & actiones suas obeant.

Atqui diversum ex Scripturis supra in θέσει hujus Quæstionis luculentissimè est demonstratum : nimirùm, nihil, nihil prorsus ex totâ rerú creatarum universitate dari posse; quod non arcanâ & efficaci divinæ providentiæ inspiratione, vegetetur & moveatur: conservetur & dirigatur. Correctione ergò hac adhibitâ, expirat propositi argumenti nervus, tanquam merum Ethnicismum sapiens : & turpi petitione principij laborans.

QUINTUM argumentum hodiè nonnulli ex Scripturis sacris movent, in hunc modum : Scriptura testatur DEUM multos dimittere secundum desideria ipsorum, ut abeant in adinventioninibus suis Act. 14, 15. Ps. 81, 13. Eadem testatur DEUM reliquisse Hominem in manu consilij sui, Ecclesiastici 15, 14. Eadem testatur deniq̄, DEO non esse curæ de bobus 1. Cor. 9, 9. Ergò Providentiæ divinæ non omnia sunt subjecta.

Respondeo. Fallit argumentum Sophisticatione non causæ ut causæ. Nam in omnibus istis actionibus, de quibus producta Scripturarum testimonia agunt, usque adeò Providentia Dei non excluditur, ut potiùs ex illis mirificè ea eluceat. Nam quoad primum Scripturæ testimonium, Deus non ita permittit quosdam abire secundum desideria ipsorum, ac si nullam prorsus ipsorum ampliùs cogitationem habeat : sed potiùs ita permittit ipsos abire in adinventionibus suis, ut tanquã justus judex, in vindictam antegressæ inexpugnabilis contumaciæ, gratiâ suam ipsis subtrahat, ut cupiditates ipsorum pravas frenet, coërceat, ad fines certos & gloriæ suæ subservientes dirigat, & tandem æternùm ipsos puniat. Quemadmodum de reprobis, & induratis subsequente Articulo nobis ex professo futura est disputatio.

Alterum dictum non indefinitè de omnibus hominibus est accipiendum, sed tantùm de primis nostris parentibus, in statu integritatis adhuc constitutis: quibus Deus ante lapsum talem concessit & rationis usum, & arbitrij libertatem, quâ tam ab bonum, quàm ad malum, liberrimè se inclinare poterant. Quâ in parte conditio Hominis plurimùm distabat à naturaliter agentibus. Hæc enim eodem semper modo agunt: Homo verò ita erat initiò conditus, ut relinqueretur in manibus consilij sui, hoc est, ut deliberando & eligendo voluntariè ageret. Ubi tamen DEI providentia nullatenus excludi, sed modis potiùs omnibus includi debet: & quidem tam ante, quàm post lapsum. Nan ante lapsum Deus ab æterno disposuit, quo remedio lapsum hominis per Filium suum restaurare velit. Eph. 1, 4. imò promulgando præceptum de arbore prohibita: item denunciando pœnam præcepti hujus transgressioni constitutam: imò conservando ipsam voluntatis facultatem: certè providentiæ suæ ἐνέργειαν satis evidentem exeruit. Post lapsum verò, DEUS non tantùm Homini Rationis usum, & aliquam voluntatis libertatem, in naturalibus & moralibus conservat, sed & voluntatem ipsius ad bonum inclinat, & tandem per Verbum & Sacramenta regenerat. In quibus sanè actionibus singulis & Universis, Providentia DEI maximè efficax deprehenditur.

In tertij Scripturæ dicti allegatione crassâ committitur Elenchi Ignoratio. Non enim absolutè, sed comparatè illud est intelligendum, facta nimirùm comparatione boum ad Homines. Haud proindè τὸ ῥητὸν, sed διάνοια loci hujus spectanda fuerit. Nam τὸ ῥητὸν infringit, ipsa textûs συνέπεια, quæ ex Deut. 25, 4. citat illud Dei mandatum maximè φερωφητικὸν: Bovi trituranti os non obturabis. Διάνοια autem dicti hujus est gemina, & quidem utraq; in comparando posita. Prior est: Non ita curæ DEO esse boves: sicut homines: nempè pro diversitate graduum. Aliàs Deus tam jumenta, quàm homines conservat: Psal. 36, 7. ita ut ne passeres quidem & pullos corvorum negligat Matth. 6, 29. Psal. 146, 9. Posterior διάνοια est: Esse quidem curam Deo de bobus: sed non πρώτως propter ipsos boves: Verùm propter hominem, cujus causa bruta animantia omnia sunt condita: δευτέρως interim propter ipsa etiam bruta. Proindè, Negatio Apostolica simplex, sensum limitatum & conditionalem, eumq́; geminum obtinet, uti jam est demonstratum.

SEXTUM argumentum tale à quibusdam profertur: Stante Universali DEI Providentia & eâ quidē tàm circa malas, quàm bonas actiones occupatâ: vix videtur dari posse ratio, quâ DEUS à causâ peccati immunis asseri queat. Etsi enim DEus non est causa peccati eo respectu, quasi vel jubeat, vel impellat, vel quovis modo alliciat hominem ad peccandum: multò minus approbat illud: tamen quatenus saltem Providentia ipsig laborare videtur, quatenus malis hominum voluntatibus, & sic peccatis ipsorum uti consuevit, ad eos producendos effectus, quos jampridem in actum deducere decreverat. Ergò satius fuerit negare universalem DEI providentiam, quàm eam asserendo, DEO peccati culpam aliquam impingere. Respondeo. 1. Evertit hoc argumentum seipsum: si enim Deus, neq; jubet peccatum, neq; ad id quovis modo hominem impellit aut allicit, nedum approbat illud: certè ab omni peccati culpâ immunis sit, necesse. Deindè fallit argumentum Sophismate gemino: partim non causæ ut causæ, partim verò vitiosi consequentis. Etsi enim Divinæ Providentiæ omnes hominum actiones, tàm malæ, quàm bonæ subjacent: tamen ipse gubernationis actus longè est diversissimus. Bonas enim efficit, adjuvat, probat, remuneratur. Malas verò odit, detestatur, improbat, punit. Et quanquam Naturam peccantem sustentat, & hominibus motum præbet: Siquidem tàm impij, quàm pii in ipso sunt, vivunt & moventur: Quia tamen peccati vis non est in ipso motu sive actu naturali, quatenus ipse in se consideratur, & à DEI virtute unicè dependet: Sed in adhærente vitio & deformitate, quæ est ex pravitate voluntatis humanæ: utiq; peccati causa DEO nullo modo adscribi potest. Deindè verò, quòd ex malis actionibus bonus sæpissimè eventus emergit, id non ipsis malis actionibus: Sed externæ & alienæ causæ imputandum est, nempè divinæ sapientiæ & bonitati, quæ novit ex malo bonum elicere, quæque, ut Augustinus alicubi loquitur, non permitteret malum fieri, nisi bonum indè finem producere posset: etiam contra impiorum consilium & propositum. Quâ in parte locum habet vulgata illa regula: Non eventus, sed voluntas mensurat facta hominum.

SEPTIMUM argumentum: Si omnia dependent à DEI providentiâ: corruit omnium causarum secundarum actio & effectus. Atqui hoc posterius affirmata prorsus absurdum fuerit. Ergò, neq; prius illud stare poterit. Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate vitiosi consequentis: subordinata enim non pugnant: Et causarum secundarum ordo usq; adèo providentiam DEI non tollit, ut eam magis stabiliat. Hoc enim proprium quasi officium est Providentiæ divinæ, efficere, ut res creatæ singulæ eum motum exerceant, easq; actiones sive effectus producant, quos ex viribus ipsis à DEO inditis exercere & producere possunt. Undè rectè Augustinus scribit, lib. 7. de Civit. Dei cap. 30. Sic administrat DEUS omnia, quæ creavit, ut ea etiam suos proprios exercere & agere motus sinat. Id quod ἐμφατικωτέρως David exprimit Psal. 119, 91. inquiens, Ordinatione tuâ res omnes PERSEVERANT usq; in hodiernum diem, quoniam inserviunt tibi: graviter innuens, non tolli, sed asseri: non aboleri, sed ordinari tantùm causas secundas, per DEI providentiam; ut eo nimirùm habeantur loco, quo ipsa eorum indigitatio, eas habendas esse monet.

Sed instant nonnulli: Si DEI Providentia ordinat causas secundas. Ergò prout se habent causæ secundæ, sic ipsa quoq; DEI Providentia, tanquam prima causa agere cogitur. Vel uti Philosophorum aliqui arguunt: Positis in actu causis secundis; sequitur talis effectus, qualis est ipsa causarum secundarum dispositio: illis verò non positis actu: non etiam sequitur effectus: Ergò necesse quidem est, primam causam concurrere ad omnem actionem causarum secundarum: sed in causis essentialiter ordinatis, secundâ agente, necessariò etiam agere primam: neq; quicquam posse agere primam, sine secundis: neq; aliter etiam quàm pro naturâ & dispositione secundarum.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate non causæ, ut causæ. Etsi enim DEUS agit per causas secundas, & in producendis certis effectibus, earum ministerio utitur: tamen illud non facit per, aut propter necessariam quandam & immutabilem connexionem causarum secundarum, cum primâ: sed ex liberrimâ voluntate: ita ut causæ secundæ non modò primæ causæ, quæ est causa causarum subsint: Sed DEUS etiam sine, imò sæpissimè contra earum dispositionem atq; ordinem, Effectus maximè insignes producat: tanquam agens liberrimum: quin etiam haud rarò ex causis secundis in actu positis alium effectum producat, quàm ipsarum natura atq; dispositio ferat: uti ex historiâ Abraha & Saræ, in senectute demùm, contra causarum secundarum dispositionem, & vires generantium: Gen. 21, 1. & 2. Item Eliæ, ad cujus preces, nubes ad pluvias dispositæ, aquam tamen emittere non poterant, 1. Reg. 18, 44. luculenter patet.

OCTAVUM argumentum. Si omnes hominum actiones tàm bonæ, quàm malæ, & vice versa, dependent à DEI providentiâ: utiq; nullus ampliùs locus relinquetur libertati voluntatis humanæ, sive deliberationibus & consilijs humanis. Atqui hoc posterius absurdum. Ergò prius illud stare non poterit.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum eadem Sophisticatione non causæ, quâ præcedens proximum. Nam hîc quoq; locum habet Regula illa Logicorum: Subordinata non pugnant: Multò minùs ἀντιφατικῶς sibi sunt opposita, sed simul sine contradictione stare possunt. Quemadmodum enim DEUS suâ providentiâ ita gubernat causas secundas, ut permittat illas suos etiam proprios exercere motus: Ita gubernat etiam & regit voluntatem hominis, ut tamen in rebus naturalibus & moralibus, aliquam agendi libertatem ei relinquat, eam nimirùm quam post lapsum valdè labefactatam adhuc homo retinuit. Circa quam ipsam tamen agendi libertatem Providentia etiam DEI efficaciter concurrit: primùm quidem conservando naturam humanam à se conditam: deindè verò consilia, deliberationes & actiones hominum, bonas quidem adjuvando & perficiendo: malas verò ita dirigendo, ut eventum sortiantur, soli ipsius voluntati congruum. Tùm quia voluntas hominis haud rarò ea sibi proponit, quæ à divinâ dissident : sit ut interdum DEUS effectum prorsus vel immediatè vel mediatè impediat: motu interim voluntatis humanæ liberrimè agente quidem: Sed alium sortiente effectum, quàm quem sibi proposuerat. Sic Paulus fatetur, se sibi proposuisse invisere Romanos, Thessalonicenses, item prædicare Evangelium in Phrygiâ & Galatiâ, indéque abire in Bithyniam: sed semper à DEO præpeditum fuisse. Rom. 1, 13. 1.Thess. 2, 18. Act. 16, 6. & 7. Hinc omnium consiliorum & actionum nostrarum mensuram rectissimè constituerimus, voluntatem DEI: sic edocti à CHRISTO, Matth. 6, 10. Fiat voluntas tua sicut in cœlo & in terrâ: Item à Jacobo cap. 4, 15. Si Dominus voluerit, & si vixerimus, faciemus hoc vel illud,


### Question I. Is there a Providence of God?: This Question, How the Freedom of the Will can stand with Providence, can be dispatched more concisely if we accurately distinguish three…

This Question, How the Freedom of the Will can stand with Providence, can be dispatched more concisely if we accurately distinguish three things.

I. The human action itself, insofar as it is natural:

II. The determination of the action itself, which tends either to good or to evil, and properly flows from the freedom of our will.

III. The success and outcome of all actions.

Regarding I. Every action of ours, insofar as it is natural, depends on GOD as the first cause. Acts 17. Rom. 11. From him, through him, and in him are all things. Eph. 1. Who works all things according to the counsel of his will.

II. The determination of an action to Good and evil is proximately ascribed to the will, Gen. 4, 7. yet the first cause is not excluded, but in good things it is introduced as leader and governor: in evil things as reformer and corrector.

III. The outcome and success of actions, if it be good, is simply ascribed to GOD; but if it be evil, it is also attributed to GOD, but as one performing a work that is not his own.

Latin:

Compendiosiùs expediri potest Quæstio hæc, Quomodo Libertas Voluntatis cum Providentiâ stare possit? Si tria accuratè distingvamus.

I. Actio ipsa humana, quatenus naturalis est:

II. Ipsa actionis determinatio, quæ vel ad bonum, vel ad malum tendit, & propriè fluit à libertate voluntatis nostræ.

III. Omnium actionum successus atq́ue eventus.

Quoad I. Omnis nostra actio, quatenus naturalis est, à DEO tanquam causa prima pendet. Act. 17. Rom. 11. Ex eo, per eum, & in ipsum sunt omnia. Eph. 1. Qui operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ.

II. Determinatio actionis ad Bonum & malum voluntati proximè adscribitur, Genes. 4, 7. neque tamen causa prima excluditur, sed in bonis tanquam dux & gubernator introducitur : In malis tanquam reformator & corrector.

III. Eventus & successus actionum si bonus sit, DEO simpliciter adscribitur; sin malus sit, etiam DEO tribuitur, sed alienum opus agenti.


### Question III. What is the Form, or by what mode is the divine providence concerning things and actions of men?

IF we consult the holy Scriptures, as is fitting: the Form of divine Providence consists chiefly in two works: of which one is of Conservation: the other indeed of Government.

Regarding the work of conservation, GOD in the first creation indeed endowed individual things with their natural powers: but in such a way that they can never exercise them, except insofar as they are moved and directed by the present hand of GOD. For example: The Sun is thus founded in the beginning, that it may rise daily, and by its motion constitute those four seasons of the year. Meanwhile, CHRIST is witness that his heavenly Father is he who causes the Sun to rise daily, Matt. 5, 45. And David, Ps. 74, 16. Thine, he says, is the day, and thine is the night: thou makest the dawn and the sun; Thou makest summer and spring. Let the opinion of those therefore be extinguished, who either entirely deny this first work of divine Providence, or certainly define it imperfectly and insufficiently, contending that GOD in the beginning created the nature of this universe, and its individual parts, in such a way that He once implanted in each its own proper powers, by the force of which they are subsequently agitated, and are carried along of their own accord and by their own motion, without the support or impulse of the supreme cause, namely GOD. The impiety of whom we have sufficiently refuted in the immediately preceding question, where we dealt with secondary causes: and we have demonstrated the contrary. We add this in this place as it were ἐκ περιουσίας. 1. That if this opinion stands, that saying of the Savior must necessarily be false, John 5:17, My Father is working until now, and I am working: 2. That by this arrangement GOD would be constituted as a sort of momentary creator of things, and only a general principle of confused motion. 3. That by this arrangement also, the providence of GOD would today differ no more from His foreknowledge: since neither would concur in the administration of created things: but would be occupied with the mere knowledge of all things. All of which, since they are prodigiously absurd, we shall have most rightly established that the first function of divine Providence is proper to conservation, namely that conservation by which He not only preserves created things from destruction: but also with a clearly fatherly and solicitous care provides and disposes that each thing may act and effect that for the sake of which it was first created.

THE OTHER work of divine Providence, which is said to be Government, consists in a perpetual, vigilant, and efficacious operation, by which GOD not only preserves the things created by Him: but also in all things that are done and carried out, He Himself holds the helm as it were, moderating and disposing each and every thing, both with respect to events and with regard to ends: indeed by effecting, assisting, and approving good actions and things: but by prohibiting, directing, and determining evil ones: so that absolutely nothing of all things that are, are done, and are carried out, can decline or escape this special dispensation of GOD.

Where, however, that distinction, already indicated in some way, deserves the most accurate observation. For although not only good, but also evil human actions, and indeed the worst actions of devils, are truly subject to the government of divine Providence: yet the act by which the good works of men are governed is very different from that which directs and moderates evil ones.

Latin:

SI Scripturas sacras, uti par est, consulamus: Forma divinæ Providentiæ, in duobus potíssimùm operibus consistit: quorum Unum est Conservationis: alterum verò Gubernationis.

Quoad conservationis opus DEUS in primâ quidem creatione, singulis rebus vires suas naturales indidit: sed ita, ut eas exercere nunquam possint, nisi quatenus præsenti DEI manu moventur & diriguntur. Exempli gratia: Sol sic initio est conditus, ut quotidiè oriatur, & motu suo quatuor illa anni tempora constituat. Interim testis est CHRISTUS, Patrem suum cœlestem esse eum; qui faciat quotidiè oboriri Solem, Matth. 5, 45. Et David Psal. 74, 16. Tuus, inquit, est dies, & tua est nox: tu facis auroram & solem; Tu facis æstatem & ver. Facescat proindè eorum opinio, qui primum istud opus Providentiæ divinæ vel prorsus negant, vel certè imperfectè ac insufficienter definiunt, contendentes, DEUM initiò naturam hujus universi, & singulas ejus partes sic condidisse, ut singulis vires suas proprias semel indiderit, quarum vi deinceps agitatæ, sponte suâ & proprio motu ferantur, sine adminiculo sive impulsu summæ causæ, nempè DEI. Quorum sanè impietatem quæstione præcedente proximâ, ubi de causis secundis egimus satis sufficienter refutavimus: & contrarium demonstravimus. Illud ἐκ περιουσίας quasi hoc loco adjicimus. 1. Quod stante hâc opinione, falsum esse necesse sit illud Servatoris, Joh. 5, 17. Pater meus usq́; modò operatur, & ego operor: 2. Quod DEUS hoc pacto momentaneus quasi rerum creator, & Generale tantùm confusi motus principium constitueretur. 3. quòd hoc etiam pacto, providentia DEI ab ipsius præscientiâ nihil hodiè ampliùs differret: quippè quarum neutra ad rerum creatarum concurreret administrationem: sed circa nudam rerum omnium notitiam occuparetur. Quæ sanè omnia, cum prodigiosè sint absurda, rectissimè statuerimus, Providentiæ divinæ munus primum, esse conservationis proprium, illius nimirùm conservationis, quâ non modò res conditas ab interitu conservat: Sed & paterna planè & sollicita cura providet, & disponit, ut res quæq́; agat & efficiat, id, cujus rei gratia primùm fuit condita.

ALTERUM divinæ Providentiæ opus, quod Gubernationis esse dicitur, consistit in perpetuâ, vigili & efficaci operatione, quâ DEUS non modò res à se conditas conservat: sed & in omnibus quæ fiunt & geruntur, ipsemet clavum quasi tenet, moderando & disponendo singula atq́; universa, tùm respectu eventuum, tùm ratione finium: bonas quidem actiones atque res efficiendo, adjuvando, approbando: malas verò prohibendo, dirigendo, determinando: ita ut dispensationem hanc DEI specialem, nihil prorsus rerum omnium, quæ sunt, fiunt & geruntur, declinare aut effugere possit.

Ubi tamen discrimen illud, jam aliquo modo indigitatum, observationem longè accuratissimam meretur. Etsi enim divinæ Providentiæ gubernationi, non bonæ tantùm: sed & malæ hominum actiones, imò diabolorum pessimæ, reverà subjacent: diversissimus tamen est actus, quo bona hominum opera gubernantur, ab eo, qui dirigit & moderatur mala.


### Question III. What is the Form: Whether the Providence of God excludes the contingency of human things and actions?

For in the effecting of those things GOD is not only present at hand, but also bestows the strength and grace of His Holy Spirit, so that they may be able to perform good works: according to that saying of the Savior in John 15:5, 'Without me you can do nothing': and of the Prophet Isaiah, chapter 26:12, 'You, O Lord, have wrought all our works in us.' In which respect, indeed, God is more rightly called and celebrated as the author of good actions than as a helper. But as regards evil actions, although God preserves nature itself founded by Him, and the natural powers of acting: for if GOD did not perform this, man could not subsist even for a moment, let alone extend a hand or move a foot from its place: yet He can never be called or thought to be, in any way, either the author or the συνεργὸς of those evil operations. Nor is it an objection that God is read in the Scriptures to permit that the wicked walk in their own ways, according to the desires and inventions of their hearts: Psalm 81:13, Acts 14:15. For not even in this way does God in any manner participate in the effect of those evil actions: since this permission has respect to the justice of GOD, by which He is accustomed to punish preceding, unconquerable contumacy in such a way that He withdraws His grace: which being withdrawn, man of his own accord involves and entangles himself more and more in the snares of impiety and sins. Furthermore, that permission also does not directly regard the sins themselves, but rather that determination or direction by which God partly sets a measure to those evil actions, and prescribes a certain limit, as it were: and partly assigns to them a far different end than that for which they were undertaken and perpetrated by the wicked. Moreover, since there is to be an express discussion for us concerning these Questions in the next article following, it does not pertain to treat of them more fully in this place. Let us rather consider that which comes into controversy most of all concerning the Form of divine Providence.

At the beginning, however, that which seems to fight against this doctrine is that, while this Universal and indeed efficacious Government of GOD stands, all contingency of human things and actions seems to be removed: which some attempt to prove by this argument: If all things are subject to divine Government, they either can be done otherwise than as GOD has decreed from eternity to govern, or they cannot be done otherwise: If the former, divine providence will be deceived: If the latter, then the providence of GOD will bring necessity to the things provided: and consequently all contingency will be removed. But both are absurd: Therefore, that Universal and indeed efficacious Providence or Government of all things will hardly be able to stand.

Concerning the dissolution of this knot, those two distinctions will be most necessary, which those theologians observed who at times explained this part of Christian doctrine more accurately.

The prior distinction is this: Everything mutable and immutable is said in two ways: One, when something by its own nature, of itself, absolutely and

simply is so constituted that it can or cannot be otherwise. But in the other way, when something, not of itself, but by accident: not absolutely and simply, but ἐξ ὑποθέσεως is either mutable or immutable. For example: GOD is good and wise immutably, of Himself, and simply or absolutely: Angels likewise are good and wise also immutably: but not of themselves, or simply: but by Accident: insofar as they are now so confirmed in good that they can no longer fall. Thus, regarding an example of Mutability: Adam was good before the fall mutably, for if he had not been such, he could not have fallen: but because he could have remained good if he had willed: it is most rightly established that this mutability was in him not simply and of itself: but finally from the condition of the will. All the faithful after the fall are likewise good mutably: but simply and of themselves. For in the state of corruption, it cannot be otherwise than that their goodness is mutable.

The posterior distinction is of the Necessary or Necessity. For in our Theology, having set aside other degrees or Divisions of Necessity, of which Logicians and Physicists treat, a twofold Necessity is established. One is Absolute or Simple: called by Logicians otherwise the Necessity of the Consequent: but by Theologians, the Necessity of Coaction: the opposite of which is simply impossible: The other is Conditioned Necessity: called by Logicians otherwise, the Necessity of Consequence, or ἀναγκαῖον ἐκ τῆς ὑποθέσεως: but by Theologians, the Necessity of Condition. That Absolute one is that by which things are so constituted that nothing at all can be changed in them: such as those things which are predicated of the Essence of GOD and His attributes. But that Conditioned one is that by which some thing indeed has a cause, by reason of which it cannot now be changed, or be otherwise: but yet by its own nature it is mutable: and could have been changed and been otherwise entirely. Whose necessity is not inconveniently constituted in three degrees: The first of those things which have been divinely foretold: The second of those things which arise from immutable causes: The third, finally, of those things which are true, even though they were contingent: as Judas betrayed Christ. Thus when the Savior says, It is necessary that scandals come: And Paul: It is necessary that there be heresies among you: in both cases the necessity of Consequence or of Condition is understood: Because, forsooth, such is the perversity of men that scandals and heresies cannot but arise, which perversity being corrected, it could happen otherwise.

These two distinctions having been premised, the latter member of the Disjunction is answered categorically and affirmatively: That those things which have been foreseen by GOD cannot be otherwise: or which is the same thing, that they are not mutable, but κατά τι and with this condition: that they are immutable, forsooth, not simply or in themselves, or by absolute necessity: but only by accident, or by the condition of the thing foreseen. For such as each thing would at some time be future and about to happen, from its causes

Latin:

In illis enim efficiendis DEUS non tantum praesto adest, sed & largitur vires & gratiam Spiritus sui Sancti, ut bona praestare valeant: secundum illud Servatoris Joh. 15, 5. Sine me nihil potestis facere : & Prophetae Jesaiae cap. 26, 12. Omnia opera nostra, Tu Domine, operatus es in nobis. Quo sane respectu Deus bonarum actionum rectius autor, quam adjutor dicitur & celebratur. Caeterum quoad malas actiones, etsi Deus naturam ipsam a se conditam, & naturales agendi vires conservat: nisi enim hoc praestaret DEUS, homo ne ad momentum quidem subsistere, nedum vel manum extendere, vel pedem loco movere posset: nunquam tamen malarum illarum operationum, sive autor, sive συνεργὸς quovis modo dici aut cogitari vel potest vel debet. Neque obstat, quod Deus in Scripturis legitur permittere, ut impij ambulent in vijs suis, secundum desideria & adinventiones cordium suorum: Psal. 81, 13. Act. 14, 15. Nam ne sic quidem Deus effectu malarum illarum actionum ullo modo participat: Siquidem permissio haec respectum habet ad justitiam DEI, qua antegressam inexpugnabilem contumaciam sic punire solet, ut gratiam suam subtrahat: qua subtracta, homo sua sponte magis magisque impietatis & peccatorum laqueis seipsum involvit & implicat. Deinde permissio etiam illa, non directe respicit ipsa peccata, sed potius determinationem sive directionem illam, qua Deus partim malis illis actionibus modum statuit, & certum quasi terminum praescribit: partim vero longe alium finem illis assignat, quam quo ab impijs susceptae & perpetratae fuerunt. Caeterum cum de hisce Quaestionibus, articulo subsequente proximo, nobis ex professo futura sit disputatio, haud attinet fusius hoc loco de illis agere. Id potius pensi habeamus, quod circa Formam divinae Providentiae potissimum in controversiam venit.

Initio autem cum doctrina hac pugnare videtur illud, quod stante hac Universali DEI & quidem efficaci Gubernatione, omnis videtur tolli rerum humanarum & actionum contingentia: id quod hoc argumento nonnulli evincere conantur: Si omnia divinae Gubernationi subjacent, aut aliter fieri possunt, quam prout DEUS ab aeterno gubernare decrevit: aut aliter fieri non possunt: Si illud, falletur divina providentia: Sin hoc: utique DEI providentia rebus provisis adferet necessitatẽ: & per consequens omnis tolletur contingentia. Atqui utrumque absurdum est: Ergo vix stare poterit Universalis illa & quidem efficax rerum omnium Providentia sive Gubernatio.

Circa nodi hujus dissolutionem, Distinctionibus illis duabus vel maxime opus fuerit, quas illi observarunt Theologi, qui aliquando accuratius partem hanc doctrinae Christianae explicarunt.

Prior distinctio est haec: Omne mutabile & immutabile duobus modis dicitur: Uno, quando aliquid natura sua, per se, absolute &

simpliciter ita est comparatum, ut aliter se habere vel possit, vel non possit. Altero verò modo, quando aliquid, non per se, sed ex accidente: non absolutè & simpliciter, sed ἐξ ὑποθέσεως est, vel mutabile, vel immutabile. Exempli gratia: DEUS est bonus ac sapiens immutabiliter, per se, ac simpliciter sive absolutè: Angeli itidem sunt boni ac sapientes etiam immutabiliter: sed non per se, sive simpliciter: verùm ex Accidente: quatenus nimirùm jam ita in bono sunt confirmati, ut prolabi ampliùs nequeant. Sic quoad Mutabilitatis exemplum: Adamus fuit bonus ante lapsum mutabiliter, nisi enim talis fuisset, labi non potuisset: quia verò bonus manere potuisset, si voluisset: rectissimè statuitur mutabilitas hæc in ipso fuisse non simpliciter & per se: sed ex conditione demùm voluntatis. Fideles quique post lapsum itidem boni sunt mutabiliter: verùm simpliciter & per se. Nam in statu corruptionis, fieri aliter nequit, quin mutabilis ipsorum sit bonitas.

Posterior distinctio est Necessarii sive Necessitatis. Nam in Theologiâ nostrâ, posthabitis alijs Necessitatis gradibus sive Divisionibus, de quibus Logici & Physici agunt, duplex Necessitas constituitur, Alia Absoluta sive Simplex: Logicis aliàs dicta Necessitas Consequentis: Theologis verò, Necessitas Coactionis: cujus nimirùm oppositum simpliciter est impossibile: Alia est Necessitas Conditionata: Logicis aliàs dicta, Necessitas Consequentiæ, sive ἀναγκαῖον ἐκ τῆς ὑποθέσεως: Theologis verò Necessitas Conditionis. Absoluta illa est, quâ res ita se habent, ut nihil quicquam in ipsis mutari possit: qualia sunt, quæ de Essentiâ DEI ejusdemque attributis prædicantur. Conditionata verò ea est, quâ res aliqua causam quidem habet, cujus gratia jam non mutari, aut aliter se habere potest: sed naturâ tamen suâ est mutabilis: & mutari atq; aliter omninò se habere potuisset. Cujus Necessitas tres gradus haud incommodè constituuntur: Primus eorum, quæ divinitùs prædicta sunt: Alter eorum, quæ oriuntur ex causis immutabilibus: Tertius denique eorum, quæ vera sunt, etsi fuerunt contingentia: ut Judas prodidit Christum. Sic quando Servator inquit, Necesse est ut veniant scandala: Et Paulus: Oportet hæreses esse in vobis: utrobique necessitas Consequentiæ sive Conditionis intelligitur: Quia nimirùm ea hominum est perversitas, ut non possint non oboriri scandala & hæreses, quâ tamen perversitate correctâ, fieri aliter posset.

Præmissis duabus istis distinctionibus, ad posterius membrum Disjuncti categoricè & affirmatè respondetur: Ea quæ à DEO provisa sunt, aliter se habere non posse: vel quod idem est, non esse mutabilia, verùm κατά τι & cum conditione hac: Immutabiliter nimirùm ea se habere, non simpliciter aut per se, sive necessitate absolutâ: sed tantùm ex accidente, sive conditione rei provisæ. Nam qualis quæque res aliquando futura & eventura esset, ex causis suis


### Question III. What is the Form: Whether Providence brings necessity upon things provided?

whether natural or voluntary: such things GOD has also provided: and now in this respect, the Providence of GOD cannot be deceived. But if they had been destined to be otherwise by their own nature, GOD would have provided for that too, and neither thus could His Providence have been deceived: and in this respect, it is most rightly denied that the things provided can be otherwise than as they have been provided.

Moreover, when the question is now asked: Does this Providence therefore bring necessity upon things provided, and consequently is contingency removed: it is most rightly answered by another distinction. For if necessity is understood as simple or absolute or of the consequent, it is simply denied that Providence brings necessity upon things provided: for thus no place would remain for natural causes, nor would any liberty be left to the will of man: both of which, however, we have demonstrated to the eye in the immediately preceding question to be subordinate to the Providence of GOD and able to stand with it without contradiction. But if the other necessity is understood, which is of condition or of the consequence: we willingly and entirely concede that things provided depend necessarily upon the Providence of GOD: because, to be sure, GOD did not provide those things otherwise than as they were to come to pass from their own causes, therefore they also come to pass just as GOD provided them. Nor, however, does that which is inferred by consequence in the argument militate against this: Therefore all contingency is removed. For because this necessity of consequence belongs to those things which by their own nature are mutable, and could have been changed and been otherwise: certainly that necessity and contingency can stand together as subordinate, although in a different respect: necessity, to be sure, insofar as some thing has a cause, on account of which it can no longer be changed or be otherwise. But contingency, insofar as that very thing is by its own nature so constituted that it could have been otherwise. For example: The betrayal of Judas, in respect to divine Providence, is called necessary by necessity of consequence: because, to be sure, GOD from eternity provided that Judas, with set malice and certain counsel, would betray Christ: but contingent, insofar as he could have resisted the depraved desires of his own will and not betrayed Christ. Which very thing, however, if Judas had done, GOD would also have provided from eternity: and thus, by not betraying, the Providence of GOD could not have been deceived.

Finally, concerning the dissolution of this argument and similar ones, this also must be accurately observed: What, to be sure, the Contingent or Contingency is or is called in this Article: lest by chance Contingent and Fortuitous be taken for the same things. It is defined, however, not only by Logicians but also by Theologians, that the Contingent is that which, when it happens, has a cause which according to its own nature could act otherwise. With this definition standing, it most rightly agrees with divine providence. For although things provided happen indeed necessarily and immutably by reason of providence: yet as far as we are concerned, they have a cause, namely a mutable will, from which they could have happened otherwise. They hallucinate childishly, therefore, who take Contingent and Fortuitous or casual things for the same. Such contingency we simply deny, and with Basil the Great we maintain that it is unworthy of the schools of Christians if those words of the Heathens, Chance and Fortune, are heard in them.

The use and practice of those things which have now been said, both in informing our judgments concerning the various events of things, and in dissolving many most intricate questions, can be very great: which I am pleased to demonstrate by certain examples.

It is asked whether the term prefixed to each life is necessary: or whether it is contingent: so that it can be increased or even diminished? And how does each respect agree with the providence of GOD, which cannot be deceived?

To which question the common run of men for the most part answer in the manner of the Stoics: namely, that a fatal and certain term of our life is so prefixed: that just as GOD has prefixed the term and hour of death for each, so he is necessarily compelled to die: For his little hour is thus set for him. Whose opinion, indeed, we rightly reject as impious and erroneous. For thus the promises of GOD concerning longevity: thus the threats concerning the shortening of the life of the Impious: thus the counsels of Physicians, and the powers of the medicines themselves: thus the prayers and vows of the pious, conceived in a just manner for longevity, would be entirely vain, void, and superfluous: nay, the blame would also redound upon GOD Himself, if anyone were to lay violent hands upon himself, because that term of life had been so prefixed for him by GOD with inevitable necessity. Therefore, in dissolving the proposed question, there will be need of greater circumspection and piety. Wherefore if we consult the scriptures, we discover it to be true, 1. That a certain fixed term is set for every man: but not a fatal one. Then, that this certainty is to be defined not by reason of any absolute decree: but partly with respect to foreknowledge: partly with respect to divine Providence, although in a different manner. With respect indeed to Foreknowledge, insofar as it is infallibly known to GOD, on what day, at what hour, or at what moment of the hour, by what kind of death everyone is to die: Which foreknowledge of GOD, however, ordains, rules, or disposes nothing of this kind: but is completed by mere knowledge: but with respect to Providence, insofar as GOD not only knows, but also pre-fixes and pre-defines for each the term of his life, and not this only, but also the kind of death. He pre-fixes it, however, not by any absolute decree, not by an inevitable law of necessity: but dispositively in consideration partly of secondary causes, which consist either in nature or in the will of man: and finally partly of those which can happen to a man from without. For the sake of example: Although GOD is not bound to secondary causes: yet for the most part He leaves the natural course of Nature: so that when in man the κρᾶσει of the humours is disturbed, the radical moisture fails, together with the native heat, then man dies.
