Insofar, therefore, as GOD now not only foreknows when this is to happen in man, and in what manner: but also by the power of His providence sustains and governs those secondary causes: certainly in this twofold respect, the death of Man is said to have been thus provided for by GOD. Where, however, all absolute and fatal necessity is excluded: But only the ordination of GOD, according to the disposition of natural causes, and that most freely, holds place. For GOD could bend the course of nature, and either promote or hinder it: which He also very often does.

Thus when someone, according to the constitution of the humours of the body, could live for a very long time, but by ἀσωτία or gluttony, accelerates both diseases and a premature death for himself: there that term of life is most rightly said to have been thus prefixed by GOD, partly in respect of His foreknowledge, partly in respect of His providence, insofar as GOD, as a punishment for either gluttony or lasciviousness, prefixes this term to them: when nevertheless He would have prefixed another term to them, had they not as it were cut short their life themselves through ἀσωτία and other wicked deeds. Where again all absolute and fatal necessity expires: Since the prefixing of this term also has a certain respect to secondary causes.

Thus when the pious are snatched away by a premature death: this again is to be thought to happen not by any inevitable law of necessity prefixed by GOD, but rather in respect of certain causes. For as Scripture teaches, the Lord sometimes calls away many who are established in infancy, or childhood, or youth, or in manly age, so that partly malice may not pervert their understanding: and partly that their eyes may not see the evils that are to come, and thus they be judged with this wicked world. Wis. 4, 10. & 11. Isa. 26, 40. & ch. 57, 1. 1 Cor. 11, 32.

Thus a certain term of life, nay even a certain kind of death, is said to be prefixed by GOD for thieves, adulterers, robbers, and other criminals of that kind: not only by reason of foreknowledge: but also in respect of divine providence: insofar as GOD prefixes a certain limit to such criminals, as to how far their impiety and how long it should rage: and at the same time, as a punishment for their preceding malice, determines for them a certain kind of death and punishment: Where again no absolute decree militates: For unless they had been about to devote effort to such wickedness: certainly GOD would have prefixed for them another and a longer and more honest term of life.

Furthermore, almost nothing is heard more frequently in the common life of men than that marriages are fatal: concerning which expression, indeed, what is to be determined is easily evident from those things which have been said thus far. For if this phrase is taken concerning some such absolute decree, by which GOD, without any respect to secondary causes, and especially to the will of man, has so associated a certain wife to any man, or vice versa, that he is compelled by inevitable necessity to join this one and no other to himself in matrimony: then indeed we simply reject it as Stoic. But when marriages are said to be fatal in this sense, that GOD so concurs in the contracting of marriages with the will of men: that in compensation for the preceding piety of the pious, He so governs their will that they desire and join to themselves as a life companion one with whom they can live in peace and tranquility: but permits the impious, as a punishment for their preceding impiety, to abuse their own will, so that they entangle themselves in an unhappy marriage: then indeed we easily admit that marriages are fatal. Where, however, in neither respect does any absolute decree or inevitable connection of causes militate. Moreover, in this part the exception of the cross can by no means or ought to be excluded: Since not rarely a Socrates has his Xantippe, and a Hercules his Omphale: which happens with the providence of GOD also bearing it so, that they may indeed be able to fight so much the more strongly in the School of the cross, and to exercise themselves in the practice of Christian virtues, especially Patience.

These things being thus established, we rightly explode that Fate of the Stoics, to which, as Augustine testifies, they contended that not only the will of men, but GOD Himself is subject: attributing partly to fatal causes that power by which they can act from themselves, and produce any effects whatsoever by their own strength: and partly inventing that the series of causes is immutable. But the same Augustine rightly answered someone who was defending this Fate of the Stoics: If your heart were not fatuous, you would not believe in Fate.

But the patrons of the Stoics fought with two arguments especially, and among these especially Boethius, book 4, On Consolation.

It previously read thus: Every provider establishes his work as best he can, so that it may nowhere fail. But GOD is supremely powerful. Therefore, an immutable necessity exists for things provided.

But Boethius later formulated it thus: Fate, proceeding from the immovable beginnings of Providence, binds all human affairs in an indissoluble connection of causes. Therefore, it leaves nothing at all contingent.

But both arguments proceed from a false hypothesis. For some such necessity of Providence is posited which depends upon secondary causes: which we have just now irrefragably proven to be most false. For although there is a certain necessity of things provided—namely, a necessity ἐξ ὑποθέσεως—it does not, however, depend upon the perpetual nexus of secondary causes, or upon some implicit series included within Nature itself, but upon the certainty of divine Providence.

For in whatever way things happen, whether necessarily or contingently, so also they are foreseen: nor is divine Providence deceived, to the certainty of which itself pertains that immutability which is in the things foreseen: but by no means to the indissoluble connection of causes, about which the patrons of the Stoics fable.

Latin:

sive naturalibus, sive voluntariis: tales etiam DEUS providit: & jam hoc respectu, Providentia DEI falli nequit. Quod si aliter ex naturâ suâ futuræ fuissent, DEUS etiam illud providisset, & neque sic Providentia ipsius falli potuisset: & hoc respectu, res provisæ, aliter, quàm prout provisæ sunt, habere se posse, rectissimè negatur.

Cæterùm quando jam quæritur: Annè igitur Providentia hæc rebus provisis afferat necessitatem: & per consequens tollatur contingentia: per alteram distinctionem rectissimè respondetur. Quòd si enim Necessitas simplex sive absoluta aut consequentis intelligatur, simpliciter negatur, Providentia rebus provisis afferre necessitatem: Sic enim nullus ampliùs locus causis naturalibus, neque etiam voluntati hominis ulla libertas relinqueretur: Quod utrumque tamen Providentiæ DEI subordinatum esse, & cum eâ sine contradictione stare posse, Quæstione præcedente proximâ ad oculum demonstravimus. Quod si verò altera intelligatur Necessitas, quæ est conditionis sive consequentis: libenter omninò concedimus, à Providentiâ DEI res provisas necessariò dependere: Quia nimirùm DEUS non aliter providit res illas, quàm prout ex causis suis eventuræ erant, Ergò sic etiam eveniunt, prout DEUS eas providit. Neque tamen proptereà militat id, quod per consequentiam in argumento infertur: Ergò omnis tollitur contingentia. Quia enim Necessitas hæc consequentiæ, est earum rerum, quæ naturâ suâ sunt mutabiles, & mutari atque aliter se habere potuissent: utique Necessitas etiam illa & contingentia, tanquàm subordinata simul stare possunt, diverso licèt respectu: Necessitas nimirùm, quatenus res aliqua causam habet, ob quam non ampliùs mutari, aut aliter se habere queat. Contingentia verò, quatenus illa ipsa res naturâ suâ ita cõparata est, ut aliter se habere potuisset. Exempli gratiâ: Proditio Judæ respectu Providentiæ divinæ, dicitur necessaria, Necessitate consequentiæ: quia nimirùm DEUS ab æterno providit Judam destinatâ malitiâ, ac consilio certo proditurum Christum: contingens verò, quatenus voluntatis suæ pravis desideriis resistere, & Christum prodere non potuisset. Quod ipsum tamen si fecisset Judas, DEUS etiam ab æterno providisset: & sic, neque non prodendo falli potuisset DEI providentia.

Tandem circa argumenti hujus & similium dissolutionem illud quoque accuratè observandum fuerit: Quid nimirùm Contingens sive Contingentia hoc in Articulo sit aut dicatur: ne fortè Contingens & Fortuitum pro iisdem accipiantur. Definitur autem non modò à Logicis, sed & Theologis, Contingens esse id, quod cum fit, causam habet, quæ secundum naturam suam aliter agere poterat. Stante hâc definitione rectissimè divinæ providentiæ cum Contingentiâ convenit. Nam licèt res provisæ fiant quidem ratione providentiæ necessariò & immutabiliter: tamen quoad nos causam habent, nempè mutabilem voluntatem, ex quâ aliter fieri poterant. Pueriliter proindè hallucinantur, qui Contingentia & Fortuita sive casualia pro iisdem accipiunt. Qualia contingentia nos simpliciter negamus, & cum Basilio Magno statuimus, Indignum esse Christianorum Scholis, si voces istæ Ethnicorum, Casus & Fortunæ in illis audiantur.

Usus & Praxis eorum, quæ jam dicta sunt, tùm in informandis judiciis nostris, de variis rerum eventibus: tùm in dissolvendis plurimis intricatissimis quæstionibus, potest esse maximus: id quod quibusdam exemplis demonstrare libet.

Quæritur, an terminus cujusquè vitæ præfixus, sit necessarius: an verò contingens: ita ut augeri, vel etiam minui possit? & quomodo uterquè respectus cum DEI providentiâ, quæ falli non potest, congruat?

Ad quam Quæstionem vulgus hominum plerumque Stoicorum more respondet: nempè fatalem & certum terminum vitæ nostræ ita esse præfixum: ut prout DEUS cuilibet terminum & horam mortis præfixerit, ita necessariò mori cogatur: Denn sein Stündlein sey ihm also auffgeseßt. Quorum sanè sententiam tanquam impiam & erroneam meritò rejicimus. Sic enim promissiones DEI de longævitate: sic comminationes de abbreviatione vitæ Impiorum: sic Medicorum consilia, & ipsorum medicamentorum vires: sic preces & vota piorum, pro longævitate justo modo conceptæ, prorsus essent vanæ, irritæ & supervacaneæ: quin culpa quoque in DEUM ipsum redundaret, si quis sibiipsi manus violentas inferret, propterea quod iste terminus vitæ, inevitabili necessitate, à DEO sic ipsi esset præfixus. Proindè in dissolvendâ propositâ quæstione, majore circumspectione & pietate opus fuerit. Quare si scripturas consulamus, verum quidem esse deprehendimus, 1. Cuilibet homini certum præfixum esse terminum: sed non fatalem. Deindè certitudine illam definiendam esse non ratione absoluti alicujus decreti: sed partim respectu præscientiæ: partim respectu Providentiæ divinæ, diversâ licèt ratione. Respectu quidem Præscientiæ, quatenus DEO infallibiliter notum, quo die, quâ horâ, quové horæ momento, quo mortis genere quilibet, sit moriturus: Quæ tamen præscientia DEI nihil hujusmodi ordinat, regit aut disponit: sed merâ notitiâ absolvitur: verùm respectu Providentiæ, quatenus DEUS non tantum novit, sed etiam præsigit & præfinit cuique vitæ suæ terminum, nec hunc modò, sed & mortis genus. Præfigit autem non absoluto aliquo de- « creto, non inevitabili necessitatis lege: sed di- « spositivè pro consideratione partim causarum secundarum, quæ vel in naturâ, vel in hominis « voluntate consistunt: partim deniquè earum « quæ forinsecùs homini evenire possunt. Exempli gratiâ: Etsi DEUS non est alligatus ad causas secundas : plerumque tamen Naturæ cursum naturalem relinquit: ita ut quando in homine turbata κρᾶσει humorum, deficit humidum radicale, unà cum calido nativo, tùm homo moriatur. Quatenùs ergò jam DEUS non modò præscit, quando hoc in homine, & quo pacto sit eventurum: sed & vi providentiæ suæ causas illas secundas sustentat ac regit: utique gemino hoc respectu, jam mors Hominis dicitur ita à DEO fuisse provisa. Ubi tamen omnis absoluta & fatalis necessitas exulat: Sed DEI tantùm ordinatio, secundum dispositionem causarum naturalium, eaque longè liberrima locum obtinet. Posset enim DEUS naturæ cursum inflectere, & vel promovere, vel impedire: id quod sæpissimè etiam facit.

Sic quando aliquis pro constitutione humorum corporis quàm diutissimè vivere posset, sed ἀσωτία sive crapulâ, tùm morbos, tùm mortem præproperam sibi accelerat: ibi terminus iste vitæ rectissimè dicitur à DEO sic esse præfixus, partim respectu præscientiæ, partim respectu providentiæ ipsius, quatenùs nimirùm DEUS in pœnam vel crapulæ, vel lasciviæ, hunc ipsis terminum præfigit: cùm tamen alium ipsis terminum præfixisse, nisi sibiipli per ἀσωτίαν & alia flagitia vitam quasi abrupissent. Ubi rursus omnis absoluta & fatalis necessitas expirat: Siquidem præfixio hujus etiam termini, certum ad causas secundas habet respectum.

Sic quando pii præmaturâ morte abripiuntur : id rursum non inevitabili quapiam necessitatis lege à DEO præfixat sed potiùs respectu certarum causarum, fieri existimandum est. Nam scriptura docente plures interdum in infantiâ, vel pueritiâ vel juventute, vel in virili ætate constitutos evocat Dominus, ut partim malitia non pervertat ipsorum intellectum: partim verò ne videant oculi ipsorum eventura mala, & sic cum impio hoc mundo judicentur. Sap. 4, 10. & 11. Jes. 26, 40. & cap 57, 1. 1. Cor. 11, 32.

Sic certus vitæ terminus, imò certum etiam mortis genus dicitur à DEO esse præfixum, furibus, adulteris, latronibus, & id genus sceleratis aliis: non modò ratione præscientiæ: sed & respectu providentiæ divinæ: quatenus nimirùm DEUS bujusmodi sceleratis certam metam præfigit, quousque ipsorum impietas, & quamdiu grassari debeat: & simul in pœnam antegrefsæ malitiæ certum mortis ac supplicii genus ipsis determinat: Ubi rursus nullum absolutum decretum militat: Nisi enim hujusmodi sceleribus operam daturi fuissent: certè alium etiam & diuturniorem & honestiorem vitæ terminum DEUS ipsis præfixisset.

Porrò nihil fermè frequentiùs in communi hominum vitâ auditur: quàm conjugia esse fatalia: de quâ sanè locutione quid sit statuendum, ex iis quæ hactenus dicta sunt, facilè patet. Nam si phrasis isthæc accipiatur, de de tali aliquo absoluto decreto, quo DEUS sine ullo respectu ad causas secundas, & cumprimis ad voluntatem hominis, cuilibet viro, ita certam uxorem, vel contrà, associârit, ut inevitabili necessitate cogatur aliquando hanc, & non aliam sibi in matrimonium jungere : tum sanè eam ceu Stoicam simpliciter improbamus. Quando verò conjugia hoc sensu dicuntur esse fatalia, quod DEUS in matrimoniis contrahendis, cum voluntate hominum ita concurrat: ut in compensationem pietatis antegressæ piorum voluntatem ita regat, ut eam sibi optent & jungant vitæ sociam, cum quâ in pace & tranquillitate vivere queant: Impios verò in pœnam antegressæ Impietatis, permittat abuti suâ voluntate, ut semetipsos infelici conjugio implicent : tum sanè facilè admittimus conjugia esse fatalia. Ubi tamen neutro respectu ullum absolutum decretum, vel inevitabilis causarum connexio militat. Cæterùm hac in parte exceptio crucis minimè excludi potest aut debet : Siquidem haud rarò priùs quoque suam fortiter Xantippem, & Hercules suam Omphalem: id quod fit DEI etiam sic ferente providentiâ, ut nimirùm sic in Schola crucis tantò fortiùs pugnare, & in exercitio virtutum Christianarum, Patientiæ cumprimis, se exercere queant.

Quibus ita constitutis, meritò explodimus Fatum illud Stoicorum, cui Augustino teste, non hominum tantùm voluntatem, sed ipsum etiam DEUM subjacere contenderunt: tribuentes partim causis fatalibus eam vim, quâ ex seipsis agere, & viribus suis quoslibet effectus producere queant: partim verò comminiscentes seriem causarum esse immutabilem. Rectè autem idem Augustinus, cuipiam, Fatum istud Stoicorum propugnanti, respondit: Si cor tuum non esset fatuum, non crederes Fatum.

Duobus autem potissimùm argumentis Stoicorum Patroni pugnabant, & inter hos cumprimis Boëthius lib. 4. de consol.

Prius sic habebat: Omnis provisor sic stabilit pro virili opus suum, ne uspiam deficiant. Atqui DEUS summè potens est. Constat Ergò rebus provisis immutabilis necessitas.

Posterius verò sic informabat Boëthius: Fatum ab immobilibus Providentiæ exordiis proficiscens, humana omnia indissolubili causarum connexione astringit. Ergò contingens nihil prorsus reliquit.

Verùm utrunique argumentum ex falsâ procedit hypothesi. Statuitur enim talis aliqua Providentiæ necessitas, quæ causis secundis dependeat: id quod falsissimum esse, jam modò irrefragabiliter evicimus. Etsi enim rerum provisarum aliqua est necessitas: necessitas videlicet ἐξ ὑποθέσεως: ea tamen non dependet à causarum secundarum perpetuo nexu, sive implicitâ quadam serie, Naturæ ipsi inclusâ: sed à Providentiæ divinæ certitudine.

Quo enim cunque modo res eveniunt, sive necessariò sive contingenter: ita etiam provisæ sunt: neque fallitur divina Providentia, ad cujus ipsius certitudinem, immutabilitas illa pertinet, quæ est in rebus provisis: neutiquam verò ad indissolubilem causarum connexionem: de quâ Stoicorum patroni fabulantur.


### Question IV. How the Foreknowledge, Providence, and Predestination of God relate to one another

In the discussion concerning the eternal Providence of God, one must accurately distinguish between Foreknowledge, Providence, and Predestination. For the confusion of these terms most easily produces such an error that God Himself is affected with contumely. At the beginning, however, Providence and Foreknowledge seem to differ as if by substance: since Foreknowledge is nothing other than that Essential idiom in God which is and is called Omniscience, and is most simply convertible with the very essence of God. Providence, however, seems to be more like a secondary affection, or an Essential Effect in God of the will, by reason of which God proceeds outwardly to creatures, and disposes, rules, and governs them in various ways: exercising now the majesty of Omnipotence, now of mercy, now of justice, now of Omniscience, most freely through the things and actions of men.

Then, although the Foreknowledge and Providence of God are of the same breadth, that is, extend equally widely, reaching themselves to all things both bad and good: yet they differ in this very much, that by the word Providence is noted the act and efficacious operation in those things and actions which are, come to be, and are carried out in this world: but by the word Foreknowledge is expressed only the habit of knowledge in the mind of God: not indeed the cause of the things foreknown. For, as Justin Martyr and Philosopher rightly argues: Foreknowledge is not the cause of that which is to be: but that which is to be is the cause of the foreknowledge: since the Future does not follow foreknowledge: but the Future follows foreknowledge. Response 58 to the Orthodox. For you would not immediately compel him to sin whom you foresaw would sin: nor would your foreknowledge itself compel him to sin, although without doubt he was going to sin: for you would not foresee it to be future otherwise: And just as you by your memory do not compel things to have happened which have passed: so God by His foreknowledge does not compel things to be done which are to be. And just as you remember certain things which you have done: nor yet have you done all things which you remember: So God foreknows all things of which He Himself is the author, nor yet is He Himself the author of all things which He foreknows: But of those things of which He is not the evil author, He is the just avenger: as Augustine once very skillfully discussed in book 3, de l. Arb. cap. 4. It would therefore be a sin, as Augustine again infers, to ascribe to God the causes of such ruins: for if from eternal knowledge He has foreknown what He is to requite for the merits of each one: yet by this, that He cannot be deceived, He has brought upon no one either the necessity or the will to sin. Response 13 to the articles falsely imposed upon him.

With these things observed, it is immediately clear that Foreknowledge is not properly predicated of God, but only κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν (after the manner of men): since speaking properly there is nothing past for God, and nothing future: but all things are present. For as Prosper of Aquitaine elegantly writes, sentent. 40 from Augustine: That which is new in time is not new to God, who created times, and without time possesses all things, which He distributes in their own times according to their variety.

Then it is clear from this that it is indeed true that divine foreknowledge cannot be deceived: but that in respect to it all things happen necessarily: by a necessity, namely, of consequence, or ἐξ ὑποθέσεως (by hypothesis), but not by a necessity of the consequent, or absolute: much less by a necessity of coercion.

Thirdly, it is clear from this also, namely that by the Foreknowledge of God contingency is not removed in human affairs. Since those things which are foreknown by God could also happen otherwise, being by their nature mutable, before they are brought to the event foreknown by God: For if they had met with another event, God would have foreknown them otherwise: In almost the same way as in Prophetic predictions, that prediction is not the cause of that which is predicted: but individual things were predicted because they were going to be. Nor does it stand in the way that which is read in John 12:38: When Jesus had done so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, that the word of Isaiah the Prophet might be fulfilled: And again in verse 39: Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again, etc. For this particle, Because, is not causal, but of event: nor because Isaiah said it, therefore they did not believe: but because they were not going to believe, therefore Isaiah said it: as Chrysostom rightly determines, Homily 6 on John.

Finally, it is evident from this also that one must distinguish between the Foreknowledge of God, insofar as it is considered in itself as an essential idiom of God: and insofar as it relates to things foreknown. For considered in the former way, it denotes the most perfect and most absolute idiom of divine Omniscience: which cannot be perfected or determined by any thing: so that if even in the greatest degree no things were created, yet it would remain most perfect in itself. But considered in the latter way, it cannot be denied that the Foreknowledge of God meets with a limitation of mode: insofar as God is said to foreknow created and future things, in the way in which they happen. Which limitation itself, however, imports no perfection or imperfection at all to the foreknowledge of God: since firstly that mutability depends only on the condition of things, which before they arrive at a certain event, are by their nature mutable, and could have met with another event: Then, whether this or that outcome human affairs may have: yet GOD would always have infallibly foreseen that: since absolutely nothing can escape His Omniscience.

Moreover, ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, that also deserves observation in this place, that the word προγνώσεως or Foreknowledge is accepted in sacred writings chiefly in three ways: First, most generally, concerning the simple knowledge of all things, as well evil as good: concerning which it has been treated thus far. Then, however, specially and as it were restrictedly or determinately to the faithful alone, or the Elect Children of GOD: In which sense it is accepted in Rom. 8, 29. Whom He foreknew, them He also predestined.

Finally, it is most specially predicated of Christ alone and His merit: as in Acts 2, 23. Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and Foreknowledge of GOD, when you had taken, you crucified. And 1 Pet. 1, 20. You were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ τῦ προεγνωσμένη foreknown before the foundation of the world. Concerning which two latter respects, there will be a future Disputation for us in the Article concerning the eternal predestination of GOD.

And in this way indeed the Providence and Foreknowledge of GOD differ very much from each other. But no lighter distinction intervenes between the same Providence and Predestination. For the Providence of GOD is concerned with all created things, and looks to the governance of all events: as was demonstrated in questions 2 and 3 above: Predestination, however, or the eternal election of GOD, pertains only to the good and elect Children of GOD: that is, to those who are finally saved and glorified: as we shall demonstrate expressly in its proper place.

These things having been thus discussed, we finally conclude, and elicit that definition of divine Providence from the things already said: PROVIDENCE is an action of GOD, by which He not only foreknows and foresees all individual and universal future things: but also partly preserves, and partly so rules and governs the natures of things and the order founded by Himself, that absolutely nothing escapes His care: and in all things which happen and are done, nothing happens without Him either not effecting and assisting: or at least not determining and disposing.

Topic V. CONCERNING THE CAUSE OF SIN. THEOLOGICAL TREATMENT. Of the Article, which is, concerning the CAUSE OF SIN.

Latin:

IN disputatione de æternâ DEI Providentiâ, accuratè inter Præscientiam, Providentiam & Præstinationem distingvendum est. Facillimè enim vocabulorum istorum confusio talem errorem parit, ut DEUS ipse contumeliâ afficiatur. Initiò autem Providentia & Præscientia ipsâ quasi substantiâ differre videntur: Siquidem Præscientia nihil est aliud, quàm Essentiale illud idioma in DEO, quod est ac dicitur Omniscientia, & cum ipsissimâ DEI essentiâ simplicissimè convertitur. Providentia autem videtur magis esse Affectus quasi secundus: sive Effectus Essentialis in DEO voluntatis, ratione cujus DEUS foràs ad creaturas progreditur, & eas disponit regit & gubernat diversimodè: jam quidem Omnipotentiæ, jam misericordiæ, nunc justitiæ, nunc Omniscientiæ Majestatem, per res & actiones hominum liberrimè exercens.

Deinè, licet Præscientia & Providentia DEI, ejusdem sint latitudinis, hoc est, æquè latè pateant, sese ad res omnes tam malas, quàm bonas extendentes: in eo tamen quàmplurimùm differunt, quòd Providentiæ vocabulo notatur actus & operatio efficax in rebus & actionibus illis, quæ sunt, fiunt, & geruntur hoc in mundo: Præscientiæ autem vocabulo exprimitur tantùm habitus notitiæ in mente DEI: non verò causa rerum præscitarum. Nam, uti rectè Justinus Martyr & Philosophus, disputat: Præscientia non est causa ejus quod futurum est: sed id, quod futurum est, causa est præscientiæ: Siquidem non præscientiam sequitur Futurum: sed Futurum consequitur præscientia. Respons. 58. ad Orthodoxos. Non enim continuò tu peccare cogeres, quem peccaturum præscires: neque ipsa præscientia tua peccare eum cogeret, quamvis sine dubio peccaturus esset: non enim aliter id futurum præscires: Et sicut tu memoria tua non cogis facta esse, quæ præterierunt: sic DEUS præscientiâ suâ non cogit facienda, quæ futura sunt. Et sicut tu quædam, quæ fecisti, meministi: nec tamen omnia quæ meministi, fecisti: Ita Deus omnia, quorum ipse autor est præscit nec tamen omnium quæ præscit ipse author est: Quorum autem non est malus autor, eorum justus est ultor: uti scitè admodum disseruit olim Augustinus lib. 3. de l. Arb cap. 4. Nefas proindè fuerit, ut rursum Augustinus infert DEO adscribere causas talium ruinarum : quiet si ex æternâ scientiâ præcognitum habet, quid uniuscujusque, meritis retributurus sit:nemini tamen per hoc, quod falli non potest, aut necefsitatem aut voluntatem intulit delinquendi. Respons. 13. ad articulos falsò sibi impositos.

Quibus observatis illud statim liquet, Præscientiam de DEO non propriè prædicari, sed κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν solummodò: cùm propriè loquendo DEO nihil sit præteritum, nihilque futurum: sed omnia præsentia. Nam uti eleganter scribit Prosper Aquitanicus, sentent. 40. ex Augustino; Id quod in tempore novum est, non est novum apud DEUM, qui condidit tempora, & sine tempore habet omnia, quæ suis quibusq; temporibus pro eorum varietate distribuit.

Deindè patet hinc verum quidem esse, quòd divina præscientia falli nequeat: sed ejus respectu omnia fiant necessariò: necessitate, videlicet consequentiæ, seu ἐξ ὑποθέσεως non autem necessitate consequentis, seu absolutâ: multò minùs autem necessitate coactionis.

Tertiò liquet hinc & illud, nempè per Præscientiam DEI non tolli in rebus humanis contingentiam. Siquidem ea quæ à DEO præscita sunt, aliter etiam fieri possent, quippè naturâ suâ mutabilia, priusquàm ad eventum à DEO præscitum perducuntur: Nam si alium eventum sortita fuissent, aliter etiam DEUS ea præscivisset: Eodem fermè modo, quo in prædictionibus Propheticis, prædictio illa non est causa ejus quod prædicitur: sed ideò singula prædicta sunt, quia futura fuerant. Neq; obstat, quod Johan. 12, 38. legitur: Tanta cùm fecisset Jesus signa coràm eis, non crediderunt in eum, ut sermo Jesaiæ Prophetæ impleretur: Et iterum versu 39. Proptereà non poterant credere, quia rursus dicit Esaias &c. Nam particula hæc, Quia, non causalis est, sed eventus: neque quia dixit Esaias, ideò non crediderunt: sed quia non credituri erant, ideò dixit Jesaias: uti rectè statuit Chrysostomus, Homil. 6. in Johannem.

Tandem constat hinc etiam distingvendum esse inter Præscientiam DEI, quatenùs ea in se, ut essentiale DEI idioma consideratur: & quatenùs sese habet ad res præscitas. Priore enim modo considerata, perfectissimum & absolutissimum notat Omniscientiæ divinæ idioma: quod nullâ re perfici aut determinari potest: ita ut si vel maximè nullæ res essent conditæ, tamen illa sibi constaret perfectissima. Posteriore verò modo considerata, negari non potest, quin Præscientia DEI limitationem modi sortiatur: quatenùs nimirùm DEUS præscire dicitur res conditas & futuras, eo modo, quo eveniunt. Quæ ipsa tamen limitatio nullam prorsus sive perfectionem, sive imperfectionem præscientiæ DEI importat: Siquidem primò mutabilitas illa dependet tantùm à conditione rerum, quæ priusquàm ad certum eventum perveniunt, naturâ suâ sunt mutabiles, & alium eventum sortiri potuissent: Deindè, sive hunc sive illum eventum res humanae fortiantur: tamen illud semper infallibiliter DEUS praescivisset: siquidem nihil prorsus Omniscientiam ipsius effugere potest.

Caeterùm ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ illud quoque hoc loco observationem meretur, quod vocabulum προγνώσεως sive Praescientiae, in sacris tribus potissimùm modis accipitur: Primò Generalissimè de simplici notitia rerum omnium tàm malarum, quàm bonarum: de quâ hactenus actum. Deindè verò specialiter & quasi restrictè sive determinatè ad solos fideles, sive Electos DEI Filios: Quo sensu accipitur Rom. 8, 29. Quos praescivit, hos etiam praedestinavit.

Tandem specialissimè praedicatur de solo Christo ejusque meritò: ut Act. 2, 23. Hunc definito consilio & Praescientiâ DEI traditum cùm accepissetis, crucifixistis. Et 1. Pet. 1, 20. Redempti estis pretioso sanguine Christi τῦ προεγνωσμένη praesciti ante mundi constitutionem De quibus duobus postremis respectibus, in Articulo de aeternâ DEI praedestinatione nobis futura Disputatio.

Et hoc quidem pacto Providentia & Praescientia DEI plurimùm à se mutuò differunt. Sed neque levius discrimen eidem Providentiae intercedit etiam cum Praestinatione. Providentia enim DEI versatur circa res creatas omnes, omniumque eventuum gubernationem respicit: uti quaestionibus 2. & 3. suprà fuit demonstratum: Praedestinatio autem, sive aeterna DEI electio, tantùm ad bonos & electos DEI Filios pertinet: hoc est, ad eos, qui tandem salvantur & glorificantur: uti suo loco ex professo demonstrabimus.

Quibus ita discussis concludimus tandem, & istam Providentiae divinae definitionem ex jam dictis elicimus: PROVIDENTIA est actio DEI, quâ non tantùm prescit ac praevidet res futuras singulas & universas: sed & naturas rerum, & ordinem à se conditum partim conservat, partim ita etiam regit & gubernat, ut curam ipsius nihil prorsus effugiat: & in omnibus quae fiunt & geruntur, nihil ipso vel non efficiente atque adjuvante: vel non determinante saltem & disponente eveniat.

Locus V. DE CAUSA PECCATI. TRACTATIO THEOLOGICA. Articuli, qui est, de CAUSA PECCATI.


## 7 On the Cause of Sin

Our Author joins also in this place two distinct articles: of which one is concerning the cause of Sin: the other concerning contingency and necessity. Great indeed is the kinship of both: so that in the conflict of disputation, they can scarcely be separated from each other. For since already from the first beginnings of the Christian Church, more sincere Theology has established that all things in general, which are, happen and are done in this world, as well evils or sins, as goods, are subject to the governance of divine providence: it began to be asked immediately: In what way or respect would Sins come under the rule of divine providence? Should GOD perhaps be established as the author and abettor of these just as of things rightly done? Should some contingency of Sins be granted, and such indeed as would exclude every necessity of sinning simply? Should finally, this being denied, a Man be able to be said to sin necessarily, and indeed with the providence of GOD so disposing? Hence therefore it happened that Philip, and those who followed him, expedited these Questions with one and the same thread of Treatment: But since in Theological Schools, not primarily the kinship of Articles, which intervenes absolutely between each and all: but rather the proper πάθος or affection of the things themselves and the objects, is to be considered by those who desire to be engaged in treating the chapters of the Christian Religion with a more accurate Method: certainly hardly anyone (whether good or sane) would turn it to our fault, if this time we, making a divorce from Philip, dispute separately concerning the cause of sin; and concerning Necessity and contingency: with the beginning indeed made from that controversy, which is clearly Classical, concerning the cause of Evil or sin, which is agitated today.

As regards the Philippean Treatment, it consists of and is completed in two parts. For in the beginning our Author recounts and rejects the frenzies rather than errors of certain Philosophers and Manichaeans concerning the cause of evil or sin: so that this former part can supply the place of an antithesis. Then, however, he proposes, confirms, and vindicates from certain Sophistications the purer doctrine: so that this latter part may deservedly be for us in the place of a Thesis. In the exposition of both parts, however, the author approved such purity and ὀρθοδοξίαν to the Church of GOD, that, if in any other, certainly in this article, he has manifestly dissented from the schools of the Calvinists and other fanatics.

We, partly following the footsteps of our author: partly, however, weighing the controversies of our own times a little more accurately, likewise constitute TWO chapters of our future Treatment: of which indeed the FORMER will weave through the Negative ἀπόφασιν showing: that GOD can in no way or respect be established as the cause of Sin. Where that solemn controversy, which intervenes in our Churches partly with certain Batavian Libertines, partly with the Calvinists, will be recalled under the anvil of Treatment.

Latin:

COnjungit & hoc loco Autor noster duos distinctos articulos : quorum alter est, de causâ Peccati: alter de contingentiâ & necessitate. Magna quidem utriusque est cognatio : ita ut in disputationis conflictu, vix à se mutuò separari queant. Nam cùm jam indè à primis Ecclesiæ Christianæ Exordiis, sincerior Theologia statuerit, omnia in universum, quæ sunt, fiunt ac geruntur hoc in mundo, tàm mala sive peccata, quàm bona, divinæ providentiæ gubernationi subesse : statim quæri cœptum fuit: Quonam pacto sive respectu, Peccata sub regimen divinæ providentiæ venirent: Nùm fortè istorum perindè ac rectè factorum autor & fautor esset constituendus DEUS? Num Peccatorum aliqua contingentia concedenda, & talis quidem, quæ omnem simpliciter peccandi necessitatem excluderet? Nùm denique hâc negatâ, Homo necessariò peccare, & quidem DEI providentia sic disponente, peccare dici posset? Hinc ergò factum, ut Philipus, & qui eum secuti, uno eodemque Tractationis filo, Quæstiones istas expediverint : Verùm cùm in Scholis Theologicis, non præcipuè Articulorum cognatio, quæ singulis atque universis prorsus intercedit indissolubilis : sed rerum potiùs ipsarum, & objectorum proprium quasi πάθος sive affectio, consideranda sit iis, qui accuratiore Methodo, in pertractandis Religionis Christianæ capitibus versari cupiunt: utique vix quisquam (sive bonus sive sanus) vitio nobis verterit, si hac iterum vice à Philippo divortium facientes, seorsim tùm de causâ peccati; tùm de Necessitate & contingentiâ disputemus : Initio quidem facto ab eâ controversia, quæ planè Classica, de Mali sive peccati causâ, hodiè agitatur.

Quoad Tractationem Philippéam, duabus ea constat & absolvitur partibus. Initiò enim tùm Philosophorum quorundam, tùm Manichæorum furores potiùs, quàm errores de causâ mali sive peccati percenset & rejicit Autor noster : ita ut prior hæc pars, ἀντιθέσεως vicem supplere possit. Deindè verò puriorem doctrinam proponit, confirmat, & à Sophisticationibus quibus dam vindicat : ita ut pars hæc posterior, meritò Theseως loco nobis esse debeat. In utriusque verò partis diexodo, eam puritatem & ὀρθοδοξίαν, Ecclesiæ DEI probavit autor, ut, si in ullo alio, certè hoc in articulo, à Calvinianorum, aliorumque fanaticorum Scholis manifestè dissenserit.

Nos partim autoris nostri secuti vestigia : partim verò nostrorum temporum controversias paulò accuratiùs pensi habentes, DUO itidem futuræ Tractationis nostræ capita constituimus : quorum quidem PRIUS ἀπόφασιν Negativam pertexet ostendens : DEUM nullo prorsus pacto aut respectu, Peccati causam posse constitui. Ubi solennis illa controversia, quæ nostris Ecclesiis partim cum Batavis quibusdam Libertinis, partim cum Calvinianis intercedit, sub Tractationis incudem revocabitur.


### That God is not the cause of sin is proved

The latter, however, will explain the κατάφασιν or Affirmative: making plain what, according to the Scriptures, ought to be truly and properly defined as the cause of sin. Where we shall examine and refute the ψευδολογίας of the philosophers in part, and of the Manichaeans in part.

CHAPTER I. That GOD can by no means or respect be constituted the cause of the evil of fault or of Sin.

That GOD is the cause of sin, we simply deny, along with our Author and all Orthodox persons. By the term cause, however, we understand not only the principal Efficient cause: but whatever can have a respect of a cause, whether Efficient, or impelling, or cooperating, or creating, or inclining, or commanding, or approving, or willing, or decreeing, or finally in any way instigating or compelling.

Similarly, by the term Sin, there comes to us whatever falls under the scope of either Original or Actual Sin: indeed, whatever obtains the name and definition of any vice or fault whatsoever.

The oracles of the Scriptures give entirely undoubted assurance to this negative of ours: and that in four ways.

For first, they proclaim GOD to be as supremely Good as He is supremely just: Matt. 19:17, Mark 10:18, Luke 18:19. One and Only GOD is good.

Now, however, GOD is immutably such: Exod. 3:14, I am who I am: And Mal. 3:6, I am Jehovah, and I do not change.

Therefore, it can by no means happen that GOD should at any time have ceased, or should cease, to be GOD, that is, that having laid aside His Essential goodness, He should undergo the nature of any Evil: which is what would entirely follow if GOD, in any way or respect, were to ordain, or will, or effect, or approve of sin, insofar as it is such.

Furthermore, Scripture describes GOD as just and perfect, so that whatever proceeds from GOD in any respect, that is both just and perfect: Deut. 32:4, The works of GOD are perfect, and all his ways are judgments: GOD is faithful, and without any iniquity, just and upright: Psalm 119:137, You are just, O LORD, and all your judgments are right.

Now, however, there is no participation of Justice with injustice: of perfection with imperfection: no fellowship of Light with darkness: no communion of Christ with Belial. 2 Cor. 6:14 and 15.

And yet Evil or sin is nothing other than injustice, than Imperfection, nay, as Damascenus speaks, it is entirely παρὰ φύσιν, καὶ μὴ ὄν:

Therefore Sin can in no way be referred to GOD as its author, nor ought it to be.

Thirdly, Scripture is witness that GOD not only does not will, but also seriously hates, forbids, detests, punishes, and finally eternally condemns sin, nay, tolerates it with great patience Psalm 5, 5. Thou art not a GOD willing iniquity: thou hatest all who work iniquity. Deut. 18, 15. & seqq. Rom. 9, 22. 1 Thess. 4, 6. The Lord is the avenger of all things &c.

But indeed GOD hates nothing of those things which He has made: For neither does He establish or make anything while hating it: Wisd. 11, 25. Therefore, that GOD cannot in any way be established as the author or cause of sin, can be a doubt to no pious person.

Finally, contradictory causes can never be mutually ὑπαλληλοι: or be recalled to the same first principle.

But indeed GOD is established in the Scriptures as the author and cause of all good: but the Devil as the author and cause of all sin. Gen. 1, 3. GOD saw all things which He had made, and they were very good: James 1, 17. Every perfect and good gift descends from above from the Father of Lights. John 8, 44. The Devil was a murderer from the beginning, and stood not in the truth, because the truth is not in him, when he speaks a lie, ἐξ ἰδιων, he speaks from his own: because he is a liar, and the Father of lies. 1 John 3, 8. He who commits sin is of the Devil, because the Devil sins from the beginning.

Therefore the cause of sin can never be ὑπαλληλος to the cause of good, and consequently, from the same first principle from which Good depends, Sin can in no way proceed.

THE OTHER foundation of our negative is built upon certain and entirely infallible hypotheses: of which the FIRST is thus: Sin is not a thing created by GOD: but rather it is a horrible destruction, or certainly the highest corruption of a most noble work created by GOD. Therefore it cannot have GOD as its author: unless perhaps someone wishes to affirm that GOD, having become weary of a work once created by Himself, wished to destroy it through some other work likewise created by Himself: or certainly to cast it down from a state of goodness and perfection to a state of evil and imperfection: which is prodigiously blasphemous.

The second sounds thus. Whatever GOD makes or creates: that is of the Genus of Beings, or something positive.

But Sin is not of the Genus of Substantials: nor is it a positive Substantial thing among Beings: But it is a defect or privation: or as we are accustomed to speak in the Schools, it is a privative Nothing. Whence not ineptly one of the Fathers wrote: That Sin lacks both its own end, and an efficient cause, and consequently, Essence. An end indeed, insofar as the will is always carried elsewhere, and never seeks evil. An efficient cause truly, because no efficient cause can be assigned for deficient Effects.

Therefore the efficient cause of Sin, as a Defect, is not to be sought in God.

The third can be such: If GOD were the author of Sin: he himself would certainly also be a sinner: and consequently, he would not even be GOD any longer.

And yet this latter is signally blasphemous. Therefore such is that former also.

Fourth. In GOD, wills that are contradictory, as well as contrary to His Essence, simply cannot exist. And yet to will good, and to will sin: likewise to hate, detest, and punish sins: and to be the author of the same: imply contradictory wills. Therefore: it is by no means possible for both to be predicated of GOD.

Fifth: If GOD is the cause of sin, it is necessary that one of these two things follow: namely, either that Sin is good in itself and by its own nature: or that GOD errs from His Object. The reason for this is: Because just as the Intellect has the true for its object: So the object of the will is that which is good.

And yet neither can be affirmed without prejudice to the analogy of faith. Therefore it would be heretical, nay even blasphemous, that from which both of these follow.

Sixth and last. If all determinations of actions are from a particular Efficient cause: It is a consequence that GOD cannot be the cause of sin. The reason for this consequence is this: Because GOD is the Universal cause of actions. Now, however, that former point is true beyond controversy. For vice, defect, or ἀταξία, is inherent in actions, not insofar as they are actions: but insofar as they are already determined in this way. But this determination does not proceed from a universal, but from a particular cause. For example: the will of Judas betraying Christ, insofar as it depends on the universal cause, is not evil: for in respect of this cause, Judas only had the ability to will, without determination toward evil. But that he now wills Evil: that does not depend on the universal cause which is GOD: but on the particular cause, which is the will now abusing itself toward evil.

THE THIRD and last foundation of our negative position is, as it were, subsidiary, taken from the unanimous consent of Orthodox Antiquity: nay, even from the judgment of the sounder Philosophers.

For the minds and ears of all have so abhorred that proposition: that GOD is the cause of sin, that outside the Church, Plato in book 2 of the πολιτεῖαι, brought forth this memorable sentiment: We must fight with all contention, lest anyone in the city, which we wish to be well governed, should either say or hear, whether old man or youth, whether in a poem or in any other narrative, that GOD is the cause of evils to anyone: Which can neither truly be said in this way, nor is it useful to the city, nor does it agree with itself in explanation. Similarly in the Church, the heretics themselves, such as the Manichaeans, preferred to invent some other evil GOD, rather than ascribe the cause of sin to GOD, who is supremely good and just.

Furthermore, Eusebius is a witness in book 5, chapter 18, around A.D. 170, or according to others, 182, that a certain Florinus, a disciple of Montanus, was for this reason struck with anathema by the Church and proclaimed a heretic, because he contended that Evil is from GOD, and that GOD commits sins not only permissively, but also effectively.

Irenaeus, under the title of heresy, noted the dogmas of the Valentinians, who contended that the hardening of Pharaoh and the blinding of the Jews were, by tradition

of the Gentiles into a reprobate mind, were works of God, imposed upon men by divine necessity to be perpetrated. lib. 4. cont. hær. cap. 47. & 48. In Eusebius, lib. 6. cap. 5. concerning the Evangelical Preparation, this is an illustrious sentiment: Truly he will be judged impious, nay, the worst of all, who thinks that some are driven by the creator of the universe to adulteries, others to rapines, and others to other vices. For from this it would follow: Either that these are not sins: or that the cause of sinning is referred to the creator: than which dogma nothing more wicked can be conceived. Augustine: By no wise author is anyone made worse, and according to the same: Those things which are necessary to be done by my authority and command, I may deservedly be considered the author of them. Those are to be held unworthy of the name of Christians who establish GOD, who is good by nature, as the cause of evil or the author of any depraved will, or action, whether exciting or impelling. lib. 83. q. 3. Chrysost. Homil. 23. in Acts of the Apostles. It is better to be buried in the earth six hundred times than that GOD should hear such things from us, that He himself is the author of evil. The thesis of our churches having been sufficiently confirmed in this manner, we conclude at length that GOD can in no way or respect whatsoever be constituted the author or cause of sin.

Moreover, a question arises at this point, and indeed one not so easy to explain. For since it is established by the calculation and confession of all sounder theologians that even evil actions or sins are subject to the government of Divine Providence: it is immediately asked: In what manner does GOD concur with the action of sin: Where learned theologians depart into diverse opinions: some erring in defect, others in excess. Therefore it will be most safe that, following the footsteps of the Scriptures, we enter upon the middle path. But this question is most rightly answered: that GOD concurs with evil actions or sins not only permissively, not only governatively or dispositively by reason of the end: but moreover in other ways and respects: none of which, however, constitutes GOD the author or cause of sin in any way.

For first, GOD concurs with such evil actions as a universal cause: providing, namely, to all, motion and the powers of acting: according to that in Acts 17:28, In him we are, and move, and live. But in this first respect, GOD is least of all constituted the cause of sin. For it is established beyond controversy among all learned men that when an action is said to be evil, that depends upon the determination of the action: insofar as the action is considered not as an action simply, but as such an action. This determination standing, two things necessarily follow: 1. That any action is named only in a modified way. 2. That this modification, and consequently Sin, insofar as it is such, cannot be ascribed to the universal cause, which does not admit this modification, but only to the particular cause. For GOD, as the universal cause, only provides that you can act:

But that you act wrongly, that redounds from a particular cause, namely your perverse will. The Scholastic Doctors, and especially the Thomists, seem to have looked to this when they define sin as an entity with a defect; when they likewise assert that the formal reason of sin consists in the privation of rectitude; that GOD concurs with the real entity of the action, but not with the privation of rectitude; when finally they write that GOD is therefore not the cause of sin, because He is not a particular cause, but a universal one, insofar as He provides a certain influx indifferent to good and evil action: which influx is determined to sin by the created will; and consequently that the created will is the cause of sin: but that the First Cause does not flow into the sin, but concurs with the action indifferent regarding goodness and malice: Therefore, that sin does not have an influx from GOD insofar as it is sin, but insofar as it is a certain operation: Thomas in 1a2ae, question 80, article 7. So that this may be better understood, Alexander Posantius not ineptly wished to explain the opinion of the Scholastics in these words. It is to be noted that, the will of man being established in the first act, it can determine itself to this or that act: and indeed, when the determination determines itself to a good act, then it has a dependent relation to the divine determination: because it cannot determine itself to good unless GOD effects this in it: But when it determines itself to evil, then it does not have a dependent relation to GOD, but to the will itself, which of itself and by its own nature is prone to evil. There is therefore a distinction between a good and an evil act: because a good act is a perfect act and includes something positive: but an evil act is an imperfect act: therefore, for the whole good act the concurrence of GOD is necessary, but for an evil act, while the concurrence of GOD is indeed necessary insofar as it is a real act, it is not [necessary] insofar as it includes imperfection: because the created will determines itself to that imperfection: And because it is an imperfection and a defect, it does not require the concurrence of GOD for this.

Another mode and respect in which GOD is said to concur in the designation of sins is that of permission. But that is expressed in the Scriptures themselves: as Psalm 81:13, 'He let them go after the desires of their hearts': and Acts 14:15, 'In past generations GOD allowed all nations to walk in their own ways.' Moreover, this very permission is to be defined neither too broadly nor too narrowly. For in both directions the matter is not without danger. Therefore, at the beginning we willingly subscribe to the Fathers and to all the Orthodox who define this permission in such a way that GOD is entirely exempted from every cause, whether efficient, or operating, or assisting, or impelling. For it is certain that that is properly called 'permitted' which another was going to do even without us: and while we permit in this way, we certainly bind the one to whom it is permitted to no necessity: but we allow him to do what he himself wills. Although, however, this modesty and circumspection of the Fathers and other theologians deserves its praise, yet in this way this divine permission is circumscribed too narrowly. But for those investigating the matter a little more deeply in the Scriptures, it cannot be obscure that this very divine permission must be described quite diligently by its certain marks and degrees.

For at the beginning, this permission of GOD differs in its whole genus from human permission. For human [permission], on account of impotence and violence, is more often coercion than permission: but this divine [permission] is joined with Omnipotence, so that if GOD willed, He could prevent that which He nevertheless permits to happen. Whence, however, no guilt of sin redounds to GOD: For this is not properly a question here about the Omnipotence of GOD, but about His efficacious will and duty. Now GOD does not will sin, but hates it: Therefore this permission does not presuppose the will of GOD regarding sin, insofar as it is such: Thus GOD owes nothing to anyone. And since He bestowed upon the first man full grace and entire powers, sufficient for obeying GOD, if only he had willed to obey: What, I ask, could there be more by which GOD might be obligated to man? What? [Consider] that this permission presupposes no efficacious action of GOD, or principle of an evil action. For the act which is permitted has its principle not from the one permitting, but from the agent.

Furthermore: Although this permission does not presuppose a pure and simple will of GOD, yet nothing seems to stand in the way of adding to this permission that which has the character neither of Will nor of Non-will simply and entirely: and can neither properly be called an action of GOD: nor yet a bare permission. For if we call the holy Scriptures and their examples into council, it certainly cannot be denied that this permission is some species of will in GOD, although it is not an efficacious or operative will. For whatever GOD permits, He permits either willingly, or unwillingly and against His will. But this latter conflicts with the Omnipotence of GOD: to which nothing at all can resist, so as to prevent Him from doing what He wills: Psalm 115, 10. Rom. 9. 10. That GOD therefore permits in some way willingly, cannot be obscure or doubtful. If anyone should object at this point that this very thing is established by us, which is ascribed to the Calvinists as heretical: That indeed it is not only of permission, but of the will and good pleasure of GOD, that men sin: it would certainly have to be considered what can and ought to be solidly answered. The Scholastic Doctors, and among these especially Peter Lombard, lib. 2. sent. dist. 45. & 46. answer that GOD, with respect to the evil of fault, does not have a positive act, either of willing or not willing, but only a negative act of not willing, which is indifferent, and signifies Permission: Since it belongs to them to permit, not who will or do not will: but only who do not will to prohibit. Which answer, although it contains no impiety: yet does not at all sufficiently solve the knot itself.

Latin:

Posterius verò κατάφασιν sive Affirmativam expediet: planum faciens, Quænam peccati causa, secundum Scripturas, verè ac propriè definiri debeat. Ubi Philosophorum partim, partim Manichæorum ψευδολογίας examinabimus & refutabimus.

CAPUT I. Quod DEUS nullo prorsus pacto aut respectu Mali culpæ sive Peccati causa constitui possit?

DEUM esse causam peccati, cum Autore nostro, & quibusvis Orthodoxis simpliciter negamus. Causæ autem appellatione non modò intelligimus causam Efficientem principalem: sed quicquid causæ sive Efficientis, sive impellentis, sive cooperantis, sive creantis, sive inclinantis, sive mandantis, sive approbantis, sive volentis, sive decernentis, sive denique quovis modo instigantis aut cogentis respectum habere potest.

Consimiliter Peccati termino nobis venit, quicquid sub Peccati vel Originalis, vel Actualis ambitum cadit: Imò quicquid vitii sive culpæ cujusvis nomen ac definitionem sortitur.

Negativæ huic nostræ fidem planè indubiam faciunt, Scripturarum oracula: idque quadrupliciter.

Primùm enim DEUM, uti summè justum, sic summè etiam Bonum deprædicant: Matth. 19, 17. Marci 10, 18. Luc. 18, 19. Unus & Solus DEUS bonus est.

Jam verò DEUS immutabiliter talis est: Exod. 3, 14. Sum qui sum: Et Malach. 3, 6. Jehovah ego sum, & non mutor.

Fieri Ergò nullâ ratione potest, ut DEUS aliquando, vel desierit, vel desinat esse DEUS, hoc est, ut depositâ Essentiale bonitate, Mali alicujus rationem subeat: id quod omninò sequeretur, si DEUS quovis modo aut respectu, peccatum, quatenùs tale, vel ordinaret, vel vellet, vel efficeret, vel approbaret.

Deindè Scriptura describit DEUM, ut justurn & perfectum, ita ut quicquid ullo respectu à DEO profiscitur, illud & justum & perfectum sit: Deut. 32, 4. Perfecta sunt opera DEI, & omnes viæ ejus judicia: DEUS fidelis, & absq; ullâ iniquitate, justus & rectus: Psalm. 119, 137. Justus es DOMINE, & judicia tua omnia recta.

Jam verò nulla est participatio Justitiæ cum injustitiâ: perfectioni cum imperfectione: nulla societas Luci cum tenebris: nulla communicatio Christi cum Belial. 2. Cor. 6, 14. & 15.

Atqui Malum sive peccatum nihil est aliud quàm injustitia, quàm Imperfectio, imò ut Damascenus loquitur, prorsus est παρὰ φύσιν, καὶ μὴ ὄν:

Ergò Peccatum ad DEUM tanquam ejus autorem nullo pacto referri potest, vel debet.

Tertiò Scriptura testis, DEUM non modò non velle, sed & seriò odisse, prohibere, detestari, punire, & tandem æternùm damnare peccatum, imò magna patientia tolerare Psalm. 5, 5. Non DEUS volens iniquitatem, tu es: odisti omnes, qui operantur iniquitatem. Deut. 18, 15. & seqq. Rom. 9. 22. 1. Tess. 4, 6. Vindex est Dominus de omnibus &c.

Jam verò DEUS nihil odit eorum, quæ fecit: Neque enim odiens aliquid constituit aut facit: Sap. 11, 25. Quin Ergò DEUS peccati autor sive causa ullo pacto constitui nequeat, dubium potest esse pio nemini.

Tandem causæ contradistinctæ nunquàm sibi invicem possunt esse vel ὑπαλληλοι: vel ad idem primum principium revocari.

Jam verò DEUS omnis boni: Diabolus verò omnis peccati autor & causa in Scripturis constituitur. Gen. 1, 3. Vidit DEUS cuncta quæ fecerat, & erant valdè bona: Jacob: 1, 17. Omne donum perfectum & bonum, sursum descendit à Patre Luminum. Joh. 9, 44. Diabolus homicida fuit ab initio, & in veritate non stetit, quia veritas non est in ipso, cùm loquitur mendacium, ἐξ ἰδιων, ex propriis loquitur: quia mendax est, & Pater mendacii. 1. Joh. 3, 8. Qui facit peccatum, ex Diabolo est, quoniam ab initio Diabolus peccat.

Ergò causa peccati nunquam potest esse ὑπαλληλος causæ boni, & per consequens, à quo primo principio Bonum dependet, ab eodem Peccatum ullo modo proficisci nequit.

ALTERUM Negativæ nostræ fundamentum certis quibusdam & prorsus infallibilibus hypothesibus superstruitur: quarum PRIMA sic habet: Peccatum non est res condita à DEO: sed potiùs est horrenda destructio, vel certè summa corruptio nobilissimi operis à DEO conditi. Ergò DEUM autorem habere nequit: nisi fortè quis affirmare velit DEUM operis semel à se conditi pertæsum, per aliud quoddam opus itidem à se conditum, illud destruere: vel certè ex bonitatis & perfectionis statu, ad statum mali & imperfectionis deturbare voluisse: id quod prodigiosè est blasphemum.

ALTERA sic sonat. Quicquid DEUS facit aut creat: illud est ex Genere Entium, sive positivum aliquid.

Atqui Peccatum non est ex Genere Substantialium: Entium sic neq́; est res positiva Substantialis: Sed est defect9 sive privatio: vel uti in Scholis loqui solemus, est Nihil privativum. Undè haud ineptè quidam ex Patribus scripsit: Peccatum carere tùm fine proprio, tùm causâ efficiente, & per consequens, Essentiâ. Fine quidem, quatenus voluntas semper aliò fertur, & malum nunquàm expetit. Causâ verò efficiente, quia deficientium Effectuum causa efficiens assignari nulla potest.

Ergò Peccati, tanquàm Defectus causa efficiens in Deo non est quærenda.

Tertia talis esse potest: Si DEUS Peccati esset autor: utiquè ipse etiam peccator esset: & per consequens, ne DEUS quidem ampliùs esset.

Atqui hoc posterius insigniter blasphemum est. Ergo tale est & illud prius.

Quarta. In DEO tam voluntates contradictoriae, quàm contrariae Essentiae esse simpliciter nequeunt. Atqui velle bonum, & velle peccatum : Item odisse, detestari & punire peccata: ac eorundem autorem esse: contradictorias inferunt voluntates. Ergo: de DEO utrumq; praedicari nullâ ratione potest.

Quinta: Si DEUS est causa peccati, alterutrum istorum sequatur necesse est : nempè vel Peccatum per se & suâ naturâ esse bonum : vel DEUM ab Objecto suo aberrare. Ratio haec est: Quia sicut Intellectus pro objecto habet verum : Ita voluntatis objectum illud est, quod est bonum.

Atqui neutrum salvâ analogiâ fidei affirmari potest. Haereticum Ergo, imò blasphemum fuerit id, ex quo utrumq; istud consequitur.

Sexta & postrema. Si omnes actionum determinationes sunt ab Efficiente particulari: Consequens est, DEUM peccati causam esse non posse. Ratio consecutionis est haec: Quia DEUS est Universalis actionum causa. Jam verò prius illud citra controversiam verum est. Nam vitium, defectus sive ἀταξία, inest actionibus, non quatenus actiones sunt: sed quatenus sic jam sunt determinatae. Haec verò determinatio non ab universali, sed particulari causâ provenit. Exempli gratia: voluntas Judae prodentis Christum, quatenus ab universali causâ dependet, non est malae: nam causae hujus respectu, Judas illud tantùm habuit ut potuerit velle, sine determinatione ad malum. Quod verò jam vult Malum: illud non dependet ab universali causâ quae est DEUS: sed à particulari, quae voluntate jam ad malum abutitur.

TERTIUM & postremum Negativae nostrae fundamentum est, quasi subsidiarium, petitum ab unanimi consensu Orthodoxae Antiquitatis : quin à saniorum etiam Philosophorum judicio.

Nam usque adeò abhorruerunt omnium mentes & aures ab eâ propositione: DEUM esse causam peccati, ut extra Ecclesiam Plato lib. 2. πολιτειῶν, memorabilem hanc sententiam prodiderit: Omni contentione pugnandum est, ne quis in civitate, quam benè regi volumus, vel dicat, vel audiat, seu senex, seu juvenis, seu in poëmate, seu in alia narratione, DEUM esse alicui causam malorum: Quod nequè sanè ita dici potest, neq; utile est civitati, neq; secum consentit in Explicatione. Consimiliter in Ecclesia, ipsi quoque haeretici, ut Manichaei maluerunt alium quempiam DEUM malum fingere, quàm DEO, qui summè bonus & justus est, causam peccati adscribere.

Testis est porrò Eusebius lib. 5. cap. 18. circa A. D. 170. vel secundum alios, 182. Florinum quendam, Montani discipulum ideò ab Ecclesia anathemate percussum, & haereticum proclamatum fuisse, quòd contenderet, Malum à DEO esse, DEUMque facere peccata non modò permissive, sed & effective.

Irenaeus haereseos titulo notavit dogmata Valentinianorum contendentium, Indurationem Pharaonis, excaecationem Judaeorum traditione

Gentilium in sensum reprobum, esse opera Dei, ex divina necessitate hominibus ad perpetranda, imposita. lib. 4. cont. hær. cap. 47. & 48. Eusebii lib. 6. cap. 5. de præparatione Evangelicâ, illustris hæc est sententia: Impius profectò judicabitur, imò pessimus omnium, qui à creatore universi alios ad adulteria, alios & rapinas, alios ad alia vitia impelli arbitratur. Hinc enim sequeretur: Aut hæc non esse peccata: aut peccandi causam in creatorem referri: Quo dogmate nihil scelestius cogitari potest. Augustinus: Nemine Sapiente autore quisquam sit deterior, & secundum eundem: Quæ me autore imperantequè fieri necesse est, eorum ego autor meritò censear, Christianorum nomine indigni sunt habendi, qui DEUM naturâ bonum, Mali causam vel pravæ cujusdam aut voluntatis, aut actionis autorem statuunt, sive excitantem, sive impellentem lib. 83. q. 3. Chryssst. Homil. 23. in Acta Apost. Satiùs est, sexcenties terrâ defodi, quàm ut DEUS talia à nobis audiat, Quòd ipse mali autor sit. Thesi Ecclesiarum nostrarum hunc in modum sufficienter confirmatâ, colligim9 tandem, DEUM peccati Autorem sive causam, nullo prorsus pacto aut respectu constitui posse.

Cæterùm oritur hoc loco statim Quæstio, & quidem non usque adeò explicatu facilis. Cùm enim omnium saniorum Theologorum calculo & confessione constet, Divinæ Providentiæ gubernationi subesse etiam actiones malas sive peccata: mox quæritur: Quonam modo DEUS cum actione peccati concurrat: Ubi Doctores Theologi in diversas abeunt sententias: quibusdam in defectu; aliis in excessu peccantibus. Proindè tutissimum fuerit, ut Scripturarum vestigia secuti, mediâ viâ ingrediamur. Rectissimè autem hanc ad Quæstionem respondetur, DEUM non tantùm permissivè, non duntaxat gubernativè sive dispositivè, ratione finis: sed aliis insuper modis & respectibus ad malas actiones, sive peccata concurrere: quorum tamen nullus DEUM Peccati autorem sive causam ullo pacto constituat.

Primùm enim ad ejusmodi malas actiones concurrit DEUS, ut causa universalis: dans nimirùm omnibus motum & vires, agendi: secundum illud Act. 17, 28. In ipso sumus, movemur & vivimus. Verùm primo hoc respectu, DEUS peccati causa minimè omnium constituitur. Nam extra controversiam apud eruditos quosvis est positum, Quando Actio dicitur esse mala; id ex Actionis determinatione dependere: quatenus nimirùm Actio non ut Actio simpliciter, sed ut Talis Actio consideratur. Stante hac determinatione, duo necessariò consequuntur: 1. Actionem aliquam, non nisi modificatè nominari. 2. Modificationem hanc, & consequenter Peccatum, quatenus tale, non causæ universali, quæ modificationem hanc non admittit, sed causæ tantùm particulari adscribi posse. DEUS enim ut causa universalis id tantùm præstat, ut possis agere:

Quod verò malè agis, illud ex causâ, particulari, nempè perversâ tuâ voluntate redundat. Doctores Scholastici, & cumprimis Thomistæ hûc respexisse videntur, quando peccatum definiunt, quod si Ens cum defectu: quando item asserunt, Rationem formalem peccati consistere inprivatione rectitudinis: DEUM verò concurrere ad entitatem realem Actionis: non ad privationem rectitudinis: quando denique scribunt: DEUM ideò non esse causam peccati, quia non est causa patticularis, sed universalis, quatenùs præbet influxum quemdam indifferentem ad actum bonum & malum: qui influxus à voluntate creatâ determinetur ad peccatum; ac proindè voluntatem creatam esse causam peccati: Causam verò primam non influere in peccatum: sed concurrere ad actum indifferentem circa bonitatem & malitiam: Itaque peccatum non habere influxum à DEO, quatenus peccatum est: sed quatenus est operatio quædam: Thomas in 1. secundæ quest. 80. art. 7. Quod ut rectiùs intelligatur, haud ineptè Alexander Posantius, Scholasticorum sententiam his verbis explicare voluit. Notandum, quòd constitutâ voluntate, hominis in actu primo, illa se potest determinare ad hunc vel illum actum: & quidem, quando determinatio se actum bonum determinat: tùm dependenter habet se à determinatione divinâ: quia non potest se determinare ad bonum, nisi DEUS hoc in illa efficiat: Quando verò se ad malum determinat, tùm non habet se dependenter à DEO: sed ab ipsâ voluntate, quæ ex se & suâ naturâ ad malum prona est. Est ergò discrimen inter actum bonum & malum: quia actus bonus est actus perfectus, & includit aliquid positivum: actus verò malus est actus Imperfectus: ideò ad totum actum bonum necessarius est concursus DEI, ad actum verò malum, necessarius quidem est concursus DEI, quatenùs est actus realis: non quatenùs includit Imperfectionem: quia ad illam imperfectionem, se determinat voluntas creata: Et quia est Imperfectio & defectus non requirit ad hoc concursum DEI.

Alter modus atque respectus quo DEUS ad designationem peccatorum concurrere dicitur, est permissionis. Exprimitur autem ille in Scripturis ipsis: ut Psalm. 81. 13. Dimisit eos secundum desideria cordium eorum: Et Act. 14, 15. Præteritis generationibus dimisit DEUS omnes gentes ingredi vias suas. Cæterùm hæc ipsa permissio, neq; nimis latè neque nimis arctè est definienda. Utrinque enim res non caret periculo. Proindè initiò libenter subscribimus Patribus & Orthodoxis quibusque qui Permissionem istam ita definiunt: ut DEUS ab omni sive efficiente, sive operante, sive adjuvante, sive impellente causâ prorsus eximatur. Certum enim est illud propriè dici Permitti, quod alius etiam sine nobis facturus erat: & dùm sic permittimus, utique illum, cui permissum est, nulli necessitati adstringimus: sed quòd ille vult, agere ipsum sinimus. Quanquàm verò hæc Patrum, aliorumque Theologorum modestia ac circumspectio, laudem suam meretur, tamen hoc pacto Permissio isthæc divina nimis arctè circumscribitur. Rem verò paulò altiùs inspiScripturis investigantibus obscurum esse nequit: hanc ipsam permissionem divinam certis suis notis atque gradibus diligenter admodum describendam esse.

Initiò enim Permissio haec DEI, ab humanâ permissione toto genere distat. Humana enim, propter impotentiam & violentiam saepiùs coactio magis est, quàm Permissio: Divina verò haec conjuncta est cum Omnipotentiâ, ut si DEUS vellet, impedire posset, quò minùs fieret, quod tamen fieri permittit. Undè tamen in DEUM nulla peccati culpa redundat: Nam non est hic propriè quaestio, de Omnipotentiâ DEI, sed de efficaci ipsius voluntate atque debito. Jam DEUS non vult peccatum, sed odit: Ergò Permissio haec non praesupponit voluntatem DEI, quoad peccatum, quatenus tale: Sic DEUS nemini quicquam debet. Et cum homini primo, plenam tribuerit gratiam & vires integras, ad obsequendum DEO sufficientes, si modò voluisset obsequi: Quid, quaesò, ampliùs esse possit, quo DEUS homini sit obstrictus? Quid? quòd Permissio haec nullam praesupponit efficacem DEI actionem: vel principium malae actionis. Nam actus qui permittitur, principium habet, non à permittente, sed ab agente.

Deindè verò: Etsi permissio haec, non praesupponit puram ac simplicem voluntatem DEI, nihil tamen obstare videtur, quò minùs Permissioni huic illud addatur, quod nec Voluntatis, nec Noluntatis rationem simpliciter & omninò habeat: & neque propriè dici possit DEI actio: neque etiam nuda permissio. Nam si Scripturas sacras, earundemque Exempla in Concilium adhibeamus, negari certè nequit, quin Permissio ista sit aliqua Species voluntatis in DEO, licèt non sit efficax, aut operosa voluntas. Nam quicquid DEUS permittit, illud vel volens permittit, vel nolens & invitus. Atqui posterius hoc pugnat cum DEI Omnipotentiâ: Cui nihil quicquam potest resistere, quò minùs faciat, quae velit: Psalm. 115, 10. Rom. 9. 10. Quin ergò aliquo modo volens permittat DEUS, obscurum aut dubium esse nequit. Si objiciat hoc loco aliquis, id ipsum hoc paà nobis statui, quod Calvinianis tanquam haereticum adscribitur: Quod nimirum apud DEUM non permissionis tantùm, sed voluntatis & beneplaciti sit, ut peccent homines: dispiciendum utique fuerit, quidnam solidè responderi possit ac debeat. Scholastici Doctores, & inter hos cumprimis Petrus Lombardus, lib. 2. sent. dist. 45. & 46. respondet, DEUM respectu mali culpae non habere actum positivum, vel volendi vel nolendi, sed tantùm actum negativum non volendi, qui sit indifferens, & Permissionem significet: Siquidem illorum est Permittere, non qui volunt aut nolunt: sed tantùm qui non volunt prohibere. Quae responsio etsi nihil impietatis continet: nodum tamen ipsum minimè solvit sufficienter.


### IV. Regarding hardening, blinding, etc

Therefore, regarding the explanation of our argument, it should be observed above all that between one who is simply willing and one who is simply unwilling, a third thing, as it were mixed from both, can and ought to be given: that which the Holy Spirit Himself expressed in Psalm 5:5, saying, 'You are not a GOD willing iniquity.' Therefore, GOD is said to permit sins not simply as Unwilling, but as Not Willing. That some distinction must be established between the 'Not Willing' and the 'Unwilling' is evident from this: that the former, namely the 'Not Willing,' contains only a negation of care, or provision, or direction in any matter, without an affirmation of an act: as when I say, 'I do not will,' for that which is, 'I do not have the will' to procure this thing or that: but the latter, namely this 'Unwilling,' has an affirmation of an act and something positive in the will, regarding not procuring, and prohibiting, or directing the proposed matter. In the former, the will does not act: but merely rests: In the latter, however, the will is moved by an internal act. The ethical doctrine of Aristotle also recognizes and confirms this distinction, when it concedes a certain middle ground between Willing and Unwilling. Most correctly, therefore, GOD is said to be neither Willing, nor Unwilling or reluctant, but rather not willing to permit sins.

The third mode and respect in which GOD is said to concur in evil actions, or sins, is that of Desertion. This mode is expressed in the Scriptures in many places: but especially in the history of King Saul. 1 Samuel 16:14, 'The Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubled him.' But not even in this manner can GOD be established as the cause of sin. For although, when the grace of GOD and the Spirit are removed, error, darkness, and sins immediately rush in of their own accord: yet GOD, by thus deserting man, does not effect the sins themselves that follow: no more than a physician can be called the cause of the most serious and sometimes increasingly worsening diseases when he departs from a sick man who is intemperate and rejects sounder advice: but rather, just as a physician does not instill vicious habits into such a patient, but leaves those already implanted: so GOD, by His desertion, does not infuse malice into sinners: but rather, since it is incorrigible, He leaves it to His just judgment. Hence, Augustine, speaking of the fall of Adam, piously infers: 'The desertion of GOD was not the cause of the Adamic fall: but this very fall was the cause of the desertion.' For GOD did not withdraw His grace from man before the fall: but man himself, through and because of the fall, lost it.

The fourth mode and respect in which GOD is said to concur in sins is clearly singular: and is proper to Hardening and Blinding. The foundations of this mode exist. Exodus 4:21, 'I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, and he will not let the people go.' Exodus 9:16, 'For this very purpose I have placed you, that I might show my power in you.' Job 12:24, 'GOD changes the heart of the princes of the people of the earth, and deceives them, and makes them wander as if drunk.' Isaiah 6:19, John 12:40, 'GOD has blinded their eyes, and hardened their,'

- so that they may not see with their eyes, and not understand with their heart, and be converted, that I might save them. Romans 1:28, 'GOD gave them over to a reprobate mind.' To this also pertains the fact that in the Scriptures such words are predicated of GOD which seem to assign some action to GOD: such as that GOD seduces and deceives, Ezekiel 14:9. Sends the efficacy of error, 2 Thessalonians 2:11. Makes to wander, Isaiah 63:17. Mixes a spirit of giddiness, Isaiah 19:14. Gives a spirit of lying, 1 Kings 22:23, 2 Chronicles 18:21: And indeed these and other places of the Scriptures of this kind have been a stumbling block for many, against which they have shamefully struck, so as to establish GOD as the cause and author of sin, if not with respect to all evil actions: yet especially of those in which GOD is accustomed to punish sins with sins. Hence that logical axiom was poorly accommodated and distorted here: Active verbs signify an action to be ascribed to him of whom they are predicated. Indeed, it was argued from the precepts of Hebrew grammarians: Do not these and similar verbs, which are predicated of GOD, imply force and most active operation, because they are taken from the Piel and Hiphil conjugations? But if we rightly explain the scriptures by the scriptures, and look to the analogy of faith as to an infallible Cynosure of truth, it will not be able to be obscure. That this Fourth mode is also so constituted that it in no way establishes GOD as the author of sin. To which end not a few theologians have determined that these words are to be explained by the negation and subtraction of Grace and illumination: so that to Harden and to Blind is nothing other than not to impart the grace of Illumination. Whose circumspection, although it deserves praise, yet does not solve the knot sufficiently, so much as it entangles it more. For if these two things, To harden: And, Not to illuminate, are convertible, or reciprocal in both their parts, so that GOD must be said to harden or blind him whom He does not illuminate: Certainly we must necessarily hold as hardened and blinded all those who perish in sins and in unbelief. But these things are manifestly repugnant to the Scriptures. For these, through Hardening and Blinding, and terms similar to these, express some singular kind of punishment, not common to all the impious: but proper to those whom GOD is accustomed to punish with the singular fury of His wrath and vengeance. Therefore, something more must be added, which implies both some evident operation of GOD, and yet such a one as completely exempts GOD from the cause of sin: which can be most rightly explained by the five following hypotheses.

I. Active verbs, although taken from the Piel and Hiphil conjugations, do not always signify an efficacious action or approval: but they more often denote those effects which are proper either to permission, or declaration, or some other indirect mode. Of which matter Chemnitz has collected very many examples in part 1 of the Loci Theologici, Article on the cause of sin: chapter 4.

II. When the literal sense, or τὸ ῥητὸν, of certain Scriptures clashes in many ways with the analogy of faith: conflicts with other more manifest passages of Scripture: and seems to inflict some injury upon both the justice and the mercy of GOD: then, having abandoned the literal sense, one must take refuge in the meaning, and seek that interpretation which is analogous to faith and consonant with the Scriptures themselves: and which does not in the least render GOD impious. Which rule having been observed with St. Augustine.

III.
