In place of a hypothesis we infer: That many works are predicated of GOD in the Scriptures which do not happen by His own working, but by His permitting them with a certain desertion: For GOD does not work the very hardness and blindness of heart in man, but is said to harden him whom He does not soften; or, as he speaks elsewhere, GOD does not harden by imparting malice: but by not imparting mercy. Likewise by deserting, not by helping. Thus He is said to blind, not by effecting blindness, but by permitting it through desertion.

IV. In the Scriptures, some work is very often attributed to GOD which nevertheless principally belongs to the Devil and the depraved will of men: this is what happens especially in those works in which action must be properly distinguished from passion, since they are things most diverse from one another. Commonly in the Schools, by the distinction between the evil of punishment and the evil of fault, this very thing is explained a little more clearly. For because GOD, in executing His judgments, uses the ministry of the devil: it happens that one and the same work is assigned in the Scriptures to GOD, and to the Devil, and to Man, but in a most diverse respect: to GOD, namely, insofar as He, as a Just Judge, punishes an antecedent, unconquerable contumacy, or other sins perpetrated against conscience: Where that action obtains the respect of an evil of punishment. But to the Devil, insofar as GOD permitting, he impels man to sin, and from time to time provides occasions for committing more grievous sins: finally to Man, insofar as he hardens and blinds himself, while he willingly and voluntarily obeys the impulses of Satan and his own depraved desires, and turns himself away from GOD by his own will. In both of which respects the evil of fault comes under consideration. Which diversity of actions Augustine expressed briefly, but with sufficient vigor, saying: The Devil suggests: Man consents: GOD deserts. The foundation of this hypothesis or observation, however, may be seen in the history of David: who is read in 2 Sam. 24:1 to have been moved by GOD to see to it that the people were numbered in Israel and Judah. Now, lest this be taken as some efficacious impulse or inspiration of GOD: but only as a just permission in punishment for David's pride, the Holy Spirit Himself, 1. Chronicles 21:1 affirms that Satan incited David to number Israel: thus most evidently distinguishing between GOD as a just judge punishing: and the Devil as the author and impeller to sin, and David himself drawing this punishment upon himself by his own insolence. Which same thing is also most clearly evident from the history of King Ahab. For when by his enormous impiety he had deserved that he should at last pay the most just penalty for his sins: the text has, 1 Kings 22:19, that GOD deceived the prophets of Ahab, so that they might persuade the King to enter into battle with the Syrians. Now, lest GOD Himself be established as having efficaciously sent a spirit of error and lying: but rather, that as a just Judge He executed these judgments of His through the Devil, it is immediately subjoined in the text: That God said: Who will deceive Ahab: Where the Devil without delay offered himself as the executor of the divine judgment, by far the most powerful. To whom GOD, having entrusted the execution, said: Go and you will do it. That these words were not of one commanding, but of one permitting, the whole context of the text clearly proves: nay, the very collation of the Scriptures most evidently demonstrates: as in Matthew 8:31, where the demons, having been cast out of some possessed man, asked Christ: If you cast us out, PERMIT us to migrate into the herd of swine: Christ, however, is read to have answered: GO. Which word certainly had not the force of a command, but the respect of a permission, as is evident both from the prayer of the demons themselves and from Luke chapter 8:32: Where that word GO is rendered thus, And HE PERMITTED THEM. Thus in the plundering of Job's goods there was both fault and punishment: and the depraved action was joined to the righteous passion. Insofar, therefore, as it was a calamity, the same plundering is referred to GOD: insofar as it was a fault, it is referred to Satan as the author.

V. And the final Hypothesis. That which belongs to men by itself: that is more often attributed to GOD in the Scriptures, but only by accident. For just as it is attributed to the Sun by accident that those who suffer from weakness of the eyes or other defects feel darkness and pain from its rising and splendor: so it happens also to God, and to His word, miracles, and benefits, by accident, that by their sum and utility and excellence, the minds of those who are stubborn and unconquerable become more hardened and stiffened. As for example, by one and the same word by which the Israelites were illuminated, Pharaoh and the Egyptians were blinded: that this happens by accident is manifest. Since GOD did not infuse blindness and contumacy into Pharaoh, which was previously absent: but elicited that which lay hidden, utterly incorrigible, in their hearts. Hence it is that Exodus 8:15 and chapter 13:15. Pharaoh is read to have hardened himself: And Rom. 1, 24, it is written that GOD delivered idolatrous nations into uncleanness through the desires of their own hearts: Thus expressly noting that those impure desires, and the uncleanness bursting forth from them, were not sent into them by GOD: but that their hearts had previously teemed with those perverse desires: but now, to avenge their most foul idolatry, GOD permitted them to entangle themselves more and more in the snares of shameful acts and crimes.

Latin:

Illud proindè circa explicationem argumenti nostri cumprimis observandum fuerit, quòd inter volentem simpliciter, & nolentem aliquid simplicer, tertium quiddam ex utroque quasi mixtum dari potest & debet: id quod ipse Spiritus Sanctus expressit. Pfalm. 5, 5. inquiens, Non volens iniquitatem DEUS, tu es. Permittere ergò dicitur, DEUS peccata non simpliciter, Nolens, sed Non Volens. Esse autem inter τὸ Non Velle, & inter τὸ Nolle discriminis aliquid constituendum, vel indè patet: Quòd prius illud nempè τὸ Non velle, negationem solùm continet curæ, vel provisionis, aut directionis in re quapiam, sine actus affirmatione: ut cùm dico, " Non volo: pro eo quod est, Non habeo voluntatem " hanc rem aut illam procurandi: Posterius verò " hoc nempè τὸ Nolle, Actus affirmationem, & positivum quiddam habet in voluntate, de non procurando, & prohibendo, aut dirigendo rem propositam. In priori voluntas non agit: sed tantùm quiescit: In posteriori verò movetùr voluntas actu interno. Quam distinctionem doctrina etiam Ethica Aristotelis agnoscit & comprobat, dùm medium quoddam concedit inter Voluntatem & Noluntatem. Rectissimè ergò neque Volens, neque Nolens aut invitus: sed potiùs non volens peccata permittere DEUS dicitur.

Tertius modus atque respectus, quo DEUS ad malas actiones, sive peccata concurrere dicitur, est Desertionis. Exprimitur autem modus iste in Scripturis multis in locis: cumprimis verò in historiâ Regis Saul. 1. Sam. 16, 14. Spiritus Domini recessit à Saul & exagitavit eum Spiritus nequam à DOMINO. Verùm neque hoc pacto DEUS peccati causa potest constitui. Etsi enim sublatâ, DEI gratiâ & Spiritu, statim error, tenebræ, peccata sponte suâ ingruunt: non tamen sic deserendo DEUS hominem, ipsa peccata, quæ consequuntur, efficit: haud magis, atque Medicus dici potest gravissimorum & subindè magis ingravescentium morborum causa, quando ab homine ægro, sed intemperante, & consilia saniora respuente discessum facit: sed potiùs, quemadmodum Medicus tali ægro vitiosos mores non inferit, sed jam insitos relinquit: Sic DEUS desertione suâ peccatoribus malitiam non infundit: sed eam potiùs, quippè incorrigibilem, justo judicio relinquit. Hinc de lapsu Adami verba faciens Augustinus piè infert: Non desertio DEI fuit causa lapsus Adamici: sed hic ipse lapsus desertionis extitit: Neq́; enim DEUS gratiam suam homini ante lapsum subtraxit: Sed Homo ipse, per & propter lapsum eam deperdidit.

Quartus modus atq́; respectus, quo DEUS ad peccata concurrere dicitur, est planè singularis: & est Indurationis & Excæcationis proprius. Fundamenta modi hujus extant. Exod. 4, 21. Ego indurabo cor Pharaonis & non dimittet populum. Exod. 9, 16. In hoc ipsum posui te, ut in te ostenderem potentiam meam. Job. 12, 24. DEUS immutat cor principum populi terræ, & decipit eos, & errare facit eos, quasi ebrios. Jes. 6, 19. Joh. 12, 40. Excæcavit DEUS oculos eorum, & induravit eorum,

- ut non videant oculis, & non intelligant corde & convertantur ut salvem eos. Rom. 1, 28. Tradidit hominibus eos DEUS in sensum reprobum. Quo pertinet etiam, quòd in Scripturis de DEO prædicantur ejusmodi verba, quæ aliquam DEO actionem assignare videntur: ut quòd DEUS seducat & decipiat, Ezech. 14, 9. Mittat efficaciam erroris, 2. Thess. 2, 11. Errare faciat. Jes. 63. 17. Misceat spiritum Vertiginis. Jes. 19, 14. det spiritum Mendacii. 1. Reg. 22, 23. 2. Paral. 18, 21: Et sanè hæc & id genus alia Scripturarum loca, multis fuerunt lapis offensionis, in quem turpiter impegerunt, ut DEUM causam & autorem peccati constituerent, si non omnium malarum actionum respectu: earum tamen potissimùm, in quibus peccata peccatis punire solet DEUS. Hinc axioma illud Logicum malè huc accommodatum & detortum fuit. Verba Activa significant actionem, adscribendam ei, de quo prædicantur. Quin ex Hebræorum Grammaticorum præceptis disputatum fuit: Annon hæc & similia verba, quæ de DEO prædicantur, vel ideò vim & operationem actuosissimam inferant, quia sint desumta ex conjugationibus Piel & Hiphil: Verùm si scripturas per scripturas ritè explicemus, & ad analogiam fidei, tanquàm ad infallibilem veritatis Cynosuram respiciamus, haud obscurum esse poterit. Modum etiam istum Quartum ita esse comparatum, ut DEUM nullo pacto autorem peccati constituat. Quem in finem haud pauci Theologorum verba isthæc per negationem & substractionem Gratiæ atque illuminationis, exponenda esse statuerunt: ita ut Indurare atque Excæcare nihil sit aliud, quàm non impertiri gratiam Illuminationis. Quorum sanè circumspectio etsi laudem meretur: nodum tamen usque adeò non sufficienter solvit, ut magis eum implicet. Nam si duo isthæc Indurare: Et, Non illuminare sunt convertibilia, sive utraque sui parte reciproca, ut DEUS eum indurare sive excæcare dici debeat, quem non illuminat: Certè pro induratis & excæcatis habeamus necesse est, omnes eos, qui in peccatis atque in incredulitate pereunt. Atqui hæc Scripturis manifestè repugnant. Hæc enim per Indurationem & Excæcationem, & his consimilia vocabula, exprimunt singulare aliquod supplicii genus, non omnibus impiis commune: sed illorum proprium, quos DEUS singulari iræ atque vindictæ suæ furore punire solet. Proindè aliquid ampliùs addendum fuerit, quod & evidentem aliquam DEI operationem, & tamen talem subinferat, quæ DEUM à causâ peccati penitùs eximat: id quod subsequentibus quinque hypothesibus rectissimè expediri potest.

I. Verba Activa, licet desumta ex conjugationibus Piel & Hiphil, non semper significant efficacem actionem aut approbationem: sed eos sæpiùs notat effectus, qui vel permissionis, vel declarationis, vel alius cujuspiam inflexi modi sunt propria. Cujus rei Exempla planè multa collegit Chemnitius part. 1. Locorum Theol. Art. de causâ peccati: cap. 4.

II. Quando quarundam Scripturae phrasium τὸ ῥητὸν, sive literalis sensus, multis modis impingit in analogiam fidei: pugnat cum aliis Scripturae locis manifestioribus: & DEI tùm justitiam, tùm misericordiam injuriâ quapiam afficere videtur: tùm relicto τῷ ῥητῷ, ad διάνοιαν est confugiendum, & ea quaerenda interpretatio, quae fidei sit analoga, Scripturis ipsis consona: neque DEUM minimè impia. Quâ observata regula cum D. Augustino.

III. Hypotheseos loco inferimus: Multa in Scripturis opera de DEO praedicari, quae non operante ipso: sed cum desertione quadam permittente eveniunt: Neque enim DEUS in homine operatur ipsam duritiem & caecitatem cordis, sed indurare dicitur, quem non emollit; vel, ut alibi idem loquitur, DEUS non indurat impertiendo malitiam: sed non impertiendo misericordiam. Item deserendo, non adjuvando. Sic excaecare dicitur, non caecitatem efficiendo, sed per desertionem permittendo.

IV. In Scripturis DEO attribuitur saepissimè opus aliquod, quod tamen Diabolo, & pravae hominum voluntati principaliter competit: id quod in illis potissimùm operibus usu venit, in quibus actio à passione probè discernenda est, quippè res inter se diversissima. Vulgò in Scholis distinctione mali poenae & mali culpae, hoc ipsum paulò liquidiùs explicatur. Quia enim DEUS in judiciis suis exequendis utitur ministerio diaboli: fit ut unum quidem idéq; opus & DEO, & Diabolo, & Homini in scripturis adsignetur, sed diversissimo respectu: DEO nimirùm, quatenus ut Justus Judex antegressam inexpugnabilem contumaciam, vel alia peccata contra conscientiam perpetrata, punit: Ubi actio illa respectum obtinet Mali poenae. Diabolo verò quatenùs permittente DEO, Hominem ad peccandum impellit, & occasiones subindè ad graviora peccata delinquenda subministrat: Homini denique, quatenùs seipsum indurat & excaecat, dùm Satanae impulsibus, suisque pravis cupiditatibus libenter & ultrò obtemperat, seque à DEO propriâ voluntate avertit. Quo utroque respectu Malum culpae sub considerationem venit. Quam diversitatem actionum breviter, sed nervosè satis expressit Augustinus, inquiens: Diabolus suggerit: Homo consentit: DEUS deserit. Fundamentum autem hypotheseos sive observationis hujus videre licet, in historiâ Davidis: qui 2. Sam. 24, 1. legitur, à DEO commotus fuisse, ut curaret numerari populum in Israele & Judâ. Jam ne de efficaci aliquo DEI impulsu sive inspiratione: sed tantum de justâ permissione in poenam superbiae Davidis accipiatur, ipse Spiritus Sanctus, 1. Paral. 21, 1 affirmat, Satanam incitasse Davidem, ut numeraret Israel: sic evidentissimè distingvens inter DEUM tanquam justum judicem punientem: & inter Diabolum, tanquam autorem & impulsorem ad peccandum, & ipsum Davidem suâ sibi insolentiâ hanc poenam artrahentem. Quod ipsum luculentissimè etiam patet ex historiâ regis Achab. Nam cum enormi impietate suâ promeritus esset, ut vel tandem peccatorum pœnam justissimam lueret: habet textus, 1. Reg. 22, 19. quòd DEUS deceperit Prophetas Achabi, ut suaderent Regi ut prælium iniret cum Syris. Jam ne DEUS ipse statueretur efficaciter Spiritum erroris & mendacii immisisse: sed potiùs, ut justus Judex per Diabolum hæc sua judicia executum esse statim subjungitur in textu: Deum dixisse: Quis decipiet Achabum: Ubi Diabolus sine morâ se executorem, Judicii divini longè potissimum obtulerit. Cui DEUS executione demâdatâ dixerit: Vade & efficies. Quæ sanè verba non præcipientis, sed permittentis fuisse: tota textus συνέπεια luculenter evincit: imò ipsarum Scripturarum collatio evidentissimè demonstrat: ut Matth. 8, 31. Ubi Dæmones ex obsesslo quopiam ejecti rogabant Christum: Si ejicis nos, PERMITTE nobis, ut migremus in gregem porcorum: Christus autem respondisse legitur: ABITE. Quod sanè verbum non præcepti vim, sed permissionis respectum habuisse, tùm ex ipsorum Diabolorum præcatione, tùm ex Cap. 8, 32. Lucæ patet: Ubi verbum illud ABITE sic redditur, Et PERMISIT EIS. Sic in direptione bonorum Jobis & culpa erat & pœna: actioque prava, rectæ passioni juncta. Quatenus igitur calamitas fuit, ad DEUM: quatenus culpa, ad Satanam autorem refertur eadem direptio.

V. Et postrema Hypothefis. Quod per se competit Hominibus: id in Scripturis sæpiùs tribuitur DEO, sed non nisi per Accidens. Quemadmodum enim per accidens tribuitur Soli, quod ex ejus ortu atque splendore, caliginem & dolorem sentiunt, qui oculorum lippitudinem vel alios defectus patiuntur: ita per accidens quoque Deo, ejusdemque verbo, miraculis & beneficiis obtingit, ut eorum summâ & utilitate & præstantiâ, eorum animi magis obrigescent, & indurentur, qui sunt pervicaces & inexpugnabiles. Ut exempli gratiâ, Uno eodemque verbo, quo illuminati sunt Israëlitæ, excoecatæ fuerunt Pharao & Ægyptii: id quod per accidens fieri, manifestum est. Siquidem DEUS non infudit cæcitatem & contumaciam Pharaoni, quæ priùs abfuerit: sed eam, quæ in cordibus ipsorum, prorsus incorrigibilis latebat, elicuit. Hinc est, quod Exod, 8, 15. & cap. 13, 15. Pharao seipsum indurasse legitur: Et Rom. 1, 24. scribitur, DEUM tradidisse gentes idololattras in immunditiem per cupiditates cordium ipsorum: Sic disertè notans, impuras illas cupiditates, & hinc erumpentem immunditiem ipsis à DEO non fuisse immissam: sed illorum corda antè scatuisse perversis cupiditatibus illis: nunc verò ad vindicandam fœdissimam illorum Idololatriam, permisisfe DEUM, ut ipsi sese, magis magisque flagitiorum atque scelerum laqueis irretirent.


### The sixth and last mode or respect is divine Governance

In which way indeed GOD ought to be called not the efficient, but rather the deficient cause of sin. And lest any scruple should remain, the Apostle himself wished to explain himself, when in Eph. 4:19 he expressly frees GOD from this suspicion, asserting that the Gentiles gave themselves over to lasciviousness to perform every uncleanness, with all greediness.

The fifth mode and respect, by which GOD concurs with sins, is that of foreknowledge. For it is placed beyond any hazard of doubt that the foreknowledge of GOD is concerned not only with good, but also with evil actions, insofar as it is nothing other than the eternal and essential Omniscience in GOD. But whether this is at the same time the cause of the things foreknown, and especially of evil things, is today a matter of controversy. Calvin and Beza indeed contend that the foreknowledge of GOD is at the same time the efficient cause of the evils foreknown: and indeed not only of the evils of punishment, but also of the evils of fault: for the reason that GOD provides and foreknows nothing, unless he also wills to effect it. But we, denying this entirely, concede it for reasons sufficiently evident. For 1. Scripture indeed attributes to GOD the foreknowledge of all things: but it does not at the same time also establish him as the efficient cause of all things: for of those things of which he himself is the

1. author, they cannot be anything but perfectly good: according to that Mosaic epiphonema: Gen. 1:31. GOD saw all things that he had made, and behold they were very good.

2. Furthermore, the foreknowledge of GOD does not immediately presuppose the operation of GOD itself. For the seat of foreknowledge is in the intellect: but operation is a property of Omnipotence in GOD.

3. Foreknowledge in GOD is a most absolute idiom, and clearly convertible with his Essence: so that GOD cannot exist unless he is Omniscient, and indeed from all eternity: but operation is a secondary act of the most free will in GOD,

4. which can either be exerted or withdrawn, without any diminution or injury to the divine Essence. Finally, the foreknowledge of GOD is an internal action of the divine mind, and considered in itself, it accomplishes nothing by an external act. But operation, or the efficient cause, is an external principle, which proceeds outward in producing an effect: as is evident from the creation of this universe, where GOD proceeded outward and outside of himself as if by a secondary act, while the internal act of foreknowledge meanwhile remained within the most absolute essence of GOD, clearly unchanged.

Therefore, the principle of the Calvinists is most false: that GOD provides and foreknows nothing, unless he also wills to effect it: From which very opinion even Augustine recoiled: It would be a crime, he says, to ascribe the causes of sins to GOD: who, even if he has foreknown from eternal knowledge what each person's mind is going to render: yet by this, that he cannot be deceived, he has brought no necessity or will to sin upon anyone. Response 13 to the articles falsely imposed upon him.

The sixth and last mode or respect is that of divine Government. For GOD, by the power of his eternal Providence, disposes, rules, orders, and governs each and every thing that is, happens, and is carried out in this world: and he moderates evils or sins in such a way that he both sets a limit for those sinning, and restrains them so that they cannot always rush where they themselves wish: and he governs the sins themselves in such a way that, beyond and against the will of the sinners, they attain that end which serves most of all for his own glory and the edification of the Church. The history of the passion of Christ provides a very illustrious example of this matter: Where the Jews, Herod, and Pilate are read to have done what the hand and counsel of GOD had predetermined: by reason, indeed, of the divine counsel and determination, which had directed their actions toward a far more wholesome end, which they had perpetrated of their own accord, with GOD in no way instigating them. And indeed it is evident from this, that GOD is to be absolved from all blame or cause of sin even in this respect, because this Government does not look to the source and origin of sin, which has its seat in the will of men: but only to its course, end, and outcome. Where that saying of Fulgentius has place: Although GOD is not the author of evil thoughts: He is nevertheless the Ordainer of evil wills: and from the evil work of any evil person, He does not cease to work good.

With these six modes and respects duly observed, it will be plain that GOD does indeed concur in evil actions, or sins: but in such a way that He can or should in no wise be called or considered their cause, or author, or abettor, or approver.

Latin:

Quo sanè pacto DEUS non efficiens, sed deficiens potiùs peccati causa debet dici. Et ne scrupulus aliquis maneret reliquus, ipse Apostolus se explicare voluit, cùm Ephes. 4, 19. expressè DEUM ab hac suspicione liberat, asserens, Gentiles semetipsos dedisse lasciviae ad patrandam immunditiem omnem, cum omni aviditate.

Quintus modus atq; respectus, quo DEUS ad peccata concurrit est praescientiae. Extra omnem enim dubitationis aleam est positum, Praescientiam DEI versari non circa bonas tantùm: sed & malas actiones, quatenùs nimirùm nihil ea est aliud, quàm aeterna & essentialis in DEO Omniscientia. Nùm verò haec simul sit causa rerum praescitarum, & cumprimis malarum, hodiè controvertitur. Calvinus quidem & Beza contendunt, Praescientiam DEI esse simul causam efficientem malorum praescitorum: & quidem non tantùm malorum poenae: sed & malorum culpae: propterea quod DEUS nihil provideat, & praesciat, nisi quod velit etiam efficere. Nos verò negantem omninò concedimus, ob causas satis evidentes. Nam 1. Scriptura tribuit quidem DEO praescientiam omnium: non autem simul etiam constituit causam efficientem omnium: quorum enim ipse est au-

1. tor, ea non nisi perfectè bona esse possunt: secundum illud, Epiphonema Mosaicum: Gen. 1, 31. Vidit DEUS cuncta quae fecerat, & ecce erant valdè bona.

2. Deindè Praescientia DEI non praesupponit ipsam statim DEI operationem. Est enim Praescientiae sedes in intellectu: Operatio autem est proprietas Omnipotentiae in DEO.

3. Praescientia in DEO est absolutissimum, & cum Essentiâ ipsius planè convertibile Idioma: ut DEUS esse nequeat, nisi sit Omniscius, & quidem jam indè ab omni aeternitate: Operatio autem est actus secundus liberrimae voluntatis in DEO,

4. qui vel exeri, vel retrahi potest, sine ullâ divinae Essentiae diminutione aut laesione. Tandem Praescientia DEI est interna mentis divinae actio, neque in se considerata, ullam rem actu externo perficit. Operatio verò, sive causa efficiens est externum principium, quod in producendo effectu foràs progredietur: uti patet ex creatione hujus universi, ubi DEUS foràs & extra se quasi actu secundo progressus est, interno interim Praescientiae actu, intra absolutissimam DEI essentiam, planè invariato, permanente.

Falsissimum Ergò est Calvinianorum principiu: DEUM nihil providere & praescire, nisi quod velit etiam efficere: A quâ ipsa sententia abhorruit etiam Augustinus: Nefas, inquiens, fuerit, DEO adscribere causas peccatorũ: qui etsi ex aeternâ scientiâ praecognitum habet, quid uniuscujusq́; mentis retributurus sit: nemini tamen per hoc, quod falli non potest, necessitatem aut voluntatem intulit delinquendi. Responsion. 13. ad articulos falsò sibi impositos.

Sextus & postremus modus sive respectus, est divinae Gubernationis. DEUS enim vi aeternae suae Providentiae, singula atque universa, quae in hoc mundo, sunt, fiunt, & geruntur, disponit, regit, ordinat & gubernat: & Mala quidem sive peccata ita moderatur, ut tùm peccantibus modum statuat, & ita coërceat, ut ne ruere semper queant, quò ipsi volunt : tùm verò peccata ipsa ita gubernat, ut præter & contra voluntatem peccantium, eum finem sortiantur, qui & gloriæ ipsius : & Ecclesiæ ædificationi plurimùm inservit. Cujus rei illustre admodùm exemplum subministrat Historia passionis Christi : Ubi Judæi Herodes & Pilatus fecisse leguntur, quod uthieret manus & consilium DEI præfiniverat : ratione nimirùm consilii & determinationis divinæ, quæ ad finem longè saluberrimam illorum actiones direxerat, quas ipsi sponte suâ, DEO minimè instigante, perpetraverant. Et profectò DEUM hujus etiam modi respectu, ab omni culpâ sive causâ peccati prorsus absolvendû esse, vel indè patet, quod Gubernatio isthæc non fontem & originem peccati, quę in hominum voluntate sedem suam habet : sed tantùm cursum, finem & exitum ejus respicit, Ubi locum habet illud Fulgentii : DEUS licèt autor non sit malarum cogitationum : Ordinator tamen est malarum voluntatum : & de malo opere cujuslibet mali, non desinit operari bonum.

Sex istis modis atque respectibus ritè observatis, planum erit, DEUM concurrere quidem ad actiones malas, sive peccata : sed ita, ut eorum causa, sive autor, aut fautor, aut approbator, nullo pacto dici possit aut debeat.


### The sixth and last mode or respect is divine Governance: Antithesis

ANTITHESIS.

Our first parents initially raised a dispute against this purer doctrine of ours, who strove to remove the cause and blame of their most sad fall from themselves, and not obscurely to transfer it to GOD Himself: Gen. 3:12. To such an extent that we, their descendants, both individually and collectively, are swifter to excuse, or rather to extenuate and cloak, than to acknowledge our sins: as Augustine piously writes, book 3, On Free Choice, chapter 2.

Furthermore, not only indirectly and obliquely, but directly and openly, the Valentinians, Manichaeans, Seleucians, Hermians, and Florians said that GOD is the cause and author of sin. Since the impiety of these is partly too atrocious to require laborious refutation, and partly because we must speak expressly about most of them in the second chapter following: having passed over them in this place, we proceed to the tenets of more recent heretics.

Moreover, in the previous century, the Libertines sought a place for themselves in the Church of GOD; having arisen in Brabant and Holland, with their zeal for religion turned into license of the flesh, yet under the very guise of religion, they referred everything to the blind lust of the flesh, and kept saying that nothing possessed the nature of sin, except at least in the opinion of those who thought they were sinning: as Pierre Viret defined their impiety. Furthermore, John Calvin is a witness, in the book published against the Libertines, that in France these Libertines were called Quintinists, after a certain Quintin, a tailor of Picardy; and he says that their theology was drawn from the ravings and abominable pleasures of the Cerdonians, Manichaeans, Marcionites, and Gnostics. But the flowers, or rather the emblems, which they produced concerning the present Article, are especially these: 1. That GOD is the author of sin: and that He Himself committed the sin of Cain, Saul, and Judas. 2. That sin by its own nature is not an evil thing, but only by the opinion of men. 3. That spiritual regeneration is to be defined by such a security of the flesh, which is touched by nothing, neither by the sting of sin, nor by the fear of GOD, nor by the terror of any judgment. 4. That all things are lawful to all men, which they please: Just as Calvin writes about the Libertines in the book already cited: Likewise Bullinger in book 2 against the Anabaptists: And finally Peter Viret in book 2 on the Ministry of the Word, who establishes these Libertines as the offspring of the Catabaptists.

The arguments by which they attempted to put a gloss upon their impiety are especially these:

I. Whatever is the cause of a cause, is also the cause of the caused. But GOD is the cause of the cause: namely, of the human will, from which sin proceeds. Therefore GOD is also the cause of the caused: namely, of the sin itself.

I answer, that the major premise suffers from the fallacy παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For it is not simply true in every kind of cause: but only in a certain respect and in part; namely, with respect to causes that are subordinated and moving of themselves, when, that is, their order is kept uninterrupted: and none fails, or declines, or deviates from the other. But with regard to a universal cause, the major proposition is for the most part false: since it (as the Scholastics say) employs a certain influence that is common and indifferent to many things. Now, however, as Thomas rightly infers, it very often happens that the second cause fails from the order of the first cause, that is, that the defect is in the second cause and not in the first. Or that the defect arises from some thing or action, insofar as it is such in species: which it has not from the first, but from the second cause. In this case, therefore, the effect of the second cause is not reduced to the first cause: as Thomas says again: that is, the universal cause is indeed the cause of the cause: but yet it is not the cause of the caused. Therefore, even though GOD is the cause of the cause, namely, of the human will which sins: He is not, however, the cause of the caused, that is, of the sin itself. For the human will does not commit sin insofar as it was made by GOD: but insofar as it fails and declines from the order of GOD. And above, where we dealt expressly with the universal cause, we demonstrated quite abundantly: That sin, insofar as it is a deformity fighting against the law of GOD, or ἀταξία, cannot be attributed to GOD, both because the defect is in the second cause alone: and because that deformity is not the action itself, insofar as it is an action, but is a vice following and adhering to the action: which it has from the second or particular cause. St. Augustine illustrates the matter not inappropriately with a comparison taken from one who limps: In one who limps, he says, there are two things: 1. The motion: 2. The limping itself, or the vice and defect in the gait. Now the motion itself is from the locomotive power of the soul: but the vice of limping cannot be referred to the same, because it depends not on the motion per se, but on the vicious motion, that is, on a broken leg or a dislocated shin.

These things having been observed concerning the major, the response to the minor is easier. For insofar as the human will depends on the first or universal cause, namely GOD, to that extent it certainly does not commit sin: but insofar as it is corrupted, and has failed and deviated from the order of the first cause through a horrible ἀταξία: to that extent it sins. Which effect, or rather defect, is to be ascribed not to the first cause itself: but to the second or particular cause. All these things having been duly weighed, we invert this first argument τῷ βιαίου thus: Whatever is the cause of the cause, is also the cause of the caused. But GOD is not the cause of the cause, namely, of the will, insofar as it is evil and sins: Therefore neither is GOD the cause of the caused: namely, of the sin itself.

II. Argument. Whoever sustains a sinful nature, and does not immediately destroy it when he can, is not undeservedly established as an approver and cause of sin. But GOD sustains the sinful human nature, and when He can, He does not immediately destroy it. Therefore.

I answer, that this argument at the outset reeks of manifest impiety. For it prescribes to GOD the way and manner by which He ought to exercise His judgments concerning sinful human nature. Furthermore, it labors under the fallacy τῷ μὴ αἰτίω. For the fact that GOD does not immediately destroy sinful human nature is not the cause or approval of sin, as the Libertines babble; but rather His immense long-suffering and patience, by which He strives to allure and recall stubborn sinners more and more to repentance.

Which cause the Apostle expressed, both in Rom. 2:4, Do you not know that the kindness of GOD leads you to repentance? and Rom. 9:22, GOD in much patience sustains the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, to show the riches of His glory. Peter supports Paul, 2 Pet. 3:9, saying, The Lord acts patiently for your sake, not wishing any to perish, but all to return to repentance.

Finally, this argument also suffers from the sophistication ἀπὸ το̃ πη καὶ ἁπλω̃ς. For GOD sustains human nature, insofar as it is a work or substance created by Him, which is something that pertains entirely to His own divine Majesty, as Creator. But insofar as this very human nature is infected by sin, that is the work of Satan: and is by no means to be ascribed to the Creator.

III. Argument: Whatever happens, that happens either with GOD knowing and willing it: or apart from the will of GOD. But this latter cannot subsist: For if anything were to happen apart from the will of GOD, then GOD would not be the universal and primary cause of all things: which is manifestly false. Now, indeed, a secondary and particular cause never acts without the primary and universal one. But the actions and motions of secondary causes are sins. Why, therefore, it should seem doubtful to anyone that they happen with GOD knowing and willing it, will hardly seem so.

Latin:

ANTITHESIS.

PUriori huic doctrinæ nostræ litem intenderunt initiò primi parentes nostri, qui tristissimi lapsus causam culpamque à se removere, & haud obscurè in DEUM ipsum transferre studuerunt : Gen. 3, 12. usque adeò ut nos, ipsorum posteri singuli & universi, velociores simus ad excusanda, vel potiùs elevanda ac pallianda, quàm agnoscenda peccata nostra : ut piè scribit Augustinus : lib. 3. de Lib. Arbitrio cap. 2.

Deindè verò non rectè tantùm & obliquè : sed directè & palam DEUM peccati causam & autorem dixerunt esse, Valentiniani, Manichæi, Seleuciani, Hermiani, Floriani. Quorum impietas cùm partim atrocior sit, quàm ut operosâ refutatione indigeat, partim verò de plerisque ipsis, cap. subseq. secundo ex professo nobis aliquid dicendum sit : utique de illis, hoc loco præteritis, ad recentiorum hæreticorum placita accessum facimus.

Locum autem superiori seculo in Ecclesiâ DEI sibi quæsiverunt Libertini, qui in Brabantia & Hollandia exorti, Religionis studio in carnis licentiam converso, sub ipsâ tamen Religionis specie, omnia ad cæcam carnis libidinem referebant, neque quicquam peccati naturam obtinere dictitabant, nisi ex eorum saltem opinione, qui se peccare arbitrarentur, : uti Petrus Vuretus impietatem istorum definivit. Testis est prætereà Johannes Calvinus, in libro contra Libertinos edito, in Galliâ Libertinos iftos, nominatos fuisse QVINTINISTAS, à quodam Quinto sartore Piccardo : horumque Theologiam petitam esse ait, ex Cerdonistarum, Manichæorum, Marcionistarum, & Gnosticorum deliriis atque abominandis voluptatibus. Flosculi verò Emblemata, quæ de præsente Articulo prodiderunt: præcipuè sunt isthæc: 1. DEVM esse autorem peccati: ipsumquè operatum esse peccatum Cain, Saul & Judæ. 2. Peccatum suâ naturâ non esse rem malam, sed tantùm opinione hominum. 3. Spiritualem regenerationem per ejusmodi carnis securitatem definiendam esse, quæ nullâ re, neq́; peccati morsu, neq́; DEI timore, neq́; ullius judicii terrore tangatur. 4. Omnia omnibus licere, quæ libent: Quemadmodum de Libertinis scribunt Calvinus libro jam citato: Item Bullingerus libro 2. contra Anabaptistas: Et tandem Petrus Viretus lib. 2. de Ministerio verbi, qui Libertinos istos Catabaptistarum prolem constituit.

Argumenta quibus impietati fucum facere conabantur, præcipua sunt isthæc:

I Quicquid est causa causæ, est etiam causa causati. Atqui DEUS est causa causæ: nempè voluntatis humanæ, ex quâ peccatum proficiscitur. Ergò DEUS est etiam causa causati: nimirùm ipsius peccati.

Respondeo, Majorem laborare Sophismate παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Neque enim simpliciter ea vera est, in omni causarum genere: sed tantùm secundum id, & ex parte; nempè respectu causarum subordinatorum, & per se moventium, quando videlicet earum ordo interruptus servatur: & nulla ab alterâ deficit, vel declinat, vel exorbitat. Verùm quoad causam universalem plerumque falsa est Major propositio: quippè quæ (ut Scholastici loquuntur) adhibet influxum quendam Communem & indifferentem ad multa. Jam verò, uti Thomas rectè infert, sæpissimè accidit, ut causa secunda deficiat ab ordine causæ primæ, hoc est, ut defectus sit in causâ fecundâ & non in primâ. Vel ut defectus oriatur ex re vel actione aliquâ, quatenùs talis est in specie: id quod habet non à primâ, sed à secundâ causâ. Hoc ergò casu Effectus causæ secundæ, non reducitur ad causam primam: uti rursum Thomas loquitur: hoc est, causa universalis est quidem causa causæ: sed tamen non est causa causati. Proindè etsi DEUS est causa causæ, nempè voluntatis humanæ, quæ peccat: non tamen est causa causati, hoc est, ipsius peccati. Non enim voluntas humana peccatum facit, quatenùs à DEO facta est: sed quatenùs ab ordine DEI deficit & declinat. Et suprà, ubi de causâ universali ex professo egimus, satis abundè demonstravimus: Peccatũ, quatenùs est deformitas pugnans cum lege DEI, sive ataξία, non posse tribui DEO, tùm quia defectus est in solâ causâ secundâ: tùm quia deformitas illa, non est ipsa actio, quatenùs actio, sed est Actionis consequens & adhærens vitium: quod habet à causâ fecundâ sive particulari. D. Augustinus rem simili à claudicante petito, haud incommodè illustrat: In Claudicante, inquiens, duo sunt: 1. Motus: 2. ipsa Claudicatio, seu Vitium & defectus in incessu. Jam motus ipse est à potentiâ animæ locomotivâ: vitium verò claudicationis ad eandem referri nequit, quia non à motu per se, sed à motu vitioso, hoc est, à fracto crure, vel luxatâ tibiâ dependet.

His de Majore observatis, adMinorem facilior est responsio. Nam quatenùs voluntas humana dependet à causâ primâ sive universali, nempè DEO, eatenùs certè non facit peccatum: sed quatenùs ea corrupta est, & ab ordine causæ primæ, per horrendam ἀταξίαν defecit & exorbitavit: eatenùs peccat. Qui sanè effectus, vel defectus potiùs, non ipsi causæ primæ: sed causæ secundæ sive particulari adscribendus est. Quibus omnibus ritè expensis, argumentum hoc primum τῷ βιαίου sic invertimus: Quicquid est causa causæ: est etiam causa causati. Atqui DEUS non est causa causæ, nempè voluntatis, quatenùs mala est, & peccat: Ergò neque DEUS est causa causati: nempè ipsius peccati.

II. Argumentum. Quisquis sustentat naturam peccatricem, nec non statim delet eam, cùm possit, is approbator & causa peccati non immeritò statuitur. Atqui DEUS sustentat naturam humanam peccatricem, & cùm possit, eam non statim delet. Ergò.

Respondeo, Manifestam initiò impietatem argumentum hoc resipit. Præscribit enim DEO viam ac rationem, quâ judicia sua circa peccatricem naturam humanam exercere debeat. Deindè verò laborat sophismate τῶ μὴ αἰτίω. Quòd enim DEUS naturam humanam peccatricem non statim delet; non causa est, approbatio Peccati, uti Libertini nugantur; sed potiùs immensa ipsius longanimitas & patientia, quâ præfractos peccatores magis magisque ad pœnitentiam allicere & revocare studet.

Quam causam expressit Apostolus, tùm Rom. 2, 4. An nescis, quod lenitas DEI ad pœnitentiam te adducit? & Rom. 9, 22, DEUS in multâ patientiâ sustinet vasa iræ aptata ad interitum, ut ostendere, divitias gloriæ suæ. Suffragatur Paulo, Petrus 2. cap. 3, 9. Patienter agit, inquiens, Dominus propter vos, nolens aliquos perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam reverti.

Tandem laborat hoc etiam Argumentum Sophisticatione ἀπὸ το̃ πη καὶ ἁπλω̃ς. DEUS enim sustentat naturam humanam, quatenùs est opus sive substantia à se creata, id quod divinæ etiam ipsius Majestati, tanquàm Creatori omninò competit. Quatenùs verò hæc ipsa natura humana peccato est infecta, illud est opus Satanæ: & Creatori minimè adscribendum.

III. Argumentum: Quicquid fit, illud fit vel DEO sciente ac volente: vel citra DEI voluntatem. Atqui posterius hoc subsistere non potest: Si enim aliquid fieret citra DEI voluntatem, tùm DEUS non esset causa universalis & prima rerum omnium: id quod manifestè falsum: Jam verò causa secunda & particularis nunquam agit, sine primâ & universali. Atqui Causarum secundarum actiones & motus sunt peccata. Quin Ergò DEO sciente & volente eafiant, dubium vix cuiquam videbitur.


### Refutation of the Libertines

I answer. In the major proposition, a confusion of two very different questions is committed. For it is one thing when I ask whether all things happen with God knowing, and another thing whether all things come to pass with Him willing. The former we readily grant; but the latter, as far as sins are concerned, we simply deny. For you are not a God who wills iniquity. Furthermore, that distinction which we explained more fully above regarding the second mode, by which God is said to concur with sins, must be referred to here. For although it is supremely and prodigiously impious if anyone wishes to affirm that God wills sins, yet it does not square with the pattern of sound words if anyone asserts that sins happen with God simply not willing them; therefore, a third point must be added to the major proposition, namely, or that sins happen with God not willing them: which is what we contend. But regarding the minor, in which the chief force of the argument consists, I answer that it suffers at the outset from a fallacy of things that are distinct, while human action is shamefully confused with the disorder adhering to it; yet these two must be most diligently distinguished. For in every sin, the action, insofar as it is an action, is indeed from God as the universal cause; and in this respect, the action is not a sin. But insofar as disorder adheres to this action, that is certainly not from God, but from a particular cause, as explained above. Whence immediately arises another fallacy of the cause, while that which is proper to the particular cause is assigned to the universal cause. Then a gross fallacy of the vicious consequent is committed; for from the whole system of this argument, it does not follow that secondary or particular causes do not act without the first or universal cause, which is a point placed beyond controversy. If anyone now wishes to infer: Therefore the disorder also, or the vice, which adheres to the action of the secondary cause, will likewise depend on the first or universal cause, he betrays a most shameful ignorance of the refutation. For one ought not to argue from actions considered in themselves to the differences and qualities of those actions, so that just as they depend on the first and universal cause, so these also must necessarily depend on it. In order that this may be better understood, those three principles of all human actions must be properly observed: The first is the UNIVERSAL, as the principle of all principles, which is GOD: For from him, through him, and in him are all things: Rom. 11:36. But because this Principle administers all things that it has created in such a way that it also allows them to exercise and perform their own motions, as Augustine speaks in Book 7 of The City of God, ch. 30, therefore the remaining principles also have a place in this discussion. Therefore, we most rightly name the second principle the COMMON, which is nothing other than NATURE: not only that common nature which fell to the human race equally after the fall of the first parents, but also that special nature by which each individual is singularly moved and affected. The third is the SINGULAR principle, implanted in individual things by nature, and that either of natural inclination or instinct, by the benefit of which all animate things seek their own preservation, or of the intellective will, which is nothing other than the faculty of desiring and willing some certain end through those means which seem to lead to that end. Since these three principles concur in the production of every single work, the mutual affection of them toward one another must be properly considered, which I choose to explain by certain hypotheses.

I. In the customary course of human actions, the higher principle does not detract anything from the lower, but leaves its powers of acting. For as shown above, God administers all things that He has created in such a way that He nevertheless allows them to exercise their own motions; thus nature moves the will in such a way that, with its liberty left to it, it never falls under the necessity of coercion.

2. The first principle in a certain way has the nature of a Genus: the second of a species: the third of a singular individual. Now, just as the whole nature of the Genus is in the species, and the whole nature of the species is in the individual, but not vice versa—the whole nature of the species is not in the Genus, nor is the whole nature of the species in the individual—so the action of the first principle is always of its own Genus, and it neither acts nor suffers vice; the action of the second principle does not of itself produce vice, just as the species does not of itself produce it, but it suffers it from the third principle; but the third principle both produces vice and suffers it.

3. The third principle acts and suffers, either by itself through its own internal power, or through another external principle coming from outside. It acts by internal power when either the intelligent faculty knows the truth by itself, or fails from the truth; or the willing faculty wills the good by itself, or fails from the good. It is moved by another principle when either a superior nature, such as the diabolical, supervenes and impels it to evil, or the same nature persuades it to desire vice. Thus, in that most sad fall of our first parents, their first internal principle was moved by a supervening nature, namely the Devil; then the internal principle of Adam was moved by the same nature, when indeed Eve deceived him. Finally, they both consented to that supervening principle from their own internal principle, and thus by their own will they fell into sin.

4. Hence it now follows that, since several subordinate causes concur for the effect of a single work, the ultimate effect follows the quality and condition not of the first, nor of the middle, but only of the proximate cause, yet with this distinction: that for good actions to be performed, it is required that all principles be good, and that they in no way deviate from the motion of the superior principle, whereas for evil actions, even one, and indeed the proximate principle, suffices. Now, since the proximate principle of human actions is the will of man, it is most clearly evident that one must judge the source and origin or cause of evil actions not from the remote universal cause, but from the proximate particular cause.

Latin:

Respondeo. In Majore propositione committitur confusio duarum diversissimarum Quæstionum. Aliud enim est, quando quæro, An sciente DEO omnia fiant: Aliud verò, An eodem volente, omnia eveniant. Priùs illud ultrò largimur: posterius verò hoc, quoad peccata, simpliciter negamus. Non enim DEUS volens iniquitatem, tu es. Deindè referenda huc est illa distinctio, quam suprà circa Modum secundum, quò DEUS ad peccata concurrere dicitur, fusiùs explicatam dedimus. Etsi enim summè & prodigiosè impium est, si quis affirmare velit, DEUM velle peccata: tamen neque illud ad ὑποτύπωσιν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων, quadrat, si quis asserat, DEO simpliciter nolente peccata fieri: proindè tertium addi debet in majore propositione, nempè aut peccata fieri DEO non volente: id quod nos contendimus. Sed quoad Minorem, in quâ præcipua argumenti vis consistit, respondeo, eam initiò laborare Sophismate disparatorum, dùm turpiter confunditur Actio humana cum adhærente ἀταξίᾳ: quæ duo tamen diligentissimè discerni debent. In omni enim peccato, Actio, quatenùs Actio, est quidem à DEO tanquàm causâ universali: & hoc respectu, Actio non est peccatum: Quatenùs verò Actioni huic adhæret ἀταξία, illa certè non est à DEO, sed à causâ particulari: uti supra explicatum. Undè statim altera oritur Sophisticatio nõ causæ, dùm quod proprium est causæ particulari: id assignatur causæ universali. Deindè crassa committitur Sophisticatio vitiosi consequentis: plus enim ex toto argumenti hujus Systemate non sequitur, quàm causas secundas sive particulares non agere sine primâ sive universali: id quod extra controversiam est positum. Si quis jam inferre velit: Ergò ἀταξία etiam, sive vitium, quod adhæret actioni causæ secundæ, itidem dependebit à causâ primâ sive universali, is turpissimam prodit Elenchi ignorationem. Neque enim ab actionibus in se consideratis, licèt argumentari ad ipsarum actionum differentias & qualitates: ut quemadmodum illæ, sic hæ quoq; dependere necesse habeant à causâ primâ & universali. Quod ut rectiùs intelligatur, Tria illa omnium actionum humanarum Principia probè observanda veniunt: Primum est UNIVERSALE tanquam principium principiorum omnium, quod est DEUS: Nam ex eo, per eum, & in ipsum sunt omnia: Rom. 11, 36. Quia autem Principium hoc ita administrat omnia, quæ creavit, ut etiam ipsa proprios exercere & agere motus sinat, ut loquitur Augustinus lib. 7. de Civit. DEI c. 30. ideò reliqua etiam principia in hac disputatione locum habent. Alterum Ergò principium rectissimè nominamus COMMUNE, quod nihil est aliud, quàm NATURA: non tantùm communis illa, quæ generi humano ex lapsu protoplastorum, æqualis planè obtigit: sed & specialis illa, quâ quodlibet Individuum singulariter movetur & afficitur. Tertium est principium SINGULARE, à naturâ rebus singulis inditum, idque vel Naturalis inclinationis sive instinctus: quo sensuum beneficio singula animata sui appetunt conservationem: vel intellectivæ voluntatis, quæ nihil est aliud, quàm facultas appetendi & volendi certum aliquem finem, per ea media, quæ ad finem illum perducere videntur. Quæ tria principia, cum in unius cujusque operis productione concurrant: utique mutua illorum erga se invicem affectio probè confideranda fuerit: id quod certis quibusdam hypothesibus expedire placet.

I. In consueto actionum humanarum cursu: Principium superius Inferiori nihil derogat: sed suas agendi vires relinquit. Nam uti suprà ostensum, DEUS ita omnia, quæ creavit, administrat, ut tamen ipsa proprios etiam exercere motus sinat: sic natura voluntatem ita movet, ut hæc libertate suâ relicta, sub coactionis necessitatem nunquam cadat.

2. Primum principium quodammodo habet rationem Generis: Secundum speciei: tertium singularis individui. Jam quemadmodum tota ratio Generis in specie: tota speciei in Individuo est: non autem vice versâ, tota ratio speciei inest Generi: aut tota speciei ratio inest Individuo: Sic primi principii Actio semper sui est Generis, vitiumque nec agit nec patitur: Secundi principii Actio vitium per se non facit, ut per se non facit species: sed à tertio principio patitur: Tertium verò principium & facit vitium & patitur.

3. Tertium principium agit & patitur, aut per se internâ suâ vi: aut per aliud principium externum, & foris adveniens. Vi internâ tùm, quando vel facultas intelligens per se cognoscit verum, aut deficit à vero: vel facultas volenti vult per se bonum, aut deficit à bono. Per aliud verò principium movetur, tùm, quando vel Natura superior, ut diabolica supervenit, & ad malum impellit: vel eadem Natura suadet ut appetat vitium: Sic in lapsu illo tristissimo primorum parentum, motum fuit principium illorum internum primum à naturâ superveniéte, nempè Diabolo: Deindè principium Internum Adami motum fuit ab eadem naturâ, quando nimirùm Eva ipsum decepit. Tandem utrique principio illi supervenienti ex proprio suo interno principio consenserunt: & sic voluntate propriâ in peccatum prolapsi sunt.

4. Hinc jam consequitur, cum ad unius operis effectum plures causæ subordinatæ concurrant: Effectum ultimum neque primæ, neque mediæ, sed solius proximæ causæ qualitatem & conditionem sequi, eo tamen discrimine, ut ullum eorum ad actiones bonas perficiendas requiratur, ut omnia principia sint bona: neque ullatenus exorbitent à motu superioris principii, ad malas autem actiones vel unum & quidem proximum principium sufficiat. Jam cùm actionum humanarum proximum principium sit voluntas Hominis: utique non ex causâ remotâ universali: sed ex proximâ particulari causâ de fonte & Origine sive causâ malarum actionum, judicandum esse, evidentissimè liquet,


### Errors concerning the Cause of Sin

IV. To whatever action the effect of sin follows, that very action is the cause of sin. But indeed, to the action of GOD withdrawing his grace and the Spirit of illumination, the effect of sin follows. Therefore, that very action of GOD will be the cause of sin. I answer: The consequence does not hold from causes by accident to the effect; but when causes in themselves are actually posited, the proper effect follows. But indeed, the subtraction of grace is not a cause in itself of sin. Rather, sin is the cause of the subtraction of grace: so that, speaking properly, sin precedes the respect of the cause; but the subtraction of grace obtains the status of an effect. But indeed, an effect can never be the cause of its own cause. Furthermore, that after grace and the spirit of illumination are withdrawn, greater sins follow of their own accord; that has in itself the status not of an effect, but of a defect: as was shown above.

But the vanities of the Libertines now being dismissed, we make a transition to the Zwinglians and Calvinists. It would be desirable in every way that they should proceed with a straighter foot toward the truth of the Gospel, and not that they themselves, in their own writings, should too clearly and perspicuously assert and attempt to defend what they condemned in the Libertines. Certainly, it is better known than to need proof that those arguments, by which we have already taught that some of the Libertines fight, are also leveled against our Churches by the very race of Zwinglians. Therefore, if any discrepancy exists between them, it will have been placed in this alone, that the Zwinglians seem to abhor that phrase of the Libertines, that sins by their own nature are not sins, but only by the opinion of men. Meanwhile, however, both not obscurely constitute GOD as the cause of sin. And although some, most especially among the recent Zwinglians, contend that their Churches are burdened in this part without merit, because none of their Doctors ever categorically said or wrote that GOD is the cause of sin, this protestation is nevertheless contrary to the fact. Calvin himself is a witness in his letter to the people of Rouen, that a certain Libertine, accused by name of horrible impiety, did not want to confess that he had constituted GOD as the author of sin, but protested that his mind was far otherwise. For even if they referred adulteries, homicides, rapines, and other crimes and wickednesses of that kind of men to GOD, they nevertheless denied that they were making GOD the author of evils, for the reason that they are not evils insofar as they are done by the impulse of GOD, but only insofar as they are judged to be such by the opinion of men. But whether the School of the Zwinglians and Calvinists today differs even a hair's breadth from this evasion of the Libertines, it would be worth the effort to repeat a little more accurately from their own writings and books.

Thus, however, Zwingli in his book on Providence, chapter 5, Vol. 1 of his Works, p. 346 and following: Since GOD or the Divine Power could in no way show injustice in himself to us, as that which is everywhere true, good, and holy by nature, he therefore produced an example of injustice through the creature, not as if the creature produced it by its own strength, which neither is, nor lives, nor operates without GOD or the Divine Power: But because the Divine Power itself is the author of that which is injustice to us, but to him is in no way injustice. And after a few words: One and the same deed, for instance adultery or homicide, insofar as it is the work of GOD as author, mover, and impeller, is not a crime; but insofar as it is of man, it is a crime and a wickedness. And after some things: GOD freely moves to some work, which is a fraud to the one performing it; yet it is not so to himself; nor does he do injury to the instrument, since all things are his. He moves, therefore, the robber to kill, even the innocent and unprepared for death. And again: Just as it is to the praise of a bull if it enters and fills the whole herd, but the master of the bull, if he knows only one woman besides his wife, is guilty of adultery, the cause is: because a law is set for this one: Do not commit adultery; but no law restrains that one (the bull): So for GOD, as if he were the head of a household, no law is set, therefore he does not sin while he does this very thing in man, which is a sin for man. And Chapter 6: Let the adultery of David be an example to you: Insofar as it pertains to GOD the author, it can no more be called a sin than if a bull mounts and fills the whole herd.

John Calvin, book 1 of the Institutes, chapter 8, § 2. Satan is said to blind the minds of the unfaithful: but whence this, unless because the efficacy of error flows from GOD himself, so that they believe lies, who refuse to obey the truth.

The same, book 2 of the Institutes, chapter 4, section 4. There are other testimonies which go further, such as those concerning the hardening of Pharaoh: I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, that he may not hear you and let the people go: Afterwards he says that he had made his heart heavy, and strengthened it. Did he harden it by not softening it? That is indeed true: but he did something more, in that he commanded Satan to make his breast firm with obstinacy. And section 5. An impure spirit is called the Spirit of God, because it responds to his nod and power, being more his instrument in acting than an author from itself. The same, book 3 of the Institutes, chapter 23, section 4. Were they not, by the ordination of God, predestined to that corruption which is now brought forward as the cause of damnation? When, therefore, they perish in their own corruption, they do nothing other than pay the penalties of that calamity into which Adam fell by his own predestination, and dragged his descendants headlong with him; is he not therefore unjust, who so cruelly mocks his own creatures? To this question Calvin answers thus: I confess indeed that all the sons of Adam fell into this misery of condition, by which they are now bound, by the will of God: and that is what I was saying at the beginning, that one must always return at last to the sole arbitration of the divine will, the cause of which is hidden in himself. The same, ibid., section. They deny that it stands in express words that it was decreed by God that Adam should perish by his own defection. As if that same God, whom Scripture proclaims to do whatever he wills, had created the most noble of his creatures with an ambiguous end. And after a few words: I confess that the decree is horrible: yet no one will be able to deny that God foresaw what end man was going to have before he created him: and therefore he foresaw it, because he had so ordained it by his decree.

Latin:

IV. Ad quamcunq; actionem sequitur Effectus peccati, illa ipsa actio causa est peccati. Jam verò ad actionem DEI subtrahentis suam gratiam, & Spiritum illuminationis, sequitur Effectus peccati. Ergò illa ipsa actio DEI erit causa peccati. Respondeo: A causis per Accidens non valet consequentia ad Effectum: sed positis actu causis per se, sequitur Effectus proprius. Jam verò subtractio gratiæ non est causa per se peccati. Quin potiùs Peccatum est causa subtractionis gratiæ: ita ut propriè loquendo, peccatum præcedens causæ respectum: Subtractio verò Gratiæ, effectus rationem obtineat. Jam verò effectus nunquam potest esse causa suæ causæ. Cæterùm quod subtractâ Gratiâ & spiritu illuminationis suâ sponte subindè majora sequuntur peccata; id non effectus, sed defectus rationem in se habet: uti suprà ostensum.

Sed Libertinorum vanitatibus jam missis, ad Zvvinglianos & Calvinianos transitum facimus. Optandum verò modis omnibus foret, ut rectiore pede ad veritatem Evangelii isti incederent: neque quod in Libertinis damnarunt, ipsimet suis in scriptis, nimis clarè & perspicuè assererent & defendere conarentur. Certè argumenta illa, quibus nonnullos ex Libertinis pugnare, jam præcepimus, ab ipsâ quoque Zvvinglianorum gente nostris Ecclesiis objici, notiùs est, quàm ut probatione opus sit. Proindè si quid discrepantiæ illis invicem intercedit, in eo solo id positum fuerit, quòd Zvvingliani abhorrere videntur ab eâ phrasi Libertinorum, quod peccata suâ naturâ non sint peccata: sed tantùm opinione hominum. Interim verò utrique DEUM peccati causam haud obscurè constituunt. Et licèt nonnulli, ex recentioribus potissimùm Zvvinglianis, hac in parte præter meritum suas gravari Ecclesias contendant: eò quod nullus suorum Doctorum categoricè unquàm vel dixerit, vel scripserit: DEUM esse causam peccati: est tamen Protestatio hæc contraria facto. Testis est ipse Calvinus in Epistolâ ad Rotomagenses, Libertinum quendam impietatis horrendæ nomine accusatum noluisse confiteri, se DEUM peccati autorem constituisse: sed contestatum esse, sibi longè aliam esse mentem. Etsi enim adulteria, homicidia, rapinas, & id genus alia hominum scelera atque flagitia in DEUM referebant: negabant tamen se facere DEUM autorem malorum, propterea quòd non ea sint mala, quatenùs DEI impulsu fiunt: sed tantùm quatenùs hominum opinione talia esse judicantur. Nùm verò vel latum pilum ab hac Libertinorum tergiversatione Zvvinglianorum & Calvinianorum Schola hodiè dissentiat: ex ipsorum Scriptis ac libris paulò accuratiùs repetere, operæ pretium fuerit.

Sic autem Zvvinglius libro de Providentiâ cap. 5. Tom. 1. Operum p. 346. & seqq. Cùm DEUS sive Numen injustitiam in sese nobis ostendere, nullâ ratione posset, ut quod undiquè verum, bonum, sanctum, naturâ sit, ideò per creaturam injustitiæ Exemplum produxit, non quasi Creatura illam suo Marte produxerit, quæ nec est, nec vivit, nec operatur sine DEO sive Numine : Sed quod Numen ipsum autor est, ejus, quod nobis est injustitia : illi verò nullatenùs est. Et post pauca : Unum atq́; idem facinus, putà adulterium, aut homicidium, quantum DEI est autoris, motoris, Impulsoris opus est, crimen non est : quantum autem hominis est, crimen ac scelus est. Et post aliqua : DEUS liberè movit ad opus aliquod, quod perficienti fraudi est : sibi tamen non est : neq́; instrumento facit injuriam, cùm omnia sint sua. Movet ergò latronem ad occidendum : innocentem etiam ac imparatum ad mortem. Et rursum : Quemadmodum Tauro, si totum armentum ineat & impleat, laudi est : Herus autem Tauri, si unam modò præter uxorem, cognoscat, reus sit adulterii : causa est : quia huic lex est posita : Ne adulterium admittas : Illum verò (Taurum) nulla lex coërcet : Ita DEO veluti patrifamiliâs non est posita lex, idcircò nec peccat, dùm hoc ipsum agit in homine, quod homini peccatum est. Et Cap. 6. Exemplo sit tibi Adulterium Davidis : Quatenùs illud ad Autorem DEUM pertinet, haud magis peccatum dici potest, quàm si Taurus totum armentum inscendit & implet.

Johannes Calvinus lib. 1. Instit. cap. 8. §. 2. Dicitur Satan excæcare infidelium mentes : sed unde hoc, nisi quod à DEO ipso manat efficacia erroris, ut mendaciis credant ; qui renuunt parére veritati.

Idem lib. 2. Instit. cap. 4. §. 4. Sunt alia testimonia, quæ ultrà procedunt, qualia sunt de Pharaonis Induratione : Indurabo cor Pharaonis, ne vos audiat ac dimittat populu : Postea dicit se aggravasse cor illius, & roborasse. An induravit non emolliendo ? Id quidem verum est : sed plus aliquid fecit, quod obstinatione pectus ejus obfirmandum Satanæ mandavit. Et §. 5. Spiritus impurus DEI Spiritus vocatur, quia ad ejus nutum potentiamquè respondet, instrumentum magis ipsius in agendo , quàm à seipso autor. Idem lib. 3. Instit. cap. 23. §. 4. Nonnè ad eam, quæ nunc pro damnationis causâ obtenditur, corruptionem, DEI ordinatione prædestinati fuerunt ? Cùm ergò in suâ corruptione pereunt, nihil aliud, quàm pœnas luunt ejus calamitatis, in quam ipsius prædestinatione lapsus est Adam, ac posteros secum præcipites traxit, an non itaquè injustus, qui creaturis suis tam crudeliter illudit : Ad hanc Quæstionem ita respondet Calvinus : Fateor sanè in hanc, quâ nunc illigati sunt, conditionis miseriam DEI voluntate decidisse omnes filios Adam : atq́; id est, quod principiò dicebam, redeundum tandem semper esse ad solum divinæ voluntatis arbitrium, cujus causa sit in ipso abscondita. Idem ibid. §. Disertis verbis hoc extare negant, Decretum fuisse à DEO, ut suâ defectione periret Adam. Quasi verò idem ille DEUS, quem Scriptura prædicat facere quæcunq́; vult, ambiguo fine condiderit nobilissimam ex suis creaturis. Et post pauca : Decretum quidem horribile fateor : inficiari tamen nemo poterit, quin præsciverit DEUS, quem exitum esset habiturus homo, antequam ipsum conderet : & ideò præsciverit, quia decreto suo sic ordinârat.


### Errors concerning the Cause of Sin: Question 1. Whether here rather the faculty and inclination alone is explained?

And after a few words: Nor should it seem absurd, what I say: that GOD not only foresaw the fall of the first man, and in him the ruin of his descendants: but also disposed it by his own will. For as it pertains to his wisdom to be prescient of all things that are to be: so it pertains to his power to rule and moderate all things by his own hand.

David Paraeus, p. 179, in the Neustadt Bible, writes: That divine foreknowledge is the supreme cause of all things that happen, the worker of good, but of evil, the enge.

Theodore Beza, in his Response to Castellio concerning the eternal predestination of GOD, in the refutation of the second calumny, discourses thus concerning the fall of Adam: GOD, being about to create man to declare the glory both of his mercy and of his severity, created Adam in his own image, that is, holy and innocent: But why indeed? Namely, because since he is good, nothing vicious can be created by him: But it is necessary that they be vicious, both those whom he determined to pity, and also those whom he justly decreed, for the sake of his glory, to condemn,

And after a few words: It was therefore necessary for GOD also to open this one way for himself, that is, to ordain the fall of Adam, but to the end which I have mentioned, which, since it is most just and most holy, it follows that his ordination of it is also just.

And a little later: The origin of vice must be sought in the spontaneous motion of the instruments, whereby it happens that GOD justly decreed what they unjustly did. But you will say, They could not resist the will of GOD, that is, his decree? I confess it, but just as they could not, so also they did not want to. But could they not have willed otherwise? I confess it, as regards the outcome and the ἐνέργειαν: But yet the will of Adam was not coerced.

The same, in his 2nd Response to the Acts of the Colloquy of Montbéliard, page 177: If we posit that it is in the power of Satan and the wicked to plot anything against us, whose malice GOD merely restrains: you will certainly have taken away as much from GOD as you have attributed of power to them.

Moreover, for the sake of obtaining victory in this unhappy war, the Adversaries write at the beginning to our Churches concerning the cause of the Adamic fall, in various and partly too curious ways and questions: which it will not be inconvenient to treat in order.

And at the beginning indeed it is asked, why GOD created Adam to that end, that in him he might have matter for exercising his glory, both as regards his justice and as regards his mercy? whether Adam did not have need to fall, so that GOD might attain that end of his?

That this question may be more solidly explained, we readily grant at the beginning that the end of the created Adam is also the glory of God: but we immediately reply to that, that in this dispute, the controversy is not primarily about the end of the 'g' [grace/glory], but about the end of the 'w' [work/will], as they speak in the Schools: that is, the question is not whether the glory of God could shine forth from the creation of man: but rather this, to what end man himself was created by God? Whether it was so that he might fall and rush into sin? Or indeed so that he might persist in a state of integrity, and at length be eternally saved. Where our adversaries dissent from us in what they call the whole camp, contending that God could never have attained that end of His, in respect to Himself, unless the first man fell: and consequently that God, thus willing and ordaining, the fall itself was. Which opinion we indeed simply reject as impious. For, 1. ἄτερ γραφῆς without the Scriptures, the adversaries affirm these things, then against the Scriptures: since they expressly affirm that God created man for eternal life, Wis. 2:23. 3. If God had never created man at all: nevertheless He would have remained in Himself alone, in every respect most just, most good, most blessed, most perfect: although He had never declared His goodness in the salvation of men, nor His justice in the damnation of the reprobate. 4. God did not need the fall of our first parents to demonstrate His justice: which He had sufficiently demonstrated in the fallen angels. 5. If no one, either of men or angels, had fallen: or if all who had fallen, as well angels as men, had been restored to their integrity: yet there would have remained sufficiently great and illustrious arguments, not only of mercy, but also of divine justice. For the Lord knows how to temper His mercy in such a way that He also satisfies justice: which He abundantly shows in the merit of the Son freely imputed to those who believe. 6. If God ordained from eternity that man should fall: it was certainly a mere mockery that He created him in His own image, and endowed him with such rectitude and integrity of all his powers, that if he had willed, he could have persisted entirely in a state of innocence: but far be it that we should imagine any such thing about God. 7. That law and the threatening of the law, by which God wished to deter man from sinning in Paradise, must necessarily have been in vain, nay, only feigned: if God ordained man to the fall itself by some eternal decree? Which again would be prodigiously absurd and impious. 8. The justice of God would labor gravely in this arrangement. For because God most atrociously punished the fall of our first parents: God would certainly have to be considered to have punished man for that to which he had been ordained by Him: which is diametrically opposed to the immutable justice of God: since the justice of God could never excuse itself in eternity, if He punished a creature with infernal and eternal torments for that which the Creator Himself willed and approved, nay, to which He impelled him. Which reasons being well weighed, it is clearer than the midday light that the opinion of the Calvinists, in whatever way it may be cloaked, in reality constitutes God as the author and approver of sin. For if, as Calvin and Beza attest, God not only foreknew from eternity that Adam would fall: but also foreknew it for this reason, because by His own will and decree He had ordained him to this very fall: who does not see that Adam was ordained from eternity not only to the ultimate end, which in their opinion is the glory of either divine justice or mercy: but also to the intermediate cause, which by the confession of the adversaries themselves is sin: the force and evidence of which collection of ours is so great, that it has extorted this confession even from an unwilling Beza:

That GOD destined Man not only to the ultimate end, namely the fall: but also to the intermediate causes. For in the booklet Quæst. & Resp. Vol. 1. page 681. he raises such a question: The sum, therefore, of those things which you have said concerning Providence, is this: That nothing at all happens either against the will or without the knowledge of GOD: but so entirely, as GOD himself from eternity decreed, most powerfully and most effectively disposing all intermediate causes, so that they are NECESSARILY carried to the destined end, as far as pertains to his own Decree: and yet that he is not the author or approver of any evil; since he always acts most justly, with whatever instruments he executes his work? Response: IT is so. Which Confession of Beza other Calvinists, and especially Hermann Rennecher in the golden chain of salvation, increases with greater impiety, writing thus on page 32: GOD DRAWS the impious by a secret force, as if by a hidden rope, otherwise unknowing, to the attaining of those ends which they themselves least contemplate. Thus the Impious, by the hidden hand of GOD, without ANY purpose and effort of their own, are directed to an end unknown to them, no differently than an arrow arrives at the target of the one who shoots it, without any sense of its own.

But perhaps someone might object, and think that the Theology of the Calvinists can be mitigated, in that they occasionally add that GOD justly, or by a just decree of GOD, Adam was ordained to the fall. But these are fig leaves, used by Libertines just as much as by Calvinists, which so far from covering the shameful parts of their dogma, that they rather uncover them. For first, they shamefully beg the question, and take for granted that which is placed in Controversy. Therefore, let them first prove from the Scriptures that GOD from eternity ordained Adam to the fall, so that he might have material for declaring his justice and mercy. If they have provided this proof, then at last room is left for that Scheme which they occasionally append concerning the justice of GOD: since it is beyond Controversy: that GOD does all things which he does, justly.

Certainly if GOD had left man, already fallen into sins by his own will and malice, along with his entire posterity, in his misery: no one surely would deny that GOD would not on that account have suffered any loss of his justice. But to ordain from eternity that Man should fall into sin: that can never be reconciled with the eternal justice of GOD: but rather implies a most shameful Contradiction, nay, it plainly overturns the very justice of GOD: as was shown a little before. Thus neither does this phrase of the Adversaries accord with the analogy of faith, when they keep saying: that GOD ordained Adam to the fall by a free, but just will, or certainly created him for that end, that from their fall, and indeed in damning the reprobate, material for declaring justice might be supplied. Perhaps an argument for power: but this could never be an argument for divine justice: as will be shown more fully in its place from the Article on Predestination.

Cast down from this stronghold, the Calvinists seek various κρησφύγετα (places of refuge). For they seek further, Why did GOD not prevent the Fall of Adam, if he did not create him for that end, that he might fall? But the vanity of this quibble can also be demonstrated in many ways. For 1. GOD was under no obligation by any right to prevent the fall of Adam: since he owes nothing to anyone. 2. If we contemplate Adam himself, as he had been created by GOD in the beginning, more accurately: it is certainly most clearly evident that GOD on his part omitted nothing at all that he could have done to prohibit and prevent the fall. For 1. he instructed him with that rectitude and faculty of all powers, by which he could have persisted in the state of integrity, and rendered the obedience due to GOD, if he had willed. 2. Lest man himself should rush into some ἐθελοθρησκείαν (will-worship) or elective cult, and thus fall from the grace of creation: he fixed a certain law for him, by the barriers of which he might be restrained within the bounds of true divine worship. 3 By adding most grave threats he deterred man from sinning. Which three things were indeed so arranged that they could have prevented Man from sinning, had not man himself of his own accord turned himself away from GOD: so that Augustine rightly said: Adam, with no one terrifying him, and furthermore against the command of the terrifying GOD, using his free will, did not stand in such happiness, in such ease of not sinning. Book on rebuke and grace, chapter 12.

Latin:

Et post pauca: Nec absurdum videri debet, quod dico: DEUM non modò primi hominis casum, & in eo posterorum ruinam prævidisse: sed arbitrio quoq́; suo dispensasse. Ut enim ad ejus sapientiam pertinet omnium, quæ futura sunt, esse præscium: sic ad potentiam, omnia suâ manu regere ac moderari.

David Paræus p. 179. Bibl. Neostad. scribit: Divinam præscientiam, summam esse causam omnium quæ fiunt, operatricem boni, mali verò enge.

Theodoretus Beza, Responsione ad Castellionem de æternâ DEI prædestinatione, in refutatione secundæ calumniæ: ita disserit de lapsu Adami: DEUS hominem conditurus ad gloriam tùm misericordiæ, tùm severitatis suæ declarandam, Adamum condidit ad imaginem suam, id est, sanctum ac innocentem: Cur nam id verò? nempè quia bonus cùm sit, non potest ab eo vitiosum quicquam creari: Vitiosi autem sint oportet, tùm, quorum constituit misereri, tùm etiam quos justè decrevit, gloriæ suæ causâ condemnare,

Et pòst pauca: Oportuit ergò DEUM quoq́; hanc unicam viam sibi aperire, id est, Adami lapsum ordinare, sed ad eum, quem dixi finem, qui cùm sit justissimus & sanctissimus, justam quoque ipsius ordinationem esse consequitur.

Et paulò pòst: Quærenda est vitii origo in Instrumentorum spontaneo motu, quo fit, ut DEUS justè decreverit, quod illi injustè fecerunt. At enim dices, Non potuerunt resistere DEI voluntati, id est, decreto? Fateor, sed sicut non potuerunt, ita etiam noluerunt. Verùm non poterant aliter velle? Fateor, quoad eventum, & ἐνέργειαν: Sed voluntas tamen Adami coacta non fuit.

Idem Respons. 2. ad Acta Colloquii Mompelg. pag. 177. Si statuamus in Satanæ & Sceleratorum potestate esse quidpiam in nos moliri, quorum duntaxat malitiam DEUS refrænet: tantùm certè DEO ademeris, quantùm illis potestatis tribueris.

Cæterùm pro obtinendâ in hoc infelici bello victoriâ, Adversarii initiò de causâ lapsus Adamici, dicam, scribunt nostris Ecclesiis, variis & partìm nimis curiosis modis quæstionibus: quas ordine pertractare haud fuerit inconveniens.

Acinitio quidem quæritur, cur DEUS eo fine considerit Adamum, ut in eo haberet materiam exercendæ suæ gloriæ, tùm quoad justitiam, tùm quoad misericordiam suam? an non ideò Adam labi necesse habuerit, ut DEUS finem illum suum assequeretur?
