Quæ Quæstio ut solidiùs explicetur, facilè initio largimur quidem, Finem creati Adami esse etiam gloriam DEI: verùm illud statim regerimus, hac in disputatione, non potissimùm de fine g: sed de fine ῶ, ut in Scholis loquuntur, esse Controversiam: hoc est, non de eo quæri, An ex creatione Hominis Gloria DEI elucere poterit: Sed illud potiùs, Ad quem finem ipse Homo à DEO creatus fuerit An ideò ut laberetur & in peccatum prorueret? An verò ut in statu integritatis persisteret, & tandem æternùm salvaretur. Ubi Adversarii à nobis totis, quod ajunt, castris dissident, contendentes, DEUM finē illum suũ, ratione sui, nunquam assequi potuisse, nisi primus homo laberetur: ac proindè DEO sic volente & ordinante ipsum lapsum esse. Quam sanè sententiam nos ceu impiam simpliciter rejicimus. Nam, 1. ἄτερ γραφῆς sine Scripturis isthæc affirmant Adversarii, Deindè contra Scripturas: quippè quæ διαρρήδην affirmant, DEUM condidisse Hominem ad vitam æternam Sap. 2, 23. 3. Si vel maximè DEUS hominem nunquam condidisset: nihilominus tamen in seipso solo permansisset, omni numero justissimus, optimus, beatissimus, perfectissimus: licèt neque bonitatem suam in salvatione hominum, neq; justitiam in damnatione reproborum nunquam declarasset. 4. Lapsu primorum parentum non indiguit DEUS, ut justitiam suam demonstraret: quam in lapsis Angelis sufficienter demonstraverat. 5. Si maximè nemo vel hominum vel Angelorum lapsus fuisset: aut si omnes lapsi, tàm Angeli quàm homines integritati suæ fuissent restituti: satis tamen magna & præclara superfuissent, non modò Misericordiæ, sed & justitiæ divinæ argumenta. Ita enim Misericordiam suam temperare novit DOMINUS, ut támen justitiæ quoque satisfaciat: id quod in merito Filii credentibus gratis imputato abundè ostendit. 6. Si DEUS ab æterno ordinavit, ut homo laberetur: certè merum ludibrium fuit, quod ipsum ad Sui imaginem creavit, eaque virium omnium rectitudine & integritate instruxit, ut si voluisset, omninò in statu innocentiæ persistere potuisset: Absit autem ut de DEO tale aliquid fingamus. 7. Frustranea fuerit, necesse est, imò simulata tátùm Lex illa & legis comminatio, quâ à peccando DEUS hominem deterrere voluit in Paradiso: Si DEUS ad lapsum ipsum æterno aliquo decreto ordinavit? id quod rursum prodigiosè absurdum & impium fuerit. 8. Justitia DEI graviter laboraret hoc pacto. Quia enim DEUS lapsum primorum parentum, atrocissimè punivit: utique statuendus esset DEUS Hominem punivisse ob id, ad quod ab ipso ordinatus fuerat: id quod cum immotâ DEI justitiâ è diametro pugnat: Siquidem in æternum justitia DEI excusare non posset, si creaturam infernalibus atque æternis suppliciis puniret, propter id quod vellet & approbaret ipse conditor, imò ad quod impelleret. Quibus rationibus probè expensis, luce meridianâ clariùs liquet, quod Sententia Calvinianorum, quocunque tandem modo pallietur, revera tamen DEUM peccati autorem & approbatorem constituit. Si enim Calvino & Beza attestantibus, DEUS non modò præscivit ab æterno Adamum lapsurum: sed ideò etiam præscivit, quia suâ voluntate & decreto ad hunc ipsum lapsum illum ordinaverat: Quis non videt, non tantùm ad ultimum finem, qui istorum opinione est Gloria vel Justitiæ vel misericordiæ divinæ: sed etiam ad causam intermediam, quæ ipsorum quoque Adversariorum Confessione est peccatum, Adamum ab æterno ordinatum fuisse: Cujus nostræ collectionis tanta est vis & evidentia, ut Bezæ vel inscio hanc Confessionem extorserit:

DEUM non modò ad finem ultimum, nempè lapsum: sed & ad causas intermedias Hominem destinasse. Nam in libello Quæst. & Resp. Vol. 1. pag. 681. talem movet quæstionem: Summa igitur eorum, quæ de Providentiâ dixisti, hæc est: Nihil prorsus vel invito vel nesciente DEO evenire: sed ita omninò, uti DEUS ipse ab æterno decrevit potentissimè & efficacissimè Causas omnes intermedias disponens, ut ad destinatum finem NECESSARIO, quod ad ipsius Decretum attinet, ferantur: nec tamē ullius mali autorem esse, vel approbatorem; quoniam justissimè semper agat, quibuscunq; instrumentis opus suum exequatur? Responsio: ITA est. Quam Bezæ Confessionem alii Calviniani, & cumprimis Hermannus Rennecherus in aureâ salutis catenâ, majore impietate auget, sic scribens pag. 32 DEUS impios arcanâ vi, tanquam occulto fune alioquin nescios, ad eos fines, quos ipsi minimè spectant, consequendos TRAHIT. Sic Impii occultâ DEI manu sine ULLO suo proposito & conatu, ad finem ipsis incognitum non secus diriguntur, quàm sagitta ad emittentis scopum, sine ullo suo sensu perveniunt.

Sed excipiat fortè aliquis, Calvinianorum Theologiam mitigari posse opinetur, eò quod subindè addunt, DEUM justè, aut justo DEI decreto, Adamum ad lapsum ordinatum esse. Sed folia hæc sunt ficulnea, Libertinis æquè ac Calvinianis usitata, quæ dogmatis ipsorum pudenda usque adeò non tegunt, ut magis detegant. Nam primò turpiter petunt principium, & pro confesso arripiunt id, quod in Controversiâ est positum. Prius ergò ex Scripturis probent, DEUM ab æterno Adamum, ad lapsum ordinasse, ut haberet materiam declarandæ suæ justitiæ & misericordiæ. Hoc si probatum dederint, tùm demùm locus relinquitur Schemati illi, quod de justitiâ DEI subindè attexunt: Siquidem extra Controversiam est: DEUM omnia, quæ facit, justè facere.

Certè si DEUS hominem propriâ voluntate & malitiâ jam in peccata prolapsum, cum universâ ipsius posteritate, reliquisset in suâ miseriâ: nemo profectò priùs inficiaretur, DEUM non proptereà justitiæ suæ jacturam ullam facturum fuisse. Cæterùm ab æterno ordinare, ut Homo labatur in peccatum: id cum æternâ DEI justitiâ nunquam conciliari potest: sed turpissimam potiùs Contradictionem implicat, imò ipsam justitiam DEI planè evertit: uti paulò antè fuit ostensum. Sic neque hæc Adversariorum phrasis analogiæ fidei congruit, quando dictitant: DEUM liberâ, sed justâ voluntate, Adamum ad lapsum ordinasse, vel certè eo fine condidisse, ut ex ipsorum lapsu, & quidem in damnandis reprobis justitiæ declarandæ materia suppeteret. Potentiæ fortassis: at nunquam justitiæ divinæ argumentum hoc esse poterat: uti suo loco ex Articulo de Prædestinatione patebit fusius.

Ab hoc dejecti præsidio Calviniani varia quærunt κρησφύγετα. Quærunt enim porrò, Cur DEUS non impediverit Lapsum Adami, si ipsum non eo fine condidit, ut laberetur? Sed & hujus argutiæ vanitas multis modis demonstrari potest. Nam 1. DEUS nullo jure tenebatur impedire lapsum Adami: Siquidem nemini quicquam debet. 2. Si ipsum Adamum, prout initio a DEO conditus fuerat, contemplemur accuratius: certe luculentissime patet, DEUM ex sua parte nihil prorsus intermisisse, quod ad prohibendum, impediendumque lapsum facere poterat. Nam 1. instruxit ipsum ea virium omnium rectitudine & facultate, qua in statu integritatis persistere, & DEO debitam obedientiam præstare potuisset, si voluisset. 2. Ne homo ipse in aliquam ἐθελοθρησκείαν sive cultum electitium prorueret, & sic gratia creationis excideret: certam ipsi legem fixit, cujus repagulis intra cancellos veri cultus divini coërceretur. 3 Additis gravissimis comminationibus a peccando deterruit hominem. Quæ sane tria ita fuerunt comparata, ut Hominem a peccando impedire potuissent, nisi homo ipse sponte sua se a DEO avertisset: ita ut recte Augustinus dixerit: Adam & terrente nullo, & insuper contra DEI terrentis imperium, libero usus arbitrio, non stetit in tanta felicitate, in tanta non peccandi facilitate. l. de corrept. & grat. cap. 12.


### Errors concerning the Cause of Sin: Question 1. Whether here rather the faculty and inclination alone is explained? (continued)

Therefore, since GOD so formed man that it was as easy for him not to sin as to sin: certainly no cause can now be given by which GOD was bound by duty not to permit the fall of the first parents.

But neither does Human curiosity rest even thus, but continues by asking, Why did GOD not prevent the fall by some external means? Why did he not, by some violent repression, pull back the hands of the first parents from the touch of the forbidden fruit? It is answered, however, that this could not have been done by any reason, nay, that it should not even have been done. For 1. The obedience of the first parents had to be spontaneous: Now such violent repression could not stand with spontaneous Obedience. And for this reason the obedience of Adam had to be spontaneous, so that it might be proved to GOD: that which D. Basil explains with this simile: Just as you, who are an earthly Lord, do not judge those to be faithful and thrifty servants who, constrained by shackles or chains, do what you command: but those who spontaneously and freely do what is their duty, strenuously: So also it is not acceptable to GOD, what is forced and expressed by some violence: but proceeds from true virtue. Virtue, however, arises from προαιρέσει (choice), not from necessity. προαίρεσις (choice) and Election requires freedom of will, and τὸ ἀυτεξέσιον (self-determination), or τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν (that which is in our power). Homily, that GOD is not the cause of sin. Augustine book 11 on Genesis to the letter, c. 7. 2. That violent repression would indeed have pulled back the hands: but it would not have corrected the internal perverse will and concupiscence itself: and therefore if the hands had been pulled back from the first parents in a violent manner even to the greatest degree: the fall itself would not yet have been prevented. The source of sin, therefore, which lay hidden in the heart of Man, had to be restrained: which GOD most conveniently performed: by those three things, or ἐμποδισμασι (hindrances), or remedies proposed, by which Man could resist perverse concupiscences, and use the free will of his volition rightly.

Human Reason further becomes tumultuous: Why did GOD leave to the first man τὸ ἀυτεξέσιον (self-determination), or the freedom of the will: and why did He not rather create him so that he could not sin? But this curiosity also labors under manifest absurdities and impieties. For 1. If GOD had not left to man τὸ ἀυτεξόσιον, or the freedom of the will: then He ought not to have granted man the use of Reason either. as Damascenus rightly infers: Along with Reason, free will is introduced: ἐυθέως τῷ λογικῷ συνεισέρχεται τὸ ἀυτεξόσιον, and these two are ἀντιςρέφοντα, which posit and remove each other. To which Basil also agrees in his Hexaëmeron: He who finds fault in our Creator, that He did not create us so that we could not sin by nature: he does nothing else but contend that it would have been better if GOD had created us irrational, or clearly immobile trunks or stones, rather than rational men. 2. Therefore GOD left man in the hand of his own counsel, who ought to have exhibited a free and spontaneous worship to GOD: such as he himself could never have performed, if he had been destitute of the faculty of Free will.

Human Reason rises up in the fifth place: Why did GOD not immediately, as soon as He created Man, at the same time confirm him in good: and so destine him to eternal life, that he could no longer fall away? But it is answered: That GOD had far weightier and most just causes for this act as well. For 1. Confirmation in good ought to have been the reward and gratuitous compensation of preceding spontaneous and free obedience: which, since Adam had not yet proven to GOD, how, I ask, could he have been made, or even ought he to have been made, a participant of this reward?

The evidence of this reason is clear from the Example of the good Angels, who were not confirmed in good by GOD before they had proven their free and spontaneous obedience to GOD: unlike the others, who did not persist in the truth, John 8:44, nor kept their own principality, but left their own habitation, for the judgment of the great day in eternal chains, kept under darkness: as the Epistle of Jude v. 6 has it. 2. Furthermore, that obedience which Man owed to his Creator, by the benefit of creation, needed in every way to be conspicuous and evident, such indeed, in which he himself would experience the faculty of his own powers bestowed in creation. Now, however, it can be a doubt to no one, that that Obedience is most regarded and illustrious, when one does not sin, when he could sin: than if one does not sin for the reason that he cannot sin. With these two reasons observed, the voice of Johannes Piscator must needs be impious, clearly and blasphemous, who in his disputation on Predestination, Thesis 27 and 33, writes thus: GOD created the first parents such that they could fall: Indeed, He created them with this counsel, that they would in fact fall.

Sixthly it is asked, Why did GOD not set another law before the first parents, which they would have kept: or, why was GOD not content with the internal worship of the mind, but demanded in addition the external obedience of the members of the body? But these evasions too are too putrid and rotten. For 1. If GOD had even greatly promulgated another law to the first parents, they would nevertheless have transgressed that one too, if they had not rightly used the freedom of choice and the powers granted. 2. If GOD had given such a law, the object of which would have been already entirely hateful and unappealing to Man, to speak with the Scholastics: certainly it would no longer have been his spontaneous Obedience, indeed, properly speaking, it would have been no obedience at all. For neither do laws even prohibit that which Men by their nature flee and avert: nor is anyone said to perform spontaneous obedience regarding such an object, which by itself and by reason of itself is so affected, that all sane people flee it and pursue it with hatred. 3. GOD could hardly have promulgated a law easier to observe. For in such a variety and abundance of most precious trees, and most noble fruits, what, I ask, was easier than to refrain from the fruit of one tree: so that if ever anywhere, certainly in Paradise GOD must be established to have promulgated a law possible and easy to observe. 4. Since Adam, regarding a Law so very easy, did not want to use the powers granted rightly: but gave place to the persuasions of the woman and the Devil: certainly it is gathered even from that: If GOD had even greatly imposed another law, nevertheless the first parents would not have kept that one either.

By the same reasoning, the other member of the proposed Question is clearly nugatory. For since Man did not consist of the mind alone, but also of the body; since also that Image of GOD, to which he had been created, regarded not only the powers of the mind, but also the rectitude of the powers of the body and of all the members; certainly Man also, not only as to the soul, but also as to the body, was bound to declare obedience to GOD the Creator. Therefore, a Law of such a kind was also required, concerning the observance of which man might declare to GOD the obedience of both parts, both of Soul and Body.

Seventhly, it is asked: Would it not have been better if GOD had given absolutely no law to our first parents? But now, since a Law was given: is it not, and consequently its author also, the cause, or at least the occasion, of the most sad fall of our first parents? But I answer that this Question 1. is utterly destitute of every refutation, at least in appearance. For he who maintains that it would have been better if no Law at all had bound our first parents, he seeks and contends for nothing else than that it would have been better, both for the glory of GOD and for the benefit of man himself, if Man had either been obliged to render no obedience at all to GOD according to the prescription of any law, or at least had performed it not according to the will of GOD, but according to his own. How both of these square with the end of Creation and the analogy of faith, ought to be weighed by the adversaries.

The end of created Man, with respect to GOD, was surely none other than that the Creator should be duly worshipped by the creature. But now, what kind of worship would be pleasing and acceptable to GOD, ought deservedly to depend not on the will of man, but on the will of GOD himself.

Therefore, so that man might not err regarding the worship to be rendered, GOD wished to promulgate a certain law, by which he might inform both the internal movement of the mind and the external obedience of the body, and even by this pact testify to his Philanthropia: so that neither the cause nor the occasion of the fall can be ascribed to GOD any more than a political Magistrate ought to be established as the cause of transgressions when subjects sin against laws promulgated in a just manner.

Eighthly, it is asked: Why did GOD not immediately after the committed fall utterly abolish the first parents and produce a new Man? But it is answered most correctly, first with the Apostle from 1 Cor. 4:6, ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ὑπὲρ ὃ γέγραπται: one ought not to be wise above that which is written. For, as Augustine aptly infers in book 11 of De Genesi ad litteram, ch. 10, GOD could have converted the will of the first parents into good, since he is omnipotent: or he could have plainly changed their nature; he could have plainly: Why then did he not do it? Because he did not wish to: Why he did not wish to, rests with him: We ought not to be wiser than we ought, Rom. 12:3.

But then, to those weighing the matter a little more deeply, causes can be at hand for which GOD ought not to have done this. For it is certain that individual species created by GOD were also created by GOD for this end, that such as they were created, they should endure until this World persisted. Therefore, the abolition of one species, and indeed a most noble one, could not have a place: and indeed immediately on that very day on which this species was created. For if we believe Irenaeus and other Fathers, the first Man fell on that very day on which he had been founded. But if, therefore, GOD had immediately after the fall abolished this species, his infinite wisdom as well as his providence would have been greatly endangered. Then, if GOD had had to create a new one once man was abolished: certainly he would have had to found one either the same in species or different in species: if the same in species: surely even that one could have fallen into sin, and thus by this pact the danger of the fall would not have been removed. But if different in species: then a true man, endowed with body and rational soul and instructed with freedom of will, would no longer have been founded: rather that former human species would have utterly ceased: that which again conflicts manifestly both with the eternal wisdom of GOD and with the end of creation. Thirdly, GOD could not create a new species of Man, because it is read that he rested on the seventh day: even by this pact testifying that he would produce no more new species of creatures thereafter. Finally, since GOD provided a remedy for the fall of the first parents, not indeed through a new creation, but through that spiritual παλιγγενεσίαν, or Regeneration of Man, by a most wise counsel: Human Reason certainly has nothing by which it can speak against GOD in this part as well: especially since this Regeneration takes away the guilt of that most sad Fall, which a New creation of Man could never have taken away.

Latin:

Proinde cum sic DEUS formaverit hominem, ut tam facile ipsi esset non peccare, quam peccare: utique causa jam dari non potest, qua DEUS ex debito obstrictus fuerit, ad lapsum primorum parentum non permittendum.

Sed neque sic quiescit Humana curiositas, quin quærendo pergit, Cur DEUS non externo aliquo modo lapsum impediverit? Cur non violenta quadam repressione, manus primorum parentum ab tactu pomi prohibiti, retraxerit? Respondetur autem, hoc nulla ratione fieri potuisse, imo ne debuisse quidem. Nam 1. Obedientia primorum parentum debuit esse spontanea: Jam talis violenta repressio, cum spontanea Obedientia stare non potuit. Idco autem debuit esse spontanea Adami obedientia, ut probaretur DEO: id, quod D. Basilius hac similitudine explicat: Quemadmodum tu, qui terrenus Dominus es, non eos pro fidelibus, & frugi servis judicas qui compedibus aut vinculis constricti, id agunt, quod jubes: sed qui sponte & libere, quod sui est muneris, strenue faciunt: Ita quoq; DEO acceptum non est, quod coacta & violentia quadam expressum est: sed ex vera virtute proficiscitur. Virtus autem ex προαιρέσει oritur, non ex necessitate. προαίρεσις autem & Electio requirit libertatem arbitrii, & τὸ ἀυτεξέσιον, sive τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν. Homilia, quod DEUS non est causa peccati. Augustinus lib. 11. de Genesi ad lit. c. 7. 2. Violenta illa repressio, manus quidem retrahere: ipsam autem internam pravam voluntatem& concupiscentiam minime correxisset: ac proinde si vel maxime manus primis parentibus violento modo retracta fuiffet: nondum tamen lapsus ipse impeditus fuisset. Fons ergo peccati, qui in corde Hominis latitabat, cohibendus fuerat: id quod DEUS cövenientissime præstitit: tribus illis sive ἐμποδισμασι, sive remediis propositis, quib9 Homo pravis concupiscentiis resistere, & libero voluntatis arbitrio recte uti poterat.

Tumultuatur porro Humana Ratio: Cur DEUS primo homini reliquerit τὸ ἀυτεξέσιον, sive libertatem voluntatis: & cur non potiùs ita ipsum condiderit, ut peccare non posset? Sed & hæc curiositas manifestis tùm absurditatibus, tùm impietatibus laborat. Nam 1. Si DEUS homini non reliquisset τὸ ἀυτεξόσιον, sive libertatem voluntatis: tùm neque quidem Homini Rationis usum concedere debuisset. Ratio enim non est absque arbitrii libertate: neque arbitrii libertas absque ratione: sed ut Damascenus rectè infert: Unà cum Ratione inducitur liberum arbitrium: ἐυθέως τῷ λογικῷ συνεισέρχεται τὸ ἀυτεξόσιον, & hæc duo sunt ἀντιςρέφοντα, quæ se mutuò ponunt & tollunt. Cui adstipulatur etiam Basilius in Hexaëmero: Qui illud carpit in Creatore nostro, quod nos non condiderit, ut naturâ peccare non possemus: is nihil aliud facit, quàm quòd contendit, melius fuisse, si DEUS nos creasset irrationales, aut planè immobiles truncos aut lapides, quàm rationales homines. 2. Ideò DEUS reliquit hominem in manu consilii sui, qui liberum & spontaneum DEO cultum exhibere debebat: qualem ipse nunquàm præstare potuisset, si facultate Liberi arbitrii destitutus fuisset.

Insurgit quinto loco Ratio humana: Cur DEUS non statim atq; creavit Hominem, simul ita in bono confirmavit: & ita ad vitam æternam destinavit, ut excidere amplius non posset? Sed Respondetur: Facti etiam hujus causas longè gravissimas & justissimas habuisse DEUM. Nam 1. Confirmatio in bono esse debuit præmium & gratuita compensatio, antegressæ spontaneæ ac liberæ obedientiæ: quam cùm Adam nondum DEO probaverit, quomodo, quæso, præmii hujus particeps reddi vel potuisset; vel etiam debuisset?

Patet rationis hujus evidentia Exemplo bonorum Angelorum, quid haud prius à DEO in bono confirmati sunt, quàm liberam & spontaneam obedientiam DEO probassent: reliquis, qui in veritate non perstiterunt, Joh. 8, 44. neque servarunt suum principatum, sed dereliquerunt suum domicilium, in judicium magni diei vinculis æternis, sub caligine custoditis: uti habet Epistola Judæ v. 6. 2. Deindè obedientiam illam, quam Homo Creatori suo, præ creationis beneficio debebat, modis omnib9 oportebat esse conspicuam & evidentem, talem nimirum, in quâ ipsemet experiretur suarum virium in creatione inditarum facultatem. Jam verò dubium nemini esse potest, quin ea Obedientia maximè sit spectata & illustris, quando quis non peccat, cùm peccare posset: quàm si quis ideò non peccat, quia peccare non potest. Quibus duabus rationibus observatis, impia, planè & blasphema, vox sit necesse est Johannis Piscatoris, qui in disputat. de Prædest. Thesi 27. & 33. sic scribit: DEUS primos parentes tales condidit, ut labi possent: Imò hoc consilio condidit, ut reipsa laberentur.

Sextò quæritur, Quare DEUS non aliam legē primis parentibus præfixerit, quam servassent: vel, cur non DEUS interno mentis cultu contento fuerit, sed insuper externam etiam membrorum corporis obedientia exegerit? Sed & isthæc effugia nimis sunt iputida & putrida. Nam 1. Si vel maximè DEUS aliam legem primis parentibus promulgasset, tamen illam quoque transgressuri fuissent, si libertatis arbitrio, & viribus concessis non rectè usi fuissent. 2. Si DEUS ejusmodi legem dedisset, cujus objectum Homini jam ante prorsus fuisset exosum & inappetibile, ut cum Scholasticis loquamur: certè non jam Obedientia ipsius fuisset spontanea, Imò propriè loquendo planè nulla fuisset obedientia. Neque enim vel leges prohibent id, quòd Homines naturâ suâ fugiunt & aversantur: neq; etiam quisquam spontaneam dicitur præstare obedientiam circa tale objectum, quod per se & ratione sui ita est affectum, ut omnes sani illud fugiant & odio prosequantur. 3. Vix legem observatu faciliorem DEUS promulgare potuisset. Nam in tantâ varietate & copiâ pretiosissimarum arborum, & nobiIissimorum fructuũ, quid, obsecro, facilius erat, quàm ab unius arboris fructu sibi temperare: ita ut si unquàm uspiam, certè in Paradiso DEUS legem observatu & possibilem promulgasse, statuendus sit. 4. Cùm circa Legem usque adeò facilem Adam viribus concessis rectè uti noluerit: sed persuasionibus mulieris & Diaboli locum dederit: certè vel indè colligitur: Si vel maximè aliam legem DEUS tulisset, tamen nec eam quoque primos parentes servaturos fuisse.

Pari ratione alterum propositæ Quæstionis membrum planè est nugatorium. Quia enim Homo non solâ mente constabat: sed & corpore: quia etiam Imago illa DEI, ad quam erat conditus, non tantùm vires mentis, sed & rectitudinem virium corporis, omniumque membrorum respiciebat; utique Homo etiam, non tantùm, quoad animam, verùm etiam quoad corpus, DEO Creatori ad obedientiam declarandam, obstrictus erat. Proindè ejusmodi etiam Lex requirebatur, circa cujus observationem utriusque partis, & Animæ & Corporis obedientiam DEO homo declararet.

Septimò quæritur: Annon satius fuisset, si DEUS planè nullam legem primis parentibus dedisset. Jam vero cùm Lex lata sit: annon ea, & per consequens, ejus etiam autor sit causa, vel satis occasio tristissimi lapsus primorum parentum? Sed Respondeo, Quæstionem hanc 1. omni vel in speciem saltem probabili ἐλέγχῳ penitùs destitui. Qui enim statuit satiùs fuisse futurum, si primos parentes nulla prorsus Lex obstrinxisset: ille nihil quærit & contendit aliud, quàm tùm è gloriâ DEI, tùm ex ipsius hominis emolumento futurum fuisses; si Homo vel nullam prorsus obedientiam DEO secundum legis alicujus præscriptum exsolvere debuisset: vel saltem illum, non secundum DEI, sed suum proprium arbitrium præstitisset. Quod utrumque quomodo cum Creationis fine, & analogiâ fidei quadret, expendendum esset adversariis.

Finis utique creati Hominis, DEI respectu, nullus erat alius, quàm ut Creator à creaturâ ritè coleretur. Jam verò quinám cultus DEO esset gratus & acceptus, non ex hominis, sed ipsius DEI arbitrio, meritò stare debuit.

Proindè ut ne homo circa cultum istum dependendum aberraret, DEUS certam legem, quâ tàm internum mentis motum, quàm externam corporis obedientiam informaret, promulgare, & vel hoc pacto suam Φιλανθρωπίαν contestari voluit: ita ut haud magis vel causa, vel occasio lapsûs DEO adscribi queat: atque Magistratus politicus transgressionum causa constitui debet, quando subditi contra leges, justo modo promulgatas peccant.

Octavò quæritur: Cur non DEUS primos parentes statim post commissum lapsum prorsus aboleverit, & novum Hominem produxerit. Sed rectissime respondetur, primò cum Apostolo ex 1. Cor. 4. 6. ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ὑπὲρ ὃ γέγραπται: non oportet sapere supra id quod scriptum est. Nam, ut scite infert August. l. 11. de Gen. ad lit. c. 10. potuisset DEUS vel voluntatem primorum parentum in bonam convertere, quoniam omnipotens est: vel naturam ipsorum planè immutare: potuisset planè: Cur Ergò non fecit? Quia noluit: Cur noluerit, penes ipsum est: Debemus non plus sapere quàm oportet Rom. 12, 3.

Deindè verò rem paulò altiùs expendentibus, causæ in promtu esse possunt, propter quas DEUS hoc facere non debuerit. Nam certum est singulas à DEO creatas species eo etiam fine à DEO creatas esse, ut tales, quales creatæ sunt, eò usque perdurarent, dùm Mundus hic persisteret. Ergò unius speciei & quidem nobilissimæ abolitio, locum habere non potuit: & quidem statim illo ipso die, quo species hæc creata fuit. Nam si Irenæo & aliis Patribus credimus, lapsus est primus Homo, illo ipso die, quo erat conditus. Quod si Ergò DEUS post lapsum statim hanc speciem abolevisset: plurimùm periclitata fuisset infinita ipsius tùm sapientia, tùm providentia. Deindè si DEUS homine abolito novum creare debuisset: certè vel specie eundem, vel specie diversum condere necesse habuisset: si specie eundem: sanè & iste in peccatum prolabi potuisset, & sic hoc pacto periculum lapsûs non fuisset amotum. Sin specie diversum: tunc non ampliùs verus homo, corpore & animâ rationali præditus, & libertate voluntatis instructus conditus fuisset: quin prior illa humana species penitùs desiisset: id quod rursum tùm cum æternâ DEI sapientiâ, tùm cum creationis fine manifestè pugnat. Tertiò novam Hominis speciem DEUS creare non potuit, propterà quòd die septimo quievisse legitur: vel hoc pacto testatus, se nullas ampliùs deinceps novas species creaturarum producturum. Tandem cùm DEUS lapsui primorum parentum, non quidem per novam creationem: sed per spiritualem illam παλιγγενεσίαν, sive Regenerationem Hominis, medicinam, consilio longè sapientissimo fecerit: utique non habet Ratio Humana, quod hac etiam in parte DEO obloqui possit: præsertim cùm Regeneratio hæc auferat Lapsus illius tristissimi reatum, quem Nova Hominis creatio auferre nunquam potuisset.


### Errors concerning the Cause of Sin: Question 1. Whether here rather the faculty and inclination alone is explained? (continued)

Ninthly, this also is asked: Why did GOD grant to the Devil that he might deceive Man? But the Answer is simple and plain, that GOD permitted it for this reason, because he had instructed Man with such powers that he could have most easily resisted all the darts and snares of the Devil, if only he had wished. Then GOD also permitted this, so that Man might have a certain exercise, as it were, by which he might exercise more and more the granted powers of body and soul, which were most sound. By both of which pacts GOD neither incited the Devil, nor armed him as an Enemy for the destruction of Man, nor impelled Man himself to assent to the suggestions of the Devil, so that the voice of Calvin in his Institutions, writing thus in his Commentary on chapter 7 of Genesis, is plainly blasphemous: GOD created Man flexible: he not only suffered him to be tempted, but willed it. For he also LENT the tongue of the Serpent to the Devil, beyond its ordinary use, just as if someone were to supply a sword and weapons to another: when the unhappy outcome was known to him beforehand, he did not bring such remedy as he could.

Tenth: there are not lacking those who argue from that eternal decree of GOD concerning sending the Son and redeeming the human race: that the fall of the first parents must necessarily have happened by the ordination of GOD: lest, forsooth, that decree be void and in vain. But a gross error arises from the confusion of cause and effect: for that decree concerning sending the Son was not the cause of the Adamic Fall: but rather this fall was the cause of that decree. Because GOD had foreseen from eternity that Adam would fall by his own will; therefore he also thought from eternity about a salutary remedy, which, when he saw that none could be found on the part of men, he certainly made the decree concerning sending the Son, and redeeming the entire human race through his death.

Finally, there are found those who complain about the gravity of the punishment with which GOD punished the fall of Adam, dreaming that the eating of the forbidden fruit is not of such moment that it would involve the entire human race, and indeed not only in temporal but also in eternal punishments. Just as Julius III, the Roman Pontiff, is read to have extenuated this deed. For when he had been admonished, forsooth, not to be angry because of the light offense of a Cook who had not replaced a roasted Peacock at dinner, he replied through the height of blasphemy: that GOD had cast the first Parents out of Paradise because of the eating of one Fruit: Why therefore should it not be permitted to him, the Vicar of Christ, to be angry because of a Peacock, a thing far more excellent than a fruit.

Thus others measure that offense by the mere violation of the prohibition: Others, elevating it even more, interpret it as having been gluttony and intemperance. But the foulness of that sin must be probed more deeply and thoroughly. I. The truth of the divine Word having been called into doubt, Eve perfidiously constituted GOD a liar. II. There followed the crime of injured Majesty, whose honors, not content with her own, Eve coveted. III. Hence Ambition, joined with detestable ingratitude. IV. Apostasy from GOD, for when, having set aside the Word of GOD, she had more faith in the Satanic promise: was not the Faith of GOD denied here? V. Contumely and lies cast upon GOD by the Devil, of which matter the first-formed became guilty as soon as they showed themselves obedient to the words of Satan: All of which things Augustine weighing, l. 14. de Civit. DEI, c. 15. In the fall of Adam, GOD was despised, who had commanded, who had created man, who had made him in His own image, who had set him over the other animals, who had established him in Paradise: who had provided an abundance of all things and of salvation: who had burdened him with precepts neither many, nor great, nor difficult to observe: but had been content with one precept, most light and most brief, for the healthfulness of obedience, by which He reminded him that He was Lord over that creature to whom free servitude was expedient, a just condemnation followed. There were, therefore, in this single fall many most sad and most atrocious sins: namely, doubt concerning the word of GOD, distrust of the truth of GOD: curiosity, not content with the knowledge of good, but desiring to know evil also: Pride: contempt of GOD: supreme ingratitude: violation of the divine command against conscience: and other things of that kind, by which they brought upon themselves, and also upon their whole posterity, an inextricable Iliad of miseries and troubles.

But enough and more than enough concerning the fall of Adam: It remains that we respond to the remaining arguments, with which the Calvinists are accustomed to fight for the maintaining of their opinion.

At the beginning, however, they gather from the Holy Scriptures individual and universal testimonies which affirm of GOD that He hardens, blinds, tempts, and leads into temptation, deceives and seduces, delivers into a reprobate sense, sends the efficacy of error, causes to err, mixes a Spirit of dizziness, sends in a Spirit of lying, and those things which are of this kind, which according to the surface of the letter seem to attribute to GOD some efficacious action with respect to sin. But since we have expressly shown above, around the fourth mode by which GOD concurs with sins or evil actions, that not even in this respect can GOD be constituted the cause of sin in any way, it is of no use to deal with it more fully in this place: rather, it will be worth the effort to weigh the remaining arguments. Those, indeed, are of such a kind that they seem to patronize the Calvinist fury by consequence and implicitly.

And indeed Theodore Beza, Respons. 2. ad acta Colloquii Mompelgartensis, gathers quite a few of this kind: and at the beginning he brings forward that, Gen. 45, 8. where Joseph says to his brothers: It was not by your counsel, but by the will of GOD that I was sent here. Therefore, it would be right to ascribe the malicious selling of Joseph not so much to the brothers as to the secret will and decree of GOD Himself.

But it is most rightly answered that a double Sophism is committed, both of the Figure of speech and of the statement according to something. For that mission is to be understood not of the efficacious operation of GOD: but partly of permission, and partly of the wonderful outcome of this mission, or the government of GOD, and direction toward a good end. The foundation of which response Joseph himself shows us most firmly, thus again to his brothers, Gen. 50, 20. You thought evil against me: but GOD turned it into good, that He might exalt me, as you see at present, and might save many peoples. Where indeed he distinguishes so expressly between the selling itself as a sin of guilt and the outcome or good end of this selling, that he clearly imputes the former to his brothers: but attributes the latter to GOD alone. Therefore that passage, which is brought forward by the Adversaries, hints at least this: That the malicious intention of the brothers, who looked to the destruction of Joseph, is not now to be attended to, but rather that eyes are to be fixed upon that wonderful providence of GOD, which by its government brought it about that their crime obtained a happier outcome than they themselves either wanted or thought.

Which same thing can and ought to be answered to the remaining passages also, which Beza produces: such as what Job says: The Lord gave, the Lord took away, ch. 1, 3. that likewise the pious are afflicted, not otherwise than by the will of GOD Rom. 8, 29. 1. Pet. 3, 17. That Herod and Pilate gathered together, that they might do whatever the hand and counsel of the Lord had defined to be done; Act. 4, 27. that Christ was delivered by the defined counsel of GOD, and by a preceding decree: Act. 2, 23. that Christ was wounded by GOD Himself Isa. 53, 5. and very many other passages of this kind, which Beza in the place already cited above gathers in great number and opposes.

For if in the refutation of each of these passages, the following notes or rules are always to be observed.

1. That phrases of this kind have not an active sense with efficacy with respect to evil: but only a permissive one with government with respect to a good end: That which is to be observed especially concerning the words of Job, and the Apostolic passage concerning the affliction of the pious: and the Prophetic passage concerning the wounding of Christ.

2. Sometimes in the Scriptures works are predicated of GOD, which likewise happen not by His working, but with a certain desertion permitting them: as when it is read that GOD Exod. 9, 16. Rom. 9, 17. stirred up Pharaoh, so that he would not let the Israelite people go. Likewise, 2. Sam. 12, 11. That He delivered David's wives to Absalom: 2. Sam. 24, 1. that He incited David to number the people. Likewise, that He commanded Shimei to curse David. 2. Sam. 16, 10. Likewise, that it is the work of GOD that the 10 Israelite tribes defected from Rehoboam. 1. Reg. 12, 24.

3. Regarding these very things and others of this kind, that customary distinction is to be maintained between the evil of punishment and the evil of fault. For in one evil work, for example, in the secession of the ten tribes of Israel, there was both punishment and fault: that is, to the just suffering and vengeance of King Rehoboam and the people combined, there was joined a wicked and unjust action. Insofar, therefore, as there was punishment in that work, it pertained to GOD: insofar as there was fault, it was the sole property of the King and the people. This same reasoning applies to the wives of the father handed over to Absalom: so that the fornication and adultery committed with Bathsheba might be punished in this way. Just as the address of the Prophet Nathan to David clearly hints at this, saying thus in 2 Sam. 12:12: Thus says the Lord: You did it secretly: but I will do this thing in the sight of all Israel, and in the sight of the sun. The same must be held regarding Shimei cursing David. What Amos says, ch. 3:6, also pertains here. Is there evil in a city, which the Lord has not done? And Prov. 16:4. That GOD created the wicked for the day of evil. Which Jeremiah also has in Lamentations ch. 3:37, 38.

Who is it that said, this happens, the Lord not commanding it? Out of the mouth of the Most High do not proceed evils, nor goods. In which individual actions GOD did not work the evil actions: but permitted them: and indeed to this end, that He might punish the preceding contumacy and impiety, as a just Judge.

4. Regarding those two passages from the Acts of the Apostles, one answers most correctly by distinguishing between the evil of guilt or the killing of Christ: and between GOD's both Universal Omniscience and His singular determination of the deed of the Jews, to a far better end: so indeed, that in the former passage, which exists in Acts 2:23 (Him, delivered by the definite counsel and foreknowledge of GOD, you have crucified), the word 'delivered' is to be understood concerning the promise of GOD: but the words 'counsel and foreknowledge' tend toward different ends. Foreknowledge indeed toward the deed of the Jews, which is the evil of guilt: which foreknowledge, however, as it never denotes the cause of evil elsewhere, so neither does it here, but only knowledge. But the counsel designates that good end, for the sake of which GOD permitted this most atrocious deed: namely, the redemption of the human race. Thus the later passage Acts 4:27. (They gathered against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your counsel had previously defined to be done.) The passage, I say, is to be understood here concerning the divine and clearly admirable governance of the deed of the Jews and its direction toward a good end. For the text does not have it that GOD decreed that Herod, Pilate, and the Jews should do these things: but it said that they gathered to do what the hand and counsel of GOD had defined to be done. Which phrase looks to that end for which GOD decreed to permit that to be done, which Herod, Pontius Pilate, and the Jews would otherwise have perpetrated of their own accord.

Finally, the Adversaries also produce two other passages from the sacred writings, one of which exists in Exodus 3:21. Where GOD commands the Israelites to despoil the Egyptians, by taking on loan gold and silver vessels and precious garments. The other, however, in Hosea 1:2. Where the Prophet is commanded to take a harlot or a wife of whoredoms.

But I answer, that in the former passage a collection is instituted from the singular to the universal: or what is the same thing, from a singular example to a universal rule. For in that command concerning the Egyptian spoil, there is the singularity of an Example. 2. Regarding the very nature of the deed, it was not properly a spoil or robbery: but a claiming of wages due: for those infinite troubles and labors which they were forced to sustain from the Egyptians, beyond what was right and deserved.

The later passage is not to be understood according to the letter: for here infinite absurdities would emerge, impious and blasphemous toward GOD Himself, as if GOD had ordered the Prophet either to commit fornication or to take a public harlot as a wife: But this passage ought to be explained typically: so that the wife of the Prophet had to bear the name of a harlot, and his children were called illegitimate: to the end that by this type the Israelite people might be admonished of their crimes and spiritual fornication: just as the coherence of the whole text clearly proves. In which part we also have Calvin himself agreeing, as is evident from his Commentary on this passage.

But the Calvinian Spirit is in an uproar against the responses given thus far, with various sought-out and devised arguments: the chief of which it would be worth the effort to examine on the scales of truth.

And at the beginning they clamor thus: He who wills the end, he also wills the means leading to the end. But GOD wills the end which results from evil actions. Therefore He also wills the means leading to this end, namely the evil actions themselves, or sins.

I answer that the major premise is true only in the case of an end and means that are proper and ordered by themselves. But when an end follows by accident to some means and actions, depending on an alien power, then it is simply false that he who wills the end also wills the means: so much so that this does not even hold true in politics and economics. For example: Good laws are born from bad morals, which the Magistrate promulgates, yet he does not therefore will or approve of the bad morals. Thus a Father wills the amendment of a prodigal son: but he does not will the prodigality itself. Thus GOD wills the conversion of sinners, but He does not will their sins: otherwise that Apostolic rule would be false: Evils are not to be done so that goods may come. Romans 3:8. Furthermore, if that major proposition is accommodated to divine Mysteries, it can be conceded only when both the means and the End are equally related to the will and nature of GOD. Now, however, regarding the present question, a great disparity presents itself. For example: The end which results from the fall of Adam is good, and in all things conformable to the will and Nature of GOD: but the medium, that is, the Fall itself and the sin, is clearly repugnant to it. Therefore it is false also in this case that he who wills the end also wills the means leading to the end. Thirdly, neither is it simply true in this argument that Sin is of itself a medium of that end: For how could that which is evil by its own nature produce a good end? That therefore a good end finally emerged from the fall of our first parents, from the betrayal and crucifixion of Christ, and other crimes and outrages of that kind: that is not to be ascribed to the sin itself of itself, as a medium or cause: but rather entirely to the most wise divine providence: which, as Augustine says somewhere, would not permit evil to be done unless it knew how to elicit a good end from it. Thus, therefore, the whole strength of the argument gives way.

Finally, concerning the dissolution of this sophism, a proper distinction must be made between the simple will of GOD and the conditional will, or that which is secundum quid. For example, GOD willed the sale of Joseph, but not simply, or in itself, or insofar as it has the nature of sin: but only secundum quid, that is, permissively: insofar as He permitted it to happen: He permitted it, however, because He willed to elicit a good end from it.

The Calvinists rise up against these things in this manner. Wherever in any deeds human will agrees with the divine: it cannot be that men sin, without GOD himself also being the approver of that sin, if not the cause. But in the passion of Christ, the sinning will of men was in agreement with the divine will. Therefore. I answer that the Passion of Christ must be accurately distinguished with respect to the agent and the patient: Or what is the same thing, with respect to the saving Passion and the unjust Crucifixion. Now, for there to be an agreement of the divine and human will, it is not enough to will the Crucifixion of Christ: but it is necessary that there be a conformity of will with respect to both, namely the action and the passion: Where indeed a greater dissonance immediately presents itself than can exist between GOD and the Devil himself. For the action of the Crucifixion is a crime enormously hateful and abominable to GOD: but the Passion of Christ suffering is a work far most pleasing to Him. Thus GOD willed the Crucifixion of the Son not simply, but in a certain respect, permissively, namely with respect to that saving end which was bound to emerge from it: but the Jews willed the same Crucifixion, but for a far different end, namely that by this pact they might remove Christ from the midst, abolish the Gospel and his doctrine, and by this punishment, which carried the mark of a curse, afflict Christ with perpetual infamy of name. As much therefore as crime and justice differ: so much do the will of GOD and the Jews mutually dissent from each other in the act of the Crucifixion of Christ.

Latin:

Nonò & istud quæritur: Cur DEUS Diabolo concesserit ut, Hominem deciperet? Sed simplex & plana est Responsio, ideò permisisse DEUM, quia Hominem, ejusmodi viribus instruxerat, ut omnibus Diaboli telis, & insidiis facillimè resistere potuisset, si modò voluisset. Deindè permisit etiam hoc DEUS, ut Homo exercitium quasi quoddam haberet, quo concessas vires corporis & animæ longè integerrimas magis magisq; exerceret. Quo utroque pacto DEUS neque Diabolum incitavit, neq; ipsum tanquam Hostem in exitium Hominis armavit, neque Hominem ipsum, ut Diaboli suggestionibus annueret, impulit, ita, ut blasphema planè sit vox Calvini in Institutionibus, sic scribentis in suo Commentario ad cap. 7. Geneseos: Flexibilem DEUS Hominem creavit: tentari non modò passus est, sed voluit. Nam & Diabolo lingvam Serpentis, præter ordinarium usum COMMODAVIT, quemadmodum, si quis alteri gladium & arma suppeditet: cùm in felix eventus illi esset præcognitus, remedium, quale poterat, non attulit.

Decimo: non desunt, qui ex æterno illo DEI decreto, de mittendo Filio, & redimendo genere humano arguût: Lapsum primorum parentum DEI ordinatione necessariò evenire debuisse: ne videlicet decretum illud esset irritum & frustraneum. Sed crassus oritur error ex confusione causæ & effectus: neque enim decretum illud de mittendo Filio fuit causa Lapsus Adamici: sed hic potiùs lapsus causa fuit decreti illius. Quia enim DEUS ab æterno præviderat Adamum propriâ suâ voluntate lapsurum; ideò ab æterno etiam de remedio salutari cogitavit, quod cùm ex hominum parte nullum inveniri posse videret, utique decretum fecit de mittendo Filio, & per hujus mortem redimendo genere humano universo.

Tandem reperiuntur, qui de pœnæ gravitate, quâ DEUS lapsum Adami punivit, conqueruntur, somniantes, esum pomi interdicti, tanti momenti non esse ut universum genus humanum, & quidem non temporalibus modò: sed & æternis suppliciis involveret. Quemadmodum Julius III. Pontifex Romanus factum hoc extenuasse legitur. Nam cùm admonitus esset, ne nimirùm irasceretur propter leve delictum Coqui, qui Pavonem assatum in cœnâ non reposuerat, respondit per summam blasphemiam: DEUM propter esum unius Pomi ejecisse primos Parentes ex Paradiso: Quin ergò sibi, Christi Vicario, non liceret irasci propter Pavonem, rem longè præstantiorem pomo.

Sic alii solâ interdicti violatione delictum illud metiuntur: Alii magis etiam illud elevantes, gulositatem atque intemperantiam fuisse, interpretantur. Sed altiùs & penitùs peccati istius fœditas rimanda est. I. Verbi divini veritate in dubium vocatâ, mendacem DEUM Eva perfidè constituit. II. Accessit læsæ Majestatis crimen, cujus honores, non contenta suis, Eva appetiit. III. Hinc Ambitio, conjuncta cum detestandâ ingratitudine. IV. Apostasia à DEO, cùm enim posthabito Verbo DEI, Satanicæ promissioni plus fidei habuit: annon hîc Fides DEI abnegata est? V. Contumelia & mendacia in DEUM projecta à Diabolo, quorũ rei protoplasti facti sunt, quamprimùm dictis Satanæ obedientes sese præbuerunt: Quæ omnia expendens Augustinus l. 14. de Civit. DEI, c. 15. In lapsu Adami contemtus est DEUS jubens, qui hominem creaverat, qui ad suam imaginem eum fecerat, qui cæteris animalibus præposuerat, qui in Paradiso constituerat: qui rerum omnium copiam salutisq; præstiterat: qui præceptis nec pluribus, nec grandibus, nec observatu difficilibus oneraverat: sed uno præcepto, levissimo, atq; brevissimo, ad obedientiæ salubritatem contentus fuerat, quo super eam creaturam, cui libera servitus expediret, se esse Dominum commonebat justa damnatio subsecuta est. Fuerunt igitur in hoc unico lapsu multa tristissima & atrocissima peccata: Dubitatio videlicet de verbo DEI, diffidentia de veritate DEI: curiositas, non contenta boni agnitione, sed malum quoq; scire desiderans: Superbia: contemtus DEI: ingratitudo summa: violatio mandati divini contra conscientiam: & id genus alia, quibus non modò sibiipsis, sed toti etiam posteritati, miseriarum & ærumnarum inextricabilem Iliada accersiverunt.

Sed de lapsu Adami plus satis: Superest, ut ad argumenta reliqua, quibus Calviniani pro obtinenda sua sententia pugnare solent, respondeamus.

Initiò autem ex Scripturis Sacris colligunt singula, atque universa testimonia, quæ de DEO affirmant, quod induret, excæcet, tentet, & in tentationem inducat, decipiat, & seducat, tradat in sensum reprobum, mittat efficaciam erroris, errare faciat, misceat Spiritum vertiginis, immittat Spiritum mendacii, & quæ sunt hujus generis illa, quæ secundum superficiem literæ DEO efficacem aliquam actionem, respectu peccati tribuere videntur. Verùm cum suprà circa modum Quartum, quo DEUS ad peccata sive malas actiones concurrat, ex professo ostenderimus, ne quidem hoc respectu DEUM, ullo pacto peccati causam constitui posse, nihil attinet hoc loco fusiùs de eo agere: quin reliqua potiùs expendamus argumenta, operæ pretium fuerit. Ea verò sunt ejusmodi, ut per consequentiam & implicitè furori Calviniano patrocinari videantur.

Et sanè Theodorus Beza, Respons. 2. ad acta Colloquii Mompelgartensis, hujus generis bene multa colligit: ac initiò quidem profert illud, Gen. 45, 8. ubi Joseph ad fratres: Non vestro consilio, sed DEI voluntate huc missus sum. Ergò malitiosam Josephi venditionẽ non tam fratrü, quã ipsig Dei arcanæ voluntati atq; decreto adscribere fas fuerit.

Sed rectissimè respondetur, committi geminum Sophisma, tùm Figuræ dictionis, tùm à dicto secundum quid. Nam missio illa, non de efficaci DEI operatione: sed partim de permissione, partim verò de mirando missionis hujus exitu, sive gubernatione DEI, & directione ad finem bonum, est accipienda. Cujus responsionis Fundamentum longè firmissimum nobis monstrat ipse Josephus, sic rursum ad fratres suos, Gen. 50, 20. Vos cogitastis de me malum: sed DEUS vertit illud in bonum, ut exaltaret me, sicut in præsentiarum cernitis, & salvos faceret multos populos. Ubi sanè inter venditionem ipsam tanquam malum culpæ: & venditionis hujus eventum sive finem bonum ita expresse distingvit, ut illam diserte fratribus suis impingat: hunc vero soli DEO tribuat. Proinde locus ille, qui ab Adversariis adducitur, hoc saltem innuit: Non jam attendendam esse malitiosam fratrum intentionem, qui interitum Josephi spectarint, sed oculos potius figendos esse, in mirandam illam DEI providentiam, quæ sua gubernatione effecerit, ut crimen ipsorum feliciorem fortitum sit exitu, quam ipsi vel voluerint, vel cogitaverint.

Quod ipsum responderi potest & debet, ad reliqua etiam loca, quæ Beza producit: ut quod Job ait: Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit, cap. 1, 3. quod item pii affliguntur, non nisi ex DEI voluntate Rom. 8, 29. 1. Pet. 3, 17. Quod convenerunt Herodes & Pilatus, ut facerent quæcunque, manus & consilium Domini definiverat, ut fierent; Act. 4, 27. quod Christus traditus est ex definito DEI consilio, & præeunte decreto: Act. 2, 23. quod Christus ab ipso DEO vulneratus Jes. 53, 5. & quæ sunt hujus generis alia loca quam plurima, quæ Beza loco jam supra citato, magno numero colligit & opponit.

Nam si singulorum istorum locorum refutatione, sequentes notæ sive regulæ semper sunt observandæ.

1. Quod ejusmodi phrases sensus habeant non activum cum efficacia respectu mali: sed permissivum duntaxat cum gubernatione respectu finis boni: Id quod cumprimis circa verba Jobi, & locum Apostolicum de afflictione pioru:& locum Propheticum de vulneratione Christi est observandum.

2. Interdum in Scripturis de DEO prædicantur opera, quæ itidem non operante ipso, sed cum desertione quandam permittente eveniunt: ut cum legitur DEUS Exod. 9, 16. Rom. 9, 17. Pharaonem excitasse, ne demitteret populum Israeliticum. Item, 2. Sam. 12, 11. Tradidisse Absolomo uxores Davidis: 2. Sam. 24, 1. incitasse Davidem, ut numeraret populum. Item, præcepisse Semei, ut malediceret Davidi. 2. Sam. 16, 10. Item, Opus DEI esse, quod 10. tribus Israeliticæ a Roboamo defecereunt. 1. Reg. 12, 24.

3. Circa hæc ipsa & id genus alia loca distinctio illa usitata est tenenda inter malum pœnæ; & malum culpæ. Nam in opere uno malo, exempli gratia, in cefessione decem tribuum Israel, & pœna fuit & culpa: hoc est, justæ passioni & ultioni Regis Roboami, atque populi simul conjuncta fuit, actio prava & justa. Quatenus Ergo in opere illo pœna fuit, ad DEUM id pertinuit: quatenus culpa, Regis & populi in solidum fuit proprium. Quæ ipsa ratio militat in traditis Absolomo uxoribus patris: ut sic puniretur scortatio & adulterium cum Bethsabea commissum. Quemadmodum diserte hoc innuit concio Prophetæ Nathanis ad Davidem, sic dicentis 2. Sam. 12, 12 Hoc ait Dominus: Tu fecisti abscondite: ego autem faciam Verbum istud in conspectu omnis Israel, & in conspectu solis. Quod ipsum tenendum de Semei maledicente Davidi. Pertinet huc etiam, quod Amos dicit, c. 3. 6. Non est malum in Civitate, quod non fecerit Domino. Et Prov. 16, 4. DEUM condidisse impium ad diem malum. Quod item Jeremias habet in Threnis cap. 3, 17. 18.

Quis est, qui dixit, fieri hoc, Domino non jubente? Ex ore Altissimi non egredi mala, nec bona. In quibus actionibus singulis DEUS non est operatus actiones malas: sed permisit: & quidem eo fine, ut antegressam contumaciam & impietatem, tanquam justus Judex vindicaret.

4. Quoad duo illa loca ex Actis Apostolicis rectissimè respondetur, distinguendo inter malum culpæ sive occisionem Christi: & inter DEI tum Universalem Omniscientiam, tum singularem determinationem facti Judæorum, ad finem longè optimum: ita quidem, ut in priore dicto, quod extat Act. 2, 23. (Hunc definito consilio, & præscientia DEI traditum, crucifixistis) vox Tradendi, de promissione DEI sit accipienda: vocabula verò (consilii & præscientiæ) ad diversos fines tendant. Præscientia quidem ad factum Judæorum, quod malum culpæ est: quæ tamen Præscientia uti nunquam aliàs, sic neque hîc mali causam, sed notitiam tantùm notat. Consilium verò finem illum bonum designet, propter quem DEUS factum hoc atrocissimum permittebat: nempè redemtionem generis humani. Sic locus posterior Act. 4, 27. (Convenerunt adversus sanctum Filium tuum Jesum, quem unxeras, Herodes & Pontius Pilatus, cum gentibus & populis Israel, ut facerent, quæcunquè manus tua & consilium tuum prius definierat, ut fierent.) Locus, inquam, hic de divina & planè admiranda gubernatione facti Judæorum ejusdemq; directione ad bonum finem est accipiendus. Neq; enim textus habet, DEUM decrevisse, ut facerent hæc Herodes, Pilatus & Judæi: sed dixit, hos convenisse ut facerent, quæ ut fierent, manus & consilium DEI definiverit. Quæ phrasis finem illum respicit, ob quem DEUS decrevit permittere, ut fieret id, quod Herodes, Pontius Pilatus, & Judæi aliàs sponte sua fuissent perpetraturi.

Tandem ex sacris producunt Adversarii etiam duo loca alia, quorum unus extat Exod. 3, 21. Ubi DEUS præcipit Ismelitis ut spoliarent Ægyptios, mutuò acceptis vasis aureis & argenteis & vestibus pretiosis. Alter verò Oseæ 1, 2. Ubi Propheta jubetur ducere meretricem sive uxorem fornicationum.

Sed respondeo, in priore loco collectionem institui à singulari ad universale: vel quod idem est, ab exemplo singulari ad regulam universalem. In mandato enim illo de spolio Ægyptiaco inest, singularitas Exempli. 2. Quoad ipsam speciem facti, propriè illud non fuit spolium aut rapina: sed mercedis debitæ vendicatio: pro infinitis illis molestiis ac laboribus, quos sustinere ab Ægyptiis, præter fas & meritum, cogebantur.

Posterior locus κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν non est accipiendus: Hic enim infinitæ emergerent absurditates, in DEUM ipsum impiæ & blasphemæ, quasi DEUS jusserit Prophetam vel scortari, vel scortum publicum in uxorem ducere: Sed Typicè locus iste exponi debet: ita ut uxor Prophetæ gerere debuerit, nomen scorti, & liberi ejus appellati sint spurii: eo fine, ut hoc typo populus Israeliticus, de suis sceleribus, & spirituali fornicatione admoneretur: quemadmodum totius textus συνέπεια luculenter id evincit. Quâ in parte adstipulantem etiam habemus ipsum Calvinum, uti patet ex ipsius ad hunc locum Commentario.

Tumultuatur verò Spiritus Calvinianus, adversus responsiones hactenus datas, variis conquisitis & excogitatis ratiunculis: quarum præcipuas ad trutinam veritatis exigere, operæ pretium fuerit.

Ac initiò quidem sic obstrepunt: Qui vult finem, ille vult etiã media, ad finem deducentia. Atqui DEUS vult finē, qui ex actionibus malis resultat. Ergò vult etiam media ad hunc finem deducentia, nempè ipsas actiones malas, sive peccata.

Respondeo, Majorem veram esse, non nisi in fine & mediis propriis, & per se ordinatis. Quando autem ad media & actiones aliquas per accidens sequitur finis, à virtute aliena dependens, tum simpliciter falsum est, ut qui vult finem, velit etiam media: adeò ut ne quidem in Politicis & Oeconomicis locũ illud habeat. Exempli gratia: Ex malis moribus nascuntur bonæ leges, quas promulgat Magistratus, neque tamen malos mores ideò vel vult, vel probat. Sic Pater vult emendationem filii prodigi: sed non vult ipsam prodigalitatem. Sic DEUS vult peccatorum conversionem, sed non vult ipsorum peccata: aliàs falsa esset regula illa Apostolica: Non sunt facienda mala, ut eveniant bona. Rom. 3, 8. Deindè si ad divina Mysteria Major illa propositio accommodetur, concedi potest ea tum, quando & media & Finis ad voluntatem DEI ac naturam pariter se habent. Jam verò, quoad præsentem quæstionem, maxima sese offert disparitas. Exempli gratia: Finis qui ex lapsu Adami provenit, est bonus, & voluntati atque Naturæ DEI per omnia conformis: Medium verò, hoc est, Lapsus ipse & peccatum eidem planè repugnat. Ergò falsum etiam hoc loco, ut qui vult finem, ille velit etiam media ad finem deducentia. Tertiò, neque illud in hoc argumento simpliciter verum est: quòd Peccatum per se sit medium finis illius: Quomodo enim quod suâ naturâ malum est, finem bonum posset producere? Quod Ergò ex lapsu primorum parentum, ex proditione & crucifixione Christi, & aliis id genus sceleribus atque flagitiis, Finis bonus tandem emersit: illud non ipsi per se peccato, tanquam medio sive causæ: sed sapientissimæ potiùs divinæ providentiæ, in solidum est adscribendum: quæ, ut Augustinus alicubi loquitur, non permitteret malum fieri, nisi bonum ex eo finem nosset elicere. Sic ergò totius argumenti nervus omnis concedit.

Tandem circa Sophismatis hujus dissolutionem, probè distinguendum fuerit inter voluntatem DEI simplicem, & conditionatam, sive eam, quæ est secundum quid. Exempli gratia, Venditionem Josephi voluit DEUS, sed non simpliciter, sive per se, vel quatenus ea peccati rationem habet: sed tantùm secundum quid, hoc est, permissivè: quatenus permisit id fieri: permisit autem, quia finem bonum indè voluit elicere.

Insurgunt adversus isthæc Calvinani in hunc modum. Ubicunque in factis aliquibus, voluntas humana congruit cum divina: fieri nequit, se peccant homines, quin ipse etiam DEUS peccati illius sit approbator, si non causa. Atqui in passione Christi, voluntas hominum peccans, congrua fuit divinæ voluntati. Ergò. Respondeo, Passionem Christi accuratè discernendam esse respectu agentis & patientis: Vel quod idem est, respectu salutaris Passionis, & injustæ Crucifixionis. Jam ut congruentia sit voluntatis divinæ & humanæ, non satis est velle, Crucifixionem Christi: sed necessum est, ut sit conformitas voluntatem respectu utriusq;, nempè actionis & passionis: Ubi sanè statim major se offert dissonantia, quàm inter DEUM & Diabolum ipsum esse queat. Nam Crucifixionis actio, est scelus DEO enormiter invisum & abominabile: sed Christi sufferentis Passio, est opus ipsi longè gratissimum. Sic DEUS voluit Crucifixionem Filii non simpliciter, sed secundum quid, Permissivè, respectu nimirùm finis illius salutaris, qui indè emergere debuit: Judæi verò voluerunt eandem Crucifixionem, sed fine longè diversissimo nempè ut hoc pacto Christum è medio tollerent, Evangelium & doctrinam ejus abolerent, & hoc supplicio, quod maledictionis notam habebat, Christum perpetua nominis infamia afficerent. Quantum Ergo differunt scelus & justitia: tantùm à se mutuò dissident voluntas DEI & Judæorum, in actu Crucifixionis Christi.


### Chapter Two

What is the true and proper cause of sin.

Our Author discusses this Question quite orthodoxly: establishing two causes of Sin: They are, he says, the cause of sin. 1. The will of the Devil: 2. The will of man, which turned themselves freely of their own accord away from GOD, with GOD neither willing nor approving that aversion, and remained wandering outside the order in objects, against the command of GOD, as the will of Eve turning itself away from the voice of GOD, and having wandered outside the order, remained in the apple. Which declaration of our Author is indeed to be noted for the reason that elsewhere he had written somewhat more harshly about the cause of Sin, and indeed in his Commentary on chapter 8 to the Romans, asserting that the adultery of David and the betrayal of Judas were the work of GOD, just as the calling of Paul. Which erroneous opinion he corrected quite clearly in those places of his, with that proposition or declaration or Retraction, with which the Church of GOD can easily be content: so that Bellarmine, Gregorius de Valentia, Andreas Fabritius and many other papist writers, who do not fear to slander Philip and our Churches because of those harsher words and to accuse them of the most atrocious heresies, ought to appear to have cast off shame along with all piety.

But to return to the causes of sin, those two are indeed rightly established: the Devil, and the will of man: but with this distinction observed, that neither the same mode nor the same force in operating can or ought to be assigned to each cause: which can be easily demonstrated by observing certain degrees of differences.

For first, that former cause, which is the Devil, is an external cause: but this latter, namely the human will, is an internal cause: as will soon be clearer.

Then that former is established as an indirect cause of sin: The Reason: because nothing can be a direct cause of sin, except that which can move the will of man from within to sin. But the latter cause, namely the will of Man, is most rightly established as the proximate and direct cause of sin: Since the proper and immediate principle of the act of sin is the will, insofar as every sin is voluntary.

Thirdly, the Will of man is moved both by itself and by the Devil: but in a far different way. For 1. the Will is moved by that which intrinsically inclines the will to will: which cannot happen, unless either by the will itself, or by GOD. For the Devil cannot move the will intrinsically, except in those who are corporally possessed. Now, however, GOD never inclines the human will to will evil: since GOD is not one who wills iniquity, as was clearly shown in the previous chapter. It remains therefore that only the will of man moves itself intrinsically, or inclines itself to evil: and therefore is the direct cause of sin. Then, however, the human will is moved objectively, as the Scholastics say: and that in three ways especially: 1. by a bare object: according to that trite saying: Objects move the senses: 2. Occasionally by him who objects and proposes the object: 3 Impulsively by him who persuades and sells the objected thing under the guise of good. In the first way, the external objects of sensible things move the will of men to sin, but indirectly, insofar as they move the sensitive appetite, which causes the object to appear suitable to the one desiring it, and thus it is also proposed to the will to be sought: which the Apostle James seems to have expressed, Chapter 1, 14. Each one is tempted by his own concupiscence, being drawn away and enticed: But concupiscence, when it has conceived, brings forth sin. Whence Augustine very skillfully writes in book 5, Against Julian, chapter 5: The parent is concupiscence: the offspring is sin: But concupiscence does not bring forth unless it has conceived; it does not conceive unless it has enticed: that is, it has obtained the assent of the will to perpetrate evil. Which same thing the Apostle also explains more significantly, Rom. 7, 23. I see, he says, another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity under the law of sin.

Moreover, the reason why the will is thus moved by the appetite is the very sympathy of the powers of the soul, arising from the fact that all these are perfections and, as it were, ornaments of one and the same substance of man: as Cajetan wrote not inappropriately in Thomas, Part 1 of the Second Part, Question 4, Disputation 2, Article 2. Regarding the second and third mode, an external cause also concurs with them, and either the Devil or even another human, who himself can also incite another human to sin. Where, however, neither the Devil nor such a human can be established as a proximate, direct, sufficient, or necessary cause of sin, but only an occasional and indirect one, insofar as, by enticing and persuading the external and internal senses, and indeed by deceiving and obfuscating the intellect itself, he obtains consent to sin from the human will. The use of this observation is indeed of the greatest importance for repelling the madness of those who, while naming the Devil or some other human as the author or at least the persuader of their own shameful deeds, and complaining that they were deceived by their fraud, immediately assume that they are immune and therefore free from all guilt of sin.

To whom Gregory of Nazianzus responds gravely, in the book of Spiritual Sentences, which he set forth in verse; saying:

Why do we always accuse the enemy, the lost one? And allow license to our morals? Accuse yourself entirely, or most of all: We have the fire: the Spirit stirs the flame.

For although the power of the Devil's suggestions is great, he can never be established as the direct cause of sins: rather, we are by nature inclined to sin, with that internal and common principle inciting us, which is and is called our corrupt and vitiated nature: so that even if it were entirely without the Devil's suggestions and persuasions, the appetite for natural things in man could still be inordinate and consequently would be sin, unless it were ordered by reason: as the Scholastics, especially Thomas, argue. The foundation of this assertion is the Fall of the first parents itself, which depends entirely on the will of man alone: and can in no way be ascribed to GOD, as a universal principle, nor to the Devil, as a principle of a superior nature, directly. For although it is read that Satan seduced the first parents, yet that was not of necessity or coercion, but only of persuasion and instigation. The same must be established regarding all actual sins, namely, that they are to be referred solely to the internal and direct principle of the human will. For although from the corruption of human nature some necessity of sinning remains with us, so that we cannot not sin, according to that most sad complaint of the Apostle, Rom. 7:14, 'We know that the Law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin,' and v. 20, 'I find this Law in me, that sin lies near me,' etc., yet this very necessity of sinning took its origin from the voluntary fall of the first parents, and never erupts into act without the assent of the will being added: so that there is no sin except that which is voluntary.

This part of the Christian Religion also has its foundations expressed in the scriptures. For regarding the Devil, that classic oracle of the Savior is known, John 8:44, 'The Devil is a murderer from the beginning; when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar, and the father of lies.' To which pertains that Apostolic saying, 1 John 3:8, 'He who commits sin is of the Devil: because the Devil sins from the beginning.' Where, however, our Author rightly admonishes that a lie must be accurately distinguished from the very substance of the Devil: just as that which he has as his own, and that which he receives from elsewhere. For the Devil does not have his substance from his own, but from elsewhere: for all Angels were created by GOD, some of whom later fell: but the Devil also has something of his own, not received from GOD, namely a lie, that is, sin, which the free will of the Devil brought forth. Nor do these things, as Philip skillfully infers, conflict with one another: that substance is created and sustained by GOD, and yet the will of the Devil and the will of man are the causes of sin: because the will could abuse its liberty and turn itself away from GOD.

Moreover, as regards the will of man, Scripture likewise clearly testifies that the primary and direct cause of sin is to be ascribed to this as to a fountain. In which part that of the Apostle militates, Rom. 5: through man sin entered into the world. 1 John 2: The concupiscence of the flesh is not of the Father, but of the world, that is, of men who are in the world.

Latin:

Quænam vera ac propria sit peccati causa.

DE hac Quæstione satis orthodoxè disserit Autor noster: duas constituens Peccati causas: Sunt, inquiens, causa peccati. 1. Voluntas Diaboli: 2. Voluntas hominis, quæ averterunt se liberè sua sponte à DEO, nec volente, nec approbante illam aversionem, & hæserunt vagantes extra ordinem in objectis, contra mandatum DEI, ut Evæ voluntas avertens se à voce DEI, & vagata extra ordinem hæsit in pomo. Quæ sanè Autoris nostri Declaratio vel ideò notanda fuerit, quòd alibi paulò duriùs de Peccati causa, & quidem in Commentario ad cap. 8. ad Romanos scripserat, asserens, fic esse opus DEI, Davidis adulterium & Judæ proditionem, ut Pauli vocationem. Quam erroneam opinionem in locis istis suis, satis perspicuè correxit, eâ propositâ sive declaratione, sive Retractatione, quâ Ecclesia DEI facilè contenta esse queat: ita ut pudorem cum omni pietate exuisse videri debeant Bellarminus, Gregorius de Valentia, Andreas Fabritius & complures pontificii Scriptores alii, qui Philippum & Ecclesias nostras propter duriora illa verba sugillare, & atrocissimarum hæresewn insimulare non verentur.

Sed ut ad peccati causas redeamus, rectè quidem duæ istæ constituuntur: Diabolus, & voluntas hominis: sed eo tamen observato discrimine, ut neque idem modus, neque eadem vis in operando, utrique causæ adsignari possit, aut debeat: id quod certis quibusdam differentiarum gradibus observatis, facilè demonstrari potest.

Primùm enim, Prior illa causa, quæ est Diabolo, causa est externa: Posterior verò hæc, nempè voluntas humana, causa est interna: uti mox clariùs patebit.

Deindè prior illa, indirectè peccati causa statuitur: Ratio: quia nihil directè potest peccati causa esse, nisi quod voluntatem hominis intus movere potest ad peccandum. Verùm posterior causa, nempè voluntas Hominis, rectissimè peccati causa propinqua & directa constituitur: Siquidem proprium & immediatum principium actus peccati est voluntas, quatenùs nimirùm omne peccatum est voluntarium.

Tertiò movetur Voluntas hominis tùm à seipsa, tùm à Diabolo: sed modo longè diversissimo. Nam 1. movetur Voluntas ab eo, quod intrinsecus inclinat voluntatem ad volendum: id quod fieri nequit, nisi vel à voluntate ipsa, vel à DEO. Diabolus enim, non nisi in corporaliter obsessis, voluntatem intrinsecus movere potest. Jam verò DEUS ad malum volendum nunquàm inclinat voluntatem humanam: siquidem non est DEUS volens iniquitatem, uti priore capite luculenter ostensum. Relinquitur ergò Solam voluntatem hominis intrinsecus semetipsam movere, sive inclinare ad malum: ac proindè Directè peccati causam esse. Deindè verò movetur voluntas humana objectivè, uti Scholastici loquuntur: idque tribus potissimùm modis: 1. per nudum objectum: secundum tritum illud: Objecta movent sensus: 2. Occasionaliter per eum, qui objectum objicit & proponit: 3 Impulsivè per eum, qui persuadet, & rem objectam sub ratione boni venditat. Primo modo objecta rerum sensilium externa, movent voluntatem hominum ac peccandum, sed indirectè quatenùs nimirùm movent appetitum sensitivum, qui facit, ut Objectum appareat conveniens ipsi appetenti, & sic voluntati etiam proponatur expetendum: id quod Apostolus Jacobus expressisse videtur, Cap. 1, 14. Unusquisque tentatur à concupiscentia sua abstractus & illectus: Concupiscentia autem, cùm conceperit, parit peccatum. Undè scitè admodùm Augustinus lib. 5. Contra Julianum cap. 5. scribit: Pariens est Concupiscentia: partus peccatum: Sed Concupiscentia non parit, nisi conceperit; non concipit, nisi illexerit: hoc est, ad malum perpetrandum obtinuerit voluntatis assensum. Quod ipsum significantiùs explicat Apostolus quoque, Rom. 7, 23. Video, inquiens, aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meæ, & captivantem me sub lege peccati.

Cæterùm cur ita voluntas moveatur ab appetitu, causa est, ipsa potentiarum animæ συμπάθεια, indè existens, quod omnes illæ sunt perfectiones, & quasi ornamenta unius & ejusdem substantiæ hominis : uti haud incommodè scripsit Cajetanus Thom 1. secundæ. Quæst. 4. disput. 2. Art. 2. Quoad secundum & tertium modum, concurrit ad illos exterior etiam causa, & vel Diabolus, vel alius etiam Homo, qui & ipse potest alium Hominem instigare ad peccandum. Ubi tamen neque Diabolus, neque talis Homo, proxima, directa, sufficiens, aut necessaria : sed occasionalis duntaxat & indirecta peccati causa constitui potest, quatenùs nimirùm sensibus exterioribus & interioribus, illectis & persuasis, imò ipso intellectu decepto, & obfuscato, consensum peccati à voluntate humanâ impetrat. Est verò observationis hujus usus longè maximus, ad retundendam illorum vesanian, qui dùm Diabolum, vel alium quempiam Hominem flagitiorum suorum autorem, vel saltem persuasorem nominant, & istorum fraude se deceptos esse conqueruntur: statim ab omni peccati reatu se immunes atque adeò liberos esse autumant.

Quibus graviter respondet Gregorius Nazianzenus, in libro Spiritualium sententiarum, quas Carmine exposuit; Inquiens:

Hostem quìd accusamus usq;, perditum? Et moribus permittimus licentiam? Te criminare prorsus ipsum, aut maximè: Nos ignem habemus : Spiritus flammam ciet.

Etsi enim suggestionum Diaboli magna est vis: peccatorum tamen causa nunquam directè constitui potest: quin potiùs nos τῇ Φύσει & naturâ ad peccandum sum9 proclives, sic instigante interno illo & communi principio, quod est ac dicitur, Natura nostra corrupta & vitiata: ita ut si vel maximè, absque Diaboli suggestionibus & persuasionibus esset: appetitus tamen rerum naturalium in homine posset esse inordinatus & consequenter peccatum esset, nisi ratione ordinaretur: uti Scholastici, Thomas cumprimis disputant. Fundamentum assertionis hujus est ipse Lapsus primorum parentum, qui à solâ voluntate Hominis in solidum dependet: & neque DEO, tanquam universali principio ullo pacto: neque Diabolo, tanquam superioris naturæ principio, directè adscribi potest. Nam licèt Satanas seduxisse primos parentes legatur: tamen id non necessitatis, vel coactionis: sed suasionis tantum & instigationis fuit. Quod ipsum de omnibus etiam peccatis actualibus est statuendum, nempè, quòd ad solum internum & directum voluntatis humanæ principium ea sint referenda. Etsi enim ex corruptione naturæ humanæ, aliqua nos manet peccandi necessitas, ita ut non possimus non peccare: secundum tristissimam illam querelam Apostoli, Rom. 7, 14. Scimus Legem esse spiritualem: at ego carnalis sum venditus sub peccatum: & v. 20.
