Invenio hanc Legem in me, quòd peccatum mihi adjacet &c. tamé hæc ipsa peccandi necessitas, ex voluntario lapsu primorum parentum ortum duxit: & nunquam in actum erumpit, quin voluntatis assensus accedat: ita ut peccatum non sit, nisi quod est voluntarium.

Pars hæc Religionis Christianæ sua in scripturis quoque expressa habet fundamenta. Nam quoad Diabolum, notum est classicum illud Servatoris oraculum Joh. 8, 44. Diabolus homicida est ab initio; cùm mendacium loquitur, ex propriis loquitur, quia mendax est, & pater mendacii. Quo pertinet illud Apostolicum 1. Joh. 3, 8. Qui facit peccatum ex Diabolo est: quoniam ab initio Diabolus peccat. Ubi tamen rectè admonet Autor noster mendacium ab ipsâ substantiâ Diaboli: sicut & id, quod proprium habet, & quod aliundè accipit, accuratè discernendum esse. Substantiam enim non ex proprio, sed aliundè habet Diabolus: Nam omnes Angeli à DEO sunt creati, quorum aliqui posteà lapsi sunt: Habet autem etiam proprium quiddam Diabolus, non à DEO acceptum, videlicet mendacium id est, peccatum, quod libera voluntas Diaboli peperit. Neque hæc, ut scitè infert Philippus, inter se pugnant: Substantiam à DEO conditam esse, & sustentari: & tamen voluntatem Diaboli & voluntatem hominis causas esse peccati: quia voluntas abuti suâ libertate potuit, seque à DEO av ertere.

Cæterùm quoad voluntatem Hominis, itidem Scriptura luculenter testatur, huic tanquam fonti primariam & directam peccati causam esse adscribendam. Quâ in parte militat illud Apostoli Rom. 5. per Hominem intravit peccatum in mundum. 1. Johan. 2. Concupiscentia carnis non est ex Patre, sed ex Mundo, hoc est, ex hominibus, qui sunt in mundo.


### Chapter Two: Part II. Ἀντιθετικὴ, of the second chapter concerning the cause of sin

PART II. Ἀντιθετικὴ, of the second chapter concerning the cause of sin.

To this purer doctrine concerning the cause of sin, Gentile philosophers, established outside the boundaries of the Church, have long since moved a dispute, whose opinions, however, partly in themselves old-womanish and ridiculous, partly manifestly impious, it is not worth the effort to expound at length: since they had as much insight into the nature and origin of evil as they did into other mysteries of the Christian religion, of which they knew not even γρῦ: so that D. Augustine truly pronounced of them altogether, What, I beseech you, could they know about this matter, who neither knew nor read that: Through one man sin entered into the world.

Our author reduces their opinions to two main heads: Philosophers, he says, partly place the causes of sin in matter: partly transfer them to fate, which they say is the necessary connection of the first cause and of all secondary causes, physical and of the will.

Moreover, the seeds of each of these errors in the progress of time in the very Church of God sprouted again: indeed in such a way that the Marcionites brought the former into the theater of the Church, and the Zwinglians the latter. For Marcion, as Augustine reports in his book on heresies, contended that sin did not arise from the free will of the first man, but was created in the beginning, and that sins are now committed not by free will—that is, by the mind judging and the will choosing—but just as a bad tree, neither knowing nor willing, but by nature produces bad fruits, so also man sins by reason of his condition and nature. Thus, in the time of Tertullian, a certain Hermogenes in express words established the cause of sin in matter, feigning that matter had existed from eternity, one part good, the other evil, and consequently that some were made good and others evil, not by the virtue or vice of the Creator, but of matter.

Regarding the latter opinion, which was properly that of the Stoics, it has just now been shown above in chapter 1 that the Libertines, and the Calvinists who support them, weave such a connection of the first and second causes that whatever the second cause does, it does and works necessarily only with the concurrence of the first and universal cause, whether that thing be good or evil. Let them see, therefore, how they can either excuse this impiety, long since condemned in the philosophers, or entirely clear themselves of it. Certainly, in the Stoics, just as in the Libertines and Calvinists, that which they established—that God is the governor of all created things, by whose nod and power the whole world is administered and ruled, and also the lives of men are cared for and provided for—easily deserved assent and approval, as Cicero explains the mind of the Stoics somewhere. But that was deservedly repudiated as impious and ὑπερβολικὸν, that they introduced a Fate of necessity from the perpetual connection and order of the first or universal cause with the second causes. Thus, in the Libertines and Calvinists, that former point also easily gains our approval, namely that nothing, whether good or evil, happens to which the governance of God, as the first and universal cause, does not concur. But that far more terrible excess savors of the view that they establish and contend that that first or universal cause concurs with the evil actions of men in such a way that they happen necessarily, not only with respect to foreknowledge but also to divine providence: thus, indeed, with God willing, ordaining, and disposing; which was shown more fully from their own writings in the previous chapter. But to proceed in compiling the catalog of heretics, the Valentinians also wickedly defiled the purity of this article, who contended that a certain force is brought upon man by divine necessity when he perpetrates crimes, as Irenaeus testifies, book 4, chapters 47 and 48.

The Manichaeans followed these, who also, removing the cause of sin from human choice or will, disseminated the seeds of the same impiety that had been scattered by the Marcionites and Valentinians concerning that double and coeternal principle of all things, or twin God: both of whom, when they had undertaken the work of creation from the matter subject to them, they claimed it happened that, because of the disagreement that arose between them, something of the matter of his own quality was sprinkled by the adverse or evil God onto the good creation of man, which had been undertaken by the good principle or God; whence afterwards the cause of all evil and sin in man took its origin.

If one may investigate more accurately the causes of these most gross errors, two especially occur, which seem to have provided the handle and occasion for heresy to the Libertines themselves and their followers.

The first is: an excessively loose confusion of particular causes with the universal. For because they saw a remarkable dissonance, or rather contrariety, in the causes of particular effects, because some turn out good and others evil, they established that a place must certainly be left for that contrariety in the first or universal cause also; or, which is the same thing, in the first principle. In which part, however, they were most shamefully hallucinating; since it is necessary that contraries do not proceed to infinity, but finally meet in one common thing; and therefore there must be one common cause, which is none other than the universal cause, which is the first and highest principle of being for the nature of the whole of being, that is, of all things that in any way exist.

A later cause of the error seems to have flowed from this, that they judged wrongly concerning the nature of evil. For they supposed that judgment ought to be made concerning it from particular effects: just as if someone were to say that the nature of fire is evil, because a house had been burned down by it and reduced to ashes. In which part they again shamefully erred: since one must not judge of the goodness or malice of any thing from its relation to some evil thing, but from the nature of the thing itself, and its relation to the whole Universe. There was also added that, which the Manichaeans did, namely that they referred evil or sin into the class of Essences themselves. But now nothing that is, insofar as it is, or by its own Essence is evil: but everything that is, insofar as it is, is Good.

What is more: evil is not except in Good: as an accident in its subject. Therefore if there were some supreme Evil, it would certainly destroy itself: since if the supreme Good were destroyed, evil itself would also be destroyed, inasmuch as it happens to and inheres in Good as its subject. Finally, such is the nature of evil, that it can never be a primary cause: since evil cannot be a cause except by accident: but now this cause, which is by itself, is always later.

However, however gross and absurd that error of the Manichaeans may have been: yet reasons and arguments were not lacking to them, with which they attempted to put a gloss upon their impiety: These indeed Thomas recounts in this order in part 1, question 19, article 3 of his Theology.

1. Of contrary effects there are contrary principles. But well and ill done deeds, or virtues and vices are

there are contrary effects. Therefore, there will be contrary principles. They were accustomed to confirm the certainty of the major premise not only from philosophy, but also from our most sacred theology, with those words of Ecclesiasticus 33:15 adapted here: Against evil, there is good: and against death, life: so also against the just man, the sinner: And thus look upon all the works of the Most High: Two against two: and one against one. And chap. 42:25. All things are double, one against one.

But it is most rightly answered that a gross fallacy of the consequent is being committed. For although contrary effects have particular contrary causes, yet it is most fallaciously inferred from that to contrary first or universal causes. The reason is: Because in this way a process of contraries into infinity would be established: which is manifestly absurd. For it is necessary that contraries eventually meet in one supreme genus and in the very nature of being: so that eventually one must arrive at one common and first cause, which is none other than the universal cause: which is the nature of the whole of Being: that is, the first and supreme principle of Being for all things that are in any way. In the allegation of both sayings of Ecclesiasticus, an ἄγνοια ἐλέγχου (ignorance of the refutation) is committed, whether you take it regarding the first creation or regarding the course and condition of human life and actions. For in the former way this sense emerges: that GOD has so made and ordered his creatures that one is in a certain way opposed to another: and each has a use distinct from the other, indeed contrary to the other: which is to be seen both in rational creatures, such as angels and men: and in brutes, indeed in plants, herbs, elements, and any other creatures whatsoever. But that a collection should not be made toward two contrary principles, the son of Sirach himself forbids, immediately adding: But all these are the works of the Most High. But then, if you take those two passages regarding the common course of human actions and mutual affection: no other sense emerges than that in all things and actions one always finds two against two: so that two goods always have two evils contrary to them: and one good and true is contrary to another evil and false. Thus, as regards the latter saying in particular, it is truly so arranged that all things are double: For there is GOD and the creature: there is spirit and body: there is true and false, just, unjust, upward, downward, right, left, virtue, vice: hot, cold: moist, dry: etc. Of all of which one is always against one, where, however, it is sufficiently clear in itself that only the dissonance and contrariety of particular causes is being noted.

II. The nature of opposites requires that, given one contrary in the nature of things, the other is immediately posited. But the cause of every good, in the nature of things, is the supreme good. Therefore, the cause of every evil will also be some supreme evil.

I answer that the major premise is true only regarding particular contrary causes: from whose condition it was just now shown above that it is most fallaciously inferred to two contrary first or universal causes. For particular causes ought not to be traced back to contrary first causes: but to one and the same, which, because of its amplitude, is the origin even of contrary causes: for it is impossible, without manifest contradiction, for several first causes to be established. Then, one must distinguish in this place between evil and good, just as between privation and habit. For evil is not some positive being: nor is it even a pure negation: but a privation, which is a negation of goodness and perfection due to a thing. Now, therefore, since evil is such a privation, it is certainly opposed only to that good to which potency is joined: but not to the supreme good, which is pure act.

III. Just as good and better are found in things: so also are evil and worse. But the former is not called such except in respect to the supreme good. Therefore, the latter is likewise called such in respect to the supreme evil.

I answer: That it is indeed true that there are degrees of comparison from the genus of evils as well as of goods; so that just as there is good and better: so also there is evil and worse: But the question lies in this, from what principle these degrees depend: or what is the same, from where each is intensified: Where it is most fallaciously presupposed by the Manichaeans that the principle of both intensification depends on a twin supreme or first principle: which conflicts with all reason. Since each, as much evil as good, is intensified only according to its own nature. For something does not become more or less evil through some accession to some greater or lesser evil: or through some participation in greater or lesser evil: but through a recession from a greater or lesser good, and thus from the supreme good, which is GOD: indeed in such a way that the further one recedes from GOD as the supreme good and principle: the more the degree of evil or sin is intensified. Thus, as regards good, it is intensified, and is said to be more or less good: insofar as one approaches more or less to the limit of perfection. The foundation for this answer is laid down from philosophy: That just as form is a certain perfection: so privation is a removal: Therefore, degrees of evil are most rightly defined by the recession from the limit of goodness or perfection: but those of good, by the accession to the limit of perfection. Hence St. Augustine, book 1 against Julian, chapter 3, quite acutely: Nature is capable of goodness by participation in the good, from which it was made: but it receives malice not by participation in evil: but by privation of good.

IV. Whatever is such by participation is reduced to that which is such by essence. But evil is not such by essence, but by participation. Therefore, evil can be reduced to that which is evil by essence.

I answer: The major premise is true concerning the Good: which has the nature of Being and Habit. The minor premise is false. For Evil is not such by the participation of some evil: but insofar as it is a Privation of the Good: as has already been shown.

V. If Evil is posited by accident, evil must also be posited in itself: Reason: Because everything that is by accident is reduced to that which is in itself. But Evil is posited by Accident. Therefore, evil must also be posited in itself.

I answer: The reasoning of the consequence is denied: For because Evil is a privation: it certainly can have no other cause, except by accident: And insofar as it can have no other; it would certainly be impossible for it to be able to be reduced to something that is a cause of Evil in itself: so far is it from being established as some first cause of Evil: But rather, since there is one first cause, and that is supremely Good: there will certainly be no other cause of Evil than a recession from this first or universal cause.

VI. The effect of evil is reduced to the evil of the cause: and in this reduction it is not permitted to proceed to infinity. Therefore, it is necessary to posit a supreme evil, which is the cause of all evil. It is answered from the preceding that this is begging the question in the argument. For in the causes of Evil or sin: one must not proceed to infinity: nor to some one first cause, which is the supreme Evil, and the cause of all evil: but the cause of Evil is reduced to some good cause: from which, when one recedes, Evil is immediately committed: and thus by accident, Evil follows from the Good: as is most clearly evident from the preceding.

The arguments of the Manichaeans having been thus refuted, there remains a single Question, which deserves some explanation on account of the superstitions of certain Astrologers. For because it is established from the above that the proximate and direct cause of sin is the will of Man: it is immediately asked: Whether by the impression of the stars or celestial bodies, by a certain fatal necessity, the wills of men are impelled to sin?

To which question we answer in the beginning simply in the Negative: Then, however, we confirm this negative with the following reasons.

For first, from the whole of sacred scripture, not even one testimony can be brought forward, which even in appearance at least probably confirms the opinion of the Astrologers: so that rather each and every thing that deals with the stars asserts the complete opposite, and clearly confirms that the stars were by no means created by God for the purpose that they should have any power over the will and intellect of man: so that the Prophet Isaiah in chapter 47, 13, even for this reason mocks the study of those who place faith in Astrological divinations, because there is absolutely no certain and necessary connection of human and contingent events with the disposition of the celestial stars: as was shown more fully and vigorously in the Article on creation. Furthermore, reasons are added that prove the opposite. For 1. The will is an immaterial thing and therefore too perfect to be able to receive directly any impression from any corporeal thing. Nor does it stand in the way that some object that some celestial body can formally concur with the act of the will, insofar as it specifies it objectively. For even if this were granted to the greatest extent: it is not yet confirmed that some celestial body directly moves the will of Man. For whatever objectively terminates and specifies the act of the will: that does not yet directly move the will of Man: but only shows some Object, around which the will can behave freely: and can either desire or avoid it.

Another reason can be given as follows: The act of the will can proceed only from that external principle which is the cause of the will itself: But the only principle of this kind is GOD. Therefore, the will can proceed from GOD alone as from a principle, as that which moves it directly to the exercise of its act, which, if the importunity of the adversaries should so demand, we are most prepared to demonstrate with more arguments.

Latin:

PARS II. Ἀντιθετικὴ, Secundi capitis de Causâ peccati.

PUriori huic de Causâ Peccati doctrinæ litem jam olim moverunt, Philosophi Gentiles, extra Ecclesiæ pomœria constituti, quorum tamen sententias partim per se aniles & ridiculas, partim manifestè impias, operosius exponere nihil attinet: Siquidem de naturâ & Origine mali, tantundem fuit ipsis perspectum, quantum de aliis Christianæ Religionis mysteriis, de quibus ne γρῦ quidem noverunt: ut verè omninò de illis pronunciaverit D. Augustinus, Quid, obsecro, hâc de re sapere potuerunt, qui nec sciverunt, nec legerunt illud: Per unum hominem peccatum intravit in mundum.

Autor noster ad duo summa capita illorum opiniones revocat: Philosophi, inquiens, partim in materiâ causas Peccati collocant: partim ad fatum transferunt, quod dicunt, esse necessariam connexionem causæ primæ, & omnium secundarum, Physicarum & voluntatum.

Cæterùm semina singulorum istorum errorum progressu temporis in ipsâ Ecclesiâ Dei repullulârut: ita quidem ut priorem illum Marcionitæ: posteriorem Zvvingliani in theatrum Ecclesiæ produxerint. Marcion enim, referente, Augustino, libro de hæresibq, contendebat, Peccatum ortum esse, non ex libero primi Hominis arbitrio: sed esse creatum in principio: & nunc committi peccata non libero arbitrio: id est, mente judicante, & voluntate eligente: sed sicut mala arbor, nec sciens, nec volens, sed naturâ profert malos fructus: ita etiam Hominem ratione conditionis & naturæ peccare. Sic tempore Tertulliani Hermogenes quidam expressis verbis peccati causam in Materiâ constituit: fingens, materiam ab æterno fuisse aliam bonam, aliam malam: ac proindè quosdam esse bonos factos, quosdam malos, non creatoris, sed materiæ vel virtute, vel vitio.

Quoad posteriorem sentétiam, quæ Stoicorum propriè fuit, jam modò supra cap. 1. ostensum est. Libertinos, & his suffragantes Calvinianos, talem connexionem causæ primæ & secundarum nectere, ut quicquid agit causa secunda, illud non nisi cum cōcursu causæ primæ & universalis sic necessariò agat & operetur, sive bonum sive malum illud sit. Viderint proindè quo pacto impietatem istam, jampridem in Philosophis damnatam, vel excusare, vel à se prorsus amoliri queant. Certè in Stoicis æque ac in Libertinis & Calvinianis, illud facilè assensum & approbationem merebatur, quod DEUM rerum omnium creatarum gubernatorem constituebant, cujus nutu ac virtute tum mund9 universus administraretur & regatur: tum vitæ etiam hominum consulatur & provideatur: uti Cicero Stoicorum mentem alicubi exponit. Illud verò tanquam impium & ὑπερβολικὸν meritò repudiabatur, quod necessitatis Fatum introduxerunt, ex perpetuo causæ primæ sive Universalis, cum secundarum nexu & ordine. Sic in Libertinis & Calvinianis etiam prius illud nostrum calculum facilè impetrat, quod nimirùm nihil vel boni vel mali fiat, ad quod non DEI, tanquam causæ primæ & universalis, concurrat gubernatio: Sed excessum illud longè teterrimum sapit, quod statuunt & contendunt, ita primam sive universalem illam causam ad actiones hominum malas concurrere, ut non modò præscientiæ, sed & divinæ providentiæ respectu, ea eveniant necessariò: sic nimirùm DEO volente, ordinante, disponente: id quod capite priore fusiùs ex ipsorum scriptis ostensum fuit. Sed ut in hæreticorum cathalogo pertexendo progrediamur, puritatem hujus Articuli nefariè etiam conspurcarunt Valentiniani, qui contendebant, divinâ necessitate vim quandam homini inferri, quando scelera perpetrat: teste Irenæo, lib. 4. capp. 47. & 48.

Hos sunt subsecuti Manichæi, qui & ipsi causam peccati ab arbitrio sive voluntate humanâ removentes, semina ejusdem impietatis disseminârunt, quæ à Marcionitis & Valentinianis sparsa fuerunt, de duplici illo & coæterno rerum omnium principio, seu DEO gemino: quorum uterque cùm ex subjectâ sibi materiâ opus creationis aggressus esset, factum p effe nugabantur, ut propter diffidium inter ipfos exortum Hominis Creationi bonæ, à Bono principio five DEO fusceptæ, ab adverfo seu malo DEO, de suæ qualitatis materiâ aliquid aspersum fuerit: Undè postmodùm in Homine omnis mali & peccati causa ortum duxerit.

Causas crassissimorum istorum errorum si accuratiùs investigare liceat: duæ potissimùm occurrunt: quæ ipsis quoque Libertinis & asseclis, hæresews ansam & occasionem præbuisse videntur.

Prior est: particularium causarum cum universali nimis laxa confusio. Quia enim videbant insignem dissonantiam, imò contrarietatem inesse causis particularium effectuum, propterea quòd alii boni, alii mali proveniant: statuerunt utique contrarietati isti locum reliquendum esse in causâ etiam primâ sive universali: vel quod idem est, in primo principio. Quâ tamen in parte turpissimè hallucinabantur: Siquidem necessum est, ut contraria non in infinitum progrediantur: sed tandem conveniant in uno communi: ac proindè detur una causa communis quæ nulla est alia, quàm causa universalis, quæ totius entis natura, hoc est, rerum omnium, quæ quocunque modo sunt, primum & summum essendi est principium.

Posterior erroris causa indè fluxisse videtur, quod de naturâ mali perperàm judicarunt. Nam ex particularibus effectibus de eâ judicium faciendum esse autumarunt: haud secòs ac si quis Naturam Ignis malam esse dicat, quia ab eo domus esset exusta & in cineres redacta. Quâ rursus in parte turpiter aberrarunt: siquidem de rei alicujus bonitate aut malitiâ non est judicandum, ex ordine ad aliquam rem malam: Sed ex rei ipsius naturâ, & ordine ad totum Universum. Accedebat & illud, quod Manichæi malum sive peccatum in classem ipsarum Essentiarum retulerunt. Jam verò nihil quod est, quatenùs est, sive suâ Essentiâ est malum: sed omne quod est, quatenùs est, est Bonum.

Quid: quòd Malum non est nisi in Bono: tanquam accidens in suo subjecto. Ergò si summum aliquod Malum esset, certè seipsum destrueret: Siquidem destructo summo Bono, malum etiam ipsum destrueretur, quippè quod Bono tanquam suo subjecto accidit & inhæret. Tandẽ ea est mali natura, ut nunquam possit esse prima causa: Siquidem malum non potest esse causa nisi per accidens: Jam verò hæc semper posterior est, ea causa, quæ est per se.

Cæterùm quantumvis crassus & absurdus fuerit error iste Manichæorum: non tamen ipsis defuerunt rationes & argumenta, quibus impietati fucum facere conabantur: Ea verò hoc ordine percenset Thomas part. 1. quæst. 19. art. 3. Theologiæ suæ.

1. Contrariorum effectuum contraria sunt principia. Atqui rectè & malè facta, sive virtutes & vitia sunt

sunt contrarii effectus. Ergò contraria erunt principia. Majoris certitudinem non ex Philosophiâ tantùm, sed & sacratissimâ nostrâ Theologiâ confirmare solebant, hùc accommodatis verbis illis Ecclesiastici 33, 15. Contra malum, bonum est: & contra mortem vita: sic & contra virum justum peccator: Et sic intuere in omnia opera Altissimi: Duo contra duo: & unum contra unum. Et cap. 42, 25. Omnia duplicia, unum contra unum.

Sed rectissimè respondetur, crassam committi Sophisticationem vitiosi Consequentis. Etsi enim contrarii Effectus causas habent particulares contrarias: tamen indè vitiosissimè colligitur, ad causas itidem primas sive universales contrarias: Ratio est: Quia hoc pacto Contrariorum processus in infinitum statueretur: id quod manifestè absurdum. Contraria enim tandem in Uno Genere summo, & in ipsâ essendi ratione conveniant, necesse est: Ita ut tandem ad unam communem & primam causam sit deveniendum, quæ nulla est alia, quàm causa universalis: quæ totius Entis natura: hoc est, rerum omnium, quæ quocunque modo sunt, primum & summum Essendi est principium. In allegatione utriusque dicti Ecclesiastici committitur ἄγνοια ἐλέγχε, sive de primâ creatione, sive de cursu & conditione vitæ & actionum humanarum communica accipias. Priore enim modo sensus emergit iste: DEUM creaturas suas ita fecisse & ordinasse, ut una alteri quodammodo sit opposita: & quælibet usum habeat ab alterâ distinctum, imò alteri contrarium: id quod tùm in creaturis rationalibus, ut Angelis & Hominibus: tùm in brutis, imò in plantis, herbis, Elementis, & creaturis quibuscunque aliis videre est. Cæterùm ne ad duo contraria principia instituatur collectio, prohibet ipse Syracides, statim subjiciens: Hæc autem omnia sunt opera Altissimi. Deindè verò si de communi actionum humanarum cursu & mutuâ affectione, loca illa duo accipias: sensus non alius emergit, quàm in omnibus rebus & actionibus semper invenire duo contra duo: ita ut duo bona semper sibi habeant contraria duo mala: & unum bonum, ac verum alteri malo & falso sit contrarium. Sic quoad in specie ad posterius dictum, reverà ita est comparatum, ut omnia sint duplicia: Est enim DEUS & creatura: est Spiritus & corpus: est verum & falsum, justum, injustum, sursum, deorsum, dextrum, sinistrum, virtus, vitium: calidum, frigidum: humidum, siccum: &c. Quorum omnium semper unum est contra unum, ubi tamen particularium duntaxat causarum dissonantiam & contrarietatem notari, per se satis liquet.

II. Oppositorum natura requirit, ut dato in naturâ rerum contrario uno, statim ponatur & alterum. Atqui omnis Boni causa, in naturâ rerum, est summum bonum. Ergò omnis etiam mali causa erit aliquod summum malum.

Respondeo, Majorem tantùm veram esse de contrariis causis particularibus: à quarum conditione vitiosissimè colligi ad duas causas contrarias primas sive universales: jam modò suprà ostensum fuit. Neque enim causae particulares debent revocari in primas contrarias: sed in unam & eandem, quae ob sui amplitudinem sit origo etiam causarum contrariarum: neque enim possunt sine contradictione manifestâ, plures constitui causae primae. Deindè distingvendum est, hoc loco inter malum & inter bonum, quemadmodum inter privationem & Habitum. Neque enim Malum est Ens aliquod positivum: neque pura etiam negatio: sed privatio, quae est negatio bonitatis atq; perfectionis alicui rei debitae. Jam ergò, cùm Malum talis sit privatio, utique illi tantùm bono opponitur, cui adjungitur potentia: non autem summo bono, quod est actus purissimus.

III. Sicut in rebus invenitur Bonum & Melius: Ita etiam Malum & Pejus. Sed illud non dicitur tale, nisi respectu summi Boni. Ergò posterius hoc, respectu summi mali itidem tale dicitur.

Respondeo: Verum quidem esse, tam ex malorum, quàm ex bonorum genere dari gradus comparationis; ita ut quemadmodum datur bonum & melius: sic etiam detur malum & pejus: Verùm in eo est quaestio, à quonám principio Gradus isti dependeant: vel quod idem est, Undénam unumquodque intendatur: Ubi vitiosissimè à Manichaeis praesupponitur, intensionis utriusque principium dependere à gemino summo sive primo principio: id quod cum omni ratione pugnat. Siquidem unumquodque tàm malum quàm bonum intenditur non nisi secundum propriam rationem. Neque enim aliquid fit magis aut minùs malum, per quandam accessionem ad majus aliquod, aut minus malum: aut per aliquam participationem majoris aut minoris mali: sed per recessum à majori vel minori bono, atque adeò summo bono, quod est DEUS: ita quidem, ut quò longiùs receditur à DEO tanquam summo bono & principio: eò magis etiam intendatur gradus Mali sive peccati. Sic quoad Bonum, intenditur illud, & dicitur magis vel minus esse Bonum: quatenùs magis aut minus acceditur ad Terminum perfectionis. Fundamentum ex Philosophiâ responsioni huic substernitur istud: Quod sicut Forma est perfectio quaedam: ita privatio est remotio: Ergò rectissimè Gradus mali definiuntur per recessum à termino bonitatis sive perfectionis: Boni verò, per accessionem ad terminum perfectionis. Hinc D. Augustinus l. 1. contra Julianum cap. 3. satis acutè: Bonitatis capax est natura participatione boni, à quo facta est: Malitiam verò capit non participatione mali: sed privatione Boni.

IV. Quicquid per Participationem est tale: illud reducitur ad id, quod est per Essentiam tale. Atqui Malum tale non est per Essentiam, sed per Participationem. Ergò Malum reduci potest ad id, quod est per Essentiam malum.

Respondeo : Major vera est de Bono : quod habet rationem Entis & Habitus. Minor falsa est. Neque enim Malum tale est, per participationem alicujus mali : sed quatenùs est Privatio Boni : uti jam ostensum.

V. Si ponitur Malum per accidens, ponendum est etiam malum per se : Ratio : Quia omne quod est per accidens, reducitur ad id, quod est per se. Atqui ponitur Malum per Accidens. Ergò ponendum est etiam malum per se.

Respondeo : Negatur ratio Consequentiæ : Quia enim Malum est privatio : utique nullam etiam aliam potest habere causam, nisi per accidens : Et quatenùs nullam aliam habere potest; utique impossibile fuerit, eam posse reduci ad aliquid, quod per se sit causa Mali : tantùm abest, ut aliqua prima causa Mali constituatur : Sed potiùs cum Una sit causa prima, eaque summè Bona : utique causa Mali alia non fuerit, quàm recessio ab hac causâ primâ sive universali.

VI. Malum effectus reducitur ad malum causæ : & in hac reductione non licet procedere in infinitum. Ergò necessum est ponere summum malum, quod sit causa omnis mali. Respondetur ex præcedentibus, peti hoc in argumento principium. In causis enim Mali sive peccati : neque in infinitum : neque ad unam aliquam primam causam, quæ sit summum Malum, & causa omnis mali, est progrediendum : sed Mali causa reducitur ad aliquam causam bonam : à quâ, quando receditur, Malum statim committitur : & sic per accidens, Malum ex Bono sequitur : uti ex præcedentibus liquidissimè patet.

Manichæorum argumentis ita refutatis, superest unica Quæstio, quæ propter Astrologorum quorundam superstitiones explicationem aliquam meretur. Quia enim ex superioribus constat, propinquam & directam peccati causam esse voluntatem Hominis : statim quæritur : An ex impressione astrorum sive corporum cœlestium, fatali quadam necessitate, voluntates hominum ad peccandum impellantur?

Ad quam quæstionem initiò simpliciter Negatè respondemus : Deindè verò hanc negativam confirmamus subseqq. rationibus.

Primùm enim ex universâ scripturâ sacrâ, ne unum quidem proferri potest testimonium, quod vel in speciem saltem probabiliter Astrologorum sententiam confirmet : ut potiùs singula atque universa, quæ de astris agunt, diversum omninò astruant, ac luculenter confirment, astra eo fine à Deo minimè esse condita, ut in voluntatem atque intellectum hominis ullum aliquod haberent imperium : ita ut Propheta Esaias cap. 47, 13. vel hanc ob causam irrideat studium illorum, qui Astrologicis divinationibus adhibent fidem, proptereà quòd nulla prorsus certa & necessaria est connexio eventuum humanorum & contingentium, cum dispositione siderum cœlestium: uti in Art. de creatione fusius & nervosius ostensum. Accedunt porrò rationes, diversum evincentes. Nam 1. Voluntas est res immaterialis atqu­ adeò perfectior, quàm ut ab ullâ re corporeâ possit recipere directè aliquam impressionem. Neque obstat, quod nonnulli objiciunt, Corpus aliquod cœleste posse formaliter concurrere ad actum voluntatis, quatenùs nimirùm objectivè ipsum specificat. Nam si vel maximè hoc “ concedatur: nondum tamen confirmatum est, “ corpus aliquod cœleste directè movere volun- “ tatem Hominis. Nam quicquid objectivè ter- “ minat & specificat voluntatis actum: illud nondum directè movet voluntatem Hominis: sed tantùm Objectum aliquod ostendit, circa quod voluntas liberè se habere: & illud vel appetere, vel aversari potest.

Altera ratio talis dari potest: Actus voluntatis ab eo duntaxat exteriori principio potest procēdere, quod est ipsius voluntatis causa: Sed hujusmodi principium solus est DEUS. E. voluntas à solo DEO potest procedere tanquam à principio, ut quod moveat eam directè ad exercitium sui actus, id quod si Adversariorum ita postulaverit importunitas, pluribus demonstrare sumus paratissimi.


### Appendix. On Astrological Fate

Every cause of evil must be removed from GOD, not only the immediate: but also any mediate one. For which reason more sincere Theologians also wish Astrological FATE to be proscribed from the Church, by which a sidereal force and celestial influence, falling upon the moments of conceptions and births: or of human counsels and actions, is irreligiously feigned to be the cause of evils and sins.

Some attempt to stroke this impiety, while they assert that they do not attribute to the stars any effective force that induces necessity, but only one that inclines; or, consulting their own interests with another more honorable escape, as they think, they repeatedly say that they deny even the faculty of inclining to the constellations, and assign to them only the power of signifying.

But Augustine refuted all these vanities to the point of sufficiency in Book 5 of The City of God, chapter 1. Where he not only breaks the arguments of those who establish the stars, in the nativities of infants, as the effective causes of the fortunes and fates of each one at their birth: but he also refutes those who attribute to the stars the power of signs concerning the future life, character, and fortune of those being born.

Latin:

REmovenda est à DEO causa omnis mali, non immediata tantùm: sed mediata etiam quælibet. Quo nomine proscriptum etiam ex Ecclesiâ sinceriores Theologi esse volunt FATUM Astrologicum, quo vis siderea & influentia cœlestis, vel inconceptuum & natalium: vel consiliorum atque actionum humanarum momenta incidens, malorum & peccatorum causa esse, parùm religiosè fingitur.

Palpum impietati huic facere aliqui conantur, dùm se astris non vim ullam effectricem, quæ necessitatem inducat: quæ duntaxat inclinet, tribuere asserunt: aut alio honestiore, ut putant, effugio sibi consulentes, etiam ipsam inclinandi facultatem se constellationibus denegare, solamque significandi vim assignare dictitant.

Verùm has omnes vanitates ad sufficientiam refutavit Augustinus l. 5. de Civit. Dei, cap. 1. Ubi non tantùm eorum rationes infringit, qui Stellas, in genituris infantium, effectrices causas suarum nascenti cuique fortium & fatorum statuunt: sed & eos refellit, qui signorum vim de futurâ nascentium vitâ, moribus, fortunâ, astris tribuunt.


### Appendix. On Astrological Fate: The impieties of certain Mathematicians

SCHONERUS p. 46 of the Isagoge sets forth a table of aspects, by which it may be safe and convenient to act with the senses, with the learned, with princes, with farmers: and for whom the use of new clothes is profitable, for whom likewise it is fitting to seek counsel, to contract marriages, to commit boys to tutors, to send ambassadors, to make treaties, etc., and the contrary.

Abenragel required certain signs for the receiving of baptism.

Bellantius predicted Savonarola's heresy and strangulation from the great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn a few months before his death.

Cardano writes that Luther was made a heretic by the stars, and by the impulse of the heavenly bodies.

Petrus Aliacus and Cardano lied about the Magi in Matthew 2, because they claimed they derived Christ's birth from the stars from the great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in the sign of Cancer six years prior: Likewise from the position of the stars of that night on which Christ was born, on which the horoscope was the eighth degree of Virgo, which denotes changes in religion, with Saturn holding the zenith of the sky, and the Sun the nadir.

Bellantius says that intemperate stars create thieves and robbers by corrupting the spirits, humors, and elements of those born.

See the Article on creation near the end. NOTE. If the stars incline toward sins: they do that either physically or acquiredly. But they do not do this acquiredly, as the astrologers themselves admit: since the stars did not finally acquire the power of acting, which they are said to exercise, through frequent practice. Therefore, they will incline toward evils by nature. But indeed, whatever the stars do by nature, they have from GOD the creator. But this latter is absurd. Therefore the former is also: and consequently it is false that the stars incline toward sins.

II. Of particular future events, especially those contingent by accident, there is no knowledge or art.

III. To know future contingent events belongs to GOD alone.

Latin:

SCHONERUS p. 46. Isagoges b. tabulam aspectuum ponit, quibus tutum & commodum sit agere eum sensibus, cum doctis, principibus, agricolis: & quibus conducat vestium novarum usurpatio, quibus item aspectibus deceat consilia petere, conjugia contrahere, pueros praeceptoribus committere, legatos mittere, foedera facere &c. & contra.

Abenragel ad baptismum suscipiendum certa signa requisivit.

Bellantius ex magnâ Conjunctione ♃. & ♄. Savanorolae heresin & strangulationem predixit paucis ante mortem mensibus.

Cardanus Lutherum scribit ex sideribus factum hereticum, & astrorum impulsu.

Petrus Aliacus & Cardanus de Magis Matth. 2. mentiti sunt, quòd ex astris Christi nativitatem habuerint ex Conjunctione magnâ ♃. & ♄. in signo Cancri sexto anno antè: Item ex positu siderum illius noctis quâ Christus natus, quâ horoscopus fuerit pars VIII. Virginis, quae Religionis mutationes notet, Culmen coeli Saturno, imum Sole tenente.

Bellantius ait intemperatas stellas, fures & latrones efficere, corrumpendo Spiritus, humores & Elementa natorum.

Vide Articulum de creatione circa finem. NOTA. Si astra inclinant ad peccata: illud faciunt vel Φυσικῶς vel ἐπικτήτως. Atqui ἐπικτήτως hoc non faciunt, fatentibus ipsis Astrologis: Siquidem astra non demùm crebrâ exercitatione acquisiverunt vim agendi, quam exercere dicuntur. Ergò Φύσει sive Naturâ inclinabunt ad mala. Jam verò quicquid astra Naturâ agunt, id habent à DEO conditore. Atqui hoc posterius est absurdum. Ergò & prius illud: & per consequens falsum est, quòd astra inclinent ad peccata.

II. Particularium futurorum, præcipuè per accidens Contingentium, nulla est notitia, aut ars.

III. Nosse futura Contingentia solius DEI est.


## 8 On Necessity and Contingency

Oikonomia or the arrangement of the TREATISE.

ON Necessity and Contingency, both in the genus of all things and human actions: and in the species of Sin or Evil, a controversy is agitated among the learned, not so much common and ancient, as it is also grave and arduous: so that not only the schools of the Philosophers, but also the schools of the Theologians, resound with the noise of this question. And indeed such is its gravity, that he who errs concerning it, does so not only in the foundation: but even in the very

may seem to err at the beginning of the Christian [doctrine]. For he will hardly ever have sufficiently known and understood the fall of our first parents, and consequently the Nature of Evil or sin: much less will he be able to be certain that the cause of sin resides not in GOD, in any pact or respect; but only in the human will, and that indeed free: unless he has most thoroughly explored whether some fatal necessity dominates created things and human actions: or whether some contingency of the same can and ought to be granted?

Our author joins the treatment of this truly difficult Question with the immediately preceding Article in such a way that he resolves it under a fourfold consideration. For first he explains the τὸ εἰ ἔςi, namely, whether Contingency is granted in human affairs: then indeed the τὸ τί ἐςι, what, to be sure, is that Contingency which is inquired about in the Schools of the Theologians? Then what ought to be established as its true and proper cause? And finally what is its proper subject?

Since all those things, both individual and universal, which can be in dispute among Theologians concerning Contingency, are comprehended within the scope of these Questions: we, following the same footsteps, shall accommodate the future Treatise, especially to the controversies of our own times, in such a way that we may appear to have held both the thesis and the antithesis in consideration.

QUESTION I.

NOT only in the Schools of the Gentile Philosophers were these voices, full of desperate impiety, heard long ago: That it is by Fate that no one is born without vices: And, That by Fate no one becomes innocent: But this impiety has so invaded the very boundaries of the Church, that there are not lacking those who invent a fatal Necessity for all things and human events, especially sins, and are not at all afraid to refer the same to GOD himself. Which opinion, indeed, the Sacramentarians defend today with furious blindness, having twisted various testimonies of Scripture into a foreign sense; as the following exodus will show more clearly. Thus, therefore, by these men all Contingency was denied and is denied today. And indeed this opinion seems to be so plausible; that it appears to have fixed its seat in the minds of almost all men, by the force of original corruption: nay, even among the regenerate, under that heavier struggle of flesh and Spirit, and under the more intense heat of afflictions, the sinews of these errors exert themselves. For when they gaze upon that enormous ἀταξίαν or confusion of all things, when they gaze upon the stupendous inequality of the lot of the pious and the impious: when they gaze upon the persecutions of the Church; it happens for the most part that the thought of some fatal necessity strikes their minds. Therefore it is not a matter of indifferent liberty, but of the highest necessity, that a pious mind should have fully known and understood that not by some Fate, or some absolute necessity, are all things done: but that the Contingency of things and human actions must be entirely established.

The first argument for confirmation is ἔγγραφον (scriptural). For Scripture confirms quite clearly that many things happen contingently and freely, and that can be reduced to almost infinite passages, which nevertheless can be recalled to five classes.

The first class contains those passages of Scripture which testify ἀυτολεξεὶ (in the very words) and according to the letter that certain things are placed in the most free power of man, as Gen. 4:7, 'Unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.' Acts 5:4, Peter says to Ananias, 'Was it not in thine own power to sell the land?'

The second class consists of those passages of Scripture which show that many things are done by men ἑκουσίως (voluntarily) or of their own will: but that is called ἑκούσιον (voluntary) or spontaneous, the principle of which is in the agent himself, and who knows the individual circumstances of the action: τὸ ἑκούσιον ἐστὶν ὅ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐν ἀυτῶ εἰδότι τὰ καθ’ ἕκαστα ἐν οἷς ἡ πρᾶξις (the voluntary is that of which the principle is in himself, knowing the particulars in which the action consists). To this pertain these passages: Exod. 35:5, 'Let everyone who is willing and of a spontaneous mind offer to the Lord.' 1 Chron. 29:9, 'The people rejoiced, because they made offerings willingly.' Luke 9:35, 'Whoever shall wish to save his soul shall lose it.'

The third class contains those passages in which an option is given to man, that he may choose what he wishes. Deut. 30:19 and 20, 'I have set before you today good and evil: choose therefore life, that you may live, etc.' Josh. 24:15, 'If it seems evil to you to serve the Lord, an option is given to you: choose today what pleases you, whom you ought most especially to serve.' Thus 2 Sam. 24:12, an option is given to David, that he may choose from three punishments which he wishes. Thus 1 Kings 3:5, Solomon is commanded by God to ask for what he wishes.

The fourth class embraces those individual and universal testimonies of the Scriptures which confirm that man very often does something against and beyond the will of God, indeed that he resists the divine will willingly: to which pertains that sad complaint, Matt. 23:37, 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered thy children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not.' Likewise that passage, Heb. 10:26, concerning those who sin and resist God voluntarily.

The fifth and final class consists of those passages of Scripture which either prescribe precepts or counsels for the actions of men: or praise or blame the deeds of men: or finally propose divine promises and threats. Which indeed all, unless men could act freely and contingently in certain things, would find no place at all. For if man were impelled to act by a fatal, or absolute, or some Stoic necessity: every promise of rewards would certainly perish; every threat of punishments would also perish: since a promise looks in the place of an object to such an action as someone does freely and spontaneously: but a threat looks to such an action as someone could have freely omitted.

The second argument for confirmation we can borrow from the following next Article, concerning Free Will, where it will be demonstrated to the eye that man, even after the fall, has innumerable

in ethical, political, economic, and in part even ecclesiastical matters, some freedom of the will has been granted, by virtue of which he acts freely and contingently: so much so that the Apostle also names the righteousness of the Law the righteousness of the Flesh, for no other reason than that man, by the powers of Nature, can perform that external discipline of the Law in some way. Those famous monuments and deeds of the Gentiles confirm this very thing: indeed the entire νομοθεσία (legislation) of the Gentiles, likewise the constitution of empires: the use of which would be clearly nothing, unless man could freely and spontaneously either obey or resist those laws.

The third argument is borrowed by our Author from the previous next Article, arguing thus from a hypothesis: If God is not the cause of sin: it follows that not all things happen necessarily: and consequently, that there is contingency in the actions of men. For whatever follows from the consequent of a good consequence: follows also from the antecedent.

The fourth is supplied by reason itself. For if the will stands: the freedom of the will certainly also stands: for will and coercion mutually exclude each other. Now if the freedom of the will stands: contingency will certainly also stand: because by this being denied, the freedom of the will itself is also denied concerning things and actions to be freely sought or avoided: which if it be denied, nothing at all is left anymore that can distinguish man from the brutes: The reason is: Because where there is no freedom of the will, there can be no use of Reason there either.

The fifth argument the sounder philosophers gather not ineptly from the condition of Matter, from which all created things in this theater of the lower world consist. For if it is true, what the Philosopher has set forth (Book 7, Metaphysics), that Matter is the cause why a thing can be or not be, then Matter will certainly be the most certain and infallible argument for contingency in created things.

The sixth is clear from the testimony of our own senses. For these bear witness, as it were, from within, that they and their operations are not driven by some fatal necessity, but are exercised freely and contingently. Whence Scotus also not ineptly wrote in Book 1 of the Sentences, distinction 39, that he who denies contingency should be coerced by torments rather than by reason, and should be tortured until he concedes that it is possible for it to happen that he is no longer tortured.

The seventh and final argument is that of orthodox antiquity, which fought with great consensus against Stoic or absolute necessity: as can be seen especially in Augustine, who expressly took upon himself the task of refuting the opinion of the philosophers and especially of Cicero: that man had written in Book 5 of De Divinatione: Either God's foreknowledge must be denied and contingency granted: or, if God's foreknowledge is affirmed and granted, contingency or the freedom of the human will is removed: but if this is denied, the state of human affairs cannot stand. Therefore, it is better to deny God's foreknowledge than the contingency of human affairs.

Latin:

Θικονομία sive TRACTATIONIS dispositio.

DE Necessitate & Contingentiâ, tùm in genere rerum & actionum humanarum omnium: tùm in specie Peccati sive Mali, controversia inter doctos agitatur, non tàm vulgata & antiqua, quàm gravis etiam atque ardua: ita ut non Philosophorum tantùm Φροντιστήρια: Sed Theologorum etiam Scholæ, quæstionis kujus strepitu personent. Et profectò tanta ejus est gravitas, ut qui circa eam aberrat, non in fundamento tantùm: sed in ipso etiam Religionis

Christianae principio errare videatur. Lapsum enim primorum parentum, & consequenter Naturam Mali sive peccati, vix unquam satis cognitam perspectamque habebit: nedum certus esse poterit, causam peccati non in DEO, ullo pacto sive respectu; sed tantùm in voluntate humanâ, & eâ quidem liberâ, residere: nisi qui exploratissimum habuerit, Nùm rebus creatis & actionibus humanis fatalis aliqua dominetur necessitas: an verò aliqua earundem Contingentia dari possit & debeat?

Cujus sanè difficilis Quaestionis tractationem Autor noster, cum Articulo praecedente proximò ita conjungit, ut sub quadruplici consideratione eam expediat. Primùm enim τὸ εἰ ἔςi explicat, An videlicet detur Contingentia in humanis: deindè verò τὸ τί ἐςι, Quid nimirùm sit Contingentia illa, de quâ in Scholis Theologorum quaeritur? Tùm qua ejus vera ac propria causa constitui debeat? Et tandem quodnam proprium ejus sit subjectum?

Quarum Quaestionum ambitu cùm ea singula atque universa comprehendantur, quae inter Theologos de Contingentiâ discrepare possunt: iisdem nos utique insistentes vestigiis futuram Tractationem, nostrorum potissimùm temporum controversiis ita accommodabimus: ut tùm θέσιν, tùm ἀντίθεσιν pensi habuisse videri queamus.

QUAESTIO I.

NON in Philosophorum tantùm Gentilium Scholis, auditae jam olim fuerunt voces hae, desperatae impietatis plenae: Fata factum esse ut nemo sine vitiis nascatur: Et, Fato neminem innocentem fieri: Sed ipsa quoque Ecclesiae pomeria impietas isthaec ita invasit, ut non desint, qui omnium rerum atque eventuum humanorum, peccatorum cumprimis Necessitatem fatalem comminiscuntur, eandemque ad DEUM ipsum referre minimè verentur. Quam sanè opinionem hodiè furiosâ caecitate tuentur Sacramentarii, detortis in alienum sensum variis Scripturae testimoniis; uti diexodus insequens clariùs ostendet. Sic ergò ab istis hominibus omnis negata fuit hodiéque negatur Contingentia. Et profectò usque adeò plausibilis haec videtur esse sententia; ut in omnium fermè hominum animis, vi originalis corruptionis sedem fixisse videatur: quin apud renatos quoque, sub luctâ illâ graviore carnis & Spiritus, & sub intensiore afflictionum aestu errorum istorum nervi sese exerant. Quando enim enormem illam rerum omnium ἀταξίαν sive confusionem, quando stupendam inaequalitatem sortis piorum & impiorum: quando Ecclesiae persecutiones intuentur; fit plerumque, ut fatalis alicujus necessitatis cogitatio animos ipsorum percellat. Proindè non adiaphoricae libertatis, sed summae necessitatis fuerit, ut mens pia ex asse habeat cognitum ac perspectum, Non Fato quodam, sive absolutâ aliquâ necessitate omnia fieri: sed Contingentiam rerum & actionum humanarum omninò esse statuendam.

PRIMUM confirmationis argumentum est ἔγγραφον. Contingenter enim & liberè multa evenire scriptura satis dilucidè confirmat, idque locis fermè infinitis, quæ tamen ad quinque classes revocari possunt.

Prima classis ea continet scripturarum loca, quæ ἀυτολεξεὶ & secundum literam attestantur, quædam esse sita in liberrimâ hominis potestate, ut Genes. 4, 7. Sub te erit appetitus, & tu dominaberis illi. Actor. 5, 4. dicit Petrus ad Ananiam, Nonne in tuâ erat potestate vendere agrum?

Altera classis illis constat Scripturæ locis, quæ ostendunt, multa ab hominibus fieri ἑκουσίως sive voluntariè: ἑκούσιον verò sive spontaneum dicitur, cujus principium est in ipso agente, & sciente singulas actionis circumstantias: τὸ ἑκούσιον ἐστὶν ὅ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐν ἀυτῶ εἰδότι τὰ καθ’ ἕκαστα ἐν οἷς ἡ πρᾶξις. Huc pertinent loca isthæc: Exod. 35, 5. Omnis voluntariè & spontaneo animo offerat Domino. 1. Paral. 29, 9. Lætatus est populus, quòd sponte vota facerent. Luc. 9, 35 Qui voluerit animam suam servare, perdet eam.

Tertia classis ea continet loca, in quib9 homini datur optio, ut eligat quod volet. Deut. 30, 19. & 20. proposui hodiè vobis bonum & malum: Eligite ergò vitam, ut vivatis &c. Jos. 24, 15. Si malum vobis videtur, ut Domino serviatis, optio vobis datur: eligite hodiè, quod placet, cui servire potissimùm debeatis: Sic 2. Sam. 24, 12. Davidi datur optio, ut ex tribus pœnis eligat, quam velit. Sic 1. Reg. 3, 5. Jubetur Salomon à DEO petere, quod velit.

Quarta classis singula atque universa illa Scripturarum testimonia complectitur, quæ cófirmant, Hominem sæpissimè contra & præter DEI voluntatem aliquid facere, imò voluntati divinæ, volenter resistere: Quò pertinet tristis illa querela, Matth. 23, 37. Jerusalem, Jerusalem, quoties volui congregare filios tuos, quemadmodum gallina congregat pullos suos sub alas suas, & noluisti. Item Locus ille Hebr. 10, 26. de voluntariè peccantibus & resistentibus DEO.

Quinta & postrema classis constat illis scripturæ locis, quæ vel præcepta, vel consilia hominum actionibus præscribunt: vel facta hominum laudant aut vituperant: vel denique promissiones & comminationes divinas proponunt. Quæ sanè omnia, nisi homines in quibusdam liberè & contingenter agere possent, locum minimè invenirent. Nam si fatali, sive absolutâ, aut Stoicâ quadam necessitate Homo ad agendum impelleretur: Omnis profectò præmiorum promissio; omnis etiam pœnarum comminatio labesceret: siquidem promissio objecti loco respicit talem actionem, quam quis liberè & spontè facit: comminatio verò talem actionem, quam quis liberè omittere potuisset.

ALTERUM confirmationis argumentum mutuari possumus, ex subsequente Articulo proximo, de Libero arbitrio, ubi ad oculum de monstrabitur, Homini etiam post lapsum, innumera

Ethicis, Politicis, Oeconomicis, & ex parte Ecclesiasticis etiam, concessam esse aliquam voluntatis libertatem, cujus virtute liberè & contingenter agat: usque adeò ut Apostolus quoque Justitiam Legis, nominet Justitiam Carnis, non aliam magis ob causam, quàm quod Homo viribus Naturæ, externam illam disciplinam Legis, utcunque præstare potest. Confirmant hoc ipsum præclara illa Ethnicorum monumenta & facinora: imò universa νομοθεσία Gentilium, Item imperiorum constitutio: quorum usus planè foret nullus, nisi Homo liberè & spontè legibus illis vel parére, vel resistere posset.

TERTIUM argumentum mutuatur Autor noster, ex Articulo superiore proximo, sic ex hypothesi arguens: Si DEUS non est causa peccati: sequitur, non omnia necessariò fieri: & per consequens, dari in actionibus hominum contingentiam. Quicquid enim sequitur ad consequens bonæ consequentiæ: sequitur etiam ad Antecedens.

QUARTUM suppeditat ipsa ratio. Stante enim voluntate: stat utique etiam voluntatis libertas: Nam voluntas & coactio se mutuò excludunt. Jam si stat voluntatis libertas: utique stabit etiam contingentia: propterea quod hâc negatâ, negatur ipsa etiam voluntatis libertas circa res & actiones liberè vel expetendas, vel aversandas: Quæ si negetur, nihil profectò relinquitur ampliùs, quod Hominem à brutis discernere possit: Ratio est: Quia ubi voluntatis nulla est libertas, ibi nec Rationis usus aliquis esse potest.

QUINTUM argumentum Philosophi saniores haud ineptè colligunt ex conditione Materiæ, ex quâ creata omnia, in hoc inferioris mundi theatro consistunt. Nam si verum est, quod Philosophus prodidit (l. 7. Metaph.) Materiam causam esse, cur res esse, vel non esse possit utique Materia certissimum & infallibile erit argumentum contingentia in rebus creatis.

SEXTUM ipsorum sensuum nostrorum testimonio liquet. Hi enim intrinsecùs quasi testimonium perhibent, se suasque operationes non à fatali quadam necessitate impelli, sed liberè & contingenter exerceri, Undè haud ineptè Scotus etiam in lib. 1. Sent. dist. 39. scripsit, Eum qui negat Contingentiam, tormentis quàm ratione coërcendu, & tamdiu excruciandum esse, dùm concedat posse fieri, ut non ampliùs crucietur.

SEPTIMUM & postremum argumentum est orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, quæ contra Necessitatem stoicam sive absolutam, magno consensu pugnavit: uti cumprimis videre est apud Augustinum, qui ex professo philosophorum & cumprimis Ciceronis sententiam sibi refutandam sumsit: Scripserat iste lib. 5. de divin. Aut negandam esse Dei præscientiam: & concedendam contingentiam: aut affirmatâ & concessâ DEI præscientia, tolli cōtingentiam sive voluntatis humanæ libertatem: Jam verò hac negatâ, rerum humanarum statum consistere non posse. Ergò rectiùs negari DEI præscientiam, quàm rerum humanarum Contingentiam.


### Is Contingency possible?

Augustine refutes this opinion of the philosophers with many excellent arguments in book 5 of The City of God, writing thus among other things: While Cicero wishes us to be free in this way, he makes us sacrilegious. For to confess that GOD exists, and to deny that He has foreknowledge of future events, is the most manifest insanity. We in the Church, against these sacrilegious and impious daring men, say: both that GOD knows all things before they happen, and that we do by our will whatever we feel and know is done by us, not except by our willing it.

Others also support Augustine, such as Justin the Philosopher and Martyr in his 2nd Apology. Let no one, he says, think that we teach that all things happen by fatal necessity because they were foreseen and foretold in Scripture.

Irenaeus in book 4 refutes the opinion of Necessity through several chapters. Tertullian does the same thing in his entire 2nd book against Marcion.

Jerome in book 5 on Jeremiah: Man is not compelled by the foreknowledge of GOD, as if by necessity, either to do something or not to do it.

Chrysostom, Homily 60 on Matthew: GOD does not subject the life of men to necessity.

Antithesis.

This part of Christian doctrine has suffered open contradiction from many: so that a certain theologian (Hyperius in his place on providence) did not hesitate to write that contingency neither has a solid foundation in the Scriptures, nor has been approved by the Holy Fathers. However, almost all those testimonies are brought forward which most correctly fight against the powers of human free will in purely spiritual matters. Where even a novice in theology understands that a gross ignorance is being exposed. For the question is not, whether freedom of the will, and consequently contingency, is granted to man in spiritual matters: but the question is about natural, ethical, political, and economic actions, concerning which our will is properly occupied: whether some fatal necessity reigns in such actions, or rather contingency? Now, therefore, from the negation of one species, the consequence does not hold for the negation of either another or all the rest.

Then they bring forward that passage from Jeremiah 10:23: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not his own, nor is it in a man to direct his steps. If, therefore, not even the freedom of ways or steps is granted to man, how will the contingency of the remaining higher actions be given?

I answer that a twofold sophism is committed: one παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως [based on the figure of speech]: while the way and direction of steps is taken in a simple sense regarding locomotion, which in a figurative sense must be referred to the power of events. The other παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον [based on the non-sequitur]: for something else is inferred than what the logic of the consequence allows. For it is not a consequence if the power of events is not placed in the will of man: Therefore, there is clearly no freedom of choice in external things in the power of the human will. The Holy Spirit Himself revealed the opposite when He says in Proverbs 16:1 and 19: It is for man to prepare the heart, but it is the Lord's to govern the tongue; the heart of man disposes his way, but it is the Lord's to direct his steps. Where the Holy Spirit certainly expressly ascribes to the heart or will of man its own free disposition, namely in external actions concerning the preservation of this life, but assigns the government and direction of the same to GOD: which, however, by no means removes that freedom of the human will, as the following second Question will show. The proper and genuine sense of the prophetic saying is therefore: Although the counsels, deliberations, choices, and actions of men proceed from the freedom of the will, nevertheless, by reason of government and direction toward a certain event, they are subject to Divine providence, and this is evident from the fact that even things best deliberated often turn out worst, and even in good causes, the desired events do not always follow: and many unforeseen slips occur, which produce difficulties inexplicable to human counsels.

Finally, they rise up with this argument also: The nature of men is moved by GOD Himself: nor does it act otherwise than as it is moved by GOD: Therefore, the freedom of the will collapses, and consequently, all contingency. The reason for the connection is: Because GOD is Omnipotent, and no creature can resist His motion.

I answer, the argument fails by the sophism παρά τό πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς [based on the confusion of the qualified and the absolute]. For the reason of the connection is true in a qualified sense, if indeed it is posited that GOD uses His absolute power in the motion and sustenance of human nature. For thus the will of man would be snatched away by the force of immense omnipotence, so that no deliberation, no choice, and consequently, no freedom of the human will could escape that divine snatching or motion. But since the providence of GOD does not concur with the actions of men in this way, but, as Augustine speaks, administers, rules, and governs creatures in such a way that He allows them to perform and exercise their own motions: and leaves to them free the kind of power of acting that He once implanted in them: the reason for the connection certainly collapses of its own accord: as was shown more fully in the Article on Providence: and will be made clearer from the exposition of the following question.

Latin:

Quam Philosophi sententiam multis egregiis rationibus refutat Augustinus lib. 5. de Civit. DEI, sic inter reliqua scribens: Dum hoc modo Cicero nos liberos esse cupit, sacrilegos facit. Nam confiteri, DEUM esse, & negare prescium futurorum, apertissima insania est. Nos in Ecclesia contra istos sacrilegos & impios ausus dicimus: & DEUM omnia scire antequam fiant, & voluntate nos facere, quicquid a nobis, non nisi volentibus, fieri sentimus & novimus.

Augustino suffragantur & alii, ut Justinus Philosophus & Martyr Apol. 2. Ne quis, inquiens, existimet nos docere, ex fatali necessitate omnia fieri, quia prævisa & prædicta sunt in Scriptura.

Irenæus lib. 4. per aliquot capita Necessitatis opinionem refutat. Quod & ipsum præstat Tertullianus, toto libro 2. contra Marcionem.

Hieron. lib. 5. in Jerem. Non cogitur homo ex præscientia DEI, quasi necessitate vel facere quid, vel non facere.

Chryfost. Homil. 60. in Matth. DEUS non subjicit necessitati hominum vitam.

Ἀντίθεσις.

Passa est pars hæc doctrinæ Christianæ apertam contradictionem a multis: ita ut quidam Theologus (Hyperius in loco de provid.) scribere non dubitaverit. Contingentiam neque in Scripturis habere solidum fundamentum, neque a Sanctis Patribus esse approbatam. Proferuntur autem ea ferme testimonia omnia, quæ contra arbitrii humani vires in rebus merè Spiritualibo rectissime pugnant. Ubi crassam committi ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχου, vel Tyro Theologiæ intelligit. Neq; enim quæstio est, Num Homini in rebus Spiritualibus concessa sit voluntatis libertas, & per consequens, Contingentia: sed de actionibus Naturalibus, Ethicis, Politicis, Oeconomicis, circa quas voluntas nostra propriè versatur, est Quæstio: An in hujusmodi actionibus regnet fatalis aliqua Necessitas: an vero contingentia? Jam ergo ex negatione unius speciei, ad negationem vel alterius, vel reliquarum omnium, non valet consequentia.

Deinde proferunt locum illum Jerem. 10, 23. Scio Domine, quod non est Hominis via ejus, nec est viri dirigere gressus suos. Si ergo ne viarum quidem aut gressuum libertas homini est concessa, quomodo reliquarum superiorum actionum dabitur contingentia?

Respondeo, geminum committi σοφισλογισμὸν: unum παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως: dum via & directio gressuum, simplici sensu de locomotiva accipitur, quæ figurato sensu ad potestatem eventuum referenda est. Alterum παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον: Aliud enim infertur, quam quod Consequentiæ ratio patitur. Neque enim Consequens est, si eventuum potestas non est in voluntate hominis posita: Ergo plane nullum Electionis arbitrium in rebus externis est penes voluntatem Hominis. Diversum prodidit ipse Spiritus Sanctus cùm Proverb. 16, 1. & 19. inquit: Hominis est, cor præparare: sed Domini est, lingvam gubernare: Cor hominis disponit viam suam: sed Domini est, dirigere gressus ejus. Ubi certè cordi sive voluntati Hominis, suam dispositionem liberam expressè adscribit Spiritus Sanctus, in actionibus scilicet externis, vitæ hujus conservationem concernentibus: DEO autem adsignat earundem gubernationem & directionem: quæ tamen libertatem illam voluntatis humanæ minimè tollit: uti subsequens Quæstio secunda ostendet. Sensus ergò dicti prophetici proprius & genuinus est: Licèt consilia, Deliberationes, Electiones, & actiones hominum proficiscantur à libertate voluntatis, nihilominus tamen ratione gubernationis, & directionis ad certum eventum, subjacere eas Divinæ providentiæ, idque vel indè patescere, quòd sæpiùs optimè etiam deliberata pessimè cadunt, & in bonis etiam causis, optati eventus non semper respondent: & multi lapsus improvisi accidunt, qui pariunt difficultates inexplicabiles consiliis humanis.

Tandem hoc etiam argumento insurgunt: Natura hominum movetur à DEO ipso: neq́; aliter agit, quàm sicut à DEO movetur: Ergò corruit voluntatis libertas, & per consequens, omnis Contingentia. Ratio connexi est: Quia DEUS est Omnipotens, & ipsius motui nulla creatura potest resistere.

Respondeo, Fallit argumentum Sophismate παρά τό πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Secundum quid enim Ratio connexi vera est, si nimirùm statuatur DEUS absolutâ suâ potentiâ in motu & sustentatione Naturæ humanæ uti. Sic enim voluntas Hominis raperetur vi immensæ omnipotentiæ, ita ut istum raptum sive motum divinum, nulla deliberatio, nulla electio, ac per consequens, Nulla libertas voluntatis humanæ possit effugere. Cæterùm cùm hoc modo DEI providentia, ad actiones hominum non concurrat: sed ea, ut Augustinus loquitur, ita administret, regat & gubernet creaturas, ut eas proprios motus agere & exercere sinat: & qualem ipsis agendi vim semel indidit, eam illis liberam relinquat: utique ratio connexi suâ sponte corruit: uti in Articulo de Providentiâ fusiùs est ostensum: & ex subsequentis quæstionis diexodo patebit luculentiùs.


### Question concerning what it is

The common herd of men, and the unlearned crowd of those who philosophize, very ignorantly confuse Contingency with Chance and Fortune, as if they were synonyms and equipollent: when nevertheless they differ greatly from one another. For Chance, as defined by the sounder philosophers, is nothing other than an accidental cause of those things which are not undertaken by a certain προαίρεσις [choice] or counsel: Just as Fortune is also an accidental cause of those things which rarely happen: but by itself and by its own force it is the cause of nothing: For although there may perhaps be certain hidden causes which fortuitous events follow: those are nevertheless not known to us: and therefore we call them Fortune, not because we attribute any force to Fortune: but because the true and proper cause is not known to us.

Whence also Cicero, book 1 of the Academic Questions, writes not ineptly: It is called Fortune, on account of the obscurity and ignorance of the other four causes.

Furthermore, Fortune and Chance are παρὰ λογόν τι, something alien to reason: a thing which, as is clear from the preceding, cannot be affirmed of Contingency. For Contingency belongs to those things which right reason, with choice or counsel, either performs or avoids. But this reason is concerned with those things which are accustomed to happen either always or for the most part: Fortune, however, with those things which happen very rarely, indeed beyond all hope and will.

Then it would be a crime to leave any place for Chance and Fortune in the Church of GOD. For since all things, the least and the greatest, are subject to divine providence, so that not even lots cast into the lap, which seem most fortuitous, escape his governance, as Solomon testifies, Prov. 16:33, surely nothing can be or be called casual or fortuitous.

Finally, Chance and Fortune exclude the Providence of GOD: Contingency, however, establishes and confirms it: a thing which we shall demonstrate presently, if we first show what Contingency is.

This definition can be established most correctly if we look to the cause and source of Contingency, which is none other than the Liberty of the will. This being established, a Contingent, or τὸ ἐνδεχόμενον, is not incongruously defined as that which, while it exists, is neither impossible nor necessary: but has a cause which could have acted otherwise by its own nature: such as the will of men, or, as others define it with words slightly changed but the same sense: A Contingent is that which by its own nature can either be or not be, and which can be or not be in this or another way: or that which can happen and not happen: And before it happens, it can be prevented from happening: but when it does exist, it has a cause which by its own nature could have acted otherwise, and whose contradictory would not be impossible. For example, the Fall of the first parents was a contingent event: because by its own nature it could either be or not be: that is, it was placed in the judgment of their own will whether to sin or not to sin: And after they had already actually sinned, there was nevertheless a cause which by its own nature could have acted otherwise: namely, the rectitude of all the powers of body and soul: and the right use of the free will granted as much to evil as to good. Thus the betrayal of Judas was a contingent event: for Judas could have abstained from that crime and not betrayed his Master: so that after he had already actually betrayed him, there was nevertheless a cause in him which by its own nature could have acted otherwise, that is, could have refrained from that deed.

This part of Christian doctrine is a stone of stumbling, against which very many today, and especially those of the Calvinist persuasion, strike themselves most dangerously. To counter this evil, it is my pleasure to divide the entire discussion, which is moved against the proposed definition of Contingency, into distinct Questions, and to treat each one separately.

And at the beginning, indeed, it is asked: How can Contingency, such as it has now been defined, stand with the eternal and infallible foreknowledge, or rather Omniscience, of GOD? For it is argued thus: Whatever things are foreknown by GOD, those cannot happen otherwise than as they are foreknown. But all things that are and happen are foreknown by GOD: and indeed foreknown in the way in which they happen. Therefore, they cannot happen otherwise: and consequently, either the Contingency of human things and actions must be denied: or, if this is granted, the eternal, universal, and infallible foreknowledge of GOD collapses.

I answer: The argument fails, 1. By the sophism of a vicious definition of divine Foreknowledge, which is imagined to bring some necessity to things foreknown, or certainly that things are foreknown by GOD in such a certain way that they can no longer, by any necessity, happen otherwise: neither of which conforms to the truth. For as each thing is by its own nature, and how it is also going to happen from itself, such is it foreseen or foreknown by GOD: so that this Foreknowledge depends upon the event: but the event does not depend upon the foreknowledge. For, as we noted above from Augustine, GOD administers all created things in such a way that he allows them to exercise their own proper motions. And as St. Jerome skillfully infers, book 3 in Ezechiel, The foreknowledge of future things does not make it immutable that GOD knows it will be: for it is not because GOD knows future things that it is necessary for us to do what he has foreknown: but because we are going to do it by our own will, he knows it will be. Thus, therefore, an eclipse of the Sun or Moon does not occur because it is foreknown and predicted by a mathematician a long time before: but, since it was going to happen nonetheless from its own natural causes even if no mathematician were foreknowing or predicting it: so that which GOD has foreknown or foreseen is not immutable, nor does it happen by fatal necessity, because He has foreknown or foreseen it: But because the will of man is not changed, acting freely in this or that way. For if this will were going to change itself, and had acted otherwise, GOD would certainly have foreknown this very thing: So that this foreknowledge follows the nature of the thing foreknown: or, as Augustine speaks in book 3 of On Free Choice, chapter 3, it acts upon itself, not upon another, nor does it perfect any thing outside of itself. With these things observed, it follows of necessity that the freedom of the human will, which we have said is the source and cause of contingency, does not abolish the foreknowledge of GOD: nor does the latter abolish the former: But that both can stand together, without any contradiction.

Furthermore, this argument fails through the confusion of disparate questions, which must be most accurately distinguished from one another. For it is one thing when I say that something is immutable, or happens necessarily, with respect to divine foreknowledge: but it is another thing when I say that a thing is immutable on account of the foreknowledge of GOD: or, which is the same thing, that foreknowledge brings necessity to the things foreknown. The former is asserted orthodoxly: the latter is not. Since this latter expression expresses a cause, on account of which a thing cannot be otherwise than it is:

The former, however, denotes only the truth and certainty of divine foreknowledge: and it intends nothing else than that GOD, being omniscient, knows from all eternity what outcome each thing is going to have. In this respect it is rightly said that things foreknown happen in the way they are foreknown, not causally with respect to foreknowledge: as if this made the foreknown things happen in this and no other way: but only conditionally, insofar as GOD did not foreknow things otherwise than as they are going to happen from their own proper causes and indeed freely. Now therefore, when some thing happens in this way, it is rightly said, when it could not have happened in another way, with respect to divine foreknowledge: according to the common rule: Everything that is, when it is, necessarily is. I see Peter limping: while I see this, it is necessarily the case that the matter is so, because vision is not deceived: and because that limping is in act, it certainly cannot be said not to be: but it is necessary that it be: Nevertheless, Peter is not to be said to limp because I see him limping: for by my vision he is neither impelled, nor is a necessity of limping imposed upon him, seeing that he would have been about to limp, not being seen by me: and he could have not limped, if his proper and natural cause had been otherwise: which, however, if it had been otherwise, I too would have seen this very thing, and not something different. In exactly the same way, although it is true that we do nothing of those things which GOD has not foreknown: yet this foreknowledge of GOD is not the cause of those actions. For those things could have been done by us otherwise, if their principle, upon which they depend, is considered. Nor, however, would the foreknowledge of GOD be deceived: For if they were going to be otherwise than they happen, GOD, to whom, speaking properly, nothing is future or past: but all things are most present, would have foreseen this very thing also: since human actions do not depend on foreknowledge, but rather foreknowledge depends on them.

The third sophism is that of vicious opposition.
