For the certainty of divine foreknowledge and the contingency of foreknown things cannot nor ought they to be opposed to one another contradictorily; since they relate to each other ὑπαλλήλως or subordinately: a fact which even the Scholastic Doctors have proved by this Syllogistic reasoning.

Whatever can objectively terminate the act of infallible divine foreknowledge: that is not removed by the certainty of divine foreknowledge.

But the contingency of future effects can objectively terminate the act of infallible divine foreknowledge.

Therefore, contingency is not removed by the certainty of divine foreknowledge.

The truth of the major premise is most clearly evident by the consensus and judgment of all who philosophize correctly, since between any Act and that which can be the object of that Act, there is always a certain ἁρμονία or congruence.

The minor premise is proved by the Scholastics and Metaphysicians thus: Whatever, with the consideration of any cognition removed, and with the reasons of the things themselves viewed in themselves, is in itself a possible Being, implying no contradiction: That can be an object of certain cognition or science, especially divine: since every Being is an object of the intellect.

Latin:

Vulgus hominum, & indocta Philosophantium turba, Contingentiam cum Casu & Fortunâ, admodùm inscitè confundit: ac si essent Synonyma, & Æquipollentia: cùm tamen plurimùm à se mutuò differant. Casus enim sanioribus definientibus Philosophis, nihil est aliud quàm Causa per accidens eorum, quæ certâ προαιρέσει sive consilio non suscipiuntur: Quemadmodum Fortuna etiam est causa per accidens earum rerum quæ rarò eveniunt: per se autem suâquè vi nullius rei est causa: Nam licèt fortassis occultæ quædam sint causæ, quas sequuntur fortuiti eventus: illæ tamen nobis notæ non sunt: ideoq́; eas Fortunam appellamus, non quòd aliquam vim Fortunæ tribuamus: sed quòd vera & propria causa nobis cognita non est.

Unde & Cicero lib. 1. Acad. quaest. haud inepte scribit: Fortuna appellatur, propter obscuritatem, ignorationemque caeterarum quatuor causarum.

Deinde Fortuna & Casus sunt παρὰ λογόν τι, a ratione quiddam alienum: id quod de Contingentia, uti ex praecedentibus patet, affirmari nequit. Siquidem Contingentia est earum rerum, quas recta ratio cum electione sive consilio, vel agit, vel aversatur. Haec vero ratio versatur in iis, quae vel semper, vel plerumque eodem modo evenire solent: Fortuna autem in illis, quae rarissime, imo praeter omnem spem ac voluntatem accidunt.

Tum nefas fuerit Casui & Fortunae in Ecclesia DEI locum aliquem relinquere. Nam cum divinae providentiae omnia, minima, maxima, subjaceant, adeo ut ne sortes quidem in sinum missae, quae vel maxime videntur fortuitae, ejus gubernationem effugiant, Salomone teste, Prov. 16, 33. utique nihil casuale, nihil fortuitum esse aut dici potest.

Tandem Casus & Fortuna excludunt DEI Providentiam: Contingentia vero eandem stabilit & confirmat: id quod mox demonstrabimus, si prius, Quid sit Contingentia, ostenderimus.

Rectissime autem Definitio haec poterit constitui, si ad causam atque fontem Contingentiae, qui non est alius, quam Libertas voluntatis, respexerimus. Quo stante haud incongrue Contingens, sive τὸ ἐνδεχόμενον definitur esse id, quod cum sit, nec impossibile, neque necessarium est: sed habet causam, quae poterat ex natura sua aliter agere: ut est voluntas hominum, vel, ut alii verbis paululum mutatis, sensu tamen eodem, definiunt: Contingens est, quod natura sua vel esse, vel non esse potest, quodque vel hoc vel alio modo se habere: vel quod fieri, & non fieri potest: Et priusquam fit, impediri potest, ne fiat: cum vero sit, causam habet, quae sua natura aliter agere poterat, & cujus contradictoria non esset impossibilis. Exempli gratia, Lapsus protoplastorum fuit eventus contingens: quia Natura sua vel esse, vel non esse poterat: hoc est, in arbitrio voluntatis ipsorum erat positum, vel peccare, vel non peccare: Et postquam jam actu peccarunt, causa tamen erat, quae sua natura aliter agere poterat: nempe Rectitudo omnium virium corporis & animae: & rectus usus concessi liberi arbitrii tam ad malum, quam ad bonum. Sic proditio Judae fuit eventus contingens: poterat enim Judas abstinere a facinore isto, & non prodere Magistrum: ita, ut postquam jam actu prodidit, causa tamen in ipso fuerit, quae sua natura aliter agere, hoc est, se a facto isto continere poterat.

Est pars haec doctrinae Christianae lapis offensionis, ad quem plurimi hodie, & cumprimis ex gente Calviniana, periculose admodum impingunt. Cui malo ut obviam eatur, placet universam disputationem, quae adversus propositam Contingentiae definitionem movetur, in distinctas Quaestiones dispescere, & seorsim singulas pertractare.

Ac initiò quidem quæritur, Quomodo Contingentia, qualis jam definita est, cum æterna & infallibili DEI præscientiâ, vel potiùs Omniscientiâ stare possit? Sic enim arguitur: Quæcunquè à DEO sunt præscita, illa non possunt aliter evenire quàm prout sunt præscita. Atqui omnia, quæ sunt & fiunt, à DEO sunt præscita: & eo quidem modo præscita, quo eveniunt. Ergò, aliter etiam illa evenire non possunt: & per consequens, vel neganda est rerum & actionum humanarum Contingentia: vel hâc concessâ corruit æterna, universalis & infallibilis DEI præscientia.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum, 1. Sophismate vitiosæ definitionis Præscientiæ divinæ, quæ fingitur rebus præscitis aliquam inferre necessitatem, vel certè, res ita certo modo à DEO præscitas esse, ut jam ex necessitate quapiam aliter fieri nequeant: Quorum neutrum cum veritate consonat. Nam qualis quæque res sua natura est, & quomodo etiam ex se eventura est, talis prævidetur sive præscitur à DEO: ita ut Præscientia hæc pendeat ab eventu: eventus verò non pendeat è præscientiâ. Siquidem, uti supra ex Augustino annotavimus, creata omnia sic administrat DEUS, ut ipsa proprios suos motus exercere sinat. Et ut D. Hieronymus scitè infert, lib. 3. in Ezech. Præscientia futurorum, non immutabile facit, quòd DEUS futurum novit: non enim quia DEUS futura cognoscit, necesse est nos facere, quod ille præscivit: sed quod nos propriâ voluntate facturi sumus, ille novit futurum. Sic ergò non ideò Eclipsis Solis aut Lunæ fit, quia à Mathematico longo tempore antè præscitur & prædicitur: sed, quippè quæ nemine etiam Mathematicorum vel præsciente vel prædicente nihilominùs ex suis causis naturalibus eventura erat: ita non immutabile est, vel fatali necessitate fit, quod præscivit aut prævidit DEUS, quia nimirùm præscivit aut prævidit: Sed quia non mutatur voluntas Hominis, liberè hoc vel illud agens. Hæc enim si se mutatura fuisset, & aliter egisset, DEUS utique hoc ipsum præscivisset: Ita ut præscientia hæc sequatur naturam rei præscitæ: vel, ut Augustinus lib. 3. de lib. arb. cap. 3. loquitur, agat in se, non in alio, neque rem ullam extra semetipsam perficiat. Quibus observatis ἐξ ἀνάγκης sequitur, Libertatem voluntatis humanæ, quam Contingentiæ fontem & causam esse diximus, non tollere præscientiam DEI: neque hanc illam: Sed simul utramque stare posse, sine ullâ ἀντιφάσει, sive contradictione.

Deindè fallit hoc argumentum confusione disparatarum quæstionum, quæ à se mutuò accuratissimè sunt discernendæ. Aliud enim est, quando dico, Præscientiæ divinæ respectu aliquid esse immutabile, aut fieri necessariò: Aliud verò est, quando dico, Rem esse immutabilem propter Præscientiam DEI: vel quod idem est, Præscientiam rebus præscitis afferre necessitatem. Prius illud Orthodoxè asseritur: Posterius hoc non item. : Siquidem posterior hæc locutio, causam exprimit, propter quá res aliter se habere nequeat:

Prior verò illa veritatem tantùm & certitudinem divinæ præscientiæ notat: neque quicquam vult aliud, quàm DEUM, quippè omnifcium, jam indè ab omni æternitate scire qualem quæque res eventum sit habitura. Quo respectu rectè dicitur, Res præscitas eo modo evenire, quo præscitæ sunt, non causaliter respectu præscientiæ: quasi hæc res præscitas hoc & non alio modo evenire faciat: sed tantùm conditionaliter, quatenùs DEUS non aliter res præscivit, quàm prout ex causis suis propriis & quidem liberè sunt eventuræ. Jam ergò, quando res aliqua hoc modo fit, rectè dicitur, quando alio modo fieri non potuerit, respectu divinæ præscientiæ: secundum vulgatam regulam: Omne quod est, quando est, cùm esse necesse est. Exemplo res hæc iterum illustrari potest. Video claudicare Petrum: id dùm video, necessum utique est, rem ita se habere, quia visio non fallitur: & quia Claudicatio illa in actu est, certè non potest dici non esse: sed necessum est esse: Veruntamen Petrus non proptereà dicendus est claudicare, quia ego illum claudicare video: Visione enim meâ nec impellitur ille, nec necessitas claudicandi ei imponitur, quippè qui claudicaturus esset, à me non visus: & poterat non claudicare, si aliter se haberet causa propria & naturalis: quæ tamen si aliter se fuisset habitura, hoc ipsum ego quoque, & non diversum visurus fuissem. Eodem planè modo, etsi verum est nihil nos facere eorum, quæ DEUS non præsciverit: tamen hæc præscientia DEI, actionum istarum non est causa. Poterant enim aliter illa à nobis fieri, si earum principium spectetur, à quo dependent. Neq; tamen falleretur præscientia DEI: Si enim aliter futuræ fuissent, quàm fiunt, utique DEUS, cui propriè loquendo, nihil est futurum aut præteritum: sed omnia præsentissima, hoc ipsum quoque prævidisset: cùm non prævisione actiones humanæ, sed ab his potiùs illa dependeat.

Tertium Sophisma est vitiosæ oppositionis. Neque enim vel possunt aut debent contradictoriè sibi invicem opponi, Præscientiæ divinæ certitudo, & rerum præscitarum contingentia: Siquidem ad se mutuò se habent ὑπαλλήλως sive subordinatè: id quod Doctores etiam Scholastici hâc ratione Syllogisticâ probârunt.

Quicquid objectivè potest terminare actum infallibilis divinæ præscientiæ: illud non tollitur à certitudine divinæ præscientiæ.

Atqui effectuum futurorum contingentia potest objectivè terminare actum infallibilis divinæ præscientiæ.

Ergò contingentia non tollitur à certitudine divinæ præscientiæ.

Majoris veritas omnium rectè Philosophantium consensu atque judicio liquidissimè patet Siquidem inter Actum aliquem, & inter id quod esse potest objectum illius Actus, semper certa quædam est ἁρμονία sive congruentia.

Minor à Scholasticis & Metaphysicis sic probatur: Quicquid remotâ consideratione cujuscúque cognitionis: & spectatis per se ipsarum rerum rationibus, per se est Ens possibile, nullam contradictionem implicans: Illud potest objectum certae cognitionis sive scientiae, cumprimis divinae: Siquidem omne Ens est objectum intellectus.


### Question concerning what it is (continued)

Now since such is the condition of future effects, that they proceed indeed from their cause, but in such a way that they can also not proceed, either because the cause can be hindered, or because it is indifferent toward either side: certainly those future effects are such a thing, which in itself, the reasons of the things themselves being viewed, is in the latitude of possible Being: and indeed without any contradiction or repugnance: in this sense; that just as that is possible in the present: so also it is possible in the future: since everything that is at some time present, is also at some time future.

Therefore, since this account of the contingency of effects is possible in itself, not only in the present but also in the future: it will certainly be able, just as in the present so also in the future, to terminate objectively the infallible divine cognition or knowledge: and consequently, through the infallibility of this divine knowledge, the contingency of things will not be removed.

Augustine expressed this argument of the Scholastics skillfully and clearly enough, in book 3 of On Free Choice, chapter 4, in these words: It does not follow that if the order of all causes is certain to God, there is nothing in the arbitration of our will: For our very wills themselves are in the order of causes, which is a certain order. And thus, he who foreknew all the causes of things, certainly could not have been ignorant of our wills among those causes, which he foreknew to be the causes of our actions.

Two things are chiefly objected to this triple response of ours: First, that there is a very great dissimilarity between divine and human foreknowledge. Therefore, one cannot be judged from the other.

Then, that it is clearly absurd if it is said that the event of things does not depend on foreknowledge, but rather the latter depends on the former: because in this way, the event of temporal things is established as the cause of the eternal foreknowledge of God: or at least it is conceded that there is something in God which depends on something outside of God.

I respond that the first objection suffers from the fallacy of ωδὲ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For no reason of consequence holds in this argument: divine and human foreknowledge differ from each other greatly. Therefore, divine foreknowledge removes the contingency of things: or, therefore, no judgment at all can be made about divine foreknowledge from human. For at the beginning we willingly concede that discrepancy: since it cannot be denied. 1. That human foreknowledge, drawn from the collection of individual things, grows and increases day by day: but the Divine, by a most pure and most perfect act of intelligence, having all things most present to itself from eternity, knows them in itself and from itself. 2. That human foreknowledge is in man as an accident in its subject: but in God it is essential, and is most simply convertible with the very essence of God: so that foreknowledge is predicated of God only improperly and κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν: since in Him it is rather the most pure and perpetual act of omniscience. 3. that human foreknowledge is imperfect regarding a few things: but Divine foreknowledge is most perfect regarding all things: 4. that finally human foreknowledge is not rarely concerned with those things which a man, unwilling and reluctant, more often even compelled, finds it necessary to permit: but Divine foreknowledge is subject to no violence or coercion whatsoever. These, even if there are other kinds of differences, we by no means deny: but that the consequence which is inferred can be elicited from thence: that we deny again and again. For however perfect, or self-sufficient, the foreknowledge of GOD may be: it by no means follows from that, that from it (except for mere knowledge) any necessity or any other affection accrues to the things foreknown: so that on account of the foreknowledge of GOD they must needs happen in this or that way. Since indeed neither the ancient nor the more recent Stoic Theologians have hitherto provided proof for this Consequence, it is manifest that they are shamefully begging the question. We rather conclude invincibly thus: Since Divine foreknowledge brings no more necessity to things foreknown than human foreknowledge does: Therefore, regarding the present question, a judgment can most correctly be made from the latter concerning the former.

The latter objection labors under the same sophistries. For even if the foreknowledge of GOD, or rather omniscience, established in a certain perpetual now of eternity, has all things, sequestered from all concretion of matter and intervals of time, most present to itself: and consequently is never perfected by the condition of time: it by no means follows, however, what the argument intends: namely, that things foreknown obtain their events not from their own nature and from a proximate free cause: but from the foreknowledge of GOD. For that this is false can be demonstrated by a twofold reason. For first, in this way the foreknowledge of GOD, considered in itself, is most shamefully confused with the limitation of foreknowledge: which two things, however, ought to be most accurately distinguished from each other. For Foreknowledge itself, considered in itself, is nothing other than the very Omniscience of GOD, most perfect in itself and from itself, and always consistent with itself equally and without any imperfection, even if there were no things created at all. And it is simply denied that this depends on the condition of the things foreknown. But regarding the limitation of foreknowledge, in respect of which GOD foreknows or foresees that things will happen in the way in which, placed outside in the state of their mutability, they happen from a free and mutable cause: certainly hardly anyone would be so absurd as to dare to deny that this limitation proceeds from the condition of the things foreknown: and that in this respect foreknowledge depends on the things foreknown. Nor is there any reason for anyone to fear that from this limitation any mutability redounds to the foreknowledge of GOD itself considered in itself. For this, being simply devoid of all mutability, however things may fall out, sees them plainly immutably: since GOD cannot but know and see all things, in whatever way they may eventually happen.

The posterior reason, by which we demonstrate the vanity of this objection, can be such: All knowledge and foreknowledge is of the genus of those things which without

are called Relatives, and always obtain some relation to one another, that is, they are always referred to another: so that the things foreknown obtain the respect and nature of the Foundation in that Relation. Therefore, either the very Order of Nature, which is in the Foundation and the Term of the Relation, would have to be inverted: or that for which the Church of GOD fights must be conceded, namely, that things do not happen because they are foreknown by GOD: but because they are to happen by the power of their own causes, therefore they are predicted, foreknown, and foreseen: that is, that foreknowledge depends on the things foreknown, not these on that.

Nor is this assertion of ours destitute of the consensus of Orthodox Antiquity: For thus Justin the Philosopher and Martyr, Response 58 to the Orthodox: Foreknowledge is not the cause of that which is to be: But that which is to be is the cause of Foreknowledge: Since indeed the Future does not follow foreknowledge: But the Future follows foreknowledge. Augustine also supports this, lib. 3 de lib. arb. c. 4: Just as your memory does not force things that have passed to have been done: So GOD by his foreknowledge does not force things that are to be to be done.

But let it suffice to have said these things concerning foreknowledge and its affection toward the contingency of human affairs.

II. In the second place, a question of no less importance is raised concerning the eternal providence of GOD. For since this is occupied not only with a bare knowledge of all things and actions, but at the same time concurs in their efficacious governance, it is asked whether and how, while the providence of GOD remains intact, the contingency of things and human actions can stand: Hence this argument has arisen: All things are subject to divine providence: Therefore no place is left for contingency. Likewise: There is nothing fortuitous: Therefore, no contingency.

I answer that the first objection fails by the fallacy of the consequent (τῷ μὴ ἑπομένῳ). For providence and contingency are most viciously opposed as if they were contradictorily opposed or contrary, when they relate to each other as subordinate, since contingency is substrated or subordinate to divine providence, so that neither hinders nor removes the other: as will be demonstrated presently. Furthermore, it involves at the same time the sophistry of taking what is said in a certain respect as said simply (καθόλου πρὸς τί καὶ ἁπλῶς). For it is not simply and absolutely, but in a certain respect true, which is hidden in that argument, namely that with respect to divine providence all things happen necessarily. In a certain respect, I say, this is true, namely with respect to the same cause. But here there is a diversity of causes. For providence, as also foreknowledge, is proper to the first and universal cause. But the contingency of actions is properly referred to secondary and singular causes. Hence it happens that one and the same action, one and the same event, can be called both necessary and contingent: Necessary indeed, when it is referred to divine providence, which cannot be deceived: But contingent, when it is weighed from its own nature, or from its own and proximate cause, which is the free will of man. But what kind of necessity is to be established with respect to divine providence, and whether it also contradicts contingency, will be clear from what follows.

The latter objection suffers from the fallacy τῆς μεταβάσεως (of shifting the category). For it posits that the Fortuitous and the Contingent are so related to each other that if one is denied, the other is immediately denied: although, however, Fortune and Contingency are contained under clearly different genera: as was shown at the beginning of this second Question. "But as regards the proposed Question," it is most correctly answered, "that the contingency of things and human actions can most correctly stand with the providence of GOD safe and unshaken, because (as has already been said) this contingency is not opposed to divine Providence, but is placed under or subordinated to it. For just as the Providence of GOD governs and determines individual and universal things: so it also governs and determines contingent actions. For hence it happens that GOD does not suffer the impious to rush where they otherwise tend by their own free will: but sets limits, up to which He will loosen the reins on their lust." Hence also, not rarely, GOD, by the power of His providence, casts and places bonds and barriers upon the impious, so that they are compelled to desist entirely from their undertakings, and clearly to omit what their unbridled lust would otherwise have perpetrated. Examples can be Esau, the brother of Jacob, who had formed a plan to kill his brother: Balaam, who with full intention of mind had already prepared himself for a journey to curse the Israelite people: Ahithophel, who had already made a decree about casting David out of the kingdom: But these individual designs, as well as very many others of that kind of the impious, GOD timely repressed, broke, and thwarted. But suppose nothing of the sort happens sometimes, but GOD suffers to be done what the will of the impious decrees: nevertheless, even from that, the singular artifice of divine providence shines forth, while from that very thing He takes the material for inflicting deserved punishments upon the impious and for overturning them: or He knows how to turn even the worst counsels into the inconveniences and salvation of the pious: Of which matter the history of Joseph and the Passion of Christ supply the most illustrious examples by far. But some rise up higher, arguing: The order of divine Providence is most certain. Therefore, contingency has no place.

Latin:

Jam cum futurorum Effectuum ea sit conditio, ut procedant quidem ex sua causa, sed ita, ut possint etiam non procedere, vel quia causa impediri potest, vel quia indifferenter ea se habet ad utrumlibet: utique Effectus illi futuri sunt talis res, quae per se, spectatis ipsarum rerum rationibus, sit in latitudine Entis possibilis: & quidem sine ulla contradictione sive repugnantia: hoc sensu; ut quemadmodum istud in praesenti est possibile: ita etiam in futuro sit possibile: Siquidem omne id, quod est aliquando praesens, etiam aliquando futurum.

Ergo, cum ista ratio contingentiae Effectuum sit possibilis per se, non solum in praesenti, sed etiam in futuro: utique poterit etiam, uti in praesenti sic etiam in futuro terminare objective infallibilem divinam cognitionem sive scientiam: & per consequens per infallibilitatem divinae hujus scientiae, non tolletur reru contingentia.

Argumentum hoc Scholasticorum dextre & perspicue satis expressit Augustinus, lib. 3. de lib. arb. cap. 4. his verbis: Non est consequens ut si DEO certus est ordo omnium causarum, nihil sit in nostrae voluntatis arbitrio: Et ipsa quippe nostrae voluntates, in causarum ordine sunt, qui certus est ordo. Atq; ita qui omnes rerum causas praescivit, profecto in eis causis, nostras etiam voluntates ignorare non potuit, quas nostrarum actionum causas esse praescivit.

Triplici huic responsioni nostrae duo potissimum objiciuntur: Primum Maximam esse dissimilitudinem inter praescientiam divinam & humanam. Ergo ex hac de illa judicari posse.

Deinde absurdum plane esse, si dicatur, quod rerum eventus non a Praescientia: sed haec potius ab illis dependeat: propterea quod hoc pacto, rerum temporalium eventus, causa statuatur aeternae DEI praescientiae: vel saltem in DEO concedatur esse aliquid, quod ab aliquo extra DEUM dependeat.

Respondeo, Prius objectum laborare Sophisticatione ωδὲ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Non enim ulla militat ratio Consequentiae in hoc argumento: praescientia divina & humana & se mutuo plurimum discrepant. Ergo praescientia divina tollit rerum contingentiam: vel, Ergo de praescientia divina, ex humana plane nullum potest fieri judicium. Nam initio discrepantiam illam libenter concedimus: siquidem negari non potest. 1. quod humana praescientia ex collectione rerum singularium hausta indies crescit & augescit: Divina vero purissimo & perfectissimo intelligentiae actu, omnia sibi ab aeterno habens praesentissima, in seipsa & a seipsa cognoscit. 2. quod praescientia humana est in Homine tanquam Accidens in suo subjecto: In DEO vero Essentialis est, & cum ipsa Essentia DEI simplicissime convertitur: ita ut improprie & κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν tantum de DEO praedicetur praescientia: Cum in ipso potius sit, purissimus & perpetuus Omniscientiæ actus. 3. quod Humana præscientia est de paucis imperfecta: Divina verò est de omnibus perfectissima: 4. quod denique Humana præscientia haud rarò versatur circa ea, quæ Homo nolens & invitus, sæpius etiam coactus permittere necesse habet: Divina verò nulli prorsus violentiæ aut coactioni est obnoxia. Hæc, etsi quæ alia sunt differentiarum genera, minimè negamus: atqui indè consequens illud elici posse, quod infertur: illud iterum atque iterum negamus. Quantumvis enim perfecta, sive ἀυτοτελὴς DEI sit præscientia: minimè tamen indè sequitur, quod ex illâ rebus præscitis (exceptâ solâ notitiâ) quicquam vel necessitatis, vel alius alicujus affectionis obtingat: ut propter DEI præscientiam hoc vel illo modo evenire necesse habeant. Quod sanè Consequens cùm neque veteres neque recentiores Stoici Theologi, hactenùs probatum dederint, manifestum est, ipsos turpiter petere principium. Nos potiùs invictè sic colligimus, Cùm Divina præscientia haud magis atq; humana, rebus præscitis ullam afferat necessitatem: Ergò ex hâc de illâ quoad præsentem quæstionem, rectissimè fieri posse judicium.

Posterius objectum iisdem Sophisticationibus laborat. Etsi enim DEI præscientia, vel omniscientia potiùs, in perpetuo quodam æternitatis τῷ νῦν constituta, res omnes ab omni concretione materiæ, & temporum intervallis sequestratas, sibi habet præsentissimas: ac proindè ex conditione temporali ea nunquam perficitur: minimè tamen omnium sequitur, quod argumentum intendit: nempè res præscitas suos sortiri eventus non ex naturâ suâ, & ex causâ propinquâ liberâ: sed ex DEI præscientiâ. Falsum enim hoc esse, duplici ratione demonstrari potest. Primùm enim hoc pacto DEI præscientia in se considerata, turpissimè confunditur cum præscientiæ limitatione: quæ duo tamen à se mutuò accuratissimè discerni de- "bent. Nam Præscientia ipsa in se considerata, "nihil est aliud quàm ipsissima DEI Omniscien- "tia, per se & ex se perfectissima, sibique semper "æqualiter, & sine ullâ imperfectione constans, si "vel maximè nullæ res essent conditæ. Et hæc à conditione rerum præscitarum pendere simpliciter negatur. Verùm quoad Præscientiæ limitationem, cujus respectu DEUS præscit vel prævidet res eo modo evêturas, quo foris in statu suæ mutabilitatis positæ, ex causâ liberâ, & mutabili eveniunt: certè vix quisquam ita absurd9 fuerit, qui limitationem hanc à conditione rerum præscitarum provenire: & hoc respectu præscientiam à rebus præscitis pendere inficias ire ausit. Neque est ut metuat aliquis, ex hâc limitatione aliquid mutabilitatis ad ipsam DEI præscientiam in se consideratam redundare. Nam hæc omnis mutabilitatis simpliciter expers utut cadant res, ita eas videt planè immutabiliter: quoniam non potest non DEUS scire & videre omnia, quocunque tandem modo illa eveniant.

Posterior ratio, quâ objecti hujus vanitatem demonstramus, talis esse potest: Omnis scientia & præscientia est ex genere eorum, quæ sine

πρός τι, Relata dicuntur, & semper aliquam πρὸς ἄλληλα σχέσιν obtinent, hoc est, ad aliud semper referuntur: ita ut res præscitæ Fundamenti respectum & naturam in istâ Relatione obtineant. Ergò vel ipse Naturæ Ordo, qui est in Fundamento & Termino Relationis invertendus fuerit: vel concedendum id, pro quo Ecclesia DEI pugnat, nempè, non evenire res, quia à DEO præsciuntur: sed quia vi causarum propriarum eventuræ sunt, ideò prædici, præsciri & prævideri: hoc est, præscientiam â rebus præscitis, non has ab illis dependere.

Neque destituitur hæc nostra assertio consensu Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis: Sic enim Justinus Philosophus & Martyr, Respons 58. ad Orthodoxos: Præscientia non est causa ejus, quod futurum est: Sed id quod futurum est, causa est Præscientiæ: Siquidem non præscientiam sequitur Futurum: Sed Futurum sequitur præscientia. Suffragatur & Augustinus lib. 3. de lib. arb. c. 4. Sicut memoria tua non cogit facta esse, quæ præterierunt: Sic DEUS præscientiâ suâ, non cogit facienda, quæ futura sunt.

Sed de præscientiâ, ejusdemque ad rerum humanarum contingentiam affectione, hæc dixisse, sufficiat.

II. Secundo loco haud levior movetur Quæstio de æternâ DEI Providentiâ. Cùm enim hæc, non in nudâ tantùm occupetur, rerum & actionum omnium notitiâ: sed simul etiam efficaci gubernatione ad easdem concurrat, Quæritur, Num & quomodo salvâ DEI providentiâ, contingentia rerum & actionum humanarum stare possit: Hinc natum est argumentum istud: Omnia subjacent divinæ providentiæ: Ergò nullus locus relinquitur contingentiæ. Item: Nullum est Fortuitum: E. nulla contingentia.

Respondeo prius objectum fallit Sophismate tᵹ͂ μὴ ἐπομένᵹ. Nam Providentia & Contingentia tanquam ἀντιφατικῶς opposita, sive contraria vitiosissimè opponuntur: cùm ad se mutuò sese habeant ut subordinata, siquidem Contingentia Divinæ Providentiæ est substrata sive ὑπεκκλήλας subordinata, ita ut neutra alteram sive impediat, sive tollat: uti mox demonstrabitur. Deindè involvitur simul Sophisticatio καθολῒ πρὸς τὶ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Non enim simpliciter & absolutè, sed secundum quid verum est, quod in argumento isto occultatur, nempè respectu divinæ Providentiæ omnia fieri necessariò. Secundum quid, inquam, verùm hoc est, nempè respectu ejusdem causæ. Jam verò diversitas hic est causarum. Providentia enim ut & Præscientia, primæ & universalis causæ est propria. Contingentia verò actionum propriè ad secundas & singulares causas refertur. Hinc fit, ut una eademque actio, unus idemque eventus dici possit & necessarius & contingens: Necessarius quidem, quando refertur ad divinam providentiam, quæ falli nequit: Contingens vero, quando ex suâ naturâ perpenditur, sive ex propriâ & proximâ causâ, quæ est libera Hominis voluntas. Cæterùm qualis Necessitas respectu divinæ Providentiæ sit statuenda: nùm etiam ea cum contingentiâ contradictoriè pugnet, patebit ex sequentibus.

Posterius objectum laborat Sophisticatione τῆς μεταβάσεως. Statuit enim Fortuitum & Contingens, ita ad se mutuò habere ut uno negato, statim negetur alterum: cum tamen Fortuna & Contingentia sub diversis planè generibus contineantur: uti sub initium Quæstionis hujus secundæ est ostensum. ” Cæterùm quoad propositam Quæstionem, ” rectissimè respondetur, contingentiam rerum ” & actionum humanarum, salvâ & inconcussâ ” DEI providentiâ rectissimè stare posse, propter- ” eà quòd (uti jam dictum) contingentia isthæc ” divinæ Providentiæ non opponitur, sed substernitur sive subordinatur. Quemadmodum ” enim Providentia DEI singula atque universa: ” ita contingentes etiam actiones gubernat & ” determinat. Hinc enim fit, ut DEUS non pa- ” tiatur ruere impios quo ipsi aliàs ex liberâ vo- ” luntate tendunt: sed metas præfigat, quousque ” frena libidini ipsorum laxaturus sit. Hinc eti- ” am haud rarò DEUS vi suæ providentiæ vincu- ” la & repagulas impiis injicit & ponit, ut prorsus à ceptis desistere, & planè omittere cogantur, quæ aliàs effrenata ipsorum libido perpetratura esset. Exemplo possunt esse, Esavus frater Jacobi, qui de occidendo fratre consilium inierat: Bileam, qui plenâ animi intentione, ad maledicendum populo Israelitico, jam itineri se accinxerat: Achitophel qui de Davide regno ejiciendo jam decretum fecerat: Sed quæ instituta singula, ut & id genus alia impiorum quàm plurima DEUS tempestivè repressit, fregit, disputavit. Sed esto nihil tale interdum eveniat, sed DEUS patiatur fieri, quæ voluntas impiorum decernit: nihilominus tamen indè quoque singulare divinæ providentiæ artificium elucescat, dùm vel indè merita supplicia impiis irrogandi, eosque evertendi materiam sumit: vel pessima etiam consilia, incommoda atque salutem piorum convertere novit: Cujus rei historia Josephi & Passionis Christi, Exempla longè illustrissima suppeditat. Sed altiùs insurgunt quidam arguentes: Ordo divinæ Providentiæ est certissimus. Ergò locum non habet contingentia.


### Question concerning what it is (continued)

But it is most correctly answered by inversion: that for this very reason contingency is not removed, because the Order of divine Providence is certain: which is proved thus: It pertains to the perfection of divine Providence that things be directed to their ends, not in any way whatsoever, but in that way which pertains to the perfection of the universe. Now, indeed, that mode is that some things are directed necessarily, as effects from causes acting by necessity of nature: and some things contingently, as effects from causes acting contingently or freely, that is, which can be hindered, or even not act of their own accord. Therefore, it is so far from the case that divine Providence imposes necessity on all things, that it rather pertains to it to leave liberty or contingency in some things. Then this very thing is proved by this reason: The execution of the order of divine providence does not always happen from His nod alone: but for the most part simultaneously from secondary causes. Therefore, according to the condition of the secondary cause, whether necessary, or contingent, or free, the effect itself of the order of divine providence is also either necessary, or free, or contingent.

But since we have expressly dealt with this very question above in the Article on Providence: it is not appropriate to deal with it more fully in this place.

III. The third question, therefore, which pertains here, is what comes into dispute: Must contingency be posited for absolutely all things and human actions? To which ζήτημα (question) we answer in the negative. For the field of contingency is not infinite, but limited and restricted, and that by those limits by which its principle and cause, namely the liberty of the human will, is circumscribed and determined: as will be shown in the third subsequent Question. Then a distinction must be made between those things which are subject to the human will as its proper and adequate objects: and those things which indeed concern Man: but do not depend on the will of Man as a cause: but only on the care and providence of GOD: such as the Resurrection of the flesh, Faith in Christ, and works of that kind, to the efficiency of which the will of Man cannot concur as a cause, whether efficient, or cooperating, or as a sine qua non, or assisting. Those things, insofar as the will of Man is not hindered, are and are called Contingent: but these latter are not.

IV. Fourthly and lastly, it is asked: Does Contingency remove all necessity whatsoever? Which question indeed has caused much labor and trouble both to the Ancients and to more recent Theologians, because neither a simple Affirmation, nor even a simple Negation, can stand. We must therefore enter upon a middle path: which can be most conveniently done by observing the various meanings and distinctions of the word Necessary. For if these are not observed, it happens that an ἀσυλλογισία (non-sequitur) is committed by moving from the undistributed to the distributed.

Moreover, of those things which are called Necessary, four kinds are commonly established: so that one necessity is called Absolute, when, to wit, a thing or proposition cannot be otherwise, and whose Contradictory is simply false, nay, destructive of the thing itself: Which necessity has place only in divine and eternal things, as also in first principles: and it is not of compulsion, but of perfection: As: it is necessary ἁπλῶς & absolutely for GOD to be just: for Spirits to be incorporeal: for the rising of the Sun to accompany the day. For the whole to be greater than its part: For twice two to be four. Another Necessity is called of Consequence, or ἐξ ὑποθέσεως, which is of those things and propositions which can by their own nature be otherwise: but become necessary, either because of preceding causes, or because they are determined. The third Necessity is Physical, of those things whose condition is indeed mutable, but yet is so constrained by a certain law of immutability, that only the first and supreme cause can dissolve it.

That which is called natural or Physical, because it is occupied mostly about the physical affection of created things, as: Fire necessarily heats: The Sun is necessarily moved. The fourth Necessity is called that of Definitions and Demonstrations, which is nothing else than a Proposition, of which if the opposite is imagined, an implication of contradiction arises: but this degree is treated primarily in Logic: nor does it properly pertain to the present discussion.

But there are those who have treated this matter more accurately, who indeed establish only two kinds of Necessity: the former of which arises from the necessity of the cause cohering with the effect: Which necessity is called simple, preceding, absolute, and of consequence: The latter, however, arises from the necessity of the Effect following the cause: And it is named of condition, also following the condition of the thing, also hypothetical and of the consequent. But (to come to the decision of the proposed question) this latter Necessity has a place in singular and contingent things, which are indeed in reality, or by their own nature, mutable: but they are not changed, because they follow from causes which are not changed, when nevertheless they could have been changed: or, because when they happen, or have happened, contradictory things cannot be true, the truth of the Assertion is clear from that common rule of contingent things (τῶν ἐνδεχομένων): by which Logicians establish that neither of them is necessary in potentiality (τῇ δυνάμει): but only in actuality (ἐνεργείᾳ). For these contingent things (ἐνδεχόμενα), considered in their principles, can either be or not be in potentiality (τῇ δυνάμει): But as soon as the potentiality (δύναμις) passes into act, it is immediately said to be necessary: according to that immovable Aristotelian Axiom: Everything that is, when it is, it is necessary that it be. This same thing is most rightly affirmed also concerning that which is future and past: For just as it is impossible that what is, should not be: so also it is impossible that what is at some time future, should not be future: and that what has been, should not have been. Concerning which matter Anselm, in his book on the Concord of Foreknowledge and Free Will, ch. 1, discourses in this manner: If it is pronounced thus: What will be, will be of necessity: necessity here signifies nothing else than that what will be, cannot at the same time not be: but at the same time it is also true, that it has been, and is, and will be something, not by necessity, but because it is necessary that everything which has been, has been, and that which is, is, and that which will be, will be. The matter can be illustrated by an example: plague, famine, war, insofar as they are punishments for our sins, can be called both contingent (ἐνδεχόμενα) and necessary (ἀναγκαῖα): contingent and necessary: so that to be affected by these punishments, and not to be affected, is to be referred to contingent things (ἐνδεχόμενα): insofar as, indeed, not both at the same time, but only one or the other can happen to men in potentiality (τῇ δυνάμει): but in actuality (τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ), only one or the other can happen. Now therefore, as regards the will of men, and those powers by which they can govern external locomotion, and set a limit to crimes against Conscience: it is contingent that men be punished, or not be punished: For neither is necessary by its own nature, and in itself, to happen. But now, when the morals of men behave most wickedly, we say it is necessary that men be punished; because, indeed, the causes are not changed, namely the wickedness and crimes by which they do not cease to provoke the anger and vengeance of GOD.

Some, from among the Sacramentarians, are in an uproar at this point, claiming that these Distinctions of the Necessary, taken from the Schools of the Philosophers, are not to be applied to the present Theological Controversy. To whom it can be sufficiently answered, if only it is demonstrated that the Terms of these Distinctions are indeed not scriptural (ἐγγράφους), but Philosophical: but that the thing itself is built upon the immovable foundations of the Scriptures. For let them explain to us, whether these statements of the Scriptures are to be accepted with one and the same degree of necessity: It is necessary that offenses come: Matt. 18, 7. And, It is necessary that Christ reign, 1 Cor. 15, 24. Now they themselves must needs admit that Christ reigns by a far different degree of necessity than that by which it is necessary that offenses come: For Christ reigns with GOD willing, approving, and ordaining, and that even if the whole world should resist: But heresies happen, with GOD neither willing nor approving, but rather most highly opposing: And yet they nevertheless happen necessarily: Namely, by a necessity of consequence or hypothetical (ἐξ ὑποθέσεως), insofar as indeed in Men and the Devil, there is always a cause for which and from which heresies arise: so that even unwillingly they are forced to admit that not one kind of Necessity is to be established. Then, unless this distinction of the degrees of Necessity is observed, it will never be possible to demonstrate that the sins, crimes, and wickedness of Men are not of absolute necessity, but only of hypothetical necessity, which does not exclude Contingency, but coincides with it: which that former, or absolute necessity, by no means permits. Finally, the use of this distinction is also most necessary for this reason, that it may thus be demonstrated what is the cause and foundation of that assertion of ours, by which without any contradiction we affirm that of Events contingent by their own nature, there is also a certain necessity: And again, that of Necessary events there is a certain contingency: but in a most diverse respect, and that a twofold one: First indeed in respect of secondary causes to the first: then, however, in respect of the distinct degrees of Necessity: of which one, which is and is called of consequence, does not remove Contingency: but the other, which is and is called of the consequent, simply excludes Contingency.

But furthermore some clamor, complaining, Since the actions of men, in their own way and respect, are also necessary, why do we not in common parlance call them necessary rather than contingent. But this easy and ready answer can be given: Actions, or the Effects and events of human actions, are denominated from the condition of their nature: such as they exist from their own nature and that of their proximate causes, not such as they are in respect of divine Foreknowledge or Providence, which is a more remote cause. The foundation of this answer appears sufficiently immovable even from the fact that any thing, any action, any event, derives its denomination not from remote and external causes, but from internal principles and proximate causes.

Latin:

Verùm rectissimè respondetur per Inversionem: quòd hanc ipsam ob causam non tollatur contingentia, quia certus est Ordo divinæ Providentiæ: id quod sic probatur: At perfectionem divinæ Providentiæ spectat, ut res dirigantur in suos fines, non quomodocunque, sed eo modo, qui pertinet ad perfectionem universi. Jam verò is modus est, ut quædam dirigantur necessariò, tanquam Effecta, à causis ex naturæ necessitate efficientibus: & quædam contingenter, tanquam effecta à causis contingenter vel liberè agentibus, id est, quę impediri possint, aut etiam sponte suâ non agere. Ergò tantùm abest, ut divina Providentia imponat necessitatem omnibus rebus, ut potiùs ad illam pertineat relinquere in quibusdam Libertatem sive Contingentiam. Deindè probatur hoc ipsum, hâc ratione: Executio Ordinis divinæ providentiæ, non semper fit, à solo ipsius nutu: sed plerumque simul à causis secundis. Ergò pro conditione causæ secundæ, vel necessaria, vel contingentis aut liberæ, ipse etiam effectus ordinis divinæ providentiæ est vel necessarius, vel liber aut contingens.

Cæterùm cùm de hâc ipsâ quæstione suprà in Articulo de Providentiâ ex professo egerimus: nihil attinet fusiùs hoc loco de eâ agere.

III. Tertia proindè quæstio quæ huc pertinet, est, quod in disceptationem venit: Num omnium prorsus rerum & actionum humanarum statuenda sit contingentia? Ad quod ζήτημα negatè respondemus. Contingentia enim campus non est infinitus, sed limitatus & restrictus, idq; iis limitibus, quibus principium & causa ejus, nempè libertas humanæ voluntatis est circumscripta & determinata: quemadmodum Quæstione subsequente tertiâ ostendetur. Deindè distinguendum est inter ea, quæ voluntati humanæ tanquam objecta propria & adæquata sunt subjecta: & inter ea, quæ Hominem quidem respiciunt: sed non ab Hominis voluntate, tanquam causâ : sed tantùm à DEI curâ atque providentiâ dependent: ut Resurrectio carnis, Fides in Christum, & id genus opera, ad quorum Efficientiam voluntas Hominis non potest, ut causa sive Efficiens, sive cooperans, sive sine quâ non, sive adjuvans concurrere. Illa, quatenùs voluntas Hominis non impeditur, sunt & dicuntur Contingentia: hæc verò non item.

IV. Quartò & postremò quæritur: An Contingentia omnem prorsus tollat Necessitatem? Quæ sanè quæstio plurimùm laboris atque negotii fecit tùm Veteribus, tùm recentioribus Theologis, proptereà quod neque simplex Affirmatio, neque simplex etiam Negatio, subsistere potest. Mediâ ergò viâ nobis ingrediendum: id quod observatis vocabuli Necessarii variis significationibus & distinctionibus, commodissimè fieri poterit. His enim non observatis fit, ut à non distributo ad distributum ἀσυλλογισία committatur.

Eorum autem, quæ Necessaria dicuntur, vulgò quatuor constituuntur genera: ita ut una necessitas dicatur Absoluta, cùm videlicèt res aut propositio aliter se habere non potest, & cujus Contradictoria simpliciter est falsa, imò ipsius rei destructiva: Quæ necessitas tantùm in divinis & æternis locum habet, ut & in primis principiis : estq; non coactionis, sed perfectionis: Ut: necesse est ἁπλῶς & absolutè DEUM esse justum: Spiritus esse incorporeos: Solis exortum comitari diem. Totum majus esse suâ parte: Bis duo esse quatuor. Altera Necessitas dicitur Consequentiæ, sive ἐξ ὑποθέσεως, quæ est earum rerum & propositionum, quæ possunt se naturâ suâ aliter habere: sed fiunt necessariò, vel propter præcedentes causas, vel quia determinatæ sunt. Tertia Necessitas est Physica earum rerum, quarum mutabilis quidem est Conditio, sed tamen lege quadâ immutabilitatis sic constrictâ, ut eam solvere non nisi causa prima & suprema possit.

Quæ naturalis sive Physica appellatur, quia circa physicam rerum creatarum affectionem, vel maximè occupatur, ut: Ignis necessariò calefacit: Sol necessariò movetur. Quarta Necessitas dicitur Definitionum & Demonstrationum, quæ nihil est aliud, quàm Propositio, cujus si fingatur oppositum, fit implicatio contradictionis: sed de hoc gradu in Logicis potissimùm agitur: neque ad præsentem disputationem propriè pertinet.

Sed sunt, qui accuratiùs materiam istam pertractârunt, quippè duo tantùm Necessitatis constituunt genera: quorum prius oritur ex necessitate causæ cum effectu cohærentis: Quæ necessitas appellatur simplex, præcedens, absoluta, consequentiæ: Posterius verò oritur, ex necessitate Effectus, ad causam consequentis: Et nominatur conditionis, Item sequens conditionem rei, item hypothetica & consequentis. Habet verò (ut ad decisionem quæstionis propositæ veniamus) posterior hæc Necessitas locum in rebus singularibus & contingentibus, quæ sunt quidem reipsâ, sive naturâ suâ mutabiles: sed non mutantur, quia sequuntur ex causis, quæ non mutantur, cùm tamen potuissent mutari: vel, quia cùm fiunt, aut factæ sunt, contradictoria veræ esse non possunt, Assertionis veritas liquet, ex vulgatâ illâ τῶν ἐνδεχομένων contingentium regula: quâ Logici statuunt, Neutrum illorum τῇ δυνάμει esse necessarium: sed tantùm ἐνεργείᾳ. Nam ἐνδεχόμενα isthæc in suis principiis considerata, τῇ δυνάμει fieri vel possunt, vel non possunt: Quam primùm autem δύναμις in actum exit, statim necessariò id esse dicitur: secundum immotum illud Axioma Aristotelicum: Omne quod est, quando est, ipsum esse necessum est. Quod ipsum de eo quoque, quod futurum & præteritum est, rectissimè affirmatur: Nam sicut impossibile est, ut, quod est, non sit: ita etiam impossibile est, ut quod aliquando futurum est, non sit futurum: & quod fuit, non fuerit. Quâ de re scitè Anshelmus lib. de Concordiâ præscientiæ & liberi arbitrii, c. 1. in hunc modum disserit: Si ita pronuncietur: Quod erit, ex necessitate erit: non aliud hic significat, necessitas, nisi quia quod erit, non poterit simul non esse: simul autem & illud verum est, quia fuerit, & est, & erit aliquid, non est ex necessitate, sed quia necesse est, fuisse omne quod fuit, & esse quod est, & futurum esse, quod erit. Exemplo res illustrari potest: pestis, fames, bellum quatenùs sunt pœnæ nostrorum peccatorum, possunt dici & ἐνδεχόμενα & ἀναγκαῖα: contingentia & necessaria: ita ut pœnis istis affici, & non affici referendum sit ad ἐνδεχόμενα: quatenùs nimirùm non utrumque simul, sed alterutrum tantùm τῇ δυνάμει hominibus obtingere potest: τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ verò, non nisi alterum evenire potest. Jam ergò quoad voluntatem hominum, & eas vires, quibus externam regere locomotivam, & sceleribus contra Conscientiam modum statuere possunt: contingens est, ut puniantur, vel non puniantur homines: Neutrum enim suâ naturâ, & per se est necessarium, ut fiat. Jam verò, quando mores hominum se habent sceleratissimè, necessarium esse dicimus, ut puniantur homines; quia nimirùm causæ non mutantur, flagitia videlicet & fcelera, quibus DEI iram & vindictam provocare non definunt.

Tumultuantur nonnulli hoc loco ex Sacramentariis, Distinctiones istas Necessarii ex Philosophorum Scholis petitas, ad præsentem Controversiam Theologicam haud esse accommodandas. Quibus fufficienter satis responderi potest, si illud modò demonstretur, Terminos quidem Distinctionum istarum non esse ἐγγράφους, sed Philosophicos: Rem verò ipsam immotis Scripturarum fundamentis esse superstructam. Edisserant enim ipsi nobis, nùm uno eodemque necessitatis gradu accipienda sint hæc Scripturarum enunciata: Necesse est, venire scandala: Matth. 18, 7. Et, Necesse est Christum regnare, 1. Cor. 15, 24. Jam ipsimet fateri necesse habent, longè alio necessitatis gradu Christum regnare, quàm quo scandala venire necesse est: Christus enim regnat DEO volente, approbante, ordinante, idque si totus mundus reluctetur: Hæreses autem eveniunt, DEO nec volente, nec approbante, sed summè potiùs repugnante: Et tamen nihilominùs necessariò eveniunt: Necessitate videlicet consequentiæ sive ἐξ ὑποθέσεως, quatenùs nimirùm in Hominibus & Diabolo, semper causa est, ob quam & ex quâ hæreses proveniunt: utique vel inviti fateri coguntur, non unum Necessitatis genus esse constituendum. Deindè nisi distinctio hæc graduum Necessitatis observetur, nunquam demonstrari poterit, quòd peccata, scelera atque flagitia Hominum non sint absolutæ necessitatis, sed duntaxat hypotheticæ, quæ Contingentiam non excludit, sed cum eâdem coincidit: id quod prior illa, sive absoluta necessitas minimè permittit. Tandem distinctionis hujus usus vel ideò etiam maximè est necessarius, ut sic demonstretur, quæ causa sit atque fundamentum illius assertionis nostræ, quâ sine ullâ contradictione affirmamus, Eventuum suâ naturâ contingentium, esse etiam quandam necessitatem: Et rursus, Necessariorum eventuum esse quandam contingentiam: sed diversissimo respectu, eoque gemino: Primùm quidem respectu causarum secundarum ad primam: deindè verò respectu distinctorum graduum Necessitatis: quorum unus, qui est, & dicitur Consequentiæ, Contingentiam non tollit: alter verò, qui est ac dicitur Consequentis, Contingentiam simpliciter excludit.

Sed porrò obstrepunt nonnulli, quiritantes, Cùm actiones hominum, suo modo atq́; respectu etiam sint necessariæ, cur non in communi loquendi consuetudine necessarias eas potiùs, quàm contingentes nominemus. Sed facilis & expedita dari potest responsio isthæc: Actiones, vel actionum humanarum Effectus & eventus denominari ex conditione suæ naturæ: quales nimirùm illi ex suâ, & proximarum causarum naturâ existunt, non quales sunt respectu Præscientiæ aut Providentiæ divinæ, quæ remotior causa est. Fundamentum responsionis hujus satis immotum patet vel indè, quòd quævis res, quævis actio, quivis Eventus, denominationem sortitur non à causis remotis & externis, sed à principiis internis & causis proximis.


### Question concerning the Cause of Contingency

CONCERNING this Question our Author says thus: The cause of the contingency of our actions is the liberty of the will: or, which is the same thing, the human will, and that free and unimpeded. The truth of the assertion is evident from the fact that even after the fall, the will of Man in external matters, and those subject to the judgment of reason, behaves itself freely and reciprocally, so that it can either choose or reject the objects, and command the locomotive powers: and hence something is either done or omitted: where contingency has a place on both sides: For that which has already been done could not have been done, and that which has not been done could have been done according to the free choice of the will. It must be observed, however, that when the will of Man is constituted the cause of contingency, it is when it is free and is not impeded by another principle approaching from the outside. For when this happens, then contingency, properly speaking, does not have a place. But it is sufficiently evident that the will of Man, and consequently contingency itself, can be impeded in many ways. For in the beginning, the Devil possesses great power over the impious, so that he bends their will according to his pleasure, and holds it as if it were enslaved: so that they often act not so much by a determined and free will, as by a blinded and captivated one, even unknowingly doing those things to which Satan impels them. Furthermore, not rarely is the vehemence of internal motions or affections so great that the will rejects every judgment of right reason and is carried away sideways, nay, is impelled to design those things which, with the use and judgment of the will standing free, it would never design. Added to this in the third place is the fact that GOD not rarely is accustomed to withdraw and impede the will of Man for reasons far better and most just, so that it cannot bring into effect what the will has freely chosen and approved. An example of which thing the Lord Apostle shows us even in his own person, writing thus to the Romans, ch. 1:13. I do not want you to be ignorant, brethren, that I have often proposed to come to you, but I have been hindered until now. What? That in the fourth place GOD sometimes delivers men into a reprobate sense, and mixes a spirit of giddiness into their heart, so that they are so far from using the right judgment of reason, or possessing the liberty of the will, that the Apostle rather calls them κατεφθαρμένους τὸν νῦν, corrupted in mind, 2 Tim. 3:8, and ἀπηλλοτριωμένους καὶ ἐσκοτισμένους τῇ διανοίᾳ, having the understanding darkened, and alienated, Eph. 4:18. Finally, such is the condition of the Regenerate that, although the flesh always struggles against the spirit, yet, aided by divine power, they leave more room for the dictation of the Holy Spirit than for the pleasure of their own will.

With these removals or impediments observed, it is easy to conclude that contingency has its own certain prefixed limits, and that the will of Man is impeded in many and various ways, so that it cannot struggle forth to contingency. It is asked in this place, since the cause of contingency can be changed, how the certain and infallible foreknowledge of GOD relates to it: or what is the same thing, how it can be demonstrated that Divine knowledge is certain, even with respect to future contingent things, the cause of which, however, is so often impeded that, with all the requirements of contingency posited, the Effect nevertheless does not follow? Which question, indeed, that it may be more correctly explained, it should be well noted: that an effect can be known or recognized in three ways: First, in its cause only: as for example: if you hear a student speaking about a future disputation, and you see him preparing himself for it: then you immediately argue from that that he will go to the disputation. Secondly, in itself, as if you now see the student actually going to the disputation. Thirdly, in itself and in the cause together: as if you see him going to the disputation, and going for that reason, because he previously decided to go. Now, since by the opinion of all, GOD knows future effects in this third way, namely in himself and in the cause: It is asked, from where precisely can it be demonstrated that the Knowledge of GOD with respect to future effects is certain, although the cause of contingency can be impeded? It is answered that it can be demonstrated in two ways: 1. From the fact that GOD, insofar as he exactly knows the disposition of a necessary, unimpedable cause, to that extent also precisely, certainly, and infallibly knows future contingent effects. Secondly, that GOD knows the disposition of a contingent cause, not only as it is in itself: but also as it is actually brought into effect by him. The truth of this assertion is evident from the fact that a cause of contingency is generally called that which can have an effect, and can also not have one: either because by its own nature it is indifferent to either, so that with all requirements for acting posited, it can still not act: such is a free cause: or, because although it is by its own nature determined to one, yet it can and is sometimes accustomed to be impeded by another cause: as has already been shown above. Therefore, in the present question, it is a matter of the Knowledge of a future contingent Effect, as it is about to be in the very act. For as it is potentially future, but does not emerge into act: there is certainly no doubt that GOD has foreknown and foreseen only the possibility, and not the act itself: so that, in whichever direction the matter falls, the foreknowledge of GOD can never be uncertain or fallible. For while the disposition of a contingent cause stands, the effect can still, and is wont to, not come to pass, or come to pass otherwise than the disposition of such a cause might otherwise seem to require. Therefore, the knowledge of such a disposition does not immediately and necessarily imply the knowledge of the actual effect itself. There is also a second reason, that divine knowledge, being infinitely perfect, does not depend upon the actual existence of a created object: but having all power and perfection in itself and from itself, it cannot depend upon the mutability of any external object: but by one perpetual act it sees and beholds all things, just as they are at some time contingently either to be or not to be.

Finally, in so far as GOD certainly and infallibly knows that a contingent cause is now being determined immediately to produce some effect, and is hindered by absolutely no other cause: to that extent He also certainly and infallibly knows that the contingent effect will be, however much it could have been changed and hindered. For just as a necessary effect follows infallibly from a necessary cause that cannot be hindered: so also a contingent effect follows infallibly and certainly from a contingent cause, one that is indeed hinderable, but yet is now determined immediately to act, and is not at all hindered by any cause.

These things having been thus discussed, let it be plain that, speaking properly and in itself, the knowledge of future contingent events belongs to GOD alone: but that our intellect does not naturally know future contingencies with certainty: where, however, we except those things which both Angels and Men know from their own natural causes: such as that the rising of the Sun is accompanied by day, or those things which ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ usually happen for the most part.

Latin:

DE hac Quæstione sic Autor noster: Causa Contingentiæ nostrarum actionum est libertas voluntatis: vel, quod idem est, voluntas humana, eaque libera & non impedita. Assertionis veritas patet vel indè, quòd post lapsum etiam, voluntas Hominis in rebus externis, & rationis judicio subjectis liberè & reciprocè se habet, ita ut vel eligere, vel aversari res objectas, & locomotivæ imperare queat : & hinc vel fiat, vel omittatur aliquid : ubi ex utrâque parte Contingentia locum habet: Nam & id, quod jam factum est, non fieri, & id, quod non factum est, pro liberâ electione voluntatis fieri potuisset. Observandum verò, quòd voluntas Hominis cùm constituitur causa contingentiæ, quando est libera, & non impeditur ab alio forinsecùs accedente principio. Hoc enim quando fit, tùm Cōtingentia propriè loquendo locum non habet. Multis autem modis & voluntatem Hominis, & per consequens ipsam Contingentiam impediri posse, satis evidenter constat. Initiò enim magnam vim in impiis possidet Diabolus, ita ut eorum voluntatem pro arbitrio inflectat, & quasi mancipatam habeat : ut non tàm destinatâ & liberâ, quàm excæcatâ & captivatâ voluntate, vel inscii agant ea sæpiùs, ad quæ ipsos impellit Satanas. Deindè haud rarò tanta est vehementia motuū internorum sive affectuum, ut voluntas prorsus omne rectæ rationis judicium respuat, & in transversum abripiatur, imò impellatur ad ea designanda, quæ aliàs libero stante voluntatis usu & arbitrio, nunquam designaret. Accedit tertio loco, quòd DEUS haud rarò voluntatem Hominis propter causas longè optimas & justissimas, ita retrahere & impedire solet, ut in effectum deducere non possit, quæ voluntas liberè elegit & approbavit. Cujus rei exemplum D. Apostolus vel in propriâ suâ personâ nobis monstrat, sic scribens ad Romanos cap. 1, 13. Nolo vos ignorare fratres, quod sæpè proposuerim venire ad vos, sed prohibitus sum usquè huc. Quid? quòd quarto loco DEUS interdum homines tradit in sensum reprobum, & Spiritum vertiginis miscet in cor eorum, ut tantùm absit ipsos recto rationis uti judicio, vel, libertate voluntatis potiri, ut potiùs, Apostolus ipsos nominet κατεφθαρμένους τὸν νῦν mente corruptos, 2. Timoth. 3, 8. & ἀπηλλοτριωμένους καὶ ἐσκοτισμένους τῇ διανοίᾳ, Obscuratum habentes intellectum, & alienatos Eph. 18. Tandem Regeneratorum ea est conditio, ut licèt caro semper reluctetur adversus spiritum, tamen divinâ virtute adjuti locum magis relinqueant Spiritus Sancti dictamini, quàm voluntatis suæ arbitrio.

Quibus remotis sive impedimentis observatis, promtum est colligere, tùm Contingentiæ suos certos præfixos esse terminos, tum voluntatem Hominis multis variísque modis impediri, quò minùs ad cõtingentiam eluctari posfit. Quæritur hoc loco, cùm causa Contingentiæ possit mutari, quomodo ad eam sese habeat certa & infallibilis DEI præscientia: vel quod idem est, quomodo demonstrari possit, Divinam notitiam esse certam, etiam respectu rerum futurarum contingentium, quarum tamen causa ita sæpiùs impediatur, ut positis omnibus requisitis contingentiæ, Effectus tamen non sequatur? Quæ sanè Quæstio ut rectiùs explicetur, probè notandum fuerit: Effectum aliquem tribus modis sciri aut cognosci posse: Primùm in suâ causâ tantùm: ut Exempli gratiâ: si audias Studiosum loqui de futurâ disputatione, & videas ipsum se ad eam comparare: tùm indè statim arguas ipsum iturum ad disputationem. Deindè in seipso, ut si jam videas studiosum actu euntem ad disputationem. Tertiò in se, & in causâ simul: ut si videas illum ad disputationem ire, & ideò ire, quoniam prius ire statuit. Jam cùm ex omnium sententiâ, DEUS cognoscat effectus futuros isto tertio modo, scilicet in se & in causâ: Quæritur, undénam præcisè demonstrari possit, Scientiam DEI respectu effectuum futurorum esse certam, licèt causa Contingentiæ impediri queat? Respondetur duobus modis illud demonstrari posse: 1. Indè, quod DEUS, quatenùs exactè novit dispositionem causæ necessariæ, non impedibilis, eatenùs etiam præcisè, certò & infallibiliter cognoscat effectus futuros contingentes. Deindè quod DEUS cognoscit dispositionem causę contingentis, non tantùm, sicut est in seipsâ: sed etiam sicut ipso actu in effectum deducitur. Assertionis hujus veritas indè patet, quòd causa contingentiæ generatim ea dicitur, quæ potest habere effectum, & potest etiam non habere: sive quia suâ naturâ est indifferens ad utrumlibet, ita ut positis omnibus requisitis ad agendum, possit adhuc non agere: qualis est causa libera: sive, quia licèt sit naturâ suâ determinata ad unum, tamen potest & solet quandoque impediri ab aliâ causâ: uti jam suprà ostensum. Proindè in præsenti quæstione agitur de Scientiâ Effectus futuri contingentis, prout in ipso actu est futurus. Nam ut est possibiliter futurus, sed in actum non emergit: dubium certè est nullum quin DEUS etiam possibilitatem tantùm, non verò actum ipsum præsciverit, & præviderit: ita, ut in quamcunque partem res cadat, DEI præscientia nunquam sit incerta aut fallibilis. Nam stante dispositione causæ contingentis, potest adhuc & solet effectus non evenire, vel aliter evenire, quàm talis causæ dispositio alioqui postulare videatur. Ergò talis dispositionis notitia, non statim necessariò subinfert notitiam ipsius effectus actualis. Accedit & altera ratio, quod divina scientia, quippè infinitè perfecta, non pendet ex actuali existentiâ objecti creati: sed in se & ex se omnem vim atque perfectionem habens, non potest ab ullius objecti externi mutabilitate dependere: sed uno perpetuo actu videt & intuetur omnia, prout aliquando contingenter vel futura, vel non futura sunt.

Tandem quatenùs DEUS certò & infallibiliter novit, causam contingentem proximè jam determinari, ad efficiendum aliquem effectum, & à nullâ prorsus aliâ causâ impediri: eatenùs etiam certò & infallibiliter novit effectum contingentem futurum, quantumvis ille mutari & impediri potuisset. Quemadmodum enim infallibiliter sequitur effectus necessarius, ex causâ necessariâ non impedibili: ita etiam infallibiliter & certò sequitur effectus contingens, ex causâ contingenti, impedibili quidem, sed tamen determinatâ jam proximè ad agendum, & minimè per ullam causam impedita.

His ita discussis planum sit, soli DEO propriè loquendo, & per se competere scientiam futurorum eventuum contingentium: Intellectum verò nostrum naturaliter futura contingentia certò non cognoscere: Ubi tamen excipimus ea, quæ & Angeli & Homines ex causis suis naturalibus sciunt: ut Solis Ortum comitari diem, vel quæ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ plerumque evenire solent.


### IV. and the Last Q U E S T I O. On the Subject of Contingency: or, of what things Contingency consists

On the Subject of Contingency: or, of what things there is Contingency.

Our Author touches upon the decision of this question in a few words: In this place, he says, we are speaking of the Contingency of human actions: not of the motions of other things, which are discussed in Physics. He therefore determines, and most rightly determines, that physical events and the motions of Elementary Nature, which wanders in a clearly uncertain course, are to be removed from this dispute, so that if we look at the first principles of those motions and events, and the condition of matter, we could more rightly call them fortuitous or necessary than contingent. For there is a clear distinction between natural things, and those acting naturally, and between voluntary things. For natural things each produce some one effect in their own way, or fail in it: but voluntary things behave otherwise, and can behave in this way or that, and are not constrained by any absolute or Physical necessity. For example: The Sun naturally moves from east to west: Fire naturally burns: iron by nature tends downward: nor can these things behave otherwise naturally, but they happen thus necessarily (namely, by physical necessity): which only GOD, and that beyond and above the condition of nature, can suspend, hinder, and break entirely, as the examples of the sacred scriptures testify: Joshua 10:13, Daniel 3:50, 2 Kings 6:6. But indeed such necessity does not dominate human will: but it acts freely, and can suspend an action, and do works that are unlike.

Our Author therefore most rightly determines that the field of contingency is not infinite, but limited and restricted, namely by those limits by which its principle and cause, that is, the Liberty of the human will, is circumscribed and determined. From which decision it is clear that one must accurately distinguish between those things which regard the human will as its proper and adequate object: and those things which indeed regard Man but not from the will of Man as a cause: but depend only on the care and providence of GOD: such as the Resurrection of the flesh, Faith in Christ, and actions of that kind, to the efficiency of which the will of Man, as a cause whether efficient, or cooperating, or without which not, can never concur.

These things having been thus considered, it remains finally that contingency belongs only to those things and actions about which the will of Man acts freely: such as ethical, political, and economic ones, and those as much evil as good: pertaining to external discipline, or conflicting with the same. Some also refer to this, but too ignorantly, those natural actions of man, to live, to eat, to drink, to sleep, and others that are of this kind. Certainly to will to live is not contingent, but is a certain necessary thing for Man, depending on the principle of common Nature, for the sake of Man himself: Thus to will to eat and drink is Natural, and therefore necessary, depending on the same principle, for the sake of life. These things therefore are necessary by reason of the principle, not by free will. But to will to drink this or that belongs to the intellective and right will, if it keeps measure and order: but to the depraved will if it fails from order: but it is always free, whether it keeps order or not: because our will is an internal principle toward many things: just as Nature is an internal principle, moving toward one thing and determined by its own inclination. Whence was born that distinction of the Natural and Voluntary principle, which has a very great use not only in Philosophy but also in Theology: so that, namely, of those things which cannot behave except in one way, the Principle is, and is called, NATURE: but of those things which can behave in various ways, the principle is, and is called, will: Because the Form, through which the will acts, is not one, but manifold, according as manifold reasons are perceived by the intellect, which are brought to the will by it.

It is, however, seriously disputed in this place what is to be determined concerning sin, whether it is contingent or voluntary: or whether it is indeed necessary: or, which is the same thing, whether man sins necessarily, or indeed contingently? In which question various people twist themselves in various ways, and there have not been lacking theologians, otherwise Orthodox, who have determined that man sins neither simply necessarily, nor simply contingently: but with a certain contingency mixed with necessity. Which opinion we leave to be defended by its authors. We determine that the proposed question must be answered by a distinction, and that twofold. For first, one must distinguish the time preceding the Adamic fall from that which followed it. For before the fall, universal contingency had a place in man: for such freedom of will was granted to Adam that he could as easily not sin as sin: and he could most freely perform individual and all actions, both natural and voluntary: and he could incline himself wherever he wished, occupying natural things by the necessity of nature, but voluntary things by the freedom of the will. The fall of our first parents, therefore, with respect to the will, was clearly contingent, that is, neither necessary nor even impossible. But after our nature was so corrupted by the fall that it is prone to evil at all times, the question arises: Is sin now necessary, or contingent? Here the latter distinction should be observed, which discerns between original and actual sin. For as regards original sin or the corruption of our nature, contingency has no place. Since it is not placed in the freedom of our will, but in the condition of nature, that we can now be infected by nothing but sin and depraved concupiscences: nor can we lay aside or cast off this natural stain and the internal depravity of all the powers of body and soul. Concerning this natural corruption, the Apostle complains most tragically in Rom. 7:23: I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity under the law of sin, which is in my members. Therefore, by reason of this natural corruption, sin is rightly called necessary: yet not by an absolute or Stoic necessity, but by a physical necessity and ἐξ ὑποθέσεως.

But as regards actual sins, and those indeed which are committed against conscience, nothing certainly prevents us from calling them contingent: because we commit them freely and spontaneously, and do not obey right reason, according to that of Medea: I see the better things and approve them, I follow the worse: when nevertheless in this or that species of sin a man could restrain his mind from perpetrating wickedness and crime: as a thief could withdraw his hand from the handling of another's property: an adulterer could abstain from another's spouse: a fornicator could put a bridle on wandering lusts: a drunkard could temper himself from the excessive gulping of wine. Hence was born that most celebrated apophthegm of Augustine: There is no sin except that which is voluntary: How this may also be true in its own respect regarding original sin, we shall expressly show in the digression of that article.

Now we shorten sail and, in place of a coronis, we add that which was anxiously sought among the Scholastic Doctors: Namely, whether contingency can also be predicated of God and divine actions?

Which question can likewise be most rightly resolved by two distinctions. For either the sense of the proposed question is: Do things, as they objectively terminate divine foreknowledge, have the nature and truth of contingency? And in this sense we hold the affirmative simply: for since God foreknows things as they are in themselves, they certainly do not lose the nature and affection of contingency with respect to foreknowledge, and insofar as they relate objectively to it. Or the sense can be given as this: Are things, as they terminate divine foreknowledge, certain: and insofar as they are certainly to be in the future, are they at that point not contingent but necessary with respect to foreknowledge: then indeed we simply deny that contingency can be predicated of God and his foreknowledge. For the status of contingency, as the Scholastics speak, is in things as they are considered in themselves and by their own nature: but it ceases in them when they are appended to the certainty of divine foreknowledge. And hence it is true what is commonly said: Propositions about the future are of determined truth according to divine foreknowledge. And again, it is also true what is likewise commonly said: There is no determined truth of contingent futures. For with respect to the extrinsic cause, namely God's determination of contingent futures, the truth is most certain: but with respect to the proper and internal cause, namely the will of man, there is certainly no determined truth of these same contingent futures. For the will of man is mutable in itself, and relates itself mutably to both objects. For example: This proposition, God foreknew that the Antichrist would come, is contingent, and is necessary. Contingent, insofar as the coming of the Antichrist itself in itself and through itself behaved contingently. For the Antichrist could have not come, if the Devil had not wished to work that mystery of iniquity, as the Apostle speaks. But necessary, insofar as God saw that the Devil would certainly at some time bring the Antichrist into the light.

Bonaventura revealed the latter distinction, which is most useful to observe, writing thus on Book 1 of the Sentences, dist. 45: Contingency is considered in act and in effect: If we speak of contingency in effect, certainly it is not only in our effect, but also in many things which are from God: for God does many things which he could not do, with nothing resisting: But if we speak of contingency in act, that the will now wills something, now either begins or ceases to will something: or now wills the opposite: that which happens in the human will, whence also there is a difference between the will and the act, so that the will is neither always in one act, nor in a uniform act: now indeed the divine will, because of its identity with the act, cannot be varied at all, nor does it have any contingency in itself: therefore God also, although he foresees contingencies, is by no means to be established as foreseeing or foreknowing contingently.

Latin:

De Subjecto Contingentiæ: sive, quarum rerum sit Contingentia.

Hujus quæstionis decisionem Autor noster paucis verbis perstringit: Hoc loco, inquiens, de Contingentiâ humanarum actionum loquimur: non de cæterarum rerum motibus, de quibus in Physicis disseritur. Statuit ergò & rectissimè statuit ab hâc disputatione removendos esse eventus physicos & motus Naturæ Elementaris, quæ incerto planè cursu vagatur, ita ut si motuum & eventuum istorum prima principia, & materiæ conditionem spectemus, rectiùs vel fortuitos, vel necessarios, quàm contingentes appellare possimus. Nam inter res naturales, & naturaliter agentes, & inter res voluntarias luculentum est discrimen. Naturales enim unum aliquem effectum suo modo singulæ pariunt, aut in eo deficiunt: voluntariæ verò aliter se habent, & vel hoc, vel illo modo se habere possunt, neque ullâ absolutâ vel Physicâ necessitate constringuntur.
