Exempli gratiâ: Sol naturaliter movetur ab ortu in occafum: Ignis naturaliter urit: ferrum naturâ tendit deorsum: neq; aliter isthæc se naturaliter habere possunt, sed necessariò (necessitate nimirùm physicâ) sic eveniunt: quam non nisi DEUS, idque præter & suprà naturæ conditionem suspendere, impedire ac prorsus infringere potest, uti sacrarum literarum exempla testantur: Josuæ 10, 13. Daniel. 3, 50. 2. Reg. 6, 6. Atqui verò voluntati humanæ talis necessitas, non dominatur: sed liberè illa agit, & potest suspendere actionem, & dissimilia facere opera.

Rectissimè proindè Autor noster statuit, contingentiæ campum non esse infinitum, sed limitatum & restrictum, iis nimirùm limitibus, quibus principium & causa ejus, nempè Libertas voluntatis humanæ est circumscripta & determinata. Ex quâ decisione liquet, accuratè distingvendum esse inter ea, quæ voluntatem humanam, tanquam objectum proprium & adæquatum respiciunt: & inter ea, quæ Hominem quidem respiciunt sed non ab Hominis voluntate tanquam causâ: sed tantùm à DEI curâ atque providentiâ dependent: ut Resurrectio carnis, Fides in Christum, & id genus actiones, ad quarum efficientiam voluntas Hominis, ut causa sive efficiens, sive cooperans, sive sine quâ non, nunquàm potest concurrere.

Quibus ita consideratis, relinquitur tandem, contingentiarn esse tantùm illarum rerum & actionum, circa quas voluntas Hominis liberè agit: quales sunt Ethicæ, Politicæ, Oeconomicæ, eæque tàm malæ, quàm bonæ: ad externam disciplinam pertinentes, vel cum eadem pugnantes. Referuntur à nonnullis hûc etiam, sed nimis inscitè, naturales illæ hominis actiones, vivere, edere, bibere, dormire, & quæ sunt hujus generis aliæ. Certè velle, vivere non contingens est, sed Homini est naturale quiddam necessarium, à principio Naturæ communis, propter ipsum Hominem dependens: Sic velle, edere & bibere Naturale est, eoque necessarium ab eodem principio dependens, propter vitam. Hæc ergò principii ratione sunt necessaria, non voluntate libera. Verùm velle hoc bibere aut illud, voluntatis est intellectivæ & rectæ, si modum & ordinem teneat: pravæ verò si ab ordine deficiat: sed semper liberæ, sive teneat ordinem sive non: quia voluntas nostra, est internum principium ad plurima: quemadmodum Natura est principium internum, ad unum quid & determinatum suâ inclinatione movens. Undè nata est distinctio illa principii Naturalis & Voluntarii, quæ non in Philosophiâ modò: sed in Theologiâ etiam usum habet longè maximum: ut nimirùm earum rerum, quæ se non nisi uno modo habere possunt, Principium sit, & dicatur NATURA: Earum verò rerum, quæ variæ se habere possunt, principium sit & dicatur voluntas: Proptereà quòd Forma, per quam voluntas agit, non est una, sed multiplex, prout rationes multiplices percipiuntur intellectu, quæ ad voluntatem ab ipso deferuntur.

Controvertitur autem hoc loco satis graviter, quid statuendum sit de peccato, An illud sit contingens sive voluntarium: An verò necessarium: vel quod idem est, An Homo peccet necessariò, an verò contingenter? In quâ Quæstione varii variè se torquent, & non defuerunt ex Orthodoxis alioqui Theologis, qui statuerunt Hominem peccare, neque simpliciter necessariò, neque simpliciter contingenter: sed mixtâ quadam cum necessitate contingentiâ. Quam opinionem nos Autoribus suis defendendam relinquimus. Nos ad propositam quæstionem respondendum esse statuimus, per distinctionem, eamque geminam. Primùm enim distinguendum est Tempus præcedens lapsum Adamicum, ab eo, quod illum insecutum est. Nam ante lapsum Contingentia universalis in homine locum habebat: Ea enim libertas voluntatis Adamo erat concessa, ut tàm facilè possent non peccare, quàm peccare: & singulas atque universas actiones tùm Naturales, tùm voluntarias liberrimè ederet: & quô vellet, sese inclinaret, res naturales necessitate Naturæ, voluntarias verò libertate voluntatis occupans. Lapsus ergò primorum parentum voluntatis respectu planè fuit contingens, hoc est, neque necessarius, neque etiam impossibilis. Cæterùm postquàm jam per lapsum Natura nostra ita est corrupta, ut prona sit ad malum omni tempore, quæritur, Utrum jam peccatum sit necessarium, an Contingens? Hic posterior distinctio observanda fuerit, quæ inter peccatum Originale, & Actuale discernit. Nam quoad peccatum Originale sive corruptionem Naturæ nostræ, Contingentia locum non habet. Siquidem, non in libertate voluntatis nostræ: sed in Naturæ conditione est positum, ut jam non nisi peccato & pravis concupiscentiis infecti esse queamus: neque etiam labem hanc Naturalem, & internam omnium virium corporis & animæ pravitatem deponere aut exuere possimus. De quâ naturali corruptione tragicè admodum conqueritur Apostolus Rom. 7, 23. Video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meæ, & caprivantem me sub lege peccati, quæ est in membris meis. Proindè rationem hujus Naturalis corruptionis, Peccatum rectè dicitur Necessarium: Necessitate autem non absolutâ, sive Stoicâ: sed necessitate Physicâ & ἐξ ὑποθέσεως.

Cæterùm quoad Peccata Actualia, & illa quidem, quæ contra conscientiam designantur, nihil certè obstat, quin Contingentia ea nominemus: proptereà quòd liberè, & spontè ea committimus, rectæque rationi non obtemperamus, secundum illud Medeæ: Video meliora proboquè, Deteriora sequor: cum tamen in hâc vel illâ specie peccati abstinere homo animum possit à scelere & flagitio perpetrando: ut fur posset abstrahere manum à Contrectatione rei alienæ: adulter posset abstinere ab alterius conjuge: Scortator posset frena injicere vagis libidinibus: ebriosus posset sibi temperare à nimiâ ingurgitatione vini. Hinc natum est illud Augustini celebratissimum apophtegma: Peccatum non est, nisi quod est voluntarium: Quod quomodo suo respectu de Peccato Originis etiam verum sit, in diexodo illius Articuli ex professo ostendemus.

Jam vela contrahimus & Coronidis vice illud addimus, de quo apud Doctores Scholasticos anxiè quæsitum fuit: An videlicet de Deo quoquè & actionibus divinis prædicari possit Contingentia?

Quæ quæstio duabus itidem distinctionibus rectissimè expediri potest. Vel enim hic sensus est Quæstionis propositæ, An res prout Objectivè terminant Præscientiam divinam, habeant Naturam & Veritatem contingentiæ? Et hoc sensu Affirmativam simpliciter tenemus: cùm enim DEUS res præsciat, sicut ipsæ in se sunt: utique respectu Præscientiæ, & quatenùs objectivè ad eam sese habent, non amittunt Contingentiæ naturam & affectionem. Vel sensus dari potest iste: An res prout terminant divinam præscientiam, sint certæ: & quatenùs certò sunt futuræ, aliquando, eatenùs respectu præscientiæ non sint contingentes, sed necessariæ: tùm sanè simpliciter negamus, Contingentiam de DEO ejusque præscientiâ prædicari posse. Nam Contingentiæ status, uti Scholastici loquuntur, est in rebus, prout in seipsis, & ex naturâ suâ considerantur: desinit verò in iisdem, quando ad certitudinem divinæ præscientiæ appenduntur. Atque hinc verum est illud, quòd vulgò dicitur: Propositiones de futuro esse determinatæ veritatis secundum præscientiam divinam. Et rursus verum etiam illud, quod itidem vulgò dici solet: Futurorum contingentium non est determinata veritas. Nam quoad causam extrinsecam, scilicet DEI determinationem futurorum contingentium certissima est veritas: sed quoad causam propriam & internam scilicet, voluntatem hominis, certè eorundem futurorum contingentium non est determinata veritas. Voluntas enim hominis in se mutabilis, & ad utrumque objectorum habet se mutabiliter, Exempli gratiâ: Propositio hæc, Antichristum venturum præscivit DEUS, est Contingens, & est Necessaria. Contingens, quatenùs ipse Adventus Antichristi in se, & per se contingenter sese habuit. Potuisset enim non venire Antichristus, si Diabolus mysterium illud iniquitatis, uti Apostolus loquitur, operari noluisset. Necessaria verò, quatenùs DEUS vidit, Diabolum certò aliquando editurum in lucem Antichristum.

Posteriorem distinctionem observatu perquàm utilem, prodidit Bonaventura super lib. 1. sent. dist. 45. sic scribens: Contingentia consideratur in actu & in Effectu: Si loquimur de contingentiâ in Effectu, certè ea, non in nostro tantùm effectu est, sed etiam in multis, quæ à DEO sunt: Multa enim facit DEUS, quæ posset non facere nullo repugnante: Si verò loquimur de Contingentiâ in actu, quod voluntas modò vult aliquid, modò vel incipit, vel desinit aliquid velle: vel modò vult oppositum: id quod accidit in voluntate humanâ, unde etiam inter voluntatem & actum est differentia, ut voluntas neque semper sit in actu uno, neque in actu uniformi: jam verò divina voluntas, propter identitatem sui cum actu, omninò variari non potest, nec habet in se aliquam contingentiam: ideò DEUS etiam, licèt contingentia prævideat, contingenter tamen prævidere aut præscire, minimè est statuendus.


## 9 On Free Will


### Prolegomena

If in no other Article of the Christian Religion do dangerous reefs present themselves, which seem to block the royal and almost military path of investigating truth: certainly we discover that this happens to us regarding the present one. For as D. Augustine also noticed in his own time, This question, by which there is a dispute concerning the Free Will of the will, and the grace of GOD, is so difficult to discern, that when Free Will is defended, the grace of GOD seems to be denied: but when the grace of GOD is asserted, Free Will is thought to be taken away, lib. 1. de Pecc. Orig. cont. Pelag. c. 47. What? That in previous years, not only between B. Luther and Erasmus of Rotterdam: but also among several other theologians, otherwise addicted to the Augsburg Confession, this Article was so discussed and ventilated: that on account of the variety, as well as the obscurity, of the questions which were being treated, it obtained almost more shadows than light or perspicuity: not indeed by the fault of our theologians, but rather of the Adversaries, who did not distinguish accurately enough things heterogeneous from homogeneous, or things alien from proper: nor did they legitimately inform the state of the controversy: but even when informed, they Sophistically exchanged it with other questions, which in no way pertained to this forum. Hence it happened, that, when the State of the controversy was proposed here primarily to the disputants, Whether Man after the fall, from the proper powers of nature, can perfectly satisfy the Law of GOD? they, in the heat of the dispute, would slip away to other questions, concerning the hidden and revealed GOD, concerning the will of GOD regarding the business of our salvation, concerning the necessity and contingency of sin, and others of this kind, which did not explain the proposed state of the controversy, but entangled it; did not illustrate it, but obscured it. Therefore, the very necessity of the matter seems to demand that, before we make a legitimate approach to the investigation of the truth itself, or to the state of the controversy, we remove from the midst those obstacles in particular which seem able to cast some delay, so that we may afterwards proceed with an unoffending foot: this we shall perform in the place of προλεγομένων, but in such a way that we reduce the whole matter to only two general heads. The first will be, as it were, a προπαρασκευαστικόν preparatory [discourse], concerning the Philippean Treatment itself, which in the different editions of the Loci presents itself regarding the present Article. The latter, however, will be both ϑετικόν and ἀφαιρετικόν, showing at the beginning what is the proper signification and affection of the otherwise ambiguous words, Free Will: what also is its Subject, what its Object, what Definition is to be established: and finally what true, proper, and legitimate state of the Controversy can and ought to be given in this Article?

Latin:

SIn nullo alio Religionis Christianæ Articulo, periculosi sese offerunt scopuli, qui regiam & quasi militarem investigâdæ veritatis viam, in tercludere videntur: certè circa præsentem id usu nobis venire deprehendimus. Nam uti D. Augustinus suo etiam tempore animadvertit, Quæstio hæc, quâ de Libero voluntatis Arbitrio, & DEI gratiâ disputatur ita ad discernendum est difficilis, ut quando defenditur Liberum Arbitrium, negari DEI gratiâ videatur: quando autem asseritur DEI gratiâ, Liberum Arbitrium putetur auferri lib. 1. de Pecc. Orig. cont. Pelag. c. 47. Quid? quod superioribus annis, non modò inter B. Lutherum, & Erasmum Roterodamum: sed & nonnullos Theologos alios, confessioni Augustanæ alioquin addictos, Articulus iste ita est discussus & ventilatus: ut ob quæstionum, quæ tractabantur, tùm varietatem, tùm obscuritatem, plus fermè tenebrarum, quàm lucis aut perspicuitatis ille nactus sit: non nostrorum quidem Theologorum, sed Adversariorum potiùs culpâ, qui ἐπεγγένα ab homogeneis, sive aliena à propriis, non satis accuratè discernebant: neque statum controversiæ legitimè informabant: sed informatum etiam, cum aliis quæstionibus, ad forum hoc minimè pertinentibus, Sophisticè permutabant. Hinc factum, ut, cum disputantibus hic potissimùm controversiæ Status esset propositus, An Homo post lapsum, ex propriis naturæ viribus, possit Legi DEI perfectè satisfacere? illi in fervore disputationis delaberentur ad Quæstiones alias, de DEO abscondito & revelato, de voluntate DEI circa salutis nostræ negotium, de Necessitate & Contingentiâ peccati: & hujus generis alias, quæ propositum controversiæ Statum non explicabant, sed implicabant: non illustrabant, sed obscurabant. Proindè ipsa rei necessitas flagitare videtur, ut priusquam ad ipsam veritatis investigationem, sive controversiæ Statu legitimum accessum faciamus: illos potissimùm scopulos è medio removeamus, qui remoram aliquam injicere posse videntur, quò minùs postmodùm inoffenso pede progredi queamus : id quod προλεγομένων loco, sed ita, præstabimus, ut rem universam, ad duo tantùm capita generalia revocemus. Prius erit, quasi προπαρασκευαστικόν præparatorium, de ipsâ nimirùm Tractatione Philippéa, quæ in diversis Locorum editionibus, circa præsentem Articulum se offert. Posterius verò erit tùm ϑετικόν, tùm ἀφαιρετικόν, initiò ostendens, quæ propria sit, vocum alioquin ambiguarum, Liberi Arbitrii, significatio & affectio : quod item ejus Subjectum, quod Objectum, quæ Definitio constituenda : & tandem quis verus, proprius ac legitimus Controversiæ status, hoc in Articulo, dari possit & debeat?


### Prolegomena: Chapter I Of the Prolegomena Concerning the Philippean Treatment

CHAPTER I.

Of the Prolegomena,

Concerning the Philippean Treatment.

That which is read to have been answered long ago by certain Philosophers who objected to themselves a shameful defection from the doctrine of their Preceptors: Plato is a friend, Socrates is a friend: but truth is a greater friend: that we can use with better right, against the insults of those who today accuse us of I know not what defection from the preceptor Philip Melanchthon. For Philip is a friend, Luther is a friend: but he is a greater friend, who is truth itself, CHRIST THE SAVIOR. But if therefore Philip, having suffered something human, deviated somewhat from the path of truth: who among the pious would blame us, if we have held a greater regard for truth than for human authority. Now indeed if we examine the Philippean Treatment, which was produced by the author himself through various editions, a little more accurately: it can certainly be denied by no reason, that Philip did not always remain sufficiently consistent with himself concerning this Article: nor that he preserved the form of sound words, and the analogy of faith, safe and sound. And at the beginning indeed in the years 21, 22, 23, 24, and 25, the Theological Hypotyposes of Philip Melanchthon were produced, printed at Wittenberg, Strasbourg, and Basel, exhibiting to us that treatment of this Place, which breathes ὀρϑοδοξίαν in every part, if you except that one thing, that he then establishes that divine predestination takes away from Man all freedom of acting whatsoever, so much so, that all things happen necessarily, nothing contingently. Which error, however, he corrected and retracted in subsequent editions, writing thus among other things: Let us flee those absurd Stoic imaginations concerning Fate which, on account of divine government, take away freedom from the will: For it must be conceded, that Apostolic Scripture attributes to man even now after the fall, some freedom of choosing those things which are subject to reason. And a little later: This Manichaean imagination is a horrible lie, and minds must be led away from this error, and taught that Free Will does something: as is evident from the Edition of the year 35 and 38, inscribed to Henry King of England: and seen, read, and approved by our B. Luther.

And would that he had remained constant in this very truth: then indeed there would be nothing that we would desire in Philip regarding the orthodoxy of the present passage: But I do not know by what fate it happened that in the passage of time, and indeed in the final edition of the places, which occurred in the year 1548: he made a divorce from Luther, and then undertook a manifest defense of Synergism: and then openly revealed an agreement with Erasmus of Rotterdam against Luther. This latter point is most clearly evident from the fact that he interpolated into those later places of his the definition of Free Will, first devised by the Scholastics, but afterwards thrust upon the Church of GOD by Erasmus: which had been rejected by Luther with great Spirit as erroneous and heretical, and commended it to the Church of GOD as Orthodox: writing among other things thus: Know that GOD wishes to convert us in this way, when, stirred by the promise of the Gospel, we struggle with ourselves, we call upon Him, and we fight against our diffidence, and other vicious affections: Therefore some ancients (Erasmus) said thus: Free Will in Man is the faculty of applying oneself to grace, that is, he hears the promise, and tries to assent, and casts away sins against Conscience.

But may the former point become clearer than the midday sun from the whole treatment, which indeed deals with human powers after the fall, regarding the act of conversion. For what? Do they not manifestly smack of Synergism, nay, Papism, which the Author wished to encrust with these words, now that Luther is dead: God institutes the ministry, so that the voice may be received, so that the mind may think upon and embrace the promise, and while we fight against diffidence, the Holy Spirit may at the same time be effective in us. Thus therefore to those who excuse their cessation, because they think that Free Will does nothing, I answer: Nay, the command of GOD is eternal and immovable, that you should obey the voice of the Gospel, that you should hear the Son of GOD, that you should acknowledge the mediator. How foul are these sins, to be unwilling to look upon the Mediator, the Son of GOD, given to the human race? I cannot, you will say: Nay, in some way you can, and when you sustain yourself with the voice of the Gospel, know that you are HELPED by GOD when you ask, and know that the Holy Spirit is effective in that consolation. And after a few words: Since the promise is universal, and there are no contradictory wills in GOD, it is necessary that there be IN US some cause of difference, why Saul is cast away, David is received, that is, it is necessary that there be some dissimilar action in these two. To which also pertain the preceding words, which sound thus: It has often been said that those thinking about GOD ought to start from the Word of GOD, not to seek GOD without His word: and when we start from the word, here three causes of a good action concur, the Word of GOD, the Holy Spirit, and the human Will assenting, and not resisting the Word of GOD. For he could cast it off, as Saul casts it off of his own accord: But when the mind, hearing and sustaining itself, does not resist, does not indulge in diffidence, but with the Holy Spirit also helping, tries to assent, in this struggle the will is not idle.

This turning or rather defection of Philip from the doctrine of our Luther became so well known that it was noted and observed by this name both by our own people and by the Romanist Adversaries. As for our own, it is manifest that the incomparable Theologian Dr. Martin Chemnitz, among others, even because of this lapse of Philip, gravely judged that his Corpus Doctrinae could not and ought not to be held as the norm and form of the purer Evangelical Doctrine, just as we have demonstrated that more fully, and indeed to the eye, in the general Prolegomena prefixed to the Treatment of the Philippic places. As for the Romanist Adversaries, it is certain that they congratulated themselves wonderfully that Philip had passed from the Lutheran to the Roman Church. Concerning which matter Wilhelmus Lindanus writes thus, book 3 of the Evangelical Panoply, chapter 16. I cannot but praise to the highest degree the ingenuousness of Melanchthon, who, having better searched out the truth, was not ashamed to change his doctrine, which in those Commonplaces, poured forth in the heat of youth in the year 21, he had so preached about the lack of any freedom of man in works both external and internal, that he had deemed this little book of Melanchthon worthy of an Ecclesiastical Canon, and having become more learned, to sing a palinode of his youthful error: as is clear in the Commonplaces published in the year 52 and elsewhere with more prudent judgment and greater erudition.

Stanislaus Hosius also greatly exaggerates this very thing, in his book on the life, sects, and dogmas of heretics, under the heading of Melanchthon: In that, he says, which is the hinge of the matter, which is the throat of the whole cause (namely, in the doctrine of Free Will), Philip and his followers, who are of the Augsburg Confession, dared to separate themselves openly from their master Martin Luther by holding different opinions: What else was this than to condemn Luther of heresy and impiety? And in truth, the hinge of Lutheran doctrine turns on this one dogma of free will, which cannot fall without all things, especially those written by him concerning Justification and matters pertaining to it, collapsing at the same movement. Robert Bellarmine also notes this very thing, in book 4 on grace and free will, chapter 5, openly accusing Philip on this account of inconstancy and defection from Luther.

Since these things are so, it should seem strange to no one that both by the authors of the Christian Concord and by any more sincere theologians, the opinion of Philip concerning Free Will, which exists today in the common copies, is rejected and condemned as Synergistic, or rather Popish.

Some fault-finders clamor at this point, and as the shield of Achilles, they hold up to us the authority of the blessed Luther, who did not hesitate to adorn the Loci of Philip Melanchthon with a far more honorable eulogy and to commend them for their purity. And indeed, it cannot be denied that Luther, in his book against Erasmus on the Enslaved Will of Man, among other things, also produced these words: It seems superfluous to reply to your arguments, which have been so often refuted by me before, and indeed trampled and utterly crushed by the invincible little book of Melanchthon, which in my judgment is worthy not only of immortality but also of an Ecclesiastical Canon. But the matter is safe, and the authority of Luther does not hinder us in the least,

Latin:

CAPUT I.

Προλεγομένων,

De Tractatione Philippéa.

Quod jam olim Philosophis quibusdam turpem defectionem à Præceptorum doctrinâ ipsi objicientibus respondisse legitur : Amicus Plato, amicus Socrates : sed magis amica veritas : illud nos potiore jure usurpare possumus, adversus eorum insultus, qui nescio cujus defectionis, à præceptore Philippo Melanchthone hodiè nos insimulant. Est enim amicus Philippus, amicus Lutherus : sed magis amicus ille, qui ipsissima est veritas CHRISTUS SERVATOR. Quod si ergò Philippus humani aliquid passus, à veritatis tramite nônihil deflextit : quis pius vitio nobis verterit, si potiorem veritatis, quàm humanæ autoritatis rationem habuerimus. Jam verò si Tractationem Philippéam, quæ per diversas editiones ab autore ipso prodita est, paulò accuratiùs expendamus : negari profectò nullâ ratione potest, neque Philippum sibi semper circa Articulum istum satis constitisse : neque etiam formam sanorum verborum, fideique analogiam, sartam tectam conservasse. Acinitiò quidem An 21. 22. 23. 24. & 25. prodierunt Hypotyposes Theologicæ Philippi MelanchthonisVVitebergæ, Argentorati, Basilææ impressæ eam nobis Loci hujus tractationem exhibentes, quæ ὀρϑοδοξίαν ex omni parte resipit, si unum illud excipias, quòd tùm statuit, divinam prædestinationem Homini adimere omnem prorsus agendi libertatem, usque adeò, ut omnia necessariò, nihil contingenter eveniat. Quem tamen errorem in subsequentibus editionibus correxit & retractavit, sic inter reliqua scribens : Stoicas illas de Fato absurdas imaginationes quæ propter divinam gubernationem adimunt libertatem voluntati, fugiamus : Concedendum enim est, quod Scriptura Apostolica tribuat homini etiam nunc post lapsum, libertatem aliquam deligendi ea, quæ sunt subjecta rationi. Et paulò post:Hæc Manichæa imaginatio, horribile mendacium est, & ab hoc errore mentes abducendæ sunt, & docendæ, agere aliquid Liberum Arbitrium : uti patet ex Editione anni 35. & 38. Henrico Regi Angliæ inscriptæ : & à B.Luth.nostro visa, lecta & approbata.

Atq; utinam in hac ipsa veritate constans perstitisset: tum sane nihil esset, quod circa praesentis Loci ὀρθοδοξίαν, in Philippo desideraremus: Sed nescio, quo fato factum, ut progressu temporis, & quidem in editione postrema locoru, quae in A. C. 1548. incidit: a Luthero divortium fecerit, & tum manifestum patrocinium Synergismi susceperit: tum consensum cum Erasmo Roterodamo contra Lutherum palam prodiderit. Posterius hoc vel inde luculentissime patet, quod definitionem Liberi Arbitrij, a Scholasticis primum excogitatam, postmodum vero ab Erasmo Ecclesiae DEI obtrusam: a Luthero autem tanquam erroneam & haereticam magno Spiritu rejectam, Locis illis suis postremis interpolavit, & tanquam Orthodoxam Ecclesiae DEI commendavit: sic inter reliqua scribens: Scito DEUM hoc modo velle nos convertere, cum promissione Evangelij excitati luctamur nobiscum, invocamus, & repugnamus diffidentiae nostrae, & alijs vitiosis affectibq: Ideo veteres aliqui (Erasmo) sic dixerunt: Liberum Arbitrium in Homine facultate esse, applicandi se ad gratia, id est, audit promissionem, & assentiri conatur, & abjicit peccata contra Conscientiam.

Priq vero illud, ex tota tractatione Sole meridiano clarius elucescat, quae quidem agit de viribq humanis post lapsum, quoad conversionis actu. Quid enim? An no Synergismum, imo Papismu manifeste resipiunt, quae defuncto jam Luthero, his verbis incrustare Autor voluit: Instituit Deus ministeriu, ut vox accipiatur, ut promissione mens cogitet, & amplectatur, & dum repugnamus diffidentiae, Spiritus Sanctus simul in nobis sit efficax. Sic igitur illis, qui cessationem suam excusant, quia putant nihil agere Liberu Arbitrium, respondeo: Imo mandatu DEI aeternum & immotu est, ut voci Evangelij obtemperes, ut Filium DEI audias, ut agnoscas mediatore. Quam tetra sunt haec peccata, nolle aspicere donatu generi humano Mediatorem Filium DEI? Non possum, inquies: Imo aliquo modo potes, & cum te voce Evangelij sustent as, ADJUVARI te a DEO petito, & scito Spiritum Sanctum efficace esse in ea consolatione. Et post pauca: Cum promissio sit universalis, nec sint in DEO contradictoriae voluntates necesse est, IN NOBIS esse aliqua discriminis causam, cur Saul abjiciatur, David recipiatur, id est, necesse est, aliquam esse actione dissimile in his duobus. Quo pertinent etiam praecedentia, quaesic sonant: Saepe dictum est, cogitantes de DEO oportere ordiri a Verbo DEI, non quaerere DEUM sine suo verbo: cumq, ordimur a verbo, hic concurrunt tres causae bonae actionis, Verbum DEI, Spiritus Sanctus, & humana Voluntas assenticus, nec repugnans Verbo DEI. Posset enim excutere, ut excutit Saul sua sponte: Sed cum mens audiens ac se sustentans, non repugnat, non indulget diffidentiae, sed adjuvante etiam Spiritu Sancto conatur assentiri, in hoc certamine voluntas non est otiosa.

Haec inflexio vel potius defectio Philippi a doctrina B Lutheri nostri ita innotuit, ut tum a nostratibus, tum ab Adversarijs Romanensibus hoc nomine notata & observata fuerit. Quoad nostros, manifestum est, incomparabilem Theologum D. Martinum Chemnitium, inter cæteros, vel hunc etiam ob lapsum Philippeum, graviter censuisse, Corpus Doctrinæ ipsius, pro normâ & formâ Doctrinæ Evangelicæ purioris, haberi nec posse, nec debere, quemadmodum fusiùs illud, in Prolegomenis generalibus, Tractationi locorum Philippicorum præmissis, à nobis est, & quidem ad oculum demonstratum. Quoad Adversarios Romanenses, mirificè illos sibi gratulatos fuisse constat, quod Philippus à Lutheranâ ad Romanam Ecclesiam transierit. Quâ de re sic scribit Wilhelmus Lindanus, lib. 3. Panopliæ Evangelicæ, cap. 16. Non possum non summoperè laudare Melanchthonis ingenuitatem, qui doctrinam suam, Locis illis Communibus, anno 21. per adolescentiæ calorem effusis, de nullâ hominis in operibus tam externis, quàm internis libertate per Lutherum adeò prædicatam, ut libellum hunc Melanchthonis Canone dignum censuerit Ecclesiastico, non erubuerit veritatem meliùs perscrutatus permutare, atq; factus eruditior, sui erroris juvenilis palinodiam canere: uti liquet Locis Communibus anno 52. & aliàs prudentiori cum judicio, ac majori cum eruditione in lucem editis.

Quod ipsum valdè exaggerat etiam Stanislaus Hosius, libro de vitâ, sectis & dogmatis hæreticorum, sub titulo Melanchthonis: In eo, inquiens, quod rerum cardo, quod totius causæ jugulu est (scilicet in doctrinâ de Libero Arbitrio) ausus est Philippus cum suis, qui Augustanæ Confessionis sunt, à Magistro suo Martino Luthero se palam, diversis sentiendo segregare: Quod quid aliud fuit, quàm Lutherum hæreseos & impietatis damnare? Et reverà cardo Lutheranæ doctrinæ vertitur, in hoc uno dogmate de libero arbitrio, quod ruere non potest, quin simul eodem motu labefactata concidant omnia, quæ de Justificatione præsertim, deq; rebus ad illam pertinentibus ab eo scripta sunt. Animadvertit hoc ipsum etiam Robertus Bellarminus, lib. 4. de gratiâ & libero Arbitrio, cap. 5. hoc nomine Philippum inconstantiæ & defectionis à Luthero apertè insimulans.

Quæ cum ita se habeant, mirum videri debet nemini, quod tùm ab autoribus Christianæ Concordiæ, tùm à quibusvis Theologis sincerioribus, sententia Philippi, de Libero Arbitrio, quæ hodiè in consuetis Exemplaribus extat, tanquam Synergistica, imò Pontificia rejicitur & damnatur.

Obstrepunt hoc loco nonnulli Φιλαπελζοντες, & ceu Achillis clypeum nobis obvertunt B. Lutheri autoritatem, qui Locos Philippi Melanchthonis longè honestiore elogio exornare, & à puritate commendare, minimè dubitaverit. Et profectò negari non potest, quin Lutherus in suo adversus Erasmum libro, de Servo Hominis Arbitrio, inter reliqua etiam isthæc prodiderit: Supervacaneum videtur tuis argumentis, antea à me quoquè toties confutatis, conculcatis verò & prorsus contritis per Melanchthonis invictum libellum, meo judicio non solùm immortalitate, sed & Canone Ecclesiastico dignum. Verùm salva res est, & nihil quicquam Lutheri autoritas nobis officit,


### On the name of Free Will

if we consider only this task, namely in what year that book of Luther against Erasmus was brought to light, it is a fact that even the Philippists themselves cannot but know was done in the year '25. It is therefore too gross an imposture if that which B. Luther judged concerning the first edition of the Loci and its sincerity is applied to that edition which was brought to light only after the death of Luther, and did not exist in the nature of things while he was alive, much less was seen, read, or approved by him. The atrocity of this imposture is evident even from the fact that the compiler of the works of Philip judged that first little book of ὑποτυπώσεων, concerning which Luther allows that encomium, to be clearly unworthy of being given a place among the other writings of Philip, but wished it to be struck from the hands and memory of posterity: a truly cunning plan. For he thought that it would come to pass that Luther's judgment would be accepted only concerning the latest edition, which today alone is commended to the Church of God. From this single fact, a judgment can and ought to be made concerning the candor of the Philippists. Furthermore, regarding the rest of the treatment of this Locus, as the latest edition has set it forth, it is completed in five parts primarily. For in the beginning, the author argues against Laurentius Valla and others who strip the human will of all freedom, on the grounds that all things happen by the decree of God. The author rightly warns, however, that this question concerning the necessity and contingency of things and human actions should not be mixed with the question of free will, since in this place the discussion is more about the infirmity than the natural faculty of the will. Then, indeed, he shows what is meant by free will in the present discussion, namely the mind and will of man together. Since this assertion has given rise and occasion to various questions, and indeed has not a little implicated the present discussion, it will certainly have to be seen how this decision of Philip can and ought to be admitted, which the second chapter of the prolegomena will explain. Thirdly, the author informs the state of the controversy, namely that which was most especially agitated between our people and the Romanists: whether, and to what extent, the human will can obey the law of God? To which question the author responds by way of a distinction, showing that for a man not yet reborn, some freedom is to be granted in external matters, but in spiritual matters, he cannot provide perfect or complete obedience to the law of God. Hence, in the fourth place, he makes a transition to the question concerning the conversion of a man not yet reborn, showing how the Holy Spirit is effective, namely through the heard or contemplated voice of the Gospel. The author treats this whole question against the Manichaeans and Enthusiasts in such a way that he indeed rightly teaches that the Holy Spirit does not work the conversion of man except through the ministry of the Gospel. But in the meantime, he entangles and implicates himself in the snares of synergism, as was shown a little earlier. Finally, he institutes a grave complaint concerning various objects and external impediments which stand in the way of even the reborn being able to use their freedom rightly, and as a kind of colophon, he responds to two sayings of Jerome which, in appearance and according to the surface of the letter, seem to suggest that the law of God is possible for man to observe even after the fall.

This entire Philippean treatment reveals those two primary states of the controversy concerning which a dispute still exists today in our churches, both with the Romanists and with the Synergists, as we shall show expressly if we have first explained the other chapter of the prolegomena.

Latin:

si illud tantùm pensi habeamus, quo nimirùm anno liber iste Lutheri contra Erasmum in lucem prodierit, id quod anno 25. factum esse, vel ipsis Philippistis, non potest non esse notißimũ. Nimis ergò crassa impostura est, si id, quod de primâ Locorum editione & sincerâ B. Lutherus judicavit, ad eam editionem accommodetur: quæ post obitum demùm Lutheri in Lucem prodijt, ac ipso vivente in rerum naturâ non extitit, nedũ ab ipso visa, lecta aut approbata fuit. Patet imposturæ hujus atrocitas vel indè etiam, quod Compilator operum Philippi, primũ istum libellum ὑποτυπώσεων, de quo Lutherus encomium istud tolerat, indignum planè judicavit, cui locum inter cætera Philippi scripta tribueret: sed manibus & memoriæ posteritatis excussum esse voluit: astuto sanè consilio. Sic enim futurum arbitratus est, ut Lutheri judicium non nisi de postremâ editione, quæ hodiè sola Ecclesiæ DEI commendatur, acciperetur. Ex quo vel unico facto de Philippistarum candore fieri potest, & debet judicium. Cæterùm quoad reliquam Loci hujus Tractationem, prout quidem postrema editio eam expedijt, quinquè potissimùm membris ea absolvitur. Initiò enim disputat Autor contra Laurentiũ Vallam, & alios, detrahentes voluntati hominis omnẽ libertatem, propterea quòd omnia fiant decernente DEO. Rectè a. admonet Autor, Quæstioné hanc de Necessitate & Contingentiâ rerum atq; actionũ humanarum, non esse miscendam quæstioni de Libero Arbitrio: Siquidem hoc loco magis de infirmitate, quàm de naturali facultate voluntatis disputetur. Deindè verò ostendit, quid in præsenti disputatione dicatur Liberum Arbitrium, nempè Mens & Voluntas Hominis conjunctim. Quæ assertio cum varijs quæstionibus ansam & occasionem præbuerit, imò præsentem disputationem haud parùm implicaverit, videndum utiq; fuerit, quomodo hæc decisio Philippi, & quatenùs admitti possit & debeat: id quod alterum προλεγομένων caput expediet. Tertiò informat Autor Statum Controversiæ, eũ nimirùm qui inter nostros & Romanenses vel maximè agitabatur: An videlicet, & quatenùs voluntas humana poßit obedire legi DEI? Ad quam quæstionem Autor per distinctionem respondet, ostendens Homini, nondum renato in externis aliquam concedendam esse libertatem: In Spiritualibus verò non posse perfectam sive integram Legi DEI præstare obedientiam. Hinc quarto loco transitum facit, ad quæstionem de Conversione hominis nondum renati: ostendens quomodo Spiritus Sanctus sit efficax: nempè per vocem Evangelij auditam seu cogitatam. Quam totam quæstionem contra Manichæos & Enthusiastas ita pertractat Autor, ut rectè quidem doceat, Spiritum Sanctum non operari Conversionem Hominis, nisi per Ministerium Evangelij. Sed interim ipse semetipsum Synergismi cassibus irretiat & implicet: uti paulò ante ostensum. Tandẽ gravem querelã instituit de varijs objectis & impedimentis externis, quæ obstant quò minùs etiam Renati suâ Libertate rectè uti possint: & Colo phonis quasi loco respondet ad duo dicta Hieronymi, quæ in speciem & secundum superficiem literę innuere videntur, Legem DEI, Homini etiam post lapsum, esse observatu possibilem.

Hæc universa Tractatio Philippéa, duos illos prodit Controversiæ Status primarios, de quibus hodieq; nostris Ecclesiis, tùm cum Romanensibus, tùm cum Synergistis intercedit Disputatio: quemadmodum ex professo, id ostendemus, si priùs alterum προλεγομένων Caput expediverimus.


### On the name of Free Will: Chapter II. Of the Prolegomena

CHAPTER II. Of the Prolegomena.

Not only concerning the thing itself, but also concerning the words or terms by which this article is designated, and their true and legitimate use and proper meaning, it has been asked and disputed long ago, and is still variously controverted today. This matter has indeed given birth to many and intricate questions, which we shall hardly be able to treat more correctly than if we examine each one in order a little more accurately.

And in the beginning, there were not lacking, nor are there lacking today, those to whom the title of this article seems too insolent and tacitly to patronize Pelagianism or at least Synergism. They prefer, therefore, to inscribe this Locus concerning human powers rather than concerning free will, so that they can hardly bear to hear the latter and commonly received term. Although the zeal of these people does not seem to be entirely worthy of disapproval, because even the smallest things that seem to be joined with some danger are to be avoided very studiously, yet if it is permitted to confess what the case is, it is most clearly evident that the danger which they fear can least of all be avoided by this method. For whether you use this title or that, the matter comes to exactly the same thing, so that upon hearing at least the term 'human powers,' someone could conceive the opinion as if man were so much the master of his own powers, and thus of his mind and will, that he could turn it in either direction, as much to good as to evil, from himself. Furthermore, in a simple term and in an abstract consideration of the thing and the words, since there is no proposition contained therein, nor is any implication of a concrete immediately made, that ancient title is certainly being dragged into suspicion by some people entirely in vain. And why, I ask, do these censors not also abstain from the appellation of the image of God in man, which seems to be joined with the same, if not greater, danger? Now if the appellation of the image of God in man ought not to seem suspicious to us for the reason that it was lost through the fall of our first parents, then certainly nothing will stand in the way of calling that faculty in man 'free will,' which, although it is not remaining now, was once most perfect in him, unless perhaps through a remarkable ἀῥῥωσίαν τῆς διανοίας someone might wish to contend that not even the appellation of some lost good ought to remain in the Church of God.

Nor does it stand in the way of this response of ours that neither the Latin word for free will nor the Greek τὸ ἀυτεξύσιον is read in the Scriptures.

For if the thing itself is not fictitious or imaginary, but has its foundations expressed in the Scriptures, why, I ask, would there be a need to wrangle over the terms of the words? Especially since we do not use them for the purpose that the human mind might grasp from this a subject for becoming puffed up: but that, having been taught from what a degree of dignity it has fallen, it might learn to acknowledge its own infirmity, to lay aside confidence in itself, to magnify the benefits acquired for the human race in healing this lethal wound by the Son of God, and to piously venerate the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, not even in this way do some Aristarchuses acquiesce, but they even carp at and gnaw at the title of this article on this account, because it clearly savors of a childish pleonasm. For since, according to the common custom of speaking, Arbitrium is nothing other than the right and power of acting according to one's pleasure, and thus by its own property, of itself, it implies the condition of Liberty: since indeed that does not deserve to be called arbitrary, for which there is not a free power of either choosing or rejecting in either direction: it certainly seems to be entirely redundant when the term Liberty is also added to the word Arbitrium, as if Arbitrium could exist without Liberty. But the reasons for this fact are also far more evident and ready at hand. For first, the ancients, in the formation of this title, looked not so much to the propriety and breadth of the words themselves as to the subject in which Free Will ought to have its seat: which, since it is twofold according to the two diverse faculties of the soul, namely the Mind or intellect, and the heart or will, they certainly wished to note those distinct subjects with two distinct words with grave counsel: in such a way indeed that the word Arbitrium is to be referred to the Mind or Reason, but the appellation of Liberty to the heart or will. For thus it is provided by nature that Reason determines or judges concerning the good or evil proposed, but the will, approaching, finally chooses what is to be followed. Hence Augustine says that Free Will is the faculty of Reason and Will: or, as Origen in book 3. περὶ ἀρχῶν, explains the matter more clearly; that it is the faculty of Reason for discerning good or evil: but of the Will for choosing either one. Then, by this doubled appellation, the ancients wished to note the excellence of the degree in the liberty of the human will: just as if someone were to name that faculty, to which no impediment is placed anywhere, not only simply Liberty, but with an anadiplosis, most free Liberty. By which method they looked especially to the will of Man, which alone comes into controversy in this place: although from the condition of this, a judgment can most rightly be made concerning the other also, namely the powers of the human intellect: which will appear more clearly from what follows.

Furthermore, there was also anxious inquiry and dispute concerning the use of the words: some constituting the will of Man as Free, others as Servile: whence a contradiction was also objected to our Theologians: as can be seen in Bellarmine, book 4, on Grace, and

on Free Will, chapter 5, who accuses the blessed Luther of inconsistency, because he now denied Free Will, and soon granted it. But this apparent contradiction is easily removed if we rightly distinguish the correct use of the words from their abuse. Because the word (Free) has a great kinship with spontaneous: but sometimes it is also opposed to simple necessity, or to coercion or the violent: therefore it happens that, according to the diverse acceptance of the word, without any implication of contradiction, Free Will can rightly be both granted and denied. So that this may be explained more conveniently, it should be observed that some Theologians oppose Free to Servile: but others to coercion or the violent: the former explaining the matter properly, the latter improperly and catachrestically. For properly and directly, Free is not opposed except to servile: but spontaneous is opposed to coercion or the violent. When therefore Luther writes that Man has a Servile Will, he then considers the proper signification of the word, and wished to intimate that the will of Man in spiritual matters is clearly servile, and can do nothing of itself. But when he grants Free Will to Man in spiritual matters, then he opposes Free to coerced. In which respect, indeed, the will of man is free, even in extreme servitude, depravity, and the necessity of sinning. Since it is not snatched to sinning by a violent or coerced motion, but by a most free one. To whose will if coercion were ascribed, then neither the true reason nor the definition of will or of sin could subsist. Thus it is asserted by Orthodox Theologians even today, that in those not yet reborn, the will is both Free and Servile, with respect to evil: Servile indeed, by reason of natural corruption: but Free by reason of the will, which is not compelled to sin by any violence; but by its own nature is prone and inclined: nor is it compelled to its own Conversion in a violent manner: as will be shown below. Therefore, since the affirmation or negation is not made concerning the same reason of the same thing, no contradiction at all is implied.

But another observation also pertains here, which must be duly noted in this place concerning the equivocation of the word will: which, not being weighed, it happens that in the writings of our own Theologians also, a great diversity presents itself, some asserting Free Will, others denying it: indeed, one and the same writer now affirming it, now denying it. The term Arbitrium or will is therefore taken sometimes for the other faculty of the soul, namely the very substance of the will: whose act is the simple to velle. By which method and respect, hardly anyone would deny Free Will to Man, unless he had dared to affirm that Man is destitute of or lacks this faculty of the Soul. Whose stupidity would deservedly be exploded by all: since the faculty or power of the Soul cannot be denied, unless the whole substance of the Soul is denied: because this is nothing other than what its faculties are: and with one faculty lost, it itself must necessarily perish. Sometimes, however, by the term of Choice and will, a certain habit or quality is denoted, which is determined for freely choosing the good and freely fleeing the evil. In which respect it is most rightly denied that Free Choice remains in man after the fall.

It is clear, however, from this dispute, what Subject of Free Choice is to be established: and indeed the proper and adequate one. There are those who contend that the whole Man must be given as the Subject of this liberty: because the whole man is the whole principle of acting: and the whole Man is said to will and not to will: which, in a confused and more general sense, perhaps no one would deny can be admitted. But if you weigh more carefully the discrete operations of Man, distinct according to the powers of the soul, it will be evident that neither the whole Man, nor even the whole Soul: But only the faculty of the will can properly be established as the adequate Subject of Free Choice: not that the judgment of the mind is entirely excluded, but rather presupposed: in the very way in which, among the faculties of the soul, every superior one does not indeed have all the inferior ones included within itself: but only presupposes them: so that from the sentient faculty there is not vegetation itself: nor is this sensation: yet each faculty and operation presupposes the other. In exactly the same way, Free Choice does not indeed have its own proper seat in the Mind: yet it is never and nowhere, unless it has the prior integrity of mind and judgment; from which it has its dependence, both from the front and from the back. For from the front of the mind is the right judgment, to which the will in free choice obediently accommodates itself: From the back, however, is the appetite and the motion of the inferior powers, which promptly attempers itself to the obedience of a good will. When, therefore, the Mind judges about desiring the good and fleeing the evil from its own proper and peculiar faculty: and the will, supervening, embraces the Good shown by the Mind, and flees and rejects the evil without any impediment, then it is most rightly established that the proper place, function, and office of Free Choice is in this operation. Hence it is that it has been not ineptly put forth by some: that Free Choice has its roots indeed in the Mind or reason: But that it shines forth most of all in the will.

Latin:

CAPUT II. Προλεγομένων.

NOn de reipsâ modò, sed & de vocabulis sive terminis, quibus Articulus iste indigitatur, eorundemq; vero ac legitimo usu, propriâquè affectione, & jam olim quæsitum disputatumq; fuit: & hodieq; variè controvertitur. Quæ sanè res, tùm benè multas, tùm intricatas peperit quæstiones, quas vix rectiùs pertractabimus, quàm si ordine singulas paulò accuratiùs examinaverimus.

Ac initiò quidem non defuerunt, neq; hodiè defunt, quibus Titulus Articuli hujus videtur insolentior esse, & Pelagianismo, vel certè Synergismo tacitè patrocinari. Malunt proindè Locum hunc de viribus humanis, quàm de Libero Arbitrio inscribere: ita ut vix posteriorem istum, & vulgò receptum Terminum audire sustineant. Quanquam verò studium istorum haud omninò videtur esse improbandum, propterea quod vel minima quæq;, quæ quidem cum periculo aliquo videntur esse conjuncta, studiosè admodum sunt vitanda: si tamen, quod res est, fateri liceat, minimè omnium, periculum quod isti metuunt, hoc pacto evitari posse, clarissimè liquet. Nam sive hoc, sive illo utaris titulo res eôdem planè recidit: ita ut audito saltem virium humanarum termino, concipere aliquis eam opinionem possit, quasi Homo virium suarum, & sic mentis atq; voluntatis suæ ita sit Dominus, ut flectere eam in utramvis partem, tàm bonam quàm malam ex seipso possit. Deindè, in termino simplici, & abstractâ rei & vocabulorum consideratione, cùm neq; enunciatio aliqua insit, neq; statim aliqua fiat concreti implicatio: utiq; frustrà omninò, antiquus ille titulus, hodiè in suspicionem à nonnullis rapitur. Et cur quæso censores isti non etiam abstinent ab appellatione imaginis DEI in homine: quæ cum eodem, si non majore periculo conjuncta videtur? Jam si non ideò Imaginis DEI in Homine appellatio, suspecta nobis videri debet, quia per lapsum protoplastorum ea est amissa: utiq; nihil etiam obstabit, quo minùs Liberum Arbitrium appelletur ea facultas in Homine, quæ licèt nunc non sit reliqua, quondam tamen in eo fuit perfectissima: nisi fortè per insignem ἀῥῥωσίαν τῆς διανοίας contendere quis velit, amissi alicujus boni ne quidem appellationem in Ecclesiâ DEI debere esse reliquam.

Neq; responsioni huic nostræ obstat, quòd neq; Latina vox Liberi Arbitrij, neq; Græca τὸ ἀυτεξύσιον, in Scripturis legitur.

Nam si res ipsa non est ficta sive commentitia, sed sua in Scripturis expressa habet fundamenta, quid, obsecro, opus fuerit de vocabulorum terminis digladiari? praesertim cùm non eo fine illis utamur, ut hinc infolescendi materiam mens humana capessat: sed ut edocta, de quanto dignitatis gradu sit delapsa, infirmitatem suam agnoscere, fiduciam sui deponere, beneficia filij DEI, in sanando vulnere hoc lethali, generi humano acquisita, magnificare, & Spiritus Sancti gratiam piè venerari discat.

Caeterùm ne sic quidem acquiescunt nonnulli Aristarchi, quin & hoc nomine Titulum articuli hujus vellicant & arrodunt, quòd puerilem planè πλεονασμὸν ille resipiat. Cùm enim secundum communem loquendi consvetudinem, Arbitrium nihil sit aliud, quàm jus & potestas agendi pro placito, & sic suâ proprietate, per se implicet Libertatis conditionem: Siquidem arbitrarium dici non meretur, cujus vel eligendi, vel respuendi non est in utramvis partem libera potestas: utiq́; redundare omninò videtur, quando ad vocem Arbitrij, apponitur etiam Libertatis terminus, quasi Arbitrium sine Libertate dari possit. Verùm facti etiam hujus rationes in promptu sunt longè evidentissimae. Primùm enim Tituli hujus informatione respexerunt veteres, non tàm ad ipsorum vocabulorum proprietatem & latitudinem: quàm ad subjectum, in quo Liberum Arbitrium sedem suam habere debeat: Quod cùm secundum duas diversas animae facultates sit geminum, nempe Mens sive intellectus: & cor, sive voluntas: utiq́; duobus etiam distinctis vocabulis distincta illa subjecta, gravi consilio notare voluerunt: ita quidem ut vox Arbitrij ad Mentem sive Rationem: Liberi verò appellatio ad cor sive voluntatem sit referenda. Sic enim naturâ comparatum est, ut Ratio statuat sive judicet de bono maloq́; proposito: voluntas verò accedens eligat demùm, quid sequendum sit. Hinc Augustinus Liberum Arbitrium dicit, esse facultatem Rationis & Voluntatis: vel, ut Origines lib. 3. περὶ ἀρχῶν, clariùs rem explicat; esse facultatem Rationis ad bonum malumvè discernendum: Voluntatis verò ad utrumvis eligendum. Deindè geminatâ hâc appellatione, excellentiam gradus in Libertate voluntatis humanae veteres notare voluerunt: proindè ac si quis eam facultatem, cui nihil impedimenti uspiam est objectum, nominet non modò simpliciter Libertatem: sed cum ἀναδιπλώσει, liberrimam Libertatem. Quo pacto potissimùm respexerunt ad Hominis voluntatem, quae etiam sola hoc loco in controversiam venit: licèt ex hujus conditione, de alterius etiam, nempè intellectus humani viribus, rectissimè fieri queat judicium: id quod ex sequentibus patebit luculentiùs.

Porrò de usu vocabulorum anxiè etiam quaesitum & disceptatum fuit: nonnullis Liberum alijs Servum Hominis arbitrium constituentibus: Undè nostris etiam Theologis objecta fuit ἀντίφασις sive contradictio: quemadmodum videre est apud Bellarminum, lib. 4. de Gratia, &

Libero Arbitrio cap. 5. qui B. Lutherum inconstantiae insimulat, quod jam Liberum Arbitrium negaverit, mox concesserit. Verum apparens haec contradictio facile tollitur, si rectum vocabulorum usum, ab eorundem abusu rite distingvamus. Quia enim vox (Liberum) magnam cognationem habet cum spontaneo: interdum vero etiam opponitur necessitati simplici, sive coactioni aut violento: ideo fit, ut pro diversa acceptione vocabuli, sine ulla contradictionis implicatione Liberum Arbitrium recte & concedi & negari possit. Quod ut commodius explicetur, observandum fuerit, quosdam Theologos Liberum opponere Servo: alios vero coactioni sive violento: illis proprie, his improprie & καταχρηστικως rem expedientibus. Nam proprie & directe Liberum non opponitur nisi servo: spontaneum vero coactioni sive violento. Quando ergo Lutherus Hominem scribit, Servum habere Arbitrium, tum propriam vocis significationem considerat, & Hominis voluntatem in spiritualibus servam plane esse, neque ex se quicquam posse, innuere voluit. Quando vero Liberum Arbitrium Homini concedit in Spiritualibus: tum Liberum coactu opponit. Quo sane respectu libera est voluntas hominis, etiam in extrema servitute, depravatione & necessitate peccandi. Siquidem non violento aut coacto, sed liberrimo motu ad peccandum rapitur. Cujus voluntati si coactio adscriberetur, jam neque voluntatis, neque peccati vera ratio, ac definitio subsistere posset. Sic ab Orthodoxis Theologis hodieque asseritur, in nondum renatis, & Liberum & Servum esse arbitrium, respectu mali: Servum quidem, ratione corruptionis naturalis: Liberum vero ratione voluntatis, quae neque ad peccandum non per violentiam quandam cogitur; sed sua natura est proclivis ac propensa: neque etiam violento modo cogitur ad sui Conversionem: ut infra ostendetur. Proinde cum non de eadem ratione ejusdem fiat affirmatio aut negatio, nulla prorsus implicatur contradictio.

Pertinet vero huc altera etiam observatio, quae de aequivocatione vocabuli voluntatis, hoc loco probe notanda venit: qua non pensi habita, fit, ut in nostrorum etiam Theologorum scriptis, magna sese offerat diversitas, aliquibus liberum Arbitrium astruentibus: alijs negantibus: Imo uno eodemque Scriptore illud modo affirmante, jam vero negante. Sumitur ergo interdum Arbitrij sive voluntatis terminus, pro altera facultate animae, ipsa nimirum voluntatis substantia: Cujus actus est simplex το velle. Quo sane pacto ac respectu Liberum Arbitrium Homini vix quisquam negaverit, nisi qui Hominem facultate hac Animae destitui aut carere, affirmare ausus fuerit. Cujus sane stoliditas merito ab omnibus exploderetur: Siquidem facultas sive potentia Animae negari non potest, nisi tota Animae substantia negetur: propterea quod haec nihil est aliud, nisi quod sunt ejus facultates: & una facultate perdita, ipsa interire necesum habet. Interdum verò Arbitrij & voluntatis termino notatur certus quidam habitus, sive qualitas, quæ ad bonum liberè eligendum, & ad malum liberè fugiendum, est determinata. Quo respectu in homine post lapsum reliquum esse Liberum Arbitrium rectissimè negatur.

Liquet verò ex hâc disputatione, Quodnam Subjectum Liberi Arbitrij sit constituendu: & quidem proprium ac adæquatum. Sunt qui totum Hominem Libertatis hujus Subjectum dandum esse contendunt: eò quòd integer homo integrum est agendi principium: & totus Homo velle, & non velle dicitur: id quod sensu confuso & generaliore admitti posse, haud fortassè quisquam iverit inficias. Cæterùm si discretas, & secundum potentias animæ, distinctas Hominis operationes pensiculatiùs expendas, patebit neq; totum Hominem, neq; totam etiam Animam: Sed solam voluntatis facultatem, propriè posse Liberi Arbitrij adæquatum constitui Subjectum: non quòd omninò excludatur judicium mentis, sed potiùs præsupponatur: eo planè modo, quo in facultatibus animæ superior quæq; inferiores omnes non quidem in se inclusas habet: sed tantùm præsupponit: ita, ut ex facultate sentiente, non sit vegetatio ipsa: neq; hæc sit sensus: utrâq; tamen facultas & operatio præsupponat alteram. Eundem planè in modum Libero Arbitrio non est quidem sua propria sedes in Mente: nunquam tamen & nuspiam est, nisi præviam habeat mentis & judicij integritatem; â quâ suam habet dependentiam, tùm à fronte, tùm à tergo. Nam à fronte mentis rectum est judicium, cui se voluntas in libero arbitrio obedienter accommodat: A tergo verò est appetitus, & inferiorum virium motus, qui se ad bonæ voluntatis obsequium promptè attemperat. Quando ergò Mens de bono appetendo, & Malo fugiendo ex facultate sibi propriâ & peculiari judicat: voluntas autem superveniens, Bonum à Mente monstratum amplectitur, malum fugit & respust sine impedimento ullo, tùm in hâc operatione Liberi Arbitrij proprium esse locum, munus & officium rectissimè statuitur. Hinc est quod ab aliquibus haud ineptè est proditum: Liberum Arbitrium in Mente quidem sive ratione habere radices: Sed in voluntate potissimùm elucere.


### On the name of Free Will: Chapter II. Of the Prolegomena (continued)

But if the opposite happens, and the Mind judges something absolutely, and no appetite follows at all: or if the will desires or is averse to something, without the prior judgment of the mind: then the appellation of Free Choice has no place. Although, therefore, the integrity of Free Choice is most rightly circumscribed by the concurrence of three things: namely, the soundness of the mind: the promptness of the will: and the ready obedience of the remaining powers: so that if one of these things is lacking, the proper affection, Nature, and integrity of Free Choice is immediately impaired: yet Free Choice does not execute its own proper hand before the operation of the will has been added. Hence, in brute animals, and in stupid and insane men, it is most rightly denied that Free Choice exists: since it is evident that they are destitute both of the judgment of reason and the Election of the will. These things having been thus discussed, that controversy which is agitated concerning the true and proper object of Free Choice is more easily explained. That, however, cannot be human Actions simply: as Laurentius Valla dreamed, asking, Is it in man's choice to move a foot, either the right or the left? But the Good and the Evil shown by right reason. But because this can never be right, unless it is conformable and consonant with the Word of GOD: Hence it happens that B. Chemnitius and other Orthodox Theologians establish that the Law of GOD is the true and proper object of Free Choice, about which inquiry is made in the Church of GOD: so that, when the Good shown in the law of GOD is chosen: and likewise the Evil prohibited is held in hatred and left behind: then at last it is to be established that Free Choice is occupied about its proper object. But because this very thing can be taken in a double sense, namely, alternated and conjoined: certainly two distinct degrees of perfection in Free Choice emerge from this. Theologians call the sense alternated when Free Choice has itself as convertible to either, as Augustine speaks: that is, when its proper action is said to be either to choose or to be averse to the Good: and likewise either to flee or to embrace the Evil: But they name the sense conjoined that by which such liberty is assigned to Choice, by which it cannot but embrace the good and hate the evil: so that it is not convertible to both. The former degree of Liberty, resulting from the alternated sense, was in the protoplasts. Where, however, it is to be noted that this Degree is not proper to Free Choice: Since, speaking properly, to desire the Good and to be averse to the Evil pertains to the condition of Free Choice: according to that of Bernard: Let no one think that it is called Free Choice because it is occupied in an equal power and faculty between good and evil: otherwise neither GOD nor the Angels would be said to be possessed of Free Choice: but it is called Free Choice rather from this, that it makes the will free in the good, since no one ought to be called good, nor is he able to be, unless he is willing. The latter degree of Liberty, which emerges from the conjoined sense, is proper to GOD and the Angels, though in a most diverse way. For Free Choice is predicated of these, not because it is occupied in an equal power and Faculty between Good and evil. (For they can never do evil for eternity) but because they have a most free will both in good and in evil: by uniquely loving the former, but by constantly and immutably shunning the latter: as Augustine demonstrates this in many places in Enchir. c. 105, and l. 22 de Civit. DEI, last chapter. Thus, at some time in eternal life, through the necessity of not sinning, the Free Will of the blessed will not be taken away, but will rather be conformed: for to be able to choose evil is not a virtue of Free Will, but a defect. Concerning which matter Thomas disputes quite vigorously in quæst. 24 de veritate art. 3, confirming with many arguments that it is not of the essence and definition of Free Will to be able to will good and evil: or to be able to will one thing now and later not to will it: or not to be able to choose unless deliberation actually precedes it: but that it is sufficient if one has an opinion of different things, and the choice is made with the full and perfect judgment of reason.

For to be able to will good and evil pertains to Free Will not simply, but as it is in a created nature, which can fail and sin: Therefore such liberty is not only not fitting for God, but neither for Angels and blessed men.

With these things observed in this manner, it will be easier to determine something certain concerning the true and perfect definition of Free Will; Philosophers certainly, insofar as they define Free Will against natural power, define it as: that which is a power indifferent to opposites, which clearly has in its own power both of the opposites, namely to do and not to do, for different instants successively, as the physicists speak, Or: Free Will is a faculty by which we either undertake or repudiate, as it pleases, those things which have been decreed by reason. Which definitions, as they are by no means disapproved by us: so, having weighed those things which we have hitherto disputed concerning the nature and essence of Free Will, we judge that it is defined more fully and plainly by our Theologians: Free Will is a faculty of the will, which, having followed the judgment of Reason, can most freely both embrace the Good and avoid the Evil: Or, Free Will is the assent and obedience of the will, as well as of the remaining inferior powers, to the right judgment of the mind.

Since these things are so, it is easy to gather what properly comes into controversy in this Article, and what does not. Questions concerning the Substance of the will are to be removed, to be sure: concerning any of its liberty in external things, concerning vicious actions: concerning the renewed liberty of the will: but especially the dispute concerning Stoic or fatal Necessity is to be removed: and concerning the immutability of providence and divine determination: and others which are of this kind.

These being removed, that state of the Controversy alone remains: Namely, whether there is in Man such a faculty of choice or will, which presupposes a right judgment of Reason, and afterwards most freely embraces the Good, but avoids the Evil. Which state of the Controversy, indeed, according to the diversity of times and related Questions, has been informed in various ways in the Church of GOD: but so that, as regards the very Substance of the matter, almost the same thing has been sought and fought over. In the time of B. Luther, this κρινόμενον was especially ventilated, Whether the human Will can from its own powers obey the Law of GOD: and satisfy it? In the progress of time, and indeed soon after the death of B. Luther, it began to be disputed among certain Theologians not so much specifically about the fulfillment of the divine Law, as about the Conversion of Man. Whence it happened that in the Book of Concord, that ancient state of the Controversy was as it were exchanged with this more recent one: Whether the intellect and will of a man not yet reborn, in the very Conversion and Regeneration, can perform anything from his own powers, and those remaining after the fall: and in some way apply himself to apprehend the grace of GOD, embrace it, and offer some assent, even a languid one, to the word of GOD heard? But this state of the Controversy is so constituted that it does not exclude the former, but necessarily presupposes it, so much so that if the latter is rightly established, whether in the Affirmative or Negative: the matter concerning the former is also settled at the same time. Therefore, we will also moderate the future Treatment in such a way that we may appear to have taken account of both states.

Moreover, that we may proceed with a right and inoffensive step in this matter, first of all those distinctions must be set forth and explained, the observation of which will bring the clearest light to this whole dispute. The former distinction, however, is of operations or actions, with which the human will can be occupied, either in seeking or in fleeing. But they are placed in a triple difference primarily: For some are EVIL, which are prohibited by the Moral Law, and therefore conflict not only with piety, but also with true honesty. But others are MIDDLE and INDIFFERENT: and these again are threefold: for they either pertain to the condition of our Nature, such as standing, sitting, sleeping, eating, drinking, and others similar: most of which are common to man with the brutes, for the most part regarding the vegetative, sensitive, appetitive, and locomotive power of the soul: or they regard Civil and Economic Conversation: such as buying, selling, judging, serving in the military, exercising certain crafts, ruling a family, and others of this kind, which pertain to external, and that either Civil or Economic life: or finally they concern the external polity and discipline of the Church: such as teaching and hearing the Word of GOD, using certain ceremonies, giving and receiving the Sacraments, and similar external works, which fall into the external senses. We name the actions of this second kind middle, or indifferent, because by their nature or in themselves they are neither good nor evil: but whatever goodness or vice they acquire, they obtain that from other accidental causes. The third and last genus is of those actions which are and are called GOOD: and that in two ways: either MORALLY, such as: living honestly: giving to each his own: not harming another: or SPIRITUALLY, such as those which properly look to the worship of GOD, sincere religion, and the eternal salvation of souls: such as to be converted to GOD, to assent to the word heard, to believe in CHRIST, to call upon GOD, in Spirit and in truth, to do works pleasing to GOD, to live according to the Spirit, to console oneself in adversities, and many others of this kind of internal, heavenly, and spiritual actions.

The subsequent distinction is of the various States of Man, according to which he can and ought to be considered. For the State of Man before the fall was far different, which is called the State of Integrity and Innocence: again, another after the fall, which is of Sin and Corruption: and indeed twofold: either before the Conversion of Man: or in the very Conversion itself: Finally, another is the State of Man now converted to GOD, which is and is called of Restoration: and this again is twofold: for either man is semi-fully restored, after regeneration: which happens here on earth, in the Church militant: or most fully and most perfectly: which happens after this life in the Church triumphant.

The present Article, and the primary Status of the controversy within it, must be resolved by a perpetual consideration of these two distinctions: so that the following may come under investigation: 1. What kind of Free Will our first parents possessed before the fall: 2. Whether and to what extent a man not yet reborn can satisfy the Law of GOD: and whether by the own powers of Free Will, before he has been regenerated by the Spirit of GOD through the word, he can apply and prepare himself for the grace of GOD in conversion. 3. Whether the now-regenerated will is a cooperating cause of the fruit of the Spirit, or of spiritual actions? Therefore, we most correctly divide and distribute the entire subsequent treatment into three distinct chapters, according to those three distinct questions.

Latin:

Quod si diversum eveniat, & Mens absolutè judicet aliquid, & nulla prorsus sequatur appetitio: vel si voluntas appetat aut aversetur aliquid, sine prævio mentis judicio: tunc Liberi Arbitrij appellatio locum non habet. Etsi igitur trium rerum concursu integritas Liberi Arbitrij rectisimè circumscribitur: nempè sanitate mentis: promptitudine voluntatis: & viriû reliquarum expedito obsequio: ita ut harum rerum unâ deficiente, statim propria Liberi Arbitrij affectio, Natura & integritas laboret: tamen haud prius Liberum Arbitrium proprium suum manų exequitur, quàm voluntatis operatio accesserit. Hinc in bruta animatia, & homines stupidos ac infanos, Liberum Arbitriů cadere rectisimè negatur: quippè quos tùm rationis judicio, tùm voluntatis Electione destitutos tui constat. His ita discussis, facilior explicata est ea Controversia, quæ de vero ac proprio objecto Liberi Arbitrij agitatur. Illud verò non possunt esse Actiones humanæ simpliciter: prout Laurentius Valla fomniavit, quærens, Num sit in hominis arbitrio movere pedem, vel dextrum, vel sinistrum? Sed Bonum Malumq́; à rectâ ratione commonstratum. Hæc verò quia recta esse nunquam potest, nisi Verbo DEI conformis sit & consona: Hinc fit, ut B. Chemnitius, & alij Orthodoxi Theologi statuant, Legem DEI verè ac proprium esse objectum Liberi Arbitrij, de quo in Ecclesiâ DEI quæritur: ita ut, quando Bonũ, in lege DEI monstratum eligitur: Malum itidem prohibitum odio habetur & relinquitur: tùm demùm Liberum Arbitrium circa suum proprium objectum versari, statuendum sit. Cæterùm quia hoc ipsum duplici sensu, alternato nimirùm & conjuncto accipi potest: Utiq; duo hinc distincti gradus perfectionis in Libero Arbitrio emergunt. Alternatum autem sensum Theologi vocant, cum Liberum Arbitrium ad utrumq; se habet vertibile, ut loquitur Augustinus: hoc est, cùm propria ejus dicitur esse actio, Bonum vel eligere, vel aversari: Malum itidem vel fugere vel amplecti: Conjunctum autem sensum nominant eum, quo talis libertas Arbitrio assignatur, quâ non potest non bonum amplecti, & malum edisse: ita ut non sit utroq; vertibile. Prioris Libertatis gradus, ex sensu alternato resultans, fuit in protoplastis. Ubi tamen notandum, Gradum istum non esse Liberi Arbitrij proprium: Siquidem propriè loquendo, Bonum appetere, & Malum aversari pertinet ad Liberi Arbitrij conditionem: secundum illud Bernhardi: Nemo putet ideò dictum esse, Liberum Arbitrium, quòd in æquâ inter bonum & malum potestate & facultate versetur: alioqui nec DEUS, nec Angeli, Liberi Arbitrij compotes esse dicerentur: sed ex eo potiùs Liberum Arbitrium dicitur, quòd in bono liberam facit voluntatem, cùm bonus quispiam dici non debeat, aut esse non valeat, nisi volens. Posterioris Libertatis gradus, qui ex sensu conjuncto emergit, proprius est DEI & Angelorum, modo tamen diversissimo. Nam de his Liberum Arbitrium prædicatur, non quod in æquâ inter Bonum & malum potestate & Facultate versetur. (Malum enim agere nunquàm in æternum possunt) sed quia tùm in bono, tùm in malo liberrimam habent voluntatẽ: illo quidem unicè diligendo: hoc autem constanter atq; immutabiliter fugiendo: uti pluribus illud demonstrat Augustinus in Enchir. c. 105. & l. 22. de Civit. DEI cap. ult. Sic aliquando in vitâ æternâ per necessitatem, non peccandi, non tolletur Liberum Arbitrium beatorum, sed conformabitur potiùs: posse enim eligere malum, non est virtus Liberi Arbitrij, sed defectus. Quâ de re satis nervosè disputat Thomas in quæst. 24. de veritate art. 3. multis confirmans, non esse de Essentiâ ac definitione Liberi Arbitrij posse velle bonum & malum: aut posse nunc velle unum, postea nolle: aut non posse eligere, nisi consuletatio reipsâ præcedat: sed satis esse, si quis habeat opinionem diversarum rerum, & Electio fiat cùm pleno atq; perfecto judicio rationis.

Nam posse velle bonum & malum, pertinet ad Liberum Arbitrium non simpliciter, sed ut est in naturâ creata, quæ deficere & peccare potest: Itaq; talis libertas non solùm DEo non convenit: sed neq; etiam Angelis & hominibus beatis.

His hunc in modum observatis faciliùs erit jâ de verâ & perfectâ Liberi Arbitrij definitione, certi quid statuere; Philosophi certè, quatenus Liberum Arbitrium contra potentiam naturalē, definiunt illud: quod sit potentia indifferens ad opposita, quæ scilicet in sua potestate babeat utrumq; Oppositorū, scilicet facere & non facere, pro diversis instantibus successivè, uti loquütur physici, Vel: Liberũ Arbitrium est facultas, quâ vel suscipimus, vel repudiamus, prout libuerit, ea, quæ à ratione decreta fuerunt. Quæ definitiones, uti à nobis minimè improbantur: sic pensi habitis illis, quæ hāctenus de naturâ & essentiâ Liberi Arbitrij disputavimus, sic pleniùs & planiùs à nostratibus Theologis, illud definiri arbitramur: Liberum Arbitriũ est Facultas voluntatis, quæ Rationis Judicium secuta, tum Bonum amplecti, tum Malum aversari liberrimè potest: Vel, Liberum Arbitrium est tum voluntatis, tum reliquarum inferiorum virium, de recto mentis judicio, assensus & obsequium.

Quæ cùm ita sese habeant, promptum est colligere, quid propriè hoc in Articulo in controversiam veniat, quid non. Removendæ nimirùm sunt quæstiones, de Substantiâ voluntatis: de qualicunq; ejus libertate in externis, de vitiosis actionibus: de renovatâ voluntatis libertate: cumprimis verò removenda est disputatio de Necessitate Stoicâ sive fatali: deq; providentiæ & determinationis divinæ immutabilitate: & quæ sunt hujus generis aliæ.

Quibus remotis, ille statη Controversiæ unicè manet reliquus: An nimirùm in Homine sit talis Facultas arbitrij sive voluntatis, quæ Rationis judicium rectum præsupponat, & postmodùm liberrimè Bonum amplectatur, Malum verò aversetur. Qui sanè Controversiæ status, fecundùm diversitatem temporum, & Quæstionum cognatarum, diversimodè in Ecclesiâ DEI informatus fuit: sed ita, ut quoad ipsam rei Substantiam, idem fermè quæsitum & pugnatum fuerit. Tempore B. Lutheri hoc potissimùm ventilabatur κρινόμενον, An Voluntas humana ex proprijs viribus possit Legi DEI obedire: eig; satisfacere? Progressu temporis, & quidem mox post obitũ B. Lutheri, non tàm in specie de impletione Legis divinæ, quàm de Conversione Hominis, inter quosdam Theologos disputari cœptum fuit. Undè factum, ut in libro Concordiæ, antiquus ille Controversiæ status cum recentiore hoc sit quasi permutatus: An Hominis nondũ renati intellectus & voluntas, in ipsâ Conversione & Regeneratione, ex propriis suis, & post lapsum reliquis viribq aliquid præstare: & ad DEI gratiã apprehendendã aliquo modo sese applicare, eam amplecti, & verbo DEI audito aliquem assensum, languidum etiã præbere possit? Est verò status iste Controversiæ ita comparatus, ut priorem illum non excludat, sed necessariò præsupponat, usq; adeò, ut si de posterioris hujus sive Affirmativâ, sive Negativâ rectè constet: de priore etiam simul res sit expedita. Proindè futuram etiam Tractationem ita moderabimur, ut utriusq; status rationem habuisse videri queamus.

Cæterùm, ut recto atq; inoffenso pede hac in materiâ progrediamur, primùm omnium eæ præmittendæ & explicandæ sunt distinctiones, quarum observatio, toti huic disputationi lucem clarissimam inferet. Prior autem distinctio est operationum sive actionum, quibus vel appetendis, vel fugiendis voluntas humana occupari potest. Sunt autem eæ in triplici potissimùm differentiâ positæ: Aliæ enim sunt MALÆ, quæ Lege Morali sunt prohibitæ, ac proinde non modò cum pietate, sed & verâ honestate pugnant.
