Aliæ verò sunt MEDIÆ atq; INDIFFERENTES: eæq; rursum triplices: vel enim ad Naturæ nostræ conditionem pertinent, quales sunt stare, sedere, dormire, edere, bibere, & consimiles aliæ: quarum pleræq; homini cum brutis sunt communes, maximam partem respicientes vegetativam, sensitivam, appetitivam & locomotivam animæ potentiam: vel Civilem atq; Oeconomicam Conversationem respiciunt: quales, emere, vendere, jus dicere, militare, opificia certa exercere, familiam regere, & quæ hujus generis sunt aliæ, quæ ad externam, eamq; vel Civilem, vel Oeconomicam vitam pertinent: vel deniq; externam Ecclesiæ politiam & disciplinam concernunt: quales sunt docere & audire Verbum DEI, uti certis ceremonijs, dare & accipere Sacramenta, & similia externa opera, in sensus exteriores incurrentia. Secundi hujus generis actiones nominamus medias, sive indifferentes, cò quod suâ naturâ sive per se neq; bonæ, neq; malæ sunt: sed quicquid vel bonitatis vel vitij sortiuntur, illud ex alijs causis accidentalibus obtinent. Tertium & postremum genus est earum actionum, quæ BONÆ sunt & dicuntur: idq; dupliciter: vel MORALITER, quales sunt: honestè vivere: suum cuiq; tribuere: alterum non lædere: vel SPIRITUALITER, quales sunt, quæ propriè spectant ad cultum DEI, sinceram religionem, æternamq; animarum salutem: ut converti ad DEUM, assentiri verbo audito, credere in CHRISTUM, invocare DEUM, in Spiritu & veritate, facere opera DEO placentia, vivere secundum Spiritum, in adversis se consolari, & quæ sunt hujus generis actionum internarum, cœlestium & spiritualium, complures aliæ.

Posterior distinctio est diversorum Statuum Hominis, secundum quos ille considerari potest ac debet. Longè enim alius fuit Status Hominis ante lapsum, qui vocatur Status Integritatis & Innocentiæ: Rursum alius post lapsum, qui est Peccati & Corruptionis: & quidem duplex: vel ante Conversionem Hominis: vel in ipsâ etiam Conversione: Tandem alius est Status Hominis jam ad DEUM conversi, qui est & dicitur Reparationis: isq; iterum geminus: vel enim semiplenè restauratur homo, post regenerationem: id quod fit hisce in terris, in Ecclesiâ militante: vel plenissimè & perfectissimè: id quod fit post hanc vitam in Ecclesiâ triumphante.

Duarum istarum distinctionum perpetuo intuitu expediri debet præsens Articulus, & primarius in eo controversiæ Status: ita ut sub disquisitionem veniat: 1. Quale Liberum Arbitrium habuerint primi nostri parentes ante lapsum: 2. An & quatenùs Homo nondum renatus Legi DEI possit satisfacere: & an proprijs Liberi Arbitrij viribus, antequam per Spiritum DEI, mediante verbo sit regeneratus, possit sese ad gratiam DEI in conversione applicare & comparare. 3. An voluntas jam regenerata sit causa cooperans fructum Spiritus, sive actionum spiritualium? proindè totam etiam subsequentem tractationem, in tria distincta capita: secundum tres istas distinctas quæstiones, rectissimè partimur & dispescimus.


### Chapter I. On the State of Integrity and Innocence: What sort of Free Will the first Man had before the Fall

On the State of Integrity and Innocence: What kind of Free Will the first Man possessed before the Fall.

That the first man was created in the image of GOD is established beyond controversy among all Christians by the testimony of the Scriptures. But what Scripture understands by the Image and Likeness of GOD in the first man: and likewise what kind of Free Will he possessed in the State of Integrity with respect to this Image of GOD: divergent opinions have long since prevailed, and prevail today. For, to say nothing now of the ancient Pelagians, who contended that the Image of GOD in our first parents before the fall was exactly the same as that which remains now after the fall: certainly the Romanists cherish a view no more tolerable. For, according to Bellarmine, in his book on the Grace of the first man, they teach that by Adam's sin, man lost neither Free Will nor other natural gifts, but only supernatural ones. What is to be determined concerning this opinion can hardly be shown more correctly than if we hear the Holy Spirit Himself speaking in the Scriptures about this image of GOD. For from this it will spontaneously become clear, What kind of Free Will was in Man before the fall? And whether all Natural things remained intact in Man after the fall? Three testimonies of Scripture occur most especially, from which a judgment can be made concerning the proposed question.

The first stands at 2 Cor. 3:18. We all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

The second is Eph. 4:24. Put on the new man, who is created according to GOD in righteousness and holiness of truth.

The third is Col. 3:10. Putting on the new man, who is renewed into knowledge, according to the image of him who created him.

The Holy Spirit clearly shows that the true definition of the first State of Man must be sought from the restoration of the lost divine Image to which the first man had been created. Now, this Restoration does not happen except through righteousness and

holiness of truth, that is, through true holiness: and holy truth: or as the Apostle speaks in Col. 3:10, through renewal εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν, into the knowledge of GOD. Therefore, that image of GOD which shone in the first man was a perfect conformity of the rational soul and all its powers with GOD, determined by true wisdom, righteousness, and holiness, so that in the mind of man there shone a perfect knowledge of the law of GOD, and in the will the highest approval of the same, joined with delight and desire, along with the most prompt and absolute obedience.

With these things thus presupposed as a foundation, it will be easy to conclude what kind of Free Will Man possessed before the fall, namely, one that was clearly excellent, to whose perfection nothing at all was lacking: so that that Definition of Free Will truly fits this first State, by which it is said to be a faculty of reason for discerning good and evil: of the will, for choosing either one: and finally of all powers, for performing either one: according to that passage of Ecclesiasticus 15:14, GOD from the beginning created man, and left him in the hand of his own counsel.

Moreover, concerning that state of innocence and integrity, two things especially come into question: First, whence could the fall and ruin have befallen man in such a perfection of all powers? Then, how could that free will of man have stood with the law of God, by which he had been bound to obedience: since these two seem to exclude one another: to be bound by some law and to be free.

To that former ζήτημα (question), a more solid answer can hardly be given than that which is sought from the already cited passage of Ecclesiasticus chapter 15: God from the beginning left man in the hand of his own counsel: that is, God conferred this supreme dignity upon man under a mutable condition. For it was placed in the powers of the protoplast that the mind might understand what was agreeable to piety, and the faculty of the will might most freely perform it: namely, to love God above all things, and to adhere to Him inseparably: which was the property of that liberty. But indeed, because mutability was added to this dignity under the aspect of an adjunct, which itself also first had a place in the angels, for so long until, a fall of many having likewise occurred, the rest were confirmed in grace: hence it came about that through a spontaneous departure man fell from that dignity.

As for the latter ζήτημα (question), the matter is sufficiently plain and straightforward. For not even the slightest amount was taken away from the liberty of man because he was bound to a certain law. For to be released from every law and to be bound by no order at all does not pertain to the definition or nature of free will, whether human or angelic: but the mode of acting ἐκ προαιρέσεως (from choice), and indeed such a one, requires the proper affection of free will, by which the will can voluntarily and of its own accord follow the judgment of the mind: which is the mark of true liberty, notwithstanding the law of order; which does not abolish or exclude liberty. Therefore, when some argue thus: Whatever is subject to law, that is not free. But the will of man even in the state of integrity and innocence was subject to law; Therefore it was not free:

They commit a shameful sophistry both by equivocation and by treating non-causes as causes. By equivocation, insofar as they take the word (Free) abusively in the common sense, but not in the ecclesiastical sense: namely, for that which is released from law and entirely free from every order obliging one to certain obedience: which kind of liberty certainly does not fall even to the angels, however much they are confirmed in good; nor, properly speaking, is it liberty, but rather unbridled and beastly license, wandering like the brutes without law and order; indeed, in truth, it despoils man of all reason and changes him into an irrational beast. For what, I ask, will be the remaining duty of reason, unless by the intuition of some certain law it discerns good from evil, true from false? Therefore, in the proposed argument, those things which are not at all opposed to each other are most viciously opposed: namely, to be Free and to be subject to Law: which two things only stand in relation as things subordinate to one another. The reason for the assertion is most evident, because true Liberty is not opposed to order and the certain prescription of a certain law, but partly to violent coercion, and partly to servile necessity: and thus consequently it presupposes a mode of acting by choice: which, if it be neither coerced nor servile, but freely uses its own election: then certainly this Liberty retains its own perfection. In which part Free Will in the first man had something in common with things acting naturally. For just as natural causes are determined to one certain mode of acting: so that with a convenient or adequate object present, they cannot but exercise their activity: as fire cannot but exercise its action on dry wood: so in the state of innocence and integrity, the will of the first man had a most free election, so that it could not but exercise its activity most freely, whether in this direction or that: so much so, that the proposed Law did not abolish or suspend the liberty of election, but showed at least how this very liberty of election ought to contain itself within order, and not ferociously exceed its bounds. Nor does that of the Apostle 1 Tim. 1:9 stand in the way: The law is not laid down for the just. For since there is a threefold use of the Law: one, to restrain external crimes: another, to show sins: a third, to be a norm for good works: of which the first pertains to the unregenerate, the third to the regenerate: the second pertains to both: certainly the Aphorism of the Apostle is to be understood concerning the first use, since the Law among the just, whether they are such originally or by Regeneration, cannot exercise that proper duty of its own, so as to be able to accuse, terrify, or condemn them: according to that of the Apostle: There is now no condemnation for those who are in CHRIST Jesus. Rom. 8:1. And who shall accuse the elect of GOD? It is GOD who justifies. Rom. 8:33. Which very thing the Greek phrase of the Apostle also hints at, who did not use the verb to be placed, but the verb to lie: which word is more emphatic, and in that way hints that the law is not placed for the Just so that it may lie, that is, so that it may restrain, terrify, accuse, or condemn him, as has already been shown. Now, however, from the negation of one use, a collection is viciously instituted to the negation of all uses simply. Since, as the Logicians attest, it is only permitted to argue from species to genus by affirming, unless a full enumeration of all species is made.

Latin:

De Statu Integritatis & Innocencentiæ: Qualenam Liberum Arbitrium habuerit primus Homo ante Lapsum.

Primum hominem ad imaginem DEI fuisse conditum, Scripturarum testimonio apud Christianos omnes extra controversiam est positum. Cæterùm quid Scriptura per Imaginem & Similitudinē DEI in primo homine intelligat: quale item Liberum Arbitrium respectu Imaginis hujus DEI, ille in Statu Integritatis habuerit: de eo discrepantes planè sententiæ jampridem obtinuerunt, hodieq́; obtinent. Nam ut de veteribus Pelagianis nihil nunc dicamus, qui contenderunt, eandem planè fuisse in primis parentibus Imaginem DEI ante lapsum, qualis nunc post lapsum est reliqua: Certè Romanenses haud tolerabiliorem fovent sententiam. Teste enim Bellarmino, libro de Gratiâ primi hominis docent, per Adæ peccatum, neq́ Liberum Arbitrium, neque alia naturalia dona, sed solùm supernaturalia Hominem perdidisse. De quâ sanè sententiâ quid statuendum sit, vix rectiùs ostendetur, quàm si ipsum Spiritum Sanctum de imagine hâc DEI in Scripturis differentem audiamus. Hinc enim ultrò planum fiet, Quale Liberum Arbitrium in Homine ante lapsum fuerit? &, nùm post lapsum Naturalia omnia in Homine manserint integra? Tria autem potissimùm occurrunt Scripturæ Testimonia, ex quibus de propositâ quæstione fieri queat judicium.

Primum extat 2. Cor. 3, 18. Nos omnes revelatâ facie gloriam Domini speculantes, in eandem imaginem transformamur, à claritate in claritatem, tanquam à Domini Spiritu.

Alterum Eph 4, 24. Induite novum hominem, qui secundum DEUM creatus est in justitia & sanctitate veritatis.

Tertium Col. 3, 10. Induentes novum hominem, eum qui renovatur in agnitionem, secundum imaginem ejus qui creavit illum.

Monstrat nimirùm Spiritus Sanctus veram definitionem primi Status Hominis petendam esse ex restitutione, amissæ Imaginis divinæ ad quam primus homo erat conditus. Jam verò Restitutio hæc non fit, nisi per justitiam &

sanctitatem veritatis, hoc est, per veram sanctitatem : & sanctam veritatem : vel ut Col. 3, 10. loquitur Apostolus, per renovationem εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν, in agnitionem DEI. Proindè imago illa DEI, quæ in primo homine refulsit, erat animæ rationalis, omniumq; virium perfecta cum DEO conformitas, verâ sapientiâ, justitiâ & sanctitate determinata, ita ut in mente hominis luxerit perfecta legis DEI notitia, in voluntate summa ejusdem approbatio, cum delectatione & desiderio, conjuncta cum promptissimâ & absolutissimâ obedientiâ.

Quibus ita fundamenti loco præsuppositis, promptum erit colligere, Quodnám & quale Liberum Arbitrium habuerit Homo ante lapsum, nempè planè eximium, cujus perfectioni nihil prorsus defuerit: ita ut primo huic Statui verè conveniat Definitio illa Liberi Arbitrij, quâ dicitur esse facultas rationis ad discernendum bonum & malum: voluntatis autem ad utrumvis eligendum: Virium deniq; omnium, ad utrumlibet præstandum: secundum illud Ecclesiastici 15, 14. DEUS ab initiò constituit hominem, & reliquit illum in manu consilij sui.

Cæterùm de statu isto innocentiæ & integritatis, duo potissimùm in quæstionem veniunt: Primùm, Undenám in tantâ perfectione virium omnium, Lapsus & ruina Homini obtingere potuerit? Deindè quomodo Liberum istud Arbitrium Hominis stare potuerit cum Lege DEI, quâ ille ad obedientiam obstrictus fuerat: Siquidem hæc duo se mutuò excludere videntur: Lege quapiam obligatum esse & liberum esse.

Ad prius illud ζήτημα vix solidiùs responsum dari potest, quàm illud quod petitur ex citato jam loco Ecclesiastici cap. 15. DEUS ab initio hominē reliquit in manu consilij sui: hoc est, sub mutabili, conditione summam istam dignitatem DEUS homini contulit. Fuit enim hoc in viribus protoplasti positum, ut quod pietati consentaneū esset, illud mens intelligeret, facultas autem voluntatis liberrimè præstare posset: DEUM nimirùm supra omnia diligere, atq; ipsi indivulsè adhærere: id quod proprium istius libertatis fuit. At verò, quia huic dignitati, sub Adjuncti ratione accesfit mutabilitas, quæ ipsa quoque primùm in Angelis locum habuit, tàm diu donec lapsu multorum itidē facto, reliqui in gratiâ confirmati sunt:hinc adeò factū, ut per spōtaneum excessum homodignitate istâ exciderit.

Quoad posterius ζήτημα, res satis est plana & expedita. Neq; enim vel tantillùm libertati hominis ideò decessit, quia legi certæ obstrictus fuit. Nam lege omni solutum esse: & nullo prorsus ordine obligari, non pertinet ad definitionem sive naturam Liberi Arbitrij, sive humani, sive Angelici: sed modū agendi ἐκ προαιρέσεως, & quidem talem, propria Liberi Arbitrij affectio requirit, quâ voluntas ultrò & suâ sponte judicium mentis sequi possit: id quod veræ libertatis est, non obstante Lege Ordinis; quæ Libertatem non tollit aut excludit. Proindè, quando nonnulli sic arguunt: Quicquid Legi subjectum est, illud liberum non est. Atqui voluntas hominis in statu etiā integritatis & innocientiæ fuit subjecta legi; Ergò non fuit Libera:

turpem Sophisticationem tùm ὁμωνυμίας, tùm non causæ ut causæ committunt. ὁμωνυμίας quidem, quatenus vocem (Liberum) καταχρηστικῶς sensu vulgari, non verò Ecclesiastico accipiunt: nimirùm pro eo, quod est solutum lege & planè liberum ab omni ordine, obligante ad certam obedientiam : Qualis certè libertas, ne quidem in Angelos, quantumvis in bono confirmatos cadit: neq; propriè loquendo libertas est, sed effrænis potiùs & belluina licentia, brutorum more sine lege & Ordine vagans: imò reverâ hominem omni ratione spolians, & in bestiam irrationalem, commutans. Quod enim obsecro Rationis erit, officium reliquum, nisi certæ cujusdam legis intuitu, bonum à malo, verum à falso discernat? Proindè in argumento proposito vitiosissimè opponuntur ea, quæ minimè omnium sibi mutuò sunt opposita: nempè Liberum & Legi subjectum esse: Quæ duo tantùm se habent, ut τὰ υπ᾽ ἄλληλα sive subordinata. Ratio assertionis evidentissima est, quòd Libertas vera non opponitur ordini & certo præscripto legis certæ, sed partim violentæ coactioni, partim servili necessitati: & sic consequenter præsupponit modum agendi ἐκ προαιρέσεως: qui si neq; coactus, neq; servilis sit, sed suâ electione liberè utatur: tunc utiq; Libertati huic sua constat perfectio. Quâ in parte Liberum Arbitrium in primo homine, commune quiddam habuit, cum naturaliter agentibus. Quemadmodum enim causæ naturales, ad unum quendam certum agendi modum sunt determinatæ: ita ut objecto conveniente sive adæquato præsente, non possint non exercere suam ἐνέργειαν: uti Ignis non potest non in ligno arido suam actionem exercere: ita in statu innocentiæ & integritatis, voluntas primi hominis Electionem habebat liberrimam, ut non posset non suam exercere ἐνέργειαν liberrimè, sive in hanc, sive in illam partem: usq; adeò, ut Lex proposita, non tolleret aut suspenderet Electionis libertatem, sed monstraret saltem, quomodo hæc ipsa Electionis libertas intra ordinem sese continere, nec ferociùs exorbitare debeat. Neq; obstat illud Apostoli 1. Tim. 1, 9. Justo non est Lex posita. Nam cùm triplex Legis usus sit: unus ut coërceat scelera externa: alter, ut peccata monstret: tertius, ut sit norma bonorum operum: quorum primus ad non renatos, tertius ad renatos: secundus ad utrosque pertinet: utiq; de primo usu Aphorismus Apostoli accipiendus est, siquidem Lex apud justos, sive illi originaliter, sive Regeneratione tales sint, officium illud suum proprium exercere nequit, ut accusare, terrere, damnare eos possit: secundum illud Apostoli: Nulla nunc condemnatio, his qui sunt in CHRISTO Jesu. Rom. 8, 1. & quis accusabit electos DEI: DEUS est qui justificat. Rom. 8, 33. Quod ipsum innuit etiam Phrasis Græca Apostoli, qui non usus est verbo τίθεσθαι positum esse: sed verbo κεῖσθαι jacere: Quod verbum ἐμφατικώτερον est, & eo modo innuit, Justo non esse positam legem, ut jaceat, hoc est, ut ipsum coërceat, terreat, accuset, damnet, uti jam ostensum. Jam verò ab unius usus negatione, vitiosè instituitur collectio ad negationem omnium simpliciter usuum. Siquidem à specie ad genus affirmando, tantùm licet argumentari, nisi plena fiat enumeratio omnium specierum: attestantibus Logicis.


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption, before conversion, and in the very conversion

The principal and classic controversy of this Article, according to that State of Man which is of Corruption, and indeed primarily before conversion, concerns this most of all. For it is asked, Whether Man not yet regenerate or converted has such Free Will that he can discern good from evil, desire the former, flee the latter: and especially in Spiritual matters can perform something of himself? The decision of this question admits neither a simple Affirmative nor Negative: but by reason of both the subject and the object, it ought to be settled by a certain limitation or distinction.

As regards the Subject, if the will of Man is considered in itself, it can certainly be called free, even in corruption, in that sense, namely, which is opposed to coercion. For the will is always carried by a spontaneous motion, so that nothing is more adverse or repugnant to it than violence and coercion.

As regards the Object, however, namely the actions about which the will of Man is occupied, whether to desire or to flee them, there is need of a distinction. For in evil and vicious actions the Liberty of the will is granted even to the greatest degree, because the will, not yet regenerate, most freely, that is, not coerced but spontaneously, wills, chooses, approves, and does what is evil. Whence it is that the voluntary enters into the definition of Sin, so that, properly speaking, there is no Sin except that which is voluntary. Hence D. Augustine, book on Nature and Grace, ch. 23, writes: For one to go into Sin, Free Will is sufficient for him. And book on the Spirit and the Letter, ch. 3: Free Will is of no avail, except to sin. And Gregory in his exposition of the morals of Job, book 13, ch. 9: We are led to perpetual evil from Free Will.

But it is asked at this point, Why this propensity to evil is called Free, nay, Liberty, when it is rather a sad and horrible servitude: and so much so, that Scripture also explicitly names men not yet regenerate Servants of Sin, Rom. 6:20. And Anselm rightly affirms that the power of sinning is neither Liberty nor a part of Liberty: And Augustine shrewdly infers: To do evil is not to have power, but rather to fail: Therefore, the will which we use to do evil, I do not think worthy to be called free. But it is most rightly answered that both are true in a different respect: namely, that this propensity of our will to evil is most rightly named both Servile and Free.

A slave, indeed, with respect to the lost Image of GOD. For after the ability to choose the good and flee the evil was taken away by the fall, there was left behind a will, which is held so captive under the tyranny of sin that it is not moved except to choose evil and flee good: according to that saying in Gen. 8:21, 'The imagination of man's heart is only evil from his youth.' And Rom. 8:7, 'The affection of the flesh is enmity against GOD.' But however slave this will may be, it is nevertheless most rightly called free, if indeed we look to the proper seat of Sin, which is in the will of man. But if anyone should wish to assign another reason, namely that the Church usurps the limit of Liberty concerning evil actions in order to set a measure for human curiosity, so that one may not seek the cause of Sin outside oneself, but rather investigate and acknowledge it in oneself: we shall certainly not object.

As for the other class of actions, which we call indifferent, and which concern either the condition of our nature, or civil society, or Ecclesiastical Polity: certainly in all these, hardly any sane person would deny that even the unregenerate will retains its own freedom to govern the locomotive power. The truth of this assertion is evident partly from the Scriptures, partly from reason. From the Scriptures, indeed, if we weigh those sayings which show that a man can do some things which he does not do, and conversely: and which contain the express condition of our will: such as are, Num. 20:14, 'It is in the man's choice whether he does it or does not do it.' And Isa. 1:19, 'If you are willing, you shall eat the good of the land.' Gen. 4:7, 'Why are you angry? And why has your countenance fallen? Under you shall be the desire, and you shall rule over it.' To which also pertains that which in the Scriptures is more often permitted to men, a free Choice and Option: as 2 Sam. 24:12. Three options are given to you: choose one, which you will, from these, that I may do it to you, etc. And Acts 5:4, Peter to Ananias, 'Was it not in your power to sell the field?'

But by reason the same can be demonstrated in this way: If in the mind of man, even after the fall, there still remains some distinction of honorable and base things in civil actions, and some judgment concerning things which are subject to sense and reason: then surely in the will also there will remain some faculty by which the locomotive power can be governed and the discipline of external manners can be performed. But the former is true: therefore the latter is also established.

The connection of the major premise is of itself of the clearest truth. For Reason and Will are so inseparably connected in Man that neither can exist without the other, but they posit each other: so that if some faculty of Reason is granted after the fall, then surely some faculty of the will must necessarily be granted: unless perhaps one wishes to posit that Reason can choose or flee something without the will, which would be prodigiously absurd.

The minor premise is confirmed quite clearly by the Polities of the Gentiles, in which the discipline of morals and civil conversation was so constituted that it deserves praise and admiration for wisdom and virtue that will never perish. But if, however, anyone should wish to except in this place the heroic deeds of some Gentiles, and clearly unusual specimens of virtues, under which peculiar inspirations of divinity, and such indeed as are to be distinguished from the general action of GOD, exerted themselves: we shall certainly not resist.

Then the certainty of the minor premise is also evident from the fact that the Apostle not obscurely attributes to the Gentiles, Rom. 2:14, that they naturally do the things which are of the Law: namely, by performing some obedience to the discipline of the Law in external matters. For as Augustine speaks, the image of GOD in the human soul has not been so worn away by the stain of earthly affections that no external lineaments, as it were, have remained in it, from which it may be deservedly said that the Gentiles, even in the very impiety of their life, do or know some things of the law. And indeed if, with the same Apostle as witness, Rom. 1:19, some wisdom and knowledge, even concerning GOD, remains in the mind of man after the fall, which is designated by the Apostle as the wisdom of the flesh, Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκος: nothing surely will prevent the will from having a faculty which can add its compliance, or expedite its dissent, in that class of things and actions which are subject to Reason and sense, and look only to external discipline. Which they commonly call the righteousness of the flesh, as can be seen in B. Luther in the Saxon Visitation, Art. on Free Will. Socrates is celebrated most of all by this name, who affirmed that he had crushed the seeds of a very bad nature with the plow of discipline, and from there had restrained its most certain motions by the cultivation of Philosophy, as Cicero testifies in his book on Fate.

Thirdly, it cannot be denied that this very righteousness of the flesh breaks forth in such effects even in the unregenerate, from which a judgment can be made concerning the remaining little sparks of the Light of Nature, regarding this class of actions. For from the visible works of GOD, they acknowledge the eternal power and divinity of GOD, Rom. 1:20; they do not doubt at all about the immortality of souls, and that there will be either rewards or punishments at some time: they also know that GOD is to be worshipped with a pure mind: indeed, they prefer that it be well with them after this life rather than ill: as the books of the Gentile Philosophers clearly attest.

Finally, the minor premise can also be confirmed quite evidently from the consideration of those men in whom Nature suffers violence, and who are delivered into a reprobate sense by the just judgment of GOD: For just as in these the use of natural faculties is so subverted that they can no longer perform what is proper to men: so by reason of the contrary, men who are free from this bond of induration can, from the faculty of natural powers, at least maintain some mode of life, provided they themselves wish, and can bring their tumultuous affections, willing or unwilling, into the circle of command: which that utterance of Caracalla proves, saying, 'I would, if it were permitted.'

These reasons having been duly weighed, it shines forth most clearly that for men not yet reborn, some freedom of the will must be conceded, not only regarding the class of actions that are despotic, when, namely, the locomotive power in the limbs is governed by the command of the will, whether or not the affections within agree: but also proairetic, when the will, with serious affection, prefers honest actions, as our Chemnitius speaks, part 1 of the Loci, page 455.

Furthermore, to the class of those intermediate and indifferent actions, we have also referred above certain external ecclesiastical works: such as the external hearing of the Word, reading, and some meditation on Holy Scripture: which works are commonly called Carnal Study: concerning which we most firmly maintain with the Book of Concord that even after the fall, some free will is not to be denied to man: so that a man not reborn can, by natural sense and the bodily organ of the ears, perceive the preached word: pursue it with some investigation of the mind, and meditate upon it according to human capacity: or hear it more sleepily, and weigh it only incidentally and perfunctorily: or, with ears stopped, altogether reject and turn away from it. The truth of this assertion is evident, partly from the Scriptures, partly from certain and immovable reasons: partly from the authority of the Fathers and Symbolic writers: and finally, partly from the examples of those who, not being converted, were held by some carnal study of knowing the divine word.

1. Regarding Scripture, it is a witness that merely carnal men can have some zeal for God: although not according to knowledge, Rom. 10:2, so that they go about from sea even to sea, and from the North even to the East, seeking the word of God, and do not find it, Amos 8:11, nay, even seek to enter through the narrow gate, Luke 13:24.

2. Regarding reasons, it cannot be denied that there remains in man, even when not yet reborn, a natural knowledge, not only of physical and worldly things, of disciplines and arts, in which God has scattered a grateful fame of Himself: but also of God Himself: which is named by the Apostle τὸ γνωστὸν θεῦ, Rom. 1:19, which, although it contains nothing in itself of saving knowledge of God: and in respect of that knowledge which is drawn from the Word of God, more rightly earns the name of darkness than of light: yet it brings such light to human reason and mind that, although it is ignorant of what kind of God it is proper to have, it nevertheless knows that one must be had, and furthermore, it is not ignorant that He must be worshipped with honesty of life and morals. If even men who are not reborn follow the guidance of this knowledge, and do not, by the corruption of life and morals, as it were, offer violence to this light of nature: or, as the Apostle speaks, do not hold back the truth of God in unrighteousness: it certainly cannot be but that, because of the desire for salvation and immortality which is ingrained in the nature of men, an ardent study of knowing God and divine things arises in their souls, so that they labor diligently according to their capacity to acquire that knowledge for themselves: as we shall demonstrate shortly by examples.

There is also the fact that God Himself, for most weighty reasons, wills that even after the fall this knowledge of Himself, and of a certain part of His law, should remain in the human mind, even when not yet reborn: not only to show and convict sin, and to govern discipline, as our author speaks, Tom. 2 of his works, p. 328. But also that through this medium He may call, convert, and regenerate men to eternal salvation. But just as this light of nature, not having suffered violence, can apply carnal study to any other religions: so God seriously commanded that this very study be applied also to the preaching of His own word: nay, through this medium, but out of mere grace, He ordained from eternity that it should work effectively for salvation. Rom. 10:17. Faith comes by hearing. Regarding the authority of the Fathers, let one Augustine suffice, who in his book De Fide ad Petrum, chapter 32, has it thus: Hold most firmly that a man, whom neither ignorance of letters nor any weakness or adversity prevents, can indeed read the words of the Law and the Gospel, or hear them from the mouth of any preacher: but that no one can obey the divine commands unless God has anticipated him with His grace; so that what he hears with the body, he may also perceive with the heart. To the same effect the Book of Concord also explicitly writes: This Word of God, a man even not yet converted to God, nor reborn, can hear with external ears, or read. For in such external matters, man, even after the fall, still has in some way free will, so that he can attend public ecclesiastical assemblies, and hear or not hear the word of God, page 671. Finally, regarding examples, Scripture is a witness that the Queen of the Ethiopians, Nicaula, traveled from the innermost ends of the kingdom to Jerusalem, so that she might know the wisdom of Solomon, the chief part of which was religion, drawn from the oracles of the Scriptures, 1 Kings 10:1, 2 Chron. 9:1, etc. That the Magi sought to be instructed from the oracles of the Scriptures where the Savior of the World was to be born, Matt. 2:2. That Herod gladly heard John the Baptist preaching, Mark 6:20. That Sergius the proconsul, an ethnic man, desired to hear Paul and Barnabas, Acts 13:7. That Felix, the governor of Judea, likewise an ethnic, for that reason called the bound Apostle to himself, so that he might hear the sermon from him, Acts 24:24. Furthermore, Josephus is a witness, book 1 against Apion, that Pythagoras burned with such a study of knowing the Jewish religion that he transferred very many of the laws of the Hebrews into his own sect: nay, finally, having traveled into Egypt and Judea, he himself also wished to be initiated into the Jewish sacred rites: which could not have happened without serious study of religion. Moreover, Justin the Philosopher and Martyr reports in his exhortation to the Gentiles that Plato transferred many things from the books of the Hebrews into his own: so that it became a proverb, what is Plato but Moses speaking Attic? Which same thing Eusebius also testifies in his Evangelical Preparation, and Theodoret on the Affections of the Greeks: nay, Aristobulus the Jew, book 1 to Philometor, cited by Eusebius, expressly writes that Plato in many things followed the Law of the Hebrews. Nor are there wanting those who affirm that Plato, for the sake of drawing wisdom, traveled into Egypt, and either heard the Prophet Jeremiah himself, or at least perused the Prophetic Scriptures.

Latin:

PRincipaliter & classica Articuli hujus Controversia, secundum istum Statum Hominis, qui est Corruptionis, & quidem primùm ante conversionem, potissimùm respicit. Quæritur enim, An Homo nondùm renatus sive conversus, habeat tale Liberum Arbitrium, ut bonũ à malo discernere, illud appetere, hoc fugere: & cumprimis in Spiritualibus ex se aliquid præstare possit? Quæsiti hujus decisio, neq; Affirmativam neq; Negativam simplicem admittit: sed ratione tùm subjecti, tùm objecti, certâ sive limitatione sive distinctione expediri debet.

Quoad Subjectum quidem, si voluntas Hominis in seipsâ consideretur, libera certè illa, etiam in corruptione dici potest, eo nimirùm sensu, qui coactioni est oppositus. Semper enim spontaneo motu fertur voluntas, ita ut nihil ipli magis sit adversum aut repugnans, quàm violentum & coactio.

Quoad Objectum verò, nempè Actiones circa quas vel appetendas vel fugiendas voluntas Hominis occupatur, distinctione opus est. In malis enim & vitiosis actionibus Libertas voluntatis vel maximè conceditur, proptereà quòd nondùm renata voluntas, liberrimè, hoc est, non coactè, sed spontaneè vult, eligit, approbat & facit, quod malum est. Undè est, quod Peccati definitionem ingreditur voluntarium, ita ut propriè loquendo, Peccatum non sit, nisi quod est voluntarium. Hinc D. Augustinus lib. de Naturâ, & Gratiâ cap. 23. scribit: Ut quis in Peccatu eat, sufficit ei Liberum Arbitriũ. Et lib. de sp. & lit. cap. 3. Liberũ Arbitrium nihil, nisi ad peccandũ valet. EtGregor. in expof. mor. Job. l. 13. c. 9. Ad perpetuum malu ducimur ex Libero Arbitrio.

Quæritur autem hoc loco, Cùr hæc ad malum propensio, dicatur Libera, imò Libertas, cùm potiùs tristis & horrenda sit servitus: utq;, adeò, ut Scriptura quoq; Homines nondùm renatos, disertè nominet Servos Peccati, Rom. 6, 20. & Anshelmus rectè affirmet, Peccandi potestatẽ neq; Libertatẽ, neq; partẽ Libertatis esse: Et Augustinus scitè inferat: Malum agere nõ est posse, sed potiùs deficere: Arbitriũ igitur, quo utimur ad malè agendũ, non arbitror dignũ, ut liberum appelletur. Sed rectissimè respondetur, diverso respectu utrumq; verũ esse: nempè propensione hanc voluntatis nostræ ad malum, rectissimè & Servam & Liberam nominari.

Servam quidem respectu amisse Imaginis DEI. Postquàm enim per lapsum sublata est facultas eligendi boni, & fugiendi mali, relicta est postmodùm voluntas, quæ sub Tyrannide peccati usq; adeò captiva tenetur, ut non feratur, nisi ad malum eligendum & bonum fugiendum: secundùm illud Gen. 8, 21. Figmentum cordis humani tantùm pravum est ab adolescentiâ. Et Rom. 8, 7. Affectus carnis inimicitia est adversò DEUM. Sed quantumvis serva hæc sit voluntas, libera tamen nihilominus rectissimè appellatur, si nimirùm sedem Peccati propriam respiciamus, quæ est in voluntate hominis. Quòd si quis alteram etiam causam adsignare velit, ideò nimirùm Ecclesiæm Libertatis terminum circa malas actiones usurpare, ut humanæ curiositati modum statuat, ne videlicet Peccati causam extra se quærat: sed in seipso potiùs investiget & agnoscat: haud profectò refragabimur.

Quoad alterum Genus actionum, quas Medias appellamus, & vel Naturæ nostræ conditionem, vel civilem societatem, vel Ecclesiasticam Politiam concernunt: certè in his omnibus, voluntati etiam non renatæ suam constare libertatem, ad regendam locomotivam, vix quisquam sanus iverit inficias. Patet assertionis hujus veritas partim ex Scripturis, partim ex ratione. Ex Scripturis quidem, si expendamus ea dicta, quæ ostendunt hominem posse aliqua facere, quæ non facit, & contra: quæq; expressam voluntatis nostræ conditionem continent: Qualia sunt, Numer. 20, 14. In arbitrio viri est, sive faciat, sive non faciat. Et Esai. 1, 19. Si volueritis, bona terræ comederis. Gen. 4, 7. Quare iratus es? & cur concidit facies tua? Sub te erit appetitus, & tu dominaberis ille. Quò pertinet etiam, quod in Scripturis Hominibus sæpiùs libera permittitur Electio & Optio: ut 2. Sam. 24, 12. Trium tibi datur optio: elige unum, quod volueris ex his, ut faciam tibi &c. Et Act. 5, 4. Petrus ad Ananiam, Nonne in tua erat potestate vendere agrum?

Ex ratione verò idem demonstrari potest in hunc modum: Si in mente hominis etiam post lapsum adhuc reliquum est, aliquod discrimen honestorum & turpium in civilibus, actionibus, & Judicium aliquod de rebus, quæ sensui & rationi sunt subjectæ: utiq; in voluntate quoq; supererit aliqua facultas, quâ locomotiva regi, & externamorum disciplina præstari possit. Atqui prius verum: Ratum ergò & posterius.

Connexum Majoris per se est liquidissimæ veritatis. Sunt enim Ratio & Voluntas in Homine ita inseparabiliter connexæ, ut neutra sine alterâ consistere possit, sed se mutuò ponant: Ita ut aliquâ Rationis concessâ facultate post lapsum, utiq; voluntatis etiam aliqua facultas necessariò sit concedenda: nisi fortè Rationem sine voluntate aliquid vel eligere, vel fugere, statuere quis velit, id quod prodigiosè foret absurdum.

Minorem satis luculenter confirmant Poilitiæ Gentilium, in quibus disciplina morum, & Civilis conversatio sic fuit constituta, ut sapientiæ & virtutis laudem atq; admirationem nunquàm interituram mereatur. Quod si tamen excipere hoc loco quis velit Heroica nonnullorum Gentilium facta, & inusitata planè virtutum specimina, sub quibus peculiares divinitatis afflatus, & tales quidem, qui à generali DEI actione sint distingvendi, sese exeruerint: haud sanè reluctabimur.

Deindè Minoris certitudo patet etiam exindè, quod Apostolus Gentilibus haud obscurè tribuit, Rom 2, 14. quod naturaliter faciant ea, quæ sunt Legis: aliquam nimirùm Legis disciplinæ præstando obedientiam in externis. Nam ut Augustinus loquitur, non usq; adeò in animâ humanâ, imago DEI terrenorum affectuum labe detrita est, ut nulla in eâ velut lineamenta externa remanserint, undè meritò dici possit, Gentiles etiam in ipsâ impietate vitæ suæ, facere aliqua legis vel sapere. Et profectò si eodem Apostolo teste Rom. 1, 19. in mente hominis sapientia & scientia aliqua, etiam de DEO post lapsum est reliqua, quæ sapientia carnis, Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκος ab Apostolo indigitatur: nihil utiq; obstabit, quò minùs voluntati insit facultas, quæ obsequium suum possit adjungere, vel diffensum expedire, in eo rerum & actionum genere, quæ Rationi & sensui subjacent, & externam tantùm disciplinam spectant. Quam Justitiam carnis vulgò nominant, uti videre est, apud B. Lutherum in visitat. Saxon. Art. de Lib. Arb. Celebratur hoc nomine vel maximè Socrates, qui naturæ pessimæ semina, aratro disciplinæ se obtrivisse, & indè certissimos ejus motus, Philosophiæ culturâ se compescuisse affirmavit, teste Cicerone lib. de Fato.

Tertiò negari non potest, quin hæc ipsa Justitia carnis, in ejusmodi Effecto in non renatis etiam erumpat, ex quibus de reliquis adhuc Luminis Naturæ scintillulis, quoad hoc actionum Genus, judicium fieri queat. Nam ex visibilibus DEI operibus, æternam DEI potentiam & divinitatem agnoscunt, Rom. 1, 20. de animarum immortalitate, & secuturis aliquando vel præmijs, vel pænis, minimè dubitant: noverunt etiam DEUM purâ mente esse colendum: quin malunt post hanc vitam sibi benè, quàm malè esse: uti Philosophorum Gentilium libri luculenter attestantur.

Tandem satis etiam evidenter confirmari potest Minor ex consideratione eorum Hominum, in quibus Natura vim patitur, quiq; in sensum reprobum, justo DEI judicio traduntur: Quemadmodum enim in his sic intervertitur naturalium facultatum usus, ut jam, quod hominum est proprium, præstare ampliùs nequeant: Ita ex ratione contrarij Homines ab hoc indurationis vinculo liberi, ex virium naturalium facultate, saltem aliquem vitæ modum, modò ipsi velint, servare, & affectus tumultuantes, volentes, nolentes, in gyrum Imperij redigere possunt: id quod vox illa Caracallæ evincit: dicentis, Vellem, si liceret.

Quibus rationibus probè ponderatis, clarissime elucescit, Hominibus nondum renatis, aliquam concedendam esse voluntatis libertatem, non modò quoad genus actionum δεσποτικόν, cùm videlicet locomotiva in membris regitur voluntatis imperio, sive intus congruant affectus, sive non: sed & προαιρετικόν, quando voluntas, serio affectu antefert honestas actiones, uti loquitur Chemnitius noster, part. 1. Locorum, pag. 455.

Cæterum ad classem actionum istarum mediarum atq; indifferentium, suprà retulimus etiam opera quædam Ecclesiastica externa: qualia sunt, externus Auditus Verbi, Lectio & Meditatio aliqua Scripturæ Sacræ: Quæ opera vulgò nominantur Carnale Studium: circa quod Homini etiam post lapsum, Liberum aliquod Arbitrium haud negandum esse cum Libro Concordiæ firmissimè statuimus: ita ut naturali sensu atq; organo aurium corporeo verbum prædicatum percipere: aliquâ indagine mentis prosequi, & pro captu humano meditari: vel somnolentiùs illud audire, atq; obiter duntaxat ac perfunctoriè expendere: vel obturatis auribus prorsus illud respuere atq; aversari Homo non renatus possit. Patet assertionis hujus veritas, partim ex Scripturis, partim ex certis ac immotis rationibus: partim autoritate Patrum & Scriptorum Symbolicorum: partim denique exemplis eorum, qui non conversi Carnali aliquo studio cognoscendi verbi divini tenebantur.

1. Quoad Scripturam, testis ea est, Homines merè carnales posse habere Zelum aliquem DEI: licèt non secundum scientiam, Rom. 10, 2. ita ut Circumeuntes à mari usq; ad mare, & ab Aquilone usq; ad Orientem, Quærant verbum DEI, & non inveniant, Amos 8, 11. imò Quærant intrare per angustam portam, Luc. 10, 24.

2. Quoad Rationes, negari non potest, quin reliqua sit in homine etiam nondum renato, notitia Naturalis, non de rebus tantùm Physicis & mundanis, de disciplinis atŏtque artibus, in quibus DEUS gratam sui famam sparsit: sed de DEo etiam ipso: quæ ab Apostolo nominatur τὸ γνωστὸν θεῦ, Rom. 1, 19. quæ licèt nihil in se contineat salutaris agnitionis DEI: & illius notitiæ, quæ ex Verbo Dei hauritur, respectu, rectiùs tenebrarum, quàm luminis nomen sortiatur: Rationi tamen & menti humanæ eam lucem adfert, ut quamvis ignoret, qualem DEum habere deceat, tamen habendum esse sciat, quin etiam vitæ morumq; honestate colendum esse, haud ignoret. Hujus notitiæ dučtum, si homines etiam non renati sequantur, neque lumini huic naturæ, vitæ morúmque consceleratione, vim quasi inferant: vel, ut Apostolus loquitur, veritatem DEI in injustitiâ non detineant: fieri certè nequit, quin pro eo, quod hominum naturæ ingeneratum est, salutis atque immortalitatis desiderio, studium ardens cognoscendi DEum & res divinas, in animis ipsorum oriatur, ut pro captu suo de notitiâ illâ sibi comparanda, sedulò laborent: quemadmodum exemplis id paulò pòst demonstrabimus.

Accedit & illud, quod DEus ipse gravissimas ob causas vult post lapsum etiam notitiam hanc de se, & parte quadam legis suae, in humanâ mente, etiam nondum renata esse reliquam: nõ modò, ut ostendat & arguat peccatum, & regat disciplinam, quemadmodum autor noster loquitur, Tom. 2. operum, p. 328. Sed & ut per hoc medium, homines ad salutem æternam vocet, convertat, regeneret. Quemadmodum verò Lumen hoc Naturæ, vim non passum, quibusvis religionibus alijs, carnale studium impendere potest: ita DEUS hoc ipsum studium, sui quoq; verbi prædicationi, ut impendatur, seriò præcepit: imò per hoc medium, sed ex merâ gratiâ, efficaciter ad salutem operari, ab æterno constituit. Rom. 10, 17. Fides ex auditu. 3. Quoad autoritatem Patrum, sufficiat unus Augustinus, qui lib. de Fide ad Petrū, cap. 32. sic habet: Firmissimè tene, posse quidem hominē, quem nec ignorantia literarū, nec aliqua prohibet imbecillitas vel adversitas, verba legis & Evāgelij, sive legere sive ex ore cujusq́; prædicatoris audire: sed divinis mandatis obedire posse neminē, nisi quē DEUS gratiâ suâ prævenerit; ut quod audit corpore, corde etiā percipiat. Quam eandem in sententiam Liber etiam Concordiæ disertè scribit: Hoc DEI Verbum, Homo etiam nondum ad DEUM conversus, nec renatus, externis auribus audire, aut legere potest. In ejusmodi enim externis rebus, Homo adhuc etiam post lapsum, aliquo modo Liberum Arbitrium habet, ut ad cœtus publicos Ecclesiasticos accedere, verbum DEI audire, vel non audire possit pag. 671. 4. Tandem quoad Exempla, testis est Scriptura, Reginam Aethiopum Nicaulam ab intimis regni finibus Hierosolymam profectam esse, ut Salomonis sapientiam, cujus præcipua pars erat Religio, ex Scripturarum oraculis hausta, cognosceret, 1. Reg. 10, 1. 2. Paral. 9, 1. &c. Magos ex Scripturarum oraculis erudiri petijsse, ubi Salvator Mundi nascendus esset Matth. 2, 2. Herodē Libenter audivisse concionanté Johannem Baptistam Marci 6, 20. Sergiū proconsulem, hominem Ethnicū desiderasse audire Paulum & Barnabam. Act. 13, 7. Felicem præsidem Judææ itidē Ethnicum, ideò ad se vocasse Apostolum vinctum, ut ex ipso audiret sermonem. Act. 24, 24. Testis prætereà est Josephus lib. 1. contra Appionem, Pythagoram tanto studio Religionis Judaicæ cognoscendæ flagrasse, ut quam plurimas Hebræorū leges in suā sectam transtulerit: imò tandē in Aegyptum: & Judæā profectus, ipse quoq; sacris Judaicis initiari voluerit: id quod citra studium Religionis seriū, fieri non potuit. Refert insuper Justinus Philosophus & Martyr in suâ ad Gentes exhortatione, Platonem ex Hebræorum libris multa in suos transtulisse: ita ut in proverbium abierit, τὶ ἐστὶ πλάτων ἢ μωυσῆς ἀττικίζων. Quod ipsum testaturetiam Eusebius in præparatione Evangelicâ, & Theodorethus de Græcorū Affectionibus: quin Aristobulus Judæus lib. 1. ad Philomet. Citante Eusebio, expressè scribit, Platonem in multis secutum esse Legem Hebræorum. Neq; desunt, qui afferment, Platonem hauriendæ sapientiæ gratia in Aegyptum profectum, vel Prophetam Jeremiam ipsum audivisse, vel saltem Scripturas Propheticas evolvisse.


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: Antithesis of the doctrine proposed

These things, which we have said thus far concerning the Liberty of Human Will regarding intermediate and indifferent actions, whether Natural, Civil, or external Ecclesiastical, are indeed of immovable certainty, but not of simple or absolute [certainty]: but rather only limited. For when GOD uses the will of unregenerate men for certain singular ends, it often happens that the outcome which men propose to themselves regarding these intermediate actions does not always follow. For as regards Natural Actions, although men can perform something without, especially, Satanic impediment, yet that they have need of the general help of GOD, the Apostle is witness, Acts 17:28. In him we live, and move, and have our being. This divine help being withdrawn, Man could not even move an arm or a foot, as is evident from the example of Jeroboam, who, ordering the Prophet to be bound with chains with his arm extended, could not draw it back. 1 Kings 13:4. Likewise the example of the Emperor Valens, who, about to issue a sentence of exile and proscription against Basil, had his hand stiffen into the hardness of wood. Whence that common saying arose: Many things fall between the cup and the lip.

As regards Civil Actions, two obstacles are chiefly opposed to the Liberty of human will: The first is the infirmity and corruption of the men themselves, which is the cause that darkness arises in the mind, lapses of judgment, and errors of counsel: To these are added the turmoils of business, the mass of dangers, and other things of that kind: concerning which Bernard rightly says in his Sermon on the Advent of the Lord: We are easy to be seduced: weak to act: fragile to resist: If we wish to discern between good and evil, we are deceived: if we attempt to do good, we fail: if we strive to resist evil, we are cast down and overcome. Hence, therefore, it happens that the mind errs in judging what is honorable and what is base: and thus consequently the will, deceived by the judgment of the mind, or swept aside by the violence of the affections, more often desires what should be avoided: and flees what should be most desired.

The latter obstacle is the Diabolical Tyranny which very often hinders us, so that we cannot arrive where we wish, and where we could otherwise arrive, if it were without it. For this is what the Tyranny of the Devil does, to move and excite the innate delight of iniquity, either in the senses or in the affections, so that in this way sin may be committed by man with his will. The testimonies of the Scriptures pertain here, which assert that the Devil is effective in the children of disobedience, Eph. 2:2, and holds them captive to his will, 2 Tim. 2:26. Nay, even blinds their minds, 2 Cor. 4:4, etc.

Finally, as regards external Ecclesiastical Actions, that deserves observation, that although ordinarily GOD confers his heavenly grace for salvation only through the medium of these, yet merit, whether of congruity or condignity, is by no means to be ascribed to them, as if through these actions any preparation were made in man for the grace of GOD or for conversion: As will be shown more fully a little later.

To this purer doctrine concerning this second kind of human actions, and concerning the free

Will of Man, old and recent Heretics have long since stirred up a dispute, and stir it up today: some of whom have erred gravely on the side of excess, others on the side of defect.

The Papist Doctors, both old and recent, sin especially in excess: whose twofold error should be noted here: The first is that they contend that for the Heathen, who did not doubt the Providence of GOD by the benefit of the light of nature, and who established that GOD, for his own goodness, would omit nothing that makes for the eternal salvation of men, this knowledge sufficed for salvation: as Andradius writes explicitly in his Explanatio Orthodoxa, book 3, p. 292. The latter is that most of the Scholastics fight along with Andradius, [claiming] that by the merit of civil works, done in the unregenerate, it happens that either a preparation is made for justification, or at least some merit of congruity for Grace: although Bellarmine, dissenting in this part from Andradius and the Scholastics, seems to hold the Negative in both cases.

Some Zwinglians pertain to this class, who extend that 'which is known of God' (γνωστὸν Θεῦ), which also came to the Heathen from the Light of Nature, so far as to maintain that it could have profited them for a sufficient and saving knowledge of GOD: as can be seen in Zwingli in his Expositio fidei Christianae to the King of France: Likewise in Gualther in his Apologia Zwinglii, page 53. The impiety of this dogma, however, is evident first from the fact that in the court of GOD, whatever is not of faith is sin: Rom. 14:23. And that it is impossible to please GOD without faith, Heb. 11:6. Therefore, it would be more absurd than the most absurd to wish to merit divine grace and heavenly goods in any way by the price of sins. Then, because not that light of Nature, however great it may be, but the Word of the Lord and that more sure prophetic word, is the only lamp to our feet (2 Pet. 1:19, Ps. 119), by the shining of which one arrives at a saving knowledge of GOD. Since the best of the Gentile philosophers were destitute of this, they were in no way able to aspire to the fellowship of blessed light. Finally, the Apostle himself is a witness, Rom. 1:18, that the Gentiles polluted that very light of Nature with extreme impiety, that is, by detaining the truth in unrighteousness, they departed very far from the salutary worship and acknowledgment of GOD: for although they acknowledged GOD, they did not glorify Him as GOD, but by attributing the outcomes of both favorable and adverse events to Fortune, Chance, the power of the stars, secondary causes, their own strengths, and to good and evil spirits, they rendered themselves guilty of detestable ingratitude toward GOD. And although they sometimes seemed to philosophize excellently about GOD and divine things in their leisure, yet how great was the vanity of opinions among them, how foul the darkness of their errors; indeed, if you consider the whole system of Ethnic worship and religion, how great was the blindness and folly everywhere? how great, finally, was the abomination in fashioning and worshipping idols that were clearly infinite? So that those who dare to attribute salutary knowledge to the Light of Nature are to be judged as clearly insane with reason.

The Stoics err at the very beginning, who imagine that all things which happen, and in whatever way they happen, happen necessarily, and that by an absolute necessity: and that no liberty is left to the human will, by which at least the honesty of external discipline and civil justice might be performed, or more gross crimes avoided by man: But rather that he is snatched away by a certain violent and brute motion to designate any crimes whatsoever. Which most absurd error Huldrych Zwingli has, as it were, recalled from hell in our century, who in Vol. 1 of his works, in the book concerning the Providence of GOD, chapter 5, page 364, expressly writes that man does not designate such crimes by his own will, but GOD in man, and yet that this cannot be imputed to Him as a fault, no more than to a bull, which impregnates the whole herd. Which very thing he repeats in the following sixth chapter. Which stupendous impiety we expressly refuted in the previous Article, which was concerning the cause of sin.

But the Manichaeans also pertain to this class, who, as Augustine testifies in his book on heresies to Quodvultdeus, around A.D. 170, spread the same error, simply taking away and denying all liberty of the human will.

In more recent times the Council of Constance, session 8, article 2, condemned this error in John Wycliffe. By this very name our author also reproves Laurentius Valla: Valla, he says, and many others, do not rightly take away liberty from the will of man, 'because all things happen by the decree of God.' But also in our own century the more recent Manichaeans, the Flacians, are indeed very closely related to this error, inasmuch as they contend that in the conversion or regeneration of man, the will is not changed by a quality, but the very substance of the old heart is abolished, and a new essence of the will is created. Which being posited, it is manifest that by them no liberty of will at all is left to the unregenerate man in any kind of action. But this base and absurd heresy was rightly exploded and condemned long ago in the ancient Manichaeans, because it did not distinguish between the work or creature of GOD and the sin adhering to it. Moreover, the arguments by which the Stoics and Manichaeans, both ancient and modern, are accustomed to fight, are chiefly these:

The first is taken from Jer. 10:23. I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself, nor is it in man to direct his steps. If therefore not even the liberty of ways or steps is to be granted to man, how in the remaining actions superior to the second of this kind will any liberty of the will be able to stand?

But it is most rightly answered that a twofold sophistry is committed: One παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως: while indeed the way and direction of steps is taken in a simple sense concerning locomotion, which in a figurative sense is to be referred to the power of events: which we have just now shown above do not always correspond to the will of man, and therefore this liberty of the will is limited or determined. Which determination of events, however, does not at all take away the liberty of the action considered in itself, as it depends on the liberty of the will as a proximate principle; but rather presupposes it.

The other sophistry is παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For something else is inferred than what the reason of the consequence allows. For it does not follow: If the power of events is not placed in the will of man: Therefore clearly no liberty, no choice, is to be granted to the will of man in these intermediate and indifferent actions. For this consequent strikes most shamefully against that most true axiom of the logicians: Subordinated things do not fight, nor do they mutually take away or exclude each other. Furthermore, the Holy Spirit Himself revealed the difference, Proverbs 16:9, saying: It is of man to prepare the heart: but it is of the Lord to govern the tongue: The heart of man disposes his way: but it is of the Lord to direct his steps. Where indeed liberty of acting is expressly ascribed to man: but the determination of those actions to God. The sense therefore of the saying of Jeremiah is: Although the counsels, deliberations, choices, and actions of men proceed from the liberty of the will: nevertheless, by reason of government and direction toward a certain event, they are subject to divine providence: which does not at all fight with our doctrine.

The other, taken from reason, is such: Where there is no contingency, there is no liberty of the will at all. But in human actions there is no contingency at all: since all things happen as GOD has constituted and decreed them. Therefore there is no liberty of the human will in general.

But this argument encounters at the beginning the same sophistries which the preceding one labored under. Furthermore, the minor proposition is simply false: and that in two ways: For first, that there is no contingency of things and human actions fights with Scripture and all reason, just as was demonstrated to the eye in the immediately preceding Article, which was concerning Necessity and Contingency. Secondly, that which the Manichaeans have taken for granted is an enormous Ψευδογράφημα in our theology, namely that the providence of GOD overturns the liberty of the will: which two, however, relate to each other as subordinated things, concerning which matter see the Article on Providence.

The third and final argument is as follows: Whatever is governed by the immutable will of GOD, that does not act freely: But the will of both Angels and men is governed by the immutable will of GOD. Therefore there is no Freedom of the will.

But the Major proposition is simply denied, which again ignorantly makes contradictories out of subordinates. For the immutable will of GOD and the will of men do not stand in a contradictory relation: for thus they could not stand together at the same time: but they are subordinate: indeed in such a way that the will of GOD, however immutable, nevertheless leaves Freedom to the will, which also acts freely without any compulsion. Furthermore, a Sophistication of equivocation lies hidden in the word (immutable) which meant the same thing to the Manichaeans as absolutely necessary and fatal. By which arrangement, indeed, the will of GOD with respect to human actions is by no means immutable, that is, it does not fatally compel men to do this or that. But in Scripture and our Theology this term signifies the same as infallible.

Latin:

Sunt hæc, quæ hactenus de Libertate Arbitrij Humani circa actiones medias ac indifferentes, tùm Naturales, tùm Civiles, tùm Ecclefiafticas externas diximus, immotæ quidem certitudinis, sed non simplicis, sive absolutæ: verùm duntaxat limitatæ. Quando enim DEUS voluntate hominum non renatorum utitur ad fingulares quosdam fines: sæpiùs fit, ut non semper ille sequatur eventus, quem Homines circa actiones istas medias sibi proponunt. Nam quoad Actiones Naturales, etsi sine impedimento præcipuè Satanico, aliquid præstare possunt Homines: tamen generali DEI auxilio illis opus esse, testis est Apostolus Actor. 17, 28. In ipso sumus, movemur & vivimus. Hoc auxilio divino subtracto, Homo ne quidem brachium aut pedem movere posset, uti constat exemplo Jeroboami, qui extenso brachio jubens vinculis constringi Prophetam, illud retrahere non potuit. 1. Reg. 13, 4. Exemplo item Valentis Imp. cui exilij sententiam & proscriptionem in Basilium expedituro, manus in ligni duritiem obriguit. Undè natum illud vulgare: Multa cadunt inter calicem supremaq́; labra.

Quoad Actiones Civiles, Libertati voluntatis humanæ duo potissimùm obstacula objiciuntur: Prius est, propria ipsorum hominum infirmitas & corruptio, quæ causa est, ut oriantur in mente tenebræ, lapsus judicij, consiliorum errores: Accedunt negotiorum turbæ, periculorum moles, & id genus alia: de quibus rectè Bernhardus Serm. de Adventu Domini: Faciles sumus ad seducendum: debiles ad operandum: fragiles ad resistendum: Si discernere volumus inter bonum & malum, decipimur: si tentamus facere bonum, deficimus: si conamur resistere malo, dejicimur & superamur. Hinc ergò fit, ut mens aberret in dijudicandis honestis & turpibus: & sic consequenter voluntas mentis judicio decepta, aut affectuum violentiâ in transversum abrepta, sæpiùs appetat fugienda: & maximè appetenda fugiat.

Posterius obstaculum est Tyrannis Diabolica quæ sæpissimè nos impedit, quo minùs perveniam9, quò volumus, & quò aliàs, si absq́; eâ esset, pervenire possemus. Hoc enim agit Diaboli Tyrannis, ut congenitam delectationem iniquitatis, vel in sensibus, vel in affectibus moveat & excitet, ut ita ab homine peccatum, voluntate committatur. Pertinent hûc ea Scripturarum testimonia, quæ asserunt Diabolum esse efficacem in filiis inobedientiæ, Eph. 2, 2. eosdemq́; captivos tenere ad suam voluntatem, 2. Tim, 2, 26. Imò eorundem mentes excæcare, 2. Cor. 4, 4. &c.

Tandem quoad Actiones Ecclesiasticas externas, illud observationem meretur, quòd licèt ordinariè DEUS, non nisi mediantibus illis, cælestem suam gratiam ad salutem conferat: minimè tamen illis meritum, vel congrui vel condigni, sit adscribendum, quasi per istas actiones, ad gratiam DEI, vel ad conversionem aliquâ in homine fiat præparatio: Quemadmodum paulò pòst fusiùs ostendetur.

Puriori huic de secundo hoc actionum humanarum genere, deque libero circa illud

Arbitrio Hominis, doctrinæ litem jam olim moverunt, hodieq́; movent veteres & recentiores Hæretici: quorum nonnulli ex parte ὑπερβολῆς in excessu, alij ex parte ἐλλείψεως in defectu graviter errarunt.

In excessu cumprimis peccant Doctores Pontificij tùm veteres, tùm recentiores: quorum geminus error hoc loco notari debet: Prior est, quod contendunt Ethnicis, qui beneficio luminis naturæ non dubitarunt de DEI Providentiâ, quiq́; statuerunt, DEUM pro suâ bonitate nihil prætermissurum, quod ad homines æternùm salvandos faciat, hanc notitiam ad salutem satisfuisse: uti disertè scribit Andradius in explic. Orth. l. 3. p. 292. Posterior est, quòd Scholasticorum pleriq́; cum Andradio pugnant, civilium operum laude, in non renatis fieri, ut vel ad justificationem fiat præparatio, vel ad Gratiam saltem de congruo aliquod promeritum: licèt Bellarminus, hac in parte ab Andradio & Scholasticis dissentiens, utrobiq́; Negativam tenere videatur.

Pertinent ad hanc classem, Zvvingliani nonnulli, qui illud γνωστὸν Θεῦ, quod ex Lumine Naturæ Ethnicis etiam obtigit, eò usq́; extendunt, ut statuant illud ipsis ad sufficientem & salutarem DEI cognitionem prodesse potuisse: uti videre est apud Zvvinglium in expof. fid. Christianæ ad Regem Galliæ: Item apud Gualtherum in Apologiâ Zvvinglij pag. 53. Dogmatis autem hujus impietas primùm vel indè patet, quod in foro DEI peccatum est, quicquid non est ex fide: Rom. 14. 23. Et quod impossibile est, sine fide placere DEO, Hebr. 11, 6. Absurdissimo proindè absurdius fuerit, peccatorum pretio, divinam gratiam & cœlestia bona quovis modo velle promereri. Deindè quod non lux illa Naturæ quantacunq́; : sed Verbum Domini & firmior ille Propheticus sermo, lucerna pedibus nostris unica est (2. Pet. 1, 19. Pf. 119.) quâ prælucente, in salutarem DEI agnitionem pervenitur. Quâ cùm destituti fuerint optimi quiq́; Gentilium Philosophi, ad beatæ lucis consortium adspirare minimè potuerunt. Tandem testis est ipse Apostolus, Rom. 1, 18. Gentiles illam ipsam lucem Naturæ extremâ impietate polluisse, hoc est, veritate in injustitiâ detentâ, à salutari DEI cultu atq́; agnitione longissimè discessisse: Siquidem DEUM agnitum, non ut DEUM glorificarunt, sed Fortunæ, Casui, virtuti siderum, causis secundis, viribus proprijs, Genijs bonis malisq́;, rerum tàm secundarum, quàm adversarum eventus acceptum referentes, detestandæ ingratitudinis erga DEUM reos sese constituerunt. Et quamvis præclarè interdum aliqua de DEO, rebusq́; divinis, in otio Philosophari viderentur: quanta tamen apud illos opinionum fuit vanitas, quàm tetræ errorum tenebræ; imò si universam cultus & religionis Ethnicæ rationem consideres, quanta passim fuit cæcitas & stultitia? quanta deniq́; abominatio in fabricandis & colendis idolis planè infinitis? ut cum ratione planè insanire censendi sint, qui Lumini Naturæ salutarem Notitiam tribuere audent.

In defectu initiò peccant Stoici, qui fingunt, omnia quæ fiunt, & quoquo modo fiunt, fieri necessariò, idq; absolutâ necessitate: neq; ullam voluntati humanæ libertatem relinqui, quâ externæ saltem disciplinæ honestas, & civilis justitia præstari, aut flagitia crassiora, vitari ab homine possint: Sed potiùs violento & bruto quodam motu illum abripi ad designanda quævis scelera. Quem absurdissimum errorem nostro seculo ab orco quasi revocavit Huldricus Zvvinglius, qui Tom. 1. operum lib. de Provid. DEI, cap. 5. p. 364. disertè scribit, Hominem non propria sua voluntate, sed DEUM in Homine designare ejusmodi flagitia, neq; tamen ipsi hoc vitio verti posse, haud magis atq; Tauro, qui totum gregem imprægnat. Quod ipsum repetit capite subsequente Sexto. Quam stupendam impietatem superiore Articulo, qui fuit de causâ peccati, ex professo refutavimus.

Pertinent verò ad hanc classem Manichæi etiam, qui teste Augustino, libro de hærefibus ad Quodvult Deum, circa A. D. 170. eundem errorem sparserunt, simpliciter omnem tollentes & negantes voluntatis humanæ libertatem.

Recentioribus temporibus errorem istum in Johanne Wiclefo damnavit Concilium Constantiense, seß. 8. art. 2. Quo ipso nomine reprehendit etiam Autor noster Laurentium Vallam: Valla, inquiens, & pleriq; alij, non rectè detrahunt voluntati hominis Libertatem, 'quia fiant omnia decernente Deo. Sed & nostro seculo recentiores Manichæi, Flaciani nimirùm errori huic admodum sunt affines, quippè qui contendunt, in Conversione sive regeneratione Hominis, non per qualitatem mutari voluntatem, sedipsam substantiam veteris cordis aboleri, novamq; essentiam voluntatis creari. Quo posito manifestum sit, ab illis homini non regenerato, nullam prorfus libertatem voluntatis, ullo in actionum genere relinqui. Sed rectè jam olim turpis & absurda hæc hæresis, in priscis Manichæis, explosa & damnata fuit, eò quòd inter opus sive creaturam DEI, & peccatum adhærens non discerneret. Cæterùm argumenta, quibus Stoici & Manichæi tùm veteres, tùm recentiores pugnare soliti, præcipuè sunt isthæc:

Primum est petitum ex Jer. 10, 23. Scio Domine, quod non est Hominis via ejus, neq; viri est, dirigere gressus suos. Si ergò ne viarum quidem aut gressuum libertas homini est concedenda, quomodo in reliquis actionibus superioribus secundi hujus generis, ulla aliqua voluntatis libertas stare poterit?

Sed rectissimè respondetur, geminam committi Sophisticationem: Unam παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως: dum nimirùm via & directio gressuum, simplici sensu de locomotivâ accipitur, quæ sensu figurato, ad potestatem eventuum referenda est: quos non semper voluntati hominis respondēre, ac proindè Libertatem hanc voluntatis, limitatam sive determinatam esse, jam modò suprà ipsi ostendimus. Quæ tamen determinatio eventuum, ipsam libertatem actionis in se consideratæ, prout ea pendet à Libertate voluntatis, tanquàm principio propinquo, minimè tollit; sed potiùs præsupponit.

Altera Sophisticatio est παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Aliud enim infertur, quàm quòd Consequentię ratio patitur. Neq; enim consequens est : Si eventuum potestas non est in voluntate Hominis posita: Ergò planè nulla Libertas, nulla electio, voluntati Hominis, in actionibus istis medijs & indifferentibus est concedenda. Impingit enim hoc Consequens turpissimè, in illud verisfimum Logicorum axioma: Subordinata non pugnant, neq; se mutuò tollunt aut excludunt. Prætereà diversum prodidit ipse Spiritus Sanctus, Proverb.16. & 9. Hominis, inquiens, est, cor preparare: sed Domini est, lingvam gubernare: Cor bominis disponit viam suam: sed Domini est, dirigere gressus ejus. Ubi sanè Homini Libertas agendi: Deo autem determinatio illarum actionum disertè adscribitur. Sensus proindè dicti Jeremiæ est : Licèt consilia, deliberationes, electiones & actiones hominum proficiscantur à libertate voluntatis : nihilo minus tamen eas ratione gubernationis & directionis ad certum eventum, subjacere divinæ providentiæ : id quod cum doctrinâ nostrâ minimè pugnat.

Alterum ex ratione petitum, tale est: Ubi nulla Contingentia: ibi nulla prorsus voluntatis Libertas. Atqui in actionibus humanis nulla prorsus est Contingentia: siquidem omnia fiunt, prout DEUS ea constituit & decrevit. Ergò nulla in universum est voluntatis humanæ Libertas.

Sed easdem Sophisticationes initiò occurrit hoc argumentum, quibus præcedens laboravit. Accedit deindè, quo minor propositio simpliciter est falsa : idq; dupliciter: Primùm enim nullam esse rerum atq; actionum humanarum Contingentiam, pugnat cum Scripturâ & omni ratione, quemadmodum ex professo Articulo præcedente proximo, qui fuit de Necessitate & Contingentiâ, ad oculum est demonstratum. Deindè enorme Ψευδογράφημα in Theologiâ nostrâ est id, quod pro confesso sumserunt Manichæi, nempè Providentiam DEI evertere Libertatem voluntatis : quæ duo tamen ad se mutuò se habent, ut Subordinata, Quâ de re videatur Articulus de Providentiâ.

Tertium & postremum argumentum sic habet: Quicquid immutabili voluntate DEI regitur, illud non agit liberè: Atqui voluntas tùm Angelorum, tùm bominum, regitur immutabili voluntate DEI. Ergò nulla est Libertas voluntatis.

Sed negatur simpliciter Major propositio, quæ rursum ex subordinatis inscitè facit contradictoria. Immutabilis enim voluntas DEI, & voluntas hominum non habent sese contradictoriè: Sic enim simul stare non possent: sed sunt subordinata : ita quidem, ut voluntas DEI, quantumvis immutabilis, relinquat tamen Libertatem voluntati, quæ etiam liberè agit sine ullâ coactione. Deindè Sophisticatio æquivocationis latet in vocabulo (immutabilis) quòd idem significavit Manichæis, ac absolutè necessarium & fatale. Quo sanè pacto voluntas DEI respectu actionum humanarum minimè est immutabilis, hoc est, non fataliter cogit homines ad hoc vel illud agendum. : Sed idem in Scripturâ & Theologiâ nostrâ sonat hic terminus, ac infallibilis.


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: Reasons against Liberty in external Ecclesiastical matters, with responses

There is, therefore, an infallible will of GOD, which concurs with our actions: but it does not compel us fatally. That infallibility and certainty of the divine will does not take away the liberty of our will in external matters, but rather presupposes, directs, and determines it.

But enough and more than enough about the Manichaeans and Stoics: rather, in this place, the opinion of those must be more accurately unfolded who, in recent years, condemned it in our theologians as erroneous, nay, even heretical, because they granted to a man not yet reborn some such liberty of the human will in external ecclesiastical matters, by which, from the powers of his own judgment, he could approach the temple and hear the word of GOD, or not hear it: he could in some way, and with a certain carnal zeal, meditate upon the heard word, or not meditate.

The reasons, however, by which those Aristarchuses or censors kept saying they were moved, so as not to concede to this opinion of our theologians, were chiefly these: 1. They said that the opinion of the Papists concerning merit of congruity is confirmed. For just as these feigned that it is altogether congruous that GOD should confer grace upon those who do what is in them: so they claimed that our men posit that it is in human powers to hear and meditate upon the word of GOD, upon which being done, GOD is then bound to confer faith upon them.

Then, that the error of the Synergists is again being recalled to the stage of the Church, who dreamed that something still remained in man after the fall, by which he could in some way prepare or apply himself to his own conversion.

Finally, that this opinion concerning the carnal zeal of those not yet reborn conflicts diametrically with the doctrine of the Formula of Concord.

But these three accusations are so constituted that if the ardor for truth, rather than for ambition, had occupied the minds of those censors, they themselves would easily recognize their futility: which it will have been worth the effort to uncover in a few words.

Regarding the first reason, therefore, those censors most shamefully confuse the order of conversion ordained by GOD from eternity with the very means or organ which GOD has determined to use in conversion: which possesses the respect and nature not of any meritorious cause, but only of an instrumental one. The order of conversion itself is as follows: First, GOD, out of mere grace, without regard for any preceding human work, determined to call men to the kingdom of grace through the word of preaching.

Then He wills that men hear this word, and indeed not coldly or sleepily: but seriously and with some zeal.

Finally, He promised that He would grant faith in Christ the Savior to those hearing in this way, not because of that hearing: but through that hearing: and therefore not out of debt, or any preceding merit, whether of congruity or condignity: but out of mere grace and mercy.

And indeed that order of conversion, in its own parts, is asserted by our theologians to be so sound and intact that they do not allow even the smallest particle of any human merit to be rubbed onto or feigned for it. Since GOD anticipates all our zeal and every effort of hearing in many ways: both because He manifested this very word to us out of mere grace: and because He offers His grace in it before we hear: and finally because He promised that He would perhaps be efficacious through this preached and heard word. Whence it follows:

1. That hearing is not, in and of itself and with respect to the work performed, as the Papists say, the instrument for conferring faith, but is so by the ordination and institution of GOD.

2. That our faith merits absolutely nothing. For if it could merit anything, then in establishing the order of conversion, GOD would necessarily have had to look to this hearing and study of ours as to an efficient or impelling cause. For between merit and the rendering of a reward, there must be an equal proportion and analogy. But in truth, GOD had so little regard for our hearing as a meritorious cause in establishing the order of conversion that if some man were to hear the word of the Gospel for a hundred years, yet GOD had not, by preventing grace, determined that it should be out of mere grace that He is merciful, then indeed all this work put into listening would be useless and in vain, nor would even the slightest bit of faith be kindled in his heart.

3. That this hearing of the word is indeed an instrumental cause of conversion, but not with respect to us, as if we could in any way merit the subsequent conversion through it; but only with respect to GOD, who has determined to use this hearing, as an instrument in effecting our conversion, most freely and not out of any debt.

We conclude, therefore, irrefutably, that this hearing of ours merits nothing at all, whether by congruity or by condignity. But just as, by the testimony of the Apostle in 1 Cor. 3:7, in preaching the word, neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only GOD who gives the increase is anything; so, by the nature of the correlate, in this external hearing also, neither he who hears, nor he who meditates, wills, or runs, is anything; but He who bestows increase and blessing upon the hearing, and through this external medium, out of most free grace, draws the hearer: without which heavenly drawing he would never otherwise come to CHRIST, even if he were to hear the word for his entire life; John 6:44.
