As for the other reason of our censors, it collapses by its own vanity and futility, provided we take into account those things which have just been answered regarding the first reason. For by the same arguments by which we refute the Papist opinion concerning the merit of congruity, we can most powerfully banish the suspicion of Synergism from our doctrine as well. For although the Holy Spirit uses the preaching and hearing of the word in effecting conversion, He does so most freely; yet the will and the mind of a man, by his own proper and natural powers, can do nothing at all, not even the slightest trifle, to perform, assist, cooperate, or in any way prepare or apply himself to grace for his own conversion, much less can he offer any assent to the Word when heard. Therefore, these two very different ζητήματα (questions) must be accurately distinguished: the former of which asks, What can a man perform before conversion, but the latter, what can he perform in the very effecting of conversion? To the former, it is answered that a man, even before any conversion, can hear the Word with his external ears and meditate upon it in a carnal manner. To the latter, it is answered that a man can contribute not even the least thing from himself toward his own conversion: but that this hearing eventually yields to the organ of conversion and faith; that this is to be attributed entirely not to the will or course of man, but to divine grace and mercy.

Regarding the third and final argument, our censors object to us two passages in particular taken from the Book of Concord: the former of which reads thus: 'Scripture, therefore, takes away from the intellect, heart, and will of natural man all aptitude, capacity, and faculty in spiritual things to think, understand, begin, will, propose, act, operate, and cooperate in anything good and right from himself.' The latter, however, is proposed by them in these words: 'Whoever feels in his heart some little spark and desire for divine grace and eternal salvation ought to know that GOD himself has kindled that beginning of true piety in his heart.'

But the response to both passages is easy, if only the state of the matter in question is weighed more diligently. For the former indeed deals with the state of a man not yet regenerate, regarding what he can do in external actions, where we have just shown above that the Book of Concord is in complete agreement with us: but the Concord there asks and expressly deals with: What can the intellect and will of a man not yet regenerate perform in the very conversion from his own powers? Where we feel, believe, and confess exactly the same as the Concord. Therefore, this former objection suffers from the fallacy of many questions. In the allegation of the latter passage, the same sophistication is shamefully committed. For the Concord does not deal with those not yet regenerate, but (as its words expressly sound) with pious minds that indeed have true faith, but one struggling with great infirmity. Therefore, in place of firm consolation for these, not only is that Apostolic passage, Phil. 2:13, 'It is God who works in you both TO WILL AND TO PERFORM,' recalled to mind: but through a certain explanation (ἐπεξήγησιν) it is shown that they themselves can be certain that God himself has kindled that beginning of true piety like a little flame in their hearts: and that He also wills to further confirm and assist them in their great infirmity, so that they may persevere in true faith until the end. p. 659.

But enough and more than enough about this second kind of human actions: There remains the third and final one, which we said to be of good actions: and those either moral or spiritual. And regarding moral ones, the Jesuits today weave a fairly long discussion, more for the sake of showing off their ingenuity than for eliciting and confirming the truth, as can be seen in Bellarmine, book five, On Grace and Free Will. Certainly, that a man even not yet regenerate can know some true moral good is clear from those things which we discussed above concerning the Light of Nature and the righteousness of the flesh. Hence those much-celebrated precepts of the Gentile philosophers, by which they reduced the whole scope or complex of good moral actions to three highest heads of things: namely: 1. To live honestly. 2. To give everyone his due. 3. To harm no one. Hence that other apophthegm of the same breadth: 'What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another': which there is hardly anyone who would deny that almost all the individual precepts of the second table of the Decalogue are comprehended in this one. Therefore, the Gentiles knew, and today men even not yet regenerate, and those who live outside the Church, know that parents, and those who are in the place of parents, are to be honored: that no one is to be killed rashly: that one must live chastely: that another's property is not to be taken away without the knowledge and against the will of the owner, that false testimony is not to be borne: and other good moral things of this kind pertaining to the second table. The Apostle confirms this very thing, Rom. 1:21, saying, 'The Gentiles knew GOD, but did not glorify Him as GOD.' And chapter 2:14. When the Gentiles, who do not have the Law, naturally do the things that are of the law, not having such a law: they are a law to themselves, who show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them.

Latin:

Est ergò DEI voluntas infallibilis, quæ concurrit ad actiones nostras : sed non fataliter nos cogit. Infallibilitas verò & certitudo illa voluntatis divinæ non tollit libertatem voluntatis nostræ in externis, sed eam potiùs præsupponit, dirigit & determinat.

Sed de Manichæis & Stoicis plus satis: illorum potiùs hoc loco accuratiùs evolvenda est sententia, qui superioribus annis proximis, in nostris Theologis tanquam erroneum, imò hæreticum damnârunt, quòd Homini nondum renato concederent talem aliquam Libertatem voluntatis humanæ in Ecclesiasticis externis, quâ ex viribus Arbitrij sui, possit adire templum & audire verbum DEI, vel non audire : possit aliquo modo, & studio quodam carnali meditari auditum verbum, vel non meditari.

Rationes autem, quibus Aristarchi sive censores illi, moveri se dictitabant, quò minùs in hanc nostratium Theologorum sententiam concederent, præcipuæ erant hæ : 1. Pontificiorum, ajebant, confirmari opinionem de merito congrui. Quemadmodum enim hi fingebant, congruum omninò esse, ut DEUS facientibus quod in se est, gratiam conferat : Ita nostros statuere, in viribus humanis positum esse audire, & meditari verbum DEI, quo facto DEUS jam Fidem ipsis conferre teneatur.

Deindè Synergistarum errorem denuò in proscenium Ecclesiæ revocari, qui somniabant, aliquid adhuc post lapsum in homine esse reliquum, quo ad sui conversionem se quodammodo præparare, sive applicare possit.

Tandem cùm doctrinâ Formulæ Concordiæ, hanc sententiam de studio Carnali nondum renatorum è diametro pugnare.

Verùm tria isthæc ἐγκλήματα ita sunt comparata, ut si veritatis magis, quàm ambitionis ardor animos, istorum censorum occupasset, ipsimet facilè eorum futilitatem agnoscerent : quam paucis detegere, operæ pretium fuerit.

Quoad primam ergò Rationem, turpissimè confundunt censores isti ordinem conversionis à DEO ab æterno sancitum, cum ipso medio sive Organo, quo DEUS in conversione uti constituit : quodq; non ullius causæ meritoriæ, sed tantùm Instrumentalis respectum & naturam obtinet. Ordo ipse conversionis sic se habet : Primùm DEUS ex merâ gratiâ, sine intuitu ullius præcedentis operis humani, constituit homines vocare ad regnum gratiæ, per verbum prædicationis.

Deindè vult, ut verbum hoc Homines audiant, & quidem non frigidè aut somnolenter : sed seriò & cum studio aliquo.

Tandem promisit, se sic audientibus donaturum Fidem in Christum Servatorem, non propter auditum illum : sed per auditum illum : idq; proindè non ex debito, sive merito aliquo præcedente, sive congrui sive condigni : sed ex merâ gratiâ & misericordiâ.

Et profectò Ordo iste conversionis, in manibus suis partibus usq; adeò à nostris Theologis sartus tectusq; asseritur, ut ne minimam quidem particulam ullius meriti humani ipsi affricari aut affingi patiantur. Siquidem DEUS omne nostrum studium, omnemq; conatum audiendi, multis modis antevertit: tum quod ex merâ gratiâ, hoc ipsum verbum nobis manifestavit: tum quòd in eo gratiam suam offert, priusquàm audiamus: tùm deniq; quòd promisit se fortè efficacem, per verbum hoc prædicatum & auditum. Undè consequitur:

1. Non auditum per se & respectu operis operati, uti Pontificij loquuntur, sed ex ordinatione & instituto DEI esse fidei conferendæ organum.

2. Nihil prorsus mereri fidem nostram. Si enim aliquid promereri posset, tum in constituendo ordine conversionis, DEUS ad auditum & studium istud nostrum, tanquam ad causam efficientem sive impellentem necessariò respicere debuisset. Nam inter meritum & præstationem mercedis, æqua debet esse proportio & analogia. Jam verò DEUS usq; adeò nullum ad auditum nostrum, tanquam ad causam meritoriam, in constituendo conversationis ordine, respectum habuit: ut si homo aliquis, centum annis audiret verbum Evangelij: DEUS verò non præveniendo constituisset per hunc auditum, ex merâ gratiâ esse misericors: tùm sanè omnis isthæc opera in auscultando posita foret inutilis & frustranea, neq; vel tantillùm fidei in corde ipsius accenderetur.

3. Auditum istum verbi, esse quidem causam instrumentalem conversionis, sed non respectu nostri, quasi nos per illum mereamur aliquo modo subsequentem conversionem: sed tantùm respectu DEI, qui hôc auditu, tanquam organo in conversione nostrâ efficienda, liberrimè, & non ex ullo debito uti constituit.

Concludimus proindè irrefragabiliter, Auditum hunc nostrum, nihil quicquam promereri, sive ex congruo, sive ex condigno: Sed quemadmodum Apostolo teste, 1. Cor. 3, 7. in prædicando verbo, nihil est, qui plantat, aut qui rigat: sed tantùm aliquid est, qui dat incrementum DEUS: ita ex naturâ correlati, in Auditu quoq; isto externo, neq; qui audit, neq; qui meditatur, vult, currit, est aliquid: Sed qui Auditui incrementum & benedictionem largitur: & per externum istud medium, ex liberrimâ gratiâ, trahit audientem: sine quo cœlesti tractu nunquam aliàs ad CHRISTUM veniret, si vel maximè, per universam vitam audiret verbum: Joh. 6, 44.

Quoad alteram Rationem censorum nostrorum, propriâ vanitate ac futilitate illâ concidit, si modò pensi habeamus ea, quæ ad primam rationem modò sunt responsa. Quibus enim argumentis Pontificiam opinionem de merito congrui: ijsdem Synergismi etiam suspicionem à doctrinâ nostrâ validissimè profligare possumus. Etsi enim Spiritus Sanctus, prædicatione & auditu verbi, in efficiendâ conversione utitur, sed liberrimè: voluntas tamen & mens hominis, propriis & naturalibus suis viribus, nihil quicquam, & ne extremum quidem modiculum, ad sui Conversionem, vel præstare, vel adjuvare, vel cooperari, vel ad gratiam ullo pacto se præparare aut applicare, nedùm ullum assensum Verbo audito præbere potest. Distinguenda proindè accuratè sunt duo hæc diversissima ζητήματα : quorum prius quærit, Quid ante Conversionem, posterius verò, quid in ipsa Conversione efficienda, Homo præstare possit? Ad prius respondetur, quòd Homo ante omnem etiam Conversionem possit externis auribus audire Verbum, & carnali studio quodammodo meditari. Ad posterius respondetur, quòd ad sui Conversionem ne minimùm quidem Homo ex se conferre possit: sed quòd Auditus iste tandem cedit in organum Conversionis & fidei: id non Hominis vel voluntati vel cursui, sed divinæ gratiæ & misericordiæ in solidum esse acceptum ferendum.

Quoad Tertiam & postremam Rationem, Objiciunt nobis censores nostri, duo potissimùm loca ex Libro Concordiæ petita : quorum prior sic habet. Scriptura igitur hominis naturalis intellectui, cordi & voluntati, omnem aptitudinem, capacitatem & facultatem in rebus spiritualibus, aliquid boni & recti ex semetipso cogitandi, intelligendi, inchoandi, volendi, proponendi, agendi, operandi & cooperandi adimit. Posterior verò his verbis ab ipsis proponitur: Qui scintillulam aliquam & desiderium gratiæ divinæ, & æternæ salutis in corde suo sentit, scire debet, quod ipse DEUS initium illud veræ pietatis in corde accenderit.

Sed facilis est ad utrumque locum responsio, si modò status de quo agitur, diligentiùs expendatur. Prior enim μὲν quidem agit, de statu Hominis nondum renati, Quidnam ille possit in externis actionibus, ubi Librum Concordiæ per omnia nobis esse ὁμόψυχον, jam modò suprà ostendimus: Sed de eo ibi quærit, & ex professo agit Concordia : Quidnam Hominis nondùm renati intellectus & voluntas in ipsa Conversione ex propriis viribus præstare possit? Ubi nos idem prorsus cum Concordia sentimus, credimus & confitemur. Laborat proindè prior hæc objectio Sophismate plurium Quæstionum. In allegatione posterioris loci, eadem Sophisticatio turpiter committitur. Neque enim de nondùm renatis agit Concordia, sed (uti verba ejus expressè sonant) de piis mentibus, quæ veram quidem fidem habent, sed cum magna infirmitate luctantem. His ergo firmæ consolationis loco non modò illud Apostolicum Philip. 2, 13. Deus est, qui operatur in vobis VELLE & PERFICERE, ad animum revocatur: sed per quandam ἐπεξήγησιν ostenditur, certos ipsos esse posse, quòd ipse Deus initium illud veræ pietatis tanquam flammulam, in cordibus ipsorum accenderit: quodque velit eos etiam in magna infirmitate porrò confirmare, & juvare, ut in vera fide ad finem usque perseverent. p. 659.

Sed de secundo isto actionum humanarum genere plus satis: Restat Tertium & postremum, quod Bonarum actionum esse diximus: earumque vel Moralium vel Spiritualium. Et de Moralibus quidem benè longam disputationem hodiè pertexunt Jesuwitæ, ostentandi magis ingenii, quàm veritatis eruendæ & confirmandæ gratia, uti videre est apud Bellarminum libro quinto de Gratia & Libero Arbitrio. Certè posse Hominem etiam nondùm renatum cognoscere verum aliquod Bonum Morale, patet ex iis, quæ supra de Lumine Naturæ & justitia carnis disputavimus. Hinc πολυθρύλλητα illa Gentilium Philosophorum præcepta, quibus ad tria summa rerum capita, universum quasi ambitum sive complexum actionum bonarum Moralium, revocarunt: nempè: 1. Honestè vivendum. 2. Suum cuique tribuendum. 3. Neminem lædendum. Hinc illud alterum ejusdem amplitudinis apophthegma: Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris: Quo vel uno singula ferrnè secundæ Decalogi tabulæ præcepta comprehendi, vix quisquam est, qui inficias iverit. Cognoverunt proindè Gentiles, hodieque cognoscunt Homines etiam nondùm renati, quique extra Ecclesiam vivunt, parentes, & qui parentum loco sunt, esse honorandos: neminem esse occidendum temerè: castè esse vivendum: non auferendam rem alienam inscio & invito Domino, non esse falsum perhibendum testimonium: & quæ sunt hujus generis Bona Moralia alia, ad secundam tabulam pertinentia. Confirmat hoc ipsum Apostolus, Rom. 1, 21. Gentes, inquiens, cognoverunt DEUM, sed non, ut DEUM glorificarunt. Et cap. 2, 14. Cùm gentes, quæ Legem non habent, naturaliter ea, quæ legis sunt, faciant, ejusmodi legem non habentes: ipsi sibi sunt Lex, qui ostendunt, opus Legis scriptum in cordibus suis, testimonium reddente illis conscientia ipsorum.


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: Reasons against Liberty in external Ecclesiastical matters, with responses (continued)

This very thing is evident from reason in this manner: Every natural power, remaining after the fall, can exercise some act regarding an adequate object: otherwise that power would be entirely idle, useless, and superfluous: which would be impious even to think, indeed highly insulting to GOD the creator himself. But the human intellect is a natural power: and its adequate object is also moral good, that is, according to reason, either in whole or in part. Therefore, the human intellect can know some moral good from its own powers.

However, two things come into question in this place: The first is, whether the grace and help of GOD is not required for this very knowledge and efficiency of some moral good? The second, however, is whether by the powers of Nature alone, a man not regenerate can fulfill all moral precepts, according to the substance of the acts, or of the work, as Bellarmine speaks, lib. 5. de grat. & lib. arb. c. 5.

The former ζήτημα is most correctly explained through the distinction between general and special grace of God. For just as for the remaining individual and universal natural actions of man, a general help of God is also required: For in him we live, and move, and have our being, Acts 17:28; so, that the same is presupposed in moral actions, can be a matter of doubt to no one. Now if the question is concerning the special grace of God, we do not deny that in certain heroic and clearly unusual examples of virtues, it most especially exerts itself: but as regards that common Theory and ethical practice, we do not doubt in the least to affirm that it is for the most part accomplished only by the general help of GOD, by the power of the Light of Nature. Nor indeed does that special grace of GOD, or the as it were peculiar inspiration of the Holy Spirit, which is sometimes perceived in the unregenerate, patronize their fury rather than their error, who trifled that those Gentiles, in whom such singular heroic deeds were observed, had been saved even without faith in Christ, by that excellence of the Light of Nature. They surely betray a plainly stupendous ignorance, since they have not yet learned to distinguish among the distinct gifts of the special grace of GOD, or of the Holy Spirit. For there are some gifts that are ministering, serving either for external discipline or for preserving the common society of men: But others are sanctifying, such as are Conversion to God, Faith in Christ, Perseverance in faith, Justification, Glorification. The former do not contribute anything to salvation, and therefore can also fall to the lot of infidels, and be joined with mortal sin. But the latter are proper only to the faithful or the Elect.

As regards the latter question, it is not yet agreed among the Papists themselves what they wish to be understood by the Substance of acts or of the work. Bellarmine indeed, and the whole Jesuitical dregs of today, understand by the Substance of the Work such an observance of the commandments of GOD as is necessary, and by which a new sin is avoided, and it is a good work, according to a certain mortal honesty: as Bellarmine teaches, in the place just cited: who immediately adds this as it were explanation:

Observance according to the substance of the work requires that the commandment be so observed that sin is not committed, and a man does not become guilty for not fulfilling the commandment. With this explanation standing, he writes that he embraces the negative: namely, that all moral commandments cannot be kept by the powers of Nature alone, according to the Substance of the Work. Although indeed this negative of Bellarmine seems to savor of orthodoxy: yet he craftily partly hides the ancient doctrine of the Romans concerning the proposed Question: and partly, fostering a hidden sore, he sophistically lies in wait for our purer doctrine. For first, the older Papists taught that a Man can, without the Holy Spirit, by the powers of nature alone, love GOD above all things; as is to be seen especially in Andradius, whose flowers and emblems we shall pluck and taste from his own writings below.

Then indeed they contended that the commandments of GOD can be done by men, according to the Substance of the acts, that is, that the external works divinely commanded can be fulfilled by man, according to that which is to be performed outwardly, even if internal motions are not applied. Whence Johannes Cochlaeus writes that from such an observance or fulfillment of the commandments of GOD, only two things are to be excepted; 1. The meritorious dignity of the deed. 2. The opinion concerning the absence of the general grace of GOD.

But this is a sink of the most absurd impieties. For that which they define by the external work alone, concerning the substance of acts in keeping the commandments of GOD, labors under an enormous absurdity, nay, a manifest falsehood. The Law of GOD surely does not command only concerning external discipline, or only external members: but demands the entire obedience of the whole man. CHRIST certainly established the substance of the Act in the commandments of the first table as this: You shall love GOD with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind, Matt. 22. 36. Thus GOD himself established the Substance of all the negative commandments of the second table: You shall not covet: Both parts of which substance of acts, since it is impossible by human powers outside of regeneration, Rom. 8, 3. Acts 15, 10. It is plainly trifling, whatever the Romanists blather about the substance of acts in external works: nay, it is heretical; because the seventh Canon of the Sixth Session of the Council of Trent too boldly vibrates the lightning bolt of anathema against those who say that all works, which are done by the unregenerate in any way whatsoever, are truly sins, or deserve the hatred of GOD.

Taking up the patronage of which heresy, Bellarmine, lib. 5. de grat. & lib. arb. cap. 9. devises a certain new little distinction at the beginning: saying that it is not altogether the same thing to do a moral good, and to observe a commandment, according to the substance of the work. For a commandment can be kept according to the substance of the work, even with sin, as if someone should return a deposit to a friend, so that he himself might be despoiled of it by thieves: But a moral good cannot be done with sin. Then indeed he flees to the special help of GOD; saying, It is most certain that not all works, which are done without faith, are sins. Finally, being ill-conscious of himself, he uses a certain limitation, saying, Meanwhile, however, we also wish to prove that some work can be done that is morally good, not only without faith, but also without special help, if no temptation urges. For we have already shown that when temptation urges, nothing good can be done by the powers of nature alone.

But these leaves are fig leaves, with which this ill-starred society strives to cover the shameful parts of its religion: which, that we may uncover, it is pleasing to comprehend the whole matter under certain hypotheses.

First, therefore, this Jesuitical dogma fundamentally undermines and overturns the ancient doctrine of the Scholastic theologians concerning the works of the unregenerate. For they taught that an unregenerate man, without faith and the Holy Spirit, can from purely natural powers fulfill the commandments of God as regards the substance of the act, and that an infidel who performs the works of the commandments in this way does not sin: Indeed, that a man even existing in mortal sin can, from purely natural powers, avoid and beware of any mortal sin, so as not to commit it anew, and that an infidel, by doing what is in him in this way—namely, by removing the obstacle of mortal sin and eliciting a good act from free will—merits by congruity that God should give him grace.

To this more than heretical opinion of the Scholastics, Bellarmine indeed opposes his own new little distinction: but in such a way that he binds himself in the snare of the same impiety, as will soon be demonstrated.

Furthermore, the Jesuit shamefully begs the question, asserting that a precept can indeed be observed with sin, but that a moral good cannot likewise be done with sin: this is what is placed in controversy and stands in need of clear proof.

Thirdly, we showed above that the claim that special help from GOD removes the character of sin from the works of such people in the case of unbelievers is simply false, once the distinction between the ministering and the sanctifying gifts of GOD is observed.

Fourthly, what the Jesuit brings forward concerning Temptation is likewise nonsensical and betrays a shameful, nay, childish babbling, as if the nature and definition of a Good Work depended on the presence of some temptation, and not rather on faith.

Fifthly, it is clearly sophistical that the Jesuit, by special help from GOD, does not understand the grace of regeneration and renewal through the Holy Spirit, but rather peculiar motions or impulses in the unregenerate, which we commonly call heroic, such as were in Scipio, Aristides, and other Gentiles.

Sixthly, a distinction must be made between the works of the unregenerate: for some are by their kind vicious and prohibited by the law of God; others, however, are not, such as practicing mechanical arts, promulgating honest laws, and studying political, ethical, or economic virtues. Works of this latter kind are not in themselves sins or vicious—that is, the very substance or matter of the actions is not evil—but if you consider them partly with respect to GOD and partly with respect to the person performing them, they are certainly nothing other than sins, not even excluding heroic motions. For first, the Gentiles or unregenerate do not set the glory of GOD, or even the salvation of their neighbor, as the end of these works, but rather pleasure, avarice, or ambition. Furthermore, the person performing them is not reconciled to GOD through faith. Now, whatever is not of faith is sin; and without faith it is impossible to please God. Rom. 14, 23. Hebr. 11, 6. Hence Augustine rightly replies to Julian, who commended the works of the Gentiles too much: You introduce a kind of human being that can please GOD by the law of nature without the faith of Christ. This is the very thing for which the Christian Church most detests your voice.

Bellarmino objects to these things that have been said with that passage from Exod. 1, 20: Because the midwives feared GOD, He built houses for them. Hence he argues thus: God rewards certain good works of the Gentiles. Therefore, some good works can be done by unbelievers, whether with special help or even by the powers of nature alone. He submits this reason for the consequence: Because GOD, who is most just, would not reward evil works, since these, by just judgment, deserve punishment, not a reward.

I answer: The argument fails, first, by the fallacy of Ignoratio Elenchi. For it is not in controversy between us and the Jesuits whether the moral works of the unregenerate are in no way and in no respect good in their own kind. For we ourselves readily admit that very many of these works, such as was also the work of the Egyptian midwives, are truly good works τῇ φύσει, that is, by nature and by reason of their substance or matter. But this is in question, whether

, these works, however much they are good τῇ φύσει, fulfill the law of GOD as regards the substance of the acts and merit grace de congruo, so that GOD might give them grace, as the Romanists have commonly taught. Then, the fallacy of non-cause as cause is committed, as well as that of the vicious consequent. For it does not follow: God rewarded their work in those midwives; therefore, there are works of the unregenerate that are so good that they fulfill the Law of GOD as regards the substance of the acts and merit grace de congruo. The reason is: Because GOD corporally rewards even works of this kind, insofar as they are good τῇ φύσει and serve external honesty and piety. Which reason the Text itself expresses: Because, it says, they feared GOD—that is, they determined that GOD must be obeyed rather than the impious and cruel mandate of the King—therefore He built houses for them. Hence Augustine aptly says: That it is written that GOD did well with the Hebrew midwives and with Rahab the harlot of Jericho, was done because they were merciful to the people of GOD. Therefore, the work itself, considered in itself, pleased GOD, although the persons were unbelievers and most displeasing to God. And consequently, the argument from a corporal blessing to the works of unbelievers, considered in the forum of GOD, is invalid, as if these were not sins because GOD rewarded them corporally.

Then the Jesuit brings forward that passage of Daniel to King Nebuchadnezzar, chap. 4, 24: Now, O King, let my counsel be pleasing to you; redeem your sins with alms. Therefore, if the alms of an unbelieving man could avert temporal punishment, certainly some good works of unbelievers will not be sins, since sins do not mitigate the wrath of GOD, but rather inflame it.

I answer: 1. Even if the text were to read exactly as the Jesuit cites it, it would prove nothing, provided that those things which the Refutation of the preceding argument set forth concerning the works of the unregenerate were taken into account. But if we consult the Chaldean sources, the name בְּצִדְקָה occurs in them, which does not mean by alms, but in righteousness: so that this is the sense of Daniel's words: Redeem your sins in righteousness, and your iniquities by mercies to the poor, then behold, there will be long-suffering over your transgression. Daniel is indeed prescribing to the King a mode of true repentance, that he might exchange his preceding impiety and pride for contrary virtues. Furthermore, nothing at all is treated in this passage concerning eternal punishments and redemption from them, which Daniel himself ascribes entirely to the Holy of Holies, namely CHRIST, chap. 9, 24. But the question concerns a temporal punishment, as the Jesuit himself admits, namely that ejection of the King from the company of men to the wild beasts: so that in this passage the word sin denotes that temporal punishment for sin, which GOD is wont not rarely to mitigate, or even to take away entirely, on account of works of charity and mercy performed for the needy: according to that of Psalm 41:1, Blessed is he that considereth the poor and needy: the LORD will deliver him in time of trouble. Which deliverance can befall even an unbelieving man, although meanwhile his works, however τῇ φύσει good, inasmuch as

Latin:

Patet hoc ipsum ex ratione in hunc modum: Omnis potentia naturalis, post lapsum reliqua, potest circa objectum adæquatum, actum aliquem exercere: alioquin otiosa planè, inutilis & supervacanea foret illa potentia: id quod vel cogitatu impium, imò in ipsum DEUM creatorem summè contumeliosum esset. Atqui Intellectus humanus est potentia naturalis: Objectum verò ejus adæquatum, est etiam Bonum morale, idǫ, secundum rationem, vel ex toto vel ex parte. Ergò intellectus humanus potest Bonum aliquod morale ex suis viribus cognoscere.

Duo autem hoc loco in quæstionem veniunt: Prius est, An non ad hanc ipsam notitiam & efficientiam Boni alicujus Moralis, requiratur DEI gratia & auxilium? Posterius verò. An solis Naturæ viribus, Homo non renatus possit adimplere omnia præcepta moralia, secundum substantiam actuum, sive operis, ut loquitur Bellarminus, lib. 5. de grat. & lib. arb.c.5.

Prius ζήτημα per distinctionem Gratiæ Dei generalis & specialis, rectissimè explicatur. Quemadmodum enim ad reliquas actiones Hominis singulas & universas Naturales etiam requiritur Generale Dei auxilium: In ipso enim sumus, movemur & vivimus, Actor. 17, 28. ita, quin in actionibus moralibus idem præsupponatur, nemini potest esse dubium. Jam si de speciali gratia Dei sit quæstio, non negamus, quin in factis quibusdan Heroicis, & inusitatis planè virtutum fpeciminibus, illa vel maximè fefe exerat: sed quoad communem illam & Theoriam & praxin Ethicam, quin plerumque Generali tantùm DEI auxilio, vi Luminis Naturæ illa absolvatur, affirmare minimè dubitamus. Neque verò fpecialis illa DEI gratia, five peculiaris quafi Spiritus fancti afflatus, qui in non renatis interdum perfpicitur, quicquam patrocinatur eorum furori potiùs, quàm errori, qui nugabantur, Ethnicos illos, in quibus ejusmodi singularia facta Heroica confpiciebantur, etiam fine fide in Chriftum, ex præstantia illa Luminis Naturæ salvatos fuiffe. Infcitiam nimirùm planè stupendam produnt, cùm inter distincta dona specialis gratiæ DEI, sive Spiritus sancti, nondùm distinguere didicerunt. Sunt enim, alia Ministrantia, vel ad externam difciplinam, vel ad communem hominum societatem confervandam facientia: Alia verò sunt Sanctificantia, qualia sunt, Conversio ad Deum, Fides in Christum, Perseverantia in fide, Justificatio, Glorificatio. Illa non faciunt quicquam ad salutem, ac proindè in infideles quoq; cadere, & cum peccato mortali conjuncta esse possunt. Hæc verò tantùm fidelium sive Electorum sunt propria.

Quoad Posterius ζήτημα, nondum inter ipsos Pontificios convenit, quid per Substantiam actuum sive operis intellectum velint. Bellarminus sanè, & universa hodiè colluvies Jesuitica, per Substantiam Operis intelligit talem observationem præceptorum DEI, quæ necessaria est, & qua novum peccatum vitatur, & sit opus bonum, secundùm mortalem quandam honestatem: sic docente Bellarmino, loco jam proximè citato: qui statim hanc quafi ἐπεξήγησιν adjicit:

Observatio secundùm substantiam operis requirit, ut sic præceptum observetur, ut peccatum non committatur, & non fiat homo reus ob præceptum non impletum. Quâ explicatione stante, Negantem se amplecti scriptitat: nempè, Non posse solis Naturæ viribus servari omnia præcepta moralia, secundùm Substantiam Operis. Quanquam verò Negativa hæc Bellarmini ὀρθοδοξίαν resipere videtur: astutè tamen partim antiquam Romanenfium doctrinam de proposita Quæstione occultat: partim verò ὕπυλον fovens, puriori nostræ doctrinæ Sophisticè insidiatur. Nam primùm Vetustiores Pontificii docuerunt, posse Hominem sine Spiritu sancto, solis naturæ viribus, DEUM super omnia diligere; uti videre est cumprimis apud Andradium, cujus flosculos & Emblemata ex ipsius scriptis infra decerpemus & delibabimus.

Deindè verò contenderunt, posse ab hominibus præcepta DEI fieri, quoad Substantiam actuum, hoc est, posse ab homine externa opem divinitùs præcepta expleri, secundùm illud, quod foris gerendum est, quamvis interiores res motus non adhibeantur. Undè Johan. Cochlæus à tali observatione sive impletione præceptorum DEI, duo tantùm excipienda esse scribit; 1. Dignitatem meritoriam facti. 2. Opinionem de absentia gratiæ DEI generalis.

Verùm sentina hæc est absurdissimarum impietatum. Nam enormi absurditate, imò manifesta falsitate laborat illud, quod substantiam actuum in præceptis DEI servandis, definiunt per externum duntaxat opus. Lex profectò DEI, non tantùm de externa disciplina, aut externis tantùm membris præcipit: sed integram totius hominis obedientiam flagitat. CHRISTUS certè substantiam Actus in primæ tabulæ præceptis hanc constituit: Diliges DEUM ex toto corde, tota anima, totaque mente Matth. 22. 36. Sic secundæ tabulæ præceptorum omnium Negativorum Substantiam DEUS ipse constituit: Non concupisces: Cujus sanè substantiæ actuum pars utraque, cùm humanis viribus extra regenerationem sit impossibilis, Rom. 8, 3. Actor. 15, 10. nugatorium planè est, quicquid de substantia actuum in externis operibus, blaterant Romanenses: imò hæreticum est; quod Canon septimus, Sessionis Sextæ Concilii Tridentini nimis audacter anathematis fulmen vibrat in eos, qui dixerint, Opera omnia, quæ à non renatis quacunque ratione fiunt, verè esse peccata, vel odium DEI mereri.

Cujus sanè hæreseως patrocinium suscipiens Bellarminus, lib. 5. de grat. & lib. arb. cap. 9. novam quandam initiò excogitat distinctiunculam: Non inquiens omninò idem est facere bonum morale, & observare præceptum, secundùm substantiam operis. Potest enim servari præceptum secundùm substantiam operis, etiam cum peccato, ut si quis amico restituat depositum, ut illo ipse à furibus spolietur: Sed bonum morale non potest cum peccato fieri. Deindè verò auxilium DEI speciale confugit; Certissimum est, inquiens, non omnia opera, quæ fiunt sine fide, esse peccata. Tandem quippè malè sibi conscius limitatione quadam utitur, inquiens, Interim tamen illud etiam probare volumus, posse fieri aliquod opus bonum moraliter, non solùm sine fide, sed etiam sine auxilio speciali, si nulla tentatio urgeat. Nam urgente tentatione nihil boni solis naturæ viribus fieri posse, jam ostendimus.

Sed folia hæc sunt ficulnea, quibus maleseriata isthæc societas, Religionis suæ pudenda tegere satagit: quæ ut detegamus, rem omnem certis quibusdam hypothesibus comprehendere placet.

Primùm igitur dogma hoc Jesuwiticum, antiquam Scholasticorum Theologorum doctrinam de operibus non renatorum fonditus subruit & evertit. Hi enim docuerunt, Hominem non renatum, sine fide & Spiritu sancto, ex puris naturalibus posse præcepta Dei implere, quoad substantiam actus, & infidelem, qui hoc modo facit opera præceptorum, non peccare: Imò, Homo etiam in peccato mortali existentem, posse ex puris naturalibus vitare, & cavere quodvis peccatum mortale, ne de novo illud committat, & infidelem, hoc modo faciendo, quod in se est, removendo scilicet obicem peccati mortalis, & eliciendo bonum actum ex libero arbitrio, mereri de congruo, ut DEUS ipsi det gratiam.

Huic Scholasticorum opinioni plusquàm hæreticæ, Bellarminus novam quidem suam opponit distinctiunculam: sed ita, ut ejusdem impietatis laqueo se constringat: uti mox demonstrabitur.

Deindè turpiter petit Jesuwita principium, asserens posse quidem observari præceptum cum peccato: sed non itidem posse fieri bonum morale cum peccato: id quod in Controversia est positum, & luculenta probatione indiget.

Tertiò auxilium DEI speciale in infidelibus peccati rationem in operibus istorum tollere, simpliciter falsum esse suprà ostendimus, observata distinctione inter dona DEI ministrantia, & Sanctificantia.

Quartò de Tentatione quod adfert Jesuwita itidem nugatorium est, & turpem imò puerilem ἀδολεσχίαν prodit, quasi verò ex tentationis alicujus præsentia, non verò ex fide, Boni Operis natura & definitio dependeat.

Quintò Sophisticum planè est, quòd Jesuwita per auxilium DEI speciale, non intelligit gratiam regenerationis & renovationis per Spiritum sanctum, sed motus seu impetus peculiares in non renatis, quos vulgò vocamus heroicos, quales fuerunt in Scipione, Aristide, & aliis Ethnicis.

Sextò distinguendum est inter opera non renatorum: Quædam enim sunt genere suo vitiosa, & lege Dei prohibita: Quædam verò non item, qualia sunt, exercere artes Mechanicas, promulgere leges honestas, studere virtutibus Politicis, Ethicis, Oeconomicis. Posterioris hujus generis opera, per se quidem non sunt peccata sive vitiosa: hoc est, ipsa substantia, sive materia actionum non est mala: sed si partim respectu DEI, partim respectu personæ operantis ea consideres, certè nihil aliud sunt, quàm peccata: ne quidem heroicis exceptis motibus. Primùm enim Ethnici sive non renati finem istorum operum non constituunt gloriam DEI, vel etiam salutem proximi: sed vel voluptatem, vel avaritiam, vel ambitionem. Deindè verò persona operans non est per fidem DEO reconciliata: Jam verò quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est: Et sine fide impossibile est placere Deo. Rom. 14, 23. Hebr. 11, 6. Hinc Augustinus rectè Juliano, Ethnicorum opera nimiùm commendanti respondet: Introducis hominum genus, quod ex lege naturæ placere DEO possit, sine fide Christi. Hoc ipsum est, undè vox maximè detestatur Christiana Ecclesia.

Objicit his, quæ dicta sunt Bellarminus, locum illum Exod. 1, 20. Quia timuerunt obstetrices DEUM, ædificavit illis domos. Hinc sic arguit? Deus remuneratur bona quædam opera Gentilium. Ergò possunt fieri aliqua bona opera ab infidelibus, sive cum auxilio speciali, sive etiam solis naturæ viribus. Rationem consequentiæ subjicit hanc: Quia DEUS, qui justissimus est, opera mala, non remuneraretur, siquidem hæc justo judicio supplicium mereantur, non præmium.

Respondeo; fallit argumentum 1. Sophismate Ignorationis Elenchi. Neque enim illud inter nos & Jesuwitas controvertitur: An opera moralia non renatorum planè nullo modo ac respectu, in suo genere sint bona? Nam nos ipsi ultro fatemur, plurima istorum opera, quale etiam fuit opus obstetricum Ægyptiacarum τῇ φύσει sive natura, & ratione substantiæ sive materiæ suæ, esse revera bona opera: Sed hoc in quæstione est, An

, opera isthæc quantumvis τῇ φύσει bona, impleant legem DEI, quoad substantiam actuum & mereantur de congruo, ut DEUS illis det gratiam: Sicuti communiter Romanenses docuerunt. Deindè committitur Sophisticatio non causæ ut causæ: & vitiosi consequentis. Neque enim sequitur: Deus remuneratus est in obstetricibus istis opus ipsorum. Ergo dantur opera non renatorum, quæ ita bona sunt, ut Legem DEI impleant, quoad substantiam actuum, & de congruo mereantur gratiam. Ratio est: Quia DEUS corporaliter remuneratur etiam opera hujusmodi, quatenùs τῇ φύσει bona sunt, & externæ honestati, ac pietati subserviunt. Quam rationem exprimit ipse Textus: Quia, inquiens, timuerunt DEUM, hoc est, statuerunt magis obediendum esse DEO, quàm impio ac crudeli Regis mandato, ideò ædificavit illis domos. Hinc scitè Augustinus: Quod scriptum est, benè DEUM fecifse, cum Hebræis obstetricibus, & cum Rahab Hierichuntica meretrice, ideò factum est, quia in homines DEI misericordes fuerunt. Placuit Ergò DEO opus ipsum in se consideratum: licèt personæ infideles Deo maximè displicerent: Ac proindè à corporali benedictione; non valet consequentia, ad opera infidelium, in foro DEI considerata: quasi hæc ideò non sint peccata, quia DEUS ea corporaliter est remuneratus.

Deindè profert Jesuwita illud Danielis ad Regem Nabuchodonosorem, cap. 4, 24. Nunc Rex consilium meum placeat tibi, peccata tua eleemosynis redime. Ergò si Eleemosynæ hominis infidelis avertere poterant pœnam temporalem: Certè bona quædam infidelium opera erunt non peccata: Siquidem peccata non mitigant iram DEI, sed magis accendunt.

Respondeo 1. Si vel maximè textus ita haberet, prout Jesuwita eum citat: nihil tamen evinceret, si modò pensi haberentur ea, quæ de operibus non renatorum præcedentis argumenti Refutatio expediit. Sed si fontes Chaldæos consulamus, occurrit in eis nomen בְּצִדְקָה quòd non significat Eleemosynis, sed in Justitia: ut hic sit sensus verborum Danielis: Peccata tua in Justitia redime: & iniquitates tuas misericordiis pauperum, tùm ecce longanimitas erit super delictum tuum. Præscribit nimirùm Daniel Regi veræ pœnitentiæ modum, ut antegressam impietatem & superbiam, contrariis cum virtutibus permutet. Deinde nihil quicquam hoc loco agitur de pœnis æternis; deque redemtione ab iisdem; quam ipse Daniel, Sancto Sanctorum nempè CHRISTO in solidum adscribit, cap. 9, 24. Sed agitur de pœna temporali, quemadmodum ipse Jesuwita fatetur, nempè de ejectione illa Regis ex hominum contubernio ad feras bestias: ita, ut hoc loco peccati vox notet pœnam illam peccati temporalem, quam DEUS haud rarò mitigare, imò penitùs auferre solet, propter opera charitatis & misericordiæ egenis præstita: secundùm illud Psalmi 41, 2. Beatus qui intelligit super egenum & pauperem: in die mala liberabit eum DOMINUS. Quæ liberatio potest obtingere homini etiam infideli, licet interim opera ipsius, quantumvis τῇ φύσει bona, quippè


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: On Actions Of Pure Spirituals

destitute of faith, are displeasing to God, and obtain the character of sin.

OF PURELY Spiritual ACTIONS.

But enough and more than enough about moral actions: There remains the last kind of human actions, which is the merely spiritual: such as those which properly pertain to the worship of GOD, the purity of Religion, and the eternal salvation of souls: such as to assent to the preached word: To be converted to God, to detest sin, to believe in Christ, to call upon God in Spirit and in truth, under the cross to hope patiently and undoubtedly for the help of GOD: To live according to the Spirit, and many others of this kind of internal, heavenly, and purely spiritual actions. Therefore, it is these actions that are properly inquired into in this place: Whether to an unregenerate man, after the fall, there is any Free Will left in spiritual matters: or, which amounts to the same thing: Whether the mind and will from their first birth have such power, such strength and faculties, that when a man reads, hears, and thinks upon the word of GOD, he can, without the Holy Spirit, from pure (as the Scholastics say) naturals, conceive such motions, and elicit such actions in the mind and will, as Scripture requires for contrition, faith, and new obedience. Concerning which the κρινόμενον (point at issue) of our Church is that they hold and defend the negative simply, being thus taught by the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, which speak negatively and expressly declare that by the fall in corrupt nature every δυναμιν (power), strength, and efficacy or faculty has been utterly lost, by which spiritual actions are either to be begun or to be effected: And indeed the Scriptures clearly attest this distinctly both concerning the mind or intellect, and concerning the heart or will of the unregenerate man. And concerning the Mind indeed, 1 Cor. 2:14: The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of GOD: nay, he cannot even do so, because they are judged spiritually.

Ephes. 2:1. In sins we are (not languid or infirm) but dead. Whence this Theological Demonstration can and ought to be sought: Just as a man who is corporally dead can neither prepare nor accommodate himself to receive temporal life, much less effect it: so a man spiritually dead in sins can in no way prepare or apply himself by his own powers to obtain spiritual and heavenly righteousness and life, much less effect or procure it. Nor does that parable in Luke 10:30, concerning the man beaten by robbers and left half-dead, prove otherwise. For it was not the Savior's purpose in that place to show what and what kind of Free Will an unregenerate man has in spiritual matters: but only who is our neighbor. Therefore a gross Ignorance of the Elenchus (refutation) is committed in the citation of this saying, which does not even whisper about the stated point of the controversy. Let the Apostle rather be heard, who affirms that we are not healed while half-dead; but that we are raised up while dead purely by the power of GOD: nay, that we are already buried and are illuminated to receive Christ, Ephes. 2:5 & 6, likewise ch. 5:14.

Ephes. 4:14, 18, & 19. They walk (the not yet regenerate) in the vanity of their mind: having the intellect darkened by reason of the ignorance that is in their nature because of the blindness of their heart.

2 Cor. 3:5. We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves: but that we are sufficient, that is from GOD.

Rom. 8:6 & 7. The τὸ Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς (mind of the flesh). The affection or prudence of the flesh is enmity against GOD, because it is not subject to the Law of GOD: nor indeed can it be.

Philip. 2, 13, It is GOD who works in us, both to will and to perform.

Joh. 15, 5. Without me you can do NOTHING. Where the particle Nothing is to be taken not privately, but Negatively: namely, that an unregenerate man can do nothing at all in spiritual matters. Concerning which matter Augustine speaks excellently, against the two epistles of Pelagius to Boniface, book 2, ch. 2. The Lord, that He might answer the future Pelagius, does not say: Without me you can do anything with difficulty: but He says, Without me you can do Nothing: and that He might answer these future ones also, in that same Evangelical sentence, He does not say: Without me you can perfect Nothing, but do: For if He had said perfect, these men could say that the help of GOD is necessary not for beginning the good, which is from us, but only for perfecting the good.

Concerning the heart or will of Man, besides those things which can be gathered from what has already been produced, its total ἀδυναμία (impotence) in spiritual matters is most strongly confirmed by that divine oracle, Gen. 6. 5. and ch. 8, 21. The imagination of the human heart is only evil from its youth. Where the Hebrew word יֵצֶר has a peculiar emphasis, which descends from the root יָצַר which signifies to conceive something studiously in the mind, or to form an idea according to the concept of the mind: thus quite evidently hinting that every motion and action of the heart, and thus what ought to be the best in it, is only evil.

But Holy Scripture proceeds, and speaks not only of the defect: but shows also that in the place of the lost powers a vicious habit has succeeded, and a most sad depravation, in the mind and will or heart of man, regarding spiritual motions or actions: so that before Conversion the heart is hard, Rom. 2, 5. A stony heart, Ezek. 11, 19. 36, 26. An iron neck, a brazen forehead, an iron sinew, Isa. 48, 4. A heart wicked above all things, Jer. 17, 9. and it can no more change itself than an Ethiopian can change his skin, or a leopard his spots, Jerem. 13, 23. A vain heart, Ps. 5, 10. Eph. 4, 17. the body of sin, Rom. 6, 6.

It is added in the third place, that Holy Scripture describes the Conversion or regeneration of Man in such a way that it denies to Man every power of acting whatsoever, and ascribes all things entirely and solely to divine Grace: as Ezek. 11, 19. and 36, 26. I, God, will take away the stony heart and will give a new heart: 2 Cor. 4, 6. God who said, let light shine out of darkness, He has shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of GOD. Deut. 29, 4. Jehovah has not given you a heart to understand, and eyes to see, and ears that could hear, unto this present day. 1 Cor. 12, 3. No one can say that Jesus is Lord, except by the Holy Spirit.

Psalm 51, 12. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Matt. 16, 17. Flesh and blood has not revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven. John 1, 13. He gave power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. John 6, 43. No one can come to me unless the Father draws him. Phil. 1, 6. He who began a good work in you will complete it. Acts 16, 14. God opens the heart of Lydia. And Luke 24, 27. Christ opens the mind to the disciples, that they might understand the Scriptures. Eph. 2, 8. By the grace of God you have been saved through faith: and this is not of yourselves; but it is the gift of GOD, so that no one may boast: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus, etc.

The prayers of the saints and the faithful pertain to this in the fourth place, by which they urgently request to be taught, illuminated, and sanctified more and more by God: as can be seen especially in Psalm 119, where David prays ten times and more that the understanding of the divine Word be given to him. For as Augustine skillfully infers in his book On Nature and Grace, ch. 18: What would be more foolish than to pray that you may do what you have in your power? And Epist. 107: We do not pray to GOD at all, but pretend that we are praying, if we think that we ourselves, and not He, do what we pray for: we do not give thanks to GOD at all, but pretend that we are giving them, if we do not think that He does that for which we give Him thanks.

With these and other similar kinds of proofs duly observed, it is most plainly evident that in spiritual actions, to an unregenerate man, nothing but mere ἀδυναμίαν (inability) is to be attributed.

Moreover, under the consideration of this state comes that truly classic question and controversy concerning the will of man in the very act of conversion, namely, how does it behave itself in conversion itself? That which occurs in the conversion of an unregenerate man, which cannot happen otherwise than that good actions concur and spiritual motions intervene, gave the handle or ἀφορμὴν (occasion) to this question: such as are: the struggle with the flesh, the fight with diffidence, the assent to the divine word, and the like. It was therefore asked, and is asked today, whether these very motions, or at least some part of them, should be attributed to the faculty of human powers?

Which question, indeed, that it may be more correctly explained, it must first be observed in general that the conversion of man to GOD is not one and the same, but that two distinct species of it can be given, according to the two distinct subjects of whom the conversion is made. For because some of those to be converted are entirely strangers to the Church, commonly noted by the title of infidels, such as are all those who live outside the Church: but others dwell in the assembly of the called, and have been inserted into the Church through baptism and were once regenerate: but afterwards, through sins against conscience, have fallen from the grace of Regeneration: hence it certainly happens that the conversion of unregenerate infidels is one thing, and the conversion of those who were once regenerate but have now fallen is another. Of which, indeed, there is a huge discrepancy between both conversions: just as he who either still persists in the covenant of divine grace, or although he has succumbed to diabolical temptation and fallen from the grace of God, has nevertheless at some time received and had the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit, differs greatly from him who is first called and admitted to the faith of Christ and the grace of the covenant. These become regenerate from unregenerate, and believers from infidels: but the condition of those who have fallen in the Church is such that, although seduced by the Devil they become liable to divine wrath and eternal damnation, yet they do not yet entirely fall from the covenant itself and the right of the adoption of the children of God with respect to God, since His gifts are ἀμεταμέλητα (irrevocable), Romans 11, 29, nor do they fall from it entirely before they finally persevere in their sins. Therefore, the conversion of these is nothing else than a return, as it were, through serious repentance to the use or enjoyment of their former grace. Besides these two species of conversion, there is also mention in the schools of theologians of a third conversion, which is called the repentance or conversion of those who stand, namely, of those who are regenerate, but subsequently, because of the adhering infirmities and falls of sin and the flesh, revive themselves through repentance: so that the conversion of these is nothing else than a certain perpetual mortification of the flesh, and a daily fight of the flesh and the Spirit, reviving, recreating, and sustaining itself by faith in Christ and the Evangelical promises. And indeed, there is no dispute or controversy in this place concerning these two latter species, namely the conversion of the fallen and of those who stand: since they pertain properly to the Article on Repentance. There remains, therefore, in the present only that remaining state of the controversy: What can an infidel man, or one not yet regenerate, perform from his own powers in his first conversion?

Latin:

fide destituta, Deo displiceant, & peccati rationem obtineant.

DE ACTIONIBUS Purè Spiritualibus.

SEd de moralibus actionibus plus satis: Restat postremum actionum humanarum Genus, quod est merè spiritualium: quales sunt, quæ proprie spectant ad cultum DEI, Religionis puritatem, æternamque animarum salutem: ut affentiri verbo prædicato: Converti ad Deum, detestari peccatum, credere in Christum, invocare Deum in Spiritu & veritate, sub cruce patienter & indubitatò sperare DEI auxilium: Vivere secundum Spiritum, quæ sunt hujus generis internarum, cœlestium & purè spiritualium actionum complures aliæ. De his ergò actionibus propriè hoc loco quæritur: An Homini non renato, post lapsum, ullum sit relictum Liberum Arbitrium in Spiritualibus: vel, quòd eôdem recidit: An mens & voluntas ex prima nativitate insitam habeant talem potentiam, tales vires & facultates, ut quando homo verbum DEI legit, audit & cogitat, possit sine Spiritu sancto, ex puris (sicut Scholastici loquuntur) naturalibus, concipere tales motus, & elicere tales actiones in mente & voluntate, quales ad contritionem, fidem & novam obedientiam Scriptura requirit. Circa quòd κρινόμενον nostræ Ecclesiæ Negativam simpliciter tenent ac defendunt, sic edoctæ S. literarum testimoniis, quæ negativè loquuntur & ἐξαρρηδην perhibent, per lapsum in natura corrupta prorsus amissam esse omnem δυναμιν, vim & efficaciam sive facultatem, qua vel inchoandæ, vel efficiendæ sint actiones Spirituales: Et quidem distinctè tùm de mente sive intellectu, tùm de corde sive voluntate Hominis non renati luculenter hoc Scripturæ attestantur. Et de Mente quidem, 1. Cor. 2, 14. Animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus DEI: imò ne potest quidem, quia de spiritualibus dijudicatur.

Ephes. 2, 1. In peccatis sumus (non languidi aut infirmi) sed mortui. Undè Theologica hæc Demonstratio peti potest & debet: Sicut homo, qui corporaliter mortuus est, seipsum ad recipiendam vitam temporalem neque præparare, neque accommodare, multò minùs eam efficere potest: ita Homo Spiritualiter mortuus in peccatis seipsum propriis viribus, ad consequendam Spiritualem & cœlestem Justitiam & vitam neque præparare, neque applicare, multò minùs eam efficere aut comparare nullo modo potest. Neque diversum evincit parabola illa Luc. 10, 30. de Homine à latronibus percuffo, & Semivivo relicto. Neque enim Servatori eo loci propositum fuit ostendere, quod & quale Liberum Arbitrium habeat Homo non renatus in Spiritualibus: sed tantùm, quis sit proximus noster. Committitur ergò crassa Elenchi Ignoratio, in citatione hujus dicti, quod de proposito statu controversiæ, ne γρῦ agit. Audiatur potiùs Apostolus, qui nos non Semivivos sanari; sed mortuos planè virtute DEI suscitari: imò jam sepultos ad recipiendum Christum illuminari affirmat Ephes. 2, 5. & 6. item c. 5, 14.

Ephes. 4, 14. 18. & 19. Ambulant (nondum renati) in vanitate mentis suæ: tenebris obscuratum habentes intellectum, propter ignorantiam, quæ est in natura ipsorum propter cæcitatem cordis ipsorum.

2. Cor. 3, 5. Non sumus idonei cogitare aliquid à nobis ipsis, tanquam à nobis ipsis: sed quod idonei sumus, id ex DEO est.

Rom. 8, 6. & 7. τὸ Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς. Affectus sive prudentia carnis, est inimicitia adversus DEUM, quia Legi DEI non subjicitur: ac ne potest quidem.

Philip. 2, 13, DEUS est, qui operatur in nobis, & velle & perficere.

Joh. 15, 5. Sine me NIHIL potestis facere. Ubi non privatimè, sed Negativè particula Nihil est accipienda: quòd nimirum Homo non renatus, nihil quicquam in rebus Spiritualibus possit. Quâ de re præclarè Augustinus, contra duas epistolas Pelagii ad Bonifacium cap. 2. lib. Dominus ut responderet futuro Pelagio, non ait: Sine me difficulter potestis quicquam facere: sed ait, Sine me Nihil potestis facere: & ut responderet futuris etiam istis, in eadem ipsa Evangelica sententia, non ait: Sine me Nihil potest perficere, sed facere: Nam si perficere dixisset, possent isti dicere, non ad incipiendum bonum, quòd à nobis est: sed tantùm ad perficiendum bonum, necessarium esse DEI adjutorium.

De corde sive voluntate Hominis, præter ea, quæ ex jam productis colligi possunt, summam ejus ἀδυναμίαν in Spiritualibus, vel maximè confirmat illud divinum oraculum, Gen. 6. 5. & cap. 8, 21. Figmentum cordis humani tantùm malum est, ab adolescentia sua. Ubi peculiarem emphasin habet vox Hebræa יֵצֶר, quæ descendit à radice יָצַר quod significat studiosè aliquid vel animo concipere, vel juxta animi conceptum ideam efformare: sic satis evidenter innuens, omnem motum & actionem cordis, & sic quod optimum in eo esse debeat, tantùm malum esse.

Sed pergit Scriptura Sacra, & non tantùm de defectu loquitur: sed ostendit etiam in locum amissarum virium successisse vitiosum habitum, & tristissimam depravationem, in mente & voluntate sive corde hominis, quoad motus sive actiones Spirituales: ita, ut ante Conversionem sit cor durum, Rom. 2, 5. Cor lapideum, Ezech. 11, 19. 36, 26. Cervix ferrea, frons ænea, nervus ferreus, Jes 48, 4 Cor pravum super omnia, Jer. 17, 9. & haud magis se mutare possit, atque Æthiops mutare potest pellem suam, aut pardus maculas suas, Jerem 13, 23. Cor vanum, Psal. 5, 10. Eph. 4, 17. corpus peccati, Rom. 6, 6.

Accedit tertio loco, quod Scriptura Sacra ita Hominis Conversionem sive regenerationem describit, ut Homini omnem prorsus agendi δύναμιν deroger, & omnia in solidum & unicè Gratiæ divinæ adscribat: ut Jezech. 11, 19. & 36, 26. Ego Deus auferam cor lapideum & dabo cor novum: 2. Cor. 4, 6. Deus qui dixit, ex tenebris lucem splendescere, ipse illuxit cordibus nostris, ad illuminationem scientiæ claritatis DEI. Deut. 29, 4. Jehovah non dedit tibi cor ad intelligendum, oculos ad videndum & aures, quæ possent audire usque in præsentem diem. 1. Cor. 12, 3. Nemo potest Jesum Dominum dicere, nisi per Spiritum sanctum.

Psalm 51, 12. Cor mundum crea in me Deus, & Spiritum rectum innova in visceribus meis. Matth. 16, 17. Caro & sanguis non revelavit tibi, sed Pater meus qui in cœlis est. Joh. 1, 13. Dedit potestatem filios Dei fieri, qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate viri, aut carnis, sed ex Deo nati sunt. Joh. 6, 43. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi pater traxerit eum. Phil. 1, 6. Qui incepit in vobis bonum opus, idem perficiet. Actor. 16, 14. Deus aperit Cor Lydiæ. Et Luc. 24, 27. Christus aperit discipulis mentem, ut intelligerent Scripturas. Eph. 2, 8. Gratia Dei salvati estis per fidem: & hoc non ex vobis; Sed DEI donum est, ne quis glorietur: Ipsius enim sumus creatura, creati in Christo Jesu &c.

Pertinent huc quarto loco Orationes Sanctorum, & fidelium, quibus à Deo magis magisque doceri, illuminari & sanctificari flagitant: uti cumprimis videre est Psalmo 119. ubi David decies & ampliùs intellectum Verbi divini sibi donari precatur. Nam uti scitè infert Augustinus lib. de nat. & grat. c. 18. Quid stultius esset, quàm orare ut facias, quod in potestate habes? Et Epist. 107. prorsus non oramus DEUM, sed orare nos fingimus, si nos ipsos, non ipsum putamus facere, quæ oramus: prorsus non gratias agimus DEO, sed agere nos fingimus, si undè illi gratias agimus, ipsum facere non putamus.

His & consimilibus aliis probationum generibus ritè observatis, planissimè constat, in spiritualibus actionibus, homini non renato; nil nisi meram ἀδυναμίαν tribuendam esse.

Cæterùm sub hujus Status Considerationem venit Quæstio & Controversia illa verè classica, de voluntate Hominis in ipso Conversionis actu, quomodo nimirùm hæc in ipsa Conversione sese habeat? Ansam sive ἀφορμὴν quæstioni huic dedit illud, quod in Conversione Hominis non renati, altero fieri nequit; quin actiones bonæ concurrant, & motus spirituales interveniant: quales sunt: Lucta cum carne, pugna cum diffidentia, assensus verbi divini, & similia. Quæsitum ergo fuit, hodièque quæritur, Nùm hi ipsi motus, aut aliqua saltem earum pars, virium humanarum facultati tribuenda sit?

Quæ sanè quæstio, ut rectiùs explicetur, prius in genere illud observandum fuerit, Conversionem Hominis ad DEUM non esse unam eandemque, sed duas distinctas ejus dari posse species, secundum duo distincta subjecta; quorum fit Conversio. Quia enim Convertendorum aliqui ab Ecclesia planè sunt extorres, vulgò infidelium titulo notati, quales sunt omnes illi, qui extra Ecclesiam vivunt: alii verò versantur in cætu vocatorum, & per baptismum Ecclesiæ inserti & semel sunt renati: sed postmodùm per peccata contra conscientiam, Regenerationis gratia exciderunt: hinc utique fit, ut alia non renatorum infidelium, alia semel quidem renatorum, sed jam lapsorum sit Conversio. Cujus sanè utriusque Conversionis ingens est discrepantia: quemadmodum plurimum is, qui vel adhuc in gratiae divinae foedere persistit, vel licet tentationi Diabolicae succubuerit, & gratia Dei exciderit, primitias tamen Spiritus sancti aliquando accepit & habuit, differt ab eo, qui ad fidem Christi, & gratiam foederis primum vocatur & admittitur. Hi ex non renatis fiunt renati, ex infidelibus fideles: Lapsorum autem in Ecclesia ea est conditio, ut quamvis a Diabolo seducti, divinae irae, & aeternae damnationis rei fiant, foedere tamen ipso & adoptionis filiorum Dei jure respectu Dei, quippe cujus dona sunt ἀμεταμέλητα, Roman. 11, 29. nondum prorsus excidant, neque prius etiam illo penitus excidant, quam si finaliter in peccatis perseverent. Istorum proinde Conversio nihil est aliud, quam ad usum sive perfruitionem pristinae gratiae, quidam quasi per seriam poenitentiam reditus. Praeter has duas Conversionis species, sit insuper in Scholis Theologorum, tertiae etiam Conversionis mentio, quae dicitur poenitentia sive Conversio stantium, eorum videlicet qui renati sunt, sed subinde propter adhaerentes peccati & carnis infirmitates & lapsus, per poenitentiam se quasi resuscitant: ita ut istorum Conversio nihil sit aliud, quam perpetua quaedam carnis mortificatio, & quotidiana pugna carnis & Spiritus, fide in Christum & promissionibus Evangelicis se resuscitans recreans ac sustentans. Et de duabus quidem posterioribus hisce speciebus, nempe Conversione lapsorum & stantium, hoc loco non disputatur sive controvertitur: quippe ad Articulum de Poenitentia proprie pertinentibus. Manet proinde reliquus in praesenti ille tantum Controversiae status: Quidnam Homo infidelis, sive nondum renatus in prima sui Conversione, ex viribus propriis praestare possit?


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: On Actions Of Pure Spirituals (continued)

To which question we answer, that man can contribute nothing at all, and not even the least bit, toward his own conversion, either to begin it or to effect it: and consequently that the beginning, the progress, and finally the entire success of this conversion to God, must be attributed entirely and solely to the operation of the Holy Spirit. That this opinion is in every way consonant with the truth is irrefragably proven by the foundations of those Scriptures, which, produced a little while ago in great number, clearly attest that the mind and will of man in spiritual matters are darkness, vanity, nay, are enmity with God: and that he can neither understand nor perform, nay, not even think of anything good in this kind of action: but is plainly dead and buried in sins: and which furthermore confirm that the grace of God in converting man does not operate in such a way as if there were still remaining in corrupt nature, from his first birth, some innate and inherent faculty either to begin, or to cooperate with, or to effect spiritual motions: so that the grace of God, coming afterward, only excites and assists that natural δύναμιν, so that he may now be able to conceive spiritual motions and actions: not otherwise than if someone, having in himself and by himself the δύναμιν of walking, were released from the chains or fetters by which he is bound and held fast: just as the Papists trifle: But that the Holy Spirit, in those whom He wills to convert, first begins to mortify and take away that depravity which He finds in the mind and will not yet reborn, regarding spiritual motions and actions: then indeed He begins to work and to grant new strength, faculty, and efficacy in the mind and will, for beginning and accomplishing spiritual actions: as is most evidently clear from the produced testimonies of the Scriptures.

Another kind of our demonstration is constituted by certain arguments, taken from the very act of conversion: the first of which can be such as this.

A subject receiving a Form cannot be the Efficient cause of that Form: or, which amounts to the same thing: A passive subject cannot be the efficient cause of the action itself. But the will of an unregenerate man behaves itself in Conversion as a passive subject or one to be converted. Therefore, it cannot be the efficient cause of Conversion.

The minor premise is proved thus: Whatever has been corrupted by the fall of our first parents, that is restored by Conversion or Regeneration. But the heart or will of Man has been corrupted by the fall of the protoplasts. Therefore, it too is restored by Conversion: and consequently, in Conversion, it cannot behave itself as an efficient cause, but only as a passive subject or one to be converted. The other argument is shown by that Apostolic passage 1 Cor. 2:14. The natural man perceives nothing of those things which are of the Spirit of GOD, nay, he is not even able to: Where indeed He takes away from the natural, or unregenerate, man not only the act, but also the δύναμιν (power). Hence one may gather thus: If that which seems more to be present is not present, much less will that be present which seems less able to be present. But in the unregenerate man, not even the intellect of divine things is present. Much less, therefore, will the assent and apprehension of those things be present: and consequently, the work of Conversion will in no part, in no way, be referable to the will or powers of Man.

Finally, it is evident that as often as flesh is opposed to Spirit in the Scriptures, it always denotes such a total corruption of all powers in man, which leaves to those not yet reborn nothing but extreme ἀδυναμίαν (impotence) in the business of Conversion and salvation. Now, indeed, Scripture expressly names the man not yet reborn 'Flesh,' John 3:6. Therefore. This is expressed by those notations of the Scriptures in which the unregenerate Man is named a Servant of sin, Rom. 6:17. Dead in sin, Eph. 2:1. A straying and lost sheep, a lost drachma, Luke 15:4 & 8, etc.

The third and last kind of proof is taken from the authority of Orthodox Antiquity, in which Augustine easily holds the first place, who, in his book On Nature and Grace, expressly treating this question against the Pelagians, finally concludes in chapter 23 as follows: for one to go into sin, Free Will is sufficient for him: but for him to return to Justice, there is need of a physician, because he is not healthy.

And in the book On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 3, he confesses it to be an error if he had said that it is our own property to consent when the Gospel is preached, and that it is from us of ourselves. For what I said, that it is ours to believe and to will, is to be understood in such a way that both are of God, who prepares the will, and both are also ours, because it does not happen unless we are willing. But how Augustine wished this very thing to be understood, he explains himself again, book 1 to Boniface, chapter 19. Christ, he says, did not say, 'Whom my Father shall LEAD,' so that we might think that our will precedes in some way: but He says: 'SHALL DRAW.' But who is drawn if he was already willing: and yet no one comes unless he wills. He is drawn, therefore, in wondrous ways, so that he may will, by Him who knows how to work within, in the very hearts of men: not so that men may believe unwillingly (which cannot happen), but so that they may be made willing from being unwilling.

And in the Enchiridion, chapter 32: He prevents the unwilling, so that he may will: He follows the willing, so that he may not will in vain. See more in Chemnitz, Exam. part 1, page 122. Concerning this purer doctrine of our Churches, various reefs and multiple questions offer themselves, which, unless they are explained more clearly, a most copious harvest of many and indeed very grave errors can arise.

For it is asked 1. Whether after the fall all powers in man are so broken, nay, extinguished in spiritual matters, that no ἱκανότης (aptitude), aptitude, or capacity has remained at all? Concerning which question a sufficiently sharp battle arose among certain Theologians: some proscribing the words Aptitude and Capacity from this Article: others, however, admitting them: neither perhaps explaining the matter sufficiently skillfully. For this battle is easily removed if only this much is considered, that these words can be taken in a twofold sense, namely, Active and Passive. Active, then, if by Aptitude and Capacity you understand such an ἐνεργητικὴν (energetic) faculty, by which Man of himself could apprehend the Grace of Conversion offered in the preached Word. Passive, however, if Man is posited to be a παθητικὸν (passive) subject, which is fit for receiving Conversion, or apt for conversion: Such a passive capacity or aptitude does not fall to a trunk or a stone: neither of which is ἱκανὸς (apt) or δεκτικὸς (receptive) of capacity. And in this latter sense our Blessed Luther rightly attributes capacity to Man, that is, a δύναμιν (power) behaving itself passively: writing thus in his defense against Eck: When the Fathers defend Free Will, they preach the Capacity of that Liberty, by which he himself can be converted to the Good through the Grace of God, and become truly Free, for which he was created. Whence Irenaeus also writes in book 5, that human flesh is capable of the gift of GOD, that is, of eternal life. And in book 4, chapter 24, that Man is a receptacle of the goodness of GOD.

Moreover, concerning this passive capacity, there is no controversy in this place: but only concerning that Active one, which (that we may answer the ζήτημα proposed) we deny to the unregenerate man so entirely, that we do not even grant him that which it has pleased some to name a Modicum: relying on the Apostolic authority, which in such a case man so entirely that we do not even grant him that which it pleased some to name a "little bit": relying on the Apostolic authority, which in such a species expressly denies to man every ἱκανότητα, or Capacity or Active Aptitude: as in 2 Cor. 3:5. From ourselves, as from ourselves, we are not ἱκανοί ἐσμεν, sufficient or apt, even to think anything good: But our ἱκανότης, our aptitude, is from God. And Col. 1:12. God makes us fit to share in the lot of the Saints, in the light.

Bernard discourses no less vigorously and orthodoxly, as well as elegantly, concerning both that capacity, at the beginning of his treatise on Grace and Free Will: saying, What, he asks, does Free Will do? I answer briefly, It is saved: Take away Free Will, there will be nothing to be saved: take away grace: there will be nothing from which it may be saved: This work cannot be done without these two: One, by whom it is done: the other, to whom or in whom it is done: God is the author of salvation: Free Will is only the recipient: nor is it able to give it, unless God, nor to receive it, unless Free Will, while it consents, that is, while it is saved: for to consent is to be saved. What then? Is this therefore the whole work of Free Will? Is this its only merit, that it consents? It is entirely: but not because the consent itself, in which all merit consists, is from itself, since we are not sufficient to think (which is less than to consent) anything from ourselves, as if from ourselves: But God prevents us by sending in a good thought, by also changing an evil will, etc.

But furthermore it is asked: Since the will of an unregenerate man can perform absolutely nothing, and not even the least thing, toward his own conversion. How then does it conduct itself in the conversion itself? To which question different answers are given by different people. Some maintain that it conducts itself merely and purely passively: just as indeed the Blessed Luther did not shrink from this phrase: writing thus somewhere among other things (in the Psalms) It is an error that Free Will has any activity in a good work, when we speak of an internal work: For to will to believe, to hope, to love, are motions, raptures, and leadings of the word of God, and a certain continuous purgation and renewal of the mind, although that passion is not always equally intense, yet it is always a passion. Behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so also is the house of Israel in my hand, Jer. 18. What activity, I pray, does clay have when the potter fashions a form for it? Is not mere passion seen there? Bellarminus, in book 6 of Grace and Free Will, chapter 9, attacks this opinion of Luther in strange ways, chiefly on the grounds that Luther thus makes man either an irrational beast or a log. For he says, to will is an immanent and vital act, just like understanding and seeing: therefore the active principle of that act ought to be the will itself. But Chemnitius answers most correctly in part 1 of the Examination, pages 125, 126. That someone might perhaps easily be offended by this phrase, who is not accustomed to the modes of speaking that are customary among Scholastic writers: as if the meaning were that the Holy Spirit so works conversion that in the will, which has begun to be renewed, no new motions follow at all: But it is plainly idle and inert, and is only tossed and extended by a brute agitation: which never entered Luther's mind. But what it is to conduct oneself merely passively can be known from Scholastic writers. For among them there was a customary dispute: That a subject receiving some form, or quality, habit, action, etc., insofar as it receives, conducts itself passively. But there are certain subjects which, besides the fact that they conduct themselves passively by receiving, also have a certain activity in themselves, which they contribute, and by which they cooperate at the same time, so that the form, quality, action, or habit is produced in that subject. And other subjects conduct themselves toward the production of a form not merely passively, but partly passively, partly actively. But there are certain other subjects which have no activity from themselves toward the production of a form: but only receive the form. And those are said to conduct themselves merely passively. Luther adapted those modes of speaking of the Scholastics, as they were customary and known in the Schools at that time, to the doctrine of Free Will. For since the mind and will of an unregenerate man are the subject in which the Holy Spirit works conversion or renewal: thus far that subject conducts itself, according to the phrases of the Scholastics, passively. But now the question is: Whether the mind and will of an unregenerate man, in this corruption of nature through sin, has any activity, that is, any δύναμιν, power or efficacy, and cooperates at the same time with the Holy Spirit, so that conversion, a holy thought, a good purpose, effort, endeavor, struggle, etc., is begun in spiritual morals and actions, that is, (as the Scholastics speak) whether the unregenerate will conducts itself toward spiritual conversion partly actively, partly passively? But now, because Scripture teaches that that δύναμιν for spiritual things has been entirely lost through sin, so that the will can do nothing of itself: therefore Luther, using the phrase of the Scholastics, explained that opinion in such a way that it conducts itself merely passively. And yet he did not teach that conversion happens without the thought of the mind and the consent of the will: but he meant this: that God draws those whom He converts by their wills, which He Himself has worked in them through the Holy Spirit.

Thus far Chemnitz, whom Bellarmine lashes without any cause and undeservedly, because through this very explanation he involves Luther's mind more than he explains it. For if that which conducts itself merely passively is entirely destitute of all actuality, then it would follow from the opinion of Luther and Chemnitz that the human will conducts itself only passively in conversion.
