But the Sophist does not notice that both Luther and Chemnitz consider the will of the man being converted, not insofar as the Holy Spirit has now just illuminated it, and from unwilling and resisting has made it willing and consenting—in which manner, indeed, neither of them ever denied that it also concurs actively—but they consider it only insofar as it is weighed from itself and its own powers, where indeed it conducts itself only as a passive subject, and cannot bring even the slightest bit of help toward its own conversion from itself. however much meanwhile it remains in respect of substance that which it is and is called. With these things observed, it is most clearly evident that Luther's phrase contains no danger at all in itself.

Latin:

Ad quam quaestionem respondemus, Hominem nihil prorsus, & ne quidem minimum, ad sui Conversionem, vel inchoandam, vel efficiendam praestare posse: ac proinde initium, progressum, successum denique omnem Conversionis hujus ad Deum, operationi Spiritus sancti, in solidum & unice tribuendum esse. Sententiam hanc veritati undiquaque esse consonam, illarum Scripturarum fundamentis irrefragabiliter evincitur, quae paulo ante magno numero producta liquido attestantur, Mentem & voluntatem Hominis in spiritualibus esse tenebras, vanitatem, imo esse inimicitiam cum Deo: & nihil quicquam boni, in hoc actionum genere, vel intelligere, vel perficere, imo ne cogitare quidem posse: sed plane in peccatis esse mortua & sepulta: quaeque porro confirmant, Gratiam Dei in convertendo Homine, non ita operari, quasi in corrupta natura, ex prima nativitate, adhuc reliqua sit, insita quaepiam & inhaerens facultas vel inchoandi, vel cooperandi, vel efficiendi spirituales motus: ita ut accedens postmodum Dei gratia, excitet tantum & adjuvet naturalem illam δύναμιν, ut possit jam Spirituales concipere motus & actiones: haud secus ac si quis hominem per se & in se habentem ambulandi δύναμιν, ex vinculis sive compedibus, quibus constrictus tenetur, solvat : quemadmodum Pontificii nugantur : Sed quod Spiritus sanctus in illis, quos vult convertere, primùm incipiat pravitatem illam, quam quoad motus & actiones spirituales, in mente & voluntate nondùm renata invenit, mortificare & auferre: deindè verò incipiat operari, & donare novam vim, facultatem, & efficaciam in mente & voluntate, ad inchoandas & efficiendas spirituales actiones: uti ex productis scripturarum testimoniis evidentissimè patet.

Alterum Demonstrationis nostræ genus constituunt certæ quæpiam rationes, ex ipso conversionis actu petitæ : quarum prima talis esse potest.

Subjectum recipiens Formam, non potest esse causa Efficiens illius Formæ : vel quod eodem recidit: Subjectum patiens non potest esse causa efficiens ipsius actionis, Atqui voluntas hominis non renata, habet se in Conversione, ut Subjectum patiens sive convertendum. Ergò non potest esse causa efficiens Conversionis.

Minor sic probatur : Quicquid per lapsum primorum parentum est corruptum : illud per Conversionem sive Regenerationem restauratur. Atqui cor sive voluntas Hominis, per lapsum protoplastorum est corrupta. Ergò illa quoque per Conversionem restauratur: & per consequens in Conversione non ut causa efficiens, sed tantum ut subjectum patiens sive convertendum se habere potest. Alteram rationem monstrat illud Apostolicum 1. Cor. 2, 14. Animalis homo nihil percipit eorum, quæ sunt Spiritus DEI, imò ne potest quidem : Ubi sanè non actum modò, sed & δυναμίαν Homini animali, sive non renato, adimit. Hinc sic licet colligere : Si quod magis inesse videtur, non inest, multò minus inerit id, quod minus inesse posse videtur. Atqui homini non renato, ne intellectus quidem inest rerum divinarum. Multò minùs ergò assensus & apprehensio illarum rerum inerit : & per consequens, Conversionis opus ad voluntatem aut vires Hominis, nulla ex parte, uko modo referendum erit.

Tandem constat, quotiescunque in Scripturis caro Spiritui opponitur semper notari ejusmodi summam in homine omnium virium corruptionem, quæ illis nondum renatis in negotio Conversionis & salutis, nil nisi extremam ἀδυναμίαν relinquat. Jam verò Scriptura Hominem nondum renatum, expressè Carnem nominat Johan. 3, 6. Ergo. Quod ipsum exprimunt eæ notationes Scripturarum, quibus Homo non renatus, nominatur Servus peccati Rom. 6, 17. In peccato mortuos. Eph. 2, 1. Ovis errans & perdita, drachma amissa. Luc. 15, 4. & 8. &c.

Tertium & postremum probationis genus, ab autoritate Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis petitur, in qua primas obtinet facilè Augustinus, qui in libro de Natura & Gratia ex professo quæstionem hanc contra Pelagianos pertractans, tandem cap 23. sic quasi concludit : ut quis in peccatum eat, sufficit ipsi Liberum Arbitrium: ut autem redeat ad Justitiam, opus est medico, quia sanus non est.

Et lib. de Prædestinatione Sanctorum, cap 3. fatetur errorem esse, sicubi dixerit, ut prædicato Evangelio consentiamus, nostrum esse proprium. & nobis ex nobis esse. Nam quod dixi, Nostrum esse credere & velle, ita est intelligendum, quod utrumq; sit Dei, qui preparat voluntatem, & utrumq; etiam sit nostrum, quia non fit, nisi volentibus nobis. Sed quomodo hoc ipsum intellectum voluerit Augustinus, rursum semetipsum explicat, lib. 1. ad Bonifacium cap. 19. Christus, inquiens, non dixit, Quem Pater meus DUXERIT, ut sic existimemus, aliquo modo præcedere nostram voluntatem: sed dicit: TRAXERIT. Quis autem trahitur, si jam volebat: & tamen nemo venit, nisi velit. Trahitur ergo miris modis, ut velit, ab illo, qui novit intus, in ipsis hominum cordibus operari: non ut homines (quod fieri non potest) nolentes credant, sed ut volentes ex nolentibus fiant.

Et in Enchiridio cap. 32. Nolentem prævenit, ut velit: volentem subsequitur, ne frustrà velit. Vide plura apud Chemnitium Exam. part. 1. pag. 122. Circa puriorem hanc Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctrinam, varii sese offerunt Scopuli & Quæstiones multiplices, quæ nisi planiùs explicentur, plurimorum & quidem gravissimorum errorum seges longè copiosissima oboriri potest.

Quæritur enim 1. Num post lapsum in homine ita vires omnes sint fractæ, imo extinctæ in Spiritualibus, ut nulla prorsus ἱκανότης, aptitudo sive capacitas remanserit? Circa quam quæstionem pugna satis acris inter Theologos quosdam oborta fuit: nonnullis vocabula Aptitudinis & Capacitatis ex hoc Articulo proscribentibus: aliis verò eadem admittentibus: neutris fortassè rem satis dextrè explicantibus. Facilè enim pugna hæc tollitur, si illud duntaxat pensi habeatur, vocabula isthæc gemino sensu posse accipi, Activo nimirùm & Passivo. Activo tùm, si per Aptitudinem & Capacitatem, talem intelligas facultatem ἐνεργητικὴν, quâ Homo ex se possit apprehendere oblatam in Verbo prædicato, Gratiam Conversionis. Passivo, verò, si Homo statuatur esse subjectum παθητικὸν, quod sit habile ad recipiendam Conversionem, sive aptum ad conversionem: Qualis passiva capacitas sive aptitudo, in Truncum aut lapidem non cadit: quorum neuter est ἱκανὸς aptus sive δεκτικὸς capacitatis. Et hoc posteriore sensu B. Lutherus noster Homini rectè tribuit capacitatem, hoc est, δύναμιν παθητικῶς se habentem: sic scribens in defensione contra Eccium: Quando Patres Liberum Arbitrium defendunt, Capacitatem illius Libertatis prædicant, quâ ipse converti possit ad Bonum per Gratiam Dei, & fieri revera Liberum, ad quod creatum est. Undè Irenæus quoque lib. 5. scribit, Carnem humanam capacem esse donationis DEI, hoc est, vitæ æternæ. Et lib. 4. cap. 24. Hominem esse receptaculum bonitatis DEI.

Cæterùm de hac passiva capacitate hoc loco non controvertitur: Sed tantùm de Activâ illâ, quam (ut ad propositum ζήτημα respondeamus) Homini non renato, usque adeò in solidum negamus, ut ne quidem illud ipsi largiamur, quod aliquibus nominare placuit, Modiculum: freti autoritate Apostolica, quæ in specie tali Homini, omnem ἱκανότητα, sive Capacitatem aut Aptitudinem Activam disertè derogat: ut in 2. Cor. 3. 5. Ex nobis ipsis, tanquam ex nobis ipsis, ne quidem cogitare quicquam boni ἱκανοί ἐσμεν idonei aut apti sumus : Sed ἱκανότης ἡμῶν aptitudo nostra ex Deo est. Et Colos. 1, 12. Deus reddit nos idoneos ad participandam sortem Sanctorum, in lumine.

De utraque ista capacitate haud minùs nervosè & orthodoxè, quàm eleganter disserit Bernhardus, in principio tractatus de Gratia & Libero Arbitrio: Quid inquiens, agit Liberum arbitrium? breviter respondeo, Salvatur : Tolle Liberum, non erit, quod salvetur : tolle gratiam : non erit unde Salvetur : Opus hoc sine duobus hoc effici non potest : Vno, à quo fit: altero, cui vel in quo fit: Deus autor est salutis : Liberum arbitrium tantùm capax: nec dare illam, nisi Deus, nec capere valet, nisi Liberum Arbitrium, dūm consentit, hoc est, dum salvatur : consentire enim salvari est. Quid igitur? Hoc ergò totum Liberi Arbitrij opus? Hoc ne solum ejus est meritum, quod consentit ? Est prorsus : sed non quòd vel ipse consensus, in quo omne meritum consistit, ab ipso sit, cùm nec cogitare, (quod minus est, quàm consentire) aliquid à nobis, quasi ex nobis sufficientes simus : Sed Deus immittendo bonam cogitationem nos prævenit, immutando etiam malam voluntatem &c.

Sed porrò quæritur: Cùm voluntas Hominis non renati nihil prorsus, & ne quidem minimum ad sui conversionem præstare possit. Quomodò ergò in ipsa conversione sese ea habeat? Ad quàm quæstionem diversimodè à diversis respondetur. Alij eam merè & purè passivè se habere dictitant: quemadmodum sanè B. Lutherus ab hac phrasi non exhorruit: sic alicubi inter reliqua scribens (in Psalmos) Error est, quod Liberum Arbitrium habeat aliquam activitatem in bono opere, quando de interno opere loquimur: Velle enim credere, sperare, diligere, sunt motus, raptus & ductus verbi Dei, & quædam continua purgatio, & renovatio mentis, licèt non semper æquè intensa sit illa passio, tamèn semper est passio. Ecce sicut lutum in manu figuli, ita & domus Israel in manu mea Jer. 18. Quid obsecro activitatis habet lutum, quandó figulus formam ei affingit ? nonne mera passio ibi cernitur ? Quam Lutheri sententiam miris modis exagitat Bellarminus lib. 6. de Grat. & Lib. arbit. cap. 9. eo potissimùm nomine, quòd sic Lutherus ex Homine vel bestiam irrationalem vel truncum faciat. Nam inquit, velle est actus immanens & vitalis, sicut intelligere & videre: proindè principium activum ejus actus debet esse ipsa voluntas. Sed rectissimè respondet Chemnitius part. 1. Exam. pag. 125, 126. Hâc quidem phrasi facilè fortassis posse offendi aliquem, qui non assuetus sit modis loquendi, qui Scholasticis scriptoribus usitati sunt: quasi sensus sit, Spiritum Sanctum ita operari Conversionem, ut in voluntate, quæ renovari cœpit, nulli omninò sequantur novi motus : Sed planè sit otiosa & iners, & tantùm bruta agitatione procellatur & protendatur: quod Luthero nunquam in mentem venit. Quid autem sit merè passivè se habere, ex Scholasticis scriptoribus notum esse potest. Usitate enim apud illos fuit disputatio: Quòd Subjectum recipiens formam aliquam, aut qualitatem, habitum, actionem &c. quatenùs recipit, habeat se passivè. Sunt verò quædam Subjecta, quæ præter quam quod recipiendo se passive habent, etiam activitatem quandam in se habent, quam conferunt, & quâ simul cooperantur, ut forma, qualitas, actio sive habitus in subjecto illo producatur. Et alia subjecta habent se ad productionem formæ non merè passive, sed partim passivè, partim activè. Sunt verò alia quædam subjecta, quæ ad productionem forma nullam ex se habent activitatem: sed tantùm recipiunt formam. Et illa dicuntur, se merè passivè habere. Illos modos loquendi Scholasticorum, Lutherus, ut tunc temporis in Scholis usitatos & notos, accommodavit ad doctrinam de Libero Arbitrio. Cùm enim mens & voluntas Hominis non renati sint subjectum, in quo Spiritus Sanctus operatur conversionem sive renovationem: hactenus habet se subjectum illud, juxta Scholasticorum phrases, passivè. Jam verò quæstio est: An mens & voluntas Hominis non renati, in hac naturæ per peccatum corruptione, habeat activitatem aliquam, hoc est, δυναμιν, vim sive efficaciam aliquam conferat, & simul cum Spiritu Sancto cooperetur, ut inchoetur conversio, sancta cogitatio, bonum propositum, studium, conatus, lucta &c. in moribus & actionibus spiritualibus, hoc est, (ut Scholastici loquuntur) an voluntas nõ renata, habeat se ad spiritualem conversionem, partim activè, partim passive? Jam verò, quia scriptura tradit, δυναμιν illam ad spiritualia per peccatum prorsus esse amissam, ita ut nihil possit voluntas ex se: ideo Lutherus Scholasticorum phrasi usus, sententiam illam ita explicavit, quòd merè passivè se habeat. Et tamen non docuit, sine cogitatione mentis, & consensu voluntatis fieri conversionem: sed hoc voluit: Deum eos, quos convertit, trahere voluntatibus eorum, quas ipsi illis per Spiritum Sanctum operatus est.

Hactenùs Chemnitius, quem sine omni causa & præter meritum flagellat Bellarminus, quòd per hanc ipsam explicationem, Lutheri mentem magis involvat, quàm explicet. Siquidem quod merè passivè se habet: illud planè omni actualitate destituitur: ac proindè ex Lutheri & Chemnitij sententia sequatur, voluntatem humanam tantùm passivè se habere in conversione, Sed non animadvertit Sophista, & Lutherum & Chemnitium considerare voluntatem Hominis convertendi, non quatenùs jam modò Spiritus Sanctus eam illuminavit, & ex nolente ac repugnante, fecit volentem ac consentientem: quo sanè pacto etiam activè eam concurrere, neuter istorum unquam negavit: sed considerare tantùm eam, quatenùs ex se, & proprijs suis viribus pensiratur, ubi sanè tantummodò se habet ut subjectum patiens, neque ex seipsa vel tantillùm adjumenti ad sui conversionem afferre potest: quantumvis interim maneat ratione substantiæ id, quod est & dicitur. Quibus observatis nihil prorsus periculi phrasin Lutheri in se continere, liquidissimè patet.


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: Is it rightly said, that a man has himself in conversion to be opposed?

But there were others who answered the proposed question, that a man in conversion behaves like some log. Which opinion indeed seemed to many, especially to the patrons of Synergism, too harsh and horrid: But this expression also, understood in a sound sense, has nothing at all of inconvenience. For although a man differs from a log in many ways, both by that faculty by which he acts with προαιρέσει in external matters and those subject to reason; and by that respect, that conversion falls upon a man, however corrupt, but not likewise upon a log or a stone: Meanwhile, however, if that δύναμις, power or faculty, is considered by which conversion can both be begun and effected: certainly in this respect, there is no difference at all between a man and a log: inasmuch as he can no more than a log do anything toward his own conversion from his own powers: But he is as clay in the hand of the potter: as Scripture itself expressly speaks, Isa. 45:9. & ch. 64:8. Rom. 9:21. What? That in this respect the condition of a log is in a way better than that of a man: inasmuch as, just as he is destitute of the faculty of willing: so he also lacks the sin and malice which adheres to an unregenerate man. And to this the blessed Luther looked, who writes in his exposition of Psalm 99: In spiritual and divine matters, concerning the salvation of the soul, an unregenerate man behaves like a statue of salt, into which Lot's wife was turned: indeed like a log, a stone, and a dead image.

Thirdly, there were others who said that the will of an unregenerate man behaves in conversion reluctantly: so that the Holy Spirit effects conversion through violent pulls, or by way of coercion, even in those who are unwilling and reluctant. Which opinion indeed contains something mixed of truth and falsehood. For it is true that a natural man can do nothing of himself but resist the Holy Spirit: For the φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς is enmity against God, Rom. 8:7. So it is also true that some were converted when they were most raging against God: as can be testified by the example of Paul. But that which is inferred is most false: That the reluctant and resisting are converted. For it is most certain that those in whom that reluctance does not cease are never converted to God. Therefore it should rather be established thus: That the Holy Spirit works in the will of a resisting man in such a way that He softens it, and from unwilling and resisting makes it willing and consenting, and thus a man, no longer resisting but willing, is converted: yet willing not from himself, but from the grace of God.

Pelagianism is objected to us in this place, because Pelagius explained himself in a way clearly similar, as can be seen in Augustine, book 4 against the two letters of Pelagius, ch. 6. For Pelagius said that grace helps the good purpose of each person: but does not instill a desire for virtue into one who is reluctant: But our opinion differs from Pelagius by a very long interval: For as Augustine rightly answers in the same place: This opinion of Pelagius could be well understood if it were not said by those whose sense is known. For to the reluctant, the approach of divine calling is first procured by the grace of God itself: and then in him, now no longer reluctant, the spirit of virtue is kindled. Which process Pelagius simply denied. But this answer of ours moves the suspicion of Synergism in many, as if we established that a man's will can incline itself to conversion: and approved simply that of Chrysostom: God draws, but the willing; and that of Basil: Only be willing, and God anticipates. But this suspicion also is clearly vain. For we do not establish that an unregenerate man can will his own conversion from himself and his own powers: which was a Synergistic delirium: But we say that the will, resisting of itself, is softened by the grace of God, and changed by the power of the Holy Spirit, so that it no longer resists: which has nothing at all in common with synergism. As for Chrysostom and Basil, if they spoke thus generally even about the unregenerate: we certainly hold that we are not at all bound by their authority: nay, we establish that the words produced are not analogous to the form of sound words. But if they spoke about the state of the regenerate and the faithful, as the Formula of Concord judges them to have spoken: then they taught nothing repugnant to us.

Fourthly and lastly, others answered that a man in conversion not only does nothing, but is converted idle and ignorant of what is being done with him. Which opinion indeed smacks of Enthusiasm and is refuted, or rather explained, by the same reasons as the one immediately preceding. For although an unregenerate man cannot know of himself and from his own powers what is being done with him: yet the Holy Spirit removes that stupor and illuminates the intellect, so that he now knows what is being done with him, and consents to the acting Holy Spirit. But enough about this second question.

The third succeeds, which has vehemently tormented many: Namely, what and how many causes are to be established, concurring in the conversion of man. Where again theologians depart into clearly diverse opinions, some establishing only two, namely the Holy Spirit and the Word of God: others establishing three, and to the two already named, adding the third, namely the will of man. Which dissension has indeed stirred up no light disturbances in the Church of God: which war, however, seems most rightly able to be settled and composed, if we accurately distinguish between those two species of men to be converted, and thus also of conversion itself: concerning which we have treated more prolixly above. For either the question is about the first conversion, which is of the impious or infidels and those never reborn, or about the second conversion, which is the daily repentance of the faithful and reborn. If therefore the question is about the first, certainly neither more nor fewer causes of conversion can and ought to be established than two: so that those who in this place pos-

Latin:

Sed fuerunt alij, qui ad propositam quæstionem responderunt, Hominem in Conversione habere se instar trunci alicujus. Quæ sanè sententia multis, præsertim patronis Synergismi, visa fuit nimis aspera & horrida : Sed & hæc locutio, sano sensu intellecta, nihil prorsus habet incommodi. Etsi enim Homo à trunco multis modis discrepat, tùm ea facultate, quâ agit cum προαιρέσει in rebus externis, & rationi subjectis: tùm eo respectu, quòd in hominem quantumvis corruptum, non item in truncum aut lapidem cadit Conversio : Interim tamen, si ea consideretur δύναμις, vis sive facultas, quâ Conversio & inchoari & effici potest : certè hoc respectu, nulla prorsus inter hominem & truncum est differentia : quippè qui haud magis atque truncus ad sui Conversionem quicquam ex proprijs viribus facere potest : Sed est quasi lutum in manu figuli : uti scriptura ipsa expressè loquitur, Jes. 45, 9. & cap. 64, 8. Rom. 9, 21. Quid ? quod hoc respectu Trunci suo quodammodo melior est, quàm Hominis conditio: quippè qui, uti facultate volendi destituitur: ita caret etiam peccato & malitia quæ homini non renato adhæret. Et huc respexit B. Lutherus, qui in enarratione Psalm. 99. scribit: In spiritualibus & divinis rebus, salutem animæ concernentibus, Homo non renatus habet se instar statuæ salis, in quam est conversa Lothi conjux : imò instar trunci, lapidis & imaginis mortuæ.

Tertiò fuerunt alij, qui dixerunt, voluntatem Hominis non renati habere se in Conversione repugnanter : ita ut per tractus violentos, sive per modum coactionis in nolentibus etiam & repugnantibus Spiritus Sanctus efficiat conversionem. Quæ sanè sententia ex veritate & falsitate mixtum aliquid continet. Verum enim est, Hominem Animalem ex seipso nihil posse, quàm repugnare Spiritui Sancto : Nam φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς est inimicitia adversus Deum Rom. 8, 7. Sic verum est & illud, quosdam, tùm conversos fuisse, quando maximè contra Deum fremuerunt : uti exemplo Paulo testatum fieri potest. Sed falsissimum est illud, quod infertur : Repugnantes & reluctantes converti. Certissimum enim est, eos, in quibus Reluctatio ista non desinit: nunquam ad Deum converti. Proindè sic potiùs statuendum : Spiritum Sanctum operari in voluntate hominis repugnantis hoc modo, ut eam emolliat, & ex nolente ac repugnante faciat volentem ac consentientem, & sic Homo non ampliùs repugnans, sed volens convertatur : volens autem non ex se, sed ex Dei gratia.

Objicitur hoc loco nobis pelagianismus, proptereà quod Pelagius simili planè modo sese explicaverit, uti videre est apud Augustinum, lib. 4. contra duas epistolas Pelagij cap. 6. Dicebat enim Pelagius, Gratiam adjuvare bonum cujusque propositum: non tamen reluctanti studium virtutis immittere : Verùm longissimo interh vallo nostra sententia a Pelagio discrepat: Nam uti recte Augustinus ibidem respondet: Posset sententia haec Pelagij bene intelligi, si non ab istis, quorum sensus notus est, diceretur. Reluctanti enim prius aditus divinae vocationis, per ipsam DEI gratiam procuratur: ac deinde in illo jam non reluctante, spiritus virtutis accenditur. Quem processum simpliciter negavit Pelagius. Sed Synergismi suspicionem multis movet haec nostra responsio, ac si Hominis voluntas ad Conversionem se inclinare posse, a nobis statuatur: & probetur simpliciter illud Chrysostomi: Trahit Deus sed volentem: & illud Basilij, Tantum velis, & Deus praecurrit. Verum & isthæc suspicio plane est frustranea. Neque enim Hominem non renatum, ex se & suis viribus sui Conversionem velle posse statuimus: id quod Synergisticum fuit delirium: Sed voluntatem ex se repugnantem, per gratiam Dei emolliri, & virtute Spiritus Sancti immutari dicimus, ut jam non repugnet amplius: id quod cum synergismo nihil prorsus habet commercij. Quoad Chrysostomum & Basilium, si generaliter etiam de non renatis sic locuti sint: sane autoritate ipsorum nos minime teneri: quin! & verba producta, forma sanorum verborum haud esse analoga, statuimus. Sin vero de statu renatorum & fidelium locuti sunt, ut ipsos locutos esse formula Concordiae censet: tum nihil nobis repugnans docuerunt.

Quarto & postremo responderunt alij, Hominem in Conversione non tantum nihil agere, sed converti otiosum & nescientem quid secum agatur. Quae sane sententiam Enthusiasmi resipit &, ijfsdem, quibus praecedens proxima, refutatur, vel potius explicatur rationibus. Etsi enim Homo non renatus ex se, & ex suis viribus scire nequit, quid secum agatur: tamen stuporem istum Spiritus Sanctus aufert, & intellectum illuminat, ut jam sciat quid secum agatur, & agenti Spiritui Sancto consentiat. Sed satis de secunda hac quaestione.

Succedit Tertia, quae multos vehementer torsit: Quæ nimirum & quot sint constituendae causae, concurrentes in Conversione Hominis. Ubi rursus in diversas plane sententias abeunt Theologi, nonnullis duas tantum, nempe Spiritum Sanctum & verbum DEI: alijs tres constituentibus, & duabus jam nominatis, Tertiam nempe voluntatem Hominis adjicientibus. Quae sane dissensio turbas haud leves in Ecclesia Dei concitavit: quod tamen bellum rectissime dirimi & componi posse videtur, si accurate distinguamus inter duas illas species convertendorum hominum, & sic ipsius etiam conversionis: de quibus supra prolixius egimus. Vel enim quaeritur de Conversione prima, qua est impiorum sive infidelium & nunquam renatorum, vel de Conversione secunda, qua est quotidiana fidelium & renatorum penitentia. Si ergo de prima fit quaestio, certe neque plures, neque pauciores Conversionis causae constitui possunt & debent, quam duae: ita, ut qui hoc loco ternari-


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: Whether Conversion begun by the Holy Spirit is perfected by the own powers of men

it a triad, and urge the will of man, are hardly strangers to the Synergistic error. But if the question is about the other, certainly nothing stands in the way of the will of man also being admitted, and a ternary finding a place: Since in that perpetual exercise of repentance, which those already reborn and faithful institute, the regenerated will συνεργει cooperates, and acts simultaneously: as we shall expressly show in the third subsequent chapter. Furthermore, the question in this place is not about this latter: But only about that first one. Therefore, if an unfaithful man who has never been reborn is to be converted, we posit that only two causes concur: But under a most diverse genus of causes: One, namely, the efficient, which is the sole and only Holy Spirit: The other, however, the organic or instrumental, which is the Word of God preached and heard, as is the right use of the Sacraments. Concerning the efficient cause, the testimonies of the scriptures are clear:

Phil. 2:13. God works in us both to will and to perform. And chap. 1, 29. To you it has been granted by God, that you may believe in Christ.

Acts 5:31. God gives repentance and remission of sins.

2 Tim. 2:25 & 26. God gives repentance for the acknowledging of the truth, etc.

John 6:29. This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent,

Deut. 29:4. It is God who gives an understanding heart, eyes that see, and ears that hear.

Concerning the Word and Sacraments, as the means which the Holy Spirit uses in initiating and effecting conversion: the Savior treats in John 6:45. Everyone who has heard from the Father, and has learned, comes to me.

Rom. 10:14. How shall they believe, if they do not hear? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And v. 17. Faith comes by hearing: And hearing by the Word of Christ. And the same Paul in general calls the Sacraments seals of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4:11. In particular, however, he names Baptism the washing of regeneration and renewal in the Holy Spirit. Tit. 3:5.

Fourthly, it is asked concerning the manner of Conversion, what and of what kind it is: or what is the order by which progress is made in the conversion of man? But here the discussion is again not about the other, but about the first species of Conversion, which is of men who have never been reborn. Now if we examine the examples of such conversions more accurately, it becomes plain by reason of both the motions themselves, and also of time, that one conversion is most rightly called sudden and as it were violent: the other, however, slow and gentle. The Scripture shows us an example of the former in the Apostle Paul in Acts 9. Weighing which, Augustine writes that he marvels at the immensity of divine goodness and mercy: For God not only calls and converts the wicked and impious to himself,

but also strives to terrify some, even while they are engaged in the act of performing impiety (like Saul), with the fear of his judgment, and to strike their hearts with the hammer of his power, so that at the very time they deserve the punishment of hell, he himself may promote the drawing of their salvation. The scripture shows an example of the latter conversion in the Magi, whom the LORD, when other heralds were lacking, drew and converted from the most remote ends of the earth to the knowledge of the Messiah by the new miracle of an unusual star appearing, with a very gentle and slow step. Matt. 2. Which example one may also see in the Ethiopian converted to Christ through Philip the Apostle. Acts 8:26 & seqq. Furthermore, in every conversion, it is necessary that the Word of God intervene as an Organ, or as the Fathers have spoken, as an ὄχημα, a vehicle of the Holy Spirit. For neither are new motions impressed upon those to be converted as a seal upon wax: nor is this conversion something brute, as when Balaam's donkey speaks: Num. 22:28. nor is it something violent, as when a stone is pushed: nor is it something Enthusiastic, as when the possessed (who are carried away by the Devil) give oracles or many things happen in the obsessed, without the application of mind and will: But through the ministry of the word, of which every conversion must be the beginning: to which men must leave a place, and admit the heard word, if indeed any conversion is to follow. Now truly, even if a man not yet reborn can hear and read the Word of GOD, can discourse about it, can conceive a part of historical faith from it, no less than the devils themselves, as James testifies in Chapter 2:19. Yet he can in no way embrace or understand the word of salvation, to such an extent that it is foolishness to him, unless the illumination of the Holy Spirit supervenes: so far is it from the case that he can from this source in any way promote the business of his own salvation by himself, or even make a beginning of it: But as the Ancients have spoken, those efforts are gross, if they are not aided by grace: nay, they are plainly null, if they are not excited: Now the Holy Spirit excites good motions, when He inspires pious thoughts, and by injecting a motion of good purpose, He prevents man with His grace. Therefore the beginning and the whole operation of Conversion is to be ascribed entirely and in its entirety to the Holy Spirit alone, who in the man hearing the Word is not idle, but moves and impels the will, so that at the very beginning of Conversion, it as it were fluctuates and hangs in the balance, and begins to struggle with the flesh, for so long, until from being resistant it becomes consenting, that is, from being a slave it becomes liberated, from being unwilling it becomes willing, so that now to will lies at hand for the man, and he delights in the Law of God, not coerced or unwilling, but κατὰ τὸ ἑκούσιον. Rom. 7, 18. & 22. Philem. verse 14.

Fifthly and lastly it is asked, Whether Conversion once begun in man by the power of the Holy Spirit, is afterwards perfected and preserved by the powers of human nature alone. Where our churches hold and defend the Negative. For neither is corrupt Nature so restored by this operation of the Holy Spirit, that it has it in its own power to change itself for the better, nor does it stand in need of the Holy Spirit's aid any longer, and by its own virtue be able to stand in grace and persevere to the very end: But all these things, no less than the beginning of Conversion, are to be ascribed to the Holy Spirit: who works in us, not only to will, but also to perform: and who completes and perfects the good which He has begun in us: and by His own virtue guards and preserves the reborn to the very end. Phil. 1, 6. and chap. 2, 13. 1 Pet. 1, 5. and chap. 5, 10.

Latin:

tim ponunt, & voluntatem Hominis urgent, à Synergistico errore haud sint alieni. Sin de altera sit quaestio, nihil certè obstat, quo minus voluntas Hominis etiam admittatur, & ternarius locum inveniat: Siquidem in perpetuo illo poenitentiae exercitio, quod jam renati & fideles instituunt, voluntas regenerata συνεργει cooperatur, & simul agit: uti capite subsequente tertio ex professo ostendemus. Caeterùm de hac posteriore hoc loco non est quaestio: Sed tantùm de prima illa. Proindè si Homo infidelis & nunquam renatus converti debeat, duas tantùm causas concurrere statuimus: Sed sub diversissimo causarum genere: Unam nimirùm efficientem, quae est, solus & unus Spiritus Sanctus: Alteram verò Organicam sive instrumentalem, quae est, Verbum Dei praedicatum auditumq́;, ut rectus usus Sacramentorum. De causa efficiente perspicua sunt scripturae testimonia:

Phil. 2 13. Deus operatur in nobis & velle & perficere. Et cap. 1, 29. Vobis à Deo donatum est, ut in Christum credatis.

Actor. 5, 31. Deus dat poenitentiam & Remissionem peccatorum.

2. Tim. 2, 25. & 26. Deus dat poenitentiam ad agnoscendam veritatem &c.

Joh. 6, 29. Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum, quem misit ille,

Deut. 29, 4. Deus est, qui donat Cor intelligens oculos videntes & aures audientes.

De Verbo & Sacramentis, tanquam medijs, quibus Spiritus Sanctus in inchoanda & efficienda conversione utitur: agit Servator Joh. 6, 45. Omnis qui audivit à patre, & didicit, venit ad me.

Rom. 10, 14. Quomodo credent, si non audiant? quomodo audient, sine praedicante? Et v. 17. Fides ex auditu: Auditus autem per Verbum Christi. Et idem Paulus in genere Sacramenta vocat sigilla Justitiae fidei, Rom. 4, 11. In specie verò Baptismum nominat lavacrum regenerationis & renovationis in Spiritu Sancto. Tit. 3, 5.

Quartò quaeritur de Conversionis modo, quinam & qualis sit: sive quis sit ordo, quo in Conversione hominis fit progressio? Agitur autem hic rursum non de altera, sed de prima Conversionis specie, quae est Hominum nunquam renatorum. Jam si exempla hujusmodi Conversiorum accuratius exdendamus, planum fit ratione tùm ipsorum motuum, tùm temporis etiam, rectissimè Conversionem aliam dici subitam & quasi violentam: aliam verò lentam atque lenem. Prioris exemplum Scriptura nobis monstrat in Apostolo Paulo Actor. 9. Quod expendens Augustinus, divinae bonitatis & misericordiae immensitatem se mirari scribit: Non solùm enim sceleratos & impios ad se vocat & convertit,

Deus, sed quosdam etiam dum in impietatis actu peragendo versantur, (uti Saulus) judicij sui metu perterrefacere, & malleo potentiæ suæ corda ipsorum pulsare satagit, ut quo tempore ipsi supplicium gehennæ merentur, salutis tractum ipse promoveat. Posterioris Conversionis exemplum scriptura monstrat in Magis, quos DOMINUS, cum alij præcones deessent, novo stellæ inusitatæ apparentis miracolo, a remotissimis terræ finibus ad agnitionem Messiæ, leni perquàm ac lento gradu pertraxit ac convertit. Matth. 2. Quale exemplum videre etiam licet in Æthiope per Philippum Apostolum ad Christum Converso. Actor. 8, 26. & seqq. Cæterum in omni Conversione, Verbum Dei tanquam Organum, sive uti Patres locuti sunt, tanquam ὄχημα vehiculum Spiritus Sancti, interveniat necesse est. Neque enim convertendis novi motus imprimuntur tanquam ceræ sigillum: neque conversio hæc est brutum aliquid, sicut cùm asina Bileami loquitur: Num. 22, 28. neque etiam violentum quid, sicut cum lapis protruditur: neque Enthusiasticum quiddam, sicut arreptitij (qui a Diabolo abripiuntur) oracula reddunt vel in obsessis fiunt multa, sine applicatione mentis & voluntatis: Sed per ministerium verbi, cujus libet Conversionis sit exordium: cui locum relinquere, & auditum verbum admittere debent homines, si modò Conversio ulla subsequi debeat. Jam verò, etsi homo nondùm renatus potest audire & legere Verbum DEI, potest de eo differere, potest partem fidei historicæ ex eodem concipere, non minus quàm Diaboli ipsi, teste Jacobo Cap. 2, 19. Verbum tamen salutis vel amplecti, vel intelligere nullo modo potest, adeò ut stultitia ipsi sit, nisi Spiritus Sancti illuminatio superveniat: tantum abest, ut ipse hinc salutis suæ negotium ex se ipso ullo modo promovere possit, vel ejus tantùm initium facere: Sed ut Veteres locuti sunt, crassi sunt conatus isti, si a gratia non adjuventur: imò planè nulli, si non excitentur: Excitat autem Spiritus Sanctus bonos motus, cùm cogitationes pias inspirat, & boni propositi motum immittendo, gratia sua hominem prævenit. Proindè initium & tota operatio Conversionis in solidum & ex asse est adscribenda soli Spiritui Sancto, qui in Homine audiente Verbum non est otiosus, sed movet & impellit voluntatem, ut sub ipso Conversionis initio, ea quasi fluctuet ac pendeat, & cum carne luctare incipiat, tam diu, donec ex repugnante fiat consentiens, hoc est, ex serva fiat liberata, ex nolente volens, ut jam velle jam adjaceat homini, & condelectetur Legi Dei, non coactus aut invitus, sed κατὰ τὸ ἑκούσιον. Rom. 7, 18. & 22. Philem. versu. 14.

Quinto & postremo quæritur, Num Conversio semel in homine virtute Spiritῥ Sancti inchoata, postmodum solis naturæ humanæ viribus, perficiatur & conservetur. Ubi Negativam nostræ tenent ac defendunt Ecclesiæ. Neque enim ex hac Spiritus Sancti operatione, Natura corrupta sic instauratur, ut in sua potestate situm habeat, mutare se in melius, neq; Spiritus Sancti auxilio amplius indigeat, suaque virtute in gratia stare & ad finem usque perseverare possit: Sed hæc omnia haud minus atque Conversionis initium, Spiritui Sancto sunt adscribenda: qui operatur in nobis, non tantum velle, sed & perficere: quique bonum quod in nobis cepit, consummat & perficit: & virtute sua ad finem usque renatos custodit ac conservat. Phil. 1, 6. & cap. 2, 13. 1. Petr. 1, 5. & cap. 5, 10.


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: The other part of the second Chapter, antithetical

The other part of the second Chapter, antithetical.

Both ancient and more recent Pelagians have wickedly defiled this purer part of Christian doctrine. By the ancients we understand those who, in the fourth century after Christ's birth, especially in the time of St. Augustine, disturbed the Church of God, having scattered various seeds of heresy. Among other things, however, regarding the present Article, they contended that man, by the aid of natural powers at least, apart from the grace of GOD and the aid of the Holy Spirit, could perform obedience to the divine law. For, as Augustine testifies in his book On Heresies, chapter 88, they were such enemies of the grace of God that they asserted that man could perform all the commandments of God without it. For which name of impiety

Pelagius, having been rebuked by the brethren because he thus attributed nothing at all to the aid of the Grace of God for performing His commandments, wished to appear to have left room for their admonition, while he conceded that the Grace of God is altogether required for free will. Where, however, with too much crafty cunning he most shamefully imposed upon the Church of God, while he did not place the Grace of God before free will, but placed it under it. For he expressly said that the Grace of God is given to men for this purpose, that what they are commanded to do through free will, they might be able to fulfill more easily through Grace. Furthermore, he acknowledged no other Grace of God than that of the possibility of nature, or of doctrine, or of the restoration of nature through Christ, who is necessary for us to do good, not by the aid of virtue, but by the example of imitation, as can be seen in Augustine's book On the Grace of Christ against Pelagius and Caelestius, chapters 33, 34, 39. Although Jerome and others among the Fathers opposed themselves to this heresy with great zeal and knowledge, yet Augustine easily surpassed all the rest in this part, who manfully uncovered the snares of the Pelagians and gravely refuted them from Holy Scripture; indeed, he most skillfully explained the whole doctrine concerning free will, which had previously been enveloped in the mire of various errors. Where, first of all, that most useful distinction of Augustine deserves observation, between preventing, preparing, operating, cooperating, and persevering grace: for by observing this, one can most rightly oppose the sophistries of those who, in the present controversy, too craftily join the Grace of God and the powers of free will. Augustine therefore opposed the first grace, namely preventing grace, to the error of those who, before Pelagius, did not fear to say that the beginning of conversion is from the powers of free will: thus showing that it is not even ours to begin: but that it depends entirely upon the preventing, or preceding, Grace of God: according to that of Psalm 21:4, 'You have prevented him with the blessings of sweetness.' And Psalm 59:11, 'My God, His mercy shall prevent me.'

The other grace, which Augustine designates as preparing, he opposed to those who conceded that the beginning of our conversion is indeed from God, but that our acquiescence or consent is to be attributed to the powers of free will. Augustine, therefore, denying this, shows that this very thing also is a gift of preparing Grace, that is, of moving and inclining our mind and will, so that it does not resist, but consents and obeys the Holy Spirit: by the example of Lydia, to whom God opened her heart, so that she might attend to those things which were said by Paul, Acts 16:14.

The third grace, namely operating, he opposed to those who maintained that it was placed in the powers of man to change his will for the better, after the Holy Spirit had already begun to work in him in conversion. He shows, therefore, that this very thing depends upon the operating Grace of God, inasmuch as it works in us both to will and to perform, Phil. 2:13.

Augustine named the fourth grace, cooperating, that which brings it about in the reborn that they consent to the law of God, Rom. 7:22, so that they may grow more and more in faith and the knowledge of God, Eph. 4:13.

He defines the fifth and last Grace by the Gift of perseverance in faith, even to the end, which likewise depends upon God alone, as was demonstrated above from the first Epistle of Peter, chap. 1:5, and chap. 5:10.

Moreover, the arguments upon which the Pelagians relied most heavily were these.

THE FIRST is taken from Rom. 2, 14. The Gentiles, which have not the Law, do by nature the things contained in the Law: these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves.

But this argument fails at the outset with the fallacy of Ignoratio Elenchi. For the Apostle does not say that the Gentiles fulfilled the Law, or that they were doers of the Law: but that they did τὰ τοῦ νόμου, that is, that they produced some specimens of virtues, and rendered obedience to the discipline of the law in some part. For although, as Augustine speaks, lib. de Spiritu & Litera, cap. 28, they were ungodly, and did not truly worship the true God, we either read, or know, or hear of certain things done by them, which, according to the rule of justice, we not only cannot blame: but even deservedly and rightly praise: although if they are examined as to the end for which they are done, they are scarcely found to be such as deserve the praise or defense due to justice. Then the argument proceeds from a part. For it is a collection from a part to the whole affirmatively, that is, from moral matters to spiritual things: where the consequence is most rightly denied. For although an unregenerate man can perform certain deeds, joined with praise, in external actions: according to that saying: 'Under you is the appetite, and you shall rule over it': yet in spiritual things he can do nothing at all: Since flesh and blood cannot reveal those things which pertain to the kingdom of Christ, Matt. 16.

The second, sought from the scriptures, consisted of a certain collection of those passages which contain precepts, exhortations, rebukes, promises, and threats. For hence they argued thus: If in spiritual matters an unregenerate man can do nothing from the faculty or powers of free will, then such precepts, promises, and threats are proposed by God altogether in vain and to no purpose. But this is absurd, nay, highly blasphemous: It remains, therefore, that there still exists in man, however corrupt, some faculty of free will, by which he can perform those things which are thus proposed by God.

I answer that a fallacy ὡ̓ς ἀπό τοῡ ἀνεπόμενον is committed. For a negative collection is made from the species to the genus, in this manner: If such precepts, promises, and threats are not proposed by God because there remains in man, even when unregenerate, a faculty of performing what God requires: Therefore, there will be absolutely no other use for those precepts, etc. Where the consequence is most rightly denied. For many other uses can be given, both with respect to God and with respect to men. For God requires from man what is owed to Him: 2. In this way, He calls to man's memory what and how great goods he lost through the fall: 3. Thus He abundantly testifies that He is not at fault that men perish and are damned. But with respect to men, a manifold use likewise emerges; 1. that the pious may recognize the atrocity of original corruption. 2. that, despairing of their own dignity, they may understand what must be begged from God with assiduous prayers. 3. that they may value all the more the most perfect obedience rendered to the Law by Christ, and apply it to themselves: but that the impious may be held partly by the threats of the Law, as if by thunderbolts, and be enticed to the amendment of life: and partly be rendered ἀναπολόγητοι, inexcusable, if they perish eternally and are damned: as the Apostle testifies, Rom. 2, 1.

Thirdly, they brought forward many testimonies of the scriptures which seemed to patronize free will even after the fall: to which, that one may answer as if by a certain compendium to each and all, it will be very profitable if they are distributed into certain classes. For they either deal with the faculty of the will in external things, and those subject to reason, in which a man, even unregenerate, can in some way command the locomotive [powers]: to which pertains that Gen. 4, 7: 'Under you shall be the appetite, and you shall rule over it': And that Rom. 2, 14: 'The Gentiles naturally do those things which are of the Law.' Some deal with the perfection of human nature before the fall: such as that Eccl. 15, 14 and following: 'God from the beginning left man in the hand of his own counsel,' etc. Some speak of the faculty which is in man, most free toward evil. Heb. 10, 26: 'For those who sin willfully there remains no sacrifice for sin': Matt. 23, 47. I wanted to gather you, but you would not. Some speak of the will in those already regenerate: of which the third chapter of our treatise will deal: To which pertain the following testimonies: Isa. 1, 19: 'If you are willing and hear, you shall eat the good of the land.' 1 John 5, 3: 'His commandments are not grievous.' 1 Cor. 9, 17: 'If I do this willingly.' Rom. 7, 19: 'The good that I will, I do not,' etc. Finally, some speak of the liberty of that glory which will one day be consummated in the Elect in the future age: Eph. 5, 27: 'The Church shall not have spot or wrinkle': and such other things.

But to leave the ancient heretics and approach the more recent ones, it is manifest that the Scholastic Doctors, and the Papists who followed them, have as it were resurrected from hell the very same heresy of Pelagius. The theology of the Scholastics certainly betrayed these emblems of the Pelagians quite openly: 1. Free will from its own natural powers can fulfill the precepts of God, as regards the substance of the act. 2. An unregenerate man, without faith and the Holy Spirit, doing the works of the precepts by free will alone, does not sin. 3. A man existing in mortal sin, without faith and the Holy Spirit, can avoid and beware of any mortal sin, so as not to commit it anew: Although some spoke more mildly and tolerably, such as P. Lombard, Thomas, and Bonaventure: yet they did not so much remove the old errors with new ones, as they confirmed them, even if unwittingly: as when Bonaventure, seeing that the Pelagian heresy was contrary to the scriptures and all antiquity, descended to a new hyperbole, feigning that men always bring with them at birth some gratuitous gifts, even before the renewal of the spirit, by whose virtue they might be able to prepare themselves to receive grace. Hence Occam did not hesitate to write: As easily as reason can have a dictate about loving God above all things, so easily can the will from pure natural powers perfectly accommodate itself to that dictate.

Latin:

Pars Capitis secundi altera, ἀντιθετικὴ.

Purjorem hanc doctrinæ Christianæ partem nefariè conspurcarunt, tùm veteres tùm recentiores pelagiani. Per veteres intelligimus illos, qui quarto post Christum natum seculo, tempore potissimum D. Augustini Ecclesiam Dei turbarunt, varijs hæresem sparsis seminibus. Inter cætera verò quoad præsentem Articulum contendebant. Hominem naturalium saltem virium adjumento, citra gratiam DEI, & Spiritus Sancti auxilium, obedientiam legi divinæ præstare posse. Nam teste Augustino l. de hære. fibus cap. 88. in tantum erant inimici gratiæ Dei, ut sine hac Hominem omnia mandata Dei facere posse, assererent. Quo impietatis nomine

Pelagius à fratribus increpatus, quod sic nihil prorsus tribueret adjutorio Gratiæ Dei, ad ejus mandata facienda: locum quidem admonitioni ipsorum reliquisse videri volebat, dùm concessit, Gratiam Dei ad Liberum arbitrium omninò requiri. Ubi tamen nimis veteratoria callidate Ecclesiæ Dei turpissimè imposuit, dùm Gratiam Dei Libero arbitrio non præposuit, sed supposuit. Expressè enim dicebat, Gratiam Dei ad hoc dari hominibus, ut quæ facere per Liberum Arbitrium jubentur, faciliùs possent implere per Gratiam. Deindè non aliam agnoscecebat Gratiam Dei, quàm possibilitatis naturæ, vel doctrinæ vel instaurationis naturæ per Christum, qui nobis neceffarius sit ad benè agendum, non virtutis auxilio, sed imitationis exemplo, uti videre est apud Augustinum lib. de Gratiâ Dei adversus Pelagium & Cælestium cap. 33. 34. 39. Quanquam verò Hieronymus & alij ex Patribus, magno studio & cognatu, hærefi huic sese opposuerunt: tamen palmam hac in parte reliquis omnibus facilè antevertit Augustinus, qui insidias Pelagianorum masculè detexit, & ex Scriptura Sacra graviter refutavit: imò doctrinam totam de Libero arbitrio quæ prius variorum errorum cæno obvoluta erat, dexterrìmè explicavit. Ubi cum primis observationem meretur utilissima distinctio illa Augustini, inter Gratiam prævenientem, præparantem, operantem, cooperantem, perseverantem: Hâc enim observata, rectissimè obviam iri potest Sophisticationibus illorum, qui Gratiam Dei & vires Liberi Arbitrij in præsenti controversiâ nimis subdolè conjungunt. Primam ergo Gratiam nempè prævenientem opposuit, Augustinus illorum errori, qui ante Pelagium dicere non verebantur, Initium Conversionis esse ex viribus Liberi arbitrij: Sic ostendens, ne quidem incipere esse nostrum: Sed dependere ex toto, à Gratia Dei præveniente, sive præcedente: secundum illud Psalmi 21, 4. prævenisti eum in benedictione dulcedinis. Et Psal. 59, 11. Deus meus misericordia ejus præveniet me.

Alteram Gratiam, quam præparantem Augustinus indigitat, opposuit illis, qui concedebant, Initum quidem Conversionis nostræ esse ex Deo, sed ut acquiescamus sive consentiamus, viribus Liberi arbitrij esse acceptum ferendum. Hoc ergò negans Augustinus, ostendit hoc ipsum quoque esse donum Dei Gratiæ præparantis, hos est, moventis & inclinantis mentem & voluntatem nostram, ne repugnet, sed consentiat & obsequatur Spiritui Sancto: exemplo Lydiæ, cui Deus cor aperuit, ut attenderet illis, quæ dicebantur à Paulo Actor. 16, 14.

Tertiam gratiam, nempè operantem, opposuit illis, qui statuebant, in Hominis viribus positum esse, voluntatem suam mutare in melius, postquàm jam in ea Spiritus Sanctus Conversione operari cepit. Ostendit ergò hoc ipsum pendere ex Gratia Dei operante, quippe quæ in nobis operetur & velle & perficere Phil. 2, 13.

Quartam Gratiam, cooperantem, nominavit Augustinus eam, quæ in renatis efficit, ut consentiant legi Dei, Rom. 7, 22. ut magis magisque in fide & agnitione Dei crescant. Ephes. 4, 13.

Quintam & postremam Gratiam definit per Donum perseverantiæ in fide, usque ad finem, quæ itidem à solo Deo dependet, uti supra demonstratum ex priore Epistola Petri cap. 1, 5. & cap. 5, 10.

Cæterùm argumenta, quibus Pelagiani vel maximè nitebantur, erant isthæc.

PRIMUM desumptum ex Rom. 2, 14. Gentes, quæ Legem non habent, naturâ faciunt ea, quæ Legis sunt: hi legem non habentes, sibi ipsi sunt Lex.

Sed fallit hoc argumentum initio Sophismate Ignorationis Elenchi. Neque enim dicit Apostolus, Gentes Legem implevisse, aut Legis factores fuisse: Sed τὰ τοῦ νόμου fecisse, hoc est, aliqua virtutum specimina edidisse, & legis disciplinæ aliqua ex parte obedientiam ipsos præstitisse. Quamvis enim, ut Augustinus loquitur, lib. de Spiritu & Litera, cap. 28. Impij fuerint, Deumque verum veraciter non coluerint, quædam ab ipsis facta vel legimus, vel novimus, vel audimus, quæ secundum Justitiæ regulam, non solùm vituperare non possumus: Verùm etiam meritò recteque laudamus: quanquam si discutiantur, quo fine fiant, vix inveniantur, quæ justitiæ debitam laudem defensionemve mereantur. Deindè ex parte procedit argumentum. Sit enim collectio à parte ad totum affirmatè, hoc est, ex moralibus ad spiritualia: ubi rectissimè negatnr consequentia. Etsi enim Homo non renatus, quædam facta, cum laude conjuncta, præstare potest, in externis actionibus: secundum illud: Subte est appetitus,& tu dominaberis illi: in spiritualibus tamen nihil quicquam potest: Siquidem Caro & Sanguis non possunt revelare ea, quæ ad regnum Christi attinent, Matth.16.

Alterùm ex scripturis petitum, congerie quadam constabat eorum locorum, quæ præcepta,exhortationes, objurgationes, promissiones & comminationes continent. Hinc enim sic arguebant: Si in rebus spiritualibus Homo non renatus nihil potest ex facultate sive viribus Liberi arbitrij, frustra omninò & abs re ejusmodi præcepta, promissiones & comminationes à DEO proponuntur. Atqui hoc absurdum imò summè blasphemum est: Relinquitur ergò restare adhuc in homine quantumvis corrupto facultatem aliquam Liberi Arbitrij, quâ præstare possit ea,quæ sic à Deo sunt proposita.

Respondeo, committi Sophisma ὡ̓ς ἀπό τοῡ ἀνεπόμενον. Nam à specie ad Genus negativa fit collectio, in hunc modum: Si non ideò ejusmodi præcepta,promissiones & comminationes à Deo proponuntur, quia in homine etiam non renato reliqua est facultas præstandi ea, quæ Deus requirit: Ergò planè nullus alius istorum præceptorum &c. erit usus. Ubi rectissimè negatur consequentia. Plures enim alij dari possunt usus, tum respectu Dei, tum respectu hominum. Deus enim requirit ab homine, quod sibi debetur: 2.in memoriam homini hoc modo revocat, quæ & quanta bona per lapsum perdiderit: 3. Sic abundè testatur, se non esse in culpâ, quòd Homines pereunt & damnantur. Hominum verò respectu usus itidem multiplex emergit; 1. ut pij agnoscant attrocitatem corruptionis Originalis. 2. ut de sua dignitate desperantes, intelligant, quid à Deo assiduis precibus flagitandum sit. 3. ut obedientiam perfectissimam à Christo Legi præstitam, tantò pluris faciant, & sibi applicent: Impij verò ut partim comminationibus Legis, tanquam fulminibus teneantur, & ad vitæ emendationem alliciantur: partim verò reddantur ἀναπολόγητοι inexcusabiles, si æternum pereant & damnentur: teste Apostolo, Rom. 2, 1.

Tertiò proferebant benè multa scripturarum testimonia, quæ Libero arbitrio etiam post lapsum reliquo patrocinari videbantur: ad quæ singula & universa, ut per compendium quasi quoddam respondeatur, plurimùm profuerit, si in certas quasi classes ea distribuantur. Nam vel agunt de facultate voluntatis in externis rebus, & rationi subjectis, in quibus Homo etiam non renatus, locomotivæ aliquo modo imperare potest: quò pertinent illud Genes. 4, 7. Sub te erit appetitus, & tu dominaberis illi: Etillud Rom. 2, 14. Gentes naturaliter ea, quæ Legis sunt, faciunt. Quædam agunt de perfectione Naturæ humanæ ante lapsum: quale est, illud Eccl. 15, 14. & seqq. Deus ab initio reliquit Hominem in manu consilij sui &c. Quædam loquuntur de facultate, quæ est in homine liberrima ad malum. Hebr. 10, 26. Voluntariè peccantibus non supereft hostia pro peccato: Matth. 23, 47. Volui te congregare, sed noluisti. Quædam loquuntur de arbitrio in renatis jam liberato : de quo tertium Tractationis nostræ caput aget: Quò pertinent seqq. testimonia: Jes. 1, 19. Si volueritis & audieritis, bona terræ comedetis. 1. Johan. 5, 3. Mandata ejus gravia non sunt. 1. Corinth. 9, 17. Si volens hoc facio. Rom. 7, 19. Bonum quod volo, non facio &c. Quædam denique loquuntur de libertate illius gloriæ, quæ aliquando in futuro seculo, in Electis consummabitur : Ephes. 5, 27. Ecclesia non habebit maculam, aut rugam: ut tale aliquid aliud.

Sed ut missis veteribus hæreticis ad recentiores accedamus, manifestum est Doctores Scholasticos, & hos secutos Pontificios, eandem planè Pelagij hæresin, ab orco quasi resuscitasse. Scholasticorum certè Theologia satis apertè hæc Pelagianorum Emblemata prodidit : Liberum arbitrium ex suis naturalibus, potest præcepta DEI implere, quoad substantiam actus. 2. Homo non renatus sine fide & Spiritu Sancto solo Libero arbitrio faciens opera præceptorum, non peccat. 3. Homo existens in peccato mortali, sine fide & Spiritu Sancto, potest vitare & cavere quodvis peccatum mortale, ne de novo illud committat : Quanquam verò nonnulli mitius & tolerabilius locuti sunt, ut P. Lombardus: Thomas & Bonaventura: tamen novis erroribus veteres tàm non sustulerunt, ut vel inscij illos confirmarent : ut quando Bonaventura videns Pelagianam hæresin, scripturis & toti Antiquitati esse contrariam, ad novam hyperbolen descendit, fingens. Homines nascentes semper afferre aliquid donorum gratuitorum, etiam ante renovationem spiritus, cujus virtute se præparare queant ad suscipiendam gratiam. Hinc Occam scribere non dubitavit. Quàm facilè ratio potest habere dictamen de diligendo Deo super omnia : tàm facile voluntas ex puris naturalibus potest se illi dictamini perfectè accommodare.


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: The other part of the second Chapter, antithetical (continued)

Although Robert Bellarmine and the remaining more recent Papist writers wish to appear to disapprove and condemn this Scholastic theology: yet to those weighing their writings and disputations more closely, it cannot be obscure that they play with perpetual sophistications and impostures, and in this part craftily impose upon the Church of God. For that they retain the thing itself and the very nerve, as it were, of Pelagianism is clearly evident from the Decrees of the Council of Trent, from the writings of Andradius the Spaniard, and from the disputations of Bellarmine and other Jesuits.

For as regards the Council of Trent, although it strives in sufficiently specious words to ward off the heresy of Pelagianism from itself: while it writes, namely, that free will is in no way sufficient to begin and accomplish spiritual actions: but that all things must be attributed to the necessity of the grace of God and divine aid, so that we cannot even desire and will any perfect good without it: nay, not even think any of those things which lead to eternal happiness, unless it be raised and confirmed by the touch and virtue of the divine Spirit:

Although finally it even brandishes the thunderbolt of anathema against those who maintain that, whether by the preventing inspiration and aid of the Holy Spirit, a man can repent, believe, love, and hope as he ought: yet it is not difficult to gather how they wish all these things to be understood, if we consider the explanation given by those who have undertaken the defense of the Council of Trent. Andradius explains the mind of the Council thus: Free Will, without the inspiration and aid of the Holy Spirit, cannot indeed perform spiritual actions: not, however, because in an unregenerate man the mind and will have absolutely no power, no strength or faculties, which are necessary for beginning and performing spiritual actions: but only because those natural strengths and faculties, although neither destroyed nor extinguished, are yet so entangled in the snares of sins that a man cannot by his own virtue extricate himself from them. And so that it may be clearer what the sense of these should be, he explains the matter with these comparisons: just as he who is bound in iron fetters has an inherent δύναμιν [power] of walking, but cannot proceed in the act itself unless the bonds are broken. And just as for a sick man, whose strength has been broken, weakened, and attenuated by disease, the strength that still remains, although attenuated, is confirmed and strengthened by a physician: and if any has been lost, it is restored: And just as a little bird has the faculty of flying, but cannot fly when tied by a little cord: and he who breaks this does not impart to the little bird a new δύναμιν [power] of flying, And just as fire is the efficient cause of burning wood, but not alone, but rather with GOD as the author and patron of nature: So since the motion of our free will depends no more on the grace of God than the burning of wood depends on divine virtue, why is it that you strip free will of the dignity and name of an efficient cause? The Council of Trent therefore thinks, with Andradius as interpreter, (as Chemnitius rightly gathers part 1. Exam. p. 118.b) that in the mind and will of an unregenerate man, from his first birth, in this corruption, there are still naturally inherent some strengths, or faculties of whatever kind, for divine things or spiritual actions; but that the motion and use of those faculties and strengths are repressed and retarded in the unregenerate through sin: but that the grace of God, and the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, do not simply effect, or work in those who are reborn, some new δύναμιν [power] or faculty of beginning and performing spiritual motions and actions which they did not already have before from the strengths of nature: but only break those bonds, so that the natural faculty, previously constricted and hindered, can now, having been excited by grace, exercise its strengths in spiritual matters. But those natural strengths, wherever they are weaker, they feel are aided and confirmed by the grace and aid of the Holy Spirit: And where they do not suffice, they say a new habit is infused, which brings with it the respect of merit.

Yet the Romanists did not always hide under such obscurities and wrappings of words, but sometimes broke forth into the light, explaining their mind more clearly: just as the same Andradius did not hesitate to write in his books of Orthodox Explanations: That many were justified by the law of Nature and the strengths of Free Will: nay, that the knowledge of GOD, which is sought from the law of Nature, can suffice for salvation: since this implicitly hides faith in CHRIST Crucified: p. 292. Nay, that it was placed in the faculty of the Gentiles to add to that knowledge of GOD, which could suffice for salvation, worship, piety, and religion toward GOD, and to understand GOD, whom they understood to be the Supreme Good, with all the strengths of the mind, etc. p. 293.

The Jesuit Bellarmine, in book 6 of On Grace and Free Will, chapter two, indeed strives to confirm with many things: That a man cannot, without the special illumination of God, believe the mysteries of faith: But soon in the following parts, like a shrew-mouse, he betrays himself, that under the coverings of words he holds the same mind and opinion as the Council of Trent and Andradius. For in chapter 3, p. 879. B., intending to refute certain objections, he writes among other things thus: To all these it will be possible to answer easily, if one observes that when we say that without special aid a man cannot believe the articles of our faith, we do not mean that he cannot believe in any way: but that he cannot, as he ought, for this to be an act of Catholic faith and the beginning of Justification. And in chapter 9 he proposes this question: Whether a man after the fall of the first man truly has free will in those things which pertain to salvation, so that although he can do nothing without the aid of grace: yet, having been excited by preventing grace and aided by GOD, he is so able to act that he can also not act? The Jesuit writes explicitly that he defends the affirmative of this question against Luther. Hence the following little flowers were also produced by him: chapter 10. B. & C. If men in pious and salutary actions did nothing properly through Free Will: but were only led and moved as mere instruments, they should not be called co-workers and co-adjutors of GOD.

2. If a man were not of free will in works of piety, it would follow that those who do not wish to believe in Christ, or do not wish to be converted from sins, or do not wish to do good works for the sake of GOD, do not sin.

3. It would follow that those who are willing to believe, to hope, to love, to be converted, and to suffer anything arduous and bitter for the sake of GOD, are not to be praised, nor are they worthy of any reward.

4. Precepts, counsels, exhortations, reproofs, examples, and other things of that kind would have no place in such matters.

Finally, all diligence and industry in increasing and cultivating faith and piety would be removed from the midst.

Indeed, in chapter 15 he writes that the Roman Church maintains this opinion in express words: Man before all Grace has free will, not only for natural and moral works, but also for works of piety and supernatural ones: because free will could not be taken away by sin, since sin could harm natural goods but not extinguish them. And it deserves observation that the Jesuit explains his mind and that of his own with almost the same comparisons as Andradius. For in chapter 10, page 904, letter C, he says among other things: Just as fire, when it is applied to wood, is not moved like a log, doing nothing, but truly the fire burns the wood: and just as a horse, when spurs are applied to it, it does not move like a post, for a horse truly walks: and yet who, unless he were insane, would command or persuade fire to burn, or a horse to walk? But fire and horse are not endowed with mind and reason: Thus no one commands or persuades a man to want to be happy or miserable: unless because he knows that a man endowed with mind and reason cannot not love happiness, and not hate misery, since for these there is no liberty of human choice. Precepts therefore and persuasions demonstrate that not only reason, but liberty also, exists in men.

Let the Church of GOD now judge whether or not modern Papists, however much they may twist themselves, are held guilty of the very Pelagianism itself: certainly, with Augustine as witness, Pelagius himself also left a place for divine grace entirely, saying: Grace helps the good purpose of each one: yet it does not instill a zeal for virtue into one who resists: nor does it inspire a desire for good into one who is unwilling: as can be seen in Augustine against the two letters of Pelagius, book 6. And just as Bellarmine, in the cited chapter 15, contends that the power of Free Will is remote and imperfect for performing works of piety: So Pelagius also tempered his discourse in such a way as to say that Man indeed has from Free Will a desire for Good, but an imperfect one. To whom, however, Augustine resisted most sharply even when he spoke thus: nay, the Church pronounced anathema, relying especially upon those oracles of the Scriptures which we produced above in great number for the confirmation of our Negative.

As regards the arguments of Bellarmine produced a little earlier, they are entirely straw, and wander off the track.

For first, as often as men are named in the Scriptures as συνεργοὶ, fellow-workers or coadjutors of GOD, the discourse is always about those already reborn, whose will has been so illuminated by the Holy Spirit that it now itself also works good: but not from some inherent natural power, as the Romanists imagine through a childish ἀγνοίαν ἐλέγχου, but from the indwelling Grace of the Holy Spirit: as was shown above.

The second argument fails by the sophistication of a childish begging of the question. For that which Bellarmine intends would follow if he had first given proof that in the powers of an unregenerate man it is as much placed to want to believe in Christ, to want to be converted from sins, to want to do good works for the sake of GOD, as it is not to want. The Jesuit therefore assumes as confessed that which is most of all placed in controversy: and thus he trifles sophistically.

The third argument is of the same futility. For those who believe are not therefore worthy of reward and praise as if they had both wanted and been able to believe from the proper powers of Free Will: but because they have not contumaciously resisted the working power of the Holy Spirit, nor refused to hear the Word. The Jesuit therefore commits the fallacy of non-cause as cause. Furthermore, the consequence from Reluctance to Assent is no more valid than it could be if someone were to conclude thus: Some blind man is able not to be reluctant, or not to resist contumaciously him who wishes to guide him as he turns from the way, and lead him onto a royal or military road. Therefore the blind man can perform this very thing from himself and his own powers. Where indeed even a boy would answer: with the privation already actually posited, the habit is actually excluded in one and the same subject: or, as the Schools of Logicians teach concerning privatively Opposites, Every privation indeed presupposes a habit: but with the habit removed, it is necessary that the privation be attributed to the Subject, especially in excellent degrees.

The fourth argument was refuted above, in the dissolution of the second argument of the Pelagians.

The last argument again institutes a collection from the nature and condition of those already converted to the powers or faculties of those not yet reborn. Where the consequence is most rightly denied. For that the reborn or converted have some diligence and industry for increasing and cultivating faith: that they have not from the natural powers of Free Will, but from the Grace of Conversion, and the perpetual motion of the indwelling Holy Spirit. Since unregenerate men are destitute of this grace, such a zeal or desire for faith, whether to be begun or to be increased, certainly does not fall upon them; for with the cause removed, the Effect is removed.

Besides those arguments, the Jesuit rises up with another argument, chapter 10, p. 905 A. Scripture, he says, teaches that we are helped in works of piety. But he is not to be called helped in the proper sense who does nothing, but he who labors in acting.

I answer, Pelagius once objected this very argument to Augustine: He who is helped, he says, acts and works something together with the one helping. The unregenerate will is helped by Grace. Therefore it contributes something from itself, and by its own natural powers, which it has from its first birth, it cooperates something toward Conversion. But D. Augustine answers most rightly in book 2 against Boniface, ch. 9. Subsequent grace indeed helps the good purpose of man: but even that would not be in man, unless grace preceded. Therefore the Holy Spirit performs and works both in man: 1. that he may want something good in spiritual matters: 2. that he may finally attain that very thing.

Then the passages from the Scriptures which the Jesuit produces from Ps. 27, 9. Be my helper: do not forsake me: Ps. 70, 1. O GOD, look to my help: O Lord, make haste to help me. Rom. 8, 26. The Spirit helps our infirmity: For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered. These, I say, and other passages of Scripture of that kind, do nothing at all for the present Controversy. For they each deal with the state of those already Reborn or Converted: from which the consequence to those not yet Reborn is not valid! as has already been shown several times. And the argument is no more valid than if I wished to argue: That blind man, who in Luke 18, 35 was restored to sight by Christ, sees: Therefore he also saw before the restoration. Where even a boy of ten years understands the fallacy of the Consequent. But also in the seventh place the Jesuit produces a new argument, one truly unworthy of a man, I do not say a theologian, but at least a literate person. For thus he says, in the place already cited above, letter D: The Holy Scriptures teach that a man called by God can fail to come. For since he can come through the grace of God, as the adversaries concede, if he can also resist grace and not come: without doubt he is convinced to have free will. Proverbs 1:24, 'I have called and you have refused'; Matthew 23:37, 'I wanted to gather your children, and you would not,' etc.; John 6:67, 'Do you also wish to go away?'; Acts 7:51, 'You always resist the Holy Spirit'; Revelation 3:20, 'I stand at the door and knock: if anyone opens to me, I will enter to him.' But this argument is clearly trivial. For first, it is a collection from the powers of free will toward evil, to establish the powers of the same will regarding good in spiritual matters. This method of arguing is childishly trivial, and through an unworthy loquacity, it takes for granted what is most strongly denied on our part, and has not yet been proven on their part. Scripture certainly testifies that man is by nature prone ONLY to evil. If only to evil, then certainly not to good in spiritual matters, by virtue of the exclusive particle 'only.' Furthermore, in the cited testimonies of Scripture, it is not shown what man can do by the natural powers of free will, but how just is the vengeance of God toward the stubborn despisers of His word, which they contumaciously neglected, and to the Holy Spirit, who was willing to work conversion, they stubbornly resisted. Therefore, a gross sophistry of ignoring the point at issue is committed. Finally, we repeat that logical axiom: when a habit is destroyed, a privation is posited in act; nor can a habit and a privation exist in one and the same subject, such as blindness and sight, or repugnance and assent, simultaneously and in the same respect.

But enough of the Pelagianism of the Romanists. There remain in this class of those who err the Synergists, who, soon after the death of the blessed Luther, with Victorinus Strigelius holding the first place in their ranks, pretended that man in spiritual matters is not entirely dead to good, but only seriously wounded and half-dead. And although free will is too weak to make a beginning, and to convert itself to God by its own powers, and to obey the law of God with the whole heart: yet if the Holy Spirit makes the beginning, and calls us through the Gospel, and offers us His grace, the remission of sins, and eternal salvation: then free will, by its own natural powers, can meet God, and in some way contribute at least something, however little and languidly, to its own conversion, assist it, cooperate, prepare and apply itself to grace, apprehend it, embrace it, yield to the Gospel, and indeed in the continuation and conservation of this work, by its own powers, together with the Holy Spirit, it can cooperate.

Our author, Philipp Melanchthon, was not entirely immune to that error, who, after the blessed Luther had already piously died, openly inserted and as it were encrusted that Synergism both into the changed Augsburg Confession and into his other writings:

- just as was demonstrated to the eye above in chapter 1 of the prolegomena. Which very inflection or depravation of the purer doctrine is perceived also in the changed Augsburg Confession, undertaken by Melanchthon by private daring and will for the sake of the Zwinglians. For in the fifth article of that Confession, Philipp says thus: 'When we console ourselves with the promise or the Gospel, and raise ourselves up by faith, at the same time the Holy Spirit is given to us. For the Holy Spirit is given and is effective through the Word and through the Sacraments, when we hear the Gospel, think about it, or handle the Sacraments, and console ourselves by faith, at the same time the Holy Spirit is effective.'

Thus in Article XVIII of the same changed Confession: 'Spiritual righteousness is effected in us when we are assisted by the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, we conceive the Holy Spirit when we assent to the Word of God, so that we may console ourselves by faith in terrors.'

Following in the footsteps of Philipp as a common teacher, many other theologians, both in this and in the neighboring Leipzig Academy, fought bitterly for Synergism: until finally, in the Weimar disputation in the year 1561, the impiety of this dogma was detected; but in the year 1580, through that golden treasure of our churches, the Book of Christian Concord, it was thoroughly crushed and trampled underfoot: while in the meantime the clandestine Philippists, who are accustomed to sting us secretly like scorpions with their poisonous tails, rage and gnash their teeth in vain; but they do not dare to come out into the public and engage with us in open warfare, by this very act betraying the vanity of their dogma too manifestly.

Latin:

Quanquam verò Robertus Bellarminus, & reliqui scriptores Pontificij recentiores hanc Scholasticorum Theologiam improbare & damnare videri volunt: pressiùs tamen, istorum scripta & disputationes expendentibus obscurum esse nequit, perpetuis Sophisticationibus & imposturis ipsos ludere, & Ecclesiæ Dei hac in parte veteratoriè imponere. Nam rem ipsam & ipsum quasi Pelagianismi nervum ipsos retinere ex Decretis Concilij Tridentini: ex scriptis Andradij Hispani: ex disputationibus Bellarmini & aliorum Jesuvitarum liquidò patet.

Nam quoad Concilium Tridentinum, etsi illud verbis satis speciosis Pelagianismi hæresin à se amoliri studet : dùm nimirùm scribit, Liberum arbitrium nullatenùs sufficere ad inchoandas & efficiendas actiones spirituales : sed Gratia Dei & divini auxilij necessitate, ita omnia acceptum esse ferenda, ut ne optare quidem & velle ullum perfectum bonum sine illo possimus: imò ne cogitare quicquam eorum, quæ ad sempiternam felicitatem ducunt, nisi divini Spiritus tu atq; virtute erigatur atque confirmetur:

Etsi deniq; Anathematis etiam fulmen vibrat in eos, quistatuunt, siue præveniente Spiritus Sancti inspiratione & adjutorio, Hominem posse pœnitere, credere, diligere, sperare sicut oportet: tamen quomodo hæc omnia velint intellecta, haud difficile est colligere, si explicationem consideremus,datam ab ijs,qui Concilij Tridentini defensionem susceperunt.
