Sic autem Andradius mentem Concilij explicat: Liberum Arbitrium sine inspiratione & auxilio Spiritus Sancti,non potest sanè efficere spirituales actiones: non quidem ideò,quod in Homine non renato mens & voluntas prorsus nullam habeat potentiam, nullas vires aut facultates, quæ ad inchoandas & efficiendas spirituales actiones necessariæ sunt: sed ideò tantùm,quia naturales illæ vires & facultates, licet nec deletæ nec extinctæ, adeò tamen peccatorum laqueis implicatæ sint,ut Homo non possit se propria virtute ab illis extricare. Et ut clariùs pateat, quis istorum sensus esse debeat, his similitudinibus rem explicat: quemadmodum qui ferreis compedibus devinctus est,habet insitam incedendi δύναμιν: sed non ipso actu prodire potest, nisi vincula rumpantur. Et sicut ægroto, cujus vires morbo fractæ,debilitatæ & attenuatæ sunt, à medico vires,quæ adhuc reliquæ sunt, licèt attenuatæ,confirmantur & roborantur:& siquiæ sunt amissæ,restituuntur: Et sicut avicula habet volandi facultatem; sed funiculo alligata volare non potest: quiq; hunc rumpit,non infert aviculæ novam volandi δύναμιν, Et quemadmodum Ignis est causa efficiens conflagrantis ligni, sed non solus, verùm cum DEO naturæ autore & patrono: Sic cùm Liberi nostri arbitrij motus,non magis à Dei gratia pendeat,quàm à divina virtute ligni exustio, quid est, quod Luberum arbitrium efficientis causæ dignitate & nomine spolies? Sentit proindè Concilium Tridentinum interprete Andradio, (ut rectè colligit Chemnitius part. 1. Exam. p. 118.b) in mente & voluntate hominis non renati, ex prima nativitate, in hac corruptione, naturaliter adhuc insitas esse vires aliquas, sive facultates qualéscunque ad res divinas, sive spirituales actiones sed illarum facultatum & virium motum & usum, per peccatum reprimi & retardari in non renatis: Gratiam vero Dei, & efficaciam Spiritus Sancti, non simpliciter efficere, sive operari in ijs, qui renascuntur, novam aliquam δύναμιν, sive facultatem inchoandi & bræstandi motus & actiones spirituales: quàm jam ante ex naturæ viribus non habuerint: sed tantùm vincula illa rumpere, ut facultas naturalis antea constricta & impedita, possit jam per gratiam excitata, vires suas in rebus spiritualibus exercere. Illas autem vires naturales, sicubi imbecilliores sunt, sentiunt adjuvari & confirmari per gratiam & auxilium Spiritus Sancti: Et ubi non sufficiunt, dicunt novum habitum infundi, qui respectum meriti afferat.

Neque tamen semper sub ejusmodi verborum obscuritatibus & involucris latitarunt Romanenses, quin interdum in lucem proruperunt, dilucidiùs mentem suam explicantes : quemadmodum idem Andradius in suis Orthodoxarum explicationem libris scribere non dubitavit: Ex lege Naturæ,& viribus Liberi Arbitrij multos fuisse justificatos: quin Notitiam DEI, quae ex Lege Naturae petitur, posse sufficere ad salutem: Siquidem haec fidem in CHRISTUM Crucifixum absconditè implicet: pag. 292. Imò in facultate Gentilium positum fuisse, ad notitiam istam DEI, quae ad salutem sufficere poterat, adjungere Cultum, pietatem, religionem erga DEUM, & DEUM, quem Summum Bonum esse intelligebant, totis animi viribus &c. pag. 293.

Jesuvvita Bellarminus lib. 6. de Grat. & Lib. arb. cap. secundo, multis quidem confirmare annititur. Non posse hominem sine speciali illustratione Dei, credere mysteria fidei: Sed mox in subsequentibus soricis instar, semetipsum prodit, se sub verborum integumentis, eandem cum Concilio Tridentino & Andradio tenere mentem atque sententiam. Nam cap. 3. p. 879. B. Objectiones quasdam refutaturus, inter reliqua sic scribit: Ad haec omnia facilè responderi poterit, si quis observet, nos cùm dicimus, sine auxilio speciali, non posse hominem credere articulos nostrae fidei, non intelligere, non posse credere ulto modo: sed non posse, ut oportet, ad hoc, ut sit actus fidei Catholicae, & initium Justificationis. Et cap. 9. proponit hanc quaestionem: An Homo post lapsum primi hominis, verè liberum arbitrium habeat in ijs rebus, quae pertinent ad salutem, ut quamvis nihil possit, sine auxilio gratiae: tamen per gratiam praevenientem excitatus, & à DEO adiutus, ita veleat operari, ut possit etiam non operari? Cujus Quaestionis Affirmativam contra Lutherum se tueri disertè scriptitat Jesuvvita. Hinc sequentes etiam flosculi ab ipso sunt proditi: cap. 10. B. & C. Si homines in actionibus pijs & salutaribus, propriè nihil agerent per Liberum Arbitrium: sed tantùm ducerentur & moverentur, ut mera instrumenta, non deberent appellari cooperatores & coadjutores DEI.

2. Si non esset homo Liberi arbitrij in operibus pietatis, sequeretur, non peccare eos, qui nolunt credere in Christum, aut nolunt converti à peccatis, aut nolunt propter DEUM bona opera facere.

3. Sequeretur, non esse laudandos, nec ullo praemio dignos eos, qui volunt credere, sperare, diligere, converti, propter DEUM quidvis arduum & acerbum pati.

4. Nullum haberent locum in ejusmodi rebus praecepta, consilia, cohortationes, reprehensiones, exempla, aliaq, id genus.

Tandem tolleretur è medio omnis diligentia, atq; industria in fide & pietate augenda & excolenda.

Quin cap. 15. hanc sententiam expressis verbis, Romanam Ecclesiam tueri scriptitat: Homo ante omnem Gratiam Liberum habet arbitrium, non solùm ad opera naturalia & moralia: sed etiam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia: propterea quòd per peccatum non tolli potuit Liberum arbitrium, quia peccatum laedere potuit naturalia, bona non tamen extinguere. Et observationem meretur, quòd, Jesuvvita ijsdem fermè similitudinibus mentem suam suorumque explicat, quibus Andradius. Nam cap. 10. pag. 904. lit. C. sic inter reliqua: Quemadmodum ignis, cùm applicatur ad ligna, non movetur instar trunci, nihil agentis, verò en mignis Comburit ligna: & quemadmodum equus, cum ei adhibentur calcaria, non movetur instar stipitis, verè enim equus ambulat: & tamen quis, nisi amens, imperaret vel suaderet igni, ut combureret, aut equo, ut ambularet? At ignis & equus non sunt mente & ratione præditi: Sic nemo imperat aut suadet homini, ut velit esse beatus aut miser: nisi quia novit, non posse hominem mente & ratione præditum, non amare beatitudinem, ac non odisse miseriam, cùm ad hæc arbitrii humani non sit ulla libertas. Præcepta igitur & suasiones, non solam rationem, sed libertatem etiam in hominibus esse demonstrant.

Judicet nunc Ecclesia DEI, an non moderni Pontificii, quantumvis etiam se torqueant, rei teneantur ipsissimi Pelagianismi: certè Augustino teste, ipse quoque Pelagius gratiæ divinæ locum omninò reliquit, dicens: Gratiam adjuvare bonum cujusque propositum: non tamen reluctanti studium virtutis immittere: neque invito inspirare boni cupiditatem: ut videre est apud Augustinum contra duas epistolas Pelagij lib. 6. Et quemadmodum Bellarminus citato cap. 15. contendit, Liberi arbitrij potentiam esse remotam & imperfectam ad opera pietatis facienda: Ita Pelagius quoque sermonem suum ita temperavit, ut diceret, habere quidem Hominem ex Libero Arbitrio cupiditatem Boni, sed imperfectam. Cui tamen Augustinus etiam sic loquenti acerrimè restitit: imò Ecclesia anathema dixit, illis potissimùm fretâ Scripturarum oraculis, quæ suprà pro confirmatione Negativæ nostræ, magno numero produximus.

Ad rationes Bellarmini, paulo antè productas quod attinet, sunt eæ prorsus stramineæ, & extra oleas vagantur.

Primùm enim, quoties in Scripturis Homines nominantur συνεργοὶ Cooperarii sive Coadjutores DEI, sermo semper est, de jam renatis, quorum voluntas per Spiritum sanctum ita est illustrata, ut jam ipsa quoque bonum operetur: sed non ex insita quadam vi naturali, uti per puerilem ἀγνοίαν ἐλέγχου, automant Romanenses: sed ex inhabitante Gratia Spiritus sancti: uti supra ostensum.

Secunda ratio fallit Sophisticatione puerilis petitionis Principii. Tùm enim sequeretur id, quod intendit Bellarminus, si probatum priùs dedisset, in Hominis non renati viribus, tam positum esse, velle credere in Christum, velle converti à peccatis, velle propter DEUM bona opera facere: quàm non velle. Sumit proindè pro confesso Jesuuvita id, quod vel maximè in controversia est positum: & sic Sophisticè nugatur.

Tertia ratio ejusdem est futilitatis. Neque enim ideò præmio & laude digni sunt, qui credunt, quasi ex propriis Liberi Arbitrii viribus, credere & voluerint & potuerint: sed quia operanti Spiritus sancti virtuti non contumaciter sunt reluctati, neque Verbum audire detrectarunt. Sophisma proindè non causæ ut causæ committit Jesuuvita. Deindè haud magis valet Consequentia, à Reluctatione ad Assensum, quàm valere potest, si quis ita colligat: Cæcus aliquis potest non reluctari, sive non contumaciter resistere illi, qui ipsum à via declinantem regere, & in regiam sive militarem viam vult perducere. Ergò Cæcus ex se & suis viribus potest hoc ipsum præstare. Ubi sanè vel puer aliquis responderet: positâ jam actu privatione, excluditur actu habitus in uno eodemque subjecto: vel, uti de privativè Oppositis Scholæ Logicorum tradunt, Omnis quidem privatio præsupponit habitum: sed detracto habitu, necesse est, Subjecto tribui privationem, in gradibus præsertim excellentibus.

Quarta ratio suprà est refutata, in dissolutione secundi argumenti Pelagianorum.

Postrema ratio rursus collectionem instituit, à natura & conditione jam conversorum ad vires sive facultates nondum renatorum. Ubi rectissimè negatur consequentia. Nam quod renati sive conversi habent aliquam diligentiam & industriam ad augendam & excolendam fidem: illud habent non ex viribus naturalibus Liberi Arbitrii, sed ex Gratia Conversionis, & perpetuo motu inhabitantis Spiritus sancti. Quâ gratiâ cùm destituantur Homines non renati, utique tale etiam studium sive desiderium fidei vel inchoandæ vel augendæ in ipsos non cadit; Sublatâ enim causa, tollitur Effectus.

Præter rationes istas alio etiam argumento insurgit Jesuuvita, cap. 10. p. 905 A. Scriptura, inquiens, docet, nos juvari in operibus pietatis. Non autem propriè juvari dicendus est, qui nihil agit, sed qui laborat in agendo.

Respondeo, Hoc ipsum argumentum olim objiciebat Pelagius Augustino: Qui, inquiens, adjuvatur, ipse una cùm adjuvante aliquid agit & operatur. Voluntas non renata adjuvatur à Gratia. Ergò ex se aliquid confert, & viribus suis naturalibus, quas habet ex prima nativitate, aliquid cooperatur ad Conversionem. Sed rectissimè respondet D. Augustinus lib. 2. contra Bonifacium c. 9. Hominis bonum propositum adjuvat quidem subsequens gratia: sed neque illud esset in Homine, nisi præcederet gratia. Utrumq; ergò præstat & operatur Spiritus sanctus in Homine: 1. ut velit aliquid bonum in Spiritualibus: 2. ut illud ipsum tandem assequatur.

Deindè loca ex Scripturis, quæ producit Jesuuvita ex Psal. 27, 9. Adjutor meus esto: ne derelinquas me: Psal. 70, 1. DEUS in adjutorium meum intende: Domine ad adjuvandum me festina. Rom. 8, 26. Spiritus adjuvat infirmitatem nostram: Nam quid oremus, sicut oportet, nescimus, sed ipse Spiritus postulat pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus. Hæc inquam & id genus alia Scripturarum loca, nihil quicquam ad præsentem Controversiam faciunt. Agunt enim singula de Renatorum jam sive Conversorum statu: à quo ad nondum Renatos non valet consequentia! uti jam aliquoties ostensum. Et haud magis valet argumentum, ac si argumentari vellem: Cæcus ille, qui Luc. 18, 35. visus à Christo est restitutus, videt: Ergo etiam ante restitutionem vidit. Ubi ἀλεονεξίαν Consequentis vel puer decem annorum intelligit. Sed & septimo loco novum producit argumentum Jesuita, Homine profectò non dico, Theologo, sed Literato saltem perquàm indignum. Sic enim ille, loco jam suprà citato, lit. D. Sacræ literæ docent, Hominem à Deo vocatum posse non venire. Nam cùm per gratiam DEI possit venire, ut Adversarii concedunt, si possit etiam Gratiæ resistere & non venire: sine dubio Liberi Arbitrii esse convincitur. Proverb. 1, 24. Vocavi & renuistis, Matth.23, 37. Volui congregare filios tuos, & noluisti &c. Johan. 6, 67. Vultis & vos abire? Actor. 7, 51. Vos semper Spiritui sancto resistitis. Apocalyp. 3, 20. Ego sto ad ostium & pulso: si quis aperuerit mihi, intraboad eum. Sed nugatorium planè est hoc argumentum. Primùm enim sit collectio à viribus Liberi arbitrii ad Malum; ad astruendas ejusdem arbitrii vires, quoad Bonum in spiritualibus. Quæ argumentandi ratio pueriliter nugatur, & per indignam ἀδολεσχίαν, pro confesso sumit, quod ex nostra parte vel maximè negatur: ex ipsorum verò parte nondùm probatum est. Scriptura certè testatur, Hominem naturâ pronum esse TANTUM ad malum. Si tantùm ad malum: utique non ad Bonum in spiritualibus: vi particulæ Exclusivæ Tantùm. Deindè in citatis Scripturarum testimoniis non ostenditur, quid Homo naturalibus Liberi Arbitrii viribus possit: Sed quàm justa sit DEI vindicta, erga præfractos contemtores verbi sui: quod contumaciter neglexerunt: & Spiritui sancto volenti conversionem operari, pertinaciter restiterunt. Committitur proindè crassa Sophisticatio Ignorationis Elenchi. Tandem repetimus illud Logicum axioma: Destructo habitu, ponitur actu privatio: neque in uno eodemq; subjecto, habitus & privatio: ut Cæcitas & visus: vel repugnantia & assensus simul & secundum idem locum obtinere possunt.

Sed de Romanensium Pelagianismo plus satis: Supersunt in classe hac errantium Synergistæ, qui mox post obitum B. Lutheri, primas in ipsorum agmine tenente Victorino Strigelio, fingebant, Hominem in rebus Spiritualibus non prorsus ad bonum esse mortuum: sed tantùm graviter vulneratum & semimortuum esse. Et quamvis Liberum Arbitrium infirmius sit, quàm ut initium facere, & seipsum proprijs viribus ad DEUM convertere, & legi DEI toto corde obedire possit: tamen si Spiritus sanctus initium faciat, & nos per Evangelium vocet, gratiam suam, Remissionem peccatorum & æternam salutem nobis offerat: tunc Liberum Arbitrium proprijs suis naturalibus viribus DEO occurrere, & aliquo modo aliquid saltem, etsi parùm & languidè, ad conversionem suam conferre, eam adjuvare, cooperari, sese ad gratiam præparare & applicare, eam apprehendere, amplecti, Evangelio redere, & quidem in continuatione & conservatione hujus operis, proprijs suis viribus, unà cum Spiritu sancto cooperari posse.

Ab isto errore haud immunis fuit Autor noster, Philippus Melanchthon, qui B. Luthero jam piè defuncto, Synergismum istum tum mutatæ Confessioni Augustanæ, tum reliquis suis scriptis palàm inseruit & quasi incrustavit:

- quemadmodum supra cap. 1. προλεγομένων, ad - oculum fuit demonstratum. Quæ ipsa purioris - doctrinæ sive inflexio sive depravatio, perspici- - tur etiam in mutata Confessione Augustana, - privato ausu ac arbitrio, à Melanchthone in - gratiam Zwinglianorum suscepta. Nam Arti- - culo quinto illius Confessionis sic Philippus: - Cùm nos consolamur promissione seu Evangelio, & - erigerimus nos fide, simul nobis datur Spiritus san- - ctus. Nam Spiritus sanctus datur & est efficax - per Verbum & per Sacramenta, cùm Evange- - lium audimus, cogitamus, aut Sacramenta tra- - ctamus, & fide nos consolamur, simul est efficax - Spiritus sanctus.

Sic Articulo XVIII. ejusdem mutatæ Confessionis: Efficitur Spiritualis Justitia in nobis, cùm adjuvamur à Spiritu sancto. Porrò Spiritum sanctum concipimus, cùm Verbo DEI afsentimur, ut nos fide in terroribus consolemur.

Vestigiis Philippi tanquàm communis præceptoris insistentes plures alii Theologi, tùm in hac, tùm vicina Lipsiensi Academia, pro Synergismo acriter pugnarunt: donec tandem in disputatione Vinariensi, Anno 61. supra sesquimillefimum, impietas hujus dogmatis detecta: Anno verò 80. per aureum illud Ecclesiarum nostrarum κειμήλιον, Librum Christianæ Concordiæ, penitùs protrita & conculcata est: frustrà interim frementibus & frendentibus clanculariis Philippistis, qui Scorpionum more venenatis suis aculeis clàm nos pungere solent: in publicum verò prodire, & aperto Marte nobiscum congredi non audent: vel hoc pacto dogmatis sui vanitatem nimis manifestè prodentes.


### Chapter II. Concerning the other State of Man, which is that of Corruption…: Of the third State of Man, which is of the Reborn or Converted

The state of the regenerate or converted is either of this life or of the other future age. Regarding the state of the regenerate in this life, since the Holy Spirit by His power, through the Word of the Gospel, has illuminated the mind of man with the knowledge of God, and has also as it were purged and sanctified the heart and will: certainly, by their own impulse, the individual and universal actions of man now progress for the better: so that they now arise from other causes, are done in another way, and are finally directed to other ends, namely to the glory of God and the edification both of himself and of his neighbor.

Pertinent here are these illustrious testimonies of Scripture, Matt. 12, 35. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things: And Matt. 7, 17. Every good tree brings forth good fruit: neither can a good tree bring forth evil fruit.

The reason for the affirmative is: Because, as is the cause, so is the effect: But the cause is good: Therefore the effect must also be such. Now the cause is 1. The Word of GOD, which shows what works please God, and which do not. 2. The will now restored, assenting to the Word of GOD: the third and chief is the Holy Spirit, who in the heart of the reborn man cannot be languid or idle, but continually instigates, moves, and impels him to perform good deeds and flee evil ones: according to that John 14, 26. The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and will suggest all things to you: and chap. 16, 13. The Holy Spirit will lead you into all truth. And Rom. 8, 14. Those who are led by the Spirit of GOD, these are the sons of God. and chap. 8, 5. Those who are spiritual, care for spiritual things. and Galat. 5, 25. If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.

These things being established, it is evident first from this, what kind of Will should be granted to a man already reborn, namely, Liberated rather than Free. For however much the will of man has begun to be repaired by the Holy Spirit: because it must nevertheless be engaged in a perpetual struggle of flesh and Spirit: and cannot yet in this life fully aspire to that integrity and perfection in which the first man was created: But is only half-restored, so that, always subject to the remnants of sins, he must work out his salvation with fear and trembling: the will of the reborn man will certainly be more correctly called Liberated than Free. And of this will sounds that of the Apostle, 2 Cor. 3, 17. where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. Thence it is evident from this, that in this third state the Reborn Man, even in external actions, has a far greater and more perfect Will than a man not yet reborn. For since the reborn man, aided by the Holy Spirit and informed by the Word of GOD, overcomes those difficulties and impediments of the flesh which can abstract the will even from moral Good, much more correctly and happily than one who is destitute of these aids. For first, such a Reborn person constitutes the Word of GOD as the norm and rule of all his actions: then he rests uniquely in the Providence of GOD, and humbly and patiently subjects the events and successes of all actions to the will of GOD: according to that of James 4, 15. If the Lord wills, if we live, we will do this and that. 1 Cor. 10, 31. Coloss. 3, 17. Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do all to the glory of God.

In the genus of Spiritual actions, the restoration of powers, which has been effected through the Holy Spirit, extends so far in the reborn that the Apostle proclaims of himself that he can do all things in the power of Christ, by whom he is strengthened, Philip. 4, 13. For the acting cause in the reborn man is the Holy Spirit himself, who effects both the Willing and the performing, so that now the man himself also works out his own salvation, from that power which the Holy Spirit bestows upon him, Phil. 2, 13. Which liberty and restoration itself, however, is imperfect in this life. For the infirmities of nature, diseases, afflictions, remnants of sin: the snares and diabolical temptations do not allow us to aspire to perfect liberty until, having finished the warfare of this life, we are transferred to that state in which, as Augustine speaks, there will be liberty without Servitude, security without fear: joy without weeping: glory without end, consolation without satiety. For in the future fatherland, as Augustine again has it, in Enchirid. chap. 105. Since we are to have supreme happiness, no kind of liberty can be desired there, unless one wishes to call Liberty the ability to sin and to fall away from God: But because this is not Liberty, but the saddest Servitude: therefore we hope that we will be most free in the fatherland: Which hope, that CHRIST the Savior may at last fulfill in us by his glorious coming; let us each pray with most ardent vows: AMEN.

Latin:

STatus Renatorum sive Conversorum vel est hujus vitæ: vel alterius futuri seculi. Quoad statum renatorum in hac vita, quoniam Spiritus sanctus virtute sua, per Verbum Evangelii, mentem Hominis agnitione DEI illuminavit: cor quoque & voluntatem quasi repurgavit, & sanctificavit: utique sua sponte jam singulæ & universæ actiones hominis in melius proficiunt: Ita ut ex aliis causis jam oriantur: alio modo fiant: ad alios denique fines dirigantur, nempè ad gloriam DEI & ædificationem tùm sui ipsius, tùm proximi.

Pertinent huc illustria isthæc Scripturæ testimonia, Matth. 12, 35. Bonus homo de bono thesauro cordis sui profert bona: Et Matth. 7, 17. Omnis arbor bona, fructus bonos profert: nec potest arbor bona malos fructus ferre.

Ratio affirmati est: Quia, qualis causa, talis effectus: Atqui causa bona: Ergo Effectus quoq; talis sit necesse est. Causa autem est 1. Verbum DEI, quod monstrat, quæ opera Deo placeant, quæ non. 2. Voluntas jam restituta, assentiens Verbo DEI: tertia & præcipua est Spiritus sanctus, qui in corde hominis renati, languidus aut otiosus esse nequit, sed subinde ad bona peragenda, & mala fugienda, ipsum instigat, movet, & impellit: secundum illud Joh. 14, 26. Paracletus Spiritus sanctus, quem Pater mittet in nomine meo, ille vos docebit omnia, & suggeret vobis omnia: & cap. 16, 13. Spiritus sanctus ducet vos in omnem veritatem. Et Rom. 8, 14. Qui Spiritu DEI aguntur, hi sunt filij Dei. & cap. 8, 5. Qui spirituales sunt, spiritualia curant. & Galat. 5, 25. Si Spiritu vivimus, Spiritu etiam incedamus.

Quibus constitutis patet primùm indè, quale Arbitrium Homini jam renato sit concedendum, nempè Liberatum magis, quàm Liberum. Nam quantumvis voluntas Hominis per Spiritum sanctum jam reparari cœpta est: quia tamen sub perpetuà lucta carnis & Spiritus versari necesse habet: & ad illam integritatem atque perfectionem, in quá primùs Homo erat conditus, nondum hac in vita, plenè adspirare potest: Sed semiplenè tantùm restauratur, ita ut peccatorum reliquiis semper obnoxia, cum timore ab tremore salutem operari debeat: utique rectiùs Liberatum, quàm Liberum nominabitur Hominis renati arbitrium. Et de hoc arbitrio sonat illud Apostoli, 2. Cor. 3, 17. ubi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas. Deindè patet hinc, in tertio hoc statu Hominem Renatum, in externis etiam actionibus, longè majus & perfectius habere Arbitrium, quàm Hominem nondùm renatum. Siquidem à Spiritu sancto adjutus homo renatus, & Verbo DEI informatus, difficultates, & impedimenta illa carnis, quæ à Bono etiam morali voluntatem abstrahere possunt, multò rectiùs & fæliciùs superat, quàm qui istis auxiliis destituitur. Nam primùm talis Renatus omnium suarum actionum normam ac regulam constituit Verbum DEI: deindè in Providentia DEI unicè acquiescit, omniumque actionum eventus ac successus DEI voluntati humiliter & patienter subjicit: secundùm illud Jacobi 4, 15. Si Dominus voluerit, si vixerimus, faciemus hoc & illud. 1. Cor. 10, 31. Coloss. 3, 17. Sive editis sive bibitis, sive aliud quid facitis, omnia ad gloriam Dei facite.

In genere actionum Spiritualium, eò se usque in renatis extendit virium restauratio, quæ per Spiritum sanctum est facta, ut Apostolus de se prædicet, se posse omnia in virtute Christi, à quo roboretur Philip. 4, 13. Causa enim agens in homine renato, est ipse Spiritus sanctus, qui efficit & Velle & perficere, ut jam ipse quoque homo operetur suam salutem, ex ea virtute, quam Spiritus sanctus ipsi largitur, Phil. 2, 13. Quæ ipsa tamen libertas & restauratio, hac in vita, est imperfecta. Nam infirmitates naturæ, morbi, afflictiones, peccati reliquiæ: insidiæ & tentationes diabolicæ, ad perfectam libertatem adspirare nos non priùs patiuntur, quàm militiâ vitæ hujus defuncti, ad eum statum transferamur, in quo, uti Augustinus loquitur, sine Servitute erit libertas, sine metu securitas: sine fletu gaudium: sine fine gloria, sine satietate solatium. In futura enim patria, uti rursus Augustinus habet, in Enchirid. cap. 105. Cum summam habituri simus fœlicitatem, nullum ibi genus libertatis desiderari potest, nisi quis Libertatem dicere velit, posse peccare & à Deo deficere: Sed quia hæc non est Libertas, sed tristissima Servitus: ideò nos in patria fore liberrimos speramus: Quam spem ut glorioso suo adventu vel tandem in nobis impleat, CHRISTVS Servator; votis ardentissimis, precemur singuli: AMEN.


## 10 On the Image of GOD and the Original Justice of the First Man

This article, which is about Sin, follows the Article on Free Will in the most convenient order. For no one will ever have judged correctly concerning the powers of Free Will, unless he has known and perceived what and what kind of corruption of human powers, both superior and inferior, followed the most sad fall of the protoplasts. But this knowledge can be drawn and borrowed only from the Schools of Theologians, and indeed from that doctrine which is handed down concerning Original sin. For although Philosophy also, and human Reason, hands down some knowledge concerning sin: insofar as it argues quite cleverly from the Light of Nature concerning vices and virtues, concerning the distinction between honorable and base things, concerning inordinate coarser affections, concerning civil punishments, concerning the causes and remedies of vices, and concerning other questions related to that kind: It is nevertheless certain that all that science of Reason, however specious, is confused, mutilated, and imperfect. For it is ignorant of the true efficient cause of sin; it is ignorant of its proper object; it is ignorant of the fountain of vices; it is ignorant of the Effect and proper End of sin; finally, it is ignorant of what the Church of GOD hands down and explains from the Sacred Scriptures concerning internal concupiscence and depraved affections, even those not breaking out into act. Hence in the writings of even the wisest Philosophers, such ἀπεράματα occur, which diametrically conflict with the doctrine of the Church: such as that which Aristotle argues, that neither virtues nor vices τῇ φύσει ἐγγίνεσθαι: that which Hortensius asserts in Cicero: That calamities in human life draw their Origin from nowhere else than from the supreme Deity: and that we are for no other end, than that we were born for the sake of paying penalties: nay, that Cicero himself in the 3rd book of the Tusculans maintains that these are born good by origin, but afterwards become evil through instruction and conversation: There are, he says, seeds of virtues implanted in our natures, which, if they were allowed to grow, nature itself would lead us to a blessed life. But now, as soon as we are brought into the light and received, we are immediately involved in every depravity and in the highest perversity of opinions, so that we seem to have sucked in error almost with our nurse's milk. But when we are returned to our parents or handed over to teachers, we are then imbued with such various errors that truth yields to vanity, and Nature itself yields to confirmed opinion, etc.

But what, I ask, could those philosophers have known about this matter, who neither knew nor read this: Through one man sin entered into the world: as Augustine once wittily replied to Julian, who was objecting the opinions of the philosophers concerning the dignity of human nature. Therefore, our most sacred theological science alone provides a solid knowledge of sin, inasmuch as it instructs and informs us most correctly concerning the Origin, Form, Matter, Object, Subject, Parts, and finally the most sorrowful Effects of this Evil. This knowledge is indeed so necessary that its ignorance is joined with the destruction of the entire Christian religion: and for this very reason our Author, Philipp Melanchthon, also instituted and completed a most accurate treatment (ἐργασίαν) of this Article. It consists, indeed, if it is recalled to the anvil of a more accurate analysis, of three parts primarily: namely, prolegomena: Definition: and Division of sin. The Philippean prolegomena are directed solely to the commendation of this Article. For by three degrees of opposition he shows that philosophy cannot rise to a solid and true knowledge of sin. For first, Reason persuades itself that Nature is entirely good: and that the source of sin is to be sought only in the disturbance of the affections. Then it maintains that only external vicious actions are to be held in the census and number of sins: understanding nothing meanwhile of internal depraved thoughts and concupiscences. Finally, it does not recognize any punishments of sin other than external and bodily calamities and miseries.

Moreover, the proper doctrine of the Church constitutes the source of sin as the very horrible depravity of human nature: then it recalls to the class of sin internal depraved concupiscence, nay, each and every work which is destitute of faith, and thus also those which deserve praise and rewards in the schools of the philosophers. Finally, it constitutes the end and effect of sin as the guilt of divine wrath and eternal damnation, of which the philosophers knew so little that they rather laughed at this part of Christian doctrine and turned it into fables: as is clearly evident from the writings of Plato and the poets.

The second part of the Philippean treatment is completed by the Definition of Original Sin, which, however, soon resolved into its parts, presents to us a sufficiently perfect exposition (diexodon) of all those things which concerning

The Cause, Nature, Subject, Form, Matter, End, Effect of sin and related affections, which are usually disputed, as will be more clearly evident from our treatment.

The third and final part consists of the division of sin into its species, which can be constituted as various and manifold according to different respects: yet so that it institutes the greatest care and disquisition concerning Mortal and Venial sin, as the principal species of Actual sins. Although we could insist on the footsteps of Philipp and make an approach with a straight foot to the exposition of the Article on Sin: yet the evidence of those controversies moves us, which were not only moved long ago by the Scholastics concerning the Image of God and the Original Justice of the first man: but are even now agitated today by the Jesuit race with great effort: so that we may deflect somewhat from the Philippean treatment and it may please us to assign a peculiar Place or Article to the disputation concerning the Image of God and Original Justice. It is added that the Article on sin can never be fully and dexterously explained or understood unless we are correctly established concerning the Image of God in the first man. What? That after the death of our Author, a new apple of contention was clearly thrown onto the stage of the Church, concerning the Image of God: which also shook and disturbed the Church quite gravely. We divide this entire controversy into two chapters, the former of which will explain the Thesis: the latter the Antithesis.

Latin:

ARticulum de Libero Arbitrio Ordine Convenientissimo excipit iste, qui est de Peccato. Neque enim de viribus Liberi Arbitrii rectè judicaverit unquam, nisi qui cognitum perspectumque habuerit, quæ & qualis corruptio virium humanarum, tàm superiorum, quàm inferiorum tristissimum protoplastorum lapsum infecuta sit. Hanc verò notitiam non nisi ex Scholis Theologorum, & quidem ex ea doctrinâ, quæ de peccato Originis traditur, haurire & mutuari licet. Etsi enim Philosophia quoque, & Ratio humana aliquam tradit de peccato notitiam: quatenùs de vitiis & virtutibus, de discrimine honestorum & turpium, de inordinatis crassioribus affectibus, de pœnis civilibus, de causis & remediis vitiorum, deque id genus quæstionibus cognatis aliis, ex Lumine Naturæ satis argutè disputat: Constat tamen universam istam, quantumvis speciosam Rationis scientiam esse confusam, mutilam, imperfectam. Ignorat enim eam veram peccati caussam efficientem; ignorat proprium ejus objectum: ignorat vitiorum fontem: ignorat peccati Effectum, Finemque proprium: ignorat denique quæ de interna concupiscentia, pravisquè affectibus, in actum etiam non erumpentibus, Ecclesia DEI ex Scripturis Sacris tradit & explicat. Hinc in sapientissimorum etiam Philosophorum scriptis, ejusmodi occurrunt ἀπεράματα, quæ cum doctrina Ecclesiæ è diametro pugnant: ut quòd Aristoteles disputat, nequè virtutes, neque vitia τῇ φύσει ἐγγίνεσθαι: quòd Hortensius apud Ciceronem asserit: Calamitates in vita humana, non aliundè, quàm à supremo Numine trahere Originem: nosque non alio fine, quàm pœnarum luendarum causa natos esse: imò quòd Cicero ipse 3. Tusculanarum statuit, hos Origine bonos nasci, sed pòstmodùm informatione & conversatione malos fieri: Sunt, inquiens, ingenijs nostris semina insita virtutum, quæ si adolescere liceret, ipsa nos ad beatam vitam natura perduceret. Nunc autem simul atq; editi sumus in lucem & suscepti, in omni continuò pravitate, & in summa opinionum perversitate versamur, ut penè cum lacte nutricis errorem suxisse videamur. Cùm verò parentibus redditi, vel magistris traditi sumus, tùm ita varijs imbuimur erroribus, ut vanitati veritas, & opinioni confirmata Natura ipsa cedat, &c.

Sed quid obsecro Philosophi illi hac de re sapere potuissent, qui nec sciverunt, nec legerunt illud: Per unum hominem peccatum intravit in mundum: uti argutè aliquando respondit Augustinus Juliano, Philosophorum sententias de dignitate Naturæ humanæ objectanti. Proindè solidam peccati noticiam, sola sacratissima nostra scientia Theologica tradit, quippè quæ de Origine, Forma, Materia, Objecto, Subjecto, Partibus, Effectis denique tristissimis Mali hujus, rectissimè nos instruit & informat. Est verò notitia isthæc tàm necessaria, ut ejus ignorantia, cum religionis Christianæ universæ interitu sit conjuncta: & vel hanc ipsam ob causam Autor etiam noster, Philippus Melanchthon, accuratissimam Articuli hujus ἐργασίαν instituerit, & expediverit. Constat verò ea, si sub accuratioris ἀναλύσεως incudem revocetur, tribus potissimùm partibus: nempè προλεγομένοις: Definitione: & Divisione peccati. προλεγόμενα Philippéa ad commendationem Articuli hujus unicè sunt directa. Tribus enim oppositionum gradibus ostendit, Philosophiam ad solidam & veram peccati Notitiam assurgere non posse. Primùm enim Ratio sibi persuadet, Naturam omninò bonam esse: & fontem peccati tantùm in perturbatione affectuum quærendum esse. Deinde statuit, in peccati censu numeroque habendas esse tantùm externas vitiosas actiones: de internis interim pravis cogitationibus & cocupiscentiis, nihil intelligens. Tandem peccati pœnas non agnoscit alias, quàm externas & corporales calamitates ac miserias.

Cæterùm doctrina Ecclesiæ propria Fontem peccati constituit ipsam horrendam Naturæ humanæ depravationem: deindè internam pravam concupiscentiam, imò singula atque universa opera, quæ fide destituuntur, atque adeò ea quoque, quæ in Philosophorum Scholis laudem & præmia merentur, sub peccati classem revocat. Tandem Finem & Effectum peccati constituit reatum iræ divinæ & æternæ damnationis, de quo usque adeò nihil noverunt Philosophi, ut hanc partem doctrinæ Christianæ potiùs riferint, & in fabulas converterint: uti ex Platonis & Poetarum scriptis liquidò constat.

Altera pars Tractationis Philippéæ absolvitur Definitione Peccati originalis, quæ tamen mox in suas partes resoluta, satis perfectam nobis exhibet diexodon omnium eorum, quæ de

Peccati Causa, Natura, Subjecto, Forma, Materia, Fine, Effectu & cognatis affectionibus, quæri disputativè solent, uti ex Tractatione nostra patebit dilucidiùs.

Tertia & postrema pars divisione constat Peccati in suas species, quæ pro diversis respectibus variæ ac multiplices constitui possunt: ita tamen ut de peccato Mortali & Veniali, tanquàm præcipuis peccatorum Actualium speciebus, potissimam curam ac disquisitionem instituat. Quanquàm verò vestigiis Philippi insistere possemus, & recto pede ad diexodon Articuli de Peccato accessum facere: movet tamen nos earum controversiarum evidentia, quæ de Imagine DEI & Justitia Originali primi Hominis, non modò jam olim à Scholasticis motæ fuerunt: sed etiamnùm hodie à gente Jesuwitica magno conatu agitantur: ut à Tractatione Philippea nonnihil deflectamus, & peculiarem Locum sive Articulum disputationi de Imagine DEI & Justitia Originali assignare libeat. Accedit, quod Articulus de peccato nunquam plenè ac dextrè vel explicari vel intelligi potest, nisi de Imagine DEI in primo Homine nobis rectè constiterit. Quid? quòd post obitum Autoris nostri, novum planè contentionis pomum, in proscenium Ecclesiæ projectum fuit, de Imagine DEI: quod Ecclesiam etiam satis graviter concussit & turbavit. Totam autem istam controversiam in duo capita dispescimus, quorum prius Thesin: posterius Ἀντίθεσιν expediet.


### Chapter I. Proposing the orthodox doctrine concerning the Image of God, or the Original Justice of the first parents

Proposing the orthodox doctrine concerning the Image of God, or the Original Justice of our first parents.

Our author most rightly determines that Original Sin cannot be defined unless it is first established what the Image of God is, and Original Justice, according to which the first man was created. Thus, however, he himself defines it. Original Justice was the acceptance of the human race before God, and in the very nature of men, a Light in the mind, by which he could firmly assent to the Word of God, and a conversion of the will to God, and obedience of the heart, congruent with the judgment of the Law of God, which was implanted in the mind. Our author confirms this definition with a twofold testimony of Scripture: one from the Old Testament, Gen. 1, 26: Let us make man in our image and likeness; the other from the New Testament, Eph. 4, 24, where the Apostle teaches that the Image of God is a mind acknowledging God, and a free will, just and congruent with the Law of God. For the Apostle calls true holiness all virtues, referred with a true heart to this end, that obedience might be rendered to God, that God might be loved and celebrated. Thus far our author; whose opinion we certainly approve in all respects.

This Philippean thesis can, however, scarcely be illustrated more correctly than from that very restoration of the divine image which the Holy Spirit works in believers in this life. Thus, moreover, the Apostle speaks on this matter, 2 Cor. 3:18: We are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory. And Col. 3:10: We are being renewed into the image of him who created us: and indeed, as the Apostle explains in Eph. 4:24, in righteousness and holiness of truth. There was, therefore, in that glory and Original Justice, first (as our author speaks) the acceptance and paternal good pleasure of GOD, for conferring upon man not only any goods of this visible world, but also the blessed immortality of heavenly life. Then, integrity and uprightness not only of the senses of the body, but also the most perfect integrity of the powers of the mind, joined with the greatest immunity and freedom from every evil. This Justice is called Original, moreover, because if our first parents had persisted in this integrity, all virtues whatsoever would have had their origin from it as from a fountain, and it would have been ours from Adam onwards by hereditary propagation. Now, however, since the first man by his own will turned himself away from GOD, and lost this Justice both for himself and for all his posterity, a most sad guilt certainly succeeded the former part, dragging with it the ruin of eternal damnation: but to the latter part, namely integrity, there succeeded corruption from sin, which, besides the lack of that Original Justice, introduced darkness in the mind instead of light, depravity in the will instead of uprightness, and contumacy in the remaining members instead of obedience. Concerning which most sad permutation, Solomon speaks briefly indeed, but quite shrewdly, in Ecclesiastes chapter 7:30. This only have I found, that God made man upright: and he himself has mixed himself with infinite inventions. This part of Christian doctrine remained sufficiently uncorrupted in the ancient Church of the Fathers, until at length the Pelagian heresy provided an opening and occasion for various disputes; which in the progress of time, and indeed in the Pontifical kingdom, now holding dominion in the Church of GOD, so grew into a nerve that not even to this day does the Roman Church cherish any purity regarding this Article, as the second chapter will now show more fully.

Latin:

Orthodoxam proponens doctrinam, de Imagine Dei, sive Justitia Originali primorum parentum.

REctissimè statuit Autor noster, Peccatum Originis definiri non posse, nisi prius constet, quid sit Imago DEI, & Justitia Originalis, ad quàm primus Homo erat conditus. Sic autem eam ipse definit. Justitia Originalis fuit acceptatio humani generis còram Deo, & in ipsa natura hominum Lux in mente, quâ firmiter assentiri Verbo Dei poterat, & Conversio voluntatis ad DEUM, & obedientia cordis, congruens cum Judicio Legis DEI, quæ menti insita erat. Cõfirmat definitionem hanc Autor noster gemino Scripturæ testimonio: uno ex Veteri Testamento Gen. 1, 26. Faciamus Hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram: Altero ex novo Testamento, Ephes. 4, 24. ubi Apostolus docet, Imaginem DEI esse mentem agnoscentem Deum, & Voluntatem liberam, justam & congruentem cum Lege DEI. Veram enim sanctitatem vocat Apostolus omnes virtutes, vero corde relatas ad hunc finem, ut DEO obedientia præstaretur, ut DEUS diligeretur & celebraretur. Hactenus Autor noster; cujus sanè sententiam per omnia approbamus.

Potest autem Thesis haec Philippea vix rectiùs illustrari, quàm ex ea ipsa imaginis divinae instaurtione, quam Spiritus sanctus in credentibus hac in vita operatur. Sic autem hac de re Apostolus, 2. Cor. 3, 18. Renotamur ad eandem imaginem de Gloria in gloriam. Et Coloss. 3, 10. Renovamur ad imaginem ejus, qui creavit nos: & quidem uti Ephes. 4, 24. explicat Apostolus, in justitia & sanctitate veritatis. Fuit pròindè in illa gloria & Justitia Originali primùm (uti Autor noster loquitur) acceptatio & beneplacitum DEI paternum, ad conferenda Homini non tantùm Bona quaelibet Mundi hujus visibilis: sed & beatam coelestis vitae immortalitatem. Deindè integritas & rectitudo non sensuum tantùm corporis, sed & Virium animi perfectissima, conjuncta cum immunitate & libertate ab omni malo maxima. Dicitur autem Justitia haec ideò Originalis, quia si primi parentes in integritate hac perstitissent, omnes omninò virtutes, ex éa tanquam ex fonte Originem habuissent, & nobis ab Adamo usque, per propagationem haereditaria fuiffet. Jam verò cum primus Homo propria voluntate se à DEO averterit, & Justitiam hanc tùm sibi, tùm posteritati universae perdiderit: utique priori parti successit reatus tristissimus, damnationis aeternae cladem secum trahens: Posteriori autem parti, nempè integritati successit, ex peccato corruptio, quae praeter carentiam Justitiae illius Originalis, pro luce, tenebras in mente: pro rectitudine, pravitatem in voluntate, pro obedientia contumaciam in reliquis membris induxit. Qua de tristissima permutatione breviter quidem, sed satis argutè Salomon in Ecclesiaste cap. 7, 30. Solummodo hoc inveni, quod fecerit Deus hominem rectum: & ipse se infinitis miscuerit adinventionibus. Mansit pars haec doctrinae Christianae incorrupta satis in antiqua Patrum Ecclesia: donec tandem Pelagiana haeresis, variis disputationibus ansam & occasionem praebuit: quae progressu temporis, & quidem regno Pontificio, jam in Ecclesia DEI dominatum obtinente, ita in neryum cruperunt, ut neque in hunc usque diem Romana Ecclesia, puritatis aliquid circa Articulum istum foveat: uti caput secundum fusiùs nunc ostendet.


### Chapter II. Anthesis

Antithesis.

To this doctrine of ours concerning the Image of God, two main hosts of enemies oppose themselves: one of which is that of the Pontificians, both ancient and modern; the other, however, is that of the Flacians. As for the Pontificians, the Scholastic Doctors initially maintained that human nature was so created in its very integrity that, because it consisted of diverse parts that by no means agreed among themselves, there followed upon it incitements and, as it were, itches—that is, such impulses and agitations that the flesh, when it desires what is pleasing and pleasant to itself, resists against the Spirit and is turned away from the prescription of Reason. To those pure or mere natural things, however, they claimed that Original Justice had been added as a supernatural gift, which would compress, restrain, and coerce the lasciviousness and affections of the flesh, and keep the flesh and the lower faculties of man in their duty. Wherefore, on the contrary, they taught that Original Sin is only a bare privation of Original Justice or of that supernatural gift, which no depravation in the mind and will followed; but that, however much Original Justice or the supernatural gift was lost, the natural things in man remained intact. Hence they contended that Original Sin inheres only in the flesh, and is propagated only through the flesh, as a morbid quality of the flesh; but that the higher part of Reason is immune from all corruption and is intact; and therefore that that depravity, whose subject is the flesh, draws and inclines the will toward lower things—that is, toward carnal and animal things—and causes Reason to err.

The Jesuitical doctrine is in no way averse to this theology of the Scholastics, as is evident from the disputation of Bellarmine, which he wove together in a single book, to which he gave the title, On the Grace of the First Man. In it, therefore, he brought forth the three following errors concerning the Image of God, which are most worthy of more accurate investigation. The first is as follows: The Image of God in Adam was the very substance of the rational soul, or the very nature of the three faculties of the rational soul, memory, intelligence, and will: but the Likeness of God, to which Adam was created, was something far other and different, namely, the conformity of man with God according to all virtues. P. Ramus was not far from this error either, writing thus in book 1 on Faith, chapter 5, page 21: God created man in his own image, that is, possessed of a rational soul.

II. Error. The Image of God was neither lost through the fall of the first man, nor made worse in any part of itself, but remained the same, and is still in all men.

III. Error. The nature of Adam considered in itself, in pure, as they call them, naturals, before the fall, was created with a certain disease and languor, namely, with a headlong inclination to vices, and the rebellion of the lower powers against the higher: nor were the pure naturals in him any sounder than they are now in men: and therefore the Rectitude of Adam, and his likeness to God, which was lost by sin, and without which all men are born after the fall, are not natural to man, but a certain supernatural gift. The end and scope of Jesuitical doctrine in this article tends solely to demonstrate that, after the fall of our first parents, all naturals in men are intact, and thus the Image of God itself has remained unharmed: but that that likeness of God, namely Wisdom and Justice only, is a supernatural gift that was lost through the fall. Since the salvation and ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxy) of the entire Christian religion are directly attacked by this dogma, it will be worth the effort to examine it a little more accurately by the balance of truth.

Latin:

Ἀντίθεσις.

PLuriori huic doctrinae nostrae, de Imagine Dei, duo potissimùm hostium agmina sese opponunt: quorum uuum est Pontificiorum tùm Veterum & recentiorum: Alterum verò est Flacianorum. Quoad Pontificios, Scholastici initiò Doctores statuebant, humanam naturam in ipsa integritate, ita conditam fuisse, ut quia propter compositionem ex diversis partibus, inter se minimè consentientibus constabat, consecuta sint eam incitamenta, & quasi prurigines, hoc est, tales pulsus & concitationes, ut caro, cùm sibi grata & jucunda concupiscit, contra Spiritum repugnet, & à praescripto Rationis sit aversa: Illis verò puris seu meris naturalibus, sitper additam fuisse Justitiam Originalem, tanquam donum supernaturale, quæ Carnis lasciviam & affectus comprimeret, compesceret, & coërceret, atque carnem, inferioresq; hominis facultates in officio contineret. Quare è contrario docebant, Peccatum Originale tantùm esse nudam privationem Justitiæ Originalis sive doni illius supernaturalis, quam nulla secuta sit depravatio in mente & voluntate: sed quantumvis amissâ justitiâ Originali, sive dono supernaturali, Naturalia in homine manserint integra. Hinc contendebant, Peccatum Originis tantùm in carne hærere, & per carnem duntaxat propagari, tanquàm morbidam carnis qualitatem: Superiorem autem partem Rationis, ab omni corruptione immunem esse, & integram: ac proindè pravitatem illam, cujus subjectum caro sit, ad inferiora, hoc est, ad carnalia & animalia, trahere & inclinare voluntatem, & facere ut erret Ratio

Ab hac Scholasticorum Theologia, nihil prorsus abhorret Doctrina Jesuuvitica, uti patet ex disputatione Bellarmini, quam unico libro pertexit, cui titulum fecit, De Gratia primi Hominis. In eo igitur tres sequentes errores de Imagine DEI, accuratiore indagine perquàm dignos, prodidit. Primus sic habet: Imago DEI in Adamo fuit ipsa Animæ rationalis substantia, sive ipsa Natura trium facultatum animæ rationalis, memoriæ, intelligentiæ, voluntatis: Similitudo verò DEI, ad quam Adam conditus erat, longè aliud ac diversum fuit, nempè conformitas hominis cum DEO, secundum omnes virtutes, A quo errore parum etiam abfuit, P. Ramus sic scribens lib. 1. de Fide, cap. 5. p. 21. DEUS creavit hominem ad imaginem suam, hoc est, animæ rationalis compotem.

II. Error. Imago DEI per lapsum primi hominis, neq; amissa, neq; ulla sui parte deterior facta est, sed eadem mansit, & adhuc in omnibus est.

III. Error. Natura Adami secundùm se, in puris, ut vocant, naturalibus, ante lapsum considerata, condita fuit cum morbo & languore quodam, videlicet cum præcipiti inclinatione ad vitia, rebellione inferiorum virium adversus superiores: nec fuerunt in ipso pura Naturalia saniora, quàm modò sunt in hominibus: ac proindè Rectitudo Adami, & similitudo ejus cum DEO, quæ peccato deperdita fuit, & sine qua omnes homines post lapsum nascuntur, non sunt Homini naturalis, sed donum quoddam supernaturale. Finis & Scopus doctrinæ Jesuiticæ hoc in Articulo eò tendit unicè, ut demonstret, post lapsum primorum parentum, Naturalia omnia in hominibus esse integra, & sic ipsam Imaginem DEI mansisse illæsam: sed similitudinem illam DEI, nempè Sapientiam & Justitiam tantùm, sive donum supernaturale esse per lapsum amissum. Quo sanè dogmate cum salus & ὀρθοδοξία universæ Religionis Christianæ directè petatur, operæ pretium fuerit, ad trutinam veritatis illud paulò accuratiùs exigere.


### Chapter II. Anthesis: On the first Jesuitical Error

The first error, therefore, separates the Image and Likeness of God as two different things: and refers the Image itself to the nature of the intelligence & of the will: But as for the likeness to wisdom & justice. Although we do not deny that Augustine, lib. 10 de Trin. cap. 12 & lib. 11 de Civit. Dei, cap. 26, establishes the image of the divine essence and of the Trinity of persons in the one soul of man, whose three faculties are memory, intellect, and will; although we are also not unaware that most of the Fathers, whom the Jesuit brings forward in great number, distinguish in this way between the image and the likeness of God: yet the authority of Scripture is far greater and holier for us, which clearly demonstrates that these two things are by no means to be distinguished. But this passage fixes for itself the primary seat of the controversy in those words of Jehovah, Gen. 1:26, Let us make man in our image and likeness: or as the Hebrew words sound, according to Pagninus's translation: Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness. And in the verse immediately following, 27. God created man in his image: in the image of God he created him. An accurate comparison of these two verses demonstrates to the eye that image and likeness denote exactly the same thing. For the latter verse omits the word likeness and repeats the word image twice, so that it may be evident even from this that what was expressed by two words in the preceding verse denotes one and the same thing. But the Holy Spirit undoubtedly wished, in the former verse, to explain the word image exegetically by the added word likeness. For because not every image is similar to its prototype, and the very nature of the image of God can be conceived in many ways: the Holy Spirit certainly did not wish to leave us in suspense as to what ought to be understood by the word image, but by the added exegetical word likeness, he shows that the first man was created such that in him the image of God the Creator shone forth similar in all respects. Hence also Gen. 5:1, with the word image omitted, it is read: In the day that God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. : 2. Furthermore, the truth of our assertion is evident from that Apostolic aphorism, Col. 3:10, You have put on the new (man) who is renewed unto knowledge, according to the image of him who created him. Which aphorism, indeed, compared with that which exists in Eph. 4:24, Put on the new man, who is created according to God, in righteousness and holiness of truth: shows an infallible ἀπόδειξιν, or demonstration, of our opinion. For 1. the equivalence of these terms must be noted: to be to the image of God, and to be created according to God.

2. The description of the new man must be observed, which in both Apostolic sayings defines his image, not by the very nature or essence of the soul: but by new qualities; namely, by the knowledge of God, righteousness, and true holiness: Hence, against the Jesuit, we infer thus invincibly.

As is the image of God in the new man after restoration: such also it was in the first man after creation before the fall.

likeness of God. Now, indeed, since the Apostle defines the new man by these qualities, he refers to the image of God. Therefore, the likeness of God is nothing other than the image of God itself.

3. There is added, moreover, the passage of Ecclesiasticus 17:2, He (God) clothed them with strength according to themselves, and created them to the image of himself. Where even a boy understands that to be created to the image of God and to be clothed with strength are equivalent terms.

4. What? That the Jesuits themselves are otherwise accustomed to condemn this opinion in the Flacians, who also themselves established that the image of God, impressed upon man in the first creation, was the very substance of the rational soul: Which opinion we shall refute expressly a little later.

5. The Apostle again, 2 Cor. 3:18, saying, We are transformed into the same image of the glory of God: provides us with such an argument.

The restoration of the image of God in man after the fall takes place κατά μεταμόρφωσιν, according to the transformation of the old form into the new, or that primary one to which the first man was created.

Therefore, the image of God does not denote the essence of the soul itself, which was not abolished and destroyed by the fall: but it denotes those qualities or virtues which man lost through sin.

6. Finally, some of the Fathers are in all respects ὁμόψηφοι with us. Let Origen suffice in this place, who in book 4, περὶ ἀρχῶν, writes thus: In man, the signs of the divine IMAGE are clearly discerned, not through the likeness of the Body, which is corrupted, but through the prudence of the Soul, through Justice, through moderation, through fortitude, through wisdom, through discipline, and finally through the whole choir of virtues, which, since they exist in GOD by substance, can exist in man through industry and the imitation of God.

With these things thus established at the beginning, we evidently gather from this that the Soul of man and the Image of GOD differ by their very definition, and that the οὐσία of the one is different from that of the other: and therefore that this Image is not to be reckoned among the parts of the Essence, but among the adjuncts: and by no means to be posited as the Essence itself. This is also evident from the fact that if the Image of GOD were abolished, the essence of man would necessarily have perished, either in whole or in part, if the Jesuit hypothesis were to stand. Furthermore, from what has already been said, it is not obscurely gathered that the term Image of GOD is not ineptly referred by some of our theologians to those words which are called by the Philosophers ἀφ' ἑνός καὶ πρὸς ἕν: in which there is a certain principal thing, and with respect to which the rest are understood to exist, just as the Philosopher explains that by the example of Being in books γ and ζ of the Metaphysics. Therefore, principally and primarily, the Image of GOD in man signifies the perfect conformity of the rational soul and all its powers with God, determined by true wisdom, justice, holiness, and the knowledge of GOD, so that in the whole mind, the whole heart, the whole will, and in all the powers of the soul, both lower and higher, there might be most integral and most perfect powers.

Moreover, there depended upon this image of God a most ardent pious love of God toward man: likewise that admirable wisdom, by which the first man contemplated this whole universe, and knew most exactly the causes of all things: Likewise a peaceful conscience, subject to no inordinate affections of the soul: and finally the highest vigor of all the powers of the body, perpetual health, without any fear of diseases and death. To these internal dignities can be added also that external dominion, which by the institution of God man obtained, far most fully, over all created things of the earth and sea. But whether this dignity and excellence of the first man was natural, or supernatural, or of what kind it was: the Refutation of the third Jesuitical error will show: if we first note a few things about the second.

Latin:

PRimus igitur error, Imaginem & Similitudinem DEI, tanquàm duo diversa dispescit: & Imaginem ipsam refert ad naturam intelligentiæ & voluntatis : Similitudinem verò ad sapientiam & Justitiam. Quanquàm verò non diffitemur, Augustinum lib. 10. de Trin. cap. 12. & lib. 11. de Civit. Dei, cap. 26. Constituere Imaginem divinæ Essentiæ, & Trinitatis personarum, in una Anima hominis, cujus tres sint facultates, Memoria, Intellectus & Voluntas; quanquàm etiam non ignoramus, plerosque Patres, quos magno numero adducit Jesusitæ hoc modo inter Imaginem & similitudinem Dei distinguere : longè tamen major & sanctior nobis est Scripturæ autoritas, quæ duo isthæc minimè distinguenda esse, evidenter demonstrat. Sedem autem primariam controversiæ hæc sibi figit, in verbis illis Jehovæ, Gen. 1, 26. Faciamus hominem in Imagine & similitudine nostra : vel uti verba Hebræa, interprete Pagnino sonant : Faciamus hominem in Imagine nostra, secundum similitudinem nostram. Et versu statim subsequente 27. Creavit Deus hominem in imagine sua : in imagine Dei creavit illum. Quorum duorum versuum accurata collatio ad oculum demonstrat, Imaginem & Similitudinem idem prorsus notare. Nam versus posterior omittit vocem similitudinis, & bis repetit vocem imaginis, ut vel indè constare possit, id quod præcedente versu duobus vocabulis expressum fuit, unam eandemque rem notare. Voluit autem sine dubio Spiritus sanctus, in priore versu vocem imaginis, per adjectam vocem similitudinis ἐξηγητικῶς explicare. Quia enim non omnis imago similis est prototypo, & ipsa ratio Imaginis DEI multiplex excogitari potest: noluit utique Spiritus sanctus in suspenso nos relinquere, quid per vocabulum Imaginis intelligi debeat, sed adjecta voce ἐξηγητικῇ Similitudinis ostendit, talem fuisse primum hominem conditum, ut in ipso imago Deo creatori per omnia similis, eluceret. Hinc etiam Genes. 5, 1. omissa voce imaginis, legitur: In die quâ creavit DEUS hominem, ad similitudinem DEI fecit illum. : 2. Prætereà assertionis nostræ veritas patet ex Aphorismo illo Apostolico, Col. 3, 10. Induistis novum (hominem) qui renovatur ad agnitionem, juxta imaginem ejus, qui condidit illum. Qui sanè Aphorismus, collatus cum eo, qui extat. Ephes. 4, 24. Induite novum hominem, qui juxta DEUM conditus est, in Justitia & sanctitate veritatis: infallibilem monstrat ἀπόδειξιν, sive demonstrationem nostræ sententiæ. Nam 1. notanda venit æquipollentia istorum terminorum, ad Imaginem DEI, & juxta DEUM conditum esse.

2. Observanda venit descriptio Novi hominis, quæ in utroq; dicto Apostolico, Imaginem illius definit, non per ipsam Animæ Naturam sive essentiam: sed per novas qualitates; nempè per agnitionem Dei, justitiam, veramque sanctitatem: Hinc adversus Jesusitam sic invictè inferimus.

Qualis est imago DEI in Novo homine, post restaurationem: talis etiam fuit in primo homine, post creationem ante lapsum.

tudinem DEI. Jam verò definiente Apostolo, Novus homo, per has qualitates, refert imaginem DEI Ergò Similitudo DEI, nihil est aliud, quàm ipsa Imago DEI.

3. Accedit insuper locus Ecclesiastici 17, 2. Induit eos (DEUS) VIRTUTE secundùm seipsos, & ad Imaginem sui eos creavit. Ubi ad imaginem DEI creatum, & virtute indutum esse, æquipollentes esse terminos, vel puer intelligit.

4. Quid? quòd sententiam hanc ipsi alioqui Jesuwtæ in Flacianis damnare solent, qui & ipsi statuerunt, Imaginem DEI, in prima creatione impressam homini, fuisse ipsam animæ rationalis substantiam: Quam sententiam paulò pòst ex professo refutabimus.

5. Apostolus rursum. 2. Cor. 3, 18. Transformamur, inquiens, in eandem imaginem Gloria DEI: tale nobis suppeditat argumentum.

Imaginis DEI Restitutio in Homine post lapsum fit κατά μεταμόρφωσιν, secundùm transformationem Veteris Formæ, in novam sive primam illam, ad quam primus homo erat conditus.

Ergò Imago DEI, non notat ipsam Animæ Essentiam, quæ per lapsum non est abolita & destructa: sed notat qualitates sive virtutes illas, quas Homo per peccatum amisit.

6. Tandem Patrum nonnulli nobis per omnia sunt ὁμόψηφοι. Sufficiat hoc loco unus Origenes, qui lib. 4. περὶ ἀρχῶν, sic scribit. In homine manifestè cernuntur divinæ IMAGINIS indicia non per effigiem Corporis, quæ corrumpitur: sed per Animi prudentiam, per Justitiam, per moderationem, per fortitudinem, per sapientiam, per disciplinam, per omnem denique virtutum chorum, quæ cùm DEO insint per substantiam, in homine possunt esse per industriam & imitationem Dei.

Quibus ita constitutis initiò evidenter inde colligimus, Animam hominis & Imaginem DEI, ipsa definitione differre, & aliam hujus, aliam illius esse ὐσίαν: ac proindè Imaginem hanc non inter partes Essentiæ, sed inter adjuncta recensendam: nullo verò pacto pro ipsa Essentia ponendam. Id quod vel indè etiam patet, quòd Imagine DEI abolita, hominis essentiam, vel ex toto, vel ex parte interire necessum fuiffet, si Jesuitica hypothesis subsisteret. Deinde ex jam dictis haud obscurè colligitur, vocem Imaginis DEI haud ineptè à nonnullis nostratium Theologorum, referri ad ea vocabula, quæ ἀφ' ἑνός καὶ πρὸς ἕν, à Philosophis nominantur: in quibus quoddam est principale, & respectu cujus reliqua esse intelliguntur, quemadmodum exemplo Entis illud explicat Philosophus lib. γ. & ζ. μεταφυσ. Principaliter ergò & primò Imago DEI in homine, significat animæ rationalis, omniumque virium ejus perfectam cum Deo conformitatem, verâ sapientiâ, justitiâ, sanctitate & agnitione DEI determinatam, ita ut in tota mente, toto corde, tota voluntate, in omnia bus potentiis animæ, càm inferioribus quàm superioribus, effent vires integerrimæ & perfectissimæ.

Dependebat autem ab hac imagine Dei, ardentissimus amor pius Dei erga hominem: item admirabilis illa sapientia, qua primus homo totum hoc universum contemplabatur, omniumque rerum causas exactissimè noverat: Item pacata conscientia, nullis inordinatis animæ affectibus obnoxia: & denique summus vigor omnium virium corporis, perpetua sanitas, sine omni morborum ac mortis metu. Quibus internis dignitatibus addi potest etiam externum illud dominium, quod ex institutione Dei in omnes res creatas terræ marisque, longe plenissimum Homo obtinebat. Cæterùm nùm naturalis, an supernaturalis, vel qualis fuerit hæc dignitas & excellentia primi hominis: Erroris tertij Jesuvvitici Refutatio ostendet: si priùs de secundo pauca nota verimus.


### Chapter II. Anthesis: On the Second Jesuitical Error, concerning the doctrine of the Image of God & Original Justice

ON THE SECOND Jesuitical ERROR, concerning the doctrine of the Image of GOD & Original Justice.

The second error of Bellarmine is that, through the fall of the first parents, the image of God was neither lost, nor made worse in any part of itself, but remained the same, and is still entire in all. What is to be determined concerning this error can only be settled through an accurate distinction of the gifts of the image of God. For either by the image of God is understood that less principal congruence and analogy of the soul of man with God, such as that it is immortal, incorporeal, spiritual, intelligent, and of free will in things subject to reason: that also, according to the Fathers, it bears as it were a certain shadow of the Mystery of the Holy Trinity: insofar as, indeed, the soul is one according to Essence, and yet according to powers it obtains a respect of the Trinity. To which also pertains the dignity of empire, which man exercises over living creatures: Likewise, those common notions about God and divine things, which are sought from the Light of nature. Or by the image of God, and indeed in the proper sense and that used by the scriptures, is understood the interior perfection of the mind and Will, and of all the powers of man, as regards divine and spiritual things both to be understood and to be desired: likewise the highest approval of the divine Law, and perfect congruence with each and all of the precepts of the same law. Now therefore, regarding the decision of this second error, if the Adversary were taking the word image of God in the first and at least less proper or principal sense: then indeed we would not resist in the least: For we ourselves confess that in this respect the image of God was not entirely lost in man through the fall: but only weakened and obscured: so that it behaves in this way like ruins, or remains, from which a judgment can be made about some most beautiful building. But concerning this first and looser meaning of the image of God, there is not properly a controversy between us and the Jesuits, as is evident from the preceding article, concerning Free Will: where we expressly disputed about those natural notions, still remaining after the fall. But if the Adversary understands the word image of God in the latter, and indeed proper sense, as he certainly does, then we simply embrace the Adversative, and undoubtedly determine that in this sense and respect the image of God has been entirely lost, so that man after the fall cannot think anything at all in spiritual matters, indeed not even anything good: but is entirely dead and buried to the good: as was demonstrated in the preceding article. Let this one thing suffice in this place, which the Lord Apostle 1 Corinthians 15, most openly testifies, that we after the fall do not bear the image of God, but the image of the earthly Adam: of him, indeed, who is turned away from God, who is destitute of the glory before God, Rom. 3, 23. who is carnal, and sold under sin, Rom. 7, 14. who is by nature a child of wrath, Eph. 2, 3. who must be renewed by the power of God, and indeed through a certain μεταμόρφωσιν, unto righteousness and holiness of truth, 2 Cor. 3, 18. Eph. 4, 24. Coloss. 3, 10. who finally is guilty of the wrath of God and eternal death, John 3, 5. Ephes. 2, 3.

To this pertains that excellent comparison of Adam and Christ, which the Apostle weaves through many points in Rom. 5. Showing that from Adam nothing but sin, death, and condemnation passes to us by hereditary right.

Latin:

DE SECUNDO ERROre Jesuvvitico, circa doctrinam de Imagine DEI & Justitia Originali.

SEcundus error Bellarmini est, quod per lapsum primorum parentum Imago Dei neq; amissa, neque ulla sui parte deterior facta sit, sed eadem manserit, & adhuc in omnibus sit integra. De hoc errore quid sit statuendum, non nisi per accuratam distinctionem donorum Imaginis Dei, expediri potest. Vel enim per Imaginem Dei intelligitur minus principalis illa congruentia & analogia Animæ Hominis cum Deo, ut quòd immortalis est, incorporea, spiritualis, intelligens, liberæque voluntatis in rebus rationi subjectis: quòd etiam secundum Patres, umbram quasi quandam gerit, Mysterij S. Trinitatis: quatenùs nimirùm, una est anima secundum Essentiam, & tamen secundum potentias Trinitatis respectum sortitur. Quò pertinent etiam Imperij dignitas, quod homo in animantia exercet: Item, communes illæ notitiæ de Deo rebúsque divinis, quæ ex Lumine naturæ petuntur. Vel per Imaginem Dei, & quidem sensu proprio ac scripturis ufitato, intelligitur interior perfectio mentis & Voluntatis, omniumq; virium hominis, quoad res divinas & spirituales tùm intelligendas, tùm appetendas: summa item approbatio Legis divinæ, & perfecta congruentia cum singulis & universis ejusdem legis præceptis. Jam ergò quoad decisionem secundi hujus erroris, si primo saltem minusq; proprio sive principali sensu acciperet Adversarius vocabulum Imaginis Dei: tùm sanè nos minimè reluctaremur: Fatemur enim ipsi hoc respectu Imaginem Dei per lapsum in homine non prorsus esse amissam: sed debilitatam tantùm & obscuratam: ita ut ea hoc pacto sese habeat instar ruderum, sive reliquiarum, ex quibus de pulcherrimo aliquo ædificio fieri queat judicium. Sed de hoc primo ac laxiore significatu Imaginis Dei, propriè inter nos & Jesuvvitas non est controversia, uti patet ex præcedente proximo Articulo, de Libero Arbitrio: ubi de Notitijs istis naturalibus, adhuc post lapsum reliquis, ex professo disputavimus. Cæterùm si posteriore, & quidem proprio sensu vocem Imaginis Dei intelligit Adversarius, ut sanè intelligit, tum nos simpliciter Adversativam amplectimur, & indubitatò statuimus, Hoc sensu & respectu Imaginem Dei prorsus esse amissam, ita ut Homo post lapsum nil quicquam in spiritualibus, imò ne quidem aliquid boni cogitare possit : sed prorsus ad bonum sit mortuus & sepultus: ut præcedente Articulo demonstratum fuit. Sufficiat hoc loco unicum istud, quod D. Apostolus 1. Corinth. 15, apertissimè testatur, Nos post lapsum non gestare imaginem Dei, sed imaginem terrestris Adami: illius nimirùm, qui aversus est à Deo, qui destituitur gloria apud Deum, Rom. 3, 23. qui carnalis est, & venundatus sub peccato, Rom. 7, 14. qui naturâ est Filius iræ, Eph. 2, 3. qui virtute Dei renovari debet, & quidem per quandam μεταμόρφωσιν, ad justitiam & sanctitatem veritatis, 2. Cor. 3, 18. Eph. 4, 24. Coloss. 3, 10. qui denique reus est iræ Dei & æternæ mortis, Joh. 3, 5. Ephes. 2. 3.

Pertinet huc egregia illa comparatio Adami & Christi, quam multis pertexit Apostolus Rom. 5. Ostendens ex Adamo nihil nisi peccatum, mortem & condemnationem in nos jure hæreditario transire.


### Chapter II. Anthesis: On the Third Jesuitical Error concerning the doctrine of the Image of God and Original Justice

Bellarmine contends in the third place, together with the Scholastics, that the image of God, or Original justice, was in Adam a supernatural gift, conferred upon man in such a way that it could be lost, while the natural things remained safe: just as if a garland were placed upon the head of a virgin, which being removed, she nevertheless remains a virgin. For to that end tend all those things which Bellarmine argues in Chap. 5, contending

1. that man consists of flesh and spirit in such a way that from this, out of contrary propensities, there exists in one man a certain struggle, and from this a huge difficulty of doing good, while one propensity hinders the other.

2. That Divine Providence, at the beginning of Creation, in order to apply a remedy to this disease or languor of human nature, added to man a certain distinguished gift, namely Original Justice, by which, as if by a golden bridle, the lower part was easily kept subject to the higher part, and the higher part to God.

3. That that rectitude of the lower part was a supernatural gift, and indeed per se, not per accidens, so that it neither flowed from the principles of nature, nor could it have flowed.

4. That with this supernatural gift removed, human nature, left to itself, began to experience that conflict of the lower part with the higher, which was going to be natural, that is, which would follow from the condition of matter, unless God had superadded the gift of Justice to man.

5. And therefore that the state of man after the fall of Adam does not differ more from his state before the fall in pure naturals, than a despoiled person differs from a naked one:

nor is human nature worse, if you take away Original sin, nor does it labor more under ignorance and infirmity than it would be and would labor if founded in pure Naturals: and therefore the corruption of Nature flowed not from the lack of any natural gift, nor from the accession of any new quality, but solely from the loss of the supernatural gift on account of sin.

This Question is indeed most worthy both of the most accurate consideration, and for other reasons, and because it confirms or destroys the very foundation of this Article according to the diversity of the decision. But at the beginning it must be well observed what properly comes into controversy in this place. The Jesuit Adversary sophistically mixes in several questions, about which, however, there is no proper controversy in this place: Such as is: Chap. 3. Whether Man in creation also received justifying Grace? For if he understands this Grace as that sum of all powers, both of Body and of mind, of rectitude and integrity, we concede it willingly to the Affirmative: yet under this law and condition, that no one may imagine some gift added to nature from without: But rather as something connatural or concreated, as will be demonstrated presently. But if in the Jesuitical manner he dreams that in the first creation some Grace of Reconciliation to God was infused into man, by which after the fall he could even return into favor with God by his own powers, either in whole or in half: then we hold and defend the negative in all respects, relying on those Oracles of the Scriptures, by which in the immediately preceding Article, to unregenerate Man every power of inclining himself to good in spiritual matters is expressly denied: by which also a little later, Chap. 2, the extreme corruption of all powers in Man will be asserted.

Furthermore, neither does this come into dispute: Whether certain Supernatural gifts were bestowed upon Man in Creation? For this was never denied by our side. For a supernatural gift was not something concreated, which the whole Sacrosanct Trinity inhabited in the first man, illuminating and confirming that concreated perfection and integrity of all powers.

But it is properly disputed in this place: Whether the Image of God or Original justice, such as has been defined above, was some Supernatural gift, so bestowed upon Man, that it could have been lost, while the naturals remained safe? To which question we answer simply in the negative, and with Blessed Luther we maintain that that rectitude and integrity of all powers was connatural to the first Man: or such a concreated power and faculty of the human soul, by which the very substance of Adam's soul was full of the knowledge of the essence and will of God, and with a most free will and most prompt obedience, it rested in the Divine Law: without any defect, without any disease, languor, and difficulty of doing well, without any concupiscence or inclination against the Law of God.

This thesis of ours consists of two members: The former asserts that that Image of God, or Original Justice, was connatural or concreated to the first man: The latter, however, affirms that this very Original Justice was immune from all that struggle of the inferior powers with the superior, from all languor, and difficulty of doing well. Both need confirmation.

The former member is most evidently clear, first indeed from the Comparison of human Nature before and after the fall. For just as the Nature of Man now after the fall behaves toward evil or sin: so the same behaved before the fall toward good. But now human Nature after the fall, by a certain connatural and concreated power, is ignorant of God, is ignorant of spiritual things, resists God, and is averse, nay, as if it were foolish, it mocks the entire doctrine concerning Christ and his merit: so that the Apostle asserts in express words, that Man is BY NATURE a child of wrath. Therefore: Human Nature before the fall likewise, by a connatural and concreated power and rectitude of mind, loved God above all things, acknowledged Him most perfectly, and rested in His will and Law, without any struggle, with a most prompt Spirit. The evidence of the consequence is by far the firmest: unless perhaps the Jesuits, through remarkable impudence, wish to deny that from a privation, no right judgment can be made concerning a habit.

The other argument of Confirmation can be sought from the consideration of the remnants of Original Justice in Man after the fall in this manner:

Of whatever condition are the remnants of the divine Image or Original Justice, which remain in the souls of men even of the Gentiles: of the same condition will be the Image of God itself, or Original Justice, bestowed upon the first man.

And yet these remnants are connatural to man even after the fall. Therefore, Original Justice was also connatural to man before the fall.

The truth of the major premise is evident from this, that it is necessary that there be a certain ὁμογένειαν (homogeneity) between these remnants and Original Justice itself, as between a whole and its parts: or the adversaries must admit that these remnants also come from without, and have the nature of some supernatural gift: but if the adversaries dare to assert this, they must necessarily concede that supernatural gifts of the Holy Spirit are conferred even upon men who are not reborn: since this is prodigiously impious and absurd: inasmuch as now after the fall all supernatural gifts of the Holy Spirit are nothing but justifying and saving: it remains that the connection of the major premise is of immovable evidence.
