The minor premise is confirmed by that statement of the Apostle, Rom. 2:14. Gentiles τῇ φύσει (by nature) do the things that are of the law. And verse 15. The work of the law is written in their hearts; their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another: then those excellent effects which proceed from those remnants: such as are the distinction between honorable and base things: the entire ethical doctrine and νομοθεσία (legislation) of the Gentiles.

The conclusion will therefore also have its own immovable certainty and truth.

Thirdly: If you maintain that Original Justice was not of nature, but a certain supernatural gift added, and that after the fall the natural faculties remained intact in man: it would follow that the Son of God assumed our nature in vain, in order to restore it to integrity: which would be most absurd even to think.

Finally, in place of a fourth argument, we produce our blessed Luther, in that golden commentary of his on Chapter 3 of Genesis, arguing thus about this question: The Scholastics dispute that Original Justice was not connatural, but like a certain ornament added to man as a gift, as if someone were to place a crown upon a beautiful girl. The crown is certainly not a part of the virgin's nature, but something separated from nature, which comes from the outside and can be taken away again without violation of nature. Therefore, they dispute concerning man and the demons that, even though they lost Original Justice, the natural faculties nevertheless remained pure, just as they were created in the beginning. But this opinion, because it diminishes Original Sin, must be fled from like poison. Rather, let us maintain this: that Justice was not a certain gift that came from the outside, separated from the nature of man, but was truly natural, so that it was the nature of Adam to love God, to believe in God, to acknowledge God, etc. These were as natural in Adam as it is natural that eyes receive light. But because if you render an eye defective by inflicting a wound, you rightly say that nature has been violated: so after man fell from justice into sin, it is rightly and truly said: the natural faculties are not intact, but corrupted by sin. For just as it is the nature of the eye to see, so it was by the nature of reason and will in Adam to know God, to trust in God, to fear God. Since it is now certain that these have been lost, who is so insane as to say that the natural faculties are still intact?

The latter part of our thesis is confirmed at the beginning by that epiphonema which Moses appends to the history of creation: God saw all that He had made, and behold, they were very good: Gen. 1:31. Now if man was very good, that struggle and strife of the lower powers with the higher, and likewise the languor and difficulty of doing good in man, could by no means have subsisted: especially since God pronounces that man was created by Him not simply good, but with the added emphatic particle, VERY good.

The reason for this consequence is most evident: For if there was in the first man a struggle of the lower powers and the higher, with the former inclining by nature to good and the latter to evil, then it is necessary that some innate force and evil faculty, worthy of God's hatred, was implanted in him. If this is so, then God did not create man very good, but must be established as the author of that evil disposition or faculty. But this is blasphemous and absurd; therefore, that which the Jesuits imagine about such a struggle in the first man would be of the same impiety.

Latin:

COntendit tertio loco Bellarminus unà cum Scholasticis, Imaginem Dei, sive Justitiam Originalem fuisse in Adamo donum supernaturale, ita Homini collatum, ut illud, salvis manentibus naturalibus, amitti potuerit : perindè ac si Virginis capiti imponatur sertum, quo ablato, ipsa nihilominus maneat virgo. Eò enim tendunt illa omnia, quæ Cap. 5. disputat Bellarminus, contendens.

1. Hominem ita constare carne & spiritu, ut hinc ex contrarijs propensionibus existat in uno homine pugna quædam, & ex hac ingens benè agendi difficultas, dùm una propensio alteram impediat.

2. Divinam Providentiam initio Creationis, ut remedium adhiberet huic morbo, sive languori naturæ humanæ : addidisse homini donum quoddam insigne, Justitiam videlicet Originalem, quâ veluti aureo quodam freno pars inferior parti superiori, & pars superior Deo facilè subjecta contineretur.

3. Rectitudinem illam partis inferioris, fuisse donum supernaturale, & quidem per se, non per accidens, ita ut neq; ex naturæ principijs fluxerit, neq; potuerit fluere.

4. Remoto dono hoc supernaturali, naturam humanam sibi relictam, cœpisse experiri pugnam illa partis inferioris cùm superiore, quæ Naturalis futura erat, hoc est, ex conditione materiæ secutura, nisi Deus Justitiæ donum homini superaddidisset.

5. Ideoque non magis differre statum hominis post lapsum Adami à statu ejusdem ante lapsum in puris naturalibus, quàm differat spoliatus à nudo:

neque deteriorem esse humanam naturam, si culpam Originalem detrahas, neq; magis ignorantia & infirmitate laborare quàm esset & laboraret in puris Naturalibus condita: ac proindè corruptionem Naturæ non ex doni alicujus naturalis carentia, neq; ex alicujus novæ qualitatis accessu, sed ex sola doni supernaturalis ob peccatum amissione profluxisse.

Dignissima verò hæc est Quæstio tùm accuratissima consideratione, tùm ob causas alias, tùm quod ea ipsum fundamentum Articuli hujus pro diversitate decisionis, vel confirmat vel destruit. Initiò autem probè observandum, quid propriè hoc loco in controversiam veniat. Jesuvvita Adversarius Sophisticè plures immiscet quæstiones, de quibus tamen hoc loco propriè non controvertitur: Qualis est: Cap. 3. An Homo in creatione acceperit etiam Gratiam gratum facientem? Nam si de summa illa virium omnium, tùm Corporis, tùm animi, rectitudine atque integritate, Gratiam hanc intelligat, in Affirmativam ultrò concedimus: eâ tamen lege & conditione, ut ne quis fingat donum aliquod ab extra additum naturæ: Sed potiùs ut connaturale sive concreatum aliquid, uti mox demonstrabitur. Sin more Esavvitico somniet in prima creatione Gratiam aliquam Reconciliationis Deo homini esse infusam, quâ post lapsum etiam se ex proprijs viribus, vel ex asse, vel ex semisse, cum Deo in gratiam redire possit: tùm negativam per omnia tenemus ac defendimus, freti ijs Scripturarum Oraculis, quibus in præcedente Articulo proximo, Homini non renato omnis prorsus δύναμις inclinandi se ad bonum inspiritualibus, expressè derogatur: quibus etiam paulò post, Cap. 2. extrema virium omnium corruptio in Homine adstruetur.

Deindè neque illud in disceptationem venit: An dona quædam Supernaturalia Homini in Creatione sint collata? Neq; enim hoc unquàm à nostris fuit negatum. Donum enim supernaturale, neque concreatum aliquid fuit, quod tota Sacrosancta Trinitas in primo homine habitavit, illustrans & confirmans concreatam illam virium omnium perfectionem & integritatem.

Sed de eo propriè hoc loco controvertitur: An Imago Dei sive justitia Originalis, qualis jam supra definita est, fuerit donum aliquod Supernaturale, ita Homini collatum, ut illud, salvis manentibus naturalibus, amitti potuerit? Ad quam quæstionem nos simpliciter negatè respondemus, & cum B. Luthero statuimus, rectitudinem illam & integritatem omnium virium fuisse Homini primo connaturalem: sive talem concreatam animæ humanæ vim ac facultatem, qua ipsa animæ Adami substantia plena fuit agnitione essentiæ & voluntatis Dei, & liberrima voluntate ac promtissima obedientia, in Lege Divina acquievit: sine ulla defectu, sine omni morbo, languore, & difficultate benè agendi, sine omni concupiscentia aut inclinatione contra Legem Dei.

Thesis haec nostra duobus constat membris: Prius asserit, Imaginem illam Dei, sive Iustitiam Originalem fuisse primo homini connaturalem sive concreatam: Posterius verò affirmat, hanc ipsam Iustitiam Originalem fuisse immunem ab omni illa pugna virium inferiorum cum superioribus, ab omni languore, & difficultate benè agendi. Utrumque confirmatione indiget.

Prius membrum evidentissimè patet, primùm quidem ex Collatione Naturæ humanæ ante & post lapsum. Quemadmodum enim Natura Hominis jam post lapsum se habet ad malum sive peccatum: ita eadem se habuit ante lapsum ad bonum. Jam verò Natura humana post lapsum ex connaturali atque concreata quadam vi ignorat Deum, ignorat spiritualia, resistit Deo, & aversatur, imò ceu stultam irridet universam doctrinam de Christo ejusque merito: ita ut Apostolus disertis verbis asserat, Hominem NATURA, esse filium iræ. Ergò: Natura Humana ante lapsum itidem ex connaturali atque concreata animi vi ac rectitudine Deum super omnia dilexit, perfectissime agnovit, inque voluntate ac Lege ipsius, absque ulla pugna, promtissimo Spiritu acquievit. Consecutionis evidentia est longè firmissima: nisi fortè Jesuvitæ per insignem impudentiam negare velint, Ex privatione, de habitu nullum posse rectum fieri judicium.

Alterum Confirmationis argumentum peti potest, ex consideratione reliquiarum Justitiæ Originalis in Homine post lapsum in hunc modum:

Cujus Conditionis sunt reliquiæ Imaginis divinæ sive Justitiæ Originalis, quæ in animis hominum etiam Gentilium supersunt: ejusdem conditionis erit ipsa etiam Imago Dei, sive Justitia Originalis, primo homini collata.

Atqui reliquiæ hæ Homini sunt connaturales etiam post lapsum. Ergò Justitia etiam Originalis ante lapsum Homini fuit connaturalis.

Majoris Veritas vel inde patet, quod necessum est, inter reliquias hasce, & inter ipsam Justitiam Originalem, tanquam inter Totum & partes esse ὁμογένειαν quandam: vel fatendum Adversariis, Reliquias etiam hasce forinsecùs accedere, & habere rationem doni alicujus supernaturalis: Quod si asserere ausint Adversarij, concedant necesse est, Hominibus etiam non renatis supernaturalia Spiritus Sancti dona conferri: Quod cùm prodigiosè impium & absurdum sit: Siquidem jam post lapsum omnia Spiritus Sancti dona supernaturalia, non sunt nisi justificantia & salvantia: Relinquitur utique Majoris connexum esse immotæ evidentiæ.

Minorem confirmattùm illud Apostoli, Rom. 2, 14. Gentes τῇ φύσει Naturâ faciunt ea, quæ legis sunt. Et vers. 15. Opus Legis scriptum est in cordibus ipsorum; unà testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuò accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus: tùm præclari illi Effectus, qui ex reliquijs illis proveniunt: quales sunt, discrimen honestorum & turpium: Universa doctrina Ethica & νομοθεσία Gentilium.

Constabit proindè conclusioni suâ etiam immota certitudo & Veritas.

Tertiò: Si statuas Justitiam Originalem non fuissè naturæ, sed donum quoddam supernaturale additum, & post lapsum in Homine Naturalia mansisse integra: consequens fuerit, frustra Filium Dei assumpsisse Naturam nostram, ut eam in integrum restitueret: id quod vel cogitatu longè absurdissimum fuerit.

Tandem quarti argumenti loco producimus B. Lutherum nostrum, in aureo illo suo commentario, super Cap. 3. Genes. sic de hac quæstione differentem: Scholastici disputant, Quòd Justitia Originalis non fuerit connaturalis: sed ceu ornatus quidam, additus homini, tanquam donum: ut si quis formosæ puellæ coronam imponat. Corona certè non est pars Naturæ Virginis: sed quiddam separatum à natura, quod ab extra accedit, & sine violatione naturæ potest iterum adimi. Quare disputant de homine & dæmonibus, quòd, etsi Originalem Iustitiam amiserint, tamen Naturalia manserint pura, sicut initiò condita sunt. Sed hæc sententia, quia peccatum Originis extenuat, ceu venenum fugienda est. Quin hoc statuamus, Iustitiam non fuisse quoddam donum, quod ab extra accederet, separatum à natura hominis: sed fuisse verè Naturalem, ita ut Natura Adæ esset, diligere Deum, credere Deo, agnoscere Deum &c. Hæc tam naturalia fuêre in Adamo, quàm naturale est, quod oculi lumen recipiunt. Quia autem si oculum vitiosum reddas inflicto vulnere, rectè dicas, Naturam violatam esse: Ita postquam homo ex justitia in peccatum lapsus est, rectè & verè dicitur: Naturalia non integra, sed corrupta esse per peccatum. Sicut enim naturæ oculi est videre: Ita naturâ rationis & voluntatis in Adamo fuit, nosse Deum, fidere Deo, timere Deum. Hæc cùm jam amissa esse constet, quis tàm amens est, qui dicat: Naturalia adhuc esse integra.

Posterius thesews nostræ membrum confirmat initiò Epiphonema illud, quod Moses creationis historiæ subjicit: Vidit Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, ecce erant valdè bona: Genes. 1, 31. Jam si valdè Bonus fuit homo, utique pugna illa & rixa inferiorum virium cum superioribus, languor item de difficultas benè agendi in homine, minimè potuit subsistere: præsertim cùm Deus non simpliciter Bonum, sed cum adjecta particula emphatica, VALDE Bonum hominem à se creatum pronunciet.

Ratio consecutionis patet evidentissima isthæc: Nam si in primo homine fuit pugna inferiorum virium & superiorum: his quidem ad Bonum, illis ad malum naturâ inclinantibus: utique innata quæpiam vis ac facultas mala, Deiquè odio digna, ipsi indita fuerit necesse est: Si hoc: Ergo Deus non valdè Bonum creavit Hominem, sed malæ illius indolis sive facultatis Autor erit constituendus. Atqui hoc blasphemum & absurdum: Ergò ejusdem impietatis fuerit & illud, quod te tali pugna in primo homine fingunt Jesuvvitæ.


### Chapter II. Anthesis: On the Third Jesuitical Error concerning the doctrine of the Image of God and Original Justice (continued)

Bellarmino objects that that struggle was indeed natural to the first man, but that it neither drew its origin from God nor was contrary to nature itself, because it existed in man not from the intention of the Author of nature, but beyond his intention. Truly, what the Jesuit says at the beginning he does not prove; he begs the question. Furthermore, he increases impiety with impiety: for what else does this Jesuitical exception mean than that God, the creator of this universe, was so impotent or weak that He could not, between matter and form, between flesh and spirit, create the most noble creature, man, from formless clay, with the best order, harmony, conformity, and concord of all powers.

Another argument of our confirmation can be such: Wherever there is an inclination to evil, from which a struggle arises against the spirit, there is the first act of corruption and sin, and of the consequent destruction or death. But in the first man, such a first act did not exist. Therefore, neither did that inclination to evil, or the struggle of flesh and spirit.

The major premise is superior to every exception, as the Apostle teaches: Rom. 5:12, Through sin death entered into the world. And chapter 6:23, The wages of sin is death.

The truth of the minor premise is evident from that saying in Wisdom 2:23, God created man in incorruption, and made him an image of his own likeness: ὁ θεὸς ἔκτισε τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπὶ ἀφθαρσίᾳ, καὶ εἰκόνα τῆς ἰδίας ἰδιότητος ἐποίησεν αὐτόν. Furthermore, it is evident from that Ecclesiastes 7:30, God made man upright. Therefore, there was no obliquity in him, no curvature, no propensity from God toward vices: finally, no defect, as much in the lower as in the higher faculties, as Augustine gathers in his book De correptione et gratia, ch. 10.

The entire argument is provided by the excellence of human Nature, by which it surpasses all other living creatures in infinite ways. For if in the first man there was such a struggle or conflict of the lower powers with the higher, he must certainly have been worse than any brute animal whatsoever: since the nature of brutes is entirely devoid of such rebellion or conflict. Nor is it for them to object a reason for the difference, taken from the use of reason, with which Man is endowed. For they ought to remember that they themselves constitute the cause and source of that conflict, not the use of reason: but the condition of matter, which even they are not unaware is common to brutes and men.

Finally, that fictitious conflict in the first man is disallowed both by his nakedness and by his constitution in paradise. For the fact that Adam and Eve walked naked was the highest adornment before God. Now after sin, we not only flee the sight of men naked: but we are ashamed even before ourselves: from which the integrity and uprightness of the lower powers, and thus of the whole of human Nature, is most rightly inferred, as our blessed Luther teaches. Had he persisted in this integrity, he would have been translated from the earthly Paradise to the heavenly, with no death or corruption intervening.

The Jesuits oppose themselves to this purer doctrine of ours with great effort, and among them especially Bellarmine: contending at the beginning that that depraved concupiscence, or rather that inclination to evil, or conflict of the lower powers against the higher is from the condition of matter. For thus he says in chapter 7, page 28, column C: the concupiscence of the flesh is indeed now a punishment for sin: but for man created in pure naturals it would have been without doubt natural, not indeed as some good of nature, but as a defect, and as it were a certain disease of nature, following from the condition of matter.

To the refutation of this sophism must first be prefixed a distinction between the twofold object of concupiscence: for either it is concerned with moral evil: so that concupiscence is nothing else than a motion, inclination, or action fighting against the law of God: or it is concerned with some physical object: as when a man desires his own preservation. Concerning which latter object there is no question in this place: since we ourselves readily admit that concupiscence considered in this way is natural to man: but the question is concerning the former object: whether concupiscence, insofar as it is directed toward moral evil, is natural to man, and depends upon the condition of matter? Where the Jesuit holds the affirmative: but we altogether concede to the negative, relying on these reasons.

1. Either they understand by matter the body, or the soul of man: but they cannot understand the soul, since it is not a material thing, but a spirit. Therefore it is necessary that they understand the body. Now, however, it is manifest, so as to need no proof, that to the body and its members, humors, and temperaments, primarily no concupiscence belongs, whether ordered or disordered. The reason is because the appetitive power or faculty is not a power or faculty of the body, but of the soul. Therefore, whatever the Jesuits blather in this place about the condition of matter is nonsensical.

2. The nature of man was so created in the beginning that it had no appetite except one that was ordered and in agreement with the law of God: which is most evidently demonstrated from the human nature of Christ the Savior, which, being indeed destitute of all sin, represented in naturals most perfectly the human nature as it was created in the beginning before the fall. But such a struggle of the lower powers with the higher was not in the human nature of Christ, but all natural passions were ordered. Therefore, there was a like reason also for human nature before the fall, so that whatever it desired, it desired in an ordered way, such as was the conjugal love in Adam, since it tended toward that end which, among others, God also looked to in the creation of man: namely, to the propagation of his species. It is added that the Jesuits, only through a stupendous absurdity, would name the nature of man, and indeed the appetitive nature, matter: if by chance they wished to retreat to this evasion, that they are speaking neither of the body nor of the soul, but of the nature of man.

3. If that inclination to evil arises from the condition of matter, and indeed in the first man before the fall: certainly it would follow that God is the author of that very inclination to evil and thus of sin: The reason is: Because God is the author of that very matter. Bellarmine indeed objects that God is free from blame in this part, because He superadded to man original justice, which would restrain that struggle and make peace between the flesh and the spirit. But I reply that not even in this way is the evidence of our reason infringed: for granted, but not conceded, that God superadded original justice to man for this end: nevertheless, there remained in the flesh that headlong inclination to vices, which man following, at length (as Bellarmine fabulates) fell into sin. Where that still remains in question, whence then that headlong inclination to vices? If the Jesuit replies, as he indeed replies, from the condition of matter: we immediately infer: But God is the author of that matter, therefore: He will also be the author of that headlong inclination to evil, since it was natural to the first man from his first creation: as the Jesuits contend.

4. Finally, in whatever subject the struggle of the lower powers with the higher reigns, or a headlong inclination to vices: there also reigns mortality, since through it is most correctly gathered the disorder of human powers. Therefore man was to die from the condition of matter, even if he had not sinned. But by the testimony of Scripture, man was created for life and immortality, which he himself also actually attained, and would have been translated from an animal life into a heavenly one, without the intervention of death, if he had persisted in integrity. Therefore, what the Romanists chatter about that struggle is fictitious and nonsensical: and consequently, the truth is most clear and immovable, that man was created in the beginning by God, not indeed so that he could not die, which immortality we attain at some time in eternal life: but so that he could not die, if indeed he had not sinned.

Bellarmine, in order to be able to extricate himself in some way from that difficulty, has woven the web of a new question, anxiously disputing whether the immortality of our first parents was a natural gift, or a condition of nature; or whether it was a supernatural gift: and at length he concludes that death and the other human defects, to which we are subject through the fall of our first parents, are from the nature of man in itself; and therefore that immortality for the first man was beyond nature, or a supernatural gift: but that mortality was natural.

Which assertion indeed teems with infinite absurdities. For 1. Death is the wages of sin. And through sin death entered into the world. Therefore it is false and erroneous that mortality was natural to that nature which was still devoid of sin. 2. If death follows the condition of nature: this condition must certainly be evil: for if it were good, it would not be subject to death: now if it is evil, it will be false for both that Moses asserts, that God saw all things that He had made, and that all were very good: but this is absurd and blasphemous. Therefore. 3. Death is the effect or wages of sin: Therefore if before the fall Death was Natural to human nature, it would follow either that Man was created in sin, or that it is false that Death is the effect of sin: But both of these are monstrously absurd: Therefore. 4. If the Jesuitical opinion stands, no use could be given for the tree of life: Now, however, the use of that tree was granted to man before the fall for this reason, that by its benefit Man might preserve the powers of his Body lively, in continuous vigor and youth, until he was transferred from this animal life to the heavenly one, at that time when it seemed good to God. 5. If the corruption of Nature depends on the condition of Matter. Therefore it does not depend on Original sin: which is what conflicts most openly with scripture. And indeed the Jesuits are so blinded that they can hardly recognize the power of Original sin. Whence Bellarmine also, from Thomas, writes no less ignorantly than impiously: chap. 5. From Original sin, which consists not in act, but in habit, there arises directly no inclination to evil: but indirectly, as a removing of that which prohibits. 5. And finally, the unanimous consensus of the Holy Fathers is repugnant: Let one Basil suffice, asserting that God the creator created human bodies in the beginning with a preparation suitable to them according to nature, so that they might have an equal temperament of all qualities, and for the maintenance of this, might have the use of the various, and most wholesome, fruits of Paradise as a Natural means.

Latin:

Excipit Bellarminus, Pugnam quidem illam fuisse primo homini Naturalem: sed eam neq; à Deo traxisse Originem, neq; Naturæ ipsi fuisse contrariam, propterea quòd non ex intentione Autoris Naturæ,sed præter ejus intentionem in homine eâ extiterit. Verum initiò quod dicit Jesuvvita, nonprobat, E.petit principium. Deindè impietatem impietate auget: Quid enim Exceptio isthæc Jesuvvitica sibi vult aliud, quàm Deum conditorem hujus universi, usque adeò impotentem aut infirmum fuisse, ut non posset, inter materiam & formam, inter Carnem & Spiritum, Ordinem longè optimum, harmoniam, conformitatem & concordiam omnium virium ex informi luto, Hominem nobilissimam Creaturam efficere potuit.

Alterum confirmationis nostræ argumentum tale esse potest: Vbicunq; est ad malum inclinatio, ex qua pugna oritur adversus spiritum: ibi est actus primus corrupti nis & peccati: & consequentis destructionis sive mortis. Atqui in primô homine talis actus primus non fuit. Ergò neq; illa ad malum inclinatio, sive pugna Carnis & Spiritus.

Major omni exceptione superior est, sic docente Apostolo: Rom. 5, 12. Per peccatum mors intravit in mundum Et cap. 6, 23. Stipendium peccati Mors.

Minoris veritas patet ex illo dicto Sap. 2, 23. Deus creavit hominem in incorruptione, & Imaginem propriæ similitudinis fecit eum: ὁ θεὸς ἔκτισε τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπὶ ἀφθαρσίᾳ, καὶ εἰκόνα τῆς ἰδίας ἰδιότητος ἐποίησεν αὐτόν. Deindè patet ex illo Ecclesiaste 7, 30. Deus fecit hominem rectum. Ergo nulla in eo obliquitas, nulla curvitas, nulla à Deo ad vitia propensio: nullus deniq; defectus, tàm in Inferioribus quàm Superioribus facultatibus, uti Augustinus colligit lib. de corrept. & grat. c. 10.

Totum argumentum subministrat præstantia Naturæ humanæ, quâ reliqua animantia omnia infinitis modis superat. Quod si enim in primo homine talis fuit pugna sive rixa virium inferiorum cum superioribus, certè quo libet bruto animante deterior ipse fuerit, necesse est: Siquidem brutorum natura, ejusmodi rebellionis sive pugnæ prorsus est expers. Neque est ut diversitatis rationem objiciant, petitam ex usu rationis, quo Homo est præditus. Meminisse enim debent, seipsos causam atque fontem pugnæ illius constituere non usum rationis: Sed conditionem materiæ, quam brutis cum hominib9 communem esse, vel ipsi haud ignorant.

Tandem fictitiam istam pugnam in primo homine non admittit tùm ipsius nuditas, tùm ejusdem in paradiso constitutio. Nam quòd Adam & Heva nudi incesserunt, fuit summus ornatus coram Deo. Nunc post peccatum, non solùm fugimus hominum conspectum nudi: Sed etiam coram nobis ipsis verecundamur: undè inferiorum etiam virium, & sic totius Naturæ humanæ integritas & rectitudo, sic docente B. Luthero nostro rectissimè colligitur. Quâ integritate si perstitisset, ex terrestri Paradiso in cœlestem, nulla interveniente morte aut corruptione translatus fuisset.

Puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ magno conatu se opponunt Jesuvvitæ, & inter hos cumprimis Bellarminus: initiò contendens, pravam illam concupiscentiā, vel potiùs inclinationē istam ad malū, sive pugnam virium inferio...um advers9 superiores esse ex conditione materiæ. Sic enim ille cap. 7. p 28. C. concupiscentia Carnis nunc quidem pœna peccati est: sed Homini condito in puris naturalibus fuisset sine dubio naturalis, non quidem, ut Bonum aliquod naturæ, sed ut defectus, & quasi morbus quidam naturæ, ex conditione materiæ consequens.

Refutationi Sophismatis hujus initiò præmittenda est distinctio inter Concupiscentiæ objectum geminum: vel enim ea versatur circa Malum morale: ita ut Concupiscentia nihil sit aliud, quàm motus, inclinatio, sive actio pugnans cum lege Dei: vel versatur circa objectum aliquod physicum: ut quando homo sui desiderat conservationem. De quo posteriore objecto hoc loco non quæritur: Siquidem ipsi ultrò fatemur, Concupiscentiam hoc modo consideratam esse homini Naturalem: Sed de priore objecto quæritur: utrum Concupiscentia, quatenùs fertur ad malum morale, sit Homini Naturalis, & à Materiæ conditione dependeat? Ubi Jesuvvita affirmantem tenet: Nos verò in Negantem omninò concedimus, his freti rationibus.

1. Aut perm Materiam intell gunt Corpus, aut Animam Hominis: Atqui Animam intelligere non possunt, quippè quæ non est materiatum aliquid, sed Spiritus. Ergo corpus intelligant necesse est. Jam verò manifestus est, quàm ut probatione indigeat, corpori ejusque membris, humoribus & temperamentis πρώτως nullam competere Concupiscentiam, sive ordinatam, sive inordinatam. Ratio est, quia vis ἐπιθυμητικὴ sive appetitiva non est δύναμις sive facultas corporis, sed Animæ. Ergo nugatorium est, quicquid de Materiæ conditione hoc loco blaterant Esavvitæ.

2 Natura hominis sic initiò condita fuit, ut appetitum non nisi ordinatum & cum Lege Dei congruenter haberet: id quod evidentissime demonstratur ex Natura humana Christi Servatoris, quæ quippè omni peccato destituta in Naturalibus perfectissimè repræsentabat Naturam humanam, qualis ea ante Lapsum initiò erat condita. Atqui talis pugna virium inferiorum cum superioribus, in Humana Natura Christi non fuit, sed omnia naturalia παθήματα fuerunt ordinata. Ergo par ratio fuit quoque Naturæ humanæ ante lapsum, ita ut quicquid appeteret, illud ordinatè appeteret, Qualis appetitus erat in Adamo Amor conjugalis, quippè qui tendebat ad eum finem, quem inter reliquos, Deus in creatione hominis etiam spectavit: nempè ad propagationem suæ speciei. Accedit quòd Jesuvvitæ non nisi per stupendam absurditatem, Naturam hominis & quidem Appetitivam nominarent Materiam: si fortè ad hoc effugium se recipere vellent, se neque de corpore, neque de Anima: sed de Natura hominis loqui.

3. Si ex Materiæ conditione oritur Inclinatio illa ad malum, & quidem in primo homine ante lapsum: Certè consequens fuerit, Deum esse autorem illius ipsius inclinationis ad malum & sic peccati: Ratio est: Quia illius ipsius materiæ autor est Deus. Excipit quidem Bellarminus, DEUM hac in parte culpa vacare, propterea quod superaddidit homini Justitiam Originalem, quæ pugnam illam coërceret, & pacem inter carnem & spiritum faceret. Sed respondeo ne sic quidem infringi Rationis nostræ evidentiam: Posito enim, sed non concesso, Deum superaddidisse hoc fine homini Justitiam Originalem: nihilominus tamen mansit in carne præceps illa ad vitia inclinatio, quam secutus homo, tandem (uti Bellarminus fabulatur) in peccatum prolapsus est. Ubi manet illud adhuc in quæstione, unde nam præceps illa ad vitia inclinatio? Si respondet Jesuvita, uti sanè respondet, Ex materiæ conditione: Nos statim inferimus: Atqui Materiæ illius Autor est DEUS, Ergo: Autor etiam erit præcipitis illius inclinationis ad malum, quippè quæ primo Homini ex prima creatione Naturalis fuit: uti Esavvitæ contendunt.

4. Tandem in quocunque subjecto regnat pugna inferiorum virium cum superioribus, sive præceps inclinatio ad vitia: ibi quoque regnat Mortalitas, quippè per quam rectissimè colligitur, virium humanarum ἀταξία. Ergò Homo ex Materiæ conditione moriturus erat, licet non peccasset, Atqui scriptura teste, Homo conditus est ad vitam & immortalitatem, quam ipse etiam actu consecutus, & ex animali vita in cælestem, sine mortis interventu, translatus fuisset, si integritate perstitisset. Ergò commentitium & nugatorium est, quod de pugna illa garriunt Romanenses: & per consequens liquidissima ac inmota est veritatis, Hominem initiò à Deo esse conditum, non quidem ut non posset mori, Quam immortalitatem aliquando in vita æterna consequemur: Sed ut posset non mori, si nimirum non peccasset?

Bellarminus ut ex ista difficultate aliquo modo se extricare possit, novæ quæstionis telam pertexit, sollicitè disputans, Anne primorum parentum immortalitas, fuerit donum Naturale, vel Naturæ conditio; An verò donum supernaturale vel Naturæ conditio; An verò donum supernaturale: & tandem concludit, Mortem & cæteros defectus humanos, quibus per lapsum primorum parentum obnoxij sumus, esse à Natura hominis per se; ac proindè immortalitatem primo homini fuisse præter Naturam, sive donum supernaturale: Mortalitatem verò Naturalem.

Quæ sanè assertio infinitis scatet absurditatibus. Nam 1. Mors est Stipendium peccati. Et per peccatum Mors intravit in mundum. Ergò falsum & erroneum: Mortalitatem fuisse naturalem ei Naturæ, quæ peccati adhuc erat expers. 2. Si mors sequitur conditionem Naturæ: hac utiq́; conditio mala sit necesse est: Nam bona si esset, Morti non subjaceret: Jam mala si est, falsum utrique erit, quod Moses asserit, vidisse Deum cuncta quæ fecerat, & omnia fuisse valdè bona: Atqui hoc absurdum & blasphemum. Ergò. 3. Mors est effectus sive stipendium peccati: Ergo si ante lapsum Mors Naturæ humanæ fuit Naturalis, consequens fuerit, vel Hominem in peccato esse conditum, vel falsum, quod Mors sit effectus peccati: Atqui utrumque hoc prodigiosè est absurdum: E. 4. Stante sententia Esavvitica, nullus posset dari usus arboris vitæ: Jam verò ideò arboris istius usus ante lapsum homini erat concessus, ut ejus beneficio vires Corporis vegetas, in continuo vigore & juventa Homo conservaret, donec ex animali hac vita ad cælestem transferretur, eo tempore, quo Deo visum esset. 5. Si corruptio Naturæ pendet ex coditione Materiæ. Ergo non pendet ex peccato Originali: id quod pugnat cùm scriptura apertissimè. Et profectò usque adeò excæcati sunt Jesuvvitæ, ut peccati Originalis vim haud agnoscere queant. Unde Bellarminus etiam ex Thoma, non magis inscitè quàm impiè scribit: cap. 5. Ex peccato Originali, quod non in actu, sed in habitu consistit, non oritur directè ulla inclinatio ad malum: sed indirectè, tanquam ex removente prohibens 5. & postremò repugnat unanimis consensus S. Patrum: Sufficiat unus Basilius asserens, Deum opificem Corpora humana initiò in conveniente ipsis secundum naturam præparatione condidisse, ut æquale omnium qualitatum temperamentum haberet, & ad hujus conversationem, variorum, eorumquè saluberrimorum fructuum Paradisi usum, tanquam medium Naturale haberet.


### Chapter II. Anthesis: On the Third Jesuitical Error concerning the doctrine of the Image of God and Original Justice (continued)

But it is asked at this point: Was not the Body of Adam corruptible by Nature for the reason that it consisted of four Elements and various humors? But it is most correctly answered that, after the fall, the corruption of our bodies is indeed most correctly inferred from this, that they necessarily have to be resolved into the four Elements because they are composed of them. But if you ask: Is this of absolute necessity, and does it depend on the condition of Nature itself primarily and immediately? Then I answer negatively: For the first cause and Origin of this mortality and corruption is sin, as Scripture testifies. Now if man had persisted in integrity, God could certainly have preserved his Body also, however much it was composed of diverse Elements and humors, without corruptibility, in perpetual health and immortality: according to that passage in Wisdom 2:23, God created man for incorruption.

But furthermore it is asked: Did not GOD himself wish to intimate that the Body of Adam was of itself subject to Mortality: in that he wished to create it from the dust of the earth, as a certain sign of corruptibility? To which question it is most correctly answered, by observing the distinction between Act and Potency. For the first man was not created so devoid of all corruption, as regards potency, as the Angels, who have absolutely no potency or power toward corruptibility: for in this way Man could never have died: But neither was he created mortal in such a way as we are now after the fall: where we die as we are born, and death depends on our origin. But he was created immortal in act itself, in such a way that he was nevertheless mortal in potency, if indeed he should transgress the commandment of God. Therefore, an evident sign of this potency or possibility toward death and corruption was that creation of Man from the dust of the earth: which potency, however, would never have erupted into act if he had not transgressed the command of God, however much he had been created from the dust of the earth. But after the fall, the potency passed into act in such a way that now we are Mortal and are born in act itself: not only because of the condition of the matter from which man is created: but primarily because of the horrible corruption of all the powers of both Soul and Body.

And this indeed is the doctrine of the Roman pseudo-Catholic Church concerning the Image of God and Original Justice: which, although it is in all ways absurd and impious, nevertheless seems so plausible to the Jesuits that they are solicitous even to the point of superstition to confirm it from the Scriptures.

And in the beginning, indeed, he brings forward that passage from Genesis 3:19, Dust you are, and to dust you shall return. He contends that the meaning of these words is this: Although I made you very glorious by my kindness, so that you could fear neither death nor any evils: nevertheless by your nature you were dust, mortal, fragile, and subject to pains and labors: and because you were despoiled of that superadded gift of mine by your own fault, and have fallen back into your natural state, therefore now you are also dust, and to dust you shall return.

I answer: An error of confusion of disparate questions is committed: and a malicious perversion of the state of the case. For the controversy at this point is about the Image of God, the seat of which was primarily in the soul of man: namely, whether such a conflict as the Adversaries imagine could have fallen into it from the first creation. Where, when the Adversaries ought to prove their affirmative, they bring forward a passage of such a kind that it deals with nothing at all concerning the condition of the Soul: but only concerning the first Origin of the human body. Now, however, from the condition of the Body to the condition of the Soul, the consequence is not valid. What is more? That not even from that formation of the human body from the slime or dust of the earth did fragility, mortality, pains, and labors follow immediately in act itself: but only the potency of those infirmities, as we showed a little earlier.

The Jesuit borrows another testimony of Scripture from chapter 17:2 of Ecclesiasticus: GOD created man from the earth, and clothed him with power according to himself.

Whence the Jesuit concludes that Original Justice, like a garment, was superadded to man by God.

I answer: 1. No ἔλεγχος can be derived from the word of clothing, since it is predicated not only of supernatural and externally occurring things, but also of natural and substantial things: as when God is read to have clothed man with flesh and skin; Job 10, 11. From which, however, it will by no means be right to conclude that flesh and skin are supernatural gifts. Next, a faulty version of the Vulgate Latin occurs. For according to himself, that is, according to God: but according to the man himself: For thus the Greek words sound: καὶ ἐνέδυσεν αὐτὸς καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸς ἰχύν: He clothed them with strength according to themselves. Therefore that strength was not supernatural, but according to the men themselves, namely, most suitable to their nature.

The Jesuit takes a third passage of scripture from that parable in Luke 10:30 concerning the man stripped and wounded: From which he concludes that the wounds inflicted on our nature do not spring from original sin, nor properly from the corruption of man's nature: but from the nature of Adam, such as it was created by itself in the beginning.

I answer: 1. Parables are not to be extended further than their own end and scope allow. Now, the end and scope of that parable in Luke 10:30 was in no way a description of either original justice or original sin: but only the love of one's neighbor. Furthermore, although it may be adapted to the present state of the controversy through some allegory: it does not at all follow that which the adversary intends. For no logic of consequence holds if the collection is set up thus: Man was first stripped, then wounded: Therefore original justice was not natural to the first man. For by equal logic someone could infer thus: A blind man is stripped of the faculty of seeing: Therefore, this faculty was not natural to him: Or: Someone possessed by the devil is stripped of the use of right reason: Therefore the use of right reason is not natural to man. Where anyone easily understands the vanity of the argument.

But the Jesuit, destitute of the protection of the Scriptures, seeks to defend his cause with certain little arguments, which it will be worth the effort to weigh in a few words.

The first reason is as follows: Whatever consists of flesh and rational spirit is subject to the struggle or fight of flesh and spirit: and indeed by the condition of nature: so that it cannot be averted and prohibited except by a supernatural gift coming from without. But the first man consisted of flesh and rational spirit. Therefore.

The Jesuit proves the connection of the major premise thus: Man, in that part where he is flesh, shares with beasts, and has a certain propensity toward bodily and sensible good, toward which he is carried by sense and appetite: On the other hand, where he is spirit, he shares with the angels, and has a propensity toward spiritual and intelligible good, toward which he is carried by intelligence and will. But from these diverse or contrary propensities there exists in one and the same man a certain struggle, and from that struggle, a huge difficulty in doing good, while one propensity hinders the other.

I answer: The argument fails, 1. by begging the question and by the fallacy of accident. For the hypothesis is false, and labors under a most faulty opposition, from which the Jesuit reasons. For bodily and spiritual, or sensible and intelligible good, ought not to be opposed to each other contradictorily as contraries: but they stand only as disparate or subordinate things, which do not acquire a contrary affection between them except by accident. 2. A sophistry of ignorance of the refutation is committed. For no refutation holds when the Jesuit argues thus: Man consists of flesh and rational spirit. Therefore, already from his first creation, he is subject to the struggle or fight of flesh and spirit: For that such a struggle is now detected in man is to be ascribed not to the first creation, but entirely to the corruption of our nature: and thus it belongs to man again by accident. Certainly the first man, although he consisted of flesh and spirit, was nevertheless so devoid of all struggle that rather a supreme harmony of the lower powers with the higher, whatever good you might consider, flourished in him: and that by the force or virtue of the divine image, to which he had been created: as was demonstrated above. Once this was destroyed, that disorder finally began, and thus by accident the flesh lusts against the spirit.

The second reason is as follows: If the corruption which is now in man proceeds neither from God, nor from the forbidden fruit, nor from the breath of the serpent, nor from pure natural faculties, it follows that it proceeds from the removal of a supernatural gift. But the former is true: therefore the latter is also established: and consequently it is posited that the efficient cause of this corruption is the condition of the matter in the first man: the meritorious cause is the sin of Adam: and finally, Divine justice, despoiling man of the supernatural gift, is the cause removing the impediment to the second act.

I answer: The argument suffers, 1. from the incompleteness of the division. For the major proposition omits the true and principal efficient cause of the corruption of our nature; which is the loss of the divine image, and the horrible destruction of that excellent and perpetual harmony of all the faculties, which obtained in the nature of man before the fall, which immediately followed this. The far most sorrowful effect of which destruction was this, that whereas before man desired nothing but what was good and right, now by nature he desires only what is evil. 2. The argument fails by the fallacy of Ignoratio Elenchi. For neither, as the Esauite sophistically argues, is the viciousness of concupiscence to be defined only by the disorder of the lower faculties, since rather, as Scripture teaches, it has its place chiefly in the higher faculties of the human mind: so that every figment, every pursuit of the human mind and heart is only evil from youth.

Which certainly most sorrowful condition of our nature does not depend upon the removal of any supernatural gift, which would have left the natural faculties intact: nor even from a natural or animal appetite, straying from the right path: but it depends entirely upon the destruction of the higher and lower powers and the harmony of all powers in Man: as the following Article will show.

Bellarmino's third argument sounds thus: The account of actual sins in the Reborn after the fall is the same as the account of the actual sin committed by Adam: But the Reborn do not lose any property of their Nature through actual sins: but only a supernatural gift: Therefore Adam also, through the actual sin committed by him, did not lose anything of the property of Nature: but while the natural things remained safe, he lost only some supernatural gift.

I answer: The error arises ὥς γε τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς [in a certain respect and simply]: and from a faulty consequence. For the major proposition is not true simply or in its entirety: but only in a certain respect, or in part. For although the sins of the reborn and of Adam agree in respect of the Genus, in that both obtain the name and definition of actual sins: yet if you look at their source and origin, a very great disparity presents itself. For in the reborn, nature itself is so polluted and corrupted by sin that it cannot but repeatedly conceive wicked desires and designate actual sins, through which they lose and forfeit a supernatural gift, namely the Grace of Regeneration, unless they repent. But in Adam, Nature was optimal and most perfect; so that he could as easily not sin as sin: and therefore he committed sin not from the condition of Nature, but from spontaneous disobedience: whence he lost and forfeited not only some supernatural gift, but the perfection and integrity of the natural powers themselves in spiritual matters, not only for himself, but also for his entire posterity, by which degrees of disparity being duly considered, the falsity of both premises and the stupendous vanity of the whole argument spontaneously shine forth.

Bellarmino's fourth argument is this: Many were recalled from death to this life, some of whom were purged from original sin, and yet lacked original justice, so that they were in all things similar to infants brought into the light by the ordinary way. Therefore original justice was a supernatural gift, which could be taken away from man while the natural things remained safe.

I answer: The Jesuit is trifling rather than arguing. For first, he takes for granted that which is most in doubt: namely, whether those resurrected lacked original sin? Where indeed we believe it must be distinguished at the outset between those resurrected who, when Christ rose from the dead, themselves also came forth from the tombs and were translated into heaven: and those who, not yet reduced to dust, were recalled to life and lived longer in these lands. That the former were purged from original sin, we indeed willingly concede: but we reply that the consequence does not hold from the condition of the latter to the state of the rest of the resurrected. For because original sin so pervaded the entire substance of man that it cannot be thoroughly extirpated unless the body is reduced to dust: certainly the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles who were resurrected before they had seen the total corruption of their flesh were by no means purged from original sin. 2. A fallacy is committed παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχꙋ [ignoring the refutation]: and that in two ways: first, when a conclusion is established from miracles to build a common rule: when yet the account of those very miracles has not yet been fully explained. But then, when some middle state of men, lacking original vice and original justice, is imagined: about which Scripture has not uttered even a γρῦ [a syllable]. 3. The Jesuit's reasoning is ἀσύ- στατον [inconsistent] and overturns itself through a shameful contradiction. For if Lazarus, if the infants and others resurrected by Elijah, Elisha, Christ, and the Apostles, had to die again: they were certainly still infected with original sin. The reason is: Because death is the wages of sin, Rom. 6:23. Now the cause being removed, the effect is removed: But they had to die: Since it cannot be demonstrated from the scriptures that they were translated alive into heaven. Therefore they were subject to original sin even after resurrection: and indeed from the condition of their nature: but not, as Pelagius dreamed, only from imitation or the examples of others.

The fifth and final argument of the Jesuit can be formed thus: The first parents were raised to that dignity, that they were Children of GOD, and certain Gods, that is, partakers of the divine nature. But it is most absurd for a created thing, such as man, to make GOD, or a child of GOD, naturally. Therefore that dignity was a supernatural gift, which could be taken away while the natural things remained safe.

I answer: The Adversary plays with a childish equivocation on the word Naturally. For either it sounds the same as to be GOD or the Son of GOD by the Essence of Nature: In which sense, indeed, our first parents were not Sons of GOD, for thus they would no longer have been Men: But would have been incorporeal Spirits: which is false and absurd: or it denotes some conformity of human Nature with the divine, by reason of concrete holiness and justice: by which Man, not by the grace of Reconciliation or Regeneration, as now after the fall: but from creation itself, and thus by some concrete grace, bore the Image and likeness of GOD: According to that: Let us make Man in our Image and Likeness. This grace of creation, since it has been lost and forfeited through sin: it comes to pass, indeed, that now we are no longer Sons of GOD by Nature (in the sense already explained) but only by Adoption: and consequently that the natural things in man are most miserably corrupted and depraved.

Finally, the Jesuit produces a good many Fathers, by whose authority he claims his opinion can be confirmed: but what ought to be answered to this kind of argument will easily appear, if we have the following hypotheses in view:

1. The Fathers are not sufficiently consistent with themselves in defining the proposed controversy: but they go off into such various opinions that nothing certain can be elicited from their own writings: as is indeed clearly evident from the treatment of Bellarmine himself in chapter 6.

2. The force of the Pelagian heresy was so great that not a few otherwise Orthodox Fathers, avoiding one extreme of Manichaeism, lapsed into the contrary hyperbole of Pelagianism: and too much extenuated Original Sin: maintaining that in Angels and Men after the fall the Natural faculties remained intact: a thing which conflicts diametrically with Scripture, as the following Article will show.

3. Some Fathers, denying that Man was holy by nature, do not treat of the mode of inherence by which holiness was conferred upon Man: But only of its Origin: namely, that they are not holy as GOD is holy by Essence, or rather that they are not Holiness itself: a thing which we also deny: but only that they received that holiness from the grace of the Holy Spirit: by no means, however, denying in the meantime that the first parents, from the origin of their creation, had a Nature endowed with this property of righteousness and Holiness pleasing to GOD, as a faculty concreated and natural, yet separable from the Essence itself.

Finally, the Fathers understood this phrase in a far different sense than the Jesuits: "The Natural faculties remained after the fall." For the Jesuits mean by this that the Nature of Man, not only according to its parts or Essential properties, such as it is even now after the fall, remained intact: but also such as it was before the fall, with respect to the powers of body and soul.

The Fathers, however, and indeed our Blessed Luther, in affirming that the Natural faculties remained intact after the fall, understand Nature as it consists of its constituent parts, the body and the rational Soul, and the natural properties of these parts: Which indeed were not destroyed or abolished by the fall: as we shall soon show against the Flacians. Now, however, from the affirmation of those Essential parts, the consequence does not hold for the affirmation of those most perfect powers which were concreated with those Essential parts, and thus were truly Natural before the fall: but are now destroyed by the fall, and transmuted into contrary qualities. Concerning which matter our Blessed Luther speaks thus excellently: When the Sophists say that the Natural faculties are intact: I concede this: But if they infer: Therefore man can love GOD, I deny the consequence, and I distinguish the Natural from the Spiritual: and I say that the Spiritual are not intact, but corrupted, nay, utterly extinguished by sin in Man and the Devil, so that there is nothing there but a depraved Intellect, and a will hostile and adversarial to GOD, which thinks of nothing but those things which are against GOD. Wherefore the Natural faculties are indeed intact: But which natural ones? That man, immersed in Impiety and a slave of the Devil, has Reason, will, Free choice, and the power of building a house, holding a Magistracy, steering a ship, and performing other duties which are subject to man. Gen. 1. These are not taken away from man, nor are generation, Politics, and Economics abolished by these words, but confirmed.

Latin:

Sed quæritur hoc loco: Annon ideò Corpus Adami fuerit corruptibile Naturâ, quia constabat ex quatuor Elementis & variis humoribus? Sed rectissimè respondetur, post lapsum quidem rectissimè hinc colligi corruptionem nostrorum corporum, ut nimirum ideò tandem in quatuor Elementa resolvi necesse habeant quia ex ijs sunt conflata. Verùm nisi quæas: An hoc absolutæ sit necessitatis, & dependeat ex ipsius Naturæ conditione πρώτως & immediatè? Tum negatè respondeo: Prima enim causa & Origo hujus mortalitatis & corruptionis est peccatum, teste Scriptura. Jam si homo in integritate perstitisset, utique Deus Corpus etiam ipsius, quantumvis ex Elementis & humoribus diversis conflatum, sine corruptibilitate, in perpetua sanitate & immortalitate conservare potuisset: secundum illud Sap. 2, 23. Deus condidit hominem επ' αφθαρσία, in incorruptione.

Sed porrò quæritur: Annon DEUS ipse innuere voluerit, Corpus Adami per se esse Mortalitati obnoxium: eò quòd illud ex pulvere terræ, tanquàm corruptibilitatis certo indicio creare voluit: Ad quod ζήτημα rectissimè respondetur, observata distinctione inter Actum & Potentiam. Homo enim primus non ita omnis corruptionis expers, quoad δύναμιν, est conditus, quemadmodum Angeli, qui nullam prorsus habent δύναμιν sive potentiam ad corruptibilitatem: Hoc enim pacto Homo nunquam mori potuisset: Sed neque ita mortalis est conditus, uti nunc post lapsum sumus: ubi Nascentes do morimur, finúque ab origine pendet Verùm sic ipso actu immortalis erat conditus, ut tamen τη δυνάμει esset mortalis, si nimirùm transgrederetur præceptum Dei. Hujus ergò δυνά- μεως sive possibilitatis ad mortem & corruptionem signum evidens erat, creatio illa Hominis ex pulvere terræ: quæ tamen δυνάμις inactum nunquam erupisset, si mandatum Dei non transgressus esset, quantumvis etiam ex pulvere terræ fuisset conditus. Ad verò post lapsum ita δυνάμις in actum transijt, ut jam ipso actu Mortalis simus & nascamur: non modò propter materiæ conditionem, ex qua homo conditus est: sed cum primis propter horrendam corruptionem omnium virium tam Animæ quàm Corporis.

Et hæc quidem Romanæ pseudo Catholicæ Ecclesiæ est doctrina de Imagine Dei, & Justitia Originali: quæ licet modis omnibus sit absurda & impia, usque adeò tamen Jesuvvitæ videtur plausibilis, ut de ea, ex Scripturis etiam confirmanda ad superstitionem usque sit sollicitus.

Ac initio quidem profert illud Genes. 3. 19. Pulvis es, & in pulverem reverteris. Quorum verborum hanc sententiam esse contendit: Quanquam te valdè gloriosum mea benignitate effeci, ita ut posses neque mortem, neq. mala ulla formidare: tamen ex natura tua pulvis eras, mortalis, fragilis, doloribus laboribusque obnoxius: & quia dono illo meo superaddito culpa tua spoliatus es, & in statum tuum naturalem recidisti, ideò nunc etiam pulvis es, & in pulverem reverteris.

Respondeo: Committitur error confusionis disparatarum quæstionum: & malitiosa status perversio. Controvertitur enim hoc loco de Imagine Dei, cujus sedes potissimum fuit in Anima hominis: An videlicet in eam ex prima creatione potuerit cadere talis pugna, qualem fingunt Adversarij. Ubi cùm Affirmativam suam probare deberent Adversarij, proferunt ejusmodi locum, qui nihil quicquam agit de conditione Animæ: sed tantum de prima corporis humani Origine. Jam verò à conditione Corporis, ad conditionem Animæ, non valet consequentia. Quid? quod ne quidem illam Corporis humani ex limo sive pulvere terræ formationem, statim sequebatur ipso actu fragilitas, mortalitas, dolores & labores: sed tantùm δυνάμις istarum infirmitatum, uti paulò antè ostendimus.

Alterum Scripturæ testimonium mutuatur Jesuvvita ex cap. 17, 2. Ecclesiastici: DEVS creavit hominem de terra, & secundum se vestivit eum virtute.

Undè colligit Jesuvvita, Justitiam Originalem tanquàm vestem, homini à Deo fuisse superadditam.

Respondeo: 1. Nullus ἔλεγχος ex verbo vestiendi peti potest, quippè quod non modò de supernaturalibus & extrinsecus accidentibus: sed & de Naturalibus & substantialibus praedicatur: ut quando Deus legitur hominem carne & cute vestivisse: Iob. 10, 11. Unde tamen haud fas erit colligere, carnem & cutem esse dona supernaturalia. Deinde occurrit vitiosa versio vulgatae Latinae. Nam in Graeco non legitur, quod Deus vestiverit hominem secundum se, hoc est, secundum Deum: sed secundum ipsum hominem: Sic enim sonant verba Graeca: καὶ ἐνέδυσεν αὐτὸς καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸς ἰχύν: Induit eos virtute secundum seipsos. Ergo virtus illa non fuit supernaturalis, sed secundum ipsos homines, Naturae videlicet eorum convenientissima.

Tertium scripturae locum desumit Jesuvvita ex parabola illa Luc. 10,30. de homine spoliato & sauciato: Ex qua colligit, Vulnera Natura nostrae inflicta, non ex peccato Originali, neque proprie ex Natura hominis corruptione: sed ex Natura Adami, qualis initio per se fuit condita, pullulare.

Se respondeo 1. Parabolae non latius sunt extendendae, quam quousque ipse finis & scopus earum admittit. Jam vero parabolae illius Luc. 10,30. finis & scopus nullatenus fuit, Descriptio vel Justitiae Originalis, vel peccati Originalis: sed tantum dilectio proximi. Deinde licet per Allegoriam aliquam ad praesentem statum controversiae accommodari ea possit: minime tamen sequitur id quod intendit Adversarius. Neque enim militat ulla Consequentiae ratio, si sic instituatur collectio: Homo prius spoliatus postea vulneratus est: Ergo Justitia Originalis non fuit primo Homini Naturalis. Pari enim Logica sic aliquis inferre posset: Caecus facultate videndi est spoliatus: Ergo, Facultas haec non fuit ipsi naturalis: Vel: Obsessus aliquis a Diabolo, spoliatur usu rectae rationis: Ergo usus rationis rectae, non est homini Naturalis. Ubi vanitatem argumenti quivis facile intelligit.

Sed Scripturarum praesidio destitutus Jesuvvita, causae patrocinium quaerit in quibusdam ratiunculis, quas paucis expendere, operae pretium fuerit.

Prima ratio sic habet: Quicquid constat ex carne & spiritu rationali: illud lucta sive pugna carnis & spiritus est obnoxium: & quidem ex naturae conditione: ita ut non nisi per extrinsecus accedens donum supernaturale averti illa & prohiberi possit. Atqui primus homo constabat ex carne & spiritu rationali. Ergo.

Majoris connexum sic probat Jesuvvita: Homo ex ea parte, qua caro est, communicat cum bestijs, & propensionem quandam habet ad bonum Corporale & Sensibile, in quod fertur per sensum & appetitum: Ex altera vero parte, qua Spiritus est, communicat cum Angelis, & propensionem habet ad bonum spirituale, & intelligibile, in quod fertur per intelligentiam & voluntatem. Ex his autem diversis vel contrarijs propensionibus existit in uno eodemque homine pugna quaedam, & ex ea pugna, ingens bene agendi difficultas, dum una propensio alteram impedit.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum 1. petitione principij, & Sophismate Accidentis. Falsa enim est hypothesis, & vitiosissimâ laborat oppositione, ex qua Jesuvvita ratiocinatur. Neque enim Bonum corporale & spirituale, vel sensibile & intelligibile ἀντιφατικῶς sibi mutuò opponi debent tanquàm contraria: sed se habent tantùm ut disparata, sive subordinata, quæ contrariam inter se affectionem, non nisi per accidens fortiuntur. 2. Committitur Sophisticatio παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε. Nullus enim ἔλεγχος militat, quando sic arguit Jesuvvita: Homo constat ex carne & spiritu rationali. Ergo jam indè à prima creatione, luctæ sive pugnæ carnis & spiritus est obnoxius: Nam quòd talis lucta in Homine jam deprehenditur, illud non Creationi primæ, sed corruptioni Naturæ nostræ, in solidum est adscribendum: & sic rursum per Accidens Homini competit. Certè primus Homo, licèt ex carne & spiritu constaret, usque adeò tamen omnis luctæ erat expers, ut summà potiùs Concordia virium inferiorum cum superioribus, quodcunque etiam Bonum consideres, in ipso vigeret: idque vi sive virtute Imaginis divinæ, ad quam ille erat conditus: uti supra demonstratum. Hâc destructâ, demum cœpit ἀταξία illa, & sic per accidens Caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum.

Secunda ratio talis est: Sic Corruptio, quæ nunc est in Homine, neq; à Deo proficiscitur, neque à pomo vetito, neq; à flatu serpentis, neq; à puris naturalibus: consequens fuerit, eam proficisci à remotione doni supernaturalis. Atqui prius est verum: Ratum ergò & posterius: ac per consequens statuitur corruptionis hujus causa efficiens esse conditio materiæ in primo homine: meritoria, peccatum Adami: Divina deniq; justitia spolians hominem dono supernaturali, esse causa removens impedimentum actus secundi.

Respondeo: Laborat argumentum 1. παρὰ τὸ ἐλλιπὲς τῆς διαιρέσεως. Major enim propositio omittit veram & præcipuam causam efficientem corruptionis Naturæ nostræ; quæ est, amissio Imaginis divinæ, & quæ hanc statim insecuta est, horribilis destructio egregij illius & perpetui consensus virium omnium, qui in Natura Hominis ante lapsum obtinebat. Cujus destructionis Effectus longè tristissimus erat iste, ut cùm antea Homo, non nisi quod bonum rectumque appetebat, jam naturâ appeteret tantùm, quod malum est. 2. Fallit argumentum Sophismate Ignorationis Elenchi. Neque enim, uti Esavvita sophisicatur, Concupiscentiæ vitiositas tantùm definienda est, per inferiorum virium ἀταξίαν, cùm potius, Scriptura sic docente, locum ea habeat præcipuè in viribus superioribus mentis humanæ: ita ut omne figmentum, omne studium mentis & Cordis humani tantùm malum sit ab adolescentia.

Quæ certè tristissima Naturæ nostræ conditio, non dependet ex remotione doni alicujus supernaturalis, quæ Naturalia reliquerit integra: neque etiam ex Naturali sive animali appetitu, aberrante à recta via: sed ex toto dependet ex destructione virium superiorum, & inferiorum & harmoniæ virium omnium in Homine:uti subsequens Articulus ostendet.

Tertia Bellarmini ratio sic sonat: Quæ est ratio peccatorum actualium in Renatis post lapsum: eadem etiam est ratio peccati Actualis, ab Adamo commissi: Atqui Renati per peccata Actualia non amittunt aliquam Naturæ suæ proprietatem: sed tantùm donum Supernaturale :. Ergo Adamus quoque per peccatum Actualle à se commissum, non amisit aliquid de proprietate Naturæ : sed salvis manentibus Naturalibus perdidit tantùm donum aliquod supernaturale.

Respondeo : Error oritur ὥς γε τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: & vitiosi consequentis. Neque enim Major propositio simpliciter sive ex toto : sed tantùm secundùm quid, sive ex parte, vera est. Etsi enim peccata renatorum, & Adami ratione Generis in eo conveniunt, quòd utraq; Peccatorum Actualium nomen ac definitionem sortiantur: tamen si fontem & originem eorum spectes, maxima sese offert disparitas. Nam in Renatis ipsa natura ita peccato est polluta & corrupta: ut non possit non pravas subindè concipere concupiscentias, & designare peccata Actualia, per quæ amittunt & perdunt donum supernaturale, nempè Regenerationis Gratiam, nisi agant pœnitentiam. Cæterùm in Adamo Natura erat optima & perfectissima; ut tam facilè posset non peccare, quàm peccare: ac proindè non ex Naturæ conditione, sed ex spontanea inobedientia peccatum commisit: undè non modò doni alicujus supernaturalis, sed ipsarum Naturalium virium perfectionem & integritatem in rebus spiritualibus non sibi tantùm, sed toti etiam posteritati perdidit & amisit, quibus disparitatis gradibus probè consideratis utriusque præmissæ falsitas, & totius argumenti stupenda vanitas ultrò elucescit.

Quarta ratio Bellarmini hæc est: Multi ex morte revocati sunt in hanc vitam, quorum aliqui purgati fuerunt à peccato Originis, & tamen caruerunt Justitia Originali, ita ut per omnia similes essent infantibus via ordinaria in lucem editis. Ergo Justitia Originalis fuit donum supernaturale, quod auferri potuit ab homine salvis manentibus Naturalibus.

Respondeo : Nugari magis quàm disputare Jesuwitam. Primùm enim pro confesso sumit id, de quo maximè dubitatur: An nimirùm resuscitati illi caruerint peccato Originis? Ubi sanè nos initiò distinguendum esse censemus inter eos resuscitatos, qui resurgente ex mortuis Christo, ipsi quoque è monumentis prodierunt, & in cœlum translati sunt: & inter eos, qui nondum in pulverem redacti, in vitam revocati fuerunt, & hisce in terris diutiùs vixerunt. Illos è peccato Originali purgatos fuisse, libenter quidem concedimus: sed ab istorum conditione, ad statum reliquorum resuscitatorum haud valere consequentiam, regerimus. Quia enim Peccatum Originis ita universam pervasit substantiam hominis, ut non nisi in pulverem redacto corpore, penitùs extirpari possit: utique à Prophetis, à Christo, ab Apostolis, qui resuscitati fuerunt, priusquàm totalem carnis suæ corruptionem viderant, à peccato etiam Originis purgati minimè fuerunt. 2. Committitur Sophisma παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχꙋ: idque dupliciter: primùm quidem, cùm collectio instituitur ex miraculis, ad communem extruendam regulam: cùm tamen illorum ipsorum miraculorum ratio nondùm plenè sit explicata. Deindè verò cùm medius aliquis status hominum, vitio Originali, & Justitia Originali vacantium, fingitur: de quo Scriptura ne γρῦ quidem movit. 3. ἀσύστατον est, & seipsum per turpem contradictionem evertit Jesuivitæ ratiocinatio. Si enim Lazarus, si infantes & alii ab Elia, Elisæo, Christo & Apostolis resuscitati, denuò mori necesse habuerunt: utiq; peccato Originis adhuc fuerunt infecti. Ratio est: Quia Mors est stipendium Peccati, Rom. 6, 23. Jam sublata causa, tollitur Effectus: Atqui mori necesse habuerunt: Siquidem illos in cœlum vivos translatos fuisse, ex scripturis demonstrari nequit. Ergo peccato originali etiam post resuscitationem fuerunt obnoxy: & quidem ex naturæ suæ conditione: non verò, uti Pelagius somniavit, tantùm ex imitatione sive Exemplis aliorum.

Quinta & postrema ratio Jesuivitæ sic informari potest: Primi parentes evecti fuere ad eam dignitatem, ut essent Filii DEI, & Dÿ quidam, id est, divinæ consortes naturæ. Atqui absurdissimum est, rem creatam, qualis est homo, DEUM, vel DEI filium naturaliter facere. Ergo Dignitas illa fuit Supernaturale donum, quod salvis naturalibus auferri potuit.

Respondeo: Ludit Adversarius puerili Æquivocatione in vocabulo Naturaliter. Vel enim illud idem sonat ac per Essentiam Naturæ esse DEUM sive Filium DEI: Quo sanè sensu primi parentes non fuerunt Filii DEI, sic enim non ampliùs Homines: Sed Spiritus incorporei fuissent: id quod falsum & absurdum: vel notat conformitatem aliquam Naturæ humanæ cum divina, ratione concretæ sanctitatis & justitiæ: quâ Homo non ex Reconciliationis sive Regenerationis gratia, uti nunc post lapsum: sed ex ipsâ creatione, & sic concretâ aliquâ gratiâ Imaginem & similitudinem DEI gestavit: Secundum illud: Faciamus Hominem ad Imaginem & Similitudinem nostram. Hæc creationis gratia, cùm per peccatum sit perdita & amissa: fit utique, ut jam non ampliùs per Naturam (sensu jam explicato) sed tantùm per Adoptionem simus Filii DEI: ac per consequens Naturalia in homine miferrimè sint corrupta & depravata.

Tandem producit Jesuivita Patres benè multos, quorum autoritate suam confirmari posse sententiam autumat: verùm quid ad hoc argumenti genus responderi debeat, facilè patebit, si subsequentes hypotheses in conspectu habuerimus:

1. Patres in definienda proposita controversia sibi satis non constant: sed usque adeo in varias abeunt sententias, ut ex ipsorum scriptis nihil certi elici possit: quemadmodum sane ex ipsius Bellarmini tractatione c. 6. luculenter patet.

2. Tanta fuit vis haereseos Pelagianae, ut haud pauci Orthodoxi alioqui Patres, vitantes unum extremum Manichaeismi, prolaberentur ad contrariam hyperbolem Pelagianismi: & Peccatum Originis nimium extenuarent: statuentes, in Angelis & Hominibus post lapsum Naturalia mansisse integra: id quod cum Scriptura e diametro pugnat, uti subsequens Articulus ostendet.

3. Nonnulli Patres negantes Hominem natura Sanctum fuisse, non agunt de modo inhaerentiae, quo in Hominem Sanctitas collata fuerit: Sed tantum de Origine illius: quod nimirum non uti DEUS per Essentiam sint sancti, vel ipsa potius Sanctitas: id quod nos quoque negamus: sed tantum quod sanctitatem illam ex Spiritus S. gratia acceperint: minime omnium interim negantes, primos parentes, ex creationis origine, habuisse Naturam praeditam proprietate hac justitiae & Sanctitatis DEO placentis, tanquam facultate concreata & naturali, separabili tamen ab ipsa Essentia.

Tandem Patres longe alio, quam Jesuwitae, sensu, intellexerunt phrasin hanc: Naturalia post lapsum manserunt reliqua. Jesuwi tae enim hoc volunt, Naturam Hominis non tantum secundum partes sive proprietates Essentiales, qualis jam post lapsum adhuc est, mansisse integram: sed etiam, qualis fuit ante lapsum, respectu virium corporis & Anima.

Patres vero, quin etiam B. Lutherus noster, affirmantes, Naturalia post lapsum mansisse integra, intelligunt. Naturam, prout ea constat ex partibus constituentibus, corpore & Anima rationali, & harum partium proprietatibus naturalibus: Quae sane per lapsum no sunt destructae aut abolitae: uti mox contra Flacianos ostendemus. Jam vero ex affirmatione istarum partium Essentialium, non valet Consequentia, ad affirmationem virium illarum perfectissimarum, quae partibus istis Essentialibus erant concreatae, & sic ante lapsum revera Naturales: sed jam per lapsum destructae, & in contrarias qualitates transmutatae. Qua de re sic praeclare B. Lutherus noster: Quando Sophistae dicunt, Naturalia esse integra: Concedo hoc: Si autem inferunt: Ergo homo potest diligere DEUM, nego consequentiam, & distinguo Naturalia contra Spiritualia: & dico, Spiritualia non esse integra, sed corrupta, imo per peccatum prorsus extincta esse in Homine & Diabolo, ibi ut nihil ibi sit; quam Intellectus depravatus, & voluntas inimica & adversaria DEI, quae nihil cogitat, quam ea, quae sunt contra DEUM. Quare Naturalia quidem integra sunt: Sed quae naturalia? Quod homo in Impietate mersus & servus Diaboli, habet Rationem, voluntatem, Liberum arbitrium, & potestatem aedificandi domum, gerendi Magistratum, gubernandi navem, & faciendi alia officia, quae homini sunt subjecta. Genes. 1. Ea non sunt adempta homini, nec est sublata generatio, Politia, Oeconomia, his dictis, sed confirmata.


### Chapter II. Anthesis: Part II Ἀντιθέσεως The Error of the Flacians

Part II.

Ἀντιθέσεως.

The Error of the Flacians.

And thus far indeed the first host of enemies has been disputed with sufficient accuracy, and the errors of both the ancient Scholastics and the recent Jesuits concerning the Image of GOD have been sufficiently refuted: It remains to address the other host of enemies, which the Flacians constitute. For these, sinning in excess, contend that Original Righteousness, or the image of GOD in Adam, was the Essential Form, or the very Substance of Man: and therefore that Original Sin, which succeeded into its place, is likewise the very Substance of Man.

But since we are to have a separate treatment of Original Sin expressly: in this place we shall examine only the former error of the Flacians concerning original righteousness. Thus, however, Matthias Flacius Illyricus himself explains his mind and opinion: We understand the Image of GOD, to which the first Man was created, to be that very thing which is restored in us: namely, the Spirit of the mind, or that new and Spiritual heart, (that is, the rational soul, which Scripture places in the heart) which is given to us divinely when the old and stony one is cut out, and is created in us by the Holy Spirit: part 1, Clavis Scripturae, under the word Image, page 408. Moreover, lest by chance anyone should think that Flacius is speaking of the spiritual renewal of the heart, but not of the very substance of the heart, it deserves noting that Flacius himself in the immediately following words expresses the sentiments of his mind thus: In these, he says, of most of all the significations, Image is placed for a certain true and real existence, or the form of the thing itself, and a living and essential expression, not merely a shadowy picture, page 409. Thus in part 2, treatise 6, page 369, he explains himself more clearly. Scripture says that God created man in His own image: afterwards, that man having died through disobedience, it says in Genesis 5:3 that he begat sons no longer in the image of God, but in his own: and he speaks not of external lineaments, or the appearance of man, which still in some way recalls that former man: But of the very intimate and most noble essence of man. Where Scripture sufficiently indicates that that image is primarily the essential form itself, in the highest and most noble parts of man, etc.

And after a few words: I speak of that most noble substantial form, to which the heart itself, or rather the rational soul, was primarily formed, so that its very essence was the image of God, page 379. And a little later: I say that this substantial form has not only perished for man, but has also been utterly inverted into its contrary: and that through a substantial change of the soul.

The same in the Triple consensus, letter B. On the reverse side: It was the Image of GOD, not a certain ornament added to man, as a gift, as the Sophists argued: but the very FORM of the whole man, consisting of soul and body, and his good NATURE.

And with a few words inserted: Therefore we affirm that the MAN HIMSELF, or (as the Dialecticians speak) the ESSENTIAL FORM of man, was the image of GOD.

Moreover, there are ready at hand the most evident reasons and arguments by which the vanity of this Dogma can be demonstrated to the eye.

And the first Reason can be formulated thus: If the Image of GOD, or Original Justice, was a Substantial Form in the first Man. It will follow that it was either some peculiar Substance, diverse and distinct from the very Substance of Man: or it was the Soul of man itself, or (if one may speak so) some part of the Soul: or the body of man: or finally, it was the whole Man himself. But the Image of GOD was nothing of the sort in the first man: Therefore it was not a substance.

The major premise consists in a perfect enumeration of those modes and respects according to which the Image of GOD could, or ought to be, defined by Substance. The minor premise, however, which denies that any of all these modes could have belonged to the Image of GOD in the first man, can be clearly demonstrated by a most evident removal and reduction to absurdity. For first, if the Flacians imagine that the Image of God was a peculiar substance, diverse and distinct from the substance of man, it would follow on the contrary that Original Sin, which succeeded in its place, is likewise a peculiar substance diverse and distinct from the substance of man. Since the reasoning for contraries is the same. Now, however, there is no creator of all substances except the one and only GOD: Therefore it is necessary that the same GOD be the creator of Original Sin, as a substance existing in Man by itself. But this is highly impious and blasphemous: Therefore that also will be of the same character, namely that Original Sin is a substance, diverse and distinct from the substance of Man.

Then, if the Image of GOD was the Soul of Man itself: it will follow that upon the destruction of the Image of God, the Soul itself is destroyed κατ̓ ὀσιαν and substantially: and consequently, that our Soul is not, by reason of substance, of the same species and ὀμουσιάς with the soul of Adam: which would be prodigiously absurd. For thus Adam would be nothing at all to us: thus he himself would no longer sustain the stock of the human race: Thus also Christ himself would have assumed a Soul consubstantial either to his, or to ours: If to his: then his entire merit is nothing to us: For what is not assumed, that is not redeemed: But if he assumed a Soul ὁμοόσιον to ours: Then for the same reason, his merit will profit the first Adam nothing. All of which are more absurd than the most absurd things.

Thirdly: The Image of GOD was not any part of the soul: 1. Because the Soul as a Spirit is ὅλως ὁλόνλι, having no part outside of part: 2. Because thus Original Sin would likewise be established as being some part of the Soul: Which being posited, it would follow that Original Sin had not pervaded the whole Nature of man, but only one part of another Essential part: and consequently, that not the whole Man is guilty of the wrath of God and eternal damnation: which again is absurd to the point of stupor.

Illyricus indeed objects that it is only a principle of Philosophy, not a doctrine of Theology, that a part of the soul cannot be utterly abolished unless the whole essence of the soul is destroyed. But it is most solidly answered that this principle is not only Philosophical, but also Theological, and indeed perpetually true in all sciences. For whatever a spirit is, it is this entirely, nor does it have a part of its Essence outside of a part, like corporeal things. For of the parts of the body I can say, Here is the hand, here is the foot; so that with the hand amputated, the foot nevertheless remains safe: But of the Soul I cannot say: Here is the intellect, where the will is not: nor does the will remain when the mind is abolished, because this Soul is all of these things entirely.
