For the Soul is nothing but all its powers: And the powers of the Soul are nothing but the Soul itself: which is whole in the whole body, and whole in any part of it: and it does everything it does as a whole, however much the powers may be truly distinct in the Essence of the Soul.

Fourthly, the Image of GOD was not the body of Man itself: 1. Because to place the Image of GOD in the body alone, and indeed considered substantially, would be clearly discordant, and would confirm the heresy of the Anthropomorphites: 2. Because upon the loss of the Image of God, man would have lost the body itself: or if the body nevertheless remained, it is necessary that it be a new one, clearly different from the former species, created by GOD and added to Man: which is manifestly false.

Finally: The Image of GOD was not the whole Man, as he consists of Soul and Body. For thus it would follow: 1. That Original Sin is also the whole Man: Which the following Article will show to be discordant with all truth. 2. That Man, by reason of his Substance, was not Man, but GOD: For whatever is the Image of God by its Substance or Essence, that is God: just as the Epistle to the Hebrews ch. 1, 3 most rightly concludes concerning the Son of GOD alone. But that also would be highly blasphemous.

These ways being therefore removed, with respect to which the Image of GOD, according to the hypothesis of Flacius, could be called Essence or substance, a judgment can easily be made concerning the stupendous vanity of this dogma.

But many other reasons can be given, by which the same thing can be demonstrated: and indeed a second Reason can be such:

Whatever things differ by definition, they differ in reality, so that they can never coincide as substance.

But the definition of man is one thing, and the definition of the image of God is another. What the latter is has been shown above from our author, namely the concreated supreme perfection of the whole man, and the rectitude and conformity of all the powers of soul and body, without any struggle of flesh and Spirit, agreeing with God himself the Archetype: In the mind, wisdom and the light of the knowledge of God: In the will, holiness and justice, most conformable to the law of God, and thus the agreement and harmony of all superior and inferior faculties and members without rebellion, agreeing exactly with the will of God: dominion and empire over created things: finally, blessed immortality. But what man is according to his essential definition is too well known to need any explanation in this place.

Therefore the image of God and man considered according to his essence differ in reality: and consequently they do not constitute one and the same substance, with respect to the question in no. 79.

III. The reason can be sought from the proper nature and affection of the image of God, insofar as it obtains respect both to matter and to form. For the material of the image of God, or original justice, is the integrity and εὐταξία of all the powers of man: but the formal is approval and acceptance before God, as our author speaks. But neither of these is substance: therefore the image of God, which consists of these two, cannot be substance.

IV. To whatever the definition of an accident applies, the defined thing itself applies to the same.

But the definition of an accident applies to the image of God in the first man.

Therefore also the defined thing itself: namely that it is an accident, however connatural.

The minor premise is evident from this: that it is the nature and property of accidents to be present or absent from their subjects. Now since original justice was in the mind, as in a subject, the light of the knowledge of God: and in the will, the supreme agreement with the law of God: certainly anyone sees of his own accord that the mind and will of man are one thing, and the image of God, which inhered in them as subjects separably, is another: so that the mind of man would not be called holiness and justice itself in the abstract: but in the concrete, holy and just. Now in the concrete there are always two distinct things: one is the substance, or the subject itself: the other is that which inheres in the substance or subject: as all logicians and theologians attest.

Latin:

Pars II.

Ἀντιθέσεως.

Error Flacianorum.

EThactenùs quidem de primo hostium agmine satis accuratè disputatum, & tùm veterum Scholasticorum tùm recentium Jesuwitarum errores de Imagine DEI sufficienter sunt refutati: Reliquum est alterum hostium agmen, quod Flaciani constituunt. Hi enim in excessu peccantes contendunt, Originalem Justitiam, sive imaginem DEI in Adamo, fuisse Essentialem Formam, sive ipsam Substantiam Hominis: ac proindè Peccatum Originis, quod in locum ipsius successit, itidem esse ipsam Substantiam Hominis.

Sed cùm de Peccato Originis ex professo seorsim futura nobis sit Tractatio: hoc loco priorem tantùm Flacianorum errorem de justitia originali examinabimus. Sic autem ipse Matthias Flacius Illyricus mentem ac sententiam suam explicat: Intelligimus Imaginem DEI, ad quam primùs Homo fuit conditus, esse illud ipsum, quòd in nobis instauratur: nempè Spiritum mentis, seu illud novum ac Spirituale cor, (hoc est, animam rationalem, quam Scriptura in corde collocat) quod nobis exciso veteri ac lapideo divinitùs donatur, & per Spiritum sanctum in nobis creatur: part. 1. Clav. Script. in voce Imaginis, pag. 408. Cæterùm ne fortè aliquis existimet, loqui Flacium de Spirituali cordis Renovatione: non verò ne ipsa substantia cordis, notationem meretur, quòd ipse Flacius in statim subsequentibus sic animi sui sensa exprimit: In his, inquiens, ex plerisq; omnibus significationibus, Imago pro quadam vera ac reali existentia, sive rei ipsius forma, ac viva, essentialique expressione, non tantùm umbratili pictura ponitur pag. 409. Sic in parte 2. Tractatu 6. pag. 369. planiùs se explicat. Scriptura dicit, DEUM hominem creasse ad imaginem suam: postea, illo homine per inobedientiam mortuo, dicit Genes. 5, 3 eum genuisse filios non ampliùs ad DEI, sed ad suam imaginem: ac loquitur non de externis lineamentis, aut specie hominis, quæ adhuc utcunque priorem illum hominem refert: Se de IPSA Intima, nobilissimaq; Essentia Hominis. Ubi Imaginem illam satis indicat Scriptura esse ipsam potissimùm essentialem Formam, in summis nobilissimisq; hominis partibus, &c.

Et post pauca: Loquor de ea nobilissima substantiali Forma, ad quam præcipuè ipsum cor, aut potiùs Anima rationalis formata erat, ita ut ipsa sua essentia esset DEI imago. pag. 379. Et paulò pòst: Hanc Substantialem Formam dico non tantùm deperiisse homini, sed etiam prorsus in contrariam esse inversam: idque per Substantialem immutationem Animæ.

Idem in consensu Triplici lit. B. Versa facie: Fuit Imago DEI, non ornatus quidam homini additus, tanquàm donum, ut Sophistæ disputarunt: sed IPSAM ET TOTIUS HOMINIS, anima constantis & corpore, FORMA integra & NATURA bona.

Et paucis interjectis: Ergo IPSUM HOMINEM, sive (ut Dialectici loquuntur) ESSENTIALEM Hominis FORMAM, imaginem DEI fuisse affirmamus.

Cæterùm in promtu sunt rationes & argumenta evidentissima, quibus Dogmatis hujus vanitas ad oculum demonstrari queat.

Et prima quidem Ratio sic informari potest: Si Imago DEI, sive Justitia Originalis fuit Substantialis Forma in primo Homine. Consequens erit, fuisse illum aut peculiarem aliquam Substantiam, ab ipsâ Hominis Substantiâ diversam & distinctam: vel fuisse ipsam Animam hominis, vel (si sic loqui liceat) partem aliquam Animæ: vel corpus hominis: vel denique fuisse ipsum totum Hominem. Atqui Imago DEI nihil tale in primo homine fuit: Ergo neque fuit substantia.

Major constat perfecta enumeratione eorum modorum atque respectuum, secundum quos Imago DEI per Substantiam definiri possit, aut debeat. Minor verò, quæ negat ullum istorum modorum omnium potuisse competere Imagini DEI in primo homine, luculenter demonstrari potest, per remotionem longè evidentissimam: & deductionem ad absurdum. Primùm enim si fingant Flaciani, Imaginem Dei fuisse Substantiam peculiarem, ab hominis substantia diversam & distinctam, consequens fuerit è contrario, Peccatum quoque Originis, quod in illius locum successit, itidem esse peculiarem Substantiam ab hominis substantia diversam & distinctam. Siquidem contrariorum eadem est ratio. Jam verò omnium substantiarum creator non est, nisi solus & unus DEUS: Ergo idem DEUS Peccati Originis, tanquàm substantiæ per se in Homine existentis, creator sit, necesse est. Atqui hoc summè est impium & blasphemum: Ergo ejusdem notæ erit etiam illud, nempe Peccatum Originis esse substantiam, ab Hominis substantia diversam & distinctam.

Deinde si Imago DEI fuit ipsa Anima Hominis: sequetur destructa Imagine Dei, ipsam Animam κατ̓ ὀσιαν & substantialiter esse destructam: & per consequens, Animam nostram, non esse ratione substantiæ, cum anima Adami ejusdem speciei & ὀμουσιάς: id quod prodigiosè foret absurdum. Sic enim Adamus nihil prorsus ad nos: sic ipse non ampliùs stirpem humani generis sustineret: Sic etiam Christus ipse vel illius, vel nostræ Animæ consubstantialem Animam assumsisset: Si illius: tum universum ipsius meritum nihil ad nos: Nam quod assumtum non est, illud ne redemtum quidem: Sin nostræ ὁμοόσιον Animam assumsit: Tum eandem ob causam, ipsius meritum nihil conducet primo Adamo. Quæ omnia absurdissimis sunt absurdiora.

Tertiò: Imago DEI non fuit pars aliqua animæ: 1. Quia Anima tanquàm Spiritus est ὅλως ὁλόνλι, partem extra partem nullam habens: 2. Quia sic peccatum Originis itidem constitueretur esse pars aliqua Animæ: Quo posito, sequeretur, Peccatum Originis non totam hominis Naturam, sed unam tantùm alterius partis Essentialis, partem pervasisse: ac per consequens, neq; totum Hominem reum esse, iræ Dei & æternæ damnationis: id quod rursus ad stuporem usque est absurdum.

Excipit quidem Illyricus, Philosophiæ tantùm principium, non verò Theologiæ doctrinam esse, quòd pars animæ non possit penitùs aboleri: nisi tota essentia animæ destruatur. Sed solidissimè respondetur, Principium hoc non modò Philosophicum, sed etiam Theologicum, & quidem perpetuò ac in omnibus scientiis verum esse. Spiritus enim quicquid est, hoc totum est, nec habet partem Essentiæ suæ extra partem, sicut res corporeæ. De corporis enim partibus dicere possum, Hîc est manus, hîc est pes; ita ut manu amputata, nihilominus pes adhuc salvus maneat: Sed de Anima non possum dicere: Hîc est intellectus, ubi non sit voluntas: neque mente abolita, voluntas remanet, quia Anima hæc omnia tota est. Nihil enim est Anima, nisi omnes ejus potentiæ: Et nihil sunt Animæ potentiæ, nisi ipsa Anima: quæ est tota in toto corpore, & in qualibet ejus parte tota: & tota facit, quicquid facit, quantumvis etiam potentiæ in Essentiâ Animæ verè sint distinctæ.

Quartò, Imago DEI non fuit corpus ipsum Hominis: 1. Quia Imaginem DEI in solo corpore, & quidem substantialiter considerato, ponere planè foret absonum, & Anthropomorphitarum hæresin confirmaret: 2. Quia Imagine Dei amissa, ipsum quoque corpus amisisset homo: vel si corpus nihilominus aliquod remansit, Novum planè, & à priore specie diversum à DEO creatum, & Homini additum sit necesse est: id quod manifestè falsum.

Tandem: Imago DEI non fuit totus Homo, prout constat Anima & Corpore. Sic enim sequeretur: 1. Peccatum etiam Originis esse totum Hominem: Quod quàm sit ab omni veritate absonum, subsequens Articulus ostendet. 2. Hominem rationem Substantiæ suæ non Hominem, sed DEUM fuisse: Quicquid enim per Substantiam sive Essentiam suam est Imago Dei, illud Deus: quemadmodum de solo Filio DEI rectissimè colligit Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 1, 3. Atqui & istud summè fuerit blasphemum.

Remotis proindè modis istis omnibus, quorum respectu Imago DEI, ex hypothesi Flacii Essentia sive substantia dici possit, facilè judicium fieri potest, de stupenda vanitate dogmatis hujus.

Sed dari possunt plures aliæ rationes, quibus idem demonstrari queat: & secunda quidem Ratio talis esse potest:

Quæcunque definitione differunt, ea reipsa differunt, ita ut Substantia nunquam convenire queant.

Atqui alia est definitio Hominis, alia verò Imaginis DEI. Hæc quid sit, supra ex Autore nostro ostensum, nempe concreata perfectio summa totius hominis, omniumq; animæ & corporis virium rectitudo & conformitas, sine omni lucta carnis & Spiritus, congruens cum ipso DEO Archetypo: In mente Sapientia & lux agnitionis DEI: In voluntate Sanctitas & Justitia, Legi DEI maximè corformis, adeòque omnium superiorum & inferiorum facultatum & membrorum sine rebellione consensio & harmonia cum voluntate DEI ad amussim congruens: dominatus & imperium in res creatas: Beata denique Immortalitas. Quid verò sit Homo secundum essentialem definitionem, notius est, quàm ut hoc loco explicatione ulla opus sit.

Ergo Imago DEI & Homo secundum essentiam consideratus, reipsa differunt: & per consequens unam eandemque substantiam non constituunt, respectu quæstionis n. 79.

III. Ratio peti potest a propria natura atque affectione Imaginis DEI, quatenùs ea tùm Materiæ tùm Formæ respectum sortitur. Materiale enim Imagine DEI, sive Justitia Originalis est Integritas & εὐταξία omnium virium Hominis: formale verò est approbatio & acceptatio apud DEUM, uti Autor noster loquitur. Atqui neutrum istorum est Substantia: Ergo neque Imago DEI, quæ ex duobus istis constat, substantia esse potest.

IV. Cuicunque competit definitio Accidentis, eidem & definitum ipsum.

Atqui Imagini DEI in primo Homine competit definitio Accidentis.

Ergo & ipsum definitum: nempè quod sit Accidens, quantumvis connaturale.

Minor vel inde constat: quòd Accidentium Natura & proprietas est, adesse vel abesse subjectis. Jam cùm Justitia Originalis fuerit IN MENTE, tanquàm in Subjecto, Lux agnitionis DEI: IN VOLUNTATE autem summa consensio cum Lege DEI: certè quilibet ultrò videt, aliud esse mentem & voluntatem Hominis: aliud verò Imaginem DEI, quæ illis tanquàm Subjectis inhærebat separabiliter: ita ut Mens Hominis non in abstracto diceretur ipsa Sanctitas & Justitia: Sed in concreto, Sancta & Justa. Jam verò in concreto semper duo distincta sunt: unum Substantia, sive subjectum ipsum: Alterum verò id, quod Substantiæ sive subjecto inest: attestantibus omnibus Logicis & Theologis.


### Chapter II. Anthesis: Part II Ἀντιθέσεως The Error of the Flacians (continued)

V. And the final reason, by far the firmest, is taken from the restoration of the image of God, which is both begun in this life and will be consummated in the other in the elect. But that, as the Apostle testifies, 2 Cor. 3, 8 Eph. 4, 24. Coloss. 3, 10, is not done by a substantial mutation: but by an accidental renewal of the mind, consisting of true justice and holiness. Therefore the image of God in the first man is not to be defined as substance, but only by qualities.

Against this purer doctrine of ours, those who take up Flacius's dogma and parts to defend arise with various contrived sophistications.

And at the beginning, indeed, they distinguish between the Physical Man and the Theological Man: contending that they speak only of the Theological Man, in whom the Image of God, and indeed considered in the concrete, was the very substance of Man, and they attempt to prove this by this argument.

If original righteousness in Adam was an accident: it follows that the Image of God in Man was not a goodness of substance, but only of an accident: and again, from the contrary sense, the loss of original righteousness was only the corruption of an accident, not of the very substance of Adam. But this latter is absurd: therefore the former is as well.

Which argument, indeed, since it contains in itself the whole weight of this dispute with the Flacians, its individual members must be unfolded more accurately. At the beginning, therefore, that distinction of man into physical and theological is nothing other than a sophistic κρησφύγετον (refuge). For 1. This distinction is clearly ἄγραφος (unwritten), destitute of all authority of the Scriptures: since it does not distinguish the Theological Man from the Physical by species: but considers one man, both physical and theological: physically, as he is propagated and generated from parents: but theologically, as the same man in number and essence is either endowed with original righteousness, or infected by sin, or liberated, justified, and saved by the benefit of Christ. Furthermore, by this distinction, Illyricus yields his own vineyard, so to speak, and refutes himself. For a man is not called theological because he is different from a physical man by reason of substance: but only on account of theology, if I may so speak, which is an accident, just like all other arts and faculties: just as a man is called musical on account of music, which is an accident in man. Thus there is one Adam, who, if he is considered simply and physically according to his essential form and matter, is and is called a physical man: but if he is considered theologically according to that which he was created in the image of God: he is and is called a theological man, who, because he is considered as a man according to theology, is not considered insofar as he is a man, that is, an animal consisting of a body and a rational soul: but insofar as he is either good or evil in the judgment of God. Then, if Illyricus disputes about the Theological Man, what need is there for the terms of form and essential substance? which have no more to do with the consideration of the Theological Man than form and essential substance have to do with the consideration of the Musical Man. A base sophistry, therefore, ὡς ἐν τῷ πῇ και ἁπλῶς (as between the particular and the absolute), is committed regarding that fictitious distinction.

The second part of the Flacian Sophistry is that it is taken for granted that the Image of GOD, considered in the concrete, or the Goodness of Adam, accepted concretely, was the very Substance of Adam. But besides the fact that this assertion labors under a begging of the question, it also crashes most shamefully into the very principles of Theology and Philosophy. For as soon as a concrete is named, the respect of two very different things is immediately involved: namely, of the substance or subject, and of the Accident. Whence it is also commonly defined by Logicians that concretes are Adjective nouns, which are regularly said of a Subject, as, Socrates is just, the wall is white. Thus Adam in the concrete was called Good, Wise, Just: not in the Abstract, Goodness, Wisdom, Justice itself. Therefore, when Illyricus asserts that the Goodness of Adam is considered in the concrete, he himself, even if unwittingly, confesses that Goodness is in Adam as an Accident, as in a Substance or subject. With which assertion he immediately fights, when he adds: That that Goodness is the Essential Form of man created in the image of GOD: For the image of GOD is in this Essential Form of man: but it is not the Essential Form itself. It is added that not only in the schools of Logicians, but also of Theologians, this axiom is placed beyond controversy: Concretes and Abstracts must be placed in the same Category. Wherefore if Goodness is in the Category of Quality: certainly the concrete 'Good' also will be in the same predicament: since it is not predicated of Adam simply, in the 'What': but in the 'What kind': which is that of Accidents.

Thirdly, it is of the same vanity that he infers in the subjoined argument: If the image of GOD in Adam was an Accident: It follows that the Image of GOD in Adam was not the Goodness of the Substance, but only of an Accident. For the consequence is most rightly denied, which has no more weight than if I were to conclude thus: If the power or visual faculty in the eye is an accident: Therefore not the eye itself, but only that Accident sees. Where certainly such a collection would be worthy of explosion: since the visual power outside the eye is nothing: Whose proper nature and affection is not to be the eye itself, according to Substance: but to be in the eye, as an Accident in its subject. Whence also that power in the eye is not properly said to see: Since it is not some Being in itself: But of a non-being there are no qualities: but the eye is said to see, because of the inherent accidental visual power: So Original Justice was nothing outside the Substance of Adam: but it was its property to be in Adam: nor could that Justice be properly said to have been just, as something subsisting by itself: But Adam is called Just, because of that inherent concreated Justice.

It is clear from this that the cause and source of the error of Illyricus was this, that he falsely persuaded himself that what is Essential is and is called not only that which in truth and properly speaking is Essence, or as the Metaphysicians speak, which is a real Being: But also that which is in Essence or inheres, and does not subsist without essence: Which respect, however, is not proper to Substances, but only to Accidents: as is clear from the doctrine of Logic.

Fourthly, there comes to be noted an Equivocation in the word corruption, under which Illyricus plays. For there is one Physical, or essential corruption, by which a thing is utterly destroyed: and is defined by Philosophers as Motion from being to non-being: as for example, when a Man dies, then such a corruption intervenes, that the body can no longer even be called a body, but rather a corpse: and Man loses the name along with the definition. But there is another accidental corruption, and improperly so called: for properly speaking, corruption is only opposed to Physical Generation: as the Philosopher testifies in book 1 of coming to be and passing away. But this accidental corruption happens where, while the substance remains, the Quality is deformed: and thus the Substance is said to be corrupted not simply, but in a certain respect. Such corruption happened to Adam, who after the fall was miserably corrupted according to his whole substance, but not simply: but only in a certain respect. For by reason of the Essential parts considered in themselves and by themselves, Adam remained the same after the fall as he was before the fall, namely a Man consisting of a true natural body, and a rational Soul: meanwhile, however, according to his concrete Qualities he was horribly corrupted, so that from Good he became evil, from just unjust, from Holy profane and a sinner. Therefore, from this second species of corruption it is not permitted to argue to the first, unless we wish to fall into a Sophism from what is said in a certain respect to what is said simply.

Finally, a shameful Sophistry of the consequent is committed when Illyricus infers: If the Image of GOD was only an Accident, it follows that its loss corrupted not the Substance or Nature of Man itself, but only some Accident. For the reason that this corruption is attributed not to Accidents, but to Nature itself, is that Accidents are not in themselves, but are in another as a Subject: But Substance is effective in itself and simply, and that either to good or to evil, but not insofar as it is Substance: but only by reason of the qualities which are in substances, either from the first creation, or from the subsequent depravity. Then the Image of GOD is not established as such an Accident that it consists in a bare relation, just as some have thought, that the Dominion which man has over the remaining creatures is this very Image of GOD: just as the Scholastics once and even today some Pontifical Writers contend, that the Image of GOD added at least an external ornament to man, like the color of a painting, or a garland to a virgin. For although it was not the mind itself: yet in the mind there was concreated and connatural perfect knowledge of GOD, and wisdom, as much as could fall to man: in the will conformity of all powers: In the body the highest εὐκρασία of all humors, and of the whole temperament.

The second argument by which Illyricus fought in this arena was as follows: A straight and whole nature is the very substance of man. But the Image of God, or Original Justice, is a straight and whole nature. Therefore, the Image of God was the very substance of man, or his essential form.

I reply, the argument fails by the fallacy of παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς (in a certain respect and simply). For the concrete is confused with the abstract: that is, the genus of the subject in the major proposition, taken simply and abstractly, is predicated of the same subject considered κατά τι καὶ συμβεβηκὸς, in a certain respect and according to accident: or, which amounts to the same thing: substance taken simply, and considered by reason of itself τῷ εἶναι (in its being), is predicated not of nature taken simply, but of nature as straight and whole: which cannot be done. For the nature of man is not therefore or called substance because it was straight and whole: but because it consisted of substantial parts, body and rational soul. Therefore, the major proposition is true in a certain respect: but understood simply, it is most false. The same must also be established regarding the minor proposition, which is likewise true only in a certain respect. For the Image of God was not the very nature of man simply, insofar as it is such: but only κατά τι (in a certain respect), insofar as this nature is straight and whole. This argument therefore labors under the πλεονεξίᾳ (excess) of four terms: of which 1. is the nature of man: 2. a straight and whole nature: 3. the substance of man: 4. the Image of God. Which weak sophistry can be eluded by a similar argument: A healthy nature endowed with a good temperament is substance: But the εὐκρασία (good temperament) of the humors is a healthy nature, and joined with a good temperament. Therefore, the εὐκρασία of the humors is the very substance of man.

The third argument of Illyricus is as follows: Whatever diminishes the Image of God and original justice ought not to be tolerated in the Church of God. But the term 'accident' diminishes the Image of God and Original Justice, and no cause urges why this term should be used. Therefore, it also ought not to be tolerated in the Church of God: but rather the term 'substance' or 'form' should be substituted.

I reply: The argument fails by the fallacy of non-cause. For the Image of God and Original Justice are not diminished by the use of the term 'accident,' especially if it is posited to be not some light or superficial accident, but a connatural and concreated one. Furthermore, if one must not do evil that good may come, according to the authentic word of the Apostle, Rom. 3:8, then one should certainly not use inconvenient and absurd phrases or locutions to assert the truth. Thirdly, such inconvenient phrases carry with them much more absurdity than they can add patronage to the truth. Finally, most grave causes urge us, on account of which we maintain that the term 'accident' must be used entirely in this dispute.

First, indeed, to show the distinction between the Creator and the creature. For God is immutable because an accident does not fall into Him: but justice and all virtues are essential in God. Man, however, is mutable: because justice and all virtues in him are accidents, which can be changed into contrary vices while the substance of man remains. The second cause is, lest God be constituted the author or Creator of sin, who is the Creator of all substances: since without Him nothing was made that was made. But God is the Creator or author of no sin. Therefore, neither this, nor the preceding Original Justice, will be substance. There is no need for disputes to be stirred up about the term 'form'. For if Illyricus understands the essential form of man considered by reason of substance: we simply deny that Original Justice, or the Image of God, was the form of man: for in this sense and respect, there is no other form of man except the rational soul. But if he understands an accidental form, then the matter will be settled. For we ourselves confess that the Image of God was the form of man, not insofar as he was man: but insofar as he was a just, wise, and perfect man. Just as Original Sin can not inconveniently be called the form of a sinful man: or rather, the deformity of the former form.

The fourth and last argument of Illyricus is taken from the authority of the blessed Luther, who several times called the Image of God connatural: indeed, he wrote expressly in his Commentary on Genesis that it was of the essence of man.

But this argument fails by the fallacy of non-cause. For our blessed Luther did not use these terms and phrases of speaking as if he maintained that the Image of God was either the whole substance of man or some essential part of it: but to show that for the constitution of a perfect, good, wise, and just man, the Image of God, or Original Justice, is necessarily required: since it gives being to a thing as a form: but to a thing or substance, not insofar as it is substance; but insofar as it is such a substance: namely, considered in the category of quality. In which respect the blessed Luther most rightly affirmed that the Image of God is of the essence of man, namely, of that intrinsic essence of man created in the Image of God, which is defined not by substance, but by qualities: so that here is simultaneously involved the fallacy of equivocation in the term 'essence,' which denotes either the substance itself by itself: or the quality or condition of the substance: as in this place. Luther explains himself quite clearly in this opinion, writing thus in chapter 3 of Genesis: As the nature of the eye is to see: so the nature of reason and will in Adam was to know God, to trust in God, to fear God. Where, indeed, that the term 'nature' or 'essence' was used by Luther in the latter signification, hardly anyone would deny, unless he dared to affirm that Luther maintained that the power of seeing in the eye is the very substance of the eye: which would be joined with the manifest crime of falsehood.

With these matters thus far expedited in Thesis and Antithesis, let it be plain that there are most weighty causes for which our Churches, in the Article concerning the Image of God and Original Justice in the first man, openly separate and segregate themselves both from the ancient and recent Romanists, and also from the Flacians: but in such a way that they have no commerce at all with the Anthropomorphites, who understood the Image of God as a bodily form: as attested by Epiphanius and Augustine in their treatise on heresies.

Latin:

V. Et postrema Ratio longè firmissima desumitur à Restauratione Imaginis DEI, quæ tùm in hac vita inchoatur, tùm in futura altera in Electis consummabitur. Ea verò teste Apostolo, 2 Cor. 3, 8 Eph. 4, 24. Coloss. 3, 10. non fit per substantialem immutationem: sed per Accidentalem Renovationem mentis, constantem verâ Justitia & Sanctitate. Ert go neque Imago DEI in primo Homine, Substantia, sed tantum Qualitatibus est definienda.

Contra puriorem doctrinam hanc nostram, variis excogitatis Sophisticationibus insurgunt, qui Flacij dogma & partes sibi defendendas sumunt.

Ac initiò quidem distinguunt inter Hominem Physicum & inter Hominem Theologicum: contendentes se tantùm loqui de Homine Theologico, in quo Imago DEI & quidem in concreto considerata, fuerit ipsa substantia Hominis, idque hoc argumento evincere conantur.

Si originalis Justitia in Adamo fuit Accidens: sequitur, Imaginem DEI in Homine, non Substantiæ, sed tantùm Accidentis fuisse Bonitatem: & rursum ex contrario sensu amissionem Justitiæ Originalis, tantùm Accidentis fuisse corruptionem, non ipsius Substantiæ Adami. Atqui posterius hoc absurdum: Ergo & prius illud.

Quod sanè argumentum, cùm omne momentum disputationis hujus cum Flacianis, in se contineat, singula ejus membra accuratiùs evolvenda veniunt. Initiò igitur distinctio illa Hominis in Physicum & Theologicum, nihil est aliud, quàm Sophisticum κρησφύγετον. Nam 1. Distinctio hæc est planè ἄγραφος, omni Scripturarum autoritate destituta: quippè quæ Hominem Theologicum à Physico non specie distínguit: sed unum hominem Physicum & Theologicum considerat: Physicè, qualis à parentibus propagatur & generatur: Theologicè verò, qualis idem Numero & Essentia Homo, vel Justitia Originali est præditus, vel peccato infectus, vel beneficio Christi liberatus, justificatus, salvatus. Deindè hac distinctione propria quod dicitur vineta cedit Illyricus, seque ipsum refutat. Neque enim Homo ideò vocatur Theologicus, quod ratione substantiæ alius sit ab homine Physico: sed tantùm propter Theologiam, ut sic loquar, quæ est Accidens, sicut omnes aliæ artes & facultates: Quemadmodum etiam Homo Musicus propter Musicam, quæ est Accidens in Homine, sic appellatur. Sic unus est Adam, qui, si secundum Formam & Materiam Essentialem simpliciter & Physicè consideratur, Homo Physicus est & dicitur: Si verò Theologicè secundum id, quòd ad Imaginem Dei fuit conditus: Homo Theologicus est ac dicitur, qui quia secundum Theologiam Homo consideratur, non quatenùs Homo, hoc est, Animal constans verò corpore & anima rationali: sed quatenùs vel Bonus, vel malus est in judicio DEI. Tùm, si Illyricus de Homine Theologico disputat, quid opus est vocabulis Formæ & Substantiæ Essentialis? quæ haud magis ad considerationem Hominis Theologici faciunt: atque Forma ac Substantia Essentialis faciunt ad considerationem Hominis Musici. Turpis proindè Sophisticatio ὡς ἐν τῷ πῇ και ἁπλῶς, circa distinctionem istam commentitiam committitur.

Alterum membrum Flacianæ Sophisticationis est, quòd pro confesso sumitur, Imaginem DEI, in concreto consideratam, vel Bonitatem Adami, concretivè acceptam, fuisse ipsam Substantiam Adami. Sed præterquàm quòd petitione principii laborat hæc assertio, insuper impingit turpissimè in ipsa principia Theologica & Philosophica. Quamprimùm enim concretum nominatur, statim duarum diversissimarum rerum involvitur respectus: nempè substantiæ sive subjecti, & Accidentis. Undè à Logicis etiam concreta vulgò definiuntur, quòd sint nomina Adjectiva, quæ de Subjecto dicuntur regulariter, ut, Socrates est justus, paries est albus. Sic Adam in concreto dicebatur Bonus, Sapiens, Justus: non in Abstracto ipsa Bonitas, Sapiencia, Justitia. Proindè quandò Illyricus asserit, Bonitatem Adami considerari in concreto, ipsemet vel inscius fatetur, Bonitatem tanquàm Accidens esse in Adamo, tanquàm in Substantia sive subjecto. Cùm qua assertione statim pugnat, quod subjicit: Illam Bonitatem esse Formam Essentialem hominis ad imaginem DEI creati: Inest enim huic Formæ Essentiali hominis imago DEI: non autem est ipsa forma Essentialis. Accedit quod non in Logicorum tantùm, sed & Theologorum Scholis axioma istud extra controversiam est positum: Concreta & Abstracta in eadem Categoria collocari debent. Quare si Bonitas est in Categoria Qualitatis: utiquè concretum etiam Bonus, in eodem prædicamento erit: quippè quod de Adamo non simpliciter prædicatur, in Quid: sed in Quale quid: id quod est Accidentium.

Tertiò ejusdem vanitatis est, quòd in subjuncto argumento infert: Si imago DEI in Adamo fuit Accidens: Sequitur Imaginem DEI in Adamo non fuisse Substantiæ, sed tantùm Accidentis Bonitatem. Nam rectissimè negatur consequentia, cui haud plus momenti inest, ac si sic colligam: Si vis sive facultas visiva in oculo est accidens: Ergo non oculus ipse, sed tantùm Accidens illud videt. Ubi certè talis collectio explosione digna foret: siquidem vis visiva extra oculum nihil est: Cujus propria natura & affectio non est, ut sit ipse oculus, secundum Substantiam: sed ut insit oculo, tanquàm Accidens suo subjecto. Undè etiam vis illa in oculo propriè non dicitur videre: Siquidem non per se est Ens aliquod: Non entis autem nullæ sunt qualitates: sed oculus dicitur videre, propter inhærentem accidentalem vim visivam: Ita Justitia Originalis extra Substantiam Adami nihil fuit: sed ejus proprium erat inesse Adamo: neque Justitia ista propriè dici potuit fuisse justa, tanquàm per se subsistens aliquid: Sed Adam dicitur Justus, propter inhærentem concreatam illam Justitiam.

Patet hinc causam & fontem erroris Illyrici fuisse istum, quod falsò sibi persuadebat, Essentiale esse & vocari non tantùm id, quòd revera & propriè loquendo Essentia est, vel ut Metaphysici loquuntur, quod est Ens reale: Sed etiam illud, quod in Essentia est sive inhæret, & absque essentia non subsistit: Qui tamen respectus non est Substantiarum, sed tantum Accidentium proprius: ubi patet ex doctrina Logica.

Quartò notanda venit AEquivocatio in vocabulo corruptionis, sub qua ludit Illyricus. Alia enim est corruptio Physica, sive essentialis, qua res prorsus destruitur: & ā Philosophis definitur Motus ab esse ad non esse: ut Exempli gratia, quando Homo moritur, tum talis corruptio intervenit, ut ne quidem corpus amplius dici possit corpus, sed cadaver potius: & Homo cum definitione nomen quoque amittat. Alia verò est corruptio accidentalis, & impropriè sic dicta: nam propriè loquendo, corruptio non nisi Generationi Physicae opponitur: teste Philosopho lib. 1 de ortu & interitu. Accidentalis verò haec corruptio fit, ubi manente substantia, Qualitas deformatur: & sic Substantia non simpliciter, sed secundum quid corrumpi dicitur. Qualis corruptio Adamo obtigit, qui post lapsum secundum totam substantiam miserè corruptus fuit, verum non simpliciter: sed tantum secundum quid. Nam ratione partium Essentialium in se & per se consideratarum, mansit Adamus idem post lapsum, qui fuit ante lapsum, nempè Homo constans vero corpore naturali, & Anima rationali: interim tamen secundum concretas Qualitates horribiliter corruptus est, ut ex Bono malus, ex justo injustus, ex Sancto profanus & peccator evaderet. Proindè ex secunda hac corruptionis specie non licet argumentari ad primam, nisi in Sophisma à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter incurrere velimus.

Tandem turpis Sophisticatio consequentis committitur, quando infert Illyricus: Si Imago DEI tantùm fuit Accidens, sequitur, ejusdem amissionem non Substantiam sive Naturam ipsam Hominis, sed tantum Accidens aliquod corrupisse. Nam quòd corruptio haec non Accidentibus, sed ipsi Naturae tribuitur, causa est, quòd Accidentia per se non sunt, sed in alio insunt tanquam Subjecto: Substantia verō est efficax per se & simpliciter, idque vel ad bonum vel ad malum, sed non quatenus est Substantia: verùm tantum ratione qualitatum, quae substantiis insunt, vel ex prima creatione, vel ex subsecuta depravatione. Deinde Imago DEI non tale statuitur Accidens, quod in nuda relatione versetur, quemadmodum quidem putarunt, Dominium, quod habet homo in reliquas creaturas, esse hanc ipsam Imaginem DEI: sicut olim Scholastici etiam ac etiamnum hodie quidam Scriptores Pontificii contendunt, quòd Imago DEI externum saltem ornatum homini addiderit, ut color tabulae, corolla virgini. Nam etsi non erat ipsa mens: in mente tamen erat concreata & connaturalis perfecta agnitio DEI, & sapientia, quanta quidem in hominem cadere poterat: in voluntate conformitas omnium virium: In corpore summa omnium humorum, & totius temperamenti εὐκρασία.

Alterum argumentum quo in hac palæstra militabat Illyricus tale erat: Natura recta & integra, est ipsius hominis substantia. Atqui Imago DEI, sive Justitia Originalis, est Natura recta & integra. Ergo Imago DEI fuit ipsa hominis substantia, sive essentialis ejus Forma.

Respondeo, fallit argumentum Sophismate παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Confunditur enim concretum cum abstracto: hoc est, Genus subjecti in majore propositione simpliciter & abstractè accepti, prædicatur de eodem subjecto, κατά τι καὶ συμβεβηκὸς, secundum quid & secundum accidens considerato: vel quod eodem recidit: Substantia simpliciter accepta, & ratione sui τῷ εἶναι considerata prædicatur de Natu ra non simpliciter accepta, sed de natura recta & integra: id quod fieri nequit. Neque enim natura hominis ideò est aut dicitur Substantia, quia recta & integra fuit: sed quia constabat ex partibus Substantialibus corpore & anima rationali. Proindè major propositio secundum quid vera est: Simpliciter verò intellecta est falsissima. Quod ipsum statuendum etiam est de minore propositione, quæ itidem secundum quid tantùm vera est. Neque enim Imago DEI fuit ipsa Natura hominis simpliciter, quatenùs ea talis est: sed tantùm κατά τι, quatenùs Natura hæc est recta & integra. Laborat proindè argumentum hoc πλεονεξίᾳ quatuor terminorum: quorum 1. est Natura hominis: 2. Natura recta & integra: 3. Substantia hominis. 4. Imago Dei. Quæ elumbis Sophisticatio simili argumento eludi potest: Natura sana & bono temperamento prædita, est substantia: Atqui εὐκρασία humorum est natura sana, & cum bono temperamento conjuncta. Ergo εὐκρασία humorum est ipsa Substantia hominis.

Tertium argumentum Illyrici sic habet: Quicquid extenuat Imaginem DEI & justitiam originalem, illud in Ecclesia DEI non est ferendum. Atqui Accidentis vocabulum extenuat Imaginem DEI & Justitiam Originalem, neque aliqua causa urget, ob quam hoc vocabulo sit utendum. Ergo illud etiam in Ecclesia DEI non ferendum: Sed substantia potiùs sive formæ vocabulum substituendum.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate non causæ. Neque enim ex usu vocabuli Accidentis extenuatur Imago DEI & Justitia Originalis, præsertim si non leve aut superficiale aliquod, sed connaturale & concreatum statuitur esse Accidens. Deindè si non sunt facienda mala, ut eveniant bona, secundum authenticam Apostoli, Rom. 3, 8. utique non utendum etiam fuerit phrasibus aut locutionibus incommodis & absurdis, ut asseratur veritas. Tertiò, ejusmodi phrases incommodæ multò plus secum trahunt absurditatis, quam veritati patrocinium addere queant. Tandem causæ gravissimæ nos urgent, propter quas vocabulo Accidentis hac in disputatione omninò utendum esse statuamus.

Primùm quidem, ad ostendendum discrimen inter creatorem & creaturam. Nam Deus ideò immutabilis est, quia in ipsum non cadit Accidens: Sed justitia & virtutes omnes in Deo sunt essentiales, Homo autem mutabilis est: quia Justitia & virtutes omnes in ipso sunt Accidentia, quæ permanente Substantia hominis in contraria vitia permutari possunt. Altera causa est, ne DEUS constituatur Autor vel Creator peccati, qui est Creator Substantiarum omnium: siquidem sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est. Atqui nullius peccati Creator sive Autor DEUS. Ergo neque hoc, neque præcedens Justitia Originalis, erit Substantia. De vocabulo Formæ non est ut litigia moveantur. Si enim Formam Essentialem Hominis ratione substantiæ confiderati, intelligat Illyricus: simpliciter negamus, Justitiam Originalem, sive Imaginem DEI fuisse Formam Hominis: Hoc enim sensu ac respectu, Forma Hominis nulla est alia, præter Animam rationalem. Sin formam Accidentalem intelligat, tum res erit expedita, Ipsi enim fatemur, Imaginem DEI fuisse Formam Hominis, non quatenus erat Homo: sed quatenùs Homo Justus, Sapiens ac Perfectus. Quemadmodum Peccatum Originis haud incommodè Forma Hominis peccatoris: vel potiùs deformitas prioris Formæ, dici potest.

Quartum & postremum Illyrici argumentum petitum est ab autoritate B. Lutheri, qui imaginem DEI aliquoties nominaverit connaturalem: imò expresse in suo Commentario in Genesin scripserit, Illam fuisse de Essentia Hominis.

Sed fallit hoc argumentum Sophismate non causæ. Neque enim B. Lutherus noster ideò his terminis & phrasibus loquendi usus est, ac si statucret, Imaginem DEI vel esse totam Substantiam hominis, vel partem ejus aliquam Essentialem: sed ut ostenderet, ad constitutionem Hominis perfecti, Boni, Sapientis & Justi, necessariò requiri Imaginem DEI, sive Justitiam Originalem: quippè quæ tanquàm Forma dat esse rei: Rei autem sive Substantiæ, non quatenùs est Substantia; sed quatenùs talis est Substantia: nempè in prædicamento Qualitatis considerata. Quo respectu rectissimè affirmavit B. Lutherus Imaginem DEI esse de essentia Hominis, scilicet de intrinseca illa Essentia Hominis ad Imaginem DEI conditi, quæ non Substantia, sed qualitatibus definitur: ita ut hic simul involvatur Æquivocationis Sophisma in vocabulo Essentiæ, quæ vel Substantiam ipsam per se: vel Qualitatem aut conditionem Substantiæ notat: ut hoc loco. Quam in sententiam semetipsum Lutherus satis perspicuè explicat: sic scribens in cap. 3. Genesews: Sicut Natura oculi est videre: ita Natura Rationis & voluntatis in Adamo fuit, nosse DEUM, confidere DEO, timere DEUM. Ubi sanè in posteriore significatione vocabulum Naturæ sive Essentiæ à Luthero usurpatum esse, vix quisquam iverit inficias, nisi qui affirmare ausus fuerit, statuisse Lutherum, vim videndi in oculo, esse ipsam substantiam oculi: id quod cum manifesto crimine falsi conjunctum foret.

HIs ita hactenus in thesi & Antithesi expeditis, planum sit, causas esse gravissimas, propter quas Ecclesiae nostrae, in Articulo de Imagine Dei & Justitia Originali in primo homine, tùm à Romanensibus priscis & recentioribus, tùm etiam à Flacianis, se palàm sejungant & segregent: sed ita, ut ne quidem cum Anthropomorphitis quicquam habeant commercij, qui Imaginem Dei de corporea forma intelligebant: teste Epiphanio & Augustino: in tractatu de haeresibus.


## 11 On Original Sin

The disputation concerning Original Sin extends by far the most widely of all because of the abundance and variety of the Questions, concerning which there was grave disputation in the Church of God long ago, and there is still disputation today: with the Jesuits casting the apple of contention onto the stage of the Church. However, these, each and all, can be conveniently reduced to four general controversies: the first of which is concerning the definition and the quasi-essential parts of Original Sin. The second, indeed, is concerning its breadth and propagation into the entire human race. The third is concerning the most sad effect of this sin, and concerning the remedy by which it can be removed and averted. The fourth, finally and lastly, is specifically concerning Concupiscence, which remains even in the Reborn: namely, whether it obtains the character of sin properly so called? Our Treatment will also consist within the ambit or scope of these four controversies: provided that we have first said certain things, as if in a place of prolegomena, concerning Sin considered in general.

And at the beginning, indeed, it is established by the authority of the Scriptures that something is propagated from the fall of the first Parents into each and all of their descendants, which, speaking properly, is and ought to be called Sin: and first of all from that classic Aphorism of the Apostle, Rom. 5:12: 'Just as through one man sin entered into this world, and death through sin: So death passed through to all men, in whom all have sinned.' Examining this passage, D. Augustine elegantly writes: 'Passed through, passed through, attend to the word: Consider what you have heard: See what it is, passed through? Hence even the little child is guilty: he did not commit the sin, but he contracted it. For the sin did not remain in the source: but it passed through: it passed through not into this one or that one, but into all men.' Also pertinent here is that which the Apostle asserts expressly in the subsequent verse, 19: 'Through the disobedience of one, many were constituted sinners': And Rom. 3:23, he excepts no one: 'All,' he says, 'have sinned, and are destitute of the glory of God.' Indeed, Gal. 3:22 introduces that general Aphorism: 'The Scripture has concluded all things under sin': And Eph. 2:3, 'We are by nature children of wrath.'

But even if it were entirely without the authority of the Scriptures: nevertheless, there are most evident reasons at hand which wonderfully confirm the same thing. For who, I ask, would be the use of the Sacraments of the Old and New Testaments? What would be the end of the passion and death of Christ our Savior? What would be the cause of punishments, calamities, and finally of death itself? If men were immune from sin? So that Justin Martyr wrote most truly in his Dialogue with Trypho: 'Christ came to the Jordan to be baptized, for the sake of the human race: which had fallen through Adam into death and the fraud and seduction of the serpent, to say nothing for the moment of the proper guilt of each one acting wickedly for himself.'

And Origen, homily 8 on Leviticus: 'Whatever soul is born in the flesh is polluted by the filth of iniquity and sin, for which reason it is said: No one is clean from filth, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is one day.'

And Jerome on chapter 6 of Hosea: 'In paradise all have transgressed in me, says the LORD, and in the likeness of the transgression of Adam. For it is not a wonder if that which preceded in the parent is condemned in the children.'

Therefore, the error of Pelagius is intolerable, who contends that the sin of Adam harmed only himself, but not his posterity. And that all who draw their origin from Adam die, happens naturally: For even Adam would have died, even if he had not sinned, as attested by Augustine in his book on heresies, chapter 88.

That which the Jesuits maintain has a great kinship with this error: that death, and all the miseries into which we have been cast by the sin of Adam, are from nature in itself, but from guilt as from a cause removing that which prevents. But we shall have to speak expressly about this error in the digression of the second Controversy of this Article. Now that which comes under consideration is rather how Sin, considered thus in general, can and ought to be defined. And indeed the Jesuit Bellarmine, in book 1 of On the loss of grace and the state of sin, chapter 1, thinks that Augustine's definition, which sounds as follows: Sin is every word, deed, or desire against the eternal law, and that nothing can be desired in that definition except that mention of the voluntary be made in it, because, as Augustine himself testifies in the book On true religion, chapter 14, Every sin is a voluntary evil, so that it is in no way a sin if it is not voluntary. Although the same Jesuit, forgetful of himself, nay, manifestly contradicting himself, writes expressly in book 5 of On the loss of grace and the state of sin, chapter 20, page 451, that Augustine's definition applies only to sin as it signifies a transient act, not as it signifies a permanent stain. But if we examine it by the balance of the analogy of faith, it will readily be evident that it is in many ways imperfect and narrower than the thing defined, since it neither notes the source and origin of this evil, nor does it apply to all species of sin. For it is certain that infants also are born with sin, upon whom, however, neither deed, nor word, nor even desire, properly speaking, falls.

Noting this, the Scholastics determined it to be impossible to explain and comprehend what sin was in clear and precise language. Hence there have been almost as many definitions of sin in the past as there have been Doctors of the Church. But if we consult the Holy Scriptures, they certainly comprehend the whole matter in a very brief summary, defining sin thus: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἀνομία, Sin is the transgression of the law, 1 John 3:4. Our author explains the brevity of this definition skillfully and sufficiently with these words: Sin is a defect, or an inclination, or an action fighting against the law of God, offending God, condemned by God, and making men guilty of eternal wrath and eternal punishments, unless remission is made on account of Christ.

Our author most rightly establishes the foundations of this definition with clear testimonies of the Scriptures, such as: Deut. 27:26, Cursed is he who does not abide in all things which are written in the law. Where sin is defined as disobedience cursed by God: and disobedience not only actual, but the whole that is in the nature of man. Likewise Rom. 1:18, The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness. And Rom. 7:13, That sin might become sin exceedingly through the law, that is, the law shows the wrath of God, by the recognition of which we understand our impurity not to be a light evil, but to be something guilty, condemned, and cursed by GOD, which is accompanied by horrible punishments.

However, there is no lack of theologians who are accustomed to rise up against both definitions already given with some arguments. And at the beginning, indeed, that Johannine definition seems to some to labor under a certain tautology, and therefore to be insufficient, in that it does not express the respect of the foundation and the term in sin.

Then there are those who argue that this definition implies a certain contradiction if it is compared with other places of Scripture. For they say, Christ himself in John 16:9 asserts that the Holy Spirit will therefore accuse the world of sin, because they do not believe in him: thus clearly hinting that sin should be defined by infidelity rather than by ἀνομία or transgression of the law: especially since the Apostle also affirms that everything that is not of faith is sin, Rom. 14:23.

But the truth of both objections will readily appear if the individual members of the Apostolic definition are weighed more accurately. Rhetoricians otherwise teach that the vice of tautology is committed when the same word is repeated without singular emphasis: now although the words ἁμαρτίας and ἀνομίας agree in terms of breadth, yet they differ greatly in emphasis and clarity. For the former, namely the word ἁμαρτίας, is more obscure and expresses the 'whether it is' rather than the 'what it is': but the latter comprehends everything that pertains to the complex of sin, consisting as it were of its own genus and specific difference: so that the privative particle and the genus denote, namely, transgression or exorbitance: but the word νόμος expresses the specific definition, showing that that alone is truly sin and transgression which is committed against the law of God. Thus, therefore, this definition is easily vindicated from the crime of tautology: indeed, it is shown that it is convertible and admits of conversion, which the philosopher requires most of all as the proper criterion of a good definition. It is clear from this also that this definition is falsely accused of any insufficiency. For as has already been shown, the word ἀνομίας defines the whole relation of sin, namely its foundation and its term, quite clearly. For since the law of God obliges man either to perfect obedience or to punishment, certainly disobedience or transgression of the law denotes the foundation, while the obligation to punishment denotes the term of the relation of sin.

The latter objection labors under the fallacy of ignoring the refutation and of 'in a certain respect.' For those two aphorisms of Christ and the Apostle do not consider sin in general and simply, but only in a certain respect, namely regarding one certain species of sin, which is and is called infidelity. Now, from the position of one species, the consequence to the negation of the others is not valid. Therefore, the consequence in the argument does not hold: Christ and the Apostle consider sin only in the species. Therefore, John, who takes sin in the universal genus, is contrary to Christ and Paul. Rather, the argument ought to be inverted in this way: Sin considered in general is whatever transgresses the law of God. Now, infidelity transgresses the law of God, which by the first commandment requires full trust in God from us. Therefore, infidelity is truly sin, and it behaves as a species to a genus, or as a part to a whole. Meanwhile, however, if another question is mixed in at this point, concerning the preeminence or excellence of sin: which sin considered in species is graver and more excellent than all other species? We willingly admit that Christ and the Apostle in the alleged places ascribe this preeminence or excellence to infidelity alone. For this is as it were the fountain and source of all other sins: because it is partly directly opposed to the mercy of God and the merit of Christ, and partly because, while infidelity stands, no remedy is prepared for other sins, according to that of John 3:18, He who does not believe is already judged: but with that removed, all guilt is removed through faith in Christ.

Some criticize the Philippian definition produced a little earlier, moved by these reasons.

1. A defect or privation is the absence of a form which can be present. But original justice cannot be present in human nature. Therefore, sin cannot be defined by a defect or privation of original justice.

2. Inclinations, motions, and actions are something positive: Sin is an inclination, motion, and action. Therefore, Sin is something positive: And consequently it ought not to be defined so universally by privation and defect: which is what Scripture also intimates, when it defines sin by positive terms, such as, the old man,

Latin:

DIsputatio de Peccato Originis longè omnium latissimè patet propter copiam & varietatem Quaestionum, de quibus & jam olim in Ecclesia Dei graviter disceptatum fuit, ac etiamnùm hodie disceptatur: pomum contentionis in proscenium Ecclesiae projicientibus Jesuiticis. Possunt autem eae singulae ac universae ad quatuor controversias generales haud incommodè revocari : quarum Prima est de Definitione & partibus quasi Essentialibus Peccati Originalis. Altera verò de ejusdem latitudine, ac propagatione in universum genus humanum. Tertia de Peccati hujus tristissimo effectu, deque remedio, quo ille tolli & averti potest. Quarta denique & postrema, est in specie de Concupiscentia, quae in Renatis etiam est reliqua: An nimirùm ea Peccati propriè sic dicti rationem obtineat? Quatuor istarum controversiarum ambitu sive complexu, Nostra quoque constabit Tractatio: si modò προλεγομένων quasi loco quaedam de Peccato in genere considerato, dixerimus.

Ac initiò quidem ex lapsu primorum Parentum propagari in posteros singulos & Universos aliquid, quod Peccatum propriè loquendo sit & dici debeat, constat primùm Scripturarum autoritate: & cùm primis ex classico illo Aphorismo Apostoli. Rom 5, 12. Sicut per unum hominem peccatum in hunc mundum intravit, & per peccatum mors: Ita in omnes homines mors pertransijt, in quo omnes peccaverunt. Quem locum expendens D. Augustinus, eleganter scribit: Pentransiit, pertransijt, Verbum attendite: Quod audivistis, considedate: Videte quid est pertransijt? Indè est & parvulus reus: peccatum non fecit, sed traxit. Etenim peccatum non in fonte mansit: sed pertransijt: non in illum, aut in illam, sed in omnns homines pertransijt. Pertinet huc & id, quòd Apostolus versu subseq. 19. expressè asserit, Per unius Inobedientiam Peccatores esse constitutos multos: Et Rom 3, 23. neminem excipit: Omnes, inquiens, peccaverunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei. Quin Galat. 3, 22. generalem istum infert Aphorismum: Conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccatum: Et Eph. 2, 3. Sumus naturâ filij irae.

Sed si vel maxime absque scripturarum autoritate esset: Rationes tamen in promptu sunt longe evidentissimae, quae idipsum mirifice confirmant, Quis enim quaeso Sacramentorum veteris & Novi Testamenti esset usus? Quis finis passionis & mortis Christi Servatoris nostri? Quae causa poenarum, calamitatum & denique ipsius mortis? Si homines a peccato essent immunes? adeo ut verissime scripserit Justinus Martyr in Dialogo cum Triphone: Christus ad Jordanem venit baptizandus, humani generis causa: quod per Adam in mortem & fraudem, seductionemq; serpentis conciderat, ut interim propriam pro se maligne agentis cujusq; culpam taceam.

Et Origenes homil. 8. in Leviticum: Quaecunque anima in Carne nascitur, iniquitatis & peccati sorde polluitur, propter quod dictum est: Nemo mundus a sorde, nec infans, cujus est unius diei vita super terram.

Et Hieronymus super cap. 6. Hoseae: In paradiso omnes praevaricati sunt in me, inquit DOMINUS, & in similitudinem praevarionis Adam Non enim mirum, si quod in parente praecessit, in filijs condemnetur.

Intolerabilis proinde error est Pelagij, qui contendit, Peccatum Adami, soli ipsi nocuisse, non autem posteritati, Quod autem omnes, qui ex Adamo originem trahunt, moriantur, fieri naturaliter: Nam etiam Adamum fuisse moriturum, quamvis non peccasset, teste Augustino lib. de haeresibus, cap. 88.

Habet cum errore isto magnam cognationem illud, quod Jesuuvitae statuant: Mortem, omnesque miserias, in quas peccato Adami conjecti sumus, esse a natura per se, a culpa vero, sicut a causa removente prohibens. Verum de errore isto ex professo dicendum nobis fuerit, in diexodo Controversiae secundae hujus Articuli. Nunc illud potius sub considerationem venit, quomodo Peccatum sic in genere consideratum definiri possit & debeat. Et sane Jesuuvita Bellarminus lib. 1. de amiss. grat. & statu peccati, cap. 1. Augustini definitionem, quae sic sonat Peccatum est omne dictum factum seu concupitum contra legem aeternam Neque quicquam in definitione ista desiderari posse existimat, quam ut voluntarij mentio in ea fiat, propterea quod ipso Augustino teste, lib. de vera religione, cap. 14. Omne peccatum est malum voluntarium, ut nullo modo sit peccatum, quod non sit voluntarium. Quanquam idem Jesuuvita sui oblitus, imo manifeste sibi contradicens, diserte scribit lib. 5. de amiss grat. & stat. pec. cap. 20. pag. 451. A. Augustini definitionem convenire tantum peccato, ut peccatum significet actum transeuntem, non ut significet maculam permanentem. Verum si ad analogiae fidei trutinam eam examinemus, ultro patebit, multis modis eam imperfectam, & definito angustiorem esse, quippe quae neque fontem atque originem mali hujus notat, neque etiam omnibus peccati speciebus competit. Constat enim Infantes quoque cum peccato nasci, in quos tamen neque factum, neq; dictum: quin nec concupitum proprie loquendo cadit.

Quod animadvertentes Scholaftici imposfibile esse statuerunt, quid peccatum esset, oratione certa & perspicua explicare ac comprehendere. Undè plures fermè, peccati Definitiones olim quàm Doctores Ecclesiæ extiterunt. Verùm si scripturas sacras consulamus, certè brevissimo compendio rem universam comprehendentes, sic peccatum definiunt: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐsτὶν ἀνομία, Peccatum est transgressio legis, 1. Ioh. 3, 4. Brevitatem Definitionis hujus, Autor noster his verbis dextrè & sufficienter explicat: Peccatum est defectus, vel inclinatio, vel actio pugnans cum lege Dei, offendens Deum, damnata à Deo, & faciens reos æternæ iræ, & æternarum pœnarum, nisi propter Christum fiat remissio.

Fundamenta autem Definitionis hujus rectissimè constituit Autor noster, perspicua Scripturarum testimonia, qualia sunt: Deut. 27, 26. Maledictus, qui non manet in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in lege. Ubi Peccatum definitur Inobedientia maledicta à Deo: inobedientia autem non tantùm aEtualis, sed universa quæ est in natura hominis. Item Rom. 1, 18. Revelatur ira Dei de cælo, super omnem impietatem. Et Rom. 7, 13. Per Legem peccatum sit excellenter peccatum, id est, Lex monstrat Jram Dei, quâ agnitâ intelligimus nostram immunditiem non esse leve malum, sed esse quiddam reum, damnatum, maledictum à DEO, quod comitantur horribiles pœnæ.

Cæterùm nón desunt Theologi, qui contra utramq; definitionem jam datam nonnullis rationibus insurgere solent. Ac initiò quidem illa Johannistica ddfinitio quibusdam videtur ταυτολογία quadam laborare, ac proindè insufficiens esse, eò quod Fundamenti & Termini respectum in peccato non exprimat.

Deindè sunt qui arguant, Definitionem istam ἀντιλογίαν quandam implicare, si cum alijs Scripturæ locis conferatur. Nam inquiunt, Christus ipse Ioh. 16, 9. asserit, Spiritum SanEtum ideò Mundum de peccato accusaturum, quia non credant in ipsum: Sic perspicuè innuens, Peccatum infidelitate potiùs quàm ἀνομία sive Legis transgressione definiendum esse: præsertim cùm Apostolus quoque omne id peccatum esse affirmet, quod non est ex fide Rom. 14, 23.

Verùm utriusque Objecti veritas ultrò patebit, si singula definitionis Apostolicæ membra accuratiùs expendantur. Tradunt alioqui Rhetores ταυτολογίας vitium tùm committi, quandò eadem vox sine singulari ἐμφάsει iteratur: Jam licèt vocabula ἁμαρτίας καὶ ἀνομίας ratione latitudinis conveniant: tamen ἐμφάsει & perspicuitate plurimùm differunt. Prius enim illud, nempè ἁμαρτίας vocabulum, obscurius est, & magis τὸ εἰ ἔsτι quàm τὸ τὶ exprimit: posterius verò hoc omne id comprehendit, quicquid ad peccati complexum pertinet: Genere quasi proprio & specificâ differentia constans: ita ut privativa particula & Genus notet, nempè transgressionem sive exorbitationem: Vocabulum autem νόμε specificam exprimat definitionem, ostendens illud demùm verè esse peccatum & transgrespœ sionem, quod contra Legem Dei committitur. Sic ergò à ταυτολογίας crimine Definitio isthæc facilè vindicatur: imò ostenditur, quòd ea sit ἀντίστρεφομένη, & conversionem admittat: id quod tanquàm proprium bonæ definitionis κριτήριον Philosophus vel maximè requirit. Patet hinc etiam frustrà insufficientiæ alicujus, definitionem hanc insimulari. Nam uti jam ostensum, vocabulum ἀνομίας, totam Peccati Relationem, fundamentum nimirùm ejus & terminum satis perspicuè definit. Cùm enim Lex Dei obliget hominem vel ad perfectam obedientiam, vel ad pœnam: certè Inobedientia sive transgressio Legis Fundamentum: Obligatio verò ad pœnam Terminum Relationis peccati notat.

Posterius objectum laborat Sophismate Ignorationis Elenchi, & secundum quid. Nam duo illi Aphorimi Christi & Apostoli, non in Genere & simpliciter, sed secundum quid tantùm Peccatum considerant, nempè quoad unam certam peccati speciem, quæ est ac dicitur Infidelitas. Jam verò à positione unius speciei, ad negationem reliquarum non valet consequentia. Proinde non militat consequentia in argumento: Christus & Apostolus in specie duntaxat considerant peccatum Infidelitatis. Ergò Johannes, qui peccatum in genere universo accipit, est contrarius Christo & Paulo. Quin potius inverti debet argumentum in hunc modum: Peccatum in genere consideratum est, quicquid transgreditur Legem Dei. Iam verò infidelitas trans greditur Legem Dei, quæ præcepto primo plenam à nobis requirit fiduciam erga Deum. Ergò Infidelitas revera est peccatum, & se habet ut species ad Genus, sive ut pars ad Totum. Interim verò si hoc loco alia immisceatur Quæstio, de ἐξοχῇ sive excellentia peccati: Quodnam peccatum in specie consideratum reliquis omnibus speciebus sit gravius & excellentius? libenter fatemur Christum & Apostolum in locis allegatis, soli infidelitati hanc ὑπεροχὴν sive ἐξοχὴν adscribere. Hæc enim est quasi fons & scaturigo reliquorū peccatorum omnium: propterea quòd ea partim directè Misericordiæ Dei & merito Christi opponitur: partim verò quòd stante Infidelitate, reliquis peccatis nullum paratum est remedium, secundum illud Joh. 3, 18. Qui non credit, jam judicatus est: Eâ verò sublata, omnis reatus per Fidem in Christum tollitur.

Definitionem Philippicam paulò ante productam vellicant nonnulli his moti rationibus.

1. Defectus sive privatio est absentia Formæ, quæ potest adesse. Atqui Iustitia Originalis non potest in Natura humana adesse. Ergò Peccatum non potest definiri per defectum sive privationem Iustitiæ Originalis.

2. Inclinationes, motus & actiones sunt aliquid positivum: Peccatum est inclinatio, motus & actio. Ergò Peccatum est aliquid positivum: Et per conséquens non debet ita universaliter definiri per privationem & defectum: id quod Scriptura etiam innuit, quando per vocabula positiva peccatum definit, qualià sunt, vetus homo,


### On Sin in General

a heart of stone, flesh, etc. Whence Thomas also maintains that sin is not a pure privation, but a certain corrupted habit.

3. Whatever diminishes the atrocity of sin ought not to be taught: Privation diminishes the atrocity of sin. Therefore.

But the force of those arguments can easily be averted and overturned. For the first labors under the sophism of a vicious and imperfect definition. For privation is not only defined by the absence of a form, which can be present, but also which ought to have been present, nay, to which it was even fitting to be present, although now, through the intervention of a most sad accident, it cannot be present. Furthermore, the minor proposition is not completely true. For although in the reborn, original justice is not fully and entirely restored, it is nevertheless restored in part; and it will be restored at some time most fully in the other life. Most rightly, therefore, is sin defined by the defect and privation of that form which can be present to man, nay, which at some time will be present in the very act most perfectly.

The second argument labors at the beginning under the sophism of composition and division. For inclination and action are not posited solitarily or nakedly, but with the added complex of opposition against the law of God. Furthermore, it labors under the sophism of the accident. For the subject of privation is confused with the privation itself. For what is said in the minor, that sin is an inclination, motion, and action, these are not understood simply as positive things; but at the same time, the ἀνομία or ἀταξία is involved and noted, which inheres in these positive things as in subjects. Therefore, in the minor, it should have been added that sin is an inclination, motion, and action against the law of God: these being added, it is readily clear to anyone that there is a distinction between the subject and the depravity which inheres in the subject by accident. In this same sense the words of the Scriptures are also to be received. For the epithets added to substantive nouns argue that the substances of natures created by God are not themselves being noted, but something in the substances, namely, the forces and the depravity, which a just reason does not allow to be confused with the nature of things. As for the authority of Thomas, we are certainly not bound by it in the least, even if it were to make against us most strongly; but his own words fight more for our opinion, which sound thus, Prima Secundae, art. 82: 'Just as bodily sickness has something of privation, in that the equality of health is removed; and has something positively, namely, the humors themselves disposed inordinately: so also sin has the privation of original justice, and with this, an inordinate disposition of the parts of the soul: whence it is not a pure privation, but is a certain corrupted habit.' Thus far Thomas. Now, however, a corrupted habit does not simply denote a positive thing, but signifies an accident in a positive thing.

The third and final argument consists of a false hypothesis, which is assumed in the minor as certain and indubitable. Whence a begging of the question emerges. For by the word privation, the atrocity of sin is not diminished, but rather exaggerated;

and it is shown what great ruin and what huge damage the human race has received from this privation. There are, however, grave reasons for which the word privation must be retained in the definition of sin: namely, so that the distinction may be seen between created things and the depravity of things not created, but drawing its origin from the devil. But not even thus is the end of the sophistications, for there have been found those to whom even that in the Philippean definition of sin was displeasing, which maintains that the guilt of sin is the wrath of God and eternal damnation. Against this, however, they rose up with three arguments.

I. That which is nothing is not worthy of eternal punishment. But sin is nothing, because it is a defect: Therefore, sin is not worthy of eternal punishment.

II. The supreme mercy of God cannot stand together with extreme rigor, or with eternal torments. But this would happen if God, being supremely merciful, were to inflict eternal punishments on account of sin. Therefore.

III. The justice of God does not allow one and the same sin to be punished twice. But most, or almost all, sins receive temporal punishments. Therefore, it is not to be maintained that the same are punished again with eternal punishments.

But neither is there any evidence in those arguments. For the first plays with a childish equivocation of the word 'nothing,' whence a πλεονεξία of four terms readily emerges. For the major considers 'nothing' as negative, which sin is not; but the minor understands 'nothing' as privative, which posits a contrary habit: concerning which 'nothing' it is false that it is not worthy of eternal punishment.

A second argument proceeds from such a hypothesis, which is not simply true. For then at last the supreme mercy of God, when it could not stand with the extreme vehemence of rigor and the eternal torments of men, if God were not at the same time supremely just, nay, by His very Essence, justice itself. Just as, however, in God essential justice and Mercy do not mutually cancel each other: So God, through the rigor of His justice, inflicts eternal torments on those who perish: but through the affection of Mercy, He saves those who believe: without any contradiction, because the nature of the objects themselves is different. Where the admirable Temperament of divine Mercy and justice shines forth: concerning which the Article of Justification expressly disputes.

The third and final argument is most easily overturned by applying a certain limitation or distinction. For the major premise is true when it is understood of such a sufficient punishment by which the infinite divine justice is fully satisfied. Certainly in this way, if God were to punish sin twice, His own justice would be flawed. Now, however, regarding the minor premise, temporal punishments do not satisfy the infinite justice of God: nay, if you look at the intention of God, they cannot properly be called punishments: but rather they are exhortations, and as it were ὁρμητήρια (incitements) to repentance in the impious: to which, if they do not repent, they subsequently yield into punishments, which are the beginning of the eternal torments of the future age.

But let these things said concerning sin considered in general suffice. Now, whether it is of one and the same, or indeed of distinct species, comes under consideration. Pelagius and those who followed him contended that one should not speak of sin except in general: indeed, they bore it very ill, noticing that certain species of sin were established by the Orthodox: wise, as it is said, in their own eyes. For they noticed that under an indistinct generality, various errors could easily be covered and hidden.

Therefore, the zeal of the Holy Fathers, Augustine above all, deserves praise, who from the sacred scriptures skillfully elicited and explained certain species of sin. Although indeed various and manifold species of sin are commonly established, yet they can all most conveniently be reduced to this one general dichotomy: namely, that one sin is called Original, another Actual. Which distinction certainly depends upon the truth of the thing itself and the authority of the divine word. For just as there is a difference between the fountain itself or the source, and the rivulets or the flowing of waters, so reason itself clearly shows that the hereditary plague of sin differs from those actions which are designated by one's own fault. Moreover, as a foundation for this distinction, there is laid down both that graphic description of Original Sin which exists in Psalm 51:7, and indeed the fifth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, which, speaking of original sin, affirms that sin entered into the world through one man, and indeed passed through to all: and a little later adds, in verse 14, that it passed through even to those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression: where it is beyond controversy that actual sin is noted. This very distinction the Scripture sets before our eyes with very emphatic comparisons: such as 1. Of the tree and the fruits. Matt. 7:17 and 18. Luke 6:43. Matt. 12:33. 2. Of the hidden treasure and the expenditures of the same: Matt. 12:35. 3. Of the foul sepulcher, which although it is whitened on the outside, yet exhales the foulest stenches. 4. Of the fountain or source, and the waters flowing from it. Matt. 15:19.

Actual sin can be subdivided into various and manifold species: so that according to quality, one is Mortal, another Venial: according to the act of designation, one is a sin of Commission, another of Omission: according to the mode of duration, one is Reigning, another not reigning: according to the condition of guilt, one is Remissible, or against the Son of Man, another indeed Irremissible, or against the Holy Spirit. Concerning which species we are to have a discussion expressly in the subsequent next Articles. But in this present Article, an inquiry is instituted only concerning the first and as it were primogenial species of sin, namely Original sin: and that under that fourfold controversy which, as was shown from the beginning of these prolegomena, chiefly exists today between our Churches and the Jesuit faction concerning this sin: as the subsequent Treatise itself will now expressly demonstrate.

Moreover, before we make an approach to those individual controversies, it will be worth the effort to respond to those trifles by which, moved, both the Pelagians and other fanatics simply denied the species of Original sin. And first indeed they argued thus: The very word Original Sin is not found in the Sacred Scriptures. Therefore, Original Sin is a new thing, which is affirmed without the word of God.

I respond: The argument fails by the fallacy of the consequent. For even if this word is not contained in the sacred writings word for word and according to the letter, yet the thing itself, which is expressed by it, is proposed in them most manifestly: as has just now been demonstrated. What of the fact that by this method, not only the term for Original Sin, but also for all the remaining species of sin, with the sole exception of the sin against the Holy Spirit, would have to be denied: since they are not expressly contained in the sacred writings.

II. To sin is an active verb, signifying an action, that is, either a word, or a deed, or a desire. Therefore, that statement of Paul, all have sinned: Rom. 3:23 and 5:12, is not to be understood except of actual sin.

I respond that the fallacy of the figure of speech is committed. For verbs, according to the idiom of the Hebrews, do not only signify actions, but more often something habitual, especially if the nature and condition of the subject itself implies not only an activity, but the habit itself, as the fountain and principle of those actions: that this is the case in this place is proven by those testimonies of the Scriptures which constitute the heart of man itself as the fountain of actual sins. Matt. 15:19.

III. Not to fear God, and not to trust in God are actual sins. Therefore, they do not define Original Sin: but only actual sins.

I respond, the argument fails by ignorance of the refutation, for these phrases are sometimes taken for an activity, but sometimes for an inability. Aristotle himself was by no means ignorant of this, who expressly warned that verbs of activity in definitions concerning natural impotence are often to be understood. Hence our theologians also, by these phrases in the definition of Original Sin, do not so much wish to note the presence of vicious actions, as rather the absence and privation of that habit from which good acts ought to have proceeded. Whence Original Sin can not inconveniently be referred to two distinct species of quality: namely, to natural impotence, and to a habit. For if you consider sin with respect to that righteousness by which we might please God, it certainly must be called a certain impotence.
