But again, it is also a habit, opposed to that habit of righteousness which man would have attained if he had not been disobedient to the command of God. For the first man before the fall was neither just nor unjust by habit or disposition: because the righteousness which was in him was a certain natural potentiality, confirmed by no habit:

For the lower powers of the soul were indeed obedient to the higher, not by habit, but by creation. Now if Man had persisted in integrity, then certainly that natural perfection would have passed into a most absolute Habit.

Latin:

cor lapideum, caro &c. Unde Thomas etiam statuit, Peccatum non esse puram privationem: sed habitumquendam corruptum.

3. Quicquid atrocitatem peccati extenuat, doceri non debet: Privatio extenuat atrocitatem Peccati. Ergo.

Sed Rationum istarum impetus facilè averti & everti potest. Prima enim laborat Sophismate vitiosæ & imperfectæ definitionis. Privatio enim non tantùm definitur per absentiam Formæ, quæ potest adesse, sed & quæ debebat adesse, imo cui etiam competebat adesse, licet nunc ex interventu tristissimi accidentis, adesse non possit. Deindè Minor propositio non est completè vera. Etsi enim in renatis Justitia Originalis non plenè & ex asse restituitur: restituitur tamen ex parte ; & restituetur aliquando plenissimè in altera vita, Rectissimè proindè Peccatum definitur per defectum & privationem illius Formæ, quæ Homini potest adesse, imò aliquando perfectissimè ipso actu aderit.

Ratio secunda laborat initiò Sophismate compositionis & divisionis. Nam Inclinatio & actio, non ponuntur solitariè sivè nudè, sed cum adjecto complexu pugnantiæ adversus Legem Dei. Deindè verò Sophismate Accidentis. Confunditur enim subjectum privationis cum privatione ipsa. Nam quod in Minore dicitur, Peccatum esse inclinationem, motum & actionem, non simpliciter hæres positivæ intelliguntur: sed simul involvitur & notatur ἀνομία sive ἀταξία, quæ rebus istis positivis, tanquàm subjectis inest. Proindè in Minore addi debebat, quod Peccatum sit inclinatio, motus & actio contra Legem Dei : Quibus adjectis, ultrò cuivis patet, Discrimen esse inter subjectum, & inter depravationem, quæ subjecto per accidens inhæret. Quo eodem sensu Scripturæ etiam vocabula sunt accipienda, Nam Epithera substantivis nominibus addita arguunt, non notari ipsas substantias naturarum à Deo conditarum: Sed aliquid in substantiis, nempè virium & depravationem, quam cum natura rerum confundere, justa ratio non patitur. Quoad autoritatem Thomæ, illâ sanè nos minimè tenemur, li vel maximè contra nos faceret: Sed verba ipsius magis pro nostra militant sententia, quæ sic sonant, prima secundæ, art. 82. Sicut ægritudo Corporalis habet aliquid de privatione, in quantum tollitur æqualitas sanitatis; & aliquid habet positivè, scilicet ipsos humores inordinatè dispositos: Ita etiam peccatum habet privationem Originalis Justitiæ, & cum hoc inordinatam dispositionem partium animæ: Vnde non est privatio pura, sedest habitus quidam corruptus. Hactenus Thomas. Jam verò habitus corruptus non simpliciter notat rem positivam: sed significat accidens in re positiva.

Tertia & postrema ratio ex falsa constat hypothesi, quæ in Minore pro certa & indubitatâ sumitur. Undè principij petitio emergit. Neque enim Privationis voce extenuatur: sed exaggeratur potiùs peccati atrocitas:

& oftenditur, quantam cladem, & quam ingens damnum Genus humanum, ex privatione hac acceperit. Graves autem sunt causae, propter quas Privationis vocabulum in definitione peccati est retinendum: nempe ut conspiciatur discrimen inter res conditas, & rerum depravationem non conditam, sed a Diabolo ortum trahentem: Sed neque sic finis est Sophisticationum, quin reperti fuerunt, quibus & illud in definitione peccati Philippea displicuit, quod statuit Peccati reatum esse iram Dei & aeternam damnationem. Tribus autem & isti rationibus insurgebant.

I. Quod nihil est, non est dignum pœna aterna. Atqui peccatum nihil est, quia est defectus: Ergo peccatum non est dignum pœna aeterna.

II. Summa Dei misericordia, cum extrema rigoris vehementia, sive cum aeternis cruciatibus non potest simul stare. Atqui hoc fieret, si Deus summe misericors, propter peccatum aeterna supplicia infligeret. Ergo.

III. Bis puniri unum idemq; peccatum, Dei justitia non patitur. Atqui peccata pleraq; ferme omnia fortiuntur pœnas temporales. Ergo aeternis pœnis eadem denuo puniri non est statuendum.

Sed neque istarum rationum ulla est evidentia. Nam prima ludit, sub puerili aequivocatione vocis Nihil: unde πλεονεξία quatuor terminorum ultro emergit. Major enim considerat Nihil Negativum: quale peccatum non est: Minor vero intelligit Nihil privativum, quod contrarium habitum ponit: de quo nihilo falsum est, quod non sit dignum aeterna pœna.

Altera ratio ex tali procedit hypothesi, quae non simpliciter vera est. Tum demum enim summa Dei misericordia, cum extrema rigoris vehementia, & aeternis hominum cruciatibus stare non posset, si Deus non simul summe esset justus, imo per Essentiam ipsissima justitia. Quemadmodum vero in Deo essentialis justitia & Misericordia se mutuo non tollunt: Ita Deus per justitiae suae rigorem infligit aeternos cruciatus illis, qui pereunt: per Misericordiae vero affectum aeternum salvat credentes: sine ulla contradictione, propterea quod ipsorum objectorum dispar est ratio. Ubi admirandum Temperamentum Misericordiae & justitiae divinae elucescit: de quo Articulus Justificationis ex professo disputat.

Tertia & postrema ratio adhibita certa limitatione, sive distinctione facillime evertitur. Major enim vera est tum, quando de tali sufficienti poena ea intelligitur, qua infinitae justitiae divinae ex toto satis fit. Hoc certe pacto, si Deus peccatum bis puniret, ipsius laboraret justitia. Jam vero quoad Minorem, poenae temporales, justitiae Dei infinitae non satisfaciunt: imo si Dei intentionem spectes, poenae proprie loquendo dici non possunt: sed potius conciones sunt, & quasi ὁρμητήρια ad poenitentiam in impijs: quibus, si non resipiscant, postmodum cedunt in poenas, quae sunt initium aeternorum suppliciorum futuri seculi.

Sed de peccato in Genere considerato haec dicta sufficiant. Nunc, num unius ejusdemque, an verò distinctarum specierum illud sit sub considerationem venit. Pelagus & qui illum secuti sunt, contendebant, de peccato non nisi in genere loquendum esse: Imò aegerrimè ferebant, animadvertentes ab Orthodoxis certas peccati species constitui: in loco, quod dicitur, sapientes. Animadvertebant enim sub indistincta Generalitate varios errores facilè tegi & occultari posse.

Laudem proindè meretur S. Patrum, Augustini cum primis studium, qui ex scripturis sacris, certas peccati species, dextrè elicuit & explicavit. Quanquam verò variae & multiplices constituuntur vulgò Peccati species: tamen ad unam hanc διχοτομίαν Generalem, singulae & universae commodissimè revocari possunt: ut nimirum Peccatum aliud dicatur Originale: aliud Actuale. Quae sanè distinctio ab ipsius rei veritate, & divini verbi autoritate dependet. Nam quemadmodum inter fontem ipsum sive scaturiginem, & inter rivulos sive decursionem aquarum discrimen est: ita haereditariam peccati luem differre ab illis actionibus, quae culpa propria designantur, ratio ipsa luculenter ostendit. Fundamenti autem loco substernitur distinctioni huic, tum graphica illa descriptio Peccati Originalis, quae extat Psalmo 51, 7. tum verò caput quintum Epistolae ad Romanos, quod de originali peccato verba faciens, Peccatum per unum hominem in mundum introijsse, imò in omnes pertransijsse affirmat: & paulò post subijcit, versu 14. etiam in eos pertransijsse illud, qui non peccaverunt in similitudine praevaricationis Adae: ubi actuale peccatum notari, extra controversiam est. Quod ipsum discrimen Scriptura similitudinibus valdè emphaticis ob oculos constituit: ut 1. Arboris & fructuum. Matth. 7, 17. & 18. Luc. 6, 43. Matth. 12, 33. 2. Thesauri reconditi, & expensarum ejusdem: Matth. 12, 35. 3. Sepulchri foetidi, quod licèt foris dealbetur, exhalat tamen foetores pessimos. 4. Fontis sive scaturiginis, & aquarum indè promanantium. Matth. 15, 19.

Peccatum Actuale in varias & multiplices species potest subdividi: ita ut secundùm Qualitatem aliud sit Mortale, aliud Veniale: secundùm actum designationis, aliud sit peccatum Commissionis, aliud Omissionis: secundùm durationis modum, aliud sit Regnans, aliud non regnans: secundùm Reatus conditionem, aliud sit Remissibile sive in Filium Hominis. aliud verò Irremissibile, sive in Spiritum Sanctum. De quibus speciebus nobis ex professo futura est disputatio, in subsequentibus Articulis proximis. Hoc autem praesente Articulo tantùm de prima & quasi primogenea peccati specie, nimirum Originali peccato, disquisitio instituitur: idque sub quatruplici illa controversia, quae, uti ab initio προλεγομένων istorum ostensum, de hoc peccato potissimum nostris Ecclesiis hodiè cum gente Jesuitica intercedit: uti ipsa subsequens Tractatio ex professo jam demonstrabit.

Cæterùm priusquàm ad singulas illas controversias accessum faciamus : operæ pretium fuerit respondere ad eas φλυαρίας, quibus moti tùm Pelagiani, tùm alij fanatici, peccati Originalis speciem simpliciter negarunt. Et primùm quidem sic arguēbant : Vox ipsa Peccati Originalis non reperitur in Scripturis Sacris. Ergo Peccatum Originale est res nova, quæ sine verbo Dei affirmatur.

Respondeo : Fallit argumentum Sophismate, παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Etsi enim αὐτολεξεὶ & κατὰ τὸ γράμμα vocabulum hoc in sacris non continetur : res tamen ipsa, quæ per illud exprimitur, proponitur in illis manifestissimè : uti jam modò demonstratum. Quid quod hoc pacto, non modò Peccati Originis, sed & reliquarum peccati specierum omnium Terminus, solo excepto peccato in Spiritum Sanctum, negandus foret : quippè qui in sacris nòn expressè continetur.

II. Peccare est verbum activum, significans actionem, hoc est, vel dictum, vel factum, vel concupitum. Ergo illud Pauli, omnes peccaverunt : Rom. 3. & 23. & 5, 12. non est intelligendum nisi de peccato actuali.

Respondeo committi sophisma παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως. Verba enim juxta idiotismum Hebræorum, non tantùm significant actiones, sed sæpiùs aliquid habituale, præsertim si ipsius subjecti natura & conditio, non ἐνέργειαν tantùm, sed ipsum habitum, tanquàm actionum istarum fontem atque principium innuat : id quod hoc loco usu venire ea evincant Scripturarum testimonia, quæ ipsum cor Hominis, fontem peccatorum actualium constituunt. Matth. 15, 19.

III. Non timere DEVM, & non confidere DEO sunt peccata actualia. Ergo non definiunt Peccatum Originis : sed tantùm peccata actualia.

Respondeo, Fallit argumentum Elenchi Ignoratione, Phrases enim hæ interdum pro ἐνεργίᾳ, interdum verò pro ἀδυναμίᾳ accipiuntur. Ignoravit hoc minimè ipse quoq; Aristoteles, qui verba ἐνεργειῶν in definitionibus de naturali impotentia sæpiùs intelligenda esse, disertè monuit. Hinc nostrates etiam Theologi, per phrases hasce in definitione Peccati Originis, non tàm notatam volunt vitiosarum actionum præsentiam, quàm potiùs absentiam & στέρησιν illius habitus, ex quo actus boni proficisci debebant. Undè haud incommodè Peccatum originis, ad duas distinctas species Qualitatis referri potest : nempè ad Naturalem impotentiam, & ad Habitum. Nam si peccatum consideres respectu illius Justitiæ, qua Deo placere queamus, certè impotentia quædam illud dici debet. Rursus verò Habitus etiam est, oppositus illi Habitui justitiæ, quam homo consecutus fuisset, si mandato Dei non fuisset inobediens. Nam primus Homo ante lapsum, neque justus neque injustus fuit Habitu aut διαθέσει : propterea quòd justitia, quæ ipsi inerat, potentia quædam fuit naturalis, nullo Habitu confirmata :

siquidem inferiores animæ vires superioribus erant obedientes, non ex habitu, sed ex creatione. Jam si Homo in integritate perstitisset, tum sanè naturalis illa perfectio, in Habitum absolutissimum transiisset.


### Chapter I. Controversy I. On the definition and quasi-essential parts of Original Sin

Controversy I. Concerning the definition and the quasi-essential parts of Original Sin.

Original Sin has obtained its name, not from the origin of time in which it was committed, which was indeed the beginning of the World: especially since the first man fell on the very day he was created, if we believe Irenaeus; nor even from the very birth of the human race, which from the first creation was by far the best and most holy: according to that Mosaic epiphonema: God saw all that He had made, and behold they were very good, Gen. 1:31. But it is derived partly from a transitive sense, because every sin, and primarily that in which we are conceived and born, drew its origin from the Sin of Adam, which was Actual; and partly from the medium of propagation, which is joined with the very principle of our birth, so that Man does not begin to be or exist before he has the evil of this sin implanted, nay, ingenerated by nature. Ps. 51:7, Eph. 2:3.

Moreover, what Original Sin is has always been variously debated. Before the times of Augustine, hardly any plain and perfect definition of this sin occurs in the writings of the Fathers: indeed, that simpler and still ruder infancy of the primitive Church does not seem to have undertaken any care for this matter, being content rather with these two Questions: Whether such a sin exists: and What are its Effects? Whence it happened later that Pelagius, abusing the simplicity of the Fathers, tried to persuade the Church that the question περι του ει (concerning whether it is), what sin might be, was not a matter of faith, but only of inquiry: until at last Augustine, detecting the snares of Pelagius, understood that labor must be spent on establishing a certain definition: defining Original Sin not indeed inconveniently, but yet imperfectly, through concupiscence. Observing which imperfection, Anselm, Bishop of Canterbury in England, gave a somewhat fuller definition in his book on the Virgin Conception, chap. 26. Original Sin, he says, I can understand as nothing else, even in infants themselves, than the very nakedness of due justice caused by the fall of Adam, through which all are children of wrath. Which definition itself, however, is found to incur the mark of imperfection for the very reason that it defined this sin from one side only, namely στερητικῆς (privatively), making no mention meanwhile of the most vicious θέσεως (positively). Therefore, not ineptly, Hugh of St. Victor judged that both should be expressed in the definition of Original Sin, namely ignorance in the mind, as a defect: and concupiscence in the flesh, as a contrary habit. And although the Scholastic Doctors, and among them primarily Peter Lombard and Thomas Aquinas, were not altogether unsuccessfully occupied with this question: yet they admitted some things that were partly less convenient, partly less Orthodox: so that the matter itself was more obscured than explained; nay, with the passage of time, every definition of original sin was entirely lost and neglected. Albert Pighius makes this assertion sufficiently clear, who in the year 1541, soon after the Colloquy of Worms instituted with B. Luther, did not hesitate to write: Three things concerning original sin have been defined in the Church: 1. That it is. 2. Whence it is: namely from propagation from Adam. 3. What its effects are in us: But what Original Sin truly is, and in what its proper nature consists, is not certain by ecclesiastical definition.

Hence the Council of Trent, in the fifth session, was so unable, or rather unwilling, to define Original Sin, that it left to everyone the freedom of thinking about this head. A witness in this part, even by the opinion of the Pontificians themselves, who is beyond all exception, is Andradius, who in book 3 of his Orthodox Explanations, page 216, wished to uncover the counsel of the Fathers of that council in these words: Since theologians labor to explain how the transgression of Adam has the nature of sin in us, and could make us sinners: the Council of Trent, when it defined Original Sin to be truly sin, proper to each one, nevertheless deliberately wrapped its proper nature in silence, and thus left it free for everyone to opine.

And after a few words. Since, therefore, what the nature and definition of sin is, is a matter of question not only among heretics, but even among Catholics, and all are distracted into contrary opinions by doubtful contention: the Council of Trent, just as certain other councils, when they defined that all draw the sin of Origin from Adam, deliberately passed over and left aside what that sin might be.

The enormity of which impiety is so great that even Bellarmine himself, in book 5 de amiss. gratiae & statu peccati, chapter 20, p. 451 A., writes that Pighius and Catharinus (add also the Council of Trent) believed that Original Sin is nothing in reality remaining in us, but only the disobedience of the first parent imputed to us.

But neither do the modern Jesuits offer us any taste of candor regarding the explanation of this Question, but rather they transmute themselves into various forms, and strive to obscure the matter itself with wrappings of words rather than explain it. A judgment can be formed by Bellarmine himself again, who in the book 5 already cited, chapter 17, page 443 D., explains his own mind and that of his companions in this way: If anyone asks us what Original sin properly is: We shall answer with a distinction in this manner: If sin is taken for an action fighting against the Law, Original Sin is the first disobedience of Adam, committed by Adam himself, not as he was a singular person, but as he bore the person of the whole human race.

Latin:

Controversia I. De definitione & partibus quasi Essentiabus Peccati Originalis.

PEccatum Originale denominationem suam fortitum est, non ab Origine temporis, in quo commissum fuit, quod fuit sanè Mundi primitivum: præsertim cùm primus homo eo ipso die, quo conditus est, lapsus est, si Irenæo credimus, neque etiam ab ortu ipso generis humani, qui ex creatione primâ longè fuit optimus, & sanctissimus: secundùm illud Epiphonema Mosaicum: Vidit Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, & ecce erant valdè bona Genes. 1, 31. Verùm partim à sensu transitivo, quia à Peccato Adami, quod fuit Actuale, originem traxit omne peccatum, & cum primis illud in quo concipimur & nascimur: partim à propagationis medio, quod cum ipso ortus nostri principio conjunctum est, ut Homo non prius esse aut existere incipiat, quàm peccati hujus malum habeat insitum, imò naturâ ingeneratum. Psal. 51, 7. Ephes. 2, 3.

Cæterùm quid sit Peccatum Originis, variè semper disceptatum fuit. Ante tempora Augustini, vix ulla in Patrum scriptis, occurrit plana, ac perfecta peccati hujus definitio: quin neque curam aliquam rei hujus suscepisse videtur, simplicior illa & adhuc rudior primitivæ Ecclesiæ infantia: contenta potiùs duabus istis Quæstionibus: An sit tale peccatum: & Quinam ejus Effectus? undè postmodùm factum, ut Pelagius Patrum simplicitate abutens, persua dere conaretur Ecclesiæ, Quæstionem περι του ει, quid peccatum esset, non esse fidei, sed tantùm Quæstionis: donec tandem Augustinus Pelagij insidias deprehendens, de definitione certa constituenda laborandum esse intellexit: Peccatum Originis haud quidem incommodè, sed tamen imperfectè definiens per concupiscentiam. Quam imperfectionem observans Anshelmus Episcopus Contuariensis in Anglia paulò pleniorem definitionem dedit lib. de conceptione Virginali, cap. 26. Peccatum Originale, inquiens, aliud intelligere nequeo in ipsis etiam infantibus, quàm ipsam factam per lapsum Adæ, justitiæ debitæ nuditatem, per quam omnes sunt filij iræ. Quæ ipsa tamen definitio vel ideò imperfectionis notam subire deprehenditur, quòd ex una duntaxat parte nempè στερητικῆς peccatum hoc definiit, nullam interim vitiosissimæ θέσεως faciens mentionem. Proindè haud ineptè Hugo de S. Victore, utrumque in definitione Peccati Originalis exprimendum esse censuit, nempe ignorantiam in mente, tanquam defectum: & concupiscentiam in carne, tanquam contrarium habitum. Et quanquam Scholastici Doctores, & inter hos cum primis Petrus Lombardus & Thomas Aquinas, circa quaestionem hanc non omnino infeliciter occupati fuerunt: tamen admiscuerunt nonnulla minus partim commoda, partim Orthodoxa: ita ut res ipsa magis obscurata, quam explicata, imo progressu temporis omnis Peccati originalis definitio, prorsus amissa & neglecta sit. Fidem assertioni huic satis luculentam facit, quod Albertus Pighius, Anno 1541. mox post Colloquium Wormatiense, cum B. Luthero institutum, scribere non dubitavit. Tria de peccato originis in Ecclesia definita sunt: 1. Quod sit. 2. Vnde sit: ex propagatione scilicet ab Adam. 3. qui sint ejus in nobis effectus: Quid vero sit Peccatum Originis, & in quo consistat propria ejus ratio, Ecclesiastica definitione certum non est.

Hinc Concilium Tridentinum sessione quinta, usque adeo Peccatum Originis definire non potuit, vel potius noluit, ut liberam cuilibet de hoc capite sentiendi potestatem relinqueret. Testis hac in parte, ipsorum etiam Pontificiorum opinione, omni exceptione major, est Andradius, qui lib. 3. Orthodoxarum explicationum, pag. 216. Patrum concilij illius consilium his verbis detegere voluit: Cum Theologi laborent, ut explicent, quomodo transgressio Adae in nobis, peccati rationem habeat, nosque peccatores efficere potuerit: Concilium Tridentinum, cum definiret Peccatum Originis, vere esse peccatum, unicuique proprium illius tamen propriam rationem consulto silentio involvit, & ita liberum reliquit cuig, opinari.

Et post pauca. Cum igitur, quae sit peccati ratio atque definitio, non inter hereticos modo, sed inter Catholicos etiam in quaestione versetur, & ancipiti contentione in contrarias sententias omnes distrahantur: Concilium Tridentinum, sicut & alia quaedam concilia, cum definierint omnes trahere Originis peccatum ex Adamo, quidnam illud peccatum sit, consulto praetereunt, & missum fecerunt.

Cujus impietatis tanta est enormitas, ut vel ipse Bellarminus, lib. 5. de amiss. gratiae & statu peccati, cap. 20. p. 451. A. scribat, Pighium & Catharinum (adde etiam Concilium Tridentinum) credidisse, Peccatum Originis nihil esse reipsa in nobis manens, sed tantum inobedientiam primi parentis nobis imputatam.

Sed neque moderni Jesuvvitae circa hanc Quaestionem explicandam candoris gustum aliquem nobis praebent, quin in varias sese formas transmutant, & verborum involucris rem ipsam obscurare magis, quam explicare student. Judicio esse potest vel ipse rursum Bellarminus, qui lib. 5. jam citato, cap 17. pag. 443. D. sua suorumq, sociorum mentem sic explicat: Siquis a nobis quaerat, quid proprie sit Originale peccatum: Respondebimus cum distinctione ad hunc modum: Si peccatum pro actione cu Lege pugnante accipiatur, Peccatu Originale est prima Adami inobedietia, ab ipso Adamo commissa, no ut erat singularis persona, sed ut persona totig generis humani gerebat.


### Chapter I. Controversy I. On the definition and quasi-essential parts of…: Foundations of the definition of original sin

If, however, sin is understood as that which resides in man after an action, and from which the same man is named not sinning, but a sinner; Original Sin is the lack of the gift of Original Justice, or the habitual aversion and obliquity of the will, which can also be called a stain rendering the mind hateful to God. Which Jesuitical definition is indeed faulty in many ways: For first, Original Sin is distinguished into species that overturn themselves, nay, that manifestly imply a contradiction. For if it is true, as it is certainly most true even by our own concession, which Bellarmine argues, in the cited book 5, chapter 4, p. 366, C. & D., that Original Sin is ἀντιδιῃρημένως contradistinguished from actual sin: How, I ask, will that former aspect of the Jesuitical distinction be able to subsist? For the disobedience of Adam, in whatever way it may finally be considered, takes the name and definition of Actual Sin, so that what was actual sin in Adam is original in us: and what was personal in him is Natural in us. Most faultily, therefore, is the disobedience of Adam constituted under a distinct species of Original Sin. Furthermore, Original Sin is defined too imperfectly by the mere privation or lack of Original Justice: which has left nothing else in man but some stain displeasing to God. For, as will soon be demonstrated, such a lack or privation of Original Justice must be established as has extremely corrupted the natural faculties in man, so that man naturally has no power at all, or force, or gifts to effect spiritual Justice toward the Law of God, whether you look at the mind or the will of man: nay, that concupiscence, ἀταξία, and the propensity to sin, which we put on together with nature, is Original Sin. Finally, the Jesuitical definition of Original Sin involves the most sad guilt in plain silence: which is 1. Death of the Body: 2. Eternal damnation. 3. The tyranny of the Devil, as will be shown in its place.

With those false and insufficient definitions removed, we establish that Original Sin cannot be defined more correctly and solidly than if we consult the sacred scriptures and investigate its Nature more fully from them. When these are weighed more accurately, four main members of observations emerge. The first is supplied by a correct consideration of Original Justice, in whose place Original Sin has succeeded: and this in this manner.

Just as Original Justice stood in relation to the Nature of Man before the fall: so Original Sin stands in relation to the same after the fall: For the principle of contraries is the same. But the Image of God or Original Justice before the fall was in the Nature of man an integrity and rectitude, not only of the senses of the Body, but also a most perfect one of the powers of the soul, joined with immunity and the greatest freedom from every evil: The effect of which was the acceptance and fatherly good pleasure of God, to confer upon man not only any goods of this visible world: but also the blessed immortality of heavenly life.

Therefore Original Sin, which succeeded into the place of Original Justice after the fall, will be nothing else than such a corruption which, besides the lack of that Original Justice, has introduced darkness for light in the mind: depravity for rectitude in the will: contumacy for obedience in the remaining members: The effect of which is the most sad guilt, dragging with it the ruin of eternal damnation.

The second member of the observation is shown by Scripture, which depicts Original Sin in its own proper and native colors so graphically that he must be considered blind who does not wish to elicit its nature and true definition from it.

The first is that in Genesis 5:3, Adam begat a Son (Seth) in HIS own image, where indeed, that external disposition or form of the body is not understood: much less that which had come to Adam by grace: But the corruption of nature and the condition of mortality which Adam had brought upon himself by sinning: which is expressed more emphatically in Genesis 8:21, The imagination of the thoughts of the heart is only evil from youth.

The Apostolic passage, Romans 5:12, pertains here most of all: Through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death passed to all men, inasmuch as all have sinned. Where at the beginning the root of sin is expressed, one Man, namely Adam: For although the Apostle in 1 Timothy 2:4 refers the beginning of sin and the cause of death to the woman: yet because in the scriptures succession is attributed to the man, and the comparison to Christ, the root of sin is most correctly referred by the Apostle in this place to one Adam. Then it is worth noting that the Apostle does not say, From one Man: but through one Man: thus indeed hinting that the principal efficient cause is Satan, by whose envy death entered into the world: Wisdom 2:24, which, although it could not serve to remove the guilt of sin, could serve much to mitigate it. Thirdly, the Origin of sin is shown: which is not to be referred to God, nor even to created nature: but that it was introduced from elsewhere and entered into the world. Fourthly, the propagation of sin is noted, not into one or another: but into all men naturally begotten: Which is also hinted at by the word World. Where the Apostolic argumentation does not even exempt infants: which can be such: Where there is death, there is sin: But death reigns even over infants: Therefore there is sin in them too: But in them, says the Apostle, sin is not in the likeness of the sin of Adam: that is, they do not yet have actual sin: Therefore they have Original Sin: and indeed their own: For as Anselm cleverly concludes thus: When an infant is damned for Original Sin, he is not damned for the sin of Adam, but for his own: For if he himself did not have his own sin, he would not be damned: So we likewise cleverly infer against the Romanists and other fanatics: If an infant dies for Original Sin, he does not die for the sin of Adam, or of his parents: but for his own: For if he himself did not have his own sin, he would not die. Fifthly and lastly, the guilt of Sin is also described, which is both death of the body and eternal damnation: verse 12 and 16. In view of these five members, a perfect and sufficient definition of sin can, and indeed must, be most rightly established and judged: as our definition will show a little later.

Scripture again provides the third member of the observation, showing what kind of man is by his nature before regeneration or conversion to God: as Ps. 51:7, Eph. 2:1 & 3. Man is conceived in sin, and by nature is a child of wrath; indeed dead in sin: verse 12, without God, without Christ, without hope: Likewise chap. 4:17 & 18. Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their heart. Hence, the restoration or reparation of man, as Scripture defines it, does not take place only in the lower parts, as the Papists trifle, but in the higher as well as the lower, indeed in each and every power of man: until at last the body of sin is abolished, Rom. 6:6. and the new man is put on, which is created after God in righteousness and true holiness, Eph. 4:24, so that from this ἀνάληψις, namely the renewal of man, an infallible judgment can be made concerning the very corruption or depravity of all the powers of body and soul in man: and that all the more certainly, the sadder the complaints are that even those who are already reborn are read to have conceived concerning the remnants of inherent sin: Rom. 7:14. We know that the Law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin. And verse 18. I know that in me dwells no good thing: For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do: and verse 23. I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members.

Scripture provides the fourth and final member of the observation when it describes sin not only στερητικῶς (privatively), in the Papist sense, but also θετικῶς (positively): as the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit: where a στέρησις (privation) is noted: but soon follows a most sad θέσις (position): The things of the Spirit of God are foolishness to the natural man, 1 Cor. 2:14. Likewise Rom. 8:6. Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, the wisdom of the flesh is enmity against God. Rom. 7:23. The law of the members wars against the law of the mind, bringing the reborn into captivity under the law of sin. Gen. 8:21. Every imagination, every intent of the human heart, is only evil from youth.

These four members of the observations having been well weighed, a sufficiently adequate and accurate definition of Original Sin can be established according to the Scriptures: and it is such: Original Sin is the corruption inborn in all who are conceived and born according to nature from Adam the first-formed: which, besides the lack of Original Righteousness, has caused not only blindness in the mind, depravity in the will, and stubbornness and aversion from God in all the remaining members: but has also rendered all mankind guilty of divine wrath and subject to death and eternal damnation, unless remission is made on account of Christ.

With this Orthodox definition standing, it is readily apparent that two parts of this sin must be established: the former of which is proper to corruption, consisting of σχέσει (relation) and θεσει (position): by privation and by position. By privation, insofar as it is sin, that is, the lack of Original Righteousness which ought to have been in man: but by position, insofar as that privation is joined with a contrary habit, namely concupiscence, which consists of such and so great a viciousness of all the powers that by nature we are only prone to evil, and by the very act we are without true knowledge, without fear and trust in God, being indeed extremely depraved through concupiscence. The latter part consists in guilt, which draws the entire human race into the society of the fault of the fall of the first-formed in such a way that God is no less angry with each one of us than with Adam himself: as if we ourselves had also eaten from the forbidden fruit. Whence the series of evils and calamities, and especially death of the body and eternal damnation, arises.

These things having been premised for the confirmation of our definition, a judgment can easily be made concerning the antithesis. For in the beginning, the negligence of those Fathers cannot be approved who, before the heresy of Pelagius was stirred up, spoke more carelessly, indeed more inconveniently, concerning Original Sin: so that Origen did not judge this article to be of such weight and moment that it should be publicly proposed in the most famous Alexandrian School: but Basil maintained that sin could very easily be separated from human nature, so that not even signs of any evil would remain: and Chrysostom expressly wrote that sins are not natural: indeed that malice is contrary to nature, comment. on Tit. 1 and on Eph. 1.

Then the heresy of Pelagius was most rightly struck by the thunderbolt of anathema, who simply denied Original Sin: contending that nothing is sin except what is committed by the proper action of the will: and that infants also have nothing of vicious defects, and nothing of depravity in the soul, before they act evilly by a determined will: as witnessed by Augustine, lib. 2 de Grat. & peccat. orig. cap. 13. Indeed, proceeding to such impiety as to deny that death is a punishment for sin: as will be shown below, where we shall dispute concerning the most sad effect of sin.

Thirdly, those also are deservedly referred to the class of those in error who, around the year of Christ 1000, taught that Original Sin is only the liability to punishment for the sin of the first man, not the guilt: and in this respect it may be conceded that sin exists, even in infants, no otherwise than as sometimes a son, according to the judgment of a court, is exiled for the crime of a parent, while he himself meanwhile participates in nothing of that sin; as M. S. reports in book 2 of his Sentences, distinction 30.

Which most foul error the Anabaptists brought back onto the stage of the Church in the fourth place, in our age or certainly that of our parents, who among other things contended that infants should not be baptized because they lack original sin, and that Christ by his death took away Original Sin entirely from human nature.

Latin:

Si verò peccatum accipiatur pro eo, quod residet in homine post actionem, & undè idem homo non peccans, sed peccator nominatur; Peccatum originale est carentia doni Iustitiæ Originalis, sive habitualis aversio & obliquitas voluntatis, Quæ & macula mentem Deo invisam reddens appellari potest. Quæ sanè Jesuitica definitio multis modis est vitiosa: Primum enim distinguitur, Peccatum originis in species, seipsas evertentes, imò contradictionem manifestè implicantes. Nam si verum est, uti certè nostrâ etiam concessione verissimum est, quod pugnat Bellarminus, lib. citato 5. cap. 4. p. 366. C. & D. Peccatum Originis, peccato actuali esse ἀντιδιῃρημένως contradistinctum: Quomodo quæso prior ille respectus Jesuviticæ distinctionis poterit subsistere? Nam inobedientia Adami quocunque tandem modo consideretur, Peccati Actualis nomen ac definitionem sortitur, ita ut, quod in Adamo peccatum fuit actuale: in nobis sit originale: & quod in ipso fuit personale, in nobis sit Naturale. Vitiosissimè ergò Inobedientia Adami sub distincta species peccati Originalis constituitur. Deindè nimis imperfectè definitur Peccatum Originis, per nudam privationem, sive carentiam Iustitiæ Originalis: quæ nihil aliud, quam maculam aliquam Deo displicentem in homine reliquerit. Nam, uti mox demonstrabitur, talis statuenda est carentia sive privatio Justitiæ Originalis, quæ Naturalia in homine extremè corruperit, ita ut Homo naturaliter nullam prorsus habeat potentiam, sive vim, sive dona efficiendi Justitiam spiritualem erga Legem Dei, sive mentem, sive voluntatem hominis spectes: imò ut concupiscentia, ἀταξία & propensio ad peccandum, quam simul cum natura induimus, sit Peccatum Originale. Tandem definitio Jesuitica Peccati Originalis tristissimum reatum, alio planè silentio involvit: qui est 1. Mors Corporis: 2. æterna damnatio. 3. Tyrannis Diaboli, uti suo loco ostendetur.

Remotis falsis istis & insufficientibus planè definitionibus, statuimus rectiùs ac solidiùs Peccatum Originis definiri non posse, quàm si sacras consulamus literas, & ex illis Naturam ejus plenius investigemus. His verò accuratiùs expensis, quatuor potissimùm observationum membra emergunt. Primum suppeditat Originalis Justitiæ, in cujus locum peccatum Originale successit, recta consideratio: idque in hunc modum.

Quemadmodum se habuit Originalis Justitia ad Naturam Hominis ante lapsum: ita se habet peccatum Originis ad eandem post lapsum: Nam contrariorum eadem est ratio. Atqui Imago Dei sive Originalis Iustitia ante lapsum fuit in Natura hominis integritas & rectitudo, non sensuum tantùm Corporis, sed & virium animi perfectissima, conjuncta cum immunitate, & libertate maxima ab omni malo: Cujus effectus erat acceptatio, & beneplacitum Dei paternum, ad conferendum homini, non tantùm qualibet mundi hujus visibilis bona: sed & beatam cælestis vita immortalitatem.

Ergò Peccatum Originale, quod in locum Iustitia Originalis post lapsum succeßit, nihil erit aliud, quàm talis corruptio, quæ præter carentiam illius Iustitiæ Originalis, pro luce in mente tenebras : pro rectitudine in voluntate, pravitatem : pro obedientia in membris reliquis, contumaciam induxit : Cujus effectus est, reatus tristißimus, æterna damnationis cladem secum trahens.

Alterum observationis membrum monstrat Scriptura, quæ peccatum Originis proprijs & nativis suis coloribus ita graphicè depingit, ut cæcutire censendus sit, qui naturam ejus & definitionem veram indè elicere nolit.

Primum est illud Genes. 5, 3. Adam genuit Filium (Sethum) ad imaginem SUAM, ubi profectò, non intelligitur externa illa dispositio sive forma corporis : multò minus id, quod ex gratia Adamo obtigerat: Sed corruptio naturæ, & mortalitatis conditio, quam Adam peccando sibi ipse accersiverat : id quod ἐμφατικωτέρως exprimitur, Genes. 8, 21. Figmentum cogitationum cordis tantùm malum est ab adolescentia.

Pertinet hûc vel maximè Locus Apostolicus, Rom. 5, 12. Per unum hominem intravit peccatum in mundum, & per peccatum mors, & sic in omnes homines mors transivit, siquidem omnes peccaverunt. Ubi initiò exprimitur stirps peccati, Homo unus, Adam scilicet : Nam licet Apostolus 1. Timoth. 2, 4. initium peccati & causam mortis referat ad mulierem : quia tamen in scripturis viro tribuitur successio, & collatio ad Christum, utique rectissimè ad unum Adamum stirps peccati ab Apostolo hoc loco refertur. Deindè observationem meretur, quòd Apostolus non dicit, Ex uno Homine : sed per unum Hominem : sic nimirùm innuens causam efficientem principalem esse Satanam, cujus invidiâ mors intravit in mundum : Sap. 2, 24. id quod licèt non ad tollendam, ad mitigandam tamen peccati culpam multùm servire poterat. Tertiò Origo peccati monstratur : quæ non ad Deum, non etiam ad naturam conditam sit referenda : sed aliundè inducta, intraverit in mundum. Quartò notatur peccati propagatio, non in unum aut alterum: sed in omnes homines naturaliter progenitos : Id quod Mundi etiam vocabulo innuitur Ubi argumentatio Apostolica ne quidem infantes eximit : quæ talis esse potest : Vbi mors ibi peccatum : Atqui mors dominatur etiam infantibus : Ergo ijs etiam est peccatum : Atqui in illis, inquit Apostolus, peccatum non est in similitudine peccati Adam : hoc est, nondum habent peccatum actuale : Ergo habent peccatum Originale : & quidem proprium : Quemadmodum enim Anshelmus scitè sic colligit : Cùm damnatur infans, pro peccato Originali, non damnatur pro peccato Adæ, sed pro suo : Nam si ipse non haberet suum peccatu, non damnaretur : Sic nos itidem contra Romanenses & alios fanaticos scitè inferim9 : Si moritur infans pro peccato Originali, non moritur pro peccato Adami, sive parentum : sed pro suo : Nam si ipse nō haberet suum peccatū, non moreretur. Quintò & postremò describitur etiam Peccati reatus, qui est tùm Mors corporis, tùm æterna damnatio: versu 12. & 16. Quinque istorum membrorum intuitu de perfecta ac sufficiente peccati definitione rectissimè statui judicarique potest, imò verò debet: uti paulò pòst nostra ostendet Definitio.

Tertium observationis membrum subministrat rursum scriptura, ostendens, qualis Homo sit Naturâ suâ ante regenerationem sive conversionem ad Deum: ut Psal. 51, 7. Eph. 2, 1. & 3. Homo concipitur in peccato, & naturâ est Filius iræ; imò mortuus in peccato: versu 12. sine DEO, sine Christo, sine Spe: Item cap. 4, 17. & 18. Obtenebratam habens cogitationem, abalienatus à vita DEI, propter ignorantiam in ipso per indurationem cordis ipsius. Hinc restitutio sive reparatio etiam hominis, definiente scriptura, non fit in inferioribus tantùm, uti Pontificij nugantur, sed cùm superioribus quàm inferioribus, imò singulis & universis viribus hominis: eò usque donec tandem aboleatur corpus peccati, Rom. 6, 6. & induatur Novus, qui secundum Deum conditus est, ad justitiam & sanctitatem veritatis, Eph. 4, 24. ita ut ex hac ἀναλήψει, nempè renovatione hominis, de ipsa corruptione sive depravatione omnium virium corporis & Animæ in Homine, infallibile fieri queat judicium: idque tantò certiùs, quantò tristiores querelas ipsi etiam jam renati, de reliquiis inhærentis peccati, concepifse leguntur: Rom. 7, 14. Scimus Legem esse spiritualem: at ego carnalis sum, venundatus sub peccatum. Et versu 18. Novi quod in me non habitet bonum: Non enim facio bonum, quod volo: sed malum, quod nolo, hoc ago: & versu 23. video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meæ, & captivantem me sub lege peccati, quæ est in membris meis.

Quartum & postremum observationis membrum suppeditat Scriptura, quando peccatum non tantùm στερητικῶς, sensu Pontificio, sed & θετικῶς positivè describit: ut Animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus: ubi στέρησις notatur: sed mox sequitur tristissima θέσις: Ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, sunt stultitia homini Animali, 1. Cor. 2, 14. Item Rom. 8, 6. Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, Sapientia carnis est inimicitia adversus DEUM. Rom. 7, 23. Lex membrorum repugnat Legi mentis, captivans renatos sub lege peccati. Gen. 8, 21. Omnis cogitatio, omne studium cordis humani, tantùm malum est, ab adolescentia.

Quatuor istis observationum membris probè expensis, satis sufficiens & accurata Peccati Originalis definitio, secundùm scripturas constitui potest: eaq; talis: Peccatum Originis est corruptio, omnibus secundum naturam conceptis & natis, ab Adamo protoplasto ingenita: quæ præter carentiam Justitiæ Originalis, non modò, tùm in mente Cæcitatem, tùm in voluntate, pravitatem, tùm in reliquis membris omnibus, contumaciam & aversionem à Deo effecit: Sed & iræ divinæ reos, ac morti æternæq; damnationi obnoxios reddidit homines universos, nisi propter Christum fiat remissio.

Stante Orthodoxâ hac definitione ultrò patescit, duas esse constituendas Peccati hujus partes: quarum prior est Corruptionis propria, constans σχεσει & θεσει: privatione & positione. Privatione quidem, quatenùs Peccatum, hoc est, Carentia Justitiæ Originalis, quæ homini inesse debebat: Positione verò, quatenùs privatio illa cum contrario habitu, nempè concupiscentia est conjuncta, qui tali ac tanta constat vitiositate omnium virium, ut naturâ simus tantum proni ad malum, & ipso actu simus sine vera agnitione, sine metu & fiducia DEI, quippè per concupiscentiam extremè depravati, Posterior pars in Reatu consistit, qui universum genus humanum, in societatem culpæ lapsus protoplastorum ita trahit, ut unicuique nostrûm non minùs irascatur DEUS, quàm ipsi Adamo: ac si vel ipsi quoque de pomo vetito comedissemus. Undè lias malorum & calamitatum, cumprimis verò Mors corporis & æterna damnatio oritur.

His ita pro Confirmatione Definitionis nostræ præmissis, facilè de Antithefi fieri potest Judicium. Initiò enim probari non potest illorum Patrum oscitantia, qui ante motam hæresin Pelagii, de Peccato Originis securiùs, imò incommodiùs locuti sunt: ita ut Origenes Articulum istum non tanti judicaret esse ponderis & momenti, ut in celeberrima Schola Alexandrina publicè proponeretur: Basilius verò statueret, Peccatum per facilè posse separari ab humana natura, ita ut nullius mali ne signa quidem remaneant: Quin Chrysostomus expressè scriberet, Peccata non esse naturalia: imò malitiam præter naturam esse, comment. ad Tit. 1. & ad Ephes. 1.

Deindè Anathematis fulmine rectissimè percussa est hæresis Pelagii, qui Peccatum Originis simpliciter negavit: contendens nihil esse peccatum, nisi quod actione propria voluntatis committitur: Infantes etiam nihil vitiosorum defectuum, nihilq́; depravationis in anima habere, priusquàm destinata voluntate malè agant: teste Augustino lib 2. de Grat & peccat.orig.cap.13. Quin eò impietatis progrediens, ut negaret Mortem esse pœnam Peccati: uti infra ostendetur, ubi de tristissimo effectu peccati disputabimus.

Tertiò ad errantium classem meritò referuntur etiam illi, qui circa An. C. 1000. circiter docuerunt; Peccatum Originis esse tantùm reatum pænæ, pro peccato primi hominis, non culpam: & hoc respectu peccatum concedi posse, in Infantibus quoque esse, haud aliter, ac interdum Filius secundum sententiam Fori, exulat pro delicto parentis, ipse interim de peccato illo nihil participans; uti refert. M. S. l.2. Sent. dist.30.

Quem fœdissimum errorem in proscenium Ecclesiæ Quarto loco, revocârunt, nostro vel certè parentum nostrûm seculo Anabaptistæ, qui inter cætera ideò infantes non baptizandos esse contendebant, quia careant peccato originali, & Christus morte sua Originale Peccatum in universum sustulerit ex humana natura.


### Chapter I. Controversy I. On the definition and quasi-essential parts of…: The Papists

Fifth, Huldrych Zwingli, in his centurion-like [or: leading] Anabaptist fashion, maintains that Original Sin is not properly a fault or sin, on account of which infants are condemned to eternal punishment: But that it is a disease, or a natural defect, such as stammering, a stone, or another hereditary disease, etc., which, because they are present by nature, cannot be called a crime.

Likewise, that this sin is called sin by metonymy, on account of the actual transgression of the first man: and that it cannot bring about damnation unless it breaks forth into an action contrary to the divine Law, which action can be found only in those who have the use of reason. And these and other such monstrosities one may read in Zwingli’s Commentary on chapter 5 of Romans. Likewise, in the book on Baptism, tract 3. Likewise, in the declaration on original sin, to Urbanus Rhegius: so that Bullinger, Bucer, Rodolphus Gualtherus, Sobnius, and other Calvinist writers, who attempt to free Zwingli from the stigma of this heresy by writing that he spoke in such a way as to distinguish Original sin from actual sin, may seem to have betrayed all shame. Whether this excuse can indeed stand, let those judge who know how to judge without partiality. But it should seem strange to no one that the Sacramentarians undertake the patronage of Zwingli, since they themselves are hardly immune from the same error. For this very thing is meant by that which they commonly teach, that infants who are born of faithful parents, even before they are regenerated through Baptism, are not held bound to the guilt of the wrath of GOD, but are in grace. Now, however, the effect ceasing, namely the guilt: the efficient cause itself ceases, namely Original sin. But in the infants of faithful parents the guilt of sin ceases, even before regeneration: Therefore in them the Efficient cause also ceases, namely Original sin, and indeed not by the grace of renewal, but by the privilege of birth.

Sixth, both Scholastic writers and more recent Jesuits belong to the class of those who err, who, as shown above, wish Original Sin to be a bare privation, and not some positive corruption or depravity inherent in human nature: because, Original Justice having been lost, the Natural faculties remained intact. Which opinion is indeed directed solely to the extenuation of this Original evil. Whence Andradius did not hesitate to break out into these words: Although we cannot deny that human nature is extremely depraved: yet this depravity is not to be amplified so much that we acknowledge nothing pious, nothing good, nothing not contaminated in it. Far differently, indeed, does the most holy Job determine, ch. 14, 4. Who, he says, will bring a clean thing out of an unclean? or: Who will be clean from filth? none, even if his life on earth is but one day. Likewise, Augustine and Anselm thought far differently, who were accustomed to call this corruption Natural Sin: not indeed in the sense as if God the Creator had conjoined this evil to Nature; as Augustine speaks in Hypognost. 4. But because it has so passed through human nature from the sinning Nature, that nothing sound is left in it, from the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head. Is. 1, 6. Moses expressed this sufficiently clearly, as shown above, Gen. 6, 5. saying, Every figment of the thoughts of the heart is only evil at all times: And lest this Aphorism be restricted to the impious alone, who lived before the flood, it is repeated in ch. 8, 21. and indeed at that time when only Noah the just lived on earth with his own: and it is accommodated to the whole human race, not even infants excepted. Of which Mosaic saying, the greater and clearer the emphasis is: the fouler is the depravity of Bellarmine, by which he attempts to obscure it: That, he says, all thoughts are said to be evil, is without doubt a hyperbole familiar to the Scriptures: For in the same sixth chapter of Genesis we read: all flesh had corrupted its way: and yet in the same place it is said: Noah was a just and perfect man in his generations. lib. 5. cap 3. de amiss. grat. & stat. peccati pag. 355. A. But the Jesuit commits a manifest crime, while he takes in a hyperbolic sense at the beginning what the Holy Spirit indicates is to be taken in a proper, literal, and most true sense: For both the analogy of faith and the comparison of all places of Scripture dealing with this sin demonstrate most evidently that Man is so corrupted according to all the powers of soul and body, that whatever he thinks from the instinct of Nature, or conceives in any way, is only evil. Then, indeed, the Example of Noah does nothing at all to the matter. For the consequence does not hold from the state of the Regenerate to human Nature itself considered in itself and in the state of sin. But the Jesuit has undoubtedly learned this depravation of the Mosaic passage from the Latin Vulgate, which committed the crime of Falsity regarding the version of the Hebrew text. For at the beginning, for Figment of the thoughts and of the heart, it corruptly rendered, Sense and thought of the heart. Whence it began to be disputed about the sensuality of the affections, and the corruption of the lower powers, namely so that the higher faculties could be speciously exempted from that corruption. 2. The exclusive particle Only [רק] it completely elided. 3. For that which was simply posited by Moses, is evil, the Vulgate version insidiously rendered: is prone and intent to evil: of which the former denotes a most present act of malice: but the latter only a power or proclivity to evil. But that incomparable Theologian Dr. Martin Chemnitz rightly warns that the greatest force and emphasis lies both in the Exclusive particle and in the word Figment. For that Exclusive leaves nothing at all to natural man, except what is evil, and thus is fighting with the will of GOD. Then the word Figment in Hebrew is יצר, which is derived from the root יצר: This, however, properly signifies to conceive something studiously in the mind, or to form it outwardly according to the idea conceived in the mind. By this word, therefore, it is implied, whether the motions are merely conceived in the heart as far as a man can, or whether they go forth into the work itself: whatever best can be done in this regard, that nowhere deserves the title of goodness.

Latin:

Quintò Huldrichus Zwinglius Anabaptiflis suecenturians statuit malum Originale propriè non esse culpam sive peccatum, propter quod infantes æterno supplicio addicantur: Sed esse morbum, sive naturalem defectum, qualis est balbuties, calculus, vel alius morbus hereditarius, &c. quæ quia naturâ adsint, in crimen vocari non possunt.

Item, Peccatum hoc vocari peccatum per Metonymiam, propter actualem prævaricationem primi hominis: neque illud posse damnationem inferre, nisi erumpat in actionem Legi divinæ contrariam, qualis actio in ijs folùm inveniri potest, qui usum rationis habent. Quæ & id genus alia portenta legere licet in Commentario Zwinglij ad cap. 5. ad Roman. Item, in libro de Baptismo, tractat. 3. Item, in declaratione de peccato originali, ad Urbanum Rhegium: ita ut pudorem omnem prodidisse videri queant Bullingerus, Bucerus, Rodolphus Gualtherus, Sobnius, & alii Calviniani scriptores, qui Zwinglium ab hac hæreseως nota liberare conantur, scriptitantes, ipsum sic locutum esse, ut peccatum Originis ab actuali discerneret. Quæ sanè excusatio nùm subsistere queat, judicetis, qui ἄνευ προsωποληψίας judicare novit. Sed mirum videri debet nemini, Sacramentarios Zwinglii patrocinium suscipere, cùm ipsimet ab eodem errore haud sint immunes? Hoc ipsum enim sibi vult illud, quod communiter docent, Infantes, qui ex fidelibus parentibus nascuntur, etiam priusquam per Baptismum regenerantur, non teneri obstrictos reatui iræ DEI, sed esse illos in gratiâ. Jam verò cessante effectu, nempè reatu: cessat ipsa causa efficiens videlicet peccatum Originis. Atqui in infantibus fidelium parentum cessat reatus peccati, etiam ante regenerationem: Ergo in ijsdem cessat etiam causa Efficiens, nempè peccatum Originis, & quidem non ex renovationis gratia, sed ex nativitatis privilegio.

Sextò pertinent ad classem errantium, tùm Scholastici Scriptores, tùm recentiores Jesuvitæ, qui, uti suprà ostensum, Peccatum Originis volunt esse nudam privationem, & non positivam aliquam corruptionem sive pravitatem, hærentem in natura humana: proptereà quòd amissa Justitia Originali, Naturalia manserint, integra. Quæ sanè sententia ad extenuandum malum hoc Originis unicè directa est. Undè Andradius in hæc verba erumpere non dubitavit: Etsi humanam naturam perquàm depravatam esse, negare non possumus: hæc tamen depravatio non tantoperè est amplificanda, ut nihil in illâ pium, nihil bonum, nihil non contaminatum agnoscamus. Longè sanè aliter statuit sanctissimus Job. cap. 14, 4. Quis, inquiens, dabit à sordibus mundum, quod ex contaminato est? vel: Quis mundus erit à sorde? nullus, etsi una dies vitæ ejus super terram. Longè item aliter senserunt Augustinus & Anshelmus, qui corruptionem hanc vocare consueverunt Peccatum Naturale: non eo quidem sensu, quasi DEus Creator Malum hoc Naturæ congenuerit; uti loquitur Augustinus Hypognost. 4. Sed quòd à peccante Natura ita Naturam humanam pertransierit, ut nihil sani in ea sit relictum, à planta pedis, usque ad verticem capitis. Jes. 1, 6. Expressit hoc satis luculenter Moses, uti supra ostensum, Genes. 6, 5. Omne, inquiens, figmentum cogitationum cordis tantum malum est omni tempore: Et ne ad solos impios, qui ante diluvium vixerunt, Aphorismus iste restringatur, repetitur ille cap. 8, 21. & quidem eo tempore, quo solus Nohahus justus, cum suis in terra viveret: & accommodatur ad totum genus humanum, ne quidem infantibus exceptis. Cujus sane dicti Mosaici, quo major & luculentior est emphasis: eo fœdior est depravatio Bellarmini, qua illud obscurare conatur: Quòd, inquiens, Cogitationes omnes dicuntur esse malæ, sine dubio hyperbole est Scripturis familiaris: Nam in eodem capite sexto Genesis legimus: omnis caro corruperat viam suam: & tamen in eodem loco dicitur: Noë vir justus atque perfectus fuit in generationibus suis. lib. 5. cap 3. de amiss. grat. & stat. peccati pag. 355. A. Sed scelus manifestum committit Jesuita, dum initio hyperbolico sensu accipit, quod Spiritus sanctus in proprio, literali ac verissimo sensu accipiendum esse innuit: Nam tum analogia fidei, tum collatio omnium locorum Scripturæ de hoc peccato agentium, evidentissime demonstrat, Hominem secundum vires omnes animæ & corporis ita corruptum esse, ut tantum malum sit, quicquid ex Naturæ instinctu cogitat, aut quoquo modo concipit. Deinde vero Exemplum Noahi nihil prorsus ad rem facit. Nam a statu Renatorum, ad Naturam ipsam humanam in se & in statu peccati consideratam, non valet consequentia. Sed didicit sine dubio Jesuita hanc loci Mosaici depravationem, ex vulgata latina, quæ circa versionem textus Hebræi tergeminum commisit crimen Falsi. Nam initio pro Figmento cogitationum & cordis, corrupte, reddidit, Sensus & cogitatio cordis. Unde disputari cœptum fuit de sensualitate affectuum, & corruptione inferiorum virium, nempe ut facultates superiores a corruptione ista speciose eximi possent. 2. Particulam exclusivam Tantummodo רק prorsus elisit. 3. Pro eo, quod a Mose simpliciter positum fuit, Malum est, vulgata versio insidiose reddidit: in malum prona & intenta est: quorum illud actum malitiæ præsentissimum: hoc vero dynamin tantum sive proclivitatem ad malum notat. Recte autem admonet incomparabilis ille Theologus D. Martinus Chemnitius, maximam vim atque emphasin tum in particula Exclusiva: tum in voce Figmenti latere. Exclusiva enim illa nihil prorsus relinquit homini naturali, nisi quod malum, & sic cum voluntate DEI pugnans est. Deinde vox Figmenti in Hebræo est יצר, quæ deducitur a radice יצר: Hæc vero proprie significat studiosè aliquid vel animo concipere, vel juxta conceptam animo ideam, foris efformare. Illud proinde hac voce innuitur, sive motus duntaxat in corde concipiatur pro virili: sive in opus ipsum exeant: quicquid optimum hac parte fieri potest, illud bonitatis titulum nuspiam mereri.


### Chapter I. Controversy I. On the definition and quasi-essential parts of…: On Flacianism

Seventhly and lastly, that Neo-Manichaeism of the Flacians also pertains here, who determine that Original Sin must be defined by the very Substance of Man, and indeed by his most noble part, namely the rational Soul, and his most excellent powers, namely the Intellect and the will. The first handle and occasion for this error was provided in the previous century by the Weimar Disputation in the year 1561, instituted between Victorinus Strigel and Matthias Flacius Illyricus concerning Free Will. For when, in the act of the Disputation, it did not immediately occur to Flacius whether and how a Substance could be corrupted by an Accident, it happened that in exaggerating the corruption of Human nature, he contended that Original Sin should be referred not to the class of Accidents, but to the Substance itself of human Nature, properly and without distinction.

Hence he produced the following flowers or Emblems.

1. Let us know that the word Sin signifies not only a work, action, or thought, nor even some evil habit: but also a certain very evil force and Essence, brought with us from the mother's womb, part 2, Clavis Scripturae, tractate 6, p. 369.

2. I feel and assert that the primary Original Sin is Substance, because the rational soul, and especially its most noble and substantial powers, namely the intellect and will, are now so utterly inverted by the fraud of Satan that they are a true and living image of Satan, not otherwise than if some most sincere mass, infected with a most poisonous ferment, had been thoroughly and Substantially changed and transformed into the mass of that same ferment. ibid p. 376.

3. Nor yet do I deny that some part of Original Sin is Accidents: for I know that Sin has so pervaded the whole man, and even the whole world, that it can be found in the whole man, and in all categories, and is almost a certain transcendent. For some sin is Substance, namely the flesh itself, the old Adam, etc.; some is Accident, such as the vain, most evil inclinations born with us. ibid.

4. It clearly appears that some original sin or part of it is the very Substance of man, not something external or accidental in him: nay (in the immediately preceding context) it is the flesh itself, it is the animal man himself, the old man himself, or the WHOLE man, AS MUCH AS he is, insofar as he is not reborn. p. 369.

5. We were once in the first creation something very good, both in Accidents and in Substance: afterwards we were changed ESSENTIALLY into a thing very evil IN ITS SUBSTANCE, page 368.

Although indeed Illyricus not rarely complained that the State of the controversy was perverted by our side, while indeed this is not the Question: Whether original sin is Substance or Accident?

But only this: Whether original sin is the very corrupted Nature of Man, and especially the Essential Form or Image of the rational soul? Yet he did not explain himself so much as to involve the matter more intricately: For if he seriously denied that Original Sin is Substance, he must certainly have also denied that Original Sin is the very corrupted Nature or Substance of man. For our people, in informing the former State of the controversy, did not ask this: Whether original sin is some substance subsisting by itself outside of man: But: Whether Original Sin is the very corrupted Substance of Man? The State of the Controversy therefore is one and the same on both sides; the Affirmative of which Illyricus held: while our Churches on the contrary fought orthodoxly for the Negative: for the Reasons or arguments which follow, which are by far the most evident.

I. Every Substance is only from GOD the creator: John 1:3. But Original Sin is not from GOD the creator: but from the Devil and the depraved will of man. Wis. 2:13. Therefore Original Sin is not Substance.

II. Every substance, created by God, is good. Gen. 1, 31. 1 Tim. 4, 4. But original sin is not good. Therefore, original sin cannot be that very substance which was created by God.

Flacius objects that the major proposition is not true simply, but only in a certain respect, insofar as the substance created by God has not yet been so changed by the fall of the first parents that it can now no longer be called good, but evil and hateful to God.

But it is most rightly answered that disparate things do not cancel each other out, but can exist together in one subject without contradiction. Now, for one and the same substance to be evil and at the same time remain a good creature of God are disparate things. Therefore, the minor premise can be demonstrated from this most evidently, that Adam in the very fall, and likewise the Devil in the very apostasy, did not cease to be a creature of God. Since God himself after the fall, however evil and perverse men may be, still expressly calls them his creature. Gen. 6, 7. Deut. 32, 7.

With this foundation presupposed, we most rightly infer two things: I. That the theology of Flacius is gross and horrendous, asserting that man is only initially, or by reason of his first creation, a creature of God: Likewise, that the Devil differs in his whole species and whole genus from the holy angels. II. That in man after the fall, and thus in sinful man, two distinct or disparate things must always be properly considered and distinguished: one of which is the very substance of man created by God: the other, however, is sin or malice, which has the Devil as its author, and happens to the created man. The former ensures that man is man: the latter, however, causes the same man to be called evil and a sinner. Although this sin has taken such deep roots in the substance of man that in this life it can never be materially separated: yet they are to be distinguished from each other as far as the work of God is distant from the work of the Devil.

This caution Scripture itself also carefully observed: GOD, it says, created man immortal: But by the envy of the Devil death entered into the world, Wis. 2, 23.

III. Argument: Whose power it is to substantially transmute rational Essences into Essences differing in species from the former: his it is also to create new essences: But this belongs to GOD alone, and never to the Devil, so that he cannot even create a louse. Exod. 8, 18. Therefore it is false and fictitious that the Devil has essentially transmuted the Substance of Man: unless perhaps Flacius, through notable impiety, wishes to sell the Devil as a creator.

But Illyricus objects that the Devil is to be called a creator only if he were to create some new Substance: Now, however, since he has merely transmuted a Substance already created by GOD into another essentially: it does not follow from that any more that the Devil is a creator, than it follows that some Woman is a creator because she transmutes Milk into Cheese or Butter, or wine into vinegar.

But I reply: This Exception fails 1. By the sophistry of begging the question: For this very thing is in controversy, 1. Whether the Devil can Essentially transmute the rational Substance of Man? 2. Whether such an Essential transmutation does not likewise presuppose divine power and a new creation? Now Illyricus answers the former affirmatively: and the latter negatively: but in both cases too unreasonably and ignorantly. For every true Essential transformation is a true creation, and belongs to GOD alone: as for example, the body of Adam existed by the essential transformation of clay: but the body of Eve by the essential transformation of a rib: But Scripture expressly testifies that they were created by GOD, Gen. 2, 7. Thus John 2, 11. The essential change of water into wine is ascribed to the works of creation: For it is read that Christ declared his glory in this way, namely that which is called, John 1, 14, the Glory of the Only-begotten from the Father. Thus the Devil himself, Matth. 4, 3, judged that the Divine nature of Christ was to be tested by the essential transformation of a stone into bread. It is therefore irrefragably established that the force and power of transforming created things Essentially is a true creation, and belongs to GOD alone.

Whence the Council of Ancyra most rightly defined: He who believes that any creature can be made, or transformed into another species, or into another likeness, except by the Creator himself, who made all things, and through whom all things were made, is without doubt an infidel, and worse than a pagan. And Damascenus lib. 2. Orth. fid. Whoever says that Angels are the founders of any substance, he is the mouth of the Devil.

As for the analogy of Illyricus, it is clearly irrelevant. For Milk and Wine are things naturally transmutable: but Spiritual Substances, such as the Souls of men and Angels, are not naturally corruptible or substantially mutable, since they lack matter: and therefore they can be created from nothing, or reduced to nothing, or transmuted into other forms only by the power of GOD.

Nor is there any reason for Flacius to object that he is not speaking of the transformation of the whole soul, but only of a more noble part of it. For the matter comes to the same thing, for as soon as it is established that either a part or the whole has been Essentially transformed by the Devil: the status of creator is immediately granted to him at the same time. 2. It is clearly unreasonable to divide the Soul into parts: which, although it is most rightly distinguished into its powers, yet it is so much nothing else in its entirety than what each power is; so that it is either preserved as a whole, or perishes as a whole.

IV. The argument of the demonstration can be such: A concrete can never be essentially the same as an Abstract. Now, however, Holy Scripture distinguishes man the sinner from sin itself, as a concrete from an abstract. Therefore, man the sinner cannot be Essentially the same as sin itself.

The minor is confirmed by those individual and universal testimonies of Scripture which show that sin as an abstract is in Man as in another: and therefore is not Man himself: as when GOD is read to have seen that the wickedness of men was great on the earth, and that every thought of the heart was prone to evil at all times. Where certainly, who does not see that a most accurate distinction is made between wickedness and Men: between thoughts and the heart: between proneness to evil and Man?

Thus David, Psal. 51, 7, writing that he was conceived in iniquities, and born in sins by his mother: most clearly distinguishes between them, or between his substance and sin.

Latin:

Septimò & postremò pertinet huc etiam Neo-Manichæismus ille Flacianorum, qui Peccatum Originis definiendum esse statuunt per ipsam Substantiam Hominis, & quidem per nobiilissimam ejus partē, Anima nimirum rationale, & præstantissimam ejus potentias, Intellectū videlicet & voluntatē. Ansam primam & occasionem errori huic præbuit, superiore seculo Disputatio Vinariensis Anno 61. supra sesquimillesimum, inter Victorinum Strigelium, & Matthiam Flacium Illyricum, de Libero Arbitrio instituta. Nam cùm in Disputationis actu Flacio non statim succurreret, An & quomodo ab Accidente posset corrumpi Substantia, factum ut in exaggeranda Humanæ naturæ corruptione, Peccatum Originis non ad classem Accidentium: Sed ad Substantiam ipsam Naturæ humanæ, propriè & sine discrimine, referendum esse contenderet.

Hinc sequentes prodidit flosculos sive Emblemata.

1. Sciamus vocem Peccati significare non tantùm opus, actionem aut cogitationem, non etiam habitum aliquem malum: sed etiam vim ac Essentiam quandam pessimam, nobiscum ex utero matris allatam, part. 2. clavis scripturæ tractatu 6. p. 369.

2. Sentio & assero, primarium Peccatum Originale esse Substantiam, quia anima rationalis, & præsertim nobilissimæ ejus substantialesq; potentiæ, nempè intellectus & voluntas, nunc fraude Satanæ ita prorsus sunt inversæ, ut sint vera ac viva imago Satanæ, non aliter ac si sincerissima quæpiam massa, venanatissimo fermento infecta, in ejusdem fermenti molem, penitùs & Substantialiter immutata ac transformata esset. ibid p. 376.

3. Neque tamen nego, partem aliquam peccati Originalis esse Accidentia: Scio enim Peccatum ita pervasisse totum hominem, ac etiam totum mundum, ut possit in toto homine, & in omnibus prædicamentis reperiri, ac sit fermè transcendens quoddam. Aliquod enim peccatum est Substantia, nempè ipsa caro, vetus Adam &c. aliquod est Accidens; ut vanæ, pessimæ inclinationes nobiscum natæ. ibid.

4. Liquidò apparet, aliquod originale peccatum aut partem ejus esse ipsam Substantiam hominis, non quiddam externum, aut accidentarium in ipso: imò (in immediatè præcedentibus) esse ipsam carnem, esse ipsum hominem animalem, ipsum veterem hominem, seu ToTUM hominem, QUANTUS, QUANTUS est, quatenùs renatus non est. p. 369.

5. Nos olim fuimus in prima creatione quiddam valdè bonum, tùm in Accidentibus, tùm in Substantia: postea mutati sumus ESSENTIALITER, in REM valdè malam SUBSTANTIA SUA, pag. 368.

Quanquàm verò haud rarò Illyricus conquestus fuit, Statum controversiæ à nostris perverti, dùm nimirùm non id in Quæstione sit: An peccatum originis sit Substantia, vel Accidens?

Sed hoc tantùm: An peccatum originale sit ipsa corrupta Hominis Natura, præsertim autem animæ rationalis Essentialis Forma aut Imago? tamen usque adeò se non explicavit, ut intricatiùs rem involveret: Si enim seriò negavit, Peccatum Originis esse Substantiam: utique negaverit etiam necesse est, Peccatum Originis esse ipsam corruptam Naturam sive Substantiam hominis. Nostri enim priorem controversiæ Statum informantes, non hoc quæsiverunt, An peccatum Originis sit aliqua substantia, extra hominem per se subsistens: Sed: An Peccatum, Originis sit ipsa corrupta Substantia Hominis? Status ergo Controversiæ utrobique unus est idemque; Cujus Affirmativam tenuit Illyricus: Nostris contrà Ecclesiis pro Negativa Orthodoxè pugnantibus: ob Rationes sive argumenta, quæ sequuntur, longè evidentissima.

I. Omnis Substantia, non est nisi à DEO conditore: Joh. 1, 3. Atqui Peccatum Originis non est à DEO conditore: sed à Diabolo, & prava hominis voluntate. Sap. 2, 13. Ergo Peccatum Originis non est Substantia.

II. Omnis Substantia, à DEO creata, bona est. Genes. 1, 31. 1. Tim. 4, 4. At Peccatum Originis non est bonum. Ergo Peccatum Originis non potest esse illa ipsa Substantia, quæ à DEO creata est.

Excipit Flacius Majorem propositionem non simpliciter esse veram, sed tantùm secundùm quid, quatenùs nimirùm Substantia à DEO creata, nondùm ita per lapsum protoplastorum est immutata, ut jam non ampliùs bona, sed mala Deoque exosa dici queat.

Sed rectissimè respondetur, Disparata se mutuò non tollere, sed simul in uno Subjecto stare posse sine contradictione. Jam verò unam eandemque Substantiam esse malam: & simul manere DEI creaturam bonam, sunt disparata. E. Minor vel indè demonstrari potest evidentissime, quòd Adamus in ipso lapsu, quòd item Diabolus in ipsa apostasia, non desiit esse DEI creatura. Siquidem Deus ipse post lapsum, Homines quantumvis malos ac perversos, suam tamen creaturam disertè appellat. Genes 6, 7. Deut. 32, 7.

Quo fundamento præsupposito, duo rectissimè inferimus: I. Crassam & horrendam esse Theologiam Flacii asserentis: Hominem tantùm initialiter, aut ratione primæ creationis, esse DEI creaturam: Item, Diabolum tota specie, & toto genere differre à Sanctis Angelis. II. In Homine post lapsum, & sic in Homine peccatore, semper duo distincta sive disparata, probè esse consideranda & distinguenda: quorum unum est Substantia ipsa hominis à DEO creata: Alterum verò est Peccatum sive malitia, quæ autorem habet Diabolum, & Homini creato accidit. Illud præstat, ut Homo sit Homo: Hoc autem efficit, ut idem Homo dicatur Malus & peccator. Quanquam verò Peccatum hoc in Substantia Hominis tàm altas radices egit, ut hac in vita nunquàm Materialiter separari possit: tamen tàm procul à se mutuò distinguenda sunt, quàm procul opus DEI distat ab opere Diaboli.

Quam cautionem ipsa quoq; Scriptura diligenter observavit: DEUS, inquiens, creavit hominem immortalem: Invidia autem Diaboli mors intravit in orbem terrarum, Sap. 2, 23.

III. Ratio: Cujus potentia est, Essentias rationales substantialiter transmutare in Essentias specie a prioribus differentes: illius etiam est creare novas essentias: Atqui hoc soli DEO, nunquam vero Diabolo competit, ita ut ne quidem pediculum creare possit. Exod. 8, 18. Ergo falsum & fictitium est, Diabolum essentialiter transmutasse Hominis Substantiam: nisi forte Flacius per insignem impietatem, Diabolum pro creatore venditare velit.

Sed excipit Illyricus, Diabolum tum demum dicendum esse creatorem, si novam aliquam Substantiam crearet: Jam vero cùm ipse Substantiam jam modò à DEO creatam in aliam saltem essentialiter transmutaverit: baud magis indè consequi, Diabolum esse creatorem, atq; non sequitur Mulierem aliquam esse creatricem, propterea quòd Lac transmutat in Caseum aut Butyrum, vel vinum in acetum.

Sed respondeo: Fallit Exceptio isthæc 1. Sophisticatione petitionis principii: Hoc ipsum enim est in controversia, 1. An Diabolus Substantiam rationalem Hominis Essentialiter transmutare possit? 2. Annon talis Essentialis transmutatio itidem divinam potentiam, novamq;, creationem præsupponat? Jam Illyricus ad prius affirmatè: ad posterius negatè respondet: sed utrobiq; nimis ἀλόγως καὶ ἀπαιδεύτως. Nam omnis vera Essentialis transformatio, est vera creatio, solique DEO competit: ut exempli gratia, Adami corpus transformatione essentiali luti: Evæ autem transformatione essentiali costæ extitit: Atqui Scriptura à DEO creatos illos esse, ἐξαρρήδην testatur, Genes. 2, 7. Sic Johan. 2, 11. Essentialis mutatio aquæ in vinum operibus creationis adscribitur: Legitur enim Christo hoc pacto declarasse gloriam suam, eam nimirùm, quæ Joh. 1, 14. appellatur, Gloria Unigeniti à Patre. Sic Diabolus ipse, Matth. 4, 3. ex essentiali transformatione lapidis in panem, Divinam Christi naturam explorandam esse judicavit. Constat proindè irrefragabiliter, vim ac potentiam transformandi Essentialiter res creatas, esse veram creationem, soliq; DEO competere.

Undè Concilium Ancyranum rectissimè definivit: Qui credit, posse fieri aliquam creaturam, aut transformari in speciem aliam, aut in aliam similitudinem, nisi ab ipso Creatore, qui omnia fecit, & per quem omnia facta sunt, sine dubio infidelis est, & pagano deterior. Et Damascenus lib. 2. Orth. fid. Quicunq; dicit, Angelos esse conditores cujusquam substantiæ, ipse est os Diaboli.

Quoad similitudinem Illyrici, illa est planè ἀπροσδιόνυσος. Lac enim & Vinum sunt res naturaliter transmutabiles: Substantiæ verò Spirituales, quales sunt Animæ hominum, & Angeli non sunt naturaliter corruptibiles, aut substantialiter mutabiles, cùm materia careant: ac proindè solius DEI virtute, vel ex nihilo creari, vel in nihilum redigi, vel in alias formas transmutari possunt.

Neque est, ut excipiat Flacius, se non de totius animæ: sed tantùm de partis ipsius portioris transformatione loqui. Nam res eodem recidit, Quamprimùm enim vel pars, vel totum Essentialiter à Diabolo transformatum esse statuitur: statim creationis vicipsi simul conceditur. 2. ἄλογον planè est, Animam in partes dividere: quæ licet rectissimè in suas potentias distinguatur, tamen usq; adeò ea nihil est aliud tota, quàm quod quælibet est potentia; ita ut aut tota conservetur, aut tota intereat.

IV. Demonstrationis argumentum tale esse potest: Concretum nunquàm essentialiter idem esse potest cum Abstracto. Jam verò Scriptura Sacra distinguit Hominem peccatorem à peccato ipso, tanquàm concretum ab abstracto.E. Homo peccator non potest Essentialiter idem esse, cum peccato ipso.

Minorem confirmant singula & universa illa Scripturæ testimonia, quæ ostendunt, peccatum tanquàm abstractum esse in Homine tanquàm in altero: ac proinde non esse ipsum Hominem: ut quando DEUS legitur vidisse, quòd multa malitia esset hominum in terra, & cuncta cogitatio cordis prona esset ad malum omni tempore. Ubi certè inter malitiam, & inter Homines: inter cogitationes & inter cor: inter pronitatem ad malum, & inter Hominem accuratissimè discerni, quis non videt?

Sic David Psal. 51, 7. scribens, Se in iniquitatibus esse conceptum, & à matre in peccatis genitum esse: luculentissimè inter se, sive substantiam suam, & inter peccatum distinguit.


### Chapter I. Controversy I. On the definition and quasi-essential parts of…: On Flacianism (continued)
