Thus the Savior, Matt. 15, 19, asserting that evils come out of the heart, and that by these a man is defiled, expressly distinguishes between the Man and the defilement itself. Thus the Apostle, Acts 17, 28, affirming that we are, live, and move in GOD, quite clearly intimates that the life, motion, and essence even of a corrupt Man are from God. Now if they are from God, they certainly cannot be from the Devil.

Thus the Apostle, Rom. 7, 17 and 21, naming Original Sin, the Evil inhabiting and Adjoining: Thus the Epistle to the Hebrews ch. 12, 1, naming the same sin ἁμαρτίαν circumstans, wonderfully confirms this distinction of ours: and expressly refers sin to the class of Accidents, and things surrounding the Substance of man.

Illyricus makes a tumult against these things, and charges us with the crime of Contradiction, in that we call one and the same Nature of man now good, now evil: But he ought to have remembered that it is not ὡσαύτως, in one and the same way and respect, that both are affirmed by us: and therefore every appearance of Contradiction utterly expires: which thing D. Augustine explains most accurately in his Enchiridion ch. 13 in these words: A wonderful thing is brought about, that because every nature, in so far as it is a nature, is good, nothing else seems to be said, when a vicious nature is called an evil nature, than that what is good is evil. But it is written: woe to those who call good, evil, or evil, good: And yet the Lord says: An evil man, out of the evil treasure of his heart, brings forth evil. But what is an evil man, if not an evil nature, because man is a Nature?

Furthermore, if man is something good, because he is a Nature: what is an evil man, if not an evil good?

However, when we distinguish these two, we find that it is not evil because it is man, nor is it good because it is wicked: but it is good because it is man, and evil because it is wicked. Therefore, every nature, even if it is vicious, in so far as it is Nature, is good; in so far as it is vicious, it is evil.

V. The argument can be formulated thus: Just as the image of GOD, or Original Justice, stood in relation to the first man before the fall, so now after the fall the contrary habit, namely Original Sin, stands in relation to corrupt man.

But the image of GOD in the first man was in no way essential to him.

Therefore, Original Sin will not be essential to man.

The minor premise is of self-evident certainty: For if the image of GOD had been essential to the first man—that is, if the justice and holiness of man had been one and the same thing most simply with his essence—then GOD would not have created a man, but a GOD; or at least He would have created such a one whose justice and holiness could not be lost forever, or be changed into the contrary habit of sin, except by the power of GOD Himself through an essential transformation. Both of which are most absurd.

VI. Argument: The Son of God assumed a human nature, ὁμοούσιον (consubstantial) with ours, or of the same species as ours. Therefore, our nature is not Original Sin itself. The reason for the consequence is firm. For 1. If it be imagined that the Son of GOD assumed another human nature, different from our species, it would follow that His entire merit would not concern our nature at all: for what is not assumed is not redeemed. 2. If the λόγος (Word) assumed our nature, and that nature, as Flacius raves, is Original Sin itself, it follows consequently that the λόγος Himself assumed Original Sin. ἄτοπον καὶ ἐπερόδοξον (absurd and heterodox).

Illyricus objects: that Christ assumed a human soul, not such as we have, but such as it was in Adam before the fall; and that one is distinguished from the other not by species or physical genus, but only by theological.

But the adversary traps himself. For if the soul of Adam after the fall does not differ in species or physical genus from the soul before the fall, it follows ex ἀναλύγκης (of necessity) that the soul of Adam after the fall was not Original Sin itself; since, by the adversary's own concession, the same species and the same physical genus of Adam's soul remained after the fall as was before the fall.

Furthermore, if the soul of Adam after the fall differs from the soul as it was before the fall only by theological genus, and if theological genus does not regard the essence of the soul itself, but only inherent qualities, whether good or vicious, then it is proven even from this: that the soul according to its essence is not Original Sin itself. If the adversary sophistically understands by theological genus the highest power or faculty of the rational soul, he will certainly incur a double absurdity: the first is that the highest power of the rational soul pertains not to physical species, but to theological. The second is that it follows consequently that the λόγος (Word) assumed a human soul similar in all things to our soul, except for that one highest power of the rational soul. From which it will again follow that our soul is not redeemed in its entirety, but only in part, and indeed in a less principal part.

VII. Argument: The nature or substance of man after the fall is regenerated, renewed, sanctified, justified, resurrected from the dead, and finally saved. But none of these things can be said of Original Sin. Therefore, human nature or substance is not Original Sin itself.

Illyricus objects that all these things happen to man through an essential mutation of the prior form. But by this arrangement, the same individual will not be regenerated, resurrected, and saved; which is diametrically opposed to the Scriptures, as was demonstrated by us more fully in the exposition of the first Article of the Book of Concord.

VIII. The following reasons provide the argument: 1. The definition of substance does not apply to Original Sin, because it is never ἀνθυπόςατον (subsistent in itself), but only the definition of a privation and of a disease or vicious habit. Therefore.

2. Original Sin is separable from man: in this life, indeed, Formally, through the grace of Regeneration: but in the other, even Materially. Therefore.

3. An act never passes into Substance, but original sin in the protoplasts was an Act. Therefore.

4. Original sin is the cause of actual sins. Therefore it is not something substantial. The reason for the consequence is: Because No Substance, insofar as it is Substance, is the cause of actions: But only insofar as it is furnished with faculties, powers, habits, or other qualities: For quality is the form through which a Substance is efficacious. Thus Man sins, not as Man: but as he is infected by the vicious quality of original evil.

IX. And the final argument is provided by the unanimous consensus of Orthodox Antiquity, and of the Symbols of the Church, both ancient and more recent: just as the Book of Concord, in the first Article, shows this more fully. We shall be content for this turn with the authority of Augustine and Luther alone: the former of whom, in Book 7 of the Confessions, chapter 12, writes thus: That evil, which I was seeking, whence it was, is not a substance: Because if it were a substance, it would be good.

And in Psalm 68. Iniquity itself is not a substance: For iniquity is not a nature, which God formed: but it is a perversity, which Man made.

And in Book 1 against Julian, chapter 3. We do not resist the Manichaeans, unless we maintain that evils have not arisen except from goods, and that those evils are not a substance, but vices of created substances, by which they fall away from the good. Blessed Luther, at the beginning in both Catechisms, Article 1 of the Apostles' Creed, confesses that body and soul, Intellect, Reason, and all senses are still given today by GOD.

…The same author, upon chapter 3 of Genesis, expressly denies that Original Sin is a change of Nature. The nature remains, he says, but corrupted in many ways: since trust toward GOD has been lost, and the heart is full of dissension, fear, and shame. Thus remain in Nature the members are the same: but those which were previously seen naked with glory, are now covered as if shameful and dishonest.

The same on chapter 4 of Genesis. Spiritual men ought to distinguish between the sin of origin and the creature.

The same on chapter 11 of Genesis. The Holy Spirit discerns between the disease of nature, vitiated by sin, and his own work. And on chapter 38. According to nature, the flesh of Christ is the same as ours: But in his conception the Holy Spirit approached, overshadowing and purifying that mass which he received from the virgin, so that it might be joined with the divine nature, etc.

The same, Tom. 1, Latin, Jena, p. 448. The inner and outer man, or the New and the Old, are not distinguished according to the difference of soul and body: but according to the affections.

But here too Flacius creates a tumult, and gathers a great number of Luther's testimonies, by which, according to the surface of the letter, he seems to affirm: That the sin of origin is of the Essence of man: that it is Natural and Essential: that it is that very thing which is conceived and begotten by father and mother: that it is the very vicious fountain of the heart: that it is the intellect obscured, the will depraved: the conscience not tranquil, etc.

However, in each and every one of these passages a fallacy is committed, παρὰ τὸ πῆ, and παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For these words of Luther are to be understood in a certain respect, namely, augmentatively and exaggeratively. For because his matter and dispute was with the Scholastics and Papists, who too much extenuated original sin, he was most rightly occupied in amplifying and exaggerating the atrocity of original sin. But now, from exaggerations of things considered according to qualities, to their essential transformation, the consequence does not hold. Hence it is that blessed Luther himself in his Sermon on the triple Justice explains himself: I said, he says, that this sin is Essential, because we contract it through Birth, and it always remains, and never passes away like actual sin. What Luther intended to be understood in a certain respect, the Flacians sophistically take absolutely and distort it to the very Essential transmutation of Man. Then the fallacy of Equivocation is committed in the word Essence, or Essential. For substance or Essence is sometimes spoken of generally concerning that by which each thing is what it is. In which sense even to Accidents their own substance or Essence is granted. Hence Augustine wrote of the Essence of charity: and Quintilian of the Substance of Rhetoric: and our Luther in the Confutation of Latomus, Tom. 2, Jena, p. 418, of the Substance of sin. But, (as Luther himself adds) speaking in the manner of Quintilian. In this respect the word Essence denotes the Quiddity of a thing, or as the Philosopher speaks, τὸ τὶ ἦν εἶναι. However, in this sense the word substance or Essence is not taken in the present dispute against Flacius: but in that stricter signification, by which for Aristotle a substance is something ἀνθυπόστατον, subsisting by itself, or having its own being, and not needing the support of another: just as Logicians are accustomed to use the word substance. Therefore, in the former general or Metaphysical sense, not in this latter Logical one, Luther understood the word Essence, just as he himself writes in his Sermon on the Triple Justice, that he is not dealing with the Logicians.

Latin:

Sic Servator, Matth. 15, 19. asserens, de corde exire mala, & his coinquinari hominem, disertè inter Hominem & coinquinationem ipsam distinguit. Sic Apostolus Actor. 17, 28. affirmans nos in DEO esse, vivere & moveri, satis dilucidè innuit, Hominis etiam corrupti, vitam, motum & essentiam ex Deo esse. Jam si ex Deo sunt, utique ex Diabolo esse nequeunt.

Sic Apostolus Rom. 7, 17. & 21. nominans Peccatum Originis, Malum inhabitans & Adjacens: Sic Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 12, 1. nominans idem peccatum ἁμαρτίαν circumstans, mirificè distinctionem hanc nostram confirmat: & peccatum in classem Accidentium, & Substantiam hominis circumstantium, expressè refert.

Tumultuatur adversum isthæc Illyricus, & Contradictionis crimen nobis objicit, eò quòd unam eandemq; Naturam hominis, jam bonam, jam malam dicamus: Sed meminisse debebat, non ὡσαύτως, uno eodemq; modo ac respectu, utrumque à nobis affirmari: ac proindè omnis Contradictionis speciem penitùs expirare: id quod D. Augustinus in suo Enchiridio cap. 13. perquàm accuratè his verbis explicat: Res mira conficitur, ut quia omnis natura, in quantum natura est, bonum est, nihil aliud dici videatur, cùm vitiosa natura, mala esse natura dicitur, nisi malum esse, quod bonum est. Scriptum est autem: væ his, qui dicunt bonum, malum, vel malum, bonum: Et tamen Dominus ait: Malus homo, de malo thesauro cordis sui, profert malum. Quid est autem malus homo, nisi natura mala, quia homo Natura est?

Porrò si homo aliquid bonum est, quia Natura est: quid est malus homo, nisi malum bonum?

Tamen cùm ista duo discernimus, invenimus, nec ideò malum, quia homo est: nec ideò bonum, quia iniquus est : sed bonum, quia homo : malum, quia iniquus. Omnis itaque natura, etiamsi vitiosa est, in quantum Natura est, bona est : in quantum vitiosa est : mala est.

V. Argumentum sic informari potest: Quemadmodum se habuit imago DEI, sive Justitia Originalis, ad primum hominem ante lapsum : sic se jam post lapsum etiam habet contrarius habitus, nempè Peccatum Originis, ad hominem corruptum.

Atqui Imago DEI in primo homine, nullo modo ipsi fuit Essentialis.

Ergo neque Peccatum Originis Homini erit Essentiale.

Minor per se immotæ est certitudinis : Si enim Imago DEI primo homini fuisset Essentialis : hoc est : Si Justitia & Sanctitas hominis cum essentia ejusdem unum quiddam fuisset simplicissimè: Jam non hominem, sed DEUM condidisset DEUS : vel certè talem condidisset, cujus Justitia & Sanctitas in æternum non amitti, aut in contrarium peccati habitum, nisi ipsius DEI virtute, mediante essentiali transformatione, permutari potuisset. Quod utrumque longè est absurdissimum.

VI. Argumentum : Filius Dei naturam humanam, nostræ ὁμοούσιον, sive ejusdem speciei cum nostra assumsit. Ergo Natura nostra non est ipsum peccatum Originis. Ratio consecutionis est firma. Nam 1. Si aliam Naturam humanam, à nostrâ specie diversam, Filius DEI assumpsisse fingatur: consequens fuerit, Universum ipsius meritum nihil prorsus nostram spectare naturam : Nam quod assumtum non est : illud neq; redemtum. 2. Si nostram Naturam λόγος assumsit : Ea verò, uti Flacius delirat, est ipsum peccatum Originis : uti consequenter. λόγον ipsum peccatum Originis assumsisse. ἄτοπον καὶ ἐπερόδοξον.

Excipit Illyricus : Christum assumsisse animam humanam, non qualem nos habemus : sed qualis in Adamo fuit ante peccatum : distingui verò unam ab alia non specie, aut genere Physico, sed tantum Theologico.

Verùm seipsum constringit Adversarius. Si enim Adami anima post lapsum non specie aut genere Physica differt, ab anima ante lapsum : Consequitur ex ἀναλύγκης, quòd neq; post lapsum Anima Adami fuerit ipsum peccatum Originis : Siquidem ex concessione Adversarii, eadem mansit species, idemque genus Physicum Animæ Adami post lapsum : quod fuit ante lapsum.

Deindè si Genere Theologico tantùm differt Anima Adami post lapsum, ab anima qualis fuit ante lapsum : Genus autem Theologicum non respicit ipsam Essentiam animæ, sed inhærentes tantùm Qualitates, easq; vel bonas vel vitiosas : utique vel hinc evincitur: quòd Anima secundùm essentiam non sit ipsum peccatum Originis. Sin Adversarius per Genus Theologicum Sophistice intelligat summam potentiam sive facultatem Animæ rationalis : certè geminam absurditatem incurret : Prior est, quòd summa potentia animæ rationalis, non ad speciem Physicam, sed Theologicam pertineat. Posterior verò, quòd indè consequenter, λόγον assumsisse Animam humanam per omnia animę nostræ similem, excepta sola summa illa potentia animæ rationalis. Undè rursus consequetur, Animam nostram non ex toto, sed tantùm ex parte, & quidem minùs principali redemtam esse.

VII. Argumentum: Natura sive Substantia Hominis post lapsum regeneratur, renovatur, sanctificatur, justificatur, resuscitatur ex mortuis, & tandem salvatur. Atqui nihil horum de peccato Originis dici potest. E. Humana Natura sive Substantia non est ipsum peccatum Originis.

Excipit Illyricus, hæc omnia obtingere homini, per Essentialem quandam mutationem prioris formæ. Atqui hoc pacto non idem individuum regenerabitur, resuscitabitur, salvabitur: id quod cum Scripturis è diametro pugnat: uti in diexodo Articuli primi Libri Concordiæ fusiùs à nobis fuit demonstratum.

VIII. Argumentum suppeditant sequentes rationes: 1. Peccato Originis non competit definitio Substantiæ, quia nunquam est ἀνθυπόςατον, sed tantùm definitio privationis, & morbi sive vitiosi habitûs. Ergo.

2. Peccatum Originis est separabile ab homine: hac quidem in vita, Formaliter, per Regenerationis gratiam: in altera verò, etiam Materialiter. Ergo.

3. Actus nunquam transit in Substantiam, At peccatum Originis in protoplastis fuit Actus. Ergo.

4. Peccatum originis est causa peccatorum actualium. Ergo non est substantiale aliquid. Ratio consecutionis est: Quia Nulla Substantia, quatenùs est Substantia causa est actionum: Sed tantùm, quatenùs facultatibus, viribus, habitibus sive qualitatibus aliis est instructa: Qualitas enim forma est, per quam Substantia est efficax. Sic Homo peccat, non quâ Homo: sed quâ originalis mali vitiosa qualitate est infectus.

IX. Et postremum argumentum subministrat unanimis consensus Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, & Symbolorum Ecclesiæ, tùm antiquorum, tùm recentiorum: quemadmodum Liber concordiæ, Articulo primo fusiùs illud ostendit. Nos contenti hac vice erimus unius Augustini & Lutheri autoritate: quorum ille lib. 7. Confess. cap. 12. sic scribit: Malum illud, quod quærebam, undè esset, non est substantia: Quia si substantia esset, bonum esset.

Et in Psal. 68. Iniquitas ipsa non est substantia: Non enim iniquitas est natura, quam formavit Deus: sed est perversitas, quam fecit Homo.

Et l. 1. adversus Julianum cap. 3. Non resistimus Manichæis, nisi obtineamus, non esse mala orta, nisi ex bonis, nec ea mala substantiam esse, sed vitia substantiarum creatarum, quibus deficiunt à bono. B. Lutherus initio in utroq; Catechismo, Art. 1. Symboli Apostolici fatetur, corpus & animam, Intellectum, Rationem, omnésq; sensus hodieq; à DEO dari.

Idem super cap. 3. Genes. disertè negat, Peccatum originale esse Naturæ immutationem. Manet quidem, inquit, natura, sed multis modis corrupta: siquidem fiducia erga DEUM amissa est, & cor plenum est dissidentia, metu, pudore. Sic manent in Natura membra eadem: sed quæ antea nuda cum gloria conspiciebantur, nunc tanquam turpia & inhonesta velantur.

Idem super cap. 4. Genes. Spirituales homines debent distinguere inter peccatum originis & creaturam.

Idem super cap. 11. Gen. Inter morbum naturæ, per peccatum vitiatæ, & suum opus Spiritus sanctus discernit. Et super cap. 38. Secundum naturam eadem est caro Christi cum nostra: Sed in conceptione ejus accessit Spiritus sanctus, obumbrans & purificans illam massam, quam accepit de virgine, ut conjungeretur cum divina natura, &c.

Idem Tom. 1. Lat. Jen. p. 448. Homo interior & exterior, seu Novus & Vetus non distinguuntur juxta differentiam animæ & corporis: sed juxta affectus.

Sed & hîc tumultuatur Flacius, & magno numero coacervat Lutheri testimonia, quibus secundùm superficiem literæ affirmare videtur: Peccatum originis esse de Essentia hominis: esse Naturale & Essentiale: esse illud ipsum, quod à patre & matre concipitur & gignitur: esse ipsum fontem vitiosum cordis: esse intellectum obscuratum, voluntatem depravatam: conscientiam non tranquillam, &c.

Cæterùm in singulis ac universis istis locis committitur Sophisma, παρὰ τὸ πῆ, & παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Secundùm quid enim sunt hæc verba Lutheri intelligenda, nempè αὐξητικῶς & exaggerativè. Quia enim ipsi res & disputatio fuit cum Scholasticis, & Pontificiis, Peccatum originis nimiùm extenuantibus: ipse in amplificanda & exaggeranda peccati originalis atrocitate, rectissimè occupabatur. Jam verò ab exaggerationibus rerum secundùm qualitates consideratarum, ad earundem essentialem transformationem non valet consequentia. Hinc est, quod B. Lutherus ipse in Serm. de triplici Justitia semetipsum explicat: ideo, inquiens, dixi, Peccatum hoc esse Essentiale, quia per Nativitatem id contrahimus, & semper manet, neque aliquando transit sicut peccatum actuale. Quod E. secundùm quid intellectum voluit Lutherus, illud Sophisticè ἁπλῶς accipiunt Flaciani, & ad ipsam Essentialem Hominis transmutationem detorquent. Deindè Æquivocationis Sophisma committitur in voce Essentiæ, sive Essentiale. Substantia enim sive Essentia generaliter interdum dicitur de eo, quo unumquodq́; est, quod est. Quo sensu Accidentibus etiam sua substantia sive Essentia conceditur. Hinc Augustinus scripsit de Essentia charitatis: & Quintilianus de Substantia Rhetorices: & Lutherus noster in Confutatione Latomi Tom. 2. Jen. L. p. 418. de Substantia peccati. Sed, (ut ipse Lutherus subjicit) Quintiliano more loquendo. Hoc respectu Essentiæ vox notat Quidditatem rei, sive ut Philosophus loquitur τὸ τὶ ἦν εἶναι. Cæterùm hoc sensu non accipitur vox substantiæ sive Essentiæ in præsenti disputatione contra Flacium: verùm in eo strictiore fignificatu, quo Aristoteli est substantia quædam ἀνθυπόστατον per se subsistens, sive proprium esse habens, neque alterius sustentatione indigens: Quemadmodum Logici vocem substantiæ usurpare solent. Priore ergo generali资re sive Metaphysico sensu, non posteriore hoc Logico, vocem Essentia intellexit Lutherus, quemadmodum ipsemet scribit, Serm. de Tripl. Just. se non cum Logicis agere.


### Chapter I. Controversy I. On the definition and quasi-essential parts of…: On Flacianism (continued)

Finally, the same Sophistication presents itself in the word Mutation or Corruption, which blessed Luther uses quite frequently. For there is one Physical or Essential Corruption, by which a thing is utterly destroyed: and it is defined by the Philosophers as Motion from being to non-being. Such a Physical corruption befell the wife of Lot, who was turned into a pillar of Salt, by reason of corporeal substance: the soul indeed having been called out of the body by sudden death. That such a physical mutation or corruption befell Man from the fall, Luther himself expressly denies: as was shown above. But there is another, accidental corruption, and improperly so called: when the Substance remaining, the Quality is deformed: and thus the substance is said to be corrupted and changed not simply or by itself according to essence: but in a certain respect. Such a corruption befell Man from the Fall of the protoplasts: namely, a corruption not of the Essential form, but of the Accidental Form. When therefore Luther writes that Man after the fall was changed into a pillar of Salt, like the wife of Lot: he understands it not simply, but in a certain respect: namely, not by reason of Substance, but by reason of powers toward the good: so that man can no more effect his own restoration to integrity by his own powers, than the wife of Lot can transform herself from her own powers into her former human form: just as the context of the whole passage clearly demonstrates.

And these indeed are the arguments by which, having been moved, we maintain that Original Sin, however much it may have invaded and infected the nature of man, nevertheless, without great blasphemy against divine truth and the endangering of most articles of faith, can in no way be called the nature or substance itself, or even the essential form of man.

But Flacius has some arguments by which he attempts to put a gloss upon his error, the chief of which are these:

1. Whatever is non-conforming to the law of God, that is sin, just as it is written: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐςὶν ἡ ἀνομία. But this whole corrupted human nature and substance after the fall is non-conforming to the law of God. Therefore, this very nature and substance is sin: And consequently: Since this very nature, which is accused as the fountain of actual sins, is substance: therefore, also Sin is substance: Colloq. Arg. page 1. Consens. tripl.

But this objection has almost more faults than words. For 1. a manifest ψεῦδος (falsehood) is committed in the major premise: For this definition is false, nor is it contained in the sacred writings: Sin is whatever is non-conforming to the Law of God, or whatever is repugnant to the Law of God. Certainly the Johannine definition, 1 John 3:4, defines sin as being ἀνομία (lawlessness). Now, however, the word ἀνομία does not mean: whatever fights against the Law of God: but it signifies a discrepancy from the Law: thus explaining the whole matter in a very brief and clever summary: namely, both the privation, and the norm, into which sin strikes by the force of this privation: For α- is privative, positing a privation: but νόμος denotes the Law as a rule: so that sin is rightly defined by ἀνομία, that is, by a discrepancy from the Law. Hence, against Flacius, one may conclude thus: No ἀνομία is a substance, sin is ἀνομία. Therefore, sin is not a substance. The truth of the major premise is evident from this, because ἀνομία is something abstract from substance, on account of which abstract, the substance is called not ἀνομία, but ἄνομος (lawless). Therefore, on account of the adjacent or adhering sin, man is called a sinner (ἄνομος), and the subject itself in the concrete is called ἄνομον (lawless), not ἀνομία: nor can that abstract ever be predicated synonymously of the concrete. Furthermore, even if we were to admit that common Latin version of the Johannine definition: yet not even then will Flacius obtain what he intends. For because that which fights against the Law of God presupposes a vicious action: certainly the privation itself of conformity to the Law will be sin formally: but an action not conforming to the Law will be sin materially: But substance, which is the principle of action, ought to be named neither sin formally nor materially: but sinning or sinful. Thirdly, if we look at the very connection of the proposed argument: in both premises a fallacy of 'in a certain respect' (secundum quid) is committed. For in the major, whatever is non-conforming to the Law of God, namely in itself and simply, that is sin. Now, however, regarding the minor, human nature is non-conforming to the Law of God, but not simply or in itself, insofar as it is nature: But only in a certain respect, namely, by reason of the inherent sin. Therefore, human nature is not sin, but sinful. Finally, these things being observed, a non-syllogism of four terms emerges. For the major speaks of simple non-conformity considered in itself and by itself. But the minor speaks of non-conformity in a certain respect, that is, not by reason of nature in itself, but by reason of something else, namely, the inherent vice.

But Illyricus objects; that this distinction cannot have a place, because Scripture does not in a certain respect, but simply, and without any exception or condition, accuse the whole nature of man, as non-conforming to the Law of God: not the accident itself adhering in nature, as when Christ says: Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh. But this

The adversary shamefully begs the question, nay, he brings forth these things beyond and against the mind of the Scriptures. Certainly, just now above in the third argument of our demonstration, it was most evidently shown how Scripture, and how accurately, distinguishes between sin and the man to whom sin adheres. Furthermore, how can it be true, what Illyricus asserts, that Scripture simply, and without any exception or condition, accuses the whole nature itself as non-conforming to the Law of God, but not the accident itself adhering in nature? What then is it? Or what will the adversary answer to that prophetic word: Your sins have divided between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he does not hear. Isa. 59:2. Certainly in this place the Prophet establishes some third thing between God and men as a medium, which is neither God, nor man, nor of the essence of God, nor of the essence of man, namely, sin. Nor does that word of the Savior, John 3:6, stand in the way: Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh. For we do not deny that the whole nature and essence of man is accused and condemned, because the whole nature with all its powers and faculties is contaminated: But not simply, insofar as it is nature, or on account of itself: but on account of something else, that is, on account of that inherent vice, which has contaminated the whole essence of man, but has not destroyed or abolished it.

Which same response ought also to be given to that Mosaic passage, Gen. 8:21: The imagination of the human heart is only evil from its youth. What? That Moses himself not obscurely distinguishes between the imagination and the heart: by the imagination of the heart understanding not the substance of the heart itself, but the thoughts which are imagined by the heart, and which are not substance but an accident. The evidence of which response is confirmed by Moses himself, who, defining the same aphorism in the preceding chapter, 6:5, expressly adds: The imagination of the thoughts of the heart is only evil every day.

Furthermore, that the Apostle, Rom. 6:6, seems to define sin by the very substance of the body does not confirm the exception of Flacius even in the slightest: as, saying, that the body of sin might be destroyed. For what kind of body is to be understood is clearly evident from the adjunct of the predicate. For such as the destruction is, such also must the body be, or of the same kind. Now, however, this destruction does not happen by reduction into nothing, or the dissolution of that bond which exists between the soul and the body. For this must happen in the living, nor is it momentary, but joined with the continuation of time. But an alteration (ἀλλοίωσις) is understood, by which the power of sin is broken; therefore, it is not the nature or substance of the body, but the vice and its power that is understood, which the Apostle says is to be destroyed, that is, weakened.

The Apostle himself confirms this explanation in the immediately subsequent verses, while he asserts that this destruction is required for this reason, that sin may no longer be served. Therefore, the destruction of the body of sin occurs when sin is no longer served: or as the Apostle speaks elsewhere: When sin does not reign in our mortal body, to obey its lusts.

II. Flacius's argument is this: Whatever is the source and root of all actual sins: or, whatever produces all other sins, that is Original sin. But the very heart of man is the source and root, indeed it produces all other sins, according to evil thoughts, adulteries, thefts, murders. Therefore, the very heart of man is Original sin.

I answer: The argument fails by the fallacy of secundum quid et simpliciter. For the major premise is not true simply, but in a certain respect: namely, so that whatever of itself, through itself, and by no other moving principle produces all actual sins: that is truly Original sin. Now as regards the minor, certainly in actual sins there are two distinct things: One, the Natural Action, which depends upon the acting substance itself: as when a thief extends his hand, the action itself is Natural. The other, however, is the vice itself, as it adheres to the action: namely, the handling of another's property. Which vice does not proceed from the Action considered in itself, and consequently not from the Nature of man simply and considered in itself: But from the corruption of Nature. Therefore, not the Heart simply, but the corrupt Heart is the source and root of all actual sins: where immediately the Heart is discovered to be one thing, and the corruption inherent in the Heart another: so that the Heart cannot be called the corruption itself: but corrupt.

III. Argument. An accident is that which can be present and absent without the corruption of the subject. But Original sin cannot be present to man without his horrible corruption. Therefore, Original sin is not an Accident.

I answer 1. That the Porphyrian definition of an Accident can be conceded, if it is understood concerning Physical corruption, which is the change of the Essence itself: as Porphyry certainly understood it. But with the major premise understood in this way, the minor is most false, and contains a shameful begging of the question: For it is false, and in no way proven by Flacius: that Original sin cannot be present to man without the essential destruction of human nature or substance. Therefore, the argument concludes nothing: Nay, it is rather inverted in this manner: Whatever can be present and absent to human substance without its physical corruption, that is an Accident. But Original sin can be present and absent to man without his physical corruption. Therefore, Original sin is an Accident.

Latin:

Tandem eadem Sophisticatio sese offert in vocabulo Mutationis sive Corruptionis, quo frequenter admodum B. Lutherus utitur. Alia enim est Corruptio Physica sive Essentialis, quâ res prorsus destruitur: & à Philosophis definitur, Motus ab esse ad non esse. Qualis Physica corruptio obtigit uxori Lothi, conversæ in statuam Salis, ratione substantiæ corporeæ: anima verò per subitaneam mortem è corpore evocatâ. Talem Physicam mutationem sive corruptionem Homini ex lapsu obtigisse, ipse Lutherus ἀλαρῥήδην negat: uti supra ostensum. Alia verò est corruptio accidentalis, & impropriè sic dicta: quando manente Substantia Qualitas deformatur: & sic substantia non simplicitèr aut per se secundùm essentiam: sed secundùm quid corrumpi ac mutari dicitur. Qualis corruptio Homini ex Lapsu protoplastorum obtigit: nempè corruptio non formæ Essentialis, sed Formæ Accidentalis. Quando Ergo Lutherus scribit, Hominem post lapsum mutatum esse in statuam Salis, sicut uxorem Lothi: non simplicitèr, sed secundùm quid intelligit: videlicet non ratione Substantiæ, sed ratione virium ad bonum: ut haud magis homo ex propriis viribus possit sui in integrum restitutionem efficere, atque uxor Lothi ex propriis se potest in pristinam formam humanam transmutare: quemadmodum totius loci συνέπεια luculenter demonstrat.

Et hæc quidem ea sunt argumenta, quibus moti statuimus, Peccatum Originis, quantumvis etiam illud Naturam hominis invaserit & infecerit: tamen absque grandi blasphemia divinæ veritatis, & discrimine plerorumque Fidei articulorum, nullo modo ipsam Naturam sive substantiam vel etiam essentialem Formam Hominis appellari posse.

Sed habet Flacius nonnulla, quibus errori suo fucum facere conatur, argumenta: quorum præcipua sunt isthæc:

1. Quicquid est inconforme legi DEI, id peccatum est, sicut Scriptum est: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐςὶν ἡ ἀνομία. Atqui tota hæc corrupta natura humana & substantia post lapsum, est inconformis legi DEI. E. hæc ipsa Natura & Substantia est peccatum: Et per consequens: Quoniam hæc ipsa Natura, quæ tanquam fons actualium peccatorum accusatur est substantia: ideò, quoque Peccatum est Substantia: Colloq. Arg. pag. 1. Consens. tripl.

Sed plura ferme vitia, quàm verba objectio hæc habet. Nam 1. in majore propositione manifestum ψεῦδος committitur: Falsa enim hæc est definitio, neque in sacris continetur: Peccatum est, quicquid est inconforme legi Dei, vel quicquid repugnat Legi Dei. Definitio certè Johannitica 1. cap. 3, 4. definit Peccatum, quod sit άνομία. Jam verò vox ἀνομίας, non significat: quicquid pugnat cum Lege Dei: sed significat discrepantiam à Lege: sic brevi admōdùm & arguto compendio rem universam explicans: nempè & privationem, & normam, in quam Peccatum vi privationis hujus impingit: Nam a. privativum est, privationem ponens: νόμος verò Legem tanquàm regulam notat: ita ut Peccatum rectè definiatur per ἀνομίαν, hoc est, per discrepantiam à Lege. Hinc adversus Flacium sic licet colligere: Nulla ἀνομία est substantia, Peccatum est ἀνομία. Ergo Peccatum non est substantia. Majoris veritas indè patet, quia ἀνομία est Abstractum aliquid à substantia, propter quod abstractum, substantia non ἀνομία, sed ἄνομος appellatur. Ergo propter adjacens sive adhærens peccatum, Homo peccator ἄνομος, & subjectum ipsum in concreto ἄνομον, non ἄνομία dicitur: neque συνωνύμως de concreto prædicari abstractum istud unquàm potest. Deindè si vel maximè vulgatam illam versionem definitionis latinæ Johanniticæ admittamus: tamen ne sic quidem obtinebit Flacius, quod intendit. Quia enim id quod pugnat cum lege Dei, actionem vitiosam præsupponit: utique privatio ipsa conformitatis ad Legem, erit peccatum formaliter: actio verò non conformis legi, peccatum erit materialiter: Substantia autem, quæ est actionis principium, neque peccatum formaliter, neque materialiter: sed peccans vel peccatrix nominari debet. Tertiô si ipsam propositi argumenti connexiouem spectemus: in utraque præmissarum committitur Sophisticatio secundum quid. Nam in Majore, Quicquid est incōforme Legi Dei, nempè per se & simpliciter, illud est peccatum. Jam verò quoad Minorem, Humana natura est inconfórmis legi Dei, sed non simpliciter aut per se, quatenùs est natura: Verùm dûntaxat secundùm quid, nempè, ratione peccati inhærentis. E. Natura humana non est peccatum, sed peccatrix. Tandem his ita observatis, emergit ἀσυλλογισία quatuór terminòrum. Nam Major loquitur de simplici inconformitate in se & per se considerata. Minor verò dè inconformitate secundùm quid, hoc est, non ratione Naturæ per se, sed ratione alterius, nempè inhærentis vitij.

Sed excipit Illyricus; distinctionem hanc non posse habere locum, Quia Scriptura non secundum quid, sed simpliciter, & sine omni exceptione aut conditione accuset Totam Naturam hominis, tanquàm inconformem Legi Dei: non ipsum Accidens in Natura hærens, ut quando Christus dicit: Quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est. Verùm hæc

Principium turpiter petit Adversarius, imò prætēr & contra Scripturarum mentem ista profert. Certè jam modò suprà argumento Demonstrationis nostræ tertio, evidentissimè fuit ostensum, quomodo scriptura, & quam accuratè distinguat inter peccatum, & inter Hominem, cui peccatum adhæret. Porrò quî verum esse queat, quòd Illyricus asserit, Scripturam simpliciter, & sine omni exceptione aut conditione accusare totam naturam ipsam, ut Legi Dei inconformem, non verò ipsum Accidens in Natura inhærens. Quid igitur est? vel quid respondebit Adversarius ad illud Propheticum: Peccata vestra diviserunt, inter Vos & Deum vestrum, & peccata vestra absconderunt faciem ejus à Vobis, ne vos exaudiat. Jes. 59, 2. Certè hoc loco Propheta, inter Deum & inter homines constituit aliquod tertium tanquàm medium, quod neque Deus, neque Homo, neque de Dei, neque de Hominis Essentia sit, videlicet Peccatum. Neque obstat illud Servatoris, Joh. 3, 6. Quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est. Neque enim negamus totam Naturam & Essentiam hominis accusari & damnari, quia tota Natura cum omnibus suis viribus & potentijs est contaminata: Sed non simpliciter, quatenùs est Natura, sive propter seipsam: sed propter aliud, hoc est, propter illud inhærens vitium, quod universam Essentiam hominis contaminavit, non verò destruxit aut abolevit.

Quæ ipsa Responsio dari etiam debet, ad illud Mosaïcum, Gen. 8, 2. Figmentum cordis humani tantùm malum est ab adolescentia sua. Quid? quòd Moses ipse haud obscurè inter Figmentum & cor distinguit: per Figmentum cordis intelligens non ipsam cordis substantiam, sed cogitationes, quæ à corde finguntur, quæque non sunt substantia sed accidens. Cujus responsionis evidentiam confirmat ipse Moses, qui eundem Aphorismum definiens, cap. præced. 6, 5. disertè addit: Figmentum cogitationum cordis tantùm malum omni die.

Prætereà Exceptionem Flacij neque illud vel tantillum confirmat, quòd Apostolus Rom. 6, 6. peccatum definire videtur, per ipsam corporis substantiam: ut, inquiens, destruatur corpus peccati Nàm quale corpus sit intelligendum, ex adjuncto prædicati liquidò patet. Qualis enim est destructio, tale etiam, vel ejusdem generis corpus etiam sit necesse est. Jam verò destructio hæc non fit per redactionem in nihilum, vel solutionem vinculi illius, quod animæ cum corpore intercedit. Nam hanc in viventibus fieri necessum est, neque momentanea est, sed cum continuatione temporis conjuncta. Verùm ἀλλοίωσις sive alteratio intelligitur, quâ vis peccati infringitur, corporis ergò non Natura, sive substantia, sed vitium, ejusdemque vis intelligitur, quæ destruenda, hoc est, infirmanda esse ab Apostolo dicitur.

Confirmat hanc explicationem Apostolus ipse, in statim subsequentibus, dum hanc destructionem ideò requiri asserit, non peccato ampliùs serviatur. Fit E. destructio corporis peccati, quando peccato non ampliùs servitur: vel ut alibi loquitur Apostolus: Quando peccatum non regnat in mortali nostro corpore, ad obediendum concupiscentijs ejus.

II. Argumentum Flacij est istud: Quicquid est fons & radix omnium peccatorum actualium: vel, quicquid efficit omnia alia peccata, illud est peccatum Originis. Atqui cor ipsum Hominis est fons & radix, imò efficit omnia alia peccata, secundum cogitationes male, adulteria, furta, homicidia. E. ipsum cor Hominis est peccatum Originis.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate ὧςφ̔ τὸ πῆ κὰι ἁπλως. Major enim non simpliciter: sed secundùm quid vera est: ita nimirùm, ut quicquid ex se, per se, & nullo alio movente principio efficit omnia peccata actualia: illud reverà sit peccatum originis. Jam quoad minorem, certè in peccatis actualibus duo distincta quædam sunt: Unum, Actio Naturalis, quæ dependet ab ipsa substantia agente: ut cum Fur extendit manum, Actio ipsa est Naturalis. Alterum verò est vitium ipsum, quoad actioni adhæret: nempè contrectatio rei alienæ. Quod vitium non ab Actione in se considerata, ac proindè neque ab ipsa Naturâ hominis simpliciter & in se considerata: Sed à corruptione Naturæ proficiscitur. Proindè non Cor simpliciter, sed Cor corruptum est fons & radix omnium peccatorum actualium: ubi statim aliud diversum esse deprehenditur Cor: aliud verò corruptio Cordi inhærens: ita ut Cor non dici queat ipsa corruptio: sed corruptum.

III. Argumentum. Accidens est quod potest adeffe & abesse præter subjecti corruptionem. Atqui Peccatum Originis non potest adesse Homini, sine horrenda ejus corruptione. E. Peccatum Originis non est Accidens.

Respondeo 1. Concedi posse Definitionem Accidentis Porphyrianam, si de corruptione Physica, quæ est ipsius Essentiæ immutatio, intelligatur: uti certè eam intellexit Porphyrius. Verùm hoc modo intellecta Majore, Minor est falsissima, & continet turpem petitionem principij: Falsum enim est, neq; à Flacio ullo pacto comprobatum: Peccatum Originis non posse adesse Homini, sine essentiali destructione Naturæ aut substantiæ humanæ. Ergo neq; quicquam concludit argumentum: Quin illud potiùs invertitur in hunc modum: Quicquid potest substantiæ humanæ adesse & abesse citra physicam ejus corruptionem, illud est Accidens. Atqui Peccatum Originis potest Homini adesse & abesse citra physicam ejus corruptionem. Ergo Peccatum Originis est Accidens.


### Chapter I. Controversy I. On the definition and quasi-essential parts of…: On Flacianism (continued)

Nor is that exception of any value, which is raised in this place concerning the death of the body, malignant fevers, and other accidents of that kind: as those which cannot be present to a subject without its physical destruction. For what the Porphyrian definition of an Accident has concerning the destruction of the subject is not to be understood efficiently, but formally: signifying this, that accidents can indeed have such Qualities as destroy the subject: meanwhile, however, the presence or absence of the accidents themselves does not of itself cause the subject to perish. In which sense sin is truly an Accident, because with it present: and removed by regeneration as regards its guilt: the subject nonetheless retains its Essence. Nor, however, is it our intention in the meantime to write against those Logicians who maintain that this Porphyrian definition does not apply to every Accident: Let it suffice to have demonstrated that that definition, under which Flacius triumphs, neither hinders us: nor helps his cause even in the slightest. But if another definition of an Accident is substituted, or that common one of Philip: An accident is that which does not subsist by itself, nor is a part of substance, but is in another mutably: or that more accurate one of Aristotle: συμβεβηκὸς ἐστὶν, ὃ ἐνδέχεται ὑπάρχειν ἢ τῷ ἓν ἑνὶ καὶ τῷ ἑαυτῷ καὶ μὴ ὑπάρχειν: An accident is that which happens to be in a thing, and not to be: Certainly our opinion will be so much the more confirmed, if those are applied to Original sin.

Nor is there any reason for Flacius to object with that feeble cuckoo-cry about Physical and Theological man. For Scripture proposes one and the same Natural man, as he is born, to be considered: not another: Whence Blessed Luther on Psalm 51 says: The proper subject of Theology is man, guilty of sin and lost. 2. A different consideration does not make a different man. And the theologian does not consider a different man than the physicist, although in a different way. Finally, if Flacius takes refuge in theological corruption, let him remember that it is not the essential destruction of the subject itself: for thus it would no longer be theological, but physical corruption: But that it is only the destruction of Qualities, that is, of the Justice and Holiness with which the first man was endowed before the fall. But this destruction of an accident, not of substance, grants the definition to Original sin. And although Blessed Luther wrote somewhere: That the definition of man in Theology is not true, which is said to be a rational animal: yet he understood that not simply concerning the Essence of man considered in itself, by reason of which this definition remains true forever: but concerning the powers of human reason in divine matters: in respect of which man, speaking theologically, is truly and rightly called an irrational animal: because the natural man does not understand the things that are of the Spirit of God: nor can he: since he is judged by spiritual things: 1 Cor. 2:14.

IV. Argument: Scripture, in describing Original Sin, always uses substantial words. Therefore, Original Sin will be the very substance of Man.

I answer, the argument fails by the fallacy of the non-cause, and of the vicious consequent. For Scripture does not therefore use substantial words because sin is the very Substance of Man: but because sin is not separately outside of Man, but in Man, and thus the substance itself sins, namely the heart of Man: although it does not sin insofar as it is a heart, but insofar as it is corrupted. From this solution it is also clear what ought to be answered to that putrid cavil of Illyricus, arguing thus: If Original sin is an Accident, therefore, only Accidents in Man, not the Nature of Man itself, will be corrupted. For the reason that this corruption is attributed not to Accidents, but to Nature itself, is not that Nature itself is substantially Original sin: but that Accidents of themselves neither are nor act: but they exist and act in another, as in a subject: but Substance is efficacious: and that either for good or for evil, but not insofar as it is substance: but only by reason of the Qualities, which are in substances either from first creation: or from subsequent corruption.

And these indeed are the principal arguments with which Flacius himself was accustomed to fight: But when his disciples noticed that the absurdity of his dogma was being demonstrated to the eye by our Theologians, chiefly from that Article which is concerning creation: with a clearly cunning plan they devised that σοφὸν φάρμακον, that they should contend that the Article of creation is by no means to be confused with the present one, which is concerning Original sin, nor is judgment to be made about this from that.

The reasons, however, by which they attempt to put a gloss on this assertion, are these principal ones.

1. Because creation preceded the fall, and creation has nothing in common with sin.

2. Because in the Article of Creation, not even a word of Original Sin is mentioned: nor does it explain either what it is, or whence it arises, or how we are freed from it.

3. Because sin was not created but, as Luther testifies, made.

4. Because man through sin was made guilty before God, who before the fall was created in the image of God.

5. Lest the error of the Manichaeans be confirmed, who posit that Sin is in creation itself as something Essential infused into human Nature.

6. Lest the Article concerning Redemption be diminished.

7. Because the Symbolic Books decree that Articles are by no means to be mixed.

But when these arguments are weighed a little more exactly against the balance of the Scriptures and the analogy of faith, they collapse by their own futility.

For the first suffers from the childish sophistry of a faulty consequence. For no reason of consequence holds in this argument: Creation preceded the fall, and creation has nothing in common with sin: Therefore, from the Article of creation, no judgment at all can be made concerning Original Sin.

For by the same logic I could infer: Creation preceded the fall: Therefore, from the Article of Creation, no judgment can be made concerning the cause of the Fall and sin. Now, indeed, since the Flacians themselves, in the Article concerning the cause of sin, draw arguments against the Manichaeans from the Article of creation, showing that God created all things very good, and therefore is not the cause of the Fall and sin: surely the stupendous vanity of the first argument is evidently apparent even from that. Thus, against the Flacians, I could rise up with the same reasoning: The Image of God preceded the fall: and the Image of God has nothing in common with sin. Therefore, the Flacians judge very faultily from the Article concerning the Image of God about original sin: as is abundantly clear from all their books and writings. Now if they themselves easily detect the futility of this collection: and judge that a judgment can be made about the subsequent corruption from the image of God, as if from a habit: What, I ask, is this stupendous vertigo, to be unwilling to admit the same concerning the Article of Creation: especially when a judgment concerning the cause, nature, and Essence of sin can scarcely be made from anywhere else than from the first creation: insofar as, indeed, truth shines forth more when opposites are placed next to each other. And certainly in this respect it is not simply true that creation has nothing in common with sin. For although this is most true regarding the cause, origin, and constitution of sin: yet insofar as creation shows that sin is not from God, and cannot likewise constitute the very Essence of man: to that extent this argument certainly admits a certain restriction, or at least a certain limitation. Next, this argument strikes against the very Analogy of faith, which subsists in that entire and in no way interrupted chain of Articles, which coheres so tightly that one always provides mutual assistance to another. Therefore, if a controversy arises concerning any one Article, and the Affirmative of the other party manifestly strikes against some other Article: then it is undoubtedly permitted to pronounce upon the falsity of that Affirmative. As when in the present controversy, the Affirmative of Flacius strikes against the analogy of faith and, specifically, against the Article of Creation; which shows that God once founded the human species in such a way that He propagates and preserves the same even today after the fall, according to that passage in John 5:17. My Father is working until now, and I am working: Now, indeed, since it is false, absurd, and impious that God propagates and preserves sin itself: surely I can now most correctly judge from that concerning the falsity of the Affirmative of Flacius, which asserts that Original Sin is the very Nature and Substance of Man, considered in itself and by itself. Thirdly, God Himself shows this method of arguing, as often as He mentions the extreme corruption of man, and yet always expressly mentions the Article of Creation: and explicitly names man, however much corrupted by sin, nevertheless His work and creature, and thus clearly distinguishes him from sin itself even after the fall: as in Genesis 6:5. God seeing that every thought of the heart was evil, it repented Him that He had made man on the earth.

And lest by chance this be understood concerning the first creation before the fall, and not concerning that secondary one, which consists after the fall in the propagation and preservation of the species; he immediately adds in the following verse 7: I will blot out man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth. Thus Moses also held the same method of arguing in Deuteronomy 32:6: A perverse and crooked generation, do you thus repay the Lord, O foolish and unwise people? Is he not your father, who possessed you, and made you, and created you? Fourthly, this first argument of the Flacians fosters something ὕπουλον [insidious]: namely, that the substance of Man after the fall no longer falls under the Article of creation. And so that this may appear more clearly, I argue thus: Either Man after the fall, and already corrupted by sin, or to speak according to the hypothesis of Flacius, insofar as his very Nature and substance is nothing else than the very sin of Origin itself; belongs also to the Article of creation: or he does not belong: If he belongs, I ask of the Flacians, whence then this Nature and substance of Man, which is the very sin of origin itself? Either from God; or from the Devil: If from God, then God will be the creator of sin, Because this (namely, the sin of origin) is the very substance of Man: which is impious. If from the Devil: then the Devil will be the creator of that human substance, which is the sin of origin itself: And this also is heretical and impious. Therefore it is necessary that they concede that Man, however much corrupted by the sin of origin, is most rightly considered also in the Article of creation: so that we may distinguish the Nature of Man, insofar as it is even after the fall a creature of God, from sin, which is the work of the Devil, and adheres intimately to the Nature of Man. But if they wish simply to deny that Man after the fall falls even under the consideration of the Article of creation, let them see 1. how they can name anything a substance, which nevertheless has not been created by God? Then what they wish to answer at some time to God and Moses, who assert that Man, however much a perverse and crooked generation, is nonetheless a creature of God: as was shown a little before. And now in this place that saying can be rightly accommodated, Creation has nothing in common with sin: Just as indeed we ourselves for that purpose, so solicitously urge the Article of creation in this dispute, so that we may demonstrate to the eye that the opinion of Flacius cannot subsist for this reason, because in this way Creation would be established as having something in common with sin. For if the Nature and substance of man itself were by Definition the sin of Origin itself: And indeed this (as it cannot piously be denied) were also after the fall a creature of God: it would certainly follow that the works of Creation comprehend sin under their scope, and thus have something in common with it, as regards its constitution or Definition: which is false and absurd.

The second argument contains nothing besides the empty and idle repetition of the first: And therefore it does not need a special Refutation: if only this be added: That arguments are not sought by us in the present controversy from the Article of creation for the purpose of showing what it is, or whence it arises, or how we are freed from it: but for other reasons, so that we may show that a clear distinction must be established even after the fall, between the Nature or substance of Man itself, since it, considered from the Article of Creation, is still a good creature of God: and between Sin, which entered into the World from elsewhere, and horribly corrupted human nature, while its essential parts, κατ᾽ οὐσίαν [according to essence], nevertheless remain intact. Therefore this argument sins περὶ τὸ ἐλλιπὲς τῆς διαιρέσεως [regarding the deficiency of the division]. For because there can be several causes for one thing, this conclusion is certainly clearly straw: There cannot be mention of the Article of Creation in a dispute about sin for either this or that cause. Therefore it ought not to be mentioned for any other cause at all.

We simply invert the third argument in this manner: Sin is not created: Yet this very thing cannot be demonstrated except from the Article of creation. Therefore, the Article concerning sin cannot be explained clearly and perfectly, according to all circumstances, unless the Article of Creation is used as an aid.

The fourth argument incurs the Sophism of non-cause as cause. For the Article of Creation is not to be passed over in silence in this dispute for the reason that Man was created before the fall in the image of God: Nay rather, for this very reason these two Articles are to be joined, so that it may be all the more evident to us concerning the Nature of sin: if, namely, it is shown, 1. That Man was created by God. 2. That he was created in the image of God, in perfect holiness and Justice before God: which nevertheless after the fall was utterly lost and forfeited. Therefore, again by inversion, the vanity of this argument also is most rightly demonstrated.

The fifth argument feigns crocodile tears, for the Flacians simulate that the heresy of the Manichaeans is most alien to them: which nevertheless they establish in every way by their absurd dogma. Then let the Church of God judge, whether we have fought against the Flacians from the Article of Creation for any other purpose than to show that sin is not the Nature and essence of Man itself, Because sin is not something created, or infused into the human Nature itself as something Essential in the Creation itself. But that incomparable Theologian rightly admonishes, part 1 of the Loci, page 645: That the Manichaeans were not condemned only because they feigned: That the Principle of evil is coeternal with the good God, and that they derived the Origin of sin from the very creation itself: but also because they established that sin is a substance. For Augustine attributes both to the Manichaeans, lib. 1. against Julian, chapter 3. We do not sufficiently resist the Manichaeans, unless we maintain that evils have not arisen except from goods, and that those evils are not Substances, but vices of created substances, by which they fall short of the good. Now since the Flacians affirm this latter point concerning the Substance of evil, they are certainly, before the whole Church of God, convicted of Manichaeism with the best right: since they seek fire in Manichaean ashes, and with new blasts stir up old embers, as Cassian speaks. The sixth argument does not touch the mark, nor does it contribute anything to the matter. For let no, or even the slightest, reason for the consequence be shown: The Article concerning Redemption is not to be diminished. Therefore, in a disputation concerning Original sin, mention of the Article of Creation ought not to be made. But perhaps they mean this, that Original Sin must be exaggerated, so that the price and merit of our Redemption may be so much the more evident? In which part we indeed willingly subscribe to them, but with this caution, that sin be exaggerated in that manner which Scripture itself prescribes. And nowhere does Scripture name Sin as the Nature or Essence of man itself: but it expressly names it an Accident, indeed as inhabiting and adjoining, Rom. 7:17 & 21, and περίστατον, surrounding, Heb. 12:1. Therefore, that method also, which the Flacians urge, does not accord with the Scriptures for the exaggeration of sin. Which method of exaggerating our Luther also wished to be most alien from himself, so that when the Parisians in their censure accused him of exaggerating Original Sin in such a way that he taught it to be the very Substance of Man, he intrepidly replied that a cruel injury was being inflicted upon our Churches by this accusation. And just as evils are not to be done so that good may come, Rom. 3:8, so truth is never rightly built up by false opinions and new monstrosities of words: for the reason of Truth is simple, and as Ambrose speaks, it is fisherman-like.

The seventh and final argument does not strike us. For he is not to be considered as mixing or confounding the Articles of faith who considers them so conjunctively that he confirms the ὀρθοδοξίαν of one from the other. Indeed, we ourselves in this part faithfully insist upon the Symbolic books of our Churches. The Augsburg Confession, certainly, in Article XIX, expressly distinguishes the matter or substance of Man itself, of which God is the creator, from the sin by which, with the Devil as author and man as agent, nature has been depraved. Thus the Epitome of the Formula of Concord, Article I, Affirmative Thesis 1. We believe, it says, that there is some distinction between the Nature of man itself, not only as man was created pure and Holy and without sin by God in the beginning: But also, what kind of nature we have now after the fall: a distinction, I say, between the Nature itself, which even after the fall is and remains a creature of God: and between Original Sin: And that the difference between Nature and Original Sin is as great as that between the work of God and the work of the Devil, etc. And in the declaration of the same Article, To retain this distinction we are moved, urged, and compelled by the principal articles of our Christian faith: For in the first Article concerning Creation, the holy Scripture teaches: that God not only created human nature before the fall: But also that the same, after the fall, is the work and creature of God, etc.

Latin:

Neque ullius teruntij est illa Exceptio, quæ de Morte Corporis, de febribus malignis, & id genus alijs Accidentibus hoc loco movetur: ut quæ subjecto citra Physicam ejus destructionem adesse non possunt. Quod enim Definitio Accidentis Porphyriana habet de subjecti destructione, non intelligendum efficienter, sed formaliter: id significans, posse quidem accidentia habere ejusmodi Qualitates, quæ destruunt subjectum: interim tamen ipsorum Accidentium præsentiam vel absentiam, per se non efficere, ut subjectum intereat. Quo sensu Peccatum revera est Accidens, quia ipso & præsente: & sublato per regenerationem quoad reatum: nihilominùs subjectum suam Essentiam retinet. Neque tamen interim dicam scribere animus nobis est, illis Logicis, qui Definitionem hanc Porphyrianam non omni Accidenti competere statuunt: Sufficiat illud demonstrasse, Definitionem illam, sub qua triumphat Flacius, neque nobis officere: neque ipsius causam vel tantillum juvare. Quod si verò substituatur alia definitio Accipentis sive vulgata illa Philippi: Accidens est, quod non per se subsistit, nec est pars substantiæ, sed est in alio mutabiliter: sive accuratior illa Aristotelis: συμβεβηκὸς ἐστὶν, ὃ ἐνδέχεται ὑπάρχειν ἢ τῷ ἓν ἑνὶ καὶ τῷ ἑαυτῷ καὶ μὴ ὑπάρχειν: Accidens est quod cõtingit alicui rei inesse, & non inesse: Certè tantò magis sententia nostra confirmabitur, si ad peccatum Originis illæ accommodentur.

Neque est ut elumbem illum κοκκυσμὸν de Homine Physico & Theologico obvertat Flacius. Nam scriptura unum eundemque Naturalem hominem, qualis nascitur considerandum proponit: non alium: Undè B. Lutherus super Psal. 51. Theologiæ, inquit, subjectum proprium est, Homo peccati reus ac perditus. 2. Diversa consideratio non alium efficit hominem. Et Theologus non alium Hominem, quàm physicus, licet aliter, considerat, Tandem si ad Theologicam corruptionem confugiat Flacius, meminerit eam non esse ipsius subjecti Essentialem destructionem: sic enim non Theologica ampliùs, sed physica foret corruptio: Verùm tantum esse destructionem Qualitatum, hoc est, Justitiæ & Sanctitatis, qua primus homo ante lapsum erat præditus. Atqui hæc destructio non substantiæ, sed Accidentis definitionem largitur Peccato Originali. Et quanquam B. Lutherus alicubi scripsit: Definitionem Hominis in Theologia non esse veram, quæ dicitur esse animal rationale: tamen illud non simpliciter de Essentia Hominis per se considerata, ratione cujus Definitio hæc in æternum manet vera: sed de viribus rationis humanæ in divinis intellexit: quarum respectu Homo Theologicè loquendo verè & rectè dicitur Animal irrationale: quia animalis homo, non intelligit eaque sunt spiritus Dei: neq; potest etiam: siquidem de spiritualibus judicatur: 1. Cor. 2, 14.

IV. Argumentum: Scriptura describens Peccatum Originis, semper utitur verbis substatialibus. Ergo Peccatum Originis erit ipsa substantia Hominis.

Respondeo, Fallit argumentum Sophismate τοῦ μὴ αἰτίου, & vitiosi consequentis. Neq; enim scriptura ideò utitur verbis substantialibus, quod Peccatum sit Substantia ipsa Hominis: sed quia peccatum non est seorsim extra Hominem: sed in Homine, & sic ipsa substantia peccat, videlicet cor Hominis: licet non quatenus cor est, sed quatenus corruptum est, peccet. Ex hac solutione patet etiam, quid ad putidum illud cavillum Illyrici responderi debeat, sic arguentis: Si peccatum Originis est Accidens. Ergo, Accidentia tantùm in Homine, non ipsa Natura Hominis erit corrupta. Nam quod corruptio hæc non Accidentibus, sed ipsi Naturæ tribuitur, causa est, non quòd Natura ipsa sit substantialiter peccatum Originis: sed quòd Accidentia per se non sunt neque agunt: sed in alio insunt & agunt, tanquàm in subjecto: Substantia verò est efficax: idque vel ad bonum vel ad malum, sed non quatenus est substantia: sed tantùm ratione Qualitatum, quæ substantijs insunt vel ex prima creatione: vel ex subsecuta corruptione.

Et hæc quidem præcipua sunt argumenta, quibus Flacius ipse pugnare consuevit: Cæterùm cùm discipuli ejus animadverterent, absurditatem dogmatis ipsius à nostratibus Theologis ad oculum demonstrari, ex eo potissimùm Articulo, qui est de creatione: astuto planè consilio illud excogitarunt σοφὸν φάρμακον, ut contenderent, Articulum creationis nullo pacto cum præsente, qui est de peccato Originis confundendum esse, neque de hoc ex illo judicium faciendum.

Rationes autem, quibus assertioni huic fucum facere conantur, sunt hæ præcipuæ.

1. Quia creatio lapsum præcessit, & creationi cum peccato nihil est commune.

2. Quia in Creationis Articulo, ne verbo quidem Peccati Originalis fit mentio: neque vel quid sit, vel undè oriatur, vel quomodo ab eo liberemur, explicat.

3. Quia peccatum non est creatum sed Luthero teste factum.

4. Quia homo per peccatum reus factus est coram Deo, qui ante lapsum conditus erat ad imaginem Dei.

5. Nec confirmetur Manichæorum error, statuentium, Peccatum in ipsa creatione esse tanquàm Essentiale quiddam infusum humanæ Naturæ.

6. Ne extenuetur Articulus de Redemtione.

7. Quia Libri Symbolici statuunt, nequaquàm Articulos miscendos esse.

Verùm ad trutinam Scripturarum & Analogiæ fidei Rationes hæ universæ paulò exactiùs appensæ, propria futilitate concidunt.

Prima enim puerili laborat Sophisticatione vitiosi consequentis. Nulla enim militat ratio consequentiæ in hoc argumento: Creatio præcessit lapsum, & creationi cùm peccato nihil est commune: Ergo ex Articulo creationis nullum prorsus potest judicium fieri de Peccato Originis.

Pari enim Logica inferre possem: Creatio præcessit lapsum: E. ex Articulo Creationis non potest judicium fieri de causa Lapsus & peccati. Jam vero cum ipsi Flaciani in Articulo de causa peccati, contra Manichæos argumenta depromant ex Articulo creationis, ostendentes Deum omnia valde bona creasse, ac proinde non esse causam Lapsus & peccati: utique vel inde stupenda vanitas Rationis primæ evidenter patet. Sic adversus Flacianos ex eadem ratione insurgere possem: Imago Dei præcessit lapsum: neque Imagini Dei cum peccato quicquam est commune. Ergo vitiose admodum Flaciani ex Articulo de Imagine Dei faciunt judicium de peccato originis: uti ex omnibus ipsorum libris & scriptis abunde patet. Jam si ipsimet futilitatem hojus collectionis facile deprehendunt: & ex imagine Dei, tanquam ex habitu, de subsecuta corruptione judicium fieri posse censent: Quænam obsecro hæc stupenda vertigo fuerit, idem de Creationis Articulo nolle admittere: præsertim cum de causa, natura & Essentia peccati, vix aliunde, quam ex creatione prima fieri queat judicium: quatenus nimirum contrarijs juxta se positis veritas magis elucescit. Et sane hoc respectu non simpliciter verum est, quod creationi cum peccato nihil sit commune. Etsi enim verissimum hoc est, quoad causam, originem & constitutionem peccati: tamen quatenus creatio ostendit, peccatum non esse a Deo, non item posse constituere ipsam Essentiam hominis: eatenus certe restrictionem quandam, vel certe limitationem quandam Ratio hæc admittit. Deinde impingit hæc ratio in ipsam Analogiam fidei, quæ subsistit in integra illa, minimeque interrupta Articulorum catena, quæ usque adeo arcte cohæret, ut semper unus alteri mutuam præstet operam. Proinde si circa unum aliquem Articulum oritur controversia, & alterius partis Affirmativa manifeste impingit in aliquem alium Articulum: tum indubitrato de illius Affirmativæ falsitate pronunciare licet. Ut quando in præsente controversia, Affirmativa Flacij impingit in analogiam fidei & in specie, in Articulum Creationis; qui monstrat, Deum ita semel speciem humanam condidisse, ut eandem hodieque post lapsum propaget & conservet, secundum illud Joh. 5, 17. Pater meus usque modo operatur, & ego operor: Jam vero cum falsum, absurdum & impium sit; Deum propagare & conservare peccatum ipsum: utique jam rectissime inde judicare possum de falsitate Affirmativæ Flacij, statuentis, Peccatum Originis esse ipsam Naturam ac Substantiam Hominis, in se & perse consideratam. Tertio Deus ipse hanc argumentandi rationem monstrat, quoties ex trema corruptione hominis, & tamen semper Articuli Creationis expresse meminit: & Hominem, quantumvis peccato corruptum, nihilominus opus & creaturam suam diserte nominat, & sic luculenter a peccato ipso etiam post lapsum distinguit: ut Genes. 6, 5. Videns Deus, quod cuncta cogitatio cordis mala esset, pœniticuit eum quod hominem fecisset in terra.

Et ne fortè hoc de prima creatione ante lapsum intelligatur, non verò de secundaria illa, quæ post lapsum in propagatione & conservatione speciei consistit; statim versu subseq. 7. addit: Delebo hominem, quem creavi, à facie terræ. Sic eandem argumentandi rationem tenuit etiam Moyses Deuter. 32, 6. Generatio prava atque perversa, Hæccine reddis Domino popule stulte & insipiens? numquid non ipse est pater tuus, qui possedit te, & fecit, & creavit te? Quartò, Ratio hæc prima Flacianorum ὕπουλον aliquid fovet: illud nimirum, quod substantia Hominis post lapsum, non ampliùs cadat sub Articulum de creatione. Et ut hoc dilucidiùs pateat, sic argumentor: Aut Homo post lapsum, & peccato jam corruptus, vel ut ex hypothesi Flacij loquar, quatenus ipsius Natura & substantia nihil est aliud, quàm ipsissimum peccatum Originis; pertinet etiam ad Articulum creationis: aut non pertinet: Si pertinet, quæro ex Flacianis, undè ergò hæc Natura & substantia Hominis, quæ est ipsissimum peccatum originis? Aut ex Deo; Aut ex Diabolo: Si ex Deo, tùm Deus erit creator peccati, Quia hoc (nempè peccatum originis) est ipsa substantia Hominis: id quod impium. Si ex Diabolo: tùm Diabolus erit creator illius substantiæ humanæ, quæ est peccatum ipsum originis: Atque & hoc hæreticum & impium. Ergo concedant necesse, Hominem quantumvis peccato originis corruptum, rectissimè considerari etiam in Articulo creationis: ita, ut distinguamus Naturam Hominis, quatenùs ea etiam post lapsum est creatura Dei, à peccato, quod est opus Diaboli, & Naturæ Hominis intimè adhæret. Quod si verò simpliciter negare velint, Hominem post lapsum cadere etiam sub considerationem Articuli creationis, viderint 1. quomodo aliquid nominare possint substantiam, quod tamen à Deo non sit creatum? Deindè quid respondere aliquando velint Deo & Mosi, qui Hominem, quantumvis Generationem pravam & perversam, nihilominus Dei creaturam esse afferunt: uti paulò ante ostensum. Et jam hoc loco rectè accommodari potest illud, Creationi cum peccato nihil est commune: Quemadmodum fanè nos ipsi eo fine, usque adeò sollicitè hac in disputatione urgemus Articulum creationis, ut ad oculum demonstremus, ideò sententiam Flacij subsistere non posse, quia hoc pacto Creatio cum peccato commune aliquid habere statueretur. Nam si Natura ipsa & substantia hominis esset Definitione ipsum peccatum Originis: Et verò hæc (uti piè negari non potest) esset etiam post lapsum creatura Dei: utique sequeretur Creationis opera sub suo ambitu comprehendere peccatum, & sic cum eo aliquid commune habere, quoad ejus constitutionem sive Definitio nem: id quod falsum & absurdum.

Altera ratio præter inanem & otiosam repetitionem primæ nihil continet: Ac proindè peculiari Refutatione non indiget: si modò illud adjiciatur: Non eo fine à nobis in præsente controversia argumenta peti ex creationis Articulo, ut oftendamus quid fit, vel undè oriatur, vel quomodo ab eo liberemur: sed alijs de caufis, ut oftendamus luculentum discrimen etiam post lapsum constituendum esse, inter Naturam sive substantiam ipsam Hominis, quippè quæ ex Articulo Creationis considerata, etiamnùm bona Dei sit creatura: & inter Peccatum, quod aliundè intravit in Mundum, & Naturam humanam horribiliter corrupit, essentialibus tamen ejus partibus, κατ᾽ οὐσίαν, integris manentibus. Proindè peccat hæc ratio περὶ τὸ ἐλλιπὲς τῆς διαιρέσεως. Quia enim unius rei plures dari possunt caufæ, utique straminea planè est hæc consecutio: Non vel ob hanc vel ob illam caufam potest fieri mentio Articuli Creationis, in disputatione de peccato. Ergo planè nullam aliam ob caufam ejus fieri debet mentio.

Tertiam rationem nos simpliciter invertimus in hunc modum: Peccatum non est creatum: Atqui hoc ipsum non nisi ex Articulo creationis demonstrari potest. E. Articulus de peccato, non planè ac perfectè, secundum omnes circumstantias explicari potest, nisi in subsidium adhibeatur Articulus Creationis.

Quarta ratio incurrit Sophisma non caufæ, ut caufæ. Neque enim ideò Creationis Articulus in hac disputatione silentio est prætereundus, Quia Homo ante lapsum conditus erat ad imaginem Dei: Quin imò vel hanc ipsam ob caufam conjungendi sunt duo isti Articuli, ut tantò evidentiùs de Natura peccati constare nobis possit: si nimirùm ostendatur, 1. Hominem à Deo esse creatum. 2. Creatum esse ad imaginem Dei, in perfecta sanctitate & Justitia coram Deo: quæ tamen post lapsum penitùs sit perdita & amissa. Proindè rursum per inversionem vanitas hujus etiam Rationis rectissimè demonstratur.

Quinta ratio lachrymas Crocodili fingit, simulant enim Flaciani hæresin Manichæorum à se esse alienissimam: quam tamen absurdo suo dogmate modis omnibus stabiliunt. Deindè judicet Ecclesia Dei, An alio fine hacte, nùs ex Articulo Creationis contra Flacianos pugnaverimus, quàm ut ostenderemus, peccatum ideò non esse ipsam Naturam ac essentiam Hominis, Quia peccatum non sit aliquid creatum, vel in ipsa Creatione, tanquàm Essentiale quiddam Naturæ humanæ infusum. Rectè autem admonet incomparabilis ille Theologus, part. 1. Locorum pag. 645. Non ideò tantùm damnatos esse Manichæos, quod finxerint: Principium mali esse coæternum bono Deo, quodque Originem peccati deduxerint ex ipsa mox creatione: sed & quod peccatum statuerunt esse substantiam. Augustinus enim utrumque Manichæis tribuit, lib. 1. contra Iulianum cap 3. Non satis resistimus Manichæis, nisi obtineamus, non esse mala orta nisi ex bonis, nec ea mala Substantias esse, sed creatarum substantiarum vitia, quibus deficiunt à bono. Jam cùm Flaciani posterius hoc de Substantia mali affirment, certè coram tota Ecclesia Dei, Manichæismi optimo jure rei peraguntur: quippè, qui in Manichæis cineribus ignem quærunt, & novis flatibus veteres favillas excitant,uti loquitur Cassianus. Sexta ratio scopum non tangit, neque quicquam ad rem facit. Monstretur enim nulla vel minima consequentiæ ratio : Articulus de Redemtione non est extenuandus. E. in disputatione de peccato Originis,non debet fieri mentio Articuli Creationis. Sed fortè illud volunt,Exaggerandum esse Peccatum Originis,ut tantò evidentiùs sit Redemtionis nostræ pretium meritumque ? Qua sanè in parte nos illis libenter subscribimus, sed cum hac cautione,ut eo modo peccatum exaggeretur, quem Scriptura ipsa præscribit. Atque nuspiam Scriptura Peccatum nominat ipsam Naturam, aut Essentiam hominis: sed disertè nominat Accidens,quippè inhabitans & adjacens Rom. 7. 17 & 21 & &περίστατον circumstans, Hebr. 12, 1.Ergo Modus etiam ille,quem urgent Flaciani, Exaggerationi peccati, secundùm scripturas non congruit. Quem etiam exaggerandi modum B Lutherus noster à se voluit esse alienissimum, ita,ut Parisiensibus in censura suâ ipsum insimulantibus, quòd Peccatum Originale ita exaggeraret, ut doceret esse ipsam Substantiam Hominis: intrepidè responderet, atrocem nostris Ecclesiis, hac criminatione inferri injuriam. Et quemadmodum non sunt facienda mala, ut eveniant bona, Rom. 3, 8. Sic falsis opinionibus, & novis verborum portentis, veritas nunquam rectè adstruitur: Veritatis enim ratio simplex, & ut Ambrosius loquitur,piscatoria est.

Septima & postrema ratio nos non ferit. Neque enim Articulos fidei miscere aut confundere censendus est, qui eos ita conjunctim considerat, ut unius ὀρθοδοξίαν ex altero confirmet. Quin nos ipsi hac in parte fideliter insistimus libellis Ecclesiarum nostrarum Symbolicis. Augustana certè confessio Articulo XIX. disertè distinguit ipsam materiam seu substantiam Hominis, cujus conditor est Deus, à peccato,quo,Diabolo autore & homine, depravata est natura. Sic Epitome Formulæ concordiæ Articulo I. Thesi Affirmativa 1. Credimus,inquit, quòd sit aliquod discrimen, inter ipsam hominis Naturam, non tantùm quemadmodum initiò à Deo purus & Sanctus, & absque peccato homo conditus est: Verùm etiam, qualem jam post lapsum naturam illam habemus: discrimen, inquam, inter ipsam Naturam,quæ etiam post lapsum est,permanetque Dei creatura: & inter Peccatum Originis: Et quòd tanta sit illa Naturæ & Peccati Originalis differentia,quanta est inter opus Dei,& inter opus Diaboli &c. Et in declaratione ejusdem Articuli, Ad retinendum hoc discrimen movemur,urgemur,atque cogimur præcipuis articulis Christianæ fidei nostræ: In primo enim Articulo de Creatione docet Scriptura sacra:Deum non modò ante lapsum, humanam naturam creasse: Verùm etiam eandem, post lapsum esse Dei opus & creaturam &c.


### Chapter II. Second controversy concerning the breadth and propagation of Original Sin

Concerning the Latitude and compass of Original sin, there is not such a great discrepancy between us and the Romanists: if you except that one single question, which is concerning the Virgin Mary, namely, whether she too was conceived and born in Original sin? Where the Jesuits hold the negative: meanwhile establishing with us that the compass of Original sin extends as widely as the condition of natural conception and generation itself extends: that is, that it has the same latitude as the human race.
