For as many as have been brought into this light from Adam by male seed, so many are likewise those whom this Original and hereditary stain has infected: so that from this catalog no one can or ought to be excepted, except for that one and only son of the Virgin Mary, who, from the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, had a singular manner of birth. That Apostolic Aphorism Rom. 5:12 confirms this thesis. Through one man Sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed through to all men, inasmuch as all have sinned. Where the Latitude of this sin is noted collectively at the Beginning by the word WORLD: then, however, distributively, by naming all men, not even infants excepted: for they are also subject to death. Now, however, where death as the saddest Effect dominates: there it is a necessary consequence that Sin also, as the efficient cause, is not absent.

The Manichaeans formerly waged a dispute against this purer doctrine, contending: That not all men are subject to the stain of this original evil: but only some, namely those who were χοϊκοὶ, that is, produced from an earthly nature: to whom were opposed those whom they imagined were formed from a nature of Light, and were thenceforth entirely alien and immune from original sin. Furthermore, they said that Sin did not enter into the world through one man, but was created in the beginning by a certain evil God. But the impiety of both these errors is too foul to need a lengthy Refutation. Let there be only a comparison of it to those testimonies of the scriptures which openly testify concerning the compass of this sin: Such as that one cited a little earlier from chapter 5 to the Romans. Likewise that of Job 14:4. Who will bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one (that is, the world is not), even if his days are short. What of the fact that David himself, certainly a Son of Light, expressly confesses that he was conceived in iniquities and born in sins: Psalm 51:7. To which pertains that Rom. 3:23. All have sinned and lack the glory of God. And Gal. 3:22. The scripture has concluded all under sin. And Eph. 2:3. We were by nature Children of wrath, even as others. Whence St. Ambrose aptly infers, chapter 11 in the Apology of David: Before we are born, we are stained with contagion: before we receive the use of light, we receive the injury of our very origin: and we are conceived in iniquity.

in paganism, still established, to be in a state of innocence. For thus Zwingli in his book on Baptism: Likewise in his declaration on original sin, near the end: As long as little ones are not capable of the law, we assert without hesitation, supported by the authority of Paul to the Romans, chapter four, that they are in a state of innocence: for where there is no law, there is no transgression: But they are tender, inexperienced in laws, and no less without law than Paul: Therefore they do not transgress, and consequently, they are not condemned, etc.

The Anabaptists also belong to the class of those in error, who, although they confess that under the Old Testament the plague of Original Sin was common to the whole human race, nevertheless contend that under the New Testament the reason for it is different, because sin was so expiated through Christ that infants are born into this light entirely immune from sin. But this opinion is also easily overturned by the same testimonies of the Scriptures. For let the Anabaptists explain why Death also rules over Infants under the New Testament: and whether any cause for Death, other than sin, can or ought to be established? Let them demonstrate how Infants have sinned and fall short of the glory of God: just as the Apostle indeed in Romans 3:23, under the note of universality, includes infants themselves: certainly if ALL have sinned, Infants are not excepted from sin: But little ones have done nothing good or evil by their own will: Therefore it is necessary that they be infected with original sin. Furthermore, since Christ died for all men whatsoever, and thus for Infants also: it follows that all without any exception of condition, sex, or age were infected with sin, and therefore stood in need of a Redeemer. But whether this Redemption has entirely removed sin from the midst with respect to Infants and the Reborn, the following third chapter will explain.

However, each and every one of these Pelagianizers has certain reasons or arguments by which they attempt to put a gloss upon their impiety.

The first is taken from Romans 4:15. Where there is no Law, there is no sin: Infants do not have the Law, because they do not understand it. Therefore neither sin. Likewise, Romans 7:8, without the Law sin was dead: But I was alive without the law once: But when the commandment came, sin revived. Now, this can be understood of no part of age other than infancy or childhood. For this alone is ignorant of laws. Therefore, as long as infants are ignorant of laws, they are in a state of innocence: nor do they contract the guilt of sin before the knowledge of the law has shone upon them.

But I reply that in the allegation of both sayings a shameful Ignorance of the Refutation is committed. For the former Aphorism, Romans 4:15, expressly does not deal with the Origin, or with the scope or breadth of original sin, but only with the sense or recognition of Sin, so that where the Law does not obtain its force, the detestable foulness of sin is never recognized. For human nature is so stupefied that, unless terrified by an external thunderbolt, it never trembles at the sense of sin. The solidity of this response is evident from the fact that the Apostle in the immediately preceding, indeed clearly coherent words, says: Through the law is the recognition of sin. Now, the consequence does not hold: Infants cannot recognize sin from the Law. Therefore they do not have sin. For by the same reasoning, the same could be inferred about hardened and stubborn sinners: since they no more than infants recognize the deformity of sin from the Law. However, the error of the argument arises from the negation of the second act to the negation of the first act: where the inference proceeds no more than if one were to infer: An infant does not recognize that it has a rational Soul. Therefore it does not have a rational Soul. The later Apostolic Aphorism, Romans 7:8, is distorted too maliciously, contrary to the mind of Paul, into a foreign sense, partly through Ignorance of the Refutation, and partly through a Figure of Speech. For sin is said to be dead without the law, not because it does not exist, or does not operate in any way at all: but because without the stimulus of the law, it is either not felt or recognized by us at all, or very little: Since, as the Apostle testifies, the strength of sin is the Law: And without the law sin is neither recognized, nor does it press upon man: but with the Law silent, sin itself sleeps as if lulled at the doors, and therefore one lives more securely. Thus the Apostle in the following does not say: Therefore I once lived without sin: but, I lived without the Law: not referring to infantile age, but to adult.

But this Anabaptist error is a rivulet of the Pelagian heresy, which, among other things, spread this delirium: Sin is not born with man, because it is exercised by man only afterwards, because it is demonstrated to be not a fault of Nature, but of the will: as testified by Augustine, book 2, On Grace and Original Sin, chapter 6.

Zwingli also attempted to defend this same impiety: Although if we thoroughly examine his writings, it is easily detected that he was less than consistent with himself. For initially in a letter to Urbanus Rhegius, he denied that the Evil of Origin is properly sin, because it is not voluntary: as was shown above toward the end of the first chapter. But then the same man said that sin is indeed damnable in itself: but that its guilt is already so removed through the death of Christ that infants, not only of the faithful but also of the Gentiles, even if not baptized, are free from the guilt of divine wrath. Thirdly, he wrote that Original Sin does not properly merit damnation, provided one has had faithful parents. Vol. 2 of his works, page 89, in the book on Baptism. These three opinions, although they differ greatly among themselves in circumstances, nevertheless agree entirely in this, that Original Sin under its scope or ambit does not include all Infants, especially those who are born of faithful parents: indeed, not only these, but indifferently and promiscuously all Infants, not yet even baptized, but

Latin:

DE Latitudine & complexu peccati Originalis haud usque adeò magna inter nos & Romanenses est discrepantia: si unicam illam quæstionem excipias, quæ est de Maria Virgine, An nimirum & hæc in peccato Originali sit concepta & progenita? Ubi negativam tenent Jesuvvitæ: Interim nobiscum statuentes tàm latè patere peccati Originalis complexum, quàm latè se extendit ipsa conceptionis & generationis naturalis conditio: hoc est, eandem ipsius esse cum genere humano latitudinem. Quotquot enim jam indè ab Adamo ex virili semine sunt hanc in lucem editi, tot sunt itidem quos labes ista Originalis & hæreditaria infecit: adeò ut ex hoc catalogo nemo excipi possit aut debeat, præter unum & solum illum Virginis Mariæ filium, qui ex obumbratione Spiritus Sancti conceptus singularem nascendi modum habuit. Confirmat Thesin hanc Aphorismus ille Apostolicus Rom. 5, 12. Per unum hominem Peccatum intravit in mundum, & per peccatum mors, & sic in omnes homines mors pertransijt, siquidem omnes peccaverunt. Ubi Latitudo peccati hujus Initio collectivè notatur vocabulo MUNDI: deindè verò distributivè, omnes homines nominando, ne infantibus quidem exceptis: quippe morti quoque obnoxijs. Jam autem ubi mors tanquàm tristissimus Effectus dominatur: ibi Peccatum quoque, tanquàm causam efficientem haud abesse, necessarium est consequens.

Puriori huic doctrinæ litem olim intenderunt Manichæi, contendentes: Non omnes homines mali hujus originalis labi esse obnoxios: sed quosdam tantùm, eos nimirum qui essent χοϊκοὶ, hoc est, ex natura terrea producti: quibus contrarij essent, quos ex natura Lucis formatos, ac exindè à peccato originali prorfus alienos atq; immunes esse fingebant. Deindè dicebant, Peccatum non per unum hominem in mundum introijsse, sed in principio esse creatum à malo quodam Deo. Sed fœdior est utriusque istius erroris impietas, quàm ut Refutatione prolixa indigeat. Fiac tantùm illius collatio ad ea scripturarum testimonia quæ de complexu peccati hujus apertè testantur: Quale illud est paulò antè citatum ex c. 5. ad Rom. Item illud Jobi 14, 4. Quis dabit mundum ab immundo? non unus (videlicet mundus est) etiamsi breves dies ejus. Quid quòd David ipse, Filius certè Lucis, disertè fatetur, se in iniquitatibus conceptum, & in peccatis gemtum esse: Psal. 51, 7. Quò pertinet illud Rom. 3, 23. Omnes peccaverunt & egent gloria Dei Et Gal. 3, 22. Conclusit scriptura omnes sub peccato. Et Eph. 2, 3. Eramus naturâ Filij iræ, sicut & cæteri. Undè scitè infert B. Ambrosius, cap. 11. in Apologia Davidis: Antequàm nascamur, maculamur contagio: antiquàm usuram lucis, originis ipsius injuriam excipimus: & in iniquitate concipimur.

in gentiliśmo, adhuc constitutos, esse in statu innocentiæ. Sic euim Zvvinglius lib. de Baptismo: Item in declaratione de peccato originis, circa fiem: Quamdiu parvuli legis capaces non sunt, in statu esse innocentiæ, nos incunctanter de nostris asferimus, fulti autoritate Pauli ad Romanos quarto: ubi enim non est lex, ibi nec prevaricatio: Sunt autem teneri, Legum inexperti, & non minùs sine lege, quàm Paulus: Ergo non transgrediuntur, proindeǫ, nec damnantur &c.

Pertinent ad classem errantium etiam Anabaptistæ, qui licet fateantur sub Vetere Testamento, Peccati Originalis luem toti generi humano communem fuisse: aliam tamen contendunt, jam sub novo Testamento ejus esse rationem, proptereà quòd per Christum peccatum Itastit expiatum, ut infantes prorsus à peccato immunes, hanc in lucem nascantur. Sed & hæc sententia ijsdem Scripturarum testimoniis facilè evertitur. Edisserant enim Anabaptistæ, cur Mors etiam dominetur Infantibus sub Novo Testamento: & nùm alia, præter peccatum, causa Mortis constitui possit aut debeat? Demonstrent, quomodo Infantes peccaverint, & egeant gloria Dei: quemadmodum sanè Apostolus Rom. 3, 23. sub nota universalitatis, ipsos quoque Infantes complectitur: certè si OMNES peccaverunt, non excipiuntur Infantes à peccato: Parvuli autem propria voluntate nihil boni, aut mali egerunt: Ergo peccato originis sint infecti, necesse est. Porrò cùm Christus pro omnibus omninò hominibus, & sic pro Infantibus quoque sit mortuus: sequitur omnes omninò sine ulla exceptione conditionis, sexus, ætatis peccato fuisse infectos, ac proindè Redemtore indiguisse. Nùm verò hæc Redemtio peccatum prorsus è medio sustulerit Infantium & Renatorum respectu, caput infequens tertium expediet.

Habent autem singuli & universi isti πελαγιάνιζοντες certas rationes sive argumenta, quibus impietati suæ fucum facere conantur.

Prima petita ex cap. Rom. 4, 15. Ubi non est Lex: ibi non est peccatum: Infantes non habent Legem, quia eam non intelligunt. Ergo neq́ peccatum. Item, Rom. 7, 8. sine Lege peccatum erat mortuum: Ego autem vivebam sine lege aliquando: Sed cum venisset mandatum, peccatum revixit. Jam verò de nulla ætatis parte, quàm de Infantia pueritiavè hoc intelligi potest. Hæc enim sola legum ignara est. Ergo quamdiu infantes legum rudes sunt, tamdiu sunt in statu innocentiæ: neque prius peccati reatum contrahunt, quàm legis notitia ipsis affulserit.

Sed respondeo in utriusque dicti allegatione turpem committi Ignorationem Elenchi. Prior enim Aphorismus Rom. 4, 15. ex professo non agit vel de Origine, vel de complexu sive latitudine peccati originalis, sed tantùm de sensu sive agnitione Peccati, ita ut ubi Lex vigorem suum non obtinet, peccati detestanda fæditas nunquàm agnoscatur. Sic enim stupet natura humana, ut nisi externo fulmine territa, ad peccati sensum nunquàm expavescat. Patet Responsonis hujus soliditas exindè, quòd Apostolus in immediatè præcedentibus imò planè cohærentibus; Per legem, dicit, est agnitio peccati. Jam verò non valet consequentia: Infantes non possunt ex Lege agnoscere peccatum. Ergo peccatum non habent. Sic enim eadem rationè de præfractis & contumacibus peccatoribus idem colligi posset: quippè qui haud magis ac infantes, ex Lege peccati, deformitatem agnoscunt. Oritur autem error argumenti ex negatione actus secundi, ad negationem actus primi: ubi haud magis procedit collectio, ac si quis inferat: Infans nõ agnoscit se habere Animam rationalem. Ergo non habet Animam rationalem. Posterior Aphorismus Apostolicus Rom. 7, 8. Præter mentem Pauli in alienum sensum, partim per Elenchi Ignorationem, partim verò per Figuram Dictionis, nimis malitiosè detorquetur. Peccatum enim sine lege dicitur mortuum, non quòd non sit, aut nullo prorsus modo operetur: sed quia sine legis stimulo, vel planè non vel perparùm à nobis sentitur aut agnoscitur: Siquidem teste Apostolo, vis peccati, Lex est: Et sine lege peccatum neque agnoscitur, neque premit hominem: sed Lege tacente ipsum quoque peccatum, quasi obsopitum ad fores dormit, ac proindè securius vivitur. Sic Apostolus in subsequentibus non dicit: Ergo quondam sine peccato vixi: sed, sine Lege vixi: non ad infantilem ætatem, sed adultam

Sed rivulus est error iste Anabaptisticus hæresews Pelagianæ, quæ inter reliqua, & istud delirium sparsit: Peccatum non cum homine nascitur, quòd demùm postmodùm exercetur ab homine, quia non Naturæ delictum, sed voluntatis esse demonstratur: teste Augustino lib. 2. de grat. & peccat. Orig. cap. 6.

Quam eandem impietatem Zvvinglius quoq, manifestè defendere conatus est: Quanquam si penitus scripta ipsius examinemus, sibi ipsi minùs constitisse facilè deprehenditur. Initiò enim in epistola ad Vrbanum Rhegium, Malum Originis propriè esse peccatum, negavit, quia non sit voluntarium: uti suprà sub finem capitis primi oftensum. Deindè verò idem peccatum per se quidem damnabile esse dixit: sed per mortem Christi ita jam sublatũ esse reatũ, ut Infantes non fidelium tantùm: sed & Gentilium, etiam non baptizati, à reatu ira divinæ sint liberi. Tertiò Peccatum Originale damnationem propriè non mereri, scripsit, si modò quis parentes fideles nactus fuerit. Tom. 2. operum pag. 89. in libro de Baptismo. Quæ tres sententiæ licèt inter se circumstantiis plurimùm discrepent, in eo tamen omninò consentiunt, quòd Peccatum Originis sub suo complexu sive ambitu non comprehendat omnes Infantes, eos præsertim, qui ex fidelibus parentibus sunt prognati: imò non hos solùm, sed indifferenter & promiscuè omnes Infantes, nondum etiam baptizatos, quin


### Chapter II. Second controversy concerning the breadth and propagation of…: Whether the Virgin Mary is without original sin?

rather, and indeed looking to that, by which, devoted to Pharisaism and a persecutor of the Christian name, he did not yet recognize his sin from the Law. Finally, the Apostle does not say that when the Law came, sin finally began to exist: but that sin revived. Now sin revives when, from the very recognition of it, a tremendous disturbance or consternation of conscience follows, by which a man sees his destruction before his eyes, and is so crushed that he feels himself nowhere equal to bearing the burden of sin.

A second argument is taken from the words of the Apostle, Romans 5:14. Death reigned from Adam even to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of the transgression of Adam. From this they argued that death is indeed drawn from the first parent, but not sin.

But this is a malicious corruption of the Apostle's words: For the Apostle is entirely concerned in this place to demonstrate that even before Moses, sin had passed into all, although the Law had not yet been promulgated: because death reigned over all before Moses: thus concluding: Death is nothing but the wages of sin: For if even one person were to die who did not have sin, it would follow that God is unjust. But all from Adam to Moses have died: And they died not only the old and adults, who by the very act, just as Adam, having committed sins, deserved death: but infants also, who, properly speaking, have committed nothing of actual sins. It is therefore a consequence that they were sinners by a common sin, namely, that which was propagated from the protoplasts thence to all posterity; which is nothing else but Original [sin].

The third and final argument is this: Nothing has the nature of sin except that which is voluntary. But the voluntary does not fall upon infants. Therefore infants are destitute of sin.

This objection caused a great deal of trouble even to the ancient Fathers: For Augustine had written that sin is so much a voluntary evil that it is in no way sin if it is not voluntary. But Augustine himself finally acknowledged of what sin this is to be understood, writing thus in book 3, chapter 5, against Julian, who was objecting this very thing about the voluntary to him. You think in vain that there is no fault in infants because it cannot exist without will, which is absent in them. For these things are rightly said of the personal sin of each one: but not of the Original contagion of the first parent. The major premise, therefore, is not simply true, but only in a certain respect, namely, concerning Actual sin: but it is false concerning Original sin, since, in order for it to be contracted, it does not require, as a personal act, that it be voluntary, that is, that it be of one who knows and wills. Moreover, if the Pelagians dispute about the subject of Original sin, certainly hardly anyone would deny that in this respect the sin of origin can be called voluntary, unless he were ignorant that the sin of origin is an aversion from GOD and a perversion in the will itself. In which respect, indeed, the sin of origin can be called voluntary in infants as well. Indeed, if we look to the first source of Original sin, which was the will of Adam, no one would deny that in this sense also it can be called voluntary. This very thing Augustine also acknowledged, writing thus in book 1 of the Retractations, chapter 13: That which is called Original sin in infants, although they do not yet use the free choice of the will, is not absurdly called voluntary also, because, contracted from the evil will of the first man, it has become in a certain way hereditary. It is not, therefore, false what I said, that sin is so much a voluntary evil that it is in no way sin unless it is voluntary.

With these things well observed, it is clear that it is not inconvenient for the sin of origin to be called voluntary, chiefly in three respects. 1. By reason of its Origin, because it drew its rise from a depraved will. 2. By reason of its Subject, because it fixed its seat, as it were, in the will of every man. 3. By reason of the second act: Because a man not yet reborn is delighted by this sin even to the greatest degree: nor does he acknowledge that Concupiscence is sin. Moreover, if 'voluntary' is taken in the Pelagian sense: that, namely, only that is sin which is contracted by one who knows and wills: then indeed we deny that the sin of origin is voluntary in this way: but at the same time, with our Author, we retort that this definition of the voluntary is true concerning civil offenses. For in the judgment of a court, an ordinary penalty is not established except for voluntary offenses: which is evident even from this; GOD Himself, Deut. 19:2. He established cities of refuge or public asylums, in which security might be provided for those who had committed some slaughter not by intended will, but by chance. Now, however, political sentences are not to be rashly mixed with the doctrine of the Church, as our Author warns.

But enough and more than enough about the Pelagians and their arguments: There remains now still an error, which gravely impinges upon the purer doctrine concerning the scope or breadth of sin.

This, however, is the position of the Romanists and especially the Jesuits, who stubbornly contend that the Blessed Virgin Mary was conceived without original sin. Regarding this question, a serious dispute once arose among the monks themselves. For the Dominicans taught that Mary was conceived and born in original sin, and they kept saying that in this matter they were following the footsteps of their master, Thomas. The Franciscans, however, carried the purity or immunity of Mary from original sin to the point of madness, moved by the authority of Alexander of Hales and Scotus. And indeed, the Council of Constance in the year 1439 took up their defense, to such an extent that in the year 1470, by the authority of the Pope, the Council of Basel in its 36th session proposed this opinion as one to be held and embraced without doubt by all Catholics, and designated a special feast of the Conception of Mary to be celebrated holily every year. Nor did the Council of Trent shrink from this opinion, which in the Appendix to the Decree of the fifth session protests in express words that it is not its intention to include the blessed and immaculate Virgin Mary under the decree concerning original sin.

The Jesuit Bellarmine, noticing that this opinion is not altogether firm, undertook its defense rather timidly, yet in such a way that he stands on the side of the Franciscans: For first, he says, it is not held among Catholics as a certain and explored matter that the Blessed Virgin Mary was conceived without sin. But he soon adds that this very opinion is in no way heretical or erroneous, but very pious and probable, and indeed far more probable than the contrary opinion: lib. 4. de amiss. grat. & statu peccati, cap. 15 p 324 C.

But the vanity of this dogma is readily apparent from those things which we have argued above from the Scriptures concerning the complexity and latitude of Original Sin, inasmuch as they indefinitely and universally conclude all men whatsoever, begotten from male seed, under sin: and they pronounce Christ alone ἄκακον ἀμίαντον, κεχωρισμένων ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν. Hebr. 7. The consensus of Orthodox Antiquity is added: For thus Augustine, lib. de fide ad Petrum cap. 23. Hold most firmly, and doubt in no way, that every man who is conceived through the intercourse of man and woman is born with Original Sin, subject to impiety, and subject to death, and for this reason is born by nature a child of wrath.

And lib. de nuptiis & concupiscentia: Therefore Christ did not wish to be born of intercourse, so that from this he might also teach that everyone who is born of intercourse is flesh of sin, since the Only One, who was not born thence, was not flesh of sin.

Ambrose in Isaiah: It has been observed that from man and woman, that is, through that commingling of bodies, no one appears to be free from fault. But he who is free from fault is also free from this conception.

And what need is there of many words, when even the very history of the Annunciation of Mary, and her canticle, removes all doubt? For to what end was there need of the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, and the power of the Most High, other than that that mass of the Virgin Mary, from which the Son of God was conceived, should be purged from the filth of Original Sin? What, furthermore, did those words of Elizabeth mean: Blessed are you who believed: that Mary's blessedness was obtained not from the holiness of her own flesh, but from Faith? Why, moreover, would Mary herself call Christ HER Savior? And my spirit rejoices, she says, in GOD MY Savior: If she had been free from Original Sin: for Christ is not a Savior except of those who have perished through sin? Why, finally, would she so greatly proclaim the mercy of God declared to her, unless she herself had also promised herself from that the Remission of all sins? Hence Augustine evidently concludes: Whoever thinks that there is or has been in this life any man, or any men, except the one Mediator of God and men, to whom the Remission of sins has not been necessary, is contrary to divine scripture, where the Apostle says: through one man sin entered into the world &c. in lib. de Perfectione Justitiæ.

And it is clearly trifling, what Bellarmine answers in this place, that the remission of sins was necessary for the B. Virgin Mary, and that Christ

was her Redeemer is not denied: but that sins were remitted to her, not into which she had fallen, but into which she would have fallen, had she not been prevented by the grace of God through the merits of Christ. Thus, indeed, the Jesuits like to play craftily in a very serious matter. The remission of sins, certainly, to whomever the individual is accommodated, relates both to the sin of Origin, and to each and every sin which was committed either by thinking, or by doing, or by speaking, or by omitting, or in any other way. But those things which were not committed, but could have been committed, are not said to be remitted, nor indeed do they even need remission. It is therefore the same as if the Jesuit said: Mary had need of the Remission of sins, because she did not sin: but she could have sinned: Than which hardly anything more absurd or more trifling could be said: Nor is there any reason for him to object to that of David, Psalm 85, 13. You have delivered my soul from the lowest hell: And Psalm 144, 10. You have redeemed your servant from the evil sword: From which, however, it does not follow that David was in the lowest hell, or had been struck by an evil sword. For the Jesuit ought to have remembered that those phrases and modes of speaking cannot be taken according to the letter: but metaphorically denote those calamities by which David was then constrained in the very act, &c.

But the Jesuit has certain reasons by which he tries to put a gloss on his opinion: And at the beginning, indeed, he flees to some singular Privilege: All men, he says, who are born from Adam through carnal generation, draw Original sin from him, unless perhaps someone is excepted from the common law by a singular privilege. He established, therefore, that the Virgin Mary had been exempted from the common census and number of the rest of men by such a singular privilege. But how weak this reason is, and how childishly it begs the question: there is hardly a boy who does not understand: especially when, driven by the force of truth, the Jesuit himself finds it necessary to confess: That this singular privilege of Mary can be proven neither from the Word of God, nor from a certain definition of the Church. What, that Scripture utterly denies this fictitious privilege, asserting that not even among the Saints is anyone pure: Job 15, 15.

Moreover, lest he seem to yield the arena, he rises up in the second place thus: Adam was a type of the future Christ: But Adam was not formed from cursed earth, but from earth still pure. Therefore Christ also had to be formed from earth not cursed, that is, from the Virgin Mother, who was devoid of all curse, and by this, of all sin.

But I reply 1. That an ἀγνοίαν ἐλέγχου, or a fallacy of faulty comparison, is committed in the application of the Type, that is, of Adam to Christ: which Type certainly ought not to be extended more widely than Scripture itself permits. The proper seat of this doctrine, however, is chapter 5 to the Romans, and chapter 15 of the first to the Corinthians: Where, since this application which the Jesuit imagines in this place is not indicated by even a single jot, we certainly reject it as fictitious.

Then, if according to the Jesuit hypothesis, there must exist between the Type and the antitype a harmony and conformity that is in every way complete and in no respect deficient, it will follow that Christ, after the example of the Type, could not—nay, indeed, ought not—to have been conceived and born of a woman: nor, once born, to have gradually grown in wisdom and stature before GOD and men: since no such thing can be affirmed of Adam. But this is absurd and contrary to the Scriptures. Therefore, such a harmony as the Jesuit imagines between the Type and the Antitype outside of the Scriptures cannot subsist. We therefore correct the error in this manner, by positing that the congruence of the Type and Antitype required that Christ should not be conceived from cursed earth, that is, not from flesh polluted by sin, which we willingly concede was accomplished by the power of the Most High and the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit. But now, from that particle of Mary's substance being purified, the consequence does not hold for her entire substance.

This very response of ours must be given to the subsequent argument of Bellarmine, taken from Eve, who served as a Type of Mary: What? That Eve, not begotten from the commingling of man and woman, obtained some privilege above Mary.

Thirdly, he brings forward passages from the Song of Songs: As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters, Cant. 2:1. And: Thou art all fair, my love, and there is no spot in thee, Cant. 4:7. And: A garden enclosed is my sister, my spouse, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, ibid. verse 12.

I answer 1. That an ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχɣ (ignorance of the refutation) is being committed. For these and similar passages do not treat of the Virgin Mary at all, but depict the state of the Church, insofar as it is sanctified and cleansed by the washing of water in the word: that is, the most perfect holiness and innocence of Christ the Savior is imputed to it: so that it may be glorious, not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing: as interpreted by the Apostle in Eph. 5:26 & 27. Furthermore, even if those passages were to be applied to Mary in the highest degree, they must nevertheless be accepted only in a qualified sense: namely, partly in respect of regeneration, by the power of which the guilt of sin was removed from Mary, as from the rest of the faithful: and partly in respect of a singular sanctification, which, however, concerns not her entire substance, but only that part or mass from which the flesh of Christ was conceived and formed. Finally, granted but not conceded: that by the power of the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit Mary's entire substance was purged from Original Sin: it does not therefore follow, as Bellarmine intends, that Mary was free from original sin from her conception and Nativity. For if that were true, there would certainly have been no need for this peculiar sanctification of Mary around the time when she was to conceive Christ.

Finally, he collects certain figurative expressions from the fathers; such as that Mary was an incorrupt virgin, that she was always in the light: and many others of this kind, from which everyone easily understands that nothing can be proven. That one passage of Augustine, which exists in his book De Natura et Gratia, chapter 36, seems to patronize this error, which reads thus: For the honor of the Lord, I wish to have no question concerning the Blessed Mary, when the subject of sins is being discussed.

But the conclusion in the Jesuit's argument is clearly weak: Augustine does not wish to have a question concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary when the subject of sins is being discussed: Therefore, he posits that she was free from original sin from her conception. For it is one thing to ἐπέχειν, or to suspend judgment—which is what Augustine does—and quite another to affirm something as certain—which is what Augustine does not do. Nay, rather, if we weigh that very passage more accurately, it is manifest that he was not of the same mind as the Jesuits. For in the immediately following words he asserts: that more grace was conferred upon Mary, for the overcoming of sin in every respect. Now, who is there who does not see that where there is need for Grace, where sin must be overcome, sin is there in actual fact? What? That Augustine, in book 5 against Julian, chapter 9, expressly writes: that the body of Mary indeed came from original concupiscence, but did not transmit it into the Body of Christ, inasmuch as He was not conceived from it.

Latin:

potiùs, & quidem eam refpiciens, quâ Pharisæismo deditus, & Christiani nominis persecutor, ex Lege nondum peccatum suum agnoscebat. Tandem non dicit Apostolus, cum Lex veniret, peccatum demùm incepit esse: sed peccatum revixit. Reviviscit autem peccatum tùm, quando ex ipsius agnitione, tremenda conscientiæ turbatio sive consternatio sequitur, quâ interitum suum homo ante oculos videt, & sic atteritur, ut oneri peccati sustinendo nusquàm se parem esse sentiat.

Altera ratio desumta est ex verbis Apostoli, Roman. 5, 14. Regnavit mors ab Adam usque ad Mosen, etiam super eos, qui non peccaverunt in similitudine transgressionis Adam. Hinc arguebant, Mortem quidem ex primo parente trahi, non autem peccatum.

Sed malitiosa hæc est verborum Apostoli corruptio: Nam in eo totus hoc loco est Apostolus, ut demonstret, etiam ante Mosen peccatum transiisse in omnes, licèt Lex nondum fuerit promulgata: quia mors in omnes ante Mosen regnaverit: sic colligens: Mors non est nisi peccati stipendium: Si enim vel unus quispiam moreretur, qui peccatum nón haberet; sequeretur, injustum esse Deum. Atqui omnes ab Adamo usque ad Mosen mortui sunt: Mortui autem sunt non tantùm senes & adulti, qui actu ipso, perindè ut Adam, peccatis admissis, mortem sunt promeriti: sed infantes etiam, qui actualium peccatorum nihil, propriè loquendo, admiserunt. Consequens est ergò, peccatores illos fuisse peccato communi, nimirùm à protoplastis indè ad omnem posteritatem propagato; quod nullum est aliud, præter Originale.

Tertia & postrema ratio est isthæc: Nihil habet rationem peccati, nisi quod est voluntarium. Atqui in Infantes non cadit voluntarium. Ergo Infantes destituuntur peccato.

Facessivit hæc Objectio plurimùm negotii antiquis etiam Patribus: Scripserat enim Augustinus, Peccatum usque adeò malum esse voluntarium, ut nullo modo sit peccatum, si non sit voluntarium. Verùm de quonam peccato hoc accipiendum sit, agnovit tandem ipse quoque Augustinus, sic scribens lib. 3. cap. 5. contra Julianum hoc ipsum de voluntario sibi objicientem. Frustra putas ideò in parvulis nullum esse delictum, quia sine voluntate, quæ in illis nulla est, esse non potest. Hæc enim rectè dicuntur de proprio cujusq; peccato: non autem de primi parentis Originali contagio. Major ergò propositio non simpliciter, sed tantùm secundum quid vera est, nempè de peccato Actuali: Falsa verò de peccato Originali, quippè quod, ut contrahatur, non requirit tanquàm proprium, ut sit voluntarium, hoc est, sit scientis & volentis. Cæterùm si de subjecto peccati Originalis disputent, Pelagiani, certè hoc respectu Peccatum Originis dici posse voluntarium, vix quisquam iverit inficias, nisi qui ignoraverit, Peccatum Originis esse aversionem à DEO, & perversionem in ipsa voluntate. Quo sanè respectu Peccatum Originis in Infantibus quoque dici potest voluntarium. Quin si ad primum fontem peccati Originalis respiciamus, qui fuit voluntas Adami, quin hoc etiam sensu illud dici possit voluntarium, nemo negaverit. Quod ipsum agnovit etiam Augustinus sic scribens lib. 1. Retractationum cap. 13. Illud, quod in parvulis dicitur Originale peccatum, cum adhuc non utantur libero arbitrio voluntatis, non absurdè vocatur etiam voluntarium, quia ex primi hominis mala voluntate contractum, factum est quodammodò hæreditarium. Non itaque falsum est quod dixi, usque adeò peccatum, voluntarium est malum, ut nullo modo sit peccatum, nisi sit voluntarium.

His probè observatis liquet haud incommodè, Peccatum Originis dici posse voluntarium, tribus potissimùm respectibus. 1. Ratione Originis, quia ex voluntate prava ortum traxit. 2. Ratione Subjecti. Quia in voluntate cujuslibet hominis propriam quasi sedem fixit. 3. Ratione actus secundi: Quia Homo nondum renatus peccato hoc vel maximè delectatur: neque agnoscit, Concupiscentiam esse peccatum. Cæterùm si voluntarium sensu Pelagiano accipiatur: quod nimirùm illud tantùm sit peccatum, quod à sciente & volente contrahitur: tùm sanè negamus, peccatum Originis hoc modo esse voluntarium: sed simul cum Autore nostro regerimus, Definitionem hanc voluntarii de civilibus delictis veram esse. Nam in judicio fori ordinaria pœna non statuitur, nisi in delicta voluntaria: id quod vel indè patet; DEUS ipse Deut. 19, 2. Civitates refugii sive asyla publica constituit, in quibus securitas præstaretur his, qui non destinata voluntate, sed fortuitò cædem aliquam commiserant, Jam verò politicæ sententiæ cum doctrina Ecclesiæ non sunt temerè permiscendæ, uti Autor noster admonet.

Sed de Pelagianis eorumque, rationibus plus satis: Superest nunc adhuc error, qui in puriorem doctrinam de complexu sive latitudine peccati graviter impingit.

Is verò est Romanensium & cumprimis Jesuitarum, qui B. Virginem Mariam sine Peccato Originis conceptam fuisse, mordicùs pugnant. Qua de quæstione inter ipsos Monachos olim gravis orta est dimicatio. Dominicani enim docebant, Mariam in peccato Originali conceptam esse, & natam: sed, hac in parte Magistri sui Thomæ vestigia sequi dictitabant. Franciscani autem puritatem sive immunitatem Mariæ à peccato Originis, ad rabiem usque afferebant, moti autoritate Alexandri de Ales, & Scoti. Et sanè istorum patrocinium suscepit Concilium Constantinum Anno 1439. usque adeò, ut Anno 1470. autoritate Pontificis Concilium Basileense Sessione 36. sententiam hanc omnibus Catholicis indubitatò tenendam & amplectendam proponeret: & singularem festivitatem Conceptionis Mariæ annis singulis sanctè peragendam destinaret. Neq; ab hac sententia abhorruit Concilium Tridentinum, quod in Appendice Decreti, Sessionis quintæ disertis verbis protestatur, suæ non esse intentionis, sub decreto de peccato Originali, comprehendere etiam beatam & immaculatam Virginem Mariam.

Jesuwita Bellarminus animadvertens sententiam hanc haud usque adeò firmam esse, timidiusculè, sed ita tamen ejus defensionem suscepit, ut à Franciscanorum stet partibus: Primùm enim, inquit, non haberi apud Catholicos pro re certa & explorata B. Virginem Mariam, sine peccato fuisse conceptam. Sed mox subjicit, hanc ipsam opinionem non ullo modo esse hæreticam vel erroneam, sed piam admòdum, ac probabilem, atq; adeò contraria sententia longè probabiliorem: lib. 4. de amiss. grat. & statu peccati, cap. 15 p 324 C.

Sed vanitas hujus dogmatis ultrò patet ex iis, quæ suprà de complexu atque Latitudine Peccati Originalis, ex Scripturis disputavimus, quippè quæ indefinitè & Universaliter omnes omninò homines, ex virili semine progenitos concludunt sub peccato: & solum Christum pronunciant ἄκακον ἀμίαντον, κεχωρισμένων ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν. Hebr. 7. Accedit consensus Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis: Sic enim Augustinus, lib. de fide ad Petrum cap. 23. Firmissimè tene, & nullatenùs dubites, omnem hominem, qui per concubitum viri & mulieris concipitur, cum peccato Originali nasci, impietati subditum, mortiq; subjectum, & ob hoc naturâ Filium iræ nasci.

Et lib. de nuptiis & concupiscentia: Ideò Christus non de concubitu nasci voluit, ut hinc etiam doceret, omnis qui de concubitu nascitur, carnem esse peccati, quandoquidem Sola, quæ non indè nata est, non fuit caro peccati.

Ambrosius in Esaiam: Servatum est, ut ex viro & muliere, id est, per illam corporum commixtionem nemo videatur esse expers delicti. Qui autem expers delicti, expers est etiam hujus conceptionis.

Et quid multis opus est, cum vel ipsa histostoria Annunciationis Mariæ, ejusdemque canticum, dubitationem omnem tollat? Quorsum enim opus erat obumbratione Spiritus sancti, & virtute altissimi, quàm ut massa illa Mariæ Virginis, ex qua Filius DEI conceptus est, à sordibus peccati Originalis purgaretur? Quid porrò sibi volebant verba illa Elisabethæ: Beata tu quæ credidisti: quâm Mariæ beatitudinem obtingere non ex propria carnis sanctitate: sed ex Fide? Cur insuper ipsa Maria vocaret Christum Servatorem SUUM? & exultat, inquiens, Spiritus meus, in DEO Salvatore MEO: Si expers fuisset peccati Originalis: Salvator enim non est Christus nisi eorum, qui per peccatum perierunt? Cur denique Misericordiam DEI sibi declaratam, tantoperè prædicaret, nisi & ipsa indè sibi peccatorum omnium Remissionem pollicita fuiffet? Hinc Augustinus evidenter colligit: Quisquis putat esse vel fuisse in hac vita aliquem hominem, vel aliquos homines, excepto uno Mediatore DEI & hominum, quibus neceffaria non fuerit Remissio peccatorum, contrarius est divinæ scripturæ, ubi Apostolus ait: per unum hominem peccatum intravit in mundum &c. in lib. de Perfectione Justitiæ.

Et nugatorium planè est, quod hoc loco respondet Bellarminus, B Virgini Mariæ necessariam fuisse remissionem peccatorum, & Christus ejus

Redemptorem fuisse non negari: sed remissa ei fuisse peccata, non in quæ inciderat, sed in quæ incidisset, nisi gratia DEI per Christi merita, præventa fuisset. Sic nimirum Jesuwitis veteratoriè ludere libet, in re admodum seria. Remissio certè peccatorum ad quocunq; Individuum accommodetur, relatè se habet, tum ad peccatum Originis, tum ad singula atque universa peccata, quæ vel cogitando, vel faciendo, vel dicendo, vel omittendo, vel quovis alio modo commissa fuerunt. Ea verò quæ commissa non sunt, sed committi potuissent, non dicuntur remitti, imò ne quidem remissione indigent. Idem proindè est ac si diceret Jesuwita: Maria Remissione peccatorum opus habuit, quia non peccavit: sed peccare potuit: Quo vix quicquam vel absurdius vel nugatorium magis dici queat: Neque est ut objiciat illud Davidis, Psalm. 85, 13. Eruisti animam meam de inferno inferiori: Et Psalm. 144, 10. Redemisti servum tuum de gladio maligno: Undè tamen non sequatur, Davidem fuisse in inferno inferiore, vel gladio maligno cœsum fuisse. Nam meminisse debebat Jesuwita, phrases istas & modos loquendi non secundum literam accipi posse: sed μεταφορικῶς notare eas calamitates, quibus tum David constringebatur ipso actu, &c.

Sed habet Jesuwita quasdam rationes, quibus sententiæ suæ fucum facere conatur: Ac initiò quidem confugit ad singulare aliquod Privilegium: Omnes inquiens homines, qui per carnalem generationem ex Adamo nascuntur, ex eodem trahunt Originale peccatum, nisi fortè singulari privilegio à communi lege aliquis excipiatur. Statuit proindè, tali singulari privilegio à communi reliquorum hominum censu numeroquè exemptam fuisse Mariam Virginem. Verùm quàm elumbis hæc sit ratio, & quàm pueriliter petat principium: vix puer est, quin intelligat: præsertim cùm vi veritatis adactus Jesuwita, ipse fateri necesse habeat: Singulare istud privilegium Mariæ, neque ex Verbo DEI, neque ex certa Ecclesiæ definitione probari posse. Quid, quod Scriptura fictitium hoc privilegium prorsus negat, asserens, ne quidem inter Sanctos aliquem esse purum: Job. 15, 15.

Cæterùm ne arenâ cedere videatur, sic secundo loco insurgit: Adam fuit typus futuri Christi: Atqui Adam non formatus fuit ex terra maledicta, sed pura adhuc. Ergo Christus quoq; formandus erat ex terra non maledicta, hoc est, ex Matre Virgine, quæ omnis maledictionis, ac per hoc, omnis peccati expers fuerit.

Sed respondeo 1. Committi ἀγνοίαν ἐλέγχη, sive Sophisma vitiosæ comparationis, in applicatione Typi, hoc est, Adami ad Christum: qui sanè Typus latiùs extendi non debet, quàm ipsa Scriptura permittit. Hujus autem doctrinæ propria sedes est, caput 5. ad Romanos, & caput 15. prioris ad Corinthios: Ubi cùm ne unico quidem apice indigitetur isthæc applicatio, quam fingit Jesuwita hoc loco: utique nos eam ceu fictitiam repudiamus.

Deindè si ex hypothesi Jesuitica, Typo cum antitypo omnimoda & nullatenùs deficiens intercedere debeat, harmonia & conformitas, sequetur, Christum ad exemplum Typi, non potuisse, imò ne debuisse quidem ex muliere concipi & nasci: neque etiam jam progenitum paulatim crescere sapientia & statura coram DEO & hominibus: Siquidem tale quid de Adamo affirmari nequit. Atqui hoc absurdum, & Scripturis adversum. Ergo talis etiam harmonia, qualem Jesuita inter Typum & Antitypum extra Scripturas fingit, subsistere nequit. Corrigimus proindè errorem in hunc modum, ut statuamus, congruentiam Typi & Antitypi hoc postulâsse, ut Christus non ex maledicta terra, hoc est, non ex carne peccato polluta conciperetur, id quod nos virtute Altissimi & obumbratione Spiritus sancti factum esse libenter concedimus. Jam verò ex particula illa substantiæ Mariæ purificata, ad totam ejus substantiam, non valet consequentia.

Quæ ipsa nostra responsio dari debet ad subsequentem rationem Bellarmini, petitam ab Eva, quæ Mariæ Typum gesserit: Quid? quòd Eva, non ex commixtione viri & mulieris procreata, privilegii aliquid præ Maria obtinuit.

Tertiò profert loca ex Canticis: Sicut lilium inter spinas, sic amica mea inter filios, Cantic. 2, 1. Et tota pulchra es amica mea, & macula non est in te. Cantic. 4, 7. Et: hortus conclusus, soror mea sponsa, hortus conclusus, fons signatus, ibid. versu 12.

Respondeo 1. Committi ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχɣ. Neq; enim hæc & similia loca quicquam agunt de Maria virgine, sed depingunt statum Ecclesiæ, quâtenùs ea sanctificatur & purgatur lavacro aquæ in verbo: hoc est, imputatur ipsi perfectissima sanctitas & innocentia Christi Servatoris: ut sit gloriosa, non habens maculam aut rugam, aut quicquam ejusmodi: Interprete Apostolo Eph. 5, 26 & 27. Deindè si vel maximè ad Mariam loca illa accommodentur, tamen secundum quid tantùm sunt accipienda: nimirùm partim respectu regenerationis, cujus virtute à Maria, uti à reliquis fidelibus, peccati reatus est sublatus: partim verò respectu singularis sanctificationis, quæ tamen non totam substantiam, sed illam tantùm partem sive massam concernit, ex qua Christi caro concepta & formata fuit. Tandem posito, non verò concesso: Obumbrationis Spiritus sancti virtute totam substantiam Mariæ à Peccato Originis purgatâm fuisse: non tamen indè sequitur, quod intendit Bellarminus, nempè Mariam à conceptione & Nativitate sua expertem fuisse peccati originalis. Quod si verum esset, non utique opus fuisset, peculiari hac sanctificatione Mariæ circa id tempus, quo Christum concipere debuit.

Tandem colligit figuratas quasdam locutiones ex patribus; ut quòd Maria fuerit incorrupta virgo, quòd semper fuerit in luce: & quæ sunt hujus generis alia complures, ex quibus nihil probari posse, quisque facilè intelligit. Unicus ille locus Augustini, qui extat in lib.de Natura & gratia cap. 36. patrocinari errori huic videtur, qui sic habet: Propter honorem Domini de B. Maria, nullam volo habere quæstionem, cùm de peccatis agitur.

Verùm infirma planè est consecutio in argumento Jesuitico: Augustinus non vult habere quæstionem, de B. Virgine Maria, quando de peccatis agitur: Ergo statuit eam à conceptione fuisse expertem peccati originalis. Aliud enim est ἐπέχειν, sive suspendere sententiam: id quod facit Augustinus: aliud verò est, certi quid affirmare: id quod non facit Augustinus: Quin imò si illum ipsum locum accuratiùs expendamus, manifestum est ipsum non fuisse ὁμόψηφον Jesuitis. Nam in immediatè subsequentibus asserit: Mariæ plus gratiæ collatum fuisse, ad vincendum omni ex parte peccatum. Jam verò ubi Gratiâ opus est, ubi peccatum vincendum est, quin peccatum ibi ipso actu sit, quis est qui non videat. Quid? quod Augustinus, lib. 5. contra Julianum cap. 9. disertè scribit: Mariæ corpus ex concupiscentia originali venisse quidem, sed non trajecisse eam in Corpus Christi, quippè quod non inde conceperit.


### Chapter II. Second controversy concerning the breadth and propagation of…: On the Propagation of Original Sin

ON THE PROPAGATION of Original Sin.

Dependent upon the question concerning the complexity and extent of original sin is that other, as it were, subordinate question: How, namely, this sin is propagated, and by the intervention of what organ or medium it occurs, whether of the body or rather of the soul, or indeed of both.

Moreover, theologians, both ancient and more recent, diverge into four principal and diverse opinions concerning this ζήτημα. The first is: that the soul is propagated by traduction; that is, that children receive from their parents, along with their bodies, their souls also: according to that saying of the Philosopher: ἄνθρωπος ἄνθρωπον γεννᾷ: Man begets man: καὶ ὁ καθ' ἕκαστος τὸν τινά: the singular or individual, the singular or individual man: lib.λ. Metaphys. cap. 3.

The second is: that Original Sin is derived into the offspring through that pleasure which parents perceive in cohabiting: just as Augustine discusses this opinion in his book De nuptiis et concupiscentia: and from the Scholastics, Peter Lombard, lib. 2. sent. dist. 31.

The third is that of those who maintain that GOD creates the soul with this vice, for the reason that it is to be the soul of a man already execrated and placed under a curse: just as we see that a canine soul is given to the body of a dog, and an asinine soul to an asinine body, etc.

The fourth and final one is that of those who teach that the soul is not created with sin, but only contracts it when it is already being infused into the body; not otherwise than as generous wine is good in itself, but as soon as it is poured into a vessel of yew, it is converted into poison. And those who hold this opinion, as do most Calvinists today, they establish that the subject of Original sin, regarding propagation, is the flesh, in which it has its seat as if in a root and principle, and from there it flows forth as if from a source to the soul itself also: Which opinion some of the Scholastics also held, contending that the sin of origin is in the body first, and in the soul afterwards, and they accommodate that book of Wisdom very ineptly to this, ch. 8, 19. I was a witty child, and I obtained a good soul: And whereas I was more good, I came to a body undefiled. And ch. 9, 15. The corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the mind that museth upon many things. Which passages, however, do nothing at all to the point. For in the allegation of the former passage a manifest crime of falsehood is committed. For in the Greek sources it is not read, I came to a polluted body: but the contrary is expressly expressed, ἦλθον εἰς σῶμα ἀμίαντον: I came to an undefiled body. Where, however, neither is hinted, either that the soul or that the body, after the fall, is good, pure, or undefiled: But the author means at least this: That there are in the souls of men certain seeds of virtues, which can be excited by good education, so that the body may be preserved and as it were fortified against manifest crimes. Thus the latter passage supports the Scholastics not at all, since it means nothing else than that a corruptible body often hinders even a wise and rightly informed soul, or rather one renewed by the Holy Spirit, from acting wisely and well: while, namely, the affections, which for the most part are wont to imitate the temperament of the body, disturb good and salutary counsels, impede a good purpose, and impel a man to design those things of which he may afterwards repent and be ashamed. Therefore, not only is the body established as the subject of Original sin in this passage: but only this is hinted: that there is occasionally some struggle of the flesh and the Spirit, as long as the affections claim for themselves some dominion over the mind of man.

Moreover, so that it may be clear to us what, in such a great discrepancy and variety of opinions, is to be established concerning the proposed question: that must be observed at the beginning, that it can never be fully or dexterously explained, unless it is first rightly clear to us concerning the origin of the soul. Pelagius once noticed this very thing: and when he saw that both questions labored under sufficiently great difficulty and perplexity: he devoted effort to completely removing, or at least enervating, the propagation of Original sin. For he took it for granted that only the body is begotten by traduction: not likewise the soul of man. Hence he argued thus: Traduction not being granted, no reason can be given by which the soul comes into the society of sin and guilt, without the Justice of GOD laboring. And yet it never labors: for it is not granted by any reason that GOD, who forgives one's own sins, should impute those of another: which is what would happen if the soul, clean in itself, were infected by the contagion of the body. Therefore, there is no guilt of Original sin.

In the progress of time, this question in the Church of the Holy Fathers seemed to be completely inexplicable: so that Gregory the Great did not hesitate to write: This is a grave question and cannot be grasped by man: For if the soul is born with the flesh from the substance of Adam, why does it not also die with the flesh? But if it is not born with the flesh, why is it held bound by sins in that flesh which was brought forth from Adam? Epistle 53. Hence it happened that Augustine also judged that a limit should be set to human curiosity concerning this question, by this otherwise most useful prescribed rule: where a most obscure matter is treated, with no certain and clear documents of the divine scriptures helping, human presumption ought to restrain itself, doing nothing by inclining to the other side, book 2, on the merits of sins, ch. 36. Nor was the doctrine of the Scholastics sounder, who contended that Original sin adheres in the flesh, because the flesh is by traduction: but that the soul, from its conjunction with the flesh, is in those appetites only which are exercised through the organs of the body: but in the higher powers, which are inorganic, the soul is free from Original sin, because it is created by GOD as good, so that it cannot be defiled by the body in those higher powers: just as Lombard discusses at length on this matter, book 2, Sentences, dist. 31. Reading the footsteps of some of the ancient Fathers, who established that new souls are so created for individual men, that as soon as the flesh is formed after conception, finally on the forty-eighth day, the soul is infused by creating, and is created by infusing, and that being so infused it is polluted by the contagion of the flesh: just as Cyprian taught, as Augustine testifies, Sermon 15 to the brothers in the desert. This very dissonance of the Doctors of the Church has caused that in this our own century there are not lacking theologians, easily primary, who have preferred to suspend judgment concerning this very question, rather than to establish anything certain without and beyond the express authority of Scripture. Our blessed Luther certainly, in his disputations, expressly professes that he wishes to affirm nothing publicly about that question, but privately holds the opinion of traduction to himself. Thus that incomparable theologian, Dr. Chemnitz, part 1 of the Loci, page 581, did not shrink from writing: Let it be enough to know concerning the efficient cause, that the first parents by their fall deserved that all their posterity should be procreated such as they themselves were after the fall, both in body and soul: But how the soul contracts that evil, can be ignored without prejudice to the faith: because the Holy Spirit did not wish to make this manifest by certain and clear testimonies of Scripture.

Moreover, if anyone should ask us whether we judge the opinion to be most in agreement with the truth, we answer fearlessly that we support the opinion of the blessed Luther entirely, and that it is consonant with the scriptures: namely, that the human soul is propagated by traduction, so that just as every thing brings forth what is similar to its own species, a lion a lion, a horse a horse: so man also generates a man, and not only the flesh or the body (which cannot be called a man) but the soul of the offspring also is essentially derived from the parents.

Latin:

DE PROPAGATIONE Peccati Originalis.

DEpendet à Quæstione de complexu & Latitudine peccati originalis, illa altera quasi subordinata, Quomodo nimirùm Peccatum hoc propagetur, & cujus organi sive medij interventu illud fiat, corporisnè an animæ potiùs, an verò utriusque.

Cæterùm Theologi tum veteres tum recentiores, in quatuor potissimùm diversas opiniones, circa hoc ζήτημα, abeunt. Prima est: Animam propagari ex traduce; hoc est; liberos à parentibus suis; unà cum corporibus, etiam animas accipere: secundum illud Philosophi: ἄνθρωπος ἄνθρωπον γεννᾷ: Homo Hominem generat: καὶ ὁ καθ' ἕκαστος τὸν τινά: singularis seu individuum, singularem sive individuum hominem: lib.λ. Metaphys.cap.3.

Altera est: Peccatum Originis derivari in sobolem, per illam voluptatem, quam parentes concumbendo percipiunt: quemadmodum de hac sententia disputat Augustinus l.bro de nuptijs & concupiscentia: & ex Scholasticis Petrus Lombardus lib.2.sent.dist.31.

Tertia est eorum, qui statuunt, DEUM creare animam cum hoc vitio, idcò quod futurum sit anima hominis jam execrati, & sub maledictione constituti: Quemadmodum videmus corpori canis dari animam caninam: & corpori asinino, animam asininam &c.

Quarta & postrema est eorum,qui docent; animam non creari cum peccato: sed eam contrahere demùm, illud cùm jam in corpus infunditur; haud secus atque generosum vinum per se bonum est, sed statim ac infunditur in vasculum taxinum, in venenum convertitur. Atque qui hanc sententiam tenent, uti plerique hodiè Calviniani, illi statuunt subjectum peccati Originalis, quoad propagationem, esse carnem, in quâ tanquàm in radice & principio sedem habeat, & indè tanquàm ex fonte ad ipsam quoque animam promanet: Quam sententiam tenuerunt nonnulli etiam ex Scholasticis, contendentes, Peccatum Originis per priùs inesse corpori, per posterius animæ, illudq́; Sapientiæ libri nimiù ineptè huc accommodantes, cap. 8, 19. Puer eram ingeniosus, & fortitus sum animam bonam: Et cùm essem magis bonus, veni ad corpus coinquinatum. Et cap. 9, 15. Corpus quod corrumpitur aggravat animam, & terrena inhabitatio deprimit sensum multùm cogitantem. Quæ tamen loca nihil quicquam ad rem faciunt. Nam in allegatione prioris loci manifestum crimen falsi committitur. Nam in fontibus Græcis non legitur, Veni ad corpus pollutum: sed contrarium disertè exprimitur, ἦλθον εἰς σῶμα ἀμίαντον: veni ad corpus impollutum. Ubi tamen neutrum innuitur, vel quòd anima, vel quòd corpus, post lapsum sit bonum, purum aut impollutum: Sed hoc saltem sibi vult autor: Esse in animis hominum, quædam virtutum semina, quæ bona educatione excitari possint, ut corpus à manifestis sceleribus præservetur quasi & præmuniatur. Sic posterior locus nihil quicquam Patrocinatur Scholasticis, cùm nihil velit aliud, quàm corpus corruptibile etiam animam sapientem & rectè informatam, quin à Spiritu sancto renovatam, sæpe impedire, quo minùs sapienter & benè agat: dùm nimirùm affectus, qui ut plurimùm imitari solent corporis temperamentum, bona & salutaria consilia perturbant, bonum propositum impediunt, & hominem eo impellunt, ut designet ea, quorum postea ipsum pœniteat atque pudeat. Haud proindè solum Corpus peccati Originalis Subjectum hoc loco constituitur: sed illud tantum innuitur: subindè esse luctam aliquam carnis & Spiritus, quamdiu affectus sibi dominium aliquod in mentem hominis vendicant.

Cæterùm ut constare nobis possit, quid in tanta sententiarum discrepantia & varietate, de proposita quæstione sit statuendum: illud initiò observandum fuerit, nunquàm plenè aut dextrè eam explicari posse, nisi priùs de Origine Animæ rectè nobis constet. Animadvertit hoc ipsum olim Pelagius: & cùm videret utramque quæstionem satis magna & difficultate & perplexitate laborare: operam dedit, ut peccati Originalis propagationem prorsùs tolleret, vel saltem enervaret. Pro confesso enim sumsit, Solum corpus gigni ex traduce: non item animam hominis. Hinc sic arguebat: Traduce non concessa, ratio reddi nulla potest, quâ anima in societatem peccati & reatum veniat, quin Justitia DEI laboret. Atqui nunquàm hæc laborat: neq́; enim ulla ratione conceditur, ut DEUS, qui propria peccata remittit, imputet aliena: id quod futurum tùm esset, si anima per se munda, contagio corporis inficeretur. Ergo reatus peccati Originalis nullus est.

Progressu temporis quæstio hæc in Ecclesia S. Patrum visa fuit prorsus esse in explicabilis: ita ut Gregorius M. scribere non dubitaverit: Gravis hæc est quæstio nec valet ab homine comprehendi: Nam si de Adami Substantia, Anima cum carne nascitur, cur non etiam cum carne moritur? Si verò cum carne non nascitur, cur in ea carne, quæ de Adamo prolata est, obligata peccatis tenetur? Epist. 53. Hinc factum, ut Augustinus quoque curiositati humanæ, circa hanc quæstionem modum statuendum esse censeret, hâc aliâs utilissimâ præscriptâ regula: ubi de re obscurissima tractatur, non adjuvantibus certis clarisq; divinarum scripturarum documentis, cohibere se debet humana præsumtio, nihil faciens in partem alteram declinando lib. 2. de peccat. meritis cap. 36. Neque sanior fuit doctrina Scholasticorum, contendentium, Peccatum Originis hærere in carne, quia caro sit ex traduce: Animam verò ex conjunctione cum carne, in illis tantùm appetitionibus, quæ exercentur per organa corporis: in superioribus autem potentijs, quæ sunt inorganica, animam liberam esse à Peccato Originali, quia à DEO creetur utique bona, ut non possit in superioribus illis potentijs à corpore inquinari: quemadmodum pluribus hac de re disputat Lombardus lib. 2. Sent. dist. 31. Veterum nonnullorum Patrum legens vestigia, qui statuerunt, singulis hominibus ita novas creari animas, ut quamprimùm post conceptum caro formata est, quadragesimo octavo demùm die, anima creando infundatur, & infundendo creetur, eaq; sic infusa carnis contagio polluatur: quemadmodum teste Augustino Serm. 15. ad fratres in eremo docuit Cyprianus. Fecit hæc ipsa Doctorum Ecclesiæ dissonantia, ut nostro hoc etiam seculo non desint Theologi facilè primarii, qui circa hanc ipsam quæstionem maluerunt ἐπέχειν, quàm citra & præter expressam Scripturæ autoritatem certi quid statuere. B. certè Lutherus noster in disputationibus disertè profitetur, se publicè nihil velle affirmare de ista quæstione, sed privatim apud se tenere sententiam de traduce. Sic incomparabilis ille Theologus D. Chemnitius part 1. Locorum pag. 581. scribere non exhorruit: Satis sit de causa efficiente scire, primos parentes lapsu suo meritos esse, ut quales ipsi erant post lapsum & corpore & anima, tales procrearentur omnes posteri: Quomodo autem malum illud contrahat anima, salva fide potest ignorari: quia Spiritus sanctus non voluit hoc certis & perspicuis Scripturæ testimonijs patefacere.

Cæterùm si à nobis quis quærat, utrum sententiam veritati maximè consentaneam esse arbitremur, intrepidè respondemus, nos B. Lutheri sententiæ ex asse suffragari, eamque scripturis consonam esse: nimirùm ex traduce animam humanam propagari, ita ut quemadmodum suæ speciei similem, res unaquæque profert, Leo leonem, equus equum: sic homo etiam hominem generet & non caro duntaxat aut Corpus (quod homo dici nequit) sed anima etiam Sobolis essentialiter à parentibus traducatur.


### Chapter II. Second controversy concerning the breadth and propagation of…: Antithesis of the Calvinists

Reasons and arguments, both philosophical and theological, most evidently confirm this thesis of ours. And that we may leave philosophical matters to be examined by philosophers, from the sacred writings there occurs at the beginning that which is read, that GOD rested on the seventh day from all immediate creation, Gen. 2:2, namely such as produces species without natural propagation.

2. That GOD himself implanted the force and power in men, so that man might generate man, and indeed the whole man: by this singular formula of blessing, not only promulgated before the fall: Increase and multiply, Gen. 1:28, but also repeated after the fall, Gen. 8:17 and chap. 9:1.

3. That Scripture specifically ascribes the production of seventy souls to the loins of Jacob, thus not obscurely hinting that souls are not divinely infused immediately, but through the natural generation of parents, Gen. 46:26.

4. That Adam is read to have begotten children not in the image of GOD, but in his own image, Gen. 5:3. Whence I conclude thus: The image of Adam, which in succession had its seat in the image of GOD, not only in the body, but most especially in the soul of Adam. The reason is: Because otherwise there would not be a perfect ἀντίθεσις κάτὰ τὸ ἀὐτὸ καὶ ἐν τῷ ἀὐτῷ: If the image of GOD had had its seat most especially in the soul of Adam, but the image of Adam subsisted only in his body. Therefore, Adam provided the origin not only of bodies but also of souls to his descendants.

5. That this assertion of ours evidently asserts the orthodoxy of this article against any corruptions whatsoever. For as soon as that opinion concerning the new creation of souls is received, immediately this article labors most dangerously. For either the soul, thus newly and immediately founded by God, will be free from sin, or already polluted by sin, or finally it will be defiled by conjunction with the body. The first of these would have to be conceded entirely, unless one wishes to establish GOD as the author of sin. But with this first member standing, the remaining two involve the matter in many absurdities: For as regards the second member, it is not undeservedly asked, Did the soul, before conjunction with the body, exist in the very act as good and devoid of all sin? The affirmative will never be confirmed from the Scriptures: rather, the contrary is clearly evinced from the fact that the image of GOD, or original righteousness, was so lost through the fall of the first parents that it cannot be made a participant of it again except through παλιγγενεσίαν or regeneration. Thus, as regards the third member, if the soul is said to be defiled by conjunction with the body, the righteousness of GOD will again labor, since he is the author of that conjunction. What? And that this will necessarily follow: that original sin adheres only to those powers of the soul which are organic and have a dependency on the body, or which communicate immediately with the body. Since all these things are more absurd than the most absurd, indeed are contradictorily opposed to the Holy Scriptures, our opinion, which affirms that the origin of the soul is by traducianism, certainly prevails among all the pious.

The Calvinists and others are in an uproar at this point, heaping up a great number of testimonies of the Scriptures which assert that the spirit of man is given and created by God. But a manifold ignorance of the point at issue is committed. For 1. It is not denied by us that the soul is also given by God, even if it is generated by traducianism; since those things which are produced mediately by God are most correctly assigned to him as the first and universal cause. But this is asked: Does GOD immediately create new souls from time to time and infuse them into the brute corporeal mass in the mother's womb? That which cannot be elicited by any reason at all from all those testimonies of the Scriptures. 2. This collection is clearly weak: GOD is read in the Scriptures to give the spirit to men: Therefore the human spirit is not by traducianism. For by equal logic I can subsume concerning the human body also: The human body is read in the Scriptures to be given by GOD: Therefore the human body is not by traducianism. The antecedent is clear from that of Job, chap. 10:8. and following. Thy hands have made me and fashioned me altogether round about: Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as clay: Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh: and hast fenced me with bones and sinews, thou hast granted me life, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit.

But they also rise up against us with certain reasons, of which the chief are two. For first they ask, How can the propagation of the soul by traducianism happen without the division or diminution of the souls of the parents? Truly, this knot is most correctly solved by the analogy of light from light, kindled without any division or diminution. For in the seed of the parents, something divine lies hidden τῇ δυνάμει, which by the benefit of the πλαστικῆς δυνάμεως is excited and kindled: not otherwise than fire lies hidden in flint, which is elicited by the friction and striking of iron. Wherefore, as body from body, so the soul is propagated from the soul, as light kindled from light.

Then they object that there cannot be a multiplication of spirits. But it is answered that this is true of spirits considered absolutely and in themselves, but not of spirits coupled or bound with bodies. For that a multiplication of these can exist, even that proves: Increase and multiply.

The question concerning the origin of the soul being settled in this manner, it is spontaneously revealed, 1. what can and ought to be answered to that former question concerning the propagation of sin: namely, that it happens through natural generation, not with only one essential part of man, but with the whole man begetting the whole: so that as soon as man begins to be by means of this natural generation, just so immediately also does the propagation of this sin occur: and Scripture also hints at this quite clearly when it refers the origin of this contagion to the very moment of conception, Psalm 51:7.

Since this purer thesis of ours stands, it is spontaneously evident what must be answered to that insolent sophism by which some attempt to prove the contrary, nay, they strive to deny the propagation of sin entirely, arguing thus: If there be a propagation of sin, it happens either by reason of the body or of the soul. But it happens in respect of neither. Therefore, in no way at all. That it does not happen according to the body is evident from the fact that the body is a brute thing: That the propagation does not happen on the part of the soul is clear from the fact that it would follow that the soul is created evil by GOD. For it is most solidly answered that in this argument the τὸ ἐλλιπὲς τῆς διαιρέσεως (deficiency of the division) is committed. For a third is given, namely, that the propagation of sin happens by reason of both Essential parts, through the medium of the natural generation of the whole man. Furthermore, the argument also labors under a false hypothesis, as if the soul, created by God, were infused from without: which the analogy of faith does not suffer.

Furthermore, it is clear from this what is to be established as the subject of this original evil: not, to be sure, the Body alone: not the Soul alone: but the whole Man, by reason of both Essential parts, as much of the Soul as of the Body: and of the Soul indeed, considered as much in respect of the higher and nobler powers as in respect of the lower. Holy Scripture confirms this thesis of ours wonderfully, not only in general, asserting the whole man to be the subject of sin and in need of the benefit of Regeneration: 1 Cor. 2:14, The natural man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of GOD: Rom. 6:6, Gal. 5:24, The old man with his lusts is to be crucified: John 3:6, Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh: But also explaining the matter by parts, in particular it constitutes both the Mind and Intellect, and the heart or will, and the body of man as the subject of sin. The Mind indeed or Intellect, Ephes. 4:18, having the intellect darkened by darkness. 2 Corinth. 3:5, We are not sufficient to think anything good of ourselves as from ourselves.

The heart indeed or the will, Gen. 6:5 & 8:21, Every figment of the heart is only Evil from his youth.

The body finally, Rom. 8:6, The wisdom of the flesh is enmity against GOD. Rom. 7:18, In my flesh dwells no good. Rom. 6:6, Our old Man is crucified together, that the body of sin might be destroyed.

Latin:

Rationes & argumenta tum Philosophica tum Theologica Thesin hanc nostram evidentissime confirmant. Et ut Philosophica Philosophis excutienda relinquamus, ex sacris initio occurrit illud, quod DEUS legitur quievisse die septimo, ab omni immediata creatione, Genes. 2, 2. tali nimirum, quæ citra naturalem propagationem species producat.

2. Quod DEUS ipse vim atq; potentiam hominibus indidit, ut Homo hominem, & quidem totum generaret: singulari hac Benedictionis formula non modo ante lapsum promulgata: Crescite & multiplicamini, Genes. 1, 2, 8. sed & post lapsum repetita. Genes. 8, 17. & cap. 9, 1.

3. Quod Scriptura in specie Animarum septuaginta productionem fæmoribus Jacobi adscribit, sic haud obscure innuens, Animas non divinitus immediate infundi, sed naturali parentum mediante generatione, Genes. 46, 26.

4. Quod Adam legitur genuisse liberos non ad DEI, sed ad suam Imaginem, Genes 5, 3. Unde sic colligo: Imago Adami, quæ successu Imagini DEI sedem suam habuit non in corpore tantum, sed potissimum in Anima Adami. Ratio est: Quia alias non perfecta esset ἀντίθεσις κάτὰ τὸ ἀὐτὸ καὶ ἐν τῷ ἀὐτῷ: Si Imago DEI sedem habuisset in Adami anima potissimum: Imago autem Adami tantum in corpore ipsius subsisteret. Ergo Adamus non solum corporum, sed & animarum originem posteris præbuit.

5. Quod hæc nostra assertio, ὀρθοδοξίαν Articuli hujus contra quasvis corruptelas evidenter asserit. Quamprimum enim opinio illa de nova creatione animarum recipitur: statim Articulus iste periculosissime laborat. Aut enim Anima, sic a Deo nova & immediate condita, libera erit a peccato: aut peccato jam polluta: aut demum ex conjunctione cum corpore inquinabitur. Primum illud omnino concedendum foret, nisi quis DEUM peccati autorem statuere velit. Sed stante hoc primo membro, reliqua duo multis absurditatibus rem implicant: Nam quoad alterum membrum, haud immerito quæritur, Anne anima ante conjunctionem cum corpore, ipso actu extiterit bona, & peccati omnis expers? Affirmativa ex Scripturis nunquam confirmabitur: quin contrarium vel inde luculenter evincitur, quod videlicet Imago DEI sive Justitia Originalis ita per lapsum primorum parentum est amissa, ut non nisi per παλιγγενεσίαν sive Regenerationem, illius denuo possit reddi particeps. Sic quoad Tertium membrum, si Anima ex conjunctione cum corpore inquinari dicatur, DEI rursus Justitia laborabit, quippe qui conjunctionis istius autor est: Quid? quod & illud necessario consequetur, Peccatum Originis in illis duntaxat animæ potentiis hærere, quæ sunt organicæ, & dependentiam habent ad corpus, sive quæ corpori immediate communicant. Quæ omnia cum sint absurdissimis abfurdiora, imo Scripturis Sacris ἀντιφατικῶς opposita: utique apud pios omnes nostra præponderat sententia, quæ Animæ originem ex traduce esse affirmat.

Tumultuantur hoc loco Calviniani & alii, magno numero coacervantes Scripturarum testimonia, quæ asserunt Spiritum Hominis à Deo dari & creari. Sed multiplex committitur Ignoratio Elenchi. Nam 1. à nobis non negatur, Animam dari etiam à Deo licet illa ex traduce generetur: siquidem quæ mediatè à Deo producuntur, rectissimè ipsi tanquàm causæ primæ & Universali assignantur. Sed hoc quæritur: An DEUS immediatè novas subindè creet animas, & illas brutæ massæ corporeæ in utero matris infundat? id quod ex universis illis Scripturarum testimoniis nullâ prorsus ratione elici potest. 2. Infirma planè est hæc collectio, DEUS in scripturis legitur dare Spiritum Hominibus: Ergo Spiritus humanus non est ex traduce. Nam pari Logicâ de corpore quoque humano subsumere possum: Corpus humanum legitur in Scripturis DEUS dare: Ergo corpus humanum non est ex traduce. Antecedens patet ex illo Jobi cap. 10, 8. & seqq. Manus tuæ fecerunt me, & plasmaverunt me totum in circuitu: Memento quæso, quod sicut lutum feceris me: Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me, & sicut caseum me coagulasti? Pelle & carnibus vestisti me: ossibus & nervis compegisti me, vitam tribuisti mihi, & visitatio tua custodivit Spiritum meum.

Sed & rationibus quibusdam adversum nos insurgunt: quarum præcipuæ sunt duæ. Primùm enim quærunt, Quomodo propagatio animæ ex traduce, sine decisione aut diminutione animæ parentum fieri possit? Verùm nodus iste similitudine luminis de lumine, sine ulla decisione aut diminutione accensi, rectissimè solvitur. In semine enim parentum, divinum quiddam latet τῇ δυνάμει, quod beneficio πλαστικῆς δυνάμεως excitatur & accenditur: haud secus atque in silice latet ignis, qui ferri attritu & percussione elicitur. Quapropter uti corpus à corpore, sic anima propagatur ab anima, tanquàm lumen à lumine accensa.

Deindè objiciunt, quòd Spirituum non possit dari Multiplicatio. Sed respondetur, verum hoc esse de spiritibus absolutè & per se consideratis: non verò de Spiritibus cum corporibus copulatis sive devinctis. Horum enim multiplicationem dari posse, vel illud evincit: Crescite & multiplicamini.

Expedita in hunc modum quæstione de Origine animæ, ultrò patescit, 1. quid ad priorem illam, de propagatione peccati quæstionem responderi possit ac debeat: nempè fieri illam per naturalem generationem, non unâ tantùm Essentiali hominis parte, sed toto homine gignente totum: ità ut quamprimùm Homo mediante hac naturali generatione incipit esse, tam statim etiam fiat Peccati hujus propagatio: idque satis luculenter etiam innuit Scriptura, quando ortum contagii hujus refert ad ipsum primitus conceptionis momentum, Psal. 51, 7.

Stante puriore hac thesi nostra ultrò patescit, quid respondendum sit ad insolens illud Sophisma, quo nonnulli diversum evincere imò peccati propagationem prorsus negare student, sic argumentati: Si sit propagatio peccati, ea aut fit ratione corporis, aut animæ, Atqui neutrius respectu fit. Ergo nullo planè modò. Quòd secundum corpus non fiat, indè constat, quia corpus est res bruta: Quòd ex parte animæ non fiat propagatio, indè liquet, quia sic sequeretur, animam à DEO creari malam.
