Solidissimè enim respondetur, in argumento hoc committi τὸ ἐλλιπὲς τῆς διαιρέσεως. Datur enim tertium, nimirùm, quòd propagatio peccati fiat ratione utriusque partis Essentialis, mediante naturali generatione totius hominis. Deindè laborat etiam argumentum falsa hypothesi, quasi anima à Deo creata, forinsecùs infundatur: id quod analogia fidei non patitur.

Deindè patet hinc, quodnám sit constituendum subjectum mali hujus originalis: non videlicet Corpus solùm: non Anima sola: sed totus Homo, ratione utriusque partis Essentialis, tàm Animæ, quàm Corporis: & Animæ quidem, tàm respectu superiorum nobiliorumq; potentiarum, quàm respectu inferiorum consideratæ. Mirificè thesin hanc nostram confirmat Scriptura Sacra, non modo in genere, Totum hominem peccati subjectum, & Regenerationis beneficio egentem asserens: 1. Cor. 2, 14. Animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus DEI: Roman. 6, 6. Gal. 5, 24. Vetus homo cum concupiscentijs suis est crucifigendus: Johan. 3, 6. Quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est: Verùm etiam rem per partes explicans, in specie tùm Mentem & Intellectum; tùm cor sive voluntatem, tùm corpus hominis peccati subjectum constituit. Mentem quidem sive Intellectum Ephes. 4, 18. tenebris habentes obscuratum intellectum. 2. Corinth. 3, 5. Non sumus idonei vel cogitare aliquid boni ex nobis ipsis tanquam ex nobis.

Cor verò sive voluntatem Genes. 6, 5. & 8, 21. Omne figmentum cordis tantùm Malum est à Juventute suâ.

Corpus denique, Rom. 8, 6. Sapientia carnis est inimicitia adversus DEUM. Rom. 7, 18. In carne mea non habitat bonum. Rom. 6, 6. Vetus Homo noster simul crucifixus est, ut destruatur corpus peccati.


### Chapter II. Second controversy concerning the breadth and propagation of…: The Second Part. Antithetical

The Second Part. Antithetical.

Against this purer doctrine of our churches, both the Manichaeans and the Pelagians have long since raised a dispute: but in this our age, the Romanists, who strive to bring back the heresy of the Pelagians, if not entirely, certainly in half, onto the stage of the Church even today.

And that we may say something about each, the Manichaeans at first denied all propagation of Original sin, positing that sin is not contracted from carnal generation: but is the work of GOD creating and forming sin itself in man. Which error is too foul and atrocious to be refuted at length, especially since it was expressly disputed in the previous article, concerning the Cause of sin. But then the Pelagians contended that the descendants of Adam were indeed infected with sin: but not through the medium of the propagation of carnal generation: but only by example, imitation, and occasion. Which heresy indeed undermines a great, nay, the primary part of the Christian Religion: but especially it is an enemy of the Grace of GOD, as Augustine speaks in his treatise on heresies, chapter 88.

However, as foul as that is, the Roman Pseudo-Catholic Church has nevertheless made it its own in great part, which writes explicitly that, with Original Justice lost, the Naturals in man nevertheless remained Integral: Likewise, that the fuel of sin as a morbid quality adheres only in the flesh, which inclines the sensitive appetite, and through it, inclines the will also to lower things: Nay, that this fuel of sin adheres so only in the sensitive appetite, that the higher part of reason is entirely immune, free, and integral from all depravity, unless perhaps it is inclined a little from elsewhere to lower things: as can be seen in the writings of Albert Pighius, Ambrosius Catharinus, Andradius, and others, whom Chemnitius cites in the Examination of the Council of Trent, part 1, title concerning Original sin, page 88 and following.

Bellarmino the Jesuit, fearing for himself because of the impiety of this dogma, wished to move nothing in his own disputations concerning the total and by far most atrocious corruption of the whole of human nature: meanwhile, revealing the sentiments of his mind not obscurely, writing thus in book 6 de amiss. grat. & statu pecc. chapter 16, page 501, A. & B.: The sectarians of our time wish there to be three other effects of Original sin, which Catholics do not acknowledge. One is the loss of Free will: Another is such a corruption of nature that a man, even when Justified, cannot but always sin. The third is to hate GOD, to flee the Judgment of GOD, to doubt the promises of GOD, &c. Since the Roman Church, as Bellarmino admits, does not acknowledge these effects of original sin, it is easily evident even from this how far it is from the heresy of the Pelagians.

Moreover, the arguments by which the ancient and more recent Pelagians strive to put a gloss upon their heresy are these principal ones.

1. From the Old Testament there was that passage, Ezek. 18. 4. & 20. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. Now truly, if parents transmitted sin to their children through carnal generation, the Son would certainly bear the iniquity of the Father. Therefore, whatever is proposed concerning the propagation of sin must be false and erroneous.

I answer: The argument fails by the fallacy παρὰ τὴν ἀγνοιαν ἐλέγχε. For the Prophet in that place wishes to counter the complaints of the Jews, who thought that they, as Holy and Just men, were being punished by GOD solely on account of the transgressions of their parents: as is evident from their own outcries, verse 2: Our fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge: by which manner of speaking they were surely calling the Justice of GOD into doubt not obscurely.

Latin:

Pars Altera. Ἀντιθετικὴ.

PUriori huic Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctrinæ litem jam olim intenderunt tùm Manichæi, tùm Pelagiani: Nostro verò hoc seculo, Romanenses, qui Pelagianorum hæresin, si non ex asse, certè ex semisse, in proscenium Ecclesiæ hodieq; revocare student.

Et ut de singulis aliquid dicamus, Manichæi initiò Omnem peccati Originalis propagationem negabant, statuentes, Peccatum non contrahi ex generatione carnali: sed esse opus DEI creantis & formantis ipsum peccatum in homine. Qui error fædior & atrocior est, quàm ut pluribus sit refutandus, præsertim cùm de eo ex professo sit disputatum in superiore articulo, de Causa peccati. Deindè verò Pelagiani contenderunt, posteros Adami infectos esse quidem peccato: sed non mediante propagatione generationis carnalis: sed tantùm exemplo, imitatione & occasione. Quæ sanè hæresis magnam, imò primariam Religionis Christianæ partem subruit: præcipuè verò Gratiæ D E I inimica est, uti loquitur Augustinus tractatu de hæresibus, cap. 88.

Cæterùm quantumvis fœda ea sit, magna tamen ex parte suam illam fecit Romana PseudoCatholica Ecclesia, quæ disertè scriptitat, amissâ Justitiâ Originali, Naturalia in homine nihilominus mansisse Integra: Item, Fomitem peccati tanquàm morbidam qualitatem hærere tantùm in carne, quæ inclinet appetitum sensitivum, & mediante eo, voluntatem etiam inclinet ad inferiora: Quin Fomitem hunc peccati ita tantùm in appetitu sensitivo hærere, ut superior pars rationis ab omni depravatione planè sit immunis, libera & integra, nisi fortè aliundè paululùm inclinetur ad inferiora: quemadmodum videre est in scriptis, Alberti Pighij, Ambrosij Catharini, Andradij & aliorum, quos citat Chemnitius in Exam. Concilij Tridentini part. 1. tit. de peccat. Orig. pag. 88. & seqq.

Bellarminus Jesuita ab impietate dogmatis hujus sibi metuens, nihil suis in disputationibus, de omnimodâ & longè atrocissima totius Naturæ humanæ corruptione movere voluit: Interim haud obscurè sensa animi prodens, sic scribens lib. 6. de amiss. grat. & statu pecc. cap. 16. pag. 501. A. & B. Sectarij nostri temporis tres alios effectus peccati Originalis esse volunt, quos Catholici non agnoscunt. Unus est amissio Liberi arbitrij: Alter tanta naturæ corruptio, ut non possit homo etiam Justificatus, non semper peccare. Tertius est, odisse DEUM, fugere Judicium DEI, dubitare de promifsionibus DEI, &c. Hos certè effectus peccati originalis, cùm Romana Ecclesia, fatente Bellarmino, non agnoscat, facilè vel indè patet, quàm procul ea absit à Pelagianorum hæresi.

Cæterùm argumenta, quibus veteres & recentiores Pelagiani hæresi fucum facere student, præcipua sunt isthæc.

1. Ex Vetere Testamento erat illud, Jezech. 18. 4. & 20. Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. Jam verò, si per carnalem generationem parentes transmitterent peccatum in liberos, utique Filius portaret iniquitatem Patris. Ergo falsum & erroneum fuerit, quicquid de propagatione peccati proponitur.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate παρὰ τὴν ἀγνοιαν ἐλέγχε. Propheta enim eo loci vult occurrere querelis Judæorum, opinantium se tanquàm Sanctos & Justos à D E O puniri duntaxat propter transgressiones parentum: uti patet ex ipsorum clamoribus, versu 2. Patres nostri comederunt uvam acerbam, & dentes filiorum obstupuerunt: Quo sanè pacto Justitiam D E I haud obscurè in dubium vocabant.


### Chapter II. Second controversy concerning the breadth and propagation of…: Of Sin

Of Sin

The Prophet therefore answers that the judgments of God are most just, and that He punishes none but those who have sinned themselves. This prophetic scope being well observed, it is clearly evident that he speaks of sins, as they call them, personal or pertaining to some one individual: not indeed of the sin of the whole species, or regarding the whole species: such as is the sin of Adam, who represented the whole species, that is, the whole human race: so that, just as his justice would have been our justice also, if he had persisted in integrity: so after he fell into sin, his sin indeed drew us all into both the fellowship and the guilt of sin: according to that, Rom. 5:12, by one man sin entered into the world, and passed through unto all. Furthermore, the argument fails by the fallacy ἀπὸ τῶ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father: if, namely, he himself has been innocent. Which condition the Prophet himself clearly explains, in the cited chapter, verse 14 and following: But if a father has begotten a son, who seeing all the sins of his father, fears, and does not do like them: he shall not die in the iniquity of his father: but he shall surely live, etc.

The Pelagians took another argument from chapter 5:19 of Romans: By the disobedience of one, many were made sinners. For if sin were propagated by means of carnal generation, the Apostle would surely not have said, Many, but, All. Now, however, because he says, Many, he wished to imply that only those were made sinners who, having imitated the example of Adam, also did evil themselves.

I answer that a fallacy of phrase is committed. For in the Hebrew phrase, by Many, all are to be understood, provided the nature of the subject admits a universal predication. Just as it is taken in this very sense, Daniel 12:2, Matthew 20:16 and 22:14. Now, however, that the nature of the subject, which is treated in this place, admits an indeterminate universality of predication, the preceding verse 12 clearly proves: Where the Apostle expresses the breadth of sin first collectively, by the word World: then distributively, by the universal particle All, explicitly: As, he says, by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; so death passed into all men, in whom all have sinned. Which same thing is also proven from the immediately preceding verse 18: As by the offense of one (namely, the transition was made) into all men to condemnation.

Furthermore, Pelagius most viciously refers the word of sinning to actual sin, so that he may prove that Adam harmed only by example, and maintains that corruption is only from the imitation of sin. But the end and scope of the Apostle protests against this, who considers the sin of Adam in this place, not insofar as it was terminated in the person of one Adam: but insofar as he sustained the nature of the whole human race: implying this especially, since the sin of Adam was not so much personal as it was in a way natural, therefore also the guilt of one sin flowed into all.

Finally, for this reason the Apostle wished to use the particle Many, because in truth there are many who are born from Adam. For some things can be all, which nevertheless are not many, as the Gospels are all four, but not many: as Augustine not ineptly answered Pelagius long ago in book 6 against Julian, chapter 12.

They borrowed a third argument from the same place, Rom. 5:12: By one man sin entered into the world. For if sin had entered into the world by carnal generation, the Apostle would not have said, by one man, but by two men. For generation requires two.

In dissolving this objection, the Fathers labored quite anxiously. Ambrose understands Eve by one man, to whom the name Adam also applies in a general sense: since the Hebrew word Adam signifies man: thinking that in this way he would reconcile Scripture, which has that the beginning of sin was made by a woman, and that through her all are subject to death; Ecclesiasticus 25:33. Likewise, that Adam was not seduced: but the woman was seduced in sin. 1 Timothy 2:14. Origen, however, understands the man by one man, because succession is attributed to him in the Scriptures. Augustine seems to incline toward a third opinion, and to understand both protoplasts, indeed as one flesh. But if we consult the scriptures, it is manifest that Adam is most correctly understood by one man in this place: which is proven by that comparison which the Apostle weaves throughout this whole chapter. Nor does it stand in the way that Eve sinned first, and seems to be the more potent cause of every evil. For because the primacy of generation rests with the man, the propagation of sin is surely attributed to Adam rather as the man, and not to Eve. In which respect the Apostle wished to name not two, but one man.

Fourthly, they argue thus: It is not necessary that accidents be propagated from parents to descendants. But sin in the first parents was an accident. Therefore, it is not necessary that sin be propagated to all descendants.

I respond to the major premise by a distinction: for some accidents belong to the whole species and to every member, but others belong only to certain individuals. The former must necessarily be propagated to all individuals, provided that the species itself is to be propagated; but the latter, indeed, not so. Now, regarding the minor premise: sin was indeed an accident in the first parents, but such a one that it belonged to the whole species, because it is the privation of that Original Justice which was to be propagated to the whole species of the human race: wherefore Original Sin is propagated to that same whole species.

The fifth argument was such: The children of pious parents are holy. 1 Cor. 7:14. Therefore, the sin of Origin is not propagated to them through carnal generation. I answer: The argument fails by the fallacy of Ignoratio Elenchi. For the Apostle is not dealing with Ecclesiastical or spiritual holiness: but only with political holiness, which even those children have who are born from one infidel parent: since the disparity of religion is no obstacle to the children born from such a marriage being considered legitimate, because a legitimate marriage is contracted not only among Christians: but also among Gentiles: so that the children of these are by no means considered spurious. Then a sophistry is committed ἀπὸ τῶν τὶ καὶ ἁπλῶς [from what is in a certain respect to what is simply]. For the major premise, which was omitted, ought to have been such: Whoever are holy, they are not subject to sin. Which proposition is indeed true, secundum quid [in a certain respect]: if, namely, you understand it of the Formal, that is, the guilt of sin: but it is false, if you take it ἁπλῶς [simply] also concerning the Material of sin. Now if you subjoin the Minor, it is most rightly denied. For the children of holy parents are not spiritually holy: but by nature they are children of wrath, Eph. 2:3. They are flesh, since they are born of flesh, John 3:6, and therefore are most infected by sin. But since the Calvinists are also accustomed to fight with this very argument for the holiness of infants born of faithful parents, with which they are endowed even before the reception of Baptism: it will perhaps not be irrelevant to observe in a few words that explanation of this passage which Wolfg. Musculus, himself a Calvinist, dissenting from his own in this part, produced on page 204 of his commentary on the first to the Corinthians. I once abused, he says, the present passage against the error of the Anabaptists, thinking that (But now they are holy) meant the same as, they are of the people of God, because of the faithful parent. But the present passage contributes nothing to this cause, in which the subject is not the holiness of the covenant and the people of God, but the purity of a legitimate marriage, even of infidels. For holiness is ascribed not only to children, to whom perhaps the holiness of a faithful parent might so pertain that they are participants of the covenant of God because of it: but also to infidel husbands and wives, even though they oppose the faith of Christ. Nor is there any other holiness and purity of children being discussed than that which also belongs to infidel parents. But to them belongs no other than that which is from a legitimate marriage.

Sixthly, they reasoned thus: The procreation of like comes from like: But Adam was received into grace, and in grace he propagated children: Therefore he procreated those like himself, without the propagation of sin.

But I answer that a sophistry is committed from a statement in a certain respect to a statement simply. For the major premise is true concerning carnal propagation. But the minor is simply false, if it is taken in such a way that Adam propagated the Grace, into which he had been received after the fall, into his children.

For Adam, as Scripture testifies, however much he was reborn, did not procreate children to that image of God which had already begun to be restored in him: but to HIS OWN image. And that rule of Antiquity is universally true: Parents procreate children not according to that from which they are reborn: but from which they are flesh.

Seventhly, they inferred thus: What parents do not have, that they cannot propagate into their children. But Christian or faithful parents do not have damning sin. Therefore, they cannot propagate into their children such sin as is said to be original sin.

I answer, an error is committed secundum quid [in a certain respect]. For the major premise is true if it is understood of that which parents have, neither by grace nor by Nature. Now, as for the Minor, it is most false that Christian and faithful parents do not have damning sin by Nature. For that sin is not imputed to them, that does not depend on their nature, but on the benefit of Christ. Therefore, this argument is more rightly inverted in this manner: Whatever Christian and faithful parents have by Nature: that they propagate into their children. But however much they are Christian and faithful, they nevertheless have original sin by Nature: For this is remitted to them, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not imputed, as Augustine speaks. Therefore.

Latin:

Peccati O

Respondet ergo Propheta, judicia Dei esse justissima, & non nisi eos ipsum punire, qui ipsimet peccaverunt. Scopo hoc prophetico probè observato, luculenter patet, ipsum loqui de peccatis, uti vocant, personalibus sive pertinentibus ad unum aliquod individuum: non verò de peccato totius speciei, sive spectante totam speciem: Quale peccatum est Adami, qui totam speciem, hoc est, totum genus humanum repræsentabat: ita ut, quemadmodum justitia ipsius, nostra etiam fuisset justitia, si in integritate perstitisset: Ita postquàm in peccatum prolapsus est, utique ipsius peccatum, nos omnes tùm in societatem, tùm in reatum peccati pertraxit: secundum illud, Rom. 5, 12. per unum Hominem peccatum intravit in Mundum, & pertransijt in omnes. Deindè fallit argumentum Sophismate ἀπὸ τῶ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Filius enim non portabit iniquitatem patris: si videlicet ipse fuerit innocens. Quam conditionem Propheta ipse luculenter explicat, citato capite, versu 14. & seqq.: Quod si pater genuerit Filium, qui videns omnia peccata patris sui, & timuerit, ac non fecerit simile eis: hic non morietur in iniquitate patris sui: sed vita vivet &c.

Alterum argumentum sumebant Pelagiani ex cap. 5, 19. Rom. Per unius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi. Si enim carnali generatione mediante peccatum propagaretur, utique non dixisset Apostolus, Multi, sed, Omnes. Jam verò quia dicit, Multi, innuere voluit, eos duntaxat peccatores constitui, qui exemplum Adami imitati, ipsi quoque malè egerunt.

Respondeo committi Sophisma phraseωs. Hebræa enim phrasi, per Multos, intelligendi sunt omnes, siquidem Subjecti natura universalem prædicationem admittit. Sicut hoc ipso sensu sumitur, Daniel. 12, 2. Matth. 20, 16. & 22, 14. Jam verò Naturam Subjecti, de quo hoc loco agitur, indeterminatam universalitatem prædicationis admittere, versus præcedens 12. luculenter evincit: Ubi Apostolus latitudinem peccati initiò collectivè, per vocabulum Mundi: mox distributivè, per particulam universalem Omnes, disertè exprimit: Sicut, inquiens, per unum hominem peccatum intravit in mundum, & per peccatum mors; ita in Omnes homines mors transijt, in quo Omnes peccaverunt. Quod ipsum evincitur etiam ex versu immediatè præcedente 18. Sicut per unius delictum (scilicet transitus factus est) in Omnes homines ad condemnationem.

Deindè vitiosissimè Pelagius verbum peccandi ad actuale peccatum refert, ut exemplo tantùm Adamum nocuisse evincat, & corruptionem tantùm ex imitatione peccati esse obtineat. Sed reclamat finis & scopus Apostoli, qui Adami peccatum hoc loco considerat, non quatenùs in unius Adami persona terminabatur: sed quatenus ipse Naturam universi generis humani sustinuit: hoc potissimùm innuens, cùm Peccatum Adami non tàm personale, quàm Naturale quodammodo fuerit, ideò etiam unius peccati reatum in omnes dimanasse.

Tandem ideò D. Apostolus uti voluit particula Multi, quia revera multi sunt, qui nascuntur ex Adamo. Possunt enim aliqua esse omnia, quæ tamen non sunt multa, ut Evangelia quatuor sunt omnia, non verò multa: uti haud ineptè jam olim respondit Pelagio Augustinus lib. 6. cont. Julian. cap. 12.

Tertium argumentum mutuabantur ex eodem loco Rom. 5, 12. Per Vnum hominem peccatum in mundum intravit. Si enim peccatum intrasset in mundum, per Generationem carnalem, non dixisset Apostolus, per Vnum hominem, sed per duos homines. Generatio enim duos requirit.

In dissolvenda hac objectione Patres satis anxiè desudarunt. Ambrosius per unum Hominem Evam intelligit, cui sub sensu generali nomen Adam etiam competat: Siquidem vox Hæbrea Adam Hominem significet: existimans, se hoc pacto Scripturam conciliaturum, quæ habet, A muliere initium factum esse peccati, & per illam omnes mori subjocere: Ecclesiastici 25, 33. Item, Adamum non fuisse seductum: mulierem autem in peccato seductam fuisse. 1. Timoth. 2, 14. Origenes verò per unum Hominem Virum intelligit, quia huic in Scripturis tribuitur successio. Augustinus in tertiam inclinare videtur sententiam, & utrumque protoplastum, quippè unam carnem intelligere. Sed si seripturas consulamus, manifestum est, per Unum hominem rectissimè hoc loco Adamum intelligi: id quod evincit σύγκρισις illa, quam toto hoc capite Apostolus pertexit. Neque obstat, quòd Heva initiò peccavit, & potior videtur esse causa omnis mali. Quia enim penes virum est principatus generationis, utique Adamo potiùs tanquàm viro, non verò Hevæ tribuitur peccati propagatio. Quo respectu non duos etiam, sed unum Hominem nominare voluit Apostolus.

Quartò sic arguunt: Non necesse est, accidentia propagari ex parentibus in posteros. Peccatum autem in primis parentibus fuit accidens. Ergo non est necesse peccatum propagari in omnes posteros.

Respondeo ad Majorem per distinctionem: Quædam enim accidentia competunt toti speciei & omni: quædam verò quibusdam duntaxat Individuis. Priora illa necesse est Propagari ad omnia Individua; dummodò ipsa species propagari debeat: posteriora verò hæc non item. Jam quoad Minorem, Fuit quidem peccatum in primis parentibus Accidens, sed tale, quod competebat toti speciei, quia est privatio illius Justitiæ Originalis, quæ propaganda erat in totam speciem generis humani: Quare Peccatum Originale propagatur in eandem totam speciem.

Quintum argumentum tale erat: Liberi piorum parentum sancti. 1. Cor. 7, 14. Ergo peccatum Originis ex carnali generatione in ipsos non est propagatum. Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate Ignorationis Elenchi. Neque enim de sanctitate Ecclesiastica sive spirituali agit Apostolus: sed tantum de Sanctitate politica quam habent illi etiam Liberi, qui ex altero infideli parente sunt prognati: Si quidem non obstat Religionis disparitas, quo minus Liberi, ex tali conjugio nati, pro legitimis censeantur, propterea quod conjugium legitimum contrahitur non tantum inter Christianos: sed & inter Gentiles: ita ut istorum liberi pro spuriis minime censeantur. Deinde committitur Sophisticatio ἀπὸ τῶν τὶ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Major enim quæ omissa est, talis esse debebat: Quicunque sancti sunt, illi peccato non sunt obnoxij. Quæ sanè propositio vera est, secundum quid: si ninirùm Formale, hoc est, reatum peccati intel ligas: falsa vero, si ἁπλῶς etiam de Materiali peccati eam accipias. Jam si Minorem subijcias, rectissime ea negatur. Neque enim Liberi Sanctorum parentum spiritualiter sunt Sancti: sed naturâ sunt Filii iræ, Eph. 2, 3. Sunt caro, quippè ex carne nati, Joh. 3, 6. ac proinde peccato vel maximè infecti. Cæterum cum hoc ipso argumento Calviniani etiam pugnare soleant, pro sanctitate infantium ex fidelibus parentibus progenitorum, qua etiam ante Baptismi perceptionem sint præditi: haud fortè abs re fuerit, paucis observare eam loci hujus explicationem, quam VVolfg. Musculus, & ipse Calvinista, hac in parte à suis dissidens, prodidit pag 204. commentarij in priorem ad Corinth. Abusus sum, inquit, aliquando præsenti loco contra errorem Anabaptistarum, putans illud (Nunc autem sancti sunt) idem esse, atque, de populo Dei sunt, propter fidelem parentem. Verùm ad hanc causam præsens locus nihil facit, in quo non de fœderis, & populi Dei sanctimonia, sed de conjugij legitimi, etiam infidelium puritate agitur. Non enim liberis tantum, ad quos forsan poterit ita pertinere fidelis parentis Sanctimonia, ut fœderis Dei propter illam sint participes: sed & maritis ac uxoribus infidelibus Sanctimonia adscribitur, ut ut fidei Christi repugnent. Nec de alia agitur Sanctitate ac puritate liberorum, quàm quæ & infidelibus parentibus competit. Illis autem non competit alia quàm quæ est ex conjugio legitimo.

Sexto sic colligebant: Procreatio similium fit ex similibus: Atqui Adam receptus est in gratiam, & in gratiâ propagavit liberos: Ergo procreavit sibi similes, absq; propagatione peccati.

Sed Respondeo committi Sophisma à dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter. Major enim vera est de propagatione carnali. Minor vero simpliciter est falsa, si sic accipiatur, quòd Adam Gratiam, in quam receptus erat per lapsum, propagaverit in liberos.

Nam Adam, Scriptura teste, quantumvis renatus, non tamen procreavit liberos ad imaginem illam Dei, quæ jam in ipso restaurari cepla fuit: sed ad SVAM imaginem Et universaliter vera est Regula illa Antiquitatis: Parentes procreant liberos non secundum id; ex quo sunt renati: sed ex quo sunt caro.

Septimò sic inferebant. Quod non habent parentes, illud non possunt propagare in liberos. Atqui Parentes Christiani sive fideles non habent peccatum damnans. Ergo nec in liberos tale peccatum, quale peccatum originis esse dicitur, propagare possunt.

Respondeo, committitur error secundum quid. Major enim vera est tum, si intelligatur de eo, quod parentes habent, neque per gratiam, neque per Naturam. Jam verò quoad Minorem falsissimum est, quòd parentes Christiani & fideles non habent peccatum damnans à Natura. Nam quód peccatum ipsis non imputatur, id non dependet ab ipsorum naturâ, sed à beneficio Christi. Proindè rectiùs invertitur argumentum hoc in hunc modum: Quicquid parentes Christiani & fideles Naturâ habent: illud propagantin liberos. Atqui quantumvis Christiani & fideles, habent tamen Naturâ peccatum originis: Hoc enim illis remittitur, non ut non sit, sed ut non imputetur, uti Augustinus loquitur. Ergo.


### Controversy III. Concerning the effect of Original Sin? and concerning the remedy by which it is taken away

Concerning the effect of Original sin? and concerning the remedy by which it is removed.

It is debated today between us and the Papists, not only concerning the Effect of Original Sin: but also concerning its remedy. We, taught by the holy scriptures, maintain that the wages and the ultimate effect of this sin is Death, and that both that first or temporal one, which is nothing else than the violent dissolution of that Natural Union which exists between Soul and Body: and the second, which is eternal damnation. God himself confirms this thesis, Gen. 2, 17. Saying, In whatever day you shall eat from this tree, you shall die the death: and then the Apostle, Rom. 6, 23. Saying, The wages of sin is Death. Moreover, the species of both deaths are expressed in Apocal. 20, 6. and ch. 21, 8. But just as there is given no Man, begotten according to nature, who is devoid of this sin: so also from this Effect, or punishment of sin: no mortal, and not even any of the infants is immune, however much these (infants) may seem to have neither increased nor aggravated the evil of this sin by any actual sin. Where, however, we by no means deny, since there will be certain and distinct degrees of heavenly glory, as well as of Infernal punishments, that the punishments of such infants will be much lighter than those of them who have exacerbated the punishments for themselves by actual sins. Two things are chiefly objected in this place: The first is. That which is nothing, is not worthy of such a punishment. But sin is nothing, because it is a defect. Therefore. But a childish Sophistry of equivocation is committed in the word Nothing: which is one thing as Negative Nothing: and another as Privative Nothing. The Major premise, however,

Latin:

De effectu peccati Originalis? deq̃ remedio, quo ille tollitur.

COntrovertitur hodiè inter nos & Pontificios, non modò de Effectu Peccati Originalis: sed de ejusdem etiam remedio. Nos sacris edocti literis statuimus stipendium & effectum peccati hujus ultimum est Mortem, eamque tum primam illam sive temporalem, quæ nihil est aliud, quàm violenta Unionis illius Naturalis, quæ Animæ & Corpori intercedit, solutio: tum secundam, quæ est damnatio sempiterna. Confirmat thesin hanc tum Deus ipse Genes. 2, 17. Quâcunq̃, inquiens, die de arbore hac comederis, morte morieris: tum Apostol9, Rom 6, 23. Stipendium, inquiens, peccati Mors est. Utriusque autem mortis species exprimitur Apocal. 20, 6. & c. 21, 8. Quemadmodum verò non datur Homo aliquis, secundum naturam progenitus, qui expers sit peccati hujus: ita ab Effectu etiam isto, sive pœna peccati: nemo mortalium, & ne quidem ullus infantum immunis, quantumvis etiam hi (infantes) peccati hujus malum, peccato aliquo actuali nullo vel auxisse, vel aggravasse videri queant. Ubi tamen minimè negamus, cùm uti gloriæ cælestis, sic pœnarum etiam Infernalium futuri sint certi & distincti gradus, multò leviora fore ejusmodi infantium supplicia, quàm eorum qui peccatis actualibus pœnas sibi ipsis exasperarunt. Duo potissimùm hoc loco objiciuntur: Prius est. Quod nihil est, non est dignum tantâ pœna. Sed peccatum est nihil, quia est defectus. Ergo. Sed puerilis committitur Sophisticatio æquivocationis, in vocabulo Nihil: quod aliud est, Nihil negativum: aliud Nihil privativum. Major E. verà


### Controversy III. Concerning the effect of Original Sin? and concerning the…: What must here in particular be explained is this: What in Baptism is taken away from sin?

is about that which is negative nothing. But the minor deals with sin, which is not a negative Nothing: but a privative one, joined with the position of a contrary habit: and therefore worthy, by the most just judgment of God, of eternal and temporal punishments.

The latter thing that is objected is this: Every effect is intended by efficient causes. But that was not Adam's intention, that he should precipitate himself and all his posterity into such great punishments. Therefore, this effect, the sin of Adam, is scarcely seen to follow.

To this argument Thomas 1.20. q. 85. art. 5 replies not ineptly as follows: A cause intending an effect is a cause per se: but a cause per accidens does not intend the effect: Thus the sin of the first parents is the cause of death and of all defects in human nature, in so far as by the sin of the first parent, Original Justice was removed: but the subtraction of Original Justice has the nature of a punishment.

Wherefore, although death and other effects were not intended by the sinner: they are nevertheless ordained according to the justice of God who punishes. The argument therefore fails by the fallacy a̓pò tōũ perí ti pròs tò ạplãs. For the major, which consists of a common philosophical axiom, is true only secundum quid, namely concerning those effects which are either placed in the power of the one intending, or depend upon the intention of the agent as from a proper and per se cause. Now, however, as regards the minor, the effect of Original sin, namely temporal and eternal death, does not depend upon the intention of Adam the agent, but upon the ordination and decree of divine Justice, as from a proper and per se cause. Whatever, therefore, may have been in Adam's intention: that could prejudice nothing against the most just decree of God.

But it is now asked in the second place concerning the means or remedy by which this most sad effect can be taken away? But for this evil no medicine could be found, either by the help of men or of Angels. Therefore, the remedy was found by the benefit of one and only divine mercy. For the eternal heavenly Father, having pity on the human race, willed that His Son should be incarnate, and that by His merit sin should be expiated, and we should be recalled into grace. But let our part be this ineffable benefit of divine compassion, not otherwise than through the remission of sins, apprehended by faith through and because of Christ: and that first and properly in Baptism, through the washing of regeneration: then, however, through the constant application of the promises of grace offered in the Gospel: which is done through faith in Christ the Savior. Concerning which matter, a discussion is to be held by us sỳn Theõ expressly. That rather should be explained in this place: What is taken away concerning sin in Baptism? Or what kind of abolition of sin is that which is done in Baptism? To which question our Churches respond partly from the Scriptures, partly from the consensus of the ancient Church: that this abolition of sin consists in remission alone, by which sin is not imputed: according to that trite saying of Augustine: Sin is remitted in Baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not imputed, lib. 1. de cons. & nuptijs, c. 34. By which formula of speaking it was shown: that the remedy of Original sin is so constituted, that the evil itself is both taken away: and yet remains: It is taken away, indeed, as regards the guilt, which the Scholastics named the formal part of Original sin: but it remains as regards the corruption of nature: which the same Scholastics called the material part. And in this sense we do not disapprove of that rule of the Scholastics: In Baptism the formal part of original sin is taken away: but the material part remains: provided that that sophistication is absent which the Jesuits are accustomed to hide under this rule: concerning which a little later. With this decision standing, it becomes plain how sin does not exist in the regenerate, namely with respect to remission, and in so far as its guilt has been abolished: and how the same sin at the same time remains: namely in so far as the corruption or concupiscence is in the act itself remaining, and is never entirely cut out in the regenerate, even the most holy, in this life.

Moreover, this remission of sin: although it seems to imply only one act: yet its mode is twofold, of which the former is ςερητικὸς, and regards the material part of sin, when indeed that which is present is not imputed: the latter is θετικὸς, and regards the formal part of sin, when, the guilt of sin having been removed, that which does not in reality inhere in man is truly imputed, namely the innocence and justice of Christ, not that essential and eternal one: but that which He acquired by fulfilling the law. Both of which modes have their proper place in the form of justification.

For by remitting the sin which is in the sinner, it is reputed by God as not being in him: but by bestowing the justice of Christ, which does not in reality exist in the reconciled sinner, it is nevertheless reputed by God as being in him, as will be demonstrated more fully elsewhere.

The nature or affection of Original sin is completely contrary to the condition of actual sins. For actual sins, such as theft, robbery, adultery, pass away in act: they remain in guilt: But the sin of origin is taken away in guilt through remission: but it remains in act through the inherence and inhabitation of corruption.

And this indeed is the purer doctrine of our Churches concerning the present controversy: to which very many and clearly discrepant opinions are opposed as if diametrically.

And at the beginning, indeed, regarding the definition of the effect of original sin, the Gentile philosophers displayed a truly stupendous ignorance, for they relegated temporal death to the class of natural conditions and traced its cause back to matter and the mixture of the elements. From this opinion the modern Jesuits do not at all shrink, who likewise dream that man, even before the fall, was subject to death by the condition of his matter: as was shown in the article concerning the image of God, to which profanity even that passage from Wisdom 2:24 may be most solidly opposed:

Latin:

est de eo, quod est nihil negativum. Minor autem agit de peccato, quod non est Nihil negativum: sed privativum, conjunctum cum positione contrarij habitus: ac proindè æternis & temporalibus pœnis, justissimo Dei judicio, dignum.

Posteriùs quod objicitur est istud: Omnis effectus intenditur à causis efficientibus. Atqui Adami non ea fuit intentio, ut in tantas pœnas serpsum & universam posteritatem præcipitaret. Ergo vix didetur Effectus iste, peccatum Adami consequi.

Ad hoc argumentum haud ineptè Thomas 1.20. q. 85. art. 5 sic respondet: Causa intendens Effectum, est causa per se: sed causa per accidens non intendit Effectum: Ita peccatum primorum parentum est causa mortis, & omnium defectum in natura humana, in quantum per peccatum primi parentis, sublata est Justitia Originalis: subtractio autem Originalis Justitiæ habet rationem pœnæ.

Quare quamvis mors & alij Effectus non sint intenti à peccante: sunt tamen ordinati secundum justitiam Dei punientis. Fallit proindè argumentum Sophismate a̓pò tōũ perí ti pròs tò ạplãs. Major enim, quæ constat axiomate communi Philosophico, vera tantùm est, secundum quid, nempè de ijs effectibus, qui sunt vel in potestate intendentis positi, vel ab intentione agentis, tanquàm à causa propria & per se, dependent. Jam verò, quoad Minorem, Effectus peccati Originalis, Mors nempè temporalis & æterna, non dependet ab intentione Adami agentis, seb ab ordinatione & decreto Justitiæ divinæ, tanquàm à causa propria & per se. Quicquid ergo in Adami intentione fuerit: illud decreto Dei justissimo, nihil præjudicare potuit.

Sed quæritur jam secundo loco de medio sive remedio, quo tristissimus iste Effectus tolli possit? Atqui malo huic nulla medicina, vel ex hominum vel ex Angelorum ope, inveniri poterat. E. unius & solius divinæ misericordiæ beneficio repertum est remedium. Æternus enim pater cælestis, misertus generis humani, Filium suum incarnari, ejusdemque merito peccatum expiari, inque gratiam revocari nos voluit. Nostrum autem sit ineffabile hoc miserationis divinæ beneficium, non nisi per Remissionem peccatorùm, per & propter Christum fide apprehensum: idque primo & propriè in Baptismo, per lavacrum regenerationis: deindè verò per jugem applicationem promissionum gratiæ, in Evangelio oblatarum: id quod fit per fidem in Christum Servatorem. Qua de re in Articulo Justificationis nobis sỳn Theõ ex professo futura est Disputatio. Illud potiùs hoc loco explicandum fuerit: Quid in Baptismo de peccato tollatur? Vel qualis sit peccati abolitio, in Baptismo facta? Ad quod zétēma nostræ respondent Ecclesiæ ex Scripturis partim, partim ex consensu antiquæ Ecclesiæ: constare illam abolitionem peccati, sola Remissione, qua peccatum non imputatur: secundum illud tritum Augustini: Peccatum in Baptismo remittitur, non ut non sit, sed ut non imputetur lib. 1. de cons. & nuptijs, c. 34. Qua loquendi formula illud ostensum fuit: Remedium peccati Originalis ita comparatum esse, ut Malum ipsum & tollatur: & tamen remaneat: Tollatur quidem, quoad Reatum, quem Scholastici, Formale peccati Originalis nominarunt: Remaneat autem, quoad corruptionem Naturæ: quam ijdem Scholastici Materiale appellarunt. Et hoc sensu non improbamus Regulam illam Scholasticorum: In Baptismo tollitur Formale peccati Originis: Materiale autem remanet: modo absit Sophisticatio illa, quam Jesuitæ sub hac regula occultare solent: de qua paulo post. Stante hac decisione planum jam fit, quomodo in Renatis peccatum non sit, nempe respectu remissionis, & quatenus ejus reatus est abolitus: & quomodo idem peccatum simul remaneat: nempe quatenus Corruptio sive concupiscentia, actu ipso est reliqua neque in renatis etiam & sanctissimis nunquam hac in vita prorsus excinditur.

Cæterum Remissio hæc peccati: etsi unum duntaxat actum innuere videtur: modus tamen ejus duplex est, quorum Prior est ςερητικὸς, & Materiale peccati respicit, cum nimirum non imputatur id, quod adest: posterior est θετικὸς, & Formale peccati respicit, cum sublato reatu peccati, revera imputatur id, quod reipsa homini non inhæret, nempe Innocentia & Justitia Christi, non essentialis illa atque æterna: sed quam ille implendo legem acquisivit. Qui uterque modus in Forma Justificationis proprium locum habet.

Remittendo enim peccatum, quo inest peccatori, non inesse imputatur a Deo: Donando autem, Justitia Christi, quæ non inest reipsa peccatori reconciliato, inesse tamen a Deo reputatur, ut alibi fusius demonstrabitur.

Contraria prorsus est hæc peccati Originalis natura sive affectio, conditioni peccatorum actualium. Nam peccata actualia, ut Furtum, latrocinium, stuprum, actu transeunt: reatu remanent: Sed peccatum Originis reatu tollitur per Remissionem: actu autem remanet per inhærentiam atque inhabitationem corruptionis.

Et hæc quidem purior est Ecclesiarum nostrarum de præsente Controversia, doctrina: cui bene multæ & discrepantes plane sententiæ e diametro quasi sunt oppositæ.

Ac initio quidem circa Effectum peccati Originalis definiendum, ignorantiam plane stupendam prodiderunt Gentiles Philosophi, qui Mortem temporalem in classem conditionum naturalium retulerunt, ejusque causam ad materiam & mixtionem Elementorum revocarunt. A qua sententia haud abhorrent moderni Jesuitæ, qui itidem Hominem etiam ante lapsum ex conditione Materiæ Morti obnoxium fuisse, somniant: uti Artic de Imagine DEI fuit ostensum, cui prophanitati vel illud Sapient. 2, 24. solidissime opponi possit:


### Controversy III. Concerning the effect of Original Sin? and concerning the…: Of the Effect and the Remedy

God created man ἐπ' ἀφθαρσίᾳ (for incorruptibility) for eternal life: But by the envy of the Devil death entered into the world. And that of Thomas, in the place already cited above: The sin of the first parent was the cause of death, and of defects in human nature, by which through him original justice was taken away, by which not only were the lower powers of the soul contained under Reason without any deordination (exorbitation or error) but also the whole body under the soul without any defect. Wherefore, Original Justice having been subtracted by the sin of Adam, just as human nature was wounded, as regards the soul, by the deordination of the powers, so it was made corruptible, by the deordination of the body itself.

Then, concerning this very question, both the ancient and the more recent Pontificians err gravely, who, for the sake of asserting that fabulous figment about the limbo of Infants, among other things, assign also this reason: that infants, being indeed innocent, cannot be constituted guilty by any law of damnation, and therefore, descending from here, they arrive neither into hell, nor into Purgatory, nor into the limbo of the Fathers: but into a fourth floor, namely such a place in which there is indeed a place of punishments, but joined with no other sense of punishments than with the deprivation of a better and perfect good. Which error the Jesuits hold even today, establishing that little ones dying without Baptism will have sorrow of mind from that fact alone, that they will understand themselves to be deprived of beatitude, alienated from the company of pious brothers and parents, thrust into the prison of hell, and to live in perpetual darkness: as Bellarmine speaks in book 6 de amiss. grat. & stat. peccati (of the grace and state of sin) chap. 6. page 476. D. But the same Jesuit adds that this sorrow in them will be very light and very mild for many reasons: both because they had a disposition to beatitude that was only most remote: and because they will understand that they did not lose so great a good by their own negligence, and therefore they will also lack the worm of conscience, and because they never tasted delights, neither heavenly nor earthly: and they can easily lack those goods to which they were never accustomed: and finally because they will see that there are many in the same prison of Gehenna much more unhappy than themselves. Ibid. & p. 480. A. Moreover, if you will ask of the Jesuit, what foundations of this opinion he can bring forward? he certainly shows not even one apex of the sacred scriptures: but he answers that he believes this because of the authority of the Holy Fathers: whom some of the Scholastic Theologians also have followed.

But this is a sink, and as it were a confluence of many most absurd impieties. For first, ἄγε γραφῆς (without scripture) certain and distinct cells of the underworld are built up by the Pontificians: as is demonstrated elsewhere. Then, it is erroneous and Pelagian to subject unbaptized Infants to eternal damnation for this reason, that they had a disposition to beatitude that was only most remote: as if indeed Beatitude depended upon the disposition of those to be saved: and not rather upon the sole grace and mercy of God, promised to us in Christ. Thirdly, it is impious and blasphemous to assert that Infants are damned, but not by their own negligence. For they are damned either by their own, or by their parents', or by God's negligence. But not by their own: as the Jesuit himself confesses: Nor also by their parents': Since there will be given no one who does not most greedily desire the eternal and temporal salvation of his offspring, and promote it by whatever means he can. And just as the Just man lives not by another's, but by his own faith, Habakkuk 2, 4. So the unjust man is damned not by another's, but by his own impiety. It remains, therefore, that Infants are damned by God's negligence: which is prodigiously blasphemous: and contradictorily opposed to that most sacred divine protestation: As I live, saith the LORD, I desire not the death of the DYING, etc. Ezekiel 18, 23. 32. & 33, 11. Finally, they argue for a very profane theology, which the Jesuit philosophizes sweetly about heavenly and earthly delights. For just as heavenly delights befall none but the Elect and the blessed: so the presence of earthly delights does not save: their absence does not damn: and consequently, a judgment is foolishly sought from the enjoyment of the latter concerning the punishments and state of Infants dying without Baptism.

We, that we may submit our ἐπίκρισιν (judgment) in a few words, establish it thus: that Baptism is indeed the ordinary medium of regeneration, by which infants are inserted into Christ and the Church: but meanwhile, if it happens that an infant is extinguished in the mother's womb, such a one is held as a transgressor of the divine ordinance, and therefore can or ought in no way to be referred to the assembly of the damned. For Baptism, because it is the washing of regeneration, certainly presupposes the first Generation. Nor is there any doubt that God, by His extraordinary and immediate power, regenerates them to eternal life, remits sins, and receives them into grace: and that through and because of Christ, who himself also willed to become an infant, and to lie hidden in the mother's womb for a just space of time, so that he might show that he can wash and sanctify even those who are extinguished while enclosed in the maternal womb from all uncleanness. The reason for this assertion can be sought sufficiently evidently from the Type, which was the circumcision of the Old Testament: where it is certain that many exhaled their soul before the eighth day, whom, however, hardly anyone would affirm to have been damned, unless he were ignorant of that, Genesis 17, 7. I will be thy God and of thy seed after thee. Which same judgment is to be held concerning those infants also who are indeed brought forth alive into the light, but, anticipated by some unexpected accident, cease to be among the living sooner than they can obtain the Sacrament of Baptism: especially if the pious prayers and supplications of the parents have come to God: which it is certain are heard: according to the immovable promise of the Savior: Amen, Amen I say to you, whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it to you, John 16, 23. And that other of Jehovah himself, Exodus 20, 6. I the God will show mercy unto a thousand generations of them that love me. Likewise Matthew 18, 14. It is not the will of my Father, that one of these little ones should perish.

The third place in the class of those who err is occupied by Franciscus Socinus the Photinian, who in part 3, chapter 8, page 294, indeed concedes that the effect or wages of sin is eternal death and the necessity of dying, but not bodily death itself: and that for two reasons above all. For first, he says, the death of the body is natural to man, and of itself follows that nature which Adam received and had in his very creation, inasmuch as he was endowed with an animal, mortal body. Then Socinus infers thus: Christ has freed us from every penalty and guilt of sin. But he has not freed us from bodily death. Therefore, this is not the effect or penalty of sin. But both reasons labor under manifest vanity. And the former indeed overturns itself. For if the necessity of dying depends on the effect of sin, then bodily death itself will certainly also depend on the same. For these two things are indissolubly joined: so that mortality after sin is nothing other than the necessity of dying, and vice versa: so much so that he who wishes to invent a real distinction between these ought to be considered as trifling, not disputing. Therefore, the first reason is simply false: for although Adam received in his first creation, and indeed before sin, a natural body which was mortal in potentiality (τῆ δυνάμει), and would have become mortal in act if he had transgressed the law of God: yet this potentiality (δύναμις) would never have passed into act if man had persisted in integrity, so that it is manifestly blasphemous against God if anyone maintains that Adam was created by God mortal in act.

The other reason fails by the fallacy of 'in a certain respect' (ὧς πρός τι) and 'absolutely' (ἁπλῶς). For Christ has freed us from every penalty and guilt in a certain respect, so that, namely, neither the death of the body nor other temporal penalties can, speaking properly, obtain the character of a penalty proceeding from an angry God and joined with eternal damnation. Now as regards the minor premise, it is false that Socinus infers simply that Christ has not freed us from bodily death. For although he has not freed us from this death in such a way that we would now be immortal: yet in other respects he has truly freed us from it, so that, namely, this temporal death is no longer for the faithful a penal death, speaking properly, but rather a passage to life (John 5:24) and the most joyful conclusion of all evils, so that it can now truly be said of them what appears in Revelation 14:13. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord: for now says the Spirit, they rest from their labors: And indeed, if the pious were not thus freed even from bodily death, then no distinction would remain between the death of the faithful and the unfaithful: which is manifestly absurd and contrary to the Scriptures.

But enough and more than enough about this error: that error rather, and indeed fourth in order, which the same Romanists cherish concerning the remedy of original sin in those already baptized and actually regenerated, stands in need of explanation. For they maintain that the formal element of original sin is removed and remitted in baptism, but the material element remains. Which manner of speaking, if you look at the letters and points of the words, seems to be in complete agreement (ὁμόψηφος) with our opinion: but if you look at the sense which the Romanists conceal under these terms, then it is indeed discovered to establish a foul error. For by the perverse use of these terms, they think that the formal element, that is, the defect of original justice, is removed and remitted: but the material element, that is, concupiscence, remains in the regenerate. Hence both old and recent Papists argued thus: The formal element, or the form of a thing, being removed, the thing itself is removed: In baptism the formal element of original sin is removed. Therefore the thing itself is removed: and consequently, what remains in the regenerate of the material element, namely concupiscence, can no longer be or be called sin. The foundation of this sophistry is situated in a vicious definition of the parts of sin, which the Church otherwise wished to express by material and formal: but the Scholastics snatched them into an entirely different sense: Thomas, in the first part of the second part, question 82, article 3, says: Original sin is materially indeed concupiscence: but formally it is the defect of original justice. Biel, in book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 10, says: In original sin, two things are considered: one, as the material, namely concupiscence, which is a certain morbid quality, especially that which inheres in the soul: the other is the formal, and it is the lack of original justice. But they refer the guilt of sin to the penalty of sin, as is in Thomas, first part of the second part, question 87, where he disputes about guilt through eight articles. Furthermore, this foul theology of the Scholastics is most rightly corrected by the substitution of a purer doctrine concerning the proper, genuine, and as it were essential parts of original sin. Such, however, are not those which the Scholastics, and the Jesuits who followed them, define as defect and concupiscence. For these two constitute only the material of sin, and therefore only one part of it, namely that which is proper to corruption. But those are the legitimate and essential parts which express both the matter and the form of sin according to the Scriptures: such as these two: 1. Corruption, which comprehends both defect and concupiscence under itself: and therefore is most rightly called the material of sin: 2. Guilt, which obtains the character of the formal.

For guilt cannot or ought not to be referred to the penalty of sin: if indeed fault is one thing, and penalty another: nor does the latter ever assume the nature of the former: except where God is read to punish sins with sins, that is, to harden men, as a singular example of his fury. Where sin sustains the character of both fault and penalty. But this does nothing for the present question. For 1. here the inquiry is not about those singular examples of divine judgment: but about sin, which is natural and congenital to all men. Then, those singular examples of divine judgments consist in actual sins: therefore, from there no consequence is valid for original sin, as regards its proper affection, which is distinct from, nay, different from actual sins. These things having been premised, it is now easy to respond to the argument of the Romanists proposed above: for in the major premise it is indeed true that, the formal cause being removed, the thing itself is removed; but under this condition, if the true form, and that which is proper to the species of the thing itself, be established. Now as regards the Minor, it is denied that the formal element of original sin is the defect of original justice, which pertains to the matter; and a true formal element is substituted, namely, the guilt of sin. Thus, therefore, the argument proceeds in this manner: When the formal element is removed, the thing itself is removed: But through baptism in the regenerate the formal element is removed, namely, the guilt of sin, from which that sin is properly called damning. Therefore, in the regenerate the thing itself, namely, the species of damning sin, is removed: For there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Rom. 8, 1. Now, indeed, if anyone should conclude: Since this form and species of damning sin is removed, clearly no nature of sin remains any longer in the regenerate: he is arguing negatively from species to genus, or from part to whole; that this is done irrationally is manifest in itself. Moreover, concerning this controversy, and especially concerning the concupiscence remaining in the regenerate, the following fourth and final part of this treatise will institute a discussion expressly.

It remains in this place that the error of the Sacramentarians also, which impinges upon the present question concerning the effect of sin, be noted in a few words. Zwingli certainly writes in a letter to Urbanus Rhegius: That original sin is indeed damnable in itself: but that through the death of Christ the guilt is now so removed that infants, not only of believers but also of Gentiles, born with the original defect, even if not baptized, are free from the guilt of divine wrath, wrongly accommodating here that Apostolic saying Rom. 5, 18 and 19: As by the offense of one (the transition was made) upon all men to condemnation: So also by the justification of one (the transition was made) upon all men to justification of life: For as by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners: so by the obedience of one many shall be made righteous. Hence, therefore, he argued: Just as without our consent we draw the corruption of Adam: so also without faith, and without the sacrament of regeneration, infants naturally have the benefit of Christ's redemption. But it is most rightly answered that the Pauline apodosis concerning Christ's redemption, however universal, must be taken determinately. For not all who are generated from Adam in sin are the same ones regenerated through Christ to grace: But it is said thus, as Augustine testifies, because just as no one's carnal generation is except through Adam: so no one's spiritual regeneration is except through Christ. Moreover, all regeneration happens from faith in Christ: For without this no one can be justified. Why, therefore, the universal Apostolic expression must be taken under the determination of regeneration or faith, can be a doubt to no one.

The remaining Sacramentarians, individually and collectively, have betrayed the same impiety, who imagine that the children of believers are so immune from the guilt of sin that they are born holy from their parents, indeed that their children, even while still enclosed in the womb, before they draw the vital spirit, have been co-opted into the covenant of eternal life, as Calvin speaks: so much so that they are not regenerated or saved through baptism: but that salvation, of which they had previously been participants, is merely sealed to them.

454, on the new method of reforming, and page 1082, defense 11, on the Sacraments. But since the refutation of this error finds its proper place in the Article on Baptism: let it suffice to have noted it in this place.

Latin:

Deus hominem condidit ἐπ' ἀφθαρσίᾳ ad vitam æternam: Invidia autem Diaboli mors intravit in mundum. Et illud Thomæ, loco jam suprà citato: Peccatum primi parentis fuit causa mortis, & defectuum in humana naturâ, quâ per ipsum sublata est justitia originalis, per quam non solùm inferiores animæ vires continebantur sub Ratione sine omni deordinatione (exorbitatione sive errore) sed & totum corpus sub animâ sine omni defectu, Quare subtractâ Justitiâ Originali per peccatum Adæ, sicut vulnerata est humana natura, quantum ad animam, per deordinationem potentiarum, ita facta est corruptibilis, per deordinationem ipsius corporis.

Deindè circa hanc ipsam quæstionem graviter errant tùm veteres, tùm recentiores Pontificij, qui pro fabuloso illo de limbo Infantium figmento asserendo, inter reliquas, hanc etiam causam adsignant, quod infantes quippè innocentes, nullo jure damnationis rei possint constitui, ac proindè hinc descendentes neque in infernum, neque in Purgatorium, neque in limbum Patrum: sed in quartam contignationem perveniant, talem nimirùm locum, in quo sit quidem pœnarum etiam locus, sed cum nullo alio pœnarum sensu, quàm cum privatione melioris & perfecti boni sit conjunctus. Quem errorem hodieque tenent Jesuitæ, statuentes, parvulos sine Baptismo decedentes, ex eo tantùm dolorem animi habituros, quòd intel ligent se beatitudine privatos, à consortio piorum fratrũ & parentum alienos in carcerem inferni detrusos, & intenebris perpetuis vitam acturos: uti loquitur Bellarminus lib. 6 de amiss. grat & stat. peccati cap. 6. pag. 476. D. Addit autem idem Jesuvvita hunc dolorem in eis levissimum mitissimumque multis de causis futurum: tùm quòd dispositionem ad beatitudinem non nisi remotissimam habuerunt:tũ quòd intelligent, non propriâ negligentiâ se tantũ bonũ amisisse, ac proindè verme conscientiæ ipsos etiam carituros, tùm, quod delitias neque cœlestes, neque terrestres unquam gustaverunt: & facilè ÿs bonis carere possunt, quibus nunquàm assueverunt: tùm denique quòd videbunt, plurimos esse in eodem gehennæ carcere, se multò infeliciores. Ibid. & p. 480. A. Cæterùm si ex Jesuvvita quæres, quænam sententiæ hujus fundamenta proferre possit? non certè scripturarum sacrarum vel unum apicem monstrat: sed respondet, se hoc credere propter autoritatem Sanctorum Patrum: quos nonnulli etiam Scholasticorum Theologorum secuti sint.

Verùm sentina hæc est, & quasi confluentia plurimarum absurdissimarum impietatum. Primùm enjm ἄγε γραφῆς certæ & distinctæ inferorum cellulæ à Pontificijs extruuntur: uti alibi demonstratur. Deindè erroneum & Pelagianum est, ideò Infantes non baptizatos æternæ damnationi subjicere, quia dispositionem ad beatitudinem non nisi remotissimam habuerint: quasi verò Beatitudo dependeat à dispositione salvandorum: & non potiùs à sola gratia & misericordia Dei, in Christo nobis promissa. Tertiò impium & blasphemum est asserere, Infantes pesse damnatos, sed non propria negligentia. Aut enim propria, aut parentum, aut Dei negligentia sunt damnati. Atqui non propria: sic fatente ipso Jesuvita: Non etiam parentum: Siquidem nullus dabitur, qui non sobolis aeternam & temporalem salutem avidissime cupiat, eamque quibus potest rationibus, promoveat. Et quemadmodum Justus non aliena, sed sua fide vivit Habacuc 2, 4. Ita injustus non aliena etiam, sed sua impietate damnatur. Relinquitur Ergo, Dei negligentia Infantes damnari: id quod prodigiose blasphemum: & contradictorie oppositum, sacratissimae illi protestationi divinae: Vivo ego DEUS, Nolo mortem MORIENTIS &c. Iezech. 18, 23. 32. & 33, 11. Tandem prophanam admodum Theologiam arguunt, quae Jesuvvita de delitiis caelestibus atque terrestribus suaviter philosophatur. Quemadmodum enim caelestes delitiae, non nisi Electis & beatis obtingunt: ita terrestrium delitiarum praesentia non salvat: absentia non damnat: & per consequens ex istarum perfruitione de poenis & statu Infantium, sine Baptismo decedentium stolide petitur judicium.

Nos ut paucis nostram ἐπίκρισιν subjiciamus, sic statuimus: Baptismum quidem esse ordinarium medium regenerationis, quo infantes inseruntur Christo & Ecclesiae: sed interim si contingat, infantem in utero matris extingui, talem pro transgressore divinae ordinationis haberi, ac proinde ad caetum damnatorum referri nullo modo posse aut debere. Baptismus enim quia lavacrum est regenerationis, utique praesupponit Generationem primam. Neque dubium est ullum, quin Deus extraordinaria & immediata virtute sua illos ad vitam aeternam regeneret, peccata remittat, & in gratiam recipiat: idque per & propter Christum, qui ipse quoque infans fieri, inque utero matris, justo temporis spatio delitescere voluit, ut sic ostenderet, se eos quoque, qui utero materno clausi extinguuntur, ab omni immundicia abluere & sanctificare posse. Potest assertionis hujus ratio satis evidens peti a Typo, qui fuit circumcisio Veteris Testamenti: ubi sane multos ante octavum diem animam exhalasse certum est, quos tamen damnatos fuisse, vix quisquam affirmaverit, nisi qui ignorarit illud, Genes. 17, 7. Ego ero Deus tuus & seminis tui post te. Quod ipsum est ferendum judicium, de illis quoque infantibus, qui in lucem vivi quidem sunt editi, sed casu quodam inopinato praeventi, citius in vivis esse desinunt, quam Sacramento Baptismi potiantur: praesertim si piae parentum preces & supplicationes ad Deum accesserint: quas exaudiri certum est: secundum immotam promissionem Servatoris: Amen, Amen dico vobis, quicquid rogaveritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis, Iohan. 16, 23. Et illam alteram ipsius Jehovae, Exod. 20, 6. Ego Deus faciam misericordiam in mille generationes eorum qui diligunt me. Item Matth. 18, 14. Non est voluntas Patris mei, ut unus pereat de pusillis istis.

Tertium in classe errantium locum occupat Franciscus Socinus Photinianus, qui parte 3. cap. 8. p. 294. concedit quidem, Effectum sive stipendium peccati esse Mortem æternam, & moriendi necessitatem: sed non mortem ipsam Corporalem: 1: idquè propter duas potissimum rationes. Primum enim inquit, Mors Corporis homini est naturalis, & per se sequitur eam naturam, quam Adam in ipsa Creatione ante peccatum accepit & habuit, ut potè Corpus animale, mortale fortitus. Deindè sic infert Socinus, Christus nos ab omni peccati pœna & reatu liberavit. Atqui nos non liberavit à morte corporali. E. hæc non est Effectus vel pœna peccati. Sed utraque ratio manifesta vanitate laborat. Et prior quidem semetipsam evertit. Nam si Moriendi necessitas pendet ab Effectu peccati: utique ab eodem pendebit etiam ipsa mors corporalis. Hæc enim duo sunt indissolubiliter conjuncta: ut mortalitas po\u01stt peccatum, nihil sit aliud, quam moriendi necessitas, & vice versa: usque adeò ut nugari, non disputare censeri debeat, qui inter hæc realem Distinctionem comminisci velit. Ratio proindè prima simpliciter falsa est: Etsi enim Adam accepit in prima creatione, & quidem ante peccatum, corpus naturale, quòd τῆ δυνάμει esset mortale, & actu evaderet mortale, si Legem Dei transgrederetur: tamen hæc δυνάμις nunquam in actum transiisset, si homo in integritate perstitisset, ita ut in Deum manifestè blasphemum sit, si quis statuat, Adamum à Deo actu mortalem fuisse conditum.

Altera ratio fallit Sophismate ὧς πρός τι πρῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Christus enim ab omni pœna & reatu nos liberavit, secundum quid, ut nimirùm, neque Mors Corporis, neque aliæ pœnæ temporales, propriè loquendo rationem pœnæ ab irato Deo Proficiscentis, & cum æterna damnatione conjunctæ obtinere possint. Jam quoad Minorem, falsum est, quod Socinus simpliciter infert, Christum nos non liberasse à morte corporali. Etsi enim non ita liberavit nos ab hac morte, ut nunc immortales essemus: tamen respectibus alijs verè nos ab ea liberavit, ut nimirùm Mors hæc temporalis, non ampliùs fidelibus sit Mors pœnalis propriè loquendo, sed potiùs transitus ad vitam Joh. 5, 24. & lætissima clausula omnium malorum, ut jam verè de illis dici queat, quod extat Apocal. 14, 13. Beati mortui, qui in DOMINO moriuntur: Jam enim dicit Spiritus, requiescunt à laboribus suis: Et sanè nisi sic liberati essent pij à morte etiam corporali, tùm inter mortem fidelium & infidèlium nihil relinqueretur discriminis: id quod manifestè absurdum & Scripturis adversum.

Sed de hoc etiam errore plus satis: Ille potiùs error, & ordine quidem quartus, explicatione indiget, quem de Remedio Peccati Originalis in Baptizatis jam, & actu regeneratis ijdem fovent Romanenses. Statuunt enim Peccati Originalis Formale in Baptismo tolli & remitti: Materiale autem remanere. Quæ sanè loquendi ratio, si verborum literas & apices spectes, nostræ sententiæ per omnia videtur esse ὁμόψηφος: Sin verò sensum, quem Romanenses sub terminis istis occultant, tùm profactò fædum errorem stabilire deprehenditur. Perverso enim Terminorum istorum usu, sentiunt, Formale, hoc est, defectum Justitiæ Originalis tolli & remitti : Materiale autem, hoc est, Concupiscentiam in renatis remanere. Hinc tùm veteres tùm recentiores Pontificij sic arguebant ;: Sublato Formali, sive Forma rei, res ipsa tollitur: In Baptismo tollitur Formale peccati Originalis. Ergo Res ipsa tollitur : ac per consequens, Quod reliquum est in Renatis de Materia: nempè Concupiscentia, Peccatum ampliùs esse aut dici non potest. Fundamentum hujus Sophistices situm est in vitiosa definitione partium peccati, quas per Materiale & Formale alioqui Ecclesia exprimere voluit : Sed Scholastici in alienum prorsus sensum rapuerunt : Thomas prima secundæ, quæst. 82. Artic. 3. Peccatum, inquit, Originale materialiter quidem est concupiscentia : Formaliter autem est defectus Originalis Justitiæ. Biel. in l. 2. sent. distinct. 10. In peccato, inquit, Originali, duo considerantur : Vnum, tanquam materiale, scilicet Concupiscentia, quæ est, Qualitas quædam morbida, maximè illa quæ inhæret animæ : Aliud est Formale, & est carentia Iustitiæ Originalis. Reatum verò peccati, referunt ad pœnam peccati, ut est apud Thomam prima secundæ, quæst. 87. ubi de reatu per octo articulos disputat Cæterùm fæda isthæc Scholasticorum Theologia rectissimè corrigitur, substitutione purioris doctrinæ de partibus peccati Originalis proprijs, genuinis, & quasi essentialibus. Tales autem sunt; non quas Scholastici, & hos secuti Jesuitæ, definiunt, Defectus & Concupiscentia. Hæc enim duo Materiale tantùm peccati, & proindè unam duntaxat ejus partem, eam nimirùm, quæ est corruptionis propria constituunt. Verùm eæ sunt partes legitimæ & Essentiales, quæ & Materiam & formam peccati secundum scripturas exprimunt: Quales sunt hæ duæ : 1. Corruptio, quæ & Defectum & Concupiscentiam sub se comprehendit : ac proindè rectissimè Materiale peccati dicitur : 2. Reatus, qui Formalis rationem obtinet.

Neque enim Reatus ad pœnam peccati referri potest, aut debet : Si quidem aliud est culpa, aliud pœna : neque hæc illius naturam unquàm induit : nisi ubi Deus, singulari furoris sui exemplo peccata peccatis punire, hoc est, homines indurare legitur. Ubi peccatum & culpæ & pœnæ rationem sustinet. Verùm nihil hoc facit ad præsentem quæstionem. Nam 1. hîc non quæritur de singulatibus illis divini judicij exemplis : sed de peccato, quod omnibus hominibus est Naturale & congenitum. Deinde singularia illa divinorum judiciorum exempla in actualibus peccatis consistunt: Ergo indè ad Originale peccatum nulla valet consequentia, quoad propriam ejus affectionem, quæ ab actualibus est distincta, imò diversa. His ita præmissis facilè jam est respondere ad Argumentum Romanensium supra propositum : Nam in Majore verum quidem est; quod sublato Formali, res ipsa tollatur : sed sub hac conditione, si vera Forma, & quæ ipsius est speciei propria constituatur. Jam quoad Minorem, negatur Formale peccati originis, esse defectus justitiae Originalis: qui ad Materiam pertinet: & substituitur verum Formale, nempè Reatus peccati. Sic ergò jam in hunc modum procedit argumentum: Sublato formali res ipsa tollitur: Atqui per Baptismum in renatis tollitur formale: nempè reatus peccati, à quo peccatum istud propriè damnans appellatur. E. in renatis res ipsa, nempè species peccati damnantis tollitur: Neque enim ulla est condemnatio in his, qui sunt in Christo Jesu. Rom. 8, 1. Jam verò si quis colligat: Sublatâ hâc damnantis peccati formâ & specie, planè nullam peccati rationem in renatis ampliùs superesse: is à specie ad Genus, sive à parte ad Totum Negativè argumentatur: id quòd ἀλόγως fieri, per se manifestum est. Caeterùm de hac controversia, & cumprimis de concupiscentia in Renatis reliqua: subsequens quarta & postrema Tractationis hujus pars, ex professo disceptationem instituet.

Superest hoc loco, ut Sacramentariorum etiam error, in praesentem quaestionem de Effectu peccati impingens, paucis notetur. Zvvinglius certè in epistola ad Urbanum Regium scribit: Peccatum Originis per se quidem damnabile esse: sed per mortem Christi, ita jam sublatum esse reatum, ut infantes non fidelium tantùm, sed & Gentilium, cum defectu Originali nati, etiam non baptizati, à reatu irae divinae sint liberi, perperàm huc accommodans illud Apostolicum Rom. 5, 18. & 19. Sicut per unius delictum (transitus factus est) in omnes homines ad condemnationem: Ita & per unius justificationem (transitus factus est) in omnes homines ad Justificationem vitae: Sicut enim per inobedientiam unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi: ita per unius obedientiam justi constituentur multi. Hinc ergò arguebat: Quemadmodum sine consensu nostro trahimus corruptionem Adae: ita etiam sine fide, & sine Sacramento regenerationis, Beneficium Redemtionis Christi Infantes naturaliter habent. Sed rectissimè respondetur, ἀπόδωσιν Paulinam de Christi redemtione, quantumvis universali, determinatè accipiendam esse. Non enim qui generantur omnes ex Adamo in peccato: ijdem ipsi omnes per Christum regenerantur ad gratiam: Sed sic id dictum est, teste Augustino, quia sicuti nullius Generatio carnalis nisi per Adam: sic spiritualis nullius regeneratio, nisi per Christum. Regeneratio autem omnis fit ex fide in Christum: Sine hac enim nemo justificari potest. Quin E. universalis locutio Apostolica sub determinatione Regenerationis sive fidei, accipienda sit, nemini potest esse dubium.

Prodiderunt eandem impietatem reliqui Sacramentarij singuli & universi, qui fingunt Fidelium liberos à reatu peccati ita immunes esse, ut sancti nascantur ex parentibus, imò adhuc utero inclusi ipsorum liberi, antequàm vitalem spiritum hauriant, cooptati sint in foedus vitae aeternae, ut Calvinus loquitur: adeò ut per Baptismum non regenerentur aut salventur: sed illis tantùm obsignetur salus, cujus prius fuerant participes

454. de nova reformandi ratione, & pag. 1082. def. 11. de Sacramentis. Verùm cùm erroris istius Refutatio propriam sedem sibi figat in Articulo de Baptismo: hoc loco illum notasse, sufficiat.


### Controversy IV. And the last concerning Original Sin: namely in the question of the species of Concupiscence which remains in the Regenerate

It is disputed between us and the Romanists: Whether concupiscence, which remains in the regenerate, properly speaking is sin: that is, something fighting against the law of God, and by its own nature worthy of eternal death: or whether it is merely the punishment of sin, or as others speak, whether it is something indifferent, which one may use either well or badly. Which status of the controversy, so that it may be more fully known, it must be noted in this place that those natural concupiscences do not come under the question, which concern the preservation of our nature, and are commonly included under the definition of appetites: Nor is this also disputed: Whether those remnants of original sin make the regenerate, who have been grafted into Christ through baptism and are in Him by faith, hateful to God and condemn them? For there is nothing of condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus: Rom. 8. Moreover, neither is this properly recalled for discussion in this place: Whether those remnants of original sin, when they acquire dominion in a regenerate man and reign, condemn? For that Apostolic saying is too manifest: If you live according to the flesh, you will die: But this only is asked, What is that concupiscence, which in the regenerate after baptism remains in this life, and from time to time lusts against the spirit Gal. 5, 17, although it is not obeyed, what, I say, is it, in itself, by itself, from itself, and by its own nature, as the Jesuits speak: Whether indeed it is a good, pure, clean, holy thing, pleasing to God and conformable to the divine law? Or whether it is evil, and has the nature of sin? The Romanists embrace the negative of this question, contending that this concupiscence remaining in the regenerate after baptism is not properly sin: but a good, pure thing conformable to the law of God: or at least not against, but at least beside the law of God. As we shall hear them speaking below. We, however, holding the affirmative, maintain that this concupiscence is a thing by its own nature evil, and displeasing to God: and therefore in itself and by itself, or properly speaking, is sin. Nor indeed is the dispute which is instituted concerning this matter a vain logomachy, as it has pleased some to cavil: But it is fought over an article of the Christian faith, and not the least among the chief ones: Whether indeed a regenerate man in this life can perfectly satisfy the law of God, and through works merit eternal life? Which is what the Romanists hide under their negative.

Moreover, this whole controversy will hardly be explained more correctly than if it is shown at the beginning: What is concupiscence in those who have not been regenerated by water and the Spirit? Then, indeed, how is this very concupiscence removed by baptism? From which it will immediately and spontaneously become clear what is to be thought concerning the concupiscence remaining after baptism.

Regarding that first point, it is placed beyond controversy that concupiscence in the not-yet-regenerate is the very thing that is accustomed to be called original sin: namely, not only the privation or lack, as they say, of the original justice that ought to be present, but also a horrible depravity of all human powers, which condemns and brings eternal death to those who are not reborn through water and the Spirit (John 3:5). This depravity, therefore, is properly called concupiscence because the old man is corrupted through the concupiscences of error, as the Apostle says (Eph. 4:22). But how this concupiscence is removed in baptism, that is indeed what is most disputed today. The Papist doctors, especially the Jesuits, maintain that it is abolished in every way, as we shall soon show in the Antithesis.
