But we, as demonstrated in the third preceding controversy, feel with St. Augustine: that the concupiscence of the flesh is dismissed in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not imputed as sin (Book 1, On Marriage and Concupiscence, ch. 25). Or, to explain our mind more clearly: since there are two things in the concupiscence of the flesh or original sin, the depravity of all powers and the guilt, we maintain that the latter is indeed entirely removed in baptism, and that nothing of it remains that would hinder the regenerate unto damnation. Meanwhile, however, the depraved powers, although they also begin to be renewed, remain as remnants, and renewal is never fully completed in this life. From which it will now be easy to conclude that this concupiscence, remaining in the regenerate, although it is not imputed to them for damnation, is nevertheless, by its nature or considered in and of itself, truly sin.

The first argument for this affirmative of ours is shown by the Apostle in the seventh chapter to the Romans, who, speaking of himself as a regenerate man, complains quite tragically that sin dwells in him and that he performs every evil. Indeed, in this one chapter, he explicitly calls the concupiscence remaining in the regenerate sin fourteen times: verses 5, 7, 8, twice in 9, 11, three times in 13, 14, 17, 20, 23, 25. Added to this is that the Apostle attributes to the concupiscence remaining in the regenerate such effects as can only belong to sin properly so-called: such as to fight against this commandment of God: 'You shall not covet' (Rom. 7:7); to be sold under sin (v. 14); to work evil (verses 17 and 20); to war against the law of the mind and to render us captives under the law of sin which is in the members (verse 23). To which also pertains that of Rom. 8:7: 'The wisdom of the flesh is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can it be.' Gal. 5:17. The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish.

With these effects considered, it is clear that the concupiscence remaining in the regenerate is called sin, not only originally or by a certain metalepsis, because it is from sin or because it produces sin—just as a hand is called a hand because it is performed by a hand, or death is called pale because it induces paleness, as the Jesuits grunt, that concupiscence in the baptized is called sin because it descends originally from sin and is the fuel of sin—but it is called sin properly and formally because it fights against the law of God, and therefore by its own nature attracts the guilt of eternal damnation; for that concupiscence is prohibited by divine law is beyond controversy.

It is therefore trifling that Bellarmine objects: 1. That concupiscence is called sin by the Apostle improperly, by the figure of metonymy, because it is the cause of sin if it is obeyed. For the Apostle does not call concupiscence sin only insofar as it is obeyed, but rather insofar as it directly fights against the law of God: 'You shall not covet.' For he speaks not only of the second act, which consists in coveting an illicit thing, but of concupiscence itself considered in itself, the Apostle expressly says: 'I did not know sin except through the law: for I would not have known concupiscence unless the law had said: You shall not covet' (Rom. 7:7). Furthermore, the Apostle does not attribute a mere appellation of sin to the remnants of concupiscence, but describes in multiple ways what he wishes to be understood by the word sin: For 1. he says: 'In my flesh dwells no good.' 2. 'To me, willing to do good, evil is present.' He describes that evil privatively: 'The good that I will, I do not do; the evil that I do not will, I find no way to perform.' 4. He also describes the same positively: 'That I hate evil, this I do: I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind,' that is, the divine law which the Holy Spirit writes in the heart of the regenerate, 'indeed, taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members.' Likewise, 'With the mind I serve the law of God, with the flesh I serve the law of sin.' 5. He says it is such an evil that it fights against the commandment: 'You shall not covet.' Likewise, that it is to be crucified, mortified, destroyed: where anyone can easily understand that the Apostle is speaking not figuratively or improperly, but most properly.

Wherefore, neither can that be admitted which Costerus and others object: that the first motions of concupiscence, to which assent is not given, are not sin. Where the Jesuits mean this, that those motions are not only not imputed to the regenerate, but that the motions themselves, in themselves, are not evil or contrary to the law of God. If this were true, why, I ask, does the Savior pronounce him also liable to judgment who is angry with his brother rashly (Matt. 5:22)? So that not only 'Raca,' or the second act, makes one liable to the council; not only does the insult 'Fool' constitute one guilty of the fire of hell; but also anger, and indeed sudden anger, flaring up rashly and as if by chance, incurs the guilt of judgment; where only a fool and a blockhead would deny that the first act of concupiscence is noted.

The second objection of the Jesuit is that the Apostle does not say that concupiscence is properly sin. But this argument is also weak: As if it were of any necessity that this adverb, 'properly,' be added! Certainly, thus there will also be no sin in the unregenerate, because the Apostle, speaking of them, nowhere affirms that in them there is sin properly. Is it not enough to have explicitly named concupiscence sin? Nay, even to ascribe to it in the regenerate such effects as do not belong to anything except sin properly so called: and by their own nature are an evil of guilt.

Bellarmino replies: Not everything that is repugnant to the law is sin, although every sin is repugnant to the law: For, he says, many things are repugnant to laws which are not sins: as a man is repugnant to the law when he sins: and yet a man is not sin properly. But this objection ignores a notable malice. For the Jesuit knows that there is a huge dissimilarity in the example. For a man sins, not insofar as he is a man: but insofar as he is a corrupt man: so that the substance of man itself is one thing and different: but sin or the vice inherent in the substance of man is another and different thing. Which distinction the Jesuit will not prove can have a place in concupiscence until he has convinced us, along with Illyricus, that concupiscence or original sin is something substantial in man, or rather the very substance of man.

Thirdly, he objects: That the Apostle in this place is not speaking of himself and his like, the righteous: but has introduced the person of impious men, who not only have the fuel of sin: but are also overcome by that very fuel and dragged into various crimes.

But the Jesuit is talking nonsense: For that the Apostle is speaking of himself is too manifest to be evaded by any artifice: For otherwise he could not have said: I delight in the law of God, according to the inward man: Likewise, With the mind I serve the law of God. And the good that I would: The evil that I would not: To me willing to do good, evil is present: and other similar things of that kind, which can never be predicated of the impious, but only of the regenerate. But such is the power of truth that even the Jesuit himself is forced to admit that that interpretation cannot stand: But that the words of the Apostle must be accepted concerning the regenerate: Yet so that concupiscence is understood to be sin only insofar as it breaks out into a second act. But this nonsense has already been discussed and refuted.

The fourth argument: Where the condition of death has a place: there also is the evil of sin properly so called. But in the regenerate the condition of death has a place. Therefore in them also is the evil of sin properly so called. He confirms the connection of the major premise with that apostolic saying, Rom. 6:23: The wages of sin is death.

The fifth: Whatever must be put off, crucified, subdued, mortified in the regenerate: that must necessarily be evil or sin by its own nature: But all these things belong to concupiscence. Rom. 6:12, Gal. 5:16, Eph. 4:22, etc. Therefore.

The sixth and final argument is provided by the consensus of orthodox antiquity; concerning which one should especially see part 1 of the Examination of the Council of Trent by Dr. Chemnitz, under the title concerning the remains of original sin.

Another argument of our confirmation can be such: Whatever obscures and as it were obliterates the image of God in the regenerate, and thus hinders its restoration, that is rightly considered sin. But this is done in the regenerate by the evil of concupiscence. Therefore.

Augustine certainly supports our opinion, writing in book 5 against Julian, chapter 3: The concupiscence of the flesh, against which the good spirit lusts, is sin, because there is in it disobedience against the dominion of the mind: And it is the punishment of sin, because it was rendered to the merits of the disobedient: And it is the cause of sin, by the defection of the one consenting, or by the contagion of the one being born.

The minor premise is clear from the sayings of Scripture already produced: as also from that most sad complaint of the Apostle in Rom. 7:24: Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? Bellarmino, intending to refute this argument, is stuck, as they say: nor does anything else occur to him than that he childishly objects that misery in the Scriptures is for the most part attributed to punishment rather than to guilt. But the Jesuit does not notice that the Apostle in this whole passage is concerned to show that one must not only struggle strenuously with the spirit of the mind against the indwelling and working sin: but that the misery with which the regenerate are necessarily forced to conflict from time to time because of indwelling sin must also be deplored with groans and pursued with anxious sighs: until at last they are delivered through death and fully restored to that perfection to which man was created in the beginning.

And lest this should perhaps seem new and strange to the Jesuit, it is worth observing that the same Augustine, with a clearly similar comparison or example, shows that one thing can simultaneously be both sin and the punishment of sin: As he says, the blindness of the heart, which only the illuminator God removes, is both sin, by which one does not believe in God; and the punishment of sin, by which the proud heart is punished with a deserved correction; and the cause of sin, when some evil is committed by the error of a blind heart: So the concupiscence of the flesh, etc. With which agrees that in Tractate 41 on John: Let not sin reign in your mortal body: He does not say; LET IT NOT BE: but let it not REIGN. For as long as you live, it is necessary for SIN to be in your members: at least let its reign be taken away: let not that be done which it commands.

Third argument: Whatever is prohibited by the precepts of the Decalogue, that is properly sin. But concupiscence is prohibited by the ninth and tenth precepts of the Decalogue. Therefore.

The major premise is self-evident, according to that passage 1 John 3:4. Sin is ἀνομία.

Bernard in his Sermon on the Lord's Supper writes thus: In the case of the first man we all fell: but we fell upon a heap of stones, and into the mud. Whence we are not only defiled; but also wounded, and grievously shaken: We can indeed be washed quickly: but for healing, there is need of much treatment.

And after a few words: We have spoken concerning Concupiscence, that although Christ has taken away the condemnation: yet to humble us, He still suffers it (Concupiscence) to live in us, and to afflict us grievously, so that we may feel what Grace provides for us, and may always recur to its aid.

The Allegory of the Canaanites is applied here by some Fathers, whom God did not utterly destroy, so that He might exercise His people in this way to amend their security.

Latin:

COntrovertitur inter nos & Romanenses: Concupiscentia, quæ in Renatis est reliqua, propriè loquendo sit peccatum: hoc est, quiddam pugnans cum lege Dei, & naturâ suâ dignum æterna morte: an verò sit duntaxat pœna peccati, vel ut alij loquuntur, sit quiddam indifferens, quo vel benè, vel malè uti liceat. Qui status Controversiæ, ut plenius cognoscatur, notandum hoc loco sub quæstionem non venire concupiscentias illas naturales, quæ Conservationem Naturæ nostræ concernunt, & vulgò sub Appetituum definitione comprehenduntur: Neque illud etiam controverti: An reliquiæ illæ peccati Originalis, renatos, qui per Baptismum Christo sunt insiti, & fide in ipso sunt, Deo exosos faciant & damnent? Nihil enim condemnationis est illis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu: Rom. 8. Quin neque illud propriè hoc loco sub disputationem revocari: An reliquiæ illæ peccati Originalis, quando dominium in homine renato acquirunt & regnant, damnent? Nam nimis manifestum est illud Apostolicum: Si secundùm Carnem vixeritis, moriemini: Sed hoc tantùm quæritur, Quid concupiscentia illa, quæ in renatis post Baptismum, hac in vita est reliqua, & adversus spiritum subindè concupiscit Gal. 5, 17. licet ipsi non obtemperetur, quid, inquam, sit, per se, in se, ex se, & suâ naturâ, sicut Jesuitæ loquuntur: An nimirum sit res bona, pura, munda, sancta, placens Deo Legi divinæ conformis? An verò sit mala, & peccati rationem habeat? Cujus Quæstionis Negativam amplectuntur Romanenses, contendentes, Concupiscentiam hanc in Renatis post Baptismum reliquam, non esse propriè peccatum: sed rem bonam, puram legiq; Dei conformem: vel certè non contra sed saltem præter Legem Dei. Uti infra ipsosmet audiemus loquentes. Nos verò Affirmativam tenentes statuimus, Concupiscentiam hanc esse rem naturâ suâ malam, Deoque displicentem: ac proindè in se & per se, sive propriè loquendo, esse peccatum. Neque verò inanis est λογομαχία, quæ hac de re instituitur disputatio, uti nonnullis cavillari libuit: Quin de Articulo fidei Christianæ inter præcipuos haud postremò pugnatur: An nimirum Homo renatus hac in vita possit perfectè Legi Dei satis facecere, & per opera promereri vitam æternam? id quod sub Negativâ suâ occultant Romanenses.

Cæterùm tota hæc Controversia vix rectiùs explicabitur, quàm si initiò ostendatur, Quidnam Concupiscentia sit in ijs, qui per Aquam & Spiritum no sunt regenerati? Deinde verò, Quomodo hæc ipsa Concupiscentia per Baptismum tollatur? Undè statim ultrò elucescet, quid de Concupiscentia post Baptismum reliquâ sit sentiendum.

Quoad prius illud, extra Controversiam est positum, Concupiscentiam in nondum Renatis idipsum esse, quod Peccatum Originis solet nominari: nempè non modò privationem, sive carentiam, ut loquuntur, Justitiæ Originalis debitæ inesse: sed & horribilem depravationem omnium virium humanarum: quæ damnet, & afferat æternam mortem his, qui non renascuntur per Aquam & Spiritum: Joh. 3, 5. Hæc ergò depravatio propriè concupiscentia nominatur proptereà quòd vetus homo per Concupiscentias erroris corrumpitur, uti loquitur Apostolus, Eph. 4, 22. Verùm quomodo hæc concupiscentia in Baptismo tollatur: id verò est, de quo maximè hodiè controvertitur. Doctores Pontificii cumprimis Jesuwitæ, omnimodè eam aboleri statuunt, uti mox in Ἀντιθέσει ostendemus. Nos verò, uti præcedenti controversia tertiâ demonstratum, sentimus cum D. Augustino: Concupiscentiam carnis dimitti in Baptismo, non ut non sit: sed ut in peccatum non imputetur: lib. 1. de nuptijs & concup. cap. 25. Vel ut clariùs mentem nostram explicemus: cùm in Concupiscentia carnis sive Peccato Originis sint duo, depravatio omnium virium & Reatus: statuimus, Hunc quidem in Baptismo planè tolli, neque quicquam ejus, quod ad damnationem Renatis obsit, remanere: Interim tamen vires depravatas, licèt & ipsæ renovari incipiant: manere reliquas: neque Renovationem hac in vita plenè unquàm absolvi. Undè jam promtum erit colligere, Concupiscentiam hanc, in renatis reliquam, licèt ad damnationem ipsis non imputetur: naturâ tamen suâ sive in se, & per se consideratam, reverà esse peccatum.

Affirmativæ hujus nostræ argumentum primum monstrat Apostolus capite septimo ad Romanos, qui de se Renato verba faciens, Peccatum in se habitare, & omne malum perpetrare, satis tragicè conqueritur: Imò hoc uno capite, reliquam in Renatis Concupiscentiam decies quater Peccatum disertè nominat: versu 5. 7. 8. bis 9. 11. 13. ter. 14. 17. 20. 23 25. Accedit quòd Apostolus Concupiscentiæ in renatis reliquæ ejusmodi tribuit Effectus, qui non nisi Peccato propriè sic dicto competere possunt: quales sunt: pugnare cum hoc præcepto DEI: Non Concupisces: Rom 7, 7. Venundare sub peccatum: v. 14. operari malum: versu 17. & 20. repugnare legi mentis, & captivos nos reddere sub Lege peccati, quæ est in membris, versu 23. Quo pertinet & illud Rom. 8, 7. Sapientiæ carnis inimicitia est adversus DEUM: Nam Legi DEI non subditur: siquidem ne potest quidem. Galat. 5, 17. Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum: Spiritus autem adversus carnem: hæc autem inter se mutuò adversantur, ut non, quæ volueritis, ea faciatis.

His effectibus consideratis, patet, Concupiscentiam in renatis reliquam, dici peccatum, non tantùm Originaliter, aut per quandam μετάληψιν, quia ex peccato est, vel quia peccatum efficit: sicut Scriptura dicitur manus, quia à manu perficitur: aut mors pallida, quia pallorem inducit: quemadmodum Jesuitae grunniunt, quod Concupiscentia in baptizatis dicatur peccatum, quia ex peccato Originaliter descendit, & est fomes peccati: Sed peccatum dicitur propriè, & formaliter, quia repugnat Legi DEI, ac proindè reatum aeternae damnationis suâ naturâ attrahit: Concupiscentiam enim lege divina prohiberi, extra controversiam est.

Nugatorium proindè est, quòd excipit Bellarminus 1. Concupiscentiam ab Apostolo nominari peccatum impropriè, per figuram Metonymiæ, quod sit causa peccati, si ei obediatur. Neque enim eatenùs tantùm Concupiscentiam nominat Apostolus peccatum, quatenùs ei obeditur: sed potiùs, quatenùs directè pugnat cum Lege DEI: Non Concupisces. Non enim de actu tantùm secundo, qui in Concupiscendo rem illicitam consistit: sed de ipsa Concupiscentia in se confiderata, expressè dicit Apostolus: Peccatum non cognovi, nisi per Legem: Nam & Concupiscentiam non novissem, nisi Lex dixisset: Non Concupisces. Rom. 7, 7. Deindè Apostolus non nudam appellationem peccati tribuit reliquiis Concupiscentiae: sed multipliciter describit, quid velit intelligi vocabulo peccati: Nam 1. dicit: In carne mea non habitat bonum. 2. Volenti mihi facere bonum, adjacet malum. 3. Malum illud describit privativè: Non quod volo bonum, hoc facio, perficere non invenio. 4. Idem describit etiam positivè: Quod odi malum, hoc facio: Video legem aliam in membris meis repugnantem legi mentis mea: id est, legi divinae, quam Spiritus sanctus scribit in corde renatorum, imò captivantem me sub lege peccati, quae est in membris meis. Item, Mente servio legi DEI, Carne servio legi peccati. 5. Dicit tale esse malum, quod pugnat cum praecepto: Non Concupisces: Item quòd sit crucifigendum, mortificandum, destruendum: Ubi sanè Apostolum non figuratè aut impropriè: sed propriissimè loqui quivis facilè intelligit.

Quapropter neque illud admitti potest, quod Costerus & alii objiciunt: Primos Concupiscentiae motus, quibus non praebetur assensus, peccatum non esse. Ubi hoc volunt Jesuwitae, Renatis illos motus non modò non imputari: sed & ipsos motus per se, non esse malos, aut Legi DEI contrarios. Hoc si verum, cur obsecro Servator illum etiam judicio obnoxium esse pronunciat, qui temerè irascitur fratri suo: Matth. 5, 22. Ita ut non solum Racha, sive actus secundus Concilio faciat obnoxium: non item Fatui tantùm convitium, Gehennae incendii reum constituat: sed & ira, & ira quidem subita, temerè & quasi fortuito exardescens, judicii reatum contrahat: ubi actum primum Concupiscentiae notari, non nisi bardus & blenno negaverit.

Altera Exceptio Jesuitae est, quòd Apostolus non dicat, Concupiscentiam propriè esse peccatum. Sed elumbis & haec est argutatio: Quasi verò necessitatis alicujus sit, ut adjiciatur hoc Adverbium, Propriè? Certè sic nullum etiam peccatum erit in non Renatis, quia de his verba faciens Apostolus, nuspiam affirmat, in illis esse peccatum propriè. Annon sufficit, Concupiscentiam disertè nominasse peccatum: Imò tales ei effectus etiam in renatis adscribere, qui non nisi peccato propriè sic dicto competunt: & ratione sui sunt malum culpae.

Respondet Bellarminus: Non omne quod repugnat legi esse peccatum, quamvis omne peccatum legi repugnet: Nam, inquit, multa legibus repugnant, quae peccata non sunt: ut Homo repugnat legi, quando peccat: & tamen Homo non est peccatum propriè. Sed insignem malitiam respit haec objectio. Novit enim Jesuita ingentem esse dissimilitudinem in Exemplo. Homo enim peccat, non quatenùs est Homo: sed quatenùs est Homo corrùptus: Ita ut áliud ac diversum sit ipsa substantia Hominis: aliud verò & diversum sit peccatum sive vitium Substantiae Hominis inhaerês. Quam distinctionem in Concupiscentia quoq; Locum habere posse, non prius probabit Jesuita: quàm cum Illyrico fidem nobis fecerit, Concupiscentiam sive peccatum Originis in Homine esse Substantiale aliquid, vel ipsam potiùs Substantiam Hominis.

Tertiò excipit: Apostolum hoc loco non loqui de se, suisq; similibus justis: sed induxisse personam hominum impiorum, qui non solùm fomitem habent: sed etiam ab ipso fomite vincuntur & pertrahuntur in varia flagitia.

Sed nugatur Jesuita: Nam Apostolum de se loqui, manifestiùs est, quàm ut ullo artificio eludi queat: Aliàs enim dicere non potuisset: Condelector legi DEI, quoad interiorem hominem: Item, Mente lege DEI servio. Et Bonum quod volo: Malum quod nolo: Bonum facere volenti mihi, malum adjacet: & id genus consimilia alia, quae nunquàm de Impiis, sed tantùm de Renatis praedicari possunt. Sed tanta est vis Veritatis, ut vel ipse Jesuita fateri necesse habeat, interpretationem illam subsistere non posse: Sed de Renatis Verba Apostoli accipi debere: Verùm ità, ut Concupiscentia tantùm intelligatur esse peccatum, quatenùs in actum secundum erumpit. Sed haec nugatio jam modò est discussa & refutata.

Quartum argumentum: Ubi mortis conditio habet locum: ibi etiam est malum peccati propriè sic dicti. Atqui in renatis locum habet Mortis conditio. Ergo in illis etiam est malum peccati propriè sic dicti. Connexam majoris confirmat illud Apostolicum Rom. 5, 23. Stipendium peccati est Mors.

Quintum: Quicquid est exuendum, crucifigendum, debellandum, mortificandum in Renatis: illud malum sive Peccatum naturâ suâ sit, necesse est: Atqui Concupiscentiae ista omnia competunt. Rom 6, 12. Gal. 5, 16. Eph. 4, 22. &c. Ergo.

Sextum & postremum argumentum suppeditat consensus Orthodoxae Antiquitatis; de quo potissimùm videatur pars 1. Examinis Concilij Trident. Doct. Chemnit. tit. de Reliquijs peccati Originalis.

Alterum confirmationis nostrae argumentum tale esse potest: Quicquid imaginem DEI in renatis obfuscat & quasi obliterat, adeoǵ, ejus resturationem impedit, id peccatum jure censetur. Atqui Concupiscentia malo in Renatis hoc fit. E.

Augustinus certè nostrae suffragatur sententiae, scribens lib. 5. contra Julian. cap. 3. Concupiscentia carnis, adversus quam bonus concupiscit spirit, Peccatum est, quia inest illi inobedientia contra dominatum mentis: Et peccati paena est, quia reddita est meritis inobedientis: Et causa peccati est, defectione consentientis, vel contagione nascentis.

Minor patet ex Scripturae dictis jam productis: ut & ex tristissima illa querela Apostoli Rom. 7, 24. Me miserum, quis liberabit me de corpore mortis hujus? Argumentum hoc refutaturo Bellarmino, aqua, quod dicitur, haeret: neque quicquam succurrit aliud, quàm quòd pueriliter excipit, Miseriam in scripturis ùt plurimùm paenae potiùs, quàm culpae tribui. Sed non animadvertit Jesuita, Apostolum in eo totum hoc loco esse, ut ostendat, non tantùm adversus inhabitans & operans peccatum, Spiritu mentis strenuè luctandum esse: sed gemitibus etiam deplorandam, & suspiriis anxiis prosequendam esse miseriam, cum qua ob inhaerens peccatum renati subindè conflictari necesse habent: donec tandem per mortem liberentur & plenè restituantur illi perfectioni; ad quam initio homo erat conditus.

Et ne fortè novum ac insolens hoc videatur Jesuitae, observationem meretur, quòd idem Augustinus accommodato planè simili sive exemplo ostendit, Unum simul posse esse & peccatum & paenam peccati: Sicut inquiens, Caecitas cordis, quam solus removet illuminator DEUS, & peccatum est, quo in DEUM non creditur; & Paena peccati, quâ cor superbum digna animadversione punitur: & causa peccati cùm mali aliquid caeci cordis errore committitur: Ita Concupiscentia carnis &c. Cum quibus consentit illud Tractatu 41. in Johannem: Non regnet peccatum in vestro mortali corpore: Non ait; NON SIT: sed non REGNET. Quamdiu enim vivis, PECCATUM necesse est esse in membris tuis: saltem illi Regnum auferatur: non fiat, quod jubet.

Tertium argumentum: Quicquid praeceptis Decalogi prohibetur, illud propriè est peccatum. Atqui Concupiscentia prohibetur nono & decimo praeceptis Decalogi. Ergo.

Major est ἀυτὸ πιστὸς, juxtà illud 1. Joh. 3, 4. Peccatum est ἀνομία.

Bernhardus in Serm. de Caena Domini sic scribit: In casu primi hominis cecidimus omnes: cecidimus autem super acervum lapidum, & in lutum. Unde non solùm inquinati; sed & vulnerati sumus, & graviter quassati: Lavari quidem citò possumus: ad sanandum verò opus est curatione multa.

Et post pauca: De Concupiscentia diximus, quòd licet damnationem abstulerit Christus: tamen ad humiliandos nos, ipsam (Concupiscentiam) adhuc patitur vivere in nobis, & graviter affligere nos, ut sentiamus, quid nobis Gratia præstet, & semper ad illius auxilium recurramus.

Accommodatur huc à Patribus nonnullis Allegoria Cananæorum, quos Deus non prorsus delevit, ut populum suum hac ratione exerceret ad emendandam ejus securitatem.


### Controversy IV. And the last concerning Original Sin: Second Part. Examining the doctrine of the Papists

Examining the doctrine of the Papists.

The Romanists in this chapter of this Article also hold a sufficiently foul error, establishing that not only is the guilt of Original sin, as well as that of the rest committed before Baptism, remitted through Baptism: which indeed we also most willingly concede: But also that a perfect and in all respects absolute Renewal takes place: so that a Man regenerated through Baptism can, even in this life, perfectly satisfy the Law of God.

The Council of Trent defined this error quite boldly in Session 5, Decree 1, on the 17th of June in the year 1546, in these words: If anyone denies that the guilt of Original sin is remitted through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is conferred in Baptism, or even asserts that all that which has the true and proper nature of sin is not taken away: but says that it is only shaved off, or not imputed, let him be anathema.

Andradius in book 3 of his Orthodox Explanations explains the matter more plainly, writing thus on page 259: When Justice has been restored to us in the sacred laver, the whole nature of sin has truly been abolished and scraped away at the same time, and the stings of Concupiscence remain, which prick and torment us, and perpetually remind us of our misery, but with the fountain of sin stopped up and blocked, they are entirely devoid of any nature of sin: And thus, the Concupiscence that remains after Baptism is entirely devoid of all filth and nature of sin.

The Colonians, against the book of the Reformation, teach that Concupiscence is not only remitted in Baptism through grace to believers, so that it is not imputed for condemnation: but that it is brought about that Concupiscence itself, in itself and in its own nature, is no longer an evil thing, and displeasing to GOD: and even if GOD wished to enter into Judgment with it, with the veil of grace removed, He could not nevertheless make it guilty of eternal condemnation. Andradius also strives to defend this very opinion against Dr. Chemnitz, in the book already cited, page 269 and following.

Hence were born those emblems full of impiety, which Johannes à Daventria produced in his Refutation of the second Article of the Augsburg Confession, writing thus: It is not commanded to the flesh, nor to the sensitive Soul, but to the intellectual, Thou shalt not covet: because that cannot but covet carnal things. And shortly after: For if it were commanded to the flesh, Thou shalt not covet, it would be the same as if GOD had commanded the Sun and Moon not to shine: the Fire, not to burn: the Water, not to flow down: a Stone cast from a sling, not to fall. For all these act by the impelling force of Nature: Thus the flesh, or the sensitive Soul, cannot be without this corruption, which it contracted from the protoparent. Bellarmine book 5 on the loss of grace. and on the state of sin, chapter 5, page 370, C. and D., explains his own mind and that of his associates thus: The whole Controversy is, whether the Corruption of nature, and especially Concupiscence in itself, and from its own nature, such as it is found even in the baptized and justified, is properly Original Sin. For the Adversaries contend that it is: But the Catholics deny it, seeing that, with the will healed through justifying grace, they teach that the remaining diseases not only do not constitute men guilty: but cannot even constitute them so, since they do not have the true nature of sin.

Furthermore, the reasons and arguments by which the Romanists were moved to undertake the patronage of this error are brought forward variously by various people. The Council of Trent appeals to the infallible authority of the Roman Church, which in this part is unaccountable. For this Concupiscence, it says, which the Apostle sometimes calls Sin, the Holy Synod declares that the Catholic Church has never understood to be called sin, because it is truly and properly sin in the Regenerate: but because it is from sin, and inclines to sin: If anyone however thinks otherwise, let him be anathema. Which decree indeed exhibits a notable specimen of stupidity in that which they add concerning their own understanding, as if it mattered much what those Fathers understand: or if it could suffice to give assurance to the error, if they say that they understand it so, the Apostle is surely more powerful to us than the authority of those Fathers. Furthermore, that decree manifestly overturns itself: while what it takes away with one hand, it immediately bestows freely with the other. For let someone explain to us: whether that which is from sin, and inclines to sin, in the sight of GOD obtains the respect of a virtue or of a vice. It has commonly prevailed in the Schools: As is the cause, so is the effect: And again: From the effect, judgment ought to be made concerning the cause: Therefore if Concupiscence in the regenerate flows from sin, as the Council confesses: then certainly it must also be Sin properly so called: unless perhaps by an unheard-of absurdity they prefer to assert that that which is properly sin can be the Efficient cause of that which is good, and does not displease God. Furthermore, if Concupiscence in the regenerate inclines to sin: then it itself will also be Evil in itself: For that which is good in itself and by its own nature: cannot incline to evil. Thus, therefore, the Fathers of that Council, together with the truth, have also lost the very use of right reason, by the just judgment of GOD.

Bellarmino, in the sixth chapter of the book already cited before, attempts to give assurance to his error from the Holy Scriptures: At the beginning indeed from chapter 1, 15 of James, arguing thus: Each one is tempted by his own concupiscence, being drawn away and enticed: Then concupiscence, when it has conceived, brings forth sin: but sin, when it is finished, brings forth death: Where James does not call Concupiscence, that is, the prone power and its first motion, Sin: But then indeed the imperfect offspring that is, pleasure not fully deliberated, he calls a sin, but not a mortal one: Finally, he defines the perfect of the parts, that is, desire with full consent, as clearly a mortal sin.

But a shameful begging of the question is committed at the beginning. For it has not been proven that Concupiscence is therefore not a sin because the Apostle does not call it a sin ἀὐτολεξεί. Nor is it as he objects, that Concupiscence begets sin. Therefore it itself is not a sin. For although the same sin is not begotten by itself, yet nothing prevents one sin from being able to be begotten by another. Concupiscence, therefore, which is proper to Original sin, when it conceives, it begets: but it begets actual sin, not itself. Now the begetter communicates with the begotten, if not always in species, at least in one and the same Genus. Just as, therefore, it does not follow: He who begets an ass is not himself an Ass: But the contrary is true: He who begets an ass, he himself is also an ass: Since everything that begets begets something similar to itself: and every begotten thing participates in the nature of its begetter: So it does not follow: Concupiscence begets sin. Therefore it itself is not a sin: But the contrary should rather be inferred by force. Then a gross Ignorance of the Refutation and a Sophism of ἐπιροζητήσεως is committed. For the Apostle is not arguing in this place how and when mortal sin begins to be born, as the Jesuit dreams: but he only shows whence it emerges: For thus he proceeds step by step: The cause of eternal death is the consummation of sin: but this sin arises from evil desires, which in turn have their root in Concupiscence: thus manifestly intending to show that the root of our damnation is in ourselves: and consequently that Concupiscence itself is in us a thing evil in itself and by its own nature: which is irrefragably proven from the words of James: If Concupiscence begets sin, then it too will be a sin. The reason for the connection is most firm: because such as the fruits are, such is the tree: Matt 7:17. And such as the Effect is, such also is the cause.

But Bellarmine insists: If simple Concupiscence is a sin, it is nevertheless not a mortal sin: because, as James testifies, this sin finally begets death when it is performed.

I answer that a Sophism παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον is committed. For a generic and common effect is removed from a remote cause beyond all reason, because it is attributed to the proximate one: For it is not the case that, because a father begets a mortal, therefore the grandfather did not beget a mortal. Thus, it is not the case that Original sin is not mortal because a performed or actual sin is a mortal sin: But because this is mortal, therefore that is too. Furthermore, the Apostle wished to call Actual sin Mortal because it proximately and more notoriously begets death than latent Concupiscence.

He seeks a second argument from Rom. 7:17, 18, where the Apostle speaks thus: But now it is not I who work it: but sin that dwells in me: For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no good. Since, therefore, the Apostle affirms that the Motion of Concupiscence is not his work, and by this cannot be imputed to him: Since he also says that such evil is not in himself, but in his Flesh: he teaches quite openly that Concupiscence in a justified Man is not properly a sin that can make one guilty.

I answer. The argument fails: 1. By the Sophism ὧδε τι π' π και ἁπλῶς. For the Apostle does not simply and entirely deny that that Motion of Concupiscence is his work: For in the verses immediately preceding, he expressly confessed that he is the operator of Evil: For what I will, he says, that I do not do: but what I hate, that I do, verse 15. Therefore, if the Apostle were now denying in the Jesuitical sense that the Motion of Concupiscence is his work, then he would be manifestly contradicting himself. Therefore, καὶ ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο must both be understood. The Apostle is dividing his person εἰς ἄλλον καὶ ἄλλον, into one and another: denying in this place that he works evil from that part by which he was reborn: but at the same time asserting that from that part by which the flesh always lusts against the spirit, he designates the evil. Then arises the Sophistication ἑ μὴ αἴτιε ὡς αἰτίε: For the Evil is not not imputed to the Apostle by God for the reason that he did not designate it in any way at all: as the Jesuit fabulates: For he himself confesses the contrary about himself: but because that which is in itself, and by itself or by its own nature, is evil and damnable, is not imputed to believers on account of the merit of Christ: For there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8:1.

Latin:

Pontificiorum doctrinam examinans.

ROmanenses in hoc etiam capite Articuli hujus satis fœdum tenent errorem statuentes, non modò Originalis peccati, ut & reliquorum ante Baptismum commissorum Reatum per Baptismum remitti: quod quidem nos quoque libentissimè concedimus: Sed & perfectam omnibusque numeris absolutam Renovationem fieri: ita ut Homo per Baptismum regeneratus, etiam hac in vita, perfectè Legi Dei possit satisfacere.

Definivit errorem istum satis audacter Concilium Tridentinum Sess. 5. Decreto 1. die 17. Junij An. 1546. his verbis: Si quis per Jesu Christi Domini nostri gratiam, quæ Baptismate confertur, reatum Originalis peccati remitti negat, aut etiam asserit, non tolli totum id, quod veram & propriam rationem peccati habet: sed illud tantùm dicit radi, aut non imputari, anathema sit.

Andradius lib. 3. Orthodoxarum explicationum planiùs rem explicat, sic scribens p. 259. Cùm in sacro lavacro Justitia nobis fuerit restituta, omnis sanè peccati ratio simul abolita & abrasa est, manentq́; Concupiscentiarum aculei, qui nos pungant & torqueant, nosq́; miseria nostræ perpetuò admoneant, sed peccati fonte obturato & oppilato, omnis rationis peccati prorsus sunt expertes: Atq; ita, quæ post Baptismum Concupiscentia manet, omni prorsus peccati turpitudine atq; ratione caret.

Colonienses contra librum Reformationis docent, Concupiscentiam in Baptismo per gratiam credentibus non tantùm remitti, ut non imputetur ad damnationem: sed effici, ut ipsa Concupiscentia in se, & sua natura non sit ampliùs res mala, & displicens DEO: & etiamsi DEUS cum illa vellet intrare in Judicium, remoto gratiæ umbraculo, non tamen posset reum facere æternæ damnationis. Quam ipsam sententiam contra D. Chemnitium defendere studet Andradius quoq;, libro jam citato, pag. 269. & seqq.

Hinc nata sunt Emblemata illa impietatis plenissima, quæ prodidit Johannes à Daventria in Refutatione Articuli secundi Confessionis Augustana, sic scribens: Non præceptum est carni, nec Animæ sensitivæ, sed intellectivæ, Non Concupisces: quia illa non potest non Concupiscere carnalia. Et mox: Si enim carni præciperetur, Non concupisces, perindè esset, ac si DEUS Soli & Lunæ præcepisset, ne lucerent: Igni, ne arderet: Aquæ, ne deflueret: Lapidi fundà emisso, ne decideret. Hæc enim omnia agunt Naturæ vi impellente: Sic caro, seu Anima sensitiva hâc corruptelâ, quàm à protoparente contraxit, carere non potest. Bellarminus lib. 5. de amiss. grat. & statu pecc. cap. 5. pag. 370. C. & D. mentem suam suorumq́; sociorum sic explicat: Tota Controversia est, utrum Corruptio naturæ, ac præsertim Concupiscentia per se, & ex natura sua, qualis invenitur etiam in baptizatis & justificatis, sit propriè Peccatum Originis. Id enim Adversarij contendunt: Catholici autem negant, quippè qui, sanâta voluntate per gratiam Justificantem, docent, reliquos morbos non solum non constituere homines reos: sed neq; posse constituere, cùm non habeant veram peccati rationem.

Cæterùm rationes atque argumenta, quibus moti Romanenses erroris istius patrocinium susceperunt, varia à variis proferuntur. Concilium Tridentinum provocat ad infallibilem Ecclesiæ Romanæ autoritatem, quæ hac in parte sit a̓νυπεύθυνος. Hanc enim, inquit, Concupiscentiam, quam aliquando Apostolus Peccatum appellat, Sancta Synodus declarat Ecclesiam Catholicam nunquàm intellexisse peccatum appellari, quod verè & propriè in Renatis peccatum sit: sed quia ex peccato est, & ad peccatum inclinat: Si quis autem contrarium senserit, Anathema sit. Quod sanè decretum insigne stoliditatis specimen exhibet in eo, quod de intellectu suo adjiciunt, quasi multùm referat, quid Patres isti intelligant: vel sufficere queat ad fidem errori faciendam, si dicant, se ita intelligere, potior sanè nobis Apostoli est, quàm Patrum istorum autoritas. Deindè decretum istud seipsum manifestè evertit: dùm quod una manu adimit, statim alterâ ultrò largitur. E disserat enim nobis aliquis, Nùmid quod ex peccato est: & ad peccatum inclinat, in conspectu DEI virtutis, an vitij respectum sortiatur. Vulgò in Scholis obtinuit illud: Qualis causa, talis effectus: Et rursum: Ex effectu de causa debet fieri judicium: Ergo si Concupiscentia in Renatis ex peccato profluit, ut fatetur Concilium: utiq; & Peccatum propriè sic dictum sit necesse est: nisi fortè per inauditam absurditatem adserere malint, id, quod propriè est peccatû, posse esse causam Efficientem ejus, quod bonum est, Deoq; nõ displicet. Porrò, si Concupiscentia in Renatis ad peccatum inclinat: utiq; & ipsa Malum per se erit: Nam quod per se & suâ naturâ bonum est: ad malum inclinare nequit. Sic ergo Patres istius Concilii unâ cum veritate, ipsum quoque rectæ rationis usum, justo DEI judicio, perdiderunt.

Bellarminus capite sexto libri jam antè citati, ex Scripturis Sacris fidem errori facere conatur: Initiò quidem ex cap. 1, 15. Jacobi sic arguens: Unusquisque tentatur à Concupiscentia sua abstractus & illectus: Deinde Concupiscentia cùm conceperit, parit peccatum: peccatum verò, cùm consummatum fuerit, parit mortem: Ubi Jacobus Concupiscentiam, hoc est, potentiam pronam, & primum ejus motum non appellat Peccatum: Deindè verò partum imperfectum, hoc est, delectationem non plenè deliberatam, peccatum vocat, sed non mortale: Deniq; partium perfectum, hoc est, desiderium cum pleno consensu, peccatum planè mortale esse definit.

Sed turpis initiò committitur petitio principii. Neq; enim probatum est, Concupiscentiam ideò non esse peccatum: quia Apostolus non ἀὐτολεξεί eam nominat peccatum. Neq; est, ut objiciat, Concupiscentiam gignere peccatum. Ergo ipsam non esse peccatum. Nam etsi peccatum idem non gignitur à seipso: tamen quô minùs peccatum unum gigni possit ab alio, nihil prohibet. Concupiscentia igitur, quæ est peccati Originalis propria, cùm concipit, gignit: sed gignit peccatum actuale, non seipsum. Gignens autem cum genito si non specie semper, saltem Genere uno eodemq; communicat. Quemadmodum ergò non sequitur: Qui gignit asinum, non est ipse Asinus: Sed contrarium verum est: Qui gignit asinum, is ipse quoque est asinus: Siquidem unumquodque gignens gignit sibi simile: & omne genitum participat naturam sui gignentis: Ita non sequitur: Concupiscentia gignit peccatum. Ergo ipsa non est peccatum: Sed contrarium potius per violentum inferri debet. Deindè crassa committitur Ignoratio Elenchi & Sophisma ἐπιροζητήσεως. Non enim Apostolus hoc loco disputat, quomodo & quando incipiat nasci peccatum mortale, prout somniat Jesuwita: sed tantùm ostendit: undè illud emergat: Sic enim gradatim procedit: Mortis æternæ causa, est peccati consummatio: peccatum verò hoc oritur ex pravis desideriis, quæ rursum radicem suam habent in Concupiscentia: sic manifestè ostensurus: Radicem nostræ damnationis in nobis ipsis esse: ac proindè ipsam quoque Concupiscentiam in nobis esse Rem malam per se & suâ naturâ: id quod ex verbis Jacobi irrefragabiliter evincitur: Si Concupiscentia gignit peccatum: utique & ipsa erit peccatum. Ratio connexi est firmissima: quia quales sunt fructus: talis & arbor: Matth 7,17. Et qualis Effectus: talis etiam causa.

Sed instat Bellarminus: Si Concupiscentia simplex est peccatum: non tamen est mortale peccatum: quia Jacobo teste, peccatum hoc peractum demum gignit mortem.

Respondeo, committi Sophisma παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Effectus enim genericus & communis præter omnem rationem removetur à causa remota, eò quòd tribuitur proximæ: Neque enim, quia pater gignit mortalem: Ideò avus mortalem non genuit. Sic non ideò Originale peccatum non est mortale, quia peccatum peractum sive actuale est peccatum mortale: Sed quia hoc mortale, Ergo & illud. Cæterùm ideò Apostolus peccatum Actuale nominare voluit Mortale, quia proximè & magis notoriè gignit mortem, quàm Concupiscentia latens.

Secundum argumentum petit ex cap. 7, 17. 18. ad Rom. ubi Apostolus sic loquitur: Nunc autem non ego operor illud: sed quod habitat in me peccate tum: Scio enim, quia non habitat in me, id est, in carne meabonum. Cùm Ergo Apostolus affirmet, Motum Concupiscentiæ non esse suum opus, ac per hoc non posse sibi imputari: Cùm item dicat, ejusmodi malum non esse in se, sed in Carne sua: satis apertè docet, Concupiscentiam in Homine justificato non esse propriè peccatum, quod reum facere possit.

Respondeo. Fallit argumentum: 1. Sophismate ὧδε τι π' π και ἁπλῶς. Neque enim Apostolus simpliciter & ex toto negat, Motum illum Concupiscentiæ esse suum opus: Nam in versibus immediatè præcedentibus, disertè fassus est, se Mali operatorem esse: Non enim quod volo, inquit, hoc facio: sed quod odi, facio versu 15. Proindè si jam sensu Jesuwitico negaret Apostolus, Motum Concupiscentiæ esse suum opus: tùm sibi ipsi manifestè contradiceret. Ergo καὶ ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο utrumq; intelligi debet. Dividit nimirùm suam personam Apostolus εἰς ἄλλον καὶ ἄλλον, in alium & alium: negans hoc loco se operari malum ex ea parte, quâ renatus erat: simul autem asserens ex ea parte, quâ caro semper concupiscit adversus spiritum, se designare malum. Deinde oritur Sophisticatio ἑ μὴ αἴτιε ὡς αἰτίε: Non enim eo respectu Malum non imputatur à Deo Apostolo, quasi illud planè nullo pacto designaverit: uti Jesuwita fabulatur: Nam contrarium ipsemet de se fatetur: sed ideò, quia id quod in se, & per se sive naturâ suâ est malum & damnabile, non imputatur credentibus propter meritum Christi: Nulla enim condemnatio est his, qui sunt in Christo Jesu, Rom. 8, 1.


### Controversy IV. And the last concerning Original Sin: Second Part. Examining the doctrine of the Papists (continued)

Finally, the error of Ignorance of the Refutation is committed: For the Apostle, asserting in this place that sin dwells not in himself, but in his flesh, does not oppose the Flesh to the Soul as one Essential part to another: as the Jesuit philosophizes too ἀπαιδεύτως: But speaking about himself as a reborn Man, he opposes Flesh and Spirit to each other: pronouncing the latter to be immune from sin. Now, that the Apostle is not speaking about the nature and Substance of the exterior flesh or visible Body, at least that is proven by the fact that he pronounces our Bodies elsewhere to be temples of the Holy Spirit. Flesh, therefore, in this place is taken for the whole Nature of man, consisting of both essential parts, but insofar as it is corrupted by the sin of Origin. Just as, conversely, by the name of Spirit, the whole man is likewise understood, but insofar as he is already regenerated. The Jesuit is therefore very much mistaken when he interprets flesh in this place as the other Substantial part of Man: and from there tries to establish that error also, as if Man had suffered corruption only of the lower faculties, while the higher ones remained uncorrupted.

Nor does the subsequent verse 23 stand in the way of this our response, where the Apostle says: I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind: And I myself with the mind serve the law of GOD: but with the flesh the law of sin.

For by the Law of the members is understood the External Man, or Man from that part by which he is repeatedly exercised by the desires of the flesh: Just as the Law of the mind denotes the interior Man, or Man from that part by which he is inclined and ready to render obedience to the divine law. By which appellations a diversity of Substance is not noted: but a distinction of faculties is sought: of which one, which pertains to regeneration, obtains the appellation of the Internal or new Man: the other, which is proper to natural depravity, is marked by the term of the External or old man or the law of the members. Thus the Apostle asserting, With the mind I serve the law of GOD: But with the flesh the law of sin: by the Mind he does not understand the human intellect or reason: but the will renewed by the holy Spirit, and repeatedly resisting the Flesh: But by the Flesh he understands the vicious desires and inordinate motions, which are always contrary to the Spirit of the mind, Galat. 5, 17.

The Jesuit seeks a third argument from chap. 1 of Romans, where the Apostle speaks thus: There is therefore now no condemnation to them who are in CHRIST JESUS. The Apostle therefore signifies not only that there is no condemnation for those Justified in Christ on account of concupiscence: but also that there is nothing in them worthy of Condemnation, or that there is no cause of condemnation in them.

But a manifest crime of Falsehood is committed. For the Apostle does not say, That there is no sin in the Elect: Or, That there is nothing condemnable in the Elect: as the Jesuit renders it: But that there is no condemnation. Now Condemnable and Condemnation differ greatly: the former denotes guilt: but the latter denotes the very act of condemnation. Now there can be guilt: where yet the punishment is not immediately placed by the act itself. As for example: if a civil Magistrate remits the punishment of a murderer: it can indeed truly be said, There is now no condemnation or punishment in that man: But it is not therefore true, if I should wish to say: There is nothing condemnable in that man. In the very same way, although condemnation does not actually have a place in the reborn, because the person is reconciled to GOD through faith: it ought not therefore to be denied: That there is nothing at all condemnable in the same: that is, that Concupiscence or the sin of Origin is not by its nature sin, worthy of eternal death. The reason is: because in Baptism the disease itself, or sin, is not removed: but the Guilt of sin: and indeed considered not with respect to the sin: but with respect to the person.

The Jesuit objects: If guilt is removed: then certainly sin is also removed: Since Guilt is that which is properly called sin. But the Sophist plays with the equivocation of the word sin: which sometimes signifies the very horrible depravity of Nature, sometimes the Guilt of sin. Now if it be taken in the latter sense, we indeed grant that the Guilt is removed, and thus sin itself: but so that that former notation of sin nevertheless remains in the Reborn: since it is never put off or removed in this life.

Furthermore the Jesuit objects: That guilt is entirely inseparable from that which by its nature is worthy of eternal condemnation: Therefore, he infers, if Concupiscence remains in the reborn, it is by its nature worthy of eternal condemnation: then Guilt also will remain in them. But this knot is easily solved, if only this is attended to, that Guilt is considered in two ways, either by reason of the sin itself: or by reason of the person sinning. In the former way Guilt is always inseparable: and therefore in the Reborn also the sin of Origin or Concupiscence is by its nature damnable. But in the latter sense, Guilt is separable, as regards the person sinning: since he, being reconciled to GOD the father through Christ apprehended by faith, is absolved from the guilt of all sins both Actual, and of that Original fault or Concupiscence.

Thirdly the Jesuit objects: That it is certain from the scriptures, that GOD never remits guilt, while its foundation remains. For the Judgment of GOD is according to truth Roman. 2, 2. And GOD hates all who work iniquity, Psal. 5, 7. But this objection also is true only in a certain respect, if indeed reigning or dominating sin is understood: which as long as it remains: so long also the guilt of them remains. The testimonies of Scripture, which are brought forward by the Adversary, are also to be understood concerning this species of sin. Now indeed the Reborn do not have such reigning sin: For thus they would not be reborn: but rather they repeatedly crucify the flesh with its Concupiscences, so that in the struggle of flesh and Spirit, the Spirit always obtains the victory.

The Jesuit takes his fourth argument from those testimonies of the Scriptures, which teach, that through Baptism a true remission of sins is made, so that not only is the debt of punishment pardoned: but also stains are washed away, purged, deleted, removed. Therefore Concupiscence in the reborn does not have the nature of sin properly so called.

But the Jesuit deceives and is deceived by a base begging of the question. For this very thing is the question, whether in Baptism not only the guilt, but also the very material of sin is taken away? The negative of which we have above demonstrated sufficiently and invincibly. Therefore, in most of the testimonies which are brought forward in this place by the adversaries from the Epistle to the Romans, Ephesians, Galatians, and to Titus, there is committed an ignorance of the refutation, and a fallacy of the consequent. For first, Scripture teaches that GOD loves the reborn, not because their nature is perfectly pure, immaculate, and harmless in every part: But because they have been received into grace, because all their sins have been freely forgiven them through and on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. And this is what that passage in Rom. 6:4 means: we are buried with Christ by baptism into his death: but so that the reborn subsequently have need to crucify the flesh with its lusts. To which also pertains that passage 1 Cor. 6:11. And such were some of you, but you are washed, but you are sanctified.

For as far as concerns the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, the baptized certainly have most perfect cleanliness in Christ: but the cleanliness of RENEWAL or SANCTIFICATION is only begun: which ought to grow daily, until it is finally perfected in the other life. Whence the Apostle himself asserts that his Corinthians were so cleansed that they nevertheless stand in need of daily cleansing, writing thus in 2 Cor. 7:1: Let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting sanctification. And in 1 Cor. 5:7: Purge out the old leaven.

Furthermore, some testimonies of Scripture do not deal with that perfection or holiness which is to be consummated in this life, but which is to be consummated in the Elect only in the future life. In which sense that passage of the Apostle in Ephesians 5:27 must be understood: He sanctified the Church, cleansing it with the washing of water by the word, that he might present it to himself glorious, not having spot or wrinkle. Explaining which passage, Augustine, Book 2 of Retractations, Chapter 18, says: Wherever, he says, in the books (On Baptism against the Donatists) I have mentioned the Church not having spot or wrinkle, it is not to be understood as if it already were so, but that it is being prepared to be so, when it shall also appear glorious. For now, on account of certain ignorances and infirmities of its members, it has cause to say daily, Forgive us our debts.

But the Romanists have certain arguments with which they are accustomed to fight.

FIRST. If the guilt, which is as it were the proper inseparable attribute of sin, is taken away in the reborn, much more will that which must be placed in the category of remnants be taken away, namely, Concupiscence. But the former takes place, therefore the latter also.

But an error is committed by ignorance of the refutation. For judgment concerning the quality of the remission of sin is not to be made from the judgment of reason or philosophical rules, but from the revealed Word of God: because this whole matter depends solely upon the most free will of God. Now, the Word of God teaches that the grace of God in Baptism does indeed confer a full and perfect remission of all sins, but that renewal or sanctification is only begun in this life, and will be more absolute and perfect only in the other. God could indeed in one moment take away not only the guilt but also the material of sin: but He does not do this, and that for a certain counsel known to Himself alone. Therefore, this dispute, which is instituted against us by the Romanists partly from the dictate of our reason and partly from the possibility of God, is clearly futile.

SECOND ARGUMENT. Natural things are not damnable, and therefore they are not truly and properly sin. But concupiscence is a natural thing. Therefore.

Latin:

Tandem committitur error Ignorationis Elenchi: Nam Apostolus hoc loco asserens peccatum non in se, sed in carne sua habitare, non opponit Carnem Animæ, tanquàm unam partem Essentialem alteri: uti Jesuwita nimis ἀπαιδεύτως philosophatur: Sed de se quippè Homine renato verba faciens, Carnem & Spiritum sibi mutuò opponit: hunc à peccato immunem esse pronuncians. Jam verò Apostolum non loqui de natura & Substantia carnis exterioris aut Corporis visibilis, saltem illud probat, quòd Corpora nostra alibi templa Spiritus sancti esse pronnnciat. Caro igitur hoc loco, pro universa Natura hominis, utraque parte essentiali constante, sed quatenùs peccato Originis est corrupta, accipitur. Sicut è diverso, Spiritus appellatione, itidem totus homo intelligitur, sed quatenùs jam regeneratus est. Fallitur Ergo longissimè Jesuwita, dùm hoc loco carnem, per partem alteram Substantialem Hominis interpretatur: atque indè errorem etiam illum stabilire conatur, quasi inferiorum tantùm facultatum corruptionem Homo passus, superiores incorruptas habeat.

Neque responsioni huic nostræ obstat subsequens versus 23 ubi dicit Apostolus: Video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meæ: Et ego ipse mente servio legi DEI: carne autem legi peccati.

Per Legem enim membrorum, intelligitur Externus Homo, sive Homo ex ea parte, quâ carnis desideriis subindè exercetur: Quemadmodum Lex mentis, notat interiorem Hominem, sive Hominem ex ea parte, qua ad obedientiam divinæ legi præstandam pronus & paratus est. Quibus appellationibus non Substantiæ diversitas notatur: sed facultatum discrimen Inquitur: quarum una, quæ ad regenerationem pertinet, Interni seu novi Hominis appellationem sortitur: altera, quæ naturalis vitiositatis propria est, Externi seu veteris hominis vel legis membrorum termino insignitur. Sic asserens Apostolus, Mente servio legi DEI: Carne autem legi peccati: per Mentem non intelligit intellectum aut rationem humanam: sed voluntatem per Spiritum sanctum renovatam, & Carni subindè resistentem: Per Carnem verò intelligit cupiditates vitiosas & motus inordinatos, qui Spiritui mentis semper sunt contrarii, Galat. 5, 17.

Tertium argumentum petit Jesuita, ex cap. 1. Rom. ubi sic loquitur Apostolus: Nihil ergo damnationis est in ijs, qui sunt in CHRISTO JESU. Significat E. Apostolus non modò nullam esse condemnationem Justificatis in Christo ob concupiscentiam: sed nihil etiam esse in eis Condemnatione dignum, sive nullam in illis esse causam condemnationis.

Sed manifestum committitur crimen Falsi. Neque enim dicit Apostolus, Nullum peccatum esse in Electis: Aut, Nihil condemnabile esse in Electis: uti Jesuita reddit: Sed Nihil damnationis esse. Differunt autem plurimùm, Condemnabile & Damnatio: quorum illud reatum: hoc verò ipsum damnationis actum notat. Jam autem potest esse reatus: ubi tamen non statim ipso actu ponitur supplicium. Ut exempli gratiâ: si Magistratus civilis homicidæ remittit pœnam: Verè quidem dici potest, Nihil jam damnationis aut supplicii est in isto homine: Non autem propterea verum est illud, si dicere velim: Nihil est damnabile in isto homine. Eodem planè modo licèt damnatio actu non locum habeat in renatis, quia persona est reconciliata per fidem DEO: non tamen propterea negari debet: Nihil prorsus damnabile esse in iisdem: hoc est, Concupiscentiam sive peccatum Originis, non esse naturâ suâ peccatum, dignum æternâ morte. Ratio est: quia in Baptismo non tollitur morbus ipse, sive peccatum: sed peccati Reatus: & quidem non respectu peccati: sed respectu personæ consideratus.

Excipit Jesuita: Si reatus tollitur: utique tollitur etiam peccatum: Siquidem Reatus est id, quod proprie dicitur peccatum. Sed ludit Sophista sub æquivocatione vocabuli peccati: quod interdum ipsam horrendam Naturæ depravationem, interdum Reatum peccati significat. Jam si posteriore sensu accipiatur, largimur quidem tolli Reatum, & sic peccatum ipsum: sed ut prior tamen illa peccati notatio, in Renatis maneat reliqua: quippe quæ hac in vita nunquam exuitur aut tollitur.

Porrò excipit Jesuuvita: Reatum omninò esse inseparabilem ab eo, quod naturâ suâ dignum est æterna damnatione: Ergo, infert, si Concupiscentia in renatis reliqua, naturâ suâ digna est æterna damnatione: utique Reatus quoque in ijsdem manebit. Sed facilè nodus iste solvitur, si illud tantùm attendatur, Reatum duobus modis considerari, vel ratione ipsius peccati: vel ratione personæ peccantis. Priore modo Reatus est semper inseparabilis: ac proindè in Renatis quoque peccatum Originis sive Concupiscentia, est naturâ suâ damnabilis. Posteriore verò sensu, Reatus est separabilis, quoad personam peccantem: quippe quæ DEO patri per Christum fide apprehensum reconciliata, absolvitur à reatu peccatorum omnium tùm Actualium, tùm Originalis illius culpæ sive Concupiscentiæ.

Tertiò excipit Jesuuvita: Certum esse ex scripturis, DEUM nunquam remittere reatum, dùm manet ejus fundamentum. Nam Judicium DEI est secundum veritatem Roman. 2, 2. Et odio habet DEUS omnes qui operantur iniquitatem, Psal. 5, 7. Sed & hæc exceptio vera est tantùm secundum quid, si nimirùm peccatum regnans sive dominans intelligatur: quod quamdiu manet: tamdiu manet etiam ipsorum reatus. De qua peccati specie etiam sunt intelligenda Scripturæ testimonia, quæ ab Adversario proferuntur. Jam verò Renati tale peccatum Regnans non habent: Sic enim non essent renati: sed potiùs subindè crucifigunt carnem cum suis Concupiscentiis, ut in lucta carnis & Spiritus, semper Spiritus victoriam obtineat.

Quartum argumentum sumit Jesuuvita ab ijs Scripturarum testimonijs, quæ docent, per Baptismum fieri veram remissionem peccatorum, ita ut non solum condonetur debitum pænæ: sed etiam maculæ abluantur, purgentur, deleantur, tollantur. Ergo Concupiscentia in renatis non habet rationem peccati propriè sic dicti.

Sed fallit & fallitur Jesuuvita turpi petitione principii. Hoc ipsum enim quæritur, An in Baptismo non modò reatus: sed & ipsum Materiale peccati tollatur? Cujus Negativam nos supra satis invictè demonstravimus. Proindè in plerisque Testimoniis, quæ ex Epistola ad Romanos, Ephesios, Galatas, & ad Titum hoc loco ab Adversariis proferuntur, committitur ἀγνοία ἐλέγχꝢ, & πλεονεξία Consequentis. Nam primùm Scriptura tradit, DEUM renatos diligere, non ideò, quòd natura ipsorum omni ex parte perfectè sit pura, immaculata & innoxia: Sed quòd in gratiam sint recepti, quòd ipsis sint gratis remissa omnia peccata per & propter Christi meritum fide apprehensum. Et hoc sibi vult illud Rom. 6, 4. consepulti sumus cum Christo per Baptismum in mortem ipsius: sedita, ut Renati subindè necesse habeant crucifigere carnem cum concupiscentijs suis. Quò pertinet etiam illud 1. Cor. 6, 11. Et hæc quidem fuistis, sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis.

Nam quod attinet ad Remissionem peccatorum, & ad imputationem Justitiæ Christi, certè Baptizati habent in Christo munditiam perfectissimam: Verùm mundities RENOVATIONIS seu SANCTIFICATIONIS, tantùm inchoata est: quæ quotidiè crescere debet, donec tandem in altera vita perficiatur. Undè Apostolus ipse asserit, ita suos Corinthios mundatos esse, ut tamen quotidiana mundatione indigeant, sic scribens 2. Corint. 7, 1. Mundemus nos ab omni inquinamento carnis, & Spiritus perficientes sanctificationem. Et in 1. Cor. 5, 7. Expurgate vetus fermentum.

Deindè nonnulla scripturæ testimonia non agunt de ea perfectione sive sanctitate, quæ hac in vita: sed quæ in futura demùm vita in Electis sit consummanda. Quo sensu accipiendum est illud Apostoli Ephes. 5, 27. Sanctificavit Ecclesiam, mundans eam lavacro aquæ in verbo, ut exhiberet ipsam sibi gloriosam, non habentem maculam aut rugam. Quem locum explicans Augustinus, lib 2. Retract. cap. 18. Ubieunq;, inquit, in libris (de Baptismo contra Donatistas) commemoravi, Ecclesiam non habentem maculam aut rugam: non sic accipiendum est, quasi jam sit: sed quòd preparetur, ut sit, quando apparebit etiam gloriosa. Nunc enim propter quasdam ignorantias & infirmitates membrorum suorum habet, undè quotidiè dicat, dimitte nobis debita nostra.

Sed habent Romanenses rationes quasdam, quibus pugnare solent.

PRIMA. Si reatus, qui est proprium quasi ἀχώριςον peccati, tollitur in renatis: multò magis tolletur id, quod in reliquiarum censu collocandum est, nempè Concupiscentia. Atqui prius illud fit, Ergo & hoc posterius.

Sed committitur error παρά τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε. Neque enim de qualitate Remissionis peccati judicium est faciendum ex judicio rationis, aut regulis Philosophicis: Sed ex Verbo DEI revelato: propterea quòd hoc totum unicè dependet à liberrima voluntate DEI: Jam verò docet Verbum DEI, Gratiam DEI in Baptismo, conferre quidem plenam & perfectam remissionem omnium peccatorum: sed Renovationem sive Sanctificationem hac in vita tantùm inchoari: sed in altera demùm absolutiorem & perfectiorem fore. Posset sanè Deus uno momento tollere non modò reatum, sed & Materiale peccati: Verum hoc non præstat: idqué certo consilio, ipsi soli cognito. Proindè frustranea planè hæc est disputatio, quæ partim ex rationis nostræ dictamine, partim verò ex possibilitate DEI à Romanensibus adversum nos instituitur.

SECUNDA RATIO. Res naturales non sunt damnabiles, ac proindè verè & propriè non sunt peccatum. Atqui Concupiscentia est res naturalis. Ergo.


### Controversy IV. And the last concerning Original Sin: Second Part. Examining the doctrine of the Papists (continued)

I answer that a feeble sophistry of equivocation is being committed. For by the term concupiscence in this place is not denoted a natural power or a motion proper to the sensitive faculty, which no sane person would affirm to be vicious or sin in itself: but it denotes disorder, which consists partly in the privation of original righteousness, and partly in the position of a contrary habit, namely, extreme depravity, not only of the lower powers of the soul but also of the higher. Therefore, four terms emerge in the argument. Moreover, since the Jesuitical tribe is accustomed to seek the patronage of its cause most especially under this argument, it will not be inappropriate to note, by way of a compendium, those distinctions and axioms by the aid of which all the sophisms that can be hidden here may be most solidly refuted; and that in this manner: The word concupiscence is taken either physically, or ethically, or theologically. Physically it denotes either the natural power of desiring or the energy itself, the act itself. That natural power is never placed in the category of sin: for it depends so simply, considered in itself and by itself, upon that faculty of the soul which is and is called the appetitive, and has God Himself as its author. But the act receives a different consideration, and one sought either from physics or from ethics. Physical, insofar as the act of concupiscence is considered absolutely, in itself and by itself. In which respect it is indifferent or middle, and in itself neither good nor evil: of the same kind clearly as eating, drinking, sleeping, standing, etc. But concupiscence receives an ethical consideration insofar as it relates to the law of nature, whose three duties are: 1. To live honestly; 2. To harm no one; 3. To give to each his own. Finally, it is considered theologically insofar as it is weighed and examined in relation to the Law of God as the sole infallible judge of all our thoughts and actions. In which respect the act of concupiscence itself is called either good or evil: Good, if it agrees with both the natural and divine law: Evil, if it differs from it. It differs, however, if it is directed toward any thing, whether one's own or another's, in an inordinate manner and end: which happens in three ways. First, by reason of the object, when the act of concupiscence is directed toward things prohibited by natural and divine law, whether it breaks out into a second act or not. For the prohibition of the Decalogue is indefinite, Thou shalt not covet: and therefore it includes both the first and the second act with respect to the prohibited object. Then by reason of the mode, when one exceeds the mode in desiring: which can happen concerning all objects that fall under the appetite. Finally, regarding the end, when someone does not desire a thing for such an end as looks to the glory of GOD, the edification of one’s neighbor, and one’s own salvation. These distinctions being observed, the proposed ζήτημα is most correctly answered: that concupiscences in the regenerate, considered physically, are not sin; but taken ethically and theologically, they are either good, or evil, and thus sin. Evil in the way that has already been stated; good, if from faith they desire a legitimate object, in a due manner and for a due end.

And if a faithful husband seeks the end of marriage which regards the procreation of offspring, not for the sake of lust, but for the sake of propagating the human race: so also he should duly observe laws both sacred and civil, in mutual, loaned, hired, bought, sold, and any other legitimate contract, concerning the thing which he seeks. Thus, in itself, that concupiscence by which a young man seeks either a bishopric or the marriage of a virgin is not placed in vice or as part of sin: at least if it be done in a legitimate manner and for a legitimate end. For he who seeks a bishopric, seeks a good work, 1 Tim. 3:1. Thus it is better to marry than to burn: 1 Cor. 7:9. Furthermore, however much concupiscences of this kind are by their nature, and in the respect we have mentioned, good in the regenerate: yet it happens by accident that, because of the corruption of nature adhering to them, they are scarcely ever without vice. Nor does any object occur, concerning which the regenerate do not also exceed the measure: except for those spiritual things which concern the glory of God, our salvation and that of our neighbor, and finally divine matters simply. With all these things observed, it may be plain what properly comes into question concerning concupiscence in the regenerate, namely, not whether concupiscibility itself, as Stapleton speaks, or the first act of concupiscence considered physically, is good or evil: nor likewise whether there can be in the regenerate a concupiscence that is good: But whether those defects, motions, itches, or concupiscence, by which the flesh fights against the Spirit, are also in the regenerate by their nature, and properly speaking, sin: which is what we affirm: the Jesuits deny.

THIRD argument: Whatever inheres in man necessarily cannot be sin: But concupiscence inheres necessarily in the regenerate even after baptism. Therefore.

I answer, an ἀγνοία ἐλέγχꙋ [ignorance of refutation] is committed again. For the major premise is true in those things which behave according to the judgment of our reason: but it is false in our theology, especially if it is accommodated to hypothetical necessity. Now, however, concupiscence inheres in man not from simple or absolute necessity: since God did not create man such in the beginning: but only from the necessity of condition and consequence; which does not render him immune from sin: because man, by his own fault, brought this law of necessity upon himself. The argument therefore suffers from the πλεονεξίᾳ [excess] of four terms.

FOURTH argument: The remission of sin does not behave like the shaving of hair, in which the roots of the hairs remain under the skin: but it is a plenary abolition of sin. Therefore, unless a contradiction is implied, so that the same thing is said to remain and to be abolished: it cannot happen that concupiscence obtains the true and proper definition of sin.

But a shameful begging of the question is committed: for it is taken for granted that the remission of sin cannot take place unless everything that can obtain the definition of sin is simply taken away and abolished: which was demonstrated to be false above from the Scriptures, and especially from the example of the Apostle Paul from chapter 7 to the Romans.

FIFTH argument: The punishment of sin cannot at the same time be guilt: But concupiscence is the punishment of the fall of our first parents. Therefore, it cannot at the same time be guilt.

I answer that the major proposition in our theology is simply false. For concupiscence is both sin, and the punishment of sin, and the cause of sin: as we showed above from Augustine.

SIXTH argument: Sanctification cannot stand together with sin in one and the same subject: But the regenerate are sanctified: Therefore.

I answer that a fallacy of ὡς πρός τι πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς [relative to something, in a respect, and simply] is committed. For the major premise is true in a respect, namely if it is understood as reigning sin: with which the sanctification or renewal of the mind can never agree. But now, the consequence does not hold from reigning sin to every kind of sin. Certainly, the regenerate in the Lord's Prayer seek the sanctification of the divine name and the fulfillment of his will: but at the same time they also daily implore the remission of sins, according to that: For this shall every saint pray to thee in a time of need. Ps. 32:6.

SEVENTH argument: If all that which has the definition of sin is not taken away and abolished in baptism: the grace of God is affected with insult: the merit of Christ is diminished: and finally the efficacy of the sacraments is enervated. For, says Bellarmine, lib. 5 de amiss. grat. & stat. pecc. cap. 9, it would follow that Christ redeemed us from sins not truly, but only imputatively: Likewise that the Devil is more powerful than Christ, since he was able to truly defile: the latter was not able to truly cleanse. But this latter is absurd: Therefore the former is also.

I reply that an error is committed, namely, treating as a cause that which is not a cause, and that which does not follow. For no logic of consequence holds: In the reborn, there remains after Baptism something which has the nature of sin properly so called: Therefore the grace of God and the merit of Christ could not take this away as well. As if, says Augustine, we were to deny that the help of God is so powerful, if He wills, that today I could have no evil desires against which we might fight even most invincibly: And yet it does not happen. But why it does not happen, who has known the mind of the Lord? Yet I know not a little, when I know, whatever that cause may be, that it is neither the iniquity of a just God nor the weakness of the Almighty. There is, therefore, something in His hidden counsel why, as long as we live in this mortal flesh, there is within us that against which our mind may fight: there is also that for which we may say: Forgive us our debts. And a little later the same Augustine: Therefore it was brought about in this place of weakness, lest we should live proudly, that we should live under the daily remission of sins. And after a few words: But whether this be the cause, or another, which is hidden from me by much more, yet that which I cannot doubt is that, however much we may progress under this burden of a corruptible body, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

But they likewise oppose Augustine with Augustine, who sometimes denies that concupiscence remaining in the reborn is sin. Since they place no small part of their victory in this objection, it must be considered more accurately what Augustine understands by the name of sin in those places which are objected to us, and what he thinks about this whole question elsewhere. Indeed, in the first book On Marriage and Concupiscence, when he had said in chapter 23 that concupiscence in the regenerate is not sin, he immediately explained in the following chapter, 25, what he wishes to be understood by the name of sin in these words: Just as of those sins which cannot remain, because when they are committed they pass away, the GUILT nevertheless remains, and unless it is remitted, it will remain forever: so of that concupiscence, when it is remitted, the GUILT is taken away: for this is what it means not to HAVE sin, not to be GUILTY of sin. So also in book 1 against the two letters of the Pelagians, chapter 13. When he had said that concupiscence is so called, not because it is sin, but because it was made by sin, he immediately adds: Sins are those things which are done, said, or thought illicitly according to the concupiscence or ignorance of the flesh: which, even when they have passed, hold men GUILTY if they are not remitted. He explains his own opinion clearly in book 2 against Julian the Pelagian: Now it is not called sin in the same way that it makes one GUILTY: but because it is the GUILT of the first man's deed, and because by REBELLING it strives to draw us to GUILT, unless the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord helps us, lest the dead SIN also rebel in this way, and by conquering, revive and reign. And in book 6 against the same, chapter 5. But who is so imprudent and impudent, so forward, stubborn, obstinate, and finally so insane and demented, who, while he confesses that SINS are EVIL, denies that the CONCUPISCENCE of sins is EVIL, EVEN IF, with the SPIRIT lusting against it, it is not allowed to lust after and produce sins.

Augustine therefore does not simply deny that concupiscence in the regenerate is sin, but only in a certain way: namely, if the word sin is taken either for guilt, or for the deeds, words, or thoughts themselves that hold us guilty. Augustine explains this very thing more clearly in book 2 against Julian the Pelagian: For this law of sin, which is in the members of the body of this death, has been remitted by spiritual regeneration, and remains in the mortal flesh. Remitted, that is, because the GUILT has been dissolved by the sacrament by which the faithful are reborn: but it remains, because it WORKS desires, against which the faithful struggle.

The EIGHTH argument is as follows: The involuntary cannot be called sin: since sin is that which is done by one who knows and wills. But the motions of concupiscence, since they depend on nature, are involuntary. Therefore they are not sins.

I answer that both premises are false. And the major is false because sin is and is called sin, not because it depends on our προαιρέσει, or the choice of the will, but because it fights against the law of God. For this is the norm of our actions. And we have already shown above, Question 2, how sin truly exists even in infants, although they possess the act of the will not at all.
