What of the fact that the philosopher also denies that the major is καθ’ ὅλꙋ or universally true: since he refers among sins, or vicious actions, even those παραπτώματα which are done ἀκꙋσίως and δι’ ἄγνοιαν. Whence that common saying drew its origin: ꙋδεὶς ἑκὼν πονηρὸς. No one is evil willingly. Now as for the minor, it is manifest that concupiscence, when it breaks out into act, has its seat most firmly fixed in the will of man. For a man can scarcely be said to desire anything unless he wills it.

But in this place, one must note the remarkable sophistry of the Romanists, who cast a veil over their error under a certain new distinction. For they distinguish between formed and unformed concupiscence. By unformed they understand evil thoughts, which indeed stimulate the sense and the will, but without the deliberate assent of the will. By formed, however, they understand evil thoughts with the full assent of the will. Therefore, they wish this alone to be sin: the other not so. But this is beyond and against the Scriptures: as they also call that unformed concupiscence sin: according to that: Thou shalt not covet. And sin is non-conformity with the law. Now evil thoughts, however much assent does not follow, are non-conformant to the Law of God: since it demands nothing but good ones. Therefore, by their nature, strictly speaking, they are sin.

Latin:

Respondeo, Elumbem committi Sophisticationem τῆς ὁμωνυμίας. Neque enim vocabulo Concupiscentiæ hoc loco notatur potentia naturalis, aut motus facultatis sensitivæ proprius, quem per se vitiosum, aut peccatum esse, nemo sanus affirmaverit: Sed notatur ἀταξία, quæ constat partim privatione Justitiæ Originalis: partim verò positione contrarii habitus, nempè depravatione extrema, non inferiorum tantùm animæ potentiarum: sed & superiorum. Emergunt ergò in argumento Quatuor Termini. Cæterùm cùm gens Jesuwitica sub hoc argumento causæ suæ patrocinium vel maximè quærere soleat, haud inconveniens fuerit, per Compendium quasi quoddam, notare eas distinctiones & axiomata, quorum adminiculo omnia Sophismata, quæ hîc occultari possunt, solidissimè refutari queant: idque in hunc modum: Vox Concupiscentiæ vel accipitur Physicè: vel Ethicè: vel Theologicè. Physicè notat vel δύναμιν φυσικὴν potentiam naturalem concupiscendi: vel ipsam ἐνέργειαν, actum ipsum. Δύναμις illa φυσικὴ in parte peccati nunquàm ponitur: dependet enim ea ita simpliciter in se & per se considerata, ab ea facultate animi, quæ est ac dicitur ἐπιθυμητικὴ: ac DEUM ipsum autorem habet. Actus verò diversam considerationem fortitur, eamque vel ex Physica, vel ex Ethica petitam. Physicam quidem, quatenùs actus Concupiscentiæ consideratur absolutè; in se ac per se. Quo respectu est ἀδιάφορος ac indifferens sive medius; & per se neque bonus, heque malus: ejusdem planè generis, cujus est, edere, bibere, dormire, stare &c. Ethicam verò considerationem fortitur Concupiscentia, quatenùs Relatè ad Legem Naturæ se habet: Cujus tria sunt officia: 1. Honestè vivere: 2. Neminem lædere; 3. Jus suum cuique tribuere. Theologicè denique consideratur, quatenùs relatè ad Legem DEI tanquàm unicum infallibilem omnium cogitationum & actionum nostrarum judicem pensitatur & exigitur. Quo respectu Actus ipse Concupiscentiæ dicitur vel bonus; vel malus: Bonus, si cum Lege & naturali & divina congruat: Malus, si ab eadem discrepet. Discrepat autem tùm, si feratur ad rem aliquam, sive propriam, sive alienam, modo ac fine inordinato: id quod fit tripliciter. Primùm ratione objecti, quando actus Concupiscentiæ fertur ad res, lege & Naturali ac divina prohibitas; sive in actum secundum erumpat, sive non. Indefinita enim est prohibitio Decalogi, Non Concupisces: ac proindè actum tam primum; quàm secundum, respectu objecti prohibiti, includit. Deindè ratione Modi, quando quis in appetendo Modum excedit: id quod circa omnia Objecta fieri potest, quæ quidem sub Appetitum cadunt. Tandem ratione Finis, quando quis non tali fine rem appetit, qui gloriam DEI, ædificationem proximi, ac salutem propriam spectet. Distinctionibus istis observatis; ad propositum ζήτημα rectissimè respondetur: Concupiscentias in Renatis Physicè consideratas non esse peccatum: Ethicè verò & Theologicè acceptas, vel esse bonas: vel malas, & sic peccatum. Malas eo, quo jam dictum est, modo: Bonas, si ex fide Objectum legitimum, modo & fine debito appetant:

et si maritus fidelis appetat finem conjugij eum, qui procreationem sobolis respicit, non libidinis causa, sed generis humani propagandi gratia: sic etiam leges tum sacras tum civiles rite observet, in mutuo, commodato, conducto, emtione, venditione, & quovis contractu alio legitimo, circa rem, quam appetit. Sic per se in vitio aut parte peccati non est posita ea Concupiscentia, qua Juvenis appetit vel Episcopatum, vel nuptias virginis: saltem id fiat modo ac fine legitimo. Qui enim Episcopatum appetit, bonum opus appetit, 1. Tim. 3, 1. Sic melius est nubere, quam uri: 1. Cor. 7, 9. Cæterum, quantumvis hujusmodi Concupiscentiæ sua natura, & eo, quo diximus respectu, bonæ sint in renatis: tamen ex accidenti fit, ut propter adhærentem naturæ corruptionem, vix unquam vitio careant. Neq; ullum occurrit Objectum, circa quod Renati etiam modum non excedant: præter spiritualia illa, quæ gloriam Dei, salutem nostram & proximi, & denique res divinas simpliciter concernunt. Quibus omnibus observatis, planum sit, quid proprie circa Concupiscentiam in renatis in quæstionem veniat, non videlicet, an ipsa concupiscibilitas, uti Stapletonus loquitur, sive actus primus Concupiscentiæ Physice consideratus, sit bonus vel malus: an item in Renatis concupiscentia dari possit, quæ bona sit: Sed an illi defectus, motus, pruritus, sive Concupiscentia, quibus caro pugnat adversus Spiritum, etiam in Renatis sint natura sua, & proprie loquendo, peccatum: id quod nos affirmamus: Jesuvitæ negant.

TERTIA ratio: Quicquid homini inhæret necessario, peccatum esse non potest: Atqui Conpiscentia post Baptismum etiam renatis inhæret necessario. E.

Respondeo, committitur rursum ἀγνοία ἐλέγχꙋ. Major enim vera est in ijs, quæ secundum rationis nostræ judicium sese habent: Falsa autem est in Theologia nostra, præsertim si ad necessitatem hypotheticam ea accommodetur. Jam vero Concupiscentia inhæret homini non ex simplice sive absoluta necessitate: Siquidem Deus talem initio hominem non condidit: sed duntaxat ex Necessitate Conditionis & Consequentiæ; quæ a peccato ipsum non immunem reddit: propterea quod Homo suapte culpa, hanc necessitatis legem sibi accessivit. Laborat Ergo argumentum πλεονεξίᾳ quatuor terminorum.

QVARTA ratio: Remissio peccati non se habet, ut rasio capillorum, in qua pilorum radices subcute remanent: sed est plenaria peccati abolitio. Ergo nisi Contradictio implicetur, ut idem dicatur remanere & abolitum esse: fieri nequit, ut Concupiscentia veram peccati & propriam rationem obtineat.

Sed turpis committitur Petitio principij: Sumitur enim pro Confesso, Remissionem peccati non posse fieri, nisi simpliciter tollatur & aboleatur omne, quod peccati rationem obtinere potest: id quod falsum esse, supra ex Scripturis, & cumprimis Exemplo Apoftoli Pauli ex cap. 7. ad Rom. fuit demonstratum.

QUINTA ratio: Pœna peccati non potest simul esse culpa: Atqui Concupiscentia est pœna lapsus protoparentum nostrorum. E. non potest simul esse culpa.

Respondeo, Majorem propositionem in Theologia nostra simpliciter esse falsam. Nam Concupiscentia est, & peccatum, & pœna peccati, & causa peccati: uti supra ex Augustino ostendimus.

SEXTA ratio: Sanctificatio cum peccato nequit in uno eodemque subjecto simul stare: Atqui renati sunt sanctificati: E.

Respondeo, committi fallaciam ὡς πρός τι πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Majorem enim vera est secundum quid, nempè si intelligatur peccatum regnans: cum quo Sanctificationi sive Renovationi mentis nunquàm convenire potest. Jam verò à peccato Regnante, ad omnem peccati speciem non valet Consequentia. Certè Renati in Oratione Dominica sanctificationem nominis divini, & voluntaris ejusdem eventum expetunt: sed simul etiam ijdem Remissionem peccatorum indies efflagitant, secundum illud: Pro hac orabit ad te omnis Sanctus in tempore opportuno. Psal. 32, 6.

SEPTIMA ratio: Si totum id, quod peccati rationem habet, in Baptismo non tollitur & aboletur: Gratia Dei contumelia afficitur: Meritum Christi imminuitur: Sacramentorum denique efficacia enervatur. Nam inquit Bellarminus, lib. 5. de amiss. grat. & stat. pecc. cap. 9. sequeretur, Christum nos non verè, sed imputativè tantùm à peccatis redemisse: Item Diabolum potentiorem esse Christo, cùm ille verè potuerit inquinare: iste non potuerit verè mundare. Atqui posterius hoc absurdum: Ergo & prius illud.

Respondeo, committi errorem ὧν δὲ ὧ μὴ ἑπόμενον καὶ τὸ μὴ αἰτιον ὡς αἰτίαν. Neque enim ulla militat ratio Consequentiæ: In renatis remanet post Baptismum aliquid, quod peccati propriè sic dicti rationem habet: Ergo Gratia Dei, & Christi meritum non potuerunt istud quoque tollere. Quasi verò, inquit Augustinus, nos negemus, Adjutoriũ Dei tantum valere, si velit, ut hodiè nullas malas Concupiscentias habere possim̃, contra quas vel invictissimè dimicemus: Et tamen non fieri. Cur autem non fiat, quis cognovit sensum Domini? Non tamen parùm scio, cum scio, quacuńq́, illa causa sit, quod nec justi Dei sit iniquitas, nec Omnipotentis infirmitas. Est igitur aliquid in abdito ejus consilio, cur, quamdiu vivimus in hac carne mortali, est in nobis, contra quod mens nostra dimicet: est etiam propter quod dicamus: Dimitte nobis debita nostra. Et paulò post idem Augustinus: Ideò factum est in loco infirmitatis hujus, ne superbè viveremus, ut sub quotidiana peccatorum remissione vivamus. Et post pauca: Sed sive ista causa sit, sive alia, qua multò ampliùs me latet, tamen quod dubitare non possum, quantumlibet proficiamus sub hoc onere corruptibilis corporis, si dixerimus, quia peccatum non habemus, nosipsos decipimus, & veritas non est in nobis.

Sed Augustino opponunt itidem Augustinum, qui aliquoties Concupiscentiam in renatis reliquam, peccatum esse negat. Qua in objectione, cùm haud postremam victoriæ partem collocent, accuratiùs considerandum fuerit, quid Augustinus Peccati nomine ijs in locis, quæ nobis obijciuntur, intelligat: & quid de hac tota Quæstione aliàs sentiat? Libro sanè primo de Nuptijs & concupiscentia, cum cap. 23. dixisset: Concupiscentiam in Regeneratis peccatum non esse: statim cap. sequente 25. quid Peccati nomine velit intelligi, his verbis explicavit: Sicut eorum peccatorum quæ manere non possunt, quoniam cùm fiunt, prætereunt, REATVS tamen manet, & nisi remittatur, in æternum manebit : sic illius Concupiscentiæ, quando remittitur, REATVS aufertur: Hoc est enim non HABERE peccatum, non REVM esse peccati. Ita etiam lib. 1. contra duas Epistolas Pelagianorum, cap. 13. Cùm concupiscentiam, non quia peccatum est, sed quia peccato facta est, sic vocari dixisset: statim subjungit: Peccata aut sunt, quæ secundum carnis Concupiscentiam vel ignorantiam illicitè fiunt, dicuntur, cogitantur: quæ transacta etiam REOS tenent, si non remittantur. Eandem planè sententiam sese explicat, lib. 2. contra Julianum Pelagianum: Iam non eodem modo appellatur Peccatū, quo facit REVM: sed quòd sit REATV primi hominis factum, & quòd REBELLANDO nos trahere nititur ad REATVM, nisi adjuvet nos gratia Dei per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, ne sic etiam mortuum PECCATVM rebellet, & vincendo, revivifcat & regnet. Et lib. 6. contra eundem cap. 5. Quis autem ita sit imprudens atque impudens, ita procax, pertinax, pervicax, ita postremò insanus & demens, qui cum PECCATA MALA esse fateatur, neget esse MALAM CONCVPISCENTIAM peccatorum, ETIAMSI adversus eam concupiscente SPIRITV peccata concupiscere ac parere non sinatur.

Non igitur simpliciter negat Augustinus Concupiscentiam in Renatis peccatum esse: sed quodam tantùm modo: Nempè si vox peccati, vel pro Reatu, vel pro ipsis Factis, dictis, sive cogitatis reos nos tenentibus, accipiatur. Quod ipsum planiùs explicat Augustinus lib. 2. contra Julianum Pelagianum: Lex quippe ista peccati, quæ in membris est corporis mortis hujus, & remissa est regeneratione Spirituali, & manet in carne mortali. Remissa scilicet, quia REATVS solutus est Sacramento, quo renascuntur Fideles: manet autem, quia OPERATVR desideria, contra quæ dimicant fideles.

OCTAVA ratio sic habet: Involuntarium non potest dici peccatum: siquidem Peccatum est, quod fit à sciente & volente. Atqui Conpupiscentiæ motus, quippè à naturâ dependentes, sunt involuntarij. Ergo non sunt peccata.

Respondeo, utramque præmissaram esse falsam. Et Majorem quidem ideò, quia Peccatum, est ac dicitur, non quod à nostra dependet προαιρέσει, sive voluntatis arbitrio: sed quod pugnat cum lege Dei. Hæc enim norma est actionum nostrarum. Et jam supra, Quæst. 2. ostendimus, Quomodo Peccatum in Infantibus etiam revera sit, licèt voluntatis actu minimè potiantur. Quid? quòd Philosophus etiam Majorem negat esse καθ’ ὅλꙋ sive universaliter veram : quippè inter peccata, sive vitiosas actiones referens ea etiam παραπτώματα, quæ fiunt ἀκꙋσίως & δι’ ἄγνοιαν. Undè originem traxit illud vulgatum: ꙋδεὶς ἑκὼν πονηρὸς. Nemo volens malus. Jam quoad Minorem, manifestum est, Concupiscentiam, quando in actum prorumpit, sedem suam vel maximè fixam habere in voluntate hominis. Vix enim unquàm appetere aliquid dici potest homo, nisi quod velit.

Notanda verò hoc loco est insignis Sophisticatio Romanensium, sub nova quadam distinctione errori fucum facientium. Distinguunt enim inter Concupiscentiam Formatam & informem. Per Informem intelligunt cogitationes malas, sensum & voluntatem stimulantes quidem, sed absque voluntatis deliberato assensu. Per Formatam verò intelligunt cogitationes malas cum pleno assensu voluntatis. Hanc Ergo solam volunt esse peccatum: Illam non item. Verùm præter & contra Scripturas: ut quæ illam quoque Informem Concupiscentiam nominant peccatum: Secundum illud: Non Concupisces. Et peccatum est inconformitas cum legi. Jam cogitationes malæ, quantumvis assensus non accedat, inconformes sunt Legi Dei: quippè quæ non nisi bonas exigit. Ergo naturâ suâ sunt propriè loquendo, peccatum..


## 12 On Actual Sin, and its several species

There are two main heads which are accustomed to come into controversy concerning Actual Sin: the first of which is concerning the nature and the proper affection, as it were, of this sin: the latter, however, is concerning its legitimate and genuine parts, which constitute the distinct species of Actual Sin.

Latin:

DUo potissimùm sunt capita, quæ de Peccato Actuali in controversiam venire solent: quorum prius est de Natura, & propria quasi affectione peccati hujus: Posterius verò de legitimis & genuinis èjus partibus, quæ distinctas peccati Actualis species constituunt.


### Chapter I. On the Nature & proper affection of Actual Sin

That Actual Sin differs from Original Sin as one species contradistinguished from another cannot be obscure to him who

Latin:

PEccatum Actuale, differre à Peccato Originis tanquàm speciem contradistinctam unam ab altera, obscurum non potest esse ei, qui paulò accuratiùs Scripturarum oracula ex-


### Chapter I. On the Nature & proper affection of Actual Sin: Why it is called actual sin

weighs the oracles of the Scriptures a little more accurately. For in the beginning, Sin is given as considered in general, which, as the Apostle John defines it, is nothing other than ἀνομία, or non-conformity with the Law of God. This, however, is considered either with respect to the lack of Original Justice, and the vicious habit, or the depravity of all the powers of soul and body, which causes man to be only prone to evil at all times: or with respect to some actual transgression, fighting against the law of God, whether that happens by the omission of a due work: or by the commission of an undue work. That former respect is and is called Original Sin: This latter, however, Actual Sin. Nor does it stand in the way that Actual sin seems to differ more from Original, as an Effect from its cause. For insofar as a privation is defined not only by defect, but also by a contrary position or habit: and indeed this habit can erupt into a separate act: to that extent they certainly not only obtain the relationship of cause and effect: but can also be considered as sub-distinct species. The foundation of this difference between both sins may be sought from the Epistle of James 1:14 and 15. Each one, when he is tempted, is drawn away by his own concupiscence, and enticed: Then Concupiscence, when it has conceived, brings forth sin: But sin, when it is finished, brings forth death.

Looking to which, the ancient fathers established five Degrees, by which this difference can be illustrated: 1. The tinder, or inherent corruption, joined with defect. 2. Suggestions of thoughts and affections, but not yet erupting into act: when indeed the Original evil never rests, but moves itself with some inclination: 3. Delight. 4. Consent. 5. The work itself. Of which degrees the first two respect the Nature of Original sin: the last three the Nature of Actual sin: Where, however, if anyone wishes to contend more stubbornly that the second degree also is proper to Original Sin, because, speaking properly, all motions, suggestions, and actions against the Law of God pertain to Actual sin: We will certainly not litigate with him, provided that a distinction is granted between the fountain itself or the Source of evil, and the streams themselves, or between the cause and the Effect: And it is established with the Blessed Luther: 1. That the sin of Origin is never idle, but always acting. 2. In this sin there are always also actual sins. 3. That the tinder is actual sin: that is, the actual privation of that Justice which ought to be present: and the actual position of the depravity of all powers, which ought to be absent.

Therefore, it deserves observation in this place, that Actual sin is not named from the species contradistinguished from Original Sin as if this were entirely immune from every act: just as the Scholastics once trifled, contending that Original Sin is an idle evil, and a torpid quality, and therefore, unless actual ones are added, the remaining Concupiscence is not sin, because it does nothing against the Law of God: But that it is so called from that condition which is proper to every act or action. For because an act is something transitory, in distinction to Original sin, this was called Actual. For in actual sin the matter does not persist or remain: but as soon as something has been committed with wickedness and crime: the offense against God, and the guilt of the action indeed remains: but the action itself, the crime having been perpetrated, immediately passes and ceases. In Original sin, however, the matter is otherwise. For its matter in this life never passes: but is in perennial motion, and thus that corruption always adheres to us, and is engaged in perpetual act, so that it is never idle: but excites both doubts in the mind, and motions in the soul against the law of God perpetually. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks: and from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, foolishness, pride, adulteries, etc. Matt. 12:34, 15:18, Mark 7:21.

The matter can be illustrated by an example taken from the Scriptures. Genesis 6:5 it is read: Every thought of man is only evil at all times, from youth. Where the perpetual act of evil thoughts is noted. But 1 Cor. 13:5, the Apostle says, Charity does not think evil: thus implying that there is someone who is free from the guilt of evil thoughts. Now, therefore, lest an ἀντίφασις (contradiction) seem to intervene between these two places, a different respect for each must be shown: Namely, that the former Mosaic passage is understood of Original evil: with respect to which not even the reborn and the faithful are free from the perpetual act of evil thoughts: but the latter Apostolic one is taken concerning Actual sin: Where indeed it is true that the reborn, by the virtue and grace of the indwelling Holy Spirit, can resist depraved desires or thoughts so that they do not erupt into act. And in this respect Charity does not think evil, insofar as it does not assent to, much less indulge in, internal evil concupiscences, so as to fulfill them in act.

Although indeed in the ancient Church of the Fathers, this appellation of Actual Sin was by no means received by usage: and in the whole of Augustine it is found only once, namely in book 5 of the Hypognosticon: although it is not without reason doubted concerning this book also, whether it is Augustine's, or whether it is supposititious; yet two reasons especially militate, which can irrefragably procure ecclesiastical right for this appellation. 1. Because those terms which the Holy Fathers used less express or attain the nature of this sin. For whether you call it Proper with Augustine: or with other Fathers, Added sin: yet you nowhere attain its nature: much less do you explain whether it consists in some bare and idle habit, or whether it consists in act. 2. Scripture itself points out this designation: in so far as in the description of this sin it uses the words ἐργάζεσθαι, καταργάζεσθαι, ἐνεργεῖν, of doing, of acting, of working, of effecting, and others of this kind, as may be seen, Matt. 7, 23.

You who work iniquity Rom 7, 8. Sin, having taken occasion, worked in me all concupiscence. And in verse 17. Sin dwelling in me works evil: and elsewhere passim. Hence sins of this kind are named in the Scriptures Works of the flesh, Gal. 5, 19. Actions of the Old man. Col. 3, 9. and similarly.

These things having been premised, we must look into the definition of this Actual Sin. The Scholastics defined Actual Sin too imperfectly and confusedly as the fruit of Original Sin, or of a vicious nature. Where, what most of all ought to have been done, neither the proximate Genus nor the specific difference is expressed. Much more correctly, therefore, D. Augustine said this Sin is every deed, or word, or desire against the law of God. lib. 22. Against Faustus. But our author Philip Melanchthon defined it most fully of all: Actual Sin, he says, is every action fighting against the Law of God, both in the mind, and in the will and heart: and having a place in the external members.

This definition consists of a proper Genus and a specific difference. The Genus is Action, and indeed every action, fighting against the Law of God, whether interior or exterior, or in whatever other way it may come. It is understood, however, as we also admonished above, as a transient action, and one joined with assent, deliberation, and purpose: to the difference of Original Sin, which is in a perpetual and never-transient motion or act, whence not ineptly that great Theologian Chemnitius refers even thoughts to the sin of Origin, when indeed they are bare suggestions, and are completed by a bare concept, without any assent or προαιρέσει: although there are not lacking Theologians who prefer to refer such wicked suggestions to the Instinct or dictation of the Devil. The place of the specific difference is supplied, both by the determination of the Action to the Law of God, so that it indeed fights with it: and by that description of the subject, or seat, in which this Sin can have a place. But this subject is either considered generally, and then the Subject of this sin is constituted as whatever obtains the power and faculty of acting. For because Actual takes its name from acting: it will certainly have a place in all the parts of man also, in which there is a δύναμις of acting. Or it is considered specially, and then according to the diversity of the actions themselves, the Subject of this sin is either the Mind or intellect: To which pertain doubts, disputations of thoughts Rom. 14, 1. Iacob. 1, 6. hesitations, errors, ignorance; forgetfulness: or the heart or will: To which are referred the concupiscences and desires of the body, Rom. 6, 12. vicious affections and perturbations, hatreds, emulations and the like: Or finally the external members: To which pertain filthy speeches, unseemly jests, Eph. 4, 29. detractions, calumnies, sorceries, murders, gluttony, lusts and the like, which are designated as crimes and flagitious acts by the ministry of the external members of the body.

Where, however, we by no means deny that there can be given such actions which can be referred not to one only, but to several powers or faculties of the Soul, as to parts of the body: Such are heresies, idolatry, perjury, and others of that kind.

And this indeed is the Nature, and as it were the proper Affection of Actual Sin: about which, however, both by Scholastic Doctors and by more recent Theologians, many and various things have been called into controversy: Which we determine can hardly be settled better than through Questions.

At the beginning, therefore, it comes under question, How Actual sin is designated. The handle and occasion for this Question was provided by both that ancient theology of the Pharisees and the more recent theology of the Scholastics and Papists, dreaming that the guilt of this Sin is not contracted except partly by an external work only, partly by the designation of one's own deed: so that evil concupiscence, and even that joined with delight, provided it is not fulfilled by the act itself, can neither be held nor ought to be held as Actual sin. Whence was born the impious German proverb: Die Gedancken sind Zollfrey. Scripture contradicts this error διαρρήδην, 1. showing that even the interior perturbation of the heart, and an inordinate affection, come under the census of this sin, so indeed that if anyone rashly conceives anger against a brother, although he does not harm him with his hand, or by some other external means: yet he is guilty of judgment, so the Savior himself judges, Matth. 5, 23. Or if anyone only looks at another's spouse, to lust after her, he has contracted the guilt of adultery: ibid. verse 29. Then also Scripture gravely refutes this error, when it demonstrates by both precepts and examples, that Actual Sin is committed, not only by the designation of one's own, but also by the communication of another's crime: according to that grave admonition of the Apostle: 1. Tim. 5, 22. Do not communicate in other men's sins. And Eph. 5, 7. and 11. Do not be partakers of their works: but reprove them.

Latin:

pendit. Datur enim initio Peccatum in genere consideratum, quòd Johanne Apostolo definiente, nihil est aliud, quàm ἀνομία, sive in conformitas cum Lege Dei. Hoc autem consideratur vel respectu carentiæ Justitiæ Originalis, & vitiosi habitus, sive depravationis virium omnium animæ & corporis, quæ efficit, ut Homo tantùm pronus sit ad malum omni tempore: vel respectu actualis alicujus transgressionis, pugnantis cum lege Dei, sive illud fiat operis debiti omissione: sive operis indebiti commissione. Prior ille respectus est ac dicitur Peccatum originale: Hic verò posterior, Peccatum Actuale. Neque obstat, quòd peccatum Actuale ab Originali magis differre videtur, tanquàm Effectus à sua causa. Nam quatenùs privatio non modò per defectum, verùm etiam per contrariam positionem sive habitum definitur: & verò habitus iste in actum separatum erumpere potest: eatenùs certè non modò rationem causæ & effectus sortiuntur: sed & tanquàm subdistinctæ species considerari possunt. Fundamentum autem differentiæ hujus inter utrumque peccatum petere licet ex Epistola Jacobi. 1, 14. & 15. Vnusquisque quando tentatur, à propria concupiscentia abstrahitur, & inescatur: Deindè Concupiscentia, postquàm conceperit, parit peccatum: Peccatum verò peractum, gignit mortem.

Quò respicientes antiqui patres, quinque constituerunt Gradus, quibus differentia hæc illustrari queat: 1. Fomitem, sive corruptionem inhærentem, conjunctam cum defectu. 2. Suggestiones cogitationum & affectuum, sed nondum in actum erumpentium: quando nimirum Originale malum nunquàm quiescit, sed aliqua inclinatione se movet: 3. Delectationem. 4. Consensum. 5. ipsum opus. Quorum graduum primi duo Naturam peccati Originalis: postremi tres Naturam Actualis peccati respiciunt: Ubi tamen si quis morosius pugnare velit, secundum etiam gradum Peccati Originalis esse proprium, propterea quòd propriè loquendo, omnes motus, suggestiones & actiones contra Legem Dei pertinent ad peccatum Actuale: Cum eo sanè minimè litigabimus, dummodò inter fontem ipsum sive Scaturiginem mali, & inter rivulos ipsos, sive inter causam & Effectum, discrimen concedatur: Et cum B. Luthero statuatur: Peccatum Originis nunquàm esse otiosum, sed semper agere. 2. In hoc peccato semper etiam esse peccata actualia. 3. Fomitem esse actuale peccatum: hoc est, actualem privationem illius Justitiæ, quæ adesse debebat: & actualem positionem depravationis omnium virium, quæ abesse debebat.

Observationem proindè hoc loco vel maximè meretur, Peccatum actuale non eo sensu nominari à contradistincta Peccati Originalis specie, quasi hæc ab omni actu prorsus sit immunis: quemadmodum olim Scholastici nugati sunt, contendentes, Peccatum Originale esse malum otiosum, & torpidam qualitatem, ac propterea, nisi accedant actualia, Concupiscentia ssentiam reliquam non esse peccatum, quia nihil agat contra Legem Dei: Verùm sic appellari ab ea conditione, quæ actus sive actionis cujusque est propria. Nam quia actus est transitorium quiddam, ad differentiam peccati Originalis, Actuale hoc appellatum fuit. In actuali enim peccato materia non perstat sive permanet: sed quamprimùm aliquod cum flagitio & scelere admissum est: offensa quidem Dei, & reatus actionis remanet: actio verò ipsa, facinore patrato statim transit & desinit. In peccato autem Originali secus res habet. Nam materia ejus hac in vita, nunquàm transit: sed in perenni motu est, & sic semper adhæret nobis illa corruptio, versaturque in perpetuo actu, ut nunquàm sit otiosa: sed tùm in mente dubitationes, tùm in animis motus contra legem Dei perpetim excitet. Ex abundantia enim cordis os loquitur: & ab intus de corde hominum exeunt mala cogitationes, stultitia, superbia, adulteria &c. Matth. 12, 34. 15, 18. Marci 7, 21.

Exemplo ex Scripturis petito res illustrari potest. Genes. 6, 5. legitur: Omnis cogitatio hominis tantùm mala est omni tempore, ab adolescentia. Ubi perpetuus actus notatur malarum cogitationum. Atqui 1. Cor. 13, 5. inquit Apostolus, Charitas non cogitat malum: sic innuens dari aliquem, qui liber sit à malarum cogitationum reatu. Jam ergò ne duobus istis locis ἀντίφασις intercedere videatur, diversus utriusque respectus monstrari debet: Iste videlicet, ut prior ille locus Mosaicus intelligatur de malo Originali: cujus respectu ne renati quidem & fideles à cogitationum malarum perpetuo actu, liberi sunt: posterior verò iste Apostolicus de peccato Actuali accipiatur: Ubi sanè verum est, quod renati virtute & gratia inhabitantis Spiritus Sancti, pravis desiderijs sive cogitationibus resistere queant quo minùs in actum erumpant. Et hoc respectu Charitas non cogitat malum, quatenùs non assentitur, nedùm indulget internis malis concupiscentijs, ut actu eas expleat.

Quanquàm verò in antiqua Patrum Ecclesia, appellatio hæc Peccati Actualis usu minimè fuit recepta: & in toto Augustino semel tantùm reperitur, nempè lib. 5. hypognosticon: licet de hoc etiam libro haud immeritò dubitetur, an sit Augustini, nùm verò supposititius; tamen duæ potissimùm militant rationes, quæ appellationi huic jus Ecclesiasticum irrefragabiliter conciliare possunt. 1. Quia termini isti quibus usi sunt S. Patres naturam hujus peccati minùs exprimunt aut assequuntur. Nam sivecum Augustino Proprium: sive cùm alijs Patribus, Peccatum additum, appellites: tamen naturam ejus nuspiam assequeris: nedùm explicas, nùm in nudo aliquo atque otioso habitu, an verò in actu consistat. 2. Scriptura ipsa hanc appellationem monstrat: quatenùs in peccati hujus descriptione utitur verbis ἐργάζεσθαι, καταργάζεσθαι, ἐνεργεῖν, faciendi, agendi, operandi, efficiendi, & hujus generis alijs, ut videre est, Matth. 7, 23.

Qui operamini iniquitatem Rom 7, 8. Peccatum accepta occasione, operatum est in me omnem concupiscentiam. Et versu 17. Peccatum in me habitans operatur malum: & passim alibi. Hinc hujus modi peccata in Scripturis nominantur Opera carnis, Gal. 5, 19. Actiones Veteris hominis. Col. 3, 9. & similiter.

His ita præmissis, de definitione Peccati hujus actualis dispiciendum fuerit. Scholastici nimis imperfectè & confusè peccatum Actuale finiverunt Peccati Originalis; sive naturæ vitiosæ fructum. Ubi, quod fieri maximè debebat, neque Genus proximum, neque differentia specifica exprimitur. Multò ergò rectius D: Augustinus, Peccatum hoc dixit esse omne factum, vel dictum, vel concupitum contra legem Dei. lib. 22. Contra Faustum. Omnium autem plenissimè illud definivit Autor noster Philippus Melanchthon: Peccatum Actuale, inquiens, est omnis actio pugnans cum Lege Dei, tum in mente, tum in voluntate & corde: tum in membris externis locum habens.

Constat hæc definitio Genere proprio, & differentia specifica Genus est, Actio & omnis quidem actio, pugnans cum Lege Dei, sive interior sive exterior, vel quocunque alio modo veniat. Intelligitur autem, uti supra etiam admonuimus, Actio transiens, & cum assensu, deliberatione & proposito conjuncta: ad differentiam peccati Originalis, quod est in perpetuo, & nunquàm transeunte motu sive actu, unde haud ineptè magnus ille Theologus Chemnitius, cogitationes etiam refert ad peccatum Originis, quando nimirùm nudæ sunt suggestiones, & nudo conceptu absolvuntur, sine assensu ullo aut προαιρέσει: quanquàm non desunt Theologi, qui ejusmodi pravas suggestiones malunt referre ad Instinctum sive dictamen Diaboli. Differentiæ specificæ locum supplet, tùm Actionis determinatio ad Legem Dei, ut nimirum cum hac pugnet: tùm descriptio illa subjecti, sive sedis, in qua Peccatum hoc locum habere potest. Subjectum autem hoc vel consideratur generaliter, & tùm Subjectum peccati hujus constituitur, quicquid agendi vim facultatemque obtinet. Nam quia Actuale ab agendo nomen habet: utique in omnibus etiam hominis partibus locum illud habebit, in quibus est agendi δύναμις. Vel consideratur specialiter, & tùm pro diversitate ipsarum actionum, peccati hujus Subjectum vel est Mens sive intellectus: Quô pertinent dubitationes, disceptationes cogitationum Rom. 14, 1. Iacob. 1, 6. hæsitationes, errores, ignorantia; oblivio: vel cor sive voluntas: Quô referuntur concupiscentiæ & desideria corporis, Rom. 6, 12. vitiosi affectus & perturbationes, odia, æmulationes & similia: Vel denique membra externa: Quô pertinent spurci sermones, illiberales joci, Eph. 4, 29. obtrectationes, calumniæ, Veneficia, cædes, crapula, libidines & similia, quæ externorum corporis membrorum ministerio designantur scelera & flagitia.

Ubi tamen minimè negamus, dari posse ejusmodi actiones, quæ non ad unam tantum, sed plures Animæ potentias sive facultates, ut corporis partes referri queant: Quales sunt hæreses, idolatria, perjurium, & id genus alia.

Et hæc quidem est Natura, & propria quasi Affectio Peccati Actualis: de qua tamen tùm à Scholasticis Doctoribus, tùm a recentioribus Theologis, bene multa ac varia, in controversiam sunt vocata: Quæ vix rectiùs, quàm per Quæstiones expediri posse statuimus.

Initiò igitur sub quæstionem venit, Quomodo peccatum Actuale designetur. Ansam & occasionem præbuit Quæstioni huic, tùm antiqua illa Pharisæorum tùm recentior Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum Theologia, somniantium, Peccati hujus reatum non contrahi, nisi partim externo tantùm opere, partim proprij facti designatione: ita ut concupiscentia mala, & cum delectatione etiam conjuncta, modò ipso opere non expleatur, pro peccato Actuali haberi neque possit, neque debeat. Undè natum impium proverbium Germanicum: Die Gedancken sind Zollfrey. Errori huic διαρρήδην contradicit Scriptura, 1. ostendens interiorem etiam perturbationem cordis, & inordinatum affectum venire sub censum peccati hujus, ita quidem ut si quis temerè iram concipiat adversus fratrem, quamvis manu, aut alia quadam exteriore ratione ipsum non lædat: tamen reus sit judicij, sic censente ipso Servatore, Matth. 5, 23. Vel si quis tantùm adspiciat alterius conjugem, ad concupiscendum eam, adulterij reatum contraxerit: ibid. versu 29. Deindè errorem hunc graviter etiam refutat Scriptura, quando & præceptis & exemplis demonstrat, Peccatum Actuale committi, non tantùm designatione proprij, sed & communicatione alieni criminis: juxta gravem illam admonitionem Apostoli: 1. Tim. 5, 22. Ne communices peccatis alienis. Et Eph. 5, 7. & 11. Ne particpetis de operibus ipsorum: sed redarguatis.


### Chapter I. On the Nature & proper affection of Actual Sin: Why it is called actual sin (continued)

But by what ways especially one can communicate in others' sins, that would be very difficult to define: both because of the infinite circumstances of the actions themselves: and because of the various and inscrutable recesses of human hearts: Commonly in the Schools nine are defined, and comprised in this distich:

1. I advise.

2. I command.

3. I consent.

4. I praise.

5. I receive.

6. I share.

7. I am silent.

8. I do not oppose.

9. I do not reveal.

Thus Achitophel is held guilty of those incests which Absalom committed with his father's concubines: by suggesting the counsel of this crime, of course: 2 Sam. 16:21. Thus by commanding, David killed Uriah, 2 Sam. 11:15. Thus by consenting to the stoning of Stephen, Paul contracted the guilt of it, Acts 7:58. Thus by praising and flattering those young counselors of Rehoboam sinned, 1 Kings 12:10. Thus, by receiving light and vagrant men, Abimelech sinned, Judges 9:4. Thus, by participating, they sinned who ran with thieves, Psalm 50:18. Thus, by keeping silent, ministers and others sin, not taxing with righteous zeal the vices of their hearers or neighbors, Ezekiel 33:8. Thus, by not opposing, but conniving at the crimes of his sons, the priest Eli sinned, 1 Samuel 3:13. Thus, finally, he who does not manifest some crime committed by others is compared to one having a part with a thief, Proverbs 29:24. He who has a part with thieves hears cursing and does not report it, he hates his own life. He who participates with a thief, hears the swearer, and does not report it, hates his own soul. It is worthy of observation, however, that in all these and other similar modes of communication, the partner in crime is always involved in equal guilt with the author of the same: as the Apostle judges, Romans 1:32. Those who do such things are worthy of death: and not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.

The second question, which is moved concerning actual sin, is: Whether it also falls upon the regenerate and children of God? The handle for this question was given primarily by that Apostolic aphorism 1 John 3:8 and 9. He who commits sin is of the Devil: but whoever is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him: nor can he sin because he is born of God. Abusing this aphorism, therefore, both the Anabaptists and Schwenkfeldians established that the regenerate are entirely immune from actual sins; and the Calvinists, denying that the regenerate can fall into such sins, by which they cast off the Holy Spirit and fall totally from the grace of God.

But both of these errors are easily overturned if we attend not so much to the ῥητὸν (literal word) as to the διάνοιαν (meaning) of the Apostle's words, namely that which the συνέπεια (coherence) of that whole passage ineffably demonstrates. Now, it is established from the beginning, beyond controversy, that the Apostle in this place is dealing expressly with the regenerate: indeed, if we examine the text more accurately, with the elect properly so called, who indeed do not just begin to believe, but retain the seed of God, that is, faith in Christ, to the very end. Now, therefore, it is asked concerning these: Can they fall into actual sins? If anyone wishes to distort the letter of the Apostle's words stubbornly into a denial: it is necessary that he accuse the Apostle himself of lying and shameful contradiction: as he who in the preceding chapter, 1:8, set forth this universal rule: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us: And verse 10. If we say that we have not sinned, we make God a liar, and His Word is not in us. Therefore, the very analogy of faith and the συνάφεια (connection) of the texts of Scripture compel us, having neglected the ῥητῷ (literal word), or the simple sense of the words, to recur to the διάνοιαν (meaning). That, however, is demonstrated by the equivocation of the word Sin: which denotes either a simple lapse of human infirmity, to which the regenerate and elect are subject even in this life: And concerning this sin, it is true that these also fall into actual sins: so that the just man falls seven times a day: Proverbs 24:16, although they do not consent to the sins, but struggle against them with groaning, as the Apostle testifies, Romans 7:19. Or it denotes the pursuit and perseverance in sinning, when sins are committed with the whole affection of the heart and full deliberation and purpose of mind.

In this way, certainly, the regenerate do not sin, as long as they retain the seed of God in themselves: For if they were to sin in this way, they would no longer be regenerate, but rather servants of sin, children of the Devil: indeed, as long as they design such sins, they are outside the grace of God, and if they die in final impenitence, they are to be held not only not as elect, but not even as regenerate. Thus, although it happens not rarely that the elect also sin enormously, and sometimes fall totally from the grace of God, which the horrible lapses of Aaron, David, Peter, and others clearly demonstrate: yet, being admonished, they soon acknowledge, confess, grieve for, and correct the sin, and anxiously and solicitously implore the mercy of God. Concerning this certain species of sin, therefore, which the Apostle rightly denied of the regenerate: that is most viciously distorted by the adversaries to the denial of the remaining species as well. For just as the regenerate, insofar as they are and remain such, do not sin with the whole affection of the heart and full deliberation of mind: So they are always subject to the remaining cases of infirmity, so that they must needs groan with the Apostle: In their flesh dwells no good thing: Who will deliver us from the body of this death? Romans 7:18 and following.

With these things thus established, the ancient Novatians erred gravely, and today some fanatics err, who imagine and dream for themselves a holiness in the regenerate void of all sin, and a Church militant in these lands, entirely free and immune from all defects. To these must be added the insanity of the Papists, who boast that the fulfillment of the divine law in the regenerate is not only possible: but also invent works of supererogation, by which they might be able to merit eternal life for others.

Finally, the error of those is also intolerable who write that the regenerate and the elect, whenever they fall into sins against conscience, do not cast off the Holy Spirit, neither totally nor finally. That the elect never fall away finally, we ourselves assert. For thus the elect would not be elect, nor would election attain its end: That both are absurd and openly false, even that single Apostolic aphorism proves, Romans 11: What Israel seeks, it has not attained: but the election has attained it. But this theme is not properly in controversy in this place: But rather this comes into question, Whether the elect and regenerate, when they design actual sins, knowingly, willingly, and with a protesting conscience; do they then cast off the Holy Spirit? Where we hold the affirmative in all respects, relying on immovable foundations.

For first, the fall of the Angels teaches this, who did not stand in the Truth. John 8:44. Next, the same is argued by the ruin of our first parents, who, having committed actual sin, namely by tasting the fruit of the forbidden tree, incurred the guilt of both temporal and eternal death. Gen. 2:17. Thirdly, the examples of Saul and David, of Judas the traitor, and of Peter denying Christ three times prove the same. 1 Sam. 1:9; 1 Sam. 16:14; 2 Sam. 11:4 & 16; Matt. 27:5 & 26:69. Finally, the manifest testimonies of the Scriptures confirm the same. Ezek. 18:26: When the righteous shall turn away from his righteousness, and commit iniquity, he shall die in them; in the injustice which he has wrought, he shall die. 1 Cor. 9:27: I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway. Heb. 6:4: Those who were enlightened have fallen away. 2 Pet. 2:20: Those who are again entangled in the pollutions of the world, the latter end is worse for them than the beginning. Rev. 2:4. You have left your first love, etc.

Nor is it an objection that the gifts of God are said to be ἀμεταμέλητα (without repentance). Rom. 11:29. For the Apostle means nothing else than that God is moved by nothing from within Himself to repent: so that, namely, He would deprive anyone of His grace, once bestowed upon him, out of His absolute will. Meanwhile, however, nothing prevents Him from being offended and provoked by men, and being led to repent of His gifts, as Scripture itself teaches: Gen. 6:6: It repented God that He had made man on the earth. Jer. 18:10: If the people shall do evil in my eyes, that they do not hear my voice, I will repent of the good which I spoke that I would do to them.

Thirdly, it is asked: Whether infants have actual sins, from which they are cleansed in and through Baptism no less than from the guilt of Original sin? And indeed we answer affirmatively, but with a clear distinction between an action προαιρετικὴν (deliberate) and that which is proper to Original sin: Certainly, with respect to the former actions, that is, ἐκ προαιρέσεως (from deliberate choice) and by set purpose, infants do not sin actually; since they are destitute of the use of reason, or the second act. In which respect it is also true that infants understand neither good nor evil, Deut. 1:39, and that they do not know the difference between their right hand and their left, Jonah 4:11. But insofar as these very infants are infected with Original sin, and the root of this, as our Luther speaks, never rests: to that extent they are certainly to be judged as sinning actually; not, however, in the way that is προαιρετικὸς (deliberate) and falls upon those who already possess the use of reason, but in the way that is proper to Original sin. And indeed, such infants provide by no means obscure indications of this fact when they are found to be subject to anger, rancor, disgust, impatience, and other inordinate movements of that kind. Looking to this, our forefathers did not hesitate to insert these words into the prayer used in the rite of Baptism: We pray that through this saving flood there may be suffocated and perish in the infant everything that is engendered in him from Adam, and what he has added besides: All that is born in him from Adam, and what he himself has added to it.

And although the actual sins of such infants differ greatly in degree of atrocity from voluntary sins, because they do not proceed from a deliberate movement of the mind; nevertheless, because infants before Baptism are destitute of the gift of regeneration, they contract the guilt of damning sin, which is not removed except through Baptism at last: so that if it happens that such infants die, that guilt can do them no harm, as long as they are established outside the years of discretion.

But furthermore it is asked at this point, how far these years of innocence extend, and in what year of age the use of reason or the act of discretion begins in infants: Or what amounts to the same: At what age do baptized infants begin to sin actually, in the former way, which is προαιρετικὸς (deliberate), so that they derive upon themselves the judgment of divine wrath and the guilt of damning and mortal sin? Which question has indeed exercised many in various ways. The Greek theologians established the term or end of the years of innocence as the twelfth year of age: moved by the example of Christ, who likewise only in the twelfth year of His age revealed the use of His intellect; while in the remaining preceding years, He kept Himself within the secret guidance, as it were, of Nature. But Gregory rightly exploded their opinion, Dial. 4, cap. 10. By the example of a certain boy who, in his fifth year of age, because of blasphemies cast against God, was miserably vexed by demons until he breathed out his blasphemous soul. We shall therefore do better if, since the Scriptures are silent on this point, we also remain silent, and do not rashly establish a certain term of age: Indeed, we should not even believe that it can be established: especially since the condition of talents is clearly as different as the method of education; and malice often outstrips age: or certainly the excessive indulgence of parents, and some silent power of evil examples, implants the most foul vices even in the tenderest children, and those endowed with the best disposition: a fact which experience itself proves clearly enough.

Latin:

Cæterùm quibus potissimùm modis alienis peccatis communicare quis possit, illud definitu admodùm difficile fuerit: tùm propter infinitas ipsarum actionum circumstantias: tùm propter varios & imperscrutabiles cordium humanorum recessus: Vulgò in Scholis novem sunt definiti, & hoc disticho comprehensi:

1. Consulo.

2. Præcipio.

3. Consentio.

4. Laudo.

5. Recepto.

6. Participio.

7. Sileo.

8. Non obsto.

9. Non manifesto.

Sic Achitophel reus peragitur eorum incestuum, quas Absolom cum concubinis patris commisit: hujus nimirùm facinoris consilium suggerens: 2. Sam. 16, 21. Sic præcipiendo David occidit Vriam, 2. Sam. 11, 15. Sic consentiendo in lapidationem Stephani, Paulus reatum illius contraxit Act. 7, 58. Sic laudando & adulando peccarunt Juvenculi illi Consiliarij Roboami, 1, Reg. 12, 10. Sic recipiendo viros leves & vagos peccavit Abimelech, Judic. 9, 4. Sic participando peccarunt, qui currebant cum furibus. Psal. 50, 18. Sic tacendo peccant ministri & alij, non taxantes justo Zelo vitia auditorum aut proximi, Iezech. 33, 8. Sic non obstando, sed connivendo ad scelera filiorum peccavit Sacerdos Eli. 1. Sam. 3, 13. Sic denique, qui facinus aliquod ab alijs patratum non manifestat, comparatur partem habenti cum fure Proverb. 29, 24. Wer mit Dieben theil hat / höret fluchen / vnnd sagets nicht an / der hasset sein Leben. Qui participat cum fure, jurantem audit, & non indicat, odit animam suam. Observationem autem meretur, quod in his omnibus & consimilibus alijs communicationis modis, semper socius criminis, cum autore ejusdem pari reatu involvitur: Judice Apostolo, Rom 1, 32. Qui talia agunt, digni sunt morte: non autem tantùm qui ea faciunt, sed etiam qui consentiunt facientibus.

Altera Quæstio, quæ de peccato Actuali movetur, est: An illud etiam cadat in renatos & filios Dei? Ansam huic quæstioni potissimùm dedit Aphorismus ille Apostolicus 1. Johan. 3, 8. & 9. Qui facit peccatum, ex Diabolo est: Quisquis autem natus est ex Deo, peccatum non facit, quoniam semen ipsius in eo manet: nec potest peccare ea quòd ex Deo natus est. Hoc ergo Aphorismo abusi tùm Anabaptistæ & Schvvenckfeldiani statuerunt, Renatos à peccatis actualibus planè esse immunes: tùm Calviniani negantes, Renatos in ejusmodi peccata prolabi posse: quibus excutiant Spiritum Sanctum, & gratiâ Dei totaliter excidant.

Cæterùm uterque iste error facilè evertitur, si non magis ῥητὸν quàm διάνοιαν verborum Apostoli, eam nimirùm, quam totius illius loci συνέπεια ineffabiliter monstrat, attendamus. Jam verò extra Controversiam initiò est positum, Apostolum hoc loco agere ex professo de Renatis: Imò si textum accuratiùs expendamus, de Electis propriè sic dictis, qui nimirùm modò incipiunt credere, sed semen Dei, hoc est, fidem in Christum ad finem usque retinent. Jam ergò de his quæritur: An in peccata Actualia prolabi possint? His si quis verborum Apostoli literam mordicùs in negantem detorquere velit: is mendacij arguat, & turpis contradictionis ipsum Apostolum insimulet, necesse est: ut qui capite præcedente, 1, 8. hanc universalem prodidit regulam: Si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas non est in nobis: Et vers. 10. Si dixerimus nos non peccasse, mendacem facimus Deum, & Verbum ejus non est in nobis. Proindè ipsa analogia fidei, & textuum Scripturæ συνάφεια nos cogit, ut neglecto τῷ ῥητῷ, sive simplici Verborum sensu, ad διάνοιαν recurramus. Eam verò monstrat Aequivocatio vocabuli Peccati: quod vel simplicem notat infirmitatis humanæ lapsum, cui Renati & Electi etiam hac in vita subjacent: Et de hoc peccato verum est, quod hi et- , iam prolabantur in peccata actualia: ita ut Iustus in die cadat septies: Proverb. 24, 16. quamvis peccatis non consentiant, sed cum gemitu illis reluctentur, teste Apostolo, Rom. 7, 19. Vel notat peccandi studium & perseverantiam, quando toto cordis affectu, plena animi deliberatione & proposito peccata peraguntur.

Hoc sane modo Renati non peccant, quamdiu semen Dei in se retinent: Nam si hoc modo peccarent, non amplius essent Renati, sed potius servi peccati, filij Diaboli: imo quamdiu talia peccata designant, tamdiu sunt extra gratiam Dei, & in finali impoenitentia decedant, non modo non pro Electis, sed ne quidem pro Renatis habendi sunt. Sic etsi haud raro contingit, ut Electi quoque enormiter peccent, & totaliter interdum excidant gratia Dei, id quod horrendi lapsus Aaronis, Davidis, Petri & aliorum luculenter demonstrant: tamen admoniti peccatum mox agnoscunt, fatentur, dolent, corrigunt, Deique misericordiam anxie & sollicite implorant. De hac ergo certa peccati specie, quod de Renatis recte negavit Apostolus: illud ad negationem reliquarum etiam specierum vitiosissime ab Adversarijs detorquetur. Quemadmodum enim Renati, quatenus tales sunt & manent, toto cordis affectu, & plena animi deliberatione non peccant: Ita reliquis infirmitatis casibus semper sunt obnoxij, ut cum Apostolo ingemiscere necessum habeant: In carne sua non habitare bonum: Quis nos liberabit de corporis mortis hujus? Rom. 7. 18. & seqq.

Quibus ita constitutis graviter errarunt Veteres Novatiani, hodieque errant fanatici nonnulli, qui omni peccato vacuam in renatis Sanctimoniam, & Ecclesia hisce in terris militantem, plane ab omnibus defectibus liberam & immunem sibi fingunt ac somniant, Quibus annumeranda est Pontificiorum etiam insania, qui legis divinae impletionem in renatis non tantum possibilem esse gloriantur: sed & opera supererogationis comminiscuntur, quibus alijs vitam aternam promereri queant.

Tandem intolerabilis illorum etiam est error, qui scriptitant, Renatos & Electos, quandocunque in peccata contra conscientiam, non excutere Spiritum Sanctum, neque totaliter neque finaliter. Electos quidem finaliter excidere nunquam, ipsi asserimus. Sic enim Electi non essent Electi, neque Electio finem suum assequeretur: Quod utrumque absurdum & palam falsum esse, vel unicus ille evincit Aphorismus Apostolicus, Rom. 11. Quod quaerit Israel, non est assecutus: Electio autem est assecuta. Sed de hoc themate hoc loco non proprie controvertitur: Sed illud potius in quaestionem venit, An Electi & Renati quando designant peccata Actualia, scientes, volentes, & reclamante conscientia; An tum excutiant Spiritum Sanctum? Ubi nos affirmativam per omnia tenemus, immotis freti fundamentis.

Primùm enim hoc docet Angelorum lapsus, qui in Veritate non steterunt. Ioh. 8, 44. Deindè arguit idem protoparentum ruina, qui peccato actuali commisso, gustato nimirùm arboris prohibitæ fructu, mortis & temporalis & æternæ reatum subierunt. Gen. 2, 17. Tertiò idem evincunt exempla Saulis & Davidis, Iudæ proditoris, Petri ter abnegantis Christum 1. Sam. 1. 9. 1. Sam. 16, 14. 2. Sam. 11, 4. & 16. Matth. 27, 5. & 26, 69. Tandem idem confirmant manifesta Scripturarum testimonia, Ezech. 18, 26. Cùm averterit se justus à Justitia sua, & fecerit iniquitatem, morietur in eis, in injustitia, quam operatus est, morietur. 1, Cor. 9, 27. Castigo corpus meum, & in servitutem redigo, ne fortè cùm alijs prædicaverim, ipse reprobus fiam. Heb. 6, 4. Illuminati prolapsi sunt. 2. Pet. 2, 20. Qui rursus implicantur coinquinationibus mundi, his facta sunt posteriora deteriora prioribus. Apoc. 2, 4. Charitatem tuam primam dereliquisti &c.

Neque obstat, quòd dona Dei dicantur esse ἀμεταμέλητα. Rom. 11, 29. Nam nihil aliud sibi vult Apostolus, quàm Deum ex seipso nullâ moveri causâ ad pœnitendum : ut nimirùm ex absoluta sua voluntate ullum gratia sua, semel in ipsum collatâ, privet. Interim verò nihil obstat, quò minùs ab hominibus offensus & irritatus, pœnitudine ducatur donorum suorum, ipsa Scriptura hoc docente: Genes 6, 6. Pœnituit Deum, quòd hominem fecisset in terra, Jerem. 18, 10. Si populus fecerit malum in oculis meis, ut non audiat vocem meam : pœnitentiam agam super bono, quod locutus sum, ut facerem ei.

Tertiò quæritur : An Infantes habeant peccata actualia, à quibus haud minùs, quàm ab Originalis peccati reatu, in & per Baptismum purgentur? Et sanè respondemus affirmatè, sed cum loculenta distinctione inter actionem προαιρετικὴν: & inter eam, quæ est peccati Originalis propria : Certè priorum actionum respectu, hoc est, ἐκ προαιρέσεως, & destinato consilio, non peccant actualiter infantes: siquidem destituuntur rationis usu, sive actu secundo. Quo etiam respectu verum est, quòd infantes neque bonum, neque malum intelligant, Deut. 1, 39. quòd nesciant discrimen dextræ & sinistræ Jonæ 4, 11. Verùm quatenùs hi ipsi infantes sunt peccato Originali infecti, hujus verò radix, ut Lutherus noster loquitur, nunquàm quiescit : eactenùs certè, actualiter etiam peccare censendi sunt: modo autem non eo, qui est προαιρετικὸς, & in eos cadit, qui rationis usu jam potiuntur: sed qui est Peccati Originalis proprius. Et sanè rei hujus indicia minimè obscura de se præbent hujusmodi infantes, quando iræ, rancoris, fastidij, impatientiæ, alijsque id genus motibus inordinatis obnoxij esse deprehenduntur. Huc respicientes Majores nostri, precationi in ritu Baptismi usitatæ, hæc verba inferere minimè dubitarunt: Oramus, ut per hoc salutare diluvium suffocetur in infante, & intereat omne, quod ab Adamo ipsi est ingeneratum, quodque ab ipso insuper additum: Alles was Im von Adam angebohren ist/vnd er selbst darzu gethan hat.

Et quanquàm peccata hujusmodi Infantium actualia, vel ideò à peccatis voluntarijs àtrocitatis gradu plurimùm discrepart, quod à deliberato animi motu non proficiscuntur: interim tamen, quia ante Baptismum Infantes regenerationis dono destituuntur, ideò peccati damnantis reatum contrahunt, qui non nisi per Baptismum demùm tollitur: ut si ejusmodi Infantes mori contingat: reatus iste nocere illis nihil quicquam possit, quamdiu quidem extra annos discretionis sunt constituti.

Sed porrò quæritur hoc loco, Quousque hi ipsi anni innocentiæ se extendant, & quoto ætatis anno Rationis usus sive discretionis actus in infantibus incipiat: Vel quod eôdem recidit: Quânam ætate Infantes baptizati incipiant peccare actualiter, priore modo, qui est προαιρετικὸς, ita ut iræ divinæ judicium, damnantis, & mortalis peccati reatum in se derivent? Quæ sane quæstio multos vàriè exercuit. Græci Theologi terminum sive finem annorum innocentiæ constituerunt annum ætatis duodecimum: moti exemplo Christi, qui itidem anno demum ætatis duodecimo, intellectus sui usum prodiderit: reliquis verò antecedentibus annis, intra arcanum quasi Naturæ ductum se continuerit. Sed istorum sententiam rectè explosit Gregorius, Dial. 4. cap. 10. Exemplo pueri cujusdam, qui anno ætatis quinto ob blasphemias in Deum projectas, à Cacodæmonibus eò usque miserè divexatus fuit, donec blasphemam animam exhalaret. Rectiùs ergò fecerimus, si scripturis hac in parte tacentibus, nos quoque taceamus, neque temerè certum ætatis terminum constituamus: Imò ne quidem statui posse credamus: præsertim cùm discrepans planè sit uti ingeniorum conditio, sic & Educationis ratio: sæpiùsque malitia ætatem superet: vel certè nimia parentum indulgentia, malorumque Exemplorum tacitâ quæpiam vis, tenerrimis etiam puerulis, ac optimæ indole præditis teterrima vitia implantet: id quod Experientia ipsa satis luculenter comprobat.


### Chapter I. On the Nature & proper affection of Actual Sin: Chapter II On the various divisions of Actual Sin

CHAPTER II.

On the various divisions of Actual Sin.

The distinction of actual sin is manifold and various, according to the diversity of those respects which the consideration of this sin acquires. For if you look to its seat, one is called external, another internal: the latter is designated chiefly by thought and the discourse of reason; the former by act. If you consider the guilt, one is called Mortal, another Venial: If the Origin: one is proper, another indeed committed by communication with another sin. If the object: one is against God, and this is again subdivided into another sin, which in general is against the whole Trinity; another which specifically is committed either against the Son of man or against the Holy Spirit; another against one's neighbor, another against oneself. If regarding knowledge, one thing is hidden, another manifest. If regarding the source, one thing is contumacy, or against conscience, another is a sin of ignorance. If regarding the mode of designation, one thing is of commission, another of omission: If regarding gravity, one thing is reigning, another not reigning: concerning which individual and universal species Chemnitz discourses quite accurately in part 1, Loc. page 634 and following. We shall treat in order only of three divisions, which indeed come most into controversy. First, indeed, concerning the distinction of sin into reigning or dominating, and not reigning; then, however, concerning the division of the same into mortal and venial sin: Finally, concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit.

But before we treat of each in particular, that scope must be removed which has rendered not only the Stoic philosophers but also certain ecclesiastical doctors not a little doubtful: Whether actual sins, considered in themselves, by themselves, and from their own nature, possess any difference: or what is the same: Whether they are equal or unequal? The handle and occasion for doubting was provided 1. because all sins are committed by deviating from the straight rule of reason; where there seems to be no inequality: as the Stoics spoke: Or because this is the proper affection of sin itself, that it fights with the Law of God: nay, is opposed to God himself. But just as this does not admit of more or less, so every sin also seems to be of equal quantity: Then, however, the equality of punishment, which is eternal damnation, divinely destined equally for all sins, seems to argue for the equality of sins. And Jovinianus indeed held this opinion, as witnessed by Augustine, chapter 81 of Heresies, and Jerome, book 2 against Jovinianus.

But these reasons, both of the Stoics and of the Jovinians, shamefully beg the question: and commit the fallacy of non-cause as cause: For although the rule of reason itself behaves equally: yet it does not follow that those things which are designated against that rule are also equal: Nay, equality does not even belong to sins for this reason, because they fail from the path of equality. For just as the straight is simple: but the crooked is manifold: so it is necessary that sins also, declining from the straight, are manifold, and therefore unequal. Then that only follows from the Stoics' reasoning: that sins are equal, if they are considered according to the most common definition or affection of sin, by which they are repugnant to the good of Reason, or to the Law of God. Now, however, there is also given a special affection proper to each sin, which depends on the diversity of objects and subjects: and which either aggravates or extenuates the deed. Thus regarding the other reason of the Jovinians; the equality of damnation does not remove the inequality of offenses, both in respect of quantity and in respect of quality, especially since there are degrees of infernal torments: as will be demonstrated shortly.

Therefore the purer Church of God holds the affirmative regarding the proposed question: and establishes that actual sins are unequal or inequal: that is, that one is graver than another: for the following most evident reasons. For first, Scripture itself is accustomed to exaggerate certain sins as graver than others. Gen. 13:13. The men of Sodom were sinners exceedingly before the Lord. Whence God himself in the 4th and 5th chapters of Leviticus instituted two distinct kinds of sacrifices: One for sin committed through imprudence or error by the ignorant: the other for sin through infirmity. And in the fifth chapter, this latter kind of sin is divided into three members: for one sins either against human things, or against divine things, or against both combined. Now if all sins were equal: certainly neither would God himself have distinguished between them thus, nor would he have wished one to be expiated more lightly than another. Then the thing itself, as it were, or certainly the diversity of the agents, clearly argues for this inequality of sins: For there are those who sin out of ignorance: There are those who know they are sinning: and yet, because of the excessive corruption of their nature, they cannot restrain themselves from sins, which they themselves neither excuse nor approve: according to that of Medea

I see the better things and approve them; I follow the worse.

There are besides others, who indulge in sins on purpose, and take delight in them: and furthermore consent to those who perpetrate similar things: and that against the testimony of conscience and the law inscribed on their heart. Those who certainly would not deny that the latter sin more gravely than the rest, unless one has lost all use of reason. Thirdly, this is evident also from the fact that not only did God wish there to be degrees of punishments in punishing civil offenses: According to that of Deut. 25:2, according to the measure of the sin shall be the number of stripes: but also there are distinct degrees of damnation in hell: as witnessed by the Savior in Matt. 11:24. For he states clearly that it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for the inhabitants of the cities of Galilee.

Which same thing He pronounces also concerning the Sodomites and Gomorrahites. Thus the same Savior established degrees among the reprobate, saying: The servant who knew the will of the LORD, and did not do it, shall be beaten with many stripes; but he who did not know, and did things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few. The Prophets and Apostles support Christ, everywhere instituting comparisons of sins in their sermons, as Ezek. chap. 16, 47. You have done more wicked things than Samaria and Sodom: And in verse 52. You have surpassed your sisters with your sins. Thus the Apostle 1 Tim. 5, 8. If anyone does not have care for his own, he is worse than an infidel.

Moreover, by what and how various ways one sin is made graver than another, Thomas discusses quite prolixly in the first part of the second part, quest. 73, art. 3, and the rest. The whole matter can be dispatched more compendiously thus. A sin is aggravated first from the Person, either the Subject or the Object: as when a friend harms a friend, just as Judas Iscariot the disciple betrayed Christ his Master. Thus the sin

Latin:

CAPUT II.

De varijs divisionibus Peccati Actualis.

MUltiplex est, & varia peccati Actualis distinctio, pro diversitate eorum respectuum, quos peccati hujus consideratio sortitur. Nam si sedem ejus respicias, aliud dicitur externum, aliud internum: quorum hoc cogitatione potissimùm, & rationis discursu: illud actu designatur. Si culpam consideres, aliud dicitur Mortale, aliud Veniale: Si Originem: aliud est propriū, aliud verò communicatione cum alterio peccato commissū. Si objectum: aliud contra Deum, & hoc rursus subdividitur in peccatum aliud, quod in genere contra totam Trinitatem: aliud quod in specie vel contra Filium hominis vel contra Spiritum sanctum committitur, aliud contra proximum, aliud in seipsum. Si notitiam, aliud est occultum, aliud manifestum. Si fontem, aliud est contumacia, sive contra conscientiam, aliud ignorantiæ peccatum. Si designationis modum, aliud est Commissionis, aliud omissionis: Si gravitatem, aliud est regnans, aliud non regnans: de quibus speciebus singulis & Universis satis accuratè disserit Chemnitius part 1. Loc. pag. 634. & seqq. Nos de tribus tantùm divisionibus, quæ nimirùm vel maximè in controversiam veniunt, ordine agemus. Primùm quidem de distinctione Peccati in Regnans sive dominans, & non regnans, Deindè verò de divisione ejusdem in peccatum mortale & Veniale: Tandem de peccato in Spiritum sanctum.

Priusquàm verò in specie de singulis agamus, removendus est ille Scopus, qui non Philosophos tantùm Stoicos, sed & Doctores Ecclesiasticos quosdam haud parùm reddidit dubios: An peccata actualia in se, per se & ex natura sua considerata, differentiam aliquam sortiantur: vel quod idem est: An ea sint paria vel imparia? Dubitandi ansam & occasionem præbuit 1. quod omnia peccata committuntur exorbitando à recta regula rationis; ubi nulla videtur esse inæqualitas: uti locuti sunt Stoici: Vel quia hæc est ipsius peccati propria affectio, ut pugnet cum Lege DEI: imò DEO ipsi adversetur. Sicut autem hic magis aut minùs non recipit, sic omne etiam peccatum, paris quantitatis esse videtur: Deindè verò pœnæ æqualitas, quæ est æterna damnatio, ex æquo omnibus peccatis divinitùs destinata, peccatorum æqualitatem arguere videtur. Et hanc quidem sententiam tenuit Jovinianus teste Augustino, cap. 81. de hæresibus, & Hieronymo lib. 2. contra Jovinianum.

Sed Rationes hæ tùm Stoicorùm, tùm Jovinianorum turpiter petunt principium: & Sophisma committunt non causæ ut causæ: Etsi enim regula ipsa rationis æqualiter se habet: non tamen ideò æqualia etiam sunt, quæ contra regulam illam designantur: Imò vel ideò peccatis æqualitas non competit, quia ab æqualitatis tramite deficiunt. Nam uti rectum est simplex: obliquum verò multiplex: ita peccata etiam à recto declinantia, multiplicia, ac proindè inæqualia sint necesse est. Deindè illud tantùm ex Stoicorum ratione sequitur: quòd peccata sint paria, si secundum communissimam peccati rationem sive affectionem considerentur, quâ bono Rationis, vel Legi Dei repugnant. Jam verò datur etiam specialis affectio unicuique peccato propria, quæ ex diversitate Objectorum & Subjectorum dependet: quæque factum vel aggravat vel extenuat. Sic quoad Jovinianorum rationem alteram; æqualitas damnationis non tollit delictorum inæqualitatem, tùm respectu quantitatis, quàm respectu qualitatis, præsertim cum gradus Cruciatuum Infernalium dentur: uti mox demonstrabitur.

Proindè purior Ecclesia Dei circa propositam quæstionem tenet affirmativam: peccataque actualia statuit esse imparia sive inæqualia : hoc est, unum altero esse gravius: ob sequentes rationes longe evidentissimas. Nam primum Scriptura ipsa quædam peccata, tanquam aliis graviora exaggerare solet. Gen. 13, 13. Homines Sodomitæ nimis erant peccatores coram DOMINO. Unde DEUS ipse Levitici 4. & 5. capitib9, duo distincta sacrificioru genera instituit: Unum pro peccato, per imprudentiam sive errorem commisso ab ignorantibus: alterum pro peccato per infirmitatem. Et capite quidem quinto posterius hoc peccati genus in tria membra dispescitur: nam aut in res humanas peccatur, aut in res divinas, aut in utrasque conjunctim. Jam si peccata omnia essent paria: certe neque DEUS ipse sic inter ea distinxiffet, neque alterum altero levius expiari voluisset. Deinde res ipsa quasi, vel certe agentium diversitas, imparitatem hanc peccatorum luculenter arguit: Sunt enim qui ex ignorantia peccant: Sunt, qui sciunt se peccare: & tamen præ corruptione nimia naturæ suæ, non possunt se cohibere a peccatis, quæ ipsa tamen nec excusant, nec approbant: secundum illud Medeæ

Video meliora proboq; Deteriora sequor.

Sunt præterea alii, qui ex proposito peccatis indulgent, iisque delectantur: atque iis insuper consentiunt, qui similia perpetrant: idque contra testimonium conscientiæ & legis cordi suo inscriptæ. Quos sane postremos reliquis gravius peccare non negaverit, nisi qui omnem rationis usum deperdidit. Tertio patet hoc exinde etiam, quod non modo DEUS in civilibus puniendis delictis, voluit esse pœnarum gradus: Juxta illud Deuter. 25, 2. pro mensura peccati erit etiam plagarum modus: sed & distincti sunt damnationis gradus in inferno: teste Servatore Matth. 11, 24. Diserte enim affirmat, Tyro & Sidoni tolerabilius fore in die Judicij, quam civitatum Galilææ incolis.

Quod ipsum de Sodomitis etiam & Gomorrhæis pronunciat. Sic idem Servator gradus inter reprobos constituit, dicens: Servus, qui agnovit voluntatem DOMINI, & non fecit illam, plagis vapulabit multis; Qui autem non cognovit, & fecit digna plagis, vapulabit paucis. Christo suffragantur Prophetæ & Apostoli, passim peccatorum comparationes suis in concionibus instituentes, ut Jezech. cap. 16, 47. Sceleratiora fecisti Samaria & Sodoma: Et versu 52. Vicisti sorores tuas peccatis tuis. Sic Apostolus 1. Timot. 5, 8. Si quis suorum curam non habet, infideli est deterior.

Cæterum quibus & quam variis modis unum peccatum altero gravius efficiatur, satis prolixe disputat Thomas prima secundæ, quæst. 73. art. 3. & reliquis. Compendiosius res tota sic expediri potest. Aggravatur primum peccatum ex Persona, vel Subjecta, vel Objecta: ut quando amicus amicum lædit, quemadmodum Judas Ischarioth discipulus Christum Magistrum suum pro didit. Sic Judæorum pecca-


### Chapter I. On the Nature & proper affection of Actual Sin: Whether Ignorance of Law and fact excuses a sin

of the Jews delivering up Christ was more grievous than the sin of Pilate and Herod, and of the remaining Gentiles and foreign soldiers. Thus, one sins less against a man than against GOD: thus, he sins more grievously who treats parents, teachers, or magistrates with contumely than one who treats equals or strangers so.

Next, sin is aggravated by the inequality of the thing itself or the object. For he sins more grievously who harms the life of another than one who harms their goods or faculties: he who corrupts the Word of GOD and the Sacraments than one who corrupts civil laws.

Thirdly, the very origin of sins also argues for the inequality of sins. For he sins more grievously who designs some wickedness out of set malice than one who sins out of ignorance of either the fact or the law, or out of a perturbation of the affections. Whence Christ prayed for his crucifiers, that they might not know what they were doing, Luke 23:34.

Finally, long-continued duration, frequent reiteration, excuse, and contumacious defense aggravate sin.

On the occasion of this question, it began to be disputed whether ignorance of law and fact excuses sin. For the prayer of Christ itself seems to intend this, praying for the crucifiers who did not know what they were doing: likewise that wish of Peter in Acts 3:17, saying: Now, brothers, I know that you crucified Christ through ignorance: likewise that saying of Paul, 1 Cor. 2:8: If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. It is added that it seems to abhor the φιλανθρωπια of the nature of GOD that He should slay an ignorant nation, Genesis 20:4.

However, in order for this question to be rightly explained, three things must be premised: 1. What ignorance is, or to do something ignorantly. 2. How many kinds of ignorance there are. 3. What and how many kinds of excuse there are that have a place in sin. For the first, it must be known that, just as one is said to act knowingly by reason of mind and intellect who has perceived and known both the matter itself or the thing which he handles, and the end for which he acts, and the remaining circumstances to be observed in every action: so, conversely, one is said to act out of ignorance, or ignorantly, who knows nothing at all of all these things which have now been noted. And this can indeed be called simple ignorance, which is very rare. For hardly, and indeed scarcely at all, except in madmen who are such either by disease or by the induction of the mind and voluntarily, are men found to be so ignorant of all these things in acting that they do not know at least something. But he is said to be mixedly ignorant in whom there are some things about the action that are known, and some that are unknown.

Now for the second, by reason of the object, ignorance of fact is commonly said to be one kind, when the agent is ignorant of certain singular circumstances in which the whole action scarcely consists, and which the agent could not have foreseen or guarded against before the action. Ignorance of law is said to be another, when the agent is ignorant in general of what is honest or dishonest, useful or useless, to be chosen or to be avoided in the action about which he is occupied: that is, when he is ignorant of the end of his action. But both of these are again twofold: one is gross, supine, desultory, and affected, which was formerly called vincible by the Scholastics, such as is in fact the case in drunkards, such as it is also written to have been in Lamech, the slayer of Cain, who is thought to have pierced Cain for a wild beast by a certain error of the eyes, and thus out of ignorance. Genesis 4:24, such as in Lot lying with his daughter, Genesis 19:33, such as was also in Judah committing incest with his daughter-in-law Tamar, Genesis 38:15. For this ignorance could have been overcome and corrected, at least by applying moderate diligence: but this ignorance of law is in those who are ignorant of those things of which knowledge can be had from the law of nature or at least from common sense itself: or they are ignorant only of those things which they both could and ought to have known, such as are the laws and statutes of the society of which everyone professes himself to be a member. If these things are ignored by anyone, either out of stupidity or to seek greater license for sin, this is likewise said to be gross and affected ignorance, such as was in Lot twice drunk, Genesis 19:32.

The other ignorance is called Probable, which the Scholastics have named by the barbarous term Invincible, which falls even upon a moderately prudent man, and creeps upon him who has done everything that was in his power: such as was in Noah when intoxicated by wine, the force and efficacy of which he had not yet learned by any experience, Gen. 9, 21. or could have learned: such as was also in Jacob when lying with Leah, who had not yet been married or betrothed to him, Gen. 29, 25.

Regarding the third member, the excuse itself can also be said to be twofold. For it is said to free either from the fault itself: or merely from the gravity of the fault: of which the former can excuse a man from the whole: the latter merely from a part.

Now these things being thus laid down, such an answer is returned to the principal question: Before GOD there is no ignorance, either of fact or of law, which excuses from sin in its entirety. For every ανομια, and committed in whatever way, makes one guilty of sin. 1 John 3, 4. But concerning GOD it stands written: Thou art not a GOD that hath pleasure in wickedness. Psalm 5, 5. The soul that hath sinned, it shall die, Ezek. 18, 20.
