But from a part, that is, from the gravity of the fault, gross or supine ignorance does not excuse by any means at all, much less affected ignorance, which aggravates the crime itself rather than mitigates it, both before GOD, and also before fair vindicators and observers of honest laws: But only that probable ignorance. The truth of this answer is established by that sentence which was pronounced by CHRIST, Luke 12, 48. The servant who did not know the will

of his Lord, and did things worthy of stripes, he shall be beaten with few. If he was ignorant of the will of his Lord, why, I ask, is he beaten? The reason is: Because when he could and ought to have known it, he neglected it: on which account, although it may not be in the greatest, it is nevertheless not in no, but at least in some fault. Whence it is that the Apostle explains this ignorance in a brief sentence, 1 Cor. 14:38: Let him who is ignorant, be ignorant: as if he were to say, let him be ignorant not only at his own fault, but also at his own peril. And the LORD in his law willed that a sacrifice should be made even for the sin of ignorance, Levit. 5:17. By which very thing he shows not obscurely that no ignorance whatsoever is free from fault. That the ignorance of the crucified Christ did not excuse from sin is evident from the very testimony of Christ's intercession, which would have been in vain if there had been no fault in the ignorance: Now, since Christ asks for the remission of the same from the Father, what, I ask, could be said more clearly regarding the guilt of the deed? This, therefore, is the reason for Christ's prayer, that the sin must be forgiven them, because it did not proceed from the worst source of sin, namely, malice induced, but was joined with at least some ignorance, namely, of the deed considered not simply, but mixedly: Because they know not that the one they are crucifying is the Son of GOD, which very thing, however, they were ignorant of through their own supine fault. The same is the sentiment of another passage alleged from the Acts. Thus, what Christ says in John 15:22 concerning the unbelief of the Jews: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin: he himself is the best interpreter of himself, who immediately adds to those words, They would not have sin: But now they have no excuse for their sin. By which saying he shows that 'not to have sin,' placed in the preceding clause, is not in a simple sense, as if they would have been immune from sin, but limited: namely, for an excuse of sin, which would not have been lacking to them: nor yet that same thing from the whole, but only from so much. But now he shows that this very thing also has been denied to them, namely, any excuse whatsoever for sin, so that their sin is most atrocious. That the infidelity of the Gentiles, who were without GOD in the world, Eph. 2:12, and were ignorant of GOD, 1 Thess. 4:5, was not a sin, no reason can be given. But that it was not excusable through ignorance in its entirety is evident from the fact that all ought to know, and in their own way can also know, natural and divine law. They were therefore also obligated to the inquiry of truth, and they had opportunities to know the doctrine of the Gospel. There are three signs of natural obligation: Natural knowledge, Romans 1:19; the baseness of ethnic religions; and the imperfection of philosophical doctrine. Now these were the opportunities for knowing the Gospel of Christ: 1. The celebrity of divine manifestations in the Church at all times. 2. The location of the land of Canaan in the center, as it were, of the habitable globe. 3. The exiles and dispersions of the Jewish people. 4. The conversion of the books of the Old Testament into the Greek language, which could be most well-known to all nations.

These things having been thus premised, it is next in order that we treat expressly of those more notable distinctions of Actual Sin.

Latin:

tum tradentium Christum gravius erat peccato Pilati & Herodis, & reliquorum gentilium ac externorum militum. Sic minus peccatur in Hominem quam in DEUM: Sic gravius peccat, qui parentes, Præceptores, Magistratus, quam qui æquales aut alienos contumelia afficit.

Deinde aggravatur Peccatum ex ipsius rei sive objecti inæqualitate. Gravius enim peccat, qui vitam, quam qui bona aut facultates alterius lædit: qui Verbum DEI & Sacramenta, quam qui leges civiles depravat.

Tertio ipsa quoque peccatorum origo inæqualitatem peccatorum arguit. Gravius enim peccat, qui ex destinata malitia scelus aliquod designat, quam qui ex ignorantia vel facti vel juris, aut affectuum perturbatione peccat. Unde Christus oravit pro crucifixoribus suis, ut qui nesciant, quid faciant, Luc. 23, 34.

Tandem peccatum aggravat diuturna continuatio, crebra reiteratio, excusatio & contumax defensio.

Occasione quæstionis hujus disputari cœptum fuit, An ignorantia Juris & facti peccatum excuset. Videtur enim hoc ipsum sibi velle Christi precatio, orantis pro crucifixoribus nescientibus quid faciant: Item votum illud Petri Act. 3, 17. dicentis: Nunc fratres scio, quod per ignorantiam Christum crucifixistis: Item illud Pauli, Cor. 2, 8. Si cognovissent, nunquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. Accedit quod a natura DEI φιλανθρωπια abhorrere videtur, ut gentem ignorantem interficiat, Genes. 20, 4.

Cæterum ut Quæstio hæc rite explicetur, tria præmittenda sunt: 1. Quid sit ignorantia aut ignorantem aliquid facere. 2. Quotuplex sit ignorantia. 3. Quæ sit & quotuplex Excusatio, quæ in peccato locum habet. Pro primo sciendum illud est, quemadmodum ratione mentis & intellectus Sciens facere aliquis dicitur, qui & materiam ipsam seu rem, quam tractat, & finem cur agat, & reliquas circumstantias, in actione quaque spectandas, perspectas atq; cognitas habet: Ita vice versa, ex ignorantia, aut ignorans agere is dicitur, qui hæc omnia, quæ jam sunt notata, minime novit. Et hæc quidem simplex ignorantia dici potest, quæ est rarissima. Vix enim ac ne vix quidem, nisi in furiosis, qui vel morbo, vel inductione animi, ac voluntarie tales sint, reperiuntur homines, rerum istarum omnium ita ignari in agendo, quin aliquid saltem sciant. Mixte autem ignorare is dicitur, in quo sunt quædam de actione, quæ sciuntur: quædam quæ ignorantur.

Jam pro secundo, ratione Objecti, vulgo Alia esse dicitur Ignorantia Facti, quando agens ignorat singulares quasdam circumstantias, in quibus totius actionis vix præcipue consistit: quasque agens ante actionem non potuit prævidere aut præcavere. Alia dicitur Ignorantia Juris, quando agens in universum ignorat, quid in actione, circa quam versatur, honestum aut inhonestum, utile aut inutile, eligendum aut fugiendum, sit: hoc est, quando finem suæ actionis ignorat. Sed hæc utraque rursus duplex est: Crassa una, supina, desultoria atque affectata, quæ vincibilis a Scholasticis olim appellata fuit, qualis de facto est in ebriis, qualis eteam fuisse scribitur in Lamecho, Caini occisore qui errore quodam oculorum, & sic ex ignorantia pro fera Cainum confixisse putatur. Genes. 4, 24. qualis in Lotho cum filia concumbente, Genes. 19, 33. qualis & in Juda fuit, cum nuru Thamar incestum committente. Genes. 38, 15. Poterat enim vinci & corrigi hæc ignorantia, mediocri saltem adhibita diligentia: De Jure autem hæc in illis est, qui vel ignorant ea, quorum ex lege naturæ, aut saltem ipso sensu communi potest haberi notitia: vel ea duntaxat ignorant, quæ nosse & poterant & debebant, qualia sunt leges & statura Societatis ejus, cujus fese membrum esse, quisque profitetur. Hæc sua quopiam ignorentur, vel ex stupore, vel ad quærendam majorem peccati licentiam: crassa & affectata hæc esse ignorantia itidem dicitur, qualis in Lotho bis ebrio fuit, Genes. 19, 32.

Altera ignorantia Probabilis appellatur, quam barbaro nomine Scholastici Invincibilem nominarunt, quæ in mediocriter etiam prudentem virum cadit, & obrepit ei etiam, qui fecit omne, quod in se fuit: qualis in Noacho fuit inebriato a vino, cujus vim & efficaciam nullo dum experimento didiceret, Genes. 9, 21. aut didicisse poterat: qualis fuit & in Jacobo cum Lea concumbente, quæ nupta ipsi nondum aut desponsata fuerat, Genes. 29, 25.

Quoad tertium membrum Excusatio ipsa quoque gemina esse dici potest. Nam vel a culpa ipsa: vel a gravitate duntaxat culpæ liberare dicitur: quarum illa a toto: hæc a tanto dantaxat excusare hominem potest.

Jam his ita positis, ad quæstionem principalem talis redditur responsio: Coram DEO nullam esse vel facti, vel Juris ignorantiam, quæ a peccato in totum excuset. Omnis enim ανομια, & quocunque & quocunque modo commissa, peccati reum facit. 1. Johan. 3, 4. De DEO autem scriptum extat: Non DEUS volens iniquitatem tu es. Psalm. 5, 5. Anima quæ peccaverit, ipsa morietur, Jezech. 18, 20. A tanto autem, hoc est, a gravitate culpæ, nullo prorsus pacto excusat crassa vel supina, multo minus affectata ignorantia, quæ crimen ipsum aggravat potius, quam mitigat, tum apud DEUM, tum etiam apud æquos honestarum legum vindices atque observatores: Sed probabilis tantum illa. Constat de responsi hujus veritate ex sententia ea, quæ est a CHRISTO pronunciata, Luc. 12, 48. Servus qui non cognovit voluntatem

Domini sui, & fecit digna plagis, vapulabit paucis. Si ignarus erat voluntatis Domini sui, quid vapulat quæso? Ratio est: Quia cùm poterat & debebat scire eam, neglexit: quo nomine licèt nõ si in maxima: non est tamen in nulla: sed aliqua saltem culpa. Undè est, quod Apostolus brevi sententia ignorantiam istam expedit, 1. Corinth. 14, 38. Qui ignorat, ignoret: quasi dicat, suâ non culpâ tantùm, sed & periculo ignoret. Et DOMINUS in lege sua pro Ignorantiæ delicto sacrificium etiam fieri voluit, Levit. 5, 17. Quo ipso non vacare culpa quamcunque Ignorantiam, haud obscurè ostendit. Quòd ignorantia Crucifixi Christi à peccato non excusavit: ipso intercessionis Christi testimonio constat, quæ frustranea fuisset, si culpa in ignorantia non fuiffet: Jam cùm dimissionem eidem à Patre Christus flagitet: quid dici in reatum facti manifestius quæso poterat? Hæc est ergò Precationis Christi ratio, dimittendum esse illis peccatum, quia non à pessimo peccati fonte, Malitia nimirùm inducta, profectum: sed cum ignorantia saltem aliqua, facti nimirùm non simpliciter: sed mixtè considerati, sit conjunctum: Quia quem crucifigunt, Filium DEI esse nesciant, quod ipsum tamen culpa supina sua ignorabant. Eadem loci alterius ex actis allegati est sententia. Sic quod Christus Johan. 15, 22. de Judæorum Incredulitate di cit: Si non venissem, & locutus fuissem eis, peccatum non haberent: ipsemet interpres sibi optimus est, qui statim verbis illis Peccatum non haberent, subjungit: Nunc autem excusationem non habent de peccato suo. Quo dicto ostendit, Peccatum non habere, in præcedenti commate positum esse non sensu simplici, quasi à peccato fuissent futuri immunes: sed limitato: nempè pro peccati excusatione, quæ ipsis non fuiffet defutura: neq; illa tamen ipsa à toto: sed à tanto duntaxat. Nunc autem hoc ipsum quoque negatum ipsis esse ostendit, nempè excusationem qualemcunque peccati, adeò ut peccatum ipsorum sit atrocissimum. Gentilium infidelitas, qui sine DEO fuerunt in mundo, Eph. 2, 12. & DEUM ignorarunt, 1. Thess. 4, 5. quinam peccatum non fuerit; ratio dari non potest. At quòd excusabile per ignorantiam ex toto non fuerit, indè constat, Quia jus naturale & divinum nosse omnes debent, & suo modo possunt etiam. Obligati ergò erant etiam ad inquisitionem veritatis, & habuerunt occasiones, ad cognoscendam doctrinam Evangelii. Obligationis naturalis tria sunt signa: Notitia naturalis Roman. 1, 19. Turpitudo religionum Ethnicarum: & Imperfectio doctrinæ Philosophicæ. Occasiones autem cognoscendi Evangelii Christi hæ fuerunt. 1. Celebritas patefactionum divinarum in Ecclesia omni tempore. 2. Situs terræ Canaan in meditullio quasi orbis habitabilis. 3. Exilia & dispersiones populi Judaici. 4. Conversio librorum Veteris Testamenti in linguam Græcam, quæ omnibus gentibus poterat esse notissima.

His ita præmissis, proximum est, ut in specie de insignioribus illis Peccati Actualis distinctionibus ex professo agamus.


### Chapter I. On the Nature & proper affection of Actual Sin: I. The distinction of Actual sin into reigning or dominating, and non-reigning

I. The distinction of Actual sin into reigning or dominating, and non-reigning.

The Epistle to the Romans, ch. 6:12 and 14, shows the foundation of this distinction, saying: Let not sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey sin in the lusts of the body: neither shall sin have dominion over you. Now, reigning sin is nothing other than some persevering error against the articles of faith or conscience, excluding from the heart the assurance of the remission of sins, and making the sinner liable to eternal destruction, unless remission is made: such as Original sin, and all actual sins in the unregenerate. Or as the Apostle defines it with sharp brevity: Reigning sin is to obey the concupiscence of the flesh. Such sin the regenerate also not rarely designate for a time: which is evident from the example of David. Non-reigning sin has a place only in the regenerate, and is nothing other than Original sin, defects, depraved inclinations, and those actual sins which are of ignorance, omission, or infirmity, which remain in the regenerate as long as they are survivors in this life: according to that of the Apostle, Galat. 5:17: The flesh always lusts against the Spirit: and the Spirit against the flesh: for these are contrary to one another: but they ought to be contrary in such a way that the Spirit dominates the flesh, lest sin acquire strength and obtain dominion. For if it happens that the regenerate loosen the reins to sin, and thus fall into reigning sins, then indeed they lose the Holy Spirit and fall from the grace of GOD, until they are reconciled again to GOD through true repentance.

Although there are not lacking theologians who opine that this distinction of sin, with the subsequent other one, which is into Mortal and Venial sin, is entirely one and the same, and therefore judge that reigning or dominating sin has an equal and the same breadth as mortal sin: nevertheless, to one weighing the matter more accurately, it cannot be obscure that some difference between each sin must be established. This is evident from the nature and, as it were, the proper affection of each sin, which is not reciprocal: but convertible only from one part of itself. For every reigning or dominating sin is also mortal: but not vice versa, every mortal sin is immediately also reigning or dominating. The reason for the statement is most manifest. For the guilt of mortal sin is contracted by at least one and that first act of designation. But dominating or reigning sin becomes so only when either the same sin is continued and committed at repeated times: or it obtains no remission through the intervention of serious repentance. The matter can be illustrated by examples. Peter, denying Christ three times, committed a mortal sin: but not a reigning sin: since he immediately performed repentance at the nod of Christ. Luke 22:61. David, committing adultery and murder, not only mortal but he also designated the reigning sin, as one who continued in wickedness for the space of almost an entire year: nor did he perform penance sooner than he was sharply rebuked by the Prophet.

With these things thus considered, it becomes plain that reigning or dominant sin is much more atrocious than mortal sin: inasmuch as it is for the most part joined with long-continued duration, not only does it not obtain forgiveness, but it more and more kindles and exasperates the wrath of God, and finally draws upon itself the punishment of divine desertion, which is proper to obduration. Therefore, let everyone take heed to himself against this sin above all, by applying those means and remedies, both from the Law and from the Gospel, which our Author most learnedly and at length points out, almost at the end of this Article concerning Actual sins: on page 366 of my copy.

Latin:

I. Distinctio peccati Actualis in Regnans sive Dominans, & non regnans.

DIstinctionis hujus fundamentum monstrat Epistola ad Romanos, cap. 6, 12. & 14. Neregnet, inquiens, peccatum in mortali vestro corpore, ut obediatis peccato in cupiditatibus corporis: neque vobis peccatum dominabitur. Est autem peccatum regnans nihil aliud, quàm perseverans aliquis error contra articulos fidei aut conscientiam, excludens ex corde fiduciam remissionis peccatorum, & obnoxium faciens peccantem exitio æterno, nisi fiat remissio: qualia sunt peccatum Originale, & omnia actualia in non renatis. Vel uti Apostolus arguta brevitate definit: Peccatum regnans est obedire Concupiscentiæ carnis. Quale peccatum designant haud rarò etiam renati ad tempus: id quod constat exemplo Davidis. Peccatum non regnans locum tantùm habet in renatis, & nihil est aliud, quàm Peccatum Originale, defectus, inclinationes pravæ, & peccata illa actualia, quæ sunt Ignorantiæ, omissionis, aut infirmitatis, quæ manet reliqua in renatis, quandiu hac in vita sunt superstites: secundum illud Apostoli, Galat. 5, 17. Caro semper concupiscit adversus Spiritum: & Spiritus adversus carnem: hæc enim sibi invicem adversantur: sed ita adversari debent, ut Spiritus dominetur carni, ne peccatum vires acquirat, & dominium impetret. Quod si enim contingat, ut renati frena laxent peccato: & sic ruant in peccata regnantia: tùm sanè amittunt Spiritum sanctum, & excidunt gratiâ DEI, donec per veram pœnitentiam reconcilientur rursus DEO.

Quanquàm verò non desunt Theologi, qui distinctionem hanc peccati, cum subsequente altera, quæ est in peccatum Mortale & Veniale, prorsus unam eandemque esse opinantur, ac proindè Regnantis sive Dominantis peccati, cum mortali peccato, parem eandemque latitudinem esse arbitrantur: tamen accuratiùs rem pensitanti obscurum esse nequit, aliquam utriusque peccati differentiam constituendam esse. Patet hoc ex natura & propria quasi affectione utriusque peccati, quæ reciproca non est: sed ex altera tantùm sui parte convertibilis. Omne enim peccatum regnans, sive dominans est & mortale: sed non vice versa, omne mortale, statim etiam est regnans sive dominans. Ratio dicti est manifestissima. Mortalis enim peccati reatus, uno saltem & ipso primo designationis actu contrahitur. Dominans autem sive regnans peccatum tùm demùm fit, quando vel idem peccatum continuatur, & iteratis vicibus committitur: vel interventu seriæ pœnitentiæ Remissionem nullam impetrat. Exemplis res illustrari potest. Petrus ter abnegans Christum, peccatum mortale commisit: sed non peccatum regnans: Siquidem statim ad nutum Christi egit pœnitentiam. Luc. 22, 61. David committens stuprum & homicidium non modò mortale, sed & dominans peccatum designavit, ut qui ad integri ferè anni spatium continuavit flagitium: neque citiùs egit pœnitentiam, quàm per Prophetam acriùs reprehenderetur.

Quibus ita consideratis, planum fit, peccatum regnans sive dominans peccato mortali multò esse atrocius: quippè quod plerumque cum diuturna continuatione conjunctum, non modò Veniam non consequitur, sed iram DEI magis magisque accendit & exasperat, & tandem desertionis divinæ pœnam, quæ indurationis propria est, attrahit. Maximoperè proindè ab hoc peccato prius quisque sibi caveat, iis tùm ex Lege, tùm ex Evangelio adhibitis mediis & remediis, quæ Autor noster perquàm eruditè & prolixè monstrat, sub finem fermè Articuli hujus de peccatis Actualibus: mihi pag. 366.


### Chapter I. On the Nature & proper affection of Actual Sin: II. The distinction of actual sin into mortal and venial

Our Author assigns a peculiar place or Article to this distinction, and he finally subjects it to the Article concerning the difference between the Old and New Testament, perhaps following his own plan. We are most thoroughly persuaded that its proper seat is most rightly established in the present Article.

The whole Philippean Treatise consists chiefly of five parts:

For first, he deplores the security of the greatest part of men, who either never at all, or only superficially and perfunctorily, think about the atrocity of sin.

Then, however, he shows that in the unregenerate there is no distinction between mortal and venial sins: but that all their sins are mortal.

Thirdly, he teaches that the Regenerate have venial sin when they resist doubt, security, depraved concupiscences, and inordinate affections through the Holy Spirit: but that they rush into mortal sin when they sin knowingly and willingly, and with purpose against their conscience.

Fourthly, he removes from the present dispute the Article concerning Election, inasmuch as it is less suited here. Finally, he discusses affected Ignorance and affected omission: showing that both come under the reckoning of mortal sins.

We, having regard for the present time and the controversies which are agitated today, will bring these two things especially back to the anvil of treatment:

I. What is the proper and genuine sense of this distinction; and what foundations for it can and ought to be established from the Scriptures.

II. By what reasoning both the Romanists and the Calvinists corrupt this distinction, and by what foundations their arguments ought to be opposed and overturned.

I. The true and genuine sense of the distinction of sin into Mortal and Venial:

What the true sense of this distinction may be can be explained by three especially noted Hypotheses: THE FIRST is such: Every sin in itself, by itself, and considered according to the judgment of the Law, is mortal, not even one or the lightest being excepted. For although the Law of GOD distinguishes among sins in such a way that one is either greater or less than another: yet regarding the guilt of the violated divine law, all are similar or equal. The reason is: Because it is not necessary to consider simply what is commanded: but who that is, who commands. Insofar, therefore, as individual and universal sins, thus absolutely considered, strike against the will of GOD the most just legislator: to that extent they certainly also lie under that sentence which GOD himself has brought forth, entirely immutable, concerning the transgressors of his laws: Deut. 27, 26. Gal. 3, 10. Cursed is everyone who has not remained in all things which are written in the book of the law, to do them. And Ezech 18, 4. The soul that has sinned, it shall die. Rom. 6, 23. The wages of sin is death. James 2, 10. Whoever shall have kept the whole law, but offends in one, has become guilty of all.

The lightest, therefore, or the most minute sin, by reason of its act, by itself, and according to the law, considered outside of grace, is worthy of eternal death, whether it breaks out into an external act, or consists within the innermost and lightest concupiscences, without the assent of the will. And in this respect, all sins, as much in the reborn as in the non-reborn, are only mortal.

The Jesuit Society contradicts this doctrine. For Bellarmine contends in his book on the loss of grace, chapter 12. 1. That Venial sins, considered by reason of their act, can indeed be absolutely and simply called sins: yet they are not perfectly sins, if they are compared with mortal ones. But this is a weak Sophistry, indeed a manifest depravation of the state of the controversy. For this is not in question, Whether Venial sins, if they are compared relatively to mortal sins, are smaller and lighter? which we ourselves grant; but this comes into controversy: Whether even Venial sins, if they are considered from themselves, and according to the law of GOD, are worthy of eternal death, no less than the sins which are called mortal? Where we certainly hold the affirmative in all respects.

For it has already been shown first that sins, considered by their own nature and regarding the guilt of the violated divine Law, are all equal. In this respect, therefore, this fictitious distinction of the Jesuit completely collapses, who contends that venial sins are indeed sins absolutely and simply, but not perfectly. 2. The Apostle in Romans 7:7 argues clearly enough that even involuntary concupiscence, which beyond controversy ought to be referred to the class of venial sins, is prohibited by the Law and can be called a sin properly and perfectly. Finally, whatever is subject to the curse of the Law, it is necessary that it be perfectly a sin. But even venial sins, by reason of their act and considered from the Law, are subject to the curse of the divine law, as the testimonies of Scripture already produced before teach: to which can be added that of the Savior in Matthew 5:19. Whoever breaks one of these least commandments will be called least in the kingdom of Heaven. But it is broken when it is not fulfilled in the way in which Christ fulfilled it, in verse 17.

The Jesuit objects that the testimonies of Scripture are to be understood only concerning mortal sins, and not concerning venial sins: and he tries to prove this first from the fact that, as if those scriptures comprehended venial sins, it would follow that just men could not only fall from the life of grace on account of venial sins alone, but also actually fall. But the Jesuit errs and is deceived under the sophism of ἐτεροζητήσεως [heterozētēseōs], and a shameful confusion of disparate questions: for it is one thing when it is asked what sins, which are called venial, are in themselves and by reason of their act, or considered from the Law? But it is another thing when it is asked what is the cause that the Reborn, designating venial sins, do not by the very act fall from the grace of God. By reason of the former question, these sins are considered as they are by their nature and by the definition of the Law. By reason of the latter question, these sins are no longer considered from their own affection, which they derive from the Law, but from the condition of the person who is reconciled with God through faith and has obtained the remission of those sins from the Gospel. Therefore, no logic of consequence holds if, from this latter respect, which concerns the person acting and reconciled to God through faith, a subsumption is made to that former one, which considers these venial sins from the property of their nature. For as much as the Law and the Gospel differ from each other, so much do these two questions also dissent from each other, of which the former receives its decision from the Law, the latter from the Gospel. The former regards the nature of sin according to the rigor of the Law; the latter regards the remission of sin from the promise of the Gospel. Now indeed, when we affirm that the venial sins of the Reborn are also mortal, we then only attend to and urge its nature from the Law, by no means denying that in persons reconciled to God by faith, they as it were lose this proper nature of theirs and by accident become venial or remissible, as the second observation will demonstrate shortly.

The second argument of the Jesuit, by which he strives to confirm his exception, sounds thus: That curse in Deuteronomy is referred to the violators of the commandments which had been delivered in that very book: for that pronoun 'this' signifies that, when it is said: 'Cursed is he who does not remain in all things which are written in the book of this law.' But those commandments are all by far the most serious, concerning avoiding idolatry, incest, homicide, and the like, which by the consent of all are mortal sins. By a like reason, Ezekiel 18:4 and following enumerates various crimes, all of which in their kind are mortal. Thus Paul in Romans 6 discusses that sin which fights against grace and cannot remain together with righteousness: and that he who has it is dead, he who does not have it is alive: such as are not all sins, but only mortal ones: for both Catholics and Lutherans admit that grace, righteousness, and life are not excluded by venial ones. St. James explains clearly enough that he is speaking of crimes which are properly and perfectly against the law of God: because he immediately adds: 'For he who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not kill,' etc. Therefore, these testimonies are not to be accommodated to venial sins.

But a shameful sophistication is committed κατὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχου [kata tēn agnoian elenchou]: which arises from the fact that the Jesuit very ignorantly posits that one and the same predicate cannot be accommodated to different species as well: so indeed that if more serious sins, according to the scriptures, ought to be called, nay truly are, mortal; then lighter or venial sins neither are by themselves in their nature, nor ought to be called, mortal. This lust for sophistry is most solidly overturned by that logical axiom: Whatever is either affirmed or denied of a genus, that also ought to be affirmed or denied in the same way of the individual species. Now, Scripture affirms of sin considered in general that it is by its nature mortal. Therefore, this is a true predicate of all its species, that is, of sins both lighter and more serious.

Then this argument labors under a manifest crime of falsehood. For Moses in Deut. 27:36 does not understand only those most serious commandments which the Jesuit enumerates, but the whole Law, as it was promulgated by God himself on Mount Sinai. This is evident even from the fact that in the preceding chapter 5. He inculcates the Moral Law upon the people in verse 21, and in it the commandment also concerning Concupiscence, which the Jesuit reckons among the lighter and Venial sins; which likewise, in chapter 6, 5, he expressly restricts the Sum of the Moral Law, as regards the first table, even to the internal motions of the mind and will, which Bellarmine holds to be adiaphora and indifferent: Thou shalt love the Lord thy GOD with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might: thus not obscurely intimating that even the lightest thought or Concupiscence, which impinges upon this love of GOD, is subject to that curse which he afterwards, in chapter 27, 36, threatens to all transgressors of this law, as much in regard to its second table as to its first.

Latin:

PEculiarem distinctioni huic locum sive Articulum adsignat Autor noster, eamque Articulo de discrimine Veteris & Novi Testamenti demùm subjicit, suum fortè secutus consilium. Nos propriam ejus sedem in præsente Articulo rectissimè constitui habemus persuasissimum.

Constat autem tota Tractatio Philippea quinque potissimùm membris:

Primùm enim deplorat securitatem maximæ partis hominum, vel omninò nunquam, vel obicer tantùm ac perfunctoriè, de atrocitate peccati cogitantium.

Deindè verò ostendit, in non renatis, nullum esse discrimen peccatorum mortalium & Venialium: sed omnia eorum peccata esse mortalia.

Tertiò docet, Renatos Veniale habere peccatum, quando dubitationi, securitati, pravis concupiscentiis & affectibus inordinatis, per Spiritum sanctum repugnant: Proruere autem eos in peccatum mortale, quando scientes & volentes, ac cum proposito contra conscientiam peccant.

Quartò removet à præsenti disputatione Articulum de Electione, quippè quæ huc minùs quadret. Tandem disputat de affectata Ignorantia & omissione affectata: ostendens utramque venire sub censum peccatorum mortalium.

Nos præsentis temporis, & controversiarum quæ hodiè agitantur, habita ratione, duo ista potissimùm sub tractationis incudem revocabimus:

I. Quis sit proprius ac genuinus Distinctionis hujus sensus; quæq; ejus fundamenta ex Scripturis constitui possint ac debeant.

II. Quâ ratione tum Romanenses, tum Calviniani distinctionem hanc depravent, & quibus fundamentis ipsorum argumenta oppugnari & everti debeant.

I. Verus ac genuinus sensus distinctionis peccati in Mortale ac Veniale:

QUis verus sit sensus distinctionis hujus, tribus potissimùm notatis Hypothesibus expedire potest: PRIMA talis est: Omne peccatum in se, per se, & secundum Legis sententiam consideratum, est mortale, ne unico vel levissimo etiam excepto. Etsi enim Lex DEI inter peccata ita distinguit, ut aliud alio vel sit majus, vel minus: tamen quoad reatum violatę legis divinę omnia sunt similia vel paria. Ratio est: Quia non simpliciter considerare oportet, quid præcipiatur: sed quisnam ille sit, qui præcipit. Quatenùs ergò singula & universa peccata, sic absolutè confiderata impingunt in voluntatem DEI legislatoris justissimi: eatenùs certè ea etiam subjacent illi sententiæ, quam DEUS ipse de transgressoribus legum suarum prorsus immutabilem tulit: Deut. 27, 26. Gal. 3, 10. Maledictus omnis, qui non permanferit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, ut faciat ea. Et Ezech 18, 4. Anima, quæ peccaverit ipsa morietur. Rom. 6, 23. Stipendium peccati mors. Jacobi 2, 10. Qui totam legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus.

Levissimum ergò sive minutissimum quodque peccatum, ratione actus sui, per se, & juxta legem, extra gratiam consideratum, æterna morte dignum est, sive illud in actum externum erumpat, sive intra intimas ac levissimas concupiscentias, sine assensu voluntatis, consistat. Et hoc respectu, omnia peccata, tàm in renatis, quàm in non renatis, tantùm mortalia sunt.

Doctrinæ huic contradicit Societas Esawitica. Contendit enim Bellarminus liber. de amiss. grat. cap. 12. 1. Venialia peccata, ratione actus sui considerata posse quidem absolutè & simpliciter nominari peccata: non tamen perfectè esse peccata, si cum mortalibus conferantur. Verùm elumbis hæc est Sophisticatio, imò manifesta depravatio status controversiæ. Non enim hoc in quæstione est, An peccata Venialia, si comparatè ad peccata mortalia conferantur, sint minora ac leviora? id quod nos ipsi largimur; sed hoc in controversiam venit: An peccata etiam Venialia, si ex se, & secundum legem DEI considerentur, sint æterna morte digna, haud minùs atque peccata, quæ dicuntur mortalia? Ubi sanè affirmativam per omnia tenemus.

Primum enim jam ostensum, peccata ratione sui considerata, & quoad reatum violatae Legis divinae, omnia esse paria. Hoc ergo respectu prorsus corruit fictitia haec distinctio Jesuitae, contendentis, Venialia peccata absolute & simpliciter quidem, sed non perfecte esse peccata. 2. Apostolus Rom. 7, 7. Concupiscentiam etiam involuntariam, quae extra Controversiam, ad classem peccatorum Venialium referri debet, a Lege prohibitam, & peccatum proprie ac perfecte nominari posse, satis luculenter arguit. Tandem, Quicquid Legis maledictioni subjacet, illud perfecte sit peccatum, necesse est. Atqui Venialia etiam peccata, ratione actus sui, & ex lege considerata, subjacent maledictioni legis divinae, sic docentibus Scripturae testimoniis, jam ante productis: Quibus addi potest & illud Servatoris Matth. 5, 19. Qui solverit unum de mandatis istis minimis, minimus vocabitur in regno Caelorum. Solvitur autem, quando non impletur eo modo, quo Christus eam implevit, versu 17.

Excipit Jesuita, Scripturae testimonia tantum de mortalibus, non autem de Venialibus peccatis esse accipienda: Idque primum inde probare conatur, Quasi scriptura illa peccata Venialia comprehenderent, sequeretur, homines justulos ob sola peccata Venialia, non solum excidere posse a vita gratiae: sed etiam reipsa excidere. Sed fallit & fallitur Jesuita, sub Sophismate ἐτεροζητήσεως, & disparatarum quaestionum turpi confusione: Aliud enim est, quando quaeritur, quid peccata, quae nominantur Venialia, sint per se, & ratione actus sui, sive ex Lege considerata? Aliud vero est, quando quaeritur, Quid causae sit, quod Renati designantes peccata Venialia, non ipso actu excidant gratia DEI. Ratione prioris quaesiti considerantur peccata haec, qualia sunt Natura sua, & ex definitione Legis. Ratione posterioris quaesiti, peccata haec non amplius considerantur, ex propria sua affectione, quam ex Lege sortiuntur: sed ex conditione personae, quae cum DEO per fidem est reconciliata: & ex Evangelio Remissionem illorum peccatorum est consecuta Ergo non militat ulla Consequentiae ratio: Si ex posteriore hoc respectu, qui personam agentem Deoque per fidem reconciliatam, concernit, fiat subsumtio ad priorem illum, qui peccata haec Venialia, ex proprietate suae naturae, consi- " derat. Quantum enim a se mutuo distant Lex " & Evangelium: tantum a se quoque invicem " dissident duae hae quaestiones, quarum prior ex " Lege, posterior ex Evangelio decisionem sor- " titur. Prior naturam peccati, secundum Le- " gis rigorem: Posterior peccati remissionem ex " promissione Evangelii respicit. Jam vero, quando affirmamus, Renatorum etiam Venialia peccata esse mortalia, tum tantum Naturam ejus ex Lege attendimus & urgemus: minime omnium negantes, in personis fide Deo reconciliatis, ea quasi Naturam hanc suam propriam amittere, & ex accidenti fieri Venialia sive remissibilia, uti secunda Observatio paulo post demonstrabit.

Altera Jesuitae ratio, quâ exceptionem suam confirmare studet, sic sonat: Maledictio illa Deuteronomy refertur ad violatores mandatorum, quae in eo ipso tradita fuerant: Id enim significat illud pronomen Hujus, cum dicitur: Maledictus, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in libro legis Hujus. Ea verò mandata sunt omnia longè gravissima, de cavenda Idololatria, de incestu, homicidio, & similibus, quae consensu omnium peccata sunt mortalia. Pari ratione Ezechiel 18, 4. & seqq. enumerat varia scelera, quae omnia genere suo sunt mortalia. Sic Paulus Rom. 6. de peccato illo disserit, quod pugnat cum gratia, & simul cum Justitia manere non potest: & quod qui habet, mortuus est: qui non habet, vivus: qualia sunt non omnia peccata, sed tantùm mortalia: Venialibus enim gratiam, Justitiam & vitam non excludi, & Catholici & Lutherani admittunt. S. Jacobus explicat satis apertè, de Criminibus se loqui, quae propriè & perfectè sunt contra legem DEI: quia statim subjicit: Qui enim dixit: Non maechaberis, dixit etiam, Non occides & c. Ergo Testimonia haec non sunt accommodanda ad peccata Venialia.

Sed turpis committitur Sophisticatio κατὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχꝢ: quae indè oritur, quòd inscitè admodùm Jesuuvita statuit, nõ posse unum idemq́; praedicatum diversis etiam speciebus accommodari: ita quidem, ut si peccata graviora, secundum scripturas, dici debeant, imò verè sint mortalia: tùm peccata leviora sive Venialia, neque per se suâ naturâ sint, neque etiam dici debeant mortalia. Quam Sophisticandi libidinem solidissimè evertit axioma illud Logicum: Quaecunq; de Genere aut affirmantur aut negantur: illa quoq; de singulis speciebus eodem modo affirmari aut negari oportet. Jam de peccato in genere considerato affirmat Scriptura, quòd suâ naturâ sit mortale. Ergò verum hoc est praedicatum, de omnibus ejus speciebus, hoc est, de peccatis tàm levioribus quàm gravioribus.

Deindè laborat haec ratio manifesto crimine falsi. Moses enim Deut. 27, 36. non intelligit tantùm gravissima illa mandata, quae percenset Jesuuvita: sed totam Legem, prout ea in monte Sinai à Deo ipso est promulgata. Patescit hoc vel indè, quod praecedente cap. 5. Legem Moralem, & in ea, praeceptum etiam de Concupiscentia, quam inter leviora & Venialia peccata refert Jesuuvita, populo inculcat versu 21. quòd item Summam Legis moralis, quoad primam tabulam, cap. 6, 5. ad internos etiam mentis & voluntatis motus, quos Bellarminus pro adiaphoris & indifferentibus habet, disertè restringit: Diliges Dominum DEUM ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota fortitudine tua: sic haud obscurè innuens, levissimam etiam cogitationem sive Concupiscentiam, quae in hanc dilectionem DEI impingit, subjacere illi maledictioni, quam postmodùm cap. 27, 36. minatur omnibus legis hujus transgressoribus, tàm quoad secundam, quàm quoad primam ejus tabulam.


### Chapter I. On the Nature & proper affection of Actual Sin: II. Hypothesis. On Venial Sin: it is not to be judged from the Law, nor from the nature of sin

3. What of the fact that the Apostle, Galatians 3:10, restricts the Mosaic passage indefinitely and universally to the whole Law and every one of its members, omitting the pronoun 'of this' and asserting indefinitely: 'Cursed is everyone who does not remain in the book of the Law to do them'.

Thus the Prophet Ezekiel recounts those more serious crimes for the reason that the people had designed such things: but the consequence does not hold on that account: Therefore the Prophet establishes that lesser sins are not in themselves and by their own nature mortal. For the vanity of this collection has already been sufficiently thrashed out before.

Regarding the Apostolic aphorism, the Jesuit again commits the crime of falsehood. For the Apostle asserts concerning both kinds of sin, both Venial and Mortal, both not reigning and reigning: 'The wages of sin is death.' For what, I ask, would this ἀνακολουθία (inconsistency) be, if the Apostle were here urging a more special meaning of the word than he himself defined in the immediately preceding verses: 'Sin,' he says, 'shall not have dominion over you: for you are not under the law, but under grace': where it is manifest in itself that he is speaking of sin not having dominion.

James's testimony is too evident to be eluded by any sophistication. For he says expressly: 'Whoever shall have kept the whole law, but offends in ONE, is guilty of all.' For even if we should understand, with Augustine and Jerome, this ONE as the single commandment of love: yet it is certain that the most perfect love, absolute in all respects, is required by the Law: both towards GOD and towards one's neighbor: both by external act and by internal Concupiscence. Therefore, if a transgression of this commandment occurs in the slightest degree, the guilt of the whole Law is immediately implicated.

II. HYPOTHESIS.

One must not judge concerning Venial Sin, neither from the Law nor from the nature of sin. The foundation of this hypothesis depends on what has already been said before. For every transgression of the law, whether it be great or slight, contracts the guilt of eternal curse: and therefore by its own nature it cannot be Venial. Furthermore, such perfection is required by the Law, which is not from a half, but from the whole, or as Scripture speaks, with all one's heart, with all one's soul, with all one's strength, that one should love GOD above all things and one's neighbor as oneself, Deut. 6:5, Matt. 22:37. Yet such perfection falls to no mortal in this life. For where there is Original guilt, there is a natural hatred of GOD and neighbor, so that by the testimony of the Apostle we are by nature children of wrath: Eph. 2:3.

Therefore. Nor do the examples of those Saints stand in the way, who are said to have walked according to all the law of GOD, who are held to have been just, holy, and perfect.

For 1. they are such and are called such, not by reason of any such inherent perfection, but by reason of the imputed holiness and perfection of Christ. But from this, the consequence does not hold for defining the Nature of sin.

2. This perfection is to be understood comparatively: namely, with respect to Hypocrites: however much it may have been lacking and imperfect in itself, according to that saying of the Savior, Luke 17:10: 'If you have done all things, say, we are unprofitable servants.'

3. This perfection is not to be extended to the whole Law: but to a certain kind of deed: just as Josiah is read to have returned to the LORD with all his heart, with all his soul, with all his might, according to all the law of Moses, 2 Kings 23:25. Where a certain kind of deed is noted, namely the Reformation of divine worship, which he instituted according to the Law of Moses in such a way that nothing at all of idolatry was left. Otherwise, Josiah was certainly not without sin, especially when he waged an unnecessary war out of curiosity against the King of Egypt, in which he also fell, 2 Kings 23:29, 2 Chronicles 35:21 & 22. Finally, this perfection is also defined by the judgment and censure of men: so that if anyone lives blamelessly, he is accustomed to be called perfect by men: In which sense in Luke 1:6, Zacharias and Elizabeth are pronounced righteous: certainly in the sight of GOD they were also sinners, redeemed by the merit of Christ and saved through faith, Luke 1:78.

The Jesuit Bellarmine, chapter 12 of the book on the loss of grace, page 114, column A, noticing the evidence of this thesis of ours, again invents a certain new distinction, saying: The love of GOD with all one's heart can be understood in two ways: In one way, that 'with all one's heart' is the same as 'above all other things,' entirely and perfectly, so that nothing is preferred or equaled to the love of GOD: In the OTHER way, that GOD is always thought of and loved in act, and that the love of GOD so occupies the mind that nothing can creep in which is (I do not say) against, but beside the charity of GOD or one's neighbor. In the former way, we admit it is commanded to us that we love GOD with all our heart: but we deny that venial sins conflict with this love. The latter love is proper to the blessed, nor is it properly commanded to us in this life: but only indicated, so that we may know where we ought to direct our hope and desires.

But this is a sink, collected from mere trifles and absurdities. For 1. those two ways of legal love for GOD are unknown to Holy Scripture, of which one could stand with sins, but the other could not. Rather, it knows only one legal way, which, devoid of all sin, requires the whole heart, the whole soul, and all one's strength, whole and perfect. 2. Be it so, let this distinction be admitted: it is certain, however, that not even the former way falls to any man in this life, that he should love GOD wholly and perfectly, nor prefer or equal anything to the love of GOD.

For the fact that the Jesuit denies that venial sins are in conflict with this love of God is trifling and begs the question. For it has just now been demonstrated that venial sins by their own nature, and by the Law of God, are also mortal, and therefore cannot stand with the perfect love of God. And why, I ask, would the most holy men also have need in this life to pray from time to time, 'Forgive us our sins': Ps. 32:5, Job 15:14, 25:4, Rom. 3:23, 1 John 1:8, if such a perfection fell to them? What of the fact that the Apostle convicts the Jesuit of a lie, stating expressly that he feels another law in his members, REPUGNANT to the law of his mind, and CAPTIVATING him under the law of sin. 3. This distinction overturns itself. For by the Jesuit's definition, the latter mode of the love of God is so constituted that God is always thought of and loved in act, so that nothing can creep in, not indeed against, but beside the charity of God or neighbor. Therefore, so that this distinction may maintain its integrity, the former mode of love will be so constituted: that God is not always thought of and loved in act; but something can creep in either against or beside the charity of God and neighbor. Is this, then, what it will be to love God with all one's heart, above all things, integrally and perfectly? Truly, indeed, there happens here to the Jesuit what Paul affirms of the Gentiles in Rom. 1:23: Φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ, ἐμωράνθησαν: Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. Finally, that which he dares to write, that this latter mode of love is not properly commanded to us in this life, is trifling. Certainly, no degree of this love can be conceived which that authentic Mosaic passage, Deut. 6:5, does not include. Thus, it is clearly ἀπροσδιόνυσον [irrelevant] what the adversary grunts in this place concerning the love of the blessed. For the Law does not bind those blessed ones in the other life, but mortals in this life, to absolute obedience: but the blessed in that eternal life will not love God most perfectly by the force of any law, but from the condition of their own nature, which, being entirely free from all sin, will be so confirmed in good that it can no longer sin.

Latin:

3. Quid quòd Apostolus, Galat. 3, 10. locum Mosaicum indefinitè & universaliter ad totam legem, singulaque ipsius membra restringit, omittens pronomen Hujus: & indefinitè asserens, Maledictus esse omnem, qui non permanserit in libro Legis, ut faciat ea.

Sic Propheta Jezechiel ideò crimina illa graviora recenset, quia populus talia designaverat: sed non propterea valet Consequentia: Ergò Propheta statuit, peccata leviora non esse per se, & suâ naturâ mortalia. Vanitas enim collectionis hujus, jam antè satis est protrita.

Quoad Aphorismum Apostolicum, rursus crimen falsi committit Jesuwita. Nam de utraque peccati Specie, cùm Veniali quàm Mortali, cùm non regnante quàm regnante, asserit Apostolus: Stipendium peccati mors est. Ecquæ enim obsecro hæc foret ἀνακολουθία, si hîc aliam specialiorem vocabuli significationem urgeret Apostolus, quàm in immediatè præcedentibus ipsemet definivit: Peccatum, inquiens, vobis non dominabitur: non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia: ubi ipsum de peccato non dominante loqui, per se manifestum est.

Jacobi testimonium evidentius est, quàm ut ulla Sophisticatione eludi queat. Disertè enim dicit: Qui totam legem servaverit, offenderit autem in UNO reus est omnium. Si enim vel maximè, per hoc UNUM cum Augustino & Hieronymo, intelligamus Unicum mandatum dilectionis: tamen constat, perfectissimam, omnibusque numeris absolutissimam dilectionem requiri à Lege: tùm erga DEUM, tùm erga proximum: tùm externo actu, tùm interna Concupiscentia. Ergo, si in minimo mandati hujus fiat transgressio, statim reatus totius Legis implicatur.

II. HYPOTHESIS.

DE Peccato Veniali, neque ex Lege, neque ex natura peccati est judicandum. Fundamentum hujus hypotheseos dependet ex jam antè dictis. Omnis enim transgressio legis, sive magna, sive levis sit, contrahit reatum æternæ maledictionis: ac proindè suâ naturâ Venialis esse nequit. Accedit deindè, quòd talis perfectio à Lege requiritur, quæ non ex semisse, sed ex asse, vel ut Scriptura loquitur, ex toto corde, ex tota anima, ex omnibus viribus DEUM supra omnia: proximum sicut seipsum diligat Deut. 6, 5. Matth. 22, 37. Atqui talis perfectio in mortalium neminem hac in vita cadit. Nam ubi est Originalis culpa: ibi est naturale odium DEI & proximi, ita ut Apostolo teste Naturâ simus filii iræ: Ephes. 2, 3.

Ergo. Neque obstant exempla eorum Sanctorum, qui secundum omnem legem DEI ambulasse, qui justi, sancti, & perfecti fuisse perhibentur.

Nam 1. tales sunt & dicuntur, nou ratione inhærentis talis alicujus perfectionis, sed ratione imparatæ sanctitatis & perfectionis Christi. Ab hac verò, ad peccati Naturam definiendam non valet Consequentia.

2. Comparatè hæc est perfectio intelligenda: nempè respectu Hypocritarum: quantumvis ea in se fuerit manca & imperfecta, secundum illud Servatoris, Luc. 17, 10. Si omnia feceritis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus.

3. Perfectio hæc non ad totam Legem est extendenda: sed ad certam speciem facti: quemadmodum Josias legitur reversus fuisse ad DOMINUM in omni corde suo, in tota anima sua, in universa virtute sua, juxta omnem legem Mosis, 2. Reg. 23, 25. Ubi certa species facti notatur, nempè cultus divini Reformatio, quam secundum Legem Mosis ita instituit, ut nihil quicquam de Idololatria relinqueretur. Aliàs certè Josias peccato non carebat, præsertim cum bellum non necessarium ex curiositate movit regi Ægyptio, in quo etiam occubuit, 2 Reg. 23, 29. 2. Paral. 35, 21. & 22. Tandem perfectio hæc definitur etiam judicio & censura hominum: ita ut si quis inculpatè vivat: is ab hominibus perfectus dici soleat: Quo sensu Lucæ 1, 6. Zacharias & Elisabeth pronunciantur Justi: certè in conspectu DEI & ipsi peccatores, Christi merito redemti & per fidem salvati, Luc. 1, 78.

Jesuwita Bellarminus cap. 12. libr. de amiss. grat p. 114. l. A. animadvertens thesews hujus nostræ evidentiam, rursus novam quandam comminiscitur distinctionem, Duobus, inquiens, modis, dilectio DEI ex toto corde, intelligi potest: Uno modo, ut idem sit ex toto corde, quod super omnia alia, integrè & perfectè, ut nihil DEI amori anteponatur aut adæquetur: ALTERO modo, ut semper actu DEUS cogitetur, & diligatur, & sic animum, DEI amor occupatum teneat, ut nihil obrepere possit, quod sit (non inquam) contra, sed præter DEI vel proximi charitatem. Priore modo fatemur imperari nobis, ut DEUM ex toto corde diligamus: sed cum hac dilectione negamus pugnare peccata Venialia. Posterior dilectio est beatorum propria, neque nobis in hac vita propriè imperatur: sed tantùm indicatur, ut sciamus, quo spem ac desideria dirigere debeamus.

Sed sentina hæc est, ex meris nugis & absurditatibus collecta. Nam 1. duo isti modi dilectionis DEI legalis, Sacræ Scripturæ sunt ignoti, quorum unus cum peccatis stare, alter verò non stare possit. Quin unicum ea novit modum Legalem, qui expers omnis peccati, totum cor, totam animam, omnesque vires requirit integras & perfectas. 2. Esto, admittatur hæc distinctio: certum tamen est, ne priorem quidem modum, in ullum cadere hominem hac in vita, ut integrè & perfectè diligat DEUM, neque quicquam DEI amori vel anteponat; vel adæquet.

Nam quòd Jesuvvita negat, Peccata Venialia pugnare cum hac Dei dilectione, nugatorium est, & principium petit. Venialia enim peccata naturâ suâ, & ex Lege Dei, etiam esse mortalia, ac proindè cum perfecta Dei dilectione stare haud posse, jam modò est demonstratum. Et cur obsecro Sanctissimi quoq; hac in vita sub indè necesse haberent orare, Dimitte nobis peccata nostra: Psal. 32, 5. Job. 15, 14, 25, 4. Rom. 3, 23. 1. Joban. 1, 8. si talis perfectio in ipsos caderet. Quid, quod Apostolus Jesuvvitam mendacij convincit, disertè afferens, se sentire aliam legem in membris suis, REPUGNANTEM legi mentis suae, & CAPTIVANTEM se sub legi peccati. 3. Distinctio haec seipsam evertit. Nam definiente Jesuvvita, posterior Dilectionis Dei modus sic est comparatus, ut semper Deus actu cogitetur & diligatur, ut nihil obrepere possit, non quidem contra, sed praeter Dei vel proximi charitatem. Ergo, ut distinctioni huic sua constet integritas, prior dilectionis modus ita erit comparatus: ut neque Deus semper actu cogitetur ac diligatur: sed possit obrepere aliquid vel contra, vel praeter charitatem Dei & proximi. Siccinè ergò hoc erit Deum ex toto corde, super omnia, integrè & perfectè diligere? Verè nimirùm hic evenit Jesuvvitae, quod Paulus Rom. 1, 23. de Gentilibus affirmat: Φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ, ἐμωράνθησαν: Arbitrantes se esse sapientes, stulti facti sunt. Tandem nugatorium est & illud, quod scribere, audet, posteriorem hunc dilectionis modum, nobis hac in vita non propriè imperari. Certè non ullus dilectionis hujus gradus excogitari potest, quem non Authentica illa Mosaica, Deut. 6, 5. includat. Sic planè ἀπροσδιόνυσον est, quod de Beatorum dilectione hoc loco grunnit Adversarius. Neque enim Lex beatos illos in altera vita, sed mortales hac in vita, ad absolutam obedientiam obligat: Beati verò in æterna illa vita, non vi legis alicujus Deum perfectissimè diligent, sed ex Naturæ suæ conditione, quæ ab omni peccato prorsus libera, sic in bono confirmabitur, ut peccare ampliùs non possit.


### Chapter I. On the Nature & proper affection of Actual Sin: III. Hypothesis

III. HYPOTHESIS.

The distinction between mortal and venial sin, in place of the subject, does not concern sin in itself, and by reason of its act, considered from the Law: but only the condition of the person sinning.

The foundation of this hypothesis is elicited most evidently from the scriptures. For because such a perfection as the Law requires does not fall even upon the regenerate: and by reason of this defect, Man can do nothing other than sin mortally: therefore God, having mercy on us, willed that that perfection be performed by the Son, and that it be truly imputed to us who believe in Him, and by means of this imputation, He willed to cover all our sins, however mortal they may be in themselves, in such a way that, the guilt of the curse having been expiated through the Son, they become now by accident venial and remissible, which by themselves, and by reason of their act, are mortal. The person, therefore, who by the mercy of God has obtained the forgiveness of all sins through and because of Christ apprehended by faith: or what is the same thing, the regenerate man does not sin mortally otherwise or sooner than when he acts against his conscience, and loses faith and repentance, and casts off the Holy Spirit: this is what happens when the regenerate man either conceives heresies concerning the foundation of faith, whether in the substance itself of the articles of Religion: or rushes with reckless rashness against his conscience: or, being clearly no longer concerned about the grace of God, the remission of sins, and the true fruits of repentance, nevertheless thinks that he, progressing in sins, can enjoy the grace of God or possess true faith. By these signs, therefore, the commission of mortal sin is discovered to have been made. And this is what Chemnitz cites from our Blessed Luther.

Mortal and venial sin is distinguished not according to the substance of the deed: or according to the difference of the sins admitted: but according to the person, or because of the difference of those admitting the sins.

And what the same Luther writes in Tom. 1, Jena edition, p. 105a: No sin is venial by its own nature: but all are damnable: but that they are venial, this is to be attributed to the grace of God. And Tom. 4, p. 172: God always hates sin; indeed, every sin, as to the substance of the deed, is mortal. But that it is not mortal to the believer is because of Christ the propitiator.

Moreover, that this distinction of sin is to be retained in one class of men, namely the regenerate, the clear testimonies of Scripture evidently confirm. God certainly himself in Leviticus 4 and 6, Numbers 15, 22 and 30, expressly distinguishes between sins committed through ignorance, which are committed, that is, by error, or infirmity, or some precipitate affection: and between sins of pride, when a man, knowingly and willingly, out of some contumacious and proud contempt, transgresses the precepts of the divine Law: Yea, for the expiation of those sins, he instituted distinct sacrifices. Leviticus 6, 6. Numbers 15, 30.

Thus David in Psalm 19, 13 and 14, expressly distinguishes between sin and sin, and shows that that which is committed through imprudence or ignorance differs from that which is designed with set will: nay, he shows that he himself (though regenerate) is not a stranger to either. Saying, Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults, and keep back thy servant from presumptuous sins: if they have not had dominion over me, then shall I be upright, and I shall be innocent from the great transgression.

Thus the Apostle in Romans 7, 19, confesses that he performs evil: and yet in Romans 8, 1, asserts that there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. The comparison of which testimonies clearly establishes this distinction of sin.

Thus John, 1. chap. 1. 8. when he speaks of the reborn: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us: at the same time in the following chapter 3, 6. he says: He who sins has not known God: And 1. John 3, 8. He who commits sin is of the Devil etc. most clearly confirms this distinction: thus showing that the reborn, by prevaricating, or by sinning mortally, fall away from faith and grace.

But if the proper affection or signification of the words which Scripture uses in describing sins be brought in as an aid: certainly the Hebrew words זָדוֹן Zaddon, מֶרֶד Mæred, אָשָׁם Ascham, רֶשַׁע Rascha, שֶׁגֶג Schagag, establish a clear distinction between the sins of the reborn: concerning which see Chemnitz part 3. of the Loci, pp. 255, 256.

Furthermore, the same Chemnitz warns that, if the Oracles of the Scriptures are examined more closely, five requirements especially pertain to the constitution of a venial sin.

I. That the reborn should resist depraved desires, whether in suggestion, or in delight, or in consent, through repentance, and not permit them to reign, so as to obey them by offering their members as weapons for sin: Rom. 6, 13. Gal. 5, 16.

II. Let them seek and determine by faith that those depraved desires, and their fires, which they resist through the Spirit, are pardoned and not imputed on account of Christ, and let them seek the help of the Holy Spirit.

III. Let them acknowledge Concupiscence itself, and its depraved motions, even if neither delight nor consent is added, nor the act itself follows: yet that they are in themselves sins according to the Law.

IV. Even if sometimes the fires of depraved affections carry the reborn captive by their vehemence, either to consent or even to some depraved operation, if they immediately grieve with true repentance, and seek the remission of sins by faith, the Holy Spirit is indeed grieved, or even exacerbated: yet He is not cast out, nor is faith or the grace of God sent away. Ephes. 4, 26. and 30. If you are angry, do not sin: nor give place to the Devil, nor grieve the Holy Spirit of God.

V. Let the reborn determine by faith, although they cannot in this life utterly put off those stains of Original sin, nor mortify its actions entirely Rom. 7, 24. and although those evils are in themselves according to the law worthy of eternal damnation: yet, because they are reborn, and remain in Christ, and do not walk according to the Flesh, there is no condemnation to be feared. Rom. 8, 1.

With which members being duly observed, it becomes manifest that sin, which can consist with the grace of God, faith, and the Holy Spirit; and is therefore called Venial, is such a sin as is committed out of ignorance, error, and infirmity, is as it were hidden, that is, it does not reign, but is mortified and crucified through the Spirit: and which the reborn, resisting, acknowledge, deplore, and pray against on account of Christ apprehended by faith, and obtain the remission of the same.

Now, from the contrary sense, it can likewise be not at all obscure what a mortal sin is in the regenerate, namely, one committed not out of infirmity, but by set purpose against conscience, by which the grace of God is lost, faith and the Holy Spirit are shaken off: the guilt of eternal damnation is contracted, unless they return to God through true repentance and obtain pardon anew. See Chemnitz, part 3 of the Loci, pages 262, 263.

Latin:

III. HYPOTHESIS.

Distinctio Peccati Mortalis & Venialis, subjecti loco non concernit peccatum in se, & ratione actus sui, ex Lege consideratum: sed tantùm conditionem personæ peccantis.

Fundamentum hujus hypotheseos ex scripturis evidentissimum elicitur. Quia enim ne quidem in renatos talis cadit perfectio, qualem Lex requirit: & ratione hujus defectus, Homo nihil potest aliud, quàm mortaliter peccare: ideò Deus nostri misertus, perfectionem illam per Filium præstari, nobis autem in ipsum credentibus, eandem verè imputare, & mediante hac imputatione omnia nostra peccata, quantumvis in se mortalia, ita tegere voluit, ut reatu maledictionis per Filium expiato, evadant jam per accidens Venialia & remifsibilia, quæ per se, & ratione actus sui sunt mortalia. Persona ergò, quæ ex misericordia Dei, veniam omnium peccatorum per & propter Christum fide apprehensum, est consecuta : vel quod idem est, Homo renatus non aliter aut priùs peccat mortaliter, quàm cùm agit contra conscientiam, & fidem ac pœnitentiam amittit, ac Spiritum Sanctum excutit : id quod fit, quando renatus vel circa fundamentum fidei errorem, sive in substāntia ipsa articulorum Religionis, hæreses concipit: vel desultoria temeritate ruit contra conscientiam : vel de gratia Dei, remissione peccatorum, & pœnitentiæ veræ fructibus, planè nihil ampliùs sollicitus, in peccatis nihilominùs se progredientem gratiâ Dei frui, aut veram fidem habere posse existimat. His ergò notis peccati mortalis commissio facta esse deprehenditur. Et hoc est, quod ex B. Luthero nostro citat Chemnitius.

Peccatum Mortale & Veniale distinguitur non secundum Substantiam facti : sive juxta differentiam peccatorum admissorum : sed secundum personam, sive propter differenciam peccata admittentium.

Et quod idem Lutherus Tom. 1. Ien. L. pag. 105, a. scribit : Nullum peccatum suâ naturâ Veniale est : sed omnia damnabilia : Quòd autem Venialia sunt, hoc gratiæ Dei tribuendum est. Et Tom. 4. pag. 172. Deus semper odit peccatum, imò omne peccatum, quoad substāntiam facti, est mortale. Quòd autem credenti non mortale, sit propter Christum propitiatorem.

Cæterùm in uno genere hominum, Renatis scilicet retinendum esse hoc peccati discrimen, luculenta Scripturæ testimonia, evidenter confirmant. Deus certè ipse Levit. 4. & 6. Num. 15, 22. & 30. expressè distinguit inter peccata per ignorantiam commissa, quæ scilicet errore, sive infirmitate, vel præcipiti aliquo affectu committuntur : & inter peccata superbiæ, cum homo sciens & volens, ex contumaci quopiam ac superbo comtemtu præcepta Legis divinæ transgreditur : Imò ad expiationem istorum peccatorum, distincta instituit sacrificia. Levit. 6, 6. Num. 15, 30.

Sic David Psal. 19, 13. & 14. expressè inter peccatum & peccatum distinguit, & id, quod per imprudentiam, aut ignorantiam committitur, ab eo, quod destinata voluntate designatur, differre : quin imò ab utroque se (Renatum licèt) non esse alienum ostendit. Delicta, inquiens, quis intelligit ? ab occultis meis munda me, & à contumacijs parce servo tuo : Si mihi non fuerint dominatæ, tum immaculatus ero, & emundabor à delicto maximo.

Sic Apostolus Rom. 7, 19. fatetur, se malum peragere : & tamen Rom. 8, 1. asserit, nihil condemnationis esse his, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Quorum testimoniorum collatio, discrimen hoc peccati luculenter adstruit.

Sic Johannes, 1. cap. 1. 8. quando de renatis dicit: Si dixerimus, quòd peccatum non habemus, ipsinos seducimus, & veritas non est in nobis: simul cap. subsequente 3, 6. dicit: Qui peccat, non cognovit Deum: Et 1. Joh. 3, 8. Qui facit peccatum, ex Diabolo est &c. luculentissimè hoc discrimen confirmat: sic ostendens, Renatos prævaricando, sive mortaliter peccando, fide & gratia excidere.

Quod si vocabulorum, quibus Scriptura in describendis peccatis utitur, propria sive affectio sive significatio, in subsidium adhibeatur: certè vocabula Hebræa זָדוֹן Zaddon, מֶרֶד Mæred, אָשָׁם Ascham, רֶשַׁע Rascha, שֶׁגֶג Schagag, luculentum discrimen inter peccata Renatorum constituunt: de quibus Vide Chemnitium part. 3. Locorum p. 255. 256.

Præterea admonet idem Chemnitius, si pressiùs Scripturarum Oracula excutiantur, quinq; potissimùm requisita, ad constitutionem peccati venialis pertinere.

I. Ut renati pravis Cupiditatibus, vel in suggestione, vel in delectatione, vel in consensu per pœnitentiam repugnent, nec regnare eas permittant, ut ipsis obediant, præbendo membra, arma peccato: Rom. 6, 13. Gal. 5, 16.

II. Fide petant & statuant, pravas illas Cupiditates, & earum incendia, quibus per Spiritum repugnant, condonari, & non imputari propter Christum, ac petant auxilium Spiritus Sancti.

III. Agnoscant ipsam Concupiscentiam, & pravos ejus motus, etiamsi non accedat, vel delectatio, vel consensus, nec sequatur ipsum opus: tamen per se juxta Legem esse peccata.

IV. Etiamsi interdum incendia pravorum affectuum sua vehementia captivos rapiant renatos, vel ad consensum, vel etiam ad operationem aliquam pravam, si statim verâ pœnitentia doleant, & fide petant remissionem peccatorum, Spiritus Sanctus quidem contristatur, vel etiam exacerbatur: non tamen excutitur, nec fides aut gratia Dei emittitur. Ephes. 4, 26. & 30. Si irascimini, nolite peccare: nec locum detis Diabolo, nec contristetis Spiritum Sanctum Dei.

V. Fide statuant renati, licet sordes illas peccati Originalis, non possint hac in vita penitùs deponere, nec actiones ejus prorsus mortificare Rom. 7, 24. & licèt illa mala per se juxta legem, digna sint æterna damnatione: tamen, quià renati sunt, & manent in Christo, nec secundum Carnem ambulant, nullam condemnationem esse metuendam. Rom. 8, 1.

Quibus membris probè observatis, manifestum evadit, peccatum, quod cum gratia Dei, fide ac Spiritu Sancto potest consistere; ac propterea Veniale dicitur, esse tale peccatum, quod ex Ignorantia, errore ac infirmitate commissum, occultum quasi est, hoc est, non regnat, sed per Spiritum mortificatur, ac crucifigitur: & quod Renati repugnantes agnoscunt, deplorant atq; deprecantur propter Christum fide apprehensum, ejusdemq; remissionem impetrant.

Jam ex contrario sensu itidem haud obscurum esse potest, Quidnam sit peccatum mortale in Renatis, nempè non ex infirmitate, sed destinato consilio contra conscientiam commissum, quo amittitur gratia Dei, excutitur fides & Spiritus Sanctus: aeternae damnatioins reatus contrahitur, nisi per verampœnitentiam redeant ad Deum, & veniam denuò impetrent. Vide Chemn. part. 3. Locorum pag. 262. 263.


### Chapter II. Or Corruptions contending with purer doctrine, on the discrimination of mortal and venial sin

Ἀντιθετικὴ. Or, corruptions warring against the purer doctrine concerning the distinction between mortal and venial sin.

This purer doctrine of ours has long since suffered a very sharp contradiction, and it suffers no lighter one even today.

The Scholastics: 1. Having formerly followed the dogmas of the Pharisees, they distinguished the precepts of the divine law into great and small: 2. They opposed mortal sins to the great, but venial sins to the small. 3. They enumerated seven mortal sins in particular, following Gregory the Great: namely, 1. Pride, or vainglory: 2. Anger: 3. Envy: 4. Sloth, or laziness: 5. Gluttony: 6. Avarice: 7. Lust, or lasciviousness: to which seven they opposed the contrary virtues: 1. Humility: 2. Patience: 3. Charity: 4. Diligence: 5. Abstinence: 6. Liberality: 7. Chastity. Fourthly, surpassing the impiety of the Pharisees, they maintained that these seven sins alone are by their own nature mortal: but that all other sins, each and every one, are so small and light that, although they themselves may displease God, yet man does not displease Him on their account: since they are not against the law, but beside the law of God.

The Master of the Sentences long ago betrayed this impiety, book 2, distinction 42, saying: A mortal sin binds us to eternal punishment: but a venial sin to a temporal punishment, yet one which is easily pardoned: A mortal sin is committed according to reason: but not every venial sin, since it exists only in the motion of sensuality.

Hence Thomas, 1. Secundae, question 89: A venial sin does not cause a stain in the soul: and it is in sensuality just as a mortal sin is in reason. So that this may be understood more clearly, they distinguished these two sins thus, as Chemnitz reports in part 3 of the Loci, page 276: When the sensual motion of the flesh conceives some allurement of sin, to which the lower portion of reason and thought, namely some delight, is for the most part present, but not for long: and if the will to perform it, which they call the superior portion of reason, does not accede, then they wish it to be a venial sin: such as first motions, and also those things which happen from some surprise, infirmity, or ignorance: so that a sudden act, not deliberate, however bad it may be, is a venial sin: nay, it may not even have the character of sin: nor is there need of contrition for such a sin: inasmuch as it cannot hinder the obedience of the reborn from being whole and perfect in this life: nay, it can even merit eternal life.

And lest this impiety should have no limit, the Scholastic Doctors recount certain remedies for venial sins: such as, 1. General confession: de pœnit. distinct. 3. c. de quotidianis. 2. Devout striking of the breast. Ibid dist. 1. c. tres sunt actiones. 3. Sprinkling of holy water: de consecrat. dist. 3. c. Aquam. 4. Contrition of heart: Antoninus part. 3. summæ, tit. 10. cap. 1. §. Quando. 5. The Lord's Prayer, especially de pœnitentia, dist. 3. §. de Quotidianis. 6. Episcopal and priestly blessing, and even that of a nun, causa 1. q. 1. c. multi, at the end. 7. Worthy communion: de pœnit. d. 2. c. cùm omne. 8. Bestowal of alms: de pœnit. dist. 1. c. Quamobrem. 9. Remission of injuries from chapter 6 of Luke. 10. Extreme Unction: c. unico. 11. Patience under scourges: 12. Any good work whatsoever.

Nor does the Roman Church, and especially its champions, the Jesuits, think or teach any more correctly today, who measure the distinction of sin into mortal and venial, not by the condition of the person sinning, but by the nature of the act itself, contending that a venial sin is that which is of itself worthy of pardon, and so constituted that on account of it there is no just cause for God to be angry: inasmuch as it does not conflict with the Law of God, and therefore does not have the character of sin: for which reason there is also no need for anyone to be affected by sorrow or contrition for it. Whence they call this kind of sin little trifles, petty vices, little sins, and stains, by which the works of the reborn are not contaminated: as defined indeed by the Council of Trent, Sess. 6, cap. 5, and Canon 25. Roman Catechism, p. 553. Censura Col. p. 194. Lindanus in panoplia p. 103.

The Jesuit Bellarmine reveals his own mind and that of his accomplices in this manner, l. 1. de amissione grat. & statu peccati, cap. 2. Some sins are called lethal, which clearly turn a man away from God, and to which eternal punishment is due: Some are venial, which hinder the course toward God somewhat, yet do not turn one away from Him, and are expiated with little effort. So that this may be better understood, he adds in the following chapter 3, a distinction of venial sin, sought (as he supposes) from its very nature: Some, he says, are venial by their own kind, which have as their object an evil and disordered thing, but which does not conflict with the charity of God or neighbor: such as an idle word, excessive laughter, and other things of that kind: And contrary to these are mortal sins by their own kind: such as perjury, adultery, and the like. Some are venial from the imperfection of the work, which although they could be mortal by their own kind: yet on account of the imperfection of the work they are made venial: because clearly the mere imperfection of the work causes them not to be judged as conflicting with charity. Contrary to these are mortal sins on the part of the agent, which indeed could have been venial by their own kind, and yet by a certain disposition of the sinner are mortal. These again are called venial by subreption, which are not perfectly voluntary, such as sudden motions of desire, anger, etc. Others are venial from the smallness of the matter, which are committed in a small and light thing: such as the theft of one penny.

The sum and head of Jesuit doctrine is that venial sins are and are called such, not because of the person himself, reconciled to God through faith, but from their very nature, without any regard to the grace and mercy of God, and the merit of Christ: or as Bellarmine speaks, a venial sin is distinguished from a mortal one by its own nature, and without any relation either to predestination, or to the mercy of God, or to the state of the reborn, is of such a kind that it indeed merits punishment, but not eternal: and offends God, but not to the point of the dissolution of friendship, lib. 1. de amiss. grat. cap. 9. l. C.

The arguments of the Jesuit taken from the Scriptures are these, the principal ones. FIRST, we read in Matthew 5, 23: Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment, whoever says Raca shall be liable to the council: whoever says fool shall be liable to the fire of hell. From these an argument of this kind is constructed: A manifest insult, with Christ as witness or judge, makes one liable to the fire of hell, and through this is a mortal sin: Anger expressed by the sound of the voice, but not reaching to the evil of an insult, makes one liable to the council, that is, it is not certain whether it merits hell, but it is worthy of either that punishment or a lesser one: Therefore there are found certain sins which are lighter than to merit the fire of hell, etc.

I answer: The argument fails, 1. by begging the question. For the Jesuit assumes many things as ἀναπόδεικτα (undemonstrated), which, however, both the scope of Christ's entire Sermon and the coherence of the text itself clearly prove to be most false. For it is false that by the words council and judgment, Christ the Savior means civil punishments: It is false that the Savior wished to note by these very words an uncertainty of punishment, as if it were not sufficiently certain by what kind of civil punishment those lighter offenses ought to be punished: which I would say is too absurd to affirm not only of God, but even of a political Magistrate. Finally, it is false that there are given certain sins which are lighter than to merit the fire of hell. The cause of these errors results from ignorance of the Elenchus, which is the other sophistication of the Jesuit argument. For the Sophist is ignorant, or certainly pretends to be ignorant, what end and scope was proposed to the Savior in this place: namely, not that which the Jesuit feigns, as if He wished to show that there are certain lighter offenses which, in themselves, by themselves, and by reason of their act, are not worthy of the eternal punishment of the underworld: nay, about which it could even be doubted by what kind of civil punishments they ought to be avenged: which never entered the mind of the Savior. But this was the genuine and proper scope set before Him, to demonstrate that not only those graver offenses which are designated by an external work,

But also that those interior motions, and the lightest inordinate affections, that is, sinning with the fifth commandment, are no less than homicide itself, in themselves and by themselves worthy of eternal death. The truth of the statement is evident from the fact that the Savior by this covenant sought to overturn and refute the corruptions of the Pharisees: who tried to persuade the people: that the fifth commandment is then at last violated, and its guilt contracted, when homicide is perpetrated by the hand or other external force: Thus also the guilt of the sixth commandment is then at last contracted, when someone inflicts adultery upon another's spouse by the act itself: the Savior therefore shows that the guilt of the violated divine law is also contracted then, when someone is merely rashly angry at his neighbor or brother, even if it does not reach the evil of railing: when likewise someone merely looks at another's spouse, to lust after her. The Savior therefore, under the terms of Judgment, Council, and Gehenna, alluding to earthly judgments, and those then customary among the Jews, wished to describe the anger and judgments of God himself against any, even lighter, transgressions of the Law: meanwhile indicating by that variety of words, that just as sins themselves are not equal, so also punishments before the Judgment of God will not be in all respects equal: although all are equally liable to the judgment of eternal damnation, with the degrees of punishments and infernal torments nevertheless preserved.

Bellarmino borrows a second argument from those testimonies of the Scriptures in which the Savior compares certain sins to things by their nature most light: such as gnats, Matt. 23, 24; a mote, Luke 6, 42; the last farthing, Luke 12, 59; wood, hay, stubble, 1 Cor. 3, 12.
