But on the contrary, he compares other sins to most grave things, such as a camel, a beam, etc. Now between a gnat and a camel there is almost no proportion: but between a mote and a beam there is such a difference by the nature of the thing, that a mote can be carried lightly, but a beam is unbearable. Thus for the debt of one farthing, no one in any tribunal is condemned to death: Thus wood, hay, and stubble indeed bring damage, and need purging: yet they do not cause one to fall from salvation. Therefore lighter or more minute sins are by their nature Venial, and not worthy of eternal death.

Latin:

Ἀντιθετικὴ. Sive Corruptelae pugnantes cum puriore doctrina, de discrimine peccati mortalis & Venialis.

PAssa est purior haec doctrina nostra, jam olim acrem omninò contradictionem, neque leviorem etiamnùm hodiè patitur.

Scholastici 1. olim Pharisaeorum secuti dogmata, distingvebant praecepta legis divinae in Magna & parva: 2. Magnis opponebant peccata Mortalia: parvis verò Venialia. 3. Mortalia in specie ex Gregorio Magno enumerabant septem: Videlicet, 1. Superbiam, sive inanem gloriam: 2. Iram. 3. Invidiam. 4. Acediam, sive ignaviam. 5. Gulam, 6. Avaritiam. 7. Luxuriam sive Lasciviam: quibus septem opponebant virtutes contrarias: 1. Humilitatem. 2. Patientiam: 3. Charitatem: 4. Diligentiam: 5. Abstinentiam: 6. Liberalitatem: 7. Castitatem. Quartò Pharisaeorum impietatem superantes statuebant haec sola septem peccata, suâ naturâ esse mortalia: reliqua verò singula ac universa ita esse parva & levia, ut licèt ipsa, per se displiceant Deo, tamen Homo propter ea minime displiceat: siquidem non sint contra legem, sed praeter legem Dei.

Prodidit hanc impietatem jam olim Magister sententiarum, lib. 2. dist. 42. Mortale, inquiens, peccatum, obligat, nos æternæ pœnæ: Veniale autem pœnæ temporali sed quæ facilè indulgetur: Secundum rationem peccatum mortale committitur: sed non omne Veniale, quippè quod in solo motu sensualitatis existit.

Hinc Thomas 1. secundae quaest. 89. Peccatum Veniale non causat maculam in anima: & est in sensualitate sicut Mortale est in ratione. Quod ut planiùs intelligatur, sic duo haec peccata distinxerunt, referente Chemnitio part. 3. locorū: pag. 276. Quando sensualis motus Carnis concipit aliquam illecebrā peccati, cui plerumq; inferior portio rationis & cogitationis, scilicet delectatio aliqua, sed non diu adest: & si non accedat voluntas perficiendi, quam dicunt esse superiorem rationis portionē, tùm volunt esse peccatum Veniale: ut sunt primi motus, itē quæ ex surreptione aliqua, infirmitate aut ignorantia fiunt: ita ut actus subitus, non deliberat⁹, quantumvis malus sit Veniale peccatum : imò non habeat rationem peccati : neque de tali peccato opus sit contritione : quippè quod impedire haud possit, quò minùs obedientia renatorum hac in vita sit integra & perfecta: imò vitam æternam promereri possit.

Et ne impietas isthæc modum haberet, recensent Scholastici Doctores, certa remedia Venialium peccatorum : ut, 1. Confessionem generalem : de pœnit. distinct. 3. c. de quotidianis. 2. devotam pectoris tunsionem. Ibid dist. 1. c. tres sunt actiones, 3. Aquæ benedictæ aspersionem : de consecrat. dist. 3. c. Aquam. 4. Cordis contritionem : Antoninus part. 3. summæ, tit. 10. cap. 1. §. Quando. 5. Orationem Dominicam, præsertim de pœnitentia, dist. 3. §. de Quotidianis. 6. Episcopalem benedictionem & sacerdotalem, quin & monialem, causa 1. q. 1. c. multi, in fine. 7. dignam communionem : de pœnit. d. 2. c. cùm omne. 8. Eleemosynarum largitionem : de pœnit. dist. 1. c. Quamobrem 9. Remissionem injuriarum ex cap. 6. Luc. 10, Extremam Unctionem : c. unico. 11. patientiam flagellorum : 12. quodlibet opus bonum.

Neque vel tantillo rectiùs hodiè sentit aut docet Romana Ecclesia, & hujus cumprimis Hyperaspistæ, Jesuvvitæ, qui discrimen Peccati in Mortale & Veniale, non ex ipsius personæ delinquentis conditione : sed ex natura ipsius actus metiuntur, contendentes, Veniale peccatum esse, quod per se venia dignum sit, & sic comparatum, ut ob id Deo non sit justa causa irascendi : quippè quod non pugnet cum Lege Dei, ac proindè peccati rationem non habeat : Quâ de causâ non opus etiam sit, ut de eo aliquis dolore aut contritione afficiatur. Vndè hoc genus peccatorum nominant Leviculav Vitiola, peccatilla, & aspergines, quibus opera renatorum non contaminentur: sic quidem definiente Concilio Tridentino, Sess. 6, cap. 5, & Canone 25. Catechismo Romano, p. 553. Censura Col. p. 194. Lindano in panoplia p. 103.

Jesuvvita Bellarminus, suam suorumquè complicum mentem hunc in modum aperit, l. 1. de amissione grat. & statu peccati, cap. 2 Dicuntur peccata quædam lethalia, quæ hominem planè avertunt à Deo, & quibus pœna debetur æterna: Quædam Venialia, quæ nonnihil impediunt cursum ad Deum, non tamen ab eo avertunt, & facili negotio expiantur. Quod ut rectiùs intelligatur, subjicit cap. subseq. 3. peccati Venialis distinctionem, ex naturâ (uti autumat) ipsius petitam : Quædam inquiens sunt Venalia ex genere suo, quæ habent pro Objecto rem malam & inordinatam, sed quæ charitati Dei vel proximi non repugnet : quale est, Verbum otiosum, risus nimius, & alia id genus : Et his contraria sunt peccata mortalia ex genere suo: ut perjurium, adulterium & similia. Quædam ex imperfectione operis, quæ tametsi ex genere suo mortalia esse possent : tamen ob imperfectionem operis Venialia efficiuntur : quià videlicet sola imperfectio operis facit, ut cum charitate pugnare non judicentur. His contraria funt mortalia ex parte agentis, quæ quidem ex genere suo Venialia esse potuissent, & tamen ex dispositione quadam peccantis mortalia sunt. Hac rursus alia dicuntur ex subreptione Venialia, quæ non perfectè sunt voluntaria, quales sunt, subiti motus cupiditatis, iræ &c. Alia ex materia parvitate, quæ in re parva ac levi committuntur: ut furtum unius oboli.

Summa & caput doctrinæ Jesuiticæ est, peccata Venialia esse ac dici talia, non propter ipsam personam, per fidem Deo reconciliatam, sed ex ipsa sua naturâ, sine ullo respectu ad gratiam & misericordiam Dei, Christíque meritum: vel ut Bellarminus loquitur, Peccatum Veniale ex natura sua distingui à mortali, ac sine ulla relatione vel ad prædestinationem, vel ad misericordiam Dei, vel ad statum renatorum, esse ejusmodi, ut pœnam quidem mereatur, sed non æternam: & Deum offendat, sed non usq; ad amicitiæ dissolutionem lib. 1. de amiss. grat. cap. 9. l. C.

Argumenta Jesuvvitæ ex Scripturis petita, hæc sunt præcipua. PRIMUM Matth. 5, 23. legimus: Qui irascitur fratri suo, reus erit judicio, qui dixerit Raca, reus erit consilio: qui dixerit fatue, reus erit gehennæ ignis. Ex his conficitur argumentum ejusmodi: Manifestum convitium, teste vel judice Christo, facit reum gehennæ ignis, ac per hoc est peccatum mortale: Iracundia sono vocis expressa, sed ad malum convitij nõ pertingens, facit reum consilij id est, non constat, an mereatur gehennam, sed aut ea pœna, aut minore digna est: Inveniuntur igitur peccata quædam, quæ leviora sunt, quàm ut gehennam ignis mereantur &c.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum 1. petitione principij. Multa enim sumit Jesuvvita tanquàm ἀναπόδεικτα, quæ tamen falsissima esse, tùm scopus totius Concionis Christi, tùm ipsius textus συνέπεια luculenter evincunt. Falsum enim est per vocabula, Consilij ac Iudicij, à Christo Servatore intelligi pœnas civiles: Falsum est, Servatorem his ipsis vocabulis notare voluisse incertitudinem pœnæ, ac si non satis constaret, quo pœnæ civilis genere leviora illa delicta puniri deberent: id quod non dico de Deo, sed vel de Magistratu politico affirmare nimis absurdum foret. Falsum denique est, dari peccata quædam, quæ leviora sint, quàm ut gehennam ignis mereantur. Errorum istorum causa resultat ex ignoratione Elenchi, quæ altera est argumenti Jesuitici Sophisticatio. Ignorat enim, vel certè ignorare simulat Sophista, quis finis ac scopus Servatori hoc loco fuerit propositus: himirùm non ille, quem fingit Jesuvvita, ac si ostendere voluisset, esse quædam leviora delicta, quæ per se, in se, & ratione actus sui non digna sint æterno inferorum supplicio: imò de quibus etiam dubitari possit, quo pœnarum civilium genere vindicari deberent: id quod Servatori nunquàm in mentem venit. Sed hic genuinus & proprius ipsi scopus erat præfixus, ut demonstraret, non tantùm graviores illas offensas, quæ externo opere designantur:

Sed & interiores illos motus, ac levissimos affectus inordinatos, hoc est, cum præcepto quinto peccantes, haud minùs atque ipsum homicidium, æterna morte, in se & per se dignos esse. Patet dicti veritas exindè, quòd Servator hoc pacto Pharisæorum corruptélas evertere ac refutare studuit: qui persuadere conabantur populo: Quintum præceptum tùm demùm violari, ejusque reatum contrahi, quando manu aut aliâ vi externa perpetratur homicidium: Sic sexti etiam præcepti reatum tùm demùm contrahi, quando quis alterius conjugi ipso facto stuprum inferat: ostendit proindè Servator, tùm quoque legis divinæ violatæ reatum contrahi, quando quis proximo sive fratri suo tantùm temerè irascatur, etiamsi ad malum convicij non pertingat: quando item quis alterius conjugem saltem adspiciat, ad concupiscendum eam. Servator proindè, sub vocabulis Judicij, Concilij & gehennæ, ad terrena, & Judæis, tùm usitata judicia alludens, ipsius Dei iram & judicia, adversus quasvis, leviores etiam Legis transgressiones, describere voluit: illud interim vocabulorum istorum varietate innuens, quemadmodum peccata ipsa non sunt paria, ita etiam pœnas coram Judicio Dei ron fore per omnia æquales: ex æquo licet omnes obnoxiæ sint æternæ damnationis judicio, servatis tamen pœnarum atque cruciatuum infernalium gradibus.

Alterum argumentum mutuatur Bellarminus ab illis Scripturarum testimoniis, in quibus Servator peccata quædam comparat rebus naturâ suâ levissimis: ut culicibus. Matth. 23, 24. festucæ, Luc. 6, 42. novissimo minuto, Luc. 12, 59. ligno, fæno, stipulis. 1. Cor. 3, 12. Contra verò alia peccata comparat rebus gravissimis, ut Camelo, trabi &c. Jam inter culicem & Camelum nulla ferè est proportio: inter festucam verò & trabem tanta est ex natura rei differentia, ut festuca leviter portari queat, trabi autem sit importabilis. Sic pro unius minuti debito, nemo in ullo tribunali damnatur ad mortem: Sic lignum, fænum, stipulæ detrimentum quidem afferunt, & purgatione indigent: non tamen à salute excidere faciunt. Ergo leviora sive minutiora peccata, ex naturâ suâ sunt Venalia, neq́; morte æterna digna.


### Chapter II. Or Corruptions contending with purer doctrine, on the discrimination of mortal and venial sin (continued)

I answer: The argument fails first by childish trifling, and by perversion of the legitimate state of the question. For it is not asked, whether from the Law of God an inequality of sins can be demonstrated, of which one is lighter than another: For this very thing we have already readily granted just now above, at the beginning of this second chapter. But this is the question: Whether those lighter sins, in themselves and by their nature, deserve pardon, or rather death. Therefore when the Jesuit concludes thus: There are lighter sins in the Scriptures: Therefore they are by their nature Venial: he commits another sophism, which is that of the vicious consequent. For nothing else follows from the antecedent, than that those lighter sins, as in the gravity of the guilt, so also in the atrocity of the infernal punishment itself, do not rise to the magnitude of mortal sins. Both of which we readily grant. Whence, however, it is not permitted to conclude: Therefore those lighter sins by themselves deserve pardon, and are not subject to eternal damnation: as the Jesuit concludes by a shameful begging of the question. We therefore correct the Jesuitical argument in this manner: Certain sins in the Scriptures are compared to gnats, a mote, the last farthing, wood, hay, stubble. But these things by their nature are light and minute. Therefore there are also certain sins, by their nature so compared, that both by reason of the fault, and by reason of the degrees of punishments, they are lighter than mortal sins are: which none of us has ever denied. Finally, that Apostolic comparison, taken from 1 Cor. 3, 12, fundamentally undermines and overturns the entire Jesuitical structure. For the Apostle expressly establishes that those lighter sins, which are compared to wood, hay, and stubble, are Venial because they are built upon the foundation, which is CHRIST JESUS: not because they are such by their nature. But Bellarmino strives to defend this latter point: and to attack the former: namely, that without any relation to Christ, and only by their nature, they are Venial. Therefore the Jesuit agrees as much with the Apostolic comparison as light can agree with darkness, truth with a lie: nay, Belial with Christ.

The third argument taken from chapter 1, 14, of the Epistle of James: in the fourth controversy of the preceding nearest Article, which was about Concupiscence, has been expressly and solidly refuted. To which, for the sake of brevity, I refer the reader.

The fourth and last argument the Jesuit takes from those places of the Scriptures in which the Scriptures speak of certain sins much more mildly than they are accustomed to speak of those which are by common consent lethal sins. Matt. 12, 36. Of every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account in the day of judgment. Now indeed it is one thing, that an idle word is not without fault, and therefore to be discussed in the day of judgment. But it is another thing: Depart into eternal fire: bind him hand and foot, and cast him into outer darkness: depart from me all ye workers of iniquity, etc.

But this collection also labors under the same sophistries which we have worn down in the resolution of the preceding ones. For from a disparity of sins, nothing more can be inferred than a disparity of degrees of punishments; now, just as it does not follow that because the servant who knew the will of his Lord and did not do it was beaten with double severity, therefore the servant who, being ignorant of the will of the Lord, did not do it, will clearly not be beaten at all, but only that he will be beaten less or more lightly; so it does not follow that because those who commit mortal sins are worthy of the eternal punishment of hell, therefore those who commit lighter sins are clearly not worthy of eternal damnation; but this only follows: therefore those who commit lighter sins will also suffer lighter torments in hell. Furthermore, a fallacy of non-cause is committed. For Scripture does not speak more mildly of certain sins because they are by their nature venial, but because other sins are more serious than others; and therefore, both by reason of the guilt and by reason of the infernal punishment, they differ greatly. And indeed, if he were worthy of being exploded who, from the words of Christ saying to Pilate, John 19:11, 'He who delivered me to you has the greater sin,' would wish to conclude thus: 'Judas, who by betraying Christ delivered him to Pilate, has the greater sin: therefore the sin of Pilate, condemning Christ to the death of the Cross, was by its nature Venial, since it was lighter than the sin of Judas': thus our Jesuits would be most worthy of being exploded, concluding in a like manner: 'Scripture speaks more mildly of certain sins: therefore those sins by their nature are Venial,' for in both cases the base πλεονεξία of the consequent and the Sophistication of the non-cause are at work.

The Jesuit draws a fifth argument from reason in this manner: 'If Venial sins were by their nature mortal, and were not imputed to the faithful only because of the faith which they have, certainly they would be imputed to infidels entirely, and would be mortal. But this is manifestly false and absurd. Therefore, that which is absurd, that Venial sins are by their nature mortal, is also false.' The proposition is conceded by the Adversaries and needs no proof. For if faith alone is the cause why some sins are Venial, without doubt all sins will be mortal to those who lack faith. The assumption of the argument, therefore, is proven: for in the same kind of sin, a faithful person offends God more gravely than an infidel: for 'the servant who knew the will of his Lord and did not prepare, shall be beaten with many stripes' (Luke 12:48). Thus the Apostle teaches that the sins of infidels are lighter because of ignorance, when he speaks of himself (1 Tim. 1:13). I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.

I reply to the proof of the Minor, which at the beginning contains a manifest ψεῦδος, if it is set forth so nakedly and generally in the Jesuitical manner. For it is false, and has never before been heard of even in rumor in the Church of God, that the faithful offend God more gravely than infidels. Certainly, if it is true what John 1:3, 9 [sic] has handed down: 'He who is born of God does not commit sin, because the seed of God remains in him'; if it is likewise true what the Apostle asserts, Rom. 8:1, that 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus': then this hypothesis of the Jesuit, which he himself takes as indubitable and constitutes as the foundation of his argument, will certainly be false. Furthermore, if the Adversary wishes to convince us of this hypothesis from the cited passages of Scripture, he commits the fallacy of Ignoratio Elenchi and ἑτεροζητήσεως. For in those passages sins are not compared insofar as one is faithful and the other is an infidel, as the Jesuit assumes; but insofar as both already agree in this, that they sin against conscience; where the reborn person sins more gravely, since he who knows the will of the LORD and does not do it, sins more than the one not reborn who commits the same sin out of ignorance. From which, however, that which the Jesuit intends by no means follows. For it is one question when it is asked, 'Does a faithful person offend God more gravely than an infidel?', where we defend the negative: for as long as a faithful person is and remains faithful, he is pleasing to God, indeed he is a friend of God (John 15:14 and 15). But it is another and different question when it is asked: 'Why does a reborn person, sinning against conscience and falling from the grace of God, receive more stripes than one who is not reborn?' Where certainly the cause is not assigned as the one the Jesuit dreams of, that this happens because he is faithful and the other is an infidel: but rather that he who was faithful could have resisted the depraved desires of the flesh by the power of the indwelling Holy Spirit: but, having spurned the prompting of the Spirit, he designed against his conscience those things which another, being ignorant, is accustomed to design. Regarding the Apostolic passage, Paul did not obtain mercy because his sin was by its nature Venial: for here he would not have had need of mercy: for that which by its nature deserves pardon does not need to receive it finally out of mercy, but [it is because] God looked upon Paul, sinning out of ignorance, with the eyes of His mercy.

Finally, what the Jesuit adds from Thomas, who writes in 1-2, q. 89, art. 5, that it is said unreasonably that those motions of sensuality which are Venial sins in the faithful are mortal in infidels, since the dignity of the person does not diminish but increases the reason for the guilt: that does not strike us in the least. For who of us has ever said or written that the cause of Venial sins depends on the dignity of the person? Since we refer it rather solely to the infinite mercy of God: as that which, not because of our dignity, but because of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, covers, remits, and indeed entirely removes the guilt of sins: and causes that which by its nature is mortal to become Venial.

But the Jesuit insists, and further argues thus: 'If we wish to speak properly, a sin is not Venial because God does not impute it to the guilt of eternal death: but God does not impute it to the guilt of eternal death because it is Venial. For that is called Venial which is worthy of pardon, or in which there is something why it should be punished less.' I ask, therefore, what is that which makes a sin to be Venial or worthy of pardon, and not imputed to the guilt of eternal death? They will answer that it is faith, with which that sin coexists. But I ask again, why does one sin coexist with faith and is Venial, while another excludes faith and is mortal? They will answer, because the former is involuntary, the latter voluntary. But what is this other than to refer the distinction between mortal and Venial sins to the very nature and reason of sin? For to be voluntary, or involuntary, pertains to the very nature and definition of sin. Indeed, the more voluntary a sin is, the more it is a sin; the less voluntary it is, the less it is a sin; and if it be in no way voluntary, it will in no way be a sin.

I answer: This argument fails by the fallacy of begging the question. For the Jesuit has not proven these two αἰτήματα [postulates]: 1. That sin is not imputed to the guilt of eternal death because it is in itself Venial: 2. That Venial is the same as worthy of pardon, or has something in itself for which it is punished more mildly. We deny both simply, asserting that the sins of the reborn, which in themselves and by their nature are mortal, become Venial, not because they are such by their nature, or because they have in themselves anything worthy of pardon: or finally, that there is any such dignity in the sinning person, but because God freely remits them and pardons the guilt on account of his Son. Then a gross ignorance of the refutation, or even of the definition, is committed. For when we answer that some sin is Venial, and can consist with faith, in that it is involuntary: then we do not look to the nature of sin itself, nor even to that natural conflict of appetite and reason, such as can exist even in the unregenerate from the Light of Nature: but we look to that spiritual conflict, by which the flesh sometimes lusts against the spirit: but the Spirit resists and breaks the desires of the flesh so that they do not begin to dominate and reign. Gal. 5.17. Now, just as this very victory of the Spirit against the flesh is not of our Nature, or of our natural powers: but the work of God's mercy alone: So from this term INVOLUNTARY, nothing at all can redound to the support of the nature of sins considered in themselves, according to Bellarmine's opinion.

Latin:

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum 1. puerili ἀδολεσχίᾳ, & perversione legitimi status. Non enim quæritur, An ex Lege Dei demonstrari possit inæqualitas peccatorum, quorum unum levius sit altero: Hoc ipsum enim jam modò supra, sub initium capitis hujus secundi, ultrò largiti sumus. Verùm hoc Quæstionis est: An leviora illa peccata, in se & suâ naturâ veniam, an verò mortem mereantur. Proindè quando Jesuuvita sic colligit: Dantur in Scripturis peccata leviora: Ergo illa suâ naturâ sunt Venalia: alterum jam Sophisma, quod est vitiosi consequentis, committit. Neque enim quicquam aliud ex Antecedente sequitur, quàm quòd leviora illa peccata, uti reatus gravitate, sic etiam ipsius supplicij infernalis atrocitate, ad magnitudinem peccatorum mortalium non assurgat. Quod utrumq; nos ultrò largimur. Undè tamen colligere hand licèt: Ergo leviora illa peccata, per se veniam merentur, neque æternæ damnationi subjacent: uti per turpem petitionem principij colligit Jesuvvita. Corrigimus proindè argumentum Jesuvviticum in hunc modum: Peccata quædam in Scripturis comparantur culicibus, festuca, novissimo minuto, ligno, fœno,stipulis. Atqui hæ res naturâ suâ sunt leves ac minutæ. Ergo sunt etiam peccata quædam, ex naturâ suâ ita comparata, ut tum ratione culpæ, tum ratione graduum pœnarum, sint leviora, quam sint peccata mortalia: id quod nemo nostrum inficiatus est unquam. Tandem comparatio illa Apostolica, petita ex 1. Cor. 3, 12. universam structuram Jesuvviticam funditùs subruit & evertit. Apostolus enim disertè statuit, ideò leviora illa peccata, quæ ligno, fœno ac stipulis conferuntur, esse Venialia, quia super fundamentum, quod est CHRISTUS JESUS, sint ædificata: non quod ex naturâ suâ talia sint. Atqui Bellarminus hoc posterius propugnare: illud verò prius impugnare studet: quod nimirùm sine ulla relatione ad Christum, & tantum suâ naturâ sint Venialia. E. Jesuvvitæ tàm convenit cum comparatione Apostolicâ, quàm convenire potest luci cum tenebris, veritati cum mendacio: imò Beliali cum Christo.

Tertium argumentum petitum ex cap. 1, 14. Epistolæ Jacobi: in præcedentis Articuli proximi controversiâ quarta, quæ erat de Concupiscentiâ, ex professo solidè est refutatum. Quô Lectorem brevitatis studio remitto.

Quartum & postremum argumentum sumit Jesuvvita ex illis scripturarum locis, in quibus de peccatis quibusdam longè mitiùs scripturæ loquuntur, quàm de ijs loqui soleant, quæ sunt omnium consensu peccata lethalia Matth. 12, 36. De omni verbo otioso, quod locuti fuerint homines, reddent rationem in die judicij. Jam verò aliud est, Verbum otiosum non esse sine culpa, & ideò discutiendum in die judicij. Aliud verò: Ite in ignem æternum: ligatis manibus & pedibus ejus, projicite eum in tenebras exteriores: discedite à me omnes operarij iniquitatis &c.

Verùm ijsdem Sophisticationibus laborat & hæc collectio, quas in præcedentium difsolutione protrivimus. Neque enim à disparitate peccatorum, plus inferri potest, quàm disparitas graduum pœnarum, Jam verò quemadmodum non sequitur, servus qui novit voluntatem Domini, & non fecerit, duplo graviùs vapulavit: Ergo, Servus, qui ignorans voluntatem Domini non fecerit, planè non vapulabit: Sed tantùm, Ergo minus aut levius vapulabit: Sic non sequitur: Qui mortalia peccata designant, æterno inferorum supplicio digni sunt: Ergo qui leviora peccata designant, planè non sunt digni æternâ damnatione: Sed hoc tantum sequitur: Ergo qui leviora peccata designant, leviores etiam cruciatus in inferno patientur. Deindè committitur Sophisticatio non causæ. Neque enim ideò scriptura de quibusdam peccatis mitiùs loquitur, quòd ea suâ naturâ sint Venialia: sed quia pecccta alia alijs sunt graviora; ac proindè tum ratione culpæ, tum ratione pœnæ infernalis plurimùm differunt. Et profectò si explosione dignus foret, qui ex verbis Christi dicentis ad Pilatum, Johan. 19, 11. Qui me tibi tradidit, majus peccatum habet; sic vellet colligere: Judas qui prodendo Christum tradidit Pilato, majus Peccatum habet: Ergò Peccatum Pilati damnantis Christum ad mortem Crucis, naturâ suâ erat Veniale, siquidem levius erat peccato Judæ: sic explosione dignissimi forent nostri Jesuitæ, pari ratione sic colligentes: Scriptura de quibusdam peccatis mitius loquitur: Ergò peccata illa naturâ suâ sunt Venialia, utrobique enim turpis πλεονεξία Consequentis, & Sophisticatio non causæ militat.

Quintum argumentum ex ratione petit Jesuvita in hunc modum: Si peccata Venialia ex naturâ suâ essent mortalia, & solùm fidelibus ob fidem, quam habent, non imputarentur, certè infidelibus omninò imputarentur, & mortalia essent. Atqui hoc manifestè falsum atque absurdum. Ergò falsum quod illud & absurdum, peccata Venialia ex natura sua esse mortalia. Propositio ab Adversarijs conceditur, neque ulla probatione eget. Nam si sola fides causa est, cur aliqua peccata sint Venialia, sine dubio peccata omnia mortalia erunt ijs, qui fide carent. Assumtio igitur argumenti probatur: Nam in eodem genere peccati gravius Deum fidelis quàm infidelis offendit: Nam Servus, qui cognovit voluntatem Domini, & non præparavit, vapulabit multis. Luc. 12, 48. Sic Apostolus peccata Infidelium, ob ignorantiam docet esse leviora, cùm de se loquitur. 1. Tim. 1, 13. Misericordiam consecutus sum, quia ignorans feci in incredulitate.

Respondeo ad probationem Minoris, quæ initio manifestum ψεῦδος continet, si more Jesuvitico ita nudè & generaliter ponatur. Falsum enim, & ante hac ne fando quidem in Ecclesia Dei auditum fuit, fideles Deum gravius offendere, quàm infideles. Certè si verum est, quod Johannes 1 cap. 3, 9. prodidit: Qui ex Deo natus est, peccatum non facit, quia semen Dei in eo manet: si verum itidem est; quod Apostolus asserit, Rom. 8, 1. Nihil jam condemnationis esse his, qui sunt in Christo Jesu: utique falsa erit hæc Jesuitæ hypothesis, quam ipse pro indubitata sumens, absin ac fundamentum sui argumenti constituit. Deindè verò si ex productis Scripturarum locis, hypothesi huic fidem facere velit Adversarius, Sophisma committit Ignorationis Elenchi & ἑτεροζητήσεως. Neque enim in illis conferuntur peccata, quatenùs ille fidelis, hic verò infidelis est, uti autumat Jesuvita; sed quatenùs utrique jam in eo conveniunt, quòd contra conscientiam peccant; ubi graviùs jam peccat renatus, quippè qui sciens voluntatem DOMINI, non facit eam, quàm quimen renatus, ex ignorantia idem peccatum committit. Undè tamen minimè sequitur id, quod intendit Jesuitæ. Nam alia est quæstio quando quæritur, An fidelis gravius Deum offendat, quàm infidelis, ubi negantem tuemur: Quamdîu enim fidelis est ac manet fidelis, tamdiu placet Deo, imò est amicus Dei Ioh. 15, 14. & 15. Alia verò & diversa est Quæstio, quà quæritur: Cur renatus contra conscientiam peccans, & gratia Dei excidens, gravius vapulet, quàm non renatus. Ubi certè causa non assignatur ea, quam Jesuitæ somniat, fieri hoc ideò, quia fidelis est, alter verò infidelis: sed ea potiùs, quòd ille, qui fidelis erat, potuisset virtute inhabitantis Spiritus Sancti resistere pravis desiderijs carnis: sed spreto Spiritus dictamine contra conscientiam designavit ea, quæ alius ignorans designare solet. Quoad locum Apostolicum, non ideo Paulus misericordiam consecutus est, quòd peccatum ipsius naturâ suâ esset Veniale: hic enim misericordiâ non opus habuisset: Nam quod ex naturâ suâ veniam meretur: illud non ex misericordia demùm illam accipiat, necesse habet, sed quod Deus oculis misericordiæ suæ respexit Paulum, ex ignorantia peccantem.

Quod denique ex Thoma annectit Jesuvita, qui 1. secundæ quæst. 89. art. 5. scribit, Irrationabiliter dici, motus illos sensualitatis, qui in fidelibus peccata sunt Venialia, in infidelibus esse mortalia: cum dignitas personæ non minuat, sed augeat rationem culpæ: illud nos minimè ferit. Quis enim nostrûm unquàm vel dixit vel scripsit, causam peccatorum Venialium dependere à dignitate personæ: cùm eam potiùs ad infinitam Dei misericordiam unicè referamus: ut quæ non propter nostram dignitatem, sed propter meritum Christi, fide apprehensum, tegit, remittit, imò penitùs tollit peccatorum reatum: & facit, ut quæ naturâ suâ sunt mortalia evadant Venialia.

Sed instat Jesuitæ, & porrò sic arguit: Si propriè loqui velimus, non ideò peccatum aliquod est Veniale, quia Deus illud ad reatum mortis æternæ non imputat: sed ideò Deus illud ad reatum mortis æternæ non imputat, quia Veniale est. Veniale siquidem dicitur, quod est Veniâ dignum, sive in quo aliquid est, cur minùs puniri debeat. Quæro igitur, Quid illud sit, quod facit, ut peccatum aliquod sit Veniale seu Veniâ dignum, & ad reatum mortis æternæ non imputetur. Respondebunt, esse fidem, cum quâ peccatum illud simul consistit. Sed rursus quæro, cur peccatum aliquod simul cum fide consistat, & sit Veniale: aliud fidem excludat & sit mortale? Respondebunt, quia illud involuntarium est, hoc voluntarium. At quid hoc est aliud, nisi discrimen peccatorum mortalium ac Venialium ad ipsam peccati naturam & rationem referre. Nam voluntarium esse, vel involuntarium, ad ipsam peccati naturam & rationem pertinet. Siquidem peccatum, quò magis est voluntarium, eò magis est peccatum: quòm inùs est voluntarium, eò minùs est peccatum: & si nullo modo voluntarium sit, nullo modo peccatum erit.

Respondeo: Fallit Ratio hæc Sophismate petit onis principij. Neque enim duo hæc αἰτήματα probavit Jesuvvita: 1. Peccatum ideò non imputari ad reatum mortis æternæ, quia in se sit Veniale: 2. Veniale idem esse, quod Veniâ dignum, vel aliquid in se habere, cur mitiùs puniatur. Utrumque simpliciter negamus, asserentes peccata renatorum, quæ in se & suâ naturâ sunt mortalia, fieri Venialia, non quod suâ naturâ talia sint, vel quod in se habeant aliquid Venia dignum: vel denique, quòd in persona peccante sit talis aliqua dignitas, sed quia Deus propter filium suum gratis ea remittit, & reatum condonat. Deinde crassa committitur ignorantia Elenchi, vel etiam Definitionis. Nam quando respondemus, Peccatum aliquod esse Veniale, & cum fide consistere posse, eò quod est involuntarium: tùm non ad ipsam peccati naturam, neq; etiam ad naturalem illam pugnam appetitus & rationis, Qualis ex Lumine Naturæ etiam in non renatis esse potest: sed ad spiritualem illam pugnam respicimus, qua caro subindè concupiscit adversus spiritum: Spiritus verò repugnat & infringit carnis desideria ne dominari & regnare incipiant. Gal 5.17. Jam verò quemadmodum hæc ipsa victoria Spiritus adversus carnem non est Naturæ nostræ, vel virium nostrarum naturalium: sed solius Dei misericordiæ opus: Ita ex termino etiam isto INVOLUNTARII, ad ipsam Naturam peccatorum in se consideratorum, pro Bellarmini sententia nihil quicquam præsidij redundare potest.


### Chapter II. Or Corruptions contending with purer doctrine, on the discrimination of mortal and venial sin (continued)

The Jesuit's third argument, taken from Thomas, collapses from the author's own vanity: and begs the question. For it is equally false that Venial sin does not avert a man from God: that it does not conflict with charity, if it is considered by its nature: as it can be false: That certain sins are Venial by themselves and by their nature.

The fourth argument is as follows: If by its nature any offense were to dissolve the friendship of God, by the same reason it would dissolve any other friendship. But if anyone harms a friend either carelessly, or in the most trivial matter, he is not considered by the judgment of all prudent men to have harmed that friendship, let alone be worthy of the punishment of death. Therefore, any fault does not by its nature dissolve even that friendship which exists between us and God.

I answer that this argument labors under a manifest ἀδολεχία [babbling] and begging of the Question, or from this one argument, a most certain judgment can be sought concerning the excellent method of disputing of the Jesuits, indeed their entire Theology. For 1. it establishes that the reason, the rights, and the laws of civil friendship, which is contracted between equals, are the same as that friendship which exists between the faithful and God: where, however, mere inequality reigns.

For on their part there is nothing but unworthiness and guilt: but on His part, mere pity and Pardon prevail. Then a manifest ψεῦδος [falsehood] is committed, when the Jesuit asserts that immoderate laughter, and idle words, are not by their nature such that they make a man otherwise just and a friend of God, worthy of eternal torment. Certainly, both the Savior in Matt. 12.36, and the Apostle in Col. 3.8, in express words refer these things to the class of those sins which deserve eternal death. And although these offenses are not imputed to the Reborn or friends of God unto death, this is not because they are Venial by their nature: but accidentally, insofar as God freely remits and pardons the guilt of those sins to them, apprehended by faith on account of the Son.

The Jesuit's fifth argument is as follows: Sin is not said univocally of mortal and Venial, but by a certain analogy, and therefore Venial sin is not perfectly sin, like mortal, but imperfectly. Therefore, the punishment of eternal death, which is simply and perfectly a punishment, or rather the most grievous of all punishments, is not due to it. The antecedent is proven 1. by the authority of Albert, Bonaventure, Thomas, and other Scholastics. 2. By reason: For two things are required primarily to constitute sin: that it be voluntary, and against the law. But every Venial sin is either not perfectly voluntary, or is not perfectly against the law of God. Therefore, there is no Venial sin that is perfectly and simply sin, but imperfectly and in a certain respect.

I answer: 1. That a manifest ψεῦδος [falsehood] is committed, most shamefully impinging upon the very art of Logic. For synonyms or univocals are those whose name is the same, and the definition of essence according to that name is the same; or synonyms are those which have one definition: as a Genus, when it is predicated of its species: and a species, when it is predicated of particulars and individuals. Therefore, to be predicated συνωνύμως [synonymously] or univocally is said of that, in respect of which the subject is said to be simply the predicate itself, or ὅπερ αὐτὸ [what it is]. Now, sin perfectly and properly so called is ἀνομία [lawlessness], or non-conformity with the Law of God: But Venial sin is such an ἀνομία, or non-conformity with the law of God. Therefore, venial sin, considered by its own nature, is sin perfectly and properly so called: and consequently it is most false that the term 'sin' is not predicated univocally of mortal and venial sin: whatever Albert, Bonaventure, and others may prattle in this regard. The minor premise is so true that the Apostle not only expressly names concupiscence dwelling in the regenerate person as sin, but also assigns to it attributes and effects that belong to nothing but sin properly so called: as was shown in the immediately preceding article, in the final controversy concerning concupiscence. Nor is it worth a farthing what the Jesuit objects, that for sin to be perfectly and properly so called, it is also required that it be voluntary. For 1. the Johannine definition does not in the least require this. Furthermore, let it be granted that this also is required: Certainly those lighter sins of the regenerate also have their seat in the will, and most especially so; in such a way that the regenerate person, in that part where he never ceases to feel the remnants of the old man, or as the Apostle speaks, Rom 7:23, according to the law of the members, wills that which is repugnant to the Law of GOD: to which, however, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he resists from time to time, lest it obtain dominion. And in this respect, venial sin, considered in itself, is perfectly voluntary: since it obtains its seat only in the will of man; although it differs in degree in this from voluntary mortal sin, that it is not committed by the regenerate with full affection of mind or with a determined will: just as mortal sins are committed by the unfaithful. Which difference of degrees, however, does not prevent venial sin, in the respect already noted, from being and being called voluntary.

These things being observed, the inference of Bellarmine is to be refuted not with a pen, but with a Tartarean stake, who asserts with too much impiety: That venial sin from its own kind, as an idle word: likewise from the imperfection of the work: or from subreption, as the desire of an illicit thing, not fully deliberated: or from the smallness of the matter, as the theft of one farthing, or of another thing valued at a most vile price, is not perfectly against the Law. This is, indeed, to set one's mouth against Heaven, and with one obelisk to slaughter and pierce through the whole Law of GOD, as that which 1. defines sin indefinitely as whatever is against the Law of GOD, without any determination of mode. 2. or a light commotion of the mind against a brother: nay, expressly an idle word, and indefinitely again every theft, every concupiscence, even that which does not break out into an external act, it recalls under the guilt of sin perfectly and properly so called, and consequently under the guilt of eternal damnation.

For the perfection of sin is not to be estimated from the quality of the deed, if indeed sin is considered in itself, and not comparatively to other sins: but only from the nature of the divine Law, which quite clearly attests that every ἀνομία [lawlessness], as well the lightest as the greatest, being contrary to the divine will, comes under the census and number of a perfect sin: as was shown expressly in the thesis above: especially since, as James testifies: He who transgresses the law of GOD in one point, has become guilty of all.

As for what Bellarmine finally adds, that venial sin in the regenerate does not exclude charity, and therefore it is not against the law of GOD: he commits a double sophistry, one of the cause, the other of the accident: for that charity can stand with venial sins in the regenerate, that does not depend on the very nature of venial sins, but on an accident, namely the mercy of GOD, which takes away the guilt of those sins.

But of the errors of the Papists and especially the Jesuits, for this time, more than enough.

There remain, however, in the class of those erring concerning the doctrine of the distinction between mortal and venial sin, both the Anabaptists and the Calvinists.

For the ANABAPTISTS have utterly exploded the distinction of sin into mortal and venial, and have branded it, as retained by Luther, as a fiction of the Schoolmen: contending that all sins in one and the same kind of men are equal: namely, mortal in the unregenerate: but venial in the regenerate.

They were, however, most shamefully mistaken in this, that they thought this distinction of sin had been devised only by the Scholastics, when nevertheless it cannot be denied that its use is much older. Tertullian certainly, who is the most ancient among the Latin ecclesiastical writers, and much older than the Scholastic Doctors, confirms quite clearly that this very distinction was already received in the usage of the Church, writing thus in his book On Modesty: Some sins are capital or mortal, some are daily and incidental, to which we are all so subject that if there were no forgiveness for these, no one would attain salvation. Therefore, there will be forgiveness for these through Christ the intercessor. Thus Augustine urged the same distinction, book 2 against Julian. Likewise the book On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 28. And epistle 89, although he does not use the term Mortal, but rather the names Lethal and Capital.

Moreover, even if it were entirely without this authority of the Fathers, this distinction would still hold its immovable foundations in the Scriptures. For what else did the Apostle wish to say, asserting: Those who do such things are worthy of death, Rom. 1:32. And if you live according to the flesh, you will die, Rom. 8:13. Than that some sins are mortal? Thus David, and the Apostle, pronouncing him blessed whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered, Ps. 32:1, Rom. 4:7, surely wished to note nothing else than that some sins are Venial, not because they are such in themselves, but because they have obtained forgiveness. This first error of the Anabaptists is therefore too gross to require a more lengthy refutation.

The other error of the same people is more plausible than the former: whence even today it has earned manifest applause in the Church of the Calvinists. For these also contend that the Reborn and the Elect commit only Venial sins, and cannot sin mortally, nor fall from the grace of GOD: so much so that even if they should commit the most grave crimes and atrocities, they nevertheless do not cast out the Holy Spirit. Just as Beza indeed contended in the Colloquy of Montbéliard that David, while perpetrating adultery and homicide, never lost, but always retained, the Holy Spirit and faith. Thus Zanchius writes in his Miscellanies, p. 242, that the remission of sins, once obtained, cannot be made void in the saints through subsequent lapses: But the Holy Spirit, once given to them, remains with them forever. Indeed, Rennecherus in his catechism, p. 157, and p. 261, did not shudder to write that there are often many from the number of the elect who lead a most wicked life: meanwhile, however, they have greater perseverance in their infirmity than Adam had in his perfection. Which opinion indeed tends solely to this, that it might fundamentally undermine and overturn the distinction of Mortal and Venial sin, as it is asserted in our churches: just as Beza indeed, again in the same colloquy, simply refused to allow that our side should distinguish between the lapses of human infirmity and manifest crimes against the Law of GOD, of which the former should be called Venial, but the latter Mortal: Indeed, into these words he broke out with great vehemence: There is no sin that is Venial, but all are mortal: Therefore this distinction of sins, as being Popish, cannot have a place here.

The sum and head of the error is: That there are absolutely no Mortal sins in the reborn, but all are Venial: just as, conversely, there are none but mortal sins in the reprobate: So that not only in these, but not even in those, can or ought this distinction of sins to be established. However, both the Anabaptists and the Calvinists are accustomed to call to the aid of this error those testimonies of the Scriptures especially, in which GOD promises that He will complete, until the day of Christ, that good work which He began in the reborn and Elect: Phil. 1, 6. and that He will not permit the just man, even when falling, to be dashed: Psalm 37, 24. that he who trusts in the LORD shall not be moved forever, Ps. 125, 1. that the bruised reed shall not be broken, and the smoking flax shall not be extinguished, Isa. 42, 8. that the Elect shall not be led into error, Matt. 24, 24. that no one shall snatch them from His hand, John 10, 28. that anyone can separate them from the love of GOD, which is in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8, 39.

But this error is also most solidly refuted, 1. by showing those foundations upon which we most evidently built this distinction of sin above in part 1 of the thesis of this chapter. 2. By producing other places of Scripture, in which mortal sins are assigned to the reborn and Elect in express words: as Luke 11, 24. When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he walks through dry places, seeking rest, and finding none, he says: I will return to my house from whence I came out: and when he comes, he finds it swept and garnished with brooms, then he goes and takes seven other spirits with him, more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there, and then the last state of that man becomes worse than the first. Thus GOD Himself affirms in Ezekiel, that a Just man can so fall from his justice, that He will no longer remember all his preceding justice. Ezek. 18, 24. Thus Rom. 11, 20: the Apostle says: You stand by faith: But do not be puffed up in mind, but fear: otherwise you also will fall away. And in 1 Cor. 9, 27. he confesses that he therefore brings his body into subjection, lest, when he has preached to others, he himself should become a castaway. 3. By noting the principal Sophistries, by which the Adversaries are accustomed to twist the testimonies of the Scriptures into a foreign sense through gross ignorance of the Elenchus, and a vicious consequence: and secundum quid. For that first saying, Phil. 1, 6, means nothing else than that not only the beginning, but also the consummation of our faith and salvation, depends upon the sole grace and mercy of GOD: which GOD wills to stand so unmoved on His part, that even if we should deny ourselves, He nevertheless remains faithful, and always wills His grace to be exposed to those returning through repentance. But what is this to the present business? Thus that other saying of Psalm 37, 24. deals with the adversities and troubles which sometimes, nay more frequently, are accustomed to press the pious than the impious. These, therefore, however great they may be, can never dislodge them from the protection of eternal salvation; since they are kept by the power of GOD unto salvation, but not except through faith, 1 Pet. 1, 5. Thus, therefore, this saying also is nothing to the present Rhombus. But if perhaps someone contends that the word (shall fall) is to be understood concerning a fall into sins, then we determine that the falls of human infirmity, and Venial sins, are noted. For concerning the remaining sins, which are committed by the Reborn against conscience with full deliberation of mind and set purpose: GOD Himself determines far otherwise, saying through the Prophet Nathan to David: You are a man of Death, 2 Sam. 12, 7.

Thus Psalm 125, 1 deals with those who and in so far as they trust in the LORD. For when these decline from the straight path of piety, then David brings a far different and clearly diverse judgment in the same Psalm, in the verse immediately following, the fifth: But those who decline into crooked ways, the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity.

The remaining testimonies of Scripture deal specifically with the Elect, whom it is certain will never finally fall away from the grace of GOD, although as long as they struggle in this life, they can more often fall into grave and mortal sins, and fall away totally from the grace of GOD: as will be demonstrated elsewhere συν θεῷ.

And thus indeed we conclude this disputation concerning the Distinction of Venial and mortal sin, establishing its use as being by far the greatest, namely that the Reborn and faithful may walk in the fear of GOD, and not rush into sins against conscience, that they may examine themselves incessantly, whether they have true faith; or at least a naked and empty persuasion of faith: that finally in daily infirmities and falls they may raise, console, and sustain themselves: certainly determining that GOD will not impute them to them, on account of Christ the Mediator: where, however, there is need of great caution, so that we do not indulge the desires of our flesh all the more freely. For a Venial sin can degenerate into a Mortal one: nay, it truly does degenerate, if it begins to please: as Augustine speaks somewhere.

Latin:

Tertia Jesuvvitæ ratio ex Thoma petita propriâ Autoris Vanitate corruit: & petit principium. Nam æquè falsum est, quòd Peccatum Veniale non avertat hominem à Deo: quòd non repugnet charitati, si ex natura sua consideretur: atque falsum esse potest: Quòd quædam peccata ex se & suâ naturâ sint Venialia.

Quarta ratio sichabet: Si naturâ suâ quævis offensio di\u017solveret amicitiam Dei, eâdem ratione di\u017solveret quamvis aliam amicitiam. Atqui si quis amicum vel incautè, vel in rê levissima lædat, is omnium prudentum judicio non censetur læsisse illius amicitiam, nedum mortis supplicio dignus. Ergò eam etiam amicitiam, quæ nobis cum Deo intercedit, non di\u017solvet ex natura sua qualibet culpa.

Respondeo Argumentum hoc manifestâ laborare ἀδολεχία & petitione Principij, vel ex hoc uno argumento, de egregia Jesuvvitarum disputandi ratione, imò universa ipsorum Theologiâ, certissimum peti posse judicium. Nam 1. statuit eandem esse rationem, eadem jura, easdem leges amicitiæ civili, quæ inter æquales contrahitur: cum amicitia illa, quæ fidelibus cum Deo intercedit: ubi tamen mera regnat inæqualitas.

Nam ex horum parte nihil aliud quàm indignitas & culpa: ex ipsius verò, mera miseratio & Venia militat. Deindè manifestum ψεῦδος committitur, quando asserit Jesuvvita, risum immoderatum, & verborum otiosum, ex naturâ suâ non esse talia, ut hominem alioqui justum & Dei amicum, dignum efficiant perpetuo cruciatu. Certè tùm Servator Matth. 12, 36. tùm Apostolus Coloss. 3, 8. disertis verbis in classem eorum peccatorum isthæc referunt, quæ æternam mortem promerentur. Et quanquam hæc delicta Renatis sive amicis Dei ad mortem non imputantur, sit hoc tamen non ideò, quod suâ naturâ sint Venialia: sed per accidens, quatenus videlicet Deus illorum peccatorum reatum, ipsis propter Filium fide apprehensum gratis remittit & condonat.

Quinta Jesuvvitæ ratio talis est: Peccatum non dicitur univocè de mortali & Veniali, sed per analogiam quandam, & proindè peccatum Veniar le non est perfectè peccatum, sicut mortale, sed imperfectè. Ergo non debetur ei pœna mortis æternæ, quæ est simpliciter, & perfectè pœna, vel potiùs pœnarum omnium gravissima. Antecedens probatur 1. autoritate Alberti, Bonaventuræ, Thomæ & aliorum Scholasticorum. 2. Ratione: Nam ad peccatum constituendum duo potissimùm requiruntur: ut sit voluntarium, & contra legem. Peccatum autem Veniale omne, aut non est perfectè voluntarium, aut non est perfectè contra legem Dei. Ergo nullum est Veniale peccatum, quod perfectè & simpliciter peccatum, sed imperfectè & secundum quid.

Respondeo: 1. Committi manifestum ψεῦδος, in ipsam etiam artem Logicam turpissimè impingens. Synonyma enim sive univoca sunt, quorum nomen est idem, & ratio Essentiæ secundum nomen illud est eadem; vel Synonyma sunt, quorum una est ratio & definitio: ut Generis, quando prædicatur de suis speciebus: & speciei, quando prædicatur de singularibus & individuis. Prædicari itaq́; συνωνύμως sive univocè id dicitur, cujus respectu subjectum simpliciter ipsum prædicatum, sive ὅπερ αὐτὸ esse dicitur. Jam verò peccatum perfectè & propriè sic dictum est ἀνομία, sive inconformitas cum Lege Dei: Atqui peccatum Veniale est talis ἀνομία, sive inconformitas cũ lege Dei. Ergo peccatum Veniale ex natura sua consideratum, est peccatum perfectè ac propriè sic dictum: ac per cõsequens falsissimum est, quòd vox Peccati, de mortali & Veniali non prædicetur univocè: quicquid etiam hac in parte garriant Albertus, Bonaventura & alij. Minor usque adeò vera est, ut Apostolus Concupiscentiam in se renato habitantem, non modò Peccatum disertè nominet, sed & ei ipsi attributa & effectus adsignet, qui non nisi peccato propriè sic dicto competunt: uti ostensum Articulo præcedente proximo, controversia ultimâ de Concupiscentia. Neque ullius est teruntij, quod excipit Jesuvvita, ad peccatum ac perfectè propriè sic dictum, requiri etiam ut sit voluntarium. Nam 1. definitio Johannitica hoc minimè requirit. Deindè esto, requiratur & istud: Certè pec cata illa etiam leviora renatorum, sedem sua m habent in voluntate vel maximè; ita ut Renatus ex ea parte, quâ veteris hominis reliquias nunquàm non persentiscit, vel ut Apostolus loquitur, Rom 7, 23. secundum legem membrorum, velit id, quod repugnat Legi DEI: cui tamen gratiâ Spiritus sancti, subindè resistit, nè dominium obtineat. Et hoc respectu peccatum Veniale in se consideratum, perfectè est voluntarium: siquidem non nisi in voluntate Hominis sedem suam obtinet; licèt gradu in eo differat à voluntario mortali, quod non pleno animi affectu, aut destinata voluntate committitur à renatis: sicuti committuntur mortalia ab infidelibus. Quæ tamen graduum differentia haud obstat, quo minùs peccatum Veniale, respectu jam notato, sit & dici debeat voluntarium.

Quibus observatis, non stylo, sed pilo tartareo refutanda venit illatio Bellarmini, impiè nimiùm asserentis: Peccatum Veniale ex genere suo, ut verbum otiosum: item ex imperfectione operis: sive ex subreptione, ut desiderium rei illicitæ, non plenè deliberatum: sive ex parvitate materiæ, ut furtum unius oboli, vel alterius rei, vilissimo pretio æstimatæ, non esse perfectè contra Legem. Hoc nimirùm est, os in Cœlum ponere, & uno Obelisco jugulare ac confodere totam Legem DEI, ut quæ 1. peccatum indefinitè definit esse, quicquid est contra Legem DEI, sine ulla determinatione modi. 2. vel levem animi commotionem contrà fratrem: imò expressè verbum otiosum, ac indefinitè rursus omne furtum, omnem Concupiscentiam, etiam in actum externum minimè erumpentem, sub peccati perfectè ac propriè sic dicti, & per consequens sub æternæ damnationis reatum revocat.

Neque enim peccati perfectio æstimanda est ex qualitate facti, si nimirùm peccatum in se, non verò comparatè ad alia peccata, consideratur: sed tantùm ex naturâ Legis divinæ, quæ omnem ἀνομίαν, tam levissimam, quàm maximam, quippè voluntati divinæ contrariam, sub perfecti peccati censum numerúmque venire, satis liquidò attestatur: uti suprà in thesi ex professo fuit ostensum: præsertim cùm Jacobo teste: Qui in uno legem DEI transgreditur; factus sit omnium reus.

Quòd denique subjicit Bellarminus, Peccatum Veniale in renatis non excludere charitatem. Ergò illud non esse contra legem DEI: Sophisticationem committit geminam, unam non causæ: alteram Accidentis: Quòd enim in Renatis cum peccatis venialibus stare potest charitas: id non dependet, ex ipsa natura peccatorum venialium: sed ex Accidente, nempè misericordia DEI, quæ peccatorum illorum reatum tollit.

Verùm de Pontificiorum ac Jesuwitarum cumprimis erroribus, hac vice, plus satis.

Supersunt autem in classe errantium circa doctrinam de discrimine peccati Mortalis & Venialis, tùm Anabaptistæ, tùm Calviniani.

ANABAPTISTÆ enim discrimen peccati in Mortale & Veniale prorsus exploderunt, idq; à Luthero retentum, tanquàm commentum Scholasticorum suggillarunt: pugnantes peccata in uno eodemque hominum genere omnia effe paria: mortalia nempè in non renatis: Venialia autem in renatis.

Hallucinabantur autem turpissimè in eo, quòd existimabant Distinctionem hanc peccati, à Scholasticis demùm fuisse excogitatam, cùm tamen negari haud possit, multò antiquiorem ejus esse usum. Tertullianus certè qui inter Latinos scriptores Ecclesiasticos vetustissimus est, & Scholasticis Doctoribus multò antiquior, hanc ipsam Distinctionem, jam tum usu Ecclesiæ receptam fuisse satis luculenter confirmat, sic scribens in libro de Pudicitia: Quædam peccata sunt capitalia sive mortalia, quædam quotidiana incursationis, quibus omnes ita simus Objecti, ut si nulla sit venia istorum, nemini salus competat. Horum ergò venia erit per exoratorem Christum. Sic Augustinus eandem distinctionem ursit, lib. 2. contrà Julianum. Item lib. de Spiritu & litera, cap. 28. Et epist. 89. licet non utatur termino Mortalis, sed illud nomine Lethale & Capitale.

Cæterùm, si vel maximè absque hac Patrum autoritate esset, sua tamen immota fundamenta Distinctio hæc in Scripturis obtineret. Quid enim aliud dicere voluit Apostolus, asserens. Qui talia agunt digni sunt morte, Rom. 1, 32. Et si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini, Rom. 8, 13. Quàm quædam peccata esse mortalia. Sic David, & Apostolus, Beatum pronunciantes eum, cui iniquitates sunt remissæ, & cujus peccata sunt tecta, Psal. 32, 1. Rom. 4, 7. nihil profectò notare voluerunt aliud, quàm peccata quædam esse Venialia, non quod in se talia sint, sed quòd veniam sint consecuta. Est ergò primus hic Anabaptistarum error crassior, quàm ut prolixiore refutatione indigeat.

Alter eorundem error priore est speciosior: undè hodieque in Ecclesia Calvinianorum applausum manifestum meruit. Contendunt enim & hi, Renatos & Electos non nisi Venialia peccata committere, neq; mortaliter peccare: aut gratiâ DEI excidere posse: adeò ut si vel maximè gravissima scelera atque flagitia designent, tamen non excutiant Spiritum sanctum. Quemadmodum sanè Beza in Colloquio Mömpelgartensi contendit, Davidem perpetrantem adulterium & homicidium, nunquàm tamen amisisse, sed semper retinuisse Spiritum sanctum & fidem. Sic Zanchius in Miscellaneis p. 242. scribit, Remissionem peccatorum semel impetratam, per insequentes lapsus, in sanctis non fieri posse irritam: Sed Spiritum sanctum semel illis datum, manere cum ipsis in æternum. Quin Rennecherus in cat. p 157. & p. 261. scribere non exhorruit, Sæpè complures ex numero electorum esse, qui vitam pessimam ducant: interim tamē eos in sua infirmitate majorem perseverantiam habere, quàm Adam in sua perfectione habuit. Quæ sanè opinio eò unicè tendit, ut discrimen peccati Mortalis & Venialis, prout quidem nostris in Ecclesiis illud asseritur, funditùs subruat & evertat: quemadmodum sanè Beza rursus in eodem colloquio simpliciter noluit permittere, ut nostri distinguerent inter infirmitatis humanæ lapsus, & manifesta scelera contra Legem DEI, quorum illa Venialia, hæc verò Mortalia dicerentur: Quin in has vaces magno impetu erupit: Nullum peccatum est Veniale, sed omnia sunt mortalia: Ideò hæc distinctio peccatorum, tanquam Papistica, hîc locum habere non potest.

Summa caputq́; erroris est: Nulla prorsus in renatis esse peccata Mortalia: sed omnia Venialia: quemadmodum contra non nisi in reprobis sint peccata mortalia: Ita ut non modò non in his, sed nec in illis etiam discrimen hoc peccatorum constitui possit aut debeat. In subsidium autem erroris ea potissimùm Scripturarum testimonia vocare solent, tùm Anabaptistæ, tùm Calviniani, in quibus DEUS promittit se perfecturum in diem usque Christi, opus illud bonum, quod in renatis & Electis cœpit: Phil. 1, 6. neque permissurum, ut justus etiam cadens collidatur: Psalm. 37, 24. ut commoveatur in æternum, qui confidit DOMINO, Psal. 125, 1. ut calamus quassatus conteratur, & linum fumigans extinguatur, Jes. 42, 8. ut in errorem inducantur Electi, Matth. 24, 24. ut quisquam eos rapiat de manu sua, Johan. 10, 28. ut quisquam eos separare possit à dilectione DEI, quæ est in Christo Jesu, Rom. 8, 39.

Verùm refutatur solidissimè hic quoq; error, 1. ostensis illis fundamentis, quibus suprà in parte 1. θέσεως hujus capitis, Discrimen hoc peccati evidentissimè superstruximus. 2. Productis aliis Scripturarum locis, quibus peccata mortalia etiam renatis & Electis, expressis verbis adsignantur: ut Luc. 11, 24. Cùm immundus Spiritus exierit de homine, ambulat per loca arida, quærens requiem, & non inveniens, dicit: Revertar in domum meam undè exivi: & cùm venerit, invenit eam scopis mundatam & ornatam, tunc vadit & assumit septem alios spiritus secum, nequiores se, & ingressi habitant ibi, & tùm fiunt novissima hominis illius pejora primis. Sic DEUS ipse apud Jezechielem affirmat, Justum ita excidere posse justitiâ suâ, ut omnis antegressa justitiæ ipsius nolit ampliùs recordari. Ezech. 18, 24. Sic Rom. 11, 20: inquit Apostolus: Tu fide stas: Ne autem efferaris animo, sed timeas: alioquin & tu excideris. Et in 1. Cor. 9, 27. fatetur, se ideò corpus suum in servitutem redigere, ut ne, cùm alijs prædicaverit, ipse reprobus efficiatur. 3 Notatis præcipuis Sophisticationibus, quibus Scripturæ testimonia in alienum sensum Adversarii per crassam ignorationem Elenchi, & vitiosum consequens: & secundum quid, detorquere solent. Nam primum illud dictum Phil. 1, 6. nihil vult aliud, quàm non modò initium, sed & consummationem fidei ac salutis nostræ, dependere à sola DEI gratia & misericordia: quam usque adeò ex sua parte DEUS velit stare immotam, ut si vel maximè nos ipsos negaverimus, ipse tamen fidelis maneat, & per pœnitentiam redeuntibus, gratiam suam semper velit esse expositam. Sed quid hoc ad præsens negotium? Sic alterum illud dictum Psalmi 37, 24. agit de adversitatibus & ærumnis, quæ interdum, imò frequentiùs pios, quàm impios premere solent. Hæ ergò quantæ quantæ sint, nunquàm tamen de salutis æternæ præsidio ipsos deturbare possunt; siquidem virtute DEI ad salutem custodiuntur, sed non nisi per fidem, 1. Pet. 1, 5. Sic ergò & hoc dictum nihil ad praesentem Rhombum. Sed si fortè verbum (ceciderit) dè lapsu in peccata, accipiendum esse, aliquis contendat, tùm sanè infirmitatis humanae lapsus, & peccata Venialia, notàri statuimus. Nam de reliquis peccatis, quae plena animi deliberatione, ac destinato consilio à Renatis contra conscientiam designantur: longè aliter DEUS ipse statuit, per Prophetam Nathanem ad Davidem dicens: Tu es vir Mortis, 2. Sam. 12, 7.

Sic Psalmus 125, 1. agit de illis, qui & quatenùs confidunt DOMINO. Nam quando hi declinant à recto pietatis tramite, tùm longè aliam ac diversam planè sententiam, fert David eodem Psalmo, versu statim subsequente quinto: Declinantes autem in curvas vias, abducet Dominus cum operantibus iniquitatem.

Reliqua Scripturae testimonia agunt in specie de Electis, quos certum est finaliter nunquàm excidere gratiâ DEI, licèt quamdiu hac in vita militant, saepiùs in gravia ac mortalia peccata prolabi, & gratia DEI totaliter excidere queant: uti alibi συν θεῷ demonstrabitur.

Et sic quidem disputationem hanc de Discrimine peccati Venialis & mortalis expedimus, usum ejus constituentes longè maximum istum, ut nimirùm Renati & fideles in timore DEI ambulent, neque ruant in peccata contra conscientiam, ut seipsos explorent indefinenter, nùm veram habeant fidem; vel saltem nudam ac inanem fidei persuasionem: ut denique in infirmitatibus & lapsibus quotidianis seipsos erigant, consolentur & sustentent: certò statuentes DEUM eos non imputaturum ipsis, propter Christum Mediatorem: ubi tamen magna cautione opus est, ut ne tantò liberius carnis nostrae desideriis indulgeamus. Potest enim Veniale peccatum degenerare in Mortale: imò reverà degenerat, si placere incipiat: uti alicubi loquitur Augustinus.


### Chapter II. Or Corruptions contending with purer doctrine, on the…: III The Distinction of Sin into Remissible and Irremissible, which is and is called the sin against the Holy Spirit

III.

The Distinction of Sin into Remissible and Irremissible, which is and is called the sin against the HOLY SPIRIT.

…A mortal sin, the nature of which we investigated a little earlier, admits a certain subdivision, by which it is divided into two diverse species, namely into Remissible and Irremissible Sin. The foundation of which subdivision the Savior Himself shows, Matt. 12, 31. Every, He says, blasphemy and sin shall be forgiven unto men, but the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven:

And whoever shall speak a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him: but whoever shall speak a word against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this nor in the future age: that is, it shall not be forgiven in eternity, but he shall be guilty of eternal judgment, as Christ himself interprets, Mark 3:28. There is therefore one Mortal sin, which is Blasphemy against the Son of Man, and another, which is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: the former is called Remissible; the latter Irremissible. Whence it is immediately evident that Mortal Sin acts indeed as a Genus to these two distinct species: but that it is not predicated of them univocally: since that former species, if serious repentance intervenes, turns out to be Venial and Remissible: nay, very many of the Saints, such as Aaron, David, Peter, and others, indeed sinned mortally: but they are by no means to be considered to have sinned against the Holy Spirit, for the reason that they obtained Pardon and Remission: which is what is simply denied by Christ to the sin against the Holy Spirit.

However, what and what specifically each of these sins is, because of the various and discrepant opinions of interpreters, would be a little more difficult to define: Now indeed, if truth shines forth more clearly when opposites are placed next to each other; it is certainly pleasing at the beginning to recall the erroneous opinions of both the ancients and the moderns to the anvil of a more accurate censure: then indeed to institute a somewhat more exact collation and Examination of the places of Scripture expressly dealing with these species of sin: and thus to make an approach to defining the Nature and ἴδιον, as it were, the persuasion of each sin.

Latin:

III.

Distinctio Peccati in Remissibile, & Irremissibile, quod est ac dicitur peccatum in SPIRITUM SANCTUM.

PEccatum mortale, cujus naturam paulò antè investigamus, subdivisionem quandam admittit, quâ in duas diversas species, nimirùm in Peccatum Remissibile & Irremissibile dispescitur. Cujus subdivisionis fundamentum monstrat Servator ipse, Matth. 12, 31. Omne, inquiens, convitium & peccatũ remittetur hominibus, at convitium in Spiritum sanctum non remittetur:

Et quicunq; dixerit verbum adversus Filium Hominis remittetur ei: Qui autem dixerit verbum contra Spiritum sanctum, non remittetur ei, neque in hoc neque in futuro seculo: hoc est, in æternum non remittetur, sed reus erit æterni judicij, sic ipso Christo interpretante, Marci 3, 28. Est ergò Mortale peccatum aliud, quod Blasphemia in Filium hominis, aliud quod blasphemia in Spiritum sanctum: illud Remissibile; hoc Irremissibile dicitur. Undè mox constat, Peccatum Mortale habere se quidem tanquàm Genus, ad duas hasce distinctas species: verùm non univocè de illis prædicari: Siquidem prior illa species, si seria interveniat pœnitentia, evadit Venialis & Remissibilis: quin imò Sanctorum benè multi, ut Aaron, David, Petrus & alii mortaliter quidem peccarunt: verùm in Spiritum sanctum peccasse minimè censendi sunt, propterea quòd Veniam ac Remissionem sunt consecuti: id quod peccato in Spiritum sanctum simpliciter à Christo negatur.

Cæterùm Quodnam, & quid propriè utrumque hoc peccatum sit, propter varias ac discrepantes interpretum opiniones, definitu paulò fuerit difficilius: Jam verò si contrariis juxta se positis veritas clariùs elucescat; placet utique initiò erroneas tùm veterum, tùm recentiorum opiniones, sub accuratioris censuræ incudem revocare: deindè verò Locorum Scripturæ de hisce peccati speciebus ex professo agentium collationem atque Examen paulò exactius instituere: & sic ad definiendam utriusque peccati Naturam ac ἴδιον quasi πεῖθὼ accessum facere.


### Chapter I. Or the Removal of false opinions

Ἄρσις. Or the Removal of false opinions.

The first and most ancient opinion of all seems to have been that of Origen, and of a certain Theognostus; who established that the sin against the Holy Spirit is any grave, enormous, and ἀναπολόγητον (inexcusable) transgression committed by a man after having received Baptism and the Holy Spirit.

For thus Origen himself, Tom. 11 of his Works, page 398, says concerning those who have sinned after receiving the Holy Spirit: It has no remission, neither in this age nor in the future: for he blasphemes by the works and words of sin in the present against the Holy Spirit, who sins while the Holy Spirit is present in his soul. For thus someone says that that saying was spoken which is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews (chap. 6): It is difficult for those who were once enlightened, etc. In the progress of time, this opinion provided an opening for the most pernicious dogma of the Novatians, who contended, μετὰ τὸ λῦτρον μηκέτι δυνάασθαι ἐλεεῖ- σθαι τὸν πεπτωκότα (that after the washing one who has fallen can no longer be shown mercy), as Epiphanius testifies, that is, that he who has fallen after the laver of regeneration cannot obtain mercy anymore. But this first error is found to impinge upon the analogy of faith in many ways.

For 1. all the lapses of Christians, especially those more serious ones, such as those of Aaron, David, and Peter, were committed after the reception of the Holy Spirit: yet no one would be so cruel as to dare to affirm that they sinned against the Holy Spirit: especially since Scripture clearly attests that they obtained forgiveness for their offenses. 2. Christ speaks of such a sin against the Holy Spirit, of which the Pharisees were already guilty, who, however, it is certain had neither Baptism nor the Holy Spirit, as far as the ἐνέργειαν τῆς χάριτος present in their soul is concerned. 3. The Apostle himself grants forgiveness of sin to that incestuous Corinthian, who committed this atrocious offense after Baptism but was doing penance, and restores to full standing the one who had been excommunicated for some time: 2 Cor. 2:7 & 8. 4. The same Apostle, Galat. 4:19, asserts that he is in labor with his Galatians as with infants, until CHRIST is formed AGAIN in them: where in the word AGAIN, one may detect the first initiation of the Galatians in the Holy Spirit; and their sad fall, which the Apostle strives to correct: as Athanasius rightly observed long ago, in his Oration to Serapion. Finally, the passage from the Epistle to the Hebrews does not deal with any, even an enormous, offense committed after baptism: but specifically and particularly with that which is called κατ' ἐξοχὴν, the sin against the Holy Spirit, as we shall show below. Now, argumentation does not proceed universally from the species to the genus.

The other opinion is less convenient, that of those Fathers who establish that this sin consists in this, that the Holy Spirit is blasphemed in express words, and His honor is detracted from: whether the name of the Holy Spirit is taken essentially, as it pertains to the whole Trinity: or notionally, or, as we say, personally, as it pertains to the third person alone in the divine. That Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, and Chrysostom did not abhor this opinion is attested by their own expositions on the words of Christ, Matt. 12, already proposed above. The error of this opinion is easily detected even from the fact that in this way every blasphemy against GOD, one and three, and uttered by anyone, would be a sin against the Holy Spirit: which is diametrically opposed to the words of Christ: as He Himself clearly distinguishes between blasphemy against the Son of Man and that which is designated against the Holy Spirit, pronouncing the former Remissible, the latter Irremissible.

What of the fact that the Lord Apostle expressly confesses that he indeed had been a blasphemer against GOD: but yet that he had obtained mercy: because he did that in ignorance in unbelief, 1 Timoth. 1:13. This cannot be affirmed of the sin against the Holy Spirit: since it does not obtain mercy. Therefore, even though blasphemy has a great kinship with the sin against the Holy Spirit: so that for the most part the destruction of eternal death draws with it: yet the terms are not convertible: but reciprocal only in one part of themselves: so that while every sin against the Holy Spirit is indeed blasphemy: yet not conversely, is every blasphemy a sin against the Holy Spirit. Gregory of Valencia therefore reveals remarkable ignorance, Tom. III. disp. 1. Quæst. 14. point 1. p. 557. A. asserting that this opinion of the Fathers is very agreeable to the Evangelical text. We certainly, just as we have now proven the contrary, do not allow ourselves to be bound in this matter by the authority of either the Jesuit or Thomas, whom he himself cites.

The third opinion is that of St. Augustine, who in Sermon 11 on the Words of the Lord, says that sin or blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is final impenitence: when, namely, someone persists in mortal sin of mouth, heart, and deed until death: as Thomas explains his mind, in the second part of the second book, question 14. Although Augustine himself in his book on Correction and Grace, chapter 12, explains himself thus, that sin against the Holy Spirit is an obstinate persistence until death, with a distrust of pardon.

Although indeed this final impenitence is an individual παρεπόμενον or Adjunct of the sin against the Holy Spirit, so that the latter is always joined with the former: yet they do not behave reciprocally. For final impenitence is given even in those who sin against the Son of Man: such as was in Saul, Absalom, and others, who died in final impenitence, whom, however, no sane person would affirm to have committed the sin against the Holy Spirit, so called κατ' ἐξοχὴν. Final impenitence therefore extends itself more widely than the sin against the Holy Spirit.

Then Gregory of Valencia rightly notes in this place that final impenitence is not properly, nor is it called, blasphemy: such as the sin against the Holy Spirit ought to be: but only extensively, no otherwise than other sins, insofar as they are in themselves repugnant to divine honor, and can be improperly and generally called blasphemies. For just as on the contrary, any good work, insofar as it pertains to divine glory, can be extensively and less properly called a certain confession of faith: so by the same reasoning any sin can be improperly called blasphemy. But the sin against the Holy Spirit must be defined by blasphemy most properly and most specially so called, as will appear a little later. 3. Finally, the sin against the Holy Spirit consists of one certain species of sin. But the definition of Augustine applies to all sins whatsoever, insofar as they can be with final perseverance in evil: which is nothing other than a certain mode or general condition of all sins, with which one departs from life. Therefore.

The fourth opinion is that of the Scholastics, who, with Thomas defining it, establish that the sin against the Holy Spirit is committed when someone sins against his appropriated good. For because goodness is appropriated to the Holy Spirit: power to the Father: wisdom to the Son: therefore they say that sin against the Father is committed when one sins out of infirmity. Against the Son, however, when one sins out of ignorance: finally against the Holy Spirit, when one sins out of certain malice, that is, out of the choice of evil, as when malice pleases for its own sake: which happens, 1. from the inclination of a vicious habit: where however it is not the same to sin out of malice as to sin against the Holy Spirit: but a certain general condition of sin is noted. 2. Then indeed it happens from this, when through contempt someone casts off and removes that by which he could have hindered the choice of sin, as if someone through contempt should cast off hope and trust, by which he could have resisted despair: or fear, by which he could have resisted presumption. But all these things, which hinder the choice of sin, are effects of the Holy Spirit in us: and therefore to sin thus out of malice is to sin against the Holy Spirit. The Master of the Sentences also held and approved this opinion, book 2, d. 43, who interprets the sin against the Holy Spirit as a sin in which a certain malice is peculiarly discerned, not indeed consisting in this, that one out of habit, or even prudently and knowingly chooses a thing which he sees to be evil: but in this, that by a certain peculiar consent he casts off and spurns those things by which men are wont to be retarded from sin, such as are the Gifts of GOD, which because they are peculiarly attributed to the Holy Spirit: therefore that sin is said to be peculiarly against the Holy Spirit.

These general hypotheses having been thus premised, both finally conclude that six distinct species of sin against the Holy Spirit can be given: namely 1. Despair, which casts off divine mercy: 2. Presumption, which casts off the justice of GOD: 3. Impugnation of the acknowledged truth, which casts off the knowledge of true faith, and what he sees to be true, he attempts to prove and persuade to be false. 4. Envy of fraternal grace, which indeed grieves if the grace of GOD, by which sins are extirpated, is communicated also to others. 5. Impenitence, which indeed is joined with a certain peculiar purpose of not repenting: by which very thing the Grace and kindness of GOD inviting sinners to repentance is cast off. 6. Finally Obstinacy, in purpose, which consists in a certain will of adhering to sin, insofar as it contains some reason of a delightful or useful good, notwithstanding that this good is brief and of small moment: by which very thing greater spiritual goods are rejected. And this indeed was the doctrine of the Scholastic Theologians concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit, certainly erroneous and vicious in many respects, however much Gregory of Valencia may strive to color and palliate it.

For 1. these sins, each and every one, in whatever way they may be designated as proceeding from malice, do not yet constitute that peculiar species of Blasphemy by which Holy Scripture demonstrates that the sin against the Holy Spirit is to be defined properly and according to specific difference: as will be shown presently in the thesis. Then, the sin against the Holy Spirit consists of a single simple species, as Scripture defines it.
