Thirdly, the species already enumerated by the Scholastics, with the exception of final Despair, can obtain pardon and remission in this life: But the sin against the Holy Spirit is such that it is not remitted either in this age or in the future, that is, never for eternity.

Fourthly: The Savior establishes such a species of sin against the Holy Spirit as can be committed in this life. But now, Final Impenitence, Obstinacy, and Despair are not committed unless one perseveres in them unto death: Therefore. Finally, Bellarmine himself seems to have acknowledged the weakness of this dogma when he writes in Vol. 2 of his Controversies, page 1527: Not every sin arising from malice is that of which the scriptures speak, which is properly and singularly called the sin against the Holy Spirit: and which is not forgiven, either in this or in the future age. Although, indeed, Augustine also at one time determined that he who envies the grace bestowed upon a brother sins against the Holy Spirit (Book 1, On the Lord's Sermon on the Mount, ch. 43), yet he himself later acknowledged that this opinion departs as far as possible from the words and scope of Christ: nay, he did not hesitate to publicly retract it: Book 1, Retractations, ch. 19.

The fifth opinion is that of the Romanists, and especially of P. Canisius, who in his Catechetical Institution, in the Article on the Sin against the Holy Spirit, did not hesitate to write: A species of sin against the Holy Spirit was indeed noted by Christ: but its form was not expressed. This sufficiently impious opinion is held also by some other Theologian, writing thus in his workshop, page 488: There is also this demonstration from the saying of Christ, that our judgment fails, since the Lord has not expressed the form of this sin. This sin is named blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: But blasphemy is put forward as Remissible: it is not blasphemy unless it is against GOD: and nothing is committed against GOD unless the same is sinned against the Holy Spirit: Therefore, neither blasphemy, nor the notation of the Holy Spirit, provides us with the form of this irremissible sin to be recognized. Wherefore it cannot be judged by us specifically. But what is this other than to look for a knot in a bulrush, and to involve a most manifest text in obscurities quite petulantly. For does not the text demonstrate and define this species of sin and its form clearly enough, provided that you weigh a little more accurately the scope of Christ's words, which was directly opposed to the impiety and contumacy of the Pharisees: as will be demonstrated presently.

The sixth opinion is that of the Blessed Jerome, who in his Epistle to Marcella, concerning blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, has it thus: Novatian is to be convinced from the whole order of Scripture, that this blasphemy is not called irremissible for those who, compelled by torments and eviscerated by various tortures, had denied the Lord: but for those who, when they see the works of GOD in his mighty works, slander them, and cry out that it is the work of a demon: and that all the signs which were done do not pertain to divine magnificence, but to the devil. And after a few words: Let Novatian therefore prove that any of those who were compelled to sacrifice answered before the tribunal of the judge that all things which are written in the Gospel were not performed by the Son of GOD, but by Beelzebub the prince of demons: and then he will be able to prove that the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is irremissible. The sum of Jerome's opinion seems to return to this, that he is to be said to sin against the Holy Spirit who, having been set before the tribunal of the Judge, not only denies Christ: but also says that he is Beelzebub. And although this denial of CHRIST is a perpetual occasion of the sin against the Holy Spirit: yet the opinion of Jerome fails in this, that it determines that this sin is not committed by men of their own accord, spontaneously and voluntarily, but only by those who have been set before the tribunal of the Judge: which is diametrically opposed to the nature of this sin.

The seventh is that of those who determine that this sin is to be defined by the denial of the recognized Evangelical Truth. But indeed, if this opinion prevails, it would be necessary to relegate the Apostle Peter, who denied CHRIST three times, to hell: whom, however, Scripture clearly testifies obtained pardon and was converted to Christ again. Thus, all those would have to be adjudged to the infernal flames who, in the primitive Church, while those most grievous persecutions lasted, terrified by the atrocity of the punishments, out of weakness denied the recognized truth of the heavenly doctrine: yet ecclesiastical history testifies everywhere that many of them, having performed serious repentance, were received into the communion of the Church with no less joy than the consent of the rest of the faithful. Therefore, Francesco Spiera of Cittadella falsely persuaded himself that he had committed the sin against the Holy Spirit, and therefore could no longer obtain pardon, because at Venice, before the Legate of the Pope, struck by a certain terror, he had denied and retracted the recognized truth.

The eighth is of those who even today keep saying that the sin against the Holy Spirit must be described solely by Unbelief. Although we do not deny that those who persevere in Unbelief are subject to the eternal punishment of hell: John 3:18, Mark 16:16. It is certain, however, that many, having cast off Unbelief, return to Christ through faith and become partakers of eternal blessedness: a fact which is evidently confirmed by the example of the Apostle Paul. But that those who have committed the sin against the Holy Spirit should be enlightened and saved again: this, indeed, Scripture pronounces to be simply impossible. Therefore, although Unbelief is joined by an individual bond to the sin against the Holy Spirit, it does not yet fully complete or constitute its nature and essence.

Ninthly and lastly, they define the sin against the Holy Spirit most viciously who, carried away by some more vehement Zeal, are accustomed sometimes in sermons to the people to amplify and exaggerate those graver crimes and outrages which publicly prevail to such a degree that they do not hesitate in the least to refer them to the census and number of the sin against the Holy Spirit. Whose zeal, indeed, although it deserves praise for the fact that it strives to kindle a desire for repentance in the hearers, nevertheless, with respect to the danger which can sometimes arise from it in the consciences of the weaker, certainly incurs the gravest censure: so that such license in the heralds of the Word can neither be tolerated nor ought to be.

For the sentence of the Savior, once pronounced concerning this sin, namely that it is irremissible, is never changed. Indeed, it is utterly impossible that he who sins in this way should be enlightened again: certainly the sinful man is easily cast into infinite and inextricable straits, nay, into an abyss of despair, if he hears that this or that sin or crime committed by him is the sin against the Holy Spirit. Whereupon such a minister will afterwards find it necessary either to revoke what he has basely said, or will lose all his pains and effort in trying to raise up such a troubled man. There will therefore be need of great circumspection and prudence if words are to be spoken publicly from the pulpit concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit. But the genuine and Orthodox doctrine concerning this sin, which the second chapter in the Thesis will now explain according to the scriptures, shows that [prudence].

Latin:

Ἄρσις. Sive Remotio falsarum opinionum.

PRima ac omnium antiquissima sententia videtur fuisse Origenis, & cujusdam Theognosti; qui statuerunt, Peccatum in Spiritum sanctum esse quodcunque grave, enorme ac ἀναπολόγητον delictum, post perceptum Baptismum ac Spiritum sanctum, ab homine perpetratum.

Sic enim ipse Origenes, Tom. 11. Operum: pag. 398. De his, qui post acceptum Spiritum sanctum peccaverint, dicitur: Non habet remissionem, neq; in hoc seculo, neq; in futuro: Blasphemat enim operibus & Sermonibus peccati in præsens in Spiritum sanctum, qui peccat Spiritu sancto præsente in ejus anima. Sic enim dicit aliquis, dictum illud fuisse, quod in epistola ad Hebræos scriptum est: (cap. 6.) Difficile factu est, ut qui semel illuminati fuerint &c. Ansam præbuit progressu temporis hæc opinio perniciosissimo dogmati Novatianorum, contendentium, μετὰ τὸ λῦτρον μηκέτι δυνάασθαι ἐλεεῖσθαι τὸν πεπτωκότα, teste Epiphanio, hoc est, qui post lavacrum regenerationis lapsus fuerit, eum non posse amplius misericordiam consequi. Verùm primus iste error multis modis in analogiam fidei impingere deprehenditur.

Nam 1. omnes Christianorum lapsus, præsertim graviores illi, quales fuerunt Aaronis, Davidis, Petri, commissi sunt post perceptum Spiritum sanctum: ubi tamen nemo ita crudelis fuerit, qui in Spiritum sanctum eos peccasse, affirmare ausit: præsertim cùm Scriptura luculenter attestetur, veniam eos delictorum consecutos fuisse. 2. Christus de tali peccato in Spiritum sanctum loquitur, cujus jam rei essent Pharisæi, quos tamen neque Baptismum, neque Spiritum sanctum, quoad ἐνέργειαν τῆς χάριτος præsentem in anima sua habuisse, certum est. 3. Apostolus ipse incestuoso illi Corinthio, post Baptismum atrox hoc delictum committenti, sed agenti pœnitentiam, veniam peccati indulget, & aliquandiu excommunicatum in integrum restituit: 2. Cor. 2, 7. & 8. 4. Idem Apostolus, Galat. 4, 19. asserit, se Galatas suos parturire tanquàm infantes, donec ITERUM formetur CHRISTUS in ipfis: ubi in vocabulo ITERUM, deprehendere licèt primam Galatarum in Spiritu sancto initiationem; tristemq; eorum prolapsum, quem corrigere studet Apostolus: uti rectè observavit jam olim Athanasius, in Oratione ad Serapionem. Tandem locus ex Epistola ad Hebræos non agit de quovis, etiam enormi delicto, post baptismum designato: sed in specie & peculiariter de eo, quod κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicitur, peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, ut infrà ostendemus. Jam à specie ad Genus, universaliter non procedit argumentatio.

Altera Sententia minùs commoda est eorum Patrum, qui statuunt, peccatum hoc consistere in hoc, ut disertis verbis blasphemetur Spiritus sanctus, ipsiusq; honori detrahatur: sive nomen Spiritus sancti accipiatur essentialiter, prout competit toti Trinitati: sivè notionaliter, vel, uti nos loquimur, personaliter, prout soli tertiæ personæ in divinis com petit. Ab hac sententia non abhorruisse Hilarium, Ambrosium, Hieronymum, Chrysostomum: ipsorum attestantur expositiones de Verbis Christi, Matth. 12. jam supra propositis. Cujus sententiæ error vel inde facilè deprehenditur, quod hoc pacto omnis blasphemia in DEUM unum & trinum; & à quocunq; prolata, esset peccatum in Spiritum sanctum: id quod cum Verbis Christi è diametro pugnat: ut qui inter blasphemiam in Filium Hominis, & inter eam, quæ in Spiritum sanctum designatur, ipsemet luculenter distinguit, illam Remissibilem, Hanc Irremissibilem pronuncians.

Quid quòd D. Apostolus disertè fatetur, se quidem blasphemum fuisse in DEUM: sed tamen misericordiam consecutū esse: eò quòd ignorans istud fecerit in incredulitate, 1. Timoth. 1, 13. Id quod de peccato in Spiritum sanctum affirmari nequit: quippè quòd misericordiam non consequitur. Proindè etiamsi blasphemia magnam cognationem habet cum peccato in Spiritum sanctum: ita ut plerumque æternæ mortis exitium secum trahat: non tamen termini sunt convertibiles: sed una tantùm sui parte reciproci: ita ut omne quidem peccatum in Spiritum sanctum sit blasphemia: non tamen vice versa, omnis blasphemia sit peccatum in Spiritum sanctum. Insignem ergo inscitiam prodit Gregorius de Valentia. Tom. III. disp. 1. Quæst. 14. puncto 1. p. 557. A. asserens, Sententiam hanc Patrum, valdè consentaneam esse textui Evangelico. Nos sanè uti diversum jam modò evicimus: ita neque Jesuitæ, neque Thomæ, quem ipse citat, autoritate, hac in parte nos teneri permittimus.

Tertia sententia est D. Augustini, qui Serm. 11. de Verbis Domini, Peccatum vel blasphemiam in Spiritum sanctum dicit, esse finalem impœnitētiam: quando scilicet aliquis, in peccato mortali oris, cordis & operis usque ad mortem perseverat: uti mentem ejus explicat, Thomas, secunda secundæ quæst. 14. Quanquàm Augustinus ipse lib. de corrept. & grat. cap. 12. sic se explicat, quòd peccatum in Spiritum sanctum sit obstinata ad mortem usque pertinacia, cum veniæ diffidentia.

Quanquàm verò finalis hæc impœnitentia individuum est παρεπόμενον sive Adjunctum peccati in Spiritum sanctum, ita ut hoc semper sit cum illa conjunctum: interim tamen reciprocè se non habent. Datur enim finalis Impœnitentia in iis etiam, qui peccant in Filium Hominis: Qualis fuit in Saule, Absolone & aliis, qui in finali impœnitentia decesserunt, quos tamen peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, κατ' ἐξοχὴν sic dictum, commisisse, nemo sanus affirmaverit. Latiùs ergò se extendit Finalis Impœnitentia, quàm peccatum in Spiritum sanctum.

Deindè rectè hoc loco annotat Gregorius de Valentia, Finalem Impœnitentiam propriè non esse neque dici Blasphemiam: qualis esse debet peccatum in Spiritum sanctum: sed tantùm extensivè, haud aliter atq; alia peccata, quatenùs illa per se repugnant divino honori, ac impropriè & generaliter dici possunt blasphemiæ. Quemadmodum enim è contrario, quodlibet bonum opus, quatenùs pertinet ad divinam gloriam, potest extensivè minusque propriè dici confessio quædam fidei: sic eadem ratione quodlibet peccatum potest impropriè dici blasphemia. Atqui peccatum in Spiritum sanctum definiri debet per blasphemiam propriissimè & specialissimè sic dictam, uti paulò pòst patebit. 3. Tandem peccatum in Spiritum sanctum constat una certa specie peccati. Atqui definitio Augustini competit omnibus omninò peccatis, quatenùs possunt esse cum perseverantia finali in malo: Quæ nihil aliud est, quàm modus quidam seu conditio generalis omnium peccatorum, cum quibus quis è vitâ excedit. Ergo.

Quarta sententia est Scholasticorum, qui definiente Thoma, statuunt, Peccatum in Spiritum sanctum committi, quando aliquis peccat contra appropriatum ejus bonum. Quia enim Spiritui sancto appropriatur bonitas: Patri potentia: Filio sapientia: ideò peccatum in Patrem dicunt committi, cùm ex infirmitate peccatur. In Filium verò, cùm peccatur ex ignorantia: In Spiritum sanctum denig, cùm peccatur ex certa malitia, hoc est, ex Electione mali, ut cùm malitia per se placet: id quod fit, 1. ex inclinatione habitus vitiosi: ubi tamen non est idem peccare ex malitia, quod peccare in Spiritum sanctum: sed notatur quædam generalis conditio peccati. 2. Deindè verò contingit ex eo, quando per comtemtum aliquis abjicit & removet id, per quod Electionem peccati poterat impedire, ut si quis per comtemtum abjiciat spem ac fiduciam, quâ desperationi: vel Timorem, quo præsumtioni resistere potuisset. Hæc autem omnia, quæ peccati Electionem impediunt, sunt effectus Spiritus sancti in nobis: & ideò sic peccare ex malitia est in Spiritum sanctum peccare. Tenuit & approbavit hanc sententiam etiam Magister sententiarum, lib. 2. d. 43. qui Peccatum in Spiritum sanctum interpretatur peccatum, in quo peculiariter cernitur quædam malitia, non quidem consistens in eo, ut quis ex habitu, vel etiam prudens ac sciens eligat rem, quam videt esse malam: sed in eo, ut peculiari quodam consensu abjiciat atq; aspernetur ea, quibus solent homines retardari à peccato, ut sunt Dona DEI, quæ quoniam peculiariter attribuuntur Spiritui sancto: ideò istud peccatum dicitur esse peculiariter in Spiritum sanctum.

His generalibus quasi hypothesibus ita præmissis, concludit tandem uterque sex distinctas species peccati in Spiritum sanctum dari posse: nempè 1. Desperationem, quæ abjiciat divinam misericordiam: : 2. Præsumptionem, quæ abjiciat DEI justitiam: 3. Impugnationem veritatis agnitæ, quæ abjiciat cognitionem veræ fidei, & quod videt esse verum, conetur probare & persuadere esse falsum. 4. Invidentiam fraternæ gratiæ, quæ nimirùm doleat, si gratia DEI, per quam extirpantur peccata, communicetur etiam alijs. 5. Impœnitentiam, quæ nimirùm conjuncta sit cùm peculiari quodam proposito non pœnitendi: quo ipso abjicitur Gratia & benignitas DEI ad pœnitentiam peccatores invitans. 6. Tandem Obstinationem, in proposito, quæ consistat in quadam voluntate adhærendi peccato, quatenùs aliquam rationem boni delectabilis vel utilis continet, non obstante, quòd id bonum sit breve & parvi momenti: quo ipso respuuntur majora bona spiritualia. Et hæc quidem Scholasticorum Theologorum de peccato in Spiritum sanctum fuit doctrina, multis certè nominibus erronea & vitiosa, quantumvis etiam Gregorius de Valentia eam fucare & palliare studeat.

Nam 1. peccata hæc singula atque universa, quocunq; modo ex malitia designentur, nondum tamen peculiarem eam constituunt Blasphemiæ speciem, quâ Scriptura Sacra Peccatum in Spiritum sanctum; propriè & secundùm differentiam specificam definiendam esse, demonstrat: ut mox in thesi ostendetur. Deindè peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, constat unica specie simplici, sic definiente Scriptura. Tertiò species jam à Scholasticis enumeratæ, exceptâ Desperatione finiali, veniam ac remissionem hac in vita consequi possunt: Atqui peccatum in Spiritum sanctum tale est, ut neque in hoc, neque in futuro seculo, hoc est, nunquàm in æternum remittatur.

Quartò: Peccati in Spiritum sanctum talem speciem constituit Servator, quæ hac in vita committi possit. Jam verò Finalis Impœnitentia, Obstinatio, Desperatio non committuntur, nisi ad mortem in illis perseveretur: Ergo. Tandem Bellarminus ipse infirmitatem hujus dogmatis agnovisse videtur, cùm scribit Tom. 2. Controversiarum pag. 1527. Non quodlibet peccatum ex malitia esse illud, de quo scripturæ loquuntur, quòd propriè & singulariter dicitur peccatum in Spiritum sanctum: & quod non remittitur, vel in hoc, vel in futuro seculo. Quanquàm verò Augustinus quoque aliquando statuit, peccare in Spiritum sanctum eum, qui Gratiæ in fratrem collatæ invidet. lib. 1. de Sermone Domini in monte, cap. 43. tamen ipse postmodùm agnovit sententiam hanc à Verbis & Scopo Christi quàm longissimè recedere: quin & publicè eam revocare non dubitavit: lib. 1. Retractat. cap. 19.

Quinta sententia est Romanensium, & cumprimis P. Canisii, qui in Institutione catechetica, Articulo de Peccato in Spiritum sanctum, scribere non dubitavit: Certi quidem peccati in Spiritum sanctum speciem à Christo esse notatam: sed formam ejus non expressam esse. Quam satis impiam opinionem tenet etiam alius quispiam Theologus, sic in sua officina, pag 488. scribens: Est etiam hæc ex dicto Christi demonstratio, quòd judicium nostrum fallat, cùm formam hujus peccati Dominus no expresserit. Nominatur hoc peccatum blasphemia in Spiritum sanctum: Blasphemia autem præmittitur Remissibilis: non est blasphemia nisi in DEUM: nihilq; in DEUM committitur, nisi eodem in Spiritum sanctum peccetur: Ergo nec blasphemia, nec Spiritus sancti notatio, formam hujus irremissibilis peccati nobis præbet agnoscendam. Quamobrem speciatim à nobis judicari non potest. Sed quid hoc est aliud, quàm nodum in scirpo quærere, & textum manifestissimum obscuritatibus satis petulanter involvere. An non enim speciem hanc peccati ejusq; formam satis liquidò textus demonstrat ac definit, dummodò scopum verborum Christi, qui Pharisæorum impietati & contumaciæ directè erat oppositus, paulò accuratiùs expendas: uti mox demonstrabitur.

Sexta sententia est B. Hieronymi, qui in Epistola ad Marcellam, de blasphemia in Spiritum sanctum, sic habet: De toto Scripturæ ordine convincendus est Novatianus, non his irremissibilem esse dictam blasphemiam, qui tormentis compulsi, & varijs eviscerati cruciatibus, dominum denegassent: sed his, qui cùm in virtutibus videant opera DEI, calumniētur, & clamitent, dæmonis esse virtutem: & omnia signa, quæ facta sunt, non ad divinam magnificentiam, sed ad diabolum pertinere. Et post pauca: probet itaq; Novatianus aliquem de his, qui sacrificare compulsi sunt, ante tribunal judicis respondisse, omnia quæ in Evangelio scripta sunt, non à Filio DEI, sed à Beelzebub principe dæmoniorum fuisse perfecta: & tunc poterit approbare irremissibilem in Spiritum sanctum esse blasphemiam. Summa Sententiæ Hieronymi eò redire videtur, ut in Spiritum sanctum peccare dicendus sit, qui ante tribunal Judicis constitutus, non solùm Christum neget: sed eum etiam dicat esse Beelzebub. Etsi verò abnegatio hæc CHRISTI perpetuum est παροχόμενον peccati in Spiritum sanctum: in eo tamen Sententia Hieronymi deficit, quod statuit, Peccatum hoc non ultrò, spontè & voluntariè ab hominibus, sed iis demùm, qui coram tribunali Judicis constituti sunt, committi: id quod cum naturâ peccati hujus è diametro pugnat.

Septima est eorum, qui peccatum hoc per abnegationem Veritatis Evangelicæ agnitæ, definiendum esse statuunt. Atqui verò hac obtinente sententia, Petrum Apostolum ter abnegantem CHRISTUM ad orcum relegemus, necesse foret: quem tamèn veniam consecutum, & ad Christum denuò conversum fuisse, Scriptura luculenter testatur. Sic omnibus illi flammis infernalibus adjudicandi essent, qui in primitiva Ecclesia, durantibus gravissimis illis persecutionibus, suppliciorum atrocitate perterriti, ex infirmitate, agnitam doctrinæ cœlestis veritatem abnegârunt: Quorum tamen plurimos seriâ actâ pœnitentia, non minore cum gaudio, quàm consensu reliquorum fidelium, in Ecclesiæ communionem receptos esse, passim Ecclesiastica testatur historia. Proindè falsò sibi ipsi persuasit Franciscus Spiera Civitatulanus, se peccatum in Spiritum sanctum commisisse, ac proindè veniam ampliùs consequi non posse, eò quòd Venetiis coram Legato Pontificis, veritatem agnitam terrore quodam perculsus abnegasset, & revocasset.

Octava est eorum, qui peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, sola Incredulitate describendum esse, hodieque dictitant. Quanquàm verò non negamus, in Incredulitate perseverantes, æterno inferorum subjacere supplicio: Johan. 3, 18. Marc. 16, 16. Constat tamen multos abjecta Incredulitate, per fidem redire ad Christum, & æternæ beatitudinis evadere participes: id quod Exemplo Pauli Apostoli evidenter constat. Arqui ut, qui peccatum in Spiritum sanctum commiserunt, denuò illuminentur & salventur: id verò Scriptura simpliciter impossibile esse pronunciat. Ergo licet Incredulitas, individuo nexu cum peccato in Spiritum sanctum sit conjuncta: nondùm tamen ejus naturam & essentiam plenè perficit aut absolvit.

Nonò & postremò vitiosissimè definiunt peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, qui vehementiore aliquo Zelo abrepti, interdum pro concionibus ad populum, graviora illa scelera atq; flagitia, quæ publicè grassantur usque adeò amplificare & exaggerare solent, ut in censum numerumq; peccati in Spiritum sanctum ea referre minimè dubitent. Quorum sanè Zelus, etsi ex eo laudem meretur, quod studium pœnitentiæ in Auditoribus accendere studet: respectu tamen periculi, quod aliquando in conscientiis infirmiorum inde oboriri potest, reprehensionem certè gravissimam incurrit: ita ut talis licentia in Verbi præconibus tolerari neque possit neque debeat.

Quia enim sententia Servatoris, de hoc peccato semel lata, quòd nimirùm illud sit irremissibile, nunquàm mutatur. Imò prorsus impossibile est, ut qui sic peccat, rursus illuminetur: certè facilè in infinitas ac inextricabiles angustias, imò desperationis abyssum Homo peccator conjicitur: si audiat hoc vel illud peccatum, aut scelus à se commissum, esse peccatum in Spiritum sanctum. Ubi postmodùm talis minister vel turpiter à se dicta revocare necesse habebit: vel in tali perturbato homine erigendo, omnem operam ac oleum perdet. Magna proindè circumspectione ac prudentia opus fuerit, si publicè pro suggestu de peccato in Spiritum sanctum verba fieri debeant. Eam verò monstrat genuina ac Orthodoxa de hoc peccato doctrina, quam alterum nunc caput in Thesi, secundum scripturas expediet.


### Chapter II. Or a purer doctrine about the sin against the Holy Spirit

St. Augustine rightly established long ago in book 1 of his Retractations, chapter 19, that the sin against the Holy Spirit must never be judged otherwise than a posteriori. But it is then rightly judged a posteriori if one weighs more accurately not what is agreeable to human reason, or in any way probable, but what both Holy Scripture and the analogy of faith admit. Mindful of this rule, we maintain that this chapter of the Christian religion can hardly be explained more conveniently than if we first premise certain general Hypotheses, drawn from the analogy of faith; afterwards, however, elicit the proper and genuine properties of this sin from the Scriptures themselves; and finally, pass an absolutely infallible judgment concerning its Nature and its proper affection.

I. First, therefore, regarding those Hypotheses, it must be observed at the outset that some sins regard the life and morals of men as their object, while others regard doctrine, or Faith. Those which concern life and morals regard only the Decalogue or the moral Law; and from this they are either Venial or mortal. Venial, if the sinning person returns to CHRIST the Mediator through true repentance; but mortal, if he perseveres in final impenitence. Both, therefore, are so constituted that they cannot be called irremissible in the same way and respect in which the sin against the Holy Spirit is said to be such. For although mortal sins can also be called irremissible in the sense that those who are finally impenitent obtain no remission of sins, yet this happens relatively, not so much by reason of the sin considered in itself, as by reason of the person sinning. But now the Savior so distinguishes the sin against the Holy Spirit from the sin against the Son of Man, that He pronounces the latter to be Remissible, but the former to be simply Irremissible: as much by reason of the power as by reason of the act, as will be shown a little later. It is therefore evident from this first hypothesis that the sin against the Holy Spirit does not regard the morals or life of a man as its object; so that no corruption of life and morals, however great it may be, can be given that falls under the definition of this sin. But just as this first Hypothesis can, and indeed ought to be, a remedy for the penitent against the danger of despair, so it by no means grants license to sin to the impenitent and stubborn despisers, because any mortal sins whatsoever contract the guilt of eternal damnation if repentance is not performed: and indeed not so much a late repentance as a true one: For He who promised grace to the penitent, did not promise tomorrow to the stubbornly impenitent: as Augustine is said to have stated.

II. Hypothesis. Sins which concern the Christian doctrine or Religion are of two kinds: for some are directed against the doctrine of the Law, while others are directed against the doctrine of the Gospel. But now the sin against the Holy Spirit regards only the doctrine of the Gospel or of grace as its object, as the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10, 28 and 29, attests: He who has despised the Law of Moses dies without mercy under two or three witnesses: of how much worse punishment, do you think, will he be thought worthy, who has trampled underfoot the Son of GOD, and has counted the blood of the Covenant as a profane thing, by which he was sanctified, and has insulted the SPIRIT OF GRACE. And in the preceding verse 16: If we sin willfully after having received the knowledge of the Truth, there is no longer any sacrifice left for sins. We conclude, therefore, that sins which impinge upon the doctrine of the Law do not properly pertain to the present dispute. For although it is possible that even with respect to the law, not indeed in morals, but in doctrine, such a sin might be committed that approaches most closely to the Nature of the sin against the Holy Spirit: as if someone in an article concerning the Law should defend some error against his conscience, and should knowingly and willingly condemn and persecute the contrary opinion, which he does not ignore to be most true, and which he hates with deliberate malice; yet because Holy Scripture constitutes nothing as the proper and adequate object of the sin against the Holy Spirit except the acknowledged truth of the Evangelical Doctrine, it is a matter of religious duty for us not to extend it more widely: meanwhile, we will not stubbornly resist those who might wish to recall errors impinging upon the doctrine of the Law, and asserted contumaciously in the manner already noted, under the definition and complex of the sin against the Holy Spirit: although with respect to the Scriptures that treat of this sin expressly, it must be maintained that this is done less properly and less principally.

III. Hypothesis: Sins which impinge directly and principally upon the doctrine of the Gospel are, again, according to the testimony of Scripture, of two kinds: for one is that which is called the Sin against the Son of Man: but the other is that which is called the Sin against the Holy Spirit. What the former is and of what kind, then finally

It will be established beyond doubt: if first it is exactly established what the sin against the Holy Spirit is, and how it is committed. But this will never be investigated more correctly than if, in the second place, we thoroughly weigh the προσκείμενα and requirements of this sin, and indeed those expressed by the oracles of the Scriptures.

Latin:

REctè jam olim statuit D. Augustinus lib. 1. Retract. cap. 19. De Peccato in Spiritum sanctum, nunquàm aliter, quam à posteriori judicandum esse. A posteriori autem tùm rectè judicatur, si non quid humanæ rationi sit consentaneum, vel quocunque modo probabile: sed quid tùm Scriptura Sacra, tùm analogia fidei admittat, accuratiùs pensitetur. Regulæ hujus memores, caput hoc Religionis Christianæ vix commodiùs explicari posse statuimus: quàm si initiò generales quasdam Hypotheses, ex analogia fidei decerptas, præmittamus: postmodùm verò propria & γνήσια προσκείμενα peccati hujus, ex Scripturis ipsis eliciamus: ac tandem de Natura, & propria ejus affectione, judicium feramus prorsus infallibile.

I. Primùm igitur, quoad Hypotheses illas, observandum initiò, Peccata alia Objecti loco respicere vitam moresque hominum: alia verò doctrinam, sive Fidem. Quæ vitam moresque concernunt, illa tantùm Decalogum sive Legem moralem respiciunt: ac exindè vel Venialia sunt, vel mortalia. Venialia si persona peccans per veram pœnitentiam redeat ad CHRISTUM Mediatorem: Mortalia verò, si in finali impœnitentia perseveret. Utraque ergò ita sunt comparata, ut eo modo ac respectu, irremissibilia dici nequeant, quo peccatum in Spiritum sanctum tale esse dicitur. Etsi enim peccata Mortalia dici etiam possunt Irremissibilia eo sensu, quo finaliter impœnitentes remissionem peccatorum nullam consequuntur: tamen hoc fit secundum quid, non tam ratione peccati in se considerati, quàm ratione personæ peccantis. Jam verò Servator peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, ita adverfus peccatum in Filium Hominis contradistinguit, ut hoc Remissibile: illud verò simpliciter Irremissibile esse pronunciet: tam ratione potentiæ, quàm ratione actus: uti paulò pòst ostendetur. Constat proindè ex prima hac hypothesi, Peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, Objecti loco nõ respicere mores aut vitam hominis: ita ut nulla possit dari vitæ morumq́; consceleratio, quanta quanta etiam illa sit, quæ sub definitionem peccati hujus cadat. Quemadmodum verò prima hæc Hypothesis remedio esse potest, imò debet pœnitentibus, contra Desperationis periculum: Ita impœnitentibus & præfractis contemtoribus, peccandi licentiam minimè concedit, propterea quòd peccata quævis mortalia, æternæ damnationis reatum contrahunt, si non agatur pœnitentia: & quidem non tàm sera, quàm vera: Nam qui pœnitenti promisit gratiam: is præfractè impœnitenti non promisit crastinum: ut dixisse fertur Augustinus.

II. Hypothesis. Peccata quæ Doctrinam sive Religionem Christianam cõcernunt, duûm sunt generum: Alia enim directè in Doctrinam Legis: alia verò in doctrinam Evangelii feruntur. Jam verò peccatum in Spiritum sanctum Objecti loco tantùm respicit doctrinam Evangelii sive gratiæ, sic attestante Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 10, 28. & 29. Qui aspernatus fuerit Legem Mosis, absq; misericordia sub duobus aut tribus testibus moritur: quantò putatis pejoribus afficietur suppliciis, qui Filium DEI conculcârit, & sanguinem Testamenti ceu rem profanam habuerit per quem fuerat sanctificatus, & SPIRITUM GRATIAE contumelia affecerit. Et versu præcedente 16. Si volentes peccaverimus post acceptam cognitionem Veritatis, non ultrà pro peccatis est reliqua hostia. Colligimus proindè Peccata, quæ in doctrinam Legis impingunt, ad præsentem disputationem propriè non pertinere. Etsi enim fieri potest, ut etiam respectu legis, non quidem in moribus, sed in doctrinâ, tale committatur peccatum, quod ad Naturam peccati in Spiritum sanctum quàm proximè accedit: ut si quis in articulo de Lege defendat errorem aliquem contra conscientiam: & contrariam sententiam, quam verissimam esse non ignorat, volens sciens, quæ destinata malitia odit, criminatur, persequitur; Quia tamen Scriptura Sacra, Peccati in Spiritum sanctum non nisi agnitam veritatem Doctrinæ Evangelicæ, Objecti proprii & adæquati loco constituit: utique Religio nobis est, latiùs etiam illud extendere: Interim haud morosiùs reluctaturi illis, qui errores in doctrinam Legis impingentes, & modo jam notato contumaciter assertos, sub definitionem ac complexum peccati in Spiritum sanctum revocare velit: licèt respectu Scripturarum de hoc peccato ex professo agentium, minùs propriè minusque principaliter illud fieri statuendum sit.

III. Hypothesis: Peccata quæ in doctrinam Evangelii directè ac principaliter impingunt, rursus Scripturâ teste, duûm sunt generũ: Aliud enim est, quod dicitur, Peccatũ in Filium Hominis: Aliud verò, quod dicitur Peccatũ in Spiritum sanctũ. Quodnam & quale sit prius illud, tùm deniũ

Indubitatō constabit: si prius Quidnam sit peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum, & quomodo illud committatur, exactè constiterit. Nunquam verò rectius hoc investigabitur, quàm si secundo jam loco προσκείμενα & requisita Peccati hujus, & quidem Scripturarum oraculis expressa, penitùs expendamus.


### Chapter II. Or a purer doctrine about the sin against the Holy Spirit: II. Member

II. Member.

CONCERNING the proper requirements and, as it were, essential marks of this sin, nothing can ever be solidly defined unless we examine more accurately the passages of Scripture that deal with it expressly.

But at the beginning, the words of Christ offer themselves, Matt. 12, 31 and 32, Mark 3, 28 and 29, Luke 12, 10. Whoever blasphemes the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age, nor in the future: that is, with Mark as interpreter, he will not have forgiveness forever, but will be held by eternal judgment. To those weighing these words of the Savior more closely, it will be clear: 1. That this species of sin is shown and argued to us confusedly by Christ in the Pharisees, who, constrained by the power and virtue of the truth preached by Christ, and convicted by its brightness in their conscience, nevertheless rage and rave against it with such malicious impiety that they do not shudder to defame it by the name of Beelzebub. This first notation expresses at the beginning the Universal Object around which this sin revolves: which is the whole and entire doctrine of the Gospel concerning Christ: which, however, does not exclude a special object or some certain part of Christian doctrine, as the seventh mark will show. Then, however, it expresses, but a little more confusedly, the manner in which it is committed: namely, that the doctrine of the Gospel is denied and opposed against the proper testimony of the heart and conscience. For in this way the Pharisees sinned, as those who, knowing Christ to be a Teacher sent from God, and that no one could do similar signs unless God were with him, John 3, 2, knowing also that Christ was truthful and taught the way of God in truth, Matthew 22, 16, nevertheless preferred to tear his doctrine to pieces with blasphemous mouth and insults, and even to pursue him furiously unto death, rather than to candidly render glory to God and testimony to the truth. Close to these in this kind of sin were the leaders of the Jews: of whom it is written, John 12, 42 and 43: Many of the leaders believed in Christ, but because of the Pharisees they did not profess it, lest they be cast out of the Synagogue: For they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God. And Jerem. 44, 16 and 17: The word which you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not hear from you: but we will certainly do every word that will go out of our mouth, to sacrifice to the queen of heaven, etc. For although the Holy Spirit did not dwell in them through grace, yet, as if assisting from the outside, he was convicting them through the Word and the miraculous signs annexed to the Word, so that they could not but acknowledge him as an undoubted Teacher of truth.

The second essential mark of this sin is expressed by Christ when, in the places already cited above, he discretely defines its form, calling it blasphemy, indeed, naming it as if it were the specific difference, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews also expressed this mark, chap. 10, 29, saying: How much more bitter punishment will they deserve who trample underfoot the Son of God and treat the Spirit of grace with contumely. For although the Son of Man is also blasphemed, as Christ himself testifies, and then the contumely redounds at the same time upon the Father and the Holy Spirit, yet this blasphemy is not yet that against the Holy Spirit, nor should it be called such, because of the evident reasons for the differences which, as will be clear of its own accord from the subsequent Requirements, intervene between each blasphemy. It has indeed commonly prevailed that blasphemy against the Son of Man is said to be committed through ignorance, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit when the conscience, being convicted and the Word of God recognized, nevertheless blasphemously cries out against it. Although this easily holds its place, it does not yet fully exhaust the nature of this blasphemy, as will be clear from what follows. Then, indeed, it is also to be noted in this place that the word Blasphemy, by reason of its etymology, is general and, as Budaeus notes, signifies every harmful statement; but by theologians in the present discussion it is used κατ̓ ἐξοχὴν, and in a most special signification, where it denotes such a sin by which something is detracted from the excellence of divine goodness and truth, by falsely saying that something is in God which is not in him, or that something is not in him which is in him, and that with a certain zeal and will to derogate in this way from the divine majesty, as Thomas has not inappropriately defined, 2. 2. q. 13. art. 1. Whence it is now clear that Blasphemy and infidelity differ greatly, and the latter cannot be defined by the former. For infidelity consists properly in some internal, but false, assent concerning God, and in an external assertion of the false, proceeding from such internal assent, and that either affirmatively or negatively; but blasphemy does not properly consist in the assent itself or the assertion of the false, but in the speaking or false signification concerning God, to which the internal assent of the mind by no means corresponds.

The third note concerns the Subject: namely, the sin of Man: so that it cannot be committed by just anyone, but by him against the Holy Spirit, who has an evident recognition of the truth of the Heavenly doctrine. This note is expressed by the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 6, 4 & 5. It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good Word of God, and the powers of the world to come, if they fall away again, to be renewed unto repentance.

Which description indeed applies only to those who have not some superficial or half-full, but an accurate and evident recognition of the heavenly doctrine sanctioned by true faith in their hearts, nay, confirmed by the hope of the inheritance of the children of GOD, and some taste of eternal life, finally sealed by the Holy Spirit, as a pledge of the inheritance of the children of God 2 Cor. 1:22, Eph. 1:14, and chap. 4:30. This very mark is confirmed in chap. 10:26 of the same epistle: For if we sin willfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins.

The fourth mark is that it is committed through ἀποστασίαν [apostasy], or as the Apostle speaks in the place just now cited in verse 6, through a certain παραπίπτωσιν [falling away] or παράπτωμα [transgression]. Therefore, a falling away from that acknowledged truth: But what is the fifth essential mark of this sin, not just any falling away or denial constitutes the species of this sin: For the Apostle Peter also denied the acknowledged truth: who nevertheless obtained mercy again: But such an ἀποστασία [apostasy], falling away or denial, which is joined with a new crucifixion and mockery of the Son of God, as the Apostle speaks in verse 6: that is, which proceeds from purpose and deliberate malice, and is joined with sarcasms against the Son of God: indeed, by which one with a set purpose deserts the gathering of the faithful: as the author of this epistle speaks in chap. 10:25.

The sixth mark is voluntary falling away. The same Epistle to the Hebrews expresses this, chap. 10:26, where it has it thus: ἑκουσίως ἁμαρτανόντων, If we sin willfully after the knowledge of the truth, there is no more sacrifice left for sins. Now indeed τὸ ἑκούσιον ἐστὶν, ᾧ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐν ἀυτῷ ἐιδότι τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστα ἐν οἷς ἡ πρᾶξις. The spontaneous or voluntary is that whose principle is in the agent himself and knowing the individual circumstances of the action. Therefore, excluded from this species of sin is that denial, or falling away, or apostasy, which proceeds either from infirmity or from fear of danger or persecution, such as was in Peter, and sixty-one years ago in Francesco Spiera, who not by deliberate purpose, not spontaneously and violently: but broken by infirmity of the flesh and fear of danger, denied the acknowledged truth of the Evangelical doctrine, yet without any blasphemy: and therefore did not yet sin against the Holy Spirit. A.D. 1548. But it must be judged otherwise concerning those who, outside the case of danger or persecution, by deliberate counsel and full will of mind, only so that they may enjoy authority and power in this world, fall away from the acknowledged truth of the Gospel, and against the testimony of their own heart and conscience treat the same with contumely, and by whatever reasons they can, harass, oppose, and persecute it. We are most persuaded that such a clearly noble apostate in our time was Johannes Pistorius.

The seventh mark is ἀυτοκατάκριμα [self-condemnation], Tit. 3:11, so that, namely, he who commits this sin may be ἀυτοκατάκριτος [self-condemned], condemned by his own judgment. Which indeed notes, although it is sometimes detected in those also who have not sinned against the Holy Spirit, but denied the acknowledged truth out of some infirmity, as can be seen in Francesco Spiera: yet this does not always happen, as can be demonstrated by the example of the Apostle Peter, who certainly was not ἀυτοκατάκριτος. Now indeed this ἀυτοκατάκριμα is so proper and perpetual a mark of the sin against the Holy Spirit: that it is most simply convertible with it, so that those sinning thus always feel the stings of damnation within: although their obstinacy is such that they do not wish to profess this in words: And it is to be noted that the Apostle in the cited place attributes this mark to Heretics, not to just anyone: but to those heresiarchs, namely, who pertinaciously defend an error concerning the head or some article of Christian doctrine, and indeed one directly striking at the very substance of faith, with a protesting conscience, having been warned and even convicted several times, and knowingly and willingly oppose, revile, and persecute against the acknowledged truth. The use of this observation is that it may be established that through the sin against the Holy Spirit, not always the whole and entire doctrine of the Gospel is opposed: but more often at least some part of it: which we have already shown to be done by heretics properly so called.

The eighth and last mark is that he who sins thus, willingly, contumaciously, and stubbornly opposes and rejects all the means of salvation through which he could be led to the acknowledgment of sin and serious repentance: and they pertinaciously resist the Holy Spirit, who is to work for salvation through the Ministry of the Word. The epistle to the Hebrews, chap. 10:29, expressed this mark quite clearly, stating that those who sin willfully after having received the knowledge of the truth, trample under foot the Son of God, count the blood of the covenant, by which they were sanctified, an unholy thing, and do despite unto the Spirit of grace. And from this it is now plain and manifest why this sin is called by way of excellence Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: not, namely, that the Holy Spirit is greater than the Father and the Son: For there is nothing first or last in the Trinity, nothing greater or lesser, as the Athanasian Creed has it: Or even that this sin is not equally adverse, hostile, and hateful to the Father and the Son: but only because conversion, illumination, Faith, repentance, and the Salvation of Man are ascribed to the Holy Spirit in works ad extra. Hence the Ministry of the word is called the Ministry of the Holy Spirit. 2 Cor. 3:8, and those who resist the Ministry of the Word are said to resist the Holy Spirit. Gen. 6:3, Isa. 64:10, Acts 7:51, 1 Thess. 4:8. When therefore in the ways now defined some Man not only opposes the Word, which is the ὄχημα [vehicle] of the Holy Spirit for kindling Faith and true repentance in Man: but also pertinaciously, knowingly, and willingly struggles against the testimony of the Holy Spirit, convicting his own conscience of the truth of the doctrine: then truly and properly such a Man is said to sin against the Holy Spirit. From these eight distinct notes therefore, not taken or considered separately, but joined together, such a perfect and essential Definition of the Sin against the Holy Spirit can and ought to be constructed, that it is a voluntary apostasy, or abnegation of the acknowledged Evangelical truth, undertaken with set purpose, either in whole or in part: against the proper testimony of the heart and conscience.

Latin:

II. Membrum.

DE proprijs requisitis, ac notis quasi essentialibus peccati hujus, nunquam solidè quid definiri poterit, nisi loca Scripturæ de eo ex professo agentia, accuratiùs excutiamus.

Initiò autem Verba Christi sese offerunt, Matt. 12, 31. & 32. Marci 3, 28. & 29. Luc. 12, 10. Quisquis blasphemaverit Spiritum Sanctum, non remittetur ei, neque in hoc, neq́, in futuro seculo: hoc est, Marco interprete, non habebit remissionem in æternum, sed æterno tenebitur judicio. Verba hæc Servatoris pressiùs expendentibus patebit. 1. Speciem hanc peccati confusè monstrari nobis arguique, à Christo, in Pharisæis, qui veritatis à Christo prædicatæ vi ac virtute constricti, & fulgore ejusdem in conscientia convicti, malitiosa tamèn impietate sic in ipsam furunt ac sæviunt, ut nomine Beelzebub eam diffamare non exhorrescant. Prima hæc notatio exprimit initiò Objectum Universale circa quod peccatum hoc versatur: quod est, tota & universa doctrina Evangelij de Christo: quod tamen speciale objectum, sive certam aliquam partem doctrinæ Christianæ non excludit: uti nota Septima ostendet. Deindè verò exprimit, sed paulô confusiùs modum, quo illud committatur: ut nimirùm doctrina Evangelij negetur & oppugnetur, contra proprium cordis ac conscientiæ testimonium. Hoc enim pacto peccarunt Pharisæi, ut qui scientes Christum esse Doctorem à Deo missum, neque quenquam consimilia signa facere posse, nisi Deus sit cum ipso, Joh. 3, 2. scientes item, Christum esse veracem, & viam Dei in Veritate docere, Matth. 22, 16. maluerunt tamen doctrinam ejus blasphemo ore convitijs proscindere, imò ad mortem usque furenter persequi, quàm Deo gloriam, & veritati testimonium candidè perhibere. Vicini his fueruntin hoc peccati genere Judæorum principes: de quibus scriptum est, Joh. 12, 42. & 43. Multi ex primoribus crediderunt in Christum, sed propter Pharisæos non profitebantur, ne Synagoga ejicerentur: Dilexerunt enim gloriam hominum magis quàm gloriam Dei Et Jerem. 44, 16. & 17. Sermonem quem locutus es ad nos, in nomine Do mini, non audiemus ex te: sed facientes faciemus omne Verbum, quod egredietur de ore nostro, ut sacrificemus reginæ cæli &c. Etsi enim Spiritus Sanctus in his non habitavit per gratiam: tamen quasi forinsecùs assistens, per Verbum, & Verbo annexa miraculosa signa illos convincebat, ut non possent non illum pro indubio veritatis Doctore agnoscere.

Altera nota Essentialis peccati hujus exprimitur à Christo, quando in locis jam suprà citatis: Formam ejus discretè definit, Blasphemiam illud appellitans, imò differentiae quasi specificē locō, blasphemiam nominans in Spiritum Sanctum. Notam hanc expressit etiam autor Epistolae ad Hebraeos, cap. 10, 29. Quantō inquiens, acerbiūs supplicium perferent illi, qui Filium Dei conculcant, & Spiritum gratiā contumelia afficiunt. Etsi enim Filius etiam Hominis, teste ipso Christo, blasphematur: tùm contumelia simul in Patrem & Spiritum Sanctum redundat: tamen haec blasphemia nondùm illa in Spiritum Sanctum est aut dici debet, proptèr evidentes diversitatum rationes, quas utrique blasphemiae invicem intercedere ex subsequentibus Requisitis ultrò patebit. Vulgò illud quidem obtinuit, ut blasphemia in Filium Hominis diceretur committi per ignorantiam: blasphemia autem in Spiritum Sanctum tùm, quando conscientia convicta, Verbo Dei agnito, blasphemè tamen obstrepit. Quod etsi locum facilè obtinet: nondùm tamen Naturam blasphemiae hujus planè absolvit uti ex sequentibus patebit. Deinde verò & illud hoc loco notandum, vocabulum Blasphemiae ratione etymi esse generale, & ut Budaeus annotat, significare omnē nocens dictum: A Theologis verò in praesente disputatione κατ̓ ἐξοχὴν, & in Specialissima significatione usurpari, ubi, tale notat peccatum, quò aliquid de excellentia divinae bonitatis ac veritatis detrahitur: dicendò falsò aliquid Deo inesse quòd non inest illi, vel non inesse quod inest: idque studio ac voluntate quadam derogandi hac ratione divinae majestati: uti haud incommodè definivit Thomas, 2. 2. q. 13. art. 1. Undè jam patescit, quòd Blasphemia & infidelitas plurimùm differant: neque haec per illam definiri queat. Nam Infidelitas consistit propriè tùm in interno aliquo, sed falso assensu de Deo: tùm in externa asseveratione falsi, ex tali interno assensu proveniente: idque vel affirmativè vel negativè: Blasphemia autem propriè non consistit in ipso assensu, vel asseveratione falsi: sed in dictione sive significatione falsa de Deo, cui internus animi assensus nequaquàm respondeat.

Tertia nota respicit Subjectum: videlicet peccatum Hominem: ut non à quovis, sed ab eo in Spiritum Sanctum possit peccari, qui evidentem habet veritatis doctrinae Coelestis agnitionem. Notam hanc exprimit Epistola ad Hebraeos cap. 6, 4. & 5. Impossibile est, ut qui semel fuerint illuminati, & gustaverunt donum coeleste, ac participes fuerunt facti Spiritus Sancti, & gustarunt bonum Dei Verbum, ac virtutes futuri seculi, si prolabuntur denuò, ut per poenitentiam renoventur.

Quae sanè descriptio non nisi illis competit, qui non superficiariam aliquam aut semi plenam, sed accuratam ac evidentem habet doctrinae coelestis agnitionem per fidem veram sancitam in cordibus ipsorum, imò confirmatam spe haereditatis filiorum DEI, ac gustus quopiam æternæ vitæ, obsignatam denique Spiritu Sancto, tanquàm arrhabone hæreditatis filiorum Dei 2. Cor. 1, 22. Eph. 1, 14. & cap. 4, 30. Confirmatur hæc ipsa nota cap. 10, 26. ejusdem epistolæ: Voluntariè peccantibus, post acceptam cognitionem Veritatis, nulla pro peccatis reliqua est hostia.

Quarta nota est, ut committatur per ἀποστασίαν, sive ut Apostolus loco jam modò citato versu 6. loquitur, per quandam παραπίπτωσιν sive παράπτωμα. Defectio ergò ab agnita illa veritate: Sed quæ Quinta essentialis peccati hujus nota est, Defectio, aut Abnegatio non quælibet, constituit peccati hujus speciem: Nam & Apostolus Petrus veritatem agnitam abnegavit: qui tamèn misericordiam denuò consecutus est: Verùm talis ἀποστασία, defectio aut abnegatio, quæ conjuncta est cum nova crucifixione ac illusione Filij Dei, uti Apostolus versu 6. loquitur: hoc est, quæ ex proposito, & destinata malitia proficiscitur, & cum Sarcasmis in Filium Dei est conjuncta: imò quâ quis destinato consilio deserit aggregationem fidelium: uti autor Epistolæ hujus loquitur cap. 10, 25.

Sexta nota est Voluntaria defectio. Exprimit hanc eadem Epistola ad Hebræos, cap. 10, 26. ubi sic habet: ἑκουσίως ἁμαρτανόντων, Qui voluntariè peccant post agnitionem veritatis, illis non est ultrà pro peccatis hostia reliqua. Jam verò τὸ ἑκούσιον ἐστὶν, ᾧ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐν ἀυτῷ ἐιδότι [!] τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστα ἐν οἷς ἡ πρᾶξις. Spontaneum sive voluntarium est, cujus principium est in ipso agente & sciente singulas actionis circumstantias. Excluditur ergò ab hac peccati specie, ea sive abnegatio, sive defectio aut apostasia, quæ provenit vel ex infirmitate, vel ex metu periculi, sive persecutionis, qualis erat in Petro, & ante annos sexaginta unum in Francisco Spiera, qui non destinato Consilio, non spontè ac violenter: sed ex infirmitate Carnis, & metu periculi fractus, agnitam doctrinæ Evangelicæ veritatem, sine ulla tamen blasphemiâ abnegavit: ac proindè in Spiritum Sanctum nondum peccavit. A. C. 1548. Secus verò censendum de ijs, qui extra casum periculi aut persecutionis, deliberato consilio, plenaque animi voluntate, tantùm, ut autoritate ac potentia hoc in mundo fruantur, ab agnita veritate Evangelij deficiunt, & contra proprium cordis ac conscientiæ testimonium eandem contumeliâ afficiunt, & quibus possunt rationibus exagitant, oppugnant, persequuntur. Qualem Apostatam planè nobilem nostro hoc tempore fuisse, Johannem Pistorium, habemus persuasissimum.

Septima nota est, ἀυτοκατάκριμα, Tit. 3, 11. ut nimirùm qui hoc peccatum delinquit, sit ἀυτοκατάκριτος, proprio judicio condemnatus. Quæ sanè notat, etsi interdum in illis quoque deprehenditur, qui in Spiritum S. non peccarunt, sed ex infirmitate aliqua agnitam veritatem abnegarût, uti in Francisco Spiera videre licet: tamen hoc non semper evenire solet uti exemplo Petri Apostoli demonstrari potest, qui certè ἀυτοκατάκριτος non fuit. Jam verò ἀυτοκατάκριμα hoc ita propria & perpetua nota est peccati in Spiritum Sanctum: ut simplicissimè cùm eo convertatur, ita ut stimulos damnationis intus semper persentiscant sic peccantes: licet tanta eorum sit obstinatio, ut verbis hoc profiteri nolint: Et notandum, quòd Apostolus loco citato hanc notam tribuit Hæreticis non quibusvis: sed Hæresiarchis ijs videlicet, qui errorem de capite sive aliquo articulo doctrinæ Christianæ, & quidem in ipsam substantiam fidei directè impingentem, reclamante conscientia, aliquòties moniti etiam ac convicti pertinaciter propugnant, & contra agnitam veritatem scientes volentesq́; impugnant, convitiantur, persequuntur. Cujus observationis usus est, nt constet, per peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum, non semper totam & universam Evangelij doctrinam: sed sæpius aliquam saltem ejus partem, oppugnari: id quod ab hæreticis propriè sic dictis, fieri, jam ostendimus.

Octava & postrema nota est, ut qui sic peccat, is universa Salutis media, per quæ ad agnitionem peccati, & seriam pœnitentiam perduci posset, volènter, contumaciter, ac præfactè oppugnet, abjiciat, contemnat: ac Spiritui Sancto, per Ministerium Verbi ad salutem operaturo pertinaciter resistunt. Expressit hanc notam satis dilucidè epistola ad Hebræos, cap. 10, 29. afferens, quòd illi, qui voluntariè post acceptam veritatis agnitionem peccant, Filium Dei conculcent, sanguinem testamenti, per quem fuerant sanctificati, profanum ducant, & Spiritum gratiæ contumeliâ afficiant. Et hinc jam sit planum ac manifestum, cur hoc peccatum, κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicatur Blasphemia in Spiritum Sanctum: non videlicet, quòd vel Spiritus Sanctus Patre ac Filio sit major: Nihil enim in Trinitate prius aut posterius, nihil majus aut minus, uti Symbolum Athanasij habet: Vel etiam, quòd hoc peccatum non æquè Patri ac Filio sit adversum, inimicum ac exosum: sed tantùm, quia Spiritui Sancto in operibus ad extra conversio illuminatio, Fides, pœnitentia, & Salus Hominis adscribitur. Hinc Ministerium verbi, appellatur Ministeriu Spiritus Sancti. 2. Cor. 3, 8. & qui Ministerio Verbi resistunt, resistere dicuntur Spiritui Sancto. Genef. 6, 3. Ies. 64, 10. Act. 7, 51. 1. Thesss. 4, 8. Quando ergò modis jam definitis Homo aliquis non solùm oppugnat Verbum, quod est ὄχημα Spiritus S. ad accendendâ in Homine Fidem & veram pœnitentiam: sed & pertinaciter sciens volensque reluctatur testimonio Spiritus Sancti, convincentis conscientiam ipsius de veritate doctrinæ: tùm verè ac propriè talis Homo dicitur peccare in Spiritum Sanctum. Ex his ergò octo distinctis notis, non divisim sumtis aut consideratis, sed simul junctis, Peccati in Spiritum Sanctum, talis perfecta, ac essentialis Definitio extrui potest ac debet, quòd sit Voluntaria, ac destinato consilio suscepta apostasia, sive abnegatio agnitæ veritatis Evangelicæ, vel ex toto, vel ex parte: contra proprium cordis ac conscientiæ testimonium ministerium


### Chapter II. Or a purer doctrine about the sin against the Holy Spirit: II. Member (continued)

The Spirit, or attacking and insulting the means of salvation.

With this definition standing, it is immediately and spontaneously revealed how the sin, or blasphemy against the Son of Man—which Christ himself clearly distinguishes from the sin against the Holy Spirit—ought to be defined: namely, that it is an attack on the Evangelical doctrine, either not yet acknowledged through ignorance, or a denial of it once acknowledged, out of infirmity and fear of danger, yet without any blasphemy of it. Although the atrocity of this sin is indeed so great that not all obtain that grace which the Apostles Paul and Peter obtained—the former of whom attacked the doctrine of the Gospel not yet acknowledged through ignorance, while the latter denied the same once acknowledged, out of infirmity and fear of danger—yet most are finally swept away with Francis Spira into the abyss of despair and perish eternally, according to that most grave warning of the Savior, Matt. 10:33. Whoever shall deny me before men, I also will deny him before my Father who is in heaven: yet with respect to blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, that is lighter; and while he does not petulantly and contumaciously reject the means and organs of salvation, he can obtain remission.

Furthermore, it is asked concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit: whether one should judge a priori concerning this sin? To which question most reply that one must judge concerning it only a posteriori. But, if I may say so with the kind permission of great theologians, I do not yet consider this answer sufficient; rather, I maintain that one must answer by a distinction between this sin considered in itself and in respect to itself, and the man sinning. For as regards this sin considered in itself and by reason of itself, one certainly can, and indeed ought to, judge concerning it a priori and according to distinct knowledge, especially since so many testimonies of the Scriptures express and define its nature most clearly.

However, if it is asked concerning some certain person or individual, here finally has place that which says that judgment must not be made except a posteriori, namely when he who seems to us to sin in such a way also finally closes his life in such a way. Two reasons for this affirmation can be assigned above all: 1. Because the recesses of human hearts are hidden from us. 2. Lest we provide any handle or occasion for despair to any individual, if we should wish to pronounce anyone in particular guilty of this sin. Therefore, to all sinners, established in whatever anguish and dread of conscience, universal promises must always be proposed fearlessly; and where that anguish is true—which is discovered to be true when it is not joined with raging against God or merely with the blind torment and torture of despair—then it must be certainly established that the species of this sin does not yet obtain in such a man, and therefore that pardon is prepared for those who believe. But if such terrified persons growl that saying of Cain, 'My iniquity is greater than that it can be remitted,' that must always be opposed: 'What is impossible with men is possible with God,' Matt. 19:26. And that angelic word, Luke 1:36: 'With God no word is impossible.' And yet this is the Word of God, Ezek. 33:11: 'I live, saith the Lord, I desire not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.' Therefore, with Him it is not impossible that a sinner, however great, may return penitent into grace with God and obtain pardon.

Furthermore, it is asked: How, and in what sense, the sin against the Holy Spirit is said to be irremissible: that it is not remitted in eternity; that it is impossible that he who has committed such a sin be renewed to repentance, Heb. 6:6; that for such a sin there is no longer any sacrifice remaining, but a certain horrible expectation of judgment and fire inextinguishable, which will torture those who sin in such a way eternally, Heb. 10:27; that, finally, for this sin one is no longer to pray, 1 John 5:16.

Thomas and the Scholastics who followed him, just as they hold less orthodox views regarding the definition of this sin, so they do also regarding this question. For they teach that this sin is called irremissible in two ways: 1. insofar as it is taken for final impenitence: 2. insofar as it in itself, and of itself, or by its own nature has the merit that it should not be forgiven. Thomas 2. secundae. q. 14, art. 3.

Gregorius de Valentia, Tom. 3 of the Theological Commentaries, Disp. 1, Quaest. 14, Puncto 3, taking up the defense of Thomas, says: if we interpret the sin against the Holy Spirit as blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, or as a sin from malice, it is clear that it is not called irremissible because it can in no way be forgiven, but because it is forgiven with the greatest difficulty and rarely, for the reason that it has in its own nature a peculiar cause why it is not forgiven. For it is peculiarly against the Holy Spirit, to whom the remission of sins is attributed peculiarly, as to love.

And Tom. 2, Disp. 8, Quaest. 3, on the division of grace, puncto 4, pag. 1184. B. He says: Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is called irremissible, not because it cannot be forgiven, or is never forgiven: but because for the most part it is not forgiven. And after a few words: This sin can be forgiven and is sometimes forgiven: indeed, it was even forgiven to some of the Jews, when the Lord Peter later preached to them, Acts 2. But this opinion of the Jesuits has this disadvantage: 1. that they establish this sin as irremissible because, as Thomas speaks, it has in itself the merit that it should not be forgiven: a thing which is partly common to every sin: but partly it not obscurely establishes that error of the Romanists, that venial sins are of themselves and by themselves worthy of the remission of sins: as was shown above. 2. that irremissible sounds to them the same as that which is rarely forgiven: yet in the meantime it is sometimes forgiven, indeed it has been forgiven. Where indeed the example of the Jews, who were converted to Christ from the preaching of Peter, is applied here very ignorantly. For these did not sin against the Holy Spirit. Since a distinction must be made between the promiscuous multitude of the Jews and the leaders of the people and the Pharisees.

For just as we readily concede regarding these that they sinned against the Holy Spirit, so regarding these we simply deny that: especially since Scripture itself testifies that they crucified Christ through ignorance, according to that saying of the Savior: Father forgive them: for they know not what they do: And 1 Cor. 2. If they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. It is added that Christ does not place the distinction between the sin against the Son of Man and the sin against the Holy Spirit in distinct degrees of Remission: as if the former were forgiven more easily, the latter with more difficulty, as the Jesuit maintains: But He simply pronounces the former Remissible, the latter Irremissible. It would therefore be a crime to call that Remissible which the Savior expressly asserts to be Irremissible.

Moreover, that we may finally open up a purer opinion, this sin is called Irremissible, not because it falls under such a simple inability of Remission that by its atrocity it surpasses and exceeds both the mercy of God the Father and the merit of Christ. For many absurdities would follow from this premise: 1. That sin abounds above Grace: the contrary of which the Apostle asserts in Rom. 5:20. 2. That the merit of Christ is not universal: which Scripture expressly denies, 1 John 2:2. Christ is the propitiation for sins, not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world. 3. That the Evangelical promises are not Universal: which Scripture again denies, John 3:16. God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life. 1 Tim. 2:4. God wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. 4. That the command of Christ to call all to the kingdom of Christ, and to absolve all truly penitent, is hypocritical. But it is called Irremissible because it is never actually forgiven: so that this term (Irremissible) is taken in some way improperly: and denotes more what happens than what is possible, more what is done than what could be done. For there are many things not impossible, which although they are never done, could nevertheless be done. But Remission does not reach this sin for this reason: 1. Because those sinning in this way voluntarily fall away from Christ Himself, outside of whom there is no sacrifice left for sin. 2. Because they do not indirectly, like other mortal sins, but directly, contumaciously, and willingly neglect, cast away, and trample underfoot the organs and means of salvation, without which the Holy Spirit never ordinarily works conversion. 3. Because this sin has an inseparable companion attached to it, the final hardening of the heart: so that, with a certain purpose afterwards hardened, they proceed knowingly and willingly to horribly impugn and blaspheme the truth once acknowledged: which the Savior wished to intimate, subjecting this warning to the description of the sin against the Holy Spirit: If the demon is expelled from a man through the acknowledgment of the truth: and afterwards is admitted again into his former lodging, that he does not come alone, but enters with seven spirits worse than himself, so that the last state of that man becomes worse than the first. For these reasons, therefore, it happens that those who sin in this way never actually obtain Remission: but finally die with a hardened mind, or certainly are absorbed into the abyss of despair without any hope of salvation, and perish eternally. Otherwise, if it were to happen that these people perform repentance; then it could by no means be pronounced of them that they had sinned against the Holy Spirit: but only against the Son of Man. Thus, therefore, it is clearly evident from these things: 1. How one must judge about this sin only a posteriori, regarding certain individuals who sin: although in theory, what its proper criteria and requirements are, one can rightly judge a priori. 2. How this sin is said to be Irremissible, namely with respect to actual Remission, which it never attains: but not absolutely by reason of power, as if it could simply and absolutely obtain no pardon.

With these things thus observed, it also becomes plain in what sense the Apostle John wrote that there is a certain sin unto death, for which one should not pray. 1 John 5:16. He understands, namely, the sin against the Holy Spirit called Mortal by way of excellence, which indeed never attains Remission: just as conversely the other reigning sins, which the Apostle enumerates in Gal. 5:19, are also mortal by their nature, but yet very often obtain pardon, as is clearly evident regarding the sins of David, Peter, Paul, and others. Regarding this sin, therefore, if anyone were to think that one should pray, he would be as absurd as if he were to maintain that one should pray that God might wish to convert and save someone without Christ, or rather against Him: likewise without true repentance and conversion to Christ, and without the means ordained for this end by God Himself: which would be not only discordant, but also impious.

Moreover, that we may shorten sail, we first establish the end of this Disputation to be this, that we abstain again and again not only from the express denial of Evangelical truth, but also from every appearance or simulation of denied truth. The second, that with the atrocity of the sin against the Holy Spirit well weighed, we diligently guard ourselves, so that neither seriously, nor for the sake of exercise, do we impugn too licentiously and vehemently the Articles of faith, especially those of whose certainty we are convinced in our heart: and that we do not place it as a part of some extraordinary erudition if we can dispute for and against, as they say, on either side of any mystery of the Christian Religion. For it can happen, indeed it happens very often, that this Pyrrhonic method of disputing gradually pleases us more and more, and contracts a kind of habit, so that nothing can be said from the Scriptures so holy, so true, and so certain, that it is not called into doubt. With this degree of impiety prevailing in a man’s mind, it usually happens that the Devil afterwards carries him away to such an extent that he degenerates entirely into atheism and Epicureanism: just as the tragic examples and tragic falls of many otherwise most learned men, especially those of Simon Simonius and others, attest more than sufficiently. Let that grave exhortation of the Apostle rather resound in our minds and ears: Do nothing against the truth, but everything for the truth. 2 Cor. 13, 8.

Latin:

Spiritus, sive media salutis hostiliter oppugnans ac contumelia afficiens.

Stante hac Definitione, statim ultro patescit, Quomodo jam Peccatum, sive Blasphemia in Filium Hominis, quam Christus ipse adversus peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum diserte contradistinguit, definiri debeat: quod nimirum sit Doctrinae Evangelicae, vel nondum agnitae per ignorantiam oppugnatio: vel jam agnitae ex infirmitate, ac metu periculi, sine ulla tamen ejus blasphemia abnegatio. Quanquam vero tanta etiam est peccati hujus atrocitas, ut non omnibus ea gratia obtingat, quae Paulo ac Petro Apostolis obtigit: quorum ille per ignorantiam Doctrinam Evangelij nondum agnitam oppugnavit: hic vero eandem jam agnitam, ex infirmitate & metu periculi abnegavit: Sed plerique tandem cum Francisco Spiera desperationis abysso abripiantur & aeternum pereant: secundum gravissimam illam comminationem Servatoris Matth. 10, 33. Qui me negaverit coram hominibus: negabo & ego eum coram Patre meo, qui in caelis est: Respectu tamen blasphemiae in Spiritum Sanctum, levius illud est: & dum media ac organa salutis non petulanter ac contumaciter rejicit, Remissionem consequi potest.

Caeterum de Peccato in Spiritum Sanctum quaeritur. Num a priori de hoc peccato judicandum sit? Ad quod quaesitum plerique respondent, de eo non aliter quam a posteriori judicandum esse. Sed quod bona venia magnorum Theologorum dixerim, nondum hanc responsionem sufficere arbitror: sed per distinctionem inter peccatum hoc, in se & respectu sui consideratum: & inter Hominem peccantem, respondendum esse statuo. Nam Quoad peccatum hoc in se, & ratione sui consideratum, certe a priori de ipso, & secundum discretam notitiam judicari potest, imo vero debet: praesertim cum tot Scripturarum testimonia naturam ejus dilucidissime exprimant & definiant.

Caeterum si de certa aliqua persona sive individuo quaeratur: hic demum locum habet illud, quod non nisi a posteriori sit judicium faciendum, quando nimirum, qui sic peccare nobis videtur, sic etiam tandem vitam claudit. Rationes autem affirmati hujus duae potissimum adsignari possunt: 1. Quia cordium humanorum recessus nobis sunt absconditi. 2. Ne ulli Individuo, desperationis ansam aut occasionem praebeamus, si peccati hujus reum aliquem in Individuo pronunciare velimus. Proinde peccatoribus omnibus, in quocunque angore & pavore conscientiae constitutis, semper intrepide sunt proponendae promissiones universales: & ubi angor iste verus est, qui tum verus esse deprehenditur, quando non conjunctus est cum fremitu adversus Deum, aut cum caeco duntaxat desperationis tormento atque cruciatu: tum certo statuendum est, peccati hujus speciem, in tali homine nondum obtinere: ac proinde veniam credentibus paratam esse. Quod si ejusmodi consternati ogganniant illud Caini: Major est iniquitas mea, quàm ut remitti queat, semper opponendum illud: Quod impossibile est apud homines, possibile est apud Deu Matth. 19, 26. Et illud Angelicum Luc. 1, 36. apud Deum non est impossibile ullum verbum: Atqui hoc est Verbum Dei Jezech. 33, 11. Vivo Deus, nolo mortem peccatoris: sed ut convertatur & vivat. Ergo apud ipsum non est, impossibile, ut peccator quantus quantus, poenitens redeat in gratiam cum Deo, & Veniam consequatur.

Caeterùm porrò quaeritur: Quomodo, & quo sensu Peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum dicatur Irremissibile: quòd in aeternum non remittatur: quod impossibile sit, ut qui tale peccatum commisit, renovetur ad poenitentiam: Hebr. 6, 6. quòd pro tali pecpato, nulla sit ampliùs reliqua hostia: sed horrenda quaedam expectatio Iudicij, & ignis inextinguibilis, qui sic peccantes aeternùm cruciatur us, Hebr. 10, 27. quod denique pro hoc peccato non ampliùs sit orandum: 1. Ioh. 5, 16.

Thomas & eum secuti Scholastici, uti de definitione peccati hujus, ita de hac etiam quaestione, minùs orthodoxè sentiunt. Docent enim peccatum hoc dici irremissibile duobus modis: 1. quatenùs illud accipitur pro finali impoenitentia: 2. quatenùs illud in se, & de se, vel ex sua natura habet meritum, ut non remittatur. Thomas 2. secundae. q. 14, art. 3.

Gregorius de Valentia Tom. 3. Commentariorum Theologicorum Disp. 1. Quaest. 14. Puncto. 3. Thomae patrocinium suspiciens, si inquit, Peccatum in Spiritum Sanctu interpretamur de blasphemia in Spiritum Sanctum, vel de peccato ex malitia, constat non dici Irremissibile, propterea quòd nullo modo remitti possit, sed quia difficillimè & rarò remittitur, eò quod ex sua ratione habet peculiarem causam, cur non remittatur. Nam peculiariter est contra Spiritum Sanctum, cui attribuitur peculiariter remissio peccatorum, ut amori.

Et Tom. 2. Disp. 8. Quaest. 3. de divisione gratiae, puncto 4. pag. 1184. B. Blasphemia inquit, in Spiritum Sanctum dicitur irremissibilis, non quòd remitti nequeat, aut nunquàm remittatur: sed quia ut plurimùm non remittatur. Et post pauca. Peccatum hoc remitti potest & interdum remittitur: Imò etiam quibusdam Judaeorum remissum fuit, cùm D. Petrus postea ad illos haberet concionem, Act, 2. Habet verò haec Jesuvvitarum Sententia illud incommodi: 1. quod statuunt Peccatum hoc ideò irremissibile, quia, uti Thomas loquitur, in se habet meritum, ut non remittatur: id quod partim commune est omni peccato: partim verò haud obscurè stabilit errorem illum Romanensium, quòd peccata Venalia de se & ex se digna sint remissione peccatorum: uti supra ostensum. 2. quòd irremissibile idem ipsis sonat, ac quod rarò remittatur: interim tamen interdum remittatur, imò remissum sit. Ubi sanè admodùm inscitè huc accommodatur Exemplum Judaeorum, ex concione Petri ad Christum conversorum. Neque enim hi peccarunt in Spiritum Sanctum. Siquidem disstinguendum est inter promiscuam Judaeorum multitudinem: & inter primores populi ac Pharisaeos.

Quemadmodum enim de his ultrò concedimus, quòd peccarint in Spiritum Sanctum: ita de his illud simpliciter negamus: præsertim cum Scriptura ipsa testetur, ipsos per ignorantiam crucifixisse Christum, secundum illud Servatoris: Pater remitte illis: nesciunt enim quid faciant: Et 1. Cor. 2. Si cognovissent, Dominum gloriæ non crucifixissent. Accedit, quòd Christus discrimen inter peccatum in Filium Hominis, & peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum non collocat in distinctis gradibus Remissionis: quasi illud facilius, hoc difficilius remittatur, uti Jesuvita autumat: Sed simpliciter illud Remissibile, hoc Irremissibile esse pronunciat. Nefas ergo fuerit, Remissibile dicere id, quod Servator Irremissibile esse expressè asserit.

Cæterùm ut puriorem sententiam vel tandem aperiamus, dicitur hoc peccatum Irremiffibile, non quòd sub talem simplicem cadat Remissionis ἀδυναμίαν, ut sua atrocitate, & misericordiam Dei Patris, & Christi meritum superet & excedat. Hæc enim pacto plurima sequerentur absurda: 1. Peccatum supra Gratiam exuberare: cujus contrarium Apostolus Rom. 5, 20. asserit: 2. Meritum Christi non esse: καθολικὸν: id quod expresse negat Scriptura, 1 Joh. 2, 2. Christus est propiciatio pro peccatis non pro nostris tantùm, sed pro peccatis totius mundi. 3. Promissiones Evangelicas non esse Universales: id quod rursus negat Scriptura, Joh. 3, 16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis, qui credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. 1. Tim. 2, 4. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire. 4. Mandatum Christi de vocandis omnibus ad regnum Christi, & absolvendis omnibus ad regnum Christi. & absolvendis omnibus verè pœnitentibus, esse hypocriticum. Verùm Irremissibile ideò dicitur, quia illud nunquàm ipso actu remittitur: ita ut Terminus iste (Irremissibile) aliquo modo impropriè accipiatur: & magis τὸ γινόμενον, quàm τὸ δυνατὸν, magis quid fiat, quàm quid fieri possit, denotet. Sunt enim non impossibilia multa, quæ licet nunquàm fiant, fieri tamen poterant. Ideò autem non obtingit huic peccato Remissio, 1. Quia hoc modo peccantes, ab ipso Christo, extra quem non ulla pro peccato reliqua est hostia, voluntariò deficiunt. 2. Quia organa ac media salutis, sine quibus Spiritus S. Conversionem nunquàm ordinariè operatur, non indirectè, ut peccata mortalia reliqua, sed directè, contumaciter & volenter negligunt, projiciunt, & pedibus conculcant. 3. Quia hoc peccatum individuam quasi comitem habet adjunctam, Finalem cordis indurationem: ita ut obfirmato postea quodam proposito, scientes volétes veritatem agnita horribiliter impugnare & blasphemare pergant: id quod innuere voluit Servator, descriptioni peccati in Spiritum Sanctum hanc statim ἐπίκωσιν subjiciens: Si dæmon per agnitionem veritatis expulsus sit ex homine: ac postmodùm denuò in pristinũ hospitium admittatur, nõ venire illum solum, sed assumtis septem deterioribq spiritibus, ingredi, ut postrema illius hominis fiant deteriora primis.
