His ergò respectibus, fit, ut sic peccantes, nunquã actu Remissionem consequantur: sed tandem indurata mente moriantur, vel certè in desperationis abyssum, sine ulla spe salutis absorbeantur, & æternum pereant. Aliàs si contingeret, hos agere pœnitentiam; tùm de illis pronunciari posset minimè, quod peccassent in Spiritum Sanctum: sed tantùm in Filium Hominis. Sic ergò ex his liquidò constat, 1. quomodo de hoc peccato duntaxat à posteriori sit judicandum, quoad certa peccantium individua: licèt in thesi, quænam propria ejus sint κριτήρια & requisita, à priori rectè judicari possit. 2. Quomodo hoc peccatum dicatur Irremissibile, nimirùm respectu actualis Remissionis, quam nunquàm consequitur: non verò absolutè ratione δυνάμεως, quòd simpliciter & absolutè veniam nullam consequi possit.

His ita observatis planum itidem evadit, quo sensu Johannes Apostolus scripserit, esse peccatum quoddam ad mortem, pro quo non sit orandum. 1. Iohan. 5, 16. Intelligit nimirùm peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν Mortale dictum, quod nimirum nunquàm Remissionem consequitur: quemadmodum vice versa reliqua peccata regnantia, quæ percenset Apostolus Gal. 5, 19. etiam sua natura sunt mortalia, sed tamen veniam sæpissimè consequuntur, uti de peccatis Davidis, Petri, Pauli & aliorum salis liquidò constat. De hoc ergò peccato, si quis orandum esse censeret, is tàm absurdus foret, ac si statueret, orandum esse, ut Deus aliquem sine Christo, aut potiùs contra illum: item sine vera pœnitentia ac conversione ad Christum, & sine medijs ad hunc finem à Deo ipso ordinatis, convertere & salvare velit: id quod non modò absonum, sed & impium foret.

Cæterùm ut vela contrahamus, Finem Disputationis hujus primùm constituimus istum, ut non modò à diserta abnegatione veritatis Evangelicæ, sed & ab omni specie sive simulatione abnegatæ veritatis, etiam atque etiam abstineamus. Alterum, ut peccati in Spiritum S. atrocitate probè pensitata diligenter nobis caveamus, ut ne sive seriò, sive exercitij gratia, Articulos fidei eos præsertim, de quorum certitudine in corde convicti sumus, licentiùs ac vehementiùs impugnemus: ac in parte eximiæ alicujus eruditionis ponamus, si de quovis mysterio Religionis Christianæ, in utramque quod ajunt partem, pro & contra disputare queamus. Fieri enim potest, imò fit sæpissimè, ut pededentim magis magisŇue Pyrrhonica hæc disputandi ratio, nobis arrideat, & habitum quasi quendam contrahat, ut nihil tàm sanctum, tamŇue verum ac certum ex scripturis dici possit, quod non in dubium vocetur. Hoc impietatis gradu in animo hominis obtinente, fieri solet, ut postmodùm eò usque Diabolus illum abripiat: ut in atheismum ac Episcureismum omninò degeneret: Quemadmodum tragica multorum aliàs doctissimorum virorum Exempla & casus tragici, Simonis præsertim Simonij, & aliorum satis superque attestantur, Personet potiùs in animis & auribus nostris, gravis illa exhortatio Apostoli: Nihil contra veritatem: sed omnia pro veritate facite. 2. Cor. 13, 8.


## 13 On the Law of GOD

The doctrine of the Law follows in a most convenient order that which has been handled by us thus far concerning sin. For since, as the Apostle testifies, the strength of sin is the Law (1 Cor. 15:56), the Law of God alone will be that most polished mirror which sets before our eyes the atrocity of sin to be thoroughly contemplated: and by the definitive sentence of the supreme Judge of all, it subjects the whole human race to the right and power of death and hell: unless, through Christ, who is the fulfillment of the Law (Rom. 10:4), a free remission of sins should be obtained for it. Whence, concerning the excellence, use, and necessity of this Article, it will not be difficult to form a correct judgment.

Moreover, its entire treatment by our Author consists of six distinct chapters: the first of which treats the Definition; the second, the Division; the third, an accurate and prolix exposition of the Decalogue, or Moral Law; the fourth, the Question concerning the Law of Nature; the fifth, certain and distinct uses of the moral Law; and the sixth, finally, the controversy concerning the Distinction between Precepts and Counsels.

Although, indeed, whatever is worth remembering concerning the law of God can easily be referred to these six chapters: yet because, partly, a more accurate account must be taken of the controversies of our age; and partly, because the thesis must be properly distinguished from the antithesis according to our accustomed Method: we have, by gradually departing from the Philippean Method, divided our future exposition into two general Chapters: the FORMER of which will treat in the thesis those things which are accustomed to come under question concerning the homonymy, Definition, Division, and the whole nature, as it were, of the Law of God, both in general and in particular. The LATTER will resolve that controversy.

CHAPTER I.

The first chapter, comprising six general Questions, is most correctly completed: the first of which will explain the polysemy of the word Law; the second, the Definition; the third, the Division; the fourth, the nature of the ceremonial Law; the fifth, the proper affection of the Mosaic forensic Laws; and the sixth, finally, the Definition and adjuncts of the Moral Law or Decalogue in general.

Latin:

LEgis doctrina ordine convenientissimo excipit eam, quæ hactenus de peccato à nobis est expedita. Cùm enim Apostolo teste, virtus peccati sit Lex; 1. Cor. 15, 56. utique Lex Dei sola erit politissimum illud speculum, quòd atrocitatem peccati penititus contemplandam ob oculos constituit: & per definitivam supremi universorum Judicis sententiam, Juri potestatique mortis ac inferni totum genus humanum subjicit: nisi per Christum, qui est Legis impletio, Rom. 10, 4. gratuita ipsi peccatorum obtingat remissio. Undè de præstantia, usu ac necessitate Articuli hujus, haud fuerit difficile rectum ferre Judicium.

Constat autem universa ejus Tractatio apud Autorem nostrum, sex distinctis capitibus: quorum Primum Definitionem; alterum Divisionem; tertium, Decalogi, sive Legis Moralis accuratam & prolixam expositionem; quartum, Quæstionem de Lege Naturæ; Quintum, certos ac distinctos usus Legis moralis; Sextum denique controversiam de Discrimine Præceptorum & Conciliorum pertractat.

Quanquàm verò ad sex isthæc capita facilè referri possunt, quæcunque de lege Dei memoratu digna sunt: quia tamen partim controversiarum nostri seculi accuratior est habenda ratio: partim verò θέσις ab ἀντιθέσει secundum consuetam nobis Methodum, probè est distinguenda: utique paulatim à Methodo Philippéa secessione facta, futuram nostram διέξοδον in duo Capita generalia dispescimus: Quorum PRIUS κατασκευαστικὸν in thesi pertractabit ea, quæ de ὁμωνυμίᾳ, Definitione, Divisione, & totâ quasi naturâ Legis Dei tùm in genere, tùm in specie, sub quæstionem venire solent. POSTERIUS ἀνασκευαστικὸν expediet controversiam illam.

CAPUT I.

CAput prius sex generalium Quæstionum complexum rectissimè absolvitur: quarum prima πολυσημασίαν vocabuli Legis: altera Definitionem: tertia Divisionem: quarta Legis ceremonialís naturam: quinta Legum Mosaicarum forensium affectionem propriam: Sexta denique Legis Moralis sive Decalogi Definitionem & προσκείμενα in genere expediet.


### Question I. On the homonymy of the term Law

That which Plato once established—that when the meaning of words is unknown, it happens that errors creep upon those who are learning—that this is most true is shown even by those controversies which have gravely shaken the Church of God concerning the present Article of the Christian faith. Soon after the ascension of Christ the Savior into Heaven, there were not lacking Pseudo-Apostles who, burning with a preposterous zeal for the Law, transformed the Gospel entirely into Law: thus most dangerously confounding two most diverse heads of Celestial Doctrine, differing in their whole genus: so that a little later the Galatian Church, planted by the Apostle Paul himself, almost entirely lost the purer Evangelical Doctrine from this confusion alone.

In the progress of time, the Scholastic Doctors poured oil on the fire, defining the Gospel concerning Christ as a Law much more difficult and burdensome than the Mosaic Law. Hence Thomas did not shrink from writing (Prima Secundae, quest. 107, art. 1): The precepts of the new Law are more burdensome, because in the new law the interior motions of the mind are prohibited, which were not expressly prohibited in the Old Law: and if they were prohibited in some, yet no penalty was attached. And Petrus Asotus, in his Catholic assertion, did not hesitate to call the Gospel the killing letter. Which error, indeed, later so invaded, nay, permeated the entire Roman Papacy, that even today the Monastics, both old and the more recent Jesuits, define the Gospel by the New Law: and seriously contend that the Law and the Gospel differ from each other not in the genus itself or the species of doctrine, but only in degree and ease: so that the Law of Moses is taught to contain easier and lighter precepts, but the Law of Christ, more perfect and difficult ones. What is more? That not even that more ancient Church of the Holy Fathers was entirely immune from this error, as Brentius demonstrates quite prolixly from the monuments of Tertullian, Hilary, Eusebius, Chrysostom, and others (Tom. 8 of his Works, page 361).

In the age of our fathers, the Anabaptists separated the Law and the Gospel as if they were contradictorily opposed to one another, at such great intervals: that they contended that neither the Patriarchs and Prophets of the Old Testament had anything in common with the Gospel, nor that we, established under the Gospel, ought to have any dealings with the Law of Moses: a fact which is clearly evident even from the acts of the Colloquy of Frankenthal.

Today the Antinomians follow in their footsteps, maintaining that the doctrine of the Moral Law or Decalogue must be banished from the field and boundaries of the Church to the political forum or to the court; indeed, even to the gallows.

From this, at length, the impious faction of the Libertines was born under a truly unhappy star: which, having completely abrogated every use of the divine Law for Christians, contends quite blasphemously that an arbitrary license for living has been granted under the New Testament.

Now if you inquire into the source and proximate cause of so many, and such various and discrepant opinions: certainly no other can be given than a shameful ignorance of the πολυσημασία or multiple signification which the word Law is discovered to obtain in the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, that we may enter upon a middle way, by which we may duly guard against the quicksands of errors: we shall more accurately weigh the way and power of the word Law: and we shall recall it to the dichotomy of generality and specialty. In the Scriptures, therefore, the Law of God is taken either Generally or Specially. Generally, it denotes first the Universal heavenly doctrine, consisting of Law and Gospel: or the whole Word of God, comprised in the Biblical codex. In which sense it is taken, Ps. 1:2, Ps. 19:8, in almost the entire 119th Psalm, Isa. 2:3, Rom. 3:27. And in this sense the Latin word for Law corresponds to the Hebrew word תּוֹרָה Thorah, which, likewise taken generally, signifies whatever makes us more certain about God and His will. From ignorance, therefore, of this first general signification, that error of the Scholastics and Papists was born. For these, noticing that the Gospel is also called Law in the Scriptures: very ignorantly and against the analogy of faith urged the Special signification of the Law, and thus introduced that foul Confusion of Law and Gospel.

2. Next, the Law of God, likewise taken more generally, denotes those Biblical books which are commonly called the Old Testament: but are distinguished by Christ into Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets. Luke 24:44. Insofar, therefore, as these books principally looked to the Old people: to that extent the Anabaptists now contend that we, with our New Testament, ought to have nothing in common with those books: as if indeed those books were so abrogated for us that they no longer pertain to us at all: thus too shamefully confusing the books viewed externally with the doctrine of the Law itself.

3. Finally, the Law of God taken generally denotes that Mosaic codex of all the commandments of God, of which the Rabbis of the Jews number six hundred and thirteen. Now since those individual and universal precepts do not bind us today: but most of them, except for the moral ones, have been abrogated: the faction of Antinomians and Libertines has stupidly defended from this an all-encompassing abrogation of the divine Law: the former indeed with respect to the reborn and the faithful: the latter, however, indifferently and promiscuously with respect to all men living under the Grace of the New Testament.

Specially, the Law of God taken in the Scriptures denotes that more excellent part of the Mosaic Law which is and is called the Moral Law, or the Decalogue.

In which sense it is taken in the Pauline and our own disputations concerning Justification, Faith, and Grace: and is then opposed to the Gospel concerning CHRIST ἀντιδιηρημένως (by way of division): so that in one and the same act, with respect to the same thing, they can never stand together. In this sense the word Law is taken in those classic passages which we oppose to the impiety of the Papists concerning the righteousness of works, Rom. 3:28, Rom.

v

6:15, Rom. 7:7, Rom. 8:3, Rom. 11:6, Gal. 2:16, Gal. 5:18, Eph. 2:8 & 9, and passim elsewhere. This special signification being observed, the errors noted above, each and all, collapse of themselves.

Latin:

QUod Plato olim statuit: ignoratâ vocabulorum significatione, contingere, ut obrepant discentibus errores: id ve- ́rissimum esse, vel eæ saltem controversiæ ostendunt, quæ circa præsentem fidei Christianæ Articulum Ecclesiam Dei graviter concusserunt. Mox ab ascensione Christi Servatoris in Cœlum, non defuerunt Pseudo Apostoli, qui præpostero Legis Zelo flagrantes Evangelium penitùs in Legem transformâruut: sic duo diversissima, & toto genere discrepantia Cœlestis Doctrinæ capita periculosissimè confundentes: ita ut paulò post Ecclesia Galatica, ab ipso Apostolo Paulo plantata, ex hac sola confusione, totius fermè purioris Doctrinæ Evangelicæ jacturam faceret.

Progressu temporis Doctores Scholastici oleum camino suffuderunt, Evangelium de Christo definientes per Legem multò difficiliorem & graviorem Lege Mosaicâ. Hinc Thomas scribere non exhorruit; prima secundæ, quæst. 107. art. 1. Præcepta novæ Legis sunt graviora, quia in nova lege prohibentur interiores motus animi, qui in Lege Veteri expressè non prohibebantur: & si in aliquibus prohibebantur, non tamen apponebatur pœna. Et Petrus Asotus in assertione Catholicâ, non dubitavit Evangelium nominare Literam occidentem. Qui sanè error universum postea Papatum Romanum ita invasit, imò pervasit, ut hodieque Monachitum Veteres tum recentiores Jesuvvitæ Evangelium per Novam Legem desiniant: & seriò contendant, Legem & Evangelium non Genere ipso, aut specie doctrinæ: sed gradu duntaxat & facilitate à se mutuò differre: ita ut Lex Mosis faciliora & leviora; Lex autem Christi, perfectiora & difficiliora præcepta continere doceatur. Quid? quòd ne quidem antiquior illa S. Patrum Ecclesia, ab hoc errore planè fuit immunis: quemadmodum ex Tertulliani, Hilarij, Eusebij, Chrysostomi, & aliorum monumentis, prolixè satis demonstrat Brentius, Tom. 8. Operum pag. 361.

Anabaptistæ Patrum nostrorum ætate, Legem & Evangelium, tanquàm α̉ντίζ αππω̂ς contradictoriè sibi mutuò opposita, tantis intervallis sejunxerunt: ut neque Patriarchis ac Prophetis Veteris Testamenti, cum Evangelio quicquam commune fuisse: neque nobis sub Evangelio constitutis, quicquam cum Lege Mosis commercij esse debere contenderent: id quod ex actis etiam Colloquij Franckenthalensis liquidò patet.

Horum vestigia sequuntur hodiè Antinomi,statuentes, Legis Moralis sive Decalogi doctrinam, ex agro & finibus Ecclesiæ, ad Forum Politicum, sive ad Curiam: imò ad patibulum relegandam esse.

Hinc tandem impia Libertinorum factio, infelici planè sidere nata est: quæ Legis divinæ usu omni Christianis in solidum abrogata, arbitrariam vivendi licentiam sub Novo Testamento concessam esse, satis blasphemè contendit.

Jam fontem atque causam proximam tot, tamque variarum ac discrepantium opinionum si inquiras: certè nulla potest dari alia, quàm turpis ignorantia πολυσημασίας sive multiplicis significationis, quam vocabulum Legis in Scripturis Sacris obtinere deprehenditur. Proindè ut media via ingressi, quâvis errorum Syrtes ritè præcaveamus: viam atque potestatem vocabuli Legis accuratiùs expendemus: & ad generalitatis ac specialitatis διχοτομίαν revocabimus. In Scripturis igitur Lex Dei vel Generatim, vel Speciatim accipitur. Generatim notat primùm Universam doctrinam cœlestem, Lege & Evangelio constantem: sive totum Verbum Dei, codice Biblico comprehensum. Quo sensu accipitur, Psal. 1, 2. Psal. 19, 8. Psalmo 119 fermè integro. Ies. 2, 3. Rom. 3, 27. Et respondet hoc sensu vox Latina Legis vocabulo Hebræo תּוֹרָה Thorah, quod itidem generaliter acceptum significat, quicquid de Deo ejusque voluntate nos reddit certiores. Ex ignorantia ergò primæ hujus significationis generalis, natus est error ille Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum. Hi enim animadvertentes in Scripturis Evangelium quoque nominari Legem: inscitè admodùm & contra analogiam fidei urserunt Specialem Legis significationem, & sic fædam illam Legis & Evangelij Confusionem introduxerunt.

2. Deindè Lex Dei itidem Generaliùs accepta, notat libros illos Biblicos, qui vulgò Vetus Testamentum nominantur: à Christo autem distinguuntur in Mosen, Psalmos, & Prophetas. Luc. 24, 44. Quatenus ergò hi libri principaliter respiciebant Veterem populum: eatenus jam Anabaptistæ nobis suo Novo Testamento nihil cum libris illis commune esse debere contendunt: quasi verò ita libri illi nobis sint abrogati, ut nihil quicquam ampliùs ad nos spectent: sic nimis turpiter libros forinsecùs spectatos, cum ipsa doctrina Legis confundentes.

3. Tandem Lex Dei generaliter sumta, notat codicem illum Mosaïcum mandatorum Dei omnium, quorum sexcenta tredecim numerant Judæorum Rabbini. Jam cùm singula atque universa illa præcepta nos hodiè non obligent: sed pleraque, exceptis moralibus, sint abrogata: stolidè hinc Antinomorum & Libertinorum factio, omnimodam Legis divinæ abrogationem propugnavit: illi quidem respectu renatorum ac fidelium: hi verò indifferenter ac promiscuè respectu omnium hominum, sub Gratia Novi Testamenti viventium.

Speciatim Lex Dei in Scripturis accepta, notat excellentiorem illam Legis Mosaicæ partem, quæ est ac dicitur Lex Moralis, sive Decalogus.

Quo sensu in disputationibus Paulinis & nostris, de Justificatione, de Fide & Gratia, accipitur: & tum Evangelio de CHRISTO ἀντιδιηρημένως opponitur: ita ut in uno eodemque actu, respectu ejusdem simul stare nunquàm possint. Hoc sensu accipitur vox Legis in classicis illis locis, quæ Pontificiorum impietati de justitia operum opponimus Rom. 3, 28. Rom.

v

6, 15. Rom. 7, 7. Rom. 8, 3. Rom. 11, 6. Gal. 2, 16. Gal. 5, 18. Eph. 2, 8. & 9. & passim alibi. Hac speciali significatione observatâ, errores suprà notati singuli & universi per se corruunt.


### Question II. On the Definition of the Law

Just as there are various significations of the word Law, according as it is taken either Generally or Specially: so one and the same Definition cannot be accommodated to the word Law, unless under an accurate distinction. Therefore, those are not entirely free from all error who, in Methodical booklets, ask generally, What is the Law of God? and immediately subjoin either this or another similar definition: Law is the supreme reason, implanted in nature, which commands what things are to be done, and forbids the contrary. Or: Law is a doctrine showing what one ought to do and what one ought to omit: just as Varinus defined Law as λόγον προστάσσοντα ἃ δεῖ, καὶ ἀπαγορεύοντα ἃ μὴ δεῖ (a word commanding what one ought to do, and forbidding what one ought not). For definitions of this kind are partly broader, partly narrower than their defined term: For 1. They define the Law of Nature more than the written Law of God. 2. They cannot be accommodated to every signification of Law. 3. They define that which is not properly asked about in this place: since it is not a matter of the Law considered absolutely and in general: but of the divine Law: which even the title of the present Article shows.

Thus they sin no less lightly who, to the Question What is the Law of God, bring forward such a Definition as belongs only to the Moral Law: such as that it is a doctrine delivered by God, commanding what kind of people we ought to be, and what we ought to do and what to omit, and requiring perfect obedience toward God, and pronouncing that God is angry and punishes with eternal death those not performing perfect obedience. This definition certainly does not fit every species of divine Law, but only the Moral. Now, however, it is inconvenient, and done contrary to reason, if a special Definition is brought forward when the Question is still about the Genus. What is more? It does not progress much beyond Philosophical definitions: which themselves express these five members: 1. To command: 2. To forbid: 3. To promise: 4. To bestow rewards: 5. To punish: as Chemnitius notes in his Loci, part 2, page 10.

The Law of God is therefore more fully and perfectly defined by those who establish that it is, from the will of God, a certain and suitable norm and rule of acting and judging, by which the judgments and actions of men, both in approving and pursuing what is right, and in reproving and shunning what is evil, are constituted in a useful and, as far as impunity is concerned, inviolable manner. This definition distinguishes the Law of God from human laws quite clearly: For 1. It expressly states the author himself, which philosophical definitions do not do. 2. It specifically posits the source and origin of divine laws, the will of God, since it is the highest and only measure of justice. 3. It notes the adequate object of the Law, which regards not only the actions of men: but even their judgments: nay, the very sense itself. 4. It agrees with every species of divine Law, as well written as unwritten.

Latin:

Quemadmodum varia sunt significata vocabuli Legis, prout illud vel Generaliter vel Specialiter accipitur: ita non una atque eadem Definitio Legis vocabulo, nisi sub accurata distinctione accommodari potest. Proindè non planè omni errore carent illi, qui in libellis Methodicis generaliter quærunt, Quid est Lex Dei? & statim subjiciunt vel hanc vel aliam consimilem definitionem: Lex est ratio summa, insita in natura, quæ jubet ea, quæ facienda sunt, prohibetque contraria. Vel: Lex est doctrina ostendens, quæ facere, quæ omittere oporteat: uti Varinus definivit Legem esse λόγον προστάσσοντα ἁδεῖ, καὶ ἀπαγορεύοντα ἁ μὴ δεῖ. Ejusmodi enim definitiones partim laxiores, partim angustiores sunt suo definito: Nam 1. Legem magis Naturæ, quàm Legem Dei scriptam definiunt. 2. Non omni significationi Legis accommodari possunt. 3. Definiunt id, de quo propriè hoc loco non quæritur: Si quidem non de Lege absolutè & in genere considerata: sed de divina Lege agitur: id quod vel ipse titulus præsentis Articuli ostendit.

Sic haud leviùs peccant, qui ad Quæstionem Quid sit Lex Dei, proferunt talem Definitionem, quæ soli Legi Morali competit: ut quòd sit doctrina à Deo tradita, præcipiens quales nos esse, & quæ facere, quæ omittere oportet, & requirens perfectam obedientiam erga Deum, ac pronuncians irasci Deum, & punire æterna morte, non præstantes perfectam obedientiam. Hæc sanè Definitio non omni speciei Legis divinæ congruit, sed Morali tantùm. Jam verò inconveniens est, & præter rationem fit, si specialis proferatur Definitio, quando de Genere adhuc est Quæstio. Quid? quòd ea ultra Philosophicas definitiones haud multum progreditur: quæ & ipsæ quinque hæc membra exprimunt: 1. Præci pere: 2. Prohibere: 3. Promittere: 4. Largiri præmia: 5. Punire: uti in Locis annotat Chemnitius, part. 2. pag. 10.

Pleniùs proinde & perfectiùs Lex Dei definitur ab ijs, qui statuunt, quòd sit ex voluntate Dei, talis quædam certa & conveniens agendi judicandique norma atq; regula, quâ judicijs & actionibus hominum, tùm in approbando sectandoq; quæ sunt recta: tùm in reprobando fugiendoq; quæ sunt mala, utilia & quoad impunitatem inviolabili modo constituitur. Discernit hæc definitio Legem Dei à legibus humanis satis luculenter: Nam 1. Autorem ipsum disertè exprimit: id quod Philosophicæ definitiones non faciunt. 2. Fontem atque originem legum divinarum in specie ponit, Dei voluntatem, quippè quæ est summa atque unica Justitiæ mensura. 3. Notat adæquatum Legis objectum, quod non tantùm actiones hominum: sed ipsorum etiam judicia: imò sensum ipsum respicit. 4. Omni speciei Legis divinæ tàm scriptæ, quàm non scriptæ convenit.


### Question III. On the division of the divine law

Our author enumerates these species: Divine Law: Law of Nature: and human Laws. Which division we leave in its place: meanwhile diligently noting these two things. 1. That no Question at all is being agitated in this place concerning human laws: but only concerning the Law of GOD. 2. If we consult the Holy Scriptures more strictly, it is much more correct that Divine Law be divided into written and unwritten Law: which division even Theological Schools commonly follow today.

But by unwritten Law, we understand that which is implanted in Man by nature by the power of the first creation: and could always have been most known to him, even if its precepts and rules had never been committed to letters. And this is that Law of Nature, concerning which the Apostle affirms that the work of the Law is written in the hearts of men: the term of writing being used metaphorically for that Natural impression: Rom. 2, 15. And concerning this species of Law, there will be a discussion for us below expressly: chapter 2. Controversy 1.

We name the Written Law of GOD that Law which, revealed at the beginning by the voice of GOD himself, was not indeed always contained in letters: but was afterwards committed to written tablets by the command of GOD himself. Therefore this appellation depends not on the continuous act of writing: but only on the event: insofar as the Precepts of this Law, having been previously promulgated to the Patriarchs by a singular revelation of GOD, and propagated to posterity by faithful tradition: were at length committed to letters: so that if it were without this writing, nothing or almost nothing of them would be known to us today.

Moreover, this written Law of GOD is divided into three parts. 1. Ceremonial: 2. Forensic: and 3. Moral. Nor are there lacking clear foundations of the Scriptures, upon which this Division can, nay indeed ought to be, built. For 1. GOD himself indicated the diversity of these three parts by three distinct appellations, differing from our custom of speaking more in the sound of the letters than in the sense. Saying, these are the Precepts, 2. Ceremonies, and 3. Judgments, which the LORD commanded, Deut. 6, 1. and 17. Hence Solomon in the dedication of the Hierosolymitan Temple alludes to this, saying, May the LORD our God incline our hearts, that we may keep his commandments, and the ceremonies, and the judgments, which he commanded our fathers, 1. Kings 8, 58.

Then the same is evident, even from the fact that each of these species was promulgated by GOD separately at different intervals of time. For first, GOD recites the Decalogue or moral Law with his own voice, while the whole people listened; and he himself inscribes the same with his own fingers upon tablets. Exod. 20, 1. and Exod. 32, 16. But then, this act of publication finished, Moses is ordered to approach alone to the darkness in which GOD was: and there he receives the pandects of the Forensic or Judicial Laws. Exod. 20, 21. and in the three following chapters. Finally, after that promulgation, Moses was recalled to the mountain, and remaining there for forty days and as many nights, he receives the ceremonial or Ecclesiastical Laws: Exod. 24, 18. and in the six entire subsequent chapters.

Thirdly, this Division is confirmed by the fact that GOD assigned a peculiar place of custody to each of these species: in which they ought to be deposited and preserved: for the Decalogue or Moral Law, the Ark of the LORD, 1. Kings 8, 9. For the Book of Ceremonials, the house of the LORD: in which it is read to have been found in the time of king Josiah: 2. Kings 22, 8. But for the Book of judicial laws, the King's archive: so that he might always have it with him, and judge cause and cause from it. Deut. 17, 18.

Finally, the different mode of administration argues not a little for the diversity of these laws. For GOD did not wish individual laws to be administered by individual persons, whether Ecclesiastical or Political: but he commanded the knowledge of the Decalogue to all: Exod. 20, 18. Deut. 6, 1. and seq. But the manner of divine worship to the Priests, according to that Malach. 2, 6. The lips of the Priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the Law from his mouth. Finally, he commanded the administration of civil judgments to the Hierosolymitan Sanhedrin, and its distinct orders: whose sentences it was a sin to resist. Deut. 17, 8. and following.

These four foundations being observed, every effort and attack of the Jews, who impugn this Division in order to give some color to their impious Talmudic fables, can be overturned without any difficulty. For it stands firm and unshaken, that whatever cannot be referred to these three species of Mosaic Law, and is neither contained in them word for word, nor can be elicited from them by an immovable consequence: that GOD is not the author of it, by whatever name or pretext it comes: according to that authentic [command] annexed to the Law: What I command thee, this only do to the LORD: neither add anything nor diminish: Deut. 12, 32.

Latin:

AUtor noster has species recenset: Legem divinam: Legem Naturæ: & Leges humanas. Quam διαίρεσιν nos suo loco relinquimus: duo hæc interim sedulò monentes. 1. De legibus humanis nullam prorsus hoc loco agitari Quæstionem: sed tantùm de Lege DEI. 2. Si pressius Scripturas Sacras consulamus, multò rectiùs Legem Divinam dividi in Legem scriptam & non scriptam: Quam divisionem Scholæ etiam Theologicæ hodiè communiter sequuntur.

Per Legem autem non scriptam, intelligimus eam, quæ Homini naturâ vi primæ creationis est insita: ipsique semper poterat esse notissima, si vel maximè ejus præcepta atque regulæ, literis nunquàm fuissent consignatæ. Et hæc est Lex illa Naturæ, de qua Apostolus affirmat, quòd opus Legis Naturâ scriptum sit in cordibus hominum: Scriptionis termino Metaphoricè pro impressione illa Naturali usurpato: Rom. 2, 15. Et de hac quidem specie Legis, infrà nobis ex professo futura est disputatio: capite 2. Controversiâ 1.

Legem DEI Scriptam nominamus eam Legem, quæ initiò ipsius DEI voce patefacta, non quidem semper literis erat comprehensa: sed postmodùm ipsius DEI jussu per Mosen in tabulas scriptas est relata. Dependet proindè hæc appellatio, non à continuo scriptionis actu: sed tantùm ab eventu: quatenùs nimirùm Præcepta Legis hujus priùs singulari DEI patefactione Patriarchis promulgata, & fideli traditione ad posteros propagata: tandem literis sunt consignata: ita ut si absque hac scriptione esset, nobis hodiè, vel parùm, vel planè nihil de illis constaret.

Cæterùm Lex hæc DEI scripta in tres partes dispescitur. 1. Ceremonialem: 2. Forensem: & 3. Moralem. Neque desunt luculenta Scripturarum fundamenta, quibus Divisio hæc superstrui potest, imò verò debet. Nam 1. DEUS ipse diversitatem trium istarum partium, tribus distinctis appellationibus indigitavit, sono magis literarum, quàm sensu à nostra loquendi cosuetudine discrepantibus. Hæc inquiens sunt Præcepta, 2. Ceremoniæ, & 3 Judicia, quæ mandavit DOMINUS, Deut. 6, 1. & 17. Hinc Salomon in dedicatione Templi Hierosolymitani huc alludit, DOMINVS DEUS noster, inquiens, inclinet corda nostra, ut custodiamus mandata ejus, & ceremonias, & judicia, quaecunq; mandavit patribus nostris, 1. Reg. 8, 58.

Deindè patet idem, vel indè etiam, quòd diversis temporum intervallis quælibet istarum specierum seorsim à DEO est promulgata. Primùm enim Decalogum sive Legem moralem DEUS voce sua, auscultante universo populo recitat; eandémque suis digitis ipse tabulis inscribit. Exod 20, 1. & Exod 32, 16. Deindè verò finito hoc publicationis actu, Moses jubetur solus accedere ad caliginem, in qua erat DEUS: & ibi Legum Forensium sive Judicialium pandectas accipit. Exod. 20, 21. & sequentibus tribus capitibus. Tandem demùm post promulgationem istam Moses in montem revocatus, ibíque quadraginta diebus, totidemque noctibus commoratus, Leges ceremoniales sive Ecclesiasticas accipit: Exod. 24, 18. & capitibus subsequentibus sex integris.

Tertiò Divisionem hanc confirmat, quòd DEUS singulis istis speciebus peculiarem Custodiæ locum adsignavit: in quo reponi & asservari deberent: Decalogo quidem sive Legi Morali, Arcam DOMINI, 1. Reg. 8, 9. Libro Ceremonialium, domum DOMINI: in qua ille tempore Josiæ regis, inventus esse legitur: 2 Reg 22, 8. Libro verò judicialium legum, Regis archivum: ita ut illud semper secum haberet, & ex eo causam & causam dijudicaret. Deut. 17, 18.

Tandem haud parum Legum istarum diversitatem arguit, diversus administrationis modus. Neque enim DEUS singulas leges à singulis, sive Ecclesiasticis sive Politicis personis administrari voluit: sed Decalogi notitiam mandavit omnibus: Exod. 20, 18. Deut. 6, 1. & seq. Cultuum autem divinorum rationem Sacerdotibus, secundum illud Malach. 2, 6. Labia Sacerdotis custodient scientiam, & Legem requirent ex ore ipsius. Judiciorum denique civilium administrationem mandavit Synedrio Hierosolymitano, ejusdémq; distinctis ordinibus: quorum sententiis reluctari nefas erat. Deut. 17, 8. & sequentibus.

Quatuor istis fundamentis observatis, nullo negotio everti potest omnis Judæorum conatus & impetus, Divisionem hanc ideò impugnantium, ut impiis suis fabellis Thalmudicis fucum aliquem faciant. Stat enim firmum & inconcussum, quicquid ad tres istas species Legis Mosaicæ referri nequit, neque in illis aut αὐτολεξεὶ continetur, aut per immotam consequentiam indè elici potest: illud DEUM non habere autorem, quocunque veniat nomine, aut prætextu: secundum authenticam illam Legi annexam: Quod præcipio tibi, hoc tantùm facito DOMINO: nec addas quicquam nec minuas: Deut. 12, 32.


### Question IV. on the Ceremonial Law

Three things especially concerning the Ceremonial Law are called into discussion in the Schools of the Theologians: First, it is asked: What is its definition. 2. What is its Cause. 3. What is the manner of its abrogation.

Latin:

TRia potissimùm de Lege Ceremoniali, in Scholis Theologorum sub disquisitionem vocantur: Primùm enim quæritur: Quæ ejus definitio. 2. Quæ Causa. 3. Quis abrogationis modus.


### Question IV. on the Ceremonial Law: II. What are the causes

Concerning the definition, it is easily agreed among Theologians that the Ceremonial Law is doctrine delivered by God concerning external rites and gestures to be observed regarding Sacrifices, clothing, food, movement, rest, and other exercises of this kind.

Therefore this Law differs greatly from the Moral Law: Since it does not deliver the internal reason for divine worship, as the Moral [Law] does: but only the external form or species: such, indeed, as constitutes the manner for the dispensation of Sacraments and Sacrifices, the observation of times, persons, places, sacred utensils, clothing, food, movement, and rest in Sacred matters: of all of which the book of Leviticus of Moses exhibits a nearly complete commentary.

II. What is its Cause.

Now, indeed, regarding the Causes; the Nature and proper affection, as it were, of the Ceremonial Laws is most rightly and solidly investigated if the Levitical ceremonies or rites are examined a little more exactly according to those four kinds of Causes: Efficient, Material, Formal, and Final.

Regarding the Efficient Cause of ecclesiastical rites, it is rightly established as the Person either acting or suffering. The acting or administering Person is either the High Priest, or the Priests, or the Prince, or the whole people, or even a private person. The suffering Person is one who either participates in the worship or in whose name the Sacrifice is offered.

The Material Cause regards either the essence itself or at least the accidents of those ceremonies. The former, the Essential Matter, is twofold: One, from which; the other, concerning which. The matter from which are either Animals: or things born from the earth. Animals are of four kinds: For they were either of the genus of oxen, such as: Calf, Cow, Ox. Or of the genus of goats; such as: He-goat, Kid: Or of the genus of sheep, such as: Lamb, Ram. Or of the genus of birds, such as: Dove, Turtledove. Of things born from the earth, some were offered dry, such as: Fine flour, Grain, Fruit, Incense, Salt: Bread, and that baked either in an oven, or in a frying pan, or on a gridiron: some liquid; such as Wine and Oil.

The matter concerning which are both benefits received from God: and offenses committed by men: as one may read in Leviticus 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

The accidents of the Levitical rites regard either Time, to which feasts and solemnities are to be referred, the treatment of which is partly διδασκαλικὴ (didactic), describing the feasts and solemnities both of days, insofar as they concern the whole people generally, Levit. 23, or the Priests alone specifically, chap. 24, and of years, namely the seventh and the fiftieth, chap. 25. Partly παραινετικὴ (exhortatory), exhorting to serious and diligent solemnity, as well as to the observation of the whole law.

The formal cause regards the different manner of administering. For burnt offerings were entirely consumed, and nothing of them was eaten: The host for sin itself was eaten only on the day of the sacrifice in the atrium of the temple: Peace offerings were eaten on the very day of the sacrifice, yet not everywhere, but only in Jerusalem. Finally, peace offerings, which were to be brought by vow, were not always eaten on the day of the offering, but also on the next following day.

The final cause of the Levitical rites was various and manifold: and that either special or general. The special consists in that legal purification which was performed either in one person who had defiled himself, whether from the eating and touching of unclean animals, Levit. 11, or from childbirth, chap. 12, or from leprosy of the body or garments, chap. 13, or from the impurity of a house, chap. 14, or from a more foul discharge, chap. 15. Or it was performed in many, namely the whole assembly of the Church, chap. 16, both regarding the various objects of uncleanness in the common life of men, chap. 17, and regarding ecumenical matters, such as the degrees of affinity and consanguinity, chap. 18, and finally regarding political matters, both with respect to subjects, chap. 19, and the magistrate, chap. 20.

The Apostle defines the general and chief final cause of the Ceremonial Law when he names it a shadow of good things to come, and a schoolmaster unto Christ. Coloss. 2:17, Hebr. 10:1, Gal. 3:24. Now, just as a schoolmaster is set over a boy, not for his whole life, but only for the years of childhood: so this Law had a finite age prefixed to it, over which it should preside, and that a weaker or ruder one, until the exhibition of CHRIST the Savior. Furthermore: Just as a schoolmaster, by instructing a pupil, looks solely to this, that by proposing childish rudiments to him, he may prepare him more and more for greater things: so this part of the Mosaic Law ought to have prepared and promoted the Jewish people only up to a certain point, until, having overcome the ruder elements, they could finally make progress worthy of a mature age under CHRIST.

This Law faithfully performed both of its duties in a likewise twofold manner. The former, by admonishing concerning sin, concerning the wrath of GOD, and concerning eternal condemnation: which was done in the slaughter and burning of victims. The latter, by shadowing forth the person, office, and benefits of CHRIST the Messiah: which was done, both by the multitude, and by the variety, and by the frequent repetition of the sacrifices. All of which could serve as an instance of a certain and infallible argument or indication that nothing firm and solid existed in such a variety of Sacrifices: but that they merely sustained the type and figure of that One and most perfect Expiatory Sacrifice, which the seed of the woman was one day to offer for the sins of the whole world. Which was the very reason why this Law was proper to one time indeed, but not to one nation. For whoever embraced the Religion of the Jews, even if he were not an Israelite, nor lived in Judea: he was nevertheless bound to the Ceremonial Law of Moses: so that it might be established that the Messiah would be the Redeemer not only of the Jews, but of all peoples whatsoever, Gen. 17, 12. Exod. 20, 9. Exod 12, 15.

Furthermore, whoever desires to know more about these causes of the Ceremonial Law, let him consult part 2 of the Locorum of Chemnitz, page 31 and the following few pages: as also the Commentary of Dr. David Chytraeus on Leviticus. We must study brevity.

Latin:

DE definitione Inter Theologos facilè conve-nit, quòd nimirùm Lex Ceremonialis sit do-ctrina à Deo tradita, de ritibus ac gestibus externis, circa Sacrificia, vestitum; cibum, motum, quietem, & alia id genus exercitia externa observandis.

Differt proindè plurimùm hæc Lex à Lege Morali: Siquidem non internam cultus divini rationem, sicut Moralis: sed externam tantùm formam sive speciem tradit: talem nimirùm, quæ dispensationi Sacramentorum, & Sacrifi-ciorum, observationi temporum, personarum, locorum, utensilium sacrorum, vestitus, cibi, motus, quietis in re Sacra modum constituit: Quorum omnium commentarium quasi inte-grum, Mosis Leviticus exhibet.

II. Quæ Causa.

JAm verò Quôad Causas; rectissimè ac solidis-simè Natura & propria quasi affectio Legum Ceremonialium investigatur; si secundum qua-tuor illa Causarum genera, Efficientem, Materia-lem, Formalem, Finalem, Ceremoniæ sive ritus Levitici paulò exactiùs examinentur.

Quoad Causam Efficientem rituum Eccle-siasticorum, ea rectè constituitur Persona vel agens, vel patiens. Persona agens sive admini-strans, est vel Pontifex, vel Sacerdotes, vel Prin-ceps, vel totus populus, vel persona etiam priva-ta. Persona Patiens est, quæ vel cultui interest, vel cujus nomine Sacrificium offertur.

Causa Materialis vel Essentiam ipsam, vel saltem accidentia Ceremoniarum istarum respi-cit. Prior illa Materia Essentialis est gemina: Una, Ex quâ: Altera, Circa quam. Materia ex qua sunt vel Animalia: vel ex terrâ nascentia. Animalia sunt quadruplicis generis: Vel enim erant de genere boum, ut: Vitulus, Vacca, Bos. Vel de genere caprarum; ut Hircus, Hœdus: Vel de genere ovium, ut: Agnus, Aries. Vel de genere avium, ut: Columba, Turtur. Ex terrâ nascentia offerebantur partim arida, ut: Simila, Granum, Fructus, Thus, Sal: Panis, isque vel in clibano, vel in fartagine, vel in craticula coctus: partim liquida; ut Vinum & Oleum.

Materia circa quam sunt tùm beneficia à Deo accepta: tùm maleficia ab hominibus patrata: uti Levitici 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. legere licet.

Accidentia rituum Leviticorum vel respiciunt Tempus, ad quod sunt referenda festa & solennitates, quarum tractatio, partim est διδασκαλικὴ, describens festa & solennitates tùm dierum, quatenùs vel generatim concernunt totum populum, Levit. 23. vel solos Sacerdotes speciatim, cap. 24. tùm annorum, Septimi nimirùm & quinquagesimi, cap. 25. Partim παραινετικὴ exhortatoria ad seriam sedulamque tùm solennitatem, tùm totius legis observationem.

Causa formalis diversum administrandi modum respicit. Holocausta enim tota comburebantur, neque quicquam ex iis comedebatur: Hostia pro peccato ipso sacrificii die comedebatur solùm in atrio templi: Hostiæ pacificæ comedebantur ipso sacrificii die, non tamen ubique, sed tantùm in Hierusalem. Hostiæ denique pacificæ, quæ ex voto afferendæ erant, comedebantur non ipso semper oblationis die, sed & subsequente proximo.

Causa finalis rituum Leviticorum fuit varia & multiplex: eaque vel Specialis, vel Generalis. Specialis consistit in emundatione illa legali, quæ fiebat vel in homine uno, qui se polluerat, sive ex esu & contactu animalium immundorum, Levit. 11. sive ex puerperio, cap. 12. sive ex lepra corporis aut vestium; cap. 13. sive ex impuritate domus: cap 14. sive ex fluxu fœdiore, cap. 15. Vel fiebat in pluribus, toto nempè Ecclesiæ cœtu, cap. 16. tùm quoad varia immundiciei objecta, in communi hominum vita: cap. 17. tùm quoad Oecumenica, ut de gradibus affinitatis & consanguinitatis, cap. 18. tùm denique quoad Politica, tàm respectu subditorum, cap. 19. quàm Magistratus, cap. 20.

Generalem eámque præcipuam Legis Ceremonialis Causam Finalem Apostolus definit, cùm eam nominat umbram futurorum bonorum, & Pædagogum ad Christum. Coloss. 2, 17. Hebr. 10, 1. Gal. 3, 24. Jam verò, quemadmodum Pædagogus præficitur puero, non in totam ejus ætatem: sed tantùm in annos pueritiæ: sic Lex hæc finitam ætatem sibi habuit præfixam, cui præesset, eamque imbecilliorem sive rudiorem, usque ad exhibitionem CHRISTI Servatoris. Deindè: Quemadmodum Pædagogus discipulum informando id unicè spectat, ut ipsum rudimentis puerilibus propositis, magis magisque ad majora præparet: sic pars hæc Legis Mosaicæ præparare ac promovere debuit populum Judaicum aliquò usque duntaxat, donec superatis rudioribus elementis, progressus virili ætate dignos sub CHRISTO demùm facere possent.

Utrumque hoc suum officium Lex hæc gemino itidem modo fideliter est executa. Prius illud, commonefaciendo de peccato, de ira DEI, de æterna condemnatione: id quod factum est in mactatione & combustione victimarum. Posterius hoc, adumbrando personam, officium & beneficia CHRISTI Messiæ: id quod factum est, tùm multitudine, tùm varietate, tùm crebra repetitione sacrificiorum. Quæ omnia certi atque infallibilis argumenti sive indicii instar esse poterant, tantæ Sacrificiorum varietati nihil firmi atque solidi inesse: sed typum duntaxat & figuram sustinere Unici illius ac perfectissimi Expiatorii Sacrificii, quod aliquando semen mulieris pro peccatis totius mundi erat oblaturum. Quæ ipsa causa fuit, propter quam Lex hæc, unius quidem temporis, sed non unius gentis fuit propria. Quisquis enim Judæorum Religionem amplexabatur, licet Israelita non esset, neq; in Judæa habitaret: ad Ceremonialem tamen Legem Mosis obligabatur: ut sic constaret, Messiam non Judæorum tantùm, sed omnium omninò populorum fore Redemtorem, Genes. 17, 12. Exod. 20, 9. Exod 12, 15.

Cæterùm qui plura de causis istis Legis Ceremonialis scire desiderat, is consulat partem 2. Locorum Chemnit. pag. 31. & seqq. aliquot: ut & Commentarium Doct. Davidis Chytrei in Leviticum. Nobis brevitati studendum.


### Question IV. on the Ceremonial Law: III. Abrogation of the Ceremonial Law

It remains that we say something concerning the Abrogation of this Law. For very many testimonies of the Scriptures prove that it was prescribed to the ancient people for a time: among which that passage of Daniel 9, v. last, easily holds the chief place. The Messiah shall confirm the covenant (the new one, that is) with many, for one week: and in the middle of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease. But since in this part the reason for the Ceremonial Law is almost the same as that which was for the Mosaic Forensic Laws: we shall treat of the abrogation of both, in the following Question 5, expressly.

Latin:

SUpereft, ut de Abrogatione Legis hujus aliquid dicamus. Ad tempus enim eam populo Veteri fuisse præscriptam, benè multa Scripturarum testimonia evincunt: inter quæ principem facilè locum obtinet illud Daniel. 9, v. ult. Messias confirmabit pactum (novum scilicet) multis, hebdomada una: & in dimidio hebdomadis cessare faciet hostiam & sacrificium. Verùm cùm hac in parte eadem fermè sit ratio Legis Ceremonialis, quæ fuit Legum Forensium Mosaicarum: nos de utriusque abrogatione, in subsequente Quæst. 5. ex professo agemus.


### Question V. on the Forensic or Mosaic Judicial Law

The Mosaic Forensic or Judicial Law contains divine precepts, by which it is prescribed how one must judge in civil causes, controversies, and offenses of the people: how likewise external discipline ought to be preserved among the Israelite people. The sum of these precepts can be restricted to two main categories: the former of which is concerning the Civil Magistrate: the latter concerning the duty of subjects. Whatever, therefore, constitutes and informs the order and process of forensic judgments concerning the species and form of various contracts, concerning the distinguishing of domains, concerning the division of an inheritance, concerning the law and rite of marriages, concerning repudiation, divorces, concerning servitudes, concerning the order and laws of the militia, concerning witnesses, concerning enemies, concerning the establishing of punishments and penalties against any criminals whatsoever, and concerning similar political matters: that can and ought to be referred to this part of the Mosaic Law. It is described, however, in Exodus, Leviticus, and most especially in Deuteronomy. But it is asked in this place, whether by this means the Forensic Law is not confused with the Moral: since both this and that prohibit those crimes and wicked acts, concerning the punishment of which the Forensic Law is said to be concerned. But the answer is easy by applying the distinction between crimes insofar as they are such: and between the same, insofar as they are subject to a certain determination of punishments. Thefts, therefore, adulteries, homicides, perjuries, and other offenses similar to these, pertain to the decalogue or Moral Law, insofar as they are repugnant to the will of GOD and disturb the society of the human race: But by what kind of punishments they ought to be restrained: that the forensic laws determine.

It can be judged most correctly from these things which have been said concerning the Final Cause of the Forensic Laws. For their proximate end was none other than the preservation of external discipline among the people. The more remote end, however, was that illustrious distinction of the Mosaic polity from the polities of any other nations whatsoever.

But perhaps someone might ask why we do not use the same forensic laws today in our own courts: But sufficiently adequate reasons for this matter can be given. 1. The diversity of commonwealths. For these laws were adapted only to the Israelites, and to their commonwealth, and not to all nations in general. If that commonwealth still existed today, perhaps it would still use those same laws in its courts (at least with the exception of those which were then established against violators of the ceremonial laws, which are today completely abrogated), especially since the Gospel takes nothing away at all, nor does it bring any change to political constitutions, insofar as they conform to the general equity which ought to prevail everywhere and always. 2. The forensic laws were not promulgated by GOD to the end that they should serve every time and every people: but only that, until the time of the Messiah, they might distinguish that ancient people from other nations. 3. With those laws abrogated through Christ, Evangelical Liberty certainly makes use of its right in this regard most correctly: so that it does not submit itself in the least to the yoke of the Jews.

Finally, it is asked in this place, how the abrogation both of the forensic and ceremonial Mosaic laws stands. This question can hardly be resolved more correctly than if the following three hypotheses are observed more accurately.

I. That both Laws were to be abrogated upon the arrival of Christ the Savior is clear first of all from the intention of GOD himself. For He willed them for a certain time only, just as they were sanctioned for the Republic of the Israelite nation alone. For which end GOD always added this sort of restriction to their very promulgation throughout Exodus and Leviticus: You shall keep these in your generations. Now, therefore, the Israelite Republic having been abolished, their laws, both Ceremonial and Forensic, certainly expired of their own accord. Furthermore, Scripture confirms this specifically regarding the Ceremonial laws, Daniel 9, v. last: The Messiah shall confirm the Covenant (the new one, that is) with many for one week, and in the middle of the week He shall cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease. Thus the Apostles in the Jerusalem Council, Acts 15, decree that the yoke of the Ceremonial Law, which not even the Jews could bear, is not to be imposed upon the Gentiles, thus Colossians 2, 16. Let no one, says the Apostle, judge you in food or in drink, or in the part of a feast day. Galatians 5, 2: If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing. But concerning the Forensic laws specifically, that passage sounds forth, Galatians 3, 28: In Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek: for you are all one in Him. And 1 Peter 2, 13: Be subject to every human ordinance. But especially from the Old Testament, that prophecy of Jacob the Patriarch, Genesis 49, 10, pertains to this, concerning the taking away of the scepter from Judah upon the arrival of Shiloh or the Messiah.

In general, however, that oracle of Jehovah, Jeremiah 31, 31 & 32, proves the abrogation of both Laws: Behold, the days are coming, and I will make a NEW covenant: not according to the covenant that I made with your fathers: but I will put my law in their inward parts. And that passage, Hebrews 8, 13: By saying new, He has made the first old: Now that which is made old and grows aged is near to destruction. Hence the Apostle infers this general Aphorism, Romans 6, 14: You are not under Law, but under Grace. And Romans 7, 6: We have been delivered from the Law.

II. Hypothesis. These laws were not abrogated as if they were evil or vicious in themselves, as Marcion once did not hesitate to blaspheme: But because the Israelite Republic itself has been abolished: and CHRIST having been brought forth in the flesh, the types, figures, and shadows of the Ceremonial Laws, which prefigured CHRIST, expired of their own accord. For in some ceremonies lay hidden most beautiful images of the benefits of CHRIST, an excellent explanation of which the Epistle to the Hebrews contains: just as the Ark of the Covenant bore a notable image of the Church. Now, however, the Ark was placed in the Sanctuary: Thus that is finally the true Church which embraces the covenant, that is, the Word of GOD. The tablets placed in the ark showed that the Church is always the guardian of Holy Scripture, in which GOD has revealed Himself. The golden tablets, by which the ark was covered, were the name of the mercy seat, by which CHRIST was signified as Mediator, by whose Propitiation the Church would be protected against the wrath and judgment of GOD. The Cherubim, having the touch of their wings and mutual sight, noted the different ministry of the doctrine in both Testaments, yet an elegant consensus in the same. By the use of poles and staves, the work of the ministers was prefigured. In the order of the Levitical Priesthood, than which there was no better or more elegant since the world was created, there was also an illustrious Example. But when the Papacy wished to express an imitation of it, it was perniciously mistaken through foul κακοζηλίᾳ (bad zeal).

III. This abrogation is not to be taken so loosely, as if no Ceremonies henceforth have a place in the Church: or that it is simply prohibited to observe some Levitical Ceremonies out of Evangelical Liberty: that which conflicts with that Apostolic decree, sanctioned concerning abstinence from things strangled and from blood: Acts 15, 20. Or finally, as if men of the New Testament ought to be subject to no government or political jurisdiction at all, as the Anabaptists rave: But this abrogation is to be understood in such a way that, namely, regarding the Ceremonial Law, the bond of necessary observation has been clearly dissolved, so that Christians are not bound to it: Thus also regarding the Forensic Law, the obedience owed to the Magistrate has by no means been abolished: For this pertains to the Moral Law: But only that special respect has been abrogated which requires nothing but the strict observation of those municipal laws prescribed for the Israelite Republic.

Rightly, therefore, Chemnitius infers that we today in our forum use the Imperial and Saxon Law, not because these legislators established their laws more wisely than GOD himself, who alone is wise, Romans 16, 27. But those Laws are preferred to the Mosaic Laws, κατὰ τι (in a certain respect), but not ἁπλῶς (simply), namely because of the circumstances of times and places: Likewise because of the different condition of nations, and the dissimilar form of Republics.

For GOD did not bring those Forensic Laws so that they would suit the discipline of all nations: but He accommodated them to the customs of the Israelite people. 2. To the condition of that land because of neighboring regions. 3. To the circumstance of that time, when the Messiah was expected, to be born in that polity. 4. To the form and state of that Republic, part 2, Locorum, page 28. But the Jews have something to object in this place, namely that GOD himself, both concerning Circumcision and the remaining laws, expressly affirms that they will be like an everlasting and perpetual covenant, Gen. 17, 7. Exod. 12, v 14. chap. 31, 16. Levit. 23, 14, 21, 31, 41. Levit. 24, 3. But it is most correctly answered that a Sophism of Figure of Diction is committed: which emerges from the Hebrew word עולם olam, which according to the condition of the thing of which it is predicated, either denotes absolute eternity, as when it is predicated of the Kingdom of Christ, of God himself, and of divine things: Or it denotes some periodic duration, and restricted to a certain time, as when it is predicated of the condition of Servants, Exod. 21, 6. and of other momentary things; and thus it is also predicated of Ceremonial and forensic Laws: which we have already demonstrated above to have been restricted to a certain interval of time by the intention of God himself.

Latin:

LEx Forensis sive Judicialis Mosaica continet præcepta divina, quibus præscribitur, quomodo in causis, controversiis, & delictis populi civilibus judicandum sit: quomodo item in populo Ismelitico externa disciplina conservari debeat. Summa verò istorum præceptorum ad duo summa genera restringi potest: quorum prius est de Magistratus Civilis: Posterius de subditorum officio. Quicquid ergo Judiciorum forensium ordinem & processum de contractuum variorum speciebus & forma, de distinguendis dominijs, de herciscunda hæreditate, de jure & ritu conjugiorum, de repudio, divortijs, de servitutibus, de ordine & legibus militiæ, de testibus, de hostibus, de pœnis ac supplicijs contra quosvis sceleratos statuendis, deque similibus rebus politicis, constituit & informat: id ad hanc partem Legis Mosaicæ referri potest & debet. Describitur autem ea in Exodo, Levitico, potissimùm autem in Deuteronomio. Quæritur autem hoc loco, Annon hoc pacto Lex Forensis cum Morali confundatur: siquidem tàm hæc quàm illa prohibet scelera atq́; flagitia illa, circa quæ punienda Lex Forensis versari dicitur. Sed facilis est Responsio adhibita distinctione inter scelera quatenùs talia sunt: & inter eadem, quatenùs certæ pœnarum determinationi subjacent. Furta ergò, adulteria, homicidia, perjuria, & his consimilia alia delicta, pertinent ad decalogum sive Legem Moralem, quatenùs DEI voluntati repugnant, & societatem generis humani turbant: Verùm quo pœnarum genere ea coërceri debeant: illud Leges forenses determinant.

Potest ex his quæ dicta sunt, de Causa Finali Legum Forensium rectissimè judicari. Finis enim earum proximus nullus fuit alius, quàm externæ disciplinæ in populo Conservatio. Remotior autem fuit, illustris illa distinctio politiæ Mosaicæ, à quarumvis aliarum gentium politiis.

Sed quærat fortasse aliquis, cur non ijsdem legibus Forensibus hodieq́; utamur in nostro foro: Verùm Causæ hujus rei satis sufficientes dari possunt. 1. Diversitas Rerumpublicarum. Solis enim Israëlitis, eorundemque Reipublicæ, non verò omnibus in universum gentibus Leges hæ erant accommodatæ. Si jam hodieque consisteret illa Respublica, fortè iisdem legibus in foro eâ adhuc uteretur (iis saltem exceptis, quæ in violatores Legum Ceremonialium, hodiè penitùs abrogatarum, tùm erant constitutæ) præsertim cum Evangelium nihil prorsus deroget, vel mutationem ullam afferat Constitutionibus politicis, quatenùs quidem illæ congruunt cum æquitate generali, quæ ubique & semper valere debet. 2. Leges forenses non eo fine à DEO sunt promulgatæ, ut omni tempori, omnique populo inservirent: sed tantùm ut ad tempus usque Messiæ, populum illum veterem ab aliis gentibus distinguerent. 3. Abrogatis per Christum Legibus illis, utiq; Libertas Evangelica hac in parte rectissimè suo jure utitur: ut Judæorum jugo se minimè submittat.

Tandem quæritur hoc loco, Quomodo abrogatio tùm Forensium, tùm Ceremonialium Legum Mosaicarum sese habeat. Quæ quæstio vix rectiùs expediri potest, quàm si subsequentes hypotheses tres accuratiùs observentur.

I. Utrasque Leges sub adventum Christi Servatoris abrogandas fuisse, ex ipsius DEI intentione primùm liquet. Voluit enim eas ad certum duntaxat tempus, ut & ad solam Gentis Israëliticæ Rempublicam sancitas. Quo fine passim in Exodo & Levit eò DEUS semper ipsarum promulgationi hanc quasi restrictionem adjecit: Servabitis hæc in generationibus VESTRIS. Jam E. Repub. Israëliticâ abolitâ, utique vel ultrò ejus expirarunt Leges tùm Ceremoniales, tùm Forenses. Deindè in specie de Ceremonialibus hoc confirmat Scriptura, Daniel. 9. v. ult. Messias confirmabit Pactum (novum scilicet) multis, hebdomada una, & in dimidio hebdomadis cessare faciet hostiam & Sacrificium. Sic Apostoli in Concilio Hierosolymitano, Actor. 15. decernunt, Gentibus non esse imponendum jugum Legis Ceremonialis, quod ne quidem Judæi portare potuerint, Sic Coloss. 2, 16. Nemo vos, inquit Apostolus, judicet in cibo aut potu, aut parte diei festi. Galat. 5, 2. Si circumcidamini, Christus nihil vobis proderit. De Forensibus autem in specie sonat illud, Galat. 3, 28. in Christo Jesu non est Judæus, neq; Græcus : Omnes enim vos unum estis in ipso. Et 1. Petr. 2, 13. Subditi estote Omni ordinationi humanæ. Cumprimis verò ex Veteri Testamento huc pertinet Vaticinium illud Jacobi Patriarchæ Genes. 49, 10. de auferendo sceptro de Juda, sub adventum Siloh sive Messiæ.

In genere autem utrarumque Legum abrogationem evincit oraculum illud Jehovæ, Jerem. 31, 31. & 32. Ecce dies venient, & faciam fœdus NOVUM: non secundum pactum, quod pepigi cum patribus vestris : sed dabo legem meam in visceribus eorum. Et illud Hebr. 8, 13. Dicendo novum, antiquavit prius : Quod autem antiquatur & senescit, propinquum est interitui. Hinc Apostolus generalem hunc infert Aphorismum, Roman. 6, 14. Non estis sub Lege, sed sub Gratia. Et Rom. 7, 6. à Lege liberati sumus.

II. Hypothesis. Leges hæ non sunt ideò abrogatæ, quasi in seipsis essent malæ aut vitiosæ, quemadmodum Marcion olim blasphemare non dubitavit: Sed ideò, quia ipsâ Respublica Israëlitica est abolita : & CHRISTO in carnem edito, ultrò expirarunt typi, figuræ & umbræ Legum Ceremonialium, quæ CHRISTUM præfigurabant. In Ceremoniis enim nonnullis pulcherrimæ latuerunt imagines de beneficiis CHRISTI, quarum egregiam explicationem continet Epistola ad Hebræos: ut Arca fœderis Ecclesiæ imaginem insignem gerebat. Jam verò Arca reponebatur in Sanctuario: Sic ea demùm vera est Ecclesia, quæ fœdus, id est, Verbum DEI amplectitur. Tabulæ in arca repositæ ostendebant, Ecclesiam semper esse custodem S. Scripturæ, in qua DEUS se patefecerit. Tabulæ aureæ, quâ arca tegebatur, propitiatorii nomen erant, quo CHRISTUS significabatur Mediator, cujus Propitiatione Ecclesia adversus iram & judicium DEI protegeretur. Cherubini tactum alarum, & conspectum mutuum habentes, doctrinæ in utroque Testamento diversum quidem ministerium : sed in eodem consensum elegantem notabant. Usu baculorum & vectium, opera ministrorum præfigurabatur. In ordine Sacerdotii Levitici, quo non fuit melior & elegantior ab orbe condito, illustre etiam Exemplum fuit. Verùm cùm Papatus vellet ejusdem imitationem exprimere, fœdâ κακοζηλίᾳ perniciosè erratum fuit.

III. Abrogatio hæc non ita laxè accipienda est, quasi vel nullæ porrò in Ecclesia Ceremoniæ locum ampliùs habeant: vel aliquas Leviticas Ceremonias ex Libertate Evangelica servare, simpliciter sit prohibitum: id quod cum decreto illo Apostolico pugnat, sancito de abstinentia, à suffocato & sanguine : Actor. 15, 20. Vel denique, ac si nulli prorsus regimini sive jurisdictioni politicæ subesse debeant Novi Testamenti homines, uti Anabaptistæ infaniunt: Sed ita hæc abrogatio est intelligenda, quòd nimirùm quoad Legem Ceremonialem, necessariæ observationis vinculum planè sit dissolutum, ut ad eam Christiani non sint adstricti: Sic etiam quoad Legem Forensem, obedientia Magistratui debita minimè sit abolita : Hæc enim ad Legem Moralem pertinet: Sed specialis tantùm ille respectus sit abrogatus, qui non nisi Legum illarum municipalium, Reipublicæ Israëliticæ præscriptarum, strictam observationem exigit.

Rectè proindè infert Chemnitius, nos hodiè nostro in foro, uti Jure Cæsareo & Saxonico, non quòd hi Legislatores sapientiùs Leges suas condiderint, quàm ipse DEUS, qui solus est sapiens. Rom. 16, 27. Sed præferri illa Jura Legibus Mosaicis, κατὰ τι, non verò ἁπλῶς, nempè propter circumstantias temporum & locorum: Item propter diversam conditionem gentium, & dissimilem formam Rerumpublicarum.

DEUS enim non tulit Leges illas Forenses, ut convenirent disciplinæ omnium gentium: sed accommodavit illas ad mores populi Israëlitici. 2. Ad conditionem illius terræ propter vicinas regiones. 3. Ad circumstantiam illius temporis, cùm expectabatur Messias, in illa politia nascendus. 4. Ad formam & statum illius Reipublicæ part. 2. Locorum, pag. 28. Sed habent Judæi quod hoc loco objiciant, nempè quòd DEUS ipse, tùm de Circumcisione, tùm de reliquis legibus disertè affirmet, fore eas instar fœderis sempiterni ac perpetui, Genes. 17, 7. Exod. 12, v 14. cap. 31, 16. Levit. 23, 14, 21, 31, 41. Levit. 24, 3. Verùm rectissimè respondetur committi Sophisma Figuræ Dictionis: quod emergit ex vocabulo Hebræo עולם olam, quæ secundum conditionem rei, de qua prædicatur, vel absolutam æternitatem notat, ut quando de Regno Christi, de Deo ipso, rebusque divinis prædicatur: Vel notat durationem aliquam periodicam, & ad certum tempus adstrictam, ut quando de conditione Servorum, Exod. 21, 6. deque aliis rebus momentaneis; & sic etiam de Legibus Ceremonialibus ac forensibus prædicatur: quas ex ipsius Dei intentione ad certum temporis intervallum suisse astrictas, jam suprà demonstravimus.


### On the Moral Law

IN the Schools of Theologians, a twofold consideration of the Decalogue, or Moral Law, is usually instituted: One General, which weighs the nature and proper affection of the whole system: The other special, which treats more accurately the exposition of the individual Precepts. Both lie open most widely in the multitude and variety of both Questions and things: We, for this occasion, having put aside those things which are usually proposed for the common people from the pulpit, will ventilate only those ζητήματα (questions), for which there can be some use in the Schools of Theologians concerning controversies.

But at the beginning we define the Moral Law or Decalogue as being the eternal and immovable wisdom and rule of Justice in GOD, implanted in men at the first Creation, and repeated on Mount Sinai, and more often declared: teaching what sort of persons they should not be, what they should do, and what they should omit: and in this requiring perfect and in all numbers absolute obedience from all men, with the promise of eternal life to those keeping it: but with the denunciation of eternal death to those violating it in any way.

But this Definition shows some axioms, most useful and most necessary to be observed concerning the Decalogue.

For first, the Moral Law is the eternal and immovable Wisdom and rule of Justice of GOD: Therefore, it is not accommodated to a time and a certain people like the two former species: nor is it likewise subject to abrogation. For although it happens by accident that it cannot Justify, since it is weakened by the flesh, and therefore in this respect, namely regarding the power of justifying, Galat. 3, 21, it is rightly said to be abrogated: although also it cannot brandish the bolts of curse and accusation against believers: since these have been redeemed from the curse of the Law, Galat. 3, 13, and the Law is not laid down for the Just, 1 Timot. 1, 9, yet it admits least of all any abrogation regarding the information of life, and regarding the debt of obedience or observance, which it seeks and demands from all men indiscriminately: as we shall show expressly below in the third controversy of the second chapter.

The other axiom is that the Moral Law is said to have been implanted in men at the first Creation: Therefore it did not begin only under Moses, but was inscribed in the hearts of men, so that it was naturally known to the Fathers before Moses, and indeed two whole millennia before the promulgation made by Moses. In view of which observation, one would not err at all if one were to constitute two Decalogues, not indeed differing in genus and matter, but only in time and the manner of revelation. One from the beginning of the World to Moses, not written: The other indeed written, from Moses to last until the very last day: nay, to remain for all eternity: not indeed by reason of laws and precepts; of which there will certainly be no use at all in the other blessed life: but by reason of that plenary and most perfect restoration, which will then befall the blessed with respect to the most absolute love of GOD and neighbor. But how the Decalogue was known to the Patriarchs before Moses by nature, partly by a singular revelation of GOD, both in general and in species, Chemnitius explains quite elegantly and learnedly, part 2. Locor. p. 52. 53.

The third axiom is: that the moral Law was repeated on Mount Sinai: and afterwards more often declared; and that from the will of GOD. Therefore it was of some necessity that to that natural and implanted knowledge of the Decalogue in men, there should be added that singular writing or revelation which was made through Moses. But evident causes of the fact can be given.

1. The corruption of our nature, which is so great that the will and appetite neglect the right judgment of reason: and spurn those natural notions concerning the distinction of honorable and base things. Therefore GOD wished to show that those things agree with the eternal and immutable norm or rule of His Justice.

2. The perverse and inveterate, nay daily worsening, license of crimes and vices has not a little obscured those Natural notions, and covered them as if with darkness: And, through a singular revelation and writing of them, GOD wished to restore them, and as it were to assert them in their entirety, and to dispel the mists of errors.

3. GOD, by His own authority, wished to restrain by this covenant human negligence in part, and in part human security, which cares little for those internal natural notions; nay, it laughs at and eludes them by various devised diversions: especially if ambition and self-admiration are added.

Finally, GOD willed that the Decalogue should exist in writing, so that it might be as a certain polished mirror, in which Man might contemplate the sad corruption of his Nature and the horrible atrocity of sin: nay, that it might be a medium and instrument through which the Holy Spirit might convict the world of sin and lead it into the acknowledgment of sin. Rom. 3, 20. Gal. 3, 24.

The fourth axiom is that the Moral Law demands from men an obedience that is perfect and absolute in every respect. Therefore, the Decalogue itself 1. is in itself most perfect. 2. It demands such an observance as consists not only in external actions, but also in internal motions, and indeed in a most perfect way. Doubts are raised concerning both these members of the consequence. The first is concerning the perfection of the Decalogue considered in itself: Namely, do those Ten commandments comprehend under their scope everything that one ought to do and everything that one ought to omit?

The occasion for doubting was provided by the fact that CHRIST Himself seems to have added another commandment besides: Mark 10, 19, saying, You know the commandments; Do not commit adultery: do not kill: do not steal: do not bear false witness: and μὴ ἀποστερήσῃς. Do not defraud: or do not inflict damage on anyone. Where indeed this last commandment is found neither in the first promulgation of the Decalogue nor in its repetition. Furthermore, it seems that many other commandments could still be added to the Decalogue if it were to be perfect, or that this could be gathered from the fact that the Apostle, Rom. 13, 9, after he reviewed the commandments of the second table in order, immediately adds these words: And if there is any other commandment: thus not obscurely hinting that there are more than Ten commandments. But that doubt is most rightly removed by the distinction between General and Special, or as it were Secondary, commandments, which flow from those General ones. For as regards these special ones, certainly no sane person would deny that many more can be given: since the Mosaic code itself recounts more than six hundred other commandments. But nothing is thereby taken away from the perfection of the Decalogue, which contains ten General commandments, so informed that no Special one can be given or devised that cannot easily be reduced to those ten, as to its source and primary spring. Moreover, the most absolute perfection of the commandments of the Decalogue is revealed from the consideration of the objects with which the entire action of Man is chiefly occupied. And those relate either to the Love of GOD or the Love of the neighbor. Now just as the commandments of the first table omit nothing at all of those things which pertain to the true worship of GOD and the true love of Him: so the mandates of the latter table define the individual things that complete the Love of the neighbor with such a brief and artificial compendium that the matter could never have been settled with a shorter compendium. For even if someone should wish to substitute or add that Aphorism of CHRIST, Matt. 7, 12, What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another: or that other one, Matt. 22, 39, You shall love your neighbor as yourself: neither would attain in its Genus that emphasis which the commandments of this second table are found to have: because both of those Aphorisms express only the end and scope of the law: but they do not distinguish the mode and the kinds of actions and things sufficiently expressly. It is, however, the property of laws and commandments to express the Modes of things to be done, and to contain the Genera of all things in which the actions of men are occupied. But if it had been said that the neighbor is not to be harmed by thought, word, or deed: the modes of acting would indeed have been distinct, but the genera of things would not yet have been expressed. For in homicide, and in adultery, and in theft, those individual things are present. Therefore, the Genera of things also had to be distinctly expressed, so that the true reason of legislation could be established.

There are, however, three kinds of things and actions in which we can have dealings with our neighbor, chiefly. For we can have dealings with our neighbor regarding order and Status: or regarding goods: or regarding Right, observing in this part not Philosophical precision: but a certain popular method of teaching. The Fourth contains the treatment regarding the Order and Status of the neighbor: the following four regarding Goods: the last two commandments regarding Right.

The other Doubt, which is raised concerning the Fourth Axiom of our Definition, is about the Obedience owed to the Law: Is this possible for Man to perform: or is it simply and absolutely impossible? Concerning which Question, indeed, in the time of both Christ and the Apostles, and in our own, a sharp Controversy has altogether emerged: then indeed with the Pharisees: but today with the Romanists who depart from the path of truth. For the Pharisees persuaded themselves that the Decalogue or Moral Law prescribed the mode of obedience only to external members, but not to the internal man: They feigned, moreover, that some of the mandates of GOD were great, others minimal, the violation of which GOD does not greatly care about. But that the observation of those great ones is entirely possible for man, provided that the external members of the Body are immune from their transgression. CHRIST Himself was engaged in correcting that error: partly by interpreting the Law, concerning even the internal wicked motions and concupiscences of the human heart: Matt. 5, 21, and following. partly by inculcating the summary of the Law from Moses, which is placed in it: That God is to be loved with all the heart, all the soul, and all the mind, and indeed above all things: And one's neighbor as oneself Matth. 22, 40. To which pertains that whole disputation of the Apostle, in which he shows gravely and at length in the Epistle to the Romans and Galatians; that Justification cannot be obtained by man from the Law: for the reason that the Law is spiritual, but we are carnal, sold under sin: &c. Rom. 7, 14.

Latin:

IN Scholis Theologorum gemina potissimum solet institui consideratio Decalogi, sive Legis moralis: Una Generalis, quæ totius systematis naturam & propriam affectionem expendit: Altera specialis, quæ singulorum Præceptorum accuratiorem pertractat diexodon. Utraque & Quæstionum & rerum multitudine ac varietate latissimè patet: Nos hac vice posthabitis iis, quæ plerumque pro suggestu ad plebem proponi solent: ea tantùm ventilabimus ζητήματα, quorum in Scholis Theologorum, circa controversias, usus aliquis esse potest.

Initiò autem Legem Moralem sive Decalogum definimus, quòd sit æterna & immota sapientia & regula Justitiæ in DEO, insita hominibus in prima Creatione, & repetita in monte Sinai, ac sæpius declarata: docens quales non esse, quæ facere, quæq; omittere oporteat: & in hac perfectam ac numeris omnibus absolutam requirens obedientiam ab omnibus hominibus, cum promissione vitæ æternæ servantibus eam: cum denunciatione autem mortis æternæ, ipsam quoquo modo violantibus.

Monstrat verò Definitio hæc aliquot axiomata, circa Decalogum observatu utilissima, maximéque necessaria.

Primùm enim Lex Moralis est æterna & immota Sapientia & regula Justitiæ DEI: Ergo non ut priores duæ species ad tempus & populum certum ea est accommodata: neque abrogationi pariter subjacet.
