Etsi enim ex accidente fit, quòd Justificare nequit, siquidem infirmatur per carnem, ac proindè hoc respectu, nempè quoad justificandi δύναμιν, Galat. 3, 21. rectè dicitur esse abrogata : etsi quoque maledictionis & accusationis fulmina vibrare non potest in credentes: siquidem hi à maledictione Legis sunt redemti, Galat. 3, 13. & Justo non est posita Lex. 1. Timot. 1, 9. minimè tamen omnium ullam admittit abrogationem, quoäd informationem vitæ, & quoäd debitum obedientiæ sive observantiæ, quod ab omnibus promifcuè hominibus sequirit & exigit: quemadmodum infra controversiâ tertiâ capitis secundi ex professo ostendemus.

Alterum axioma est, quôd Lex Moralis dicitur insita fuisse hominibus in prima Creatione: Ergò non sub Mose demùm cœpit, sed inscripta fuit in cordibus hominum, ita ut naturaliter nota esset Patribus ante Mosen, & quidem duobus integris millenariis ante promulgationem à Mose factam. Cujus observationis intuitu minimè erraret, si quis duos, non genere quidem & materiâ: sed tempore tantùm & patefactionis modo discrepantes Decalogos constitueret. Unum ab initio Mundi, ad Mosen, non scriptum: Alterum verò scriptum, à Mose duraturum ad diem usque novissimum: imò in omnem æternitatem permansurum: non quidem ratione legum & præceptorum; quorum certè in altera vita beata nullus prorsus erit usus: sed ratione plenariæ illius & perfectissimæ restaurationis, quæ tùm obtinget beatis respectu absolutissimæ dilectionis DEI & proximi. Cæterùm quomodo Patriarchis ante Mosen naturâ partim singulari patefactione DEI, tùm in genere, tùm in specie cognitus fuerit Decalogus, fatis eleganter & eruditè explicat Chemnitius, part. 2. Locor. p. 52. 53.

Tertium axioma est: quòd Lex moralis repetita sit in monte Sinai: & postea sæpiùs declarata; idque de voluntate DEI. Ergò necessitatis alicujus fuit, ut ad naturalem illam insitamque hominibus, Decalogi notitiam, accederet singularis scriptio sive patefactio illa, quæ per Mosen facta est. Causæ autem facti dari possunt evidentes.

1. Naturæ nostræ corruptio, quæ tanta est, ut rectum rationis Judicium, voluntas & appetitus negligat: & naturales illas notitias de discrimine honestorum & turpium aspernetur. Ostendere ergo voluit DEUS congruere illas, cum æterna ac immutabili normâ sive regula Justitiæ suæ.

2. Perversa & inveterata, imò indies ingravescens scelerum vitiorumq; licentia, Naturales illas notitias haud parùm obfuscatit, & quasi tenebris obduxit: E, per singularem earum patefactionem scriptionemq; DEUS eas restaurare, & quasi in integrum asserere, errorumq; nebulas propulsare voluit.

3. DEUS autoritate sua coërcere voluit hoc pacto humanam partim oscitantiam, partim securitatem, quæ internas illas notitias naturales parùm curat; imò variis excogitatis diverticulis ridet & eludit: præsertim si ambitio, & sui ipsius admiratio accedat.

Tandem voluit DEUS extare Decalogum scriptum, ut esset ceu politum quoddam speculum, in quo Homo Naturæ suæ tristem corruptionem, & horrendam peccati atrocitatem contemplaretur: imò ut esset medium ac instrumentum per quod Spiritus sanctus mundum argueret de peccato, & in agnitionem peccati adduceret. Rom. 3, 20. Gal. 3, 24.

Quartum axioma est, quòd Lex Moralis perfectam ac numeris omnibus absolutam exigit obedientiam ab hominibus. Ergò Decalogus ipse 1. in se est perfectissimus. 2. Talem exigit observantiam, quæ non in externis tantùm actionibus: sed motibus etiam internis, & quidem longè perfectissima consistat. De utroque isto consecutionis membro Dubia moventur. Primum est de perfectione Decalogi in se considerati: An nimirùm Decem illa præcepta sub suo ambitu comprehendant universa, quæ facere, quæque omittere oporteat?

Ansam dubitandi præbuit illud, quòd CHRISTUS ipse aliud insuper præceptum addidisse videtur: Marci 10, 19. inquiens, Mandata nosti; Ne mœchator: ne occidito: ne furator: ne falsum testimonium dicito: & μὴ ἀποστερήσῃς. Ne fraudem facito: vel ne damno quempiam afficito. Ubi sanè postremum hoc præceptum, neque in prima Decalogi promulgatione, neque in ejusdem repetitione invenitur. Deindè plura adhuc alia præcepta Decalogo addenda esse, si perfectus esse debeat, vel indè etiam colligi posse videtur, quòd Apostolus Rom. 13, 9. postquàm præcepta secundæ tabulæ ordine recensuit, statim hæc verba subjicit: Et si quod aliud est mandatum: sic plura quàm Decem esse præcepta, haud obscurè innuens. Sed dubitatio ista rectissimè tollitur per distinctionem inter præcepta Generalia & Specialia, sive Secundaria quasi, quæ ex Generalibus illis profluunt. Nam quoad hæc specialia, certè multò plura dari posse, nemo sanus iverit inficias: cùm vel ipse codex Mosaicus fexcenta ampliùs præcepta alia recenseat. Verùm nihil indè decedit perfectioni Decalogi, qui decem præcepta Generalia, ita informata continet, ut Speciale nullum dari vel excogitari possit, quod non ad decem illa, tanquam ad fontem & scaturiginem primam facilè reduci queat. Patescit autem præceptorum Decalogi absolutissima perfectio, ex consideratione objectorum, circa quæ actio Hominis universa præcipuè est occupata. Ea verò vel Dilectionem DEI, vel Dilectionem proximi respiciunt. Jam quemadmodum primæ tabulæ præcepta nihil quicquam omittunt eorum, quæ ad verum DEI cultum, veramque ejus dilectionem pertinent: Sic posterioris tabulæ mandata usq; adeò brevi & artificioso compendio singula definiunt, quæ Dilectionem proximi absolvunt, ut breviore compendio res expediri nunquàm potuerit. Nam si vel maximè aliquis substituere vel addere velit Aphorismum illum CHRISTI, Matth.7, 12. Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris: vel illum alterum, Matth. 22, 39. Diliges proximum, sicut teipsum: neuter tamen Genere suo eam emphasin assequeretur: quam secundæ hujus tabulæ præcepta habere deprehenduntur: propterea quòd uterque iste Aphorismus finem tantùm & scopum legis exprimit: modum autem & genera actionum rerumque non satis expressè distinguit. Est autem legum & præceptorum hoc proprium, Modos rerum agendarum exprimere, & Genera rerum omnium continere, in quibus actiones hominum occupantur. Quod si dictum fuisset, Proximum cogitatione, dicto, factové lædendum non esse: modi quidem agendi distincti, sed genera rerum nondum expressa fuissent. Nam & in homicidio, & in mœchatione, & in furto, singula ista insunt. Genera ergò rerum etiam distinctè fuerunt exprimenda, ut vera νομοθεσίας ratio constare posset.

Sunt autem genera rerum & actionum, in quibus res nobis esse potest cum proximo, tria potissimùm. Nam vel cum ordine & Statu: vel cum bonis: vel cum Jure proximi nobis res esse potest, observatâ hac in parte non ἀκριβείᾳ Philosophicâ: sed populari quasi quadam docendi ratione. De Ordine & Statu proximi, Quartum: de Bonis, sequentia quatuor: de Jure, postrema duo præcepta, tractationem continent.

Alterum Dubium, quod de Quarto Definitionis nostræ Axiomate movetur, est de Obedientia Legi debita: An hæc Homini sit præstitu possibilis: an verò simpliciter & absolutè impossihilis? De qua sanè Quæstione, tempore tùm Christi & Apostolorum, tùm nostro, acris omninò emersit Controversia: tùm quidem Pharisæis: hodiè verò Romanensibus à veritatis tramite discendentibus. Pharisæi enim sibi persuadebant, Decalogum sive Legem Moralem, externis tantùm membris, non autem interno homini, obedientiæ modum præscribere: Fingehant insuper, mandatorum DEI alia esse magna, alia minima, quorum violationem DEUS non magnoperè curet. Magnorum autem illorum observationem homini omninò esse possibilem, dummodò externa Corporis membra, ab eorum transgressione sint immunia. In corrigendo isto errore CHRISTUS ipse versatus est: partim interpretando Legem, de internis etiam pravis motibus ac concupiscentiis cordis humani: Matth. 5, 21. & seqq. partim summam Legis ex Mose inculcando, quæ in eo est posita: Ut diligatur Deus ex toto corde, tota anima, totaque mente, & quidem super omnia: Proximus autem sicut ipse quisque Matth. 22, 40. Quò pertinet tota illa disputatio Apostoli, quà in Epistola ad Romanos & Galatas, multis graviter ostendit; Justificationem non posse obtingere homini ex Lege: eò quòd Lex spiritualis sit, Nos autem carnales, venundati sub peccato: &c. Rom. 7, 14.


### On the Moral Law (continued)

The Romanists even in our own time cherish a no milder error, contending that, formerly in the Law of Moses, only the beginning of Justice was handed down: but that a more perfect account of the same was reserved for the Gospel: and therefore that that interpretation of the Law, proposed by Christ in Matth. 5, was a kind of ἐπανόρθωσιν, by which Christ wished to show a more excellent degree of perfection to his disciples: but one also so constituted that it consists only in the external observation of the Law. Moreover, the scope and end which Christ had uniquely set before himself in Matth. 5 manifestly opposes this error from the beginning: namely, to show that the inward wicked concupiscence of the heart is also prohibited in the Law: and therefore that the most absolute obedience of not only the external, but also the internal man is required. Furthermore, this opinion of the Romanists constitutes Christ as a New legislator: whom, however, Scripture acknowledges and proclaims only as a faithful interpreter of the divine Law. Thirdly, there was absolutely no need for a correction of the Law. For God never has repented, nor does he repent, of that norm of living which he once caused to be published through Moses in his Law.

What? That Moses himself rightly ascribes perfection to his Law for life, having solemnly and religiously testified: that he had set before his own people life and death: so that whoever shall do these things, shall have life in them. Fourthly, if there was no perfection of the Mosaic Law: Why, I ask, is God commanded in it to be loved and worshipped with all the heart, and with all the strength: and one's neighbor, as anyone himself. Whence the Apostle also does not affirm that the Law is weak in itself: but pronounces that it is weakened by the flesh, so that it cannot provide salvation for us. Rom. 8, 3. Finally, it is worth noting that Christ, acting as an interpreter of the Law, does not say in Matth. 5: Thus it is written in the Law: but: You have heard that it was said to the ancients: that saying, namely, that only the external letter of the Law is to be observed. He therefore adds; But I say to you: as if he were saying: I advise that a far higher sense of the Law must be sought: and I declare to you that the precepts of this Law are violated as often as something is committed against God and one's neighbor, whether by word or gesture, or thought, or any other internal motion of the heart.

Moreover, regarding the Question itself, Whether the Moral Law is impossible for man to perform and fulfill in this life? The Jesuits indeed, in the manner of the Pelagians, defend the affirmative: but our Churches defend the negative. And indeed these are the reasons and foundations of our negative.

I. The authority of the Scriptures: Christ certainly in John 7, 19 attributes this imperfection equally to the Jews: saying, Did not Moses give you the law: and yet none of you does the law. Stephen does the same thing also in Acts 7, 38, 39, 53. In particular, however, this Question was debated by the Apostles themselves in the Council of Jerusalem, and defined in this manner: Why do you tempt God to put a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither our Fathers, nor we were able to bear. Acts 15, 10. Thus the Apostle in Rom. 8, 3. It is impossible for the Law, he says, to justify anyone, because it is weakened by the Flesh. And in Gal. 3, 21 he affirms διαῤῥήδην, that the Law was not given which could give life: not indeed that it suffers this ἀδυναμίαν by itself: but by accident, because clearly no mortal can provide perfect obedience to the Law.

II. The reason is the horrible and extreme corruption of our nature and all its powers, which fights no less diametrically with the perfection of the Law: and they are as mutually distant as truth and falsehood, Light and darkness: Spirit and Flesh. The Apostle looked to this in Rom. 7, 14, saying: The Law is Spiritual: but we are carnal, and sold under sin.

III. The reason is the satisfaction of CHRIST, which would have been entirely superfluous and vain if we could have satisfied the Law of God. But he himself came into the world for this reason, that he might fulfill the Law for us, Matth. 5, 17, Rom. 8, 3, and then, that he might free us from the Curse of the Law. Gal. 4, 5. Whence the Apostle infers this general conclusion: Gal. 2, 21. If righteousness is from the Law, CHRIST died in vain.

IV. And the final reason is subsidiary, taken from the unanimous consent of Orthodox Antiquity: especially of Augustine, who says that we will fulfill this first precept of Justice, by which we are commanded to love God with all our heart &c., and the other following it, about loving one's neighbor, only in that life where we shall see God face to face. And he immediately adds: therefore this is commanded to us even now, that we may be reminded of what we ought to seek by faith, to which we ought to send our hope ahead. But by this, as much as it seems to me, in that Justice which is to be perfected, he makes much progress in this life who recognizes how far he is from the perfection of justice, by making progress. De Sp. & Lit. To which Bernard agrees: Serm. 50. in Cant. Charity, which is commanded in the law, can in no way be, or could have been, fulfilled by any man in this life. For who would dare to arrogate to himself that which Paul himself confesses he has not apprehended?

But two things here again come into question: The first: Is the Law therefore simply and absolutely impossible to keep? The latter: To what end do the precepts of the moral Law, so solicitously inculcated upon men, pertain, if they are simply impossible to perform? To that first point we answer at the beginning in the negative: that, namely, not a simple or absolute impossibility, but only a conditional one has a place in this question. But that condition depends not upon God the creator, but upon the corruption of the human race, which inheres in it not of itself, but accidentally. Furthermore, if a simple and absolute impossibility were established, then certainly Man could not perform any external discipline, which nevertheless cannot be denied even to the unregenerate: and it is called the righteousness of the flesh, Heb. 9, 10. Thirdly, one must accurately distinguish between the regenerate and the unregenerate.

For as regards the unregenerate, the Law is impossible for them ἁπλῶς & secundum quid: 1. Because from their own powers, they are not only unable to perform the inward obedience of the heart without faith and the Holy Spirit, but they cannot even begin it. 2. Because even their external discipline does not please God, for the reason that they are destitute of faith. Rom. 14, 23. Hebr. 11, 6. But as regards the regenerate, we maintain that the Law is fulfilled by them in two ways: 1. Imputatively, insofar as the active obedience of Christ, performed for the Law, is truly imputed to them through faith. 2. Inchoatively, insofar as not indeed from their own powers, but from the grace and operation of the Holy Spirit, they begin to perform obedience to the Law: which itself, however, because it is imperfect, certainly satisfies the Law neither in part nor in whole: Since he who fails in one is guilty of all the precepts, James 2, 10. Meanwhile, however, it pleases God on account of Christ. And as Blessed Luther speaks in the Smalcald Articles: Just as the faithful person is reckoned righteous through faith, although sin clings to the flesh: So also the good works of believers are reckoned righteous and holy out of grace on account of Christ.

To the latter ζήτημα (question) we answer with St. Augustine, that the Law is commanded to us now, however impossible it may be to keep, so that we may be admonished what we ought to seek by faith, and whither we ought to direct our hope. For neither, as St. Bernard adds, did the weight of the precept escape the preceptor, as exceeding the powers of men: but he judged it useful that they be admonished by this very thing of their own insufficiency, and that they might know truly to what end of righteousness they ought to strive with all their might. Therefore, by commanding the impossible, he did not make men transgressors against God, but humble: so that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become subject to God, serm. 50. in Cant.

But there is objected to us in this place, like the head of a Gorgon, that saying of Blessed Jerome: Let him be anathema who says that GOD has commanded the impossible. But it is doubted 1. whether this sentence acknowledges Jerome as its author 2. We oppose Jerome to Jerome, writing thus on chapter 23 of Matthew, Whatever does not have authority from the Scriptures is despised with the same ease with which it is approved. 3. the reason

τὰ τὶ (in a certain respect) it is true that God has not commanded the impossible. Namely, to human nature, insofar as it is weighed before the fall in a state of integrity and innocence. But if the subsumption is made to corrupt Nature, πλεονεξία (covetousness/excess) is committed.

4. Many things are proclaimed both in the Scriptures and in the monuments of the Fathers concerning Man, not because they are already present in him: but because he is prepared for them through Renewal. Thus Man is prepared through the Word and the Sacraments, or at some time in the other blessed life, no precept will be impossible for him to keep.

But the Papists proceed, and from the Scriptures they bring forward partly that 1 John 5, 3: The commandments of God are not grievous: but partly they scrape together very many testimonies of the Scriptures, which according to the surface of the letter seem to assign a perfect fulfillment of the Law to certain holy and regenerate men: such as that David was a man after God's own heart, that he did all his wills: 1 Sam. 13, 14. That Josiah had no equal, as one who turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses: 2 Kings 23, 25. That Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and justifications of the LORD without blame. Luke 1, 6.

But an evident answer is at hand to both of the objections. For as regards the Johannine passage; one must see at the beginning concerning what commandment the Apostle is speaking in that place. That, however, is clear from chapter 3, 23. This is the commandment of God, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he commanded us. Now, however, 2, this commandment is said not to be grievous, κατὰ τὶ (in a certain respect), namely συγκριτικῶς (comparatively), if it is compared with the Law of Moses: although meanwhile its own difficulty also remains for it. For that commandment is not grievous to the Regenerate, because they are already children of God, and are led by the Spirit of God, and whatever is lacking in their obedience is easily remitted through and on account of Christ. Therefore, John is not speaking of an absolute fulfillment of the law, but only of an inchoate one. For if anyone wishes to refer these words to an absolute act of fulfillment, in the Papist sense, he must necessarily accuse John of a shameful contradiction: as one who in the same Epistle, chapter 1, 8, did not hesitate to write: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

As regards the remaining testimonies of the Saints, a double sophistry is committed in their allegation: The first is of homonymy. For these phrases: With all the heart, with all the soul, etc., obtain not a Legal, but an Ecclesiastical sense: which denotes a perfection not absolute in all numbers, such as could not fall to either David or Josiah in this life, as their own histories attest: For the former, guilty of most grievous mortal sins, had need to beg incessantly for the remission of sins: The latter, however, moving a war not necessary against the King of Egypt out of some curiosity,

He immediately experienced the vengeance of God, so that he fell in that battle: But in an Ecclesiastical sense those phrases, Sincerity and Candor, denote that which is alien from all hypocrisy and simulation. Thus Zacharias and Elisabeth were righteous, not with a legal righteousness, but an Evangelical one, which consists in the gratuitous imputation of the Holiness of Christ, and the Remission of sins, which Zacharias himself proclaims most wonderfully in his canticle, Luke 1:78. And indeed that Zacharias was not immune from sin, his own Dissent quite clearly argues, on account of which he had also been deprived of the use of his tongue for some time. Whence Augustine aptly infers in his book on the merits of sins, chapter 3, and Epistle 93: Zacharias was a sinner, because he was a Priest. For the duty of the Priests of the Old Testament was to sacrifice for sins, both of the people and also their own. The latter is a Sophistication ὥςγε τὸ πηγὴ ἁπλῶς. For those sayings about the Holiness of certain people are to be understood κατὰ τι, according to a certain probable preservation among men: but not according to the perfection of Righteousness. Thus Paul boasts of himself that he was without blame before all: and yet he compares this righteousness to dung, and denies that he is justified in it. Furthermore, they are to be taken comparatively, instituted συγκρίσει in relation to other men. Finally, they are to be taken not concerning the whole life of the Saints, but concerning a certain kind of deed. Thus Josiah is said to have returned to the Lord according to all the law of Moses: namely, with regard to that special Reformation of divine worship, which he instituted according to the law of God in such a way that he might root out and exterminate Idolatry from the kingdom of Judah. Now, however, the Consequence does not hold from a species to the whole genus. Finally, the question is asked: Whether the Moral Law belongs to the Old, or to the New Testament: and if to the Old: Whether it has been abrogated? But this knot is most rightly solved if one affirms both things concerning the moral law, both that it belongs to both Testaments, and that it has undergone abrogation, and has not undergone it. For it belongs to the Old Testament, 1. With regard to the continuous and more rigid inculcation of the precepts of the Decalogue. 2. With regard to the more obscure tradition of the same precepts. 3. With regard to the alternative denunciation of the sentence, either to salvation and justification, if it were kept in its entirety: or to condemnation, if it were violated. Now therefore, in the way in which it belongs to the Old T., the moral Law is antiquated, especially with regard to justification and condemnation. For the Law has no power to condemn those who are in CHRIST JESUS. Rom. 8:1. And by the works of the Law shall no flesh be justified. Galat. 2:16 Again, Because the New T. embraces not only the Remission of sins, but also Renewal: since we are a new creature in Christ, created for good works: Ephes. 2:10, the norm of which is proposed most perfectly in the Decalogue: hence it comes about that by reason of New Obedience the Decalogue belongs to the New T. Furthermore, since the Decalogue is the immutable rule of divine justice, implanted in the Nature of men at their very creation, certainly, just as the Nature of Man itself remains, and all things that are Natural in it: so the Decalogue also, which itself is also from natural things, suffers no antiquation.

Latin:

Romanenses nostro etiamnum tempore haud mitiorem fovent errorem contendentes, Olim in Lege Mosis, initium duntaxat Justitiæ fuïsse traditum: perfectiorem autem ejusdem rationem Evangelio esse reservatam: ac proindè interpretationem illam Legis, Matth. 5. à Christo propositam, fuisse quandam quasi ἐπανόρθωσιν, quâ Christus excellentiorem perfectionis gradum discipulis suis monstrare voluerit: sed illum quoque ita comparatum ut in externa Legis observatione tantùm consistat. Cæterùm errori huic initiò manifestè repugnat scopus ac finis, quem Christus Matth. 5. sibi unicè habuit præfixum: ut nimirùm ostenderet, intimam etiam cordis concupiscentiam pravam in Lege prohiberi: ac proindè non externi tantùm, sed interni etiam hominis obedientiam absolutissimam requiri. Deindè sententia hæc Romanensium Christum constituit Novum legislatorem: quem tamen Scriptura fidelem tantùm Legis divinæ interpretem agnoscit, & prædicat. Tertiò correctione Legis prorsus nulla opus fuit. Deum enim nunquàm pœnituit aut pœnitet illius vivendi normæ, quam in Lege sua semel per Mosen publicari curavit.

Quid? quòd Moses ipse Legi suæ perfectionem ad vitam diterrè adscribit, solenniter ac religiosè contestatus: se proposuisse suo etiam populo vitam & mortem: ita ut qui facturus sit hæc, vitam habiturus sit in illis. Quartò si perfectio Legis Mosaicæ nulla fuit: Cur, quæso, Deus jubetur in ea diligi colique ex toto corde, & ex omnibus viribus: & proximus, sicut ipsus quilibet. Undè Apostolus etiam non affirmat Legem in seipsa infirmam esse: sed per carnem infirmari pronunciat, ne salutem nobis præstare possit. Rom. 8, 3. Tandem observationem meretur, quòd Christus Legis interpretem agens, Matth. 5. non dicit: Sic scriptum est in Lege: sed: Audistis, quod dictum sit veteribus: illud nimirùm dictum, quòd externa tantum Legis litera sit observanda. Subjicit proindè; Ego verò dico vobis: quasi dicat: Ego moneo longè altiorem Legis sensum inquirendum esse: & edico vobis, violari Legis hujus præcepta, quoties aliquid contra Deum & proximum, vel verbo vel gestu, vel cogitatione, vel quovis alio interno cordis motu committitur.

Cæterùm quòd Quæstionem ipsam, An Lex Moralis Homini hac in vita præstitu & impletu sit impossibilis? Jesuvitæ quidem Pelagianorum more affirmativam : Nostræ verò Ecclesiæ Negantem propugnant. Et sanè Negativæ nostræ rationes & fundamenta sunt hæc.

I. Scripturarum autoritas : Christus certè Joh. 7, 19. Judæis hanc imperfectionem ex æquo tribuit : Nonne inquiens Moses dedit vobis legem : sed nemo ex vobis facit legem. Quod ipsum facit Stephanus etiam Actor. 7, 38, 39. 53. In specie autem hæc Quæstio ab Apostolis ipsis in Concilio Hierosolymitano ventilata, & hunc in modum definita fuit : Quid tentatis Deum imponere jugum cervicibus discipulorum, quod neque Patres nostri, neq; nos portare potuimus. Actor. 15, 10. Sic Apostolus Rom. 8,3. Impossibile est Legi, inquit, ut quempiam justificet, quia infirmatur per Carnem. Et Gal. 3, 21. διαῤῥήδην affirmat , quòd non data sit Lex, quæ possit vivificare : non quidem quòd per se hanc ἀδυναμίαν patiatur : sed per accidens, quia videlicet nemo mortalium Legi perfectam præstare potest obedientiam.

II. Ratio est, Naturæ nostræ horrenda & extrema omnium ejus virium corruptio , quæ cum perfectione Legis haud minùs è diametro pugnat : atque à se mutuò distant , veritas & mendacium, Lux & tenebræ : Spiritus & Caro. Respexit hûc Apostolus, Rom. 7, 14. Lex inquiens Spiritualis est : Nos autem carnales, & venundati sub peccato.

III. Ratio est, CHRISTI satisfactio, quæ prorsus supervacanea & frustranea fuisset, si nos Legi Dei satis facere potuissemus. Ipse autem ideò in mundum venit, ut pro nobis impleret Legem, Matth. 5,17, Rom 8,3. deinde, ut nos à Legis Maledictione liberaret. Gal. 4,5. Unde generalem hanc conclusionem infert Apostolus : Gal. 2, 21. Si ex Lege est Justitia , CHRISTVS frustrà mortuus est.

IV. Et postrema ratio est subsidiaria, petita ex unanimi consensu Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis : Augustini cumprimis, qui primum hoc præceptum Justitiæ, quo diligere jubemur Deum ex toto corde &c. & alterum consequens, de diligendo proximo, in illa demum vita nos impleturos dicit, ubi videbimus Deum à facie ad faciem. Et statim subjicit : ideò nobis hoc etiam nunc præceptum est , ut admoneamur quid fide exposcere, quò spem præmittere debeamus. At per hoc, quantum mihi videtur , in ea, quæ præficiendo, est Justitia , multum in hac vita ille proficit, qui quàm longè sit à perfectione justitiæ, proficenda cognoscit. De Sp. & Lit. Cui adstipulatur Bernhardus : Serm. 50. in Cant. Charitas, quæ in lege jubetur, minimè in vita ista ab aliquo hominum potest, vel potuit adimpleri. Quis enim id arrogare sibi audeat, quod se Paulus ipse fatetur non apprehendisse ?

Sed duo hîc rursum in Quæstionem veniunt: Prius: Annè ergo simpliciter & absolutè Lex fit servatu impossibilis? Posterius: Quorsum attineant Legis moralis præcepta adeò sollicitè inculcata hominibus, si præstitu simpliciter sint impossibilia? Ad prius illud respondemus initiò negatè: quòd nimirùm non simplex aut absoluta impossibilitas: sed conditionata tantùm locum in hac Quæstione habeat. Conditio autem illa dependet non à Deo conditore, sed à corruptione generis humani, quæ non per se, sed per accidens illi inest. Deindè si simplex & absoluta impossibilitas statueretur: tùm certè Homo non posset aliquam externam disciplinam præstare, quæ tamen ne quidem non renatis negari potest: & justitia carnis appellatur, Heb. 9, 10. Tertiò accuratè distinguendum inter renatos & non renatos.

Nam quoad non renatos, ἁπλῶς & secundum quid Lex ipsis est impossibilis: 1. Quia ex proprijs viribus, interiorem cordis obedientiam, sine fide & Spiritu Sancto non modò non præstare, sed ne quidem inchoare possunt. 2. Quia externa etiam ipsorum disciplina Deo non placet, propterea quòd destituuntur fide. Rom. 14, 23. Hebr. 11, 6. Cæterùm quoad renatos, statuimus ab his Legem impleri duobus modis: 1. Imputativè quatenùs per fidem ipsis revera imputatur obedientia Christi activa, Legi præstita. 2. Inchoativè, quatenus non ex proprijs quidem viribus, sed ex gratia & operatione Spiritus Sancti, inchoant præstare Legi Obedientiam: quæ ipsa tamen quia imperfecta est, utique Legi neque ex parte, neque ex toto satisfacit: Siquidem qui in uno deficit, omnium præceptorum reus est, Iacob. 2, 10. Interim autem Deo placet propter Christum. Et ut B. Lutherus loquitur in articulis Schmalchaldicis: Sicut persona fidelis reputatur justa per fidem, licet peccatum hæreat in carne: Ita & opera bona credentium reputantur justa & sancta ex gratia propter Christum.

Ad posterius ζήτημα respondemus cum D. Augustino, ideò nobis, quantumvis servatu impossibilem Legem, nunc quoque præcipi, ut admoneamur, quid fide exposcere, quò spem præmittere debeamus. Neque enim, ut D. Bernhardus subjicit, latuit præceptorem, præcepti pondus, hominum vires excedere: sed judicavit utile ex hoc ipso suæ illos insufficientiæ admoneri, & ut scirent sanè, ad quem Justitiæ finem niti pro viribus oporteret. Ergò mandando impossibilia, non prævaricatores fecit Deo homines, sed humiles: ut omne os obstruatur, & subditus fiat omnis mundus Deo serm. 50. in Cant.

Sed obijcitur nobis hoc loco ceu Gorgonis caput, illud B. Hieronymi: Anathema sit, si quis dixerit, DEVM præcepisse impossibilia. Verùm dubitatur 1. an hæc sententia Hieronymum autorem agnoscat 2. Opponimus Hieronymum Hieronymo, sic ad caput. 23. Matthæi scribentem, Quicquid de Scripturis autoritatem non habet, eâdem facilitate contemnitur, quâ probatur. 3. ratio

τὰ τὶ verum est, quòd Deus non praeceperit impossibilia. Naturae scilicet humanae, quatenus ea ante lapsum in statu integritatis & innocentiae pensitatur. Si verò subsumtio fiat ad Naturam corruptam, πλεονεξία committitur.

4. Multa tùm in Scripturis, tùm in Patrum monumentis praedicantur de Homine, non quòd jam ipsi insint: sed quod ad ea per Renovationem praeparetur. Sic Homo per Verbum & Sacramenta praeparatur, aut aliquando in vita beata altera, nullum praeceptum ipsi futurum sit servatu impossibile.

Sed pergunt Pontificii, & ex Scripturis proferunt partim illud 1. Ioh. 5, 3. Mandata Dei non sunt gravia: partim verò corradunt benè multa Scripturarum testimonia, quae secundum superficiem literae, sanctis ac renatis quibusdam perfectam Legis impletionem adsignare videntur: ut quod David fuerit vir secundum Cor Dei, quod fecerit omnes voluntates ejus: 1. Sam. 13, 14. Quòd Josias similem non habuerit, ut qui reversus ad DOMINVM in omni corde suo, & in tota anima sua, & in universa virtute sua, juxta omnem legem Mosis: 2. Reg. 23, 25. quòd Zacharias & Elisabeth fuerint justi coram Deo, incedentes in omnibus mandatis & justificationibus DOMINI sine querela. Luc. 1, 6.

Sed in promptu est evidens Responsio ad utrumque objectorum. Nam quoad locum Johanniticum; videndum initiò de quo mandato Apostolus eo loci agat. Id verò patet ex capite 3, 23. Hoc est mandatum Dei, ut credamus nomini Filij ejus Jesu Christi, & diligamus alij alios, sicut mandavit nobis. Jam verò 2, Mandatum hoc dicitur non Grave, κατὰ τὶ, nempè συγκριτικῶς, si cum Lege Mosis conferatur: licet interim sua quoque ipsi difficultas constat. Mam mandatum illud Renatis non est grave, quia jam sunt filij Dei, & ducuntur Spiritu Dei, & quicquid illorum Obedientiae deest, facilè remittitur per & propter Christum. Proindè non de absoluta impletione legis, sed de inchoata tantùm loquitur Johannes. Nam si ad absolutum impletionis actum, sensu Pontificio, verba haec aliquis referre velit, is turpis Contradictionis Johannem insimulet necesse est: ut qui eâdem Epistola cap. 1, 8. scribere non dubitavit: Si dixerimus, nos peccatum non habere nosipsos fallimus, & veritas non est in nobis.

Quoad reliqua Sanctorum testimonia, gemina in eorum allegatione committitur Sophisticatio: Prior ὁμωνυμίας. Nam phrases hae: Ex toto corde, ex tota anima &c. non Legalem, sed Ecclesiasticum sensum obtinent: qui notat perfectionem non omnibus numeris absolutam, qualis neque in Davidem, neque in Iosiam hac in vita cadere potuit, uti ipsorum historiae attestantur: Ille enim gravissimorum peccatorum mortalium reus, Remissionem peccatorum indefinenter efflagitare necesse habuit: Hic verò ex curiositate quapiam bellum non necessarium Regi Aegyptio movens,

Dei vindictam statim expertus est, ut in prælio illo occumberet: Sed sensu Ecclesiastico notant phrases illæ, Sinceritatem & Candorem, ab omni hypocrisi & simulatione alienam. Sic Zacharias & Elisabeth erant justi, justitia non legali, sed Evangelica, quæ consistit in gratuita imputatione Sanctitatis Christi, & Remissione peccatorum, quam mirificè in suo cantico Zacharias ipse prædicat Luc. 1, 78. Et sanè Zachariam à peccato non fuisse immunem, Dissidentia ipsius satis luculenter arguit, ob quam etiam linguæ usu aliquandiu privatus fuerat. Vndè scitè infert Augustinus l. de peccatorum meritis, cap. 3. Et Epistola 93 Zacharias fuit peccator, quia fuit Sacerdos. Sacerdotum enim Veteris Testamenti officium fuit, sacrificare pro peccatis tùm populi, tùm suis etiam. Posterior Sophisticatio est ὥςγε τὸ πηγὴ ἁπλῶς. Dicta enim illa de quorundam Sanctitate, sunt intelligenda κατὰ τι, secundum quandam inter homines conservationem probabilem: non verò secundum perfectionem Justitiæ. Sic Paulus de se gloriatur, quòd apuod omnes sine querela fuerit: & tamen hanc justitiam stercoribus comparat, inq́ne illa se justificari negat. Deindè sunt accipienda comparatè, instituta συγκρίσει ad alios homines. Tandem accipienda sunt non de universa vita Sanctorum, sed de certa specie facti. Sic Iosias dicitur juxta omnem legem Mosis, reversus esse ad Deum: nempè quoad specialem illam Reformationem cultus divini, quam secundum legem Dei ita instituit, ut Idololatriam è regno Juda radicitùs evelleret & exterminaret. Jam verò à specie ad universum genus non valet Consequentia. Tandem quæritur: An Lex Moralis ad Vetus, an ad Novum Testamentum pertineat: & si ad Vetus: Nùm sit abrogata? Sed nodus iste rectissimè solvitur, si utrumque de lege morali affirmetu, rtùm quòd ad Testamentum utrumque pertineat: tùm quòd abrogationem passa, & non passa sit. Pertinet enim ea ad Vetus Testamentum, 1. Quoad continuam & rigidiorem præceptorum Decalogi inculcationem. 2. Quoad obscuriorem eorundem præceptorum traditionem. 3. Quoad alternativam sententiæ denunciationem, vel ad salutem & justificationem, si ex toto servata esset: vel ad damnationem, si violata. Jam ergò, eo modo, quo ad ad Vetus T. pertinet, antiquata est Lex moralis, præcipuè quoad justificationem & damnationem. Nam Lex nullam habet potestatem condemnandi eos, qui sunt in CHRIISTO JESU. Rom. 8, 1. Et ex operibus Legis non justificatur omnis caro. Galat. 2, 16 Rursus, Quia Novum T. non modò Remissionem peccatorum, sed & Renovationem complectitur: siquidem nova sumus creatura in Christo, conditi ad bona opera: Ephes. 2, 10. quorum norma in Decalogo perfectissima est proposita: hinc fit ut ratione Novæ Obedientiæ Decalogus ad Novum T. pertineat. Præterea cùm Decalogus sit immutabilis divinæ justitiæ regula, hominum Naturæ in ipsâ creatione insita, certè, quemadmodum ipsa Natura Hominis manet, & in ea, quæ sunt Naturalia omnia: ita Decalogus etiam, qui & ipse est ex naturalibus, antiquationem nullam patitur.


### On the Moral Law: Chapter II

Chapter II.

Latin:

Caput II.


### Chapter II. Controversy concerning the Law of Nature, and about natural notions, innate to Man by nature

Controversy concerning the LAW OF NATURE, and concerning natural notions, implanted in Man by nature.

The Law of Nature, not only to Philosophers but also to Theologians, is and is called that knowledge of both Divine Law and of God and divine things, which was not sought from sacred Scriptures, nor revealed externally by the Holy Spirit: but which was partly inscribed and as it were impressed upon human minds in the first Creation, but now after the fall is indeed obscured, but not utterly extinguished: and partly is acquired by the use of reason, and therefore is common to all: inasmuch as by it men are not distinguished from the pious, nor the elect from the reprobate: but only men from brutes: granted to man for this end, that he himself, being subject to this natural light, might be able to rule himself Ἀνθρωπικῶς: and thus civil public peace, justice, and discipline might be preserved among men. And indeed in the state of innocence, the human heart was as it were a golden tablet, upon which this most perfect norm of divine justice was originally inscribed and shone forth in the human mind with most brilliant rays. Although indeed through the most sad fall of our first parents this Light of Nature has been horribly obscured, and covered over with the densest darkness of ignorance and errors: yet God did not will that it should utterly perish: but that some relics of it should remain: while not only in the first few centuries of the world, in diverse ways and times, by a living voice externally through certain proposed laws, He polished this Light of Nature in some part: but also in the Year 2449, He caused a public and solemn promulgation of this Law to be made through Moses, and to be recorded on tablets. Exod. 20. The Law of Nature therefore differs from the Divine not in author: not in the matter or object of the notions: but partly in degree and perfection: and partly in the mode of revelation. For which reason the very appellation of the Law of Nature does not obtain an exclusive sense, as if it were not likewise concerning God and divine things: but only a subalternated sense, insofar as it becomes known to men not through a singular and external revelation of God; but through Nature and human Reason itself, as if through a certain Natural principle.

Moreover, since today there are not wanting those who dare to deny this Light of Nature entirely, or at least to relegate it to the class of sins, even when considered in itself: to blunt their madness, three things especially must be observed concerning its definition.

I. Whether, even after the fall, some Light of Nature or some natural knowledge of God and divine things should be granted to all men?

II. How far does the breadth of these natural notions extend?

III. What use of it can and should be established among unregenerate men, especially Gentiles?

Latin:

Controversia de LEGE NATURAE, deq́; notitijs naturalibus, Homini naturâ insitis.

LEx Naturæ non Philosophis modò, sed & Theologis, ea est ac dicitur tùm Leg Divinæ, tùm Dei rerumque divinarum notitia, quæ non ex Scripturis sacris petita, vel à Spiritu Sancto extrinsecus revelata est: sed quæ mentibus humanis, partim in prima Creatione insculpta, & quasi impressa fuit, nunc autem post lapsum obscurata quidem, sed non penitùs extincta est: partim verò usu rationis acquiritur, ac proindè omnibus communis: quippè quâ non pij ab impijs, non electi à reprobis: sed tantùm à brutis homines discernuntur: eo fine homini concessa, ut ipse lumini isti naturali subditus, regere possit se Ἀνθρπικῶς: sicque conservetur, pax, justitia & disciplina civilis publica inter homines. Et sanè in statu innocentiæ, fuit cor humanum aurea quasi tabula, cui perfectissima hæc justitiæ divinæ norma primitùs insculpta nitidissimis radijs in mente humana refulsit. Quanquam verò per tristissimum lapsum protoparentum Lumen hoc Naturæ horribiliter est obfuscatum, & densissimis ignorantiæ errorumque tenebris obductum: tamen Deus illud non penitùs interire: sed aliquas ejus reliquias permanere voluit: dùm non modò primis aliquot mundi seculis, modis ac temporibus diversis, vivâ voce extrinsecùs legibus quibusdam propositis, Lumen istud Naturæ aliqua ex parte expolivit: sed & Anno M. 2449. publicam & solennem Legis hujus promulgationem per Mosen fieri, inque tabulas referri curavit. Exod. 20. Differt proindè Lex Naturæ à Divina non autore: non notitiarum materia sive objecto: sed partim gradu & perfectione: partim verò revelationis modo. Quam ob causam ipsa etiam appellatio Legis Naturæ, non sensum obtinet exclusivum, quasi illa non itidem sit de Deo, rebusque divinis: sed sensum duntaxat subalternatum, quatenùs non per singularem ac externam Dei revelationem; sed per ipsam Naturam & Rationem humanam, tanquàm per Naturale quoddam principium, hominibus innotescit.

Cæterùm cùm hodiè, non desint, qui Lumen istud Naturæ penitùs negare, vel certè in classem peccatorum, etiam per se consideratum, referre ausint: ad retundendam ipsorum vesaniam, Tria potissimùm circa ejus definitionem observanda veniunt.

I. Nùm post lapsum etiam, Hominibus quibusq́; Lumen aliquod Naturæ sive Notitia aliqua naturalis de Deo, rebusq́; divinis sit concedenda?

II. Quousq́; Notitiarum istarum Naturalium latitudo se extendat?

III. Quisnam usus ejus apud Homines non Renatos, Gentiles cumprimis, statui poßit ac debeat?


### Chapter II. Controversy concerning the Law of Nature, and about natural…: On the First

ON THE FIRST.

That even to man after the fall, and indeed considered in the state of corruption, some Light of Nature, that is, a certain knowledge of God and divine things, must be granted, the Apostle confirms quite evidently: and that in many ways.

For 1. He categorically affirms that the Gentiles had knowledge of God: Rom. 1:19, τὸ γνωστὸν τῧ θε̄ φανερόν ἐσιν ἐν αὐτοῖς: That which can be known of God is manifest in them.

Then he asserts that God himself manifested this to them: ὁ γὰρ θεὸς αὐτοῖς ἐφανέρωσε: For God manifested it to them: ibid.

Thirdly, he expressly notes the material from which they drew some knowledge of God, not the book of Scripture, but the book of Nature: saying that from the creature, and through the creatures, they understood: v. 20. And indeed, David was also very diligent in unfolding that book of Nature, as is evident from Psalms 104 and 148, likewise the most holy Job in chapters 35 and 36. By which one book alone Anthony the Hermit once said he was so excellently content that he confessed the loss of other books was not grievous to him, as witnessed by the Tripartite History, book 8, chapter 1.

Fourthly, the Apostle also defines certain degrees of this natural knowledge: first indeed generally asserting that the ἀόρατα θε̄ (invisible things of God) were known to the Gentiles: but soon, lest this be taken too loosely, restricting it to certain species: namely, to the ἀΐδιον δύναμιν καὶ θειότητα ᾿θ θε̄, to the eternal power and divinity of God, v. 20.

Fifthly, he implies that not even the will of God was entirely hidden from the Gentiles, as they knew the τὸ δικαίωμα θε̄ (the righteous judgment of God), v. 32.

Sixthly, he describes more clearly the Effect of this natural knowledge, chap. 2, 14. & 15. For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law (that is, the written one), do by nature the things that are of the law: these, not having the law, are a law unto themselves: Who show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness and their thoughts accusing or even excusing one another. Finally, the Apostle also explains the Final cause; saying that for this reason

this knowledge of God came to them, εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυτὸς ἀναπολογήτες, that they might be without excuse Rom. 1, 20. because they held back the truth in Injustice, and did not glorify God, whom they acknowledged, as God, or give thanks: but became vain in their reasonings &c. Rom. 1, 18. & 21. & seqq. Thus, therefore, the Apostle sets forth as it were an entire Commentary, omitting nothing at all of those things which can come into Controversy concerning the Law of Nature, as will be evident from what follows.

Our Author borrows another argument of proof from the End and Creation of the human race. For Man is said to have been created in the Image of God for this reason, because the image of God shone in him, that is, the knowledge of God, and a certain likeness of the divine mind, that is, the distinction between honorable and base things: and the powers of man corresponded with these notions: And although in the corruption of Nature, the Image of God being deformed, these notions do not shine so brightly, they nevertheless remain: For the natural knowledge of God has not been completely extinguished.

A third Argument can be sought from those most excellent Effects, which one may detect and admire in Gentile Philosophers and others, living even outside the Church and the grace of regeneration. For from nowhere else, but from this Light of Nature alone, flowed the distinctions of honorable and base things, κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι, that is, those common notions concerning the just and the good. Hence flowed Ethical doctrine, and the entire legislation of the Gentiles, which sanctions some worship of God, and especially informs Man not unsuitably concerning the precepts of the second table. Hence the Father of Roman Eloquence did not hesitate to write: That God is innate in all and as it were engraved, and there is no race of men, neither so untamed, nor so wild, that does not know, even if it is ignorant of what kind of God it is fitting to have, that one must be had, book 1. de Leg.

The fourth is shown by the very justice of God, which might seem to labor, if the Gentiles could have had no knowledge of God at all: and for this very reason were later condemned. For they could have put forward an excuse of ignorance, that they did not worship God for the reason that they were ignorant that God existed. Hence the Apostle Rom. 1. v. 20. not obscurely hints, that if at least the worship of God among the Gentiles had corresponded to that knowledge which they had of God from natural things, then they could have had at least some excuse regarding their total impiety. But now, since they did not exercise that knowledge of God, such as it was, through the observance of divine worship, there was certainly no excuse left for them anymore: because God imprinted this knowledge upon their Nature for this very end, that they might rightly use it for the glory and worship of God. To which Apostolic Argumentation, indeed, all force and vigor is cut away, as soon as this Light of Nature is either denied entirely: or is referred to among the works of the flesh and mortal sins.

The contemplation of this universe provides a fifth [argument], indeed the daily experiments of the senses themselves, which do not allow those natural notions to be deserted: so much so that the most holy Job does not hesitate to invoke this external testimony in chapter 12, 7. Saying, Ask the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee: Speak to the earth, and it shall answer thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee. For who is ignorant that the hand of the Lord hath made all these things. Moreover, purer theologians establish certain degrees of this contemplation, which can come under observation.

THE FIRST is the clearly wonderful structure, both of the whole world: and especially of man himself: both as regards the structure of the body, and the most convenient symmetry of all its members: as well as regards the powers or faculties of the rational soul, and their most absolute harmony.

The second is the clearly miraculous preservation and propagation of the order, both political and economic: amidst so many and such great furies of the Devil, and ruins of the world.

The third is the internal torments of conscience, which exercise even the most wicked, and torture and torment them more cruelly than any executioner, so much so that if such men escape the punishments of men, yet at length, overcome by the vehemence of those agonies and torments, they either lay violent hands upon themselves, or certainly end their lives most miserably amidst perpetual agonies and terrors.

The fourth is the apparitions of various portents and prodigies, for the most part joined with the most certain presages of most sad events.

The fifth and last can be established as the certain order and connection of causes, which, unless a progress into infinity be granted, infallibly proves that there is one first and universal cause upon which all other things depend.

These indeed and other clear testimonies of that kind argue quite evidently that even today certain rays of divine light shine forth in the human mind.

The sixth and last argument we have borrowed from the unanimous consent of the doctors of the Church, both ancient and modern.

From the ancients, Jerome says thus: Therefore God has moderated all things by a struggle, and has ordered the elements to serve human uses, so that men, seeing these things, might understand that there is a providence, and might fear from the face of God, while from the equality, course, order, and constancy of things they understand the Creator, in chapter 3 of Ecclesiastes. Ambrose on chapter 1 of Romans: From the very structure of the heaven God is seen: for he created the stars so beautiful for this reason, that from them, how great and how admirable their Creator is might be able to be known, and he alone be adored: Hence it is written in Psalm 19, 1: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth his handiwork.

Augustine, book 25, chapter 4, on the Trinity: Not only the authority of divine books proclaims that there is a God: but the whole nature of things, which surrounds us, to which we also belong, proclaims that it has a most excellent creator, who gave us mind and natural reason.

The same in John: From the perpetuity of creatures the eternal Creator is understood, from their magnitude the omnipotent, from their order and disposition the wise, from their governance the good.

From the moderns, B. Luther says thus in his exposition on the Decalogue, Tom. IV, German, Jena, page 527b: That the Gentiles had the Law, reason and conscience itself dictate: just as Paul says in Romans 1 that the Gentiles have knowledge of God: since God manifested it to them, so that from the visible creatures of this world they might recognize the invisible things of God, namely his eternal power and divinity: By which words the Apostle wished to signify that all Gentiles had knowledge of God, namely that he created all things, bestows all things, sustains all things, and preserves them. For which cause their own conscience urges them to give glory to God, and to give thanks to him for all benefits. Therefore, even if Moses had not written the Law, all men would nevertheless have the Law, inscribed by nature upon their hearts. Moreover, out of abundance, God gave the Jews also a written Law, namely the Decalogue, which is nothing else than the Law of Nature, which is naturally inscribed upon our hearts, so that whatever Moses wrote in the Decalogue, we find that naturally in our conscience.

Philipp Melanchthon, Philosophical Disputation 1, Vol. 1 of the Latin works of Luther, Wittenberg, p. 470. Philosophy is a good creature of God, and the chief among all natural gifts: And it is a thing necessary in this bodily and civil life, just as food, drink, and public laws: Moral philosophy is the very Law of God concerning civil morals.

And p. 471. Aristotle said that he had attained this from philosophy, that he would do willingly those things which most people do only when compelled by the fear of laws: We assert that this is rightly and truly said. For man can in some way, by the powers of nature and reason, perform civilly good works, and can in some way command his will and his members to obey honesty and avoid base deeds: And philosophy excites and illuminates these natural notions, according to the saying of the lyric poet: 'But instruction promotes the innate power.'

And p. 473. Philosophy is true doctrine and a gift of God, and a notable testimony of divine providence. And when this doctrine (namely, of the arts) is called philosophy, it is a true sentiment that philosophy is Truth and a gift of God, given to the human race for the sake of many utilities. Which same thing is frequently repeated and illustrated on p. 474.

Dr. Chemnitz, Part 2 of the Loci, p. 162. Let us give thanks and acknowledge that benefit, that God did not wish the light of the law to be entirely extinguished by the fall, but wished certain remnants to survive, etc. Let us also learn to love, venerate, and magnify moral sentences congruent with the Law of Nature, wherever they exist and are read among poets, historians, philosophers, lawgivers, etc. Because they are DIVINE JUSTICE and the TRUTH OF GOD divinely revealed. Thus Paul was not afraid in a most serious matter to cite a sentence from Menander, 1 Cor. 15:33: 'Evil communications corrupt good manners,' etc.

With these things thus established, we conclude at last with Philipp, that those are not only ungrateful to God himself, but also insulting, who today do not blush to deny natural notions, or to call their most excellent effect, namely Philosophy, a work of the flesh, or Sin.

established: and he calls Heaven the highest dwelling place of God. Thus, therefore, this knowledge of God, drawn from the book of Nature, shows that God exists, that He is an eternal and immutable substance, separated from sensible things, having infinite power and nature: since no finite thing has infinite power, as regards the first cause of the existence of all things, as Aristotle speaks in book 12, chapter 7 of the Metaphysics. Finally, if the question is about the will of God, the Apostle answers that the righteous judgment of God was known to the Gentiles.

Nor does it stand in the way that David in Psalm 14:1 affirms that the impious deny that God exists. For that is to be understood not of the habit of nature, but of the affection of malice. For although the impious strive either to cover this natural knowledge of God and divine things with a certain cunning hypocrisy, or to hide or suppress it with a certain blind fury: yet it does not allow itself to be extinguished in the mind: And whatever they may pretend or dissemble outwardly, yet inwardly the judgment stands that God exists, since by the testimony of their own conscience they are convicted of error and impiety. Rom. 2:15.

Latin:

DE PRIMO.

HOmini post lapsum etiam, & quidem in statu corruptionis considerato, Lumen aliquod Naturæ, hoc est, Notitiam quandam de Deo, rebusq́; divinis concedendam eße: D. Apostolus satis evidenter confirmat: idque multipliciter.

Nam 1. Categoricè affirmat, Gentiles habuisse notitiam Dei: Rom.1, 19. τὸ γνωστὸν τῧ θε̄ φανερόν ἐσιν ἐν αὐτοῖς: Quod de Deo cognosci potest, manifestum est in ipsis.

Deindè asserit, Deum ipsum hanc ipsis maninisestasse: ὁ γὰρ θεὸς αὐτοῖς ἐφανέρωσε: Deus eim illis manifestavit: ibid.

Tertiò, Materiam ex qua Notitiam aliquam de Deo hauserint, disertè notat, non librum Scripturæ: sed librum Naturæ: Ex Creatura inquiens, & per Creaturas intellexerunt: v. 20. Et profectò in evolvendo isto libro Naturæ admodum diligens etiam erat David, uti patet ex Psalmis 104. & 148. item, Sanctissimus Jobus capp. 35. & 36. Quo uno etiam libro ita se præclarè contentum olim Antonius Eremita dixit, ut aliorum librorum jacturam sibi non gravem esse, fateretur, teste Tripartitâ lib 8. cap. 1.

Quartò, Apostolus certos etiam Gradus Notitiæ hujus Naturalis definit: primùm quidem Generaliter G ἀόρατα θε̄ nota fuisse Gentilibus afferens: sed mox, ne nimis laxè hoc accipiatur, ad certas species id restringens: nempè ad ἀΐδιον δύναμιν καὶ θειότητα ᾿θ θε̄, ad æternam tùm potentiam tùm Divinitatem Dei v. 20.

Quintò, ne quidem voluntatem Dei simpliciter Gentiles latuisse innuit, ut qui τὸ δικαίωμα θε̄ jus Dei noverint v. 32.

Sextò, dilucidiùs Effectum notitiæ istius naturalis describit, cap. 2, 14. & 15. Quando enim Gentes, qua legem (scriptam scilicet) non habent, naturâ ea, quæ legis sunt, faciunt: hi legem non habentes, sibi ipsis sunt Lex: Qui ostendunt opus Legis scriptum esse in cordibus ipsorum, attestante ipsorum conscientiâ & cogitationibus sese invicem accusantibus, vel etiam excusantibus. Tandem causam etiam Finalem exponit Apostolus; ideò inquiens, hanc

Dei notitiam ipsis obtigisse, εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀυτὸς ἀναπολογήτες, ut sint inexcusabiles Rom. 1, 20. propterea quòd veritatem in Injustitiâ detinuerunt, & Deum, quem agnoverunt, non ut Deum glorificaverunt, aut gratias egerunt: sed vani facti sunt in suis rationibus &c. Rom. 1, 18. & 21. & seqq. Sic ergò integrum quasi Commentarium expedit Apostolus, nihil quicquam omittens eorum, quæ de Lege Naturæ in Controversiam venire possunt, uti ex subsequentibus patebit.

Alterum probationis argumentum mutuatur Autor noster à Fine & Creationis Generis humani. Ideò enim Homo ad Imaginem Dei conditus esse dicitur, quia in eo lucebat imago Dei, hoc est notitia Dei, & similitudo quædam mentis divinæ, hoc est, discrimen honestorum & turpium: & cum his notitijs congruebant vires hominis: Et quanquàm in Naturæ corruptione, deformata Imagine Dei, non ita fulgent notitiæ, manent tamen: Neque enim extincta est penitùs notitia naturalis de Deo.

Tertium Argumentum peti potest ex præclarissimis illis Effectis, quæ in Gentilibus Philosophis & alijs, etiam extra Ecclesiam & regenerationis gratiam viventibus deprehendere & admirari licet. Nam non aliundè, quàm ex solo hoc Lumine Naturæ profluxerunt discrimina honestorum & turpium κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι, hoc est, communes illæ de æquo & bono notiones. Hinc defluxit doctrina Ethica, & universa Gentilium νομοθεσία, quæ aliquem Dei cultum sancit, & cumprimis Hominem circa secundæ tabulæ præcepta haud incommodè informat. Hinc Romanæ Eloquentiæ Pater scribere non dubitavit: Deum e\u017sse omnibus innatum & quasi insculptum est, & nulla de hominibus gens est, neque tam immansueta, neque tam fera, quæ non, etiamsi ignoret, qualem Deum habere deceat, tamen habendum sciat, lib. 1. de Leg.

Quartum monstrat ipsa Dei justitia, quæ laborare videri posset, si Gentes nullam prorsus Dei notitiam habere potuissent: & ob hoc ipsum postmodùm damnarentur. Excusationem enim ignorantiæ prætendere possent, se ideò Deum non coluisse, quia Deum esse ignoraverint. Hinc Apostolus Rom. 1. v. 20. haud obscurè innuit, si saltem cultus Dei apud Gentiles respondisset illi notitiæ, quam de Deo ex naturalibus habuerunt, tùm aliquid saltem illos excusationis, quoad summam impietatem habere potuisse. Nunc autem, cùm qualemcunque illam Dei notitiam non per cultus divini observantiam exercuerint, nihil utique excusationis illis ampliùs esse relictum: propterea quòd Deus hoc ipso fine Naturæ ipsorum Notitiam hanc impresserit, ut ad gloriam & cultum Dei eâ rectè uterentur. Cui sanè Argumentationi Apostolicæ omnis vis ac nervus inciditur, quamprimùm Lumen hoc Naturæ vel prorsus negatur: vel inter opera carnis & peccata mortalia refertur.

Quintum suppeditat Contemplatio hujus universi, imo ipsorum sensuum quotidiana experimenta, quæ Notitias illas naturales deseri non patiuntur: adeò ut hoc externum Testimonium provocare non dubitet sanctissimus Jobus cap. 12, 7. Interroga inquiens jumenta, & docebunt te volatilia cœli, & indicabunt tibi: Loquere terræ, & respondebunt tibi, & narrabunt pisces maris. Quis enim ignorat, quòd omnia hæc manus Domini fecerit. Constituunt autem puriores Theologi Contemplationis hujus certos quosdam Gradus, qui sub observationem venire possunt.

PRIMUS est, Miranda planè fabrica, tùm Mundi universi: tùm inprimis ipsius Hominis: tùm quoad corporis structuram, ac omnium membrorum convenientissimam συμμετρίαν: quàm quòad Animæ rationalis vires sive potentias, earumque absolutissimam harmoniam.

Alter est Miraculosa planè conservatio & propagatio Ordinis tùm Politici, tùm Oeconomici: inter tot tantosque Diaboli furores, Mundique ruinas.

Tertius est Interni Cruciatus conscientiæ, qui etiam sceleratissimos exercent, & vel quovis carnifice sævius torquent & excruciant, adeò, ut tales si maximè Hominum pœnas effugiant: tamen tandem angorum ac cruciatuum istorum vehementiâ superati, vel manus violentas sibi ipsis inferant, vel certè inter perpetuos angores ac terrores vitam miserrimè finiant.

Quartus est variorum ostentorum ac prodigiorum apparitiones, plerumque conjunctæ cum certissimis tristissimorum eventuum præsagiis.

Quintus & postremus constitui potest certus Causarum ordo & connexio, quæ nisi progressus detur in infinitum, infallibiliter evincit, dari Unam primam & universalem Causam à quâ reliqua omnia dependeant.

Hæc sanè & id genus alia luculenta testimonia satis evidenter arguunt, hodiéque lucis divinæ radios quosdam in mente humana elutescere.

Sextum & postremum argumentum mutuati licet ex unanimi consensu Doctorum Ecclesiæ tùm veterum, tùm recentiorum.

Ex veteribus sic Hieronymus: Iccircò Deus certatione cuncta moderatus est, & jussit humanis usibus Elementa servire, ut Homines hæc videntes, intelligant esse providentiam, & timeant à facie Dei, dum ex rerum æqualitate, cursu, ordine atque constantia intelligunt Creatorem, in cap. 3. Eccles. Ambrosius ad cap. 1. Rom. Ex ipsa Cæli Fabrica Deus videtur: idcircò enim tam pulchra astra condidit, ut ex his, quantus & quàm admirabilis Creator eorum est, possit agnosci, & solus adorari: Indè scriptum est Psal. 19, 1 Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opera manuum ejus, annunciat firmamentum.

August. l. 25. cap 4. de Trinit. Non divinorum tantummodò librorum autoritas esse Deum prædicat: sed omnia, quæ nec circumbstat, ad quam nos etiam pertinemus, universa rerum natura proclamat, habere se præstantissimum conditorem, qui nobis mentem rationemque naturalem dedit.

Idem in Johannem: Ex perpetuitate Creaturarum intelligitur Creator æternus, ex magnitudine omnipotens, ex ordine & dispositione sapiens, ex Gubernatione bonus.

Ex recentioribus sic B. Lutherus in exposuit in Decalogũ, Tom. IIII. Germ. Jenens. pag. 527. b. Gentes Legem habuisse, ipsa dictat ratio & conscientia: quemadmodum Paulus Rom. 1. dicit Gentes notitiam habere de Deo: siquidem Deus illud ipsis manifestaverit, ut ex visibilibus hujus mundi Creaturis agnoscerent invisibilia Dei, nempe æternam ipsius potentiam & divinitatem: Quibus Verbis Apostolus significare voluit, omnes Gentes habuisse notitiam Dei, quòd videlicet omnia creaverit, omnia largiatur, omnia sustentet, & conservet. Quâ de causa propria ipsorum Conscientia illos urget, ut dent gloriam Deo, ipsiq; pro omnib9 beneficijs agant gratias. Proindè si vel maximè Moses Legem non scripsisset: omnes tamen Homines haberent Legem, naturâ cordibus ipsorum inscriptam. Ex superabundanti autem Deus Judæis quoque dedit Legem scriptam, nempè Decalogum, qui nihil est aliud, quàm Lex Naturæ, quæ naturaliter cordibus nostris est inscripta, ita, ut quicquid in Decalogo Moses scripserit, illud naturaliter inveniamus in nostra conscientia.

Philippus Melanchthon Dispu. 1. Philosophicâ, Tom. 1. operum Lutheri Lat. VVItt. p. 470. Philosophia est bona Creatura Dei, & inter omnia naturalia dona præcipuum: Et est res hac in vita corporali ac civili necessaria, sicut cibus, potus, sicut publicæ leges: Philosophia de moribus est ipsa Lex Dei de civilibus moribus.

Et pag. 471. Aristoteles dixit, se id ex Philosophia consecutum esse, ut volens faceret ea, quæ pleriq; metu legum coacti: Id nos rectè & verè dictum asserimus. Nam Homo potest aliquomodo viribus naturæ & rationis facere civiliter bona opera, & potest aliquo modo imperare voluntati suæ, atque membris, ut honestati obediant, turpia facta vitent: Et eas naturales notitias excitat atq; illustrat Philosophia, juxta dictum Lyrici: Doctrina sed vim promovet insitam.

Et pag. 473. Philosophia est doctrina vera & donum Dei, & insigne testimonium divinæ providentiæ. Et cum hæc doctrina (artium scilicet) dicitur Philosophia, vera est sententia, Philosophiam Veritatem & Dei donum esse, multarum utilitatum causa datum generi humano. Quod ipsum aliquoties repetitur & illustratur pag. 474.

D. Chemnitius part. 2. Locorum pag. 162. Grati agnoscamus illud beneficium, quòd Deus non voluerit Lucem legis totam extinctam per lapsum, sed voluit reliquias quasdam superesse &c. Discamus etiam amare, venerari & magnificare sententias morales congruentes Legi Naturæ, ubicunque extent & legantur apud Poëtas, Historicos, Philosophos, Legumlatores &c. Quia sunt JV STIVINUM & VERITAS DEI divinitùs patefacta. Ita Paulo non est veritus in gravissima causa ex Menandro citare sententiam, 1. Cor. 15, 33. Corrumpūt bonos mores, colloquia prava &c.

Quibus ita constitutis, concludimus tandem cū Philippo, in Deum ipsum non ingratos modò, sed & contumeliosos esse, qui vel notitias naturales negare, vel præstantissimum earum Effectum, Philosophiam nimirùm, opus carnis, sivè Peccatum nominare hodiè non erubescunt.

constituta: & Cœlum vocat τὸ ἀνώτατον 9εῦ οἰκητήριον. Sic ergo Notitia hæc Dei, hausta ex libro Naturæ Ostendit, quòd sit Deus, quòd sit æterna & immutabilis substantia, à sensilibus separata, infinitam habens potentiam & naturam: siquidem nullum finitum infinitam habet potentiam, quoad causam primam existentia rerum omnium, uti loquitur Aristoteles lib. 12. cap. 7. Metaphys. Tandem si de voluntate Dei sit Quæstio, respondet Apostolus, notum fuisse Gentilibus τὸ δικαίωμα ϑεῦ Ius Dei.

Neque obstat, quòd David Psalmo 14, 1. Impios affirmat negare Deum esse. Neque enim de habitu naturæ, sed de affectu malitiæ illud est intelligendum. Nam licet vel astutâ quadam hypocrisi tegere, vel cæco quodam furore, Notitiam hanc naturalem de Deo ac rebus divinis, impij vel occultare vel opprimere fatagunt: tamen illa sese extingui in animo non patitur: Et quicquid foris isti fimulent aut diffimulent, intus tamen stat sententia, esse Deum, siquidem Conscientiæ propriæ testimonio, erroris & impietatis convincuntur. Rom. 2, 15.


### Chapter II. Controversy concerning the Law of Nature, and about natural…: II. on the Scope or Breadth of the Law of Nature

II. ON THE SCOPE or Breadth of the Law of Nature.

But how far this righteous judgment extends, the Apostle himself immediately explains, restricting it to the judicial justice of God, by which He repays good things to the good, evil things to the evil, decrees rewards for the just, and punishments for the unjust. For he immediately adds: Who, when they knew the righteous judgment of God, that they who do such things are worthy of death, etc. From this knowledge of the divine will flowed all that Law of the Gentiles, which Philosophers call the Law of nature, and Jurists call the Law of Nations: whose precepts are three positive ones. 1. To live honestly. 2. To harm no one. 3. To give each his own: But one negative one, and that a general one: That he who violates this Law is worthy of hatred and death. But this law arises, as our Author rightly warns, first from natural notions, such as the common notions concerning principles that are both contemplative or speculative, such as these axioms: The effect argues the cause: The whole is greater than its part: Nothing can be true and not true at the same time: concerning any subject there is a true affirmation or negation, and other axioms of that kind in Mathematics, Logic, and Physics: and then from Practical Principles, which concern the whole natural distinction between honorable and shameful things.

The Apostle restricts the scope or breadth of the knowledge of God, the natural knowledge of God and divine things, to two quasi-highest genera: one of which he calls truth: the other, however, the righteous judgment of God, Rom. 1:18 and 32. Moreover, he so distinguishes these two from each other, that the former is concerned with the knowledge of the Essence of God: the latter, however, with the knowledge of the Will of God: so that for the Gentiles also, who are constituted outside the Church, according to the opinion of the Apostle, there can and must be assigned not absolutely and simply that confused knowledge, that there is a Divinity, or some celestial God, but also in part a distinct one, both regarding the question of whether He exists, and what He is: but yet limited in many ways.

Then, however, this law arises from the use of reason, by means of a more accurate contemplation of this universe: as when reason concludes: That it is impossible that Heaven and earth could have existed by chance, or coalesced from the atoms of Democritus into this most absolute and beautiful structure: But that there is some divine Divinity, which created, orders, disposes, and preserves all things: and therefore is to be worshipped purely in the mind.

For regarding the question, whether God exists, not only the Apostle in chapter 1 to the Romans: but also M. Tullius in the place already cited above, place it beyond controversy, that it is innate to all by nature, and as it were inscribed: nor is any nation so savage that it has not known that God exists. Then regarding the question of what God is, the Apostle is a witness that the Gentiles knew from the Light of Nature those attributes or properties of God, the power of which is seen especially in the Creation and Government of this Universe. But the Apostle restricts them both to the eternal Divinity and to the power of God: which two he later calls the known of God and the invisible things of God, v. 19 and 20. Hence the sounder Ethnic Philosophers, Plato especially in the Timaeus, Theaetetus, and elsewhere, discourse wisely on many things concerning the nature, power, and wisdom of God, and finally describes God as being an eternal mind, the cause of good in nature. Hence Aristotle in the book on the world, chapter 6, calls God a living, eternal, best being: And in book 12 of the Metaphysics, chapters 6 and 7, he asserts that it is the hereditary fame of all mortals that all things are from God and through God.

And up to this point indeed extends the knowledge of God and divine things, drawn from the Light or Law of Nature: limited and restricted to the known of God, insofar as and to the extent that it is weighed in the scope of created or visible things and their contemplation.

With these things thus established, all those things must be removed from this knowledge which are by nature unknown to us: and which can neither become known by nature, nor be investigated or acquired by the benefit of reason: but have need of the singular revelation of God, if indeed they are to become known to men. For example.

I. It is by nature and human reason unknown to us that God is one in essence and three in Persons: for the fact that some think that this mystery was known to the Platonists, to Mercury, or to Hermes Trismegistus, that is manifestly false and fictitious. tium : or if true, from the reading of Moses and the Prophets : as it is certain from conversation with the Jews that this was established for them. For that saying of the Savior stands firm and unshaken : No one knows the Son, except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father, except the Son and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal him, Matt. 11, v. 27.

2. It is unknown to us and to human intellect that the Decalogue or Law of GOD subjects not only the external obedience of the members of the body in every way, but also the internal thoughts and disordered and vicious affections of the mind and will, to the curse of the Law: whereas, on the contrary, that Aristotelian maxim holds among philosophers : Because of affections no one is called either bad or good, nor is anyone either praised or blamed.

3. It is unknown to us and to human reason that the entire doctrine of the Gospel, concerning CHRIST, concerning the promises of grace, concerning the way and manner of eternal salvation, Rom. 16, 25. Coloss. 1, 26.

4. Finally, it is unknown to human Nature that the whole System of the Articles of Faith, when considered both jointly and separately. For if the reason of man or universal Philosophy wishes to define anything in these, immediately a shameful transition into another kind is committed, or a confusion of most diverse Principles. For as much as knowledge and faith differ, so much do the Articles of Faith differ from Philosophical Principles, so that just as faith ceases to be what it is as soon as knowledge or science arrives: since no one is said to believe, but to know that which he recognizes through apodictic causes: So the Articles of Faith immediately cease to be what they are as soon as they are demanded or examined according to Philosophical Principles, by whatever name they may come.

With these things well observed, we infer three corollaries most worthy of observation.

I. Even though natural notions are by no means to be despised, much less denied, but are to be granted in a certain order and degree of limitation: yet they are very imperfect, and produce an assent not only languid, but also involved in horrible doubts from time to time: as is evident from the testimony of Cicero arguing about the immortality of souls, book 1 of the Tusculans, where Cicero says to Antonius: Carefully unfold the book of Plato which is about the soul, and you will desire nothing more; there will be nothing. Antonius replies: By Hercules, I have done so, and indeed often: but I do not know how, while I am reading, I assent, but when I have put the book down, and have begun to think with myself about the immortality of the soul, all that assent slips away. Whence Aristotle also affirms that the Mind itself labors under such darkness that it behaves no differently toward the good and the true than the eyes of bats do toward the light of day. book 2, Metaphysics 1.

II. Even though the assertions of the Gentiles concerning GOD are not to be argued as false or lying because they proceed from infidels: as some today too impiously maintain: but are to be held entirely as true and certain: yet they are destitute of a firm foundation.

dation. For the hearts of men are so depraved by Nature through Original sin, and the judgment of right reason is so distracted and troubled, indeed perverted, by the impetus of the affections, by the power and snares of the Devil, by the wicked examples of others, and finally by the hope of impunity, that, neglecting the worship of GOD which they ought to render to GOD from this natural knowledge, they slide spontaneously and of their own accord into the most shameful crimes: according to that of Medea: I see the better things and approve them, I follow the worse: which the Apostle, in chapter 1 of Romans, enumerating the sins of the Gentiles, proves and confirms quite laboriously.

What? That not even Aristotle himself dared to deny that that recognition of the distinction between honorable and shameful things is attacked by a perpetual struggle of Reason and the affections, and all but completely overwhelmed: writing thus, book 1 of the Ethics, last chapter: It appears also that there is something else besides reason, innate in nature, which fights and resists reason, for just as the paralyzed members of the body, when one chooses to move them to the right, are carried off in the opposite direction to the left, so it happens in the soul. It appears also that there is something else different from reason, innate in nature, which resists and struggles against reason: just as members resolved by paralysis, when they are moved to the right parts, are carried off on the contrary to the left: So it happens also in the mind: And he immediately adds: in bodies indeed this struggle is seen: but in the mind, although it may not be seen, it exists in reality.

For this very reason the same Philosopher, book 7 of the Ethics, chapter 2, denies that the continent man is a good man, because he has wicked affections, even if he does not produce them into effect. These wicked affections, therefore, dragging the mind into contrary things, cause it to be that even those who, by the guidance of the Light of nature, do not rush into external crimes: yet consent to and patronize those who do such things.

III. Although the governance of locomotive power, according to the dictate of right reason and natural notions, is not our righteousness before GOD: yet it is necessary; and is required even from the unregenerate: Because it is the ordinance of God, which the Gentiles recognize and are bound to follow, so that they may satisfy their own Conscience, and so that human society may be preserved, which by the violation of external discipline is easily dissolved, indeed completely overturned.

Moreover, three questions most worthy of explanation are raised in this place: THE FIRST is: What is to be determined concerning the virtues of the heathens, which have proceeded from that Light of Nature? Whether they were in reality either good or evil; or as we speak in the Schools of the Theologians: Whether they were truly good works pleasing to GOD: Or whether they were sins? There are not a few among the Zwinglians who extend the Light of Nature so loosely that they affirm it could have sufficed for a sufficient and saving knowledge of GOD, even for men not reborn and for heathens: and consequently that they were truly good works, and pleasing to God; as one may read in Zwingli in his exposition of the Christian faith: as also in Gualther in his Apology for Zwingli, page 53, part 2, who brings forward as a foundation that passage of Isaiah 55:10 and 11: As the rain descendeth, and the snow from Heaven, and returneth not thither; but it drenches the earth, and makes it bring forth: So shall my Word be, which shall go forth from my mouth, it shall not return to me void but shall do whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in those things to which I sent it. Hence Gualtherus now infers thus: Yet the Word of GOD is not only that Mosaic and Prophetic writing: but every suggestion, as well external as internal, by which men can be drawn into the knowledge of GOD: Yet the Gentiles had such suggestions, Rom. 1. τὸ γνωστὸν θεꙋ, that is, all that which can be known and understood about GOD, was revealed to them, and GOD revealed this to them, not a malignant Spirit.

Moreover, this assertion labors under many notable sophistries. The first is τῆς ἐτεροζητήσεως, or the confusion of disparate questions. For it is one thing when it is asked, Could the Gentiles have been justified by the power of the Light of Nature?
