The negative of which we hold, and we prove it invincibly, both from what has already been noted, and from those things which we shall discuss shortly in the third member concerning the use of this Light. But it is another thing when it is asked, Were the virtues of the Gentiles truly good works, and pleasing to God? Where the question ought to be resolved by a clear distinction: whence arises the other sophistry, which is τῆς ὁμωνυμίας? For in the Schools of the Theologians, works are considered in two ways, either by reason of Φύσεως or Nature: namely, as to the substance of the deeds, which in itself is either good, as virtues, or evil, as vices: or they are considered by reason of πίςεως or Faith in Christ. Now therefore, the virtues of the Gentiles in the former way and respect were indeed good works, since they not only agreed with the precepts of the Decalogue according to the substance of the deeds: but were also excited in them by the singular grace of GOD. And in this respect, hardly anyone would easily deny that those works also pleased GOD in a certain way: so that GOD not only compensated them with the rewards of temporal goods in this life: but they were also to have security from a more severe punishment of damnation. But in the latter respect, both are most rightly denied, both that they were truly good works: and that they pleased GOD. For because they contracted vice in various ways, partly from the adjuncts, and partly from the very persons of the doers: certainly it cannot be affirmed that they were simply good or pleasing to God: but rather it must be pronounced that they were contaminated in many ways, and if not for other causes, at least for this one they were ungrateful to GOD, and thus abominable, because the persons were not reconciled to GOD through faith. The reason for this pronouncement is taken from the testimonies of Scripture, Matt. 11, 18. A bad tree cannot make good fruits. Rom. 14, 23. Whatever is not of Faith, is sin. Heb. 11, 6. Without faith it is impossible to please GOD. The third sophistry is παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἄιτιον, καὶ παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For it does not follow: GOD revealed that γνωστὸν to the Gentiles, or, GOD worked those virtues in the Gentiles, and excited those singular heroic motions: Therefore they ought to be referred to the class of works which are said in the Scriptures to be simply and absolutely good, and to please God. For a distinction must be made between the ministering or ministerial gifts of GOD, which GOD is accustomed to confer even upon men who are infidels and not reborn, for the sake of preserving human society more rightly: and the sanctifying gifts, which befall only the reborn and the faithful, and which simply please GOD, not indeed because they are good by the substance of the deed: but because they are done by the good, that is, by the reborn and those reconciled to GOD through faith, or, as Scripture speaks, because they are done from GOD and in GOD. John 3, 21.

Fourthly, the fallacy of the consequent is committed: For τό γνωσὸν τῶ θεῶ is extended too loosely beyond the mind and scope of the Apostle to the salvific knowledge of GOD: when it ought to be restricted only to the eternal Divinity and power of GOD, and that judiciary justice of GOD, as was shown above. Finally, what Gualtherus discourses here about internal suggestions or enthusiasms, defined outside the revealed Word of GOD, is un-theological and fanatical.

We conclude therefore with D. Augustine from Epistle 99 and book 4 against Julian, chapter 3: Even if the virtues of the heathens delight us by a certain nature of their own: and for that reason we do not willingly condemn them: yet because for a truly good work, pleasing to God, it is required not only that something be done which is good in its own kind: but especially that it be done well, that is, from faith in Christ: Because also virtues are to be distinguished from vices, not only by duties, but also by their ends; and the duties themselves are weighed not by the acts, but by the ends; we pronounce that those were indeed sins, and displeased God, following the Apostle in this part, because he calls his works performed in Judaism σκύβαλα, Phil. 3. And the Prophet Isaiah, who weighs the justice of works apart from faith, calls it a menstruous cloth, chapter 64.

The other question, which is agitated in this place, is about that saying of the Apostle Rom. 2, 14. The Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do those things which are of the law. For since here the Apostle seems, according to the surface of the letter, to assign to the Gentiles some fulfillment of the Law, performed by the benefit of Nature, it was variously disputed among interpreters about this passage: so much so that D. Augustine, by the name of Gentiles, understands Christians under the New Testament, converted from the Gentiles to the evangelical faith, lib. de Sp. & lit. c. 26 & 27.

Moreover, perhaps all obscurity or difficulty is most easily removed if we examine the words of the Apostle a little more closely. For the Apostle does not say that the Gentiles by nature do τὸν νόμον the Law: but τὰ τῦ νόμγ, that is, certain works which are of the law: namely, in governing external locomotion, and in performing certain external actions which agree with political honesty.

But indeed, a consequence from a part to the Whole is not valid: and therefore it is most viciously concluded: Some deeds of the Gentiles agree with the Decalogue, according to the substance of the deed: Therefore the Gentiles have clearly fulfilled the Law of God, and their works, even according to that spiritual mode of fulfillment, were absolutely good.

THE THIRD & final Question is: Should natural notions drawn from the Light of Nature concerning GOD and divine things be called true or false? There are and are found today some who maintain that those notions, and the propositions concerning God that flow from them: such as that He is an eternal mind, is omnipotent, is a just avenger of crimes, is the cause of good in Nature: these, I say, and similar propositions, if they are brought forth by the Gentiles, are false, because they are the concepts of unregenerate men. To whose opinion we can by no means subscribe: moved especially by the evident Apostolic assertion: Rom. 1, 21. which is as follows: The wrath of God is revealed from Heaven against all impiety and injustice of those men, who hold the TRUTH in injustice. But what ought to be understood by this TRUTH, the Apostle himself explains immediately, while he defines it partly by γνωστὸν τῦ θεῦ, and partly restricts it expressly to the knowledge of eternal divinity, power, and divine Justice. Now, indeed, the Apostle calls this knowledge of God, or τὸ γνωστὸν τῦ θεῦ, TRUTH. It would therefore be a sin to call that a lie and falsehood which the Apostle in express words calls truth. And how, I ask, would the evidence of the Apostolic intention stand, if one should wish to exchange the term Truth with the epithet of Falsehood. For he says that this Truth was held by the Gentiles in injustice: that is, that force was as it were brought upon that divine cognition, and the TRUTH, which they had concerning God, was oppressed by works of Injustice. For such is otherwise the nature of Truth, that it conciliates love for itself in the mind. Now if the opposite happens, namely that we are not carried toward the love of the good: but, having neglected the true and the good, we choose the false and the evil, as the Apostle reports the Gentiles to have done: then certainly it is not falsehood, but truth that is oppressed in the mind: therefore the Truth was known to them, and it is absolutely necessary that their propositions concerning God, however much they were drawn from the Light of Nature by the unregenerate, are true by their own Nature. Therefore, those who maintain the opposite to us ought to have accurately distinguished the notions themselves from the Persons of the Gentiles: and to have assigned truth to the former, but to the latter, with the Apostle, ἀδικίαν or injustice. While they do not do this, but proceed to judge the notions themselves, which were implanted in nature by God, from the condition of the Persons, they entangle and involve themselves and others in a shameful Sophistication of τῆς ἑτεροζητήσεως.

Latin:

II. DE COMPLEXU sive Latitudine Legis Naturæ.

Quousque autem hoc δικαίωμα se extendat, ipse statim Apostolus explicat, restringens illud ad Justitiam Dei judiciariam, quâ bonis bona, malis mala rependit, justis præmia, injustis pœnas decernit. Statim enim addit: Qui cùm Jus Dei nôrint, quòd qui talia faciunt, digni sunt morte &c. Ex hac notitiâ voluntatis divinæ defluxit universum illud Jus Gentilium, quòd Philosophi Jus naturæ, Jure Consulti Ius Gentium appellant: cujus præcepta tria sunt θετικά. 1. Honestè vivendum. 2. Neminem lædendum. 3. Jus suum cuiq; tribuendum: Unum verò ἀποφασικὸν, idque genérale: Hoc Jus qui violat, illum odio & morte dignùm esse. Oritur verò hoc jus, uti rectè Autor noster admonet, primùm ex notitijs naturalibus, quales sunt κοιναὶ ἐννοίαι de principijs tùm contemplativis sive speculabilibus, ut sunt axiomata hæc: Effectus arguit causam: Totum majus suâ parte: Plus uno verum esse nequit: de quolibet Subjecto vera ex vel affirmatio vel negatio, & id genus alia exiomata Mathematica, Logica & Physica: tùm de Principijs Practicis, quæ spectant totum discrimen Naturale honestorum & turpium.

COmplexum sive Latitudinem τῆς γνώσεως ϑεῦ, Notitiæ Naturalis de Deo, rebusque divinis, restringit Apostolus ad duo summa quasi genera: quorum unum nominat ἀλήθειαν Veritatem: alterum verò τὸ δικαίωμα ϑ θεῦ Jus Dei, Rom. 1, 18. & 32. Quin etiam duo hæc à se mutuò ità distinguit, ut prius illud versetur circa notitiam de Essentia Dei: Postérius verò hoc, circa notitiam de Voluntate Dei: ita ut Gentilibus etiam extra Ecclesiam constitutis, ex sententia Apostoli assignari possit & debeat non absolutè, ac simpliciter confusa illa notitia, esse Numen, sive Deum aliquem cælestem, sed & ex parte discreta, tùm quoad Quæstionem τὸ ὄτι, tùm τὸ τί: sed tamen multis modis limitata.

Deindè verò oritur hoc Jus ex usu rationis, mediante accuratiore contemplatione hujus universi: ut quando ratio colligit: Impossibile esse Cœlum & terram casu potuisse existere, aut ex atomis Democriti in absolutissimam & pulcherrimam istam compagem coalescere: Sed esse Numen aliquod divinum, quod omnia creavit, ordinet, di sponat, consérvet: ac proindè purè mente esse colendum.

Nam quoad Quæstionem, an sit Deus, non Apostolus modò capite 1. ad Romanos: sed & M. Tullius loco jam supra citato, extra controversiam ponunt, illam naturâ omnibus innatam, & quasi insculptam esse: neq; ullam gentem tam feram esse, quæ ignoravexit, esse Deum. Deindè quoad Quæstionem & τί, Quid sit Deus, testis est Apostolus, ex Lumine Naturæ novisse Gentes, ea attributa sive proprietates Dei, quarum vis præcipuè in Creatione & Gubernatione hujus Universi conspicitur. Restringit autem eas Apostolus tùm ad ἀίδιον θειότητα æternam Divinitatem, tùm ad δύναμιν ϑεῦ potentiam Dei: Quæ duo postmodùm nominat τὸ γνωστὸν τῦ ϑεῦ & τὰ ἀόρατα ϑεῦ ν. 19. & 20. Hinc saniores Philosophi Ethnici, Plato cum primis in Timæo, Theæteto & passim plurima sapienter de Dei natura & potentiâ, ac sapientia disserit, ac tandem Deum describit, quod sit mens æterna, causa boni in natura. Hinc Aristoteles lib. de mundo cap. 6. Deum vocat, ζωον ἀίδιον ἄριsτον, vivens æternum optimum: Et lib. 12. Metaphys. cap. 6. & 7. asserit, hæreditariam esse famam omnium mortalium, universa à Deo & per Deum esse

Et huc usque quidem se extendit Notitia Dei, rerumque divinarum, ex Lumine sive Lege Naturæ hausta: limitata ac restricta ad γνωσὸν τῦ ϑεῦ, quatenus & in quantum illud complexu rerum creatarum sive visibilium, earumque contemplatione pensitatur.

Quibus ita constitutis, removenda sunt ab hac notitia, omnia ea, quæ nobis naturâ sunt ἄγνωτα: & neque naturâ innotescere, neque rationis beneficio investigari aut acquiri possunt: sed singulari Dei revelatione opus habent, si modò hominibus innotescere debeant. Exempli gratia.

I. Ἄγνωστον naturâ nobis & rationi humanæ est, unum esse Deum essentia, trinum Personis: Quòd enim nonnulli arbitrantur, Platonici Mercurio sive Hermeti Trismegisto mysterium hoc innotuisse: illud vel manifestè est falsum ac fictitium : vel si verum, ex lectione Moysis & Prophetarum : ut ex conversatione cum Judæis hoc ipsis constitisse certum est. Stat enim firmum & inconcussum illud Servatoris : Nemo novit Filium, nisi Pater, neq; Patrem aliquis novit, nisi Filius & cui Filius voluerit revelare, Matth. 11. v. 27.

2. Ἄγνωστον nobis & intellectui humano est, Decalogum sive Legem DEI non externam tantùm membrorum Corporis omnimodam obedientiam, sed & internas animi voluntatisq; cogitationes & affectus inordinatos ac vitiosos, Legis maledictioni subjicere: cùm econtra apud Philosophos illud obtineat Aristotelicum : Propter affectus nemo vel malus vel bonus dicitur, neque vel laudatur, vel vituperatur.

3. Ἄγνωστον nobis & rationi humanæ est universa Evangelii doctrina, de CHRISTO, de promissionibus gratiæ, de viâ ac ratione salutis æternæ, Rom. 16, 25. Coloss. 1, 26.

4. Tandem ἄγνωστον Naturæ humanæ est totum Systema Articulorum Fidei, cùm conjunctim quàm separatim consideratorem. In his enim si ratio hominis sive Philosophia universa quicquam definire velit, statim turpis committitur μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος, sive diversissimorum Principiorum confusio. Quantum enim differunt γνῶσις & πίστις, tantùm differunt Articuli Fidei, à Principiis Philosophicis, ita ut quemadmodum πίστις desinit esse, quod est, quamprimùm accedit γνῶσις sive ἐπιστήμη: Siquidem nemo dicitur credere, sed scire id, quod per causas Apodicticas cognoscit : Ita Articuli Fidei statim desinunt esse, quod sunt, quamprimùm ad Principia Philosophica, quocunque etiam ea veniant nomine, exiguntur sive examinantur.

Quibus probè observatis tria inferimus πορίσματα observatu dignissima.

I. Etiamsi Notitiæ naturales minimè sunt contemnendæ, nedùm negandæ, sed certo ordine ac limitationis gradu concedendæ: tamen admodùm sunt imperfectæ, & assensionem pariunt non modò languidam, sed & horrendis subindè dubitationibus involutam : quemadmodum illud patet testimonio Ciceronis disputantis de Immortalitate animarum lib. 1. Tusc. ubi Cicero ad Antonium: Evolve diligenter librum Platonis, qui est de anima, amplius quid desideres; nihil erit. Respondet Antonius : Feci mehercule & quidem sæpius: sed nescio, quomodo, dum lego, assentior, cùm posui librum, & mecum ipse de immortalitate animæ cogitare cœpi, omnis illa assensio elabitur. Undè Aristoteles etiam Mentem ipsam eâ caligine laborare affirmat, ut ad bonum & verum non secus se habeat, quàm vespertilionum oculi ad lumen diei. lib. 2. Metaphys. 1.

II. Etiamsi assertiones Gentilium de DEO, non ideò falsitatis aut mendacii sunt arguendæ, quia ab infidelibus proficiscuntur : uti quidam hodiè nimis impiè statuunt: sed pro veris ac certis omninò sunt habendæ: tamen immoto fun-

damento destituuntur. Sunt enim corda hominum Natura peccato Originis ita depravata, & Judicium rectæ rationis, affectuum impetu, potentia ac insidiis Diaboli, pravis aliorum exemplis, spe denique impunitatis, ita distractum & turbatum, imò perversum, ut neglecto DEI cultu, quem ex Notitia hac naturali DEO præstare deberet; ad turpissima scelera sponte ac ultrò prolabatur: juxta illud Medeæ: Video meliora proboq́, Deteriora sequor: id quod Apostolus cap. 1. Rom. enumerans peccata Gentilium, satis operosè probat ac confirmat.

Quid? quòd ne ipse quidem Aristoteles negare ausus fuit, Agnitionem illam discriminis honestorum ac turpium, perpetuâ pugnâ Rationis & affectuum oppugnari, ac tantùm non penitùs obrui: sic scribens, lib. 1. Ethic. cap. ult. Φαίνεται καὶ ἄλλο τι παρὰ τὸν λόγον πεφυκὸς, ὃ μάχεταί τε καὶ ἀντιτείνει τῷ λόγῳ, ἀτεχνῶς γὰρ καθάπερ τὰ παραλελυμένα τῶν σώματος μόρια εἰς τὰ δεξιὰ προαιρομένων κινῆσαι, τὰναντίον εἰς τὰ ἀριστερὰ παραφέρεται καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ψυχῆς ὕτως. Apparet etiam aliud quid à ratione diversum; naturæ inditum, quod rationi repugnat ac reluctatur: planè ut membra paralysi resoluta, cùm in dextras partes moventur, ipsa econtrariò ad sinistras feruntur: Sic & in animo evenit: Et statim subjicit: in corporibus quidem hæc pugna spectatur: in animo autem tametsi non videatur, reverà tamen existit.

Quam ipsam ob causam idem Philosophus lib. 7. Ethic. cap 2. negat Continentem esse virum bonum, proptereà quòd pravos habeat affectus, licet eos in effectū non producat. Hi proindè affectus pravi in contraria abripientes animum, efficiunt, ut etiam ii, qui ductu Luminis naturæ, in externa scelera non ruunt: tamen τοῖς ταῦτα πράττουσι συνευδοκῶσι talia facientibus consentiant & patrocinentur.

III. Etsi gubernatio locomotivæ, secundum rectæ rationis dictamen & notitias naturales, non est Justitia nostra coram DEO: tamen necessaria est; & requiritur etiam à non renatis: Quia est δικαίωμα θεῦ, quòd Gentes agnoscunt & sequi tenentur, ut Conscientiæ propriæ satisfaciant, & ut conservetur societas humana, quæ violatione externæ disciplinæ facilè solvitur, imò planè evertitur.

Cæterùm moventur hoc loco tres potissimùm Quæstiones explicatu dignissimæ: PRIMA est. Quidnam de Ethnicorum virtutibus, quæ ex Lumine isto Naturæ sunt profectæ, sit statuendum? Anfuerint reverà vel bonæ vel malæ; vel ut in Scholis Theologorum loquimur: An fuerint opera verè bona DEO placentia: An verò peccata? Sunt ex Zwinglianis haud pauci, qui ita laxè Lumen Naturæ extendunt, ut ad sufficientem & salutarem DEI cognitionem, hominibus etiam non renatis & Ethnicis prodesse potuisse: ac proindè opera verè bona, Deoque placentia fuisse, affirmant; uti legere licet apud Zwingl. in exposit. fidei Christianæ: ut & apud Gualtherum in Apologia Zwinglij pag. 53. part. 2. qui fundamenti loco profert illud Esaiæ 55, 10. & 11. Sicut pluvia descendit, & nix de Cœlo, & illuc non revertitur; sed inebriat terram, & germinare eam facit: Sic erit Verbum meum, quod egredietur de ore meo, non revertetur ad me vacuum sed faciet quæcunq; volui, & prosperabitur in his, ad quæ misi illud. Hinc jam sic infert Gualtherus: Atqui Verbum DEI non est tantùm Mosaicum & Propheticum illud scriptum: sed omnis suggestio, tàm externa, quàm interna, quâ Homines in DEI agnitionem trahi possunt: Atqui tales suggestiones habuerunt Gentes, Rom. 1. τὸ γνωστὸν θεꙋ, hoc est, omne illud, quod de DEO sciri & cognosci potest, illis revelatum fuit, & DEUS hoc illis revelavit, non malignus Spiritus.

Cæterùm laborat hæc assertio multis insignibus Sophisticationibus. Prima est, τῆς ἐτεροζητήσεως, sive confusionis Disparatarum Quæstionum. Aliud enim est, quando quæritur, An Gentes virtute Luminis Naturæ justificari potuerint? Cujus negativam nos tenemus, & tùm ex jam annotatis, tùm ex iis, quæ de usu Luminis hujus mox membro tertio disputabimus, invictè adstruimus. Aliud verò est, quando quæritur, An virtutes Gentilium fuerint opera verè bona, Deoq; placentia? Ubi per luculentam distinctionem Quæstio expediri debet: undè altera Sophisticatio, quæ est τῆς ὁμωνυμίας oritur? Nam in Scholis Theologorum Opera duobus modis considerantur, vel ratione Φύσεως sive Naturæ: nempè quoad substantiam factorum, quæ in se vel bona est: ut virtutes, vel mala, ut vitia: vel considerantur ratione πίςεως sive Fidei in Christum. Jam ergò virtutes Gentilium priore modo atque respectu, utique fuerunt opera bona, quippè quæ non modò secundùm substantiam factorum, cum præceptis Decalogi conveniebant: sed & singulari DEI gratia in ipsis sunt excitata. Et hoc respectu, DEO etiam suo quodam modo Opera illa placuisse, vix quisquam facilè negaverit: ita, ut DEUS illa non modò bonorum temporalium præmiis hac in vita compensaverit: sed & à graviori damnationis supplicio securitatem sint habitura. Verùm posteriore respectu, utrumq; rectissime negatur, tùm quòd fuerint Opera verè bona: tùm quòd DEO placuerint. Quia enim partim ab Adjunctis, partim ab ipsis personis operantium, variè vitium contraxerunt: certè simpliciter Bona, aut Deo placita fuisse, affirmari non potest: sed multis potiùs modis contaminata, & si non ob causas alias, ob hanc saltem DEO ingrata, & sic abominabilia fuisse pronunciandum est, quia Personæ cum DEO per fidem non fuerunt reconciliatæ. Ratio pronunciati ex testimoniis Scripturæ sumitur, Matth. 11, 18. Non potest arbor mala, bonos fructus facere. Rom. 14, 23. Quicquid non est ex Fide, peccatum est. Hebr. 11, 6. Sine fide impossibile est placere DEO. Tertia Sophisticatio est παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἄιτιον, καὶ παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Non enim sequitur: DEUS revelavit Gentilibus illud γνωστὸν, vel, DEUS operatus est in Gentilibus illas virtutes, & motus illos singulares Heroicos excitavit: Ergò referri debent ad classem Operum, quæ simpliciter & absolutè bona esse, Deoque placere in Scripturis dicuntur. Nam distinguendum est inter Dona D E I Ministrantia sive Ministerialia, quæ in homines etiam infideles, ac non renatos D E U S conferre solet, humanæ societatis rectiùs conservandæ gratia: & inter Dona Sanctificantia, quæ solis renatis ac fidelibus obtingunt, quæq; D E O simpliciter placent, non quidem quòd per substantiam facti bona sint: sed quòd à bonis, hoc est, renatis & cum D E O per fidem reconciliatis, fiunt, aut, ut Scriptura loquitur, quòd ex DEO, & in DEO facta sunt. Joh. 3 21.

Quartò committitur πλεονεξία Consequentis: Nam τό γνωσὸν τῶ θεῶ præter mentem ac scopum Apostoli nimis laxè ad salvificam D E I notitiam extenditur: cùm ad æternam tantùm D E I Divinitatem ac potentiam, & Justitiam illam D E I judiciariam restringi debeat, uti supra ostensum. Tandem ἀθεόλογον & fanaticum est, quod de internis suggestionibus sive Enthusiasmis, extra D E I Verbum revelatum definitis, Gualtherus hoc loco differit.

Concludimus proindè cum D. Augustino ex Epistola 99. & lib. 4. contra Julianum: cap. 3. Etsi Ethnicorum virtutes suâ quadam indole animi delectant: ac propterea non libenter illas damnamus: quia tamen ad Opus verè bonum, Deoƣ placens requiritur, non tantùm, ut aliquid fiat, quod suo genere bonum sit: sed præcipuè ut benè, hoc est, ex fide Christi fiat: Quia etiam virtutes à vitiis discernendæ sunt, non officiis duntaxat, sed & finibus; ipsa quoque officia, non actibus, sed finibus pensitantur; utique peccata illa fuisse, Deoque displicuisse, pronunciamus, secuti hâc in parte Apostolum, quia Opera sua in Judaismo peracta nominat σκύβαλα, Phil. 3. Et Prophetæ Jesaiæ, qui Justitiam Operum extra fidem pensitatam, vocat pannum menstruatæ, cap. 64.

Altera Quæstio, quæ hoc loco agitatur, est de dicto illo Apostoli Rom. 2, 14. Gentes, quæ legem non habent, naturâ faciunt ea, quæ legis sunt. Cùm enim hîc videatur Apostolus secundùm superficiem literæ, Gentilibus assignare aliquam Legis impletionem, Naturæ beneficio præstitam, variè inter interpretes de hoc loco disputatum fuit: adeò ut D. Augustinus appellatione Gentium, Christianos sub Novo Testamento, ex Gentilibus ad fidem Evangelicam conversos, intelligat lib. de Sp. & lit. c. 26. & 27.

Cæterùm omnis fortassis sive obscuritas, sive difficultas facillimè tollitur, si verba Apostoli Paulò pressiùs examinemus. Non autem dicit Apostolus, Gentes naturâ facere τὸν νόμον Legem: sed τὰ τῦ νόμγ, hoc est, quædam Opera quæ legis sunt: nempè in Gubernanda externa locomotiva, & externis quibusdam actionibus edendis, quæ cum honestate Politica congruunt.

Jam verò à parte ad Totum non valet Confequentia: ac proindè vitiosissimè colligitur: Quædam facta Gentilium cum Decalogo congruunt, secundum Substantiam facti: Ergo Legem Dei gentiles planè impleverunt, ipsorumq; opera etiam secundum spiritualem illum impletionis modum, fuerunt absolutè bona.

TERTIA & postrema Quæstio est: An Notitiæ naturales ex Lumine Naturæ de DEO rebusq́; divinis haustæ, dici debeant veræ an falsæ? Sunt & reperiuntur hodiè nonnulli, qui statuunt, Notiones istas, & quæ indè profluunt propositiones de Deo: ut quòd sit mens æterna, sit omnipotens, sit justus scelerum vindex, sit causa boni in Natura: has inquam & similes propositiones, si proferantur à Gentilibus, esse falsas, eò quòd sint conceptus Hominum non renatorum. Quorum sanè sententiæ nullo pacto subscribere possumus: moti potissimùm evidenti assertione Apostolica: Rom. 1, 21. quæ sic habet: Revelatur ira Dei de Cœlo super omnem impietatem & injustitiam eorum hominum, qui VERITATEM in injustitia detinent. Quid verò per hanc VERITATEM intelligi debeat, ipse statim Apostolus explicat, dùm eam partim definit, per γνωστὸν τῦ θεῦ, partim verò ad notitiam æternæ divinitatis, potentiæ, & Justitiæ divinæ expressè restringit. Jam verò notitiam hanc Dei sive τὸ γνωστὸν τῦ θεῦ Apostolus nominat VERITATEM. Piaculum proindè fuerit, mendacium ac falsitatem nominare id, quod Apostolus disertis verbis veritatem appellitat. Et quomodo quæso intentioni Apostolicæ sua constaret evidentia, si Veritatis terminum, cùm Falsitatis epitheto commutare quis velit. Dicit enim Veritatem hanc à Gentilibus in injustitia fuisse detentam: hoc est, cognitioni illi divinæ vim quasi illatam, & VERITATEM, quam de Deo habebant, Injustitiæ operibus oppressam esse. Ea enim aliàs Veritatis est natura, ut amorem sui in mente conciliet. Jam si diversum eveniat, ut nimirùm non ad amorem boni feramur: sed neglecto vero bonóque, falsum maluḿque eligamus, uti Gentes fecisse perhibet Apostolus: tùm certè non falsitas, sed veritas in animo opprimitur: Veritas ergò ipsis cognita fuerit, ac propositiones etiam ipsorum de Deo, quantumvis à non renatis, ex Lumine Naturæ haustæ, veræ suâ Naturâ sint, omninò necesse est. Debebant proindè illi, qui diversum à nobis statuunt, Notitias ipsas à Personis Gentilium accuratè distinguere: & illis veritatem, his verò ἀδικίαν sive injustitiam cum Apostolo assignare. Quod dùm non faciunt, sed ex conditione Personarum, de ipsis notitiis, à Deo naturæ insitis, judicare pergunt, turpi Sophisticatione τῆς ἑτεροζητήσεως seipsos & alios implicant & involvunt.


### Chapter II. Controversy concerning the Law of Nature, and about natural…: On the Use of the Light, or Natural Law, among Men not Regenerate

The Apostle defines the twofold use of natural notions or Principles among the infidel and not yet regenerate: One proper and as it were Essential: The other Accidental. The proper one is that it bears clear Testimony concerning GOD and divine things: such as concerning the eternal divinity, power, Providence, Justice and Wisdom of GOD, all of which are known and perceived by nature to the Gentiles, indeed to every Man: so that even by this knowledge alone you distinguish Man from the brutes: it shows the sources of Political laws, and of all Justice and Order in human society: it informs the judgment of right reason, it rules the τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν, lest it rush into horrible crimes and wickedness against conscience.

The accidental use is that, by the judgment of this very natural light, men become ἀναπολόγητοι, inexcusable, before GOD, because their own conscience tells them that GOD is good, just, holy, the avenger of all crimes, and therefore that GOD is also to be worshipped justly, piously, and holily. Now, indeed, because the Gentiles did not glorify the GOD whom they knew, nor give thanks: but changed the glory of the incorruptible GOD into the imaginary likeness of a corruptible man, and of birds, and of quadrupeds, and of serpents, or reptiles. Roman. 1, 21. & 23. Hence it comes about that every excuse for the stupendous impiety with which they polluted themselves is entirely cut off from them.

But there are those who rise up against this latter use in this way: Natural notions are in themselves ineffective for attaining salvation: Therefore, they also could not render the Gentiles inexcusable. The reason for the connection seems to be this: That those to whom a saving and sufficient knowledge of GOD is not granted, they seem to still have some pretext for their impiety. I answer: The argument fails by the Sophism of a faulty Consequent, and of a non-cause. For the reason of the connection would hold if, indeed, GOD himself had simply denied a sufficient and saving knowledge of GOD to the Gentiles. But since they themselves, by their own fault, lost the sacrosanct deposit of the divine Word, and in this way involved themselves and their descendants in the darkness of ignorance, they have certainly, even for that reason, bound themselves with the guilt of most just damnation, and have cut off from themselves every pretext of excuse.

Furthermore, ignorance of one's own making and voluntarily attracted excuses no one: as Aristotle himself testifies in book 3 of the Ethics, chapter 1. Now, indeed, GOD at no time placed his Church in such illustrious worship, so that the fame of the true divine worship would

Latin:

GEminum usum notitiarum sive Principiorum naturalium apud infideles ac nondum renatos, definit Apostolus: Unum proprium & quasi Essentialem: Alterum Accidentarium. Proprius est, quòd luculentum perhibeat Testimonium de DEO deque rebus divinis: ut de æternâ divinitate, potentiâ, Providentiâ, Justitiâ & Sapientiâ DEI, quæ omnia Gentilibus, imò cuilibet Homini, naturâ sunt cognita & perspecta: adeò, ut vel hæc sola notitia discernas Hominem à brutis: ostendat fontes legum Politicarum, omnisq; Justitiæ & Ordinis in societate humanâ: informet judicium rectæ rationis, regat τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν, ne in horrenda scelera atque flagitia ruat contra conscientiam.

Usus accidentarius est, ut hujus ipsius naturalis luminis judicio, homines coram DEO fiant ἀναπολόγητοι inexcusabiles, propterea, quòd propria ipsorum conscientia illis dictitat, DEUM esse bonum, justum, sanctum, vindicem omnium scelerum, ac proindè ut DEUM etiam justè, piè, sanctè esse colendum. Jam verò quia Gentiles DEUM, quem cognoverunt, non ut DEUM glorificaverunt, aut gratias egerunt: sed mutarunt gloriam incorruptibilis DEI in similitudinem imaginariam corruptibilis hominis, & volucrum, & quadrupedum, & serpentum, sive reptilium. Roman. 1, 21. & 23. Hinc adeò fit, ut omnis prorsus excusatio stupendæ impietatis, quâ se polluerunt, ipsis sit præcisa.

Sed sunt, qui contra usum istum posteriorem sic insurgunt: Notitiæ naturales per se ad consequendam salutem sunt inefficaces: E. illæ quoq; non potuerunt Gentes reddere inexcusabiles. Ratio connexi videtur esse hæc: Quòd quibus non conceditur notitia DEI salutaris & sufficiens, ij videntur aliquem adhuc habere impietatis suæ prætextum. Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate vitiosi Consequentis, & non Causæ. Tùm enim ratio connexi militaret, si nimirùm sufficientem & salutarem DEI notiam, DEUS ipse Gentilibus simpliciter negasset. Jam verò cùm ipsimet propria culpâ sacrosanctum Verbi divini depositum perdiderint, seque & posteros ignorantiæ tenebris hoc pacto involverint, utique vel ideò justissimæ damnationis reatu se obstrinxerunt, omnemque excusationis prætextum sibi ipsis præciderunt.

Deindè Ignorantia ἰδιώτητος & sponte attracta neminem excusat: teste ipso Aristotele lib. 3. Eth. cap. 1. Jam verò DEUS nullo tempore Ecclesiam suam in tàm illustri cultu collocavit, ut fama de vero cultu divinâ dimâ-


### Chapter II. Controversy concerning the Law of Nature, and about natural…: Error in defect

flow out to all nations, so that, if they had wished, they could have inquired after the GOD of Israel: Nay, He even took care that the Gospel should be announced by the work and zeal of the Apostles to the whole world, indeed to every creature which is under heaven, Coloss. 1, 23. They could have, therefore, if they had wished, inquired into the true worship of GOD, by the examples of the Gibeonites, the Ninevites, the Persians converted by Mordecai, the Oriental Magi, and very many others, who from Gentilism converted themselves to the GOD of Israel, a thing which today can likewise be affirmed of the Turks and other infidel peoples: for it is sufficiently known and evident to them what and what kind of worship Christians offer to their GOD. Finally, this very Light of Nature ought to have been to them as a starting point and a certain incitement, so that they might inquire with greater zeal about the true worship of that GOD, of whom they had drawn some knowledge from visible creatures. Now since they have as it were stifled this very Light of Nature and the Truth of GOD, and have detained it in injustice: since they have basely neglected and repudiated the offered means of salvation, since they prefer Mahometan trifles, while their conscience protests, to the writings of the Prophets and Apostles: the Apostle's judgment is most true, that they are the more inexcusable, the more clearly they knew from the Light of Nature not only that GOD exists: but also that He must be glorified as GOD.

Antithesis Or erroneous opinions concerning natural knowledge, or the Light of Nature.

The crop of those erring concerning this head of the Christian Religion is very fruitful: some indeed erring quite dangerously in excess: others in defect.

They sin at the beginning in defect, who, having simply denied natural knowledge, compare the human soul to a blank slate, on which nothing is inscribed, yet everything can be inscribed: that is, which is devoid of all knowledge of GOD and divine things. These, since they either do not see the light of Paul's disputation, or certainly do not grasp it: nay, since they make the Justice of GOD labor greatly in condemning the Gentiles, they overturn their own opinion by their own vanity.

A similar error is fostered today by the more recent Samosatenians, or Photinians, asserting that GOD is known neither by nature nor from the contemplation of creatures: but that the Gentiles learn only from Fame externally that there is some GOD, because, forsooth, GOD revealed Himself to men from the beginning, as Christopher Ostorodius explicitly writes in Confess. Germ. Year 1604.

He fights for this thesis of his with three reasons primarily: For first, he says, very many Gentiles, to whom this Fame about GOD has not reached, are ignorant that there is a GOD, as is evident concerning the peoples of the new World, Brazil, the East Indies, etc. Then, very many of the Philosophers simply denied either that there is a GOD, or that GOD is affected by any care for human affairs. Finally, the Apostle in Rom. 1, v. 20, does not speak of the knowledge of GOD from the works of the first Creation, or of the World: but of the revelation of GOD through the works of the new Creation, that is, through doctrine and works.

But these reasons collapse by their own futility: For the first basely begs the question: nor does it prove what it says. The testimony of all historians, and especially of those who have traversed the history of the New World and the East Indies, certainly confirms the opposite. For what does that mean, that those Gentiles worship even the most abject and vile things, indeed even the Devil himself, or the Sun, and the Moon, and the stars of heaven as a deity, other than that their own Conscience convinces and reproves them that there is some GOD, and that He must be worshipped as GOD?

The second reason labors under the Sophism of accident. For that some of the Philosophers denied both GOD and the Providence of GOD, that came from an accident, namely from a deliberate malice, by which they preferred to obscure, cover, and hide the sparks of divine knowledge latent in the mind, rather than bear witness to the truth: so that the School of the remaining sounder Philosophers, especially Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero, has vigorously refuted the stupidity of those: but it is one thing to be simply ignorant of something, and another to maliciously deny that which you know: according to that of Psalm 14, 1: The fool has said in his heart, there is no GOD.

The third reason again begs the Question: for that the Apostle speaks not of the secondary, but of the first Creation of this World, is clearer from the text than to need any laborious proof. For he makes express mention of the creation of the world: likewise of visible Creatures: or works of Creation: nay, he explicitly affirms that the Work of the Law is written by nature in their hearts.

Thirdly: Certain Moderns also pertain to this former class of those erring by defect, who think so contemptuously and abjectly concerning the Light of Nature, or natural Notions, and the most noble Effect of these, namely sounder Philosophy, that although they do not deny that some Light of Nature remains after the fall: yet they desire that it be banished, nay, thoroughly proscribed from the field and borders of Christians as a work of the Flesh and of Satan. Hence those Emblems have been produced by them, which heretofore had not even been heard of by report, nay, almost of a sound terrible to an outsider: Such as were these.

1. Philosophy must be reckoned among the Works of the Flesh, concerning which the Apostle pronounces in Galatians 5:21 that he who does such things cannot become an heir of the kingdom of GOD. Hof. Pref. to the disputation on GOD.

2. Philosophers are the patriarchs of heretics, introducing more pestilential dogmas through Philosophy than any Carpocratianism, Mahometanism, or Manichaeism has ever scattered. Mall. p. 9.

3. Philosophy in its true, truer, and truest use, and when it is in its office, is to be condemned in Theology. Mall p. 10.

4. When Philosophy teaches that there is a GOD, that He is just, good, omnipotent, eternal, the cause of good in Nature, etc.: then all these things are lies in Theology. p. 12.

5. Philosophers are unregenerate men, and therefore everything that Philosophy says about GOD is a lie. p. 13.

6. The devils do not know that there is a GOD, or even if they know it to the highest degree, they nevertheless do not believe that there is a GOD. p. 16.

7. It will be more tolerable in the final Judgment for the most wicked scoundrel of the whole world than for the most excellent and modest philosopher of all. p. 17.

8. Logic is to be cast out from the doctrine of the Church. p. 19. Hof. 9. 30. on GOD.

These paradoxes are too absurd to be credible that it could have happened that men, otherwise not at all unlearned, would undertake their defense. But some have undertaken it, relying chiefly on these reasons.

I. Those natural notions concerning GOD and divine things were a part of the divine Image, to which the first Man was created. But this image of GOD has been utterly lost. Therefore, those natural notions have been utterly lost.

I answer: A shameful παραλογισμὸς τῆς ὁμωνυμίας (fallacy of equivocation) is committed in the word Image of GOD, which denotes first a certain general congruence and analogy by which the soul of Man expresses certain divine things: such as that it represents in some way the mystery of the Trinity, because it is one in Essence, but manifold in virtues or powers: that it is immortal, incorporeal, spiritual, intelligent, and of free will in matters subject to its own power. That this Image of GOD was lost after the fall, no one would affirm, unless he dared to deny that Man is Man, that is, that he is endowed with a rational soul.

Furthermore, the Image of GOD in the Scriptures also denotes that dominion which was granted to Man over brute animals, both individual and universal. That this part of the divine Image was diminished and weakened after the fall, we do not deny: but that it was utterly removed or abolished, we deny again and again.

Thirdly: The image of God under its scope also includes natural notions, about which inquiry is made in this place, and which we have demonstrated above from the Apostle to have been known to man by nature, and not to have been entirely extinguished by the fall.

Finally, the image of God κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of excellence) denotes that interior perfection of mind and will, and of all human powers, joined with true holiness, justice, and harmony or congruence with the Law of God. We willingly grant that this was utterly destroyed and lost in man through the fall of our first parents. But, just as it does not follow from that: Therefore that congruence of the human soul with divine things was simultaneously destroyed: or that dominion over brute animals: So it does not follow in any way: The image of God according to its principal and nobler part was lost through the fall. Therefore, no remains of the divine image survive at all. For from the negation of one part, the consequence does not hold for the negation of all the rest.

The other argument of those critics is as follows. The Apostle, after he said: that to the Gentiles τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ (that which is known of God) was known by nature, or from the visible things of this world, immediately adds, v. 21, ἐματαιώθησαν ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς αὑτῶν: They became vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened. Therefore: Those natural notions are either clearly nothing, or certainly they are false, so that if a Gentile philosopher affirms: That there is a God, that he is just, wise, eternal, good, omnipotent: then he lies and speaks falsely.

I answer: more is inferred in the consequent than the antecedent allows: That also only follows: Therefore those reasonings, by which the Gentiles were, as it were, doing violence to the light of nature concerning God, are false and mendacious. This is most clearly evident from the Apostolic text, which in the cited verse coheres thus: First, the Apostle says that the Gentiles knew God: but did not glorify him as God, or give thanks. Then he adds an etiology. Why did they not glorify God as God? Namely, because they became vain in their reasonings. By those reasonings, therefore, he does not understand those principles or natural notions: for thus the Apostolic text would nowhere cohere; and the sense would emerge as clearly inept and absurd, namely such as this: The Gentiles knew God, but did not glorify him as God: Why? Because they knew God falsely. Which opinion is not only absurd: but also diametrically opposed to the Apostolic purpose, which is entirely concerned with demonstrating: That the Gentiles are therefore justly condemned, because they indeed knew God by nature, but for that reason did not glorify him as God: because they subsequently obscured that light of nature with their own vanities and reasonings: so that those natural notions and those reasonings are not taken as the same and equivalent: but are opposed to one another: the former are placed on the side of goodness and truth: the latter, however, on the side of vanity and falsehood. For example: The natural notions in Socrates concerning God and the immortality of the soul were most excellent: But after he, about to die, took care that a cock be offered to Aesculapius: here he truly became vain in his reasoning, while he took care that worship due to God alone be rendered to a man. Next, I answer that a fallacy is committed ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ

and simply. For if even those διαλογισμοὶ (reasonings) are taken in the highest degree concerning the natural Principles themselves: yet it is true only in a certain respect that the Gentiles were made vain. 1. Insofar as they corrupted and depraved those natural principles in various ways. 2. In respect of that Divine knowledge which can be obtained by us from the revealed Word of GOD. Now, however, since both of these respects do not depend upon the very nature or substance of those natural principles: but upon the Condition and Quality of the Subject: namely, Man not reborn: certainly the subsumption is made most viciously from the Accident to the Substance: or from the vice of the Subject to the nature of the Natural principles themselves considered in and by themselves. Therefore those principles remain and are in themselves, and by reason of themselves, good and true: although afterwards from an Accident, namely the blindness and vanity of the men themselves, they contract much stain and viciousness.

The third argument of the Critics is this: Rom. 8. 7. it is written: τὸ Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, ἔχθρὰ εἰς θεὸν: The mind of the Flesh is enmity against GOD. Therefore, those natural notions are false, are a lie, are a work of the Flesh and therefore worthy of eternal damnation.

I answer: 1. A Sophistry of Begging the Question is committed: for it has not yet been proven that natural notions are called by the Apostle in this place Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, the mind or wisdom of the Flesh. We certainly deny that simply: and we ask for the reason, from that opposition by which they are mutually opposed to each other, Φρόνημα τοῦ πνεύματος, and Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός. But what each Φρόνημα is, the Apostle illustrates by Effects and adjuncts: defining the Φρόνημα τοῦ πνεύματος by that good motion of mind and will in a reborn Man, conformable to the divine law, excited by the Holy Spirit. But the Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς by the motion and endeavor of the mind and will in a man not reborn, contrary to the Law of GOD. Which is the reason why the Apostle did not simply say: τὸ Φρόνημα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, the mind or prudence of Man: but looking directly to the perverse will of Man, he said, τὸ Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, the prudence of the Flesh. The notation of the Cause proves this very thing, on account of which this Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς is enmity against GOD: Because, namely, it is not subject to the Law of GOD: that is, it institutes life and morals, as also the worship of GOD, not according to the prescription of the Divine Law, but according to its own διαλογισμοὺς (reasonings): that is, interpreting the same Apostle, it does not the will of GOD: but of the flesh and of thoughts. Now if from this Φρονήματι τῆς σαρκὸς a subsumption is made to natural notions considered in themselves, there immediately emerges a Sophism of ἑτεροζητήσεως (heterozeteseos), and a πλεονεξία (pleonexia) of four terms: as also a Paralogism of a vicious definition.

The fourth argument is as follows: The Apostle writes in Coloss. 2, 8: Beware, lest anyone despoil you through Philosophy and vain deception. Therefore, Philosophy is a work of the Flesh, is a vain deception, is the most fruitful mother of all errors and heresies.

I answer not with my own words: but with those of our Author Philip, who in the disputation concerning the distinction between the Gospel and Philosophy, Tom. 1. Lat. Witteb of the Works of B. Luther p. 470. answers thus: When Paul says: See that no one deceives you through Philosophy, he does not disapprove of Philosophy, but the abuse, as if someone should say: Beware, lest you be deceived by wine, he does not disparage wine, but the abuse. But Paul speaks of that abuse which is most harmful in the Church, namely, when Scripture is so received, as if it taught nothing else, except the doctrine of human reason. For it is easy for crafty men by a cunning interpretation to transform the Gospel into Philosophy, or the doctrine of human reason. Thus far Philip, to whom we add that great Chemnitz, whom these Critics are otherwise accustomed to esteem highly: But he says this in part 2. of the Loci, page 261. Candor must be employed in judging, lest those things which have been rightly and usefully handed down be petulantly disturbed and torn apart in the name of Philosophy.

If anyone were to bend the interpretation of the Decalogue, and restrict it only to the Natural notions of the Law, so that he would contend that only those sins which are known by nature are reproved by the Law of GOD, and that the Decalogue is satisfied by whatever obedience which reason dictates from the Law of Nature and can perform: he, because he would be going beyond the true boundaries, would rightly be said to despoil, Coloss. 2, 8. Therefore, in this argument a Fallacy of Accident is committed, and of 'in a certain respect': while what the Apostle pronounces concerning the abuse of Philosophy, that is most ignorantly accommodated to every use of Philosophy, even the legitimate, or true, truer, and truest. But that the Apostle speaks of the abuse, the subsequent words clearly prove, while namely he prohibits that Philosophical principles be so mixed with divine dogmas, that divine mysteries be explained according to human traditions, and the Elements of the world, that is, the doctrine of worldly Wisdom: and not according to CHRIST. From which most foul abuse of Philosophy all the sounder Philosophers today rightly abhor: mindful of that Aristotelian oracle lib 2 post. anal. 8 δεῖ μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος (one must not cross into another genus). But nothing is lost thereby to the true use of Philosophy, even regarding the τρόπον παιδείας (manner of instruction) in Theological matters: provided it behaves like the handmaid Hagar, who renders service only to the mistress Sarah, that is, to Theology. In which part we have all the sounder Philosophers with us in all things ὁμοψήφως (with one mind).

Finally, they bring forward the authority of certain Ecclesiastical Doctors, especially Tertullian, who was accustomed to call philosophers the patriarchs of heretics, but this argument also is frivolous: For it proceeds from that part, and that in two ways: For 1. Tertullian and others noted certain Philosophers, not each and every one, but those who supplied arms to heretics from Philosophy badly distorted, as is clearly evident from that whole Disputation of Tertullian.

Latin:

naret ad omnes gentes, ut, si voluissent, potuifsent inquirere DEUM Israëlis: Quin curavit etiam Evangelium operâ & studio Apostolorum annunciari universo mundo, imò omni creaturæ quæ sub cœlo est, Coloss. 1, 23. Potuifsent ergò, si voluissent, inquirere in verum cultum DEI, exemplis Gibeonitarum, Ninivitarum, Persarum à Mardocheo conversorum, Magorum Orientalium, & plurimorum aliorum, qui ex Gentilitate ad DEUM Israëlis se converterunt, id quod hodièque de Turcis aliiśque infidelibus populis affirmari itidem potest: quippè quibus satis est cognitum ac perspectum, quem & qualem cultum Christiani DEO suo præstent. Tandem debuisset hoc ipsum Lumen Naturæ ipsis esse tanquàm ὁρμητήριον & incitamentum quoddam, ut majori studio inquirerent de vero cultu illius DEI, cujus aliquam notitiam ex visibilibus creaturis hauserant. Jam cùm hoc ipsum Lumen Naturæ, & Veritatem DEI quasi suffocârint, & in injustitia detinuerint: cùm media salutis oblata turpiter neglexerint, ac repudiârint, cùm nugas Mahometicas, reclamante conscientia, scriptis Prophetarum & Apostolorum anteponant: utiq; verissima est Apostoli sententia, quòd tantò magis sint inexcusabiles, quantò clariùs ex Lumine Naturæ sciverunt non modò DEUM esse: sed & ut DEUM glorificandum esse.

Ἀντίθεσις Sive erroneæ opiniones de notitiis naturalibus, sive Lumine Naturæ.

FOecunda admodùm seges est errantium circa hoc Religionis Christianæ caput: nonnullis quidem in excessu: aliis in defectu satis periculosè errantibus.

In defectu initiò peccant, qui notitiis naturalibus simpliciter negatis, animam humanam rasæ tabulæ comparant, cui nihil sit inscriptum, omnia tamen inscribi possint: hoc est, quæ omnis de DEO, rebusque divinis notitiæ sit expers. Hi cùm disputationis Paulinæ lucem vel non videant, vel certè non assequantur: quin Justitiam DEI in damnandis Ethnicis valdè laborare faciant, propriâ utique vanitate suam ipsi evertunt sententiam.

Consimilem his errorem hodiè fovent recentiores Samosateniani, sive Photiniani asserentes, neq; à naturâ, neq; ex creaturarum contemplatione DEUM cognosci: sed tantùm Famâ extrinsecus addiscere Gentes, quòd aliquis sit DEUS, quoniam videlicet DEUS ab initio hominibus se patefecerit, uti disertè scriptitat Christophorus Ostorodius Confess. Germ. Anno 1604.

Tribus autem potissimùm rationibus militat pro sua hac obtinenda thesi: Primùm enim inquit, Gentes plurima, ad quas Fama isthæc de DEO non pervenit, ignorant esse DEUM, ut constat de populis novi Orbis, Brasiliæ, Indiæ Orientalis &c. Deindè plurimi Philosophorum partim esse DEUM, partim DEUM humanarum rerum curâ aliquâ affici, simpliciter negarunt. Tandem Apostolus Rom. 1. v. 20. non de notitia DEI ex operibus Creationis primæ, sive Mundi loquitur: sed de patefactione DEI per opera novæ Creationis, hoc est, per doctrinam & opera.

Verùm propriâ futilitate rationes hæ concidunt: Prima enim turpiter petit principium: neque quod dicit probat. Diversum certè tùm omnium historicorum, tùm cumprimis eorum testimonia confirmant, qui historiam Novi Orbis, & Indiæ Orientalis pertexuerunt. Quid enim sibi vult illud, quòd Gentes illæ, res etiam abjectissimas ac vilissimas, imò ipsum etiam Cacodæmonem, vel Solem, ac Lunam, Cœliq; sidera pro numine adorant, quàm quòd propria ipsorum Conscientia eos convincit & redarguit, esse DEUM aliquem, & ipsum ut DEUM esse colendum?

Altera ratio laborat Sophismate ὕ συμβεβηκότος. Quòd enim Philosophorum nonnulli, & DEUM & DEI Providentiam negârunt, id provênit ex accidente, nempè ex destinata malitiâ, quâ igniculos divinæ notitiæ in animo latentes, obscurare, tegere & occultare maluerunt, quàm veritati testimonium perhibere: ita ut istorum stuporem reliquorum saniorum Philosophorum, Platonis potissimùm, Aristotelis & Ciceronis Schola nervosè refutaverit: Aliud autem est, aliquid simpliciter ignorare, aliud verò, id quod noveris, malitiosè negare: secundúm illud Psalmi 14, 1. Dixit impius in corde suo, non est DEUS.

Tertia ratio rursus petit Principium: Apostolum enim non de secundaria, sed de prima Creatione Mundi hujus loqui, ex textu dilucidiùs patet, quàm ut ullâ operosâ probatione indigeat. Facit enim expressè mentionem τῆς κτίσεως τῦ κόσμε: item visibilium Creaturarum: sive ποιημάτων operum Creationis: quin disertè affirmat, Opus Legis Naturâ scriptum esse in cordibus ipsorum.

Tertiò: Pertinent ad priorem hanc classem errantium in defectu, etiam Recentiores quidam, qui de Lumine Naturæ, sive Notitiis naturalibus, & harum nobilissimo Effectu, Philosophiâ nimirùm saniore, usque adeò contemtim & abjectè sentiunt, ut licèt non negent, superesse post lapsum aliquod Lumen Naturæ: tamen illud ex agro & finibus Christianorum tanquàm opus Carnis & Satanæ cupiant relegatum imò penitùs proscriptum. Hinc ea ab ipsis prodita sunt Emblemata, quæ antehac ne fando quidem audita fuerunt, imò Externo ponè tremenda sono: Qualia fuerunt isthæc.

1. Philosophia referenda est inter Opera Carnis, de quibus Apostolus Gal. 5, 21. pronunciat, quòd, qui talia faciat, regni DEI haeres evadere nequeat. Hof. Praef. disputationis de DEO.

2. Philosophi sunt Patriarchae haereticorum, pestilentiora dogmata per Philosophiam introducentes, quàm ullus Carpocratianismus, Mahometismus, Manichaeismus unquam sparserit. Mall. p. 9.

3. Philosophia in vero, veriore, verissimo suo usu, & quando in suo officio est, in Theologia est damnanda. Mall pag. 10.

4. Quando Philosophia docet, esse DEUM, esse ipsum justum, bonum, omnipotentem, aeternum, causam boni in Natura, &c: tùm omnia haec in Theologia sunt mendacia. p. 12.

5. Philosophi sunt Homines non regenerati, ideoquè omnia, quae de DEO dicit Philosophia, sunt mendacia. p. 13.

6. Diaboli nesciunt esse DEUM, vel si sciant maximè, tamen non credunt esse DEUM. p. 16.

7. Sceleratissimo totius orbis nebuloni tolerabiliùs erit in extremo Judicio, quàm praestantissimo & modestissimo omnium Philosopho. p. 17.

8. Logica ex doctrina Ecclesiae ejicienda est. p. 19. Hof. 9. 30. de DEO.

Absurdiora sunt haec paradoxa, quàm ut credibile sit, potuisse fieri, ut eorum patrocinium Viri, aliàs minimè indocti, susciperent. Sed susceperunt tamen nonnulli his potissimùm freti rationibus.

I. Notitiae illae naturales de DEO & rebus divinis, fuerunt pars Imaginis divinae, ad quam primus Homo erat conditus. Atqui imago haec DEI penitùs est amissa. E. & notitiae illae naturales penitùs sunt amissae.

Respondeo: Turpis committitur παραλογισμὸς τῆς ὁμωνυμίας in voce Imagine DEI, quae notat primùm generalem quandam congruentiam & analogiam, quâ anima Hominis quaedam divina exprimit: ut quòd aliquo modo repraesentat mysterium Trinitatis, quia per Essentiam una est, per virtutes verò sive potentias, multiplex: quòd immortalis est, incorporea, spiritualis, intelligens, & liberae voluntatis in rebus suae potestati subjectis. Hanc Imaginem DEI post lapsum amissam esse, nemo affirmaverit, nisi qui negare ausit, Hominem esse Hominem, hoc est, praeditum esse animâ rationali.

Deindè verò Imago DEI in Scripturis notat etiam Dominium illud, quod Homini in bruta animantia singula & universa est concessum. Hanc Imaginis divinae partem post lapsum imminutam & labefactatam esse non imus inficias: sed penitùs sublatam aut abolitam, iterum atq; iterum negamus.

Tertiò: Imago DEI sub suo ambitu comprehendit etiam notitias naturales, de quibus hoc loco quaeritur, & quas Homini naturâ cognitas, neque per lapsum prorsus extinctas esse, supra ex Apostolo demonstravimus.

Tandem, Imago DEI κατ' ἐξοχὴν notat interiorem illam perfectionem mentis & voluntatis, omniumque virium humanarum, conjunctam cùm verâ sanctitate, justitiâ & harmoniâ sive congruentiâ cum Lege DEI. Hanc per lapsum protoparentum penitùs destructam & amissam esse in Homine, libenter largimur. Cæterùm, quemadmodum indè non sequitur: Ergò simul destructa est congruentia illa Animæ humanæ cum divinis: vel Dominium illud in animantia bruta: Sic nullo pacto sequitur: Imago DEI secundùm præcipuam & nobiliorem partem est per lapsum amissa. E. nullæ prorsus supersunt Imaginis divinæ reliquiæ. Ex negatione enim unius partis, ad reliquarum omnium negationem non valet Consequentia.

Altera ratio Criticorum istorum talis est. D. Apostolus postquam dixit: Gentilibus τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, natura, sive ex visibilibus hujus Mundi cognitum fuisse, statim subjicit, v. 21. ἐματαιώθησαν ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς αὑτῶν: Vani facti sunt in suis ratiocinationibus, & obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum. Ergò: Notitiæ illæ naturales vel planè nullæ funt, vel certè sunt falsæ, ita ut si Gentilis Philosophus affirmet: Esse DEUM, esse eundem justum, sapientem, æternum, bonum, omnipotentem: tùm mentiatur & falsum dicat.

Respondeo: plus infertur in Consequente, quam patitur Antecedens: Illud etiam tantùm sequitur: Ergò illi διαλογισμοί, quibus Lumini Naturæ de DEO, vim quasi Gentiles inferebant, sunt falsi & mendaces. Patet hoc luculentissimè ex textu Apostolico, qui versu citato sic cohæret: Primùm Apostolus dicit, Gentes cognovisse DEUM: sed non ut DEUM glorificasse, aut gratias egisse. Deindè αιτιολογίαν subjicit. Quare DEUM non ut DEUM glorificaverint? nempè quia vani facti sunt in suis ratiocinationibus. Per διαλογισμούς ergò istos non intelligit principia illa sive notitias naturales: sic enim textus Apostolicus nuspiam cohæreret; & ineptus planè ac absurdus prodiret sensus, talis nimirùm: Gentes DEUM cognoverunt, sed non ut DEUM glorificaverunt: Quare? Quia DEUM falsò cognoverunt. Quæ sententia non modò absurda est: sed & scopo Apostolico è diametro repugnat, qui in eo totus est, ut demonstret: Gentiles ideò justè damnari, quia ex naturâ cognoverunt quidem DEUM, sed ideò ipsum non ut DEUM glorificaverunt: quia Lumen illud Naturæ, suis postmodùm vanitatibus ac ratiocinationibus obscurarunt: ita ut Notitiæ illæ naturales, & διαλογισμοὶ isti, non pro iisdem & æquipollentibus accipiantur: sed sibi mutuò opponantur: illæ in parte bonitatis & veritatis: hi verò in parte veritatis & falsitatis ponantur. Exempli gratia: Notitiæ naturales in Socrate fuerunt præclarissimæ de DEO, deque immortalitate animæ: At postquàm jam moriturus curavit Æsculapio gallum gallinaceum offerri: hic sanè vanus factus est in suo διαλογισμῷ, dùm nimirùm cultum soli DEO debitum, Homini præstari curavit. Deindè respondeo, committi Sophisma ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ

καὶ ἁπλῶς. Nam si vel maximè διαλογισμοὶ isti, de ipsis Principiis naturalibus accipiantur: tamen secundum quid tantùm verum est, vanos factos fuisse Gentiles. 1. quatenùs principia illa naturália variis modis corruperunt, & depravarunt. 2. respectu agnitionis illius Divinæ, quæ ex Verbo DEI revelato nobis potest obtingere. Jam verò cùm uterque iste respectus, non dependeat ex ipsâ naturâ, sive substantiâ principiorum illorum naturalium: sed ex Conditione & Qualitate Subjecti: nempè Hominis non renati: utique vitiosissimè ab Accidenti ad Substantiam: sive ex vitio Subjecti, ad naturam ipsorum principiorum Naturalium in se & per se confideratorum, fit subsumtio. Manent proindè & sunt principia illa in se, & ratione sui bona & vera: licèt postmodum ex Accidente, nempè cæcitate & vanitate ipsorum hominum, plurimùm labis ac vitiositatis contrahant.

Tertia ratio Criticorum est hæc: Rom. 8. 7. scriptum est: τὸ Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, ἔχθρὰ εἰς θεὸν: Affectus Carnis est inimicitia adversus DEUM. E. Notitiæ illæ naturales sunt falsæ, sunt mendacium, sunt opus Carnis & proindè æterna damnatione dignæ.

Respondeo: 1. Committitur Sophisticatio Petitionis Principii: Notitias enim naturales hoc loco appellari ab Apostolo Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, Affectum sive Sapientiam Carnis, nondum probatum est. Nos certè illud simpliciter negamus: & rationem petimus, ex oppositione illa, quâ sibi mutuò opponuntur, Φρόνημα τοῦ πνεύματος, & Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός. Quid verò utrumque sit Φρόνημα, illustrat Apostolus ab Effectis & adjunctis: definiens Φρόνημα τοῦ πνεύματος per bonum istum motum mentis & voluntatis in Homine renato, conformem legi divinæ, excitatum à Spiritu sancto. Φρόνημα autem τῆς σαρκὸς per motum ac conatum mentis & voluntatis in Homine non renato, contrarium Legi DEI. Quæ causa est, quòd Apostolus non simpliciter dixit: τὸ Φρόνημα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, Affectus sive prudentia Hominis: sed directè ad perversam voluntatem Hominis respiciens dixit, τὸ Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, prudentia Carnis. Evincit hoc ipsum notatio Causæ, propter quam hoc Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς est inimicitia adversus DEUM: Quia nimirùm Legi DEI non subjicitur: hoc est, vitam moresq;, ut & cultum DEI, non secundùm præscriptum Legis Divinæ, sed secundùm proprios διαλογισμοὺς instituit: hoc est, interprete eodem Apostolo, facit voluntatem non DEI: sed carnis & cogitationum. Jam si ab hoc Φρονήματι τῆς σαρκὸς fiat subsumtio ad notitias naturales in se cosideratas, emergit statim Sophisma ἑτεροζητήσεως, & quatuor terminorum πλεονεξία: ut & vitiosæ definitionis Paralogismus.

Quarta ratio sic habet: Apostolus Coloss. 2, 8. scribit: Cavete, ne quis vos deprædetur per Philosophiam & inanem deceptionem. E. Philosophia est opus Carnis, est inanis deceptio, est errorum & haeresewn omnium foecundissima mater.

Respondeo verbis non meis: sed Autoris nostri Philippi, qui disputatione de discrimine Evangelij & Philosophiae, Tom. 1. Lat. Witteb Operum B. Lutheri p. 470. sic respondet: Cùm Paulus ait: Videte, nè quis vos decipiat per Philosophiam, non improbat Philosophiam, sed abusum, ut si quis dicat: Cave, ne vino decipiaris, is non vituperat vinum, sed abusum. Loquitur autem Paulus de illo abusu, qui maximè nocet in Ecclesia, videlicet, cùm ita accipitur Scriptura, quasi nihil aliud doceat, nisi rationis humanae doctrinam. Facile est enim astutis hominibus callida interpretatione Evangelium transformare in Philosophiam, seu doctrinam rationis humanae Hactenus Philippus, cui adjungimus magnum illum Chemnitium, quem Critici isti aliàs magni-facere solent: Sic autem iste part. 2. Locorum, pag. 261. Candor adhibendus est in judicando, ne petulanter nomine Philosophiae turbentur & convellantur, quae rectè & utiliter tradita sunt.

Si quis interpretationem Decalogi inflecteret, & restringeret tantùm ad Naturales Legis notitias, ita ut contenderet, Lege DEI argui tantùm illa peccata, quae naturâ nota sunt, & satisfieri Decalogi qualicunque obedientia, quam ratio ex Lege Naturae dictat & praestare potest: is, quia egrederetur veras metas, rectè diceretur depraedari, Coloss. 2, 8. Committitur proindè in hoc argumento Fallacia Accidentis, & secundùm quid: dùm quod de abusu Philosophiae pronunciat Apostolus, illud admodùm imperitè ad omnem usum Philosophiae, etiam legitimum, sive verum, veriorem, verissimum accommodatur. De abusu autem loqui Apostolum, subsequentia luculenter evincunt, dùm nimirùm prohibet, ne principia Philosophica cum dogmatibus divinis ita permisceantur, ut juxta traditiones humanas, & Elementa mundi, hoc est, mundanae Sapientiae doctrinam: & non secundùm CHRISTUM divina mysteria explicentur. A quô foedissimo Philosophiae abusu saniores quique Philosophi hodiè meritò abhorrent: memores oraculi illius Aristotelici lib 2 post. anal. 8 δεῖ μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος. Verùm nihil indè decedit vero Philosophiae usui, etiam quoad τρόπον παιδείας in Theologicis: dummodò se habet instar ancillae Agar, quae servitium tantùm praestat Dominae Sarae, hoc est, Theologiae. Qua in parte Philosophos saniores omnes nobis habemus per omnia ὁμοψήφως.

Tandem proferunt Doctorum quorundam Ecclesiasticorum, cumprimis Tertulliani autoritatem, qui Philosophos nominare solitus fuerit Patriarchas haereticorum, sed frivola est & haec ratio: Nam ex parte ea procedit, idque dupliciter: Nam 1. Tertullianus & alii quosdam notarunt Philosophos, non singulos & universos, sed eos, qui haereticis ex Philosophia malè detorta, arma subministrabant, quemadmodum ex tota illa Disputatione Tertulliani luculenter patet.


### Chapter II. Controversy concerning the Law of Nature, and about natural…: II. Error in excess

They censured only the abuse, not indeed the legitimate, much less the true, truer, or truest use of it. Whence the consequence is not valid either for all philosophers without exception or for every use of philosophy. For just as it does not follow that, because certain philosophers today, through a shameful abuse of philosophy, provide weapons to the Calvinists against the Orthodox: and on this account can rightly be called patriarchs of the Calvinist heresy: Therefore all philosophers without exception are such, or Therefore philosophy even in its legitimate use is the mother, source, and origin of Calvinism: So also it does not follow that, because the Fathers called certain philosophers who abused philosophical principles patriarchs of heretics: and called the abuse of philosophy the cause of all heresies. Therefore they understood this of all philosophers, and of philosophy even when rightly and legitimately used. For in both cases the consequence is denied, because a just inference is not granted from a part to the whole, from an abuse to a true and legitimate use, or from an accident to the cause per se. What is more, it is not the science of philosophy, but rather ignorance of it, that has always been the cause of most heresies.

But enough and more than enough concerning the errors in defect that sin against the present question. There follow those who, deviating from the mean, hallucinate gravely in excess. For there are those who extend natural notions so loosely that they affirm that that light implanted in nature is profitable to a man even not reborn for a sufficient and saving knowledge of God.

A certain monk of the Franciscan Order betrayed this impiety, as Sleidanus testifies in book 23, at the Council of Trent, asserting that those who did not have knowledge of Christ, provided they lived piously, were saved.

Andradius himself also supports this, writing in this manner: There is no doubt that faith is necessary for righteousness and eternal life, for the righteous shall live by faith: But that faith and true knowledge of God can be had not only from the sacred scriptures and divine oracles, but also from those things which are subject to the senses. Will you say that the philosophers, who sought and worshipped the one God with all their might, were destitute of that faith and knowledge of God by which the ungodly is justified?

The Zwinglians do not shrink from this opinion either. For thus Zwingli himself in his exposition of the Christian faith, to the King of France: Here (in eternal life) you are going to see Hercules, Theseus, Socrates, Aristides, Antigonus, Numa, Camillus, the Catos, the Scipios: Here you will see your ancestors, and as many of your forefathers as have migrated hence in the faith, etc.

Gualtherus attempts to defend this impiety of Zwingli on page 53 of his Apology, as we learned above from his own words, where the discussion was about the breadth and scope of the law of nature.

To this stupendous profanity, besides the reasons which we produced and explained above to the contrary, it is now pleasing to oppose the single authority of Augustine, who in book 1 to Boniface, chapter 21, and book 4 against Julian, chapter 3, addresses the Pelagians thus: Are you perhaps going to allow the Fabricii, the Reguli, the Fabii, the Scipiones, the Camilli some place between damnation and the kingdom of heaven, where they are not in misery, but in eternal blessedness: Who did not please God, whom it is impossible to please without faith, which they had neither in their works nor in their hearts. I do not think your perdition can leap to that impudence.

And although it can scarcely be thought of, much less pronounced, without a groan, that no hope of salvation is left to the heathens who have lived outside the fellowship of the Church: meanwhile, however, that God has most just reasons for the fact in condemning them, from those things which the Apostle discusses at length in chapter 1 to the Romans, can be obscure to no pious person.

Since these things are so, we abhor with our whole heart not only the atheism of the Zwinglians, but also the opinion of Andradius and his associates, while they do not shudder to write: that for the Gentiles who did not doubt the providence of God, and thus understood that God for his goodness would omit nothing that makes for the eternal blessing of men, for those Gentiles, I say, that notion was sufficient for salvation: Nay, it is not even to be said that they were entirely ignorant of Christ Jesus, the crucified.

For these are the words of Andradius, lib. 3. Orth. explic. p. 292. I confess indeed that the knowledge of Christ was necessary for salvation in all preceding centuries, although obscure and involved: but he who shall have diligently considered how widely the providence of God extends, and with how much vigilance it provides for human affairs, will sufficiently understand that the redemption of the human race through Christ is contained implicitly and hiddenly in the divine administration. Wherefore those who had this providence of God perceived and explored, certainly understood at the same time that God would omit nothing so that men might enjoy eternal happiness, and thus they are to be said not to have been entirely ignorant of Christ Jesus crucified, even if they had by no means discovered the method which God was about to enter upon for the sake of caring for human salvation.

And a little before, page 291. Nor can any cruelty or inhumanity be more hideous than to consign men to eternal torments on account of the lack of that Faith to which no access lay open, and which they could attain by no way and by no reason.

With these impious and clearly detestable Paradoxes, I say, relegated to hell, we maintain that not Philosophical Principles, not natural notions, or that Light of Nature, however great that may be able to fall upon Man: but only the Word, and that more firm Prophetic Discourse, is the sole Lamp to our feet, by the shining of which one may arrive at the saving knowledge of God. Psal. 119, 105. 2. Pet. 1, 19.

Latin:

2. Abusum tantum, non verò legitimum, nedùm verum, veriorem, verissimum ejus usum reprehenderunt. Vndè vel ad omnes omninò Philosophos, vel ad omnem Philosophiæ usum non valet consequentia. Quemadmodum enim non sequitur, Philosophi quidam hodiè per turpem abusum Philosophiæ, arma subministrant Calvinianis contra Orthodoxos: & hoc nomine rectè appellari possunt Patriarchæ hæreseos Calvinianæ: E. omnes omninò Philosophi tales sunt, vel E. Philosophia in legitimo etiam suo usu est mater, fons & origo Calvinismi: Sic etiam non sequitur, Patres Philosophos quosdam abutentes Philosophicis Principiis, nòminârunt Patriarchas hæreticorum: & Philosophiæ abusum nominarunt causam omnium hæresewn. E. de omnibus Philosophis, deque Philosophia etiam rectè ac legitimè usurpata, hoc intellexerunt. Vtrobique enim negatur Consequentia, quia ex parte ad totum, ab abusu ad usum verum ac legitimum, ab accidentiad Causam per se, non datur justa collectio. Quid quòd non Philosophiæ scientia, sed ejus potiùs ignorantia, plurimarum hæresewn causa semper extitit.

Cæterùm de erroribus in defectu circa præsentem quæstionem peccantibus plus satis. Sequuntur ij, qui à medio nimirùm deflectentes, in excessu graviter hallucinantur. Sunt enim, qui ita laxè Notitias naturales extendunt, ut ad sufficientem & salutarem Dei cognitionem homini etiam non renato lucem illam naturæ insitam prodesse affirment.

Prodidit hanc impietatem teste Sleidano lib. 23. in Concilio Tridentino. Monachus quidam Ordinis Franciscani, asserens, Eos, qui Christi cognitionem non habuerunt, si modò piè vixerunt, salvatos esse.

Suffragatur huic ipse quoque Andradius scribens in hunc modum: Fidem necessariam esse ad Iustitiam, & vitam æternam, nullum dubium est, Iustus enim ex fide vivet: Illa verò fides & vera Dei cognitio, non ex sacris tantùm literis, divinisq́; oraculis: sed ex rebus etiam ij, quæ sensibus subjiciuntur, haberi potest. Philosophos, qui unum Deum totis viribus inquisiverunt & venerati sunt, nùm tu illa fide Deiq́; cognitione destitutos dices, per quam impius justificatur?

A qua opinione neque Zvvingliani abhorrent. Sic enim Zvvinglius ipse in expositione fidei Christianæ, ad Regem Galliæ: Hic (in vita æterna) visurus es Herculem, Theseum, Socratem, Aristidem, Antigonum, Numam, Camillum, Catones, Scipiones: Hic Antecessores tuos, & quotquot in fide hinc migrârunt, Majores tuos videbis &c.

Quam Zvvinglij impietatem defendere conatur Gualtherus pag 53. Apologiæ, uti supra ex ipsius verbis cognovimus, ubi disputatum fuit de latitudine & complexu legis Naturæ.

Cui stupendæ profanitati, præter rationes, quas supra in contrarium produximus & expedivimus, jam unicam Augustini autoritatem opponere placet, qui lib. 1. ad Bonifacium cap. 21. & lib. 4. contra Iulianum cap. 3. sic alloquitur Pelagianos: An fortè vos Fabritijs, Regulis, Fabijs, Scipionibus, Camillis, permissuri estis aliquam locum inter damnationem regnumq; Cælorum, ubi non sint in miseria, sed beatitudine sempiterna: Qui Deo non placuerunt, cui sine fide impossibile est placere, quam nec in operibus, nec cordibus habuerunt. Non opinor perditionem vestram, ad istam impudentiam posse prosilire.

Et quanquam vix sine gemitu cogitari potest, nedùm pronunciari, Ethnicis extra consortium Ecclesiæ versatis, spem salutis nullam relinqui: interim tamen Deo in illis damnandis constare justissimas facti rationes, ex ijs, quæ Apostolus cap. 1. ad Rom. prolixè disputat, pio cuivis obscurum esse minimè potest.

Quæ cùm ita se habeant, non Zvvinglianorum modò ἀθεότητα, sed & Andradij & Sociorum ipsius sententiam toto pectore execramur, dum scribere illi non exhorrescunt: Gentilibus, qui de Dei providentia non dubitarunt, & sic intellexerunt, Deum pro bonitate sua nihil prætermissurum, quod ad homines æternùm beandos faciat, Gentilibus, inquam istis, notionem istam ad salutem satis fuisse: Imò neque dicendum esse, quòd prorsùs Christum Iesum, crucifixum ignoraverint.

Hæc enim sunt verba Andradij lib. 3. Orth. explic. p. 292. Fuisse quidem Christi cognitionem, omnibus antè seculis ad salutem necessariam, quamvis obscuram & involutam, fateor: sed qui diligenter consideraverit, quàm latè pateat Dei providentia, & quantâ cum vigilantia provideat rebus humanis, satìs intelliget humani generis per Christum redemptionem in divina procuratione, implicatè & absconditè contineri. Quare qui hanc Dei providentiam perspectam habebant & exploratam, simul sanè intelligebant, nihil Deum prætermissurum, ut homines sempiterna felicitate perfruerentur, atq; ita non prorsus ignorasse Christum Iesum crucifixum dicendi sunt, etsi rationem, quam Deus esset initurus humanæ salutis curandæ, compertam minimè habuissent.

Et paulò antè pag. 291. Neq; diritas, atque immanitas tetrior ulla esse potest, quàm sempiternis cruciatibus homines mancipare, propter Fidei illius inopiam, ad quam nullus patebat aditus, & quam consequi nulla via, nullâq́; ratione poterant.

His inquam impijs & planè detestandis Paradoxis ad orcum relegatis, statuimus, non Principia Philosophica, non notitias naturales, sive Lucem illam Naturæ, quanta quanta etiam illa in Hominem cadere possit: sed solum Verbum, & firmiorem illum Sermonem Propheticum esse unicam Lucernam pedibus nostris, quâ prælucente, in salutarem Dei agnitionem perveniri possit. Psal. 119, 105. 2. Pet. 1, 19.


## 14 On the Gospel


### Disposition of Philippean Treatise and oikonomia (future tradition) of ours

THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE PHILIPPEAN TREATISE & the economy of our future treatise.

The Philippean treatise is completed in five parts: the first of which deals with the very etymology of the word Gospel, which in the common language of the Greeks generally signifies a joyful message about something reported and good. Nor indeed is it to be thought that the use of this word began only with John the Baptist and the beginnings of the New Testament: just as certain ancient heretics contended, that before the preaching of John and Christ no mention of the Gospel was made in the Scriptures at all: but rather it is to be established that the use of this word drew its origin from the Greek translation of the Interpreters. For where the Prophets prophesied about the grace and happiness of the New Testament, they generally used the Hebrew verb בָּשַׂר, which signifies the same as to announce new and good things: there the LXX Interpreters rendered that by the verb εὐαγγελίζειν, to evangelize: as is evident from Isaiah 40:9, 41:27, 52:7, 61:1, Nahum 1:15. Psalm 68:12, so that the Hebrew בְּשׂוֹרָה and the Greek τὸ εὐαγγέλιον denote one and the same thing. Furthermore, those prophetic passages are to be accepted as being about nothing other than the grace of the New Testament: we have as witness and author the Apostle in Romans 10:15 and 16, where he says concerning the ancient people that not all had obeyed the Gospel: namely, that one about which Isaiah chapter 52:7 and Nahum 1:15 had preached long ago.

(To the Hebrews the verb בָּשַׂר and to the Greeks εὐαγγελίζειν does not signify just any message of a joyful thing simply: but generally that joy which was conceived from the news of enemies routed and defeated, as is evident from 2 Samuel 18:10, 2 Kings 7:10. According to this meaning, the use of these words is most especially suited to the preaching and doctrine concerning the redemption accomplished through Christ the Liberator.)

The SECOND part sets forth the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, divided into three degrees of difference: namely, 1. By knowledge: for the Law is known by nature: but the Gospel is not. 2. By the mode of promise: the Law promises eternal life with the condition of perfect obedience: but the Gospel with the condition of faith. 3. By efficacy: the Law works wrath, indeed it kills: but the Gospel brings joy and gives life.

The THIRD part proposes the definition of the Gospel, which the Author expresses in these words: Christ in the last chapter of Luke defines the Gospel, clearly like a master craftsman, when he commands to preach repentance and the remission of sins in his name. The Gospel is therefore the preaching of repentance and a promise, which reason does not hold naturally, but which is revealed divinely, in which God promises that he forgives sins on account of Christ his Son, and pronounces us righteous, that is, accepted, and gives the Holy Spirit and eternal life, provided that we believe, that is, trust, that these things certainly come to us on account of Christ.
