And these things he promises freely, so that they may be certain. This definition has been called, and indeed not undeservedly, under more accurate censure by various theologians, with some simply rejecting it as imperfect, too general, or even erroneous: while others, having applied various distinctions, defend it quite solicitously. Concerning which controversy we shall have a discussion expressly below.

The FOURTH part weaves a clearly lucid and vigorous exposition of that question: namely, whether it is not a manifold and diverse Gospel, but one and the same Gospel that has sounded in the Church of the faithful ever since the first fall of our human parents, by which alone also the saints and all the faithful in all times have been saved? Our Author rightly holds the affirmative of this question, and confirms it excellently by an induction of the times. For that proto-Gospel, by which our first parents were raised up from their most sad fall, Genesis 3:15, as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews chapter 11:4 and 5 testifies, shone forth to the patriarchs and to all up to the times of the flood. Afterwards, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the very same Gospel concerning the blessed seed was repeatedly stated and inculcated. Genesis 12:3, 22:18, 26:5, 28:14, etc. By a similar reason, the Mosaic age, through the types and shadows of the Levitical sacrifices, prefigured the Gospel concerning Christ, that Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world, Revelation 13.

Thus the prophecies of the prophets propose such illustrious sermons of the Gospel concerning Christ that some of them are almost more rightly called Evangelists than Prophets. Hence the Council of the Apostles, Acts 15:11, most rightly pronounced that there is clearly one grace, faith, and hope in both, in the Old and New Testament, by which we are saved and by which the ancients were saved long ago.

Which observation indeed shows a most firm refutation, and a double one at that: one against certain ancients who established three different Gospels: so that before Moses, men could be saved by the Law of Nature: after him, by the Levitical Law: under the New Testament by the Evangelical Law. Justin Martyr, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, and many others were involved in this error, until finally Augustine, in the case of Pelagius, who was using this error as a pretext for his impiety, gravely refuted it, showing that at all times there was one and the same Gospel, one and the same way of obtaining eternal salvation. Nor does it stand in the way that the Apostle affirms in Romans 16 that the Gospel is a mystery kept silent for eternal times: but now finally manifested through Christ. For neither ought that to be understood concerning the very substance of the Evangelical doctrine: but concerning a clearer and more illustrious mode of tradition or revelation: in respect of which the doctrine of the Gospel, under the types and shadows of the Old Testament, lay as it were hidden.

Another refutation of those refutes the error of those who refer the doctrine of the Gospel only to the books of the Evangelists and Apostles: just as, conversely, they dream that the Prophetic books contain nothing other than the doctrine of the Law: so that they consider that common distinction of the Biblical Code more than the very matter contained in those books. The cause, however, of this error was the many heresies concerning the Law and the Gospel disseminated long ago. It must therefore be established that the Gospel is proposed in both Testaments, as much by Moses and the Prophets as by the Apostles, although in a most diverse mode of revelation, namely, one that was more obscure, thinner, and more meager then than now under the New Testament.

The fifth and final part contains a Disputation concerning the Promises: Where the author, at the beginning, accurately distinguishes Legal promises from Evangelical ones: ascribing to the latter a purely gratuitous compensation, but to the former a meritorious retribution. Then, indeed, he confirms from the Scriptures that the Evangelical promises are universal, and he explains their practical use quite dexterously against dangerous imaginations concerning Predestination.

Although this Philippean Treatise embraces almost everything that can come into question concerning the Gospel: we, however, having regard especially to the controversies of our own time, will recall the whole exposition of this Article under the complex of three distinct Questions or controversies. The FIRST will be concerning the Definition of the Gospel, specifically so called, opposed both to the Jesuits and to certain more recent Anti-Lutherans or Philippists. The SECOND will be concerning the distinction between Law and Gospel against the Antinomians. The THIRD, concerning the form of the Gospel, that is, concerning the Evangelical promises, both purely gratuitous and universal: against the Epavvites and Calvinists.

Latin:

DISPOSITIO TRACTATIONIS PHILIPPEÆ & οἰκονομία Futuræ Tractationis nostræ.

TRactatio Philippéa quinque absolvitur partibus: quarum Prima agit de ipso etymo vocabuli Evangelij, quod vulgari Græcorum lingua plerunq́ue significat faustum de relata & bona nuncium. Neque verò existimandum est, usum vocabuli hujus demùm cum Iohanne Baptista, & primordijs Novi Testamenti cœpisse: quemadmodum Veteres quidam hæretici contenderunt, ante prædicationem Johannis & Christi nullam prorsus fieri mentionem Evangelij in Scripturis : quin potiùs statuendum, usum vocabuli hujus originem traxisse ex translatione Græca Interpretum. Nam ubi Prophetæ de Gratiâ & felicitate Novi Testamenti vaticinati sunt, plerunque usi sunt Hebræo verbo בָּשַׂר, quod idem significat, ac res novas & bonas nunciare: ibi LXX. Interpretes illud reddiderunt, per verbum εὐαγγελίζειν Evangelizandi: uti patet ex Esaia 40, 9. 41, 27. 52, 7. 61, 1. Nahum. 1, 15. Pfal. 68, 12. ita ut Hebræum בְּשׂוֹרָה, & Græcum τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, unum idemque notent. Cæterùm loca ista Prophetica, non nisi de gratia Novi Testamenti esse accipienda: testem & autorem habemus Apostolum Rom. 10, 15. & 16 ubi de veteri populo dicit, non omnes auscultasse Evangelio: illi nimirùm, de quo Esaias cap. 52, 7. & Nahum 1, 15. concionati jam pridem fuerint.

(Hebræis verbum בָּשַׂר & Græcis εὐαγγελίζειν, non quodvis simpliciter lætæ rei nuncium: sed plerunq́ue illud gaudium significat, quod concipiebatur ex nuncio de profligatis & devictis hostibus, uti patet ex 2. Sam. 18, 10. 2. Reg. 7, 10 Secundùm hanc significationem vel maximè usus verborum istorum competit prædicationi & doctrinæ de redemtione per Christum Liberatorem facta.)

ALTERA pars tradit discrimen Legis & Evangelij, tribus differentiarum gradibus distinctum: nempè. 1. Notitiâ: Lex enim naturâ nota: Evangelium verò non item. 2. Promissionis modo: Lex cum conditione perfectæ obedientiæ: Evangelium verò cum conditione Fidei promittit vitam æternam. 3. Efficaciâ: Lex iram operatur, imò occidit: Evangelium verò lætificat & vivificat.

TERTIA pars proponit Definitionem Evangelij, quam Autor his verbis exprimit: Christus Lucæ ultimo definit Evangelium, planè ut artifex, cùm jubet docere pœnitentiam & remissionem peccator tum in nomine suo. Est igitur Evangelium prædicatio pœnitentiæ & promissio, quam ratio non tenet naturaliter, sed revelata divinitùs, in qua Deus pollicetur, se propter Christum Filium suum remittere peccata, & nos pronunciat justos, id est, acceptos, & donat Spiritum Sanctum, & vitam æternam, modò ut credamus, hoc est, confidamus, hæc nobis propter Christum certò contingere. Atq; hæc gratis pollicetur, ut sint certa. Vocata est, & quidem haud immeritò Definitio hæc à diversis Theologis sub accuratiorem censuram, nonnullis simpliciter eam ceu imperfectam, nimis generalem, imò erroneam reijcientibus: alijs eam, varijs adhibitis distinctionibus, satis sollicitè propugnantibus. Quâ de Controversia nobis infra ex professo futura est Disputatio.

QVARTA pars luculentam planè & nervosam pertexit diexodon illius Quæstionis: An videlicet non multiplex ac diversum: sed unum atque idem Evangelium jam indè à primis lapsus humani parentibus, semper in Ecclesia fidelium sonuerit, quo etiam solo Sancti & fideles quiq; omnibus temporibus sint salvati? Cujus Quæstionis Affirmativam Autor noster rectè tenet, eamque inductione facta temporum, egregiè confirmat. Nam Prot Evangelium illud, quo primi parentes à tristissimo lapsu erecti fuerunt, Gen. 3, 15. teste Autore Epistolæ ad Hebræos cap. 11, 4. & 5. patriarchis omnibusque usque ad tempora diluvij, præluxit. Postmodum Abrahamo, Isaaco, Iacobo idem planè Evangelium de semine benedicto itentidem repetitum & inculcatum fuit. Genes. 12, 3. 22, 18. 26, 5. 28, 14. &c. Pari ratione seculum Mosaicum per Typos & umbras Leviticorum Sacrificiorum, præfigurabat Evangelium de Christo Agno illo, qui occisus est ab origine mundi Apoc. 13.

Sic Prophetarum vaticinia tàm illustres proponunt Evangelij conciones de Christo, ut nonnulli ipsorum fermè rectiùs Evangelistarum, quàm Prophetarum nomen sortiantur. Hinc Concilium Apostolorum Actor. 15, 11. rectissimè pronunciavit, unam planè utrobique, & in Veteri & Novo Testamento esse Gratiam, Fidem & Spem, quâ salvamur & nos, & salvati olim fuerunt Veteres.

Quæ sanè observatio firmissimum monstrat ἔλεγχον, eumque geminum: Unum contra Veteres quosdam, qui statuerunt tria diversa Evangelia: ita ut ante Moysen, Homines per Legem Naturæ: post ipsum, per Legem Leviticam: sub Novo Testamento per Legem Evangelicam salvari potuerint. Quo in errore versati sunt Justinus Martyr, Tertullianus, Clemens Alexandrinus, & alij plures, donec tandem Augustinus in Pelagio errorem istum, suæ impietati prætexente graviter illum refutavit, ostendens, omnibus temporibus unum idemq; fuisse Evangelium, unam eandemque salutis æternæ consequendæ rationem. Neq; obstat, quod Apostolus affirmat Rom. 16. Evangeliu esse mysteriū æternis temporibus tacitum: nunc autem demùm, per Christum manifestatum. Neque etim de ipsa doctrina Evangelica substantia: sed de traditionis sive revelationis clariore ac illustriore modo illud intelligi debet: respectu cujus doctrina Evangelij, sub typis & umbris Veteris Testamenti quasi latuit.

Alter ἔλεγχος illorum refutat errorem, qui Evangelij doctrinam tantum ad libros Evangelistarum, & Apostolorum referunt: quemadmodum vice versa libros Propheticos, nihil aliud quam Legis doctrinam continere, somniant: ita ut distinctionem magis illam vulgatam Codicis Biblici considerent, quam ipsam materiam libris illis contentam. Causa autem fuit error iste plurimarum hæreseon de Lege ac Evangelio jam olim disseminatarum. Statuendum proinde Evangelium in utroque Testamento proponi, tam a Mose & Prophetis, quam ab Apostolis, licet diversissimo revelationis modo, obscuriore videlicet, tenuiore, atque exiliore tum, quam nunc sub Novo Testamento.

QVINTA & postrema pars continet Disputationem de Promissionibus: Ubi autor initio, accurate discernit promissiones Legales ab Evangelicis: his mere gratuitam compensationem: illis vero meritoriam retributionem ascribens. Deinde vero promissiones Evangelicas Universales esse, ex Scripturis confirmat, earumque usum Practicum, contra periculosas imaginationes de Prædestinatione, satis dextre explicat.

Quanquam vero Tractatio hæc Philippea, pleraque omnia complectitur, quæ de Evangelio in Quæstionem venire possunt: nos tamen, nostri potissimum temporis Controversiarum habita ratione, sub trium distinctarum Quæstionum sive controversiarum complexum, totam Articuli hujus diexodon revocabimus. PRIMA erit de Definitione Evangelij, specifice sic dicti, opposita tum Jesuvitis, tum recentioribus quibusdam Anti-Lutheranis sive Philippistis. ALTERA erit de discrimine Legis & Evangelij contra Antinomos. TERTIA, de forma Evangelij, hoc est, de promissionibus Evangelicis tum mere gratuitis, tum universalibus: contra Epavvitas & Calvinianos.


### I. Question or Controversy, concerning the Definition of the Gospel

Concerning the definition of the Gospel specifically so called, it will then finally be judged most correctly if it is first exactly established what its proper Object is: or the Matter about which it properly revolves. For a matter is given at the beginning that is as it were remote and General: as when the Gospel is said to be the doctrine of salvation. Which matter certainly belongs to the divine Law also, when it is considered in itself and by itself, without the determination of a limitation. For the Law was given so that he who does it might be saved by it: but it is weakened by the flesh, and thus it happens by accident that it cannot save Man. Therefore, some constitute the proper Matter of the Gospel too generally as the doctrine of salvation. Nor can this opinion be admitted or defended in any way, unless some evident Limitation is added, namely such a one as defines the proximate, special, proper, and as it were essential matter of the Gospel: Such as is the universal promise concerning the gratuitous Remission of sins, through and on account of the merit of CHRIST, apprehended by true faith. The consideration of this matter produces a twofold Doctrine of salvation: one Legal, and impossible for human nature: the other Evangelical, and joined with the possibility of men, not indeed proper, but only imputative: The former mercenary: the latter purely gratuitous, in respect of us. Then this very proximate matter shows that the Doctrine of the Gospel, properly so called, is nothing other than the preaching of most joyful news. For if its End is looked at, certainly the news of salvation is contained in it. If the means are considered, we are declared to be redeemed by nothing but the precious blood of the Son of God. If, finally, the Principle itself and the cause, as it were, προκαταρκτικὴ (pre-initiating) is weighed, nothing other than grace, charity, and a merciful will toward us is announced in it. He who does not feel himself refreshed and as it were exhilarated by the most sweet preaching of all these things, is most correctly called ἀνόητος (foolish) or senseless: just as the Apostle points out the Galatians, after they had fallen away somewhat from the doctrine of the Gospel, chapter 3, 1. Finally, the consideration of this very proximate Matter shows the most firm foundation from which a true and essential definition of the Gospel can be constructed, nay, indeed, truly ought to be: Which is, not a Legal and mercenary promise, not a sermon of repentance, which is joined with sorrow and terror: but that sole Universal promise concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, apprehended by true faith through and on account of CHRIST. Hence such a perfect and Essential Definition can be constructed, that namely the Gospel is that most noble part of Celestial doctrine, which, contradistinguished from the Law of God, is not known to Man by nature: but brought forth from the secret bosom of the Father through the Son of God, contains a sermon concerning the immense mercy of GOD provided through the Son the redeemer, and which promises and exhibits to those believing in CHRIST gratuitous remission of sins, Justice, and eternal life.

Opposed to this purer doctrine is a twofold crowd of those who err: One of the Romanists: The other of the Crypto-Calvinists, who sell themselves as disciples of Philip. I. For the Romanists, shamefully confusing the proper or specific matter of the Gospel with that general one, wickedly transform the doctrine of the Gospel, properly so called, into the doctrine of the Law. For they contend that the Gospel is a doctrine concerning the righteousness of works: for thus the Cologne censors did not hesitate to write on p. 204: The Law imposed works and precepts, but grace to fulfill them: but the Gospel also enjoins works, but adds grace and strength to fulfill them: for the doctrine of the Gospel is: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. In the same manner, Bellarmine also did not shudder to write: book 4 de Justif. chap. 2, p. 1171. If we speak of the grace of the New Testament, the Law is not distinguished from the Gospel in that the Law requires works and the Gospel does not require works, but in that the Law teaches what is to be done, but the Gospel provides the strength to do it.

And after a few words: We contend that the Gospel contains all those things which our adversaries attribute to the Law alone, which are chiefly three: Laws properly so called, threatenings, and promises with the condition of obedience.

This error is too pernicious to be sufficiently exaggerated in words: for it fundamentally destroys and overturns the whole system of the articles of faith; indeed, it wickedly corrupts the business of our justification and salvation, as we shall expressly show in the following next article. It should only be observed in this place that this Jesuitical dogma is contradictorily opposed to the Holy Scriptures. For the Apostle, opposing the Law and the Gospel to each other, simply denies that the Gospel, thus properly and specifically accepted, is a doctrine concerning the righteousness of works. For Rom. 10:5 he differs thus: Moses describes the righteousness which is from the Law, The man who has done these things shall live by them: But the righteousness which is from faith speaks thus: If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. And Galat. 3:11 and 12. The just shall live by faith: but the Law is not of faith, but he who has done them shall live by them. Rom. 4:5. And, to him who does NOT work, but BELIEVES in Him who justifies the ungodly, faith is imputed for righteousness. That apostolic decision, which utterly destroys the Jesuitical dogma, pertains here. For when certain ones of the sect of the Pharisees were urging, besides faith, also the observance of the Mosaic Law as necessary for salvation, the Apostles in the Council of Jerusalem brought forth this decision: Why do you tempt GOD to put a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, just as they also were saved, Acts 15:10 and 11.

Hence Dr. Jerome excellently infers in book 1 of his Dialogue against the Pelagians: In that (the Law) the foundations of works are laid: but in this (the Gospel) the summit of faith and grace is imposed.

But enough and more than enough concerning this error. More in the Article on Justification.

ANOTHER error is that of the Crypto-Calvinists, who contend that the Gospel, properly so called, must be defined as a sermon of repentance. And indeed our author himself is read to have used this very definition both in this place and here and there elsewhere. Nor can it be denied that in the first times of the purified religion, many of the more sincere doctors did not abhor this definition. What more? That in the very writing of the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, this manner of speaking was not repudiated. Which is the reason why blessed Luther also is nowhere read to have disapproved of this definition in express words. And indeed, if those men who today foist the same definition upon our churches possessed the same sincerity of doctrine and sentiment that those ancient theologians possessed most sincerely, perhaps no one would more scrupulously stir up a dispute on this account: especially since Philip himself sometimes explained his mind more correctly than he spoke: as is evident primarily from the disputation on the Jubilee, held in the year 49, thesis 14, 32, and 36, Vol. IV of the Works of Philip, p. 551, 553. Likewise the disputation on the distinction between Law and Gospel, of the year 1550, thesis 5, 6, and 7. But those times soon followed which suffered a most serious Interimistic confusion in the Church, where the necessity was offered to some of observing Philip's sermons and writings more diligently. And since there were not a few who, with little prudent zeal, thought that they must swear by the words of the Master, and furthermore poured oil on the fire, that is, stubbornly contended that the Gospel, properly so called, is a sermon of repentance arguing sins: finally this question flared up into a public conflagration of strife. Therefore, the purer theologians fought bitterly against this definition of the Gospel, contending that through it the Law and the Gospel, or at least the proper and as it were essential offices of both, are shamefully confused: indeed, that the Gospel is utterly exterminated and the fury of the Antinomians is strongly established. Thus, therefore, at last, a controversy arose among theologians, even those addicted to the Augsburg Confession, not about goat's wool or an empty nut, as the saying goes, but about a matter of far greater gravity: an accurate treatment of which is provided by the Fifth Article of the Book of Christian Concord, which we have also woven together quite prolixly and clearly in our commentary on the same, and indeed we have also vigorously refuted the arguments of the Philippists. For this time, to contract the matter into a few words, we establish that two things especially must be well observed concerning this controversy: the former of which regards the state of the question itself, but the latter the propositions about which the question is raised. As to the State, we have just now admonished that some have used this Definition out of a certain received and, as it were, common custom of speaking, and in simplicity of sense, harboring nothing ὕπουλον, much less craftily seeking the patronage of any error: but others, no longer content with simplicity of sense, have fought sharply in the affirmative concerning the propriety and truth of this Definition. As to the Propositions about which there was dispute, some commonly [called it] the Gospel: or as Philip in his theses sometimes speaks, the Ministry of the Gospel, they called the Preaching of repentance: but others asserted that by the word Gospel sins are furthermore reproved. Those former ones deservedly obtain συγγνώμην pardon among all, especially if we look at the condition of those times in which this Question had not yet been called into Controversy, much less ventilated or explained. And because the word Gospel taken loosely or generally, not rarely denotes the whole complex of Celestial Doctrine: hence some understood by Gospel under this definition, the whole ministry of Christ and the Apostles. In which part that the Gospel is also a Sermon of repentance, no Orthodox person would ever have denied: provided that it be observed, that in this sense the word Gospel is taken generally, and less properly for the whole doctrine of salvation, or the whole ministry of Christ and the Apostles. What? Because, if the word Gospel is taken even strictly and specially, it is nevertheless to be preached not to Hypocrites and the stubborn: but to the penitent and those crushed by the sense of divine wrath. Which if those simpler Theologians looked at under this Definition: then they deserve pardon all the more. Finally, it is added, that the word Repentance is also equivocal in the Scriptures: For sometimes it denotes only one part of Conversion, namely that which arises from the reproof of sins, and is commonly called Contrition: But sometimes indeed the whole Conversion of Man, and thus it concludes Faith in Christ most of all. In the former way and respect, certainly, the Gospel in its proper and strict signification, taken for doctrine, distinguished διχότο- μως from the law, can never be defined by the preaching of repentance, without corruption of doctrine. But in the latter way and respect, neither the Gospel, nor the Law alone, will be truly called the preaching of repentance: But those parts of the office are to be referred respectively to each part of celestial Doctrine. But if indeed under the word Repentance, only Faith, that other and nobler part of Repentance is understood, then truly a different judgment must be rendered. For because Faith, which is the proper and adequate object of the Gospel, constitutes the other part of Repentance, and that the principal one: certainly in this respect also, we would not unwillingly concede that the Gospel was formerly called the preaching of Repentance not altogether inconveniently, both in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession: and by others.

Moreover, as for those who stubbornly contended that by the word Gospel sins are reproved, we determine that they can in no way be defended. And we oppose to the error of those that Decision; which was made in the Book of Concord, and is most conveniently restricted to these six heads.

I. The distinction of Law and Gospel must be diligently retained in the Church: But this is not retained, as soon as the accusation of sins is assigned to the Gospel, and indeed to the Gospel ἀντιδιῃρημένως opposed to the Law.

II. The Law is properly Doctrine, which teaches about works, and reproves sins: For from the Law is the knowledge of sin: Rom. 3, 20. Therefore this very office does not belong to the Gospel properly so called, unless it be transformed into the Law.

III. Whatever in sacred Scripture reproves sins, when and however that may happen, that, speaking properly, pertains to nothing but the doctrine of the Law.

IV. The Gospel properly and strictly so called, is the doctrine of Faith, of the promise of Grace, and of the benefits of CHRIST the Savior.

V. Such is the ἀντίθεσις or comparison of Law and Gospel, that to reprove sins, to work wrath, to condemn, and at the same time to propose Faith and the benefits of CHRIST the Savior, or to announce the gratuitous Remission of sins, are so incompatible, that they can by no reason be attributed to one and the same special doctrine. In the antithesis therefore of Law and Gospel, neither can be attributed to the Gospel either properly or primarily, so that it is said either to preach repentance, or to reprove sins.

VI. The Passion of Christ, although it is a part of evangelical history: nevertheless, insofar as the atrocity of sin and divine wrath is shown from it, it is joined to the legal sermon only by a secondary reduction.

Therefore, although before this Controversy was stirred up, some Theologians used this Definition, but under a sound sense, which was explained a little earlier, and they deserve pardon: yet after this very Definition later produced various disputes and scandals: certainly the ὑποτύπωσις ὑγιαινόντων λόγων should have been firmly retained and asserted with no less diligence than the sincerity of the doctrine itself.

Latin:

DE definitione Evangelij specifice sic dicti, tum demum rectissime judicabitur, si prius exacte constiterit, quodnam proprium ejus sit Objectum: sive Materia, circa quam proprie illud versatur. Datur enim initio Materia quasi remota & Generalis: ut quando Evangelium dicitur esse doctrina salutis. Quæ sane materia Legi quoque divinæ competit, quando ea in se & per se, sine limitationis determinatione consideratur. Data enim est Lex, ut qui fecerit eam, salvetur per eam: infirmatur autem per carnem, & sic ex accidente fit, quod salvare Hominem nequit. Proinde Materiam Evangelij propriam nimis generaliter nonnulli constituunt Doctrinam salutis. Neque etiam ullo pacto sententia hæc admitti aut defendi potest, nisi evidens aliqua Limitatio adjiciatur, talis nimirum, quæ Materiam propinquam, specialem, propriam & Evangelio quasi essentialem definiat: Qualis est universalis promissio de gratuita peccatorum Remissione, per & propter meritum CHRISTI, vera fide apprehensum. Hujus materiæ consideratio geminam prodit Doctrinam salutis: unam Legalem, & naturæ humanæ impossibilem: Alteram Evangelicam, & ratione hominum cum possibilitate non quidem propria, sed tantum imputativa conjunctam: Illam mercenariam: hanc pure gratuitam, ratione nostri. Deinde hæc ipsa materia propinqua ostendit, Doctrinam Evangelij proprie sic dicti, nihil esse aliud, quam lætissimi nuncij prædicationem. Si enim Finis ejus spectetur, certe salutis nuncium in ea continetur. Si media considerentur, non nisi pretioso sanguine Filij Dei redempti esse perhibemur. Si denique Principium ipsum & causa quasi προκαταρκτικὴ expendatur, nihil aliud, quam gratia, charitas & misericors erga nos voluntas, in eadem annunciatur. Quarum certe rerum omnium dulcissima prædicatione, qui se non recreari & quasi exhilarari sentit, ἀνόητος sive insensatus rectissime dicitur: quemadmodum Galatas indigitat Apostolus, postquam a doctrina Evangelij nonnihil defecissent cap. 3, 1. Tandem hujus ipsius Materiæ propinquæ consideratio, firmissimum fundamentum monstrat, ex quo vera & essentialis definitio Evangelij extrui possit, imo vere etiam debeat: Quod est, non promissio Legalis & mercenaria, non concio pœnitentiæ, quæ cum dolore & terrore est conjuncta: sed sola illa Universalis promissio de gratuita remissione peccatorum, per & propter CHRISTUM vera fide apprehensum. Hinc talis perfecta & Essentialis extrui potest Definitio, quod nimirum Evangelium sit nobilissima illa doctrinæ Cœlestis pars, quæ a Lege Dei contradistincta Homini non est natura nota: sed ex arcano sinu Patris per Filium Dei prolata, concionem continet, de immensa DEI misericordia per Filium redemptorem præstita, quæque gratuitam peccatorum remissionem, Iustitiam & & vitam æternam in CHRISTUM credentibus promittit atq; exhibet.

Puriori huic doctrinæ ex adverso gemina errantium turba est, opposita: Vna Romanensium: Altera Crypto-Calvinistarum, qui se Philippidiscipulos venditant. I. Romanenses enim propriam sive specialem Evangelij materiam, cum generali illa turpiter confundentes, doctrinam Evangelij propriè sic dicti, in Doctrinam Legis nefariè transformant. Contendunt enim, Evangelinm esse doctrinam de Justitia operum : Sic enim Efavvitæ Colonienfes p.204. Censuræ scribere non dubitârunt : Lex imposuit opera atquè præcepta, sed gratiam ea implendi : Evangelium verò etiam opera injungit, sed addit gratiam & vires implendi : Est enim Evangelij doctrina : Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Eundem in modum Bellarminus quoque scribere non exhorruit : l. 4. de Justif. cap. 2. p. 1171. Si loquamur de Gratia Novi Testamenti, non distinguitur Lex ab Evangelio, quòd Lex requirat opera : Evangelium non requirat opera : sed quòd Lex doceat, quid sit faciendum : Evangelium autem præbeat vires, ad faciendam.

Et post pauca : Nos contendimus, Evangelio contineri illa omnia, quæ Adversarij soli Legi tribuunt, quæ sunt præcipuè tria : Leges propriè dictæ, Comminationes & promissiones cum conditione Obedientiæ.

Perniciosior est error iste, quàm ut verbis sufficienter exaggerari possit : Totum enim Systema Articulorum fidei funditùs disjicit & evertit : imò negòcium Justificationis & salutis nostræ nefariè corrumpit : quemadmodum in subsequenti Articulo proximo, ex professo ostendemus. Illud duntaxat hoc loco observandum fuerit, Dogma hoc Jesuuviticum Scripturis Sacris contradictoriè esse oppositum. Apostolus enim Legem & Evangelium sibi invicem opponens, simpliciter negat, Evangelium sic propriè & specificè acceptum, esse doctrinam de Justitiâ operum. Nam Rom. 10, 5. sic differit : Moyses describit Iustitiam, quæ ex Lege est, Qui fecerit hæc homo, vivet in eis : Quæ autem ex Fide est Justitia, sic dicit : Si confitearis in ore tuo Dominum Jesum, & in corde tuo credideris, quod Deus illum suscitavit à mortuis, salvus eris. Et Galat. 3, 11. & 12. Iustus ex Fide vivet : Lex autem non est ex Fide, sed qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis. Rom. 4, 5. Et, qui NON operatur, CREDENTI autem in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur fides ad justitiam. Pertinet hùc decisio illa Apostolica, quæ Jesuvviticum dogma penitùs destruit. Nam tùm quidam de secta Pharisæorum, præter fidem etiam observantiam Legis Mosaicæ, tanquàm ad salutem necessariam urgerent, Apostoli in Concilio Hyerosolymitano hanc decisivam tulerunt : Quid tentatis DEUM imponere jugum cervices discipulorum, quod neque Patres nostri, neq; nos portare potuimus ? sed per gratiam Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI credimus nos salvari, quemadmodum & illi salvati fuerunt, Actor. 15, 10. & 11.

Hinc præclarè infert D. Hyeronymus lib. 1. Dial. adversus Pelag. In illa (Lege) operum fundamenta jaciuntur : hic (in Evangelio) Verò Fidei & gratiæ culmen imponitur.

Sed de errore isto hoc pacto plus satis. Plura in Articulo de Justificatione.

ALTER error est Crypto-Calvinistarum, qui contendunt, Evangelium propriè sic dictum definiendum esse per Concionem pænitentiæ. Et sanè ipse Autor noster, tum hoc loco, tum passim alibi hac ipsa definitione usus esse legitur. Neq; negari potest, primis repurgatæ Religionis temporibus multos sinceriores Doctores, ab hac Definitione non abhorruisse. Quid? quòd in ipsa Apologia Confessionis Augustanæ scribenda, modus iste loquendi non fuit repudiatus. Quæ causa est, quòd B. Lutherus etiam nuspiam Definitionem hanc disertis verbis improbasse legitur. Et profectò, si hominibus illis, qui eandem Definitionem hodie nostris Ecclesiis obtrudunt, eadem constaret doctrinæ & sententiæ sinceritas, quæ priscis illis Theologis constitit sincerissima, nemo fortassis scrupulosiùs litem hoc nomine moveret: præsertim cùm Philippus ipse rectiùs interdum mentem suam explicârit, quàm locutus sit: uti cum primis patet ex disputat: de Jubilæo, Anno 49. habita thef. 14. & 32. & 36. Tom. IIII. Operum Philippi p. 551. 553. Item disputat: de discrimine Legis & Evangelij, Anni 1550. thesi 5. & 6. & 7. Sed secuta sunt mox ea tempora, quæ σύῤῥαξιν Interimisticam in Ecclesia gravissimam passa fuerunt, ubi oblata nonnullis fuit necessitas, Philippi sermones scriptaque diligentiùs observandi. Cumque non pauci essent, qui zelo parum prudente, existimarent jurandum sibi esse in verba Magistri, & insuper oleum igni suffunderent, hoc est, mordicus contenderent, Evangelium propriè sic dictum, esse Concionem pænitentiæ arguentem peccata: tandèm Quæstio hæc in publicum certaminis incendium exarsit. Puriores proindè Theologi acriter contra Definitionem hanc Evangelij pugnabant, contendentes, per eam Legem & Evangelium, vel certè propria & quasi Essentialia utriusque officia turpiter confundi: imò Evangelium penitùs exterminari & Antinomorum furorem fortiter stabiliri. Sic ergò tandem non de lana caprina, aut cassa nuce, quod dici solet: sed de re longè gravissima inter Theologos, etiam Confessioni Augustanæ addictos orta fuit Controversia: cujus accuratam omninò pertractationem subministrat Articulus Quintus, Libri Christianæ Concordiæ, quam etiam in nostro Commentario in eundem satis prolixè & perspicuè pertexuimus, quin argumenta etiam Philippistarum nervosè refutavius. Hâc vice; ut rem in pauca contrahamus, duo potissimùm circa hanc Controversiam probè observanda esse, statuimus: Quorum prius respicit statum ipsum, de quo quæritur: Posterius verò propositiones, de quibus quæritur. Quoad Statum, jam modò admonuimus, quosdam Definitione hac usos fuisse, ex recepta quadam, & vulgata quasi loquendi consuetudine, & in simplicitata sensus, nihil ὕπουλον foventes, nedùm erroris alicujus patrocinium subdolè quærentes: Alios verò non ampliùs simplicitate sensus contentos, de propietate ac veritate hujus Definitionis acriter in affirmantem pugnasse. Quoad Propositiones, de quibus disputabatur, Alij vulgariter Evangelium: vel ut Philippus in thesibus aliquoties loquitur, Ministerium Evangelij, appellarunt Prædicationem pœnitentiæ: alij verò voce Evangelij Peccata argui insuper afferuerunt. Priores illi meritò apud omnes συγγνώμην veniam consequuntur, præsertim si temporum illorum conditionem spectemus quibus hæc Quæstio nondùm in Controversiam vocata, nedùm ventilata aut explicata erat. Et quia vox Evangelij laxè sive generaliter accepta, haud rarò totum Cœlestis Doctrinæ complexum notat: hinc nonnulli per Evangelium sub hac definitione, totum ministerium Christi & Apostolorum intellexerunt. Quâ in parte Evangelium etiam esse Concionem pœnitentiæ, nemo Orthodoxus unquàm negaverit: modò illud observetur, hoc sensu vocem Evangelij generaliter, minusque propriè accipi pro tota doctrina salutis, sive toto ministerio Christi & Apostolorum. Quid? quod, si strictè etiam & specialiter vox Evangelij accipiatur, illud tamen non Hypocritis & pervicacibus: sed pœnitentibus & sensu iræ divinæ contritis prædicandum est. Quòd ipsum si simpliciores illi Theologi sub hac Definitione spectarunt: tùm tantò magis veniam merentur, Tandem accedit, quòd vox Pœnitentiæ etiam in Scripturis est æquivoca: Interdum enim unam tantùm Conversionis partem, illam nimirùm notat, quæ ex redargutione peccatorum oritur, & vulgò Contritio appellatur: Interdum verò totam Hominis Conversionem, & sic Fidem in Christum vel maxi mè concludit. Priore modo ac respectu, nunquàm profectò, Evangelium in propria & stricta significatione, pro doctrina, à lege διχότομως distincta, acceptum, per prædicationem pœnitentiæ, sinè corruptela doctrinæ, definiri potest. Posteriore verò modò ac respectu, neque Evangelium, neque Lex sola, pœnitentiæ prædicatio verè appellabitur: Sed partes istæ muneris, respectivè ad partem utramque cœlestis Doctrinæ referendæ sunt. Quod si verò sub voce Pœnitentiæ, tantùm Fides, altera illa & nobilior Pœnitentiæ pars intelligatur, tùm sanè aliter ferendum est judicium. Quia anim Fides, quæ proprium & adæquatum Evangelij objectum est, partem Pœnitentiæ alteram, eamque præcipuam constituit: utique hoc respectu etiam, Evangelium tùm in Apologia Confessionis Augustanæ: tùm ab alijs prædicationem Pœnitentiæ non omninò incommodè appellatum olim fuisse, haud inviti concederimus.

Cæterùm quod Posteriores has, qui mordicits contenderunt, voce Evangelij peccata argui, nullatenùs eos defendi posse statuimus. Et istorum errori eam Decisionem opponimus; quæ in Libro Concordiæ facta est, & ad sex istæ hæc capita commodissimè restringitur.

I. Discrimen Legis & Evangelij in Ecclesiâ diligenter est retinendum: Atqui hoc non retinetur, quamprimùm Evangelio, & quidem Legi ἀντιδιῃρημένως opposito, peccatorum accusatio assignatur.

II. Lex propriè est Doctrina, quæ docet de operibus, & arguit peccata: Nam ex Lege est agnitio peccati: Rom. 3, 20. Ergo hoc ipsum officium Evangelio propriè sic dicto non competit, nisi illud in Legem transformetur.

III. Quicquid in Scriptura sacra peccata arguit, quando & quomodocunque illud fiat, id propriè loquendo, non nisi ad doctrinam Legis pertinet.

IV. Evangelium propriè & strictè sic dictum, est doctrina de Fide, de promissione Gratiæ, & beneficijs CHRISTI Servatoris.

V. Ea est ἀντίθεσις sive collatio Legis & Evangelij, ut peccata arguere, iram operari, condemnare, & simul Fidem ac beneficia CHRISTI Servatoris proponere, sive gratuitam Remissionem peccatorum annunciare, ita sint incompetibilia, ut doctrinæ speciali uni atque eidem tribui nulla ratione possint. In antithesi ergò Legis & Evangelij neutrum vel propriè, vel primò Evangelio tribui potest, ut vel prædicare pœnitentiam, vel arguere peccata dicatur.

VI. Passio Christi, quamvis historiæ Evangelicæ pars est: tamen quatentis ex illa peccati & iræ divinæ atrocitas monstratur, secundariâ demùm reductione legali concioni adjungitur.

Proindè etsi ante motam istam Controversiam, Definitione hac, sed sub sano sensu, qui paulò antè explicatus est, nonnulli Theologi usi sunt, & veniam merentur: postquàm tamen hæc ipsa Definitio postmodùm varias disceptationes & scandala peperit: utique ὑποτύπωσις ὑγιαινόντων λόγων non minori diligentia, quàm ipsa doctrinæ sinceritas firmiter retinenda & afferenda fuerit.


### Or Controversy, concerning the Distinction of Law and Gospel

How much it matters to handle the Word of God ὀρθοτομεῖν, so that the Law may keep itself within its own boundaries, and the limits of neither the Gospel nor the Law be shifted through some confusion, is shown by those struggles which, while the Apostles were still living, were stirred up by those who, claiming to be inflamed with zeal for the Law, were transforming the Gospel into the Law.

This very damage is still occurring today in the Church of God, with those same two parts of the Heavenly Doctrine being poorly proposed and defended by the idle Jesuits: as will be more clearly evident from the following Article on Justification. In this place, however, those distinctions which certain more accurate theologians have discovered from the Scriptures to exist between the Law and the Gospel must be noted with great diligence: and indeed six in particular.

For, in the first place, they differ in the mode of notice or knowledge: For the moral Law or Decalogue is in some way naturally known to men, inasmuch as it is implanted and inscribed in their very minds. Rom. 2:15. But the nature of the Gospel is entirely different: Since, apart from revelation, nothing at all could be known to Man concerning it: But it was necessary that the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, should declare it to us, John 1:18. For which very reason the Gospel is defined by the Apostle as a mystery kept silent from eternal times, or hidden in God, from ages past. Rom. 16:25. Eph. 3:9. Col. 1:26.

Next, they differ in the object of Persons: For the Law is to be proposed to the impious, the secure, the stubborn, and other wicked and unruly sinners, a long list of whom the Apostle has woven together in 1 Tim. 1:9, 10, and 11. I know that the law is not laid down for the just: but for the despisers of the law, and for those who will not be subject, for the impious and sinners, for the wicked and profane, for patricides and matricides, for murderers, for those who lie with males, for kidnappers and liars, for the perjured, and if there is anything else that is opposed to sound doctrine. But the Gospel is to be announced to those who are already laboring and are burdened, and who have need of refreshment, as Christ speaks in Matt. 11, that is, those who are already seriously grieving over committed sins, and, dismayed by the sense of divine wrath, groan with David: A contrite and humbled heart, O God, do not despise, Ps. 51.

Thirdly, they differ in the object of things: For the Law urges the righteousness of works according to that saying: He who shall have done these things shall live in them, Rom. 10:5. But the Gospel urges the righteousness of Faith, resulting from free remission and, on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith. Concerning which the Apostle says in Rom. 4:5: To him who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the impious, faith is imputed for righteousness. Therefore, as far as the meritorious and the gratuitous are distant from each other, so far also do the Law and the Gospel differ from each other, nor can they ever coalesce in this respect. For they can never stand together in the same way, at the same time, without implying a manifest contradiction: just as the Apostle explains this excellently in Rom. 11:6. If, he says, righteousness is obtained by grace, it is no longer from works: otherwise grace is no longer grace: But if from works, it is no longer from grace: otherwise work is no longer work.

Fourthly, they differ in the Form of the Promises: For the Law has promises that are, in relation to us, purely meritorious and compensatory by debt: For he alone obtains eternal life from the Law who has done all things that are written in it, Lev. 18:5, Deut. 30:15, and following. But the Gospel has promises that are, in respect to us, merely gratuitous and purely donative, according to that saying in Eph. 2:8: By grace you are saved through faith, and this not of yourselves: for it is the gift or δῶρον of God. And Rom. 4:16: Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise might be firm according to grace to all the seed.

Fifthly, they differ in their proper and entirely distinct offices: For the Law commands, threatens, terrifies, condemns, and kills. Rom. 3:20 and ch. 4:15, 2 Cor. 3:6. But the Gospel raises up, comforts, absolves, vivifies, and exhilarates the conscience, Isaiah 61:2 and 3, Luke 4:18, Rom. 1:16.

Finally, they also differ in Effect, as far as we are concerned: For although the Law is good and holy in itself, Rom. 7:12, and if anyone were to keep it, it would indeed grant him righteousness before God: yet it obtains mere ἀμηχανίαν, or as the Apostle speaks, mere ἀδυναμίαν: and it can never reach that effect of its own: Since it is weakened by the flesh, that is, the horrible corruption of our Nature, it thoroughly debilitates and breaks that condition added to the promise of the Law, Rom. 8:3, Gal. 3:21, so that it is impossible for the Law to save anyone. But the Gospel attains its end, because in it the righteousness without the Law is revealed, Rom. 1:17 and ch. 3:21. Concerning which matter the Apostle discourses excellently in Rom. 9:30, 31, 32: The Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained righteousness: but the righteousness which is from faith: Israel, however, who pursued the law of righteousness, did not arrive at the law of righteousness: Why? Because they sought it not from faith, but from the works of the law. To which also pertain those classic passages in Rom. 10:3: ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God: For Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone WHO BELIEVES. And Gal. 3:10: Whoever are from the works of the Law are under a curse: For it is written: Cursed is everyone who has not remained in all things which are written in the book of the law, to do them. But since no one is justified before God by the Law, it is manifest that the Just shall live by faith. But the Law is not from faith: but he who shall have done them shall live in them.

With these marks of the differences well observed, it is invincibly evident that these two kinds of doctrines are as far distant from each other as Heaven and earth, Light and darkness, day and night, as our Luther says somewhere; indeed, he even adds, I wish we could distinguish them even further.

Nor indeed does any patronage accrue from this to the fury of the Antinomians, who elicited a manifest ἀντίφασιν or conflict of contradiction from these differences, so that in the Church

God at the same time both Doctrines cannot have a place: but the Law simply ought to be relegated from the field and boundaries of the Church to the court, nay, to the gallows. For no such thing either came into the mind of Luther, or is asserted by us. Most wisely, however, the Antinomians establish that different things are contradictory: for the Law and the Gospel are indeed opposed to each other as different: but not as contradictory. Hence the Apostle himself Gal. 3. v. 21. expressly writes: The Law is not against the promises of the Gospel, and Rom. 3, 31. We do not evacuate or make void the Law by faith: but we establish it.

of our [faith], do they stand? 2. It is false that the Law and the Prophets only expressly promise temporal goods. Moses refutes the Jesuit of a lie Deut. 30, 19: I call heaven and earth to witness this day, he says, that I have set before you this day life and death: blessing and cursing, etc. Thirdly, it is a lie that the Gospel, as it is opposed to the Law, regards moral laws in the place of the object: as has already been shown above.

The Jesuit borrows a second distinction from the annexed matters, where he mentions many things which have nothing at all to do with the matter: a few which touch the scope of the controversy: and finally one which properly pertains here: contending that the Gospel, just as much as the Law, is properly concerned with the threats and terrors of the Law: thus intending to demonstrate that the Gospel also urges the necessity of works, in the business of Justification, book 4. chap. 4. But this comment was partly discussed in the immediately preceding Article: and partly in the next following one, we shall have to examine it expressly. In this place, only this comes under observation, that Holy Scripture so distinguishes Moses and Christ, and consequently the Law and the Gospel, that they cannot be referred under one and the same kind of doctrine. John certainly asserts that the Law was given through Moses John 1, 17. Thus the Apostle attests, that THIS is a faithful saying, and worthy that we should embrace it in all ways, that Christ came into the world, not to bring laws of works, but to save sinners, 1 Tim. 1, 15. Therefore, the voice of the Cologne Jesuits is to be detested, asserting that that mercy, which the Gospel properly celebrates, and in which the salvation and life of us all consists, is this, that God added this promise to the Law of Moses in the Gospel: He who shall do these things, shall live in them: For the sum, they say, of the mercy of GOD is that He promises eternal life to those who act rightly, page 26 of the censure. This, indeed, is to deny the nature and essence of the Gospel sacrilegiously, and to utterly undermine and overturn its proper form: what this is, the third Question will now expressly explain.

For the benefits of Christ, which are offered to us in the Gospel, are nothing other than the satisfaction owed to the Law. For Christ, of whom the Gospel preaches, was therefore made subject to the Law, Galat. 4, 4. so that the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us, (but not by us) Rom. 8, 4. So that the righteousness of the Law is at once different and the same. Different indeed in us, and with respect to us: For it is not from the Law for us, Phil. 3, 9. that is, it is not acquired by our observation of the Law. Yet it is the same again in Christ, and with respect to Christ, who rendered completed obedience to the Law. Hence our same Luther rightly pronounced that the Law and the Gospel ought to be most closely joined in the heart of every Christian. Commentary on chap. 3 of the Epistle to the Galatians.

And this indeed is our Orthodox doctrine, concerning the distinction of the Law and the Gospel, drawn and constructed from nowhere else than from clear testimonies of the Scriptures: concerning which again our Blessed Luther on chap. 2 of Galatians: He who knows well how to distinguish the Law from the Gospel, let him give thanks to GOD, and know that he is a theologian.

Moreover, from this a judgment can be made concerning the doctrine of the Jesuits, who, according to Bellarmine, posit at least two distinctions between the Law and the Gospel: from which, however, many others follow. For first he writes; book 4 on Justification, chap. 3, page 1177. That this is the difference between the Law and the Gospel, which is between an inchoate and a perfect doctrine: for the Gospel is contained in the Law, as a tree is contained in a seed. Hence he infers that the Old Testament indeed clearly teaches the unity of God: but that it rather adumbrates than expresses the Trinity of persons and the Incarnation of the Word only obscurely and imperfectly. Then that the Law and the Prophets expressly promise temporal goods: but the kingdom of heaven figuratively: whereas Christ and the Apostles manifestly promise the kingdom of heaven and eternal life. Finally, that the moral laws are the same in the Law and the Gospel.

Latin:

QUantum referat, Verbum Dei ὀρθοτομεῖν, ita ut Lex intra suos cancellos se contineat, neque vel Evangelij, vel Legis termini, per Confusionem quandam transferantur, ostendunt certamina illa, quæ viventibus adhuc Apostolis, ab ijs mota sunt, qui Legis Zelo se flagrare dictitantes, Evangelium in Legem transformabant

Quod ipsum damnum hodiéque datur in Ecclesia Dei, eandem duarum istarum partium Doctrinæ Cœlestis μεταμόρφωσιν malè feriatis Jesuvvitis proponentibus & defendentibus: uti ex subseq. Articulo de Justificatione clariùs patebit. Hoc autem loco diligenter admodùm notanda veniunt ea discrimina, quæ Legi & Evangelio invicem intercedere, Theologi quidam accuratiores ex Scripturis deprehenderunt: & quidem sex potissimùm.

PRIMUM enim differunt Notitiæ sive cognitionis modo: Nam Lex moralis sive Decalogus aliquo modo naturaliter notus est hominibus, quippè mentibus ipsorum insitus atque insculptus. Rom. 2, 15. Evangelij verò planè diversa est ratio: Siquidem extra revelationem de eo nihil quicquam Homini constare poterat: Sed necessum erat, ut Filius, qui est in sinu patris, illud nobis enarraret Joh. 1, 18. Quàm ipsam ob causam Evangelium definitur ab Apostolo mysterium ab æternis temporibus tacitum, sive absconditum in Deo, jam indè à seculis. Rom. 16, 25. Eph. 3, 9. Col. 1, 26.

Deindè differunt objecto Personarum : Lex enim est proponenda impijs, securis pervicacibus, & alijs sceleratis ac præfractis peccatoribus, quorum Catalogum benè longum pertexuit Apostolus 1. Tim. 1, 9. 10. & 11. Scio quod lex justo non est posita: sed legis contemtoribus, & ijs, qui subjici nolunt, impijs & peccatoribus, nefarijs & profanis, patricidis & matricidis, homicidis, masculorum concubitoribus, plagiarijs & mendacibus, perjuris, & si quid aliud est, quod sanæ doctrinæ sit oppositum. Evangelium verò annunciandum est illis, qui jam laborant & onerati sunt, & qui refocillatione opus habent, uti loquitur Christus Matth. 11. hoc est, qui jam seriò dolent de admissis peccatis, & sensu iræ divinæ consternati, cum Davide ingemiscunt: Cor contritum & humiliatum Deus ne despicias Psal. 51.

Tertiò differunt objecto rerum: Lex enim urget Justitiam operum secundùm illud: Qui fecerit hæc vivet in eis Rom. 10, 5. Evangelium verò urget Justitiam Fidei, resultantem ex gratuita remissione & propter meritum Christi, fide apprehensum. De qua Apostolus Rom. 4, 15. Non operanti, credenti autem in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur fides ad justitiam. Quantum ergò à se distant meritorium & gratuitum: tantum quoque invicem differunt Lex & Evangelium, neque hoc respectu unquàm coalescere possunt. Nam simul, ratione ejusdem uno eodemque modo stare nunquàm possunt, quin manifestam contradictionem implicent : quemadmodum Apostolus egregiè id explicat, Rom. 11, 6. Si, inquiens, per Gratiam Iustitia obtingit, non jam ex operibus: alioquin gratia jam non est gratia: Sin ex operibus, jam non est ex gratia: alioquin opus jam non est opus.

Quartò differunt Promissionum Formâ: Lex enim habet promissiones ratione nostri purè meritorias, & ex debito compensatorias: Nam is demum vitam æternam ex Lege consequitur, qui fecerit omnia, quæ scripta sunt in ea Levit. 18, 5. Deut. 30, 15. & seqq. Evangelium verò habet promissiones respectu nostri merè gratuitas & purè donativas, secundùm illud Ephes. 2, 8. Gratia estis salvati per fidem, & hoc non ex vobis: Dei enim donatio sive δῶρον, est Et Rom. 4, 16. Ideò ex fide, ut secundum gratiam firma sit promissio omni semini.

Quintò differunt proprijs & toto genere discrepantibus officijs: Lex enim mandat, minatur, terret, damnat, occidit. Rom. 3, 20. & cap. 4, 15. 2. Cor. 3, 6. Evangelium verò erigit, solatur, absolvit, vivificat & exhilarat conscientiam, Iesaiæ 61, 2. & 3. Luc. 4, 18. Rom. 1, 16.

Tandem differunt etiam Effectu, quoad nos: Lex enim etsi in se bona est & sancta Rom. 7, 12. & si quis eam servaret, utique Justitiam quoque ipli coram Deo tribueret: tamen meram ἀμηχανίαν, sive ut Apostolus loquitur, meram ἀδυναμίαν obtinet: & ad Effectum illum suum nunquàm potest pertingere: Siquidem infirmatur per carnem, hoc est, Naturæ nostræ horrenda corruptio, conditionem illam Legis promissioni additam, penitùs debilitat & infringit Rom. 8, 3. Gal. 3. 21. ut impossibile sit Legi quempiam salvare. Evangelium verò finem suum assequitur, quia in eo revelatur Justitia sine Lege Rom 1, 17. & cap. 3, 21. Quâ de re præclarè disserit Apostolus Rom. 9, 30. 31. 32. Gentes quæ non sectabantur Iustitiam, assecuti sunt Iustitiam: Iustitiam autem eam, quæ est ex fide: Israel verò, qui sectabatur Legem Iustitiæ, ad legem justitiæ non pervenit: Quare? Quia non ex fide, sed ex operibus legis eam quæsivit. Quô pertinent classica etiam illa loca Rom. 10, 3. ignorantes justitiam Dei, & suam quærentes statuere, justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti: Finis enim legis Christus est, ad Justitiam omni CREDENTI. Et Gal. 3, 10. Quicunque ex operibus Legis sunt, sub maledictione sunt: Scriptum est enim: Maledictus est omnis, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, ut faciat ea. Quoniam autem nemo in Lege justificatur apud Deum, manifestum est, quia Justus ex fide vivet. Lex autem non est ex fide: sed qui fecerit ea, vivet in illis.

Notis istis differentiarum probè observatis, invictè constat, duo hæc doctrinarum genera, tam procul à se mutuò distare, quàm procul à se invicem distant Cœlum & terra, Lux & tenebræ, dies & nox, uti alicubi Lutherus noster loquitur; imò subijcit etiam, utinam adhuc longius ea distinguere possemus.

Neque verò Antinomorum furori hinc quicquam accedit patrocinij, qui ex istis differentijs, manifestam ἀντίφασιν sive contradictionis pugnam eliciebant, ita ut in Ecclesia

Dei simul atraq; Doctrina locum habere haud possit: sed Lex simpliciter ex agro & finibus Ecclesiæ ad curiam, imò ad patibulum relegari debeat. Tale enim quid neque Luthero in mentem venit, neque à nobis asseritur. Virossissimè autem Antinomi Diversa statuunt esse Contradictoria: Lex enim & Evangelium sibi invicem opponuntur quidem ut Diversa: sed non ut Contradictoria. Hinc Apostolus ipse Gal. 3. v. 21. disertè scribit: Lex non adversatur promissionibus Evangelij, & Rom. 3, 31. Legem 8 καταργ̃ε̃- μεν non evacuamus vel irritam reddimus per fidem: sed stabilimus.

nis nostræ, se habent? 2. Falsum est, Legem & Prophetas tantùm polliceri expressè bona temporalia. Mendacii Jesuvvitam arguit Moses Deut. 30, 19: Testes, inquiens, hodiè invoco Cælum & Terram, quòd proposuerim vobis hodiè vitam & mortem: benedictionem & maledictionem, &c. Tertiò Mendacium est, Evangelium pròut Legi opponitur, Objecti loco respicere Leges morales: uti jam supra ostensum.

ALTERUM discrimen ex annexis mutuatur Jesuvvita, ubi multa commemorat, quæ nihil prorsus ad rem faciunt: pauca, quæ scopum Controversiæ attingunt: Unum denique quod propriè huc pertinet: contendens, Evangelium æquè atque Legem versari propriè circa comminationes & terrores Legis: sic demonstraturus, Evangelium quoque urgere necessitatem operum, in negocio Justificationis, lib. 4. cap. 4. Verùm de hoc commento partim Articulo præcedente proximo fuit disputatum: partim in subsequente proximo, ex professo nobis dispiciendum fuerit. Hoc loco illud tantùm sub observationem venit, quòd Scriptura Sacra Mosen & Christum, & consequenter Legem & Evangelium ita disterminat, ut sub unum îdemque doctrinæ genus referri non possint. Johannes certò Legem asserit per Mosen datam esse Job. 1, 17. Sic Apostolus attestatur, HUNC sermonem esse certum, dignumquè, quem modis omnibus amplectamur, quòd Christus venit in mundum, non ut Leges operum ferret, sed ut peccatores salvos faceret, 1.Timoth. 1, 15. Detestanda proindè vox est Jesuwitarum Coloniensium asserentium, Misericordiam illam, quam Evangelium propriè celebrat, & in quâ omnium nostrûm salus ac vita consistit, esse hanc, quòd Deus Legi Mosis, in Evangelio hanc adjecit promissionem: Qui fecerit hæc, vivet in eis: Summa enim, inquiunt, DEI misericordia est, quòd rectè operantibus vitam æternam promittit, pag. 26. censuræ. Hoc nimirùm est, Naturam & Essentiam Evangelii sacrilegè negare, & propriam ejus formam penitùs subruere & evertere: quæ qualis sit, Tertia jam Quæstio ex professo expēdiet.

Nam beneficia Christi, quæ in Evangelio nobis offeruntur, nihil sunt aliud, quàm Satisfactio Legi debita. Christus enim, de quo Evangelium concionatur, ideò Legi factus est subditus, Galat. 4, 4. ut Justitia Legis impleretur in nobis, (sed non à nobis) Rom. 8, 4. Ita, ut Justitia Legis diversa simul sit, atque eadem. Diversa quidem in nobis, & respectu nostri: Nam non ex Lege nobis est, Phil. 3, 9. hoc est, nostra observatione Legis non est acquisita. Eadem tamen rursus est in Christo, & respectu Christi, qui Legi consummatam præstitit obedientiam. Hinc rectè pronunciavit idem Lutherus noster, Legem & Evangelium, in cujusque Christiani corde debere esse conjunctissima. Commentario ad cap. 3. Epistolæ ad Galat.

Et hæc quidem Orthodoxa est doctrina nostra, de Discrimine Legis & Evangelij, non aliundè, quàm ex perspicuis Scripturarum testimoniis hausta & extructa: de qua rursum B. Lutherus noster ad cap. 2. Galat. Qui benè novit discernere Legem ab Evangelio, is gratias agat DEO, & sciat se esse Theologum.

Potest autem hinc judicium fieri de doctrina Jesuvvitarum, qui, interprete Bellarmino, duo saltem ponunt discrimina Legis & Evangelii: ex quibus tamen multa alia consequantur. Primùm enim scribit; l. 4. de Justif. cap. 3. pag. 1177. Id, illud interesse inter Legem & Evangelium, quod inter doctrinam inchoatam & perfectam: Contineri enim Evangelium in Lege, uti arbor continetur in semine. Hinc infert, Vetus Testamentum unitatem quidem Dei manifestè docere: Trinitatem verò personarum, & Incarnationem Verbi non nisi obscurè & imperfectè adumbrare potiùs, quàm exprimere. Deindè Legem & Prophetas polliceri expressè bona temporalia: figuratè autem regnum Cælorum: Christum verò & Apostolos manifestè regnum Cælorum & vitam ætetnam polliceri. Tandem Leges Morales easdem esse in Lege & Evangelio.


### Question III. or Controversy On the Evangelical Promises

The formal cause of the Gospel properly so called, consists in promises that are merely gratuitous and unmerited: and therefore not limited by any merit of works at all, as the Papists contend: but neither are they simply absolute, as the Calvinists dream: But determined by the condition of faith in Christ, which indeed is in a certain way opposed to these promises alternately.

This is indeed to trifle rather than to dispute about the Articles of faith. For 1. the question is not about the mode of cognition, such as it happens to men under the Law and the Gospel, but about the proper office of each, and how these two stand toward each other, and especially in the business of salvation and Justification

Three things, however, are especially wont to come into controversy regarding these promises. 1. Their nature or essence. 2. Their scope or breadth. 3. Their quality or determination.

I. We have just now said that the nature and essence of these promises is that they are purely gratuitous with respect to us, that is, not on account of any dignity, intention, work, merit, or any other disposition of ours, do they promise us the grace and mercy of God, and the remission of all sins, through and on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith. Therefore, Evangelical promises differ in this respect from Legal promises, which indeed also promise these spiritual goods, but under the condition of our merits, and indeed of most absolute obedience performed to divine commands: as was shown in the immediately preceding question. Hence the Apostle, intending to distinguish Evangelical promises from Legal ones, throughout his Epistles, scarcely deigns to call the Law by the term 'promise': but for the most part he uses the word 'promise' absolutely, understanding no others than the promises of the Gospel: thus not obscurely implying that that promise is truly and properly so called, which with respect to us is purely and simply gratuitous, unowed, and spontaneous, and does not partake of anything from the condition of a legal promise. As Rom. 4:13 and 14: 'The promise to Abraham did not come through the Law, but through the righteousness of faith.' And Gal. 3:18: 'If the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from promise: but God gave it to Abraham through promise.'

Moreover, it deserves observation that we said Evangelical promises are purely gratuitous, not absolutely and simply, but only with respect to us. Therefore, just as they exclude all merit on our part, so on the part of God they include: 1. That movement of divine mercy. 2. The most absolute merit of Christ the Savior. Therefore, if the parts of God the Father and of Christ the Mediator are considered, nothing is truly less gratuitous than the acquisition of eternal salvation: for it consists both of the most perfect active obedience performed to the law by Christ, and of his passive obedience, or his precious blood, as Scripture attests in Isa. 43:24: 'You have made me serve in your sins, you have provided me labor in your iniquities,' 1 Cor. 6:20: 'You were bought with a great price,' 1 Pet. 1:19. You were redeemed not with corruptible gold and silver, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.

Hence the immovable certainty and unshaken firmness of our salvation is evident: For although it is so ordered in human affairs that, on account of the inconstancy and mutability of human wills, nothing is more uncertain or unstable than if one wishes to entrust oneself to the promises of others, especially if no consideration of debt, merit, or obligation intervenes: yet with respect to God we most rightly conclude that the anchor of our faith, hope,

and salvation stands immovable, because God has determined to save us out of grace, and by no merit of ours. For since God is an agent who is indeed most free, but yet subject to absolutely no mutability: and indeed has holily testified in His word to this His will of acting, concerning receiving, justifying, and saving believers, and indeed freely, without any merit of their own: it is necessary that heaven and earth should collapse sooner than even one iota of this will of His should be changed. Hence the Apostle concludes by the same reasoning: Therefore salvation is by mere grace, so that the promise may be firm, ratified, and immovable to all the seed, Rom. 4:16. Hence Bernard elegantly infers, in his Commentary on Psalm 31. In whose hands, he says, does the certainty of our salvation rest more safely than in those which created heaven and earth: in those which can never be shortened: in those, finally, which abound with the bowels of mercy, nor are there lacking openings through which they flow.

The second thing that comes into controversy regarding these Evangelical promises is concerning their scope or breadth: namely, whether they are universal or indeed particular. We, with Scripture, affirm that they are merely universal, and extend themselves to the whole world or the breadth of the entire human race: without any exception or distinction of nations, or ranks, or ages. For thus do the Scriptures preach concerning the love of God: concerning the work of redemption, consummated through Christ, and concerning the means of Evangelical vocation, that in all these works they clearly attest that not even a single individual has been neglected or passed over: as Matt. 11:28, and ch. 28:19, Mark 16:15, John 1:29, and ch. 3:16, 1 Tim. 2:4, 2 Pet. 3:9, 1 John 2:2.

Away, therefore, with those evasions of the Calvinists, by which they restrict that universality, either to the universality of the elect: or they take 'world' for the better part of the world, or they understand that universality to be taken not of individuals of the kinds, but of the kinds of individuals. For although the universality of the elect and believers is not excluded by these promises: yet this stricter universality does not take away that general one, which is proper to Evangelical promises. But concerning this controversy, we are to have a discussion expressly in the Article on Predestination.

The third member remains, in which the question is asked concerning the quality of this very Universality: whether it is simple and absolute, or indeed ordered and determined? There are those who deny that the Evangelical promises are conditional, and for this reason they think they can be distinguished from the Legal promises: yet this is not simply true concerning every condition, but only in a certain respect, namely concerning that species of condition which is proper to the Law, and includes a regard for merit or human work.

Therefore it is more correctly answered that the Evangelical promises are not simply and absolutely universal: for thus no mortal would perish: indeed, there would not even be any need for faith in Christ the Mediator: but that they are limited by a certain condition of their own, namely, faith in CHRIST the Mediator. It must be observed, however, that this answer is true concerning those promises which embrace the entire act of our salvation: in which the condition of faith is always to be understood, even if it is not always found explicitly added, as in John 3:16, Acts 10:43, Galatians 3:14.

But besides these promises there are also others, which do not define the whole complex of our salvation: but only a part of it, and describe either the universal love of GOD and His Φιλανθρωπία (philanthropy) toward the human race: or the universal merit of Christ, separately in such a way that no respect is involved of that saving application which occurs through faith. These promises are indeed simply universal, and do not admit any determination or limitation by reason of themselves.

But furthermore it is asked: Do those former promises not cease to be universal as soon as the condition of faith is added? For because this faith is not of all: certainly those promises do not seem to be universal. But it is answered negatively through a distinction between restriction and limitation, or determination or even modification. For every restriction respects quantity, and makes a particular out of a universal: as when I say, according to the opinion of the Calvinists, GOD wills all to be saved, except those for whom Christ did not die. Here this restriction of the predicate causes the universal subject in reality not to be universal but particular. But limitation or determination or modification respects quality only, as when Christ says in John 3:16. So GOD loved the world, that everyone who believes in the Son might not perish: Here this determination of the predicate does not restrict the universal subject, but only limits or modifies it, that is, it shows the manner how GOD wills all men whatsoever to be saved, namely, through faith in the Son. For the same GOD, who wills all men to be saved, also wills all to conceive faith through the word, and to believe in CHRIST, as is shown more fully elsewhere.

From this, however, it becomes clear: 1. How this condition of faith stands, namely, that it does not obtain the respect of a work, or of an efficient or assisting cause: or even of a cooperating one: much less of any merit, which kind of affection legal promises obtain: but that it only has the nature of a mode and instrument by which the universal promise of the Gospel is received. For the promise and faith are correlatively opposed to each other: so that the doctrine of the Gospel is designated by the Holy Spirit Himself as the word of faith, likewise the preaching of faith, Romans 10:8, Galatians 3:2, 1 Timothy 4:6.

It is clear then from this also what must be determined concerning the vain talk of Huber, who contends that the Evangelical promises, each and all, are simply universal, and that there is no promise from GOD which concerns ONLY BELIEVERS, and excludes unbelievers. For if he himself in his response to the censure of the Tübingen theologians, page 4: Although the passages cited by them make mention of faith, yet the promises considered in themselves, and as they emanate from the counsel and heart of GOD, are not particular: but are extended to ALL MEN, with respect to the Decree or Counsel of GOD: they become particular only in effect, not by reason of the Counsel and purpose. Which vain talk being granted, three absurdities follow, fighting against the analogy of faith.

1. That GOD from all eternity has made no distinction between believers and unbelievers: but has held all indiscriminately in equal estimation and number.

2. That by reason of the eternal decree and counsel of God, eternal life pertains also to the impenitent. Which two flowers of thought fight diametrically against the immutable justice of GOD.

3. That either false, or certainly contradictorily opposed to that former eternal counsel of GOD, is some later decree: such as that of Mark 16:16: He who believes will be saved: he who does not believe will be condemned. Which calls the truth of GOD into doubt. But concerning these, in their own place, σὺν θεῷ (with God) in the Article of Predestination, we shall have to examine expressly.

Latin:

CAusa formalis Evangelii propriè sic dicti, consistit in promissionibus merè gratuitis & immeritis: ac proindè nullo prorsus operum merito limitatis, uti Pontificii contendunt: sed neque simpliciter etiam absolutis, uti Calviniâni somniant: Verùm Fidei in Christum conditione determinatis, quippè quæ promissionibus hisce ἐνάλλαξ quodammodo est opposita.

Hoc nimirùm est de Articulis fidei nugari potiùs, quàm disputare. Nam 1. non quæritur de cognitionis modo, qualis sub Lege & Evangelio hominibus obtingat, sed de proprio cujuslibet officio, & quomodo hæc duo ad se mutuò, & cumprimis in negotio salutis, atque Justificatio-

Tria autem potissimùm circa promissiones hasce in Controversiam venire solent. 1. Natura earum sive Essentia. 2. Complexus sive latitudo. 3. Qualitas sive determinatio.

I. Naturam & Essentiam quasi istarum promissionum, jam modò diximus esse eam, quòd sint purè gratuitæ, respectu nostri, hoc est, non propter ullam nostram dignitatem, intentionem, opus, meritum aut quamcunq; aliam dispositionem, nobis promittant Gratiam & Misericordiam DEI, omniumque peccatorum Remissionem, per & propter meritum CHRISTI, fide apprehensum. Differunt proindè hac ratione Promissiones Evangelicæ δις δια πασῶν a promissionibus Legalibus, quæ quidem spiritualia etiam isthæc bona promittunt, sed sub conditione nostrorum meritorum, & quidem absolutissimæ obedientiæ mandatis divinis præstitæ: uti Quæstione præcedente proxima est ostensum. Hinc D. Apostolus promissiones Evangelicas à Legalibus distincturus, passim suis in Epistolis, Legem vix dignatur vocabulo Promissionis: sed plerunque promissionis vocem absolutè ponit, nullas alias, quàm Evangelii promissiones intelligens: sic haud obscurè innuens, eam demùm promissionem verè ac propriè sic appellari, quæ ratione nostri purè ac simpliciter est gratuita, indebita, ultronea neque de conditione legalis promissionis quicquam participat. Ut Rom. 4, 13. & 14. Non per Legem promissio Abrahæ obtigit, sed per Justitiam fidei. Et Galat. 3, 18. Si ex Lege est hæreditas, jam non ex promissione: Abrahæ autem per promissionem donavit DEUS.

Cæterùm observationem meretur, quòd promissiones Evangelicas purè gratuitas esse diximus, non absolutè & simpliciter, sed tantùm respectu nostri. Quemadmodum ergò ex excludunt ex nostra parte omne meritum, sic ex parte DEI includunt. 1. Motum illum misericordiæ divinæ. 2. Meritum absolutissimum CHRISTI Servatoris. Proindè sitùm DEI Patris, tùm CHRISTI Mediatoris partes spectentur, nihil profectò minùs est gratuitum, quàm æternæ salutis acquisitio: quippè quæ constat tùm perfectissimâ obedientiâ activâ à Christo legi præstitâ: tùm obedientiâ ipsius passivâ, sive pretioso ipsius sanguine, sic attestante Scripturâ Jes. 43, 24. Servire me fecisti in peccatis tuis, præbuisti mihi laborem in iniquitatibus tuis, 1. Cor. 6, 20. Emti estis pretio magno. 1. Pet. 1, 19. Redemti estis non corruptibili auro & argento, sed pretioso sanguine Christi, tanquàm agni immaculati & incontaminati.

Patet hinc salutis nostræ immota certitudo & inconcussa firmitas: Etsi enim in humanis ita comparatum est, ut propter inconstantiam ac mutabilitatem voluntatum humanarum nihil sit incertius aut instabilius, quàm si quis aliorum promissionibus se committere velit, præsertim si nulla debiti, meriti aut obligationis ratio interveniat: tamen respectu DEI rectissimè concludimus, vel ideò immotam stare fidei, spei

& salutis nostræ anchoram, quia DEUS ex gratiâ, & nullo nostro merito nos salvare constituerit. Nam cùm DEUS agens sit liberrimum quidem, sed tamen mutabilitati prorsus nulli obnoxium: & verò hanc suam agendi voluntatem, de recipiendis, justificandis & salvandis credentibus, & quidem gratis, sine ullo ipsorum merito, in verbo suo sanctè testatus sit: citiùs profectò Cœlum & terra collabantur necesse est, quàm vel unus apex de hac ipsius voluntate mutetur. Hinc Apostolus pari ratione concludit: Ideò ex merâ gratia esse salutem, ut firma, rata atque immota sit promissio omni semini, Rom. 4, 16. Hinc eleganter Bernhardus infert, Commentario in Psalmum 31. In quibus, inquiens, manibus salutis nostræ certitudo tutiùs consistat, quam in ijs, quæ Cœlum & terram condiderunt: in ijs, quæ nunquam abbreviari possunt: in ijs denique quæ affluunt misericordiæ visceribus, nec desunt foramina, per quæ fluunt.

ALTERUM, quod circa promissiones istas Evangelicas in Controversiam venit, est de Complexu sive latitudine earum: Utrum nimirum sint Universales an verò particulares. Nos cum Scriptura affirmamus, merè Universales eas esse, & ad totum mundum sive universi generis humani latitudinem se extendere: sine ulla vel gentium, vel ordinum, vel ætatum exceptione aut distinctione. Sic enim Scripturæ de Dilectione DEI: de redemtionis opere, per CHRISTUM consummato, de vocationis Evangelicæ mediis concionantur, ut in istis operibus omnibus, ne unicum quidem Individuum neglectum aut præteritum fuisse liquidò attestentur: ut Matth. 11,28. & cap. 28, 19. Marci 16. 15. Johan. 1, 29. & cap. 3, 16. 1. Timoth. 2, 4. 2. Pet. 3, 9. 1. Johan. 2, 2.

Facessant proinde elusiones illæ Calvinianorum, quibus Universalitatem illam restringunt, vel ad Universalitatem Electorum: vel Mundum pro meliori mundi parte accipiunt vel non de singulis generum, sed de generibus singulorum, Universalitatem istam accipi intelligunt. Nam licet Electorum & Credentium Universalitas ab his promissionibus non excludatur: strictior tamen hæc Universalitas generalem illam, & promissionum Evangelicarum propriam, non tollit. Verùm de hac Controversia in Articulo de Prædestinatione nobis ex professo futura est disputatio.

Restat membrum tertium, quo quæritur, de hujus ipsius Universalitatis Qualitate: An simplex & absoluta ea sit, an verò ordinata & determinata? Sunt, qui negant promissiones Evangelicas esse conditionales, & hac ratione eas à promissionibus Legalibus distingui posse existimant: tamen non simpliciter hoc verum est, de omni conditione: sed tantùm secundùm Quid, nempè de ea Conditionis specie, quæ est Legis propria, & meriti sive operis humani respectum includit.

Proindè rectius respondetur, Promissiones Evangelicas non esse simpliciter & absolutè universales: Sic enim nemo mortalium periret: imò ne quidem ulla Fide in Christum Mediatorem opus esset: sed esse sua quadam conditione limitatas, nempè ad Fidem in CHRISTUM Mediatorem. Observandum tamen, Responsionem hanc veram esse de illis promissionibus, quæ integrum salutis nostræ actum complectuntur: in quibus semper Conditio Fidei est intelligenda, sivel maximè non semper explicitè ea adjecta reperiatur, ut Joh. 3. 16. Actor. 10. 43. Gal. 3, 44.

Sunt autem præter has promissiones etiam aliæ, quæ non totum salutis nostræ complexum definiunt: sed ejus duntaxat partem, & vel universalem DEI dilectionem, & Φιλανθρωπίαν erga genus humanum: vel universale Christi meritum, seorsim ita describunt, ut nullus respectus involvatur salutaris illius applicationis, quæ fit per fidem. Hæ sanè promissiones simpliciter sunt universales, neque ullam determinationem aut limitationem ratione sui admittunt.

Sed porrò quæritur: An priores illæ promifsiones non desinant esse universales, quamprimùm Fidei conditio additur? Quia enim hæc Fides non est omnium: utique nec promissiones illæ videntur esse Universales. Verùm negatè respondetur per distinctionem inter Restrictionem & Limitationem, sive determinationem vel etiam modificationem.
