Restrictio enim omnis Quantitatem respicit, & ex Universali facit particulare: ut quando dico ex sententia Calvinianorum, DEUS vult omnes salvos, exceptis ijs, pro quibus Christus non est mortuus. Hîc restrictio hæc prædicati efficit, ut Subjectum Universale revera non sit Universale sed particulare. Cæterùm limitatio sive determinatio aut modificatio Qualitatem tantùm respicit, ut quando Christus inquit Johan. 3, 16. Sic DEUS dilexit mundum, ut omnis, qui credit in Filium non pereat: Hîc Determinatio hæc prædicati, non restringit Subjectum Universale, sed limitat tantùm sive modificat, hoc est, modum oftendit, quomodo DEUS velit omnes omninò homines salvos, nempè per fidem in Filium. Nam idem DEUS, qui omnes homines vult salvos, vult etiam omnes per verbum concipere Fidem, & credere in CHRISTUM, uti alibi fusiùs oftenditur.

Patescit autem hinc: 1. Quomodo sese habeat conditio hæc Fidei, nempe quòd non obtineat respectum operis, vel causæ efficientis aut adjuvantis: vel etiam cooperantis: nedùm meriti alicujus, qualem affectionem obtinent promissiones Legales: sed quòd tantùm rationem habeat modi & organi, quo universalis promifsio Evangelii accipitur. Nam promissio & Fides correlativè sibi invicem opponuntur: ita ut doctrina Evangelii ab ipso Spiritu sancto indigitetur Verbum fidei, item prædicatio fidei, Roman. 10, 8. Galat. 3, 2. 1. Timoth. 4, 6.

Patet deindè hinc etiam, quid statuendum de Matæologia Huberi contendētis, Promissiones Evangelicas singulas & universas esse simpliciter Universales, neque ullam esse promissionem ex DEO, quæ SOLOS CREDENTES concernat, & incredulos excludat. Si enim ipse in responso ad censuram Tübingensium pag. 4. Quanquam loci ab ipsos citati, fidei faciunt mentionem, non tamen promissiones in sese consideratæ, & sicut emanant ex consilio & pectore DEI, sunt particulares: sed extenduntur ad OMNES HOMINES, respectu Decreti vel Consilij DEI: fiuntẽ; effectus tantùm, non ratione Consilij & propositi, particulares. Qua Matæologia concessa, Tria sequuntur absurda, contra Analogiam fidei pugnantia.

1. Quòd DEUS jam indè ab omni æternitate nullum fecerit discrimen inter Credentes & Incredulos: sed pari censu numeroq̃ omnes promescuè habuerit.

2. Quòd ratione æterni Decreti & Consilij Dei, vita æterna ad impœnitentes quoque pertineat. Qui uterque flosculus cum immutabili DEI justitia è diametro pugnat.

3. Quòd vel falsum, vel certè priori illi æterno Consilio DEI, contradictoriè sit oppositum posterius aliquod Decretum: Quale est illud Marci 16, 16. Qui crediderit salvus erit: qui non crediderit, condemnabitur. Id quòd veritatem DEI in dubium vocat. Sed de his suo loco, σὺν θεῷ in Articulo Prædestinationis, nobis ex professo dispiciendum fuerit.


## 15 On the Justification of sinful Man before God: Against the Papists and the more recent Photinians


### Disposition of the Philippic Treatise: and the oikonomia of our future Treatise

Our author institutes a treatment of this article that is indeed sufficiently prolix and accurate, but accommodated more to the ecclesiastical or practical forum than to the academic or theoretical, having instituted a consideration of that one question alone which was then being agitated most of all: Namely, whether a man is justified before GOD from works, or indeed by faith alone? The latter part of which question the Author pursues and corroborates affirmatively, and indeed with a fourfold kind of arguments.

For first he shows that the term Justification can have no other than a forensic meaning in this article: and therefore signifies nothing else than a gratuitous absolution from sins.

Then, however, he explains at length the Apostolic phrase, which asserts that a man is justified by faith without the works of the Law, and elicits and confirms its genuine sense, both from the Greek word πίστεως, and from the Scriptures themselves, and from Orthodox Antiquity.

Thirdly, he enters into a dispute against the Scholastics concerning the word Grace: and demonstrates from the Sacred Scriptures that in this Article it signifies nothing else than the gratuitous mercy of GOD. Finally, he asserts and corroborates the entire doctrine concerning the gratuitous Justification of a sinful man before GOD, quite vigorously, from the Pauline disputations of the Epistle to the Romans: at the same time he also explains and confirms clearly and solidly what the true use of the Exclusive Particles is in this matter.

And indeed this whole Philippean Treatise is so arranged that it is by no means possible to find what might be desired in it regarding ὀρθοδοξίαν. Perhaps it has one bit of inconvenience, that toward the end of his Treatise the Author judges that the Article concerning eternal Predestination should be entirely removed from the present dispute. If the Author understood this as instituting a distinct treatment of each Article, we certainly support him willingly: but if he was of the opinion—which his words show not obscurely that he indeed was—as if the Article of Predestination brings some obscurity to the business of Justification: or infringes upon the Universal Evangelical promises: or finally renders the πληροφορίαν of faith more languid: then we frankly profess that we feel differently from Philippus. Where, however, we do not deny that our Author also easily deserves pardon. For, such was the condition of those times, most theologians thought that the Decree of Predestination was more obscure, and joined with some secret or hidden will of GOD.

Now, however, since by the benefit of GOD, in this our time, this opinion has been removed from the minds of our people: and it is clearer than the midday sun from the Scriptures that the Decree of Predestination is not one thing or different, and the Decree of Justification another: but that one and the same will of GOD concerning the salvation of men is comprised in both: nay, that the causes of both are clearly the same: and that these two Articles do not differ from each other otherwise than as a Decree and the execution of a Decree: certainly there is no reason why we should fear anything from the Article of Predestination in the present business of Justification: but rather we should maintain that neither can be rightly asserted and solidly defended in the conflict of dispute without the other: which is easily understood by those who have perceived a not-at-all common taste of both controversies.

However, no matter how Orthodox and accurate the Philippean Treatise may be: the variation of that State of the Controversy, which today exists for us especially with the Jesuits, makes it so that we do not insist upon his footsteps in all things. For that is not directly controverted between us and the Romanists today, as it was in the time of Philippus: Whether a man is justified before GOD by works? For the Jesuits themselves today notice that a simple Affirmative is too crude, and ἀντιφατικῶς opposed to the Sacred letters. Therefore, having changed their attire, that is, having varied the State of the Controversy, they descend into the arena: and partly they themselves deny that a man is justified by Works in any way in the sight of GOD, if, that is, you understand that Justification which they call First, and they grant that it is accomplished by faith alone: but partly they contend that this first Justification is finally accomplished and absolved by works: so that a man can be justified before GOD neither by faith alone: nor by Works alone: but by Faith and Works: or as they are accustomed to speak, by Faith and Charity: that is, by formed faith. And this State of the Controversy will be especially set before us in our future Treatise.

Moreover, since besides the Jesuits, that infernal Dragon the Devil has thrust another kind of heretics, and indeed a far most pestilent one, onto the stage of the Church, namely the more recent Photinians, who through Poland and other places, strive to wickedly defile the most holy Deposit of purer doctrine concerning our Justification, nay, a golden κειμήλιον as it were, to agitate it with most atrocious blasphemies, and finally to attack, nay, to storm and all but entirely excise it with various weapons, sought both from Sacred Scripture, and from the Analogy of Faith, and from reason: certainly the very salvation of the Church of GOD, nay, the purity of the Christian Religion seems to demand that it be shown with what weapons the wicked attempts of these men can and ought to be intercepted, overturned, and entirely suppressed: and that all the more accurately: by how much greater effort these ill-disposed men strive to disseminate this virus of theirs through our Germany, and especially through this very Academy of ours.

Therefore, may CHRIST the Savior command that which is happy and auspicious, and useful and salutary to the Church of GOD: we divide the entire treatment of this Article into two General Controversies: The former of which is of those more recent Arians, or rather Photinians: The latter of the Romanists,

Latin:

Articuli hujus Tractationem satis quidem prolixam & accuratam, sed Ecclesiastico magis sive Practico, quàm Academico sive Theoretico foro accommodatam, Autor noster instituit, illius solius Quæstionis, quæ tum vel maximè agitabatur, instituta consideratione: Nùm videlicet Homo ex operibus, an verò sola fide justificetur coram DEO? Cujus Quæstionis membrum posterius Affirmatè, & quidem quadruplici argumentorum genere Autor persequitur & corroborat.

Primùm enim ostendit, vocabulum Justificationis non nisi forensem significationem hoc in articulo obtinere posse: ac proindè nihil aliud, quàm gratuitam absolutionem à peccatis, significare.

Deindè verò Phrasin Apostolicam, quæ Fide sine operibus Legis Hominem justificari afserit, prolixè explicat, & genuinum ejus sensum, tùm ex Græco vocabulo πίστεως, tùm ex Scripturis ipsis, tùm ex Orthodoxa Antiquitate eruit & confirmat.

Tertiò, disputationem ingreditur contra Scholasticos, de vocabulo Gratiæ: illudq́; hoc in Articulo nihil aliud, quàm gratuitam DEI misericordiam significare, ex Sacris demonstrat. Tandem universam doctrinam de gratuita Justificatione Hominis peccatoris coram DEO, ex disputationibus Paulinis Epistolæ ad Romanos, satis nervosè asserit, & corroborat: simul etiam, quis verus sit Particularum Exclusivarum, hoc in negotio, usus, perspicuè solidèque explicat & confirmat.

Et profectò tota hæc Tractatio Philippea ita est comparata, ut quidnam in ea, quoad ὀρθοδοξίαν desiderari possit, minimè invenire liceat. Unum fortassis illud incommoditatis aliquid habet, quòd sub finem Tractationis suæ censet Autor, Articulum de æterna Prædestinatione, à præsente disputatione penitùs esse semovendum. Quod, si de distincta utriusq; Articuli Tractatione instituenda intellexit Autor, ultrò sanè ipsi suffragamur: Sin verò in ea fuit sententiâ, in qua sanè ipsum fuisse, verba ipsius haud obscurè ostendunt, ac si Articulus Prædestinationis obscuritatis aliquid Justificationis negocio inferat: vel promissiones Universales Evangelicas infringat: vel denique πληροφορίαν Fidei, languidiorem reddat: tùm sanè diversum nos à Philippo sentire, ingenuè profitemur. Ubi tamen Autorem etiam nostrum veniam facilè mereri, haud inficiamur. Nam, quæ illorum temporum erat conditio, pleriq; Theologi opinabantur, Prædestinationis Decretum esse obscurius, & cum arcana aliqua, sive abscondita DEI voluntate conjunctum.

Jam verò, cùm DEI beneficio, nostro hoc tempore, opinio isthæc animis nostrorum sit exempta: & Sole meridiano clariùs ex Scripturis constet, non aliud aut diversum Prædestinationis, aliud verò Justificationis esse Decretum: sed unam eandemq́; voluntatem DEI, de salute hominum, in utroque comprehendi: quin easdem planè utriusque esse causas: neque aliter à se mutuò duos istos Articulos differre, quàm ut Decretum, & Decreti executionem: utique non est, utin præsente negocio Justificationis, quicquam nobis ab Articulo Prædestinationis metuamus: quin potiùs statuamus, neutrum sine altero, in conflictu disputationis rectè asseri, solideq́; defendi posse: id quod facilè intelligunt, qui utriusque Controversiæ gustum minimè vulgarem perceperunt.

Cæterùm quantumvis Orthodoxa & accurata sit Tractatio Philippéa: Quô minus tamen vestigiis ejus, per omnia insistamus, facit variatio illius Status Controversiæ, qui nobis hodiè cum Jesuwitis potissimùm intercedit. Neque enim illud directè hodiè, sicut tempore Philippi, inter nos & Romanenses Controvertitur: Num Homo coram DEO justificetur operibus? Nam ipsi Jesuwitæ hodiè animadvertunt, simplicem Affirmativam nimis crassam, & Sacris literis ἀντιφατικῶς oppositam esse. Proindè mutato habitu, hoc est, variato Controversiæ Statu, in palæstram descendunt: ac partim ipsi negant, Operibus ullo pacto Justificari Hominem in conspectu DEI, si videlicet eam Justificationem intelligas, quam ipsi Primam appellitant, & sola Fide perfici largiuntur: partim verò contendunt, primam hanc Justificationem perfici demùm & absolvi operibus: ita ut Homo neque sola fide: neque solis Operibus: sed Fide & Operibus: vel ut ipsi loqui solent, Fide & Charitate: hoc est, Fide formata, justificari possit coram DEO. Et hic quidem Controversiæ Status, nobis potissimùm in futura Tractatione nostra erit præfixus.

Cæterùm cùm præter Jesuwitas, aliud insuper hæreticorum genus, & quidem longè pestilentissimum, Draco ille infernalis Diabolus, in proscenium Ecclesiæ protruserit, recentiores nimirùm Photinianos, qui per Poloniam & loca alia, Sacrosanctum purioris doctrinæ, de Justificatione nostra, Depositum, imò aureum quasi κειμήλιον, nefariè conspurcare, blasphemiis atrocissimis exagitare, variis denique armis, tùm ex Scriptura Sacra, tùm ex Analogia Fidei, tùm ex ratione petitis, oppugnare, imò expugnare, ac tantùm non penitùs excindere student: certè vel ipsa Ecclesiæ DEI salus, imò Religionis Christianæ puritas flagitare videtur, ut quibus armis nefarii istorum hominum conatus interverti, everti, ac penitùs opprimi possint ac debeant, ostendatur: idque tantò accuratiùs: quantò majore conatu male-feriati isti homines, virus hoc suum per Germaniam nostram, & cumprimis per hanc ipsam Academiam nostram disseminare student.

Proindè quod felix ac faustum, Ecclesiæque DEI utile & salutare jubeat esse CHRISTUS Servator: Universam Articuli hujus Tractationem dispescimus in duas Controversias Generales: Quarum prior recentiorum illorum Arianorum, vel potiùs Photinianorum: Posterior Romanensium,


### Status of the Controversy

And especially he will examine the heresies, blasphemies, tricks, and sophistries of the Jesuits concerning this Article, by the standard of Prophetic and Apostolic truth, both logically and theologically.

I. General Controversy, Against the Recent Photinians.

If in any other dispute, certainly in this present one against the recent Photinians, it must always be accurately considered: What is the true, proper, and legitimate Status of the Controversy, at which both the Adversary directly aims, and to which it behooves us ourselves to look back from time to time, provided we wish to proceed with an unoffending foot. But that will appear more clearly if we hear the recent Photinians themselves explaining their opinion concerning the matter of our Justification.

Thus, however, Faustus Socinus of Siena, an Italian, in book 1 of 'On Christ the Savior', chapter 1, page 1: 'I judge, and consider it to be the Orthodox opinion: that JESUS CHRIST is our Savior for this reason, because He announced to us the way of eternal salvation, confirmed it, and in His own person, both by the example of His life and by rising from the dead, manifestly showed it, and that He Himself will give us eternal life, if we have faith in Him: but I affirm that He neither satisfied for our sins the Divine Justice, through which we deserved to be condemned, nor was there any need that He should satisfy.'

And a little later, page 10: 'I confess that not only the first parents, but the entire human race also, is subject to death, and indeed eternal death, on account of sin: But that did not flow necessarily from any justice of GOD, but from His free will. Wherefore, just as GOD could have, and indeed by Right, not consigned men, even though they were sinners, to eternal death: so after He consigned them to death by His edict, He can again, and indeed by Right, exempt them from His command by His SOLE will.'

And page 13: 'If someone asks how it happens that, having deserved eternal death, we nevertheless arrive at eternal life: the genuine answer is not: Because we have Christ as Savior: but, because the punishment of eternal death was pardoned for us by GOD, by whose free will and decree we had deserved it, for the sake of His infallible goodness, and in its place the reward of eternal life was given: provided we repent, and having renounced all impiety, we devote ourselves to a life of innocence and holiness.'

And page 15: 'Christ is called our Savior for the reason that He announced to us the way of eternal salvation': that which is repeated on page 22. 'For that Christ reconciled GOD to us is nowhere written,' page 51. 'Neg. Christ appeased GOD for us: but only showed Him appeased.' page 55. 'Nor was there any need for any satisfaction to be performed by anyone: since the offense is not imputed by GOD.' page 56. 'And that Christ is said to have redeemed us, that has no weight for concluding that Christ satisfied for our sins.' page 69.

The sum of the impiety or heresy of the Photinians in this Article comes down to this: That a man is justified before GOD, not on account of the merit or satisfaction of Christ: since indeed neither did the Justice of GOD require it, nor did Christ perform it by His death: but on account of the mere pardon of sins, which GOD bestows not because of any merit of the Son, but out of His most free will to those who believe the word of Christ and devote themselves to a life of innocence.

Concerning this Status, the recent Photinians hold the affirmative in all things and strive to defend it: so that even from the single treatise of Faustus Socinus 'On Christ the Savior', it is permitted to extract the following flowers of blasphemy, which are also inserted in the index prefixed to that book.

No Justice of GOD at all demanded that our sins be punished. part 1, cap. 1.

Christ the Savior is called Savior for the reason that He announced to us the way of eternal salvation: and not because He satisfied for us by His death and passion. part 1, cap. 2 & 3.

This is the way of eternal salvation, if we imitate Christ, that is, if we order our life holily and justly, just as he lived, part 1. chap. 4. pag. 17.

The resurrection of Christ is nothing other than his eternal life, since it is established that the resurrection of Christ was that which his ascension into heaven and immortality followed. He is not, however, said to be our Savior for that reason, that he merited eternal life for us by his resurrection. p. 1. c. 5. p. 33.

Christ is called our Savior, not because he merited life for us: but because he received power from the Father to grant us eternal life, without any preceding λύτρῳ, merit or satisfaction. s. p. 1. cap. 6.

The term Mediator, when it is predicated of Christ, signifies no satisfaction exhibited to divine justice, nor even any appeasement of divine wrath. pag. 1. cap. 7.

7. Our redemption performed through Christ is metaphorical: that is, in it, as regards things to be done, no true λύτρον or price intervenes: nor was anything paid to anyone on our behalf. page 2. chap. 1. & 2. & 3.

8. From the passages of Scripture in which it is simply said either that Christ bore our sins or something similar, it should by no means be concluded that Christ endured all the punishments which we had deserved by our sins. p. 2. c. 4. & the following four.

9. From the foreshadowing of Christ's death in the Levitical expiatory sacrifices, it can in no way be gathered that Christ's death satisfied divine justice for our sins. p. 2. c. 10. 11. 12. 13. 14. & some following up to chap. 21.

10. The expiatory offering of Christ was performed not on the altar of the cross, but in Heaven: insofar as, namely, having entered the Heavens, he presents himself as it were to his Father for us, that is, he exercises all his power in the preservation of the ministry and the gathering of the Church, until the last day, so that thus through his doctrine (and not indeed through any merit) he might take away the sins of men. p. 2. chap. 15. & chap. 21. & chap. 23.

11. Christ, no less than the Levitical High Priest, offered a sacrifice for himself as well: since he himself was bound to fulfill the Law and to prove himself obedient to GOD: and therefore he by no means expiated any of our sins through Satisfaction. part 2. chap. 22. & part 3. chap. 5.

12. GOD both could and would forgive us all our sins, without having accepted any true Satisfaction for them. part 3. chap. 1. & 2.

13. Christ could not provide a payment of punishments which we were not bound to undergo by the Law of GOD. part 3. chap. 4. & 5. & 6.

14. This commends the justice of GOD most of all, that Christ indeed died, yet our sins were not imputed to him. part 3. chap. 9. & 10.

15. It is false and heretical that any Satisfaction of Christ, performed to GOD the Father for our sins, is imputed to us through Faith. part 4. chap. 1. & following.

16. Those who desire to become partakers of eternal salvation have need to be truly pious, and not merely imputatively: but to live truly holily and innocently. part 4. chap. 7.

17. Faith which believes that Christ by his merit has expiated and taken away our sins is not true justifying faith. part 4. chap. 9.

This is a Lerna, and a sink of such blasphemies, at which every pious person, nay, Heaven and the Elements, must needs shudder, nay, be struck dumb. But yet there are not wanting those who spread them: and indeed not in some obscure corner of the European world: but in the most noble kingdom of Poland, and in certain parts of the most flourishing kingdom of Hungary, or at least Transylvania: nor do they spread them simply, nakedly, or perfunctorily: but under the protection of the Holy Scriptures, the analogy of faith, and sounder reason.

Moreover, that we may proceed in refuting that impiety in the right order and a suitable method, we divide the general state of the question just now proposed into three special and, as it were, subordinate controversies. The first of which is concerning the mercy of God, which the Photinians contend: 1. Is not natural or essential to God, but contingent. 2. Is simply absolute with respect to sinful men, and not founded upon any satisfaction whatsoever, whether of Christ or our own.

The second is concerning the vindicatory justice of God, or that which punishes the sins of men, which the Photinians pretend is plainly non-existent in God, or ever was: to such an extent that in the Scriptures, God is not even read to be angry with sinners, or to have been angry anywhere.

The third is concerning the satisfaction and merit of Christ our Savior: for they simply deny both, contending in a most blasphemous manner.

1. That there was no need for any satisfaction at all, nor is any mention made in the Scriptures of either satisfaction or merit. Smaltz. p. 261.

2. That the passion of Christ neither is, nor could have been, a satisfaction or merit for our sins: and indeed in our stead or place. Smalz. p. 268.

4. That the remission of sins comes to us without the shedding of the blood of Christ: by the sole, free, simple, and absolute will of divine mercy, by which He wills to forgive us our sins, and truly does forgive them, if we perform true repentance.

Indeed, more states of controversy could be formed, which depend upon those four already enumerated by an almost indivisible connection: as concerning sin, that they contend it is propagated into children only by the imitation and example of their parents: and that we, conversely, are transferred from a state of sin into a state of innocence also by the sole imitation of the life of Christ. Likewise concerning bodily death, which Socinus, part 3, c. 8, p. 294, denies to be the wages of sin, for the reason that the death of the body is natural to man, and follows nature of itself. Which errors, indeed, are likewise directed solely to this end, that they may undermine and overturn the purer doctrine concerning gratuitous justification coming to men through and on account of the satisfaction or merit of Christ.

Latin:

& cumprimis Jesuitarum, circa hunc Articulum hæreses, blasphemias, strophias, ac Sophismata, ad trutinam veritatis Propheticæ & Apostolicæ, tùm Logicè, tùm Theologicè examinabit.

I. Controversia Generalis, Contra Recentiores Photinianos.

SI in quavis disputatione alia, certè in præsenti hac cōtra recentiores Photinianos, semper & accuratè dispiciendum fuerit: Quis sit verus, proprius ac legitimus Controversiæ Status, ad quem tùm Adversarii directè collimet: tùm nos ipsos subindè respicere deceat: dummodò inoffenso pede progredi velimus. Patebit autem ille dilucidiùs, si de Justificationis nostræ negocio, ipsos Photinianos recentiores, sententiam suam exponentes, audiamus.

Sic autem Faustus Socinus Senensis Italus lib. 1. de Christo Servatore cap. 1. pag. 1. Censeo ego, & Orthodoxam sententiam esse arbitror: JESUM CHRISTUM ideò Servatorem nostrum esse, quia salutis æternæ viam nobis annunciaverit, confirmaverit, & in sua ipsius persona, tùm vita exemplo, tùm ex mortuis resurgendo, manifestè ostenderit, vitamq́; æternam nobis, ei fidem habentibus ipse daturus sit: Divinæ autem Justitiæ, per quam peccatores damnari mereremur, pro peccatis nostris, neque illum satisfecisse, neque ut satisfaceret, opus fuisse, affirmo.

Et paulo pòst pag. 10. Fateor, non primos parentes tantùm, sed universum etiam genus humanum, propter peccatum, morti, & quidem æternæ, obnoxium esse: Verùm id, non ex aliqua DEI justitia necessariò fluxit, sed ex libera ejus voluntate. Quocirca, quemadmodum potuisset DEUS, & quidem Jure, homines, licet peccantes, morti æternæ non mancipare: sic postquàm illos morti, edicto suo mancipavit, ex illius imperio iterum eximere, & quidem Jurè, sua SOLA voluntate potest.

Et pag. 13. Quærente aliquo, qui fiat, ut mortem æternam meriti, nihilominus ad vitam æternam perveniamus: non est germanum responsum: Quia Christum Servatorem habemus: sed, quia supplicium mortis æternæ à DEO, cujus liberâ voluntate atque decreto, eam meriti fueramus, nobis pro infallibili ipsius bonitate, condonatum fuit, atque ejus loco datum vitæ æternæ præmium: dummodò resipiscamus, & abnegatâ omni impietate, vita innocentiæ, ac sanctimoniæ studeamus.

Et pag. 15. Christus Servator noster dicitur, ob id, quod salutis æternæ viam nobis annunciavit: id quod repetitur pag. 22. Christum enim DEUM nobis reconciliasse, nusquàm scriptum extat pag. 51. Neg. Christus DEUM nobis placavit: sed placatum tantùm ostendit. pag. 55. Neque etiam satisfactione ulla à quoquam præstari opus erat: siquidem delictum à DEO non imputatur. pag. 56. Et quòd Christus nos redemisse dicitur, id nihil momenti habet ad concludendum, quòd Christus pro nostris peccatis fatisfecerit. pag. 69.

Summa impietatis sive hæresens Photinianæ hoc quidem in Articulo eò redit: Justificari coram DEO hominem, non propter meritum aut satisfactionem Christi: quippè quam neque Justitia DEI exegerit, neque Christus sua morte præstiterit: sed propter solam peccatorum condonationem, quam DEUS non ob meritum aliquod Filii; sed ex liberrima voluntate largiatur iis, qui Christi verbo credunt, & vitæ innocentiæ student.

Circa hunc Statum Photiniani recentiores Affirmativam per omnia tenent, ac defendere student: ità ut vel ex uno Fausti Socini tractatu de Christo Servatore, sequentes blasphemiarum flosculos, ipsi etiam indici, libro illi præfixo, insertos excerpere liceat.

Nulla DEI Justitia omninò postulavit, ut peccata nostra punirentur. part. 1. cap. 1.

Christus Servator ob id dicitur Servator, quòd salutis æternæ viam nobis annunciavit: nō verò quòd morte ac passione sua pro nobis satisfecerit. part. 1. cap. 2. & 3.

Hæc est salutis æternæ via, si Christum imitemur, hoc est, sanctè & justè, quemadmodum ille vixit, vitam componimus, part. 1. cap. 4. pag. 17.

Resurrectio Christi nihil est aliud, quàm æterna ipsius vita, cum constet, Resurrectionem Christi eam fuisse, quam in Cœlum ascensus & immortalitas consecuta est. Neg. tamen ideò Servator noster dicitur, quòd resurrectione sua vitam æternam nobis promeruerit. p. 1. c. 5. p. 33.

Christus dicitur Servator noster, non quod vitam nobis promeruerit: sed quòd potestatem acceperit à patre, donandi nobis vitam æternam, sine ullo præcedente λύτρῳ, merito aut Satisfactione. s. p. 1. cap. 6.

Vox Mediatoris, quando de Christo prædicatur, nullam divinæ justitiæ exhibitam Satisfactionem, quin nec ullam ira divina placationem significat. pag. 1. cap. 7.

7. Redemtio nostra per Christum præstita, est metaphorica: hoc est, in ea per agenda, nullum verum λύτρον sive pretium intervenit: neque quicquam cuiquam pro nobis solutum est. pag. 2. cap. 1. & 2. & 3.

8. Ex locis Scripturæ, in quibus simpliciter dicitur, aut Christum portasse peccata nostra, aut quippiam simile, minimè concludi debet, Christum omnes pœnas pertulisse, quas nos peccatis nostris præmeriti eramus. p. 2. c. 4. & sequentibus quatuor.

9. Ex adumbratione mortis Christi in Sacrificiis Leviticis expiatorijs, nullo modo potest colligi, Christi mortem pro peccatis nostris divinæ justitiæ satisfecisse. p. 2. c. 10. 11. 12. 13. 14. & aliquot seqq. usque ad cap. 21.

10. Oblatio Christi expiatoria, non in ara crucis, sed in Cœlo peracta est: quatenùs nimirùm ipse Cœlos ingressus, patri suo pro nobis se quasi præsentat, hoc est, omnem potestatem suam, in ministerij conservatione & Ecclesiæ collectione exercet, usque ad ultimum diem, ut ita per doctrinam suam (non verò per meritum aliquod) tollat peccata hominum. p. 2. cap. 15. & cap. 21. & cap. 23.

11. Christus non minùs, quàm Pontifex Leviticus, pro se quoque obtulit Sacrificium: Siquidem ipsemet devinctus erat Legem adimplere, ac DEO se comprobare obedientem: ac proinde per Satisfactionem aliqua peccata nostra minimè expiavit. part. 2. cap. 22. & part. 3. cap. 5.

12. DEUS & potuit & voluit nobis condonare omnia peccata nostra, nullâ pro ipsis verâ Satisfactione accepta. part. 3. cap. 1. & 2.

13. Christus non potuit præstare solutionem pœnarum, quas non ex Lege DEI subire tenebamur. part. 3. cap. 4. & 5. & 6.

14. Hoc vel maximè commendat DEI justitiam, quòd Christus mortuus quidem est, neque tamen ipsi peccata nostra imputata fuerunt part. 3. cap. 9. & 10.

15. Falsum & Hæreticum, quòd ulla aliqua Satisfactio Christi, DEO Patri pro peccatis nostris præstita, per Fidem nobis imputetur. part. 4. cap. 1. & seqq.

16. Qui salutis æternæ participes fieri desiderant, necesse habent, ut revera sint pij, & non imputativè tantùm: sed reverâ sanctè atque innocenter vivant part. 4. cap. 7.

17. Fides, quæ credit, quòd Christus suo merito peccata nostra expiaverit & sustulerit non est vera fides justificans. part. 4. cap. 9.

Lerna hæc est, & sentina ejusmodi blasphemiarum, ad quas pius quisque, imò Cœlum & Elementa exhorrescere, imò stupescere necesse habent. Sed tamen non desunt, qui eas spargunt: & quidem non in obscuro aliquo Orbis Europæi angulo: sed in nobilissimo regno Poloniæ, & partibus quibusdam florentissimi regni Hungariæ, vel certè Transylvaniæ: neque etiam simpliciter nudè aut perfunctoriè: sed sub præsidio Sacrarum scripturarum, analogiæ fidei, & sanioris rationis eas spargunt.

Cæterùm, ut in refutanda impietate ista recto ordine & conveniente Methodo progrediamur, Statum Generalem jam modò propositum, dispescimus in tres Controversias Speciales & quasi subordinatas. Quarum PRIMA est de MISERICORDIA DEI, quam Photiniani contendunt. 1. DEO non esse Naturalem, sive Essentialem: sed Contingentem. 2. Esse eam respectu hominum peccatorum simpliciter absolutam, neque fundatam in ulla aliquâ Satisfactione, sive CHRISTI, sive nostra.

ALTERA est de JUSTITIA DEI vindicatrice, sive puniente peccata hominum, quam Photiniani fingunt planè nullam in DEO esse, vel fuisse unquàm: usque adeò, ut in Scripturis, DEUS ne quidem peccatoribus irasci, aut iratus fuisse uspiam legatur.

TERTIA est de Satisfactione & MERITO CHRISTI Servatoris nostri: Utrumque enim simpliciter negant, blasphemè admodùm contendentes.

1. Quòd nulla prorsus Satisfactione opus fuerit, neque etiam in Scripturis ullius vel Satisfactionis, vel meriti fiat mentio Smaltz. p. 261.

2. Quòd Passio Christi neque sit, neque potuerit esse Satisfactio, aut meritum pro peccatis nostris: & quidem vice, aut loco nostri Smalz. p. 268.

4. Quòd Remissio peccatorum nobis obtingat, sine effusione Sanguinis CHRISTI: solâ, liberâ, simplici & absolutâ voluntate misericordiæ divinæ, qua nobis peccata velit condonare, & verè condonet, si veram agamus pœnitentiam.

Possent profectò plures formari Status Controversiæ, qui à quatuor istis jam enumeratis, indiviso quasi nexu dependent: ut de Peccato, quòd contendant, illud imitatione tantùm & exemplo Parentum in liberos propagari: nosque vice versâ sola etiam imitatione vitæ Christi, ex Statu peccati in Statum innocentiæ transferri. Item de Morte Corporali, quam Socinus part. 3. c. 8. p. 294. negat esse stipendium peccati, propterea, quòd Mors Corporis sit Homini naturalis, & naturam per se sequatur. Qui sanè errores itidem eò unicè sunt directi, ut doctrinam puriorem de gratuitâ Justificatione per & propter Satisfactionem sive Meritum CHRISTI, hominibus obtingente subruant & evertant.


### Whether Mercy is an essential property in God

Moreover, since the vanity of the former error concerning sin will be most manifest from the subsequent discussion, and since we have already expressly refuted the latter fabrication concerning the bodily death above in the Article on the Image of God, it will be most appropriate if our future treatment confines itself within the three defined special Controversies.

THE FIRST Special Controversy, with the modern Photinians, concerning the Mercy of God, insofar as it is predicated in this Article concerning God.

There are two main heads of errors which the Photinians spread today concerning the Mercy of God. For first, they contend that the Mercy of God, insofar as it enters into the act of our Justification, is not a natural or essential property in God, but only a secondary act, as it were, or a contingent effect of His own free will. Then, indeed, they struggle very anxiously that this very mercy of God is simply absolute, and not founded upon any λύτρῳ or satisfaction of Christ.

THE FORMER ERROR.

Faustus Socinus betrayed this error in part 1 of 'On Christ the Savior,' chapter 1, page 9, in these words: 'The same consideration holds place also in mercy itself, insofar as it is opposed to severity and vengeance, namely, that it is not a property of God, but only an effect of His will,' see Schmaltz, p. 264.

And in part 3, chapter 1, a little more clearly: 'If you say that it can be proved by the same reasoning that mercy does not reside in God—for if it resided in God, He would never inflict punishment on anyone, since mercy is nothing other than forgiving those who offend—I will answer that it is most true that mercy, insofar as it is opposed to justice, that is, to severity and vengeance, does not reside in God, but is an effect of His will.' Therefore, when the sacred scriptures testify that God is merciful, they mean nothing other than that God very often and very easily forgives sins.

Moreover, in order that this mystery of iniquity may be better understood, it should be noted that the same Socinus invents a twofold mercy in God, writing thus: 'One is the mercy of God by which He forgives all crimes to those who repent, as His promises declare, and bestows salvation and life; the other is that by which He plainly anticipates men and calls and entices them when they are immersed in sins. He uses the former perpetually; but the latter only when it pleases Him. The former seems to signify nothing other than that God is indeed most inclined toward mercy and toward forgiving sins to men, but yet that He does not absolve those who continue to be guilty and rebellious and do not repent. The latter, however, denotes nothing other than that most free act of the divine will by which He sometimes, nay, more often, forgives sins,' as Socinus explains himself (page 122).

The end and scope of this error is this one thing, that he may thus demonstrate that the Mercy of God, which remits sins, has no regard at all either to any justice in God that avenges sins, or to any satisfaction whatsoever; for the reason that it is only some contingent act or effect of free will in God. Now, indeed, that which is contingent, and which proceeds from the mere liberty of the will, cannot be determined to any certain Decree of Satisfaction, but can be retracted and changed by that same liberty of the will—that is, it can either be exercised or not exercised—as will be more clearly evident from the latter error of this heretic.

But that which must be examined more deeply in this place is: Whether Mercy, by which God in any way whatsoever has mercy on men, is a natural or essential property in Him, and thus something distinct from the very will of God; or whether it is only a secondary act, or, as Socinus speaks, an effect of free will in God.

To the first member of this Question, we respond affirmatively against Socinus: namely, that the Mercy of God, in whatever way it is considered within the very essence of God, is a Natural or Essential property of God: that is, it is that Natural goodness, and Φιλανθρωπίαν, by which God is God, that is, by His own nature He is prone and inclined to pity, to help, and to do good to all men. This Natural property in God is distinct from His very will, since it serves as it were all the Essential properties in God, and by itself, without the concurrence of the others or of one or more of them, produces no Effect. For whatever God does, He does it willingly: yet the principle of acting depends on nothing but some Natural property in God.

Therefore the principle of Pity is Natural and Essential to God: so that God would not be God, unless He were Merciful. I said, however, that this assertion of ours is true, if the Mercy of God is considered within the very essence of God: and denotes that Natural ςοργὴν or as it were fatherly affection of God toward men. But when this mercy of God proceeds outwardly in the act itself, and exerts some ἐνέργειαν: then indeed we by no means deny that it happens from the free will of God. Therefore one must distinguish between the first Act and the second Act of the mercy of God; the first Act is simply Essential to God, and does not depend at last upon the will of God, but is simply convertible with the Essence of God, even to the point that Scripture even attributes to God σπλάγχνα ἐλέες Luc. 1.78.

thus figuratively implying that God is merciful by Essence, and is affected by an essential Φιλανθρωπία towards men that is clearly singular, and indeed by His own Nature. The second act, however, can either be exercised or not exercised, and thus has its dependence upon the will. Which dependence, however, does not cause Mercy to be constituted as twofold in God, and one such that it is not natural to God, as Socinus raves: but it only determines the Effect of divine mercy. For example: The creation of this Universe is an Effect of omnipotence: which Effect depends to that extent upon the Freedom of the will in God, insofar as He did not wish to create the world from eternity, but at that moment of time in which it seemed good to God: insofar as He could also have withdrawn this very Effect, and not created the world. Where no one is so insane as to gather from that already that there is a twofold Omnipotence in God, and one that is not Natural to God: but this is rather gathered from it, that there is one omnipotence in God in number and Essence: yet its Effect, or second act, is of the free will, since indeed He could most freely either exercise or withdraw it. Thus when God forgives sins to certain men, He does this indeed out of the Freedom of the will: but from that, the very mercy of God, insofar as it is the principle of this Action, is not called a Contingent Effect of the free will in God: much less is it denied that it is essential to God: but this only follows, that this second act of divine Mercy depends also in its own respect upon the Free will of God: while in the meantime the principle of acting itself, or the power, resides clearly Essentially in God.

Shamefully, therefore, and too ignorantly does Socinus confuse power and act, or the first act and the second act: nay, the Effect itself with the cause, when clearly and un-theologically they name the Mercy that forgives sins an Effect of the will: when it rather stands in the manner of a Cause: and the concurring will only determines or modifies the cause: but does not produce it.

But Socinus has certain little arguments by which he tries to put a gloss on his raving. And at the beginning indeed, on page 5, he brings forward that Apostolic saying Rom. 9, 15. God, whom He wills He has mercy on: Therefore Mercy is an Effect of the free will.

But a Sophistry is committed by the fallacy of the consequent: For from the determination of the second act, or Effect, the Consequence does not hold for defining the Nature or Essence of the first act in itself, as has already been demonstrated before.

II. God always uses natural things: But He does not always use Mercy, because indeed He does not forgive sins to all: but to whom He wills: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy. Therefore, Mercy forgiving sins is not a natural property of God.

I answer: that in the Major premise a fallacy is committed by the confusion of the relative and the absolute. For it is not simply true: but only in a certain respect, namely if it is understood of that internal, perpetual, and altogether invariable act, by which God, according to all natural properties, is to Himself what He is. For natural properties of God are considered in two ways: First, insofar as within the simplest complex of the divine Essence, they are, with the Essence of God itself, something simply One and the same. And indeed, insofar as they are considered in this way and complete the Essence of God, to that extent the Major proposition is most true, that God always uses natural things. For if God did not always use these, then the Essence of God would cease to be what it is.

Then, however, they are considered insofar as they proceed outward from the respect of creatures; where it is false what Socinus affirms, that God always uses natural things, or always exercises them. For that divine properties proceed outward, and exert some act or Effect in creatures: that does not depend upon the most absolute perfection of the Essence of God, and therefore neither is that of absolute necessity: but it depends upon the most free will. From which, however, it is not permitted to gather: Therefore those properties cease to be Natural: just as a little before we made that attested by the Example of divine Omnipotence. And thus our heretic shamefully begs the question, and presupposes a false hypothesis: that indeed those properties, which God does not always use in the government of creatures, are not natural to God: which we have already often evidently demonstrated to be most false.

To the Minor premise we will answer expressly in the Examination of the second Error, where we will show: That God does not forgive sins to all: that this indeed depends upon the free will, but not an absolute or simple one: but an ordered one, which is, that He wills to forgive sins to all who apprehend the merit of Christ through faith. But if He does not now forgive sins to many, this happens indeed from His own will, but one determined, likewise to the Order, by which He has sanctioned that He does not wish to forgive sins to the incredulous: nor to have mercy on them. Let the Sacramentarians see, however, how they wish to repel from themselves the suspicion of Photinian heresy in this part, as long as they contend just as they do: That the Foundation of Election and Reprobation, or of Salvation and damnation, consists in the simple and absolute will of God: so that Paraeus, in the dissolution of this argument, does not find what he can or ought to answer to the Minor premise: as is evident from his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, page 926. D.

III. Whatever is freely in God, that is not natural to Him: Mercy is freely in Him. Therefore. But the major premise is simply false: For just as God is most freely what He is: so all His properties, however essential, are most freely what they are. Then there is involved an abuse of the word Free, which to Socinus denotes the same as Contingent or Accidental: whence a shameful equivocation arises: when Free is opposed in this place, and indeed properly, to that which is forced, and is as it were called servile. Just as under the word (Natural) the Sophist likewise plays craftily: understanding Natural as a certain forced constitution of Nature: when yet in God he notes the most free condition of Essence, such as it exists itself, not from forcing causes: but from most free and most absolute perfection depending.

some study divinely blessed: they pretend that the rest are likewise divinely, and indeed by mere and simple will, cursed. But of this matter elsewhere.

V. Properties do not inhere in God unequally: But mercy and Justice inhere in God unequally: For it is said that He is plenteous in mercy: but slow to anger: Therefore neither inheres in God naturally, and they err gravely who say that both are infinite.

IV. The properties of God are not contrary: Mercy is contrary to vindicatory Justice, James 2:13. Mercy rejoices against judgment. Therefore neither is a property of God.

I answer: that in the Major premise a Sophism of equivocation is committed in the word Unequally, which denotes either some contrariety. In which respect we concede the Major: or it is opposed to identity, and then the Major is false. For although the properties in God within the most absolute ὐσίαν [essence] of God are a most simple thing, ταυτὸ [the same], and are most simply convertible with the Essence itself: yet by reason of predication they do not admit identity: so that it may be lawful to say; The Mercy of God is the Omnipotence of God, the Justice of God is the eternity, or the wisdom of God: but as they obtain a distinct manner of predication: so they obtain some inequality, not indeed by reason of Essence: but by reason of predication only. Whence it happens that if these properties afterwards erupt into act: it is not lawful to predicate just anything of just anything: but as the properties themselves are distinct in themselves: so they are also distinctly predicated of those Effects. And this is the very cause for which the Effect of Creation is ascribed not to Justice: but to divine Omnipotence: the work of Salvation not to Eternity, but to Mercy: the ἔργον [work] of Damnation, not to Mercy: but to divine Justice.

I answer: that the Minor premise is simply false. For if the Mercy and Justice of God were contrary to each other: then the essence of God would consist of Contraries: and thus it would not be a most simple thing, ταυτὸ [the same] and identical: which is prodigiously absurd and blasphemous. But if you look to those diverse Effects of Justice and Mercy in men: then indeed some diversity offers itself: but no contrariety at all. The reason is, Because those diverse Effects depend not on some absolute or simple will of God: but on subordinate causes: so that the mercy of God wills to forgive sins, but not except to those believing in Christ. Inasmuch as many now do not believe, to that extent Justice exerts another and diverse Effect, namely Damnation: but not simply: but orderly: because they do not believe.

Which consideration of Subordinate causes removes all contrariety, and rather proposes to us to contemplate that admirable temperament of Justice and Mercy in God, so that without any Contradiction, or conflict, God can save some, but damn others: of which more fully in the following. But neither can the Calvinists solidly answer this argument of the Photinians, as long as they teach and champion the absolute salvation of a few certain ones: and conversely the absolute Condemnation of the many. Just as indeed, as it is said, Paræus is stuck in the mud in the dissolution of this argument, first conceding that the Effects are indeed contrary: but not the attributes themselves: then however explaining himself thus, in a sense clearly Photinian: Just as the sun with the same heat melts wax, hardens mud: effecting contrary things in diverse, or contrarily disposed [objects]: So God by the same will (NB: THE SAME) has mercy on whom He wills, hardens whom He wills: effecting contrary things in diverse, or contrarily disposed Objects. Where it is to be noted, that according to the mind of the Calvinists, God effects this very contrariety in men: while of certain men the Minor is most false, and is simply denied by us: nor will Socinus ever prove that Mercy and Justice inhere in God unequally, and that one inheres more, the other less: Nor does any patronage redound to him from the fact that in the Scriptures God is held to be plenteous in mercy: but slow to anger. For in such places Mercy and justice are not considered, insofar as they inhere in God, that is, insofar as they are Essential properties of God: but insofar as they are viewed in execution by reason of the second act: where God is found to be swifter to show mercy, than to punish. Whence, however, the Consequence is not valid for constructing either a majority or a minority in the properties themselves, according to their nature, and in the complex of the divine Essence, considered in themselves and through themselves.

For those ἐνεργείαι [energies] or executions of the divine properties, as they are of the most free will, so they can also obtain inequality: while in the meantime the equality of the divine Essence, and of the individual properties, remains.

Latin:

Cæterùm cùm prioris erroris de peccato vanitas ex subsequente disputatione futura sit manifestissima: posterius autem commentum de morte Corporali, supra in Articulo de Imagine Dei ex professo refutaverimus, convenientissimum fuerit, si intra definitas tres Controversias speciales, futura nostra Tractatio se contineat.

PRIMA CONTROVERsia Specialis, cum Recentioribus Photinianis, de Misericordia Dei, quatenùs in Articulo hoc de Deo prædicatur.

DUo sunt errorum capita præcipua, quæ de Misericordia Dei hodiè spargunt Photiniani. Primum enim contendunt, Misericordiam Dei, quatenùs ea ingreditur actum Justificationis nostræ, non esse Naturalem sive Essentialem proprietatem in Deo, sed tantummodò Actum quasi secundum, sive Contingens Effectum, liberæ voluntatis ipsius. Deindè verò sollicitè admodùm pugnant, Hanc ipsam Deimisericordiam esse simpliciter absolutam, neq́; fundatam in ullo λύτρῳ sive satisfactione Christi.

PRIOR ERROR.

Prodidit hunc errorem Faustus Socinus part. 1. de Christo Servatore cap. 1. pag. 9. his verbis: Eadem consideratio locum habet in ipsa quoque misericordia, quatenùs severitati opposita est atq́; vindictæ, ut scilicet Dei proprietas non sit, sed Effectus tantum voluntatis ejus, vide Schmaltz. p. 264.

Et part. 3. cap. 1. paulò dilucidiùs: Si dixeris, eadem ratione probari posse, misericordiam in Deo non residere: Nam si ea in Deo resideret, u nemini unquàm pœnam irrogaret, cùm misericordiæ nihil aliud sit, quàm delinquentibus ignoscere: Respondebo, verißimum esse, misericordiam, quatenùs esti Justitiæ, hoc est, severitati & vindictæ opponitur, in Deo non residere, sed effectum esse voluntatis ejus. Cùm igitur sacræ literæ testantur, Deum misericordem esse, nihil aliud sibi volunt, quàm Deum sæpißimè & facillimè peccata condonare.

Cæterùm ut mysterium hoc iniquitatis rectiùs intelligatur, notandum fuerit, quòd idem Socinus duplicem in Deo comminiscitur misericordiam, sic scribens: Vna Dei misericordia est, quâ respiscentibus, ut ipsius promissa ferunt, omnia scelera condonat, & salutem vitamq́; largitur: Altera, quâ planè homines prævenit, & peccatis immersos ad se vocat & allicit: Illa perpetuò utitur: hâc verò tùm demum, cùm sibi libuerit. Illa nihil aliud significare videtur, quàm Deum propensißimum quidem ess ad misericordiam, & addelicta hominibus condonanda: sed tamen eos non absolvere, qui nocentes & rebelles esse pergunt, neq́; respiscunt. Hæc verò nihil notat aliud, quàm liberrimum illum voluntatis divinæ actum, quò interdum, imò sæpiùs peccata condonat, ut (pag. 122.) semetipsum Socinus explicat.

Finis & scopus Erroris hujus est unicus iste, ut sic demonstret, Misericordiam Dei, quæ remittit peccata, nullum prorsus habere respectum, vel ad Justitiam aliquam in Deo, vindicantem peccata, vel ad ullam aliquam satisfactionem; propterea quòd sit tantùm Contingens aliquis actus, sive Effectus liberæ voluntatis in Deo. Jam verò, quod Contingens est, quodque ex merâ libertate voluntatis provenit: id non potest esse determinatum ad certum aliquod Satisfactionis Decretum: sed eâdem voluntatis libertate retrahi & immutari, hoc est, vel exerceri, vel non exerceri potest: quemadmodum ex posteriore Errore, Intentio hæretici hujus patebit luculentiùs.

Illud autem hoc loco altiùs dispiciendum fuerit: An Misericordia, quâ Deus quocunq́; modo miseretur hominibus, ipsi sit Naturalis sive Essentialis proprietas, & sic distinctum quid ab ipsa voluntate Dei: an verò sit tantùm Actus secundus, sive ut Socinus loquitur, Effectus liberæ voluntatis in Deo.

Ad priùs membrum Quæstionis hujus, nos contra Socinum affirmatè respondemus: nempè Misericordiam Dei, quocunque modo illa intra ipsam Dei essentiam consideretur, esse Naturalem sive Essentialem proprietatem Dei: hoc est, esse Naturalem illam bonitatem, ac Φιλανθρωπίαν, quâ Deus est Deus, hoc est, naturâ suâ pronus ac proclivis est ad miserandum, juvandum, benefaciendum omnibus hominibus. Distincta est hæc proprietas Naturalis in Deo ab ipsa ejus voluntate, quippè quæ omnibus proprietatibus Essentialibus in Deo quasi inservit, & per se, sine reliquarum vel unius, vel plurium concursu, Effectum nullum producit. Quicquid enim Deus facit, illud volens facit: agendi tamen principio, non nisi ab aliquâ proprietate Naturali in Deo dependente.

Proindè principium Miserationis est Deo Naturale & Essentiale: ita ut Deus non esset Deus, nisi esset Misericors. Dixi autem hanc assertionem nostram veram esse, si intra ipsam Dei essentiam, Misericordia Dei consideretur: & Naturalem illam Dei erga homines ςοργὴν sive affectum quasi paternum denotet. Quando verò hæc Dei misericordia ipso actu forâs progreditur, & ἐνέργειαν aliquam exerit: tùm sanè minimè negamus, illud fieri ex libera voluntate Dei. Distinguendum proindè inter Actum primum & Actum secundum misericordiæ Dei, Actus primus simpliciter Deo est Essentialis, neque à voluntate Dei demùm dependet, sed cum Essentia Dei simpliciter est convertibilis, usq; adeò, ut Scriptura Deo etiam tribuat σπλάγχνα ἐλέες Luc. 1.78.

sic figuratè innuendo, Deum per Essentiam esse misericordem, & Φιλανθρωπία Essentiali erga homines planè singulari, & quidem per Naturam suam affici. Actus verò secundus potest vel exerceri, vel non exerceri, & sic suam à voluntate habet dependentiam. Quæ dependentia tamen non facit, ut Misericordia in Deo duplex constituatur, & altera quidem talis, quæ Deo non sit naturalis, uti Socinus delirat: sed tantùm Effectum misericordiæ divinæ determinat. Exempli gratia: Creatio hujus Universi est Effectus omnipotentiæ: qui Effectus dependet eatenùs ex Libertate voluntatis in Deo, quatenus non ab æterno, sed in eo temporis principio, quo Deo visum fuit, mundum creare voluit: quatenùs etiam hunc ipsum Effectum retrahere, & mundum non creare potuisset. Ubi nemo ità insanit, ut indè jam colligat, Geminam esse Omnipotentiam in Deo, & alteram quidem Deo non Naturalem: sed hoc potiùs indè colligitur, quod una numero & Essentiâ in Deo sit omnipotentia: Effectus tamen ejus, sive actus secundus sit liberæ voluntatis, dùm nimirùm illum vel exercere, vel retrahere liberrimè potuit. Sic quando Deus quibusdam hominibus condonat peccata, facit hoc quidem ex Libertate voluntatis: sed indè ipsa Dei misericordia, quatenùs est Actionis hujus principium, non dici Contingens Effectum liberæ voluntatis in Deo: nedùm negari, quod ipsa Deo sit essentialis: sed hoc tantùm sequitur, quòd actus iste secundus Misericordiæ divinæ dependeat suo etiam respectu, à Liberâ voluntate Dei: ipso interim agendi principio, sive δυνάμει planè Essentialiter in Deo residente.

Turpiter proindè, & nimis inscitè confundit Socinus δύναμιν & ἐνέργειαν, sive actum primum & actum secundum: imò Effectum ipsum cum causâ, cùm videlicet ἀθεολόγως planè Misericordiam condonantem peccata nominant Effectum voluntatis: cùm potius ea se habeat instar Causæ: & voluntas concurrens, causam tantùm determinet, sive modificet: non verò efficiat.

Sed habet Socinus ratiunculas quasdam, quibus delirio suo fucum facere conatur. Ac initiò quidem pag. 5. profert illud Apostolicum Rom. 9, 15. Deus, cujus vult miseretur: Ergo Misericordia est Effectus liberæ voluntatis.

Sed committitur Sophisticatio παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον: A determinatione enim actus secundi, sive Effectus, non valet Consequentia, ad definiendam Naturam sive Essentiam Actus primi per se, uti jam antè demonstratum.

II. Naturalibus Deus semper utitur: Atqui Misericordiâ non semper utitur, quia nimirùm non omnibus condonat peccata: sed quibus vult: Miseribor, cujus miserebor. E. Misericordia condonans peccata non est naturalis proprietas Dei.

Respondeo: in Majore committi Sophisma παρὰ τὸ πῇ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Non enim simpliciter ea vera est: sed tantùm secundum quid, nempè si intelligatur, de interno illo perpetuo, ac prorsus invariabili actu, quô Deus secundum omnes proprietates naturales, sibi est, quod est. Duobus enim modis considerantur Naturales Dei proprietates: Primùm, quatenùs intra simplissimum Essentiæ divinæ complexum, cùm ipsa Essentia Dei, sunt quiddam simpliciter Unum & ταυτὸ. Et profectò, quatenùs hoc modo consideratæ Essentiam Dei absolvunt, & perficiunt, eâtenùs verissima est Major propositio, quòd Deus naturalibus semper utatur. Nam si Deus istis non semper uteretur, tùm Essentia Dei cessaret esse, quod est.

Deindè verò considerantur, quatenùs ex respectu creaturarum forâs progrediuntur; ubi falsum est, quod Socinus affirmat, Deum naturalibus semper uti, vel semper eas exercere. Nam ut proprietates divinæ forâs progrediantur, & actum aliquem sive Effectum in creaturis exerant: id non de pendet ab absolutissima perfectione Essentiæ Dei, ac proindè neque absolutæ etiam illud est necessitatis: sed dependet à liberrima voluntate. Vndè tamen non licet colligere: Ergò proprietates illæ desinunt esse Naturales: quemadmodum paulò antè Exemplo Omnipotentiæ divinæ illud testatum reddidimus. Et sic hæreticus noster turpiter petit principium, & falsam præsupponit hypothesin: quòd nimirùm proprietates illæ, quibus Deus non semper in creaturarum gubernatione utitur, non sint Deo naturales: id quod falsissimum esse jam sæpè evidenter demonstravimus.

Ad Minorem ex professo respondebimus in Examine secundi Erroris, ubi ostendemus: Quòd Deus non omnibus condonet peccata: illud dependere quidem à libera voluntate, sed non absolutâ sive simplici: sed ordinatâ, quæ est, quòd velit condonare peccata omnibus, per fidem apprehendentibus meritum Christi. Quòd si jam multis non condonat peccata, fit hoc ex voluntate quidem ipsius, sed determinata, itidem ad Ordinem, quô sancivit, se nolle condonare peccata incredulis: neque istorum misereri. Viderint autem Sacramentarij, quomodo suspicionem hærefeως Photinianæ hâc in parte à se propulsare velint, quamdiu æquè ac hi contendunt: Fundamentum Electionis & Reprobationis, sive Salutis & damnationis consistere in simplici & absoluta voluntate Dei: ita ut Paræus in dissolutione hujus argumenti non inveniat, quid ad Minorem respondere vel possit vel debeat: uti patet ex ipsius Commentario in Epist. ad Rom. pag. 926. D.

III. Quicquid liberè Deo inest, id ipsi non est Naturale: Misericordia liberè ipsi inest. E. Sed Major simpliciter est falsa: Quemadmo. dum enim Deus liberrimè est, quod est: ita proprietates omnes, quantumvis Essentiales, liberrimè sunt, quod sunt. Deindè involvitur abusus vocis Liberi, quæ Socino idem notat ac Contingens sive Accidentarium: undè turpis æquivocatio oritur: cùm Liberum opponatur hoc loco & quidem propriè ei, quòd coactum est, & servum quasi dicitur. Quemadmodum sub voce (Naturale) itidem veteratoriè Sophista ludit: Naturale intelligens pro coactiva quadam Naturæ constitutione : cùm tamen in Deo notet liberrimam conditionem Essentiæ, qualis ipsa, non ex causis cogentibus: sed ex liberrima absolutissimáque perfectione dependentibus, existit.

num studium divinitùs benedictum : reliquorum itidem divinitùs, & quidem merâ ac simplici voluntate maledictum esse fingunt. Sed hac de re alibi.

V. Proprietates Deo non insunt inæqualiter: At misericordia & Justitia Deo inæqualiter insunt: Dicitur enim multus misericordiâ : sed tardus ad iram: E. neutra Deo inest naturaliter, & graviter errant, qui utramq, infinitam esse dicunt.

IV. Proprietates Dei non sunt contraria: Misericordia est contraria Justitiæ vindicatrici, Iacob. 2, 13. Misericordia gloriatur adversus judicium. Ergo neutra est Dei proprietas.

Respondeo: in Majori committi Sophisma ὁμωνυμίας in voce Inæqualiter, quæ vel contrarietatem aliquam notat. Quo respectu Majorem concedimus: vel opponitur identitati, & tunc falsa est Major. Etsi enim proprietates in Deo intra ὐσίαν Dei absolutissimam, sunt simplicissimum quiddam ταυτὸ, & cùm ipsa Essentiâ simplicissimè convertuntur: tamen ratione prædicandi non admittunt identitatem: ut dicere fas sit; Misericordia Dei est Omnipotentia Dei Justitia Dei est æternitas, vel sapientia Dei: sed uti distinctam prædicandi rationem sortiuntur : ita inæqualitatem aliquam obtinent, non quidem ratione Essentiæ: sed ratione tantùm prædicationis. Undè fit, ut si proprietates hæ postmodùm in actum erumpant: non fas sit quidvis de quavis prædicare: sed uti proprietates ipsæ in se sunt distinctæ: ita distinctè etiam de Effectis illis prædicentur. Et hæc ipsa causa est, propter quam Creationis Effectus non Justitiæ: sed Omnipotentiæ divinæ: Salvationis opus non Æternitati, sed Misericordiæ: Damnationis ἔργον, non Misericordiæ: sed Justitiæ divinæ adscribitur.

Respondeo: Minorem simpliciter esse falsam. Si enim Misericordia & Justitia Dei sibi contrariarentur: tùm Dei essentia constaret ex Contrarijs: & sic non esset quiddam simplicissimum ταυτὸ ac idem: id quod prodigiosè absurdum & blasphemum. Quòd si verò Effectus illos diversos Justitiæ & Misericordiæ in hominibus respicias: tùm sanè diversitas aliqua sese offert: sed nulla prorsus contrarietas. Ratio est, Quia diversi illi Effectus dependent non ab absoluta aliqua sive simplici voluntate Dei: sed à causis subordinatis: ita ut misericordia Dei velit condonare peccata, sed non nisi credentibus in Christum. Quatenùs jam non credunt plurimi, eatenùs Justitia alium ac diversum exerit Effectum, nempè Damnationem: verùm non simpliciter: sed ordinatè: quia non credunt.

Quæ causarum Subordinatarum confideratio omnem tollit contrarietatem, & potiùs contemplandum nobis proponit admirandum illud temperamentum Iustitiæ & Misericordiæ in Deo, ita ut sine ulla Contradictione, sive pugna, Deus quosdam salvare, quosdam verò damnare possit : de quo fusiùs in sequentibus. Sed neque ad hoc argumentum Photinianorum Calviniani solidè respondere possunt, quamdiu absolutam paucorum quorundam salvationem: & rursus absolutam plurimorum. Condemnationem docent propugnant. Quemadmodum sanè Paræo aqua, quod dicitur, hæret, in dissolutione hujus argumenti, primùm concedens Effectus quidem esse contrarios: sed non attributa ipsa: deindè verò sic se, sensu planè Photiniano, explicans: Sicut sol eodem calore ceram liquat, lutum indurat: contraria efficiens in diversis, vel contrariè se habentibus: Ita Deus eâdem voluntate (NB: EADEM) miseretur quorum vult, indurat quos vult: contraria efficiens in diversis, vel contrariè se habentibus Objectis. Ubi notandum, quod secundùm Calvinianorum mentem hanc ipsam contrarietatem in hominibusDeus efficit: dum quorundam homiMinor est falsissima, & simpliciter à nobis negatur: neque in æternum probabit Socinus, Misericordiam & Justitiam Deo inæqualiter, & unam magis, alteram minus inesse: Neque quicquam patrocinij ex eo redundat ad ipsum, quòd in Scripturis Deus perhibetur esse multus in misericordia: tardus verò ad iram. Nam in hujusmodi locis non considerantur Misericordia & justitia, quatenùs Deo insunt, hoc est, quatenùs Essentiales sunt Dei proprietates: sed quatenùs in executione ratione actus secundi spectantur: ubi Deus deprehenditur esse celerior ad miserendum, quàm ad puniendum. Vnde tamen ad extruendam vel majoritatem vel minoritatem in ipsis proprietatibus, secundùm naturam suam, & in complexu Efsentiæ divinæ, in se & per se consideratis, non valet Consequentia.

Nam ἐνεργείαι illæ sive executiones proprietatum divinarum, uti sunt liberrimæ voluntatis, ita inæqualitatem etiam sortiri possunt : salva interim Essentiæ divinæ, & singularum proprietatum manente æqualitate.


### Whether Mercy is an essential property in God: VI. Wretched-

VI. WretchedVI. Mercy is a sickness of the mind, sadness and pain conceived from the misery of another, or from the evils of others: But such a sickness does not fall into the nature of God. Therefore, mercy is also not a natural property of God.

I answer: a shameful sophistry of homonymy is committed in the word Mercy, which is either Human or Divine. Human mercy admits that definition of mercy which Cicero proposes in book 4 of the Tusculan Disputations. Divine mercy does not. For this is nothing other than essential love, favor, goodness, and philanthropy, devoid of all mental pain or perturbation. Nothing. Therefore, the argument concludes.

Latin:

VI. MiseriVI. Misericordia est ægritudo animi, tristitia & dolor ex aliena miseria, sive ex alienis malis conceptus: Atqui talis ægritudo non cadit in naturam Dei. E. Misericordia etiam Deo non est proprietas naturalis.

Respondeo: turpem committi Sophisticatinem ὁμωνυμίας in voce Misericordiæ, quæ vel Humana, vel Divina est. Humana admittit definitionem illam Misericordiæ, quam proponit Cicero l. 4. Tusc. Divina non item. Hæc enim nihil est aliud, quam Effentialis amor, favor, bonitas & Φιλανθρωπία omni destituta animi dolore sive perturbatione. Nihil. Ergo concludit argumentum.


### Subsequent Error of the more recent Photinians Concerning the Mercy of God in the act of justification

That the mercy of God is the antecedent cause, indeed the impulsive cause of our justification, is clearer than to need any proof. For the testimonies of the Scriptures confirm this most evidently. Eph. 2:8, By grace you have been saved. 2 Tim. 1:9, He saved us according to His own purpose and grace, which was given to us in CHRIST JESUS. Tit. 3:7, Being justified by His grace, we are made heirs of eternal life. However, the purer Church of God maintains that this mercy of God is not absolute, but founded solely in CHRIST and His merit and satisfaction. The chief foundations of this our faith are these.

I. God is not only supremely merciful, but also supremely just, which Valentinus Schmalz admits that he and his accomplices willingly grant, although he later contends that neither is natural to God. But this justice of God demanded from the whole human race those punishments which God Himself had denounced in Paradise to our first parents if they should transgress the proposed law. Namely, death or eternal condemnation, as we shall expressly establish with invincible arguments below in the third Controversy. Therefore, there could be no place for the mercy of God before the divine justice had been satisfied; which, if it has not yet been sufficiently accomplished through Christ the Mediator and His merit, let the heretics at last show who has either accomplished it or is ever going to accomplish it, which, however, they can never show. It remains, therefore, settled, firm, and fixed that this mercy of God could have had no place except with respect or regard to the satisfaction of Christ. And indeed, such is the force of this argument that, since the Photinians cannot find anything they can solidly bring forward to infringe upon it, they have devised these two fallacies, not even heard of before in speech, and indeed horrible by their mere external sound: 1. That God was never angry at sin. 2. That there is no vindicatory justice in God, or justice that punishes sins, concerning which the other Controversy will expressly institute a discussion.

II. Scripture itself shows the foundation, which, in describing the act of our justification, almost always expressly joins the mercy of God with the Redemption and Satisfaction of Christ, and indeed with such a satisfaction that consists not merely in showing the way of salvation, as the Photinians grunt, but in the shedding of Blood and the acquisition of salvation. Where that which the Apostle affirms in Rom. 3:24 and 25 holds almost the primary place: that God set forth Christ as a propitiation in His BLOOD; the very words of the Apostle, which are very emphatic, are as follows: Being justified freely by His grace, through the redemption that is in JESUS CHRIST, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith, in His blood, to demonstrate His JUSTICE, through the remission of sins. Which certainly is a unique Apostolic aphorism that, like a thunderbolt, strikes down the blasphemy of these heretics.

For 1. it teaches that we are justified freely by the Grace of God, where all our merit, and thus also repentance by way of Contrition and New obedience, is excluded. 2. It shows that this very Grace of God is not absolute, but founded on the Redemption which was made in Christ. 3. It demonstrates that this Redemption was made or accomplished through the shedding of the blood of Christ. 4. It explains the end for which this Redemption was accomplished through shed blood, and indeed a twofold end: one with respect to God, so that He might thus demonstrate His mercy, and indeed a mercy consistent with the tempering of Justice, since He did not spare His only-begotten Son, but delivered Him up for us; the other with respect to us, so that, namely, through this Redemption of Christ, the Remission of sins might be obtained by us.

The more recent Photinians oppose themselves to this purer doctrine with clearly blasphemous mouth and pen, contending that the mercy of God, by reason of the Effect or our Justification, is simply absolute, and is not in any way founded on the merit, ransom, or Satisfaction of Christ.

The words of Faustus Socinus sound thus in part 3 of his work on Christ, p. 230, chapter 1: Nothing can be devised that is almost more impious than to think that sins are not remitted by God unless they are clearly satisfied for Him.

And a little later: In the sacred writings, he is understood to be just who has lived purely or innocently, but not he who has believed that satisfaction for his sins would either be made to God by Christ at some time, or had already been made.

And p. 235. Unless we wish to maintain that God, in that time which in the divine scriptures is called a time of grace and kindness, was more restricted than in that which, by comparison, can be called a time of severity and wrath: it seems we must absolutely conclude that, in the salvation procured for us by divine providence through Christ, God willed to accept no true satisfaction for our offenses from anyone: but most liberally forgave all those things to us as we were repenting and returning to our senses.

I. God has mercy on whom he wills. Rom. 9, 15. & 18. Exod. 33, 20. Therefore he remits sins by his own mere will and mercy, without any regard for any satisfaction performed through Christ.

And page 236. If only repentance is present, I constantly affirm, and now especially contend, that God, out of his immense goodness, willed to remit our sins without any true satisfaction being accepted, in the new covenant which he deigned to strike with us through Christ. For how would God have been propitious to our iniquities if, when he could remit them to us without any satisfaction intervening, he had taken care that satisfaction be most fully made to him for them? Or how would he not have remembered our sins if he had exacted the punishments for them all so rigidly and exactly from human nature in Christ? Or rather, what is the wonder that he does not impute our iniquities to us, and no longer remembers our sins, if satisfaction has already been made to him most abundantly for our crimes, and he has already remembered them in such a way that he has not left even the least bit unpunished? What kind of munificence and liberality of his is this, which he proclaims so highly, if he was unwilling to remit even the slightest bit of his right?

I reply that a sophism is committed παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχꙋ. For the merciful will of God and the satisfaction of Christ are opposed as if they were contradictories, which are, however, subordinate. Therefore, let the rule of the logicians hold good here too: Subordinate things do not fight, nor do they mutually exclude each other. Now, indeed, that these two things behave as subordinates, even those testimonies of Scripture prove, by which we proved a little earlier that the grace of the remission of sins is founded in the blood, or satisfaction, of Christ. Furthermore, the will in God indeed presupposes liberty: since it is clearly not a will that is not free: but it does not exclude the determination of the will. For that is also a will which acts freely according to a certain order: as when God wills the salvation of all men: but according to an order sanctioned by himself, namely that all should also believe in Christ: thus he wills by the very act to remit sins to all, but to those who believe, that is, to those who apply the satisfaction of Christ to themselves by firm faith: where God always acts freely indeed, but not absolutely. Paraeus sweats in the refutation of this argument, and because he sees snares hidden here, by which the absolute Calvinistic decree of predestination could be bound under the guilt of the same impiety by the Photinians, he devised a clever remedy, distinguishing between a twofold mercy of God concerning the remission of sins and our salvation: one antecedent, which is absolute and constitutes election: the other consequent, which has respect to the merit of Christ, faith, and repentance. To this perversity we oppose with Scripture this immovable axiom: that in God from all eternity there was never any will or mercy with respect to men that was absolute, by which he made any absolute decree of election without regard for the means of salvation. But about this matter elsewhere.

Moreover, before we examine the reasons of these heretics, it must be properly considered: What exactly comes into the question or controversy? In the beginning, therefore, this is not asked: Whether there is in God some absolute goodness and mercy which is founded neither in the merit of Christ nor in any satisfaction? For we ourselves also hold the affirmative. For it is of the absolute will, goodness, and mercy of God that he created this visible world, that he created animals, that he created rational man: that he propagates and preserves the human race to this day: and that he exercises other works of his mercy of that kind, which do not depend at all on the satisfaction of Christ.

Then neither is this controverted: Whether the mercy of God, insofar as it is understood as that divine affection of love by which he is paternally affected toward the human race, is absolute by reason of its principle, or whether it is founded in something else? For here too we reply that mercy in this way, namely with respect to its essential principle, is no less absolute than God himself is a most absolute and most pure being.

II. Isa. 43, 25. I, I am, says the Lord, who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins: Therefore, God remits sins to us absolutely for his own sake, and not for the sake of any satisfaction of Christ.

But this comes into controversy: Whether the mercy of God, insofar as it no longer remains within the most absolute complex of the divine essence, but proceeds as if by a second act outward toward the fallen human race, and remits the punishments due to our sins by the just judgment of God without any regard for divine justice, and thus without any satisfaction rendered to divine justice, exerts the acts and effects of this mercy of His? Concerning which question we hold the negative, moved by those reasons which we explained a little before. The Photinians, however, strive to defend the affirmative, relying chiefly on these arguments.

I answer: again the ἔλεγχον of things wrongly opposed is committed: for the heretics imagine that God Himself and the satisfaction of Christ mutually destroy one another: when nevertheless, by reason of subordination, they agree most correctly. For when Jehovah says: I blot out your iniquities for my own sake, He implies nothing else than that He blots out sins, not for our sake or our repentance, but for His own sake, that is, for this very satisfaction of His. For Christ is that very Jehovah, who with His blood blots out the handwriting that was against us, and cleanses us from all sin Coloss. 2, 14. 1. Joh. 1, 7.

HI. If God did not remit sins absolutely, but on account of the preceding satisfaction of Christ, then the mercy and goodness of God would be preached in the Scriptures clearly in vain. For where there is satisfaction for a debt, there is no gratuitous remission. But this latter is absurd; therefore, the former is as well.

I answer that a fallacy of the vicious consequent is committed. For the mercy of God is not preached in the Scriptures in vain because it is founded upon the satisfaction of Christ, but rather it shines forth more clearly from that very fact. For this very satisfaction of Christ is a truly gratuitous effect of divine mercy. For, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 5:8 and 10, in this God commends his love most especially, that when we were enemies, and every satisfaction was lacking on our part, he not only had mercy on us and thought paternally about receiving us into favor, but also, so that his justice, which demanded eternal punishments from us on account of sin, might be satisfied, he satisfied himself, having delivered his only-begotten Son to death, who in our place and stead would expiate every offense. This truly stupendous mercy of God is so great that the Holy Spirit is everywhere most occupied in preaching it, especially in John 3:16. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. And Rom. 8:32: God spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us.

Then, the proof of the major premise is not simply and absolutely true.
