For even these, of themselves and by themselves, are by nature children of wrath, and stained with sin, and therefore, according to the immutable justice of GOD, considered in this way, they can in no way be either purified or judged as innocent. Whence Isaiah also compares his own righteousness, and that of all the penitent, to a menstruous cloth, Isa. 64, and Paul to dung, Philip. 3. Therefore this first foundation of Socinus collapses, by which he thought he would confirm that first species of divine Justice, restricted to the impenitent alone.

The second Testimony, by which Socinus wishes to confirm that second and indeed mutable species of divine Justice, he seeks from Exodus ch. 33, v. 19. I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious. Likewise Rom. 9:18. He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens. Therefore there is some Justice in GOD not perpetual, but mutable, which He uses according to His own pleasure, now rigidly without indulgence, now indeed more leniently with indulgence.

But this argument was answered above, in the Examination of the second Error of the Photinians concerning the Mercy of GOD: Objection 1. In this place, this must be kept in mind, that an agnoia elenchou and a Sophistry of the vicious Consequent is being committed. For neither did Moses or the Apostle wish to signify this, nor does it follow in any way from their words: GOD exercises His mercy toward the penitent by His free will, and not so toward others: Therefore a peculiar Justice ought to be established in GOD, namely a mutable one, by which He uses it toward the penitent: but only this follows: Therefore there are distinct degrees of one and the same immutable divine Justice: so that He acts more leniently with the penitent: more harshly and rigidly with the impenitent, in both cases freely indeed, but not absolutely, as was shown above. Then it must also be noted that Socinus wishes this will of GOD, by which He freely has mercy, to be bound to the mere repentance of men, without any respect to faith, relying on the Satisfaction of Christ: And conversely, he wishes the will of GOD, by which He freely hardens, to be bound to mere impenitence, without regard for unbelief, despising the Satisfaction of Christ: which Socinus has not yet demonstrated from the Scriptures, nor will he ever be able to demonstrate in eternity. We have irrefragably proven the contrary above from the oracles of the Scriptures: But enough concerning the second argument of the Photinians. III. He adds an argument: Whomever God has always loved from eternity: He could not at the same time be angry with them: For thus two contraries would exist in God with respect to one and the same object, which is blasphemously absurd. But God has loved the entire human race, however much corrupted and polluted by sin, from all eternity, as is evident from chapter 5 to the Romans, v. 8, 9, 10. God commends his love, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us: much more therefore, now justified in his blood, we shall be saved from WRATH through him: For if when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son: much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved in his life. And Eph. 1, 4. He chose us in him before the foundation of the world. Therefore God could not at the same time be angry with the human race, being indeed eternally loved and reconciled, on account of the sin adhering to it. I answer that a fallacy is committed ὥς πῃ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς: For the major premise is true only concerning the absolute love of God, but not concerning the ordered love. Now as for the minor premise, God indeed loved the entire human race from all eternity, but not absolutely and simply: but in an ordered manner, namely in his beloved Son. Which ordered love includes and respects the Son likewise not absolutely, or only in that respect ordered, insofar as God willed him to be the Teacher of the human race: but also thus ordered, insofar as he himself took upon himself the guilt of our sins, and satisfied for the whole human race, the wrath or divine Justice. This ordered Charity or love of God therefore necessarily presupposes His Wrath, so that this love could not have had a place in God before this wrath or divine Justice had been satisfied at the same time from all eternity through the Son, who offered himself as Mediator between God and men from eternity. This is evident from those very passages of the Scriptures which are produced by the Adversaries. For the Apostle hints at both: 1. That this Charity of God is ordered, or determined to the death of the Son. 2. That the WRATH OF GOD is taken away through Christ in his blood. Thus Eph. 2 likewise does not say absolutely: God chose us before the foundation of the world: but in an ordered manner, God chose us in Christ: and soon he adds the mode of this ordered Election: in Christ, saying, we have Redemption through his Blood etc. We conclude therefore that God loved men from eternity, but not absolutely: not likewise, insofar as they were sinners: but insofar as they are redeemed by the blood of the Son, and reconciled to God: where the Charity and Wrath of God could stand together without any contradiction, namely in a different respect: Wrath, to wit, with regard to Men considered in themselves, by themselves, and from their own nature, as sinners: for in this way they are by nature children of wrath Eph. 2, 3. But Charity and love, with regard to Men, no longer considered from themselves and by themselves, but in

Christ and his Satisfaction, as the redeemed and reconciled.

THE FOURTH and last argument is that Socinus contends that the Justice by which God loves justice and hates iniquity, and destroys those who sin, is not of the nature of God, nor is it any Essential and infinite property of God, but belongs to God contingently, as an effect of free will, which he can freely will or not will, just as he can freely will to rain tomorrow, or not to rain. Therefore he infers that there was no necessity that the Justice of God should be satisfied through Christ.

I answer that Socinus is babbling and basely begging the question. For what he says, he does not prove. For although he seems to contend with three reasons, as 1. That if such Justice were natural to God, then he could not remit even the least sin, because the Natural attributes of God behave immutably, 2. That to punish sins and to pardon sins are things clearly contrary, and incompatible with one divine Nature. 3. That God cannot be said to be slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy: yet he wanders outside the olive groves and does not touch the nerve. For these and other similar reasons do not contend except against that absolute Justice of God, by which he is most absolutely just in himself. Now, however, since this vindicatory Justice of God exerts itself towards men not absolutely, but under a certain condition and in an ordered manner: while indeed he testifies in his word that he will not punish eternally except the impenitent and unbelievers: but towards the faithful he will declare his gentleness, which is tempered both by mercy and by the Satisfaction of Christ: certainly these reasons prove nothing at all.

Moreover, there are ready at hand most evident reasons by which it can be demonstrated that that vindicatory Justice of God is an Essential attribute of God, and not some Contingent Effect of the will: where, however, it is to be noted that the Controversy in this place is not about the Effects themselves, which proceed from the vindicatory Justice of God: but about the cause or acting Principle, which we simply deny to be contingent in God.

1. In God there are no affections distinct from his Essence: Therefore much less is Contingency granted in him. The antecedent is evident from this, Because God is devoid of all change, as he is of Composition: and therefore those things which obtain the status of affections in Creatures, those in God are not really distinct from God himself. Now if such divine attributes were to undergo the definition of Contingent things, they would certainly be something really distinct from the Essence of God: which is absurd. For whatever God is, that he is by absolute necessity, on account of the most simple purity of his Essence. But every Contingent thing is opposed either to the necessity of coercion: or to immutable necessity. Therefore a Contingent thing cannot stand with that immutable Simplicity of the divine Essence.

2. Every Contingent thing derives its denomination from Causes, which by reason of the Effect could have behaved otherwise in time, before they

are deduced from the effect. And yet the Mercy and Justice of God depend upon a cause which cannot be otherwise, nor do they derive their denomination from the effect, which finally comes to pass in time. Therefore, the Mercy and Justice of God reject every nature of contingency. The minor premise is evident from the fact that Scripture names the Mercy of God everlasting mercy (Is. 54:8; Jer. 31:3). Now, indeed, with respect to us, it cannot be called eternal, because it exerts itself toward us only in time, and indeed can even be shaken off and completely extinguished through impenitence. It remains, therefore, that Mercy and Justice are predicated of God as eternal because they inhere in Him essentially.

3. Rom. 1:32, the Apostle says: It is known to men by nature that the Justice of God is such that those who do such things are worthy of death. Hence I conclude thus: If this vindicatory Justice of God is known to men by nature, it is certainly necessary that it be natural to God as well. But the former is true, as the Apostle testifies. Therefore, the latter is also true. I prove the connection of the major premise thus: The natural preconceptions (προλήψεις) of men, such as that God punishes sinners according to His justice, are universal and immutable. But for them to be such, it is necessary that they rest upon a universal and immutable foundation, such as can neither be given nor conceived in eternity other than the NATURE of God, which does not contingently, but by the condition of its own Nature, punish and pursue with hatred all iniquity.

Furthermore, this is irrefragably evident from the scope and intention of the Apostle. For he wishes to prove that the Gentiles are therefore without excuse (ἀναπολογήτους), because they knew by nature that this is that Justice of God which vindicates, that those who pollute themselves with crimes are worthy of death; yet they, with this natural knowledge of divine Justice protesting, did not glorify as God the God whom they acknowledged, but treated Him with contumely; certainly, he infers even from this that their condemnation is just. Now, if according to the opinion of Socinus, this vindicatory Justice were not natural to God, but only contingent, so that He might also freely not punish sins, then indeed the entire nerve of the Apostolic argumentation would have been cut. Let the Photinians see, therefore, whether they are not even worse than the Gentiles for this reason, that the latter always acknowledged and believed in the vindicatory Justice of God in God, while they themselves stubbornly deny it.

4. The highest and most perfect equality of all essential divine properties in no way admits any contingent Justice in God, such that they, considered within the most simple essence (ὐσία) of God, receive neither more nor less. Nor does it stand in the way that God is reported in the Scriptures to be slow to anger and readier to show mercy. For in such sayings, Justice and Mercy are considered not within that most absolute essence (ὐσία) of God, insofar as they are a certain most pure, most simple act, differing in no part, but insofar as they now proceed outward in a second act. Now, just as in the effects of divine Omnipotence, the first act, namely omnipotence, is of most absolute necessity, but the second act is of most free will, and He can declare His omnipotence either more or less; so the first act of divine Justice, which turns away from all iniquity and loves all Justice, is of most absolute necessity in God, but the second act depends upon His free will, so that He may punish sins either more or less. Therefore, when God is readier and swifter to exercise works of Mercy than works of Justice, this does not constitute any contingent justice in God, but only shows that God, outwardly according to His most free will and with regard to the second act, prefers that works of mercy preponderate over works of Justice; a fact which, however, detracts nothing at all from the natural and vindicatory Justice of God. Hence God, in Is. 28:21, is said to perform a strange work when He is angry and inflicts punishments upon men: not simply (ἁπλῶς), as if He were acting in this way contrary to His nature, but in a certain respect and comparatively (κατὰ τὶ), because God is indeed so loving toward us that if at any time He has need to punish, He then seems to perform a work that is, as it were, strange; or because for this very reason He mostly sends punishments, so that there may subsequently be room for His beneficence.

5. If the Law of God is the immutable norm of divine Justice, then this Justice which punishes transgressions of the law will not be some contingent effect of the divine will, but will be an immutable and, consequently, a natural property in God. The reason is that to be immutable and contingent with respect to one and the same cause and effect implies a contradiction. But the antecedent is true. Therefore, the consequent is valid.

6. The attribute of will is predicated of God improperly and figuratively according to human passion (κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν), and not as in men, either as an affection, or some motion, or a desire for the good or the apparent good with reason (τῆς ἀγαθῆς, ἢ φαινομένης ἀγαθῆς μετὰ λόγου ὄρεξιν); but, as Damascenus speaks, it denotes a providential, cohesive, and creative power (δύναμιν προνοητικὴν, συνεκτικὴν, ποιητικὴν), namely an essential virtue or power by which God both in general wills and most wisely effects, rules, and governs individual and universal human actions, pursuits, and counsels by a most free act, or most justly detests, punishes, and directs them to the end serving His glory; and in particular, He wills, cares for, ordains, perfects, and completes the salvation of the Elect. It would therefore be absurd to posit the Mercy of God forgiving sins and the Justice of God vindicating them as a contingent effect of this will.

Latin:

Deindè turpiter confundunt Adversarii actum primum Justitiæ DEI, cum actu secundo. Neque enim, quia actus secundus est liberrimæ voluntatis in DEO; vel exerceri vel retrahi potest, ideò quoque in DEO statuenda est peculiaris aliqua Justitiæ species, quæ mutabilitati subjaceat. Nam Justitia DEI, quatenùs est attributum DEI, semper cum Essentia convertitur, & haud magis atque Essentia DEI est in species dividua. Actus verò secundus est liberæ voluntatis: verùm non absolutus, sed determinatus, hinc quidem ad pœnitentes, illinc ad impœnitentes. Horum respectu, cum ira ac furore: illorum verò cum misericordia conjunctus. Misericordiæ enim divinæ, & quidem cum Justitia quadam temperata est, si pœnitentes etiam interdum corripiat, ut tantò studiofius cum timore ac tremore operentur salutem, neq; cum mundo condemnentur, 1. Cor. 11, 32. Cæterùm quòd DEUS pœnitentes non semper pœnis affligit, provenit id non ex singulari quâdam Justitiæ divinæ specie: sed ex temperamento illo Justitiæ & misericordiæ divinæ: ratione cujus DEUS erga pœnitentes rigorem Justitiæ suæ non exercet: propterea, quòd illas CHRISTUS ipsorum vice sustinuit, sic attestante Jesaia cap. 53, 5. Disciplina pacis super eum, & livore ipsius sanati sumus.

Sed excipit Socinus, & ex Scripturis Sacris duo profert Testimonia: Unum ex cap. 34. Exodi v. 6. & 7. Jehovah, Jehovah fortis, misericors & miserator, tardus ad iram, & multus misericordiâ & veritate: servans misericordem millibus: auferens iniquitatem & prævaricationem, & peccatum, & qui absolvendo non absolvat. Hic, inquit Socinus, postquàm se impensè misericordiam esse, peccataq; condonare professus est, ait: Quique absolvendo non absolvat. Ea autem nihil aliud significare videntur, quàm Dominum propensissimum quidem esse ad misericordiam, & ad delicta hominibus condonanda: sed tamen eos non absolvere, qui nocentes & rebelles esse pergunt, propter primam illam suam & immutabilem Justitiam.

Respondeo: 1. Extra oleas vagati hæreticum. Nam de Justitia hac DEI immutabiliter puniente præfractos & contumaces peccatores, nos litem nemini movemus. Hanc ipsam eum nos ipsi urgemus & defendimus, sed hoc in Quæstione est: An præter hanc perpetuam & immutabilem Justitiam DEI, alia species Justitiæ divinæ constitui possit & debeat, quæ non sit perpetua, sed mutabilis? id quod nos adversus Socinimterum atque iterum negamus. Duo autem hoc loco observanda veniunt. 1. άσυστασία sive inconstantia Socini, qui sibi ipsi turpiter contradicit. Nam hoc loco pugnat, Esse in DEO Justitiam perpetuam & immutabilem, quâ puniat nocentes & rebelles: sed part. 3 cap. 1. p. 224. expressè scribit: Nullam in DEO esse justitiam, quæ peccatum omninò puniri debere dictitet. Imò pag. 10. scribit: Genus humanum morti æternæ obnoxium esse, non ex aliquâ DEI Justitia necessariò: sed ex libera ejus voluntate. Deindè verò notanda venit gemina depravatio dicti Mosaici, quod Socinus citat. Nam 1. existimat illud agere tantùm de impœnitentibus: id quod cum toto contextu è diametro pugnat, qui in eo unicè occupatus est, ut demonstret immensam DEI misericordiam, non certè erga impœnitentes: sed pœnitentes: quemadmodum Moses ipse se explicat Deut. 5, 9. asserens, DEUM facere misericordiam in multa millia, sed eorum, qui diligunt eum, & præcepta ejus custodiant. Quam notacionem non nisi pœnitentibus competere, per se manifestum est. Altera textus depravatio Sotini est, quòd verba Hebræa, Exod. 34. vers. 7. וְנַקֵּה לֹא יְנַקֶּה Venakkeh lo Jenakkeh reddit, absolvendo non absolvam, hoc est, peccatum remittendo non remittam: ut sic sententiæ suæ fucum faciat, nempè, solos impœnitentes esse Objectum immutabilis illius divinæ Justitiæ: cùm hic potiùs verus & germanus sit verborum Mosis sensus, peccatum non agnoscam pro non peccato: vel peccatum purificando non purificabit DEUS: vel ut alii reddiderunt: innocentem judicando, non innocentem judicabit. Quæ sanè omnia ad pœnitentes quoque accommodari debent. Nam & hi ex se & per se, naturâ sunt filii iræ, & peccato inquinati, ac proindè secundum immutabilem DEI justitiam, hoc modo considerati, nullo pacto vel purificari, vel pro innocentibus judicari possunt. Undè Jesaias quoque, suam & omnium pœnitentium justitiam comparatam, confert cum panno menstruatæ Jesa. 64. & Paulus cum stercoribus. Philip. 3. Corruit proindè primum hoc fundamentum Socini, quò primam illam Justitiæ divinæ speciem, ad solos impœnitentes restrictam se confirmaturum opinatus est.

Alterum Testimonium, quò secundam illam & quidem mutabilem Justitiæ divinæ speciem, vult confirmare Socinus, petit ex cap. 33. Exod. v. 19. Miserebor, cujus miserebor, & clemens ero, in quem clemens ero. Item Rom. 9, 18. Cujus vult miseretur, & quem vult indurat. Ergò est aliqua Justitia in DEO non perpetua, sed mutabilis, quâ nimirùm pro libitu suo utitur, nunc rigidè sine indulgentia, nunc verò remissiùs cum indulgentia.

Sed ad hoc argumentum supra responsum est, in Examine Erroris secundi Photinianorum de Misericordia DEI: Objectione 1. Hoc loco illud pensi habendum, quòd committatur ἀγνοια ἐλέγχε & Sophisticatio vitiosi Consequentis. Neque enim vel Moses vel Apostolus hoc significare voluerunt, vel etiam ex verbis ipsorum ullo pacto sequitur: DEUS libera sua voluntate erga pœnitentes exercet suam misericordiam, erga alios non item: Ergò peculiaris constitui debet in DEO Justitia, nempè mutabilis, quâ erga pœnitentes utatur: sed illud tantùm sequitur: Ergò unius ejusdemq; immutabilis Justitiæ divinæ sunt distincti gradus: ita ut remifsiùs agat cum pœnitentibus: duriùs & rigidiùs cum impœnitentibus, utrobiq; liberè quidem, sed non absolutè, uti supra ostensum. Deindè notandum quoque, quòd Socinus hanc voluntatem DEI, quâ liberè miseretur, vult esse alligatam ad solam hominum pœnitentiam, sine ullo respectu fidei, nitentis Satisfactione Christi: Et vice versa voluntatem DEI, quâ liberè indurat, vult esse alligatam ad solam impœnitentiam, sine intuitu incredulitatis, contemnentis Satisfactionem Christi: id quod Socinus nondum ex Scripturis demonstravit, neque in æternum demonstrare poterit. Diversum nos supra ex Scripturarum oraculis irrefragabiliter evicimus: Sed satis de argumento Photinianorum secundo. HI. Argumentum supplet: Quoscunque Deus semper ab æterno dilexit: illis non potuit simul irasci: Sic enim duo contraria respectu unius ejusdemq́; objecti, in Deo essent, quòd est blasphemè absurdum. Atqui Deus universum genus humanum, quantumvis peccato corruptum & pollutum, jam indè ab omni æternitate dilexit, uti patet ex cap. 5. ad Rom. v. 8, 9, 10. Commendat charitatem suam Deus, quoniam cùm adhuc peccatores essem9, Christus pro nobis mortuus est: multò igitur magis nunc justificati in sanguine ipsius, salvi erimus ab IRA per ipsum: Si enim cùm inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus cum Deo, per mortem Filij ejus: multò magis reconciliati salvi erimus in vita ipsius. Et Ephes. 1, 4. Elegit nos in ipso ante mundi constitutionem. Ergò Deus non potuit simul generi humano, quippe æternùm dilecto & reconciliato, propter peccatum adhærens irasci. Respondeo committi Sophisma ὥς πῃ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἅπλῶς : Major enim vera tantùm est de absoluta Dei dilectione, non verò de ordinata. Jam quoad Minorem, dilexit quidem Deus jam indè ab omni æternitate universum genus humanum, sed non absolutè & simpliciter : sed ordinatè nempè in Filio suo dilecto. Quæ ordinata dilectio, includit & respicit Filium itidem non absolutè, vel eo tantùm respectu ordinatè, quatenus Deus ipsum voluit esse Doctorem generis humani : sed & sic ordinatè, quatenus ipse peccatorum nostrorum reatum in se recepit, & pro toto genere humano, iræ sive Justitiæ divinæ satisfecit. Præsupponit ergò ordinata hæc Charitas sive dilectio Dei, necessariò Iram ipsius, ita ut dilectio hæc in Deo non potuerit prius habere locum, quàm simul ab omni æternitate iræ huic sive Justitiæ divinæ esset satisfactum per Filium, qui Mediatorem se inter Deum & homines ab æterno obtulit. Patet hoc ex illis ipsis Scripturarum locis, quæ ab Adversarijs producuntur. Nam utrumque innuit Apostolus: 1. Quòd Charitas hæc Dei sit ordinata, sive determinata ad mortem Filij. 2. Quòd IRA DEI sit sublata per Christum in sanguine ipsius. Sic Ephes. 2. itidem non absolutè dicit: Deus nos elegit ante constitutionem mundi : sed ordinatè, Deus in Christo nos elegit : & mox subijcit Ordinatæ hujus Electionis modum : in Christo, inquiens, habemus Redemptionem per Sanguinem ejus &c Concludimus proindè Deum ab æterno dilexisse homines, sed non absolutè : non item, quatenus erant peccatores: sed quatenus sanguine Filij sunt redempti,& Deo reconciliati : ubi Charitas & Ira Dei simul stare potuerunt sine ulla contradictione, diverso nimirum respectu : Ira videlicet, quoad Homines in se, per se, & ex sua naturâ consideratos, ut peccatores : hoc enim modo sunt naturâ Filij iræ Ephes. 2,3. Charitas verò & dilectio, quoad Homines, non ampliùs ex se & per se consideratos, sed in

Christo ejusdemque Satisfactione, ut redemtos & reconciliatos.

QVARTUM & postremum argumentum est, quòd Socinus contendit, Iustitiam illam, quâ Deus justitiam diligit & iniquitatem odit, & peccantes destruit, non esse de naturâ Dei, neq; esse aliquam Essentialem ac infinitam Dei proprietatem, sed Deo contingenter inesse, ut effectum liberæ voluntatis, quem liberè possit velle vel non velle, quemadmodum liberè potest velle, cras pluere, vel non pluere. Ergò subinfert, nihil necessum erat, ut Justitia Dei per Christum satisfaceret.

Respondeo, Socinum ἀδολεχεῖν ac turpiter petere principium. Nam quod dicit, non probat. Etsi enim tribus rationibus militare videtur, ut 1. Quòd si talis Justitia esset Deo naturalis, tum nec minimum ipse peccatum remittere posset, quia Naturalia Dei immutabiliter se habent, 2. Quòd peccata punire & peccata condonare, res sint planè contrariæ, ac uni Naturæ divinæ incompetibiles. 3. Quod non possit Deus dici tardus esse ad iram, & multus misericordiâ: tamen extra oleas vagatur & nervum non tangit. Hæ enim & consimiles rationes aliæ non militant, nisi contra absolutam illam Dei Justitiam, quâ ipse in seipso absolutissimè est justus. Jam verò cùm hæc Justitia Dei vindicatrix non absolutè, sed certâ conditione & ordinatè sese exerat erga homines: dum nimirum in verbo suo attestatur, se non nisi impœnitentes & incredulos æternùm puniturum: erga fideles verò τὸ ἐπιεικὲς declaraturum, quod temperatum sit tum misericordia, tum Satisfactione Christi: utique rationes hæ prorsus nihil evincunt.

Cæterùm in promptu sunt rationes evidentissimæ, quibus demonstrari queat, Justitiam illam Dei vindicatricem, esse Essentiale Dei attributum, non verò Contingens aliquod voluntatis Effectum: ubi tamen notandum, Controversiam hoc loco esse non de Effectis ipsis, qui ex Justitia Dei vindicatrice proveniunt: sed de causa sive Principio agente, quòd in Deo contingens esse, simpliciter negamus.

1. In Deo nullæ dantur affectiones, ab ipsius Essentia distinctæ: Ergò multò minus conceditur in ipso Contingentia. Antecedens indè patet, Quia Deus omnis uti mutationis: sic Compositionis est expers: ac proinde ea quæ in Creaturis affectionum rationem obtinent, ea in Deo ab ipso Deo realiter non sunt distincta. Jam verò si Contingentium definitionem hujusmodi divina attributa subirent, utique essent aliquid ab Essentia Dei realiter distinctum: id quod absurdum. Quicquid enim Deus est, id absoluta necessitate est, propter simplicissimam Essentiæ puritatem. Atqui omne Contingens opponitur vel necessitati coactionis: vel necessitati immutabili. Ergò Contingens cum immutabili illa Simplicitate Essentiæ divinæ stare nequit.

2. Omne Contingens denominationem fortitur, à Causis, quæ ratione Effectus in tempore aliter se habere potuissent, priusquàm in

Effectum sunt deductæ. Atqui Misericordia & Justitia Dei dependent à causâ, quæ aliter se habere nequit, neque ab Effectu demùm, qui fit in tempore, denominationem sortiuntur. Ergò Misericordia & Justitia Dei omnem Contingentiæ naturam respuunt, Minor vel indè patet, quod Scriptura Misericordiam Dei nominat Misericordiam sempiternam Es. 54, 8. Jerem. 31, 3. Jam verò ratione nostri, non potest dici æterna, quia in tempore saltem erga nos ea sese exerit, quin etiam per impœnitentiam excuti & planè extingui potest. Relinquitur ergò Misericordiam & Justitiam æternam ideò de Deo prædicari, quia Essentialiter ipsi insunt.

3. Rom. 1, 32. inquit Apostolus: Hominibus naturâ notum est Jus Dei, quod qui talia agunt, digni sunt morte. Hinc sic colligo: Si Justitia hæc Dei vindicatrix hominibus naturâ est nota: utiq; Deo etiam naturalis ea sit necesse est: Atqui prius verum, teste Apostolo. Ergo & posterius Connexum Majoris sic probo: Naturales προλήψεις hominum; qualis est, quòd Deus secundùm justitiam suam puniat peccatores, sunt Universales & immutabiles. Atqui ut tales sint, Universali iidem & immutabili fundamento nitantur necesse est: Quale in æternum nullum aliud dari aut excogitari potest, præter NATURAM Dei: quæ non contingenter, sed ex conditione Naturæ suæ puniat & odio prosequatur omnem iniquitatem.

Deindè patet hoc irrefragabiliter, ex scopo atque intentione Apostoli. Vult enim probare, ideò Gentiles esse ἀναπολογήτους, quia naturâ noverint, hoc esse Jus illud Dei vindicantis, quòd qui sceleribus se pollunt, digni sint morte: ipsi verò reclamante hac naturali Justitiæ divinæ notitiâ, Deum quem agnoverunt, non ut Deum glorificaverint: sed contumeliâ affecerint: utique vel indè infert, damnationem ipsorum esse justam. Jam si ex sententia Socini, Justitia hæc vindicatrix Deo non esset naturalis, sed tantùm Contingens: ita ut liberè etiam peccata non puniat: tum profectò argumentationi Apostolicæ nervus omnis esset incisus. Viderint proindè Photiniani, an non vel ideò Gentilibus sint deteriores, quòd illi Justitiam Dei vindicatricem, in Deo semper agnoverunt, & crediderunt, ipsi verò eam mordicus negant.

4. Contingentem aliquam Justitiam in Deo, summa & perfectissima æqualitas omnium proprietatum Essentialium divinarum nullatenùs admittit: ita ut eæ intra simplicisfimam Dei ὐσίαν consideratæ, neq; magis neque minus recipiant. Neque obstat, quod Deus tardus ad iram, & promptior ad misericordiam esse, in Scripturis perhibetur. Nam in hujusmodi dictis considerantur Justitia & Misericordia, non intra absolutissimam illam Dei ὐσίαν, quatenùs sunt actus quidam purissimus, simplicissimus, nullaque ex parte discrepans: sed quatenùs jam foràs progrediuntur actu secundo. Jam jam quemadmodum in Effectis Omnipotentiæ divinæ, actus primus, nempè omnipotentia absolutissimæ est necessitatis: actus verò secundus, est liberrimæ voluntatis: & vel magis vel minùs, Omnipotentiam suam declarare potest: Ita actus primus Justitiæ divinæ, aversantis omnem iniquitatem, & diligentis omnem Justitiam, est absolutissimæ necessitatis in Deo: actus verò secundus dependet à libera ipsius voluntate, ut vel magis vel minùs peccata punire possit. Proindè quando Deus promptior & celerior est ad exercenda opera Misericordiæ, quàm ad opera Justitiæ: id non Contingentem aliquam in Deo justitiam constituit: sed tantùm ostendit, Deum ad extra pro liberrima sua voluntate, & quoad actum secundum, malle misericordiæ opera præponderare operibus Justitiæ: id quod tamen Justitiæ Dei naturali & vindicatrici, nihil quicquam derogat. Hinc Deus Ies. 28. 21. perhibetur alienum opus exequi, quando iratus hominibus pœnas infligit: non ἁπλῶς, quasi præter naturam suam hoc pacto agat: sed κατὰ τὶ & comparatè, quòd nimirum usque adeò Deus sit amans nostri, ut si quando punire necessum habet, tunc quasi alienum opus exequi videatur: vel quod hanc ipsam ob causam pœnas plerumque immittat, ut deinceps locus esse queat ipsius beneficentiæ.

5. Si Lex Dei est immutabilis norma Justitiæ divinæ: utique Justitia hæc puniens transgressiones legis, non erit Contingens aliquis Effectus voluntatis divinæ, sed erit immutabilis, & per Consequens, naturalis proprietas in Deo: Ratio est: quia immutabiliter & Contingenter se habere, respectu unius ejusdemque Causæ & Effectus, Contradictionem implicant. Atqui antecedens verum. Ratum ergò & posterius.

6. Voluntatis attributum, impropriè planè & figuratè κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν de Deo prædicatur, neque ut in hominibus, vel affectum, vel motum aliquem, vel τῆς ἀγαθῆς, ἢ φαινομένης ἀγαθῆς μετὰ λόγου ὄρεξιν; sed, ut Damascenus loquitur, notat δύναμιν προνοητικὴν, συνεκτικὴν, ποιητικὴν Essentialem nimirùm virtutem, sive potentiam, quâ Deus tùm in genere singulas atque universas hominum actiones, studia, consilia, liberrimo actu vel vult, & sapientissimè efficit, regit, gubernat: vel justissimè detestatur, punit, & ad finem gloriæ suæ servientem dirigit: in specie verò Electorum salutem vult, curat, ordinat, perficit, absolvit. Absurdum proindè fuerit voluntatis hujus Effectum Contingens statuere Misericordiam Dei condonantem, & Justitiam Dei vindicantem peccata.


### A Special Controversy Against the recent Photinians, On the Satisfaction for our Sins

On SATISFACTION FOR our Sins.

But what need is there of many words, when it is permitted to perceive this stupendous blasphemy of these heretics more than enough, and even to the point of astonishment, from the very reasonings and arguments of theirs, with which they are accustomed to fight in this place. The legitimate status of this controversy emerges as follows: Whether God forgives sins to men on account of the most sufficient Satisfaction of Christ, apprehended by faith: Or indeed without any such Satisfaction from the mere good pleasure of His own will? We embrace the former part of this status affirmatively, intending to set forth its foundations shortly in the refutation of the objections: but we simply deny the latter: which the Photinians strive with all their might to obtain by these arguments in particular.

We have thus far dispatched the primary foundation which the modern Photinians lay beneath their heresy, or rather their blasphemy, in the present article. For the fact that they have thus far argued that the Mercy of God forgiving sins is simply absolute, and not founded upon any merit; and likewise that they have contended that there is no natural vindicatory Justice in God, or one that punishes sins, aims solely at this: that they might thus persuade the more incautious that, for the reconciliation of the human race and the perfecting of its Justification and salvation, there was no need at all for any Satisfaction to be rendered, either through Christ or through anyone else. For they maintain and write that sins are forgiven, and men are saved from eternal death, by the sole free will and absolute grace of God, provided that the men themselves repent and do penance. These are their principal flowers and emblems.

I. Christopher Osterodus of Goslar proposes the argument thus. The first reason why we maintain this is that in Holy Scripture there is nowhere any mention of that Satisfaction, not even in one little word, nor anywhere of any other thing that would have the same meaning: which could happen to be very strange if the opinion concerning merit were true: Indeed, it would not be enough if it were mentioned a few times, but it would be necessary that it be mentioned as often and as many times in Holy Scripture as we see it being incessantly inculcated in the writings and sermons of our adversaries. Socinus has this same reasoning also in book 2 on Christ, chapter 26, page 219.

The second argument coincides with this first one, by which they contend that nowhere in the Scriptures is there found an equivalent doctrine that Christ by His death reconciled God to us, that He paid to divine justice the penalties due to our sins: that He gave His blood to divine justice as the λύτρον (ransom) of our redemption: and that He freed us from the hands of God: that He compensated for our disobedience with His obedience: that He merited for us the remission of sins: or finally that He appeased the wrath of God for us: Therefore they infer that the Satisfaction of Christ is asserted without and beyond the authority of the Scriptures.

1. Not only does the word 'satisfaction,' or 'making satisfaction,' nowhere appear in the Holy Scriptures when the subject is the salvation obtained for us through Christ: but nothing of the kind is found written in them expressly, not even once. For it is nowhere read that Christ reconciled God to us by His death: that by dying He paid to divine justice all the penalties due to our iniquities: that He freed us from the hands of divine justice by giving His blood to it as the price of our redemption: that He compensated for our crimes by His obedience, or that He truly merited that God should bestow upon us the remission of sins: or finally, at least, that He appeased the wrath of God for us in any way. Faustus Socinus, part 2, on Christ the Savior, chapter 26, page 218.

I answer: the whole structure of these arguments is faulty. 1. With the fallacy of the consequent: for besides the fact that the demand is altogether impudent, by which they insist that we demonstrate where the word 'satisfy' and the term 'satisfaction' exist in the Scriptures αὐτὸ γράφμα (in the very writing) and αύτολεξεί (in the very words): yet the argument concludes nothing, even if the matter were exactly so. For if the Satisfaction of Christ were to be denied because that term is not found in the letters and syllables of the sacred texts regarding this matter; then certainly the Photinians themselves would have to abjure most of their own dogmas, since they are not expressed in the same letters and syllables in the Scriptures. But now, since they themselves maintain that one should look not so much to the tips of the letters as to the sense of the Scriptures regarding the constitution of the articles of faith: as Faustus Socinus himself judges in the disputation on the invocation of Christ, instituted against Franciscus Davidis, chapter 1. What, I ask, is this, whether it be perversity or impudence, to prescribe to others laws of unworthy servitude which one refuses to bear oneself?

2. That God could rightly forgive us, without any true satisfaction for our sins being accepted, can be established from the fact that our offenses render us liable to God, and can be seen to require that satisfaction be made to Him for them, insofar as they are an offense against His own majesty: so that for God to forgive sins, without a true satisfaction for them being accepted, is nothing other than for Him to remit His own right. Moreover, it is permitted for everyone to remit as much of their own right as they wish. God, therefore, without a true satisfaction for them being accepted, could rightly pardon our sins. part 3. cap. 1. pag. 221.

3. Holy Scripture confirms nothing other than this throughout, that God remits our sins, out of the full liberty of His will, and out of mere grace freely, out of great love and mercy, without any recompense or satisfaction, which excludes that supereminent grace of God. Christoph: Osterodus cap. 36.

Nay, what blindness is this, to deny the Satisfaction of Christ for the reason that the forensic term itself of Satisfaction or Satisdation does not exist in the Scriptures, when nevertheless the thing itself is expressed in them more clearly than the sun by equivalent terms, such as λύτρον, ἀντίλυτρον, λύτρωσις, ἀπολύτρωσις, ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, ἀνταπόδοσις, and others of that kind, as will be demonstrated a little later.

Furthermore, it is a notable lie that they keep writing that the equivalent doctrine concerning the Satisfaction of Christ is not contained in the Scriptures. In order to overturn and trample this to the ground, the principal foundations of our doctrine must be drawn from the Scriptures and opposed to their impiety.

We seek the FIRST from chapter 2, 17 of Genesis: On whatever day you eat from this tree, you shall die the death. This threat had to be fulfilled necessarily after the fall of our first parents, because the truth and Justice of God is immutable, and God knows not how to lie. But if God had remitted this truth of His, or as the Photinians say, had remitted His Right, and had embraced the human race with His mercy without any Satisfaction, then God would have lied, saying: You shall die the death. Therefore, while this truth and justice of God stands unmoved, the human race either had to perish eternally, or could not be redeemed from this punishment except by the intervention of a most absolute Satisfaction: But this could be accomplished by no mortal. Therefore, it was necessary that it be accomplished through the Son of God, Christ the Savior.

The second foundation of our assertion is shown by that first promise of the Gospel in Genesis 3, 15: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent: Therefore, the remission of sins and the pardon of eternal punishment could not reach the human race unless the head of the serpent were crushed. But this crushing was performed by Christ alone: nor was any of the nations with Him, Isaiah 63, 3. For although the Apostles also trampled serpents and cast out the Devil, both by preaching the Gospel and by performing miracles, yet they performed that partly not by their own power, but by another's, namely Christ's power working in them; and partly they did not themselves destroy that kingdom of the Devil, to which the whole human race was enslaved, but announced that it had been destroyed through Christ. Concerning this matter, the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 2, 14 and 15, discourses excellently. Saying, The Son of God, in like manner as the children, partook of flesh and blood, that through death He might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil, and might deliver them who through fear of death were all their life subject to bondage. And 1 John 3, 8: For this the Son of God appeared, that He might destroy the works of the Devil.

Our third foundation is supplied by those Evangelical promises concerning the Seed of Abraham, in whom all the nations of the earth were to be blessed, Genesis 22, 18 and chapter 28, 14. Moreover, this blessing is diametrically opposed to that legal curse, and therefore it must be defined not by some temporal happiness, but by the remission of sins and the pardon of the eternal curse. But this blessing cannot reach us except through Christ, and indeed, insofar as He Himself, hanging on the tree, having been made a curse for us, took away every curse. Therefore, it is vain, false, fictitious, and blasphemous to maintain that God pardons sins and remits eternal punishments without any Satisfaction of Christ. The Apostle confirms the minor premise more clearly than the midday sun in Galatians 3, 13, 14, and 16. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having been made a curse for us: because it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree: that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the Gentiles in Christ Jesus. For the promises were spoken to Abraham and his seed: He does not say, And to seeds, as of many, but as of one, And to your seed, which is Christ.

The FOURTH foundation is provided by the Sacrifices and victims of the Old Testament, each of which were Types of the Satisfaction to be paid at some time by Christ for our sins: Whence we argue thus.

If the blood of brute animals, offered to God in the Old Testament through Sacrifices, purified men, not only from Levitical uncleanness, which was of the flesh, but also from spiritual uncleanness, namely from sin and its guilt: much more will the blood of Christ avail for the purification of our souls before God.

Latin:

De SATISFACTIONE PRO Peccatis nostris.

Sed quid multis opus, cum stupendam hanc haereticorum istorum blasphemiam plus satis, & ad stuporem usque cernere liceat, ex ipsorum ratiunculis & argumentis, quibus hoc loco pugnare solent. Status autem hujus Controversi siae legitimus emergit iste: An Deus hominibus condonet peccata, propter sufficientissimam Satisfactionem Christi, fide apprehensam: An vero sine ulla tali Satisfactione ex mero voluntatis suae beneplacito? Priorem status hujus partem, nos Affirmate amplectimur, fundamenta ejus mox in refutatione objectionum expedituri: Posteriorem vero simpliciter negamus: quam Photiniani his potissimum argumentis obtinere summopere student.

Expedivimus hactenus primarium fundamentum, quod in praesente articulo haeresi vel potius blasphemiae suae substernunt recentiores Photiniani. Quod enim hactenus pugnarunt, Misericordiam Dei condonantem peccata, simpliciter esse absolutam, neq; in ullo aliquo merito fundatam: quod item contenderunt: Nullam naturalem in Deo esse Justitiam vindicatricem, sive punientem peccata, eo unice spectat, ut sic incautioribus persuadeant, ad reconciliationem generis humani, ejusdemque Justificationem & salutem perficiendam, nulla prorsus opus fuisse Satisfactione sive per Christum, sive per quemvis alium praestanda. Statuunt enim & scriptitant, peccata condonari, & homines a morte aeterna servari, sola libera voluntate, & absoluta gratia Dei, modo ipsi homines resipiscant & agant poenitentiam. Flosculi & Emblemata ipsorum praecipua sunt haec.

I. Argumentum sic proponit Christophorus Osterodus, Goslariensis. Prima causa, cur nos ita statuamus, est, quod in Scriptura sacra, illius Satisfactionis nuspiam, etiam ne uno verbulo sit mentio, nec uspiam alicujus alterius rei, quae perinde haberet: id quod, perquam mirum accidere posset, si opinio de merito esset vera: Immo non satis esset, si aliquoties, sed necesse esset, ut quam saepe & quam multoties, in Sacra Scriptura ejusdem mentio fieret, sicut videmus in Scriptis & concionibus adversariorum indefinenter inculcari. Quam ipsam rationem habet etiam Socinus l. 2. de Christo cap. 26. p. 219.

Coincidit cum primo hoc Argumento illud II. Alterum, quo contendunt, nusquam in Scripturis reperiri aequipollentem doctrinam, quod Christus morte sua Deum nobis reconciliaverit, quod poenas peccatis nostris debitas, divina justitiae persolverit: quod sanguine suum, tanquam λύτρον redemptionis nostrae, divina justitia dederit: nosque ex manibus Dei liberaverit: quod sua obedientia nostram inobedientiam pensaverit: quod remissionem peccatorum nobis meruerit: vel deniq; quod iram Dei nobis placaverit: Ergo inferunt, citra & praeter Scripturarum autoritatem, Satisfactio Christi asseritur.

1. Non solum Satisfactionis, seu faciendi verbum, cum de salute nobis per Christum parta, agitur, in Sanctis Scripturis nusquam apparet: sed nibil ejusmodi, ne semel quidem expresse in eis Scriptum reperitur. Nuspiam enim legitur, quod Christus nobis morte sua Deum reconciliaverit: quod poenas universas nostris iniquitatibus debitas, moriendo justitiae divinae persolverit: quod nos e manibus justitiae divinae, sanguinem suum redemtionis nostrae pretium illi dans, liberaverit: quod scelera nostra sua obedientia compensaverit, vel quod, ut remissionem peccatorum nobis Deus largiretur, digne commeritus fuerit: vel denique saltem, quod aliqua ratione Dei iram nobis placaverit. Faustus Socinus part. 2. de Christo Servatore cap 26. p. 218.

Respondeo: totam compagem istorum argumentorum laborare. 1. Sophismate Consequentis: praeterquam enim, quod impudens omnino est postulatum, quo a nobis demonstrari flagitant, ubinam verbum Satisfacere & Satisfactionis vocabulum in Scripturis αὐτὸ γράφμα, & αύτολεξεί extet: nihil tamen argumentum concludit, si vel maxime res ita sese habeat. Quod si enim Satisfactio Christi ideo neganda fuerit, quia terminus iste secundum literas & Syllabas in sacris de hac materia non reperitur; tum sane ipsi quoque Photiniani pleraque sua dogmata abjurent, necesse habebunt, quippe ijsdem literis ac Syllabis in Scripturis non expressa. Jam vero cum ipsimet statuant, non tam apices literarum, quam sensum Scripturarum circa Constitutionem articulorum fidei, spectandum esse: sic censente ipso Fausto Socino in disputatione de invocatione Christi, contra Franciscum Davidis instituta cap. 1. Quae obsecro haec fuerit sive protervia, sive impudentia, indigne servitutis leges praescribere alijs, quas ipse ferre recusat?

2. Deum nobis ignoscere jure potuisse, nulla pro peccatis nostris vera Satisfactione accepta, ex eo constare potest, quod delicta nostra eatenus nos Deo obnoxios reddunt, utq; pro ipsis ei satisfiat, requirere videri possint, quatenus offensa sunt majestatis ipsius: ita ut peccatis, vera pro ipsis Satisfactione non accepta, Deum ignoscere, nihil aliud sit, quam eum de jure suo remittere. Unicuique autem de jure suo, quantum velit, remittere licet. Deus igitur, vera pro ipsis Satisfactione non accepta, peccata nobis condonare jure potuit part 3. cap. 1. pag. 221.

3. Sacra scriptura nihil aliud, quam hoc passim confirmat, Deum remittere nobis peccata, ex plena libertate voluntatis, & ex mera gratia gratis, ex magna dilectione & misericordia, sine ulla recompensatione sive Satisfactione, quae supereminentem illam Dei gratiam excludit. Christoph: Osterodus cap. 36.

Imò, quæ hæc cæcitas, Christi Satisfactionem idcò negare, quia ipsum vocabulum forense Satisfactionis sive Satisdationis in Scripturis non exter, cùm tamen æquipollentibus res ipsa ipfo Sole clariùs in ijsdem sit expressa, qualia sunt λύτρον, ἀντίλυτρον, λύτρωσις, ἀπολύτρωσις, ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, ἀνταπόδοσις & id genus alia, uti paulò post demonstrabitur.

Deindè insigne mendacium est, quòd scriptitant æquipollentem doctrinam de Satisfactione Christi in Scripturis non contineri. Quod ut funditùs evertamus & proteramus, præcipua doctrinæ nostræ fundamenta ex Scripturis eruenda, & istorum impietati sunt opponenda.

PRIMUM petimus ex cap. 2, 17. Genef. Quocunque die comederis de arbore hac, morte morieris. Hæc comminatio post lapsum Protoparentum nostrorum necessario impleri debuit: propterea quòd veritas ac Justitia Dei est immutabilis, & Deus mentiri nescit. Atqui, si Deus de hac veritate suâ, vel uti Photiniani loquuntur, de Jure suo remisisset & sine ulla Satisfactione genus humanum misericordiâ suâ complexus esset, tùm mentitus esset Deus, dicens: Morte morieris. Ergò stante immota hac veritate ac justitiâ Dei, generi humano vel æternùm pereundum fuit, aut ab hac pœna, non nisi interventu absolutissimæ Satis factionis redimi potuit: Atqui hoc à nemine mortalium expediri poterat. E. per Filium Dei, Christum Servatorem expediretur, necessum erat.

Alterum assertionis nostræ fundamentum monstrat prima illa Evangelij promissio Genes. 3, 15. Semen mulieris, conteret caput serpentis : Ergò Remissio peccatorum & pœnæ æternæ condonatio generi humano obtingere non potuit, nisi contrito capite serpentis. Atqui hæc contritio à solo Christo est peracta: neque ullus de gentibus erat cum ipso Jes. 63, 3. Etsi enim Apostoli quoque conculcarunt serpentes, & Diabolum ejecerunt, tùm prædicando Evangelium: tùm verò edendo miracula: tamen partim non propriâ, sed alienâ, Christi nimirùm virtute in ipsis operante illud præstiterunt: partim verò etiam regnum illud Diaboli, cui mancipatum erat universum genus humanum, non destruxerunt ipsi, sed per Christum destructum esse, annunciarunt. Qua de re præclarè disserit Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 2, 14. & 15. Filius Dei, inquiens, sicut pueri, participavit carne & sanguine, ut per mortem destrueret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est, Diabolum, & liberaret eos, qui timore mortis per totam vitam obnoxii erant servituti. Et 1. Joh. 3, 8: In hoc apparuit Filius Dei, ut opera destrueret Diaboli.

Tertium fundamentum nostrum suppeditant promissiones illæ Evangelicæ, de Semine Abrahæ, in quo benedicendæ essent omnes gentes terræ, Genes. 22, 18. & cap. 28, 14. Cæterùm hæc benedictio è diametro est opposita maledictioni illi legali, ac proindè non per felicitatem aliquam temporalem, sed per remissionem peccatorum, & condonationem æternæ maledictionis definiri debet. Atqui hæc benedictio nobis non nisi per Christum, & quidem, quatenùs ipse pendens in ligno, maledictum pro nobis factus, omnem maledictionem sustulit, potest obtingere. Ergò vanum, falsum, fictitium, blasphemum est, statuere, Deum condonare peccata, & remittere æternas pœnas, sine ulla Satisfactione Christi. Minorem Sole meridiano clariùs confirmat Apostolus Gal. 3, 13, & 14. & 16. Christus nos redemit de maledicto legis, factus, pro nobis maledictum: quia scriptum est: Maledictus omnis, qui pendet in ligno: ut in gentibus benedictio Abrahæ fieret in Christo Iesu. Abrahæ enim dictæ sunt promissiones & semini ejus: Non dicit: Et seminibus, quasi in multis, sed quasi in uno & semini tuo, qui est Christus.

QUARTUM fundamentum subministrant Sacrificia & victimæ Veteris Testamenti, quæ singulæ fuerunt Typi Satisfactionis aliquando per Christum pro peccatis nostris exolvendæ: Undè sic argumentamur.

Si sanguis brutorum animantium, Deo in Veteri Testamento, per Sacrificia oblatorum homines purgabat, non à Leviticâ tantùm immunditie, quæ carnis erat: sed etiam ab immundicie spirituali, nempè à peccato ejusdemq; reatu: multò magis sanguis Christi vale bit ad purificationem animarum nostrarum coram Deo.


### A Special Controversy Against the recent Photinians, On the Satisfaction for our Sins (continued)

But the blood of brutes obtained that power, not indeed in itself and by itself, or because of the merit and dignity of those Sacrifices, but because those victims pointed the finger toward Christ, who by His truly propitiatory sacrifice expiates the sins of the world. Therefore, much more will the Blood of Christ avail for the purification of our souls from sin and its guilt.

The connection of the major premise is self-evident: for the major premise: if the strength of the body is greater than that of the shadow or figure, what then? Since whatever Types are and whatever they are worth, they obtain that solely from the virtue of the Antitype, so that the argument proceeds correctly from the lesser to the greater affirmatively. The Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 9, 13 and 14, also used this very method of argumentation: If the blood of goats, bulls, and calves sanctifies the defiled for the cleansing of the flesh: how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works.

The minor premise is most evidently clear from the Old and New Testament. Hence it is declared concerning those victims, that they are offered for sins, that they carry the iniquities of men, that they expiate sins, that they please God to the earth and to men, Leviticus 1, 2, 4, and 5. Likewise chapter 4, 3, chapter 16, 21 and 22, chapter 17, 11, and elsewhere passim. Hence the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews introduces this general aphorism: Every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. And in this respect, Revelation 13, 8, Christ is named that Lamb, who was slain from the foundation of the world.

Therefore, there remains for the Conclusion its own immovable certainty, which we can confirm from superabundance from chapter 10 of the Epistle to the Hebrews, where these noteworthy things are proposed concerning Christ. 1. That Christ alone is he of whom it is written in the head of the book, that is, in Moses and the Prophets, that he would offer himself as the High Priest of the New Testament for the sins of the world: verse 7. 2. That we are sanctified or cleansed from sins by that will by which the Father willed CHRIST to become a victim. For these words mean this to themselves, verse 7: Behold, says Christ, I come, that I may do, O God, thy will: For saying first that thou didst not desire sacrifices, offerings, and burnt offerings for sin, nor are they pleasing to thee, which are offered according to the Law, Then I said (and indeed in that eternal counsel of the Trinity) Behold I come, that I may do, O God, thy will: But soon he explains what this will of God is, through which we are sanctified, verse 10, saying: In which will we are sanctified through the OFFERING OF THE BODY OF JESUS CHRIST once. 3. That Christ, through his own sacrifice offered for sins, takes away sins, verse 12. 4. That by ONE OFFERING he has perfected forever those who are to be sanctified, verse 14. 5. That Christ performed this offering through his own BLOOD, and through this very blood, obtained for us power and confidence for entry into the holy places, v. 19. That is, with the same Epistle interpreting in chapter 9, 12, that Christ acquired eternal Redemption for us through his own blood.

The FIFTH foundation may be borrowed from chapter 9, 22 of the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the Author, among other things, has this Authentic statement: Without the shedding of blood there is no remission: Hence one may argue thus: If in the Old Testament remission of sins could not take place without the shedding of blood and the death of victims, much more does the truth and substance of the New Testament require the blood and death of a better testator. But such blood cannot be given by any other than him who was shed by Christ the Savior. Therefore, without the shedding of this blood, the remission of sins can be obtained by no one. The connection of the major premise is evident in many ways: For 1. The Old Testament had only a shadow of future goods, not the very image of the things: But the blood of calves and goats constituted the substance of the Old Testament. Therefore, the blood of Christ, which it foreshadowed, constitutes the Substance of the New Testament, Heb. 10, 1. & chapter 9, 13. & 14. & 18. 19. 20. 23. from which it is evidently gathered that God does not remit sins except on account of the Blood of Christ, as the whole Scripture testifies. Rom. 3, 24. he set forth Christ as a propitiation in his blood. Ephes. 1, 6. We have redemption in Christ through his Blood. 1 John 1, 7. The blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God cleanses us from all sin. The truth of the minor premise is clear from the Apostolic inference which follows immediately in the same chapter 9, 24. and following: For Jesus did not enter into holy places made by hand, the copies of the true ones, but into Heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us.

Nor that he should offer himself often, as the High Priest enters into the Holy places every year with the blood of another: otherwise he would have needed to suffer frequently from the foundation of the world: but now once in the consummation of the ages, for the destruction of sin, he has appeared through his own sacrifice.

The SIXTH foundation is most rightly sought from those oracles of the Scriptures which assert that Christ served in our sins, labored in our iniquities, blotted out our sins for his own sake, and will no longer remember our sins, Isa. 43, 24. & 25. that he bore our infirmities, carried our sorrows, was wounded for our iniquities, was bruised for our transgressions: that the discipline of our peace was upon him, and we are healed by his stripes, because he himself cast all our iniquities upon himself, so that as a lamb led to the slaughter, he laid down his soul as a Sacrifice for sin. Isa. 53, 4. 5. 6. 7. & 10. That Christ also, being killed, finished transgression and abolished sin, blotted out iniquity, and brought in everlasting righteousness, Dan. 9, 24. That Christ came to give his soul as a ransom for many. Matth. 20, 28. that he is that Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. John 1, 29. that his name alone is given under heaven to men, by which it is necessary for us to be saved, Acts 4, 12. That God the Father reconciled the world to himself in Christ, not imputing their sins to them, because he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the Righteousness of God in him. 2 Cor. 5, 19. & 21. And there are six hundred other testimonies of this kind which could be produced from the sacred writings, invincibly asserting: 1. That the remission of sins has never happened to anyone, either in the Old or New Testament, without Christ. 2. That Christ alone gave himself as the price of redemption for the whole human race. 3. That the reconciliation of the world with God consists in the remission of sins through and on account of Christ alone apprehended by faith, and not, as the Photinians trifle, through the satisfactory penance of men. 4. & finally that it pleased God the Father to reconcile all things to himself through Christ, both those on earth and those in heaven, having made peace through the blood of his cross, as the Apostle speaks, Col. 1, 20. & 1 Pet. 1, 19. & chapter 2, 24.

With these things standing thus, the gloss of the Photinians is more than heretical, asserting that Christ expiated our sins only insofar as he covered our sins with his doctrine, that is, he taught us to cover them through penance; or insofar as we have seen the will of God toward us concerning the remission of sins expressed in him; or insofar as he moderates and rules all things by his powerful command, as Socinus writes, part 2, chapter 20, page 176.

But it is pleasing to add also a Seventh foundation, derived from our Justification in this manner. In the same way that we are justified before God, in that same way we also obtain the Remission of sins. But we are not justified except through faith, which certainly believes and maintains that Christ paid to God the Father a most sufficient λύτρον or price for the sins of the whole world, and indeed through the shedding of his blood. Therefore, through the mediation of that same faith, and not through holiness of life, the Remission of sins also falls to our lot.

The major premise is manifest in itself: For Justification and the Remission of sins cohere adamantly, and they posit and remove one another.

The minor premise is evident from a twin Apostolic Aphorism: the former of which holds thus: Rom. 3, 24. & 25. We are justified freely by the grace of God, through the Redemption, which is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth ἱλαςήριον, a placation or propitiatory, through Faith in his blood, to show his Justice, in the remission of sins. The latter, Rom. 8, 3. because of the infirmity of the law, for it was made infirm through the Flesh, God sent his son, in the likeness of the flesh of sin, and concerning sin condemned sin in the flesh, so that the Justice of the law might be fulfilled in us. The proper sense of which latter Aphorism is this: Because a Sacrifice for sin was required to expiate sins, but the Sacrifice of goats and calves could not provide that expiation: since the Law argues, accuses, and condemns not the nature of brute animals, but human nature: therefore God sent his Son, that περὶ ἁμαρτίας, that is, by such a Sacrifice for sin, namely the victim of his own body, which owed nothing to sin, he might condemn sin in that very human flesh, namely which sin had subjected to condemnation. Whence the Sacrifice of Christ has such force and efficacy that the Justification of the Law might be fulfilled in us. But how? For, as if we might obtain the remission of sins through our own repentance: as the Photinians trifle? By no means, but that the δικαίωμα of the Law, that is, the most absolute Justice, which the Law demands and requires from us, might be fulfilled not by us, but ἐν ἡμῖν, in us: Because Christ, who fulfilled the Law for us, is in us, that is, he dwells in us through faith. Ephes. 3, 17.

The eighth and final foundation of our assertion is constituted by those two Greek words which are predicated of Christ, namely that he paid a λύτρον and ἀντίλυτρον to God the Father for the sins of the whole world, as in Matth. 20, 28. Christ came, that he might give his soul a λύτρον for many. And in 1. Timoth. 2, 5. & 6. One God, one also Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself an ἀντίλυτρον, a price of redemption for all. Now truly λύτρον, as all and every Greek author attests, signifies the price which is paid for a redemption, and by which satisfaction is made for the man being redeemed: so that the Greek word λύτρον can, nay must, be most rightly rendered by the word Satisfaction. Hence Herodotus: ὡς μισθὸς ἔιν καὶ λύτρα μοι ἀντὶ της καταδίκης, so that it may be for me a reward and a price of liberation for the judged matter. Now truly Christ himself is this λύτρον and ἀντίλυτρον, not insofar as he shows us the way of salvation through repentance: For by this pact he would not be an ἀντίλυτρον for ALL, as the Apostle holds. Since he could not show this way to the fathers of the Old Testament, because he was not yet exhibited in the Flesh: Therefore he will be such insofar as he paid the price of redemption for us, and liberated us from the power of sin, death, and hell, by his own death. Let the Photinians go now and, if they please, blather further that the word Satisfaction does not exist in the Scriptures concerning Christ. For what is it to pay a satisfactory price, if not to satisfy?

Latin:

Atqui brutorum sanguis vim illam obtinebat, non quidem in se & per se, sive propter meritum atque dignitatem eorum Sacrificiorum, sed quia victimæ illæ digitum intendebant ad Christum, sacrificio suo verè propitiatorio expiantem peccata mundi. Ergò multò magis Sanguis Christi valebit ad purgationem animarum nostrarum à peccato, ejusdemq; reatu.

Majoris connexum per se patet: Major enim: st vis corporis, quàm umbræ sive figuræ, quid? quòd Typi quicquid sunt & valent, illud unicè obtinent ex virtute Antitypi, ita ut argumentum rectè procedat à minori ad majus affirmatè. Quò ipso argumentandi genere usus est etiam Autor Epistolæ ad Hebræos cap. 9, 13. & 14. Si sanguis bircorum, taurorum & vitulorum inquinatos sanctificat ad emundationem Carnis: quantò magis Sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum Sanctum semetipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo, emundabit conscientiam nostram ab operibus mortuis.

Minor ex Veteri & Novo Testamento patet evidentissimè. Hinc de victimis illis prædicatur, quòd offerantur pro peccatis, qòud portent iniquitates hominum, quòd expient peccata, quod Deum placent terræ ac hominibus Levit. 1, 2, 4. & 5. Item cap. 4, 3. cap. 16, 21. & 22. cap. 17, 11. & passim alibi. Hinc Autor Epistolæ ad Hebræos generalem hunc infert Aphorismum: Omnis Pontifex ex hominibus assumtus, pro hominibus constituitur in ijs, quæ sunt ad Deum, ut offerat dona & sacrificia pro peccatis. Et hoc respectu Apocal. 13, 8. Christus nominatur Agnus ille, qui occisus ab origine mundi.

Constat proindè Conclusioni sua quoque immota certitudo, quam ex superabundanti confirmare possumus ex cap. 10. Epistolæ ad Hebræos, ubi de Christo hæc ἀξιομνημόνευτα proponuntur. 1. Quòd Christus solus sit is, de quo in capite libri, hoc est in Mose & Prophetis sit scriptum, quòd tanquam Pontifex Novi Testamenti seipsum sit oblaturus pro peccatis mundi: versu. 7. 2. Quòd sanctificemur sive purgemur à peccatis, per eam voluntatem, quâ Pater voluit CHRISTUM victimam fieri, Hoc enim sibi volunt hæc verba verf. 7 Ecce, inquit, Christus, venio, ut faciam Deus voluntatem tuam: Prius enim dicens, quia hostias, oblationes, & holocautomata pro peccato noluisti, nec placita sunt tibi, quæ secundum Legem offeruntur, Tunc dixi (& quidem in æterno illo Trinitatis consilio) Ecce venio, ut faciam Deus voluntatem tuam: Sed mox quæ sit hæc voluntas Dei, per quam sanctificamur explicat vers. 10 inquiens. In quâ voluntate sanctificati sumus per OBLATIONEM CORPORIS JESU CHRISTI semel. 3. Quòd Christus per suam hostiam, pro peccatis oblatam, peccata auferat vers. 12. 4. Quòd UNA OBLATIONE in sempiternum consummaverit sanctificandos vers. 14. 5. Quod Christus hanc oblationem præstiterit per SANGUINEM suum, & per hunc ipsum sanguinem, potestatem nobis impetraverit, atque fiduciam ad introitum in sancta, v. 19. hoc est, interprete eâdem Epistolâ cap. 9. 12. quòd Christus per proprium sanguinem æternam Redemptionem nobis acquisiverit.

QUINTUM fundamentum mutuari licet ex cap. 9, 22. Epistolæ ad Hebræos, ubi Autor inter reliqua hanc habet Authenticam: Sine Sanguinis effusione non sit remissio: Hinc sic licet argumentari: Si in Veteri Testamento citra sanguinis effusionem, & victimarum mortem, Remissio peccatorum fieri non potuit, multò magis, Novi Testamenti veritas & substantia, potioris testatoris sanguinem & mortem requirit, Atqui talis sanguis non potest dari ullus alius, præter eum, qui effusus est à Christo Servatore. Ergò sine hujus sanguinis effusione Remissio peccatorum nemini potest obtingere. Majoris connexum multis modis patet: Nam. 1. Vetus Testamentum umbram tantùm habuit futurorum bonorum: non ipsam rerum imaginem: Atqui sanguis vitulinus & hircinus constituebat substantiam Veteris Testamenti. E. Sanguis Christi, quem ille adumbrabat, constituit Substantiam Novi Testamenti Heb. 10, 1. & cap. 9, 13. & 14. & 18. 19. 20. 23. ex quibus evidenter colligitur, quòd Deus non remittat peccata, nisi propter Sanguinem Christi, uti universa Scriptura testatur. Rom. 3, 24. proposuit Christumn ἱλαστήριον in sanguine suo. Ephes. 1, 6. Habemus in Christo redemtionem per Sanguinem ipsius. 1. Ioh. 1, 7. Sanguis Jesu Christi Filij Dei emundat nos ab omni peccato. Minoris veritas liquet ex illatione Apostolica, quæ statim eodem cap. 9, 24. & seqq. sequitur: Non enim in manu facta sancta Jesus introivit, exemplaria verorum, sed in ipsum Cælum, ut appareat nunc vultui Dei pro nobis.

Neque ut sæpò offerat semetipsum, quemadmodum Pontifex intrat in Sancta, per singulos annos, in sanguine alieno: alioquin oportebat eum frequenter pati ab origine mundi: nunc autem semel in consummatione seculorum, ad destructionem peccati, per hostiam suam apparuit.

SEXTUM fundamentum rectissimè petitur ex ijs Scripturarum oraculis, quæ asserunt, Christum servijsse in peccatis nostris, laborasse in iniquitatibus nostris, delevisse peccata nostra propter se: & peccatorum nostrorum non ampliùs recordaturum Jes. 43, 24. & 25. languores nostros tutisse, dolores nostros portasse, vulneratum esse propter iniquitates nostras, attritum esse propter sceleranostra: disciplinam pacis nostræ fuisse super ipsum, & nos livore ipsius sanatos esse, propterea quòd ipse lebovab omnes iniquitates nostras in ipsum conjecerit, ita ut sicut agnus ad mactationem ductus, animam suam posuerit Sacrificium pro delicto. Jes. 53, 4. 5. 6. 7. & 10. Christum item occisum consummasse prævaricationem & abolevisse peccatum, delevisse iniquitatem, adduxisse æternam justitiam Dan. 9, 24. Christum venisse, ut daret animam suam λύτρον pro multis. Matth. 20, 28. esse Agnum illum Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi. Joh. 1, 29. solum ipsius nomen sub cælo datum esse hominibus, per quod oporteat nos salvari Actor. 4, 12. Deum Patrem in Christo reconciliasse sibi mundum, non imputando eis peccata ipsorum, propterea quòd eum, qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis fecit peccatum, ut nos efficeremur Justitia Dei in ipso. 2. Cor. 5, 19. & 21. Et quæ sunt hujus generis sexcenta testimonia alia, quæ ex sacris produci possent, invictè asserentia. 1. Remissionem peccatorum nemini unquam vel in Veteri vel in Novo Testamento contigisse, citra Christum. 2. solum Christum dedisse seipsum precium redemptionis, pro toto genere humano. 3. Reconciliationem mundi cùm Deo consistere in remissione peccatorum, per & propter solum Christum fide apprehensum, non verò, uti Photiniani nugantur, per satisfactoriam hominum pænitentiam. 4. & tandem placuisse Deo Patri, per Christum reconciliari sibi omnia, tùm quæ in terra, tùm quæ in cælis, factâ pace per sanguinem crucis ejus, ut loquitur Apostolus Coloß. 1, 20. & 1. Pet. 1, 19. & cap. 2, 24.

Quibus ita stantibus, plusquàm hæretica Photinianorum est glossa, asserentium, Christum expiasse peccata nostra, tantùm quatenùs suâ doctrinâ peccata nostra texit, hoc est, per pænitentiam tegere nos docuit; vel quatenus Dei voluntatem erga nos, de peccatorum remissione, in ipso expressam vidimus: vel quatenus omnia potenti suo jussu moderatur & regit, uti scribit Socinus part. 2. cap. 20. pag. 176.

Sed placet Septimum etiam adjicere fundamentum, petitum à Justificatione nostra in hunc modum. Quo pacto justificamur coram Deo, eodem etiam consequimur Remissionem peccatorum. Atquinon justificamur nisi per fidem, quæ certò credit ac statuit, Christum exolvisse Deo Patri sufficientissimum λύτρον sive precium pro peccatis totius mundi, & quidem per effusionem sanguinis sui. Ergò eâdem fide mediante, & non per vita sanctitate, nobis obtingit Remissio etiã peccatoriũ.

Major per se est manifesta: Nam Justificatio & Remissio peccatorum ἀδαμαντίνως cohærent, & se mutuò ponunt ac tollunt.

Minor patet ex gemino Aphorismo Apostolico: quorum prior sic habet: Rom. 3, 24. & 25. Justificamur gratis gratia Dei, per Redemtionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus ἱλαςήριον placamentum sive propitiatorium, per Fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad ostendendam suam Iustitiam, in remissionem peccatorum. Posterior Rom. 8, 3. propter infirmitatem legis, nam infirmabatur per Carnem, Deus misit filium suum, in similitudine carnis peccati, & de peccato damnavit peccatum in carne, ut. Ius legis compleretur in nobis. Cujus posterioris Aphorismi hic proprius est sensus: Quia ad expianda peccata requirebatur Sacrificium pro peccato, Sacrificium autem hircorum & vitulorum, non poterat expiationem illam præstare: siquidem Lex non brutorum animantium, sed humanam arguit, accusat & damnat naturam: ideò Deus misit Filium suum, ut περὶ ἁμαρτίας, hoc est, tali Sacrificio pro peccato victima scilicet sui corporis, quod peccato, nihil debebat, peccatum damnaret in illa ipsa carne humana, scilicet quam peccatum damnationi subjecerat. Unde Sacrificium Christi tantam habet vim & efficaciam, ut Justificatio Legis in nobis impleretur. Sed quomodo? Nam, ut per nostram pœnitentiam, peccatorum remissionem impetraremus: uti Photiniani nugantur? Minimè, sed ut δικαίωμα Legis, hoc est, Justitia absolutissima, quam Lex à nobis flagitat, & requirit, impleretur non à nobis, sed ἐν ἡμῖν in nobis: Quia Christus, qui Legem pro nobis implevit, in nobis est, hoc est, per fidem in nobis habitat. Ephes. 3, 17.

Octavum & ultimum assertionis nostræ fundamentum constituunt duo illa vocabula Græca, quæ de Christo prædicatur, quòd nimirum λύτρον & ἀντίλυτρον Deo patri exolverit pro peccatis totius mundi, ut Matth. 20, 28. Christus venit, ut daret animam suam λύτρον pro multis. Et in 1. Timoth. 2, 5. & 6. Unus Deus, unus etiam Mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Jesus, qui semet ipsum dedit ἀντίλυτρον pretium redemptionis pro omnibus. Jam verè λύτρον, attestantibus singulis & universis Græcis autoribus, significat pretium, quod pro redemtione ex olvitur, & quò pro homine redimendo satis fit: ita ut Græca vox λύτρον per Satisfactionis vocabulum rectissimè reddi, possit imò debeat. Hinc Herodotus: ὡς μισθὸς ἔιν καὶ λύτρα μοι ἀντὶ της καταδίκης, ut sit mihi merces & pretium liberationis pro re judicata. Jam verò Christus ipse est λύτρον & ἀντίλυτρον hoc, non quatenùs nobis per pœnitentiam viam salutis monstrat: Hoc enim pacto non esset ἀντίλυτρον pro OMNIBUS, ut Apostolus habet. Siquidem patribus Veteris Testamenti, viam hanc ipse monstrare non potuit: quippè nondum in Carnem exhibitus: Ergò talis erit, quatenùs precium redemtionis pro nobis exolvit, nosque ex potestate peccati, mortis & inferni, suâ morte liberavit. Eant nunc Photiniani & porrò si lubet, blaterent, Satisfactionis vocabulum de Christo in Sacris non extare. Quid enim est pretium satisfactorium exolvere, quàm satisfacere?


### A Special Controversy Against the recent Photinians, On the Satisfaction for our Sins (continued)

Moreover, the Photinians have very many reasons by which they strive to overturn these eight Foundations of ours. For first, they attempt to elude that Commination of Jehovah in Gen. 2, 17, contending that it cannot be understood of bodily death, because this is natural to Man, and not the Wages of Sin, but a proper consequence of our Nature, which Adam himself received in Creation: as Socinus writes, part 3, c. 8, p. 294. But this cavil does not touch the nerve. For first, it is not so much about Natural death, as that Spiritual one, that is, eternal damnation, which Jehovah threatened to our first parents if they should eat from the forbidden tree, that is properly controverted in this place: Namely, whether God could, with the truth and Justice of God remaining intact, remit or pardon this punishment to them without any Satisfaction? Where the Photinians have not yet given their affirmative as proven. Then, regarding the Question about the Death of the body, that it was Natural to Man even in the State of Integrity, we answer simply in the negative, if the Question is understood concerning the act of mortality itself, as we have evidently demonstrated our Negative in the Article on Creation against Bellarmine. Finally, it is clearly trifling that they distinguish between Death itself and the necessity of dying, saying that the necessity of dying is indeed the Effect of that Commination: but not Death itself, because this was Natural to Adam: For what, I ask, is natural death, if not the necessity of dying: as that which, according to their own hypothesis, depends on the condition of human nature after the fall, so that the Holy Spirit willed that this necessity of dying be common to the pious with the impious. Heb. 9, 27. It is appointed for all once to die. Therefore it is false and absurd that the pious die not necessarily, but only naturally: while the impious die both naturally and necessarily: As if that Apostolic Aphorism, Rom. 6, 23, did not apply Universally and equally to the pious and the impious regarding the death of the Body and its necessity: The wages of sin is Death: Where we establish that whatever comes under the name of Death is to be understood, although it is subsequently by Accident that this Bodily death is for the impious the beginning of eternal death or damnation: but for the pious a transition from death to life, Joh. 5, 24.

They falsely mock our other foundation, taken from that first Evangelical promise concerning the Seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the Serpent, and they contend with a more than heretical style that it is not a promise, but a curse, and indeed a temporal one, which signifies the enmities of men and serpents, which did not exist before the fall. Iob. Sommerus of Pirna, l. 2, against Petrus Carolius, cap. 3, pag. 73. Moreover, it is evident that this interpretation is blasphemous and twisted. 1. even from the fact that this prophecy, which, in figurative words in this place, is proposed concerning the destruction of the Satanic kingdom, has subsequently obtained its illustrious fulfillment. Furthermore, unless the destruction of the Satanic kingdom is understood through the crushing of the serpent's head, it follows that GOD indeed dictated a punishment to the first parents: but dictated absolutely none to the serpent or the Devil: who nevertheless was the primary impelling cause of that most sad fall: a thing which simply conflicts with the Justice of GOD. Then by this arrangement GOD would have left them destitute and devoid of all consolation, and fluctuating in perpetual doubt. But that this is most false is evident even from the fact that Eve understood by that Seed of the woman that man Jehovah, who, having been promised by GOD, ought to provide redemption from sin and eternal damnation. Whence chap. 4, 1. having brought forth Cain, she exclaims: I have acquired a man, Jehovah: thinking that she had now brought forth that promised Seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the Serpent 4. Furthermore, the coherence of the words of God would be clearly inept, nay, entirely null: if it be posited that GOD first threatened that natural enmity of serpents and men: and soon after, as if by a certain correction, added that Man was in some way endowed with such powers that he could sometimes either entirely prevent, or certainly mitigate or heal, the bite of serpents. What, I ask, would this have to do with the fall already committed? What with the Threat itself? What with the Consolation? Nay, what with the Devil, the Architect of all evil? Nothing, absolutely nothing. 5. Moreover, this corruption standing, it would follow that the condition of that Original or primeval Church was worse than it was in all subsequent ages and times: in which, always from the times of Abraham onwards, solemn Evangelical promises were proposed concerning liberation from death and eternal damnation, to be provided through Christ. But the original Church alone would have lacked such a promise after the fall, if this present promise concerning Christ is not to be accepted: which is prodigiously absurd. 6. Furthermore, it is manifest that Jehovah distinctly and separately dictates his sentence to the natural serpent also, in the preceding [verses]: Because, he says, you have done this, cursed shall you be among all animals and beasts of the earth: upon your breast you shall walk, and earth you shall eat all the days of your life.
