Et ubi nulla est Legis transgressio, ibi nullâ Legis impletione opus est. Atqui peccati omnis expers erat Christus. E. nihil etiam Juris in ipsum Legis maledictio obtinebat. Sic Scriptura asserit quidem, quòd Christus devinctus fuerit ad præstandam Patri obedientiam: sed simul explicat, hanc ipsam obedientiam non pro se, sed loco nostri, Legi divinæ esse præstitam. Undè ipsemet Psal. 69, 5. exclamat: Quæ non rapui, reddidi. Et Jes. 43, 24. & 25. Servire me fecisti in peccatis tuis, laborare fecisti me in iniquitatibus tuis: Ego, ego sum, qui deleo prævaricationes tuas propter me.


### A Special Controversy Against the recent Photinians, On the Satisfaction for our Sins (continued)

The third argument fails by the fallacy of non-cause as cause. For the merit of Christ is not of infinite value because Christ did not undergo eternal death: for just as the sins of our disobedience are finite in act, but infinite in guilt, since they strike against the infinite justice of God: so the obedience and death of Christ were indeed finite in act, insofar as they were circumscribed by a certain period of time, namely the days of His emptying; but by reason of merit, it is infinite, since it proceeds from an infinite person, namely the only-begotten Son of God Himself.

Furthermore, it is not simply true that the curse of the law must be defined only by eternal death. For if this were so, the Apostle would have defined that curse of the law very inconveniently by that Mosaic passage in Deut. 21:23, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. Then, eternal death is defined not only by the perpetual continuation or suffering of infernal torments: but also by the sense of infernal pains, joined with rejection or desertion by God: so that he who sustains such pains even for a moment may be said to have experienced eternal death. Just as indeed Christ truly underwent the sense of those infernal pains not for a moment or some small space of time, but throughout the whole time of His emptying, so that at last He had to exclaim, My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? But the reason He did not undergo eternal death in the latter way was that He, being innocent, had satisfied the law by dying. Finally, the Apostle clearly inverts this argument of the heretics in Rom. 5:10, saying: If, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of His Son: much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by His LIFE: hinting not obscurely: If Christ had remained in death, He could neither have merited righteousness nor conferred it upon us, and therefore the resurrection and life of Christ were altogether necessary for our justification, so that thus death might be to death 1 Cor. 15, 54. Hos. 13, 14. and through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil: and might deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage, Heb. 2, 14. and 15. Hence that epiphonema of the Apostle Rom. 4, 25. Christ was delivered for

And these are the principal reasons by which the more recent Photinians strive to impugn the sixth foundation of our doctrine, but with vain effort. Now follows the seventh, and that is sought from those places of the Scriptures in which Christ is said to have been made by the Father ἱλαστήριον or a placation in his blood, for the remission of sins. This foundation, therefore, they impugn chiefly by this reasoning, that Christ is said to be ἱλαστήριον, a placamen or placation, in the same sense as the Ark of the Covenant was once called כפרת, the propitiatory, Exod. 25, 21. and 22. Now, indeed, the Ark was so called, not because it did not placate God for the people of Israel: but because God, offering himself in it as propitious and placated to his people, and indeed of his own accord, gave answers. Therefore (they infer) Christ also is called a placation, not because he himself has placated God for us: but because not only does God show himself most placated to us in him, but also, whatever he wished us to know, he has revealed through him.

I answer that this argument also suffers from perpetual ἀσυλογίαις or begging of the question. For first, the heretics have not yet proved that Christ is called ἱλαστήριον in the same way that the Ark was once so designated. The contrary is rather evident from the whole of Scripture: for because the Ark bore the type of Christ the Savior, certainly the same power could not of itself reside in the Type that resides in the Antitype: for otherwise the Type would not be a Type. Then, neither is it proved that Christ is called ἱλαστήριον only insofar as God shows himself placated to us in him, and not that he has rendered the Father placated to us by his blood. For again, the contrary shines forth from the Type itself. For to the Ark of the Covenant is expressly attributed the power of propitiating and justifying, as is evident from the Epistle to the Hebrews ch. 9, 1 and 5. It indeed had also the former justifications, for above the ark were the Cherubim of glory overshadowing the propitiatory. Now, indeed, this power and efficacy of the Ark did not reside in it of itself and in respect to itself, but only insofar as it bore the Type of Christ: or as the Epistle to the Hebrews ch. 8, 5 speaks, insofar as it served the likeness, pattern, and shadow, that is, it prefigured that most full and most perfect Satisfaction of Christ, which of itself, and by the work performed, merited the remission of sins for the faithful, and made them perfect according to the conscience, Heb. 9, 9. Therefore it follows infallibly that Christ, effectively, and indeed by reason of merit and Satisfaction, is and is called ἱλαστήριον or a placation: whence also the Apostle Rom. 3, 25 does not name him nakedly and simply ἱλαστήριον, but at the same time involves the merit of Satisfaction or propitiation, when he adds, in his blood for the remission of sins. Which very response must also be held against the frequent triflings of Socinus, by which he contends that Christ is called our propitiation in the same sense as the Sacrifices of the Old Testament. For this assertion must be simply denied, or certainly inverted. For if it held ground, it would follow: 1. That the Sacrifices of the Old Testament did not bear the Type of Christ. 2. That Christ is not the mediator of the New, and indeed a better Testament, but 3. That another Antitype is still to be expected, which confers the Remission of sins not typically, but properly. 4. And lastly, that the Remission of sins comes to us without the shedding of blood. Every pious person understands that all these things are more absurd than the most absurd things.

Our eighth and last foundation, they strive to impugn likewise with many reasons: the principal of which it will be worth the effort to examine more deeply.

And at the beginning, indeed, they demand of us that we show where it exists in the sacred writings that Christ was made λύτρον to the FATHER? or that he satisfied the Father. But this very thing has been demonstrated invincibly thus far: let that Apostolic Aphorism suffice in this place, Ephes. 5, 2. Christ loved us and gave himself for us, προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν, an offering and a VICTIM TO GOD (the Father) for a sweet-smelling savor. And Hebr. 9, 14. Christ offered himself without fault to God. And more clearly Apocal. 5, 9. You have redeemed us TO GOD in your blood.

The second argument of the Photinians is this: Moses, and the liberation provided through him, was a type of Christ, and of the salvation acquired through him. But Moses, with God so commanding, redeemed the people of Israel from Egyptian servitude, not by the payment of any price, but by power and authority handed to him by God. Therefore, Christ also, by supreme power and authority granted to him by God, redeemed us from the servitude of sin and death, with God so commanding, with no true price paid to anyone, and claimed us for God himself.

They confirm the connection of the major premise from a comparison of Psalm 111:9 with the Canticle of Zechariah, Luke 1:68. For what the Psalm has concerning the Egyptian liberation, 'He sent redemption to his people': that Zechariah repeats in almost the same words: saying, 'He has wrought redemption for his people': Therefore the nature of Christ's redemption, which was once that of the Mosaic redemption, is the same.

I reply that a fallacy of ignoring the refutation and of a faulty consequent is being committed. For even if we might perhaps not unwillingly concede that Moses and the Egyptian liberation acted in some way as a type of Christ and of the redemption provided through him: nevertheless, we simply deny that the nature of both is one and the same. For Moses, if we look at the history, liberated his people from bodily servitude: Christ from spiritual servitude. Therefore, as much as body and spirit differ, so much do these two redemptions differ from one another. Furthermore, Moses is read to have liberated his people by the power of God; but Christ has redeemed us with his own blood, and indeed for the remission of sins: as has been demonstrated several times thus far. Thirdly, this argument overturns itself: For if the Mosaic liberation was a Type of the redemption of Christ: Therefore, there cannot be one and the same reason for both: Otherwise, the Type would not be a Type: nor would the Antitype be an Antitype: or certainly the Type would be a Type of itself, which is absurd. Finally, Scripture inculcates a clear distinction between the redemption of both in Hebrews 9:15.

For this reason, Christ is the Mediator of the New Testament, that death might intervene εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν for the redemption of transgressions, etc. And in the preceding verse, 12: Christ, not through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, entered once into the Holy places, αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν ἑυράμενος, having found eternal redemption. Although, therefore, Moses and Christ agree in that both were Mediators: yet the Mediation of the one differs from the Mediation of the other in its entire genus. For Moses was a typical, temporal, bodily Mediator, without the shedding of his own blood, for the acquisition of the promised land: but Christ is a true or real, eternal, spiritual Mediator, delivering us through his own blood from the wrath of God, the curse of the law, sin, and eternal death, for the remission of sins and the acquisition of a heavenly and eternal inheritance.

The third reason is as follows: The word 'to redeem' almost always obtains a metaphorical meaning among the sacred writers, so that 'to redeem' is nothing other than 'to deliver' or 'to claim for oneself,' even if no true payment of a true price intervenes. Therefore, it also obtains a similar meaning when this word is predicated of the death of Christ in the Scriptures.

I answer: A consequence from a part to the whole is not valid. Thus, it does not follow that because the word 'to redeem' obtains a metaphorical meaning in certain places of Scripture, it must therefore be understood metaphorically everywhere. The consequence is denied, because spiritual redemption, such as was performed by Christ, could not be accomplished without the shedding of blood and thus without the payment of a true and real λύτρον or price: as has been shown thus far. Such a λύτρον is not required in bodily liberations.

Latin:

Tertia ratio fallit Sophismate non causæ ut causæ. Neque enim ideò meritum Christi non est infiniti pretij, quia Christus non æternam mortem subiit: Quemadmodum enim inobedientiæ nostræ peccata sunt actu finita, reatu verò infinita: siquidem impingunt in infinitam Dei justitiam: Sic obedientia & mors Christi fuit quidem actu finita, quatenùs certi temporis periodo, diebus nimirùm Exinanitionis fuit circumscripta: meriti verò ratione est infinita, siquidem ab infinita persona proficiscitur, ipso nimirùm unigenito Filio Dei.

Deindè neque illud simpliciter verum est, quod execratio Legis tantùm definienda sit per mortem æternam. Hoc enim si esset, perquàm incommodè Apostolus Execrationem illam legis definiuisset per illud Mosaicum Deut. 21, 13. Execrabilis omnis, qui pendet in ligno. Tùm Mors æterna non modò definitur perpetuâ continuatione sive perpessione cruciatuum infernalium: sed & sensu dolorum infernalium, cum abjectione sive desertione à Deo conjuncto: ita ut qui vel ad momentum saltem hujusmodi dolores sustinet, is æternam mortem sensisse, dici queat. Quemadmodum sanè Christus non ad momentum, vel exiguum aliquod temporis spatium, sed per omne tempus Exinanitionis, sensum dolorum istorum infernalium verè subijt, ita ut tandem exclamare necessum haberet, Deus meus, Deus meus, quare me dereliquisti? Quod verò posteriore modo æternam mortem non subijt, in causa fuit, quod ipse innocens moriendo Legi satisfece rat. Tandem rationem hanc hæreticorum planè invertit Apostolus Rom. 5, 10. Si, inquiens, cum inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filij ejus: multò magis reconciliati salvi erimus in VITA ipsius: haud obscurè innuens: Si Christus in morte mansisset, ipsum neque Justitiam promereri, neque nobis conferre potuisse, ac proindè ad nostri Justificationem omninò necessariam fuisse Resurrectionem & vitam Christi ut sic morti esset mors 1. Cor. 15, 54. Hos. 13, 14. & per mortem destrueret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, id est, Diabolum : & liberaret eos, qui timore mortis, per totam vitam obnoxij erant servituti, Heb. 2, 14. & 15. Hinc illud Epiphonema Apostoli Rom. 4, 25. Christus traditus est propter delicta nostra, & resurrexit propter Justificationem nostram.

Et hæ sunt præcipuæ rationes, quibus recentiores Photiniani sextum nostræ doctrinæ Fundamentum, sed irrito conatu impugnare student. Sequitur jam Septimum, idque petitum ex illis Scripturarum locis, quibus Christus dicitur factus esse à Patre ἱλαστήριον sive placamentum in sanguine suo, ad remissionem peccatorum. Hoc ergo fundamentum impugnant ipsi hac potissimum ratione, quod Christus eodem sensu dicatur ἱλαστήριον placamen sive placamentum, quò olim Arca fœderis dicebatur כפרת propitiatorium Exod. 25, 21. & 22. Jam verò Arca sic dicebatur, non quòd Deum populo Israelitico non placaverit: sed quia Deus in ea se propitium & placatum populo suo, & quidem sua sponte præbens, responsa dedit. Ergo (inferunt) Christus quoq́; dicitur placamentum, non quod Deum ipse nobis placaverit: sed quia non modò Deus in ipso se nobis placatissimum ostendit, sed etiam, quicquid nos scire voluit per ipsum patefecit.

Respondeo, hoc quoque argumentum perpetuis laborare ἀσυλογίαις sive principij petitionibus. Primùm enim nondùm probarunt hæretici, Christum eodem modo dici ἱλαστήριον, quô Arca olim sic indigitabatur. Contrarium potiùs ex universa Scriptura patet: Quia enim arca typum gessit Christi Servatoris, utique non eadem vis potuit per se inesse Typo, qui inest Antitypo: alioqui enim Typus non esset Typus. Deindè neque illud probatum est, Christum dici tantùm ἱλαστήριον, quatenùs Deus in ipso se nobis placatum ostendit, non verò quod nobis suo sanguine Patrem placatum reddiderit. Nam rursus contrarium ex ipso Typo elucet. Nam arcæ fœderis tribuitur expressè vis propitiandi & justificandi, ut patet ex Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 9. 1. & 5. Habuit quidem & prius justificationes, nam super arcam erant Cherubim gloriæ obumbrantia propitiatorium. Jam verò hæc vis & efficacia Arcæ non per se & respectu sui inerat, sed tantùm, quatenùs Typum gessit Christi: vel ut Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 8, 5. loquitur, quatenus inservijt similitudini, exemplari & umbræ, hoc est, præfiguravit plenissimam illam perfectissimamque Satisfactionem Christi, quæ ex sese, & ex opere operato promeruit remissionem peccatorum fidelibus, eosque secundum conscientiam perfectos effecit Hebr. 9, 9. Ergò infallibiliter sequitur, quòd Christus effectivè, & quidem ratione meriti ac Satisfactionis, sit & dicatur ἱλαστήριον sive placamentum: Undè etiam Apostolus Rom. 3, 25. ipsum non nudè ac simpliciter nominat ἱλαστήριον, sed simul Satisfactionis sive propitiationis meritum involvit, quando addit, in sanguine suo ad remissionem peccatorum. Quæ ipsa responsio tenenda etiam est contra crebras Socini nugationes, quibus contendit, Christum eodem sensu dici nostram propitiationem, quo Sacrificia Veteris Testamenti. Hæc enim assertio simpliciter negari, vel certò inverti debet. Nam si ea locum obtineret, sequeretur, 1. Sacrificia Veteris Testamenti non gessisse Typum Christi. 2. Christum non esse mediatorem Novi, & quidem melioris Testamenti, sed 3. expectandum adhuc esse alium Antitypum, qui non typicè, sed propriè Remissionem peccatorum conferat. 4. & postremò, Remissionem peccatorum sine effusione sanguinis nobis obtingere. Quæ omnia absurdissimis quibusque absurdiora esse, pius quisque intelligit.

Octavum & postremum nostrum Fundamentum, multis itidem rationibus impugnare student: quarum præcipuas altiùs examinare, operæ pretium fuerit.

Ac initiò quidem flagitant à nobis, ut ostendamus, ubi in sacris extet, quòd Christus sit factus λύτρον PATRI? vel quòd Patri satisfeccrit. Sed hoc ipsum hactenùs invictè demonstratum: sufficiat hoc loco Aphorismus ille Apostolicus Ephes. 5, 2. Christus dilexit nos & tradidit semetipsum pro nobis, προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν, oblationem ac VICTIMAM DEO (Patri) in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ. Et Hebr. 9, 14. Christus seipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo. Et clariùs Apocal. 5, 9. Redemisti nos DEO in sanguine tuo.

Altera Photinianorum ratio hæc est : Moses, & liberatio per eum præstita, fuit typus Christi, & salutis per eum acquisitæ. Atqui Moses, Deo ita jubente, populum Israëlis ex servitute Ægyptiaca redemit, non pretiij alicujus solutione, sed potentia & autoritate sibi à Deo tradita. E. Christus etiam suprema potentia & autoritate sibi à Deo concessâ, nos ex peccati & mortis servitute, Deo ita jubente, nullo vero pretio cuiquam persoluto redemit, & ipsi Deo asseruit.

Connexum Majoris confirmant ex collatione Psalm. 111. 9. cum Cantico Zachariæ, Luc. 1, 68. Quod enim Psalmus habet de liberatione Ægyptiaca, Redemptionem misit populo suo: illud repetit Zacharias ijsdem penè verbis: Fecit inquiens redemptionem plebis suæ: Ergò par est ratio Redemptionis Christi, quæ fuit olim redemptionis Mosaïcæ.

Respondeo committi Sophisma ignorationis Elenchi & vitiosi Consequentis. Etsi enim haud fortassis inviti concesserimus, Mosen & liberationem Ægyptiacam gessisse aliquo modo Typum Christi, & Redemptionis per ipsum præstitæ: tamen unam eandemque utriusque esse rationem, simpliciter negamus. Moses enim, si historiam spectemus, liberavit populum suum ex servitute corporali: Christus ex servitute Spirituali. Quantum ergò differunt Corpus & Spiritus: tantum à se mutuô discrepant duæ hæ redemptiones. Deindè Moses legitur liberasse populum suum virtuteDei: Christus verò redemisse nos propriô suo sanguine, & quidem in remissionem peccatorum: uti aliquoties hactenus est demonstratum. Tertiò argumentum hoc seipsum evertit: Si enim liberatio Mosaica, fuit Typus redemtionis Christi: Ergò non potest esse una eademque utriusque ratio: Alioquin enim Typus non efset Typus: neque Antitypus esset Antitypus: vel certè Typus sui ipsius esset Typus, id quod absurdum. Tandem luculentum discrimen inter utriusque redemtionem inculcat Scriptura Hebræorum 9, 15.

Ob id Novi Testamenti Mediator est Christus, ut mors interveniret εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν ad redemptionem transgressionum &c. Et versu præced. 12. Christus non per sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum sed per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in Sancta, αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν ἑυράμενος, æternâ redemptione inventâ. Etsi proindè Moses & Christus in eo conveniunt, quòd uterque fuit Mediator: unius tamen Mediatio ab alterius Mediatione toto genere discrepat. Moses enim erat Mediator typicus, temporalis, corporalis, sine effusione proprij sanguinis, ad acquisitionem terræ promissæ: Christus verò est Mediator verus sive realis, æternus, spiritualis, per proprium sanguinem liberans nos ab ira Dei, maledictione legis, peccato & morte æterna, in remissionem peccatorum, & acquisitionem cœlestis & æternæ hæreditatis.

Tertia ratio sic habet: Redimendi verbum sermè semper apud sacros Scriptores metaphoricam significationem obtinet, ut nihil sit aliud redimere, quàm liberare, aut sibi asserere, licèt veri pretij vera solutio aliqua non interveniat. E. parem significationem etiam obtinet, quando de morte Christi in Scripturis verbum hoc prædicatur.

Respondeo, Ex parte ad totum non valet consequentia. Sic non sequitur, verbum redimendi in quibusdam Scripturæ locis, metaphoricam obtinet significationem. Ergo ubique metaphoricè est intelligendum. Negatur Consequentia, quia Redemptio Spiritualis, qualis à Christo fuit præstita, sine effusione Sanguinis & sic sine persolutione veri ac realis λύτρει sive pretij expediri non potuit: uti hactenus ostensum. Quale λύτρον in corporalibus liberationibus non requiritur.


### A Special Controversy Against the recent Photinians, On the Satisfaction for our Sins (continued)

FOURTH reason: By the same reason that Christ himself is said to be redeemed by God when he was raised from the dead, by that same reason we also are said to be redeemed through Christ. But Christ was redeemed without the payment of a price: according to that prayer of Christ in Psalm 31:6: 'Into your hand I commit my spirit: You have redeemed me, O Jehovah, God of truth.' Therefore, we also are said to be redeemed through Christ without a price.

I answer: The argument fails by the same sophism as the one immediately preceding: For although the word 'to redeem' is taken improperly regarding Christ in that Psalm, it does not follow that it must be taken so everywhere. Furthermore, this very redemption of Christ, which is celebrated in the Psalm, has a respect to the λύτρον or price, paid by the death of Christ. For although he did not need to pay any λύτρον for himself or his own person, by which he might deliver himself from death: yet both the Resurrection and the entire exaltation of Christ are described in the Scriptures as a consequence of the preceding λύτρον, as in Psalm 110:7: 'He shall drink of the brook in the way: THEREFORE he shall lift up the head.' Luke 24:26: 'Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and SO to enter into his glory?' Philippians 2:8 and 9: 'Christ humbled himself, becoming obedient unto the death of the cross: WHEREFORE GOD also hath highly exalted him,' etc.

FIFTH reason: Redemption is said to be properly done by him who holds captives. But we are said to be redeemed, either from our iniquities (Titus 2:14), or from our vain conversation (1 Peter 1:18), or from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13), by which we were held captive: but never from God, or from the judgment of God, or from that divine justice by which we deserved to be condemned as sinners. Therefore, we are not said to be properly redeemed through Christ.

I answer: The assumption is simply false: For Scripture clearly demonstrates that we were in reality held captive both by the guilt of our sins, and by the curse of the law, and by death and the Devil. The prophet Isaiah, certainly, about to describe the redemption to be paid through Christ, affirms that it consists in this, that liberation would come to the captives: saying, 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives' (Isaiah 61:1), which Christ the Savior testifies was clearly fulfilled in himself (Luke 4:19 and 21). The Holy Spirit also expressed this very thing in Psalm 68:19 and Ephesians 4:8: 'Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive.' What kind of captivity this was, the Apostle explains in Colossians 2:13, 14, and 15. And you, being dead in your sins (behold here the atrocious captivity of sin), God has quickened together with Christ, having forgiven you all trespasses, blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross: and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it. What? That the same Apostle in 2 Timothy 2:26 expressly names sins as the snares or bonds of the Devil, by which we are held captive to his will. Since Christ has redeemed us from these, we have certainly been redeemed not improperly, but properly, through the most sufficient payment of a price, from a captivity that was most sad.

SIXTH reason: He from whom the price has not been paid is improperly said by us to be redeemed: But the price for the curse of the Law has not been paid: since

For this is nothing other than the very punishment established by the Law. Now, it is absurd to establish that a price is paid for a punishment. Therefore, we have been redeemed from the curse of the Law improperly, that is, without a λύτρον or price. Thus, when in the Scriptures we are said to be redeemed from wrath, by wrath nothing else can be understood than the punishment owed to the impious. Now, to pay a λύτρον for a punishment would be inconsistent and ridiculous. Therefore, by the death of Christ, no price was paid for us.

I answer: This argument proceeds first from a false hypothesis, by which the adversaries imagine that redemption, speaking properly, does not occur unless from the one primarily detaining, to whom the payment of a price is made: As if redemption were not likewise properly made from chains, from prison, from capital punishment, even if a price is accustomed to be paid not to those things as punishments in themselves, but for those things, so that, namely, someone may be freed from them. They play childishly, therefore, when they infer thus: a price is not paid for the punishments themselves. Therefore, liberation from punishment is redemption improperly so called: when even a child understands that a captive is properly liberated and redeemed from Turkish captivity when a sufficient λύτρον is paid for him. Where certainly this λύτρον is not paid to the captivity itself, but yet is paid with respect to the captivity. Thus Christ by his λύτρον redeemed us from the curse of the Law, not that he paid it to the punishment itself: but that he truly paid the price to GOD the Father, who was bringing a condemnatory sentence through the Law, and thus with respect to that punishment and torment.

Finally, it is false what the adversaries take for granted: that wrath, when it is predicated of GOD in the Scriptures, only signifies by metalepsis the effect of wrath, that is, torment and punishment: when it rather signifies the very vindicatory justice of GOD: as we showed in the second controversy from chapter 1. 18. and 32. and other places of Scripture.

Seventh argument: Just as we are said to be sold under sin, that is, enslaved: So we are said to be redeemed from the same through Christ, that is, liberated. But we are said to be sold under sin with no true price intervening. Therefore, we are also redeemed through Christ, although no price truly and properly intervened.

I answer, that the connection of the major premise is clearly null. For it is not necessary that the reason for selling and buying be always equal and the same, especially under tyrannical rule: Such was the rule that pressed us when we were still established in the power of the Devil. Furthermore, we readily grant that the word 'sold' is taken improperly and metaphorically in the Scriptures, when the Apostle in Rom. 7. 14. affirms that he was sold under sin: and Isaiah affirms that we were sold in our iniquities in chapter 50. 1. Nor does it follow from that, however, that the word 'redemption' must likewise be taken improperly. But Scripture, by the word 'sold', looks to the power and tyranny of sin: For just as a buyer has a right in a thing sold to him, so sin arrogated to itself right and dominion over men; this most sad sale caused by the rashness of the Adamic fall. Thirdly, if we weigh the matter a little more accurately, we will most rightly deny the minor premise. For when our first parents, and thus the entire human race, had to be sold under sin: certainly the Devil promised a great price of purchase. Namely, that we would be like God, so that we were not sold under sin without a great price of purchase promised by the Devil: which price, however, he could by no means pay. Finally, if according to the precepts of the philosophers, every true comparison must be made in equal degrees; then the argument will proceed only when both sale and redemption are considered with respect to men, in this manner: We were sold freely under sin with respect to our price. Therefore, we were also redeemed freely, likewise with respect to our price, when absolutely none was paid by us! Which conclusion we readily grant, since it has the Holy Spirit himself as its author in Isa. 52, 3. You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money. We grant, however, that it is not absolutely so, with respect to every degree of comparison, but only insofar as men are considered from themselves and in themselves. For we were redeemed freely and without a λύτρον, with respect to us, partly because we were redeemed with no merit of ours intervening: partly, because to the Devil, as the buyer, nothing of reward accrued for the taken prey. But with respect to GOD, our redemption is not so gratuitous that it did not consist of not gold and silver, but the most precious blood of the only-begotten Son. 1 Pet. 1, 18. Apoc. 5, 9.

Eighth argument: In true redemption, he who detains the captive receives the price: But in the redemption of Christ, the Devil, who detained the human race as captive, did not receive a price: indeed, no one at all received a price: Therefore, the redemption of Christ is not a true and proper redemption; that is, it does not consist of a true λύτρον or price of satisfaction.

I answer: The major premise is true only in a certain respect, namely concerning him who primarily detains the captive: and in whose power it is placed to release the captive or not to release him. Otherwise, certainly, lictors are also said to detain a captive: to whom, however, the price of redemption is not paid: since it is not placed in their power to release the captive or not to release him. Thus, neither the Devil, nor sin, nor death, nor hell: but GOD himself was the one primarily detaining the captive human race, as one who had enslaved it to the infernal prison through this sentence: You shall die the death. The Devil, however, only sustained the role of the lictor, sin was like the chains: death and hell like the prison. Therefore, the price of redemption was to be paid not to the Devil, not to sin, not to death or hell, but to GOD, in whose power alone it was placed to pronounce the human race free once again, and to redeem it by His grace: provided that His Justice had been satisfied in full. Now as regards the Minor premise, Socinus lies, asserting that Christ clearly paid the price of redemption to no one: nay rather, he paid it to GOD the Father, as the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 9, 14, testifies: The blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to GOD the Father, cleanses our consciences from dead works. Hence the Father is said to be appeased in the blood of the Son, Rom. 3, 25; likewise, to have condemned sin in the flesh of the Son, Rom. 8, 3; to have made the Son, who knew no sin, a sin offering for us, 2 Cor. 5, 21. Nay, to be uniquely well-pleased in this Son, Matt. 17, 5. Why, therefore, no pious person can have any doubt that Christ paid a most sufficient λύτρον to the Father's wrath and Justice: for otherwise he could not be well-pleased in the Son.

Latin:

QUARTA ratio: Qua ratione Christus ipse dicitur redemptus à Deo, quando est excitatus à mortuis: eâdem ratione nos quoų dicitur per Christum redempti. Atqui Christus sine persolutione pretij est redemptus: secundum precationem illam Christi Psalmo 31, 6. In manum tuam commendo Spiritum meum: Redemisti me Jehovah Deus veritatis. Ergo nos quoų per Christum dicimur redemti sine pretio.

Respondeo, Fallit argumentum eodem Sophismate, quò proximè antecedens: Nam licet verbum redimendi in illo Psalmo improprie de Christo accipiatur, non tamen sequitur, quod ubique sic accipi debeat. Deinde haec ipsa quoque redemtio Christi, quae in Psalmo celebratur, habet respectum ad λύτρον sive pretium, morte Christi exolutum. Etsi enim pro seipso, sive sua persona non opus habuit, ut λύτρον aliquod exolveret, quo seipsum ex morte liberaret: tamen tum Resurrectio, tum universa exaltatio Christi in Scripturis tanquam Consequens praecedentis λύτρου describitur, ut Psal. 110, 7. De torrente in via bibet: PROPTEREA exaltabit caput. Luc. 24, 26. Oportuit pati Christum & SIC intrare in gloriam suam. Phil. 2, 8. & 9. Humiliavit Christus seipsum, factus obediens usque ad mortem crucis: PROPTER QUOD & DEUS ipsum exaltavit &c.

QUINTA ratio: Redemtio proprie fieri dicitur ab eo, qui detinet captivos. At nos dicimur redemti, vel ab iniquitatibus nostris Tit. 2, 14. vel ex vana conversatione nostra 1. Petr. 1, 18. vel ab execratione legis Gal. 3, 13. a quibus nos detinebamur captivi: nusquam vero a Deo, vel a judicio Dei, vel ab ea justitia divina, per quam peccatores damnari merebamur. Non igitur proprie dicimur redemti per Christum.

Respondeo, Assumtionem simpliciter esse falsam: Nam nos revera tum a peccatorum nostrorum reatu, tum a maledictione legis, tum a morte & Diabolo, captivos detentos fuisse, Scriptura luculenter demonstrat. Propheta certe Jesaias descripturus Redemtionem per Christum aliquando exolvendam, in eo illam consistere affirmat, quod captivis tum obventura sit liberatio: Spiritus inquiens Domini super me, eo quod unxerit Dominus me, ut predicarem captivis indulgentiam Jes. 61, 1. id quod Christus Servator in se impletum esse luculenter testatur, Luc. 4, 19. & 21. Hoc ipsum etiam Spiritus Sanctus expressit, Psalmo 68, 19. Ephes. 4, 8. Ascendisti in altum, captivam duxisti captivitatem. Quae captivitas qualis fuerit, explicat Apostolus Coloss. 2, 13. 14. & 15. Vos cum mortui essetis in delictis (en tibi atrocem captivitatem peccati) convivificavit vos Deus cum Christo, qui donat vobis omnia delicta, delens quod adversum nos erat cheirographum decreti, quod erat contrarium nobis, & ipsum tulit de medio, affigens illud cruci: & expolians Principatus ac potestates, traduxit confidenter palam triumphans de illis in semetipso. Quid? quod idem Apostolus 2. Timoth. 2, 26. peccata expresse nominat laqueos sive vincula Diaboli, quibus captivi teneamur ad ipsius voluntatem Ab his ergo cum redemerit nos Christus, utique non improprie, sed proprie per sufficientissimam exolutionem pretij redemti sumus ex captivitate longe tristissima.

SEXTA ratio: Cui non est persolutum pretium, ab eo improprie dicimur redemti: Atqui execrationi Legis non est persolutum pretium: siquidem

Siquidem hæc nihil est aliud quàm ipsa pœna à Lege statuta. Jam verò absurdum est statuere pœna persolvi pretium. Ergo ab execratione Legis impropriè, hoc est, sine λύτρῳ sive pretio sumus redemti. Sic quando in Scripturis dicimur redemti ab ira, per iram nihil intelligi potest aliud, quàm supplicium impiis debitum. Jam verò supplicio persolvere λύτρον, inconveniens & ridiculum foret. Ergò per mortem Christi nullum pretium pro nobis solutum fuit.

Respondeo: Argumentum hoc primùm procedere ex falsa hypothesi, quâ fingunt Adversarij, Redemtionem propriè loquendo no fieri, nisi à principaliter detinente, cui fiat solutio pretii: Quasi verò non itidem propriè fiat redemtio à vinculis, à carcere, à pœna capitis, licet non istis, tanquàm pœnis per se, tamen pro istis, ut nimirùm ab iis liberetur aliquis, pretium exsolvi soleat. Pueriliter proindè ludunt, quando sic inferunt: pœnis ipsis non exolvitur pretium. E. liberatio à pœna est redemtio impropriè sic dicta: cùm vel puer intelligat, propriè ex captivitate Turcica liberari ac redimi captivum, quando sufficiens λύτρον pro eo exolvitur. Ubi certè λύτρον hoc non ipsi captivitati, sed tamen respectu captivitatis solvitur. Sic Christus suo λύτρῳ redemit nos ab execratione Legis, non quòd ipsi pœnæ illud exolverit: sed quòd DEO patri per Legem, damnatoriam ferenti sententiam, & sic respectu pœnæ ac supplicii illius, reverâ pretium exolverit.

Tandem falsum est, quod pro confesso sumunt Adversarii: Iram, quando in Scripturis de DEO prædicatur, tantùm metalepticè significare Effectum iræ, hoc est, supplicium & pœnam: cùm potiùs ipsam DEI justitiam vindicatricem significet: uti Controversiâ secundâ ex cap. 1. 18. & 32. & aliis Scripturæ locis ostendimus.

Septima ratio: Quemadmodum venditi dicimur sub peccatum, hoc est, mancipati: Sic ab eodem per Christum dicimur redemti, hoc est, liberati. At qui venditi dicimur sub peccatum nullo vero pretio interveniente. Ergo etiam per Christum redemti, quamvis pretium nullum verè & propriè intervenerit.

Respondeo, Connexum Majoris planè nullum esse. Neque enim necessum est, ut par semper & æqualis sit ratio venditionis & emptionis, præsertim sub imperio Tyrannico: Quale imperium nos premebat, cum adhuc essemus constituti in potestate Diaboli. Deindè venditionis vocabulum, in Scripturis impropriè & metaphoricè accipi ultrò largimur, quando Apostolus Rom. 7. 14. affirmat, se venundatum esse sub peccato: & Esaias, venditos nos esse in iniquitatibus nostris affirmat cap. 50. 1. Neque tamen indè sequitur, Redemptionis vocabulu itidem impropriè esse accipiendum. Respicit autem Scriptura, venditionis vocabulo, ad potestatem ac tyrannidem peccati: Quemadmodum enim Emtori jus est in re sibi venditam, ita peccatum sibi jus ac dominium in homines arrogavit; tristissimam hanc venditione cautisam temeritate lapsus Adamici. Tertiò, si paulò accuratiùs rem expendamus, rectissimè negabimus Minorem. Nam cùm primi nostri parentes, & sic universum genus humanum vendi debuit sub peccatum: certè Diabolus grande emtionis pretiū promisit. Quòd nimirum Deo futuri essemus similes, ita ut non sine grandi emtionis pretio à Diabolo promisso venditi simus sub peccatum: quod tamen pretium nequaquam exolvere haud potuit. Tandem si secundum præcepta Philosophorum, omnis vera cõparatio fieri debet in gradibus æqualibus; tùm demùm procedet argumentum, quando & venditio & redemtio respectu hominum consideratur, in hunc modum: Gratis venundati sumus sub peccato respectu nostri pretij. Ergò Gratis etiam redemti, itidem respectu nostri pretij, quando à nobis planè nullum est exolutum! Quam consecutionem ultrò concedimus, quippè quæ ipsum Spiritum S. autorem habet Jes. 52, 3. Gratis venundati estis, & sine argento redimemini. Concedimus autem eam non ἁπλῶς, respectu cujuslibet gradus comparationis, sed tantùm quatenùs Homines ex se & & in se considerantur. Gratis enim & sine λύτρῳ redemti sumus, respectu nostri, partim quia nullo nostro merito interveniente redemti sumus: partim, quia Diabolo, tanquàm Emtori, pro ablata prædâ, premij nihil accessit. Verùm respectu D E I usque adeò Gratuita non est nostra redemtio, ut potiùs ea constiterit non auro & argento, sed pretiosissimo sanguine Filij unigeniti. 1. Pet. 1, 18. Apoc. 5, 9.

Octava ratio: In verâ Redemtione precium accipit is, qui captivum detinet: Atqui in Christi Redemtione pretium non accepit Diabolus, qui captivum detinuit genus humanum: imò nemo prorsus accepit pretium: Ergò Redemtio Christi non est vera ac propria redemtio; hoc est, non constat vero λύτρῳ sive Satisfactionis pretio.

Respondeo: Majorem esse tantùm secundum Quid veram, nempè de eo, qui principaliter captivum detinet: & in cujus potestate positum est, dimittere captivum vel non dimittere. Aliàs certè lictores quoq; dicuntur detinere captivum: quibus tamen redemtionis pretium non exolvitur: siquidem in ipsorum potestate non est positum, dimittere captivum, vel non dimittere. Sic neque Diabolus, neque peccatum, neque mors, neque infernus: sed D E U S ipse erat principalis detinens captivum genus humanum, ut qui carceri infernali mancipaverat illud, per hanc sententiam: Morte moriêris. Diabolus autem tantùm lictoris partes sustinuit, peccatū erat instar vinculorum: mors & infernus instar carceris. Proindè non Diabolo, non peccato, non morti aut inferno, sed DEO pretium redemtionis exolvendum erat, in cujus solius potestate erat positum liberum denuò pronunciare genus humanum, idque in gratiam redimere: dummodò Justitiæ suæ ex asse esset satisfactum. Jam quoad Minorem, mentitur Socinus, asserens, Christum planè nemini exolvisse redemptionis pretium: imò verò DEO Patri exolvit, sic attestante Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 9, 14. Sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum Sanctum semetipsum obtulit immaculatum DEO Patri, emundat conscientias nostras ab operibus mortuis. Hinc Pater dicitur placatus in Sanguine Filij Rom. 3, 25. item, condemnasse peccatum in carne Filij Rom. 8, 3. fecisse Filium, qui non noverat peccatum, pro nobis victimam pro peccato 2. Cor. 5, 21. Imò in hoc Filio unicè acquiescere, Matth. 17, 5. Quin ergò Patris iræ ac Justitiæ, Christus sufficientissimum λύτρον exolverit, pio nemini potest esse dubium: Alioquin enim in Filio non acquiescere posset.


### A Special Controversy Against the recent Photinians, On the Satisfaction for our Sins (continued)

And thus far, indeed, we have invincibly asserted those eight Foundations, by which we demonstrated above the meritorious Satisfaction of Christ, against the blasphemies of the Photinians: It remains that, as a kind of finishing touch, we examine certain general Objections, with which they are accustomed to gnaw at and carp at the entire doctrine concerning the Satisfaction and merit of Christ.

THE FIRST Objection is this: Christ died only for this reason: and is therefore also said to be Mediator, and to have brought eternal salvation from Heaven, because he brought the doctrine of salvation from Heaven, and he died for the confirmation of this doctrine of his, but not for any other end.

The ninth reason: Even if the death of Christ were a Satisfaction, yet it would not be a merit on that account: For no Satisfaction can at the same time be a merit: because Satisfaction is a due work, or the payment of a debt by right. But merit is an undue work.

But I answer that this is true κατά τι, in a certain respect, namely concerning such a Satisfaction by which someone pays his own debt for himself: But it is false concerning that by which someone pays a debt not by right, but freely, not for himself, but for another, not his own, but another's. Where, indeed, by this payment of his, he can merit for another a release from prison, or obtain another grace. In this way, Christ by his free will paid the debt for the human race, and acquired its remission by his blood: and thus, in this respect, his Satisfaction is most truly called Merit, both with respect to GOD and with respect to us. With respect to GOD, insofar as the Father set forth the Son to us as a ἱλαστήριον through faith in his blood, for the remission of sins, Rom. 3, 25. With respect to us, insofar as through his death the gift of grace abounded unto all for justification, Rom. 5, 16, 17, 18, 19.

I answer. 1. What they say, they do not prove. Therefore, they basely beg the question. 2. It is manifestly false, which the heretics seize upon as a confession: For since Christ was declared to be the Son of GOD from Heaven, and this command was prescribed to the whole human race: HEAR HIM: certainly it was necessary for all to place faith in his doctrine, without the intervention or consideration of any death or merit. Furthermore, if Christ had died only for confirmation, and as it were in testimony of his Doctrine: then his death could not be called λύτρον, ἀντίλυτρον, ἀπολύτρωσις, ἱλαστήριον: but it would be only μαρτύριον. In which part the death of Christ would differ in no way from the death and passion of other martyrs, who likewise shed their blood for the confirmation of, and in testimony to, the Gospel concerning Christ. Thirdly, it would be false, which Scripture so often inculcates, that Christ died for our sins, for the remission of sins, for our justification and salvation. We correct, therefore, the error, asserting that Christ is named Mediator in the Scriptures in a triple respect. 1. Insofar as he is the interpreter of the divine will: for no one has ever seen GOD: but the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known, John 1, 18. To which pertain also other sayings of Scripture, Matt. 11, 17, John 15, 15, and chapter 17, 8, Heb. 12, 25. Then, insofar as Christ as Priest, through prayers and the Sacrifice of his Body, was Mediator between GOD and men, Rom. 8, 34, Heb. 2, 17, chapter 9, 15, 1 John 2, 1, and 2 John 4, 10. Finally, insofar as he himself is the medium reconciling us to GOD, and joining us to him. John 14, 20. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you. John 17, 21. That they all may be one, as you Father are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us, that the world may believe that you sent me. It is added that Scripture expressly expresses the Form and manner of Christ's mediation: while it names him the only Mediator, and at the same time defines his Sacrifice: There is, it says, one Mediator of GOD and men, the Man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a price of redemption for all, 1 Tim. 2, 5, and indeed in his Blood. Rom. 3, 25, Heb. 9, 22.

The tenth and final reason: Scripture makes no mention of Merit. Therefore.

I answer that a fallacy of non-cause as cause is committed, and the vice of the consequent. For the merit of Christ is not to be denied just because the word 'merit' does not appear literally in the Scriptures.

For equivalent and more emphatic words are found in them, which most evidently establish the concept of Merit: Such is the word 'acquisition,' which Scripture uses very frequently in describing the work of our Redemption. Acts 20, 28, Eph. 1, 14, 1 Thess. 5, 9. Such likewise is the word 'reconciliation,' 'sanctification,' 'justification,' 'glory,' 'propitiation,' 'appeasement,' 'redemption': which each clearly confirm the meritorious Satisfaction of Christ. We therefore simply deny the major proposition, as manifestly false.

THE SECOND is as follows. God reconciled himself to us in Christ 2 Cor. 5:18. Col. 1:21. But the doctrine of Satisfaction attributes the work of reconciliation to Christ, as if he had rendered God appeased to us. Therefore this doctrine conflicts with the Scriptures.

I answer that a fallacy of ignorance of the refutation (ignoratio elenchi) is committed. For every contradiction expires if both are brought forward in a different respect: namely, that God reconciled himself to us in Christ as the source and primary cause; and that Christ appeased God the Father for us as Mediator and meritorious cause. For these are subordinate. Therefore they do not conflict: and this is the less so, the more clearly Scripture asserts both; the former indeed concerning the Father in Col. 1:19, 'It pleased the Father through him to reconcile all things to himself.' But the latter concerning the Son in verses 21 and 22, 'When you were once alienated and enemies, now he has reconciled you in the body of his flesh through death.'

THE THIRD. The doctrine of the Satisfaction of Christ establishes a lack of mercy in us: because we are commanded to imitate God in the forgiveness of injuries toward others. Eph. 5:1. But if God does not remit sins to us without Satisfaction, we also, by the example of God, ought not to remit offenses to our neighbor without punishment. But this latter is impious and absurd. Therefore the former is as well.

I answer that a fallacy of 'in a certain respect and simply' (secundum quid et simpliciter) is committed. For what is most true concerning private injuries and lighter offenses, namely that we should forgive them to our neighbor without any punishment or Satisfaction, is viciously distorted to apply to any and all, even public, injuries. For that same God who prohibited private vengeance, he grants that legitimate contracts between men be kept intact, that to each his own be given, that no one be harmed, and that rash transgressors be punished. Furthermore, this argument does not fight against just any satisfaction, but against our satisfaction. If, therefore, a legitimate opposition is made, as certainly ought to be done, then the argument proceeds thus: God commands that we forgive offenses to our neighbor without Satisfaction being made by the offender. Therefore God also forgives our sins without any satisfaction of ours. But when the Satisfaction of Christ is opposed to the remission which we owe to our neighbor, then the opposition is illegitimate and a fallacy of ignorance of the refutation is committed.

THE FOURTH. If God the Father required satisfaction for our sins, two absurdities follow. 1. That the mercy of the Son is greater than that of the Father, as he required none, but the Father required exact satisfaction. 2. By this very fact, that the will of the Son is different from the will of the Father.

I answer: that neither follows: if it is only attended to that the Son, by satisfying the justice of the Father, has also satisfied his own Justice completely: and therefore there is one will for both: since there is one essential Justice in number for both. Hence Christ also is read to have satisfied himself, Isa. 43:25, 'I, even I, blot out your transgressions FOR MY OWN SAKE.' And Tit. 2:14, 'Christ gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto HIMSELF a peculiar people.'

THE FIFTH. That which God most requires in those to whom he forgives sins, for that reason he also forgives our sins. But God in those to whom he forgives sins only requires repentance and innocence of life. Therefore, repentance and sincerity of life alone is also the cause why God mercifully forgives sins without Satisfaction.

I answer: that the major premise is not simply true, but only in a certain respect, if indeed that which is required of man can be performed by him, then finally God would forgive us our sins for that very reason. But God requires of men not just any obedience, but a perfect one, absolute in all respects, and owed to his law. Now since no mortal can perform this, it follows automatically that God does not forgive sins for the sake of such obedience. Then we invert the argument: God cannot forgive or remit the curse of the law unless the Law is fulfilled by us completely. But this could not be performed by us. Therefore, either we had to perish eternally, or it was necessary that another's Satisfaction be paid in our stead. Thirdly, this fallacy overturns itself: for if Man can sufficiently perform the innocence of life which God requires of him, then there would be no need for the forgiveness of sins, since that necessarily presupposes the omission of those things which God requires. Then a fallacy of 'not a cause as a cause' (non causa ut causa) is committed: for God requires innocence of life, or serious repentance, from us, not so that through it we may obtain Remission of sins, but so that our light may shine before men, and they may see our good works, and glorify our Father who is in heaven, Matt. 5:16, and so that we may show, that is, declare before men our internal faith, by which we are justified before God, James 2:18. With these things thus observed, the assertions of Socinus are impious and blasphemous, affirming: 1. That our obedience is Satisfactory. 2. That faith is preserved by purity and innocence of life. 3. That very many of the saints even outside of Christ obtained remission of sins, and if there are any other such monstrous tales.

For first, our repentance or obedience is lacking, is imperfect, is defiled by the filth of sins. Therefore, for meriting the forgiveness of sins, it is clearly useless, Luke 17:10. Next, the purity and innocence of life is an effect of faith. Therefore, it cannot be a cause, either efficient or preserving, of faith. Hence the Apostle says, you are kept BY THE POWER OF GOD unto salvation THROUGH FAITH, 1 Pet. 1:5. And Paul, THROUGH FAITH we stand in Grace, Rom. 5:2.

Finally, it is false that any remission of sins, or pardon of punishments, has come to men apart from Christ. For even if mention of Christ and faith in Christ is not always expressed in the promises of grace, it is nevertheless always implicitly understood. For the assertion of the Apostle stands firm and immovable: ALL the promises of GOD in CHRIST are Yes and Amen. 2 Cor. 1, v. 20. What is more, repentance and other good works cannot please GOD except in Christ. Whence the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, although in chapter 11 he recounts various objects of divine promises, nevertheless shows clearly enough that each and every one of those promises is uniquely founded in Christ: when he chose to prefix this general aphorism in verse 6: Without faith it is impossible to please GOD: for it is necessary that he who approaches GOD should believe. And yet this faith in both Testaments apprehends nothing other than Christ: whence it is called the faith of Christ, Rom. 1, 17 and ch. 3, 25. And Christ himself is said to be yesterday and today and the same forever, Heb. 13, 8. And Apoc. 13, 8: The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world: To whom, our only Mediator and Redeemer, be glory, honor, and blessing for all the infinite eternities of ages, AMEN.

Latin:

Et hactenùs quidem octo illa Fundamenta, quibus meritoriam Christi Satisfactionem suprà demonstravimus, contra Photinianorum blasphemias invictè asseruimus: Superest, ut coronidis quasi vice, generales quasdam Objectiones examinemus, quibus universam doctrinam de Satisfactione & merito Christi arrodere & vellicare solent.

PRIMA Objectio hæc est: Christus tantum ideò mortuus est: & ideò etiarn Mediator esse, & salutem æternam de Cælo attulisse dicitur, quia doctrinam salutis de Cælo attulit, & in hujus suæ doctrinæ confirmationem, non verò ob finem ullum alium mortuus est.

Nona ratio: Si vel maximè mors Christi esset Satisfactio, tamen non propterea esset meritum: Sit quidem nulla Satisfactio potest simul esse meritum: propterea quòd Satisfactio est opus debitum, sive solutio debiti de jure. Meritum verò est opus indebitum.

Sed respondeo, verum hoc esse κατά τι, secundum Quid, de tali nimirùm Satisfactione, qua quis pro seipso exolvit debitum proprium: Falsum verò de ea, qua quis non ex jure, sed gratis, non pro se, sed pro alio, non suum, sed alienum exolvit debitum. Ubi sanè sua hac solutione alteri potest promereri liberationem ex carcere, vel aliam impetrare gratiam. Hoc pacto Christus libera voluntate pro genere humano exolvit debitum, ejusq; remissionem suo sanguine acquisivit: & sic hoc respectu, Satisfactio ipsius verissimè dicitur Meritum, tum respectu DEI, tum respectu nostri. Respectu DEI, quatenus Pater proposuit nobis Filium ἱλαστήριον per Fidem in sanguine, suo ad remissionem peccatorum Rom. 3, 25. Respectu nostri, quatenus per ipsius mortem donum gratiæ redundavit in omnes ad Justificationem, Rom. 5, 16. 17. 18. 19.

Respondeo. 1. Quod dicunt, non probant. E. turpiter petunt principium. 2. manifestè falsum est, quòd pro Confesso arripiunt hæretici: Cum enim Christus fuerit Filius DEI de Cœlo declaratus, & hoc mandatum universo generi humano præscriptu: HUNC AUDITE: certè ab omnibus fidem ipsius doctrinæ adhiberi necesse erat, sine ullius mortis aut meriti interventu sive intuitu. Deinde sitantum pro confirmatione, & quasi in testimonium Doctrinæ suæ Christus mortuus esset: tum mors ipsius non posset dici λύτρον, ἀντίλυτρον, ἀπολύτρωσις, ἱλαστήριον: sed esset tantum μαρτύριον. Quâ in parte mors Christi nihil prorius differret, a morte & passione aliorum martyrum, qui itidem pro confirmatione, & in testimonium Evangelij de Christo, sanguinem suum effuderunt. Tertio falsum esset, quod Scriptura toties inculcat, Christum mortuum esse pro peccatis nostris, pro remissione peccatorum, pro Justificatione, & salute nostra. Corrigimus proinde errorem, asserentes, Christum triplici respectu in Scripturis nominari Mediatorem. 1. quatenùs interpres est voluntatis divinæ: DEUM enim nemo vidit unquam: sed Filius, qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarravit Iob. 1, 18. Quò pertinent & alia Scripturæ dicta Matth. 11, 17. Ioh. 15, 15. & cap. 17, 8. Hebr. 12.25. Deinde quatenùs Christus ut Sacerdos, per preces & Sacrificium sui Corporis, Mediator fuit inter DEUM & homines Rom. 8, 34. Hebr. 2, 17. cap. 9, 15. 1. Ioh. 2, 1. & 2, 1. Ioh. 4, 10. Tandem quatenus ipse est medium reconcilians nos DEO, eique nos conjungens. Joh. 14, 20. In illo die cognoscetis, quòd ego sum in Patre meo, & vos in me, & ego in vobis. Joh. 17, 21. Ut omnes unum sint, sicut tu Pater in me, & ego in te, ut & ipsi in nobis unum sint, ut credat mundus, quòd tu me misisti. Accedit, quòd Scriptura Formam ac modum mediationis Christi disertè exprimit: dum ipsum nominat unicum Mediatorem, & Sacrificium ipsius simul definit: Unus est, inquiens, Mediator DEI & hominum, Homo Iesus Christus, qui dedit seipsum in Redemtionis pretium pro omnibus, 1. Timoth. 2, 5. & quidem in Sanguine suo. Rom. 3, 25. Hebr. 9, 22.

Decima & postrema ratio Scriptura nullam Meriti facit mentionem. Ergò.

Respondeo, committi Sophisma non causæ ut causæ, & vitio Consequentis. Neque enim ideo meritum Christi negandum, quia vox meriti secundum literam in Scriptutis non extat.

Nam æquipollentia & ἐμφατικώτερα vocabula in illis reperiuntur, quæ Meriti rationem evidentissimè adstruunt: Quale est vocabulum acquisitionis, quo frequenter admodum Scriptura utitur, in describendo Redemtionis nostræ opere. Actor. 20, 28. Ephes. 1, 14. 1.Thess. 5, 9. Quale item vocabulum est Reconciliationis, Sanctificationis, Iustificationis, gloriæ, propitiationis, placationis, redemptionis: quæ singulas Satisfactionem Christi meritoriam lucutenter confirmant. Negamus proinde simpliciter Majorem propositionem, ceu manifestò falsam.

ALTERA sic habet. Deus seipsum nobis reconciliavit in Christo 2. Cor 5,18. Col. 1,21. At doctrina de Satisfactione, tribuit reconciliationis opus Christo, quasi Deum nobis placatum dederit. Ergò pugnat haec doctrina cùm Scripturis.

Respondeo, committi Sophisma παρὰ τὴν ἀγνοιαν ἐλέγχε. Expirat enim omnis contradictio, si diverso respectu utrumque afferatur: nempè quòd Deus seipsum nobis reconciliaverit in Christo, tanquàm fons & causa προηγυμένη: & quòd Christus nobis Deum Patrem placârit, tanquàm Mediator & causa meritoria. Subordinata enim haec sunt. E. non pugnant: idque tantò minus, quantò clariùs utrumque Scriptura asserit; Prius quidem illud de Patre Col. 1, 10. Placuit Patri per eum sibi reconciliare mundum. Posterius verò hoc de Filio versu 21. & 22. Cùm essetis aliquando alienati & hostes, nunc reconciliavit vos in Corpore illo carnis suae, per mortem.

TERTIA. Doctrina de Satisfactione Christi stabilit immisericordiam in nobis: quia jubemur Deum imitari ignoscentia injuriarum erga alios. Ephes. 5, 1. Atqui si Deus non remittit nobis peccata absq; Satisfactione, etiam nos exemplo Dei non debemus proximo remittere offensas, sine vindicta. Sed hoc posterius impium & absurdum. Ergo & prius illud.

Respondeo, committi Sophisma παρὰ τὸ πῇ καξ ἁπλῶς. Nam quod de injurijs privatis, & levioribus offensis verissimum est, ut nimirùm sine ulla vindicta aut Satisfactione eas proximo condonemus: illud ad quasvis, etiam publicas injurias vitiosè detorquetur. Nam ille ipse Deus, qui privatam vindictam prohibuit: ille concedit, ut contractus legitimi inter homines sarti tecti conserventur, suum cuique tribuatur, nemo laedatur, & temerarij transgressores puniantur. Deindè militat hoc Argumentum non contra quamlibet, sed contra Satisfactionem nostram. Si ergò legitima fiat oppositio, uti certè fieri debebat, tüm sic procedit argumentum. Deus jubet ut proximo condonemus offensas, sine Satisfactione, quae fiat ab offendente. Ergò Deus nobis etiam condonat peccata sine ulla Satisfactione nostra. Quando verò Satisfactio Christi opponitur remissioni, quam nos debemus proximo: tum illegitima est oppositio & committitur ignoratio Elenchi.

QUARTA. Si Deus Pater Satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris requisivit, duo sequuntur absurda. 1 Majorem esse misericordiam Filij, quàm Patris, ut qui nullam, Pater verò exactam Satisfactionem, requisiverit. 2. Hoc ipso pacto, diversam esse voluntatem Filij, à voluntate Patris.

Respondeo: neutrum sequi: Si illud tantùm attendatur, Filium Satisfaciendo justitiae Patris, suae quoque Justitiae ex asse satisfecisse: ac proindè unam utrique esse voluntatem: Siquidem una numero essentialis utrique est Justitia. Hinc Christus quoque sibi ipsi satisfecisse legitur Jef. 43, 25. Ego, ego deleo peccata tua PROPTER ME. & Tit. 2, 14. Christus dedit semetipsum pro nobis, ut nos redimeret ab omni iniquitate, & mundaret SIBI populum acceptum.

QUINTA. Quod Deus in illis, quibus condonat peccata, maximè requirit, propter id etiam condonat nobis peccata. Atqui Deus in illis, quibus condonat peccata, tantùm requirit resipiscentiam & innocentiam vita. Ergo sola etiam resipiscentia & sinceritas vitæ causa est, cur Deus clementer peccata condonet absq; Satisfactione.

Respondeo: Majorem non simpliciter veram esse, sed tantùm secundum Quid, si nimirùm ab homine praestari possit id, quod ab ipso requirit, tüm demùm Deum etiam propter illud ipsum condonaturum nobis peccata. Atqui Deus non qualem qualem, sed perfectam, & omnibus numeris absolutam obedientiam legi suae debitam, ab hominibus requirit. Jam cùm hanc nemo mortalium praestare possit, sequitur ultrò, Deum etiam propter talem obedientiam non condonare peccata. Deinde invertimus argumentum: Deus non potest condonare aut remittere maledictionem legis, nisi Lex ex asse impleatur à nobis. Atqui hoc à nobis praestari non potuit. Ergò vel aeternum nobis pereundum fuit, vel aliena Satisfactio vice nostri exolvatur, necessum erat. Tertio Sophisma hoc seipsum evertit: Si enim Homo praestare sufficienter potest innocentiam vitae, quam Deus ab ipso requirit, tùm peccatorum condonatione non opus fuerit, quippè quae necessariò praesupponit omissionem eorum, quae Deus requirit. Tùm committitur Sophisticatio non causae ut causae: Requirit enim Deus à nobis innocentiam vitae, sive seriam resipiscentiam, non ut per eam Remissionem peccatorum consequamur, sed ut luceat lux nostra coram hominibus, & videant bona nostra opera, & glorificent Patrem nostrum, qui in Coelis est, Matth. 5, 17. & ut ostendamus, hoc est, coram hominibus declaremo internam fidem nostram, quâ justificamur coram Deo Iacob. 2, 18. His ita observatis impiae & blasphemae sunt assertiones Socini affirmantis. 1. Obedientiam nostram esse Satisfactoriam. 2. Fidem conservari puritate & innocentia vita. 3. Sanctorum plurimos etiam extra Christum consecutos esse remissionem peccatorum, & si quae his sunt consimilia τερατολογήματα alia.

Primùm enim nostra poenitentia sive obedientia est manca, est imperfecta, est peccatorum fordibus polluta. Ergò ad condonationem peccatorum promerendam planè est inutilis Luc. 17, 10. Deindè Puritas & innocentia vitae est Effectus fidei. E. non potest esse Causa vel Efficiens vel Conservans fidei. Hinc Apostolus, VIRTVTE DEI, inquit, custodimini ad salutem PER FIDEM. 1. Petr. 1, 5. Et Paulus, PER FIDEM stamus in Gratia Rom. 5, 2.

Tandem falsum est, quòd ulla remissio peccatorum, vel condonatio pœnarum, citra Christum hominibus obtigerit. Etiamsi enim non semper in promissionibus gratiæ expressa sit mentio Christi, & fidei in Christum: tamen implicitè semper intelligitur. Stat enim firma & immota asseveratio Apostoli: OMNES promissiones DEI IN CHRISTO sunt etiam & Amen. 2. Cor. 1. v. 20. Quid, quòd pœnitentia & reliqua bona opera DEO placere non possunt nisi in Christo. Unde Autor Epistolæ ad Hebræos, etsi cap. 11. varia objecta promissionum divinarum recenset, satis tamen dilucidè ostendit, singulas ac universas illas promissiones unicè fundatas esse in Christo: quando generalem hunc aphorismum versu 6. præmittere voluit: Sine fide impossibile est placere DEO: credere enim oportet accedentem ad DEUM. Atqui hæc fides in utroque Testamento nihil aliud apprehendit quàm Christum: Undè fides Christi dicitur, Rom. 1, 17. & cap. 3, 25. Et Christus ipse dicitur esse heri & hodie & idem in secula, Hebr. 13, 8. Et Apoc. 13, 8. Agnus occisus ab origine mundi: Cui Mediatori ac Redemtori nostro unico sit gloria honos & benedictio in infinitas seculorum omnium æternitates, AMEN.


### A Special Controversy Against the recent Photinians, On the Satisfaction for…: The Second General Controversy, concerning Justification with the Romanists

The Second General Controversy, concerning Justification with the Romanists.

There is no Article of the Christian Religion which, ever since the world was created, or at least since the human race fell, has been subject to more disputes and corruptions than that which concerns the Justification of a sinful man before GOD. Among these, however, each and every one, none was ever more fruitful than that which exists between our Churches and the Papacy. For no part of this Article can be given, indeed not even the smallest appendage of any part, which has not suffered a most sad and most dangerous servitude and depravation under the Papacy, so much so that our Theologians have long since collected over thirty Popish errors concerning this one Article. Added to this is that notable polycephaly of the Romanists, or that frequent change in the State of the Controversy, which is so customary for them that not even to this day can it be determined with sufficient certainty where they finally wish to plant their feet, and which opinion they wish to consistently maintain and assert.

Certainly, soon after the times of the Apostles, that Son of perdition, the mystery of iniquity, began to act, though somewhat timidly: when some established a triple method of justification, namely that the Patriarchs were saved before Moses by the Law of Nature: the subsequent Fathers, however, by the Law of Moses: and finally we under the New Testament are saved by

the Law of Christ. Justin Martyr and Philosopher, Clement of Alexandria, and others did not at all shrink from this opinion.

In the progress of time, a purer Doctrine indeed shone upon the Fathers by the benefit of GOD: but in such a way that it can by no means be denied, nor should it be, that the seeds of Popish impiety were sown even then. For although most established that the Form of our Justification consists in the sole gratuitous Remission of sins, through and on account of the merit of CHRIST, apprehended by faith, just as Chemnitz confirms this at length from the Fathers, both in his Examen and in his Loci: yet there were by no means lacking those who defined Justification itself by its Effect or Consequent, that is, by the Renewal or Sanctification of the mind, quite dangerously confusing the Law of faith with the Law of works. Hence, without a doubt, was born that rather inconvenient explanation of the words of the Apostle Rom. 3, 24 (Justified freely by his grace) which was brought forth by Augustine in his book On the Spirit and the Letter, ch. 26, in these words: What else is 'justified' than 'made just' by him, namely, who justifies the ungodly, so that from ungodly he BECOMES just? And in the preceding chapter 13: From these we conclude that a man is not justified by the precepts of a good life, except through the Faith of Jesus Christ.

Thirdly, there followed the Scholastic Doctors, who likewise departed into opinions clearly different, and indeed such as are today in part distasteful even to the Papists themselves. For although Peter Lombard, the Patriarch of the Scholastics, passed over this Article as if with dry feet, and barely tastes it with his extreme lips, in book 2 of his Sentences, dist. 26, with this aphorism alone proposed: Prevenient grace is Faith with love: yet Thomas later in the first part of the second book, question 113, and likewise Bonaventure in book 4 of his Sentences, dist. 17, undertook an explanation of this passage expressly: but such a one as would square in every way with the Physical Doctrine of motion. For 1. they defined the Justification of the ungodly as a motion from injustice to justice: to be the making of a just man out of an unjust one: to be the transmutation of the ungodly from the state of guilt to the state of justice, according to the definition of motion, which is from one contrary to the other.

Then they brought forward this reason for those definitions: Because, forsooth, a motion is denominated more from the term to which it tends than from the term from which it departs: Therefore they inferred that this transmutation also, by which someone is transmuted to a state of innocence through the remission of sin, derives its name from the term to which it tends, and is called the Justification of the ungodly. Thirdly, they taught that the word to justify in this place signifies actively indeed the infusion of justice, and thus only GOD justifies: But passively, that it is the same as to be prepared for justice, or to receive justice: And thus the soul of man is justified, that is, is disposed and prepared so that it may admit or undergo the infusion of justice. Fourthly, they established certain requirements, four in number, which perfect and complete the Justification of Man; namely 1. The infusion of Grace. 2. Free will. 3. Contrition or

Latin:

Altera Controversia Generalis, de Justificatione cum Romanensibus.

Nullus est Religionis Christianæ Articulus, qui jam indè à condito mundo, vel lapso saltem genere humano, pluribus disceptationibus & corruptelis fuerit obnoxius, quàm qui est de Justificatione Hominis peccatoris coram DEO. Inter has verò singulas ac universas, nulla fœcundior fuit unquàm, quàm quæ Ecclesiis nostris cum Papátu intercedit. Neq; enim ulla dari potest Articuli hujus pars: imò ne quidem ullius partis appendicula minima, quæ non tristissimam pariter ac periculosifsimam servitutem & depravationem, sub Papátu passa sit, usque adeò, ut nostrates Theologi, ultra triginta errores Pontificios, circa hunc unum Articulum jampridem collegerint. Accedit insignis illa πολυκεφαλία Romanensium, sive crebra illa Status Controversiæ mutatio, quæ ipsis ita solennis est, ut neque in hunc usq; diem, satis certò constare queat, ubinam tandem pedem figere, & quámnam sententiam constanter tueri atque asserere velint.

Certè mox post Apostolorum tempora, Filius ille perditionis, mysterium iniquitatis, sed timidiusculè peragere cœpit: cum triplicem justificandi rationem nonnulli statuerent, Patriarchas nimirùm ante Mosen salvatos esse per Legem Naturæ: Patres subsequentes verò, per Legem Mosis: Nos deniq; sub Novo Testamento salvari per

Legem Christi. A qua sententia minimè abhorruerunt Justinus Martyr & Philosophus, Clemens Alexandrinus & alii.

Progressu temporis purior quidem Doctrina Patribus DEI beneficio illuxit: sed ita, ut negari minimè vel possit vel debeat, etiam tùm impietatis Pontificiæ semina fuisse sparsa. Etsi enim plerique statuebant, Justificationis nostræ Formam consistere in sola gratuita peccatorum Remissione, per & propter meritum CHRISTI, fide apprehensum, quemadmodum prolixè hoc ex Patribus confirmat Chemnitius, tùm in Examine: tùm in locis: minimè tamen defuerunt, qui Justificationem ipsam, per ejus Effectum sive Consequens, hoc est, per Renovationem sive Sanctificationem mentis definirent, satis periculosè Legem fidei, cùm Lege operum confundentes. Hinc procul dubio nata est satis incommoda illa explicatio verborum Apostoli Rom. 3, 24 (Justificati gratis per gratiam ipsius) quæ prodita ab Augustino lib. de Spiritu & litera cap. 26. his verbis: Quid est aliud Justificati, quàm justi FACTI ab illo scilicet, qui justificat impium, ut ex impio FIAT justus? Et cap. præced. 13. Ex his colligimus, non justificari hominem præceptis bonæ vitæ, nisi per Fidem Jesu Christi.

Tertiò, subsecuti sunt Doctores Scholastici, qui itidem in diversas planè abierunt sententias, & tales quidem, quæ ipsis quoque Pontificiis hodiè ex parte sordent. Etsi enim Petrus Lombardus Patriarcha Scholasticorum, sicco quasi pede Articulum istum præteriit, & vix extremis labris ipsum degustat, lib. 2. Sent. dist. 26. hoc duntaxat proposito Aphorismo: Gratia Præveniens voluntatem est Fides cum dilectione: tamen Thomas postmodùm in prima secundæ quæst. 113. item Bonaventura in l. 4. Sent. dist. 17. Loci hujus explicationem ex professo instituerunt: sed talem, quæ ad Doctrinam Physicam de motu per omnia quadraret. Nam 1. definiverunt Justificationem impij esse motum ab injustitia ad justitiam: Esse facere justum de injusto: esse transmutationem impij de statu culpæ, ad statum justitiæ, juxta rationem motus, qui est de contrario in contrarium.

Deindè Definitionum istarum causam protulerunt istam: Quia nimirùm motus denominatur magis à termino ad Quem, quàm à termino à quo: Ergo inferebant, transmutatione etiam hanc, quâ aliquis transmutatur ad statum innocentiæ per Remissione peccati, sortiri nomen à termino ad Quem, & vocari Justificationem impij. Tertiò docuerunt, verbum Justificare hoc loco activè quidem significare, Justitiæ infusionem, & sic solum DEUM justificare: Passivè verò idem esse, ac præparari ad Justitiam, vel suscipere Justitiam: Et sic animam hominis justificari, hoc est, disponi & præparari, ut admittat sive patiatur infusionem justitiæ. Quartò constituerunt certa requisita, & quidem numero quatuor, quæ Justificationem Hominis perficiant & absolvant; nempè 1. Infusionem Gratiæ. 2. Liberum arbitrium. 3. Contritionem sive detesta-


### Investigation of the State of the Controversy

detestation of sin, 4. The remission or expulsion of sin. Two of which, namely the infusion of Grace and the expulsion of sin, proceed from GOD as from a moving Cause: but the other two from the sinner being justified, as from a mobile subject receiving Justification.

Fifthly, they disputed: Whether the Justification of the ungodly is instantaneous or successive: And they answered: That the whole Justification of the ungodly consists originally in the infusion of Grace: indeed, by which the free will is moved and guilt is remitted: but that the infusion of Grace occurs in an instant without succession. Finally, they established the meritorious end of Justification: For they argued that Grace is infused by GOD so that the justified person may thus be able to merit eternal life. Since this Justification precedes all merit: nor does anyone have the merit of eternal life unless he is justified in such a way.

And these were those shadows which, in the course of a very long succession of many centuries, invaded and indeed occupied the Church of GOD regarding the business of our salvation in a miserable manner, and even today, alas, hold it as if captive in many places under the papacy: as will be evident a little later, where almost more states of Controversy emerge than there are members of the impiety itself.

Moreover, now in the fourth place, since this Scholastic Theology seemed too crude to many, because there was clearly a deep silence in it concerning Christ and his most holy merit: it again produced a new state of Controversy for the Papacy, contending that Christ also enters into the act of our Justification as Mediator: but only in part, not in full. For that he satisfied only for Original sin: but that the remaining Actual sins must be expiated by us.

But not even in this way was any mode of change found: but in the fifth place, when some noticed that Scripture, wherever it deals with the Justification of Man before GOD, always mentions Faith in CHRIST: therefore that dogma was devised concerning Faith formed by the habit of love infused as a form, in which the whole power of our Justification would consist.

Sixthly, regarding this Faith, they were again split into differing opinions. For some maintained that Faith does this in us, that minds are prepared and accommodated to receive Justification in themselves: Others ascribed this not to Faith alone, but also to charity, alms, and penance: Others stripped Faith simply of its native and proper office, asserting that the benefits of the merit of Christ can be applied by the zeal and merit of Works. Christ. Lautherius, Bavarian Theologian, in a public writing.

Seventhly, there were not lacking those who ascribed the whole power of justifying to works: yet on the condition that if they were imperfect, then finally the merit of Christ would supply their defect. In which sentiment Joh. Polandus wrote in his method of helping the dying, page 27. b. Supply, LORD JESUS, the imperfection of my actions: Join, I beseech you, my most unworthy service with all that you have done and suffered, and deign to offer it to the eternal Father.

Eighthly, a little before the Council of Trent, indeed in the Council itself, certain Pontifical Writers and Monks concocted a completely profane method of Justification: contending that Abraham had no other doctrine concerning Christ than Socrates, Plato, and other Heathens had: a thing which Latomus was not ashamed to defend in his writings: contending also that Men, even without the knowledge of Christ, provided they lived an honest life, could have been saved by the law of Nature alone: as Sleidanus attests in book 23, indeed, as Andradius himself writes in book 3, Orth. expl. p. 291. & 292. Where the Monk does not shudder to disseminate into the Christian world that even the Emperor Trajan, an enemy and persecutor of the Christian name, was delivered from the punishments of hell, in which he was, by the prayers of Gregory, on account of the JUSTICE and piety which he exercised toward a widow woman. Bellarminus does not deny this same thing entirely, but in such a way that he judges the merit of Trajan's Liberation should be ascribed not to his own work, but to the prayers of Gregory. book 2, on Purgatory, chap. 8.

Ninthly, the Council of Trent itself, Sess. 6. cap. 7, with the state again changed, contends that the sole formal cause of Justification is the Justice of GOD, not that by which he himself is just, but that by which he makes us just, by which, namely, being gifted by him, we are renewed in the spirit of our mind: and we are not only reputed, but are truly named and are just, with Justice received into us and the habit of Justice diffused in our hearts, which inheres in us.

And Can. 32. of the same Session, If anyone shall say that the good Works of a justified man are so the gifts of GOD that they are not also the good MERITS of the justified man himself, or that the justified man himself, by the good works which are done by him through the grace of GOD and the merit of Jesus Christ, of whom he is a living member, does not TRULY MERIT the increase of grace, ETERNAL LIFE, and the attainment of that eternal life itself, if however he shall have departed in grace, and also the increase of glory, let him be anathema.

And so that it might be clear in what place Faith in Christ was for those Fathers: they produced two canons worthy of note, of which the former, ninth in order, is as follows: If anyone shall say that the ungodly is justified by Faith alone, so that he understands that nothing else is required which cooperates toward obtaining the grace of Justification, and that it is not necessary in any part for him to be prepared and disposed by the motion of his own will, let him be anathema.
