The eleventh in the subsequent order reads thus: If anyone shall say that man is justified either by the sole imputation of the righteousness of Christ, or by the sole remission of sins, to the exclusion of the grace and charity which is poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit, and cleave to them, or also that Grace, by which we are justified, is only the favor of GOD, let him be anathema.

Tenthly, the Jesuit Society, intending to explain more clearly this intricate theology of the Fathers of the Council of Trent, today fabricates a twofold Justification: The first, which consists in this, that Christ by his death merited that believers should be imbued and adorned with Charity and other virtues. The second, which is placed in this, that Man, having received those new qualities, on account of the merit of Christ, now furthermore by that inherent Justice, merits a greater, fuller, more exact justice, reconciliation and adoption, and finally eternal life. Censur. Colon. p. 148. 149. 159.

And this is that citadel which the Jesuit Society today strives with great effort to defend and restore to its former liberty. Therefore, our future Treatise will serve to storm, nay, to utterly overthrow this, and so that it may keep itself within legitimate bounds, we remove at the beginning those questions about which there is no proper controversy between us and the Jesuits, such as these.

I. Whether in the man being justified the Holy Spirit, through the word, as he kindles and excites faith, so also kindles and excites the fruits of faith, Charity, repentance, and other virtues of that kind? Or whether Charity, Contrition, detestation of sin, a good purpose, and other works of that kind must exist in the Man being justified?

II. Whether the Grace of GOD, in many places of Scripture, denotes an infused habit of Renewal or Sanctification?

Tertiò: Whether Faith, by reason of its essence, is a virtue, a quality, and a habit, or indeed even some act?

Quartò: Whether those justified by faith through the Grace of GOD are renewed in the spirit of their mind, so that they may offer new obedience to GOD?

Quintò: Whether this Renewal of the mind is a part of the merit of Christ: and that those destitute of it cannot be saved?

For concerning these Questions we ourselves also hold the affirmative in all respects. Therefore, the entire dispute between us and them is properly and principally agitated only about the true and proper Causes of Justification: which, however, can be conveniently recalled to two members.

THE FORMER is: What is that for which GOD receives Man into favor, forgives him his sins, and finally saves him eternally?

THE LATTER is: What is the proper and adequate Instrument by which we may apprehend the Grace of GOD offered to us in Christ, and salutarily apply it to ourselves: Whether faith alone in Christ performs this: Or whether Works, either alone, or joined with faith?

Our treatise will therefore directly regard this twofold state: following the footsteps of the Jesuit Bellarmine, we divide it into four special questions or controversies.

The FIRST will be concerning the proper and genuine meaning of the word to justify, which it obtains in this very article: where we shall at the same time expressly examine that Jesuitical fiction concerning a twofold justification.

II. Concerning the Efficient Cause of Justification: under the compass of which belongs also both the MERITORIOUS Cause with respect to GOD, which is Christ: and the instrumental Cause, and that either offering and sealing the grace of GOD, which is the Word of GOD and the Sacraments: or apprehending the offered grace, which is FAITH ALONE IN CHRIST.

III. The question or controversy will be concerning the MATERIAL CAUSE, which is man himself fallen through sin.

IV. And the last concerning the FORMAL CAUSE of justification: where the very acropolis of the Jesuitical dogma will have to be attacked and overturned.

Latin:

tionem peccati, 4. Remissionem sive expulsionem peccati. Quorum duo, nempe infusio Gratiæ, & expulsio peccati proveniant à D E O, tanquam à Causa movente_: Duo verò reliqua, à peccatore justificando, tanquàm à subjecto mobili, suscipiente Justificationem.

Quintò disputârunt: An Justificatio impij sit instantanea, an verò successiva: Et responderunt: Totam Justificationem impij originaliter consistere in infusione Gratiæ : quippe, per quam liberum arbitrium moveatur, & culpa remittatur: Gratiæ autem infusionem fieri in instanti absq; successione. Tandem, Finem Justificationis côstituerunt meritorium: Ideò enim infundi à D E O Gratiam, ut sic justificatus mereri possit vitam æternam. Siquidem Justificatio hæc antecedat omne meritum: neq; quisquam habeat meritum vitæ æternæ, nisi qui sit tali modo justificatus.

Et hæ fuerunt tenebræ illæ, quæ benè longo multorum seculorum decursu, Ecclesiam DEI, circa salutis nostræ negotium, miserandum in modum invaserunt, imò occupârunt, ac etiamnum hodiè proh dolor, multis in locis sub papatu, captivam quasi tenent: uti paulò post patebit, Ubi plures fermè emergunt Controversiæ status, quàm ipsius impietatis sunt membra.

Cæterùm quarto jâm loco, cùm hæc Scholasticorum Theologia nimiùm crassa multis videretur, eò quòd Christi, ejusq; Sacrosancti meriti, altum planè in ea esset silentium: rursus novum peperit Papatus Controversiæ statum, contendens, Christum quoque ingredi Justificationis nostræ actum, tanquam Mediatorem: sed ex semisse tantùm, non ex asses. Nam pro Originali tantùm peccato ipsum satisfecisse: nobis verò reliqua peccata Actualia expianda esse.

Sed neq; sic mutabilitatis modus ullus inventus: verùm quinto loco, cùm nonnulli animadverterent, Scripturam, ubicunque agit de Justificatione Hominis coram DEO, semper meminisse Fidei in CHRISTUM: ideò excogitatum est dogma illud de Fide formata, per formam intellecto dilectionis infuso habitu, in quo tota vis Justificationis nostræ consisteret.

Sextò circa Fidem hanc rursus in discrepantes scindebantur opiniones. Nonnulli enim statuebant, Fidem hoc in nobis agere, ut preparentur atq; accommodentur animi ad Justificationem in se recipiendam: Alii Fidei non soli, sed & charitati, eleëmosynis, pœnitentiæ hoc adscribebant: Alii Fidem, simpliciter suo nativo, ac proprio spoliabant officio, asserentes, Operum studio meritoq; applicari posse beneficia meriti Christi. Christ. Lautherius Theolog. Bavaricus in scripto publico.

Septimò non defuerunt, qui operibus totam vim justificandi adscribebant: eâ tamen conditione, ut sicubi ea essent imperfecta, tum demùm eorum defectum suppleret meritum Christi. Quam in sententiam scripsit Joh. Polandus in methodo adjuvandi moriturus pag. 27. b. Supple DOMINE JESU imperfectionem actionum mearum: Conjunge obsecro indignissimum obsequium meum, cum omnibus, quæ tu egisti, & passus es, & patri æterno illud offerre digneris.

Octavò, paulò ante Concilium Tridentinum, imò in ipso Concilio, Scriptores & Monachi quidam Pontificii, prophanam prorsus Justificandi rationem confinxerunt: conten dentes, Abrahamum non aliam de Christo doctrinam habuisse, quàm Socrates, Plato, alijq́; Ethnici habuerunt: id quod Latomus suis in scriptis propugnare non erubuit: contendentes item, Homines etiam sine cognitione Christi, modò honestam vitam egerint, salvari potuisse solâ lege Naturæ: sic attestante Sleidano lib. 23. imò, sic scribente ipso Andradio lib. 3. Orth. expl. p. 291. & 292. Ubi Monachus non exhorrescit in orbem Christianum disseminare, quòd etiam Trajanus Imp. hostis & persecutor Christiani nominis, propter JUSTITIAM & pietatem, quam erga mulierem viduam exercuit, orationibus Gregorij, à pœnis inferni, in quibus erat, liberatus fuerit. Quod ipsum non per omnia negat etiam Bellarminus, sed ita, ut meritum Liberationis Trajani, non ipsius operi, sed Gregorij precibus adscribendum esse censeat. lib. 2. de Purgatorio, cap. 8.

Nonò, Concilium ipsum Tridentinum Sess. 6. cap. 7. rursus mutato statu contendit, Justificationis causam formalem unicam esse Justitiam DEI, non quâ ipse justus sit sed quâ nos justos facit, quâ videlicet ab eo donati, renovemur spiritu mentis nostræ: & non modò reputemur, sed & verè justi nominemur, & simus, Justitia in nobis receptâ, diffusoq́; in cordibus nostris Justitiæ habitu, qui nobis inhæreat.

Et Can. 32. ejusdem Sessionis, Si quis dixerit, Hominis justificati bona Opera ita esse dona DEI: ut non etiam sint bona ipsius justificati MERITA, aut ipsum justificatum, bonis operibus, quæ ab eo per DEI gratiam & Jesu Christi meritum, cujus membrum vivum est, fiunt, non VERE MERERI augmentum gratiæ, VITAM ÆTERNAM, & ipsius vitæ æternæ, si tamen in gratia discesserit, consecutionem, atq; etiam gloriæ augmentum, Anathema sit.

Et ut constaret, quo loco Patribus istis esset Fides in Christum: duos notatu dignos prodiderunt Canones, quorum prior, ordine nonus, fic habet: Siquis dixerit, solâ Fide justificari impium, ita ut intelligat, nihil aliud requiri, quòd ad Justificationis gratiam consequendam cooperetur, & nullâ ex parte necesse esse, eum suæ voluntatis motu præparari atq; disponi, anathema sit.

Posterior ordine undecimus sic sonat: Si quis dixerit, Hominem justificari, vel solâ imputatione Justitiæ Christi, vel solâ peccatorum remissione, exclusa gratia & Charitate, quæ in cordibus eorum per Spiritum sanctum diffundatur, atq; illis inhæreat, aut etiam Gratiam, quâ justificamur, tantùm esse favorem DEI, Anathema sit.

Decimò intricatam hanc Patrum Concilii Tridentini Theologiam, clariùs explicatura Societas Esawitica, geminam hodiè confingit Justificationem: Unam primam, quæ in eo consistat, quòd Christus morte sua hoc meruerit, ut credentes imbuantur & ornentur Charitate & alijs virtutibus. Alteram secundam, quæ in eo sit posita, quòd Homo acceptis novis illis qualitatibus, propter meritum Christi, jam porrò inhærente illa Justitiâ, promereatur majorem, pleniorem, exactiorem justitiam, reconciliationem & adoptionem, & tandem vitam æternam. Censur. Colon. p. 148. 149. 159.

Et hæc est acropolis illa, quam magno conatu Societas Jesuŵitica hodiè propugnare, & pristinæ libertati restituere studet. Huic proindè expugnandæ, imò funditùs evertendæ, futura nostra inserviet Tractatio, quæ ut intra legitimos sese contineat cancellos, removemus initiò eas quæstiones, de quibus inter nos & Jesuŵitas propriè non controvertitur, quales sunt.

I. An in homine Justificando Spiritus sanctus per verbum, uti fidem, sic etiam fidei fructus Charitatem, pœnitentiam & id genus alias virtutes accendat & excitet? vel an in Homine justificando esse debeat Charitas, Contritio, peccati detestatio, Bonum propositum, & id genus opera alia?

II. An Gratia DEI in multis Scripturæ locis, notet infusum Renovationis, sive Sanctificationis habitum?

Tertiò: An Fides ratione suæ essentiæ sit virtus, qualitas, & habitus, imò actus etiam aliquis?

Quartò: An justificati fide per Gratiam DEI, Spiritu mentis suæ renoventur, ut novam præstent DEO obedientiam?

Quintò: An Renovatio hæc mentis, sit pars meriti Christi: & quod eâ destituti, salvari nequeant?

Nam circa has Quæstiones nos ipsi quoque Affirmativam per omnia tenemus. Ergo propriè & principaliter non nisi de Causis Justificationis veris atque propriis, universa inter nos & ipsos disputatio agitatur: Quæ tamen ad duo membra haud incommodè revocari potest.

PRIUS est: Quodnam sit id, propter quod DEUS Hominem in gratiam recipit, ipsiq; peccata remittit, & tandem æternùm salvat?

POSTERIUS est: Quodnàm sit proprium & adæquatum Organon, quô Gratiam DEI, in Christo nobis oblatam, apprehendere, nobisq; salutariter applicare queamus: Nùm hoc præstet sola fides in Christum: An verò Opera vel sola: vel cum fide conjuncta?

Geminum proindè istum statum Tractatio nostra directè respiciet: quam secuti vestigia Jesuwitæ Bellarmini, in quatuor Quæstiones sive Controversias Speciales dispescimus.

PRIMA erit de verbi Justificandi propria ac genuina significatione, quam hoc quidem in articulo obtinet: Ubi simul commentum illud Jesuwiticum de duplici Justificatione, ex professo examinabimus.

II. De Causa Efficiente Justificationis: sub cujus complexum pertinet etiam tùm Causa MERITORIA respectu DEI, quæ est Christus: tùm Causa instrumentalis, eaque vel offerens & obsignans Gratiam DEI, quæ est Verbum DEI & Sacramenta: vel apprehendens oblatam Gratiam, quæ est SOLA FIDES IN CHRISTUM.

III. Quæstio sive Controversia erit de CAUSA MATERIALI, quæ est ipse Homo per peccatum lapsus.

IV. Et postrema de CAUSA FORMALI Justificationis: ubi ipsa acropolis dogmatis Esawitici oppugnanda & evertenda erit.


### Special Controversy, concerning the word Justifying, and its true and genuine meaning in the present Article

It is controverted today between us and the Jesuits, concerning the true and proper sense of the word to be justified in this very article: where they indeed contend that it signifies the same thing as, first, to be made just from being impious through preparatory dispositions, faith, love of GOD, hatred of sin and of one's past state, repentance, hope of pardon: and through infused grace of justice, or the habit of charity: which they call FIRST justification: Then indeed, this grace cooperating with the free will of man, for one who is justified to be made more justified, through works of justice, and through the observance of the commandments of GOD: which they call SECOND, actual, material, and meritorious justification before GOD: just as Stapleton defines in his Antidotes: and Costerus in his Enchiridion chapter 6. Bellarmine book 1 on Justification chapter 1. and book 2 chapter 2. The sum and head of which Jesuitical opinion comes down to this, that to justify is the same as, by infused qualities of virtues and the habit of justice itself being put in, to make one in reality just from being unjust.

Making a divorce from this doctrine, our churches maintain that the word to justify obtains a forensic meaning, or at least has been transferred from forensic usage to the cause of salvation, so that a man is said to be justified by GOD when, having been absolved from the guilt of sins, through the remission of sins, through and on account of the merit of CHRIST, he is reckoned and pronounced just by GOD.

But that we may be able to be fully certain of the truth of our doctrine, the equivocation, or variety of meanings, which the word to justify is found to obtain in the scriptures, must be unfolded at the beginning: as he himself also thinks. Bellarmino, book 1, chapter 1. Moreover, this equivocation is produced by the very diversity of the adjuncts, or causes and things, to which this word is attributed. For it is said not only that God justifies man, but also that man justifies God, and indeed even that man justifies man, and that either himself or another. Thus it is read in the Scriptures that faith, or indeed that works also, justify. Where, certainly, unless the manifold meaning of the word 'justify' is most accurately unfolded and explained according to the diversity of the causes or adjuncts, a most dangerous precipice of error is prepared for us.

In the beginning, therefore, we willingly grant that this word, wherever it occurs in the Scriptures, always denotes some act concerning justice.

Then, however, we maintain that what or what kind of act is noted must be judged not from the preconceived dogmas of the Jesuits, but from the quality of the adjunct. When this is considered more closely, eight different meanings of this word emerge, none of which, however, can establish or confirm that fictitious dogma concerning an infused habit of justice.

First, therefore, 'to justify' denotes the same as to exercise an act of judgment, or to discern between a good and a bad cause, as when Absalom says: 'Who will make me a judge in the land, that all who have a cause may come to me, and I may justify them?' 2 Sam. 15:4. In the same sense Christ complains that Wisdom is justified by the children of men, that is, pronounced unjust, or as it were called to account concerning justice.

Then this word obtains the sense of acknowledgment, preaching, and declaration: as when David says: 'That you may be justified in your words,' Ps. 51:9, and Christ is read to have been justified by all the people, that is, acknowledged, preached, and declared to be just, Luke 7:29. Thus this word is also accepted concerning men, when Christ asserts that everyone is to be justified by his own words, Matt. 12:37, and likewise when James asserts that Abraham and believers are justified by works, chap. 2:21 and 24. Where the sense of declaration can only be granted, as the circumstance of time in the person of Abraham, already justified by faith, the analogy of faith and the perpetual harmony of the Scriptures, and finally the very phrase of James, chap. 2:18 and 20, irrefragably prove, as will be shown more fully below.

Thirdly, 'to justify' means the same as to promote others to justice by teaching and instructing, as in Daniel 12:3 teachers are said to justify their hearers, that is, to instruct them in justice.

Fourthly, this word denotes strenuous progress or increments in acquiring justice: as in Rev. 22:11, 'He who is just, let him be justified still.'

Fifthly, this word involves a respect of comparison to others: as when it is read in Ezek. 16:51: 'You have justified your sisters in all your abominations which you have committed.' There, 'to justify' means the same as to surpass in injustice or malice, the prophet explaining himself thus when he immediately adds: 'Samaria has not committed half of your sins, but you have surpassed them in your crimes,' ibid.

Sixthly, it denotes Pharisaical arrogance of holiness, as when it is read in Luke 10:29 that a lawyer wished to justify himself; and likewise when in Luke 16:15 the Pharisees are said to have justified themselves before men.

Seventh, this word takes on the sense of liberation, Rom. 6:7. He who has died has been justified from sin: where the Greek δεδικαίωται is most correctly rendered by Basil with the word ἠλευθέρωται, he has been liberated. For this phrase is taken from common usage, where the word to be justified is used of those who are subjected to punishments on account of crimes: to be judged: For just as these can no longer commit crimes of that kind, so he who has died is so liberated that he can no longer sin.

Eighth and lastly, to justify signifies to absolve someone from crimes charged and to pronounce them just: as when someone is made guilty of some iniquity by another, but is pronounced just by a judge through a sentence, and is absolved from all guilt. And in this sense the word to justify is most frequently used in the Scriptures, as Gen. 44:16. What shall we say, or how shall we be justified, that is, absolved from the guilt of the crime committed against our brother Joseph? Exod. 23:7. You shall not kill the innocent and the just: for I will not justify the wicked. Deut. 25:1. When there is a dispute between men, and they come to the judges, justify the just and condemn the wicked. Prov. 17:15. He who justifies the wicked, and condemns the just, both are an abomination before GOD. And we indeed maintain that the word to justify in this article must be taken in this forensic signification: and that for the following evident reasons.

I. In the Old Testament this word, or the Hebrew הִצְדִיק, never and nowhere signifies to make a just person out of an unjust one, but in the present and any related matter it everywhere denotes to pronounce or hold someone as just, and to absolve: whether universally or particularly: whether in court or outside of court: whether truly or falsely. Nor can the Jesuits bring forward even a single testimony of a contrary signification, although they labor to the point of sweating blood in this regard, as will be most evidently clear a little later in the Refutation of their opinion.

II. Whatever signification the contrary words obtain, namely הִרְשִׁיעַ Hirschia to make wicked, to condemn the impious or evil: the opposite word to justify will also obtain the same: which the nature and affection of contraries evince.

And yet that word (malificare) nowhere in the entire Biblical Code signifies to make evil out of good, or to infuse a habit of malice: but according to the forensic custom of speaking, it signifies to hold someone as evil or guilty, or even to condemn someone. Therefore, by equal reasoning, the word Justifying will also obtain a forensic signification in this matter, so that it denotes the same as to absolve from sins.

which corresponds both to the Hebrew הִצְדִיק, and to the Greek δικαιοῦσθαι. Now, indeed, even among the Pontifical writers, Lambinus, in his annotations on chapters 5 and 9 of book 5 of Aristotle's Ethics, notes that the verb δικαιᾶν and δικαιοῦσθαι is properly taken of a Judge and Magistrate, who gives to each his own. And Suidas says, δικαιῶν signifies two things: both to punish, and to deem or pronounce just.

III. In the New Testament, the Greek verb δικαιοῦσθαι, to be justified, is opposed to the verb κατακρίνεσθαι, to be condemned: and where the matter of salvation is concerned, it is always taken in a forensic sense, nor can any dissimilar example be brought forward: with the exception, perhaps, of that one place which Bellarmine urges from chapter 22, verse 11 of the Apocalypse: He that is just, let him be justified still: concerning which, a little later.

VII. In the Scriptures, not only Justification is attributed to God, but also Condemnation: the former with respect to those to be saved: the latter with respect to those to be damned. Therefore, just as God is said to condemn, not by infusing vicious and damnation-worthy qualities, but by passing a condemnatory sentence upon the reprobate: so He must also be established to Justify, not by infusing a habit of Justice, but by absolving from the guilt of sin, and pronouncing the faithful just. The connection of the argument is firm from the nature of opposites, and indeed all the more firm because the Apostle opposes Justification not only to condemnation, but also to accusation, by which the guilt of sin is leveled against Man, Rom. 8:33. Who shall accuse the elect of God? It is God who justifies: as if he were to say: It is God who absolves: Therefore no one can accuse the Elect. But this accusation can only be made by imputing the guilt of sin. Therefore, this absolution also is made by not imputing iniquity. The argument from the position of one Contrary to the removal of the other is certainly valid in immediate opposites.

IV. The synonyms confirm this forensic signification. For not rarely in the Scriptures, to impute justice is put for the word to justify. Rom. 4:3 & 5. Faith is imputed to the believer for justice. Likewise, not to impute, but to cover sins, Ps. 31:1, Rom. 4:7. Thus the Apostle interprets the term of Justification by the remission of sins, Acts 13:38, Rom. 4:3; by salvation, Matt. 1:21, John 3:17, Acts 4:12, Acts 15:11, Eph. 2:5. Likewise by translation from the power of darkness to the kingdom of the Son, and from death to life, Col. 1:13, 1 John 3:14. Which phrases, each and all, so far from arguing for some infused habit of Justice, rather simply deny that it habitually exists in man.

Latin:

COntrovertitur hodiè inter nos & Jesuuitas, de vero ac proprio sensu verbi Justificari in hoc quidem Articulo: ubi illi quidem contendunt, significare illud idem, quod primò ex impio justum effici per dispositiones præparatorias, fidem, amorem DEI, odium peccati & status præteriti, pœnitentiam, spem veniæ: & per infusam Justitiæ gratiam, sive habitum Charitatis: quam vocant Justificationem PRIMAM: Deindè verò hac Gratiâ coöperante cum libero Hominis arbitrio, ex justificato magis justificatum fieri, per opera justitiæ, & per observationem mandatorum DEI: quam vocant Justificationem SECUNDAM, actualem, materialem & meritoriam coram DEO: quemadmodum definiunt Stapletonus in Antidotis: & Costerus in Enchiridio cap. 6. Bellarm. lib 1. de Justif. cap. 1. & lib. 2. cap. 2. Cujus sententiæ Esawiticæ summa & caput eò redit, quòd Justificare idem sit, ac infusis virtutum Qualitatibus, & habitu Justitiæ ipso indito, reipsâ ex injusto justum facere.

Ab hac doctrina divortium facientes nostræ Ecclesiæ statuunt, verbum Justificare forensem obtinere significationem, vel certè ex usu forensi ad Causam salutis esse translatam, ut justificari tùm dicatur homo à DEO, cum à peccatorum reatu absolutus, per remissionem peccatorum, per & propter CHRISTI meritum, justus à DEO reputatur & pronunciatur.

Cæterùm ut de certitudine doctrinæ nostræ ex asse nobis constare possit, evolvenda initiò fuerit æquivocatio, sive significationum varietas, quam verbum Justificare in sacris obtinere deprehenditur: sic ipso etiam censente Bellarmino lib. 1. cap. 1. Parit autem hanc æquivocationem ipsa adjuncto rum, sive Causarum & rerum diversitas, quibus verbum hoc attribuitur. Dicitur enim non modò Deus justificare Hominem: sed & Homo justificare Deum, quin etiam Homo hominem justificare, & quidem vel seipsum vel alium. Sic in Scripturis legitur, quòd Fides: imò quòd opera etiam justificent. Ubi sanè nisi pro causarum sive adjunctorum diversitate, multiplex significatio verbi Justificare accuratissimè evolvatur & explicetur, paratum nobis est periculosissimum erroris præcipitium.

Initiò igitur ultrò largimur, verbum hoc ubicunque in Scripturis occurrit, semper denotare actum aliquem circa Justitiam.

Deindè verò, quisnám vel qualis actus notetur, non ex præconceptis Jesu vvitarum placitis: sed ex Adjuncti qualitate judicandum esse statuimus. Hâc autem pressiùs consideratâ, octo potissimùm emergunt diversa verbi hujus significata: quorum tamen nullum, fictitium illud de infuso Justitiæ habitu dogma stabilire aut confirmare potest.

Primùm igitur Justificare idem notat, ac exercere actum judicii, sive discernere inter Causam bonam & malam, ut quando Absolon dicit: Quis me constituat Judicem super terram, ut ad me veniant omnes, qui habent causam, & ego justificem eos. 2. Sam. 15. 4. Eodem sensu conqueritur Christus, Sapientiam justificari à filijs hominum, hoc est, pronunciari injustam, sive de justitia in jus quasi vocari.

Deindè verbum hoc agnitionis, prædicationis, & declarationis sensum obtinet: ut quando David inquie: Ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis, Psal. 51, 9. & Christus ab universo populo justificatus, hoc est, justus agnitus, prædicatus & declaratus fuisse legitur, Luc. 7, 29. Sic de hominibus quoq; hoc verbum accipitur, quando ex verbis suis quemque justificandum esse, Christus perhibet Matth. 12, 37. quando item Abrahamum & credentes ex operibus, Justificari asserit Jacobus cap. 2, 21. & 24. Ubi Declarationis sensum tantùm concedi posse, tùm circumstantia temporis in persona Abrahami, jam fide justificati: tùm analogia fidei & Scripturarum perpetua harmonia: tùm denique phrasis ipsa Jacobi, cap. 2, 18. & 20. irrefragabiliter evincit, uti infra fusiùs ostendetur.

Tertiò idem significat Justificare, ac docendo & instituendo ad justitiam promovere alios, ut Daniel. 12, 3. dicuntur Doctores Justificare suos auditores, hoc est, ad justitiam instituere.

Quartò notat verbum hoc strenuos progressus sive incrementa, in acquirenda justitiâ: ut Apocal. 22, 11. Qui justus est, justificetur adhuc.

Quintò verbum hoc involvit respectum comparationis alicujus ad alios: ut quando Jezech. 16, 51. legitur: Justificasti sorores tuas, in omnibus abominationibus tuis, quas operatus es. Ultibi Justificare idem significat, quod injustitiâ sivè malitiâ superare, sic semetipsum explicante Prophetâ, quando statim subjicit: Samaria dimidium peccatorum tuorum non peccavit : sed vicisti eas in sceleribus tuis. ibid.

Sextò notat Pharisaicam Sanctitatis arrogantiam, ut quando Luc. 10, 29. Legisperitus seipsum justificare voluisse legitur: quando item Luc. 16, 15. Pharisaei seipsos coram hominibus justificasse perhibentur.

Septimò Liberationis sensum verbum hoc sortitur, Rom. 6, 7. Qui mortuus est, justificatus est à peccato: ubi Graecum δεδικαίωται rectissimè à Basilio redditur per verbum ἠλευθέρωται, liberatus est. Deprompta enim est haec phrasis ex communi loquendi usu, ubi verbum Justificari usurpatur de his, qui propter maleficia suppliciis afficiuntur: Gericht werden: Quemadmodùm enim hi, non ampliùs ejusmodi scelera patrare possunt: ita qui mortuus est, is ita liberatus est, ut ampliùs peccare non possit.

Octavò & postremò Justificare significat, absolvere aliquem à criminibus objectis, & pronunciare justum: ut quando aliquis ab alio reus factus est alicujus iniquitatis, à Judice verò per sententiam Justus pronunciatur, atque à reatu omni absolvitur. Et hoc sensu Justificandi verbum frequentissimè in Scripturis usurpatur ut Genes. 44, 16. Quid loquemur, aut quid justificabimur, hoc est, absolvemur à reatu facinoris, in fratrem nostrum Josephum commissi? Exod. 23. v. 7. Innocentem & justum non occides: quia non justificabo impium. Deut. 25, 1. Cùm fuerit lis inter viros, & accesserint ad Judices, justificate justum & reprobate malum. Proverb. 17, 15. Qui justificat impium, & improbat justum, abominatio sunt ambo coram DEO. Et hâc quidem in significatione forensi verbum Justificandi hoc in articulo accipiendum esse nos quidem statuimus: idque ob sequentes rationes evidentes.

I. In Veteri Testamento verbum hoc, sive Hebraeum הִצְדִיק nunquàm & nusquam significat ex injusto justum efficere, sed in praesente & cognata quavis materia ubique notat aliquem pronunciare seu habere justum, & absolvere: sive universaliter, sive particulariter: sive in foro, sive extra forum: sive verè, sive falsò. Neque contrariae significationis testimonium vel unicum proferre possunt Jesuïtae, licèt ad sudorem etiam Sanguinis hac in parte allaborent, uti paulò post in Refutatione ipsorum sententiae evidentissimè patebit.

II. Quam significationem obtinent verba contraria, nempè הִרְשִׁיעַ Hirschia malificare, reprobare impium sive malum: eandem obtinebit etiam verbum oppositum Justificare: id quod contrariorum natura & affectio evincit.

Atqui verbum illud (malificare) nuspiam in toto Codice Biblico fignificat ex bono malum facere, vel malitiæ habitum infundere: sed secundum forensem loquendi consuetudinem fignificat malum sive reum habere, vel etiam condemnare aliquem. Ergo pari ratione forensem etiam significationem Justificandi verbum in hoc negotio obtinebit, ut idem notet, ac absolvere à peccatis.

quod & Hebræo הִצְדִיק, & Græco δικαιοῦσθαι respondeat. Jam verò ex scriptoribus etiam Pontificiis, Lambinus ad cap. 5. & 9. lib. 5. Ethic. Aristotelis annotat, verbum δικαιᾶν & δικαιοῦσθαι propriè accipi de Judice & Magistratu, qui suum cuique tribuit. Et Suidas δικαιῶν, inquit, δύο δηλοῖ, τό τε κολάζειν, καὶ τὸ δίκαιον νομίζειν: Justificare duo significat, vel punire, vel justum reputare sive pronunciare.

III. In Novo Testamento verbum Græcum δικαιοῦσθαι Justificari, opponitur verbo κατακρίνεσθαι condemnari: & ubi de negotio salutis agitur, semper in forensi significatione accipitur, neque ullum dissimile exemplum potest proferri: unico fortassis isto loco excepto, quem urget Bellarminus ex cap. 22, 11. Apocalypscos: Qui justus est justificetur adhuc: de quo paulò post.

VII. In Scripturis tribuitur Deo non modò Justificatio, sed & Condemnatio: Illa respectu salvandorum: hæc respectu damnatorum. Ergo quemadmodum Deus dicitur condemnare, non infundendo vitiosas & damnatione dignas qualitates, sed ferendo sententiam damnatoriam de reprobis: Sic Justificare etiam statuendus est, non infundendo Justitiæ habitum: sed absolvendo à peccati reatu, justosque pronunciando fideles. Connexum argumenti firmum est ex natura oppositorum, & quidem eò firmiùs, quòd Apostolus Justificationem non tantùm opponit condemnationi, sed etiam accusationi, quâ peccati reatus Homini intentatur, Rom. 8. 33. Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat: quasi dicat: Deus est qui absolvit: Ergo nemo potest Electos accusare. Accusatio verò hæc fieri potest, tantùm imputando reatum peccati. Ergo absolutio etiam hæc fit, non imputando iniquitatem. Valet utique argumentum à positione Contrarii unius, ad remotionem alterius, in immediatis.

IV. Confirmant forensem hanc significationem τὰ συνώνυμια Haud rarò enim in Scripturis pro verbo Justificandi ponitur, Justitiam imputare. Rom. 4. 3. & 5. Fides credenti imputatur ad Justitiam. Item, non imputare, sed tegere peccata, Psal 31, 1. Rom. 4, 7. Sic Apostolus Justificationis vocabulum interpretatur per remissionem peccatorum, Actor. 13, 38. Rom. 4, 3. per salvationem, Matth. 1, 21. Joh. 3, 17. Actor. 4, v. 12. Actor. 15, 11. Ephes. 2, 5. Item per translationem à potestate tenebrarum, ad regnum Filii, & à morte ad vitam, Coloss. 1, 13. 1. Joh. 3, 14. Quæ phrases singulæ & universæ tàm non infusum aliquem Justitiæ habitum arguunt, ut eum potiùs homini habitualiter inesse, simpliciter negent.


### Special Controversy, concerning the word Justifying, and its true and genuine meaning in the present Article (continued)

VIII. The Consensus of Orthodox Antiquity fights for our opinion: For thus Oecumenius in chapter 3 of the Epistle to the Romans: The justice of God is Justification from God, absolution and liberation from sins, from which the Law itself could not absolve. But how is it Justification? By the remission of sins, which we obtain in Christ Jesus.

Augustine in Psalm 31: If the ungodly is justified, he is made just from ungodly: But how? You have done nothing good and the remission of sins is given to you.

V. The Apostle, when about to describe the matter of our Justification expressly, continually demands and declares it according to a forensic act or process. For first, he shows that the entire human race is guilty of eternal damnation on account of sins, Rom. 1 & 2. Then he shows that no flesh can be justified before the tribunal of God by the works of the Law, Rom. 3:20. Finally, he submits that it is liberated from eternal damnation only through the Justification of Faith, that is, through the gratuitous remission of sins and the imputation of another's Justice, namely that of Christ the Savior, Rom. 4 & 5 and the following chapters.

The same, book 2 against Julian, says that he is justified from sin to whom all sins are remitted through Baptism.

VI. In no Hebrew, nor Greek, nor Latin, nor our own vernacular idiom does to justify signify to make someone actually just by infused qualities of virtues and an implanted habit of Justice. Therefore, such a signification is deservedly exploded. And although we willingly concede to Bellarmine that this word was unknown to Cicero and Terence, and that the term of Justification is not found in either this or that signification among the authors of the Latin language: yet nothing is lost from our opinion thereby: For that word was made Latin by Theologians, and received into use in the Church, for the very reason that no other occurred,

And although Augustine sometimes seems to explain the word Justify through the gift of inherent or habitual righteousness, yet it must be noted that in such places he uses the term Justification for Sanctification or the renewal of the mind, and thus expresses the effect of our justification rather than the cause. Furthermore, Augustine willingly grants that Justify obtains a relative signification, so that it denotes the same as to reckon as just, just as he writes in Tom. 3, de Spiritu & litera, cap. 26: They shall be justified freely, as if it were said, they shall be held as just, they shall be reckoned as just: just as it was said of a certain man, he wishing to justify himself, that is, that he might be held and accounted as just. Finally, Augustine also interprets this phrase, To make a just man out of an ungodly one, through the remission of sins, as is evident from what was cited before.

Having duly weighed these reasons, we finally define Justification from the Scriptures as the Action of GOD, by which He absolves a sinful man, yet one who believes in CHRIST, freely on account of the merit of the Son, from sins, and having remitted all sins, receives him into grace, and endows him with the righteousness of CHRIST, so that, being thus adopted into the Son, and liberated from every debt of sin and the punishment of condemnation, he may attain eternal blessedness.

The Jesuit faction, intending to bring a lawsuit against this purer doctrine of ours, produces two most pestilential heads of errors. THE FIRST is concerning the Definition of Justification, which they imagine to be a change or motion toward Righteousness: so that to Justify is the same as to give or infuse righteousness: just as Heating is a motion toward heat, as Costerus holds in Enchirid. cap. 6. p. 223. Or as Bellarmine explains with another similar example: Just as air, when it is illuminated by the Sun, through the same light which it receives, ceases to be dark and begins to be bright: So also Man, through Righteousness given and infused into him by the sun of Righteousness, ceases to be unrighteous, lib. 2. de Justif. c. 2. pag. 1034 B.

But this opinion labors under two very gross errors. For first, it is constructed not from the oracles of the Scriptures, but from the rancid and obsolete dogmas of the Scholastics, especially those of Thomas. For they all commonly dispute about Justification purely physically, as if about some Generation, which is the induction of a form into matter, sufficiently disposed through alterations, as Thomas speaks, prima secundæ quæst. 113. art. 1.

Then a shameful Confusion of Justification and Sanctification is committed. For those things which they bring forward concerning the dispositions for receiving righteousness pertain to Sanctification or the renewal of the mind: which we do not deny can be called habitual: although we depart from the Romanists in two things. 1. That they imagine this very inherent Holiness to be our Justification before GOD. 2. That they establish that those dispositional habits proceed not from the mere grace of GOD, or the sole operation of the Holy Spirit, but from the powers of free will. Both of which clash diametrically with the analogy of faith, as will be evident.

But the Jesuits have some passages of Scripture with which they are accustomed to fight: And Bellarmine indeed argues thus at the beginning: Scripture uses the words to Magnify, to vivify, to mortify, to conglorify, which are altogether similar to the word to Justify. But no one would deny that to Magnify is to make great: to vivify, to make alive: to Mortify, to make dead: to conglorify, to make glorious with another. Why therefore should to Justify not also be to make just? Bellarm. lib 2. de Justif. cap. 9. p. 1066. C.

I answer that the true and genuine sense of Biblical words and phrases must be sought not from Grammar, but from Holy Scripture: and as Basil warns somewhere, our study and concern should be not for the letter, but for the Scripture. According to grammatical analogy, we might perhaps concede that words composed of an adjective and the verb FACIO generally signify the habitual effect in the Subject of that quality which the epithet denotes, with the removal of the contrary: But in the mysteries of faith, and indeed in the present Article, the analogy of faith does not admit this sense. Nay, rather, the verb I Justify is excepted from this rule, which, by Bellarmine's own admission, was unknown to Cicero and Terence and the rest of the authors of the Latin language. And since it has been translated into Latin from the Hebrew and Greek language, it certainly follows the signification of these languages as well.

Then this collection is utterly trifling: The remaining words obtain the sense of the Latin signification: Therefore also the word to Justify. For words of this kind do not always obtain their signification from the property of the etymology, but rather from the nature of the Adjunct.

Finally, it is not even simply true that such compound words always obtain a grammatical signification. GOD is certainly said to be magnified, glorified, sanctified by us, Psalm 34:4, Luke 1:46, Exod. 15:6. But who would be so impious or so alien to reason as to affirm, following the grammatical rule, that we do not make the great out of GOD, make the glorious out of the inglorious, make the holy out of the profane. Let the property of Grammatical Composition therefore cease in this part.

Furthermore, the propriety of the Latin language can or ought to prejudice no other languages.

The Jesuit's second argument is taken from the Hebrew verb, הִצְדִּיק, which, because it is in the third conjugation, Hiphil, therefore signifies nothing else than to make a just person out of an unjust one through an infused habit of justice. But our Chemnitz has long since responded most soundly that that rule of the grammarians, that verbs of the Hiphil conjugation so intend the meaning that they attribute or infuse a quality to another, is not universally true, because contrary examples can be given from the Scriptures. For if an unrighteous judge, by justifying the wicked, were to infuse into him the quality of justice, it would not be an abomination before GOD, Prov. 17, 15, nor would GOD adjudge such a one to eternal malediction, Isa. 5, 23. We therefore correct this rule of the grammarians with the same Chemnitz in this manner, that verbs of the third conjugation attribute the quality of the first conjugation to another, not only by infusion, as the Jesuits rave, but either by permission, or by judgment, or by words, testimony, asseveration, declaration: and as Paul defines, by imputation or λογισμῷ. See Chemnitz, part 2 of the Loci, pages 631, 632.

It is ridiculous, however, that the Jesuit produces in support of his cause that passage in Isa. 53, v. 11, 'My servant in his knowledge shall justify many.' For even if we grant to Jerome and the Jesuit that Christ justifies men in various ways, and that one of those ways is doctrine: nevertheless not immediately can any infusion of new habits be constructed from that. For neither does he who teaches or instructs another unto righteousness, just as Daniel 12, 3. Doctors are said to justify many in this way: he immediately infuses new qualities of righteousness. Furthermore, nowhere in the entire Scripture is the infusion of new qualities established as the medium or organ of this Justification: but only the preaching of the word, which is therefore also called the ministry of reconciliation, as God exhorting us through it. 2 Cor. 5, 19 & 20. Just as therefore Christ binds, looses, retains or remits sins mediately through the ministry of the word: so also through the same he confers the knowledge or recognition of himself to many unto righteousness. Finally, the Holy Spirit himself utterly overturns the Jesuitical gloss, who interprets this Prophetic phrase not through the infusion of new qualities, but through the remission of sins: Luke 1, 77. He will give the knowledge of salvation through John his forerunner, which is in the remission of sins. Finally, no reason of consequence holds. The word to justify in this or that saying of Scripture does not obtain a forensic meaning: Therefore neither will it obtain such in those places which expressly deal with the Justification of Man before God. For the equivocation of this word having been shown, the vanity of the Jesuitical collection spontaneously lies open and collapses,

Thirdly, the Jesuit brings forward two other places from the Scriptures, the former of which stands in Ecclesiasticus 18, 22. Do not fear to be justified until death, for the reward of the Lord remains forever. The latter in Apocalypse 22, 11. He who is just, let him be justified still. Therefore, says the Jesuit, he is said to be justified, who from just becomes more just.

Latin:

VIII. Militat pro nostra sententia Consensus Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis: Sic enim Oecumenius in cap. 3. Epistolæ ad Rom Justit a Dei est Justificatio ex Deo, absolutio ac liberatio à peccatis, à quibus Lex ipsa absolvere non potuit. Quomodo autem sit Justificatio? per remissionem peccatorum, quam in Christo Jesu consequimur.

Augustinus in Psal. 31. Si justificatur impius, ex impio fit justus: Sed quomodo? Nihil boni fecisti & datur tibi remissio peccatorum.

V. Apostolus ex professo Justificationis nostræ negotium descripturus; ad actum sive processum forensem subinde istud exigit & declarat. Primùm enim universum Genus humanum, ob peccata reum esse ostendit æternæ damnationis, Rom. 1. & 2. Deindè ostendit, ex operibus Legis coram tribunali Dei non posse Justificari ullam carnem, Rom. 3, 20. Tandem subjicit liberari illud ab æterna damnatione non nisi per Justificationem Fidei, hoc est, per gratuitam remissionem peccatorum, & imputationem alienæ Justitiæ, nimirùm Christi Servatoris, Rom. 4. & 5. ac subsequ. capitibus.

Idem lib. 2. contra Julianum, eum dicit justificari à peccato, cui per Baptismum peccata remittuntur omnia.

VI. Nullo nec Hebraico, nec Græco, nec Latino, nec vernaculo nostro Idiomate Justificare significat, infusis virtutum qualitatibus, & indito Justitiæ habitu, aliquem reipsa justum facere. Ergò meritò talis fignificatio exploditur. Et quanquàm Bellarmino libenter concedimus, verbum hoc Ciceroni & Terentio ignotum fuisse, & Justificationis vocem apud Latinæ linguæ authores, neque in hac, neque in illa significatione reperiri: nihil tamen inde sententiæ nostræ decedit: Est enim illud verbum à Theologis vel ideò Latinum factum, & in Ecclesia usu receptum, quia nullum succurrit aliud,

Et quanquam interdum Augustinus videtur verbum Justificare, per inhærentis sive habitualis justitiæ donationem exponere: tamen notandum, ipsum in ejusmodi locis Justificationis vocabulum, pro Sanctificatione sive renovatione mentis usurpare, & sic Effectum magis, quàm causam Justificationis nostræ exprimere. Deindè ultrò largitur Augustinus, Justificare, relativam obtinere significationem, ut idem notet, ac justum reputare: quemadmodum scribit Tom. 3. de Spiritu & litera cap. 26. Justificabuntur gratis, ac si diceretur, justi habebuntur, justi reputabuntur: sicut dictum est de quodam, ille volens se justificare, id est, ut justus haberetur, & deputaretur. Tandem Augustinus quoque hanc phrasin, Ex impio facere justum, interpretatur, per remissionem peccatorum, uti ex antè citatis patet.

Rationibus istis probè expensis definimus tandem ex Scripturis Justificationem, quòd sit Actio DEI, quà Hominem peccatorem, sed credentem in CHRISTUM, gratis propter meritum Filij à peccatis absolvit, omnibusq́; peccatis remissis in gratiam recipit, & justitiâ CHRISTI donat, ut sic in Filium adoptatus, & ab omni peccati reatu ac damnationis supplicio liberatus, æternam beatitudinem consequatur.

Puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ factio Jesuitica litem intendens duo prodit errorum capità longè pestilentissima. PRIUS est de Definitione Justificationis, quam fingunt esse mutationem sive motum ad Justitiam: ita ut Justificare idem sit, quòd justitiam dare sive infundere: sicut Calefactio est motus ad calorem, uti habet Costerus in Enchirid. cap. 6. p. 223. Vel ut Bellarminus alio quodam simili explicat: Sicut aër cum illustratur à Sole, per idem lumen, quod recipit, desinit esse tenebrosus, & incipit esse lucidus: Sic etiam Homo per Justitiam sibi à sole Justitiæ donatam atque infusam, desinit esse injustus lib. 2. de Justif. c. 2. pag. 1034 B.

Sed laborat hæc opinio duobus crassissimis erroribus. Primùm enim extructa ea est, non ex Scripturarum oraculis, sed ex rancidis & obsoletis Scholasticorum Thomæ cumprimis dogmatibus. Disputant enim communiter omnes de Justificatione planè Physicè, tanquàm de Generatione aliqua, quæ sit inductione formæ in materiam, per alterationes sufficienter dispositam, uti loquitur Thomas prima secundæ quæst. 113. art. 1.

Deindè turpis committitur Confusio Justificationis & Sanctificationis. Quæ enim de habitibus ad justitiam recipiendam dispositivis proferunt: ea ad Sanctificationem sive renovationem mentis pertinent: quam habitualem dici posse, non imus inficias: licèt in duobus à Romanensibus discedamus. 1. quòd fingunt, hanc ipsam inhærentem Sanctitatem, esse Justificationem nostram coram DEO. 2. quòd statuunt, habitus illos dispositivos, non à mera DEI gratia, sive solâ operatione Spiritus sancti: sed à viribus liberi arbitrij provenire. Quod utrumque cum analogia fidei è diametro pugnat, uti patebit.

Sed habent Jesuitæ nonnulla Scripturæ loca, quibus pugnare solent: Ac Bellarminus quidem initiò sic arguit: Scriptura verbis Magnificandi, vivificandi, mortificandi, conglorificandi utitur, quæ sunt omninò similia verbo Justificandi. Nemo autem negaret, Magnificare esse magnum facere: vivificare, vivum facere: Mortificare, mortuum facere: conglorificare, gloriosum cum alio facere. Cur igitur Justificare non sit etiam justum facere? Bellarm. lib 2. de Justif. cap. 9. p. 1066. C.

Respondeo, non ex Grammaticâ, sed ex Scripturâ Sacra, verum ac genuinum vocum ac phrasium Biblicarum sensum petendum esse: & ut alicubi Basilius admonet, non τη̃ γραμματη̃: sed τη̃ς γραφη̃ς stadium nobis debere esse curecordiq́;. Secundum analogiam Grammaticam fortassis concederimus, plerumque verba composita ex nomine adjectivo, & verbo, FACIO, significare, effectionem habitualem in Subjecto ejus qualitatis, quam Epitheton denotat, cum remotione contrariæ: Verùm in mysteriis fidei, & quidem in præsente Articulo sensum hunc analogia fidei non admittit. Quin potiùs excipitur ab hac regula verbum Justifico, quod, fatente ipso Bellarmino, Ciceroni & Terentio ac reliquis Latinæ linguæ autoribus ignotum fuit. Et cum illud ex Hebræa & Græca lingua in Latinum translatum sit, utique harum etiam linguarum significationem sequitur.

Deindè nugatoria prorsus isthæc collectio: Reliqua verba obtinent sensum Latinæ significationis: Ergò & verbum Justificandi. Neq; enim semper ex proprietate etymi, sed potiùs ex Adjuncti natura, verba ejusmodi composita significationem sortiuntur.

Tandem ne quidem illud simpliciter verum est, quod ejusmodi verba composita significationem Grammaticam semper obtineant. Dicitur certè DEUS à nobis magnificari, glorificari, sanctificari, Psalm. 34. 4 Luc. 1, 46. Exod. 15, 6. Quis verò ita vel impius vel à ratione foret alienus, qui Grammaticam secutus regulam affirmaret, nos ex DEO non magno facere magnum: ex inglorio facere gloriosum, ex profano facere sanctum. Facesfat proindè hac in parte Grammaticæ Compositionis proprietas.

Accedit, quòd Latinæ linguæ proprietas, reliquis linguis nihil præjudicare potest vel debet.

Alterum Jesuitæ argumentum petitum à verbo Hebræo, הִצְדִּיק, Quod quia sit in tertia Conjugatione Hiphil, ideò nihil aliud illud significare, quàm ex injusto justum facere per infusum Justitiæ habitum. Sed jampridem solidissimè respondit noster Chemnitius, Regulam illam Grammaticorum, quod verba Conjugationis Hiphil ita intendant significationem, ut tribuant vel infundant qualitatem alteri, non esse universaliter veram, propterea quod exempla contraria ex Scripturis dari possint. Si enim judex iniquus justificando impium, infunderet ipsi qualitatem justitiæ, non esset abominatio coram DEO, Prov. 17, 15. neque DEUS talem æternæ maledictioni adjudicaret. Jes. 5, 23. Corrigimus proindè cùm eodem Chemnitio regulam hanc Grammaticorum in hunc modum, quòd verba tertiæ Conjugationis, qualitatem primæ Conjugationis tribuant alteri, non tantùm per infusionem, uti Jesuitæ delirant, sed vel permissione, vel judicio, vel verbis, testimonio, asseveratione, declaratione: & ut Paulus definit, imputatione sive λογισμῷ. Videatur Chemnit. part. 2. Locorum pag. 631. 632.

Ridiculum autem est, quod Jesuita in subsidium Causæ producit locum illum Jes. 53. v. 11. Servus meus in scientia sua justificabit multos. Etsi enim Hieronymo & Jesuitæ largimur, Christum variis modis justificare homines, atq; unum ex modis illis esse doctrinam: tamen non statim infusio aliqua novorum habituum indè extrui potest. Neque enim qui docet aut informat alterum ad justitiam, quemadmodum Daniel 12, 3. Doctores hoc modo multos justificare dicuntur : ille statim novas qualitates Justitiæ infundit. Deindè nuspiam in universa Scriptura Justificationis hujus medium sive Organum constituitur infusio novarum qualitatum : sed tantùm prædicatio verbi, quæ ideò etiam dicitur ministerium reconciliationis, tanquàm Deo exhortante nos per illud. 2. Cor. 5, 19. & 20. Quemadmodum ergò Christus ligat, solvit, retinet aut remittit peccata mediatè per ministerium verbi : sic etiam per idem scientiam sive agnitionem sui confert multis ad justitiam. Tandem glossam Jesuvviticam funditùs evertit ipse Spiritus Sanctus, qui phrasin hanc Propheticam non per infusionem novarum qualitatum, sed per remissionem peccatorum interpretatur : Luc. 1, 77. Dabit scientiam salutis per Johannem præcursorem suum, quæ est in remissione peccatorum. Tandem nulla militat Consequentiæ ratio. Verbum Justificandi in hoc vel illo Scripturæ dicto non obtinet forensem significationem: Ergo neque talem obtinebit in illis locis, quæ ex professo de Justificatione Hominis coram Deo agunt. Nam ostensâ æquivocatione verbi hujus, vanitas collectionis Jesuvviticæ ultrò patescit & corruit,

Tertiò profert Jesuvvita duo ex Scripturis loca alia, quorum prior extat Ecclesiastici 18, 22. Ne verearis usque ad mortem justificari, quoniam merces Domini manet in æternum. Posterior Apocal. 22, 11. Qui justus est, justificetur adhuc. E. inquit Jesuvvita, Justificari dicitur is, qui ex justo fit justior.


### Special Controversy, concerning the word Justifying, and its true and genuine meaning in the present Article (continued)

But the answer is easy: For in the allegation of the former place, the sophistication of a vicious Latin version is detected. For if we consult the Greek text, this place ought to be rendered thus: Do not delay to be justified until death: μὴ μείνης ἕως θαυάτου δικαιωθῆναι: The sense therefore emerges as nothing other than that true repentance is not to be delayed until death: which does nothing at all for the Jesuitical cause.

The citation of the latter place suffers from Ignoratio Elenchi: For it is to be understood concerning the Righteousness of New obedience in the pious, which comes about through faith according to the Law: but it still labors under many infirmities. The sense therefore is: He who is just, let him be justified still, that is, let him incessantly continue to study good works, so that in this way he may declare the internal righteousness of Faith before men: but not so that he may thereby merit eternal life: which is what the Jesuits invent of their own accord. But if someone should stubbornly contend that this Apocalyptic place must be accepted concerning the righteousness of faith: then not even so will anything depart from our opinion. For we answer that the continuation or perseverance in faith is commended to us. But if the Jesuits now infer that this perseverance consists in an infused habit of charity, or in our own virtues: we say that they are begging the question. For they do not prove what they say. Now Scripture prescribes another mode or organ of this perseverance or

continuation, namely, incessant prayer for the remission of sins: according to that of David, Psalm 32, 6. For this (remission of sins) every Saint will pray to you.

Finally, the Jesuit brings forward quite many places of the scriptures, which seem to construct that the Formal Cause of our Justification consists in some inherent righteousness: But we shall deal with those expressly in the fourth Special Controversy.

The latter error, which they foster concerning the present dispute, is about that twofold Justification, First and second, which Bellarmine describes in different places in this manner: Justification is twofold: one first, by which a man is made just from impious: The other is called Second, by which a just man is made more just. According to this twofold justification, Paul rightly says that a man is justified without works: but James, that he is justified by works. For just as no one can by his own work beget himself, or recall himself from death: but once begotten, or recalled from death, he nourishes and increases himself by eating and drinking: so also a man dead through sin cannot by the merit of his own works justify himself: but after he has been made just by God, he can by living rightly nourish and increase righteousness in himself, and thus be justified by works, book 4 on Justification, chapter 18, page 1227, C. D.

Franciscus Costerus explains the matter a little more clearly, in Enchiridion, chapter 6, 224. We say that there is a twofold justification, from a twofold term, from Which: One, which Theologians call First, when someone is made just from unjust, good from a sinner, a friend and son of God from an enemy of God: concerning which Justification the Apostle Paul was accustomed to dispute in his epistles against the Jews. The other, which they call Second Justification, when a just man is increased with greater righteousness and holiness, according to that which is in the Apocalypse chapter 22, He who is just, let him be justified still, and let the Holy be sanctified still.

But the Jesuit theologians of Cologne most clearly revealed the sentiments of their minds in these words: Justification is twofold: First and Second. For Christ by his ignominious and bitter death obtained this from the Father, that whoever should embrace his death by faith, they should be imbued with true righteousness, which is holiness, virtue, or a new quality inherent in the man himself. And this is the first justification. Now, however, having been accepted by those new qualities on account of the merit of Christ, then furthermore the man himself, with that righteousness of his inherent, merits greater and increased righteousness, reconciliation and adoption, and finally eternal life, which it is agreed is given as a due reward and just remuneration for our works done in the love of God. And this is the Second Justification, which indeed comes to us by the grace of God, but in such a way that faith and good works, which flow from love, bring no small amount of assistance.

Moreover, the causes of justification, if we speak of the first, can be found in no way in us, although it is ours to accommodate our mind to receive that divine gift: for we are disposed by faith, fear, hope, some love, and repentance. Cens. Colon. p. 141. & seqq.

But this figment teems with as many errors as it contains sentences.

For in the first place, that is a new thing, and before the arrival of those men, not even heard of by report: in which sense indeed it is urged by them today, that forsooth the FIRST is the infusion of justifying charity before GOD, formally. The SECOND is the performance of justifying works before God, meritoriously.

Then, it recalls as if by right of postliminy into the Church that impious and blasphemous dogma of the Scholastics, who imagine that CHRIST merited for us only the first grace, so that forsooth we ourselves, with free will concurring, might be able to merit the remission of sins, salvation, and eternal life. For in the same manner the Cologne Jesuits write with a sufficiently blasphemous pen, that Christ merited this only for us, that we ourselves might be able to merit reconciliation, adoption, and eternal life.

Thirdly, this figment concerning a double distinction is so much the more impious, by how much greater blasphemy it is joined, because they do not shudder to assert that the Second justification, which consists in our own merits, is greater, fuller, and more increased than that First one, which is given freely on account of Christ.

Fourthly, it is contradictorily opposed to the sacred Scriptures. For they know not a twofold, but only one way of salvation and Justification. Certainly from the first cradles of the Church of God, salvation came to the pious and faithful only through Faith in the Seed of the woman who would crush the head of the Serpent, Gen. 3:15, in the seed of Abraham, through whom and in whom all the families of the earth were to be blessed, Gen. 22:17 and 18, which seed was none other than Christ, as the Apostle interprets, Gal. 3:16, who was foreshadowed through the figures, types, and shadows of the Levitical sacrifices and rites, Heb. 9:9 and ch. 10:1.

Fifthly, this distinction labors under a shameful confusion of Cause and Effect. The Scriptures certainly consider begun Holiness and the new obedience of the justified as an Effect of the preceding Justification. But the Jesuits wish it to be the Cause and (which is impious to think) the meritorious cause of our justification. Which depravation certainly can no more stand than if you were to say that an Effect is the Cause of its Cause: or that a consequent is the cause of an antecedent.

Sixthly, the Scriptures define our Justification, and indeed a plenary one, by the sole remission of sins and the imputation of the Justice of Christ: But the Jesuits define it by our own meritorious habit. Therefore they oppose the Scriptures, and defend a manifest falsehood, joined with horrible impiety.

Seventhly, the things they prattle about preparatory dispositions surpass the preceding impiety of this dogma in many ways. For if all those things which the Jesuits enumerate, namely hope, faith, fear, some Love, repentance, etc., are our own: and all these, according to their own hypothesis, are in us before that first Justification is given to us: truly nothing more is left which can be ascribed to the merit of CHRIST, even with respect to the first Justification: which even a boy understands.

Eighthly, the Jesuits betray a spirit of giddiness in this place: while they do not agree at all among themselves concerning the number of these dispositive or preparatory motions. Bellarmine, following the authority of the Council of Trent, counts seven, namely Faith, fear, Hope, Love, repentance, the purpose and desire of receiving the Sacrament in reality, the purpose of a new life, and of the observation of all the commandments, lib. 1 de Justif. cap. 13. Concil. Trid. Sess. 6. cap. 6. Stapleton counts Six: Faith, love of God, hatred of sin and of the past state, repentance, Hope of pardon, and Charity. Costerus counts only three, namely Faith, Hope, and repentance: concerning which he writes most impiously: Justification therefore is ordinarily accomplished in this way, that into the soul of a sinful Man, prepared by the already mentioned reasons, God himself through the Sacraments infuses justice, and with it the remaining virtues also, so that with vices wiped away, and surrounded by a new adornment, through all the faculties of the soul, it may be entirely beautiful and a friend of God. Enchirid. cap. 6. pag. 257 and 264.

Ninthly, sacred Scripture nowhere predicts of Faith that it disposes to Justification: but that it itself justifies, or that it is imputed for justice: Nay, it attributes to this alone the power or faculty of apprehending the merit of Christ.

Tenthly, they establish things that are clearly inconsistent and nowhere coherent: for they wish Charity to be the form and inherent habit of justice: It is false, therefore, that it is a preparatory disposition. Thus they are not at all consistent with themselves, while they wish the remaining dispositive motions, such as fear, Hope, repentance, etc., sometimes to be preparatory acts for finally receiving Justification: but at other times they ascribe to these very things the Cause and merit of our Justification.

Eleventh, God is said in the Scriptures to justify us while we are ungodly, not yet loving, and indeed freely remitting sins, and imputing righteousness without works through faith, Rom. 4. 5. & 6. Therefore it is false and fictitious that God justifies us only after we are formally disposed to righteousness through Charity: it is also false that the first Justification is Grace formally infused: finally, it is false that Charity is the Form of Justification, because it is only an Effect of faith, according to that passage in Galatians: Faith works through Charity: Indeed, because it is only a part of inherent and legal righteousness, it certainly cannot be the whole righteousness.

Twelfth: Scripture ascribes the whole of Justification to Faith, and commands us to rest in it alone, according to that passage, Being justified by faith we have peace with God Rom. 5, 1. It is false, therefore, that Faith is empty and null without the second: indeed, that it is only a dispositive beginning of righteousness.

Finally, this fictitious distinction utterly overturns and undermines the entire merit of Christ. For if an infused habit of charity reconciles us to God, then surely the death of the Son of God will not accomplish this. Yet according to the Scriptures, this death alone accomplishes this: Rom. 5, 10. Being justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath much more now: for if, when we were reconciled, we were reconciled by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. Therefore. Furthermore, if the merits of a second justification finally make us perfectly just, then these merits of ours will be more excellent than the merit of Christ, nay, they will surpass it in many ways: which is impious and blasphemous.

Latin:

Sed facilis est responsio: Nam in prioris loci allegatione deprehenditur vitiosæ versionis Latinæ Sophisticatio. Nam si textum Græcum consulamus, sic reddi debet locus iste: Nedifferas justificari, usque ad mortem: μὴ μείνης ἕως θαυάτου δικαιωθῆναι: Sensus ergo emergit nullus alius, quàm quòd vera pœnitentia non ad mortem usque sit differenda: id quod nihil quicquam facit ad causam Jesuvviticam.

Posterioris loci citatio laborat Ignoratione Elenchi : Est enim ille intelligendus de Justitia Novæ obedientiæ in pijs, quæ fit per fidem secundum Legem: sed multis adhuc infirmitatibus laborat. Sensus ergo est : Qui justus est justificetur adhuc, hoc est, indefinenter pergat studere bonis operibus, ut hoc pacto internam Fidei justitiam coram hominibus declaret: non verò ut indè vitam æternam promereatur : id quod de suo affingunt Jesuvvitæ. Quod si locum istum Apocalypticum de Justitia fidei accipiendum esse, mordicùs aliquis contendat : tùm ne sic quidem aliquid nostræ sententiæ décedet. Respondemus enim Continuationem sive perseverantiam in fide nobis commendari. Quod si jam inferant Jesuvvitæ, Perseverentiam hanc constare infuso charitatis habitu, sive nostris virtutibus : dicimus ipsos petere principium. Neq; enim quòd dicunt probant. Jam Scriptura alium hujus perseverantiæ aut

Continuationis modum sive organum præscribit, nempè indefinentem precationem pro remissione peccatorum: secundùm illud Davidis Psal. 32, 6. Pro hac (remissione peccatorum) orabit ad te omnis Sanctus.

Tandem profert Jesuvvita benè multa scripturarum loca, quæ adstruere videntur, Causam Formalem Justificationis nostræ consistere in inhærente aliquâ justitiâ: Verùm de illis Controversia Speciali quartâ ex professo agemus.

Posterior error, quem circa præsentem disputationem fovent, est de gemina illa Justificatione, Primâ & secundâ, quam utramque Bellarminus diversis in locis hunc in modum describit: Duplex est Iustificatio: una prima, quâ homo ex impio fit justus: Altera dicitur Secunda, quâ justus efficitur justior. Secundùm geminam hanc justificationem rectè Paulus dicit justificari hominem sine operibus: Jacobus verò, justificari ex operibus. Quemadmodum enim nemo potest opere suo se ipse procreare, aut à morte revocare: procreatus autem, vel à morte revocatus ipse se, comedendo & bibendo nutrit & auget: sic etiam homo per peccatum mortuus, non potest meritò operum suorum, se justificare: sed postquam à Deo justus factus est, potest rectè vivendo justitiam in se alere & augere, atque ita operibus justificari lib. 4. de Justif. cap. 18. pag. 1227. C. D.

Franciscus Costerus paulò dilucidius rem explicat, in Enchirid. cap. 6. 224. Dicimus duplicem esse justificationem, à duplici termino, à Quo: Unam, quam Theologi Primam vocant, quando aliquis ex injusto fit justus, ex peccatore bonus, ex inimico Dei, amicus & filius Dei: de qua Iustificatione ferè D. Apostolus Paulus in epistolis suis contra Iudæos disputare consuevit. Alteram, quam Iustificationem appellant Secundam, quando justus majore justitia & sanctitate augetur, juxta illud, quod est in Apocalypsi cap. 22. Qui justus est, justificetur adhuc, & Sanctus sanctificetur adhuc.

Omnium verò clarissimè animi sensa prodiderunt Iesuvvitæ Colonienses his verbis: Duplex est Iustificatio: Prior & Secunda. Nam Christus ignominiosâ suâ ac acerbâ morte hoc à Patre impetravit, ut, quicûq; Fide mortem ejus amplecterentur, illi Iustitiâ verâ imbuerentur, quæ est Sanctitas, virtus, seu nova qualitas inhærens in ipso homine. Et hæc est prior Iustificatio. Iam verò acceptus novis illis qualitatibus propter meritum Christi, tùm porrò homo ipse, inhærente illâ suâ justitiâ, promeretur majorem & auctiorem justitiam, reconciliationem & adoptionem, & tandem vitam æternam, quam operibus nostris in charitate Dei factis, tanquàm debitum præmium, ac justam remunerationem donari constat. Et hæc est Secunda Iustificatio, quæ gratiâ quidem Dei nobis obtingit, sedita, ut fides & bona opera, quæ à charitate profluunt, non parum adjumenti adferant.

Cæterùm Iustificationis Causa, si de priore loquamur, in nobis nullæ reperiri possunt, quamvis nostru hoc sit, ut animum ad divinum illud munus accipiendum accommodemus: Disponimur enim fide, timore, spe, dilectione aliquâ & pœnitentia. Cens. Colon. p. 141. & seqq.

Sed scatethoc figmentum tot erroribus, quot complectitur sententias.

Primùm enim novum illud est, & ante istorum hominum adventum,ne fando quidem auditum: quo quidem sensu ab illis hodiè illud urgetur, quòd nimirùm PRIMA sit infusio charitatis justificantis coram DEO, formaliter. SECUNDA sit præstatio operum Justificantium coram Deo, meritoriè.

Deindè,postliminiò quasi in Ecclesiam revocat impium & blasphemum illud dogma Scholasticorum, fingentium, CHRISTUM primam tantùm gratiam nobis promeruisse, ut nimirum nos ipsi concurrente libero arbitrio, possimus promeriremissionem peccatorum,salutem & vitam æternam. Eundem enim in modum scriptitant blasphemo satis calamo Jesuitæ Colonienses, Christum hoc tantùm nobis meruisse, ut nos ipsi possemus promereri, reconciliationem, adoptionem & vitam æternam.

Tertiò, eò tantò magis impium est hoc figmentum de duplici distinctione, quantò majore cum blasphemia est conjunctum, quod asserere non exhorrescunt, Secundam justificationem, quæ nostris constat meritis, esse majorem, pleniorem & auctiorem, Primâ illâ, quæ gratis propter Christum donatur.

Quartò, Scripturis sacris contradictoriè est oppositum. Neque enim geminam, sed unam tantùm salutis & Justificationis viam eæ noverunt. Certè à primis Ecclesiæ Dei incunabulis salus obtigit pijs ac fidelibus, non nisi Fide in Semen mulieris contriturum caput Serpentis, Genes. 3, 15. in semen Abrahæ, per quod & in quo benedicendæ essent omnes familiæ terræ Genes 22. 17. & 18. quod semen nullum erat aliud, quàm Christus, interprete! Apostolo, Gal. 3. 16. qui per figuras, typos & umbras sacrificiorum & rituum Leviticorum erat adumbratus. Heb. 9. 9. & cap. 10, 1.

Quintò laborat hæc distinctio turpi confusione Causæ & Effectus. Scripturæ certè inchoatam Sanctitatem & novam obedientiam justificatorum considerant, ut Effectum antecedentis Justificationis. At verò Jesuitæ eam volunt esse Causam & (quod cogitatu impium est) causam meritoriam justificationis nostræ. Quæ sanè depravatio haud magis potest consistere, quàm si dicas, Effectum esse Causam suæ Causæ: vel consequens esse causam antecedentis.

Sextò, Scripturæ Justificationem nostram & quidem plenariam definiunt solâ remissione peccatorum, & imputatione Justitiæ Christi: Atque Jesuitæ eam definiunt habitu nostro meritorio. Ergo Scripturis adversantur, & propugnant manifestam falsitatem, cum horrenda impietate conjunctam.

Septimò, Quæ de dispositionibus præparatorijs garriunt,præcedentem dogmatis hujus impietatem multis modis superant. Si enim illa omnia, quæ Jesuitæ enumerant, nempè spes, fides,timor, Dilectio aliqua, pœnitentia &c. nostra sunt propria: & hæc omnia, secundùm ipsorum hypothesin, nobis insunt priusquàm nobis donatur prima illa Iustificatio : nihil profectò, ampliùs relinquitur, quod merito CHRISTI, etiam respectu primæ Justificationis possit adscribi : id quod vel puer intelligit.

Octavò, Spiritum vertiginis hoc loco produnt Iesuvvitæ: dum de numero motuum istorum dispositoriorum sive præparantium illis minimè convenit. Bellarminus secutus autoritatem Concilij Tridentini numerat septem, nempè Fidem, timorem, Spem, Dilectionem, pœnitentiam, pròpositum ac desiderium percipiendi Sacramentum reipsâ, propositum novæ vitæ, & observationis omnium mandatorum lib. 1. de Justif. cap. 13. Concil. Trid. Sess. 6. cap. 6. Stapletonus numerat Sex: Fidem, amorem Dei, odium peccati & status præteriti, pœnitentiam, Spem veniæ & Charitatem. Costerus numerat tantùm tres, nempè Fidem, Spem & pœnitentiam: de quibus nimis impiè scribit: Justificatio igitur ordinariè hoc modo perficitur, ut in animam Hominis peccatoris, jam dictis rationibus præparatam, Deus ipse per Sacramenta infundat justitiam, & cum eá virtutes quoque reliquas, ut vitijs absterfis, novoque circumfusa cultu, per omnes animi facultates, tota puchra sit amica Dei. Enchirid. cap. 6. pag. 257. & 264.

Nonò, Scriptura sacra nuspiam de Fide prædicat, quòd disponat ad Iustificationem: sed quod ipsa justificet, vel quòd imputetur ad justitiam: Quin huic soli tribuit vim sive facultatem apprehendendi meritum Christi.

Decimò, Ἀσύστατα ptanè & nuspiam cohærentia statuunt: Volunt enim Charitatem esse formam & habitum inhærentem justitiæ: Falsum igitur, quòd sit dispositio præparatoria. Sic sibi ipsi minimè constant, dùm reliquos motus dispositorios, ut timorem, Spem, pœnitentiam &c. modò volunt esse actus præparatorios ad recipiendam demùm Iustificationem: modò verò his ipsis Causam & meritum Iustificationis nostræ adscribunt.

Undecimò, Deus in Scripturis dicitur nos justificare impios existentes, nondum diligentes, & quidem gratis remittens peccata, ac imputans justitiam absque operibus per fidem, Rom. 4. 5. & 6. Ergò falsum ac fictitium, quòd Deus nos per Charitatem formaliter ad justitiam dispositos, demùm justificet: falsum etiam, quòd Iustificatio prima sit Gratia formaliter infusa: falsum denique, quòd Charitas sit Forma Iustificationis, quia est Effectus tantùm fidei, secundum illud Galat. Fides per Charitatem operatur: Imò quia est pars tantùm justitiæ inhærentis & legalis, utique non poterit tota esse justitia.

Duodecimò: Scriptura Fidei adscribit totam Iustificationem, inque ea sola nos acquiescere jubet, secundum illud, Iustificati fide pacem habemus apud Deum Rom. 5, 1. Falsum igitur, quod Fides sit inanis & nulla, absque secunda: imò tantùm initium justitiæ dispositivum.

Tandem fictitia hæc distinctio universum meritum Christi funditùs evertit & subruit.. Nam si infusus Charitatis habitus nos Deo reconciliat: utique mors Filij Dei hoc non præstabit. Atqui secundum Scripturas sola hæc mors hoc præstat: Rom. 5, 10. Iustificati sanguine ejus servabimur nunc multò magis ab ira: si reconciliati sumus per mortem Filij ejus, multò magis reconciliati servabimur per vitam ipsius. Ergo. Porrò, si merita secundæ justificationis nos demùm perfectè justos faciunt. Ergò merita hæc nostra erunt præstantiora merito Christi, imò hoc multis modis superabunt: id quod impium & blasphemum.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification

The Jesuit Bellarmine, in book 1 of Justification, chapter 2, not ineptly posits that the entire act of our justification can be most correctly and fully explained according to those four causes of all things, namely the Final, the Efficient, the Material, and the Formal. And as we do not struggle against this opinion too stubbornly, so we too shall follow the same order of causes: but in such a way that we make a beginning of the controversy concerning the Efficient Cause of our justification. For as regards the Final Cause, perhaps there would not remain a great controversy, if only we were in agreement with each other concerning the remaining causes. The Jesuit himself certainly establishes a twofold end of justification, namely 1. The glory of God and Christ. 2. The eternal salvation of those who are justified. Our churches do not abhor this opinion, for they themselves also consider the end of justification in two ways: either with respect to God, or with regard to us. And indeed, as regards God, the Apostle is witness that this whole work is directed to the praise of his glory, Eph. 1, 6. But this glory looks partly to the mercy of God: Eph. 1, 6 and chapter 2, 7; partly to his justice, Rom. 3, 25, for the declaration of which God allowed himself to be moved as much as possible to act in this work. For although some interpreters think that the word 'justice' in this passage is used for 'mercy' through a certain ἀλλοίωσιν ἢ ἑτέρωσιν (change or substitution), since there is a great kinship of virtues in God: yet if it is considered a little more accurately: that the remission of sins could not have come to us otherwise than by the most full expiation of them made through CHRIST: nor could the adoption of the human race before God stand otherwise than by the perfect obedience rendered to the Law by CHRIST: if it is also weighed that God pours out this benefit not only upon very many, but also confers it upon those who are by nature children of wrath. Eph. 2, 3.

and who are ungodly. Rom. 4, 5. that a huge momentum of praise and glory is added to divine justice, hardly anyone will doubt.

With respect to men, the end of justification is, first, the pursuit of piety and holiness. Tit. 2, 12. For the saving grace of God has appeared, that, denying ungodliness, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world. 1 Pet. 2, 24. therefore Christ bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might live to righteousness: and second, the salvation of souls and the inheritance of eternal life to be conferred by grace, Rom. 8, 30. 1 Pet. 1, 9 and chapter 5, 4. Tit. 3, 7.

But since there is no controversy between us and the Jesuits concerning these ends in general, but rather all the dispute is chiefly partly about the Efficient Cause and partly about the Formal Cause of justification, we too make a more accurate approach to the consideration of these: having made a beginning with the Efficient Cause, and having considered it both in general and in particular.

General EFFICIENT CAUSE.

But Bellarmine himself also rightly warns that one efficient cause is primary, another is efficient by way of merit, and another by way of instrument. Book 1 of Justification, ch. 2, p. 936 C. For by the consensus of the philosophers themselves, instrumental causes are rightly referred to the efficient. Now since the act of justification consists of its own certain means, organs, and instruments, we certainly also refer the τὰ ὀργανικὰ (the organic things) under the consideration of the efficient cause: which are some with respect to God, others with respect to men.

With respect to God, the organs are threefold: one is meritorious, which is CHRIST the Savior, with all his merit: another is the organ that offers, which is the word of God heard and preached: the third is the organ that seals, which are the Sacraments.

With respect to men, the sole organ or instrument, in the act of Justification, has a place by the Decree of God: namely Faith apprehending, and applying to itself the merit of Christ.
