Since we and the Jesuits today by no means agree concerning these individual and universal causes: it will certainly be necessary to examine each one separately as well.

Latin:

JEsuvvita Bellarminus lib. 1. de Iustif. cap. 2. haud ineptè statuit, secundum quatuor illas rerum omnium causas, Finalem nimirùm, Efficientem, Materialem & Formalem, universum Iustificationis nostræ actum rectissimè plenissimèque explicari posse. Cujus sanè sententiæ uti haud morosius reluctamur: ita eundem Causarum ordinem nos quoque sequemur: sed ita, ut controversiæ auspicium faciamus, de Efficiente Iustificationis nostræ Causa. Nam quoad Causam Finalem, fortè haud magna reliqua esset Controversia, si modò de reliquis Causis nobis invicem conveniret. Constituit certè ipse Jesuvvita, Finem Iustificationis geminum, nempè 1. Gloriam Dei & Christi. 2. Salutem æternam eorum, qui justificantur. A quâ sententia non abhorrent nostræ Ecclesiæ: quæ & ipsæ Finem Iustificationis bifariam considerant: vel respectu Dei: vel ratione nostri. Et quidem quoad Deum, in laudem gloriæ ejus, totum hoc opus directum esse, testis est Apostolus, Eph. 1, 6. Gloria autem hæc respicit partim Misericordiam Dei: Ephes. 1, 6. & cap. 2, 7. partim ejusdem justitiam, Rom. 3, 25. pro qua declaranda, Deus in hoc opere se quam maximè ad agendum moveri passus est. Etsi enim nonnulli interpretes, hoc loco Iustitiæ vocabulum, per quandam ἀλλοίωσιν ἢ ἑτέρωσιν, pro Misericordia positum esse autumant, cùm in Deo magna virtutum sit cognatio: si tamen paulò accuratiùs consideretur: Remissionem peccatorum aliter nobis obtingere haud potuisse, quàm plenissimâ eorundem per CHRISTUM facta expiatione: neque aliter hominum generi adoptionem constare apud Deum, quàm præstita Legi à CHRISTO perfecta obedientia: si illud quoque expendatur, quòd beneficium hoc non tantùm in quamplurimos Deus effundit; sed in eos etiam confert, qui sunt natura filij iræ. Ephes. 2, 3.

quique sunt ἀσεβεῖς. Rom. 4, 5. ingens profectò laudis ac gloriæ momentum Iustitiæ divinæ accedere,vix quisquàm dubitaverit.

Hominum respectu, Finis Iustificationis est, tùm pietatis & sanctimoniæ studium. Tit. 2, 12. In hoc apparuit salutaris Dei gratia,ut abnegatâ impietate, sobriè, justè, & piè vivatur in hoc seculo. 1. Pet. 2, 24. ideò Christus peccata nostra tulit in corpore suo, super ligno, ut justitiæ à nobis vivatur : tùm Salus animarum,& vitæ æternæ hæreditas ex gratiâ conferenda, Rom.8,30. 1. Pet. 1, 9. & cap. 5,4. Tit. 3,7.

Cæterùm cùm de finibus istis universis propriè nobis & Jesuvvitis non intercedat controversia: sed potiùs omnis disputatio præcipuè sit,partim de Causâ Efficiente, partim de Causâ formali Justificationis : nos quoque ad istarum considerationem accuratiorem accessum facimus : initio facto à Causâ Efficiente, eâque tùm tùm in genere, tùm in Specie consideratâ

CAVSA EFFICIENS Generalis.

REctè autem ipse quoque Bellarminus admonet, Causam Efficientem aliam esse primàriam: aliam Efficientem per modum meriti: aliam per modum Instrumenti. l. 1. de Iustif. c. 2. p. 936. C. Nam ipsorum etiam Philosophorum Consensu, Causæ Instrumentales, ad Efficientem rectè referuntur. Jam cùm Justificationis actus, suis certis constet medijs, Organis & Instrumentis : utique sub considerationem Causæ Efficientis, referimus etiam τὰ ὀργανικὰ : quæ alia sunt respectu Dei : alia respectu hominum.

Respectu Dei organa sunt triplicia : Unum est meritorium, quod est CHRISTUS Servator, cum universo suo merito : Alterum est ὄργανον offerens, quod est verbum Dei auditum & prædicatum : Tertium est ὄργανον obsignans quod sunt Sacramenta.

Respectu hominum, Organum sive Instrumentum unicum, in actu Iustificationis, ex Decreto Dei locum habet : nempè Fides apprehendens, sibique applicans meritum Christi.

De causis istis singulis ac universis, cùm nobis & Jesuvvitis hodiè minimè conveniat: utique de singulis etiam seorsim dispiciendum fuerit.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: I. The Primary Efficient Cause

The primary Efficient cause therefore is GOD ALONE, one in Essence, three in persons. For although each person of the Divinity, in a peculiar manner and respect, concurs in the act of Justification, so that to GOD the Father, To the Father, compassion: to the Son, mediation: to the Holy Spirit, both the operation of faith and the renewal or sanctification of the mind, as far as the distinction of ministry is ascribed in the Scriptures: yet they concur jointly to produce one result.

Moreover, the Scriptures themselves prove clearly enough that the work of our justification must be attributed to God alone, or rather not only to him alone, but also entirely, with respect to the primary Efficient Cause. Is. 43:25. I, even I, says Jehovah, am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. Rom. 3:26. God is both just and justifies him who is of the faith of Jesus. Rom. 8:33. It is God who justifies. Jer. 31:18 & 19. Turn me, O LORD, and I shall be turned, for you are the Lord my God: After I was turned, I repented: and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh. Phil. 2:13. It is God who works in us, both TO WILL and TO DO.

The Fathers have been accustomed, not inappropriately, to argue frequently from the work of Creation to the business of Justification, so that this, no less than that, must be ascribed to God alone by some incommunicable property: and it would be clearly a sin to attribute the work of either Creation or Justification to anyone other than God: according to that passage in Is. 42:6. I the LORD Jehovah have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand. But just as God himself appends such an epiphonema to the work of Creation, completed by himself, 'I am Jehovah, this is my name, and my glory I will not give to another': so we, relying on the authority of the Holy Spirit, rightly say anathema to those who are accustomed to divide the work of Justification between God and us in such a way that they do not shrink from ascribing to our works a place, however last, in the number of the Efficient Causes of our salvation. To whose impiety that distich, also common in antiquity, was opposed:

He who made you without you, and redeemed you without you, He also, O Man, will justify you without you.

This purer doctrine of ours has suffered a sufficiently sharp contradiction, and did so long ago under the Papacy, and still suffers it today, with the Jesuits contending that the act of our justification is accomplished by human powers and merits, if not entirely, at least by half. The coming treatise will fully set forth the refutation of this impiety. In this place, we oppose to the adversaries that single and indeed memorable sentiment of Augustine, writing thus in Tractate 72 on John: 'It is a greater work to justify the ungodly than to create heaven and earth: for heaven and earth will pass away: but the salvation and justification of the elect will remain: in the former there are only the works of God: but in the latter there is the image of God.' Let him understand, therefore, who can, and let him judge, who can, whether it is greater to create the just or to justify the ungodly. For certainly, if both are of equal power, the latter is of greater mercy. So far Augustine, from whom we infer thus against the Jesuits: If he incurs the crime of blasphemy who wishes to assign the Work of Creation to man: much more must those be held guilty of this crime who attribute the Work of Justification to him: which is what the Jesuits do. But the former is true, not only in Augustine's judgment, but also confirmed by the very analogy of faith: for to whom that which is less does not belong, such as the act of Creation: to him much less does that which is greater belong, namely the act of Justification. Therefore, this latter point is also established.

Moreover, to the consideration of this Cause also pertains the προηγυμένη or impelling cause for God to enter into any counsel concerning the accomplishment of the work of our justification, which was certainly none other than the GRACE or MERCY OF GOD, as Scripture teaches. Eph. 2:8. By grace you have been saved. 2 Tim. 1:9. He saved us, not according to our works: but according to his grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus. Tit. 3:7. Justified by grace, we become heirs of eternal life.

But what this Grace of God is, and how it ought to be defined, is today disputed quite sharply. We, following the Scriptures, define with our Author this Grace of God as that fatherly favor of divine love, and the mercy itself, and the gratuitous acceptance, by which God, moved to compassion for the human race, redeemed all through his Son, and forgives sins to all who believe in him, and grants eternal life. In this sense and respect, the word 'Grace' in the Article of Justification is opposed to dignity, our works, and our merits: for according to that saying of Augustine in Psalm 34: 'It is not grace in any way, if it is not gratuitous in every way.' The Apostle vehemently urges this opposition in the matter of Predestination, Rom. 11:6. Saying, if election comes to us by grace, it is no longer of works: otherwise grace is no longer grace: But if it is of works, it is no longer of grace: otherwise work is no longer work. This Apostolic collection holds good in the Article of Justification as well: since the Causes are the same on both sides, the same means, the same end, according to the Apostle: Whom he predestined, these he also justified. Therefore, we conclude invincibly thus: If justification is by grace, it is not of works: But it is by grace: Therefore, it is not of works. The reason for the connection: otherwise a work would not be a work, that is, meritorious: this is, a manifest αντίφασις or implication of contradiction would follow, that is, the affirmation and negation of the same thing, according to the same. For a work would be feigned to be not a work, a debt not a debt, a merit not a merit. They cannot deny the minor premise, unless they wish, with brazen face, to call into doubt, or even deny, the manifest testimonies of Scripture, just now produced.

Other far more evident arguments are added. For first, Scripture is witness that GOD had regard for nothing at all in the whole world, by which He was moved to pity us, other than Himself, that is, Scripture being the interpreter, the bowels of His Mercy, through which the sunrise from on high has visited us. Luke 1:78. Whence Isaiah proclaims concerning Him that He blots out the iniquities of His people for His own sake, chap. 43, 25. Next, this sense is confirmed by the equivalent terms by which Scripture is accustomed to explain this grace of God, and which exclude every inherent dignity in men: such as are, Mercy Eph. 2, 4. Tit. 3, 5. Good pleasure, Eph. 1, 5. Love, Kindness, Φιλανθρωπία Eph. 2, 7. Tit. 3, 4. Thirdly, it is also supported by the τὸ εἰς οὐδὲν μέγα, which lies hidden in the particle, GRATIS. Rom. 3, 24. They are justified Gratis by the grace of God: Now, the emphasis and native meaning of this adverb expires immediately, as soon as the word grace is taken to mean anything other than the gratuitous affection of mercy.

prescribed twice Daniel 9, 18. We do not pray in our own righteousness, but in thy great mercy for the Lord's sake. And in the preceding verse 7. To thee, O Lord, righteousness: but to us confusion of face. Fourth and last: That the distinction between Law and Gospel may be seen: Which two kinds of doctrine are immediately confused, where the least bit of the merits of works is attributed to the word grace in this question.

This purer doctrine of ours was long ago impugned by the Pelagians, who, in the present dispute, referred the word grace to the goods of Nature, granted to men by God, among which they counted most especially the faculty of Free Will. They contended, therefore, that a man is justified by the grace of God if, rightly using the powers of Free Will, which remain even after the fall, he procures for himself a habit of righteousness through the pursuit of piety and good works. Their error was the more atrocious the more absurd a theology it introduced, which, namely: 1. Shamefully confused natural things with spiritual. 2. Held the pious and the impious in the same estimation and number, and granted the same grace to all equally and indiscriminately, although it admitted some difference between them in the exercises of this grace. 3. Openly contradicted the sacred Scriptures, which define the grace of God by eternal mercy, prepared for us in Christ alone. 4. and lastly: Blasphemously excluded Christ with his merit from the act of Justification, nay, utterly emptied it.

Fourthly: Scripture defines the word grace by something eternal, which is given in Christ before the secular times. 2 Tim. 1, 9. Therefore, it is necessary that something divine, and not anything human, be denoted by grace.

Fifthly: The grace by which we are justified is something superabundant over sin Rom. 5, 20. nay, it is πλοῦτος ὑπερβάλλων ἐν χρηστότητι, the superabundant wealth of divine kindness in Christ. Eph. 2, 7. But no virtue, no infused habit, can in any way reach this superabundance: God alone is able to perform this, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us Eph. 2, 4. Let that meaning, therefore, by which the merit or dignity of men is involved, be banished from this place.

Sixthly: Our Author concludes thus. Rom. 4, 4. & 5. the Apostle says: to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned according to grace. Where he clearly understands by grace a gratuitous imputation, or benevolence. For it is an antithesis: To labors a reward is owed: To the ancient believer, even if he does not bring merits, yet there is an imputation of righteousness, out of grace. Therefore, grace excludes our labor.

But neither do the Jesuits hold a milder error today concerning this very word grace, who, from the Scholastic Doctors, especially Biel in 4. sent, dist. 27. q. 1. art. 1. as also from Scotus, likewise in 4. sent. dist. 27. q. 1. have borrowed a more than sacrilegious error, contending that by justifying grace is denoted not the gratuitous favor of God: but an infused habit of charity, formally inherent in a beatifiable nature, through which it itself becomes a friend of God, and through which its elicited act is meritorious of eternal life. Or as the Compendium of Theological Truth explains lib 5. cap. 3. Grace, making one pleasing, is a gift divinely given for adhering.

Latin:

CAusa proindè Efficiens primaria est SOLUS DEUS, unus Essentiâ, trinus personis. Etsi enim quælibet Divinitatis persona, peculiari modo atque respectu, ad Iustificationis actum concurrit, ita ut DEO Patri, Patri Miseratio: Filio, Mediatio: Spiritui Sancto, tum Fidei operatio, tum mentis Renovatio sive Sanctificatio, quoad discrimen ministerij in Scripturis adscribatur: tamen ad unum producendum ἀποτέλεσμα conjunctim concurrunt.

Cæterùm Deo soli, imò non soli tantùm, sed & in solidum, respectu Causæ Efficientis primariæ, Justificationis nostræ opus acceptum ferendum esse, Scripturæ ipsæ satis luculenter comprobant. Jes. 43, 25. Ego sum, ego sum ipse, inquit Jehovah, qui deleo iniquitates tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordor. Rom. 3, 26. Deus & justus est, & justificat eum, qui est ex fide Iesu. Rom. 8, 33. Deus est, qui justificat, Jerem. 31, 18. & 19. Converte me DOMINE & convertar, quia tu Dominus Deus meus: Postquàm tu convertisti me, egi pœnitentiam: & postquàm tu ostendisti mihi, percussi femur meum. Phil. 2, 3. Deus est, qui operatur in nobis, & VELLE & PERFICERE.

Consueverunt Patres haud ineptè ex Creationis opere, ad Justificationis negocium frequenter argumentari, ita ut hoc, non minus quàm illud, soli Deo, proprietate quapiam incommunicabili sit adscribendum: & nefas planè sit, cuiquam alteri præter Deum, vel Creationis vel Justificationis opus acceptum referre: secundum illud Jes. 42, 6. Ego DOMINVS Iehovah vocavi te in justitia, & servavite. Quemadmodum verò Deus ipse Creationis operi, â se consummato, tale Epiphonema subjungit, Ego Iehovah, hoc nomen meum, Gloriam hanc meam alteri non dabo: Ita nos meritò, freti autoritate Spiritus Sancti, anathema dicimus illis, qui opus Justificationis inter Deum & nos ita partiri solent, ut operibus nostris locum minimè postremum, in numero Causarum Efficientium salutis nostræ, adscribere non exhorrescant. Quorum impietati antiquitùs etiam vulgatum illud Distichon fuit oppositum:

Qui sine te fecit te, te sine teq; redemit, Is sine te quoq; te justi ficabit Homo.

Contradictionem purior hæc doctrina nostra satis acrem & jam olim sub Papatu passa est, ac etiamnùm patitur, contendentibus Jesuvvitis, humanis viribus atque meritis, si non ex toto, ex dimidio saltem, Justificationis nostræ actum perfici. Cujus impietatis refutationem futura Tractatio plenè expediet. Opponimus hoc loco Adversarijs unicam & quidem memorabilem illam Augustini sententiam, sic scribentis Tractatu 72. in Johannem: Majus opus est justificare impium, quàm Creare Cœlum & terram: Cœlum enim & terra transibunt: Electorum autem Salus & justificatio permanebit: In illis tantùm sunt opera Dei: in his autem est imago Dei. Intelligat ergò qui potest, judicet, qui potest, utrùm majus sit justos creare, quàm impios justificare. Certè enim si æqualis utrumque est potentiæ, hoc majoris est misericordiæ. Hactenùs Augustinus, ex quo contra Jesuvvitas sic inferimus: Si blasphemia e crimen incurrit, qui homini Opus Creationis adsignare velit: multò magis criminis hujus peragi debent, qui eidem Opus Iustificationis tribuunt: id quod faciunt Iesuvitæ: Atqui prius verum, non Augustino modò sic censente, sed ipsa quoque fidei analogiâ confirmante: Cui enim non competit id quod minus est, ut actus Creationis: illi multò minus' competit id, quod majus est, nempè actus Justificationis. Ergo ratum hoc etiam posterius.

Cæterùm ad Causæ hujus considerationem pertinet etiam Causæ προηγυμένη sive impellens Deum, ut de Justificationis nostræ opere perficiendo Consilij aliquid iniret, quæ sanè nulla fuit alia, quàm GRATIA sive MISERICORDIA DEI, sic quidem docente Scripturâ. Ephes. 2, 8. Gratiâ salvati estis. 2. Tim. 1, 9. Salvos nos fecit, non secundum opera nostra: sed secundum gratiam, datam nobis in Christo Jesu. Tit. 3, 7. Iustificati gratiâ, hæredes evadimus vitæ æternæ.

Cæterùm quidnam sit hæc Gratia Dei, & quomodo illa definiri debeat, satis acriter hodiè controvertitur. Nos scripturas secuti, cum Autore nostro definimus Gratiam hanc Dei per paternum illum divini amoris favorem, ipsamque misericordiam, & gratuitam acceptationem, quâ Deus ad miserationem generis humani permotus, omnes per Filium suum redemit, omnibusque in eundem credentibus peccata remittit, & vitam æternam donat. Hoc sensu atque respectu vocabulum Gratiæ in Articulo Justificationis, opponitur dignati, operibus ac meritis nostris: Nam secundùm illud Augustini in Psal. 34. Gratia non est ullo modo, si non est gratuita omni modo. Quam oppositionem vehementer in negocio Prædestinationis urget Apostolus, Rom. 11, 6. Si inquiens, per Gratiam nobis obtingit Electio, non jam ex operibus: alioqui gratia jam non est gratia: Sin ex operibus, jam non ex gratia: alioquin opus jam non est opus. Quæ Collectio Apostolica valet in Articulo etiam Justificationis: siquidem eædem utrobique sunt Causæ, eadem media, idem finis, secundum illud Apostoli: Quos prædestinavit, hos, & justificavit. Invictè proindè sic colligimus: Si justificatio est ex gratia, non est ex operibus: Atqui est ex gratia: Non. E. ex operibus. Ratio Connexi: alioqui opus non esset opus, scilicet meritorium: hoc est, manifesta sequeretur αντίφασις Contradictionis implicatio, hoc est, affirmatio & negatio ejusdem, secundum idem. Fingeretur enim Opus non opus, debitum non debitum, meritum non meritum. Minorem negare non possunt, nisi manifesta Scripturæ testimonia, jam modò producta, perfricta fronte in dubium vocare, imò negare velint.

Accedunt alia longè evidentissima argumenta. Primùm enim Scriptura testis est, DEUM nihil quicquam in toto mundo respexisse, quô ad miserationem nostri impulsus fuerit, quàm Seipsum, hoc est, Scripturâ interprete, viscera Misericordiæ suæ, per quæ nos visitavit oriens ex alto. Luc. 1, 78. Undè Jesaias de ipso prædicat, quòd propter seipsum deleat iniquitates populi sui cap. 43, 25. Deindè confirmant hunc sensum vocabula æquipollentia, quibus Scriptura Gratiam hanc Dei explicare solet, & quæ omnem inhærentem hominibus dignitatem excludunt: Qualia sunt, Misericordia Eph. 2, 4. Tit. 3, 5. Beneplacitum, Eph. 1, 5. Dilectio, Benignitas, Φιλανθρωπία Eph. 2, 7. Tit. 3, 4. Tertiò suffragatur etiam τὸ εἰς οὐδὲν μέγα, quæ latet in particula,, GRATIS. Rom. 3, 24. Justificantur Gratis Gratia Dei: Jam verò Emphasis & nativa significatio hujus Adverbij statim expirat, quamprimum Gratiæ vocabulum, de alio aliquo, quàm gratuita Misericordiæ affectu accipiatur.

bis præscriptam Daniel. 9, 18. Non in nostra justitia precamur, sed in misericordia tua magnâ propter Dominum. Et versu præced. 7. Tibi Domine justitia: nobis autem confusio faciei. Quarta & postrema: Ut conspiciatur discrimen Legis & Evangelij: Quæ duo doctrinarum genera statim confunduntur, ubi vocabulo Gratiæ, hac in Quæstione vel minimum de meritis operum affingitur.

Puriorem doctrinam hanc nostram jam olim impugnarunt Pelagiani, qui Gratiæ vocabulum, in præsente disputatione, retulerunt ad bona Naturæ, hominibus concessa divinitùs, inter quæ vel maximè numerarunt Liberi Arbitrij facultatem. Contenderunt proindè, Gratiâ Dei tùm Hominem justificari, si viribus Liberi Arbitrij, post lapsum etiam reliquis, rectè utens, habitum justitiæ, per studium pietatis & bonorum operum, ipse sibi comparet. Quorum error tantò atrocior fuit, quantò absurdiorem Theologiam invehebat, quæ nimirum. 1. Naturalia cum spiritualibus turpiter confunderet. 2. Pios & impios eodem censu numeroque haberet, eandamque gratiam omnibus ex æquo, ac promiscuè concederet, licet in exercitijs hujus gratiæ aliquam inter eos dissimilitudinem admitteret. 3. Scripturis sacris, Gratiam Dei per æternam misericordiam, in solo Christo nobis paratam, definientibus apertè contradiceret. 4. & postremo: Christum cum suo merito, blasphemè ex actu Justificationis excluderet, imò penitùs evacuaret.

Quartò: Scriptura definit Gratiæ vocabulum per quiddam æternum, quod est in Christo datum ante tempora secularia. 2. Timoth. 1, 9. Ergò divinum quiddam, nihil verò humanum, per Gratiam notetur, necesse est.

Quintò: Gratia, quâ justificamur, est superabundans quiddam supra peccatum Rom. 5, 20. imò est πλοῦτος ὑπερβάλλων ἐν χρηστότητι, superabundans opulentia divinæ benignitatis in Christo. Ephes. 2, 7. Atqui nulla virtus, nullus infusus habitus, ad hanc superabundantiam, ullo pacto potest pertingere sea: solus Deus hoc præstare valet, qui dives est misericordiâ, propter multam charitatem suam, quâ dilexit nos Ephef. 2, 4. Facesfat proindè hoc loco significatio illa, quâ Hominum meritum aut dignitas involvitur.

Sextò: Sic colligit Autor Noster. Rom. 4, 4. & 5. dicit Apostolus: operanti non imputatur merces secundum Gratiam. Ubi perspicuè per Gratiam intelligit Gratuitam imputationem, sive benevolentiam. Est enim antithesis: Laboribus debetur merces: Antiqui credenti etiam si non affert merita, tamen sit imputatio justitiæ, ex gratia. E. Gratia excludit nostrum laborem.

Sed neque mitiorem hodiè errorem circa hoc ipsum Gratiæ vocabulum tenent Jesuitæ, qui ex Doctoribus Scholasticis, cumprimis Biele. in 4. sent, dist. 27. q. 1. art. 1. ut & ex Scoto, itidem in 4. sent. dist. 27. q. 1. errorem plusquàm sacrilegu mutuati sunt contendentes, per Gratiam justificantem notari non gratuitum Dei favorem: sed habitum charitatis infusum, formaliterque inhærentem naturæ beatificabili, per quem ipsa fit amica Dei, & per quem actus ejus elicitus, sit meritorius vitæ æternæ. Vel ut Compendium Theologicæ veritatis explicat lib 5. cap. 3. Gratia, Gratum faciens, est donum divinitùs datum adhærendum.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: I. The Primary Efficient Cause (continued)

Seventhly, the Apostle subjoins in the same place: Therefore it is of faith according to grace, that the promise might be sure to all the believers, that is, that the reconciliation might be certain. For if our salvation were to rest upon the merits of works, then it would clearly hang upon an uncertain foundation. Now since it resides in the hands of Him alone, who created heaven and earth, there can certainly be no uncertainty or doubt remaining.

Which blasphemies the Council of Trent judged worthy of a canon, so that it brandished the thunderbolt of anathema against those who say that the grace by which we are justified is only the favor of God. Sess. 6. Can. 11

Finally, our Author collects four causes for which one must contend for the purity of that meaning of the word Grace.

The first is: That due honor may be attributed to Christ, from whose merit just as much is detracted as is attributed to human powers, merits, or any works whatsoever. The second: that the conscience may have certain and firm consolation, and need not doubt concerning the certainty of salvation. The third: that true invocation may be performed, according to the formula by the Prophet Daniel no- Hence the Jesuit Costerus, chapter 6 of the Enchiridion, page 228, defines this grace of God as being a certain quality, divinely infused into the soul, by which sins are put to flight no differently than darkness by the arrival of light, and through which the soul receives brightness and divine beauty, by which it is not only now called, but truly is pleasing to GOD and is named as endowed with grace, so that it is a friend, nay, a son of God. And Bellarmine, book 1, on grace and free will, chapter 3, page 526, B. The common opinion of theologians, he says, is that grace which makes one pleasing is some supernatural habit, and that it is infused into us by God, so that the soul may be adorned and perfected, and thus rendered just and pleasing and acceptable to God.

But in order that it may be exactly established what is properly being disputed, the ambiguity of the word 'grace' must first be unfolded.

For first, it denotes the favor and gratuitous mercy of God regarding the act of justification, as was shown a little earlier.

Then, sometimes in the Scriptures it signifies those gifts which come to believers and the reborn through the Holy Spirit: Rom. 12:6, 'We have gifts that differ, according to the grace that is given to us'; 1 Cor. 15:10, 'The grace of God in me was not in vain, for I labored more than all of them.'

Third, it signifies more often the compensation for a gift given freely: as when it is said, 'I give you thanks.' Luke 17:9, 'Does he have thanks for that servant?'

Fourth, not rarely it denotes a gift given to someone out of grace: such are all the gifts which God confers upon us freely: and these are either natural, which depend on creation and are common to the pious and the impious; or some are spiritual, which come to men from the benefit of regeneration, such as faith, hope, charity, and other χαρίσματα of prophesying, working miracles, speaking in various tongues, and similar peculiar gifts granted for the time of the Church. 1 Cor. 12.

Fifth: in the form of alms, they are named grace by the Apostle. 1 Cor. 16, 'That I may carry your τὴν χάριν ὑμῶν to Jerusalem.'

And it is not properly disputed here about these last four meanings, but only about that first one, by which we indeed contend that the word 'grace,' wherever it denotes the cause of our justification in the Pauline Epistles, denotes only the goodness and mercy of God; the Jesuits, on the contrary, define it by an infused habit or quality. And therefore they philosophize about this grace in this manner. First, they divide it into grace freely given and grace that makes one pleasing. They say that grace freely given is a supernatural gift without any debt, conferred primarily for the spiritual salvation of others. 1 Cor. 12:4, 'There are divisions of graces, etc.' They say that grace that makes one pleasing is a supernatural gift, without any debt, given primarily for the spiritual salvation of each individual. 2 Cor. 12:9, 'My grace is sufficient for you, etc.' They write that the difference between these two types of grace is that grace that makes one pleasing is given primarily for the salvation of each individual; secondarily for that of others, namely so that we ourselves may first be made just and perfect; then that others may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven. Finally, they subdivide grace that makes one pleasing into permanent or habitual grace, and the grace of special assistance. They say that permanent grace is the infused habits of faith, hope, and charity, and especially of charity. They define the grace of special assistance as being a motion of God by which a man is helped toward operations that in some way exceed his nature. Bellar. book 1, on grace and free will, chapter 2, page 521, etc.

But this is a sink of most absurd impieties: for first, these partitions of divine grace are concocted without the authority of Scripture in support of the Jesuit dogma.

Then, by that one exclamation of the Savior, they are utterly overturned. Luke 17:10. When you have done all things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants, for we have done what we ought to have done: so far is it from the case that any grace making one pleasing inheres in us; but this grace is solely the gratuitous mercy of God, by which in the Son He has made us beloved and acceptable to Himself. Ephesians 1:6.

Thirdly: Whatever of thanks, or of gifts, is in us, that pertains to grace given gratuitously, and does not constitute a contradistinguished species of grace making one pleasing, and habitually inhering in us.

Fourthly: The Apostle himself most clearly distinguishes the grace of God, by which we are justified, from infused gifts, when he says in Romans 5:15, 'The grace of God, and the gift by grace': by χάριν understanding the gratuitous love of God toward us, as the preceding verse explains. 5, by δωρεὰν ἐν τῇ χάριτι, all the salutary effects of grace.

Fifthly: The same Apostle not only asserts that we are justified by the grace of God, but adds furthermore that this is done GRATUITOUSLY, Romans 3:24. Now if we are justified by an infused habit of charity, we are certainly not justified gratuitously. For these two mutually exclude each other.

Sixthly: All those testimonies of Scripture are repugnant, by which it was demonstrated above that the grace of God in the present matter denotes nothing other than the gratuitous mercy of God: whence also this grace is not named absolutely, but always the grace of God: likewise grace in Christ: likewise grace, which is the cause of our redemption according to that in John 3:16: 'God so LOVED the world, that He gave His only begotten Son.' Therefore, that grace no more inheres in us than the redemption of Christ.

Seventhly: Thomas himself, overcome by the force of truth, is compelled to admit this interpretation of ours, writing thus: 1. 2. quest. 110. art. 1. 'Sometimes the grace of God is called the eternal love of God itself: according to which it is also called the grace of predestination: in as much as God gratuitously, and not from merits, predestined or chose some.' Albert Pighius, a writer otherwise Papist, supports this in book 5 de lib. arb., saying: 'We shall seek the various acceptation of grace, not from the Schools, but from the Scriptures.' For some imagine that the grace of God is some quality created in our soul, by God, or the same with the habit of Charity, or distinct from the same. All of which I consider to be fabricated, nor to have any authority from the Scriptures.

Finally, if it were without all these reasons, yet that single Apostolic Aphorism, which stands at Phil. 2:13, would utterly overturn the entire Jesuitical structure. For if it is GOD alone who works in us not only the willing: but also the performing: certainly whatever the Romanists blather about this infused habit of Grace, and its merits and dignity, is nonsensical. And although the Jesuits, noticing the force of this argument, immediately object at this point: that they do not maintain that infused Grace, without some special aid, is sufficient either for performing or for persevering: yet they shamefully beg the question. For this very thing is in controversy: Whether any special aid is granted to man, which can so strengthen and confirm infused Grace, that it, being thus confirmed, can perform salvation, persevere to the very end, and overcome all temptations. We certainly do not doubt that GOD can instruct men with such Grace in this life: but what GOD wills, not what He can do, must be discerned from the scriptures. Furthermore, the Jesuits take refuge in this Special aid quite ineptly, since from the entire human race they cannot name even one man, however holy, who, endowed with such an infused habit of Grace, could either begin or perform the business of his salvation. Nay, rather, Christ taught these to pray: Forgive us our sins: And John affirms that those who say they do not have sin in themselves are liars, 1 John 1:8. Hence Solomon universally infers: There is no one who does not sin, nor can anyone say: I have purged my heart, I am clean from sin. Now, truly, where there is sin, there inherent perfect Justice, meriting eternal life, cannot have a place. For opposites cannot subsist together in the same Subject: but one excludes the other.

The Jesuits are in an uproar at this point, objecting 1. That by this reasoning we strip the pious of all infused habitual grace: and consequently leave no distinction between the pious and the impious. But I answer that they themselves are deceived and deceive under a gross ignorance of the Elenchus, and the Sophism of ἑτεροζητήσεως (changing the subject). For we do not strip the pious and faithful of all infused grace: but we deny that they obtain Justification and adoption by this infused grace. It is one thing, however, to take away all infused grace from the pious, which we by no means do: it is another to remove the merit of Justification from this grace: which Scripture and we with it do most openly.

Furthermore, Bellarmine objects with those testimonies of Scripture which affirm that Grace is diffused and poured out in our hearts, Rom. 5:5. The Charity of GOD is diffused in our hearts. And Tit. 3:6. He poured out the Holy Spirit upon us abundantly.

I answer that the Sophists are playing again under ignorance of the Elenchus; while, namely, they

think that the Charity of God in this place is to be understood passively, namely, of such Charity by which GOD is loved by us: when the same Apostle confirms, in the verse immediately following, 8, that it is to be understood actively, of that Charity by which GOD pursues us. Where he determinately names this Charity of GOD ἀγάπην τẽ θεẽ εἰς ἡμᾶς, the Charity of GOD towards us, by which He Himself loved us, not by which He is loved by us. Furthermore, the scope of the Apostle confirms the same, which turns on this, that he wants this Charity of GOD to be for us like a base and foundation, on which we ought to found and stabilize the matter of our boasting. But such a foundation cannot be our charity towards GOD: since it is imperfect, and polluted with many filthinesses of sins. What? That the Lord Apostle elsewhere pronounces indefinitely that nothing at all inheres in us of which we can boast before GOD: so that he who wishes to boast, can and ought to boast only in the LORD. 1 Cor. 1:3. Nor does it stand against this answer of ours that the Apostle affirms that this Charity is diffused in our hearts. For although by reason of its origin it is outside us in GOD alone: yet by reason of relation and term, it is carried to our hearts, the nobler part of man, put for the whole Man. Furthermore, the Charity of GOD is also said to be diffused in our hearts because of those most noble Effects of Grace, which consist in the Sanctification or renewal of our mind, and which do not justify man, but follow one who is already freely justified.

As for the word Diffusing or Pouring out, it is not taken properly in this place, but metaphorically denotes the amplification and abundance of the love of GOD: In which sense not only the gifts of the Holy Spirit: but the Holy Spirit Himself is read to have been poured out: Joel 2:28. Where he would be very absurd who would infer from that, that the Holy Spirit habitually inheres in believers, which Bellarmine himself denies, lib. 1. de Grat. & lib. arb. cap. 8. pag. 548. C.

Thirdly, Bellarmine brings forward other passages of Scripture, in which Grace is compared to a pledge, a seal, an anointing, or a seed, namely to created and permanent things, as 2 Cor. 1:21-22: 'He who anointed us is GOD, and he sealed us, and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.' And 1 John 2:27: 'The anointing which you received from him, ABIDES in you.' And chapter 3:9: 'He who is born of GOD does not commit sin, because his seed abides in him.' For what else, Bellarmine infers, is the Seed of GOD abiding in us, if not habitual Charity, from which the fruits of good works are born?

I answer that the Jesuit is trifling and begging the question. For what reason of consequence will be given in this argument: The Grace of GOD is compared to Created and permanent things. Therefore, the Grace of GOD ought to be defined by an infused habit of Charity, and one inhering Subjectively. For thus this consequence would also be valid: The Holy Spirit is compared in the places cited to a pledge, a security, a seed. Therefore the Holy Spirit is habitually infused, and subjectively inheres in believers. Since Bellarmine himself explodes and rejects this collection as futile and weak in chapter 8 of book 1 of De Gratia et Libero Arbitrio, he does not even consider it worth a penny in this place. For a consequence does not hold from similarities or metaphors to the very nature or definition of things: otherwise infinite absurdities would follow from the Scriptures, which are accustomed to compare even God himself to created things at times.

Finally, Bellarmine objects with the authority of the Fathers, which nevertheless does not hinder our opinion in the least. For what they understand concerning the grace of sanctification, which we concede with them habitually inheres in us, the Jesuit maliciously transfers to the grace of justification: and thus he plays childishly under the sophism of equivocation. What? That the authority of Scripture is more powerful for us than that of the Fathers, even if they were to side with the Jesuits in the highest degree: which, however, we by no means grant.

Latin:

Septimò, subijcit ibidem Apostolus: Ideò ex fide secundum gratiam credentibus imputatur justitia, ut sit firma promissio: hoc est, ut sit certa reconciliatio. Nam si salus nostra operum meritis niteretur, tunc ab incerto planè penderet fundamento. Jam cùm in illius solius manibus ea versetur, qui cælum terramque condidit, nihil utique incertitudinis aut dubitationis potest esse reliquum.

Quas blasphemias Concilium Tridentinum Canone dignas esse censuit, ita ut anathematis fulmen vibraret in eos, qui dicant, Gratiam, quâ justificamur, esse tantùm favorem Dei. Sess. 6. Can. 11

Tandem colligit Autor noster Causas quatuor, propter quas pro puritate istius significationis vocabuli Gratiæ pugnandum.

Prima est: Ut debitus honos Christo tribuatur: cujus merito tantundem derogatur, quantum humanis viribus meritis aut operibus quibuscunque attribuitur. Secunda: ut conscientia certam ac firmam habeat consolationem: neque de certitudine salutis dubitare necesse habeat. Tertia: ut vera invocatio præstari possit: secundum formulam à Propheta Daniele noHinc Jesuitæ Costerus cap. 6. Enchiridij pag. 228. Gratiam hanc Dei definit, quòd sit qualitas quædam, divinitùs infusa animæ, quâ non aliter fugentur peccata, quàm tenebræ adventu luminis, & per quam accipiat anima nitorem, divinamque pulchritudinem, quâ non modò jam dicatur, sed revera sit grata DEO & homogratiâ præditæ jam nominetur, ut sit amicus, imò filius Dei. Et Bellarminus lib. 1. de gratia & libero arbitrio cap. 3. pag. 526. B. Communis est, inquit, Theologorum sententia, Gratiam gratum facientem esse habitum aliquem supernaturalem, eumque nobis infundi à Deo, quò anima exornetur & perficiatur, atque adeo justa Deo què grata & accepta reddatur.

Cæterùm ut exactè constare possit, Qua de re propriè controvertatur, evolvenda initiò fuerit æquivocatio vocabuli Gratiæ.

Primùm enim notat favorem, & gratuitam misericordiam Dei, circa actum Justificationis, ut paulò antè ostensum.

Deindò, interdum in Scripturis ea significat dona, quæ credentibus & renatis per Spiritum Sanctum obveniunt: Rom. 12,6. Habemus dona differentia, juxta Gratiam, quæ data est nobis, 1. Cor. 15,10. Gratia Dei in me non fuit inanis, plus enim laboravi istis omnibus.

Tertiò, significat sæpiùs Compensationem doni gratis dati: ut cum dicitur: ago tibi gratias. Luc. 17, 9. Nùm gratiam habet servo illi?

Quartò, haud rarò notat Donum alicui ex gratia datum: Qualia sunt omnia dona, quæ Deus in nos gratis confert: eaque vel naturalia, quæ à Creatione dependent & communia sunt pijs & impijs: Quædam vel Spiritualia, quæ ex regenerationis beneficio hominibus obtingunt, qualia, sunt, Fides, Spes, Charitas, & alia χαρίσματα prophetandi, faciendi mi racula, loquendi varijs linguis, & similia dona peculiaria, ad tempus Ecclesiæ concessa. 1. Co. rinth. 12.

Quintò: in Specie Eleemosynæ ab Apostolo nominantur Gratia. 1. Cor. 16. Ut perferam τὴν χάριν ὑμῶν in Hierusalem.

Et de quatuor hisce postremis significationibus hoc loco propriè non controvertitur, sed tantùm de primâ illâ, quâ nos quidem contendimus, vocabulum Gratiæ, ubicunque in Epistolis Paulinis Iustificationis nostræ causam notat, solam Dei notare bonitatem & misericordiam: Jesuvitæ contra per Habitum sive Qualitatem infusam, illud definiunt. Ac proindè hunc in modum de Gratia hac philosophantur. Primùm eam dividunt in Gratiam gratis datam, & in Gratiam gratum facientem. Gratiam gratis datam dicunt esse donum supernaturale absque ullo debito, ad aliorum spiritualem salutem præcipuè collatum. 1. Cor. 12, 4. Divisiones Gratiaru sunt &c. Gratiam gratum facientem dicunt esse donum supernaturale, absque ullo debito, ad propriam uniuscujusq, spiritualem salutem potissimùm datum. 2. Cor. 12, 9. Sufficit tibi Gratia mea &c. Inter utramque hanc Gratiam hoc interesse scriptitant, quò dGratia gratum faciens, detur potissimùm ad propriam uniuscujusque salutem: secundariò ad aliorum, nimirùm ut nos ipsi primùm justi perfectique efficiamur: deindè cæteri videant opera nostra bona, & glorificent Patrem nostrum, qui in Cœlis est. Tandem Gratiam gratum facientem, subdividunt in Gratiam permanentem, sive habitualem: & in Gratiam auxilij speciali. Gratiam permanentem dicunt esse infusos habitus Fidei, Spei, Charitatis: ac præcipuè Charitatis. Gratiam auxilij specialis definiunt, quòd sit motio Dei, quâ homo ad operationes, quæ naturam suam aliquo modo superant, ad juvatur. Bellar. l. 1. de gratia & lib. arb. cap. 2. pag. 521 &c.

Sed sentina hæc est absurdissimarum impietatum: Primum enim sine Scripturæ auroritate partitiones hæ Gratiæ divinæ, in subsidium dogmatis Jesuitici confinguntur.

Deindè unico illo Servatoris Epiphonemate funditùs evertuntur. Luc. 17, 10. Si omnia feceritis, quæ præcepta sunt vobis: dicite: Servi inutiles sumus, nam quod debuimus facere, fecimus: tantùm abest, ut nobis inhæreat Gratia aliqua gratum faciens: sed hæc Gratia est sola gratuita Dei miseratio, quâ in Filio nos sibi fecit dilectos & acceptabiles. Ephes. 1, 6.

Tertiò: Quicquid in nobis est gratiarum, sive donorum: illud ad Gratiam gratis datam pertinet, neque contradistinctam Speciem Gratiæ gratum facientis, nobisque habitualiter inhærentis constituit.

Quartò: Apostolus ipse Dei gratiam, quâ justificamur, à donis infusis apertissimè distinguit, cum dit Rom. 5,15. Gratia Dei, & donum per Gratiam: per χάριν intelligens gratuitam Dei erga nos dilectionem: uti explicat versus præcedens. 5. per δωρεὰν ἐν τῇ χάριτι, omnia salutaria effecta gratiæ.

Quintò: idem Apostolus non solùm asserit, nos justificari gratia Dei, sed addit insuper, fieri hoc GRATIS, Rom. 3, 24. Jam si per infusum Charitatis habitum justificamur, utique non Gratis justificamur. Hæc duo enim se mutuò excludunt.

Sextò: repugnant omnia ea Scripturæ testimonia, quibus suprà demonstratum fuit, Gratiam Dei in præsente negocio, nihil aliud quàm gratuitam Dei misericordiam denotare: Undè etiam Gratia hæc non absolutè nominatur, sed semper Gratia Dei: Item Gratia in Christo: Item Gratia, quæ Causa sit redemtionis nostræ secundum illud Johan : 3, 16. Sic Deus DILEXIT mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum dederit. Illa ergò Gratia non magis in nobis inhæret, quàm Christi redemtio.

Septimò: ipse etiam Thomas vi veritatis victus, nostram hanc interpretationem admittere cogitur, sic scribens. 1. 2. quæst. 110. art. 1. Quandoque Gratia Dei dicitur ipsa æterna Dei dilectio: secundum quod etiam dicitur Gratia Prædestinationis: in quantum Deus gratuitò, & non ex meritis aliquos prædestinavit, sive elegit. Cui suffragatur Albertus Pighius, Scriptor alioqui Pontificius lib. 5. de lib. arb. Gratia inquiens, acceptionem variam, non ex Scholis sed ex Scripturis petemus. Imaginantur enim aliqui, Gratiam Dei esse qualitatem aliquâ increatam animæ nostræ, à Deo, vel eandem cum Charitatis habitu, vel distinctam ab eodem. Quæ commentitia universa existimo, nec ex Scripturis ullam autoritatem habere.

Tandem si absque omnibus istis rationibus esset, tamen unicus ille Aphorismus Apostolicus, qui extat Phil. 2, 13. universam structuram Jesuwiticam funditùs everteret. Si enim solus DEUS est, qui in nobis operatur non tantùm τὸ velle: sed & τὸ perficere: certè nugatorium est, quicquid de infuso isto Gratiæ habitu, ejusque meritis ac dignitate blaterant Romanenses. Et quanquàm Jesuwwitæ argumenti hujus vim animadvertentes, hoc loco statim excipiunt: se non statuere, quòd Gratia infusa, absque speciali quodam auxilio, vel ad perficiendum, vel ad perseverandum sufficiat: tamen turpiter petunt Principium. Nam hoc ipsum Controversitur: An homini aliquod speciale auxilium concedatur, quod Gratiam infusam ita confortare & confirmare possit, ut ea sic confirmata salutem perficere, ad finem usque perseverare, & omnes tentationes superare possit, Non sanè dubitamus, quin DEUS possit hac in vita homines tali Gratiâ instruere: sed quid velit DEUS, non quid possit, ex scripturis dispiciendum est. Deindè prorsus ineptè ad auxilium hoc Speciale confugiunt Jesuwwitæ, cùm ex universo genere humano, ne unum quidem nominare possint Hominem, quantûvis sanctum, qui tali aliquô infuso Gratiæ habitu donatus salutis suæ negocium vel inchoare, vel perficere potuerit. Quin hos potiùs Christus orare docuit: Remitte nobis peccata nostra: Et Johannes affirmat, mendaces esse, qui dixerint, se non habere in se peccatum, 1. Joh. 1, 8. Hinc Salomon universaliter infert: Nemo est qui non peccet, nec quisquam dicere potest: purgavi animum meum, mundus sum a peccato. Jam verò ubi peccatum est, ibi inhærens perfecta Justitia, vitam æternam promerens, locum habere non potest. Contraria enim in eodem Subjecto simul subsistere nequeunt: sed unum alterum excludit.

Tumultuantur hoc loco Jesuwwitæ, objicientes 1. Nos hac ratione pios spoliare omni infusa gratia habituali: & per consequens nullum relinquere discrimen inter pios & impios. Sed respondeo, ipsos falli ac fallere sub crassa ignoratione Elenchi, & Sophismate ἑτεροζητήσεως. Neque enim pios ac fideles omni infusâ gratiâ spoliamus: sed eos hâc infusâ gratiâ Justificationem atque adoptionem consequi, negamus. Aliud verò est, omnem piis infusam gratiam detrahere, quod nos minimè facimus: aliud est, Justificationis meritum ab hac gratia removere: quod apertissimè Scriptura & nos cum ipsa facimus.

Porrò objicit Bellarminus ea Scripturæ testimonia, quæ affirmant, Gratiam diffundi & effundi in cordibus nostris, Rom. 5, 5. Charitas DEI diffusa est in cordibus nostris. Et Tit. 3, 6. Spiritum sanctum effudit in nos abundè.

Respondeo, rursum sub ignoratione Elenchi Sophistas ludere: dùm nimirùm Charitatem

Dei hoc loco passive intelligendam esse opinantur, de tali nimirum Charitate, qua DEUS a nobis diligitur: cùm activè potiùs, de ea Charitate, qua DEUS nos prosequitur, eam intelligendam esse, confirmet idem Apostolus, versu statim subseq. 8. Ubi hanc Charitatem DEI determinatè nominat ἀγάπην τẽ θεẽ εἰς ἡμᾶς, Charitatem DEI erga nos, quâ ipse dilexit nos, non quâ à nobis ipse diligitur. Deindè idem confirmat Scopus Apostoli, qui in eo vertitur, quòd Charitatem hanc DEI vult nobis esse instar basis & fundamenti, in quo gloriationis nostræ materiam fundare ac stabilire debeamus. Tale autem fundamentum nostra erga DEUM charitas esse nequit: quippè quæ imperfecta, multisq; peccatorum sordibus polluta. Quid? quòd D. Apostolus alibi indefinitè pronunciat, nihil quicquam inhærere nobis, de quo coram DEO gloriari possimus: ita, ut qui gloriari velit, non nisi in DOMINO gloriari possit & debeat. 1. Cor. 1, 3. Neque responsioni huic nostræ obstat, quod Apostolus affirmat, Charitatem hanc diffusam esse in cordibus nostris. Etsi enim eâ ratione originis est extra nos in solo DEO: tamen ratione σχέσεως & termini, fertur ad corda nostra, nobiliore hominis parte, pro toto Homine posita. Deindè diffundi etiam dicitur Charitas DEI in cordibus nostris propter nobilissimos illos Effectus Gratiæ, qui in Sanctificatione sive renovatione mentis nostræ consistunt, quique Hominem non justificant, sed jam Gratis justificatum consequuntur.

Quoad verbum Diffundendi sive Effundendi, non propriè illud hoc loco accipitur, sed metaphoricè notat amplificationem & ubertatem amoris DEI: Quo sensu non dona modò Spiritus sancti: sed & ipse Spiritus sanctus legitur effusus: Joel. 2, 28. Ubi perquàm absurdus foret, qui indè colligeret, Spiritum sanctum habitualiter, inhærere credentibus, id quod negat ipse Bellarminus lib. 1. de Grat. & lib. arb. cap. 8. pag. 548. C.

Tertiò profert Bellarminus aliæ Scripturæ loca, in quibus Gratia comparatur pignori, sigillo, unctioni, vel semini, rebus videlicet creatis & permanentibus, ut 2. Cor. 1, 21. & 22. Qui unxit nos DEUS, & signavit nos, & dedit pignus Spiritus in cordibus nostris. Et 1. Johan. 2, 27. Unctio, quam accepistis ab eo, MANEAT in vobis. Et cap. 3, 9. Qui natus est ex DEO, peccatum non facit, quia semen ejus manet in eo. Quid enim, infert Bellarminus, aliud est Semen DEI in nobis manens, nisi Charitas habitualis, ex qua fructus bonorum operum nascuntur?

Respondeo, nugari Jesuwitam, & petere principium. Quæ enim dabitur ratio consehentiæ in hoc argumento: Gratia DEI comparatur rebus Creatis & permanentibus. E. Gratia DEI definiri debet per habitum Charitatis infusum, & Subjectivè inhærentem. Sic enim valeret & hæc consecutio: Spiritus sanctus comparatur in tocis citatis arrhaboni, pignori, semini. Ergo Spiritus sanctus habitualiter infunditur, & Subjectivè inhæret credentibus. Quam collectionem, cùm ipse Bellarminus tanquàm futilem & elumbem explodat & rejiciat cap 8. libri 1. de Grat. & lib. arb. meminerit, neque hoc loco eam vel unius esse teruntii. Ex similitudinibus enim sive Metaphoris ad ipsam rerum naturam sive definitionem non valet Consequentia: alioqui infinita ex Sa cris sequerentur absurda, quæ ipsum quoque Deum rebus creatis interdum comparare solent.

Tandem objicit Bellarminus autoritatem Patrum, quæ tamen nostræ sententiæ nihil quicquam officit. Nam quod de Gratia Sanctificationis, quam nos cum ipsis habitualiter nobis inhærere concedimus, ipsi intelligunt: illud Jesuwita malitiosè transfert ad Gratiam Justificationis: & sic sub Sophismate Æquivocationis pueriliter ludit. Quid? quòd potior nobis Scripturæ, quàm Patrum est autoritas, si vel maximè cum Jesuivitis facerent: id quod tamen minimè largimur.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: II. The Efficient Instrumental Cause is the Merit of Christ

We have said that the efficient cause of our justification is one thing as the principal efficient cause, and another as the organic or instrumental efficient cause. Christ obtains the respect of both of these causes. For he is the principal efficient cause of our justification, insofar as he himself, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, having had mercy on the human race, determined from eternity to receive it into grace at last, and to reconcile it to himself, 2 Cor. 5:18 and 19. But the same Christ is also the organic efficient cause, insofar as in that eternal decree of the adorable Trinity, he took upon himself the parts of mediation. Whence he also received the respect and title of meritorious cause. And it is concerning this latter respect that the question properly exists in this place.

Moreover, the Romanists do not wish to seem to deny that Christ our Savior sustained, or rather accomplished, the parts of mediation and redemption for the whole human race. For the Scriptures confirm too evidently that Christ was set forth by God as a propitiation in his blood, Rom. 3:25. And that we have redemption in Christ, Rom. 3:24, and that the same was given and made for us by the Father as righteousness and redemption, 1 Cor. 1:30. Which part of Christian doctrine the previous general controversy against the Photinians has invincibly asserted and confirmed.

That rather should be considered more deeply in this place: What controversy exists for us today with the Jesuits concerning this very merit of Christ? For although they seem to proclaim it quite splendidly in words, in the very act, however, they fundamentally undermine and overturn it: which I wish to make plain for the sake of method according to distinct questions.

At the beginning, however, it is asked: In what matter do the parts of the office of Christ consist by reason of merit? The Jesuits respond that he is not only Mediator and Redeemer, but also a new legislator, according to that sacrilegious 21st Canon of the sixth session of the Council of Trent: If anyone shall say that Christ Jesus was given by God to men as a Redeemer in whom they should trust, but not also as a legislator whom they should obey, let him be anathema. It must be noted, however, that it is not asked in this place in general concerning the office of Christ, by reason of which it was necessary for him also to be a teacher of the Church and a reformer of the moral law from Pharisaical corruptions: but specifically concerning the office of Christ by reason of the merit of our salvation and justification? Where we, having followed the oracles of the Scriptures, constantly assert that he was not a new legislator, but only Redeemer and Mediator. Whence the benefit or effect of the office of Christ so considered is always named in the Scriptures as redemption, liberation, John 19:25, 1 Tim. 2:5, Heb. 9:15 and ch. 12:24, Rom. 3:24, 1 Cor. 1:30. And although the Savior, in Matthew 5 and the two subsequent chapters, sustained the parts of a legal preacher, while he vindicated the doctrine of the Law from various corruptions: nowhere, however, is he read to have handed down new laws, by the observation of which men might merit salvation and eternal life.

There is objected to us in this place that saying of the Savior in John 13:34: A new commandment I give unto you, that you love one another, as I have loved you. But this objection overturns itself. For thus it would follow that before the coming of Christ no commandment at all concerning mutual love had been promulgated: which the Papists themselves know to be false. Therefore, this commandment is not called new by Christ, as the Jesuits pretend, because he wished to prescribe to us some new law necessary for salvation: but it is called new because of the novelty of the manner in which it is inculcated by Christ. For the old Law commands us to seek the manner of love from ourselves, by saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Christ, however, recalls us to higher things, to the manner of love with that purpose which shines forth in his own example, as one who loved us more than himself, his life having been poured out for us, even for enemies, more than for friends, which is hardly found, who would pour it out. In which there is something new, there is no one who does not understand. Nor, however, is it immediately a consequence from this, as the Jesuits pretend, that Christ is a new legislator: or that the Gospel itself concerning Christ can properly be called a Law.

Latin:

Efficientem Justificationis nostræ Causam, aliam diximus esse Efficientem Principalem: aliam Efficientem Organicam sive Instrumentalem. Utriusque hujus Causæ respectum sortitur Christus. Est enim is Causa Efficiens principalis Justificationis nostræ, quatenùs & ipse cum Patre & Spiritu sancto, misertus generis humani, ab æterno constituit demùm in gratiam illud recipere, sibique ipsi reconciliare, 2. Cor 5,18. & 19. Est verò idem ipse Christus, Causa etiam Efficiens Organica, quatenùs in æterno illo adorandæ Trinitatis Decreto, Mediationis partes in se recepit. Undè Causæ etiam Meritoriæ respectum & appellationem accepit. Et de posteriore hoc respectu, hoc loco propriè est Quæstio.

Cæterùm Christum Servatorem nostrum, Mediationis & Redemtionis partes pro toto genere humano non tàm sustinuisse, quàm expedivisse, ne ipsi quoque negare videri volunt Romanenses. Nimis enim evidenter confirmant Scripturæ, Christum à Deo propositum esse Propitiatorium in sanguine ipsius, Roman. 3, 25. Et nos habere redemptionem in Christo, Rom. 3, 24. eundemq; à Patre nobis datum factumque esse, Justitiam & Redemtionem, 1. Corinth. 1, 30. Quam doctrinæ Christianæ partem Controversia prior Generalis, contra Photinianos invictè asseruit & confirmavit.

Illud potiùs hoc loco altiùs considerandum fuerit: Quid Controversiæ nobis hodiè cum Jesuwitis, de hoc ipso merito CHRISTI intercedat? Etsi enim verbis satis splendidè illud prædicare videntur, ipso tamen facto, funditùs illud subruunt & evertunt: id quod Methodi gratiâ secundum distinctas Quæstiones planum facere libet.

Initiò autem quæritur: Qua in re partes officij Christi, ratione meriti, consistant? Respondent Jesuwitæ, ut non saltem Mediator & Redemtor; sed & novus legislator sit, secundum sacrilegum illum Canonem 21. Sessionis sextæ Concilii Tridentini: Siquis dixerit, CHRISTUM JESUM à DEO hominibus datum fuisse, ut Redemtorem cui fidant: non etiam ut legislatorem, cui obediant, anathema sit. Notandum autem est hoc loco non quæri in genere de officio CHRISTI, ratione cujus ipsum quoque Doctorem Ecclesiæ, & Legis moralis à corruptelis Pharisaicis Reformatorem esse oportuit: sed in Specie de officio CHRISTI, ratione meriti, salutis & justificationis nostræ? ubi nos Scripturarum oracula secuti, non novum legislatorem, sed tantùm Redemtorem & Mediatorem fuisse, constanter asseveramus. Unde beneficium etiam sive ἀποτέλεσμα Officii Christi sic considerati in Scripturis semper nominatur Redemtio, Liberatio, Job. 19, 25. 1. Tim 2, 5 Hebr. 9, 15. & cap. 12, 24. Rom. 3, 24. 1. Cor. 1, 30. Et quanquàm Servator, Matth. 5. & duobus subsequentibus capitibus, Concionatoris legalis partes sustinuit, dùm à variis corruptelis doctrinam Legis vindicavit: nusspiam tamen novas leges tradidisse legitur, quarum observatione Homines salutem & vitam æternam promereri possint.

Objicitur hoc loco nobis illud Servatoris Joh. 13, 34. Novum mandatum do vobis, ut diligatis vos invicem, sicut ego dilexi vos. Sed semetipsam evertit hæc objectio. Sic enim sequeretur, ante adventum Christi nullum prorsus mandatum de mutua dilectione fuisse promulgatum : id quod falsum esse ipsi noverunt Pontificii. Proindè mandatum hoc non, uti Jesuwitæ fingunt, à Christo dicitur novum, quòd ipse novam aliquam legem nobis observatu ad salutem necessariam, præscribere voluerit: sed novum dicitur, propter novitatem modi, quô illud à Christo inculcatur. Nam Lex vetus dilectionis modum, ex nobis ipsis petere jubet, dicendo: Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Christus autem ad altiora nos revocat, modò dilectionis cô propositô, qui in ipsiusmet exemplo relucet, ut qui nos magis, quàm seipsum dilexit, vita pro nobis profusâ, etiam pro inimicis, quàm pro amicis vix reperitur, qui profundat. In quo novi quiddam esse, nemo est, qui non intelligit. Neque tamen hinc statim est Consequens, quòd fingunt Jesuwitæ, novum Legislatorem esse CHRISTUM: Quin ipsum quoque Evangelium, de CHRISTO, Legem propriè nominari posse.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: Question: Whether Christ and indeed alone fully and perfectly performed the parts of the Redemption of his Mediator

For it is not the Law itself: but merely the mode of the law, to which novelty is here assigned by CHRIST, while the Law itself remains in itself entirely the same, which was delivered by Moses, Levit. 19:18. Therefore this is clearly that which the Apostle John writes in a somewhat enigmatic way: Brethren, I write no new commandment unto you: but an old commandment. And presently he adds: A new commandment I write unto you: which is to be understood concerning the commandment of love, which is both old and new. Old indeed, if you attend to the substance of the Law: but New, if you regard the mode of the commandment. Therefore, no support for that first Jesuitical error can redound from the words of CHRIST: which it is evident was devised for this reason, that something from the observance of legal precepts might be attached to the meritorious causes of our Justification.

Furthermore it is asked: Whether Christ, and indeed He alone, so fully and perfectly discharged and completed the work of Redemption or Mediation, that nothing at all further is required for its consummation? To which we answer simply in the affirmative, asserting with the Scriptures, that CHRIST has delivered us from ALL our enemies, Luke 1:71, and from the hand of ALL that hate us, verse 74, from the curse of the law, Gal. 4:5, from the servitude and fear of death, nay even from him who had the power of death, that is, from the Devil, Heb. 2:14 & 15, and finally from sin, thus indefinitely posited, that is, from every sin, and whatever can bear the character and guilt of sin. Tit. 2:14. Christ redeemed us from ALL iniquity. To which also pertain other testimonies of Scripture, such as exist, Rom. 3:24, Heb. 9:15, Eph. 1:7, Col. 1:14, Luke 21:28. Whence this Redemption is also not simply called λύτρωσις, but ἀπολύτρωσις, as Chrysostom rightly noted, to signify, of course, a plenary, perfect, and in all respects absolute redemption.

And lest by chance some scruple might arise, Scripture also notes the very kind of actual sins, from the guilt of which we have been redeemed by CHRIST, as 1 Cor. 6:9 & 10. Such were you formerly, namely fornicators, adulterers, covetous, drunkards, revilers: but you have been washed, you have been sanctified, you have been justified by the NAME OF THE LORD JESUS. 1 John 2:1 & 2. If any man sin, etc., there you have actual sins. Heb. 9:14. The blood of Christ purges us from dead WORKS.

Furthermore, that CHRIST satisfied not only for the guilt, but also for the punishment, Scripture is witness, Isa. 53:5. The chastisement of peace was upon him, and with his stripes we are healed. Gal. 3:13. CHRIST redeemed us from the curse of the law. What? Since Scripture enumerates the very kinds of punishments, and confirms that we have been delivered from them by CHRIST: such as the power of Satan, Heb. 2:14. Death and hell, Hos. 13:14. Eternal damnation, Rom. 5:9, 1 Thess. 1:10. And what need is there of many words, when reason itself dictates that when the guilt expires, the punishment itself also expires.

Moreover, that CHRIST ALONE claims for Himself entirely the most sufficient and most absolute merit of Redemption and propitiation, and does not communicate even the smallest particle of it with our merits or those of any Saints whatsoever; is evident not only from the Type of the Old Testament, where there was but one mercy-seat: but also from that grave attestation of Christ the Saviour, Isaiah 63:3. I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the people there was no man with me.

Departing enormously from this doctrine, the Romanists have brought forth various errors, and some even horrible to hear.

First: That Christ indeed delivered us from eternal punishment, but that the punishment of temporal afflictions must be paid by us.

2. That the Body of Christ was offered once on the cross for Original debt: that it is offered continually in the Mass for daily sins: as Thomas writes in the book on the Sacrament of the Altar.

3. That the passion of Christ satisfied only for original sin, and for those actual sins which preceded Baptism: but that the Mass satisfies for sins following Baptism and first Justification: as Ambrosius Catharinus, Bishop of Conza, or Minoriensis, determines in a book printed at Rome.

4. That the merit of Christ is indeed the universal cause of our salvation: but that particular ones must also be added to it, such as the Sacraments and the prayers of the Church: And that this is the reason why we invoke not only Christ, but also his Saints, by whose merits and prayers we may perceive the help of Christ: as Thomas most blasphemously judged, 1. secundæ dist. 19. §. 2. Hence Keiserspergius in Conc. de Ascens. Christi. p. 73. Just as Christ ascended into heaven by his own power, that is, by his own merit: so it behooves everyone to ascend by his own merit. For the merit of Christ is not the total cause of our salvation: You must also add your own contribution and help to it: it is necessary that you also add something of your own.

5. That the passion of Christ is indeed the principal merit for which grace is conferred: yet it is never the sole and total meritorious cause: because some operation always concurs with the merit of Christ as a merit of congruity or of condignity, as the Scholastic Doctors commonly taught, and the Cologners in the Censura p. 186.

6. That only supplementary parts belong to the merit of Christ: so that if anything is lacking in our merits, then at last the merit of Christ can supply it: just as we showed above in the Prolegomena, from the method for the dying by the Jesuit Johannes Polandus, printed at Venice in the year 77, page 27.b.

7. That Christ, by his passion and death, obtained for us only the merit of first grace, that is, the facility of pardon, by which sins are remitted to the penitent: as Ludovicus Granatensis opines, in Volume 4 of his Postilla, page 604, in the first sermon for the 21st Sunday after Trinity.

8. That Christ, by his passion and death, merited for us only the first Grace, or grace freely given, that is, the infusion of Charity: as the Jesuits write today, and as was demonstrated above from the Cologne Censorship: Controversy 1. Special.

These monstrous opinions are too atrocious to require a more lengthy refutation; indeed, they are so constituted that even the Jesuits themselves are ashamed of them, and against the testimony of their own heart and conscience, they repeatedly rattle on with splendid words that the merit of CHRIST alone efficiently and meritoriously justifies and saves us, and merits everything that is necessary for us for salvation. But it is all too manifest that they are presenting us with mere tricks of words, devoid of any substance. For let us ask the Jesuits: When did Christ merit this plenary justice and salvation for us? If they answer that this is done daily through the Sacrificial Mass, then they are immediately caught in that impiety which they so strongly wish to disavow: namely, that the plenary Redemption of the human race was not accomplished on the Cross. For if it were fully accomplished, then there would be no further need for the repetition of any sacrifice as a supplement. But if they answer that it was done in the very work of the passion and death of CHRIST, by the force of the words spoken on the cross, IT IS FINISHED, then that entire structure which they labor with such effort to erect concerning our own merit, and concerning the works of charity and justice by which we might merit eternal life, immediately collapses. For there can be no place for our merit in relation to eternal life if CHRIST merited it for us most sufficiently many centuries ago. For where there is a most exuberant and absolute merit, there can be no place left for any further merit of our own.

Furthermore, we argue against the Jesuits' evasions as follows: If the justice of Christ is our justice, it is ours either by inherence or by imputation, for a third option is not given. But it is not by inherence, because this justice of CHRIST consists in the work of CHRIST, performed most sufficiently and most fully many centuries ago outside of us. Therefore, it is by imputation, which we maintain. But since the Jesuits simply reject and mock this, it becomes plain that they utterly deny that the justice of CHRIST is our justice.

But if perhaps the Sophists retreat to that κρησφύγετον [hiding place], to say that the passion and death of CHRIST did not immediately merit for us eternal life itself, but only the infusion of virtues, by which virtues we then merit a fuller and more exact justice, and eternal life itself: surely he would be a fool who did not understand that by this very arrangement, that sublime office of salvation is distributed between us and CHRIST according to distinct parts, so that CHRIST indeed immediately merited for us by his passion that which is LESS, namely the infusion of virtues. But we, by an immediate and proximate merit, merit that which is incomparably GREATER and more august, namely eternal life itself.

What? Why, the Jesuits do not even candidly ascribe the merit of the first Grace to CHRIST the Savior. For Bellarmine expressly assigns this to the powers and works of those not yet reborn in book 5 of Justification, chapter 22. He says, 'A man not yet reconciled can, through WORKS OF PENANCE, obtain and merit the Grace of Justification by congruity.' This one sentence of Bellarmine certainly excludes the merit of CHRIST from the act of our Justification entirely. For I argue thus: Whatever is the Cause of a Cause is also the (mediate) Cause of the Caused. But the works of the unregenerate, done without true faith and charity, are, according to Bellarmine's opinion, the meritorious cause of the first grace and justification by congruity. Therefore, they are also the (mediate) Cause of the caused, namely eternal life; for it depends entirely upon that first grace and justification which those works merit.

But the Jesuit objects that he is discussing only merit of congruity in this place, and not merit of condignity. But not even in this way does any help come to his cause, because the doctrine of the Roman Church concerning merit of condignity is no more tolerable than that concerning merit of congruity; which can be demonstrated evidently even from that.

I. Whatever can ABSOLUTELY merit eternal life, that also merits the same by condignity. But any works of charity, according to the Romanists, merit eternal life ABSOLUTELY. Therefore, also by condignity.

The connection of the major premise is manifest in itself: for that which is absolute admits of no limitation or restriction whatsoever.

The minor premise has as its author Thomas, who in 1st of the 2nd part, q. 114, art. 7, writes thus: 'Any act of charity merits eternal life absolutely.' And in book 2 of the Sentences, dist. 27, question 3, he further explains the mind of the Romanists more clearly: 'Some say that one cannot merit eternal life by condignity, but by congruity. Others, however, say that one can also merit eternal life by condignity through acts of virtue. And those who say that we can merit eternal life by condignity seem to speak more truly.'

And lest our Jesuit perchance be able to call into doubt the authority of Thomas in this matter, let him remember that the Council of Trent has not merely disapproved of this very impiety, but has rather fortified it with an anathema in these words: If any one shall say that the good works of a justified man are in such a way the gifts of God that they are not also the good merits of the justified man himself; or that the justified man himself, by the good works which are done by him through the grace of God and the merit of Jesus Christ, whose living member he is, does not truly merit increase of grace, eternal life, let him be anathema. Sess. 6 Can. 32.

Latin:

Nam non Lex ipsa est: sed modus duntaxat legis, cui novitas hîc à CHRISTO adsignatur, Lege ipsâ in se pròrsus manente eâdem, quæ est à Mose tradita, Levit. 19, 18. Itaque hoc est illud planè, quod Johannes Apostolus quodammodò αἰνιγματικῶς scribit: Fratres, non novum mandatum scribo vobis: sed vetus mandatum. Et mox subjicit: Novum mandatum scribo vobis: id quod de mandato dilectionis est accipiendum, quod & vetus est, & novum. Vetus quidem, si substantiam Legis attendas: Novum autem, si modum mandati respicias. Nihil proindè præsidii ad primum istum errorem Jesuwiticum ex verbis CHRISTI redundare potest: quem ideò excogitatum esse constat, ut Justificationis nostræ causæ meritoriæ, aliquid de observatione præceptorum legalium affricari posset.

Porrò quæritur: An Christus & quidem solus ita plenè & perfectè Redemtionis sive Mediationis opus expedierit & absolverit, ut nihil quicquam amplius ad ejus consummationem requiratur? Ubi nos simpliciter affirmatè respondemus, cum Scripturis asserentes, CHRISTUM liberasse nos ab OMNIBUS inimicis nostris, Luc. 1. 71. & à manu OMNIUM, qui oderunt nos, versu 74. à maledictione legis Galat. 4, 5. à servitute & metu mortis, imò ab eo quoque, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est, à Diabolo, Heb. 2, 14. & 15. à peccato denique, sic indefinitè posito, hoc est, ab omni peccato, & quicquid peccati rationem & reatum præ se ferre potest. Tit. 2, 14. Christus nos redemit ab OMNI iniquitate Quò pertinent etiam alia Scripturæ testimonia, qualia, extant, Rom. 3, 24. Heb. 9, 15. Ephes. 1, 7. Coloss. 1, 14. Luc. 21, 28. Undè Redemtio etiam hæc non simpliciter λύτρωσις, sed ἀπολύτρωσις dicitur, uti rectè annotavit Chrysostomus, ad significandam nimirùm plenariam, perfectam, omnibúsq; numeris absolutam redemtionem.

Et ne fortè scrupulus aliquis oboriri possit, Scriptura ipsam quoque notat speciem peccatorum actualium, à quorum reatu per CHRISTUM redemti sumus, ut 1. Cor. 6, 9. & 10. Hæc eritis quondam, scilicet scortatores, adulteri, avari, ebriosi, maledici: sed abluti estis, sanctificati estis, justificati estis per NOMEN DOMINI JESU. 1. Johan. 2, 1. & 2. Si quis peccaverit &c. en tibi actualia peccata. Heb. 9, 14. Sanguis Christi purgat nos ab OPERIBUS mortuis.

Præterea non pro culpa tantùm, sed & pro pœna CHRISTUM satisfecisse, Scriptura testis est, Jes 53, 5. Castigatio pacis super eum, & livore ejus sanati sumus. Galat. 3, 13. CHRISTUS nos redemit à maledictione legis. Quid? quòd ipsas pœnarum species recenset Scriptura, & ab iisdem nos per CHRISTUM liberatos esse confirmat: quales sunt Satanæ potestas. Hebr. 2, 14. Mors & infernus. Hos. 13, 14. æterna damnatio. Rom. 5, 9. 1. Thess. 1, 10. Et quid multis opus, cùm ipsa ratio dictet, expirante culpâ ipsam quoq; expirare pœnam.

Cæterùm CHRISTUM SOLUM Redemtionis & propitiationis meritum sufficientissimum & absolutissimum sibi ex asse vindicare, neque vel minimam ejus particulam cum nostris, vel Sanctorum quorumvis meritis communicare; non modò patet ex Typo Veteris Testamenti, ubi non nisi unum fuit propitiatorium: sed & ex grâvi illâ attestatione Christi Servatoris, Jesaiæ 63, 3. Ego solus calcavi torcular, & de gentibus non fuit vir mecum.

Ab hac doctrinâ enormiter planè deflectentes Romanenses, varios & vel auditu horrendos errores prodiderunt.

Primùm: Christum ab æterna quidem pœnâ nos liberasse, sed temporalium suppliciorum pœnam nobis luendam esse.

2. Corpus Christi semel oblatum esse in cruce pro debito Originali: in Missa offerri jugiter pro quotidianis peccatis: uti scribit Thomas in libro de Sacramento Altaris.

3. Christi passionem tantùm satisfecisse pro originali peccato, & pro illis peccatis actualibus, quæ Baptismum antecesserunt: Missam verò satisfacere pro peccatis, Baptismum & primam Justificationem sequentibus: uti statuit Ambrosius Catharinus, Episcopus Compsanus, sive Minoriensis in libro Romæ impresso.

4. Christi meritum esse quidem Causam Universalem nostræ salutis: sed ad quam particulares etiam oporteat accedere, sicut sunt Sacramenta, & Orationes Ecclesiæ: Et hanc causam esse, propter quam non tantùm CHRISTUM invocemus, sed & Sanctos ejus, quorum meritis & precibus auxilium CHRISTI percipiamus: uti nimis blasphemè censuit Thomas, 1. secundæ dist. 19. §. 2. Hinc Keiserspergius in Conc. de Ascens. Christi. p. 73. Sicut Christus propria virtute, hoc est, proprio merito ascendit in Cælos: Sic quemq; SUO PROPRIO merito ascendere oportet. Nam meritum Christi non est Causa totalis nostræ salutis: Du must deine Steur vnd Hülffe auch darzu thun: necesse est, ut de tuo etiam aliquid addas.

5. Christi passionem esse principale quidem meritum, propter quod conferatur gratia: nunquàm tamen esse solam & totalem causam meritoriam: quia semper cum merito CHRISTI concurrat aliqua operatio tanquàm meritum de congruo, vel de condigno, uti communiter docuerunt Doctores Scholastici, & Colonienses in Censura p 186.

6. Christi merito competere tantùm partes suppletorias: ita ut si quid nostris decedat meritis, tùm demùm meritum CHRISTI illud supplere possit: quemadmodum supra in Prolegomenis, ex Jesuwitæ Johannis Polandi methodo pro morituris, Venetijs Anno 77. impressa, pag. 27.b. osten dimus.

7. Christum suâ passione & morte, nobis tantùm primæ Gratiæ meritum consecutum efse, hoc est, veniæ facilitatem, quâ pœnitentibus peccata remittantur: uti opinatur Ludovicus Granatensis, Tomo 4. Postillæ pag. 604. Concione primâ Dominicæ XXI. Trinitatis.

8. Christum sua passione & morte, nobis tantum meruisse primam Gratiam, vel gratiam gratis datam, hoc est, infusionem Charitatis: uti hodie scriptitant Jesuitae, & supra ex Censura Coloniensium demonstratum fuit: Controversia 1. Speciali.

Atrociora sunt haec opinionum portenta, quam ut prolixiore refutatione indigeant: quin ita omnino comparata, ut ipsos etiam Jesuitas eorum pudeat, & contra proprium cordis ac Conscientiae testimonium splendidis subinde verbis crepent, CHRISTI meritum solum nos efficienter & meritorie Justificare & Salvare, & mereri omne, quod ad salutem nobis est necessarium. Meras autem verborum praestigias, omni re destitutas, nobis objici ab ipsis, nimis manifestum est. Quaeramus enim ex Jesuwaitis: Quando Christus hanc plenariam nobis justitiam & salutem sit meritus? Si respondeant, quotidie hoc fieri per Sacrificium Missaticum, tum statim illius impietatis rei deprehenduntur, quam tantopere a se amoliri volunt: quod nimirum Redemtio plenaria, generis humani in Cruce non sit peracta. Si enim plene esset peracta: Tum ad supplementum nulla repetitione ullius Sacrificii esset amplius opus. Sin respondeant, in ipso opere passionis & mortis CHRISTI id esse factum, vi verborum in cruce prolatorum, CONSUMMATUM EST, tum statim concidit universa illa structura, quam de nostro merito, deque operibus Charitatis & justitiae, quibus aeternam vitam mereamur, tanto conatu erigere laborant. Neque enim nostro merito, ratione vitae aeternae, locus esse potest, si CHRISTUS ante multa secula nobis eam sufficientissime est promeritus.
