Ubi enim est meritum exuberantissimum & absolutissimum, ibi nostro alicui ulteriori merito locus nullus potest esse reliquus.

Porro contra Jesuwitarum tergiversationes sic argumentamur: Si Christi justitia, est nostra justitia, aut per inhaesionem, aut per imputationem nostra est, Tertium enim non datur: Sed non per inhaesionem: quia Justitia haec CHRISTI consistit in opere CHRISTI, ante multa secula extra nos, sufficientissime plenissimeque praestito. Ergo per imputationem, quam nos statuimus. Hanc vero cum simpliciter rejiciant ac rideant Jesuwitae, planum fit, ipsos prorsus negare, Justitiam CHRISTI, nostram esse Justitiam.

Quod si fortassis ad illud κρησφύγετον se recipiant Sophistae, ut dicant, passionem & mortem CHRISTI non immediate nobis meruisse ipsam vitam aeternam, sed infusionem solum virtutum, quibus deinde virtutibus, nos pleniorem & exactiorem justitiam promereamur, & vitam ipsam aeternam: bardus profecto foret, qui non intelligeret, hoc ipso pacto, sublime illud officium salvationis inter nos & CHRISTUM ita secudum distinctas partes distribui, ut CHRISTUS quidem immediate nobis sua passione promeritus sit id, quod MINUS est, videlicet infusionem virtutum. Nos autem merito immediato & propinquo mereamur id, quod incomparabiliter MAJUS & augustius est, nempe ipsam vitam æternam.

Quid? quòd ne quidem primæ Gratiæ meritum CHRISTO Servatori candidè adscribunt Jesuwitæ. Hoc enim Bellarminus disertè adsignat viribus ac operibus nondum renatorum lib. 5 de Justif. cap. 22. Potest, inquiens, homo nondum reconciliatus per OPERA POENITENTIÆ impetrare, & mereri ex congruo Gratiam Justificationis. Quæ certè una Bellarmini sententia CHRISTI meritum ex actu Justificationis nostræ simpliciter excludit: Sic enim argumentor: Quicquid est Causa Causæ, est etiam Causa (mediata) Causati. Atqui Opera non renatorum sine vera fide & Charitate facta, sunt ex sententia Bellarmini, causa meritoria primæ gratiæ & justificationis ex congruo. Ergò sunt etiam Causa (mediata) causati videlicet vitæ æternæ: quippè quæ ab illa prima gratia & justificatione, quam merentur Opera illa, ex asse dependet.

Sed excipit Jesuwita, se de merito tantùm Congrui, non verò de merito Condigni hoc loco disserere. Verùm ne sic quidem ipsius causæ quicquam præsidii accedit, propterea quòd haud tolerabilior est Ecclesiæ Romanæ de merito etiam Condigni doctrina, quàm de merito Congrui; id quod vel indè evidenter demonstrari potest.

I. Quicquid Absolutè potest mereri vitam æternam, illud etiam de Condigno eandem meretur: Atqui quælibet opera Charitatis secundum Romanenses merentur ABSOLUTE vitam æternam. Ergo etiam de Condigno.

Connexum Majoris per se est manifestum: Absolutum enim quod est, illud vel limitationem vel restrictionem prorsus nullam admittit.

Minor autorem habet Thomam, qui 1. secundæ q. 114. art. 7. sic scribit: Quilibet actus charitatis meretur absolutè vitam æternam. Et in librum 2. Sent. dist. 27. quæst. 3. sic porrò clariùs Romanensium mentem explicat. Quidam dicunt, quòd aliquis vitam æternam non potest mereri ex Condigno, sed ex congruo: Alij verò dicunt, quòd quis etiam ex Condigno vitam æternam possit mereri per actus virtutum: Et hi, qui dicunt, nos ex Condigno vitam æternam mereri posse, veriùs dicere videntur.

Et ne fortè Jesuwita noster Thomæ autoritatem hac in parte in dubium vocare possit, meminerit Concilium Tridentinum hanc ipsam impietatem tantùm non improbasse, ut potiùs eam anathemate muniverit his verbis: Si quis dixerit: Hominis justificati bona Opera ita esse dona DEI, ut non sint etiam bona ipsius justificati merita; aut ipsum justificatum, bonis operibus, quæ ab eo per DEI gratiam, & Jesu Christi meritum, cujus membrum vivum est, fiunt, non verè mereri augmentum gratiæ, vitam æternam, anathema sit. Sess. 6 Can. 32.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: III. Question: According to what nature is our Christ Mediator?

II. The argument from the opinion of William of Auxerre, book 3, tract 12, Golden Summa, is as follows: By the works of the virtues man tends toward blessedness, and wisely. Therefore, he can come to that through these: And rightly: Therefore, through good works man can rightly acquire blessedness, and only by way of merit. Therefore, through good works man merits eternal life, by the right reason of meriting. And after a few words the same, ibid.: Service bestowed freely obliges the recipient, and this is a common reception of the mind, since liberality does not receive its contrary: for to do otherwise would be ingratitude: But service bestowed upon God out of charity is bestowed FREELY (that is, unduly). Therefore, it obliges GOD to remuneration: He is therefore bound to render a reward, otherwise He would be ungrateful, and would act unjustly toward such a one, unless He rendered it.

III. Bellarmine himself, forgetful of his own exception, writes expressly that the works of the Just, done out of charity, are meritorious of eternal life, and indeed by condignity: as the title of the sixteenth chapter, book 5, on Justification, has it. And finally he adds, The common opinion of the Theologians admits simply merit of Condignity, which opinion is most true. And a little later: That some distinguish between dignity and Condignity, and admit merit from dignity, but not from Condignity, is too trivial.

But let it suffice to have noted these things concerning the vanity and impiety of the Romanists regarding the meritorious Cause of our Justification.

There follows now the third Question, by which it is asked: According to which nature is our Christ mediator? To which, taught by the oracles of the Scriptures, we answer that this work of mediation and redemption is to be assigned to the whole Christ, not to either nature in Christ separately: nor even to the person according to one nature only: but according to both. For in this place also that Ecclesiastical rule holds: Actions and Passions are not of the natures, but of the whole suppositum, that is, the person: so that in performing such works the Person acts, in both, and through both natures, not separately, but conjunctively: each one nevertheless acting with the communication of the other, which is proper to each. And although the Principal agent in this work was the divine Nature of the Word: but the Principle, by which this Work of salvation was done by the Mediator, was the human Nature, nevertheless the Mediator and Redeemer himself, or the principle which worked the parts of mediation, was not either God alone, or Man alone: but both together: the Divinity of the Word indeed always employing the assumed nature to expedite and perfect any works and duties of our salvation: but the Flesh nowhere working, except by the power, command, and will of the Word: so that thus human things were done by Christ, not humanly, but divinely: just as divine things were not done divinely, but humanly: there being meanwhile one Christ, who would work both divine things humanly, and human things divinely.

It is added that neither could God alone have undergone death: nor could man alone have overcome it.

Therefore, in proportion to the twofold substance, Man is said to have undergone it, God to have overcome it. Now, that the passion and death of the assumed Flesh might be salutary, it was brought about by the communication of the Divinity: since to work salvation is not proper to human, but to divine power. Furthermore, that this passion and death might be not more human than divine, it was brought about by the Communication of the assumed flesh. Hence in the Scriptures, cleansing from sins, which is indeed a work proper to the Divinity, is attributed even to the Blood of Christ in the abstract, 1 John 1:7, not indeed in the sense as if it had this power of itself, through itself, or alone without the divinity: but that it may be signified that, for the parts of the office of Mediation to be executed, of which part cleansing from sins is also one, the assumed flesh is also employed. And that it may be seen whence the blood of Christ has this power: God himself is said to have acquired his church with his own blood. Acts 20:28. and the Son of God is read to have redeemed the human race with his precious blood. 1 Pet. 1:19. Hence Christ is also named as Jehovah our righteousness. Jer. 23:5 and 7.

Nor does it stand in the way that in 1 Tim. 2:5 our Christ is called Man as Mediator. For the Apostle did not use this manner of speaking to show that Christ is Mediator only according to his human nature: For if he had wished to imply this, he would then have formed his words either exclusively or at least abstractly: neither of which was done. Therefore he wished primarily to express the human nature. 1. Because it could be doubted concerning it, whether it also concurred to perform this work. 2. That he might point out, as with an index finger, that most close conjunction of ours with God.

This doctrine of ours, which is purer, has also suffered sharp contradiction: first indeed from Andreas Osiander, a Theologian of the Academy of Königsberg in Prussia, contending that Christ is our righteousness only according to his divine nature: Then from Francesco Stancaro of Mantua, referring the work of Mediation to the human nature of Christ. But since we have expressly disputed concerning both these errors in our Commentary on Article III of the Book of Concord: we supersede refuting them at greater length in this place.

But neither does the Roman Church deserve the praise of ὀρθοδοξίας regarding this Question either. For Lombard, in book 3 of his Sentences, distinction 19, openly blurted out that Christ is our Mediator only according to His Humanity, not according to His Divinity. Indeed, Bellarmine also, in book 5 of *De Christo*, chapter 3, rebukes Chemnitz because he includes among absurd opinions even this one, that Christ is Mediator according to the human nature only: nay, he accuses our doctrine of falsehood because we maintain that Christ, according to both natures, is our Righteousness.

Latin:

II. Argumentum ex sententia Guilelmi Antisidiorensis lib. 3. tract. 12. summa aurea, sic habet: Operibus virtutum tendit homo ad beatitudinem, & sapienter. E. potest per ista venire ad illam: Et rectè: E. per bona opera potest Homo rectè acquirere beatitudinem, nec nisi per modum meriti. E. per bona opera meretur homo vitam æternam, rectâ ratione merendi. Et post pauca idem ibid. Servitium gratis impensum obligat recipientem, & hæc est communis animi receptio, quoniam contrarium ejus non recipit liberalitas: aliter enim facere esset ingratitudo: Sed servitium impensum Deo ex charitate, est GRATIS (hoc est indebitè) impensum. Ergò obligat DEUM ad remunerationem: Tenetur igitur reddere præmium, aliter esset ingratus, & injustè faceret cum tali, nisi redderet.

III. Ipse Bellarminus exceptionis suæ immemor disertè scriptitat, opera Justorum ex charitate facta, esse meritoria vitæ æternæ, & quidem ex condigno: uti habet titulus capitis decimi sexti, lib. 5. de Justif. Et tandem subjicit, Communis sententia Theologorum admittit simpliciter meritum de Condigno, quæ sententia verissima est. Et paulò post: Quòd quidam distinguunt inter dignum & Condignum, & meritum ex digno admittunt, non verò ex Condigno, nimis leve est.

Sed de Romanensium κενεξίᾳ & impietate quoad Causam meritoriam Justificationis nostræ hæc annotasse sufficiat.

Sequitur jam tertia Quæstio, quâ quæritur: Secundum quam naturam Christus noster sit mediator? Ad quam Scripturarum oraculis edocti, respondemus, opus hoc mediationis & redemtionis toti Christo, non alterutri naturæ in Christo seorsim: neque personæ etiam secundum alterutram tantùm naturam: sed secundum utramque assignandum esse. Nam hoc etiam loco valet regula illa Ecclesiastica: Actiones & Passiones non sunt naturarum, sed totius suppositi, hoc est, personæ: ita ut in hujusmodi operibus perficiendis Persona agat, in utraque, & per utranque naturam, non separatim, sed conjunctim: unâ quâque tamen agente cum communicatione alterius, quod cujusq; proprium est. Et quanquam agens Principale in hoc opere fuit Natura divina tῦ λόγy: Principium autem, quô Opus hoc salutis à Mediatore fiebat, fuit Natura humana, tamen Mediator & Redemtor ipse, sive principium, quod operatum fuit partes mediationis, non fuit vel Deus solus, vel Homo solus: sed utrumque simul: Divinitate nimirùm tῦ λόγy assumtam naturam adhibente semper ad expedienda & perficienda quælibet salutis nostræ ópera atque munia: nuspiam autem operante Carne, nisi ex vi, imperio ac voluntate Verbi: ut sic humana à Christo fierent, non ἀνθρωπίνως, sed θεϊκῶς: perindè atque divina non fiebant θεϊκῶς, sed ἀνθρωπίνως: uno interim existente Christo, qui & divina ἀνθρωπίνως, & humana θεϊκῶς operaretur.

Accedit, quòd neque mortem solus Deus subire: neque solus homo superare potuisset.

Ergo pro ratione geminæ substantiæ, Homô eam suscepisse, Deus superasse dicitur. Jam ut passio & mors assumtæ Carnis salutifera esset, communicatione Divinitatis factum est: siquidem salutem operari non est humanæ: sed divinæ virtutis proprium. Cæterùm ut passio & mors ista, non humana magis, quàm divina esset, Communicatione carnis assumtæ factum est. Hinc in Scripturis mundatio à peccatis, quæ sanè est opus Divinitatis proprium, Sanguini Christi etiam in abstracto tribuitur, 1. Joh. 1. v. 7. non eo quidem sensu, quasi ex se, per se, aut solùm vim istam haberet absque divinitate: sed ut significetur, ad partes officii Mediationis exequendi, cujus pars est etiam Mundatio à peccatis assumtam etiam carnem adhiberi. Et ut unde sanguis Christi vim istam habeat, conspici possit: Deus ipse Ecclesiam suam proprio sanguine acquisivisse. Actor. 20, 28. & Filius Dei genus humanum suo pretioso sanguine redemisse legitur. 1. Pet. 1, 19. Hinc Christus etiam ut Jehovah nostra justitia nominatur. Jerem. 23, 5. & 7.

Neque obstat, quod 1. Tim. 2, 5. Homo Christus noster Mediator esse dicitur. Nam hoc loquendi genere non ideò usus est Apostolus, ut ostenderet, Christum tantùm secundum naturam humanam esse Mediatorem: Hoc enim si innuere voluisset, tùm vel exclusivè, vel abstractè saltem verba informafset: quorum neutrum factum est. Exprimere ergò potissimùm voluit humanam naturam. 1. Quia de ea dubitari poterat, an ad hoc opus perficiendum etiam concurreret. 2. Ut arctissimam illam nostram cum Deo conjunctionem, ceu digito indice commonstraret.

Passa est hæc etiam doctrina nostra purior acrem contradictionem: primùm quidem ab Andrea Osiandro Theologo Acad. Regiomontana in Borussia, contendente, Christum tantùm secundum divinam naturam, nostram esse justitiam: Deindè à Francisco Stancaro Mantuano, referente Mediationis opus ad humanam Christi naturam. Cæterùm cùm de utroque isto errore, in Commentario nostro ad Articulum III. Libri Concordiæ ex professo disputaverimus: prolixiùs illis hoc loco refutandis supersedemus.

Sed neque circa hanc etiam Quæstionem Romana Ecclesia ὀρθοδοξίας laudem meretur. Nam Lombardus lib. 3. sent. dist. 19. palàm effutiit, Christum esse Mediatorem nostrum tantùm secundum Humanitatem, non secundum Divinitatem. Quin Bellarminus etiam lib. 5. de Christo cap. 3. reprehendit Chemnitium, quòd ipse inter absurdas sententias referat etiam hanc, quòd Christus sit Mediator secundum humanam naturam tantùm: quin nostram doctrinam falsitatis arguit, quòd statuimus, Christum secundum utramque naturam, nostram esse Justitiam.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: IV. Question. Of what parts does the merit of Christ consist?

This error is indeed burdened with the same absurdities as Stancarus'. For it utterly evacuates the mystery of our Redemption, while it ascribes it to the Man alone. Furthermore, it establishes the Nestorian heresy, tearing the one person of Christ into two. For to act and to suffer belongs not to the natures, but to the person. Therefore, if the human nature alone performed the office of Mediation, it is necessary that it constitute the person.

Bellarmino objects: The Divinity is not thereby entirely excluded, but included. 1. Insofar as Christ is GOD and man. 2. Insofar as Satisfaction for the sins of men is owed to the Divinity: although meanwhile, if the question is about the formal principle, our Christ is Mediator only according to his human nature.

But these things are inconsistent and imply a manifest contradiction. For if Christ, insofar as he is Mediator, is both man and GOD, then it would follow that this work of Mediation must be referred to both natures: and indeed not only in respect of the suppositum, but also by reason of the formal principle. For the Divine nature had to be in the Mediator no less than the human, although in a different respect. For although the human could suffer death, yet by itself it was sufficient neither in virtue nor in value, but that it would have succumbed to death in this process. Therefore, the work required the Divine Nature also. Again, the Divine nature alone could not undergo death. Therefore, the human was required. Such a victim was therefore required, which would be a medium between GOD and men, so that it could both undergo death and overcome the same. Nor should it seem absurd to the Jesuit that it follows from this opinion of ours: that Christ is not only the Mediator himself, but also Mediator to himself. For it must be observed that a twofold consideration falls upon the Divinity of the Son: One which considers the Nature simply; the other which considers the same Nature, but determined by the parts of the office. Without any absurdity, therefore, it is said that CHRIST is the Mediator himself, and Mediator to himself. He is the Mediator himself indeed by reason of his office, which does not befit the Father or the Holy Spirit; but by reason of the Nature considered simply, since he has this in common with the other persons, he is said to be Mediator to himself, that is, as the Apostle speaks, Mediator between GOD and man, 1 Tim. 2:5. Whence also he is read to have reconciled the world to himself (ἑαυτῷ), 2 Cor. 5:18 and 19.

There remains the fourth and final Question, by which it is asked, of what parts does the λύτρον or merit of CHRIST the Savior consist? To which we answer that it is defined in the Scriptures chiefly by two things: namely, Satisfaction and Obedience: the former of which is named passive obedience in the Schools of the Theologians, consisting indeed in the toleration of punishments; but the latter is called active obedience, consisting indeed in the most exact observation and fulfillment of the divine law. Some today laugh at and cavil at this distinction, especially Piscator of Herborn, as also Pareus in his

Commentary on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Romans, page 514 B, contending that the entire λύτρον is ascribed in the Scriptures to the Blood and death of Christ alone. But the Sophists do not notice that this is done by way of eminence (καθ' ἐξοχὴν) and synecdoche (συνεκδοχὴν). Because the Blood of Christ exceeds and surpasses all other adjuncts of Mediation by many parasangs, since it is the Blood of the Son of God himself, and his death placed the final seal upon the whole passion of Christ, according to that which was uttered on the cross: It is finished: therefore the entire merit of Christ is also more often ascribed to this by way of excellence. But the active obedience is not thereby excluded, but rather presupposed: so indeed that the passive could never have attained the effect of Redemption, unless the most absolute obedience to the divine laws had preceded.

It is added that clear testimonies exist in the Scriptures concerning both kinds of obedience of Christ: And concerning the Active indeed, Rom. 10:4, Christ is the end or perfection of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes. Rom. 5:19, As by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one, many are made righteous. But the disobedience of Adam consisted in the transgression of the law. Therefore, the obedience of Christ must be defined in this place by the force of the antithesis (ἀντιθέσεως), through the fulfillment of the law. Matt. 5:17, I came not to destroy, but to fulfill the law.

Concerning the passive obedience of Christ, Gen. 3:15, The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the Serpent, but it shall bite his heel. Ps. 69:5, What I did not steal, I restored. Isa. 53:4 and 5, He himself bore our infirmities, and carried our sorrows, he was wounded for our iniquities, and bruised for our transgressions.

Rom. 3:25, They are justified freely, by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a reconciler through faith, by the intervention of his blood. Rom. 5:9, Christ died for us: much more therefore, being justified by his blood, we shall be saved by him from wrath.

Phil. 2:8, He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father, even unto the death of the Cross.

The excellent harmony of both these kinds of obedience shines forth most evidently from the consideration of divine Justice. For just as the Justice of God demanded one of two things from man, that he should either satisfy the law entirely, or sustain the guilt of eternal damnation: So Christ had to perform both. 1. That he should render perfect obedience to the divine law. 2. That he should take away the punishments which were to be sustained by us eternally, the former of which was accomplished by fulfilling the law: the latter, however, was most fully performed by Christ by suffering and dying: and thus both the defect of omission was restored by his obedience, and the sins of commission were expiated by his passion and death.

Moreover, both these kinds of obedience of Christ are expressed in the Schools of the Theologians by the single term of Righteousness: so that, indeed, Christ is said to be our righteousness, just as Scripture itself teaches. Jerem. 23. v. 6. This is the name by which they shall call him, Jehovah Justitia nostra and 1 Cor. 1:30. Christ is made unto us by the Father Righteousness, and that in two ways: 1. by reason of merit, insofar as He alone acquired for us the Righteousness that is valid before God. 2. by reason of the formal Cause, insofar as He truly and really imputes that Righteousness, acquired by His own obedience, to us who believe in Him: as will be expressly shown below in the fourth and final Question.

Latin:

Qui sanè error iisdem, quibus Stancari scater absurditatibus. Nam Redemtionis nostræ mysterium prorsus evacuat: dùm illud soli Homini adscribit. Deindè Nestorianam hæresin stabilit, unam personam Christi in duas discerpens. Nam agere & pati non est naturarum, sed personæ, Ergo si Humana natura sola officium Mediationis expediit, utique personam ea constituat necesse est.

Objicit Bellarminus: Non propterea penitùs excludi Divinitatem, sed includi. 1. Quatenùs Christus est DEUS & homo. 2. Quatenùs Divinitati debetur Satisfactio pro peccatis hominum: licèt interim, si de principio formali sit quæstio, Christus noster sit Mediator tantùm secundum humanam naturam.

Sed ἀσύστατα hæc sunt, & manifestam ἀντίφασιν implicant. Si enim Christus, quatenùs Mediator est, & homo est, & DEUS est: utique consequens fuerit, Mediationis hujus opus ad utramque naturam esse referendum: & quidem non tantùm respectu suppositi, sed etiam ratione principii formalis. Neque enim Divina minùs, quàm humana natura in Mediatore esse debuit, diverso licèt respectu. Humana enim licèt mortem oppetere poterat, sola tamen neque virtute, neque valore erat sufficiens, quin hoc pacto morti succubitura fuisset. Fuit igitur opus Naturâ etiam Divinâ. Rursus sola Divina natura mortem subire haud poterat. E. requirebatur humana. Talis proindè requisita fuit hostia, quæ media esset inter DEUM & homines, ut & mortem subire, & eandem superare posset. Neque absurdum videri debet Jesuivitæ, quòd ex nostra hac sententia sequitur: quòd Christus non modò sit Mediator ipse, sed & Mediator ad seipsum. Observandum enim, quòd in Divinitatem Filii duplex cadit consideratio: Una quæ Naturam simpliciter: altera, quæ eandem Naturam, sed partibus officii determinatam considerat. Absque omni ergo absurditate dicitur CHRISTUS esse Mediator ipse, & Mediator ad seipsum. Mediator ipse quidem ratione officij, id quod neque Patri, neque Spiritui sancto convenit; sed ratione Naturæ simpliciter consideratæ, quoniam hanc cum reliquis personis communem habet, dicitur esse Mediator ad seipsum, hoc est, ut Apostolus loquitur, Mediator inter DEUM & hominem, 1. Tim. 2, 5. Undè etiam sibiipsi ἑαυτῷ Mundum reconciliasse legitur, 2. Cor. 5, 18. & 19.

Superest quarta ac postrema Quæstio, quâ quæritur, quibus partibus constet λύτρον sive meritum CHRISTI Servatoris? Ad quam respondemus duabus potissimùm illud in Scripturis definiri: nempè Satisfactione & Obedientiâ: quarum illa passiva nominatur obedientia in Scholis Theologorum, quippè suppliciorum toleratione constans: hæc verò Activa dicitur obedientia, quippè in exactissima legis divinæ observatione & impletione consistens. Rident nonnulli hodiè & cavillantur hanc distinctionem, cumprimis Piscator Herbornensis, ut & Paræus in suo

Commentario ad cap. 5. Epistolae ad Rom. pag. 514. B. contendentes, soli Sanguini & morti Christi universum λύτρον in Sacris adscribi. Sed non animadvertunt Sophistae, hoc fieri καθ' ἐξοχὴν & συνεκδοχὴν. Quia enim Sanguis Christi reliqua omnia Mediationis adjuncta, multis parasangis excedit & superat, quippè qui est Sanguis ipsius Filii Dei, & mors ipsius laetum colophonem toti passioni Christi imposuit, secundum illud in cruce prolatum: Consummatum est: ideò huic per excellentiam universum etiam meritum Christi saepiùs adscribitur. Verùm non propterea obedientia illa activa excluditur, sed potiùs praesupponitur: ita quidem ut passiva illa nunquàm Redemtionis effectum consequi potuisset, nisi absolutissima legum divinarum obedientia praecessisset.

Accedit, quod de utraq; obedientia Christi luculenta in Scripturis extant testimonia: Ac de Activa quidem, Rom. 10, 4. Christus est finis sive perfectio legis, ad justitiam omni credenti. Rom 5, 19. Sicut per inobedientiam unius hominis, peccatores constituti sunt multi: ita per obedientiam unius, justi constituuntur multi. Atqui inobedientia Adami constabat transgressione legis. E. Obedientia Christi definienda est hoc loco ex vi ἀντιθέσεως, per impletionem legis. Matth. 5, 17. Non veni solvere, sed implere legem.

De obedientia Christi passiva, Genes. 3, 15. Semen mulieris conteret Caput Serpentis, sed illud mordebit calcaneum ejus. Psal. 69, 5. Quae non rapui, exolvi. Jes. 53, 4. & 5. Languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse portavit, vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, & attritus propter scelera nostra.

Rom. 3, 25. Justificantur gratis, per illius gratiam, per redemtionē, quae est in Christo Jesu, quem proposuit Deus reconciliatorem per fidem, interveniente sanguine ejus. Rom. 5. & 9. Christus pro nobis mortuus fuit: multò magis ergò justificati sanguine ejus servabimur per eum ab ira.

Phil. 2, 8. Humiliavit semetipsum factus obediens Patri, usque ad mortem Crucis.

Utriusque hujus obedientiae egregia harmonia, ex consideratione Justitiae divinae evidentissimè elucet. Quemadmodum enim Justitia Dei alterutrum ab homine flagitabat, ut vel legi ex toto satisfaceret, vel aeternae maledictionis reatum sustineret: Ita Christus utrumque expedire debuit. 1. Ut perfectam legi divinae praestaret obedientiam. 2. Ut poenas quae nobis aeternùm sustinendae erant, auferret, quorum illud implendo legem: hoc verò patiendo & moriendo plenissimè per Christum est expeditum: & sic tùm omissionis defectus per ipsius obedientiam restitutus: tùm Commissionis peccata per ipsius passionem & mortem expiata.

Exprimitur autem utraque haec obedientia Christi in Scholis Theologorum unico termino Justitiae: ut nimirùm Christus dicatur esse justitia nostra, sic ipsâ docente Scripturâ. Jerem. 23. v. 6. Hoc est nomen, quo vocabunt eum, Jehovah Justitia nostra & 1. Cor. 1, 30. Christus factus est nobis à Patre Iustitia, idque dupliciter: 1. ratione meriti, quatenùs Justitiam coram Deo valentem, nobis ipse solus acquisivit. 2 ratione Causæ formális, quatenus Justitiam illam utraque suâ obedientiâ acquisitam, nobis in ipsum credentibus, verè ac realiter imputat: uti infra Quæstione quarta & postrema ex professo ostendetur.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: III. the Efficient Cause Instrumental, Offering and obliging

That the τά όργανικά (organic means) pertain to the Efficient Cause is established beyond controversy. These, however, regarding the business of Justification, are considered either with respect to God who justifies, or with respect to men who are to be justified. With respect to God, the instruments are twofold: one is meritorious, which is Christ, of whom we have just disputed; the other is that which offers and seals the Merit of Christ, which is THE WORD AND THE SACRAMENTS, of which, however, we do not properly dispute in this article. For that these two means are as it were the workshop of the Holy Spirit, in which the benefits of Christ are stored up and kept, and are sold and distributed without price to believers, is too manifest from the holy Scriptures. The excellent description of the Prophet Isaiah, chapter 55, 1 and following, pertains to this. All you who thirst, come, and you who have no silver, hasten, buy and eat: Come, buy without silver: Hearken, you who listen to me, incline your ear, and come to me: hear and your soul shall live, and I will strike with you an everlasting covenant, etc.

Moreover, in this Question it deserves observation that as often as the Word of God is said to be the Organic Cause of our Justification with respect to God, and indeed an Organic Cause offering the Grace of God and the Merit of Christ, then not just any Word of God is understood, nor even just any part of the divine word: but only that which is proper to the Gospel specifically so called, that is, which proposes and offers the Grace or Mercy of God, prepared equally for all, and the benefits of Christ the Mediator equally to all, and which finally, by the power of the Holy Spirit, kindles justifying Faith in Man. This is indeed that Word which, as the Apostle defines, is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, Rom. 1:16, through which we are saved, 1 Cor. 15:2, and which finally can save our souls, James 1:21.

This Word is named in the Scriptures sometimes HEARING, as Isa. 53:1, Lord, who has believed our Hearing? Rom. 10:13, Faith comes from hearing. It is confessed that this denomination is made metonymically: so that Hearing denotes the Audible thing itself, that is, the Word. The foundation of this denomination, however, depends on the fact that God exerts the power and efficacy of His Word only in those who hear it: not indeed that hearing, by itself, insofar as it consists of a natural action, deserves such a thing: but that God Himself established this hearing as the medium through which He wills to kindle faith in men. But if it were without this decree of God, then no mortal would conceive faith in Christ, even if he were to hear this Word throughout his whole life, even with the greatest zeal: so much so that this Hearing by itself can deserve nothing, as was expressly shown in the dispute concerning Free Will.

Regarding the Sacraments, the matter is likewise straightforward. For that through these means Righteousness and Salvation come to believers, Scripture likewise clearly testifies, Mark 16:16, Tit. 3:5, 1 Pet. 3:21.

The Roman Papacy has sprinkled no light stain of impurity upon this orthodox doctrine, and that a threefold one. 1. Contending that not only the hearing of the Gospel, but also the observance of the Law is the power of God unto salvation, so that a reborn Man can fulfill the Law of God, and by this means be justified. 2. That the Sacraments confer grace and the remission of sins, ex opere operato, as the Council of Trent has it, Sess. 7, Can. 8. 3. That besides the Word of the Gospel and those two Sacraments of the New Testament, there is also, as a medium of conferring grace and our Justification, the remaining fictitious Sacraments, and especially that Mass-idol, which they pretend is propitiatory for the sins of the living and the dead: and that it profits for the remission not only of guilt, but also of punishments.

Thus, therefore, the Roman Papacy has left no part of this Article, not even the least, uncorrupted. But we shall have to look into these individual errors in the article on the Sacraments.

Latin:

AD Causam Efficientem pertinere etiam τά όργανικά extra Controversiam est positum. Hæc vero, quoad Justificationis negotium, considerantur vel respectu Dei Iustificantis: vel respectu hominum Iustificandorum. Respectu Dei Organa sunt duplicia: Vnum meritorium, quod est Christus, de quo modò disputatum: alterum est Offerens & obsignans Meritum Christi, quod est VERBUM ET SACRAMENTA, de quibus tamen in hoc articulo propriè non disputatur. Nam duo hæc media esse quasi Officinam Spiritus Sancti, in qua beneficia Christi recondita asservantur, & sine pretio divenduntur ac distrahuntur credentibus, ex Scripturis sacris nimis manifestum est. Pertinet huc egregia illa descriptio Prophetæ Jesaiæ cap. 55, 1. & seqq. Omnes qui sititis, venite, & qui non habetis argentum, properate, emite & comedite: Venite, emite absque argento: Audite audientes me, inclinate aurem vestram, & venite ad me: audite & vivet anima vestra, & feriam vobiscum pactum sempiternum &c.

Cæterùm hac in Quæstione illud observationem meretur, quòd quoties Verbum Dei dicitur esse Causa Organica Justificationis nostræ, respectu Dei, & Causa quidem Organica, offerens Gratiam Dei & Meritum Christi: tùm non quodlibet Verbum Dei intelligitur, neque etiam quævis verbi divini pars: sed ea tantùm, quæ est Evangelij specificè sic dicti propria, hoc est, quæ Gratiam sive Misericordiam Dei, omnibus ex æquo paratam, quæ beneficia Christi Mediatoris omnibus ex æquo proponit & offert, quæ denique virtute Spiritus Sancti Fidem Justificantem in Homine accendit. Hoc nimirùm est Verbum illud, quod definiente Apostolo, est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti Rom. 1, 16. per quod salvamur, 1. Cor. 15, 2. quod denique salvare potest animas nostras Jacob. 1, 21.

Nominatur hoc Verbum in Scripturis aliquoties AUDITUS ut Jes. 53, 1. Domine quis credit Auditui nostro. Rom. 10, 13. Fides est ex auditu. Quam denominationem Metonymicè fieri in confesso est: ita, ut Auditus notet ipsum Audibile, hoc est, Verbum. Fundamentum autem denominationis hujus dependet ex eo, quòd Deus Verbi sui vim atq; efficaciam exerit, non nisi in audientibus illud: non quidem quod auditus, per se, quatenùs naturali actione constat, tale quid promereatur: sed quòd Deus ipse hunc auditum constituit medium, per quod fidem in hominibus accendere velit. Quod si absque hoc Dei decreto esset, tùm nemo mortalium fidem conciperet in Christum, si vel maxime per omnem vitam Verbum hoc, etiam summo studio audiret: usque adeò Auditus iste perse nihil promereri potest, quemadmodum in disputatione de Libero Arbitrio ex professo fuit ostensum.

De Sacramentis res itidem est expedita. Nam his mediantibus Justitiam & Salutem credentibus obtingere, Scriptura itidem luculenter testatur, Marc. 16, 16. Tit. 3, 5. 1. Petr. 3, 21.

Orthodoxæ huic doctrinæ impuritatis maculam haud levem aspersit Papatus Romanus, eamque tergeminam. 1. contendens, non solùm auditum Evangelij, sed & observationem Legis esse potentiam Dei ad salutem, ita, ut Homo renatus Legem Dei implere possit, & hoc pacto justificari. 2. Sacramenta conferre gratiam & remissionem peccatorum, ex opere operato, ut habet Concil Trid. Sess. 7. Can. 8. 3. præter Verbum Evangelij & duo illa Novi Testamenti Sacramenta, medium conferendæ gratiæ & Iustificationis nostræ esse, etiam reliqua fictitia Sacramenta, cumprimis verò idolum illud Missaticum, quod fingunt esse propitiatorium pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum: & prodesse ad remissionem non culpæ tantùm, sed etiam pænarum.

Sic ergò nullam, ne minimam quidem Articuli hujus partem incorruptam reliquit Papatus Romanus. Sed de erroribus istis singulis in articulo de Sacramentis nobis dispiciendum fuerit.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: IV. the Efficient Cause, is Organic apprehending on the part of Man: and that is faith in Christ

God offers His Grace, as also the merit of His Son, to Man in the Word and Sacraments: for Man to apprehend this, and apply it to himself, no other medium has been left to us besides faith in Christ.

This, therefore, in the Schools of the Theologians, has deserved to be called an Organic Cause with respect to us, and indeed an apprehending one.

The truth of this assertion is evident from the beginning from the clear oracles of the Scriptures: such as are, Rom. 1:17. The righteousness of God is revealed through the Gospel from faith to faith: for the just shall live by faith. Habakkuk 2:4. Rom. 3:22. The righteousness of God (with that word understood actively) through the faith of Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all them that believe. And verse 26. God is just, and justifies him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ. And verse 28. λογιζόμεθα, we conclude by firm collection, that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law.

Rom. 4, 2. & seqq. It is asserted ten times over that Abraham was justified by faith alone: And finally this general aphorism is proposed: To him that worketh, the reward is not reckoned according to grace, but according to debt: But to him that worketh not, but believeth only in him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness, according to the purpose of the grace of God, v. 4. & 5.

Rom. 5, 1. Being justified by faith, we have peace with God.

Galat. 2, 16. We know that a man is not justified by the works of the Law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ.

Galat. 3, 8. God justifies men by faith. And verse 22. The Scripture hath concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe.

Ephes. 2, 8. By grace you are saved through faith.

And what need is there of many words, when St. Peter, Acts 10, 43, expressly confesses that this is the unanimous consent of all the prophets, that whosoever believes in him shall receive remission of sins in the name of Christ.

The other foundation of our assertion consists of certain and immovable reasons, and those drawn from the analogy of faith and the authority of the Scriptures.

The first reason, drawn from the example of the father of all believers from chapter 4, 2 of Romans and chapter 3, 6 and 7, can be formed thus.

In the same way that Abraham was justified before God, in the same way are all justified who are justified. But Abraham was justified before God, not otherwise than by faith in Christ. Therefore.

The connection of the major premise is sufficiently evident in itself, or from this, that as there is one God, so there is one faith and method of salvation for all who are saved. Acts 15, 11. Ephes. 4, 5. Furthermore, that Abraham is called by the Apostle the father of all who are to be saved, not indeed effectively, in which way God alone is the Father of the faithful: but analogically, so that just as he himself received salvation only through the imputation of faith for righteousness: so by the same method all his children, that is, believers, would receive the same.

Confirmed by the authority of the minor Scriptures, it is entirely ἔγγραφος (written). For in Genesis 15:6 it is expressly said: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. The Apostle repeats and inculcates this very thing in Romans 4:3, and especially in Galatians 3:6 and 7, and from there he gathers that all those who are of the faith of Christ are sons of Abraham, and are to be blessed with the same, verse 9.

Bellarmino attacks this argument with several sophistries he has devised, by which he tries to obscure it: First, indeed, in this manner: We concede, says the Jesuit, that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness; but we do not admit the gloss that for faith to be reckoned for righteousness is for the righteousness of Christ to be imputed to us, if we apprehend it by faith. For this gloss is repugnant to the Apostle for two reasons: 1. Because the Apostle says that faith itself is imputed for righteousness, but faith is not the righteousness of Christ, that is, that by which Christ is righteous: but our righteousness, that is, that by which we are righteous by the gift of God. 2. Because the word (to impute) in this place does not signify a bare estimation, but an estimation to which truth in the thing itself corresponds.

I reply that both reasons are devoid of any true refutation. For first, although we willingly admit that faith is not the righteousness of Christ itself, by which He is essentially righteous in Himself: nevertheless, faith is that instrument which apprehends that other righteousness of Christ, which we call acquired. When, therefore, faith is said to be imputed for righteousness to the believer, no other sense can be elicited than that this acquired righteousness of Christ is then at last imputed to man for salvation, when he has apprehended it by faith and applied it to himself.

Then it is false and fictitious that the Jesuit writes that the term righteousness in this place is to be understood of that righteousness by which we are righteous by the gift of God: where the sophist understands that inherent and infused holiness. For the Apostle denies this very thing διαρρήδην (expressly): saying, Not to him who works, but to him who believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, faith is imputed for righteousness. Therefore, it cannot be understood materially, as the sophist wishes, as if either the dignity of faith or the perfection of inherent righteousness made Abraham righteous: for thus he would have been justified by his own work: but it must be understood relatively, that righteousness was imputed to Abraham believing, and indeed not inherent or his own, but another's, namely the righteousness of the promised seed of the woman, in whom he believed: Or, which amounts to the same thing, that Abraham, believing in the promised Messiah, was reckoned righteous by grace, although he lacked in himself righteousness availing before God. We conclude, therefore, irrefragably, that the righteousness imputed to Abraham was not legal conformity or inherent perfection: but the gratuitous remission of sins, and acceptance into grace, on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith.

The latter reason of the Jesuit harbors something ὕπουλον (ulcerous/insidious). For we also readily grant that the word to impute does not signify a bare estimation, but such a one to which truth in the thing itself corresponds. But here immediately emerges that κρινόμενον (point at issue), in what thing that truth consists which ought to correspond to the estimation, which the Jesuit does not explain in this place: but tacitly, by begging the question, he understands that inherent righteousness of which he had spoken before. We, however, strenuously deny that very thing: and we build the truth or reality of this imputation upon a twofold foundation according to the Scriptures: The first is that this imputation has its foundation and seat, not in the judgment of man: but in the mind, decree, and will of God, which is the highest and most firm principle of all things that are. The other is, that this imputation does not rest on nothing, but has regard to the Obedience and Satisfaction made through Christ, whose merit and acquired Righteousness God truly and really imputes to believers, although He does not habitually infuse it: as will be shown more fully in the final Question.

But the Jesuit continues, and in the second place contends that the Lord Apostle is describing in Abraham only the first Justification, which consists solely of the merit of Christ, as when one is made righteous from being ungodly, and is enlightened from not yet being reborn.

But this is a most impudent lie: for the Holy Spirit, intending to show through Moses and Paul an example of true Justification in Abraham, by a certain counsel did not wish to define that time when Abraham was first called and converted from Chaldean idolatry to the truer worship of God, Genesis 12. But rather that time when, already for many good years, he had obeyed God by faith through various exercises, and indeed in the midst of that course, when he had been adorned by the Holy Spirit with many most excellent mighty works. Thus, therefore, the Holy Spirit considers Abraham as already converted, enlightened, and faithful, and affirms that, if to him who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, faith was imputed for righteousness, and blessedness came to him, according to that Davidic saying: Blessed is he to whom God imputes righteousness without works: and Blessed is he whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered, Psalm 32, 1. Romans 4, 6 and 7.

The Jesuit objects that Abraham was indeed reborn at that time of which the Apostle speaks: but that the Apostle, when he says he was justified by faith, not by works, rejects only those works which were not done from faith: but does not reject those which were done from faith, but rather affirms that those works were done from faith.

But this argument overturns itself: for if the Apostle considers Abraham as already reborn and faithful—which the Jesuit is forced to concede—he will certainly also consider his works as those of a reborn and faithful man, and insofar as they were done from faith, unless perhaps by an unheard-of absurdity he wishes to establish that Abraham was reborn and not reborn at the same time, faithful and unfaithful at the same time. Furthermore, if the Jesuitical Sophism stands, the scope and intention of the Apostle would clearly collapse, which turns on that twin hinge.

1. That he opposes the faith and works of Abraham, and indeed as a reborn man, to one another: he denies the imputation of Righteousness to the latter, but ascribes it entirely to the former, namely to faith.

2. That he opposes Grace and debt to one another in such a way that if Salvation came to Abraham from works, then it necessarily follows that it came from debt: But the Apostle infers, not from debt, but from Grace. Therefore, righteousness came to Abraham not from works, but from faith. Where the Apostolic text testifies too evidently that all works indefinitely, both those done from faith and those not done from faith, are excluded. It is therefore evident that he shamefully lies twice.

tiri the Jesuit. 1. That he contends that Paul wished to show in this place what kind of Works those of Abraham were. 2. That Paul wished to teach that the Works of Abraham were from faith. To utterly destroy both of which Sophistries, we argue thus: The Lord Apostle opposes every Worker to every believer. Therefore, he also opposes all Works, of whatever kind they may be, to faith. The argument holds from Conjugates. From the evidence of the Major premise, which has the Apostle as its author, we further infer thus: Every debt is opposed to Grace and Faith: But debt is given to every Worker. Therefore, every worker is opposed to the Believer, and to the one receiving gratuitous righteousness, in the matter of Justification.

Latin:

GRatiam suam, ut & meritum Filij sui, in Verbo & Sacramentis, Deus Homini offert: Hanc ut Homo apprehendat, sibique applicet; nullum aliud nobis relictum est medium, præter fidem in Christum.

Hæc ergò in Scholis Theologorum Causa Organica respectu nostri & quidem apprehendens dici meruit.

Assertionis hujus veritas initiò patet ex perspicuis Scripturarum oraculis: qualia sunt, Rom. 1, 17. Justitia Dei per Evangelium patefit ex fide in fidem: Justus enim ex fide vivit. Habacuc. 2, 4. Rom. 3, 22. Iustitia Dei (activè isto vocabulo intellecto) per fidem Iesu Christi, in omnes & super omnes credentes. Et vers. 26. Justus est Deus, & justificat eum, qui est ex fide Iesu Christi. Et vers. 28. λογιζόμεθα collectione firma statuimus, Fide justificari Hominem, absq; operibus legis.

Rom. 4, 2. & seqq. Abrahamus per fidem tantùm justificatus fuisse, decies ampliùs asseritut : Et tandem generalis iste Aphorismus proponitur : Ei qui operatur, merces non imputatur secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum : Ei verò, qui non operatur, credenti autem tantùm in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur fides ejus ad justitiam, secundum propositum Gratiæ Dei v. 4. & 5.

Rom. 5, 1. Iustificati fide, pacem habemus apud Deum.

Galat. 2, 16. Scimus non justificari Hominem ex operibus Legis, nisi per fidem Iesu Christi.

Galat. 3, 8. Deus ex fide homines justificat. Et vers. 22. Conclusit Scriptura omnia sub pecca tum, ut promissio ex fide Iesu Christi daretur credentibus.

Ephes. 2, 8. Gratiâ estis salvati per fidem.

Et quid multis opus, cum D. Petrus Actor. 10, 43. disertè fateatur, hunc esse unanimem consensum omnium Prophetarum, quòd remissionem peccatorum in nomine Christi accipiat, omnis qui credit in ipsum.

Alterum assertionis nostræ fundamentum, certis ac immotis constat rationibus, ijsque ex analogia Fidei & Scripturarum autoritate petitis.

Prima ratio ab exemplo Patris omnium credentium ex cap. 4, 2. Rom. & cap. 3, 6. & 7. petita, sic informari potest.

Quo pacto justificatus est Abraham coram Deo, eôdem pacto omnes justificantur, qui justificantur. Atqui Abraham9 justificatus est coram Deo, non nisi per fidem in Christum. Ergo.

Connexum Majoris evidens satis est per se i. vel indè, quòd ut unus est Deus, sic una est fides & ratio salutis omnium qui salvantur. Actor. 15, 11. Ephes. 4, 5. Deindè quod Abrahamus ab Apostolo dicitur Pater omnium salvandorum, non profectò Effectivè, quo pacto solus Deus est Pater fidelium : sed analogicè, ut quemadmodum ipse salutem accepit non nisi per imputationem fidei ad justitiam : Sic eâdem ratione omnes ipsius filij, hoc est, credentes eandem acciperent.

Minor Scripturarum autoritate firmata, tota est ἔγγραφος. Nam Genes 15. 6. expressè dicitur : Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est illi ad Iustitiam. Quod ipsum repetit & inculcat Apostolus Rom. 4, 3. & cumprimis Galat. 3, 6. & 7. indè colligit, omnes eos, qui ex fide Christi sunt, esse filios Abrahami, & cum eodem benedicendos vers. 9.

Vellicat hoc Argumentum Bellarminus, aliquot excogitatis Sophisticationibus, quibus illud obscurare conatur : Primùm quidem in hunc modum : Fidem reputatam esse Abrahæ ad justitiam, concedimus inquit Jesuuvita : sed non admittimus glossam, quòd reputari fidem ad justitiam, sit nobis imputari Christi justitiam, si fide illam apprehendamus. Nam glossahæc repugnat Apostolo duas ob causas, 1. Quoniam Apostolus ipsam fidem dicit imputari ad justitiam, fides autem non est justitia Christi, id est, quâ Christus justus est : sed Iustitia nostra, id est, quâ nos justi sumus ex dono Dei. 2. Quoniam verbum (imputare) hoc loco non significat nudam existimationem, sed existimationem, cui veritas in reipsa respondeat.

Respondeo, utramque rationem omni verô Elencho destitui. Primùm enim, etsi libenter fatemur, Fidem non esse ipsam justitiam Christi, quâ ipse in se justus est essentialiter: tamen Fides est Organum illud, quod apprehendit justitiam illam Christi alteram, quam acquisitam nominamus. Quando ergo Fides imputari dicitur ad justitiam credenti, sensus nullus potest elici alius, quàm quòd Justitia hæc Christi acquisita tùm demum Homini imputetur ad salutem, quando eam Fide apprehenderit, sibique applicaverit.

Deindè falsum ac fictitium est, quòd Jesuvvita scriptitat, Justitiæ vocabulum hoc loco accipiendum esse de eâ Justitia, quâ nos justi sumus, ex dono Dei: Ubi inhærentem & infusam illam Sanctitatem, intelligit Sophista. Nam Apostolus hoc ipsum διαρρήδην negat: Non inquiens operanti: sed credenti in eum, qui justificat impium, fides imputatur ad justitiam. Non ergò materialiter, uti Sophista vult, hoc intelligi potest, quasi vel Fidei dignitas, vel Justitiæ inhærentis perfectio Abrahamum justum effecerit: Nam sic opere suo fuisset justificatus: sed intelligi debet Relativè, quod Abrahamo credenti, fuerit imputata Justitia, & quidem non inhærens sive propria, sed aliena, nempè Justitia promissi seminis mulieris, in quod credebat: Vel quod eôdem recidit, quòd Abrahamus credens in promissum Messiam, ex gratia fuerit justus reputatus, licet ex se Justitiâ coram Deo valente caruerit. Concludimus proindè irrefragabiliter, Justitiam Abrahamo imputatam, non fuisse legalem conformitatem, aut inhærentem perfectionem: sed Gratuitam remissionem peccatorum, & acceptionem in gratiam, propter meritum Christi fide apprehensum.

Posterior Jesuvvitæ ratio ὕπουλον aliquid fovet. Nam nos quoque ultrò largimur, imputandi verbum non nudam significare existimationem, sed talem cui veritas reipsa respondeat. Verùm hîc statim emergit illud κρινόμενον, Quâ in re consistat veritas illa, quæ existimationi respondere debeat, id quod hoc loco non explicat Jesuvvita: sed tacitè per petitionem principij intelligit inhærentem illam Justitiam, de quâ prius verba fecerat. Nos verò idipsum strenuè negamus: & veritatem sive realitatem imputationis huj9 gemino fundamento secundum Scripturas superstruimus: Primum est, quòd imputatio hæc fundamentum & sedem suam habet, non in hominis judicio: sed in mente, decreto ac voluntate Dei, quæ est summum & firmissimum rerum, quæ sunt, omnium Principium. Alterum est, quòd imputatio hæc non in nihilo recumbit, sed respectum habet Obedientiæ & Satisfactionis per Christum factæ, cujus meritum ac Justitiam acquisitam, Deus credentibus verè ac realiter imputat, licet non habitualiter infundat: uti Quæstione ultimâ fusiùs erit ostendendum.

Sed pergit Jesuvvita, & secundo loco contendit, D. Apostolum describere in Abrahamo tantum primam Iustificationem, quæ constet solo merito Christi, ut quando ex impio fit justus, ex nondum renato sit illuminatus.

Sed impudentissimum hoc est mendacium: Spiritus enim Sanctus per Mosen & Paulum monstraturus exemplum veræ Justificationis in Abrahamo, certo consilio noluit definire illud tempus, quò Abrahamus primùm ex idololatria Chaldaica, ad veriorem Dei cultum vocatus & conversus fuit Genes. 12. Sed illud potiùs, quô jam annis benè multis, per varia exercitia Deo fide obedierat, & quidem in medio illo cursu, cùm multis præstantissimis virtutibus à Spiritu Sancto ornatus fuerat. Sic ergo Abrahamum jam conversum, illuminatum ac fidelem considerat Spiritus Sanctus & affirmat, i, si non Operanti, sed credenti in eum, qui justificat impium, fidem imputatam fuisse ad justitiam, & beatitudinem ipsi obtigisse, secundum illud Davidicum: Beatus, cui Deus imputat justitiam sine operibus: & Beatus, cui remissæ sunt iniquitates, & cujus tecta sunt peccata, Psal. 32, 1. Rom, 4, 6. & 7.

Excipit Jesuvvita, Abrahamum quidem eo tempore, de quo loquitur Apostolus, renatum fuisse: Apostolum autem, cùm dicit, eum justificatum esse ex fide, non ex operibus: reijcere tantùm ea opera quæ non ex fide facta sunt: non autem reijcere ea, quæ ex fide facta sunt, sed potiùs affirmare, opera illa facta esse ex fide.

Sed semetipsam evertit hæc argutatio: Si enim Apostolus considerat Abrahamum, ut jam renatum & fidelem : id quod concedere cogitur Jesuvvita: certè considerabit etiam ejusdem opera, ut renati & fidelis, & quatenùs illa ex fide facta sunt, nisi fortè per inauditam absurditatem statuere velit, Abrahamum fuisse renatum, & non renatum simul, fidelem & infidelem simul. Deindè stante Sophismate Jesuvvitico, scopus & intentio Apostolica planè concideret, quæ in gemino illo cardine vertitur.

1. Quòd fidem & opera Abrahami, & quidem ut renati sibi mutuò opponit: his imputationem Justitiæ derogat, illi verò nempè fidei in solidum adscribit.

2. Quòd Gratiam & debitum sibi ita opponit, ut si Abrahamo obtigerit Salus ex operibus, tùm ex debito obtigisse necessariò consequatur: Atqui infert Apostolus, non ex debito, sed ex Gratia Ergo non ex operibus, sed ex fide Abrahamo obtigit justitia. Ubi opera indefinitè omnia tàm ex fide, quàm non ex fide facta, excludi textus Apostolicus nimis evidenter testatur. Constat proindè bis turpiter men-

tiri Jesuvvitam. 1. Quod contendit, Paulum hoc loco oftendere voluisse, qualia Opera fuerint Abrahami. 2. Quod Paulus docere voluerit, Opera Abrahae fuisse ex fide. Quæ utraque Sophisticatio, ut penitus proteratur, sic argumentamur: D. Apostolus omnem Operantem opponit omni credenti. E. etiam omnia Opera, qualia qualia illa sint, opponit fidei. Valet argumentum à Conjugatis. Ex evidentia Majoris, quæ Apostolum autorem habet, porrò sic inferimus : Omne debitum opponitur Gratiæ & Fidei: Atqui omni Operanti datur debitum. Ergo omnis operans opponitur Credenti, & gratuitam justitiam accipienti, in negocio Justificationis.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: IV. the Efficient Cause, is Organic apprehending on the part of Man: and that is faith in Christ (continued)

Seek the remaining Sophistries of the Papists from our Commentary on the third Article of the Book of Concord.

The second reason for our Confirmation can be such: If the promise of eternal life comes to men through the Law: It is a consequence that the promise has been made void on the part of God: and consequently, from the nature of relatives, faith has also been made void on our part.

And yet both of these are absurd, and even impious to think. Therefore the promise does not come from the Law: Now if it is not from the Law, certainly it is from faith: A third option cannot be given.

The connection of the major premise has the Apostle himself as its author. Gal. 3, 18. If the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from the promise: The reason is that the Law is not from faith Gal. 3, 12. Because the Law was not given which could make alive, verse 21. Because the Law only works wrath, and therefore constitutes us not righteous, but guilty before God. Rom. 4, 15. Because the Law only brings a curse. Gal. 3, 10. Because if those who are from the Law are heirs, then faith is made void and the promise abolished Rom. 4, 14. There is also this, that faith is of things to be believed, but the Law is of things to be done. Therefore, if salvation is from the Law, no place will be left for faith: Furthermore, the Law looks to the legal justice of God: Faith, however, to His mercy: Therefore, if salvation is from the Law, there will be no further use for faith. Furthermore, the covenant of God with Abraham is nothing other than that God wills to bless and save those who are of the faith of the Son of Abraham: only on account of the promised seed, who is Christ. Gal. 3, 7, 9, 16. Therefore, a contrary covenant, that God wills to impart salvation to those who work, cannot subsist. And indeed this argument is of such firmness and evidence that our Jesuit finds nothing to oppose to it, except that stale refuge, pretending that the Apostle excludes only the works of the Law which are done without faith, which is what has already been discussed and worn out by us before.

The third reason can be formulated thus. If besides one and only faith in Christ nothing can be given by which all glory for our salvation is ascribed to God alone and to divine grace: Certainly faith also will be imputed for righteousness over works.

But faith alone and only does this. Therefore.

The connection of the major premise is clear from Rom. 4, 2. If Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about: but not before God: whence I argue thus from the text of the Apostle: If Abraham was justified by works, he has whereof he may boast, but not before GOD. Therefore the righteousness of one's own works ascribes glory not to God, but to men: Yet this is affirmed to be impious. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory before God. Rom. 3, 23. And if we have done all things, we are unprofitable servants, we have done what we ought, Luke 17, 10. Therefore the righteousness of works cannot subsist in the business of salvation.

The minor premise can likewise be most evidently confirmed from the Scriptures. For 1. Faith believes in hope against hope: Rom. 4, 18. that is, it rests solely and peacefully in the promise of God, even though the things promised are beyond all human hope, nay, even simply conflict with our reason. 2. Faith resists all the doubts of the Flesh, by the example of Abraham, who not considering his own body now dead, nor the barrenness of Sarah, nor other things, believed the divine promise. Rom. 4, 19. 3. Faith certainly determines that God both wills and is able to perform whatever He promises.

The fourth reason: In the mouth of two witnesses consists all truth: Yet the Prophets and Apostles testify that the just man lives only by his faith, as Habakkuk 2, 4. Paul Rom. 1, 17. Gal. 3, 10. Heb. 10, 38. Therefore salvation and our righteousness are to be assigned not to works, but to faith. Nor can that Jesuitical exception have any place, that this Prophetic assertion is to be understood only of initial justification. For the nature of the subject does not allow this in the least, since the matter here is not about the life of a man not yet converted, but about the life of the just man, how such a one can finally live eternally? Where the chorus of the Prophets answers: That they live, but only through faith.

But our Jesuit seeks another escape, asserting that the meaning of the Prophet's words is that the Just man lives a spiritual life by faith: namely, by such faith as is in just men, that is, by faith formed by Charity. And as Francis Coster explains, that the just man lives, or forms his life to the norm of faith, no otherwise than as someone might be said to live medically, that is, to live according to the prescription of medicine.

I answer that manifest violence is done both to the Prophet and to the Apostle. For neither of them deals at all with a spiritual life to be instituted according to the precepts of the divine law here on earth, but deals with that eternal life or happiness which is the end of faith, and which arises from the Gospel, which is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believes. And it is worth noting that the Apostle immediately prefaced these words: The righteousness of God is revealed by the Gospel, from faith to faith. For even by this means that Jesuitical fiction, concerning some righteousness mixed from faith and works, or from Faith into works, so that it begins by faith but is completed by Works, is rooted out. For the Apostle teaches that righteousness is revealed from faith to faith, not from Faith into Works: so that the beginning, progress, and end of our Justification is to be ascribed to faith alone, as the Apostle excellently explains himself in Rom. 5, 1 and 2.

The fifth reason: The entire Evangelical history assigns salvation to the faith of those who, despairing of their own dignity, placed all their trust in the mercy of Christ alone, and clearly testifies that for this very reason they obtained the remission of sins. As Matt. 8, 10 and 13, ch. 9, 2, ch. 15, 28, Mark 2, 5, ch. 5, 34, ch. 10, 52, Luke 5, 20, ch. 7, 50, ch. 8, 48, ch. 18, 13, John 1, 12, ch. 3, 16 and 18, ch. 6, 29, 35, 40, ch. 11, 25 and 26, ch. 12, 46, etc. Therefore.

The Jesuits object that faith in these places is taken not as it properly regards the mercy of God and the promise concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, through and because of Christ the Mediator, apprehended by faith: but that only that faith is understood by which they hoped for miraculous healings of various diseases from Christ. But this exception is frivolous and weak. For 1. This very faith also proceeded from that saving faith which determined that Christ was that promised Messiah of the World: which is evident from the response of Christ repeated more often: Be of good cheer, son, thy sins are forgiven thee: Or Thy faith hath made thee whole. 2. In the places already cited, Christ expressly reproves the Pharisaical righteousness of works, and establishes and confirms that which comes to Man from the mercy of God alone, without any regard for his own merits: which that parable in Luke 18 concerning the Pharisee and the Publican most evidently proves: Added to this is that notable Sermon of Christ in John 6 concerning the Faith which alone feeds Man unto eternal life.

The sixth reason is derived from the nature of opposites: or from the fact that works and faith, Law and Grace, in one and the same act of Justification, by reason of one and the same ultimate end, behave as immediate opposites, of which, one being posited, the other is necessarily excluded from the same end.

Now indeed, with the whole Scripture as witness, it is divinely ordained that Man is justified by faith, without the Works of the Law, as has been demonstrated sufficiently at length above. Therefore it is necessarily concluded that the same person cannot be justified by the Law or by Works, and those either alone or mixed with faith.

The author of the connection of the Major premise is the Apostle himself, who reasons in this manner. Rom. 11, 6. Salvation is obtained by grace, no longer from works, otherwise grace is no longer grace: But if from works, it is no longer from grace: otherwise work is no longer work.

Nor does anything detract from the evidence of this argument, because the Apostle is not discussing primarily Justification in this place, but rather Gratuitous Election. For it is certain and can by no means be denied that the Apostle in this very verse 6 and following rises from the hypothesis to the Universal Thesis, so that he may show that there is a homogeneity in the business of Election and Justification, indeed of salvation as a whole. Therefore, by whatever reason Election and salvation came to those few remnants of Israel, by that same reason it must needs come to each and every one who is to be saved.

However, it well deserves observation that the Apostle opposes grace diametrically

On works proceeding from Man. We conclude therefore from this irrefragably, that by the word Grace in this place is understood nothing at all that proceeds in any way from Man, but that which descends solely from God, namely that mere mercy and gratuitous love, as was also demonstrated above. Therefore, whatever the Jesuits prattle in this place about inherent Grace, about infused qualities, and about the newness of life generated through the Holy Spirit, collapses and vanishes into smoke. For the works of the reborn are nonetheless works, and they come under the same complex of genus as any other works whatsoever. But now the Apostle distinguishes works not some, but indefinitely all, against Grace in the act of Justification ἀντιδιῃρημένως (by way of division). Therefore, under the complex of this Grace, no works of ours at all, of whatever kind they may be, can come. Whence Augustine somewhere says no less elegantly than truly: Grace is not grace in any way, unless it be gratuitous in every way. And Bernard: Whatever you attribute to merits is lacking to Grace: I do not want, therefore, a merit that excludes Grace.

Nor do the Romanists succeed when they write: That works are also, according to the opinion of the Lutherans, effects of Grace: Therefore these two cannot be contradictorily opposed to each other. For it cannot be unknown to them that we do not even extend that contrariety simply to every respect whatsoever. For Grace and works are not, in themselves, or in respect of their Essence, opposed to each other. For in this way they are and ought to be most closely joined: but only by reason of one and the same Effect, or by reason of one and the same ultimate end, which is Salvation and eternal life. For if you attribute the Effect of Salvation, with the Apostle, to Grace alone, you certainly cannot and ought not, with the Romanists, against the Apostle, refer the same to Works.

In place of a conclusion, a Seventh Reason may be added, taken from the Orthodox Antiquity, concerning which let Chemnitz be consulted, both in his Examination of the Council of Trent and in his Loci: Let it suffice to have noted this in this place, that such is the power of truth, that the Council of Trent itself is forced to confess that Faith is the beginning and foundation of human salvation, and the root of all Justification, without which it is impossible to please God and to come into the fellowship of his sons. Sess. 6. cap. 8.

Hence it is that some of the Adversaries rhetoricate quite splendidly and magnificently concerning Justifying Faith, especially in those places in which they construct quite ruinous snares and dangers for our purer doctrine. But meanwhile they are found to differ from the Apostolic doctrine δὶς διὰ πασῶν (through and through), which will now appear more clearly from the ἀντιθέσει (antithesis).

Latin:

Reliquas Pontificiorum Sophisticationes pete ex Commentario nostro ad Articulum tertium libri concordiæ.

Altera Confirmationis nostræ ratio, talis esse potest: Si promissio vitæ æternæ hominibus obtingit per Legem: Consequens est, quod irrita sit facta promissio ex parte Dei: & consequenter ex natura relativorum, irrita etiam sit facta fides, ex parte nostri.

Atqui utramque hoc est absurdum, & vel cogitatu impium. Ergò non ex lege obtingit promissio: Jam si non ex Lege, utiq; ex fide: Tertium dari nequit.

Connexum Majoris ipsum Apostolum autorem habet. Gal. 3, 18. Si ex Lege est hæreditas, non jam est ex promissione : Ratio, quia Lex non est ex fide Gal. 3, 12. Quia non data est Lex, quæ possit vivificare vers. 21. Quia Lex tantùm iram operatur, ac proindè non justos, sed reos nos coram Deo constituit. Rom. 4, 15. Quia Lex maledictionem tantùm affert. Gal. 3, 10. Quia si ex Lege qui sunt, hæredes sunt, tùm exinanita est fides & abolita promissio Rom. 4, 14. Accedit & illud, quod Fides est τῶν πισῶν, Lex autem τῶν πρακτῶν. E. si salus ex Lege, nihil ampliùs loci relinquetur Fidei: Porrò Lex respicit justitiam Dei legalem: Fides verò ejusdem misericordiam : E. si ex Lege est salus, nullus ampliùs usus erit fidei. Præterea fœdus Dei cum Abrahamo est nullum aliud, quàm quòd Deus velit benedicere & salvare eos, qui sunt ex fide Filij Abrahæ: tantùm propter semen permissum qui est Christus. Gal. 3, 7. 9 16. E. fœdus contrarium, quod Deus velit salutem impertire operantibus subsistere nequit. Et profectò hoc argumentum tantæ est firmitudinis atque evidentiæ, ut quid ei opponat Jesuvvita noster non inveniat, præter rancidum illud κρησφύγετον, fingens, Apostolum excludere tantùm Legis Opera, quæ facta sunt sine fide, id quod jam ante à nobis est discussum & protritum.

Tertia ratio sic informari potest. Si præter unam & solam fidem in Christum nihil dari potest, quó omnis gloria de salute nostra soli Deo & gratiæ divinæ adscribitur: Utiq; Fides etiam imputabitur ad justitiam præ operibus.

Atqui sola & una Fides hoc facit. Ergo.

Connexum Majoris patet ex cap. 4, 2. Rom. Si Abraham ex operibus est justificatus, habet de quo glorietur: sed non apud Deũ: undè sic arguo ex textu Apostol: Si Abrahamus justificatꝰ est operibus, habet de quo gloriari possit, sed non apud DEUM. Ergo Justitia propriorum operum Gloriam non Deo, sed hominibus adscribit: Atqui hoc impium affirmatur. Nam omnes peccaverunt & destituuntur gloria apud Deum. Rom. 3, 23. Et si omnia fecerimus, servi sumus inutiles, fecimus quod debuimus, Luc. 17, 10. Ergo Justitia Operum in negocio salutis subsistere nequit.

Minor ex Scripturis itidem evidentissimè confirmari potest. Nam 1. Fides credit in spem contra spem: Rom. 4, 18. hoc est, in promissione Dei unicè & placidè acquiescit, licet res promifsæ sint præter omnem spem humanam, imò cum ratione nostra simpliciter pugnent. 2. Fides resistit omnibus dubitationibus Carnis, exemplo Abrahami, qui non considerans Corpus suum jam emortuum, neque sterilitatem Saræ, neque alia, credidi promissioni divinæ. Rom. 4, 19. 3. Fides certo statuit, Deum quæcunque promittit, & velle & posse præstare.

Quarta ratio: In ore duorum actrium consistit omnis veritas: Atqui Prophetæ & Apostoli testantur, Justum vivere non nisi suâ fide, ut Habacuc. 2, 4. Paulus Rom. 1, 17. Gal. 3, 10. Hebr. 10, 38. Ergo non operibus, sed fidei adsignanda est salus & justitia nostra. Neque Exceptio illa Jesuvvitica locum habere potest, quòd assertio hæc Prophetica sit intelligenda tantùm de justificatione prima. Nam Subjecti ratio hoc minimè patitur, siquidem non agitur hoc loco de vita hominis nondum conversi, sed de vita justi, quomodo talis tandem æternùm vivere possit? Ubi respondet Prophetarum chorus: Vivere ipsos sed non nisi per fidem.

Sed aliud effugium quærit Jesuvvita noster, asserens, sensum verborum Prophetæ esse, quòd Iustus vivat vitam spiritualem ex fide: nimirùm ex fide, qualis est in hominibus justis, hoc est, ex fide formatâ per Charitatem. Et ut Franciscus Costerus explicat, quòd justus vivat, sive vitam informet ad normam fidei baud secus, ac si aliquis dicatur medicè vivere, hoc est, ex præscripto medicinæ vivere.

Respondeo, vim manifestam inferri & Prophetæ & Apostolo. Uterque enim nihil quicquam agit de spirituali vita secundùm præcepta legis divinæ instituendâ hisce in terris, sed agit de æterna illa vita sive felicitate, quæ finis est fidei, quæque oritur ex Evangelio, quod est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Et notationem meretur illud, quòd Apostolus immediatè præmisit hæc verba: Justitia Dei revelatur per Evangelium, ex fide in fidem. Nam vel hoc pacto commentum illud Jesuvviticum, de justitia aliquâ, ex fide & operibus mixtâ, sive ex Fide in opera, ita ut fide incipiat, Operibus autem abfolvatur, radicitùs evertitur. Docet enim Apostolus, Justitiam revelari ex fide in fidem, non ex Fide in Opera: ita, ut initium, progressus & finis Justificationis nostræ soli fidei sit adscribendus, uti semetipsum egregiè explicat Apostolus Rom. 5, 1. & 2.

Quinta ratio: Vniversa historia Evangelica salutem adsignat fidei eorum, qui de propria dignite desperantes, omnem fiduciam in solam Christi misericordiam collocarunt, & hu hanc ipsam ob causam Remissionem peccatorum obtigisse, luculenter testatur. ut Matth. 8, 10. & 13. cap. 9, 2. cap. 15, 28. Marci 2, 5. cap. 5 34 cap. 10. 52. Luc. 5, 20. cap. 7, 50. cap. 8, 48. cap. 18, 13. Iob. 1, 12. cap. 3. 16. & 18. cap. 6, 29. 35. 40. cap. 11, 25. & 26. cap. 12, 46. &c. Ergo.

Excipju nt Jesuvvitæ, fidem in his locis accipi, non ut propriè respicit misericordiam Dei, & promissionem de gratuita peccatorum R missione, per & propter Christum Mediatorem, fide apprehensum: sed eam tantùm fidem intelligi, qua miraculosas sanationes variorum morborum à Christo sperabat. Verùm frivola & elumbis hæc est Exceptio. Nam 1. Fides hæc ipsa quoque proficiscebatur ex fide illa salvificâ, quæ statuebat, Christum esse promissum illum Mundi Messiam: id quod patet ex responso Christi sæpiùs repetito: Confide fili, remissa sunt tibi peccata tua: Vel Fides tua salvum te fecit. 2. In locis jam citatis, Christus ex professo Pharisai cam Operum justitiam reprobat, eamque stabilit & confirmat, quæ ex sola Dei misericordia, sine ullo intuitu propriorum meritorum Homini obtingit: id quod parabola illa Luc 18. de Pharisæo & Publicano evidentissimè adstruit: Accedit insignis illa Concio Christi Joh. 6. de Fide, quæ sola Hominem pascat ad vitam æternam.

Sexta ratio desumitur à natura contrariorum: sive ab eo, quòd opera & fides, Lex & Gratia, in uno eodeg, actu Iustificationis, ratione unius ejusdemq; finis ultimi, habent se ut immediatè contraria, quorum uno posito, alterum necessariò ab eodem fine excludatur.

Iam verò Scripturâ universâ teste sic divinitùs sanctum est, ut Homo justificetur fide, absque Operibus Legis, uti supra prolixè satis est demonstratum. E. necessariò conficitur, non posse eundem justificari Lege vel Operibus, ijsque vel solis, vel cum fide mixtis.

Connexum Majoris autorem habet ipsum Apostolum, qui hunc in modum ratiocinatur. Rom. 11, 6. Super Gratiam salus obtingit, non jam ex Operibus, alioqui Gratia jam non est Gratia: Sin ex operibus, jam non ex gratia: alioquin opus jam non est opus.

Neque argumenti hujus evidentiæ quicquam decedit, quod Apostolus non πρώτως de Justificatione, sed potiùs de Gratuita Electione hoc loco disserit. Constat enim & negari nullâ ratione potest, Apostolum hoc ipso versu 6. & seqq. ab hypothesi ad Thesin Universam assurgere, ut sic ὁμογένειαν, esse ostendat, in Electionis & Justificationis imò salutis universæ negotio. Quâ ergò ratione Electio & salus paucis illis reliquijs Israelis obtigit: eâdem singulis & universis salvandis eâ obtingat necesse est.

Observationem autem probè meretur, quòd Apostolus Gratiam è diametro opponit

Operibus ab Homine profectis. Colligimus ergò hinc irrefragabiliter, Gratiæ vocabulo hoc loco nihil quicquam intelligi, quod ab Homine quovis modo proficiscitur, sed id, quod à Deo unicè descendit, nimirùm meram illam misericordiam & amorem gratuitum, uti supra etiam demonstratum. Corruit proindè & in fumum evanescit, quicquid Jesuvitæ hoc loco de Gratia inhærente, de infusis qualitatibus, & per Spiritum Sanctum ingeneratâ novitate vitæ blaterant. Nam Opera renatorum nihilominus sunt opera, atque sub eundem generis complexum, cum alijs quibusvis operibus veniunt. Jam verò Apostolus opera non quædam, sed indefinitè omnia, contra Gratiam in actu Justificationis ἀντιδιῃρημένως distinguit. Ergo sub Gratiæ hujus complexum, nulla prorsus opera nostra, qualia qualia etiam sint, venire possunt. Undè haud minùs eleganter, quàm verè alicubi Augustinus: Gratia non est gratia ullo modo, nisi sit gratuita omni modo. Et Bernhardus: Deest Gratiæ, quicquid meritis deputas: Nolo ergo meritum, quod Gratiam excludat.

Neque proficiunt Romanenses, quando scriptitant: Opera etiam ex Lutheranorum sententia esse effectus Gratiæ: Ergo non posse Contradictoriè sibi invicem hæc duo esse opposita. Nam ignotum ipsis esse nequit, ne nos quidem simpliciter ad omnem prorsus respectum contrarietatem istam extendere. Neque enim Gratiam atque opera, per se, sive Essentiæ suæ respectu, sibi invicem opponuntur. Hac enim ratione sunt & esse debent conjunctissima: sed tantùm ratione unius ejusdemque Effectus, sive ratione unius ejusdemque finis ultimi, qui est Salus & vita æterna. Salutis enim Effectum, si cum Apostolo soli Gratiæ tribuas, eundem certè cum Romanensibus, contra Apostolum ad Opera referre nec potes nec debes.

Coronidis loco addi potest Ratio Septima, ab Orthodoxa Antiquitate petita, de quâ videatur Chemnitius, tùm in Examine Concilij Tridentini: tùm in Locis: Illud hoc loco annotasse sufficiat, quòd tanta est veritatis, ut ipsum quoq; Concilium Tridentinum fateri necesse habeat, Fidem esse salutis humanæ initium & fundamentum, & radicem omnis Justificationis, sine qua sit impossibile placere Deo, & ad filiorum ejus consortium venire. Sess. 6. cap. 8.

Hinc est, quod nonnulli ex Adversarijs de Fide Justificante satis splendidè & magnificè rhetoricantur illis præsertim in locis, in quibus puriori nostræ doctrinæ insidias & pericula struunt satis exitiosa. Atqui interim à doctrina Apostolica δὶς διὰ πασῶν discrepare deprehenduntur, id quod ex ἀντιθέσει jam patebit luculentiùs.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: Anti-thesis Jesuitical, concerning the Justifying Faith

The controversy which is agitated today between us and the Jesuits concerning Justifying Faith

may most rightly be recalled to three Questions: of which the FIRST asks, What and what kind is Justifying Faith? The SECOND, Whether it justifies ALONE? The THIRD, How it justifies?
