Whether by way of disposition or preparation for Justification, whether by some dignity of its own quality, as the Jesuits commonly opine today: or indeed by way of true and real reconciliation with God, which has joined to it the gratuitous remission of sins and the imputation of Righteousness: so that Faith in the act of Justification only behaves itself ὀργανικῶς (organically) and Relatively: as our Churches teach. Since the whole treatment of this Controversy is completed in the explanation of these three chapters, we shall see about each one in order.

Latin:

COntroversia quæ de Fide Justificante inter nos & Jesuvitas hodiè agitatur ad tres

Quaestiones rectissimè revocari : quarum PRIMA quærit, Quæ & quid sit Fides justificans? ALTERA, Num SOLA justificet? TERTIA, Quomodo justificet? Nùm per modum dispositionis sive præparationis ad Justificationem, nùm aliquâ suæ qualitatis dignitate, uti Jesuvvitæ hodiè communiter opinantur : an verò per modum veræ & realis cum Deo reconciliationis, quæ adjunctam habet gratuitam peccatorum remissionem & imputationem Justitiæ : ita ut Fides in actu Justificationis tantùm se habeat ὀργανικῶς & Relativè : uti nostræ docent Ecclesiæ. In trium istorum capitum explicatione, cùm tota hujus Controversiæ Tractatio absolvatur, de singulis ordine videbimus.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: I. Question. What and Which Is the Justifying Faith

The word Faith in the Scriptures is πολύσημον (polysemous), and receives various meanings: For either it denotes truth and constancy in words and deeds, both of God and of Men: as Ps. 33:4, Isa. 11:5, Jer. 5:1 & 3, Hos. 5:9, Rom. 3:3. Or sometimes it signifies the doctrine of the Gospel itself: as Rom. 3:31, We do not destroy the Law through Faith: or it denotes the fulfillment of a promised thing, as Gal. 3:25, After faith came, that is, Christ, the promised Messiah of the World. Or it is taken for the profession and assent to the Evangelical doctrine concerning Christ, as Acts 13:8, They sought to turn the proconsul away from the Faith: Or it denotes knowledge of the history concerning Christ, indeed of the whole Holy Scripture, such as falls even to the impious, indeed to the Devils, as will be shown presently: or it denotes an unmoved and certain trust and confidence in that which is believed: Which meaning belongs to justifying faith alone: as will appear presently. Or finally it denotes the gift of miracles, as Matt. 17:20, If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, etc. 1 Cor. 13:2. From these diverse meanings arise also various and diverse species of Faith. For one is called General or Historical Faith: Another Special or Justifying: Another miraculous, which, as Christ testifies, falls even upon those whom he never knew. Matt. 7:23. And this Faith was proper partly to the times of Christ, partly to the times of the Apostles: but today it has no place in the Church. Furthermore, another Faith is dead, concerning which James 2:14 & 17, which ought rather to be called a vain boast or persuasion. Near to which is feigned and simulated Faith 2 Tim. 1:5, Tit. 1:16, both of which fall even to Demons James 2:19, Mark 5:6, Luke 8:28, Acts 19:15. And this is always in vice.

Moreover, it is properly concerning only the first two species that there is controversy in this place: namely, concerning the General and the Special; or, which amounts to the same thing, concerning Historical and Justifying faith. Now, each is so named partly from its subjects, partly from the objects: from the subjects indeed, insofar as Historical Faith is common to all Christians equally. Tit. 1, 4. To his beloved son according to the common Faith. But justifying [faith] is the property of a few. 2 Thess. 3, 2. Faith is not of all.

But from the Object, insofar as Historical [faith] is concerned with every Word of God, as much of the Law as of the Gospel: but justifying [faith] strictly holds itself, and only respects the promises proper to the Gospel.

Regarding the former species, namely Historical Faith, the following three Aphorisms concerning it are to be observed.

1. Historical Faith is to be defined not by bare knowledge, but also by assent.

2. This Faith always concurs with Justifying faith in adults; although by its nature it is separable from it: which can be illustrated by an example taken from the powers of the soul: Where the superior always presupposes the inferior: but not vice versa, the inferior includes the superior. Thus justifying Faith always presupposes Historical Faith: but not vice versa, the latter includes the former.

3. Historical Faith, therefore, is never, nor can it be called, Justifying Faith. For whether you look at bare knowledge, or assent: not only the ungodly, but also the Demons are those who have that Faith, James 2, 19. It would therefore be no light sacrilege to affirm that Historical Faith can justify, and to maintain that the ungodly and the Devils are endowed with justifying faith. What is more, this alone distinguishes Christians themselves among one another, that some have only Historical Faith: others have Historical and Justifying [faith] at the same time: And thus no other Essential mark can be given by which a believer is distinguished from a believer, that is, a Christian from a Christian, except this special or Justifying Faith.

With these things observed, Bellarmine errs plainly and enormously, who asserts that Historical Faith and Justifying Faith are absolutely the same: The Catholics teach, he says, that the historical faith and that of miracles, and of promises, is one and the same, lib. 1. de Iustif. cap. 4. p. 941. C.

Now indeed if we consult the Scriptures themselves, it will not be so very difficult to demonstrate that Justifying Faith is a certain peculiar species of Faith, consisting of a proper and plainly singular specific difference, or Formal reason.

For first, Scripture establishes as a mark of justifying faith, as it were proper and Essential, that it believes beyond hope under hope Rom. 4, 18. that is, without all hesitation or doubt, it relies with certain confidence upon the promised things, however much they may seem to fight with our reason. In which part certainly this faith differs very much from Historical Faith, as one which assents to those things which are νοητὰ, but only fall under knowledge. Scripture is accustomed to express this first mark with the term πληροφορίας.

The second mark of Justifying Faith is that it does not respect every Word of God in the place of an Object: nor even any promises whatsoever: but only those proper to the Gospel: which indeed act and preach concerning the merit of Christ acquired for us, and concerning the free remission of sins through and on account of the same. For which reason this Faith is also called κατ’ ἐξοχὴν in the Scriptures, THE FAITH OF CHRIST, Gal 3.12.

Thirdly, so that one may judge more correctly concerning the Subject of justifying faith, that Apostolic Definition, Hebr. 11, 1. is to be noted, which holds thus: Faith is the substance of things which are hoped for, the basis and foundation, the argument or demonstration, or Conviction of those things which are not seen: πίστις ἐστὶν ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόσασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος ὀυ βλεπομένων. For in so far as this Faith includes or at least presupposes the knowledge of those things which are revealed both in the Law and in the Gospel, to that extent the Subject of justifying faith is established to be the Mind or intellect of Man: But in so far as this very Faith justifies only when the knowledge in the mind is followed by ὑπόσασις and assent in the will, likewise ἔλεγχος or movement in the heart, a true confidence apprehending and applying to itself the good proposed in the Evangelical promise, namely the Mercy of God forgiving sins, through and on account of CHRIST the Mediator: to that extent certainly the Subject of justifying Faith is the heart or will of Man.

This third note serves to refute the calumny of the Papists: For they trifle, claiming that such a faith is taught by us as is not Catholic, that is, which does not regard all, but only one Article of the Christian Religion. Now, however, we have just shown the contrary, asserting that the former part of Justifying Faith, namely Knowledge, is concerned with every Word of God, as much of the Law as of the Gospel, and consequently also with every Article of faith. That this may be understood more clearly, it must be established thus: that there is a twofold adequate Object or Correlate of Faith: One General: the other special: The General is every Word of God, but especially every divine promise: The Special is only the promise of Grace, concerning the gratuitous remission of sins through and on account of Christ. Now this Special Object does indeed presuppose that General one also, but it does not justify in respect of that General Object or Correlate: But only in so far as it is a firm confidence resting solely and indubitably in the merit of Christ. For this alone adds the complement of the form or specific difference, by which faith becomes truly justifying, and is distinguished from all other superstitions or persuasions. The Apostle expressed this specific difference quite clearly, Rom. 4, 23, 24, and 25, asserting that the doctrine concerning the righteousness imputed to Abraham was recorded in the Scriptures for this reason, that it might be evident therefrom that the same righteousness is to be imputed likewise to all who believe in him who raised

Jesus our Lord from the dead, delivered for our sins, and raised again for our iniquities.

There are some theologians who consider justifying faith in two ways, either absolutely or relatively, according to how it justifies: absolutely, indeed, insofar as by reason of knowledge and assent, it is concerned with every Word of God, either in general or in particular: but insofar as it is concerned with the proper promise of the Gospel, and the confidence of the heart, πληροφορίας, approaches, to that extent they say faith is considered relatively, insofar as it is that which justifies. We do not stubbornly resist their opinion, since it does not conflict with ours: provided that this is observed, that for faith considered absolutely only two things are required: namely, knowledge and assent, and indeed an assent that is not cold or sleepy, but joined with some πληροφορίᾳ, or certain and undoubted persuasion: but for justifying faith, besides these two, a third is also required, namely πεποίθησιν or confidence. Furthermore, it is also to be noted that ignorance, negation, and doubt are opposed to faith considered absolutely; but to justifying faith, there is also opposed, in addition, distrust of the grace of God, which is called unbelief κατ' ἐξοχὴν.

From these observations has arisen among certain ancient and recent theological writers that enigmatic phrase by which they said that faith is necessary in faith. The meaning of which they intended to be this: in one and the same faith, two faiths are as it were hidden: one, by which we believe; the other, which we believe: the faith by which we believe is the πληροφορία of assent, devoid of all doubt: the faith which we believe is the Word of God or the dogmas of the divine Word: the πληροφορία of which cannot stand unless the knowledge of the same precedes it.

With all these things weighed, we deservedly explode that implicit or 'coal-heaver' faith, which Hofius in book 3 on the authority of Scripture, page 190, wonderfully praises, and determines to be sufficient alone for those about to die, so that they may believe only that those things are true which the Church believes, even if they themselves do not know what the Church believes. Such a faith is truly not faith, but a cold and empty opinion.

We, having observed all those things which we have hitherto discussed concerning the proper affection and essential marks of justifying faith, are most persuaded that it can be defined in this manner both most perfectly and most briefly: Justifying faith is both a certain knowledge and firm assent to the divine word, and an unmoved and singular confidence in the mercy of God, certainly establishing that sins are freely forgiven through and on account of Christ the Mediator to all who believe in him.

This definition shows the true distinction between those phrases of Scripture: to believe God, to believe to God, to believe in God. God is believed even by infidels, indeed by devils. One believes to God alone, that is, assent is given to his promises, which is something that also falls under general faith. But one believes in God when a man with full confidence of soul rests in the mercy of God. And in this respect alone does faith justify.

Thus one believes Christ, one believes to Christ, one believes in Christ, in a very different respect. He believes Christ who establishes that he is true God and man, and the true Messiah. He believes to Christ who has faith in any saying of his. He believes in Christ who, with full confidence of soul, rests in his merit and redemption, and from this, because of the promises, expects for himself any good things from Christ.

Latin:

FIdei vocabulum in Scripturis est πολύσημον, & varias recipit significationes: Vel ehim notat veritatem ac constantiam in dictis & factis, tàm Dei, quàm Hominum: ut Psal. 33, 4. Jes. 11, 5. Jerem. 5, 1. & 3. Hos. 5, 9. Rom. 3, 3. vel interdum significat ipsam doctrinam Evangelij: ut Rom. 3, 31. Legem non destruimus per Fidem: vel notat impletionem rei promissæ, ut Gal. 3, 25. Postquam venit fides, hoc est, Christus, promissus Mundi Messias. Vel sumitur pro professione & assensu doctrinæ Evangelicæ de Christo, ut Actor. 13. 8. Quærebant proconsulem avertere à Fide: Vel notat notitiam historiæ de Christo, imò totius Scripturæ Sacræ, qualis cadit etiam in impios, imò Diabolos, uti mox ostendetur: vel notat immotam certamque fiduciam ac confidentiam in id quod creditur: Quæ significatio soli fidei justificanti competit: uti mox patebit. Vel denique notat donum miraculorum, ut Matth. 17, 20. Si habueritis fidem, ut granum sinapi & c. 1. Cor. 13, 2. Ex diversis istis significatis oriuntur variæ etiam & diversæ species Fidei. Alia enim dicitur Fides Generalis sive Historica: Alia Specialis sive Iustificans: Alia miraculosa, quæ teste Christo in eos etiam cadit, quos ipse nunquàm novit. Matth. 7, 23. Et hæc Fides partim Christi, partim Apostolorum temporibus fuit propria: hodiè autem in Ecclesiâ locum non habet. Porrò alia Fides est mortua, de qua Iacob. 2, 14. & 17. quæ inanis potiùs jactantia sive persuasio dici debet. Cui vicina est Fides ficta & simulata 2. Timoth. 1, 5. Tit. 1, 16. quæ utraque cadit etiam in Dæmones Iacob. 2. 19. Marc. 5, 6. Luc. 8, 28. Actor. 19. 15. Et hæc semper est in vitio.

Cæterùm de duabus tantùm primis Speciebus hoc loco propriè controvertitur: de Generali nimirùm & Speciali: vel quod eodem recidit, de fide Historica & Iustificante. Utraque autem sic appellatur partim à Subjectis, partim ab Objectis: A Subjectis quidem, quatenus Fides Historica Omnibus ex æquo Christianis est communis. Tit. 1, 4. Filio suo dilecto secundum communem Fidem. Justificans verò paucorum propria est. 2. Thess. 3, 2. Fides non est omnium.

Ab Objecto verò, quatenùs Historica versatur circa omne Verbum Dei, tàm Legis quàm Evangelij: Justificans autem strictè sese habet, & tantùm respicit promissiones Evangelij proprias.

Quoad priorem speciem, Fidem nimirum Historicam, sequentes tres Aphorismi de ea observandi veniunt.

1. Fides Historica definienda est non per nudam notitiam, sed & per assensum.

2. Hæc Fides semper concurrit cum fide Justificante in adultis; licet naturâ suâ ab eâ sit separabilis: id quod Exemplo à potentijs animæ petito illustrari potest: Ubi superior semper præsupponit inferiorem: non verò vice versâ, inferior includit superiorem. Sic Fides justificans semper præsupponit Fidem Historicam: non verò vice versâ, Hæc includit illam.

3. Fides ergo Historia, nunquàm est aut dici potest Fides Justificans. Sive enim notitiam nudam spectes, sive assensum: non impij tantum, sed & Dæmones sunt, qui Fidem istam habent Iacob. 2, 19. Haud ergò levius sacrilegium fuerit affirmare, Fidem Historicam posse justificare, atque statuere, impios & Diabolos fide justificante esse præditos. Quid quòd Christianos ipsos inter se hoc unicum discernit, quod alij Fidem tantùm Historicam: alij Historicam & Justificantem simul habent: Et sic Essentialis nota quâ Fidelis à fideli, hoc est, Christianus à Christiano discernitur, nulla potest dari alia, præter Fidem hanc specialem sive Justificantem.

Quibus observatis enormiter planè errat Bellarminus, qui Fidem Historicam cum Fide Justificante prorsus eandem esse asserit: Docent, inquiens, Catholici Fidem historicam & miraculorum, & promissionum unam & eandem esse lib. 1. de Iustif. cap. 4. p. 941. C.

Jam verò si Scripturas ipsas consulamus, haud usque adeò difficile erit demonstrare, Fidem Justificantem esse peculiarem quandam Fidei speciem, propriâ ac planè singulari differentiâ specificâ, sive ratione Formali constantem.

Primùm enim Fidei justificantis notam quasi propriam ac Essentialem Scriptura constituit, quòd credat præter spem sub spe Rom. 4, 18. hoc est, sine omni hæsitatione sive dubitatione, certâ fiduciâ innitatur rebus promissis, quantùmvis eæ cum ratione nostra pugnare videantur. Quâ certè in parte plurimùm jam discrepat hæc fides à Fide historicâ, ut quæ assentitur ijs, quæ sunt νοητὰ, sed sub notitiam tantùm cadunt. Primam hanc notam Scriptura πληροφορίας termino exprimere solet.

Altera nota Fidei Iustificantis est, quod ea Objecti loco, non omne Dei Verbum respicit: neque etiam promissiones quasvis: sed tantum Evangelij proprias: quæ nimirum de Christi merito nobis acquisito, deque gratuita peccatorum remissione per & propter eundem agunt & concionantur. Quam ob causam Fides etiam hæc κατ’ ἐξοχὴν in Scripturis nominatur, FIDES CHRISTI, Gal 3.12.

Tertio ut de Subjecto Fidei justificantis rectius judicari possit, notanda venit Apostolica illa Definitio, Hebr. 11, 1. quæ sic habet: Fides est rerum quæ sperantur, substantia, basis & fundamentum, argumentum sive demonstratio, aut Convictio eorum, quæ non cernuntur: πίστις ἐστὶν ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόσασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος ὀυ βλεπομένων. Nam quatenus hæc Fides includit vel saltem præsupponit notitiam eorum, quæ tum in Lege tum in Evangelio sunt revelata, eatenus Subjectum fidei Iustificantis constat esse Mentem sive intellectum Hominis: Quatenus vero hæc ipsa Fides tum demum Iustificat, quando notitiam in mente sequitur ὑπόσασις & assensus in voluntate, item ἔλεγχος sive motus in corde, vera fiducia apprehendens, sibique applicans bonum in Evangelica promissione propositum, nimirum Misericordiam Dei remittentem peccata, per & propter CHRISTUM Mediatorem: eatenus certe Subjectum Fidei justificantis est, cor sive voluntas Hominis.

Servit tertia hæc nota refutandæ Pontificiorum calumniæ: Nugantur enim talem a nobis doceri fidem, quæ non sit Catholica, hoc est, quæ non omnes, sed unum tantum Articulum Religionis Christianæ respiciat, Iam vero Contrarium jam modo ostendimus asserentes, priorem illam Fidei Iustificæ partem, nempe Notitiam versari circa omne Verbum Dei, tam Legis, quam Evangelij, ac per Consequens etiam circa omnem Articulum fidei. Quod ut planius intelligatur, sic statuendum est: Geminum esse Objectum sive Correlatum Fidei adæquatum: Vnum Generale: alterum speciale: Generale est omne Verbum Dei, præcipue vero omnis promissio divina: Speciale est tantum promissio Gratiæ, de gratuita remissione peccatorum per & propter Christum. Iam Speciale hoc Objectum præsupponit quidem etiam illud Generale, sed respectu Generalis illius Objecti sive Correlati non justificat: Sed tantum quatenus est firma fiducia in merito Christi unice & indubitate acquiescens. Hæc enim sola addit complementum formæ sive differentiæ specificæ, qua fides fit vere justificans, atque a superstitionibus sive persuasionibus alijs omnibus discernitur. Expressit differentiam hanc specificam satis dilucide Apostolus. Rom. 4, 23. 24. & 25. asserens doctrinam de Iustitia fidei Abrahamo imputata, ideo annotatam esse in Scripturis, ut inde constet, eandem Iustitiam omnibus itidem imputandam esse, qui credunt in eum, qui excitavit

Jesum Dominum nostrum à mortuis, traditum propter peccata nostra, & resuscitatum propter iniquitates nostras.

Sunt nonnulli Theologi, qui Fidem Justificantem duobus modis considerant, vel Absolute, vel Relatè, prout justificat: Absolutè quidem, quatenùs ratione notitiæ & assensus, versatur circa omne Verbum DEI vel in communi vel in particulari: Quatenùs verò est circa promissionem Evangelii propriam, & accedit πληροφορίας fiducia Cordis, eâtenùs dicunt, Fidem considerari Relatè, quatenùs nimirùm ea justificat. Quorum sententiæ quippè nostræ non repugnanti haud morosius reluctamur: modò illud observetur, ad Fidem absolutè consideratam duo tantùm requiri: nempè notitiam & assensum, ac assensum quidem non frigidum aut somnolentum: sed cum πληροφορίᾳ aliqua, sive certa ac indubiâ persuasione conjunctum: ad Fidem verò Justificam, præter hæc duo requiri etiam tertium, nempè πεποίθησιν sive fiduciam. Porrò & illud notandum, Fidei absolutè consideratæ opponi ignorantiam, negationem, dubitationem: Fidei verò justificanti insuper opponi etiam diffidentiam de Gratiâ DEI, quæ κατ' ἐξοχὴν incredulitas dicitur.

Ex his observationibus orta est apud veteres quosdam & recentiores Scriptores Theologos, ænigmatica illa phrasis, quâ dixerunt, Fidem neceffariam esse in Fide. Cujus sensum voluerunt esse istum: in unâ eadémque Fide, duas quasi occultari fides: Unam, quâ credimus: Alteram, quam credimus: Fides quâ credimus est πληροφορία assensus, omnis dubitationis expers: Fides, quam credimus, est Verbum DEI sive dogmata Verbi divini: quorum πληροφορία stare nequit, nisi præcedat eorundem notitia.

Quibus omnibus pensi habitis meritò explodimus Fidem illam implicitam sive carbonariam, quam Hofius lib. 3. de autoritate Scripturæ pag. 190. mirificè prædicat, & morituris solam sufficere statuit, ut nimirùm tantùm credant vera esse ea, quæ Ecclesia credit, licèt ipsi nesciant, quid credat Ecclesia. Talis profectò Fides non est Fides, sed frigida & inanis opinio.

Nos observatis illis omnibus, quæ de propria affectione & notis Essentialibus Fidei Justificantis hactenùs disputavimus, hunc in modum eam & perfectissimè & brevissimè definiri posse, habemus persuasissimum: Fides Justificans est tum certa notitia & firmus assensus verbi divini, tum immota ac singularis fiducia in misericordiam DEI, certò statuens, gratis remitti peccata, per & propter CHRISTUM Mediatorem omnib. in ipsum credentibus.

Monstrat hæc definitio verum discrimen inter phrases illas Scripturæ, Credere DEUM, credere DEO, credere in DEUM. Creditur DEUS ab infidelibus etiam, imò Diabolis: Creditur soli DEO, hoc est, promissis ipsius adhibetur assensus, id quod cadit etiam in fidem Generalem. Creditur autem in DEUM, quando Homo plenâ animi fiduciâ recumbit in misericordia DEI. Et hoc tantùm respectu Fides justificat.

Sic creditur Christus, creditur Christo: creditur in Christum, diversissimo respectu. Credit CHRISTUM qui ipsum statuit verum esse DEUM ac Hominem, & verum Messiam. Credit CHRISTO, qui cuivis dicto ejus fidem habet. Credit in CHRISTUM, qui plenâ animi fiduciâ, in meritum ac redemptionem ipsius recumbit, & ex hac, propter promissiones, quævis sibi bona à CHRISTO pollicetur.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: Antithesis

Antithesis.

The Romanists, and especially the Jesuits, err in many ways concerning this first question about the definition of justifying faith; whose dogmas it will be worth the effort to examine in order.

And at the beginning, indeed, they contend that the object of justifying faith, considered in any way, is the whole Word of God, and that it extends as widely as the Word of God extends: nay, that the certain promise of special mercy pertains not so much to faith as to empty presumption, as Bellarmine wrote in book 1 on Justification, chapter 4, page 941 D, and chapter 5, page 945 A.

The following reasons argue against and evidently refute the impiety of this error. For 1. Scripture expressly excludes the Word of the Law from faith, and assigns to it only the promises of the Gospel. Gal. 3, 12 The law is not of faith. Where, however, we shall always observe these two things. 1. That the question here is not about faith taken generally, but only taken specially, insofar, of course, as it justifies. Then, that the question in this place is not about the exercises of faith in those already justified, how, of course, it exercises itself through patience, what faith performs in afflictions, in prayers, in the expectation of help, and of any benefits whatsoever, and similar exercises: For in these cases we by no means deny that there are various objects, concerning which the exercise of the faith of those already justified may be occupied: But that the question is about the act of justification, what that object is, in respect of which it can justify: Where indeed we maintain with Scripture that no other can be given, except the promise of the Gospel alone, by which one distinction those arguments can be repressed and overturned, which Bellarmine in chapter 5 brings forward from the eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews, where we by no means deny that very many and discrepant objects and exercises of faith are described.

The second reason is this: If justifying faith, and indeed taken specially, regards every Word of God in the place of an object, it would follow that it, insofar as it is directed toward gratuitous mercy and the most holy passion of the Son, does not justify otherwise, nor even more or more principally, than insofar as it is directed toward the doctrine concerning devils and hell, since this also is revealed in the Word of God. How horrible this is even to hear, every pious person easily understands.

Third: All those testimonies of Scripture, which in the third question of the exodus concerning faith we shall invincibly demonstrate, overturn this impiety,

That faith cannot justify a man, except only insofar as it apprehends the mercy of GOD, offered to believers, nay to the whole world, in the merit of the Son.

Fourthly: We oppose to Bellarmine the Master of the Sentences, who in book 3, distinction 19, writes in the manner of the Lutherans thus: We are also said to be justified otherwise through the death of Christ, because through faith in his death we are cleansed from sins. Whence the Apostle: The justice of GOD is through the faith of Jesus Christ. And the same, whom GOD proposed as a propitiatory through faith in his blood, that is, through faith in his passion: as formerly those looking upon the bronze serpent erected on the wood were healed from the bites of serpents. If therefore we rightly look with the intuition of faith upon him who hung for us on the wood, we are loosed from the bonds of the Devil, that is, from sins, and are so freed from the Devil that not even after this life does he find anything to punish.

Cassander supports Lombard in his Consultation to Emperor Ferdinand, page 20. This is beyond controversy, that that Justice by which we are justified consists in the Remission of sins: that is, when on account of the merit of the passion of Christ, which he undertook for our sake, sins are no longer imputed to us: which is nothing other than that the merit of Christ itself is imputed to us for the remission of sins. And this is what Paul so often inculcates, that faith is imputed to us for justice, namely that faith by which we believe in him who raised Christ from the dead, who was delivered up for our offenses, and rose again for our Justification.

And much more clearly on the preceding page 12. We call living faith the motion of the Holy Spirit, by which those who are truly penitent for their old life are raised up to GOD, and truly apprehend the mercy promised in CHRIST, so that they now truly feel that they have received the remission of sins and reconciliation on account of the merit of CHRIST, by the gratuitous goodness of GOD.

Finally, the impiety of the Jesuitical doctrine strives to entangle and obscure the Pauline assertions concerning Justifying faith. For when the Apostle says, Faith justifies: the Jesuits oppose, nay, it does not justify: Why? Because faith believes every Word of GOD. Therefore, he who seriously believes it to be true that which is written, Cursed is he who has not remained in all things which are written in the book of this law, to do them: will he be justified by this very thing? The Apostle expressly denies this, asserting that these things were written so that every mouth might be stopped, and the whole world might become guilty before GOD. Furthermore, because faith also apprehends this Word of GOD: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments of GOD. Therefore (the Jesuits infer) faith justifies, not insofar as it apprehends Christ, but insofar as it brings forth good works. To this, undoubtedly, tends the first error of the Jesuits concerning Justifying faith.

But Bellarmine has certain arguments by which he tries to put a gloss upon this impiety of his. And at the beginning indeed, chapter 8, book 1, on Justification, pages 951 D, 952 A, he argues thus: The faith which Christ demanded, and for whose confirmation he performed miracles, was justifying faith. But Christ, Matt. 9:28, demands faith in his Omnipotence and divinity, saying, Do you believe that I can do this for you? So Matt. 16:17, again in Peter he commends the faith by which he confessed that Christ is the Son of GOD. Therefore, the Faith which in the place of an Object looks to the divinity of Christ is that very faith which grants both justice and eternal life.

I answer: The argument fails by the Sophism of ignoring the refutation and of ἑτεροζητήσεως (seeking something else). For this is not what is asked: Whether Justifying Faith in the place of an Object also looks to the Divinity of Christ, and other things of that kind revealed in Scripture? For this we ourselves willingly admit: But this is in the Question: Since Justifying Faith has various Objects, does it justify insofar as it believes all those Objects to be true? That which we deny, the Jesuit asserts: Or does it only justify insofar as it believes the promise of the Gospel concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, through and on account of Christ? That which we assert, and have hitherto proven: the Jesuits, however, deny. Therefore, since the Jesuit's argument proves no more than that Justifying Faith, with respect to knowledge and assent, also looks to other Objects, on account of the proper promise of the Gospel, it is manifest that it wanders off the track, nor does it conclude anything against us.

But if the Jesuit insists: If Justifying Faith also looks to other Objects, it will surely justify also with respect to these Objects: he shamefully begs the question, and confuses the Essential parts of Justifying Faith, while that which is owed uniquely to Trust, the more principal part and as it were the Soul of justifying faith, he himself sophistically assigns to the less principal part, namely knowledge and assent, which two, however, can exist even outside the act of Justification in unbelievers.

The other argument of Bellarmine sounds thus, Mark 1:40. To the Leper saying, Lord if you will, you can cleanse me, Christ answers, I will, be cleansed. But this leper was without doubt doubting concerning the will of the LORD, and through this concerning special mercy: And yet because he did not lack faith in Omnipotence and divinity, he obtained what he asked. Therefore, that faith also which is destitute of certainty concerning Special mercy is such faith as the Lord demands, and for whose confirmation he performed miracles: and as a Consequence, it can be Justifying Faith, which in the place of an Object looks to the special mercy of GOD.

I answer, this argument also consists of mere παρελέγχοις (irrelevant conclusions). For 1. the Consequence from miraculous faith to justifying faith is not valid, to such an extent that the former can fall even upon unbelievers, according to that Matt. 7:23 and John 6:26 and 27. Amen I say to you, you seek me, because you ate those loaves, Work for the food which remains unto eternal life: This is indeed that work, that you believe in him whom he sent. Then, this Leper doubted concerning the special mercy of the Lord, regarding the curing of leprosy: but that he doubted concerning that special mercy promised in the Gospel to believers, the Jesuit has not yet proven: And even if he were to prove this to the greatest extent, yet it would immediately follow that this leper to have been destitute of justifying faith, and therefore this argument is entirely ἄλλοτριον [alien/irrelevant].

Thirdly, there is no reason for the consequence: Many believers in the omnipotence of Christ obtained bodily benefits. Therefore, justifying faith can be that which is even most destitute of certainty concerning special mercy. For that faith in divine omnipotence, and faith in the evangelical promise, are not ἀντιφατικῶς [contradictorily] opposed: but only subordinated: indeed so that faith in the evangelical promise always presupposes faith in divine omnipotence: although the latter can exist without the former. The ten lepers can be an example, nine of whom certainly believed that Christ could heal them: but meanwhile were destitute of justifying faith.

Finally, the entire inference of the Jesuit proves nothing more than that there is some faith, for the confirmation of which the Lord performed miracles: which, however, on the part of men is destitute of certainty concerning the special mercy promised to sinners in the Gospel: a thing which we by no means deny.

For we have learned from the Gospel a twofold end of the miracles of Christ: One with respect to unbelievers, so that they might at some time be rendered ἀναπολογήτους [without excuse], Matt. 11:20 and following. If such mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon, etc. The other with respect to believers, so that they might be more and more confirmed in faith in Christ.

Latin:

Ἀντίθεσις.

Multivariàm circa primam hanc Quæstionem de Definitione Fidei Justificantis, errant Romanenses, & cumprīmis Jesuivitæ: quorum dogmata ordine examinare operæ pretium fuerit.

Ac initiò quidem contendunt, Fidei Justificæ quovis modo consideratæ, Objectum esse omne Verbum DEI, ac tàm latè patere illud, quàm latè patet Verbum DEI: quinimò certam promissionem specialis misericordiæ, non tàm ad fidem, quàm ad inanem præsumtionem pertinere, uti scripsitat Bellarminus lib. 1. de Justif. cap. 4. p. 941. D. & cap. 5. p. 945. A.

Cujus erroris impietatem sequentes rationes arguunt & evidenter refellunt. Nam 1. Verbum Legis à fide Scriptura expressè excludit, & promissiones Evangelii duntaxat eidem adsignat. Gal. 3, 12 Lex non est fide. Ubi tamen duo hæc semper observabimus. 1. Quæstionem hic esse non de Fide generaliter, sed tantùm specialiter acceptâ, quatenùs nimirùm ea justificat. Deindè non Quæstionem hoc loco esse de exercitiis fidei in jam justificatis, quomodo nimirùm per patientiam ea se exerceat, quid in afflictionibus, in precibus, expectatione auxilii, & beneficiorum quorumvis, & similibus exercitiis præstet fides: Hisce enim casibus minimè negamus, varia esse Objecta, circa quæ exercitium fidei jam justificatorum versetur: Sed quæstionem esse de actu justificationis, quodnam illud sit objectum, cujus respectu ea justificare possit: Ubi sanè nullum aliud, præter solam promissionem Evangelii, dari posse cum Scriptura statuimus, Quâ unâ distinctione reprimi & everti possunt ea argumenta, quæ Bellarminus cap. 5. ex capite undecimo Epistolæ ad Hebræos profert, ubi plurima ac discrepantia Fidei Objecta & exercitia describi minimè inficiamur.

Altera ratio hæc est: Si Fides Justificans & quidem Specialiter accepta, Objecti loco respicit omne Verbum DEI, Consequens fuerit, eam, quatenùs fertur in gratuitam misericordiam & sacrosanctam passionem Filii, non aliter, neq, etiam magis aut principaliùs justificare, quàm quatenùs fertur in Doctrinam de Diabolis & inferno, siquidem & hæc in Verbo DEI revelata est. Quòd quàm sit vel auditu horrendum, pius quisque facilè intelligit.

Tertia: Evertunt impietatem hanc universa illa Scripturæ testimonia, quibus in diexodo tertiâ Quæstione de fide, invictè demonstrabimus,

Fidem non posse justificare Hominem, nisi quatenùs tantùm apprehendit misericordiam DEI, in merito Filii credentibus, imò toti mundo oblatam.

Quartò: Opponimus Bellarmino Magistrum Sententiarum, qui lib. 3. distinct. 19. Lutheranorum more sic scribit: Dicimur quoque aliter per mortem Christi justificari, quòd per fidem mortis ejus à peccatis mundamur. Undè Apostolus: Justitia DEI est per fidem Jesu Christi. Et idem, quem DEUS proposuit propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ipsius, id est, per fidem passionis: ut olim aspicientes in serpentum æneum in ligno erectum, à morsibus serpentum sanabantur. Si ergò rectè fidei intuitu in illum respicimus, qui pro nobis pependit in ligno, à vinculis Diaboli solvimur, hoc est, à peccatis, & ita à Diabolo liberamur, ut nec post hanc vitam inveniat, quòd puniat.

Lombardo suffragatur Cassander in Consultatione ad Ferdinandum Imp. pag. 20. Hoc extra controversiam est, Justitiam illam, quâ justificamur, consistere in Remissione peccatorum: hoc est, cùm propter meritum passionis Christi, quam suscepit nostrâ causâ, peccata nobis non ampliùs imputantur: quod nihil aliud est, quàm ipsum Christi meritum ad remissionem peccatorum nobis imputari. Atque hoc est, quod Paulus toties inculcat, imputari nobis fidem ad justitiam, eam videlicet fidem, quâ credimus in eum, qui Christum suscitavit à mortuis, qui traditus est propter delicta nostra, & resurrexit propter Justificationem nostram.

Et multò clariùs præcedente pag. 12. Vocamus fidem vivam, motum Spiritus sancti, quo verè pœnitentes veteris vitæ, eriguntur ad DEUM, & verè apprehendunt misericordiam in CHRISTO promissam, ut jam verè sentiant, quòd remissionem peccatorum & reconciliationem propter meritum CHRISTI, gratuitâ DEI bonitate acceperunt.

Tandem impietas doctrinæ Jesuiticæ, assertiones Paulinas de fide Justificante involvere & obscurare studet. Quando enim Apostolus dicit, Fides justificat: Jesuitæ opponunt, imò non justificat: Quare? Quia fides credit omni Verbo DEI, Ergóne qui seriò credit verum esse illud, quod scriptum est, Maledictus, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis hujus, ut faciat ea: is hoc ipso justificabitur: Negat hoc disertè Apostolus, ideò hæc scripta esse asserens, ut omne os obturetur, & totus mundus reus fiat DEO. Porrò quia fides apprehendit & hoc Verbum DEI: Si vis in vitam ingredi serva mandata DEI. Ergò (inferunt Jesuitæ) fides justificat, non quatenus Christum apprehendit, sed quatenùs profert bona opera. Hùc nimirùm tendit Jesuitarum error primus de fide Justificante.

Sed habet Bellarminus argumenta quædam quibus impietati huic suæ fucum facere conatur. Ac initiò quidem cap. 8. lib. 1. de Justif. pag. 951. D. 952. A. sic arguit: Fides, quam Christus exigebat, & in cujus confirmationem miracula faciebat, fides erat justificans. Atqui Christus Matt. 9, 28 exigit fidem Omnipotentiæ & divinitatis suæ, inquiens, Creditis, quòd hoc possim facere vobis: Sic Matth. 16, 17. rursus in Petro commendat fidem, quâ confessus est, Christum esse Filium DEI. Ergo Fides quæ Objecti loco respicit Christi divinitatem illa est, ipsa fides, quæ & justitiam & vitam æternam tribuit.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum Sophismate ignorationis Elenchi & ἑτεροζητήσεως. Non enim hoc quæritur: An Fides Justificans Objecti loco respiciat etiam Divinitatem Christi, & alia id genus in Scriptura revelata? Hoc enim nos ipsi ultrò fatemur: Sed hoc in Quæstione est: Cùm Fides Justificans varia habeat Objecta, nùm justificet, quatenùs credit omnia illa Objecta vera esse? id quod nos negamus, Jesuïwita asserit: An verò tantùm justificet, quatenùs credit promissioni Evangelii de gratuita remissione peccatorum, per & propter Christum? id quod nos asserimus, & hactenùs probatum dedimus: Jesuïwitæ verò negant. Proindè cùm argumentum Jesuïwitæ plus non probet, quàm Fidem Justificantem, respectu notitiæ & assensus, respicere etiam alia Objecta, propter promissionem Evangelii propriam, manifestum est, illud extra oleas vagari, neq; quicquam contra nos concludere.

Sin instet Jesuïwita: Si Fides Justificans respicit alia etiam Objecta, utiq; horum etiam Objectorum respectu Justificabit: turpiter petit principium, & confundit partes Essentiales Fidei Justificantis, dùm quòd Fiduciæ, parti principaliori, & tanquàm Animæ Fidei justificantis unicè debetur, illud ipse Sophisticè adsignat parti minùs principali, nempè notitiæ & assensui, quæ duo tamen etiam extra actum Justificationis in incredulis esse possunt.

Alterum Bellarmini argumentum sic sonat, Marc. 1, 40. Leproso dicenti, Domine si vis, potes me mundare, Christus respondet, volo mundare. Atqui leprosus iste de voluntate DOMINI, ac per hoc de misericordia speciali, sine dubio ambigebat: Et tamen quia non defuit illi fides Omnipotentiæ & divinitatis, impetravit quod petijt. E. Illa etiam fides, quæ destituitur certitudine de misericordia Speciali est talis fides, qualem Dominus exigit, & in cujus cõfirmationem miracula faciebat: ac per Consequens, potest esse Fides Justificans, quæ Objecti loco respicit misericordiam DEI specialem.

Respondeo, hoc quoque Argumentum meris constare παρελέγχοις. Nam 1. à fide miraculosa ad fidem justificantem non valet Consequentia, usque adeò, ut illa in infideles etiam cadat, secundum illud Matth. 7, 23. & Joh. 6, 26. & 27. Amen dico vobis, quæritis me, quia comedistis panes illos, Operemini cibum, qui permanet in vitam æternam: Hoc est verò illud opus, ut credatis in eum, quem misit ille. Deindè Leprosus iste dubitavit de speciali misericordia Domini, quoad curationem lepræ: sed quod dubitaverit de speciali illa misericordia, in Evangelio credentibus promissa, id nondùm probavit Jesuwita: Et si vel maximè hoc probaret, tamen statim sequeretur, leprosum hunc destitutum fuisse Fide Justificante, ac proindè argumentum hoc prorsus esse ἄλλοτριον.

Tertiò nulla est ratio Consequentiae: Multi credentes omnipotentiam Christi impetrarunt beneficia corporalia. Ergo Fides justificans esse potest, quae vel maximè destituitur certitudine de misericordia speciali. Nam Fides illa omnipotentiae divinae, & fides promissionis Evangelicae, non sunt ἀντιφατικῶς opposita: sed tantùm subordinata: ita quidem ut fides promissionis Evangelicae semper praesupponat Fidem omnipotentiae divinae: licèt haec sine illa esse possit. Exemplo possunt esse decem leprosi, quorum novem credebant certè Christum se posse sanare: sed interim destituebantur fide justificante.

Tandem universa collectio Jesuitae plus non infert, quàm dari Fidem aliquam, ad cujus confirmationem Dominus miracula ediderit: quae tamen ex parte hominum destituatur certitudine de speciali misericordia in Evangelio peccatoribus promissa: id quod nos minimè negamus.

Nam geminum miraculorum Christi finem ex Evangelio didicimus: Unum respectu infidelium, ut sic aliquando reddantur ἀναπολόγητοι, Matth. 11, 20. & seqq. Si in Tyro & Sidone facta essent ejusmodi virtutes, &c. Alterum respectu fidelium ut magis magisque in fide Christi confirmarentur.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: Antithesis (continued)

The third and final argument is as follows: In the last chapter of Mark, Christ says: Signs shall follow them that have believed; in my name they shall cast out demons, they shall speak with tongues, etc. Therefore, the faith of miracles is one and the same with justifying and saving faith. Now, however, that [faith] does not regard as its object the special mercy of the remission of sins, but the omnipotence and divinity of the Son of God.

I reply that this argument also suffers from the same παρελέγχοις [fallacious refutations]. For we simply deny the consequence, which is futile and weak, indeed clearly null: for it proceeds thus: Believers performed various signs. Therefore, justifying faith in the act of justification regards the same object which miraculous faith regards. For the futility of this inference is easily seen even from the fact that these signs followed not only believers, but also unbelievers and children of hell, who it is most certain were simply lacking in justifying faith: as in Matt. 7:22. Many will say in that day, Lord, Lord, in thy name have we cast out demons, etc. And then I will confess to them: I never knew you, depart from me, etc. Thus 2 Thess. 2:9, the Apostle testifies that the coming of the Pontiff or the Roman Antichrist will be according to the working of Satan in all power and signs and wonders, etc. That he is nevertheless destitute of justifying faith is as certain as it is certain that the Pontiff is the Antichrist, indeed the slave and excrement of Satan.

But enough and more than enough concerning the first error of the Romanists regarding justifying faith.

Another and indeed a hardly more tolerable error of the Jesuits is that they define justifying faith, not by a certain and indubitable trust in divine mercy promised for Christ's sake: but merely by a general knowledge and assent of historical faith. Whence they do not shudder to write that common faith can be shared by the pious with the impious and wicked: as one may read in the Censura Coloniensium, pages 92 and 111, and in the Jesuit Hieronymus Torrensis, book 2 of the Confessio Augustiniana, chapter 5, § 4.

Bellarmino betrayed and increased this error with notable impiety in book 1 de Justif. chapter 10. Faith, he says, ought to aim at nothing else except the Word of God. For it cannot be certain and infallible unless it rests upon the authority of Him who can neither be deceived nor deceive. But in the Word of God, salvation or the remission of sins is never found announced to ME or to YOU in particular, except to a few, as to the paralytic in Matt. 9:2. Therefore, other men cannot believe, unless altogether rashly, as if from the Word of God, that their sins have been remitted to THEM. And after a few lines, letter C. Nowhere does Scripture say, He who believes that his sins have been remitted to him has eternal life, or is justified: but he who believes in the Son has eternal life. That, however, to believe in the Son is to believe that one's sins have been remitted to oneself through the Son, the adversaries do not have from the Word of God, but from their own interpretation. And after some things: page 960 B. From these conditional propositions a conditional Conclusion is gathered: Therefore I, IF I BELIEVE, have justification and eternal life. But the absolute Conclusion, which the Adversaries want, requires an absolute assumption, namely this: But I BELIEVE in the son. Which absolute assumption is not in the Word of GOD, but in my OPINION. Moreover, this opinion of mine is not only not the Word of GOD, but it can also be fallacious.

And this is the reason for which the Romanists commonly all explode the Trust, which we require as the soul and Form of Justifying Faith, and call it Carnal presumption: but on the contrary, they praise and defend Doubt concerning the Grace of GOD, and concerning the remission of sins and salvation.

This error is too atrocious to be exaggerated enough in words. For first, it is contradictorily opposed to the Scriptures, which do not define justifying Faith through mere and naked knowledge or assent, but also through πεποίθησιν, ἔλεγχον, a certain and immovable trust: as was demonstrated above.

Then Scripture defines this very Trust, not only through the assent of general pronouncements, but also through a special, or as the Jesuit speaks, an absolute confidence, by which each of the faithful applies to himself individually the promises of the Gospel: as will be demonstrated a little later with Examples.

Thirdly, the undoubted truth of the divine promise, confirmed by an oath, sanctions and establishes this immovable trust and individual πληροφορίαν of faith. Ezek. 33, 11. As I live, says GOD, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that he may turn and live.

Fourth, he explodes this Jesuitical conjecture or doubt, that internal and infallible testimony of the Holy Spirit, which, as Scripture testifies, it bears to all believers, as 1 John 5, 10. He who believes in the Son of GOD, has the testimony of GOD IN HIMSELF. Rom. 8, 16. The Spirit bears testimony to our Spirit, that WE ARE the children of GOD.

Fifth, there is added that Effect of Faith, which Scripture assigns to believers, such as that they have PEACE toward GOD, Romans 5, 1. that they OUGHT to approach with CONFIDENCE to the throne of grace, that they may obtain mercy, and help in time of need, Ephes. 3, 12. Heb. 4, 16.

Sixth, there are given from the Scriptures most evident examples of those who, not conditionally or conjecturally but absolutely, assumed that they were in the Grace of GOD, and that their sins were individually forgiven them, as Gal. 2, 16. We know that a man is not justified by the works of the Law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ. And we have believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the Law: because by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified. Gal. 2, 16.

And soon the Apostle repeats the same absolute assumption, verse 20. I live by the faith of the Son of GOD, who loved and delivered himself for ME.

Thus in Rom. 4 the Apostle vehemently urges the same absolute assumption, verses 23, 24. This is not written for his (Abraham's) sake alone, that this was imputed to him. But also for our sake, to whom it shall be imputed, to those who believe in him who raised CHRIST from the dead. The argument of the Apostle proceeds from the hypothesis to the thesis in this manner.

Abraham believed GOD, and this was imputed to him for righteousness. Therefore also any one of us shall be justified in this way. But the faith of Abraham consisted in this, not that he believed generally in every Word of GOD: But that in particular he applied to himself the promises of GOD, concerning the Seed of the woman, or the Messiah, in whom all the Families of the earth were to be blessed, and thus he believed in hope, against hope. Therefore any one of the faithful ought to subsume with Abraham not only conditionally: IF I BELIEVE: but also absolutely: I believe that Christ was delivered for MY sins: and raised for MY iniquities: Rom. 4, 24. last part. Therefore this very faith shall be imputed to ME, no less than to Abraham, for righteousness. The most evident reason of the connection lies in the words of the Apostle already cited: Because this is written not for Abraham alone, but for all who believe in CHRIST. Whence Chrysostom aptly asks, Homily 9. Why is this written thus, unless that we may learn that we also are justified in the same manner? The Apostle inculcates the same absolute assumption, Rom. 10, 9. not saying indefinitely: He who shall have confessed with his mouth, and shall have believed with his heart, shall be saved: but he says emphatically: If YOU shall have confessed with YOUR mouth, IF YOU shall have believed with YOUR heart, YOU shall be saved.

CHRIST himself showed the same absolute assumption, as often as he repeated that: Be of good cheer Son, your faith has made you whole. Nor will the Jesuitical exception have any place here, unless he first shows some evident reason for a difference intervening between the rest of the believers and those to whom Christ said: Be of good cheer, your sins are forgiven you. Which the Adversary will never give. Noting which, the Cologne Jesuits in their Censure, page 122, did not shudder to write: Faith is of general pronouncements, if we contemplate and measure these our times. They certainly wished to say this: That in the times of Christ and the Apostles these absolute assumptions were true. Your faith has made you whole: your sins are forgiven you: but in our time the truth of these assumptions has expired. But may GOD rebuke you, Satan, and quickly crush you under his feet.

Seventh, there were not lacking from among the Pontifical writers themselves those to whom this wicked dogma of the Jesuits, concerning the uncertainty of salvation and perpetual doubt, was most displeasing. Around the year of our Lord 1536, certain Canons of the Provincial Council of Cologne were published, of which Gropper, an otherwise distinguished Pontifical author, is said to have been the author, in which on page 170 this dogma concerning doubt is expressly rejected and disapproved.

Eighth, let the Jesuits explain: Whether the faithful in the Apostles' Creed can and ought truly to profess that they believe in the forgiveness of sins, if they must needs always doubt about it, and ought not to use this absolute assumption: I believe in the forgiveness of sins because of CHRIST: Therefore all my sins are truly forgiven me. We say that we believe in the Forgiveness of sins for this very reason, because we do not doubt it.

Furthermore, for this one reason we pray in the Lord's prayer that our debts be forgiven us: namely, that we may not doubt, according to that of James: He who prays, let him ask with confidence, nothing wavering, James 1, 6. Therefore we confirm our faith with the Sacraments, that we may not doubt: therefore we seek private and public Absolution, that we may not doubt, according to that: Whose sins you shall forgive, they shall be forgiven them.

Finally, we oppose to this impiety even the single eighth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, where the πληροφορία and immovable certainty of justifying faith is asserted several times against the ἐποχήν or Jesuitical doubt, as:

Vers. 1. There is now no Condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Now where there is no Condemnation, there the wrath of GOD has no place: But where there is not the wrath of GOD, there is His Grace: And where this is, there is salvation and life.

Latin:

Tertium & postremum argumentum sic habet: Marci ultimo dicit Christus: Signa ante haec sequentur eos, qui crediderint, in nomine meo daemonia ejicient, linguis loquentur &c. Ergo Fides miraculorum una & eadem est cum fide justificante & salvante. Jam autem illa non respicit tanquàm Objectum Specialem misericordiam remissionis peccatorum, sed Omnipotentiam & Divinitatem Filij Dei.

Respondeo iisdem παρελέγχοις laborare & hoc argumentum. Negamus enim simpliciter Consequentiam, quae futilis & elumbis, imò planè nulla est: Sic enim ea procedit: Credentes ediderunt varia signa. E. Fides justificans in actu Justificationis idem respicit Objectum, quod respicit Fides miraculosa. Futilitas enim hujus collectionis facilè patet vel indè, quòd signa haec secuta sunt non tantùm credentes, sed & incredulos, ac filios gehennae, quos fide Justificante simpliciter caruisse certissimum est: ut Matth. 7, 22. Multi dicent in die illa, Domine Domine, in nomine tuo daemonia ejecimus &c. Et tunc confitebor illis: Nunquàm novi vos, discedite à me, &c. Sic 2. Thess. 2, 9. testatur Apostolus, quòd adventus Pontificis sive Antichristi Romani futurus sit, secundum operationem Satanae in omni virtute & signis & prodigiis &c. Quera tamen fide justificante destitui, tàm certum est, quàm certum Pontificem esse AntiChristum, imò mancipium & excrementum Satanae.

Sed de primo errore Romanensium circa fidem Justificantem plus satis.

Alter & quidem haud tolerabilior error Jesuwitarum est, quòd Fidem Justificantem definiunt, non per certam ac indubitatam fiduciam misericordiae divinae, propter Christum promissae: sed per generalem duntaxat fidei historicae notitiam & assensionem. Undè scribere non exhorrescunt, Fidem communem esse posse pijs cum impijs & sceleratis: uti legere licet in Censura Coloniensium pag. 92. & 111. & apud Jesuwitam Hieronymum Torrensem lib. 2. Confessionis Augustiniana cap. 5. § 4.

Prodidit & insigni impietate auxit hunc errorem Bellarminus lib. 1. de Justif. cap 10. Fides, inquiens, in nihil aliud collimare debet, nisi in Verbum DEI. Non enim potest esse certa & infallibilis, nisi ejus autoritate nitatur, qui nec falli potest, nec fallere. At in Verbo DEI nunquàm reperitur annunciata salus vel remissio peccatorum, MIHI aut ILLI in particulari, nisi paucis quibusdam, ut Paralytico Matth. 9, 2. Non igitur possunt reliqui Homines credere, nisi omninò temerè, tanquàm ex Verbo DEI, SIBI esse remissa peccata. Et post pauca lit. C. Nusquam dicit Scriptura, Qui credit sibi remissa esse peccata, habet vitam aeternam, aut justificatur: sed qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam. Quòd autem credere in filium, sit credere, sibi remissa esse peccata per filium, non habent Adversarij ex Verbo DEI, sed ex interpretatione sua. Et post aliqua: pag. 960 B. Ex his conditionatis propositionibus colligitur conditionata Conclusio: Igitur ego, SI CREDO, habeo justificationem & vitam aeternam. Absoluta verò Conclusio, quam Adversarij volunt, requirit assumtionem absolutam, videlicet illam: Atqui EGO CREDO in filium. Quae assumtio absoluta non est in Verbo DEI, sed in OPINIONE mea. Opinio autem ista mea non sola non est Verbum DEI, sed etiam fallax esse potest.

Et hac causa est, propter quam Romanenses communiter omnes, Fiduciam, quam nos tanquàm animam & Formam Fidei Justificantis requirimus explodunt, & Carnalem praesumtionem nominant: contrà verò Dubitationem de Gratia DEI, deǵ; remissione peccatorum & salute laudant & propugnant.

Atrocior est hic error, quàm ut verbis satis exaggerari possit. Primùm enim Scripturis Contradictoriè adversatur, quae Fidem justificam non definiunt, per solam ac nudam sive notitiam, sive assensum, sed & per πεποίθησιν, ἔλεγχον, certam ac immotam fiduciam: uti supra demonstratum.

Deindè hanc ipsam Fiduciam definit Scriptura, non tantùm per assensum generalium pronunciatorum, sed & per specialem, sive ut Jesuwita loquitur, per absolutam confidentiam, quâ quilibet fidelium sibi in individuo applicat promissiones Evangelii: uti paulò post Exemplis demonstrabitur.

Tertiò, Immotam hanc fiduciam ac πληροφορίαν fidei individualem, sancit ac stabilit indubia veritas promissionis divinae, juramento confirmatae. Jezech. 33, 11. Vivo ego DEUS nolo mortem impij, sed ut convertatur & vivat.

Quartò, explodit Jesuwiticam hanc Conjecturam sive dubitationem, internum illud ac infallibile testimonium Spiritus sancti, quòd Scriptura teste, omnibus credentibus perhibet, ut 1. Joh. 5, 10. Qui credit in Filium DEI, habet testimonium DEI IN SE. Rom. 8, 16. Spiritus testimonium perhibet Spiritui nostro, quòd SIMUS filij DEI.

Quintò, accedit Effectus ille Fidei, quem credentibus adsignat Scriptura, ut quòd PACEM habeant erga DEUM, Roman. 5, 1. quod cum CONFIDENTIA DEBEANT accedere ad thronum gratiæ, ut misericordiam consequantur, & auxilium in tempore opportuno, Ephes. 3, 12. Hebr. 4, 16.

Sextò, Dantur ex Scripturis exempla evidentissima, eorum, qui non conditionaliter aut Conjecturaliter sed absolutè assumserunt, se esse in Gratia DEI, sibi in individuo remissa esse peccata, ut Gal. 2, 16. Scimus non justificari Hominem ex operibus Legis, sed per fidem Jesu Christi. Atqui & nos in Christum Jesum credidimus, ut justificemur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus Legis: propterea quòd non justificabitur ex operibus legis ulla caro. Gal. 2, 16.

Et mox eandem assumtionem absolutam repetit Apostolus, vers. 20. Ego vivo in fide Filij DEI, qui dilexit & tradidit semetipsum pro ME.

Sic Rom. 4. eandem assumtionem absolutam vehementer urget Apostolus, vers. 23, 24. Non scriptum est hoc propter eum solum (Abrahamum) quòd hoc imputatum fuerit ei. Sed etiam propter nos, quibus futurum est, ut imputetur ijs, qui credunt in eum, qui suscitavit CHRISTUM a mortuis. Argumentum Apostoli procedit ab hypothesi ad thesin in hunc modum.

Abrahamus credidit DEO, & imputatum hoc est illi ad justitiam. Ergo & quilibet nostrum ita justificabitur. Atqui fides Abrahæ in eo consistebat, non quòd generaliter credebat omni Verbo DEI: Sed quod in specie sibi applicabat promissiones DEI, de Semine mulieris, sive Messia, in quo benedicendæ omnes Familiæ terræ, & sic credebat in spem, contra spem. Ergo quilibet fidelium cum Abrahamo subsumere debet non tantùm Conditionaliter: SI CREDO: sed & absolutè: Ego credo Christum esse traditum propter peccata MEA: & resuscitatum propter iniquitates MEAS: Rom. 4, 24. ult. Ergo hæc ipsa fides, haud minùs MIHI, atque Abrahamo imputabitur ad justitiam. Ratio Connexi evidentissima latet in verbis jam citatis Apostoli: Quia hoc scriptum est non propter Abrahamum solum, sed propter omnes, qui credunt in CHRISTUM. Unde seitè quæriti Chrysostomus Homil. 9. Cur hoc ita scriptum est, nisi ut discamus, quòd & nos ad eundem modum justificemur? Eandem absolutam assumtionem inculcat Apostolus, Rom. 10, 9. non indefinitè dicens: Qui confessus fuerit ore, Corde autem crediderit, salvabitur: sed ἐμφατικῶς dicit: Si TU confessus fueris ore TUO, SI TU credideris corde TUO, TU salvaberis.

beEandem absolutam assumtionem monstravit CHRISTUS ipse, quoties repetiit illud: Confide Fili, fides tua salvum te fecit. Neq; locum hic habebit exceptio Jesuitica, nisi prius ostenderit evidentem aliquam diversitatis rationem, intercedere reliquis credentibus, cum his, quibus Christus dixit: Confide, remissa sunt tibi peccata. Quam in æternum non dabit Adversarius. Quod ipsum animadvertentes Jesuitæ Colonieses Censura pag. 122. scribere non exhorruerunt: Fides est generalium pronunciatorum, si hæc nostra contemplemur & metiamur tempora. Illud nimirùm dicere voluerunt: Temporibus Christi & Apostolorum veras fuisse absolutas hasce assumtiones. Fides tua salvum te fecit: remissa tibi sunt peccata tua: nostro verò tempore expirasse veritatem istarum assumtionem. Sed increpet te DEUS Satan, & sub pedibus suis conterat citò.

Septimò, non defuerunt ex ipsis Scriptoribus Pontificiis, quibus flagitiosum hoc Jesuwitarum dogma, de incertitudine salutis & dubitatione perpetua maximè displicuit. Circa annum Domini 1536. editi sunt Canones quidam Concilii Provincialis Coloniensis, quorum Gropperus, insignis alioqui Pontificius autor fuisse dicitur, in quibus pag. 170. Dogma hoc de dubitatione disertè rejicitur & improbatur.

Octavò, edisserant Jesuitæ: Nùm fideles in Symbolo Apostolico verè profiteri possint & debeant, se credere remissionem peccatorum, si de ea semper subdubitare necessum habeant, neq; absolutâ hac assumtione uti debeant: Ego credo remissionem peccatorum propter CHRISTUM: Ergò verè remissa sunt mihi omnia peccata mea. Ideò profectò dicimus nos credere Remissionem peccatorum, quia de ea non dubitamus.

Insuper hanc unam ob causam in oratione Dominica precamur remitti nobis debita nostra: ne videlicet dubitemus secundùm illud Jacobi: Qui orat, postulet cum fiducia nihil hæsitans, Jac. 1, 6. Ideo Sacramentis fidem nostram confirmamus, ne dubitemus: ideò Absolutionem privatam & publicam expetimus, ne dubitemus secundùm illud: Quibus remiseritis peccata, remissa ipsis erunt.

Tandem impietati huic opponimus vel unicum caput octavum Epistolæ ad Romanos, ubi aliquoties πληροφορία ac immota certitudo fidei justificantis contra ἐποχήν sive dubitationem Jesuiticam asseritur, ut:

Vers. 1. Nulla nunc Condemnatio ijs, qui sunt in Christo Jesu. Jam ubi nulla est Condemnatio, ibi nec ira DEI locum habet: Ubi autem non est ira DEI, ibi illius est Gratia: At ubi hæc, ibi salus & vita.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: Antithesis (continued)

Vers. 3. GOD, by sending His own Son for sin, condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteousness of GOD might be fulfilled in us. Now if all those things which the law demands of us, have been fulfilled by the Son of GOD, and indeed fulfilled in us, that is, the fruit of this fulfillment is so imputed to us, as if it had been acquired by our own operation: Why, I beseech you, should it be necessary for believers to doubt further concerning the certainty of their salvation?

Vers. 10. If Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin: but the Spirit is life because of righteousness. Such, therefore, is the spiritual κοινωνία (communion) of the faithful with Christ, that they are certain of eternal life, all doubt and fear of condemnation being set aside.

Vers. 15. You have not received the Spirit of bondage again to fear, but the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry Abba Father. And vers. 16. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of GOD. The Apostle is indeed expressing the most noble effect of our adoption through faith, which is filial confidence, the cry and invocation of the most merciful Heavenly Father. Directly opposed to this, however, is fear, doubt, and servile trepidation, such as the Jesuits urge. And indeed this adoption ought to be so much the more certain to us, by how much more precious an earnest it is confirmed, namely by the Spirit, and indeed not the Spirit of the law or of bondage or of fear, but the Spirit of the Gospel, of liberty and of confidence, which dictates an infallible testimony in the hearts of the faithful, that they are children of GOD, so that they may exclaim with the Apostle: I KNOW whom I have believed: That I live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of GOD, who loved me, and gave himself for me. Concerning which matter Chrysostom very elegantly says: If a man, an Angel, an Archangel had promised something, perhaps someone would have doubted: But the Supreme Essence, the Spirit of GOD, who makes us pray, promises to all, bestows what is promised, and bears witness to us within: What place then is there for doubt? But who, he says, makes me certain that this is not a vain persuasion? Either it will be a persuasion of the flesh or of the Spirit: Not of the flesh, for this does not lead to divine things. It is therefore a persuasion of the Spirit: The Spirit of GOD does not lie, wherefore when this attestation is felt in the heart, it is from the Spirit of GOD, it is true, even if sometimes it may be languid.

Vers. 38. & 39. I know πέπεισμαι (I am persuaded), that neither life, nor death, &c. can separate us from the love of GOD. Where the Apostle pronounces indefinitely, that there is nothing in the whole world by which the love of GOD can be intercepted for the pious, or be affected by doubt and uncertainty.

The Jesuit cohort objects that these things pertain only to the Apostle, who could therefore be certain because this was revealed to him peculiarly. I answer that this is most false. For 1. The Apostle attributes this certainty not to any revelation, but to faith, which relies upon the Word of GOD. 2. What the Apostle had from singular revelation, he says were ῥήματα ἄῤῥητα (ineffable words), which it is not lawful for a man to utter. But these things concerning the certainty of his salvation were not ἄῤῥητα (ineffable), because he uttered them. 3. He speaks not only of his own certainty of salvation, but of the common certainty of all believers and the elect. For he delivers in this place a general consolation for all the faithful, by which they ought to sustain and raise themselves against temptations.

Furthermore they object: It is nowhere written: You are blessed, for you there is no condemnation. I answer, in the thesis this is written in the Word of GOD: Every one who believes in Christ shall be saved: As regards the hypothesis and individual persons, that very thing is written incessantly by the Holy Spirit in our hearts, who bears witness with our spirit, that we are the children of GOD.

The faithful believe that θετικὸν (thetic) truth: the faithful experience this hypothetical truth: that is faith: this is the sense of faith. For those who believe know that they believe: he who has a zeal for piety feels that he has it. It is therefore true, as the Jesuits frequently harp on, that nothing is to be believed except what is contained in the Word of God: if you look at universals. Now if you descend to particulars, and inquire about the sense of faith, and about its certainty in the hearts of the faithful, there one must have recourse to the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, who transfers the thesis to the hypothesis.

Thirdly they object, that the Greek word πέπεισμαι (I am persuaded) does not denote a certain confidence, but only some probable opinion or persuasion. But this is also a vain quibble. For the Apostle himself joins the word πείθεσθαι (to be persuaded) with the word for knowing in Romans 14:14, οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι, I know and am persuaded in the LORD. And Phil. 1:25, τοῦτο πεποιθὼς οἶδα, being confident of this I know. Thus 2 Tim. 1:10, to know and to be persuaded are placed as synonyms, and even from that it is clearly hinted that this confidence of faith is not joined with some probable opinion, but with certain knowledge, οἶδα. I know whom I have believed, says the Apostle, and πέπεισμαι, I am persuaded, that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.

Fourthly, Bellarmine objects: That the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit produces only a conjectural certainty: But that conjectures are fallacious and can deceive, lib. 3. de Justif. cap. 9. pag. 1123. e. But the Sophist is caught being a liar and vain, since the Apostle himself elsewhere renders this πεποίθησιν (confidence) by πληροφορίαν (full assurance), speaking of Abraham in this manner: And πληροφορηθεὶς (being fully assured) most fully knowing or determining, that what GOD had promised, he was able also to perform &c. Thus everywhere this word is rendered by a word of knowing. Rom. 6:9, and chap. 8:28, 2 Cor. 5:1, &c.

But the Jesuit brings forward many testimonies from the Scriptures, which he adapts to confirm his dogma.

It is Proverbs 20:9. Who can say, My heart is clean, I am pure from sin.

Ecclesiastes 9:2. Man knows not whether he is worthy of hatred or love.

Ecclesiasticus 5:5. Concerning forgiven sin, be not without fear.

Job 9:20. If I wish to justify myself, my own mouth will condemn me, &c.

David Psalm 19:13. Who understands his faults? Cleanse me from my secret ones.

VI. 1 Cor. 4:4. I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not hereby justified.

VII. Daniel 4:24. Perhaps GOD will forgive your offenses.

VIII. Joel 2:14. Who knows if he will turn and GOD will forgive.

IX. Jonah 3:9. Who knows whether GOD will forgive.

X. Acts 8:22. Repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to GOD, if perhaps it may be forgiven you.

XI. Proverbs 28:14. Blessed is the man who is always fearful.

XII. 2 Cor. 10:18. Not he who commends himself is approved, but whom GOD commends.

XIII. Phil. 2:12. Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.

XIV. 1 Pet. 1:17. Conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourning.

XV. 2 Pet. 1:10. Be diligent, that by good works you may make your calling and election sure.

XVI. And finally the Prophets require various conditions for our Justification: namely, that we seek the Lord with our whole heart, Deut. 4. v. 29. that we turn to the LORD with our whole heart, 2. Chron. 6, 38. that we desist from sin, do good, and seek justice, Isa. 1, 16. that we repent, do judgment and justice, Ezek. 18, 19. that we do what Christ has commanded us, &c. John 15, 14. From all of which it is clear that something is required IN US, in order that we may be justified. But no one can be certain, especially with the certainty of faith, that he has turned to the LORD with his whole heart, and has faith and repentance of the kind that is required. Therefore, no one can be certain, with the certainty of faith, that his sins have been forgiven him.

And this indeed is that structure upon which the Jesuit builds his dogma concerning the uncertainty of salvation. We answer, however, that each and every one of these arguments suffers from a shameful Ignorance of the Refutation. For, regarding the 1st testimony, Solomon is dealing with holiness and justice that is begun and inherent, which certainly is never perfected in this life, but is polluted with various stains of sin, and therefore cannot justify us. Now, however, from the condition and quality of justice that is begun and inherent, to the holiness and justice of Christ, which is imputed to us for salvation through faith, the Consequence does not hold: and an ἀσυλλογισία (non-syllogism) of four terms emerges.

The second suffers from the defect of the common version: For in the Hebrew it is held thus: Whether it be love or hatred, man does not know, whoever is before them, because all things happen equally to the just and the impious. The sense therefore emerges as this: From the happiness or unhappiness of men, it cannot be certainly established or judged whether someone before GOD is just or unjust, pious or impious? dear or hated? which the context proves, since it immediately adds: For all things happen equally to these and those. Furthermore, Solomon in this place does not deal with the certainty by which someone might be certain of his own salvation: but he deals with the judgment of another: Namely, whether someone can be certain and indubitable concerning the faith and salvation of another? Where we ourselves indeed readily grant that such a judgment can and ought to be made only under a condition, and therefore that it is not absolute.

The third suffers from the same defect. For in the Greek it is read: περὶ ἐξιλασμõ μὴ ἀφοβῶ γίνυ, i.e. Do not be secure concerning expiation: or do not be without fear concerning propitiation, so that you add sin upon sin. The sense therefore is that repentance and the expiation of sins are not to be procrastinated, nor are sins to be heaped upon sins. Therefore, what the son of Sirach argues against carnal security, the Jesuit perfidiously twists toward the certainty and πληροφορίαν (full assurance) of faith.

The fourth is again opposed to proper and inherent holiness, or the confidence of one's own works, concerning which we ourselves also maintain that one must not only doubt, but also utterly despair in the act of Justification: by the example of Job, who although he does not dare to trust in his own works, or to defend his innocence before the LORD, nevertheless shows quite evidently that he was most certain concerning the imputed justice and his own salvation: saying, I KNOW that my Redeemer lives, and he will raise me up, &c. And I am going to see him in this FLESH of mine, I and not another. Who would be so impudent as to dare to affirm that there is any doubt in these words?

Latin:

Vers. 3. DEUS misso suo ipsius Filio pro peccato condemnavit peccatum in carne, ut justitia DEI impleretur in nobis. Jam si omnia ea, quæ lex a nobis efflagitat, sunt impleta a Filio DEI, & quidem impleta in nobis, hoc est, impletionis hujus fructus ita nobis imputatur, quasi nostrâpte operatione acquisitus sit: Quorsum obsecro opus fuerit porrò dubitare credentes de salutis suae certitudine?

Vers. 10. Si Christus in vobis est, Corpus quidem mortuum est propter peccatum: Spiritus autem vita est propter justitiam. Ea est ergo Spiritualis κοινωνία fidelium cum Christo, ut certi sint de vita aeterna, omni dubitatione & metu condemnationis seposito.

Vers. 15. Non accepistis Spiritum servitutis amplius ad metum, sed Spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus Abba Pater. Et vers. 16. Qui ipse Spiritus testimonium perhibet Spiritui nostro, nos esse filios DEI. Exprimit nimirum Apostolus nobilissimum Effectum adoptionis nostrae per fidem, qui est filialis fiducia, clamor & invocatio clementissimi Patris Caelestis. Huic verò è diametro est oppositus metus, dubitatio & trepidatio servilis, qualem Jesuitae urgent. Et quidem tanto certior nobis esse debet haec adoptio, quantò pretiosiore arrha est confirmata, nempe Spiritu, & Spiritu quidem non legis sive servitutis aut timoris, sed Spiritu Evangelii, libertatis & fiduciae, qui in cordibus fidelium infallibile dictat testimonium, quòd sint filii DEI, ut cum Apostolo exclamare possint: SCIO, cui crediderim: Quod vivo in carne, vivo per fidem Filii DEI, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Quâ de re eleganter admodùm Chrysostomus: Si homo, Angelus, Archangelus aliquid promiserit, fortè aliquis dubitaverit: Suprema verò Essentia Spiritus DEI, qui orare facit, omnibus promittit, promissum largitur, testimonium nobis intùs perhibet: Quisnám ergò dubitationi locus? Sed quis, inquit, me certum facit, non esse inanem suasum? Aut Carnis aut Spiritus ea erit persuasio: Non carnis, haec enim ad divina non inducit. Est ergò Spiritus persuasio: Spiritus DEI non mentitur, ubi igitur contestatio haec sentitur in corde, ex Spiritu DEI est, vera est, licet aliquando sit languida.

Vers. 38. & 39. Scio πέπεισμαι, quòd neque vita, neque mors, &c. possit nos separare à dilectione DEI. Ubi indefinite pronunciat Apostolus, nihil esse in universo mundo, quo piis interverti, aut dubia atq; incerta affici possit dilectio DEI.

Excipit cohors Jesuitica, haec ad Apostolum tantùm spectare, qui ideò potuerit esse certus, quia hoc peculiariter ipsi sit revelatum. Respondeo falsissimum hoc esse. Nam 1. Apostolus non revelationi alicui, sed fidei, quae Verbo DEI nititur, certitudinem istam tribuit. 2. Quae ex revelatione singulari habuit Apostolus, ea dicit fuisse ῥήματα ἄῤῥητα verba ineffabilia, quae fas non sit homini proferre. At ista de certitudine salutis suae non fuerunt ἄῤῥητα quia protulit. 3. Non de sua tantùm, sed communi credentium atque electorum omnium certitudine salutis loquitur. Tradit enim hoc loco generalem consolationem pro omnibus fidelibus, quâ se adversus tentationes sustentare atq; erigere debeant.

Porrò excipiunt: Nuspiam scriptum esse: Tu es beatus, tibi nulla est Condemnatio. Respondeo, in thesi hoc scriptum esse in Verbo DEI: Omnis credens in Christum, salvabitur: Quoàd hypothesin & singulares personas, scribitur illud ipsum indesinenter à Spiritu sancto in cordibus nostris, qui dat testimonium Spiritui nostro, quòd simus filii DEI.

Illud ergo θετικὸν fideles credunt: hoc hypotheticon fideles sentiunt: Illud est fides: hoc est sensus fidei. Qui enim credunt, sciunt se credere: Qui habet studium pietatis, habere se sentit. Verum proindè est, quod subindè crepant Jesuwitae: Nihil esse credendum, nisi quod in Verbo DEI continetur: si Universalia respicias. Jam si ad singularia descendas, & quaeras de sensu fidei, deq; ejus certitudine in cordibus fidelium, ibi ad internum Spiritus sancti testimonium, est recurtendum, qui thesin transfert ad hypothesin.

Tertiò excipiunt, Verbum Graecum πίπεισμαι non notare certam fiduciam, sed tantum verisimilem aliquam existimationem sive persuasionem. Sed inanis & haec est nugatio. Nam Apostolus ipse verbum πείθεσθαι jungit Verbo sciendi Roman. 14, 14. οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι, Scio & persuasus sum in DOMINO. Et Phil. 1, 25. τοῦτο πεποιθὼς οἶδα, hoc planè persuasus scio. Sic 2. Tim. 1, 10. Scire & persuasum habere pro Synonymis ponuntur, & vel indè liquidò innuitur, Fiduciam hanc fidei, non cum verisimili aliqua existimatione, sed cum certa scientia conjunctam esse, οἶδα. Scio cui crediderim; inquit Apostolus, & πέπεισμαι, persuasum habeo, quòd potens sit depositum meum custodire usq; in diem illam.

Quartò, excipit Bellarminus: Testimonium Spiritus sancti internum gignere tantùm certitudinem conjecturalem: Atqui Conjecturas esse fallaces & posse fallere lib. 3. de Justif. cap. 9. pag. 1123. e.
