Sed mendax & vanus deprehenditur Sophista, siquidem Apostolus ipse πεποίθησιν hanc alibi reddit per πληροφορίαν de Abrahamo verba faciens in hunc modum: Et πληροφορηθεὶς plenissimè sciens sive statuens, quòd quae promisit DEUS, possit ettam praestare &c. Sic passim verbum hoc redditur per Verbum sciendi. Rom. 6, 9. & cap. 8, 28. 2. Cor. 5, 1. &c.

Sed profert Jesuita ex Scripturis benê multa testimonia, quae ad confirmandum dogma suum accommodat.

Est Proverb. 20, 9. Quis potest dicere, mundum est Cor meum, purus sum à peccato.

Ecclesiastae 9, 2. Nescit homo, utrùm odio aut amore dignus sit.

Ecclesiastici 5, 5. De propitiato peccato noli esse sine metu.

Job. 9, 20. Si Justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me, &c.

David Psalm. 19, 13. Delicta quis intelligit? Ab occultis meis munda me.

VI. 1. Cor. 4, 4. Nihil mihi conscius sum, sed in hoc non sum justificatus.

VII. Daniel. 4, 24. Forsan ignoscet DEUS delictis tuis.

VIII. Joel. 2, 14. Quis scit si convertatur & ignoscat DEUS.

IX. Jonæ 3, 9. Quis scit an ignoscat DEUS.

X. Actor. 8, 22. Pœnitentiam age ab hac nequitia tua, & roga DEUM, si fortè remittatur tibi.

XI. Proverb. 28, 14. Beatus homo, qui semper est pavidus.

XII. 2. Cor. 10, 18. Non qui seipsum commendat, ille probatus est, sed quem DEUS commendat.

XIII. Phil. 2, 12. Cum metu & tremore salutem vestram operemini.

XIV. 1. Pet. 1, 17. In timore incolatus vestri tempore conversamini.

XV. 2. Petr. 1, 10. Satagite, ut per bona opera, vocationem vestram & Electionem certam faciatis.

XVI. Et postremò requirunt Prophetæ varias conditiones ad nostri Justificationem: ut nimirùm quæramus Dominum toto corde, Deut. 4. v. 29. ut convertamur ad DOMINUM toto corde nostro, 2. Paral. 6, 38. ut desistamus à peccato, benefaciamus & quæramus justitiam, Jes. 1, 16. ut agamus pœnitentiam, faciamus judicium & justitiam, Jezech. 18, 19. ut faciamus quæ Christus præcepit nobis, &c. Joh. 15, 14. Ex quibus omnibus patet, requiri aliquid IN NOBIS, ut justificemur. At nemo certus esse potest, præsertim certitudine fidei, se toto corde conversum esse DOMINUM, & fidem ac pœnitentiam habere, qualis requiritur. E. nemo certus esse potest, certitudine fidei, sibi remissa esse peccata.

Et hæc quidem est structura illa, cui Jesuwita dogma suum de incertitudine salutis superstruit. Respondemus autem singula ac universa hæc argumenta turpi laborare ignoratione Elenchi. Nam, quoad 1. testimonium, agit Salomon de inchoata ac inhærente Sanctitate, & justitia, quæ certè hac in vita nunquàm perficitur, sed variis peccatorum sordibus est polluta, ac proindè nos etiam justificare nequit. Jam verò à Conditione & qualitate justitiæ inchoatæ, ac inhærentis, ad Sanctitatem & justitiam Christi, quæ ad salutem per fidem nobis imputatur, non valet Consequentia: & emergit ἀσυλλογισία quatuor terminorum.

Alterum laborat vitio vulgatæ versionis: In Hebræo enim sic habetur: An dilectio sit, an odium, nescit homo, quisquis coram illis est, eò quòd universa æquè eveniant justo & impio. Sensûs proindè emergit iste: Ex felicitate vel infelicitate hominum, non posse certò statui aut judicari, nùm aliquis coram DEO sit justus an injustus, pius an impius? carus an exosus? id quod contextus evincit, cùm statim subjicit: Nam his & illis ex æquo omnia eveniunt. Præterea Salomon hoc loco non agit de certitudine, quâ quis de propria sua salute certus esse queat: sed agit de judicio alterius: Nùm videlicet aliquis de alterius fide & salute certus ac indubius esse possit? Ubi certè nos ipsi ultrò largimur, tale judicium non nisi sub conditione fieri posse ac debere, ac proindè absolutum illud non esse.

Tertium eodem vitio laborat. In Græco enim legitur: περὶ ἐξιλασμõ μὴ ἀφοβῶ γίνυ, i. e. Noli securus esse de expiatione: vel de propitiatione ne sis sine timore, ut apponas peccatum super peccatum. Sensus proinde est, pœnitentiam & peccatorum expiationem non essi procrastinandam, neg; peccata peccatis cumulanda. Quæ ergò contra carnalem securitatem disputat Syracides, illud ad certitudinem & πληροφορίαν fidei perfidè torquet Jesuwita.

Quartum rursus oppositum est propriæ atque inhærenti Sanctitati, sive confidentiæ propriorum operum, de quâ nos ipsi quoq; statuimus, non modò esse dubitandum, sed & penitùs desperandum in actu Justificationis: exemplo Jobi, qui licèt non ausit suis operibus confidere, aut innocentiam suam coram DOMINO defendere, tamen de imputatâ justitia & salute sua se certissimum fuisse satis evidenter ostendit: SCIO, inquiens, quòd Redemtor MEUS vivit, & ipse ME resuscitabit, &c. Et EGO visurus sum ipsum in Carne hac MEA, EGO & non alius. Quibus verbis dubitationis aliquid subesse, vix quisquam ita impudens fuerit, qui affirmare ausit?


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: Antithesis (continued)

The fifth has nothing at all to do with the matter: For what if we do not even understand all our transgressions, but many escape our memory, are all sins therefore not going to be forgiven us? Nothing of the sort. For we ask with David to be cleansed even from hidden ones, because we know that the blood of Christ cleanses us from all sin. And just as known sins are not forgiven us because they are known to us: so neither are unknown ones not forgiven because they are hidden: but both these and those are forgiven through the merit of Christ alone apprehended by faith.

The sixth clearly betrays a spirit of giddiness in the Jesuits. For above they conceded that Paul was most certain of his salvation, and that from a singular revelation: Here, however, they deny that very thing, and prattle that he doubted, because he writes in 1 Cor. 4, 4: I am conscious of nothing, but in this I am not justified. A liar ought to have a good memory. But to the point: A gross Ignorance of the Refutation is committed. For Paul does not at all deny that he is certain of his justification: but he denies that he is justified from the fact that he was conscious of nothing against himself. But what has this to do with the present matter?

The seventh and the following three urge those dubitative words: Perhaps, perchance, Who knows? concerning which two things are to be noted. 1. That they are not predicated of the remission of sins and the certainty of the same; but of the remission of bodily punishments, which it is certain that GOD sometimes remits to those who repent, and sometimes does not remit. Therefore, concerning the remission of these, just as we readily concede that we must doubt, and that one must pray for it only under a condition: so we simply deny that any firm conclusion can be drawn from there concerning doubt about the remission of sins. For the reason for the diversity is clearly evident from the very diversity of the bodily and spiritual promises themselves. Furthermore, it is also to be noted that the phrases produced by the Adversary cannot generate any thesis or universal Rule concerning the salvation of believers and its certainty, because in all those places the Prophet and the Apostle are not speaking with believers, or those justified through faith: but with the impious and manifest hypocrites, as in Acts 8:22 with Simon Magus: or certainly with such men about whom it was quite uncertain whether they were truly or feignedly doing penance. Therefore, just as nothing certain can be pronounced concerning the salvation of these, so from that no consequence is valid for those justified through faith.

The eleventh, XIII, and XIV. They are shamefully deceived by ignorance of the refutation. For first, in the warnings and exhortations which are general and are directed to the whole Church, one must see what is appropriate for each person. For there are many who deceive themselves with a false opinion and imagine for themselves an excellent faith, of which, however, they have not perceived even the first beginnings. Therefore, those admonitions are deservedly inculcated upon them, that they may be fearful, that they may work out their salvation with fear and trembling, that they may conduct themselves with fear during the time of their sojourn. Furthermore, the Saints themselves must also be diligently admonished to flee carnal security, to guard against the attacks of Satan, and to be solicitous about their salvation. But this does not at all hinder them from being meanwhile most certain of their salvation. For there is a double fear: Servile and filial: Servile cannot stand with true faith: But filial does not at all exclude the certainty of faith, but only prohibits carnal security. Finally, the pious and faithful, however certain they may be of the Remission of sins, nevertheless work out their salvation with fear and trembling, insofar as they are subject to the perpetual temptations of the flesh and of Satan.

The twelfth does not contribute anything to the matter: Since that passage is expressly opposed to the vain boasting and arrogance of the Pseudo-Apostles, who used to boast of their own labors and thought contemptuously and abjectly of the studies and labors of the Apostles. Therefore, the Apostle wishes that he who wishes to boast, should boast in the Lord, because he who commends himself detracts from the glory due to God and assigns it to himself. Such self-commendation renders no one approved, but rather suspected of imposture, and more to be despised and fled from than to be looked up to.

The fifteenth labors at the beginning with a manifest crime of falsehood. For these three words (through good works) are not found in the Greek copies, but have been interpolated by the Papists. Furthermore, I pray the Jesuits to show us the reason for the consequence in this argument: Peter admonishes that we make our calling and Election firm. Therefore he teaches that one must doubt the certainty of the remission of sins. Rather, we invert the argument in this manner: where there is the firmness of our calling and Election, there is also the certainty of salvation. But Peter demands from believers the firmness of calling and Election. Therefore, he also demands from them the certainty of salvation. The connection of the major premise is evident in itself. For hesitation or doubt concerning salvation or the Remission of sins does not produce the firmness of calling: but rather enervates it, indeed, utterly overturns it.

The sixteenth and last is deceived by the Sophism of heterozētēseōs (asking other questions). For it is not asked in this place: what is required both for the Justification of a man, and from a Man already justified through faith: whether, namely, he ought to declare his faith through works of piety, both toward God and toward his neighbor? For we ourselves do not at all deny this. But this is the question: Whether a Man justified through faith can be certain of the grace of God and his own salvation? or whether he ought to doubt both? Now the Jesuit will not have given his affirmative proof until he has shown what is the nerve of the consequence in this argument, which, according to his own opinion, ought to be formed thus: The Lord must be sought with the whole heart, and our conversion to the same must be done with the whole heart, likewise, penance is to be done, judgment and justice are to be performed. Therefore, we must doubt the certainty of our salvation, which is truly an argument from a stick to a corner.

If the Jesuit infers: But no one can be certain that he is converted to the Lord with his whole heart, or that he has such faith as is required. Therefore, he cannot be certain of his salvation either. We answer that he is begging the question and is shamefully trifling. For this very thing is placed in Controversy: Whether the certainty of our salvation depends upon the quality and dignity of our conversion and faith: which we simply deny. The Adversary, however, sophistically accepts it as confessed: and thus from false presuppositions infers a false consequence.

Moreover, the Jesuit continues, and strives to confirm his same thesis with various reasons, which it would be worth the effort to examine briefly.

The first is such: Nothing can be certain with the certainty of faith unless it is either immediately contained in the Word of God, or is deduced from the Word of God by an evident Consequence: For it is not faith unless it rests upon the authority of the divine word. But this particular proposition is not contained in the Word of God: Such or such a Man is truly justified. Furthermore, this cannot be proven by an evident Consequence: For the reasoning by which one would conclude the certainty of faith concerning his own justification from the Word of God ought to be this: The Word of God testifies that all who are truly converted to God and seriously doing penance obtain the indulgence and grace of sins. But my conversion and penance are evident to me. Therefore, it is certain to me, with the certainty of faith, that I have received indulgence and grace. Now, however, this subsumption is not only false, but also impossible.

I reply. 1. The major premise being granted, the minor is simply false. For the certainty of our salvation, besides the fact that it rests upon universal and entirely indubitable promises, is moreover also clearly expressed in a particular way in Rom. 10, 9: If you believe in your heart that God raised Christ from the dead, you will be saved. Where the emphasis of the second person must be observed: for the Apostle did not say indefinitely: He who believes in his heart etc. will be saved: but he says emphatically: If YOU shall believe with your heart &c: You shall be saved. Where he certainly addresses individuals, so that individuals separately, and thus each one in the individual or particular, may certainly promise salvation to himself believing.

Then as regards the evident Consequence, we are certainly not destitute of it from the word of God, although we reason much otherwise than Bellarmine would wish. For our reasoning proceeds thus: Universal promises of grace are to be safely and undoubtedly believed and trusted. Now, however, universal promises of Grace promise salvation and eternal life, not to this one or that one only, but to all believers whatsoever. Therefore it would be a crime and a sin to doubt even in the slightest about the certainty of those promises. Now the subsumption in the particular is made by all believers: I truly believe that God for Christ's sake will forgive me all my sins, and will receive me into grace. Therefore I can be most certain of my salvation. The reason for the connection is most evidently clear, because the Evangelical promises are not restricted to certain individuals only: but are universally diffused to all believers whatsoever, so that whoever shall have believed in Christ, can, nay indeed ought to, be certain of his own salvation.

But Bellarmine insists: Many think they have true faith, which however they do not have, and therefore they are deceived. I answer, that we are not disputing about the faith of these either: For those who are either Hypocrites, or are swollen with a vain persuasion of faith, they certainly are nothing to us: nor do we assign any certainty of faith to them: but the Question is about those who, namely, peacefully and solely acquiesce in the promises of grace, and promise salvation to themselves only through and because of the merit of Christ? That the faith of these is as true as it is joined with πληροφορίᾳ or certainty of salvation, we are most persuaded. For these, by the example of Paul, can truly affirm: I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day. 2 Tim. 1:12. Added to this is the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, who testifies to the Spirit of believers that they are the Children of God.

Latin:

Quintum nihil quicquam ad rem facit: Quid enim? si vel maximè non intelligamus omnia delicta nostra, sed plurima nostram memoriam fugiant, nùm ideò non omnia peccata nobis erunt remissa? Nihil profectò minùs. Ideò enim petimus cum Davide, ab occultis etiam mundari, quia scimus, Christi sanguinem mundare nos ab omni peccato. Et sicut non ideò cognita peccata nobis remittuntur, quia sunt nobis cognita: ita neque incognita non remittuntur, quia sunt occulta: sed tam hæc quàm illa remittuntur per solum Christi meritum fide apprehensum.

Sextum Spiritum vertiginis in Jesuwitis manifestè prodit. Nam suprà concesserunt, Paulum fuisse certissimum de salute sua, idq; ex singulari revelatione: Hic verò idipsum negant, & dubitasse eum garriunt, propterea, quòd 1. Cor 4, 4. scribat: Nihil mihi conscius sum, sed in hoc non sum justificatus. Mendacem oportebat esse memorem. Sed ad rem: Crassa committitur Ignoratio Elenchi. Nam minimè omnium negat Paulus se certum esse de justificatione sua: sed negat, se ex eo justificatum esse, quòd nullius rei conscius sibi fuerit. Sed quid hoc ad rhombum præsentem.

Septimum & sequentia tria, urgent vocabula illa dubitativa: Fortè, forsan, Quis scit? de quibus duo sunt notanda. 1. Prædicari illa non de remissione peccatorum ejusdemq; certitudine; sed de remissione pœnarum corporalium, quas DEUM interdum pœnitentibus remittere, interdum verò non remittere certum est. De harum ergò remissione, uti dubitãdum nobis, quin pro ea etiam non nisi sub conditione orandum esse facile concedimus: ita indè ad dubitationem de remissione peccatorũ collectionem aliquam firmam institui posse simpliciter negamus. Ratio enim diversitatis, ex ipsarum etiam promissionum corporalium ac Spiritualium diversitate, luculenter patet. Deindè & illud notandum, quod phrases ab Adversario productæ non possunt thesin sive Regulam aliquam universalem, de salute credentium, ejusque certitudine gignere, propterea quod in omnibus illis locis sermo est Prophetis & Apostolo non cum credentibus, sive per fidem justificatis : sed cum impijs & hypocritis manifestis, ut Actor. 8, 22. cum Simone Mago : vel certè cum ejusmodi hominibus, de quibus admodum incertum erat, nùm verè an simulatè agerent pœnitentiam. De horum ergò salute etiam, uti nihil certi pronunciari potest, ita indè ad justificatos per fidem nulla valet Consequentia.

Vndecimum, XIII. & XIV. Ignoratione Elenchi turpiter fallunt. Primùm enim in comminationibus, atque exhortationibus, quæ generales sunt, & ad totam Ecclesiam diriguntur, videndum est, quid cuique conveniat. Sunt enim multi qui falsâ opinione seipsos fallunt, & egregiam sibi fidem imaginantur, cujus tamen ne prima quidem initia perceperunt. His ergò meritò inculcantur admonitiones illæ, ut sint pavidi, ut salutem cum timore & tremore operentur, ut cum timore versentur, incolatus sui tempore. Deindè ipsi etiam Sancti sedulò admonendi sunt, ut securitatem carnalem fugitant, Satanæ impetus præcaveant, & de salute sua sint solliciti. Hoc verò nihil impedit, quò minus de salute sint interim certissimi. Duplex enim est timor: Servilis & filialis: Servilis cum fide vera stare nequit: Filialis verò fidei certitudinem minimè excludit, sed securitatem tantùm carnalem prohibet. Tandem pij & fideles, quantumvis certi de Remissione peccatorum, cum timore tamen & tremore salutem suam operantur, quatenùs perpetuis tentationibus carnis & Satanæ sunt obnoxij.

Duodecimum nihil quicquam ad rem facie : Siquidem vanæ gloriationi atque jactantiæ Pseudo-Apostolorum locus ille ex professo est oppositus, qui suos jactitabant labores, deque Apostolorum studijs & laboribus contemtim & abjectè sentiebant. Vult proindè Apostolus, ut qui gloriari velit, in Domino glorietur, propterea quòd qui seipsum commendat, gloriam Deo debitam detrahat, sibique adsignet. Qualis propria commendatio probatum reddit neminem, sed suspectum potiùs de impostura, magisque contemnendum ac fugiendum, quàm suspiciendum.

Decimum quintum laborat initiò manifesto crimine falsi. Nam tria hæc vocabula (per bona opera) in Græcis exemplaribus non reperiuntur, sed interpolata sunt à Pontificijs. Deindè ostendant obsecro Jesuvvitæ nobis rationem Consequentiæ in hoc argumento, Petrus admonet, ut vocationem & Electionē nostram firmam efficiamus. Ergo docet dubitandum esse de certitudine remissionis peccatorum. Quin invertimus potiùs argumentū in hunc modū: ubi est vocationis & Electionis nostræ firmitudo, ibi salutis etiā certitudo. Atqui Petrus à credentibus exigit vocationis & Electionis firmitudinem. E- | ab ijsdem etiam exigit salutis, certitudinem. Majoris connexum per se patet. Nam hæsitatio sive dubitatio de salute sive Remissione peccatorum non parit vocationis firmitudinem : sed eam potiùs enervat, imò penitùs evertit.

Decimum sextum ac postremum fallit Sophismate ἑτεροζητήσεως Non enim hoc loco quæritur: quid requiratur tùm ad Justificationem hominis, tùm ab Homine per fidem jam justificato: utrum nimirum fidem suam per opera pietatis, tùm erga Deum, tùm erga proximum declarare debeat? Hoc enim nos ipsi minimè negamus. Sed hoc quæstionis est, An Homo per fidem justificatus, de gratia Dei & salute sua certus esse possit? an verò de utraque dubitare debeat? Jam Affirmativam suam probatam haud priùs dederit Jesuvvita, quàm oftenderit, quis sit nervus Consequentiæ in hoc argumento, quod ex ipsius sententia sic informari debet: Quærendus est Dominus ex toto corde, & Conversio nostra ad eundem debet fieri ex toto corde, item, pœnitentia est agenda, faciendum judicium & justitia. Ergo de salutis nostræ certitudine nobis est dubitandum, nimirum argumentum à baculo ad angulum.

Si inferat Jesuvvita: At nemo certus esse potest, se toto corde esse conversum ad Dominum, vel talem habere fidem, qualis requiritur. Ergo neq; de salute etiam certus esse potest. Respondemus, ipsum petere principium &turpiter nugari. Hoc ipsum enim est in Controversia positum: Num salutis nostræ certitudo à nostræ conversionis ac fidei qualitate & dignitate pendeat : id quod nos simpliciter negamus. Adversarius autem pro confesso Sophisticè accipit: & sic ex falsis præsuppositis falsam infert consequentiam.

Cæterùm pergit Jesuvvita, & varijs rationibus eandem suam thesin confirmare studet, quas paucis examinare operæ precium fuerit.

Prima talis est: Non potest aliquid certum esse certitudine fidei, nisi aut immediatè contineatur in Verbo Dei, aut ex Verbo Dei per evidentem Consequentiam deducatur: Fides enim non est, nisi verbi divini autoritate nitatur. Atqui in Verbo Dei non continetur particularis ista propositio: Talis vel talis Homo verè justificatus est. Deindè per evidentem Consequentiam probari hoc non potest: Nam ratiocinatio, quâ quis certitudinem fidei de sua justitia, ex Verbo Dei cõcluderet, hæc esse deberet: Verbum Dei testatur, omnes verè conversos ad Deum, & pœnitentiam seriò agentes, peccatorum indulgentiam & gratiam obtinere. Mihi autem evidens est mea Conversio & pœnitentia. Ergo mihi certum est, certitudine fidei, me indulgentiam & gratiam accepisse. Iam verò subsumtio hæc non modò falsa, sed & impossibilis est.

Respondeo. 1. Concessâ Majore, Minorem simpliciter esse falsam. Certitudo enim salutis nostræ, præterquàm quòd innititur Universalibus & prorsus indubijs promissionibus, insuper etiam particularis evidenter expressa est Rom. 10, 9. Tu credideris in corde tuo, quòd Deus excitavit Christum à mortuis, salvaberis. Ubi observanda venit Emphasis secundæ personæ: Non enim indefinitè dixit Apostolus: Qui corde crediderit &c. salvabitur: sed ἐμφατικῶς dicit: Si TV credideris corde tuo &c : Tu salvaberis. Ubi certè singulos compellat, ut singuli seorsim, & sic quisque in individuo sive particulari, sibi credenti salutem certò polliceri possit.

Deindè quoad evidentem Consequentiam, certè ea ex verbo Dei non destituimur, licèt multò aliter ratiocinemur, quàm Bellarminus velit. Sic enim procedit nostra ratiocinatio: Promissionibus gratiæ universalibus tutò & indubitatè est credendum & confidendum. Jam verò promissiones Gratiæ universales salutem & vitam æternam compromittunt, non huic vel illi tantùm, sed omnibus omninò credentibus. Ergò scelus & piaculum fuerit, de certitudine istarum promissionum vel tantillum dubitare. Iam subsumtio in particulari fit ab omnibus credentibus: Egò verè credo, Deum propter Christum mihi remissurum omnia peccata mea, mequè in gratiam recepturum. Ergo de salute mea possum esse certissimus. Ratio connexi evidentissimè patet, quòd promissiones Evangelicæ non sunt restrictæ ad quædam tantùm individua: sed universaliter sunt diffusæ ad omnes omninò credentes, ut quisquis in Christum crediderit, de salute suâ certus esse possit, imo verò debeat.

Sed instat Bellarminus: Multi putant se habere veram fidem, quam tamen non habent, ac proindè falluntur. Respondeo, neque de horum etiam fide nos disputare: Qui enim vel sunt Hypocritæ, vel inani persuasione fidei turgent, illi profectò nihil ad nos: neque etiam ullam fidei certitudinem illis assignamus: sed de istis est Quæstio, qui nimirùm in promissionibus gratiæ, placidè ac unicè acquiescunt, & salutem sibi pollicentur tantùm per & propter meritum Christi? Horum certò fidem uti veram, ita cum πληροφορίᾳ sive certitudine salutis conjunctam esse, habemus persuasissimum. Hi enim exemplo Pauli verè affirmare possunt: Scio cui crediderim, & mihi persuasum est, eum posse depositum meum in illum diem servare. 2. Timoth. 1, 12. Accedit internum Spiritus Sancti testimonium, qui contestatur Spiritui credentium, quòd sint Filii Dei.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: Antithesis (continued)

The other Jesuitical argument is this: No article of faith in any Symbol of faith commands one to believe certainly, so that each one may establish for himself in particular that his sins have been forgiven. Therefore no one is even bound to believe certainly with the certainty of faith that his sins have been forgiven.

I answer: That even from this one argument it is evident that the Jesuits are to be held as atheists and unbelievers, while they dare to assert so rashly: That nowhere, either in the Scriptures or in the Canons of the Church, does a precept exist concerning the certainty of salvation in particular. For 1. such a precept exists in the sacred writings. Acts 16:31. BELIEVE IN THE LORD JESUS, and you shall be saved, you and your house: Thus the Savior himself to the ruler of the synagogue: Do not fear, μόνον πίςευε only believe. Mark 5:36. Luke 8:50.

Then let the Jesuitical [party] explain to us, whether or not the Church commands everyone to believe for himself in the individual that his sins have been forgiven: when in the Apostolic Symbol everyone confesses for himself. 1. I believe the forgiveness of sins. 2. I believe life everlasting. Either therefore let the Jesuits expunge this πληροφορικὸν word I believe from the Apostolic Symbol and the rest: or by an unheard-of gloss let them show this word to mean the same as I doubt or I hesitate. And let the impious Canon of the Tridentine Conventicle, which the Jesuit brings forward, be gone from this place, to which we oppose the Canon of the provincial Council of Cologne, of the year 1536, which expressly rejects and disapproves of this Jesuitical dogma.

Finally, he repeatedly brings up this cuckoo-song: Where there is fear, there is no certainty: But Believers and the Elect ought always to fear, according to that. Rom. 11:20. Do not be high-minded, but fear: Therefore in Believers and the Elect there cannot be certainty.

I answer, that it has already been shown above, that one must accurately distinguish between servile fear, such as the Jesuits attribute to Believers contrary to the mind of the Apostle, and filial fear, which alone the Apostle requires in Believers. Now, however, just as servile fear cannot stand with the certainty of faith: For such is in the Devils, who believe and tremble: so filial fear rather fosters, preserves, and increases the certainty of faith: For it causes the faithful to grieve seriously, as often as they offend God by their sins, and to fear lest they offend Him further: And yet they are perpetually persuaded of God's love toward them. Furthermore, that fear is falsely defined by doubt concerning the Grace of God, when it ought to be defined by the flight from sins, pride, and the offense of God.

But there still remain arguments by which Bellarmine strives to confirm that justifying faith is not trust. And first, indeed, from Rom. ch. 4, 19 and the three following, where the faith of Abraham is described, he infers thus: Abraham did not consider his own body dead: but he was fully persuaded that God was also able to do what He had promised. But consideration pertains to the intellect, to which trust does not pertain. Thus the Greek πληροφορηθεὶς is to know most fully. But to know most fully is of the intellect, not of the will: just as, on the contrary, to have trust is of the will, not of the intellect. Therefore, the faith of Abraham, and consequently all justifying faith, is not trust, but only a certain assent.

I answer, the argument is flawed. 1. παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. For from the position of one part, the consequence does not hold for the negation of the other. Thus this collection does not hold: The Apostle, in the word 'considered,' expressed one part of faith, namely assent: Therefore, he excluded the other, namely trust. 2. The sophist plays with an inconvenient translation. For the Greek word πληροφορηθεὶς, even if it might perhaps denote the same thing somewhere as 'to know most fully,' as the Jesuit renders it: nevertheless, in this place it obtains a more evident meaning, namely one which shows that the faith of Abraham was certain, infallible, invincible, and not to be overcome by any doubts or difficulties: where surely he would be a fool who does not see that trust is denoted. And what, I ask, does it mean otherwise, that the Apostle renders this word πληροφορηθεὶς in the preceding verse, 18, by this phrase, that Abraham believed in hope, against hope. If against hope, certainly not through the Intellect: For thus he believed not against hope, but through an immovable Trust in the truth of the divine promises.

Finally, that clear explanation of the Apostle approaches in verse 20: he did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief: Where not simple incredulity is noted, as Bellarmine chatters, but such doubt and hesitation as wavers somewhat concerning the truth of God's promises. That against this, full assurance and immovable trust are opposed, even against hope, is too manifest to require laborious proof.

II. Argument, the Apostle, 1 Cor. 13:13, distinguishes faith and hope as two things different from each other. But trust is nothing other than strengthened hope. Therefore, trust indeed arises from faith, but it cannot be the same as faith, unless we wish to confuse what the Apostle himself has so openly distinguished.

I answer, the argument fails by a fallacy of equivocation. For faith and hope differ only in a certain respect, not absolutely. As 1. by reason of order: For faith is by nature always prior to hope, because unless something is believed, it cannot be hoped for: But something is believed which is not hoped for: although nothing can be hoped for which is not believed, as Augustine teaches in book 8 of the Enchiridion. 2. Faith is of evil things equally as of good things: indeed, even of past things: Hope is only of good and future things: just as fear is of evil things. 3. Faith properly in place of an object regards the promise of good things: But hope regards the good things themselves promised: for a man does not hope for, but believes, the promise of eternal life: but he hopes for eternal life itself. And to that extent we agree with the Jesuit, that faith and hope are things that are different. But as to his arguing from that, that faith is not trust, because trust is nothing other than strengthened hope: he commits the fallacy of the consequent. For although there is some discrepancy between hope and faith, yet the kinship of both is such that Scripture, through a certain permutation of words, calls faith hope, and hope faith: so that to hope in God is frequently put for to believe in God: Thus Abraham is said to have believed in hope against hope, having accepted the hoped-for, for the believed.

Then these two virtues are so subordinated, and so cohere, that they cannot be torn apart. Whence Augustine in the place just now cited: Faith working through love cannot be without hope, nor love without hope, nor hope without love, nor both without faith. Furthermore, the Apostle in Romans 5 shows that hope also has its origin from faith. And what will the Jesuit answer to the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11:1, who defines faith as being the substance of things hoped for, the firm trust of those things which are hoped for. Relying on which reasons we invincibly infer that faith and hope are indeed distinct, but virtues so related, that he would be worthy of hellebore who would wish to expunge trust, or strengthened hope, from justifying faith.

III. Argument: Paul says that through faith the intellect is led captive into the obedience of Christ. Therefore, faith pertains only to the intellect and not to the will: and consequently is not trust.

I answer: There is more in the consequent than in the antecedent. For this only follows: Therefore faith pertains to the intellect, which we by no means deny. Now if the sophist subsumes, Therefore it pertains only to the intellect, we retort that: From the affirmation of one part, the consequence to the negation of the other is not valid.

IV. Argument: Faith is the cause of trust: For through faith we have trust. Ephesians 3:12. Therefore faith is not trust itself.

I answer: Faith is taken in two ways, either absolutely or relatively. Considered absolutely, insofar as it assents to the Evangelical promises, it is the cause of trust, and not trust itself. But considered relatively, insofar as it now fully acquiesces in those very promises: to that extent Faith is now trust itself. For Faith has its own degrees, and when it attains its full form, and as it were ἐντελέχειαν, it is and is called πεποίθησις and πληροφορία or trust. And the Apostle hints at this very thing, Rom. 1, 17. The righteousness of God, he says, is revealed in the Gospel from faith to faith, from faith that is undoubtedly weak, to faith that is robust, acquiescing with full trust of mind in the merit of Christ.

V. And the last: The act of faith in the Scriptures is said to be, To believe, but not To trust. Therefore, Faith is only assent, but not trust.

I answer: The act of faith in the Scriptures is defined either generally, according to objects of every kind: and then we do not deny that its act is To believe: or it is defined specially, and indeed by reason of Justifying Faith: and then we simply deny that its act is only To believe or to assent. For Scripture names such faith πληροφορίαν, πεποίθησιν, παῤῥησίαν, that is, certain trust, persuasion, confidence, by which one confidently acquiesces in the promise of Grace: and this is justifying Faith, Hebr. 10, 22. Let us draw near with a true heart and certain persuasion of faith. And verse 35. Do not cast away your παῤῥησίαν, your boldness or confidence, as the old version has it, etc.

But Bellarmine continues, and adds a third error in chapter 7 of book 1 on Justification: contending that Faith is not knowledge, but assent, and that to believe is nothing other than to assent to the doctrines of the Church, even if you are ignorant of what kind it is, using chiefly a double kind of argument.

The former is such: Faith is a way and a step toward understanding, according to that of Is. 7, 9. Unless you believe, you shall not understand. Therefore, Faith is not understanding.

The latter sounds thus: Knowledge is something distinct from faith. 1 Cor. 13, 2. Therefore, Faith is not knowledge.

I answer: Both objections betray a great ἀῤῥωσίαν διανοίας (weakness of mind) in the Adversary. He fought before that Faith is not trust, but only assent. Now, however, he denies that Faith is knowledge. And yet there is no assent without knowledge. For no one assents to that which he does not know and understand, and indeed either through the discourse of reason or through a revelation made in the word of God. But as for the former objection, we do not read in Isa. 7: If you do not believe, you shall not understand: but you shall not be faithful, or as others render it, you shall not be stable, which does nothing for the Jesuit's cause.

The latter objection betrays remarkable stupidity. For what is the logic of the consequence: Knowledge is something distinct from faith. Therefore, faith is not knowledge. A boy in the schools would certainly refute this petulance of reasoning and show that all definitions consist of a genus: which, considered in itself, is something distinct from its defined term: as Animal is something distinct from Man: Therefore, will Man not be an Animal? Thus, a habit is something distinct from Liberality and the other virtues: Therefore, will the virtues not be habits? We oppose to the Jesuit in this place that single passage of the sixth chapter to the Romans: where the Apostle names faith γνῶσιν (knowledge) and λογισμὸν (reasoning) in verses 6, 9, 11. Thus, he expressly assigns knowledge to the faith of Abraham and in general of all believers, and indeed not some cold or superficial knowledge: but certain and immovable, which is joined with πληροφορία (full assurance); as in Rom. 4:21, he knew fully. And Rom. 8:28, We know that to those who love God. Rom. 14:14, I know and am confident in the Lord. 2 Cor. 5:1, We know that after, etc.

But the Jesuit also betrays a fourth error, contending that Faith has its seat only in the intellect: moved chiefly by this reason.

It is impossible that one virtue should be in two faculties that are distinct in genus. Therefore, neither can Faith be in the intellect and in the will at the same time.

I answer: This argument fights expressly against that Apostolic one. Rom. 10:10, With the heart one believes unto righteousness. Therefore, the subject or seat of justifying Faith is not the brain or the intellect only, but also the Heart or the will. For with the heart, says the Apostle, not with the intellect, one believes unto righteousness: because in the intellect there can be excellent knowledge, excellent assent, but not unto righteousness, unless the faith of the heart, that is, trust, is present. As for the philosophical axiom upon which the Jesuit relies, I answer:

1. That this question which is being discussed is not of philosophy but of faith: and therefore it can and ought not to be judged even from philosophical principles. 2. The Jesuit has not yet explained whether and how the δυνάμεις (faculties) or powers of one soul by essence, namely the mind or intellect, and the heart or will, differ in genus itself, or as others speak, in their subjects.

Certainly, even in the schools of the philosophers, it is placed beyond the hazard of doubt that the motions of the faculties of the soul, namely of the mind and the will, correspond to each other, so that such as the assent and knowledge are in the mind, such are the motions that the will itself conceives. Furthermore, among the Scholastic Doctors, Bonaventure especially, this rule has long since prevailed: It is no inconvenience to posit one habit both in the reason and in the will: especially since in this place the mind or intellect is understood not as merely theoretical, but practical, insofar as it is joined to the appetitive part. Finally, Scripture itself does not always observe this philosophical ἀκρίβειαν (precision), as when it attributes to the heart not only trust, but also knowledge, which properly pertains to the intellect, as Ps. 119:11, The Saint hides these words in his Heart. Luke 24:25, Slow of heart to believe.

And thus far we have dispatched the first Controversy concerning justifying Faith, which is namely: What is justifying Faith? The second Controversy follows:

Latin:

Altera Jesuiticæ ratio est hæc: Nullus articulus fidei in ullo Symbolo fidei jubet certò credere, ut quisque statuat sibi in particulari esse remissa peccata. Ergo nemo etiam tenetur certò credere certitudine fidei, sibi esse remissa peccata.

Respondeo: Vel ex hoc uno argumento patescere Jesuitas pro ἀθέοις καὶ ἀπίστοις esse habendos, dum usque adeò temerè asserere audent: Nuspiam vel in Scripturis, vel in Canonibus Ecclesiæ præceptum extare de certitudine salutis in particulari. Nam 1. tale præceptum extat in sacris. Actor. 16,13. CREDE IN DOMINUM IESVM, & salvus eris tu & domus tua: Sic Servator ipse ad archisynagogam: Noli timere, μόνον πίςευε tantummodò crede. Marci 5,36. Luc. 8, 50.

Deindè edisserat nobis Jesuitica, an non Ecclesia jubeat quenque pro se in individuo credere sibi remissa esse peccata: quando in Symbolo Apostolico quisque pro se profitetur. 1. Credo remissionem peccatorum. 2. Credo vitam æternam. Aut ergo verbum hoc πληροφορικὸν Credo, expungant ex Symbolo Apostolico & reliquis, Jesuvitæ : aut per inauditam glossam verbum hoc ostendant idem significare ac Dubito sive hæsito. Et facessat hoc loco impius Canon Conciliabuli Tridentini, quem profert Jesuvita, cui opponimus Canonem Concilij provincialis Coloniensis, Anni 1536, qui dogma hoc Jesuviticum disertè rejicit & improbat.

Tandem subindè repetit hunc κοκκυσμὸν : Ubi timor, ibi nulla certitudo : Atqui Credentes & Electi semper timere debent, secundum illud. Rom. 11,20. Noli altum sapere, sed time : Ergo in Credentibus & Electis non potest esse certitudo.

Respondeo, jam supra ostensum esse, quòd accuratè distinguendum sit inter timorem servilem, qualem Jesuvitæ Credentibus præter mentem Apostoli affingunt, & inter timorem filialem, quem solùm Apostolus in Credentibus requirit. Jam verò uti timor servilis cum fidei certitudine stare nequit : Talis enim est in Diabolis, qui credunt & contremiscunt : ita Timor filialis certitudinem fidei magis fovet, conservat & auget : Efficit enim ille, ut fideles seriò doleant, quoties peccatis suis Deum offendunt, & metuunt, ne porrò offendant ipsum : Et tamen de Dei amore erga se perpetuò persuasi sunt. Deindè falsò definitur Timor iste per dubitationem de Gratia Dei, cùm definiri debeat per fugam peccatorum, superbiæ & offensionis Dei.

Sed supersunt adhuc argumenta, quibus Bellarminus confirmare studet, Fidem Iustificantem non esse Fiduciam. Et primùm quidem ex Rom. c. 4. 19. & seqq. tribus, ubi fides Abrahæ describitur, sic infert: Abraham non consideravit corpus suum emortuum: sed planè persuasum habuit, Deum, quod promiserat, posse etiam facere. Atqui Consideratio pertinet ad intellectum, ad quem non pertinet fiducia. Sic Græcum πληροφορηθεὶς est plenißimè scire. Atqui plenißimè scire est intellectus non voluntatis : sicut contra, fiduciam habere, voluntatis est, non intellectus. Ergo fides Abrahæ, & per consequens omnis fides Iustificans, non est fiducia, sed certus tantum assensus.

Respondeo, fallit argumentum. 1. παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Nam à positione unius partis non valet Consequentia ad negationem alterius. Sic non valet collectio hæc : Apostolus in verbo Consideravit, expressit unam fidei partem, nempè assensum : E. exclusit alteram, nempè Fiduciam. 2. Incommoda versione ludit Sophista. Nam verbum Græcum πληροφορηθεὶς, etsi alicubi fortassis idem notare possit, quòd plenissimè scire, uti reddit Jesuvvita : tamen hoc loco evidentiorem significationem sortitur, eam nimirum, quæ ostendat, Fidem Abrahæ fuisse certam, infallibilem, invictam, nullis dubitationibus aut difficultatibus superabilem : Ubi profectò Fiduciam notari bardus fuerit qui non videat. Et quid quæso sibi vult aliud, quod Apostolus verbum hoc πληροφορηθεὶς, versu præcedente 18. reddit per hanc phrasin, quòd Abraham crediderit sub spe, contra spem. Si contra stem, utique non per Intellectum : Sic enim non contra spem, sed per Fiduciam immotam, in veritatem promissionum divinarum credidit.

Tandem luculenta illa accedit Apostoli ἐπεξήγησις vers. 20. adversus promissionem Dei non disceptavit diffidentia : Ubi non simplex notatur incredulitas, ut Bellarminus garrit, sed talis dubitatio & hæsitatio, quæ de veritate promissionum Dei nonnihil ambigat. Cui ex adverso πληροφορίαν & fiduciam immotam, etiam contra spem opponi, manifestius est, quàm ut operosâ probatione indigeat.

II. Argumentum, D. Apostolus. 1. Cor. 13, 13. Fidem & spem tanquàm duo quædam diversa à se invicem distinguit. Atqui fiducia nihil est aliud, quàm spes roborata. E. Fiducia ex fide quidem oritur, sed non potest esse idem cum fide, nisi confundere velimus, quæ tam apertè Apostolus ipse distinxit.

Respondeo, fallit argumentum παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Nam secundum Quid tantùm differunt Fides & Spes, non verò ἁπλῶς. Ut 1. ratione ordinis : Fides enim τῇ φύσει semper prior est spe, quia nisi credatur aliquid, non potest sperari: Creditur autem aliquid, quod non speratur : licèt nihil sperari possit, quod non creditur, uti docet Augustinus lib. 8. Enchiridij. 2. Fides malarum pariter ac bonarum rerum est: quin & præteritarum : Spes bonarum duntaxat est & futurarum: sicut metus est rerum malarum. 3. Fides propriè objecti loco respicit promissionem bonorum : Spes verò respicit ipsa bona promissa : neque enim sperat, sed credit homo promissionem vitæ æternæ : sperat autem ipsam vitam æternam. Et eaténus consentimus Jesuvvitæ, quòd Fides & Spes sint quædam diversa. Cæterùm quòd inde arguit, Fidem non esse fiduciam, propterea quòd Fiducia nihil sit aliud, quàm Spes roborata: πλεονεξίαν Consequentis committit. Etsi enim aliqua est & Spei & fidei discrepantia, tanta tamen est utriusque cognatio, ut Scriptura per quandam permutationem vocabulorum, Fidem nominet Spem, & Spem Fidem : ita ut sperare in Deum pro credere in Deum frequenter ponatur: Sic Abrahem dicitur credidisse in spem contra spem, τῷ ἐλπιςῷ accepto, pro τῷ πισῷ.

Deindè duæ hæ virtutes sic sunt subordinatæ, & sic cohærent, ut divelli non possint. Undè Augustinus loco jam modò citato : Fides operans per dilectionem sine spe esse non potest, nec amor sine spe, nec sine amore, spes, nec utrumque sine fide. Præterea Apostolus Rom. 5. Spem ex fide etiam ortum suum habere ostendit. Et quid respondebit Jesuvvita Autori Epistolæ ad Hebræos cap. 11, 1. qui Fidem definit, quòd sit ὑπόςασις τῶν ἐλπιζομένων, firma fiducia eorum, quæ sperantur. Quibus freti rationibus invictè inferimus, Fidem & Spem esse quidem distinctas, sed ita cognatas virtutes, ut helleboro dignus sit, qui fiduciam sive Spem roboratam, ex Fide Justificante expungere velit.

III. Argumentum: Paulus dicit, per fidem intellectum captivum duci, sub obsequium Christi. E. Fides tantum pertinet ad intellectum. & non ad voluntatem: ac per Consequens non est fiducia.

Respondeo: Plus est in Consequente, quàm in Antecedente. Nam hoc tantùm sequitur. E. Fides pertinet ad intellectum, id quod nos minimè negamus. Jam si subsumat Sophista, E. tantùm ad intellectum pertinet, regerimus illud: Ex affirmatione unius partis non valet Consequentia ad negationem alterius.

IV. Argumentum: Fides est Causa Fiduciae: Nam per fidem habemus fiduciam. Ephes. 3, 12. Ergo Fides non est ipsa fiducia.

Respondeo: Fides duobus modis accipitur, vel absolutè: vel relatè. Absolutè considerata, quatenùs assentitur promissionibus Evangelicis, est causa fiduciae, & non fiducia ipsa. Relatè autem considerata, quatenùs videlicet jam plenè acquiescit in illis ipsis promissionibus: eatenùs Fides jam est fiducia ipsa. Fides enim suos habet gradus, & quando plenam suam assequitur formam, & quasi ἐντελέχειαν, est & dicitur πεποίθησις & πληροφορία sive fiducia. Et hoc ipsum innuit Apostolus. Rom. 1, 17. Justitia Dei, inquiens, revelatur in Evangelio ex fide in fidem, ex fide nimirùm infirma, in fidem robustam, plenâ animi fiducia acquiescentem in merito Christi.

V. Et postremum: Actus fidei in Scripturis dicitur esse, Credere, non verò Fidere. E. Fides est tantum assensus, non verò fiducia.

Respondeo: Actus fidei in Scripturis definitur vel Generaliter, secundum omnis generis objecta: & tum actum ejus esse, Credere non negamus: vel definitur Specialiter, & quidem ratione Fidei Justificantis: & tum actum ejus esse, tantùm Credere sive assentiri, simpliciter negamus. Scriptura enim talem fidem nominat πληροφορίαν, πεποίθησιν; παῤῥησίαν, hoc est, certam fiduciam, persuasionem, confidentiam, quâ in promissione Gratiae confidenter acquiescitur: & haec est Fides justificans Hebr. 10, 22. Accedamus cum vero corde & certa persuasione fidei. Et vers. 35. Ne abjicite παῤῥησίαν libertatem sive confidentiam vestram, uti habet vetus versio &c.

Sed pergit Bellarminus, & tertium adjicit errorem cap. 7. libri. 1. de Justificat: contendens, Fidem non esse notitiam, sed assensum, & credere nihil esse aliud, quàm assentiri doctrinis Ecclesiae, etiam si ignores qualis sit, duplici potissimùm usus argumentorum genere.

Prius tale est: Fides est via & gradus ad intelligendum, secundum illud Ies. 7, 9. Nisi credideritis, non intelligetis. E. Fides non est intelligentia.

Posterius sic sonat: Notitia est quiddam distinctum à fide. 1. Cor. 13, 2. E. Fides non est notitia.

Respondeo: Utrumque objectum prodere magnam ἀῤῥωσίαν διανοίας in Adversario. Pugnârit is antea, Fidem non esse fiduciam, sed tantùm assensum. Jam vero negat Fidem esse notitiam. Atqui assensus non est sine notitia. Neque enim quisquam assentitur ei, quod non novit & intelligit, & quidem vel per discursum rationis, vel per revelationem factam in verbo Dei. Sed quoad prius objectum, non legimus Jes 7. Si non credideritis, non intelligetis: sed non eritis fideles, vel ut alij reddunt, non eritis stabiles, id quod nihil facit ad causam Jesuvvitæ.

Posterius Objectum insignem stoliditatem prodit. Quæ enim est ratio Consequentiæ: Notitia est distinctum quid à fide. E. fides non est notitia. Puer certè in Scholis redargueret hanc colligendi petulantiam, & ostenderet, Definitiones omnes constare Genere: quod in se consideratum, est aliquid distinctum à suo definito: ut Animal est quiddam distinctum ab Homine: Ergone Homo non erit Animal: Sic Habitus est aliquid distinctum à Liberalitate & reliquis virtutibus: Ergone virtutes non erunt Habitus? Opponimus hoc loco Jesuvvitæ unicum illud capitis sexti ad Romanos: ubi Apostolus fidem nominat γνῶσιν scientiam & λογισμὸν ratiocinationem vers. 6, 9. 11. Sic Fidei Abrahami & in genere omnium credentium expressè adsignat scientiam, & quidem non frigidam aliquam sive superficiariam: sed certam & immotam, quæ cum πληροφορία sit conjuncta; ut Rom. 4, 21. plenè sciebat. Et Rom. 8, 28.. Scimus quòd diligentibus Deum Rom. 14, 14. Scio & confido in Domino. 2. Cor. 5, 1 Scimus quod postquam &c.

Sed Quartum etiam errorem prodit Jesuvvita contendens, Fidem habere suam sedem tantùm intellectu: hâc potissimum motus ratione.

Fieri non potest, ut una virtus sit in duabus potentijs, genere distinctis. Ergò neque Fides potest es se in intellectu, & in voluntate simul.

Respondeo: διαῤῥήδην pugnat hoc argumentum, cum illo Apostolico. Rom. 10, 10 Corde creditur ad justitiam. Ergò Fidei Justificantis Subjectum sive sedes non est cerebrum aut intellectus tantùm, sed & Cor sive voluntas. Corde enim, inquit Apostolus, non intellectu creditur ad justitiam: propterea quòd in intellectu potest esse præclara notitia, præclarus assensus, sed non ad justitiam, nisi adsit fides cordis, hoc est, fiducia. Quoad axioma Philosophicum, quô Jesuvvita nititur, respondeo.

1. Quæstionem hanc de qua agitur, non esse Philosophia sed fidei: ac proindè ex Principijs etiam Philosophicis dijudicari eam nec posse nec debere. 2. Nondum explicatum dedit Jesuvvita, An & quomodo unius per essentiam animæ, δυνάμεις sive potentiæ, Mens scilicet sive intellectus, & cor sive voluntas, ipso Genere, vel ut alij loquuntur, Subjectis differant

Certè in Scholis etiam Philosophorum extra dubitationis aleam est positum, motus potentiarum animæ, mentis scilicet & voluntatis sibi mutuò correspondere, ut qualis est assenssio & notitia in mente, tales etiam motus ipsa voluntas concipiat. Porrò apud Doctores Scholasticos, Bonaventuram cumprimis, jampridem obtinuit hæc regula: Nullum est inconviens: Unum habitum ponere & in ratione & in voluntate: præsertim cùm hoc loco mens sive intellectus non merè theoricus, sed practicus intelligatur, quatenùs nimirùm ille jam parti appetitivæ jungitur. Tandem Scriptura ipsa hanc ἀκρίβειαν Philosophicam non semper observat, ut quoties cordi non modò tribuit fiduciam, sed & notitiam, quæ propriè ad intellectum pertinet, ut Psal 119, 11. Recondit Sanctus hæc verba in Corde suo. Luc. 24, 25. Tardi corde ad credendum.

Et hactenus quidem primam Controversiam de Fide justificante expedivimus, Quæ nimirùm &: Quid sit Fides justificans: Sequitur Controversia altera:


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: II. Question Concerning Justifying Faith, Does Faith alone justify?

II. Question Concerning JUSTIFYING FAITH, Does Faith alone justify?

Concerning this Question also, a very sharp controversy exists today between our Churches and the Jesuits. For although they speak quite splendidly about justifying faith, so that Bellarmine did not hesitate to write that faith is of such value that even when separated from Charity (which is nothing else than if you were to say, Faith alone) it has the power of justifying: yet everything is uniquely composed for the purpose of deception, since they are accustomed to explain this assertion of theirs by way of disposition and impetration, as we shall show in the third question concerning faith. But in this place, the controversy is properly about the exclusive particles. And indeed, we fight most rightly from the Scriptures for their genuine sense and use, both against the Jesuits and the Interimistic authors, in this manner.

I. Whatever phrase expresses the doctrine of the Gospel most significantly, that can and ought not to be accused of impiety or falsehood. But this phrase, WE ARE JUSTIFIED BY FAITH ALONE, evidently accomplishes this very thing. Therefore. The truth of the assumption is clear even from this, that whatever Scripture hands down concerning the justification of man, that it is done by faith and mercy, by grace, without the law, without the works of the law, and through the imputation of the righteousness of Christ: that produces no other sense at all than if the Apostle had said: THAT MAN IS JUSTIFIED BY FAITH ALONE: so much so, that if anyone considers the matter more exactly, he must necessarily admit that by Pauline expressions the justification of works is more strongly denied and excluded than by the particle ALONE: as is evident from Rom. 3, 21. & 24. chap. 4. 6. Gal. 3, 21. Eph. 2, 8. & 9. Tit. 3, 5. and very many other places. For the Apostle pursues this one argument in not by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ. For if (he says) a Law had been given which could give life, truly righteousness would be from the Law: But Scripture has concluded all under sin, that the promise might be given by faith of Christ to those who believe, but not to those who work, for the reason that to him who works the reward is not imputed according to grace, but according to debt: But to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed for righteousness. Therefore we know that a man is not justified by the works of the Law, except through the faith of Jesus Christ.

II. That the Scripture itself confirms this phrase of speaking by synonymy, it should not be disapproved. But the Scripture confirms this very exclusive phrase (By faith alone) by synonymy in the place just now cited. Gal. 2, 16. We know that a man is justified not by the works of the Law, except through the faith of Jesus Christ. Therefore.

The Jesuits object that these words are to be taken not exclusively, but conjunctively, so that works are simultaneously implied, in this sense: We know that a man is not justified by works otherwise than if faith in Christ is added.

But this objection is vain and frivolous. For 1. it directly fights with the intention of the Apostle, who is entirely occupied in demonstrating that justification does not come to us from the works of the Law either without or with faith: as has already been demonstrated before. Then, the Apostle's inference would be clearly irrelevant, nay, entirely null, who in the immediately following words subsumes thus: Therefore we also believe in Christ, that we may be justified by faith, and not by works: whereas according to the Jesuit gloss he should have subsumed thus: Therefore we also believe in Christ, that we may be justified by works joined with faith.

Finally, the Apostle adds such an epiphonema, which utterly overturns the Jesuit objection: Wherefore by works no flesh is justified. The evidence of the Greek phrase also approaches: for the Apostle does not say, ἐι μὴ διὰ πίςεως, which phrase might perhaps seem in some way to hint at that connected or implicit sense: but ἐὰν μὴ διὰ πίςεως, which phrase other places of Scripture demonstrate to possess an exclusive force, as John 6, 44. No one can come to me, ἐὰν μὴ unless the Father draws him. And John 15, 4. The branch cannot bear fruit of itself, ἐὰν μὴ unless it remains in the vine: so neither can you, ἐὰν μὴ, unless you remain in me. Where it is too manifest that that implicit or connected sense expires.

III. Reason: The exclusive particle 1. uncovers and refutes the grossest impiety of the Romanists concerning the merits of works. 2. It represses the depravations of the Scriptures. 3. It asserts the glory of God uniquely. 4. It rightly distinguishes the Gospel from the Law. 5. It produces firm consolation. 6. It excites the ardor of divine invocation. 7. It places and confirms the hope of our salvation, which is absolutely infallible, in Christ alone. Therefore it cannot be accused of either impiety or novelty. The antecedent is evident from the entire doctrine which we have hitherto asserted concerning justifying faith against the sophistries of the Jesuits.

IV. Reason: The entire Orthodox Antiquity uses this exclusive phrase everywhere, not only as to the sense, but also as to the letter, and indeed to exclude personal merits. It would therefore be rash that the Jesuits accuse this phrase of novelty, and constitute our blessed Luther as its first author. The truth of the antecedent is most evidently apparent from the writings of our own, especially those of Chemnitz: from whence testimonies can be sought.

Moreover, regarding the action of B. Luther, in that he expressly inserted into the German version of the Apostolic passage Rom. 3. 28 the exclusive particle 'Alone,' which is not held as such in the Greek, that deserves not only excuse but even praise. For it was in no way his intention to add even one iota to the Holy Scriptures or to correct the language of the Holy Spirit: but by consulting for his own people, he wished to accommodate himself as closely as possible to the condition of our vernacular language. Now, such is the condition of our language that when, in any proposition, a negation is made concerning either many or one, and an affirmation is placed concerning one or the other, the discourse is most conveniently expressed by an added exclusive particle. For example, what the Hebrew says: 'One must not glory in wisdom, strength, riches: but in the Lord,' Jer. 9. 23, 1 Cor. 1. 31, our vernacular language enunciates most correctly: 'One must glory in the Lord alone.' Thus, what the Greek language says: 'There is no one good, except one God, namely,' our language expresses most correctly: 'There is no one good, except God alone, or only God,' Matt. 19. 17. It is added in the second place that such liberty has been left to the Church, indeed, such is the proper mark, as it were, of the Prophetic gift, or of interpreting the Scriptures, that the Scriptures should be so translated and explained that every nation may understand in its own language what is the proper and native meaning of the words of the Holy Spirit. Thirdly, that received custom of the ancient Church, by which it used clearly equal liberty in interpreting passages of Scripture, wonderfully approves Luther's action: As that which is read in Gen. 3. 11, 'Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat,' the LXX interpreters rendered it thus, so that they followed the sense rather than the number of the words: ἔφαγες ἀπὸ τῦ ξύλυ, ὗ ἐνετειλάμην σοι τέτυμόνε μὴ φαγεῖν: 'Hast thou eaten of the tree, of which I had commanded thee ALONE, that thou shouldest not eat.' Thus 2 Chron. 20. 12, the Hebrew text renders this sense: 'When we do not know what we ought to do, we have this of remainder, that we direct our eyes to thee.' And yet the Latin Church, through an inserted exclusive particle, rendered it thus: 'We have THIS ALONE of remainder.' Thus Rom. 4. 5, the Chaldean paraphrase inserted the exclusive word Calchud, 'only,' reading thus: 'To him who does not work, but only to him who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, is his faith imputed for righteousness.' Finally, Christ himself confirmed this very liberty of the Church by his own example. For in Deut. 6. 13, Moses has: 'Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God and shalt serve him': but Christ, with the exclusive particle inserted, rendered it thus: 'Thou shalt serve him ALONE.' Matt. 4. 10.

Latin:

II. Quæstio De FIDE JUSTIFICANTE, Nùm Sola Fides justificet?

DE hac etiam Quæstione acris omninò Controversia nostris Ecclesiis hodiè cum Jesuvvitis intercedit. Etsi enim illi satis splendidè loquuntur de fide justificante, ita ut Bellarminus scribere non dubitaverit, Fidem tanti esse pretij, ut à Charitate etiam disjuncta (id quod nihil est aliud, quàm si dicas, Sola fides) vim habeat justificandi: tamen ad decipiendum omnia unicè sunt composita, cum assertionem hanc suam, per modum dispositionis & impetrationis explicare soleant, uti Quæstione tertiâ de fide, ostendemus. Verùm de particulis Exclusivis hoc loco propriè controvertitur. Et sanè nos pro earum sensu ac usu genuino tùm contra Jesuvvitas, tùm autores Interimisticos rectissimè ex Scripturis pugnamus, in hunc modum.

I. Quæcunq; phrasis doctrinam Evangelij propriam significantissimè exprimit, ea impietatis aut falsitatis argui nec potest nec debet. Atqui phrasis hæc, SOLA FIDE justificamur, hoc ipsum evidenter præstat. Ergo. Assumtionis veritas vel indè patet, quòd quicquid Scriptura tradit de Justificatione hominis, quòd fiat fide ac misericordia, ex gratia, sine lege, sine operibus legis, & per imputationem justitiæ Christi: illud nullum prorsus sensum parit alium, quàm si dixisset Apostolus: SOLA FIDE justificari Hominem: adeò, ut si quis rem exactiùs consideret, fateri necessum sit habiturus, Paulinis locutionibus operum justificationem fortiùs negari & excludi, quàm per particulam SOLA: uti patet ex Rom. 3, 21. & 24. cap. 4. 6. Gal. 3, 21. Ephes. 2, 8. & 9 Tit. 3, 5. & locis alijs quàm plurimis. Hoc enim unum argumentum in omnibus istis locis persequitur Apostolus: Omnes in universum homines non ex operibus legis: sed ex fide Jesu Christi justificantur. Si enim (inquit) data esse Lex, quæ posset vivificare, verè ex Lege esset justitia: Sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato, ut promissio ex fide Christi daretur credentibus, non verò operantibus, propterea quòd operanti non imputatur merces secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum: Ei verò qui non operatur, sed credit in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur ejus fides ad justitiam. Ergo scimus non justificari Hominem, ex operibus Legis, nisi per fidem Iesu Christi.

II. Quam phrasin loquendi ipsa confirmat Scriptura συνωνυμίᾳ, ea improbanda haud fuerit. Atqui hanc ipsam phrasin exclusivam (Sola fide) confirmat Scriptura Synonymia in loco jam modò citato. Gal. 2, 16. Scimus justificari Hominem non operibus Legis, nisi per fidem Jesu Christi. Ergo.

Excipiunt Jesuvvitæ non exclusivè, sed conjunctim hæc verba esse accipienda, ita ut opera simul implicentur, hoc sensu: Scimus, operibus non aliter justificari Hominem, nisi Fides in Christum accedat.

Sed vana & frivola hæc est exceptio. Nam 1. ea διερρήδην pugnat cum intentione Apostoli, qui in eo totus est, ut demonstret, ex Legis peribus neque sine neque cum fide nobis obtingere justificationem: uti jam antè demonstratum. Deinde impertinens planè, imò prorsus nulla foret illatio Apostoli, qui in immediatè subsequentibus sic subsumit: Ideò & nos in Christum credimus, ut justificemur ex fide, & non ex operibus: cùm secundum glossam Jesuvviticam sic subsumere debuisset: Ideò & nos credimus in Christum, ut justificemur ex operibus cum fide junctis.

Tandem subjicit Apostolus tale Epiphonema, quod Jnsuvviticam exceptionem funditùs evertit: Quapropter ex operibus non justificatur ulla caro. Accedit & Græcæ phraseos evidentia: non enim dicit Apostolus, ἐι μὴ διὰ πίςεως, quæ phrasis fortè aliquo modo sensum illum connexum sive implicitum innuere videri posset: sed ἐὰν μὴ διὰ πίςεως, quam sanè phrasin vim obtinere exclusivam, alia Scripturæ loca demonstrant, ut Joh. 6, 44. Nemo potest venire ad me, ἐὰν μὴ nisi pater traxerit eum. Et Joh. 15, 4. Palmes non potest fructum à seipso ferre, ἐὰν μὴ μείνῃ nisi manserit in vite: ita nec vos, ἐὰν μὴ, nisi in me manseritis. Ubi implicitum illum sive connexum sensum expirare, nimis manifestum est.

III. Ratio: Particula exclusiva 1. crassissillam impietatem Romanensium de meritis operum detegit & retundit. 2. Depravationes Scripturarum reprimit. 3. gloriam Dei unicè asserit. 4. Evangelium à Lege rectè discernit. 5. firmam consolationem parit. 6. excitat ardorem divinæ invocationis. 7. Spem salutis nostræ in solo Christo infallibilem prorsus collocat & confirmat. Ergo vel impietatis, vel novitatis insimulari nequit. Antecedens constat ex universa Doctrina, quam de fide justificante adversus strophas Jesuvvitarũ hactenus asseruimus.

IV. Ratio: Vniversa Antiquitas Orthodoxa, non modò quoad sensum,sed & quoad literã, phrasi hac Exclusiva passim utitur, & quidem ad excludenda propria merita. Temerariũ ergo fuerit,quòd Jesuvvitæ hanc phrasin novitatis arguunt, ejus primum autorem B. Lutherum nostrum constituunt. Antecedentis veritas evidentissimè patet, ex nostrorum, Chemnitij cumprimis scriptis: Undè testimonia peti possunt.

Cæterùm quoad factum B. Lutheri, quod ver sioni Germanicæ loci Apostolici Rom. 3. 28. particulam exclusivam Solùm expressè inseruit, quæ talem in Græco non habetur,illud non modò excusationem, sed laudem etiam meretur. Neque enim Scripturæ sacræ vel unum apicem addere, vel linguam Spiritus Sancti corrigere, ullo modo ipsi fuit propositum: sed genti suæ consulendo ad linguæ nostræ vernaculæ conditionem se quàm proximè accommodare voluit. Ea autem est linguæ nostræ conditio, ut cum in propositione aliqua, vel de plurib9 vel de uno factâ negatione, de uno vel altero affirmatio ponitur, per adjectam particulam exclusivá Oratio cōmodissimè efferatur. Exempli gratia, quod Hebræus dicit: Non esse gloriandum in sapientia fortitudine, divitijs: sed in Domino: Ier. 9. 23. 1. Corinth. 1. 31. id lingua nostra vernacula rectissimè enunciat: Gloriandum esse in solo Domino. Sic quod Græca lingua dicit: Non est bonus, nisi unus Deus scilicet: id nostra rectissimè exprimit: Nemo est bonus, nisi solus Deus, vel tantùm Deus Matth. 19. 17. Accedit secundo loco, quòd Ecclesiæ ea relicta est libertas, imò ea est doni Prophetici, sive interpretandi Scripturas propria quasi nota, ut sic vertantur, explicenturque Scripturæ, ut quævis gens in lingua sua intelligat, quæ sit verborum Spiritus Sancti propria & nativa sententia. Tertio Lutheri factum mirificè comprobat recepta illa veteris Ecclesiæ consuetudo, quâ pari planè libertate in interpretandis Scripturæ locis usa est: Ut quod Genes. 3. 11. legitur, Ex ligno, de quo præceperam tibi, ne comederes, comedisti, id LXX. interpretes sic reddiderunt, ut sensum magis, quàm verborum numerum sequerentur: ἔφαγες ἀπὸ τῦ ξύλυ, ὗ ἐνετειλάμην σοι τέτυμόνε μὴ φαγεῖν: Comedisti de ligno, de quo Solo præceperam, ne comederes. Sic 2. Paral. 20, 12. Hebræus textus hunc reddit sensum: Cùm ignoramus, quid agere debemus, hoc habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te. Atqui Latina Ecclesia per insertam particulam exclusivam sic reddidit: Hoc SOLVM habemus residui. Sic Rom. 4. 5. paraphrasis chaldæa inseruit vocem Exclusivam Calchud, solùm, sic legens: Non operanti, sed solùm credenti in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur fides sua ad justitiam. Tandem Christus ipse suo exemplo hanc ipsam libertatē Ecclesiæ confirmavit. Nam Deuter. 4, 14. habet Moses: Adorabis Dominum Deum tuum & ipsi servies: Christus verò intersertâ particulâ exclusivâ sic reddidit: ipsi SOLI servies. Matth. 4, 10.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: What is the use of the exclusive particles

Thus, he wished to express this phrase of Mark 13:32, 'No one knows except the Father,' as Christ himself did in Matthew chapter 24:26: 'No one knows, except the Father alone.'

However, a question is raised at this point: what exactly can be the use of this exclusive particle in this Article, or against what things to be excluded is it opposed? For since it is established that we are justified no less by the grace of God and the merit of Christ than by faith, who could not not undeservedly doubt whether, perhaps, by this exclusive phrase, 'FAITH ALONE,' the remaining causes of justification are excluded? We answer, however, in the negative. For this exclusive particle does not remove the diverse kinds of causes, such as the principal and προηγουμένη [preceding] cause, which is the grace of God, or the meritorious cause, which is Christ; but in its own order alone, it excludes all other organic causes, and those apprehending the merit of Christ, which are devised by the Papists, and it ascribes this apprehensive power to faith alone, uniquely and entirely. Therefore, the same exclusive particle can also very rightly hold a place in the remaining orders of causes: as 'The grace of God alone justifies us,' if the question is about the προηγουμένη [preceding cause]; 'Christ alone justifies us,' if the matter concerns the meritorious cause. In vain, therefore, and without merit, do the Papists object to us an implication of contradiction, since the opposition is not in the same, but in different orders of causes.

Furthermore, this exclusive particle expresses a determination not of the subject, but only of the predicate, and therefore it is opposed to works, not because they ought not to be present, but because they cannot justify. For our churches do not imagine such a faith that would permit to anyone a free license for any crimes whatsoever. For we ourselves maintain with James chapter 2:17 that faith without works is dead. We also believe with blessed Luther that faith is never alone, since it is not conferred without spiritual renewal. For it is the same grace that both gives us faith and regenerates us to the newness of the children of God: yet in such a way that good works do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the justified, as Augustine speaks somewhere. Therefore, 'faith alone justifies' and 'faith is solitary' differ. The former we defend: the latter we reject with Augustine and Chrysostom, who rightly denied that faith alone, that is, solitary or dead faith, justifies.

The Jesuits bitterly oppose this purer doctrine of ours, relying chiefly on this argument: If faith alone justifies, then it will certainly justify even if it were alone, without love, fear, hope, and the other virtues. But even the Lutherans themselves deny that justifying faith is without love and the other virtues. Therefore, faith alone does not justify.

But I answer from what was said a little earlier: 1. The particle 'alone' determines not the subject but the predicate, that is, it does not mean that justifying faith is solitary, that is, that it does not have the remaining virtues joined to it, but that it justifies alone, without the help of the remaining virtues, however present they may be. 2. They foolishly imagine

the adversaries: that the act of a subject subsists even when the subject is destroyed; that is, they imagine some justifying faith that is without charity, and thus that faith is not faith: for faith without works is not living faith, but dead, no less than an ear torn from the body is a dead ear, and an eye torn out is a dead eye.

Therefore, the Sophists reveal no less foolishness by this argument than if someone were to conclude thus: if ears alone hear, eyes alone see, the mind of man alone understands, therefore they also perform this without the body. Finally, just as it does not follow: 'Ears joined to the body hear; therefore, it is equally the act of the body as it is of the ears,' so the Jesuitical collection is childish: 'Faith is never alone without charity and the other virtues; therefore, it does not justify alone.' The vice of the collection arises from that false hypothesis which the Sophists hide, and it is such: 'Things that are joined together also act together as one and the same thing,' which it is clear of itself is most false. Certainly the soul and body are most closely joined, and yet the body does not reason: thus the powers and faculties of the soul are most closely joined, nay, in essence they are one: and yet the will does not understand the objects of intellect, nor does the mind will the objects of desire, or perform the duties of the remaining powers. We therefore correct that error, substituting this most true rule: Many things can be joined: nevertheless, because they are distinct in and by themselves, they can certainly be occupied with distinct energies about distinct objects: Thus Faith and Charity, however much they may be joined in the justified, yet differ greatly in definition, objects, and energies, so that the proper energy of faith is to believe and trust in God: but the proper energy of Charity is to love God and one's neighbor. With these things observed, those things which Bellarmine argues from chapter 12 of book 1. on Justification to the very end, and too anxiously, but without an adversary, confirms: That faith is never alone, nor can it be separated from Charity and the other virtues.

They object furthermore to that passage Gal. 5, 6. Faith is effective through Charity. Therefore, they say, we are not justified by unformed or solitary faith, but by formed faith, that is, by Faith and Charity together.

I answer 1. That the Jesuits are not attacking any opinion of ours, but a figment of their own brain. For none of us has ever dreamed of any unformed justifying faith, or one that is imperfect: since we know and confess that it generates from itself both Charity and the remaining Christian virtues. 2. The adversaries presuppose a false hypothesis, namely that Charity informs faith, a thing which no sane person would ever concede, unless perhaps he dared to assert that a Cause is informed by its Effect: which would be far most absurd. But Faith receives its justifying Form not from Charity, but from CHRIST himself, whom it apprehends: afterwards, being thus formed, it itself forms Charity and the remaining virtues, so that they may please GOD. 3. The Apostle does not say that Faith justifies through Charity: but that it works, which are two very different things: For we are not justified by working: but the justified work. Therefore, the Apostle describes true and living faith as a sign or effect, and in this place shows not how we are made just, but how we, having already been made just, act and work: so that, indeed, it may shine forth from works as from fruits that we have already been justified beforehand by faith. Finally, a distinction must be made between the twofold ἐνέργεια of faith. For one operation of it is proper and native, and absolutely incommunicable to all other virtues, which is to apprehend the merit of CHRIST and apply it to oneself. The other and, as it were, subsequent operation of justifying faith is to exert itself into various acts of virtues, such as charity, hope, fear, and repentance. With respect to the former ἐνέργεια, it is said to justify, in the sense which will be explained in the subsequent third special controversy concerning faith. With respect to the latter, it is not.

The adversaries press and object: that a much more excellent action or ἐνέργεια is assigned in the Scriptures to charity than to faith. Therefore, we are justified also by charity and not by faith alone. They confirm the antecedent from that apostolic passage, 1 Cor. 13: Now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three: but the greatest of these is charity.

I answer: 1. That the adversaries are deceived and deceive again through a false hypothesis, which is that the greatest virtue justifies the most: or certainly that the noblest ἐνέργεια performs this act. The subsequent controversy will show that both of these are far from the truth. 2. Regarding the apostolic passage, the sophists commit a παραλογισμὸν παρὰ τὸ πῇ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For the Apostle does not establish charity as greater than faith and hope ἁπλῶς, simply and in every way, but only κατά τι, in a certain respect: because, indeed, as Chrysostom also observes, charity remains even in the other life, for which faith and hope have no function or office after this life. Finally, they commit the sophism of ἑτεροζητήσεως. For the controversy is not which virtue is more lasting and, by reason of its duration, more excellent, faith or charity: but which one apprehends CHRIST, and by so apprehending him, justifies. But it is certain that Christ is apprehended by faith, and not by charity, and this will be proved later.

Latin:

Sic phrasin hanc Marci 13, 32. Nemo novit nisi Pater, Christus ipse apud Matthæum cap. 24, 26. sic efferre voluit: Nemo novit, nisi solus pater.

Movetur autem hoc loco Quæstio. Quisnam potissimum particulæ hujus exclusivæ usus hoc in Articulo esse possit, vel quibus rebus excludendis ea opponatur. Nam cùm constet, Nos haud minùs Gratiâ Dei, & merito Christi, quàm Fide justificari, dubitare haud immeritò, quis posset, Nùm fortè, per hanc phrasin exclusivam, SOLA FIDE, reliquæ Iustificationis Causæ excludantur? Respondemus autem negatè. Neque enim particula hæc exclusiva tollit diversa Causarum genera, ut efficientem principalem ac προηγυμένην, quæ est Gratia Dei: vel meritoriam, quæ est Christus: sed in suo tantùm ordine excludit omnes alias causas organicas, & apprehendentes meritum Christi, quæ à Pontificijs excogitantur, & hanc vim apprehensivam soli fidei unicè & in solidum adscribit. Locum proindè etiam rectissimè obtinere potest eadem particula exclusiva, in reliquis Causarum ordinibus : ut Sola Gratia Dei nos justificat, si de προηγυμένῃ sit quæstio: Solus Christus nos justificat, si de Causa meritoria agatur. Frustra ergò, & præter meritum Pontificij nobis ἀντιφάσεως implicationem objiciunt: siquidem non in eodem, sed in diversis Causarum ordinibus sit oppositio.

Deindè exclusiva hæc particula non Subjecti, sed prædicati tantùm determinationem exprimit, ac proindè operibus opponitur, non quòd adesse non debeant, sed quod justificare nequeant. Neque enim talem fidem nostræ fingunt Ecclesiæ, quæ cuivis liberam quorumvis flagitiorum licentiam permitteret. Statuimus enim ipsi cum Jacobo cap. 2, 17. Fidem sine operibus esse mortuam. Credimus etiam cum B. Luthero, Fidem nunquàm esse solam, quippè quæ non confertur sine spirituali renovatione. Eadem enim est Gratia, quæ & fidem nobis donat, & ad novitatem filiorum Dei regenerat: sic tamen ut bona opera justificandum non præcedant, sed sequantur justificatum, ut Augustinus alicubi loquitur. Differunt proindè, fides sola justificat, & Fides est solitaria.
