Prius illud defendimus: Posterius hoc reijcimus cum Augustino & Chrysostomo, qui rectè negârunt, Fidem solam, hoc est, solitariam sive mortuam justificare.

Puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ acrite se opponunt Jesuitæ: hoc potissimùm freti argumento: Si sola fides justificat, utique justificabit etiam si fuerit sola, absque dilectione, timore, spe, cæterisq́; virtutibus. Atqui vel ipsi Lutherani negant Fidem justificantem esse sine dilectione & cæteris virtutibus. Ergo Fides sola non justificat.

Sed respondeo ex paulò antè dictis. 1. Particulam Solam determinare non Subjectum sed prædicatum, hoc est, non velle, quòd Fides justificans sit solitaria, hoc est, non habeat adjunctas reliquas virtutes: sed quòd Sola justificet, sine auxilio reliquarum virtutum, quantumvis præsentium. 2. Stolidè fingunt

Adversarij: Actum subjecti subsistere etiam destructo subjecto: hoc est, fingunt, fidem aliquam justificantem, quæ sit sine charitate, & sic fidem non esse fidem: Fides enim sine operibus, non est fides viva, sed mortua, non minùs quam auris avulsa à corpore, est mortua auris, & oculus avulsus est mortuus oculus.

Haud leviorem ergo hoc argumento stoliditatem produnt Sophistæ, quàm si quis ita colligit: si Aures solæ audiunt: oculi soli vident: Mens hominis sola intelligit. E. hoc etiam præstant sine Corpore. Tandem quemadmodum non sequitur: Aures conjunctæ corpori audiunt: Ergo Corporis actus æquè est audire atque aurium. Sic puerilis est collectio Jesuitica: Fides nunquàm est sola sine charitate & cæteris virtutibus. E. Sola etiam non justificat: Vitium Collectionis oritur ex falsa illa hypothesi, quam occultant Sophistæ, & talis est: Quæ sunt conjuncta, conjunctim etiam unum idemquè agunt, quod falsissimum esse ultrò liquet. Certè Anima & Corpus sunt conjunctissima, neque tamen Corpus ratiocinatur: Sic potentiæ & facultates animæ sunt conjunctissimæ, imò οὐσίἁ unum sunt: neque tamen voluntas intelligit νοητὰ neque mens vult τὰ βυλητὰ, aut reliquarum potentiarum officia obit. Corrigimus proindè errorem istum, substituentes verissimam hanc regulam: Multa possunt esse conjuncta: nihilominus tamen, quia in & per se sunt distincta, utique distinctis ἐνεργείαις circa distincta objecta versari possunt: Sic Fides & Charitas, quantumvis in justificatis sint conjunctæ, Definitione tamen, objectis & ἐνεργείαις plurimùm differunt, ita, ut propria ἐνέργεια fidei sit, credere & confidere Deo: propria autem ἐνέργεια Charitatis sit diligere Deum & proximum. Quibus observatis ultrò corruunt ea, quæ à capite 12. libri. 1. de Iustif. ad finem usque disputat Bellarminus, & nimis anxiè, sed sine Adversario confirmat: Fidem nunquàm esse solam, neque à Charitate cæterisquè virtutibus posse separari.

Objiciunt præterea locum illum Gal. 5, 6. Fides per Charitatem est efficax. E. inquiunt, non fide informi sive sola, sed fide formata, hoc est, Fide & Charitate simul justificamur.

Respondeo 1. Jesuitas non nostram aliquam sententiam, sed proprium cerebri figmentum impugnare. Nemo enim nostrum Fidem aliquam informem justificantem, vel perfebrim unquàm somniavit: quippè quam tùm Charitatem, tùm reliquas virtutes Christianas ex se gignere novimus & fatemur. 2. Falsam hypothesin præsupponunt Adversarij, quòd videlicet Charitas informet fidem, id quod nemo sanus unquàm concesserit, nisi forte Causam per Effectum informari asserere ausit: id quod longè esset absurdissimum. Accipit autem Fides justificant Formam suam non à Charitate, sed à CHRISTO ipso, quem apprehendit: postmodùm sic formata, format ipsa Charitatem & reliquas virtutes, ut DEO placeant. 3. Apostolus non dicit, Fidem justificare per Charitatem: sed operari, quæ duo diversissima sunt: Non enim operantes justificamur: sed justificati operantur. Ergò tanquàm à signo sive Effectu veram ac vivam fidem Apostolus describit, ac non quomodo justi fiamus, sed quomodo jam modò justi facti agamus & operemur, hoc loco ostendit: ut nimirùm ex operibus tanquàm ex fructibus illucescat, nos per fidem jam antè justificatos esse. Tandem distinguendum inter duplicem fidei ἐνέργειαν. Una enim ejus operatio est propria & nativa, & reliquis virtutibus omnibus prorsus incommunicabilis, quæ est, apprehendere CHRISTI meritum, sibique applicare. Altera & quasi ἐπομένη operatio Fidei justificantis est, in varios actus virtutum, ut Charitatis, spei, timoris, pœnitentiæ, se exerere. Respectu prioris ἐνεργείας Justificare dicitur, eo sensu, qui subseq. Controversia tertia Speciali de Fide explicabitur. Respectu posterioris non item.

Instant & excipiunt Adversarii: Multò præstantiorem actionem sive ἐνέργειαν in Scripturis adsignari Charitati, quàm Fidei. Ergo, Charitate etiam & non sola fide nos justificari. Antecedens confirmant ex illo Apostolico. 1. Cor. 13. Nunc manet Fides, Spes, Charitas, tria hæc: Major autem horum Charitas.

Respondeo: 1. falli ac fallere Adversarios rursum per falsam hypothesin, quæ est, quòd maxima virtus maximè justificet: vel certè nobilissima ἐνέργεια hunc actum perficiat. Quod utrumq; longè falsissimum esse, subsequens Controversia ostendet. 2. Quoad locum Apostolicum committunt Sophistæ παραλογισμὸν παρὰ τὸ πῇ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Charitatem enim Apostolus non ἁπλῶς simpliciter & omni modo, sed tantùm κατά τι Fide ac Spe majorem constituit: quia nimirùm, ut Chrysostomus etiam animadvertit, Charitas in altero etiam seculo permánet, cui fidei atque spei nullum sit post hanc vitam munus sive officium. Tandem committunt Sophisma ἑτεροζητήσεως. Non enim controvertitur, utra virtus sit diuturnior, & diuturnitatis ratione præstantior, Fides an Charitas: sed utra CHRISTUM apprehendat, & sic ipsum apprehendendo justificet. Jam autem Fide, non verò Charitate Christum apprehendi constat, & postmodùm probabitur.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Efficient Cause of Justification: III. Question Concerning Justifying Faith

How is faith in Christ said to justify?

It is disputed between us and the Jesuits in the third place concerning the office itself of faith in the work or act of justification. For since faith possesses a twofold condition: one absolute, the other relative: it is asked, with respect to which condition is faith established to justify us? Faith is considered absolutely when it is estimated in itself and of itself, as some virtue and quality or habit. In which respect, indeed, the excellence of faith is great, inasmuch as it leads captive every judgment of our reason and senses, contemns the powers of natural causes, believes against hope in hope, resists any impediments and temptations whatsoever with strength, conquers the Devil, and finally most rightly asserts its glory to GOD. But it is considered relatively when it is not weighed as a work, virtue, or quality, but only as an organ apprehending the merit of Christ. And it is only in this latter respect that faith is said to justify, so that not the subject, but the object of faith performs the act of justification. But that object is nothing other than the gratuitous promise of divine mercy concerning the remission of sins and the adoption of believers, through and on account of Christ the Mediator. For justifying faith embraces this object not merely by bare knowledge, nor by simple assent of the mind alone, but by a true and undoubted confidence of the heart.

Moreover, the testimonies of the Scriptures confirm this opinion of ours, which prove that this phrase 'to be justified by faith,' or 'through faith,' or 'from faith,' is to be taken in the same sense as other equivalent ones are taken, which assert that we are justified through the redemption of JESUS CHRIST, through the blood and death of Christ, through the obedience of Christ, Rom. 3:24 and 25, ch. 5:9 and 19. The reason is evident, that the manner of justifying is not manifold or various, but only one. Therefore, if we are justified only by the blood and merit of Christ, then to be justified by faith will be nothing else than to be justified by the merit of Christ alone, apprehended by faith: and consequently, faith ought to be considered in the act of justification only relatively, and not absolutely. Meanwhile, however, we do not deny that there is a metalepsis in this phrase (we are justified by faith), while indeed the effect of the principal cause is attributed to the instrumental. For by faith we receive the remission of sins on account of the blood of Christ: not on account of the dignity or excellence of faith. With this observed, that axiom most worthy of note also emerges, that faith confers righteousness upon us, not effectively, as if it made us habitually just, or, as the Jesuits speak, that it disposes or informs toward habitual righteousness: nor even materially, as if faith itself were that by which we are accounted just: but partly objectively, insofar as it looks to Christ, who alone is our righteousness: and partly organically, insofar as it apprehends the righteousness of CHRIST imputed to those who believe freely.

The Romanists bitterly contradict this purer doctrine, having brought forth a threefold error. For first, they insist that faith in the act of justification must be considered insofar as it is an inherent virtue or habit, the dignity of which is so great that it can justify a man.

Bellarmino also betrayed this error, lib. 1. de Justif. cap. 3. p. 938. writing thus: We disagree about the manner in which faith justifies. For they (the Lutherans) contend that faith is of no value and merit, and justifies relatively: We assert that Faith, even when separated from Charity, is of some value, and has the power of justifying, by way of disposition and impetration.

But what Bellarmino says, he does not prove: nay rather, he lies splendidly at the beginning, asserting that Faith is held by the Lutherans to be of no value. For although we derogate from the ἐνέργειαν (energy) of justifying, as if it were a virtue and quality: we nevertheless meanwhile assign to it effects or acts, which are certainly so excellent that no other virtue can rise to their excellence: as we have enumerated certain ones above, and attributed them to faith even when considered absolutely. Then, indeed, this Jesuitical opinion labors under manifest impiety, nay, it seems to recall from hell that old, long-since condemned error of the Gnostics, who assigned all power of justifying to the very dignity and excellence of faith: so that those who at least profess it, although they live most wickedly, obtain justification from it. To which, indeed, both the error of the Gnostics and the Jesuits, we oppose those things which we have just drawn from the Scriptures as the Foundations of our doctrine: and even the little book of Augustine, which he wrote long ago against the Gnostics, concerning faith and works, in a clearly Lutheran sense. However, the ἀνθομολογία (inconsistency) or inconstancy of the Romanists deserves observation in this place. For in the previous century they feigned such a worthlessness of faith that they extended it even to a trifle: but now they slip into an hyperbolic preaching of it, according to that saying: Fools, while they avoid vices, run into the contrary.

Another error of the Jesuits is that they contend that Faith justifies not objectively or relatively: but by way of disposition: as Bellarmino speaks, lib. 1. de Justif. cap. 3. p. 938. C. D. and explains himself more fully in cap. 12. p. 973 B. saying: The Catholics enumerate seven acts by which the ungodly are disposed toward justice, namely, Faith, Fear, Hope, Love, repentance, the purpose of receiving the Sacrament, and the purpose of a new life, and the observation of the commandments of GOD. Therefore, the Jesuit inserts, in the following chapter 13. l. C. D., that Faith justifies as the beginning and the first root of justification.

To this error we oppose: 1. That Justification is used or accepted neither in the Scriptures, nor in any idiom, for a disposition and motion toward receiving justice in itself. But now Scripture expressly ascribes justification to faith. Therefore, it expresses not a disposition toward justice, but the act of Justification itself.

Then every disposition, by whatever name it comes, falls under the genus of works, and therefore derives its nature and estimation from the Law of GOD: since the Law informs all our actions which are done, either with respect to GOD or our neighbor.

Now, indeed, Justification is not from the Law, but from the promise only, Gal. 3, 21. Therefore, Faith, by which we are justified, cannot or ought not to be defined from the Law, either by habit, or by disposition toward a habit.

Thirdly: Most dispositions are nothing other than new motions pertaining to the Renovation or sanctification of the mind, and indeed following Justification in the order of nature, such as Hope, Charity, Fear, and other similar ones.

Fourthly: Nowhere in the entire Scripture is justification attributed to Fear, or Hope, or Charity, as it is to Faith. Therefore, Faith, insofar as it justifies, cannot be recalled under the same genus of dispositions.

Fifthly: The Jesuits establish contradictions: For they commonly teach that Charity is the very form or habit inherent in justice. Therefore, it is false that Bellarmino contends it is a disposition to justice along with faith.

Sixthly: The Apostle is a witness that GOD justifies us while we are ungodly, not yet loving, and freely without the consideration of any work, imputing justice through faith, Rom. 4, 5. and 6. It is therefore fictitious and trifling that the Romanists grunt, that GOD does not justify unless formally disposed beforehand through Faith, Hope, Charity, repentance, etc.

Seventhly: No motion toward a thing is the thing itself, nor does it generate a disposition, but it is a way toward generation. Therefore, Faith does not justify by way of disposition: The reason is: Because Scripture assigns to faith not a motion toward Justification, but justification itself.

Eighthly: Justification does not occur through motion, like heating, but through imputation: Therefore, Faith, by which we are justified, cannot or ought not to be defined by motion or disposition.

Ninthly: In the Scriptures, there is ascribed to Faith not only the beginning, or the first root of justification: but all perfection, that is, the beginning, middle, and end: as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 5:1. Being justified by faith, we have peace with GOD: but where there is peace with GOD: there is the perfection of salvation: For nothing else can be added beyond this peace to righteousness and eternal life. Thus, regarding the middle and the end, that is, the progress and continuation of Justification, all those things are owed to faith alone. For by faith, says the Apostle in Rom. 5:2, we have not only been brought into this grace: but also by it we stand, nay, by it we glory in the hope of the glory of GOD. To which pertains also that of Peter 1. ch. 1. 5. By the power of GOD THROUGH FAITH you are kept for salvation. Therefore, these trifles are more vain than Sicilian nonsense, that Faith justifies only as the first root and by way of disposition. Let the Jesuit also remember that Augustine indeed names Faith a root, but not of justification, but rather of good work, in Psalm 31.

The third and last error of the Jesuits, which pertains to this, is that they contend partly that that apprehensive power belongs not so much to Faith as to the works of the reborn: and partly that Faith justifies, not only because it looks to the promise and apprehends it by believing: but because it obtains Remission, and in a certain way of its own merits it, as Bellarmine writes in book 1 on Justification, chapter 17, page 998. C. That the former part of this error is manifestly false will be readily apparent if only that is considered, how grace and justice are offered to us. For from that it will not be difficult to judge concerning the medium or apprehensive Organ. But that Justice or Grace of GOD is offered only through gratuitous promises. Now, however, it is not the promise and Works: but only Faith and the promise that look to each other as correlates. Therefore, it is necessary that the promise be apprehended not by works, but by Faith. The assumption is most evidently established from that Apostolic antithesis, Rom. 11:6, by which Grace and Works are so opposed to each other in the act of Justification that one excludes the other. Furthermore, it is worthy of observation that works are nowhere in the Scriptures compared to hands: but to feet: since in the stadium of good works and the newness of life we are commanded to walk and run. Just as, therefore, in the human Body feet are not suitable organs for apprehending something, but for walking and running. So good works in the business of salvation cannot have the use or power of apprehending justice: but they only perform this, that after we have already been justified by faith, we may walk worthily of the Gospel, or the Grace which we have received. As for the latter error, the Jesuits trifle shamefully. For they have not given, nor will they ever give, proof that Faith justifies not only organically or relatively: but also meritoriously. And this opinion fights contradictorily and plainly with those phrases of Scripture in part, which assert that Man is justified GRATUITOUSLY, without works, where indeed Faith also, insofar as it takes on the respect of a virtue or some work, is expunged from the act of justification no less than the rest of the works: and in part with other equivalent phrases of Scripture, which hint clearly enough what it is to be justified by Faith, such as: Faith is imputed for justice: Item, we are justified from faith to faith: Item, through faith, concerning which [I have spoken] more prolixly above. Then this assertion opposes itself expressly to the Apostle affirming that Faith is imputed to him who DOES NOT WORK: but only to him who believes. For merit and works behave themselves correlatively, as the Apostle explains in the same place: The reward, he says, is imputed to him who WORKS not from Grace, but from debt. But faith is imputed to him who BELIEVES not from debt, but only from Grace. Therefore Faith, insofar as it is imputed for justice, is not a work, and consequently neither is it a merit. Thirdly: The phrase THROUGH FAITH Διὰ πίστεως, which Bellarmine urges so strongly, denotes not an efficient or meritorious cause, but only an instrumental or Organic one: and thus Faith is opposed to reason, science, Law, works, virtues, dispositions, and other movements of that kind, through which the Jesuits falsely opine that justification is brought about.

Finally, the reasons which Bellarmine produces are altogether straw. For although in Luke 7:50 it is said to the woman: Thy faith hath saved thee: yet the word to make does not denote merit, but expresses only the Organ through which Salvation and justice were imputed to her, namely through Faith. What? That in the Greek the word to make is not present at all: but it is read simply, ἡ πίστις σꭢ σεσωκέ σε, Thy faith hath saved thee. Therefore the Jesuit wastes his effort and oil while he strives so solicitously to rub a meritorious cause of Faith onto the word to make. Thus, that Faith obtains salvation is beyond doubt; but it does not immediately follow from this what the Jesuit intends: Faith obtains salvation. Therefore, it obtains it under the reason of its own dignity and merit. For the Apostle denies this consequence, as has been shown several times thus far. And another mode is given, which is and is called instrumental or Organic.

Latin:

Quomodo Fides in Christum justificare dicatur?

COntrovertitur inter nos & Jesuïtas tertio loco de officio ipso Fidei, in opere sive actu Justificationis. Cùm enim Fides geminam fortiatur conditionem: Unam absolutam: Alteram relatam: quæritur, cujus conditionis respectu Fides nos justificare statuatur? Absolutè autem consideratur Fides tùm, quando in se & ex se, ut virtus & qualitas sive Habitus aliquis æstimatur. Quò sanè respectu magna est fidei præstantia, quippè quæ omne rationis nostræ & sensuum judicium captivum ducit, causarum naturalium vires cõtemnit: contra spem in spem credit: impedimentis & tentationibus quibusvis fortiter resistit: Diabolum vincit: DEO denique gloriam suam rectissimè asserit. Relatè autem, quando non ut opus, virtus aut qualitas: sed tantùm ut organum apprehendens meritum Christi expenditur. Et tantùm hoc posteriore respectu Fides justificare dicitur, ita ut non Subjectum: sed Objectum fidei Justificationis actum perficiat. Objectum autem illud nullum est aliud, pręter gratuitam misericordiæ divinæ promissionem de remissione peccatorum & adoptione credentium, per & propter Christum Mediatorem. Hoc enim Objectum Fides Justificans non nudâ tantùm notitiâ, neque simplici duntaxat assensu mentis: sed verâ ac indubitatâ cordis fiducia amplectitur.

Confirmant autem sententiam hanc nostram Scripturarum testimonia, quæ evincunt, phrasin hanc Justificari fide, vel per fidem, vel ex fide, eôdem planè sensu accipiendam esse, quô accipiuntur æquipollentes aliæ, quæ asserunt, nos justificari per ἀπολύτρωσιν JESU CHRISTI, per sanguinem & mortem Christi, per obedientiam Christi, Rom. 3, 24. & 25. cap. 5, 9. & 19. Ratio evidens est, quòd non multiplex aut varia est justificandi ratio, sed Una tantùm. Ergo si sanguine ac merito Christi tantùm justificamur: utique Fide etiam justificari nihil erit aliud, quàm solo Christi meritô, fide apprehensô, justificari: ac per Consequens relatè tantùm non verò absolutè Fides in actu Justificationis considerari debet. Interim tamen non imus inficias, phrasi huic (Fide justificamur) inesse sensum metalepticum: dùm nimirùm Effectus causæ principalis tribuitur instrumentali. Fide enim accipimus remissionem peccatorum propter sanguinem Christi: non propter fidei dignitatem aut præstantiam. Quo observatô, altorum etiam illud emergit axioma notatu dignissimum, quòd nimirùm Fides Justitiam nobis conferat, non Effectivè, quasi habitualiter justos nos efficiat, vel, ut Jesuuitæ loquuntur, quòd ad justitiam habitualem disponat aut informet: neque etiam materialiter, quasi Fides ipsa sit id, quô justi censemur: sed partim Objectivè, quatenùs Christum, qui solus nostra est justitia respicit: partim Organicè, quatenùs Justitiam CHRISTI gratis credentibus imputatam, apprehendit.

Puriori huic Doctrinæ acriter contradicunt Romanenses, triplici potissimùm prodito errore. Primùm enim fidem in actu Justificationis considerandam esse dictitant, quatenùs est virtus sive habitus inhærens, cujus tanta sit dignitas, ut Hominem justificare possit.

Prodidit hunc errorem Bellarminus quoque, lib. 1. de Justif. cap. 3. p. 938. sic scribens: Dissentimus de modo, quo fides justificat. Ipsi enim (Lutherani) contendunt, fidem nullius esse pretij & meriti, & situm relative justificare: Nos afferimus, Fidem etiam à Charitate disiunctam, alicujus esse pretij, & vim habere justificandi, per modum dispositionis & impetrationis.

Sed quod dicit Bellarminus, non probat: quin potiùs initiò splendidè mentitur, afferens Fidem à Lutheranis nullius pretij instar haberi. Etsi enim justificandi ἐνέργειαν ipsi, tanquàm virtuti & qualitati derogamus: nos tamen interim affignamus ei effectus sive actus, qui certè usque adeò sunt excellentes, ut nulla virtus alia, ad illorum præstantiam affurgere possit: uti suprà quosdam enumeravimus, & fidei etiam absolutè consideratæ tribuimus. Deindè verò opinio hæc Jesuitica manifesta impietate laborat, quin veterem illum jampridem damnatum Gnosticorum errorem ab orco revocare videtur, qui & ipsi dignitati & præstantiæ fidei, omnem justificandi vim assignârunt: ita ut qui eam saltem profiteantur, licèt pessimè vivant, justificationem indè fortiantur. Cui sanè utrique tùm Gnosticorum & Jesuitarum errori opponimus ea, quæ modò doctrinæ nostræ ex Scripturis depromsimus Fundamenta: quin etiam Augustini libellum, quem de fide & operibus, sensu planè Lutherano, contra Gnosticos jam olim scripsit. Observationem autem hoc loco meretur Romanensium ἀνθομολογία sive inconstantia. Nam superiore seculo eam fidei nauoitatem cofinxerunt, ut ad titivilitium usque eam extenuarent: nunc verò in hyperbolicam ejus prædicationem delabuntur, secundum illud: Stulti dùm vitant vitia, in contraria currunt.

Alter error Jesuitarum est, quòd contendunt, Fidem justificare non vel objectivè, vel relativè: sed per modum dispositionis: uti loquitur Bellarminus lib. 1. de Justif. cap. 3. p 938. C. D. & uberiùs se explicat cap. 12. p 973 B. Catholici inquiens, Septem actus enumerant, quibus impij ad justiciam disponuntur, videlicet, Fidei, Timoris, Spei, Dilectionis, pœnitentiæ, propositi suscipiendi Sacramenti, & propositi novæ vitæ, atq, observationis mandatorum DEI. Insert proindè Jesu wita, cap. subseq. 13. l. C. D. Fidem justificare ut initium & radicem primam justificationis.

Erroti huic opponimus: 1. Id, quod Justificatio neque in Scripturis, neque in ullo idiomate, pro dispositione ac motu ad justitiam in se recipiendam, usurpatur aut accipitur. Jam autem Scriptura disertè adscribit fidei justificationem. E. non dispositionem ad justitiam, sed actum ipsum Justificationis exprimit.

Deindè omnis dispositio, quocunq; veniat nomine, cadit sub genus operum, ac proindè ex Lege DEI naturam ac æstimationem suam fortitur: siquidem Lex omnes nostras actiones informat, quæ fiunt, vel DEI vel proximi respectu.

Jam verò Justificatio non est ex Lege, sed ex promissione tantùm, Gal. 3, 21. Ergo Fides, quâ justificamur non potest aut debet definiri ex Lege, vel per habitum, vel per dispositionem ad habitum.

Tertiò: Dispositiones pleræque nihil sunt aliud, quàm motus novi ad Renovationem sive sanctificationem mentis pertinentes, & quidem ordine naturæ Justificationem demùm sequentes, quales sunt Spes, Charitas, Timor & Consimiles aliæ.

Quartò: Nuspiam in universa Scriptura Timori, aut Spei, aut Charitati tribuitur justificatio, quemadmodum Fidei. Ergo Fides, quatenùs justificat, sub idem genus dispositionum revocari nequit.

Quintò: ἀντιφατικὰ statuunt Jesuitæ: Communiter enim docent, Charitatem esse ipsam formam sive habitum inhærentem justitiæ. Ergo falsum, quòd eam cum fide Bellarminus contendit esse dispositionem ad justitiam.

Sextò: Apostolus testis est DEUM justificare nos impios existentes, nondum diligentes, & gratis sine intuitu ullius operis, imputare justitiam per fidem, Rom. 4, 5. & 6. Fictitium ergò & nugatorium est, quòd grunniunt Romanenses, DEUM non justificare, nisi formaliter priùs dispositos per Fidem, Spem, Charitatem, pœnitentiam, &c.

Septimò: Nullus motus ad rem est res ipsa, neque dispositio generat, sed est via ad generationem. Ergo Fides non justificat per modum dispositionis: Ratio est: Quia Scriptura fidei adsignat non motum ad Justificationem, sed justificationem ipsam.

Octavò: Justificatio non sit per motum, sicut Calefactio, sed per imputationem: Ergò Fides, quâ justificamur, non potest aut debet definiri per motum sive dispositionem.

Nonò: in Scripturis adscribitur Fidei non initium tantùm, sive prima radix justificationis: sed omnis perfectio, hoc est, initium, medium & finis: teste Apostolo Rom. 5, 1. Justificati fide, pacem habemus apud DEUM: sed ubi pax cum DEO: ibi perfectio salutis: Neqs enim ultra pacem hanc quicquam aliud ad justitiam & vitam æternam adjici potest. Sic quoad medium & finem, hoc est, progressum & continuationem Justificationis, illa omnia soli debentur fidei. Nam per fidem inquit Apostolus Rom 5, 2. non modò adducti sumus in hanc gratiam: sed etiam per eam stamus, imò per eam gloriamur sub spe gloriæ DEI. Quò pertinet & illud Petrir. c. 1. 5. Virtute DEI PER FIDEM custodimini ad salutem. Nugæ ergo gerris Siculis vaniores sunt, quòd Fides tantùm justificet, ut radix prima & per modum dispositionis. Meminerit etiam Jesuwita, quòd Augustinus Fidem quidem nominat radicem, sed non justificationis, verùm boni operis, in Psal. 31.

Tertius & Postremus error Jesu vvitarum, qui huc pertinet, est quòd contendunt partim vim illam apprehensivam, non tàm Fidei, quàm operibus etiam renatorum competere: partim verò Fidem justificare, non tantùm quia respiciat promissionem, & illam credendo apprehendat: sed quia Remissionem impetret, & suo quodam modo mereatur, uti scribit Bellarminus lib. 1. de Justif. cap. 17. pag. 998. C. Priorem erroris hujus partem manifestè falsam esse, ultrò patebit, si illud modò consideretur, quomodo gratia & justitia nobis offeratur. Indè enim de medio sive Organo apprehensivo haud difficile erit judicare. Offertur autem illa Justitia sive Gratia DEI, non nisi per promissiones gratuitas. Jam verò non promissio & Opera: sed tantùm Fides & promissio se mutuò ut correlata respiciunt. Ergo non operibus, sed Fide promissio apprehendatur necesse est. Assumtio evidentissimè constat ex ἀντιθέσει illa Apostolica, Rom. 11, 6. quâ Gratia & Opera in actu Justificationis ita sibi opponuntur, ut unum alterum excludat. Præterea observatione dignum est, quòd opera nusquàm in Scripturis comparantur manibus: sed pedibus: siquidem in stadio bonorum operum & novitate vitæ jubemur ambulare & currere. Quemadmodum ergo in humano Corpore pedes non sunt idonea organa ad apprehendendum aliquid, sed ad ambulandum & currendum. Ita opera bona in negocio salutis non possunt habere usum aut vim apprehendendi justitiam: sed id tantùm præstant, ut postquàm jam fide justificati sumus, dignè ambulemus Evangelio, sive Gratiâ, quam accepimus. Quoad posteriorem errorem, turpiter nugantur Jesuitæ. Neque enim probatum dederunt, vel dabunt unquàm, Fidem justificare non tantùm organicè sive relatè: sed etiam meritoriè. Et pugnat hæc sententia contradictoriè planè cum iis partim Scripturæ phrasibus, quæ asserunt, Hominem GRATIS justificari, sine operibus, Ubi sanè Fides etiam, quatenùs virtutis aut operis alicujus respectum induit, haud minùs atq; reliqua opera ex actu justificationis expungitur: partim aliis Scripturæ phrasibus æquipollentibus, quæ quid sit Fide justificari, satis dilucidè innuit, quales sunt: Fides imputatur ad justitiam: Item, justificamur ex fide in fidem: Item, per fidem, de quibus suprà prolixiùs. Deindè adversatur hæc assertio Ἐξαρῥήδως Apostolo affirmanti, quòd Fides imputetur NON OPERANTI: sed tantùm credenti. Nam meritum & opera habent se correlatè, uti ibidem Apostolus explicat: Merces, inquiens, imputatur Operanti non ex Gratia, sed ex debito. Atqui fides imputatur Credenti non ex debito, sed tantùm ex Gratia. Ergo Fides quatenùs imputatur ad justitiam non est opus, ac per consequens neq; meritum. Tertiò: Phrasis PER FIDEM Διὰ πίστεως, quam Bellarminus tantoperè urget, non causam efficientem aut meritoriam, sed instrumentalem tantùm sive Organicam notat: & sic Fides opponitur rationi, scientiæ, Legi, operibus, virtutibus, dispositionibus, & id genus motibus aliis, per quos Jesuitae justificationem fieri falsò opinantur.

Tandem rationes, quas producit Bellarminus, prorsus sunt stramineae. Etsi enim Luc. 7. ult. dicitur mulieri: Fides tua salvam te fecit: tamen verbum facere non notat meritum, sed exprimit tantùm Organum, per quod ipsi imputata sit Salus & justitia, nempè per Fidem. Quid? quòd in Graeco verbum facere prorsus non habetur: sed simpliciter legitur, ἡ πίστις σꭢ σεσωκέ σε, Fides tua salvavit te. Ergo operam & oleum perdit Jesusuwita, dùm ex verbo facere, usque adeò sollicitè Fidei causam meritoriam affricare studet. Sic quòd Fides impetret salutem; extra dubium est; sed hoc non statim sequitur, quod intendit Jesuwita: Fides impetrat salutem. E. sub ratione suae dignitatis atꝙ meriti impetrat. Hanc enim consecutionem negat Apostolus, uti aliquoties hactenùs ostensum. Et datur modus alius, qui est & dicitur instrumentalis sive Organicus.


### III. Special Controversy, On the Material Cause of Justification

We establish the material cause, or rather the Subject to be justified, to be One and Only Man, and indeed insofar as he has fallen through sin and is subject to eternal damnation. For if man had persisted in the concreated justice and Holiness of the divine Image, he would certainly have propagated the same by transmission to all his posterity, and would have had no need of any Mediator or Redeemer.

With this thesis standing, it is prompt to gather from it that the entire Angelic order is excluded from Justification. For the good Angels, who stood in the truth and proved their obedience to GOD the creator, were confirmed in that very Justice in which they were created, without Redemption and Justification. But the evil ones, who did not stand in the truth, were so rejected by GOD that no hope of salvation remains for them, but they are addicted to eternal damnation.

Therefore, gross and horrendous was the error of the Origenists, who raved that the punishments of reprobate men, as also of the Devils themselves, would not be eternal, but would be finished in the space of a thousand years, and that they would each at last be saved, but that the Elect would then be damned in their place. Concerning which error Augustine rightly says in On Heresies, chapter 43: What Catholic Christian, whether learned or unlearned, would not vehemently shudder at this purgation of the wicked and of demons? But let the prolix disputation of the same Augustine be seen, opposed to this most vain impiety, in the books on the City of GOD, especially book 20, chapters 7 and 9, and book 21, chapter 23, and book 22, passim.

But neither is Otto Brunfels found to have fostered a more tolerable error among the more recent ones, who in his Theological Pandects, printed at Strasbourg in the year 1529, page 16, expressly He writes that Christ also died for the angels and demons, and redeemed them. His own words are these: In Christ dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead, who redeemed us with his blood, Apocal. 5. and 15. also the angels in the heavens and the demons. And on the same page, he sets this title: Christ also died for the spirits and angels. For the sake of confirming this opinion of his, he brings forward the following passages of Scripture.

Ephes. 1, 10. Christ has summed up all things which are in the heavens, and which are on the earth.

Ephes. 3, 9. 10. Who created all things through Christ, so that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to all principalities and powers in the heavens through the Church.

Coloss. 1, 20. Making peace through the blood of his cross, whether they be things in the heavens, or things on the earth.

1. Pet. 3, 19. In which he also went and preached to the spirits who were in prison, who were once disobedient.

1. Pet. 4, 6. The Gospel was preached also to the dead.

Apocal. 5, 9. You were slain, say the angels, and you have redeemed us to GOD in your blood.

But in most of these passages, an ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꞢ and a fallacy of the figure of speech are shamefully committed. For regarding the passage in Ephes. 1, 10 and Coloss. 1, 20, the Apostle, by the ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν and εἰρηνοποίησιν, the restoration or pacification of all things, both those which are in the heavens and those which are on the earth, wished to include all those things which either needed restoration or had to be reconciled with the human race. First, therefore, there was discord between GOD and men: For our sins have divided between us and our GOD. Isa. 59, 2. Then, discord also arose between the good and evil angels. For just as, if man had persisted in integrity, the greatest union and concord would have flourished between men and angels: so after man turned himself away from GOD through sin, immediately the angels themselves also became hostile. Both this discord was removed through Christ, and through his blood we were so reconciled to GOD the Father that those heavenly spirits, who were previously alienated from us, have been made our friends again, indeed our ministers and fellow-servants. And this is what the Apostle says, that Christ restored even those things which were in the heavens, which is very ignorantly snatched and twisted toward the redemption of the angels. For as the Epistle to the Hebrews testifies: Christ did not take hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham, Heb. 2. v. 16. Therefore, he did not redeem angels either, but the seed of Abraham, according to that saying of Nazianzen: τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον: ὁ δὲ ἥνωται τῷ θεῷ, τοῦτο καὶ σώζεται: That which is not assumed is not healed: but that which is united to GOD, that is also saved.

It is added that that ἀνακεφαλαίωσις of those things which are in the heavens can not ineptly be understood of the Church of the Elect Triumphant, which, no less than the one militant on these earths, has been redeemed by Christ and, as it were, restored to its entirety.

The passage Eph. 3, 9. & 10. labors with the same word through ελεγχω. For there is no other sense of the Apostle's words than that those hidden mysteries of divine wisdom, which are now revealed in the Gospel in the Church, were also made known to the blessed Angels, but were previously unknown to them. But what has this to do with the redemption of the Angels?

Two passages from 1 Pet. 3, 19. & 4, 6. deal not with Angels, but with the spirits of men who perished in the waters of the flood in the times of Noah, and paid the penalties for their disobedience. Furthermore, if the Gospel was preached to the dead, it was certainly not preached to the Angels, since they are not subject to mortality.

The Apocalyptic passage again has nothing at all to do with the Angels: for that song which is described in that place was not sung by angelic spirits, but by those twenty-four Elders, that is, by all the Saints, who pursue their redemption with ardent prayers, and desire to be finally and fully liberated from this prison.

But not even the Romanists hold to orthodoxy in all things regarding the matter or Subject of Justification. For although they concede that Man is the subject or matter of Justification, they nevertheless require such a man who, by the powers of free will, can dispose himself to receive Justification, and indeed prepare himself in such a way that GOD, if not by merit of condignity, is nevertheless bound by merit of congruity to bestow justification upon him in place of a reward. Therefore, according to the opinion of the Romanists, the subject of justification is not an ungodly man, but one who is already pious and penitent. For Bellarmine himself means this, saying, The mind of man, or his very will, in which justice dwells as in its subject and proper seat, can be called the Material Cause. Dispositions, which prepare the matter to receive the form, also pertain to the material Cause. Moreover, those acts of grace and free will by which the gift of justification itself is acquired are called dispositions to justification, such as, according to the opinion of the Council of Trent, Sess. 6, Can. 6, are the acts of faith, fear, hope, love, and repentance. Thus far Bellarmine, lib. 1, de Justif. cap. 2, pag. 937. D.

This is a Lernaean swamp of the grossest errors, to which we oppose Apostolic Authority from Rom. 4, 5, where the subject or material cause of Justification is defined as Man, with a manifest determination of ungodliness: To him who believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, faith is imputed for righteousness. From which a universal conclusion is built: that all are ungodly before justification, and that no one brings preparatory dispositions of free will to the grace of justification. And what, I ask, would the ungodly bring, being void of the fear of GOD, piety, and faith? Where also that point deserves observation, that the Apostle does not say that God justifies the unjust ἀδίκως, where perhaps someone might dream of merely a privation of justice: but the ungodly (ἀσεβεῖς), where the term for ungodliness (ἀσεβείας) expresses the very idea of injustice sufficiently and more than enough: and indeed not only that external and grosser kind, such as is found in the manifestly wicked, as the Romanists are accustomed to cavil: but also that internal impurity of the heart, with which we all labor before GOD before justification: according to that of Job 14, v. 4: Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean seed? We conclude therefore with the Blessed Ambrose, commenting on this very Apostolic passage as follows:

Manifestly blessed are those to whom, without any labor or work, iniquities are remitted and sins are covered, with no work of penance required of them, except only that they believe.

Latin:

CAusam materialem vel Subjectum potiùs justificandum, statuimus esse Unum & Solum Hominem, & quidem quatenus per peccatum lapsus, aeternae damnationi subjacet. Quòd si enim in concreata justitia & Sanctitate Imaginis divinae perstitisset homo, certè eandem per traducem ad omnem posteritatem propagasset, neque Mediatore aut Redemtore ullo opus habuisset.

Stante hac thesi, promptum est indè colligere, à Justificatione excludi universum ordinem Angelicum. Nam boni Angeli, qui in veritate steterunt, suamque DEO conditori obedientiam comprobarunt, in ea ipsâ, quâ conditi fuerunt, Justitiâ confirmati sunt, citra Redemtionem & Justificationem. Mali verò qui in veritate non steterunt, ita rejecti sunt à DEO, ut nulla spes salutis ipsis sit reliqua, sed aeternae damnationi sint addicti.

Crassus proindè & horrendus fuit error Origenistarum delirantium, poenas reproborum hominum, ut & Diabolorum ipsorum non fore aeternas, sed mille annorum spatio finiendas, eosꝙ singulos tandem salvatum iri, Electos verò tùm illorum loco damnatum iri. De quo errore rectè Augustinus de haeresibus cap. 43. Quis Catholicus Christianus, vel doctus vel indoctus non vehementer exhorreat hanc malorum & daemonum purgationem? Videatur autem prolixa ejusdem Augustini disputatio, vanissimae huic impietati opposita, in libris de Civitate DEI, libro praesertim 20. capp 7. & 9. & lib. 21. cap 23. & lib. 22. passim.

Sed nec tolerabiliorem errorem ex recentioribus fovisse deprehenditur Otto Brunfelsius, qui in Pandectis suis Theologicis, Argentorati Anno 29. supra sesquimillesimum excusis pag. 16. disertè Christum etiam pro Angelis & dæmonibus mortuum esse, eosq́; redemisse scribit. Verba ipsius sunt hæc: In Christo inhabitavit omnis plenitudo Divinitatis, qui nos redemit sanguine suo, Apocal. 5. & 15. etiam Angelos in cælestibus & dæmones. Et eâdem pagina, titulum ponit istum: Christus etiam pro Spiritibus & Angelis mortuus est. Cujus suæ sententiæ confirmandæ gratia profert sequentes Scripturæ locos.

Ephes. 1, 10. Christus summatim instauravit omnia quæ in cælis sunt, & quæ in terra.

Ephes. 3, 9. 10. Qui in universa condidit per Christum, ut nota fiat omnibus principatibus & potestatibus in Cælestibus per Ecclesiam, multiformis Sapientia Dei.

Coloss. 1, 20. Pacificans per sanguinem crucis ipsius, sive quæ in Cælis sunt, sive quæ in terra.

1. Pet. 3, 19. In quo etiam abiit, & Spiritibus, qui erant in carcere prædicavit, qui inobedientes erant quondam.

1. Pet. 4, 6. Mortuis quoque prædicatum est Evangelium.

Apocal. 5, 9. Occisus es, inquiunt Angeli, & redemistinos DEO in sanguine tuo.

Verùm in plerisq; istis locis turpiter committitur ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꞢ, & Sophisma Figuræ Dictionis. Nam quoad locum Ephes. 1, 10. & Coloss. 1, 20. Apostolus per ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν κ, εἰρηνοποίησιν restitutionem sive pacificationem omnium, tum quæ in Cælis, tùm quæ in terra sunt, complecti voluit universa ea, quæ vel instauratioue ind gebant, vel cum genere humano reconcilianda erant. Primùm ergo discordia erat inter DEUM & homines: Nam peccata nostra diviserunt inter nos & DEUM nostrum. Jes. 59, 2. Deindè discordia etiam oborta fuit inter Angelos bonos & malos. Quemadmodum enim, si homo in integritate perstitisset, summa floruisset conjunctio & concordia inter Homines & Angelos: ita pòstquàm Homo per peccatum à DEO se avertit, statim Angeli quoque ipsi facti sunt infensi. Ultraq; hæc discordia per Christum sublata est, perq; ipsius sanguinem ita DEO Patri reconciliati sumus, ut cœlestes illi Spiritus, qui prius abalienati à nobis erant, denuò nobis amici, imò ministri & conservi facti sint. Et hoc est, quod Apostolus dicit, Christum restaurasse etiam ea, quæ in Cælis emnt, id quod inscitè admodum ad Angelorum redemtionem rapitur & detorquetur. Nam teste Epistolâ ad Hebræos: Non Angelos, sed Semen Abrahæ Christus affumsit, Heb. 2. v. 16. E. Non Angelos etiam, sed Semen Abrahæ redemit, secundum illud Nazianzeni: τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον: ὁ δὲ ἥνωται τῷ θεῷ, τοῦτο καὶ σώζεται: Quod assumtum non est, nec redemtum est: Quod verò unitum est DEO, illud & sanatur.

Accedit, quòd illa ἀνακεφαλαίωσις eorum, quæ in Cælis sunt, haud ineptè intelligi potest, de Ecclesia Electorum Triumphante, quæ haud minùs, atq; in his terris militans, à Christo est redemta, & quasi in integrum restituta.

Locus Eph. 3, 9. & 10. eôdem per ελεγχω laborat. Sensus enim verborum Apostoli nullus est alius, quàm beatis quoque Angelis innotuisse arcana illa divinæ sapientiæ mysteria, quæ in Evangelio jam in Ecclesia revelantur, sed antea ipsis erant incognita. Sed quid hoc ad redemtionem Angelorum?

Loca duo ex 1. Pet. 3, 19. & 4, 6. agunt non de Angelis, sed de Spiritibus hominum, qui temporibus Noæ in aquis diluvii periêrut, & ἀπειθείας suæ pœnas luerunt. Porrò si mortuis prædicatum est Evangelium, utiq; Angelis non est prædicatum: quippè qui mortalitati non subjacent.

Locus Apocalypticus rursus nihil quicquam ad Angelos: Canticum enim illud, quod eo loci describitur, non cecinerunt Spiritus Angelici, sed viginti illi quatuor Seniores, hoc est, Sancti quique, qui ardentibus precibus suam redemtionem profequuntur, & vel tandem plenè ex hoc ergastulo liberari desiderant.

Sed ne quidem Romanenses per omnia ὀρθοδοξίαν tenent, circa materiam sive Subjectum Justificationis. Etsienim Hominem concedunt esse Subjectum sive materiam Justificationis: tamen talem Hominem requirunt, qui ex viribus liberi arbitrii semetipsum possit disponere ad recipiendam Justificationem imò ita sese præparare, ut DEUS si non ex condigno, ex congruo tamen teneatur, ipsi retributionis loco impertire justificationem. Ex sententia ergo Romanensium Subjectum justificationis non est homo impius: sed jam pius & pœnitens. Hoc ipsum enim vult Bellarminus, Materialis, inquiens, Causa dici potest animus hominis sive ipsa ejus voluntas, in qua justitia tanquàm in Subjecto & sede propria commoratur. Pertinent quoq, ad materialem Causam dispositiones, qua materiam præparant ad recipiendam formam. Dicuntur autem dispositiones ad justificationem, omnes illi actus gratia & liberi arbitrij, quibus donum ipsum justificationis acquiritur, quales sunt ex sententia Concilij Tridentini Sess. 6. Can. 6. actus fidei, timoris, Spei, dilectionis, pœnitentiæ. Hactenus Bellarminus lib. 1. de Justif. cap. 2. pag. 937. D.

Lernâ hæc est crassissimorum errorum, cui Apostolicam Autoritatem opponimus ex Rom. 4, 5. ubi Justificationis subjectum sive causa materialis definitur Homo, cum manifesta determinatione impietatis: Credenti in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur fides ad justitiam. Unde universalis extruitur Collectio, Omnes ante justificationem esse impios: neq; quenquam ad justificationis gratiam, dispositiones præparatorias liberi arbitrii afferre. Et quid quæso afferrent impii, timore DEI, pietate & fide vacui? Ubi & illud obier vationem meretur, quòd Apostolus nó dicit, Deum justificare ἀδίκως injustos, ubi fortè privationem duntaxat justitiæ somniare aliquis posset: sed ἀσεβεῖς, ubi ἀσεβείας terminus ipsam etiam injustitiæ ἰδέαν satis superque exprimit: & quidem non externam tantùm eam & crassiorem, qualis deprehenditur in manifestè flagitiosis, uti cavillari solent Romanenses: sed & internam illam cordis immunditiem, quâ ante justificationem coram DEO laboramus omnes: secundum illud Jobi 14. v. 4. Quis dabit mundum, de immundo conceptum semine? Concludimus proindè eum B. Ambrosio in hunc ipsum locum Apostolicum sic commentante:

Manifestè beati sunt, quibus sine labore vel opere aliquo remittuntur iniquitates, & peccata teguntur, nullo ab his requisito pænitentiæ opere, nisi tantùm, ut credant.


### IV. and the Final Special Controversy: On the Formal Cause of our Justification

This is the acropolis of the whole war which is waged most fiercely with the Jesuits concerning the Justification of Man. For if there were agreement on both sides concerning the Formal Cause of Justification, all the rest of the Controversy would surely expire of its own accord. However, the state of the Controversy is not that which the Jesuits often Sophistically and insidiously clamor about: namely, whether in the Justification of Man, through the grace of GOD, some renewal or Sanctification of the mind takes place? For no such thing has ever been denied by us. Likewise, it is not disputed whether that very renewal or sanctification of the mind can be named an inherent Quality and habitual Justice. For although all such holiness and justice is like a menstruous cloth, Isa. 64:6, nay, to be reckoned as dung, Phil. 3:8, because in the sight of GOD, or in the court of heaven, it cannot stand on account of the impurity and imperfection adhering to it: much less merit eternal life either in whole or in part: yet because the person himself is reconciled to GOD through faith, and the works of the reborn are done out of obedience owed to GOD, Rom. 6:17, Phil. 3:9, therefore they are sometimes designated in the Scriptures by the term Justice. Phil. 3:9, 1 John 3:7 and 10.

But this is what properly comes into Controversy: Whether the Formal Cause of our justification should be placed only in the merit or Satisfaction of CHRIST, imputed to us through faith, along with the gratuitous remission of all sins, apprehended through and because of CHRIST by faith? Where we concede to the Affirmative: the Papists, however, to the negative, contending that in place of the Formal Cause must be established those virtues which the Holy Spirit and the grace of GOD work in us, and in which the reborn and Children of GOD cooperate with divine grace, or as Bellarmine speaks, that it is inherent Justice.

Furthermore, in order that the chief foundations of our Affirmative may be better perceived, it should be noted that the word 'to impute' in this place is not taken Physically concerning the infusion of justice, just as shoots are said to be imputed to plants: But Relatively, concerning λογισμός or acceptance, as for example: when a victory against the Turks is imputed or ascribed to an Emperor, although he himself was not present at the battle. Now, although we by no means deny that there can be found in the Scriptures such places in which the foundation of imputation is something inherent in those to whom the imputation is made: the term, however, being either guilt or reward: as when 2 Sam. 19:19, Shimei says: Let not the King impute iniquity to me: And the Apostle 2 Tim. 4:16, all deserted me, may it not be imputed to them. And Rom. 4:4. To him who works, the reward is imputed as a debt: in the present matter, however, the Apostle uses this word in another and different signification, namely, when in the one to whom the imputation is made, no regard is established for the Foundation by whose dignity the imputation is made: but when it is made out of the gratuitous mercy of GOD, without our merit, nay, contrary to what we have merited, so that a foundation clearly contrary adheres to the one to whom the imputation is made: which the following reasons taken from Scripture irrefragably prove.

Reason 1. It has the Apostle as its author, Rom. 4:3, 4, and 5. Abraham believed GOD, and it was imputed to him for justice: But to him who works, the reward is not imputed according to grace, but as a debt: But to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed for justice. The argument can be such: If Abraham was justified by the imputation of faith, it could not be that he was justified for inherent justice, or from works. But Abraham obtained justice only by the imputation of faith. Therefore, not for inherent justice, or from works, and consequently, the Formal Cause of our Justification is not inherent proper justice: but imputed alien justice, namely, that of CHRIST.

The Apostle himself confirms the connection of the Major premise from proper contraries, adjuncts, and consequences. For those things whose contraries are proper, adjuncts, and consequences, and which exclude each other, those very things must also be contrary. Now, such contraries can be given in the opposition of faith and works: or of imputed and inherent justice. For 1. in imputation the subject to be justified is ἀσεβής, ungodly: in meritorious justification, therefore, it is necessary to be εὐσεβής. 2. In imputation, Faith is regarded: but in merit, works are regarded. 3. In imputation, grace alone has a place: but in meritorious, justice, debt. 4. In imputative, justice is a gift: but in meritorious, a reward. Since all these things are surely contrary, it is necessary that their subjects and antecedents also mutually exclude each other: so that neither can the one be truly predicated of the other, nor both of a third: that is, that to whom justice is imputed through faith, to him the same cannot be imputed on account of the inherent justice of his own merits.

He relies on the authority of the Scriptures, Gen. 15, 6. Rom. 4, 3. Therefore the truth of his conclusion remains unshaken.

Pererius objects in his Commentary on chapter 15 of Genesis: that faith was therefore imputed to Abraham for righteousness, because it was a work or a most perfect and excellent thing: and consequently that Abraham was justified by inherent righteousness. But the sophist inflicts manifest violence upon the Apostolic text, which expressly opposes faith ἀνυποδιηγημέρως to works indefinitely of all kinds: For not to him that worketh, but to Abraham that believeth, was faith imputed for righteousness, and indeed by grace. Therefore the faith of Abraham does not denote an act or work by which he might have merited to be justified, or by which he might be formally justified: for the Apostle simply denies this: but it denotes that firm confidence by which he rested solely in the promise of God, or in the promised Seed of the woman, and thus believed in hope against hope: as the Apostle himself explains, Rom. 4.

II. The argument can be as follows: Scripture assigns blessedness to those to whom GOD imputes righteousness without works. Therefore, the Formal Cause of our Justification does not consist in inherent habitual righteousness, but only in the gratuitous imputation of the alien righteousness of CHRIST.

Or it can be formulated in another way as follows: The Holy Spirit defines the righteousness of those to be saved by imputation alone, and indeed by imputation without works. Therefore, works and imputation are rightly established as mutually exclusive in the act of justification. The entire antecedent is ἕγγραφον, since it is taken from Psalm 32:1: Blessed is he whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered: Blessed is the man to whom the LORD has not imputed sin. The consequent has the Apostle himself as its author, Rom. 4:6, inferring thus: Therefore David says this is the blessedness of man, if GOD imputes righteousness to him without works. Therefore, and consequently, without inherent habitual righteousness.

III. The argument is constructed from the same passages as follows: Whoever is justified by the remission of sins, to him righteousness cannot come from the works of inherent righteousness. But all who are to be saved are justified by the remission of sins: Therefore, righteousness does not come to them from the works of inherent habitual righteousness. The connection of the major premise is evident from the fact that where there is inherent habitual righteousness, there the remission of sins has no place, and vice versa. The minor premise rests on the authority of David and Paul, in the passages already cited: Therefore.

IV. Argument: In whatever [person or thing] CHRIST is not our righteousness, that cannot be the formal cause of our justification. But Christ is not our righteousness by reason of the virtues and works which the Holy Spirit works in us, and which inhere in us, but only in his obedience, righteousness, and blood, through the remission of sins. Therefore, our inherent virtue or righteousness also cannot be the formal cause of our justification.

The connection of the major premise is self-evident: For since Christ alone has been made for us by the Father Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification, Redemption: certainly the formal cause of this righteousness of ours cannot be that in which Christ is not our righteousness.

The minor premise is clearly evident from the testimonies of the Scriptures, such as these:

Rom 3:25. GOD set forth Christ as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness, through the remission of sins.

Rom 5:19. Just as through the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners: so through the obedience of one, many shall be made righteous.

Coloss. 1:14. In Christ we have redemption through the remission of sins.

1 John 1:7. The blood of JESUS CHRIST the Son of GOD cleanses us from all sin.

Luke 1:77. Christ will give the knowledge of salvation to his people, which is in the remission of sins.

Nor can even one testimony be brought forward by the Adversaries, by which it might be confirmed, even probably in appearance, that Christ is our righteousness by reason of any righteousness or virtue of our own that is inherent.

V. Argument: In whatever a man cannot safely rely during any temptations, even Satanic ones, and indeed in the very hour of death; which likewise cannot be opposed to the most severe divine judgment; in that it is impossible for the formal cause of our justification to consist. But our inherent righteousness and any other virtue whatsoever can consist neither in temptations nor in the judgment of God: Therefore, the formal cause of our justification cannot be established in it either.

The minor premise, which contains the τὸ κρινόμενον, is evident from the fact that all our righteousness in the sight of God is like a menstruous cloth. Isa. 64:6. And if you have done all things, say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done. Luke 17:10.

VI. Argument: The righteousness of Christ, by which we are saved, is the righteousness revealed in the Gospel, without the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe. Rom. 3:22. Now, an infused habit of righteousness cannot be called revealed without the law. For the law commands legal righteousness, that is, charity and the fulfillment of works, in the highest degree. Therefore, the righteousness of Christ, by which we are saved, is other than infused charity or inherent righteousness: it is, namely, that which God imputes to the sinner freely without works, Rom. 4:6.

VII. Argument: No formal cause can consist of contraries. Therefore, neither can the formal cause of our justification consist of the righteousness of faith and the righteousness of the law or of works: The reason is that these two righteousnesses behave as contraries. Therefore, they cannot consist together in one and the same subject in respect to one and the same end. That they are contraries is evident from the fact that the righteousness of the law is inherent: but the righteousness of faith is not inherent, but imputed: The former is obtained by the worker: the latter by the believer: The former is by debt: the latter is by grace: The former is a reward: the latter is truly a gift.

From these and other arguments of this kind, we finally conclude invincibly: 1. That the formal cause of our justification is not any righteousness inherent in us, but the alien righteousness of Christ, which the Apostle names imputative righteousness. 2. That this imputed righteousness is not legal conformity or inherent perfection, but the gratuitous remission of sins and acceptance in the judgment of God on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. For what is imputed gratuitously, that neither inheres nor is owed. But righteousness is imputed to believers gratuitously, and indeed without works. Therefore, it neither formally inheres in them, nor is it owed by right as a reward.

Moreover, a new question arises here: namely, how the form of this very imputation itself behaves? Or by what parts is it completed? The decision, however, is most correctly sought from the very act or motion of our justification. Just as in it there are two different terms: one is of the evil from which we are freed: the other is of the good to which we are transferred: so also a twofold form of this imputation is given: One privative, by which that which is within is not imputed: The other positive, by which that which is not within is imputed. Hence likewise emerge two parts of one and the same Formal Cause in justification: one privative, which is and is called the Remission of sins, so that to those being justified in the act of justification, inherent iniquities and sins are not imputed: The other part is positive, which is called the Donation or imputation of the Righteousness of Christ: so that to those being justified, an alien righteousness is imputed, namely the Righteousness of Christ, not that eternal and essential one: but this ἐπίκτητος [acquired] one, that is, acquired by the merits of Obedience. By the combination of both these parts, therefore, the Formal Cause of our Justification is completed: and it is expressed in the Schools of the Theologians by the single term of imputative Righteousness.

Moreover, this assertion of ours rests upon certain and immovable foundations, sought from the analogy of faith.

THE FIRST is derived from the condition of that state from which, through justification, we are transferred to a better state. For outside of Justification we dwell in a State of Corruption, in which a twofold evil lies upon us: The one θετικόν [positive] or positive, namely the damnable guilt of our sins: The other στερητικόν [privative] or privative, namely the lack of righteousness which ought to have been within. The Formal Cause of our Justification brings a remedy to both these evils. For the Remission of sins takes away the former; the Donation or imputation of the righteousness of Christ compensates for the latter.

At this point the Jesuits object to a dissonance in our Churches, because Lutheran Theologians not rarely assign the Form of our Justification to only one part: and some indeed to the Remission of sins alone: others, however, to the Righteousness and merits of Christ. But this dissonance does not arise from any discrepancy of faith, which is truly one for all, but from another cause. For since in one motion there is a twofold term, and the effect of the same Formal Cause is twofold, it thus happens that one is established as being included by the other, or at least presupposed. For, just as when the Sun has risen, night is understood to have been dispersed, and with night dispersed, it is doubted by no one that the day has shone forth: where indeed only one thing is posited, but two are understood, even if they are not expressed: So when one is said to have been made righteous from being ungodly through the remission of sins, the imputed righteousness of Christ is spontaneously understood, since without it he could not be reckoned righteous. Thus, conversely, if you say that someone is reckoned righteous on account of the imputed righteousness of Christ, the Remission of sins is immediately presupposed, as that without which he could not likewise be reckoned righteous.

The second Foundation is sought from the parts of the Mediation by which righteousness and salvation have been restored to us by Christ. For this Mediation consists of.

1. The Obedience of Christ, performed for us to the divine Law.

2. but by Satisfaction, by which Christ paid the penalties due to our sins by his passion and death. The former part earned for us the imputation

of righteousness: the latter, however, the remission of both sins and the penalties due to them. By both of which merits our Justification is completed.

We can borrow a third foundation from the Mediator Christ himself: For just as he, who knew no sin, was made sin for us, 2 Cor. 5:21, not by an inherent vicious quality: but only by the mode of imputation, by which the Father cast upon him the sins of us all, Isa. 53:6. So we are Righteousness in him, not by an inherent habit: but by the gift of imputation: so indeed, that the sins which intimately inhere in us are not imputed to us: but the Righteousness of Christ is imputed, however extrinsic it may be, and does not inhere in us.

But furthermore it is asked: Since this imputative Righteousness does not inhere in us, but is placed outside of us, how can we be certain of it? And indeed the Jesuits attack it in strange ways, while they call it an imaginary Form, a shadowy one, a title without a thing, or a thing of a title only, a thing unworthy of the truth and righteousness of God.

But this is a most vain Cavil. For first, this λογισμὸς [reckoning] or imputation is not human: but has its foundation and seat in the divine mind and will, which is the supreme principle of all things, and which calls those things which are not, that they might be. Rom. 4:17. Secondly, this divine λογισμὸς does not rest on nothing: but has a foundation of the obedience and satisfaction made through Christ, whose most precious merit God, as a most free agent, according to his own will, which is the sole rule of Justice, can apply to whom he wills. Just as therefore the imputation of our sins placed upon Christ was not something shadowy or titular: but such a burden, which made Christ labor and serve, Isa. 43:24, which made him sweat blood, Luke 22:44, which finally made him the last of men, Isa. 53:3. Thus the condition of this imputation is not shadowy or imaginary, or without substance: but it is the greatest of all things: namely, the Justice of Christ, by which we are rendered acceptable to God, and obtain the remission of sins. Finally, this imputation alone provides firm material for consoling troubled minds. For because even the holiest of men must needs struggle with sins from time to time, and while they are in the world, can never be immune from the stains of sins: certainly they can promise themselves no help or comfort from their own justice: Therefore, there is no other means left to them but to take refuge in this divine imputation of another's Justice.

Finally, there cannot be given any other mode of Justice, which could have a place in restoring men to integrity after the fall. Certainly not that original habit of Justice: since indeed it

Latin:

Acropolis hæc est totius belli, quod de Justificatione Hominis cum Jesuwitis longè acerrimum geritur. Quod si enim de Causa Formali Justificationis utrinque conveniret, omnis profectò reliqua Controversia ultrò expiraret. Status autem Controversiæ non est ille, quem Sophisticè & insidiosè satis subindè Jesuwitæ crepant: An videlicet in Justificatione Hominis, per Gratiam DEI fiat renovatio aliqua sive Sanctificatio mentis? Neque enim tale quid unquàm à nobis fuit negatum. Sic neque de eo controvertitur: An illa ipsa mentis renovatio sive sanctificatio inhærens Qualitas & Justitia habitualis nominari possit? Nam licèt omnis talis Sanctitas & justitia sit instar panni menstruata, Jes. 64, 6. imò pro stercoribus reputanda, Phil. 3, 8. propterea quòd in conspectu DEI, sive in foro poli, propter impuritatem ac imperfectionem adhærentem consistere nequit: nedùm vitam æternam vel ex asse, vel ex semisse promereri : quia tamen persona ipsa per fidem DEO est reconciliata, & renatorum opera fiunt ex obedientia DEO debita. Rom 6, 17. Phil. 3, 9. ideò interdum in Scripturis Justitiæ termino indigitantur. Phil. 3, 9. 1. Joh. 3, 7. & 10.

Verùm hoc propriè in Controversiam venit: An Causa Formalis Justificationis nostræ, ponenda sit tantùm in merito sive Satis factione CHRISTI, per fidem nobis imputata, cum gratuita omnium peccatorum remissione, per & propter CHRISTUM fide apprehensum? Ubi nos in Affirmantem concedimus: Pontificii verò in negantem, contendentes, Causæ Formalis loco constituendas esse virtutes illas, quas Spiritus sanctus, & Gratia DEI in nobis operantur, & in quibus renati ac Filii DEI, Gratia divina cooperantur, vel ut Bellarminus loquitur, esse Justitiam inhærentem.

Cæterùm Affirmativæ nostræ fundamenta præcipua ut rectiùs percipiantur, notandum fuerit, Verbum imputandi hoc loco non accipi Physicè de infusione justitiæ, quemadmodum plantis dicuntur imputari surculi: Sed Relativè, de λογισμῷ sive acceptatione, ut exempli gratia: quando Imperatori victoria contra Turcas imputatur sive transcribitur, licèt ipse prælio non interfuerit. Jam licèt minimè negemus dari posse ex Scripturis ejusmodi loca, in quibus fundamentum imputationis est aliquid inhærens in illis, quibus fit imputatio: Terminus verò sit vel reatus, vel præmium: ut cum 2.Sam. 19. v 19. dicit Semei: Non imputet mihi Rex iniquitatem: Et Apostolus 2. Tim. 4, 16. omnes me deseruerunt, utinam illis non imputetur. Et Rom. 4, 4. Operanti imputatur merces ex debito: in præsente tamen negocio Apostolus hoc verbo utitur in alia ac diversa significatione, quando videlicet in eo, cui fit imputatio, non instituitur respectus ad Fundamentum, cujus dignitate fiat imputatio: sed quando ea fit ex gratuita misericordia DEI, sine nostro merito, imò contrà, quàm meriti sumus, ita ut Fundamentum planè contrarium inhæreat ei, cui fit imputatio: id quod sequentes rationes ex Scriptura petitæ irrefragabiliter evincunt.

Ratio 1. Apostolum autorem habet, Rom. 4, v. 3. 4. & 5. Credidit Abraham DEO, & imputatum est ipsi ad justitiam: Ei autem, qui operatur, merces non imputatur secundum gratiam, sed ex debito: Ei verò qui non operatur, sed credit in eum, qui justificat impium, imputatur fides sua ad justitiam. Argumentum tale esse potest: Si imputatione fidei justificatus est Abraham, fieri non potuit, ut ob inhærentem justitiam, sive ex operibus idem justificatus sit. Atqui tantùm imputatione fidei justitiam Abrahamus obtinuit. E. non ob inhærentem justitiam, sive ex operibus, ac per Consequens, Causa Formalis Justificationis nostræ non est inhærens propria: sed imputata aliena justitia, nempè CHRISTI.

Connexum Majoris confirmat ipse Apostolus à contrarijs proprijs, adjunctis & consequentibus. Quarum enim rerum contraria sunt propria, adjuncta & consequentia, & se invicem excludunt: illas ipsas quoque res contrarias esse oportet. Jam verò talia contraria dari possunt in oppositione fidei & operum: vel justitiæ imputatæ & inhærentis. Nam 1. in imputatione subjectum justificandi est ἀσεβὴς impius: in justificatione ergò meritoria, εὐσεβὴς esse necessum est. 2. In imputatione respicitur Fides: in merito verò respiciuntur opera. 3. In imputatione locum habet sola gratia: in meritoria verò justitia, debitum. 4. In imputativa justitia est donum: in meritoria verò merces. Hæc sanè omnia cùm contraria sint, utiquè eorum etiam subjecta & antecedentia sese mutuò excludant necesse est: ita, ut neque alterum de altero, neque ambo de tertio prædicari verè possint: hoc est, ut cui per fidem imputatur justitia, ei propter inhærentem justitiam propriorum meritorum, eadem imputari nequeat.

Minor autoritate Scripturarum nititur, Genes. 15, 6. Rom. 4, 3. Constat proindè Conclusioni sua immota veritas.

Objicit Pererius in Comment. ad caput 15. Geneseos: Fidem ideò esse imputatam Abrahæ ad justitiam, quia fuerit opus sive res perfectissima & bræstantissima: ac proindè inhærente justitiâ Abrahamum fuisse justificatum. Sed manifestam vim infert Sophista textui Apostolico, qui expressè Fidem ἀνυποδιηγημέρως opponit operibus indefinitè omnibus: Non enim Operanti, sed Credenti Abrahamo imputata est fides ad justitiam, & quidem ex Gratia. Fides ergò Abrahæ non notat actum vel opus, quo meritus sit justificari, vel quo formaliter sit justificatus: Hoc enim simpliciter negat Apostolus: sed notat firmam illam fiduciam, qua in Dei promissione, sive in promisso Semine mulieris unice acquievit, & sic credidit in spem contra spem: ut ipse explicat Apostolus, Rom. 4.

II. Ratio talis esse potest: Scriptura beatitudinem illis adsignat, quibus DEUS justitiam imputat sine operibus. Ergo Causa Formalis nostra Justificationis non consistit in inhaerente habituali justitia, sed tantum in imputatione gratuita alienae justitiae CHRISTI.

Vel alia ratione in hunc modum informari potest: Spiritus sanctus definit justitiam salvandorum, sola imputatione, & quidem imputatione sine operibus. E. Opera & imputatio in justificationis actu se invicem excludere, merito statuuntur. Antecedens totum est ἕγγραφον, quippe petitum ex Psal. 32, 1. Beatus cui remissa sunt iniquitates, & cui tecta sunt peccata: Beatus vir cui non imputavit DOMINUS peccatum. Consequens ipsum Apostolum autorem habet, Rom. 4, 6 sic inferentem. Ergo David hanc esse dicit beatitudinem hominis, si ipsi DEUS imputet justitiam sine operibus. Ergo & Consequenter, sine inhaerente justitia habituali.

III. Ratio ex iisdem locis extruitur talis: Quisquis remissis peccatis justificatur, ei Justitia ex operibus inhaerentis justitiae esse nequit. Atqui omnes salvandi justificantur remissis peccatis: E. Justitia ipsis non obtingit ex operibus inhaerentis habitualis justitiae. Connexum Majoris vel inde patet, quod ubi est inhaerens justitia habitualis, ibi remissio peccatorum locum non habet, & vice versa. Minor Davidis & Pauli nititur autoritate, locis jam ante citatis: Ergo.

IV. Ratio: In quocunque CHRISTUS non est justitia nostra, illud non potest esse causa formalis justificationis nostrae. Atqui Christus non est nostra justitia ratione Virtutum & Operum, quae Spiritus sanctus in nobis operatur, quaeque nobis inhaerent, sed tantum in obedientia, justitia & sanguine suo, per remissionem peccatorum. Ergo inhaerens etiam nostra virtus sive justitia, non potest esse Causa formalis justificationis nostrae.

Connexum Majoris per se liquet: Nam cum Solus Christus nobis a patre factus sit Sapientia, Justitia, Sanctificatio, Redemtio: utique Justitiae hujus nostrae Causa formalis non poterit esse id, in quo Christus non est nostra justitia.

Minor luculenter patet ex Scripturarum testimoniis, qualia sunt:

Rom 3, 25. DEUS proposuit Christum propitiationem per fidem in sanguine ipsius ad ostensionem justitiae sua, per remissionem peccatorum.

Rom 5, 19. Sicut per inobedientiam unius hominis, peccatores constituti sunt multi: ita per unius obedientiam justi constituentur multi.

Coloss. 1, 14. In Christo habemus redemtionem per remissionem peccatorum.

1. Joh. 1, 7. Sanguis JESU CHRISTI Filii DEI emundat nos ab omni peccato.

Luc. 1, 77. Christus dabit scientiam salutis plebi suae, quae est in remissione peccatorum.

Neq; potest ab Adversariis vel unum proferri testimonium, quo in speciem probabiliter saltem confirmari possit, Christum esse justitiam nostram, ratione inhaerentis alicujus nostrae justitiae, aut virtutis.

V. Ratio: In quocunque Homo in tentationibus quibusq;, Satanicis, atq; adeo in ipsa hora mortis tuto considere nequit: quod item severissimo judicio divino opponi nequit, in eo impossibile est, consistere Formalem Justificationis nostra Causam. Atqui inhaerens nostra justitia & virtus qualiscunq; alia neq; in tentationibus, neq; in judicio DEI potest consistere: Ergo neque in ea potest constitui Formalis justificationis nostra Causa.

Minor, quae continet τὸ κρινόμενον, vel inde patet, quod omnis nostra Justitia in conspectu Dei est instar panni menstruata. Jes. 64, 6. Et si omnia feceritis, dicite, Servi inutiles sumus, fecimus, quod debuimus, Luc. 17, 10.

VI. Ratio: Justitia Christi, qua salvamur, est justitia in Evangelio patefacta, absq; lege, per fidem Jesu Christi, in omnes & super omnes credentes. Rom. 3, 22. Jam habitus justitia infusus, non potest dici patefactus absq; lege. Lex enim justitiam legalem, hoc est; charitatem & impletionem operum maxime praecipit. E. Justitia Christi, qua salvamur est alia, quam Charitas infusa sive justitia inhaerens: ea nimirum, quam DEUS peccatori gratis imputat absque operibus, Rom. 4, 6.

VII. Ratio: Causa nulla formalis potest constare ex Contrarijs. Ergo neque Causa formalis Justificationis nostrae potest constare ex justitia fidei & ex justitia legis sive operum: Ratio est, quia haec dua justitia habent se ut contraria. E. simul in uno eodemq; subjecto ratione unius ejusdemq; finis consistere nequeunt. Quod sint contraria patet inde, quia Legis justitia est inhaerens: Fidei autem justitia est non inhaerens, sed imputata: Illa obtingit operanti: haec credenti: Illa ex debito: haec ex gratia: Illa est merces: haec vero est donum.

Ex his & id genus rationibus aliis invicte tandem colligimus, 1. Causam Formalem justificationis nostrae, non esse justitiam aliquam nobis inhaerentem: sed justitiam alienam Christi nimirum, quam Apostolus nominat Justitiam imputativam. 2. Justitiam hanc imputatam non esse legalem conformitatem aut inhaerentem perfectionem, sed gratuitam remissionem peccatorum, & acceptationem in judicio DEI propter Christi meritum fide apprehensum. Nam quod gratuito imputatur, id nec inest, nec debetur. Justitia autem Credentibus, & quidem absque operibus gratuito imputatur. Non ergo vel formaliter eis inhaeret, vel jure tanquam merces debetur.

Caterum nova hic oritur Quaestio: Quomodo nimirum hujus ipsius imputationis Forma sese habeat? vel quibus partibus ea absolvatur? Decisio autem ejus rectissime petitur ex ipso justificationis nostrae actu sive motu. Quemadmodum in eo duo diversi datur Termini: Unus est mali, a quo liberamur: alter vero est Boni, ad quod trasferimur: Ita gemina etia datur forma imputationis hujus: Una privativa, quâ non imputatur id, quod ineft: Altera positiva, quâ imputatur id, quod non inest. Hinc emergunt itidem partes duæ, unius, & ejusdem Causæ Formalis in justificatione: una privativa, quæ est ac dicitur Remissio peccatorum, ita ut justificandis in actu justificationis non imputentur iniquitates & peccata inhærentia: Altera pars est positiva, quæ dicitur Donatio sive imputatio Iustitiæ Christi: ita ut justificandis imputetur aliena, Christi nimirùm Justitia, non æterna illa & essentiâlis: sed ἐπίκτητος hæc, hoc est, Obedientiæ meritis acquisita. Utriusque proindè partis hujus complexu absolvitur Causa formalis Justificationis nostræ: & uno termino Justitiæ imputativæ in Scholis Theologorum exprimitur.

Nititur autem hæc assertio nostra certis atque immotis fundamentis, ex analogia fidei petitis.

PRIMUM desumitur à conditione illius status, ex quo per justificationem, ad statum meliorem transferimur. Nam extra Justificationem versamur in Statu Corruptionis, in quo duplex malum nobis incumbit: Vnum θετικὸν sive positivum, nempè damnabilis peccatorum nostrorum reatus: Alterum steρητικὸν privativum, nempè defectus justitiæ, quæ inesse debebat. Utrique huic malo medicinam affert Causa Formalis Justificationis nostræ. Nam priùs illud tollit Remissio peccatorum: posteriùs compensat Donatio sive imputatio justitiæ Christi.

Objiciunt hoc loco Jesuvvitæ nostris Ecclesijs dissonantiam, propterea quòd Theologi Lutherani baud rarò uni tantùm parti Formam Iustificationis nostræ adsignent: & alij quidem soli Remissioni peccatorum: alij verò Iustitiæ & meritis Christi. Verùm dissonantia hæc non oritur ex discrepantia aliqua fidei, quæ fanè omnibus una est, sed ex causa alia. Quoniam enim in uno motu duplex est terminus, & ejusdem Causæ formalis geminus esti effectus, hinc adeò fit, ut unum ab altero includi, vel certè præsupponi statuatur.
