Nam, sicut orto Sole, nox dispussa esse intelligitur, & nocte dispussâ, diem affulsiffe à nemine dubitatur: ubi profectò Unum saltem ponitur, sed duo intelliguntur, licèt ea non exprimantur: Ita cùm ex impio dicitur esse factus justus per remissionem peccatorum, ultrò justitia Christi imputata intelligitur, quippè sine qua justus reputari non posset. Sic vice versâ si dicas, aliquem reputari justum propter imputatam justitiam Christi, statim præsupponitur Remissio peccatorum, ut sine qua Justus ille itidem reputari non posset.

Alterum Fundamentum petitur à partibus Mediatonis, quâ justitia & salus à Christo nobis reparata est. Constat enim Mediatio hæc.

1. Obedientiâ Christi, Legi divinæ pro nobis præstitâ.

2. verò Satisfačione, quâ pœnas peccatis nostris debitas, Christus suâ passione & morte exolvit. Prior illa pars promeruit nobis imputationem

justitiæ : posterior verò hæc remissionem & peccatorum, & pœnarum illis debitarum. Quo utroque merito Justificatio nostra absolvitur.

Tertium fundamentum mutuati possumus ex ipso Mediatore Christo: Quemadmodum enim is, qui non noverat peccatum, pro nobis factus est peccatum, 2. Cor. 21. non inhærente qualitate vitiosa : sed duntaxat per imputationis modum, quô Pater in ipsum conjecit omnium nostrûm peccata. Jes. 53, 6. Ita nos in ipso sumus Justitia, non inhærente habitu : sed imputationis dono: sic nimirùm, ut peccata, quæ intimè nobis inhærent, nobis non imputentur : imputetur autem Justitia Christi, quantùmvis extrinseca ea sit, & nobis non inhæreat.

Sed porrò quæritur : Cùm Justitia hæc imputativa nobis non inhæreat, sed extranos sit posita, quomodo nos de ea certi esse possimus? Et profectò Jesuvvitæ miris modis eam exagitant, dum eam nominant Formam imaginariam, umbratilem, titulum sine re, vel rem de solo titulo, rem veritate & justitia Dei indignam.

Verùm vanissima hæc est Cavillatio. Primùm enim λογισμὸς iste sive imputatio non humana est : sed fundamentum ac sedem suam habet in mente & voluntate divina, quæ est summum rerum omnium principium, quæque vocat ea, quæ non sunt, ut sint. Rom. 4, 17. Deindè divinus iste λογισμὸς non in nihilo recumbit : sed fundamentum habet obedientiæ & satisfactionis per Christum factæ, cujus meritum pretiosissimum Deus, agens liberrimum, pro sua voluntate, quæ est Justitiæ unica regula, potest applicare, quibus vult. Sicut ergò peccatorum nostrorum imputatio super Christo posita, non fuit umbratile aut titulare quiddam : sed onus tale, quod laborare & servire fecit Christum Jes. 43, 24. quæ ipsum fecit sudare sanguinem Luc. 22, 44. quæ denique ipsum fecit novissimum virorum. Ies. 53, 3. Ita non est hujus imputationis conditio umbratilis aut imaginaria, sive sine re : sed res est omnium maxima : Justitia nimirùm Christi, quâ nos Deo reddimur acceptabiles, & peccatorum remissionem consequimur. Tandem hæc sola imputatio suppeditat firmam in consolandis consternatis mentibus materiam. Quia enim sanctissimi quique cum peccatis subindè conflictari necesse habent, & dùm in mundo sunt, à peccatorum sordibus immunes nunquam esse possunt: utique de propria etiam justitia nihil sibi auxilij aut solarij polliceri possunt: Quin ergò ad divinam hanc alienæ Justitiæ imputationem confugiant, unicum relictum ipsis est medium.

Tandem non dari potest ullus Justitiæ modus alius, qui post lapsum in hominibus in integrum restituendis locum habere posset. Non certè originalis ille Justitiæ habitus: siquidem cum Naturæ corruptione stare ille


### IV. and the Final Special Controversy: The foundation of errors concerning the formal cause of justification

cannot stand with the corruption of Nature, and will not be obtained by us except in the other life. Nor is that habit of Angelic Justice immutable. For here 1. it does not depend on the merit of Christ: but on the most free will of God. 2. It does not depend on nature: but on the grace of Confirmation, without any regard for committed sin. It is not a moral or Ethical habit of Justice act justly and perform works pleasing to God, unless the person first pleases God, that is, is already justified before God: so that just works do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the one who is justified. It is not that communicative one, which has a place only in the person of Christ with respect to the assumed Humanity: For no sinful man is united personally with the λόγῳ. There remains, therefore, only that imputative mode of Justice, by which a sinner can return into favor with God, and be eternally saved.

And such is the force of this purer doctrine of ours, that many of the Papist Writers bear witness to the truth for us in this Question: among whom is Albertus Pighius, as Bellarmine himself even admits in book 2, On Justification, chapter 1. The Authors of the Cologne Antididagma also did the same thing; again, as Bellarmine acknowledges. What of the fact that in that very ancient little book, which is titled, The Garden of the Soul: this same doctrine of ours is asserted quite clearly. For the dying were directed to that one righteousness of CHRIST, acquired long ago outside of us, but imputed to us for justification and salvation, with this admonition repeatedly pressed upon them from the meditations of Anselm: Act, while your precious soul is still in the Body, you must place all your hope and trust NOT IN ANYTHING else: than in the merit and death of JESUS CHRIST: Commit yourself wholly to this death of his, cover yourself with it, and wrap yourself in it.

ANTITHESIS.

Andreas Osiander bitterly opposed this purer doctrine of ours, who contends that a man is formally just by the very essential justice of God, and that it dwells within the man himself. When, therefore, a man is incorporated into Christ through faith and Baptism, and becomes his member and a partaker of his divine nature: then this very indwelling of the divine nature, which is the essential justice of God, is the formal justice of man. This justice, just as it was lost through Adam, so it was, said Osiander, indeed acquired and restored again by Christ through his death and satisfaction, and proposed to the world in the preaching of the Gospel, so that through faith there might be an apprehension of the benefits and death of Christ: But up to this point, the man has business with the work of Redemption, as if with a preparation and cause for preparing justice; because it is thus most alien to justification. And thus, by the work of redemption apprehended through faith, it comes to pass that Christ, nay GOD himself and the very eternal and essential justice of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit dwells in our hearts, which thus dwelling finally and really makes us just.

But this fanatical opinion mixes what is called Heaven with earth, and indeed hell itself with Heaven. For the work of essential justice in God is not to save men, but to judge. 2. By the same, God has to do not with the pious, for justifying, but with the impious for damning. 3. All the Saints pray against it, since it cannot save, Psalm 143. 4. The work of Mediation in Christ is completely dissolved by this opinion, and what is proper to the Divinity from the parts of the office of one person, is indiscriminately scattered among all the persons, not without enormous confusion of the articles of faith.

Moreover, that also is to be noted in Osiandrism, that although he constituted the Formal Cause of our Justification in the essential indwelling of divine justice: he nevertheless declared this indwelling in such a way that through it the Charity of God is poured out in our Hearts, by which essential Charity we are inflamed to love him, and our neighbor for his sake: in disputat. θ. 63. and that that justice moves, excites, urges, and makes us eager to do justly, and is one and the same divine essence, which it is necessary to be in us by grace, to dwell in us, to vivify and justify us: and that that justice is that very thing which moves the just man to act justly, and without which he could neither be just nor act justly in Confess. F. 3. Hence he says it is an error, and a horrible one, if it is taught that we are reputed just and accepted for eternal life by faith only. Confess. I. 3. and the word to justify is understood only as to repute and pronounce just, in the forensic manner, and not for that which is to make one just in reality and in truth. Confess. F. 2. T. 3. They teach things colder than ice, says Osiander in disputat. θ. 73., whoever teaches that we are reputed just only on account of the remission of sins. Finally, he says that the justice of faith, which frees from death, and by which the impious is justified before God for eternal life, is infused justice, in which all virtues are included, which makes us do just things, which mortifies sins. This justice, however, he says is the divine essence, dwelling in believers, and indeed, because it makes us do just things. Confess. G. 1, 2. I. lastly and elsewhere.

But this is the very same doctrine which, with slightly changed words and a tortuous manner of teaching, the Council of Trent recently approved according to its custom. Sess. 6. cap. 7. in these words: The only formal cause is the Justice of God, not that by which he himself is just, but that by which he makes us just, by which, namely, being gifted by him, we are renewed in the Spirit of our mind: and we are not only reputed: but we are truly named and are just, receiving justice in ourselves, each one his own, according to the measure which the Holy Spirit distributes to each as he wills, and according to the proper disposition and cooperation of each. For although no one can be just, unless he to whom the merits of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ are communicated: this, however, happens in this justification of the ungodly, while by the merit of the same most holy passion, through the Holy Spirit, the Charity of God is poured forth in the hearts of those who are justified, and inheres in them. Whence in justification itself, with the remission of sins, man receives through Jesus Christ, into whom he is grafted, all these things infused at the same time: Faith, Hope, Charity.

A twofold observation in this chapter is worthy of mention. The first is concerning the power of Heavenly truth, which sometimes exerts itself even in heretics in such a way that, whether unwilling or at least ignorant, they are compelled to bear witness to it. The Papists in this chapter are an example to us. For in describing the form of justification, although they wish the merit of the passion, or the justice of Christ and the remission of sins, to be excluded; yet they cannot commit themselves to passing over both in silence. The second is concerning the perfidious and stubborn impiety of the Romanists, who by this very act insert into their own dogma the doctrine of our Church, which they have long condemned as impiety: and they do not wish to appear to have said what they say openly, and they prefer to entangle themselves in inextricable knots of absurdities and contradictions rather than yield to manifest truth. For what answer will be given to the Apostle, who uses the term imputation more than ten times in this Question, and indeed in the single fourth chapter to the Romans, which they desire to be utterly exterminated? Now, having repudiated the imputation of the merit and justice of Christ, and the non-imputation of sins, which Scripture teaches, yet to hand down and establish a communication of the merit of Christ and an infusion of the remission of sins, which is unknown to Scripture, clearly betrays a Spirit of Giddiness. What? That the merit of Christ is said by them to be something extrinsic, which cannot inhere. Bellarm. lib. 2. de Iustif. cap. 2. p. 1033. C. Now, to posit it as communicated and infused, which, however, being extrinsic, does not inhere, would be absurd and contradictory.

But that we may make a closer approach to the error of the Romanists concerning the formal cause of our Justification: Bellarmine explains his own opinion and that of his followers thus: The intrinsic Formal Cause of Justification is the very habit of grace or charity infused: The extrinsic formal cause, which is also called Exemplary, is the justice of Christ itself, lib. 1. de Iustif. cap. 2. D. p. 637. And he explains his mind a little more fully, lib. 2. de Iustif. cap. 2. p. 1033. C. If, he says, you look at the Formal Cause, we maintain that we are justified on account of the newness inherent in us, not on account of the merit of Christ, which cannot inhere. But if you look at the meritorious Cause, we say we are justified on account of the merit of the Son of God, not on account of the newness inherent in us: If, finally, you look at the cause in general, we assert that a man is justified on account of both, but on account of the merit of the Son of God meritoriously, and on account of the newness inherent in us, formally.

But the Jesuit puts forward loose arguments: For although it is most true that the Form of our justification is not the merit of Christ itself considered absolutely, it is nevertheless necessary that this Form should lean upon a certain principle or foundation, by whose virtue or intuition or respect it can justify us? Now if, according to the opinion of Bellarmine, there is given an inherent newness of life, it would follow that it is also the foundation and meritorious principle of our justification. For a formal cause cannot subsist unless it includes a sufficient merit under itself. But if the merit of Christ is given, then our inherent newness of life ceases to be a Formal Cause. Since the merit of Christ is so sufficient and absolute that it does not need the supplement of our inherent newness to constitute the form of our justification: but without any intuition of this, being imputed to us, it can perfectly justify those who believe, nay, it truly justifies: so that the Jesuit entangles himself in a manifest contradiction, insofar as he assigns the Form of Justification, which gives being to a thing, entirely to our newness: but says the meritorious cause is Christ: which he himself, however, believes to be not at all true, as we have evidently demonstrated above in the disputation concerning the meritorious Cause.

Latin:

nequit, & non nisi in altera vita nobis obtinget. Non etiam immutabilis ille habitus Justitiae Angelicæ. Hıc enim 1. non à Christi dependet merito: sed liberrima Dei voluntate. 2. Non dependet à natura: sed à Confirmationis gratia, extra ullum peccati admissi respectum. Non moralis sive Ethicus Justitiæ habitus, per crebras actiones comparatus: Siquidem justè agere, & Deo placita opera præstare nemo potest, nisi prius Deo persona placeat, hoc est, jam sit coram Deo justificata: ut opera justa non justificandum præcedant, sed justificatum sequantur. Non communicativus ille, qui in sola Christi persona respectu assumtæ Humanitatis locum habet: Neque enim ullus homo peccator cum λόγῳ unitur personaliter. Relinquitur ergò solus ille Justitiæ modus imputativus, quo peccator in gratiam cum Deo redire, ac æternùm salvari potest.

Et tanta quidem vis purioris hujus doctrinæ nostræ, ut multi ex Scriptoribus Pontificijs, nobis in hac Quæstione Testimonium veritatis perhibeant: inter quos est Albertus Pighius, ipso etiam fatente Bellarmino lib. 2. de Justif. cap. 1. Quod ipsum fecerunt Autores etiam Antididagmatis Coloniensis; rursus id agnoscente Bellarmino. Quid quod in vetustiffimo illo libello, cui titulus est, Hortulus Animæ: eadem doctrina nostra satis perspicuè asseritur. Nam morientes ad unicum illam CHRISTI justitiam, extra nos olim acquisitam, nobis autem in justificationem & salutem imputatam, remittebantur, hâc subindè ipsis ex Anselmi meditationibus inculcatâ admonitione: Age, dum adhuc pretiosa anima tua est in Corpore, debes omnem tuam spem & fiduciam NON IN QUICQUAM aliud collocare: quàm in meritum & mortem JESU CHRISTI: Huic ipsius morti te totum committe, hac te contege, & in illam te involve.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ.

Puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ acriter se opposuit Andreas Osiander, qui contendit, Formaliter hominem esse justum, ipsâ Dei essentiali justiciâ, eâque in homine ipso inhabitante. Quandò ergo per fidem & Baptismum Christo incorporatus homo, membrum ejus, & divinæ ejus naturæ particeps fiat: tum ipsam hanc divinæ naturæ, quæ essentialis Dei sit justitia, inhabitationem, esse justitiam hominis formalem. Hanc justitiam, uti per Adamum sit deperdita, ita à Christo, dixit Osiander, esse quidem morte ac satisfactione sua rursus acquisitam & reparatam, & in Evangelij prædicatione mundo propositam, ut fide fiat beneficiorum & mortis Christi apprehensio: Sed hactenùs cùm Redemtionis opere, tanquam cum præparatione & causa justitiæ parandæ, homini esse negotium; quòd sic à justificatione alienissimum. Sic autem redemtionis opere per fidem apprehenso, fieri, ut Christus, imò DEUS ipse & ipsa æterna atquè essentialis Dei Patris, Filij & Spiritus Sancti justitia in cordibus nostris inhabitet, quæ sic inhabitans tando formaliter demùm & realiter justos nos efficiat.

Sed fanatica hæc opinio Cœlum quod dicitur, terræ, adeoque infernum ipsum Cœlo miscet. Nam justitiæ essentialis in Deo opus est, non salvare homines, sed judicare. 2. per eandem Deo res est non cum pijs, ad justificandum, sed cum impijs ad damnandum. 3. Omnes Sancti eam deprecantur, quoniam ea salvare non potest, Psal. 143. 4. Opus Mediationis in Christo hac opinione prorsus solvitur, & quod ex partibus officii personæ unius, in Divinitate est proprium, promascuè in omnes personas, non sine enormi confusione articulorum fidei, spargitur.

Cæterùm illud quoque in Osiandrismo notandum, quòd quamvis Formalem Causam Justificationis nostræ constituerit in essentiali justitiæ divinæ inhabitatione : hanc tamen inhabitationem sic declaravit, quòd per eam Charitas Dei diffundatur in Cordibus nostris, quâ essentiali Charitate inflammemur ad diligendum ipsum, & proximum propter ipsum: in disputat. θ. 63. quodque justitia illa nos moveat, exsuscitet, urgeat atque alacres faciat ad justè faciendum, & una atque eadem sit essentia divina, quam ex gratia in nobis necesse sit esse, in nobis habitare, nos vivificare & justificare : quodque illa justitia sit illud ipsum, quod justum ad justè agendum movet, & sine quo nec justus esse, nec justè agere possit in Confess. F. 3. Hinc errorem esse ait, eumque horribilem, si fide tantùm reputari justos, & acceptari nos ad vitam æternam doceatur. Confess. I. 3. & justificandi verbum, tantùm pro justum reputare & pronunciare, forensi more intelligatur, & non pro eo, quod est reipsa & in veritate justum efficere. Confess. F. 2. T. 3. Glacie, inquit Osiander in disputat. θ. 73. frigidiora docent, quicunque docent, nos tantum propter remissionem peccatorum reputari justos. Justitiam denique fidei, quæ liberat à morte, quaq; impius justificetur coram Deo ad vitam æternam, inquit esse infusam justitiam, in qua omnes virtutes includantur, quæ faciat, ut justos faciamus, quæ peccata mortificet. Hanc autem justitiam esse ait divinam essentiam, inhabitantem in credentibus, & quidem, quoniam efficiat, ut justa agamus. Confess. G. 1, 2. I. ultimò & alibi.

Hæc verò ipsissima est doctrina, quam inflexis paulisper verbis, & tortuoso docendi genere, pro more suo Concilium Tridentinum nuper approbavit. Sess. 6. cap. 7. his verbis : Unica formalis causa est Justitia Dei, non quâ ipse justus est, sed quâ nos justos facit, quâ videlicet ab eo donati, renovamur Spiritu mentis nostræ: & non modò reputamur : sed verè justi nominamur & sumus, justitiam in nobis recipientes, unusquisque suam, secundum mensuram, quam Spiritus Sanctus partitur singulis, prout vult, & secundum propriam cujusq; dispositionem & cooperationem. Quanquàm enim nemo possit esse justus, nisi cui merita passionis Domini nostri Jesu Christi commuficantur: id tamen in hac impij juftificatione fit, dum ejusdem sanctissimæ passionis merito, per Spiritum Sanctum Charitas Dei diffunditur in cordibus eorum, qui justificantur, atque ipsis inhæret. Vnde in ipsa justificatione cum remissione peccatorum, hæc omnia simul infusa accipit homo per Jesum Christum, cui inseritur, Fidem, Spem, Charitatem.

Digna est memoratu hoc in capitulo gemina Observatio. Prior de vi Cœlestis veritatis, quæ se ita quandoque in hæreticis etiam exerit, ut vel inviti, vel ignari saltem eidem testimonium perhibere cogantur. Exemplo nobis sunt Pontificij in hoc capitulo. Nam in forma justificationis describenda, quamvis meritum passionis, sive justitiam Christi & remissionem peccatorum exclusam velint; ut tamen utramque silentio prorsus prætereant, committere non possunt. Altera est de perfida & pervicace Romanensium impietate, qui hoc ipso facto & doctrinam Ecclesiæ nostræ, quam diu impietatis damnarunt, suo dogmati tamen inserciunt: & quod dicunt apertè, dixisse tamen videri nolunt, & sese inextricabilibus absurditatum & contradictionum nodis implicare malunt, quàm veritati manifestæ cedere. Quid enim Apostolo respondebitur, imputationis termino, plus decies in hac Quæstione, & quidem unico capite quarto ad Romanos utenti quam isti prorsus exterminatam cupiunt? Jam meriti & justitiæ Christi imputatione, peccatorum autem non imputatione, quam Scriptura docet, repudiatâ, Communicationem tamen meriti Christi, & infusionem remissionis peccatorum Scripturæ incognitam, tradere & statuere, Vertiginis Spiritum manifestè prodit. Quid? quod meritum Christi ab ipsis quiddam extrinsecum esse dicitur, quod inhærere non possit. Bellarm. lib. 2. de Iustif. cap. 2. p. 1033. C. Jam verò communicatum & infusum ponere, quod tamen, quippè extrinsecum non inhæreat, absurdum & contradictorium fuerit.

Sed ut propiùs ad Romanensium errorem de causa formali Justificationis nostræ accessum faciamus: sic suam, suorumque sententiam explicat Bellarminus: Causa Formalis intrinseca Justificationis est ipse habitus gratiæ sive charitatis infusus: Causa formalis extrinseca, qua & Exemplaris dicitur, est ipsa Christi justitia lib. 1. de Iustif. cap. 2. D. p. 637. Et paulò pleniùs mentem suam explicat, lib. 2. de Iustif. cap. 2. p. 1033. C. Si inquiens Causam formalem respicias, statuimus, nos justificari propter novitatem nobis inhærentem, non propter meritum Christi, quod inhærere non potest. Si verò Causam meritoriam, dicimus nos justificari propter meritum Filij Dei, non propter novitatem in nobis inhærentem: Si denique causam in communi, asserimus justificari hominem propter utrumque, sed propter meritum Filij Dei meritoriè, propter novitatem in nobis inhærentem, formaliter.

Sed scopas dissolutas apponit Jesuvvita: Etsi enim verissimum est, Formam justificationis nostræ non esse ipsum Christi meritum absolutè consideratum, necesse tamen est, ut Forma hæc certo innitatur principio sive fundamento, cujus virtute sive intuitu aut respectu nos justificare possit? Jam si ex sententia Bellarmini datur inhærens vitæ novitas, Consequens fuerit, eam quoque esse fundamentum ac principium meritorium justificationis nostræ. Causa enim formalis subsistere nequit, nisi meritum sufficiens sub se complectatur. Sin verò detur meritum Christi, tum nostra inhærens vitæ novitas, desinit esse Causa Formalis. Siquidem meritum Christi usque adeò est sufficiens & absolutum, ut ad formam constituendam justificationis nostræ, non indigeat supplemento inhærentis nostræ novitatis: sed absque hujus intuitu, nobis imputatum, perfectè credentes justificare possit, imò verè justificet: ita ut Jesuvita manifestâ contradictione semetipsum implicet, quatenùs Formam Justificationis, quæ dat esse rei, nostræ novitati in solidum assignat: Causam verò meritoriam dicit esse Christum: quod ipsum tamen minimè verum esse credit, uti supra in disputatione de Causa meritoria, evidenter demonstravimus.


### IV. and the Final Special Controversy: The foundation of errors concerning the formal cause of justification (continued)

Furthermore, this assertion fights manifestly with the Scriptures, which confirm that justice did not inhere in Abraham, but was imputed to him: Since to him who does not work, but only believes, faith is imputed for justice. Rom. 4.

Thirdly: If infused grace, or newness inherent in us, were the Formal Cause of our Justification, and could bring true justice to us, certainly it would have to be both perfect and in all things agreeable to the divine law. The reason is: because this Formal Cause ought to confer upon us such justice as would free us from the curse of the law and the immense wrath of God against sin. Now, since the Jesuits themselves fear to ascribe such perfection to our inherent newness, what an impiety would it be to assign it as the form of our justification? Again, since the obedience of Christ alone obtains this perfection, we most rightly attribute to it every respect of both the meritorious and the Formal Cause. Nor is there any reason for the Adversaries to have recourse to a Special help of God: For the question is not whether God can endow a man with such grace that he cannot sin. But it is disputed what God wills. Ineptly, therefore, do the Adversaries in this place betake themselves to some special help of God, unless they show us such a man who, instructed by this special grace, has never sinned thereafter.

Fourthly, God is a consuming fire, nor can anyone stand before Him to whom anything is lacking for perfect justice. For what is not perfect is vicious in its own kind. If, therefore, God could be appeased by our inherent justice, and that imperfect, something vicious would please God. For why is justice called imperfect, unless because it is not at all free from vice? Therefore, he who [has] imperfect righteousness and, relying on this inherent righteousness of theirs, they approach God; and they promise themselves eternal life from it, and set this against the most just judgment of God, they demand God by their own supreme righteousness, and inflict the greatest insult upon Him. For how could God acknowledge as just anything that did not conform to His own most perfect will?

Finally, all those arguments which we have already produced to confirm our thesis serve to refute this error.

Moreover, Bellarmine fights for the defense of his error with very many arguments, the chief of which are these:

THE FIRST, from chapter 5, verse 19 of Romans, is as follows: As the disobedience of the first Adam condemns us: So the obedience of the second Adam, namely Christ, justifies us: or to use the words of Bellarmine: In the same way that we are constituted just through the obedience of Christ, in that same way we were constituted unjust through the disobedience of Adam. But through the disobedience of Adam, we were constituted unjust, with injustice truly and in reality inherent in us, and not indeed with the injustice of Adam merely imputed to us. Therefore, through the obedience of Christ also, we are constituted just, with righteousness truly and in reality inherent in us.

I answer: the Jesuit errs and is deceived by the fallacy of ignoring the point at issue. For 1. He extends the Apostolic comparison too widely, beyond what the scope and intention of the whole passage admits. 2. He confuses the thing with the mode of the thing. For the Apostle looks only at the thing itself, namely, what flows to us from the disobedience of Adam and the obedience of Christ opposed to it, namely, sin from the former, righteousness from the latter. The Jesuit, however, subsumes the mode of the thing, contending that righteousness is conferred upon us from Christ in the exact same way that sin flowed into us from Adam, namely, through an inherent habit or quality: which is what the Apostle least of all intended to demonstrate. Therefore, as in other places of Scripture, so also in the present particle SICUT ὥσπερ, it designates not an absolute equality of all degrees, but some similarity of at least one or another. Otherwise, by the same Jesuitical artifice, one could conclude from chapter 6, verse 36 of Luke: As our Heavenly Father is merciful, so we also ought to be merciful. But mercy in us is an inherent habit and quality. Therefore, mercy in God will likewise be an inherent habit, which the Jesuit himself understands to be absurd, and easily perceives that the thing is being confused with the mode of the thing: while a subsumption is made to absolute equality from at least some degree of comparison: let him remember, therefore, that in this place also, an absolute equality of all degrees of comparison cannot be inferred from the particle SICUT. 3. The Apostle himself clearly expressed the diversity of the mode in this very chapter, asserting that sin passed into us through natural participation, verse 12. For he says εἰσῆλθε and διῆλθεν, thus showing that sin does not have its origin from God, nor was it created in the nature of man, but was introduced into all from elsewhere, namely from Adam, which could not have happened except through that natural propagation.

But concerning the righteousness which flows from Christ into us, the Apostle does not say διῆλθεν (it passed through): but he names it χάρισμα (gift) verse 15, περισσείαν χάριτος (abundance of grace), and δωρεὰν τῆς δικαιοσύνης (gift of righteousness) verse 17, δωρεὰν ἐν χάριτι (gift by grace), which from one man Christ has exuberated (ἐπερίσσευσε) into many, verse 15, δικαίωσιν ζωῆς (justification of life) verse 18. Fourthly, we rightly distinguish between τὸ δικαιῶσθαι (to be justified) and τὸ δίκαιον κατασταθῆναι (to be constituted just). The former is nothing other than to be absolved from the guilt or condemnation of sin, freely through the imputation of the righteousness of Christ: but the latter is also to be sanctified by habitual righteousness. Both of these flow from the obedience of Christ, but to a very different end: the former regarding our justification and salvation: the latter regarding the regeneration or renewal of our mind. If the Jesuit takes his argument from this latter effect, then we concede it entirely. For just as sin habitually inheres in us: so this righteousness of sanctification also exists in us as a quality. But if the adversary now subsumes: Therefore the form of our justification is inherent righteousness, we deny the consequent, which is inferred from a false presupposition: for it is false that we are justified before God by the righteousness of sanctification or the renewal of our mind: since this is rather an effect of the antecedent justification: and not its cause. Thus, therefore, the adversary also begins shamefully. And that which the Apostle, speaking in this place or verse 19 about the righteousness and sin flowing into us, does not use the same tense in both cases, well deserves observation: but concerning sin, he affirms that through Adam many have already been constituted (καθεστάθησαν) sinners: where he notes a completed act: but concerning the righteousness of our renewal or sanctification, he uses a verb of the future tense, many shall be constituted (κατασταθήσονται) just, so as to show that the benefit of regeneration is indeed begun in this life, but is only completed in the future.

II. The argument taken from 1 Cor. 6:11 is as follows: The Apostle says: Such were you, but you were washed: but you were sanctified, but you were justified. And yet the Corinthians were such, namely fornicators, idolaters, adulterers by the inherent quality of their vices. Therefore, the washing, sanctification, and justification opposed to these vices is also brought about by an inherent habit of justice: and consequently, the formal cause of our justification is inherent justice.

I answer. 1. The same fallacy of comparison is committed as in the preceding argument. 2. We admit the whole argument, if the discussion is about the regeneration and sanctification of our mind. But if he subsumes it to the formal cause of justification itself

Adversary, we deny the consequence. For the Apostle himself shows that the gift of Justification is distinct from the benefit of Sanctification: saying not only that he sanctified, but also justified us, as Chrysostom also explains in Homily 16 on 1 Corinthians, οὐδὲ τοῦτο μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐδικαίωσε. 3. The Apostle did not wish in this place to express the form of our justification: but only to show in what things Christianity consists, namely in Baptism, Sanctification, and Justification. Where, however, he by no means denies that these three differ not only in word, but also in reality and in number. Nor was the Apostle concerned in this place with showing the order, how one follows from the other. For although the beginning of our Conversion and Justification depends on Baptism, yet the latter follows the former not indeed in time, but in the order of Nature: Sanctification, however, is posterior to both Baptism and Conversion in terms of order.

III. The argument consists of many places of Scripture, which assert that many have obtained the Testimony of Justice: Likewise that the Elect are made conformable to the image of the Son of God, Heb. 11, 4. and following. Rom. 8, 29. But these and other sayings of this kind have nothing to do with the matter. For the State of the Controversy is not: Whether the Saints and faithful are gifted with some Justice, and whether in respect of the tribulations to which they are subject, they represent in some way the image of the Son of God, who also himself entered into his glory through death. But this is the Question. 1. Whether this justice of the Saints is perfect and absolute, such as is required by God in the law. 2. Whether this conformity of the Elect presupposes the absolute perfection of some inherent justice. Both we deny. The former for this reason, because that habitual Justice is indeed begun in this life, and also grows through the increments of virtues: but it is not completed, nor does it become perfect, until it is finally purged of every spot and wrinkle in the other life. The groans and complaints of the most holy testify to this, and indeed the very sense of our conscience, as it were, dictates this imperfection to each of us; he who does not feel it in himself is stupid, he who does not acknowledge it is a hypocrite. For each and all of us must exclaim with Paul: I delight in the law of God, according to the inward man: but I see another law in my members, captivating me under the law of sin, which is in my members. Likewise: The good that I will, I do not: but the evil which I will not, that I do: Likewise, in my flesh dwells no good, etc. Rom. 7, 18. 19. 22. 23. And with the most holy David: Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight no living man is just. Ps. 143, 2.

We deny the latter for this reason, because the Apostle himself restricts that συμμόρφωσιν with a double limitation. 1. By asserting that Christ remains the firstborn in it, so that not an arithmetical, but only a geometrical conformity has place. 2. By defining it only through the likeness of the cross and tribulations, in respect of which the pious bear some likeness of Christ: which, however, has nothing to do with the present Controversy.

Fourthly, the Jesuit brings forward that passage of chapter 6, 2. Rom. We who are dead to sin, how shall we live any longer in it? Hence the Adversaries are accustomed to infer thus.

Those who, dead to sin, live to justice, are entirely renewed and clothed with a new justice, by which they please God, and obtain eternal life. But the effect of the grace of Christ is that, being dead to sin, we live to justice. Therefore, the effect of the grace of Christ is that we please God by a new inherent justice, and not by an imputed one.

I answer: The major proposition begs the question, or rather is simply false, if it is taken concerning the renewal of the Saints in this life. For this can perform neither: that we perfectly die to sin, nor that we perfectly live to justice, as has just now been confirmed by the example of David and Paul.

Then in the minor, a sophistry is committed according to what is said in a qualified sense versus absolutely. For it is true that the effect of the grace of Christ brings it about that believers are perfectly dead to sin in a qualified sense, namely as to the formal aspect, that is, guilt and condemnation: but it is false that this effect of the Grace of Christ brings it about that believers are dead to sin absolutely, even as to the material aspect. For this always remains remaining, even in the most holy. The reason is: because this perfection will be the least final part of eternal life. Because if this perfect renewal of our mind stood, Death would no longer have dominion over Believers: since this is nothing but the wages of sin. Rom. 6, 23.

Some Jesuits insist that the righteousness of believers is called perfect, not because it is such in itself, and can stand as perfect in the judgment of God: but because it is accepted by God as perfect, on account of the perfection of Christ. But this cavil is also feeble, maliciously perverting the state of the question. For this is not what is asked: Whether the new obedience of the pious, however imperfect in itself, pleases God on account of the perfection of Christ: but this is what is disputed: Whether this new obedience is accepted by God as the formal cause by which we can be justified before God, which is clearly most false from what has already been said. For justification before God cannot be had except from perfect righteousness, according to that: He who shall have done these things shall live in them. But such cannot be given except for the one and only righteousness of Christ, by the imputation of which alone the regenerate are accounted as holy and perfect. For God justifies us not when we are upright or holy, but while we are still ungodly. Rom. 4, 5. Therefore we are not justified finally by a new inherent righteousness.

Sixthly, the Jesuit objects that neither in the Scriptures nor in the Fathers is it read anywhere that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us for righteousness: or that we are righteous through the righteousness of Christ imputed to us. But the Jesuit would be worthy of hellebore to purge his head. For is not the term of imputation used eleven times in one chapter, Romans 4, is it repeated? Do not Paul and David there attest that righteousness was imputed to Abraham, and righteousness indeed not of works, but of faith, which is the righteousness of Christ, which faith apprehends? Does not David declare him blessed to whom God does not impute sins? And what, I ask, is the righteousness which is imputed, other than righteousness imputed or imputative? Therefore, let the Jesuits learn at last to argue from the place of Conjugates. But let the Jesuit show us, where in the whole Scripture even a single iota is found concerning infused and inherent righteousness, by which we are justified?

Finally, our Jesuit is very prolix in gathering arguments by which he may demonstrate that Justification does not consist in the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, because Scripture everywhere confirms that in the pious sin is taken away, they themselves are renewed, sanctified, the Spirit of adoption is given to them, and charity and other virtues are required in them: But since all these do not touch the nerve and sophistically pervert the State of the Dispute, and the foundations of the responses can be sought from what has already been said, we sound the retreat, and for the purity of this Article, which in these last times has shone upon the Church as if returned from exile, we give immortal thanks to the merciful God. Amen.

Latin:

Deindè pugnat hæc assertio manifestè cum Scripturis, quæ confirmant, Abrahamo non inhæsisse, sed imputatam esse justitiam: Siquidem non operanti, sed credenti tantùm imputata est fides ad justitiam. Rom. 4.

Tertiò: Si gratia infusa, sive inhærens nobis novitas Formalis esset Causa Justificationis nostræ, & veram nobis justitiam afferre posset, certè eam & perfectam & legi divinæ per omnia consentaneam esse oporteret. Ratio est: quia hæc Causa Formalis conferre nobis debet talem justitiam, quæ nos à legis maledictione, & immensâ Dei in peccatum ira liberet. Jam cùm talem perfectionem nostræ inhærenti novitati adscribere ipsi vereantur Jesuvitæ, quæ obiecro impietas fuerit, Formam justificationis nostræ illi adsignare? Rursus cùm sola obedientia Christi perfectionem hanc obtineat, rectissimè utique nos omnem respectum Causæ & meritoriæ & Formalis, illi acceptum ferimus. Neque est, ut ad Speciale Dei auxilium recurrant Adversarij: Non enim quæritur, an Deus tali gratia possit donare hominem, ut peccare nequeat. Sed quid velit Deus disputatur. Ineptè ergò hoc loco ad auxilium aliquod Dei speciale se recipiunt Adversarij, nisi monstrent talem nobis hominem, qui speciali hac gratia instructus, nunquam deinceps peccârit.

Quartò, Deus est ignis consumens, neque coram ipso consistere potest, cui aliquid ad perfectam justitiam deest. Quod enim non est perfectum, id in suo genere vitiosum est. Si ergò Deus inhærente nostrâ justitiâ eâq; imperfectâ placari posset, Deo aliquid placeret vitiosum. Cur enim justitia imperfecta dicitur, nisi quod vitiô minimè careat? Ergò qui imperfecta hâc suâ justitiâ inhærentefreti ad Deum accedunt; vitamque æternam sibi ex ea pollicentur, & hanc justissimo Dei judicio opponunt, ij Deum suâ summâ justitia postulant, & maximâ contumeliâ afficiunt. Quomodo enim Deus aliquid pro justo agnosceret, quod non ipsius perfectissimæ voluntati congrueret?

Tandem refutando errori huic subserviunt omnia ea argumenta, quæ pro thesi nostra confirmanda jam antè produximus.

Cæterùm pugnat Bellarminus pro defensione sui erroris, argumentis benè multis, quorum præcipua sunt hæc:

PRIMUM ex cap. 5, 19. Rom. tale est: Sicut inobedientia primi Adami nos condemnat: Sic obedientia secundi Adami, nempè Christi nos justificat: vel ut verbis Bellarmini utamur: Eôdem modo constituimur justi per obedientiam Christi, quô modô constituti sumus injusti per inobedientiam Adami. Atqui per inobedientiam Adami, constituti sumus injusti, injustitiâ in nobis verè ac reipsa inhærente, non verò injustitia Adaminobis tantùm imputatâ. Ergò per Christi etiam obedientiam constituimur justi, justitiâ in nobis verè ac reipsa inhærente.

Respondeo: fallit & fallitur Jesuuvita sub Sophismate ignorationis Elenchi. Nam 1. Similitudinem Apostolicam nimis latè extendit, ultra quàm totius loci scopus & intentio admittit. 2. Confundit rem cum modo rei. Apostolus enim rem ipsam tantùm spectat, Quid nimirùm ex inobedientia Adami, & huic oppositâ Obedientiâ Christi ad nos redundet, nempè illinc peccatum, hinc justitia. Jesuuvita verò subsumit ad modum rei, contendens, eôdem planè modô in nos conferri justitiam ex Christo, quô modô in nos redundavit peccatum ex Adamo, nempè per inhærentem habitum sive Qualitatem : id quod tamen Apostolus minimè omnium demonstrare voluit. Proindè ut in alijs Scripturæ locis, sic in præsenti quoque particula συγγκριτικὴ SICUT ὥσπερ non absolutam omnium graduum æqualitatem, sed unius saltem aut alterius similitudinem aliquam designat. Aliàs pari artificio Jesuuvitico liceret colligere ex cap. 6, 36. Lucæ: Sicut Pater noster Cælestis misericors est, sic & nos misericordes esse debemus. Atqui misericordia in nobis est habitus & qualitas inhærens. E. misericordia in Deo itidem erit ha bitus inhærens, id quost absurdum esse intelligit ipse Jesuuvita, & rem cum modo rei confundi facile animadvertit: dùm ex aliquo saltem Comparationis gradu ad absolutam æqualitatem fit subsumtio: Meminerit ergò hoc etiam loco, ex particula SICUT absolutam æqualitatem omnium graduum comparationis inferri haud posse. 3. Apostolus ipse diversitatem modi hoc ipso capite luculenter expressit, asserens, peccatum in nos transjisse per participationem naturalem, vers. 12. Dicit enim εἰσῆλθε & διῆλθεν, sic ostendens, peccatum non habere ortum à Deo, neque in natura hominis conditum esse, sed aliundè, nempè ex Adamo esse inductum in omnes, id quod non nisi per naturalem illam propagationem fieri potuit.

Cæterùm de Justitia, quæ ex Christo in nos redundat, non dicit Apostolus διῆλθεν pertransijt: sed nominat eam χάρισμα Donum vers. 15. περισσείαν χάριτος abundantiam gratiæ, καὶ δωρεὰν τῆς δικαιοσύνης Donum justitiæ vers. 17. δωρεὰν ἐν χάριτι donum per gratiam, quæ ex uno homine Christo in multos ἐπερίσσευσε exuberavit vers. 15. δικαίωσιν ζωῆς justificationem vitæ vers.18. Quartò distinguimus meritò inter τὸ δικαιῶσθαι justificari, & inter τὸ δίκαιον κατασταθῆναι justum constitui. Illud nihil est aliud, quàm à reatu sive Condemnatione peccati absolvi, gratis per imputationem Justitiæ Christi: Hoc verò est etiam justitia habituali sanctificari. Utrumque hoc ex Christi obedientia fluit, sed fine longè diversissimo: Illud quoad justificationem & salutem nostram: hoc verò quoad regenerationem sive renovationem mentis nostræ. De hoc posteriore effectu, si argumentum suum accipiat Jesuvvita, tùm illud concedimus totum. Nam quemadmodum peccatum nobis habitualiter inhæret: ita Justitia etiam hæc Sanctificationis nobis inest ut qualitas. Verùm si jam subsumat Adversarius: Ergo Forma Justificationis nostræ est inhærens justitia, negamus Consequens, quod ex falso præsupposito infertur: Falsum enim est, nos justitia Sanctificationis aut renovationis mentis nostræ coram Deo justificari: Siquidem hæc potiùs est Effectus antecedentis justificationis: non verò ejus Causa. Sic ergo principium etiam turpiter Adversarius. Et observationem probè meretur illud, quod Apostolus hoc loco sive vers. 19. de Justitia & peccato in nos redundante, verba faciens, non utrobique eodem tempore utitur: sed de peccato affirmat, quod ex Adamo jam καθεστάθησαν cōstituti sint peccatores multi: ubi actum perfectum notat: de justitia autem Renovationis sive Sanctificationis nostræ, utitur verbo Futuri temporis κατασταθήσονται constituentur multi justi, ut sic ostendat, Regenerationis beneficium in hac vita inchoari quidem, sed absolvi demùm in futura.

II. Argumentum ex 1. Cor. 6, 11. petitum sic habet: Dicit Apostolus: Hæc eratis, sed abluti estis: sed sanctificati estis, sed justificati estis. Atqui erant Corinthij tales, nempè scortatores, idololatræ, adulteri per inhærentem vitiorum qualitatem. Ergo his vitijs opposita ablutio, Sanctificatio, justificatio fit etiam per inhærentem justitiæ habitum: & per Consequens, Formalis Iustificationis nostræ Causa est Iustitia inhærens.

Respondeo. 1. eundem committi elenchum comparatorum, qui in præcedenti argumento. 2. admittimus argumentum totum, si de regeneratione & Sanctificatione mentis nostræ sit disputatio. Si verò ad Justificationis ipsius Causam formalem subsumat

Adversarius, negamus Consequentiam. Nam ipse Apostolus ostendit, Justificationis donum esse distinctum à Sanctificationis beneficio: Non tantùm inquiens sanctificavit, sed & justificavit nos, uti Chrysostomus etiam explicat Homil. 16. in 1. ad Corinth. οὐδὲ τοῦτο μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐδικαίωσε. 3. Apostolus hoc loco non formam justificationis nostrae exprimere voluit: sed ostendere tantùm quibus in rebus consistat Christianismus, nempè in Baptismo, Sanctificatione & Justificatione. Ubi tamen minimè negat, tria haec non λόγῳ tantùm, sed & reipsa atque numero differre. Neque etiam de ordine monstrando, quomodo unum ex altero sequatur, hoc loco sollicitus fuit Apostolus. Etsi enim à Baptismo dependet initium Conversionis & Justificationis nostrae, tamen haec illum non tempore quidem, sed ordine Naturae posterior sequitur: Sanctificatio autem tùm Baptismo, tùm Conversione ratione ordinis est posterior.

III. Argumentum constat multis Scripturae locis, quae asserunt, Multos consecutos esse Testimonium Justitiae: Item Electos fieri conformes imagini Filii Dei, Hebr. 11, 4. & seqq. Rom. 8, 29. Sed haec & id genus dicta alia nihil quicquam ad rem faciunt. Nam Status Controversiae non est: An Sancti & fideles donentur Justitia aliquâ, & num respectu tribulationum quibus obnoxii sunt, repraesentent aliquo modo imaginem Filii Dei, qui & ipse per mortem intravit in gloriam suam. Sed hoc Quaestionis est. 1. An justitia haec Sanctorum sit perfecta & absoluta, qualis à Deo in lege requiritur. 2. An haec conformitas Electorum praesupponat absolutam perfetionem inhaerentis alicujus justitiae. Utrumque nos negamus. Prius illud ideò, quia Justitia illa habitualis hac in vita inchoatur quidem, & per incrementa virtutum augescit etiam: sed non absolvitur, nec fit perfecta, donec in altera demum vita ab omni macula & ruga plenè purgetur. Testantur id gemitus & querelae Sanctissimorum, quin singulis nobis ipse quasi Conscientiae nostrae sensus dictat imperfectionem hanc, quàm qui in se non sentit, stupidus, qui non agnoscit, hypocrita est. Singulis nimirùm & universis cum Paulo exclamandum: Condelector quidem lege Dei, quoad interiorem hominem: sed video aliam legem in membris meis, captivantem me sub lege peccati, quae est in membris meis. Item: Bonum quod volo, non facio: sed malum quod nolo, illud perago: Item, in carne mea non habitat bonum &c. Rom. 7, 18. 19. 22. 23. Et cum sanctissimo Davide: Ne ingrediaris in judicium cum servo tuo, quia coram te non est justus ullus vivens Psal. 143, 2.

Posterius hoc negamus ideò, quia Apostolus ipse συμμόρφωσιν illam duplici limitatione restringit. 1. quidem asserens, Christum in ea manere primogenitum, ita ut non arithmetica, sed geometrica tantùm conformitas locum habeat. 2. Definiens eam tantùm per similitudinem crucis & tribulationum, respectu quarum pij aliquam Christi similitudinem gerunt: id quod tamen nihil quicquam ad præsentem facit Controversiam.

Quartò profert Jesuvita locum illum capitis 6, 2. Rom. Qui mortui sumus peccato, quomodo adhuc vivemus in eo? Hinc sic inferre solent Adversarij.

Qui mortui peccato vivunt justitiæ, illi toti renovati novâ justitiâ induuntur, quâ placent Deo, vitamq́; æternam consequuntur. Atqui effectus gratiæ Christi est, ut mortui peccato vivamus justitiæ. Ergo Effectus gratiæ Christi est, ut novâ justitiâ inhærente placeamus Deo, non autem imputatâ.

Respondeo: Majorem propositionem petere principium, imò simpliciter esse falsam, si de renovatione Sanctorum hac in vita accipiatur. Hæc enim neutrum præstare potest, vel ut perfectè moriamur peccato: vel ut perfectè vivamus justitiæ, uti exemplo Davidis & Pauli jam modò est confirmatum.

Deindè in minore committitur Sophisticatio secundum Quid ad dictum simpliciter. Verum enim est, quod effectus gratiæ Christi præstat, ut credentes perfectè sint mortui peccato secundùm Quid, nempè quoad formale, hoc est, reatum & condemnationem: falsum verò est, quod effectus iste Gratiæ Christi præstet, ut simpliciter Credentes sint mortui peccato, etiam quod Materiale. Hoc enim semper manet reliquum, etiam in sanctissimis. Ratio est: quia perfectio hæc erit pars minimè postrema æternæ vitæ. Quia stante hâc perfecta renovatione nostræ mentis, Mors non ampliùs haberet in Credentes dominium: Siquidem hæc est non nisi peccati stipendium. Rom 6, 23.

Instant Jesuvitæ nonnulli, Credentium justitiam, nominari perfectam, non quod in se sit talis, & in Dei judicio tanquàm perfecta consistere possit: sed quo pro perfecta gratiâ à Deo acceptetur, propter perfectionem Christi. Sed elumbis & hæc est cavillatio, malitiosè statum quæstionis pervertens. Non enim hoc quæritur: An piorum Nova Obedientia, quantumvis in se imperfecta, placeat Deo propter perfectionem Christi: sed hoc controvertitur: An hæc Nova Obedientia acceptetur à Deo tanquàm Causa formalis, quâ coram Deo justificari queamus, id quod falsissimum esse ex jam dictis patet. Nam justificatio coram Deo haberi non potest, nisi ex perfecta justitia, secundum illud: Qui fecerit hæc, vivet in eis Talis verò non potest dari præter unam & solam Christi justitiam, cujus solius imputatione renati pro sanctis & perfectis reputantur. Justificat enim nos Deus non probos aut sanctos, sed adhuc impios existentes. Rom. 4, 5. Non igitur novâ justitiâ inhærente demùm justificamur.

Sextò objicit Jesuvvita neq́; in Scripturis, neque in Patribus uspiam legi, Christi justitiam nobis imputari ad justitiam: vel nos justos esse per Christi justitiam nobis imputatam. Sed hel leboro dignus foret Jesuvvita, quò caput expurgaret. An non enim in uno capite 4. ad Romanos, Terminus imputationis undecies repetitur? An non ibi Paulus & David attestantur, Abrahamo fuisse imputatam justitiam, & justitiam quidem non operum, sed fidei, quæ est justitia Christi, quam fides apprehendit? An non David beatum prædicat, cui Deus non imputat peccata? Et quid quæso aliud est Justitia quæ imputatur, quàm justitia imputata vel imputativa? Itaque discant vel tandem Jesuvvitæ ex loco Conjugatorum argumentari. Sed edifferat nobis Jesuvvita, Ubinam in universa Scriptura vel unicum Jota reperiatur, de infusà & inhærente justitia, quâ justificemur?

Tandem valdè prolixus est Jesuvvita noster in conquirendis argumentis, quibus demonstret, Justificationem non consistere in imputatatione justitiæ Christi, propterea, quòd Scriptura passim confirmet, in pijs tolli peccatum, renovari, sanctificari ipsos, dari ipsis Spiritum adoptionis, requiri in ipsis charitatem & alias virtutes: Verùm cùm hæc omnia nervum non tangant & Statum Disputationis Sophisticè pervertant, & ex jam dictis responsionum fundamenta peti possint, receptui canimus, & pro Articuli hujus puritate, quæ postremis hisce temporibus postliminiò quasi Ecclesiæ affulsit, misericordi Deo gratias agimus immortales Amen.


## 16 On Good Works

Philip has set forth a sufficiently prolix and accurate exposition of this Article, consisting of two parts. The one positive, which is completed in four questions, the first of which asks, Whether good Works are necessary, or not? The second, what are truly good Works? The third, How can good Works be done? The fourth, What is the final Cause of good works? Or, Why should they be done? The other is entirely refutatory, being solely occupied in refuting the Objections of the Romanists. We, having regard for those Controversies which are agitated today, will set forth our Treatment in three Questions: THE FIRST will be concerning the nature and essence or definition: THE SECOND, concerning the efficient Cause: THE THIRD concerning the final Cause of Good Works. By these three questions we establish that all those things which are today controverted between us and the Jesuits can be comprehended. For as regards that Controversy, which was agitated soon after the death of Blessed Luther among the Theologians addicted to the Augsburg Confession concerning the necessity of Good Works, with some contending that they are necessary for salvation: while others fought that they are pernicious to salvation: both sides deviating enormously from the path of truth: that

in our Commentary on the Fourth Article of the Book of Concord, we have expressly treated. Therefore, this time our Dispute will be only with the Romanists.

Latin:

SAtis prolixam & accuratam Articuli hujus διέξοδον Philippus expedijt, duabus constantem partibus. Unà ϑετικῆ, quæ quatuor absolvitur quæstionibus, quarum Prima quærit, An bona Opera necessaria sint, nec ne? Altera, quænam sint Opera verè bona? Tertia, Quomodo fieri possint Bona Opera? Quarta, Quæ sit Causa finalis bonorũ operum? Sive, Cur ea sint facienda? Altera tota est ἀνασκευαστικὴ, quippè in refutandis Romanensium Objectionibus unicè occupata. Nos earum Controversiarum, qua hodiè agitantur, habitâ ratione, Tractationem nostram tribus Quæstionibus expediemus: PRIMA erit de natura & essentia sive definitione: ALTERA, de Causa efficiente: TERTIA de Causa finali Bonorum Operum. Tribus istis quæstionibus statuimus comprehendi posse universa ea, quæ inter nos & Jesuvvitas hodiè controvertuntur. Nam quoad eam Controversiam, quæ mox post obitum B. Lutheri, inter Theologos Augustanæ Confessioni addictos de necessitate Bonorum Operum agitata fuit, nonnullis contendentibus, ea necessaria esse ad salutem: alijs verò pugnantibus, ea esse perniciosa ad salutem: utrisq; à veritatis tramite enormiter aberrantibus: eam ista

- in Commentario nostro ad Articulum Quartum libri Concordiæ, ex professo pertractavimus. Nobis ergò hâc vice cum Romanensibus tantùm erit Disputatio.


### Question I. On the Nature and Essence, or Definition of Good Works

By the complex of three hypotheses especially, the Nature or Definition of Good Works can be most fully set forth according to the Scriptures, so that if one of these is lacking, then a fault is committed either in excess or in defect.

The first hypothesis is, Good Works are only those which are prescribed and comprehended in the Word of God, and indeed in the legal part of it, namely the Decalogue. For thus God through Moses. Num. 15, 39. & 40. They shall not follow their own thoughts, but rather being mindful of the precepts of the Lord, let them do them for Him.

Deut. 4, 2. Keep the commandments of the Lord your God, which I command you.

And chap. 12, 32. What I command you, this ONLY do to the LORD, neither add anything nor diminish.

Ezek. 20, 19. Walk in my statutes v. 18. Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers.

Matt. 15, 9. In vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments of men.

Rom. 12, 2. In the pursuit of good works, one must consider what is the good, acceptable, and perfect will of God.

This hypothesis is as if naturally ingrained in the minds of men, so that even the philosophers of the Gentiles in this respect determined more soundly than our Romanists, that every god is to be worshipped according to his own pleasure, and as he himself wills. Whence that saying among the Greek comic poets: Θεὸν σέβων καὶ πάντα πράξης εὐθέως, θνητὸς πεφυκὼς, μὴ φρονῆς ὑπέρθεα: By worshipping God you will do all things straightway, nor, being mortal, strive to be wise above the divine.

II. Hypothesis: Under the census and number of truly good works, there must be called not only external works, which strike the eyes and which offer an external appearance of piety of themselves: and are more often hypocritical: but also, and indeed even especially, internal works: such as are piety, fear of God, faith, hope, charity: for just as the adoration of God, so also any worship of God is then finally judged to be truly good, when hypocrisy is absent, and man strives to worship God in spirit and in truth, as Christ himself teaches in John 4, 23. For the judgment is the same concerning similar things. Hence the Apostle demands from the Romans and all believers a λογικὴν λατρείαν, a rational worship, consisting indeed more in spiritual than in external exercises of piety, Rom. 12, 1. To which David also seems to have looked, Psal. 51, 19, saying, The sacrifice acceptable to GOD is a contrite and humbled spirit. And Isaiah chap. 66, 2, To whom shall I look, but to the humble and contrite spirit, and him who trembles at my words.

III. Hypothesis: In the whole category of good works or divine worship, faith or trust in GOD holds the primacy: both for other reasons, and especially because no action of man can be given that is more divine or more excellent than to believe and trust in the LORD. For if you wish to worship GOD, if you wish to implore GOD's help in undertaking the greatest works and functions, if you wish to promise yourself with certainty GOD's presence and help in more serious temptations; if, finally, you wish to institute and exercise other acts of piety with GOD: it is necessary that faith, as the basis and foundation, and the true use of the same, be always presupposed: For whatever is not of faith cannot please GOD, Rom. 14, 23.

The explanation of that controversy which was raised concerning the works of the Gentiles depends upon the decision of this question: Namely, whether those works can and ought to be called truly good? And if they were good, whether they pleased GOD or not? Where indeed it has been anxiously disputed by many: some, however, on the side of deficiency, simply stripping their works of all goodness whatsoever; others, on the side of excess, assigning absolute goodness to them, so that by their virtue they attained eternal life, just as Zwingli, Andradius, and others have philosophized concerning the virtues of the Gentiles. We, having more rightly entered upon a middle path, shall be able to remove and take away all difficulty by a certain distinction. We therefore establish that a twofold goodness can be given in the consideration of good works: For there is one goodness which only regards the substance of the deed or work, whether it is conformable to the divine law or not; but it does not consider the quality of the person himself, whether he is reconciled to GOD or not. But there is another goodness, which regards not only the substance of the deed, but also the quality of the person: and in the schools of the theologians it is called absolute goodness. If, therefore, the works and virtues of the Gentiles are considered in the former way, we answer that they were relatively good, namely, as regards the substance of the work, which agreed with the precepts of GOD, and in its own way pleased GOD; who also rewarded them with the prizes of temporal goods, and provided security from the more severe punishment of damnation, as Augustine speaks, lib. 4, contra Julian. cap. 3. Now if Zwingli, or some other of the fanatics, should infer from this goodness that these very works of the Gentiles pleased GOD in such a way that He granted them eternal life, we deny the consequence: Since there is no progression from relative goodness to absolute goodness. Absolute goodness indeed presupposes relative goodness: but the latter does not presuppose the former: just as that which is true in a certain respect cannot immediately be said to be true simply and according to all parts and degrees. Let it be, therefore, that the goodness of the works of the Gentiles was great, and that they pleased GOD in a certain respect, namely, as regards the substance of the deed: because, however, the person himself was not reconciled to GOD through faith: absolute goodness certainly cannot be assigned to them, much less can it be affirmed that they pleased GOD simply. For in this latter respect that Apostolic axiom stands firm and immovable, Rom. 14, 23: Whatever is not of faith is sin. And Hebr. 11, 6. It is impossible for anyone to please GOD without faith. The work of the Gentiles, therefore, considered in itself, pleased GOD: but the person working displeased Him: the former was approved; the latter was disapproved, nay, utterly rejected and adjudged to eternal damnation. Moreover, from this very decision, a judgment can also be made concerning the various questions which are wont to be raised about the works of the reborn or believers: For it is asked: 1. What and of what kind is the goodness of these works? Where, following the Scriptures, we answer that they are not only relatively, but also absolutely good, and therefore please GOD. Those eulogies by which the works of the reborn are designated in the Scriptures prove this, such as that they are called living sacrifices, holy, pleasing to GOD. Rom. 12, 1. Ephes. 5, 9. Coloss. 3, 20. 1. Timot. 5, 4. Hebr. 13, 16. 1. Joh. 3, 22. Next it is asked: Whence do the works of the reborn please GOD? Where we distinguish between the work and the person: The work pleases GOD because, according to the substance of the deed, it agrees with the Law of GOD: then because it proceeds from a person reconciled with GOD. Therefore, the work does not please GOD simply, as the Romanists wish, insofar as it is a work performed. But the person likewise does not please GOD simply and of himself, since he is contaminated by sin: but insofar as he is reconciled to GOD through faith, and therefore his works are done not so much from man as from GOD, or in GOD, as the Savior defined, Joh. 3, 21.

Thirdly it is asked: For what reason do the works of the reborn please GOD? Where, with the blessed Luther, we answer that they please GOD not because of their excellence, which in the eyes of GOD is nothing: or because of their perfection, which in the eyes of GOD is mere imperfection, Luc. 17, 10. But only through and because of CHRIST, in whose faith the reborn truly do good works. Scripture hints at this, asserting quite evidently that Abel offered a more excellent sacrifice to GOD by FAITH, Hebr. 11, 4. Likewise, that our spiritual sacrifices are made acceptable to GOD through Jesus Christ. 1. Pet. 2, 5. The Romanists object in this place to many good passages of Scripture, in which the reborn are named just, holy, perfect, immaculate, unpolluted, pure in heart, sincere, blameless, etc. But the meaning is to be regarded more than the letter of these passages. That meaning, however, receives a threefold respect: One imputative, which consists not in one's own, but in another's perfection, holiness, and righteousness, namely that of CHRIST, which is truly imputed to believers for righteousness through faith, as was shown in the preceding Article. The second is the comparative, insofar as those saints are compared with others who perform the exercises of divine worship with a hypocritical and only half-hearted heart. The third and final preparatory, insofar as it is shown through those sayings of Scripture what the pious are to be in the other life, where Christ will present His Church to GOD the Father glorious, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing, Eph. 5:27, so that the condition of the Church Triumphant rather than the Militant is expressed in those sayings. To which opinion Augustine, book 3, On Christian Doctrine, ch. 34, says: It is not, he says, to be understood as if the Church were already such, but that it is being prepared to be so, when it will also appear glorious. Moreover, regarding inherent holiness and perfection, the Prophets and Apostles themselves esteemed it so deficient, imperfect, and contaminated that they compared it to a menstrual cloth, Isa. 64:6, and to σκυϐάλοις (refuse), Phil. 3:8, so that they seriously lamented the filth and manifold imperfections which they perceived their works to suffer from the vice of indwelling sin: as is evident even from the single seventh chapter to the Romans, where the Apostle, considering his own imperfection, finally breaks out into this tragic cry: Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death, verse 24.

Fourthly, it is asked: In what way and how far do the works of the reborn please GOD? Where we establish that a most accurate distinction must be made between that which is from GOD and in GOD, and the vice which, because of the infirmity and corruption of our flesh, adheres to those works: according to that Apostolic assertion, Rom. 7:21, 'To me who wishes to do good, evil lies near.' Therefore, good works, insofar as they are the ἐνέργεια (energy) or fruits of the Holy Spirit Himself, and proceed from a conscience purified and sanctified by faith, to that extent they certainly please GOD and are not sins. For that same GOD who approves faith in believers as His own work will also approve the fruits of that same faith as His own work. But the vice which adheres to those works, and which in itself does not please GOD at all, He covers, pardons, and forgives with the mantle of divine mercy.

Finally, this is also asked: How do the good works of the reborn please GOD? Where a plain and clear answer can be sought from what has already been said: namely, that they please GOD, not as if the person were rendered acceptable to GOD through or because of them, as the Romanists suppose: but rather the reverse, that they please GOD because the person is reconciled to GOD: so that the pleasing of the person does not depend on the works, but on faith: but the pleasing of the works depends on the condition of the person, insofar as that person pleases GOD through faith.

The Pseudo-Catholic Roman Church has long since declared war on this purer doctrine of ours, betrayed by a twofold and most gross error. The FORMER is that they contend that truly good works are not only those which are commanded in the Word of GOD, but also those which, apart from the authority of the divine Word, are ordained by the Pope and the Church with some good intention, or are undertaken and done by men themselves of their own motion.

Whence that immense heap of ἐθελοθρησκειῶν (will-worships) or cults devised by men, and consisting mostly in external gesticulations or exercises, took its origin.

To this error we oppose even that one saying of the Savior, Matt. 15:9, 'In vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments of men': Which ought to strike the adversaries all the more forcefully, the more ancient authority it obtained in the Old Testament also from the mouth of GOD, saying: 'This people draws near with their mouth, and honors me with their lips: but their heart is far from me, and they have worshipped me with the commandments and doctrines of men,' Isa. 29:13.

The LATTER error is that they establish that men are in themselves and by themselves just and acceptable to GOD by the dignity and merit of their own works. To this error, for the present, we oppose only those testimonies of Scripture which deal with the essential justice of GOD. For such is the ἀκρίβεια (precision) of this divine justice that it finds remnants of sins even in the most holy, and those both many in number and atrocious in weight, so that the most holy of all confess themselves to be far inferior to them in dignity, whether in acknowledging or lamenting them. To this pertain these testimonies of Scripture. Deut. 4:24, 'The Lord thy GOD is a consuming fire.' Job 4:18, 'Behold, those who serve Him are not stable, and in His angels He finds perversity.'

Job 9:2 & 3. 'I know that a man composed before GOD is not justified: For if he should wish to contend with Him, he will not be able to answer Him one for a thousand.'

Ps. 19:13. Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others.

Ps. 32:6. For the remission of sins, every saint will pray to you at an opportune time.

Ps. 130:3. Lord, if you should mark iniquities, Lord, who will stand?

Ps. 143:2. Do not enter into judgment with your servant: for no one living will be justified in your sight.

Dan. 9:7. To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness: but to us confusion of face: and following.

Luke 17:10. If you have done all things, say: we are unprofitable servants: we have done what we ought to have done.

Rom. 7:23. I see another law in my members, taking me captive under the law of sin.

1 John 1:8. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

And v. 10. If we say that we have not sinned, we make God a liar, and his Word is not in us.

But by what arguments the Jesuits fight for this later error of theirs, we shall show below in the exegesis of the third Question.

Moreover, regarding that former one, the Jesuits today bring forward many good arguments in its defense: the chief of which are these:

I. They contend that that Mosaic precept, by which addition to the word is prohibited, is to be understood of those additions which are made: 1. Against the Word of GOD. 2. By private men. 3. By the Jewish people. 4. Without the authority and consent of the Church.

I answer that manifest violence is done to the Mosaic precept, which, not only being placed indefinitely, obtains the force of universality and does not admit restrictions of this kind at all, but also, through the added exclusive particle 'Only', completely undermines and overturns the Jesuit exceptions. Furthermore, it is to be observed that not only those additions are against the Word of GOD which are directly and contradictorily opposed to it, but also those which, by human whim, add something to the Word of GOD regarding divine worship with good intention, without a command of GOD, or institute a worship that is clearly new, or exercise that which is commanded in a manner other than it is prescribed: such are the additions of the Romanists concerning the celibacy of priests, concerning the Lenten fast, concerning pilgrimages to the chapels of the Saints. Thirdly, Moses promulgated this precept not to one order of men, namely the common people, but to all of Israel, as is clear from chapter 4. Deut. 5:2, and therefore he forbade both the Priests and the political Magistrate, as well as private individuals, from adding anything to the prescribed worship of GOD by private whim. Fourthly, the Decalogue is the eternal, immutable norm of the divine will. Just as, therefore, He did not wish to be worshipped by the Jews except through those works which He had commanded in the Decalogue: so He also wishes to be worshipped by Christians under the New Testament by the same works, and not by human traditions. Finally, the Church is equally bound to this Mosaic precept as any private individual, so that as soon as it sanctions certain works necessary for observance outside the prescription of the divine Word, it immediately degenerates into a false church and one of the malignant.

II. The argument is such: Subordinated things do not conflict: But the Word of GOD and works devised by humans are subordinated. Therefore, they do not conflict, much less are they contradictorily opposed.

I answer: That the minor premise is true only in a certain respect, namely regarding external, civil, economic, or even external ecclesiastical matters: but it is most false when it is applied to the Question concerning Good Works, or the true worship of GOD. For in order for that to please GOD, it is necessary that it rely solely on His word.

- not prescribed. But it is briefly answered that the intentions which are called 'good' must be distinguished. For not everything that someone does with a good intention is immediately approved by the Lord: but what it is that is undertaken must be examined first, and indeed if that which is undertaken is in itself evil and prohibited, it will never become good, with whatever intention it is performed: since we have an express command of God: Not what seems good to us is to be done, but what the Lord has prescribed. But if that which is undertaken is by its nature a medium and indifferent, so that someone can use it either well or badly: then indeed a good intention, that is, the end of that action which is in itself indifferent, related to the glory of God, makes the action itself good.

Moreover, the Anabaptists also belong to the class of those erring regarding this first Question, who, having neglected and repudiated the word of God, rave that such works are to be done as some internal rapture or Enthusiasm, or as the more prudent among them are accustomed to speak, as some singular and secret instinct of the Holy Spirit shall have suggested or dictated. But not only the oracles of the Scriptures, already produced above, but also experience itself as an avenger has hitherto refuted this madness.

The error of the Antinomians must also be referred here, by which they contend that there can no longer be any use of the divine law among the regenerate, because they do good works from the instinct of the Holy Spirit: and not from the impulse of the Mosaic Law. As if the Holy Spirit Himself did not show through the Law a certain norm to which the regenerate, in exercising themselves according to the will of God, should conform. What? That not every movement of the regenerate can or ought to be immediately referred to the instinct of the Holy Spirit. For there is usually a great force of depraved concupiscences in them as well, so that according to the inner man they delight in the law of God: but according to the outer man they feel the law of sin, so that they do not always do the good that they want: as the Apostle teaches by his own example. Rom. 7:22 and 23. It is added that no more certain rule of Good Works can be given than that which was once dictated by the Master of eternal justice Himself, and established with the most serious counsel for the conferring of eternal life as well, if only it could be kept. Let that Prophetic saying, therefore, also prevail in this place, Isa. 8:20, To the Law and to the Testimony, etc.

Latin:

TRium potissimùm hypotheseων complexu, plenissimè secundum Scripturas expediri potest Natura sivè Definitio Bonorum Operum, ita ut si harum una deficiat, tùm vitium vel in excessu vel in defectu committatur.

Prima hypothesis est, Bona Opera ea tantùm sunt, quæ in Verbo Dei, & quidem parte ejus legali, nempè Decalogo sunt præscripta & comprehensa. Sic enim Deus per Mosen. Num. 15, 39. & 40. Non sequentur cogitationes suas, sed magis memores præceptorum Domini faciant ei.

Deut. 4, 2. Custodite mandata Domini Dei vestri, quæ Ego præcipio vobis.

Et cap. 12, 32. Quod præcipio tibi, hoc TANTUM facito DOMINO, nec addas quicquam neq; minuas.

Jezech. 20, 19. Jn præceptis meis ambulate v. 18. In præceptis Patrum vestrorum nolite incedere.

Matth. 15, 9. Frustra colunt me docentes mandata hominum.

Rom. 12, 2. In studio bonorum Operum spectandum, quæ sit voluntas Dei bona, placens & perfecta.

Est hypothesis hæc hominum animis naturâ quasi ingenerata, ita ut Philosophi etiam Gentilium hac in parte Romanensibus nostris saniores statuerunt, Unumquemque Deum pro suo placito, & prout ipse velit, colendum esse. Vndè illud apud Græcos Comicos: Θεὸν σέβων καὶ πάντα πράξης εὐθέως, θνητὸς πεφυκὼς, μὴ φρονῆς ὑπέρθεα : DEUM colendo cuncta facies protinùs, Nec supra numen sapere mortalis stude.

II. Hypothesis: Sub censum numerumque Operum verè bonorum, vocari debent non tantùm opera externa, inque oculos incurrentia, quæque externam pietatis speciem de se præbent: & sæpiùs hypocritica sunt: sed &, imò vel maximè interna Opera: qualia sunt, Pietas, Timor Dei, Fides, Spes, Charitas: Quemadmodum enim Adoratio Dei, sic quilibet etiam cultus Dei, tùm demùm verè bonus esse censetur, quando hypocrisis abest, & Homo Deum colere studet in Spiritu & veritate, sic docente ipso Christo Joh. 4, 23. De similibus enim idem est judicium. Hinc Apostolus à Romanis & quibusque fidelibus exigit λογικὴν λατρείαν cultum rationalem, spiritualibus nimirum magis, quàm externis exercitiis pietatis constantem, Rom. 12, 1. Quò respexisse etiam videtur David, Psal. 51, 19. Sacrificium, inquiens, DEO gratum est Spiritus contritus & humiliatus. Et Jesaias cap. 66, 2. Ad quem respiciam, nisi ad humilem & contritum Spiritum, & trementem sermones meos.

III. Hypothesis: In universo genere bonorum Operum sive Cultus divini, principatum obtinet Fides sive fiducia in DEUM: tùm ob causas alias, tùm etiam potissimùm, quòd nulla divinior aut præstantior actio Hominis dari potest, quàm Credere & Confidere in DOMINO. Si enim DEUM colere, si in obeundis maximis quibusq; Operibus & functionibus DEO auxilium implorare, si in gravioribus tentationibus DEI præsentiam & auxilium tibi certò polliceri; si denique alios cum DEO actus pietatis instituere & exercere velis: semper tanquàm basis & fundamentum, unica fides ejusdemque verus usus præsupponatur, necesse est: Quicquid enim non est ex fide, DEO placere nequit, Rom. 14, 23.

Dependet à Quæstionis hujus decisione, illius controversiæ explicatio, quæ mota fuit de Operibus Gentilium: Annimirùm Opera illa verè bona dici possint & debeant? & si bona fuerunt, Nùm DEO placuerint nec ne? Ubi sanè anxiè à multis disputatum fuit: nonnullis tamen ex parte ἐλλείψεως sive defectus omnem prorsus bonitatem ipsorum Operibus simpliciter derogantibus; aliis verò ex parte ὑπερβολῆς sive excessus absolutam bonitatem illis adsignantibus, ita ut eorum virtute vitam æternam sint consecuti, quemadmodum Zwinglius; Andradius & alii de Gentilium virtutibus sunt philosophati.
