Rectiùs nos mediâ viâ ingressi, per distinctionem quandam omnem difficultatem tollere & amovere poterimus. Geminam ergo Bonitatem in consideratione bonorum Operum dari posse statuimus: Alia enim est Bonitas, quæ tantùm respicit substantiam facti sive Operis, utrum ea legi divinæ sit conformis, nec ne? non verò ipsius personæ qualitatem considerat, utrum ea sit DEO reconciliata; nec ne? Alia est verò Bonitas, quæ non modò substantiam facti, sed & qualitatem Personæ respicit: & in Scholis Theo logorum dicitur Bonitas absoluta. Priore ergo modo si considerentur Opera & virtutes Gentilium, respondemus eas fuisse relatè bonas, nempè quoad substantiam Operis, quæ præceptis DEI cõgruebat, & suo quodammodo DEO placebat; qui bonorum etiam temporalium præmiis eas remuneratus est, & à graviori damnationis supplicio securitatem præstitit, uti loquitur Augustinus lib. 4. contra Julian. cap. 3. Jam si ex hac bonitate subsumat Zwinglius, vel phanaticorum alius aliquis, Hæc ipsa Gentilium Opera sic placuisse DEO, ut vitam ipsis æternam donaverit, negamus Consequentiam: Siquidem à bonitate relata, ad bonitatem absolutam non datur progressus. Absoluta quidem bonitas præsupponit bonitatem relatam: hæc verò non præsupponit illam: haud secus atq; id, quod secundum Quid verum est, non statim simpliciter, & secundum omnes partes atq; gradus verum esse potest. Esto ergò, magna fuerit bonitas Operum Gentilium, eaque DEO placuerint secundum Quid, nempè quoad Substantiam Facti: quia tamen persona ipsa non erat per fidem DEO reconciliata: utiq; absoluta Bonitas illis adsignari non potest, nedùm affirmari, quòd DEO simpliciter placuerint. Stat enim posteriore hoc respectu firmum & immotum axioma illud Apostolicum, Rom. 14, 23: Quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est. Et Hebr. 11, 6. Impossibile est sine fide quenquam placere DEO. Placuit ergò DEO opus Gentilium in se consideratum: displicuit verò persona operans: illud approbatum: hæc improbata, imò penitùs reprobata & æternæ damnationi adjudicata. Cæterùm ex hac ipsa decisione judicium etiam fieri potest, de variis quæstionibus, quæ circa renatorum sive fidelium Opera moveri solent: Quæritur enim: 1. Quæ & qualis sit bonitas istorum Operum? Ubi Scripturas secuti respondemus, ea non modò relatè, sed & absolutè bona esse, ac proinde DEO placere. Evincunt hoc elogia illa, quibus Renatorum Opera in Scripturis indigitantur, ut quòd nominantur hostia viva, sancta, placens DEO. Rom. 12, 1. Ephes 5, 9. Coloss 3, 20. 1. Timot. 5, 4. Hebr. 13, 16. 1. Joh. 3, 22. Deindè quæritur: Undenam Renatorum Opera placeant DEO? Ubi distinguimus inter Opus & Personam: Opus placet DEO, quia secundum substantiam facti congruit cum Lege DEI: deindè quia proficiscitur à persona cum DEO reconciliata. Ergo non simpliciter Opus placet DEO, uti Pontificij volunt, quatenùs est Opus operatum. Persona autem itidem non simpliciter, & per se placet DEO, quippè quæ peccato est contaminata: sed quatenus per fidem DEO est reconciliata, ac proindè Opera ejus, non tàm ex Homine, quàm ex DEO, sive in DEO facta sunt, uti definivit Servator, Joh. 3, 21.

Tertiò quæritur: Propter quid renatorum Opera placeant DEO? Ubi cum B. Luthero respondemus, placere illa DEO non propter suam vel præstantiam, quæ in oculis DEI nulla est: vel propter suam perfectionem, quæ in oculis DEI mera est imperfectio, Luc. 17, 10. Sed tantùm per & propter CHRISTUM, in cujus fide vera Renati benè operantur. Innuit hoc Scriptura, satis evidenter asserens, Abelem FIDE præstantiorem hostiam obtulisse DEO, Hebr. 11, 4. Item, Spirituales nostras hostias acceptabiles reddi DEO per Jesum Christum. 1. Pet. 2, 5. Objiciunt hoc loco Romanenses benè multa Scripturarum loca, in quibus Renati nominantur justi, sancti, perfecti, immaculati, impolluti, mundi corde, sinceri, inoffensi, &c. Sed διάνοια magis, quàm τὸ ρητὸν istorum locorum est spectanda. Illa verò διάνοια triplicem sortitur respectum: Unum imputativum, qui non in propria, sed alienà consistit perfectione, Sanctitate atque justitia, CHRISTI nimirùm, quæ credentibus per fidem verè imputatur ad justitiam, uti præcedente Articulo ostensum. Alterum συγκριτικὸν Comparativum, quatenùs nimirùm sancti isti comparantur cum aliis, qui hypocritico & dimidiato tantùm Corde, cultus divini exercitia tractant. Tertium ac postremum præparativum, quatenùs nimirùm per dicta illa Scripturæ ostenditur, quid pii sint futuri in altera vita, ubi Ecclesiam suam Christus DEO Patri exhibebit gloriosam, non habentem maculam, aut rugam, aut aliquid hujusmodi, Ephes. 5, 27. ita ut Triumphantis potiùs, quàm militantis Ecclesiæ conditio in illis dictis exprimatur. Quam in sententiam Augustinus lib. 3. de Doctrina Christiana cap. 34. Non, inquit, sic accipiendum est, quasi jam talis sit Ecclesia, sed quòd præparetur, ut sit, quando etiam apparebit gloriosa. Cæterùm quoad inhærentem Sanctitatem & perfectionem ipsi quoque Prophetæ, & Apostoli eam usque adeò mancam, imperfectam, contaminatam æstimarunt, ut eam compararent cum panno menstruatæ, Jes. 64, 6. cum σκυϐάλοις stercoribus, Phil 3, 8. ut seriò deplorarent sordes & imperfectiones multiplices, quibus ex adhærentis peccati vitio, Opera sua laborare animadverterunt: uti vel ex unico capite septimo ad Romanos evidenter patet, ubi Apostolus imperfectionem sui considerans, tandem in tragicam hanc vocem erumpit: Me miserum, quis eripiet me ex Corpore isto mortis, vers. 24.

Quartò quæritur: Quatenùs & quousq́; DEO placeant Renatorum Opera? ubi accuratissimè distinguendum esse statuimus inter id, quod ex DEO, & in DEO sit; & inter vitium, quod propter Carnis nostræ infirmitatem & Corruptionem, Operibus illis adhæret: secundum assertionem illam Apostolicam, Rom. 7, 21. Volenti mihi facere bonum, malum adjacet. Bona ergò opera, quatenus sunt ἐνέργεια sive fructus ipsius Spiritus sancti, & ex Conscientiâ fide purgatâ ac sanctificatâ proficiscuntur, eatenùs certè placent DEO, neque sunt peccata. Idem enim ille DEUS, qui Fidem in credentibus, tanquàm suum opus probat: probabit etiam ejusdem fidei fructus, tanquàm suum opus. Vitium autem, quod operibus illis adhærescit, quodque DEO per se minimè placet, pallio misericordiæ divinæ tegit, condonat & ignoscit.

Tandem & illud quæritur: Quomodo renatorum Opera bona DEO placeant? Ubi ex jam dictis Responsio plana ac perspicua peti potest: placere nimirùm illa DEO, non quasi per aut propter ista, persona DEO accepta reddatur uti Romanenses autumant: sed vice potiùs versa, placere illa DEO ideò, quia Persona DEO est reconciliata: ita ut placentia personæ non dependeat ab Operibus: sed à fide: placentia autem Operum dependeat à Conditione Personæ, quatenùs ea per fidem DEO placet.

Puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ jampridem bellum indixit Pseudo-Catholica Ecclesia Ro- - mana : gemino eoque crassissimo errore prodito. PRIOR est, quòd contendunt, Opera verè bona esse non modò ea, quæ in Verbo DEI sunt mandata: sed & quæ citra Verbi divini autoritatem, Bonâ aliqua intentione, vel à Pontifice & Ecclesia ordinantur, vel ab ipsis hominibus proprio motu suscipiuntur & fiunt.

Undè immensa illa strues ἐθελοθρησκειῶν sive cultuum humanitùs excogitatorum, & in externis potissimùm gesticulationibus sive exercitiis positorum, traxit originem.

Cui errori vel unicum illud Servatoris obvertimus, Matth. 15, 9. Frustra colunt me, docentes mandata hominum: Quod tantò fortiùs ferire debet Adversarios, quantò antiquiorem illud autoritatem, in Veteri etiam Testamento ex ore DEI obtinuit: dicentis: Populus iste ore suo appropinquat, & labijs suis honorat me: Cor autem ejus longè est à me, & coluerunt me mandatis & doctrinis hominum, Jes 29, 13.

POSTERIOR error est, quòd statuunt, Homines in se & per se justos & DEO acceptos esse, propriorum Operum dignitate atq; merito. Cui errori hâc vice ea tantùm Scripturæ testimonia, quæ de essentiali DEI justitiâ agunt, opponimus. Ea enim est Justitiæ hujus divinæ ἀκρίβεια, ut in sanctissimis quibusq; etiam peccatorum reliquias inveniat, easque tùm numero multas, tùm pondere atroces, ut illis pro dignitate vel agnoscendis vel deplorandis multò inferiores se fateantur sanctissimi quique. Quo pertinent hæc Scripturæ testimonia. Deut. 4. v. 24. Dominus DEUS tuus ignis consumens est. Job, 4, 18. Ecce qui serviunt ei, non sunt stabiles, & in Angelis suis reperit pravitatem.

Job. 9, 2. & 3. Scio, quòd homo DEO compositus non justificetur: Si enim voluerit contendere cum eo, non poterit ei respondere unum pro millibus.

Psal. 19, 13. Delicta quis intelligit: ab occultis meis munda me, & ab alienis parce servo tuo.

Psal. 32, 6. Pro remissione peccatorum orabit ad te omnis Sanctus in tempore opportuno.

Psal. 130, 3. Domine si iniquitates observaveris, Domine quis sustinebit.

Psal. 143, 2. Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo: quia non justificabitur in conspectu tuo ullus vivens.

Daniel. 9, 7. Tibi DOMINE justitia: nobis autem confusio faciei: & seqq.

Luc. 17, 10. Si omnia feceritis, dicite servi inutiles sumus: fecimus quod debuimus.

Rom. 7, 23. Video aliam legem in membris meis, captivantem me sub lege peccati.

1. Joh. 1, 8. Si dixerimus, quod peccatum non habeamus, ipsi nos seducimus, & veritas non est in nobis.

Et v. 10. Si dixerimus, quod non peccavimus, mendacem facimus DEUM, & Verbum ejus non est in nobis.

Quibus verò argumentis pro posteriore hoc errore suo pugnent Jesuitae, infra in diexodo Quaestionis tertiae ostendemus.

Caeterùm quoad priorem illum, proferunt Jesuitae hodiè in ejus defensionem argumenta benè multa : quorum praecipua sunt haec :

I. Contendunt praeceptum illud Mosaicum, quô prohibetur additio ad verbum, intelligendum esse de ijs additionibus, quae fiunt. 1. Contra Verbum DEI. 2. ab hominibus privatis. 3. à populo Judaico. 4. Sine autoritate & consensu Ecclesiae.

Respondeo, vim manifestam inferri praecepto Mosaico, quod non modò indefinitè positum, Universalitatis vim obtinet, & restrictiones hujusmodi prorsus non admittit, sed & per adjectam particulam exclusivam Tantùm, exceptiones Jesuiticas prorsus subruit & evertit. Deindè observandum, non eas tantùm additiones esse contra Verbum DEI, quae ei directè & contradictoriè sunt oppositae : sed etiam quae arbitrio humano, bona intentione aliquid Verbo DEI, quoad cultum divinum adjiciunt, sine mandato DEI, vel cultum planè novum instituunt, vel eum, qui mandatus est, alio, quàm praeceptum est, modo, exercent : quales sunt additiones Romanensium de coelibatu Sacerdotum, de jejunio quadragesimali, de peregrinationibus ad sacella Sanctorum. Tertiò Moses praeceptum hoc non uni hominum ordini, nempè plebejo, sed toti Israëli promulgavit, uti patet ex cap. 4. Deut. v. 2. ac proindè tàm Sacerdotibus & Magistratui politico, quàm privatis interdixit, ut ne quicquam privato arbitrio cultui DEI praescripto adderent. Quartò Decalogus est aeterna norma immutabilis voluntatis divinae. Quemadmodum ergo à Judaeis non nisi per ea opera, quae in Decalogo praeceperat, coli voluit : Ita à Christianis quoque sub Novo Testamento, iisdem operibus, non verò humanis traditionibus coli vult. Tandem Ecclesia aequè est alligata ad hoc praeceptum Mosaicum : atque privatorum quilibet, ut quamprimùm citra praescriptum Verbi divini Opera quaedam observatu necessaria sancit, statim in Ecclesiam falsam ac malignantium degeneret.

II. Argumentum tale est : Subordinata non pugnant: Atqui Verbum DEI, & Opera humanitùs excogitata, sunt subordinata. E. non pugnant, multò minùs contradictoriè sunt opposita.

Respondeo : Minorem veram esse tantùm secundum Quid, nempè quoad externa, civilia, Oeconomica, vel etiam quoad externa, Ecclesiastica: falsissimam verò esse, quando ad Quaestionem de Bonis Operibus, sive vero cultu DEI, accommodatur. Ut enim iste DEO placeat, solo ipsius verbo nitatur necesse est.

- non præscripta. Verùm breviter respondetur, distinguendas esse intentiones, quæ Bonæ vocantur. Non enim statim quod quis bona intentione facit, id probatur Domino: sed quale id sit, quod suscipitur, dispiciendum prius est, & quidem si per se malum & prohibitum sit, quod suscipitur, nunquàm bonum fiet, quacunque intentione peragatur: cùm expressum Dei mandatum habeamus: Non quod nobis videtur, id faciendum esse, sed quod præscripsit Dominus. Sin autem id quod suscipitur, naturâ suâ sit medium & indifferens, ut eo vel benè vel malè aliquis uti possit: tùm verò bona intentio, hoc est, finis illius actionis per se mediæ, ad gloriam Dei relatus, bonam ipsam actionem efficit.

Cæterùm pertinent ad classem errantium circa primam hanc Quæstionem, etiam Anabaptistæ, qui neglecto & repudiato verbo Dei, ejusmodi Opera facienda esse delirant, quæ internus aliquis raptus aut Enthusiasmus, vel ut prudentiores ex ipsis loqui solent, quæ singularis aliquis atque arcanus instinctus Spiritus sancti suggesserit sive dictârit. Sed furorem istum non modò Scripturæ oracula, jam supra producta: sed ipsa quoq; experientia vindex hactenùs refutavit.

Referendus huc etiam est Antinomorum error, quô contendunt, nullum ampliùs usum legis divinæ esse posse apud renatos, propterea quòd bona Opera faciant ex instinctu Spiritus sancti: non verò ex impulsu Legis Mosaicæ. Quasi verò Spiritus sanctus ipse non per Legem monstraret certam normam, ad quam sese juxta voluntatem Dei exercendo, renati conformarent. Quid? quòd non quilibet motus renatorum, statim ad instinctum Spiritus sancti referri potest aut debet. Magna enim in ipsis quoque solet esse vis pravarum concupiscentiarum, ut secundum interiorem quidem hominem condelectentur lege Dei: secundum exteriorem verò sentiant legem peccati, ut bonum quod volunt, non semper faciant: uti suo docet exemplo Apostolus. Rom. 7, 22. & 23. Accedit, quòd nulla certior bonorũ Operum dari potest regula, quàm quæ ab ipso æternæ justitiæ Magistro semel est dictata, & ad vitam etiam æternam conferendam, si modò servari posset, gravissimo consilio constituta. Valeat ergò & hoc loco illud Propheticum, Jes. 8, 20. Ad Legem & ad Testimonium, &c.


### Question II. Concerning the Efficient Cause of Good Works

The question is how Good Works can be performed? Where the inquiry concerning the Efficient Cause is selfevident. That this may be duly expedited, there will be need of the observation of two Theological Aphorisms.

The first Aphorism is this: External locomotive [actions] or external manners can in some way be governed by human diligence and the faculties of one's own powers. We say, however, that this can be done only in some way: for the human mind and locomotive [faculty], even in the wisest of this age, has its difficulties, delays, and obstacles, with which reason must necessarily struggle. When, therefore, reason presides, but appetite obeys, then man can to some extent emerge from these difficulties. Those illustrious examples of the Gentiles, Aristides, Scipio, Camillus, and the like, show this. But whether these Works, and how they were good before GOD and pleased Him: was sufficiently demonstrated in the first question above.

The other Aphorism is this: The interior obedience of the heart, such as the Law of GOD necessarily requires for the performing of a truly good work, and with which it delights in the law of GOD, Rom. 7, 22, and whose end is charity, 1 Tim. 1, 5, man by his own powers not only cannot perfect, but cannot even begin, without illumination, which is through the doctrine of the Gospel, by the power of the Holy Spirit. The Savior Himself confirms this, John 14, 5: Without me you can do nothing. Where the Savior does not understand only that general help of GOD, which consists in the preservation of human nature, as the Jesuits wish: But also this special help, which works both the willing and the perfecting of a good work in man: and without which he cannot even think anything good. Phil. 2, 13. 2 Cor. 3, v. 5. However, this operation of special help does not have a place except in those already reborn, or reconciled with GOD: but this reconciliation is not known except from the Gospel. From this, therefore, when true trust in divine mercy is conceived, and terrified minds are raised up by faith: immediately at the same time the Holy Spirit is given, who imbues us with the love of GOD, and with the law of GOD written in the hearts of believers, excites in us new motions, agreeing with the divine law. Whence at last truly good Works are made, and thus from a good tree, good fruits arise. We conclude, therefore, that truly good Works, and interior obedience and worship, proceed not from the faculty of human powers: but solely from the operation and efficacy of the Holy Spirit. And indeed this divine help of the Holy Spirit is required both by our infirmity: and by that perpetual hatred of the Devil, by which he strives to lead men away from the true path of piety to the byways of vices.

Moreover, since this very Question was expressly debated against the Jesuits in the digression of the Article on free will: to weave it through at greater length in this place would be clearly superfluous.

Latin:

Quæritur quomodo fieri possint Bona Opera? Ubi de Causa Efficiente quæri per se manifestum est. Hæc ut ritè expediatur, duorum Aphorismorum Theologicorum observatione opus fuerit.

Aphorismus primus est iste: Externa locomotiva sive mores externi aliquo modo regi possunt humana diligentia, & virium propriarum facultates. Dicimus autem, Aliquo modo tantùm hoc fieri posse: Habet enim mens humana & locomotiva etiam in sapientissimis hujus seculi, suas difficultates, remoras, atque obstacula, cum quibus ratio conflictari necessum habet. Quando ergò ratio præest, appetitus verò obtemperat, tùm ex difficultatibus istis quadantenùs homo emergere potest. Monstrant hoc exempla illa illustria Gentilium, Aristidis, Scipionis, Camilli & similium. Nùm verò hæc Opera, & quomodo coram D E O bona fuerint, ipsique placuerint: superiore quæstione prima sufficienter fuit demonstratum.

Alter Aphorismus est iste: Interiorem cordis obedientiam, qualem quidem Lex DEI ad præstandum opus verè bonum, necessariò requirit, quaq; condelectatur legi DEI, Rom. 7, 22. & cujus finis est charitas, 1. Tim. 1, 5. Homo proprijs viribus non tantùm non perficere: sed ne quidem inchoare potest, sine illuminatione, quæ sit per doctrinam Evangelij, virtute Spiritus sancti. Confirmat hoc Servator ipse, Johan. 14, 5. Sine me nihil potestis facere. Ubi non generale tantùm illud auxilium D E I, intelligit Servator, quòd consistit in conservatione naturæ humanæ: uti Jesuwitæ volunt: Sed & speciale hoc, quod & velle & perficere bonum opus in homine operatur: & fine quo ipse ne quidem cogitare potest aliquid boni. Phil. 2, 13. 2. Cor. 3. v. 5. Hæc operatio autem auxilii specialis non locum habet nisi in jam renatis, sive cum D E O reconciliatis: Reconciliatio autem hæc non ni si ex Evangelio innotescit. Ex hoc ergò, quando vera fiducia misericordiæ divinæ concipitur, & mentes perterrefactæ eriguntur fide: statim simul datur Spiritus sanctus, qui dilectione D E I nos imbuit, & lege D E I in cordibus credentium scriptâ, in nobis novos motus, legi divinæ congruentes excitat. Undè demùm fiunt Opera verè bona, & sic ex arbore bona, boni fructus enascuntur. Colligimus proindè, Opera verè bona, & obedientiam cultumque interiorem, non ab humanarum virium facultate: sed ab operatione & efficacia Spiritus sancti unicè proficisci. Et profectò divinum hoc Spiritus sancti auxilium requirit tùm infirmitas nostra: tùm perpetuum illud Diaboli odium, quô homines à vero pietatis tramite, ad vitiorum devia abducere studet.

Cæterùm cùm de hac ipsa Quæstione in diexodo Articuli de libero arbitrio, ex professo contra Jesuwitas sit disputatum: pluribus hoc loco eam pertexere, planè foret supervacaneum.


### Question III. Concerning the Final Cause of Good Works

That the pursuit of good Works is not indifferent, or adiaphorous: but highly necessary, is placed beyond Controversy in our Churches, so that the theology of those who determined that good Works are harmful and pernicious to salvation would be clearly crude. This necessity, however, partly respects the command of GOD, who seriously demands repentance and newness, Matt. 9, 13, Luke 13, 5, 1 Cor. 6, 9 and 10, 1 John 3, 8, and partly the condition of order and Consequence between Causes and effects. For it is certain that we are not so regenerated and justified by faith, as if we felt no alterations of our minds: but that as new creatures, we are also occupied with new pursuits of good Works, and our light shines before men, that they may see our good Works, and glorify our Father, who is in Heaven. Matt. 5, v. 15, 2 Cor. 5, 17, Gal. 6, 15, Eph. 2, 10. Just as therefore according to the Philosophers, the Cause being placed in act, the Effect cannot but follow: So faith and justification being placed, the fruit of good Works cannot but follow.

Moreover, here a Question immediately emerges: If good Works are necessary, what is the End of this Necessity, or for what Causes are good Works to be done? Now if we examine the Scriptures, three final Causes are given most especially. THE FIRST respects GOD Himself, who partly commanded them, John 13, v. 34, 1 Thess. 4, 3, and partly wishes this glory of obedience to be rendered to Him by us, that thence He Himself may be glorified among others, Matt. 5, 16, 1 Pet. 4, 11.

The other Cause respects the Man himself working well: both that they may testify of their faith and justification among others, Matt. 7, 16, By their fruits you shall know them: and that they may be made partakers of those promises, which Piety has concerning the rewards of this and eternal life, 1 Tim. 4, 8: and that temporal and eternal punishments and torments may be avoided, Rom. 8, 13, If you live according to the Flesh, you shall die: and finally, that they may not afflict with sadness the Holy Spirit, by whom they are sealed, Eph. 4, 30, Psalm 51, 13. But some infer very poorly from the nature of contraries, that by good Works faith or the Holy Spirit is retained, just as indeed our author in this very place does not entirely abhor this opinion. For of contrariety, as far as opposites are concerned, there is not an equal and like reason on both sides: nor does the form of sound words admit that. For we are kept by the power of GOD through faith unto salvation, 1 Pet. 1, 5. & we stand in faith, & we glory in the hope of the children of GOD, Rom. 5, 2.

Furthermore, just as we conceive faith only through the Word and Sacraments, so also it is retained and preserved only through these same things.

The THIRD and final Cause concerns the Neighbor, and him either good or evil: that we may not offend either with impiety, but may assist them with the pursuit of good Works, and incite them to similar piety. Philip. 2, v. 15. 1. Pet. 2, 12. & ch. 3, 1. 16. Tit. 2, 8.

The Roman Church has mixed a manifest corruption into this purer doctrine; besides the ends already enumerated, it also reckons a Fourth, namely that which concerns our Justification and salvation. For Bellarmine fights today: 1. That Works are necessary for salvation: 2. That good Works preserve salvation. 3. That the same are meritorious and worthy of retribution in themselves. Bellar. b. 4. on Justification, throughout.

The impiety of the former error can be demonstrated by these reasons. 1. The doctrine of Works ought to be distinguished from the Article of Justification, as Cause and Effect, or as Antecedent and Consequent, and not be confused. But these two Articles are confused as soon as necessity for salvation is ascribed to good works.

2. This error is contradictorily opposed to the Holy Scriptures: which expressly separate and exclude Works from the business of our Justification and salvation, Rom. 3, 28. Rom. 4, 6. Ephes. 2, 9. Galat. 2, v. 16.

3. The dignity of the merit of Christ is enervated, nay, it is plainly overturned by this pact: For as much as is attributed to our Works in the act of salvation, so much is derogated from the merit of Christ.

4. For consciences crushed and prostrated by the sense of divine wrath, all the foundations of true consolations, and especially that unshaken confidence resting solely in the mercy of GOD, are not only shaken, but are also undermined and overturned.

The authority of the Scriptures likewise refutes and dissipates the other error. For it establishes the progress, end, and every consummation of our salvation, not in Works, either in part or in whole, but in the sole gratuitous mercy of GOD, apprehended through faith, as 1 Cor. 1, 8. GOD will establish you even to the end, Phil. 1, 6. He who began a good Work in you, will finish it, even to the day of Jesus Christ, 1 Thess. 3, 13. & ch. 5, 23. 1 Pet. 1, 5. Furthermore, the same Scripture pronounces Christ alone to be the author and finisher of our faith and salvation, Heb. 12, 2. Hence that full assurance of the Apostle, from which he says he is certain, not from Works, but from the love of GOD, that nothing can separate him from GOD and eternal salvation, Rom. 8, 38.

The third error collapses by its own, and that a plainly stupendous, vanity and impiety: which shines forth abundantly even from the mere enumeration of the dogma of the Jesuits. For they imagine that the merit which good works obtain for effecting and meriting our salvation is threefold: of Congruity, of Worthiness, and of Condignity. Merit of Congruity to them is an act freely elicited by man, accepted by God to reward something, not from a debt of justice, but from the sole liberality of the one accepting. And this merit, indeed, they say obtains a place especially in sinners and those not yet reborn, who first merit the grace of God from Congruity: For if a sinner does what is in him, that is, abandons the act and will of sinning, and strives for good as much as possible: then it is fitting for God, and it is congruous and convenient, that He Himself, out of His own liberality and goodness, should confer His grace upon such a sinner.

They call the merit of Worthiness the fitness of the Worker to attain that which he merits. And this merit, they say, has a place in the just and reborn, when they work for others, as when they pray for the conversion of a sinner. For they say it is just before God that the just man should be heard before God when he makes vows for a sinner. Hence arose among the Romanists Suffrages, Prayers, and votive Masses for the sins of both the living and the dead.

They call the merit of condignity an act of the righteous, elicited by the will through the grace of God, for a reward or recompense to be rendered according to the debt of justice. These things being thus presupposed as if in the place of a foundation, the Romanists proceed, and are accustomed to apply this excellent theology of theirs to the work of our justification and salvation in this manner, so that they do not fear to write: If a meritorious work is considered, according to that which proceeds from the grace of the Holy Spirit, then it is meritorious of eternal life: and a man established in grace can merit eternal life, of condignity, as Thomas has it, in the first part of the second part at the end: and Bellarmine, book 5 on Justification, chapter 16.

The impiety of this doctrine is too atrocious to be sufficiently exaggerated in words: it is also too gross to need refutation by many. For 1. it inflicts a manifest and indeed sufficiently blasphemous injury upon the most holy merit of Christ: to which whatever is attributed to the merits of human works, even from the least, is detracted. 2. It involves and overturns itself in open contradiction. For this is a statement of an opposite in an adjective, that a man can merit eternal life by his own works out of the grace of God. For that statement of the Apostle is certain and immovable; that human merit and divine grace simply exclude each other in the act of justification, Rom. 11, 6.

3. It is clearly inconsistent, and nowhere holds together. For partly it pits man, although reborn, yet a sinner, against the justice of God, which all the saints have always prayed against, and have appealed from the court of divine justice to the court of mercy: but partly they do not so much join as confuse grace with justice, and indeed with respect to merit, while from the due works of the reborn they elicit a certain merit as if it were undue; and from the repayment of their debt, they make GOD a debtor to man. By a path clearly contrary to this, all the holy and pious in the Scriptures have stripped all merit of eternal life from all their own works and sufferings, as well as those of other reborn persons: and they have sought all dignity, if they desired any, in the mercy of GOD: finally, they have sought all boasting from the merit and cross of CHRIST, as one who alone has been made for us by the Father Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification and Redemption, so that he who boasts, may boast in the LORD, 1 Cor. 1.

Finally, not even the Romanists themselves agree on this doctrine, but even the chief among the Scholastics have manifestly contradicted it, such as:

Thomas Aquinas in Epist. ad Rom. cap 4. Works are not the Cause that anyone is righteous before GOD: but rather they are executions and manifestations of righteousness. For no one is justified before GOD by Works: but by the habit of faith, not indeed acquired, but infused: And therefore whoever wishes to be justified by Works are under a curse, because sins are not removed by Works, nor is anyone justified before GOD: but by the habit of faith, informed by charity.

The same in Epist. ad Gal. cap. 3. Human works are considered in two ways: In one way, according to the Substance of the works, and thus they do not have anything Worthy, so that the eternal reward of glory may be rendered to them. In another way they can be considered according to their principle, namely, as they are done from the impulse of GOD: and according to this, a reward is owed to them according to debt. How Thomas understood this, he explains in quest. 3 in 27 distinct. GOD, he says, becomes a debtor to us from his promise, because he himself promised a reward to those doing well, so that we are said to merit, because he promised.

Bonaventura lib. 5. Compendij Theologiæ cap. 13. posits eight causes why we merit eternal life by worthiness. 1. The efficacy of the gift of the Holy Spirit, cooperating toward merit. 2. The truth of GOD promising. 3. The persuasibility of free will consenting and finally persevering. 4. The difficulty of the state of meriting. 5. The dignity of Christ our head intervening, who ought to be glorified in his members. 6. The liberality of GOD rewarding, whom it does not befit to render small things. 7. The service of one faithfully obeying him. 8. The nobility of the Work, which proceeds from charity.

Latin:

STudium bonorum Operum non esse indifferens, sive adiaphorum: sed summè necessarium, extra Controversiam in Ecclesiis nostris est positum, ut cruda planè Theologia fuerit eorum, qui statuerunt, Bona Opera ad salutem esse noxia & perniciosa. Necessitas autem hæc partim respicit mandatum DEI, qui pœnitentiam & novitatem seriò exigit, Matth. 9, 13. Luc. 13, 5. 1. Cor. 6, 9. & 10. 1. Joh. 3, 8. partim conditionem ordinis atque Consequentiæ inter Causas atque effecta. Constat enim non sic nos regenerari, & justificari fide, quasi nullas animorum alterationes sentiamus: sed ut novæ creaturæ, novis etiam bonorum Operum studiis occupemur, & lux nostra luceat coram hominibus, ut videant bona Opera nostra, & glorificent Patrem nostrum, qui in Cœlis est. Matth. 5. v. 15. 2. Cor. 5, 17. Gal. 6, 15. Eph. 2, 10. Quemadmodum ergò secundum Philosophos, Causa in actu positâ, non potest non sequi Effectus: Ita positâ fide & justificatione non potest non sequi fructus bonorum Operum.

Cæterùm hîc statim emergit Quæstio: Si necessaria sunt bona Opera, quis sit Necessitatis hujus Finis, vel propter quas Causas facienda sint bona Opera? Jam si Scripturas excutiamus, tres potissimùm dantur Causæ finales. PRIMA respicit DEUM ipsum, qui partim mandavit, Joh. 13. v. 34. 1. Thess. 4, 3. partim hanc à nobis gloriam obedientiæ sibi præstari vult, ut indè apud alios ipse glorificetur, Matth. 5, 16. 1. Pet. 4, 11.

Altera Causa respicit Hominem ipsum benè operantem: tùm ut de fide & justificatione sua apud alios testentur. Matth. 7, 16. Ex fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos: tùm ut reddantur participes earum promissionum, quas Pietas habet de hujus & æternæ vitæ præmiis. 1. Tim. 4, 8. tùm ut evitentur pœnæ & supplicia temporalia & æterna, Rom. 8, 13. Si secundum Carnem vixeritis, moriemini: tùm denique, ut ne tristitiâ afficiant Spiritum sanctum, quo sunt obsignati. Ephes. 4, 30. Psalm. 51, 13. Pessimè autem ex contrariorum naturâ inferunt nonnulli, per Bona Opera retineri fidem sive Spiritum sanctum, quemadmodum sanè ab hac sententia non planè etiam abhorres Autor noster hoc loco ipso. Nam contrarietatis, quoad opposita non est æqualis & par utrinque ratio: neque sanorum verborum forma id admittit. Nam virtute DEI custodimur per fidem ad salutem. 1. Pet. 1, 5. & in fide stamus, & gloriamur in spe filiorum DEI, Rom. 5, 2.

Porrò quemadmodum non nisi per Verbum & Sacramenta fidem concipimus: ita etiam non nisi per hæc eadem, illa retinetur & conservatur.

TERTIA & postrema Causa respicit Proximum, eumque vel bonum vel malum: ut neutrum impietate offendamus: sed bonorum Operum studiis juvemus, & ad similem pietatem incitemus. Philip. 2. v. 15. 1. Petr. 2, 12. & cap. 3, 1. 16. Tit. 2, 8.

Puriori huic doctrinæ manifestum corruptelam admiscuit Romana Ecclesia; præter fines jam enumeratos, recensens etiam Quartum, illum nimirùm, qui Justificationem & salutem nostram concernit. Nam pugnat hodiè Bellarminus. 1. Opera esse necessaria ad salutem: 2. Bona Opera conservare salutem. 3. Eadem esse meritoria & ex se digna esse retributione. Bellar. l. 4. de Justif. integro.

Prioris erroris impietas his demonstrari potest rationibus. 1. Doctrina Operum ab Articulo Justificationis, ut Causa & Effectus, vel ut Antecedens & Consequens distingui, neque confundi debet. Confunduntur autem duo hi Articuli, quamprimùm bonis operibus necessitas ad salutem adscribitur.

2. Scripturis Sacris error iste contradictoriè est oppositus: quæ Opera à Justificationis & salutis nostræ negocio, expressè separant & excludunt, Rom. 3, 28. Rom. 4, 6. Ephes. 2, 9. Galat. 2. v. 16.

3. Dignitas meriti Christi enervatur, imò planè hoc pacto evertitur: Quantum enim in actu salutis, nostris tribuitur Operibus, tantum derogatur merito Christi.

4. Conscientiis sensu iræ divinæ contritis & prostratis, omnia firmamenta verarum consolationum, præcipuè autem immotæ illius fiduciæ in misericordia DEI unicè acquiescentis, non concutiuntur modò: sed & subruuntur atque evertuntur.

Alterum errorem itidem Scripturæ autoritas retundit & dissipat. Hæc enim progressum, finem atque consummationem omnem salutis nostræ, non in Operibus, vel ex parte, vel ex toto: sed in sola gratuita DEI misericordia, per fidem apprehensâ constituit, ut 1. Cor. 1, 8. DEUS stabiliet vos usq; ad finem, Phil. 1, 6. Qui cœpit in vobis Opus bonum, consummabit, usque ad diem Jesu Christi, 1. Thess. 3, 13. & cap. 5, 23. 1. Pet. 1, 5. Porrò eadem Scriptura solum Christum pronunciat esse δι ἀρχηγὸν & τελειωτὺν fidei nostræ & salutis, Heb. 12, 2. Hinc illa Apostoli πληροφορία, ex qua certum se esse dicit, non ex Operibus, sed ex dilectione DEI, quòd nihil ipsum separare possit à DEO & salute æterna, Rom. 8, 38.

Tertius error propriâ suâ, eâque planè stupenda vanitate & impietate corruit: id quod vel ex sola enumeratione dogmatis Jesuuitarum abundè elucescit. Fingunt enim, Meritum illud, quòd Bona opera ad salutem nostram efficiendam & promerendam obtinent, esse triplex: Congrui, Digni & Condigni. Congrui meritum illis est actus liberè elicitus ab homine, acceptatus à Deo ad aliquid retribuendum, non ex debito juftitiæ, sed ex sola acceptantis liberalitate. Et hoc quidem meritum dicunt, locum præcipuè obtinere in peccatoribus & nondum renatis, qui gratiam Dei primùm ex Congruo mereantur: Nam si faciat peccator, quod in se est, hoc est; actum & voluntatem peccandi deserat, & pro possibili conetur in bonum: tùm decere Deum, & congruum esse, ac conveniens, ut ipse ex liberalitate & bonitate sua gratiam suam tali peccatori conferat.

Meritum Digni nominant Idoneitatem Operantis ad assequendum id, quod meretur. Et meritum hoc, dicunt, locum habere in justis & renatis, quandò hi operantur pro aliis, ut cùm orant pro conversione peccatoris. Justum enim apud Deum esse dicunt, ut justus exaudiatur apud Deum, vota faciens pro peccatore. Hinc ortum apud Romanenses traxerunt Suffragia, Orationes, & Missæ votivæ pro peccatis tùm vivorum tùm mortuorum.

Meritum Condigni vocant actum justorum, per gratiam Dei à voluntate elicitum, ad præmium sive mercedem, secundum debitum justitiæ retribuendam. His ita fundamenti quasi loco præsuppositis, pergunt Romanenses, & egregiam hanc suam Theologiam ad opus Justificationis ac salutis nostræ, hunc in modum applicare solent, ut scribere non vereantur: Si opus meritorium consideretur, secundum quod procedit ex gratia Spiritus sancti, tùm esse meritorium vitæ æternæ: & hominem constitutum in gratia posse mereri vitam æternam, ex Condigno, ut habet Thomas, prima secundæ in fine: & Bellarminus lib. 5. de Justif. cap. 16.

Impietas doctrinæ hujus atrocior est, quàm ut verbis satis exaggerari possit: crassior etiam est, quàm ut multis refutari debeat. Nam 1. injuriam manifestam & quidem blasphemè satis infert Sacro-Sancto Christi merito: cui derogatur, quicquid Operum humanorum meritis, vel ex minimo etiam tribuitur. 2. Seipsam apertâ Contradictione implicat & evertit. Nam oppositi in adjecto hæc est enunciatio, quòd Homo ex gratia Dei possit suis Operibus promereri vitam æternam. Certum enim & immotum est illud Apostoli enunciatum; quòd meritum humanum, & gratia divina se in actu justificationis simpliciter excludant, Rom. 11, 6.

3. Ἀσύστατον planè est, & nuspiam cohæret. Nam partim Hominem licèt renatum, peccatorem tamen cum Justitia Dei committit, quam omnes Sancti semper deprecati sunt, & à foro Justitiæ divinæ, ad forum misericordiæ provocârunt: partim verò Gratiam cum Justitia, & quidem quoad respectum meritorium non magis conjungunt, quàm confundunt, dùm ex operibus renatorum debitis, meritum quoddam quasi indebitum eliciunt; & ex redditione debiti sui, DEUM homini debitorem faciunt. Contrafiâ planè viâ Sancti & pii quique in Scripturis ingressi, omnibus tùm suis, tùm aliorum renatorum operibus & passionibus omnem condignitatem promerendi vitam æternam derogârunt: omnemq; dignitatem, si quam optârunt in DEI misericordia quæsiverunt: omnem denique gloriationem, ex merito & cruce CHRISTI petiêrunt, ut qui solus factus sit nobis à Patre Sapientia, Justitia, Sanctificatio & Redemtio, ut qui gloriatur, in DOMINO glorietur, 1. Cor. 1.

Tandem ne ipsi quidem Romanenses de doctrina ista conveniunt, quin ex Scholasticis etiam præcipui ei manifestè contradixerunt, ut:

Thomas Aquinas in Epist. ad Rom. cap 4. Opera non sunt Causa, quòd aliquis sit justus apud DEUM: sed potius sunt executiones & manifestationes justitiæ. Nam nullus per Opera justificatur apud DEUM: sed per habitum fidei, non quidem acquisitum, sed infusum: Et ideò quicunq; ex Operibus justificari volunt, sub maledicto sunt, quia per Opera non removentur peccata, nec aliquis quoad DEUM justificatur: sed per habitum fidei, charitate informatum.

Idem in Epist. ad Gal. cap. 3. Opera humana considerantur dupliciter: Uno modo, secundum Substantiam Operum, & sic non habent aliquid Condignum, ut eis merces æterna gloriæ reddatur. Alio modo possunt considerari secundum suum principium, prout scilicet èa ex impulsu DEI aguntur: & secundum hoc debetur eis merces secundum debitum. Quod quomodo Thomas intellexerit, explicat quæst. 3. in 27 distinct. DEUS ex promisso, inquiens, debitor nobis fit, quòd ipse benè agentibus præmium promisit, ut mereri dicamur, quoniam promisit.

Bonaventura lib. 5. Compendij Theologiæ cap. 13. ponit octo causas, quamobrem ex condigno mereamur vitam æternam. 1. Efficacia doni Spiritus sancti, cooperantis in meritum. 2. Veritas DEI promittentis. 3. Persuasibilitas liberi arbitrij consentientis & finaliter perseverantis. 4. Difficultas status merendi. 5. Dignitas Christi capitis nostri intervenientis, quod glorificari debet in membris suis. 6. Liberalitas DEI retribuentis, quem non decet parvà reddere. 7. Obsequium sibi fideliter obtemperantis. 8. Nobilitas Operis, quod ex charitate procedit.


### Question III. Concerning the Final Cause of Good Works (continued)

Johan. Gerson. in Serm. de Verbis Domini: Venite ad me omnes, &c. part 2. If perhaps that ancient Adversary resists, and will slander, that it is unjust that anyone should be saved by the prayers of others, and not by their own Works: I confess, I would shudder at that word, unless I recognized my great merits. For I have two great and valid merits, And the first indeed is the passion of my Lord: but the second is my own and his operation, even if I have worked even the least thing, even if I have uttered but one groan at the end of my life. The first work the Lord worked for me and without me. The second work the LORD works with me and in me.

-willing, he says: Nor is there need that you remind me of my sins, inferring from this that I am unworthy of heavenly rewards. For I know that, but I also know that that pious Father of mine JESUS CHRIST paid my debt, and will blot out all my sins, as often as they have displeased me, and has gained and bought for me the heavenly kingdom with his most precious blood. From this title and no other do I await the possession of that thing.

Moreover, the Romanists bring forward very many testimonies of the Scriptures, by which they strive to palliate the impiety of their dogma in some way: and at the beginning indeed they urge those which attribute great dignity and perfection to Works.

But I reply that a fallacy is committed παρὰ τὸ πη̃ καὶ ἀπλω̃ς [in a certain respect and absolutely]. For such dignity is not understood, which might inhere in the Substance of good works by their own nature: or be obtained from the perfection and holiness of the Person Working: but only that which is accessory, or happens to the good works of the reborn by accident, both from the faith shining before, which always relies solely on the merit of Christ, and from the benevolence and good pleasure of GOD, who allows the works of his Elect, whatever they may be, to be approved with fatherly affection: and finally from the calling, by which the people of GOD excel by far any other men, since GOD receives the obedience of believers on account of his son and calls them sacrifices, that is, Works, by which GOD judges himself to be honored, and which he himself adorns, or as the Psalm speaks, crowns with the promises of rewards.

Then the Adversaries bring forward those testimonies of Scripture, which promise a retribution of corporal and Spiritual rewards to good works, such as Isaiah 1, 19. If you hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land. Matt. 10, 42. Whoever shall give to one of these little ones a cup of cold water, shall not lose his reward. Luke 14, 14. it will be repaid to you in the resurrection of the just. And in chapters 11 and 28 of Deuteronomy a long Catalog of rewards is woven, with which GOD wishes to compensate good Works. 1 Tim. 4, 8. Piety has promises of this and the future life.

But I reply that a fallacy is committed both of Ignorance of the Refutation, and of a vicious Consequent, when the Romanists institute from there a collection of the merits of good Works. For these rewards are not promised to those working well on account of any dignity and merit of good Works considered in themselves, which certainly always labor under the greatest imperfection in this life, and are polluted with the filth of sins: But only from the Grace of GOD, to whom all things must be attributed. But Grace and the merit of Works exclude each other immediately or Contradictorily, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 11, 6. And Luke 17, 10. If you have done all things, say, we are unprofitable servants. To which pertain also those most noble testimonies of scripture, which strip from any works whatsoever the power of justifying: as Job 9, 2 and 20. A man is not justified before God, if I wish to justify myself, my mouth will condemn me. Proverbs 20, 9.

Who can say, my heart is clean, I am pure from sin. Ecclesiastes 7:20. There is no just man on earth, who does good and does not sin. Isaiah 64:6. All our righteousnesses are as a menstruous cloth. Therefore when and as often as God rewards good works, he does nothing else than crown his own gifts in us. For all the good works of the reborn are not so much the works of the reborn as of God himself. Isaiah 26:12. Lord, you have wrought all our works in us. Philippians 2:13. It is God who works in us both to will and to perform good. Whence any good works are named by the Apostle the Fruit of the Spirit Galatians 5:22.

The Jesuits therefore commit a shameful begging of the question, arguing thus: God in the Scriptures promises bodily and spiritual rewards to good works. Therefore good works are of themselves meritorious. For the vanity of the collection shines forth of its own accord from what has already been said.

Thirdly, they urge most strongly those testimonies which assign to our works the reward of eternal life, such as Matthew 5:12. Your reward is great in heaven.

But I reply that a fallacy of equivocation is committed in the word reward. For the Scriptures, not as the Jesuits suppose, in the business of justification and good works, do not denote by this word that mercenary reward by reason of which eternal life, as a reward, would be owed to works, and indeed from condignity. For all those testimonies of Scripture disprove and overthrow this meaning, as many as exclude works from the act of our justification and argue their imperfection and ἀδυναμίαν [inability]: just as the Apostle also expressly denies that righteousness came to Abraham from reward: because it is given not according to grace, but according to debt: but to Abraham not working, but believing, faith was imputed for righteousness, not according to debt, but according to grace. Romans 4:4. But generally and commonly in the Scriptures, whatever is repaid is called a reward, whether it be in some proportion analogous to labor or work, or not. An example of this thing may be seen in the parable of the laborers in the vineyard: Matth. 20, where that is called a reward which was paid out to the laborers not for the labor of the vinedressers, but out of the good pleasure of the householder. And in this sense the word reward is used Gen. 15, 1, when the Lord says to Abraham: I am your reward very great. Moreover, eternal life is called a reward because it was obtained by immense labor, not indeed our own, but Christ’s. It is therefore called our reward, not with respect to our merit, but to the imputed merit of another. Furthermore, it is so named on account of the promise made to believers, which falls into the category of debt: not indeed by reason of our merit, but with respect to the immutable divine truth. Whatever therefore is understood under the word reward, whether eternal life itself, or degrees of heavenly glory in it, or even bodily benefits: then it does not denote a due retribution of our labors, where there is a due proportion between reward and work: but a gratuitous and clearly undue compensation, depending not on the dignity of our works, but on the mere grace and liberality of the promising God. Whence this is also named in the Scriptures: The reward of the inheritance. Colossians 3:24. Because by that sole limitation the Apostle implies that he understands this word not of merit, but of the free and undue gift of God: just as he explains himself in Romans 6:23. Eternal life, he says, is the gift of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

But the Jesuits insist, and contend that that former meaning of the word reward must be interpreted by a mercenary or meritorious reward, because both Scripture itself and all Antiquity have explained the word reward by the word merit.

I reply 1. The word merit, in that sense indeed in which it is accepted by the Romanists, and insofar as it makes God a debtor to us, has always been held as detestable both in this and in the preceding article; which, however, in evil works is, alas, too proper and authentic. Furthermore, in the entire canonical Holy Scripture, the word merit is not found even once regarding the present business. The Jesuits therefore incur the charge of falsehood.

Thirdly, the word merit does indeed exist in the Apocryphal book of Ecclesiasticus, namely 10:31 and 38:18. But in both places it does not denote any merit of ours toward God, but only merit toward men: as in the former place: Son, give honor to your soul according to its merit: in the latter, however: Make mourning according to his merit for one day. But this is nothing to the point. Thus the passage which Bellarmine objects from Ecclesiasticus chapter 16:14, where it is read: Let every mercy make a place for each one according to the merit of his works, does not make anything to the matter. For in this place also a gross crime of falsehood is committed in a vicious translation: The Greek has it thus, πάσῃ ἐλεεμοσύνῃ ποιήσει τόπον, he will make a place for every alms: ἕκαστος κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ εὑρήσει: each one will find according to his works. Therefore no meaning emerges other than that God rewards beneficence and alms, but punishes unmercifulness.

To which opinion the Apostle also writes in Rom. 2:6: "Who will render to every man according to his deeds." Whence if anyone wished to construct a meritorious justice of works, he would be fighting diametrically against the Pauline purpose, which is entirely directed toward detracting the praise of justice from works. 2. The Apostle would have had to say ἀντιδώσει, which word denotes merit and a mercenary reward: but he says ἀποδώσει, which in a general sense signifies a bestowal or retribution not always owed, but also gratuitous. 3. He would have had to say ἐξ ἔργων, or διὰ τὰ ἔργὰ, which phrases would imply a respect for a meritorious cause:

And yet he says κατὰ τὰ ἔργα [according to works], which phrase only obtains the respect of a sign, so that it may show that the judgment of each person will be such as his own works are: If good: testifying, namely, of a true faith, then a great retribution from God will follow: But if evil, an evil judgment also is to be expected for works of this kind. Which reasons being observed, it is plain that they are sophistical under the fallacy of non-cause as cause, while good works constitute the cause of eternal life: when they perform only the office of a sign and testimony in this part.

But the Romanists do not rest even so, but clamor that the word 'to merit' is found most frequently even in the canonical Scriptures: and therefore they infer that the word 'merit' itself, from the place of conjugates, is also canonical and ἐλλογιμον [imputable].

Latin:

Johan. Gerson. in Serm. de Verbis Domini: Venite ad me omnes, &c. parte 2. Si obsister fortassis antiquus ille Adversarius, & calumnia bitur, injustum esse, ut alienis precibus, & non proprijs Operibus quisquam salvetur: ad verbum illud, fateor, exhorrescerem, nisi magna merita mea recognoscerem. Habeo autem duo merita magna & valida, Et primum quidem est, Domini mei passio: secundum verò, mei est & ipsius operatio, etiamsi vel minimum quid operatus fuero, etiamsi vel unum in fine vitæ gemitum edidero. Primum opus operatus est Dominus pro me & sine me. Secundum opus operatur DOMINUS mecum & in me.

-volentibus inquit: Nec opus est, ut mihi peccata mea commemoretis, inferentes hinc, me caelestibus praemijs esse indignum. Id enim scio, sed & scio, quod pius ille meus Pater JESUS CHRISTUS meum debitum solvit, & mea omnia, quotiescunq; mihi displicuerint, peccata delebit, mihiq; suo pretiosissimo sanguine caeleste regnum lucrifecit & emit. Ex hoc titulo & nullo alio possessionem ejus rei praestolor.

Caeterum proferunt Romanenses bene multa Scripturarum testimonia, quibus impietatem dogmatis sui aliquo modo palliare student: ac initio quidem ea urgent, quae magnam Operibus dignitatem & perfectionem tribuunt.

Sed respondeo committi Sophisma παρὰ τὸ πη̃ καὶ ἀπλω̃ς. Non enim talis dignitas intelligitur, quae Substantiae bonorum ex sua natura insit: vel ex Personae Operantis perfectione & sanctimonia concilietur: sed tantum ea, quae accessoria est, sive per accidens obtingit bonis renatorum Operibus, tum ex fide praelucente, quae merito Christi unice semper nititur, tum ex benevolentia & beneplacito DEI, qui sibi Electorum suorum Opera, qualiacunque etiam paterno affectu probari patitur: tum denique ex vocatione, qua populus DEI quibusvis aliis hominibus plurimum antecellit, cum DEUS credentium obedientiam propter filium recipiat & vocet sacrificia, hoc est, Opera, quibus DEUS judicat se honore affici, & quae ipse ornat, vel ut Psalmus loquitur, coronat promissionibus praemiorum.

Deinde proferunt Adversarii illa Scripturae testimonia, quae Operibus bonis retributionem praemiorum corporalium ac Spiritualium pollicentur, qualia sunt Esaiae 1, 19. Si audieritis me, bona terrae comedetis. Matth. 10, 42. Qui dederit uni ex minimis istis calicem aquae frigidae, non perdet mercedem suam. Luc. 14, 14. retribuetur tibi in resurrectione justorum. Et Deut. 11. & 28. capitibus longus pertexitur Catalogus praemiorum, quibus bona Opera DEUS compensare velit. 1. Tim. 4, 8. Pietas promissiones habet hujus & futurae vitae.

Sed respondeo committi Sophisma tum Ignorationis Elenchi, tum vitiosi Consequentis, quando Romanenses inde ad merita bonorum Operum collectionem instituunt. Neque enim praemia haec promittuntur bene operantibus propter aliquam dignitatem & meritum bonorum Operum in se consideratorum, quae certe imperfectione maxima hac in vita semper laborant, & sordibus peccatorum sunt polluta: Sed tantum ex Gratia DEI, cui omnia sunt acceptum ferenda. Excludit autem sese invicem immediate sive Contradictorie Gratia & meritum Operum, teste Apostolo Rom. 11, 6. Et Luc. 17, 10. Si omnia feceritis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus. Quo pertinent nobilissima etiam illa scripturae testimonia, quae operibus quibusq; justificandi δύναμιν derogant: ut Job. 9, 2. & 20. Non justificatur Homo compositus Deo, si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me. Prover. 20, 9.

Quis potest dicere, mundum est Cor meum, purus sum à peccato. Ecclesiastæ 7, 20. Non est homo justus in terra, qui faciat bonum & non peccet. Jes. 64, 6. Quasi pannus menstruatæ omnes justitiæ nostræ. Proindè quando & quoties Deus bonis operibus retribuit, nihil facit aliud, quàm quòd sua propria dona in nobis coronat. Nam omnia bona Renatorum opera, non tàm renatorum, quàm ipsius Dei sunt opera. Jesaiæ 26, 12. Omnia opera nostra tu in nobis operatus es Domine. Phil. 2, 13. Deus est, qui operatur in nobis & velle & perficere bonum. Undè bona quævis opera ab Apostolo nominantur Fructus Spiritus Gal. 5, 22.

Turpem ergo petitionem Principij committunt Jesuvvitæ, sic arguentes: Deus in Scripturis promittit bonis operibus præmia Corporalia & Spiritualia. E. bona opera ex se sunt meritoria. Vanitas enim Collectionis ex jam dictis ultrò elucescit.

Tertiò urgent vel maximè ea testimonia, quæ operibus nostris Mercedem vitæ æternæ adsignant, ut Matth. 5, 12. Merces vestra copiosa est in Cælis.

Sed respondeo committi Sophisma ὁμωνυμίας in vocabulo Mercedis. Nam Scripturæ non uti Jesuvvitæ autumant, in negocio justificationis & bonorum operum per hoc vocabulum notant mercedem illam mercenariam, ratione cujus vita æterna tanquàm merces, operibus debeatur, & quidem ex condigno. Hanc enim significationem universa ea Scripturæ testimonia improbant & convellunt, quotquot opera ex actu justificationis nostræ excludunt, eorundemque imperfectionem & ἀδυναμίαν arguunt: Quemadmodum etiam disertè Apostolus negat, Abrahamo obtigisse justitiam ex mercede: propterea quòd detur non secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum: Abrahamó verò non operanti, sed credenti imputata fuerit fides ad justitiam, non secundum debitum, sed secundum gratiam. Rom. 4, 4. Sed generatim & communiter in Scripturis Merces nominatur, quicquid rependitur, sive illud labori aut operi sit proportione aliqua analogum, sive non. Cujus rei exemplum videre licet in parabola de operarijs in vinea: Matth. 20, ubi merces vocatur, quod non pro labore vinitorum: sed ex beneplacito patris familias operarijs est exsolutum. Et in hac significatione usurpatur vox Mercedis. Gen. 15, 1. cùm Dominus dicit ad Abrahamum: Ego sum merces tua valdè magna. Nominatur autem vita æterna merces, quia ea immenso labore constitit, non quidem nostro, sed Christi. Dicitur ergò merces nostra, non respectu meritorio nostro, sed imputativo alieno. Deindè sic nominatur propter promissionem factam credentibus, quæ cadit in debitum: non quidem ratione nostri meriti, sed respectu immutabilis veritatis divinæ. Quicquid proindè sub vocabulo Mercedis intelligitur, sive ipsa vita æterna, sive gradus gloriæ cælestis in illa, sive etiam beneficia corporalia: tùm non notatur debita nostrorum laborum retributio, ubi inter mercedem & opus debita est proportio: sed gratuita & planè indebita cõpensatio, dependens non ex dignitate nostrorum operum : sed ex mera gratia & liberalitate Dei promittentis. Undè Merces etiam hæc in Scripturis nominatur. Merces hereditatis. Coloss. 2, 24. Quia sola limitatione Apostolus innuit, se vocem hanc intelligere non de merito, sed de libero ac indebito Dei dono: quemadmodum ipse se explicat Rom. 6, 23. Vita æterna, inquiens, est donum Dei in Christo Jesu Domino nostro.

Sed instant Jesuvitæ, & priorem illam significationem vocabuli Mercedis, per mercedem mercenariam sive meritioram interpretandam esse contendunt, eò, quod tùm Scriptura ipsa, tùm universa Antiquitas, vocabulum Mercedis, per vocabulum Meriti explicaverit.

Respondeo 1. Meriti vocabulum eô quidem sensu, quô à Romanensibus accipitur, & quatenùs Deum nobis facit debitorem, tùm in hoc, tùm in præcedente Articulo proximo, pro detestabili semper fuisse habitum : quod tamen in malis operibus, nimis, pro dolor, proprium & authenticum est. Deindè in universa sacra Scriptura Canonica, ne semel quidem vox Meriti reperitur, quoad præsens negocium. Falsi ergò crimen incurrunt Jesuvitæ.

Tertiò Meriti quidem vox extat in libro Apocrypho Ecclesiastico nimirum 10, 31. & 38, 18. Sed utrobique non notatur aliquod nostrum meritum erga Deum: sed tantùm meritum erga homines: ut in priore loco: Fili da animæ tuæ honorem secundum meritum suum : in posteriore verò: Fac luctum secundum meritum ejus uno die. Sed nihil hoc ad rhombum. Sic nihil quicquam ad rem facit locus, quem objicit Bellarminus ex Ecclesiastico cap. 16, 14. ubi legitur : Omnis misericordia faciat locum unicuique secundum meritum operum suorum. Nam & hoc loco committitur crassum crimen falsi, in vitiosa versione: Græca sic habet, πάσῃ ἐλεεμοσύνῃ ποιήσει τόπον, omni Eleemosynæ faciet locum : ἕκαστος κτ τὰ ἔργα ἀυτᾶ εὑρήσει : unusquisque secundum opera sua inveniet. Sensus ergo nullus emergit alius, quàm quòd Deus beneficentiam & eleemosynam remuneretur : immisericordiam verò puniat.

Quam in sententiam etiam Apostolus scribit Rom. 2, 6. Qui reddet unicuig, secundum opera ipsius. Undè si quis operum justitiam meritoriam extruere vellet, is pugnaret è Diametro cum scopo Paulino, qui in eo totus est, ut operibus laudem justitiæ deroget. 2. dicendum fuisset Apostolo ἀντιδώσει, quæ vox meritum, mercedemque mercenariam denotat : Atqui dicit, ἀποδώσει, quod in genere significat largitionem sive retributionem non semper debitam, sed etiam gratuitam. 3. dicendum fuisset ἐξ ἔργων, vel διὰ τὰ ἔργὰ, quæ phrases causæ meritoriæ respectum innuerent :

Atqui dicit κατὰ τὰ ἔργα, quæ phrasis tantùm Signi respectum obtinet, ut tale cujusque judicium futurum ostendat, qualia sunt ipsius opera: Si bona: testantia nempè de fide verâ, tùm magnam à Deo retributionem secuturam esse: Sin mala, malum etiam judicium operibus hujusmodi expectandum esse. Quibus rationibus observatis, planum sit Sophisticari ipsos sub Sophismate non Causæ ut Causæ dùm bona opera Causam constituunt vitæ æternæ: cùm signi tantùm & testimonij officio, hac in parte funguntur.

Sed neque sic quiescunt Romanenses, quin verbum Merendi in Scripturis etiam Canonicis frequentissimè reperiri clamitant: ac proindè ipsum etiam Meriti vocabulum, ex loco Conjugatorum, Canonicum & ἐλλογιμον esse, inferunt.


### Question III. Concerning the Final Cause of Good Works (continued)

I answer that a manifold ignorance of the refutation is committed. For although we do not deny that the word 'to merit' occurs here and there in the Scriptures: yet it is nowhere accepted concerning the merit of eternal life: but it is used either concerning the punishments of sins; as Deut. 7:10, 'He will render to the impious according to what they merit.' Thus Judg. 20:10, it is said that it ought to be rendered to the tribe of Benjamin for the wickedness which it merits: or as the Hebrew has it: 'He will render to him according to all the filthiness which he did in Israel.' Thus 2 Chron. 19:2, the Prophet Jehu says to Jehoshaphat: 'You will merit the wrath of the Lord.' Esther 16:18, God is said to have rendered to Haman what he had merited. Job 6:2, he says his sins have merited wrath. Thus it is accepted also in Job 11:6. Furthermore, this word is snatched into a foreign sense by a vicious Latin version: as Gen. 4:13, 'My iniquity is greater than that I may merit pardon': where it is read in the Hebrew: 'My iniquity is greater than that I may be spared, or that I may bear it.' Which is the voice of one despairing, from which, if they please, the Romanists can learn the way of salvation from us. Thus Josh. 11:20, it is said concerning the Hivites: 'that they might not merit clemency': Where in the Hebrew it sounds simply: 'that there might be no mercy for them.' Nor have the Jesuits been able to bring forward any contrary and evident testimony of Scripture to this very day for confirming their signification, so that as regards the word 'merit' in this Article, they are utterly destitute of all authority of canonical Scripture.

As regards the Fathers, we concede that they used the word 'merit' and 'to merit' quite frequently, both in this and in the preceding Article, but we simply deny that the Pontifical sense can be elicited from their own discourses. For it is evident from their writings that they used these words quite generally, and according to the common and then-received idiom of their language: so that 'to merit' meant the same to them as 'to obtain': as their notable sentences attest.

Ambrose certainly, in book 1 of 'On the Calling of the Gentiles,' chapter 7, explains himself thus: 'It is manifest that every good merit of man, from the beginning of faith to the consummation of perseverance, is a divine gift and work.'

Jerome, in chapter 64 of Isaiah: 'If we consider our merits, we must despair: but if we consider your clemency, we dare to pour forth prayers.' Augustine, Epistle 46: 'That the grace of God is given according to our merits is most false.' And in book 50 of homilies: Homily 14: 'When God crowns your merits, he crowns nothing but his own gifts.' Preface to Psalm 31: 'If you wish to be a stranger to grace, boast of your merits.' In Psalm 139: 'The Saints attribute nothing to their own merits: They attribute everything to nothing but your mercy, O God.' Bernard, Sermon 61 on the Song of Songs: 'My merit is the mercy of the Lord: I am clearly not destitute of merit, as long as He is not destitute of mercies.' Sermon 68: 'It suffices for merit to know that merits do not suffice.' Sermon 15 on Psalm 91: 'This is the whole merit of man, if he places his whole hope in Him, who makes all things safe.'

The Jesuits take their fourth and final argument chiefly from the Epistle of James: where the Apostle says: 'Was not Abraham our father justified by works, offering his son upon the altar &c.'

I answer that a gross ignorance of the refutation is committed. For the Apostle is not dealing with the obtaining of justice, but with the demonstrating of it: whence he sometimes says: 'Show me your faith without your works, and I will show you my faith from my works': Therefore James is not dealing with the causes of Justification, but with its effects that strike the eyes: and consequently he does not dispute against us, who with Paul establish the gratuitous justification of faith without works: but against those who boasted of faith but testified by the impiety of their life and morals that they were destitute of true and justifying faith. Furthermore, James considers man not in the sight of God: but of men. 3. He deals with those already justified by faith, not with those yet to be justified: where that saying of Augustine truly has a place: 'Works do not precede the one to be justified: but follow the one already justified.' Finally, James is not dealing with the first act of justification, which consists in the sole gratuitous imputation of the justice of faith: but with the second act, which consists in the judgment of works, and is an effect of justification, not indeed its cause.

As for the example of Abraham, it seems to be brought forward inconveniently in this place, so much so that the ancients even for this very reason referred the Epistle of James among the ἀντιλεγόμενα writings. For verse 21, which Bellarmine cites, cannot be reconciled with the history of Genesis: James asserts that the Scripture, which says, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness, v. 23, was then finally fulfilled when he wished to offer his son Isaac upon the altar: but in truth the faith of Abraham, which was imputed to him for righteousness in Genesis 15:6, is celebrated in the 84th year of his age, whereas Isaac was born only in his hundredth year, and as the circumstances of the whole history show, was offered by Abraham in his 115th year. Therefore, by a full thirty years, Abraham was justified by faith, applied to the promise concerning the multiplication of his seed, before he was willing to offer Isaac. It seems, therefore, to be false what the author of the Epistle of James says, that in the final immolation of Isaac that Scripture was fulfilled which says, Abraham believed God &c. Nor does Bellarmine explain himself out of that difficulty when he says that in every act of Abraham's faith, that which says, Abraham believed God &c., was fulfilled. Since faith was always imputed to him for righteousness. For this is not in question, whether faith is imputed for righteousness to any act of faith: but this comes into controversy: whether that Scripture was fulfilled which says, Abraham believed God &c. when he was willing to immolate his son Isaac? Where James holds the affirmative: but the Mosaic Scripture refers this fulfillment of Scripture not to that act of immolation, but to that faith by which Abraham believed the promise concerning that Seed, in whom all the families of the earth are to be blessed, Gen. 15:6. Which very thing Paul also does, Rom. 4:18, asserting that Abraham believed in hope against hope. And this is the principal cause on account of which Blessed Luther asserted that the Epistle of James seemed straw-like, if indeed it is compared to the Pauline Epistles. For which very reason we also, in the present disputation, do not allow ourselves to be constrained by the authority of this Epistle: although it cannot harm our cause, provided the scope itself is attended to, as we have just now shown.

Furthermore, Bellarmine disputes quite prolixly in the entire fifth book concerning Justification, and strives to confirm the righteousness of our own merits or works, both from the Scriptures, and from Antiquity, and finally from reason. However, so that we may provide for time as if by some compendium, and set a limit to excessive prolixity, it is pleasing to propose certain rules, the observation of which may be able to show a sufficiently certain way of refuting almost all Jesuitical sophisms.

I. Rule I. The proper and legitimate state of the controversy must always be well considered, lest either another be foisted upon us: or it be involved in extraneous questions, just as it is too trite and familiar for the Jesuits today to sin against this rule through the Sophistry of Ignorance of the Refutation: as when he repeatedly intermixes questions about the necessity of good works, about the gift of regeneration, Sanctification, and Renewal, about the rewards of the good after the righteousness of faith has already been obtained.

II. Because the word Grace, Faith, Righteousness, and also the word Justify admits various meanings, effort must always be made so that the polysemy is unfolded, and the Sophistry of the Figure of speech or of homonymy, which is to be noted in the objections of the Jesuits.

III. One must accurately distinguish between the legal sayings of Scripture, which indeed urge the righteousness of Works, but by no means establish that it is possible for human nature: and between the Evangelical sayings, which define and explain the proper and genuine causes of our justification and salvation.

IV. Evangelical sayings again are not of one and the same kind: For some, as has already been said, reveal the causes of justification; such as are most of those which we cited, both in this and in the preceding Article, from the Pauline Epistles for the gratuitous justification of faith. Others, however, treat of the Effects and signs of our true justification, such signs being the pursuit of good works and new obedience: as when John says in chapter 3, verse 7, He who does righteousness is righteous: and some Saints are said to have walked in all the commandments and justifications of the Lord blamelessly. Where it is not shown by what things righteousness not yet acquired is obtained, but what it works in believers once it is already obtained: that is, the cause of righteousness is not expressed: but only a sign is placed, from which a judgment concerning the certainty of righteousness might be made.

V. Certain sayings are adapted to the specific persons of those who were seeking righteousness from the Law and Works, to whom Scripture responds: Do this and you shall live: or, How do you read in Moses? From which, however, a general rule for the causes of our Justification can neither be constructed nor ought to be.

VI. Sayings of Scripture concerning the rewards and wages of good works are either understood absolutely, insofar as the judgment of the law is proposed in them, and the exquisite righteousness of the divine will: but then a condition of observation is always annexed, He who shall do them shall live in them: which condition, however, both Scripture itself and our conscience openly testify to be impossible: Or they are understood in a certain respect, namely in a certain subject, that is, in the person of the reborn and believers. In which latter respect, three things always come to be noted: 1. That the reward which is promised to the faithful does not proceed from the perfection or merit of the work itself, but from the grace and liberality of God who compensates. 2. That the person does not please God because of the work itself: but the work pleases because of the person reconciled to God by faith. 3. In compensating good works, God does not deal with the reborn according to the rigor of the law: for thus no work, however good, would obtain a reward in the reborn: since whatever is by its nature imperfect, is owed and sordid.

VII. It must be well observed with what faith, or rather with what perfidy, the Romanists are accustomed to allege the sayings of Scripture. For sometimes they bring forward a faulty version, which must be corrected according to the Hebrew and Greek sources: or they add what should not be added, or omit what should not be omitted: or they attach a foreign meaning to the words of Scripture.

VIII. And the final Rule may be this, That Romanists are accustomed to bring forward many things from the Apocryphal books for the establishing of their error, concerning which that judgment of Jerome is most true, that the Church reads books of this kind, not for the confirming of the authority of Ecclesiastical dogmas: but only for the edification of the people. Hieron. præfat. in libros Salomonis.

Latin:

Respondeo, multiplicem committi ἀγνοίαν ἐλέγχυ. Etsi enim non negamus, Merendi verbum in Scripturis passim occurrere: tamen nusspiam de merito vitæ æternæ accipitur: sed vel de pœnis peccatorum usurpatur; ut Deut. 7, 10. reddet impijs secundum quod merentur. Sic Judic. 20, 10. dicitur, quod tribui Benjamin reddi debeat pro scelere, quod meretur: vel ut Hebræum habet: reddet ei secundum omnem turpitudinem, quam fecit in I srael. Sic 2. Paralip. 19, 2. Jehu Propheta dicit Josaphato: Iram Domini mereberis. Esther. 16, 18. Hamano reddidisse Deus dicitur, quod meruerat. Job. 6, 2. peccata sua iram meruisse dicit. Sic accipitur etiam Job. 11, 6. Deindè verò verbum hoc in alienum sensum, per vitiosam versionem latinam rapitur: ut Genes. 4, 13. Major est iniquitas mea, quàm ut veniam merear: ubi in Hebræo legitur: Major est iniquitas mea, quàm ut mihi parcatur, vel ut ego eam feram. Quæ vox est desperantis, ex qua, si lubet, Romanenses viam salutis per nos addiscere possunt. Sic Jos. 11, 20. de Hevæis dicitur: ut non mererentur clementiam: Ubi in Hebræo simpliciter sonat: ut non esset eis misericordia. Neque contrarium aliquod & evidens Scripturæ testimonium in hunc usque diem pro confirmanda sua significatione Jesuitæ proferre potuerunt, ita ut quoad Meriti vocabulum in hoc Articulo, prorsus destituantur omni Scripturæ Casonicæ autoritate.

Quoad Patres, concedimus, eos, vocabulo Meriti & merendi, tum in hoc, tum in præcedente Articulo frequenter admodum usos esse, sed sensum Pontificium ex ipsorum sermonibus elici posse, simpliciter negamus. Constat enim ex Scriptis ipsorum, planè generaliter, & secundum vulgarem, ac tum receptum linguæ suæ idiotismum, vocabulis istis ipsos usos esse: ita ut Mereri idem illis valeret, ac consequi: quemadmodum insignes ipsorum sententiæ attestantur.

Ambrosius certè lib. 1. de vocat gentium cap. 7. sic se explicat: Manifestum est, omne hominis bonum meritum, ab initio fidei, usq; ad perseverantiæ consummationem, donum atq; opus esse divinum.

Hieron. in cap. 64. Jesaiæ: Si nostra consideremus merita, desperandum est: si tuam autem clementiam, audemus preces fundere. Augustin. Epist. 46. Gratiam Dei secundum merita nostra dari omninò falsissimum est. Et lib. 50. homiliarum: Homilia 14. Cum coronat Deus merita tua, nihil coronat, nisi dona sua. Præfat. in Psal. 31. Si vis esse alienus à gratiâ, jacta tua merita. In Psal. 139. Meritis suis nihil tribuunt Sancti: Totum, non nisi misericordiæ tuæ tribuunt, ô Deus. Bernh. Serm. 61. in Cant. Cant. Meum meritum, miseratio Domini: Non planè sum inops meriti, quamdiu inops ille miserationum non fuerit. Serm. 68. Sufficit ad meritum scire, quod non sufficiant merita. Serm. 15. in Psal. 91. Hoc est totum hominis meritum, si totam spem suam ponat in eo, qui totum salvum facit.

Quartum & postremum argumentum præcipuè ex Epistola Jacobi sumunt Jesuvvitæ: ubi Apostolus inquit: Abraham pater noster nonne ex operibus justificatus est, offerens filium suum super altare &c.

Respondeo crassam committi ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχꙋ. Agit enim Apostolus non de consequenda, sed de demonstranda justitia: undè aliquoties dicit: Ostende mihi tuam fidem absque operibus tuis, & ego ostendam tibi ex operibus meis fidem meam: Ergo non de causis Justificationis, sed de ejusdem effectibus in oculos incurentibus agit Jacobus: & per consequens non disputat contra nos, qui cum Paulo gratuitam fidei justificationem absque operibus statuimus: sed contra eos, qui de fide gloriabantur sed vitæ morumque impietate testabantur, se destitui fide vera ac justificante. Deindè considerat Jacobus hominem non in conspectu Dei: sed hominum. 3. Agit cùm jam justificatis fide, non verò demum justificandis: ubi revera locum habet illud Augustini: Opera non præcedunt justificandum: sed sequuntur jam justificatum. Tandem Jacobus non agit de actu primo justificationis, qui consistit in sola gratuita imputatione justitiæ fidei: sed de actu secundo, qui in operum judicio consistit, & justificationis effectus, non verò causa est.

Quoad Exemplum Abrahami illud incommodè hoc loco adduci videtur, ita ut Veteres etiam vel hanc ipsam ob causam, Epistolam Jacobi inter scripta ἀντιλεγόμενα retulerint. Versus enim 21. quem citat Bellarminus, conciliari nequit cum historia Geneseos: Asserit Jacobus, Scripturam, quæ dicit, Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ipsi ad justitiam, v. 23. tùm demùm impletam esse, cùm Isaacum filium suum super altare offerre voluit: Jam verò Fides Abrahæ, quæ ipsi imputata est ad justitiam Genes. 15, 6. celebratur anno ætatis ejus 84. Isaac autem centesimo demùm natus, & ut circumstantiæ totius historiæ ostendunt, anno 115. Abrahæ oblatus est. Totis igitur triginta annis, Abraham per Fidem, promissioni de multiplicatione seminis sui adhibitam, ante justificatus est, quam Isaacum offerre voluit. Falsum proindè esse videtur, quòd autor Epistolæ Iacobeæ dicit, in immolatione demùm Isaaci Scripturam illam impletam esse, quæ dicit, Credidit Abraham Deo &c. Neqs ex ista difficultate se explicat Bellarminus, quando dicit, in quolibet actu fidei Abrahæ, impletum esse illud, Credidit Abraham Deo &c. Siquidem semper Fides ipsi fuerit imputata ad justitiam. Nam hoc non in Quæstione est, An ad quemlibet actum fidei, fides imputetur ad justitiam: sed hoc in controversiam venit: antùm Scriptura impleta fuerit, quæ dicit, Credidit Abraham Deo &c. quando voluerit immolare filium Isaac? ubi Jacobus affirmativam tenet: Scriptura autem Mosaica impletionem hanc Scripturæ non ad actum istum immolationis, sed ad fidem illam, qua Abraham credidit promissioni de Semine illo, in quo benedicenda omnes familiæ terræ, refert, Gen.15,6. Quod ipsum facit etiam Paulus Rom. 4, 18. asserens, Abrahamum credidisse in spem contra spem. Et hæc præcipua causa est propter quam Epistolam Jacobi B. Lutherus Stramineam videri asseruit, si nimirùm ad Epistolas Paulinas conferatur. Quam ipsam ob causam nos quoque in præsente disputatione, autoritate Epistolæ hujus constringi non patimur: licet ea causæ nostræ obesse non possit, modò scopus ipse attendatur, uti jam modò ostendimus.

Disputat porrò Bellarminus satis prolixè libro quinto integro de Iustificatione, & Justitiam propriorum meritorum sive operum nostrorum confirmare studet tùm ex Scripturis, tùm ex Antiquitate, tùm deniquè ex ratione. Cæterùm ut compendio quasi quodam tùm tempori consulamus, tùm prolixitati nimiæ modum statuamus, libet certas quasdam proponere regulas, quarum observatio viam pleraque omnia Jesuiticæ sophismata refutandi, satis certam monstrare possit.

I. Regula I. Status Controversiæ proprius ac legitimus semper probè considerandus est, ne vel alius nobis obtrudatur: vel alienis quæstionibus involvatur, quemadmodum Jesuitis hodiè per Sophisticam Ignorationis Elenchi contra hanc regulam peccare, nimis tritum & familiare est: ut quando subindè immiscet Quæstiones de necessitate bonorum operum, de dono regenerationis, Sanctificationis, & Renovationis, de præmijs bonorum post impetratam jam fidei justitiam.

II. Quia Vocabulum Gratiæ, Fidei, Iustitiæ, item Verbum Iustificare varias admittit significationes, semper danda est opera, ut evolvatur πολυσημασία, & Sophisticatio Figuræ dictionis vel ὁμωνυμίας, quæ in Jesuiticarum objectionibus notetur.
