III. Accuratè distinguendum inter dicta Scripturæ legalia, quæ justitiam quidem Operum urgent, sed eam hominum naturæ possibilem esse, minimè astruunt: & inter dicta Evangelica, quæ causas justificationis & salutis nostræ proprias & genuinas definiunt & explicant.

IV. Dicta Evangelica rursus non unius ejusdemq; sunt generis: Quædam enim, ut jam dictum, causas justificationis aperiunt; qualia sunt pleraque illa, quæ tùm in hoc, tùm in præcedente Articulo, ex Epistolis Paulinis pro gratuita justificatione fidei citavimus, Alia verò agunt de Effectibus, & signis veræ justificationis nostræ, qualia signa sunt Studium bonorum Operum, & Nova obedientia: ut quando Johannes dicit 1. cap. 3. 7. Qui justitiam facit, justus est: & nonnulli Sancti dicuntur ambulasse in omnibus mandatis & justificationibus Domini inculpatè. Ubi non ostenditur, quibus rebus justitia nondùm acquisita comparetur, sed quid jam comparata, in credentibus operetur: hoc est, non causa justitiæ exprimitur: sed signum tantùm ponitur, ex quo de certitudine justitiæ judicium fieret.

V. Quædam dicta sunt accommodata ad certas personas eorum, qui ex Lege & Operibus justitiam quærebant, quibus respondet Scriptura: Fac hoc & vives: vel, Quomodo legis in Mose? Undè tamen generalis regula ad causas Justificationis nostræ, extrui neque potest neque debet.

VI. Dicta Scripturæ de præmijs & mercede bonorum operum, vel absolutè intelliguntur, quatenùs nimirùm judicium legis in illis proponitur, & voluntatis divinæ exquisita justitia: sed tùm semper annexa est conditio observationis, Quifecerit ea, vivet in eis: Quam tamen conditionem impossibilem esse, tùm ipsa Scriptura, tùm nostra conscientia apertè testatur: Vel intelliguntur secundum quid, nempè in certo subjecto, hoc est, in persona renatorum & credentium. Quo posteriore respectu, tria semper notanda veniunt: 1. Mercedem, quæ fidelibus promittitur, non ex operis ipsius sive perfectione, sive merito, sed ex Dei compensantis gratia ac liberalitate provenire. 2. Personam non placere Deo propter opus ipsum: sed opus propter personam fide Deo reconciliatam. 3. In compensandis bonis operibus, Deum non agere cum renatis, secundum rigorem legis: sic enim nullum opus, quantumvis bonum, in renatis retributionem consequeretur: siquidem quodvis naturâ suâ imperfectum, debitum & sordidum est.

VII. Probè observandum, quâ fide, vel potiùs quâ perfidiâ Romanenses allegare soleant Scripturæ dicta. Interdum enim vitiosam proferunt versionem, quæ secundum fontes Hebræos & Græcos corrigenda est: vel addunt noh addenda, Vel omittunt non omittenda: Vel alienam sententiam verbis Scripturæ affingunt.

VIII. Et postrema Regula potest esse hæc, Quod Romanenses ex libris Apocryphis multa pro errore suo stabiliendo proferre solent, de quibus verissimum est illud Hieronymi judicium, quod Ecclesia hujusmodi libros legat, non ad autoritatem Ecclesiasticorum dogmatum confirmandam: sed tantùm ad ædificationem plebis. Hieron. præfat. in libros Salomonis.


### Appendix, On the sins of the regenerated, and which sort and in what way they are in them

Since our Author adds the decision of this question also to the Article concerning good Works, it was necessary to explain in a few words what is to be determined concerning it. This question arises from the preceding matters. For because it is established from what has already been said that the obedience of the regenerate is imperfect in this world, on account of the remnants of sins: It is asked: what and of what kind are those sins? We answer with our Author, that they are not sins or lapses against the conscience: The reason is: 1. because sins of this kind expel the Holy Spirit: they shake off faith and the grace of God. 2. The righteousness of the regenerate is joined with a good conscience: 1 Tim. 1:5. The sum of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned, and verse 18. Wage the good warfare, having faith and a good conscience. 1 Pet. 3:16. Have a good conscience, 1 John 3:21. If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God.

Moreover, there remain in the Regenerate from the class of sins. 1. Original corruption, and that root of actual sins, concupiscence, which the Apostle calls indwelling sin, and evil lying near. Rom. 7:17 and 21. Then, depraved motions, or vicious affections of the flesh, which always lusts against the Spirit, Gal. 5:17. Thirdly, sins of omission. Fourthly, errors in vocations, which frequently creep upon the incautious: yet so that by these sins neither is the conscience harmed: nor is faith, or the Holy Spirit, and with these, the righteousness and grace of God lost.

But furthermore it is asked, How do these sins remain in the regenerate? I answer that they remain in this way, not that they are cherished, or that the pious take delight in them: but 1. under groans and sighs of burning displeasure. Rom. 7:24. Wretched man that I am: who will deliver me from the body of this death. 2. Under battle and struggle, indeed a perpetual agony as it were of the Spirit, Gal. 5:17. The flesh lusts against the Spirit: but the Spirit against the flesh: for these are contrary to one another. 3. Under the assiduous mortification of the actions of the flesh. Rom. 8:13. If by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you will live. Finally, under the unceasing imploration of heavenly aid: as David can especially be an example to us in the Psalms.

Latin:

CUm Autor noster, hujus etiam quæstionis decisionem adjicias Articulo de bonis Operibus, paucis, quid de ea statuendum sit, expediendum fuerit. Resultat autem hæc quæstio ex superioribus. Quia enim obedientiam renatorum constat ex jam dictis esse imperfectam, in hoc mundo, propter reliquias peccatorum: Quæritur: quanam & qualia illa sint peccata? Respondemus cum Autore nostro, ea non esse peccata aut lapsus contra conscientiam: Ratio est: 1. quia peccata ejusmodi expellunt Spiritum Sanctum: excutiunt fidem & Gratiam Dei. 2. Justitia renatorum conjuncta est cum bona conscientia: 1. Tim. 1, 5. Summa mandati est dilectio ex corde puro, conscientia bona, & fide non ficta, & vers. 18. Milita bonam militiam, habens fidem & bonam conscientiam. 1. Pet. 3, 16. Conscientiam habete bonam, 1. Joh. 3, 21. Si cor nostrum non condemnat nos, fiduciam habemus apud Deum.

Cæterùm remanent in Renatis ex peccatorum genere. 1. Originalis lues, & radix illa peccatorum actualium, concupiscentia, quam Apostolus inhabitans peccatum, & malum adjacens appellat. Rom. 7, 17. & 21. Deindè, pravi motus, sive vitiosi affectus carnis, quæ semper concupiscit adversus Spiritum Gal. 5, v. 17. Tertiò, delicta omissionis. Quartò errata in vocationibus, quæ incautis subindè plurima obrepunt: ita tamen, ut ne peccatis istis vel lædatur conscientia: vel fides, aut Spiritus Sanctus, & cum his, justitia & gratia Dei amittatur.

Sed porrò quæritur, Quomodo in renatis ista peccata maneant? Respondeo sic ea manere, non quod foveantur, aut pij istis condelectentur: sed 1. sub gemitu & suspirijs displicentiæ ardentibus. Rom. 7, 28. Miser ego homo: quis me eripiet de corpore mortis hujus. 2. Sub pugna & lucta, imò perpetuo quasi Spiritus agone, Gal. 5, 17. Caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum: Spiritus autem adversus carnem: hæc enim sibi invicem adversantur. 3. Sub mortificatione assidua actionum carnis. Rom. 8, 13. Si Spiritu opera carnis mortificaveritis, vivetis. Tandem sub imploratione indefinente cœlestis auxilij: uti cumprimis exemplo nobis esse potest David in Psalmis.


## 17 On the Distinction of the Old and New Testament

Our Author pursues this Article quite prolixly, having settled four questions primarily, the first of which argues that the doctrine of the Church of all times has been one and the same, ever since the Creation of man, and the published Evangelical promise, after the fall of our first parents: that is, ever since the beginnings of the Church of the Old Testament: but that that doctrine is of two kinds: one, namely, of the Law, the other, however, of the Gospel. The second explains, What properly is and is called the Old Testament, namely the promulgation of the law, or the covenant, by which the people of Israel were bound to the Law, and to this form of polity for this end, that in this polity the promise concerning the coming Messiah might be preserved and propagated, on account of which also the true Church of the Elect was in this people. The third proposes the Definition of the New Testament, that it is nothing else than the preaching of the remission of sins, and the donation of eternal life, and of new righteousness, with sin deleted, and death deleted, on account of Christ the Mediator. The fourth finally and lastly examines in some way the distinction of the Old and New Testament, which our Author seeks from there primarily, that the Old is abrogated, with the Levitical ceremonies.

Although indeed this whole Philippean Treatment in its own kind, and, if you consider the state of the Church of former times, can easily be admitted and tolerated, although we cannot approve the Philippean definition of both Testaments in all respects, as will evidently appear from the subsequent exposition: but if, however, you examine more accurately the Controversies of this our age, and consider more carefully whom, and how gross errors, the Sacramentarians, Jesuits, Anabaptists, and Schwenkfeldians cherish today concerning this very Article: it will spontaneously appear that it cannot be held against us as a fault, if on this occasion also, departing a little from the footsteps of Philip, we have greater care and regard for the controversies of our own time.

We therefore divide the whole exposition of this Article into two general chapters: the former of which, the positive, will investigate more accurately both the Nature and Definition of both Testaments: and will make plain in what matters the distinction of the Old and New Testament can, indeed ought to be, established according to the Scriptures.

The latter, the antithetical, will more diligently examine and refute the various errors, both ancient and more recent, of the Sacramentarians, and especially of the Jesuits.

But before we make an approach to the actual treatment of these chapters, certain general matters concerning the words Testament, Covenant, pact, and concerning the kinship and discrepancy of the same: and furthermore concerning the very polysemy of the word Testament, seem to be premised: lest a confusion of these should produce either difficulty or some error.

Initiò igitur Testamentum secundum communem loquendi consuetudinem, &

Latin:

PRolixè satis l Articulum hunc persequitur Autor noster, quatuor potissimùm expeditis quæstio nibus, quarum prima disputat, Unam eandemq; fuisse doctrinam Ecclesiæ omnium temporum, jam indè à Creatione hominis, & edita promissione Evangelica, post lapsum proto-parentum nostrorum: hoc est, jam indè à primordijs Ecclesiæ Veteris Testamenti: Doctrinam verò illam duûm esse generum: Aliam nimirùm Legis, aliam verò Evangelij. Altera explicat, Quid propriè sit & dicatur Vetus Testamentum, nempè promulgatio legis, sive pactum, quo populus Israel ad Legem, & hanc formam politiæ obligatus erat ad hunc finem, ut in hac politia conservaretur & propagaretur promissio de venturo Messia', propter quam & in hoc populo erat vera Electorum Ecclesia. Tertia proponit Definitionem Novi Testamenti, quòd illud nihil sit aliud, quàm prædicatio remissionis peccatorum, & donatio vitæ æternæ, ac novæ justitiæ, deleto peccato, & deleta morte, propter Christum Mediatorem. Quarta denique ac postrema expendit aliquo modo discrimen Veteris & Novi Testamenti, quod exindè præcipuè petit Autor noster, quòd Vetus est abrogatum, cum ceremonijs Leviticis.

Quanquàm verò tota hæc Tractatio Philippéa in suo genere, &, si statum Ecclesiæ superiorum temporum consideres, facilè admitti & tolerari potest, licèt utriusque Testamenti definitionem Philippéam per omnia approbare non possimus, uti ex subsequente diexodo evidenter patebit: quod si tamen Controversias nostri hujus seculi, accuratiùs expendas, & quos, quamque crassos errores, circa hunc ipsum Articulum hodiè foveant Sacramentarij, Jesuvitæ, Anabaptistæ, Schvvenck feldiani, pensiculatiùs consideres: ultrò patebit, vitio nobis verti haud posse, si hac etiam vice, à vestigijs Philippi paulisper secedentes, potiorem controversiarum nostritemporis, curam rationemque habeamus.

Partimur proindè totam Articuli hujus diexodon in duo capita generalia: quorum prius θετικόν tùm Naturam ac Definitionem utriusque Testamenti accuratiùs investigabit: tùm verò quibus in rebus discrimen Veteris & Novi Testamenti secundum Scripturas constitui possit, imò debeat, planum faciet.

Posterius α̉ντιθετικόν varios errores, tùm Veteres, tùm recentiores Sacramentariorum, cum primis & Jesuvvitarum diligentiùs expendet & refutabit.

Priusquàm verò ad ipsam capitum istorum tractationem accessum faciamus, generalia quædam de vocabulis Testamenti, Fæderis, pacti, de que eorundem cognatione ac discrepantia: quin etiam de ipsa πολυσημασίᾳ vocabuli Testamenti, præmittenda videtur: ne istorum confusio vel difficultatem vel errorem aliquem pariat.

Initiò igitur Testamentum secundum communem loquendi consuetudinem, &


### On the Vocabularies of Covenant and Pact

According to the doctrine of the jurists, a disposition is called a matter left behind, lawfully declared either by words or consigned to tablets: whence they call one nuncupative, the other written: or a Testament is a disposition concerning the final will of one about to die, by which he distributes his goods among heirs: Or it is the expression of our will concerning that which one wishes to be done after his death. l. 1. ff. de verborum & rerum significationibus.

Covenants, which the Greeks call συνθήκας, as defined by Suidas and others, are a natural obligation by which dissenting parties agree upon certain conditions to be mutually performed concerning alliance, commerce, peace, truces, and other things of that kind.

Now these were made either by words conceived in a certain form according to the will and consent of the contracting parties: and recorded in tablets, and confirmed on both sides by the seals of the contracting parties: Or they were made by deeds, such as victims, the custom of slaughtering which, in the ratifying of covenants, once obtained even among the Israelite people: as one may read in Gen. 15, 9. Jerem. 34, 18. And Cyril is a witness, in his book against Julian, that the ancients observed this custom in entering into covenants, that they would divide either a bull or a calf, and pass through the divided parts; imprecating such things upon themselves: Unless I keep the covenant, may I myself be thus divided: Or they were made by hands, or right hands, by the joining of which they stipulated that faith should be religiously kept: or finally they were made by hostages given on both sides. And among historians, covenants of this kind were understood as warlike pacts, ratified either before or after a battle was joined: whence the Greeks also divided a covenant into an offensive alliance (ἐπιμαχίαν) and a defensive alliance (συμμαχίαν).

A pact is commonly said and called a promise or consent of two or more concerning any matter whatsoever, either to be given or to be done, conceived in express words.

These three terms are by some taken indifferently and as equivalent, especially by the Sacramentarians, for whom it is very solemn and familiar, as often as the two Testaments of the Church are discussed, to use the terms not of Testaments, but of covenants and pacts: not without a notable stratagem, by which they easily impose upon the more imprudent, so that they allow themselves to be persuaded that, just as there is only one covenant of grace which God has entered into with us concerning our salvation: so also each Testament is to be properly defined by this very covenant of grace, and consequently that the substance of both Testaments is one and the same: the mode of dispensation only being different and diverse on each side. Which single error arises from the confusion of these terms, and begets many other errors in our Theology, sufficiently gross and intolerable: as will be evident from the discourse itself.

Although indeed we cannot deny that the Hebrew word בְרִית is general, and to Greek and Latin interpreters sounds indiscriminately the same as Testament, Covenant, and pact: just as indeed, according to Jerome, Aquila, the most ancient interpreter of the Hebrew Bibles, rendered it by the Greek συνθήκην, but the LXX interpreters, and the Apostles who followed them, by διαθήκην: even though there is also a great kinship among these three terms, especially if you consider the nature of the disposition and dispensation, which is wont to be conceived as articulated in all of them: yet if you weigh more accurately the proper nature of each, and its as it were peculiar property, and indeed their twin requirements: it will readily be evident that a great difference exists between them.

For first, every testament does not acquire its force unless the death of the testator intervenes: according to that of the Epistle to the Hebrews 9, 16. Where there is a testament, it is necessary that the death of the testator intervene: for a testament is confirmed in the dead: otherwise it is not yet valid, while he who has testified is still alive.

But pacts and covenants among men are not so confirmed by the death of the contracting parties: rather they are immediately dissolved as soon as even one party of the contractors dies: unless perhaps by the will and consent of the contracting parties, the heirs and all descendants are also bound and obligated by the same federal right: which we know to have been observed in the Peace of Religion, or the Transaction of Passau, by all the orders of the Roman Empire.

Then, in treaties and covenants, a confirmation is accustomed to be made by a religious oath sworn on both sides: so that just as in other cases an oath is the end of all controversy, so the same oath secures firm strength for all agreements, treaties, and transactions, as the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 6, verse 16, teaches. Yet in a testamentary action, no sane person ever demands an oath from a testator.

Finally, all covenants consist of a certain natural obligation, where there is a certain proportion and analogy between the contracting parties. But to invent such a thing between God and men, Creator and creatures, would be too discordant and blasphemous.

We conclude, therefore, that a testament and a covenant in the Church of God are two very different things, and differ by their very definition: provided that you view each of these according to its own proper nature and essence, as certainly it ought to be viewed in this place.

However, if you take the word testament in a broad sense, generally and improperly, then we do not at all deny that it can be referred to the covenant sanctioned by God with men, in some way and respect; provided it is conceded that this is done improperly. For we ourselves know, and readily grant, that God entered into such a covenant with His people, which also obtains some respect of a testament. For 1. The people of God, on account of this covenant, are adorned in the Scriptures with the title of sons, because of those reciprocal conditions of the pacts, of which we shall speak shortly. 2. The goods which were promised to that people from this covenant receive the name of inheritance in the Holy Scriptures. But we cannot be heirs intestate: since by nature we are children of wrath. Eph. 2. Therefore, by testament. 3. That eternal covenant of God was confirmed in no other way than by the destination and intervention of the death of CHRIST. These three respects being observed, we do not indeed deny

That this divine covenant, which God struck with His people, can also be called the Testament of God, since it is a certain attestation of the divine will; and indeed one that is purely donative; but that the word Testament is taken in a somewhat more general and less proper sense, will be most evidently clear from those things which we shall discuss in chapter 1 concerning the nature of both Testaments. And this is indeed the first equivocation of the word Testament, which is sometimes, but improperly and outside the present Disputation concerning the distinction of both Testaments, taken for the Covenant of God itself. Furthermore, this very word Testament is accommodated still much more generally even to those three requirements which concur in every covenant between God and Man. THE FIRST is: The divine promise, and that purely gratuitous with respect to men: so that no natural covenant, but only a Covenant of Grace can consist between God and Men. The second is, the reciprocal Obedience of Faith, by which the promises are firmly believed by men, and by which, according to the due pact, one lives piously, justly, and soberly, Tit. 2, 12. The third is, an external sign or instrument, or the testimony of the tables. Now if we consult the Scriptures, it becomes plain that all these three requirements, even when placed separately, are named בְּרִית, διαθήκην, Testament. The Apostle certainly, Gal. 3, 17, expressly calls the divine promise made to Abraham a Testament. Thus David, Psalm 77, 10, names that reciprocal obedience of faith a Testament: saying, They did not keep the Testament of God: and refused to walk in his law. Thus, finally, Stephen the protomartyr names the external sign of the New Testament a Testament: saying, He gave them the Testament of Circumcision. Acts 7, 8. Thus the federal tables themselves, that is, the Prophetic and Apostolic books, are likewise named a Testament: and indeed on account of the difference of time, the Old and New Testament. Hence the reading of the books of Moses is indicated by the Apostle as the reading of the Old Testament: 2 Cor. 3, 14. Hence the Apostles are said to be constituted ministers of the New Testament: 2 Cor. 3, 6.

sidered. This one distinction being observed, it is clearly evident that the Calvinists, as often as they define the word Testament by the nature of the Covenant in the present disputation, are shamefully deceived and deceive others under the sophism of Equivocation.

Then, that we may press our Adversaries more strongly, it pleases us to argue thus from the very nature and, as it were, the proper affection of the divine Covenant.

The Covenant of God, which He struck with His people, is nothing other than the promise of Grace, offering and applying the remission of sins, salvation, and eternal life to all through and on account of the Messiah who was then to come, but now has been exhibited, and in both cases apprehended by true faith: with the restipulation of obedience and gratitude to be rendered to God by men.

And yet this Covenant of God, from the very first times of the world's creation, is one and the same in number, is perpetual, eternal, and immutable, according to all its Essential parts: which, as they do not admit of abrogation and innovation, or mutability, so also they do not admit of the reasons of Oldness and Newness, nay, they cannot even admit them in any way, because the reason of eternal Salvation was, is still, and will be in all coming ages, one in number and the same: and consequently the Substance of this Covenant is also one and the same, always like itself.

Now, however, Holy Scripture in many places not only makes express mention of two Testaments, but also names one the Old, and the other the New; nay, it expressly confesses that the former Old one has been antiquated; but that the New was begun and confirmed only at the advent of Christ. Therefore, even from this, it is irrefragably evinced that these two Testaments can neither be nor ought to be properly defined by that eternal Covenant of God, of which we have already treated. Moreover, it is elicited from this that we are dealing in this place with such Testaments as are not the Covenant of Grace itself: but which, under one and the same reason of the divine Covenant in number and substance, receive some diversity, and indeed an Essential one, and from thence derive their proper reason of Oldness and Newness.

But whence this very diversity of both Testaments arises, and how it can and ought to be defined, the following digression will now expressly show.

It is therefore evident from what has already been said that there is a polysemy or multiple signification of the word Testament: which is sometimes taken for the Covenant itself: or also for its requirements, even when considered separately.

Latin:

JCtorum doctrinam dicitur dispositio de rebus relictis, legitimè vel verbis nuncupata, vel tabulis consignata: Undè aliud nuncupativum, aliud scriptum appellant: vel Testamentum est dispositio de extrema morituri voluntate, quâ bona sua inter heredes dispensat: Vel est voluntatis nostræ sententia de eo, quod quis post mortem suam fieri velit. l. 1. ff. de verborum & rerum significationibus.

Fœdera Græcis συνθήκας Definiente Suida & alijs, sunt naturalis obligatio, quâ partes dissidentes certis conditionibus mutuò præstandis conveniunt de societate, de commercijs, de pace, de inducijs, deq́; id genus rebus alijs.

Fiebant autem hæc vel verbis pro voluntate & consensu paciscentium certâ formâ conceptis: inque tabulas relatis, & sigillis paciscentium utrinque confirmatis: Vel fiebant factis, ut victimis, quárum cædendarum consuetudo, in sanciendis fœderibus, etiam in populo Jsraelitico olim obtinebat: uti legere licet Gen. 15, 9. Jerem. 34, 18. Et testis est Cyrillus lib. contra Julianum, veteres inferiendis fœderibus, morem hunc observasse, ut vel taurum, vel vitulum dividerent, & per partes divisas medij transirent; talia sibi imprecati: Nisi fœdus serváro, ipse sic dividar: Vel fiebant manibus, sive dextris, quibus invicem junctis, de fide religiosè servandâ, stipulabantur: vel denique fiebant obsidibus utrinque datis. Et apud historicos fœdera hujusmodi intelligebantur de pactis bellicis, vel ante, vel post commissum prælium sancitis: undè Fœdus etiam Græci dividebant in ἐπιμαχίαν & συμμαχίαν.

Pactum vulgò est ac dicitur promissio sive consensus duorum aut plurium de re quacunque vel dandâ vel faciendâ, expressis verbis conceptus.

Tria hæc vocabula à nonnullis indifferenter & pro æquipollentibus accipiuntur, cumprimis à Sacramentarijs, quibus solenne admodum & familiare est, quoties de duobus Testamentis Ecclesiæ agitur, non Testamentorum, sed fœderum & pactorum uti terminis: non sine insigni Stratagemate, quo imprudentioribus facilè imponunt, ut persuaderi sibi patiantur, quemadmodum unum tantum est fœdus gratiæ, quod Deus de salute nostra nobiscum inijt: Ita utrumque etiam Testamentum, propriè definiendum esse, per hoc ipsum fœdus gratiæ, & per consequens Unam eandemque esse utriusque Testamenti Substantiam: modum tantùm dispensationis utrinque alium & diversum. Qui vel unus error ex confusione istorum vocabulorum oritur, & pluros alios in Theologia nostrâ parit errores, satis crassos & intolerabiles: uti ex ipsa dixeodo patebit.

Quanquàm verò negare non possumus, vocabulum Hebræum בְרִית esse generale, & Græcis ac Latinis interpretibus promiscuè idem sonare, ac Testamentum, Fœdus, & pactum: quemadmodum sanè Hieronymo teste, Aquilas Bibliorum Hebræorum interpres antiquißimus, per Græcum συνθήκην, LXX. verò interpretes, & hos secuti Apostoli per διαθήκην reddiderunt: etsi quoque trium istorum vocabulorum, magna est cognatio, præsertim si dispositionis & dispensarionis rationem consideres, quæ in omnibus istis articulata solet concipi: quod si tamen propriam cujuslibet naturam, & ἴδιον quasi κτῆμα, quin & gemina eorum requisita accuratiùs expendas: magnam illis invicem diversitatem intercedere, ultrò patebit.

Primùm enim omne Testamentum vim suam non acquirit, nisi interveniente morte testatoris: secundum illud Epistolæ ad Hebr. 9, 16. Vbi est Testamentum, mors testatoris interveniat necesse est: Testamentum enim in mortuis confirmatum est: alioqui nondum valet, dùm adhuc vivit, qui testatus est.

Atqui pacta & fœdera inter homines usque adeò morte paciscentium non confirmantur: ut potiùs statim solvantur, quamprimùm vel una tantùm pars contrahentium, moritur: nisi fortè de voluntate & consensu, paciscentium, hæredes etiam & universi posteri, eodem jure fœderali constringantur & obligentur: id quod in pace Religionis, sive Transactione Passaviensi, ab universis Imperij Romani ordinibus, observatum fuisse novimus.

Deinde in fœderibus & pactis religioso juramento utrinque præstito, fieri consuevit Confirmatio: ita ut quemadmodum aliàs jusjurandum finis est omnis controversiæ: sic idem omnibus etiam pactis, fœderibus, transactionibus robur firmum conciliet, sic docente Epistola ad Hebr. cap 6, 16. Atqui in Testamentaria actione nemo sanus à Testatore Juramentum unquám exigit.

Tandem Fœdera omnia constant naturali quadam obligatione, ubi inter paciscentes est quædam proportio & analogia. Talem verò inter Deum & homines, Creatorem & creaturas comminisci, nimis foret absonum & blasphemum.

Concludimus proindè Testamentum & Fœdus in Ecclesia Dei esse duo diversissima, & ipsâ definitione differentia: Si modò quodlibet istorum secundum propriam suam naturam & Essentiam spectes, uti certè hoc loco spectari debet.

Cæterùm si vocem Testamenti ἐν πλάτει generaliter & impropriè accipias, tùm ad Fœdus etiam Dei cum hominibus sancitum, aliquo modo ac respectu, referri illud posse, minimè negamus; modò impropriè illud fieri concedatur. Novimus enim ipsi, & ultrò largimur, Deum tale fœdus cum populo suo inijsse, quod aliquem etiam Testamenti respectum obtinet. Nam 1. Populus Dei, propter hoc fœdus, filiorum elogio in scripturis exornatur, propter reciprocas illas pactorum conditiones, de quibus paulò post. 2. Bona, quæ ex fœdere hoc populo isti sunt promissa, Hæreditatis appellationem in Sacris sortiuntur. Hæredes autem non possumus esse ab intestato: Siquidem natura sumus filij iræ. Eph. 2. Ergò ex Testamento. 3. Fœdus illud Dei æternum non aliter confirmatum erat, quàm destinatione & interventu mortis CHRISTI. Tribus istis respectibus observatis, non negamus quidem

Fœdus hôc divinum, quod Deus cum populo suo pepigit, Testamentum etiam Dei appellari posse, quippè in quo voluntatis divinæ testatio quædam; & quidem merè donativa existit; verum Testamenti vocabulum generaliùs quodammodo & minùs propriè accipi, evidentissimè patebit ex ijs, quæ de natura utriusque Testamenti cap. 1. disputabimus. Et hæc quidem prima est æquivocatio vocabuli Testamenti. quod interdum, sed impropriè & extra præsentem Disputationem de discrimine utriusque Testamenti, pro ipso Fœdere Dei accipitur. Porrò hæc ipsa vox Testamenti multò adhuc generalius accommodatur etiam ad tria illa requisita, quæ in omni fœdere inter Deum & Hominem concurrunt. PRIMUM est: Promissio divina, eaque merè gratuita respectu hominum: ita ut nullum Fœdus naturale, sed tantùm Fœdus Gratiæ inter Deum & Homines possit consistere. Alterum est, Fidei reciproca Obedientia, quâ ab hominibus promissionibus firmiter creditur, & ex pacto debito, piè, justè, & sobriè vivitur, Tit. 2, 12. Tertium est, externum vel signum vel instrumentum, seu testimonium tabularum. Jam si Scripturas consulamus, planum fit, omnia hæc tria requisita, etiam seorsim posita nominari בְּרִית, διαθήκην, Testamentum. Apostolus certè Gal. 3, 17. promissionem divinam Abrahæ factam, disertè appellat Testamentum. Sic David Psal. 77, 10. reciprocam illam fidei obedientiam nominat Testamentum: Non in quiens, custodierunt Testamentum Dei: & in lege ejus noluerunt ambulare. Sic denique Stephanus protomartyr Novi Testamenti, Signum externum nominat Testamentum: Dedit, inquiens, illis Testamentum Circumcisionis. Actor. 7, 8. Sic tabulæ ipsæ fœderales, hoc est, libri Prophetici & Apostolici, itidem nominantur Testamentum: & quidem propter discrimen temporis, Testamentum Vetus & Novum. Hinc lectio librorum Mosis, indigitatur ab Apostolo lectio Veteris Testamenti: 2. Cor. 3, 14. Hinc Apostoli dicuntur constituti ministri Novi Testamenti: 2. Cor. 3, 6.

siderata. Quâ unâ distinctione observatâ, patet luculenter, Calvinianos, quoties in præsenti disputatione, Testamenti vocabulum, per naturam Fœderis definiunt, turpiter decipi & decipere sub sophismate Aequivocationis.

Deindè, ut fortiùs premamus Adversarios, fic lubet ex ipsâ Fœderis divini naturâ & propriâ quasi affectione sic argumentari.

Fœdus Dei, quod cum populo suo pepigit, nihil est aliud, quàm promissio Gratiæ, offerens & applicans remissionem peccatorum, salutem & vitam æternam omnibus per & propter Messiam tùm venturum, jam verò exhibitum, utrobique autem verâ fide apprehensum: cum restipulatione obedientiæ & gratitudinis ab hominibus Deo præstandæ.

Atqui hoc Fœdus Dei jam indè à primis conditi mundi temporibus, est numero unum atque idem, est perpetuum, æternum & immutabile, secundum omnes suas partes Essentiales: quæ uti abrogationis & innovationis, sive mutabilitatis: ita quoque Vetustatis & Novitatis rationes non admittunt, imò ne quidem admittere ullo modo possunt, propterea, quòd una numero, eademque fuit semper, estque etiamnùm, & futura est seculis venturis omnibus, Salutis æternæ ratio: ac proindè una etiam eademque Fœderis hujus Substantia, sibi semper similis.

Jam verò Scriptura Sacra multis in locis non modò duorum Testamentorum expressam facit mentionem, sed & unum nominat Vetus, alterum verò Novum; imò Vetus illud antiquatum; Novum autem sub Christi demùm adventu inchoatum confirmatumque esse, disertè fatetur. Ergò vel hinc irrefragabiliter ecvincitur, duo hæc Testamenta, per æternum illud Fœdus Dei, de quo jam egimus, propriè definiri nec posse nec debere. Quin & illud indè elicitur, de ejusmodi Testamentis hoc loco agi, quæ non sint Fœdus ipsum Gratiæ: sed quæ sub unâ numero, & per substantiam eâdem Fœderis divini ratione, diversitatem aliquam, & quidem Essentialem recipiant, ac exindè Vetustatis & Novitatis rationem propriam sortiantur.

Undè verò hæc ipsa Utriusque Testamenti diversitas, & quomodo definiri possit ac debeat, insequens diexodus jam ex professo ostendet.

Patet proindè ex jam dictis πολυσημασίας sive multiplex fignificatio vocabuli Testamenti: quod vel pro Fœdere ipso interdum sumitur: vel etiam pro ejusdem requisitis, etiam seorsim consideratis.


### On the Vocabularies of Covenant and Pact: Chapter I Θετικον

CHAPTER I.

ΘΕΤΙΚΟΝ.

Moreover, none of those meanings, regarding the present discussion on the distinction between the Old and New Testament, can or ought to be referred to, strictly speaking. For first, these two Testaments are not considered in this place insofar as they have any kinship to the Covenant of God entered into with us concerning our salvation: or even insofar as the designation of Testament is attributed in the Scriptures loosely, and as it were καταχρηστικῶς, both to the Covenant itself and to the federal requirements: but insofar as these two Testaments, opposed to one another ἀντιδιῃρημένως, obtain diverse and specifically different natures and definitions: and indeed not σχετικῶς, or relatively to another: but ὀσιωδῶς essentially, and in themselves and by themselves. We divide this chapter into two Questions: the former of which will elicit from the Scriptures and most plainly explain the very nature, essence, and definition of both Testaments: the latter, however, will reveal the true and essential distinctions of the same Testaments, and will confirm them from the Scriptures.

Latin:

CAPUT I.

ΘΕΤΙΚΟΝ.

Cæterùm nulla istarum significationum, ad præsentem disputationem de discrimine Veteris & Novi Testamenti, propriè loquendo, referri potest aut debet. Primùm enim duo hæc Testamenta hoc loco non considerantur, quatenùs ad Fœdus Dei, de salute nostra nobiscum initum, aliquam cognationem habent: vel etiam quatenùs laxè, & quasi καταχρηστικῶς tùm Fœderi ipsi, tùm requisitis fœderalibus in Scripturis appellatio Testamenti tribuitur: sed quatenùs duo hæc Testamenta, sibi invicem ἀντιδιῃρημένως opposita, diversas ac specie differentes naturas ac definitiones fortiuntur: & quidem non σχετικῶς, sive respectivè ad aliud: sed ὀσιωδῶς Essentialiter, ac in se & per se conPArtimur hoc caput in duas Quæstiones: quarum prior ipsam naturam, Essentiam ac Definitionem utriusque Testamenti ex Scripturis eruet, & planissimè explicabit: Posterior verò eorundem Testamentorum discrimina vera ac Essentialia aperiet, & ex Scripturis confirmabit.


### On the Definition of the Testament. Question I. on the Nature, Essence, and definition of the Two Testaments

ON THE NATURE, ESSENCE and definition of both Testaments.

That there are two distinct Testaments, and indeed diverse ones by the ordinance of GOD Himself, can be clearly demonstrated from the Scriptures: as in Jeremiah 31:31. Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah, a NEW Covenant: NOT according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. Thus Christ Himself, as if about to expedite this promised New Testament and its sealing and consummation, says in the institution of the Eucharist: This is my Blood of the New Testament, Matthew 26:28, Mark 14:24. Or as Luke has it, chapter 22:20, and Paul, 1 Corinthians 11:25: This cup is the New Testament in MY Blood. Thus the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 3:6, asserts that Christ made the Apostles ministers of the New Testament, by this assertion surely expressing not obscurely the negation or abrogation of the Old Testament, and Galatians 4:24. He says that these two diverse Testaments were prefigured in the wives of Abraham: the one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating unto bondage; the other, however, from Mount Sion, asserting unto liberty.

Thus the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews has woven together a commentary, as it were, on the nature and essence of both Testaments: having made an opposition between the former or first, that is, that Old one, and between the latter or other, that is, this New Testament: constituting Moses the mediator of the Old, but Christ the mediator of the New, and indeed of a BETTER Testament: chapter 7:22, chapter 8:6, chapter 9:15, chapter 12:24. Nay, this very BETTER Testament, he later, chapter 10:28, calls κατ' ἐξοχὴν nakedly and simply: and indeed by reason of its excellence, ETERNAL, chapter 13:20. Whence it is easy to gather that two distinct, nay, diverse Testaments can be elicited. For where there is a former and a latter: where there is also a good and a better: where finally an end and an eternity are given: there simple Unity cannot have a place: For nothing admits these diverse degrees of comparison with respect to itself: But these always necessarily exist in at least two.

These things being thus presupposed, it is infallibly evinced: that the Old and New Testaments are rightly constituted as two diverse things: not only as to Number: but also as to excellence; not only in name, but also as to Substance.

But here a Question soon arises: Whence can and ought the Nature, or Essence, or proper affection, as it were, of any Testament to be derived? In which Question, since most writers labor under some confusion, and join together things that ought to be properly distinguished, and make one mixed thing out of two corrupt ones: whence no small difficulty also befalls the Question: we, in order to explain the matter most clearly, will proceed κατ' ἄρσιν to θέσιν, intending to descend from the removal of false modes to the position of the true.

In the beginning, therefore, we remove that mode which seeks the nature and condition of both Testaments from the division of the Biblical books: defining the Old indeed by the books of Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets: the New, however, by the books of the Evangelists and Apostles. The vanity of this error is evident even from this, that both these and those books extend more widely than to be able to be referred to only one Testament: Nay, rather, the new lies hidden in those: but in these, the Complement of the Old is handed down: as Augustine speaks somewhere.

Then the Nature of both Testaments is most viciously sought from the doctrine itself of the Law and the Gospel. For neither in itself and by itself can obtain the reason of Oldness or Newness: Since the will of God is eternal and immutable, revealed as much in the Law as in the Gospel concerning the business of our salvation: and it is so far from the case that the doctrine of the Law is today antiquated, that salvation and eternal life can be obtained by no mortal without the perfect fulfillment of the Law, and that either one's own, or another's imputed. Therefore, to the doctrine of the Law, as to the Old Testament, antiquation or abrogation cannot be attributed: and consequently, the doctrine of the Law, considered in itself and by itself, cannot or ought not to be defined by the Old Testament, provided we wish to speak properly.

Thirdly, one must not judge of the proper nature and affection of both Testaments from that twin tradition of the Law: of which one was ruder before Moses, and not yet expressed and comprehended by certain laws: the other, however, was more polished and perfect after the doctrine of the whole Law had already been promulgated divinely. Which error surely falls of its own accord: for the reason of Oldness, which, as Scripture testifies, has abrogation as its companion, regards and defines not only the mode of the thing, but the thing itself: so that not only that more imperfect mode, which was of an accident: but the thing itself, or the Substance of the Old Testament, has been utterly abrogated.

Fourthly, they also hallucinate most shamefully who determine that the nature and definition of the Old and New Testament must be explained through two distinct, nay, clearly diverse modes of justification. The Apostolic decision in the Council of Jerusalem, Acts 15:11, and the Pauline inference in Ephesians 4:4, clearly prove the contrary: One God, One Faith, One Baptism.

Fifthly, those also err who maintain that the Old Testament consisted only of promises of corporal or external things, but the New of spiritual and heavenly things

Latin:

DE NATUR, ÆSSENtiâ ac definitione Utriusq; Testamenti.

DUo distincta & quidem ex ordinatione ipsius DEI, diversa esse Testamenta, ex Scripturis luculenter demonstrari potest: ut Jerem. 31, 31. Ecce dies venient, dicit DOMINUS, & feriam cum domo Israel, & cum domo Juda, Fœdus NOVUM: NON secundum pactum, quod pepigi cum patribus eorum, in die, quâ apprehendi manum eorum, ut educerem eos de terrâ Ægypti. Sic Christus ipse promissum hoc Novum Testamentum, ejusque obsignationem & consummâtionem quasi expediturus, dicit in institutione Eucharistica: Hic est Sanguis meus Novi Testamenti, Matth. 26, 28. Marci 14, 24. Vel ut habet Lucas cap. 22, 20. & Paulus 1. Cor. 11, 25. Hic calix est Novum Testamentum in MEO Sanguine. Sic Apostolus 2. Cor. 3, 6. asserit, Christum fecisse Apostolos ministros Novi Testamenti, hac profectò assertione, Veteris Testamenti negationem, sive abrogationem haud obscurè exprimens, Et Gal. 4, 24. Duo hæc diversa Testamenta in Conjugibus Abrahæ præfigurata fuisse dicit: Unum quidem à monte Sinai, in Servitutem generans: alterum verò, ex monte Sion, in libertatem asserens.

Sic Autor Epistolæ ad Hebræos integrum quasi commentarium de utriusque Testamenti naturâ & essentiâ pertexit: factâ oppositione inter prius sive primum, hoc est, Vetus illud, & inter posterius sive alterum, hoc est, Novum hoc Testamentum: Mosen Veteris: Christum verò Novi Mediatorem constituens & quidem MELIORIS Testamenti: cap. 7, 22. cap. 8, 6. cap. 9, 15. cap. 12, 24. Quin hoc ipsum MELIUS Testamentum, postmodùm cap. 10, 28. κατ' ἐξοχὴν nudè & simpliciter nominat: & quidem ratione præstantiæ suæ ÆTERNUM, cap. 13, 20. Undè duo distincta, imò diversa Testamenta elici posse, promptum est colligere. Nam ubi prius est & posterius: ubi bonum etiam est & melius: ubi denique datur finis & æternitas: ibi simplex Unitas locum habere nequit: Nihil enim respectu sui ipsius, diversos istos comparationis gradus admittit: Sed hi ut minimum in duo semper necessariò existunt.

His ita præsuppositis infallibiliter evincitur: Vetus & Novum Testamenta, rectè duo diversa constitui: non modò quoad Numerum: sed & quoad præstantiam; non nominetenùs saltem, sed & quoad Substantiam.

Cæterùm mox hic oritur Quæstio: Undenám Natura, sive Essentia vel propria quasi affectio cujuslibet Testamenti erui possit & debeat? Qua in Quæstione cum plærique Scriptores confusione aliqua laborent, & probè distinguenda conjungant, & ex duobus corruptis, Unum faciant mixtum: Undè Quæstioni etiam difficultas haud exigua obvenit: nos ut planissimè rem explicemus, κατ' ἄρσιν àd θέσιν progrediemur, per remotionem falsorum modorum, ad positionem veri descensuri.

Initiò igitur eum removemus modum, qui utriusq; Testamenti naturam & conditionem petit ex divisione librorum Biblicorum: Vetus quidem per libros Mosis, Psalmorum & Prophetarum: Novum verò per libros Evangelistarum & Apostolorum definiens. Erroris hujus vanitas vel indè liquet, quòd latiùs patent tùm hi, tùm illi libri, quàm ut ad unum tantùm Testamentum referri possint: Quin potiùs in illis latet novum: in his verò traditur Complementum Veteris: uti alicubi loquitur Augustinus.

Deindè Natura utriusq; Testamenti vitiosissimè petitur ex doctrina ipsa Legis & Evangelii. Neutra enim in se & per se, Vetustatis aut Novitatis rationem sortiri potest: Siquidem æterna ac immutabilis est voluntas Dei, tàm in Lege, quàm in Evangelio, de salutis nostræ negocio revelata: & tantùm abest, ut Legis doctrina hodiè sit antiquata, ut nemini mortalium salus & vita æterna sine perfecta Legis impletione, eaque vel propria, vel imputata aliena obtingere possit. Ergò Legis doctrinæ, non uti Veteri Testamento, tribui potest antiquatio sive abrogatio: & per consequens, Legis etiam doctrina, in se, & per se considerata, non potest aut debet definiri per Vetus Testamentum, dummodò propriè loqui velimus.

Tertiò, non judicandum est de propria utriusq; Testamenti natura, & affectione, ex gemina illa Legis traditione: quarum una ante Mosen fuit rudior, & nondùm certis legibus expressa & comprehensa: altera verò fuit expolitior & perfectior post promulgatam jam divinitùs Legis universæ doctrinam. Qui sanè error sua sponte concidit: Vetustatis enim ratio, quæ Scriptura Teste, comitem habet abrogationem, non modum tantùm rei, sed rem ipsam respicit & definit: ita ut non tantùm modus ille imperfectior, qui accidentis erat: sed res ipsa, sive Substantia Veteris Testamenti penitùs sit abrogata.

Quartò turpissimè etiam hallucinantur, qui Veteris & Novi Testamenti naturam ac Definitionem per duos distinctos imò planè diversos Justificandi modos, explicandam esse statuunt. Contrariam planè evincit decisio Apostolica in Concilio Hierosolymitano, Act. 15, 11. & illatio Paulina Ephes. 4, 4. Unus Deus, Una Fides, Unum Baptisma.

Quintò errant & illi, qui Vetus Testamentum, rerum tantùm corporalium sive externarum: Novum verò spiritualium ac cœlestium rerum promissionibus constitisse so-


### On the Definition of the Testament. Question I. on the Nature, Essence, and…: What is the Old Testament?

mniant. As if indeed today, the Old Testament being entirely antiquated, all the promises of corporal things had expired at once? Absurdly and impiously. Since even today Piety has promises of this life and of the eternal life: 1 Timothy 4:8.

Finally, there were also those who maintain that both Testaments must be defined by the doctrine of salvation itself simply, or by the promise of Grace offered in Christ, administered only in one way and another. Which opinion, proper to the Calvinist people, we have partly worn down in the Prolegomena, and will expressly refute in the second chapter.

These erroneous opinions being thus removed, we shall duly proceed to investigate the true nature and definition of both Testaments: if 1. we have weighed what a Testament is in general considered in the Scriptures. 2. What specifically is either the Old or the New Testament, and whence the reason for either antiquity or novelty is obtained for them, so that it can be named either Old or New. 3. And lastly, what is the proper and native Substance of any Testament, giving it Form and Essence.

Regarding I. A Testament in general is a divine disposition, both concerning the legitimate dispensation of religion itself and concerning the government of the Church or the people of God, instituted with this end and purpose, that the people of God might not wander by their own will and stray in some mere ἀταξίᾳ or confusion, but be contained within a certain form of polity, distinct from all other peoples.

This general definition provides two πορίσματα, or corollaries, the use and observation of which can bring great light to this whole discussion.

I. It is: that a Testament is not religion, or faith or the doctrine itself, but something occupied with its legitimate dispensation.

II. That a Testament neither delivers nor informs the doctrine of salvation itself, insofar as it is considered in itself, but rather instructs the ecclesiastical polity, by which the people of God, as if surrounded by certain limits, constitute a peculiar polity, distinct from the flocks of other peoples.

Regarding the II. member, the Old Testament is that most ancient solemn disposition by which GOD, after the Israelite people were led out of Egyptian captivity, amidst thunders and lightnings, delivered the entire administration of both religion and polity, described in a certain form of rites and laws or constitutions, on Mount Sinai.

The New Testament, indeed, is a new and solemn disposition by which GOD, the former Old Testament having been abrogated, announced to His people the universal promulgation of the Gospel, and its most clear propagation into the whole world, from Zion and Jerusalem, and instituted and ordained a new administration of evangelical doctrine, through two Sacraments, Baptism and the Lord's Supper: not indeed that the doctrine concerning the reconciliation of men on account of Christ was entirely unknown in antiquity, but that now it has been revealed in another mode of dispensation, more full and more plain. Thus, therefore, the nature and proper affection of the New Testament does not regard the thing itself proper to the Gospel, that is, the very doctrine of our salvation: but the mode of delivering and administering this thing, properly and solely: just as, conversely, the nature and proper affection of the Old Testament regards indeed the law also, or the Decalogue, but not the doctrine of the Law itself considered in itself: but only the mode of delivering the thing, that is, the legitimate dispensation of the promulgated Law, according to the form prescribed by God himself.

It is evident from what has already been said: Whence the reason for Oldness and Newness comes to these two Testaments.

For 1. it is placed beyond doubt that the Jewish people were other and entirely different from the Christian people. Therefore, GOD also, by a certain and good counsel, willed that there be one disposition of Religion and another: as well as a form of the polity itself: And indeed the Israelitic people, whom GOD had chosen before all the peoples that are upon the earth, Deut. 7, 6, He enclosed in a certain Ecclesiastical, and Civil, or forensic, and Economic polity, which would endure as long as a new face of the ages should approach: that is to say, by which the Messiah, exhibited in the flesh, this polity being abrogated, would introduce another form and polity of living and acting. And this is that solid Foundation, from which the diversity of the two Testaments, distinguished by appearance, emerges and depends: so indeed, that the former is called the Old: but the latter, the New Testament.

Moreover, the very reason for this appellation rests upon certain respects or causes: and those chiefly three. The first respect is of Time. For that external and solemn promulgation of the law, and the whole constitution of the Israelitic polity, is older than that public and universal promulgation of the Gospel by at least two thousand years. Therefore, the former is rightly designated Old: the latter, New: as Scripture itself teaches, Jerem. 31, 31. Hebr. 8, 8.

The second respect is of the Object. For that whole Mosaic polity, as it was in itself most burdensome, being indeed almost infinite in rites and ceremonies constant: It served primarily for curbing and restraining the old man: but this public and universal propagation of the Gospel contributes most to the forming of the New Man.

The third and final respect is that of the Subject. For the principle of Laws is inscribed in us at creation, whence the Law is said to be known to us by nature. But the principle of the Gospel relies solely on revelation. Therefore, by as much as the first Creation is older than the Promulgation which finally happened in time, by so much is the Law also older than the Gospel itself: not only by reason of the doctrine of each, but also by reason of the dispensation by which it is fitting that both be administered according to the prescription of GOD.

Regarding the third member, which asks, What is the true Substance of each Testament? Scripture itself explains the matter quite clearly and perspicuously. And indeed, as regards the Old Testament, it was sealed and consummated by the blood of cattle.

For after GOD had delivered that old Disposition to his people with a solemn rite; it is read that Moses, by the command of GOD, having taken the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, sprinkled both the volume of the law itself and the people, using this solemn formula: This is the Blood of the Testament, which GOD has commanded to you, Exod. 24, 8. Hebr. 9, 18. 19. 20. The blood of cattle therefore constitutes the Substance of the Old Testament.

Moreover, Christ the Savior, about to carry out the sealing and consummation of the New Testament, willed to use this formula: This is MY Blood of the New Testament, Matth. 26, 28. Marc. 14. v. 24. Or, as Luke and Paul have it: This cup is the New Testament in MY Blood, Luc. 22, 20. 1. Cor. 11, 25. The blood of Christ, therefore, shed for us for the remission of sins, constitutes the Substance of the New Testament.

Latin:

mniant. Quasi verò hodiè, Veteri Testamento prorsus antiquato, omnes simul promissiones rerum corporalium expiraverint? Absurdè & impiè. Siquidem hodieque Pietas promissiones habet hujus & æternæ vitæ: 1. Timoth. 4, 8.

Tandem erant quoque, qui Utrumque Testamentum definiendum esse autumant, per ipsam simpliciter doctrinam salutis, sive per promissionem Gratiæ in Christo oblatam, alio tantùm atque alio modo administratam. Quam opinionem, Gentu Calviniana propriam, tùm in Prolegomenis ex parte protrivimus, tùm capite secundo ex professo refutabimus.

Erroneis istis opinionibus ita remotis, ad veram utriusque Testamenti naturam ac definitionem investigandam ritè progrediemur: si 1. expenderimus, Quid sit in Sacris Testamentum in genere consideratum. 2. Quodnam in specie sit vel Vetus vel Novum Testamentum, & Undè vel Vetustatis vel Novitatis ratio illis obtingat, ut vel Vetus, vel Novum nominari possit. 3. & postremò, Quænam sit cujuslibet Testamenti propria ac nativa Substantia, dans ei Formam & Essentiam.

Quoad I. Testamentum in genere est Dispositio divina, tùm de ipsius Religionis legitimâ dispensatione: tùm de gubernatione Ecclesiæ sive populi Dei, hoc fine ac consilio instituta, ut ne populus Dei proprio suo vagetur arbitrio, & in merâ quapiam ἀταξίᾳ sive confusione oberret: sed intrà certam politiæ formam, à reliquis omnibus populis distinctam contineatur.

Generalis hæc Definitio πορίσματα, sive corollaria duo subministrat, quorum usus ac observatio magnam lucem toti huic disputationi inferre potest.

I. Est: quòd Testamentum non est Religio, sive fides aut doctrina ipsa, sed aliquid circa legitimam ejus dispensationem occupatum.

II. Quòd Testamentum non doctrinam salutis ipsam vel tradit vel informat: quatenùs quidem ea in se consideratur: sed politiam magis Ecclesiasticam instruit, quâ populus Dei, tanquàm certis limitibus circumdatus, peculiarem, & à reliquorum populorum gregibus distinctam politiam constituat.

Quoad II. membrum, Vetus Testamentum est antiquissima illa solennis dispositio, quâ DEUS, populo Israëlitico ex captivitate Ægyptiacâ educto, inter tonitrua & fulgura, universam tùm Religionis, tùm Politiæ administrationem, certâ rituum ac legum sive constitutionum formâ descriptam in monte Sinai tradidit.

Novum vero Testamentum, est nova & solennis dispositio, quâ DEUS, priore vetere Testamento abrogato, populo suo universalem Evangelij promulgationem, ejusq; clarissimam propagationem in universum orbem terrarum, ex Sion & Jerusalem annunciavit, & novam doctrinæ Evangelicæ administrationem, per duo Sacramenta, Baptismum & Cœnam Domini, instituit & ordinavit: non quidem, quòd doctrina de reconciliatione hominum propter Christum, antiquitùs prorsus fuerit ignota:sed quòd nunc alio dispensationis modo, pleniore ac planiore fuerit revelata. Sic ergò Novi Testamenti natura & affectio propria, non rem ipsam Evangelii propriam, hoc est, ipsam salutis nostræ doctrinam: sed Rei hujus tradendæ & administrandæ Modum, propriè & unicè respicit: Quemadmodum vice versa, Veteris Testamenti Natura & affectio propria, legem quidem etiam respicit, sive Decalogum, sed non ipsam doctrinam Legis in se consideratam: verum tantùm Modum tradendæ rei, hoc est, Legis promulgatæ legitimam dispensationem, secundum formam à Deo ipso præscriptam.

Patet ex jam dictis: Undenam Vetustatis & Novitatis ratio duobus istis Testamentis obveniat.

Nam 1. populum Judaicum alium ac planè diversum fuisse, à populo Christiano extra dubium est positum. Ergò DEUS quoque certo bonoœque consilio aliam atque aliam esse voluit tùm dispositionem Religionis: tùm ipsius politiæ formam: Et populum quidem Israëliticum, quem præ cunctis populis, qui sunt super terram, DEUS elegerat, Deut. 7, 6. certæ tùm Ecclesiasticæ, tùm Civili, sive forensi, tùm Oeconomicæ politiæ inclusit, quæ tamdiu duraret, donec nova seculorum facies ingrueret: ea nimirùm, quâ Messias in carnem exhibitus, abrogatâ hac politia, aliam vivendi, agendique formam & politiam introduceret. Et hoc est solidum illud Fundamentum, ex quo duorum Testamentorum specie distinctorum diversitas, emergit & dependet: ita quidem, ut prior illa dicatur Vetus: posterior verò hæc, Novum Testamentum.

Cæterùm ipsa appellationis hujus ratio certis nititur respectibus sivè causis: iisque potissimùm tribus. Primus respectus est Temporis. Nam externa illa & solennis promulgatio legis, totaœq; constitutio politiæ Israëliticæ, antiquior est publicâ illâ & universali Evangelii promulgatione, annis ut minimum bis mille. Ergò illa Vetus: hæc Novum rectè indigitatur: sic docente ipsâ Scripturâ, Jerem. 31, 31. Hebr. 8, 8.

Alter respectus est Objecti. Nam tota illa politia Mosaica, uti in se erat molestissima, quippè infinitis fermè ritibus ac ceremoniis constans: Veteri homini frenando & compescendo, potissimum inserviebat: publica autem hæc & universalis Evangelii propagatio, Novo Homini formando, plurimùm conducit.

Tertius & postremus respectus est Subjecti. Nam Legum ratio nobis in creatione est insculpta, Undè Lex naturâ nobis nota esse dicitur. Evangelii verò ratio, patefactione sola nititur. Quantò ergò antiquior est Creatio prima, Promulgatione quæ in tempore demùm evenit: tantò vetustior etiam est Lex, ipso Evangelio: non modò ratione doctrinæ utriusque: sed & ratione dispensationis, quâ utramque ex præscripto DEI administrari convenit.

Quoad III. membrum, quod quærit, Quænam sit vera utriusq; Testamenti Substantia? Scriptura ipsa satis dilucidè ac perspicuè rem explicat. Et quidem quoad Vetus Testamentum obsignatum & consummatum illud fuit, Sanguine pecuino.

Postquàm enim DEUS populo suo Dispositionem illam veterem solenni ritu tradiderat; legitur Moses, ex mandato DEI, sumto sanguine vitulorum & hircorum, cum aquâ, lanâ Coccina & hyssopo, tùm volumen ipsum legis, tùm populum aspersisse, hac solenni formulâ usus: Hic est Sanguis Testamenti, quod mandavit vobis DEUS, Exod. 24, 8. Hebr. 9, 18. 19. 20. Sanguis ergò pecuinus constituit Substantiam Veteris Testamenti.

Cæterùm Christus Servator obsignationem & consummationem Novi Testamenti expediturus, hâc uti voluit formulâ: Hic est Sanguis MEUS Novi Testamenti, Matth. 26, 28. Marc. 14. v. 24. Vel, ut Lucas & Paulus habent: Hic calix est Novum Testamentum in MEO Sanguine, Luc. 22, 20. 1. Cor. 11, 25. Substantiam ergò Novi Testamenti constituit Sanguis Christi, effusus pro nobis in remissionem peccatorum.


### Question II. of the First Chapter. Concerning Similitude and Dissimilarity; or rather concerning the Substantial Difference of the Old &…

SUCH is the mutual affection of these two Testaments toward each other, that they differ indeed according to their very Substance, as will be shown presently: But yet they communicate with each other in certain respects.

For first, they communicate regarding the unity of the Covenant which God struck with the human race, if you consider its reciprocal stipulation, but not the mode of dispensation. For just as God bound himself to the Fathers of the Old Testament, that he wills to be their God: and they in turn were bound to God, that they will to be his people: so these are the same heads of the covenant under which we are contained today. Nor does that Prophetic passage, Jerem. 31. verse 31, where one Covenant and another is described, stand in the way. For the Prophet there considers the Covenant not in itself, but only in respect of the dispensation or administration, or external Form: which we readily admit is most diverse.

Then they agree, or rather communicate, regarding the doctrine itself concerning the business of our Justification and salvation, which is clearly one and the same in both; and it is not one or different under the Old Testament, and another under the New. That Canon of the Council of Jerusalem, Act. 15, 11, confirms this, which holds as follows: We believe that we are saved by the grace of Jesus Christ, just as the Fathers were saved, who could not bear the yoke of the law.

Thirdly, these two Testaments also communicate by the Communion of Saints, or the Unity of the Church. For there is one and the same Church of the Saints in both, whose foundation is one Christ: although the excellence, splendor, and clarity of the Church of the New Testament is greater, which nevertheless does not take away the Unity of the Church, but only modifies it.

And thus indeed stands the agreement of those two Testaments. They differ, however, in various and manifold ways: and I. indeed in the Mediator. For the Old Testament has Moses as mediator: but the New acknowledges Christ alone. Now therefore, as much difference as intervenes between Moses and Christ, so much difference also intervenes between the Old and the New Testament. But Moses and Christ differ as minister and Lord; as Servant and Son. Therefore. The following testimonies of Scripture confirm the minor premise.

Num. 12, 7. My servant Moses is most faithful in all my house.

Hebr. 3, 3. & seqq. For this man was counted worthy of more glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who hath builded the house hath more honour than the house itself. For every house is builded by some man; but he that built all things is God. And Moses verily was faithful in all his house, as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken after; But Christ as a son over his own house.

Hebr. 8, 6. Christ has obtained a ministry as much better, as he is the mediator of a better covenant, which has been established upon better promises.

Hebr. 9, 15. Christ is therefore the mediator of the New Testament, that by means of death for the redemption of those transgressions that were under the former Testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance.

Then they differ in the time of their promulgation. For that old one was established on the day that the Lord took the hand of the Israelites to lead them out of the land of Egypt, Jer. 31, 32. But the new one was promulgated at the end of times, according to the prophecies of the Prophets, Isa. 2, verse 2. Mic. 4, 1.

Thirdly, they differ in the place of their promulgation. For the old was promulgated on Mount Horeb, in the desert of Sinai, Exod. 19, 18. But the new went forth from Zion and Jerusalem, Isa. 2, 2. Mic. 4, 1. Gal. 4, 24.

Fourthly, they differ in duration. For the old was to be abrogated and ended with the Israelite polity itself: which obsolescence also befell it by the very act, as soon as the new was established: as the Epistle to the Hebrews 8, 13 teaches. By saying new, he has made the old obsolete. But the new is eternal: that is, it will never yield to any other Testament to be established later: and it will not find its end until Christ himself on the last day delivers the kingdom, that is, the government of the Church, to his Father, 1. Cor. 15, 24.

Fifthly, they differ in breadth and scope. For the old was bounded by the very narrow borders of the Israelite people. Whence GOD, at its solemn promulgation, repeatedly added this limitation: You shall keep these in YOUR generations. But the new extends as widely as the globe of the earth spreads itself: according to the constitution of Christ: Go into all the world, teach all nations, etc. Matt. 28, 19.

Sixthly, they differ in the manner of their dispensation, and that in many ways. For in the promulgation of the Old, GOD willed to use the ministry of angels, Gal. 3, v. 19. Acts 7, 53. In the constitution of the New, the Lord himself descended from Heaven and carried out its solemnity. Then, that was promulgated amidst thunders and lightnings, full of horror and stupor, and indeed into bondage: but this was established and confirmed by the sweetest propagation of the Gospel, into the liberty of the children of GOD. Gal. 4, 24 and 26. Then the promulgation of the former consisted of an immense and almost innumerable multitude of laws, rites, and ceremonies, joined with infinite burdens of works: but the institution of this has rites, as Augustine writes somewhere, very few in number: easiest to perform, most august in understanding, and most chaste in observation. Finally, that one consisted of external purifications and for the most part bloody sacrifices: But this one consists of internal purification, with the blood of Christ apprehended by faith, our hearts are purged from dead works, Hebr. 9, 14. It also consists of victims or unbloody sacrifices, namely the calves of lips confessing the name of the LORD: from the exercises of which, neither intervals of places, nor any hardships can exclude anyone, Rom. 12, 1. Hebr. 13, 15.

Seventhly, they differ in the perfection of their benefits. For the old did not have the very image of the things, or the future goods: that is, the very flesh and blood of Christ the Savior: but only a shadow or type, Hebr. 10, v. 1. But the new has the very body of CHRIST, Col. 2, 17.

Eighthly, they differ in clarity, in which the New in many ways surpasses the obscurity of the Old, as it, with the mists of shadows and types dispelled, dwells in the clearest light of heavenly truth and divine mysteries: and contains the Messiah no longer to come, but already sent and incarnate.

Finally, they differ in tradition and ministry or effect. For the Old Testament, by reason of the law, whose solemn promulgation was the principal part of the Old Testament, was written on stone tablets: but the New, by reason of the Gospel, whose universal preaching is likewise a primary part of the New Testament, is written in the hearts of men: That was of the letter that kills: But this of the Spirit that gives life: as the Prophet teaches, Jer. 31, v. 34. The Apostle 2. Cor. 3, 6.

Moreover, from what has already been said, some more difficult questions emerge, which are most worthy of explanation. THE FIRST is that which is today especially controverted: Whether these two Testaments differ in their very substance, or indeed only in accidents, or in one and another mode of dispensation. We answer, from what has already been presupposed, that they differ in their very substance, not only in accidents. However, this substance is most viciously defined by the Sacramentarians through the very doctrine of our justification and salvation: which substance, to be sure, we readily admit to be one and the same in both; but the substance which is inquired about in this place is, as Scripture defines it, either the shadow of things to come, that is, of the Body and Blood of Christ, or these very goods themselves now exhibited and present in act: the former is proper to the Old Testament, the latter to the New. Just as, therefore, a shadow or Type differs in reality and according to substance, from the Body and Antitype itself: thus, by equal reasoning, it is necessary that these two Testaments differ among themselves. But concerning this question, more fully in the ἀντιθέσει itself. Furthermore, it is asked at this point: To what extent or how far has the Old Testament been abrogated: whether entirely, or only in part? We answer that it has been abrogated entirely, as far as its substantials are concerned. But these substantials, as was also shown above, ought not to be defined by the doctrine of the Decalogue itself: but by those things which pertain to the state of the Polity and Church, proper to the Israelite people. In which part the Ceremonial and forensic Law are chiefly placed. But now a third, more difficult Question arises: if the Moral Law does not pertain to the Substance of the Old Testament, is it therefore proper to the New Testament? And again: If it does not pertain to the New Testament: should it be established whether and how it ought to be referred to the Old, and to have been abrogated? I answer that the Moral Law pertains to both Testaments, and therefore it has been both abrogated and not abrogated: but with a very different respect. For it pertained to the Old, 1. as regards the continuous and more rigid inculcation, by which we were kept shut up as if in a prison, unto that faith which was to be revealed through Christ, Galat. 3, 23. Then, as regards the more obscure and less clear tradition of the precepts of the Decalogue, which received the light of clarity from the interpretation of the law proposed by Christ, in the 5th, 6th, and 7th chapters of Matthew. Thirdly, as regards that alternative sentence, either to salvation, if it were kept: or to condemnation, if it were violated. By these three ways and respects, therefore, by which the moral law pertains to the Old Testament, it is most rightly established that it has also been abrogated or made obsolete: especially as regards Justification and condemnation. For the Law has no power to condemn those who are in Christ Jesus: Roman. 8, v. 1. and by works no flesh can be justified, Galat. 2, 16. Indeed, the Law was not given, which could justify, Galat. 3, 21. But, because the New Testament embraces both the Remission of sins and the Renewal of the mind: since we are a new creature in CHRIST, created unto good works, Ephes. 2, 10. the norm of which is proposed most perfectly in the Decalogue: hence it comes about that now the Decalogue, by reason of New obedience, pertains also to the New Testament. And indeed, since the Decalogue is nothing other than the immutable rule of divine Justice, implanted in the nature of men in creation itself: certainly in this respect the Decalogue admits no more obsolescence than the Nature of man itself, and in these, Natural things can admit no abrogation at all. Thus, therefore, without any Contradiction, it can be established that the Moral Law can be referred to both the Old and the New Testament, and be both abrogated and not abrogated.

Fourthly, it is asked, Did the Ceremonial Law have nothing concerning Christ: and if it was abrogated entirely, does not something of the doctrine of the Gospel depart from it, since it contains only Christ.

I answer affirmatively, that the Ceremonial Law indeed contained many things concerning Christ and his benefits within itself, but only under the aspect of type and shadow: not, however, under the aspect of the thing itself, or the body. For example: The Ark of the covenant bore the type of the Church, which would be true only if it embraced the covenant, that is, the Word of GOD. Thus the Tables of the Decalogue, placed in the ark, showed that the Church would always be the guardian of the Holy Scripture, in which GOD has revealed himself. But the golden tables, by which the ark was covered, were the name of the Mercy-seat, by which Christ the Mediator was signified, by whose propitiation the Church would be protected against the wrath and judgment of GOD. Two Cherubim, having a mutual view, noted the ministry of the doctrine in both Testaments, indeed different: but in the same elegant consensus. By the use of the staves and poles, the work of the ministers was prefigured. But since these images and figures have now been fulfilled, there can be no further use for them.

But here, in the fifth place, a more difficult question arises. For since, as is evident from what has already been said, the Ceremonial Law contains the doctrine concerning the person, office, and benefits of Christ, and thus proper to the Gospel: it is asked; Should it not rather be referred to the substance of the New, than of the Old Testament: and how can it be established that it has been abrogated? But I answer with the Apostle, that the Ceremonial Law, considered generally, was a schoolmaster unto Christ, Gal. 3, 24. Likewise, that Christ is the end of the law, Rom. 10, 4.

Now, indeed, the End cannot be a part of the thing itself of which it is the end: but it is something outside the Substance of that thing. Therefore, the Legal doctrine, whose end is Christ, is proper to the Old Testament; but that it might be conspicuous that the end was finally impending over this very doctrine; it certainly could not have happened in any other way than if some Evangelical things, and indeed those proper to the New Testament, had been sprinkled upon this very doctrine. But since in these the thing itself differs much, through substance: and the mode of the thing delivered, which is in part an Accident: hence we now answer to the proposed ζήτημα: that the thing itself is to be judged proper not to the Law, but to the Gospel; not to the Old, but to the New Testament: but the mode of the thing ought to be referred to the Old Testament, and therefore it is subject to abrogation, indeed to plenary obsolescence: indeed, it has truly been abrogated. There are other Theologians who are accustomed to answer by distinguishing otherwise; that Levitical ceremonies are considered in a twofold way: 1. as pedagogical works and exercises of sermons concerning sin, concerning the wrath of God, and similar matters: In which respect they pertain to the Law and to the Old Testament: But then as types of Christ: In which respect they pertain to the Gospel and the New Testament. Which answer is indeed true and squares with the analogy of faith: but it does not yet seem to suffice for solving the knot of the proposed question. For that scruple always remains: If the Levitical ceremonies, insofar as they were types, pertain to the New Testament, why is it that they could not be abrogated? Therefore, so that you may be able to fully extricate yourself from this difficulty, that further point must be observed, that you distinguish most accurately between the thing and the mode of the thing. For the type is not the thing itself: but only the mode of the thing shadowed forth: Which mode of the thing is clearly proper to the Law, and therefore, now that Christ, who is the thing itself, has been exhibited, it is abrogated in all respects.

Sixthly, it is also asked in this place concerning the time at which the New Testament was first begun? The Apostle, Galatians 2:17, provides a handle for doubting, when he asserts that the Gospel is older than the Law, when he argues that that promise of the Gospel, concerning the Seed in whom all the families of the earth are to be blessed, was not abrogated by the Law, as that which was promulgated only four hundred and thirty years later. But I answer that a distinction must be made between any evangelical promise whatsoever and the solemn and universal preaching or propagation of the Gospel into the whole world. The promises of the Gospel indeed concerning the seed of the woman and of Abraham were proposed to our first parents immediately after the fall in Paradise: and the same sounded forth at all times among the ancient people, even before Moses. And in this respect it is true what the Apostle affirms, that these promises are older than the Law, but not simply so: since the Law was promulgated in Paradise itself, where there was not yet need for an evangelical sermon: but only in a qualified sense, namely with respect to that solemn disposition by which it was prescribed and ordained by God himself, by what rites and ceremonies the doctrine of the Law ought to be proposed and exercised among the people of God: Which one and only disposition is and is called the Old Testament. Furthermore, as regards the solemn and universal preaching and propagation of the Gospel into the whole world, from which the New Testament also received its name most especially: it is certainly much later than the promulgation of the Old Testament. And because that solemn promulgation of the Gospel could not take place until the Messiah was exhibited and the work of redemption was consummated, and the Synagogue or Jewish polity was first honorably buried: we establish the beginning of the New Testament, although it obtained some beginning and splendor from the times of John the Baptist; yet we hold that the fuller revelation, and that which is proper to the New Testament, is to be referred to those times which followed the Ascension of Christ into the heavens, and which had the dispersion of the Apostles into the whole world as a genuine and adequate sign and symbol joined to it.

Finally, it is also asked whether the Forensic Law is so proper to the Old Testament, and so abrogated, that nothing of it remains under the New Testament. I answer again by a distinction between the thing and the mode of the thing. I call the thing the natural equity itself, implanted in the natures of men at the first creation. But I call the mode of the thing that certain form to which the Israelite people were bound in exercising forensic judgments: and which mode alone was proper to the Old Testament. The thing itself, therefore, is no more abrogated than the nature of man could be abrogated. Nay, rather, the Gospel and the New Testament do not abolish this thing itself, but rather confirm it, as that in forensic judgments natural equity is to be regarded, and faith, patience, love, and other virtues of that kind are to be exercised. But the mode which was to be observed by the ancient people according to the prescription of God concerning forensic judgments, being indeed proper to the Old Testament, is simply abrogated today.

Latin:

EA est duorum istorum Testamentorum mutua ad se invicem affectio, ut secundum Substantiam ipsam differant quidem, uti mox ostenderut : Sed in quibusdam tamen inter se communicent.
