Primùm enim communicant quoad Fœderis, quod Deus cum humano genere pepigit, unitatem, si reciprocam ejus stipulationem, non verò dispensationis modum, consideres. Nam quemadmodum Patribus Veteris Testamenti se obstrinxit Deus, quòd velit Deus ipsorum esse: & iidem rursus Deo fue. unt obstricti, quòd velint populus ipsius esse: ita eadem sunt capita fœderis, sub quo nos hodiè continemur. Neque obstat illud Propheticum, Jerem.31. vers. 31. ubi aliud atque aliud Fœdus describitur. Nam Propheta ibi Fœdus non in se, sed tantùm respectu dispensationis sive administrationis, aut externæ Formæ considerat: quam diversissimam ultrò fatemur.

Deindè conveniunt, vel potiùs communicant quoad doctrinam ipsam, de Justificationis & salutis nostræ negotio, quæ utrobique planè una est, & eadem: neque alia aut diversa sub Vetere, alia sub Novo Testamento. Confirmat hoc Canon ille Concilii Hierosolymitani, Act. 15, 11. qui sic habet: Credimus nos salvari per gratiam Jesu Christi, quemadmodum & Patres salvati sunt, qui legis jugum portare non potuerunt.

Tertiò communicant etiam duo hæc Testamenta Communione Sanctorum, sive Unitate Ecclesiæ. Una enim est atq; eadem utrobique Sanctorum Ecclesia, cujus fundamentum est, unus Christus: licèt Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti major sit præstantia, splendor & claritas, quæ tamen Ecclesiæ Unitatem non tollit, sed tantum modificat.

Et sic quidem se habet duorum istorum Testamentorum convenientia. Differunt aumul variè & multipliciter: & I. quidem Mediatore. Vetus enim Testamentum Mediatorem habet Mosen: Novum autem agnoscit solum Christum. Jam ergò quantum discriminis intercedit Mosi cum Christo, tantum etiam differentiæ intercedit Veteri cum Novo Testamento. Atqui Moses & Christus differunt ut minister & Dominus; ut Servus & Filius. Ergò. Minorem confirmant sequentia Scripturæ testimonia.

Num. 12, 7. Servus meus Moses fidelissimus in omni domo mea.

Hebr. 3, 3. & seqq. Tantò ampliore gloria præ Mose hic dignus est habitus, quantò majorem honorem habet is, qui construxit domùm quàm domus ipsa. Omnis enim domus construitur ab aliquo: qui verò condidit hæc omnia, Deus est. Et Moses quidem fidus fuit in tota domo ipsius ut minister, in testimonium eorum, quæ dicenda erant. Christus autem, tanquàm filius in domo sua.

Hebr. 8, 6. Christus tantò melius est fortitus ministerium, quantò melioris Testamenti mediator est, quod in melioribus promissionibus sancitum est.

Hebr. 9, 15. Christus ideò Novi Testamenti mediator est, ut morte intercedente in redemptionem earum prævaricationum, quæ erant sub priore Testamento, repromissionem accipiant, qui vocati sunt, æternæ hæreditatis.

Deindè differunt Promulgationis tempore. Nam vetus illud sancitum fuit in die ea, quâ Dominus apprehendit manum Israelitarum, ut educeret eos de terra Ægypti, Jeremiæ 31, 32. Novum verò promulgatum est in fine temporum, secundum vaticinia Prophetarum, Esa. 2. vers. 2. Mich. 4, 1.

Tertiò differunt promulgationis Loco. Vetus enim in monte Horeb, in deserto Sinai fuit promulgatum, Exod. 19, 18. Novum verò exivit ex Sion & Jerusalem, Esa. 2, 2. Mich. 4, 1. Gal. 4, 24.

Quartò differunt Duratione. Vetus enim cum ipsa politia Israëlitica abrogandum & finiendum erat: quæ etiam antiquatio ipso actu ei obtigit, quamprimùm Novum est sancitum: sic docente Epistola ad Hebr. 8, 13. Dicendo novum, antiquavit Vetus. Novum verò æternum est: hoc est, nulli alii Testamento, ulteriùs sanciendo, unquàm cedet: & haud priùs finem suum sortietur, quàm Christus ipse in die novissimo regnum, hoc est, Ecclesiæ regimen tradet suo patri, 1. Cor. 15, 24.

Quintò differunt Latitudine & Complexu. Vetus enim angustis admodum populi Israëlitici finibus terminabatur. Undè DEUS solenni ejus promulgationi subindè adjecit hanc limitationem: Servabitis hæc in generationibus VESTRIS. Novum verò tàm latè se extendit, quàm latè se diffundit Orbis terrarum: secundum constitutionem Christi: Euntes in mundum universum, docete omnes gentes, &c. Matth. 28, 19.

Sextò differunt Dispensationis modo, eóque multiplici. Nam in promulgatione Veteris Angelorum ministerio DEUS uti voluit, Galat. 3. v. 19. Actor. 7, 53. In constitutione Novi Dominus ipse de Cœlo descendit, & ejus solennitatem expediit. Deindè illud promulgabatur inter tonitrua & fulgura, horroris ac stuporis plenissima, & quidem in servitutem: hoc verò sancitum & confirmatum dulcissima Evangelii propagatione, in libertatem filiorum DEI. Galat 4, 24. & 26. Tùm illius promulgatio constabat immensâ & fermè innumerâ, legum, rituum, ceremoniarum multitudine, cum infinitis operationum molestiis conjunctâ: Hujus verò institutio, ritus habet, ut Augustinus alicubi scribit, numero paucissimos: factu facillimos, intellectu augustissimos; observatione castissimos. Tandem illud constabat purgationibus externis, & sacrificiis ut plurimùm cruentis: Hoc verò constat purgatione interna, cum sanguine Christi fide apprehenso, purgantur corda nostra ab operibus mortis, Hebr. 9, 14. constat etiam victimis sive sacrificiis incruentis, nempè vitulis labiorum consentientium nomini DOMINI: à quorum exercitiis, neque locorum intervalla, neq; aerumnae quaevis quempiam possunt excludere, Rom. 12, 1. Hebr. 13, 15.

Septimò differunt Beneficiorum perfectione. Vetus enim non habuit ipsam rerum imaginem, sive futura bona: hoc est, ipsam carnem & sanguinem Christi Servatoris: sed tantùm umbram sive typum, Hebr. 10. v. 1. Novum verò habet ipsum corpus CHRISTI, Col. 2, 17.

Octavò differunt Claritate, quâ Novum multis modis superat Veteris obscuritatem, ut quod depulsis umbrarum & typorum nebulis, in clarissima coelestis veritatis, & mysteriorum divinorum luce versatur: & Messiam non ampliùs venturum: sed jam missum atque incarnatum continet.

Tandem differunt Traditione & Ministerio sive effectu. Nam Vetus Testamentum ratione legis, cujus solennis promulgatio praecipua fuit Veteris Testamenti pars, tabulis lapideis inscriptum fuit: Novum verò, ratione Evangelij, cujus universalis praedicatio itidem pars est Novi Testamenti primaria, in cordibus hominum scribitur: Illud fuit literae occidentis: Hoc verò: Spiritus vivificantis: sic docente Propheta, Jer. 31, v. 34. Apostolo 2. Cor. 3, 6.

Caeterùm ex his quae jam dicta sunt, difficiliores nonnullae emergunt Quaestiones, explicatu dignissimae. PRIMA est, de qua hodiè potissimùm controvertitur, An duo haec Testamenta differant ipsa substantiâ, an verò tantum accidentibus, sive alio atq; alio dispensationis modo. Respondemus nos ex jam praesuppositis, differre ea ipsâ substantiâ, non tantùm accidentibus. Substantia autem haec vitiosissimè definitur à Sacramentariis, per ipsam doctrinam justificationis & salutis nostrae: quam certè substantiam, utrobique unam & eandem esse, ultrò admittimus: Sed substantia, de qua hoc loco quaeritur, est, definiente Scriptura, vel umbra rerum futurarum, hoc est, Corporis & Sanguinis Christi: vel ipsifsima haec bona ipso actu jam exhibita & praesentia illud Veteris: hoc Novi Testamenti proprium est. Quemadmodum ergò umbra sive Typus reipsa & secundum substantiam differt, ab ipso Corpore & Antitypo: sic pari ratione duo hæc Testamenta inter se differre necessum est. Sed de hac quæstione in ipsa ἀντιθέσει fusiùs. Porrò quæritur hoc loco: Quatenùs sive quousq́; abrogatum sit Vetus Testamentum: num ex toto, an ex parte tantum? Respondemus abrogatum illud esse ex toto, quoad substantialia ejus. Substantialia verò hæc, uti suprà etiam ostensum fuit, non definiri debent per ipsam doctrinam Decalogi: sed per ea, quæ pertinet ad statum Politiæ, & Ecclesiæ, populi Israelitici proprium. Quâ in parte præcipuè collocantur Lex Ceremonialis & forensis. Sed difficilior jam oritur tertia Quæstio, si Lex Moralis non pertinet ad Substantiam Veteris Testamenti, an ergo ea Novi Testamenti sit propria. Et rursum: Si ad Novum Testamentum non pertinet: an & quomodo ad Vetus referri, & abrogata esse, statui debeat? Respondeo Legem Moralem ad utrumque Testamentum pertinere, ac proindè & abrogatum, & non abrogatum esse: respectu autem diversissimo. Ad Vetus enim pertinuit, 1. quoad continuam & rigidiorem inculcationem, qua conclusi tanquàm in carcere custodiebamur, in eam fidem, quæ per Christum revelanda erat, Galat. 3, 23. Deindè, quoad obscuriorem, minusque perspicuam præceptorum Decalogi traditionem, quæ claritatis lucem accepit, ex interpretatione legis, à Christo proposita, Matth. 5, 6. & 7. capitibus. Tertiò, quoad alternativam illam sententiam, vel ad salutem, si servata esset: vel ad damnationem, si violata. Tribus ergò istis modis ac respectibus, quibus ad Vetus Testamentum lex moralis pertinet, rectissimè etiam statuitur abrogatam sivè antiquatam esse: præcipuè quoad Justificationem & damnationem. Nam Lex nullam habet potestatem condemnandi eos, qui sunt in Christo Jesu: Roman. 8. v. 1. & ex operibus non potest justificari omnis caro, Galat. 2, 16. Imò non est data Lex, quæ possit justificare, Galat. 3, 21. Cæterùm, quia Novum Testamentum, & Remissionem peccatorum, & Renovationem mentis complectitur: siquidem nova sumus in CHRISTO creatura, conditi ad bona opera, Ephes. 2, 10. quorum norma in Decalogo longè perfectissima est proposita: hinc adeò fit, ut jam Decalogus ratione Novæ obedientiæ, ad Novum etiam Testamentum pertineat. Et profectò cum Decalogus nihil sit aliud, quàm immutabilis divinæ Justitiæ regula, hominum naturæ in creatione ipsa insita: utique hoc respectu Decalogus etiam haud magis antiquationem admittit, quàm Natura ipsa hominis, inque ea Naturalia abrogationem planè nullam admittere possunt. Sic ergò sine ulla Contradictione Lex Moralis, & ad Vetus & ad Novum Testamentum referri, & abrogata & non abrogata esse, statui potest.

Quartò quæritur, Annè Lex Ceremonialis nihil de Christo habuerit: & si ea abrogata ex toto, annon indè decedat aliquid doctrinæ Evangelij, quippè quæ solum Christum continet.

Respondeo affirmatè, Legem nimirùm Ceremonialem multa de Christo, ejusdemque beneficiis in se continuisse quidem, sed tantùm sub ratione typi & umbræ: non verò sub ratione ipsius rei, sive corporis. Exempli gratia: Arca fœderis typum gessit Ecclesiæ, quæ tùm demùm vera sit futura, si fœdus, hoc est, Verbum DEI complectatur. Sic Tabulæ Decalogi in arca repositæ, ostendebant Ecclesiam semper fore custodem Scripturæ Sacræ, in quà DEUS se patefecerit. Tabulæ verò aureæ, quà arca tegebatur, Propitiatorii nomen erant, quo Christus Mediator significabatur, cujus propitiatione Ecclesia adversus iram & judicium DEI protegeretur. Duo Cherubim, conspectum mutuum habentes, doctrinæ in utroque Testamento diversum quidem ministerium: sed in eodem consensum elegantem notabant. Usu baculorum & vectium, opera ministrorum præfigurabatur. Verùm cùm hæ imagines & figuræ jam sint impletæ, nullus earum ampliùs usus esse potest.

Verùm hic quinto loco difficilior oritur quæstio. Cùm enim, uti ex jam dictis constat, Lex Ceremonialis doctrinam de persona, officio & beneficiis Christi, & sic Evangelii propriam contineat: quæritur; Annòn potiùs ea ad Novi, quàm ad Veteris Testamenti substantiam referri debeat: & quomodo ea abrogata esse, statui possit? Sed respondeo cum Apostolo, Legem Ceremonialem generatim consideratam, fuisse pædagogum ad Christum, Gal. 3, 24. Item, finem esse legis Christum, Rom. 10, 4.

Jam verò Finis non potest esse pars ipsius rei cujus est finis: sed est aliquid extra Substantiam illius rei. Legalis ergò doctrina, cujus finis est Christus, propria est Veteris Testamenti; ut verò finem huic ipsi doctrinæ tandem imminere, conspicuum esset; fieri certè illud alià ratione non potuit, quàm si huic ipsi doctrinæ, Evangelica quædam, & quidem Novi Testamenti propria essent aspersa. Verùm cùm in his multùm differat res ipsa, per substantiam: & modus rei traditæ, qui est in parte Accidentis: hinc jam ad propositum ζήτημα respondemus: quod res ipsa, non Legis, sed Evangelii; non Veteris sed Novi Testamenti propria sit judicanda: Modus verò rei ad Vetus Testamentum referri debeat, ac proindè abrogationi etiam, imò plenariæ antiquationi subjaceat: imò verè sit abrogatus. Sunt alii Theologi, qui aliter distinguendo respondere solent; dupliciter considerari Ceremonias Leviticas 1. tanquàm opera pædagogica, & exercitia concionum de peccato, de ira Dei, & similibus rebus: Quo respectu eæ ad legem pertineant, & ad Vetus Testamentum: Deindè verò tanquàm Typos Christi: Quo respectu ad Evangelium, & Novum Testamentum pertineant. Quæ Responsio, vera quidem est, & ad analogiam fidei quadrat: sed propositæ Quæstionis nodo solvendo nondùm planè sufficere videtur. Nam semper manet ille scrupulus: Si Ceremoniæ Leviticæ, quatenùs Typi fuerunt, pertinent ad Novum Testamentum, quòd nimirùm abrogari non potuerint? Proindè ut ex difficultate hâc te plenè expedire possis, illud præterea observandum fuerit, ut inter rem, & modum rei accuratissimè distinguas. Nam typus non est res ipsa: sed modus tantùm rei adumbratæ: Qui modus rei planè Legis proprius est, ac proindè jam exhibito Christo, qui es res ipsa, per omnia abrogatus.

Sextò quæritur etiam hoc loco de Tempore, quo Novum Testamentum primùm sit inchoatum? Ansam dubitandi movet illud, quòd Apostolus Galat 2, 17. Evangelium asserit antiquius esse Lege, cum disputat, promissionem illam Evangelii, de Semine, in quo benedicendæ omnes familiæ terræ, non esse abrogatam per Legem, ut quæ quadringentis triginta annis demùm pòst, fuerit promulgata. Sed respondeo, distinguendum esse inter quamlibet promissionem Evangelicam: & inter solennem ac universalem Evangelii prædicationem, sive propagationem in universum terrarum orbem. Promissiones quidem Evangelii de semine mulieris & Abrahæ, statim post lapsum in Paradiso, protoparentibus proponebantur: eædemque omnibus temporibus in Veteri populo, etiam ante Mosen sonuerunt. Et hoc respectu verum est, quòd Apostolus affirmat, promissiones hasce antiquiores esse Lege, non verò simpliciter: Siquidem Lex in ipso Paradiso promulgata est, ubi Concione Evangelica nondùm opus erat: sed tantùm secundum quid, nempè respectu solennis illius dispositionis, quâ à DEO ipso præscriptum & ordinatum fuit, quibus ritibus ac ceremoniis Legis doctrina in populo DEI proponi & exerceri debeat: Quæ una etiam atque sola dispositio, est ac dicitur Vetus Testamentum. Cæterùm quoad solennem atque universalem Evangelii prædicationem & propagationem in totum orbem terrarum, à quâ Novum etiam Testamentum appellationem suam potissimùm accepit: certè multò posterior est, promulgatione Veteris Testamenti. Et quia non nisi exhibito Messia, & Redemtionis Opere consummato, ac Synagogâ sive politiâ Judaica priùs honorificè sepulta, Solennis illa Evangelii promulgatio fieri potuit: statuimus inchoationem Novi Testamenti, licèt ea à temporibus Johannis Baptistæ, initium aliquod & splendorem sit sortita; plenè niorem tamen, & Novi Testamenti propriam revelationem ad ea tempora referendam esse, quæ Ascensionem Christi in Cœlos sunt secuta, quæque dispersionem Apostolorum in universum terrarum orbem, tanquàm Signum ac Symbolum γνήσιον & adæquatum, conjunctum habuerunt.

Tandem & illud quæritur, Nùm Lex Forensis ita sit Veteris Testamenti propria, ita etiam sit abrogata, ut nihil ampliùs de ea, sub Novo Testamento sit reliquum. Respondeo rursus per distinctionem inter Rem & modum Rei, Rem voco, ipsam æquitatem naturalem, in primâ creatione hominum naturis ingeneratam. Rei verò modum voco, certam illam formam, ad quam in exercendis judiciis forensibus, populus Israëliticus erat alligatus: & qui modus solus Veteris Testamenti erat proprius. Res ergò ipsa, haud magis est abrogata, atque Natura hominis abrogari potuit. Quin imò hanc rem ipsam etiam Evangelium, & Novum Testamentum non abolent, sed potiùs confirmant, ut quòd in judiciis forensibus spectanda sit æquitas naturalis, exercenda fides, patientia, dilectio, & id genus virtutes aliæ. Modus autem, qui veteri populo ex præscripto DEI, circa judicia forensia erat observandus, quippè Veteris Testamenti proprius, simpliciter hodiè est abrogatus.


### Chapter II. Antiobetikon. On the Various Corruptions of This Article

We assign the first place in the class of those who err, along with our author, to the Jews, who are found to have fostered three distinct but far most terrible errors concerning this article: of which

PRIMUS was concerning the condition of the New Testament, or the kingdom of the Messiah, which they dreamed was entirely corporal: establishing that the promised Messiah would be an earthly King, distinguished by the abundance and splendor of all things: and understanding nothing at all concerning eternal goods, concerning the redemption of the human race, concerning sin, death, the Devil, concerning righteousness and the salvation of souls.

ALTER their error was concerning the quality of the obedience demanded by the Law, which they understood only as external discipline, being meanwhile not at all solicitous about the motions of the mind, which directly fight against the Law of God, and thus against the will of God and the rule of righteousness: as if they were not sins, or did not deviate from the divine law.

The third error concerned the use and value of the Levitical ceremonies, especially the sacrifices, to which they attributed a clearly meritorious power in the expiation of sins. Deceived by this opinion, therefore, they accumulated sacrifices; indeed, they even devised new ceremonies or adopted heathen ones: they progressed so far in superstition that, under the opinion of worship and merit, they slaughtered their own children and sacrificed them to the idol Molech. To correct this threefold impiety, the study and works of the Prophets were of great service, teaching 1. That the Jewish polity was established by God for this end, that it might be a certain seat of the Church, in which, with the distinction of families preserved, it could stand, from whence the Messiah was to be born, who, having abolished sin and death, was to assert his people into the true liberty of the sons of God. 2. In the Law of God, internal and perfect obedience is chiefly required, which, being impossible for men to perform, the Messiah would eventually fulfill for God, by which divine justice would be satisfied. 3. Finally, that the use and value of the ceremonies were not meritorious or expiatory: but were partly signs and types of the future redemption and propitiation for the sins of the whole human race through the Messiah: and partly testimonies of profession and exercises of faith and invocation: Jer. 7, 22. I did not speak with your fathers, and I did not command them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. Thus Psalm 50 is almost entirely consumed with this argument. Psalm 51, 18. If you had desired sacrifice, I would have given it: you will not delight in burnt offerings. Amos 5, 21. & 22. The Lord says that he hates these things. Isa. 66, 3. He who sacrifices an ox, as if he were killing a man: he who slaughters a beast, as if he were braining a dog, etc. And this very thing was the cause for which the most grievous persecutions and accusations were moved and agitated against the Prophets, as if they were abrogators of the divine law.

Latin:

PRimum in classe errantium locum, cum Autore nostro adsignamus Judæis, qui tres distinctos, sed longè teterrimos errores circa hunc articulum fovisse deprehenduntur: quorum

PRIMUS fuit de conditione Novi Testamenti, sive regni Meffiæ, quod prorsus Corporale somniabant: statuentes, Messiam promifsum, fore Regem terrenum, omnium rerum affluentia & splendore insignem: & nihil quicquam intelligentes de bonis æternis, de redemtione generis humani, de peccato, morte, Diabolo, de Justitia & salute animarum.

ALTER error ipsorum fuit de qualitate Obedientiæ à Lege flagitatæ, quam de externa tantùm disciplinâ intelligebant, nihil interim solliciti, de motibus animi, cum Lege DEI, & sic cum voluntate DEI ac justitiæ regula directè pugnantibus: quasi non essent peccata, aut à lege divina exorbitarent.

TERTIVS error fuit de usu & valore Ceremoniarum Leviticarum, præcipuè Sacrificiorum, quibus isti vim planè meritoriam in expiatione peccatorum tribuebant. Hac ergò decepti opinione, cumulabant Sacrificia; imò & novas ceremonias excogitabant, aut Ethnicas recipiebant: eò usque superstitionis progressi, ut sub opinione cultus & meriti, proprios suos mactarent, & Idolo Molech sacrificarent liberos. Impietati huic triplici corrigendæ plurimùm inservijt Prophetarum studium & Opera, docentium 1. Politiam Judaicam eo fine à Deo constitutam esse, ut esset certa Ecclesiæ sedes, in qua conservato familiarum discrimine constare posset, undè nasciturus esset Messias, qui abolito peccato & morte, ad veram libertatem filiorum Dei, populum suum asserturus efset. 2. In Lege Dei præcipuè requiri internam, eamque perfectam obedientiam, quam hominibus præstitu impossibilem, Messias Deo tandem exoluturus esset, quâ justitiæ divinæ satisfieret. 3. Tandem Ceremoniarum usum ac valorem, non esse meritorium aut expiatorium: sed partim signa esse ac typos futuræ per Messiam redemtionis & propitiationis pro peccatis totius generis humani: partim verò testimonia professionis atque exercitia fidei & invocationis: Jer. 7, 22. Non sum locutus cum Patribus vestris, & non præcepi eis in die, quâ eduxi eos de terra Ægypti, de holocaustis & victimis. Sic Psalmus 50. fermè totus in hoc argumento consumitur. Psalm. 51, 18. Si voluisses Sacrificium, dediffem tibi: holocaustis non delectaberis. Amos 5, 21. & 22. Odio sibi ista esse, dicit Dominus. Jes. 66, 3. Qui immolat bovem, quafi qui interficiat virum: qui mactat pecus, quasi qui excerebret canem &c. Et hæc ipsa causa fuit, ob quam in Prophetas, tanquàm abrogatores legis divinæ, gravissimæ persecutiones ac criminationes motæ & agitatæ fuerunt.


### Chapter II. Antiobetikon. On the Various Corruptions of This Article: II. Certain Ancient Fathers

We assign the second place among the erring to certain older Fathers, who, embracing the tenets of the Gentile philosophers a little too greedily, finally descended into such a hyperbole that they concocted not just two, but three distinct Testaments, and from that, a threefold method of justification. They described the first Testament as the age of the Patriarchs, up to Moses: and they contended that it consisted solely of the Law of nature and the observance of the same: and that by this pact the Patriarchs were also saved. They included the second Testament in the age of Moses: in which the Law of Moses prevailed, and by its observance the Israelites were saved. Finally, the third

Testament they established as proper to Christ, who promulgated a certain new law, by the observance of which men must now be saved. The champions of this error were chiefly Justin the Philosopher and Martyr: and Clement of Alexandria. In our own century, Zwingli, Andradius, Isengrinius, and many others, having emerged partly from the school of the Sacramentarians and partly from that of the Romanists, have made this error for the most part their own, establishing that philosophers and other wiser Gentiles were justified and saved before God by the Law of Nature alone. But we have dealt with that error expressly elsewhere, namely in the Article on the justification of man before God. Only two things, which pertain to the present Article, are to be well observed here: I. By this error, the very method of our justification and salvation is most viciously confused with the proper nature and Essence of a Testament properly so called: which two things, however, it was abundantly shown above, differ greatly from each other. II. By this error, different modes of justification are established, or rather concocted: the contrary of which Scripture clearly proves: which, just as it acknowledges One in number Christ and Mediator: 1 Tim. 2, 5. so it also defines and confirms One in number Church, one faith, one way of salvation, Ephes. 4, 4. Acts 15, 11. The Apostle evidently asserts this very thing in Rom. 4, having brought forward as examples from both preceding ages, namely Abraham and David, who were saved only by faith in the Messiah, by which all who similarly believe in him today are also saved: so much so that the Epistle to the Hebrews, for this very reason, extends Christ to both Testaments, saying, Christ is yesterday and today, and forever: chap. 13, 8.

Latin:

Alterum inter errantes locum tribuimus Patribus quibusdam vetustioribus, qui Gentilium Philosophorum placita, paulò avidiùs amplectentes, in eam tandem descenderunt hyperbolen, ut non duo tantùm, sed Tria distincta Testamenta, indè triplicem Justificandi rationem, confinxerint. Primum Testamentum describebant seculo Patriarcharum, usque ad Mosen: idque solâ Lege naturæ, ejusdemque observatione constitiisse: & hoc pacto Patriarchas etiam salvatos fuisse, contendebant. Alterum Testamentum seculo Mosis includebant: in quo Lex Mosis viguerit, & ejus observatione Jsraelitæ salvati fuerint. Tertium denique

Testamentum statuebant esse Christi proprium, qui novam quandam legem promulgaverit, cujus observatione jam homines salvari oporteat. Erroris hujus propugnatores præcipuè fuerunt Iustinus Philosophus, & Martyr: & Clemens Alexandrinus. Nostro verò seculo errorem hunc maximam partem suum fecit Zvinglius, Andradius, Isengrinius, & alij complures partim ex Sacramentariorum, partim ex Romanensium scholâ egressi, statuentes, Philosophos, & alios sapientiores Gentiles, solâ Lege Naturæ coram Deo justificatos & salvatos fuisse. Sed de errore isto alibi ex professo egimus, nempè in Articulo de Justificatione hominis coram Deo. Duo tantùm hoc loco, quæ ad præsentem Articulum faciunt, probè observanda veniunt: I. Errore isto vitiosissimè ipsam Justificationis & salutis nostræ rationem confundi cum propria natura atque Essentia Testamenti propriè sic dicti: quæ duo tamen inter se plurimum differre, supra abundè fuit ostensum. II. Errore isto, diversos constitui, vel confingi potiùs justificationis modos: cujus contrarium Scriptura luculenter evincit: quæ uti Unum numerum Christum & Mediatorem agnoscit: 1. Timoth. 2, 5. ita Unam etiam numero Ecclesiam, fidem unam, unam salutis viam definit, & confirmat Ephes. 4, 4. Actior 15, 11. Quod ipsum evidenter admodùm adstruit Apostolus Rom. 4. productis in medium exemplis, ex utroque seculo antegresso, Abrahami nimirùm & Davidis, qui non nisi fide in Messiam salvati sint, quâ salventur hodieque omnes consimiliter in ipsum credentes: usque adeò ut Epistola ad Hebræos, Christum hanc ipsam ob causam ad utrumque Testamentum extendat, Christus, inquiens, est heri & hodiè, & in secula: cap. 13, 8.


### Chapter II. Antiobetikon. On the Various Corruptions of This Article: III. Pontificians and Scholastics

Since some of the Fathers taught less appropriately concerning the nature of the Testaments, it happened that in the progress of time the Scholastic Doctors, following in their footsteps, contended that both Testaments, as much the New as the Old, were to be defined by nothing but mere legal doctrine: yet with this distinction, that the Law of Moses or the Old Testament proposed precepts that were imperfect and easier to keep, since they dealt only with external and bodily things and benefits: but the Law of Christ, or the New Testament, delivers precepts that are more perfect and more difficult, since they deal with internal and spiritual virtues.

But there are some among the Papists who heap error upon error, establishing that the Old with the New:

And that the New has always been mixed with the Old Testament: indeed in such a way that when the Law is proposed to the old man, and sin is increased thereby: there the nature of the Old Testament prevails: But when the Holy Spirit inscribes the Law in the renewed mind of man, beginning a New Obedience according to the Law, then it is called the New Testament. But this is nothing other than making one confused and corrupt thing out of two whole ones: that is: to mix heaven with earth, and to offer manifest violence to the Scriptures. For 1. Christ is nowhere in the whole Scripture described as a new lawgiver, or even as another Moses: but only as Redeemer, Mediator, and Savior. And although Christ himself also wished to be engaged in the interpretation of the Mosaic law in the fifth chapter of Matthew: he did not, however, oppose his own doctrine to the Mosaic doctrine, or wish to add any such ἐπανόρθωσιν (correction) to the Mosaic law, as if he had bound the mandates of his law to a higher degree of perfection than had been done by Moses, or even than could have been done. But the Savior fights there solely for the true and genuine sense of the Mosaic law, against the depravations of the Pharisees. Nor was it ever his intention to change even a single apex of the law. 2. This error fights against the very doctrine of the Mosaic law. For it prescribes such a norm of living that to those observing it, eternal life ought to be conferred as a reward and a debt. For this is the sum of that law: You shall love God with all your heart, etc., and your neighbor as yourself. Now let the Papists show: Whether any greater or more perfect, or more difficult precept can be added to this Mosaic Law? Which they will never demonstrate. 3. Christ himself nowhere prescribes new mandates to be kept by men: but refers them to the precepts of Moses: if you wish, he says, to enter into life, keep the commandments of God. Matt. 19, 17. 4. The Apostle does not say the Law is weak in itself: but calls it holy, good, just: and pronounces that it is weakened only through our flesh. Rom. 8, 3. 5. That error is blasphemous against God himself, the author of the Mosaic Law. For it imagines that God, through Moses, wished to inform only the eyes, hands, feet, and the remaining external members of man: and indeed only for some external appearance of piety. By which manner, indeed, the Justice and Wisdom of God are quite blasphemously called into doubt. 6: The Law of Moses itself, even according to the external letter, beats back this insanity of the Papists: as when Moses prohibits the internal desire for vengeance: Levit. 19, 18. You shall not seek revenge: nor will you be mindful of the injury of your citizens: and v. 17. you shall not hate your brother in your heart. Finally, this error defines the Testament most viciously through the doctrine of the law itself: which was demonstrated above to be false.

IV. ANABAPTISTS.

The faction of the Anabaptists, judaizing not obscurely in this article, defines the nature of both Testaments through external things, through the form of polity, and public laws. Upon this false hypothesis, they build that other, falser one, by which they contend most absurdly: Since the people of the Old Testament were bound by laws, and likewise subject to a political Magistrate, and on this account overwhelmed by various burdens of servitude: but that Old Testament is now not only abrogated: but also Christ under the New Testament has asserted us into liberty: therefore Christians are now so free that they ought not to obey civil laws, nor be subject to a political Magistrate, nor undergo political burdens, such as Wars, Oaths, Tributes, and other things of that kind. A solid refutation of which horrendous error will be set forth, God willing, in the Article concerning civil Magistrates. In this place, it deserves observation that the New Testament is indeed rightly defined by Evangelical Liberty: but not such that it is any ἀνομία (lawlessness) or ἀναρχία (anarchy), and which permits to anyone the license to live in external matters according to their own will: but which is the faculty of acting and living according to the norm, according to which the Reborn, and those liberated through Christ, ought to institute the reasons of their life and morals. Now, however, the Gospel does not take away the Laws of the Decalogue, nor does it abolish polities: Matt. 22, 21, Luke 22, 25. Rom. 13, 1. 1 Tim. 6, 1. 1 Pet. 2, 13 & 18. All of which places would certainly not subsist if, by the right of the New Testament, all were indiscriminately asserted into external or political liberty. Whence we most firmly conclude that the condition or nature of the Testament in both peoples, as much in the New as in the Old, is by no means to be referred to the external or political state itself.

Latin:

Cùm Patrum nonnulli minùs commodè de natura Testamentorum docerent, factum est, ut progressu temporis Doctores Scholastici, illorum vestigia secuti, Utrumque Testamentum, tàm Novum, quàm Vetus definiendum esse, contenderent, non nisi per meram doctrinam legalem: sub eo tamen discrimine, quòd Lex Mosis sive Vetus Testamentum proposuerit præcepta imperfecta, & servatu faciliora, quippè de rebus ac beneficijs tantùm externis & corporalibus agentia: Lex verò Christi, sive Novum Testamentum tradat præcepta perfectiora, & difficiliora, quippè de interioribus & spiritualibus virtutibus agentia.

Sed sunt nonnulli ex Pontificijs, qui errorem errore cumulant, statuentes, Vetus cum Novo:

& Novum cum Veteri Testamento semper fuisse permixtum: ita quidem, ut quando Veteri homini Lex proponitur, & indè augetur peccatum: ibi veteris Testamenti ratio obtineat: Quando verò Spiritus Sanctus in mente hominis renovata, Legem inscribit, inchoantem Novam Obedientiam juxta Legem, tum vocari Novum Testamentum. Verùm hoc nihil est aliud, quàm ex duobus integris, facere unum confusum corruptum: hoc est: Cœlum terræ miscere, & vim manifestam Scripturis inferre. Nam 1. Christus nuspiam in universâ Scriptura describitur ut novus legis lator, vel ut alter quidem Moses: sed tantùm ut Redemtor, Mediator, & Salvator. Et quanquàm in interpretatione legis Mosaicæ Christus quoque ipse versari voluit Matthæi quinto capite: non tamen suam doctrinam, doctrinæ Mosaicæ opposuit, vel legi Mosaicæ talem aliquam ἐπανόρθωσιν addere voluit, quasi ad altiorem quendam perfectionis gradum, legis suæ mandata alligaverit, quàm à Mose factum sit, aut fieri etiam potuerit. Sed pro vero & genuino sensu legis Mosaicæ, adversus depravationes Pharisæorum, unicè ibi depugnat Servator. Neque unquàm ipsi fuit propositum vel unicum legis apicem mutare. 2. Pugnat hic error, cum ipsa doctrina legis Mosaicæ. Ea enim ejusmodi normam vivendi præscribit, ut observantibus illam vita æterna, tanquàm merces ac debitum, conferri debeat. Hæc enim est summa legis illius: Diliges Deum ex toto corde &c. & proximum sicut teipsum. Jam ostendant Pontificij: Vtrum ullum majus aut perfectius, aut difficilius præceptum, Legi huic Mosaicæ addi possit? Id quod in æternum non demonstrabunt. 3. Christus ipse nuspiam nova mandata hominibo servanda præscribit: sed ad præcepta Mosis eos ablegat: si vis in quiens, ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata Dei. Matth. 19, 17. 4. Apostolus Legem non dicit in se esse infirmam: sed nominat eam sanctam, bonam, justam: & non nisi per carnem nostram infirmari pronunciat. Rom. 8, 3. 5. Error iste blasphemus est in Deum ipsum, Legis Mosaicæ autorem. Fingit enim Deum per Mosen informare tantùm voluisse, oculos, manus, pedes, & reliqua externa tantùm hominis membra: & quidem ad externam tantùm aliquam pietatis speciem. Quo sanè pacto Justitia & Sapientia Dei satis blasphemè in dubium vocantur. 6: Ipsa Lex Mosis, etiam secundum externam literam, hanc Pontificiorum insaniam retundit: ut quando Moses internam vindictæ cupiditatem prohibet: Levit. 19, 18. Ne quæras ultionem: nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum: & v. 17. non oderis fratrem tuum in Corde tuo. Tandem error iste definit vitiosissimè Testamentum, per ipsam doctrinam legis: id quod falsum esse, supra demonstratum fuit.

IV. ANABAPTISTAE.

Anabaptistarum factio, hoc in articulo haud obscurè judaizans, definit utriusque Testamenti rationem, per res externas, per formam politiae, & jura publica. Falsae huic hypothesi, superstruunt falsiorem istam alteram, quâ nimis absurdè contendunt: Cùm Veteris Testamenti populus legibus fuerit devinctus, item Magistratui politico subjectus, & hoc nomine varijs servitutis oneribus obrutus: Vetus autem illud Testamentum jam non modò sit abrogatum: sed & Christus sub Novo Testamento, in libertatem nos asseruerit: ideò Christianos jam ita esse liberos, ut neque legibus civilibus parere, neque Magistratui politico subesse, neque onera politica, qualia sunt, Bella, Iuramenta, Tributa, & id genus alia subire debeant. Cujus horrendi erroris solida refutatio σὺν Θεῷ in Articulo de Magistratibus civilibus expedietur. Hoc loco illud observationem meretur, quòd Novum Testamentum rectè quidem definitur, per Libertatem Evangelicam: verùm non talem, quæ sit ἀνομία sive ἀναρχία aliqua, quæque in externis pro arbitrio vivendi licentiam cuivis permittat: sed quæ sit facultas agendi & vivendi, secundum normam, ad quam Renati, & per Christum liberati, vitæ morumque suorum rationes instituere debent. Jam verò Evangelium non tollit vel Leges Decalogi, vel abolet politias: Matth. 22, 21, Luc. 22, 25. Rom. 13, 1. 1. Tim. 6, 1. 1. Petr. 2, 13 & 18. Quæ sanè loca omnia non subsisterent, si Novi Testamenti jure, in libertatem externam sive politicam promescuè omnes assererentur. Vndè firmissimè colligimus, Conditionem sive naturam Testamenti in utroœ, populo, tàm Novo, quàm Veteri, ad statum ipsum externum sive politicum, minimè referendum esse.


### Chapter II. Antiobetikon. On the Various Corruptions of This Article: V. Sacramentarians, or Calvinists

The Sacramentarian tribe contends that the distinction of the Testaments of God into Old and New is not one of Genus into species, but merely of Subject into Accidents: and therefore that these two Testaments differ not in substance itself but only in qualities or the accidental mode of revelation or dispensation: just as Petrus Martyr writes, part 1 of the Theological Commonplaces: Place XVI. §. 2. But this error arises from a false Definition of the Testaments, while, namely, the Adversaries think that the whole nature of the Testament is to be referred to the doctrine of salvation itself, and the promise of grace made to the human race in Christ. Now, however, just as this is one and the same, and has been from the time of the first published Evangelical promise perpetual and immutable: so they insist that the Testament is also one and the same, and that it is invariable: Indeed, just as the Church of the Saints is one before and after Christ was born, one way to the Heavens, one religion of all the Saints, one Christ: so they contend that there is also one, perpetual and immutable Testament of God: namely that which God struck with Abraham in Genesis 17: as Szegedinus repeatedly writes in his Common Places, pages 72 and 76, as also Wolfgang Musculus in his Common Places, page 178. Now if it be objected by our opponents that the nature and definition of a Testament ought to be referred not to the doctrine of salvation itself, but to the diverse dispensation which, according to the counsel of divine wisdom, was instituted differently before and after the birth of Christ, they indeed readily profess to grant this; but they immediately object with Calvin that this is done improperly, and that that diverse dispensation is to be considered only as an accident, which in no way detracts from the Testament or covenant in its substance, which is one and the same. This error is too intricate for anyone to be able to extricate himself from it so easily; and truly, as the saying goes, here the snake lurks in the grass. For while this error stands, they immediately infer: 1. That there is one and the same thing, or substance, of the Sacraments of both Testaments. 2. Sacramental signs, namely the elemental part of the Sacraments of the Old Testament, were indeed changed by the counsel of God: but the heavenly thing remained the same in both with respect to substance. 3. Therefore, in the Sacraments of the New Testament, the very Body and Blood of Christ are not really present and dispensed: but that substance is present which was also proper to the Sacraments of the Old Testament; namely, typical sacramental signs, or figurative symbols, shadowing forth the Body and Blood of Christ, absent from the Sacrament dispensed here on earth by as great an interval as the highest Heaven is distant from the lowest earth: as Beza speaks in the Colloquy of Poissy. And this is that acropolis whose foundations the Calvinists, with great effort indeed, strive to lay in the present article.

But that we may happily extricate ourselves from that labyrinth, a most accurate distinction must be made between the things themselves, which the adversaries lay down as a foundation, and the application of those same things to the present question concerning the nature and definition of the Testaments.

As for the things themselves which they bring forward in this opinion of theirs, it is true in itself and separately that there is one way of salvation, one promise of grace, one covenant of God regarding the business of our justification and salvation: one faith; and finally, one eternal life. Thus it is also true that there was one dispensation of this very doctrine of salvation in the Old Testament, and another in the New. But as for the two things they infer from this: 1. That the Testaments of God are to be properly defined by the same doctrine of salvation: 2. That the Testament is one in substance: we simply deny both; and we are most persuaded that neither can be elicited from the presuppositions by any artifice of truth.

For the flaw in the accommodation is detected to be manifold. For first, it was demonstrated above in the thesis that the doctrine of salvation and the promise of grace in the present passage can neither be called, nor ought to be called, a Testament, for the reasons alleged there.

Then it is also false what they contend, that that diverse dispensation of religion is only improperly called a Testament, and that it does not pertain to its substance, but only happens to it as a certain external accident. Now, it was likewise demonstrated most evidently above that the proper nature and affection, or ἴδιον πάθος, of any Testament regards that diverse dispensation of doctrine only properly and principally, and that this constitutes not an accident, but the very substance of the Testaments.

Thirdly, Scripture utterly overturns the opinion of the Calvinists, in express words counting not one, but two diverse Testaments. Jer. 31:31; Gal. 4:24; and it elicits this binary number not merely from the name alone, but accurately accommodates it to the very mysteries of our religion: as is especially to be seen in the cited passage from the Epistle to the Galatians.

Fourthly: The doctrine of salvation is common to diverse peoples: the individual Testaments are proper to individual peoples. Therefore, one and the same substance and reason for both is not to be established.

Fifthly: Testaments admit of variation: whence it is that they have been given the names of Old and New. What of the fact that for the one, namely the Old Testament, abrogation and an end have already long since occurred? Heb. 8:13. Yet neither of these falls upon the doctrine of salvation, or the promises of grace, which is clearly immutable, and has always stood by itself, and will stand equably until the end of the world. Therefore, the nature of the Testaments can in no way be defined by this doctrine of salvation.

Sixthly: as much as the blood of a calf and the blood of Christ differ from each other, so much do these two Testaments also differ from each other. The reason for the connection is that the blood of a calf constituted the substance of the Old Testament. Exod. 24:8. But the blood of Christ constitutes the substance of the New Testament: Matt. 26:28; Mark 14:24; Luke 22:20; 1 Cor. 11:25. Yet they differ in species, or substance. Therefore, these two Testaments also differ in species and substance: and consequently, they cannot be properly defined by one doctrine in number.

Seventhly: The opinion of the Sacramentarians overturns itself: and it tacitly asserts that very thing which it presumes to deny. For what, I ask, is it to concede a twofold and diverse dispensation of religion in one covenant of divine grace in substance, than to establish a twofold testamentary disposition in the business of the heavenly inheritance, which we ourselves also readily grant to be one in substance? For just as that disposition by which the same goods are to come to the heirs, And indeed by the law of nature, those who are to arrive: yet it is provided by the Testator, in what manner, in what order, and with what distinction those things ought to come to the heirs through the will of the testator, just as, I say, such a disposition is named a Testament: So that disposition also is most rightly called a Testament, by which God, under the cause and business of the same heavenly inheritance, according to the diversity of peoples and times, instituted one mode of religion after another, according to the counsel of divine wisdom. Now therefore, just as he would be clearly absurd who argued that a testamentary constitution is not but one, in entering upon and dividing the same inheritance: so he is no more rightly wise who, on account of the same doctrine of salvation, has concluded that a diversity of divine Testaments, as regards the thing and the substance itself, cannot have a place.

Eighthly and lastly, this opinion of the Sacramentarians is to be rejected for this reason alone, because it manifestly strikes against the analogy of faith, while it lays snares for the Truth and Substance of the Sacraments of the New Testament: and denies and destroys the real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ.

The Sacramentarians object, using this argument especially: In both Testaments, the benefits are the same, the salutary fruit is the same: and finally, the salvation is the same. But in the Old Testament, no other participation took place than that of the merits of Christ, applied through faith. Therefore, in the New Testament also, no other communication takes place than that of the merit of Christ, and indeed only through faith: nor should the Essential presence of the Body of Christ, as the substance of the New Testament, be urged by any pact.

I answer. 1. To the Major, a fallacy is committed παρὰ τὸ πῆ, καὶ ἁπλῶς [in a certain respect and simply]. For it is true that in both Testaments the benefits are the same, and the fruits are the same: but in a certain respect: namely, with respect to the benefits themselves, considered in themselves and by themselves. But now, if you look at the means and organs through which the communication of those benefits can reach us through the substance of the same: then indeed the Major proposition is most false. Now as for the Minor, although it may be true, it labors under such an imperfection that it is very apt to deceive the more inexperienced. For it sophistically defines only that one medium which is proper to the Gospel, namely Faith: which we easily grant to be one and the same for all believers in both Testaments: But it omits quite insidiously, and craftily conceals, those sealing and confirming Media, the promises of Grace; which are proper to the Sacraments, concerning which, however, the chief controversy is in this place. Unless, therefore, the Adversaries wish to foist upon us an Assumption of this kind, which labors under the manifest vice of παρὰ τὸ ἐλλιπὲς διαιρέσεως [deficiency of division], in the insufficient enumeration of the means of salvation: then they have a necessity to form the Assumption thus: But in the Old Testament, no other participation took place than that of the merits of Christ, applied through faith: nor was the promise of grace sealed by any other means and

Sacramental organs: than those by which it is sealed today in the New Testament. Now if the Minor is formed thus, then its latter member is detected to be most false and to labor under a shameful begging of the question: since these means and organs are not the same, but far different, indeed different in species, and therefore different according to substance. For in the Old they were typical and figurative, namely the blood of calves and goats: But in the New they are exhibitive means and organs, and containing the thing itself, namely the true and Essential Body: the true and essential Blood of Christ: by which, in the use of the Sacrament, the true and real Sealing of the promise of Grace reaches us. Now therefore, unless the Type of the Old Testament is imagined to have been a̓́τυπος [without type], it follows ἐξανάγκης [of necessity] that in the New Testament, not a Type any longer: but an Antitype, namely the Body and Blood of Christ itself, must be established as the Substance of the New Testament. Finally, an insidious ignorance of the refutation is also hidden in this argument: while, namely, the Sacramentarians sophistically refer the Body and Blood of Christ among the fruit and Spiritual goods: that which cannot subsist in the doctrine of the Sacraments. Since the Body and Blood, by the force of the words of Institution, must be referred to the class of means: indeed to the class of substantial parts of the Sacrament: that which the Adversaries themselves also, outside of this conflict, willingly confess: as will be demonstrated expressly, σὺν θεῷ [with God], in its proper place in the doctrine concerning the Sacraments.

Latin:

Contendit gens Sacramentaria, distinctionem Testamentorum Dei in Vetus & Novum, non esse Generis in species, sed duntaxat Subjecti in Accidentia: ac proindè duo hæc Testamenta, non ipsâ Substantiâ sed tantùm qualitatibus sive revelationis aut dispensationis accidentaria modo differre: quemadmodum scribit Petrus Martyr, part. 1. Locorum Theologicorum: Loco XVI. §. 2. Oritur autem error iste ex falsâ Testamentorum Definitione, dùm nimirùm Adversarij opinantur, omnem Testamenti rationem, ad ipsam doctrinam salutis, & promissionem gratiæ in Christo, generi humano factam, esse referendam. Jam verò, quemadmodum hæc una est atque eadem, & jam indè à tempore editæ primæ promissionis Evangelicæ perpetua atque immutabilis: ita unum quoque atque idem, idque invariabile Testamentum esse dictitant: Imò quemadmodum una est ante & post Christum natum Sanctorum Ecclesia, una ad Cœlos via, una Sanctorum omnium religio, unus Christus: ita unum etiam, perpetuum atque immutabile Testamentum Dei esse, contendunt: nempè illud, quod Genes. 17. cum Abrahamo Deus pepigerit: uti scriptitant Szegedinus inLocis Communibus, pag. 72, & 76. ut & Wolff. Musculus, in Locis Communibus, p. 178. Jam si à nostris illis obijciatur, Testamenti Naturam ac definitionem, non ad doctrinam ipsam salutis: sed ad diversam dispensationem esse referendam, quæ pro Consilio divinæ sapientiæ, aliter atque aliter ante & post Christum natum fuerit instituta: tùm ultrò se hoc largiri quidem dictitant: sed statim cum Calvino excipiunt, impropriè istud fieri: & diversam illam dispensationem in parte duntaxat accidentis, esse habendam, quæ Testamento aut fœderi, per substantiam, uni atque eidem nihil prorsus deroget. Intricatior est error iste, quàm ut quisque ita facilè se expedire possit:& verè quod dicitur hîc latet anguis in herba. Nam stante errore isto, mox inferunt: 1. Unam eandemq;, etiam esse Sacramentorum utriusq; Testamenti Rem, sive substantiam. 2. Signa Sacramentalia, nempè Sacramentorum Veteris Testamenti partem Elementarem, Dei consilio esse quidem mutata: Sed rem Cælestem utrobiq; ratione Substantiæ eandem mansisse. 3. In Sacramentis ergò Novi Testamenti non realiter adesse, & dispensari, ipsum Corpus & Sanguinem Christi:sed adesse eam substantiam, quæ etiam Sacramentorum Veteris Testamenti fuerit propria: nempè Signa Sacramentalia typica, sive Symbola figurativa, & adumbrantia Corpus & Sanguinem Christi, tanto intervallo à Sacramento hisce in terris dispensato absentia, quanto distat summum Cœlum ab imâ terrâ: uti loquitur Beza in Colloquio Possiaceno. Et hæc est acropolis illa, cujus fundamenta in præsente articulo, magno certè conatu, ponere student Calviniani.

Cæterùm ut ex isto labyrintho nos feliciter expediamus, accuratissimè distinguendum fuerit, inter res ipsas, quas fundamenti loco substernunt adversarij: & inter earundem rerum applicationem ad præsentem quæstionem, de natura ac definitione Testamentorum.

Quoad res ipsas, quas in hac opinione sua proferunt, per se, & seorsim verum est, Unam esse viam salutis, Unam promissionem Gratiæ, Unum fœdus Dei, quoad Justificationis & salutis nostræ negocium: Unam fidem; Unam denique Vitam æternam. Sic verum est & illud, hujus ipsius unius doctrinæ salutis aliam fuisse dispensationem in Veteri: aliam in Novo Testamento. Cæterùm quod indè duo inferunt: 1. Testamenta Dei, per eandem salutis doctrinam propriè esse definienda: 2. Vnum per substantiam esse Testamentum: id verò utrumque simpliciter negamus: neque ex præsuppositis ullo veritatis artificio elici posse habemus persuasissimum.

Nam vitium in accommodatione multiplex deprehenditur. Primùm enim supra in thesi demonstratum est, Doctrinam salutis & promissionem gratiæ in præsenti loco Testamentum appellari nec posse, nec debere, ob causas ibi allegatas.

Deindè falsum est & illud, quod contendunt, diversam illam religionis dispensationem impropriè tantùm dici Testamentum, & pertinere eam non ad Substantiam ejus, sedeantùm ut accidens quoddam forinsecus ei abtingere. Jam verò propriam naturam atque affectionem, sive ἴδιον πάθος, cujuslibet Testamenti, tantùm propriè ac principaliter respicere, diversam illam doctrinæ dispensationem, & hanc non accidens, sed ipsam Testamentorum Substantiam constituere, itidem supra evidentissimè fuit demonstratum.

Tertiò Calvinianorum sententiam prorsus evertis Scriptura, disertis verbis, non unum, sed duo diversa Testamenta numerans. Jerem. 31, 31. Galat. 4, 24. & binarium istum numerum, nō ex nuda tantùm appellatione eliciens; sed ad mysteria ipsa religionis nostræ, accuratè accommodans: uti cumprimis videre est citato loco ex Epistola ad Galatas.

Quartò: Doctrina salutis diversorum populorum communis est: Testamenta singula, singulorum sunt propria. Non est ergò una atque eadem utriusque Substantia atque ratio constituenda.

Quintò: Testamenta Variationem recipiunt: Undè est, quod Vetustatis & Novitatis appellationem eadem sunt fortita. Quid quod alteri, nempè Veteri Testamento antiquatio & finis jampridem obtigit: Hebr. 8, 13. Atqui neutrum horum cadit in doctrinam salutis, sive promissionum gratiæ, quæ planè est immutabilis, & sibi semper constitit, & ad finem usque mundi constabit æquabiliter. Ergò Testamentorum etiam natura, per doctrinam hanc salutis definiri nullo modo potest.

Sextò: quantum à se mutuò differunt Sanguis vitulinus: & sanguis Christi: tantum à se mutuò etiam differunt duo hæc Testamenta. Ratio connexi est, quia sanguis vitulinus constituebat substantiam Veteris Testamenti. Exod. 24, 8. sanguis autem Christi constituit Substantiam Novi Testamenti: Matth. 26, 28. Marc. 14, 24. Luc. 22. 20. 1. Cor. 11, 25. Atquî differunt ipsa specie, sive Substantia. Ergò ipsa quoque duo hæc Testamenta differunt speciei & substantia: ac per consequens, per unam numero doctrinam, propriè definiri non possunt.

Septimò: Opinio Sacramentariorum seipsam evertit: & illud ipsum quod negare præsumit, tacitè astruit. Quid enim obsecrò est, concedere geminam ac diversam Religionis dispensationem, in uno per substantiam Gratiæ divinæ fædere: quam in hæreditatis cœlestis negotio, quod per substantiam unum esse, nos ipsi quoque ultrò largimur, dispositionem testamentariam geminam constituere? Nam quemadmodum dispositio ea, quâ de bonis ijsdem ad hæredes perventuris, & quidem jure naturæ, perventuris: cavetur tamen à Testatore, quo modo ad hæredes, quo ordine,quo discrimine per voluntatem testantis ea venire debeant, quemadmodum inquam talis dispositio nominatur Testamentum: Ita ea quoque dispositio rectissimè Testamentum appellatur, qua Deus, sub hæreditatis cœlestis causa & negotio eodem, pro diversitate populorum & temporum Religionis modum alium atque alium, pro divinæ sapientiæ consilio instituit. Jam ergo quemadmodum absurdus planè foret, qui testamentariam constitutionem non nisi unam esse pugnaret, in adeundâ, & herciscundâ hæreditate eâdem : ita nihilo rectiùs sapit, qui propter doctrinam salutis eandem, diversitatem divinorum Testamentorum, quoad rem ac Substantiam ipsam, locum habere non posse, collegerit.

Octavò & postremò vel hanc solam ob causam opinio hæc Sacramentariorum repudianda est, quia manifestè impingit in analogiam fidei, dùm Veritati ac Substantiæ Sacramentorum Novi Testamenti insidias struit: & Corporis ac Sanguinis Christi realem præsentiam negat, ac destruit.

Excipiunt Sacramentarij, hoc potissimùm usi argumento: In utroque Testamento, eadem sunt beneficia, fructus salutaris idem: eadem deniq; salus. Atqui in Veteri Testamento nulla alia, quàm meritorum Christi, per fidem applicatorum, fiebat participatio. Ergò in Novo quoq; Testamento, nulla alia, quàm meriti Christi & quidem non nisi per fidem fit communicatio: neq; Essentialis Corporis Christi præsentia, tanquàm Novi Testamenti substantia,ullo pacto urgeri debet.

Respondeo. 1. ad Majorem, committi Sophisma παρὰ τὸ πῆ, καὶ ἁπλῶς. Verum enim est, quòd in utroque Testamento eadem sint beneficia, ijfdemque fructus: sed secundum quid: nempè respectu ipsorum beneficiorum, in se & per se consideratorum. Jam verò si media atque organa spectes, per quæ beneficiorum istorum, per substantiam eorundem, nobis obtingere potest Communicatio : tùm sanè Major propositio est falsissima. Jam quoad Minorem, ea licèt vera sit, imperfectione tamen tali laborat, quæ ad decipiendum imperitiores valdè est apta. Nam Sophisticè unum tantùm illud medium, quòd est Evangelij proprium,nempè Fidem, definit: quam in utroque Testamento omnibus fidelibus unam eandemque esse, facilè largimur: Verùm insidiosè satis omittit, & subdolè occultat Media illa obsignantia & Confirmantia, promissiones Gratiæ; quæ Sacramentorum sunt propria, de quibus tamen hoc loco præcipua est controversia. Nisi ergò ejusmodi Assumtionem nobis obtrudere velint Adversarij, quæ laboret manifesto vitio παρὰ τὸ ἐλλιπὲς διαιρέσεως, in sufficientis enumerationis mediorum salutis: tùm necessè habent, ut Assumtionem sic informent : Atqui in Veteri Testamento, nulla alia, quàm meritorum Christi, per fidem applicatorum fiebat participatio: nullis etiam alijs medijs atque

Organis Sacramentalibus obsignabatur promissio gratiæ: quàm quibus hodieque in Novo Testamento obsignatur. Jam si sic informetur Minor,tùm posterius ejus membrum deprehenditur esse falsissimum & laborare turpi petitione principij: siquidem non eadem,sed longè diversissima, imò specie, ac proindè secundum substantiam differentia sunt media & organa isthæc. In Veteri enim erant typica & figurativa, nempè sanguis vitulinus & hircinus : In Novo verò sunt media & organa exhibitiva, & ipsam rem continentia, nempè verum & Essentiale Corpus: verus & essentialis Sanguis Christi: quibus nobis in Sacramenti usu,obtingit vera ac realis Obsignatio promissionis Gratiæ. Jam ergò nisi Typus Veteris Testamenti, fingatur fuisse a̓́τυπος, utique ἐξανάγκης consequitur, in Novo Testamento non ampliùs Typum: sed Antitypum, ipsum nimirum Corpus & Sanguinem Christi, constituendum esse Novi Testamenti Substantiam. Tandem occultatur etiam insidiosa Elenchi ignoratio in hoc argumento: dùm nimirum Sacramentarij Corpus & Sanguinem Christi Sophisticè referunt, inter fructum, & bona Spiritualia: id quod in doctrina Sacramentorum non potest subsistere. Siquidem Corpus & Sanguis, vi verborum Institutionis in classem mediorum: imò in classem partium Sacramenti substantialium referenda sunt: id quod aliàs ipsi quoque Adversarij, extra istum conflictum, ultrò fatentur: uti in doctrina de Sacramentis suo loco, σὺν θεῷ ex professo demonstrabitur.


### Chapter II. Antiobetikon. On the Various Corruptions of This Article: V. Sacramentarians, or Calvinists (continued)

But there are others among the Sacramentarians who propose this very argument in another, but cruder form: in this manner:

The goods and fruits of both Testaments are the same. But in the Old Testament, the Sacraments had nothing but types and figures of Christ. Therefore, the Sacraments of the New Testament also contain not the substance, the Body and Blood of Christ: but only signs and figures of the same; although now incarnate. But this sophistry incurs the same absurdities which we noted in the former. But above all, the whole connection of the argument proceeds from a false hypothesis, namely that which the Adversaries repeatedly carry in their mouths as a rule ἀναπόδεικτον [undemonstrable] and αὐτόπιστον [self-evident]: namely: that the Nature and Substance of the Sacraments of both Testaments is the same: and therefore one ought to judge of the Substance of the Sacraments of the New Testament from the condition of the Sacraments of the Old Testament: Which hypothesis, indeed, is built from mere falsehoods and absurdities, is clearly evident from those things which have been argued thus far: Certainly it is manifestly absurd if it is posited that the substance of both Testaments is one, and such a substance indeed that consists of mere figures, types, and shadows: For thus it would follow that obscurity is a part of both Testaments: indeed it would be false that the Old Testament, with Christ now exhibited, has been abrogated: it would be false: that the Old Testament had only a shadow, but the New contains the very image itself, that is, the body of Christ. Furthermore, through a gross ignorance, the argument proceeds again from the types of the Sacraments to the goods and substance of the same. Finally, Types look to their archetypes, Shadows look to their Bodies: when these are removed, types become non-types, and shadows clearly vanish into nothing. Therefore, the Adversaries labor under a notable weakness of mind when they require the same types and shadows in the New Testament as they do in the Old Testament. For this is nothing other than if they were to say: The types of the Old Testament are non-types, that is, without an archetype: or: The shadows of the Old Testament are without a Body: that is: they are and are not: Which absurd theology and method of disputing we willingly leave to them, while they refuse to be wiser.

But the Calvinists insist: Where there is a Shadow, there is a Body: Therefore, if the Old Testament had a shadow, it certainly also had a Body.

I answer that an ignorance of the refutation is being committed: for the Apostle does not understand just any shadow, such as that which a body placed opposite a light casts and projects from itself: where shadow and body mutually posit and remove each other: but he understands only an adumbration or prefiguration of a body or a thing absent, and finally to come: which is what its antitype demonstrates, namely the image, which the Apostle expressly opposes to the shadow: alluding to the manner and custom of painters, who, when about to create some image, first put forward a shadow or a certain shadowy delineation: (A sketching/or drafting) and with darker lines, place the form of the image to follow before the eyes. But just as he would be absurd who would call such a delineation the Body or Image itself: so the Calvinists ought deservedly to seem absurd, who are accustomed to call those darker lines of the Old Testament the Body itself: and indeed the more absurd in that they themselves contend otherwise, and rightly so: that the Old Testament did not have the Body of Christ itself: but only its shadow and figure.

Furthermore, the Adversaries argue thus: An effect cannot precede its cause. Therefore, if the Fathers had the Effect of the Body of Christ, they certainly had the Body of Christ itself, equally in their Sacraments as we do: But they had it in a Type: Therefore we do likewise.

I answer that the philosophical axiom of the major premise is true only in natural causes and effects: but not always in voluntary ones. For example: Some debtor is set free if someone pledges in his place concerning a payment that will occur only after a certain time. Where indeed the liberation from debt is the Effect of the payment, which the guarantor indeed pledges in the present: but performs only in the future. Thus, liberation from sin and hell is the Effect of the incarnation and passion of the Son of God, which the eternal Father indeed pledged immediately from the fall of our first parents, but performed in act only in the fullness of time. Furthermore, the Sacramentarians bring forward, and brandish as the shield of Achilles, that more obscure passage of the first to the Corinthians 10. from verse 1 up to the fifth: which Beza rendered from the Greek thus: I would not have you ignorant, brethren, that our fathers were all under that cloud, and all passed through the sea: and all were baptized into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea: And all ate the same spiritual food (the same, that is, as we, as Beza adds in the glosses) And all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the following spiritual rock: But that rock was Christ. Therefore, Beza infers, regarding the matter and substance, the Sacraments of the ancients were equal to ours, as those which also looked to one Christ: which Christ offered himself to them in various types. I answer that this argument fails through a perpetual ignorance of the refutation: which, so that it may be better perceived, must be explained in parts. In the beginning, therefore, Beza takes for granted that in this place the Apostle is dealing with the Sacraments of the Old Testament: and he strives to confirm this. 1. from the fact that the Apostle calls the cloud and the sea Baptism: Then: that the Apostle makes mention of Water, which is proper to our Baptism: to which the Word and Grace have been added: Inasmuch as the cloud and the spread-out Sea were symbols of divine Grace. We answer 1. to the proposition itself, and we deny it most simply, relying on these reasons: 1. If we have recourse to the history of Moses, which clearly describes these things to which the Apostle alludes in this place, it is immediately and spontaneously clear that those histories possess the nature and condition not of any sacrament, but of a notable miracle. But the analogy of faith does not permit making sacraments out of miracles, besides the fact that the number of sacraments of both Testaments would increase immeasurably. 2. No sacrament can be given that consisted of only one, and indeed momentary, act: but such is the nature of sacraments that they require perennial acts of each church. Thus Circumcision was a durable act, extending itself to all newly born infants of the old people. Thus the Paschal Lamb was an act to be celebrated solemnly every year. But nothing of the sort can be affirmed of those acts which the Apostle touches upon in this place. For the crossing of the Red Sea was only something momentary: which happened once: indeed, which did not comprehend all the Israelitic people: but only those who had gone out of Egypt. But sacraments are and ought to be for all. Thus the Cloud provided itself as a companion to the Israelites only while they were wandering in the desert: not so to their descendants. Therefore, neither can this obtain the status of a sacrament. 3. Every sacrament is dispensed through the ministry of men. But neither in that crossing, nor in the company of the cloud, did human ministry have a place. Therefore 4. The fruit of all sacraments is obtained by none but believers: which the Adversaries themselves admit with us. But the benefit, use, and fruit, both of that crossing through the sea, and also of the Cloud accompanying them, came to the impious as well as to the pious: as well to those who, as the Apostle testifies, were overthrown in the desert, as to those who had arrived in the land of promise. Therefore, these were by no means sacraments properly so called.

Next, we respond to the means of proof by which Beza strives to confirm the proposition: And indeed, regarding the former, he errs and is himself deceived by the fallacy of homonymy. For the fact that the Apostle designates that crossing, as also the cloud, by the term Baptism, that is done figuratively by a certain metaphor or transference. Just as the Savior also, by the same figure, calls the sufferings of the saints a Baptism: Mark 10:38. From which, however, the consequence does not hold for a sacrament properly so called. Regarding the latter argument of Beza, it suffers from the fallacy of the consequent and an insufficient enumeration of the parts pertaining to the constitution of the substance of a sacrament. For 1. not just any element, but only that which enjoys divine institution, constitutes the elemental part of a sacrament. But the water of the Red Sea and the cloud, in Moses and Paul, do not enjoy such divine institution. Therefore, neither can this be understood, nor ought it to be, of sacramental water, properly so called.

Next, not just any word immediately constitutes a sacrament: but only the Word of command and promise. Since those things are destitute of both these words, it is evidently clear that they cannot be held as a sacrament even properly so called. Finally, even if both the crossing and the cloud did not lack the presence of God and singular grace, yet they lacked that grace which is proper to the Gospel, and which seals and confirms to everyone using a sacrament that promise concerning the gratuitous remission of sins through and on account of Christ apprehended by faith. Therefore, the entire rationale and nature of a sacrament properly so called expires entirely in this place. And this is the one ignorance of refutation with which Beza's argument is found to labor enormously.

The other results from the fact that Beza assumes the Apostle in this place is comparing the sacraments of the Old Testament with our sacraments. The falsity of which assertion is abundantly clear from what we have already said. For the Apostle does not compare sacraments with sacraments; much less does he affirm that there was one and the same substance of the sacraments of both Testaments: but the Apostle compares those miracles which happened to the Israelites with our or evangelical sacraments: not indeed absolutely, but only in a certain respect, insofar as some analogical rationale at least intervenes between them; while those Israelite miracles bore a certain type of our sacraments. From which, however, no support whatsoever accrues to the cause of the Calvinists. For if those miracles bore only a certain type: therefore they did not contain the archetype itself: for neither can type and archetype be the same in respect of substance: but they differ by definition or by the word, and we therefore invert Beza's collection in this manner: Between those Israelite miracles, as types, there intervened some analogy with our sacraments: Therefore, each meanwhile had its own peculiar word or substance, clearly different from the other: For in those, there was a type: in these, therefore, it is invincibly concluded that the antitype or archetype itself, that is, the substance of the body opposed to the shadow, must be constituted; so much so that if those Israelite ones had been similar to our sacraments in substance, then there would have been no need for the institution of the new sacraments.

But Calvin proceeds in book 4 of the Institutes, ch. 14, § 23 and 26, and urges that phrase, They ate the same food and drank the same drink; and from there he collects thus: The Israelites ate the same food WITH US, or the same which we eat in the sacrament: and they drank the same drink which we drink. But the Israelites did not eat the substantial body of Christ itself, nor did they drink his substantial blood. Therefore, neither do we eat the substantial body of Christ itself in our sacrament; or drink his substantial blood: and consequently: these two Testaments do not differ in substance itself.

But I respond 1. to the major premise: and I deny it as simply false. For 1. it is established from what has already been said that the Apostle is dealing with nothing at all concerning the sacraments of the Old Testament. Next, although we have already conceded that those Israelite miracles, because of a certain analogy, are compared by the Apostle with evangelical sacraments: we deny again and again that that absolute and simple comparison, which the adversaries urge, has a place here. For 1. the consideration of the subject itself argues for a difference, which is determinedly posited by the Apostle himself: and is restricted to the fathers, and indeed all the fathers, as many as were in the desert, however dissimilar they were among themselves: and it is predicated of all these that they ate the same food and drank the same drink. Which determination of the subject indeed admits a comparison, but such a one by which those fathers are not compared with us, but among themselves. Which comparison the Apostle himself also immediately explains excellently, when he affirms that most of them, because of impiety, were overthrown in the desert. Next, the adversaries commit a manifest crime of falsehood when they stuff in that WITH US of their own: which is nowhere in the text. 3. The very first verse immediately overturns this Calvinistic interpretation, which asserts that all those of whom the Apostle speaks were under the cloud and passed through the Red Sea: Which if, therefore, in the following verse, according to the Calvinian hypothesis, an absolute comparison of the fathers with the evangelical people were instituted: then certainly this first verse also would admit this comparison. But neither that crossing through the sea, nor the cloud, can be absolutely accommodated to the evangelical people.

E. That absolute Comparison itself also falls, which the Calvinists urge in this place. 4. From the hypothesis of the Calvinists, I wish to argue against them thus. That food, which the Fathers of the Old Testament, not only among themselves, but also, (according to the Calvinist hypothesis) ate as absolutely one and the same with us; was either the very Substantial Body of the Lord: or only the fruit and merit of the death of Christ. But neither of those can be adapted to those Fathers, who were struck down in the desert on account of impiety: Which I prove from the Theology of the Calvinists thus: If those Fathers ate one and the same food, where indeed they ate by the testimony of the Apostle: and truly this food was the very substantial Body of Christ: then it will follow that the Unworthy also, and those who were struck down in the desert, became participants of the substantial Body of Christ. But the Theology of the Calvinists does not admit this; as it establishes that the Unworthy become participants only of the Elemental thing: and not of the Lord's Body. Therefore they must necessarily either concede that those Israelites did not all eat the same spiritual food, and drink the same spiritual drink: which is diametrically opposed to the Apostolic affirmation: or that this Apostolic passage cannot be understood of the Sacraments properly so called: which is what we are fighting for.

Then if they understand that same food, and same drink, as the benefits of the merit of Christ, it would again follow as an absurdity, that undoubtedly all those Israelites, and thus those also who were struck down in the desert by an angry GOD, nevertheless pleased GOD, remained in His grace, and were rendered participants of the merit of Christ: which is diametrically opposed both to the Apostolic text and to the very doctrine of the Calvinists. We conclude therefore, and indeed with Oecolampadius himself, who, dissenting from Calvin in this part, writes thus upon this very passage: A comparison is not to be made with us, as some explain, that they ate the same food as we do: But the Comparison is among those Israelite Fathers themselves, that undoubtedly the food which Moses ate was not denied to Core, nor to Abiram, nor to the women.

But the Adversaries reply with two things; first, that the Apostle names not just any food, or any drink: but both Spiritual.

Then, that the Apostle himself asserts that they drank of Christ: because they drank of the Spiritual rock: which was Christ.

I answer, that a Sophism is committed in the former argument, παρὰ τὸ σχη̂μα τη̃ς λέξεως. For the Adversaries think that only that is said and is Spiritual in the Scriptures, which is such according to its nature and Essence. Which false opinion we can overwhelm and overturn with infinite examples. For Manna is called in this place by the Apostle, spiritual food, which nevertheless served not for nourishing the soul, but the Body, and for preserving it from hunger. Which same thing must be established concerning the drink leaping from the rock, so much so,

, that from it, not only men, but also beasts quenched their thirst. Num. 20. We therefore correct that former argument, by giving the true definition of the word, Spiritual, or Spiritually, which denotes not only that which is such by its nature and substance: but also, that which is, and can be called, Spiritual, either by origin, or by inherent mystery, or finally by respect of use. Just as therefore Flesh and Carnal is called in the Scriptures, whatever falls under φρόνημα σαρκός, Rom. 8. and savors of carnal Works, Gal. 5. although sometimes such Carnal works are internal and do not proceed outwardly: but Idolatry, wicked Concupiscences: So conversely, whatever proceeds from the Holy Spirit, or is destined by the same for the use of human salvation, is called Spiritual: although it be visible, corporeal, palpable: Of which condition was the Manna sent down from Heaven: and the water leaping from the rock.

In the latter argument a Sophism of begging the Question and a vicious consequence is committed: For it does not follow, That rock accompanying the Israelites was Christ, Therefore the substance of the Sacraments of both Testaments is the same. For the Apostle in this place does not speak of a simple or natural rock. Of this no one could say that it was or had been Christ: but that it only signified the same: But of that Spiritual rock. When therefore they drank of the waters leaping from the rock: they drank indeed of Christ, but only in type: since that rock was a type of the Spiritual rock, which accompanied the Israelites, and which was Christ. When therefore between that external rock, pouring forth waters: and between the mystical rock, which was Christ, it is accurately distinguished: then the vanity of the Objection emerges of its own accord.

Latin:

Sed sunt ex Sacramentarijs alij,qui hoc ipsum argumentum, in alia,sed rudiore forma proponunt: in hunc modum:

Bona & fructus utriusq; Testamenti sunt ijdem. Atqui in Veteri Testamento, Sacramenta non nisi typos & figuras de Christo habuerunt. Ergò Novi etiam Testamenti Sacramenta, non Substantiam, Corpus & Sanguinis Christi: sed signa tantùm & figuras ejusdem; licèt jam incarnati, continent. Sed eafdem absurditates incurrit hæc Sophisticatio, quas in priore notavimus.
