Cumprimis autem totum argumenti connexum, ex falsa procedit hypothesi,eâ nimirum,quam tanquàm regulam ἀναπόδεικτον & αὐτόπιστον subindè in ore ferunt Adversarij: nempè: quòd eadem sit Sacramentorum utriusque Testamenti Natura & Substantia: ac proindè ex Sacramentorum Veteris Testamenti conditione judicari debeat, de Substantia Sacramentorum Novi Testamenti: Quam sanè hypothesin,ex meris falsitatibus & absurditatibus esse extructam, luculenter patet ex ijs, quæ hactenus sunt disputata: Certè manifestè absurdum est, si statuatur una esse substantia utriusque Testamenti, & talis quidem substantia, quæ constat, meris figuris,typis & umbris : Sic enim sequeretur, partem esse utriusque Testamenti obscuritatem: imò falsum esset, Vetus Testamentum jam exhibito Christo, esse abrogatum: falsum esset: quod Vetus Testamentum tantùm Umbram habuerit : Novum autem ipsam imaginem, hoc est, corpus Christi contineat. Porrò per crasssam rursus ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε procedit argumentum à typis Sacramentorum, ad eorundem bona & substantiam. Tandem Typi respiciunt suos archetypos, Umbræ respiciunt sua Corpora : quibus sublatis , τύποι evadunt ἄτυποι, & umbræ planè in nihilum abeunt . Insigni proindè ἀῤῥωστίᾳ διανοίας laborant Adversarij, quando eosdem in Novo Testamento haud minùs typos & umbram, atque in Veteri Testamento requirunt. Hoc enim nihil est aliud, quàm si dicerent : Veteris Testamenti typi sunt ἄτυποι, hoc est, sine archetypo : vel: Veteris Testamenti Umbræ sunt sine Corpore : hoc est : sunt & non sunt : Quam absurdam Theologiam & disputandi rationem, nos illis libenter relinquimus , dùm rectiùs sapere nolunt.

Sed instant Calviniani : Vbi Vmbra : Ibi Corpus : E. si Vetus Testamentum habuit umbram : habuit utiq; etiam Corpus.

Respondeo, Committi Ignorationem Elenchi : non enim quamlibet umbram intelligit Apostolus, qualis est, quam Corpus lumini oppositum, de se spargit ac proijcit: Ubi umbra & Corpus, se mutuò ponunt, & tollunt : sed intelligit tantùm adumbrationem sive præfigurationem Corporis aut rei absentis, & demùm futuræ : id quod demonstrat ἀντίτυπον ejus, nempè εἰκὼν Imago, quam Apostolus disertè τῇ σκιᾷ sive Umbræ opponit : alludens ad morem & consuetudinem pictorum, qui imaginem aliquam efficturi, priùs σκιὰν sive delineationem quandam umbratilem præmittunt : (Eine abreissung/oder entwerffung) & lineis obscurioribus, formam secuturæ imaginis, oculis subijciunt. Quemadmodum verò absurdus foret, qui ejusmodi delineationem nominaret ipsum Corpus sive Imaginem : ita absurdi meritò vidèri debent Calviniani, qui lineas illas obscuriores Veteris Testamenti, ipsum Corpus nominare solent : & eò quidem absurdiores, quòd ipsimet aliàs contendunt, & rectè quidem : Vetus Testamentum non habuisse ipsum Corpus Christi: sed ejus tantùm umbram atque figuram.

Porrò sic arguunt Adversarij : Effectus non potest causam suam antevertere. E. si Patres habuerunt Effectum Corporis Christi, habuerunt utiq; ipsum Corpus Christi, æquè in suis Sacramentis, atq; nos : Sed habuerunt in Typo : Ergò & nos consimiliter.

Respondeo, Axioma Majoris Philosophicum verum tantùm esse in Causis & effectis naturalibus : non verò semper in Voluntarijs . Exempli gratia : Debitor aliquis liber dimittitur, si quis ipsius loco spondeat, de solutione, post certum demùm tempus futurâ. Ubi profectò liberatio à debito, est Effectus solutionis, quam fidejussor spondet quidem in præsenti : præstat autem demùm in futuro. Sic liberatio à peccato, & inferno est Effectus incarnationis & passionis Filij Dei, quam æternus Pater jam indè statim à lapsu proto - parentum spospondit quidem, sed demùm in plenitudine temporis actu præstitit. Proferunt præterea Sacramentarij, & ceu Achillis clypeum obvertunt, locum illum obscuriorem; prioris ad Corinth. 10. à v. 1. usq; ad quintum: quem Beza ex Græco sic reddidit: Nolim vos ignorare fratres, Patres nostros omnes sub illa nube fuisse, & omnes per mare transivisse: & omnes in Mosen baptizatos esse, nube & mari: Et omnes eandem escam spiritualem edisse (eandem videlicet, atque nos, uti in glossis addit Beza) Et omnes eundem potum spiritualem bibisse. Bibebant enim ex sequente spirituali petra: Petra verò illa erat Christus. Ergò infert Beza, quoad rem & substantiam, paria fuerunt Veterum Sacramenta cum nostris, ut quæ ipsa quoq; in unum Christum respicerent: qui Christus varijs typis se illis ingerebat. Respondeo, Fallit hoc argumentum perpetua ignoratione Elenchi: quæ, ut rectiùs percipiatur, per partes explicanda fuerit. Initiò igitur Beza pro confesso sumit, quod hoc loco D. Apostolus agat de Sacramentis Veteris Testamenti: idque confirmare annititur. 1. exindè, quòd Apostolus nubem & mare nominat Baptismum: Deindè: quòd Apostolus mentionem facit Aquæ, quæ propria sit Baptismi nostri: ad quam accesserit Verbum, & Gratia: Siquidem nubes & Mare diffusum, fuerint Symbola divinæ Gratiæ. Respondemus nos 1. ad propositionem ipsam, eamque simplicissimè negamus, his freti rationibus: 1. Si ad historiam Mosis, quæ res hasce, ad quas hoc loco alludit Apostolus, luculenter describit, recurramus, statim ultrò liquet, historias illas non Sacramenti alicujus, sed insignis miraculi, naturam ac conditionem sortiri. Atqui ex miraculis facere Sacramenta, analogia fidei non permittit, præterquàm quòd in immensum excreturus esset Sacramentorum utriusque Testamenti numerus. 2. Nullum potest dari Sacramentum, quod uno tantùm, & quidem momentaneo constiterit actu: sed ea est Sacramentorum natura, ut perennes requirant actus cujusque Ecclesiæ. Sic Circumcisio erat actus durabilis, Veteris populi ad omnes infantes recens natos, se extendens. Sic Agnus Paschalis erat actus, quotannis solenniter celebrandus. Verùm nihil tale potest affirmari, de illis actibus, quos Apostolus hoc loco tangit. Nam transitus maris rubri, momentaneum duntaxat quiddam fuit: qui semel evenit: imò, qui non omnem populum JIsraeliticum comprehendebat: sed eum tantùm, qui ex Ægypto exierat. Atqui Sacramenta sunt & debent esse omnium. Sic Nubes, in deserto tantùm peregrinantibus JIsraelitis comitem se præbuit: posteris non item. Ergò neque hæc Sacramenti rationem obtinere potest. 3. Omne Sacramentum dispensatur per ministerium hominum. Atqui neque in transitu illo, neque in comitatu nubis, ministerium humanum locum habuit. Ergò 4. Omnium Sacramentorum fructus, obtingit non nisi credentibus: id quod nobiscum fatentur ipsi Adversarij. Atqui beneficium, usus & fructus, tùm transitus illius per mare, tùm Nubis etiam concomitantis, obveniebat tàm impijs, quàm pijs: tàm illis, qui teste Apostolo, in deserto prostrati fuerunt: quàm qui in terram promissionis pervenerant. E. Sacramenta propriè sic dicta, isthæc minimè fuerunt.

Deindè respondemus ad probationum media, quibus Beza propositionem confirmare studet: Et quidem quoad priorem; fallit & fallitur ipse Sophismate ὁνωνυμίας. Quòd enim Apostolus, Transitum illum, ut & nubem, Baptismi termino indigitat: illud fit figuratè per quandam μεταφορὰν, sive Translationem. Quemadmodum Servator quoque per eandem figuram, passiones Sanctorum nominat Baptisma: Marc. 10, 38. Undè tamen ad Sacramentum propriè sic dictum non valet consequentia. Quoad posteriorem Bezæ rationem, laborat ea πλεονεξία Consequentis, & insufficiente enumeratione partium, ad constituendam Sacramenti substantiam pertinentium. Nam 1. non quodlibet Elementum; sed illud tantùm, quod divina institutione gaudet, constituit partem Sacramenti Elementarem. Atqui Aqua Maris rubri, & Nubis, apud Mosen & Paulum, tali divina institutione non gaudent. Ergò neque hæc potest aut debet intelligi, de Aqua Sacramentali, propriè sic dicta.

Deindè non quodvis statim verbum, Sacramentum constituit: Sed Verbum tantùm Mandati, & promissionis. Quo utroque Verbo cùm res illæ destituantur: liquet evidenter, pro Sacramento etiam propriè sic dicto, eas haberi non posse. Tandem etsi tùm transitus, tùm Nubes, non caruit præsentia Dei, & singulari gratiâ: tamen caruit eâ gratiâ, quæ est Evangelij propria, quæque obsignat & confirmat cuilibet Sacramento utenti, promissionem illam, de gratuita peccatorum remissione per & propter Christum fide apprehensum. Ergò omnis Sacramenti propriè sic dicti ratio atque natura, hoc loco, prorsus expirat. Et hæc una est ἄγνοια ἐλέγχε, quâ Bezæ argumentum enormiter laborare deprehenditur.

Altera ex eo resultat, quòd autumat Beza, Apostolum hoc loco, conferre Sacramenta Veteris Testamenti, cum nostris Sacramentis. Cujus assertionis falsitas ex ijs, quæ jam diximus, abundè liquet. Neque enim Sacramenta cum Sacramentis comparat Apostolus; multò minùs, unam eandemque Sacramentorum utriusque Testamenti fuisse Substantiam, affirmat: Sed miracula illa, quæ Israelitis obtigerunt, confert Apostolus, cum nostris sive Evangelicis Sacramentis: non verò ἁπλῶς, sed tantùm secundùm quid, quatenùs nimirùm aliqua salteὰm analogica ratio illis invicem intercedit: dùm miracula illa Israelitica, Typum quendam nostrorum Sacramentorum gesserunt. Undè tamen ad causam Calvinianorum nihil quicquam præsidij accedit. Si enim miracula illa, typum tantùm aliquem gesserunt: E. non continuerunt ipsum Archetypum: Neque enim typus & Archetypus, ratione substantiæ, idem esse possunt: sed definitione sive τῷ λόγῳ differunt, invertimus proindè Collectionem Bezæ in hunc modum: Miraculis illis Israeliticis, tanquàm Typis intercessit aliqua analogia cum Sacramentis nostris: Ergò unicuique suus interim peculiaris λόγος, sive substantia fuit, ab altero planè diversa: In illis enim, Typus fuit: in his ergo ἀντίτυπον sive ἀρχέτυπον ipsum, hoc est, Substantiam Corporis, Umbræ oppositam, constituendam esse, invictè colligitur; usque adeò, ut si Israelitica illa, nostris Sacramentis per substantiam fuissent similia, tùm Novorum Sacramentorum institutione opus non fuissent.

Sed pergit Calvinus l. 4. Institut. c. 14. §. 23. & 26. & urget phrasin illam, Eandem escam comederunt, & eundem potum biberunt; atque indè sic colligit: Israelitæ eandem escam comederunt NOBISCUM, sive eandem, quam nos in Sacramento comedimus: eundemque potum biberunt, quem nos bibimus. Atqui Israelitæ non ipsum substantiale Corpus Christi comederunt, neque substantialem ipsius sanguinem biberunt. Ergò neque in nostro Sacramento ipsum substantiale Corpus Christi comedimus; aut substantialem ipsius sanguinem bibimus: ac per consequens: duo hæc Testamenta, non ipsâ Substantiâ differunt.

Sed respondeo 1. ad Majorem: eamquè ut simpliciter falsam, nego. Nam 1. ex jam dictis constat, de Sacramentis Veteris Testamenti, nihil quicquam agere Apostolum. Deindè licet jam concesserimus, miracula illa Israelitica, propter quandam analogiam, conferri ab Apostolo cum Sacramentis Evangelicis: absolutam tamen & simplicem illam Comparationem, quam urgent Adversarij, locum hîc habere, iterum atque iterum negamus. Nam 1. diversum arguit ipsius SUBJECTI consideratio, quod ab ipso Apostolo, determinatè ponitur: & restringitur ad Patres, & Patres quidem omnes, quotquot in deserto fuerunt, quantumvis inter se dissimiles: & de his universis prædicatur, quòd eandem escam comederint, eundemque potum biberint. Quæ subjecti determinatio, admittit quidem Comparationem, sed talem, quâ Patres illi non nobiscum: sed inter se ipsos conferuntur. Quam comparationem etiàm ipse Apostolus statim egregiè explicat, dùm affirmat, plurimos ipsorum, propter impietatem in deserto prostratos fuisse. Deindè crimen falsi manifestum committunt Adversarij, dùm de suo infarciunt, illud NOBISCUM: id quod in textu nuspiã habetur. 3. Evertit hanc interpretationem Calvinisticam versus statim primus, qui asserit, Omnes illos, de quibus loquitur Apostolus, sub nube fuisse, per mare rubrum transÿsse: Quod si ergo in subsequente versu secundum hypothesin Calvinianam, Comparatio institueretur absoluta Patrum cum populo Evangelico: utique versus etiam iste primus, Comparationem hanc admitteret. Atqui neque transitus ille per mare, neque Nubes ad populum Evangelicum absolutè accommodari potest:

E. cadit ipsa quoque illa absoluta Comparatio, quam Calviniani hoc loco urgent. 4. Ex hypothesi Calvinianorum, contra ipsos sic libet arguere. Esca illa, quam Patres Veteris Testamenti, non modò inter se, sed &, (secundum hypothesin Calvinianam) nobiscum prorsus unam atque eandem comederunt; aut fuit ipsum Substantiale Corpus Domini: aut tantùm fructus & meritum mortis Christi. Atqui neutrum istud ad Patres illos, qui in deserto propter impietatem prostrati fuerunt accommodari potest: Id quod ex Theologia Calvinianorum sic probo: Si Patres illi, unam atq; eandem escam comederunt, ubi sanè teste Apostolo comederunt: & verò esca hæc fuit ipsum substantiale Corpus Christi: utique consequetur, Indignos etiam & eos, qui prostrati fuerunt in deserto, Corporis Christi substantialis evasisse participes. Atqui hoc Theologia Calvinianorum non admittit; ut quæ statuit, Indignos evadere tantùm participes rei Elementaris: non verò Corporis Dominici. Ergò vel concedant necesse est, Israelitas illos non omnes eandem escam spiritualem comedisse, eundemq; potum spiritualem bibisse: id quod Apostolicæ affirmationi è diametro repugnat: vel locum istum Apostolicum de Sacramentis propriè sic dictis non posse accipi: id quod nos pugnamus.

Deinde si escam illam eandem, & potum eundem, de beneficiis meriti Christi intelligant, rursus consequens fuerit illud absurdum, quòd nimirum omnes illi Israelitæ, & sic ii quoque, qui ab irato DEO in deserto prostrati sunt, nihilominùs tamen placuerint DEO, manserint in ipsius gratia, & redditi fuerint participes meriti Christi: id quòd tum cum textu Apostolico, tum cum ipsa Calvinianorum doctrina è diametro pugnat. Concludimus proindè & quidem cum ipso Oecolampadio, qui à Calvino hac in parte dissidens, super hunc ipsum locum sic scribit: Non est facienda collatio cum nobis, sicut quidam exponunt, quòd eandem, quam nos, escam comederint: Sed inter ipsos Patres illos Israelitas est Comparatio, quòd nimirum esca, quam Moses manducavit, neque Core, neque Abiramo, neque mulieribus sit denegata.

Sed duo regerunt Adversarii; primùm illud, quòd Apostolus, non quamlibet escam, aut quemlibet potum: sed utrumq; Spirituale m nominet.

Deinde, quòd Apostolus ipse asserat, bibisse illos de Christo: propterea quòd biberint de Spirituali petra: quæ erat Christus.

Respondeo, Committi in priore ratione Sophisma, παρὰ τὸ σχη̂μα τη̃ς λέξεως. Opinantur enim Adversarii, illud duntaxat in Scripturis, dici & esse Spirituale, quod secundùm naturam & Essentiam suam tale est. Quam falsam sententiam infinitis exemplis obruere & evertere possumus. Nam Manna dicitur hoc loco ab Apostolo, esca spiritualis, quæ tamen non animæ, sed Corpori nutriendo, & à fame præservando, inserviebat. Quod ipsum de potu quoque è petra saliente est statuendum, usque adeò,

, ut ex eo, non homines tantùm, sed & jumenta sitim restingerent. Num. 20. Corrigimus proindè priorem istam rationem, data vera definitione vocis, Spiritualis, sive Spiritualiter, quæ non tantùm notat id, quod natura & substantia sua tale est: sed &, quod vel originis, vel mysterii inhærentis, vel denique respectu usus, Spirituale est, & dici potest. Sicut ergo Caro & Carnale in Scripturis vocatur, quicquid cadit sub φρόνημα σαρκός, Rom. 8. & Opera carnalia sapit, Gal. 5. licèt interdum ejusmodi Carnalia opera sint interna & foras nõ progrediantur: at Idololatria, pravæ Concupiscentiæ: Ita vice versa, Spirituale appellatur, quicquid vel à Spiritu sancto proficiscitur, vel in usum salutis humanæ ab eodem destinatur: licèt illud sit visibile, corporeum, palpabile: Cujus conditionis fuit Manna Cælitus demissum: & aqua è petra saliens.

In posteriore ratione committitur Sophisma petitionis Principii & vitiosi consequentis: Non enim sequitur, Petra illa concomitans Israelitas erat Christus, Ergò eadem substantia Sacramentorum utriusq; Testamenti. Nam Apostolus hoc loco, non loquitur de simplici aut naturali petra. De hac nemo dicere poterat, quòd esset aut fuerit Christus: sed quòd eandem duntaxat notârit: Verùm de Spirituali illa petra. Quando ergo biberunt de aquis salientibus è petra: biberunt utique de Christo, sed non nisi in typo: siquidem petra illa erat typus Spiritualis petræ, quæ comitabatur Israelitas, quæque erat Christus. Quando proinde inter externam illam petram, profundentem aquas: & inter petram mysticam, quæ erat Christus, accuratè distinguitur: tum vanitas Objectionis ultrò emergit.


## 18 Of the Church

Just as, by the testimony of Lactantius, lib. 4. Instit. last chapter, the boasting of no thing was more frequent among all peoples than that of the Church: so that every single assembly of heretics contended that they were Christians above all others; and that their Church was truly Catholic and Apostolic: So the Romanists also have chosen this one Article, out of the entire Theology of the Christian Religion, under which they might seek patronage for their most desperate cause, that is, for their most crass errors: and thus under the august title of the Church, they might hostily attack the Church of Christ, indeed with a cunning plan. For when they perceived well that the sum of this Article is both of great breadth and difficulty, since it can never be understood accurately enough, except by one who has perceived a clearly solid and exact knowledge of all the remaining parts of Christian doctrine: they therefore opined that they could hide so much more safely under this as it were hiding-place. Added to this is that external splendor and adornment of the Roman Synagogue, its external majesty and celebrity: which

Latin:

QUemadmodùm Lactantio teste, lib. 4. Institut. cap. ult. nullius rei apud populos omnes frequentior fuit gloriatio, quàm Ecclesiæ: adeò ut singuli quique hæreticorum cœtus, se potissimum Christianos; & suam Ecclesiam verè esse Catholicam, Apostolicam contenderint: Ita Romanenses quoque, hunc vel unum Articulum, ex universa Religionis Christianæ Theologia, sibi delegerunt, sub quo perditissimæ suæ causæ, hoc est, crassissimorum errorum patrocinium quærerent: & sic sub augusto Ecclesiæ titulo, Ecclesiam Christi hostiliter impugnarent, astuto sanè consilio. Cùm enim probè animadverterent, summam esse Articuli hujus & amplitudinem & difficultatem, quippè qui nunquam satis accuratè intelligi possit, nisi ab eo, qui reliquorum doctrinæ Christianæ locorum omnium notitiam planè solidam ac exactam perceperit: ideóque sub hoc quasi latibulo tantò tutiùs latitare se posse, opinati sunt. Accedit externus ille Synagogæ Romanæ splendor & ornatus, externa majestas & celebritas: quæ


### Philippic Treatment

has hitherto obtained, and today still obtains, so much the greater power for seducing the more unskilled, by how much more confidently the Romanists have been accustomed to appeal repeatedly to the judgment and authority of the Church. Now, apart from that conflict also with the Romanists, such is both the necessity and the utility of this Article, that Gregory the Great speaks in Morals 35, but only on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem can salvation be obtained by us: Joel 2:32. Therefore, the very reason for our salvation demands most highly that he who desires not so much to appear as to be a true member of the Church should have its true nature well known and understood. For those who are established outside of this are altogether alien from God, and from Christ, and from the Testaments, from the promises, from the polity of Israel, and finally from the hope of the sons of God, and they fall away entirely from eternal salvation, as the Apostle defines, Ephesians 2:12. In which sense the Ancients not badly said: He who does not have the Church as mother, does not have God as Father. Which, however, if it be accommodated in the Papal sense to the Roman Synagogue, we invert entirely in this manner: He who does not have God as Father, him the mother will not save, and he who does not hear the bridegroom, him the bride will not help.

Our Author instituted a treatment of this Article that is sufficiently prolix, but suitable to his own age: which can be resolved analytically into the following members.

For first he discourses on the question of whether, whether there is a Church on this earth? And he gathers into the affirmative part, where there is a visible assembly of the called, in which the preaching of the Gospel and the administration of the Sacraments resounds, there is the invisible Church of the Elect: according to that of the Apostle, Rom. 8:30, Whom he chose, these he also called.

Then he defines the visible Church, that it is an assembly of those embracing the Gospel of Christ, and rightly using the Sacraments, in which God is effective through the ministry of the Gospel: and regenerates many to eternal life: in which assembly, however, there are many not reborn, but consenting to the true doctrine.

Thirdly, he disputes about the ordinary succession of Bishops and Colleges, to which the Church is not bound.

Fourthly, he responds to the question about the judge of Ecclesiastical Controversies, and shows such to be only the Word of God, and the Confession or consensus of all the pious.

Fifthly, he discourses on the foundation of faith, and judges it to be so rashly [held], when the Articles of faith are handed down whole and without corruptions, and manifest worship of Idols is not defended.

Sixthly, a certain comparison having been instituted, he demonstrates what is the difference between the Church and political government.

Seventhly, he refutes the fury of the Donatists, who contended that neither the Word nor the Sacraments have any efficacy if the life of the ministers is contaminated by crimes.

Eighthly, he shows the true marks of the Church to be the pure Doctrine of the Gospel and the legitimate administration of the Sacraments: but that the false marks are both the ordinary succession of Bishops and the observance of human traditions.

Ninthly and lastly, he adds certain things concerning the gift of interpreting the Scriptures, and shows that it is not bound to a certain order of men, but is a gift of God; and at the same time, he gives some admonitions concerning the similarity of traditions and the laws of Bishops.

Although we by no means disapprove of this whole Philippean treatment, as it is suitable for the previous century, it cannot be held against us as a fault if, having regard both to an easier Method and to the Controversies of our own century, we reduce this scattered material to four general chapters: and thus recall every controversial Question, treated by our author, to its own proper place.

The first chapter, therefore, will be concerning the Nature and Essence of the Church. Where that controversy will come under investigation, which especially exists today between our Churches and the Jesuit faction concerning the Invisible Church.

The second chapter will examine the axioms and eulogies, or, as others say, the attributes or adjuncts, or even the ornaments and privileges of the Church. Where we shall have to dispute expressly concerning the Unity, perpetuity, and Holiness of the Catholic Church, and concerning its authority and power.

The third chapter will explain that noble dispute concerning the Government of the Church. Where the following will come under question: 1. What head or Foundation of the Church is to be established? 2. What Form of Government or Administration is suitable for the Church? Whether Monarchical, or rather Democratic or Aristocratic? 3. With what weapons or means is this Ecclesiastical Government to be administered?

The fourth and last chapter will treat the classic and easily primary Controversy concerning the Marks of the true Church, against the Jesuits.

And we maintain that each and every thing which is accustomed to come into controversy today, both concerning the nature and definition and concerning the quality of the Church, can be recalled to these four chapters. For as to the question of ei ἑστι, Whether there is a Church on this earth, that is, some assembly which God acknowledges as His own people, and which He rules in this life by the word and Sacraments, and which He is to endow with eternal blessedness after this life? We certainly do not think we would be doing something worth the effort if, in treating that, we wished to spend any care or labor at this time. For long since, by the benefit of God, that Epicurean profanity has been exploded, which impiously imagined that God, occupied only with heavenly things, is affected by no care at all for human affairs; as well as the empty talk of certain people who dream that the whole world is the Church, and that everyone can be saved in their own religion. Thus, it has not yet earned the applause of certain sharp-witted men, or the wisdom of politicians, who, seeing the disorder and confusion of all things, and especially the countless sects and opinions regarding the matter of faith, take up the subject of doubting of divine promises restrains the petulance of all these people from the beginning, by which the Savior solemnly promised that He would be with us all days even to the consummation of the age. Matt. 28, 29. Indeed, not even the gates of hell would prevail against the Church. Matt. 16, v. 18. Now, if the Church were ever to cease to be in the world, it would necessarily follow that these promises would expire, which is absurd. 2. And why, I ask, would the Apostle assert that the death of Christ is to be announced and commemorated in this world until He Himself comes, if the Church were ever to perish on this earth? 1 Cor. 11, 26. 3. Furthermore, since in the Apostles' Creed we profess that we believe in the Church: and since faith cannot be terminated except with this very world, and is changeable only with eternity itself: surely from this alone an absolutely infallible argument can be drawn, that the Church in this world can no more be completely abolished or interrupted than faith itself. 4. Finally, the continuous series and succession of the Patriarchs before the flood gives no uncertain assurance to this assertion of ours: likewise the calling of Abraham after the flood, from whom the Israelite people originated. Now, while the polity of this people still stood, the promised Messiah came and was exhibited, who gathered a Church from Jews and Gentiles through the ministry of the Gospel, which is to endure until that other, or most recent, coming of Christ for judgment. D. Augustine described this series of the Church in a most beautiful commentary and illustrated it through all ages in that excellent work of his, The City of God, which ought to be most highly recommended to all theologians.

CHAPTER I.

Latin:

tantò majorem vim ad seducendos imperitiores obtinuit hactenus, hodieque obtinet: quantò confidentiùs Romanenses, ad Ecclesiæ judicium atque authoritatem subindè provocare consueverunt. Jam extra conflictum etiam istum cum Romanensibus, ea est Articuli hujus tùm necessitas, tùm utilitas, ut extra Ecclesiam non sit salus, sicut loquitur Gregorius M. Morali 35. sed tantùm in monte Sion, & in Hierusalem salvatio nobis obtingere possit: Joel. 2, 32. Ipsa proindè salutis nostræ ratio summoperè efflagitat, ut Ecclesiæ veræ naturam probè cognitam perspectamque habeat, qui verum ejus membrum non tàm videri, quàm esse, exoptat. Extra hanc enim qui sunt constituti, illi & à Deo, & à Christo, & à Testamentis, à promissionibus, à politia Israelis, à spe deniq; filiorum Dei, prorsus sunt alieni, & salute æterna planè excidunt, sic definiente Apostolo, Ephes 2, 12. Quo sensu Veteres haud malè dixerunt: Qui Ecclesiam non habet matrem, Deum non habet Patrem. Quod tamen si sensu Pontificio ad Romanam Synagogam accommodetur; invertimus planè illud in hunc modum: Qui Deum non habet Patrem, hunc mater non salvabit, & qui sponsum non audit, hunc sponsa non juvabit.

Tractationem Articuli hujus Autor noster satis prolixam, sed suo seculo convenientem instituit: quæ α̉ναλυτικῶς in sequentia membra resolvi potest.

Primùm enim disserit de Quæstione ei ἑἰ, An sit in terris bisce Ecclesia? & in partem affirmantem colligit, ubi est cætus vocatorum visibilis, in quo sonat prædicatio Evangelii & Sacramentorum administratio, ibi esse invisibilem Electorum Ecclesiam: secundum illud Apostoli, Rom. 8, 30. Quos elegit, hos & vocavit.

Deindè Ecclesiam visibilem definit, quòd sit cœtus amplectentium Evangelium Christi, & rectè utentium Sacramentis, in quo Deus per ministerium Evangelii sit efficax: & multos ad vitam æternam regeneret: in quo cœtu tamen multi sint non renati, sed de vera doctrina consentientes.

Tertiò disputat de ordinaria successione Episcoporum & Collegiorum, ad quam Ecclesia non sit alligata.

Quartò respondet ad quæstionem de judice Controversiarum Ecclesiasticarum, & talem esse ostendit, solum Verbum Dei, & omnium piorum Confessionem sive consensum.

Quintò disserit de fundamento fidei, illudque tùm temerè censet, quando Articuli fidei integri & sine corruptelis traduntur, & non defenduntur manifesti cultus Idolorum.

Sextò σύγκρισιν quadam instituta, quid sit inter Ecclesiam & regimen politicum discriminis, demonstrat.

Septimò Donatistarum furorem refutat, qui contendebant, neg, Verbum, neg, Sacramenta, ullam habere efficaciam, si ministrorum vita sceleribus sit contaminata.

Octavo ostendit veras Ecclesiæ notas esse puram Evangelii Doctrinam, & legitimam Sacramentorum administrationem: falsas verò esse notas tùm Ordinariam Episcoporum successionem, tùm traditionum humanarum observantiam.

Nonò ac postremò subjicit quædam de dono interpretandi Scripturas, illudq; non ad certum quendam hominum ordinem alligatum, sed Dei donum esse ostendit, simulque de similitudine traditionum, de que Episcoporum legibus, quædam admonet.

Quanquam verò totam hanc tractationem Philippæam, quippè superiori seculo convenientem, minimè improbamus: vitio tamen verti nobis haud poterit, si tùm facilioris Methodi, tùm Controversiarum nostri seculi habita ratione, dispersam hanc materiam, ad quatuor capita generalia redigamus: & sic quamlibet Quæstionem controversam, ab autore nostro pertractatam, ad propriam suam sedem revocemus.

Caput proindè primum erit de Natura atq; Essentia Ecclesiæ. Ubi sub disquisitionem veniet ea potissimùm Controversia, quæ de Ecclesia Invisibili, nostris hodiè Ecclesus, cum gente Jesuwitica intercedit.

Caput alterum expendet axiomata & elogia, vel, ut alii loquuntur, attributa sive adjuncta, vel etiam ornamenta ac privilegia Ecclesiæ. Ubi disputandum ex professo nobis fuerit, de Unitate, perennitate, & Sanctitate Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, deq; ejusdem autoritate ac potestate.

Caput tertium explicabit nobilem illam disputationem de Regimine Ecclesiæ. Ubi sub quæstionem veniet. 1. Quodnám sit constituendum caput sive Fundamentum Ecclesiæ? 2. Quænam Regiminis sive Gubernationis Forma Ecclesiæ conveniat? nùm Monarchica, an verò Democratica vel Aristocratica? 3. Quibus armis sive mediis Regimen hoc Ecclesiasticum administretur?

Caput quartum ac postremum classicam & facilè primariam Controversiam de Notis veræ Ecclesiæ, contra Jesuwtias pertractabit.

Et ad hæc quatuor capita revocari posse statuimus singula & universa, quæ tùm de natura ac definitione, tùm de qualitate Ecclesiæ, in controversiam hodiè venire solent. Nam quoad quæstionem ei ἑστι, An sit in terris bisce Ecclesia, hoc est, cœtus aliquis, quem Deus pro suo populo agnoscat, quemque hac in vita, verbo & Sacramentis regat, post hanc verò æterna beatitate sit donaturus? haud sanè operæ precium nos facturos arbitramur, si in ea pertractanda, hac vice, curæ aliquid operæque infumere vellemus. Jampridem enim Dei beneficio explosa est, tùm Epicuræa illa prophanitas, quæ Deum cœlestibus tantum occupatum, rerum humanarum curâ planè nullâ affici, impiè confinxit; tùm quorundam matæologia, qui somniant, universum mundum esse Ecclesiam, & quemque in sua religione salvari posse. Sic applausum etiam nondum meruit, nasutulorum quorundam, sive Politicorum sapientia, qui rerum omnium ἀταξίαν & Confusionem, cumprimis verò innumeras sectas atque opiniones de negocio fidei, conspicientes, subdubitandi materiam capessunt, Nùm aliqua in mundo sic Ecclesia? Istorum enim omnium petulantiam initiò coërcet promifsionum divinarum evidentia, quibus Servator sanctè compromisit, se nobiscum futurum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi. Matth. 28, 29. imò ne quidem portas inferorum contra Ecclesiam quicquam prævalituras. Matth. 16. v. 18. Jam si unquam Ecclesia in mundo esse desineret, utique promissiones has expirare necessum foret, id quod absurdum. 2. Et cur quæso Apostolus assereret, mortem Christi hoc in mundo annunciandam & commemorandam esse, usq; dùm ipse veniat, si aliquando his in terris Ecclesia esset interitura? 1. Cor. 11, 26. 3. Porrò cùm in Symbolo Apostolico credere nos profiteamur Ecclesiam: Fides autem non nisi cum ipso hoc mundo sit terminabilis, cumque ipsa æternitate commutabilis: utique vel indè argumentum prorsus infallibile peti potest, Ecclesiam hoc in mundo, haud magis, atque fidem ipsam, vel abrogari penitùs, vel interrumpi posse. 4. Tandem assertioni huic nostræ fidem minimè dubiam facit, continua series & successio Patriarcharum ante diluvium: similiter vocatio Abrahæ post diluvium, ex quo populus Israëliticus oriundus fuit. Jam stante adhuć politia hujus populi, venit & exhibitus est promissus Messias, qui Ecclesiam ex Judæis & gentibus ministerio Evangelii collegit, quæ est duratura ad alterum illum, sive novissimum Christi adventum ad judicium. Hanc Ecclesiæ seriem pulcherrimo commentario descripsit, & per omnes ætates illustravit D. Augustinus, in egregio illo suo opere, De Civitate DEI, quod omnibus Theologis debet esse commendatissimum.

CAPUT I.


### On the Nature and Essence of the Church

As in any other, so especially in the present discussion, that precept of the Philosopher is found to be most true, lib. 1. Top. cap. 14. & l. 1. de Cælo, cap. 11. t. 10. It is easy to understand what that is which is being inquired into, if it has been explained in what ways it is spoken of. Therefore, for those investigating the Nature and Definition of the Church, both the etymology of the word itself, its polysemy, and finally its varied and manifold division must be properly weighed.

The etymology of the Church, therefore, is Greek in origin, and properly signifies an evocation: noting, however, the Object of the Calling—that is, the assembly of the called—more than the act of calling. The seventy interpreters generally rendered the Hebrew קָהָל, which signifies a congregation or assembly, by the Greek word συναγωγῆς, looking especially to the condition of the ancient people, namely the Jewish. For because religion was, as it were, born at home for the Jews—that is, God dwelt in their midst in such a way that they did not need an evocation from elsewhere to learn divine worship—the name Synagogue suited them most correctly. But since after the Ascension of Christ, all tongues and nations from the whole world were finally to be called to the worship of God, as they were previously entirely ignorant of the true worship of God: it thus came about that the Apostles themselves in their writings designated the assembly of the called Gentiles with the term ἐκκλησίας, Church, thus distinguishing it from the Jewish Synagogue. Bellarmine himself also rightly admonishes, lib. 3. de Ecclesia militante, cap. 1. pag. 1225. l. B., that the people of God are called an assembly of the called, because no one joins himself to this people by himself and by his own instinct: but all, as many as come, are anticipated by the calling of God.

Moreover, the use of the word Church, both in the Scriptures and in the disputes of adversaries, is found to be twofold: improper, that is, catachrestic, and proper. When it is taken improperly, it admits almost the same meaning that the word City obtains in the books of Politics. For just as this does not always signify an assembly of citizens living together, but sometimes also the place in which that assembly lives: so the Church sometimes, but less properly, denotes the Place in which the called gather for sacred worship: as 1 Cor. 11, 18. Thus, this word is used improperly and quite abusively by the Pontificians for the Clergy alone, so that they say that what has been done or decreed by only one of its orders has been done by the Church.

When the word Church is used properly, it takes on a triple meaning: One most general, when it denotes any assembly or congregation. In which sense Apoc. 2, 9. & 3. 9. it is called the Synagogue of Satan: and Psalm 26, 5. the Church of the malignant, ἐκκλησία πονηρευομένων. To which, perhaps, that passage in Acts 19, 32 can not ineptly be referred: The assembly was confused, συγκεχυμένη, and the majority did not know for what reason they had gathered.

The other [is] special, when it is taken for the whole assembly of the called, or of those who are called to the kingdom of Christ through the Word and Sacraments, and who leave a place for this calling, as far as the external use of the ministry is concerned, although very many of them do not believe in Christ, but perish eternally. In this sense, therefore, if the word Church is taken so simply, we readily concede that the members of the Church are not only the Elect and the piously faithful; who nevertheless, outside this assembly of the called, never (except in a case of necessity and violence) are nowhere to be found: but that they are all those who, enjoying the benefit of the calling, profess the faith of Christ in any way whatsoever, and use the Sacraments. For someone to be said to be in this Church, it is enough that he is a Christian by profession, or is in the assembly of the called. And insofar as such a person professes the faith of Christ, to that extent he is named a Faithful one, in distinction to Infidels and pagans, because they utterly abhor the Christian Religion. The term Faithful being accepted in this general sense, the Church is defined by some as the assembly or congregation of the faithful. Although, however, it is by no means sufficient for salvation that you are in the Church speaking in this general way, and only as regards the external profession of the Christian faith: yet salvation itself cannot be obtained by anyone outside this assembly. And here that comparison of the Church with Noah's ark has its place. For just as no one was saved outside of this during the flood: and yet not all who were in the ark were saved eternally: So no one is saved outside this Church of the called: yet not all are saved, as many as are contained in this most ample assembly of the Church. Therefore, this Church admits a distinction between Truth and Falsehood: so that it matters a great deal, both for faith and for salvation, of which Church, whether true or false, someone is a member. Concerning which distinction more will be dealt with below in its proper place.

The word Church takes on a third and final meaning, and that the most special one, when it is taken for the assembly of the Elect and the piously faithful: And then the Church is rightly defined as being the Pillar and foundation of the Truth. 1 Tim. 3, 15.

With those three meanings properly weighed, it will become plain what is to be judged concerning that whole and sufficiently prolix disputation of Bellarmine, which he institutes concerning the members of the Church, book 3 of the Church militant from chapter 1 up to chapter eleven. For in chapter 2 he defines the Church as being an assembly of men, bound together by the profession of the same Christian faith, and the communion of the same Sacraments, under the government of legitimate pastors, and especially of one vicar of Christ on earth, the Roman Pontiff. He subsequently submits that from this Church are excluded first all infidel gentiles, Jews, Turks, Pagans: Then Catechumens and the excommunicated: Thirdly Schismatics, who have the faith and the Sacraments, but are not subject to a legitimate pastor, and therefore profess the faith and receive the Sacraments outside. Which theology is indeed found to be false and absurd in many ways. For 1 it labors under manifest obscurity. For not any profession of faith: just as not any Communion of Sacraments constitutes the Church of God. For Hypocrites have, and Heretics also have, the profession of faith and the use of Sacraments: whom, however, we believe with David, Psalm 26, 5, not to be the Church, but to be of the malignant.

Furthermore, this definition does not even suit the Roman Church itself. For the Laity are deprived of the full use of the Sacraments: Therefore, either these do not belong to the Church, that is, to the assembly of men using the Sacraments, and indeed bound together under the communion of the same Sacraments: or this communion of Sacraments does not constitute the specific difference of the Church. Let it be, according to the doctrine of the Papists, that Marriage is a Sacrament: Yet Clerics under the Papacy abhor this Sacrament. Therefore they are not members of the Church, that is, of that assembly which is bound together by the communion of the same (NB. THE SAME) Sacraments.

Thirdly, this definition suits only the visible Church; that is, only those who already profess the faith by an external act. How gross this error is, will have to be said below, where we will expressly dispute concerning the Invisible Church. And that which Bellarmine writes in this place deserves observation: Although all virtues, Faith, Hope, Charity, and the rest, may be found in the Church: yet so that someone may be absolutely called a part of the true Church, of which the Scriptures speak, we do not think any internal virtue is required, but only an external profession of faith and Communion of Sacraments, in which sense it is itself perceived. Thus, therefore, the true members of the true Church, according to Bellarmine's sense, are the worst of all hypocrites, provided they join themselves to the external society.

Fourthly, what kind of monster is it that he writes that Schismatics are excluded from the Church because, although they have the faith and the Sacraments, they are not nevertheless subject to a legitimate pastor. Thus, therefore, according to Bellarmine, a Church will be True which has neither faith nor Sacraments, if it only has obedience to the Roman Pontiff. And again, a Church will not be True which indeed has Faith and Sacraments: but is nevertheless destitute of this third thing, namely the obedience of the Roman Pontiff.

Finally, Bellarmine indeed disputes at length concerning Catechumens, that they are not in the Church: but he entangles both himself and the whole matter in perpetual contradictions.

It is a shameful contradiction that he writes at the end of chapter 2: that Catechumens can have faith and charity, indeed that they are of the Soul of the Church; but meanwhile that they are not of the Body of the Church. Likewise, in chapter 3, he asserts: that Catechumens are faithful and can be saved: but nevertheless that they are not in the Church actually and properly: but only in potentiality, just as a man conceived, but not yet formed and born, is not called a man, except in potentiality. The Sophist surely looks only to the external act, which consists in the external profession of faith and the external use of the Sacraments: Which he himself names from Augustine the Body of the Church. To extricate ourselves from which contradictions, we establish that a distinction is needed. For at the beginning we willingly grant to Bellarmine that there is, as it were, a twofold form of the Church: One, which is of the Soul, and concerns those internal gifts of the Holy Spirit, Faith, Hope, Charity: The other, which is of the Body, and regards the external profession of faith and the communication of the Sacraments. But what the Jesuit concludes from that, that those who are not of the body, that is, who are not yet admitted to the external profession of faith and the participation of the Sacraments, although they may have faith and can be saved,

Latin:

Cum in quavis aliâ, tùm præsente potissimùm disputatione verissimum deprehenditur præceptum illud Philosophi, lib. 1. Top. cap. 14. & l. 1. de Cælo, cap. 11. t. 10. Facilè quid sit id, de quo quæritur, potest intelligi, si explanatum sit, quod modis illud dicatur. Ecclesiæ ergò Naturam ac Definitionem investigaturis, tùm ipsum vocis ἔτυμον, tùm ejusdem πολυσυμασία, tùm denique variá ac multiplex ejus divisio probè expendenda fuerit.

Ecclesiæ igitur ἔτυμον origine Græcum est, & evocationem propriè significat: notato tamen magis Vocationis Objecto, hoc est, cœtu vocatorum, quam Vocandi actu. Septuaginta interpretes Hebræum קָהָל quod congregationem sive cœtum significat, plerumque reddiderunt per vocem Græcam συναγωγῆς: ad conditionem veteris populi, Judaici nimirum præcipuè respicientes. Quia enim Judæis Religio domi quasi nata fuit, hoc est, Deus in medio ejus ita habitavit, ut non demum aliundè ad cultum divinum addiscendum, evocatione aliquâ opus haberet: ideò Synagogæ appellatio rectissimè illis conveniebat. Cæterùm cùm post Ascensionem Christi, ad cultum Dei omnes linguæ & gentes ex universo terrarum orbe, demùm evocandæ essent, quippè quæ verum Dei cultum priùs planè ignorabant: hinc adeò factum, ut ipsi Apostoli suis in scriptis Cœtum vocatorum Gentilium, ἐκκλησίας Ecclesiæ termino indigitarent: sic illum à Synagoga Judaica discernentes. Rectè autem ipse quoque Bellarminus admonet, lib. 3. de Ecclesia militante, cap. 1. pag. 1225. l. B. populum Dei dici cœtum vocatorum, quia nemo ad hunc populum se adjungit perse, & suo proprio instinctu: sed omnes quotquot veniunt, à Dei vocatione præveniuntur.

Cæterum usus vocabuli Ecclesiæ tùm in Scripturis, tùm in disputationibus Adversariorum, deprehenditur geminus: Improprius nimirum sive καταχρηστικὸς: & proprius. Impropriè quando accipitur, tùm eandem fermè admittit significationem, quam obtinet vocabulum Civitatis in libris Politicorum. Quemadmodùm enim hoc non semper significat cœtum civium simul viventium: sed interdùm etiam locum, in quo cœtus ille vivit: Ita Ecclesia interdum, sed minùs propriè notat Locum, in quo vocati ad cultus sacros conveniunt: ut 1. Cor. 11, 18. Sic impropriè & planè abusivè vocabulum hoc à Pontificiis accommodatur ad solum Clerum, ita ut ab Ecclesia factum esse dictitent, quod ab uno tantùm ejus ordine est actum aut decretum.

Propriè quando usurpatur vox Ecclesiæ, triplicem significationem sortitur: Unam Generalissimam, quando notat quemlibet cœtum sive congregationem. Quo sensu Apoc. 2, 9. & 3. 9. Satanæ Synagoga nominatur: & Psal. 26, 5. Ecclesia malignantium, ἐκκλησία πονηρευομένων. Quô fortassis haud ineptè referri potest locus ille, Actor. 19, 32. Erat Ecclesia confusa συγκεχυμένη, & plures nesciebant quam ob causam convenissent.

Alteram specialem, quando accipitur pro toto cœtu vocatorum, sive eorum, qui per verbum & Sacramenta ad regnum Christi vocantur, & vocatione huic, quoad externum usum ministerii, locum relinquunt, licèt plurimi ipsorum non credant in Christum, sed æternùm pereant. Hoc ergò sensu, si Ecclesiæ vox ita simpliciter accipiatur, ultrò concedimus, Ecclesiæ membra non esse Solos Electos, & piè fideles; qui tamen extra cœtum istum vocatorum nunquàm (excepto necessitatis & violentiæ casu) & nusquam reperiuntur: sed esse universos eos, quo quot vocationis beneficio fruentes, fidem Christi quoquo modo profitentur, & Sacramentis utuntur. Hac in Ecclesia ut aliquis esse dicatur, satis est, ipsum professione Christianum, sive in coetu vocatorum esse. Et quatenus talis fidem Christi profitetur, eatenus Fidelis nominatur, ad differentiam Infidelium & paganorum, quia a Christiana Religione penitus abhorrent. Quo generali sensu accepto termino Fidelium, Ecclesia a nonnullis definitur coetus sive congregatio fidelium. Quanquam vero ad salutem minime sufficit, ut sic generaliter loquendo, & tantum quoad externam fidei Christianae professionem sis in Ecclesia: Salus tamen ipsa, extra hunc coetum, nemini obtingere potest. Et hic locum habet Comparatio illa Ecclesiae cum arca Noahi. Quemadmodum enim extra hanc nemo servatus fuit, durante diluvio: neque tamen omnes, qui in arca fuerunt, aeternum salvati sunt: Ita extra hanc vocatorum Ecclesiam nemo salvatur: non servantur tamen omnes, quotquot in amplissimo isto Ecclesiae coetu continentur. Proinde haec Ecclesia, Veritatis & Falsitatis distinctionem admittit: ut tum ad fidem, tum ad salutem plurimum intersit, utrius Ecclesiae, Veraene an falsae aliquis membrum sit. Qua de distinctione infra suo loco pluribus agetur.

Tertiam & postremam significationem, eamque specialissimam sortitur Ecclesiae vocabulum, quando pro coetu Electorum, pieque fidelium accipitur: Et tum Ecclesia recte definitur, quod sit Columna & firmamentum Veritatis. 1. Tim. 3, 15.

Tribus istis significationibus probe expensis planum fiet, quid judicandum sit de universa illa, & prolixa satis disputatione Bellarmini, quam de membris Ecclesiae instituit, lib. 3. de Ecclesia militante a cap. 1. usq; ad caput undecimum. Nam cap. 2. definit Ecclesiam, quod sit coetus hominum, ejusdem Christianae fidei professione, & eorundem Sacramentorum communione colligatus, sub regimine legitimorum pastorum, ac praecipue unius Christi in terris vicarij Romani Pontificis. Subjicit postmodum ab hac Ecclesia excludi primum omnes infideles gentiles, Judaeos, Turcas, Paganos: Deinde Catechumenos & excommunicatos: Tertio Schismaticos, qui habent fidem & Sacramenta, sed non subduntur legitimo pastori, & ideo foris profitentur fidem, & Sacramenta percipiunt. Quae sane Theologia multis modis falsa & absurda deprehenditur. Nam 1 obscuritate manifesta laborat. Non enim quaelibet professio fidei: ut neq; quaelibet Communio Sacramentorum constituit Ecclesiam Dei. Habent enim Hypocritae, habent & Haeretici, professionem fidei, & Sacramentorum usum: quos tamen Ecclesiam nonesse, sed malignantiuim esse, cum Davide credimus, Psalm 26, 5.

Deinde Definitio haec nec ipsi Romanae Ecclesiae competit. Nam integro Sacramentorum usu privantur Laici: Ergo vel hi non pertinent ad Ecclesiam, hoc est, ad coetum hominum, utentium Sacramentis, & quidem sub eorundem Sacramentorum communione colligatorum: vel haec Sacramentorum communio, non constituit differentiam specificam Ecclesiae. Sit secundum doctrinam Pontificiorum, Conjugium est Sacramentum: Atqui Clerici ab hoc Sacramento sub Papatu abhorrent. Ergo non sunt illi membra Ecclesiae, hoc est, coetus illius, qui eorundem (NB. EORUNDEM) Sacramentorum communione est colligatus.

Tertio competit haec definitio soli Ecclesiae visibili; hoc est, iis tantum, qui fidem jam externo actu profitentur. Qui error, quam crassus sit, infra dicendum fuerit, ubi de Ecclesia Invisibili ex professu disputabimus. Et observationem meretur id, quod Bellarminus hoc loco scribit: Etsi in Ecclesia inveniantur omnes virtutes, Fides, Spes, Charitas, & caetera: tamen ut aliquis absolute dici possit pars verae Ecclesiae, de qua Scripturae loquuntur, non putamus requiri ullam internam virtutem, sed tantum externam professionem fidei, & Sacramentorum Communionem, quo sensu ipso percipitur. Sic ergo Vera Ecclesiae vera membra ex sensu Bellarmini sunt pessimi quique hypocritae, modo exte. nae societati se adjungant.

Quarto quid illud monstri est, quod Schismaticos ideo ab Ecclesia excludi scribit, quia licet fidem & Sacramenta habeant, non tamen subduntur legitimo pastori. Sic ergo Bellarmino Vera erit Ecclesia, quae nec fidem nec Sacramenta habet, si tantum habeat obedientiam Romani Pontificis. Et rursum, Vera Ecclesia non erit, quae Fidem quidem & Sacramenta habet: sed tamen tertio hoc, nempe obedientia Romani Pontificis destituitur.

Tandem prolixe quidem disputat Bellarminus de Catechumenis, quod non sint in Ecclesia: sed perpetuis contradictionibus & seipsum, & rem totam implicat.

Turpis contradictio est, quod cap. 2 circa finem scribit: Catechumenos posse habere fidem & charitatem, imo esse de Anima Ecclesiae; sed interim illos non esse de Corpore Ecclesiae. Item, cap. 3. asserit: Catechumenos esse fideles & salvari posse: at nihilominus ipsos non esse in Ecclesia actu & proprie: sed tantum in potentia, quomodo homo conceptus, sed nondum formatus, & natus, non dicitur homo, nisi in potentia. Respicit nimirum Sophista Actum tantum externum, qui in externa professione fidei, externoq;e usu Sacramentorum consistit: Quem ipse ex Augustino nominat Corpus Ecclesiae. Ex quibus contradictionibus ut nos extricemus, distinctione opus esse, statuimus. Nam initio Bellarmino libenter largimur, duplicem quasi esse Ecclesiae formam: Unam, quae sit Animae, & concernat interna illa dona Spiritus sancti, Fidem, Spem, Charitatem: Alteram, quae sit Corporis, & respiciat externam professionem fidei & communicationem Sacramentorum. Caeterum quod inde colligit Jesuita, eos, qui non sunt de corpore, hoc est, qui nondum sunt admissi ad externam professionem fidei, & Sacramentorum participationem, licet habeant fidem & salvari possint,


### On the Nature and Essence of the Church: Various distinctions of the Church

are not, however, in the very act and properly of the Church, that we certainly deny simply. For that emerges only from that twofold form of the Church, namely that the Church can be considered in two ways: Either properly and oppositely according to the internal and external form: or absolutely and commonly according to both persons, according to that external form, who in the external participation of the Sacraments, to which they are not immediately admitted according to the custom of the Church, are not members of the Church: yet if they have faith, they are certainly members of the Church, according to that internal form, or internal act, and are more in the true Church than very many others, who indeed carry before them the external form of members of the Church, but are hypocrites within and are destitute of faith. For the internal form of a thing is an essential part of the thing itself: but the external accompanies the former; through the internal a thing is and acts: but through the external it is known. Thus faith is as it were the form of the Church considered in particular members. The analogy concerning a man who is indeed conceived, but not yet formed, clearly limps in this place. For Catechumens, if they have true faith in Christ, are not finally formed by the external use of the Sacraments: but they are already fully formed and born, namely by that one justifying medium: namely by faith, which afterwards is not finally formed and born through the Sacraments; but being already formed and born, it is only sealed and confirmed. We therefore invert Bellarmine's analogy in this manner: Just as a man is and is called [a man], not only he who has shown by an external act that he is endowed with an intelligent soul: but also he who truly has a rational soul within, however invisible: So a true member of the true Church is he who has true faith in Christ, although he has not yet been admitted to the external participation of the Sacraments, or to a public profession of faith.

A second contradiction is that Bellarmine concedes that definition of the Fathers, that the Church is a congregation of the faithful: And yet, soon forgetting himself, he concedes that Catechumens can indeed be faithful: but he nevertheless denies that they are members of the Church. For if the Church is a congregation of the faithful: then those who constitute the Church will certainly be the faithful. But such are the Catechumens, of whom the Jesuit treats. Therefore these also, as faithful, must necessarily constitute the true Church. Or, if the Jesuit persists in stubbornly denying this, he must confess: that the Church is indeed a congregation of the faithful: but not of all the faithful: but that there are faithful ones established outside the bosom of the true and Catholic Church: which is absurd to the point of being a prodigy, and utterly overturns and destroys the nature of the Catholic Church.

A third contradiction is that he concedes that Catechumens who are faithful can indeed be saved: but nevertheless are not members of the true Church. Is salvation then to be outside the Church? The Jesuit tries to struggle out of this difficulty by a certain newly devised distinction, writing: Outside the order

of the Church no one is saved, [this] ought to be understood of those who are neither in reality nor by desire of the Church: Now indeed, because Catechumens, if not in reality, are at least by vow in the Church; therefore they can be saved. But the Jesuit constrains himself. For he who is by vow in the Church; he is of the Church by Spirit, or by soul: but he who is by Spirit, he is in the Church by the very act, indeed by an internal act.

Moreover, this whole dispute can hardly be resolved more correctly; than if various divisions of the Church are premised, then a solid and perfect definition of it is subjoined, and thus at last a judgment may be formed concerning the members of the Church.

First, therefore, a manifold distinction happens to the Church on account of diverse consideration, which draws its origin from the matter itself, from the state, from the time, from the form, and from the respect of condition.

From the matter, which is the assembly of the called, the Church is divided into Universal and Particular. And the Universal is either absolutely such, or κατὰ τὶ. That which is absolutely such denotes the universal assembly of the faithful, which was from the beginning of the world, and still is, and will be until the end of the world. That which is Universal κατὰ τὶ contains that assembly of all the faithful who now live dispersed on earth throughout the whole Christian world.

A particular [Church] likewise is either looser or narrower: Looser, which is of a whole kingdom or people, or of some city: Narrower, however, which is proper to one house only, or to a few individuals: such as that Church of Aquila and Priscilla is written to have been. Rom. 16, 5. 1. Cor. 16, 19.

Then the Universal Church, although it is one and the same in its genus and its complexity: yet for diverse causes it comes about that a various and manifold distinction of it can be given. For with respect to state and consummation it is divided into Triumphant and Militant: of which the former contains that part of the Elect who, having finished this mortal life, have already migrated to the blessed and heavenly fatherland, eternally triumphing over sin, death, the flesh, the world, and Satan. That is called the Militant Church, which, having professed the religion of CHRIST, still has the necessity to fight in this world against adverse powers, under the auspices of the divine calling.

This militant [Church] is again subdivided according to the consideration of time, into the Church of the Old and New Testament. The former contains the assembly of those who, before the times of the Messiah exhibited in the flesh, were gathered under the Patriarchs and especially from the Israelite people. The latter, however, signifies that people which, after CHRIST was born, is gathered from the whole world through the preaching of the Gospel.

Furthermore, the militant Church of both Testaments is again divided into the visible and invisible Church: or internal and external. Which distinction, however, is not taken from any natural diversity of the subjects, or any other natural property or difference: but only from the ἀνέκτως or knowledge, which concerning the visible and invisible Church, is made partly by the external judgment of the eyes; but partly by the hidden and invisible, or internal κριτηρίῳ of faith. For example; truly faithful or

The elect constitute the Church both invisible and visible, but in a different respect. Invisible, insofar as their true faith is then invisible, and to the eyes of no man: but is known and perceived by the eyes of GOD alone, the Searcher of hearts: and insofar as the same elect are known not to us, but to GOD alone. Again, the same elect constitute the visible Church, insofar as they dwell in an external and visible assembly of the called, and use the external and observable ministry of the Word and Sacraments: insofar, finally, as the elect are not invisible spirits while they live in these lands: but as men, as called, as inaugurated by the Sacraments, they are seen by all. For vision is properly and primarily terminated only by a physical object: but it is attributed to spiritual things improperly and only by way of contemplation. But this distinction is to be treated expressly below.

Finally, the visible Church, by reason of its form, is divided into true and false. For because this visible Church is that which is bound together by the same profession of the Christian faith, and by the same use of the Sacraments, or at least an external and observable one, and one perceptible to the senses themselves: and indeed, truth and falsehood can befall both this profession of faith and the use of the Sacraments: hence it comes about that the visible Church is distinguished into true and false: in almost the same way as a true Christian is accustomed to be distinguished from a false one. For just as it is not enough to be a Christian, nor to be among the people of GOD: but it is required that each one be a true Christian, and that he be of the people of GOD: so also it is by no means enough to be a Church, and to be in the Church. For the name of Church also applies to the false congregation or the congregation of the malignant: Psalm 26:5. and those who are either atheists regarding their morals, or heretics regarding their doctrine, are not entirely outside the Church.

Moreover, the estimation of this truth and falsehood is not sought from the morals and life or piety or impiety of those who are in the assembly of the Church. For a certain and infallible judgment can never be sought from this, because of the many recesses of human hearts, and the frequent vicissitudes of changes: so that if the truth of the Church depended on this, we could never be certain of it. Furthermore, from the piety of men, a judgment is formed more correctly concerning the invisible than the visible Church. For if someone is truly pious, it is certainly concluded from that, that such a one is a member of that invisible Church of the elect. It is added that in these lands the condition of the Church, both true and false, is always mixed. For in the assembly of the true Church are found the impious, who are members of the false Church, and vice versa: in the assembly of the false Church, there are also the pious, who constitute members of the true Church, and belong to it by right. But the judgment of this truth and falsehood in the Church depends entirely upon the purity of heavenly doctrine faithfully retained, and upon the preservation of the legitimate use of the Sacraments, so that the true Church of Christ is that which preserves and propagates the pure doctrine of the Word and the uncorrupted use of the Sacraments: from which Church it is as impossible for the truly pious to be absent, as it is impossible that rain descending from Heaven should not water the earth: as the Lord himself asserts, Isaiah 55:10. But the false Church is that which depraves heavenly doctrine and wickedly corrupts the use of the Sacraments. In which assembly, although it is possible that some pious people also exist and are found: yet that is not a matter of necessity, but only of contingency.

Besides the distinctions already enumerated, the Romanists have devised a certain other and monstrous one, while they distinguish the Church into virtual, representative, and visible. They call the Church of the holy Angels and the blessed in heaven the virtual. They name the Roman Pontiff, and the rest of the shaven and anointed colluvies of bishops and cardinals, the representative. Finally, they call the rest of the assembly or multitude of Christians, whom they designate as laymen, the visible. Bellarmine, Vol. 1 of Controversies, pages 1132, 1163, 1276, 1279.

Latin:

non tamen ipso actu & propriè esse de Ecclesia, id certè simpliciter negamus. Illud enim tantùm ex gemina illâ Ecclesiæ formâ emergit, quòd videlicet Ecclesia duobus modis considerari possit: Aut propriè atq; oppositè secundum internam & externam formam: aut absolutè & communiter secundum utramque formam simul. Ergò licèt Catechumeni,& excommunicati resipiscentes, secundum externam illam formam, qui in externa participatione Sacramentorum, ad quam pro more Ecclesiæ non statim admittuntur, non sint membra Ecclesiæ: tamen si fidem habeant, certè sunt membra Ecclesiæ, secundum internam illam formam, sive actu interno, & magis sunt in Ecclesia vera, quàm plurimi alii, qui externam quidem formam membrorum Ecclesiæ præ se ferunt, sed intùs sunt Hypocritæ & fide destituuntur. Nam Forma rei interna est pars Essentialis ipsius rei: Externa autem priorem comitatur per internam res est, & agit: per externam verò cognoscitur. Sic Fides est quasi forma Ecclesiæ in membris particularibus consideratæ. Similitudo de Homine concepto quidem,sed nondùm formato, planè hoc loco claudicat. Nam Catechumeni, si veram fidem in Christum habeant, non demùm formantur, per externum usum Sacramentorum: sed jam sunt plenè formati & nati, nempè per unicum istud medium Justificans: nempè per Fidem, quæ postmodùm per Sacramenta non demùm formatur & nascitur; sed jam formata & nata, obsignatur tantùm & confirmatur. Invertimus proindè simile Bellarmini in hunc modum: Quemadmodum Homo est & dicitur, non tantùm qui externo actu prodidit, se esse præditum anima intelligente: sed & qui intus revera habet Animam rationalem, quantumvis invisibilem: Ita verum veræ Ecclesiæ membrum est, qui habet veram fidem in Christum, licèt ad externam Sacramentorum participationem, vel publicam fidei professionem nondùm sit admissus.

Alterà Contradictio est, quod Bellarminus concedit definitionem illam Patrum, quòd Ecclesia sit congregatio fidelium: Et tamen mox sui oblitus, Catechumenos fideles quidem esse posse concedit: sed membra Ecclesiæ illos esse inseitè negat. Nam si Ecclesia est congregatio fidelium: utique fideles erunt illi, qui constituunt Ecclesiam. At tales sunt Catechumeni, de quibus agit Jesuwita. Ergò & hi, tanquàm fideles; Ecclesiam veram constituant necesse est. Vel, si hoc præfractè negare pergat Jesuwita, fateatur oportet: Ecclesiam esse congregationem quidem fidelium: sed non omnium fidelium: verùm dari fideles, extra Ecclesiæ veræ ac Catholicæ gremium constitutos: id quod ad prodigium usque absurdum est, & naturam Catholicæ Ecclesiæ penitùs evertit ac destruit.

Tertia Contradictio est, quòd concedit Catechumenos fideles salvari quidem posse: sed nihilominùs non esse membra veræ Ecclesiæ. Siccine ergò extra Ecclesiam erit salus? Ex hac difficultate eluctari conatur Jesuwita, novâ quâdam excogitatâ distinctiunculâ, scriptitans: Extra ordinem

Ecclesiam neminem salvari, intelligi debere de ijs, qui neq; reipsa, nec desiderio sunt de Ecclesia: Jam vero, quia Catechumeni, si non re, saltem voto sunt in Ecclesia; ideo salvari possunt. Verùm seipsum constringit Jesusvita. Qui enim voto est in Ecclesia; ille Spiritu, sive animâ est de Ecclesia: sed qui Spiritu est, ille ipso actu est in Ecclesia, verùm actu interno.

Cæterùm vix rectiùs tota hæc disputatio expediri potest; quam si præmittantur variæ divisiones Ecclesiæ, deindè subjungatur solida & perfecta ejus Definitio, & sic tandem judicium informetur de membris Ecclesiæ.

Primùm igitur Ecclesiæ propter diversam considerationem multiplex distinctio accidit, quæ tùm ex materia ipsa, tùm ex statu, tùm tempore, tùm forma, tùm respectu conditionis ortum trahit.

Ex materia, quæ est cœtus vocatorum, dividitur Ecclesia in Universalem & Particularem. Et Universalis quidem vel absolutè talis est, vel κατὰ τὶ. Quæ absolutè talis est, notat universum fidelium cœtum, qui fuit ab origine mundi, estq; etiamnùm, & futurus est ad finem mundi. Quæ κατὰ τὶ est Universalis, eum continet cœtum fidelium omnium, qui nunc in terris per totum orbem Christianum dispersi vivunt.

Particularis itidem vel laxior est, vel angustior: Laxior, quæ totius vel regni vel populi, vel civitatis alicujus: Angustior autem, quæ unius tantùm domus, aut paucorum individuorum est propria: qualis fuisse scribitur illa Ecclesia Aquilæ & Priscillæ. Rom. 16, 5. 1. Cor. 16, 19.

Deindè Ecclesia Universalis, quamvis genere & complexu suo una sit atquè eadem: diversis tamen causis fit, ut varia & multiplex ejus dari possit distinctio. Nam Status & Consummationis respectu dispescitur ea in Triumphantem & Militantem: quarum illa partem Electorum eam continet, qui vitâ hâc mortali functi, jam ad beatam & cœlestem migrârunt patriam, de peccato, morte, carne, mundo, Satanâ devictis æternùm triumphantes. Militans illa vocatur Ecclesia, quæ Religionem CHRISTI professa, hoc in mundo adhuc contra potestates adversarias, sub auspiciis divinæ vocationis, pugnare necessum habet.

Militans hæc rursus temporis ratione subdividitur, in Ecclesiam Veteris & Novi Testamenti. Illa continet cœtum eorum, qui ante tempora Messiæ in carne exhibiti, sub Patriarchis, & ex populo Israëlitico præcipuè collectus fuit. Hæc verò eum populum significat, qui post natum CHRISTUM, per prædicationem Evangelii, ex toto terrarum orbe congregatur.

Porrò Militans Ecclesia utriusq; Testamenti, rursus dispescitur in Ecclesiam Visibilem & Invisibilem: sive internam & externam. Quæ tamen distinctio non sumitur vel à diversitate aliqua naturali Subjectorum, vel quacunq; alia naturali proprietate aut discrimine: sed tantùm ἀνέκτως sive notitiâ, quæ de visibili & invisibili Ecclesia, partim fit externo oculorum judicio; partim verò occulto & invisibili, sive interno fidei κριτηρίῳ. Exempli gratiâ; Verè fideles sive

Electi constituunt Ecclesiam & Invisibilem & Visibilem, sed diverso respectu. Invisibilem, quatenùs tùm vera ipsorum fides infe est invisibilis, & nullius hominis oculis: sed solius DEI, Scrutatoris cordium, oculis est cognita & perspecta: tùm quatenùs iidem Electi, non nobis, sed soli DEO sunt cogniti. Rursus iidem Electi Visibilem constituunt Ecclesiam, quatenùs in externo atque visibili vocatorum cœtu versantur, atque externo & adspectabili Verbi ac Sacramentorum ministerio utuntur: quatenùs denique Electi non sunt Invisibiles Spiritus, dùm in his terris degunt: sed ut homines, ut vocati, ut Sacramentis inaugurati ab omnibus visuntur. Visio enim propriè & primò non nisi Objecto physico terminatur: Spiritualibus autem rebus impropriè καὶ ἐποψίως duntaxat tribuitur. Sed de hac distinctione infrà ex professo agendum.

Tandem Ecclesia Visibilis ratione Formæ, disjungitur in Veram & Falsam. Quia enim Visibilis hæc Ecclesia ea est, quæ fidei Christianæ professione eâdem, & Sacramentorum usu eodem, vel externo saltem & adspectabili, ipsisque sensibus perceptibili colligata est: & verò tùm professioni huic fidei, tùm Usui Sacramentorum Veritas & Falsitas potest obtingere: hinc adeò fit, ut in Veram & Falsam Ecclesia Visibilis distinguatur: eodem fermè modo, quo Christianus verus à falso distingui solet. Quemadmodum enim neque Christianum esse, neque in populo DEI esse, sufficit: sed ut verè Christianus quisque sit, & ut de populo DEI sit, requiritur: Ita quoque Ecclesiam esse, & in Ecclesia esse, minimè sufficit. Nam & falsæ sive malignantium congregationi, nomen Ecclesiæ competit: Psalm. 26, 5. & non sunt extra Ecclesiam prorsus, qui aut quoad mores sunt ἄθεοι, aut quoad doctrinam, hæretici.

Cæterùm Veritatis hujus atque falsitatis æstimatio, non petitur à moribus & vitâ vel pietate aut impietate eorum, qui sunt in cœtu Ecclesiæ. Ex hac enim certum & infallibile judicium nunquàm peti potest, propter plurimos cordium humanorum recessus, & crebras mutationum vicissitudines: ut si Ecclesiæ veritas indè dependeret, nos nunquàm de ea certi esse possemus. Quid quòd ex pietate hominum, rectiùs de invisibili, quàm de visibili Ecclesia informatur judicium. Si enim verè pius aliquis sit, indè certè colligitur, talem invisibilis illius Electorum Ecclesiæ esse membrum. Accedit, quòd in his terris semper est mixta conditio Ecclesiæ tàm veræ quàm falsæ. Nam in cœtu veræ Ecclesiæ reperiuntur impii, qui sunt membra falsæ Ecclesiæ, & vice versa: In cœtu falsæ Ecclesiæ, sunt & pii, qui membra Veræ Ecclesiæ constituunt, & ad hanc jure pertinent. Verùm ex Doctrinæ cœlestis puritate fideliter retentâ, & ex conservatione legitimi usus Sacramentorum, Veritatis istius & falsitatis in Ecclesia judicium in folidum dependet, ut vera sit Ecclesia Christi, quæ doctrinam Verbi puram, usumque Sacramentorum incorruptum cõservat & propagat: à quâ Ecclesiâ verè pios abesse, tàm est impossibile, quàm impossibile est, ut imber de Cœlo descendens non inebriet terram: sic asserente ipso Domino, Jes. 55. 10. Falsa autem sit Ecclesia, quæ doctrinam cœlestem depravat, & usum Sacramentorum improbè corrumpit. In quo cœtu, tametsi pios etiam aliquos esse atque inveniri possibile est: non id tamen est necessitatis, sed contingentiæ duntaxat.

Præter distinctiones jam enumeratas, novam quandam aliam & monstrosam excogitarunt Romanenses, dùm Ecclesiam distinguunt in Virtualem, Repræsentativam, & Visibilem. Virtualem vocant Sanctorum Angelorum, & beatorum cœlitum Ecclesiam. Repræsentativam nominant Pontificem Romanum, ac reliquam Episcoporum atq; Cardinalium rasam unctamq; colluviem. Visibilem denique appellant reliquum Christianorum, quos illi Laicos indigitant, cœtum sive multitudinem. Bellarm. Tom. 1. Controversiarum pag. 1132. 1163. 1276. 1279.


### On the Nature and Essence of the Church: Various distinctions of the Church (continued)

But the vanity of this distinction is detected in many ways. For first, it is not a division of a genus into species, such as every true and legitimate division ought to be. For that virtual Church of the Angels does not fall under the same genus as the Church of men: as those who constitute a Church with us neither by any calling, nor by the means of calling, namely the Word and Sacraments.

Then it is sacrilegious, while one Order of sacrificers seizes for itself alone the august title of the Church, with a nefarious and sacrilegious daring. Scripture certainly names not the clergy alone, but all the faithful entirely, scattered here and there throughout the whole Christian world, a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of GOD, living stones, built upon the cornerstone, which is CHRIST: 1 Peter 2:5 & 9.

Finally, it is profane and smacks of something worldly, namely this: that just as the Philosopher in book 9 of the Ethics, chapter 9, considers that to be a city most of all which is principal in it: and just as the whole city is said to do and feel what its princes and governors do and feel: so under the title, decree, and authority of the Church, whatever that shaven and anointed crowd of sacrificers wills, commands, and decrees is held as ratified and holy. From which tyranny, while GOD willed our Churches to be asserted by the blessed Luther, there is certainly cause for us to give eternal thanks to His infinite mercy.

The adversaries bring forward two passages from the Scriptures to confirm their opinion:

One from book 1 of 1 Kings 8:14, where King Solomon is read to have blessed the whole Church, that is, the Priests and Pontiffs, at the dedication of the Temple: Another from chapter 19:8 of Exodus, where it is read that all the people, that is, the Priests and Levites, answered Moses: 'All that the Lord has spoken we will do.' Therefore, they say, the title of the whole Church is assigned in the Scriptures to the Priests and Levites. But I reply that a manifest crime of falsehood is committed in both places. For in neither place is the title of the whole Church attributed to the Priests and Levites alone. For in the former place it is not read that only the Priests and Pontiffs were gathered then: but verses 2, 3, and 4 expressly affirm that then all Israel, and all the Elders of Israel, gathered to King Solomon, with the princes of the tribes and the leaders of the families. Thus in the latter place, not only the Priests and Levites, but also, as verse 7 has it, all the elders of the people are read to have been summoned by Moses. Here, therefore, it could truly be said that it was thus answered to Moses by all the people, although not all the people were present then, because those elders or seniors of the people, having first explored the mind of the people and having agreed, had answered thus.

Moreover, to return to our purpose, today it is fought most especially between us and the Jesuits concerning the True Church: whose definition, such as Bellarmine has produced, we showed a little earlier. We are most persuaded that the True Church can be defined most correctly and plainly as follows: The True Church of the New Testament is the assembly of all those men who, through the ministry of the Gospel purely preached and the Sacraments legitimately administered, are called and gathered into the society of the kingdom of Christ, in which there cannot but be the elect, and those truly believing in Christ, and thus to be saved eternally: yet so that the evil and unholy are mixed with them, though professing the same doctrine.

With this Definition standing, that question immediately arises which Bellarmine also moves at length: Of what men does the Church consist? In order for this question to be explained dexterously, first, in general, the subject itself of the Question must be properly noted: concerning which Church, indeed, the controversy properly exists: whether of the Church simply so called: or truly, specifically, of the true Church? While Bellarmine does not observe this, it happens that he discourses about this question like a blind man about colors. We, first in general, concerning the Church simply so called, insofar as it promiscuously denotes the assembly of the called, whom God calls by the voice of His Gospel to the society of His people, we establish that, taken in this sense, it extends as widely as the Christian world itself spreads, that is, the assembly of the called who profess the Christian faith. For in order for any assembly to deserve the title of Church, it is enough if it has the doctrine of the Gospel and the use of the Sacraments, even if both are most corrupt. This is evident from chapters 2 and 3 of the Apocalypse, where the appellation of Church is attributed to the Ephesian, Pergamene, Thyatiran, Sardian, and Laodicean assemblies, of which, however, the Holy Spirit affirms that they had left their first love, that they had fallen, that they had in their midst those holding the doctrine of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, that they had permitted the woman Jezebel to teach and seduce the servants of the Lord, that they were neither cold nor hot, etc.

Therefore, the members of the Church simply so called are not only the elect themselves and the piously faithful, who indeed are never and nowhere found outside this assembly of the called: but also, in the same complex, are included as many as have coalesced into one by the same vocation and the same profession of the Christian name. For just as Augustine, in his book on the Unity of the Church, rightly denies that those are in the Church who do not believe that Christ came in the flesh, from the Virgin Mary of the seed of David, or that He rose in the same body in which He was crucified and buried: so those who believe this, as many as are baptized, as they indeed profess to believe, are all to be judged to be in the Church.
