In this respect, the whole world is commonly and rightly distinguished into believers and unbelievers, so that as many as have not received the faith of Christ are held for unbelievers or pagans and Gentiles, and are said to be outside the church and on the outside. But all the others, who are called in the name of Christ, who are initiated by the Sacrament of Baptism, who finally are joined even by an external profession of the Christian faith: they are to be held entirely as parts and members of the Church simply so called: and they are called believers, with the term 'believers' taken ἐν πλάτει (broadly) and opposed to the profanity of the Gentiles.

Moreover, if one asks about the Church specifically, and indeed about the True Church, who are its members and parts, we answer first that all the Elect have a place in it, insofar as they dwell in the external and visible society of the Church: which Bellarmine himself also admits in chapter 7 of the third book.

Then we establish that the members of this Church are also the Catechumens, who, although not yet dipped in Baptism, are kept while remaining in the learning of the dogmas of the Christian faith: an example of which thing Ambrose shows in the case of Emperor Valentinian in his Oration on his death. Bellarmine indeed denies this in chapter 3, book 3, but without any evident reason, as has already been shown above.

Thirdly, the weak in faith and the imperfect in life pertain here. For just as faith does not save insofar as it is either firm or weak, but only insofar as it apprehends the merit of Christ: so also the weakness of faith can remove no one from the society of the true Church. Thus, the imperfection of life, insofar as the reins are not loosened to crimes against conscience, does not overturn faith itself.

…Fourthly, those whom the Roman Synagogue holds as Excommunicated cannot be separated from the census and number of the members of the True Church. For not Excommunication itself, but for the sake of communion, deprives one of the society of the true Church. Therefore, a diligent distinction must be made among the excommunicated, some of whom are justly and legitimately excommunicated, while others are cast out of the Church by the injury and tyranny of the Papists, beyond what is right and deserved, solely on account of their profession of the Evangelical Truth. Just as, therefore, we willingly concede to Bellarmine that those who are justly and legitimately excommunicated are removed from the fellowship of the true Church—although they remain members of the church simply so called, insofar as they are baptized; insofar as they may return to the true Church through repentance, not being baptized again; and insofar as they are not separated from the people of God, whom the Church brings to a better mind through repentance by either degrading or excommunicating them—so too, the force and tyranny of the Papists can no more deprive those who are unjustly and undeservedly excommunicated of the fellowship of the true Church than Rome can bestow the faith and title of the true Church upon any mortal of eminence. And Bellarmine is clearly an inept disputant when, in chapter 6 of book 3, he simply and indefinitely denies that all excommunicated persons are in the Church: for if this is understood of the church simply so called, it is manifestly false; but if it is taken of the true Church, it can be admitted κατὰ τι (in a certain respect) only, namely, regarding those who are justly excommunicated, as has already been shown.

Finally (which must be placed in the category of the accidental), there are in the same true Church, mixed with the Elect and the truly pious, those who are not holy, who err in religion itself, and indeed have even fallen into heresies, and what is greater, even into infidelity itself, but as yet hidden, and neither manifested by open apostasy nor marked by the censure of excommunication. Augustine confirms this opinion in book 3, chapter 19, of On Baptism, asserting that heretics are in the Church before they are separated by obstinacy and pertinacity, so that they are called not so much heretics as erring while they are still in the Church. Scripture confirms this very thing with various similitudes: of the chaff and the wheat, Matt. 13:12; of the wheat and the tares, Matt. 13:24; of the dragnet or seine containing good and bad fish, Matt. 13:47; of the wedding, at which good and bad guests are present, Matt. 22:10; of the wise and foolish virgins, Matt. 25:1. A sheepfold in which there are sheep and goats, John 10; a great house, in which there are vessels of the most diverse kinds, some for honor, some for dishonor, 2 Tim. 2:20.

Moreover, it must be well noted in this place that the condition of the wicked and of heretics is not one and the same regarding the true Church, which is of the Elect and the piously faithful. Indeed, the wicked are in the true Church, just as the Elect are sometimes in the false church; but neither these nor those are of the Church in which they are, but both are in that church of which they are not. For these two things differ, to be IN the Church and to be OF the Church, in the same way that, according to the opinion of the Savior, it differs to be IN the world and to be OF the world, John 17. To be in the world is nothing other than to live in the midst of the children of this world; to be of the world is to follow and approve the perverse pursuits of the world. Thus, to be in the true Church is nothing other than to live in the assembly of those who, through the preaching of the Word and the administration of the Sacraments, constitute the true Church. To be of the Church is to agree entirely regarding the doctrine of the Word and the Sacraments. Now, those who follow a different opinion, discrepant from the purity of doctrine, as heretics do, they indeed cease to be of the true Church, but they do not cease to be in the true Church, as long as they are not cast out by the Church and do not themselves make a public secession to a false church. There are Orthodox Theologians who explain this matter a little differently, but they differ from what we have just said more in the sound of the words than in the sense. For they establish that these two phrases, to be IN the Church and to be OF the Church, differ as a part and a member of the Church. For it is one thing to be a part, another to be a member of the Church. For the name of a part is spread more widely; the name of a member is narrower. A part is referred to any whole whatsoever; a member looks toward an animated body, or at least something similar and analogous. Thus, a part is found without life, as in a stone, wood, or metal; but a member truly and properly cannot even be understood without life. Therefore, heretics and those who are not holy are indeed parts of the true church while they live and move in its bosom, as it were; but they are by no means to be called members of the same, just as the pious who cling to a false Church are indeed parts of it while they move in its external fellowship, but they are by no means to be considered members of the same.

Clearer testimonies of Scripture confirm this very thing, as when the Apostle expressly writes: 'There must be heresies ἐν ὑμῖν, among you, that those who are approved may be made manifest among you,' 1 Cor. 11:19. And elsewhere he predicts that the Antichrist will sit in the temple of God, 2 Thess. 2:4. Hence it is that the Blessed Luther writes that the Pope and the Cardinals are in the Church, generally so called, but he denies that they are of the Church, that is, the true one. Thus, conversely, there are today in the Roman church, which we are most persuaded is false, many who think rightly concerning religion. These, therefore, although they are in the assembly of the false church, are nevertheless members of the true Church. Thus, heretics are indeed a part of the true Church in which they live and move, but they are members of the false church with which they think and teach.

Bellarmine, Stapleton, Pistorius, and others are in an uproar at this point, objecting various things to us: and first, indeed, they keep saying that by this doctrine of ours it could be elicited by the same reasoning that Jews, Mahometans, and others who nevertheless reject the Christian religion are also in the true Church, because it happens that such people not rarely live in the midst of the faithful? But we answer that the consequence is simply false, because of the huge reason for the diversity that exists between heretics and Jews, Mahometans, and other peoples of this kind. For the reason that we do not simply cut off a place for heretics in the true Church is because they are through the sacrament of initiation grafted into the Church: because they retain the external profession of the Christian faith, and because they themselves can also administer the true Sacraments. Since all these things do not apply to Jews, Mahometans, and other infidel peoples, it happens that they are not in the Church, even if they live in the very midst of Christians.

Furthermore, the adversaries clamor, and accuse us of I know not what vanity, while we concede in this question that the Roman Church is a Church, and that in it there are many who are piously faithful or elect: yet at other times we deny that there is a Church among the Papists.

I answer that no mark of confusion or contradiction can be imputed to us at all, since we predicate both things most truly of one and the same Roman or Papal Church: but not in the same way, but in one respect and another. For we cannot deny that there is a Church among the Papists, because we argue that it is a false one. For from species to genus, the inference is rightly affirmative. But in the meantime, it does not follow: The Papists are a Church: Therefore they are a true Church: For from one disparate species to another, there is no affirmative inference: but only a negative one, in this way: The Papists are a false Church: Therefore they are not a true one. Therefore, without contradiction, we both concede and deny that the Papists are a Church. But when they themselves infer thus: The Papists are a Church: Therefore they are a true Church: then they infer affirmatively from genus to species: which neither the precepts of Logic nor the truth of the matter itself permit.

But do they rise higher? Do we think that there are some good and elect people in the Roman Church? Yet we grant this very thing willingly: For if there were no elect there, it could hardly happen that God would not immediately cut off that Church. And if there were no elect there from the assembly of adults, at least the infants, who cease to be among the living after being baptized before they can give assent to Papal idolomania, would constitute a true Church of the elect in the midst of the Papacy. But from that, there is no inference to the Roman Church itself, that it is itself a true Church of the elect: certainly no more than it follows by any reason: The good are always mixed with the evil in external conversation: Therefore the evil themselves are those good ones: Or, Truly pious and Orthodox people have always been mixed with the assembly of Arians: Therefore the Arians themselves were a true and Orthodox Church.

Here, with what has been said so far about the members of the true Church properly observed, the things which Bellarmine disputes especially in chapter 4 of the third book concerning Heretics, and simply denies that they are in the true Church, can be refuted without difficulty. Where, besides what has already been said, this also must be observed by those who are disputing, that in this whole dispute about the True Church, the question is not properly: Who are the saints? For that we may know this undoubtedly, it is not discerned by external signs: But that it is uniquely sought and disputed: Where is the truth of Christian doctrine, where is the legitimate use of the Sacraments; And by what means does it come about that men can rightly aspire to true holiness? While the Jesuit does not weigh this, but immediately takes it for granted that the Roman Church is a true Church, and that heretics are not in the Church, it happens that he disputes about this grave matter like a blind man about colors.

However, the things which he disputes in the following fifth chapter concerning Schismatics seem more probable, provided that the definition of a Schismatic is rightly established for us, and the Jesuit understands those who (as the etymology of the word itself suggests) cut themselves off and tear themselves away from the body of the true Church, and make a secession to a false Church. For in this case and respect, we would easily concede that such Schismatics are neither in the true Church nor of the true Church. And to these, that Apostolic saying is most rightly applied, 1 John 2:19: They went out from us, but they were not of us: for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us: but that they might be manifest that they are not of us, they went out from us. But if Schismatics are taken according to the customary and received definition of Schism: namely, that a Schism is committed when they indeed agree on doctrine, but are split into factions in the matter of external and indifferent things, those who ought to have been most closely joined: then I certainly deny that Schismatics are not in the true Church. For since the members of the true Church coalesce into one body only by the unity of purer doctrine: and indeed Schism is about ceremonies, rites, and external things: certainly because of dissonance in these things, the unity of faith is not taken away: and consequently, such Schismatics also do not cease to be in the Church and of the true Church.

But let these things said about the present question, namely who are the members of the true Church, suffice: from which, by the contrary sense, it will now be easy to infer: Who are not members of the true Church? They are excluded from it, first of all, all unbaptized infidels, Jews, Mahometans, Gentiles, and all open enemies of the Christian faith. Apostates are also excluded, since they have made a manifest secession from the true Church to a false one. Furthermore, the excommunicated are also excluded from here, since they have been ejected from the fellowship of the true Church: although in the meantime they are not simply eliminated from the universal Church, or from the assembly of the called. Finally, Heretics are also excluded from here, but those already convicted of error several times, condemned, and yet nevertheless, they have and maintain either the true doctrine polluted and adulterated by various depravations, or the Sacraments by horrendous abuses, or finally both Doctrine and Sacraments by wicked corruptions. The assembly and congregation of these, whatever and however great the appearance of external piety may be, can in no way be held or ought to be held as the True Church: since it has made a secession from the true Church, and has degenerated into a false or malignant Church.

Latin:

Verùm Distinctionis hujus vanitas multis modis deprehenditur. Primùm enim non est divisio Generis in species, qualis esse debet omnis vera ac legitima Divisio. Nam virtualis illa Angelorum Ecclesia, sub idem genus cum Ecclesiâ hominum non cadit: ut qui neque ex vocatione aliquâ, neque ex Vocationis mediis, Verbo nimirùm & Sacramentis, Ecclesiam nobiscum unam constituunt.

Deindè sacrilega est, dùm unus Sacrificulorum Ordo, augustum Ecclesiæ titulum sibi soli rapit, ausu nefario & sacrilego. Scriptura certè non Clericos solos, sed omnes omninò fideles hinc indè per totum orbem Christianum disperfos, nominat Genus electum, regale Sacerdotium, gentem sanctam, populum DEI, vivos lapides, ædificatos super lapidem angularem, qui est CHRISTUS: 1. Pet. 2, 5 & 9.

Tandem prophana est & mundani aliquid resipit, illud videlicet: ut quemadmodum Philosophus lib. 9. Eth. cap. 9. Civitatem id maximè esse censet, quod in ea principale est: & quemadmodum tota Civitas id facere & sentire dicitur, quod principes & gubernatores ejus faciunt & sentiunt: ita sub Ecclesiæ titulo, decreto atq; autoritate, ratum ac sanctum habeatur, quicquid rasa illa & uncta Sacrificulorum caterva vult, jubet, decernit. A quâ Tyrannide dùm nostras Ecclesias per B. Lutherum assertas voluit DEUS, est sanè quod infinitæ ipsius misericordiæ æternas agamus gratias.

Proferunt Adversarii duo loca ex Scripturis pro confirmanda sua sententia:

Unum ex libr. 1. Reg. 8, 14. Ubi Salomon rex in dedicatione Templi toti Ecclesiae, hoc est, Sacerdotibus & Pontificibus benedixisse legatur: Alterum ex cap. 19. 8. Exodi, ubi legatur Omnis populus hoc est, Sacerdotes & Levitae respondisse Mosi: Cuncta quae locutus est Dominus faciemus. Ergo, inquiunt illi, Sacerdotibus & Levitis, totius Ecclesiae titulus in Scripturis adsignatur. Sed respondeo, manifestum crimen falsi in utroque loco committi. In neutro enim solis Sacerdotibus & Levitis & Levitis, Ecclesiae totius titulus tribuitur. Nam in priore loco non legitur, quod duntaxat Sacerdotes & Pontifices tum fuerint congregati: sed versus 2. & 3. & 4. diserte affirmant, quod tum universus Israel, cunctique Seniores Israel convenerint ad regem Salomonem, cum principibus tribuum, & ducibus familiarum. Sic in posteriore loco non soli Sacerdotes & Levitae, sed & ut versus 7. habet, omnes majores natu populi, a Mose convocati fuisse leguntur. Hic ergo vere dici potuit, ab omni populo Mosi sic responsum fuisse, licet non omnis populus tum praesens adesset, quia illi natu majores vel seniores populi explorata prius populi mente consensique, sic responderant.

Ceterum, ut ad institutum nostrum redeamus, de Vera Ecclesia hodie vel maxime inter nos & Jesuvvitas pugnatur: Cujus definitionem, qualem Bellarminus prodiderit, paulo ante ostendimus. Nos Veram Ecclesiam sic rectissime ac planissime definiri posse, habemus persuasissimum: Ecclesia Vera Novi Testamenti est coetus eorum hominum omnium, qui per ministerium Evangelij, pure praedicati, & Sacramentorum legitime administratorum, ad societatem regni Christi vocantur, congreganturque, in quo non possunt, non esse electi, & vere in Christum credentes, & sic aeternum salvandi: sic tamen ut istis sint permixti mali & non sancti, eandem tamen doctrinam profitentes.

Stante hac Definitione, oritur statim quaestio illa, quam Bellarminus etiam prolixe movet: Ex quibus hominibus constet Ecclesia? Quaestio haec ut dextre explicetur, primum in genere subjectum ipsum Quaestionis probe est notandum: de qua nimirum Ecclesia proprie sit controversia: num de Ecclesia simpliciter sic appellata: an vero in specie de Ecclesia vera? Hoc dum non observat Bellarminus, fit, ut de quaestione hac differat, tanquam caecus de coloribus. Nos primum in genere, de Ecclesia simpliciter sic dicta, quatenus ea promiscue coetum vocatorum notat, quos Evangelij sui voce, ad societatem populi sui Deus vocat, sic statuimus, quod hoc sensu accepta, tam late pateat, quam late se diffundit ipse orbis Christianus, hoc est, coetus vocatorum, qui Christianam fidem profitentur. Nam ut Ecclesiae titulum mereatur coetus quispiam, satis est, si Evangelij doctrinam & usum Sacramentorum habeat, licet utrumque corruptissimum. Constat hoc ex cap. 2. & 3. Apocalypseos, ubi coetui Ephesino, Pergamensi, Thyatirensi, Sardensi, Laodicensi, tribuitur Ecclesiae appellatio, de quibus tamen Spiritus Sanctus affirmat, quòd charitatem primam reliquerint, quòd exciderint, quòd in medio sui habuerint tenentes doctrinam Balaam, & Nicolaitarum, quòd permiserint mulierem Jezabel docere & seducere servos Domini, quòd neque frigidi neque calidi fuerint. &c.

Membra ergò Ecclesiæ simpliciter sic dictæ, non tantùm sunt electi ipsi, & piè fideles, qui quidem extra cœtum istum vocatorum, nunquàm & nuspiam reperiuntur: sed & ejusdem complexu comprehenduntur, quotquot eâdem vocatione, eâdemque professione Christiani nominis in unum quali coaluerunt. Nam uti Augustinus, lib. de Vnit at. Ecclesiæ rectè negat in Ecclesia esse eos, qui non credunt Christum in carne venisse, de virgine Maria ex semine David, aut in eo corpore resurrexisse, in quo crucifixus & sepultus fuit: Ita qui hoc credunt, quod sanè credere se profitentur, quotquot baptisati sunt, utique illi omnes in Ecclesia esse censendi sunt. Hoc respectu universus mundus vulgò rectè in fideles & in infideles distinguitur, ut quotquot fidem Christi non receperunt, illi pro infidelibus sive paganis & Ethnicis habeantur, ac extra ecclesiam & foris esse dicantur: Cæteri verò omnes, qui in Christi nomine sunt vocati qui Sacramento Baptismi anaugurati, qui denique vel externâsaltem fidei Christianæ professione sunt conjuncti: ij pro partibus & membris Ecclesiæ simpliciter sic dictæ, omninò sint habendi: & fideles dicantur, fidelium termino ἐν πλάτει accepto, & Gentilium prophanitati opposito.

Cæterùm si de Ecclesia in specie, & quidem de Vera Ecclesia quæratur, Quinam ejus sint membra & partes, respondemus primùm in ea locum sortiri Electos omnes, quatenùs in societate Ecclesiæ externa atque adspectabili versantur: id quod Bellarminus ipse quoque fatetur, capite 7. libri tertij.

Deindè membra hujus Ecclesiæ statuimus etiam esse Catechumenos, qui, licet Baptismo nondum tincti, in fidei tam en Christianæ dogmatibus addiscendis commorantes servantur: Cujus rei exemplum in Valentiniano Imp. monstrat Ambrosius in Orat. de ejusdem obitu. Negat quidem hoc Bellarminus cap. 3. l. 3. sed præter omnem evidentem rationem, uti jam suprà est ostensum.

Tertiò huc pertinent infirmi in fide, in vita imperfecti. Quemadmodum enim fides non salvat, quatenùs vel firma vel infirma est: sed tantùm quatenùs apprehendit Christi meritum: ita fidei etiam infirmitas ex societate veræ Ecclesiæ, neminem removere potest. Sic vitæ imperfectio, quatenùs quidem non contra conscientiam sceleribus frena laxantur, fidem ipsam non evertit.

Quartò à censu numeroque membrorum Veræ Ecclesiæ segregari non possunt illi, quos Synagoga Romana pro Excommunicatis habet. Non enim Excommunicatio ipsa, sed communicationis causa privat societate Ecclesiæ veræ. Diligenter proindè inter Excommunicatos est distinguendum, quorum aliqui justè ac legitimè sunt excommunicati, alij verò per Injuriam ac Tyrannidem Pontificiorum, præter fas ac meritum, tantùm ob professionem Veritatis Evangelicæ, Ecclesiâ ejiciuntur. Quemadmodum ergò Bellarmino libenter concedimus, quòd justè ac legitimè excommunicati, à Consortio Veræ Ecclesiæ sint eliminati: licèt ecclesiæ simpliciter sic dictæ membra maneant, quatenùs nimirùm sunt baptizati: quatenùs per pœnitentiam ad veram Ecclesiam reverti, non iterùm baptizantur, quatenus denique à populo Dei non separantur, quos vel degradando, vel excommunicando ad meliorem mentem per pœnitentiam adigit Ecclesia: Ita injustè ac præter meritum excommunicatos, tàm non vis ac tyrannis pontificia, Ecclesiæ veræ consortio privare potest, quàm non ulli mortalium Fidem & titulum veræ Ecclesiæ, Romana eminentiæ impertire potest. Et ineptus planè est disputator Bellarminus, dùm cap. 6. libri 3. simpliciter ac indefinitè omnes Excommunicatos negat esse in Ecclesia: quòd si de Ecclesia simpliciter sic dicta intelligatur, manifestè falsum est: si verò de Ecclesia vera accipiatur, κατὰ τι tantùm, nempè de justè excommunicatis, admitti potest, uti jam ostensum.

Tandem (id quod in parte accidentis est reponendum) sunt in eâdem vera Ecclesiâ, Electis ac vere pijs mixti non sancti, in religione ipsa errantes, imò in hæreses etiam, & quod majus est ad ipsam usque prolapsi infidelitatem, sed occultam adhuc, & neque manifesta Apostasia manifestatam, neque excommunicationis censurâ notatam. Confirmat hanc sententiam Augustinus l. 3 c. 19. de Baptismo, asserens, hæreticos esse in Ecclesia, antequàm per obstinationem & pertinaciam separentur: ita ut non tam hæretici, quàm errantes dicantur, dum sunt adhuc in Ecclesia. Confirmat hoc ipsum Scriptura, varijs similitudinibus palearum & tritici, Matth. 13, 12. tritici & zizaniorum, Matth. 13, 24. verriculi sive sagenæ continentis pisces bonos & malos, Mat. 13. 47. nuptiarum, quibus intersunt hospites boni & mali, Matth. 22, 10. Virginum prudentum & fatuarum, Matth. 25, 1. Ovilis in quo sunt oves & hirci. Joh. 10, 1 magna domus, in qua sunt vasa diversissima, quædam ad honorem, nonnulla ad ignominiam. 2. Timoth. 2, 20.

Cæterùm hoc loco probè notandum, non unam eandemque esse tùm malorum, tùm hæreticorum conditionem, quoad veram Ecclesiam, quæ est Electorum & piè fidelium. Sunt quidem in Ecclêsiâ vera, etiam mali, sicut in Ecclesia falsa interdum sunt Electi: sed neque hi, neque illi sunt de Ecclesia, in qua sunt: sed utrique sunt in ea Ecclesia, de qua non sunt. Differunt enim ista duo, Esse IN Ecclesia, & esse DE Ecclesiâ: eodem modo, quo differunt ex sententia Servatoris, esse IN mundo, & esse DE mundo, Joh. 17. Esse in mundo nihil aliud est, quàm in medio filiorum hujus mundi vivere: Esse mundo, est perversa mundi studia sectari & approbare. Sic esse in Ecclesia vera nihil est aliud, quàm vivere in cœtu eorum, qui quà prædicationem Verbi & administrationem Sacramentorum, veram constituunt Ecclesiam. Esse de Ecclesia, est planè consentire de doctrina Verbi & Sacramentorum. Jam qui diversam sectatur sententiam discrepantem à puritate doctrinæ, uti faciunt Hæretici; illi desinunt quidem esse de ecclesia vera, sed non desinunt esse in Ecclesia vera, quamdiu quidem non Ecclesiâ, ejiciuntur, & ipsi publicè ad falsam ecclesiam secessionem faciunt. Sunt Orthodoxi Theologi qui paulo aliter rem istam explicant, sed verborum magis sono quàm sensu ab ijs quæ jam diximus, discrepantes. Statuunt enim duas hasce phrases, Esse IN Ecclesia, & esse DE Ecclesia, differre ut Partem & Membrum Ecclesiæ. Aliud enim est, Esse partem, aliud, esse membrum Ecclesiæ. Nomen enim partis latiùs diffunditur: nomen membri est angustius. Pars ad totum quodvis refertur: membrum ad corpus animatum, vel saltem simile quiddam & analogum respicit. Ita pars sine vita invenitur, ut in lapide, ligno, metallo: Membrum autem verè & propriè sine vita ne intelligi quidem potest. Sunt ergò hæretici & non Sancti, partes quidem ecclesiæ veræ, dùm in ejus quasi gremio vivunt & versantur: membra autem ejusdem nullo modo appellandi sunt: perindè ut in falsa Ecclesia hærentes pij, partes quidem ejus sunt, dùm in consortio ejus externo versantur, pro membris autem ejusdem nequaquam sunt habendi.

Confirmant hoc ipsum & talia luculentiora Scripturæ testimonia, ut eum Apostolus exprefse scribit: Oportet esse hæreses ἐν ὑμῖν, inter vos, ut qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant in vobis 1. Cor. 11, 19. Et alibi prædicit, Antichristum sessurum in templum Dei 2. Thess. 2. 4. Hinc est, quod B. Lutherus scribit, Papam & Cardinales esse in Ecclesia, generatim sic dicta; sed de Ecclesia, vera scilicet eos esse, pernegat. Sic vice versa sunt hodiè in ecclesia Romana, quam Falsam esse, persuasissimum habemus, de Religione rectè sentientes plurimi. Hi ergo, licet sint in falsæ ecclesiæ cœtu: Veræ tamen Ecclesiæ membra sunt. Sic Hæretici sunt quidem pars Ecclesiæ veræ, in qua vivunt, & versantur: sed sunt membra Ecclesiæ falsæ, cum qua sentiunt & docent.

Tumultuatur hoc loco Bellarminus Stapletonus, Pistorius & alij, varia nobis objicientes: ac primùm quidem dictitant, pari ratione ex doctrina hac nostra elici posse, Iudæos quoq;, Mahometistas & alios, qui tamen religionem Christianam aversantur, esse in Ecclesia vera, propterea quòd tales haud rarò in medio fidelium vivere contingat? Sed Respondemus simpliciter falsam esse consequentiam, propter ingentem diversitatis rationem, quæ Hæreticis, cũ Judæis, Mahometistis, & alijs hujusmodi populis intercedit. Nam quòd hæreticis locum in Ecclesia vera non simpliciter præcidimus, sit ideò, quòd sunt per Sacramentum initiationis Ecclesiæ inferti: quòd externam fidei Christianæ professionem retinent, quòd denique & ipsi vera Sacramenta administrare possunt. Quæ omnia cum Judæis, Mahometistis & alijs infidelibus populis non competant, fit, ut in Ecclesiâ non sint, li vel maximè inter medios Christianos vivant.

Porrò clamitant Adversarij, & nescio cujus vanitatis nos infimulant, dùm videlicet hac in quæstione concedamus, Romanam Ecclesiam esse Ecclesiam, inquè ea multos esse piè fideles sive electos: Aliàs verò negamus apud Pontificios esse Ecclesiam.

Respondeo, nullam prorsus vel ἀσυγχυσίας vel ἀντιφάσεως notam nobis impingì posse: siquidem utrumque verissimè, de unâ eâdemque Romanâ sive Pontificiâ Ecclesia prædicamus: verùm non ὡσαύτως, sed alio atque alio modo sive respectu. Ecclesiam enim apud Pontificios esse, negare non possumus, quia falsam illam esse pugnamus. A specie enim ad genus ritè affirmativa sit collectio. Sed interim non sequitur: Pontificij sunt Ecclesia: Ergò sunt Ecclesia vera: Ab una enim disparata specie, ad alteram non datur collectio affirmativè: sed tantùm negativè, hoc modo Pontificij sunt Ecclesia falsa: E. non sunt Vera, E. sine contradictione Pontificios esse Ecclesiam & concedimus & negamus. Quando verò ipsi sic colligunt: Pontificij sunt Ecclesia: E. sunt Ecclesia vera: tùm à genere ad speciem affirmatè colligunt: id quod tum præcepta Logica, tùm rei ipsius Veritas non permittunt.

Sed altiùs insurgunt? Num bonos & Electos aliquos in Romanâ Ecclesiâ esse arbitremur? Atqui hoc ipsum ultrò largimur: Si enim nulli ibi essent electi, fieri vix posset, quin Ecclesiam istam Deus protenùs excinderet. Et si ex adultorum cœtu nulli ibi essent electi, saltem infantes, qui baptizati in vivis priùs esse desinunt, quàm Idolomania Pontificiæ assensum præbeant, veram Electorum Ecclesiam in medio Papatu constituerent. Verùm indè non datur collectio ad ipsam Ecclesiam Romanam, quòd ipsa sit vera Electorum Ecclesia: haud profectò magis, atque nulla ratione sequitur: Malis semper in externa conversatione sunt admixti boni: E. Mali ipsi sunt illi boni: Vel, Arianorum cœtui semper permixti fuerunt verè pij & Orthodoxi: E. Ariani ipsi fuerunt vera atquè Orthodoxa Ecclesia.

Hic, quæ hactenùs de membris veræ Ecclesiæ dicta sunt, probè observatis, nullo negocio refutari possunt, quæ Bellarminus cumprimis capite 4. libri tertij, de Hæreticis disputat, eosque in Ecclesia vera esse, simpliciter negat. Ubi præter jam dicta, illud etiam disputantibus cumprimis observandum fuerit, in tota hac disputatione de Verâ Ecclesiâ, non illud propriè in controversiam venire, Quinam Sancti sint? De hoc enim ut indubitatò nobis constare possit, externis signis non dignoscitur: Sed illud unicè quæri & controverti, Vbinam sit doctrina Christianæ veritas, ubinam sit legitimus Sacramentorum usus; Et quibus mediis fiat, ut ad veram sanctitatem homines rectè aspirare queant? Hoc dùm non peusi habet Jesuvvita, sed pro confesso statim sumit, Romanam Ecclesiam esse veram Ecclesiam, neque Hæreticos in Ecclesia esse, fit ut de gravi hoc materia disputet, tanquàm cæcus de coloribus.

Cæterùm quæ capite subsequente quinto de Schismaticis disputat, probabiliora videntur, dummodò de Definitione Schismatici nobis rectè constet, & eos Jesuvvita intelligat, qui (quod etymon ipsum vocabuli innuit) à corpore Ecclesiæ veræ seipsos scindunt quasi & avellunt, & ad falsam Ecclesiam secessio nem faciunt. Hoc enim casu ac respectu facilè concesserimus, tales Schismaticos, neque in Ecclesia vera, neque de Ecclesia verâ esse. Et ad hos rectissimè accommodatur illud Apostolicum, 1. Joh. 2, 19. Ex nobis exierunt, sed non erant ex nobis: si enim fuissent ex nobis, permansissent utique nobiscum: sed ut manifefti sint, quòd non sunt ex nobis, exierunt à nobis. Verùm si Schismatici secundum usitatam ac receptam Schismatis definitionem accipiantur: quòd nimirùm Schisma tùm committatur, ubi de doctrinâ quidem consentiunt, sed in causa rerum externarum & indifferentium, in partes scinduntur ij, qui debebant esse junctissimi: tùm sanè nego, Schismaticos non esse in Ecclesia vera. Cum enim membra veræ Ecclesiæ in unum corpus coalescant, non nisi Unitate doctrinæ purioris: & verò Schisma sit de Ceremonijs, ritibus, & rebus externis: utique propter dissonantiam in istis rebus, Unitas fidei non tollitur: ac per Consequens, tales etiam Schismatici, in Ecclesia, & de Ecclesia verâ esse non desinunt.

Sed hæc de præsente quæstione, Qui nimirùm sint membra veræ Ecclesiæ, dicta sufficiant: ex quibus per contrarium sensum facilè jam licebit colligere: Quinam non sint membra veræ Ecclesiæ? Excluduntur nimirùm eb eâ primùm infideles omnes non baptizari, Iudæi, Mahometistæ, Gentiles, & omnes aperti hostes fidei Christianæ. Excluduntur etiam Apostatæ, quippè qui à vera Ecclesia ad falsam manifestam secessionem fecerunt. Porrò excluduntur etiam hinc excommunicati, quippè à consortio veræ Ecclesiæ sunt ejecti: licet interim non simpliciter ex universa Ecclesia, sive ex cœtu vocatorum sint eliminati. Tandem excluduntur etiam hinc Hæretici, sed jam erroris aliquoties convicti, damnati, & tamen nihilominùs, vel veram doctrinam varijs depravationibus, vel Sacramenta horrendis abusibus, vel denique & Doctrinam & Sacramenta nefandis corruptelis polluta & adulterata habent atque tuentur. Horum sanè cœtus & congregatio, quæ & quantacunque etiam sit externæ pietatis species, pro Vera Ecclesia haberi nullo modo potest aut debet: Siquidem à verâ Ecclesia secesssionem fecit, & in falsam sive malignantium Ecclesiam degeneravit:


### On the Nature and Essence of the Church: What is the invisible Church?

With these things thus settled. One thing alone remains to be settled regarding this first general Question: How, namely, is that controversy to be defined which today exists between us and the Jesuits concerning the Invisible Church? Which Bellarmine treats in three chapters, 11, 12, and 15 of the third book on the Church militant, in such a way that he simply denies the Invisible Church.

Moreover, we have just now shown above what we understand by the Invisible Church, namely the Elect alone: whose election itself is invisible, and whose faith cannot be perceived by the senses: but as the Apostle speaks, who are in secret, and whose profession is not in the letter, but in the Spirit. Rom. 2:29. In which sense and respect we rightly define the Invisible Church as being the assembly of those who are truly faithful and predestined to eternal life. This Church, therefore, admits no more of the impious, hypocrites, or heretics than heavenly blessedness receives the damned and the reprobate: although such is the condition of the Elect in this life that they never live apart or alone, nor possess any peculiar place distinct or separated from the rest of the visible assembly and congregation of the called: but sometimes they have the necessity to live in the midst of a perverse nation, in a promiscuous congregation of the wicked and hypocrites, Phil. 2:15.

The following testimonies of Scripture confirm this Invisible Church of the Elect.

Furthermore, Christ the Savior says in Luke 17:20, The kingdom of God does not come with observation. In evading this statement, the Jesuit entangles himself more than he explains. For he contends that by the Kingdom of God is understood either Grace, through which God reigns in the hearts of men: or Christ himself with his kingdom. But the Kingdom of Grace, which Christ begins in these lands, and which he will one day deliver to God the Father, 1 Cor. 15:24, is nothing other than the true Church. Now, the Savior says: This kingdom does not come with observation: but it is WITHIN YOU: Therefore, the true Church of the Elect cannot be judged by the visible sight of the eyes: but lies hidden in the hearts of the Elect.

of the Church, the adornment of the spouse of Christ, is from within or internal: Ps. 45:14. Which statement our Jesuit also silently passes over.

Finally, we repeat that which the Apostle asserts in Rom. 2:28 & 29, that the true profession of faith has its power not in the manifest or open, but in the secret: just as the same Apostle testifies that the life of the Saints is also hidden with Christ in God, Col. 3:3, and St. Peter calls it the hidden man of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest Spirit, which is rich in the sight of God (he does not say in the sight of men), 1 Pet. 3:4. But the Jesuit passes over this statement too with blind eyes: meanwhile fighting in vain about other testimonies of Scripture, in which, however, we do not primarily place the defense of our cause in this place.

We seek a second argument for confirmation from the fact that in the Apostolic Creed we profess that we believe the Catholic Church. But Faith is of things which are not seen, Heb. 11:1. Therefore, if the Catholic Church of the Elect were visible, it would certainly not be believed, but seen.

And indeed, the force of this argument is so great that it has extorted this confession from the Jesuit who was about to refute it, whether he was unaware or certainly unwilling: I say that the holiness of the Church is without doubt invisible. But I say better, that in the Church something is seen, and something is believed. For we see that assembly of men which is the Church: but that that assembly is the very true Church of Christ, we do not see but believe. This confession of Bellarmine we seize with both hands and willingly grant that the true, Holy, Catholic Church is visible and is invisible: in a different respect, namely. For it is visible, 1. by reason of its parts, which individually and all separately can be viewed, although the whole itself never comes under human sight all at once and in one glance: just as the individual parts of this world are viewable separately: but the whole universe itself is perceived by no one. Then it is visible on account of the preaching of the Word and the administration of the Sacraments, and other works and worship, the execution of which falls into the eyes and the other external senses. Again, the same Church is invisible partly by reason of the whole: (For the whole Church was never seen at once, except in that extreme rarity of the human race at the time of the Protoplasts, and in the ark of Noah at the time of the flood) partly on account of faith and Election, neither of which falls under human sight: as we have already proven from the Scriptures.

But the Jesuit race is in an uproar in this place, and contends that the Church is simply visible and conspicuous, primarily for the purpose that it may not be forced to concede that in the previous centuries under the Papacy, there was nevertheless a true Church, but an invisible one. This society therefore fights for the visible Church alone, as if for hearth and home, having scraped together from here and there some arguments, but of very light armor.

And at the beginning indeed Bellarmine in chapter 11 of the third book censures our theologians, primarily B. Luther, because at first he acknowledged only an invisible Church, but afterwards, when he saw the absurd consequences that followed from it, he decided by secret counsel that the Church should also be called visible, and therefore he accuses him of a shameful contradiction.

But I reply that the mark of contradiction is unjustly branded upon our side: since in a very different respect, they always maintained that the Church is both visible and invisible: as was explained a little earlier. But that blessed Luther fought so strongly for the Invisible Church, was done on the occasion of the struggle which he then had with the Papists: and therefore he was not fighting simply but only in a certain respect that the true Church is invisible, namely with respect to the Elect, insofar as they are such and are called so. For thus the Papists then argued: if Luther's doctrine is true, then there was no Church before Luther, no Elect at all, no true members of Christ. Here therefore Luther replied, and rightly indeed, that this Church of the Elect is only invisible. Where he considered the Elect not by reason of nature, in which respect Luther never denied that they were indeed visible: but by reason of faith or purity in the doctrine and faith of Christ. Thus therefore Luther noted not the external, but the internal form of the Elect, that is, the essential parts of the Elect, which constitute them, not insofar as they are visible men, but insofar as they are invisible believers. Which two do not conflict, but have themselves as things subordinated one to another. Thus therefore blessed Luther is free from all blame of inconstancy and contradiction.

But Bellarmine continues, and in chapter 12 brings forward these arguments.

1. Wherever the name of the Church is found in the Scriptures, a visible congregation is always signified: nor could or can one passage be brought forward where this name is attributed to an invisible congregation. Therefore.

I reply that the antecedent is most false. For I bring forward in the beginning all those testimonies of Scripture, already brought forward a little before for the establishing of the invisible Church of the Elect, which the Jesuit indeed barks at, but does not refute. Then I bring forward that passage Heb. 12, 22 and 23. You have approached Mount Zion, and the city of the living God, to the heavenly Jerusalem, and the Church of the firstborn, who are enrolled in the heavens. Where it is clearly nonsensical, what the Jesuit replies in chapter 15, that in this place only the Church triumphant in the heavens is described. For the whole coherence of the text clearly proves the contrary. For there the Apostle compares the indignation of the Law with the sweetness of the Gospel, and the Church of the Old people with the Church of the Christians under the New Testament, this is evident even from the fact that he expressly says with those to whom he had directed his Epistle, to whom he attributes this, that they had approached Mount Zion, that is, to the Church of the New Testament. For the Jesuit knows, or certainly ought to know, that in the Scriptures, as often as Mount Sinai and Mount Zion are opposed, the Law and the Gospel, the Old and New Testament, the Church of the Jews and of the Christians are always opposed. And what, I pray, would this harshness be, if the Apostle understood by Mount Zion, in this place, the Triumphant Church in the heavens: For the text would hang together nakedly: no apodosis or accommodation could be given: unless perhaps this one, which is far most inept: You my Hebrews be at peace, be holy, be solicitous for the salvation of your brothers, because you have not approached Mount Sinai, formidable with lightnings and thunder, but to Mount Zion, that is, to the Church triumphant in the heavens, as the Jesuit interprets. Where even a ten-year-old boy understands that the Triumphant Church is not opposed by the Apostle to the Church of the Old people: but the Church of the New Testament still militant here on earth. This, however, he calls the heavenly Church, because the heavenly kingdom, in this age also, is begun in the faithful. Now indeed the description of the Elect is too manifest and evident, whom the Apostle calls the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven: Where certainly hardly anyone would be so dull as not to understand that the invisible Church of the Elect is described. Nor does it stand in the way that the Apostle makes mention of many thousands of Angels, and the spirits of just men: For this is solemn to the Holy Spirit, that with the description of the militant Church, he joins the description of the Triumphant Church, so that even from that it may be clear that the dignity of the Elect is to be fully perfected and completed only in the other heavenly life.

Furthermore, I also bring forward that passage from chapter 5, 26 and 27 of the Ephesians, where the Apostle describes the Church, that it does not have a wrinkle, or a spot, or anything of this kind. If the Jesuit wishes this passage to be understood of the visible Church, let him show us such a Church, which has ever been without a wrinkle or spot. And indeed Bellarmine himself admits that such a visible Church cannot be given, while he argues in chapter 7, that not only the Elect belong to the true and Catholic Church, but also the reprobate, not perfect ones, grave sinners, and not only hidden ones, but manifest ones, nay even hidden infidels. But where such are, there is the most ample crop of wrinkles and spots. Therefore the species of Church opposed to this, which is free of wrinkles, must be invisible. But if the Jesuit understands this Apostolic passage of the Triumphant Church, in the sense of Turrianus, we ask him to demonstrate two things to us.

Latin:

His ita expeditis. Unum illud circa primam hanc generalem Quæstionem expediundum restare videtur: Quomodo nimirùm definienda illa controversia, quæ nobis hodiè cum Jesuvitis, de Ecclesia Invisibili intercedit? Quam Bellarminus tribus capitibus, 11.& 12,& 15. libri tertij de Ecclesia militante, ita pertractat, ut Ecclesiam Invisibilem simpliciter neget.

Cæterùm jam modò supra oftendimus, Quidnàm per Ecclesiam Invisibilem intelligamus, nempè solos Electos: quorum tùm Electio ipsa est invisibilis, tùm fides, sensibus percipi non potest: sed ut Apostolus loquitur, qui in occulto sunt, & quorum professio non est in literâ, sed in Spiritu. Rom. 2, 29. Quo sensu ac respectu Ecclesiam Invisibilem rectè definimus, quòd sit cœtus verè fidelium, & prædestinatorum ad vitam æternam. Hæc proindè Ecclesia haud magis impios, hypocritas aut hæreticos admittit, quàm beatitudo cœlestis, damnatos & reprobos recipit: licèt ea sit Electorum hac in vita conditio, ut nunquàm seorsim aut soli degant, vel peculiarem aliquem locum, à reliquo visibili vocatorum cœtu ac congre gatione distinctum, aut separatum possideant: sed interdum in medio nationis pravæ, in promiscua malorum & hypocritarum congregatione vivere necesfum habeant, Phil. 2,15.

Confirmant verò hanc Invisibilem Electorum Ecclesiam, sequentia Scripturæ testimonia.

Porrò Christus Servator Luc. 17, 20. Regnum Dei inquit, non venit cum observatione. In quo dicto eludendo, magis se Jesuvvita implicat, quàm explicat. Contendit enim per Regnum Dei vel intelligi Gratiam, per quam Deus regnat in cordibus hominum: vel ipsum Christum cum regno ipsius. Atqui Regnum Gratiæ, quod his in terris inchoat Christus, & quòd aliquando in die novissimo tradet Deo Patri, 1. Cor. 15,24. nihil est aliud quam Ecclesia vera. Jam verò dicit Servator. Hoc regnum non venit cum observatione: sed illud INTRA VOS est: Ergò Ecclesia vera Electorum non potest visibili oculorum scioq dijudicari: sed latet abscondita in Electorum cordibus.

siæ, sponsæ Christi ornatum, ab intus sive internum esse prædicat: Psal. 45,14. Quod ipsum quoq; dictum Jesuvvita noster tacitè præterit.

Tandem repetimus illud, quòd Apostolus Rom. 2, 28. & 29. asserit, veram fidei professionem, non in manifesto sive aperto, sed in occulto vim suam habere: prout vitam etiam Sanctorum cum Christo, in Deo absconditam esse, idem Apostolus perhibet, Coloss. 3, 3. & D. Petrus nominat absconditum hominem cordis, in incorruptibilitate quieti & modesti Spiritus, qui sit in conspectu Dei (non dicit in conspectu hominum) locuples. 1. Pet. 3,4. Sed & hoc dictum cæcis oculis præterit Jesuvvita: frustra interim de alijs Scripturæ testimonijs pugnans, in quibus tamen principaliter causæ nostræ præsidium, hoc loco, minimè ponimus.

Alterum Confirmationis argumentum indè petimus, quòd in Symbolo Apostolico profitemur, nos credere Ecclesiam Catholicam. Atqui Fides est rerum quæ non videntur. Hebr. 11, 1. Ergò si Catholica Electorum Ecclesia esset visibilis, non certè crederetur, sed videretur.

Et sanè hujus etiam argumenti tanta est vis, ut Jesuvvitæ illud refutaturo, hanc vel inscio, vel certè invito confessionem extorserit: Sanctitatem Ecclesiæ dicô sine dubio invisibilem esse. Sed melius dico, in Ecclesia aliquid videri, & aliquid credi. Videmus enim eum cœtum hominum, qui est Ecclesia: sed quòd ille cœtus sit ipsa vera Christi Ecclesia, non videmus sed credimus. Quam Bellarmini confessionem nos utrâque manu arripim9, & ultrò largimur, Ecclesiam veram, Sanctam, Catholicam, esse visibilem & esse invisibilem: diverso nimitum respectu. Visibilis enim est, 1. ratione partium, quæ singulæ atque omnes seorsim aspectari possunt, licet ipsum totum, nunquàm simul & uno intuitu sub aspectum humanum veniat: perindè ut mundi hujus partes singulæ seorsim sunt aspectabiles: totum autem ipsum universum à nemine cernitur. Deindè visibilis est, propter prædicationem Verbi & administrationem Sacramentorum, aliaque opera & cultus, quorum expeditio, in oculos, sensusque reliquos externos incurrit. Rursus Ecclesia eadem est Invisibilis partim ratione totius: (Tota enim Ecclesia, nunquàm, nisi in summâ illa raritate generis humani tempore Protoplastorum, & in arca Noæ tempore diluvij simul visa fuit) partim propter fidem & Electionem, quæ neutra sub aspectum humanum cadit: uti ex Scripturis jam evicimus.

Sed tumultuatur hoc loco gens Jesuvvitica, & Ecclesiam simpliciter visibilem ac conspicuam esse contendit eó potissimùm fine, ut ne concedere cogatur, superioribus seculis sub Papatu, nihilominus veram fuisse Ecclesiam, sed invisibilem. Pugnat proindè societas hæc, pro sola visibili Ecclesia, tanquàm pro aris & focis, corrasis hinc indè aliquot, sed levis admodùm armaturæ rationibus.

Acinitiò quidem Bellarminus cap. 11. libri tertij suggillat nostros Theologos, cum primis B. Lutherum, quòd primùm invisibilem tantùm Ecclesiam agnoverit, sed postea, cùm videret absurda, quæ indè sequebantur, secreto consilio statuerit, ut Ecclesia etiam visibilis diceretur, ac proindè turpis contradictionis eum insimulat.

Sed respondeo præter meritum contradictionis notam nostris impingi: Siquidem respectu diversissimo, Ecclesiam semper statuerunt esse, & visibilem & invisibilem: uti paulò antè est explicatum. Quod verò B. Lutherus pro Invisibili Ecclesia tantoperè pugnavit, factum est occasione certaminis, quòd ipsi tùm cum Pontificijs intercedebat: ac proindè non ἁπλῶς sed κᾴ τί tantùm pugnabat Ecclesiam veram esse Invisibilem, nempè respectu Electorum, quatenùs tales sunt & dicuntur. Sic enim tùm argumentabantur Pontificii: si Lutheri doctrina vera est, tùm nulla ante Lutherum fuit Ecclesia, nulli omninò Electi, nulla vera membra Christi. Hîc ergò respondebat Lutherus, & rectè quidem, hanc Electorum Ecclesiam tantùm esse invisibilem. Ubi Electos consideravit non ratione φύσεως, quo respectu utique visibiles illos fuisse, nunquàm negavit Lutherus: sed ratione πίςεως sive puritatis in doctrina & fide Christi. Sic ergò non externam, sed internam Electorum formam notabat Lutherus, hoc est, partes Essentiales Electorum, quæ ipsos, non quatenùs homines visibiles, sed quatenùs credentes invisibiles, constituunt. Quæ duo non pugnant, sed habent se ut ὑπ᾽ ἀλλήλως subordinata. Sic ergò omni inconstantiæ & contradictionis culpâ vacat B. Lutherus.

Sed pergit Bellarminus, & cap. 12. hæc profert argumenta.

1. Ubicunq; in Scripturis invenitur nomen Ecclesiæ, semper visibilis congregatio significatur: nec unus locus proferri potuit aut potest, ubi hoc nomen tribuatur congregationi invisibili. Ergo.

Respondeo Antecedens esse falsissimum. Profero enim initiò omnia ea Scripturæ testimonia, jam paulò ante pro astruenda invisibili Electorum Ecclesiâ, prolata, quæ Jesuvvita allatrat quidem, sed non refutat. Deinde profero illud Hebr. 12, 22. & 23. Accessistis ad montem Sion, & civitatem Dei viventis, ad cælestem Hierofolymam, & Ecclesiam primitivorum, qui in cælis conscripti sunt. Ubi nugatorium planè est, quod Jesuvvita cap. 15. respondet, hoc loco describi tantùm Ecclesiam modò in cælis triumphantem. Contrarium enim tota textus συνέπεια luculenter evincit. Confert enim ibi Apostolus Legis indignationem cum suavitate Evangelij, & Ecclesiam Veteris populi, cum Ecclesia Christianorum sub Novo Testamento, patet hoc vel indè, quòd expressè ait cum ijs, ad quos Epistolam suam direxerat, quibus hoc tribuit, quòd accesserint ad montem Sion, hoc est, ad Ecclesiam Novi Testamenti. Novit enim Jesuvvita, vel certè nosse debet, in Scripturis, quoties opponuntur Mons Sinai, & mons Sion, semper opponi Legem & Evangelium, Vetus ac Novum Testamentum, Judæorum ac Christianorum Ecclesiam. Et quæ obsecro hæc foret τραχύτης sive asperitas, si per montem Sion, hoc loco, Triumphantem Ecclesiam in cælis intelligeret Apostolus: Nudùm spiam enim cohæreret textus: nulla dari posset ἀπόδοσις sive Accommodatio: nisi fortè hæc longè ineptissima: Vos mei Hebræi sellemini pacem, sitis sancti, sitis solliciti pro fratrum vestrorum salute, quia nõ accessistis ad montem Sinai, fulminibus & tonitru formidabilem, sed ad montem Sion, hoc est, ad Ecclesiam in cælis triumphantem, uti interpretatur Jesuvvita. Ubi vel puer decennis intelligit, Ecclesiæ Veteris populi, non opponi ab Apostolo Ecclesiam Triumphantem: sed Ecclesiam Novi Testamenti hisce in terris adhuc militantem. Hanc autem Ecclesiam cœlestem nominat, eò, quòd regnum cæleste, in hoc quoque seculo, inchoetur in fidelibus. Jam verò nimis manifesta & evidens est descriptio Electorum, quos Apostolus vocat primogenitos, qui in cœlo inscripti sint: Ubi certè invisibilem Electorum Ecclesiam describi, vix quisquam ita bardus fuerit, quin intelligat. Neque obstat, quod Apostolus multorum millium Angelorum, & justorum spirituum facit mentionem: Nam solenne hoc est Spiritui S., ut cum descriptione Ecclesiæ militantis, cõjungat descriptioné Ecclesiæ Triumphantis, ut vel indè constet dignitatem Electorum, in altera demùm cœlesti vitâ planè perficiendam & absolvendam esse.

Porrò profero etiam locum illum ex cap. 5, 26. & 27. Ephesiorum, ubi Apostolus describit Ecclesiam, quòd non habeat rugam, aut maculam, aut quicquam hujusmodi. Si de Ecclesia visibili locum istum velit intelligi Jesuvvita, monstret ille nobis talem Ecclesiam, quæ unquàm fuerit sine ruga aut macula. Et sanè talem Visibilem Ecclesiam dari non posse, fatetur ipse Bellarminus, dùm cap 7. disputat, ad Ecclesiam veram & Catholicam pertinere non solos Electos, sed & reprobos, non perfectos, graves peccatores, & non solùm occultos, sed manifestos, imò infideles occultos, Atqui ubi tales sunt, ibi rugarum & macularum amplissima est seges. Ergò huic opposita Ecclesia species, quæ sit rugarum expers, invisibilis sit necesse est. Sin Jesuvvita de Triumphante Ecclesia, sensu Turriani, locum istum Apostolicum intelligat, duo quæsumus nobis demonstret.


### On the Nature and Essence of the Church: What is the invisible Church? (continued)

1. With what face, therefore, have the Romanists hitherto dared to accommodate this passage to the visible Roman Church, and from that to prove that the Church cannot err.

2. How the verse immediately preceding, and cohering in an undivided connection, ought to be explained, is that also to be accommodated to the Triumphant Church? If he answers affirmatively: it would follow that the Triumphant Church is finally sanctified by the washing of water, in the word: Which is absurd. If negatively: then let him show the coherence of the text, which is such: Christ gave himself for the Church, that he might sanctify it by the washing of water in the word, that he might present it to himself glorious, that it might be holy and immaculate, not having a wrinkle. If the former is to be accepted concerning the militant Church, as certainly it cannot be accepted otherwise: why not also this latter. The sense of this passage therefore emerges as this: That the fruit of the passion of Christ is among the rest, also that, that by the washing of water he so sanctifies His Church, as washed by His own blood and thoroughly cleansed by the laver of regeneration, may now have no spot or wrinkle of sins: not indeed in the Schwenckfeldian and Anabaptist sense, but in the Orthodox sense: insofar as Christ truly bestows His righteousness upon the Church, and through faith cleanses consciences from dead works, so that with all sins remitted, the wrinkles or spots of adhering infirmities are covered. Now, however, let Bellarmine make the attempt whether he can see this imputed righteousness of Christ in the Elect, and point it out to us. As long as he has not pointed it out to us—as indeed he will never point it out in this life—so long will it remain settled and firm that the Church of the Elect, and thus of those purified through faith, is invisible. Meanwhile, however, we by no means deny that the Apostolic passage διέξοδως can also be understood concerning the state of the Triumphant Church in the other life: where at last this holiness and purity of the Church of the Elect will be perfect and absolute.

sensible. Therefore, the Church itself is also always sensible. Where the major premise stands in need of clear proof. For if it ought to be true, then it is necessary that it be such κτα παντός. But it is not such: since it fails in many things: for the foundation of the Church is sinless, is omnipotent, is immortal. Therefore, will the Church itself also be such? Does the Jesuit therefore peddle trifles, not dispute? Thirdly, if by the rock you understand the confession of faith, was it visible? Not so. Observing this, therefore, the Jesuit craftily substitutes 'the Sensible' for 'the visible': so that a little loophole for escaping might lie open. Thus, therefore, from now on the Jesuits will dispute not so much for a visible as for a sensible Church. Finally, what the Jesuit narrates concerning the Roman Pontiff as the vicar and successor of Christ and Peter are fables long since worn out by our people.

But the Jesuit makes a commotion, from Numbers ch. 20, 4, and 1 Kings 8, 14, where the whole assembly of Israel was seen.

The Jesuit borrows another argument from Psalm 19:5, where David says of the Church: 'He has set his tabernacle in the Sun': that is, in the manifest, so that just as the Sun cannot be hidden at all, so neither can the Church be concealed. Likewise, the Church is compared to a great and conspicuous mountain, which in no way can be hidden: according to that, Matthew 5:14: 'A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.'

I answer that the Disputant is wandering off the track. For the question is not whether this or that particular Church is visible: nor is it disputed whether the Elect, insofar as they are men and move in the external assembly of the called, are visible. For we readily grant both of these: but this is properly the point in question: whether the Elect, insofar as they are Elect, can be seen, so that you can be certain by your eyes that this or that person is truly elect? Or that these or those are truly faithful, constituting on this earth the true Church of the Elect? Where we hold the negative: which the testimonies produced do not infringe. For let the Jesuit explain: Did Moses and the King of Israel, in the whole multitude which they beheld with their eyes, also see in the individual who were the Elect and who were not? While he cannot demonstrate this, the Jesuit stumbles like a blind gladiator.

But this argument also labors under a shameful ignorance of the point at issue and the fallacy of 'answering another question.' For each of these testimonies deals with the external assembly of the visible Church, which has never been obscure in the world, although it has flourished more at one time and less at another: concerning which matter there is no dispute in this place. Therefore, it is rather for the Jesuit to prove that the Elect themselves, insofar as they are defined by internal faith, are also conspicuous, just as they are and remain conspicuous insofar as they move as the called in the visible flock of the called. While the Jesuit does not prove this, his entire argument is wandering off the track.

But the Jesuit shows a more subtle sharpness of disputation when, from the passage Matthew 16:18, 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,' he infers thus in the same chapter 12 of the third book on the militant Church: 'By the name of rock, whether you understand Christ, or the confession of faith, or Peter, the foundation of the Church is always something sensible: Therefore, the Church itself is sensible, or visible: and indeed today, in the Roman Pontiff, the vicar of Christ and Peter.'

In particular, however, it is to be noted that the passage in Psalm 19 does not deal literally with the Church: but with the created Sun, for which God has placed a tent or seat in the heavens: as the Hebrew sources clearly confirm. Nor can or should Augustine prejudice us here, who, having followed the faulty Vulgate, interpreted that passage concerning the Church: although even this interpretation cannot harm our cause in the least.

The Jesuit takes a third argument from the very origin and progress of the Church, of the Old and New Testament, which has always been visible: just as the Israelites, the Apostles, and the remaining faithful have always been visible.

I answer to the antecedent, and I deny it as false. For that the foundation of the Church is always something sensible or visible is most false. Christ was certainly just as much the foundation of the Old Jewish Church as He is today: yet that was not then sensible or visible, for the Son of God had not yet assumed flesh: nor had He yet established any visible vicar. Therefore, it is false that the foundation of the Church is always visible or sensible. Furthermore, the reasoning of the consequence is most futile: that which is more clearly evident if the entire syllogism is formed, which will be such: 'Whatever is the nature or condition of the foundation of the Church, the same is also of the Church itself: But the foundation of the Church is always'

I answer: That the same ignorance of the point at issue and 'answering another question' is committed, which we noted in the second argument. 2. It is manifestly false that in the times of Christ the entire Catholic Church was in the Apostles and disciples of Christ: as if, indeed, besides these, there was no one among the Jews who acknowledged Christ, although they did not dare to confess Him openly. The contrary is clearly evident even from the example of Nicodemus, John 3. And I beg the Jesuit to explain what reason there is why the Apostles themselves, when Christ was preaching about His betrayer, so diligently they inquired, Who that might be. Certainly all saw Judas Iscariot: But whether he was of the Elect or the reprobate, they could not see. Therefore even by this example it can be irrefragably demonstrated that the Church of the Elect is Invisible.

The Jesuit takes the fourth argument from the very definition of the Church: for the Church is a certain society, not of angels nor of souls, but of men. But it cannot be called a society of men which cannot be seen. Therefore. But this argument is too futile to need a more lengthy refutation: for that twofold consideration of the Elect, of which mention has been made several times, completely represses and refutes all its force. Furthermore, it is horrible to hear what the Jesuit adds, that there is no society unless those who are called associates recognize one another. Is it so, then, that no society exists for us with the angels, and with the Elect already triumphing in heaven? Is it so, then, that what we showed a little earlier from chapter 12 of the Epistle to the Hebrews is false, that the Church even militant on this earth has been admitted to the company of many thousands of angels and the spirits of just men? Is it so, then, that we shall no longer believe in the Apostolic Creed the Communion of Saints, where all Saints are understood, as well those who are still on the way as those who are now in the homeland, as the Scholastics speak.

The fifth argument is as follows: In the time of Christ (as the Lutherans maintain) the true Church was only in Zacharias, Hannah, Mary, and a few other pious people. But these communicated with the high priests in the temple, in sacrifices, etc. Therefore, either they did wrong by communicating with a false Church, or the Lutherans do wrong by not communicating with the Papists and not obeying the Pope.

I answer, the argument fails: 1. By ignorance of the point at issue. For it concludes nothing at all for the visibility of the Church of the Elect: but only deals with the communication of the True Church with the false, about which nothing is being discussed in this place. 2. The minor premise is true not simply, but only in a certain respect. For those Saints communicated with the high priests in certain points at least, namely those which were ordained in the Law of God: and only up to the time until the Synagogue of the Jews was buried with honor, and the public ministry of the Church was begun by the Apostles in the whole world.

The sixth argument is as follows: We are all bound under peril of eternal death to join ourselves to the true Church and to persevere in it. But this cannot be done if the Church is invisible. Therefore, the true Church must necessarily be simply visible.

I answer, the argument fails under the confusion of disparate questions: For it is one thing to ask, Where is the true Church of the Elect? It is another thing, Which in particular is that Church of the Elect? To the former it is rightly answered: The true Church of the Elect is where there is a visible assembly of the called, where the pure doctrine of the Gospel sounds, where the Sacraments are legitimately administered. Therefore, whoever wishes to join himself to the true Church, it is necessary that he associate himself with that visible assembly of the called. For in this assembly there cannot but be those who are truly Elect.

ci

But to the latter question we answer that those constitute the true Church of the Elect who have faith in Christ and persevere in this faith: But to be able to point out such Elect as if with a finger and say, These are they: that is indeed impossible. Wherefore it remains firm and settled that this Church of the Elect is Invisible.

Furthermore, the minor proposition is not completely true. For the exclusive particle 'only' should be added, in this manner: But this cannot be done if the Church is invisible only. But we deny this, for we even willingly grant the Church of the Elect its own visibility, in those ways and respects which have been explained several times.

The seventh argument is as follows: If the Church is a congregation of men using the same Sacraments and professing the faith of Christ, under the government of legitimate pastors, it follows necessarily that it is visible.

I answer that a fallacy is committed by incomplete division. For there are required for the constitution of the true Church not only those things which the Jesuit enumerates: since those things fall even to hypocrites, nay even to heretics: but it is required in addition that in the same assembly there be also some Elect, against whom the gates of hell cannot prevail. But who such persons are, that is certainly not conspicuous to our eyes: but known only to God, because that true faith which perseveres to the end, and the remaining internal gifts of the Holy Spirit which perfect such Elect, cannot be judged by our eyes.

The eighth and last, not indeed of Bellarmine, but of the Jesuit Turrianus, is what sounds thus: All particular churches are visible. All particular churches are one Catholic Church. Therefore, the Catholic Church, gathered into one body from all those particulars, was also visible.

I answer 1. that the fallacy of secundum quid and simpliciter is committed in the major premise: For all particular churches are visible, secundum quid, namely with respect to the calling and the called men: but they are invisible with respect to election or the elect, who are in any true particular church, although they are not seen. Therefore the same must be established concerning the whole Catholic Church, even if it could be gathered into one place. Furthermore, the definition of the Catholic Church by the aggregation of all particular ones is too plebeian and childish: since it ought to be defined theologically by the unity or communion of faith and Spirit. Thirdly, that very aggregation of all particular churches argues more for an invisible than a visible Catholic Church. For since this aggregation can never actually take place in this world, it certainly consists not in the operation of the eyes, but of the mind. Fourthly, it labors under a manifest absurdity: For if what the Jesuit dreams of, the aggregation of all particular churches, could actually take place, then they would cease to be particular churches: and one visible church would emerge in number church would emerge in number. Again, as long as there are and remain many particular Churches, the Catholic Church itself, which by thought alone constitutes one whole, will certainly not be visible but invisible. For with the philosophers themselves supporting it, the τὸ καθ᾽ ὅλꙋ (the universal) is conceived only by the operation of the mind. Fifth, a shameful tautology is committed. For it is asked, whether the whole Catholic Church is visible? The Jesuit answers that it is: Because, forsooth, all particular Churches are visible. But this is nothing else than to prove the same thing by itself. For all particular Churches taken together are the Catholic Church itself: Whence such a tautology emerges: The whole Catholic Church is visible: because the whole Catholic Church is visible. If the Jesuit corrects the major premise in this way: All particular Churches considered separately are visible: then the minor proposition will be manifestly false. For not all particular Churches separately, but taken jointly and collectively, are the Catholic Church. If in the minor premise he substitutes 'jointly' or 'collectively' for 'separately', then a fallacy of four terms will result. Sixth, an error occurs ꚙρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως (according to the figure of speech), in the copula 'is': For in the major premise it is taken existentially, 'All Churches are visible', that is, they exist visibly: But in the minor it is taken by collection, collectively in this sense: All particular Churches are one whole Catholic Church, that is, they compose and constitute, when taken together, one whole Catholic Church. Finally, however the minor is taken, it is found to be false, indeed impossible. For since very many particular Churches have ceased to exist throughout almost the entire East: indeed, the whole Israelite Church has long since expired: How, I ask, will it be true that all particular Churches are actually visible at the same time, and thus actually constitute one visible Catholic Church. For not only those that exist today, but also those particular Churches that have passed away, constitute one universal comprehended by the mind, or the whole Catholic Church.

Latin:

1. Quâ fronte ergò locum istum Romanenses hactenùs ad Ecclesiam visibilem Romanam accommodare, & exindè probare ausi fuerint, Ecclesiam errare non posse.

2. Quomodo versus immediatè præcedens, & indiviso nexu cohærens, explicari debeat, nùm & ille ad Triumphantem Ecclesiam sit accommodandus? Si affirmatè responderit: consequens fuerit, Ecclesiam Triumphantem demùm sanctificari per lavacrum aquæ, in verbo: Quod absurdum. Sin negatè: tùm ostendat textus cohærentiam, quæ talis est: Christus dedit seipsum pro Ecclesia, ut sanctificaret eam per lavacrum aquæ in verbo, ut sisteret eam sibi gloriosam, ut esset sancta & immaculata, non habens rugam. Si prius illud de melitante Ecclesia est accipiendum, uti certè aliter accipi non potest: cur non & hoc posterius. Sensus proindè loci istius emergit iste: Quòd fructus passionis Christi sit inter reliquos, & ille, quod per lavacrum aquæ ita sanctificet Ecclesiam suam, ut sanguine ipsius lota, & regenerationis lavacro perpurgata, nullam jam habeat peccatorum maculam aut rugam: non quidem sensu Schvvenckfeldiano & Anabaptistico: sed sensu Orthodoxo: quatenus nimirum Christus Ecclesiæ suam donat justitiam, & per fidem purgat conscientias ab operibus mortuis, ut remissis omnibus peccatis, contectæ sint rugæ sive maculæ adhærentium infirmitatum. Jam verò faciat periculum Bellarminus, utrùm imputatam hanc justitiam Christi in Electis videre possit, & illam nobis monstret. Hanc quamdiu nobis non monstraverit, uti certè hac in vita eam monstrabit nunquàm, tamdiu ratum firmumq; manebit, Ecclesiam Electorum, & sic per fidem purificatorum esse invisibilem. Interim tamen minimè negamus locum Apostolicum διέξοδως etiam accipi posse, de statu Ecclesiæ Triumphantis in altera vita: ubi demùm hæc sanctitas & puritas Ecclesiæ Electorum erit perfecta & absoluta.

sensibile. E. ipsa quoque Ecclesia semper est sensibilis. Ubi major propositio luculenta probatione indiget. Vera enim si esse debeat, tùm κτα παντός talis sit, necesse est. Atqui talis non est: Siquidem in multis deficit: Nam fundamentum Ecclesiæ est ἀναμάρτητον, est omnipotens, est immortale. Ergone talis etiam erit Ecclesia ipsa. Nugas ergò venditat, non disputat Jesuvvita? Tertiò si per petram intelligas Fidei confessionem, annè visibilis ea fuit? Haud ita. Hoc ergò animadvertens Jesu vvita callidè pro visibili, substituit τὸ Sensibile: ut sic elabendi rimula pateret. Sic ergò deinceps non tàm pro visibili, quàm pro sensibili Ecclesia disputabunt Jesu vvitæ. Tandem quæ de Christi ac Petri vicario & successore Pontifice Romano narrat Jesuvvita, fabulosa sunt dudum à nostris protrita.

Sed tumultuatur Jesuvvita, ex cap. 20, 4. Numerorum, & lib. 1. Reg. 8, 14. Vbi omnis Ecclesia Israel conspecta fuerit.

Alterum argumentum mutuatur Jesuvvita, ex Psalm. 19, 5. ubi David de Ecclesia: in Sole posuit tabernaculum suum: hoc est, in manifesto, ut sicut Sol non potest omninò latere, ita nec Ecclesia possit abscondi. Item Ecclesia comparatur monti magno & conspicuo, qui nullo modo potest latere: secundum illud, Matth. 5, 14. Non potest civitas abscondi supra montem posita.

Respondeo extra oleas vagari Disputatorem. Non enim quæritur, An hæc vel illa particularis Ecclesia sit visibilis: Neque etiam illud controvertitur, An Electi quatenus sunt homines, & in externo vocatorum cœtu versantur, sint visibiles. Utrumque enim istud ultrò largimur: sed hoc propriè est ζητόμενον: An Electi, quatenus Electi, videri possint, ut certus esse possis ex oculorum nescio hunc vel illum esse verè electum? vel hos aut illos verè fideles, constituere in terris hisce, veram Elestorum Ecclesiam? Ubi nos pegantem tenemus: quam etiam producta testimonia non infringunt. Edisserat enim Jesuvvita, Num Moses & Rex Israëlis in universa multitudine, quam oculis aspexerant, etiam in individuo viderint, quinam sint Electi, quinon? Hoc dùm demonstrare nequit, Andabatarum more cespitat Jesuvvita.

Sed laborat & hoc argumentum turpi ignoratione Elenchi, & Sophismate ἑτεροζητήσεως. Agunt enim singula hæc Testimonia, de externo cœtu visibilis Ecclesiæ, qui nunquam fuit obscurus in orbe terrarum, licet aliàs magis, aliàs minùs floruerit: Quâ de re hocloco non controvertitur. Illud proindè potiùs probandum esse Jesuvvitæ, ipsos quoque Electos, quatenus per internam fidem desiniuntur, esse conspicuos, prout conspicui sunt & manent, quatenus ut vocati in visibili vocatorum grege versantur. Quod dùm non probat Jesuvvita, utique extra oleas tota ipsius vagatur disputatio.

Sed subtilius disputandi acumen prodit Jesuvvita, quando ex loco Matth. 16, 18. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, sic infert eod. cap. 12. libri tertij de Ecclesia militante. Nomine petræ sive intelligas Christum, sive fidei confessionem, sive Petrum, semper fundamentum Ecclesiæ est aliquid sensibile: E. Ecclesia ipsa est sensibilis, sive visibilis: & quidem hodiè, in Christi ac Petri vicario, Pontifice Romano.

In specie verò notandum, quòd locus Psal. 19. non agat quoad literam de Ecclesia: sed de Sola creato, cui Deus tentorium sive sedem posuerit in cœlis: uti fontes Hebræi evidenter confirmant. Neque hîc quicquam præjudicare nobis potest aut debet Augusting, qui vitiosum vulgatum secutus, de Ecclesia locum illum interpretatus est: licèt & hæc interpretatio nostræ causæ nihil quicquam incommodare possit.

Tertium argumentum sumit Jesuvvita ex ipso ortu & progressu Ecclesiæ, Veteris & Novi Testamenti, quæ semper fuerit visibilis: uti Israëlitæ, Apostoli, & reliqui fideles semper fuerunt visibiles.

Respondeo ad Antecedens,illudque ut falsum nego. Nam fundamentum Ecclesiæ semper esse aliquid sensibile, sive visibile, falsissimum est. Christus certè æquè fuit fundamentum Veteris Judaicæ Ecclesiæ, atque hodiè est: Atqui sensibile illud aut visibile tùm non erat, neque enim Filius Dei carnem modò assumserat: neque etiam vicarium aliquem visibilem tum constituerat. E. falsum quod Ecclesiæ fundamentum semper sit visibile aut sensibile. Deindè ratio Consequentiæ est futilissima: id quod clariùs patet, si integer formetur Syllogismus, qui talis erit. Qualis est ratio sive conditio Fundamenti Ecclesiæ, eadem quoque est ipsius Ecclesiæ: Atqui Fundamentum Ecclesiæ semper est

Respondeo: Eandem committi ἀγνοιαν ἐλέγχε & ἑτεροζήτησιν, quam in secundo argumento notavimus. 2. manifestè falsum, quòd temporibus Christi tota Catholica Ecclesia fuerit in Apostolis & discipulis Christi: quasi verò præter hos nemo quisquam ex Judæis fuerit, qui Christum agnoverit, licèt apertè illum confiteri non fuerint ausi. Diversum sanè vel ex Nicodemi Exemplo, Johannis 3. luculenter patet. Et edisserat obsecro Jesuvvita, quid causæ sit, quod Apostoli ipsi Christo concionante de proditore suo tàm deligenter inquisiverint, Ecquis ille esset. Certè omnes videbant Judam Ischariotem : Sed nùm ex Electis an reprobis esset, videre non potuerunt. Ergò vel hoc exemplo irrefragabiliter demonstrari potest,Ecclesiam Electorum esse Invisibilem.

Quartum argumentum desumit Jesuwita, ex ipsa ratione Ecclesiæ: Ecclesia enim est societ as quædam,non Angelorum neq; animarum, sed hominum. Atqui non dici potest societas hominum, quæ videri nequit. E. Sed futilius est hoc argumentum, quam ut refutatione prolixiore opus sit: Gemina enim illa cosideratio Electorum, de qua aliquoties dictum, omnem ejus impetum penitissimè reprimit ac refellit. Deindè verò auditu horrendum est, quòd subjicit Jesuwita, nullam esse societatem, nisi se agnoscant ij, qui dicuntur socij. Siccinè ergò nobis nulla societas intercedit cum Angelis, cumq́; Electis in cælo jam triumphantibus? Siccine ergò falsum fuerit, quod paulo ante ex cap. 12. Epistolæ ad Hebræos ostendimus, Ecclesiam etiam militantem in his terris admissam esse ad frequentiam multorum millium Angelorum, & Spirituum justorum? Siccinè non ampliùs in Symbolo Apostolico credemus Comunionem Sanctorum,ubi omnes Sancti intelliguntur,tam illi qui adhuc sunt In via, quàm qui modò sunt in patria, uti Scholastici loquuntur.

Quintum argumentum tale est: Tempore Christi, (uti volunt Lutherani) Ecclesia vera solùm erat in Zacharia,Hanna,Maria, & paucis aliis piis. Atqui hi communicabant cum Pontificibus in templo,in sacrificiis &c. E. vel malè faciebant isti communicando falsæ Ecclesiæ: vel malè faciunt Lutherani,non communicando cum Pontificiis, & non obediendo Pontifici.

Respondeo, fallit argumentum : 1. Ignoratione Elenchi. Nihil enim quicquam concludit, pro visibilitate Ecclesiæ Electorum : sed tantùm agit de cōmunicatione Veræ Ecclesiæ cum falsa, de qua hoc loco nihil agitur. 2. Vera est minor non simpliciter, sed tantùm secundum quid. Communicarunt enim Sancti illi cum Pontificibus in quibusdam saltem capitibus, iis nimirùm quæ in Lege D E I erant ordinata : & duntaxat ad tempus usque dùm Judæorum Synagoga cum honore est sepulta, & ministerium Ecclesiæ publicum per Apostolos in toto mundo inchoatum.
