Sextum argumentum sic habet : Tenemur omnes sub periculo mortis æternæ, nos veræ Ecclesiæ adjungere, & in illa perseverare. At hoc fieri non potest, si Ecclesia est invisibilis. E. Ecclesia vera simpliciter visibilis sit necesse est.

Respondeo, Fallit argumenum sub confusione disparatarum quæstionum: Aliud enim est quærere? Ubi sit vera Electorum Ecclesia? Aliud est, Quænam in individuo sit illa Electorum Ecclesia? Ad priorem rectè respondetur: Ibi veram efse Electorum Ecclesiam, ubi est cœtus visibilis vocatorum, ubi sonat pura doctrina Evangelii, ubi legitimè administrantur Sacramenta. Ergò qui veræ se Ecclesiæ adjungere velit, cœtui isti visibili vocatorum se adsociet, necesse est. In hoc enim cœtu non possunt non esse verè Electi.

ci

Verùm ad posteriorem quæstionem respondemus, eos constituere veram Electorum Ecclesiam, qui fidem habent in Christum, inq; fide hac perseverant: Sed ut in individuo ac digito quasi monstrare possim hujusmodi Electos ac dicere, Hi sunt illi: id verò impossibile est. Quare hanc Electorum Ecclesiam, esse Invisibilem adhuc firmum ratumque manet.

Deindè minor propositio non est completè vera. Addenda enim esset particula exclusiva tantùm, in hunc modum: At fieri hoc non potest, si Ecclesia est invisibilis tantùm. Verùm hoc nos negamus, quin Electorum etiam Ecclesiæ suam visibilitatem ipsi ultrò largimur, iis modis atque respectibus, qui aliquoties sunt explicati.

Septimum argumentum sic habet: Si Ecclesia est congregatio hominum utentium Sacramentis ijsdcm, & fidem Christi profitentium, sub regimine legitimorum pastorum, sequitur necessario eam esse visibilem.

Respondeo committi sophisma ἀπὸ τὸ ἐλλιπὲς διαιρέσεως. Requiruntur enim ad constitutionem veræ Ecclesiæ, non duntaxat ea, quæ enumerat Jesuita: Siquidem ea cadunt etiam in Hypocritas, imò in hæreticos etiam: sed requiritur insuper, ut in eodem cœtu sint etiam aliqui Electi, adversus quos portæ inferorum prævalere haud queant. Qui verò tales sint, id certè oculis nostris non est conspicuum: sed soli Deo notum, propterea quòd fides illa vera & ad finem perseverans, & reliqua interna Spiritus sancti dona, quæ ejusmodi Electos perficiunt, oculorum nostrorum περὶ judicari haud possunt.

Octavum & postremum, non quidem Bellarmini, sed Turriani Jesuitæ est, quod sic sonat: Omnes Ecclesiæ particulares sunt visibiles. Omnes Ecclesiæ particulares, sunt una Catholica Ecclesia. E. Catholica Ecclesia, ex particularibus illis omnibus in unum congregata corpus, erat etiam visibilis.

Respondeo 1. committi Sophisma τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς, in Majore: Omnes enim Ecclesiæ particulares sunt visibiles, secundùm quid, nempè respectu Vocationis, & hominum vocatorum: Sunt verò invisibiles, respectu Electionis sive Electorum, qui in quavis vera particulari Ecclesia sunt, licet non videantur. Ergò idem statuendum est de tota Catholica Ecclesia, si vel maximè in unum locum ea congregari posset. Deindè nimis plebeja & puerilis est Definitio Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, per aggregationem omnium particularium: cùm Theologicè definiri debeat, per unitatem sive communionem fidei ac Spiritus. Tertiò illa ipsa aggregatio omnium particularium magis arguit Invisibilem, quàm visibilem Ecclesiam Catholicam. Cùm enim aggregatio hæc, ipso actu nunquàm in hoc mundo fieri possit: utique non in oculorum, sed mentis operatione ea constitit. Quartò absurditate manifestâ laborat: Si enim quod Jesuita somniat, omnium particularium Ecclesiarum aggregatio ipso actu fieri posset, tùm desinerent esse Ecclesiæ particulares: & una numero prodiret visibilis Ecclesia. Rursus quamdiu sunt & manent plures Ecclesiæ particulares, utique ipsa Catholica Ecclesia, quæ νοήσει tantùm Unum totum constituit, non erit visibilis sed invisibilis. Nam ipsis quoque Philosophis suffragantibus τὸ καθ᾽ ὅλꙋ, non nisi mentis operatione concipitur. Quinto turpis ἀδολεσχία committitur. Quæritur enim, an tota Catholica Ecclesia sit visibilis? Respondet Jesuwita quòd sic: Quia nimirùm omnes particulares Ecclesiæ sunt visibiles. Atqui hoc nihil est aliud, quàm idem probare per seipsum. Nam omnes particulares Ecclesiæ simul sumtæ, sunt ipsa Catholica Ecclesia: Unde talis emergit ἀδολεσχία: Tota Catholica Ecclesia est visibilis: quia tota Catholica Ecclesia est visibilis. Sin Majorem in hunc modum corrigat Jesuwita: Omnes particulares Ecclesiæ seorsim consideratæ sunt visibiles: tùm minor propositio manifestè falsa erit. Nam non omnes Ecclesiæ particulares seorsim, sed junctim & collectivè sumtæ, sunt Catholica Ecclesia. Sin in Minore pro seorsim, substituat junctim aut collectivè, tùm prodibit paralogismus quatuor terminorum. Sextò occurrit error ꚙρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως, in copula Est: Nam in Majore sumitur ὑπαρκτικῶς, Omnes Ecclesiæ sunt visibiles, hoc est, existunt visibiliter: In minore verò sumitur per συναθροισμὸν collectivè hoc sensu: Omnes particulares Ecclesiæ sunt Una tota Catholica Ecclesia, hoc est, componunt ac constituunt simul sumtæ unam totam Catholicam Ecclesiam. Tandem minor quocunq́; modo accipiatur, falsa tamen deprehenditur, imò impossibilis. Cùm enim plurimæ particulares Ecclesiæ, per totum fermè Orientem esse defierint: imò tota Israëlitica Ecclesia jam pridem expiraverit: Quomodo quæso verum erit, quòd omnes particulares Ecclesiæ sint actu simul visibiles, & sic actu unam visibilem Catholicam Ecclesiam constituant. Nam non modò eæ, quæ hodiè extant, sed & illæ quæ præterierunt particulares Ecclesiæ, Unum constituunt καθόλꙋ mente comprehensum, sive totam Catholicam Ecclesiam.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes, or ornaments or privileges of the Church

In the Holy Scriptures the Church receives various and many appellations, from which a judgment can be made concerning the attributes and axioms of the Church: such as that it is the City of God, Ps. 46:5. New Jerusalem, Rev. 3:12. Kingdom of God, Matt. 13:41. Temple of God, 1 Cor. 3:16. Vineyard of the Lord, Isa. 5:2. Granary of Christ, Luke 3:17. Fold of Christ, John 10:16. And it is indicated by other encomiastic appellations of that kind: but among these, those epithets or attributes which are defined in the Ecumenical Creeds, primarily the Nicene and the Apostolic, hold a place of honor, as it were: such as that the Church is named 1. One, 2. Holy, 3. Catholic, 4. Apostolic. For from these attributes the proper affection of the true Church can be investigated. Which is the very reason that today a sharp controversy is being waged between us and the Jesuits concerning these four attributes or axioms. Therefore, we must also examine each one a little more accurately.

Latin:

IN Scripturis Sacris Ecclesia varias & multas appellationes sortitur, ex quibus de attributis & axiomatis Ecclesiæ fieri queat judicium: ut quòd Civitas DEI, Psal. 46, 5. Nova Hierosolyma, Apoc. 3, 12. Regnum DEI, Matth. 13, 41. Templum DEI, 1. Corint. 3, 16. Vinea Domini, Jes. 5, 2. Horreum Christi, Luc. 3, 17. Ovile Christi, Joh. 10, v. 16. & id genus aliis appellationibus encomiasticis indigitatur: sed inter has principem quasi locum obtinent ea epitheta sive attributa, quæ in Symbolis Oecumenicis, Niceno cumprimis & Apostolico sunt definita: ut quòd Ecclesia nominatur 1 Una. 2. Sancta, 3. Catholica, 4. Apostolica. Ex hisce enim attributis investigari potest, propria affectio Ecclesiæ veræ. Quæ ipsa causa est, quòd de quatuor istis attributis sive axiomatis hodiè inter nos & Jesuuitas acris omninò agitatur controversia. Proindè de singulis etiam paulò accuratiùs nobis dispiciendum fuerit.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: The First Attribute of the Church or axiom is that which is predicated: One

That the true Church is one in number and essence, and divided only by accidents, Holy Scripture confirms clearly everywhere: as in Song of Songs 6:8, 'My dove is one, my perfect one is one.' Scripture likewise explains by what things this unity is completed: as in Ephesians 4:3 and following, 'Strive to keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace: there is one body, and one Spirit: just as you were also called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one Baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in all.' Therefore, six distinct members of this unity are most correctly established by Apostolic authority.

I. One God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

II. One Faith, namely because the doctrine of faith or the Gospel has always been, is, and will be one from the origin of the Church until the end of the age.

III. One Foundation of Salvation and Lord, namely Christ.

IV. One Baptism, One Sacrament of the Supper: which are equally seals of the righteousness of faith, just as the Sacraments of the Old Testament were formerly: Rom. 4:11.

V. One Hope of eternal Life.

VI. Of the mystical body itself, in the highest conjunction of members, a simple unity also, which the Apostles' Creed names the communion of Saints.

Moreover, the whole rationale of this Unity is perceived much more clearly if those things which seem able to destroy, or at least to weaken, the Unity of the Church are accurately removed: such as are: 1. The dispersion of particular churches, or of the Elect or faithful themselves, regarding the intervals of places, throughout the whole world. 2. The huge dissimilarity of the members of the Church themselves, according to the three Hierarchical states. 3. The great discrepancy of ecclesiastical ceremonies and rites everywhere. 4. Dissensions concerning matters pertaining to the faith, provided they do not overturn the substance itself, or the foundation of the faith. 5. And lastly, the association of the wicked and hypocrites.

For first, regarding the dispersion of the Elect or faithful, or of particular churches, that certainly does not oppose the Unity of the Church; because neither differences of times, nor intervals of places, nor any other conditions of any external or perishable thing pertain to establishing the Unity of the Church: nor are they required in any pact or respect: But it is completed by one society of faith and communion of the Spirit. Whence also the Church has obtained the appellation of the Communion of Saints, and of Spiritual Unity.

Furthermore, the vast dissimilarity of the members of the Church themselves, according to three distinct Hierarchical statuses, does not dissolve this Unity; just as the dissimilarity of various members does not dissolve or destroy the unity of the human body. But just as these concur into one correct and elegant symmetry of one body: so too the diverse members of the Church constitute the harmony of one most perfect mystical body. For this perfection is completed by One Spirit, by which the individual members are vivified: by One hope, by which they are destined to one and the same end: by One Lord, by which they are governed: by One faith, by which, as the eye of the body, all things are directed to the goal and end: by One baptism, by which, as an external testimony of faith, all members are associated and bound together: Which Unity exists entirely among those who are true and living members of the body of Christ. Away then with the Anabaptist fury, which removes the distinctions of hierarchical orders or statuses from the midst of the Church: and rashly, partly foolishly, fabricates a common and identical promiscuous lot for all men.

Thirdly, the dissimilarity of ceremonies and rites of the Churches in no way detracts from the praise of this Unity, so much so that St. Jerome does not hesitate to affirm that the Church of the Old and New Testament was and is one in Essence, and that it should not be distinguished into two, differing in Essence, on account of the times, because GOD has associated both by the same faith and the same Spirit, although a very great discrepancy of rites is seen on both sides. Nor can any time be given since the age of the Apostles when a universal conformity of rites has prevailed in the Church. Indeed, not even the Roman Church can boast of such conformity of rites to this very day: of which fact the diverse and almost infinite orders of Monks—of which the Papists today count more than 130—as well as the diverse offices of celebrating the Missatic sacrifice, can be evidence. What? That such conformity of rites in the Church is neither possible, nor useful, nor necessary. It is impossible, because of the vast diversity of the causes from which those ceremonies draw their origin. For 1. The judgment of human will is variable and inconstant according to the diversity of subjects or men. 2. The discrepancy of times and objects in no way admits such equality or similarity of rites. Furthermore, it is also useless, not only because of the danger of a new Jewish servitude, which we would draw upon ourselves by this pact, contrary to the admonition of the Apostle, Galatians 5:1. But also because of the fear of Scandals, which would arise in great numbers and magnitude due to the slightest intermission of this or that ceremony.

Finally, it is even less necessary, because human traditions contribute nothing to salvation: and therefore, for the sake of Christian liberty,

, they can either be observed or omitted. And if such conformity were simply or even in some respect necessary for salvation, certainly the Roman Church would have long since fallen from salvation itself. For Platina is a witness that the Apostle Peter celebrated the Eucharist with the Lord's Prayer alone, without so many ceremonies, rites, and gesticulations, and indeed even without that Canon which the Romanists otherwise call the Soul of the Mass.

The Jesuits object, and clamor that one must distinguish between Universal and Special rites: contending that not the latter but the former ought always to be conformable in the Church. But I answer: if by Universal rites they understand those which GOD himself instituted, namely the administration of the Sacraments: then we readily grant that the observation of those Sacramental rites is so necessary, as far as the dispensation of the visible Elements is concerned, that for this very reason we accuse the Roman Church of the foulest apostasy, because it has sacrilegiously stolen the Chalice from the Laity regarding the administration of the Eucharist. But if by Universal rites they understand such Ceremonies as were devised only by Roman Pontiffs and foisted upon all Churches to be observed: then we certainly deny that they are Universal: since it has not yet been proven that the Roman Pontiff is the Universal head of the Catholic Church. Furthermore, regarding special rites, we again distinguish between the Genus itself and this or that species of human rites. We readily concede that the Genus itself, that is, some order and decorum, must be observed in the Church, being so taught by the Apostle, 1 Cor. 14:40; but as far as this or that rite in particular is concerned, which the Papists and other superstitious people foist upon us: I judge that we must use the Christian liberty into which we have been asserted through Christ, and not allow ourselves to be entangled again in the yoke of ceremonies, since GOD is worshipped in vain, or rather not at all, through the observation of such human rites, Matt. 15:9. Finally, this exception of the Jesuits is contrary to the fact: for they contend that these special or particular rites, which the Roman Church holds, are just as necessary and proper to divine worship as the universal ones are, so that a priest who lives in marriage sins no less than one who keeps several hundred prostitutes: or certainly sins more gravely who eats meat during the Lenten season than one who has committed adultery. Thus, therefore, with this doctrine of the Jesuits standing, the condition and necessity of these particular and Universal rites will be equal and the same: For whatever is proper to divine worship: that is absolutely necessary. Therefore, this distinction of the Jesuits, under which they seek a defense for their cause, expires.

Fourthly, dissensions which sometimes arise concerning such matters as do not concern the very foundation of religion and faith do not detract from the Unity of the Church. This is evident from the example of the Corinthian Church, which indeed had many Schisms; but nevertheless did not fall away from the Bond of Ecclesiastical Unity: as is clearly evident from the comparison of chapter 1, 4, and 5 with the chapter and with chapter 11, 18. Frivolous, therefore, is the insult of the Jesuits, which they seek against the Lutheran Church from this chapter, writing that from the one doctrine of Luther have proceeded the Anabaptists, Schwenkfeldians, Calvinists, Libertines, and other sectarians of this flour. For this one calumny manifests the genius and character of the adversaries clearly enough: namely that which Blessed Augustine describes, book on the Sheep, chapter 15: This alone, he says, has remained for the slanderous heathens, that they say against us: Why do you not agree among yourselves? The Gentile pagans, who have remained having nothing to say against the name of Christ, object to the dissension of Christians. But that we may engage with the Jesuits at close quarters, we appeal to their own conscience, that they may declare to us, whether they seriously maintain that sectarians of this kind are members of the Lutheran Church? If they assert it: let them show us, I beseech you, why Luther and the Lutheran theologians oppose themselves to them with such great force, and segregate themselves from their synagogue as much as can be done? If they deny it: then they convict themselves of levity and lying. Let the Jesuits therefore remember that the unity, and consequently the truth, of the Lutheran Church is not to be judged either from the writings of this or that private man, or even of many who think wrongly: which we cannot deny contain many things said inconveniently: but from the public confession of our churches, the public Symbolic books, examined by the norm of the Scriptures, and approved by the calculation of all genuine Lutherans: such as we know those symbols to be, which are comprised in the Book of Christian Concord. Meanwhile, however, if the Jesuits so wish and urge, we do not unwillingly concede that sectarians of this kind have gone out from us: but we immediately retort that they were not of us, 1 John 2:19. Nor will this seem absurd to them, provided they take to heart that of the Apostle, Acts 20:30: From among yourselves men will arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them.

Latin:

UNam numero atque essentiâ esse Ecclesiam veram, & non nisi accidentibus dividuam, Scriptura Sacra passim evidenter confirmat: ut Cantie 6, 8. Una est columba mea, Una est perfecta mea. Unitas verò hæc quibus rebus absolvatur, itidem Scriptura explicat: ut Ephes. 4, 3. & seqq. Studete servare Unitatem Spiritus, per vinculum pacis: Unum est corpus, & unus Spiritus: quemadmodum & vocati estis in unam spem vocationis vestræ. Unus Dominus, una fides, unum Baptisma, unus DEUS & Pater omnium, qui est super omnia, & per omnia, & in omnibus. Sex proindè distincta Unitatis hujus membra, Apostolica autoritate rectissimè constituuntur.

I. Unus DEUS, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus S.

II. Una Fides, nempè quia doctrina fidei sive Evangelium, unum semper ab origine Ecclesiæ fuit, est & erit ad finem usque seculi.

III. Unum Salutis Fundamentum & Dominus, CHRISTUS scilicet.

IV. Unus Baptismus, Unum Sacramentum Cœnæ: quæ æquè sunt sigilla justitiæ fidei, atque olim fuerunt Sacramenta Veteris Testamenti: Rom. 4, 11.

V. Una Spes Vitæ æternæ.

VI. Corporis ipsius mystici, in summa membrorum conjunctione, simplex etiam unitas, quam Symbolum Apostolicum nominat communionem Sanctorum.

Cæterùm tota Unitatis hujus ratio multò evidentius perspicitur, si accuratè removeantur ea, quæ Unitatem Ecclesiæ tollere, vel saltem labefactare posse videntur: qualia sunt: 1. Ecclesiarum particularium, sive ipsorum Electorum aut fidelium, quoad locorum intervalla, per totum terrarum orbem dispersio. 2 Ipsorum Ecclesiæ membrorum, secundum tres status Hierarchicos, ingens dissimilitudo. 3. Ceremoniarum & rituum Ecclesiasticorum magna passim discrepantia. 4. Dissensiones de rebus ad fidem pertinentibus, modò ipsam substantiam, sive fundamentum fidei non evertant 5. & postremò, Malorum & hypocritarum conversatio.

Primùm enim, quoad Electorum aut fidelium, sive Ecclesiarum particularium dispersionem, ea certè Unitati Ecclesiæ non adversatur; eò quòd neque discrimina temporum, neque locorum intervalla, neque ullæ aliæ cujusquam rei externæ aut caducæ conditiones ad Unitatem Ecclesiæ constituendam pertinent: aut ullo pacto aut respectu requiruntur: Sed unâ societate fidei & communione Spiritus illa absolvitur. Undè etiam Communionis Sanctorum, & Unitatis Spiritualis appellationem Ecclesia sortita est.

Deindè Unitatem hanc etiam non solvit, ipsorum membrorum Ecclesiæ, secundum tres distinctos status Hierarchicos, ingens dissimilitudo: haud magis atque Unitatem corporis humani non solvit aut tollit, variorum membrorum dissimilitudo. Sed quemadmodum hæc in unam rectam atque elegantem unius corporis συμμετρίαν concurrunt: Ita diversa etiam Ecclesiæ membra, unius perfectissimi corporis mystici harmoniam constituunt. Perfectio enim hæc absolvitur Uno Spiritu, quo membra singula vivificantur: Una spe, quâ ad finem unum eundemque destinantur: Uno Domino, quo gubernantur: Una fide, quâ ceu corporis oculo, ad scopum & finem omnia diriguntur: Uno baptismo, quo tanquàm externâ fidei testatione, membra omnia consociantur colliganturque: Quæ Unitas ex asse intercedit iis, qui vera vivaque corporis Christi membra sunt. Facessat proindè furor Anabaptisticus, distinctiones ordinum sive statuum hierarchicorum è medio Ecclesiæ tollens: & communem eandemque omnium hominum sortem promescuam, temerè partim, partim stolidè confingens.

Tertiò Unitatis hujus laudem Ecclesiæ etiam minimè derogat, ceremoniarum & rituum Ecclesiarum dissimilitudo, adeò ut B Hieronymus affirmare non dubitet, Veteris quoque & Novi Testamenti Ecclesiam, fuisse & esse per Essentiam unam, neque temporibus illam in duas, secundum Essentiam differentes, distinguendam esse, propterea quod eâdem fide, eodemque Spiritu DEUS utramq; consociaverit, licèt rituum utrinq; maxima conspiciatur discrepantia. Neque etiam jam indè ab Apostolorum ætate, tempus potest dari ullum, quo universalis rituum conformitas in Ecclesia obtinuerit. Quin nè quidem Romana Ecclesia in hunc usque diem de tali rituum conformitate gloriari potest: cujus rei indicio esse possunt, tùm diversi & fermè infiniti Monachorum ordines: quorum 130. ampliùs hodiè numerant Pontificii: tùm diversa etiam celebrandi sacrificii Missatici officia. Quid? quòd neque possibilis, neque utilis, neque necessaria est, talis rituum in Ecclesia conformitas. Impossibilis est, propter caussarum, ex quibus ceremoniæ istæ suam trahunt originem, ingentem diversitatem. Nam 1. Arbitrii humani judicium, pro diversitate subjectorum sive hominum est variabile & inconstans. 2. Temporum & objectorum discrepantia, ejusmodi æqualitatem sive similitudinem rituum nullo modo admittit. Porrò inutilis etiam eadem est, non tantùm propter periculum novæ servitutis Judaicæ, quam hoc pacto nobis attraheremus, cotra admonitionem Apostoli, Gal 5, 1. Sed & propter metum Scandalorum; quæ ob levissimam hujus aut illius ceremoniæ intermissionem, plurima & maxima oborirentur.

Tandem, minus etiam necessaria est, propterea quòd traditiones humanæ ad salutem nihil faciunt: ac proindè pro libertate Christiana

, vel observari vel omitti possunt. Et si simpliciter vel etiam secundum quid ad salutem talis conformitas esset necessaria, certè salute ipsa jampridem excidisset Romana Ecclesia. Testis enim est Platina, Petrum Apostolum solâ Oratione Dominicâ Eucharistiam celebrasse, sine tot ceremoniis, ritibus, gesticulationibus, imò etiam sine Canone illo, quem aliàs Animam Missæ nominant Romanenses.

Excipiunt Jesuivitæ, & distinguendum esse clamitant inter ritus Universales & Speciales: non hos sed illos Ecclesiæ semper conformes esse debere contendentes. Sed respondeo: si per Univerfales ritus intelligant eos, quos DEUS ipse instituit, nempè administrationem Sacramentorum: tùm ultrò largimur, usque adeò necessariam esse rituum istorum Sacramentalium observationem, quoad dispensationem Elementorum visibilium: ut vel ideò Ecclesiam Romanam fœdifsimæ apostasias insimulemus, quòd circa administrationem Eucharistiæ, Calicem sacrilegè Laicis suffurata est. Sin autem per ritus Universales intelligant ejusmodi Ceremonias, quæ à Pontificibus demùm Romanis sunt excogitatæ & omnibus Ecclesiis ad observandum obtrusæ: tùm sanè negamus eos esse Universales: Siquidem nondùm probatum est, Pontificem Romanum esse caput Universale Catholicæ Ecclesiæ. Deindè quoad speciales ritus, rursum distinguimus inter Genus ipsum & inter hanc vel illam speciem rituum humanorum. Genus ipsum, hoc est, ordinem aliquem, & decorum in Ecclesia observandum esse, ultrò concedimus, sic edocti ab Apostolo, 1. Cor. 14, 40. sed quod in specie hos vel illos ritus attinet, quos Pontificii, & superstitiosi alii nobis obtrudunt: judico utendum esse libertate Christiana, in quam per Christum asserti sumus, neque committendum, ut denuò ceremoniarum jugo implicemur, siquidem frustrà, imò planè non colitur DEUS, per observationem ejusmodi humanorum rituum, Matt. 15. v. 9. Tandem exceptio hæc Jesuwitarum facto est contraria: Contendunt enim speciales sive particulares istos ritus, quos Romana tenet Ecclesia, aquè necessarios, cultusq́; divini proprios esse atque sunt universales, ita ut haud leviùs peccet sacerdos, qui in conjugio vivat, quàm qui aliquot centenas meretrices alat: vel certè graviùs peccet, qui tempore quadragesimali carnibus vescatur, quam qui adulterium commiserit. Sic ergò stante hac Jesu witarum doctrinâ, par erit & æqualis particularium istorum, & Universalium rituum conditio ac necessitas: Quicquid enim cultus divini proprium est: illud absolutè est necessarium. Expirat proindè distinctio hæc Jesuwitarum, sub quâ causæ præsidium quærunt.

Quartò Unitati Ecclesiæ nihil derogant diffensiones, quæ gliscunt interdum de ejusmodi rebus, quæ fundamentum ipsum religionis & fidei non concernunt. Patet hoc exemplo Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ, quæ quidem Schismata benè multa habebat; sed tamen à Vinculo Unitatis Ecclesiasticæ minimè excidebat: uti evidenter patet ex collatione capitis 1, 4. & 5. cum cap. & eum capite 11, 18. Frivola proindè est Jesu-witarum insultatio, quam adversus Ecclesiam Lutheranam ex hoc capite petunt, scriptitantes ex una Lutheri doctrinâ prodiisse Anabaptistas, Schvvenckfeldianos, Calvinistas, Libertinos, & hujus farinæ sectarios alios. Hæc enim vel una calumnia genium & ingenium Adversariorum satis manifestè prodit: nimirùm illud quod B. Augustinus describit, lib. de Ovibus, cap. 15: Hoc solum, inquiens, maledicis Ethnicis remansit, ut contranos dicant: Quare inter vos non consentitis? Gentiles pagani, qui remanserunt no habentes, quod dicant contra Christi nomen, dissensionem Christianorum objiciunt. Sed ut cominùs cum Jesu-witis congrediamur, provocamus ad propriam ipsorum conscientiam, ut edicant nobis, nùm seriò statuant, Sectarios hujusmodi esse Lutheranæ Ecclesiæ membra? Si asserunt: ostendant nobis obsecro, cur Lutherus & Lutherani Theologi, tantis viribus sese illis opponant, & ab illorum Synagoga, quantum fieri potest, se segregent? Sinegent: Tùm semetipsos levitatis & mendacii arguunt. Meminerint proindè Jesuwitæ, de Unitate, & consequenter Veritate Ecclesiæ Lutheranæ, non esse judicandum, vel ex hujus vel alterius privati hominis, vel plurium etiam malè sentientium scriptis: quibus multa incommodiùs dicta contineri, negare haud possumus: sed ex publicâ Ecclesiarum nostrarum confessione, libellis publicis Symbolicis, ad normam Scripturarum examinatis, ac omnium γνήσιως Lutheranorum calculo approbatis: Quales novimus ea esse Symbola, quæ libro Christianæ Concordiæ comprehenduntur. Interim verò, si ita velint & urgeant Jesuwitæ, haud inviti concesferimus, Sectarios hujusmodi exiisse è nobis: sed statim regerimus, ipsos non fuisse de nobis, 1. Joh. 2, 19. Neque hoc absurdum illis videbitur, modò pensi habeant illud Apostoli, Act. 20, 30. Ex vobis ipsis exurgent viri, loquentes perversa, ut abducant discipulos post se.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: The First Attribute of the Church or axiom is that which is predicated: One (continued)

darkness, and associates and reconciles Christ with Belial: Nay, they even object the authority of Augustine, who in book 2 against Parmenianus, the last chapter, affirms: The wicked are not in the body of Christ, which is the Church, although they may become bodily participants of the sacraments of Christ. But I reply that the Jesuits are talking nonsense. For Augustine himself is the interpreter; that the wicked do not indeed belong to the structure of the house, which is the Church: but that they are nevertheless in that house, although they are in it no differently than chaff is said to be in a heap of wheat, as he speaks in book 7 against the Donatists, chapter 51. Furthermore, in what way the upright and the wicked constitute one and the same people: and yet there is no fellowship of light with darkness, or agreement of Christ with Belial: that same thing Augustine explains excellently against the Donatists after the conference, chapter 6. Whether, he says, they call the Church a body, or bread, or wheat, or a house, or any similar things: these are names which belong to the good by themselves: But through the good they belong also to that people, whose primary parts are the good. Concerning which matter he disputes more lengthily also in book 3 of Christian Doctrine, chapter 32. We are accustomed commonly in the schools to reply that the denomination is made from the better part, by synecdoche, which is most customary even to the Scriptures themselves: as we shall show more lengthily below, where we shall dispute concerning the holiness of the Church.

Moreover, from this first attribute of the Church depends the ventilation of that most grave question or controversy, which is agitated today concerning the perpetuity of the Church, and other questions depending therefrom. For from unity an argument is sought that is clearly infallible for the perpetuity of the Church: since that which is one by essence, and invariable: that easily obtains also a respect of perpetuity. For if the Church were ever to perish completely, then it could not be believed to be one in number, and the same by essence. Now, however, we profess in the Nicene Creed that we believe in ONE Church: the reason for which profession of ours must be examined more deeply.

Therefore, the Christian faith does not command us to believe in the Church: since, with Augustine as interpreter, to believe in something is, by believing, to love, and by believing, to seek after that thing: which is a thing that belongs to GOD alone. But the Church is not GOD, but a gathering gathered to GOD, as Rufinus holds.

Fifthly and lastly, it does not take away the unity of the Church if there are found in it those who do not keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, and who neither coalesce among themselves through true love, nor adhere to the head of the Church, CHRIST, through true faith. For as long as such are not excluded from the Church, although they are destitute of true faith: or they themselves do not depart at least from the external profession of the purer religion: it is enough that in them there is one baptism, one profession of faith and religion, the same society of sacraments, so that they may be said to be in one Church.

Then also in the Creed we do not profess that we believe the Church. In which part the authority of the Church is inferior to apostolic authority: for we believe the prophets and apostles when they speak or write, and indeed not under the condition of faith made elsewhere: but with absolute assent, as the legates of the LORD, through whom the Holy Spirit himself has spoken, 2 Timothy 3:16, 2 Peter 1:21. But we never believe the Church with such absolute assent, but only with conditional assent, namely insofar as its words and decrees agree entirely with the oracles of the prophets and apostles.

The Romanists grunt here, and try to overwhelm us with an absurdity, writing that such a unity of the Church is taught by the Lutherans as constitutes the same citizens of both Jerusalem and Babylon, which makes the same members of Christ and of the Devil, which makes light agree. Away then with the Jesuit Bellarmine's vain babbling, who attributes to the Church such authority that it is to be believed in matters of religion not conditionally, but absolutely: so that the truth of faith, as far as we are concerned, rests upon the authority of the Church: and whatever the Church approves is true: whatever it disapproves is false, lib. 3. de Ecclesia militante, cap. 14. But of this question below in its proper place.

Finally, we profess in the Creed that we believe the Church, which is nothing else than to establish beyond doubt that God has not abandoned the whole human race: but that there is some perennial Church, which, as it began in Paradise, and has been preserved always until now: so it is to endure until the end of the world. Where, however, no Platonic idea, or some spectrum hovering in the air and in the gathering of atoms is conceived in the mind: but eyes are turned to a certain gathering: a gathering, namely, of those who have been recalled to the kingdom of the Son of God through the Word and Sacraments: in which gathering there are always the Elect: For whom God chose, these He also called, Rom. 8, 30. Thus, therefore, by the word BELIEVE, not some external condition of the Church, but its perpetual duration is noted. For because faith will not cease before this visible world itself has met its end: the Church certainly can no more be completely abolished or interrupted than faith itself. But if any time could be given in which the duration or continuation of the Church had been either broken or interrupted in this world: certainly not only faith and the truth of the divine word would have been endangered regarding their unshaken certainty: but Christ himself also would have deserted the parts of his office, while he would have ceased to be the head of his Church, Ephes. 1, 22. and cap. 5, 23. Yet neither of these do the Promises admit, by which CHRIST himself has solemnly pledged the perpetual duration and conservation of his Church: as Matth. 16, 18. that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Matt. 28, 20. that he himself will be with it all days, even unto the consummation of the age. To which pertains also that illustrious Prophecy, Jes 59, 21. This is my covenant with them, says the Lord, My spirit which is in you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, and from the mouth of your seed, from now and unto the age. Whence in the Scriptures not only the kingdom of Glory, but also the kingdom of Grace is proclaimed as Eternal: Luc. 1, 33. Psalm. 45, 7. Psalm. 48, 9. Psal. 89, 37. Daniel. 2, 44. and cap. 7, 14. etc.

Away then with the profanity of the Epicurean herd, which imagines that GOD is affected by absolutely no care for human affairs: and partly the Pyrrhonic Theology of those who dream that everyone is to be saved in his own religion, even outside the gathering of the faithful and the reborn.

But some in this place object with very many testimonies of the Scriptures, which seem to hint that the Church has completely failed in this world: as what is said in Jes. 1, 6. concerning Israel (outside of whom there could not even then be a Church): from the sole of the foot even to the top of the head there is no soundness in it: Israel has not known me. Likewise what is read in Jerem. 2. v. 26, the house of Israel is confounded, they and their kings, Princes and Priests, and Prophets, saying to wood: You are my father: and to stone, You have begotten me: Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the LORD. And indeed the Donatists fought with these arguments in the time of Augustine. For when they could not bring forward the consensus of previous centuries for the confirmation of their doctrine, they immediately feigned that the true Church had completely failed, as Augustine reports, lib. de Unit. Eccles. cap. 12.

But I answer that complaints of this kind by the Prophets are not to be understood so absolutely and simply, but Synecdochically. For since, by instituting some comparison of the impious to the pious, such a multitude of the former is discovered that hardly any good or faithful people appear: therefore Scripture rebukes the whole people with one designation of the impious, although there are some Elect and faithful in it, but very few. The matter can be illustrated by an example. Jeremiah and Ezekiel were contemporaries, and directed their Prophecies to the house of Israel at one and the same time. Now Ezekiel cap. 3, 7. complains thus: The house of Israel will not listen to you: because they will not listen to me. For all Israel is of a brazen forehead, and hard of heart. What then? Did the whole Church of the Israelites then completely fail? Not at all: For GOD himself, in the same Prophet, immediately following cap. 9. 4. thus restricts this complaint: Mark with the letter Than the foreheads of the men who sigh and grieve over all the abominations that are done in the midst of it.

Thus David Psalm 12, 1 prays: Save me O GOD, for the Saint has failed? Was there therefore no Saint left besides David? Not so: For David himself restricts this, immediately in verse 6 adding: Because of the misery of the needy, and the groaning of the poor, now will I arise. And verse 8. You O Lord will keep us from this generation.

Thus the Apostle Philip. 2, 21. says, All seek their own, not the things that are of JESUS CHRIST. Where, however, he did not wish to hint as if the whole Church of the Philippians had failed: For both the inscription and the Epilogue of the Epistle insinuate the contrary: Where he mentions the Saints in that Church: cap. 1, 1. and cap. 4, 21.

Therefore that Rule of Augustine has place here, lib. de Unit. Eccles. cap. 12. The divine discourse often rebukes the impious crowds of the Church as if all were such, and none at all remained: for thence we are admonished that in a certain number of their own they are all called, that is, all children of hell.

Moreover, in this place arise three most serious controversies, highly celebrated in the writings of the Jesuits: the first of which is concerning the hidden Church: The second concerning the Lutheran Church, namely, what kind it is and where it existed in previous centuries under the Papacy, before the rise of Luther? The third and last is concerning the ordinary succession of Bishops, which the Romanists deem so necessarily required for the essence and perpetuity of the true Church, that where it cannot be shown, there it must be established that not even a true Church has remained.

Latin:

tenebris, & Christum cum Belial consociet & conciliet: Quin & Augustini autoritatem objiciunt, qui lib. 2. contra Paul.c.ult. affirmat: Malos non esse in CHRISTI corpore, quod est Ecclesia, licèt Sacramentorum Christi corporaliter participes fiant. Sed respondeo nugari Jesuwitas. Nam Augustinus ipse interpres est; Malos non quidem pertinere ad compagem domus, quæ est Ecclesia: sed esse tamen in illa domo, quamvis in ea non secus sint, quàm paleæ dicuntur esse in acervo tritici, ut loquitur lib. 7. contra Donatum, cap. 51. Cæterùm quo pacto probi atque improbi eundem omninò populum constituant: nec fiat tamen lucis ad tenebras societas, vel Christi ad Belial conventio: id idem Augustinus egregiè explicat contra Donat. post collat.cap.6. Sive inquiens Ecclesiam Corpus dicant, sive panem, sive triticum, sive domum, aut similia quævis: nomina hæc sunt, qua bonis per se conveniunt: Sed per bonos illi etiam populo, cujus partes primariæ sunt Boni. Quâ de re prolixiùs etiam disputat lib. 3. de doctr. Christ. c. 32. Nos vulgò in Scholis respondere folemus, à potiori fieri denominationem, per Synecdochen, ipsis quoque Scripturis usitatissimam: uti infrà prolixiùs ostendemus, ubi de Sanctitate Ecclesiæ disputabimus.

Cæterùm dependet à primo hoc Ecclesiæ attributo, ventilatio gravissimæ illius quæstionis sive Controversiæ, quæ de Perennitate Ecclesiæ, & quæstionibus aliis indè dependentibus, hodiè agitatur. Ex Unitate enim ad perennitatem Ecclesiæ, argumentum planè infallibile petitur: Siquidem quod per Essentiam Unum est, & invariabile: illud perennitatis etiam respectum facilè sortitur. Si enim aliquandò penitùs interiret Ecclesia, tùm Una numero, & per Essentiam eadem credi non posset. Jam verò profitemur in Symbolo Niceno, Credere nos UNAM Ecclesiam: Cujus sanè professionis nostræ, quæ sit ratio, altiùs dispiciendum fuerit.

Institò igitur Fides Christiana non jubet ut credamus in Ecclesiam: Siquidem Augustino interprete, credere in aliquid, est credendo amare, & credendo in illud quæsirere: id quod Soli DEO competit. Ecclesia verò non DEUS est, sed cœtus DEO congregatus, uti Ruffinus habet.

Quintò & postremò, Unitatem Ecclesiæ non tollit, si in ea reperiantur, qui non servant Unitatem Spiritus in vinculo pacis, quique nec inter se, per verum amorem coalescunt, neque capiti etiam Ecclesiæ CHRISTO per veram fidem adhærescunt. Quamdìu enim tales ab Ecclesia non sunt exclusi, licèt verâ fide destituantur: vel ipsimet à professione saltem externâ Religionis purioris non discedunt: satis est, in illis unum esse Baptisma, unam esse fidei & religionis professionem, eandem Sacramentorum societatem, ut in Una Ecclesia esse dicantur.

Deindè in Symbolo etiam non profitemur, Nos credere Ecclesia. Quâ in parte inferior est autoritas Ecclesiæ autoritate Apostolica: Prophetis enim & Apostolis loquentibus, aut scribentibus credimus, & quidem non sub conditione factæ aliundè fidei: sed assensu absoluto, tanquàm DOMINI legatis, per quos ipse Spiritus sanctus locutus est, 2. Timoth. 3, 16. 2. Petr. 1, 21. Cæterùm Ecclesię tali assensu absoluto nunquàm credimus, sed tantùm assensu conditionato, quatenùs videlicet ejus verba & decreta, cum Oraculis Prophetarum & Apostolorum ex asse

Grunniunt hîc Romanenses, & absurdo nos obruere conantur, scriptitantes talem Ecclesiæ Unitatem à Lutheranis doceri, quæ eosdem cives constituat & Hierosolymæ & Babylonis,quæ Christi & Diaboli membra eadem faciat, quæ lucem cum congruunt. Facessat proindè Jesuvita Bellarmini ματαιολογία, qui Ecclesiæ eam afsingit autoritatem, quâ ei non ex conditione, sed absolutè sit credendum in Religionis negocio: ita ut Veri tas fidei, quoad nos nitatur Ecclesiæ autoritate: & verum sit, quicquid Ecclesia probat: falsum, quicquid illa improbat lib 3. de Ecclesia militante, cap. 14. Sèd de hac quæstione infrà suo loco.

Tandem, profitemur in Symbolo nos credere Ecclesiam, quod nihil est aliud, quàm indubitato statuere, non objectum esse à Deo totum genus humanum: sed esse Ecclesiam áliquam perennem, quæ uti in Paradiso cœpit, & hactenus semper conservata fuit: ita ad finem usque mundi sit duratura. Ubi tamen non idea aliqua Platonica, aut in aëre atque atomorum cœtu obvolitans quoddam spectrum animo concipitur: sed ad certum quendam cœtum convertuntur oculi: cœtum nimirùm eorum, qui per Verbum & Sacramenta ad regnum Filii Dei revocati sunt: in quo cœtu semper sunt Electi: Siquidem quos Deus elegit, hos & vocavit, Rom. 8, 30. Sic ergò CREDENDI verbo non externa aliqua Ecclesiæ conditio, sed perpetua ejus duratio, notatur. Quia enim fides non priùs cessabit, quàm mundus ipse hic aspectabilis finem sortitus fuerit: Ecclesia certè nihil magis, quàm fides ipsa abrogari penitùs vel interrumpi potest. Quod si dari tempus ullum posset, quo duratio sive continuatio Ecclesiæ vel abrupta, vel interrupta in hoc mundo fuisset: certè non fides tantùm & Veritas verbi divini, de immota sua certitudine periclitata fuisset: sed Christus etiam ipse officii sui partes deseruisset, dùm caput Ecclesiæ suæ esse desiisset, Ephes. 1, 22. & cap. 5, 23. Atqui neutrum horum admittunt Promissiones, quibus Ecclesiæ suæ perpetuam durationem & conservationem CHRISTUS ipse sanctè recepit: ut Matth. 16, 18. quod portæ inferorum adversus eam non sint prævalituræ. Matt. 28, 20. quod ipse ei adfuturus sit omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Quô pertinet illustre etiam illud Vaticinium, Jes 59, 21. Hoc fœdus meum cum eis, dicit Dominus, Spiritus meus qui est in te, & verba mea quæ posui in ore tuo, non recedent de ore tuo, & de ore seminis tui, amodo & usque in seculum. Undè in Scripturis non modò regnum Gloriæ, sed & regnum Gratiæ Æternum prædicatur: Luc. 1, 33. Psalm. 45, 7. Psalm. 48, 9. Psal. 89, 37. Daniel. 2, 44. & cap. 7, 14. &c.

Facessat proindè tum Epicurei gregis profanitas, qui fingit, DEUM rerum humanarum curâ prorfus nullâ affici: Partim Pyrrhonica Theologia eorum, qui quemque in sua Religione, etiam extra cœtum fidelium & renatorum salvandum esse somniant.

Objiciunt verò hoc loco nonnulli benè multa Scripturarum testimonia, quæ Ecclesiam hoc in mundo penitùs defecisse, innuere videantur: ut quod Jes. 1, 6. de Israële (extra quem ne quidem tùm poterat esse Ecclesia) dicitur : à planta pedis usque ad verticem capitis non est in eo sanitas: Israël non cognovit me. Item quòd Jerem. 2. v. 26. legitur, confusi sunt domus Israël, ipsi & reges eorum, Principes & Sacerdotes, & Prophetæ, dicentes ligno: Pater meus es tu: & lapidi, Tu me genuisti: Quid vultis mecum judicio contendere? Omnes dereliquistis me, inquit DOMINUS. Et sanè his argumentis tempore Augustini pugnabant Donatistæ. Nam cùm pro doctrinæ suæ confirmatione proferre non possent superiorum seculorum consensum, statim fingebant, Ecclesiam veram penitùs defecisse, sic referente Augustino, lib. de Unit. Eccles. cap. 12.

Verùm respondeo querelas hujusmodi Propheticas, non ita absolutè & simpliciter, sed Synecdochicè esse intelligendas. Quoniam enim comparatione aliquâ impiorum ad pios institutâ, tanta illorum deprehenditur copia, ut vix boni aut fideles ulli appareant: ideò Scriptura unâ impiorum notatione totum populum reprehendit, licèt in eo aliqui sint Electi & fideles sed paucissimi. Exemplo res illustrari potest. Erant Jeremias & Jezechiel σύγχρονοι, & ad domum Israël uno eodemque tempore sua dirigebant Vaticinia. Jam Jezechiel cap. 3, 7. sic conqueritur: Domus Israël noluit audire te: quia nolunt audire me. Omnis quippè Israël attrita fronte est, & duri cordis? Quid igitur? Anné tota Israëlitarum Ecclesia tùm penitùs defecit? Minimè verò: Nam DEUS ipse apud eundem Prophetam, statim subseq. cap. 9. 4. sic querelam hanc restringit: Signa literâ Than frontes virorum gementium & dolentium super cunctis abominationibus, quæ fiunt in medio ejus.

Sic David Psalm. 12, 1 orat: Salvum me fac DEUS, quoniam defecit Sanctus? Ergóne præter Davidem Sanctorum nullus ampliùs erat reliquus? Haud ita: Nam David ipse hoc restringit, statim vers. 6. subjiciens: Propter miseriam inopum, & gemitum pauperum nunc exsurgam. Et vers. 8. Tu Domine servabis nos à generatione hac.

Sic Apostolus Philip. 2, 21. Omnes, inquit, quæ sua sunt quærunt, non quæ sunt JESU CHRISTI. Ubi tamen non hoc innuere voluit, ac si Ecclesia Philippensium tota defecisset: Diversum enim tùm inscriptio, tùm Epilogus Epistolæ insinuat: Ubi Sanctorum in illa Ecclesia meminit: cap. 1, 1. & cap. 4, 21.

Locum ergò hîc habet Regula illa Augustini, lib. de Unit. Eccles. cap. 12. Sermo divinus plerumque impias turbas Ecclesiæ sic redarguit, tanquam omnes tales sint, & nullus omninò remanserit: indè quippe admonemur, in suo quodam numero eos dici omnes, hoc est, omnes filios gehennæ.

Cæterùm hoc loco oriuntur tres gravissimæ controversiæ, Jesuwitarum scriptis admodùm celebratæ: quarum prima est, de Ecclesia latente: Altera de Ecclesia Lutherana, Nùm, qualis & ubi ea superioribus seculis sub Papatu, ante exortum Lutheri extiterit? Tertià ac postrema est, de Ordinaria Episcoporum successione, quam ad essentiam & perennitatem veræ Ecclesiæ ita necessariò requiri autumant Romanenses, ut ubi ea monstrari non queat, ibi ne quidem veram Ecclesiam mansisse statui debeat.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: Controversy Concerning the Latent (hidden) Church

The Jesuits, concerning the doctrine of the duration and perpetuity of the Church until the last day, indeed agree with us: But they differ greatly in defining the form of this duration. For they imagine that the duration or perpetuity of the Church must be defined by its uniform state, and that one indeed perpetually flourishing and always like itself. Whence Bellarmine also, in book 3 on the Church militant, chapter 13, argues that even the visible Church cannot simply and absolutely fail.

We establish it thus: 1. The true or Catholic Church never fails entirely: Since this properly consists of the invisible assembly of the Elect known to GOD alone. 2. The true visible Church, with respect to its external form, that is, as regards the pious, and indeed as regards the public ministry itself, fails so often that hardly any traces of it appear, and if it were possible, the Elect themselves might be led into error. Therefore, the Church endures and will endure until the consummation of the age, the gates of hell never prevailing against it: But this duration must be defined with the exception of vicissitude, as regards increases and decreases. For just as the Moon, from its recession from the Sun and approach to the Sun, either grows or wanes, or suffers an eclipse or some defect: So the Church, according as it approaches closer to or recedes further from the Sun of righteousness, feels no small change: which is accustomed to happen not only in the particular, but even in the Universal Church itself. The Israelite Church flourished in the Old Testament not rarely, like a full moon: But sometimes it suffered a sad defect and obscuration: as in the times of Eli the Priest, in which the Word of the Lord is said to have been rare and precious: 1 Sam. 3:1; in the times of the impious King Ahab, in which the Prophet Elijah complained that he alone of the faithful remained, 1 Kings 19:18. Likewise in the times of

the Prophet Azariah, according to whose prophecy many days passed in Israel without the true GOD, without a Priest, without a Teacher, without a law. 2 Chron. 15:3. Likewise in those times in which the book of the law was clearly lost among the Israelite people: 2 Kings 22. Furthermore, in those times in which CHRIST was manifested in the flesh: also in those times in which the Arian heresy, by the permission of GOD, so prevailed in the Church that it seemed to have occupied the whole Christian world. In these and other times of this kind, who is there who does not see that the Church did not indeed fail entirely, but nevertheless suffered a sad obscuration? Concerning which matter, Lord Jerome says excellently somewhere: The whole world groaned and marveled to find itself Arian: But when no hope remained, the Lord is awakened, He commands the tempest, the beast dies, tranquility returned. I shall speak more clearly. All the Bishops who had been exterminated from their own sees return to the Churches. Then Egypt receives its conqueror Athanasius: then the Church of the Gauls embraced Hilary returning from the battle: then Italy changed its mourning garments for the return of Eusebius, etc. Therefore, the principal Bishops and Orthodox Prelates were indeed exiled from their Churches. But the Church of CHRIST was not exiled from the World.

But that we may approach more closely to the contest with the Jesuits, we solemnly protest at the beginning that the Lutherans are burdened with a notable injury by certain Pontifical writers, as if they taught that the Catholic Church could fail entirely. For the contrary is sufficiently clear both from the writings of our own people and from those things which we have argued thus far concerning the perpetuity of the Church. Therefore, that which is properly disputed between us and the Jesuits is: Whether a particular Church: this one or that one: indeed whether all particular Churches can be reduced to such straitness and obscurity that even as regards the external pure and legitimate ministry it does not publicly become known to us, Where the true particular visible Church of CHRIST is? Where we hold the affirmative, instructed by those testimonies of the Scriptures which we have just produced: But the Jesuits strive to defend the negative, relying chiefly on those arguments which Bellarmine proposes in this order: book 3 on the Church militant, chapter 13.

I. He takes the argument from Matthew 16:18: The gates of hell shall not prevail against the Church. And 1 Tim. 3:15: The Church of the living God is the Pillar and foundation of the Truth.

I answer: The state of the controversy is maliciously perverted, while the Jesuit sophistically applies to the visible [Church] those testimonies of Scripture which expressly treat of the invisible Church of the Elect, inasmuch as it alone is founded upon the rock, and is the pillar and ground of the truth.

He applies it to the Church: which, even according to its external ministry, so far falls away from the truth that it is not founded upon the rock, nor does it remain a pillar of Truth: although meanwhile the gates of hell do not prevail against the invisible Church of the Elect.

The second argument heaps up several testimonies, in which are contained promises concerning the preservation of the Church, in that Christ promised that He would be present with the pious even to the consummation of the age, Matt. 28:20; that He therefore gave to the Church pastors, Doctors, Apostles, etc., for the consummation of the Saints, Eph. 4:11, 12, 13; that God founded it forever, Ps. 47:7; that God entered into an everlasting covenant with His people, etc.

But I reply that these and similar sayings confirm nothing more than that the Church of God never completely fails in this world; which very thing we also concede. For faith will never fail in its entirety, but it will endure in certain members of the Church until the end of the age, although they are not always known and perceived by us. But from these, the consequence does not hold for the rest of the multitude of the Church.

For it does not follow: The Church of the Elect is perpetual and will never fail. Therefore, any visible Church will never fail. Furthermore, Christ, ascending into the heavens, indeed promised in Eph. 4 the perpetual use of the ecclesiastical ministry: but He did not bind that to this or that Church or visible assembly: rather, according to the good pleasure of His will, He gives pastors and Doctors, whom, such as, when, and how He wills: so that faithful Doctors are sometimes not known to all, nor are they established in some ordinary and visible Succession: as the Romanists otherwise dream, but they lie hidden as if concealed.

The Jesuit takes the third argument from those parables by which the Church is compared to a threshing floor, in which there are grains and chaff: to a net, in which there are good and bad fish: to a field, in which there are tares and wheat, etc. But these things denote the visible Church, and indeed show that it will never perish. Therefore.

I reply that loose brooms are being thrown at us. For what connection, I ask, is there in this argument? The visible Church is compared to a threshing floor, a field, etc. But this threshing floor will remain until the last day, when Christ will finally purge His threshing floor and separate the wheat from the chaff. Therefore, the visible Church will never fail. For we ourselves also readily grant this very thing, that even the visible Church will never completely perish. But this is the question: Can the visible Church not sometimes be so pressed and obscured by the force and tyranny of persecution that you can scarcely see or recognize any form of it? Furthermore, whether that which Scripture affirms concerning the universal Church ought to be immediately twisted and applied to this or that particular Church: just as the Romanists indeed falsely twist it to their own Roman Church (which is particular),

are proper to the Catholic Church. Certainly, since the Savior Himself expressly affirms that the wheat must be separated from the chaff, and the sheep from the goats, only on the last day: He surely hints clearly enough that such is the form of the Church here on earth that it can by no means be established to us according to distinct knowledge who are the sheep, who the goats, who the wheat, who the chaff: Nay, He asserts that the pious and the Elect lie hidden in such a way that if the tares were to be eradicated by men in this world, it could easily happen that the wheat would be uprooted at the same time: because, of course, the truly Elect cannot be judged by our eyes.

He seeks the fourth argument from those places of Scripture in which an everlasting Kingdom is promised to Christ.

But this argument also incurs the same sophistications with which the preceding ones labored. For 1. that which we do not deny is proven. 2. that which is most true concerning the internal glory of the Kingdom of Christ is ineptly applied to the external, visible, and always equally flourishing form of the Church: which is not an essential mark of the True Church: 3. it is profane that the Jesuit sweetly raves that the Kingdom of Christ is to be judged by the multitude of citizens or men gathered into one place: as if the Spirit of God were so weak and impotent that He could not reign in those who are dispersed far and wide throughout the whole world, and cannot be seen by us, but lie hidden, sometimes concealed in dens and caves. 4. the Jesuit ought to have proven that the visible Church is always equally glorious as it is perpetual: but he proves nothing other than that there will always be some visible Church in the world. Whence a judgment can be made concerning the candor of this disputant.

The Jesuit borrows the fifth argument from the authority of the Fathers: which, however, does not refute us, as is evident even from those things which we noted above from Augustine and Jerome.

The Jesuit seeks the sixth and final argument from reasons; of which he brings forward three.

The first is: If at any time the invisible Church alone remains in the world: the salvation of those who are outside the Church will be impossible. For they cannot be saved unless they enter into the Church: But they cannot enter into it if they are ignorant of it.

I answer that the fallacy of ἐπερώτησις is being committed: while two very different questions are shamefully confused. For it is one thing when it is asked, Whether the visible Church can be so hidden that it lacks every visible form entirely, so that no Church can any longer be recognized on earth.

It is another thing, however, when it is asked, Whether the true Church of the Elect always exerts its visible form uniformly?

The former we have never affirmed, namely that the Church is sometimes so hidden that no visible form of the Church appears at all any longer.

We affirm this latter point fearlessly, namely that the Church of the Elect does not always exert its external form in such a way that it can be known through it. Therefore, those who desire to associate themselves with the Church should approach the visible assembly of the called, wherever it may be, and however it may appear, whether glorious or calamitous. For just as external glory is not the medium through which the Holy Spirit works faith, so that miserable and sad face of the Church cannot hinder the power of the Holy Spirit.

The second Jesuit argument sounds like this: It is of the nature of the one true Church that it be visible. Therefore, if the visible Church perishes, no true Church remains.

I reply that the antecedent is false: for it is of the nature of the true Church not that it be seen, but that it be believed to exist, as the Apostles' Creed testifies. 2. From visibility to its uniform glorious state, there is no progression. Granted: there may always be some visible assembly of the called: it does not follow from that: Therefore it is visible in one and the same way and respect: just as it does not follow: The solar body is visible. Therefore it is always visible in one and the same degree of brightness. Let the adversaries, therefore, distinguish between the thing and the mode of the thing. We do not deny the thing itself, that is, the visibility and glory of the Church: but that there is always one and the same mode and degree of this visibility and glory: that we deny again and again. And indeed, the adversaries cannot even prove regarding their own Roman Church that its status has always been the same.

The third reason is as follows: The Elect either issue a profession of their faith or they do not: If they issue it: then the Church is always visible, because a confession is always being issued: If they do not issue it: then there is no Church. For it is not a true Church in which there are none who issue their confession and are saved.

I reply that the former part of this dilemma suffers from the base fallacy of Ignoratio Elenchi. For it is not the confession of faith, which certainly never strikes the eyes, that ensures the Church is always visible: but the condition of the men themselves, which is visible. Nor is it required that the true and faithful confessors of Christ should always come into the sight of tyrants and voluntarily expose themselves to dangers. For God nowhere commands this. Indeed, the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles testified to the contrary by their own example, who even took flight to provide for their own safety. And what will the Jesuit answer regarding those seven thousand, in the time of the impious King Ahab, who were hidden and could not even be seen by the Prophet Elijah? Did these issue a confession of faith or not? If he answers affirmatively: let him show how their Church was visible then. But if negatively: then according to the Jesuit's opinion, were these seven thousand damned because they did not issue a confession of faith? We conclude, therefore, that a confession of faith can be issued by the Elect, even if that is not known to everyone: and therefore the Church does not fail on this earth, even if their confession is invisible and unknown to us.

Bellarminus objects: Thus the Church will lack a visible form: And because it will lack this, the Church will no longer be in the world: For it implies a contradiction: for the Church to exist and to lack every visible form.

I reply that the fallacy of the accident is committed. For it is not if it lacks a sincere ministry, but only if the Church lacked every ministry entirely, that it would suffer the loss of an observable or visible form. Now, that visible form of the Church can obtain for a time even with a Ministry corrupted in doctrine: as Christ himself teaches, who asserts that the Scribes and Pharisees, not only flagitious in life and morals but also imbued with the foulest errors, nevertheless sit in the Chair of Moses. An example can be the Ministry in the Old Testament, which was most corrupt at various times: In the New Testament, however, the Arian heresy, which spread through the entire East and West, occupied the very summit of the ecclesiastical ministry in such a way that nothing sound, nothing integral appeared anywhere in it. Here, therefore, we affirm that the Church was hidden indeed, but did not fail. Hilary supports us, who in his own century also believed the true Church was hidden rather than saw it, when he responds thus to those urging the visible form of the Church, in the manner of the Pontiffs, under Arianism, in his book against Auxentius near the end: A love of walls has wrongly seized us; you wrongly venerate the Church of God in roofs and buildings; you wrongly bring the name of Peace under these; is it ambiguous that the Antichrist is to sit in them? Mountains and forests and lakes and prisons and chasms are safer for me. For in these the Prophets, either remaining or submerged, were still prophesying. Athanasius supports us, who did not hesitate to seek the Church among the pious faithful, in the manner of the Prophets, and following the example of other Bishops wandering in deserts, in forests, caves, cisterns, and caverns of the earth. But it must also be observed that the true Church often lies hidden in one part of the world, which nevertheless flourishes greatly in another part, just as in previous centuries the true Church lay hidden in the West under the Papacy, which nevertheless flourished then in the East: as we shall show a little later. Otherwise, outside of a state of persecution, we readily concede that the Church is a City set upon a hill, which cannot be hidden: that it is a lamp, placed not under a bushel but upon a lampstand.

Latin:

JEsuwitæ circa doctrinam de duratione & perpetuitate Ecclesiæ usque ad diem novissimum, nobiscum quidem consentiunt: Sed in durationis hujus Formâ definiendâ plurimùm dissentiunt. Fingunt enim, durationem sive perennitatem Ecclesiæ definiendam esse, per æquabilem ejus statum, & eum quidem perpetuò florentem, sibiq; semper similem. Undè Bellarminus etiam lib. 3. de Ecclesia militante, cap. 13. disputat, Ecclesiam etiam visibilem, simpliciter & absolutè non posse deficere.

Nos sic statuimus, 1. Ecclesiam Veram sive Catholicam nunquàm totam deficere: Siquidem hæc propriè constat invisibili Electorum cœtu soli DEO cognito. 2. Ecclesiam veram visibilem externæ formæ respectu, hoc est, quoad pios, imò quoad ipsum ministerium publicum ita sæpiùs deficere, ut vix ulla ejus appareant vestigia, & si fieri posset, ipsi quoque Electi in errorem inducantur. Durat proindè & durabit quidem Ecclesia usque ad consummationem seculi, portis inferorum nunquàm adversus illam prævalentibus: Sed Duratio hæc definienda est, cum exceptione vicissitudinis, quoad incrementa & decrementa. Nam sicut Luna ex recessu à Sole, & accessu ad Solem vel augescit, vel minuitur, aut ecclipsin sive defectum aliquem patitur: Ita Ecclesia, prout ad Solem justitiæ vel propiùs accedit, vel longiùs recedit, mutationem haud parvam persentiscit: id quod in particulari tantùm, sed ipsâ etiam Universali Ecclesiâ evenire solet. Floruit in Veteri Testamento non rarò Ecclesia Israëlitica, instar plenilunij: Interdum verò tristem defectum & obscurationnem passa est: ut temporibus Eli Sacerdotis, quibus rarus & carus fuisse dicitur Sermo Domini: 1. Sam. 3, 1. temporibus impii Regis Achabi, quibus Elias Propheta se solum ex fidelibus superesse quiritabatur, 1. Reg. 19, 18. Item temporibus

Prophetæ Azariæ, secundum cujus vaticinium, multi dies transierunt in Israël absq; verò D E O, absque Sacerdote, absque Doctore, absque lege. 2. Paralip. 15, 3. Item illis temporibus, quibus liber legis in populo Israëlitico planè fuit amissus: 2. Reg. 22. Illis præterea temporibus, quibus C H R I S T U S in carnem est exhibitus: illis etiam temporibus, quibus Ariana hæresis, D E I permissu, in Ecclesia ita invaluit, ut totum orbem Christianum occupasse videretur. His sanè & id genus aliis temporibus, Ecclesiam non quidem totam defecisse, sed tamen tristem obscurationem passam esse, quis est qui non videat? Quâ de re præclarè alicubi D. Hieronymus: Ingemuit totus orbis, & Arianum se esse miratus est: Sed cùm nihil superesset spei, Dominus excitatur, imperat tempestati, bestia moritur, tranquillitas rediit. Manifestiùs dicam. Omnes Episcopi, qui de propriis sedibus fuerant exterminati, ad Ecclesias redeunt. Tunc Triumphatorem suum Athanasium Ægyptus excipit: tunc Hilarium de prælio revertentem, Galliarum Ecclesia complexa est: tunc ad reditum Eusebii lugubres vestes Italia mutavit, &c. Exulabant ergò quidem Ecclesiis suis præcipui Episcopi, & Antistites Orthodoxi. At non exulabat Orbe, Ecclesia C H R I S T I.

Sed ut propiùs ad certamen cum Jesuwitis accedamus, solenniter initiò protestamur, insigni injuria à quibusdam Scriptoribus Pontificiis gravari Lutheranos, quasi docerent, Ecclesiam Catholicam penitùs deficere posse. Contrarium enim tùm ex nostrorum scriptis, tùm ex iis, quæ hactenùs de perennitate Ecclesiæ disputavimus, satis liquidò patet. Illud proindè propriè inter nos & Jesuwitas controvertitur: An Ecclesia particularis: vel hæc vel illa: imò an omnes particulares Ecclesiæ, in eam angustiam & obscuritatem redigi possint, ut etiam quoad externum purum ac legitimum ministerium publicè nobis non innotescat, Ubi sit vera C H R I S T I Ecclesia particularis Visibilis? Ubi nos affirmantem tenemus, iis edocti Scripturarum testimoniis, quæ modò produximus: Negantem verò tueri student Jesuwitæ, iis potissimùm freti argumentis, quæ Bellarminus hoc ordine proponit: lib. 3. de Eccl. mil. cap. 13.

I. Argumentum sumit ex cap. 16, 18. Matthæi: Portæ inferorum non prævalebunt adversus Ecclesiam. Et 1. Tim. 3, 15. Ecclesia Dei vivi, est Columna & stabilimentum Veritatis.

Respondeo: Statum controversiæ malitiosè perverti, dùm Jesuwita ea Scripturæ testimonia, quæ ex professo agunt de Electorum Ecclesia invisibili, quippè quæ sola est fundata supra petram, & est columna ac stabilimentum veritatis; Sophisticè ad visibilem

Ecclesiam accommodat: quæ secundum externum etiam ministerium, ità à veritate deficit, ut non sit fundata super petram, neque columna Veritatis maneat: licèt interim adversus Ecclesiam invisibilem Electorum, portæ inferorum non prævaleant.

Alterum argumentum plura coacervat testimonia, in quibus continentur promissiones de conservatione Ecclesiæ, eò quòd Christus promiserit, se adfuturum pijs usque ad consumma tionem seculi, Matth. 28, 20. quòd dederit ideò Ecclesiæ pastores, Doctores, Apostolos &c. ad consummationem Sanctorum, Ephes. 4, 11. 12. 13. quòd Deus fundaverit eam in æternum Psal. 47, 7. quòd Deus fædus perpetuum inierit cum populo suo &c.

Sed respondeo hæc & similia dicta non plus confirmare, quàm Ecclesiam Dei nunquàm penitus in hoc mundo deficere; Quodipsum & nos concedimus. Siquidem nunquàm deficiet fides in toto, sed in quibusdam Ecclesiæ membris ea durabit usque ad finem seculi, licèt illi nobis non semper sint cogniti atque perspecti. Ab his verò ad reliquam Ecclesiæ multitudinem non valet Consequentia.

Neque enim sequitur: Ecclesia Electorum est perpetua neque unquàm deficiet. E. quælibet Ecclesia visibilis nunquàm deficiet. Deindè Christus in cœlos ascendens, promisit quidem Ephes. 4. perpetuum ministerij Ecclesiastici usum: sed non vel ad hanc, vel ad illam Ecclesiam sive cætum visibilem illud alligavit: verùm pro voluntatis suæ beneplacito dat pastores & Doctores, quos, quales, quando, & quomodo vult: ita ut fideles Doctores interdum non omnibus sint cogniti, neque in Ordinaria, aliqua & visibili Successione sint constituti: uti aliàs somniant Romanenses, sed lateant quasi absconditi.

Tertium argumentum desumit Jesuvvita ex parabolis illis, quibus Ecclesia comparatur areæ, in qua sunt grana & paleæ: reti, in quo sunt boni & mali pisces: agro, in quo sunt Zizania & triticum &c. Atqui res hæ notant Ecclesiam visibilem, & quidem ostendunt eam nunquàm interituram. E.

Respondeo scopas dissolutas nobis obijci. Ecquæ enim obsecro connexio est in hoc argumento. Ecclesia visibilis comparatur areæ, agro &c. Atqui area hæc permanebit ad diem usq; novißimum, ubi demum purgabic Christus aream suam, & segregabit triticum à paleis. E. Ecclesia visibilis nunquam deficiet. Nam hoc ipsum nos quoque ultrò largimur, quòd Ecclesia etiam visibilis nunquàm planè sit interitura. Sed hoc quæstionis est. An Ecclesia visibilis non ita interdùm persecutionem vi atq; tyrannide premi & obscuri poßit, ut vix ullam ejus formam videre aut cognoscere queas? Deindè an, quod de universa Ecclesia affirmat Scriptura, illud vel ad hanc vel ad illam particularem Ecclesiam statim torqueri & accommodari debeat: quemadmodum sanè Romanenses ad Romanam suam Ecclesiam, (quæ particularis est) falsò detorquent,

Catholicæ Ecclesiæ sunt propria. Certè cùm Servator ipse disertè affirmet, triticum à paleis, oves ab hædis, demùm in die novissimo segregari debere : utique satìs perspicuè innuit, talem esse Formam Ecclesiæ hisce in terris, ut nobis secundum discretam notitiam constare minimè possit, qui sint oves, qui hædi, qui triticum, qui paleæ: Imò ita pios & Electos latere asserit, ut si ab hominibus Zizania hoc in mundo eradicari deberent, facilè fieri posset, ut triticum simul evelleretur: quia nimirum verè Electi, nostrorum oculorum κειρὸν dijudicari, non possunt.

Quartum argumentum petit ex ijs Scripturæ locis, quibus Christo Regnum perpetuum promittitur.

Sed easdem Sophisticationes incurrit & hoc argumentum, quibus laborarunt præcedentia. Nam 1. probatur id, quod nos non negamus. 2. quod de interna gloria Regni Christi veriffimum est, ineptè accommodatur ad externam, visibilem & æqualiter semper florentem Ecclesiæ formam: quæ non est essentialis nota Veræ Ecclesiæ: 3. prophanum est, quod Jesuvvita Regnum Christi ex multitudine civium sive hominum, in unum locum congregatorum judicandum esse, suaviter delirat: quasi Spiritus Dei, usque adeò infirmus & impotens sit, ut non possit regnare in ijs, qui per totum terrarum orbem longè lateque sunt dispersi, & à nobis videri non possunt, quin in latebris interdum & cavernis occultati latirant. 4. probare debebat Jesuvvita, Ecclesiam visibilem semper pariter esse gloriosam, uti perpetuam: sed ipse probat nihil aliud, quàm semper in mundo fore Ecclesiam aliquam visibilem. Unde de Candore Disputatoris hujus judicium fieri potest.

Quintum argumentum mutuatur ab autoritate Patrum : quam tamen nobis non refragari, vel ex ijs patet, quæ supra ex Augustino & Hieronymo notavimus.

Sextum ac postremum argumentum petit Jesuvvita ex rationibus; quarum tres profert.

PRIMA est: Si aliquando sola Ecclesia invisibilis in mundo manet: impossibilis erit salus eorum, qui sunt extra Ecclesiam. Nam salvari non possunt, nisi in Ecclesiam ingrediantur: At in eam ingredi non possunt, si eam ignorant.

Respondeo committi Sophisma ἐπερώτησεως: dùm duæ diversissimæ quæstiones turpiter confunduntur. Aliud enim est, quando quæritur, An ita latere possit Ecclesia visibilis, ut omni prorsus careat forma aspectabili, ita ut in terris nulla amplius Ecclesia agnosci possit.

Aliud verò est, quando quæritur, An veræ Electorum Ecclesia, Formam suam visibilem semper æquabiliter exerat?

Prius illud nos nunquam affirmavim9, quòd videlicet ita Ecclesia interdù lateat, ut nulla prorsus amplius visibilis Ecclesiæ forma appareat.

Posterius hoc affirmamus intrepidè, quòd nimirùm Electorum Ecclesia, suam externam formam non semper ita exerat, ut per eam cognosci queat. Qui ergò Ecclesiæ se associare cupiunt, illi accedant visibilem vocatorum cœtum, ubi ubi etiam ille, & qualis qualis appareat, sive gloriosus, sive calamitosus. Nam uti externa gloria non est medium, per quod Spiritus Sanctus fidem operatur: ita misera & tristis illa Ecclesiæ facies, non potest remorari virtutem Spiritus Sancti.

Altera argumentatio Jesuitica sic sonat: De ratione unius veræ Ecclesiæ est, ut sit visibilis. E. si Ecclesia visibilis perit, nulla vera Ecclesia remanet.

Respondeo, Antecedens esse falsum: De ratione enim veræ Ecclesiæ est, non ut videatur, sed ut credatur esse, teste Symbolo Apostolico. 2. A visibilitate ad æquabilem ejus statum gloriosum, non datur processus. Esto: semper sit cœtus aliquis visibilis vocatorum: non tamen indè sequitur: Ergò uno eodemque modo & respectu ille est visibilis: quemadmodum non sequitur: Corpus solare est visibile. E. uno eodemque semper claritatis gradu est visibile. Distinguant ergò adversarij inter rem, & modum rei. Rem ipsam, hoc est, visibilitatem & gloriam Ecclesiæ non negamus: sed unum semper eundemque visibilitatis & gloriæ hujus esse modum ac gradum: illud iterum atque iterum negamus. Et profectò ne quidem de Ecclesia sua Romana probare possunt Adversarij, quod semper idem ejus fuerit status.

Tertia ratio talis est: Electi aut edunt fidei suæ professionem aut non edunt: Si edunt: utique Ecclesia semper est visibilis, quia semper editur confessio: Si non edunt: tum nulla est Ecclesia. Nam non est Ecclesia vera, in qua nulli sunt, qui edunt confessionem suam, & salvantur.

Respondeo priorem Dilemmatis hujus partem laborare turpi Sophismate Ignorationis Elenchi. Nam ut Ecclesia semper sit visibilis, non præstat confessio fidei, quæ certè in oculos nunquàm incurrit: sed ipsorum hominum conditio quæ est visibilis. Neque etiam requiritur, ut veri ac fideles Christi confessores, semper prodeant in conspectum Tyrannorum, & sese ultro periculis objiciant. Hoc enim nuspiam præcepit Deus. Quin suo exemplo diversum testati sunt Prophetæ, Christus & Apostoli, qui fugâ etiam arreptâ saluti suæ consuluerunt. Et quid respondebit Jesuitica de illis septem millibus, tempore impij Regis Achabi, quæ occultata erant, & ne quidem ab Elia Propheta conspici poterant. Anne hi confessionem fidei ediderunt, nec ne? Si affirmatè responderit: ostendat, quomodo tùm illorum Ecclesia fuerit visibilis. Sin negatè: tùm ex sententia Jesuitvitæ, fuerunt hæc septem millia damnata, propterea quòd fidei confessionem non ediderunt? Concludimus proindè Fidei confessionem edi posse ab Electis, licèt non omnibus illud innotescat: ac proindè non deficere hisce in terris Ecclesiam, licèt illorum confessio nobis sit invisibilis & ignota.

Excipit Bellarminus: Sic cavebit Ecclesia, Formâ visibili: Et quia hâc carebit, Ecclesia non ampliùs erit in mundo: Contradictionem enim implicat: Ecclesiam esse, & carere omni ad formâ visibili.

Respondeo committi Sophisma τῶ συμβεβηκότος. Non enim si sincero: sed si planè omni ministerio careret Ecclesia, tùm demùm formæ adspectabilis sive visibilis jacturam faceret. Jam verò forma illa visibilis Ecclesiæ, etiam quoad doctrinam corrupto Ministerio, ad tempus obtinere potest: sic docente ipso Christo, qui Scribas & Pharisæos, non tantùm in vitâ ac moribus flagitiosos: sed & erroribus fœdissimis imbutos, in Cathedra tamen Mosis sedere asserit. Exemplo esse potest in Veteri Testamento Ministerium diversis temporibus corruptissimum: In Novo verò Testamento, Ariana hæresis, quæ universum Orientem & Occidentem est pervagata, ipsum culmen Ecclesiastici ministerij ita occupavit, ut in eo nihil sanum, nihil integrum uspiam appareret. Hîc ergó latuisse quidem, sed non defecisse Ecclesiam affirmamus. Suffragatur nobis Hilarius, qui suo etiam seculo latentem Ecclesiam veram credebat potiùs, quàm videbat, cùm quibusdam Ecclesiæ formam visibilem, more Pontificio, sub Arianismo urgentibus, sic respondet, lib. contra Auxentium circa finem: Malè nos parietum amor cepit: malè Ecclesiam Dei in tectis ædificijsque veneramini: malè sub his Pacis nomen ingeritis: anne ambiguum est, in ijs Antichristum esse sessurum? Montes mihi & sylvæ, & lacus, & carceres, & voragines sunt tutiores. In his enim Prophetæ aut manentes aut demersi etiam prophetabant. Suffragatur Athanasius, qui Ecclesiam in piè fidelibus, Prophetarum more, aliorumque Episcoporum exemplo in desertis oberrantibus, in sylvis, speluncis, cisternis, terræq; cavernis, quæreie non dubitavit. Sed & illud observandum, multoties in una Orbis parte latere Ecclesiam veram, quæ tamen in alia parte maximè floreat, quemadmodum superioribus seculis in Occidente sub Papatu latuit Ecclesia vera, quæ tamen in Oriente tùm floruit: uti paulò post ostendemus. Alioquin extra persecutionis statum, Ecclesiam esse Civitatem supra montem positam, quæ abscondi non possit: esse lucernam, non sub modio sed sub candelabro positam, facilè concedimus.
