Seventhly: Eugenius IV, who presided over the Roman seat, was not only deposed from the papacy by the Council of Basel in the year of our Lord 1430, but was also convicted and condemned with his entire sect of schism and heresy.

Eighthly, this papal succession receives heretics, indeed downright Epicureans, in doctrine; and in morals, wicked men. Liberius was an Arian: Honorius was a Eunomian: Anastasius followed the heresy of the Photinians: Marcellinus sacrificed to idols: John XXII denied the immortality of the soul, and was therefore struck with an anathema by the theologians of Paris: and so on.

Ninthly and lastly I argue thus: Of a non-entity there are no qualities. But in the Roman Church there are absolutely no Bishops. Therefore, neither is there any succession of Bishops there. I prove the minor premise thus. Every true Bishop of the Church, according to Apostolic ordination, ought 1. to hold the form of sound doctrine. 2. to be διδακτικὸς, 3. the husband of one wife. 4. Powerful to refute adversaries. But these κριτήρια do not belong to the Bishops of the Romanists any more than a lyre to a Cuman ass. Therefore, the title of Bishop does not rightly belong to them either. For to whom the definition does not apply, to him the defined does not apply either.

Latin:

AD propositam hanc Quæstionem, simpliciter negare respondemus, ob sequentes rationes, longè evidentissimas.

Nam 1. caret hæc fictitia Romanorum Episcoporum successio, suo capite, quod volunt esse Petrum Apostolum. De hoc enim incertum est, An Romam unquàm pervenerit: incertius an ibi 25. annis manserit: incertissimum quòd Episcopum ibi egerit. Jam quia ex Sacris citra omnem dubitationem constat, Petrum multis annis præfuisse Ecclesiæ Antiochenæ: consequens fuerit, Successionem Episcoporum Ordinariam dummodò à Petro tanquam capite dependeat, ad Antiochenam Ecclesiam, non verò ad Romanam esse adstrictam: & per consequens, non Romam, sed Antiochiam, esse successionis Apostolicæ sedem propriam. Vel si hoc largiri nolint Jesuuvitæ, fateantur necesse est, duas diversas esse sedes Apostolicas, ac proindè geminam etiam ordinariam Episcoporum successionem. Quo concesso, corruit statim tota structura figmenti hujus, de Una sede Apostolica, deque una, indè emanante perpetua Episcoporum successione.

Deindè successio hæc Pontificia multoties fuit interrupta. Anno certè Domini 1045. tres fuerunt Papæ, vel potiùs Antipapæ simul, qui omnes uno eodemque tempore sellam Pontificalem affectabant, imò occupabant, nempè Benedictus VI. Sylvester III. & Gregorius VI. qui singuli plures ordinaverunt Episcopos, à quibus alij rursus sunt creati.

Tertiò, hi tres Antipapæ postmodùm tetro quodam excitato Schismate, omnes à Synodo fuêre damnati, & de sede Pontificali dejecti: in Pontificem electo Præsule Bambergensi, Clemente II.

Quartò, Papalis sella aliquoties ad biennium vacua fuit: teste Platina & Volaterrano.

Quintò, Sedem Pontificalem tenuit infame quoddam Scortum, Papissa meretricula, quæ Johannis I I X. nomen ementita fuerat. Sic ergò Episcoporum Romanensium successio, in suum ordinem cooptat fœminas meretrices, fortassis exemplo Christi in gratiam recipientis peccatricem Mariam Magdalenam, & mulierem & adulteram, Iohan. 8, 11.

Sextò: Loco suo mota fuit Sedes papalis, & ex Italia in Galliam migravit, ibidemque ultra annos septuaginta commorata.

Septimo: Eugenius IV. qui sedi Romanæ præfuit, à Concilio Basiliensi, Anno D. 1430. non modò à Pontificatu fuit abdicatus: sed cum universâ suâ Sectâ Schismatis atque hæresews convictus & damnatus.

Octavò, Successio hæc Pontificia recipit etiam tùm in doctrina hæreticos, imò planè Epicuræos; tùm in moribus sceleratos. Liberius fuit Arianus : Honorius fuit Eunomianus : Anastasius secutus est hæresin Photinianorum: Marcellinus sacrificavit Idolis : Johannes XXII. negavit immortalitatem animæ,ac ideò à Theologis Parisiensibus anathemate percussus: & sic deinceps.

Nonò & postremò sic arguo: Non entis nullæ sunt qualitates. Atqui in Romana Ecclesia nulli prorsus sunt Episcopi. E. neque ulla ibi est Episcoporum successio. Minorem sic probo. Omnis verus Ecclesiæ Episcopus, secundum ordinationem Apostolicam, debet 1. tenere formam sanæ doctrinæ. 2. esse διδακτικὸς, 3. Unius uxoris maritus. 4. Potens ad refutandum adversarios. Atqui Episcopis Romanensium haud magis κριτήρια hæc competunt, atque lyra asino Cumano. Ergò neque ipsis Episcopi titulus jure competit. Cui enim non competit definitio, eidem nec definitum.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: Jesuitical Solution

JESUITICAL Solution.

The Jesuits fashion and paint such a face of the true Church, which is not only always like itself, but in which there can also be shown an ordinary and never-interrupted succession of Bishops: and they contend that this is a proper and Essential mark of the True Church: as is evident from book 4, chapter 8 of Bellarmine on the Marks of the Church. They fight, however, chiefly with these arguments.

The first and principal one is that which they take from the authority of Irenaeus, Tertullian, Epiphanius, Augustine, and others, who very frequently in their writings against heretics appealed to the ordinary succession of Bishops. But I answer 1. that a gross ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχy is committed, and a sophistical treatment of a non-cause as a cause. For the cause or occasion by which the Fathers were led to appeal to the ordinary succession of Bishops must be diligently noted. For they had business and controversy with wicked and cunning heretics, who partly brought monstrous and prodigious errors onto the stage, and boasted speciously that they had been revealed to them by God: as the Montanists were accustomed to do above all: and partly, according to their own pleasure and whim, received some books of Apostolic Scripture and rejected others. In this case, therefore, the Orthodox Fathers rightly appealed to those Churches in which there was then an ordinary succession of Bishops, derived from the Apostles themselves. For in this way they showed to the eye the very original copies, or ἀυτόγραφα of the Holy Apostles: and they thought they were rendering it testified that those writings were consigned by no one but the Apostles themselves through a continuous tradition of hands. But now, since by the grace of God the Canon of Biblical writings has been established, and there is no danger that new books will be foisted upon the Church under the authority of the Apostles: the example of the Holy Fathers is surely in this part objected against us. What of the fact that at that time this appeal was easy and possible, since there were still among the living those who were partly hearers of the Apostles themselves; and partly indeed preserved the doctrine of the Apostles uncorrupted. Since neither of these can be affirmed of the Bishops devastating the Church under the Roman Antichrist, the Jesuits in vain continue to trouble us with this argument. Then, a distinction must be made between true or principal succession, which is the Truth of doctrine, and the less principal or secondary, which is of persons and places. To the former, therefore, the Fathers appealed, not to this latter, whenever a controversy arose concerning the heads of the Christian Religion. Now, however, from that former to this latter, the consequence does not hold. Thus Irenaeus, book 4, against heresies, chapters 43 and 44. It is necessary, he says, to obey those Presbyters who are in the Church, those who have succession from the Apostles, who with the succession of the Episcopate have received the certain charisma of Truth, according to the good pleasure of God the Father. And after a few words: It is necessary to adhere to those who guard the doctrine of the Apostles.

Thus Tertullian, challenging heretics to demonstrate their origin by the example of the Orthodox through the succession of Bishops from the Apostles: Let the heretics, he says, invent something of the sort: For what is illicit for them after blasphemy? But even if they have invented it, they will accomplish nothing: For their very doctrine, when compared with the Apostolic, will declare by its diversity and contrariety that it is not of any Apostolic author, nor of an Apostolic man. Book on prescription against heretics.

Thus Augustine, who most often opposed legitimate succession to both the Manichaeans and the Donatists, openly protests that he is speaking of that Church which constantly retains the purity of Doctrine received from the Apostles. Whence he writes explicitly: Let us seek the Church in the Holy Scriptures. Book on the Unity of the Church, chapter 3. And afterwards, chapter 10, he says, Let no one tell me what Donatus or Parmenianus said, because one must not agree even with Catholic Bishops if they are deceived anywhere, so that they think something contrary to the canonical Scriptures.

Thus Chrysostom, homily 49 on Matthew. When you see the impious heresy, which is the army of Antichrist, standing in the holy places of the Church, then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains: that is, those who are in Christendom, let them betake themselves to the Scriptures: because from the time that heresy obtained those Churches, there can be no proof of true Christianity, nor any other refuge for Christians wishing to know the Truth of the faith, except the divine Scripture.

The second argument is such: The true Church cannot be without Pastors and Bishops: so that it is not a Church which does not have Priests. Therefore, there is a perpetual succession of Bishops.

I answer that the Antecedent is true κατ' ἄλλο: for a twofold possibility is given: one of right, the other of fact. If you look at the possibility of right, certainly the Church cannot be without Pastors and Bishops. For divine Law commands otherwise: which wills that there should always be Pastors in the Church. But from the possibility of Right to the possibility of fact, the consequence does not hold. For it very often happens that they are removed either by death, or are not appointed over Churches through the carelessness or sloth of patrons: or because of the cruelty of tyrants, Pastors cannot be appointed over Churches. In these cases, therefore, the Church is in fact without pastors, which by divine right should never be without them. Then a distinction must be made between a free Church using its own right, which always has its own Pastors: and a Church pressed by Tyranny, which sometimes has clearly none, and sometimes has Pastors and Bishops who are wicked both in life and in doctrine: which is better known to have happened under the Papacy than it needs to be demonstrated. Where, however, we have shown above that the true Church nevertheless remained.

The third argument sounds thus: Christ chose twelve Apostles: the Apostles chose and ordained Bishops, and gave these the power of ordaining others in turn: and so on. Therefore, there are no true Pastors and Bishops except those who, ordained by Bishops, legitimately succeed the Apostles.

I answer that more is inferred in the consequent than the Antecedent permits. For this only follows: Therefore some legitimate succession of Bishops is necessary. But what the Jesuit infers, that this legitimate succession is that which is restricted both to the city of Rome and to the Bishops of the Romans: that does not follow from the Antecedent in the least. Since it is certain that both the city of Rome and the Roman Bishops have degenerated greatly from the true and legitimate Apostolic succession, and have defected to the Antichrist. Then, the Truth of doctrine does not depend on the act of ordination itself, as if from an opus operatum, as the Romanists dream. Judas was called to the Apostleship by Christ himself: but he defected from Christ, having become a son of sin and Satan. Thus it could happen, and indeed truly happened, that those ordained by Orthodox Bishops, having later fallen into errors, have shamefully lost their legitimate Apostolic succession. Whoever, therefore, hold the Truth of Apostolic doctrine: they enjoy legitimate Apostolic succession, wherever and by whomever they may have been ordained.

The Jesuit Bellarmine objects that for a true ordination it is required that he who is a Bishop be ordained by three Bishops, who themselves are also ordained by others, and those by others, until one comes to the Apostles. But this does not apply to Lutheran pastors. Therefore, they are not in the legitimate Apostolic succession.

I reply to the Major premise, that it rests upon no principle of the Holy Scriptures, but only upon human tradition. 2. That custom of ordaining Bishops could have been retained in a free and flourishing Church: not likewise in an oppressed Church. 3. Nor was this custom always observed in the Church in such a way, Bellarmine himself being witness. 4. The argument itself concludes nothing: For it does not follow: that man is a Bishop ordained by three others, who themselves were also ordained by three others, until one arrives at the Apostles, therefore that Bishop, who was so ordained, is a true Bishop, and enjoys an ordinary Apostolic succession. Otherwise, indeed, Arian Bishops throughout Greece and Asia would have been true Bishops, and in the Apostolic succession, since they succeeded those who had been ordained by the Apostles through continuous succession and ordination. Finally, we do not delay over the canons which the Jesuit produces, as well as the Decretals and the Epistles of Anacletus, since they were forged by the Roman Pontiffs themselves for the protection of their own cause. The Jesuit presses further, bringing forward the words of the Apostle from 1 Timothy 4:14: 'Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.' For (Bellarmino writes) by the name of presbytery he understands the assembly of bishops, who together with the ordainer laid hands upon the head of the one being ordained.

I answer: The Jesuit's gloss is false. For a comparison of Scripture clearly demonstrates that by presbyters in this place, bishops cannot be understood. For Scripture acknowledges several presbyters of one church, as of the Ephesian church, Acts 20:17. Now, it is indeed absurd to constitute several bishops for one church, such as the Jesuit understands in this place. Furthermore, the Apostle protests when he commands Titus to constitute presbyters town by town: that is, ministers, pastors, and teachers of the church. This having been demonstrated, the Jesuit's inference collapses, by which he derogates the title of legitimate apostolic succession from blessed Luther and the remaining Lutheran doctors, because they were not ordained by the bishops of the Romanists: such an ordination, certainly, Timothy had never even received. Add that the Apostle deals with such presbyters who were subject to Timothy's inspection and were his fellow workers in the Word. Whence, toward the end of the same chapter, the Apostle shows that he is dealing with those presbyters who rule well and labor in the Word, and for whom Timothy ought to provide their stipends, and against whom he ought not easily admit an accusation: all of which in no way applies to bishops, such as the Jesuit imagines for himself in this place. For neither do such men constitute them town by town, nor do several rule the same church at once, nor does one receive a salary from another, much less is one subject to the jurisdiction of another, as the Jesuits themselves contend elsewhere. Therefore, the Lutheran ministers or pastors are legitimately ordained, although Luther himself, who ordained them, was not a bishop but only a presbyter.

Latin:

Αυσις JESUVITICA.

Jesuvitæ talem Ecclesiæ veræ faciem fingunt & pingunt, quæ non modò sibi semper sit similis, sed in qua monstrari possit etiam ordinaria & nunquàm interrupta Episcoporum successio: & hanc contendunt esse propriam atq; Essentialem Veræ Ecclesiæ notam: uti patet ex libro 4. cap. 8. Bellarmini de Notis Ecclesiæ. Argumentis autem præcipuè pugnant istis.

Primum & principale est, quod desumunt ab autoritate Irenæi, Tertulliani, Epiphanij, Augustini & aliorum, qui frequenter admodum in suis adversus hæreticos scriptionibus ad ordinariam Episcoporum Successionem provocarunt. Sed respondeo 1. crassam committi ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχy, & Sophisticationem non causæ ut causæ. Diligenter enim notanda causa sive occasio, quâ adducti Patres ad ordinariam Episcoporum successionem & provocarent. Erat autem illis negocium & controversia, cum improbis & callidis hæreticis, qui partim monstrosos & prodigiosos errores in theatrum proferebant, eosque divinitiùs sibi revelatos esse, speciosè gloriabantur: uti cum primis Montanistæ consueverant: partim verò pro suo libitu & arbitrio, quosdam Scripturæ Apostolicæ libros recipiebant, quosdam repudiabant. In hoc igitur casu Patres Orthodoxi meritò provocabant ad eas Ecclesias, in quibus ordinaria tùm erat Episcoporum Successio, jam indè ab Apostolis deducta. Hoc enim pacto ad oculum monstrabant ipsa originalia Exemplaria, sive ἀυτόγραφα Sanctorum Apostolorum: & testatum putabant reddere, scripta illa per continuam manuum traditionem, non nisi ab Apostolis ipsis esse confignata. Jam verò cum Dei beneficio Canon Scriptorum Biblicorum sit constitutus, neque periculum sit, ut novi libri sub Apostolorum autoritate obtrudantur Ecclesiæ: frustra utique S. Patrum exemplum hac in parte nobis objicitur. Quid quòd illo tempore Provocatio hæc facilis erat & possibilis, Siquidem in vivis adhuc erant, qui partim ipsorum Apostolorum fuerunt Auditores; partim verò Apostolorū doctrinam incorruptam conservarunt. Quod utrumq; cum de Episcopis sub Antichristo Romano Ecclesiam devastantibus affirmari nequeat, frustra utique nobis hoc argumento molesti esse pergunt Jesuitæ. Deindè distinguendum inter Successionem veram sive principalem, quæ est Veritas doctrinæ, & minùs principalem sive secundariam, quæ est personarum & locorum. Ad priorem ergò illam provocarunt Patres, non ad posteriorem hanc, quoties de Religionis Christianæ capitibus incidebat controversia. Jam verò à priore illâ ad posteriorem hanc non valet Consequentia. Sic Irenæus lib. 4. contra hæreses. cap. 43. & 44. Oportet, inquit, eis qui in Ecclesia sunt Presbyteris obedire, his qui successionem habent ab Apostolis, qui cum Episcopatus successione, charisma Veritatis certum, secundū placitum Dei Patris acceperunt. Et post pauca: Adhærere oportet his, qui Apostolorum doctrinam custodiunt.

Sic Tertullianus hæreticos provocans, ut Orthodoxorum exemplo Originem suam, per Episcoporum inde ab Apostolis successionem demonstrent: Confingant, inquit, tale quid hæretici: Quid enim illis post blasphemiam illicitum? Sed etsi confinxerint nihil promovebunt: Ipsa enim doctrina eorum cum Apostolica comparata ex diversitate & contrarietate sua pronunciabit, non esse Apostoli alicujus autoris, neq; Apostolici. lib. de præscr. adversus hæreticos.

Sic Augustinus, qui & Manichæis & Donatistis Successionem legitimam sæpissimè opposuit, apertè protestatur, sed de ea Ecclesia loqui, quæ Doctrinæ puritatem ab Apostolis acceptam cōstanter retineat. Undè disertè scribit: In Scripturis Sanctis Ecclesiam requiramus. l. de Vnit. Eccl. c.3 Et postea cap. 10. inquit, Nemo mihi dicat, quid dixerit Donatus, aut Parmenianus, quia nec Catholicis Episcopis consentiendum, sicubi falluntur, ut contra canonicas Scripturas aliquid sentiant.

Sic Chrysostomus homil. 49. in Matth. Cùm videritis hæresin impiam, quæ est exercitus Antichristi, stantem in locis sanctis Ecclesiæ, tunc, qui in Judæa sunt fugiant ad montes: id est, qui sunt in Christianitate, conferant se ad Scripturas: quia ex quo Ecclésias illas hæresis obtinuit, nulla probatio esse potest veræ Christianitatis, neq; refugium Christianorum aliud volentium cognoscere fidei Veritatem, nisi Scriptura divina.

Alterum argumentum tale est: Ecclesia vera non potest esse sine Pastoribus & Episcopis: ita ut Ecclesia non sit, quæ non habeat Sacerdotes. Ergò datur perpetua Episcoporum successio.

Respondeo, Antecedens verum esse κατ' ἄλλο: Gemina enim datur possibilitas: Vna juris: altera Facti. Si possibilitatem juris spectes, certè Ecclesia non potest esse sine Pastoribus & Episcopis. Diversum enim præcipit Jus divinum: quod vult ut semper in Ecclesia sint Pastores. Cæterùm à possibilitate Juris ad possibilitatem facti non valet consequentia. Sæpissimè enim accidit, ut vel morte tollantur, vel patronorum incuriâ sive ignaviâ Ecclesiis non præficiantur: vel ob tyrannorum crudelitatem Ecclesiis Pastores præfici non possint. His ergò casibus ut Ecclesia ipso facto sit sine pastoribus, quæ jure divino nunquàm sine illis esse deberet. Deindè distinguendum est inter Ecclesiam liberam & suo jure utentem, quæ semper suos habet Pastores : & inter Ecclesiam Tyrannide pressam, quæ interdum planè nullos, interdum verò quà vitam, quà doctrinam flagitiosos Pastores & Episcopos habet : id quod sub Papatu evenisse notius est, quàm ut demonstrari debeat. Vbi tamen nihilominùs veram mansisse Ecclesiam supra oftendimus.

Tertium argumentum sic sonat: Christus elegit duodecim Apostolos : Apostoli elegerunt atg, ordinarunt Episcopos, & his alios deinceps ordinandi potestatem dederunt: & sic deinceps. Ergò nulli veri sunt Pastores & Episcopi, nisi qui per Episcopos ordinati, Apostolis legitimè succedunt.

Respondeo, plus inferri in consequente, quàm permittat Antecedens. Hoc enimtantùm sequitur : Ergò neceffaria est legitima aliqua successio Episcoporum. Sed quod infert Jesuvvita, legitimam hanc successionem esse illam, quæ sit adstricta tùm ad urbem Romam, tùm ad Romanensium Episcopos : illud ex Antecedente minimè sequitur. Siquidem constat tùm urbem Romam, tùm Romanos Episcopos, à vera ac legitima successione Apostolica plurimùm degenerasse, & ad Antichristum defecisse. Deindè Veritas doctrinæ non pendet ab ipso ordinationis actu, tanquàm ab opere operato, uti somniant Romanenses. Judas ab ipso Christo ad Apostolatum erat vocatus : sed defecit à Christo, factus filius peccati & Satanæ. Sic fieri potuit, imò verè factum, ut ab Orthodoxis Episcopis ordinati, in errores verò postmodùm prolapsi successione legitimâ Apostolicâ turpiter exciderint. Quicunq, ergò Veritatem doctrinæ Apostolicæ tenent : illi gaudent legitimâ successione Apostolica, ubicunqs & à quocunq; etiam sint ordinati.

Excipit Jesuvvita Bellarminus, ad veram ordinationem requiri, ut qui sit Episcopus, ordinetur à tribus Episcopis, qui & ipsi sint ab aliis ordinati, & illi ab aliis, donec ad Apostolos veniatur. Atqui hoc non competit Lutheranis pastoribus. E. illi non sunt in legitima successione Apostolica.

Respondeo ad Majorem, illam nullo Sacrarum literarum principio, sed tantùm humana traditione niti. 2. Consuetudinem illam ordinandi Episcopos retineri potuisse in Ecclesia libera ac florente : non itidem in Ecclesia pressa. 3. Neque hanc consuetudinem sic semper in Ecclesia fuisse observatam, teste Bellarmino ipso. 4. Argumentum ipsum nihil concludit : Neque enim sequitur : ille Episcopus est ordinatus à tribus aliis, qui & ipsi ab aliis tribus sunt ordinati, donec ad Apostolos perveniatur, E. Episcopus ille, qui sic ordinatus fuit, est verus Episcopus, & gaudet ordinaria successione Apostolica. Alioquin n. Ariani Episcopi per Græciam &, Asiam veri fuissent Episcopi, inq; successione Apostolica, quoniam ijs succedebant, qui ab Apostolis per continuam successionem, & ordinationem ordinati fuerant. Tandẽ, canones quos producit Jesuvvita, ut & Decretales, & Anacleti Epistolas, nó moramur : quippè ab ipsis Pontificib9 Romanis in causæ sua præsidium confictas. Amplius instat Jesuvvita, proferens verba Apostoli ex 1. Tim. 4, 14. Noli negligere gratiam, quæ in te est, quæ data est tibi cum impositione : manuum presbyterij. Nam (scribit Bellarminus) nomine Presbyterij intelligit cœtum Episcoporum, qui simul cum ordinante imponebant manus super caput ordinandi.

Respondeo : Glossam Jesuvvitæ esse falsam. Per Presbyteros enim hoc loco non posse intelligi Episcopos, collatio Scripturæ evidenter demonstrat. Scriptura enim plures unius Ecclesiæ Presbyteros agnoscit, ut Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ, Actor. 20, 17. Jam verò absonum est, Unius Ecclesiæ plures Episcopos constituere, quales quidem hoc loco intelligit Jesuvvita. Deindè reclamat Apostolus, quando præcipit Tito, ut oppidatim constituat Presbyteros: hoc est, Ministros, Pastores & Doctores Ecclesiæ. Quo sic demonstrato corruit Jesuvitæ illatio, qua B. Luthero & reliquis Lutheranis Doctoribus, Legitimæ successionis Apostolicæ elogium, ideo derogat, quia non sint ab Episcopis Romanensium ordinati : Qualem certè Ordinationem ne quidem Timotheus unquàm acceperat : Adde quòd de ejusmodi Presbyteris agit Apostolus, qui Timothei inspectioni erant subjecti : ejusdemque σύνεργοι in Verbo. Undè sub finem ejusdem capitis, se de illis Presbyteris agere ostendit Apostolus, qui benè præsint, & laborent in Verbo, & quibus stipendia sua curare debebat Timotheus, & adversus quos haud facilè accusationem admittere debeat: Quæ omnia in Episcopos, quales Jesuvvita hoc loco sibi imaginatur, minimè cadunt. Neque enim tales oppidatim constituunt: neque plures simul eidem Ecclesiæ præsunt: neque unus ab altero accipit Salarium: nedùm unus alterius Jurisdictioni subjacet: uti aliâs ipsi contendunt Jesuvvitæ. Sunt ergò Ministri sive Pastores Lutherani legitimè ordinati, licèt Lutherus ipse, qui eos ordinavit, non Episcopus, sed Presbyter tantùm fuerit.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: Jesuitical Solution (continued)

The Jesuit continues, and thus impugns the vocation and ordination both of blessed Luther and of others who defected from the Papacy: 'Lutherans have neither ordination nor succession. Therefore, much more impudently than any other heretics ever, they usurp for themselves the name and office of bishop.' He proves the antecedent thus: 'The church cannot be without bishops, as we have shown. Among the Lutherans there are no bishops, for they have neither ordination nor succession from the Apostles. Therefore, among them there is no church.' And indeed, that neither Luther nor other doctors who defected from the Papacy were ordained by three bishops, nor by dispensation by one with abbots assisting, is most well-known, nor do they themselves deny it: therefore they are not or were not bishops.

I answer that the proof of the antecedent consists of mere vanities and begging the question. For first, what he asserts, that the church cannot be without bishops, is highly equivocal. Where, if by the title and description of bishop he understands such a one who has given his name to the Roman Pontiff, who has sworn to his decrees, who is destitute of all those apostolic marks with which a true bishop of the church ought to be adorned: that is, who is not the husband of one wife, not apt to teach, nay, who performs no part of ecclesiastical ministry at all, but who lives in impure celibacy, who lords it like princes, who exercises not only ecclesiastical but also political jurisdiction over many provinces, who neither preaches nor baptizes, nor administers the Sacrament, but in the church prepares chrism, and distributes it like the mark of the beast partly on the forehead, partly on the hand to those being ordained and confirmed, but outside the church leads a courtly life: if, I say, he understands such a one by the title of bishop, then it is most false that the Jesuit affirms, that the church cannot be without bishops. For such bishops were unknown to Peter and Paul, unknown to all the Apostles, unknown to the entire primitive church, unknown to Christ and His holy Spirit. Furthermore, such bishops are not what they wish to be and appear, true bishops, but are masks of Satan and the Roman Antichrist. For to whomever the apostolic definition of a true bishop does not apply, the defined does not apply to him either. But the apostolic definition of a bishop, such as indeed exists in the Pauline epistles to Timothy and Titus, does not apply to the bishops of the Romanists. Therefore, they are not true bishops, but masks of bishops and slaves of Satan and the Antichrist.

However, if in the proof of the antecedent we understand by bishops the pastors and teachers of the church who teach the Word of God and administer the Sacraments, then we willingly concede that the church cannot be without such bishops. Where, however, it is to be noted that these bishops and their ministry are sometimes most corrupt, as we showed above in the disputation concerning the hidden church. Such a ministry existed even under the densest Papacy, and thus the church even then was not without bishops, that is, priests who administered the entire Sacrament of Baptism, although their ministry was most defiled by many horrible errors.

Furthermore, it is false and trifling what the Jesuit adds in the proof of the antecedent: 'Among the Lutherans there are no bishops, because they have neither ordination nor succession from the Apostles, and consequently among them there is also no church.' For although we freely confess that the Lutherans have neither Pontifical bishops nor Pontifical ordination and succession, it does not therefore follow that they are destitute of either true bishops or apostolic ordination or succession. For they have true teachers of the divine Word and dispensers of the Sacraments, to whom, according to the apostolic definition of a bishop, it is certain that the definition of a bishop truly and properly belongs, in preference to those mitred slaves of the Antichrist. Then the Lutherans have apostolic ordination, and they retain it as a salutary ceremony, which consists of the laying on of the hands of the presbytery, that is, of those who rule the church both by teaching and by governing. Finally, they have a true and legitimate apostolic succession, which is not restricted to a certain place, nor to a certain and never-interrupted order of Bishops succeeding one another: but is restricted to conformity of Doctrine; as was shown above. But (Bellarmino objects) neither Luther, nor other Lutheran Theologians were ordained by three Bishops, nor by dispensation by one, with Abbots assisting. I reply that this was not necessary either: For just as the Ministry itself with all its parts is highly necessary: and indeed a right and legitimate Vocation, which is made by the voice of the Church, is likewise highly necessary for a Minister: being commanded by divine precept: so Papal Orders are not necessary, as they are neither of divine command, nor of Apostolic tradition: Ambrose also supporting this, on the 4th chapter to the Ephesians. Thus that Ordination of a Presbyter by a Bishop, and of a Bishop by two or three Bishops, although perhaps it was introduced at first with good counsel, was nevertheless by no means a divine precept, but a free custom, which could be changed, and still can be, according to the diversity of the condition of the Churches, especially if a case of necessity arises: such as was the case in the time of Blessed Luther, when all the Papal Bishops had degenerated into most rapacious wolves, and tyrants or persecutors of the true Church. In such a state, therefore, if the Church is destitute of a faithful and Orthodox Pastor, nothing prevents the whole flock of the faithful from consenting to a certain person as their Minister, who is fit for teaching, and from calling and choosing him as their Minister, while the service of either a Presbyter or a Bishop, from whom he might receive Ordination, cannot be had. Such a Minister, thus named and Elected by the voice of the Church, is undoubtedly a true Pastor of the Church, who has a legitimate vocation, and can duly perform all the duties of his office. And let the Jesuit answer whether he can show any other ordination in the Apostleship of Matthias, besides vocation and election. But if at that time this Vocation and Election were sufficient for Apostolic ordination, with the prayers of the Church added, so that not even the laying on of hands is read to have been used, and much less did Episcopal anointing, or chrism, or tonsure, or insufflation occur: why would such a legitimate Vocation and Election of the Church not be equally sufficient for the ordination of Luther and the Lutheran Theologians? Thus Paul and Barnabas in Acts 13 were sent out to preach to the Gentiles without all those Papal rites. And indeed hands are read to have been laid upon them, but not so that they might be ordained anew, who had been ordained from heaven before: but so that by this rite the disciples might pray for good fortune for them. To this can most rightly be accommodated that Apostolic saying, 1 Tim. 4:14: Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy, with the laying on of hands, by the authority of the PRESBYTERY: or rather, as the Greek text has it: μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τῶ πρεσβυτερίε: with the laying on of the hands of the Presbytery: Therefore Timothy was ordained to the ministry of the Church not by Paul alone, but also by the Presbytery. Nothing therefore is lacking to the ordination of the Lutheran Theologians, although Luther, from whom they received their ordination, was not

a Bishop, but only a Presbyter. What? Since Scripture teaches that all those who teach the Gospel of Christ come under the name of Bishops, although they are called Bishops κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of excellence) in a special signification, to whom inspection over other Pastors is entrusted. This is evident primarily from 1 Tim. 3: If anyone desires the Episcopate, he desires a good work. Where the whole context of the text clearly proves that the office of ecclesiastical teaching is defined by the Apostle in general as the Episcopate. From which it follows that Presbyters also come under the census and number of Bishops in this place according to the Apostle. For if you exclude Presbyters from the name of Bishop, it is not without reason asked, since he indeed recounts the marks and properties of Bishops, and likewise of Deacons, and expressly instructs what kind of men both ought to be in office, how and why the Apostle could or would want to forget the Presbyters, the intermediate order? and why the same Apostle, writing to the Philippians, prays for greetings for the Bishops and Deacons, but is completely forgetful of the Presbyters, if he has not also included them under the title of Bishops? Certainly the Romanists themselves today fight tooth and nail that Peter was a Bishop: And yet he calls himself a Presbyter. From which single passage, that fictitious distinction which the Papists invent between Bishops and Presbyters can be refuted of vanity. D. Jerome also supports us, arguing thus learnedly in his Epistle to Titus:

"A bishop must be without crime, as the steward of God. The Presbyter is therefore the SAME as the Bishop: and before, by the instinct of the Devil, schisms were made in religion, and it was said among the people: I am of Paul, I of Apollo, but I of Cephas, the Churches were governed by the common counsel of the Presbyters. But after each one thought that those whom he had baptized were his own, not Christ's, it was decreed in the whole world that one chosen from the Presbyters should be set over the others, to whom the whole care of the Church should pertain, and the seeds of schisms might be removed. If anyone thinks that it is our opinion, and not that of the Scriptures, that a Bishop and a Presbyter are one, and that one is a name of age, the other of office: let him reread the words of the Apostle to the Philippians saying: Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the Saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the Bishops and Deacons: Grace to you and peace etc." Philippi is one city of Macedonia, and certainly in one city there could not be more (as they are called) Bishops, but because they called the SAME BISHOPS at that time, WHOM THEY ALSO CALLED PRESBYTERS, for that reason he spoke indifferently of Bishops as if of Presbyters. To some this still seems ambiguous, unless it is proven by another testimony. In the Acts of the Apostles it is written that when the Apostle had come to Miletus, he sent to Ephesus, and called the PRESBYTERS of that same Church: to whom afterwards among other things he spoke: Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you BISHOPS, to feed the Church of GOD, which he has acquired by his own blood. And here observe more diligently how, calling the Presbyters of the one city of Ephesus, he afterwards called the same ones Bishops. And a little later, the same Jerome. Just as therefore Presbyters know that they are subject by the custom of the Church to him who has been set over them: So let Bishops know that they are greater by custom than by the truth of the Lord's disposition than Presby-

Latin:

Pergit Jesuvvita, & tum B. Lutheri, tum aliorum, qui à Papatu defecerunt, vocationem & ordinationem sic impugnat: Lutherani neque ordinationem, neq; successionem habent. E. longè invercundius, quàm ulli unquam hæretici alij, sibi nomen & munus Episcopi usurpant. Antecedens sic probat: Ecclesia non potest esse sine Episcopis, ut ostendimus. Apud Lutheranos non sunt Episcopi, nam non habent ordinationem, nec successionem ab Apostolis. E. apud eos non est Ecclesia. Et quidem quod nec Lutherus, nec alij, qui à Papatu defecerunt Doctores, ordinati sint à tribus Episcopis, neq; ex dispensatione ab uno assistentibus Abbatibus, notissimum est, nec ipsi negant: Ergò non sunt aut fuerunt Episcopi.

Respondeo Antecedentis probationem meris constare vanitatibus & principij petitionibus. Primùm enim valdè æquivocum est, quod asserit, Ecclesiam non posse esse sine Episcopis. Ubi si Episcopi titulo & elogio intelligit talé, qui Pontifici Romano nomina sua dedit: qui in hujus placita juravit, qui destituitur omnibus illis notis Apostolicis, quibus verus Ecclesiæ Episcopus insignitus esse debet: hoc est; qui non unius uxoris est maritus, non aptus ad docendum, imò qui nullam prorsus ministerij Ecclesiastici partem obit: sed qui in impuro cœlibatu vivit, qui principum more dominatur, qui non Ecclesiasticam duntaxat, sed & politicam exercet jurisdictionem in multas provincias, qui nec concionatur nec baptizat, nec Sacramentum administrat: sed in Ecclesia conficit Chrisma, illudque tanquam characterem bestiæ partim in fronte, partim in manu ordinandis & confirmandis tribuit: Extra Ecclesiam verò aulicam agit vitam: Si inquam Episcopi titulò talem intelligit, tùm falsissimum est, quod Jesuvvita affirmat, ecclesiam non posse esse sine Episcopis. Tales enim Episcopi ignoti fuerunt Petro & Paulo, ignoti omnibus Apostolis, ignoti primitivæ Ecclesiæ universæ, ignoti Christo & sancto ipsius Spiritui. Deindè tales Episcopi, non sunt, quod esse & videri volunt veri Episcopi, sed sunt larvæ Satanæ & Antichristi Romani. Cuicunque enim non convenit Definitio Apostolica veri Episcopi, illi nec convenit definitum. Atqui Romamensium Episcopis non convenit Definitio Apostolica Episcopi, qualis quidem extat in Epistolis Paulinis ad Timotheum & Titum. E. non sunt veri Episcopi, sed Episcoporum larvæ, & Satanæ ac Antichristi mancipia.

Cæterùm si in Antecedentis probatione, per Episcopos intelligamus Pastores & Doctores Ecclesiæ, qui Verbum Dei doceant, & administrent Sacramenta: tùm libenter concedimus, Ecclesiam non posse esse sine hujusmodi Episcopis. Ubi tamen notandum est, Episcopos hosce, ipsorumque ministerium, interdum esse corruptissimum: uti suprà ostendimus in disputatione de Ecclesia latente. Tale ministerium fuit etiam sub densissimo Papatu, & sic ecclesia etiam tùm non fuit sine Episcopis, hoc est, Sacerdotibus, qui integrum administrarent Sacramentum Baptismi, licet ministerium ipsorum multis horrendis erroribus fuerit conspurcatissimum.

Porrò falsum ac nugatorium est, quod in Antecedentis probatione subjicit Jesuvvita: Apud Lutheranos non esse Episcopos, quia neq́; Ordinationem neq́; Successionem habeant ab Apostolis: ac per consequens apud illos etiam non esse Ecclesiam. Nam licet ultrò fateamur, Lutheranos neque episcopos Pontificios, neque Ordinationem & Successionem Pontificiam habere: tamen non propterea sequitur, eos destitui aut Episcopis veris, aut Ordinatione aut Successione Apostolica. Habent enim veros Verbi divini Doctores, & Sacramentorum dispensatores, quibus secundum definitionem Apostolicam definitionem Episcopi, præ insulatis illis Antichristi mancipijs verè ac propriè competere, certum est. Deindè habent Lutherani Ordinationem Apostolicam, eamq́; tanquàm Ceremoniam salutarem retinent, quæ constat impositione manuum Presbyterij, hoc est, eorum, qui Ecclesiæ tùm docendo, tùm gubernando præsunt. Habent denique veram ac legitimam successionem Apostolicam, quæ non ad certum locum, neque ad certum quendam, eumq́; nunquàm interruptum Episcoporum sibi invicem succedentium, Ordinem: sed ad Doctrinæ conformitatem est adstricta; uti supra ostensum fuit. Sed(objicit Bellarminus) neque Lutherus, neq́, alij Theologi Lutheranorum ordinati sunt à tribus Episcopis, neq́, ex dispensatione ab uno, assistentibus Abbatibus. Respondeo neque hoc necesse fuisse: Quemadmodum enim Ministerium ipsum cum omnibus suis partibus summè est necessarium: quin Vocatio quoque recta & legitima, quæ fit voce Ecclesiæ, itidem Ministro summè est necessaria: quippè divino præcepto mandata: ita Ordines Pontificii, non sunt necessarii, ut qui neq; divini sunt mandati, neq; traditionis Apostolicæ: ipso quoq; suffragante Ambrosio, super 4. caput ad Ephesios. Sic Ordinatio etiam illa Presbyteri per Episcopum, Episcopi verò per duos vel tres Episcopos, licèt fortassis primitùs bono consilio fuerit introducta, minimè tamen divini fuit præcepti, sed consuetudinis liberæ, quæ pro diversitate conditionis Ecclesiarum mutari potuit, & adhuc potest, præsertim si casus necessitatis accedat: qualis fuit tempore B. Lutheri, ubi Episcopi omnes Pontificii degeneraverant in lupos rapacissimos, & Ecclesiæ veræ Tyrannos sive persecutores. Tali ergò statu, si Ecclesia fideli & Orthodoxo Pastore destituatur, nihil prohibet, quò minùs totus fidelium grex in certam personam Ministri alicujus consentiat, qui sit ad docendum idoneus, & hunc sibi vocet ac eligat Ministrum, dûm non potest haberi opera sive Presbyteri, sive Episcopi, a quo accipiat Ordinationem. Talis Minister sic voce Ecclesiæ nominatus & Electus, indubiè est verus Ecclesiæ Pastor, qui legitimam vocationem habeat, omniaq; sui muneris officia ritè obire queat. Et respondeat Jesusvita, nùm quam aliam ordinationem in Apostolatu Matthiæ possit ostendere, præter vocationem & electionem. Si verò tùm sufficiebat ad Apostolicam ordinationem Vocatio hæc & Electio, accedentibus Ecclesiæ precibus, ita ut ne quidem manuum impositio adhibita legatur, multò verò minus, unctio Episcopalis, vel chrisma, vel tonsura, vel insufflatio accesserit: quidnî ad Lutheri & Lutheranorum Theologorum ordinationem, talis legitima Ecclesiæ Vocatio & Electio pariter sufficeret? Sic Paulus & Barnabas Actor. 13. sine omnibus istis ritibus Pontificiis emissi sunt ad prædicandum gentibus. Et quidem impositæ ipsis leguntur manus, verùm non ut de novo ordinarentur, qui priùs cœlitùs ordinati erant: sed ut hoc ritu fausta precarentur eis discipuli. Huc rectissimè accommodari potest illud Apostolicum, 1. Tim. 4. v. 14. Ne neglexeris, quod in te est donum, quod datum est tibi per Prophetiam, cum impositione manuum, autoritate PRESBYTERII: vel potiùs, ut textus Græcus habet: μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τῶ πρεσβυτερίε: cum impositione manuum Presbyterij: E. Timotheus non à solo Paulo, sed etiam à Presbyterio ad Ecclesiæ ministerium est ordinatus. Nihil ergò decedit Ordinationi Lutheranorum Theologorum, licèt Lutherus, à quo suam ordinationem acceperint, non fuerit

Episcopus, sed Presbyter duntaxat. Quid? quòd Scripturâ docente, omnes illi, qui docent Evangelium Christi, veniunt nomine Episcoporum, quamvis κατ' ἐξοχὴν Episcopi dicantur in speciali significatione, quibus inspectio super cæteros Pastores est concredita. Patet hoc cumprimis ex 1. Tim. 3. Siquis Episcopatum desiderat, bonum opus desiderat. Ubi munus docendi Ecclesiasticum ab Apostolo in genere definiri per Episcopatum, tota textus συνέπεια luculenter evincit. Undè consequitur Presbyteros quoque, sub censu numeroque Episcoporum hoc loco venire Apostolo. Si enim ab Episcopi nomine Presbyteros secludas, haud abs re quæritur, cum Episcoporum quidem notas proprietatesq; recenseat, Diaconorum itidem, & utrosque, quales in officio esse deceat, ex professo erudiat, quomodo & cur Apostolus vel potuerit, vel voluerit oblivisci Presbyterorum, ordinis intermedii? & cur idem Apostolus ad Philippenses scribens, salutem precatur Episcopis & Diaconis, Presbyterorum autem penitùs oblitus, si eos non etiam Episcoporum titulo complexus est? Certè Romanenses ipsi hodiè mordicùs pugnant, Petrum fuisse Episcopum: Atqui is se Presbyterum nominat. Ex quo vel unico loco, fictitium illud discrimen, quod inter Episcopos & Presbyteros fingunt Pontificii, Vanitatis redargui potest. Suffragatur nobis & D. Hieronymus, sic eruditè disserens, in Epistolam ad Titum:

"Oportet Episcopum sine crimine esse, tanquàm Dei "dispensatorem. IDEM ergò est Presbyter qui Episco- "pus: & antequam Diaboli instinctu, Schismata in "religione fierent, & diceretur in populis: Ego sum "Pauli, ego Apollo, ego autem Cephæ, communi Pres- "byterorum consilio Ecclesiæ gubernabantur. Postea- "quàm verò unusquisque eos, quos baptizaverat, suos "putabat esse, non Christi, in toto orbe decretum est, ut "unus ex Presbyteris electus, superponeretur cæteris, "ad quem omnis Ecclesiæ cura pertineret, & Schisma- "tum semina tollerentur. Putat aliquis non Scriptura- "rum, sed nostram esse sententiam, Episcopum & Pres- "byterum unum esse, & aliud ætatis, aliud officij esse "nomen: relegat Apostoli ad Philippenses verba dicen- "tis: Paulus & Timotheus servi Jesu Christi, omnibus "Sanctis in Christo Jesu, qui sunt Philippis, cum Epi- "scopis & Diaconis: Gratia vobis & pax &c. Philippi "una est urbs Macedoniæ, & certè in una civitate plu- "res (ut nuncupantur) Episcopi esse non poterant, sed "quia EOSDEM EPISCOPOS illo tempore, QUOS "ET PRESBYTEROS appellabant, propterea indif- "ferenter, de Episcopis, quasi de Presbyteris, est locu- "tus. Adhuc alicui hoc videtur ambiguum, nisi altero "testimonio cõprobetur. In actibus Apostolorum scri- "ptum est, quòd cùm Apostolus venisset Miletum, emi- "serit Ephesum, & vocaverit PRESBYTEROS Ec- "clesiæ ejusdem: quibus postea inter cætera sit locutus: "Attendite vobis & omni gregi, in quo vos Spiritus S. "posuit EPISCOPOS, pascere Ecclesia DEI, quam "acquisivit per sanguinem suum. Et hîc diligentiùs ob- "servate, quomodo unius civitatis Ephesi Presbyteros "vocans postea eosdem Episcopos dixerit. Et paulò "pòst, idem Hieron. Sicut ergò Presbyteriscium, se "ex Ecclesiæ consuetudine, ei qui sibi præpositus fuerat, "esse subjectos: Ita Episcopi noverint se magis consuetu- "dine, quàm dispositionis Dominicæ veritate Presby-


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: Jesuitical Solution (continued)

to be greater, and in common ought to rule the Church.

Thirdly, it is not observed even among the Romanists themselves, what they so vehemently demand of us. For how few are the Papist Presbyters who are ordained by any Bishop? Since it is confessed that it is not the Bishops themselves, but their Vicars, whom they call Suffragans, who are accustomed to confer ordination upon Presbyters: and it is not the Bishop, but the Suffragans, who breathe the breath into those to be ordained, and it is not the Bishop, but the Suffragans, who lay their vicarious hands upon them. Therefore, among the Romanists also, it is not of absolute necessity that ordination be conferred by a Bishop. Which being granted, it follows that ordination can be rightly performed not only by a Bishop, but also by Presbyters, with the laying on of the hands of the Presbytery: as the Apostle speaks.

Finally, this whole structure of the Jesuit proceeds from false presuppositions. For they presuppose as indubitable, and confessed on both sides, that the power and efficacy of the Ecclesiastical Ministry depend upon the Episcopal title and ordination. For to what end would there otherwise be a need to dispute so laboriously for the bringing in of Episcopal Ordination, unless the Adversaries maintained that by this, a certain singular virtue—which they are accustomed to call an indelible character—is infused and imprinted upon those ordained by a Bishop, by which the Word and Sacraments would finally be rendered efficacious. But this is nothing else than to accumulate error upon errors, and impiety upon ever greater impieties. For Scripture being witness, the entire power of the Ecclesiastical Ministry depends upon GOD alone; for He alone gives the increase, and grants power to His thunder. For the Word of GOD, provided it is preached purely by the Ministers of the Word, does not cease to be the Word of GOD, even if they are not ordained by Bishops, nor by their Suffragans: indeed, even if they are not ordained at all, provided they are legitimately called by the Church: But it remains the Word of GOD by whomever it is preached. But if it remains the Word of GOD, it will not vanish without fruit, nor will it return empty, according to that promise of Jehovah, Isaiah 55. The same must also be firmly established concerning Luther, and his colleagues and legitimate successors, since it is certain that, having repudiated the Papist traditions, they have urged the one Word of GOD, and have preached it purely, and even today still preach it: which is evident all the more clearly from the fact that they constitute no other judge of their doctrine than the Holy Spirit speaking in the Word: which, since the Romanists reject, and delegate these parts of the judge to the Roman Pontiff, and make him both the actor, witness, and judge in his own cause, they are certainly convicted by this alone, that they do not teach the Word of GOD purely: but have made shipwreck of the faith.

But furthermore, the Jesuit makes a tumult, and tries to press us with the authority of the Fathers, especially Cyprian, who recognized no ordination as true unless conferred by a Bishop. But the Jesuit beats the air. For the Fathers speak of the custom of their own times, namely, that a Presbyter was accustomed to be ordained by a Bishop. But the Fathers nowhere write that this was or is of absolute necessity, especially if those times occur in which Bishops degenerate into wolves. But even if the Fathers were to affirm such a thing, namely, that not even in a case of necessity could a Presbyter be ordained by a Presbyter: yet the authority of Scripture would be more powerful for us than that of these Fathers. But what Scripture thinks about this matter was explained a little earlier.

The Jesuit proceeds, and brandishes another dart of his argumentation at us, taken from ordinary Succession. For he says that it is most certain that Lutheran Theologians did not succeed ancient Bishops in the Episcopate, both because they invaded the place of Bishops who were still living and not yet deposed. But one does not succeed unless the Bishops are dead, or legitimately deposed: and also, because they themselves confess that they are the first Bishops of their own places.

I answer to the first part of the argument by a distinction between Singular and Common Succession. Singular is when a person succeeds a person in doctrine, in function, in place: Which is otherwise accustomed to be called succession into the head. And this succession has a place, both when the Church is constituted outside a state of persecution, and uses the ministry of true Bishops. But it is otherwise if Bishops turn into heretics, and the Church is enveloped in the darkness of errors: Where indeed this former succession cannot or ought not always be urged: as is evident from the example of those who succeeded Arian Bishops. Common succession is when one succeeds into the Ecclesiastical body itself, and into the order of the body, with heretical Bishops ejected: which entirely fits the Lutheran Theologians, who succeeded into the body of the Church itself, and into the Order of the Body, that is, into the Order of the Ministry, although they did not succeed in the doctrine of their predecessors. For because these were wolves, were mercenaries, were heretics, and therefore, the damage which they were inflicting upon the Church being recognized, they were soon deposed, condemned, and ejected by the remaining Orders of the Church: and Orthodox Doctors were called into their place. Nor was there any need here that the consent of the Roman Pontiff should be awaited, who in canon law ambitiously claims for himself alone the Right of deposing Bishops: can. Accusatus: and can. seq. 3. q. 6. For no place of Scripture can be brought forward which commands one to await the consent of the Roman Pontiff, as one wolf, to destroy another wolf. The Apostles certainly, in choosing and calling Bishops of the Churches who would succeed Pseudo-apostles, did not first seek the Consent of Caiaphas, or of any other high Priest: but on the contrary, and against his inhibition, they preached the Gospel concerning Christ: Acts 4, 6, 7, and 20.

Finally, every effort of Bellarmine, Stapleton, and the remaining Jesuits is concluded in this, that they contend that Luther was sent or called by no one to initiate a new kind of doctrine, against the consent of the entire Catholic Church.

I reply first that the Jesuits lie. For was not Luther legitimately called to teach the Word of God purely and incorruptly, at the time when he was initiated into holy orders, made a Presbyter, and according to the rite of the Roman Church, the power was granted to him of preaching and administering the Sacraments, in these words: "Consecrating, most beloved brethren, to the office of the Presbyterate, you should strive to receive it worthily, and having received it, to execute it laudably: for it behooves a Priest to offer, to bless, to preside, to preach, and to baptize. With great fear, therefore, one must ascend to so great a degree, and it must be provided that heavenly Wisdom, upright morals, and long-continued observance of justice may commend those elected to this office." And after a few words: "Let the doctrine of your life be spiritual medicine for the people of GOD: May it be the odor of your life, the delight of the Church of Christ, so that by prayer and example you may build up the house, that is, the family of GOD: etc. as can be seen in the Roman Pontifical, page 17, a and b, printed at Venice, in the year 1572. Thus, therefore, Luther, and thus the rest of his colleagues who were alive at the beginning of the Reformation, were legitimately called and sent to teach the Gospel: so that not even the Papists themselves can find anything to desire in the calling and ordination of these men, as far as the essentials are concerned. But that, while so diligently performing their duty, they eventually discovered, disapproved of, uncovered, and finally completely defected from the errors of the Roman Pontiff: that is accidental, and does not in any part vitiate the calling itself in its essentials. Now, since the Evangelical Magistrate substituted these men in the place of the Romanist Bishops, as persecutors of the true doctrine, and gave them the power of calling, choosing, and ordaining other pure Doctors of the Gospel: certainly, there can be no reason to doubt the legitimate calling of their successors.

Furthermore, it is established that the blessed Luther, by the command and urgency of the most Illustrious Magistrate, with the consent and agreement of the Church, and in a manner entirely orderly and legitimate, was solemnly declared a Doctor of Theology, where, by means of a religious attestation of an oath, he had to give assurance that he would faithfully assert and defend the doctrine divinely revealed in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles against its treacherous enemies and deniers: That this same Luther also performed this manfully, with a great Spirit and with the salvation of many thousands of souls, is evidently demonstrated by that insatiable hatred with which Satan and the Roman Antichrist, with the entire Papist cohort, raged and fumed against him.

Thirdly, the Jesuits also lie in this, that they pretend that Luther began a new kind of doctrine. For he did not begin a new one, but he skillfully asserted and vindicated that truly ancient and truly Apostolic deposit of doctrine from the new and absurd, and entirely impious, trifles and impostures of the Roman Antichrist. Where the same thing happened to the Church of GOD that once happened to it at the time of the raging Arian heresy. Certainly, the Arian Bishops did not establish, much less confirm, the orthodox prelates or their kind of doctrine: but the Church, usurping its own right, when it emerged everywhere from the filth of the heretics, having shaken off the Arian yoke, chose and called orthodox Ministers who would vindicate the ancient kind of doctrine from the novelties of the Arians.

Finally, we distinguish between the ordinary office of teaching and the singular Reformation of the Church. For the fact that the blessed Luther, as a Doctor of the Church, preached the Word of GOD, administered the Sacraments, refuted errors and heresies, and did not even spare the Roman Pontiff in this regard: that depended on his ordinary calling and ordination to the Presbyterate, conferred upon him by the Papists themselves.

almost, he undertook this great work of the Reformation of the Church, nay, he happily completed it, so that now throughout almost all of Germany the Pope is held in contempt, and that light of Apostolic Evangelical truth shines upon the Church of GOD with, as it were, full radiance: that was extraordinary and something entirely singular. For by the singular counsel of GOD, Luther was called and stirred up to perform this work: so that in him that Apocalyptic vision was truly fulfilled, by which John, ch. 14, 6, after the description of the Papal kingdom, testifies that he saw an Angel flying through the midst of heaven, having the eternal Gospel, to preach to those who dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and tribe, and tongue, saying with a loud voice: Fear GOD, and give him honor, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the fountains of waters. And ch. 18, 1 and 2. After this I saw another Angel, descending from heaven, having great power, and the earth was illuminated by his brightness: and he cried out with strength, saying: Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen, and has become a habitation of demons, and a prison for every unclean and hateful bird, because all nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication, etc.

But here the Romanists object two things. 1. That all who were extraordinarily called were so confirmed by GOD that they were immune from errors in doctrine: a thing which cannot be affirmed of Luther, even by the admission of the Lutherans themselves. 2. That there is no extraordinary Calling which has not been confirmed by certain signs or miracles: Which, however, cannot be shown in Luther.

I answer: That the former is not absolutely and universally true. The Apostles were certainly called immediately by Christ himself, and yet they were not immune from all errors (before they received the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost). For they erred concerning the kingdom of Christ, which they imagined to be earthly and corporal for themselves: they erred concerning the Truth of the Lord's Resurrection, which, even though preached by Angels and women, they held for a fable: they erred concerning association with the Gentiles, and concerning their gathering into the Church. Therefore, that absolute and nowhere-failing immunity from errors was not an infallible mark of an immediate and extraordinary Calling. Thus, regarding Luther, we certainly do not deny that at the beginning of the struggle he was still involved in many errors, which he had drawn from Papist doctrine. But we also fearlessly assert that the Holy Spirit of GOD so wonderfully guided and illuminated the mind of the blessed Luther that he emerged from all those errors into the clearest light of truth, and proposed a heavenly doctrine, chastened and free from every error.

Regarding the latter part of the objection concerning signs and wonders, neither is that universally true. Certainly, most of the Prophets were called extraordinarily: but the confirmation of this Calling, with a few exceptions, is nowhere read to have been done through Miracles. The Calling of John the Baptist was extraordinary; but of him, John 10:41, it is written: That he did no sign. Furthermore, let the Jesuits remember what answer Augustine once gave to the Donatists, when they attempted to establish the truth of the Church and of their Calling from miracles, in book 1 of On the Unity of the Church, chapter 16. That very answer, namely: Putting all things aside, let them not demonstrate their Church by notable signs and deceptive prodigies: because even against these things we have been prepared and rendered cautious by the Word of the Lord: but rather in the prescription of the law, in the predictions of the Prophets, in the songs of the Psalms, in the voices of the Shepherd himself, in the preachings of the Evangelists, that is, in all the canonical authorities of the holy books. 3. This very thing ought to have been a certain proof of the revealed Antichrist in these latter times, that his coming was to be according to the working of Satan in great power, in signs and lying wonders, 2 Thess 2:9. Finally, not even this extraordinary calling of Luther is entirely destitute of all signs and miracles. It is miraculous that the Holy Spirit willed to show this work of Luther's Reformation to John in the Apocalypse, chapter 14:6, many centuries before. It is miraculous that this very Reformation of Luther was predicted long before by John Huss and Hieltenius. It is miraculous that a peaceful and unarmed man with his pen so shook, weakened, and overturned the Roman seat that it has not been able to resume its strength even to this day. Finally, it is miraculous that his doctrine could not be conquered amidst so many and such great furies of the Devil and of heretics, especially the Jesuits and the Calvinists: but like a palm tree, the more strongly it was pressed, the more illustriously it flourished, and flourishes today.

Latin:

" teris esse majores, & in commune debere Ecclesiam " regere."

Tertiò, ne apud ipsos quoq; Romanenses observatur, quod à nobis tantoperè efflagitant. Quotus enim quisque Presbyter Pontificius est, ordinatus ab aliquo Episcopo? siquidem in confesso est, non ipsos Episcopos, sed horum Vicarios, quos Suffraganeos vocant, solere ordinationem conferre Presbyteris: & non Episcopi, sed suffraganei halitum insufflari ordinandis, & non Episcopi, sed Suffraganei vicarias manus eis imponi. Proindè apud Romanenses quoq; non est absolutæ necessitatis, ut ordinatio conferatur ab Episcopo. Quo concesso, sequitur Ordinationem non tantùm ab Episcopo, sed & à Presbyteris ritè posse perfici, cum impositione manuum Presbyteri: uti loquitur Apostolus.

Tandem ex falsis præsuppositis procedit universa hæc structura Jesuwitter.…. Præsupponunt enim tanquàm indubium, & utrinque confessum; vim & efficaciam Ministerij Ecclesiastici pendere ab Episcopali titulo ac ordinatione. Quorsum enim aliàs opus foret, tam operosè disputare pro afferenda Episcopali Ordinatione, nisi statuerent Adversarii, per hanc ordinatis ab Episcopo singularem quandam virtutem, quam ipsi indelebilem characterem appellitare solent, infundi & imprimi, quâ Verbum & Sacramenta redderentur demùm efficacia. Verùm nihil hoc est aliud, quàm errorem erroribus, & impietatem impietatibus subindè majoribus accumulare. Scripturâ enim teste, à solo DEO dependet universa vis Ministerij Ecclesiastici; quippè qui solus dat incrementum, & tonitrui suo largitur virtutem. Verbum quippè DEI, modò purè prædicetur à Verbi Ministris, non definit esse Verbum DEI, licèt neq; ab Episcopis, neqs ab horum Suffraganeis sint ordinati: imò si maximè planè non sint ordinati,modò ab Ecclesia sint legitimè vocati: Sed manet DEI Verbum à quocunq; prædicetur. Si verò manet DEI Verbum, non evanescet absq; fructu, nec revertetur vacuum, secundum promissionem illam Jehovæ, Jes. 55. Quod ipsum de Luthero, ejusdemq; Collegis ac successoribus legitimis firmiter etiam est statuendum, ut quos constat, repudiatis traditionibus Pontificiis, Unum Verbum DEI ursisse, purèq; prædicasse, ac etiamnùm hodiè prædicare: id quod vel indè tantò evidentiùs patet, quòd doctrinæ suæ Judicem nullum alium constituunt, quàm Spiritum S. in Verbo loquentem: quem cum rejiciant Romanenses, & has judicis partes subdelegent Pontifici Romano, ipsumq; in causa propria & actore, & testem & judicem faciant, certè vel hoc solo convincuntur, quòd Verbũ DEI nō purè doceant: sed fidei naufragium fecerint.

Sed porrò tumultuatur Jesu vvita, & Patrum Cypriani cumprimis autoritate nos premere conatur, qui Ordinationem non nisi ab Episcopo collatam, pro verâ agnoverint. Verùm aërera verberat Jesuwita. Loquūtur n. Patres de consuetudine suorū téporū, quòd videlicet Presbyter per Episcopum solitus fuerit ordinari. Nuspiam a. scribunt Patres, absolutæ hoc fuisse vel esse necessitatis, præsertim si ea incidant tempora, quibus Episcopi in lupos degenerant. Quin si maximè Patres tale aliquid affirmarent, nempè ne quidem in casu necessitatis, Presbyterū à Presbytero posse ordinari: tamen potior nobis Scripturæ, quàm Patrum istorum esset autoritas. Quid verò Scriptura hać de re sentiat, paulò antè fuit explicatum.

Pergit Jesuwita, & alterum argumentationis suæ telum in nos vibrat, defumtum à Successione ordinaria. Quod enim inquit, Lutherani Theologi non successerint in Episcopatu antiquis Episcopis,certissimum est, tùm quia locum viventium adhuc, & nondum depositorum Episcoporum invaserunt. Non autem succeditur, nisi Episcopis defunctis, aut legitimè depositis:tùm etiam, quia ipsi fatentur se primos esse suorum locorum Episcopos.

Respondeo ad prius argumenti membrū per distinctioné inter Successionem Singularem & Comunē. Singularis est cùm persona personæ succedit in doctrinâ, in functioné, in locum: Quæ aliàs nominari consuevit Successio in caput. Et locū habet hæc Successio, tùm, quâdo Ecclesia extra statū persecutionis est cōstituta, & verorū Episcoporū ministerio utitur. Secus vero si Episcopi in hæreticos evadant, & Ecclesia errorum tenebris involvitur: Ubi sanè prior hæc successio nō semper urgeri potest aut debet: uti exemplo eorum patet, qui Arianis Episcopis succefferūt. Comunis succesfio est, quâdo in corpus ipsum Ecclesiasticū, & in ordine corporis, ejectis Episcopis hæreticis succeditur: id quod Lutheranis Theologis omninò convenit, qui in corpus ipsum Ecclesiæ, & in Ordinem Corporis, h. e. in Ordinem Ministerii successerūt, licèt nō successerint in doctrinâ Antecessoru. Quia n. hi lupi erant, mercenarii erant, hæretici erant, ideoq; damno, quod Ecclesiæ inferebât, cognito, mox à reliquis Ecclesiæ Ordinib. sunt depositi, damnati, ejecti: inq; istorū locū Orthodoxi Doctores evocati. Neq; opus hîc erat, ut Romani Pontificis cōsensus expectaretur, qui in jure canonico sibi soli Jus deponédi Episcopos, ambitiosè vindicat: can. Accusatus:&' can. feq.3. q. 6. Nam nullus Scripturæ locus proferri potest, qui jubeat, Romani Pontificis, tanquàm unius lupi, ad alterū lupū profligandū expectare cōsensum. Apostoli certè in eligendis & vocâdis Ecclesiariū Episcopis, qui Pseudoapostolis succederent, non priùs petierunt Consensum Caiphæ, aut alterius cujusdam summi Pontificis: quin cōtra & præter hujus inhibitioné, prædicarunt Evangelium de Christo: Actor.4, 6,7. & 20.

Tandem omnis conatus Bellarmini, Stapletoni & reliquorū Jesu vvitarum in eo absolvitur, quod contendunt, Lutherum à nemine missum, aut vocatum esse, ut novum doctrinæ genus inchoaret, con tra consensum totius Ecclesiæ Catholicæ.

Respondeo initiò mentiri Jesuwitas. An non n. Lutherus legitimè vocatus fuit ad docēdum Verbum DEI purè & incotruptè, tùm cùm ordinibus sacris initiatus, Presbyter factus fuit & secundū ritum Ecclesiæ Romanæ, potestas ipsi faćta est prædicandi & Sacramenta adiministrandi: his verbis: Consecrandi fratres charissimi in Presbyteratus officium, illud dignè suscipere, atq; susceptū laudabiliter exequi studeatis: Sacerdotem n. oportet offerre, benedicere, præesse, prædicare & baptizare. Cum magno itaq; timore, ad tantū gradū ascendēdum est atq; providēdum, ut cœlestis Sapientia, probi mores & diuturna justitiæ observatio, ad hoc munus electos commendet. Et post pauca: Sit doctrina vestra spiritualis medicina populo DEI: Sit odor vitæ vestræ, delectamentum Ecclesiæ Christi, ut precatione atq; exemplo ædificetis domum, id est, familiam DEI: &c. uti videre est in Pontificali Romano, pag. 17. a & b. Venetijs excuso, Anno 1572. Sic ergò Lutherus, sic reliqui ipsius collegæ, qui sub initium reformationis in vivis fuerunt, legitimè fuerunt vocati & missi ad docendum Evangelium: ut ne quidem Pontificii ipsi, in istorum vocatione & ordinatione, quòad Substantialia, quicquam desiderare possint. Quòd verò sic gnaviter facientes officium, errores Pontificis Romani tandem deprehenderunt, improbarunt, detexerunt, & tandem ab eo planè defecerunt: id accidentis est, neque vocationem ipsam in Substantialibus ulla ex parte vitiat. Jam cùm Magistratus Evangelicus, istos in locum Episcoporum Romanensium, tanquàm veræ doctrinæ persecutorum substituit, iisque potestatem dedit alios puros Evangelii Doctores vocandi, eligendi, ordinandi: utiq; neq; de successorum legitimâ vocatione dubitari ulla ratione potest.

Deindè constat B. Lutherum, sic jubente & urgente Illustrissimo Magistratu, sic consente etiam & consentiente Ecclesiâ, & sic ordinariâ planè ac legitimâ ratione, Theologiæ Doctorem solenniter renunciatum esse, ubi mediante religiosâ Juramenti attestatione fidem dare necesse habuit, se doctrinam scriptis Prophetarum & Apostolorum divinitùs patefactam, contra perfidos illius hostes & abnegatores fideliter afserturum ac propugnaturum : Quod ipsum Lutherum quoque magno Spiritu, & cum multarum millium animarum salute, masculè præstitisse, vel insatiabile illud odium evidenter demonstrat, quo Satanas & Antichristus Romanus, cum universa cohorte Pontificiâ adversus ipsum flagravit & desæviit.

Tertiò in eo etiam mentiuntur Jesuwitæ quòd fingunt, Lutherum novum Doctrinæ genus inchoasse. Neque enim novum inchoavit, sed verè antiquum illud, vereque Apostolicum Doctrinæ depositum, à novis & absurdis, planeque impiis Antichristi Romani nugis & imposturis, dextrè asseruit & vindicavit. Ubi idem Ecclesiæ DEI tùm obvenit, quod olim eidem obtigit tempore grassantis Arianæ hæreseωs. Certè Ariani Episcopi orthodoxos Antistites, aut istorum doctrinæ genus minimè constituerunt, nedúm confirmarunt: sed Ecclesia jus suum usurpans, cùm passim ex sordibus hæreticorum emergeret, excusso jugo Ariano, Ministros orthodoxos elegit & vocavit, qui antiquum Doctrinæ genus, ab Arianorum novitatibus vindicarent.

Tandem distinguimus inter ordinarium docendi munus, & inter singularem Reformationem Ecclesiæ. Nam quòd B. Lutherus, ut Doctor Ecclesiæ prædicavit Verbum DEI, administravit Sacramenta, errores atque hæreses refutavit, & ne quidem hac in parte pepercit Pontifici Romano: id pendebat ab ordinaria ipsius vocatione & ordinatione ad Presbyterium, ab ipsis etiam Pontificiis in eum collatâ.

lus fermè, grande hoc opus Reformationis Ecclesiæ molitus est, imò feliciter perfecit, ut jam per totam fermè Germaniam sordeat Pontifex, & lux illa Apostolocæ veritatis Evangelicæ, pleno quasi jubare, Ecclesiæ DEI affulgeat: id extraordinarium & quiddam planè singulare fuit. Singulari enim DEI consilio ad hoc opus patrandum vocatus & excitatus fuit Lutherus: ut verè in ipso impleta visio illa Apocalyptica, quâ Johannes c. 14, 6. post descriptionem regni Pontificii, testatur, se vidisse Angelum volantem per medium cæli, habentem æternum Evangelium, ut evangelizaret habitantibus super terram, & omni genti, & populo, & linguæ dicentem voce magna: Timete DEUM, & date illi honorem, quia venit hora judicij ejus, & adorate eum, qui fecit cælum & terram, mare & fontes aquarum. Et cap. 18, 1. & 2. Posthæc vidi alium Angelum, descendentem de cælo, habentem potestatem magnam, & terra illuminata est à claritate ejus: & exclamavit in fortitudine dicens: Cecidit, cecidit Babylon magna, & facta est habitatio Dæmoniorum, & custodia omnis volucris immundæ & invisæ, quia de vino iræ fornicationis ejus bibêrunt omnes gentes, &c.

Sed duo hîc regerunt Romalenses. 1. Omnes extraordinariè vocatos, sic à DEO fuisse confirmatos, ut immunes fuerint ab erroribus in doctrinâ: id quod de Luthero affirmari nequeat, vel ipsis fatentibus Lutheranis. 2. Nullam dari extraordinariam Vocationem, quæ non certis signis sive miraculis fuerit confirmata: Quæ tamen in Luthero monstrari non possint.

Respondeo: Prius illud non absolutè & universaliter verum esse. Apostoli certè immediatè à Christo ipso erant vocati, neque tamen ab omnibus erroribus (antè acceptum in die Pentescostes Spiritum sanctum) erant immunes. Errabant enim de regno Christi, quod terrênum ac corporale sibi imaginabantur: errabant circa Veritatem Resurrect. Dominicæ, quam ab Angelis etiam & mulieribus prædicatam habebant pro fabula: errabant de conversatione cum gentilibus, deque horum congregatione ad Ecclesiam. Haud proindè infallibilis nota immediatæ & extraordinariæ Vocationis fuerit, absoluta illa & nuspiam deficiens ab erroribus immunitas. Sic quoad Lutherum, minimè profectò diffitemur, ipsum in primordio certaminis multis adhuc erroribus fuisse involutum, quos ex doctrinâ Pontificiâ hauserat. Sed & illud intrepidè asserimos, ipsum Sanctum DEI Spiritum ita mirabiliter B. Lutheri mentem rexisse & illuminasse, ut ex omnibus illis erroribus, in clarifsimam veritatis lucem emerserit, doctrinamque cœlestem ab omni errore castigatam ac liberam, proposuerit.

Quoad posterius objectionis membrum de signis & prodigiis, neque illud universaliter verum est. Certè Prophetæ plerique extraordinariè vocati sunt: at Vocationis hujus Confirmatio, paucis exceptis, per Miracula nuspiam facta legitur. Johannis Baptistæ extraordinaria fuit Vocatio; sed de eo, Job. 10, 41. scriptum est: Quod signum nullum fecerit. Deindè meminerint Jesuvitæ, quid olim responsi Donatilis ex miraculis, veritatem Ecclesiæ & Vocationis stabilire conantibus, dederit Augustinus, lib. 1. de Unit. Eccl. cap. 16. Istud nimirum : Remotis omnibus, Ecclesiam suam non demonstrent insignis & prodigijs fallacibus : quia etiam contra isthæc Verbo Domini præparati & cauti redditi sumus: sed in præscripto legis, in Prophetarum prædictis, in Psalmorum cantibus, in ipsius Pastoris vocibus, in Evangelistarum prædicationibus, hoc est, in omnibus Canonicis Sanctorum librorū autoritatibus. 3. Hoc ipsum potiùs postremis hisce temporibus certum debuit esse τεκμήριον revelati Antichristi, quòd nimirùm adventus ipsius futurus erat secundum operationem Satanæ in magna potentia, in signis, & prodigiis mendacibus, 2. Thess 2, 9. Tandem, ne quidem extraordinaria hæc Lutheri vocatio omnibus prorsus signis ac miraculis destituitur. Miraculosum est, quod Spiritus sanctus Opus hoc Reformationis Lutheri, multis seculis ante, Johanni in Apocalypsi monstrare voluit, cap. 14, 6. Miraculosum est, quod per Johannem Hussum, & Hieltenium hæc ipsa Reformatio Lutheri, multò antè fuit prædicta. Miraculosum est, quod imbellis & inermis homo calamo suo sedem Romanam ita concussit, labefactavit, evertit: ut nec in hodiernum usq; diem vires resumere possit. Miraculosum denique est, quod Doctrina ipsius, inter tot tantosq; Diaboli & hæreticorum, Jesuitarum cùmprimis & Calvinianorum furores, expugnari non potuit : sed palmæ instar, quò fortiùs pressa fuit, eò illustriùs effloruit, hodièq; efflorescit.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: The Second Axiom of the Church is that it is declared Holy in the Apostolic Creed

With respect to this second axiom, the Church is adorned in the Scriptures with illustrious titles, such as that it is the Spouse of the Son of GOD, 2 Cor 11:2; a spiritual house, Heb 3:6, 1 Pet 2:5; a holy priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, a chosen race, 1 Pet 2:5 & 9; the house of the living GOD, 1 Tim 3:15; the Council of the Saints, Ps 89:8; a tabernacle sanctified by GOD, Ps 46:5; an acceptable people, Tit 2:14. Which titles, and others of this kind, as they cannot and ought not to be assigned to Turks, modern Jews, and other infidel peoples, so the Church is distinguished from their company when we profess in the Apostles' Creed that we believe in the holy Church.

Moreover, concerning the nature and definition of this holiness, what it is and in what it consists, is today especially contested. The Romanists attribute to the Church a holiness of such a kind that it surpasses even the Holy Scriptures themselves, and consequently procures for the Church a certain absolute and clearly unaccountable authority: as will be demonstrated a little later in the antithesis. We, taught by the oracles of the Scriptures, grant a twofold holiness to the Church: One is alien, namely that which depends on Christ, the head of the Church. For Christ alone is the one who sanctifies his Church, Eph 5:26.

who calls it with a holy calling, 2 Tim 1:9; who informs and confirms it in the Truth of the Evangelical Word, John 17:17; who cleanses it with the washing of water in the Word, Eph 5:26; who gives it the Holy Spirit as a pledge of the heavenly inheritance: 2 Cor 1:22, Eph 1:14; who purifies it through faith: Acts 15:9; who finally was given by the Father to the Church for Sanctification, 1 Cor 1:30. This holiness the schools of theologians commonly name imputed holiness, the reason for this appellation being sought primarily from the form of communication by which this holiness comes to the Church from GOD. We can name the other holiness of the Church its own. This, however, is that by which the Church, occupied with holy things and pursuits, serves GOD in holiness: Luke 1:75; by which it is holy in all conversation, 1 Pet 1:15; by which, finally, it strives toward that goal which it will one day attain in eternal life, so that it may be glorious, not having a wrinkle, or a spot, or anything of that kind: but may be holy and blameless: Eph 5:27.

Both these kinds of holiness differ from each other in the greatest degree. For the former is perfect and absolute in every respect: but this latter is only begun, and must be perfected before this corruptible puts on incorruption. Furthermore, it is more with respect to that former one than to this latter one that the Church is called holy in the Creed. Whence it follows that that Church also is and is called holy where there is not solid purity and perfection of life and morals: which the Anabaptists, and before them the Novatians, ignorantly denied. Furthermore, it also follows that it is not necessarily required that all who dwell in the bosom of the Church be holy: just as the Donatists of old imagined for themselves a Church consisting of merely holy people.

Finally, it also follows from this that the opinion of those who establish that a place in the Church is to be granted only to those predestined to glory cannot stand.
