For the oracles of the Scriptures protest against all these and similar errors, which testify that there was present at the royal wedding even he who lacked a wedding garment, and was therefore cast into outer darkness: Matt 22:11. Likewise, that to the kingdom of heaven, which is gathered in these lands, that is, the Church, there was also joined a congregation of virgins, not only five wise ones, but also five foolish ones: Matt 25:2. To which also pertains that parable of the fishing net, by which fish of every kind are gathered, the separation of which will take place only on the shore, that is, at the end of the world, Matt 13:47. Hence the Apostle shows that in the Church, not all walk with an equal pace of holiness, just as in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware: and some indeed for honor, but others for dishonor, 2 Tim. 2:20. What? That Christ himself compares the Church to a threshing floor, in which wheat is so gathered that chaff is mixed in, until, having been cleansed by the winnowing fan and sieve, it is finally stored in the barn, but the chaff is burned with unquenchable fire, Matt. 3:12.

Furthermore, if it were necessary that the Church be perfect in its individual members and free from every vice or blemish, then we would no longer have any Church at all on earth; indeed, there never would have been any on earth, since it is undoubtedly established from the Scriptures that there is no man who does not sin, 1 Kings 8:46, Psalm 130:3, and Psalm 143:2, Proverbs 20:9, 1 John 1:8, etc.

Thirdly, Scripture describes the Church nowhere from predestination, but from the present grace of Christ the Savior, as also from the presence of faith: As in Eph. 2:12, 'At that time you were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.' And 1 Pet. 2:10, 'In time past you were not a people: but now you are the people of GOD.' Thus, regarding the presence of faith, John says, 'He gave power to become the sons of GOD, to them that believe on his name,' John 1:12. Thus the Apostle defines the Body of the Church, not by the narrow limits of the Predestined, but by that most wide flock of the baptized: saying, 'We being many are one body in Christ,' 'By one Spirit are we all baptized into one body,' Rom. 12:5, 1 Cor. 12:13.

Finally, illustrious examples also confirm our assertion, such as those of Aaron, David, and Peter, who certainly were neither perfect in life, nor (regarding Peter and Aaron) were they walking in a straight path toward the Truth of the Gospel, Gal. 2:14, Exod. 32:2, and following. Thus the Apostle rebukes very many and grave vices in the Corinthians and Thessalonians, as also in the Galatians: whom, however, he himself clearly shows were by no means alien from the bosom of the Church.

The sum of what has been said thus far tends to this: that for the Church to be holy, it is not necessary that all those who are its parts be holy; but it is sufficient that some, and a certain number, and many in it are holy, and that the true nature of holiness is taught and shown in it; and that these, who are holy in the Church, are lacking neither in true faith in Christ, nor in the true fruits of the same.

We conclude, therefore, that although the eulogy of Holiness, as well as other honorable praises of this kind which are proclaimed in the Scriptures concerning the Church, properly belong to one and the only assembly of the truly faithful or Elect, who alone are the Body, are the Complement, are the Spouse of Christ: yet by a synecdoche of the whole for the part, it is referred to the whole Church and the entire visible assembly of the called; and this for two reasons primarily. 1. Because in this very visible assembly the purity of the heavenly word sounds forth: and where this sounds, there the Holy and Elect are never not found. 2. Because this whole visible assembly of the called, established apart from the rest of the peoples outside the Church, is dedicated to GOD, is consecrated to Christ through Baptism: where no one fails to see that a regard for some holiness is at work. In this very synecdochical sense, the Apostle wished to call that whole assembly of the Corinthians, though polluted with many vices, nevertheless 'called saints'.

The Jesuit Bellarmine himself also acknowledges the firmness of this doctrine of ours, writing in book 3, 'On the Church Militant,' chapter 9, that the Church is called Holy first because all things that pertain to constituting it are holy: such as Baptism, the Christian profession, the union of members among themselves and with the head; 2. that it is so called on account of the saints whom it has: since denomination is always made from the better part; and that to have saints is proper to the Church, as it alone has the truly holy; but that to have the wicked belongs also to other assemblies. 3. Finally, that it is so called because it is entirely consecrated to GOD, and because its head, Christ, is the Holy of Holies.

But what the Jesuit explained not badly in this place, he wickedly corrupts a little later, when in the following chapter, 14, he extends this holiness of the Church so far as to show that the Church cannot simply and absolutely err in the dogmas of faith and in deciding theological controversies; so that in questions of faith, one must appeal to none but the Church, and one must stand by its judgment and authority alone in this matter.

Thus, therefore, the Question concerning the Holiness of the Church has provided an occasion between us and the Jesuits for two distinct and most grave Controversies: the former of which is concerning the authority of the Church, whether it is greater than the authority of the Holy Scriptures, as indeed the Jesuits commonly contend today. The latter is concerning the infallibility of the Church: namely, whether it cannot simply err in interpreting the Scriptures and deciding Controversies, as the Adversaries argue.

Latin:

SEcundi hujus axiomatis respectu, Ecclesia in Scripturis præclaris omninò elogiis exornatur, ut quòd sit, Sponsa Filij DEI. 2. Cor 11, 2. domus spiritualis, Hebr. 3, 6. 1. Petr. 2, 5. Sacerdotium sanctum, gens sancta, populus acqui sitionis, genus electum, 1. Pet. 2, 5. & 9. domus DEI vivi, 1. Tim. 3, 15. Concilium Sanctorum, Psal. 89, 8. tabernaculum à DEO sanctificatum : Psal. 46, 5. populus acceptabilis, Tit. 2, 14. Quæ, & id genus alia elogia, uti Turcis, Judæis modernis, aliisq; infidelibus populis afsignari nec possunt nec debent: ita ab istorum consortio Ecclesia discernitur, quando in Symbolo Apostolico profitemur, nos sanctam credere Ecclesiam.

Cæterùm de naturâ atque definitione sanctitatis hujus, quid ea sit, & quà in re consistat, hodiè potissimùm pugnatur. Romanenses ejusmodi Sanctitatem affingunt Ecclesiæ, quæ ipsas quoque Scripturas Sacras superet, ac proindè absolutam quandam, & planè ἀνυπεύθυνον autoritatem Ecclesiæ conciliet: uti in ἀντιθέσει paulò pòst demonstrabitur. Nos Scripturarum oraculis edocti, duplicem largimur Ecclesiæ Sanctitatem: Unam alienam, eam nimirùm, quæ à Christo capite Ecclesiæ dependet. Christus enim solus est, qui sanctificat Ecclesiam suam, Eph. 5, 26.

qui vocat eam vocatione sancta, 2. Tim 1, 9. qui in Veritate Verbi Evangelici eam informat & confirmat, Joh. 17, 17. qui eam mundat lavacro aquæ in Verbo, Ephes. 5, 26. qui donat ei Spiritum sanctum, tanquàm arrham cœlestis hæreditatis: 2. Cor. 1, 22. Ephes. 1, 14. qui per fidem eam purificat: Actor. 15, 9. qui denique à Patre datus est Ecclesiæ in Sanctificationē, 1. Cor. 1, 30. Hanc Sanctitatem vulgò Scholæ Theologorum nominant Sanctitatem imputatam, appellationis hujus ratione potissimùm petita, à formâ communicationis, quâ Ecclesiæ à DEO sanctitas hæc obtingit. Alteram Sanctitatem Ecclesiæ nominare possumus propriam. Hæc vèrò ea est, quâ rebus & studiis sanctis occupata Ecclesia servit DEO in sanctitate: Luc. 1, 75. quâ in omni conversatione Sancta est, 1. Pet. 1, 15. quâ denique ad eum scopum contendit, quem aliquando in vita æterna assequetur, ut sit gloriosa, non habens rugam, aut maculam, aut quicquam istiusmodi: sed sit sancta & inculpata: Ephes. 5, 27.

Utraq; hæc Sanctitas inter se vel maximè differt. Nam prior illa est perfecta, & omnibus numeris absoluta: hæc verò posterior, inchoata duntaxat est, ac priùs perficienda, quàm corruptibile hoc, incorruptibilitatem induat. Deindè magis respectu prioris illius, quàm posterioris hujus, Ecclesia dicitur in Symbolo Sancta. Undè consequens est, illam etiam Ecclesiam esse & dici sanctam, ubi non est solida vitæ morumque puritas & perfectio: id quod Anabaptistæ, & ante hos Novatiani inscitè negarunt. Deindè consequens etiam est, necessariò non requiri, ut omnes sancti sint, qui in Ecclesiæ gremio versantur: uti Donatistæ olim Ecclesiam ex meris Sanctis constantem sibi imaginabantur.

Tandem consequens etiam hinc est, haud subsistere posse eorum sententiam, qui statuunt, solis prædestinatis ad gloriam, locum in Ecclesia esse concedendum. Omnibus enim istis & consimilibus erroribus reclamant Scripturæ oracula, quæ testantur, Nuptiis regiis interfuisse etiam illum, qui carebat veste nuptiali, ac ideo missum in tenebras exteriores: Matth. 22, 11. Item, regno cœlorum, quod in his terris colligitur, hoc est, Ecclesiæ adjunctã etiam fuisse congregationem virginum non quinq; tantùm prudentum: sed etiam quinq; fatuarum: Matth. 25, 2. Quò pertinet parabola etiam illa retis piscatorii, quo omnis generis pisces colliguntur, quorum in littore demùm, h. e. in fine mundi fiet segregatio, Matth. 13, 47. Hinc Apostolus in Ecclesia, non pari omnes sanctitatis passu ambulare ostendit, perindè ut in magna domo non sint aurea solùm & argentea vasa: sed & lignea & fictilia: & alia quidem in honorem, alia verò ignominiam, 2. Tim. 2, 20. Quid? quod Christus ipse Ecclesiam confert cum area, in qua sic collectum est triticum, ut admixtæ sint paleæ, donec vanno & cribro repurgatum, recondatur tandem in horreum, paleæ autem comburantur igni inextinguibili, Matth. 3, 12.

Deindè, si Ecclesiam in singulis membris perfectam esse, omníq; vitio aut labe vacare, necessum foret: jam nullam prorsus in terris Ecclesiam ampliùs essemus habituri: imò nequè fuiffet ulla unquàm in terris, cùm indubitatò constet ex Scripturis, Non esse hominem, qui non peccet, 1. Reg. 8, 46. Psal. 130, 3. & Psal. 143, 2 Prov. 20, 9. 1. Joh. 1, 8. &c.

Tertiò, Scriptura nuspiam à prædestinatione, sed à præsente gratiâ Christi Servatoris, ut & à præsentia fidei describit: Ut Eph. 2, 12. Eratis illo tempore sine Christo, abalienati à politia Israëlis, alieni à fœdere promissionis, spem non habentes, & impÿ in mundo. Et 1. Pet. 2, 10. Olim non eratis populus: nunc autem estis populus DEI. Sic quoad præsentiam fidei inquit Johannes, Dedit potestatem filios DEI fieri, his qui credunt in nomen ejus, Joh. 1, v. 12. Sic Apostolus Corpus Ecclesiæ definit, non per angustos Prædestinatorum limites: sed per latissimum illum baptizatorum gregem: Unum, inquiens, Corpus multi sumus in Christo: In uno Spiritu omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus: Rom. 12, 5. 1. Cor. 12, 13.

Tandem illustria etiam Exempla assertionem nostram confirmant, ut Aaronis, Davidis, & Petri, qui certè neque perfecti erant in vita, neque (quoad Petrum & Aaronem) recto tramite ad Veritatem Evangelii ambulabant, Galat. 2, 14. Exod. 32, 2. & seqq. Sic benè multa ac gravia vitia in Corinthijs & Thessalonicensibus Apostolus reprehendit, ut & in Galatis: quos tamen ab Ecclesiæ gremio minimè fuisse alienos, ipsemet dilucidè ostendit.

Summa tandem hactenùs dictorum eò tendit, ut Ecclesia sit sancta, non oportet omnes eos esse sanctos, qui illius partes sunt: sed satis est nonnullos, & aliquam, multos in eà sanctos esse, & veram in illa sanctitatis rationem tradi & monstrari: & hos, qui sunt in Ecclesia sancti, neque verâ in Christum fide, neque veris ejusdem fructibus vacare.

Concludimus proindè, licèt Sanctitatis elogium, ut & alia id genus honorifica encomia, quæ in Scripturis de Ecclesia prædicantur, propriè uni & soli cœtui verè fidelium sive Electorum conveniant, qui soli sunt Corpus, sunt Complementum, sunt Sponsa Christi: per Synecdochen tamen totius pro parte, ad totam Ecclesiam, & universum visibilem vocatorum cœtum referri: idǻ; duas potissimùm ob causas. 1. Quia in hoc ipso visibili cœtu sonat verbi cœlestis puritas: Ubi verò hæc sonat, ibi verè Sancti & Electi nunquàm non reperiuntur. 2. Quia totus iste vocatorum cœtus visibilis, præ reliquis populis extra Ecclesiam constitutus, est DEO dicatus, est Christo per Baptismum consecratus: Ubi sanctitatis alicujus respectum militare nemo non videt. Quo ipso sensu Synecdochico Apostolus totum illum Corinthiorum cœtum, multis licèt vitiis pollutum, Sanctos tamen vocatos appellare voluit.

Agnoscit doctrinæ hujus nostræ firmitatem ipse quoq; Jesuita Bellarminus, scribens lib. 3. de Ecclesia militante, cap 9. ideò primùm dici Ecclesiam Sanctam, quia omnia, quæ ad ipsam constituendam pertinent, sint sancta: qualia sint Baptismus, professio Christiana, Unio membrorum inter se, & cum capite 2. sic dici propter Sanctos, quos habet: Siquidem denominatio semper fiat à meliori: & habere sanctos, proprium sit Ecclesiæ, ut quæ sola habeat verè sanctos: sed habere malos aliis etiam cœtibus conveniat. 3. Tandem sic eam dici, quia tota est consecrata DEO, & quia caput ejus Christus sit Sanctus Sanctorum.

Cæterùm quod hoc loco haud malè explicavit Jesuita, illud paulò post nefariè corrumpit, cum capite subseq 14. Sanctitatem hanc Ecclesiæ eo usq; extendit, ut ostendat Ecclesiam simpliciter & absolutè errare non posse, in dogmatibus fidei; & in decidendis controversiis Theologicis: ita ut in quæstionibus fidei, non nisi ad Ecclesiam sit provocandum, ipsiusque solius judicio & autoritate hac in parte standum.

Sic ergò Quæstio de Sanctitate Ecclesiæ, inter nos & Jesuwitas ansam præbuit duabus distinctis & gravissimis Controversiis: quarum prior de autoritate Ecclesiæ, Num major ea sit, quàm Scripturarum Sacrarum Autoritas, uti quidem communiter hodiè contendunt Jesuivitæ. Posterior est de infallibilitate Ecclesiæ: An videlicet ea in interpretandis Scripturis, & decidendis Controversiis, simpliciter errare non possit? uti pugnant Adversarii.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: Whether the authority of Scripture or of the Church is greater?

It is asked between us and the Jesuits, since on both sides in the Apostolic Creed we profess that we believe in the Holy Church, and from that a great authority of the Church altogether emerges: What and of what kind is the authority and power of the Church, and how far does it extend? We maintain that a solid decision of this question can be sought from a consideration of the Right which the Church possesses over the things entrusted to it:

However, an observation deserves to be made here immediately from the very threshold, that by the name of the Church, in this dispute, we do not understand any part of it exclusively, in the manner and sense of the Papists, namely only the order of Clerics or of the Mass-priests: But the whole assembly of the faithful; and this considered either with respect to the Catholic or Universal Church, dispersed throughout the whole world: or also with respect to any particular Churches whatsoever.

First, therefore, we concede to the Church some right and power in the custody of the Biblical books. For the fact that these have been transmitted down to these our times is certainly to be attributed solely to the care and benefit of the Church, after GOD. Insofar, therefore, as the Church today testifies that these books are divine beyond all doubt, to that extent it certainly exercises some right and authority over the Scriptures: but no greater than that which belongs to a truthful witness. Whence it comes about that every faithful person gives assent to the testimony of the Church in this matter, following the example of Augustine, who asserted that he would not believe the Gospel (namely, that it is by those authors who, by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, wrote it) unless the authority of the Church moved him; and that by reason of the testimony which it has always borne with one voice to the books of the Evangelists, book against the Epistle of the Foundation of the Manichaeans, chapter 5.

Then some right and authority belongs to the Church in judging spirits: 1 John 4:1, 1 Thess. 5:21. The Apostle expressed this right, warning the Corinthians that two or three prophets should speak, and the others should judge. Where, however, it must be observed that this right is not understood by the Apostle concerning those things which are brought forth from the Scriptures themselves according to the letter, which the Church or any of the faithful ought to judge: for every pious person is bound to apprehend these with simple faith: But only concerning doctrines which are brought forth by the teachers or ministers of the Church (whom the Apostle in the cited passage calls prophets), which he wishes to be examined and judged according to the norm of faith, that is, the divine Word. The Beroeans can be an example, who searched the Scriptures to see if those things which had been said to them were so: Acts 17.

Thirdly, the Church obtains some right and authority in assessing and judging both morals and deeds: according to that saying of Christ, Matt. 18:17, where He wishes those things to be referred to the Church which cannot be brought into order by the judgments of private men. Where also such authority is assigned to the Church that he who has not heard it, that is, has not stood by its judgment, ought to be held as a Gentile or a tax collector.

Fourthly, the Church also obtains a clearly exceptional right and authority concerning the power of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, the use of which it can both exercise by itself and also commit to others, namely to the ecclesiastical ministry, to be used piously and legitimately: by the example of the Corinthian Church, which had excommunicated the incestuous man by the use of the binding key, 1 Cor. 5:1 and following.

Fifthly, finally, the Church also has the right and power in legitimately choosing and calling suitable ministers of the Word: as also in removing reprobate and false pastors and teachers.

But it is immediately asked here, how great is this power and authority of the Church, or how far does it extend? We, being thus taught by the Holy Scriptures, maintain that all this authority is limited and determined by the prescription of the divine Word, so that in exercising it, it must uniquely contain itself within the bounds of the Word, according to that saying: If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, John 8:31.

From these things which have been said, that question which is debated today can be decided. Whether the authority of the Church is greater than that of Scripture, both in dogmas of faith and in judging controversies? We hold the negative in all respects, and we contend that the authority of Scripture is greater, relying on these three reasons.

I. The dignity or authority of Holy Scripture does not consist of the Church: but vice versa, the authority of the Church consists of Scripture, as a thing measured from its measure: and Scripture is not judged by the Church, but the latter by the former. All those passages of the Scriptures confirm this opinion, in which Scripture is not bound to the Church, but the Church to Scripture, and in the matter of salvation and heavenly truth, we are referred not to the Church, but uniquely to the Scriptures, as Deut. 4:2: You shall not add to the word which I speak to you, nor take away from it: keep the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you. Deut. 12:32: What I command you, this ONLY do to the Lord: neither add anything nor diminish. Isa. 8:20: To the Law and to the Testimony: If they do not speak according to these, there will be no morning light for them. Gal. 1:8: If an angel from heaven should preach a gospel to you beyond that which you have received, let him be anathema.

II. Scripture is not built upon the foundation of the Church: but the Church is built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, Eph. 2:20. Therefore, Holy Scripture, which has the place and reason of a foundation, does not have its firmness from the Church: but rather it is necessary that the Church has its stability from it. And although the Church, out of an infinite number of writers and books, has approved only the canonical Scriptures by its testimony: it did not, however, make them true, certain, and holy from false, doubtful, and profane ones: but because they were such by themselves, the Church certainly confirmed by its calculation that they were such, and wished them to be committed to its custody. Just as, therefore, a witness in a political court does not finally make a cause good by his testimony, but at least testifies that it is good: so nothing is conferred upon Holy Scripture beyond testimony and custody.

III. The truth of our opinion is evident even by the consent and testimony of the Papists themselves, as many as have retained some sound mind from extreme blindness and insanity. Among these was Gerson, whose opinion is celebrated: One who is learned in the Holy Scriptures and brings forth canonical authority is to be believed more than a general council. Thus Panormitanus on the canon: Sanctificasti, title on Elections: A simple layman bringing forth Scripture is to be believed more than a whole council together. The same thing is also established by Alphonsus de Castro, in whose book 1 against heresies, chapter 8, these are the words: We have this from the Church, that we may know which is the divine Scripture. But when it has been established to us that Scripture is divine, it now has from itself that we are bound to believe it in all things. While the Church discerns that Scripture is the revelation of God, it does only that which witnesses do, bearing testimony about some matter. For the truth of Scripture is Catholic, not because of the witnesses: but because of itself: and not because the Church receives it: but because GOD published and revealed it. But if the contrary is maintained, and it is said that this matter depends on the judgment of the Church, what will follow, I ask? Namely this, that the truth of Scripture would be recognized either by experience or by natural reason: and thus our faith would rest on the principle of experience and natural reason. To which that Pauline passage, 1 Cor. 2:4, clearly objects: My speech and my preaching were not in the persuasive words of human wisdom: but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power: and our faith is not in the wisdom of men: but in the power of GOD. This cause can also be elegantly illustrated by the example of the Samaritans. For just as these men, moved by the testimony of the woman, had first gone out to hear Christ: but afterwards, having heard Him and acknowledged Him as the Messiah, they said to the woman: Now we believe not because of thy saying, for we have heard Him ourselves and know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world, the Christ: Joh. 4, 42. So from the Church's testimony Scripture is first accepted: after it has once been accepted, it suffices for itself for the proof of Truth by divine power.

The Jesuits bitterly contradict this purer doctrine of ours, objecting various things: and first of all that Apostolic passage in 1 Tim. 3:15, where the Church is called the pillar and foundation of the living God's Truth.

I reply that a fallacy is committed, παρα τό τῆ και ἁπλῶς [from the particular to the absolute]. For the Church is called the pillar and foundation of Truth by reason of its faithful custody, by which it guards with the utmost fidelity the Oracles of the divine Word (which alone is truth itself, John 17:17) committed to it, while remaining itself built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, that is, upon canonical Scripture. Now when the Romanists infer from this custody an absolute infallibility and a greater authority for the Church than Scripture has, they immediately fall into another fallacy, which is τῶ μή αἰτίω ὡς αἰτίῳ [treating the non-cause as the cause], & παρα το μη ἑπόμενον [and the non-sequitur]. The evidence of this response, to make it clearer, comes to be noted in three things especially concerning the present Apostolic dictum: 1. Its genuine sense. 2. The cause. 3. The mode. Regarding the sense, the Apostle does not say that the Church is the foundation, but only the pillar or stabilizer of the truth. The cause of the assertion is not what the Jesuits falsely attribute to it, that truth depends absolutely upon the Church: but because it is built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, with Christ being the chief cornerstone, Eph. 2:20, while indeed, like a pillar, it supports the truth by its ministry, by preaching it among men, and by preserving and defending it from errors and destruction, and indeed by faithfully transmitting it to posterity. 3. The mode of the matter as limited by the Apostle himself is this: The house of God, namely that Church of the living God, is the pillar and foundation of the truth. Where the Apostle limits the subject of the proposition, and determines it by a certain reason of his own. For he does not speak of just any Church, or assembly of men, nor even simply of the Christian Church, in whatever state it may be: but of the Church, insofar as it is the house of God, or insofar as God dwells in it by His word, grace, and Spirit, insofar, finally, as God lives and reigns in it. Of this Church, therefore, limited in this way from the side of the subject, he predicates that it is the pillar and foundation of the truth. A manifold depravation is therefore committed against the Apostolic passage by the Papists: and indeed, besides the two fallacies already noted, also παραλογισμός ἐπερωτήσεως [a fallacy of questioning]. For what the Apostle said about the pillar and foundation, they interpret as if the Church were called the foundation of the truth: when yet it is named the pillar and foundation of the truth only because it is sustained on the foundation of the truth, and the rock of salvation, which is Christ: and not that it itself sustains the building of the truth either alone or primarily: as has been shown.

Another argument of the Jesuits is usually such: The Church is prior to Scripture. Therefore, the authority of the Church is also superior or greater.

I reply that in the antecedent a fallacy is committed, παραλογισμὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ τὶ καὶ ἁπλῶς [a fallacy from the particular to the absolute]. For the Church is prior to the Word of God, not simply, but only insofar as it is written. Which writing happened to the Word of God only as a certain accident. But the Word of God, considered in itself, was before the Church, was before Scripture, and indeed will remain when Scripture is abolished. Although, therefore, the Church was prior with respect to Scripture: it is not granted that it was prior to the Word of God: indeed, it is expressly denied by the Apostle, who asserts that the Church was constituted from incorruptible seed, through the Word of the living God, 1 Pet. 1:23.

Thirdly, they object that, from book 1 of Pighius, De Ecclesia Hierarchia, chap. 2: The Church has bestowed canonical authority upon the Scriptures, which they did not have from themselves, nor from their authors. Which if the Church had done, Scripture would have no greater authority than the fables of Aesop.

I reply that the whole structure of this argument is woven from falsehoods and blasphemies. It is false that the authority of the holy Scriptures is from the Church, or from men. For if the whole world were to condemn the Word of God, it would never cease to be what it is: just as God does not cease to be God, although the wicked say in their heart, There is no God: Ps. 14:1. But the authority of Holy Scripture, or the Word of God, stands from God Himself, by whom it is inspired, 2 Tim. 3:16, 2 Pet. 1:21. Therefore, we do indeed have this from the Church, that we know which is the divine scripture: But after it is established which it is, it now has from itself, indeed from God, that we are bound to believe it in all things, as we have already explained above from Alphonso de Castro. Another and indeed more recent Papist writer, Michael Medina the Spaniard, subscribes to these in a book printed at Venice, writing: From the fact that the Church points out the Scriptures, it is as weakly inferred that it is greater in authority than the Scriptures, as if someone were to assert that he is more excellent than a King who, in a most crowded throng of men, points out the King to someone: or if someone were to conclude that John the Baptist is greater than Christ, because he pointed out Christ with an extended finger, and bore witness of Him.

At last, as if it were the shield of Achilles, the Papists repeatedly hold up that passage of Augustine, book against the Epistle of Manichaeus called Fundamental, chapter 5: 'I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved me.'

I answer ϰατ᾽ εὖ and that the saying of Augustine must be accepted with a certain moderation. For 1. he speaks of the true, and indeed the Catholic Church: but not of a false and particular one, such as the Roman is. 2. he speaks of the primitive Church, which partly saw and heard Christ and the Apostles, which [attested] the truth of these writings, through the authors themselves, or their most intimate associates had most thoroughly: which transmitted the knowledge of this matter to posterity: which finally, in an uninterrupted series of times, by the continuous testimony of leaders and other trustworthy men, received and preserved the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles. 3. He does not say that he believes because of the Church: but that he is moved by its testimony to believe that the Evangelical books were divinely handed down through the Apostles, because they have been propagated in the Church by a certain series of succession. 4. The occasion which led Augustine to write such a thing confirms this answer. Faustus the Manichaean had brought forward an epistle which he called 'The Foundation': and he had contended that the same, as if written by some one of the Apostles, should be held and received in the same place and rank as the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles. Here, therefore, Augustine most rightly appealed to the testimony of the Church, asserting that he could not receive that Epistle because it was destitute of the testimony of the primitive and Catholic Church, which he himself values so highly that he would not even believe the Gospel to have been written by the Evangelists themselves, unless the Church testified to this by unanimous consent. 5. Although Augustine grants great authority to the Church in this part: yet so much cannot be elicited from it, as if the truth and certainty of the books and of the Evangelicals depended more on the authority of the testifying Church than on the divine truth itself. 6. The fallacy of the Figure of Diction occurs. For that the Gospel is to be understood not of the doctrine of the Gospel itself considered in itself, as the Papists wish: but of the Evangelical books, is evident even from the scope of that book. For in it Augustine expressly disputes about the certainty of those books, namely, that they are from the Evangelists themselves whose names they bear. He writes, therefore, that he was moved, and is still moved, to believe that those books are Evangelical, that is, divinely written and handed down by the Apostles and Evangelists, because they have been propagated in the Church by a certain series of succession: as Augustine himself explains himself more fully and clearly, lib. 28. contra Faust. Manich. cap. 2. & c.

Finally, we oppose to the Papists other Papist writers who are in this part of the same mind as we are: such as Nicholas de Clemanges, who in his disputation on the matter of a general Council asserts that the words of Augustine are to be understood not of the power and judgment of the Church over Scripture: but only of its testimony. Gerson also supports this, lib. de vita animae Spirituali, lect. 2. coroll. 7., writing that those err who abuse these words of Augustine to prove that the Pope, a Council, or the Church can change what has been handed down by the Evangelists and Apostles. Durandus also approaches this, lib. 3. sent dist. 24. q. 1., who interprets the words of Augustine as referring only to the pristine or primitive Church. Which Andradius writes is a capital and destructive statement, page 107 of his second writing.

Latin:

QUæritur inter nos & Jesuwitas, cùm utrinque in Symbolo Apostolico profiteamur nos credere Sanctam Ecclesiam, & inde magna omninò autoritas Ecclesiæ emergat: Quænam & qualis sit Ecclesiæ autoritas ac potestas, & quousq; ea se extendat? Nos solidam quæstionis hujus decisionem peti posse statuimus, ex consideratione Juris, quod Ecclesia in res sibi concreditas obtinet:

Observationem autem hoc loco mox à limine primo meretur illud, quòd nomine Ecclesiæ, hac in disputatione, non aliquam ejus partem exclusivè intelligamus, more ac sensu Pontificio, nempè solùm ordinem Clericorum, sive Sacrificulorum Missaticorum: Sed totum cœtum fidelium: & hunc quidem vel respectu Ecclesiæ Catholicæ sive Universalis, per totum orbem dispersæ: vel etiam respectu Ecclesiarum quarumvis particularium, consideratum.

Primùm ergò Jus aliquod atque potestatem Ecclesiæ concedimus, in custodiendis libris Biblicis. Quòd enim hi ad hæc nostra usquè tempora sunt transmissa, illud certè curæ atque beneficio Ecclesiæ, post DEUM unicè acceptum fertur. Quatenùs ergò Ecclesia hodieq; testatur, hos libros citra omnem dubitationem esse divinos, eantenùs certè jus aliquod atq; autoritatem in Scripturas exercet: sed non majorem, quàm quæ testi veraci competit. Undè fit, ut Ecclesiæ etiam testimonio, hac in parte, fidelis quisque assensum præbeat, exemplo Augustini, asserentis, se Evangelio non crediturum (scilicet esse illorum autorum, qui instinctu Spiritus S. scripserunt) nisi Ecclesiæ autoritas se commoveret: neque ratione testimonii, quòd libris Evangelistarum uno semper ore perhibuit, l. contra Epist. Funda menti Manichæorum, cap. 5.

Deindè jus aliquod atque autoritas competit Ecclesiæ, in judicandi Spiritibus: 1. Joh. 4, 1. 1. Thess. 5, 21. Jus hoc expressit Apostolus, monens Corinthios, ut Prophetæ duo vel tres loquantur: cæteri autem dijudicent. Ubi tamen observandum, Jus hoc ab Apostolo non intelligi de illis rebus, quæ ex Scripturis ipsis, secundum literam proferuntur; quas Ecclesia, vel fidelium quisquam judicare debear: Has enim fide simplici apprehendere pius quisque tenetur_: Sed tantùm de dogmatibus, quæ à Doctoribus sive Ministris Ecclesiæ, (quos Apostolus loco citato, Prophetas appellitar) proferuntur, quæ vult examinari & judicari secundum normam fidei, hoc est, Verbi divini. Exemplo possunt esse Berrhæenses, qui scrutati sunt, nùm in Scripturis ita se haberent, quæ ipsis essent dicta: Actor. 17.

Tertiò, Jus aliquod autoritatemque obtinet Ecclesia in censendis judicandisque tùm moribus, tùm factis: secundum illud Christi, Matt. 18, 17. ubi ad Ecclesiam vult deferri ea, quæ privatorum hominum judiciis in ordinem redigi non possunt. Ubi etiam tanta autoritas Ecclesiæ adsignatur, ut qui eam non audierit, hoc est, ejus judicio non steterit, is Ethnici aut publicani instar haberi debeat_.

Quartò, Jus etiam autoritatemque planè eximiam obtinet Ecclesia, circa potestatem clavium regni cœlestis, quarum usum ipsa tùm per se exercere, tùm aliis etiam, nempè ministerio Ecclesiastico usurpandam piè ac legitimè committere potest: exemplo Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ, quæ hominem incestuosum ex usu clavis ligantis excommunicaverat, 1. Cor. 5, 1. & seqq.

Quintò, tandem Jus etiam atque potestatem habet Ecclesia in legitimè eligendis vocandisque idoneis Verbi Ministris: ut & in reprobis falsisque Pastoribus ac Doctoribus removendis.

Cæterùm statim hîc quæritur, Quanta sit, vel quousque se extendat potestas hæc, & autoritas Ecclesiæ? Nos Scripturis Sacris sic edocti, omnem hanc autoritatem limitatâ, & Verbi divini præscripto determinatam esse statuimus, adeò ut in ea exercenda intra cancellos verbi unicè se continere debeat, juxta illud: Si manseritis in sermone meo, verè discipuli mei eritis, Johan. 8, 31.

Potest ex his quæ dicta sunt decidi Quæstio ea, quâ hodiè controvertitur. Nùm major sit Ecclesiæ, quam Scripturæ autoritas, tùm in dogmatibus fidei, tùm in dijudicandis Controversiis? Nos negativam per omnia tenemus, & majorem Scripturæ autoritatem esse contendimus tribus hisce freti rationibus.

I. Scripturæ S. dignitas sive autoritas sua non constat ab Ecclesia: Sed vice versa, Ecclesiæ sua constat autoritas à Scriptura, tanquàm rei mensuratæ, à sua mensura:& non judicatur Scriptura ab Ecclesia: sed hæc ab illa_. Confirmant hanc sententiam loca illa Scripturarum omnia, quibus non Scriptura ad Ecclesiam: sed hæc ad illam alligatur, & in negocio salutis, ac veritatis cœlestis causâ, non ad Ecclesiam, sed ad Scripturas unicè remittimur, ut Deut. 4, 2. Non addetis ad verbum, quod vobis loquor, nec auferetis ex eo: custodite mandata Domini DEI vestri, quæ EGO præcipio vobis, Deut. 12, 32. Quod præcipio tibi, hoc TANTUM facito Domino: nec addas quicquam nec minuas, Jes. 8, 20. Ad Legem & ad Testimonium: Si non dixerint secundum hæc, non erit eis lux matutina. Galat. 1, 8. Si Angelus de cælo evangelizet vobis præter id, quod accepistis, anathema sit.

II. Scriptura non est superstructa super fundamentum Ecclesiæ: sed Ecclesia est superstructa super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, Eph. 2, 20. E. Scriptura S. quippè, quæ fundamenti locum & rationem habet, suam firmitatem non ab Ecclesia: sed hæc potiùs ab illa stabilitatem suam habeat necesse est. Et quanquàm Ecclesia ex infinito Scriptorum ac librorum numero, solas canonicas Scripturas testificatione sua approbavit: minimè tamen ex falsis, dubiis & prophanis, veras, certas, & sanctas effecit: sed quia tales per se erant, utique Ecclesia eas tales esse, suo calculo confirmavit, & suæ custodiæ commendatas esse voluit. Quemadmodum ergò Testis aliquis in foro politico, Causam rei suo testimonio nõ demùm bonam efficit: sed saltem testatur esse bonam: ita Scripturis S. præter testimonium & custodiam nihil confertur.

III. Constat sententiæ nostræ Veritas ipsorum etiam Pontificiorum consensu atq; testimonio, quotquot quidem aliquid sanæ mentis ab extrema cæcitate, & insania retinuerūt. Inter hos fuit Gerson, cujus hæc celebratur sententia: In Sacris literis erudito, atque autoritatem Canonicam proferenti, plus est credendum, quàm generali Concilio. Sic Panormitanus ad cano: Sanctificasti, tit de Electionibus: Plus est credendum vel simplici laico, Scripturam proferēti, quàm toti cōcilio simul. Quod ipsum statuit etiam Alphonsus de Castro, cujus lib. 1. adversus hæreses, cap. 8. hæc sunt verba: Hoc ex Ecclesia habemus, ut sciamus, quæ sit Scriptura divina. At cum Scripturam esse divinam nobis constiterit, jam ex se ipsa habet, ut ei per omnia credere teneamur. Ecclesia dum discernit, Scripturam esse Dei revelationem, id tantùm facit, quod testes, ferentes de re quapiam testimonium. Nam Veritas Scripturæ est Catholica, non propter testes: sed propter se: & non quia Ecclesia recipit: sed quia DEUS edidit & revelavit. Quòd si diversum statuatur, & ex Ecclesiæ arbitrio pendere dicatur hoc negotium, quid sequetur quæso? nempè hoc, quod aut per experientiam, aut per naturalem rationem Veritas Scripturæ esset agnita: & sic fides nostra principio experientiæ & rationis naturalis niteretur. Cui manifestè repugnat Paulinum illud, 1. Cor. 2, 4. Sermo meus & prædicatio non in persuasibilibus humanæ sapientiæ verbis: sed in ostensione Spiritus & virtutis: & fides nostra non est in sapientia hominum: sed in virtute DEI. Potest etiam causa ista exemplo Samaritanorum eleganter illustrari. Nam quemadmodum hi, mulieris testimonio moti ad Christum audiendum, primùm exierant: sed postmodùm eo audito, & pro Messia agnito, dicebant mulieri: Non jam propter Sermonem tuum credimus ampliùs, sed quia ipsi audivimus & vidimus, quòd iste reverà sit Servator mundi, Christus: Joh. 4, 42. Ita ex Ecclesiæ testimonio primùm accipitur Scriptura : postquàm semel accepta est, ipsa sibi ad Veritatis documentum ex virtute divina sufficit.

Puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ acriter contradicunt Jesuvvitæ varia objicientes : ac primùm quidem lcum illum Apostolicum, in 1. Tim. 3, 15. ubi Ecclesia Dei viventis nuncupatur columna & firmamentum Veritatis.

Respondeo committi Sophisma παρα τό τῆ και ἁπλῶς. Ecclesia enim dicitur columna & firmamentum Veritatis, ratione fidelis custodiæ, quâ Oracula Verbi divini (quod solum veritas ipsa est, Joh. 17, 17.) sibi commissa, summa fide custodit, interim ipsa manens superstructa super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, hoc est, super Scripturam canonicam. Jam quando Romanenses ex hac custodia colligunt absolutam infallibilitatem, & majorem autoritatem Ecclesiæ, quàm sit Scriptura, statim incidunt in alteram Sophisticationem, quæ est τῶ μή αἰτίω ὡς αἰτίῳ, & παρα το μη ἑπόμενον. Responsionis hujus evidentia, ut fiat manifestior, tria potissimùm circa præsens dictum Apostolicum notanda veniunt: 1. Sensus ejus genui nus. 2. Causa. 3. Modus. Quoad sensum, non dicit Apostolus, Ecclesiam esse fundamentum: sed duntaxat columnam sive stabilimentum veri tatis. Causa assertionis est, non quam Jesuvvitæ affingunt, quòd ab Ecclesia veritas absolutè dependeat : sed quia ipsa superstructa est super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, summo angulari lapide existente Christo, Ephes. 2, 20. dùm nimirùm columnæ instar veritatem suo ministerio suffulcit, prædicando eam inter homines, & ab erroribus atque interitu conservando ac vindicando, quin & ad posteros fideliter transmittendo. 3. Modus rei ab ipso Apostolo limitatus hic est : Domus Dei, Ecclesia nempè illa Dei vivi, est columna & firmamentum veritatis. Ubi Apostolus Subjectum propositionis limitat, & sua quadam certa ratione determinat. Non enim de quavis Ecclesia, sive cœtu hominum, neque etiam simpliciter de Ecclesia Christiana, quoque modo se habente loquitur : sed de Ecclesia, quatenùs est domus Dei, vel quatenùs Deus suo verbo, oratia & Spiritu in ea habitat, quatenùs denique vivit & regnat in illa Deus. De hac ergò Ecclesia, ex subjecti parte sic limitata prædicat, quòd sit columna & firmamentum veritatis. Multiplex ergò in locum Apostolicum depravatio committitur à Pontificijs : & quidem præter duas Sophisticationes jam notatas, etiam παραλογισμός ἐπερωτήσεως. Nam quod Apostolus de columna & firmamento dixit, id isti interpretantur, quasi fundamentum veritatis Ecclesia appellata sit : cùm tamen ideò tantùm nominetur Columna & firmamentum veritatis, quia ipsa in fundamento veritatis, & petra salutis, quæ est Christus, sustentatur : non verò quòd ipsa ædificium veritatis vel sola, vel primariò sustineat : uti ostensum.

Alterum argumentum Jesuvvitarum tale esse solet: Ecclesia prior est, quàm Scriptura. Ergò potior etiam sive major Ecclesiæ autoritas.

Respondeo in Antecedente committi παραλογισμὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ τὶ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Ecclesia enim prior est verbo Dei, non simpliciter, sed tantùm quatenùs Scriptum est. Quæ Scriptio Verbo Dei tantùm obtigit, ut Accidens quoddam. Verùm Verbum Dei in se consideratum fuit ante Ecclesiam, fuit ante Scripturam, quin & manebit, cùm Scriptura abolebitur. Quamvis ergò respectu Scripturæ prior fuerit Ecclesia: Verbo tamen Dei prior esse, non conceditur: imò disertè negatur ab Apostolo, asserente Ecclesiam constitutam esse ex semine incorruptibili, per Verbum Dei vivi 1. Petr. 1, 23.

Tertiò illud objiciunt, ex lib. 1. Pighij de Eccleshier cap. 2. Ecclesia præcipuù Scripturis Canonicam impertita est autoritatem, quam non ex se, neque ex suis autoribus habebant. Quod si fecisset Ecclesia, Scriptura non major foret autoritas, quàm fabularum Æsopi.

Respondeo, totam structuram hujus argumenti, ex falsitatibus & blasphemijs esse contextam. Falsum est, quòd Scripturæ sacræ autoritas sit ab Ecclesia, vel ab hominibus. Quod si totus mundus damnaret Verbum Dei, nunquàm tamen desineret esse, quod est: sicut nec Deus desinit esse Deus, licèt impij dicant in corde suo, Non est Deus: Psal. 14. 1. Verùm constat S. Scripturæ, sive Verbo Dei sua autoritas ab ipso Deo, à quo est inspirata, 2. Timoth. 3, 16. 2. Petr. 1, 21. Proindè hoc quidem habemus ab Ecclesia, ut sciamus quæ sit scriptura divina: At postquàm, quænam illam sit, constat, jam ex seipsa, imò ex Deo habet illa, ut ei per omnia credere teneamur, uti jam supra ex Alphonso de Castro explicavimus. Subscribit his alius etiam & quidem recentior Scriptor Pontificius, Michael Medina Hispanus, in libro Venetijs excuso, scribens: Ex eo, quòd Ecclesia Scripturas monstrat, Scripturis eam autoritate majorem esse, càm infirmè colligitur, quàm si quis asserat, eum esse præstantiorem Rege, qui in confertissima hominum turbâ Regem alicui monstret: aut si quis colligat, Johannem Baptistam esse Christo majorem, quia is digito extento Christum monstravit, & de eo testimonium perhibuit.

Tandem ceu Achillis clypeum subindè obvertunt Pontificij illud Augustini lib. contra Epistolam Fundamenti Manichæorum, cap. 5. Evangelio non crederem, nisi me Catholicæ Ecclesiæ moveret autoritas.

Respondeo ϰατ᾽ εὖ & cum certa moderatione Augustini dictum accipiendum esse. Nam 1. loquitur de verâ, & quidem Catholicâ Ecclesia: non autem de falsa & particulari, qualis est Romana. 2. loquitur de primitiva Ecclesia, quæ partim vidit & audivit Christum atque Apostolos, quæ horum Scriptorum veritatem, per ipsos autores, vel familiarissimos illorum habuit exploratissimam : quae notitiam hujus rei ad posteros transmisit: quae denique non interrupta serie temporum, contestatione continua praepositorum & aliorum fide dignorum hominum, scripta Evangelistarum & Apostolorum accepit & conservavit. 3. Non dicit, se propter Ecclesiam credere: sed ejus testimonio moveri, ut credat libros Evangelicos divinitus per Apostolos esse traditos, quia certa successionis serie in Ecclesia propagati sint. 4. Confirmat hanc responsionem, occasio, qua factum, ut Augustinus tale quid scriberet. Protulerat Faustus Manichaeus epistolam, quam vocabat, Fundamentum: ac eandem tanquam ab Apostolorum quopiam conscriptam pari loco consuque cum scriptis Evangelistarum & Apostolorum haberi & recipi contenderat. Hic ergo rectissime ad Testimonium Ecclesiae provocavit Augustinus, afferens, se Epistolam illam recipere non posse, propterea quod destituatur Ecclesiae primitivae atq; Catholicae testimonio, quod tanti ipse faciat, ut ne quidem Evangelium crederet, ab ipsis Evangelistis esse conscriptum, nisi unanimi consensu hoc testaretur Ecclesia. 5. Licet hac in parte magnam autoritatem Ecclesiae largiatur Augustinus: tamen tanta inde elici non potest, quasi librorum & Evangelicorum veritas atque certitudo, ab autoritate testantis Ecclesiae magis, quam a veritate ipsa divina dependeat. 6. Occurrit Sophisma Figurae Dictionis. Evangelium enim non de ipsa doctrina Evangelij in se considerata, uti Pontificij volunt: sed de libris Evangelicis intelligendum esse, vel ex scopo illius libri evidenter patet. Siquidem in eo de certitudine librorum istorum, quod nimirum ab ipsis Evangelistis, quorum nomina praese ferunt, ex professo disputat Augustinus. Motum ergo se esse scribit, & moveri adhuc, ut credat libros istos esse Evangelicos, hoc est, divinitus per Apostolos & Evangelistas scriptos atque traditos, quia certa successionis serie in Ecclesia sint propagati: uti ipse Augustinus fusius ac clarius se explicat, lib. 28. contra Faust. Manich. cap. 2. & c.

Tandem opponimus Pontificijs, alios Scriptores Pontificios, nobis hac in parte óμοψήφες: ut Nicolaum de Clemangijs, qui in disputat. super materia Concilij generalis asserit, Verba Augustini non de potestate & judicio Ecclesiae in scripturam: sed de testimonio tantum intelligenda esse. Suffragatur etiam Gerson, lib. de vita animae Spirituali, lect. 2. coroll. 7. scribens, Eos errare, qui his verbis Augustini abutantur, ad probandum, quod Papa, Concilium, vel Ecclesia possit immutare, qua ab Evangelistis & Apostolis, sunt tradita. Accedit Durandus lib. 3. sent dist. 24. q. 1. qui verba Augustini, de sola pristina sive primitiva Ecclesia interpretatur. Quam Andradius capitalem & exitiosam esse orationem scribit, pag. 107. Scripti sui secundi.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: II. Controversy. Concerning the Holiness of the Church: concerning its infallibility: namely, Can the Church err, or could it err?

This controversy depends on the one immediately preceding. For the Jesuits attribute to the Church such authority that one must believe it not under a certain condition, but absolutely in the business of religion, so that the truth of faith, as far as we are concerned, rests upon the authority of the Church: and it is true, whatever the Church approves: false, whatever it disapproves, as Bellarmine writes in express words: l. 3. de Ecclesia militante, cap. 14. p. 1277. A. In order to persuade readers of this, with a truly crafty art, he is accustomed to proceed in this manner: The Church cannot err in believing. But not only could the ancient Church not err in faith: but not even the Church which now is, or which will be until the end of the age. Furthermore, not only does the Universal Church, that is, the collection of all the faithful, have this eternal spirit of truth: but the princes and pastors of the Church also have the same, so that they cannot err in faith. Whatever, therefore, the Pastors and Princes teach, which pertains to the faith of Christ, that is most true, and all Pastors and Doctors can never wander from the faith. To undermine this Jesuitical structure from its very foundations, as they say, there will be need of analysis; since, because of the indefinite and equivocal nature of the Jesuitical speech or pronouncements, no small perplexity and difficulty is detected.

At the beginning, however, that hypothesis (pre-supposition) comes under consideration, whether absolute infallibility can or ought to be granted to the Church in the cause of faith? We, with Dr. Augustine, have learned to defer this fear and honor to the books of the Scriptures alone, which are called canonical, so that we most firmly believe that no author of them erred in writing, and therefore that they deserve absolute faith and authority in the business of religion. Augustine, Epist. 19. Such, therefore, is the holiness and excellence of the canonical Scriptures, that no other writings or dogmas, by whatever name they may come, can be compared or equaled to them: so much so, that even if the same truth is found in these also, yet the authority is far unequal: as Augustine writes again, lib. 1. contra Faust. Manich. c. 5.

Perhaps the Jesuits might object that Augustine wrote that concerning only a few Doctors, and not concerning the whole University of Doctors or Bishops. But not even in this way will they obtain anything: For Augustine looked not to the number, but simply to the authority of the Bishops, which he expressly denies to be absolute for men, however great their number, however great their holiness and learning: so that nothing is to be thought true for the reason that they themselves thought so; but only because they were able to persuade [others] through canonical authors that what they said or wrote was true.

2. Furthermore, every prophecy or doctrine of all men ought to be analogous to the faith, according to the precept of the Apostle, Rom. 12:6; it ought to be consonant with the law and the testimony, according to the admonition of the Prophet Isaiah 8:20. Which, indeed, as well as other sayings of this kind, just as they deny absolute authority and infallibility in matters of faith to all men and to any orders of men whatsoever, so they grant to the Church only a conditional authority, namely, that which ought to be tested and measured against the Canon of the Scriptures.

The Jesuits object: Thus no authority is attributed to the Church; thus everything that has ever been defined by the Church, or is defined today, is rendered ambiguous; nay, thus one even goes into an infinite uncertainty, because the exception is always at hand that the Church can be mistaken in that it understands the Scriptures wrongly. But who then will be the judge? Whether the Church interprets Scripture rightly or not? Indeed, it follows from this that even every private individual must be believed when he pronounces according to the Scriptures: because all these things are too absurd.

I answer: These are presented as absurdities not of faith but of human reason. For faith, with Scripture so teaching, believes that the Ecclesiastical order is also sometimes punished by God by a just judgment of God with such an efficacy of errors that all the watchmen of the Church are blind (2 Chron. 15:2), and that those who sit in the temple of God believe a lie and the seduction of iniquity, because they did not receive the love of the truth that they might be saved (2 Thess. 2:4, 10, & 11). Thus faith determines, with Scripture warning again, that the Church of Christ, as a disciple and bride, hangs upon the mouth of her master and bridegroom in such a way that she ought to know nothing at all from herself, but ought to set the limit of her wisdom where Christ the Master has made an end of speaking.

Regarding the judgment of interpretation and controversies, although we do not maintain that it falls to any layman or private individual whatsoever, yet it cannot be denied that it has very often happened that the opinion of at least one man has prevailed over the judgment of the whole Church in a matter of religion: which is manifest by the example of Elijah in the Israelite Church, likewise of Paphnutius in the Council of Nicaea, and of Athanasius in the Eastern Church. It is added that, with Scripture teaching again, every just man, whether he be private or public, whether cleric or layman, can live and be saved not by the faith of the Church, but by his own faith: Habakkuk 2:4, Rom. 1:17. Therefore it matters greatly that any private believer can be certain and secure in his own mind, from the Word of God, concerning the truth of his faith. And to no one, as the Romanists opine, is the discernment of those things which are necessary to be known for salvation clearly impossible for every believer, even a private one or a layman. For he can use two means in this regard, which are by far the most suitable: one internal, which is the Spirit of truth, who is promised to every one of the faithful by Christ no less than to the Church herself (John 14:16, John 16:13, Luke 11:13). Every one of the faithful can therefore obtain this for himself by prayers, which, once obtained, leads a man into all truth.

The other medium is external, which those undoubted and common principles of the Christian religion provide, which can furnish the faithful with a sufficiently safe and exact rule and standard for judging any spirits whatsoever.

And indeed a more certain and firmer method of judging dogmas can be sought from these very principles than from the decrees of bishops; especially since it is common for any heretics whatsoever to boast that they hold the true opinion of the Church.

But there remains a third argument for our proof, which we seek from the Apostolic Creed, in which we by no means profess that we believe IN THE CHURCH: which is what would have to be done entirely if the absolute authority and infallibility of the Church were established in matters of faith. The Nicene Creed does indeed have this phrase, but it is less approved and accepted, which Rufinus also noted: It is not said, he says, in the Holy Church, but that the Holy Church is to be believed, not as God, but as a Church gathered by God. In which very sense Augustine writes: We believe Peter, we believe Paul; we do not believe in Peter or Paul; for to believe in someone is, by believing, to love, and by believing, to go into him. What of the fact that the same Apostolic Creed wished to decline this formula of speaking also, so that we might say we believe the Church, [just as] we believe the Scriptures, the Prophets, and the Apostles? For the writings of these are to be read not with the freedom of judging, but with the necessity of believing. In these, therefore, the Word of God demands an absolute assent for itself, so that one believes them not under the condition of a faith made elsewhere, but one believes these, sent by the Lord, as if [they were] the Lord himself. For he who hears them hears the Lord himself (Luke 10:16). The Apostolic Creed wished to intimate by this arrangement that the Church has not yet been raised to this pinnacle of dignity, as Augustine discusses more fully on this matter, lib. 11 contra Faustum Manich. cap. 5.

With these things having been premised concerning the absolute infallibility of the Church, which the Papists invent, the dispute will be easier: Whether the Church errs, or can err? Which itself, however, in order to be explained more solidly, would have to proceed in order by parts.

And at the beginning, indeed, the subject of the Question comes under consideration, which the Jesuits posit indefinitely, asserting that the Church cannot err. Bell. l. 3. de Eccl. mil, cap. 14. But the Church is understood in many ways: for it is understood either as the visible Church, or the invisible: or Universal, or particular: or finally it denotes the whole, or some part of it, or individual members.

Then, regarding the predicate, the Sophists speak ambiguously again. For error is twofold: either in morals and life: or in Doctrine. Again, error in doctrine either strikes at the foundation, or at least at some circumstance of the faith: Or that error is Universal and final, which is defined by a lasting apostasy; or particular and temporary, which is finally amended and cast off in the progress of time by the knowledge of true doctrine.

Finally, in the whole predication, that also lies hidden, which the Jesuits, contending that the Church cannot err, do not sufficiently explain, how they wish this to be understood: Namely, whether simply and absolutely: or indeed only in a certain respect, and with a certain condition, the Church cannot err?

We, therefore, intending to set forth our mind and opinion more explicitly, shall encompass the whole matter with these four hypotheses:

I. The Invisible Church, which is the assembly of the Elect, and indeed this whole Church, never errs all at once: For thus the Church of Christ would plainly fail and perish on this earth: which cannot happen.

II. The Catholic Church, which is that universal assembly of all and individual men professing the name of Christ on this earth, has never erred all at once, if you except the single fall of our first parents: Nor can it err all at once.

III. The impossibility of erring is attributed to both Churches, the Invisible and the Catholic or Universal, not in the Papal sense, that is, absolute, as if it could not simply err on account of some absolute infallibility: but in a composite sense, and under a certain condition, insofar as it is indeed a true Church: insofar as it follows the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and uniquely hears and embraces the voice of the Shepherd and Spouse Christ. Those clear promises favor and support this opinion: Matt. 16, 18. The gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Matt. 24, 24. It is impossible that the elect be led into error (namely, a final one, and one which overturns the foundation of salvation). Eph. 2, 20. The Church built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, whose cornerstone is Christ, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. 1 Tim. 3, 15. The Church of the living God is the pillar and foundation of Truth.

IV. Any Visible and particular Church, and that either in its entirety, or in its individual parts and members, errs and can err: even with an error that fights against the foundation and overturns salvation.

Now since we have the dispute and controversy primarily with the Jesuits concerning this fourth hypothesis: we demonstrate its affirmative most evidently to the eye with the following reasons.

Latin:

DEpendet hæc Controversia à præcedente proxima. Nam Ecclesiæ eam affingunt autoritatem Jesuvvitæ, quâ ipsi non sub certa conditione, sed absolutè in negocio religionis credendum sit, ita ut veritas fidei, quoad nos innitatur Ecclesiæ autoritati : & verum sit, quicquid Ecclesia probat: falsum, quicquid illa improbat, uti expressis verbis scribit Bellarminus: l. 3. de Ecclesia militante, cap. 14. p. 1277. A. Hoc ut persuadere possit lectoribus, arte planè veteratoria, hunc in modum solet progredi: Ecclesia in credendo errare non potest. Non solùm autem Ecclesia, antiqua in fide errare non potuit: sed ne Ecclesia quidem, quænunc est, quæve futura est ad consummationem seculi. Porrò non solùm Ecclesia Vniversalis, hoc est, Collectio omnium fidelium, hunc veritatis spiritum sempiternum habet: sed eundem habent etiam Ecclesiæ principes ac pastores, ut in fide errare non possint. Quicquid proindè docent Pastores atque Principes, quod ad fidem Christi attineat, id est verissimum, & Pastores ac Doctores omnes à fide nunquàm aberrare possunt. Hanc structuram Jesuvviticam, ut ex imis, quod ajunt, fundamentis subruamus, ἀναλύσεως opus fuerit; siquidem propter indefinitum & æquivocum Orationis sive pronunciatorum Jesuvviticorum Cothurnum, non mediocris & perplexitas & difficultas deprehenditur.

Initiò autem hypothesis illa προϋπόθεσις sub considerationem venit, An Ecclesiæ in causa fidei absoluta infallibilitas concedi possit aut debeat? Nos cum D. Augustino, solis Scripturarum libris, qui canonici appellantur, hunc timorem honoremque deferre didicimus, ut nullum eorum autorem scribendo aliquid errasse, ac proindè absolutam fidem ac autoritatem, in religionis negocio promereri firmissimè credamus. Augustinus Epist. 19. Tanta proindè est canonicarum Scripturarum sanctitas & excellentia, ut cum ea, nulla alia scripta aut dogmata, quot unque etiam veniant nomine, comparari, vel coæquari possint: usque adeò, ut si vel maximè in his quoque eadem inveniatur veritas : longè tamen impar sit autoritas: uti rursum scribit Augustinus lib. 1. contra Faust. Manich. c. 5.

Excipiant fortassis Jesuvvitæ, de paucis tantùm Doctoribꝫ, non verò de toto Vniversitate Doctorum aut Episcoporum istud scripsisse Augustinum. Sed neque sic quicquam obtinebunt: Neque enim ad numerum, sed ad autoritatem Episcoporum simpliciter respexit Augustinus, quam absolutam hominibus, quantovis numero, quantalibet sanctitate doctrinaque præpollentibus disertè derogat: ut nihil verum putetur ideò, quia ipsi ita senserunt; sed tantùm quia per autores canonicos persuadere potuerunt, quod verum dixerint scripserintve.

2. Porrò omnis omnium hominum prophetia sive doctrina debet esse analoga fidei, secundum præceptum Apostoli, Rom. 12, 6. debet consona esse legi & testimonio, juxta admonitionem Prophetæ Jesaiæ 8, 20. Quæ sanè ut & id genus dicta alia, uti absolutam autoritatem & infallibilitatem in causa fidei, omnibus hominibus, & quibusvis hominum ordinibus derogant: ita Ecclesiæ non nisi conditionatam autoritatem concedunt, eam nimirùm, quæ ad Scripturarum Canonem exigi ac mensurari debeat.

Excipiunt Jesuvitæ: Sic nullam Ecclesiæ tribui autoritatem: sic omnia reddi ambigua, quæ ab Ecclesia unquàm sunt definita, aut hodiè definiantur: Imò sic etiam in infinitam abiri incertitudinem, quia semper in promptu sit Exceptio, Ecclesiam posse falli in eo, quod Scripturas perperam intelligat. Ecquis verò tum judex erit? An Ecclesia ritè Scripturam interpretetur, nec ne? Quin sic illud etiam consequi, etiam privato cuig; fidem esse habendam, quando pronunciaverit secundum Scripturas: Quia omnia nimis sunt absurda.

Respondeo; Non fidei sed rationis tantùm humanæ absurda proferri. Fides enim Scriptura sic docente, credit, Ordinem etiam Ecclesiasticum interdum justo Dei judicio, tantâ errorum efficaciâ puniri à Deo: ut omnes Ecclesiæ speculatores sint cæci. 2. Paral. 15, 2. ut qui in templo Dei sedent, credant mendacio, & seductioni iniquitatis, eò quòd charitatem veritatis non receperunt, ut salvi fierent. 2. Thess. 2, 4. 10. & 11. Sic Fides statuit, monente iterum Scriptura, Ecclesiam Christi, tanquàm discipulam & sponsam ab ore magistri & sponsi sui sic pendere, ut ex se nihil quicquam sapere, sed ibi sapientiæ suæ terminum statuere debeat, ubi Christus Magister loquendi finem fecerit.

Quoad judicium interpretationis & controversiarum, etsi neque nos statuimus, in quemlibet Laïcorum sive privatorum hominum illud cadere: negari tamen minimè potest, sæpissimè evenisse, ut unius saltem hominis sententia, totius Ecclesiæ judicio, in causa religionis prævaluerit: id quod Eliæ exemplo in Ecclesia Jsraëlitica: item Paphnutij in Concilio Niceno, & Athanasij in Ecclesia Orientali sit manifestum. Accedit quòd Scriptura rursus docente, Justorum quisque, sive sit privatus sive publicus, sive Clericus sive Laïcus, non fide Ecclesiæ, sed sua propria fide vivere & salvari potest: Habacuc 2, 4. Rom. 1, 17. Ergò plurimùm interest, ut privatorum credentium quilibet in animo suo certus & securus esse possit ex Verbo Dei, de fidei suæ veritate. Nemini que, uti Romanenses opinantur, planè impossibilis est cuique credenti, etiam privato, sive Laico, earum rerum, quæ ad salutem scitu sunt necessariæ, dijudicatio. Nam duobus hac in parte medijs, longè convenientissimis uti potest: Vno interno, quod est Spiritus veritatis, qui haud minus fidelium cuique à Christo est promissus, quàm ipsi Ecclesiæ. Joh. 14, 16. Joh. 16, 13. Luc. 11, 13. Hunc ergò fidelium quisque precibus sibi comparare potest, qui comparatus, hominem inducit in omnem veritatem.

Alterum medium est externum, quod suppeditant indubitata illa, & communia Religionis Christianæ principia, quæ satis tutam & exactam ad judicandos quosvis Spiritus regulam & amussim fidelibus præstare possunt.

Et profectò certior ac firmior dijudicandi dogmata ratio, ex his ipsis principijs peti potest, quàm ex Episcoporum decretis: præsertim cùm quibusvis hæreticis hoc sit familiare, ut se veram Ecclesiæ sententiam tenere dictitent.

Sed superest & tertium probationis nostræ argumentum, quod ex Symbolo Apostolico petimus, in quo minimè profitemur, nos IN ECCLESIAM credere: id quod omninò faciendum, si in rebus fidei, absoluta constaret Ecclesiæ autoritas atque infallibilitas. Habet quidem phrasin hanc Symbolum Nicenum: sed minùs probatam & receptam: quod Ruffinus etiam annotavit: Non dicitur, inquiens, in Sanctam Ecclesiam: Sed Sanctam Ecclesiam credendam esse, non ut Deum: sed ut Ecclesiam Deo congregatam. Quo ipso sensu scribit Augustinus: Credimus Petro, Credimus Paulo: In Petrum aut Paulum non credimus: credere enim in aliquem, est credendo amare, & credendo in eum ire. Quid quòd idem Symbolum Apostolicum, hanc etiam loquendi formulam declinate voluit, ut diceremus nos credere Ecclesiæ Scripturis, Prophetis & Apostolis credimus. Horum enim Scripta, non cum judicandi libertate, sed cum credendi necessitate sunt legenda. In his ergò absolutum assensum Verbum Dei sibi flagitat, ut credatur ipsis non sub conditione factæ aliundè fidei: sed credatur istis, à Domino missis, tanquàm ipsi Domino. Qui enim bos audit, Dominum ipsum audit: Luc. 10, 16. Ad quod dignitatis fastigium nondum evectam esse Ecclesiam, Symbolum Apostolicum hoc pacto innuere voluit: uti fusiùs hac de re disputat Augustinus, lib. 11. contra Faustum Manich. cap. 5.

His de absoluta, quam fingunt Pontificij, Ecclesiæ infallibilitate ita præmissis, facilior erit disputatio, An Ecclesia erret, aut errare possit? Quæ ipsa tamen, ut solidiùs explicetur, ordine per partes progrediendum fuerit.

Ac initiò quidem Quæstionis subjectum sub considerationem venit, quod Jesuitæ indefinitè ponunt, asserentes Ecclesiam non posse errare. Bell. l. 3. de Eccl. mil, cap. 14. Jam verò Ecclesia multifariàm accipitur: vel enim intelligitur Ecclesia visibilis, vel invisibilis: vel Vniversalis, vel particularis: vel denique notat totum, vel partem ejus aliquam, aut singula individua.

Deindè, quoad prædicatum, rursus ambiguè loquuntur Sophistæ. Error enim duplex est: vel in moribus & vita: vel in Doctrina. Rursus error in doctrina vel impingit in fundamentum, vel in aliquam saltem circumstantiam fidei: Vel error iste est Vniversalis & finalis, qui per apostafiam durabilem definitur; vel particularis & temporaneus, qui tandem progressu temporis, veræ doctrinæ cognitione emendatur & abijcitur.

Tandem in prædicatione tota illud etiam ὕπυλον κρύφιεt, quod Jesuitæ contendentes Ecclesiam errare non posse, non satis explicant, quomodo hoc intellectum velint: Num videlicet simpliciter & absolutè: an verò tantùm secundum quid, & cum certa conditione, Ecclesia errare non possit?

Nos proindè explicatiùs nostram mentem atque sententiam expedituri, quatuor hisce hypothesibus rem totam comprehendemus:

I. Ecclesia Invisibilis, quæ est cœtus Electorum, & quidem Ecclesia hæc tota, nunquam simul errat: Sic enim planè deficeret & interiret Ecclesia Christi in his terris: id quod fieri nequit.

II. Ecclesia Catholica, quæ est universalis ille cœtus omnium & singulorum hominum, Christi nomen in his terris profitentium, nunquam tota simul erravit, si unicum lapsum proto-parentum nostrorum excipias: Neq; etiam tota simul errare potest.

III. Errandi impossibilitas tribuitur utriq; Ecclesiæ, Invisibili & Catholicæ sive Vniversali, non sensu Pontificio, hoc est, absoluto, quasi ob absolutam quandam infallibilitatem simpliciter errare non possit: sed sensu composito, & sub certa conditione, quatenùs nimirùm vera est Ecclesia: quatenus ductum Spiritus Sancti sequitur, & vocem Pastoris & Sponsusui Christi unicè audit & amplectitur. Favent huic sententiæ & patrocinantur promissiones illæ luculentæ: Matth. 16, 18. Portæ inferorum non prævalebunt adversus eam. Matth. 24, 24. Impossibile est, ut in errorem (finalem nimirùm, & qui salutis fundamentum evertat) inducantur electi. Ephes. 2, 20. Ecclesia superstructa fundamento Prophetarum & Apostolorum, cujus angularis lapis Christus, crescit in templum sanctum in Domino. 1. Timoth. 3, 15. Ecclesia Dei vivi est columna & firmamentum Veritatis.

IV. Ecclesia Visibilis & particularis qualibet, eaq; vel tota, vel in singulis ejus partibus atq; membris, errat & errare potest: errore etiam pugnante cum fundamento, & salutem evertente.

Jam cùm de quarta hac hypothesi nobis potissimùm lis & controversia sit cum Jesuvvitis: nos ejus affirmativam sequentibus rationibus ad oculum, evidentissimè demonstramus.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: Can err

can err.

1. The reason is taken from the example of the first parents, who as the beginning of the human race and the Church erred most gravely.

2. What happened to the Israelite Church, which erred gravely several times in its foundation, and even today still errs in such a way that it has been clearly rejected by God: that can happen to any particular Church.

3. The examples of the once most noble Churches of both the East and the West, of which not even traces remain any longer, demonstrate the same.

4. The same is evident from the example of the Apostles, who for some time were imbued with the error concerning the worldly kingdom of Christ and the exclusion of the Gentiles from it,

5. The Church at Corinth proves this very thing, in which the article of the Resurrection seems to have suffered either denial or certainly doubt, from the fact that the Apostle labors so painstakingly in confirming it, 1 Cor. 15, 36.

6. The Ephesian Church confirms the same, concerning which it is held in Apoc. 2, 5: Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the former works: if not, I will come to you quickly and will move your lampstand from its place.

7. Hardly any of all the Fathers can be found who has not been entangled in some error: a fact which not even the Romanists themselves can deny, as is clearly evident from the disputations of Bellarmine.

8. The most sorrowful complaints and threats of the Prophets confirm the same, by which they complain that the watchmen of the Church, that is, all the Bishops and Prelates, are blind, do not know, that is, all err, are dumb dogs, not willing to bark, seeing vain things, sleeping and loving dreams; ignorant of understanding, all turning aside to their own way, each one to his own greed, from the highest even to the lowest, Isa. 56, 10 & 11. To which pertains that 2 Chron. 15, 3: Many days shall pass in Israel without the true God, and without a Priest, a Teacher, and without law. And Jer. 5, 1: Go about the streets of Jerusalem and look, and consider, and seek in its squares, if you can find a man who does justice and seeks truth: and I will be propitious to him. Jer. 6, 13: From the prophet even to the priest, all deal falsely. Jer. 8, 8: How do you say, We are wise, and the Law of the Lord is with us? Truly the lying stylus of the Scribes has worked a lie: The wise are confounded, they are terrified and taken: for they have rejected the Word of the Lord, and there is no wisdom in them. Ezek. 7, 26: They shall seek a vision from the Prophet, and the Law shall perish from the Priest: and counsel from the Elders.

9. Unless any particular Church could fall into error, the Apostolic exhortations would be in vain, by which it is warned to beware of Idolatry, of the worship of images, of false prophets, of the Antichrist, lest it be seduced into error, lest anyone take away its prize, lest anyone impose upon it with persuasive words, or philosophy, or empty deception, according to the tradition of men.

10. The Apostle in the case of the Roman Church predicts that it can err to such an extent that it may be entirely cut off: Rom. 11, 20. & seqq. Do not be high-minded, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, see to it that it does not happen that He does not spare you: Behold the goodness and severity of God: on those indeed who fell, severity: but toward you goodness, if you continue in goodness; since you also may be cut off.

11. Councils, both Ecumenical and National, have erred most gravely and dangerously in matters of faith. The Council of Jerusalem, over which the Supreme Pontiff presided, and at which Scribes, Priests, and Pharisees assisted, condemns Christ and His doctrine.

The Council of the four hundred Prophets, convened by King Ahab, had the Devil himself as president, who was a lying Spirit in the mouth of all the Prophets, and therefore in it the Truth was condemned by the votes of all, the Prophet of the Lord, Micaiah, was proclaimed a heretic, was struck, and was thrown into prison. 1 Kings 22, 6. 22. 24. & 27.

The Second Council of Ephesus, with Dioscorus, Bishop of Alexandria, presiding, subscribed to the Eutychian heresy; Flavian, an Orthodox Bishop, having been condemned and removed from the government of the Church of Constantinople.

The Council of Constance committed sacrilege against the Testament of Christ: the Council of Trent approved more errors than it promulgated Canons: indeed, almost no council can be shown which has not produced some notable error, either new or established an old one.

12. Finally, an argument can be sought from the place of equals, in this manner: Any particular Church can fall into most grave sins, as regards life and morals. Therefore, it can also fall into most dangerous errors, as regards doctrine. The reason for the connection is this: Because both these and those flow from one and the same principle and source, namely, from the perverse will of man and the instigation of Satan.

With these things thus established in the thesis, the very antithesis of the Romanists must be more accurately weighed. And at the beginning, it is an altogether gross delirium that Bellarmine contends his thesis, that the Church cannot err, can be understood as much of the University of Bishops as of the University of the faithful, so that the sense of this proposition is: the Church cannot err, that is, that which all the faithful hold is necessarily true and of faith: and similarly, that which all Bishops teach, as pertaining to faith, is necessarily true and of faith, lib. 3. de Eccl. milit. cap. 14. pag. 1177. l. A. But that fraud is especially to be noted in this place, that by the university of Bishops he understands only the university of all Romanist Bishops, just as also by the Church he understands simply the Roman Church.

Then, however, it is simply false that the university of Bishops deserves the same faith and authority as the Universal Church of the faithful

can deserve. For it happens, and has happened several times, that the University of Bishops errs, even with one presbyter or layman protesting. And in this part a great sacrilege is committed by the Papists, while they do not fear to ascribe to the one and only order of Clerics that which belongs to all the faithful indiscriminately: You, says Peter, as many of you as are my hearers and readers of my Epistle, you, I say, are that chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, who may announce the mighty works of Him who called you out of darkness 1. Pet. 2, 9.

Then, with various little arguments scraped together from here and there, the Jesuit rises up against our arguments already proposed: and at the beginning indeed he carps at that which we took from the fall of our first parents, saying, if the whole Church then failed, then the invisible Church also failed, which conflicts with the doctrine of the Lutherans. 2. Two men do not constitute a Church: Therefore this example is impertinently applied here.

I answer to the former reason. We do not teach that the invisible Church never fails simply and absolutely: but after man is once received into grace after the fall, we certainly attribute the perpetuity of the Church to it. Thus no contradiction of our doctrine can be truly charged. As for the latter reason, it is too childish what the Jesuits object concerning the binary number. For does not Christ Himself testify that a gathering of two or three is such a congregation to which He will always be present with His grace, Matt. 18, 20. But let us concede to the Jesuit that those two first men can be called the beginning of the Church rather than the Church; is it not rightly inferred from this that the beginning of the Church erred, and consequently that hardly a better condition of the subsequent Church was to be hoped for: so that it itself could err: and although not in its entirety, yet it could fail in its parts, as is evident from the example of the Church at the time of the suffering and dying Christ, where very few remained immune from error and falling in matters of faith.

Then, to the passages of the Prophets produced by us, Bellarmine replies that those are to be understood as referring to false prophets.

I reply that we readily grant this very thing: but we immediately add that, since those very false prophets in the time of King Ahab were the teachers and leaders of the entire visible Church that was in the kingdom of Israel: it certainly follows evidently from this, that some entire particular visible Church, and all its pastors, both here and elsewhere, can generally err.

Thirdly, he criticizes that which we produced from chapter 56, 10 of Isaiah: All his watchmen are blind, etc., and he replies that 'all' in this place denotes the same as 'many'.
