However, what the Jesuit says, he does not prove. We urge the note of universality (all) which the Prophet expressed. What? Since, by the testimony of Jerome, the Israelite Church had such teachers who were the authors and instigators to King Manasseh to order the Orthodox Prophet Isaiah to be sawn asunder.

Fourthly, he attempts to evade the example of the Church at the time of the suffering and dying Christ by excepting that those Jews who perpetrated such wicked deeds against Christ were not the whole Church, since there were other Jews elsewhere who did not assent to these things.

But I reply: 1. The Jesuit is again begging the question. For it has not yet been proven that there were indeed Jews at that time who were Judaizing and who did not assent to the rest of the Jews in persecuting Christ. 2. He perverts the state of the controversy. For the question is not whether there can be Orthodox people elsewhere who do not err along with others—a thing which we ourselves grant not unwillingly—but this comes into controversy: Is there any particular Church whose leaders and Doctors can all err at the same time? Where we hold the affirmative, pointing to the Church of Jerusalem at the time of the suffering Christ.

He therefore answers nothing, but the Jesuit wanders off the point, saying that there could have been Jews elsewhere outside of Jerusalem who did not agree with the Jerusalemite Jews. For the question is not what kind of church the Hebronite one was, but what kind the Jerusalemite one was at that time. What is more, the Jesuit will not even be able to show that there were Jews, and Doctors of the Jews, living elsewhere who did not supremely hate the doctrine of Christ and persecute both him and his disciples. Acts 9:1; 1 Thess. 2:14.

Finally, to the example of the Apostles, who themselves also erred before the feast of Pentecost, the Jesuit replies: 1. That the Apostles were not yet Bishops, except as designated. 2. That the Church only began in the Apostles at the feast of Pentecost. 3. That they themselves did not lose the faith of the Resurrection, since they did not have it.

I reply: First, that is nonsensical; for it is manifestly false that the Apostles were ever constituted as Bishops of the kind the Papists imagine; since such an Episcopate removes the entire rationale of the Apostolate...

The other thing that the Jesuit brings forward is absurd. For it has not even been heard of that the Church of the New Testament did not have its beginning before the feast of Pentecost. It is indeed true that that solemn gathering of the New Testament Church from Jews and Gentiles began at Jerusalem at the feast of Pentecost; but that the Apostles did not previously constitute some Church together with the faithful adhering to Christ, that certainly cannot be elicited from there by any reason.

The third point is too diluted a κρησφύγεῖον [hiding place]. For although, speaking properly, the Apostles cannot be said to have lost the faith of the Resurrection, which they did not have, they are nevertheless rightly and properly said to have erred concerning that which they did not believe. But Bellarmine has other arguments by which he strives to confirm that the Church cannot err: lib. 3 de Eccl. mil. cap. 14.

He takes the first from 1 Tim. 3:13, where the Church is called the pillar and foundation of the truth. But we have already responded sufficiently to this argument above.

Latin:

errare possit.

1. Ratio sumitur ab exemplo protoplastorum, qui tanquam principium generis humani & Ecclesiæ gravissimè errarunt.

2. Quod obtigit Ecclesiæ Jsraeliticæ, quæ aliquoties in fundamento graviter erravit, ac etiamnum hodiè ita errat, ut planè à Deo sit rejecta: illud cuivis Ecclesiæ particulari obtingere potest.

3. Idem demonstrant exempla nobilissimarum quondam tùm Orientis, tùm Occidentis Ecclesiarum, quarum ne vestigia quidem amplius supersunt.

4. Patet idem Apostolorum exemplo, qui errore de mundano Christi regno, de gentibus ab eodem excludendis, aliquandiu imbuti erant,

5. Probat hoc ipsum Ecclesia Corinthiaca, in quâ articulus Resurrectionis, vel negationem, vel certè dubitationem passus fuisse videtur ex eo, quod in isto confirmando, tàm operosè Apostolus laborat 1. Cor. 15, 36.

6. Confirmat idem Ecclesia Ephesina, de qua Apoc. 2, 5. habetur: Memor esto, undè excideris, & resipisce, & priora opera facito: sin minùs, veniam adversus te citò & movebo candelabrum tuum, de loco suo.

7. Nullus fermè Patrum omnium dari potest, qui non errore aliquo intricatus fuerit: id quod ne quidem Romanenses ipsi negare possunt: uti ex disputationibus Bellarmini luculenter patet.

8. Comprobant idem querelæ & comminationes tristissimæ Prophetarum, quibus conqueruntur, speculatores Ecclesiæ, hoc est, Episcopos & Antistites omnes esse cæcos, nescire, hoc est, errare universos, esse canes mutos, non volentes latrare, videntes vana, dormientes & amantes somnia; ignorantes intelligentiam, omnes in viam suam declinantes, unumquemq; ad avaritiam suam, à summo usq; ad novissimum Jes. 56, 10. & 11. Quo pertinet illud 2. Paral. 15, 3. Multi dies transibunt in Israel absq; Deo vero, & absq; Sacerdote, Doctore & absq; lege. Et Jerem. 5, 1. circuimite vias Jerusalem & aspicite, & considerate, & quærite in plateis ejus, an inveniatis virum, facientem judicium, & quærentem fidem: & propitius ero ei. Jerem. 6, 13. A propheta usq; ad Sacerdotem, cuncti faciunt dolum. Jerem. 8, 8. Quomodo dicitis, Sapientes nos sumus, & Lex Domini nobiscum est? Verè mendacium operatus est Stylus mendax Scribarum: Confusi sunt sapientes, perterriti & capti sunt: Verbum enim Domini projecerunt, & Sapientia nulla est in eis. Jexech. 7, 26. Quærent visionem de Propheta, & Lex peribit à Sacerdote: & consilium à Senioribus.

9. Nisi Ecclesia quælibet particularis, in errorem incidere posset, frustraneæ forent exhortationes Apostolicæ, quibus monetur, ut caveat sibi ab Idololatria, à Simulachrorum cultu, à pseudo-prophetis, ab Antichristo, ne seducatur in errorem, ne quis ei palmam intervertat, nè quis imponat ei verbis probabilibus, vel philosophia, vel inani deceptione, juxta traditionem hominum.

10. D. Apostolus in specie Ecclesiæ Romanæ prædicit, posse illam ita errare, ut tota excindatur: Rom. 11, 20. & seqq. Ne efferaris animo, sed time. Nam si Deus naturalibus ramis non pepercit, vide, ne quà fiat, ut nec tibi parcat: Ecce bonitatem & severitatem Dei: in eos quidem, qui ceciderunt, severitatem: in te verò bonitatem, si permanseris in bonitate; quoniam & tu excindere.

11. Concilia tùm Oecumenica tùm Nationalia errarunt in rebus fidei gravissimè & periculosissimè. Concilium Hierosolymitanum, cui præerat summus Pontifex: cui assistebant Scribæ, Sacerdotes, Pharisæi, damnat Christum & doctrinam ejus.

Concilium quadringentorum Prophetarum, à Rege Achabo coactum, præsidem habuit ipsum Diabolum, qui erat Spiritus mendax in ore omnium Prophetarum, ac proindè in eo omnium suffragijs damnabatur Veritas, Micha Propheta Domini hæreticus proclamabatur, percutiebatur, conijciebatur in carcerem. 1. Reg. 22, 6. 22. 24. & 27.

Concilium Ephesinum II. præside Dioscoro Alexandriæ Episcopo, subscripsit hæresi Eutychianæ; damrnato & à gubernatione Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitanæ remoto Flaviano, Orthodoxo Episcopo.

Concilium Constantiense Sacrilegium commisit in Testamentum Christi: Tridentinum plures upprobavit errores, quàm promulgavit Canones: imò nullum fermè monstrari potest, quod non insignem aliquem errorem, vel novum prodiderit, vel veterem stabiliverit.

12. Tandem argumentum peti potest ex loco parium, in hunc modum: Quælibet Ecclesia particularis potest incidere in peccata gravissima, quoad vitam ac mores. Ergò incidere etiam potest in errores periculosissimos, quoad doctrinam. Ratio Connexio ist: Quia ex uno eodemque principio ac fonte, tam hi, quàm illa promanant, nempè ex perversa voluntate hominis, & instinctu Satanæ.

His in thesi ita constitutis ipsa Romanensium ἀντίθεσις accuratiùs expendenda venit. Acinitiò quidam crassum omninò delirium est, quod Bellarminus thesin suam, Ecclesiam errare non posse, contendit tàm intelligi posse de Universitate Episcoporum, quàm de Universitate fidelium, ut sensus sit propositionis hujus, Ecclesia non potest errare, hoc est, id quod tenent omnes fideles, necessario verum est, & de fide: & similiter, id, quod docent omnes Episcopi, tanquàm ad fidem pertinens, necessariò est verum & de fide lib. 3. de Eccl. milit. cap. 14. pag. 1177. l. A. Est autem illa fraus cumprimis hoc loco observanda, quod per universitatem Episcoporum tantum intelligit universitatem omnium Episcoporum Romanensium, quemadmodum etiam per Ecclesiam simpliciter intelligit Ecclesiam Romanam.

Deindè verò simpliciter falsum est, quòd universitas Episcoporum eandem fidem autoritatemque mereatur, quàm Universa fidelium

Ecclesia mereri potest. Fit enim, & factum aliquoties, ut Universitas Episcoporum erret, vel uno saltem reclamante presbytero aut Laico. Et hac in parte grande Sacrilegium committitur à Pontificijs, dùm, quod omnibus promiscuè fidelibus competit, illud soli atque uni ordini Clericorum adscribere haud verentur: Vos, inquit Petrus, quotquot mei estis auditores, meæque Epistolæ lectores, Vos inquam estis genus illud electum, regale Sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis, qui virtutes annunciet ejus, qui de tenebris vocavit eos 1. Petr. 2, 9.

Deindè varijs hinc indè corrasis ratiunculis, adversus argumenta nostra jam proposita, insurgit Jesuvvita: ac initiò quidem vellicat illud, quod à lapsu protoparentum desumsimus, si inquiens, Ecclesia tota tùm defecit, tùm invisibilis etiam Ecclesia defecit, id quod cum Lutheranorum doctrina pugnat. 2. Duo homines non constituunt Ecclesiam: Ergò impertinenter hoc exemplum huc accommodatur.

Respondeo ad priorem rationem. Nos non docere Ecclesiam invisibilem simpliciter & absolutè nunquàm deficere: sed postquam homo post lapsum semel in gratiam est receptus, utique perennitatem Ecclesiæ illi tribuimus. Sic nulla nostræ doctrinæ ἀντίφασις sive Contradictio verè impingipotest. Quoad posteriorem rationem, puerile nimis est, quod de numero binario obvertunt Jesuvvitæ. Annon enim Christus ipse testatur, conventum duorum aut trium talem esse congregationem, cui gratiâ suâ semper sit adfuturus, Matth. 18, 20. Sed concedamus Jesuvvitæ, duos illos primos homines initium potiùs Ecclesiæ, quàm Ecclesiam dici posse; annon rectè indè colligitur initium Ecclesiæ errasse ac proindè vix meliorem subsequentis Ecclesiæ conditionem sperandam fuisse: ita ut & ipsa errare: & licet non tota, secundum partes tamen deficere possit, uti patet ex emplo Ecclesiæ, tempore patientis & morientis Christi, ubi paucissimi extiterunt, in rebus fidei ab errore & lapsu immunes.

Deindè ad loca Prophetarum, à nobis producta, respondet Bellarminus, illæ esse intelligenda de Pseudo Prophetis.

Respondeo, hoc ipsum nos facilè largiri: sed statim subsumere, cum illi ipsi Pseudo prophetæ tempore Regis Achab fuerint Doctores & Antistites totius visibilis Ecclesiæ, quæ erat in regno J srael: utique vel indè evidenter consequi, Ecclesiam aliquam visibilem particularem totam, ipsiusque Pastores omnes, & hîc, & alibi generaliter errare posse.

Tertiò vellicat illud quod ex cap. 56, 10. Jesaiæ produximus: Omnes speculatores ej9 sunt cæci &c. & respondet, omnes hoc loco idē notare ac multos. Cæterùm quod dicit Jesuvvita, nō probat. Nos urgemus notā Universalitatis (omnes) quam expressit Propheta. Quid? quod Hieronymo teste, Ecclesia J sraelitica ejusmodi Doctores habebat, qui autores & instigatores erant Regi Manassæ, ut Prophetam Orthodoxum Jesaiam, serra disfecari juberet.

Quartò Exemplum Ecclesiæ, tempore patientis & morientis Christi, sic eludere conatur, ut excipiat, Iudæos illos, qui tam nefanda in Christum perpetrarunt, non fuisse totam Ecclesiam, cum alibi essent alij Iudæi, qui his non assentiebantur.

Sed respondeo 1. Jesuvvitam rursum petere principium. Nam fuisse Judæos verò tùm judaizantes, qui reliquis Judæis in persequendo Christo non assentirentur, nondùm probatum est. 2. pervertit statum controversiæ. Non enim hoc in quæstione est, an alibi locorum possint esse Orthodoxi, qui cum alijs non errent? id quod ipsi haud inviti largimur: sed hoc venit in Controversiam, An detur particularis aliqua Ecclesia, cujus præsules & Doctores simul omnes errare possint? Ubi nos Affirmativam tenemus, monstrantes Ecclesiam Hierosolymitanam, tempore patientis Christi.

Nihil ergo respondet, sed extra oleas vagatur Jesuvvita, dicens, extra Hierosolymam alibi potuisse esse Judæos, qui cum Iudæis Hierosolymitanis non convenirent. Neque enim qualis ecclesia Hebronitica, sed qualis Hierosolymitana tùm fuerit, quæritur. Quid, quod ne quidem monstrare poterit Jesuvvita, Judæos, Judæorumq; Doctores, alibi etiam viventes, qui non doctrinam Christi summè odissent, & tùm ipsum, tùm ejus discipulos persequerentur. Actor. 9, 1. 1. Thess. 2, 14.

Tandem ad exemplum Apostolorum, qui & ipsi errarint, ante festum Pontecostes, respondet Jesuvvita, 1. Apostolos tùm non fuisse Episcopos, nisi designatos. 2. Ecclesiam in Apostolis demùm cœpisse in festo Pentecostes. 3. ipsos fidem Resurrectionis non amisisse, quippè quam non habuerint.

Respondeo, Primùm illud esse nugatorium: Apostolos enim unquam fuisse Episcopos constitutos, quales fingunt Pontificij, manifestè falsum est: Siquidem Episcopatus talis, tollit omnem Apostolatus rationem...

Alterum quod profert Jesuvvita est absurdum. Nam ante festum Pentecostes Ecclesiam Novi Testamenti non habuisse initium, ne fando quidem auditum est. Illud quidem verum est, quod solennis illa collectio Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti, ex Judæis & gentibus cœperit Hierosolymis in festo Pentecostes: sed quod prius Apostoli non constituerint Ecclesiam aliquam unà cum fidelibus Christo adhærentibus: id certè indè elici nulla ratione potest.

Tertium illud nimis dilutum est κρησφύγεῖον. Etsi enim propriè loquendo Apostoli non possunt dici amisisse fidem Resurrectionis: quam non habuerunt: rectè tamen ac propriè dicuntur errasse circa id, quod non credebant. Sed habet Bellarminus alia argumenta, quibus confirmare studet, Ecclesiam errare non posse: lib. 3. de Eccl. mil. cap. 14.

Primum desumit ex 1. Tim. 3, 13. Ubi Ecclesia dicitur columna & firmamentum veritatis. Sed ad hoc argumentum jam supra sufficienter respondimus.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: Can err

can err.

The other is such: The Church is governed by Christ as by its head and Spouse, and by the Holy Spirit as by its soul. Therefore, if the Church were to err in dogmas of faith or morals, the error would be attributed to Christ and the Holy Spirit.

I reply: 1. The whole argument is granted if it is understood of the Universal and Invisible Church of the Elect, which never errs as a whole at the same time. But if the argument is accommodated to any particular Church, then its vanity can easily be shown. For Christ governs the Church, but not immediately or absolutely; rather, he does so mediately through the Word. This therefore being repudiated, or depraved, the operation of Christ and the Holy Spirit immediately expires; and when that ceases, the darkness of errors creeps in of its own accord, even in Paradise itself. Therefore, that proposition of the Jesuits concerning the governance and illumination of the Church by Christ and the Holy Spirit must always be taken in a composite sense: namely, in this sense, that the Church, governed and illuminated by the teaching of Christ and the Holy Spirit—insofar as it follows the lead of that teaching and walks in the light of God—does not err and cannot err. But if now this hypothesis is exchanged with the contrary, that is, if the Church, having shaken off the dictates of Christ and the Holy Spirit, loosens the reins for its own desires and opinions (a thing which no one will deny happens quite often), it is spontaneously evident that, in this case, the Church is both able to err, and does err in the very act.

Stapleton insists and objects that the faithfulness of the bridegroom and shepherd Christ requires this, that he never desert his bride and his sheep.

I reply that a fallacy of ἑτεροζητήσεως is being committed, and a shameful ἀγνοιαν ἐλέγχε: for the question here is not about the faithfulness of Christ toward the Church, since no one except the extremely impious doubts that.

Furthermore, this faithfulness of the Bridegroom and Shepherd Christ exerts itself effectively toward the invisible and Catholic Church, which is the communion of saints, of those who truly believe in Christ the Bridegroom and in turn prove their faithfulness to him. But neither is there a controversy in this place about this Church, namely, whether it errs in this faithfulness of Christ? For we ourselves hold the negative. For who would err in that, which by following Christ the Bridegroom and Shepherd, does not walk in darkness: but has the light of life, John 8.12. But the question is agitated primarily about the visible and particular Church, and it is debated whether it always proves its faithfulness to Christ the Bridegroom. Where we have already proven before with very many examples and testimonies of Scripture that it very often fails in this faithfulness which it owes to the Bridegroom.

The third argument of Bellarmine sounds thus: We are obligated under penalty of anathema to believe the Church in all things, as is evident in Matthew 18:17. If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. Therefore it is necessary that whatever the Church decrees be true and in no way false. For it would be unjust to be obligated under such a grave penalty to assent to things uncertain, and sometimes false.

I reply 1. That the Jesuit commits the crime of forgery when he adds from his own store, that in all things one must believe the Church. 2. A refutation of his ignorance [ἀγνοιας ἐλέγχꝢ]. For Christ does not treat in Matthew 18:17 of the dogmas of faith, of the interpretation of Scripture, or of the business of religion: but of fraternal correction and admonition, which ought to observe certain degrees, until it is referred to the Church, and the judgment of that body is sought concerning the neighbor's offense. 3. Even if this passage is taken as referring to faith, it nevertheless admits of a restriction, namely, that the Church is to be heard only insofar as it follows the footsteps of Scripture. Otherwise, that saying of the Apostle in Galatians 1:8 militates against it: If an angel from heaven should announce to you a gospel other than that which has been preached to you, let him be anathema.

The fourth argument is as follows: The Apostles' Creed teaches that the Church is holy. But this holiness consists in the profession of dogmas. Therefore, the Christian profession contains nothing except what is holy, that is, true with regard to doctrine, and just with regard to morals.

I answer 1. to the Major premise, which is simply true. For the Church is called Holy, partly with respect to the invisible Church of the Elect, which also never errs in its entirety: partly with respect to the means of calling, through which the Church is gathered here on earth, which in themselves are most holy. But from this, the consequence does not hold for any visible particular Church. For although it is of simple necessity that in the visible assembly of the called there should always be some Elect, to whom the title of Holiness truly belongs: it is not, however, of the same necessity that that very visible assembly, in every part either of Teachers or of Hearers, should be holy and unable to err.

Then the consequence is plainly futile: The Church is holy, therefore it cannot err. For thus it would also be right to argue: The Church is holy, therefore it cannot sin. And yet it can sin, 1 Joh. 1, 8: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us; therefore it can also err.

Finally, in the minor premise, the Sophism of Definition is committed. For the Holiness of the Church cannot, nor ought it to be, defined by some simple and absolute Holiness in the profession of dogmas: since, as the Prophet testifies, it is possible for the Spouse of Christ to degenerate into an adulteress and a harlot, Isa. 1, 21; 2 Cor. 11, 2, et seqq. But it must be defined by a conditional Holiness, which consists partly in that imputed Holiness of Christ, and partly in that Holiness which is begun, but imperfect, and subject to many infirmities of errors, a fact which we have already attested above by the examples of many.

Bellarmino’s fifth argument is as follows: If the Church can err and does err, the greatest part of dogmas could be called into doubt: for we believe many things which are not absolutely necessary for salvation: such as that the histories of the Old Testament, or the Gospels of Mark and Luke, are canonical writings, etc. But this latter is absurd. Therefore, so is the former.

I answer that the fallacy ὠς διὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον is being committed. For even that historical faith, concerning the certainty of the Canonical books of both Testaments, does not depend absolutely upon the Church: but only in a certain respect, namely by reason of testimony, while in the meantime those books bear witness to themselves of divine certainty and truth. Furthermore, it is an altogether gross and intolerable error of Bellarmine that he writes that it is not necessary for salvation to believe that there is some Canonical Word of GOD: and indeed, specifically, that this or that Prophetic and Apostolic writing is that very Canonical Word of GOD which points out the way of salvation without doubt. Nay, more, it was scarcely ever heard of even by hearsay before this, what Bellarmine adds, that without this faith many heathens and barbarians have been saved.

Certainly those who deny or are ignorant of this are not Christians, nor can they even be saved: for salvation comes to no one without faith: but faith comes to no one except through the Word of GOD, and indeed that of the Gospel. Therefore, he who is ignorant that this is the canonical Word of GOD, that he who believes in the Son may have eternal life, he does not have faith, and consequently cannot be saved. Thus, he who doubts that the writings of the Prophets and Apostles have canonical authority, he must necessarily doubt the truth of their dogmas as well. But he who doubts in this way cannot be saved eternally, unless perhaps the Jesuits wish to affirm, through an unheard-of ἀῤῥησίαν ἀγνοίας, that it is possible to be saved for those who do not believe that the Gospel of John is canonical, and consequently do not believe it to be true that which is written in it, that Christ is the true GOD: that the Son of GOD was made flesh, and that everyone who believes in Him will have eternal life. But the Jesuit insists: Before there were Scriptures, it was not necessary to believe them. I reply that the point at issue here is not the Scriptures insofar as they are Scriptures, which is a matter of accident, but insofar as they are the Word of God. 2. The question is not whether those who lived before the Scriptures were necessarily obliged to believe the Scriptures; for we ourselves know that a non-existent thing has no qualities. But this is what is asked: since the Scriptures have now been written down by God’s command, are we necessarily bound to believe them? To which we answer in the affirmative. If the Jesuit maintains the negative, he reveals a staggering and more than heretical vanity of mind.

The sixth and final argument Bellarmine takes from the authority of Tertullian and Augustine, who in the question concerning matters of faith appealed to the Church: which they certainly would by no means have done, if they had thought that the Church could err.

I reply 1. The fallacy τὸ μὴ ἀιτίᾳ is committed. For the infallibility of the Church cannot be asserted for the reason that many Fathers appealed to its judgment. Thus, one appeals to a political judge: is he therefore unable to be deceived or to err? There is no connection, no reason. 2. The error ῶδὲ τὶ ῶῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς is committed. The Fathers appealed to the Church, not simply to any visible and particular one, but to the one which they determined to be most true and to hold the sense of Scripture correctly. 3. The Fathers appealed to the Church, not because they determined that it simply could not err, but because they thought that heresies could be repressed and refuted all the more strongly by the consensus and agreement of many churches.

But other Jesuits bring forward many other reasons for their opinion, the chief of which are these: 1. Christ gave the Church clear promises concerning its perpetual preservation in the Truth: Therefore, these promises remaining safe, no error can have a place in the Church.

I answer. 1. Christ makes equally clear promises not only to the Church, but also to individual believers. Now, indeed, no one who has been a stranger to the Scriptures, or who has been ignorant that renewal in this life is not perfect and that the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit remains, would doubt that individual believers, even if divinely illuminated and governed by the Holy Spirit, can err.

2. Those promises, however clear, are nevertheless not absolute or simple: but conditional, namely, if the Church hears and follows the voice of its Spouse and shepherd: Just as this condition is expressly stated. John 8:31, if you abide in my word, you will truly be my disciples. And John 15:10, if you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love. And verse 14, You are my friends, if you do what I command you.

3. Whatever has been promised to the Church is rightly applied to individual believers: just as, conversely, what has been said to individual believers is not inappropriately reduced to the Church itself. For there is in this respect a certain homogeneity of the whole and the parts. For the promise is made to the Church for no other reason than that the individual members may participate in the promised goods; nor is anything brought forward in this regard to individual members, except what pertains by common reason to the whole Church.

4. Now, indeed, it has been said to individuals, if you abide in my word: Therefore, that promise also pertains to all, that is, to the whole Church. For what is the Church other than a multitude of individual believers?

5. Hence, therefore, it is finally inferred that, just as individual believers, endowed with the Holy Spirit, can err and often do err if they abandon the word of God: so the Church likewise can err if it does not abide in the word of the Lord.

6. Moreover, it is further subsumed: Individual members of the Church considered by themselves can err: whole particular churches can err: the entire ministry of a particular church: whole councils can err. Therefore, the assertion of the Papists is false, that the Church, by the power of the promises made to it, cannot err.

II. The Jesuitical argument is usually of this kind: The Church is called in the Scriptures the Kingdom of God. But in the kingdom of God, not error, but truth reigns. Therefore, the Church cannot err.

I answer that the major premise is true: For the Church is the kingdom of heaven and the kingdom of Truth, insofar as it is subject to its king, Christ, and to his word, which is truth. In which sense the Church is called the kingdom not only of Truth, but also of righteousness. Now, indeed, just as it does not follow: The Church is called the kingdom of righteousness: Therefore it cannot sin: So it does not follow at all: The Church is called the kingdom of truth. Therefore it cannot err.

Then, indeed, granted but not conceded that what the Jesuits intend can be gathered from these titles: it could not, however, be accommodated to any church, but only to the true Church. But what is this to the Roman Church, which is a Lerna of heresies and a brothel of supposed Truth?

III. This Jesuitical argument is brought forward: What was said to the supreme Rector of the Church, Peter, that pertains to the whole Church: But Christ said to Peter, Luke 22:32, I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. Therefore, the same also pertains to the Church, and consequently the Church cannot fail in faith.

I reply to the major premise, that it is false from the beginning that the Adversaries presuppose that Peter was the supreme Ruler and universal Bishop of the Church.

2. Even if he were such: nevertheless the consequence can neither be, nor ought to be, extended to this or that particular Church: but only to the whole Universal Catholic Church, as also to the invisible Church of the elect: Where we willingly concede that it is rightly attributed to the prayers of Christ that it can never, as a whole, err at the same time, or does err.

3. What Christ said to Peter was personal: and therefore cannot be referred to the whole species.

4. A fallacy of figure of speech is committed in the phrase: I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: the sense of which is not that the faith of Peter could not possibly fail, or did not truly fail. For it certainly failed when he thrice denied Christ: it failed when he did not believe in the Resurrection of Christ: it failed when he denied that the Gentiles pertained to the fellowship of Christ: it failed concerning the doctrine of the right use of Christian liberty, in his conversation with the Gentiles, erring dangerously, Gal. 2, 11. But this is the sense of the words of Christ, that He prayed for Peter, that his faith might not finally fail, and that he himself might not perish in his fall, but being restored, might be saved. Therefore, the faith of Peter is said not to have failed, on account of the subsequent restoration, which Christ obtained by His prayers: in the very same sense in which it is said in Luke 8, 52, of the daughter of Jairus: she is not dead: namely, on account of the miracle of resuscitation that was to follow.

5. And lastly: if the Jesuits infer from the example of Peter to the Pope, that on account of the prayers of Christ the faith of the latter also cannot fail: the consequence is no more valid than from a stick to a corner. Since between Peter the Apostle and the Roman Pontiff, both by reason of person, and of office and doctrine, there exists no greater agreement than exists between Christ and Belial, between light and darkness, between truth and a lie.

Latin:

errare possit.

Alterum tale est : Ecclesia gubernatur à Christo, tanquàm à capite Sponso suo, & à Spiritu Sancto, tanquàm ab anima. E. si Ecclesia in dogmatibus fidei vel morum erraret, Christo & Spiritui Sancto error tribueretur.

Resp. 1. Argumentum totum concedi, si de Ecclesia Universali & Invisibili Electorum intelligatur, quæ nunquàm tota simul errat. Si verò ad Ecclesiam quamlibet particularem argumentum accommodetur, tùm ejus vanitas facilè monstrari potest. Christus enim gubernat Ecclesiam, sed non immediatè sive absolutè: Verùm mediatè per Verbum. Hoc ergò repudiato, sive depravato, expirat statim Christi & Spiritus Sancti operatio : quâ cessante, errotum tenebræ sua sponte obrepunt, etiam in ipso Paradiso. Proindè semper in sensu composito accipienda est illa Jesuvvitarum propositio, de gubernatione & illuminatione Ecclesiæ per Christum & Spiritum Sanctum: hoc nimirùm sensu, ut Ecclesia magisterio Christi & Spiritus Sancti gubernata ac illuminata, quatenùs nempè magisterij illius ductum sequitur, & in lumine Dei ambulat, non erret nec errare possit. Quod si jam hypothesis hæc cum contraria permutetur, hoc est, si Ecclesia, excusso dictamine Christi & Spiritus Sancti, suis cupiditatibus & placitis frena laxet, (id quod sæpiusculè fieri nemo negaverit) ultrò patet, hoc casu, Ecclesiam & posse errare, & errare ipso actu.

Instat Stapletonus & obijcit, fidem sponsi & pastoris Christi hoc requirere, ut Sponsam & oves suas nunquàm deserat.

Respondeo committi Sophisma ἑτεροζητήσεως, & turpem ἀγνοιαν ἐλέγχε : Non enim de fide Christi in Ecclesiam hîc quæritur, quippè de quâ nemo nisi extremè impius dubitat.

Deindè fides hæc Sponsi & Pastoris Christi ad Ecclesiam invisibilem & Catholicam, quæ est communio Sanctorum, in Christum Sponsum verè credentium, & fidem illi suam vicissim probantium se efficaciter exerit. Sed neque de hac Ecclesia hoc loco controvertitur, Vèrum hàc in fide Christi erret ? Nam nos ipsi negativam tenemus. Qui enim ista erraret, quæ Christum Sponsum & Pastorem sequendo, non ambulat in tenebris : sed habet lumen vitæ, Iob 8.12. Verùm de visibili & particulari Ecclesia quæstio potissimùm agitatur, & nùm ea Christo Sponso fidem suam semper probet, controvertitur. Ubi sæpissimè hanc fidem, quam Sponso debet, fallere, jam ante exemplis bene multis, & Scripturæ testimonijs evicimus.

Tertium argumentum Bellarmini sic sonat: Obligamur sub anathematis pœna, credere Ecclesiæ in omnibus, ut patet Matth. 18, 17. Quod si Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi velut Ethnicus & publicanus. Ergò necessum est, ut quicquid Ecclesia decernit, sit verum minimeq; falsum. Nam iniquum foret, sub tam gravi pœna obligari ad assentiendum rebus incertis, & interdum falsis.

Respondeo 1. Crimen falsi committere Jesuvvitam cum de suo addit, in omnibus credendum esse Ecclesiæ. 2. ἀγνοιας ἐλέγχꝢ. Non enim agit Christus Matth. 18, 17. de dogmatibus fidei, de interpretatione Scripturæ, aut de Religionis negocio: sed de fraternæ correptione & admonitione, quæ certos gradus observare debeat, usquedùm ad Ecclesiam deferatur, & de delicto proximi illius sententia exquiratur. 3. Si maximè de fide accipiatur locus iste, tamen restrictionem patitur, ut nempè Ecclesia audiatur eatenùs, quatenùs Scripturæ vestigia sequitur. Aliàs militat illud Apostoli, Gal. 1, 8. Si angelus de cælo aliud vobis annunciet Evangelium, præter id, quod vobis est prædicatum, Anathema sit.

Quartum argumentum tale est: Ecclesiam esse sanctam docet Symbolum Apostolorum. Atqui Sanctitas hæc in profeßione dogmatum consistit. Ergo Christiana profeßio nihil continet, nisi sanctum, id est, verum quoad doctrinam, & justum quoad mores.

Respondeo 1. ad Majorem, quæ ἅπλως vera est. Dicitur enim Ecclesia Sancta, partim respectu invisibilis Electorum Ecclesiæ, quæ etiam nunquam tota errat: partim respectu mediorum vocationis, per quæ Ecclesia his in terris colligitur, quæ in se longè sunt sanctißima. Cæterùm hinc ad quamvis visibilem particularem Ecclesiam non valet consequentia. Etsi enim de necessitate simplici est, ut in visibili vocatorum cœtu, semper sint aliqui Electi, quibus Sanctitatis elogium verè competit: non tamen ejusdem est necessitatis, ut ille ipse cætus visibilis, ex omni parte vel Doctorum, vel Auditorum sit sanctus, & errare nequeat.

Deinde futilis planè est Consequentia: Ecclesia est sancta, Ergo errare non potest. Sic enim fas etiam foret argumentari: Ecclesia est sancta. Ergo peccare non potest. Atqui peccare potest 1. Joh. 1, 8. Si dixerimus, quod peccatum non habeamus, ipsi nos seducimus, & veritas non est in nobis, Ergo & errare potest.

Tandem in minore committitur Sophisma Definitionis. Neque enim Sanctitas Ecclesiæ definiri potest, aut debet, per simplicem & absolutam aliquam Sanctitatem in professione dogmatum: siquidem Propheta teste, fieri potest, ut Sponsa Christi degeneret in adulteram & meretricem, Jes. 1, 21. 2. Cor. 11, 2. & seqq. Sed definienda est per Sanctitatem conditionatam, quæ consistit partim in imputata illâ Sanctitate Christi: partim verò in inchoatâ illâ, sed imperfectâ, & multis errorum infirmitatibus obnoxia, id quod plurimorum exemplis suprâ testatum dedimus.

Quintum argumentum Bellarmini sic habet: Si Ecclesia errare potest & errat, maxima pars dogmatum in dubium vocari posset: nam multa credimus, quæ non absolutè necessaria sunt ad salutem: Ut historias Veteris Testamenti, vel Evangelia Marci & Lucæ esse Canonica Scripta &c. Atqui hoc posterius absurdum. Ergò & prius illud.

Respondeo committi Sophisma ὠς διὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Nam fides etiam illa historica, de certitudine librorum Canonicorum Utriusq; Testamenti, non absolute pendet ab Ecclesia: sed tantùm secundum quid, ratione videlicet testificationis, cùm interim libri illi, sibiipsis divinæ certitudinis atque veritatis perhibeant testimonium. Deinde crassus omninò & intolerabilis error est Bellarmini, quòd scriptitat, non esse necesse ad salutem credere, esse aliquod Verbum DEI Canonicum: & quidem in specie hoc vel illud scriptum Propheticum & Apostolicum, esse illud ipsum Verbum DEI canonicum, quod salutis viam indubitato monstret. Quin imô vix unquam antehac vel fando auditum fuit, quod Bellarminus subjicit, sine hac fide multos Ethnicos & barbaros fuisse servatos.

Certè hoc qui negant aut ignorant, Christiani non sunt, neque salvari etiam possunt: Salus enim nemini obtingit sine fide: Fides au tem nemini obtingit, nisi per Verbum DEI, & quidem Evangelij. Ergò qui ignorat hoc esse Verbum DEI Canonicum, ut qui crediderit in Filium, habeat vitam æternam, is fidem non habet, ac proindè salvari nequit. Sic qui dubitat Scripta Prophetarum & Apostolorum habere canonicam autoritatem, is de eorundem dogmatum Veritate itidem dubitet, necessum habet. Qui vero sic dubitat, in æternum salvari nequit, nisi fortè per inauditam ἀῤῥησίαν ἀγνοίας affirmare velint Jesuitæ, salvari posse, qui non credant Johannis Evangelium esse Canonicum, ac proindè neque credunt verum esse, quod in ipso scriptum est, Christum esse verum DEUM: Filium DEI carnem factum esse, & omnem qui crediderit in ipsum, habiturum vitam æternam. Sed instat Jesuvvita: Antequàm erant Scripturæ, non erat necessarium ijs credere. Respondeo, non de Scripturis, quatenùs sunt Scripturæ, id quod accidentis est: sed quatenus sunt Verbum DEI, hoc loco disputari. 2. Non quæstio est, An qui vixerunt ante Scripturas, credere necessariò debuerint Scripturis? Nam ipsi novimus, Non entis nullas esse qualitates: Sed hoc quæritur, Cùm nunc DEI mandato Scripturæ sint exaratæ, an nos necessariò teneamur illis credere? Ubi nos affirmatè respondemus. Negativam si tenet Jesuvvita, stupendam & plusquàm hæreticam prodit animi vanitatem.

Sextum & ultimum argumentum Bellarminus desumit ab autoritate Tertulliani & Augustini, qui in quæstione de rebus fidei, ad Ecclesiam provocarunt: quod certè nullo modo fecissent, si Ecclesiam errare posse existimassent.

Respondeo 1. Committi Sophisma τὸ μὴ ἀιτίᾳ. Non enim ideò infallibilitas Ecclesiæ adstrui potest, quia multi Patres ad ejus judicium provocarunt. Sic provocatur ad judicem politicum: Ergòne propterea falli ille aut errare non potest? Nullus nexus, nulla ratio. 2. error committitur ῶδὲ τὶ ῶῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Provocarunt Patres ad Ecclesiam, non simpliciter, ad quamvis visibilem & particularem, sed quam statuerunt maximè veram esse & Scripturæ sensum rectè tenere 3. provoearunt Patres ad Ecclesiam, non quod statuerunt eam simpliciter errare non posse, sed quod tantò fortiùs hæreses ex consensu & onovoia plurimum Ecclesiarum, reprimi ac refelli posse arbitrarentur.

Sed proferunt alij Jesuvitæ plures alias rationes, pro sua sententia, quales præcipuæ sunt hæ: 1. Christus dedit Ecclesiæ promissiones luculentas, de perpetua conservatione in Veritate: Ergò promissionibus hisce salvis permanentibus, nullus in Ecclesia error locum habere potest.

Respondeo. 1. Non Ecclesiæ tantùm, sed & singulis fidelibus æquè luculentas promissiones facit Christus. Jam verò, quin singuli fidelium, etiam divinitùs illuminati, & Spiritu Sancto gubernati, errare possint, nemo dubitaverit, nisi qui hospes fuerit in Scripturis, aut ignoraverit, renovationem in hac vita non esse perfectam, & manere luctam carnis & Spiritus.

2. Promissiones illæ, quantumvis luculentæ non tamen sunt absolutæ sive simplices: sed conditionatæ, nempè si Ecclesiæ vocem Sponsi & pastoris sui audiat & sequatur: Quemadmodum hæc conditio disertè exprimitur. Joh. 8. 31. si manseritis in sermone meo, verè discipuli mei eritis. Et Johan. 15, 10. si præcepta mea servaveritis, manebitis in dilectione mea Et vers. 14 Vos amici mei estis, si feceritis, quæ ego præcipio vobis.

3. Quæcunque Ecclesiæ sunt promissa, rectè ad singulos credentes applicantur: sicut vice versa, quæ singulis credentibus dicta sunt, haud incongruè ad Ecclesiam ipsam reducun tur. Est enim hac in parte ὁμοιουμέρεια quædam totius atque partium. Nam non alio nomine Ecclesiæ fit promissio, nisi ut promissis bonis singula membra participēt; nec ad singula membra hoc in genere quicquam profer tur, nisi quod communi ratione ad totam Ecclesiam spectat.

4. Jam verò singulis dictum est, si manseritis in sermone meo: Ergò ad universos, hoc est Ecclesiam totam promissio etiam illa pertinet. Quid est enim Ecclesia aliud, quàm singulorum credentium multitudo.

5. Hinc ergò illud tandem infertur, sicut singuli fideles, Spiritu Sancto donati errare possunt, & sæpiùs errant, si verbum DEI deserant: sic Ecclesiam etiam pariter errare, si in sermone Domini non permaneat.

6. Quin & ampliùs subsumitur: Singula Ecclesiæ membra per se considerata errare possunt:totæEcclesiæ particulares errare possunt:totumEcclesiæ particularis ministerium: tota concilia errare possunt. Falsa est ergò Pōtificiorum assertio, Ecclesiam vi promissionum ipsi factarum, errare non posse.

II. Ratio Jesuvitica talis plerumque esse solet: Ecclesia in Scripturis appellatur Regnum DEI. Atqui in regno DEI non error, sed veritas regnat. E. Ecclesia errare non potest.

Respondeo, Majorem veram esse: Nam Ecclesia regnum Cœlorum & regnum Veritatis est, quatenus regi suo Christo, & verbo ejus, quod est veritas, subjacet Quo ipse sensu non Veritatis modò, sed & justitiæ regnum appellatur Ecclesia. Jam verò quemadmodum non sequitur: Ecclesia dicitur regnum justitiæ: Ergò peccare non potest: Sic nullatenùs sequitur: Ecclesia dicitur regnum veritatis. Ergò errare non potest.

Deindè verò posito, non autem concesso, posse ex istis elogijs colligi id, quod intendunt Jesuvitæ: non tamen ad quamlibet, sed ad veram tantùm Ecclesiam illud accommodari posset. Quid autem hoc ad Romanam Ecclesiam, quæ est hæresium lerna, & Veritatis putadum prostibulum?

III. Ratio Jesuvvitica hæc affertur: Quod dictum est summo Ecclesiæ Rectori Petro,id pertinet ad totam Ecclesiam: Atqui Christus ad Petrum, Luc. 12, 32. Rogavi pro te, ut non deficiat fides tua. Ergò idem quoque ad Ecclesiam pertinet, & per consequens Ecclesia in fide deficere non potest.

Respondeo ad majorem, initiò falsum esse, quod præsupponunt Adversarij Petrum fuissse summum Rectorem, & universalem Episcopum Ecclesiæ.

2. Si maximè talis fuerit: tamen consequentia extendi nec potest, nec debet, vel ad hanc, vel ad illam particularemEcclesiam: sed tantùm ad totam Universalem Catholicam ut & invisibilem Electorum Ecclesiam: Ubi nos libenter concedimus, precibus Christi meritò acceptum referri, quod ea, nunquàm simul tota errare possit, aut erret.

3. Quod Christus Petro dixit, erat personale: ac proindè ad totam speciem referri nequit.

4. Sophisma committitur figuræ dictionis, in phrasi: Rogavi pro te, ne deficiat fides tua: Cujus sensus non est, Quòd fides Petri planè non potuerit deficere, aut verè defecerit. Defecit enim certè ter abnegans Christum: defecit. Resurrectionem Christi non credens: defecit, negans Gentes ad societatem Christi pertinere: defecit circa doctrinam de recto usu libertatis Christianæ, in conversatione cum gentilibus, periculosè errans, Gal. 2, 11. Verùm iste est sensus verborum Christi, quòd oraverit pro Petro, ne fides ipsius finaliter deficeret, & ipse in suo lapsu periret, sed restauratâ fide salvaretur. Dicitur proindè fides Petri non defecisse, propter subsecutam restaurationem, quam Christus suis precibus impetravit: eodem planè sensu, quo Luc. 8, 52. de filia Jairi dicitur:non est mortua:scilicet propter subsecu turum resuscitationis miraculum.

5. Et postremò: si ab exemplo Petri, ad Papam colligant Jesuvvitæ, quòd propter preces Christi hujus etiam fides deficere non possit: haud magis valet Consequentia, atque à baculo ad angulum. Siquidem Petro Apostolo cum Pontifice Romano, tùm personæ, tùm officij ac doctrinæ ratione, haud major intercedit convenientia, atque Christo intercedit cum Belial, luci cum tenebris, veritati cum mendacio.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: On the Catholic Church

CATHOLIC.

The Church of the New Testament is called Catholic or Universal, the denomination being derived not from a community of subjects in the human race—which the very name of Church implies, as it denotes the calling out of certain persons—but from the universality of times, places, and orders that exist in the human race, for all of whom there is a place in the Church, so that now under the kingdom of Christ it is by no means bound to any certain place, or time, or order of men, but is always diffused throughout the whole world and all orders of men.

It must be noted, however, that by this title is understood not an absolute universality, but only that which is proper to the New Testament; and consequently this epithet of the Church is not primarily opposed to particular churches, which can be named κατ' οικον, κατ' πολιν, and similarly, but rather to the Church of the Old Testament, which kept itself within the confines of the Jewish land, and was destined to last only until the time appointed for the advent of Christ the Savior, and which, being ordinarily gathered from one and only the Jewish people, could be called τοπικη η μερικη, and indeed in a certain way μερικη, not καθολικη.

The Church of the New Testament, however, diffused into the universality of places, times, and all peoples, is called Catholic by a very fitting epithet. Peter expressed the reason for this epithet, Acts 10:35, saying: In truth I perceive that GOD is no respecter of persons: but in every nation he that feareth GOD, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.

Moreover, there is found in the writings of ancient and recent theologians another notation of this epithet, namely, that that Church is called Catholic which faithfully holds and embraces the heavenly doctrine, approved by the unanimous consent and suffrage of the Prophets and Apostles.

As many, therefore, as are dispersed throughout the whole world, who coalesce into one body of Christ by the profession of one Orthodox Apostolic faith, or as the Apostle speaks, by one and the same Spirit, and are inserted into the one Head, Christ, or have ever been inserted, or are yet to be inserted; they constitute the Catholic Church of Christ, and are true Catholics. Thus, therefore, the Catholic Church, taken in this second sense, is not of the same breadth as the Catholic Church understood in the former sense: since very many of those who are called never fail from the true faith, and fall away from the title and eulogy of Catholics.

Furthermore, this appellation of the Catholic Church, taken in this second sense, is not proper to the New Testament alone, but is equally common to the assembly of the faithful of both the Old and the New Testament. For one faith, one Mediator, one salvation and eternal life obtains for both. Eph. 4:5.

From this second signification flowed a third, very common among the Fathers, namely, that Catholic is opposed to heretical: that is, to false and erroneous dogmas and heresies, and that a Catholic is one who is not a heretic. Hence it came about that the pious Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius wrote that the name of Catholics should be attributed to those who followed that faith and religion which St. Peter delivered to the Romans, that is, who according to the Apostolic discipline and the doctrine of the Gospel believed in the one Deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, under equal Majesty and under a pious Trinity. Cod. tit. de summa Trinitate & fide Catholica l. cuncto populos. Histor. Tripart. lib. 9. cap. 7.

Finally, according to the common custom of speaking, καθολικον, Universal, is opposed to τοπικω, particular: so that the Catholic Church is that which contains all particular churches under its ambit or complex, as members of the whole. Such a Catholic Church is understood as νοητη (intelligible) rather than αισθητη (sensible); nor does it exist as such in actual fact: but all particular churches, comprehended in the mind, constitute one Catholic Church in the human intellect. Whatever Church, therefore, may be given; whether Roman, or Corinthian, or Jerusalemite, or any other: that in this last meaning is only particular: although with respect to the preceding three significations it can be called Catholic, provided it guards and retains the unity of faith and Spirit safe and sound. The Jesuits therefore betray remarkable stupidity by binding the Catholic Church to the city of Rome alone, which is nothing other than a monster without example, a portent without reason, and as they say in the Schools, to invent an Oppositum in adjecto: no differently than if someone wished to define the city of Rome as being throughout the whole world.

The Romanists betray a notable error concerning this attribute of the Church as well, contending that the Church is called Catholic from the approbation of a doctrine which at all times sounds forth equally throughout the whole world: having followed in this part Vincent the Lyrinensian monk, who writes: That is truly and properly called Catholic which has been believed in the Catholic Church itself everywhere, always, and by all. Although the same Lyrinensian dissents from himself elsewhere: He, saying, is a true and genuine Catholic, who loves God, who loves the Church, who loves the Body of Christ, who prefers nothing to divine religion, nothing to the Catholic faith, not the authority of any man, not love, not talent, not eloquence, lib. against profan. nov. chap. 25.

Moreover, the Romanists, relying on this faulty definition, immediately infer that since the Pontifical doctrine is of such a nature that it has always been and is today spread equally throughout the whole world: or, as Stapleton speaks, since the Roman Church has always, through individual ages, communicated with the whole Christian world, and communicates today: therefore the title of Catholic properly and uniquely belongs to the Roman Church as well.

But all things which the Romanists bring forward in this regard are vain, false, and fictitious.

For 1. it is not required for the property of the Catholic Church that it always be actually dispersed throughout the whole world: but it is enough if it is not tied to any certain place, but rather, according to the diversity of time, it extends itself now more, now less widely. For if such an actual dispersion throughout the whole world were necessarily required for the definition of the Catholic Church: certainly the Church gathered by Christ himself could not be called Catholic: just as neither could that which, after the ascension of Christ, was gathered in those first years when the Apostles were preaching the Gospel in Judea, Galilee, and part of Samaria: since neither was actually dispersed into all parts of the world. Which was the very reason why the Apostle Peter is read to have doubted whether the Gentiles also belonged to the fellowship of the Church, until he was more correctly taught about this matter by a heavenly oracle. And yet, perhaps not even the Pontificians themselves would deny that this Apostolic Church was truly Catholic.

2. The definition of Catholic which the adversaries urge is clearly inept and absurd. For if that is Catholic which has always been, which has been everywhere, and which has been most widely received and believed by all: certainly Arianism will be most Catholic, since it occupied almost the whole world for a long time: thus Mahometanism will be most Catholic, as it pervaded and infected the whole East, and in it the principal kingdoms of the world: and indeed more equally and consistently than Popery, which has never ceased to stab and slaughter itself through perpetual schisms and contradictions. Thus, finally, Idolatry will be most Catholic, since it has almost always pervaded the whole world.

3. No time can be shown by the Pontificians themselves when the Universal World received and approved the doctrine of the Romanists. For example, the Mass Sacrifice, that acropolis of the Pontifical kingdom, was clearly unknown for many centuries from the times of the Apostles: the Canon of the Mass itself was finally collected by some Scholastic after several centuries. Thus the invocation of the dead, the primacy of the Pope, the celibacy of priests, the prohibition of certain days, the sacrilegious mutilation of the Lord's Supper: and other Pontifical dogmas of that kind, were not only never received and approved by the Eastern Church: but even in the West itself there have always been very many who contradicted these βδελύγμασι (abominations) of the Romanists with full mouth, even with their own shed blood.

4. If, according to the Pontifical definition, that is finally Catholic which is received by all and which sounds most equally throughout the whole world: certainly the doctrine and Church of Christ will be least Catholic: as it was never approved by all, but there have always been very few who followed it: so much so that the Savior himself calls his Church a little flock, Luke 12:32, and the way that leads to life, narrow and very strait: but that which tends to destruction, broad and spacious. Matt. 7:13 and 14.

5. Scripture everywhere measures the assembly of those who err by their multitude: but the Church of the truly Catholic or Elect by their fewness. For many, as the Savior testifies, will arise under the reign of the Anti-Christ, pseudo-Christs and pseudo-prophets, so that many may be seduced: Matt. 24:5. Indeed, such a small number of the Elect is predicted to be around the coming of Christ, that it is doubtful whether the Savior will find faith on earth. Luke 18:8. What of the fact that the Son of God predicted that all the nations of the earth were to be made drunk with the cup of errors and abominations, and with the wine of the fornication of the Roman harlot, Apoc. 17:2 and chap. 18:3. And St. Peter announces that most will be seduced by pernicious sects that are to come. Either, therefore, the Catholic Church will then fail, which the Romanists deny, and rightly deny: or it must be false that Catholic is to be defined by that which is mostly, and by the many, believed and received.

6. It is false and fictitious that the Roman Church has always, through individual ages, communicated with the whole Christian world, and communicates today. For as it never communicated with the Eastern Church: so neither does it communicate today with our Churches, as many as there are throughout all Germany that abhor the Papacy and its Idolomania.

It is added that we have already learned from the Apocalypse that this Communication, spreading itself widely through the kingdoms and nations of this world, is a proper mark of the kingdom of the Antichrist.

7. And finally. The Catholic Church extends more widely than the Roman. Therefore, the Roman Church falsely arrogates to itself the title of Catholic Church. The antecedent is clear, because the true and Catholic Church are most simply convertible. Now the true Church extends as widely as the assembly of the baptized extends. Therefore, the Catholic Church is also of the same breadth. I prove the minor from this, because 1. Where there is Baptism, there is the washing of regeneration: Tit. 3, 5. Where there is the washing of regeneration, there is the true and Catholic Church, being cleansed by the washing of water in the word, Ephes. 5, 26. Then the same is clear from the very practice of the Roman Church, which does not rebaptize those baptized outside the Roman Church among the Lutherans and others protesting against the Papacy: even by this agreement showing that those so baptized are truly baptized, and therefore that it is a true Church: unless perhaps by an unheard-of absurdity it wishes to establish that those who are not the true Catholic Church are also truly baptized and regenerated.

Latin:

CATHOLICA.

C Reditur Ecclesia Novi Testamenti Catholica sive Universalis, petita denominatione, non a communitate Subjectorum in genere humano, id quod vel ipsum Ecclesia nomen innuit, quod certarum quarundam personarum evocationem notat: sed ab Universitate temporum, locorum atque ordinum, qui sunt in genere humano, quibus omnibus, ita in Ecclesia locus est, ut jam sub regno Christi, ad certum vel locum, vel tempus, vel hominum ordinem ea minime sit alligata: sed semper per totum terrarum orbem, omnesque hominum ordines sit diffusa.

Notandum autem est, quod hoc titulo non absoluta universalitas: sed ea duntaxat intelligatur, quae est Novi Testamenti propria: ac proinde epitheton hoc Ecclesiae, non principaliter opponatur Ecclesiis particularibus, quae κατ' οικον, κατ' πολιν & similiter nominari possunt: sed potius Ecclesia Veteris Testamenti, quae intra angustias terrae Judaicae, se continuit, & non nisi ad tempus adventui Christi Servatoris destinato, durare debuit, quaeque ex uno ac solo populo Judaico ordinarie collecta, τοπικη η μερικη, quin & μερικη quodammodo appellari potuit, non καθολικη.

Novi autem Testamenti Ecclesia, in universitatem, tum locorum, tum temporum, tum populorum omnium diffusa, convenienti admodum Epitheto Catholica appellatur. Expressit epitheti hujus rationem Petrus, Actor. 10, 35. inquiens: In veritate comperi, quod DEVS non est personarum acceptor: sed in omni gente, quit timet DEVM, & operatur justitiam acceptus est illi.

Cæterum reperitur in scriptis veterum ac recentiorum Theologorum, alia quoque Epitheti hujus notatio, ut videlicet ea Ecclesia dicatur Catholica, quae doctrinam coelestem, unanimi Prophetarum & Apostolorum consensu & suffragio approbatam, fideliter tenet & amplectitur.

Quotquot ergo per universum terrarum orbem dispersi, unius fidei Apostolicæ Orthodoxa professione, sive ut Apostolus loquitur, uno eodemque Spiritu, in unum corpus Christi coalescunt, unique Capiti Christo inseruntur, vel unquam inferti sunt, aut adhuc inferentur; illi constituunt Catholicam Christi Ecclesiam, & veri sunt Catholici. Sic ergo Ecclesia Catholica, secundo hoc sensu accepta; non ejusdem latitudinis est, cujus est Ecclesia Catholica, priore sensu intellecta: Siquidem nunquam non vocatorum plurimi a vera fide deficiunt, & Catholicorum titulo atque elogio excidunt.

Deinde appellatio haec Ecclesiæ Catholicae, secundo hoc sensu accepta, non Novi Testamenti tantum est propria, sed ex æquo communis cœtui fidelium tam Veteris, quam Novi Testamenti. Una siquidem fides utrinque, unus Mediator, una salus & vita æterna obtinet. Ephes. 4, 5.

Ex secunda hac significatione, profluxit & tertia, Patribus admodum usitata, ut nempe Catholicum opponatur hæretico: hoc est, fallisa tque erroneis dogmatibus, & hæresibus, & Catholicus sit, qui non est hæreticus. Hinc factum, ut pij quoque Impp. Gratianus, Valentinianus & Theodosius Catholicorum nomen illis tribuendum esse rescriberent, qui eam sectarentur fidem & religionem, quam D. Petrus Romanis tradidit, hoc est, qui secundum disciplinam Apostolicam, & doctrinam Evangelij, Patris, Filij ac Spiritus Sancti unam Deitatem, sub pari Majestate, & sub pia Trinitate crederent. Cod. tit. de summa Trinitate & fide Catholica l. cuncto populos. Histor. Tripart. lib. 9. cap. 7.

Tandem secundum communem loquendi consuetudinem καθολικον Universale opponitur τοπικω particulari: ut Catholica sit Ecclesia, quae omnes particulares sub suo ambitu sive complexu continet, tanquam membra totius. Qualis Ecclesia Catholica νοητη magis, quam αισθητη intelligitur: neque ipso actu talis extat: sed particulares omnes νοητω comprehensae, in mente hominis unam constituunt Catholicam Ecclesiam. Quæcunque ergo detur Ecclesia; sive Romana, sive Corinthiaca sive Hierosolymitana, sive quaevis alia: illa hoc postremo significatu tantum est particularis: licet respectu præcedentium trium significationum Catholica dici possit, dummodo Unitatem fidei & Spiritus, sartam tectam custodiat ac retineat. Insignem ergo stoliditatem produnt Jesuvvitæ, Catholicam Ecclesiam, ad solam urbem Romam alligantes, id quod nihil est aliud, quam monstrum sine exemplo, portentum sine ratione, & ut in Scholis loquuntur, Oppositum in adjecto comminisci: haud aliter, ac si quis urbem Romam per totum terrarum orbem definire velit.

Romanenses circa hoc etiam Ecclesiæ attributum insignem errorem produnt, contendentes, Ecclesiam appellari Catholicam, a propatione doctrinæ, quæ omnibus tẽporibus semper æqualiter, per totum terrarum orbem sonet: secuti hac in parte Vincentium Monachum Lyrinensem, qui scriptitat. Catholicum vere ac proprie appellari id, quod in ipsa Catholica Ecclesia ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus est creditum. Quanquam idem Lyrinensis alibi a seipso dissentit: Ille, inquiens, est verus & germanus Catholicus, qui verit stem DEI, qui Ecclesiam, qui Christi Corpus diligit, qui divina religioni, qui Catholicae fidei nihil praeponit, non hominis cujusquam autoritatem, non amorem, non ingenium, non eloquentiam, lib. adversus profan. nov. cap. 25.

Caeterum Romanenses vitiosae huic definitioni innixi statim subfumunt, cum doctrina Pontificia talis sit ratio, ut ea aequaliter per totum terrarum orbem semper fuerit hodieque sit diffusa: vel, ut Stapletonus loquitur, cùm Romana Ecclesia, semper per singulas aetates, cum toto orbe Christiano communicaverit, hodieque communicet: ideò Romanae etiam Ecclesiae, elogium Catholicae propriè ac unicè competere.

Verùm vana, falsa ac fictitia sunt omnia, quae hâc in parte proferunt Romanenses.

Nam 1. ad proprietatem Catholicae Ecclesiae non requiritur, ut ea semper sit per totum orbem, ipso actu dispersa: sed satis est, si ad nullum certum locum sit alligata, verùm pro diversitate temporis, nunc magis, nunc minus latè se extendat. Quod si enim talis actualis dispersio per totum orbem, ad definitionem Catholicae Ecclesiae necessariò requireretur: certè Ecclesia à Christo ipso collecta, Catholica dici non posset: sicut nec ea, quae post ascensum Christi, primis illis annis, quibus in Judaea, Galilaea, & parte Samariae praedicabant Evangelium Apostoli, fuit coacta: siquidem neutra in omnes partes orbis terrarum ipso actu erat dispersa. Quae ipsa causa fuit propter quam Apostolus Petrus dubitasse legitur, an etiam gentes ad societatem Ecclesiae pertinerent, donec hac de re caelesti oraculo rectiùs esset edoctus. Atqui Apostolicam hanc Ecclesiam, fuisse verè Catholicam, fortassis ne ipse quidem negaverint Pontificij.

2. Inepta planè & absurda est Definitio Catholici, quam urgent Adversarij. Si enim Catholicum est, quod semper, quod ubique fuit, quòdque ab omnibus maximè receptum & creditum: certè maximè Catholicus erit Arianismus, quippè qui longo tempore totum fermè terrarum orbem occupavit: Sic maximè Catholicus erit Mahometismus, ut qui totum Orientem, & in eo praecipua orbis terrarum regna, pervasit & infecit: & quidem magis aequaliter ac consonanter, quam Papismus, ut qui seipsum nunquàm non perpetuis Schismatis, & contradictionibus confodit & jugulavit. Sic denique maximè Catholica erit Idololatria, quippè quae fermè semper totum terrarum orbem pervasit.

3. Nullum potest ab ipsis Pontificijs monstrari tempus, quo Orbis Universus Romanensium doctrinam receperit & approbarit. Exempli gratiâ, Sacrificium Missaticum, acropolis illa regni Pontificij, multis seculis ab Apostolorum temporibus erat planè incognitum: Canon ipse Missaticus, demùm post aliquot secula à Scholastico quodam collectus. Sic mortuorum invocatio, primatus Pontificis, caelibatus Sacerdotum, prohibitio certorum dierum, sacrilega mutilatio Coenae Dominicae: & id genus alia dogmata Pontificia, non modò ab Orientali Ecclesia nunquàm fuerunt recepta & approbata: sed & in ipso Occidente semper extiterunt quamplurimi, qui hisce Romanensium βδελύγμασι pleno ore contradixerunt, suo etiam profuso sanguine

4. Si ex definitione Pontificia, illud demùm Catholicum fuerit, quod ab omnibus recipitur & quod per totum terrarum orbem maximè aequaliter sonat: certè doctrina & Ecclesia Christi, minimè erit Catholica: ut quae nunquàm ab omnibus approbata fuit, sed paucissimi semper fuerunt, qui eam sequerentur: adeò ut Servator ipse, Ecclesiam suam nominet Gregem pusillum, Luc. 12, 32. & viam, quae ad vitam ducit, angustam & valdè arctam: eam verò quae tendit ad interitum, latam, & spatiosam. Matth. 7. 13. & 14.

5. Scriptura passim ex multitudine metitur coetum errantium: ex paucitate verò, verè Catholicorum sive Electorum Ecclesiam. Multi enim, teste Servatore, sub regno Anti-Christi, exurgent pseudo-Christi & pseudopropheta, ut plurimi seducantur: Matth. 24, 5. imò tanta futura praedicitur Electorum paucitas, circa adventum Christi, ut dubium sit futurum, an Servator fidem in terris sit reperturus. Luc. 18, 8. Quid quòd Filius DEI praedixit, omnes gentes terrae inebriandas esse, poculo errorum & abominationum, ac vino scortationis Romanae meretricis, Apocal. 17, 2. & cap. 18, 3. Et D. Petrus Plerosque seductum iri annunciat, à sectis perniciosis, quae sint eventurae. Aut ergò Catholica Ecclesia tùm deficiet, id quod negant, & rectè negant Romanenses: aut falsum sit necesse est, Catholicum definiendum per id, quod plerumque, & à pluribus creditur, & recipitur.

6. Falsum & fictitium est, Romanam Ecclesiam semper per singulas aetates communicasse cum toto orbe Christiano, & hodiè communicare. Nam cum Orientalis Ecclesia nunquam communicavit: sic neque hodiè communicat cum nostris Ecclesijs, quotquot quidem per totam Germaniam, à Papatu ejusque Idolomania abhorrent.

Accedit quòd jam ex Apocalypsi didicimus, Communicationem hanc, latè se per regna & gentes hujus mundi diffundentem, esse propriam notam regni Antichristi.

7. Et postremò. Ecclesia Catholica latiùs patet, quàm Romana. Ergò Ecclesiæ Catholicæ titulum Romana Ecclesia sibi falsò arrogat. Antecedens patet, Quia vera & Catholica Ecclesia simplicißimè convertuntur. Jam vera Ecclesia tàm latè patet, quàm latè patet baptizatorum cœtus. Ergò Ecclesia etiam Catholica ejusdem est latitudinis. Minorem probo indè, quia 1. Ubi est Baptismus, ibi est lavacrum regenerationis: Tit. 3, 5. Ubi lavacrum regenerationis, ibi Ecclesia vera & Catholica, quippè mundata lavacro aquæ in verbo, Ephes. 5, 26. Deindè idem patet ex ipsa praxi Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quæ extra Romanam Ecclesiam apud Lutheranos, & alios Papatui reclamantes, baptizatos: non rebaptizat: vel hoc pacto ostendens, sic baptizatos, verè esse baptizatos, ac proindè veram esse Ecclesiam: nisi fortè per inauditam absurditatem statuere velit, verè baptizaros, & regeneratos esse etiam eos, qui non sint vera Catholica Ecclesia.


### Chapter II. Of the attributes: IV. And the final axiom of the Church is that which is declared in the Nicene Symbol, Apostolic

APOSTOLIC.

According to the prescription of the Nicene Creed, besides the epithets already explained, we believe the Church is also Apostolic. Which axiom is nothing other than a kind of declaration and explanation of the Catholic: so that there may be noted that καθολικότης of the Church which was introduced by the Apostles themselves through the preaching of the Gospel. Therefore, the Church is called Apostolic, not with respect to any ordinary succession, deduced from the times of the Apostles down to our own times, and tied to a certain and by no means interrupted series of persons or Bishops: but only with respect to Apostolic Doctrine: which the true Church keeps safe and sound and propagates, being built indeed upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, of which the highest cornerstone is Christ, in whom all the building grows into a holy temple in the Lord: Ephes. 2, 20. and 21. For whoever walks according to this Apostolic rule; peace be upon them and mercy, Gal. 6, 16.

Moreover, those traditions do not belong to this Apostolic Canon which are today thrust upon the Church of GOD by the Papists, and are confirmed by I know not what Apostolic Canons.

For 1. they have not yet convinced us, nor will they ever, that the Apostles handed down anything other and different by word of mouth than what they included in their writings.

2. Those Canons produce such trifles that whoever wishes to attribute them to the Apostolic Spirit ought to be held guilty of the crime of lèse-majesté against the divine Majesty: such as are, in Canon 16, 17, 25, concerning the celibacy of Priests: also Can. 68, concerning the Lenten fast: and other ineptitudes of that kind, which expressly fight against Apostolic precepts, Coloss. 2, 16, 20, and following, 1 Tim. 4, 1 and 3.

From these it is easy to gather that the epithet of the Apostolic Church can no more be applied to the Roman Church than to the Church of the Pharisees or any other heretics: which can be demonstrated without any difficulty if some comparison is made between Apostolic doctrine and that of the Romanists: so that this statement of Tertullian, in his book on prescription against heretics, is most true in this place: It remains for us to demonstrate whether our doctrine is reckoned from the tradition of the Apostles: and from this very fact, whether the others come from a lie. We communicate with the Apostolic Churches, because there is no different doctrine: This is the testimony of Truth. But there, the adulteration of both Scriptures and expositions must be reckoned, where a diversity of doctrine is found. Which opinion of Tertullian strips the Roman Church of the epithet of Apostolic truth all the more strongly, the more alien its doctrine is from the Apostolic Canon: indeed, the more vehemently it resists any judgment of its doctrine being made from the writings of the Prophets and Apostles.

Latin:

APOSTOLICA.

SEcundum præscriptum Symboli Niceni, præter explicata jam elogia, credimus Ecclesiam etiam Apostolicam. Quod axioma nihil est aliud, quàm quædam quasi declaratio, & explicatio Catholici: ut sic notetur ea καθολικότης Ecclesiæ, quæ ab Apostolis ipsis, per prædicationem Evangelij est introducta. Dicitur proindè Ecclesia Apostolica, non respectu Ordinariæ alicujus succeßionis, jam indè ab Apostolorum temporibus, ad nostra usque tempora deductæ, & ad certam, minimeque interruptam personarum, sive Episcoporum seriem alligatæ: sed tantùm respectu Doctrinæ Apostolicæ: quam sartam tectam vera Ecclesia conservat, & propagat, ædificata quippè super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, cujus summus angularis lapis est Christus, in quo omnis ædificatio crescit in templum sanctum Domino: Ephes. 2, 20. & 21. Quicunq; enim secundum regulam hanc Apostolicam incedunt; pax super eos & misericordia, Gal. 6, 16.

Cæterùm ad hunc Canonem Apostolicum non pertinent Traditiones illæ: quæ à Pontificijs hodiè Ecclesiæ DEI obtruduntur, & nescio ex quibus Apostolorum Canonibus confirmantur.

Nam 1. fidem nobis nondùm fecerunt, neque facient unquàm, Apostolos aliud acdiversum vivâ voce tradidisse, quàm scriptis comprehenderit.

2. Ejusmodi nugamenta produnt illi Canones, ut qui ad Spiritum Apostolicum ea referre velit, criminis laesae divinae Majestatis reus peragi debeat: Qualia sunt, Canone 16, 17 25. de caelibatu Sacerdotum: Jtem Can. 68. De jejunio Quadragesimali: deque id genus ineptijs alijs, quae διαρρήδην pugnant cum praeceptis Apostolicis, Coloss. 2, 16. 20. & seqq. 1. Tim. 4, 1. & 3.

Ex his promptum est colligere, Elogium Ecclesiae Apostolicae, haud magis ad Romanam, atq; ad Pharisaeorum, aut aliorum quorumvis haereticorum Ecclesiam accommodari posse: id quod nullo negocio demonstrari potest, si inter doctrinam Apostolicam, & Romanensium aliqua instituatur comparatio: ut verissimum hoc loco sit illud Tertulliani, lib. de praescript. adversus haereticos: Superest ut demonstremus, an nostra doctrina, de Apostolorum traditione censeatur: & ex hoc ipso, an caeterae de mendacio veniant. Communicamus cum Ecclesijs Apostolicis, quia nulla diversa doctrina: Hoc est testimonium Veritatis. Jllîc verò & Scripturarum & expositionum adulteratio deputanda est, ubi diversitas invenitur doctrinae. Quae Tertulliani sententia tantò fortiùs Romanam Ecclesiam, Apostolicae veritatis elogio spoliat, quantò alienior ejus est doctrina, à Canone Apostolico: imò quantò vehementiùs repugnat, quo minus de sua doctrina, ex scriptis Prophetarum & Apostolorum fiat dijudicatio.


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church

It is debated today quite sharply, between us and the Jesuits, from where the κριτήρια [criteria], or infallible γνωρίσματα [distinguishing features] of the true Church, can and ought to be sought? In rightly deciding which controversy, it will be most advisable that we proceed from the more general to the more special, from the better known to the less known, by a certain ἀφαίρεσιν [abstraction] or removal of the false κριτήρια [criteria] of the true Church. We therefore remove at the beginning that carnal and political dream, by which some wise men of this age suppose that the judgment concerning the true Church is to be taken, 1. from the multitude and number of men approving any religion whatsoever: so that that Church and Religion ought to be considered the truest, which the greatest part of men follows. 2. from the power, nobility, and wisdom of the men who adhere to a religion: 3. from the happiness and prosperity of the outcomes. 4. and lastly, from the external appearance and the dignity of the titles and axioms. For this method of judging is clearly false and deceptive.

As to widows, or concerning the Elect themselves, the question is who the Elect are, or by what marks they are to be distinguished from the remaining members of the Church; for the distinct knowledge of these does not at all fall under the sight and κρίσιν of men: and it is GOD alone who knows those who are His, 1 Tim. 2, 19. Whence we also showed above in chapter 1 that these constitute the invisible Church. That there are indeed in the true Church of GOD some Elect, and truly faithful, is not at all ambiguous: and in whom for the time being there is true faith, and the present grace of the Holy Spirit, is gathered not obscurely, at least by some confused knowledge. But because faith in many is προσκαιρος, and the grace of the Holy Spirit is not an ἀδιαβλητον good in men, indeed because the recesses of human hearts are manifold, and the images of things are exceedingly deceptive: and therefore, a priori and as regards certainty or distinct knowledge, nothing can be determined concerning this ζητήματι.

For the Savior himself refutes the first γνώρισμα, calling the true Church a little flock, Luc. 12, 32. Likewise, teaching that the gate is narrow and the way constricted which leads to life, and that there are few who find it: whereas, on the contrary, the gate is wide and the way spacious which leads to destruction, and there are many who walk through it: Matth. 7, 13. & 14. The history of the Universal Church confirms this very thing. In the times, certainly, of Noah, Elijah, Christ, the Apostles, and Athanasius, the false Church had so prevailed by the multitude of men that scarcely any traces of the true Church appeared any longer: and the Prophet Elijah complained that he alone remained.

The Apostle refutes the second γνώρισμα in 1 Corinthians 1:26: "For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong." Furthermore, the vanity of this mark is also argued by the fact that the Pharisees reasoned against the Church of Christ in the same way, deeming it false for the reason that none of the rulers or the Pharisees believed in him, John 7:48.

But this point also is beyond controversy in this place, whether the Church, simply so called, can be known by whatever preaching of the divine Word, and whatever use of the Sacraments? For perhaps the Romanists themselves will not unwillingly concede this to us in the affirmative: and yet they will deny that one can immediately be elevated from there to the true Church. For they differ greatly, to be some Church: in which even falsehood can exist: and to be a true Church: just as Christ distinguishes between disciples, and those who are truly His disciples, Joh 8 31: and it is easily acknowledged that there is a huge difference commonly between believers, and those who are truly believers.

The third γνώρισμα, when it comes to the true Church’s own condition, fights diametrically against this, for, as Scripture testifies, it is nothing other than a rose among thorns: according to that passage in Canticles 2:2, "As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters." The Church is that poor little one which, pressed by tempests of every kind, seems to be devoid of all consolation, Isaiah 54:11. And in treating this very type of argument, David is expressly engaged throughout the entire 37th Psalm; Asaph, throughout the entire 73rd Psalm; James, chapter 2; Jeremiah, chapter 12; Habakkuk, chapter 1.

But the question is strictly concerning the universal assembly of the Church, in which GOD gathers to Himself either a great part, or at least some pious part of the faithful and of those to be saved: Which assembly ought to be recognized and held as the true Church of Christ; by what marks, and indeed infallible ones, it may be judged? Now, in order for any mark to be infallible, to be characteristic, to be true, proper, and certain, two things especially are required προσονειλυτα.

1. That such a mark may be, by that thing which it ought to mark, more known.

1. To show the same thing certainly and infallibly: which happens only then, 1. If it belongs solely and always to the thing to be noted. 2. If it distinguishes the same from all other things. 3. If it is of the same extent as it, that is, if it is neither broader nor narrower. 4. If it is clearly inseparable from the thing to be noted.

The fourth γνώρισμα (mark) is that the criterion of a false Church is generally its own, as the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles testify. Jeremiah certainly replies to the Jewish Church, which was boasting too insolently about the Temple of the Lord: Do not trust in lying words, saying, The Temple of the Lord, &c. Jerem. 7, 4. Thus Christ warns the Scribes and Pharisees who were boasting of the Chair of Moses, but in such a way that, meanwhile, one should not act according to their works, Matth. 23, 2. & 3.

If we inquire into such marks with the greatest diligence possible, we shall find no more than two, by which indeed the true and Orthodox Church of Christ may be infallibly recognized, and distinguished and judged from all other assemblies.

THE FORMER is: The pure preaching of heavenly doctrine:

THE LATTER is: The legitimate use of the sacraments instituted by CHRIST.

We then remove the error of the Romanists, which they cherish as far the most pernicious regarding the present question. In order that it may be examined more accurately, it must first be seen, What properly comes into controversy in this place?

Now when an investigation is instituted concerning the true Church, it is not concerning the persons themselves in di-

It is most certain that the properties of infallible marks enumerated a little earlier belong uniquely to these two, and to no more and no fewer. For 1.
