That the purity of the Word is a proper good of the Church, which is never found outside of it, and without which the Church can in no way be true, is evident from the fact that the Apostle declares the Church of GOD (where he denotes only the true one) to be the pillar and foundation of the Truth, 1 Tim. 3:15; and also because Christ prayed to the heavenly Father for this, that He might sanctify it in the truth, that is, in His own discourse and Word: the depravation of which cannot be called Truth, nor can it be pronounced of the same that it is the discourse or Word of GOD, John 17:17. As for the legitimate use of the Sacraments, it is clearly subordinate to the purity of the Word: and therefore its condition is the same as that of the purity of Doctrine.

Furthermore, these very two marks most clearly distinguish the true Church of Christ both from the church of the malignant and from any other assemblies whatsoever: which is most manifest in itself.

Finally, these marks are clearly adequate and inseparable from the true Church of Christ. For although the true Church, and the purity of doctrine, and the legitimate use of the Sacraments are not synonyms or equivalent, yet they are altogether consequent upon one another.

Moreover, the reasons or arguments by which we evidently demonstrate this thesis of ours are these principal ones.

I. In whatever thing the proper office of the Church consists, in that same thing the condition of its true and proper marks is most rightly placed. But to exercise, preserve, and defend the pure preaching of the Gospel and the legitimate use of the Sacraments is the proper office of the Church. Therefore, the condition of the true and proper marks of the Church consists in these two things as well. The reason for the connection in the Major premise can hardly come into doubt for anyone who has weighed the matter with an even scale. For although in natural things, effects are separable from their causes through the intervention of impediments, and in the doctrine of morals, obedience often differs greatly from duties, yet in the Ordinances of the divine will, from the notation of an effect and a proper office, a most firm inference is made to the notation of the proper cause and subject itself.

The truth of the Minor premise is clearly evident from the fact that the Apostle names the Church the pillar and foundation of the truth, 1 Tim. 3:15; therefore, the argument stands with its certain and immovable truth.

II. Argument: Through whatever things GOD Himself is accustomed to work the salvation of the Church ordinarily; nay, even gathers, preserves, and propagates the Church itself and the assembly of those to be saved: in those very things the clearly infallible and characteristic marks of the true Church are most rightly constituted. But through the legitimate Ministry of the Word and Sacraments, GOD ordinarily effects both of those things; therefore. The reason for the Major is most

evident. For because Salvation is a proper adjunct of the Church, it is certainly very fitting that the infallible mark of the Church be placed in that through which salvation is uniquely acquired. Just as in principles, by which every thing is constituted, the signs and marks for judging and discerning the thing itself are most rightly placed. The Minor is manifest in itself and has the Apostle Peter as its author, 1 Pet. 1:23; therefore, the inference of the whole argument is firm.

III. Argument: In whatever thing the mark of truth is placed regarding each and every individual of the true Church, in that same thing the infallible mark of the whole true Church is also most rightly placed. But in the hearing of the divine Word and the embracing of heavenly doctrine, the infallible mark of each and every Christian is placed. Therefore. The connection of the Major is evidently clear from the fact that the true Church is nothing other than a collection or multitude of those who are truly Christians and those to be saved. Now, the judgment concerning the whole and the parts cannot be different. The Minor is most clearly evident from the testimonies of Scripture: as,

John 8:47. He who is of GOD hears the words of GOD. John 10:27. My sheep hear my voice. Gal. 1:8. If even we, or an Angel from heaven, should preach a Gospel to you besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema. 2 Thess. 3:7. Withdraw yourselves from every brother who does not walk according to the doctrine which he received from us. 2 John verses 9 and 10. Whoever does not remain in the doctrine of Christ does not have GOD: and if anyone comes to you who does not bring this doctrine, do not even receive him into your house, or say GREETINGS to him.

But since the Sacraments are not only seals and signets of the Word, Rom. 4:11, but also, as it were, tokens of the Church itself: certainly for this reason it is evident that they can in no way be excluded from the characteristic marks of the Church.

Furthermore, it is asked in this place, from whence ought the judgment to be made concerning the purity and sincerity of those two marks? We answer, not from the canons which are circulated under the name of the Apostles, nor primarily from the decrees of councils, nor even simply from the monuments of the Fathers, and much less from the responses of the Roman Pontiffs: but from the Holy or canonical Scriptures alone, which are that Lydian stone to which alone all dogmas are to be examined; so that those which accord with this may be acknowledged without any doubt as pure and true, and those which dissent may be freely rejected as false. Concerning which matter, St. Augustine disputes most excellently in his book De Unitate Ecclesiæ, chapter 2, saying: Between us and the Donatists the question is, where is the Church? What, therefore, are we to do? Are we to seek it in our own words, or in the words of its head, our Lord? of Jesus Christ: I think we ought to seek him rather in his Word, who is the Truth, and knows his own body best. For the Lord knows who are his.

And ch. 3. But as we had begun to say, let us not hear: I say this, you say that: but let us hear: Thus says the Lord: There are certain books of the Lord, to whose authority we both consent, we both believe, we both serve: there let us seek the Church, there let us discuss our cause. Let those things therefore be removed from the midst, which we recite against one another not from the divine Canonical books, but from elsewhere. Perhaps someone may ask, and say to me, why then do you wish these things to be removed from the midst, when your communion, even if they are brought forward, is unconquered? Because I do not want the holy Church to be demonstrated by human documents, but by divine oracles.

And ch. 16. With all such things removed, let them demonstrate their Church, if they can, not in the sermons and rumors of the Africans, not in the councils of their Bishops, not in the letters of any disputants whatsoever, not in deceptive signs and wonders, because we have been prepared and rendered cautious even against these by the Word of the Lord: but in the prescription of the law, in the predictions of the Prophets, in the songs of the Psalms, in the very voices of the Shepherd, in the preachings of the Evangelists, in the labors of the Apostles, that is, in all the Canonical authorities of the Holy books.

Concerning the Sacraments the same Augustine in Epist. 118 thus supports us: By sacraments most few in number, most easy to observe, most excellent in signification, he bound together the society of the new people, such as is Baptism, consecrated in the name of the Trinity: The communion of his own body and blood.

Chrysostom agrees with Augustine, Homil. 49 on ch. 24 of Matthew, writing: When you see the impious heresy standing in the holy place of the Church: then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, that is, those who are in Christianity, let them betake themselves to the Scriptures. Because from the time that heresy took possession of the Churches, there can be no proof of true Christianity, nor any other refuge for Christians who wish to know the truth of the faith, except the divine Scriptures. I do not want the holy Church to be demonstrated by human document, but by divine oracles.

But furthermore it is asked whether those who are outside the Church: nay, and those who are indeed involved in the assembly of the Church, but are destitute of the gift of interpreting and understanding the Scriptures, can judge concerning these marks of the true Church? I answer affirmatively. For as for those who are involved outside the Church, even if they are not yet taught or led by the Holy Spirit regarding the knowledge of the articles of faith; meanwhile, however, they are by no means destitute of the sharpness and intelligence of natural judgment. This natural intelligence, although it cannot apprehend the dogmas of the Christian Religion in such a way that a faithful assent is provided to them. For this is the work of God alone, and it happens to those who are θεοδίδακτοι: Matt. 16, 16. yet it can achieve this, that it conceives a bare knowledge κατὰ ἄληψιν of those things which are contained in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles: especially if the knowledge of languages, which falls even to the infidels, is added. These therefore in some way can know and judge in what assembly those things are done, taught, and believed, which are contained written in the books of the Prophets and Apostles. Therefore, no total ἀδυναμία

of judging concerning the marks of the Church can or ought to be ascribed even to infidels, especially the more learned.

But as for the other order of those who are members of the Church, and have received the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit, even if they are not all endowed with the gift of interpreting and understanding all the Scriptures: even if they are also destitute of the knowledge of Theological controversies: yet the discernment of those things which make for the purity of heavenly doctrine is neither so difficult, nor entirely impossible. If only they have examined the doctrine of the Church against the catechetical heads. This certainly, even by itself, the ἐξέτασις can provide a sufficiently safe and exact rule and standard for discerning any Spirits whatsoever: provided that someone has not been entirely ignorant regarding the principles of the Christian Religion, and he himself rightly knows the way of salvation.

Latin:

COntrovertitur hodiè satis acriter, inter nos & Jesuvvitas, Undenàm peti possint ac debeant κριτήρια, sive infallibilia γνωρίσματα verae Ecclesiae? Jn qua controversia ritè decidenda, consultissimum fuerit, ut à generalioribus ad specialiora, à notioribus ad minus nota, per quandam ἀφαίρεσιν sive remotionem fallorum κριτηρίων verae Ecclesiae progrediamur. Removemus proindè initiò somnium illud carnale & politicum, quo nonnulli sapientes hujus seculi, judicium de Ecclesia vera sumendum esse autumant, 1. ex multitudine & numero hominum, religionem quampiam approbantium: ita ut ea Ecclesia & Religio censeri debeat verissima, quam maxima pars hominum sequatur. 2. ex potentia, nobilitate & sapientia hominum religioni adhaerentium: 3. ex felicitate & eventuum prosperitate. 4. & postremò, ex specie externa, & titulorum atque axiomatum dignitate. Nam falsa planè ac fallax haec est judicandi ratio.

viduis, aut de Electis ipsis quaeritur, Quinàm sint Electi, aut quibus notis à reliquis Ecclesiae membri sint dignoscendi; Notitia enim istorum discreta sub hominum aspectum & κρίσιν minimè cadit: & solus DEUS est, qui novit suos, 1. Tim. 2, 19. Undè supra etiam cap. 1. ostendimus, hos invisibilem constituere Ecclesiam. Esse quidem in vera Ecclesia DEI aliquos Electos, verèque fideles, minimè est ambiguum: & in quibus pro tempore vera sit fides, & praesens Spiritus Sancti gratia, saltem confusâ aliquâ notitiâ haud obscurè colligitur. Verùm quia fides in multis est προσκαιρος, & gratia Spiritus Sancti non est bonum in hominibus ἀδιαβλητον, imò quia multiplices sunt cordium humanorum recessus, & imagines rerum perquàm fallaces: ideoque à priori & quoad certitudinem sive scientiam discretam, nihil de hoc ζητήματι statui potest.

Primum enim γνώρισμα refutat Servator ipse, Ecclesiam veram nominans pusillum gregem, Luc. 12, 32. Jtem portam angustam, & viam arctam esse docens, quae ducat ad vitam, & paucos esse qui eam inveniant: contra verò latam esse portam, & viam spaciosam, quae ducat ad interitum, & multos esse qui ambulent per eam: Matth. 7, 13. & 14. comprobat hoc ipsum Universalis Ecclesiae historia. Temporibus certè Noëas, Eliae, Christi, Apostolorum, Athanasii, falsa Ecclesia, hominum multitudine ita praevaluerat, ut vix nulla verae Ecclesiae ampliùs apparerent vestigia: & ProphetaElias se solum superesse quiritaretur.

Alterum γνώρισμα refellit Apostolus 1. Corinth. 1, 26. Videte fratres vocationem vestram, non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles: sed quae stulta, infirma, ignobilia sunt mundi, elegit DEUS. Praeterea vanitatem notae hujus arguit etiam illud, quod eodem modo Pharisaei contra Christi Ecclesiam argumentati sunt, pro falsâ eam reputantes ideò, quòd nemo ex principibus & Pharisaei credat in ipsum, Joh. 7, 48.

Sed illud etiam extra controversiam hoc loco est, Nùm Ecclesia simpliciter sic dicta, nota esse possint, qualiscunque Verbi divini praedicatio, qualiscunque etiam Sacramentorum usus? Nam in affirmantem fortè ipsi quoque Romanenses nobiscum haud inviti concedent: & tamen indè ad veram sta im Ecclesiam sublumi posse, negabunt. Differunt enim plurimùm, esse Ecclesiam aliquam: cui inesse potest etiam falsitas: & esse Ecclesiam veram: perindè atque Christus inter discipulos, & verè discipulos suos, Joh 8 31. distinguit: & vulgò inter fideles, & verè fideles, ingens esse discrimen, facilè agnoscitur.

Tertiam γνώρισμα cùm propriâ affectione verae Ecclesiae è diametro pugnat, quippe quae Scripturâ teste, nihil est aliud, quàm rosa inter spinas: secundum illud Cantici 2, 2. Sicut lilium inter spinas, sic amica mea inter filias. Est Ecclesia paupercula illa, quae omni generis tepestatibus pressa, consolationu omnis expers esse videtur. Jes. 54, 11. Et in hoc ipso argamenti genere tractando, ex professo versatur David Psalmo 37. integro: Asaphus, Psalmo 73. integro. Jacobus cap. 21. Jeremias cap. 12. Habacuc, cap. 1.

Verùm quaestio est propriè de coetu Ecclesiae universo, in quo vel magnum, vel aliquam saltem piè fidelium, & salvandorum partem DEUS sibi colligit: Quisnam coetus, pro vera Christi Ecclesia agnosci & haberi debeat: ex quibus notis, & quidem infallibilibus ea dijudicari possit? Jam verò ut nota aliqua, sit infallibilis, sit characteristica, sit vera, propria ac certa, duo potissimùm requirantur προσονειλυτα.

1. Ut talis nota sit eâ re, quam notare debet, notior.

1. Ut eandem certò atque infallibiliter ostendat: id quod sit tùm demùm, Si 1. rei notandae soli ac semper competat. 2. Si eandem à rebus omnibus alijs discernat. 3. Si ejusdem cum ea sit latitudinis, hoc est, neque sit latior, neque angustior. 4. Si à re notanda planè sit inseparabilis.

Quartum γνώρισμα plerumque falsae Ecclesiae proprium esse κριτήριον, Prophetae, Christus & Apostoli testantur. Jeremias certè Ecclesiae Judaicae de Templo Domini insolentiùs glorianti respondet: Nolite confidere in verbu mendacii, dicentes, Templum Domini &c. Jerem. 7, 4. Sic Christus Scribas & Pharisaeos de Cathedra Mosis gloriari admonet, sed ita, ut interim secundum opera ipsorum non sit faciendum, Matth. 23, 2. & 3.

Tales notas si studio, quo fieri potest, summo inquiramus, non nisi duas inveniemus, quibus quidem vera atque Orthodoxa Christi Ecclesia, infallibiliter dignosci, & à coetibus reliquis omnibus discerni, dijudicarique possit.

PRIOR est: Pura doctrinae coelestis praedicatio:

POSTERIOR est: Sacramentorum à CHRISTO institutorum legitimus usus.

Removemus deindè errorem Romanensium, quem longè perniciosissimum circa praesentem quaestionem fovent. Qui ut accuratiùs excutiatur, cum primis videndum fuerit, Quid propriè in Controversiam hoc loco veniat?

Jam quando de vera Ecclesia investigatio instituitur, non de ipsis personarum in di-

Duabus istis, & neque pluribus, neque paucioribus notis, unice competere affectiones notarum infallibilium paulò antè enumeratas, certissimum est. Nam 1. Verbi puritatem proprium Ecclesiæ bonum esse, quod extra eam nunquàm reperitur, & sine quo Ecclesia esse vera nullo modo potest, vel indè constat, quod Apostolus Ecclesiam DEI (ubi veram duntaxat notat) columnam & firmamentum Veritatis esse prædicat Timoth. 3. 15. quòd item Christus pro hac rogavit Patrem cœlestem, ut sanctificaret eam in veritate, hoc est, in sermone & Verbo suo : cujus depravatio Veritas dici nequit, neque de eadem pronunciari potest, quòd sit Sermo sive Verbum DEI, Johan. 17. 17. Quoad Sacramentorum usum legitimum, ille puritati Verbi planè est ὑπάλληλος: ac proindè eadem ejus est, quæ puritatis Doctrinæ conditio.

Porrò hæ ipsæ duæ notæ, veram Christi Ecclesiam, tùm ab Ecclesia malignantium: tùm á quibusvis aliis cœtibus, liquidissimè distinguunt: id quod per se est manifestissimum.

Tandem sunt notæ hæ planè adæquatæ, & inseparabiles à vera Christi Ecclesia. Etsi enim Ecclesia vera, & puritas doctrinæ, ac legitimus Sacramentorum usus, non sunt Synonyma aut æquipollentia: tamen invicem prorsus sunt consectanea.

Cæterùm rationes sive argumenta, quibus θέσιν hanc nostram evidenter demonstremus, præcipua sunt hæc.

I. In quo proprium Ecclesiæ consistit officium, in eodem rectissimè etiam ponitur verarum ac propriarum ejus notarum conditio. Atqui exercere, conservare, propugnare puram Evangelij prædicationem & legitimum Sacramentorum usum, proprium est Ecclesiæ officium. Ergò in duobus etiam istis consistit verarum ac propriarum notarum Ecclesiæ conditio. Ratio connexi in Majore vix in dubium apud quenquam venire potest, qui rem æqua lance expenderit. Etsi enim in rebus naturalibus, effectus à suis causis, interventu impedimentorum sunt separabiles: & in doctrinâ morum ab officijs interdum obsequia plurimùm distant: tamen in divinæ voluntatis Ordinationibus, à notatione effectus & officij proprij, ad ipsius causæ propriæ & subjecti notationem, firmissima infertur collectio.

Minoris veritas luculenter patet ex eo, quòd Apostolus Ecclesiam nominat columnam & firmamentum veritatis, 1. Tim. 3, 15. constat ergò argumento sua certa ac immota veritas.

II. Argumentum, Per quæcunq; res DEVS ipse Ecclesiæ salutem ordinariè operari consuevit: imò etiam Ecclesiam ipsam, & salvandorum cœtum colligit, conservat, propagat: in illis ipsis rectissimè etiam constituuntur notæ Ecclesiæ veræ planè infallibiles & characteristicæ. Atqui per Verbi & Sacramentorum Ministerium legitimum, DEUS utrunq; illud ordinariè efficit, Ergò. Ratio Majoris est evidentissi-

ma. Nam quia Salus, proprium Ecclesiæ est adjunctum: utique convenienter admodum, nota Ecclesiæ infallibilis ponitur in eo, per quod salus unicè acquiritur. Sicut & in principiis, quibus res quæque constituitur, ipsius rei judicandæ dignoscend æque signa atque notæ rectissimè collocantur. Minor per se est manifesta, & autorem habet Apostolum Petrum, 1. Petr. 1, 23. firma est ergò totius argumenti collectio.

III. Argumentum : In quacunque re, nota veritatis, quoad singula atque omnia Ecclesiæ veræ in dividua ponitur: in eadem totius etiam Ecclesiæ veræ nota infallibilis rectissimè ponitur. Atqui in Verbi divini auditu & cælestis doctrinæ amplexu, singulorum atque omnium Christianorum nota infallibilis ponitur. Ergò. Majoris connexum indè evidenter patet, quòd Ecclesia vera nihil aliud est, quàm verè Christianorum & salvandorum collectio sive multitudo. Jam verò de toto atque partibus non dispar potest esse judicium. Minor Scripturam testimoniis clarissimè liquet: ut.

Johan. 8. 47. Qui ex DEO est, Verba DEI audit. Johan 10, 27. Oves meæ vocem meam audiunt. Gal. 1, 8. Si vel nos, vel Angelus de cælo prædicaverit Evangelium, præter id quod nos prædicavimus vobis, anathema sit. 2. Thess. 3, 7. Subtrahite vos ab omni fratre, qui non ambulat secundum doctrinam, quam à nobis traditam. 2. Johan. vers. 9. & 10. Quicunque non permanet in doctrinâ Christi, DEUM non habet: & si quis venit ad vos, qui hanc doctrinam non affert, eum ne domo quidem recipite, aut AVE dicitc.

Sacramenta autem cùm sint non Verbi tantùm σφραγῖδες & signacula Rom. 4, 11. Sed ipsius etiam Ecclesiæ quasi tesseræ: certè vel hac ratione constat, ea à notis Ecclesiæ characteristicis, excludi nullo modo posse.

Cæterùm quæritur hoc loco, undenàm de puritate & sinceritate duarum istarum notarum, fieri debeat judicium? Respondemus, non ex canonibus, qui sub Apostolorum nomine circũferuntur, non etiam primò ex conciliorum de cretis, non etiam simpliciter ex Patrum monumentis: multò minùs ex Pontificum Romanorum responsis: sed ex solis Scripturis Sacris sive canonicis, quæ sunt Lydius ille lapis, ad quem unum omnia dogmata sunt examinanda: ita ut, quæ huic concordant, sine ulla dubitatione, pro puris ac veris agnoscantur, quæ dissentiunt, liberè tanquàm falsa rejiciantur. Qua de re, præclarè admodùm D. Augustinus disputat, libr. de Vnitate Ecclesiæ, cap. 2. Inter nos, inquiens, & Donatistas quæstio est, ubi sit Ecclesia? Quid ergò facturi sumus? In Verbis nostris eam quæsituri, an in Verbis capitis Domini Jesu Christi: puto in illius potius Verbo eum quaerere debeamus qui est Veritas, & optime novit corpus suum. Novit enim Dominus, qui sunt ejus.

Et cap. 3. Sed ut dicere coeperamus, non audiamus: Haec dico, hec dicis: sed audiamus: Haec dicit Dominus: Sunt certi libri Dominici, quorum autoritati utrique consentimus, utrique credimus, utriq; servimus: ibi quaeramus Ecclesiam, ibi discutiamus causam nostram. Auferantur ergo illa de medio, quae adversus nos invicem non ex divinis Canonicis libris, sed aliunde recitamus. Quaerat fortasse aliquis, & dicat mihi, ur ergo vu ista auferri de medio, quando communio tua, etsi proferantur, invicta est? Quia nolo humanis documentis, sed divinis oraculis, sanctam demonstrari Ecclesiam.

Et cap. 16. Remotis omnibus talibus Ecclesiam suam demonstrent, si possunt, non in sermonibus & rumoribus Afrorum, non in conciliis Episcoporum suorum, non in literis quorumlibet disputatorum, non in signis & prodigiis fallacibus, quia etiam contra ista Verbo Domini praeparati & cauti redditi sumus: sed in praescripto legis, in Prophetarum praedictionibus, in Psalmorum cantibus, in ipsis Pastoris vocibus, in Evangelistarum praedicationibus, in Apostolorum laboribus, hoc est, in omnibus Canonicis Sanctorum librorum autoritatibus.

De Sacramentis idem Augustinus Epist. 118. sic nobis suffragatur: Sacramentis numero paucissimis, observatu facillimis, significatione praestantissimis, societatem novi populi colligavit, sicuti est Baptismus, Trinitatis nomine consecratus: Communicacio corporis & sanguinis ipsius.

Augustino adstipulatur Chrysostomus, Homil. 49. in cap. 24. Matthaei, scribens: Cùm videritis haeresin impiam stantem in loco sancto Ecclesiae: tunc qui in Judaea sunt, fugiant ad montes, hoc est, qui sunt in Christianitate, conferant se ad Scripturas. Quia ex quo haeresis obtinuit Ecclesias, nulla probatio potest esse verae Christianitatis, neq; refugium Christiano um aliud, volentium cognoscere veritatem fidei, nisi Scripturae divinae. Nolo humano documento, sed divinis oraculis Ecclesiam sanctam demonstrari.

Sed porrò quaeritur An illi, qui sunt extra Ecclesiam: imò & illi, qui versantur quidem in Ecclesiae coetu, sed dono interpretandi intelligendiq; Scripturas destituuntur, de Notu hisce Ecclesiae veræ judicare possint? Respondeo affirmatè. Nam quoad illos, qui versantur extra Ecclesiam, etiamsi hi Spiritu S. quoad notitiam articulorum fidei nondùm docentur, aut ducuntur; interim tamen naturalis judicij acumine & intelligentia minimè destituuntur. Hæc naturalis intelli gentia, licèt Religionis Christianæ dogmata non sic apprehendere possit, ut ijs fidelis assen sus præbeatur. Hoc enim solius DEI opus est, & obtingit ijs, qui sunt θεοδίδακτοι: Matth. 16, 16. illud tamen præstare potest, ut nudam scientiam κατὰ ἄληψιν concipiat earum rerum, quæ in scriptis Prophetarum & Apostolorum continentur: præsertim, si linguarum notitia, quæ in infideles etiam cadit, accedat. Hi ergò aliquo modo scire & judicare possunt, in quo cœtu fiant, doceantur & credantur ea, quæ in libris Prophetarum & Apostolorum scripta continentur. Haud proindè totalis ἀδυναμία

judicandi de notis Ecclesiæ, infidelibus etiam, præsertim doctioribus adscribi potest aut debet.

Verùm quoad alterum ordinem eorum, qui sunt membra Ecclesiæ, & Spiritus S. primitias acceperunt, etsi hi non omnes valent dono interpretandi & intelligendi omnes Scripturas: etsi etiam controversiarum Theologicarum notitiâ destituuntur: tamen neque difficilis adeò, neque planè impossibili est earum rerum, quæ ad puritatem doctrinæ cœlestis faciunt, dijudicatio. Si modò ad capita catechetica doctrinam Ecclesiæ examinaverint. Hæc certè vel sola ἐξέτασις satis tutam & exactam discernendi quosvis Spiritus regulam & amussim præstare potest: modo circa Religionis Christianæ principia aliquis non planè rudis fuerit, & ipse salutis viam rectè calleat.


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church: Antithesis

ANTITHESIS.

The Romanists, and among them Bellarmine, descend into the arena against us by a double path: at the beginning indeed, intending to impugn the foundations of our doctrine with various weapons sought out: then truly, intending to confirm the fifteen marks of the Church which they invent.

The reasons by which he attacks our thesis are chiefly these:

I. The marks which are established by the Lutherans are in no way sufficient, because they do not declare which is the true Church, except probably: For we cannot know from this who are the elect or the righteous, but rather we learn where the Church lies hidden, rather than which it is.

I answer that the Jesuit is talking nonsense. For the judgment concerning the true Church is sought from these marks not of probability, but of certain and infallible evidence. For where the Gospel is purely taught and the Sacraments are rightly administered, it is as certain that it is the true Church as it is undoubtedly certain that there is life where motion is detected. Furthermore, it does nothing for the judgment of the true Church to know who are the elect or the righteous, since this knowledge is impossible in this life: and the elect constitute the invisible Church, concerning whose marks there is no controversy in this place, as was shown above. For if such marks of the elect could be established as would fall under the κρίσιν of the senses, then the invisible Church would degenerate into a visible one, which cannot happen. Finally, we ourselves freely grant that from these two marks, a certain and infallible judgment concerning individual persons regarding election and righteousness can neither be sought nor ought to be: because one who is neither elect nor righteous can have a sense of purity in doctrine and a legitimate use of administration in the Sacraments. Hence the Apostle, speaking of himself, says, I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway. 1 Cor. 9:27, which, however, cannot be true in the same way of the whole Church.

Bellarmino continues, and contends that from these notes of ours, not even that can be sufficiently declared, where the Church lies hidden: and this for the following three reasons.

THE FIRST is such: Notes must be proper, not common. And yet the sincere preaching of the truth is a note most common to all sects, at least by their own opinion and boasting. For what sect has there ever been that did not say it possessed the sincere preaching of the truth, the promise of which, as Augustine testifies, is customary and usual for all heretics. Book against the Epistle of Manichaeus, chapter 4.

I answer 1. That this commonality is not true or real: but merely titular and opinionated: even the Jesuit himself admits this. And yet the falsity of opinions prejudices the truth not at all, unless one wishes to leave no truth remaining in the nature of things. 2. If this Papal argument stands, no note of the Church can ever be given at all: which heretics might not also dare to claim for themselves, if opinion, or mere boasting, is sufficient in this regard. Indeed, the individual and universal notes of the Papists themselves, which they are accustomed to give, would be utterly overturned by this one argument; for they will have them in common not only with heretics and sectarians, but even with infidels and heathens themselves, if opinion and vain boasting ought to prejudice the truth itself. Here, therefore, Christ requires prudence from his own, Matt. 10. 16, and commands them to προσέχειν, to take heed, Matt. 7. 15. And the Apostle requires the δοκιμασίαν (testing) of doctrines and the Spirit: 1 Thess. 5. 21, 1 John 4. 1. For which indeed there would be no need of such προσοχῇ (heed) and δοκιμασία (testing) or κρίσει (judgment), if false boasting and empty vanity regarding such notes of the true Church had no place: and if the certain discernment of these notes were subject only to the external senses, and not to the discretion of judgment and faith.

But Bellarmino insists, and attacks the former note, namely the purity of the Word, thus: Either the Lutherans understand purity as being from every error: or only from essential and fundamental ones. If the former: the consequence will be that the Church exists among none of the Lutherans: for they themselves admit that their churches are not without flaws. If the latter: then this note will be common to many sects: and the Lutherans will constitute the true Church along with the Zwinglians and Pelagians: since they do not disagree concerning the Trinity, the Incarnation of the Son of God, and other primary articles.

I answer, concerning the dissolution of this knot, which seems to be Gordian in appearance, that there is need for the observation of certain hypotheses.

1. Almost all particular churches have a certain infancy of their own, in which if certain rudiments manifest themselves, the praise of truth is not on that account to be taken away from them: which is what was well observed by the Apostle himself in the Corinthian and Galatian Church, which he names holy Churches of God, although they labored under no small rudeness of their initial training, as is clearly evident from the Epistles written to each Church.

2. The Church behaves, regarding the purity

of preaching, like the Moon. For just as it has its increases and decreases of light according to the diversity of its approach to or recession from the Sun: so the Church also has its degrees in the doctrine of purity. An example is the primitive and Apostolic Church itself, in which the articles concerning the Resurrection, concerning the propagation of the kingdom of Christ to the Gentiles, and similar ones, did not have as much light as they later attained. Nor, however, will any pious person on that account derogate from its testimony of either truth or purity in doctrine.

3 There is a great difference among those things which are contained in Christian doctrine. Some things can be ignored and disputed by some for a time without harm, which indeed do not directly touch the very foundation of religion and the substance of the articles of faith: such as those which are sometimes disputed concerning the use of indifferent things, often even among members of the true Church: where often both sides decline somewhat from the mean of truth, although neither directly attacks the foundation of faith, let alone causes the loss of truth. But others are so constituted that they cannot be ignored or disputed, especially with some pertinacity, without the loss of Christian faith and truth immediately occurring: to which pertain the articles of faith and the chief heads of Religion.

4. Errors, which proceed from private men, or adhere to individual members of the Church, do not prejudice the public confession of any whole Church: just as the errors of Hymenaeus and Alexander did not overturn the purity and truth of the Ephesian Church.

Now therefore, when the Jesuit objects blemishes to our Churches, let him remember that we do not acknowledge just any blemishes in our Churches, but only those which are committed regarding conduct, or are peculiar to the doctrine of individual men, or of certain specific individuals. In both of which cases, however, nothing is detracted from the public confession and purity of doctrine of our Churches. Since judgment concerning its purity ought to be made not from one or another private man, but from the public confession of the Church.

2. To establish unity or conformity in doctrine with some other Church, consensus on one or another article of faith, or head of Religion, is not sufficient. For thus there would never have been any departure or defection from the true Church by any heresy whatsoever. The reason is this: Because there was no heresy which did not retain, in some articles, a purity of consensus with the orthodox Church. And it is not heresy, but apostasy, which makes a universal denial of the Christian faith. Therefore, because the Zwinglians do not dissent from us in some articles of faith, they no more constitute the same Church with us than they themselves, or the Papists with the Lutherans—between whom on both sides a similar consensus intervenes—come in any way into ecclesiastical unity.

Bellarmino's second argument is as follows: A mark must be better known than the thing of which it is a mark; otherwise, they are not marks, but unknown things. But the pure preaching of the Word is not such a thing: for without doubt, it is better known what the true Church is than what the true preaching of the Word is. Therefore, this cannot be a mark of the true Church.

I respond by a distinction of knowledge: for one kind is confused, another is distinct. There is no controversy here about confused knowledge. For even if, according to this confused knowledge, the true Church becomes known to us before the nature of the preaching itself, yet in the order of nature, and according to distinct knowledge, the knowledge of the true preaching of the Word is prior to that of the true Church. For from the former, the latter is finally born, constituted, and judged. If, therefore, the argument is understood concerning distinct knowledge, as it certainly ought to be understood, then the minor proposition suffers from manifest falsity and contains nothing but a begging of the question. 2 By the term distinct knowledge, one is not always to understand an exquisite knowledge, which falls only to those who have reached the pinnacle of theological cognition, but also that which has at least some knowledge of the principles and the chief chapters of Religion and Holy Scripture. It is indeed consistent that such was the knowledge of the Beroeans, who searched the Scriptures to see whether those things which were proposed by the Apostles were consistent with them. Such distinct knowledge is that which follows directly the guidance of Scripture, the series of the chapters of the Christian Religion, and the order of nature itself. Hence it is that, by the dictation of Scripture itself, we are sent to the law and to the testimony, Isa. 8:20. Whence that saying of Augustine, Epist. 166: In the Scriptures we have learned Christ, in the Scriptures we have learned the Church. And although there are many things in the Scriptures which have obscurity and difficulty, and not a few at that, yet that Scripture at least, from which the Church is known, is better known and easier than the Church itself. 3. The very series of the articles of faith, both in all methodical books and in the Creeds themselves, delivers a great part of the chapters of Religion before it informs the pious about the Church and its condition. 4. Finally, the order of nature itself always places causes before their effects, and principles before those things which derive their origin from principles. The order of learning, which we see observed in the Church, also follows this order of nature. For the treatment of Doctrine is always undertaken prior to that of the Church. Whence the rudiments of the Christian faith, which are as it were the fifth essence of Religion itself, become known to us as children, while the discussion concerning the Church is offered only to adults, and to those very few and most practiced.

Latin:

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ.

Romanenses, & inter hos Bellarminus, duplici via adversum nos in arenam descendit: initiò quidem doctrinæ nostræ fundamen ta, varijs conquifitis armis impugnaturus: deindè verò suas quas comminiscuntur, Ecclesiæ notas quindecim confirmaturus.

Rationes quibus nostram θέσιν impugnat, præ cipuæ sunt hæ:

I. Notæ quæ constituuntur à Lutheranis non sunt ullo modo sufficientes, quia non declarant, Quæ sit vera Ecclesia, nisi probabiliter: Non enim hinc scire possumus, qui sint electi vel justi, sed potius discimus, ubi lateat Ecclesia, quàm qua sit.

Respondeo, Nugari Jesuvvitam. Non enim probabilitatis, sed certæ & infallibilis evidentiæ judicium ex his notis petitur de Ecclesia vera. Nam ubi purè docetur Evangelium, & ritè administrantur Sacramenta, ibi tàm certum est, veram esse Ecclesiam, quàm indubitatè certum est vitam esse, ubi motus deprehenditur. Deindè nihil hoc facit ad judicium veræ Ecclesiæ scire, qui sint electi vel justi, cum hæc notitia hac in vita sit impossibilis: & Electi constituunt invisibilem Ecclesiam: de cujus notis hoc loco propriè non controvertitur, uti suprà ostensum. Si enim tales notæ constitui possentElectorum, quæ sub sensuum κρίσιν caderent; tùm invisibilis Ecclesia degeneraret in visibilem, id quod fieri nequit. Tandem ipsi ultrò largimur ex notis istis duabus, de individuis singulis ad Electionem & justitiam, certum ac infallibile judicium peti nec posse nec debere: Proptereà quod puritatis in doctrina sensum, & usum administrationis legitimum in Sacramentis habere potest, qui neque electus neque justus est. Hinc Apostolus de seipso verba faciens, castigo, inquit corpus meum, & in servitutem redigo, ne fortè, cum aliis prædicaverim, ipse reprobus fiam. 1. Cor. 9, 27 id quòd tamen de Ecclesia tota itidem verum esse nequit.

Pergit Bellarminus, & ex notis istis nostris, ne illud quidem satis sufficienter declarari posse contendit, ubinam lateat Ecclesia: idq; propter sequentes rationes tres.

PRIMA talis est: Notæ debent esse propriæ, non communes. Atqui sincera prædicatio veritatis est nota communissima omnibus sectis, saltem opinione ipsarum: & gloriatione. Quæ enim secta nunquam fuit, quæ non diceret, se habere sinceram prædicationem veritatis, cujus pollicitatio, teste Augustino, hæreticis omnibus usitata & consueta est. lib. contra Epist. Fundamenti. cap. 4.

Respondeo 1. Communitatem istam non veram esse aut realem: sed titularem duntaxat atque opinabilem: ipso fatente etiam Jesuvita. Atqui opinionum falsitas, veritati nihil omnino præjudicat, nisi veritatem in rerum natura nullam relinquere ampliùs libeat. 2. Stante hoc argumento Pontificio nulla prorsus ampliùs Ecclesiæ nota dari poterit: quam non hæretici sibi quoque vendicare ausint, si opinio, aut gloriatio nuda, hâc in parte sufficiat. Imò ipsorum Pontificiorum notæ singulæ ac universæ, quas dare solent, hoc uno argumento funditùs everterentur: quippè quas non cum hæreticis tantùm & sectarijs: sed ipsis etiam infidelibus atque Ethnicis communes habebunt, si opinio & vana jactatio veritati ipsi præjudicare debeat. Hic ergò Christus à suis prudentiam requirit, Matth. 10. 16. & jubet προσέχειν attendere, Matth. 7. 15. Et Apostolus δοκιμασίαν dogmatum & Spiritum exigit: 1. Thess. 5, 21. 1. Joh. 4. 1. Qua sanè προσοχῆ & δοκιμασία sive κρίσει minimè foret opus, si falsa gloriatio & inanis jactantia, de ejusmodi notis veræ Ecclesiæ, locum non haberet: sique notarum istarum certa dijudicatio, sensuum tantùm externorum, non verò judicij & fidei discretioni subjaceret.

Sed instat Bellarminus, & priorem notam, nempè Verbi puritatem sic impugnat: Vel intelligunt Lutherani puritatem ab omni errore: vel solùm ab essentialibus & fundamentalibus. Si prim: Consequens fuerit, apud nullos Lutheranorum esse Ecclesiam: nam ipsi fatentur, suas Ecclesias non carere nævis. Si posterius: jam nota hæc erit communis multis sectis: & Lutherani cum Zvvinglianis & Pelagianis veram Ecclesiam constituent: Siquidem de Trinitate, Incarnatione Filij DEI, & alijs primarijs Articulis non dissentiunt.

Respondeo, circa dissolutionem hujus nodi, qui secundum speciem videtur esse Gorgoneus, certarum quarundam hypotheseωn observatione opus esse.

1. Ecclesiarum particularium ferè omnium sua quædam est infantia, in quâ si se rudimenta quædam exerant, non propterea veritatis laus illis est abroganda: id quod in Ecclesia Corinthiaca & Galatica ab ipso Apostolo probè est observatum, quas ille sanctas DEI Ecclesias nominat, licèt tyrociniòrum ruditate haud mediocri laboraverint, ut ex Epistolis, utrique Ecclesiæ inscriptis luculenter patet.

2. Habet se Ecclesia, quoad puritatem

prædicationis, instar Lunæ. Quemadmodum enim hæc, pro diversitate accessus, vel recessus à Sole, sua habet lucis incrementa & decrementa: ita gradus etiam suos habet Ecclesia in doctrinâ puritatis. Exemplo est, Ecclesia ipsa primitiva & Apostolica, in qua Articuli de Resurrectione, de regno Christi ad gentiles propagando, & similes, tantam lucem non habuerunt, quantam postea sunt adepti. Neque tamen propterea vel veritatis, vel puritatis in doctrina Testimonium, quisquam pius ei derogabit.

3 Magnum est inter ea, quæ in doctrina Christiana continentur, capita, discrimen. Non nulla à quibusdam ad tempus sine damno ignorari & disceptari possunt, quæ nimirum fundamentum ipsum religionis, & substantiam articulorum fidei non directè attingunt: qualia sunt, quæ interdum circa usum rerum indifferentium, sæpius etiam inter veræ Ecclesiæ membra disceptantur: ubi sæpius utraque pars à veritatis medio nonnihil declinat, licet neutra fundamentum fidei directè impugnet, nedùm veritatis jacturam faciat. Alia verò ita comparata sunt, ut ignorari, aut controverti, præcipuè cum pertinacia aliquâ non possint, quin fidei Christianæ & veritatis statim jactura fiat: Quô pertinent Articuli fidei, & summa Religionis capita.

4. Errores, qui à privatis hominibus proficiscuntur, aut in membris Ecclesiæ singularibus hærent, publicæ confessioni totius alicujus Ecclesiæ non præjudicant: sicut Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ puritatem & veritatem, Hymenæi & Alexandri errores non everterunt.

Jam ergò, quando Jesuvvita nostris Ecclesijs nævos obijcit, meminerit, nos non simpliciter quosvis, sed illos tantùm nævos, in nostris Ecclesiis agnoscere, qui vel circa conversationem committuntur, vel in doctrina singularium hominum, sive certorum quorundam individuorum sunt proprij. Quo utrôque tamen casu, publicæ Ecclesiarum nostrarum confessioni & doctrinæ puritati nihil derogatur. Siquidem non ex unius aut alterius privati hominis, sed ex publica Ecclesiæ confeffione, de ejus puritate fieri debet judicium.

2. Ad unitatem vel conformitatem in doctrina cum Ecclesiâ aliâ aliquâ constituendam, non sufficit consensus de uno aut altero fidei articulo, vel capite Religionis. Sic enim ab Ecclesia vera, nullus unquàm discessus, aut defectiò fuisset facta, per quamcunque hæresin. Ratio hæc est: Quia nulla hæresis fuit, quæ non in aliquibus articulis, puritatem consensus, cum Ecclesia orthodoxa retinuerit. Et non hæresis, sed apostasia est, quæ universalem fidei Christianæ abnegationem facit. Zuvingliani ergò quòd à nobis, in aliquibus fidei articulis non dissentiunt, tam non eandem nobiscum Ecclesiam constituunt, quàm non vel ipsi cum Pontificijs, vel Pontificij cum Lutheranis, quibus utrobique similis consensus intercedit, in unitatem Ecclesiasticam ullo modo veniunt.

ALTERA Bellarmini ratio sic habet: Nota debent esse notiores ea re, cujus sunt nota: alioquin enim non sunt nota, sed ignota. Atqui pura Verbi prædicatio talis non est: Sine dubio enim notius est, qua sit vera Ecclesia, quam qua sit vera prædicatio Verbi. Ergò hæc nota vera Ecclesia esse nequit.

Respondeo per distinctionem notitiæ: Alia enim est confusa: alia verò discreta. De confusa hoc loco non controvertitur. Ut ut enim secundum confusam hanc notitiam nobis prius vera innotescat Ecclesia, quàm prædicationis ipsius ratio. Naturæ tamen ordine, & secundum discretam notitiam, prior est veræ verbi prædicationis, quàm Ecclesiæ veræ cognitio. Nam ex illa hæc demùm nascitur, constituitur & dijudicatur. Quod si ergò de discreta notitia intelligatur argumentum, uti certè de ea intelligi debet, tum minor propositio manifestâ falsitate laborat, & nil nisi principij petitionem continet. 2 Discretæ notitiæ termino, non exquisita semper est intelligenda, quæ non cadit nisi in eos, qui ad fastigium cognitionis Theologicæ pervenerunt: sed ea etiam, quæ saltem aliquam principiorũ & præcipuorum Religionis & Scripturæ Sacræ capitum cognitionem habet. Qualem notitiam Berrhoensium fuisse, verò consentaneum est, qui scrutati sunt Scripturas, utrum ea, quæ ab Apostolis proponebantur, illis essent consòanea Talis discreta notitia est, quæ Scripturæ ductum, capitum Religionis Christianæ seriem, & Naturæ ipsius ordinem rectà sequitur. Hinc est, quòd ipsius Scripturæ dictatu, remittimur ad legem & ad testimonium Jes. 8, 20. Undè illud Augustini Epist. 166. In Scripturis didicimus Christum, in Scripturis didicimus Ecclesiam. Et quamvis multa sunt in Scripturis quæ obscuritatem & difficultatem habent, haud sanè exiguam: tamen illa saltem Scriptura, ex qua Ecclesia noscitur, Ecclesiâ ipsâ notior est & facilior. 3. Ipsa quoque series articulorum fidei, tùm in libris omnibus metho dicis, tùm in ipsis etiam Symbolis, magnam capitum Religionis partem tradit, priusquàm de Ecclesia, ejusķ; conditione pios informet. 4. Tandem ordo ipse naturæ, causas effectis suis, & principia rebus ijs, quæ ex principijs ortum ducunt, semper anteponit. Quem ordinem naturæ sequitur etiam discendi ordo, quem in Ecclesia observari videmus. Semper enim prior Doctrinæ, quàm Ecclesiæ tractatio suscipitur. Undè nobis pueris innotescunt fidei Christianæ rudimenta, quæ sunt ipsius Religionis, quinta quasi essentia: dùm vix adultis, ijsķ; paucissimis & exercitatissimis offertur disceptatio de Ecclesia.


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church: Antithesis (continued)

Furthermore, what the Jesuit-life prattles about the reception of the Word, that no one can know for certain where the Word is truly believed, these things have nothing to do with the matter and are directed solely toward perverting the state of the controversy. For the question is not: Who truly receive the Word and who do not? Who believe the Word and who do not? But this is the question: Where is the Word of GOD purely preached, and where is it not? This is what can become known to us.

Finally, what he blathers about some external preaching is fabricated by him for the sake of deception. For we know only one preaching of the Word, which we call public; and from the quality of this, we establish that a judgment concerning the truth of the Church must be made.

The Jesuit-life insists: We have learned from the Church what is the true preaching of the Word and what is not. Therefore, it is better known what the true Church is than what the true preaching of the Word is.

I respond: The antecedent is false, if it is understood concerning distinct knowledge of the Church and of the true preaching of the Word. For neither becomes known to us primarily and indubitably from the testimony of the Church. But only from the Holy Scriptures, as we have demonstrated above. We believe, therefore, primarily and absolutely in the Scriptures; then, indeed, and κατ’ ἄλλο, in the testimony of the Church, insofar as it agrees with the magisterium of Scripture. Furthermore, even if not rarely a judgment can be made about a cause from its effect, it does not follow from that: Therefore the effect is better known than its cause. For one effect can have several causes; among which, however, one is the principal efficient cause, from which a certain judgment about the effect can and ought to be made.

But the Jesuit-life confirms this argument by another reason besides, which is as follows: True preaching is the preaching and interpretation of the true divine Scripture: But we cannot know what is the true Scripture, and what is its true sense, except from the testimony of the true Church. Therefore, the Church is more a mark of true preaching than true preaching is a mark of the true Church.

I respond, the minor is simply to be denied, as it is most false. For what is truly divine Scripture, and what is its true sense, can be known to us certainly and indubitably only from the Scriptures; but from the testimony of the Church, only probably and conditionally, as we demonstrated above concerning the question of the Authority of the Church. Thus, this argument is clearly puerile and trifling: The Church has the right of interpreting the Scriptures: Therefore, one must judge concerning the true sense of Scripture only from the testimony of the Church. For the antecedent is true only κατ’ ἐπι, but not absolutely and simply. The Church has the right of interpreting the Scriptures, but not an absolute one; rather, a conditional one: namely, that that interpretation must be analogous to the faith. Therefore, certainty concerning the true sense of Scripture becomes known to us primarily and apodictically from the Scriptures, which are to be believed absolutely.

Furthermore, the Jesuit-life clamors for the defense of his second argument, in this manner: The guardian of the Treasury must be known before the Treasury: and the Doctor before the doctrine, since doctrine is sought from the Doctor, not the contrary: Therefore the Church is a mark of true preaching rather than true preaching being a mark of the true Church,

I answer, that the antecedent is true, concerning confused knowledge: but not concerning distinct knowledge: I can perhaps opine in a confused way, that this one or that one is

The true guardian of the treasure: to be a true Doctor: but I can be very much deceived and err in this: unless a discrete knowledge is added: for this to be obtained by me, it is necessary that I first be certain about the doctrine itself, whether it is certain and true, and then at last I will also be able to be certain that the Doctor is pure and sincere. Thus the Roman Church sells itself as the guardian of the most sacred treasure, namely the divine Word: But if you now examine this Word, and weigh it against the analogy of faith, it will immediately be evident that it performs not the place and office of a guardian, but of a traitor and heretic: however much, according to a confused knowledge, another thing may seem to us concerning the Roman Church.

Bellarmino's third and final argument is as follows: True marks are inseparable from the true Church: But the Church of the Corinthians and Galatians, to which Paul was writing, were true Churches: and yet there was sometimes not a sincere preaching of the word there. For the Corinthians and Galatians are rebuked because they thought wrongly about the doctrine of truth. Therefore, the purity of the preached word is not a mark of the true Church.

I answer 1. that a distinction must be made between the universal and the particular Church. The latter can fall away from the purity of doctrine, by the example of the Galatian and Corinthian Church: But the former cannot. For thus the whole universal Church would fall away, which cannot happen: And thus the purity of doctrine is an inseparable mark of the universal Church; not indeed simply and absolutely, but in the way that was said above, in the question, Whether the Church can err? Next, a distinction must also be made between those who err, and the errors themselves: which is clear from those hypotheses which we explained above in the refutation of Bellarmino's first argument. For there is in individual particular Churches, first a certain infancy, as it were, which sometimes suffers from crudeness and ignorance: and for the most part errors cling to private men, which are not to be imputed to the church itself simply: And it is one thing to err, but meanwhile to be prepared to learn: but it is another thing for one who errs to be unwilling to learn and to stubbornly persevere in errors: the former can happen to a particular Church without the loss of truth: but this latter cannot, but the one that errs in this way immediately suffers the loss of truth itself. The former must also be established concerning the Corinthian and Galatian Churches: which is clear from the praises with which the Apostle wished to distinguish them in the inscription of his epistles: he would never have done this otherwise, if they had erred in the latter way, and had suffered the loss of truth.

Bellarmino now proceeds to the refutation of the second mark, which we said is the legitimate use of the Sacraments: fighting with the same reasons with which he wished to attack the former mark: but with a vain attempt. These therefore being passed over, that cavil rather comes to be examined, by which he accuses B. Luther, that he took great care that he might not receive any mark of those which are in the Constantinopolitan Symbol: but invented seven others: in his book on councils.

& Church. namely 1. the pure preaching of the Word. 2. the legitimate administration of Baptism. 3. the legitimate use of the Eucharist. 4. the authority of the keys. 5. the ordination of ministers. 6. public prayer, psalmody and the Catechism. 7. the mystery of the cross, that is, persecution or Martyrdom.

I answer: 1 The Jesuit lies. For Luther was so far from abhorring the marks of the Church defined in the Constantinopolitan Symbol, that he rather established that the remaining marks of the Church, each and all, which he added by way of declaration, were to be examined against those four: namely that the Church be one: 2. Holy 3. Catholic. 4. Apostolic. Just as we also know that those two essential marks, which we posit, are so constituted that they demonstrate and confirm these four praises of the true Church. Next, these very epithets of the Constantinopolitan Symbol show more what the true Church is: than by what marks it ought to be recognized and judged. Finally, Luther and others did indeed establish more marks of the true Church, but they nowhere contended that they were to be held with a similar degree of necessity and certainty: Nay, Luther himself explicitly writes that if at least the first mark, namely the pure preaching of the Word, is present and seen, it is enough to convince minds that the holy Catholic Church is there. Thus therefore Luther and others of our side themselves distinguished between essential and perpetual marks: and between those which are ὡς ἐπι τὸ πολὺ, that is, for the most part they are so, but yet they are mutable and separable. But we in this place are disputing only about those perpetual and essential marks: to which all the rest can easily be referred.

After the Jesuit has agitated our doctrine concerning the marks of the Church, but in vain, he now proposes the Roman Church's opinion concerning the same: in which we note two things in general at the beginning. First indeed the πολυκεφαλίαν (multi-headedness) of the Pontiffs, in establishing the marks of their Church: and in defining their quantity, or number: concerning which such diversity and dissimilarity exists among Pontifical Doctors, that it hardly agrees between any two: which Bellarmino himself is forced to admit, chap. 3. of book 4. on the marks of the Church. p. 1299. D.

The other thing, which we note as erroneous in general, is that Bellarmino writes that those marks are so constituted that they do not indeed make it evidently true: but yet evidently credible, that the Roman Church is the true Church of GOD. But now, whatever marks do not demonstrate the former, so that they might indeed make it evidently true that this or that Church is the true Church of GOD: those marks are certainly not true, proper, and ἀνασιώδειϛ (essential), nor inseparable, such as he himself demanded from us. Such marks therefore the Jesuit brings forward, which only show probably that the Roman Church is the true Church. But what kind those are, it will have to be examined a little more deeply.

Latin:

Quæ Jesu vvita porrò garrit de receptione Verbi, nemini posse esse certò notum, ubi vere credatur Verbum? ea nihil ad rem faciunt, & ad pervertendum statum controversiæ unicè sunt directa. Neque enim quæstio est, Quinam verè recipiant Verbum, qui non? Quinam credant Verbo, qui non? Sed hoc quæstionis est: ubinam purè prædicetur Verbum DEI, ubi non? id quod nobis innotescere potest.

Tandem, quæ blaterat de externa aliqua prædicatione, sunt ab ipso ad decipiendum conficta. Unam enim tantùm nos novimus prædicationē Verbi, quam nominamus publicam: & ex hujus qualitate, de veritate Ecclesiæ judicium faciendum esse statuimus.

Instat Jesuitavita: Didicimus ab Ecclesia, quæ sit Vera prædicatio Verbi, quæ non. Ergò notius est, quæ sit vera Ecclesia, quàm quæ sit vera prædicatio Verbi.

Respondeo: Antecedens falsum esse, si de discreta notitia Ecclesiæ, & veræ prædica, tionis Verbi, illud intelligatur. Neutrum enim ex Ecclesiæ testimonio, nobis primò & indubitatò innotesčit. Sed tantùm ex Scripturis Sacris, uti suprà demonstravimus. Credimus ergò primò & absolutè Scripturis: deindè verò & κατ’ ἄλλο testificationi Ecclesiæ, quatenùs cum Scripturæ magisterio ea consentit. Deindè etsi haud rarò ex effectu de causa fieri potest judicium: non tamen indè sequitur: Ergò Effectus notior est sua causâ. Nam unius effecti plures possunt esse causæ: inter quas tamen una est principalis efficiens, ex quâ de ef fectu judicium certum fieri potest & debet.

Sed aliâ insuper ratione secundum hoc argumentum confirmat Jesuitavita, quod tale est: Vera prædicatio, est prædicatio & interpretatio veræ Scripturæ divina: Qua sit autem vera Scriptura, & quis ejus verus sensus, non possumus scire, nisi ex testimonio veræ Ecclesiæ. Ergò potius Ecclesia est nota veræ prædicationis, quam vera prædicatio sit nota ve ræ Ecclesiæ.

Respondeo, Minorem simpliciter esse negandam, quippè falsissimam. Quæ enim sit Scriptura verè divina, & quis verus ejus sen sus, certò ac indubitatè non nisi ex Scripturis, nobis constare potest: ex Ecclesiæ verò testificatione tantùm probabiliter & conditionatè: uti supra demonstravimus circà quæstionem de Autoritate Ecclesiæ. Sic puerile planè est & nugatorium hoc argumentum: Ecclesia habet jus interpretandi Scripturas: Ergò de vero Scripturæ sensu non nisi ex Ecclesiæ testimonio, judicandum est. Nam Antecedens κατ’ ἐπι tantùm verum est, non verò absolutè & simpliciter. Habet Ecclesia jus interpretandi Scripturas, sed non absolutum: verùm conditionatum: ut nimirùm illa interpretatio sit analoga fidei. Certitudo ergò de vero sensu Scripturæ, primò & apodicticè ex Scripturis nobis innotescit, quibus absolutè est credendum.

Porrò obstrepit Jesuitavita pro defensione secundi sui argumenti, in hunc modum: Prius debet esse notus custos Thesauri, quàm Thesaurus: & Doctor, quàm doctrina, cùm à Doctore, petatur doctrina, non contra: Ergò Ecclesia potius est nota veræ prædicationis quàm vera prædicatio sit nota veræ Ecclesiæ,

Respondeo, Antecedens verum esse, de confusa notitia: sed non de discreta: Confusè fortassis opinari possum, hunc vel illum esse

Thesauri custodem verum: esse Doctorem verum:sed in eo plurimùm falli & errare possum:nisi accedat discreta notitia: quæ ut mihi obtingat,necessum est,ut de doctrina ipsa mihi prius constet,an sit certa & vera, & tùm demùm certus etiam esse potero,Doctorem esse purum & sincerum.SicRomanaEcclesia venditat se pro custode thesauri sacratissimi,nem pè Verbi divini: Sed si jam Verbum hoc examines,& ad analogiam fidei appendas,statim patebit, illam non custodis, sed proditoris & hæretici loco ac munere fungi: utut secundum confusam notitiam, aliud de Romana Ecclesia nobis videatur.

Tertium & postremum Bellarmini argumentum sic habet: Veræ notæ sunt inseparabiles à vera Ecclesia:Sed Ecclesia Corinthiorum & Galatarũ, ad quas scribebatPaulus,veræEcclesiæ erant: & tamen ibi aliquando non erat sincera prædicatio ver bi. Arguuntur enim Corinthij & Galatæ,quod perperàm sentirent de doctrina veritatis. Ergò puritas prædicati verbi,non est nota veræ Ecclesiæ.

Respondeo 1. distinguendum esse, inter Ecclesiam universalem & particularem.Hæc à puritate doctrinæ,exēplo Ecclesiæ Galaticæ & Corinthiacæ,deficere potest: Illa verò non potest.Sic enim totaEcclesia universalis deficeret, quod fieri nequit: Et sic puritas doctrinæ est nota inseparabilis universalis Ecclesiæ; non id quidem simpliciter & absolutè,sed eo,quo suprà dictum est modo,in quæstione, An Ecclesia errare possit ? Deindè distinguendum etiam inter errantes, & errores ipsos: id quod ex ijs hypothesibus liquet, quas suprà in refutatione primi argumenti Bellarminiani expedivimus. Est n. singularum Ecclesiarum particularium, primùm quædam quasi infantia, quæ ruditatem & ignorantiam aliquando patitur: & plerumque in privatis hominibus errores hærent,qui non sunt ecclesiæ ipsi simpli citer imputandi: Et aliud est, Errare quidem, sed interim paratum esse ad discendum:aliud verò est, errantem nolle discere & contumaciter in erroribus perseverare:illud prius potest cadere in Ecclesiam particularem, sine jactura veritatis: hoc autem posterius non potest, sed quæ hoc modo errat, statim ipsius veritatis jacturam patitur. Prius illud statuendum etiam deEcclesijs Corinthiaca & Galatica: id quod patet ex elogijs,quibus easApostolus in inscriptione suarum epistolarum insignire voluit: nunquàm hoc aliàs facturus,si posteriore modo errassent, & veritatis jacturam fecissent.

Progreditur jam Bellarminus ad refutationem secundæ notæ,quam diximus esse legitimum Sacramentorum usum: ijsdem plane rationibus pugnans, quibus priorem notam petere volui: sed irrito conatu. His proindè præteritis, Cavillum potiùs illud examinandvm venit,quo insimulat B. Lutherum, quòd ualdè caverit, ne ullam notam reciperet earum, quæ sunt in Symbolo Constantinopolitano: sed septem alias confinxerit: in libro de concil.

& Eccles. nempè 1. puram Verbi prædicationem. 2. Baptismi legitimam administrationem. 3. Eucharistiæ usum legitimum. 4. Autoritatem clavium. 5. ministrorum ordinationem. 6. Orationem publicam, psalmodiam & Catechismum. 7. Mysterium crucis, hoc est, persecutionem sive Martyrium.

Respondeo: 1 Mentiri Jesuvvitam. Lutherus enim usque adeò non à notis Ecclesiæ, in Symbolo Constantinopolitano definitis, abhorruit, ut potiùs statueret, reliquas Ecclesiæ notas singulas ac universas, quas declarationis loco adjecit, examinandas ad quatuor illas: nempè ut Ecclesia sit una: 2. Sancta 3. Catholica. 4. Apostolica. Quemadmodum & nos, duas illas Essentiales notas, quas ponimus, sic comparatas esse novimus, ut quatuor hæc Ecclesiæ veræ elogia, demonstrent & confirment. Deindè hæc ipsa Symboli Constantinopolitani epitheta, magis ostendunt, quid sit Ecclesia vera: quam ex quibus notis illa agnosci & judicari debeat? Tandem Lutherus & alij, plures Ecclesiæ veræ notas constituerunt quidem, sed simili necessitatis atq; certitudinis gradu, eas habendas esse nuspiàm contenderunt: Quin Lutherus ipse disertè scribit, si prima saltem nota, nempè pura Verbi prædicatio adsit & conspiciatur, satis esse, ad convincendos animos, quòd ibi sit Ecclesia sancta Catholica. Sic ergò Lutherus & alij ex nostrabus ipsimet distinxerunt inter notas Essentiales & perpetuas: & inter eas, quæ sunt ὡς ἐπι τὸ πολὺ, hoc est, plerunqve ita se habent, sed tamen sunt mutabiles & sperabiles. Nos verò hoc locò de perpetuis illis atque essentialibus notis tantùm disputamus: ad quas reliquæ omnes facile referri possunt.

Postquàm Jesuvvita nostram de notis Ecclesiæ doctrinam, sed frustrà, exagitavit, jam Romanæ Ecclesiæ sententiam de ijsdem proponit: in quâ nos initiò in genere duo notamus. Primum quidem πολυκεφαλίαν Pontificorum, in constituendis notis suæ Ecclesiæ: earumque definienda quantitate, sive numero: de quo tanta Pontificijs Doctoribus intercedit diversitas ac dissimilitudo, ut vix duobus invicem conveniat: id quod fateri necesse habet ipse Bellarminus, cap. 3. libri 4. de notis Ecclesiæ. pag. 1299. D.

Alterum, quod tanquàm erroneum in genere notamus, est, quod scribit Bellarminus, Notas istas sic esse comparatas, ut non quidem efficiant evidenter verum: sed tamen evidenter credibile, Romanam Ecclesiam esse veram DEI Ecclesiam. Jam verò quæcunque notæ prius illud non demonstrant, ut nimirùm evidenter verum efficient, hanc vel illam Ecclesiam, esse veram DEI Ecclesiam: illæ profectò notæ non sunt veræ, propriæ & ἀνασιώδειϛ, neque inseparabiles, quales tamen ipse à nobis efflagitavit. Tales ergò Jesuvvita profert notas, quæ verisimiliter tantùm ostendunt, Romanam Ecclesiam esse veram Ecclesiam. Sed quales illæ sint, paulò altiùs dispiciendum fuerit.


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church: I. The mark of the Church according to Bellarmine

I. The mark of the Church according to Bellarmine.

In examining these marks, two things especially must be considered: 1. Whether they are true, proper, and essential, nay, inseparable. 2. Whether they are found in the Roman Pontifical Church.

Bellarmine establishes the first mark as the very name of the Catholic Church and of Christians. Yet this mark 1. commits a shameful begging of the question. For the question between us and the Romanists is, whether the Roman Church is the true Catholic Church? Bellarmine answers that it is: and that this can be discerned from the fact that the Roman Church is Catholic, and bears the name of the Catholic Church. 2. It argues for stupidity: for it is vain to estimate the praise of truth from the mere usurpation of names and titles. 3. The Jesuit will hardly show any heretics who have not prided themselves on this same title and name: as is evident regarding the Angelics, Apostolics, Cathars, Encratites, Euchites, and similar heretics whose heresy was condemned by the Church, as witnessed by Augustine in De hæresibus, heresy 39, 38, 25, 40, 57. Finally, if Bellarmine should except that truth is joined to the name, he involves himself in a contradiction by this appellation. For that is Catholic which agrees entirely with the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles. Now, he previously denied that this pure doctrine, or the preaching of the Word, is a mark of the true Church. He must therefore necessarily deny that 'Catholic', etc., is also a mark of the true Church: or if he urges 'Catholic', he must also include the pure preaching of the Word among the proper marks of the Church. For these two cannot be separated from each other, but are ἀδιασπάτως (inseparably) connected. Now, we have demonstrated above to the eye that the Catholic eulogy does not belong to the Roman Church, where the third axiom of the Church was disputed.

appealed to antiquity, they admitted it only as limited, so that not just any antiquity, or one accepted simply and nakedly, but one limited by the first principle, could have any value for the proof of truth: just as we have already shown from Tertullian.

Both this antiquity, both that which consists in the reason of the foundation in the doctrine of Apostolic truth, and that which is proper to the principle itself and to extreme antiquity, the Roman Pontifical Church can by no right claim for itself. For it is established that it is a new Church, and one later and worse than the Apostolic Church, not in respect of time, but in purity of doctrine, and therefore not the most ancient. Nor is it for Bellarmine to demand from us either a definite circumstance of time when Papism began: or the place where it first began: or the name of the first author, or other things of that kind which can be demonstrated in every notable mutation. For although in simple heresy such circumstances can be easily demonstrated, as Bellarmine demonstrates that regarding the Arian heresy: yet regarding the Roman Church and doctrine this cannot be demonstrated: The reason for the diversity is this, because the Papacy or Papism is not a simple heresy: but Antichrist, or Antichristianism. Scripture, however, proposes this to us to be viewed not under the image of a single person: but of an entire kingdom: nay, under the picture of such an empire and monarchy, by which not a few or insignificant kingdoms of this world are to be subjugated. To which matter the efforts not of one person, but of many, pertain: and not a moment of time, but some duration is required. What? That Scripture is a witness that that kingdom of Antichrist is to be constituted by fraud and indeed secretly, as a mystery of iniquity, which is finally to be revealed, 2 Thess. 2:7. But there would be no need for revelation if this mystery were operating openly and in the sight of men. Furthermore, Scripture is likewise a witness that this kingdom is to be constituted not at one certain moment of time: but gradually and in the progress of time: since the Apostle testifies that the mystery of iniquity was already effective in his own time, and that it was being restrained from elsewhere, so that it had not yet broken out into full force: 2 Thess. 2:7. And John in his own time affirms both, that there are many Antichrists now, and yet that the true Antichrist is finally to come: 1 John 2:18. Finally, Daniel also wished to intimate that an exact and definite certainty of time regarding the beginnings of the Papacy could not be had, when he prophesied concerning the efforts of Antichrist in changing times and laws. It must, however, be denied not at all in the meantime that it was done most correctly by those who wished to assign the six-hundredth year from the birth of Christ to the emerging kingdom of Antichrist. For around that century, this mystery of iniquity began to be most effective, by adulterating the doctrine of Christ, by introducing primacy into the Church, and by fixing its seat at Rome.

Latin:

I. Nota Ecclesiæ secundum Bellarminum.

IN examinandis notis istis, duo potissimum pensi sunt habenda: 1. Vtrùm ea sint veræ, propriæ & essentiales, imò inseparabiles. 2. Vtrùm in Romana Pontificia Ecclesia eæ inveniantur.

PRIMAM notam constituit Bellarminus, Ipsum Catholica Ecclesiæ & Christianorum nomen. Atqui hæc nota 1. committit turpem petitionem principij. Quæritur enim inter nos & Romanenses, an Romana Ecclesia sit vera Catholica Ecclesia? Respondet Bellarminus, quod sit: & il ud indè dignosci posse, quia Ecclesia Romana sit Catholica, & Catholicæ Ecclesiæ nomen præ se ferat. 2. Stohditatem arguit: Vanum est enim.veritatis laudem ex sola nominum & titulorum usurpatione æstimare 3. Vix ullos Jesuvvita monstrabit hæreticos, qui hoc eodem titulo ac nomine non superbierint:uti patet de angelicis, apostolicis, Catharis, Encratitis, Euchetis & similibus hæreti cis quorum ab Ecclesia damnata est hæresis teste Augustino de hærefibus, hærefi 39. 38. 25. 40. 57. Tandeim si excipiat Bellarminus, veritatiem nomini conjunctam,hac appellatione intelligi, seipsum contradictione implicat. Catholicum enim est, quod cum doctrinâ Prophetarum & Apostolorum ex asse concordat. Jam verò negavit antea, puram istam doctrinam sive prædicationem Verbi, esse notam veræ Ecclesiæ. Neger ergò necesse est, Catholicum etc iam non esse notam veræ Ecclesiæ: Vel si Catholicum urgeat, puram etiam prædicatione Verbi, inter notas Ecclesiæ proprias referat, oportet. Hæc enim duo dvelli non possunt à se mutuò, sed ἀδιασπάτως sunt connexa. Jam verò Romanæ Ecclesiæ Catholicum elogium non competere, supra ad oculum demonstravimus, ubi de tertio Ecclesiæ axiomate disputatum fuit.

ad antiquitatem provocarunt, illi non nisi limitatam admiferunt, ita ut non antiquitas quævis, aut simpliciter ac nudè accepta: sed primo principio limitata,ad probationem ve ritatis aliquid valere possit: Quemadmodum ex Tertulliano jam ostendimus.

Utramque hanc antiquitatem, tùm quæ ratione fundamenti consistit in doctrina veri tatis Apostolicæ,tum quæ principij ipsius, & extremæ vetustatis est propria, Romana Ponti ficia Ecclesia nullo jure sibi vendicare potest. Novam enim, &Apostolicâ Ecclesiâ, non respectu temporis,sed doctrinæ puritate & posteriorem & deteriorem,ac proindè non antiquissimam eam esse constat. Neque est, ut Bellarminus à nobis exigat,vel definitam tem poris circumstantiam,quo cœperit Papismus: vel locum, ubi primum cœperit: vel autoris primi nomé vel id genus alia,quæ in omni insigni mutatione demonstrari possunt. Nam licèt in hærefi simplici,hujusmodi circumstan tiæ facilè demonstrari possint,uti de Ariana hæresi illud demonstrat Bellarminus: tamen de Romanâ Ecclesiâ&doctrinâ hoc demonstrari nequit: Ratio diversitatis est hæc, quia Papatus sive Papismus non est simplex hæresis: sed Antichristus, sive Antichristian ismus.Hûc autem Scriptura non sub ûnius personæ: sed sub totius regni imagine spectandum nobis proponit:imò sub pictura imperij & monar chatus talis, à quo regna mundi hujus non pauca aut exigua sint subjuganda. Quam ad rem non unius personæ,sed plurium conatus pert nent: neque momentum temporis, sed diuturnitas aliqua requiritur. Quid? quod Scriptura testis est, fraude & quidem occulta regnum illud Antichristi constituendum esse, quippè mysterium iniquitatis, quod tandem sit revelandum, 2. Thess. 2. 7. Revelatione autem opus non foret,si palàm mysterium istud & in conspectu hominum operaretur. Porrò Scriptura itidem testis est, non uno quopiam certo temporis momento : sed paulatim & progressu temporis regnum istud constituendum esse: Siquidem Apostolus jam suo tempore mysterium iniquitatis efficax esse, idq; aliundè adhuc coëceri testatur, quo minus jam tùm in nervum eruperit: 2. Thess. 2.7. & Johannes suo jam tempore utrumque assirmat, & multos modo esse Antichristos, & tamen verum Antichristum demùm venturum : 1. Johan. 2. 18. Tandem neque temporis exactam ac defi nitam certitudinem de Papatus initijs haberi posse,innuere voluit Daniel, quando vaticinatus est de conatibus Antichristi, in mutandis temporibus & legibus. Negandum tamen interim est minimè, rectissimè factum esse ab ijs, qui annum Christi nati sexcentesimũ, emergenti regno antichristi, adsignare voluerunt. Nam circa illud seculum, mysterium Hoc iniquitatis maximè cœpit esse efficax, doctrinam Christi adulterando, primatum inEcclesiam introducendo, & Romæ sedem suam figendo,


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church: II. The mark of the Roman Church

II. The mark of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes Antiquity as the second mark of the true Church. Which mark 1. Is also common to falsehood and lying: and therefore does not specifically distinguish the true Church from the false. 2. Regarding particular churches, however true they may be, this mark of antiquity is lacking, and therefore it is a separable mark. 3. The most ancient Fathers rejected this mark: For Tertullian does not say that everything most ancient is most true, as this sentence is commonly cited: But everything first is most true. Let the Romanists therefore demonstrate that their Church is first, that is, Apostolic, or built solely upon Apostolic doctrine, then they will also obtain the praise of true antiquity. To which opinion Ignatius speaks excellently, in his epistle to the Philadelphians: ἐμοί ἀρχεῖα ἐςὶν ἰησῦς ὁ χριςὸς & παραφανται πεισόηλα Cν ὀλεθρῷ:. For me, the one and true antiquity is Christ, not to hear whom is joined with manifest destruction. 4. If any from the parts

III. Note of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes the third note as long duration, and never interrupted: that is, a Church that will never perish: a thing which we ourselves also grant concerning the true Church. But it is not yet proven from that, that the Church which lasts for a long time and for many centuries is the true Catholic Church. For this can happen to the churches of heretics, as is evident concerning Arianism, which flourished for an entire century, where nevertheless it would have been a very weak collection, if anyone had wished to pronounce from that time for the truth of the Arian Church. Furthermore, this note is not proper and adequate to the true Church. Certainly the Antiochene, Alexandrian, Constantinopolitan, Corinthian, Galatian, and Ephesian churches were without doubt true churches: yet they could not boast of long duration, but suffered grave interruptions; indeed, some of them have perished entirely, now serving Mohammedanism. Thus that old Roman one, which had the Apostle Paul as its teacher, was indeed Orthodox, but it experienced such vicissitudes that it has now lapsed and degenerated into an Antichristian one. Although this may seem similar to itself in the abominations of its dogmas, nevertheless it has suffered conversions and almost tragic mutations, a thing which the history of the schisms of the Roman Church clearly proves: concerning which see Illyricus's book on the Sects and dissensions of the Roman Church.

Finally, although the Roman Church has lasted for many centuries, and perhaps will last until the end of the age: yet the eulogy of truth cannot be attributed to it for that reason, because Scripture predicted this perpetuity of the Antichristian kingdom, as often as it speaks of the efficacy of that error, and that that man of perdition is finally to be abolished by the coming of Christ. The Roman Church therefore has this as something peculiar compared to all other heresies. But concerning that duration in the East, Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians, and especially Mohammedans can boast equally today, whose boasting in this part is so similar to that of the Pontificians that an egg cannot be more similar to an egg.

Latin:

II. Nota Romanæ Ecclesiæ.

ALTERAM Ecclesiæ veræ notam constituit Bellarminus Antiqui atem A.qui hæc nota 1. Communis etiam est falsitati & mendacio: ac proindè veram à falsa Ecclesia non specificè distinguit. 2. Quoâd Ecclesias particulares quantumvis veras, nota hæc antiquitatis deficit,ac proindè est nota separabilis. 3. Antiquissimi Patres hanc notam rejecerunt:Neque enim Tertullianus ait, Antiquissimum quodque esse verissimum,uti vulgo citatur hæc sententia:Sed primum quodq; est verißimum Demonstrent ergò Romanenses suam Eccle. siam esse primâ,hoc est,Apostolicam,sive do ct inæ Apostolicæ unicè superstructam, tùm antiquitatis etiam veræ laudem obtinebunt. Quam in sententiam præclarè Ignatius, epist. ad Philadelphos : ἐμοί ἀρχεῖα ἐςὶν ἰησῦς ὁ χριςὸς & παραφανται πεισόηλα Cν ὀλεθρῷ:. Mihi antiquitas una atq; vera est Christus quem non audire, eum manifesto exitio cõjunctũ est.4.Si qui ex partib.

III. Nota Romanæ Ecclesiæ.

TErtiam notam constituitBellarminusDurationem diuturnam,neq; unquàm interruptā: hoc est, nunquàm interituram Ecclesiam : id quod nos ipsi quoque largimur,deEcclesia ve ra: Sed nondum illud indè evincitur,illamEcclesiam esse veram Catholicā Ecclesiam, quæ diu & multis seculis durat. Potest enim hoc hæreticorum Ecclesiæ obtingere,uti de Arianismo constat,quod per integrum seculumflo - ruerit,ubi tamen infirmissima fuisset collectio, si quis indè tùm pro veritate Ecclesiæ Arianæ pronunciare voluisset. Deindè nota hæc non est veræ Ecclesiæ propria & adæquata.
