Ecclesia certè Antiochena, Alexandrina, Constantinopolitana,Corinthiaca,Galatica,Ephesina,veræ sine dubio fuerunt Ecclesiæ : Atqui de duratione diuturna gloria non potuerunt,sed graves passæ sunt interruptiones,imò nonnullæ earum pe nitùs defierunt,Mahometismo jam servientes. Sic Romana illa vetus,quæ Pau umApostolū Doctorem habuit, Orthodoxa quidem fuit, sed tales vicissitudines experta est, ut jam in Antichristianam defecerit & degeneravit. Hæc quamvis in abominationibus dogmatū similis sibi videatur, tamen conversiones, & tragicas quasi mutationes perpessa est,id quod historia Schismatum Ecclesiæ Romanæ luculenter comprobat:de qua vide Illyrici librum de Sectu & dissensionibus Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

Tandem licèt Romana Ecclesia multis seculis duraverit, & duratura fortassis ad finē usque seculi: veritatis tamen elogium ideò perhiberi ipsi nequit, propterea quòd hanc perpetuitatem regni Antichristiani prædixit Scriptura, quoties de efficaciâ illius erroris,& quod homo ille perditionis, Christi demum adventu plenè sit abolendus, verba facit. Habet ergòRomanaEcclesia hoc quasi peculiare præ cæteris hæresibus omnibus. Sed de ea duratione in oriente hodiè æquè gloriari possunt Ariani,Nestoriani, Eutychiani, præcipuè Mahometani,quorum hæc in parte eum Pon - tificijs, tàm similis est gloriatio, ut ovum ovo non magis simile esse queat.


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church: IV. Note of the Roman Church

IV. Note of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes the fourth note as the amplitude or multitude and variety of believers. And yet this note is not essential to the true Church, but only accidental. For it is of an accident that now there is a great multitude of believers, but sometimes a great rarity of the same. 2. The primitive Apostolic Church could not boast of this note. Was it therefore not a true Church? Thus CHRIST defines His Church by few, and by a little flock, Matt. 7:14, Luke 12:32. 3. Opposed to this amplitude is the fact that it is contained everywhere in the Scriptures concerning the cross and afflictions to which the Church is to be subjected in this world: Acts 14:22, 2 Tim. 3:12; and that the glory and amplitude of the Church is predicted to be from within, Psalm 45:14. Finally, this glory does not even belong to the Roman Church, as it is evident that ever since the reformation of B. Luther, it has suffered such a sad defection that it has lost the greater part of many kingdoms: France, Denmark, Scotland, England, Sweden, and the whole of Germany. But let it be, if the Roman Church surpasses all other particular ones in amplitude: it would not therefore be Catholic: a thing which is evident from those things which we discussed above concerning the third axiom of the Church: so that we can truly exclaim with Nazianzen: πῦ πότε ἐσιν οἱ τῶ πλήθει τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ὁρίζοντες, καὶ τὸ βραχὺ ποίμνιον τες ποιμένιον: where are those who define the Church by multitude, and despise the little flock? Naz. in sermon against the Arians concerning himself.

V. Note of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes the fifth note as the succession of Bishops in the Roman Church, traced from the Apostles down to us. And yet this is entirely lacking in any testimony of Scripture: and it smacks partly of Judaism, partly of all things carnal, and Scripture itself teaches what is to be hoped or thought concerning it, which predicts that lying ministers will come into the Church, subintroducing pernicious sects, 2 Pet. 2:1, that the Antichrist will sit in the very temple of God, 2 Thess. 2:4, and that from the Apostolic Church itself will emerge ravenous wolves, and men speaking perverse things: Acts 20:30. 2. This note is more unknown than the Church itself: and we have already discussed its vanity sufficiently and more than sufficiently above. The sum returns to this: [1] That no rectitude of succession can be given without the truth of doctrine, in which alone is founded whatever can be said or thought about true succession in the Church, which being presupposed, the Lutheran Church rightly enjoys the title of true Apostolic succession, in preference to the Roman Pontifical: as demonstrated above. 3. This mark is not proper to the true Church. For there was a true Church before there was a succession of Bishops, and indeed the Apostolic one itself, and therefore it is false, what the Jesuit so boldly affirms, that the Church is called Apostolic on account of succession from the Apostles. 4. This mark is not ἀντίσροφος (convertible) with the true Church: Otherwise it would follow: The Jewish Synagogue, in the time of Christ, had an ordinary succession of Bishops. Therefore it was a true Church: which the Romanists themselves acknowledge to be false. Finally, this mark does not even belong to the Roman Church καθ' ἁυτὸ (in itself). [2] For how often this fictitious succession of Bishops has been interrupted, has been most clearly demonstrated above, where we disputed about this succession professedly.

Latin:

IV. Nota Romanæ Ecclesiæ.

QUArtam notam constituit Bellarminus, Amplitudinem sive multitudinem &varietatem credentium Atqui &hæc nota non estEssen tialis veræ Ecclesiæ, sed tantùm accidentalis. Accidentis enim est,quòd nunc magna est cre dentium multitudo,interdum verò magna eo rundem raritas. 2. Ecclesia primativa Apostolica, de hac nota gloriari non potuit. Ergonè vera Ecclesia non fuit ? Sic CHRISTUS Ecclesiam suam definit per paucos, & per pusillum gregem,Matth. 7.14. Luc. 12,32. 3. Amplitudini huic adversatur, quòd passim in Scripturis de cruce&afflictionibus, quibus Ecclesia hoc in mundo sit subjicienda, continetur: Actor. 14, 22. 2. Timoth. 3, 12. quòd Ecclesiæ gloria & amplitudo, ab intus fore prædicitur, Psal. 45, 14. Tandem ne quidem Ecclesiæ Romanæ hæc gloria competit, ut quam constat, jam indè à reformatione B. Lutheri, tàm tristem defectionem passam esse, ut plurimorum regnorum, Galliæ, Daniæ, Scotiæ, Angliæ, Sueciæ, & totius Germaniæ maximam partem jacturam fecerit. Sed esto, superet Romana Ecclesia omnes alias particulares, amplitudine: non tamen proptereà Catholica fuerit: id quod constat ex ijs, quæ de tertio axiomate Ecclesiæ suprà disputavimus: ita ut verè cúm Nazianzeno exclamare possimus: πῦ πότε ἐσιν οἱ τῶ πλήθει τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ὁρίζοντες, καὶ τὸ βραχὺ ποίμνιον τες ποιμένιον: ubinam illi sunt, qui Ecclesiam multitudine definiunt, & gregem pusillum aspernantur? Naz. in serm. contra Arianos de se ipso.

V. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

QUintam notam constituit Bellarminus, Successionem Episcoporum in Romana Ecclesia ab Apostolis deductam usq; ad nos Atqui hæc prorsus caret omni Scripturæ testimonio: & partim Judaismum, partim carnalia omnia resipit, & quid de ea sperandum aut cogitandum sit, Scriptura ipsa docet, quæ prædicit, venturos in Ecclesia ministros mendaces, subintroducentes sectas perniciosas 2. Petr. 2, 1. Antichristum in ipso templo Domini sessurum, 2. Thess. 2, 4. & ex ipsa Apostolica Ecclesia emersuros lupos rapaces, & viros perversa loquentes: Actor. 20, 30. 2. Nota hæc ignotior est ipsâ Ecclesiâ: & de ejus vanitate jam suprà satis superque disputavimus. Summa huc redit: Successionis rectitudinem dari nullam posse absque Doctrinæ veritate, in qua sola fundatur, quidquit de vera Successione in Ecclesia dici aut cogitari potest, Quo præ supposito, Ecclesia Lutherana veræ Successionis Apostolicæ titulo, præ Romanâ Pontificiâ jure gaudet: uti supra demonstratum. 3. Nota hæc non est Ecclesiæ veræ propria. Fuit enim vera Ecclesia, antequàm fuit successio Episcoporum, & quidem ipsa Apostolica, ac proindè falsum, quod usque adeò audacter affirmat Jesuvvita, Ecclesiam dici Apostolicam, propter successionem ab Apostolis. 4. Nota hæc cùm Ecclesiâ vera non est ἀντίσροφος convertibilis: Aliàs sequeretur: Synagoga Judaica, tempore Christi habuit Successionem Episcoporum ordinariam. Ergò vera fuit Ecclesia: id quod falsum esse, ipsi agnoscunt Romanenses. Tandem ne Romanæ quidem Ecclesiæ Nota hæc καθ' ἁυτὸ competit. Quoties enim interrupta fuerit ficticia hæc Episcoporum successio, suprà demonstratum luculentissimè, ubi de successione hac ex professo disputavimus.


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church: VI. Mark of the Roman Church

VI. Mark of the Roman Church.

…[5] Bellarmine constitutes the sixth mark as conspiracy in doctrine with the ancient Church, where We initially embrace both, as it is called, that which the Jesuit brings forward from Tertullian; namely, that the true Church is called Apostolic, not only because of the succession of Bishops from the Apostles, but also because of the consanguinity of doctrine: because, clearly, it retains the doctrine which the Apostles delivered. But this mark is not better known than the Church itself: nor is it a mark at all. For if it were, then that very ancient Church would not be the true Church, because it is destitute of this mark. 2. It is impious: for it detracts from the Apostolic Writings that authority which it assigns to the writings and doctrine of antiquity. 3. It is uncertain and doubtful: for not every consensus in doctrine and worship is approved by GOD: but it must first be demonstrated that the doctrine itself is true and heavenly. 4. This mark does not belong to the Roman Church καθ' αυτὸ: so much so, that the Roman Pontiff does not approve the writings of the Holy Fathers unless they are castrated: as the expurgatory index of the Roman Church demonstrates to the eye,

VII. Mark of the Roman Church.

Bellarmine establishes the seventh mark, the union of members among themselves and with the head, that is, the Roman Pontiff. But the true union of members among themselves consists, as the Apostle teaches, in the unity of faith, Eph. 4:4. This, however, properly belongs to the invisible Church, not indeed to the visible. Therefore, by this arrangement, the Jesuit concedes the invisible Church, even without knowing it: Or if he contends that it belongs to the visible Church, it is manifest that he is proving the unknown, namely, where the true Church is and what it is, by something much more unknown, namely, by the union of members among themselves, which cannot be established as indubitable and infallible from external signs. 2. How truly the Romanists glory in this union, the histories of previous times show, concerning the contradictions, struggles of writers, schisms, wars, and persecutions of the members of the Roman Church itself among themselves. 3. That today a greater concord is perceived among the Romanists, the cause is not piety, not the truth of faith and religion: but partly the pursuit of malice, by which they strive more sharply to harm the true Church; partly the fear of danger, which could not be most present if the Roman Church were still bursting apart with its former dissensions and discords. 4. It is impious and profane, whatever the Jesuit blathers about the Roman Pontiff as the head of the Church. For just as, according to Hilary, that unity alone provides peace to the Church which is of Christ: so also Christ alone is the Head of the Church, who redeemed it with His own blood, as is demonstrated more fully elsewhere. Eph. 1. 5. This mark does not belong to the true Church alone: but also to the church of the malignant: for the members of the Jewish and Mohammedan churches have coalesced among themselves with a tighter bond of unity than any that can ever fall to the Romanists.

Bellarmine establishes the eighth mark of the Church; the holiness of doctrine. But if the Jesuit understands the purity of the divine Word and its preaching, then he confirms our opinion, which he nevertheless attacked above quite hatefully and bitterly. For doctrine cannot be holy which is not pure and consonant with the sacred Scriptures. But if he dreams of some other holiness of doctrine besides this, the Jesuit acts as a trickster and an absurd sophist, as one who impiously maintains that some holiness of ecclesiastical doctrine can consist in dissonance from the Scriptures.

Latin:

VI. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

SExtam notam constituit Bellarminus conspirationem in doctrinâ cum Ecclesia antiqua, ubi nos initiò utraque quod dicitur manu, amplexamur illud, quod ex Tertulliano profert Jesuvvita; nempè veram Ecclesiam dici Apostolicam, non tantùm propter successionem Episcoporum ab Apostolis: sed etiam propter doctrinæ Consanguinitatē: quia videlicet doctrinam retinet, quam Apostoli tradiderunt. Atqui nota hæc non est notior ipsâ Ecclesiâ: neque nota omninò est. Si enim esset, jam ipsa illa antiqua Ecclesia, vera Ecclesia non esset, quia notâ hac destituitur. 2. impia est: derogat enim Scriptis Apostolicis eam autoritatem, quam scriptis & doctrinæ antiquitatis assignat. 3. Incerta & dubia est: non enim omnis in doctrina Consensus & Cultus DEO probatur: sed prius demonstrandum est, doctrinam ipsam esse veram ac Cælestem. 4. Ecclesiæ Romanæ nota hæc non competit καθ' αυτὸ : usque adeò, ut Pontifex Romanus Sanctorum Patrum Scripta, non nisi castrata, approbet: uti index Ecclesiæ Romanæ expurgatorius ad oculum demonstrat,

VII. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

Septimam notam constituit Bellarminus, unionem membrorum inter se & cum capite, hoc est, Pontifice Romano. Atqui vera unio membrorum inter se, consistit docente Apostolo, in unitate fidei, Ephes. 4, 4. Hæc verò propriè competit Ecclesiæ invisibili, non verò visibili. Ergò hoc pacto invisibilem Ecclesiam concedit Jesuvvita, etiam nesciens: Aut si visibili Ecclesiæ eam convenire contenderit, manifestū est, ipsum probare ignotum, nempè ubi sit, & quæ sit vera Ecclesia, per multò jgnotius, videlicet, per unionem membrorum inter se, quæ indubia & infallibilis ex signis externis constitui non potest. 2. Quam verè Romanenses glorientur de hac unione, ostendunt superiorum temporum historiæ, de antilogijs, certaminibus Scriptorum, Schismatibus, bellis & persecutionibus ipsius Romanæ Ecclesiæ mem brorum inter se. 3. Quòd hodiè major inter Romanenses deprehenditur concordia, in causa est, non pietas, non fidei & Religionis veritas: sed partim malitiæ studium, quo Ecclesiæ veræ acriùs nocere satagunt; partim metus pe riculi, quod non posset esse præsentissimum, si Romanæ Ecclesiæ pristinis dissidijs ac discordiis etiamnum dissiliret. 4. Impium & prophanum est, quicquid de Pontifice Romano, tanquàm capite Ecclesiæ blaterat Jesuvvita. Quemadmodum enim Hilario teste, illa sola unitas pacem Ecclesiæ præstat, quæ Christi est: Ita solus etiam Christus est Caput Ecclesiæ, qui eam suo sanguine redemit, uti alibi fusitùs demonstratur. Ephes. 1. 5. Nota hæc soliEcclesiæ veræ non competit: sed etiam Ecclesiæ malignantium: Ecclesiæ enim Judaicæ & Mahomethanæ membra arctiore unitatis vinculo inter se coaluerunt, quàm quale unquàm in Romanenses cadere potest.

Octavam Ecclesiæ notam constituit Bellarminus; sanctitatem Doctrinæ. Quod si puritatem Verbi divini, ejusque prædicationis intelligit Jesuvvita, tùm confirmat nostram sententiam, quam tamen suprà odiosè satis & acerbè sugillavit. Sancta enim doctrina esse nequit, quæ pura non est, & Scripturis sacris consona. Quod si præter hanc aliam aliquam Sanctitatem Doctrinæ somniat, veteratorem agit Jesuvvita & absurdum Sophistam, ut qui in dissonantia à Scripturis, Sanctitatem aliquam Doctrinæ Ecclesiasticæ consistere posse, impiè autumat.


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church: IX. Mark of the Roman Church

IX. Mark of the Roman Church.

Bellarmine establishes the ninth mark, the efficacy of doctrine in converting nations. But this mark does not belong to every particular true Church: but partly only to the primitive one by reason of time: then also to others by reason of place, namely those which are situated today in those climates of the earth which are closer to barbarian and infidel nations. Concerning the conversion of the new world and especially the Indies, there is no reason for the Papists to glory. For 1. it was not the desire to propagate religion, but to subjugate the region, that drove the Papists to those places. Concerning which matter, a Papist writer, Ludovicus Granatensis, says thus in Tom. 4 of his postil, page 27, Sunday 1 after Pentecost, sermon 2. It has come to this, that among many barbarian nations the name of Christians is so execrable that if monks are ever sent to them, it is necessary to say, so that they do not detest them with similar hatred, that they are not Christians, but Fathers who have come to care for their salvation. For they have used such monstrous cruelty toward them that the most holy name of Christian has been held not as a name of piety and religion, but of cruelty and inhumanity. Thus it has been brought about that whoever hears 'Christian' understands a certain executioner, wild and inhuman, and a plague, devastation, and ruin of the human race. It is commonly reported to be believed by the Indians that Christians are not men born of men: but certain dregs of the sea, and monsters concreted from the foam of a barbarian element, and cast out: and it is written that they prefer to slaughter with their own hand the children born of them, rather than to raise them as slaves for the Spaniards. 2. Note that this applies also to heretics: for they too have an efficacy of doctrine when they deceive and seduce many; and it is assigned by the Apostle to Antichrist as his own mark in particular, the efficacy of error: 2 Thess. 2:9 and 11; 2 Tim. 3:13. Finally, it is evident that the Papists have attempted the conversion of other peoples, not through the preaching of the divine Word, but through wars, arms, and threats; just as Boniface is indeed read to have converted the Germans, and especially the Thuringians, as the Ecclesiastical Century 8, chapter 10, testifies in the Isenacense Chronicle. A similar instance of such violent conversion was seen a few years ago in Upper Germany, and especially in Donauwörth, where by prisons, swords, and cannons, by an impious army

The wretched common people were forced to embrace the Papal faith in Bavaria. If the Reformation of our blessed Luther—who, a miserable monk, was fortified by no protection of arms, but by his writing pen alone, and by his voice converted not only Germany but many kingdoms besides to the faith of Christ—is compared to this conversion, it will soon be clear of its own accord whether our Church or that of the Papists can rightly boast of this mark, provided that it ought to be reckoned among the essential marks of the true Church.

Latin:

IX. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

Nonam notam constituit Bellarminus Efficaciam doctrinæ in convertendis gentibus. Atqui non omni veræ Ecclesiæ particulari nota hæc competit: sed partim primitivæ tantùm ratione temporis: deindè aliis etiam ratione loci, illis nimirùm, quæ ad ea terræ climata ho diè sitæ sunt, quæ barbaris & infidelibus gentibus sunt viciniora. De novi orbis & cumprimis Indiarum conversione, non est, cur Pontificij glorientur. Nam 1. non Religionis propagandæ, sed regionis subjugandæ studium, ad loca illa Pontificios expulit. Qua de re sic Scriptor Pontificius, Ludovicus Granatensis Tom. 4 postillæ pag. 27. Dominicæ 1. post Pentecoft. concione 2. Eò deventum est, ut apud multas barbarorum gentes adeò sit Christianorum nomen execrabile, ut si quando ad eos monachi mittantur, ne illos simili odio detestentur, necesse sit dicere, quidem no Christianos, sed Patres esse, qui ad eorum salutem curandam venerint. Ea enim crudelitatis immanitate erga illos usi sunt, ut sanctissimum Christiani nomen, non pietatis&religionis, sed crudelitatis & immanitatis nomen habitum sit. Ita effectum est, ut qui Christianum audiat, Carnificem quendam, ferum & immanem, ac generis humani pestem, vastitatem & perniciem intelligat. Vulgó ab Indis credi perhibetur, Christianos non homines ex hominibus ortos: sed purgamenta quædam maris, & monstra ex Elementi barbari spumis concreta, ejectaque esse: scribunturque, malle illos ex se natos liberos sua manu trucidare, quàm mancipia Hispanis alere. 2. Nota hæc competit etiam hæreticis: Nam & hi habent efficaciam doctrinæ, quando multos decipiunt & seducunt: & cumprimis Antichristo tanquàm propria nota, ab Apostolo assignatur Efficacia erroris: 2. Thess. 2, 9. & 11. 2. Tim. 3, 13. Tandem constat Pontificios conversionem aliorum populorum molitos esse, non per Verbi divini prædicationem: sed per bella, arma, minas: quemadmodú sanè Bonifacius Germanos, & cumprimis Thuringos convertisse legitur, in Chronico Isenacensi sic testante centuria Ecclesiastica 8. cap. 10. Cujus violentæ conversionis simile quid vidit paucos ante annos superior Germania, & cumprimis Donavverda, ubi carceribus, gladiis & bombardis, ab impio exercitu

Bavaro, ad amplexandam fidem Pontificiam misera plebecula coacta fuit. Ad quam conversionem, si conferatur Reformatio B. Lutheri nostri, qui misellus monachus, nullis armorum præsidiis munitur, sed solo calamo scriptorio, & voce sua non Germaniam modò, sed multa insuper regna ad fidem Christi convertit: mox ultrò patebit, utrùm nostra, an Pontificiorum Ecclesia, de hac nota, jure gloriari possit, dummodò ea inter notas veræ Ecclesiæ essentiales referri debeat.


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church: X. The tenth mark of the Roman Church

X. The tenth mark of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes the tenth mark as the holiness of life of the authors, or the first fathers of the Papal religion, in whose number he includes Bernard, Dominic, and Francis. Yet this mark is more unknown than the Church itself, indeed much more uncertain, because holiness sometimes seems to us to be what is mere hypocrisy. 2. This mark is sometimes separable, which is apparent in the person of Judas Iscariot, whose impiety nevertheless does not prejudice the truth of the Church of Christ. 3. It is manifestly false: for that the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles are the authors and first fathers of the Roman religion is as certain as it is certain that the Apostle Peter presided at Rome as Bishop for 25 years. A more vain fiction than this can scarcely be devised. Meanwhile, let the Romanists keep the founders of their Church, Dominic, Francis, Benedict, and other monks of this flour, whom we do not care about. Christ suffices for us, and the sacred chorus of the Apostles, who are the true authors and first fathers of the Church of the New Testament. The holiness of the life of these was so sacrosanct that the sanctity of all the other Fathers, when compared with this, seems almost like impurity and profanity. 4. This mark signifies only an invisible Church. Since the external appearance of holiness very often deceives. Finally, this mark does not fit the Roman Pontiffs, as it is established that they were idolaters, magicians, pimps, and the makers and architects of all crimes and villainies, as testified by Platina and Nauclerus themselves, who are Papal writers.

XI. The eleventh mark of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes the eleventh mark as the glory of miracles. But such lips, such lettuce: the religion of the Papists is new; therefore, if it wishes to deserve any assent and authority, it is necessary that it be confirmed by new miracles. Our Church, indeed, resting in the ancient doctrine of Christ and the Apostles, and likewise in the glory of miracles, has no need of new miracles, about which we will have to labor only when we have brought ourselves to the mind to superinduce some new dogma upon the doctrine of Christ. 2. This mark is not essential to the true Church, but is common to the false Church with the true, as can be seen in the Egyptian magicians, Exodus 7. 3. This mark is established as a property, as if it were a criterion of the Antichrist, Matthew 24, 2 Thessalonians 2, P. Matthew 6.

XII. The twelfth mark of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes the twelfth mark as the Prophetic Light, which he claims shone most brightly in Bernard, Francis, Gregory Thaumaturgus, Anthony, Abbot John, and Benedict, who issued many prophecies. But who will give us assurance, 1, that such prophecies were either issued by them in that way, or that the outcome always corresponded? We are content with the oracles and predictions of the Holy Spirit; we gladly do without those predictions, partly false and partly doubtful, boasted of by the Jesuit faction. 2. This mark falls even upon the church of the malignant, and those whom Christ orders to depart from him into eternal fire, Matthew 7:22.

Latin:

X. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

Decimam notam constituit Bellarminus, Sanctitatem vitæ autorum, sive primorum Patrum Religionis Pontificiæ: in quorum numerum refert Bernhardum, Dominum, & Franciscum. Atqui hæc nota ignotior est ipsâ Ecclesiâ, imò multò incertior: propterea quòd Sanctitas interdum nobis esse videtur, quæ mera est hypocrisis. 2. Nota hæc interdum est separabilis, id quod in persona Judæ Ischariotæ apparet, cujus tamen impietas veritati Ecclesiæ Christi non præjudicat. 3. Manifestè falsa est: Nam Patriarchas, Prophetas & Apostolos, Romanæ religionis autores & primos patres esse, tàm certum est, quàm certum, Petru Apostolum præsedisse Romæ ut Episcopum, annis 25. Quo figmento vix vanius ullum excogitari potest. Retineant interim Romanenses, suæ Ecclesiæ fundatores, Dominicum, Franciscum, Benedictum, & hujus farinæ monachos alios, quos non moramur. Sufficit nobis Christus, & sacer Apostolorum chorus, qui veri sunt autores, & primi patres Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti. Horum vitæ sanctitas adeò fuit Sacro sancta, ut reliquorum Patrum omnium sanctimonia, cum hac collata, more videatur impuritas & prophanitas. 4. Nota hæc invisibilem Ecclesiam tantùm signat. Siquidem externa sanctitatis species sæpissimè fallit. Tandem in Pontifices Romanos nota, hæc nó quadrat, ut quos constat fuisse idololatras magos, lenones, omniumque scelerum & flagitiorum fabros & architectos, teste ipso Platina & Nauclero, scriptoribus Pontificiis.

XI. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ

UNdecimam notam constituit Bellarminus, Miraculorum gloriam. Sed qualia labra, tales lactucæ: Religio Pontificiorum est nova: Ergò si assensum aliquem & autoritatem demereri velit, miraculis novis confirmetur necesse est. Nostra Ecclesia, quippè in Veteri Christi & Apostolorum uti doctrinâ, sic & miraculorum gloriâ acquiescens: novis miraculis non est opus, de quibus tùm demùm nobis erit laborandum, quando Christi doctrinæ, novum quodda dogma superinducere, in animū induxerimus. 2. Nota hæc non est veræ Ecclesiæ Essentialis, sed falsæ Ecclesiæ cum vera communis: quemadmodum videre est in Magis Ægyptiis, Exodi 7. 3. Constituitur hæc nota proprium, quasi κριτήριον Antichristi Matth. 24, 2. Thess. 2. P. Matth. 6.

XII. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

DUodecimam notam constituit Bellarminus, Lumen Propheticum, quod in Bernardo, Francisco, Gregorio θαυμαλργῷ Antonio, Abbate Johanne Benedicto maximè enituerit, qui plurima vaticinia ediderint. Sed quis nobis 1. fidem faciet, talia vaticinia vel sic ab illis edita fuisse, vel eventum semper respondisse? Nos contenti oraculis & vaticinijs Spiritus Sancti prædictionibus illis partim falsis, partim dubijs, à Jesuvitarum factione jactatis, libenter caremus. 2. Cadit hæc nota in Ecclesiam etiam malignantium, & eos, quos jubet Christus à se in ignem æternum secedere Matth. 7, 22.


### Chapter III. Concerning the notes and signs or marks of the Church: XIII. The thirteenth mark of the Roman Church

XIII. The thirteenth mark of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes the thirteenth note as the confession of adversaries. But be it so? That there has always been, and still is under the Papacy, a true Church of Christ: neither of which we deny: Does it therefore follow that the Papacy itself will be the true Church? Certainly no more than if I were to argue thus: Antichrist sits in the very temple of GOD, 2 Thess. 2. Therefore Antichrist himself is the true Church. For these are different expressions: There is a true Church under the Papacy. And the Papacy itself is the true Church. Since the Jesuit does not distinguish between these, he clearly and impertinently alleges our confession: which is none other than that the Papacy is the very Antichristianism itself.

XIV. Note of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes the fourteenth note as the unhappy exit, or end, of those who oppose the Roman Church. Where the wicked apostate 1. understands that most holy choir of martyrs, whom the tyranny of Antichrist removed from the midst by various kinds of punishments. But it is well: such was also the exit and destruction of Stephen, the first martyr of the New Testament; such was the exit of almost all the rest of the Apostles: whose exit, however, is said to be unhappy only in the opinion of men, but in reality is by far the most happy. For precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints, Ps. 116:15, and of all those who, contradicting the Papacy, bear witness to the Evangelical truth even with the shedding of blood. 2. B. Luther's death was not sudden, as the Jesuit lies, and even if it had been, it should by no means be judged unhappy on that account. The tragic ends of Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Karlstadt, and other Sacramentarians, which the Jesuit brings forward, he commits to the fallacy of the cause. For they are not to be considered to have paid those penalties by the just judgment of GOD because they opposed the Papacy, but because they opposed the light of the Gospel.

XV. A mark of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino establishes the fifteenth and final mark as the temporal happiness of those who have defended the Roman Church. Indeed, this mark reveals the genius and character of the Romanists; nay, it evidently demonstrates that their Church is false, inasmuch as they barked about temporal happiness just as the Jews once did in the time of Jeremiah, which they were permitted to enjoy as long as they sacrificed to the queen of heaven: Jer. 44:17. But the Savior testifies that this would be the peculiar lot of his faithful in this world, that they should have cause for grief from time to time, while the world exults and rejoices in happy successes, John 16:20. This is evident from the example of the Israelite, Apostolic, primitive, and subsequent Church, which refused to bend its knees before the Roman Antichrist, and therefore had to endure, and still endures today, all the assaults of persecution and cruelty in those places where that son of perdition holds sway. That the most merciful heavenly Father has kept our churches safe and immune from his tyranny is truly a reason for us to give thanks to his infinite goodness, thanks that should never end. AMEN.

Latin:

XIII. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

DEcimam tertiam notam constituit Bellarminus, confessionem adversariorum. Sed sit ita? Fuerit semper, & adhuc sit sub Papatu vera Christi Ecclesia : quorum neutrum negamus : Nùm ideò Papatus ipse vera erit Ecclesia? Haud certè magis, atque si ita colligam: Antichristus sedet in ipso templo DEI, 2, Thess. 2. Ergò Antichristus ipse est vera Ecclesia. Diversæ enim sunt locutiones: Sub Papatu est Ecclesia vera. Et papatus ipse est vera Ecclesia. Quas cùm non distinguat Jesuvvita, inscitè plane ac impertinenter nostram allegat confessionem: quæ nulla est alia, quàm quòd Papatus sit ipsissimus Antichristianismus.

XIV. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

DEcimam quartam notam constituit Bellarminus Infelicem exitum, seu finem eorum, qui Ecclesiam Romanam oppugnant Ubi sceleratus Apostata 1. intelligit sanctissimum illum martyrum chorum, quos Antichristi Tyrannis varijs suppliciorum generibus è medio sustulit. Sed bene habet: talis fuit etiam exitus & interitus Stephani Proto martyris Novi Testamenti; talit fuit reliquorum Apostolorum ferè omnium : Quorum tamen exitus, opinione tantum hominum infelix esse dicitur, reipsa verò longé est felicissimus. Pretiosa enim in conspectu Domini mors sanctorum ejus, Psal. 116, 15. & omnium eorum, qui Papatui contradicentes, veritati Evangelicæ etiam cum profusione sanguinis, testimonium perhibent. 2. B. Lutheri mors repentina non fuit, uti mentitur Jesuvvita, & si talis maximè fuisset, infelix tamen propterea minimè censenda esset. Zvvinglij, Oecolampadij, Carolostadij, & aliorum Sacramentariorum tragicos exitus, quòd profert Jesuvvita, fallaci am causæ con mittit. Neque enim, quia Papatui, sed quia luci Evangelicæ sese opposuerunt, pœnas istas justo DEI judicio, luisse existimandi sunt.

XV. Nota Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

DEcimam quintam & ultimam notam constituit Bellarminus, Felicitatem temporalem eorum, qui Ecclesiam Romanam defenderunt. Prodit verò hæc nota genium & ingenium Romanensium: imò falsam eorum esse Ecclesiam, evidenter demonstrat: quippè quæ haud secus, atque olim apud Jeremiam Judæi felicitatem temporalem subindè ogganniebant Prophetæ, quâ frui ipsis licuerit, quamdiu reginæ cœli sacrificaverint: Jerem. 44, 17. Verùm testatur Servator, hoc suorum fidelium, hoc in mundo, proprium fore πείσθελον, ut subindè habeant, quod doleant: mundus verò in felicibus successibus exultet & lætetur, Johan 16, 20. Patet hoc exemplo Ecclesiæ Israëliticæ, Apostolicæ, primitivæ, & subsequentis, quæ coram Antichristo Roano genua flectere detrectavit, & ideò quosvis persecutionum & crudelitatis impetus sustinere necessum habuit, hodièque sustinet, illis in locis, ubi filius ille perditionis rerum potitur. A cujus Tyrannide, quòd Ecclesias nostras tutas ac immunes præstitit clementissimus Pater cœlestis, est sanè, quòd infinitæ ipsius bonitati, gratias agamus nullis seculis finiendas. AMEN.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy

Among the remaining epithets by which the Holy Spirit designates the Church in the Scriptures, it is almost primary that He attributes to it the name of KINGDOM throughout, especially in the New Testament. Now, where a Kingdom is given, no one can doubt that a certain government and a certain form of government must also be given there. Nor is it a matter of dispute that Christ the Savior both could and would govern his Church in that manner and mode which is the best and most useful of all. But since various forms of government are established by both philosophers and theologians, it is today disputed and debated which of all is the best and most useful, and which is appropriate for the Church of Christ. The Jesuits, and their leader Robert Bellarmino, fight for a Monarchical government of the Church, with the primary aim and purpose that he might the more easily and evidently confirm the primacy and Monarchy which the Roman Pontiff arrogates to himself over the Church. We, however, contend that an Aristocratic form of government is the best, and most rightly belongs to the Church militant in these lands.

But so that the state of the controversy may be more correctly informed, both the subject and the predicate of the question must be properly observed. The subject is the Church; where it is understood not as the invisible Church of the elect, nor any particular visible one, but the visible universal Church, insofar as it fights under the banner of the cross of Christ in these lands, and is proper to the New Testament. The predicate is Government: of which three forms are commonly established, even with Bellarmino himself admitting it: namely, 1. Monarchical, when the highest authority is in the hands of one in a praiseworthy manner, with the consent of the subjects: to which is opposed Tyranny, which is the less praiseworthy rule of one, without the consent of the subjects. 2. Aristocratic, which is the praiseworthy rule of the best: to which is opposed Oligarchy, which is the unpraiseworthy rule of a few, caring more for private than public advantage. 3. Democratic, which is the rule of the whole people, yet distinct and ordered according to the ability and condition of each. Its excess usually degenerates into sedition. Although we could rightly bid farewell to these terms in theological schools, because one should not seek an Aristotelian but an Apostolic form of government in the Church, yet so that we do not appear to be avoiding the debating arena, we will use and retain the terms which the Jesuits are accustomed to use today: and we will examine more accurately whether the form of Ecclesiastical government is Monarchical or Aristocratic. For there is no question here about a Democratic one, which both sides confess does not belong to the Church.

With these things concerning the subject and predicate of the question established in this manner, the very scope of the whole question also comes under consideration. But it is not asked: Whether the universal militant Church has a certain universal Monarch, and is governed by him Monarchically, namely, the one and only Christ Jesus, whom the Father gave as head of his Church, Eph. 1:22, Col. 1:18. For the Jesuits do not wish to appear to deny this at all. Furthermore, it is not disputed whether the Church has been administered by Christ and the Apostles in the best and most useful mode of government, and whether it ought to be administered today by Doctors and ministers. For we readily concede this very thing to the Jesuits. But that which is properly disputed between us and the Romanists today is this: Whether both Scripture itself and the salvation and edification of the Church require that, besides that highest and universal invisible head of the Church, CHRIST JESUS, another general and visible Bishop be set over the Church, who as a Monarch presides over all Christians dispersed throughout the whole world, who has and exercises absolute power and jurisdiction over all, both secular and spiritual, and who, finally, can and ought to judge each and every one, while he himself can be judged by no one, so much so that it is not permitted to appeal from his sentence to anyone else? Here our Church and that of the Romanists depart into clearly different and repugnant opinions. Ours is that the form of Ecclesiastical Government is the best and most useful of all, if the Church, under one universal head CHRIST, and under one equal ministry of Doctors and Pastors, or Bishops of the Church, coalesces into one mystical body in the unity of the faith and of the Spirit.

The opinion of the Romanists, however, is this: that the best and most useful form of Ecclesiastical Government is if the Church, besides Christ, also acknowledges another visible head here on earth, namely the Roman Pontiff, who obtains dominion over the whole Universal Church, who fixes and unfixes the form of teaching, of administering the Sacraments, of governing the people, and of laws for the remaining Bishops and inferior Pastors, and who has absolute power and jurisdiction over the whole Christian flock, both secular and spiritual.

We divide, however, this whole discussion, which is otherwise very extensive in the multitude and nobility of its questions, into three distinct chapters: the first of which will be concerning the true head of Ecclesiastical Government; the second, concerning the best form or mode of this government; and lastly, the third, concerning the means by which this Ecclesiastical government is administered here on earth.

Latin:

INter reliqua Epitheta, quibus Spiritus Sanctus in Scripturis Ecclesiam indigitat, primarium fermé est, quòd REGNI appellationem, præsertim in Novo Testamento, passim ei tribuit. Jam verò ubi Regnum datur, quin ibi certum quoque regimen, certa q; regiminis forma dari debeat, nemini potest esse dubium. Neque illud etiam ambigitur, quin Christus Servator & potuerit, & voluerit Ecclesiam suam ea ratione & modo gubernare, qui sit omnium optimus & utilissimus. Cæterùm cùm variæ gubernationis formæ tùm à Philosophis, tùm à Theologis constituantur, disputatur hodiè & controvertitur, Quænam omnium sit optima & utilissima, & quænam Ecclesiæ Christi conveniat. Jesuvvitæ, & horum Antefignanus Robertus Bellarminus pugnat pro Regimine Ecclesiæ Monarchico, eo potissimùm fine ac consilio, ut primatum & Monarchiam, quam Pontifex Romanus in Ecclesiam sibi arrogat, tantò faciliùs ac evidentiùs confirmare possit. Nos verò contendimus, Formam Regiminis Aristocraticam esse optimam, & Ecclesiæ in his terris militanti, rectissimè competere

Verùm ut status controversiæ rectiùs informetur, probè observandum fuerit Quæstionis tùm subjectum, tùm prædicatum. Subject est Ecclesia; ubi non intelligitur vel Ecclesia Electorum invisibilis, vel visibilis aliqua Particularis: Sed visibilis Ecclesia universalis, quatenùs illa hisce in terris, sub vexillo curcis Christi militat, & Novi Testamenti est propria. Prædicatum est Regimen: cujus tres vulgò formæ constituuntur, ipso quoque Bellarmino fatente: nempè 1. Monarchica, quando summa rerum est penes unum laudabiliter, consentientibus subditis: cui opponitur Tyrannis, quæ est, unius dominatus minùs laudabilis, præter consensum subditorum. 2. Aristocratica, quæ est dominatus optimatū laudabilis: cui opponitur Oligarchia, quæ est paucorum dominatus illaudabilis, privatum magis, quàm publicum curans commodum. 3. Democratica, quæ est totius populi imperium, distinctum tamen, & secundum cujuslibet facultatem ac conditionem ordinatum. Cujus excessus plerumq́; in seditionem degenerat. Quanquam verò termini istis in Scholis Theologicis jure nuncium remittere possemus, propterea quòd in Ecclesia non quærenda est forma Regiminis Aristotelica, sed Apostolica: ne tamen arenam disputatoriam subterfugere videamur, eos usurpabimus & retinebimus terminos, quibus hodie Jesuvitæ uti consueverunt: & num Regiminis Ecclesiastici Forma sit Monarchica, an verò Aristocratica, accuratiùs dispiciemus. Nam de Democratica hoc loco non est quæstio, quam Ecclesiæ non cōpetere, utrinque in cōfesso est.

His de subjecto & prædicato Quæstionis hunc in modum constitutis, ipsum quoq; totius Quæstionis complexum sub considerationem venit. Non autem illud quæritur: An Ecclesia militans universalis, habeat universa, lem quendam Monarcham, & ab eo Monarchicè gubernetur, nempè solùm atq; unum Christum Jesum, quem Pater dedit caput Ecclesiæ suæ, Ephes. 1, 22. Col. 1, 18. Nam Jesuvitæ hoc minimè negare videri volunt. Deindè neq; de eo etiam controvertitur, An Ecclesia optimo & utiliffimo regiminis modo administrata sit à Christo & Apostolis, hodieq́; à Doctoribus & ministris administrari debeat? Nam hoc ipsum quoq; Jesuvitis ultrò concedimus. Sed illud propriè inter nos & Romanenses hodiè controvertitur: An & scriptura ipsa, & Ecclesiæ salus ac ædificatio requirat, ut præter summum illud ac universale invisibile caput Ecclesiæ, CHRISTUM JESUM, alius insuper generalis ac visibilis Ecclesiæ præficiatur Episcopus, qui tanquàm Monarcha, omnibus per totum terrarum orbē dispersis Christianis præsit, qui absolutam in omnes & secularem & spiritualem potestatem ac jurisdictionem habeat & exerceat, qui deniq; singulos ac universos judicare, ipse verò à nemine judicari possit & debeat, adeò ut ab ipsius sententia ad neminem alium provocare liceat? Hic jam in diversas ac repugnantes planè sententias, nostræ & Romanensium Ecclesiæ abeunt. Nostra est, quòd omnium optima ac utilissima Regiminis Ecclesiastici sit forma, si Ecclesia, sub uno universali capite CHRISTO, & sub uno æquali ministerio Doctorum & Pastorum, sive Episcoporum Ecclesiæ, in unitate fidei & Spiritus in unum corpus mysticum coalescat.

Romanensium verò sententia est hæc: quòd omnium optima ac utilissima Regiminis Ecclesiastici sit forma, si Ecclesia præter Christum, aliud etiam visibile caput hisce in terris agnoscat, nempè Pontificem Romanum, qui in totam Vniversalem Ecclesiam dominatum obtineat, qui reliquis Episcopis & Pastoribus inferioribus, formam docendi, administradi Sacramenta, gubernandi populum, leges figat & refigat, quique absolutam in totum Christianorum gregem potestatem & jurisdictionem, tam secularem quàm spiritualem habeat.

Partimur autem totam hanc disputationem, quæstionum aliàs multitudine & nobilitate amplissimam, in tria distincta capita: quorum I. erit, de vero Regiminis Ecclesiastici capite. II. de optima Regiminis hujus forma sive modo III. ac postremùm, de mediis, quibus regimen hoc Ecclesiasticum hisce in terris administratur.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: Chapter I. On The True Head of Ecclesiastical Government

SINCE the kingdom of the Church is a certain body, consisting of a structure of members, warming each other only by the life-giving virtue of the Holy Spirit, it certainly cannot by any reason be ἀκέφαλον (headless) and lack a certain head: from which vigor may flow into the members, and by which they may not only be ruled and preserved, but also receive their own growth. Now, indeed, the very analogy between the Head and the body requires that this head should not be foreign, but proper and native: it should not be double, but unique: it should not be sluggish, useless, and brute, but efficacious and life-giving. For first, just as no body is moved and animated except by its own proper head, to which, whatever foreign head you may impose, the body will nevertheless remain devoid of all life, sense, and motion: So also, unless life and salvation consist for the Church from its own proper and native head, these can never reach it from a foreign head. Therefore, it is necessary that the Church have its own proper and native head.

Next, the Church cannot be πολυκέφαλος (many-headed), or have more heads than one. For if it could have more, it would either have them at the same time, or successively. Not at the same time: for thus the Church would degenerate into some two-headed or three-headed monster; and that would happen contrary to nature: since God himself, the maker of nature, naturally added only one head to one body. Nor does τὸ ὑπανάληλον (the subordinate head) have a place here, by which another is added to the principal head as a vicar. For this would argue the impotence of that principal head, since it would have to be assisted by another head: which is absurd and blasphemous: for thus

GOD himself would have provided less correctly for his Church, since he would have added to it such a head, from which, because of its infirmity, it could not sufficiently perceive life, sense, and motion. Therefore, such a vicarial head has no place. 2. Thus, neither can a succession of heads be admitted, unless death intervenes, and indeed intervenes as often as a new head grows up. But the Church, having once died with its head, and having once been resurrected with the same, does not die again. Rom. 6. 4 & 9. Therefore, just as the unity of the Church is established, so too is the unity of the head, never to be exchanged for plurality.

Finally, it is necessary that the Church have a life-giving and efficacious head: otherwise the Church would not be a body, but a brute and lifeless corpse. Therefore, from whomever the Church cannot receive life, Spirit, and motion—and indeed not animal or worldly, but spiritual, heavenly, and divine—that can in no way be held or acknowledged as the head of the Church.

Having weighed these three marks and requirements more accurately, we establish and firmly believe that such a proper, unique, life-giving, and efficacious head of the Church is CHRIST JESUS our Savior alone. By way of confirmation, we bring forward these testimonies of Scripture:

Ephesians 1:10. It pleased GOD to ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι (recapitulate) and restore all things in Christ.

And verse 22. GOD gave CHRIST as head over all things to the Church, which is his body.

Ephes. 4. 15. Let us grow up in him (CHRIST) in all things, who is the head, CHRIST.

Ephef. 5. 23. CHRIST is the head of the Church, and he himself is the Savior of the body.

Coloff. 1. 18. CHRIST is the head of the body, which is the Church.

Reason itself also supports these Scriptures, which, weighing the proper office of a true head, argues thus.

To a true and native head belongs primacy not only of place and dignity: but also of power, of government, and even of total animation, or vivification.

But all these things most rightly belong to CHRIST alone with respect to the Church, and the same are clearly attributed to him alone by the Apostle in the places already alleged. Therefore, the primary dignity of the Church depends on this, that it uniquely rejoices in and enjoys CHRIST as its Head.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ.

The Romanists and their allies the Jesuits, not content with one supreme and universal head, CHRIST, still invent another, namely the Roman Pontiff, but under this limitation, that they say CHRIST is the primary head: but the Pope is the secondary and vicarious head. Although the futility of this distinction has already been worn thin, it may nevertheless shine forth more and more clearly if it is weighed a little more deeply, with what impudence of words the Romanists describe this very primacy or

Latin:

CVM Ecclesiæ regnum, corpus quoddam sit, constans compage membrorum, non nisi virtute Spiritus Sancti vivificâ, invicem calescentium, certè ἀκέφαλον illud esse, certoque capite carere nulla ratione potest: ex quo vigor in membra influat, & à quo non regantur tantùm illa, conserventurque: sed & incrementum suum accipiant. Jam verò ipsa inter Caput & corpus analogia requirit, ut caput hoc non sit alienum, sed proprium ac nativum: non sit geminum: sed unicum: non sit ignavum, inutile ac brutum: sed efficax ac vivificum. Primùm enim, quemadmodum corpus movetur & animatur nullum, nisi à suo capite proprio, cui quodcunque alienum imponas caput, corpus tamen omnis vitæ, sensus motusque manebit expers: Ita quoque, nisi Ecclesiæ ex suo proprio ac nativo capite, vita salusque constet, nunquam ex alieno capite hæc ipsi obtingere possunt. Suum ergò proprium ac nativum caput Ecclesia habeat, necesse est.

Deinde Ecclesia πολυκέφαλος esse, vel plura capita, præter unum habere nequit. Nam si plura habere posset, aut simul illa haberet, aut successivè. Non simul: sic enim in monstrum aliquod biceps aut triceps degeneraret Ecclesia: & præter naturam illud fieret: Siquidem naturaliter corpori uni, non nisi caput unum, Deus ipse naturæ opifex addidit. Neque locum hîc habet τὸ ὑπανάληλον, caput Subordinatum, quo principali capiti, alterum tanquàm vicarium sit adjunctum. Hoc enim capitis illius principalis impotentiam argueret, quippè cui per caput alterum succurri deberet: id quod absurdum & blasphemum: sic enim

DEUS ipse Ecclesiae suae minus rectè prospexiffet, quippè cui tale caput addidiffet, ex quo, propter infirmitatem ejus, non possit vitam, sensum atque motum ad sufficientiam usque percipere. Proindè vicarium tale caput locum non habet. 2. Sic neque successio capitum potest admitti, nisi mors interveniat, & quidem toties interveniat, quoties novum caput succrescit. Atqui Ecclesia semel capiti suo commortua, semel cum eodem resuscitata, ampliùs non moritur. Rom. 6. 4. & 9. Ergò, quemadmodum Ecclesiae, sic capiti quoque sua constat Unitas, cum pluralitate nunquàm permutabilis.

Tandem vivificum etiam atque efficax caput habeat Ecclesia necesse est: alioqui non corpus, sed cadaver brutum atque exanime effet Ecclesia. A quocunque ergò vitam, Spiritum ac motum, & quidem non animalem aut mundanum, sed spiritualem, cœlestem ac divinum accipere non potest Ecclesia: id pro capite etiam Ecclesiae haberi aut agnosci nullo mode potest.

Tribus istis notis ac requisitis accuratius expensis, statuimus & firmiter credimus, Tale caput Ecclesiae proprium, Unicum, vivificum atque efficax, esse solum CHRISTUM JESUM Servatorem nostrum Confirmationis loco proferimus isthaec Scripturae testimonia:

Ephef. 1. 10. placuit DEO omnia ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθ recapitulare atque instaurare in Chri sto.

Et vers. 22. CHRISTUM dedit DEUS caput super omnia Ecclesiae, quae est corpus ipsius.

Ephes. 4. 15. Adolescamus in ipso (CHRISTO) per omnia, qui est caput, CRISTUS.

Ephef. 5. 23. CHRISTUS est caput Ecclesiae, & ipse est Salvator corporis.

Coloff. 1. 18. CHRISTUS est caput corporis, quod est Ecclesia.

Suffragatur Scripturis hisce ipsa quoque ratio, quae proprium capitis veri officium expendens, fic argumentatur.

Capiti vero ac nativo convenit principatus non loci tantùm atque dignitatis: sed potestatis etiam, regiminis, atque adeò totius animationis, sive vivificationis.

Atqui haec omnia soli CHRISTO rectissimè competunt respectu Ecclesiae, idemque soli ab Apostolo, locis jam allegatis luculenter tribuuntur. Pendet ergò hinc primaria Ecclesiae, dignitas, quòd Capite CHRISTO unice gaudet atque fruitur.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ.

Romanenses & horum σύμμαχοι Jesuvvitae, non contenti Uno summo ac Universali capite CHRISTO, aliud adhuc fingunt, nempè Pontificem Romanum, sed sub hac limitatione, ut CHRISTUM dicant esse caput primarium: Papam verò esse caput secundarium & vicarium. Quanquàm verò distinctionis hujus futilitas, jam modò est protrita: magis tamen & clariùs ea elucescat, si paulò altiùs expendatur, quanta verborum impudentia hunc ipsum sui Pontificis primatum sive Mo-


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: What kind of primacy is ascribed to the Pope

monarchy over the entire Church of Christ the Romanists describe. Whence it becomes manifest by midday light that they ascribe to the Pontiff power plainly equal to Christ.

The Popes therefore write repeatedly that this is the first privilege, that he is the supreme and sole head of the universal Church, having primacy and principate over the whole Church. The Florentine Archbishop, Summa, part 3, tit. 23, c. 3, § 2. And that the power of this head is greater than any other created power, after the power of Christ, extending itself in some way to celestial, terrestrial, and infernal things, so that that of Psalm 8 may be verified of him: Thou hast put all things under his feet, sheep and oxen, the beasts of the field, the birds of the air, and the fish of the sea. And aptly: Because he himself is the vicar of Christ, as regards infernal things, he says fish of the sea. The same, ibid., tit. 22, c. 5.

And lest we seem to stand too much by the overly flattering opinions of the Canonists, we bring forward the writings of modern Jesuits, by which they attempt to establish the same impiety. Bellarmine certainly, book 2, On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 31, defines the same Pontiff thus, that he is: 1. Pope. 2. Father of Fathers. 3. Pontiff of Christians. 4. Supreme Priest. 5. Prince of Priests. 6. Vicar of Christ. 7. Head of the body of the Church. 8. Foundation of the building of the Church. 9. Pastor of the Lord's sheepfold. 10. Father and Doctor of all the faithful. 11. Rector of the house of GOD. 12. Keeper of the vineyard of GOD. 13. Spouse of the Church. 14. Prelate of the Apostolic See. 15. Finally, universal Bishop. Hence the same Bellarmine, in the entire fourth book On the Roman Pontiff, argues that the supreme and infallible decision of all theological controversies is to be sought and expected from the Roman Pope alone, for the reason that he cannot err in doctrine and faith: furthermore, that there belongs to the same Roman Pontiff also a coercive power, so that he may even pass laws which bind men in conscience, and compel them to believe or act as it has seemed good to the supreme Pontiff: and finally, in book 5, he contends that besides this spiritual power, a secular or temporal power that is plainly absolute also belongs to him.

Moreover, this fictitious Monarchy of the Roman Pontiff fights, I pass over the Holy Scriptures, then with the purer Antiquity.

And indeed as regards Antiquity, nothing of this primacy of the Roman Pope was known to any of the Fathers before Boniface VIII, who first boasted of this sacrilegious impiety with a wicked daring, as is evident in Decretals, book 6, On the immunities of Churches, chapter Quoniam. Which constitution, however, other kingdoms repudiated, and France expressly rejected.

Augustine, Epistle 58 to Boniface, writes thus: The Catholic Church alone is the body of CHRIST, of which He is the head, the Savior of His body.

And in Psalm 56: The whole Church, consisting of all the faithful, has that head placed in the heavens, which governs its body, which although separated by vision, is nevertheless joined by charity.

He bears most indignantly that the Apostle Paul is called by some the head of those whom he had planted in the faith of CHRIST: O human rashness and pride, he says, why not rather [call him] the bosom, so that CHRIST may be the head of the Christian? How could he be the head of them also, when he says: We being many are one body in CHRIST, and he most openly proclaims in many places that CHRIST himself is the head of the universal body.

Cyril has similar things, book 11, Thesaurus, chapter 26.

But especially clear and worthy of mention is the testimony of Gregory the Great, who himself was also a Roman Pontiff, in book 4 of his Epistles, chapter 86. For when John, Bishop of Constantinople, had dared to arrogate to himself the name of universal Bishop and head in the Church, Gregory, in an epistle given to Eulogius, Bishop of Alexandria, and Anastasius, Bishop of Antioch, says that this is a novelty, the pride of his fellow priest (thus Gregory, the Roman Bishop, names John of Constantinople), by which the bowels of the whole universal Church could be disturbed, which is entirely contrary to the Lord's commands, the Apostolic precepts, and the rules of the Fathers, all of which, which cohere to the one and only head, namely CHRIST, through the elation of pompous speech, the members of the same Christ are being subjected to himself by that man: He commands them to resist this elation in such a way that they should never presume to give or receive writings or epistles containing the falsehood of the universal name, and even by dying, if any persecution should arise on account of this name, they ought to show that they love nothing in this defilement.

The same, chapter 82, in an epistle sent to the same John of Constantinople, writes further as follows: The Apostle Paul, when he heard some saying, I am of Paul, I of Apollo, I of Cephas, most vehemently shuddering at this tearing apart of the Lord's body, through which they were associating its members with other heads in a certain way, exclaimed: Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul? If, therefore, he avoided subjecting the members of the Lord's body to certain heads outside of Christ, even to the Apostles themselves, in a particular way: what will you say to Christ, the head of the universal Church, in the examination of the final judgment, you who attempt to subject all his members to yourself by the title of universal Bishop? In this so perverse term is proposed the imitation of Lucifer, who said in Isaiah 14: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven.

As for the Holy Scriptures, they cannot bring forward even one clear testimony which proves according to the letter that which the Romanists desire. Whence it happened that some of them dared to seek proof from the state and condition of the Old Testament, where, although God was the head and supreme Monarch of the Church, nevertheless it is read that a visible head also, namely the high Priest or Pontiff, was constituted by GOD himself, to whom one had to flee in doubtful cases and ecclesiastical controversies, and by whose judgment, as if infallible, one had to abide. But after it was shown by our side that a shameful ignorance of the refutation is being committed, and the state of the question is sophistically perverted, because the question is not properly about the Church of the Old, but of the New Testament: and therefore that deed was done in the Old Testament, because that Levitical High Priest had to bear the type of the supreme and unique High Priest of the New Testament, CHRIST the Savior: so that now, CHRIST having been brought to light, and most presently governing His Church in every place, there is no need for another new typical and vicarious High Priest and head: soon the more recent Papal Doctors, especially the Jesuits, having bidden farewell to proofs from the Old Testament, as if they were irrelevant, fled to the New Testament.

Now, in order that they might be able to conclude something probably from that, they premised two hypotheses, but manifestly impious and false.

The former is that CHRIST, ascending to the heavens and sitting at the right hand of GOD the Father, so left these lands that He is now no longer present to His Church according to His humanity.

The latter is that CHRIST, as if to compensate for the absence of His body and to appoint a Vicar for His Church, constituted Peter as the supreme and Universal Bishop and Head of the Church: and granted to him, as also to his successors the Roman Pontiffs, absolute power over all Christians.

The stupendous vanity of the former hypothesis has been elsewhere thrashed and trampled upon by us, namely in the exposition of the Article concerning the Person of CHRIST.

The Jesuits strive to confirm this latter one with two passages of Scripture especially accommodated to this purpose.

The former exists in Matthew 16:18: You are Peter, and upon this Rock I will build my Church.

The latter, John 21:15: Feed my sheep. Concerning both of which passages, because of the various sophistries of the Jesuits, it will be necessary for us to examine more deeply.

And at the beginning, indeed, we respond to both in general, that nothing certain can be gathered from figurative or metaphorical phrases of Scripture, unless that very thing is handed down elsewhere in the Scriptures properly and clearly. Hence Augustine also, in his book On the Unity of the Church, chapter 5, warns that those things which are placed obscurely and wrapped in the veils of figures, and can be explained according to us and according to them, should be set aside. And in chapter 16 he writes: Let them not collect and commemorate those things which have been said either obscurely, or ambiguously, or figuratively, which each person interprets according to his own sense as he wishes. For such things cannot be rightly understood and explained unless those things which have been said most openly are first held with firm faith. Bring forward something, he says in the same place, which does not need an interpreter at all.

Then, indeed, I respond specifically, first to the former passage, Matthew 16:18, from which they gather that Peter was constituted by Christ as the foundation and head of the Church.

Where it is to be noted at the beginning, that the name of Foundation is accepted in two ways: first properly, when that is denoted, upon which a building is founded, and by which it is sustained. In this way Christ alone is the foundation of the Church, according to that of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 3. 11. No man can lay another foundation, besides that which is laid, which is CHRIST JESUS.

Then improperly, when that is called a foundation, upon which some thing in any way rests. In this sense, everything that sustains the Church in any way, or that is occupied in building the Church, can be called the foundation of the Church. In which sense all the Apostles are called Foundations of the Church, Ephes. 2. 20. Apocal. 21. 14. Otherwise the Apostles differ from Christ, as Architects from a foundation, 1 Cor. 3. 10.

Similarly the word Head is equivocal. For it signifies him who excels others either in authority, or age, or zeal, or dignity, or doctrine. Thus the Synod of Ephesus, in the Epistle to the Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, calls Cyril the Head of the assembled Bishops. Thus Chrysost. Homil. 18. to the Romans, names Elijah the head of the Prophets. Thus Gregory in book 1 of Kings, book 4, chapter 5, calls Paul the head of the nations. Yet neither was Elijah a Monarch among the Prophets, nor Cyril among the Bishops, nor Paul among the nations.

Latin:

narchatum in universam Christi Ecclesiam describant Romanenses. Unde luce meridiana fit manifestius, ipsos æqualem planè cum Christo potestatem Pontifici adscribere.

Scriptitant ergò Papæ primum hoc esse privilegium, quòd sit caput summum & unicum universalis Ecclesiæ, habens primatum & principatum super totam Ecclesiam. Archiepiscopus Florentinus summæ part. 3. tit. 23. c. 3. §. 2. Et potestatem capitis hujus majorem esse, omni alia creatâ, post potestatem Christi, aliquo modo extendens se ad cœlestia, terrestria & infernalia, ut de eo possit verificari illud Psal, 8. Omnia subjecisti sub pedibus ejus, oves & boves, pecora campi, volucres cœli & pisces maris. Et aptè: Quia ipse est vicarius Christi, quoad infernalia, dicit pisces maris. Idem ibid. tit. 22. c. 5.

Et ne Canonistarum sententijs nimis adulatoriis tantùm stare videamur, proferimus modernorum Jesuuvitarum scripta, quibus eandem impietatem stabilire conantur. Bellarminus certè lib. 2. de Pontifice Romano, cap. 31. eundem Pontificem sic definit, quòd sit Papa. 2. Pater Patrum. 3. Christianorum Pontifex. 4. Summus Sacerdos. 5. Princeps Sacerdotum. 6. Vicarius Christi. 7. Caput corporis Ecclesiæ. 8. Fundamentum ædificij Ecclesiæ. 9. Pastor ovilis Domini. 10. Pater & Doctor omnium fidelium. 11. Rector domus DEI. 12. Custos vineæ DEI. 13. Sponsus Ecclesiæ. 14. Apostolicæ sedis præsul. 15. Episcopus denique universalis. Hinc idem Bellarminus, toto libro quarto de Pontifice Romano disputat, summam & infallibilem omnium controversiarum Theologicarum decisionem à solo Papa Romano petendam & expectandam esse, eò quòd ipse in doctrina & fide errare non possit: quin eidem Pontifici Romano competere etiam potestatem coactivam, ita ut etiam leges ferre possit, quæ homines in conscientia obligent, & cogant credere aut agere, prout summo Pontifici visum fuerit: actandem libro 5. præter Spiritualem hanc, etiam secularem sive temporalem potestatem planè absolutam competere contendit.

Cæterum pugnat fictitius iste Pontificis Romani Monarchatus, mittò cum Scripturis S. deindè cum puriore Antiquitate.

Et quidem quoad Antiquitatem, nihil cuiquam Patrum quicquam de hoc primatu Papæ Romano cognitum fuit, ante Bonifacium IIX. qui primus sacrilegam istam impietatem, ausu nefario jactitavit, ut patet Decretal. lib. 6. de immunitatibus Ecclesiarum, capit. Quoniam. Quam constitutionem tamen tùm alia regna repudia runt: tum Gallia expressè rejecit.

Augustinus Epist. 58. ad Bonifacium sic scribit: Ecclesia Catholica sola est corpus CHRISTI, cujus ille caput est, Salvator corporis sui.

Et in Psal. 56. Tota Ecclesia constans ex omnibus fidelibus, habet illud caput positum in cœlestibus, quod gubernat corpus suum, quod etsi separatum est visione, annectitur tamen charitate.

gnissimè fert, Paulum Apostolum à nonnullis appellari caput eorum, quos in fide CHRISTI plantaverat: ô humana temeritas & superbia, inquit, cur non sinu potius, ut CHRISTUS Christiani sit caput? Caput etiam eorum, quomodo esse poterat, cùm dicat: Nos multos unum esse corpus in CHRISTO, ipsumq́ CHRISTUM caput esse corporis universi, pluribus locis apertissimè prædicet.

Similia habet Cyrillus, lib. 11. thes. cap. 26.

Sed luculentum cumprimis & memoratu dignum est, hac de re Gregorij M. qui ipse quoque Romanus fuit Pontifex, testimonium, lib. 4. Epistolarum, cap. 86. Nam cùm Johannes Episcopus Constantinopolitanus, universalis Episcopi, & capitis in Ecclesia nōen sibi ausus fuisset arrogare, Gregorius ad Eulogium Episcopũ Alexandrinum & Anastasium Episcopum Antiochenum datâ Epistolâ Novam hanc ait esse, Consacerdotis sui (sic Johannem Constantinopolitanũ, Gregorius Episcopus Romanus nominat) superbiam, ex qua tota universalis Ecclesia viscera perturbari queant, quæ sit mandatis Dominicis, Apostolicis præceptis, regulis Patrum prorsus contraria, quæ omnia, quæ soli & uni capiti cohæreant, CHRISTO videlicet, per elationem Pompatici Sermonis, Christi nimirùm ejusdem membra sibi ab isto subjungentur: Cui elationi ita jubet eos resistere, ut scripta vel epistolas, cùm universalis nominis falsitate, nec dare unquàm, nec recipere præsumant, & moriendo etiam, si qua hoc nomine persecutio ingruat, ostendere debeant, quòd in ista inquinaitone nihil ament.

Idem cap. 82. Epistola ad eundem Johannem Constantinopolitanum missâ, sic porrò scribit: Apostolus Paulus, cùm audiret quosdam dicere, Ego sũ Pauli, ego Apollo, ego Cephæ, hanc dilacerationem corporis Dominici, per quæ membra ejus aliis quodammodo capitibus sociabant, vehementissimè perhorrescens exclamavit: Numquid Paulus pro vobis crucifixus est, aut in nomine Pauli baptizati estis? Si ergò ille membra Dominici corporis, certis extra Christum quasi capitibus, & ipsis quidem Apostolis, subjici particulariter evitavit: Tu quid Christo, universalis scilicet Ecclesiæ capiti, in extremi judicij examine es dicturus, qui cũcta ejus membra tibimet conaris universalis Episcopi appellatione supponere? Proponitur in hoc tàm perverso vocabulo, imitatio Luciferi, qui dixerit Jes. 14. In cœlum ascendam, super astra cæli eexaltabo solium meum.

Quoad, Scripturas Sacras, ne quidem unum perspicuum proferre possunt testimonium, quod κατα τό ῥητὸν astruat id, quod volunt Romanenses. Undè factum, ut nonnulli ipsorum probationem petere ausi fuerint à statu & conditione Veteris Testamenti, ubi licèt Deus caput & summus Monarcha fuerit Ecclesiæ, nihilominus tamen caput etiam visibile, nempè summus Sacerdos sive Pontifex à DEO ipso constitutus fuisse legitur, ad quem in casibus dubijs & controversiis Ecclesiasticis confugiendum, & ipsius judicio tanquàm infallibili standum erat. Verùm postquàm à nostratibus ostensum fuit, turpem committi ἀγνοιαν ἐλέγχε: & statũ quæstionis Sophisticèperverti, propterea quòd non de Ecclesia Veteris, sed novi Testamenti propriè sit quæstio: & ideò factum illud sit in Veteri Testamento, quia Leviticus ille Pontifex typū gerere debuit summi & unici Pontificis Novi Testamenti CHRISTI Servatoris: ita ut jam CHRISTO in lucem edito, & præsentissimè ubiq; locorum, Ecclesiam suam gubernante, non novo alio typico, & vicario Pontificè & capite opus sit: mox recentiores Doctores Pontificij, Jesuvvitæ cumprimis, valere jussis probationibus ex Veteri Testamento, tanquàm nihil ad rem facientibus, ad Novum Testamentum confugerent.

Jam ut ex eo probabiliter aliquid concludere possent, duas præmiserunt hypotheses, sed manifestè impias & falsas.

Prior est, CHRISTVM ad cælos ascendentem, & considentem ad dextram DEI Patris, ita reliquisse hasce terras, ut jam non ampliùs adsit suæ Ecclesiæ, secundum humanitatem suam.

Posterior est, CHRISTVM corporis sui absentiam compensaturum quasi, & Vicarium Ecclesiæ suæ ordinaturum, constituisse Petrum, summum & Universalem Episcopum ac Caput Ecclesiæ: ipsiq; ut & Successoribus ejus Pontificibus Romanis, absolutam concessisse potestatem in omnes Christianos

Prioris hypothesews stupenda vanitas alibi à nobis protrita & conculcata est, nempè in diexodo Articuli de Persona CHRISTI.

Posteriorem hanc confirmare student Jesuvvitæ, duobus potissimùm huc accommodatis Scripturæ locis.

Prior extat, Matth. 16. 18 Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam.

Posterior, Joh. 21. 15. Pasce oves meas. De quo utroque loco, propter varia Jesuvvitarum Sophismata, altiùs nobis dispiciendum fuerit.

Ac initiò quidem ad utrumque in genere respondemus, ex figuratis sive Metaphoricis Scripturæ phrasibus nihil certi colligi posse, nisi idipsum alibi propriè & perspicuè in Scripturis tradatur. Hinc Augustinus quoque lib. de Vnit. Ecclesiæ c. 5. monet illa seponenda esse, quæ obscurè sunt posita & figurarum velaminibus involuta, & secundum nos, & secundum illos possunt explicari. Et cap. 16. scribit: Non colligant & commemorent ea, quæ vel obscurè vel ambiguè, vel figuratè dicta sunt, quæ quisq; sicut voluerit, interpretatur secundum sensum suum. Talia enim rectè intelligi exponiq; non possunt, nisi priùs ea, quæ apertissimè dicta sunt, firma fide teneantur. Aliquid proferte, inquit ibidem, quod interprete omninò non egeat.

Deindè verò in specie respondeo, primùm ad locum priorem Matth. 16. 18. ex quo colligunt, Petrum à Christo fundamentum & caput Ecclesiæ constitutum fuisse.

Ubi initio notandum, Fundamenti nomen bifariam accipi: primùm propriè, quando notatur id, super quod ædificium fundatur, & à quo id sustinetur. Hoc modo solus Christus Ecclesiæ fundamentum est, secundum illud Apostoli, 1. Cor. 3. 11. Fundamentum aliud nemo ponere potest, præter id, quod positum est, quod est CHRISTVS JESVS.

Deinde impropriè, cum id fundamentum dicitur, quo res aliqua quovis modo nititur. Hoc sensu Ecclesiæ fundamentum dici potest omne id, quod Ecclesiam quovis modo sustentat, vel quod in ædificanda Ecclesia occupatum est. Quo sensu omnes Apostoli dicuntur Fundamenta Ecclesiæ, Ephes. 2. 20. Apocal. 21. 14. Aliâs Apostoli à Christo differunt, ut Architecti à fundamento, 1. Cor. 3. 10.

Similiter vox Capitis est æquivoca. Significat enim eum, qui vel dominatu, vel ætate, vel Zelo, vel dignitate, vel doctrina cæteris præstat. Sic Synodus Ephesina, in Epist. ad Theodofium & Valentinianum Impp. Cyrillum vocat Caput congregatorum Episcoporum. Sic Chrysost. Homil. 18. ad Rom. Eliam nominat Prophetarum caput. Sic Gregorius in librum 1. Regum l. 4. c. 5. Paulum appellat caput nationum. Neque tamen vel Elias inter Prophetas, vel Cyrillus inter Episcopos, vel Paulus nationum Monarcha fuit.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: What kind of primacy is ascribed to the Pope (continued)

These things having been premised, if the Jesuits argue thus: He whom Christ placed as the foundation of the Church is rightly believed to be its head. But Christ, Matth. 16. 18, placed Peter as the foundation of the Church. Therefore Peter is rightly believed to be the head of the Church: then the Major premise would be false, if foundation is accepted in the second signification. For not everyone who is occupied in building the Church upon Christ is immediately the Head and Monarch of the Church, for all the Apostles did that: yet they were not constituted heads or Monarchs over the Church. But if the word foundation is accepted in the former, namely the proper signification, then the Minor premise will be false. For Christ alone in that way is the Foundation and Head of the Church, 1 Cor. 3. 11. Isa. 28. 16.

But the Jesuits insist, and urge the tenor of the words of Christ, Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church: But not even thus will they obtain anything. For neither is asserted by the words of Christ, either that the Church is to be built upon Peter: or that Peter is the foundation of the Church. For Christ did not say to Peter, Upon thee I will build my Church, just as a little later he said: To thee I will give the keys etc. Nor did Christ say that: Thou art a Rock, and upon this rock I will build my Church: But between Peter who was confessing Christ: and the Rock upon which he was about to build the Church, he clearly distinguished, by saying: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build, etc. From this Rock, Peter has obtained his name, says St. Jerome, in chapter 7 of Matthew: and Augustine on the Words of the Lord, Sermon 13. He was called Simon, it was imposed upon him by the LORD, so that by that figure he might signify the Church. For because Christ is the Rock: Peter is the Christian people. For Rock is the primary name. Therefore Peter is from the rock, not the rock from Peter, just as Christ is not called from Christian: but the Christian is called from Christ. You therefore, says Christ to Peter, are Peter (I understand from the rock which you have confessed) and upon this very rock, which you have confessed, upon this rock, which you have acknowledged, saying, You are Christ the son of the living GOD, I will build my Church: that is, upon me myself the Son of the living GOD, I will build my Church: upon me I will build you: not me upon you. For men wishing to be built upon men were saying: I am of Paul, I of Cephas. But others who did not wish to be built upon Peter, were saying, I am of Christ.

But if the Adversaries do not wish to acquiesce in this interpretation, let them explain, I pray, what difference they think exists between these two propositions, when it is said, Peter builds the Church upon CHRIST: and CHRIST builds the Church upon Peter.

The former, even with the Adversaries themselves conceding, is most true and proper. Therefore, by the same witnesses, Peter is not the foundation of the Church in the way that Christ is. But Christ is the foundation of the Church in that way, and for that reason, that it is founded upon him. Therefore Peter cannot be called the foundation of the Church for the same reason, and in the same sense. We conclude, therefore, irrefragably, that from the words of Christ in Matthew 16, verse 1, it can in no way be brought about that Peter was constituted the Foundation and Head of the Universal Church.

Furthermore, there is also this, that if the Papal interpretation were to differ from the propriety of the words of Christ, or the dogma itself from the truth, not even so much: this would still contribute nothing to the Roman Pontiffs.

The Jesuits indeed say that this Primacy of Monarchy, and the dignity of Head over the Church, was confirmed in Peter, and in all his successors. But this is partly nonsensical, and partly manifestly false. Nonsensical, because from one individual they constitute an entire species, and from those singular particles, I SAY TO YOU YOU are Peter: and upon THIS etc., they make universals: but in such a way that they babble that it is to be gathered not from the Individual of Peter to the remaining Apostles: but to all Roman Pontiffs. But how do so many Pontiffs lie hidden under those singular particles, under which not even the eleven Apostles could be comprehended? The Jesuits therefore trifle with trifles more vain than Sicilian nonsense. But as this is manifestly false: for Peter, as an Apostle, has no successors. For to the office of the Apostleship an immediate calling is required, Galatians 1:1.

2. Peter had the universal mandate of preaching the Gospel. But the Roman Pontiff has neither an immediate calling, nor such a mandate of preaching. Therefore.

3 For the succession of a good right, witnesses are needed, and documents worthy of faith, and those beyond exception. But the Roman Pontiff is destitute of both this support.

4. Even if the Pope were the successor of Peter: a successor has no more right than the predecessor transferred to him. But Peter had no right over the remaining Apostles. It is therefore a consequence that the Pontiff, the successor of Peter, can have no right whatsoever over the remaining Bishops, who are themselves likewise successors of the Apostles.

5. Peter was not the only supreme one of the Apostles: but in this order he had several associates: and he was not superior to Paul, who calls himself the least of the Apostles, 1 Corinthians 15:9. 2 Corinthians 11.

5. Therefore, that the Roman Pontiff has clearly no primacy and dignity of Head, either over the Church or among the Bishops, by divine right, is made clearer than the midday light.

Bellarmino is in an uproar against these things which we have annotated concerning the words of Christ in Matthew 16:18, in various ways: and indeed he contends that by the Rock, Peter himself must be understood: and this for two reasons: 1. Because the relative pronoun THIS must necessarily refer to some Rock: Now, indeed, it could not have referred to any other except the Peter to whom Christ said: You are Peter. 2. Because Christ spoke in Syriac: and Kephas in Syriac denotes the same thing as Rock: as witnessed by Jerome on chapter 2 of Galatians.

I answer that the former reason begs the question. For it does not follow that the pronoun THIS refers to some visible Rock.
