Therefore Peter was that Rock: As if Christ himself did not refer this to himself, and thus show himself to be the Rock, which Peter and others interpret. 2. It is false that the pronoun THIS is a relative. For in Greek it is, ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ. Now, indeed, ὗτος, αὕτη, τῦτο are not relatives, depending on what precedes: but they are demonstratives, denoting a present thing.

The latter reason is likewise faulty in many ways. For 1. In doubtful matters one must not have recourse to the Syriac version, especially the one we have in our hands: but to the Greek sources themselves, which the Apostles left to us, as Bellarmino himself also judges: book 2 on the Word of God, chapter 4. 2. The Syriac version does not even support the Jesuits. For the word Kephas does not signify both Peter and a rock indifferently to the Syrians: that is, it does not denote an appellative and a proper noun at the same time. For a proper noun is distinguished from an appellative by gender itself. Now in that Syriac version the words of Christ sound thus: דנת הו כאפא Danth hu Kepha, that is, You are that Peter: which is proven by the pronoun of the masculine gender, Hu: which denotes not an appellative, but a proper noun. Otherwise, according to Bellarmino's gloss, it should have been said: דַּנתּ הִיא כֵּאפָא that is, Danth hi Kephah, Thou art that Rock: Which words, however, are not found in the Syriac. Thus in the following, the Chaldean or Syriac version does not have: Upon this Peter: but upon this Rock ועל הדא כאפא Veal hadah Kephah. But Da or Denah דא or דנה, and emphatically with the He Hajedah, היא Hadah, that is, this very one, are always signs of the feminine gender. If, therefore, they obtained a relative force to Peter, the pronoun would certainly have had to agree in gender also with the preceding. But it does not agree in gender: for the antecedent is masculine, but the following pronoun is feminine. It is false, therefore, that the pronoun This is relative to Peter.

Finally, regarding this saying, Bellarmine especially urges that which Christ immediately entrusted to Peter alone, the right of the keys of the Kingdom of heaven: Where the primacy of Peter was confirmed.

I answer, the argument fails by the fallacy of the consequent (τῷ παρὰ τὸ ἑπόμενον). For it does not follow: Christ said to Peter alone: I will give you the keys. Therefore Peter was constituted Monarch and head of the whole Church.

1. nothing here was given to Peter, but only promised. Now, however, not the promise, but the fulfillment or performance of the promise, completes the promise.

2. When Christ, what he promised here, afterwards performed in fact, then he entrusted the keys not to Peter alone, but to all the Apostles equally. John 20:22, Matthew 18:28. Therefore.

3. The power of the keys does not designate Monarchical Empire over the Church. Otherwise there would be as many Heads of the Church as there are pastors and ministers of the Church: to whom this power has been entrusted equally.

But the Jesuit moves on to another saying of Scripture, taken from John 21:15, where Peter is commanded several times to feed the sheep of Christ.

But I answer, that the reason for the consequence is weak, nay, clearly null. For the argument will be such: He to whom the power of feeding the sheep of Christ is entrusted: he is the Head and Monarch of the Church. But this power was given to Peter. Therefore. Where the major proposition is simply false. For a pastor, not a monarch, is he to whom the care of feeding the sheep is handed over. The minor is indeed true concerning Peter: but not him alone. For in Matthew 28:19, Mark 16:16, the same care was likewise entrusted to all the remaining Apostles. If, therefore, Peter, by reason of this pastorate, is the head and Monarch of the Church: then it is necessary that all the Apostles were of equal dignity: and consequently the Church at that time had twelve heads, and twelve Monarchs, not Monarchs.

The Jesuit objects, that the care of feeding the sheep of Christ was indeed entrusted to the remaining Apostles likewise, but all, or the Universal Church of Christ, that is what was entrusted to Peter alone.

I answer, that this also is most false. For the Apostles were all commanded equally to teach all nations, to preach the Gospel to every creature, and likewise to be witnesses of Christ to the very ends of the earth. Matthew 28:19, Mark 16:15, Acts 1:8.

Latin:

His ita præmissis si sic colligant Jesuvvitæ: Quem Christus Ecclesiæ fundamentum posuit, is caput ejus rectè creditur. Atqui Christus Matth. 16. 18. Petrum posuit Ecclesiæ fundamentum. Ergò Petrus rectè creditur caput Ecclesiæ: tùm Major falsa fuerit, si fundamentum in secunda significatione accipiatur. Non enim quisquis in Ecclesia super Christum ædificandâ occupatus est, statim Caput & Monarcha est Ecclesiæ, Fecerunt enim illud omnes Apostoli: neque tamen capita aut Monarchæ super Ecclesiam sunt constituti. Sin in priori, nempé propria significatione vox fundamenti accipiatur, tùm Minor erit falsa. Solus enim Christus isto modo est Fundamentum & Caput Ecclesiæ, 1, Cor. 3. 11. Jes. 28. 16.

Cæterùm instant Jesuvvitæ, & urgent tenorem verborum Christi, Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam: Verùm ne sic quidem aliquid obtinebunt. Neutrum enim verbis Christi asseritur, vel quòd Ecclesia super Petrum ædificanda sit: vel quòd Petrus Ecclesiæ fundamentum sit. Non enim dixit Christus Petro, Super te ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, quemadmodum paulò post dixit: Tibi dabo claves &c. Neque illud dixit Christus: Tu es Petra, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam: Sed inter Petrum qui Christum confitebatur: & Petram super quam ædificaturus erat Ecclesiam, diserte distinxit, dicendo: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo &c. Ab hac Petra, Petrus nomen est sortitus, inquit D. Hieronymus, in cap. 7. Matthæi: & Augustinus de Verbis Domini, Serm. 13. Simon vocabatur, ei a DOMINO impositum est, ut ea figura significaret Ecclesiam. Quia enim Christus Petra: Petrus populus Christianus. Petra enim principale nomen est. Ideò Petrus à petra, non petra à Petro, quemadmodum non à Christiano Christus: sed à Christo Christianus vocatur. Tu ergò, inquit Christus Petro, es Petrus (intelligo à petra quam confessus es) & super hanc ipsam petram, quam confessus es, super hanc petram, quam cognovisti, dicens, Tu es Christus filius DEI vivi, ædificabo Ecclesiam meam: hoc est, super me ipsum Filium DEI vivi, ædificabo Ecclesiam meam: super me ædificabo te: non me super te. Nam homines volentes ædificari super homines dicebant: Ego sum Pauli, lego Cephæ. Alij vero qui nolebant ædificari super Petrum, dicebant, Ego sum Christi.

Verùm si interpretatione hâc nolint acquiescere Adversarij, edisserant quæso, quid existiment discriminis intercedere, duabus hisce propositionibus, cùm dicitur, Petrus ædificat Ecclesiam super CHRISTVM: & CHRISTVS ædificat Ecclesiam super Petrum.

Prior ipsis etiam Adversarijs concedentibus, est verissima & propria. Ergò ijsdem testibus, Petrus non est modo Ecclesiæ fundamentum, quo Christus. Sed Christus eo modo, & ideò Ecclesiæ fundamentum est, quòd hæc super eum est fundata. Ergò Petrus eandem ob causam, & eodem sensu, fundamentum Ecclesiæ dici non potest. Concludimus ergó, irrefragabiliter, verborum Christi Matth. 16. v. 1, nullo modo effici posse, quòd Petrus Universalis Ecclesiæ Fundamentum & Caput constitutus sit.

Accedit porrò & illud, quòd, si vel maximè interpretatio Pontificia à proprietate Verborum Christi: vel dogma ipsum à veritate non usque adeò discreparent: nihil tamen hoc faceret ad Pontifices Romanos.

Dicunt quidem Jesuvvitæ, Primatum hunc Monarchiæ, & dignitatem Capitis super Ecclesiam, in Petro, successoribus ejus omnibus confirmatum esse. Sed partim nugatorium hoc est, partim manifeste falsum. Negatorium, Quia ex individuo uno, constituunt universam speciem, & ex particulis illis singularibus, DICO TIBI TV es Petrus: & super HANC &c. universales faciunt: sed ita, ut ab Individuo Petri, non ad reliquos Apostolos: sed ad omnes Pontifices, Romanos colligendum esse garriant. Quomodo verò tam multi Pontifices, sub particulis istis singularibus lateant, sub quibus ne quidem undecim Apostoli comprehendi potuerunt. Nugas ergò gerris Siculis vaniores nugantur Jesuvvitæ. Sed ut manifesté falsum hoc est: Petrus enim, ut Apostolus successores non habet. Nam ad Apostolatus officium immediata vocatio requiritur, Gal. 1. 1.

2. Petrus mandatum universale prædicandi Evangelij habuit. Atqui neque immediatam vocationem, neque tale mandatum prædicandi, habet Pontifex Romanus. Ergò.

3 Ad successionem boni juris, testibus opus est, & tabulis fide dignis, & exceptione majoribus. Sed utroque hoc subsidio destituitur Romanus Pontifex.

4. Si maximè Papa Petri successor sit: successor plus juris non habet, quàm in ipsum antecessor transtulit. Atqui Petro in reliquos Apostolos juris nihil fuit. Consequens est ergò, Pontifici, Successori Petri, in reliquos Episcopos, ipsos itidem Apostolorum successores, nihil quicquam juris esse posse.

5. Petrus neque solus summus fuit Apostolorum: sed in hoc ordine socios complures habuit: & Paulo, qui se minimum Apostolorum vocat, 1. Cor 15. 9. non fuit superior. 2. Cor. 11.

5. Pontifici ergò Romano primatum & Capitis dignitatem, planè nullam, vel in Ecclesiam, vel inter Episcopos, jure divino competere, luce meridiana clariùs efficitur.

Tumultuatur adversum hæc, quæ de Verbis Christi Matth. 16. 18. annotavimus, varijs modis Bellarminus: ac quidem contendit, per Petram intelligendum esse ipsum Petrum: idque deo: 1. Quia pronomen relativum HANC referat se necessario ad aliquam Petram: Jam verò ad nullam aliam referri potuisse, præter Petram, ad quem Christus dixerit: Tu es Petrus. 2. Quia Christus Syriacè sit locutus: Kephas autem Syriacè idem notet atq; Petra: teste Hieron. ad cap. 2. Galat.

Respondeo, rationem priorem petere principium. Neque enim sequitur, Pronomen HANC refert se ad visibilem aliquam Petram. Ergo Petrus fuit illa Petra: Quasi verò non Christus ipse ad semetipsum hoc retulerit, & sic se monstraverit esse Petram, quam Petrus & alij interpretantur. 2. Falsum est pronomen HANC esse relativum. Nam in Græco est, ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ. Jam verò ὗτος, αὕτη, τῦτο, non sunt relativa, à præcedente dependentia: sed sunt demonstrativa, rem præsentem notantia.

Ratio posterior itidem multis modis est vitiosa. Nam 1. in dubijs non recurrendum est ad versionem Syriacam, eam cumprimis, quam nos in manibus habemus: sed ad ipsos fontes Græcos, quos Apostoli nobis reliquerunt, sic censente ipso quoque Bellarmino: lib. 2. de Verbo DEI, cap. 4. 2. Ne quidem Syriaca versio Jesuitis patrocinatur. Neque enim vox Kephas Syris indifferenter & Petrum & Petram significat: hoc est, Appellativum simul notat, & proprium. Proprium enim ab appellativo distinguitur ipso Genere. Jam in versione illa Syriaca verba Christi sic sonant. דנת הו כאפא Danth hu Kepha, hoc est, Tu es ille Petrus: id quod evincit pronomen masculini generis, Hu: quod non appellativum, sed proprium notat. Aliàs secundum Bellarmini glossam dicendum fuisset: דַּנתּ הִיא כֵּאפָא idest, Danth hi Kephah, Tu es illa Petra: Quæ tamen verba in Syriaco non reperiuntur. Sic in subsequentibus Chaldæa sive Syriaca versio non habet: Super istum Petrum: sed super istam Petram ועל הדא כאפא Veal hadah Kephah Da autem vel Denah דא vel דנה, & emphaticè cum He Hajedah, היא Hadah, idest, hæc ipsa, semper sunt notæ fæminini generis. Quod si ergò relativam vim obtinerent ad Petrum, utique genere etiam cum præcedente convenire pronomen debuisset. Atqui genere non convenit: Antecedens enim masculinum: pronomen verò subsequens fæmininum est. Falsum ergò quod pronomen Hoc sit relativum ad Petrum.

Tandem circa hoc dictum præcipuè etiam urget Bellarminus illud, quod Christus statim soli Petro commiserit jus clavium Regni cœlorum: Vbi primatus Petri fuerit confirmatus.

Respondeo, Fallit argumentum τῷ παρὰ τὸ ἑπόμενον. Neque enim sequitur: Christus soli Petro dixit: Tibi dabo claves. Ergò Petrus constitutus est Monarcha & caput totius Ecclesiæ.

1. nihil hîc Petro datum est, sed tantùm promissum. Jam verò non promissio, sed promissi solutio sive præstatio, promissionem implet.

2. Cūm Christus quod hîc promisit, postmodùm ipso facto præstitit, tùm non soli Petro, sed omnibus ex æquo Apostolis claves commisit. Joh. 20. 22. Matth. 18. 28. Ergo.

3. Potestas clavium non designat Imperium Monarchicum in Ecclesiam. Aliâs tot essent Capita Ecclesiæ, quot pastores & ministri Ecclesiæ: quibus ex æquo potestas hæc est concre dita.

Sed ad alterum Scripturæ dictum transit Jesuwita, petitum ex Johan. 21. 15. Vbi aliquoties jubetur Petrus pascere oves Christi.

Sed Respondeo, elumbem, imò planè nullam esse rationem Consequentiæ. Tale enim erit argumentum: Cui potestas pascendi oves Christi est commissa: ille Caput est & Monarcha Ecclesiæ. Atqui Petro hæc potestas data est. Ergò. Vbi major propositio simpliciter falsa est. Pastor enim, non monarcha sit, cui summa pascendarum ovium traditur. Minor vera est quidem de Petrò: sed non solo. Nam Matth. 28. 19. Marc. 16. 16. cura eadem reliquis Apostolis omnibus itidem est commissa. Si igitur Petrus, ratione pastoratus hujus, caput est & Monarcha Ecclesiæ: tùm in pari dignitate omnes fuerint Apostoli necesse est: & perconsequens Ecclesia tùm temporis duodecim habuit capita, & duodecim Monarchas, non Monarchas.

Excipit Jesuvvita, Reliquis quidem Apostolis itidem commissam esse curam pascendi oves Christi, sed omnes, sive Vniversam Ecclesiam Christi, id quod soli Petro commissum fuerit.

Respondeo, falsissimum & hoc esse. Nam omnes gentes docere, omni creaturae Evangelium praedicare, item testes esse Christi ad ultimas usque terras, jussi fuerunt Apostoli ex aequo omnes. Matth. 28. 19. Marc. 16. 15. Actor. 1. 8.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: What kind of primacy is ascribed to the Pope (continued)

Furthermore, it is most false that 'to feed' in this passage signifies the same as to rule over the Church in the manner of a monarch. A kind of dominion which the Savior willed to be simply absent from his Apostles: Luke 22:25. Moreover, the pasturing of the sheep was not committed simply and exclusively to Peter alone, nor to the Apostles alone: but it is incumbent upon the ministers of all the churches. Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2. This pasturing Peter, in the place already alleged, so commends to the bishops that he wishes all dominion, and much more kingdom and monarchy, to be most alien from it.

Finally, there is also this: that Peter is commanded to feed sheep, not his own, but CHRIST'S, and thus another's. But this, with respect to Peter and other pastors, is nothing other than to serve and to minister. Therefore, by the commendation of this office, no dominion over the sheep is handed over and committed to Peter or to other pastors, but only service or ministry.

Bellarmino approaches in this place also that trite dispute concerning Peter: 1. That he was at Rome. 2. That he presided there for 25 years as the Head and universal Bishop of the Church. But since we have treated the detailed examination of both these questions in a separate and indeed publicly printed disputation, it is not relevant to deal with them at greater length in this place.

That rather must be weighed a little more accurately, which Bellarmino, from the presupposed false hypothesis that Peter presided at Rome for 25 years as Monarch of the Universal Church, gathers: that the Roman Pontiff succeeds Peter in the Roman episcopate, or in the primacy of the Universal Church, as Bellarmino speaks: lib. 2 de Rom. Pont. cap. 12, page 740 D.

But to pass over for now other arguments of our theologians by which the vanity of this fiction can be refuted, I will urge that one argument which is taken from that interval which intervened between the death of St. Peter and St. John of at least thirty years. For it is evident from book 3, chapter 18 of Eusebius that the Apostle John died in the hundredth year almost after Christ was born, so that his death falls in the times of the Emperor Trajan: and thus he survived Peter by at least thirty years. Let Bellarmino therefore now explain to us, who succeeded Peter in the monarchy over the Universal Church of Christ? If he answers either Linus, or Anacletus, or someone else (for the Papists themselves fight among themselves about the first successor)

I ask why the Apostle John did not succeed, who by divine right ought surely to have succeeded? For it would be too blasphemous and impious to assert that a simple Bishop, who is not an Apostle, while the Apostles were still alive, or at least one of them, arrogated to himself power and jurisdiction over the Universal Church of Christ, and thus over the Apostle John himself. By what reasoning, certainly, would the Apostles, and indeed that Apostle whom Christ is read to have loved above the rest, have been inferior to a simple Bishop? The Bishop would have been the Head; the Apostle, however, a member of the Bishop, in an order clearly inverted and preposterous. But if a Council had to be convened even then, certainly either Linus, or Cletus, or Anacletus, or some other person who, according to the Jesuits' hypothesis, had succeeded Peter in the primacy of the Church, would have held the role of president, while the Apostle John would have held the place of some simple Bishop: and thus Linus or Cletus would have had greater authority than the Apostle John, that son of thunder, as he was named by Christ. Since all these things are more absurd than any absurdities whatsoever, it is spontaneously clear that whatever Bellarmine chatters about the Succession of the Roman Pontiff in the primacy of the universal Church is the most trifling of trifles. We therefore argue as follows.

Whichever Bishop wishes to succeed Peter (according to the Papal hypothesis) in the primacy over the universal Church of Christ, and indeed while some one or more Apostles are alive: it is necessary that he have supreme authority even over those still surviving Apostles: so that they, as members, are subject to that Bishop, as to a Universal head.

But no Bishop ever arrogated to himself such authority while the Apostles were still alive, let alone usurped it. Therefore, it is false and fabricated that the Roman Bishop, whoever he may be, succeeded to such a primacy over the Apostle Peter, even if he had been constituted such a Monarch of the Church, while any Apostle was still alive.

The Romanists themselves will not deny the connection to the major premise, provided they wish to establish the Monarchy and primacy for which they fight. Let the Jesuits deliberate whether they wish to concede the minor premise. If they answer affirmatively, then our Cause is stated and proven. For thus the entire Jesuit structure concerning the Pope as the successor of Peter and his primacy will collapse of its own accord. If they answer negatively, then they will render themselves guilty of manifest blasphemy and impiety. For what is more absurd and blasphemous than to prefer the order of Romanist Bishops to the power and authority of the Apostles, whose order, however, Christ established as the highest in the Church, as Paul testifies: Christ established Apostles first in the Church: Eph. 4:11.

Perhaps some one of the Jesuits might object that the Apostle John was then banished to Patmos: and therefore he could not have succeeded: and consequently: it was of the highest necessity that, with no Apostle surviving besides John, some other Roman Bishop should succeed, lest, forsooth, the see

Apostolic should be vacant and deprived of its certain head.

But not even in this way will they find any protection for their most lost cause. For histories testify that that banishment occurred in the last times of John's life, and that he was not absent for more than three years, being recalled later a little before the reign of Trajan. Whence it is evident that John, after the death of Lord Peter, presided over the Churches of Greece and Asia Minor for a full 24 years in the greatest peace and tranquility.

There are some among the Jesuits who perhaps might object that the Apostle John, or some other Apostle, was the Head of the Church after the death of Peter, in such a way that the Roman Bishop yielded for a time. But I reply that this could not have happened either: Since an Apostle does not succeed an Apostle: For thus the Apostolate would endure to this very day by virtue of ordinary succession: which, however, Christ the Savior willed to expire with the Apostles themselves constituted by Him: but only Bishops succeed the Apostles: just as the Apostle Paul willed not an Apostle, but a Bishop to succeed him on the island of Crete: and likewise willed Bishops to preside over the Church in the Ephesian Church. Tit. 1:5; Acts 20:28. Which very thing Cyprian also and most of the Fathers, and indeed the Jesuits themselves elsewhere, outside of this conflict, readily grant.

Furthermore, this Jesuit exception fights diametrically against the catalog or Chronology of the Roman Pontiffs, which asserts that Linus succeeded Peter immediately, and as Platina trifles, by Peter's testamentary ordination: Where there is clearly no mention of the Apostle John. Nay, Onuphrius Panvinius reports that the Pontificate of Linus was in the year of Christ 57, and writes that he presided for eleven years: To whom, upon his death, succeeded Clemens, in the year of Christ 68. To him Cletus, in the year of Christ 77. To him Anacletus, in the year of Christ 84. To him finally Evaristus, in the year of Christ 96. So that according to the Chronology of the Pontificians themselves, the Apostle John outlived five Roman Pontiffs. How, therefore, can it be true that the Roman Bishops yielded to the Apostles in the primacy of the Church as long as they were alive.

Nor is it as the Adversaries say, that an Apostle succeeded an Apostle, not in the Apostolate, but in the prefecture or primacy of the Church. For not even in the prefecture of the Church could an Apostle succeed an Apostle, because Bellarmine writes expressly that in this, succession was made to Peter alone, and indeed not by any of the Apostles: But by the Roman Bishops only. To which pertains that which the same Bellarmine writes, book 2 on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 12, page 543 C. That the Roman Bishop, because he is the Roman Bishop, is the successor of Peter, had its origin from the fact of Peter. For Peter could have chosen no particular see for himself ever, just as he did for the first five years, and then upon Peter's death; neither the Roman Bishop nor the Antiochene would have succeeded, but he whom the Church had chosen for itself: he could also have always remained at Antioch, and then the Antiochene would have succeeded without a doubt:

But because he fixed his seat at Rome and held it until his death, it came about from that, that the Roman Bishop succeeds him. Furthermore, the same Bellarmine contends that it was said to Peter alone, and to his successors the Roman Bishops, Feed my sheep, and I will give you the keys. But now, no one of the Apostles was the Roman Bishop; therefore, when Peter died, no Apostle succeeded Peter in the Prefecture of the Church, nor was any one of them ever the Head of the Church. 3. If an Apostle, either John or James, was the Head of the Church: therefore the Roman Bishop was not the head: and consequently he did not succeed Peter in the prefecture. If this is so, it will necessarily follow that no one of the Roman Pontiffs can affirm that he succeeded Peter in the prefecture of the Church by hereditary right, in such a way that the succession was not interrupted. For if it is interrupted: a legitimate and hereditary succession does not exist. 4. When John or James of Jerusalem had died, if one of them had been the successor of Peter, then the Roman Bishop could clearly not have succeeded, because he would not have succeeded in the place: but he would have received his monarchical succession, not from Peter, but from either the Ephesian or the Hierosolymitan Pontiff: and thus the seat of Peter would not have remained at Rome, but would have been transferred to the East to those cities. Therefore, according to the argumentation of Bellarmine, proposed a little earlier, if any Bishop had wished to succeed legitimately in the primacy, it is necessary that he should have been either the Ephesian or the Hierosolymitan Bishop: namely, of that city in which the last surviving Apostle presided. By which arrangement it becomes most manifest that Rome and the Roman Bishops possess no right of legitimate succession.

There are some among the Romanists who, in the fourth place, object that the Apostles administered the universal Church by common councils, so that from the death of Peter there was an interregnum until the death of all the Apostles. I answer: the former is more against the Jesuits. For thus it would follow 1. that the Church then lacked a certain visible head. 2. That all the Apostles were endowed with equal power and equal jurisdiction, and thus the government of the Church was Aristocratic: which they constantly deny, contending that the government of the Church has always been Monarchical. 3. The division of the Apostles, which was made while Peter was still alive, proves the contrary, so that the Apostles, dispersed and separated very far from each other throughout the whole world, could not after the death of Peter jointly undertake the administration of the Universal Church: but rather each one cared for those Churches which he had founded, and to which he had arrived by occasion.

The latter reason likewise overturns itself: For if there was an interregnum from the death of Peter until the death of all the Apostles; it was either in the Roman Episcopate, or in the prefecture over the whole Church. It was not in the Episcopate, because, as the Jesuits contend, from the death of Peter there were always Roman Bishops succeeding one another in an uninterrupted order, until the death of John, or the time of Trajan. Therefore, it is necessary that the interregnum was in the prefecture itself. But this very thing is most especially against Bellarmine. For from that it would necessarily follow that no one of those who sat in the Roman Episcopate after the death of Peter, until the death of John and all the Apostles, was the Head of the whole militant Church, and consequently neither was he the successor of Peter in the primacy of the whole Church. We conclude therefore that there has never been any succession in the prefecture and Monarchy over the whole militant Church among the Roman Bishops from the death of Peter; nor is there to this day. For to prove succession in the prefecture of the Church, it is necessary that individuals residing in the chair be able to show that their individual predecessors had the same right which he arrogates to himself and exercises: Which indeed cannot be done in this place. For that Roman Bishop who held the Chair at the time when the last Apostle died, could not show that his immediate predecessor had such power; if indeed it is true that from the death of Peter until the death of the remaining Apostles, there was an interregnum regarding that monarchical power: and thus he could not say that he was made Head of the Church after the death of Peter by hereditary succession from Peter. Therefore the succession was interrupted: If it was interrupted, and neither Linus, nor Cletus, nor Anacletus succeeded Peter in the prefecture of the Church, because there was an interregnum then: Therefore much less could Pius V, the Head of the Council of Trent, or anyone else, say that which Bellarmine fights for, that he has that Monarchical power by hereditary right from Peter, and that Christ and Peter gave all their things to each and every Roman Bishop.

Moreover, since the adversaries never concede that the succession was interrupted, they must certainly also concede that there was no interregnum at that time.

The Jesuit Bellarmine, intending to extricate himself from these difficulties, devised a certain new plausible refuge: about which he speaks thus: lib. 1. de Pont. Rom. cap. 9. pag. 632. C. & D. The supreme Ecclesiastical power was not only given to Peter, but also to the other Apostles: but it was given to Peter as an Ordinary Pastor, to whom there would be perpetual succession: but to the others as delegates, to whom there would be no succession: Therefore, when the Apostles were dead, the Apostolic authority remained in the successor of Peter alone. For no Bishop except the Roman ever had the care of all the Churches, and he alone is called by all the Apostolic Pontiff, and his seat is simply Apostolic, etc.

I answer

I answer 1. The Jesuit is babbling or trifling. For he proves nothing of those things which he says. 2. He maliciously perverts the state of the controversy, and omits that which is most in question, namely, concerning the hereditary right, and concerning the immediate successor of Peter immediately after his death: but he only says that Apostolic authority remained in the sole successor of Peter, the Apostles being dead. Where he neither names a successor, nor mentions hereditary succession. From this one thing it is detected how insidiously and sophistically the Sophist treats this cause. For if he had wished to defend his opinion candidly, which he otherwise proposes in book 2, de Rom. Pont. chapter 12, then he ought to have said thus: The Apostles all being dead, Apostolic authority by hereditary right remained in the sole immediate successor of Peter, the Roman Bishop. But this is simply false, as has been evidently demonstrated hitherto. These things having been thus demonstrated, we conclude this first Question or Controversy with this refutatory syllogism.

Whatever right in the inheritance of a deceased person is not found at the very time of death: it is necessary that he also did not have that while alive.

But the right of prefecture or primacy over the whole militant Church, left in the inheritance of St. Peter, that is, in the immediate successors, Linus and Cletus and Anacletus, Roman Bishops, did not appear, nor was it found.

Therefore, Peter never had the right of prefecture or primacy over the whole militant Church: and consequently, what he did not have, he could not transmit to any successor.

The connection of the major premise is absolutely true, unless it can be demonstrated that someone either resigned or gave his right, which he had while alive, to some other person, or that it was taken from him either by force or by law, or at least that it was personal and extinguished at the same time as he died.

We have hitherto proven the minor premise in such a way that the Jesuits themselves doubt whether Linus, or Cletus, or Anacletus, or Evaristus, or some other person first succeeded in the Pontificate, both Peter and the remaining Apostles being dead, who were still surviving from the time of Peter's death. Thus the Jesuits themselves will by no means affirm that this right of prefecture was either taken from Peter or resigned by him to Linus or Clement or Cletus. For this was not permitted to the prejudice of those Apostles who were surviving after him: indeed, Peter could not even give this right to any of the Apostles: since, by Bellarmine's own testimony, it was said to Peter alone, Feed my sheep. Furthermore, this right was also not personal, nor extinguished at the same time as he died, the Jesuits themselves again contending.

Latin:

Praeterea falsissimum est, quod Pascere hoc loco idem significet, atque dominari in modum Monarchae super Ecclesiam. Qualem dominatum a suis Apostolis simpliciter abesse voluit Servator: Luc. 22. 25. Insuper pastura ovium non soli Petro, non solis Apostolis simpliciter & exclusive est commissa: sed ministris Ecclesiarum omnium incumbit. Actor. 20. 28. 1. Petr. 5. 2. quam pasturam Petrus loco jam allegato ita Episcopis commendat: ut omne dominium, multo magis regnum & Monarchiam velit ab ea esse alienissimam.

Tandem accedit & illud, quod Petrus jubetur pascere oves, non suas: sed CHRISTI, & sic alienas. Atqui hoc Petri & aliorum pastorum respectu, nihil aliud est, quam servire & ministrare. Ergo officij hujus commendatione, neque Petro, neque alijs pastoribus, dominium aliquod in oves: sed tantum servitium sive ministerium est traditum & commissum.

Aggreditur Bellarminus hoc loco etiam tritam illam disputationem de Petro, quod 1. fuerit Romae. 2. quod ibi praesederit annis 25. tanquam Caput & Episcopus universalis Ecclesiae. Verum cum peculiari & quidem typis publicis impressa disputatione, utriusq; hujus Quaestionis diexodon pertractaverimus: nihil attinet prolixius de illis hoc loco agere.

Illud potius paulo accuratius expendendum, quod Bellarminus ex praesupposita falsa hypothesi, Petrum Romae ut Monarcham Universalis Ecclesiae, praesedisse annis 25. colligit, Romanum Pontificem succedere Petro in episcopatu Romano: sive in primatu Universae Ecclesiae, uti loquitur Bellarminus: lib. 2. de Rom. Pont. cap. 12. pag. 740. D.

Caterum ut alias rationes Theologorum nostrorum, quibus commenti hujus Vanitas retundi potest, jam praeteream: illud unum urgebo argumentum, quod sumitur ex illo intervallo, quod inter mortem D. Petri, & D. Johannis ad minimum annorum triginta intercessit. Constat enim ex lib. 3. cap. 18. Eusebij. D. Apostolum Johannem, anno centesimo ferme post Christum natum obijsse, ita ut mors ipsius incidat in tempora Trajani Imperatoris: & sic triginta annis ad minimum Petro supervixerit. Edisserat ergo nobis jam Bellarminus, Quisnam succefferit Petro in Monarchia super Universam Ecclesiam Christi? si responderit, vel Linum, vel Anacletum, vel alium quempiam (nam ipsi Pontificij de primo successore invicem digladiantur )

Quæro cur Johannes Apostolus non successerit, qui jure divino succedere utique debuisset? Blasphemum enim nimis & impium foret asserere, Episcopum simplicem, qui non sit Apostolus, viventibus adhuc Apostolus, vel uno saltem, sibi potestatem & jurisdictionem arrogasse in Universam Christi Ecclesiam, & sic in ipsum quoque Apostolum Johannem. Qua certè ratione Apostolis, & Apostolus quidem ille, quem Christus præ reliquis dilexisse legitur, minor fuisset Episcopo simplici? Episcopus fuisset Caput; Apostolus verò mē- brum Episcopi, ordine planè inverso & præpostero. Quod si jam tùm convocandum fuisset Concilium, certè vel Linus, vel Clemens, vel Anacletus, vel alius quispiam, qui secundum Jesuitarum hypothesin, Petro successerat in primatu Ecclesiæ, præsidis partes, Apostolus verò Johannes simplicis alicujus Episcopi locum sustinuisset: & sic majorem autoritatem habuisset Linus vel Cletus, quàm Johannes Apostolus filius ille tonitrui, ut à Christo nominabatur. Quæ omnia cum absurdissimis quibusvis absurdiora sint, ultrò liquet, nugas nugacissimas esse, quicquid de Successione Romani Pontificis in primatu universæ Ecclesiæ garrit Bellarminus. Nos proindé sic argumentamur.

Quicunq́; Episcopus velit succedere Petro (ex hypothesi Pontificia) in primatu super universā Ecclesiam Christi, & quidem vivo aliquo vel pluribus Apostolis: necesse est, ut is summam habeat autoritatem etiam supra illos adhuc superstites Apostolos: ita ut hi tanquàm mēbra subsint illi Episcopo, tanquàm capiti Vniversali.

Atqui nullus Episcopus talem nunquàm autoritatem viventibus adhuc Apostolis sibi arrogavit, ne dum usurpavit. Ergo falsum & commentitium est, quòd Apostolo Petro, si vel maximè is, talis Monarcha Ecclesiæ constitutus fuisset, Episcopus Romanus, quicunque illo sit, in tali primatu successerit: vivente adhuc Apostolo aliquo.

Majori connexum non negabunt ipsi Romanenses, dummodò Monarchiam & primatum, pro quo pugnant, stabilire velint. Minorem utrum concedere velint, deliberent Jesuvvitæ. Si affirmatè responderint, tùm dicta & evicta est Causa nostra. Sic enim universa structura Jesuvvitica, de Papa successore Petri, ejusq́; primatu ultrò corruet. Sin negatè, tùm manifestæ blasphemiæ & impietatis reos seipsos constituent. Quid enim absurdum & blasphemum magis, quàm ordinem Episcoporum Romanensium, præferre potestati & autoritati Apostolorum, quorum tamen ordinem Christus in Ecclesia summum constituit: teste Paulo: Christus in Ecclesia primùm constituit Apostolos: Ephes. 4, 11.

Excipiat fortassis Jesuvvitarum aliquis, Johannem Apostolum, tùm relegatum fuisse in Pathmum: ac proinde ipsum succedere non potuisse: & per consequens: summæ fuisse necessitatis, ut nullo ampliùs præter Johannem superstite Apostolo, alius quispiam Episcopus Romanus succederet, nè videlicet sedes

Apostolica vacaret, & certo suo capite destitueretur.

Sed neque sic causæ perdidissimæ præsidium aliquod invenient. Testantur enim historiæ, Relegationem illam contigisse ultimis vitæ Johannis temporibus, neque triennio ampliùs abfuisse, revocatum postea paulò ante imperium Trajani. Undè constat Johannem post mortem D. Petri, totu 24. annis summa in pace & tranquillitate præfuisse Græcis & Asiæ minoris Ecclesiis.

Sunt ex Jesuvvitis, qui fortè illud objiciant, Johannem Apostolum, vel alium quempiam Apostolum, post mortem Petri superstitem fuisse Caput Ecclesiæ, ita ut Episcopus Romanus cesserit ad tempus. Sed respondeo, neque hoc fieri potuisse: Siquidem Apostolo non succedit Apostolus: Sic enim in hunc usque diem vi successionis ordinariæ duraret Apostolatus: quem tamen Christus Servator, cum ipsis Apostolis à se constitutis rursus expirare voluit: sed Apostolis succedunt Episcopi tantùm: quemadmodum Apostolus Paulus non Apostolum, sed Episcopu in insula Creta sibi succedere: & in Ecclesia Ephesina Episcopos itidem Ecclesiæ præesse voluit. Tit. 1. 5. Actor. 20. 28. Quod ipsum Cyprianus quoque & Patres plerique, quin ipsi quoque Jesuitæ aliàs, extra istum conflictum, ultrò largiuntur.

Præterea exceptio hæc Jesuvvitica è diametro pugnat cùm catalogo sive Chronologia Pontificum Romanorum, quæ Linum Petro immediatè, & ut Platina nugatur, ex Petri ordinatione testamentaria successisse asserunt: Ubi Johannis Apostoli planè nulla sit mentio Quin imò Onuphrius Panvinius refert, Pontificatum Lini ad A. C. 57. eundemq́; annis undecim præsedisse scribit: Cui mortuo successit Clemens, Anno C. 68. Huic Cletus, A. C 77. Isti Anacletus A. C. 84. Huic denique Evaristus A. C. 96. Jta ut secundum Chronologiam ipsorum Pontificiorum, Apostolus Johannes quinque Pontifices Romanos supervixerit Quomodo E. verum esse poterit, Episcopos Romanos cessisse Apostolis in primatu Ecclesiæ, quamdiu hi in vivis erant.

Neque est ut dicunt Adversarij, successisse Apostolum Apostolo, non in Apostolatu, sed in præfectura sive primatu Ecclesiæ. Nam ne quidem in præfectura Ecclesiæ Apostolus Apostolo succedere potuit, quia Bellarminus disertè scribit, in hac non nisi soli Petro successum esse, & quidem non ab Apostolorum quopiam: Sed ab Episcopis Romanis tantùm. Quo pertinet illud, quod idem Bellarminus scribit, l. 2. de Rom. Pont. cap. 12. p. 543. C. Quòd Romanus Episcopus, quia Episcopus Romanus est, sit Petri successor, ex facto Petri ortum habuit. Nam potuisset Petrus nullam sedem particularem sibi unquam eligere, sicut fecit primis quinque annis, & tunc moriente Petro; non Episcopus Romanus, neque Antiochenus successisset, sed is quem Ecclesia sibi elegisset: potuisset quoque semper manere Antiochiæ, & tunc Antiochenus sine dubio successisset:

Quia verò Romæ sedem fixit & tenuit usque ad mortem, factum indè est, ut Romanus Episcopus ei succedat. Præterea contendit idem Bellarminus, Soli Petro, & successoribus ejus Episcopis Romanis dictum fuisse, Pasce oves meas, & dabo tibi claves. Jam verò nullus Apostolorum fuit Episcopus Romanus, mortuo Petro E. nullus etiam Apostolus Petro successit, in Præfectura Ecclesiæ, neque ullus nunquam eorum fuit Caput Ecclesiæ. 3. Si Apostolus vel Johannes vel Jacobus fuit Caput Ecclesiæ: E. Episcopus Romanus non fuit caput : ac per consequens non successit Petro in præfectura. Si hoc, consequetur necessariò nullum Romanorum Pontificum affirmare posse, quòd in præfectura Ecclesiæ successerit Petro, jure hæreditario, ita ut successio non fuerit interrupta. Nam si interrupta est : Successio legitima & hæreditaria non est. 4. Mortuo Johanne vel Jacobo Hierosolymitano, si alter eorum fuisset successor Petri, tum Episcopus Romanus succedere planè non potuisset, quia nó successisset in loco: sed suam monarchicã successionem, non à Petro, sed vel ab Ephesino, vel Hierosolymitano Pontifice accepisset: & sic sedes Petri Romæ non mansisset, sed in Orientem ad urbes translata fuisset. Ergò secundú argumentationem Bellarmini, paulò antè propositam, si Episcopus aliquis voluisset succedere legitimè in primatu, is vel Ephesinus, vel Hierosolymitanus Episcopus fuerit, necesse est: illius videlicet urbis, in qua superstes ultimus Apostolus præsedit. Quo pacto Romam & Romanos Episcopos nullo legitimæ successionis jure potiri, evadit manifestissimum.

Sunt ex Romanensibus, qui quarto loco objiciant, Apostolos communibus consiliis administrasse Ecclesiam universam, ita ut à morte Petri fuerit interregnum usq; ad mortem omnium Apostolorum. Respondeo : prius illud magis esse contra Jesuvitas. Sic enim sequeretur 1. tùm Ecclesiam caruisse certo capite visibili. 2. Apostolos omnes pari potestate & æquali jurisdictione fuisse præditos, & sic Ecclesiæ regimen fuisse Aristocraticum: quod constanter illi per negant, contendentes, Regimen Ecclesiæ semper fuisse Monarchicum. 3. Contrarium evincit divisio Apostolorum, quæ vivo adhuc Petro facta est, ut Apostoli per totum terrarum orbem longissimè à se mutuò dispersi & dissiti non potuerint post mortem Petri, conjunctim Universalis Ecclesiæ administrationem suscipere: sed potius quilibet illas curabat Ecclesias, quas fundaverat, & ad quas per occasionem pervenerat.

Posterior ratio itidem seipsam evertit: Si enim fuit interregnum à morte Petri, usque ad mortem omnium Apostolorum ; fuit illud vel in Episcopatu Romano, vel in præfectura super omnem Ecclesiam. Jn Episcopatu non fuit, quia sic contendentibus Jesuvvitis, jam indè à morte Petri, fuerunt semper sibi ordini minùs interrupto, succedentes Episcopi Romani, usque ad mortem Johannis, sive tempore Trajani. Ergo interregnum in ipsa præfectura fuerit necesse est. Atqui hoc ipsum vel maximè est contra Bellarminum. Nã inde sequeretur necessariò, nullum eorum qui in Episcopatu Romano post mortem Petri, usque ad mortem Johannis, omniumq́; Apostolorum sedebant, fuisse Caput militantis universæ Ecclesiæ, ac proindè neque successorem Petri primatu universæ Ecclesiæ. Concludimns proindè successionem in præfectura & Monarchia super universam Ecclesiam militantem, apud Episcopos Romanos à morte Petri nullam unquam fuisse; neque in hodiernum esse diem. Nam ad successionem probandam in præfectura Ecclesiæ, necesse est, ut singuli residentes in cathedra, possint ostendere singulos prædecessores suos habuisse idem jus, quod ille sibi arrogat & exercet: Quod quidem hoc loco fieri non potest. Nam is Episcopus Románus, qui Cathedram tenus it tùm, cùm ultimus Apostolus moreretur, nõ potuit ostendere, prædecessorem suum proximum habuisse talem potestatèm; siquidem verum est, quod à morte Petri, usque ad mortem reliquorum Apostolorum, fuerit interregnum, quoad potestatem illam monarchicam: & sic non potuit dicere, se post mortem Petri factum esse Caput Ecclesiæ successione hæreditaria à Petro. Ergò interrupta fuit successio: Si interrupta, & nec Linus, nec Clemens, nec Anacletus successerunt Petro in præfectura Ecclesiæ, quia tùm erat interregnum: Ergò multò minus Pius V. Caput Concilij Tridentini, vel quisquam alius potuit dicere id, quod Bellarminus pugnat, se habere potestatem illam Monarchicam, jure hæreditario à Petro, & quòd Christus ac Petrus omnia sua dederint singulis & omnibus Episcopis Romanis.

Cæterùm cùm adversarij nunquàm concedant, Succeßionem fuisse interruptam, utique concedant etiam necesse est, nullum fuisse eo tempore interregnum.

Jesuvvita Bellarminus ex difficultatibus istis se extricaturus, novum quoddam plausibile excogitavit κρησφύγετον: de quo sic fabulatur: lib. 1. de Pont. Rom. cap. 9. pag. 632. C. & D. Summa potestas Ecclesiastica, non solum data est Petro, sed etiam aliis Apostolis: sed Petro data est, ut Ordinario Pastori, cui perpetuò succederetur: aliis verò tanquàm delegatis, quibus non succederetur: Mortuis ergò Apostolis, Apostolica autoritas in solo Petri successore permansit. Nullus enim Episcopus præter Romanum, solicitudinem habuit unquam omnium Ecclesiarum, & solus ipse vocatus est ab omnibus Apostolicus Pontifex, & sedes ejus Apostolica simpliciter &c.

Respondeo

Respondeo 1. Jesuvvitam ἀδολεσχεῖν sive nugari. Nihil enim eorum, quæ dicit, probat. 2. pervertit malitiosè statum Controversiæ, & omittit id, de quo maximè quæritur, nempè de jure hæreditario, & de proximo successore Petri statim post ejus mortem : sed tantùm ait in solo Petri successore permansisse Apostolicam autoritatem, mortuis Apostolis. Ubi neque successorem nominat, neque hæreditariæ succefsionis meminit. Ex quo uno deprehenditur, quàm insidiosè & Sophisticè causam hanc tractet Sophista. Nam si candidè suam sententiam, quam aliàs lib. 2. de Rom. Pont. cap. 12. proponit, tueri voluisset, tùm sic dicere debuisset: Mortuis omnibus Apostolis, Apostolica autoritas jure hæreditario, in solo proximo Petri successore Episcopo Romano permansit. Atqui hoc simpliciter falsum est, uti hactenùs evidenter demonstratum. His ita demonstratis primam hanc Quæstionem sive Controversiam hoc Syllogismo ἀνασκευαστικῶ concludimus.

Quodcunq; jus in hæreditate defuncti, ipso mortis tempore inventum non est: illud etiam in vivis illum non habuisse necesse est.

Atqui jus præfecturæ sive primatus super omnem militantem Ecclesiam, in hæreditate S. Petri relictæ, hoc est, in successoribus proximis, Lino & Clemente & Anacleto Episcopis Romanis non apparuit, neque inventus est.

Ergò jus præfecturæ sive primatus super omnem militantem Ecclesiam, Petrus nunquam habuit: & per Consequens, quod non habuit, ad successorem quempiam transmittere non potuit.

Majoris connexum absolutè verum est, nisi demonstrari possit, aliquem jus suum, quod in vivis habuit, vel alteri cuipiam resignasse, aut donasse, vel illud ipsi sive per vim, sive per jus ablatum, vel saltem personale fuisse, & cum ipso moriente simul extinctum.

Minorem hactenus ita probavimus, ut ipsi Jesuvvitæ dubitent, nùm Linus an Cletus, an Anacletus, an Evaristus, vel alius quispiam primus successerit in Pontificatu, mortuo & Petro & reliquis Apostolis, à Petri morte adhuc superstitibus. Sic ipsi Jesuvvitæ minimè affirmabunt, Jus hoc præfecturæ Petro vel ablatum, vel ab ipso resignatum fuisse, Lino aut Clementi, aut Cleto. Hoc enim non licebat in præjudicium eorum Apostolorum, qui post ipsum superstites erant: Imò nec quidem Apostolorum cuipiam jus hoc donare poterat Petrus: Siquidem Bellarmino teste, Soli Petro dictum fuit, Pasce oves meas. Insuper jus hoc etiam non Personale fuit, nec cum ipso moriente simul extinctum, ipsis rursum contendentibus Jesuvvitis.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: Chapter II. On the Best Form or Mode of Ecclesiastical Government

This whole dispute, which is treated quite prolixly by Bellarmine in book 1 de Pontifice Romano, can most correctly be expedited by the inclusion of two questions: THE PRIOR is: What is the best form of Republic? THE LATTER, Whether ecclesiastical government ought to be monarchical.

Latin:

TOta haec disputatio, quae satis prolixe à Bellarmino lib. 1. de Pontifice Romano pertractatur, duarum Quaestionum complexu rectissime potest expediri: PRIOR est: Quaenam optima sit Resp. Forma? POSTERIOR, An regimen Ecclesiasticum debeat esse Monarchicum.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: Question I. What is the Best Government

Bellarmine, being quite solicitous about the foundations upon which he might build the kingdom of the Roman Antichrist, informs the decision of the prior question in such a way that he pronounces in favor of monarchical government, in book 1 de Pont. chapter 2 and the following two. But the arguments by which he confirms this opinion of his, he seeks from Hebrew writers, Philo especially, from Greek and Latin theologians, from the disputes of philosophers, orators, historians, poets, and finally from various reasons, concerning which later.

We, however, at the very threshold of this dispute, desire candor in the Jesuit, while he, too astutely, with the state of the controversy bent and perverted, takes upon himself to prove something other than that which is in controversy. The question between us and him is not concerning government considered absolutely and in itself, or concerning any government: which one excels the other: which question belongs to the schools of politicians: but concerning government limited to the Church: namely, whether the monarchical government of the Church is the best? The decision of which question cannot or ought not to be defined from profane writers, just as the Church has nothing in common either with the Stoa of Plato or with the Areopagus of the Athenians. We therefore oppose to the Bellarminian dispute, regarding this prior question, two immovable theological foundations.

THE FIRST is: The best government of the Church is not to be judged, except from that form by which CHRIST himself willed it to be ruled and administered. And yet Christ willed a Monarchical government to be most alien to his Church.

Therefore neither can nor ought this to be judged or held as the best government of the Church.

The major premise is most true, even he himself admitting

Bellarmino, book 1, chapter 1, in these words: No one can doubt that our Savior JESUS CHRIST both could and would govern His Church in that manner and way which is the best and most useful of all. I prove the minor premise by two reasons above all.

The former is: that Christ Himself willed that the manner of administering the Republic and the Church be clearly different, so that a Monarchical government can in no way befit the Church: as will be clear a little later, from our second Foundation.

The latter is ἔγγραφος, consisting of clear oracles of Scripture, by which the Savior simply forbade Monarchical government for the Church, such as:

Luke 22:25. The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, but you not so. Where the Savior expressly deals with the Kingdom, which is convertible with simple Monarchy, and removes it from the Church.

2 Tim. 2:4. No one serving as a soldier for Christ entangles himself in secular affairs. Now if a Monarch of the Church were given, who would exercise the use of both swords: such a one would certainly be entangled in secular affairs.

Bellarmino attempts to refute both this saying, however evident it may be, and indeed regarding the former, he makes two exceptions: 1. That Christ by these words only institutes mere ecclesiastical princes, and wishes that they preside over subjects, not in the manner of kings, but in the manner of Fathers and pastors. 2. That lordship is not prohibited to Bishops by Christ, such as can be that of pious kings: but such as is that of kings who are ignorant of GOD, who are Tyrants rather than Kings: which he attempts to prove from the Greek word κατακυριεύειν.

I answer: both exceptions fail through a shameful ignorance of the Elenchus. For 1. the distributed is taken for the undistributed: that is, the mode of the thing for the thing itself: when the text in verse 24 expressly shows that the question had arisen among the disciples, not only about the mode of the thing: but about the thing itself also: For they were arguing, not by what pact or in what manner: but simply, which of them ought to be seen and held as the greatest? 2. The Jesuit openly contradicts the Savior: who wishes lordship over the Church and the Episcopate to be separated, in verse 25. The Jesuit, however, contends that they can be joined in a Bishop. 3. These two are foolishly separated: to preside in the manner of kings: and to preside over subjects in the manner of Fathers and pastors: which in reality is known to be one and the same in the sense of all peoples, by whom Kings and princes are called fathers of the country, and ποιμένες λαῶν. 4. This Jesuitical reasoning overturns itself, and turns all political power into Tyranny: For if that is the sense of the words of Christ, namely that Bishops ought to preside in the manner of fathers and pastors: it will follow from the contrary sense that it is not the duty of political princes to preside in the manner of fathers: but that they exercise power with Tyranny: Since a middle ground between those two cannot be given.

Finally, the latter exception affirms that lordship is granted to Bishops, such as that of pious kings: but the former denies this very thing simply, namely that Bishops ought not to preside in the manner of kings: but only in the manner of Fathers and Pastors. In this way the Disputant entangles himself in a shameful Contradiction. Nor does the Greek word κατακυριεύειν stand in the way of these. For although this word sometimes signifies immoderate Empire: Luke, however, in this place, having omitted the preposition κατά, used the simple verb κυριεύειν and ἐξουσιάζειν: not κατεξουσιάζειν. And yet κυριεύειν and ἐξουσιάζειν are said of those who obtain power and lordship: not those who rule insolently or tyrannically. Thus Mark has the verb ἄρχειν, which signifies just and legitimate rule. Nor does the preposition κατά always argue for something evil or preposterous in compounds. GOD commands man κατακυριεύσαι τῆς γῆς, as the Septuagint rendered it: yet Adam was not constituted a tyrant of the earth, but Lord.

Finally, Christ says those kings of whom He speaks are called εὐεργέτας: Which word does not befit Tyrants, nor is it attributed by subjects. Whence it is evidently gathered what is the genuine mind and meaning of the words of CHRIST, namely, not that which the Jesuit feigns, lest the Apostles covet tyrannical lordship: but lest they dream of any kingdom or monarchy at all.

Bellarmino attempts to elude the Apostolic aphorism, contending that by secular business is understood only the care of providing a living, and not indeed political government.

I reply that the Jesuit is trifling and begging the question. For this very thing is in question, whether by secular business he understands political government: which Bellarmino indeed denies, but without reason. We hold the affirmative for this reason: 1. because the Apostle made mention of secular business with no other purpose than to distinguish between these and the parts of the Episcopal office, inasmuch as he who is to serve God alone, that is, ought to be occupied only in treating sacred things.

Then the Apostolic comparison between a soldier and a bishop renders the sense of the Apostle's words clearer. For he wishes that a soldier should not handle all those things which lie outside of military service, but should be entirely in military work. Therefore he wishes the office of a bishop also to be only to handle those things which are proper to the Evangelical ministry, and to abstain from handling secular things or business.

THE LATTER Foundation, which we oppose to the disputation of Bellarmino, is the distinction of orders, political and ecclesiastical: which two orders so differ from each other that they can in no way fall under one and the same form of government, and indeed the best one. These two orders may be considered either absolutely and simply, according to their constituent causes, both internal and external: or concretively, with respect to the subject or man, upon whom both powers, ecclesiastical and political, ought to fall.

These two governments therefore differ at the outset according to their internal causes, which are two: Matter and Form. By reason of the Matter, Ecclesiastical government is concerned with internal and spiritual goods, primarily regarding the soul of man. Whence the Savior says: John 18:36, My kingdom is not of this world. The matter of political government, however, is concerned with goods of the body and of fortune, and with the preservation of external discipline: according to that passage, Matthew 22:21, Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's.

That bishop noted this distinction, who said to the Emperor: To you GOD has committed the empire: but to us, Christ has committed those things which are of the Church.

Regarding the other internal cause, namely the Form, these two distinctions likewise differ greatly from one another: For the Form of Ecclesiastical government consists in the preaching of the word, the administration of the Sacraments, and the use of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, according to the instruction given by Christ himself to the Apostles:

Matthew 28:19. Go, TEACH all nations: and BAPTIZE them, etc.

Mark 16:15. Go, PREACH the Gospel to every creature.

And verse 20. They went forth and PREACHED everywhere.

2 Corinthians 10:4. The weapons of our warfare are not carnal: but mighty through GOD to the pulling down of strongholds, etc.

The form of political government consists of civil laws and the use of the external sword.

Romans 13:4. The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain: for he is the minister of GOD, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that does evil.

The use of this external or material sword is strictly forbidden to Ecclesiastical government, in the person of Peter himself, Matthew 26:52. Put up again your sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.

Next, these two governments differ according to external causes, which are likewise two: namely, the efficient and the final.

By reason of the efficient cause, Ecclesiastical government is immediately from Christ, according to that: John 20. 21. As the Father hath sent me, even so send I you. Political government is indeed also from GOD: For there is no magistrate but of GOD: But not immediately: rather mediately by the law of nations, according to that Luke 22. 25. The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship. Which reason alone proves that, if a Monarchical kingdom belongs to the Pope, then it belongs to him not by divine law, but by human: namely, because it is proper to the law of nations, and therefore human.

According to the final cause, Ecclesiastical government looks to the end, spiritual righteousness, peace of conscience with GOD: and the eternal salvation of souls: as the Apostle teaches, Rom. 1. 16. The gospel is the power of GOD UNTO SALVATION to every one that believeth. And Rom. 14. 17. The kingdom of GOD is righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. But Political government looks to the end, civil righteousness, temporal peace, and the tranquility of this life: that under the rule of the kings of this age, we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty, 1. Timothy 2. 2.

But if these two governments are considered concretely or by reason of the subject, it is manifest that both cannot fall upon one and the same man at the same time: the possibility of law being understood: as the Scripture teaches.

Luke 22. 25. The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors: But ye shall not be so.

1. Pet. 5. 3. Peter himself prohibits dominion and the use of political power to Bishops in general: Not as being lords, he says, over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.

We conclude therefore from what has already been said, that the best government of the Church is not to be judged from the forms of Political Kingdoms: but partly from the very institution, or rather the first foundation of the Church of the New Testament, which has Christ himself as its author: and partly from the nature of the Church itself, as it is described from its causes. When therefore the Jesuit argues from a Political type of government to an Ecclesiastical one, he commits a μεταβασιν εις ἀλλο γένος.

Latin:

BEllarminus de fundamentis, quibus regnum Antichristi Romani superstruat, admodum sollicitus, Decisionem prioris quastionis ita informat, ut pro Regimine Monarchico pronunciet, lib. 1. de Pont. cap. 2. & sequentibus duobus. Argumenta vero quibus hanc suam confirmet sententiam, petit ex Scriptoribus Hebraeis, Philone cumprimis, ex Graecis, & Latinis Theologis, ex disputationibus Philosophorum, Oratorum, Historicorum, Poetarum, & tandem ex rationibus varijs, de quibus postea.

Nos autem in limine statim disputationis hujus candorem in Jesuvvita desideramus, dum astute nimis, inflexa & perverse Controversiae statu, aliud sibi probandum sumit, quam de quo controvertitur. Quaestio est inter nos & ipsum, non de Regimine absolute & in se considerato, vel de quolibet regimine: Quodnam altero praestet: Quae quaestio ad Politicorum Scholas pertinet: Sed de Regimine limitato ad Ecclesiam: An videlicet Regimen Ecclesiae Monarchicum sit optimum? Cujus Quaestionis decisio ex Scriptoribus prophanis, tam non potest aut debet definiri, quam non Ecclesia quicquam vel cum Stoa Platonis, vel cum Areopago Atheniensium habet commune. Opponimus proinde Disputationi Bellarminianae, quoad priorem hanc Quaestionem duo immota fundamenta Theologica.

PRIUS est: De Optimo Regimine Ecclesiae non est judicandum, nisi ex ea forma qua CHRISTVS ipse eam regi & administrari voluit. Atqui Christus regimen Monarchicum ac Ecclesia sua voluit esse alienissimum.

Ergo neque hoc, pro optimo Ecclesiae regimine judicari aut haberi potest vel debet.

Major est verissima, ipso etiam fatente

Bellarmino, lib. 1. cap. 1. his verbis Nemini dubium esse potest, quin & potuerit & voluerit Salvator noster JESUS CHRISTUS, Ecclesiam suam ea ratione & modo gubernare, qui sit omnium optimus & utilissimus. Minorem probo duabus potissimùm rationibus.

Prior est: quòd Christus ipse disparem plane esse voluit Reipublicæ, & Ecclesiæ administrandæ rationem, ita ut Regimen Monarchicum Ecclesiæ nullo modo possit competere: quemadmodum paulò post patebit, ex Fundamento nostro secundo.

Posterior est ἔγγραφος, perspicuis constans Scripturæ oraculis, quibus Servator Regimen Monarchicum Ecclesiæ simpliciter interdixit, ut:

Luc. 22. 25. Reges gentium dominantur, Vos autem non fic. Ubi de Regno, quod cum Monarchia simplici convertitur, ex professo agit Servator, illudque ab Ecclesia removet.

2. Tim. 2, 4. Nemo Christo militans implicat se negotiis secularibus. Jam si daretur Monarcha Ecclesiæ, qui utriusque gladij usum exerceret: utiq; talis implicaretur negotijs secularibus.

Utrumque hoc dictum, quantumvis evidens, elidere conatur Bellarminus, & quidem quoad prius illud, excipit duo: 1. Christum his verbis solum instituere meros principes Ecclesiasticos, ac velle, ut illi præsint subditis, non more regum, sed more Patrum & pastorum. 2. Non prohiberi à Christo Dominatum Episcopis, qualis esse potest regum piorum: sed qualis est regum, ignorantium DEUM, qui Tyranni potiùs sint, quàm Reges: id quod ex verbo Græco κατακυριεύειν evincere conatur.

Respondeo: fallit exceptio utraque turpi ignoratione Elenchi. Nam 1. distributum sumitur, pro non distributo: hoc est, modus rei, pro reipsa: cum textus versu 24. disertè ostendat, quæstionem ortam fuisse inter discipulos, non de modo rei tantùm: sed de reipsa quoque: Pugnabant enim, non quo pacto, aut quo modo: sed simpliciter, quis ipsorum maximus videri & haberi debeat? 2. Jesuvvita apertè contradicit Servatori: qui dominatum in Ecclesiam & Episcopatum vult esse separata, versu 25. Jesuvvita autem contendit, ea in Episcopo posse esse conjuncta. 3. Stolidè separantur hæc duo: More regum præesse: & more Patrum ac pastorum præesse subditis: quæ reipsa unum atque idem esse sensu omnium populorum constat, à quibus Reges & principes appellantur partes patriæ, & ποιμένες λαῶν. 4. Seipsam evertit hæc ratio Jesuvvitica, & omnem potestatem politicam verit in Tyrannidem: Si enim is sesus est verborum Christi, quòd nimirùm Episcopi more patrum & pastorum præesse debeant: sequetur ex sensu contrario, politicorum principum munus non esse, ut more patrum præsint: sed potestatem exerceant cum Tyrannide: Siquidem medium inter duo ista dari non potest.

Tandem posterior exceptio affirmat Episcopis concessum esse dominatum, qualis est regum piorum: Prior vero hoc ipsum negat simpliciter, quòd nimirum Episcopos non praeesse debeant more regum: sed tantùm more Patrum ac Pastorum. Quo pacto Disputator seipsum turpi Contradictione implicat. Neque his obstat verbum Graecum κατακυριεύειν. Etsi enim hoc verbum interdum significat Imperium immoderatum: Lucas tamen hoc loco omissa praepositione κ' usus est verbo simplici κυριεύειν & ἐξουσιάζειν: non κατεξουσιάζειν. Atqui κυριεύειν & ἐξουσιάζειν de ijs dicuntur, qui potestatem & dominationem obtinent: non qui infolenter aut tyrannicè imperant. Sic Marcus habet verbum ἄρχειν, quod justum ac legitimum imperium significat. Neque praepositio x' semper in compositis malum aut praeposterum aliquid arguit. DEUS hominem jubet κατακυριεύσαι τῆς γῆς, uti reddiderunt Septuaginta: non tamen Adamus tyrannus terrae, sed Dominus constitutus est.

Tandem Christus eos Reges, de quibus loquitur, ait vocari εὐεργέτας: Quae vox Tyrannis non competit, neque à subditis tribuitur. Undè evidenter colligitur, quae sit genuina mens & sententia verborum CHRISTI, nempè, non eùm, quem Jesuvvita fingit, ne Apostoli tyrannicum dominatum ambiant: sed ne omninò regnum aliquod aut monarchiam somnient.

Aphorisnum Apostolicum eludere conatur Bellarminus, contendens per Negotia secularia intelligi tantùm curam parandi victum, non verò Regimen politicum.

Respondeo Jesuvvitam nugari & petere principium. Hoc ipsum enim quaeritur, An per negotia secularia intelligat Regimen Politicum: id quod negat quidem Bellarminus: sed sine ratione. Nos affirmativam tenemus ideò, 1. quia non alio consilio Apostolus negotiorum secularium fecit mentionem, quàm ut inter haec, & inter partes muneris Episcopalis distinguat, quippè quod soli DEO militare, hoc est, in solis rebus sacris tractandis occupatum esse debeat.

Deinde collatio Apostolica inter militem & Episcopum, sensum verborum Apostoli reddit clariorem. Vult enim ut miles ea omnia, quae extra militiam versantur, non tractet, sed in opere militari totus sit. Ergò Episcopi etiam munus vult esse, tantùm tractare ea, quae ministerij Evangelici sunt propria, & abstinere à rebus sive negotijs tractandis secularibus.

POSTERIUS Fundamentum, quod Disputationi Bellarmini opponimus, est Distinctio ordinum, Politici & Ecclesiastici: Qui duo ordines ita à se mutuo discrepant, ut sub unam eandemque Regiminis formam, & quidem optimam, cadere nullo modo possint. Possunt autem duo isti ordines considerari vel absolute atque simpliciter, secundum causas constituentes, tum internas, tum externas: Vel Concretive, respectu subjecti sive hominis, in quem Utraque Potestas, Ecclesiastica & politica cadere debeat.

Discrepant ergo initio duo haec regimina, secundum causas internas, quae duae sunt: Materia & Forma. Ratione Materiae, Regimen Ecclesiasticum versatur circa Bona interna & Spiritualia, animam hominis potissimum concernentia. Unde Servator inquit: Joh. 18. 36. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Materia autem Regiminis politici, versatur circa Bona Corporis & Fortunae, & circa conservationem externae disciplinae: secundum illud Matth. 22. 21. Date Cæsari, quæ sunt Cæsaris.

Distinctionem hanc attendit Episcopus ille, qui ad Imperatorem dicebat: Tibi DEUS imperium: nobis autem ea, quae sunt Ecclesiae, Christus commisit.

Quoad alteram causam internam, Formam nimirum, plurimum itidem a se mutuo duo haec discrimina discrepant: Nam Forma Ecclesiastici Regiminis consistit in praedicatione verbi, dispensatione Sacramentorum, & usu clavium regni cœlorum, secundum instructionem ab ipso Christo datam Apostolis:

Matth. 28. 19. Euntes DOCETE omnes gentes: & BAPTIZATE eos &c.

Marc. 16. 15. Ite, PRAEDICATE Evangelium omni Creaturae.

Et vers. 20. Illi profecti PRAEDICAVERUNT ubique.

2. Cor. 10. 4. Arma militiae nostrae non sunt carnalia: sed potentia DEO, ad destructionem munitionum &c.

Forma regiminis Politici, constat legibus civilibus, & usu externi gladij.

Rom. 13. 4. Magistratus non sine causa gladium gestat: DEI enim minister est vindex in poenam ei, qui malum egerit.

Usus gladij hujus externi sive materialis, Regimini Ecclesiastico, in persona ipsius Petri prorsus est interdictus, Matth. 26. 52. Converte gladium in locum suum: Qui enim gladium sumit, gladio peribit.

Deinde discrepant duo haec regimina secundum causas externas, quae itidem duae sunt: efficiens nimirum & Finalis.

Ratione Causae efficientis, Regimen Ecclesiasticum immediate est a Christo secundum illud: Joh. 20. 21. Sicut misit me Pater: ita & ego etiam mitto vos. Regimen Politicum est quidem etiam a DEO: Non enim est magistratus nisi a DEO: Verum non immediate: sed mediate demum jure gentium, secundum illud Luc. 22. 25. Reges Gentium dominantur. Quae vel sola ratio evincit, si regnum Monarchicum competat Pontifici, tum illud ipsi competere non jure divino, sed humano: eo nimirum, quod est Juris gentium proprium, ac proinde humanum.

Secundum Causam Finalem, Regimen Ecclesiasticum finem spectat, Justitiam spiritualem, Pacem Conscientiæ cum DEO: & æternam animarum salutem: sic docente Apostolo, Rom. 1. 16. Evangelium est potentia DEI, AD SALVTEM omni credenti. Et Rom. 14. 17. Regnum DEI est justitia, & pax, & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto. Regimen verò Politicum finem spectat Justitiam civilem, Pacem temporalem, & tranquillitatem hujus vitæ: ut sub regum hujus seculi imperio, tranquillam & quietam vitam agamus, in omni modestia & pietate, 1. Timoth. 2. 2.

Quod si duo hæc regimina Concretivè sive ratione Subjecti considerentur, manifestum est, in unum eundemque hominem utrumque simul non posse cadere: possibilitate juris intellecta: sic docente Scripturâ.

Luc. 22. 25. Reges gentium dominantur, & qui in potestate sunt, benefici appellantur: Vos autem non sic.

1. Pet. 5. 3. Petrus ipse dominatum & usum potestatis politicæ Episcopis in universum prohibet: Non dominantes, inquiens, in clero, sed forma facti gregis.

Concludimus proindè ex jam dictis, de optimo Regimine Ecclesiæ, non esse judicandum ex formis Regnorum Politicorum: sed partim ex ipsa institutione, vel potiùs primâ fundatione Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti, quæ Christum ipsum autorem habet: partim verò ex naturâ ipsius Ecclesiæ, prout ea ex causis suis est descripta. Quando proindè Jesuvvita à Politico Regiminis genere ad Ecclesiasticum argumentatur, committit μεταβασιν εις ἀλλο γένος.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: Question II. Whether Ecclesiastical government ought to be Monarchical

Question II. Whether Ecclesiastical government ought to be Monarchical.

The sense of this question is not this: Whether the Church has a Universal Head, and one Monarchical κατ' ἐξο- χην, namely CHRIST the Savior? which is confessed on both sides, as was demonstrated above: But this is asked: Whether Christ, about to ascend into Heaven, willed and appointed either the Apostle Peter, or some other, as universal Bishop of the whole Church, who should act as his deputy here on earth: and upon whose nod all members of the Catholic Church, dispersed here and there throughout the whole world, ought to depend: and consequently whether he founded a Monarchical government of the Church? The Jesuit faction maintains the affirmative: We concede entirely to the negative: relying on these reasons:

1. Christ himself expressly prohibited such a Monarchy: as was shown in the immediately preceding Question.

Christ is nowhere read to have appointed any one of his disciples, or other Bishops, as Monarch and Head of the whole Church. For as regards that passage in Matthew 16:18, 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church': the stupendous vanity of the Papal collection, which is wont to be built up from there, has just now been demonstrated to the eye above.

Christ granted equal power to all the Apostles: since he chose them all equally and immediately, before his ascension, to the Apostleship: according to that passage, Luke 6:13, 'He called his disciples, and chose twelve from them, whom he also named Apostles.'

He sent out all twelve Apostles together and equally to preach the Gospel and to perform the office of the Apostleship: as the Scripture testifies: Matthew 28:19, 'Going, teach all nations, baptizing them, etc.' John 20:21, 'AS the Father sent me, SO I also send you.' Luke 9:1, 'Having called together the twelve Apostles, he gave them power over all demons, that they might cure diseases, and sent them to preach the kingdom of GOD.'

He entrusted the power of the keys equally to all twelve Apostles: Matthew 18:18 and John 20:23.

None of the Apostles ever arrogated to himself any preeminence, but they governed the Church in equal form, manner, and power with which they had been instructed by Christ: so that Paul expressly testifies that Peter is by no means greater than he, writing thus, Galatians 2:6, 7, 9: 'From those who seemed to be something, nothing was conferred upon me: But conversely, when they had seen that the Gospel of the uncircumcision was entrusted to me, just as that of the circumcision to Peter, and when they had recognized the grace which was given to me, James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship.' Now among those for whom there is a fellowship of government, equality prevails among them, and consequently among those very ones, every rationale of Monarchs and Subjects expires.

All the Apostles equally designated Bishops as their successors: as Paul did Titus for the Cretans: Timothy for the Ephesians: The remaining Apostles appointed presbyters and Bishops town by town, Acts 14:22. Thus Paul writes that he left Titus in the island of Crete for this reason, that he might appoint presbyters town by town. Thus by common counsel they chose Deacons, Acts 6:3. Thus by common counsel they made laws concerning blood and things strangled: Acts 15:20. Thus by common counsel they decreed that we cannot be justified by the works of the law: but by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as also the Fathers, who could not bear the yoke of the law. Acts 15:11.

Christ himself willed that the final and supreme judgment concerning controversies of faith (according to the Jesuit hypothesis) should be, not in the power of Peter alone or any other Apostle, but in the power of the Church: according to that passage in Matthew 18:17, 'Tell it to the Church: If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a Publican.'

Christ appointed no general Monarch: but gave some as Apostles, others as Pastors, others as Teachers, etc. Ephesians 4:11. Thus Paul, describing the entire hierarchy of the Church, makes no mention at all of any Monarch: but, he says, 'GOD has placed some in the Church: first Apostles, secondly Prophets, thirdly Teachers: then mighty works, then gifts of healings, kinds of tongues, interpretations of speeches,' 1 Corinthians 12:28.

The prophetic Scripture, Daniel 7:9, predicts the fourth Monarchy, namely the Roman, which will endure until the coming of the Son of GOD. Therefore, either the Roman Pontiff is not the Monarch of the whole universal Church, and indeed in secular matters as well as in ecclesiastical: or there will be two Monarchs: which implies a contradiction or an opposite in the adjective, and fights expressly against the prophecies of the Prophets. Now since the same prophecies predict that that King, who was prefigured under the person of Antiochus, Daniel 11:36, that is, the Antichrist, would affect a universal Monarchy, and as Paul has it, would exalt himself above everything that is called God, 2 Thessalonians 2:3. And indeed, since the Roman Pontiff has long since manfully attempted all these things, and attempts them today, what else shall we suspect than that he is that great Antichrist, designated by those prophecies? And consequently, that his affected Monarchy is not from GOD, but from the Devil.

Two species of Monarchy are commonly counted by politicians: Tyranny and Kingdom. Christ instituted neither: Not Tyranny, because he wills that he who presides over the Church should not flay, but feed the sheep, and should contribute everything to the utility and increase of the Church. Not Kingdom: Because 'The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship, but you not so.' Luke 22:12. The Apostle, explaining all those things which pertain to the true Unity of the Church, nowhere says, 'There is one Monarch, or King, or prince of the Church': But he has it thus, 'Be solicitous to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, One Body, and One Spirit, as you were called in one hope of your calling, One Lord, One faith, One baptism,' Ephesians 4:3 and following. And it is too diluted, what the Jesuit writes, that the Roman Pope is understood in these words: 'One Body.' For he either understands that mystical Body, whose head is Christ, Ephesians 1:22, or he takes Body absolutely, without relation to a head. But in the former sense, with the Apostle so defining it, not any one man: but the whole fullness of the Church, that is, all its members, constitute that mystical Body. But neither does that latter absolute sense suit the Pontiff: for thus he could no longer be the Head of the Church: unless perhaps by an unheard-of absurdity the Body is the same as the Head: and the head the same as the body.

Christ himself, whom even the Romanists themselves acknowledge as the primary Head of the Church, at the time of his visible conversation here on earth, neither was, nor wished to be, a Monarch of the Church, such as the Romanists indeed pretend their Pontiff to be: as John 18:36, 'My kingdom is not of this world.'

Luke 17:20. The kingdom of GOD does not come with observation: that is, with visible form and magnificence.

Matthew 20:28. The Son of man did not come to be served, but to serve.

Luke 22:27. I am in the midst of you as one who serves. Hence he paid the tribute to Caesar for himself and Peter, Matthew 17:27; hence he had nowhere to lay his head, Matthew 8:20, Luke 9:58.

Although the Roman Pontiff may also proclaim this humility about himself in words, while he calls himself the servant of the servants: he nevertheless betrays mere hypocrisy and peddles mere smoke: as one who meanwhile calls himself the Lord of Lords, and claims for himself the supreme and absolute power of both swords: a thing which it is nowhere read that Christ did. For although in John 13:13 he says to the disciples: You call me Master and Lord, and you do rightly, for so I am: yet it is never read that he arrogated to himself any Mastership or Dominion in spiritual and divine matters at least, but certainly not in temporal or worldly ones: so much so that in Luke 12:13, when asked for the division of an inheritance between two brothers, he warded off this political task from himself, as being alien to his office, saying, Man, who made me a judge or divider between you?

Whence it happened that the Apostles also wished political administration to be so alien to them that they did not even wish to be occupied with distributing public alms, Acts 6:2.

Bellarmino objects that by the example of Christ, it is only implied that Pontiffs and Princes of the Church should not be so occupied with minute and base duties that they are forced to omit greater ones. Book 5, On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 10.
