I reply that the Jesuit lies. For Christ in Luke 12 did not distinguish between actions of one and the same kind in such a way that he did not want minute and base things to be handled by Pontiffs and Bishops: but he denies to them in general every secular principate whatsoever: a fact which is evident even from this, that he accurately distinguishes between one kind of business and another, namely political and ecclesiastical, and indicates that they are disparate subjects.

He further objects that the Apostles did not abstain from political matters to such an extent that they were not solicitous about collecting and bringing alms from here and there, Acts 11:29, Galatians 2:10.

I reply 1. that this argument proceeds from a part, and therefore the consequence is clearly weak.

For there is no strength in this connection: The Apostles took care of alms. Therefore they exercised temporal jurisdiction. 2. Taking care of alms is an office, properly speaking, not political, but ecclesiastical. Hence, therefore, the consequence does not hold again for the political.

Finally, we can distinguish between political businesses, some of which are ecclesiastical political, namely those pertaining to the polity of the Church: while others are civil political, from the handling of which the Evangelical history abundantly testifies that the Apostles simply abstained.

14. Finally, the truth of our opinion is evident from the practice of the Orthodox Church of all times: Where ecclesiastical power in judging dogmas and deciding Theological Controversies, as well as the government of the Church, was not in the hands of one, but in the hands of many gathered Bishops: as

Paul of Samosata was proscribed by the entire Church which is under Heaven, Niceph. bk. 6, ch. 28.

Novatus was refuted throughout the whole world and removed from the fellowship of the priests of God, Cypr. bk. 3, epist. 13.

The four Ecumenical Councils testify to the same: where the definitive sentence was not in the power of one Pontiff, but in the power of all the Bishops.

Thus, in the electing of Bishops, not even the votes of the people were neglected, as is evident from Cyprian, bk. 3, Epist. 9 and 14, and from the Decree of Gelasius I, Innocent I, Leo IV, etc., concerning which see the Canon Law: dist. 63.

Moreover, two questions most worthy of explanation are raised in this place: The first is, whether by human law a primacy over the Universal Church might be permitted to any one person? And indeed, Philip at the Schmalkaldic assembly does not seem to have altogether abhorred the affirmative, although under this condition: if the Gospel is admitted and true and saving doctrine is presupposed. For his words sound thus: Concerning the Pontiff, I decide that if he were to admit the Gospel, for the sake of peace and the common tranquility of Christians who are now under him and will be under him in the future, the superiority over the Bishops, which he otherwise has, could be permitted to him by us also by human law.

But, the gravity of the matter in question having been weighed more carefully, just as the footsteps of both blessed Luther and other most illustrious theologians, we descend into the simple negative: and this for the causes and reasons which are assigned by them, which are by far the most evident.

The first is: Because such a monarchy or primacy over the Universal Church of Christ is simply repugnant to the sacred Scriptures, and consequently to divine law, as was demonstrated above quite prolixly from Luke ch. 22, 1 Peter 5, and other places. Now, however, human law, as being inferior, can or ought to derogate nothing from divine law, as being superior. Therefore, such a primacy can neither be granted nor ought to be granted by human law.

II. Reason: Such a primacy redounds not a little to the insult of God himself. For if that form of government which God himself instituted through his Son is thus neglected, another, and in our judgment a much better one, would be chosen. Whereby the wisdom and power of God are called into doubt. The former, because he did not establish the ecclesiastical order wisely enough, while he did not set some monarch over the Church. The latter, because God cannot rule and defend his Church through the orders instituted by himself, without a monarchy being added as if for a supplement.

Latin:

Quæstio II. An Regimen Ecclesiasticum debeat esse Monarchicum.

QUæstionis hujus sensus non est iste: An Ecclesia habeat Caput Vniversale, & κατ' ἐξοχην Monarchicum, CHRISTVM nimirùm Servatorem? id quod utrinque inconfesso est, uti supra demonstratum: Sed hoc quæritur: An Christus in Cœlum conscensurus, vel Petrum Apostolum, vel alium aliquem voluerit & constituerit Episcopum universalem totius Ecclesiæ, qui vices suas hisce in terris agat: & à cujus nutu omnia Catholicæ Ecclesiæ membra per totum terrarum orbem hinc inde dispersa, pendere debeant: & per consequens Monarchicum Ecclesiæ regimen fundaverit? Factio Jesuvvitica affirmantem tuetur: Nos in negantem omninò concedimus: his freti rationibus:

1. Christus ipse talem Monarchiam expressè prohibuit: uti Quæstione præcedente proximâ ostensum.

2. Christus nuspiam legitur, Unum quempiam ex suis discipulis, vel aliis Episcopis, Monarcham & Caput totius Ecclesiæ constituisse. Nam quoad illud Matth. 16, 18. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam : jam modò suprà stupenda vanitas Collectionis Pontificiæ, quæ indè extrui solet, ad oculum demonstrata fuit.

3. Christus æqualem potestatem omnibus Apostolis concessit: dùm omnes pariter & immediatè, antè ascensionem, ad Apostolatum elegit: secundum illud, Luc. 6, 13. Vocavit discipulos suos, & elegit duodecim ex ipsis, quos & Apostolos nominavit.

4. Omnes duodecim Apostolos unà & pariter emisit ad prædicandum Evangelium, & Apostolatus munus peragendum : sic testante Scriptura : Matth. 28, 19. Euntes docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos &c. Joh. 20, 21. SICVT misit me Pater, ITA & ego mitto vos. Luc. 9, 1. Convocatis duodecim Apostolis, dedit illis potestatem super omnia dæmonia, ut languores curarent, & misit eos prædicare regnum DEI.

5. Omnibus duodecim Apostolis potestatem clavium ex æquo commendavit : Matthæi 18, 18. & Joh. 20, 23.

6. Apostolorum nullus sibi præminentiam aliquam, unquàm arrogavit, sed pari formâ, modo, atque Potestate, quâ à Christo instructi erant, Ecclesiam gubernarunt : ita ut Paulus disertè testetur, Petrum se majorem minimè esse, sic scribens, Gal. 2, 6. 7. 9. Ab iis qui videbantur esse aliquid, nihil in me collatum : Sed vice versa, cùm vidissent, quòd creditum mihi sit Evangelium præputii, ficuti Petro circumcisionis, & cum cognovissent gratiam, quæ mihi data est, Jacobus, Cephas, & Johannes, qui videbantur columnæ esse, dextras dederunt mihi, & Barnabæ societatis. Jam inter quos gubernationis est societas, inter eosdem æqualitas militat, & per Consequens inter illos ipsos, Monarchæ & Subditorum ratio omnis expirat.

7. Apostoli pariter omnes designarunt Episcopos sibi successores : ut Paulus Titum Cretensibus : Timotheum Ephesiis: Reliqui Apostoli oppidatim constituerunt presbyteros & Episcopos, Actor. 14, 22. Sic Paulus scribit, se ideò Titum reliquisse in insula Creta, ut oppidatim constituat presbyteros. Sic communi consilio elegerunt Diaconos, Actor. 6, 3. Sic communi consilio tulerunt leges de sanguine & suffocato: Actor. 15, 20. Sic communi consilio decreverunt, nos non posse justificari per opera legis: sed gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi, quemadmodum & Patres, qui legis jugum portare non potuerunt. Actor. 15, 11.

8. Christus ipse ultimum & summum judicium de Controversiis fidei (secundum hypothesin Jesuiticam) voluit esse, non penes solum Petrum vel alium quempiam Apostolum, sed penes Ecclesiam : secundum illud Matth. 18, 17. Dic Ecclesiæ: Si Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus.

9. Christus nullum constituit generalem Monarcham: sed alios dedit Apostolos, alios Pastores, alios Doctores, &c. Ephes. 4, 11. Sic Paulus universam Ecclesiæ hierarchiam describens, nullam prorsus ullius Monarchæ facit mentionem: sed quosdam, inquit, posuit DEUS in Ecclesia primò Apostolos: deinde Prophetas, tertiò Doctores: tùm virtutes, exindè gratias curationum, genera linguarum, interpretationes sermonum, 1. Cor. 12, 28.

10. Scriptura prophetica Daniel. 7, 9. prædicit quartam Monarchiam, Romanam scilicet, duraturam ad adventum usque Filij DEI. Ergò aut Romanus Pontifex non est Monarcha totius universalis Ecclesiæ, & quidem tàm in secularibus, quàm in Ecclesiasticis: aut duo erunt Monarchæ: id quod contradictionem sive oppositum in adjecto implicat, & cum vaticiniis Prophetarum disertè pugnat. Jam cùm eadem vaticinia prædicant, Regem illum, qui sub persona Antiochi, Daniel. 11, 36. præfiguratus fuit, hoc est, Antichristum affectaturum universalem Monarchiam, & ut Paulus habet elevaturum se super omne quod dicitur Deus, 2. Thess. 2, 3. Et verò hæc omnia Romanus Pontifex jampridem masculè tentaverit, hodieq; tentet, quid aliud suspicabimur, quam ipsum esse magnum illum Antichristum, per vaticinia illa designatum? ac proindè affectatam ipsius Monarchiam, non esse à DEO, sed à Diabolo.

11. Duæ à politicis vulgò numerantur Monarchiæ species: Tyrannis & Regnum. Neutram instituit Christus: Non Tyrannidem, quia vult, ut qui præest Ecclesię, non deglubat, sed pascat oves, & ad utilitatem ac incrementum Ecclesiæ omnia conferat. Non Regnum: Quia Reges gentium dominantur, vos autem non sic. Luc. 22, 12. D. Apostolus enarrans omnia ea, quæ ad veram Ecclesiæ Unitatem pertinent, nuspiam dicit, Unus est Monarcha, vel Rex, vel princeps Ecclesiæ: Sed sic habet, Solliciti sitis servare unitatem Spiritus, in vinculo pacis, Unum Corpus, & Unus Spiritus, sicut vocati estis in una spe vocationis vestræ, Unus Dominus, Vna fides, Vnum baptisma, Ephes. 4, 3. & seqq. Et nimis dilutum est, quod Jesuuvita scribit, Papam Romanum intelligi in his verbis: Vnum Corpus. Nam aut Corpus intelligit illud mysticum, cujus caput est Christus, Ephes. 1, 22. aut Corpus accipit absolutè, absq; relatione ad caput. Atqui priore sensu, sic definiente Apostolo, non unus aliquis homo: sed plenitudo tota Ecclesiæ, hoc est, omnia ejus membra, constituunt Corpus illud mysticum. Sed neq; posterior ille absolutus sensus competit Pontifici: Sic enim ille non Caput ampliùs esse posset Ecclesiæ: nisi fortè per inauditam absurditatem Corpus idem sit quod Caput: & caput idem quod corpus.

12. Christus ipse, quem primarium Ecclesiæ Caput vel ipsi agnoscunt Romanenses, tempore visibilis suæ in terris hisce conversationis, neque fuit, neque esse voluit Monarcha Ecclesiæ, qualem quidem Romanenses suum fingunt esse Pontificem: ut Joh. 18, 36. Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo.

Luc. 17, 20. Regnum DEI non venit cum observatione: visibili scilicet forma & magnificentia.

Matth. 20, 28. Filius hominis non venit ministrari, sed ministrare.

Luc. 21, 27. Ego sum in medio vestri, sicut qui ministrat. Hinc tributum persolvit Cæsari pro se & Petro, Matth. 17, 17. hinc non habuit, ubi reclinaret caput suum, Matth. 8, 20. Luc. 9, 58.

Quam humilitatem licèt Pontifex Romanus verbis quoque de se prædicet, dùm seipsum nominat servum servorum: meram tamen hypocrisin prodit, merosque fumos venditat: ut qui interim Dominum Dominantium se nominat, & summam atque absolutam utriusque gladii potestatem sibi vendicat: id quod Christum fecisse nuspiam legitur. Etsi enim Joh. 13, 13. ad discipulos inquit: Vos vocatu me Magistrum & Dominum, & recte facitis, Sum etenim: tamen in spiritualibus saltem & divinis, non verò in temporalibus aut mundanis ullum unquàm sibi Magisterium aut Dominium arrogasse legitur: adeò ut Luc. 12, 13. requisitus ad divisionem hæreditatis inter duos fratres, politicum hoc opus, quippè à munere suo alienum, à sese amoliretur, Homo, inquiens, quis me constituit judicem, aut divisorem inter vos?

Undè factum, ut Apostoli quoque politicam administrationem ita à se voluerint esse alienam, ut ne quidem dispensandis eleemosynis publicis vacare vellent, Actor. 6, 2.

Excipit Bellarminus, exemplo Christi, illud tantùm innui: ut Pontifices & Principes Ecclesiæ, minutis ac vilibus officiis, non ita occupentur, ut omittere cogantur majora. lib. 5. de Pont. Rom. c. 10.

Respondeo mentiri Jesuvvitam. Neque enim Christus Luc. 12. ita inter unius ejusdemq́; generis actiones distinxit, ut minuta duntaxat & vilia à Pontificibus & Episcopis tractari noluerit: Sed in genere omnem omninò secularem principatum ipsis neget: id quod vel indè patet, quod inter genus & genus negotiorum, Politicum scilicet & Ecclesiasticum accuratè distinguit, eaque subjectis disparata esse indicat.

Excipit porrò, Apostolos non ita à Politicis rebus abstinuisse, quin solliciti essent de colligenda, & hincindè deferenda Eleemosyna, Actor. 11, 29. Gal. 2, 10.

Respondeo 1. argumentum hoc ex parte procedere, ac proindè consequentiam planè elumbem esse.

Nullus enim nervus inest connexo huic: Apostoli curarunt Eleemosynas. E. Jurisdictionem temporalem exercuerunt. 2. Curare Eleemosynas officium est, propriè loquendo non politicum, sed Ecclesiasticum. Hinc ergò rursum ad politicum non valet consequentia.

Tandem distinguere possumus inter negotia politica, quorum alia sunt politica Ecclesiastica, nempè ad Ecclesiæ politiam pertinentia: alia verò sunt civilia politica, à quibus tractandis Apostolos simpliciter abstinuisse, historia Evangelica abundè testatur.

14. Tandem patet nostræ sententiæ veritas, ex praxi Ecclesiæ Orthodoxæ omnium temporum: Ubi potestas Ecclesiastica in dijudicandis dogmatibus, & decidendis Controversiis Theologicis, ut & gubernatio Ecclesiæ nó fuit penes unum, sed penes plures Episcopos congregatos: ut

Paulus Samosatenus, ab universa, quæ sub Cælo est, Ecclesia proscriptus est, Niceph. l. 6. cap. 28.

Novatus refutatus per totum orbem, & à Sacerdotum DEI consortio remotus fuit, Cypr. lib. 3. epist. 13.

Idem testantur quatuor Concilia Oecumenica: Ubi sententia definitiva non fuit penes Unum Pontificem: sed penes omnes Episcopos.

Sic in eligendis Episcopis, ne plebis quidem suffragia fuerunt neglecta: uti patet ex Cypriano lib. 3. Epist. 9. & 14. ex Decreto Gelasii I. Innocentii I. Leonis IIII. &c. de quibus videatur Jus Canonicum: dist. 63.

Cæterùm duæ hoc loco moventur Quæstiones explicatu dignissimæ: Prior est: Annon jure humano, primatus Universalis Ecclesiæ, possit Vnalicui permitti? Et sanè Philippus in conventu Schmalcaldico non omninò ab affirmativa abhorruisse videtur, licèt sub hac conditione, si Evangelium admittatur, & vera salutarisque doctrina præsupponatur. Sic enim sonant illius verba: De Pontifice statuo, si Evangelium admitteret, posse ei, propter pacem & communem tranquillitatem Christianorum, qui jam sub ipso sunt, & in posterum sub ipso erunt, superioritatem in Episcopos, quam alioquin habet, jure humano à nobis etiam permitti.

Cæterum rei gravitate, de qua quæritur, pensiculatiùs expensâ, sicuti vestigia tùm B. Lutheri, tùm aliorum præclarissimorum Theologorum, in negantem simpliciter descendimus: idque ob causas, & rationes, quæ ab illis adsignantur, longè evidentissimas.

Prima est: Quia talis Monarchia sive primatus super Universam Christi Ecclesiam, Scripturis sacris, & consequenter juri divino, simpliciter repugnat: uti supra satis prolixè ex cap. 22. Luc. ex 1. Petr. 5. & aliis locis evidenter fuit demonstratum. Jam verò jus humanum, velut inferius, nihil potest aut debet derogare juri divino, tanquàm superiori. E. Talis primatus jure humano concedi nec potest, nec debet.

II. Ratio: Talis primatus cedit haud parùm in ipsius DEI contumeliam. Siquidem sic neglectâ ea gubernationis forma, quam DEUS ipse per Filium suum instituit, alia, & nostro judicio, multò melior eligeretur. Ubi DEI sapientia simul & potentia in dubium vocatur. Illa, quòd non sapienter satis ordinem Ecclesiasticum constituerit, dùm Monarcham aliquem Ecclesiæ non præfecit. Hæc verò, quòd Deus per Ordines à se institutos Ecclessiam suam regere, & defendere haud possit: quin in supplementum quasi addatur Monarchia.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: Question: whether the Form of government in the Church can be monarchical?

III. Such a primacy is not necessary. For Christ, who is the Head of the Church, is wise enough, and also powerful enough, that he can sustain and administer the government of his whole body without a vicar: nor does he stand in need of any other human aid than that which he himself instituted, giving some as Apostles, others as Teachers, etc.

And although Christ is not visibly present, he is nevertheless truly present to the Church invisibly, even according to his humanity: Matt. 28:20, and ch. 28:20, John 6:56, and ch. 14:23, Mark 16:20, Acts 23:11, 1 Cor. 15:8, Rev. 1:3.

IV. Reason. Such a primacy is impossible. For such great wisdom does not fall to one man that he could suffice for all cases and controversial questions to be decided throughout the whole world: by the example of Moses, for whom it was impossible to rule even a single people, circumscribed within narrow borders. Exod. 18.

And if one man could sustain such a great province, why was there a need for Christ to call so many Apostles, to send them out into the whole world? For what can be done by fewer, there is no need to be done by more.

Nor is it for the Jesuits to object that there is no need for the decisions of all questions and cases to be sought and expected from one Pontiff: for in this regard the help of legates and Bishops, whom the Pontiff might station here and there throughout the world, could be implored. For always in more serious controversies, appeal will be made from those legates and Bishops to the Pope himself as the supreme judge. Where the same difficulty arises again and again: and one must run all the way to Rome even from the furthest India, if they wish to hear the undoubted decision of the Pontiff: or in those more remote places, the Church will always remain in suspense and doubt regarding a matter of faith, as it cannot hear the Pope himself.

V. And the final reason: Such a primacy would be joined with infinite dangers and inconveniences. For 1. If such a Monarch were to lapse into error, certainly the whole Church could be led into error. 2. With the Pontifical seat vacant, any King or prince would covet its possession by whatever means possible: whence infinite contentions, slaughters, wars, and finally the total destruction of the Church would follow.

The subsequent question which emerges at this point is: If the form of Ecclesiastical government cannot be Monarchical, what then has a place in the Church? To which question I believe one should not answer simply and categorically, but proceed distinctly, according to the triple respect which the Church sustains. For 1. the Church can be considered with respect to its supreme and only Head, which is CHRIST JESUS alone. In this respect we confess the government of the Church to be simply and absolutely Monarchical: as was shown above.

Then the Church can be considered by reason of the mystical Body, which from the whole structure of called believers coalesces into one body, and is vivified by one Holy Spirit. Now, insofar as in the election and vocation of ministers the votes and suffrages of all that people and of all three hierarchical orders are required, and insofar also as the privileges, goods, rights, and dignities of the Church are not tied to this or that order alone, nor to this or that man, but have been handed down and committed by Christ and the Apostles to the whole Church: to that extent certainly Flacius Illyricus, in his book on the Election of Bishops, not ineptly judged that the government of the Church has something similar to a Democracy. Which very thing Bellarmine also acknowledges in some way, lib. 1 de Pont. Rom. ch. 3, Col. 604, asserting that the Papal Monarchy is mixed with Democracy, insofar as from the whole people, all the best men can be raised to pastoral and Episcopal dignities. But meanwhile, we do not unwillingly grant to the Jesuits that if the Church is viewed outside of such cases, its government is not Democratic.

Finally, the Church is also considered with respect to ministers and pastors. But in such a way that the Universal Church is one thing, and the particular Church another. For a particular Church can have one certain pastor, or overseer, as an Inspector of the other ministers. Where it seems that not indeed a Monarchical government, but one in some part analogous to a Monarchical one, has a place. But concerning such a government of a Particular Church, there is properly no question between us and the Jesuits. But only concerning the government of the Universal or Catholic Church: whether this, as regards Pastors and Bishops, is Monarchical, and depends upon one? Where we maintain the negative for the reasons already alleged: and we believe and teach that this government is Aristocratic, or at least similar to an Aristocratic one: relying on these arguments.

The proof of this assertion of ours is this: In the same way that the primitive Church was governed by the Apostles, in the same way will the Church be administered at all times. But the Apostles governed it aristocratically. Therefore.

Not even the Jesuit himself will deny the connection of the major premise, seeing that in book 1, chapter 1, of 'De Pontifice Romano', he freely admits that it is beyond doubt that the Apostolic government was the best of all, and therefore the norm and rule of all ecclesiastical government.

The minor premise is established most of all from Acts 15:6. For when some disagreement had arisen in the Church, the Apostles and elders gathered to deliberate about that matter. Peter is indeed read to have spoken in that council, v. 7, but he did not speak until after much disputation: and not he himself: but James is read to have pronounced the definitive judgment. Acts 15:13 and 19. From which it appears that James was president of the council more than Peter: yet the Jesuits themselves would not concede that he was a monarch of the Church. II. The proof is as follows: That which is administered by a few, namely, the chief ones, with equal right, is governed aristocratically: But the Church is administered by a few and the best with equal right. Therefore, the definition of aristocracy proves the major premise to be true. For it is such a government in which the best, referring all things to the common utility, hold sway. Aristot. book 3, politics, chap. 5. Scripture confirms the minor premise in many ways. For 1. the care of all the Apostles and the inspection of the Churches was equal: as was shown above. For no monarch among them held sway over the rest: but all and each alike taught the Churches, decided controversies, and jointly performed the remaining things pertaining to the care of the Church. 2. All were equally sent to the Church, Matt. 18, 17. Where by the Church not some monarch, but many are noted. 3. The Apostle wishes the care and inspection to be common to all Bishops. Take heed, he says, to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as Bishops, to rule the Church of GOD, which He acquired with His own blood. Acts 20, 28. 1 Pet. 5, 2.

III. Proof can be sought from the practice of the primitive Church, which was governed by Bishops, common councils, studies, and works: and this process was observed: that 1. if any controversy or doubtful case had arisen, then a neighboring Bishop would inform another neighboring Bishop about it, who would inquire what needed to be done. 2. If the matter could not be settled privately, then some Synod of Bishops would be instituted throughout that province. 3. If the Bishops did not agree on all things in this either, then the cause would be deferred to a general council: the power of convening which, however, would rest only with the Emperor: and in it, from the Holy Scriptures, something certain would be defined concerning that controversy, and the execution against heretics would be demanded of the Emperors and the political Magistrate.

IV. And the final proof can be brought forth from the consensus of Antiquity. Cyprian, having been appointed Bishop, writes about himself in this manner: book 3, epist. 19. Since this matter concerns the counsel of us all, I do not dare to prejudge it and claim the whole matter for myself alone. Ambrose on 1 Tim. c. 3. Both the Synagogue and afterwards the Church had elders, without whose consent nothing was then done. Jerome to Tit. 1. Before dissensions in religion were made by the instinct of the Devil, the Churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters. Hence in the canons of the Apostles, Can. 37, it is read to have been established thus: Let a synod of bishops be held twice a year, and let them examine among themselves the dogmas of piety, and let them dissolve the ecclesiastical controversies that occur. And in the Nicene Council, Can. 5. It seemed good that a synod be held twice a year in each province, so that with all the Bishops of the province gathered together in the same place, such questions might be examined.

And indeed all these things are so manifest to the Truth, that even the adversaries ought to confess this very thing: But lest the confession be pure, they except that this custom existed in antiquity, and that it was useful and salutary: but not necessary. Where they slay themselves. For if it was useful and salutary, it certainly ought to have been retained. For all things must be referred to edification, that is, to the salvation and utility of the people. And thus it was entirely necessary.

We therefore conclude our thesis with this general Syllogism.

Whatever GOD instituted, was always observed by the Apostles, confirmed by the practice of the Ancient Church, and was finally useful and salutary to the Church: that must be held as necessary, and constantly retained in the Church.

But the Government of the Church, as regards Bishops and Doctors, is such an Aristocratic one, as has been shown hitherto. Therefore, it must be held as necessary, and constantly retained, and in no way changed into a Monarchical one.

Latin:

III. Talis primatus non est necessarius. Christus enim, qui est Caput Ecclesiæ, satis est sapiens, satis etiam potens, ut sine vicario, totius corporis sui gubernationem sustinere & administrare possit: neque ullo humano auxilio indigeat alio, quàm quod ipsemet instituit, dans alios Apostolos, alios Doctores &c.

Et quanquàm Christus visibiliter non adest: adest tamen Ecclesiæ reverà invisibiliter, etiam secundum humanitatem suam: Matth. 28, 20. & cap. 28, 20. Johan. 6, 56. & cap. 14, 23. Marc. 16, 20. Actor. 23, 11. 1. Corinth. 15, 8. Apocal. 1. v. 3.

IV. Ratio. Talis primatus est impossibilis. Neque enim in unum hominem tanta cadit sapientia, ut ipse omnibus casibus, & quæstionibus controversis per totum orbem decidendis, sufficere possit: exemplo Mosis, cui impossibile erat, vel unicum, & angustis finibus circumscriptum populum regere. Exod. 18.

Et si unus homo tantam provinciam sustinere posset, quorsum opus erat, ut Christus tot vocaret Apostolos, ut eos in orbem terrarum emitteret. Nam quod fieri potest per pauciora, non opus est ut fiat per plura.

Neque est, ut excipiant Jesuvitæ, Non opus esse, ut ab uno Pontifice omnium quæstionum ac casuum decisiones petantur & expectentur: Posse enim hac in parte implorari opem legatorum & Episcoporum, quos Pontifex hinc indè per terrarum orbem disponat. Nam semper in gravioribus controversiis, à legatis illis & Episcopis ad ipsum Papam tanquam summum judicem provocabitur. Ubi eadem subindè difficultas oboritur: & ab extrema etiam Indiâ excurrendum Romam usque, si decisionem Pontificis indubitatam audire velint: vel in illis remotioribus locis, Ecclesia semper in suspenso & dubio hærebit, de negocio fidei, ut quæ ipsum Papam audire non possit.

V. Et postrema ratio: Talis primatus cum infinitis periculis atque incommodis esset conjunctus. Nam 1. Si talis Monarcha prolaberetur in errorem, utique universa Ecclesia in errorem induci posset. 2. Vacante sede Pontificiali, quilibet Rex aut princeps illius possessionem, quâ fieri posset, ratione ambiret: Undè infinitæ contentiones, cædes, bella ac totalis tandem Ecclesiæ interitus sequeretur.

Posterior Quæstio, quæ hoc loco emergit, est: Si Forma Regiminis Ecclesiastici Monarchica non possit subsistere: quænam ergò in Ecclesia locum habeat? Ad quàm quæstionem haud simpliciter Categoricè respondendum, sed distinctè progrediendum esse existimo, secundum triplicem respectum, quem Ecclesia sustinet. Nam 1. considerari potest Ecclesia, respectu summi & unici Capitis, quod est Solus CHRISTUS JESUS. Hoc respectu fatemur Ecclesiæ regimen simpliciter & absolutè esse Monarchicum: uti supra ostensum.

Deinde considerari potest Ecclesia ratione Corporis mystici, quod ex universa vocatorum fidelium compage, in unum corpus coalescit, & uno Spiritu Sancto vivificatur. Jam quatenùs in electione & vocatione ministrorum, totius istius populi, & omnium trium ordinum hierarchicorum vota atque suffragia requiruntur, quatenùs item privilegia, bona, jura, & dignitates Ecclesiæ, non ad hunc, vel ad illum ordinem solum, non ad hunc vel illum hominem sunt alligatæ: sed toti Ecclesiæ à Christo & Apostolis sunt traditæ & commissæ: eatenus certè Regimen Ecclesiæ cum Democratia aliquid simile habere, haud ineptè Flacius Illyricus censuit lib. de Electione Episcoporum. Quod ipsum aliquo modo etiam agnoscit Bellarminus, lib. 1. de Pont. Rom. cap. 3, Col. 604. afferens Monarchiam Papalem ex Democratia mixtam esse, quatenùs ex universo populo, Optimi quique ad pastorales & Episcopales dignitates evehi possunt. Sed interim haud inviti largimur Jesuuvitæ, si extra ejusmodi casus spectetur Ecclesia, ejus regimen non esse Democraticum.

Tandem consideratur etiam Ecclesia respectu ministrorum & pastorum. Sed ita ut alia sit Ecclesiæ Universalis, alia particularis. Nam particularis Ecclesia potest habere unú certum pastorem, sive præpositum, tanquàm reliquorum ministrorum Inspectorem. Ubi non quidem regimen Monarchicum, sed Monarchico aliqua ex parte ἀνάλογον videtur locum habere. Verùm de tali Regimine Particularis Ecclesiæ, propriè inter nos & Jesuvvitas non est quæstio. Sed tantùm de Regimine Universalis sive Catholicæ Ecclesiæ: Nùm hoc quoad Pastores & Episcopos sit Monarchicum, & ab uno dependeat? Ubi nos negativam tuemur propter causas jam allegatas: & regimen hoc Aristocraticum, vel certè Aristocraticæ simile esse credimus ac docemus: his freti argumentis.

Assertionis hujus nostræ probatio 1. est hæc: Quo modo primitiva Ecclesia ab Apostolis gubernata est, eodem omnibus temporibus Ecclesia administrabitur. Atqui Aristocraticè eam Apostoli gubernarunt. Ergo.

Majoris connexum ne ipse quidem negabit Jesuvvita, ut qui libr. 1. de Pont. Rom. c. 1. ultrò fatetur, extra dubium esse, Apostolicam gubernationem omnium fuisse optimam, ac proindè omnis Ecclesiasticæ gubernationis normam & regulam.

Minor constat vel maximè ex Actor. 15, 6. Cùm enim obortum esset dissidii quippiam in Ecclesia, convenerunt Apostoli & presbyteri, ut de negocio illo dispicerent. Locutus quidem in isto Concilio Petrus fuisse legitur, v. 7. sed non locutus, nisi post magnam disceprationem: Et non ipse: Verùm Jacobus definitivam pronunciaffe legitur. Actor. 15, 13. & 19. Ex quo Jacobum magis quàm Petrum Concilii præsidem fuisse apparet: neque tamen Ecclesiæ Monarcham fuisse, vel ipsi concesserint Jesuvvitæ. II. Probatio talis est: Quod à paucis, ing̃, præcipuis pari jure administratur, id regitur Aristocraticè: Atqui Ecclesia à paucis & optimatibus pari jure administratur. E. Majorem veram esse comprobat Definitio Aristocratiæ. Est enim ea tale imperium, in quo Optimates, omnia ad communem utilitatem referentes dominantur. Aristot. libr. 3. polit. cap. 5. Minorem Scriptura multipliciter confirmat. Nam 1. æqualis erat omnium Apostolorum cura, & Ecclesiarum inspectio: uti supra ostensum. Neque enim Monarcha aliquis inter eos reliquis dominabatur: sed omnes & singuli Ecclesias pariter docebant, controversias decidebant, reliquaq́; ad Ecclesiæ curam spectantia conjunctim agebant. 2. æqualiter omnes ablegabantur ad Ecclesiam Matth. 18, 17. Ubi per Ecclesiam non Monarcha aliquis: sed plures notantur. 3. D. Apostolus curam & inspectionem omnibus Episcopis vult esse communem. Attendite inquiens vobis, & universo gregi, in quo vos Spiritus Sanctus posuit Episcopos, ut regatis Ecclesiam DEI, quam acquisivit sanguine suo. Actor. 20, 28. 1. Petr. 5, 2.

III. Probatio ex praxi primitivæ Ecclesię peti potest, quæ ab Episcopis, communibus consiliis, studiis, operis gubernata fuit: & hic processus observatus fuit: ut 1. si controversia aliqua, vel casus dubius obortus esset, tùm vicinus Episcopus, vicinum alterum Episcopum de eo certiorem faceret, qui quid facto opus esset, quæreret. 2. Si privatim res componi non posset, tùm aliquod Episcoporum, per illam provinciam institueretur Synodus. 3. Si neque in hac consentirent per omnia Episcopi, tùm causa ad generale concilium deferretur: cujus tamen convocandi potestas, non esset nisi penes Imperatorem: inq́; eo ex Scripturis Sacris de Controversia illa certi quid definiretur, & executio in hæreticos Imperatoribus, politicoque Magistratui demandaretur.

IV. Et postrema probatio, ex Antiquitatis consensu proferri potest. Cyprianus constitutus Episcopus, de se in hunc modum scribit: lib. 3. epist. 19. Hæc res cùm omnium nostrûm consilium spectet, præjudicare ego, & soli mihi rem omnem vendicare non audeo. Ambrosius in 1. Tim. c. 3. Et Synagoga, & postea Ecclesia seniores habuit, sine quorum consensu tùm nihil agebatur. Hieronymus ad Tit. 1. Antequàm Diaboli instinctu dissidia in religione fierent, communi presbyterorum consilio Ecclesiæ gubernabantur. Hinc canonibus Apostolorum, Can. 37. sic constitutum fuisse legitur: Δεύτερον τῶ̃ ἔτος σύνοδος γινέσθω τω̃ν ἐπισκόπων, καὶ ἀνακρινέτωσαν ἀλλήλοις τὰ δόγματα τῆς εὐσεβείας, καὶ τὰς ἐμπιπτούσας ἐκκλησιαστικὰς ἀντιλογίας διαλυέτωσαν. Et in Concilio Niceno, Can. 5. καλῶς ἔχειν ἔδοξεν, ἑκάσυ ἐνιάυτε καθ᾽ ἑκάσην ἐπαρχίας δὶς τῦ ἔτες συνόδος γίνεσθαι, ἵνα κοινῇ πάντων τῶν Ἐπισκόπων τῆς ἐπαρχίας ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ συναγομένων, τὰ τοιαῦτα ζητήματα ἐξετάζοιτο.

Et profectò sunt hæc omnia Veritatis ita manifestæ, ut adversarios etiam hoc ipsum confiteri oporteat: Verùm ne pura sit confessio, illud excipiunt, antiquitùs quidem consuetudinem istam fuisse, eamque utilem & salutarem: sed non necessariam. Ubi seipsos jugulant. Si enim utilis & salutaris fuit, utique retineri debuit. Omnia enim ad ædificationem, hoc est, ad salutem & utilitatem populi referenda sunt. Et sic omninò necessaria fuit.

Concludimus proindè θέσιν nostram generali hoc Syllogismo.

Quicquid DEUS instituit, ab Apostolis semper observatum, à praxi Veteris Ecclesiæ confirmatum, Ecclesiæ denique utile & salutare fuit: istud pro necessariò est habendum, & in Ecclesia constanter retinendum.

Atqui Gubernatio Ecclesiæ, quoad Episcopos & Doctores, Aristocratica talis est, uti hactenùs ostensum. E. pro necessaria est habenda, & constanter retinenda,neque in Monarchicam ullo pacto commutanda.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: Antithesis

ANTITHESIS.

The Jesuit Bellarmine, fighting for a monarchical but mixed government of the Church, contends mainly with these arguments.

1. Monarchy is the best and most excellent form of government. But it is certain that the Church is governed by the best and most excellent form of government. Therefore, its government ought to be Monarchical. lib. 1. de Pont. Rom. cap. 2. & cap. 9.

I answer 1. That the fallacy τῆς μὴ ἀιτίας is committed. For the government of the Church ought not to be Monarchical because this form of government seems to men to be the best and most excellent: but its form ought to be such as Christ himself willed it to be in respect of the Bishops. But he did not will it to be Monarchical: but Aristocratic: as has been shown in the preceding. Therefore.

Furthermore, if the argument is understood concerning simple Monarchy, and indeed with respect to the Head, Christ the Savior, we concede all that willingly.

Finally, it is not ἁπλῶς but κατὰ τί true, what Bellarmine says. For since, according to the teaching of politicians, a distinction must be made between τὸ βέλτιον and τὸ ἀιρετὸν: and between Monarchy in the abstract, by reason of itself or its essence, and in the concrete, considered by reason of men or its existence: certainly Monarchy is then the best and most excellent government, when it is estimated in itself and by reason of its quiddity, and all the requirements of a good Monarch are presupposed. Now the requirements of a Monarch are that, instructed with the due virtues, he be supremely wise, pious, industrious, and of carnal affections devoid of [partiality], devoted solely to the pursuit of justice and truth, taking the greatest care of his subjects equally, dispatching most matters by his own industry, referring everything to the public good with private interest clearly set aside. In this respect, in the person of Christ alone, in whom all these requirements concur most perfectly, the Monarchy of the Church excellent government. But if, however, the infirmity of men who conduct the care of the Church by the institution of Christ is attended to, and thus Monarchy is considered by reason of its existence, such as it usually is and can be, not such as it ought to be: then it is not simply true that Monarchy excels the other forms of government in excellence and utility. Bellarmine himself notices this, and therefore in book 1, chapter 3, he prefers a mixed government, tempered by Aristocracy, to a simple Monarchy, if indeed the circumstances and the reason of this life are considered: thus he himself refuting those things which he had argued concerning the simple Monarchical state in the preceding chapter 2, no more fruitfully than if he had argued about a Platonic Idea. For such a simple and absolute Monarchy cannot obtain a place among men. Hence the Republics of the Athenians and Romans most laudably always preferred an Aristocratic or Democratic form of government to Monarchy: Just as today free Republics congratulate themselves greatly that they are forced to be subject to no Monarch, whether prince or King, so much so that they would sooner suffer their lives to be taken from them than permit Aristocracy or Democracy to be changed into Monarchy.

II. Bellarmine's argument is as follows: In whatever way the Church which is in heaven is governed, in the same way is that which is on earth governed. But the Church of the immortal Angels is governed by one head, which is in heaven: namely, by Michael the Archangel: Therefore the Church militant is also governed by one head which is on earth: namely, the Roman Pontiff.

I answer that the antecedent is true if it is understood of the head Christ, who alone and one is the head even of the Angelic Church. For although we do not at all deny that there are certain orders among the Angels: yet the Jesuit has not yet proved that the Archangel Michael is the Monarch of the rest. For thus it would follow that there are two Monarchs in heaven: One Christ: The other Michael: which implies a contradiction. And it is clearly impertinent that he cites from chapter 12, 7 of the Apocalypse: where it is read: Michael and his Angels. For that Christ the Savior is indicated there by the name of Michael is more certain than to need laborious proof. Furthermore, he proves the unknown by the more unknown. For the Angelic hierarchy is more unknown to us than that of the Church. That is invisible: This falls under sight, as far as external government is concerned. That is confirmed in good: This is not so. Finally, the Jesuit wanders clearly off the track when he adapts here that passage from Heb. 8, 5. Priests serve the copy and shadow of heavenly things. For that passage does not deal with the heavenly polity of Angels: but with Christ himself, and his heavenly benefits, which were foreshadowed through the figures and shadows of the Old Testament: indeed to be exhibited only in the New Testament.

III. The argument sounds thus: The Old Testament was a figure of the New: However, at the time of the Old Testament there was always one who presided over all in those things which pertained to the Law and Religion. Therefore it is necessary that the Church of the New Testament also have one visible Monarch or ruler.

I answer that the minor premise is not universally true. For after the Church had grown in the families of the Patriarchs after the flood, it is nowhere read in the Scriptures that a Monarchical government was then introduced, so that all the Churches of the Patriarchs had to depend on the nod of one: but each of them ruled his own Church, and performed the worship of GOD, as he had learned from divine revelation. Furthermore, in the subsequent time, the government of the Church was in the hands of the elders of the people, who would judge both political and ecclesiastical controversies by certain laws: so that GOD himself sent Moses to these elders, Exod. 3, 16. and 18. and Moses himself would communicate the command of the Lord with these elders. Which elders, since they were undoubtedly the nobles from the families of the Patriarchs: it is most rightly gathered from this that the government of the Church was then Aristocratic. Thirdly, after the exit of the people from Egypt, Moses was indeed appointed leader and prince of the Israelites: and therefore he dispatched all business, both ecclesiastical and political: but in such a way that, according to the counsel of his father-in-law Jethro, he divided the judicial tasks in lesser causes among the elders: reserving for himself the judgment of the more serious causes. Where again the form of government was Aristocratic, or certainly similar to an Aristocracy. Finally, although GOD later caused Aaron to be chosen, anointed, and confirmed as high Priest or Pontiff, who indeed as the first of the priests and Levites, and his successors, ought to be the first: yet it is nowhere read that such a Monarchy or primacy was commended to him by GOD, or usurped by him.

For 1. in secular matters he arrogated no dominion to himself: but this was reserved for political judges. Whence the Pontiff of the Priests with the rest of the Priests at the time of the Passion of Christ cried out: It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death, John 18, 31. Nay, the Priests themselves were subject to Kings and the political Magistrate, so that King Solomon removed the priest Abiathar from his place, 1 Kings 2, 27. and substituted the Pontiff Zadok in his place. But the Roman Pontiffs deny all obedience to the political Magistrate to such an extent that they have rather expelled Kings from their seats and stripped them of all dignity.

2. The High Priest of the Old Testament did not have all power even in ecclesiastical matters, such that he would not even dare to assemble a council by his own judgment. For it was not Aaron, but Moses: not Eleazar, but Joshua: not the priests but the judges who summoned the people. Thus David assembled two synods: 2 Sam. 1, 15. Solomon 1 Kings 8, 1. Thus Asa, Jehoshaphat, and the rest of the kings of the Jews exercised the same power, with the priests willingly obeying.

3. The High Priest of the Old Testament did not have absolute power, but limited, so that in deciding controversies of religion, he would not dare to pronounce otherwise than according to the law, according to the constitution prescribed by God himself, Deut. 17, 10 & 11, chap. 27, 21. Which was the very reason that God, as often as the High Priest and priests strayed from the norm of the divine law, always raised up prophets, outside the tribe of Levi, who censured the errors and recalled the erring to the way of truth.

4. Nor did he have supreme and final power alone, as a monarch: or as they are wont to speak commonly, mere and mixed authority: but he had to decide and judge controversies that had arisen together with the rest of the priests and with the judge: according to the precept of the Lord, Deut. 17, 9. You shall come to the priests of the Levitical race, and to the judge who shall be at that time, and you shall inquire of them, who shall tell you the truth of the judgment: And you shall do whatever they shall say, and TEACH you ACCORDING TO HIS LAW. Hence Christ himself was ordered to plead his case not before Caiaphas alone, but before the whole Council of Elders: Matt. 26, 57. Mark 14, 53. just as the Apostles were, Acts 4, 6 & seqq. Hence the Jews' Sanhedrin drew its origin, which was divided into three judicial orders: of which elsewhere.

Furthermore, as for the system of this whole Jesuit argument, it is not worth even a farthing. For 1. from the state of the Old Jewish Church, which was one of servitude, to the state of the New Testament, which is one of liberty, the consequence does not hold: But we must rather stand in that liberty into which we have been asserted through Christ, Gal. 5, 1. 2. That High Priest of the Old Testament, whatever power he may have had, was a type and figure of Christ the Savior. In Christ, therefore, now exhibited, all that system of figures and types has expired: so that, as the Epistle to the Hebrews teaches, chap. 7, 15, chap. 16, 23 & 24, as also chap. 9, 24 & 25, that pontifical power shines forth much more excellently and exactly in Christ, now the unique supreme head of the Church. 3. The Old Testament was a figure of the New, not in every respect: but by reason of the types, which are fulfilled in the New: Meanwhile, by reason of ecclesiastical discipline and government, it had many singular things which have been abrogated under the New Testament. Nor does that 1 Cor. 10, 11 stand in the way. All these things happened to them in a figure. For the Apostle is not dealing with the ceremonial or forensic law, but with the moral: and by the example of the Jews he deters the Corinthians from similar crimes impinging upon the Decalogue. 4. The system of the Israelite Church was other and clearly different from that which is the Church of Christians under the New Testament. That was enclosed by the narrow borders of Palestine or Judea: it was also tied to one nation, and therefore as a certain particular Church it could easily be governed by one man, especially since the priests, Levites, and judges lived in the same city, namely Jerusalem. But the Church of the New Testament is now so dispersed throughout the whole world, and through all nations, peoples, and tongues, that it is impossible for the Catholic Church to be ruled by one man, and to follow the prescription and opinion of this one man in all doubtful causes. 5. Christ himself has now constituted another form of ecclesiastical government under the New Testament, and one clearly different from that old one, as demonstrated evidently above.

Latin:

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ.

Jesuvvita Bellarminus pro Monarchico, sed mixto Ecclesiæ regimine pugnans, his præcipuè militat argumentis.

1. Monarchia est optimum & præstantissimum regimen. Atqui certum est Ecclesiam optimo & præstantissimo regimine gubernari. E. ejus regimen debet esse Monarchicum. lib. 1. de Pont. Rom. cap. 2. & cap. 9.

Respondeo 1. Committi Sophisma τῆς μὴ ἀιτίας. Neque enim ideò Ecclesiæ Regimen debet esse Monarchicum, quia hæc gubernationis forma hominibus videtur optima & præstantissima:Sed talis debet esse ejus forma, qualem Christus ipse ratione Episcoporum esse voluit. At non voluit eam esse Monarchicam: sed Aristocraticam: uti in præcedentibus ostensum. Ergò.

Deindè si de Monarchia simplici, & quidem respectu Capitis, Christi Servatoris, argumentum intelligatur, totum illud ultrò concedimus.

Tandem non ἁπλῶς sed κατὰ τί verum est, quod dicit Bellarminus. Cùm enim sic docentibus Politicis distinguendum sit inter τὸ βέλτιον & τὸ ἀιρετὸν: & inter Monarchiam in abstracto, ratione sui, vel essentiæ, & in concreto, ratione hominum vel existentiæ confideratam: utique Monarchia tùm est optimum & præstantissimum regimen, quando in se, & ratione quidditatis suæ æstimatur, & omnia Monarchæ boni requisita præsupponuntur. Requisita autem Monarchæ sunt, ut debitis virtutibus instructus, summè sit sapiens, pius, laboriosus, affectuum carnalium expers, soli justitiæ & veritatis studio addictus, subditorum curam ex æquo maximam agens, pleraque propria industria expediens, omnia ad publicum bonum privato planè postposito referens. Hoc respectu in sola persona Christi, in quo omnia hæc requisita perfectissimè concurrunt, Monarchia Ecclesiæ est optimum & præstantissimum regimen. Sin autem hominum, Ecclesiæ curam ex institutione Christi agentium infirmitas attendatur, & sic Monarchia consideretur ratione existentiæ, qualis esse solet & potest, non qualis esse debet: tùm haud simpliciter verum est, quòd Monarchia reliquis gubernationum formis excellentiâ & utilitate præstet. Animadvertit hoc ipse Bellarminus, ac proindè lib. 1. cap. 3. Monarchiæ simplici præfert mixtam, & ex Aristocratia temperatam, si nimirùm circumstantiæ & ratio hujus vitæ consideretur: sic ipse refutans ea, quæ de simplici statu Monarchico, capite præcedente 2. disputaverat, haud magis fructuosè, ac si de Idea Platonica disputasset. Siquidem talis simplex & absoluta Monarchia locum inter homines obtinere nequit. Hinc laudatissimè Atheniensium & Romanorum Respublicæ, formam Regiminis Aristocraticam, vel Democraticam Monarchiæ semper prætulerunt: Quemadmodum hodieq; liberę Respublicæ plurimùm sibi gratulantur, quod nulli subesse coguntur Monarchæ sive principi, sive Regi, adeò ut citiùs vitam sibi eripi patiantur, quàm permittant, ut Aristocratia vel Democratia in Monarchiam permutetur.

II. Argumentum Bellarmini tale est: Quo pacto Ecclesia, quæ in cælis est, regitur, eodem regitur & ea, quæ in terris est. Atqui Ecclesia immortalium Angelorum ab uno capite regitur, quod in cælis est: nempè à Michaele Archangelo: Ergò Ecclesia etiam militans regitur ab uno capite quod in terris est, nempè Pontifice Romano.

Respondeo Antecedens verum esse, si de capite Christo intelligatur, qui solus atque unus, Ecclesiæ etiam Angelicæ caput est. Etsi enim inter Angelos ordines quosdam esse, minimè inficiamur: Archangelum tamen Michaelem esse Monarcham reliquorum, nondùm probavit Jesuvvita. Sic enim sequeretur, duos esse Monarchas in cælis: Unum Christum: Alterum Michaelem: id quod contradictionem implicat. Et impertinens planè est, quod ex cap. 12, 7. Apocalypseos citat: ubi legitur: Michael & Angeli ejus. Nam Christum Servatorem ibi Michaelis nomine indigitari, certiùs est, quàm ut operosa probatione indigeat, Deindé ignotum probat per ignotius. Ignotior enim nobis est hierarchia Angelica, quam Ecclesiæ. Illa invisibilis est: Hæc sub aspectum, quoad externum regimen cadit. Illa in bono confirmata: Hæc non item. Tandem extra oleas planè vagatur Jesuvvita, quando huc accommodat illud Hebr. 8, 5. Sacerdotes deserviunt exemplari & umbræ cæleftium. Neque enim eo loci agitur de cælefti Angelorum politia: fed de Christo ipso, ejusdemque cælestibus beneficiis, quæ per figuras & umbras Veteris Testamenti fuerunt adumbrata: quippè in Novo demùm Testamento exhibenda.

III. Argumentum fic fonat: Testamentum Vetus fuit figura Novi: Tempore autem Testamenti Veteris femper fuit unus, qui omnibus præerat in iis, quæ ad Legem & Religionem pertinebant. Ergò Ecclesia quoq; Novi Testamenti, unum visibilem habeat Monarcham five rectorem necesse est.

Respondeo Minorem non esse universaliter veram. Postquàm enim Ecclesia in familiis Patriarcharum excreverat post diluviũ, nuspiam Scripturis legitur, quod tùm introductum fuerit Regimen Monarchicum, ut ab unius nutu omnes Patriarcharum Ecclesiæ pendere necessum haberent: sed quilibet ipsorum suam regebat Ecclesiam, & cultum DEI peragebat, prout ex divina revelatione didicerat. Porrò subsequente tempore gubernatio Ecclesiæ erat penes seniores populi, qui certis legibus, & politicas & Ecclesiasticas controversias dijudicarent: ita ut DEUS ipse Mosen ad seniores istos ablegaret, Exod. 3, 16. & 18. & Moses ipse cum senioribus istis, mandatum Domini communicaret. Qui seniores, cùm sine dubio fuerint optimates ex familiis Patriarcharum: utique regimen Ecclesiæ tùm Aristocraticum fuisse, rectissimè hinc colligitur. Tertiò post exitum populi ex Ægypto Moses dux quidem & princeps Israelitarum constitutus fuit: ideoq́; negocia omnia, tùm Ecclesiastica, tùm politica expedivit: sed ita, ut secundum consilium soceri Jethronis, operas judiciales in causis minoribus, inter seniores divideret: ipse sibi graviorum causarum dijudicationem sibi reservans. Ubi rursus forma regiminis Aristocratica, vel certè Aristocraticæ similis fuit. Tandem etsi DEUS postmodùm summum Sacerdotem sive Pontificem eligi, inungi & confirmari curavit Aaronem, qui quidem primi ut & successores ejus primi esse deberent Sacerdotum & Levitarum omnium: nusquàm tamen legitur ipsi talis Monarchia vel primatus à DEO commendatus, vel ab ipso usurpatus fuisse.

Nam 1. in secularibus nullum sibi dominium arrogabat: sed hoc politicis judicibus erat reservatum. Undè Sacerdotum Pontifex cum reliquis Sacerdotibus tempore Passionis Christi clamabat: Nobis non licet quempiam interficere, Johan. 18, 31. Quin ipsi Sacerdotes Regibus & politico Magistratui erant subditi, ita ut SalomonRex loco moveret SacerdotemAbiathar, 1. Reg 2, 27. inque ejus locum substituit Pontificem Sadoc. Atqui Pontifices Romani usque adeò Magistratui politico omnem obedientiam denegant, ut ipsi potiùs Reges sedibus suis expulerint & dignitate omni exuerint.

2. Pontifex Veteris Testamenti non habebat in rebus etiam Ecclesiasticis omnem potestatem, ita ut ne quidem proprio arbitratu auderet concilium congregare. Non enim Aaron, sed Moses: non Eleazar, sed Josua: non Sacerdotes sed Judices convocabant populum. Sic David duas Synodos congregavit: 2. Sam. 1, 15. Salomon 1. Reg. 8, 1. Sic Asa, Josaphat & reliqui Judæorum Reges, eandem potestatem exercebant, Sacerdotibus spontè obtemperantibus.

3. Non habuit Pontifex Veteris Testamenti absolutam potestatem, sed limitatam, ut in decidendis controversiis Religionis, non aliter, quàm secundùm legem auderet pronunciare, secundum constitutionem ab ipso D E O præscriptam, Deut. 17, 10. & 11. cap. 27, 21. Quæ ipsa causa fuit, quòd Deus, quoties Pontifex & Sacerdotes à norma legis divinæ aberrarunt, semper excitavit Prophetas, extra tribum Levi, qui errores taxarunt, errantes verò in viam veritatis revocarent.

4. Neque solus, tanquàm Monarcha, summam & ultimam habuit potestatem: vel ut vulgò loqui solent, merum ac mixtum imperium: sed unà cum reliquis Sacerdotibus, & cum Judice controversias obortas, decidere ac dijudicare debuit: secundum præceptum Domini, Deut. 17, 9. Venies ad Sacerdotes Levitici generis, & ad Judicem, qui fuerit illo tempore, quaresq́; ab eis, qui indicabunt tibi judicii veritatem: Et facies quodcunque dixerint, & DOCUERINT te JUXTA LEGEM ejus. Hinc Christus ipse non coram solo Caipha, sed coram toto Concilio Seniorum causam dicere jussus est: Matth. 26, 57. Marc. 14, 53. quemadmodum & Apostoli, Actor. 4, 6. & seqq. Hinc ortum suum traxit Judæorum Sanhedrin, quod in tres ordines judiciales erat divisum: de quo alibi.

Cæterùm quoad Systema totius hujus argumenti Jesuitici, illud ne unius quidem est teruntii. Nam 1. à statu Veteris Ecclesiæ Judaicæ, qui Servitutis erat, ad statum Novi Testamenti, qui libertatis est, non valet consequentia: Sed standum potiùs nobis est ea libertate, in quam per Christum asserti sumus, Gal. 5, 1. 2. Pontifex ille Veteris Testamenti quamcunque etiam habuerit potestatem, Typus fuit, & figura Christi Servatoris. In Christo ergo jam exhibito, omnis illa figurarum & Typorum ratio expiravit: ita ut docente Epistola ad Hebr. cap. 7, 15. cap. 16, 23. & 24. ut & cap. 9. 24. & 25. multo excellentius & exactius in Christo jam unico summo Ecclesiæ capite, potestas illa Pontificalis eluceat. 3. Vetus Testamentum fuit figura Novi non χτὶ πτεντὸς: sed ratione Typorum, qui in Novo sunt adimpleti: Interim ratione disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ & regiminis, multa habuit singularia, quæ sub Novo Testamento sunt abrogata. Neque obstat illud 1. Cor. 10, 11. Hæc omnia evenerunt eis in figura. Nam non de ceremoniali aut forensi Lege agit Apostolus, sed de morali: & Judæorum exemplo deterret Corinthios à similibus sceleribus in Decalogum impingentibus. 4. Alia & diversa planè fuit Ecclesiae Israeliticae ratio, quàm quae est Christianorum Ecclesiae sub Novo Testamento. Illa angustis Palaestinae sive Judaeae finibus includebatur: ad unam item gentem erat alligata, ac proindè tanquàm particularis quaepiam Ecclesia ab uno homine facilè gubernari poterat, praesertim cum Sacerdotes. Levitae & judices, eâdem urbe, nempè Hierosolymis habitarent. Verùm Ecclesia Novi Testamenti jam per totum terrarum orbem, perq́; omnes gentes, nationes & populos ita est dispersa, ut impossibile sit, Catholicam Ecclesiam ab uno homine regi, & hujus unius praescriptum ac sententiam in omnibus causis dubiis sequi. 5. Christus ipse aliam jam sub Novo Testamento, & à Veteri illa planè diversam regiminis Ecclesiastici formam constituit, uti suprà evidenter demonstratum.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: Antithesis (continued)

But let someone object against what has been said, that it is nevertheless clear from the Old Testament that the use of both governments, namely ecclesiastical and political, was granted to the priests.

But I answer, that was a matter of the time, not of divine law or precept. For although these two were not incompatible under the old law of the Israelites: but those who were the leaders of religion and sacred things also held political leadership: which is manifest by the example of Melchizedek, who was both King of Salem and Priest of the Most High, Gen. 14. Likewise of the Patriarchs, as also of Moses, who also sat to judge the people, Exod. 18, 13, and burned incense to the Lord, Exod. 40. Likewise Eli, who was both Priest of the Lord and Judge among the people, 1 Sam. 1 & 4, yet this custom was later changed by divine law, so that it was a crime for both priests and kings to administer both powers, which the laws of Scripture show, Num. 18, likewise the example of King Uzziah, 2 Chron. 28. Although this law of the Lord is also read to have been again antiquated in the time of the Maccabees: yet no support can redound from there to the cause of the Jesuits: because Christ the Savior, reforming the polity of his Church under the New Testament, recalled the old law into use, and willed that both powers be distinct for the subjects: according to that, Luke 22, 25. The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, but you not so.

IV. Bellarmine's argument can be formed thus: Just as a sheepfold, an army, a house, a ship, a bride have one head: so also it is necessary that the Church, which is compared to these things throughout the Scriptures, have one head.

I answer 1. the whole argument is conceded, as far as Christ is the head of the Church. 2. But as for the Roman Pontiff, whether he be Peter or Paul, we simply deny it. For that comparison is not to be understood simply and generally, even as regards external government: otherwise the Church would no longer be a mystical and spiritual body. Now because it is such, it certainly requires such a body, so that there may be a just analogy between the head and the body. Therefore the comparisons produced are to be taken as παρὰ τὴν: And the whole argument constructed from Allegories proves nothing.

V. Argument: When Christ was living on earth, He visibly governed the Church as its supreme Pastor and Ruler. Therefore, even now the Church must have an external and visible Monarchical government: otherwise it would not be the Church, which is now the same City of GOD as that which CHRIST Himself governed.

I answer that the fallacy ἀπὸ τοῦ μὴ ἑπομένου is committed: which is evident in many ways. For 1. the comparison between Christ and the Roman Pontiffs has not yet been proven. 2. No other universal Bishop succeeded Christ in the ecclesiastical government: nor could he succeed: which the very Unity and consistency of the subsequent Church with the former required. For Christ, ascending into heaven, did not abdicate His Pontifical office, but still remains the Head, Pontiff, Archpastor, Bishop, and Foundation of His Church, 1 Cor. 3:11, 2 Cor. 11:2, Col. 2:19, Heb. 7:21 & 24, 1 Pet. 5:4. That, however, in which one is succeeded is always derived to the successor. If, therefore, a Pontiff succeeded Christ, then Christ would no longer be King: which is blasphemous. 2. In a Monarchy, one does not succeed unless the King is dead. But Christ always lives, and death no longer has dominion over Him. Therefore. 3. Christ is not absent from His Church, not even according to His humanity, but is always most present to it. But to Him who is present, and who presently administers His kingdom, one does not succeed, nor is it necessary that one should succeed. 4. Visibility has nothing to do with the matter: For even according to the Logicians, the Mode does not vary the thing. Therefore, one and the same Church remains, and one and the same is its government, although there is a certain difference in the mode, insofar as Christ formerly presided over His Church visibly, but now invisibly. 5. If the forms of governments are changed, so that a Monarchy passes into an Aristocracy or Democracy: then in that case that Aristocratic principle obtains in a certain way, and the specific unity seems to be shaken. But this did not happen in the time of the New Testament, since the government of the Church, by reason of Christ, is still Monarchical, and by reason of the disciples of Christ, it was then Aristocratic. 6. Finally, the Unity of the Church, not as Bellarmine opines, is to be estimated from the same and always self-similar mode of government: since the form of the Church's government was different before the exodus from Egypt than it was afterwards, and nevertheless the Church remained one. But where there is the Unity of the Spirit and of faith: there also is the true unity of the Church, although concerning the mode of government, there may appear to be some diversity.

VI. Argument: One Bishop is set over one specific diocese: One Archbishop over one specific province, and the Bishops of the same province: One Patriarch over Archbishops and many provinces. Therefore, one Pontiff is set over all provinces and the whole Catholic Church.

I answer 1. that it is begging the question: For we simply deny that this very constitution of Bishops, Archbishops, and Patriarchs depends upon the ordination of Christ. Therefore, what is gathered from it cannot stand as authentic. 2. The collection is made from the particular to the universal: If one is set over one or many: Therefore one also ought to be set over all. Where the consequence is rightly denied: Since the rationale of the whole world is not the same as that of one or another province. Thus, otherwise, there ought to be given one Emperor of the whole world, who never was given, and never will be given. 3. This method of arguing conflicts with the constitution of Christ, who simply abolished Monarchy as far as the Governors or Bishops established in these lands are concerned, as was shown more fully above.

VII. Argument: Most Churches throughout England, Franconia, and Germany were planted by those whom the Roman Pontiffs sent out. Therefore, the Roman Pontiff is deservedly held to be the supreme prelate and Monarch of the Church.

I answer; that the fallacy παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον is committed. For the consequence from the mission of Pastors to the establishing of the primacy of the sender is not valid. For not only the Pontiff has this right: but also any particular Church, so that if there is need, it may send Heralds and Pastors to other dioceses and Churches that are in need of their help. For the rule of charity demands this from all Churches and their leaders. 2. It is manifestly false that Churches were planted only by the authority of the Roman Pontiff. Ecclesiastical history is a witness that the Constantinopolitan Bishops sent heralds of the word to the Getae, Persians, and Scythians: Sozom. bk. 2, ch. 23. Thus, concerning the Germans, especially the Saxons and the Franks, it is most true that they do not owe their conversion to the Roman Pontiff, but to Charlemagne. On which matter, as also on the conversions of the Gentiles, let the Ecclesiastical histories be consulted, and especially the Magdeburg Centuries.

VIII. Argument: It is necessary that all the faithful think exactly the same thing in matters of faith. But there cannot be one faith in the Church if there is not one supreme Judge, to whom all are bound to acquiesce. Therefore.

I answer that the whole argument is granted concerning Christ the Savior, who, just as He alone is the head of the Church, so He alone is also the supreme judge of all controversies, whom the faithful continue to hear speaking in the Scriptures as long as they persevere in the unity of faith. But when they attribute more faith to private dreams or human traditions than to the Word of GOD, then it happens that they fall away from the Unity of faith: which is a matter of accident, and in the meantime, it can prejudice the Unity of the Head in no way. And whence, I ask, so many sects, schisms, and dissensions among the Papists themselves, if the Unity of faith depends upon the Roman Pontiff as the head of the Universal Church? On which matter see the book of Illyricus, concerning the dissensions of the Roman Church.

Bellarmino fights with these soldiers of light armor: nor can he bring stronger ones into the battle line. Therefore, let us also sound the retreat, and let us unfold the third chapter's exposition.

However, before that is done, we shall still unfold one question concerning the worldly clerics, the bishops of the Romanists: Whence, and by what right, do they have their temporal jurisdiction, which seems to be opposed to the spiritual, and therefore incompatible for one man to hold both? Bellarmino, in book 5 of 'On the Roman Pontiff', chapter 6, determines: Not indeed by divine, but by human right: and thus not mediately and directly, but immediately and indirectly, bishops have the power to dispose of things not merely temporal, but as it were mixed in order to the spiritual good. But the truer opinion is that of the Evangelicals, who maintain that the Romanist bishops have the administration of temporal goods by human right indeed, and thus mediately, granted namely by kings and princes, but not indirectly: but illegitimately: they have not a mixed, but a confused power. For it was not permitted for bishops, as religious persons destined for divine worship, to receive from kings any temporal dominion over cities and provinces, much less to usurp it for themselves, and least of all to claim it by war and arms: but all that power should have been left to the political magistrate. Since they have not done this, it is evident that while temporal power is possessed by them by human right, they have ceased to be what they were before. For having assumed temporal power and dominion, they fell away from the ecclesiastical order; so that they have nothing episcopal, except a bare and empty name. For by the ordinance of Christ, episcopal power consists in the preaching of the Word, in the administration of the Sacraments, and in the care of ecclesiastical discipline, not by an external sword, but according to the prescription of the divine Word, through the right use of the keys of the Church. Yet such bishops perform nothing of this kind. Therefore they are such only in name, not in reality. Concerning which matter, let Bernard be consulted, Volume 2, page 131b, 'On Dominion and Temporal Goods', addressing Pope Eugenius, speaking in this manner: 'Grant that you claim these for yourself by some other reason: yet not by apostolic right. For Peter could not give you what he did not have. What he had, he gave: solicitude over the churches. Did he give dominion? Hear him (1 Peter 5): Not lording it, he says, over the clergy, but being made a pattern to the flock. Go therefore, and dare to usurp for yourself either a lordship while being an apostle, or an apostleship while being a lord. You are clearly forbidden from either one. If you wish to have both at the same time, you will lose both: this is the apostolic pattern, lordship is forbidden, ministry is enjoined. Your power is in crimes, not in possessions. Since it was for the former, not for the latter, that you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven.' Which dignity seems greater to you, forgiving sins or dividing estates? There is no comparison. This lowest and earthly matter has its own judges, the kings and princes of the earth. Why do you invade the boundaries of others?

You have been made a superior, but for what? Not for lording, I suppose? We, therefore, so that we may think highly of you, have perceived a ministry imposed, not a dominion given: Learn that you have need of a hoe, not a scepter, so that you may do the work of a Prophet. Thus far Bernard.

Latin:

Excipiat verò aliquis contra jam dicta, constare tamen ex Veteri Testamento, Sacerdotibus usum utriusq́; regiminis, Ecclesiastici nimirùm & Politici fuisse concessum.

Sed respondeo, temporis illud fuisse, non verò juris aut praecepti divini. Etsi enim duo haec Veteri Israelitarum jure non erant incompetibilia: sed principatum etiam politicum obtinebant ii, qui Religionis & sacrarum rerum erant antistites: id quod Melchisedeci exemplo est manifestum, qui & Rex Salem erat, & Sacerdos Altissimi, Genes. 14. Patriarcharum itidem, ut & Mosis, qui & sedit ut judicaret populum, Exod. 18, 13. & adolevit Domino incensum, Exod. 40. item Heli, qui & Sacerdos Domini, & Judex fuit in populo, 1. Sam. 1, & 4. tamen consuetudo haec lege divina postmodùm fuit mutata, ita ut nefas esset, & Sacerdotibus & regibus utramque administrare potestatem, quod ostendunt leges Scripturae, Num. 18. item exemplum Regis Usiae, 2. Paral. 28. Quanquàm etiam lex haec Domini tempore Macchabaeorum rursus antiquata fuisse legitur: nihil tamen indè praesidii, ad causam Jesuvvitarum redundare potest: propterea quòd Christus Servator, Ecclesiae suae politiam reformans sub Novo Testamento, veterem legem in usum revocavit, & utramq; potestatem subjectis distinctam esse voluit: secundum illud, Luc. 22, 25. Reges gentium dominantur, vos autem non sic.

IV. Argumentum Bellarmini sic informati potest: Quemadmodum ovile, exercitus, domus, navis, sponsa habent unum caput: sic etiam Ecclesia, quae his rebus passim in Scripturis comparatur, unum habeat caput necesse est.

Respondeo 1. totum argumentum concedi, quoad Christum caput Ecclesiae. 2. Verò quoad Pontificem Romanum, sive is sit Petrus, sive Paulus, illud simpliciter negamus. Comparatio enim illa nõ simpliciter & generaliter est intelligenda, etiam quoad externum regimen: alioquin enim Ecclesia non ampliùs esset corpus mysticum & spirituale. Jam quia tale est, utiq; tale etiam requirit corpus, ut inter caput & corpus justa sit analogia. ergò productæ similitudines παρὰ τὴν accipiendæ: Et argumentum totum ex Allegoriis conflatum nihil probat.

V. Argumentum, Christus cùm in terris degeret, visiboliter gubernavit Ecclesiam, ut summus ejus Pastor & Rećtor. Ergò etiam nunc habere debet Ecclesia externum & visibile regimen Monarchicum: alioqui non esset Ecclesia, quæ nunc est eadem Civitas DEI, cum illa, quam CHRISTUS ipse gubernavit.

Respondeo, committi Sophisma ἀπὸ τῶ μὴ ἑπόμενον: id quod patet multipliciter. Nam 1. comparatio inter Christum & Pontifices Romanos nondum est probata. 2. Christo in regimine Ecclesiastico, non successit alius Episcopus universalis: nec succedere potuit: id quod ipsa Unitas & convenientia Ecclesiæ subsequentis cum priori exigebat. Nam Christus in cœlum ascendens, suo se munere Pontificali non abdicavit, sed adhuc manet Ecclesiæ suæ Caput, Pontifex, Archipastor, Episcopus & Fundamentum, 1. Corinth. 3, 11. 2. Corinth. 11, 2. Coloss. 2, 19. Hebr. 7, 21. & 24. 1. Petr. 5, 4. Id autem in quo succeditur, in successorem semper derivatur. Si igitur Christo successit Pontifex, tùm Christus non ampliùs Rex esset: quod blasphemum. 2. In Monarchia non succeditur, nisi Rege mortuo. At Christus semper vivit, & mors ipsi non ampliùs dominatur. Ergò. 3. Christus ab Ecclesia sua, nec etiam secundum humanitatem abest, sed illi semper præsentissimè adest. Illi autem qui præsens est, & præsenter suum administrat regnum, non succeditur, nec ut succedatur necessum est. 4. Visibilitas nihil ad rem facit: Nam secundum Logicos etiam, Modus rem non variat. Una igitur eademque manet Ecclesia, unum quoque idemque ejus regimen, licèt differentia quædam sit in modo, quatenùs Christus primò visibiliter, nunc verò invisibiliter suæ Ecclesiæ præest. 5. Si formæ regiminum mutentur, ita ut Monarchia in Aristocratiam vel Democratiam transeat: ibi tùm quodammodo ratio illa Aristocratica obtinet, & unitas specifica labefactari videtur. Atqui hoc non factum tempore Novi Testamenti, cum regimen Ecclesiæ ratione Christi & adhuc sit Monarchicum, & ratione discipulorum Christi tùm fuerit Aristocraticum. 6. Tandem Unitas Ecclesiæ, non uti Bellarminus opinatur, est æstimanda ex eodem sibique semper simili regiminis modo: quandoquidem alia erat gubernationis Ecclesiæ forma, ante eductionem ex Ægypto, quàm postea fuit, & nihilominùs una mansit Ecclesia. Sed ubi est Unitas Spiritus & fidei: ibi vera etiam est unitas Ecclesiæ, licèt circa modum regiminis, aliqua videatur esse diversitas.

VI. Argumentum: Unus Episcopus præficitur uni certæ diœcesi: Unus Archiepiscopus uni certæ provinciæ, & ejusdem provinciæ Episcopis: Unus Patriarcha, Archiepiscopis & multis provinciis. E. Unus Pontifex omnibus provinciis, & toti Catholicæ Ecclesiæ est præfectus.

Respondeo 1. peti principium: Nam hanc ipsam Episcoporum, Archiepiscoporum, Patriarcharum constitutionem, ex Christi ordinatione dependere, simpliciter negamus. Ergò quod indè colligitur, subsistere nequit tanquàm authenticum. 2. A particulari ad universale sit collectio: Si unus uni vel multis præficitur: Ergò unus quoque omnibus debet præfici. Ubi rectè negatur consequentia: Siquidem non est eadem totius orbis, quæ unius aut alterius provinciæ ratio. Sic aliàs dari deberet unus totius orbis Imperator, qui nunquàm datus fuit, & nunquàm dabitur. 3. Pugnat hæc argumentandi ratio cum constitutione Christi, qui Monarchiam simpliciter sustulit, quoad Gubernatores sive Episcopos hisce in terris constitutos, uti suprà copiosiùs ostensum.

VII. Argumentum: Pleræq; Ecclesiæ per Angliam: Franconiam, Germaniam sunt plantatæ ab iis, quos emiserunt Pontifices Romani. Ergò Romanus Pontifex meritò habetur pro summo Ecclesiæ præsule & Monarcha.

Respondeo; committi Sophisma παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Nam à missione Pastorum ad primatum mittentis stabiliendum, non valet consequentia. Nam hoc jus habet non modò Pontifex: sed etiam quælibet Ecclesia particularis, ut si opus sit. Præcones & Pastores mittat ad alias diœceses & Ecclesias, quæ istorum ope indigent. Hoc enim exigit charitatis regula ab omnibus Ecclesiis, earundemq; pręfectis. 2. Manifestè falsum, quòd tantùm autoritate Pontificis Romani sint plantatæ Ecclesiæ. Testis est historia Ecclesiastica, Episcopos Constantinopolitanos misisse verbi præcones ad Getas, Persas, Scythas: Sozom. l. 2. c. 23. Sic de Germanis, Saxonibus præsertim & Francis verissimum est, quòd sui conversionem non debeant Pontifici Romano, sed Carolo Magno. Qua de re, ut & de conversionibus Gentium, videantur historiæ Ecclesiasticæ, & cumprimis Centuriæ Magdeburgenses.

IIX. Argumentum: Necesse est, ut omnes fideles idem omninò sentiant in rebus fidei. At una fides in Ecclesia esse non potest, si non sit unus summus Judex, cui omnes acquiescere teneantur. E.

Respondeo, concedi totum argumentum de Christo Servatore, qui uti solus est caput Ecclesiæ: ita solus etiam est summus judex omnium controversiarum, quem quamdiu in Scripturis loquentem audiunt fideles, tamdiu in unitate fidei perseverant. Quando verò privatis magis somniis, vel humanis traditionibus plus fidei tribuunt, quàm Verbo DEI: tùm sit, ut ab Unitate fidei excidant: id quod Accidentis est: & ipsi interim Unitati Capitis nihil potest præjudicare. Et undè quæsò tot sectæ, schismata & dissensiones inter ipsos Pontificios, si Unitas fidei dependet à Pontifice Romano, tanquàm capite Universalis Ecclesiæ. Qua de re videatur liber Illyrici, de dissensionibus Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

Et his quidem levis armaturæ militibus pugnat Bellarminus: neque fortiores in aciem producere potest. Ergò & nos receptui canamus, & Tertiâ capitis diexodon expediamus.

Ceterùm priusquàm id fiat, unam adhuc expediemus Quæstionem, de Romanensium Episcopis mundano Clericis: Vndé nam, & quo jure suam habeant temporalem Iurisdictionem, quæ spirituali opposita esse, & proindè utraque uni homini incompetibilis videtur? Bellarminus lib.5. de Rom. Pontif. cap. 6. statuit: Non divino quidem, sed humano jure: & sic non mediatè atque directè: sed immediatè atque indirectè, non merè quidem temporalem, sed quasi mixtam in ordine ad bonum spirituale disponendi potestatem Episcopos habere. Sed verior Evangelicorum est sententia, quist atuunt, Romanenses Episcopos humano quidem jure, & sic mediatè, donatam nimirùm à regibus & principibus, habere temporalium bonorum administrationem, verum non indirectè: sed illegitimè: non mixtam, sed confusam habere potestatem. Neque enim licuit Episcopis, tanquàm personis religiosis, & cultui divino destinatis, accipere à Regibus ullum aliquod temporale dominium in urbes & provincias, multo minùs sibi ipsis usurpare, minimè omnium bello atque armis vendicare: sed potestatem illam omnem politico magistratui fuisse relinquendam. Hoc cùm non fecerint, constat potestatem quidem temporalem, jure humano ab ipsis possideri: sed desiisse illos esse, quod prius fuerant. Suscepta enim potestate & dominio temporali, Ecclesiastico ordine exciderunt; ita ut Episcopale nihil habeant, præter nudum & inane nomen. Nam ex ordinatione Christi Episcopalis potestas consistit in prædicatione Verbi, in administratione Sacramentorum, & in curandâ disciplina Ecclesiastica, non externo gladio, sed secundum præscriptum Verbi divini, per rectum usum clavium Ecclesiæ. Atqui nihil hujusmodi præstant tales Episcopi. Ergò nominetenus saltem tales sunt, non reipsâ. Qua de re videatur Bernhardus, Tomo 2. pag. 131. b. de dominio & bonis temporalibus, ad Eugenium Pontif. Rom. verba hunc in modum faciens: Esto, ut alia quacunque ratione hæc tibi vendices: non tamen jure Apostolico. Neque enim Petrus dare tibi, quod non habuit, potuit. Quod habuit, dedit, solicitudinem super Ecclesias. Numquid dominationem? Audi ipsum (1. Petr. 5.) Non dominantes, ait, in clero, sed forma facti gregis. Ito ergò tu, & tibi usurpare aude aut dominans Apostolatum, aut Apostolicus dominatum. Planè ab alterutro prohiberis. Si utrumque simul habere voles, perdes utrumque: Forma Apostolica hæc est, Dominatio interdicitur, indicitur ministratio. In criminibus, non in possessionibus vestra est potestas. Quoniam propter illa, non propter has accepistis claves regni cælorum. Quænam tibi major videtur dignitas, dimittendi peccata, an prædia dividendi? nulla comparatio. Habet hæc infima & terrena judices suos, Reges & principes terræ. Quid fines alienos invadit?
