Factus es superior, sed ad quid? Non ad dominandum opinor? Nos igitur, ut multum sentiamus de vobis, impositum senserimus ministerium, non dominium datum: Disce sarculo tibi opus esse, non sceptro, ut opus facias Prophetæ. Hactenus Bernhardus.


### Chapter IV. and last. On the Government of the Church against the Roman Primacy: Chapter III. On the Organs or Means of Ecclesiastical Government

The government of the Church, even from its very first beginnings, has always been mediate by ordinance, inasmuch as it was governed through certain means or instruments: Just as CHRIST himself, about to ascend into heaven, solemnly confirmed those very means: John 20:21 and following. As the Father has sent me, so I also send you: Receive the Holy Spirit: Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you retain, they are retained. Matthew 28:19. Going, teach all nations: baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Mark 16:15. Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature: He who believes and is baptized shall be saved: He who does not believe shall be condemned. 1 Corinthians 11:25. Do this, as often as you shall eat this bread, and drink the cup of the LORD, you shall announce his death, UNTIL HE COMES.

There are therefore three organs or means by which the government of the Church is completed: 1. The pure preaching of the Word. 2. The legitimate administration of the Sacraments. 3. The right use of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Excluded, therefore, from the census of these means are arms and the material sword, by which the Roman Pontiff strives to amplify his kingdom: who borrowed this madness, rather than error, from the ancient and long-since condemned heretics, the Circumcellions, who, as Augustine reports in his book 'On Heresies', chapter 69, as a rustic kind of men, and of most famous audacity, not only perpetrated monstrous crimes against others throughout Africa: but did not even spare themselves in their insane ferocity, so much so that the same Augustine writes, in book 3 'Against Cresconius the Grammarian', chapter 42, that the deeds of any robbers and brigands were lesser and lighter than the crimes of these heretics.

Following these, therefore, the Roman Pontiff, at the instigation of the Devil, abusing the authority of the evangelical passage, Luke 22:38, 'Behold, two swords here', established a canon through Boniface VIII concerning superiority and obedience: which exists in that part of the Pontifical Law which is called by the ominous name of the Extravagantes, of which these are the words: In the power of the Pontiff

that there are two swords, the spiritual to wit and the temporal, is established by the Evangelical saying: For when the Apostles said, Behold here are two swords, in the Church to wit, when the Apostles were speaking, the Lord did not answer, That it is too much: but enough. Certainly he who denies that the temporal sword is in the power of Peter, ill attends to the Word of the Lord commanding, Put up thy sword into the sheath. Therefore both are in the power of the Church: the spiritual sword to wit and the material: but the latter is indeed to be exercised for the Church: the former however by the Church: the former by the hand of the priest, the latter by the hand of kings and soldiers: but at the beck and sufferance of the priest.

This cruel canon is repugnant to the Holy Scriptures, which expressly declare that the weapons of ecclesiastical warfare are not carnal: 2 Cor. 10. 4. and that no sword has been left to the Church other than the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of GOD, more penetrating than any two-edged sword, Eph. 6. 17. Heb. 4. 12.

Moreover, the Apostle defines the persons to whom the use of spiritual weapons pertains in the Church, Eph. 4. 11, naming Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists, Pastors and Doctors. Of all these, the three former orders were proper only to the primitive Church: to which must also be referred most of those who are enumerated in 1 Cor. 12. 28, powers, gifts of healings, kinds of tongues. The remaining two yielded to the establishing of the ordinary and perpetual office of ecclesiastical ministry, and between them there is this difference, that the duties of both preaching the Gospel and administering the Sacrament devolved upon the Pastors: 1 Cor. 4. 1. Tit. 1. 9. Acts 20. 28. It was, however, the duty of the Doctors to interpret Scripture, so that sound doctrine might be retained among the faithful: which would often falter and contract the stain of various errors, unless by the care and vigilance of the Doctors, the Pastors were restrained within the boundaries of Truth. These two orders are therefore distinct indeed, but not sundered: nay, they are both necessary for the bringing of the Church to an integral body, so that they allow for human weakness, or at least reveal themselves to be scorched by the flames of ambition, who imagine that the two orders are not only distinct, but so mutually sundered from each other, that they attempt to persuade themselves and others, against the express assertion of the Apostle, that the Doctors ought to have nothing in common with the governing of the Church. Although, however, these two orders, according to the Apostle, are distinct: nothing nevertheless prevents them from being sometimes comprised in one and the same order.

Moreover, in the progress of time, other persons were added, following the example of the primitive Church, to whom some part of ecclesiastical government fell: such as Governors and helpers, 1 Cor. 12. 28, namely Elders, who together with the Bishops presided over the censure of morals: Rom. 12. 8. Also Deacons, who as helpers sustained the care partly of the poor, partly of the sick, Acts 6. 1. As regards the appellation of Bishops and Presbyters, it [pertains] to all equally

to Doctors and Pastors (though in distinct grades), is clearly evident both from chapter 20, 17 & 28 of Acts, and from chapter 1 to Titus: where several Bishops are named for one city and province: although the appellation of Presbyters is sometimes not rarely attributed to the Elders of the Church and the Prefects of the ecclesiastical treasury, as was demonstrated more fully in the article on the Church: and it is not denied even in Canon law and by the Scholastic Doctors, dist. 93. c. legimus, dist. 21. cap. Cleros, dist. 95. cap. olim. P. Lombardus. l. 4. sent. dist. 24. Sect. 8.

Latin:

REgimen Ecclesiæ jam indè à primis initiis semper ex ordinatione fuit mediatum, quippè per certa media sive instrumenta gubernatum: Quemadmodum & CHRISTUS ipse, in cœlum ascensurus, illa ipsa media solenniter confirmavit: Johan. 20, 21. & seqq. Sicut misit me Pater, ita & ego mitto vos: Accipite Spiritum Sanctum: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis; & quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt. Matth. 28, 19. Euntes docete omnes gentes: baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti. Marc. 16, 15. Euntes in mundum universum prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur: Qui non crediderit, condemnabitur. 1. Cor. 11, 25. Hoc facite, quotiescunque manducabitis panem hunc, & bibetis calicem DOMINI, mortem ejus annunciabitis, USQUE DUM VENIAT.

Sunt ergò tria organa sive media, quibus regimen Ecclesiæ absolvitur: 1. Verbi prædicatio pura. 2. Legitima Sacramentorum administratio. 3. Rectus usus clavium regni cœlorum. Excluduntur ergò ex censu istorum mediorum, arma & gladius materialis, quo regnum suum amplificare studet Pontifex Romanus: qui furorem hunc potiùs, quàm errorem mutuatus est, à Veteribus ac jam pridem damnatis hæreticis, circumcellionibus, qui Augustino referente libr. de hæres. cap. 69. tanquàm genus hominum agreste, & famosissimæ audaciæ, non solùm in alios per Africam immania facinora perpetrabant: sed nec sibiipsis insana feritate parcebant, adeò, ut idem Augustinus scribat, libr. 3. contra Cresconium Grammaticum, c. 42. quorumvis latronum & prædonum facta fuisse minora & leviora, quàm istorum hæreticorum facinora.

Hos ergò secutus Pontifex Romanus, instinctu Diaboli, abusus autoritate loci Evangelici, Luc. 22, 38. Ecce duo gladii hîc, per Bonifacium IIX. canonem condidit de majoritate & obedientia: qui extat parte Juris Pontificii ea, quæ ominoso nomine Extravagantium appellatur, cujus hæc sunt Verba: In potestate Pontifi-

duo, esse gladios, spiritualem scilicet & temporalem, Evangelico dicto instituitur: Nam dicentibus Apostolis, Ecce duo gladii hîc, in Ecclesia scilicet, cùm Apostoli loquerentur, non respondit Dominus, Nimis esse: sed satis. Certè qui in potestate Petri, temporalem gladium esse negat, male Verbum attendit Domini proferentis, converte gladium tuum in vaginam. Uterque ergò est in potestate Ecclesiæ: Spiritualis scilicet gladius & materialis: sed hic quidem pro Ecclesia: ille verò ab Ecclesia exercendus: ille Sacerdotis, hic manu regum & militum: sed ad nutum & patientiam Sacerdotis.

Repugnat crudelis iste canon Scripturis Sacris, quæ disertè perhibent, Arma militiæ Ecclesiasticæ non esse carnalia: 2. Cor. 10. 4. & gladium Ecclesiæ relictum esse nullum alium præter gladium Spiritus, qui est Verbum DEI omni gladio ancipiti penetrantius, Ephes. 6. 17. Heb. 4. 12.

Cæterùm personas, quibus in Ecclesia competit usus armorum spiritualium, definit Apostolus, Ephes. 4. 11. nominans Apostolos, Prophetas, Evangelistas, Pastores & Doctores. Ex quibus omnibus, tres priores ordines, primitivæ Ecclesiæ duntaxat proprij fuerunt: ad quos recerendi sunt plerique etiam ij, qui 1. Cor. 12. 28. recensentur, potestates, dona sanationum, genera linguarum. Reliqui duo ad ordinarium & perpetuum Ecclesiastici ministerij munus constituendum cesserunt, atque inter eosdem hæc est differentia, quòd Pastoribus simul & prædicandi Evangelij, & Sacramenti administrandi partes incubuerunt: 1. Cor. 4. 1. Tit. 1. 9. Actor. 20. 28. Doctorum autem fuit Scripturam interpretari, ut sana doctrina inter fideles retineatur: quæ sæpius labasceret & labem errorum variorum contraheret, nisi Doctorum cura ac vigilantia, Pastores intra crepidines Veritatis coercerentur. Sunt ergò hi duo ordines distincti quidem, sed non divulsi: quin ad Ecclesiæ corpus integrum afferendum, utrique necessarij, ut humani liquid patiantur, vel certè nimina ambitionis flammulis se ustulari prodant, qui duos ordines non modò distinctos, sed ita à se mutuò divulsos esse opinentur, ut Doctoribus nihil cum Ecclesia regenda commune esse debere, contra expressam Apostoli assertionem, sibi & alijs persuadere conentur. Quanquàm verò duo hi ordines, secundum Apostolum, sunt distincti: nihil tamen prohibet, quò minùs nonnunquàm uno atque eodem ordine comprehendantur.

Cæterùm progressu temporis, ad exemplum Ecclesiæ primitivæ accesserunt, & aliæ personæ, quibus pars aliqua regiminis Ecclesiastici cessit: quales sunt Gubernatores & opitulatores, 1. Cor. 12. 28. nempè Seniores, qui unâ cum Episcopis censuræ morum præfuerunt: Rom 12. 8. Item Diaconi, qui tanquàm opitulatores, pauperum partim, partim ægrorum curam sustinuerunt, Actor 6. 1. Quoàd Episcoporum & Presbyterorum appellationem, eam omnibus ex æquo

Doctoribus ac Pastoribus (distinctis licet gradibus) competere, tum ex cap. Actor. 20, 17. & 28. tum ex cap. 1. ad Titum luculenter liquet: ubi unius civitatis & provinciæ, plures Episcopi nominantur: licet Presbyterorum interdum appellatio, Ecclesiæ Senioribus, & ærarij Ecclesiastici Præfectis, haud raro tribuatur, uti in articulo de Ecclesia fusius fuit demonstratum: & in jure etiam Canonico ac Doctoribus Scholasticis minime negatur, dist. 93. c. legimus, dist. 21. cap. Cleros, dist. 95. cap. olim. P. Lombardus. l. 4. sent. dist. 24. Sect. 8.


## 19 On the Sacraments in General

THE ECONOMY of the whole subsequent Treatment of this Article.

We shall, with God's help, resolve the controversy concerning the Sacraments considered in general—a controversy equally most useful and most vast in the multitude and difficulty of its questions—following partly the footsteps of our Author Philip Melanchthon, and partly looking to the controversies of our own age, by the inclusion of four principal chapters. The first will treat of those things which are proper to the Definition, that is, which concern the very nature and essence of the Sacraments, as regards the principles or causes, both constitutive of their nature and efficient.

THE SECOND will explain a little more accurately the noble Question, which is today debated quite sharply among us and our Adversaries, both Jesuits and Calvinists, concerning the effect of the Sacraments.

THE THIRD will expressly discuss the agreement and discrepancy of the Sacraments of both Testaments: and concerning those two Sacraments of the Old Testament, circumcision and the Paschal Lamb.

THE FOURTH, finally and lastly, will resolve that classic controversy which, concerning the number of the Sacraments, still exists for us today with the Jesuit faction.

In each and every one of these chapters, we shall conduct ourselves in such a way, both in the proper treatment of the thesis and of the antithesis, that if any cases of conscience occur—and indeed very many do occur regarding the exposition of this Article—we shall examine them.

But before we proceed to the discussion of the first chapter, it will be worth the effort, as if in the place of a prolegomenon, to ventilate in a few words those things which, partly concerning the ecclesiastical use of the term Sacrament, and partly concerning its etymology and πολυσημασίᾳ, have been variously disputed among theologians in previous years, and perhaps even today do not suffer the same judgment from everyone.

Latin:

OIKONOMIA totius subsequentis Tractationis hujus Articuli.

Utilissimam pariter ac quæstionum multitudine & difficultate amplissimam de Sacramentis in genere consideratis controversiam, secuti partim vestigia Autoris nostri Philippi Melanchthonis, partim vero nostri seculi controversias intuiti, quatuor potissimum capitum complexu, συν θεω expediemus. Primum pertractabit ea, quæ Definitionis sunt propria, hoc est, quæ ipsam naturam & essentiam Sacramentorum, quoad principia sive αίτια tum συςατικά της Φυσεως, tum ποιητικά propriè concernunt.

ALTERUM nobilem Quæstionem, quæ de effectu Sacramentorum hodie inter nos & Adversarios, tum Jesuvitas, tum Calvinianos satis acriter agitatur paulo accuratius explicabit.

TERTIUM de Sacramentorum utriusq; Testamenti & convenientia & discrepantia: deque duobus illis Veteris Testamenti Sacramentis circumcisione & Agno Paschali, ex professo disseret.

QUARTUM denique ac postremum expediet classicam illam controversiam, quæ de Sacramentorum numero, nobis hodieq; cum gente Jesuvitica intercedit.

In singulis vero & universis istis capitibus, tum quoad θεσιν, quam quoad αντιθεσιν recte pertractandis ita versabimur, ut si qui occurrut casus conscientiæ, qui sane circa Articuli hujus diexodon occurrunt plurimi, eos discutiamus.

Priusquam verò ad primi capitis disputationem accessum faciamus, operæ precium fuerit, προλεγομένων quasi loco, sed paucis ventilare ea, quæ partim de usu Ecclesiastico vocabuli Sacramenti, partim verò de ejusdem etỹmo & πολυσημασίᾳ inter Theologos, superioribus annis variè disputata fuerunt, & fortassis etiamnum hodiè non unam omnium eandem que censuram patiuntur.


### I. on the Use of the Vocable Sacrament in the Church. Year 1525

ON the ecclesiastical use of the term (Sacrament), soon after the beginning of the Evangelical Reformation, happily undertaken by our B. Luther, a serious controversy was stirred up, as can be seen from the second part of that golden little book which Luther published against the celestial Prophets. For Carlstadt then contended that the term Sacrament was not found in the holy Scriptures: and since GOD himself imposed names upon his creatures, it was a sin if names were imposed upon divine things by man.

But Luther responded most correctly that this term is indeed ἄγραφον, and that the Supper was neither called so by CHRIST, nor was it commanded that it be called so: But neither was it ever prohibited by the same Savior that it be called so: and therefore it was not lawful for Carlstadt to interdict the use of this term to the Church: but rather, with a safe conscience, the most free use of this term, as an adiaphorous thing, could and ought to be granted to the Church. For just as (says the same Luther) various names are given to CHRIST himself by the pious, such as, crown of the heart, jubilation, gem, etc., which do not exist in the Scriptures: so nothing prevents one from being allowed to use this term as well. What? That one would have to renounce the use of many terms if only ἐγγράφοις terms were always to be used: such as the term Trinity, Hypostatic Union: Communication of Natures and Idioms in the Person of CHRIST, and many others, which although they do not exist in the Scriptures, have nevertheless long since earned ecclesiastical right, even by the calculation and suffrage of the Sacramentarians themselves. Finally, since Christian

liberty ought to be in the same place for us as the articles of faith, so that for its safe retention we ought to do whatever is prohibited by the Adversaries against it: and conversely, we ought to omit whatever is commanded against it by the enemies of truth: Now indeed, the usurpation of that term pertains entirely to Christian liberty: certainly, even for the hatred and contempt of Carlstadt and his followers, LUTHER most correctly concludes that the term Sacrament must be used; so that he who criticizes that liberty in the faithful ought to appear to be exercising tyranny in the Church.

But as for the censorious rod which Carlstadt had once rather boldly taken up against the term Sacrament: it is only that his successors have either cast it aside, or at least mitigated it, so that they might rather reheat the same cabbage from time to time, and indeed not without offense to the weak.

Zwingli certainly in his book on true and false religion, chapter on the Sacraments, among other things has this: I would greatly wish that this word Sacrament had never been accepted by the Germans. And in the next following chapter, which is on Matrimony, he writes thus: What if this word Sacrament had never been heard by Christian ears: would not Baptism have been content with its own name: similarly the Lord's Supper? Although where this name has been accepted, we would not wish to cause a stir: Yet the nomenclature of Sacrament is more obscure and more confused. For we are almost all ignorant of what a Sacrament is. Thus no one is ignorant of what Baptism is, but few know what a Sacrament is.

John Calvin, insisting on the footsteps of his predecessors, writes that the Doctors of the Church attached a new meaning to the term Sacrament, saying, The ancients, who gave the name of Sacraments to signs, did not at all consider what the use of this word was among Latin writers: but they attached this new meaning for their own convenience, by which they might simply designate sacred signs. Book 4, Instit. chap. 14. §. 13.

But these critics are wise before the time, as it is said. For although the word Sacrament is Latin, and is found neither in the Hebrew of the Old Testament nor in the Greek of the New Testament codex: yet because usage has prevailed in the Latin Church that sacred signs should be called Sacraments by the term of a single word: and it is established that words are valid by usage, just as coins are: we certainly do not undeservedly retain the most ancient custom of the Church regarding the use of this word also, nor do we renounce it for the sake of the Zwinglians. Moreover, this custom is proven by the authority of Tertullian in his prescriptions against heretics, and book 1 against Marcion: Cyprian, book 2, Epist. 3 and Sermon on the Lord's Supper: Hilary, around the beginning of Psalm 66 and on those words of Psalm 122, 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem': Ambrose in his books on the Sacraments: Lactantius, book 4, chapter 17: Jerome on those words of chapter 44 of Ezekiel: This gate shall be shut: Augustine, book 2 on Christian doctrine and chapter 3 and Epist. 118, and elsewhere passim: and finally of all the Fathers, as many as have been famous in the Latin Church.

Furthermore, since the thing itself, which is understood in the Church by the name of Sacrament, has express foundations in the Scriptures, and no other name can be given by which that thing might be more conveniently expressed: it would certainly be rash if we allowed ourselves to be prohibited from the use of that word for the sake of the Calvinists. For although we willingly grant to them that the word for sign, seal, and mark exists in the Scriptures: yet it is also established that these words have a wide application and do not express the connotation of the sacred.

But before we leave this point, we must also note the utterly profligate lust for slander with which the Jesuit Bellarmin was not afraid to scourge the blessed Luther, as if he had protested, partly in the prelude to his book on the Babylonian Captivity, published in the year 1520, and partly in his book on the Abrogation of the Mass, published immediately in the following year, 1521, that it displeased him greatly that we use the word Sacrament in the Church. But the blessed soul of Luther is easily absolved from this most iniquitous accusation, both by the Sacramentarians, who were most hostile to Luther because of his approved use of this word, and indeed by Luther's own words, when examined and weighed in their proper places. For the former passage cited by the Jesuit exists in Volume 2 of the Jena Latin edition, page 284 in my edition. And it reads thus: The whole of Holy Scripture does not have this name 'Sacrament' in the meaning that we use, but in the opposite; for everywhere it signifies not a sign of a sacred thing, but a sacred, secret, and hidden thing. The latter passage, however, offers itself in the same volume, page 470 in my edition, which reads as follows: A pious and faithful conscience ought rightly and worthily to fear to call this a sacrifice, or to believe it to be one, which is not called a sacrifice before God and in the Scriptures. And it calls only that a sacrifice which is established to be called a sacrifice by GOD. For what rashness is more frantic than to set one's mouth against heaven in such a way as to call that a sacrifice and worship of GOD, which He does not call a sacrifice and worship of GOD. The Jesuit therefore commits a double crime of falsehood: one, that he writes that the use of the word Sacrament was highly displeasing to Luther, when nevertheless he neither said nor wrote anything other than that the word Sacrament, in the meaning in which it is used today in the Church, is nowhere to be found in the Scriptures. The other, that the Jesuit wickedly distorts what Luther wrote about the use of the word 'sacrifice' to apply to the use of the word 'Sacrament.' To both of these Jesuitical lies, by way of a conclusion, we oppose that clear protestation of Luther which exists in the same Volume 2 of the Jena Latin edition, page 59b, where in his Greater Confession he writes thus: I heartily allow that the Lord's Supper is a Sacrament, even though it is not so named in Scripture.

Latin:

DE Ecclesiastico vocabuli (Sacramenti) usu, mox sub initium Reformationis Evangelicæ, per B. Lutherum nostrum feliciter susceptæ, gravis mota fuit controversia, uti videre licet, ex parte 2. aurei illius libelli, quem contra cœlestes Prophetas, Lutherus in lucem edidit. Contendebat enim tum Carolostadius, vocabulum Sacramenti in sacris Scripturis non reperiri: & cum DEUS ipse creaturis suis nomina imposuerit, nefas esse, si rebus divinis ab homine nomina imponantur.

Cæterùm rectissimè respondit Lutherus, vocabulum hoc esse quidem ἄγραφον, & à CHRISTO neque sic appellatam esse Cœnam neq; ut sic appellaretur, præceptum esse: Sed neq; ab eodem Servatore, ne sic appellaretur, uspiam prohibitum esse: ac proindè neque Carolostatio licitum esse, usum vocabuli hujus Ecclesiæ interdicere: quin potiùs, salvâ conscientiâ liberrimum vocabuli hujus, tanquàm rei adiaphoræ usum, Ecclesiæ concedi posse & debere. Quomadmodum enim (inquit idem Lutherus) ipsi CHRISTO à piis varia induntur nomina, qualia sunt, corona cordis, jubilum, gemma &c. in Scripturis non extantia: ita nihil prohibet, quin isto etiam vocabulo uti liceat. Quid? quòd multorum vocabulorum usui renunciandum esset, si solis vocabulis ἐγγράφοις semper sit utendum: ut vocabulo Trinitatis, Unionis Hypostaticæ: Communicationis Naturarum & Idiomatum in Persona CHRISTI, & compluribus aliis, quæ licèt in Scripturis non extent, jus tamen Ecclesiasticum, ipsorum etiam Sacramentariorum calculo & suffragio jam pridem meruerunt. Tandem cum libertas

Christiana, pari cum articulis fidei loco nobis esse debeat, ita ut pro eâ salvâ retinendâ, facere debeamus, quæcunque ab Adversariis contra ipsam prohibentur: & vice versa, omittere debeamus, quæcunque contra ipsam ab hostibus veritatis præcipiuntur: Jam verò usurpatio istius vocabuli ad libertatem Christianã omninò pertineat: utique vel in Carolostadij & gregalium odium & comtemtum, vocabulo Sacramenti utendum esse, rectissimè colligit LUTHERUS; ita ut Tyrannidem in Ecclesia exercere videri debeat, qui libertatem istam in fidelibus reprehendit.

Cæterùm quam virgulam censoriam contra vocabulum Sacramenti sibi semel satis audacter sumserat Carolostadius: eam tantùm est, ut successores ipsius vel abjecerint, vel saltem mitigârint, ut potiùs eandem crambem subindè, & quidem non sine infirmorum offensione recoquerent.

Zvvinglius certè in libr. de vera & falsa religione, cap. de Sacramentis, inter reliqua sic habet: Votem istam Sacramentum magnoperè cupiam Germanis nunquàm fuisse receptam. Et capite subsequente proximo, quod est de Matrimonio, sic scribit: Quid si ista vox Sacramentum nunquàm esset Christiani auribus audita: an non Baptismus suo nomine contentus erat: similiter cœna Dominica? Quanquam ubi receptum est nomen hoc, nos nihil tumultuari velimus: Tamen Sacramenti nomenclatura obscurior est & confusior. Omnes enim fermè ignoramus, quid sit Sacramentum. Sic nemo ignorat, quid sit Baptismus, sed pauci sciunt, quid Sacramentum sit.

Johannes Calvinus antecessorum suorum vestigijs insistens, vocabulo Sacramenti novam plane significationem Doctores Ecclesiæ affinxisse scribit, Veteres, inquiens, qui Sacramentorum nomen signis indiderunt, minimè respexerunt, quis esset Verbi hujus usus apud Latinos Scriptores: sed novam hanc significationem pro suo commodo affinxerunt, quâ simpliciter sacra signa designarent. lib. 4, Instit. cap. 14. §. 13.

Verùm ante tempus, quod dicitur, Critici isti sapiunt. Etsi enim Sacramenti vox est Latina, neque vel in Hebræo Veteris, vel in Græco Novi Testamenti codice reperitur:quia tamen in Ecclesia Latina usus obtinuit, ut sacra signa, unius vocis termino, Sacramenta appellarentur: Vocabula verò ita usu valere constat, sicut nummos: utique antiquissimam Ecclesiæ consuetudinem haud immeritò, circa hujus etiam vocabuli usum retinemus, neque ei, in gratiam Zvvinglianorum nuncium remittimus. Probatur autem consuetudo ista autoritate Tertulliani de præscriptionibus adversus hæreticos, & lib. 1. contra Marcionem: Cypriani lib. 2. Epist. 3 & Serm. de Cœna Domini: Hilarij circa principium Psalmi 66. & super verba illa Psalmi 122. Rogate quæ sunt ad pacem Jerusalem: Ambrosij in libris de Sacramentis: Lactantij libr. 4. cap. 17. Hieronymi super verba illa capitis 44. Jezechielis: Porta hæc clausa erit: Augustini libr. 2. de doctrina Christiana & cap. 3. & Epist. 118. alibí passim: omnium deniq; Patrum, quotquot in Latina Ecclesia claruerunt.

Præterea cùm res ipsa, quæ Sacramenti nomine in Ecclesia intelligitur, expressa in Scripturis habeat fundamenta, neque ullum aliud nomen dari possit, quo commodiùs res ista exprimatur: temerarium utique foret, si in gratiam Calvinianorum, vocabuli istius usu nos prohiberi pateremur Etsi enim ipsis libentèr largimur, vocabulum signi Sigilli, signaculi in Scripturis extare: tamen & illud constat, voces has latè patere, neque sacri connotationem exprimere.

Priusquàm verò hinc abeamus, notanda etiam venit profligata planè calumniandi libido, quâ Jesuvvita Bellarminus B. Lutherum flagellare non fuit veritus, quasi is partim in præludio libri de capt. Babylonica, anno 1520. editi partim in l. de abrogandâ Missa, anno statim in sequente 1521. publicato, protestatus fuerit, sibi summopere displicere, ut vocabulo Sacramenti in Ecclesia utamur. Verùm ab iniquissima hac accusatione beatam Lutheri animam facilè absolvunt, tùm Sacramentarij, qui ob approbatum vocabuli hujus usum Luthero erant infensissimi: tùm verò ipsa Lutheri verba, in proprijs suis sedibus inspecta & expensa. Locus enim prior à Jesuvvita citatus, extat Tom. 2. Lat. Jen. pag. mihi 284. & sic sonat: Non habet universa Scriptura Sancta hoc nomen Sacramentum in ea significatione, quâ noster usus, sed in contraria: ubiq́; enim significat non signum rei sacræ sed rem sacram, secretam, & absconditam. Posterior verò locus, eodem Tomo p mihi 470. sese offert, qui sic habet: Pia & fidelis conscientia meritò & dignè pavere debet, ne hoc sacrificiũ appellet, aut credat, quod apud Deũ & in Scripturis non dicitur sacrificium Et hoc solùm appellat sacrificium, quod constat à DEO vocari sacrificium. Quæ enim furentior est temeritas, quàm sic os in cœlum ponere, ut hoc sacrificium & cultum DEI dicas, quod ille non dicit sacrificium & cultum DEI. Geminum ergò crimen falsi committit Jesuvvita: Unum quod scribit, Luthero usum vocabuli Sacramenti summè displicuisse: cùm tamen is nihil aliud vel dixerit, vel scripserit, quàm vocem Sacramenti eâ in significatione, quâ hodiè in Ecclesia usurpatur, nuspiam in Scripturis reperiri. Alterum, quòd quæ de usu vocis sacrificij Luthero scripsit, Jesuvvita nequiter ad usum vocabuli Sacramenti detorquet. Cui utrique mendacio Jesuvvitico coronidis vice opponimus, dilucidam illam protestationem Lutheri, quæ extat eod. Tom. 2. Lat. Jen. pag. 5. 9. b. ubi in Majore Confessione sua sic scribit: Ich lasse es von Hertzen gern zu/daß das Abendmal ein Sacrament sey: obs wol nicht in der Schrifft also genennet wird.


### I. on the Use of the Vocable Sacrament in the Church. Year 1525: II. On the various meanings of the word Sacrament

II. On the various meanings of the word SACRAMENT.

The meaning of the word Sacrament is found to be primarily twofold: one political, the other ecclesiastical. The political is again twofold: for it either denotes a pledge or some deposit, upon the loss of which litigants formerly tested their rights, as Varro writes in his book on the Latin language and the origin of words, book 4, near the end; or it denotes an oath, or the religious obligation that arises from an oath. In which sense it is most frequently used in both civil and canon law, as is evident in Cause 2, questions 4 and 5. Whence the oath of soldiers also came to be called a military Sacrament.

This meaning also applies to Baptism, not indeed equivocally, but analogically; for it is the stipulation of a good conscience with GOD, 1 Peter 3:21. The ecclesiastical sense of this word is likewise twofold: for it signifies either some secret or occult or hidden thing, called by the Greeks μυςήριον. In which sense the word Sacrament is hardly ever found used among profane authors; but among ecclesiastical writers, as also in the Latin Vulgate edition of the Bible, it is by far the most frequent: so that wherever the word μυςήριον occurs in the Greek code of the Bible, the Latin version has the word Sacrament, as can be seen in Tobit 12:7, 'It is good to hide the Sacrament of a king.' Wisdom 2:22, 'They knew not the Sacraments of GOD.' Ephesians 1:9, 3:3, 5:32, Colossians 1:27, 1 Timothy 3:16, and elsewhere passim. In this more general sense, the Fathers also called the mystery of the Lord's Incarnation a Sacrament. Or it denotes not so much the hidden sacred thing itself, as rather some external sign by which the secret itself is contained and shown. This latter meaning is proper to the present Article; which is what Augustine also wished to intimate, Epistle 5 to Marcellinus, when he says that signs, when they pertain to divine things, are called Sacraments.

[Grammatical writers contend with one another regarding the derivation of the word Sacrament; some wish SACRAMENTUM to be said as if it were 'sacrans mentem' (consecrating the mind), just as jurists wish TESTAMENTUM to be said as if it were 'testans mentem' (testifying the mind). But sounder grammarians rightly protest. For it is certain that verbal nouns ending in MENTUM are not composed from 'mens' (mind). Hence Aulus Gellius, book 6, chapter 12, criticizes the jurist Servius Sulpicius because he said that 'Testamentum' was composed from 'testatio' and 'mens': 'What then,' says Gellius, 'of 'calceamentum' (shoe)? What of 'paludamentum' (military cloak)? What of 'pavimentum' (pavement)? What of 'vestimentum' (garment)? What of a thousand others produced by this form?' Hence also Laurentius Valla, book 6, chapter 36, warns that words ending in MENTUM previously ended in MEN, to which termination the syllable TUM was later added, so that for 'spiramen' (breath) one says 'spiramentum,' for 'medicamen' (remedy) 'medicamentum,' for 'velamen' (covering) 'velamentum,' and so on for the rest. To Thomas Aquinas, Sacrament seems to be derived from 'sacrando' (consecrating), just as 'medicamentum' from 'medicando' (healing), and 'ornamentum' from 'ornando' (adorning). And indeed not ineptly. But let this dispute be left to the grammarians.]

Moreover, in this place also a great diversity of opinions presents itself, even among the theologians themselves, who disagree on whether this fourth and final meaning is proper to this Article.

Zwingli, in his book on true and false religion, chapter on the Sacraments, having rejected this fourth meaning, embraces both as political; writing: It is not established that the term Sacrament was used by the ancients for a sacred and secret thing: whence we have not given place to this acceptation: and we are led to see that a Sacrament is nothing other than an incitement or a pledging. For just as those who were about to litigate deposited a certain weight of money which was not permitted to be taken away, unless they were the victors: thus those who are initiated into the Sacraments bind themselves, pledge themselves, and receive as it were an earnest, so that it is not permitted to retreat. Hence the same Zwingli in the same place contends that the Sacraments are nothing other than tokens by which Christians are distinguished from infidels. But this impiety will be refuted ex professo below, where our future discussion will be concerning the ends of the Sacraments.

John Calvin invents a completely new meaning for the word Sacrament, lib. 4. Instit. cap. 14. §. 13. If, he says, we wish to argue more deeply, the Fathers may seem to have applied the name of Sacraments to sacred signs by the same analogy by which the name of faith was transferred to the sense in which it is now used. For since faith is truth in fulfilling promises, yet they called faith the certainty, or certain persuasion, which one might have concerning that very truth: in the same way, since a Sacrament is a soldier's oath by which he vows himself to his Commander, the Fathers nevertheless in a reciprocal sense called it a Sacrament by which GOD, or the Commander, binds Himself to His faithful as if they were soldiers. But this meaning is too cold and jejune, and does not in any way attain the nature and proper office of the Sacraments, as will soon be evident.

Almost all Romanists seize upon a third meaning, and contend that Sacrament for the Latins is the same as μυστήριον is for the Greeks: deceived by the Vulgate Latin version, which rendered the Greek μυστήριον by the word Sacrament, as was shown above. However, they do not notice that these two words are not reciprocal, nor of the same breadth, but that the word μυστήριον is much broader than the word Sacrament. For there are many mysteries of our Religion, that is, secret things, which nevertheless you would not rightly call Sacraments. What is more, the word mystery is even applied by the Apostle to hidden and great wickedness. 2 Thess. 2:7; Apocal. 17:5. Some of the Papists noticed this very thing, and therefore, intending to restrict the generality or looseness of the word Mystery to some extent, they fled to the Greek derivation of this word, asserting that the word μυστῆς, and its conjugate, μυστήριον, descend from the verb μύεω, μυῶ, which means the same as to instruct in sacred things, or to initiate: so that Sacrament has the meaning of sacred things by which men are initiated.

[Dominicus à Soto, in l. 4. sent. dist. 1. artic. 2., quite ridiculously deduces the word μυστήριον from the verb μύω, which is to close, and from the noun στόμα, that is, mouth, because, forsooth, those to whom a secret is entrusted are ordered to close their mouths. Which derivation Eustathius also recites, but without censure. More ridiculously, Claudius Xaintes repeats it, 4. c. 3. pag. 90, and deduces this word from μύες, that is, mice, because, forsooth, mice frequently live in secret places. It is more correctly derived from μυέω, μυῶ: whence descends μυστής, that is, he who has been initiated into sacred things: Hence μυστήριον, that is, a secret thing which is entrusted to those initiated into sacred things.]

But although it cannot be denied that Sacraments properly so called, insofar as secret things and things placed above human understanding are contained in them, can not ineptly be called mysteries: whence Dionysius the Areopagite writes in De hierarch. Eccles. cap. 1. that it is not right for the signs of our mysteries (Sacraments) to reach profane men: yet this word is applied quite improperly to explain the nature of the Sacraments: since it pertains only to some part, or indeed to the use of only one Sacrament, namely Baptism, which is the Sacrament of initiation: but does not fit the Eucharistic Sacrament in this meaning. And indeed we can the less admit this third meaning as proper, the more dangerous the snares are that are laid under it against our purer doctrine by the Sacramentarians, who repeatedly shout with full mouth that Sacraments are mysteries, and therefore should be participated in as mysteries: where they foster ὕπηλόν τι, and strive to undermine and overturn the oral manducation of the body and blood of CHRIST, and every real presence of the same in the Supper.

These things having been thus premised and explained, it becomes plain that we are moved by no light reasons for which we acquiesce in that fourth and simplest meaning, which the etymon of the word Sacrament itself suggests, and believe that Sacrament is said from sacrando (consecrating): because by the use of the Sacraments men are consecrated to GOD: the appellation of the name being taken from the instrumental office of consecrating and conferring grace and holiness. For the Sacraments, if you look at their proper function and office, are not signs only, but also causes or organs of grace. Meanwhile, however, we by no means deny that the Sacraments also have some respect to the remaining meanings: but a less proper and principal one. For according to the first meaning, those who are initiated into the Sacraments truly pledge themselves to GOD: but according to the second, Sacraments are as it were oaths, by which we both bind our faith to GOD, and by which GOD in turn binds Himself to us in a certain way, that He will confer grace upon those to whom the Sacraments are conferred: and finally according to the third meaning, they are also mysteries, insofar as they contain many things that are abstruse and secret in themselves. The primary and most proper, however, is the fourth meaning: as has already been shown. Although this is not taken from Varro and other approved authors of the Latin language, who indeed had no knowledge of the thing itself which is dealt with in the Church: yet it is not lacking in the authority of Ecclesiastical writers, who assigned the name of Sacrament to Baptism and the Lord's Supper, as things clearly new, and revealed only in the New Testament, as being most proper.

Latin:

II. De varia significatione vocabuli SACRAMENTI.

SEnsus vocabuli Sacramenti duplex potissimùm deprehenditur: alius Politicus: alius Ecclesiasticus Politicus rursus duplex: vel enim notat pignus aut depositum aliquod, sub cujus jactura litigantes olim jure experiebatur, ut scribit Varro de lingva lat. & verborum origine, l. 4. sub finem: vel notat jusjurandum, sive religiosam obligationem, quæ ex juramento nascitur. Quo sensu frequentissimè usurpatur in Jure tùm civili, tùm canonico: ut patet causa 2. q. 4. & 5. Undè juramentum etiam militum, vocari cõsuevit Sacramentum militare.

Quae significatio convenit etiā Baptifmati, nō quidem æquivocè, sed analogicè; quippè qui est stipulatio bonae conscientiae cum DEO, 1. Petr. 3, 21. Ecclesiasticus vocabuli hujus sensus itidem duplex est: Vel enim rem aliquam secretam sive occultam aut absconditam significat: Græcis μυςήριον dictam. Quo sensu usurpata vox Sacramenti apud prophanos Autores vix uspiam occurrit: apud Ecclesiasticos autem Scriptores, ut & in latinâ vulgatâ Bibliorum editione longè est frequentissima: ita ut ubicunque in Græco Bibliorum codice occurrit vox μυςήριον, ibi Latina versio habeat vocem Sacramenti: uti videre est, Tobiæ 12, 7. Sacramentum regis abscondere bonum est. Sap. 2, 22. Nescierunt Sacramenta DEI. Eph. 1, 9. c. 3, 3. c. 5, 32. Coloss. 1, 27. 1. Tim. 3, 16. & passim alibi. Sensu hoc generaliore Patres etiam Incarnationis Dominicæ mysterium appellarunt Sacramentum. Vel notat non tàm rem ipsam sacram latentem, quàm externum potiùs aliquod signum, quo secretum ipsum continetur & ostenditur. Quæ postrema significatio præsentis Articuli est propria: id quod Augustinus etiam innuere voluit, epist. 5. ad Marcellinum, signa inquirens, cùm ad res divinas pertinent, Sacramenta appellantur.

[De derivatione vocabuli Sacramenti Grammatici Scriptores invicem digladiantur, volunt aliqui SACRAMENTUM dictū esse, quasi sacrans mentem: Sicut Juris Consulti volunt TESTAMENTUM dici, quasi testans mentem. Sed rectè reclamant saniores Grammatici. Certùm enim est verbalia, desinentia in MENTUM, non esse à mente composita. Hinc A. Gellius libr. 6. c. 12. reprehendit Servium Sulpitium Juris Consultum, quod Testamentum dixit compositum esse à testatione & à mente: Quid igitur, inquit Gellius, calceamentum? quid paludamentum? quid pavimentum? quid vestimentum? quid alia mille per hujusmodi formam producta. Hinc etiam Laurentius Valla libr. 6. c. 36. monet, vocabula in MENTUM desinentia, anteā exiisse in MEN, cui terminationi Syllaba TUM postmodum sit adjecta, ut pro spiramen dicatur spiramentum, pro medicamen, medicamentum, pro velamen, velamentum, & sic de cæteris. Thoma Aquinati Sacramentum videtur dici à sacrando, sicut medicamentum à medicando, ornamentum ab ornando. Et quidem non ineptè. Sed hæc lis sit penes Grammaticos.]

Cœterùm & hoc loco magna se offert sententiarum diversitas, inter ipsos etiam Theologos, in eo dissentientes, utrùm quarta hæc & postrema significatio, hujus Articuli sit propria?

Zvvinglius lib. de vera & falsa relig. cap. de Sacramentis, repudiata quarta hac significatione, politicam utramque amplectitur: scribens: Sacramentum pro re sacra & arcana apud veteres accipi, non constat: undè huic acceptioni locum non dedimus: & adducimur, ut Sacramentum nihil aliud esse videamus, quàm incitationem aut oppignorationem. Sicut enim qui litigaturi erant, certum pecuniæ pondus deponebant, quod auferri nō licebat, nisi vincent: sic qui Sacramentis initiantur, sese adstringunt, oppignorant, ac velut arrhabonem accipiunt, ut referre pedem non liceat. Hinc idem Zvvinglius ibidem contendit. Sacramentanihil esse aliud, quam tesseras, quibus Christiani ab infidelibus discernantur. Sed hæc impietas ex professo refutabitur infrà, ubi de Sacramentorum finibus, nobis futura disputatio.

Johannes Calvinus novam planè vocis Sacramenti significationem comminiscitur, lib. 4. Instit. cap. 14. §. 13. Si, inquiens, altius argutari volumus, videri possunt Patres eâdem analogiâ, Sacramentorum nomen signis sacris indidisse, qua nomen fidei translatum fuit ad eum sensum, in quo nunc usurpatur. Cùm enim fides sit in præstandis promissis veritas: fidem tamen dixerunt certitudinem, sive certam persuasionem, quæ de ipsa veritate haberetur: ad eundem modum, cùm Sacramentum sit militis, quo se suo Imperatori vovet: Patres tamen reciprocato sensu vocarunt Sacramentum, quo DEUS seu Imperator, fidelibus suis tanquàm militibus se obstringit. Verùm hæc significatio nimis frigida & jejuna est, neque Sacramentorum naturam ac officium proprium ullatenùs assequitur: uti mox patebit.

Romanenses plerique omnes tertiam significationem arripiunt, & Sacramentum Latinis idem esse contendunt, quod Græcis est μυστήριον: decepti vulgata versione Latina, quæ Græcum μυστήριον, per vocem Sacramenti reddidit, uti suprà ostensum. Cæterùm non animadvertunt isti, duo hæc vocabula non esse reciproca, neque ejusdem latitudinis: sed vocem μυστήριον multò latiùs vocabulo Sacramenti. Multa enim sunt Religionis nostræ mysteria, hoc est, res secretæ, quæ tamen non rectè vocaveris Sacramenta. Quid quòd vox mysterij etiam ad occultam & magnam nequitia ab Apostolo accommodatur. 2. Thess. 2, 7. Apocal. 17, 5. Animadverterunt hoc ipsum nonnulli ex Pontificijs, ac proindè generalitatem sive laxitatem vocis Mysterij aliquatenùs restricturi, ad Græcam vocabuli hujus derivationem confugerunt, asserentes, vocem μυστῆς, & hujus συζυγον, μυστήριον, descendere à verbo μύεω, μυῶ, quod idem significat, ac sacris instruere, sive initiare: ita ut Sacramentum significationem sacrorum habeat, quibus initiantur homines.

[Ridiculè nimis Dominicus à Soto, in l. 4. sent. dist. 1. artic. 2. deducit vocem μυστήριον, à verbo μύω, quod est claudo, & à nomine σῶμα, id est, os, quia nimirùm os claudere jubentur, quibus secretum committitur. Quam derivationem recitat etiam Eustathius, sed sine censura. Magis ridiculè Claudius Xaintes repetit. 4. c. 3. pag. 90. deducit hanc vocem à μύες, id est mures, quia nimirùm mures frequenter degant, in locis secretis. Rectius derivatur à μυέω μυῶ: undè descendit μυστής, hoc est, is, qui sacris initiatus est: Hinc μυστήριον, hoc est, res secreta, quæ sacris initiatis est concredita.]

Sed licèt negari non possit, Sacramenta propriè sic dicta, quatenùs in ijs res etiam secretæ, & supra intellectum humanum positæ continentur, haud ineptè mysteria posse nuncupari: Undè Dionysius Areopagita de bierarch. Eccles. cap. 1. scribit, fas non esse, ut prophanis hominibus mysteriorum (Sacramentorum) nostrorum signa contingant: tamen impropriè admodum ad explicandam Sacramentorum naturam hæc vox accommodatur: cùm partem tantùm aliquam, imò unius duntaxat Sacramenti usui competat, nempè Baptismo, qui est Sacramentum initiationis: Sacramento autem Eucharistico, in hoc significatu, non conveniat. Et quidem tantò minus tertiam significationem hanc, tanquàm propriam admittere possumus, quantò periculosiores insidiæ sub ea, puriori nostræ doctrinæ struuntur à Sacramentarijs, pleno ore subindè clamantibus, Sacramenta esse mysteria, ac proindè tanquàm mysteria participanda esse: ubi ὕπηλόν τι fovent, & oralem manducationem corporis & sangvinis CHRISTI, omnemque realem eorundem præsentiam in Cœná, subruere & evertere student.

His ita præmissis & explicatis, planum fit, nos haud levibus moveri rationibus, propter quas in quarta illa & simplicissima significatione, quam ipsum vocabuli Sacramenti ἔτυμον suggerit, acquiescamus, & Sacramentum à sacrando dictum esse existimemus: propterea quòd Sacramentorum usu homines consecrentur DEO: nominis appellatione petitâ, ab officio instrumentali sacrandi, & gratiam ac sanctimoniam conferendi. Sacramenta enim, si proprium ipsorum munus atque officium spectes, non signa tantùm: sed & causæ sive organa sunt gratiæ. Interim tamen minimè negamus, quòd Sacramenta reliquarum etiam significationum respectum aliquem sortiantur: sed minùs proprium ac principalem. Nam secundum primam significationem Sacramentis qui initiantur, illi verè DEO se oppignorant: juxta secundam verò, Sacramenta sunt veluti juramenta, quibus & nos fidem obstringimus DEO, & quibus DEUS se vicissim nobis quodammodo obstringit, se collaturum gratiam ijs, quibus Sacramenta conferuntur:ac tandem juxta tertiam significationem, sunt etiam mysteria, quatenùs in se abstrusa & secreta multa continent. Primaria tamen & maximè propria est quarta significatio: uti jam ostensum. Hæc licèt ex Varrone & alijs probatis lingvæ Latinæ autoribus non sit petita, quippè qui rei ipsius, de quâ in Ecclesia agitur, notitiam nullam habuerunt: non tamen caret autoritate Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum, qui Baptismo & Cœnæ Dominicæ, tanquàm rebus planè novis, & in Novo demùm Testamento revelatis, Sacramenti nomen, ut maximè proprium assignârunt.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments

CHAPTER I. ON the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments.

Just as the nature and essence of any thing, whether sacred or profane, is most correctly elicited from its own proper definition, so too is that of the Sacraments. Now, indeed, among theological writers, very many definitions occur everywhere, differing not so much in words as in sense; it is a matter of conscience for us to recount each of these in this place. There are, however, three principal ones, which, being drawn partly from the writings of the Holy Fathers, partly from those of the Scholastics, and finally partly from those of our own theologians, are today most especially accustomed to come into controversy between us and the Calvinists.

The first acknowledges St. Augustine as its author, who in book 10 of The City of God, chapter 5, defines a Sacrament as a sign of a sacred thing. This definition we can more truly call nominal than essential, since it contains only the notation and interpretation of the name. Of the same kind and value is the fact that the same Augustine defines a Sacrament as a visible Word, in Tractate 80 on John.

The second is that of the Scholastics, for whom a Sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace, in such a way that it bears its likeness and exists as its cause; as can be seen in Lombard, Thomas Aquinas, and Albert the Great, book 4 of the Sentences, distinction 1, as also in Hugh of St. Victor, book 1, part 9, chapter 2, On the Sacraments, who, explaining Lombard's definition not at all, says: A Sacrament is a corporeal element, proposed outwardly in a sensible manner, representing by likeness, signifying by institution, and conferring some invisible and spiritual grace by sanctification.

Scotus defines it thus: A Sacrament is a sensible sign, effectively signifying the grace of GOD, or its gratuitous effect, by divine institution, ordained for the salvation of man as a wayfarer.

These, indeed, like other definitions of this kind, define the Sacrament only in part, insofar as they consist of an element and a word; but they do not explain the whole nature of the Sacrament from every kind of cause. Furthermore, under the guise of invisible grace, of which they wish the Sacrament to be the visible sign or form, they foster and conceal a horrendous error, which we must examine expressly below in chapter 2.

The third definition, and indeed that of our own theologians, seems to labor under no small difficulty, because of the significant discrepancy in the words and phrases of which it consists.

Our author Philip defines a Sacrament as a sign of grace, that is, of the gratuitous reconciliation which is given on account of CHRIST and is preached in the Gospel. And towards the beginning of this Article, he says: A Sacrament is called a ceremony instituted in the Gospel, that it may be a testimony of the promise, which is the promise of the Gospel, namely, of the promised reconciliation or grace. More recent theologians define a Sacrament as a ceremony or action divinely instituted, consisting of Word and Element, by which, as by a Seal, the promise of the Gospel proper, concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, is applied and sealed through and on account of CHRIST. Others, again, say that a Sacrament is a visible form or sign of invisible grace, divinely instituted for this purpose, that it may not only bear the image or likeness of that grace, but also exist as its cause, and confer the same upon those who use it legitimately.

These definitions, although they consist of very different words and phrases—and both of Philip's definitions seem to be both more general and more obscure, and indeed to be easily adaptable to the dogma of the Calvinists—nevertheless, nothing prevents us from eliciting, from each of these and others of this kind, not indeed separately but taken together, certain degrees, as it were, by which the entire nature and essence of the Sacraments can be fully constituted and completed; and indeed according to the four kinds of causes, which perfect the essential definition of any thing that is being discussed.

In the beginning, therefore, a true and legitimate Sacrament is not one unless it has been divinely instituted: that is, whose author and efficient cause, the principal one, is GOD alone. Furthermore, as regards matter and form, a Sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing, and indeed a visible sign: but not a sign of just any sacred thing, but only of invisible grace, which is proper to the Gospel. Finally, we elicit this as the final cause of a Sacrament, that it both confers and confirms this invisible grace in the faithful. Whence a full and perfect definition of a Sacrament arises, namely that it is a visible sign divinely ordained, of invisible evangelical grace, concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, through and on account of CHRIST, and that it confers, confirms, and seals the same in all who legitimately use the Sacrament.

Nor indeed is this definition destitute of the authority of the Scriptures, but rather the Lord Apostle in Romans 4:11 seems to have encompassed with ingenious brevity the individual things that perfect the nature of a Sacrament, stating that Abraham received circumcision, which for him, as regards matter and form, was a sign: but as regards the final cause or use, it was a seal of the righteousness of faith. For these two words (sign and seal) are not the same or equivalent in meaning: for thus the Apostle could be accused of idle ταυτολογίας, as if he had defined the same thing by itself: but they are clearly different in sense: which both the Greek words σημεῖον and σφραγὶς and the thing itself prove: so that this Apostolic definition, as also our own now proposed, applies συνωνύμως or univocally to every Sacrament of both the Old and New Testament. For the Levitical Sacraments also, specifically so called, namely circumcision and the Paschal Lamb, were σημεῖα signs, that is, they signified a sacred thing, namely the grace of the promise concerning the seed of the woman, in whom all the nations of the earth were to be blessed, which is proper to the Gospel: they were also σφραγίδες seals of the righteousness of faith, that is, they conferred and sealed that grace in all, as many as used the Sacraments by faith in CHRIST, not yet indeed at that time incarnate: but yet to be incarnate in his own time: the type of which future work those Sacraments also contained in themselves at the same time.

Moreover, since those things which we have hitherto touched upon concerning the nature and essence of a Sacrament are still somewhat obscure: certainly the very purity of the Christian Religion most especially demands that the individual members of the proposed definition be examined more accurately and separately: and that according to the four kinds of causes by which the definition itself is completed.

Latin:

CAPUT I. DE Natura atque Essentia Sacramentorum.

QUemadmodum cujuslibet rei tam sacræ, quàm prophanæ: sic Sacramentorum etiam natura atque Essentia, ex propria eorundem definitione, rectissimè elicitur. Jam verò apud Scriptores Theologos benè multæ, & nõ tam verbis, quàm sensu discrepantes definitiones passim occurrunt: quas singulas hoc loco percensere, religio nobis est. Tres tamen sunt præcipuæ, quæ ex S. Patrum partim, partim ex Scholasticorum, partim denique ex nostrorum Theologorum Scriptis petitæ, hodiè potissimùm inter nos & Calvinianos sub controversiam venire solent.

Prima D. Augustinum agnoscit autorem, qui lib. 10. de Civit. DEI, cap. 5. Sacramentum definit, quòd sit rei sacræ signum. Quam definitionem ὀνοματώδη veriùs, quàm ὀσιώδη nominare possumus, quippè quæ nominis tantùm notationem & interpretationem continet. Cujus generis & valoris est etiam, quòd idem Augustinus Sacramentum definit esse Verbum visibile. Tractatu 80. in Johannem.

Altera est Scholasticorum, quibus Sacramentum est invisibilis gratiæ visibilis forma, ita ut ejus similitudinem gerat, & causa existat: uti videre est apud Lombardum, Thomam Aquinatem, & Albertum M. libr. 4. sent. dist. 1. ut & apud Hugonem de S. Victore l. 1. par. 9. c. 2. de Sacramentis, qui Lombardi definitionem nonn hil declarans, Sacramentum est, inquit, elementum corporale, foris sensibiliter propositum, ex similitudine repræsentans, ex institutione significans, ex Sanctificatione aliquam gratiam invisibilem & spiritualem conferens.

Scotus sic definit: Sacramentum est signum sensibile, gratiam DEI, vel ejus effectum gratuitum, ex institutione divina efficaciter significans, ordinatum ad salutem hominis viatoris.

Quæ sanè, ut & hujus generis definitiones aliæ, Sacramentum ex parte tantùm definiunt, quatenùs nimirùm constant elemento & verbo: totam autem Sacramenti naturam, ex omni causarum genere, non explicant. Quid quòd sub gratia invisibili, cujus visibile signum aut formam volunt esse Sacramentum, horrendum errorem fovent & occultant: de quo infrà cap. 2. ex professo nobis dispiciendum.

Tertia & quidem nostrorum Theologorum definitio, haud exiguâ videtur laborare difficultate, propter insignem verborum ac phrasium, quibus constat, discrepantiam.

Autor noster Philippus definit Sacramentum, quòd sit signum gratiæ, hoc est, reconciliationis gratuitæ, quæ propter CHRISTUM donatur, & in Evangelio prædicatur. Et sub initium Articuli hujus, Sacramentum, inquit, vocatur ceremonia in Evangelio instituta, ut sit testimonium promissionis, quæ est Evangelii propria videlicet promissæ reconciliationis seu gratiæ. Recentiores Theologi definiunt Sacramentum: quòd sit ceremonia seu actio divinitùs instituta, constans Verbo & Elemento, quâ tanquàm Sigillo, promissio Evangelii propria, de gratuitâ peccatorum remissione, per & propter CHRISTUM applicatur & obsignatur. Rursus alii, Sacramentum, dicunt, esse formam sive signum visibile gratiæ invisibilis, divinitùs in hoc institutum, ut Gratiæ illius non tantùm imaginem sive similitudinem gerat: sed & causa ejus existat, eandemq́; legitimè utentibus conferat.

Quæ definitiones, licèt verbis & phrasibus constent diversissimis: & utraque Philippica tùm generalior, tùm obscurior esse, quin etiam Calvinianorum dogmati facilè accommodari posse videatur: nihil tamen obstat, quò minùs ex singulis istis, & hujus generis aliis, non quidem seorsim, sed simul sumtis, certos quasi gradus eliciamus, quibus universa Sacramentorum natura & essentia, plenè constitui & absolvi queat: & quidem secundum quatuor causarum genera, quæ essentialem cujuslibet rei, de qua disputatur, definitionem perficiunt.

Initiò igitur Sacramentum verum & legitimum non fuerit, nisi quod divinitùs sit institutum: hoc est, cujus autor & causa efficiens, principalis sit solus DEUS. Deindè verò quoad materiam & formam, Sacramentum est rei sacræ signum, & signum quidem visibile: Sed non rei cujusvis sacræ signum, verùm tantùm Gratiæ invisibilis, quæ Evangelii est propria. Tandem causam finalem Sacramenti elicimus hanc, ut Gratiam hanc invisibilem & conferat, & confirmet in fidelibus. Undè plena & perfecta Sacramenti definitio exurgit, quod nimirùm sit signum visibile divinitùs ordinatum, invisibilis gratiæ Evangelicæ, de gratuita peccatorum remissione, per & propter CHRISTUM, eandemq́; conferat, confirmet & obsignet in omnibus legitimè Sacramento utentibus.

Neque verò Definitio hæc Scripturarum destituitur autoritate, quin D. Apostolus Rom. 4, 11. argutâ brevitate complexus esse videtur singula, quæ Sacramenti naturam perficiunt, afferens, Abrahamum accepisse circumcisionem, quæ ipfi, quoad materiam & formam fuerit signum: quoad causam finalem verò sive usum, fuerit signaculum justitiæ fidei. Neque enim duo hæc vocabula (signum & signaculum) significatione sunt eadem aut æquipollentia: Sic enim Apostolus otiosæ ταυτολογίας infimulari posset, quasi idem per se ipsum definivisset: sed sensu planè sunt diversa: id quod tùm vocabula Græca σημεῖον & σφραγὶς tùm res ipsa evincit: ita ut Definitio hęc Apostolica, ut & nostra jam proposita, omni Sacramento tàm Veteris, quàm Novi Testamenti συνωνύμως sive univocè côveniat. Nam & Levitica Sacramenta specificè sic appellata, circumcisio scilicet & Agnus Paschalis, erant σημεῖα signa, hoc est, significabant rem sacram sacrātem, nempè gratiam promissionis de semine mulieris, in quo benedicendæ erant omnes gentes terræ, propriam: erant etiam σφραγίδες signacula justitiæ fidei, hoc est, conferebant, & obsignabant gratiam illam in omnibus, quotquot Sacramentis uterentur fide in CHRISTUM, nondum quidem tunc incarnatum: sed incarnandum tamen suo tempore: cujus operis futuri typum etiam simul Sacramenta illa in se continebant.

Cæterùm cùm obscuriora adhuc sint, quę de natura atque essentia Sacramenti hactenùs delibavimus: certè ipsa Religionis Christianæ puritas vel maximè efflagitat, ut definitionis propositæ membra singula seorsim accuratiùs excutiantur: idque secundum quatuor causarum genera, quibus definitio ipsa absolvitur.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: The efficient cause of Sacraments

Two things especially come under question in this place: First, who is the author and founder of the Sacraments. Second, what the person dispensing the Sacraments may work, and what power and efficacy he may provide regarding the effect of the Sacraments.

Regarding the former question, the founder or author of the Sacraments, upon whom the institution and ordination itself solely depends, is GOD alone, both in the Old and the New Testament: who in the circumcision of Abraham Gen. 17, 10 and in the Paschal Lamb, prescribed to Moses, Exod. 12, 3, similarly in the Sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper, showed clearly enough which Sacraments ought to be in the Church, what also is their matter, form, what end, what effect. And God willed to found the Sacraments for this reason, because since we were corporeal, and by our nature could not become participants of spiritual and incorporeal gifts, therefore it was necessary for GOD to συγκαταβαίνειν, and to lower himself to our infirmity, and to include spiritual gifts in corporeal things: as Chrysostom has it in homily 60 to the people of Antioch. Then, since our mind borrows the knowledge of all things from the senses according to that saying: There is nothing in the intellect which was not first in the sense: therefore GOD also willed that that which He decreed to impart to us as spiritual should first be perceived through the ministry of the senses.

With these reasons standing thus, it is a consequence that it is not placed in the power of any man to found any Sacrament. D. Thomas recognized this very thing long ago, writing thus in part 3, quest. 62, art. 5. Because the sanctification of man is in the power of the sanctifying GOD, it does not pertain to man to assume by his own judgment the elements by which he may be sanctified: but this must be determined by divine institution. Which decision of Thomas indeed provides us with the first reason, on account of which we maintain that nothing at all can have the nature of a Sacrament properly so called, unless it is that which was instituted by God Himself either in the Old Testament or by CHRIST in the New. For because the Sacraments are efficacious signs of grace: but it belongs to no man to found the means through which grace may be conferred: much less can any man confer Grace itself principally: certainly it would not be placed in the power of any man to found any new Sacrament, besides those which it is clear by the confession of all were instituted divinely. Looking to which the Apostle says, Were you baptized in the name of Paul? 1 Cor. 1, 13.

Then indeed that also deserves observation, that Christ instituted all the Sacraments immediately by Himself, not only by prescribing and commanding what is the matter and form of the Sacraments: but also by promulgating the institution itself: But He instituted no Sacrament either mediately through the Apostles: or promulgated later in a peculiar way any Sacrament instituted by Himself separately: which is clearly evident by the induction of all the Sacraments of both Testaments.

Thirdly, the Apostles never instituted or promulgated any Sacrament: But they only administered or dispensed those instituted and promulgated by Christ: Which administration is to be held as a matter of accident, and contributes nothing to the institution of the Sacraments themselves. Hence the Apostle himself says, Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of GOD, 1 Cor. 4, 1.

Fourthly: in whose power it is not placed to found new Articles of faith, in his power it will also not be to found Sacraments. But the former was not placed in the power of any man, nor indeed even in the power of any Apostle: but it belongs to GOD alone. Therefore this latter does as well.

The connection of the major premise is evident from this, that grace is given no less through the Sacraments than through the word and the articles of faith: and that also in every Sacrament something is given to be held by faith.

No one will easily deny the minor premise, unless the Roman superstition has long since bewitched his mind with the spell of error. Certainly it is Christ alone who founded the Church, and by Himself established all its foundations: upon which indeed our salvation and liberation from sins depends: as has been shown expressly in the article concerning the Church.

We conclude therefore that CHRIST the Savior alone is the sole true author and most perfect founder of the Sacraments: and that it is not permitted either to the whole Church or to any mortal to add any Sacrament whatsoever to those which have been ordained by Christ. Nor does it in the least hinder this assertion that the Savior Himself did not dispense all the Sacraments: just as it is read in John 4:2, that He did not baptize. For this dispensation is accidental, and nothing is added to or taken away from the plenary institution of the Sacraments by it. Add that the administration of the Sacraments is a clearly distinct and peculiar act from their institution.

Moreover, the solution to that question depends on this decision, in which it is disputed whether it is in the power of the Church or of any man to so change the matter and form, or anything pertaining to the essence of a Sacrament, that in place of that which Christ instituted, another thing is substituted? For we maintain that a distinction must be properly made between those things which constitute the essence of a Sacrament, and those circumstances constituted, as it were, outside and beyond the matter of the Sacraments. In the former, it is not permitted to change anything at all, not even the slightest thing, to such an extent that even the Apostles themselves would no more have changed the institution of Christ in any part than they would have presumed to establish a new article of faith. Hence it is that neither the Church of any times,

Latin:

DUo potissimùm hoc loco sub quæstionem veniunt: Primum, quis sit autor & conditor Sacramentorum. Alterum, quid operetur, quamque vim & efficaciam circa Sacramentorum effectum præstare possit, persona dispensans Sacramenta.

Quoad prius ζήτημα, conditor sive autor Sacramentorum, à quo ipsa institutio & ordinatio unicè dependet, est solus DEUS, tàm in Veteri, quàm Novo Testamento: qui in circumcisione Abrahamo Gen. 17, 10 & in Agno Paschali, Mosi præscripto, Exod. 12, 3. similiter in Baptismi & Cœnæ Dominicæ Sacramentis, satis dilucidè ostendit, quænam Sacramenta in Ecclesia esse debeant, quæ etiam eorum sit materia, forma, quis finis, quis effectus. Idcò autem Deus Sacramenta condere voluit, quia cùm nos corporei essemus, & ex naturâ nostrâ spiritualium & incorporeorum donorum participes evadere haud possemus, ideò oportuit DEUM συγκαταβαινειν, & ad infirmitatem nostram sese demittere, & spiritualia dona rebus corporeis includere: uti habet Chrysostomus homil. 60. ad pop. Antioch. Deindè cùm rerum omnium notitiam mens nostra à sensibus mutuetur secundum illud: Nihil est in intellectu, quod non prius fuerit in sensu: ideò DEUS etiam id, quod nobis spirituale impertire decrevit, sensuum etiam ministerio prius percipi voluit.

Quibus rationibus ita stantibus consequens est, in nullius hominis potestate situm, ut Sacramentum aliquod condat. Agnovit hoc ipsum jam olim quoque D. Thomas, sic scribens part. 3. quæst. 62. art. 5. Quia sanctificatio hominis est in potestate DEI sanctificantis, non pertinet ad hominem, suo judicio assumere elementa, quibus sanctificetur: sed hoc debet esse ex divina institutione determinatum. Quæ sanè Thomæ decisio primam nobis rationem subministrat, ob quam statuimus, nihil prorsus posse habere rationem Sacramenti propriè sic dicti, nisi quod vel in Veteri Testamento à Deo ipso vel in Novo, à CHRISTO est institutum. Quia enim Sacramenta sunt signa efficacia gratiæ: hominis autem nullius est, condere media, per quæ conferatur gratia: nedum hominum quisquam Gratiam ipsam conferre principaliter potest: utique in nullius etiam hominis potestate fuerit positum, novum aliquod condere Sacramentum, præter ea, quæ divinitùs instituta esse, omnium confessione liquet. Quò respiciens Apostolus, Nùm, inquit, in nomen Pauli baptizati estis? 1. Cor. 1, 13.

Deinde verò & illud obfervationem meretur, quòd Christus omnia Sacramenta instituit immediatè per seipsum, non solùm præscribendo præcipiendoq;, quæ sit materia & forma Sacramentorum : sed etiam promulgando ipsam institutionem : Nullum verò Sacramentum, vel mediatè per Apostolos instituit : vel à se seorfim institutum, peculiariter postmodùm per Apostolos promulgavit: id quod inductione omnium Sacramentorum utriusque Testamenti, liquidò constat.

Tertiò, Apostoli nullum unquàm Sacramentum instituerunt aut promulgârunt : Sed à Christo instituta & promulgata, tantùm administrarunt sive dispensarunt: Quæ administratio in parte accidentis est habenda, neque ad ipsam Sacramentorũ institutionem quicquam confert. Hinc Apostolus ipse, Sic nos, inquit, astimet homo, tanquam ministros Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum DEI, 1. Cor. 4, 1.

Quartò: in cujus potestate non est positum condere novos Articulos fidei, in illius etiam potestate non erit, condere Sacramenta. Atqui prius illud in nullius hominis, imò ne quidem in ullius Apostoli potestate erat positum : sed soli DEo competit. Ergò & hoc posterius.

Connexum majoris vel indè patet, quod per Sacramenta non minus datur gratia, quàm per verbum & articulos fidei : quòd etiam in quolibet Sacramento datur aliquid fide tenendum.

Minorem nemo facilè negaverit, nisi cujus animum Romana superstitio erroris fascino jam pridem perstrinxit. Certè solus Christus est, qui fundavit Ecclesiam, & per seipsum omnia ejus fundamenta constituit: à quibus quidem salus nostra & liberatio à peccatis pendet: uti ex professo ostensum, artic. de Ecclesia.

Concludimus proindè, solùm CHRISTUM Servatorem, esse unicum verum autorem, & conditorem perfectissimum Sacramentorum : neq; vel toti Ecclesiæ, vel cuipiam mortalium fass esse, ullum aliquod Sacramentum, illis, quæ à Christo ordinata sunt, superaddere. Neque assertioni huic vel tantillum obstat, quòd Servator ipse non omnia Sacramenta dispensavit : quemadmodum Johan. 4, 2. legitur, quòd non baptizaverit. Nam dispensatio hæc accidentis est, & institutioni plenariæ Sacramentorum nihil ex ea vel accedit vel decedit. Adde quod administratio Sacramentorum ab eorundem institutione, distinctus planè & peculiaris actus est.

Cœterùm ab hac decisione dependet illius Quæstionis solutio, quâ controvertitur, An vel in Ecclesiæ, vel cujusquam hominis potestate sit, ita mutare materiam & formam, aut aliquid pertinens ad essentiam Sacramenti, ut loco ejus, quod instituit Christus, aliud substituatur? Distinguendum enim probè esse statuimus inter ea quæ Sacramenti essentiam constituunt: & inter circumstantias, foris quasi, & extra Sacramentorum materiam constitutas. In illis nihil quicquam, ne mini. mum quidem mutare licet, usque adeò, ut ipsi quoque Apostoli, Christi institutionem ulla ex parte haud magis mutaverint, quàm novum fidei articulum condere præsumserint. Hinc est, ut neque Ecclesia quorumvis temporum,


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: Whether all Christians have the power to administer the Sacraments?

nor can any mortal bring it about that any elemental water cannot be the matter of Baptism, or that wine or something similar of the same kind is its matter: or that any wine cannot be the matter of the Eucharist: or that water, milk, or beer can be the matter of the same. The reason is, because Christ invisible grace.

Moreover, that it is permitted to change something in the circumstances, provided that the intention of Christ the institutor and the proper end of the Sacrament remain intact, can be confirmed by the authority and practice of Orthodox Antiquity, provided, however, that the twofold caution which is expressed in the same place is observed. For example: In the primitive Church, the triple immersion of the infant to be baptized was customary. And yet Cyprian rightly argues in book 4, epistle 7, that it is lawful for the Church to use Baptism performed by mere aspersion: because it is evident from the examples of the Scriptures that complete purification and expiation are effected no less by affusion or aspersion than by immersion; and that both these modes of baptizing, as regards power and efficacy, amount to the same thing. He also adds that the Apostles themselves in the Acts administered baptism in both ways.

Furthermore, the causes for which the Church can change something regarding the institution of the Sacraments, as regards circumstances, as also regarding other precepts of the Lord, are chiefly two: The former is that of necessity, by which David, being compelled, lawfully ate the loaves of proposition, which it was otherwise forbidden to eat, 1 Sam. 21:6. It is thought that it was for this cause that sprinkling regarding Baptism prevailed, which they believe was first used for the sick.

Which mode of baptizing, observed in adults, was finally, when the necessity ceased, retained in the Church in the baptizing of infants, who are not unjustly compared to the sick, lest it be thought that it is always necessary to return to the original law, once the cause of necessity, on account of which one had departed from the law, has been removed.

The other cause is departure from heretics, to avoid the danger of scandal that would otherwise be inevitable. For while the integrity of the Sacrament and the end of the institution remain safe, it is better to depart rightly from certain external ceremonies than to have any commerce with heretics regarding religion, which is asserted and defended not only by word but also by deed. CHRIST taught this by the example of his own action, who omitted the washing of hands before a meal, and did not abstain from the company of sinners: testifying by both actions that he had nothing in common with the error of the Pharisees, who were persuaded that they were polluted by the company of even repenting sinners, but were expiated by external washings. Thus, as long as the heresy of the Sabellians and other Anti-trinitarians raged, the purer antiquity solicitously retained the rite of triple immersion. But after the Arian heresy crept in, which with a clearly contrary impiety divided the nature of the Divinity, just as the persons, into many: the triple immersion being omitted, a different rite obtained in the Church. This is established by the decree of the Fourth Council of Toledo, can. 5, in these words: To avoid the scandal of schism, or the use of heretical dogma, let us hold to a single immersion of baptism. Gregory expressed this more clearly in book 1, Epist. 41, to Leander: Because until now the infant was immersed three times in baptism by heretics, I do not think it should be done among us, lest, while they count the immersions, they divide the divinity, and while they do what they were doing, they boast that they have overcome our custom.

The Ebionites, out of zeal for the Mosaic law, contended that the Eucharist must be celebrated only in unleavened bread. To weaken this error, Leo the Great decreed, as Richard of St. Victor testifies, that henceforth the celebration should take place not in unleavened, but in leavened bread. Again, the Greeks fought against the Latins that the use of leavened bread was of simple necessity: the Latins, who felt the contrary, they called Azymites. To obviate this stubbornness, it was decreed that henceforth the celebration of the Eucharist should take place from unleavened bread alone. The Church today still usurps this liberty, and although it cannot establish Sacraments, it can nevertheless sanction those things which pertain to the solemnity and reverence of the Sacrament: such as: prayers, psalms, rites, and ceremonies, directed partly to excite devotion, partly to suggest pious admonitions. To which also pertains the rite of Exorcism, regarding the action of Baptism: as also the ringing of bells, which in some reformed Churches is put into use regarding the recitation of the words of institution: Likewise kneeling, and other external ceremonies of that kind.

And let these things said about the principal efficient sacramental cause suffice: It remains that we examine in a few words what is to be determined regarding both the office and the operation of the ministers who dispense them. This whole dispute can be conveniently expedited by three Questions.

THE FIRST is: Do all CHRISTIANS have the power of administering the Sacraments? Regarding which question both the Anabaptists and the Calvinists err gravely today. The Anabaptists indeed, when they teach that the use or power of administering the Sacraments is common to all. The Calvinists indeed, when they simply reject Baptism conferred in a case of necessity by some private person, especially by a woman. We, in order to walk the middle path, so that we may sin neither in excess nor in defect, will encompass the whole matter in a few hypotheses.

I. The Holy Spirit in the Scriptures does not intend for the parts of the Ecclesiastical Ministry to be common to all who are present in the assembly of the Church: but proper only to those who are legitimately called to teach, as Rom. 10, 15. How shall they preach, unless they are sent? Heb. 5, 4. No one takes this honor to himself, unless he is called by GOD, Rom. 12, 6. & 7. likewise 1. Cor. 12, 5. Eph. 4, 11.
