The Apostle asserts that there are diverse offices and ministries in the Church, which do not belong indifferently to all. Furthermore, neither could the Apostle, Acts 14, 23. Tit. 1, 5. have appointed Bishops and Presbyters, nor could he have commanded that the same be done by them, if that power were common to all. What is more, if such a communion were granted, no order would any longer obtain, but mere confusion in the Church: otherwise than the Apostle commands, 1. Cor. 14, 40. that all things in the Church be done decently and in order.

II. The minister dispensing the Sacraments, although he contributes nothing at all to constituting the essence of the Sacraments, since they [consist] in matter and form its own, consists and is perfected by the will and power of the institutor alone: yet for the truth of the Sacrament, the Minister in ordinary dispensation is so necessary that without him it cannot consist. The reason is: 1. Because this dispensation depends upon the ordinance of Christ, not upon the own will of the ministers. Whence the Apostle testifies that he performs an embassy for Christ, 2 Cor. 5:20. 2. Because the power of administering the Sacraments is not natural or human: but supernatural and divine: whence John the Baptist, speaking of the administration of Baptism, says, No one, he says, can take anything for himself, unless it has been given to him from heaven, John 3:27. 3. Because the office of the Ministry is joined with efficacy and power, especially in the dispensation of the Sacraments, in which the words of the Ministry are not merely speculative, or merely significant: but as it were practical, and efficient of that which they signify: not indeed from the dignity of the person, or from any magical force which might underlie the recitation of the Words of Institution: but because of the ordinance of Christ, who through these words of the minister, effectively effects and works in those using the Sacrament what He promised. Which virtue and promise the words of any private man lack, and therefore effect nothing.

III. A distinction must be made with the blessed Luther between these two: 1. To have the power. 2. To exercise the same. Thus where there are several ministers in one Church, all indeed have the power of administering the Sacraments: but not all exercise it, lest, clearly, any confusion should arise in the Church. Now just as for the sake of order, one can have the power who nevertheless does not exercise the same: so conversely in a case of inevitable necessity, one can exercise the use of the power who nevertheless does not ordinarily have the power of exercising that thing. In which case a woman, any Christian, but not just any man, can be a minister or dispenser of the Sacrament, provided that he observes those things which have been instituted by Christ.

IV. A distinction must, however, be made in this place between the Sacraments themselves. For Baptism admits the ministry even of those who are not ordinarily called to the Ecclesiastical ministry. But the Sacrament of the Eucharist does not admit such a thing. The reason for the diversity is this, that the necessity of Baptism is inevitable, according to that saying of the Savior, John 3:5: Unless one has been born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, in whatever way the supply of Baptism can be had, effort must be made that no Christian be destitute of its reception. But the necessity of the Sacrament of the Eucharist is not equal: but in its defect the rule of Augustine holds: Believe and you have eaten.

THE SECOND question, which is moved in this place, is this: Do evil ministers and heretics also confer true Sacraments? (In Africa, 1300 years ago, there were found Bishops who thought that heretics and Schismatics, after the unity of the Church was broken, did not confer true Sacraments. Augustine thinks that they were induced into this opinion by hatred of Schisms and by a very great zeal for preserving Ecclesiastical unity. Augustine attributes the origin of this error to Agrippinus, a predecessor of Cyprian, and to certain other Bishops of Africa, who preferred to devise some name rather than hold to a custom whose defense they did not understand, book 2, On Baptism against the Donatists, ch. 7. Into which opinion Saint Cyprian later descended, writing several letters for the same to Jubaianus, Quintius, and Pompeius: which, however, he would never have done, as the following chapter Augustine says, unless it had been previously defined by his predecessors: on account of whose authority this error later took greater increments, with a conventicle of 71 Bishops having been gathered in addition, in which a foundation for this error was sought through a definition: the acts of which council are refuted by Augustine, book 2, On Baptism against the Donatists, ch. 2 and following. Which error was rejected by the Nicene council, canon 8: and finally was solemnly condemned by the first Council of Carthage (for the earlier ones are considered as having been stripped of authority). It is to be noted, however, that there was such a dispute by the blessed Cyprian over this error with Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, that no evil of Schism arose between them: nor did he ever presume to condemn the contrary opinion, as Augustine proves from his writings in the book already cited, 2, chapters 2, 3, 4, and book 5, chapter 17. and 25. Indeed, according to Augustine, there were not lacking those who denied entirely that Cyprian had been in this error: which, however, is not proven by Augustine, Epistle 48. Meanwhile, Cyprian is excused by the same in four ways, in these words: Furthermore, Cyprian either did not think at all what you recite that he thought: or he later corrected this in the rule of truth: or he covered this as it were a mole on his most candid breast with the abundance of charity, while he defended the unity of the Church, growing in the whole world, most copiously, and most perseveringly retained the bond of peace. For it is written, charity covers a multitude of sins. There was added to this also, that as a most fruitful Sacrament, if anything in it was to be amended, the Father purged it with the sickle of passion. In later times the Donatists arose, and abusing the authority of Cyprian, undertook to defend this error more perniciously. For they both condemned the contrary opinion as heresy: and what had been defined by a plenary council, as Augustine says, they themselves rejected: and what Cyprian had asserted only concerning heretics and Schismatics, these, having progressed further, referred to all impious ministers: that this was specifically Cresconius the Grammarian, Augustine is the witness, to whom in book 2 written against the same, ch. 28, Augustine replies thus: You said, you also did not fear to write, that whoever is a sinner among all men, let him not usurp for himself the right of Baptism. If therefore you have not yet been baptized, either correct this most vain opinion: or seek Angels by whom you may be baptized. At length, in the previous century, some are reported to have overcome the error of the Donatists, who denied that true Sacraments could be conferred not only by sinners who were then hidden or manifest, but even by those who were however upright, yet destined to die in mortal sin (i.e., not the elect, whom those men called the foreknown). In this our century, the Anabaptists maintain the same error. If there is anyone who requires an industrious refutation of that error from the Scriptures, let him read Thomas Waldensis, Tom. 2, de Sacramentis, from chapter 1 up to 17, and especially those things which were written long before him by Augustine in his seven books de Baptismo contra Donatist., likewise in his three books contra epist. Parmeniani, and in his four books contra Cresconium Grammaticum.

Latin:

neq; mortalium quisquam queat efficere, ut quævis aqua elementaris non possit esse materia Baptismi, aut ut vinum vel simile quid ejusdem sit materia: vel ut quodvis vinum non possit esse materia Eucharistiæ: aut ut aqua, lac, vel cerevisia possit esse ejusdem materia. Ratio est, Quia Christus in Baptismo aquam simpliciter: in Eucharistia verò, panem & vinum, instituit & ordinavit signa invisibilis gratiæ.

Cæterùm, quòd in circumstantijs aliquid mutare liceat, dummodò salva maneat Christi instituentis intentio, & finis Sacramenti proprius, confirmari potest autoritate & praxi Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, observatâ tamẽ geminâ cautione, quæ ibidem exprimitur. Exempli gratia: In primitiva Ecclesiâ usitata fuit trina immersio infantis baptizandi. Atqui Cyprianus rectè disputat l. 4. epist. 7. licitum esse Ecclesiæ, uti Baptismo, per solam aspersionem facto: propterea quòd Scripturarum exemplis constet, purificationem & expiationem integram, non minùs perfusione aut aspersione fieri, quàm immersione: atq; hunc utrumq; baptisandi modum, quoad vim & efficaciam in idem recidere. Addit etiam, Apostolos ipsos in Actis utroq; modo baptismum administrasse.

Porrò causæ, ob quas Ecclesia mutare potest aliquid circa institutionem Sacramentorum, quoad circumstantias, ut & circa alia præcepta Domini, sunt duæ potissimùm: Prior est necessitatis, qua David coactus, licitè comedit panes propositionis, quibus aliàs vesci nefas fuit, 1. Sam. 21 6. Hâc causâ factum fuisse putatur, ut aspersio circa Baptismum invaluerit, quam propter ægros primùm usurpatam fuisse existimant.

Qui modus baptizandi in adultis observatus, tandem cessante necessitate, in baptizandis infantibus, qui ægris haud injuriâ comparantur, retentus fuit in Ecclesia, ne putetur semper necessarium esse, ad jus pristinum redire, sublatâ necessitatis causâ, propter quam à jure discessum fuerat.

Altera causa est, discessio ab hæreticis, ad vitandum inevitabile aliàs scandali periculum. Nam salvâ integritate Sacramenti, & fine institutionis potiùs à ceremonijs quibusdam externis rectè disceditur, quàm cum hæreticis commercij aliquid habetur circa religionem, quæ non verbo tantùm: sed & facto asseritur & defenditur. Docuit hoc CHRISTUS exemplo sui facti, qui manuum lotionem ante prandium omisit, & à peccatorum consortio non abstinuit: utroq; facto nihil sibi communionis esse testificans cum errore Pharisæorum, qui se peccatorum etiam resipiscentium consortio pollui, externis autem lotionibus expiari, persuasum habebant. Sic quandiu Sabellianorũ atq; aliorũ Antitrinitariorũ hæresis grassata fuit, trinæ immersionis ritum antiquitas purior solicitè retinuit. At postquàm Ariana hæresis irrepsit, quæ contrariâ planè impietate, Divinitatis naturam, sicut personas, in plura diremit: immersione trinâ omissâ, diversus ritus in Ecclesia obtinuit. Constat hoc Concilij Toletani Quarti decreto, can. 5. his verbis: Propter vitandũ Schismatis scandalu, vel hæretici dogmatis usum, simplã teneamq baptismatis immersione. Expressit hoc planiùs Gregorius lib. 1. Epist. 41. ad Leandrū: Quia nunc huc usq́; ab hæreticis infans in baptismate tertiò mergebatur, fiendum apud nos esse non censeo, ne, dum mersiones numerant, divinitatē dividant, dumq́; quod faciebant, faciunt, se morē nostru vicisse glorientur.

Ebionitæ legis Mosaicæ studio, Eucharistiæ non nisi in azymo pane celebrandā esse, contendebant. Pro quo errore enervando, Leo M. decrevit, teste Richardo de S. Victore, ut deinceps non in azymo, sed ex fermentato pane celebratio fieret. Rursus Græci pugnabant contra Latinos, usum fermentati panis esse de necessitate simplice : cujus contrarium sentientes Latinos, Azymitas nominabant. Cui pervicaciæ ut obviam eatur, constitutum fuit, ut deinceps ex solo azymo, Eucharistiæ celebratio fieret. Hanc libertatem Ecclesia hodieq́; usurpare, & licèt Sacramenta condere non possit, potest tamen sancire ea, quæ ad solennitatem & reverentiam Sacramenti pertinent: qualia sunt: Orationes, psalmodiæ, ritus & ceremoniæ, partim ad devotionem excitandam, partim pias admonitiones suggerendas, directæ. Quo pertinet etiam ritus Exorcismi, circa actionem Baptismi: ut & campānæ pulsus, qui in Ecclesiis nonnullis reformatis, circa recitationem verborum institutionis, in usu est positus: Item genuflexio, & id genus aliæ externæ ceremoniæ.

Et hæc de causa Efficiente principali Sacramentali dicta sufficiant: Restat, ut quid de dispensantium ministrorum tùm officio, tùm operatione sit statuendum, paucis dispiciamus. Tribus verò Quæstionibus tota hæc disputatio commodè expediri potest.

PRIMA est: Num CHRISTIvANI omnes habeant potestatem administrandi Sacramenta? Circa quam quæstionem graviter hodiè errant tùm Anabaptistæ, tùm Calviniani. Anabaptistæ quidem, dum docent, usum sive potestatem administrandi Sacramenta esse communem omnibus. Calviniani verò, dum Baptismum in casu necessitatis à privato aliquo, cumprimis à muliere collatum, simpliciter rejiciunt. Nos ut mediâ viâ ingredi, neq; in excessu, neq; in defectu peccemus, paucis quibusdam hypothesibus rem omnem complectemur.

I. Spiritus S. in Scripturis Ministerij Ecclesiastici partes non vult esse communes omnib9 in Ecclesiæ cætu versantibus: sed illis tantùm proprias, qui ad docendum legitimè sunt vocati, ut Rom. 10, 15. Quomodo prædicabunt, nisi mittantur? Heb. 5, 4. Nemo sibi sumit honorem, nisi qui vocatus est à DEO, Rom. 12, 6. & 7. item 1. Cor. 12, 5. Eph. 4, 11. D. Apostolus diversa esse asserit in Ecclesia officia & ministeria, quæ non indifferenter omnibus competant. Præterea neq; Apostolus, Act. 14, 23. Tit. 1, 5. Episcopos & Presbyteros constituere, neq; ut idem ab istis fieret, præcipere potuisset, si potestas ista communis esset omnium. Quid quòd tali aliquâ communione concessa, nullus ampliùs ordo, sed mera confusio in Ecclesia obtineret: secus quàm Apostolus præcipit, 1. Cor. 14, 40. ut omnia in Ecclesia fiant ordine & decenter.

II. Minister dispensans Sacramenta, etsi nihil quicquam confert ad constituendam essentiam Sacramentorum, quippè quæ materiâ & formâ sua, ex solius instituentis voluntate & virtute constat & perficitur: ad veritatem tamen Sacramenti, Minister in ordinaria dispensatione sic est necessarius, ut sine eo constare illa non possit. Ratio est: 1. Quia dispensatio haec ex ordinatione Christi, non ex propria ministrorum voluntate dependet. Unde Apostolus se legatione pro Christo fungi, testatur, 2. Cor. 5, 20. 2. Quia potestas administrandi Sacramenta non est naturalis aut humana: sed supernaturalis & divina: unde Johannes Baptista, de Baptismi administratione verba faciens, Nemo, inquit, potest sibi sumere quicquam, nisi datum ipsi sit de caelo Joh. 3, 27. 3. Quia Ministerij officium, cum efficacia & potestate est conjunctum, præcipuè in dispensatione Sacramentorum, in qua verba Ministerij non sunt merè speculativa, aut nudè duntaxat significativa: sed practica quasi, & id quod significant, efficientia: non quidem ex dignitate personæ, vel ex magica aliqua vi, quæ recitationi Verborum Institutionis subsit: sed propter ordinationem Christi, qui per hæc ministri verba, efficaciter in Sacramento utentibus efficit & operatur, quod promisit. Quâ virtute & promissione verba privati alicujus hominis carent, ac proindè nihil efficiunt.

III. Distingvendum est cum B. Luthero inter hæc duo: 1. Habere potestatem. 2. Exercere eandẽ. Sic ubi plures ministri sunt in unâ Ecclesia, omnes quidem habent potestatem administrandi Sacramenta: sed non omnes eam exercent, ne videlicet confusio aliqua oriatur in Ecclesia. Jã quemadmodum ordinis causa, potestatem habere potest, qui tamen eandem non exercet: ita vicissim in casu inevitabilis necessitatis, usum potestatis exercere potest, qui tamen potestatem illius rei exercendæ ordinariè non habet. Quo casu potest fœmina, potest quivis Christianus, non autem homo quivis, Sacramenti esse minister sive dispensator, dummodò ea observet, quæ à Christo instituta sunt.

IV. Distingvendum autem hoc loco inter Sacramenta ipsa. Nam Baptismus admittit ministerium etiam eorum, qui non sunt ordinariè ad ministerium Ecclesiasticum vocati. Evcharistiæ autem Sacramentũ tale quid non admittit, Ratio diversitatis est hæc, quod Baptismi inevitabilis est necessitas, secundum illud Servatoris Joh. 3, 5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest intrare in regnum cœlorum. Ergò quocunque modo Baptismi copia haberi potest, danda fuerit opera, ut ejus perceptione nemo Christianus destituatur. Evcharistiæ autem Sacramenti non par est necessitas: verùm in ejus defectuvalet regula August. Crede & manducasti.

ALTERA quæstio, quæ hoc loco movetur, est hæc: Num mali ministri & hæretici etiam vera Sacramenta conferant? (In Africa ante annos 1300. reperti sunt Episcopi, qui hæreticos & Schismaticos post solutam Ecclesiæ unitatem, vera Sacramenta non conferre opinati sunt. In quam sententiam ipsos odio Schismatum: & zelo conservandæ unitatis Ecclesiasticæ maximo inductos fuisse, Augustinus existimat. Hujus erroris originem Agrippino B Cypriani prædecessori, & alijs quibusdam Africæ Episcopis Augustinus tribuit, qui maluerunt aliquod nomen moliri, quàm tenere consuetudinem, cujus defensionem non intelligebant, l. 2. de Bapt. contra Donat. c. 7. In quam sententiam postea descendit S. Cyprianus scriptis pro eâdem aliquot epistolis ad Jubajanum, Quintium, Pompejum: quod nunquam tamen fecisset, ut cap.seq. Augustinus loquitur, nisi id prius à suis prædecessoribus definitum fuisset: propter cujus viri autoritatem, majora postea error iste incrementa sumpsit, coacto insuper 71. Episcoporum conciliabulo, in quo per definitionem errori isti stabilimentum quæsitum fuit: cujus concilij acta ab Augustino refutantur, lib. 2. de Bapt. cont. Donatist. cap. 2. & seqq. Quierror concilij Niceni can. 8. rejectus: tandem concilio Carthaginensi primo (priora enim pro exautoratis habentur) solenniter damnatus fuit. Notandum tamen est, sic fuisse à B. Cypriano super hoc errore, cum Stephano Pont. Rom. disceptatum, ut nullum inter ipsos Schismatis malum ortum sit: neq́; contrariam sententiam unquàm damnare præsumserit, quemadmodum ex scriptis ejus probat Augustinus lib. jam citato 2. capp. 2. 3. 4. & lib. 5. cap. 17. & 25. imò teste Augustino non defuerunt, qui in hoc errore Cyprianum fuisse, prorsus negarunt: quod tamen non probatur ab Augustino, Epist. 48. Interim quatuor modis ab eodem Cyprianus excusatur, his verbis: Porrò Cyprianus, aut non sensit omninò, quod eum sensisse recitatis: aut hoc posteà correxit in regula veritatis: aut hunc quasi nævum sui candidissimi pectoris cooperuit ubere charitatis, dum unitatem Ecclesiæ, toto orbe crescentis & copiosissimè defendit, & perseverantissimè retinuit vinculum pacis. Scriptum est enim, charitas operit multitudinem peccatorum. Accessit huc etiam, quod tanquam Sacramentum fructuosissimum, si quod in eo fuit emendandum, purgavit Pater falce passionis. Posteris temporibus exorti Donatistæ, & Cypriani autoritate abusi, errorem istum pernitiosiùs defendendum susceperunt. Nam & contrariam sententiam hæreseos damnarunt: & quod à concilio plenario definitum erat, ut dicit Augustinus, ipsi reprobarunt: & quod de hæreticis & Schismaticis duntaxat Cyprianus asseruerat, hi ulterius progressi ad omnes impios ministros referebant: quod nominatim Cresconium Grammaticum fuisse, testis est Augustinus, cui lib. 2. contra eundem scripto, c. 28. sic respondet August. Tu dixisti, tu etiam scribere minimè timuisti, ut quisquis peccator inter omnes homines fuerit, jus sibi Baptismatis non usurpet. Si ergò nondum baptizatus es, aut hanc vanissimam sententia corrige: aut à quibus baptizeris, Angelos quære. Tandem superiori seculo errorem Donatistarum aliqui superasse feribuntur qui non tantùm peccatores tùm occultos, tù manifestos: sed etiam quantumvis probos: morituros tamen in peccato mortali: (h e. nõ electos, quos præscitos isti appellabant) vera Sacramenta conferre negarunt. Nostro hoc seculo eundẽ errorem Anabaptistæ tuetur, Siquis est, qui errores istius ex Scripturis operosam refutationem requirit, Thomã Waldensem legat, Tom 2. de Sacramentis, à c. 1. usq́; ad 17. & præcipuè ea quæ sunt longè ante istum scripta ab Aug. libris septem de Baptismo contra Donatist. item libris tribus cõnt. epist. Parmeniani: & libris totidem contra literas Petiliani: & libris quatuor contra Cresconium Grammaticum.)


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: Whether all Christians have the power to administer the Sacraments? (continued)

We maintain the affirmative against the Donatists and Anabaptists, relying chiefly on two arguments: The first is this. The entire virtue and truth of a Sacrament depends not on the quality of the minister, but on the institution of CHRIST. Therefore, whatever the minister may be like, the Sacrament will retain its virtue. The reason for the connection is manifest: for if virtue is not conferred upon the Sacrament by the minister, then certainly his qualities will not hinder the virtue and efficacy of the Sacrament. The antecedent, however, is proven: 1. Because it is not the minister, but GOD, who confers virtue upon the Sacrament. For it is He who baptizes with the Holy Spirit, John 1:33. Hence the Apostle, 1 Cor. 1:13, says: Were you baptized in the name of Paul? And 1 Cor. 3:7: Neither he who plants, nor he who waters, is anything: but GOD who gives the increase. And this, as Augustine testifies, was very necessary, so that we would not place our confidence of salvation in the merits of others: which would seem necessarily to have to be done if the virtue of the remedies of our salvation (such as the Sacraments) depended on the goodness or malice of the minister. 2. The antecedent is proven in this way: Other things, however much they proceed from God, are nevertheless attributed to men, for example, that which the Apostle says: My ministry, my Gospel. But the Sacraments are attributed to GOD alone. For no one has ever said, My Sacrament, my Baptism. Therefore. 3. One is said to be better, more learned, or more eloquent in preaching than another. But no one baptizes better than another: for Christ, who baptizes, is everywhere the same. 4. The Fathers declare the same with comparisons. 1. Of the planter or gardener in planting herbs. 2. Of the Sun or Light, diffused through muddy places, yet contracting nothing of the filth. 3. Of the conduit through which water flows, whether it be wooden, leaden, or silver. Augustine, book 3, commentary against Cresconius, ch. 8, and book 3, on baptism against the Donatists, ch. 10.

The second argument is as follows: Those gifts of GOD which are bestowed for the benefit of others rather than for the benefit of the one who possesses them, namely for the common good of the whole Church, are not lost or corrupted by the malice of the one who possesses them: But such a gift is the power of administering the Sacraments. Therefore.

In order that the truth of the major premise may be better understood, it must be noted that there are two kinds of gifts of GOD bestowed upon men in the Church. Some are for the good of the one who has them, which are called by the Scholastics graces that make one pleasing to God: Others are destined for the uses of others, which are called graces freely given. Between these two kinds of gifts there is this difference, that the former are lost through infidelity and mortal sins (for by his own fault, by which GOD is offended, a man merits that his own grace be lost). The latter, since they are not so much one's own goods as they are common to others, and bestowed for the sake of others, are certainly not vitiated by the private sin of the one who has or possesses those gifts, to the detriment of the Church. The truth of the assertion is evident even from this, because these gifts can exist even in the wicked, Matt. 7:22, 1 Cor. 13:1, and 2. The minor premise is clear by its own light. For in administering the Sacraments, one serves none but others. The conclusion therefore remains most firm: and consequently the error is deservedly to be rejected, by which it is feigned that true Sacraments are not conferred by wicked ministers and heretics.

The third and final question is this: Whether the intention of the minister is necessary for the truth and efficacy of the Sacraments? To which question one must respond by a distinction: for either this intention, about which the question is asked, concerns the action itself or the administration of the Sacrament, so that the minister knows what he wishes to do. Which intention certainly can hardly be absent, if the minister of the Church has any will at all, unless perhaps he degenerates into a completely brute animal. This intention the Scholastics call actual: which, however, if it be absent, can detract nothing from either the truth or the efficacy of the Sacraments. For this intention is not simply necessary, although it is good, and the minister who neglects it sins not lightly. Or this intention concerns the End of the Sacrament, as in Baptism, regeneration; in the Lord's Supper, spiritual union with CHRIST. Moreover, because this end depends not on the intention of the minister, but on the truth and certainty of both the institution and the divine promise, it certainly matters nothing what the minister may think, or believe, or intend, provided he administers the Sacraments according to the institution of CHRIST.

In the Papacy, a completely different opinion has prevailed in previous times. For although Lombard, indeed, and some others felt that for the truth and integrity of the Sacrament it is not necessarily required what the minister knows, feels, or believes concerning the substance and effect of the Sacrament: nay, even if he believes the contrary, the Sacrament is nevertheless true, provided he administers it according to the institution of CHRIST. On which account, concerning a ludicrous and jocular action, if someone is immersed in a bath or river in the name of the Trinity, he writes that it has been disputed that it is not a true Baptism, because it was not done with the intention of baptizing, and at the same time he adds, In this and other Sacraments, just as the form is to be observed: so also the intention of celebrating it is to be had: which intention is understood by him to be about the act of baptizing itself, not about the end and effect of Baptism. However, these things being little observed, most doctors of the Papists have judged that the Sacrament is not true and efficacious if the minister maliciously withdraws his interior intention, even if he observes the form of the institution in the administration, as Alexander of Hales has it in book 4 of the Sentences, q. 13, memb. 1, art. 2. To which opinion Biel also writes, likewise in book 4 of the Sentences, dist. 6, q. 1, concl. 3, that for the truth of Baptism the intention of the minister is required, not only with respect to the act of baptizing, as the Object: but also with respect to its end and term. Which impiety the Council of Trent also, session 7, canon 11, although timidly and with a reservation of escape, approved, decreeing thus: If anyone shall say that in ministers, while they perform and confer the Sacraments, there is not required at least the intention of doing what the Church does, let him be anathema. For the particle (at least) shows a condition, that indeed everything which has been handed down concerning Intention under the Papacy is approved by that Council: if, however, everything cannot be obtained: at least one must settle for the second degree. Moreover, the reason for which that council allowed the impiety of this dogma to be approved by itself is worthy of mention, which is as follows. sess. 6. t. 9. they decreed,

That no pious person can know with the certainty of faith, which cannot be subject to falsehood, that he is in the grace of GOD, or in possession of the remission of sins. The reason for this dogma is rendered thus: Because the promise of the Gospel is a general pronouncement: not proper to individuals. Now because the use of the Sacraments here is that the promise of the Gospel, proposed generally, should be applied to individual believers, which that Pyrrhonian dogma concerning doubt denies with an opposing front: therefore, in order to cut the nerves of certainty and faith, they invent that the truth and efficacy of the Sacraments do not depend solely upon divine institution: but that the intention of the minister is also required for the same, concerning which no one receiving the Sacraments can have any certainty.

Moreover, that this dogma rests upon no foundation of truth is evident from the following arguments:

I. The efficacy of the Sacraments is to be established in the truth and power of GOD who institutes and promises: and not to be suspended from the thought of a man or minister. Therefore.

II. If that intention of the minister were necessary, a man could never be certain that he obtains the effect of the Sacrament: because no one can look into the mind of another. But the latter is false, and conflicts with the very principal use of the Sacraments: Therefore the former is also.

III. Lombard, book 4, dist. 5, crushes this dogma with the most beautiful words of Augustine: Let the ministers be just, if they wish: But if they do not wish to be just, who sit in the Chair of Moses, my master CHRIST makes me secure, of whom the Holy Spirit says: This is he who baptizes: likewise those whom Judas baptized, Christ baptized. Likewise, Baptism is such as he is in whose power it is given: not such as he is, through whose ministry it is given.

IV. This matter is also illustrated by a comparison. For if a servant makes a contract by the will of his master, the contract is valid and firm, even if the servant has no will or intention for that matter. Similarly, the matter concerning the intention of ministers, regarding the administration of the Sacraments, is compared.

Latin:

Affirmativam contra Donatistas & Anabaptistas tuemur, duabus potissimùm nixi rationibus: Prior est. Tota virtus & veritas Sacramenti non à qualitate ministri: sed ab institutione CHRISTI dependet. Ergò qualis qualis sit minister, Sacramento sua virtus constabit. Ratio connexi est manifesta: si enim Sacramento non confertur virtus à ministro: utique qualitates etiam ejus non impedient virtutem & efficaciam Sacramenti. Antecedens autem probatur, 1. Quia non minister, sed DEUS est, qui Sacramento virtutem confert. Hic est enim, qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto, Johan. 1, 33. Hinc Apostolus 1. Cor. 1, 13. Non, inquit, in nomine Pauli baptizati estis. & 1. Cor. 3, 7. Nequè qui plantat, nequè qui rigat, est aliquid: sed qui dat incrementum DEUS. Et hoc, teste Augustino, valdè fuit necessarium, ne fiduciam salutis poneremus in alienis meritis: quod necessariò faciendum videretur, si remediorum salutis nostræ (qualia sunt Sacramenta) virtus à bonitate aut malitia ministri dependeret. 2. Probatur Antecedens hoc modo: Aliæ res, quantumvis à Deo profectæ, tamé tribuuntur hominibq verbi gratia, quòd Apostolus dicit, Ministerium meum, Evangelium meum. At Sacramenta soli DEO tribuuntur. Nemo enim unquam dixit, Sacramentum meum Baptisma meum. Ergò. 3. Uno altero dicitur melior, doctior, in prædicando facundior esse. Atqui nemo altero baptizat melius: Christus enim qui baptizat, ubique idem est. 4. Patres idem declarant similitudinibus. 1. plantatoris sive hortulani in plantandis herbis. 2. Solis aut Lucis, per cœnosa loca diffusæ, nec tamen sordium quicquam contrahentis. 3. Canalis, per quam aqua labitur, seu ligneus, sed plumbeus seu argenteus sit. Augustinus, lib. 3. com. Cresc. c. 8. & l. 3. de bapt. cont. Donatist. c. 10.

Secunda ratio talis est: Illa dona DEI, quæ tribuuntur ad aliorum potiùs, quàm ad habentis utilitatem, nempè propter commune bonum totius Ecclesiæ, non amittuntur aut corrumpuntur per malitiam habentis illa: Atqui tale donum est potestas administrandi Sacramenta. Ergò.

Majoris veritas ut rectiùs intelligatur, notandum est, duplicia esse dona DEI, hominibus collata in Ecclesia. Alia bono sunt ei, qui habet ista, quæ à Scholasticis nominantur Gratiæ gratum facientes: Alia aliorum usibus destinata sunt, quæ appellantur Gratiæ gratis datæ. Inter quæ duo donorum genera hoc est discriminis, quòd priora illa per infidelitatem & peccata mortalia amittuntur, (propriâ enim culpâ, quâ DEUS offenditur, meretur homo, ut gratia propria amittatur) Posteriora cùm non tàm sint bona propria, quàm aliorum communia, & propter alios collata, utique propter habentis sive possidentis illa dona peccatum privatum, in Ecclesiæ detrimentum, non vitiantur. Assertionis veritas vel indè constat, quia hæc dona malis etiam inesse possunt, Matth. 7, 22. 1. Cor. 13, 1. & 2. Minor sua luce patet. Nam Sacramenta administrando, non nisi alijs servitur. Cõclusio ergò manet firmissima: ac proindè meritò rejiciendus error, quo à malis ministris & hæreticis vera Sacramenta non conferri fingitur.

Tertia & postrema quæstio est hæc: Num intentio ministri sit ad veritatem & efficaciam Sacramentorum? Ad quam quæstionem per distinctionem respondendum fuerit: vel enim intentio hæc, de quâ quæritur, respicit ipsam actionem sive administrationem Sacramenti, ut nimirùm sciat minister quid velit agere. Quæ sanè intentio vix abesse potest, si maximè velit minister Ecclesiæ, nisi fortè in brutum planè animal degeneret. Quam intentionem Scholastici actualem nominant: Quæ tamen, si absit, nihil quicquam vel veritati vel efficaciæ Sacramentorum derogare potest. Neque enim simpliciter necessaria est hæc intentio, licèt bona sit, & minister istam negligens, haud leviter peccet. Vel Intentio hæc respicit Finem Sacramenti, ut in Baptismo regenerationem; in Cœna Domini, spiritualem coalitionem cum CHRISTO. Cæterùm, quia finis iste non ex ministri intentione, sed ex veritate & certitudine tùm institutionis, tùm promissionis divinæ dependet, utique nihil refert, quicquid minister vel cogitet, vel credat, vel intendat, modò secundum institutionem CHRISTI Sacramenta administret.

In Papatu diversa planè sententia obtinuit superioribus temporibus. Nam tametsi Lombardus quidem, & nonnulli alij senserunt, ad veritatem & integritatem Sacramenti non necessariò requiri, quid minister sciat, sentiat, aut credat de Sacramenti substantiâ & effectu: imò si contrarium credat, tamen verum esse Sacramentum, dummodò juxta institutionem CHRISTI administret. Quo nomine de ludicra & joculari actione, si quis in balneum vel flumen mergatur in nomine Trinitatis, sic disputatum fuisse scribit, quòd non sit verus Baptismus, quia non intentione baptisandi illud gestum sit, & simul addit, In hoc & alijs Sacramentis, sicut forma est servanda: ita & intentio illud celebrandi est habenda: quæ intentio de ipso actu baptizandi, non de fine & effectus Baptismi ab eodem intelligitur. His tamen parùm observatis, Pontificiorum doctores plerique judicarunt, Sacramentum non esse verum & efficax, si minister malitiosè subtrahat intentionem interiorem, etiamsi in administratione servet formam institutionis, ut habet Alexander ab Ales in lib. 4. sent. q. 13. memb. 1. art. 2. In quam sententiam Biel etiam scribit, itidem in lib. 4. sent. dist. 6 q. 1. concl. 3. Ad veritatem Baptismi requiri intentionem ministri, non tantùm respectu actus baptizandi, ut Objecti: sedetiam respectu ejus, & finis & termini. Quam impietatem Concilium etiam Tridentinum, sess. 7. can. 11. quamvis timidè, & cum reservatione effugij approbavit, sic decernens: Si quis dixerit, in ministris, dum Sacramenta conficiunt & conferunt, non requiri intentionem saltem faciendi, quod facit Ecclesia, anathema sit. Nam particula (saltem) conditionalis ostendit, probari quidem Concilio isti promiscuè omnia, quæ de Intencione sub Papatu tradita fuerunt: Si tamen omnia obtineri nequeant: saltem in secundo gradu consistendum esse. Est autem memoratu digna causa, ob quam concilium istud impietatem dogmatis hujus sibi probari passum fuit, quæ talis est. sess. 6. t. 9. sanxerüt,

Neminem pium scire posse certitudine fidei, cui non possit subesse falsum, se ingratia DEI, aut remissionis peccatorum compotem esse. Ratio dogmatis hæc redditur: Quia promissio Evangelij sit pronunciati generalis: non individuorum propria. Jam quia Sacramentorum hic est usus, ut promissio Evangelij generaliter proposita, ad singulos fideles applicetur, id quod Pyrrhonicum istud dogma de dubitatione, adversa fronte negat: ideò ut certitudinis & fidei nervos incidant, veritatem & efficaciam Sacramentorum non ex divina tantùm institutione pendere: sed ad eandem etiam requiri intentionem ministri comminiscuntur, de qua nemo Sacramenta suscipiens, certitudinis quicquam habere potest.

Cæterùm dogma hoc nullo veritatis fundamento niti, argumentis his sequentibus constat:

I. Sacramentorum efficacia est constituenda in veritate, & virtute DEI instituentis, & promittentis: non autem à cogitatione hominis vel ministri suspendenda. Ergò.

II. Si ista intentio ministri esset necessaria, non posset homo unquàm esse certus, quod consequatur effectum Sacramenti: quia mentem alterius nemo potest introspicere. Atqui falsum, & cum usu ipso principali Sacramentorum pugnans est posterius: Ergò & prius.

III. Lombardus lib. 4. dist. 5. dogma istud pulcherrimis Augustini verbis conculcat: Sint ministri justi, si volunt: Sin autem noluerint esse justi, qui sedent in Cathedra Mosis, securum me facit magister meus CHRISTUS, de quo Spiritus Sanctus dicit: Hic est qui baptizat: item quos baptizavit Judas, Christus baptizavit. Item Baptismus talis est, qualis est ille, in cujus potestate datur: non qualis ille est, per cujus ministerium datur.

IV. Similitudine etiam res ista illustratur. Si enim servus facit contractum ex voluntate heri sui, contractus ratus est & firmus, etiamsi servus ejus rei voluntatem aut intentionem nullam habeat. Similiter res de intentione ministrorum, circa administrationem Sacramentorum comparata est.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: II. On the matter and form of the Sacrament

Our Definition placed above expressed the Matter and Form of the Sacrament, when it defined a Sacrament as a sign or visible form of an invisible grace. Where, however, it must be observed immediately from the threshold, that the word Form in this place is not taken in the sense in which it is dichotomously distinguished against matter: but rather for a singular species, and a certain essential whole, composed of matter and form. For every Sacrament, as much of the New as of the Old Testament, is not something simple: but composite, namely consisting of those things which behave like matter and form.

The prior part of the composite or of this form is always an element or something elementary: as in the Old Testament it was the flesh of the foreskin, consisting in the shedding of blood: and the flesh and blood of the lamb. In the New Testament it is Water, Bread and Wine.

The posterior part of the composite is the heavenly thing, namely the flesh and blood of Christ: and that either typical, such as it was in the Sacraments of the Old Testament, when the Substance of the Lord's body and blood was not yet in the nature of things: Or essential, such as it is in the Sacraments of the New Testament. This form, therefore, or this whole composite, is properly the Sacrament and is so called, which is distinguished from the Thing of the Sacrament, as they are commonly named, that is, from the grace itself and the effect of the Sacrament in the whole genus. Whence it is commonly said: That some receive the Sacrament only: others the Thing of the Sacrament only: others both at once, namely the Sacrament and the Thing of the Sacrament. They receive the Sacrament only, as many as take that whole composite of matter and form, of which neither part alone is properly called the Sacrament, as will be shown more clearly a little later. But they receive the Thing of the Sacrament only, who, while they anxiously desire to receive the Sacrament itself, are prohibited by some necessary and inevitable impediment. If these apply the promise of the Gospel to themselves by true faith, they certainly receive no less of the grace and power of the Sacrament, through the mediation of divine power, than if they had been made participants of the Sacrament itself, which could truly be affirmed in the primitive and older Church concerning all those believers who were either affected by martyrdom beforehand, or were prevented by unexpected death before they could obtain the Sacrament of Baptism. For here that which Augustine once said concerning the inevitable lack of the Eucharistic Sacrament has a place: believe and you have eaten. Finally, however, they receive the Sacrament and the Thing of the Sacrament at once, who use the Sacrament worthily: as will be shown more fully in its own place in the article concerning the Sacrament of the Supper.

Moreover, in order that the whole otherwise intricate dispute concerning the Nature of any Sacrament, which cannot be correctly known except from its matter and form, may be examined with the greatest possible clarity: the following members especially will have to be weighed:

I. What are the essential parts of a Sacrament, and in what sense is a Sacrament called a visible Form, and whether the Word, whether of command or of promise, can be called a Form or an essential part of a Sacrament?

II. In what sense and respect is a Sacrament a sign, how and what it signifies: what is its Signified: and how this differs from the sign?

III. By what means do two most diverse things, and things differing in their whole kind, concur to constitute one sacramental τό δε τι, if it be permitted to speak thus, or one Sacrament in number and species.

IV. What mode of predicating, partly concerning the whole composite, and partly concerning the constituent parts themselves, can and ought to be admitted mutually.

Latin:

MAteriam & Formam Sacramenti expressit Definitio nostra suprà posita, quando definivit Sacramentum, quòd sit signum sive forma visibilis, gratiæ invisibilis. Ubi tamen statim à limine observandum, Formæ vocabulum hoc loco non accipi eo sensu, quo contra materiam διχοτόμως distingvitur: sed potiùs pro specie singulari, & toto quodam essentiali, ex materia & forma composito. Sacramentum enim omne tàm Novi, quàm Veteris Testamenti, non est quiddam simplex: sed compositum, nempè ex ijs constans, quæ se habent instar materiæ & formæ.

Prior pars compositi sive formæistius semper est elementum seu elementare, quippiam: ut in Veteri Testamento fuit caro præputij, sanguinis profusione constans: & caro ac sanguis agni. In Novo Testamento est Aqua, Panis & Vinum.

Posterior pars compositi est res cœlestis, nempè caro & sanguis Christi: isq; vel typic9, qualis fuit in Sacramentis Veteris Testamenti, cùm nondum in rerum natura esset Substantia corporis & sanguinis Dominici: Vel essentialis, qualis est in Sacramentis Novi Testamenti. Forma ergò hæc, seu totum hoc compositum, propriè Sacramentum est & dicitur, quod à Re Sacramenti, uti vulgò nominantur, hoc est, à gratia ipsa & effectu Sacramenti toto genere discernitur. Undè vulgò dici solet, Quosdam accipere Sacramentum tantùm: alios Rem duntaxat Sacramenti: alios utrumquè simul, Sacramentum scilicet & Rem Sacramenti. Sacramentum tantùm accipiunt, quotquot totum illud compositum ex materia & forma sumunt, cujus neutra pars sola Sacramentum propriè dicitur, uti paulò post dilucidiùs ostendetur. Rem autem Sacramenti tantùm accipiunt, qui cum Sacramentum ipsum accipere anxiè quidem desiderent, sed impedimento aliquo necessario ac inevitabili prohibentur. Hi si verâ fide promissionem Evangelij propriam sibi applicent, haud profectò minus gratiæ & virtutis Sacramenti, divinâ mediante virtute accipiunt, quàm si ipsius Sacramenti redditi fuissent participes, id quod in primitiva & antiquiore Ecclesia verè affirmari potuit, de omnibus istis fidelibus, qui vel martyrio priùs sunt affecti, vel morte inopinata præventi sunt, antequàm Baptismi Sacramentum consequi poterant. Hîc enim locum habet illud, quod de Sacramenti Eucharistici defectu inevitabili, dixit olim Augustinus, crede & manducasti. Tandem verò Sacramentum & Rem Sacramenti simul accipiunt, qui dignè Sacramento utuntur: uti suo loco fusius ostendetur in articulo de Sacramento Cœnæ.

Cæterùm ut tota alioqui intricata disputatio de Natura cujuslibet Sacramenti, quæ non nisi ex ejus materia & forma, rectè cognosci potest, summâ, quâ fieri potest perspicuitate excutiatur: sequentia potissimùm membra expendenda erunt:

I. Quæ sint partes essentiales Sacramenti, & quo sensu Sacramentum dicatur Forma visibilis, & num Verbum sive mandati sive promissionis, possit dici Forma aut pars essentialis Sacramenti?

II. Quo sensu & respectu Sacramentum sit signum, quomodo & quid signet: quodnam ejus Signatum: & quomodo hoc à signo differat?

III. Quo medio duæ diversissimæ res, & toto genere discrepantes concurrant ad constituendum unum Sacramentale τó δε τι, si sic loqui liceat, sive unum numero & specie Sacramentum.

IV. Quis prædicandi modus, partim de toto composito, partim verò de ipsis partibus constituentibus ad se mutuò admitti possit & debeat.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: What are the essential parts of a Sacrament: and in what sense is a Sacrament called a visible Form?

Since any Sacrament is a thing composed of two things as parts, differing in their entire genus: one earthly and visible; the other heavenly and invisible: It is asked, in respect of this or that part is the Sacrament called a visible Form? Which question can be most correctly defined by the distinction between Act and Potency. For if you understand Potency, the Sacrament is a visible Form according to both parts of the composite: But if you inquire about the act itself, the Sacrament is a visible Form, only from the other part: namely the earthly or elementary, primarily indeed and immediately. Meanwhile, however, indirectly and secondarily also from the other part: and that because of the closest conjunction or union, which intervenes between the heavenly thing and the earthly. For although the very substance of the heavenly thing does not fall under the sight of the eyes: yet it is sufficient that it is perceived through the elementary species, with which that thing, by means of the Sacramental union, has been made most united and joined: so that in the use of the Sacrament, the attribute of one part may truly be assigned to the other part also, and it may be truly affirmed that with the bread eaten the body of Christ itself is eaten, and with the bread seen, the body of Christ itself is seen: no less than when the dove was seen over the baptized CHRIST, the Holy Spirit himself could be said to have been seen: the former primarily and immediately: the latter, however, secondarily and mediately.

It is evident from this what must be determined concerning the opinion of certain Theologians, who maintain that the word is an essential part, indeed the Form of a Sacrament.

For first, the word is never united Sacramentally either with the earthly thing or with the heavenly thing: and therefore it neither constitutes nor enters into the Substance of the Sacrament. Therefore the word can be called neither the matter nor the Form of the Sacrament.

Then this word is twofold: One of command: such as Baptize, Take, eat, drink: The other of promise: and that again is twofold: One by reason of the Sacrament itself considered in itself: This is my Body: This is my Blood: The other, by reason of use and fruit: He who shall have been baptized and shall have believed, shall be saved. But neither of these words is an essential part of the Sacrament. The word of Command is not: because that looks more to the external action than to the essence of the Sacrament: The word of Promise is not, because although by the virtue of these words, This is my Body, This is my Blood, the very Sacramental union of the earthly and heavenly thing comes to be by the institution of Christ: yet this word never enters into this union, or the very constitution of the whole composite, as any essential part. Thus the other word of Promise, looking to the use and fruit of the Sacrament, does not constitute or complete the Matter and Form of the Sacrament to such an extent that the Sacrament can rather be received whole as to its Substance, although the use and fruit of the Sacrament is not present or does not follow: which is most manifestly clear from the eating of the unworthy. Nor does that of Augustine in Tractate 80 on John stand in the way: Let the word be added to the Element, and it becomes a Sacrament. For Augustine did not wish to denote by these words an αἴτιον συστατικὸν or essential part: but at least an αἴτιον ποιητικὸν. But I call that an αἴτιον ποιητικὸν, which does not enter into the substance of the whole composite, since it consists of nothing but the earthly and heavenly thing: although this very composition of these two things never happens without this word. For example: The Sacrament of the Eucharist, by the consent of all Orthodox Theologians, as a whole composite, consists of an earthly or elementary thing: Bread and Wine: and of a heavenly thing, the Body and Blood of Christ, Sacramentally united. Therefore if I resolve this composite into its essential parts, certainly this resolution is not made into Element and Word: but into Element and heavenly thing. Whence it follows irrefragably that the αἴτια συστατικὰ or essential parts of this composite are the Earthly thing and the heavenly thing: from which two taken together and united, one whole Sacramental thing finally emerges.

Now indeed because the force or virtue of this Union does not depend on any natural action, nor on the recitation of words: but on the promise of Christ the institutor, so that if this word of promise were absent, This is my Body, This is my blood, those two parts could never concur into one Sacrament: therefore I say that this word is an αἴτιον ποιητικὸν, that is, it causes those two essential parts to constitute one Sacrament in the use of the Sacrament: although that word does not constitute the essence of the Sacrament as an essential part.

The matter can be illustrated in some way by an example. The essential parts of man as a whole composite are Body and Soul. Now indeed, that in natural generation these two parts concur to constitute one man, that depends on the virtue of the divine word of promise: Increase and multiply. Therefore this word of promise causes the Soul and body to constitute one Man, and to be the αἴτια συστατικὰ or essential parts of Man: yet this word itself does not enter into the Substance of Man, or constitute any essential part of him. Similarly, it should be judged concerning the essential parts of the Sacrament, in the way that has already been shown before.

And hence it is that the Church, by unanimous consent always, [holds] the Sacrament [to consist] of things neither more, nor other, than these two, namely the earthly or elementary thing, and the heavenly, believed to consist of these as essential parts. Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 34, against Valentinus: Just as bread which is from the earth, receiving the calling of GOD, is no longer common bread, but the Eucharist, consisting of two things, earthly and heavenly: so also our bodies receiving the Eucharist are no longer corruptible, since they have the hope of the resurrection. Augustine, as the Canon Law has it, on consecration, distinction 2, chapter 48: This is what we say, what we strive to approve by all means, that this Sacrament is accomplished by two things, consists of two things, the visible appearance of the Elements, and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord JESUS CHRIST. Damascene, book 4 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 14: Just as in Baptism GOD joined the grace of the Holy Spirit to the water, and made it the laver of regeneration: in the same way, because it is the custom for men to eat bread and drink wine, He joined His divinity and grace to these very things, and made them His body and blood. And indeed, this combination or union of these two essential parts can be demonstrated to the eye from the Sacraments of both the Old and the New Testament. In circumcision, the earthly and visible thing was the foreskin cut off with the shedding of blood. The heavenly and spiritual thing was the typical Blood of Christ. In the Paschal Lamb, the earthly and visible thing was the flesh and blood of the Lamb: the spiritual thing, however, was the typical Flesh and Blood of Christ. In Baptism, the earthly and elementary thing is Water: the heavenly thing is the Blood of Christ, without which no regeneration can take place. In the Lord's Supper, the earthly and visible thing is Bread and Wine: the heavenly thing is the essential Body and Blood of Christ. Nor is it without a certain reason that God willed that every Sacrament should consist of these two essential parts. For because God willed to deal in the Sacraments not only with the external but also with the internal man: therefore He willed that there should also be two parts of the Sacraments, suitable for the consideration of every man: of which the heavenly would concern the faith of the internal man: but the earthly would concern the senses of the external man. The Sacramentarians do not walk with a straight foot regarding the purity of this doctrine. For although they themselves assert quite splendidly in words that the Sacraments consist of two things: yet by the very fact itself it can be evidently demonstrated that they deny this. For first, they ascribe the name and office of a Sacrament to the external elements or Symbols: which is clearly evident from their own dogma concerning the Manducation of the Unworthy. For they contend that the unworthy do indeed receive the Sacrament: but do not receive the Body and Blood of the Savior Himself. Therefore, the Sacrament is for them even where the heavenly thing is not: and consequently, the essence of the Sacrament will now consist of only one part, namely the elementary or earthly. Observing this, Joh. Jacob Grynaeus did not shrink from writing, in part 2 of his problems, page 203: That the Sacraments of faith are Sacraments only for the faithful. Of which paradox, however, as far as I know, he has no supporter from the entire Calvinist crowd.

Then it is manifest that the Sacramentarians reckon the Heavenly Thing, as for example the body and blood of the Lord, now as the fruit and use, now as the very substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament. But indeed, no essential part of a Sacrament can at the same time be its use and fruit: as that which always consists outside the substance of the Sacrament.

Latin:

CUm Sacramentum quodlibet sit quiddam compositum ex duabus rebus tanquàm partibus, toto genere discrepantibus: unâ terrenâ ac visibili; alterâ coelesti & invisibili: Quaeritur, nùm hujus aut illius partis respectu Sacramentum dicatur Forma visibilis? Quae quaestio rectissimè definiri poterit, per distinctionem inter Actum & Potentiam. Si enim Potentiam intelligas, Sacramentum est Forma visibilis secundum utramque partem compositi: Sin de actu ipso quaeras, Sacramentum est Forma visibilis, ex parte duntaxat altera: terrena nimirùm sive elementari, πρώτως quidem καὶ ἀμέσως. Interim tamen ἐμμέσως καὶ δευτέρως etiam ex parte altera: idque propter arctissimam conjunctionem sive unionem, quae rei coelesti, cum terrenâ intercedit. Etsi enim ipsa substantia rei coelestis sub aspectum oculorum non cadit: satis tamen est, per species elementares eam cerni, quibus illa, mediante Sacramentali unione facta est unitissima & junctissima: ita ut in usu Sacramenti, unius partis attributum, alteri etiam parti revera assignetur, & manducato pane ipsum corpus Christi manducari, viso pane, ipsum corpus Christi videri, verè affirmari possit: haud minùs atque visâ columba super CHRISTO baptizato, ipse Spiritus Sanctus visus fuisse perhiberi potuerit: illa quidem primò & immediatè: hic verò secundariò & mediatè.

Patet hinc, quid statuendum sit de ea Theologorum quorundam sententia, qui statuunt, verbum esse partem essentialem, imò Formam Sacramenti.

Primùm enim verbum nunquàm, vel cum re terrena, vel cum re coelesti Sacramentaliter unitur: ac proindè Sacramenti Substantiam neque constituit, neque ingreditur. Ergo verbum neque materia, neque Forma Sacramenti dici potest.

Deindè verbum hoc est geminum: Unum mandati: ut Baptizate, Accipite, comedite, bibite: Alterum promissionis: idque rursus geminum: Unum ratione ipsius Sacramenti in se considerati: Hoc est Corpus meum: Hic est Sanguis meus: Alterum, ratione usus & fructus: Qui baptizatus fuerit & crediderit, salvabitur. Atqui neutrum hoc verbum, est pars essentialis Sacramenti. Verbum Mandati non: quia illud magis externam actionem, quàm Sacramenti essentiam spectat: Verbum Promissionis non, quia licèt virtute verborum istorum, Hoc est Corpus meum, Hic est Sanguis meus, ex institutione Christi fiat ipsa unio Sacramentalis rei terrenae & coelestis: tamen unionem hanc, vel ipsam constitutionem totius compositi verbum hoc nunquàm ingreditur, tanquàm pars aliqua essentialis. Sic verbum Promissionis alterum, respiciens usum & fructum Sacramenti, usque adeò Materiam & Formam Sacramenti non constituit aut absolvit, ut potiùs Sacramentum quoad Substantiam integrum accipi possit, licèt usus & fructus Sacramenti non adsit aut subsequatur: id quod ex manducatione indignorum manifestissimè liquet. Neque obstat illud Augustini Tractatu 80. in Johannem: Accedat verbum ad Elementum, & fit Sacramentum. Nam non αἴτιον συστατικὸν sive partem essentialem: sed αἴτιον ποιητικὸν saltem Augustinus his verbis notare voluit. Αἴτιον ποιητικὸν autem voco illud, quod ipsam substantiam totius compositi non ingreditur, quippè quæ non nisi ex re terrena & cœlesti constat: licèt hæc ipsa duarum istarum rerum compositio, sine verbo hoc nunquàm fiat. Exempli gratia: Sacramentum Eucharistiæ, consensu omnium Orthodoxorum Theologorum, tanquàm totum compositum, constat ex re terrena sive elementari: Pane & Vino: & ex re cœlesti, Corpore & Sanguine Christi, Sacramentaliter unitis. Ergò si hoc compositum in partes suas essentiales resolvo, certè resolutio hæc non fit, in Elementum & Verbum: sed in Elementum & rem cœlestem. Undè irrefragabiliter sequitur, αἴτια συστατικὰ aut partes essentiales hujus compositi esse Rem terrenam & rem cœlestem: quibus duabus simul sumtis & unitis, unum demùm emergit totum Sacramentale.

Jam verò quia Unionis hujus vis sive virtus non dependeat ex naturali aliqua actione, neque ex recitatione verborum: sed à promissione Christi instituentis, ita ut si abesset verbum hoc promissionis, Hoc est Corpus meum, Hic est sanguis meus, nunquàm duæ illæ partes in unum Sacramentum concurrere possent: ideò dico, verbum hoc esse αἴτιον ποιητικὸν hoc est, efficere, ut duæ illæ partes essentiales unum Sacramentum constituant in usu Sacramenti: licèt verbum istud essentiam Sacramenti, tanquàm pars essentialis non constituat.

Exemplo aliquo res illustrari quodammodo potest. Hominis tanquàm totius compositi partes essentiales sunt, Corpus & Anima, Jam verò ut in generatione naturali, duæ hæ partes concurrant ad unum constituendum hominem, id dependet ex virtute verbi promissionis divinæ: Crescite & multiplicamini. Facit ergò verbum hoc promissionis, ut Anima & corpus unum constituant Hominem, & sint αἴτια συστατικὰ sive partes essentiales Hominis: ipsum tamen verbum hoc Substantiam Hominis ingreditur, vel partem ejus aliquam essentialem constituit. Consimiliter de partibus essentialibus Sacramenti judicandum fuerit, eo modo, quo jam antè ostensum.

Et hinc est, quòd Ecclesia unanimi semper consensu, Sacramentum ex rebus neque pluribus, neque aliis, quàm duabus hisce, re nimirùm terrena sive elementari, & cœlesti, tanquam partibus essentialibus constare credidit. Irenæus lib. 4. cap. 34. cont. Valent. Quemadmodum qui est a terra panis, percipiens vocationem DEI, jam non communis panis est: sed Eucharistia, ex duabus rebus constans, terrena & cælesti: sic & corpora nostra percipientia Eucharistiam, jam non sunt corruptibilia, quippe spem resurrectionis habentia. Augustinus, uti habet jus Canonicum, de consecrat. distinct. 2. cap. 48. Hoc est, quod dicimus, quod modis omnibus approbare contendimus, Sacramentum hoc duobus confici, duobus constare, visibili Elementorum specie, & invisibili Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI carne & sanguine. Damasc. lib. 4. Orth. fidei cap. 14. Quemadmodum in Baptismo DEUS conjunxit aquæ gratiam Spiritus Sancti, & fecit illud lavacrum regenerationis: eodem modo, quia mos est hominibus, manducare panem, & vinum bibere, conjunxit his ipsis divinitatem & gratiam suam, & fecit hæc corpus & sanguinem suum. Et sanè potest hæc duarum istarum partium essentialium combinatio sive unio, ex Sacramentis tam Veteris, quàm Novi Testamenti ad oculum demonstrari. In circumcisione res terrena & visibilis fuit, Præputium cum Sanguinis effusione recisum. Res cælestis & spiritualis fuit, Sanguis Christi typicus. In Agno paschali, res terrena & visibilis fuit, Caro & Sanguis Agni: Res spiritualis verò erat Caro & Sanguis typicus Christi. In Baptismo, res terrena & elementaris est Aqua: Res cælestis est Sanguis Christi, sine quo nulla regeneratio fieri potest. In Cœna Domini res terrena & visibilis est Panis & Vinum: res cælestis est Corpus & Sanguis Christi essentialis. Neque verò certâ ratione caret, quòd Deus quodvis Sacramentum duabus istis partibus essentialibus constare voluit. Quia enim Deus non cum externo duntaxat: sed cum interno etiam homine, in Sacramentis agere voluit: ideò duas etiam partes cuilibet hominis considerationi convenientes, Sacramentorum esse voluit: quarum cælestis circa interni hominis fidem: terrena verò circa externi hominis sensus versaretur. Circa doctrinæ hujus puritatem non recto pede incedunt Sacramentarii. Etsi enim & ipsi verbis satis splendidè asserunt, Sacramenta rebus duabus constare: ipso tamen facto hoc eos negare, evidenter demonstrari potest. Primùm enim externis elementis sive Symbolis Sacramenti nomen & officium adscribunt: id quòd ex ipsorum dogmate, de Manducatione Indignorum, luculenter patet. Contendunt enim, Indignos Sacramentum quidem percipere: non autem percipere ipsum Corpus & Sanguinem Servatoris. E. Sacramentum ipsis etiam est, ubi non est res cælestis: & per consequens, Sacramenti essentia, jam ex una tantùm parte Elementari nimirùm sive terrenâ constabit. Animadvertens hoc Joh. Jacob. Grynæus, scribere non exhorruit, part. 2. problematum, pag. 203. Sacramenta fidei solis fidelibus esse Sacramenta. Cujus tamen paradoxi suffragatorem, quod ego sciam, ex universa turba Calviniana, habet neminem.

Deindè manifestum est, Sacramentarios Rem Coelestem, ut exempli gratia corpus & Sanguinem Domini, jam pro fructu & usu, jam pro ipsa substantia Sacramenti Eucharistici computare. Atqui verò nulla pars essentialis Sacramenti, simul potest ejusdem esse usus & fructus: ut qui semper extra Sacramenti substantiam consistit.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: II. Question. How sacraments are Signs: and what is their Signatum

No one is ignorant that the Sacraments have been designated by the name of Signs at all times, unless he has never, not even in passing, inspected or known the disputes of the Holy Fathers, and indeed the controversy of our own century regarding this Article. Our blessed Luther certainly did not shrink from this term, who in Article XIII of the Augsburg Confession willed to define the Sacraments as Signs and testimonies of the will of GOD toward us, proposed to excite and confirm the faith in those who use them. But in what sense and respect the Sacraments are and are called Signs: and also what they signify, or what is their proper and adequate Signified: that is indeed what is most especially disputed today. Hence also there is not one opinion of all as to what a Sign is, and how many-fold it is. D. Augustine, book 2 on Christian Doctrine, chapter 1. A sign, he says, is that which, beyond the appearance which it brings to the senses, makes something else come into knowledge. Augustine himself establishes that signs of this kind are twofold: ibid., chapters 1 and 2. Some are natural, which by their own nature represent something, as smoke represents fire, a footprint a foot: Others are given signs, such as words uttered by men to signify something, the sound of trumpets, the ringing of bells, and the like. If this division is attended to, the Sacraments certainly cannot or ought not in any way be referred to natural signs: but to given signs, since they are divinely promulgated to signify or signify something. But this doctrine of Augustine concerning sacramental signs is still more general, although it contains nothing of error. Therefore, that we may descend step by step to more special things, we distinguish both these signs defined by Augustine, again into two genera: of which some have a likeness with the thing signified, as the image of a man with the man himself: others, however, have no likeness. This distinction, if it is accommodated to the Sacraments properly so called, we establish that they can and ought to be referred to the species of given Signs, and indeed of those which have a likeness with the thing signified. Which Augustine also acknowledged in Epist. 23 to Boniface; saying, If Sacraments did not have a certain likeness of those things of which they are Sacraments, they would not be Sacraments at all. And Hugo of St. Victor in book 1 of the Sacraments, part 9, chapter 1, A Sacrament is that which represents by likeness. However, Sacraments have this power of signifying, not from any inherent natural power, but only from divine institution. Wherefore, although the water of Baptism, by which the external washing of the body is done, may seem by its own nature to have a certain aptitude for signifying the internal washing of the soul: yet it does not signify it in act, unless after it was decreed by divine ordinance that the external baptismal washing should signify the internal cleansing of the soul.

Moreover, that this whole discussion concerning Sign and Signified may be vindicated from the sophistries of the Sacramentarians, three things especially deserve observation: 1. whether Sign and Seal can be held as synonyms in this matter: where we hold the negative simply. For although Chrysostom and others contended that σημεῖον and σφραγῖδα, Sign and Seal, are synonyms and obtain exactly the same signification: yet, being thus taught by the Apostle in Rom. 4:11, we determine that these two words differ as the Thing or substance of the Sacrament, and the use or fruit of the Sacrament: so indeed that the word σημεῖον or Sign embraces the whole essence of the Sacrament; but the word σφραγῖδος or seal denotes the use and fruit of the Sacrament. For the Apostle expressly names Circumcision, insofar as it was a Sacrament, a σημεῖον; but he names its use or effect a seal of the righteousness of faith.

Hence another observation now emerges, which is: Just as the name and definition of a Sacrament belong not to one of the essential parts, whether earthly or heavenly, but to both taken together and composed or united into one: so again the appellation of Sign and the office of Signifying belong not to one part separately, but to both together, and with respect to the whole composite. For example, Bread and Wine in the Eucharist, and elemental Water in Baptism, are indeed the visible form of invisible grace: but they are not the whole matter of the Sacrament or sign, but only one part of it: and therefore they are also not a Sacrament, because they are not an integral sign: but only a part of the Sacramental sign: which nevertheless, with respect to the other part, also obtains its own peculiar manner of Signifying. Whence a twofold manner or faculty of Signifying arises in every Sacrament. That this may be asserted against the Sophistications of the Sacramentarians, the equivocation of the word Sacrament, which occurs most frequently in the writings of the Fathers, must first be noted. For sometimes they attribute the appellation of Sacrament to only one essential part, whether earthly or heavenly: which, however, that it is done improperly, becomes manifest from what has already been said; since it is not a Sacrament unless it is composed of both parts. Nor yet does any advantage redound to the Sacramentarians from this. For the Fathers did not speak thus in a Calvinistic sense, as if these Elements or Symbols exhaust the whole rationale of a Sacrament, or its entire nature and essence. But they looked to the other, heavenly part, which the earthly or Elemental thing also signifies in its own way. Nor indeed Sacraments do not only, by reason of both essential parts, obtain the power of signifying something outside themselves: but also one part, such as the earthly, signifies the other, namely the heavenly, with which it is sacramentally united. And indeed, unless this twofold manner of Signifying is granted to every Sacrament, and the twofold distinction of Sign and Signified resulting thence is properly attended to, no one will either successfully engage in unfolding the writings of the Fathers, or rightly avoid the tricks and Sophistications of the Sacramentarians. There is therefore one manner of Signifying for the whole Sacrament: Where the Signified is the use and fruit of the Sacrament, and thus something placed outside the substance of the Sacrament itself. Thus the whole Sacrament of circumcision, by reason of both essential parts, signified that spiritual circumcision, or adoption into the covenant, which the Apostle names circumcision made without hands in Coloss. 2:11. Thus the whole Sacrament of the Paschal Lamb, by reason of both essential parts, signified the Spiritual food of the Flesh of Christ. Thus the whole Sacrament of Baptism by reason of both essential parts signifies the Regeneration or Renewal of the Holy Spirit, Tit. 3:5. Thus the whole Sacrament of the Eucharist by reason of both essential parts signifies the spiritual coalition of all His benefits. Where the signified is always something placed outside the essence of the Sacrament.

Then, however, there is another Sacramental signification by reason of one part only toward the other. For because the use and fruit of the Sacraments is sealed not only by external and perishable elements, but also by heavenly things, as certain pledges: but these heavenly things are not visible, therefore there was need of this other signification also, which external and visible elements perform: which are therefore called by the Fathers Symbols, Types, figures, tokens, not because they alone signify the use or fruit of the Sacrament, as the Calvinists suppose. For to this task of signifying, external elements alone would be too weak: but because they signify the other essential part of the Sacrament, namely the heavenly and invisible; not indeed (as the Calvinists again impiously contend) as clearly remote and absent, or as Beza blurted out in the Colloquy of Poissy, as far distant from those external Symbols as the highest heaven is distant from the lowest earth: but most present, and most united to those external Symbols,

From these things which we have now said, a Third observation results, which is concerning the mode of Signifying, which, according to the diverse manner of Signifying, is not one and the same, but varies greatly. For when one essential part of a Sacrament signifies the other, then the mode of signifying is not merely σημαντικὸς significative or adumbrative: but at the same time it is προσφερόμενος καὶ διαδοτικὸς collative or exhibitive. For because an intimate and most strict Sacramental union intervenes between the external elements and the heavenly thing, hence it comes about that the external Symbols not only signify the heavenly thing, but at the same time truly confer and exhibit the same. But when the whole Sacrament, by reason of both essential parts, signifies something placed outside its essence, namely the use or fruit of the Sacrament: then it is indeed always a significative sign: but not always προσφερόμενον. For because that saving use of the Sacrament, by reason of the act or enjoyment, does not simply depend upon the essence of the Sacrament: for thus all, as many as participate in the Sacrament, would also participate in its saving use: which is manifestly false: but because that depends by the power of divine ordination upon the faith of those using it: hence it comes about that the Sacraments with respect to unbelievers are not always προσφερόμενα regarding the saving use, although from the intention of GOD they could and ought always to be such, unless the unbelief of those using them were to hinder, nay, to take away this saving διάδοσιν καὶ ἐνέργειαν.

There depends upon this observation also that which, according to this diverse mode of signifying, can and ought to be defined in diverse ways regarding the Signified. For if the whole Sacrament, by reason of both essential parts, is a Sign, that is, signifies the use or fruit of the Sacrament: then the Signified is not any essential part of the Sacrament: for thus the part and the whole: the Sign and the Signified would be the same: which is absurd. But the signified is, and is called, something placed outside the substance of the Sacrament: namely the use or fruit of the Sacrament.

Vice versa, if one essential part of the Sacrament is called a Sign, that is, signifies the other essential part: then the Signified is something constituted within the very substance of the Sacrament: nay, necessarily pertaining to the integrity of the same: namely the other essential part: the heavenly and invisible thing. This diversity of Sign and Signified, unless it is well attended to, one will never happily extricate himself from the tricks of the Calvinists, which they are accustomed to weave under the indiscriminate and confused use of these terms.

The matter will become clearer by an example: If the whole Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, as it consists and is considered from both essential parts, earthly and heavenly, namely bread and wine, the body and blood of Christ, is and is called a Sign: then the Signified is the spiritual use or fruit of the Sacrament, which does not pertain to the essential integrity of the Sacrament. And thus it is true that those participating unworthily in the Sacrament receive the Sign but not the Signified. But if only one part of this Sacrament, namely the earthly thing, bread and wine, is called a Sign: as is most customary for the Fathers and other writers: then the Signified is not something placed outside the essence of the Sacrament, as they deceitfully pretend

Calvinists: but the Signified is the other essential part of the Sacrament, namely the heavenly thing, the Body and Blood of CHRIST: which, with the earthly or elementary part, is always sacramentally united, and most unitively present. And in this sense it is now most false that those using the Sacrament unworthily receive indeed the Sign, but not the Signified, as the Sacramentarians wish. For it cannot happen that anyone using the Sacrament receives only one essential part, namely the elementary: but not the other also, namely the heavenly: because neither part separately or without the other, but always both together constitute the essential integrity of the Sacrament. Therefore, let the Calvinists either confess that the unworthy do not possess the Sacrament at all: or that the essence of the Sacrament is perfected and completed by only one part of it, namely the earthly: both of which would be joined with stupendous absurdity.

And these things indeed, concerning the twofold mode of signifying, as also concerning the diverse usurpation of Sign and Signified, on account of the controversies of our century, and especially the sophistications of the Calvinists, I have chosen to note a little more accurately: otherwise, outside of this conflict with the Sacramentarians, the doctrine of the purer theologians concerning sacramental signs was informed a little differently: which, however, does not so much overturn or weaken our previous disputation, as it rather wonderfully establishes it.

Some, therefore, considering the nature of signs in general, have elicited three kinds of signs from the sacred writings: of which some are federal signs, Bundszeichen; such as Circumcision and Baptism: and since these signs are testimonies of the Divine will toward us, according to the promise of the Gospel, they have rightly determined that they be named Sacraments. Others are signs of truth, and of things either done or to be done, Warzeichen: such as were: the fleece of Gideon, likewise the fire consuming the sacrifices: the napkins in the sepulcher after the resurrection of CHRIST. And to such signs they have rightly determined that the definition of Sacraments properly so called does not apply. Finally, there are others which are memorial signs or μνημονευτικά Gedenckzeichen: such as the Passover, and the Supper of the Lord: to which they have also rightly determined that the name of Sacraments can be truly and properly attributed.

Other theologians have treated this doctrine concerning Sacramental signs a little more strictly, having that especially in mind, that in the definition of Sacraments, the Genus which is expressed by the term Sign is not extended to just any thing (in which generic meaning indeed in the Mosaic Law very many signs can be given) but is restricted, as it were, so that a Sacrament is not, unless it is a sign of a sacred thing. Therefore, following the footsteps of these theologians, we have determined that this is especially to be noted, that the mode of signifying, by which Sacraments are said to signify, is not one and the same: but especially threefold. For every Sacrament signifies according to the diversity of the parts of time; both of the past, and of the present, and of the future. By reason of past time, Sacraments are commemorative signs: by reason of present time, they are exhibitive and προσφερόμενα [offered] signs: by reason of future time, Sacraments are, as it were, prognostic signs. Dionysius in Ecclesiastical Hierarchy discourses at great length on these three respects of signifying. Damascene in book 4 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 10. But also Holy Scripture has not obscurely expressed these very diverse respects of signifying in some Sacraments. Concerning Baptism, that it is a commemorative sign, it is held in Rom. 6:3. Whosoever of us have been baptized into Christ Jesus, have been baptized into his death.

Then, that it is a demonstrative sign of present grace is clear in the same place, verse 7. He who is dead is justified from sin. Finally, that it is a prognostic of partly future holiness, and partly also of future glory, is taught in the same place, verse 11. Reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin: but alive to GOD, in CHRIST JESUS: and verse 5, If we have been made planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection.

Concerning the Lord's Supper, that it is primarily a commemorative sign of the death of Christ, the Apostle is witness, 1 Cor. 11:26. As often as you drink from this cup, you shall announce the Lord's death, until he comes: Likewise, do this in remembrance of me. That it is a demonstrative and προσφερόμενον [offered] sign of present grace conferred is shown by these words: This is my body, which is given for you: This is my blood, which is shed for you, for the remission of sins. Matt. 26:28. That it is finally a prognostic sign of future glory, by reason of its salutary use and fruit, John teaches at great length in chapter 6. He who eats me, shall live because of me.
