Thus circumcision 1. signified the guilt of original sin, on account of which the human race had been worthy of excision. 2. the present grace of the covenant and adoption into the people of GOD. 3. future abstinence from sins.

Thus the Paschal Lamb denoted. 1. liberation from Egyptian servitude. 2. the present expiation of sins. 3. the future slaughter of the blessed lamb.

Now although all Sacraments are signifying in such a varied respect: yet κατ̓ έξοχὴν [pre-eminently], by reason of present time, insofar as they are indeed signs προσφερόμενα [offered] and exhibitive, they are and are called signs: because indeed they confer the grace of Sanctification, or the Sanctifying thing. However, the essence or nature of the Sacraments consists not in this, that they are signs of a sanctifying thing simply, or in any way whatsoever: but rather in this, that they signify grace and the sanctifying thing in the one legitimately using, or receiving the Sacrament. For if it were enough for the essence of a Sacrament to signify a sanctifying thing: then all the sacrifices of the Old Testament would be Sacraments, because they signified the death of Christ: which was indeed a sanctifying thing. But in the Old Testament there were three distinct things: Sacred things: Sacrifices: Sacraments. Sacred things were, Vessels, the temple, Vestments and the like. Sacrifices consisted of offerings of animals and other things. There were only two Sacraments; Circumcision and the Paschal Lamb.

Furthermore, it is to be noted in this place, that for a sign of invisible grace to be truly Sacramental, it is not enough that something be applied to signify grace: but that it be so applied that it is instituted by GOD, to signify always, and to effect grace and sanctification. For not everything that signifies in any way is immediately a Sacrament: as for example, those words in Matt. 9:2, Luke 7:48, Thy sins are forgiven thee: were a sign of grace conferred through Christ: yet they were not a Sacrament. The reason for this is, because those words were indeed a sign from a present will to signify the merciful affection of Christ: but they were not instituted by Christ as a sign, to signify always, and to confer grace.

Finally, the proper signification of the Sacraments is of grace, but not just any grace: but of Evangelical grace alone, and indeed that which internally and immediately sanctifies. For example: Manna in the desert, and the bronze serpent, were signs of most sacred things: the former indeed of CHRIST, in the Eucharist: the latter of the same on the cross. But none of these was a Sacrament. The reason is this, because by these signs, by divine institution, there was not signified a thing internally and immediately sanctifying: but they were rather figures of sacred things, denoting an extrinsic and mediate cause of sanctification. Thus the dove at the Baptism of CHRIST, Matt. 3:16, and the tongues of fire appearing over the Apostles on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2:3, were indeed signs of the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit: yet they were not Sacraments. The manifest reason for this was, because those signs did not signify the sanctification proper to Evangelical grace. For Christ was not made holier by the coming of the dove: nor was this instituted then as a sign of a sanctifying thing: but it was a document of the peculiar presence of the Holy Spirit, and a figure of the sanctification to be conferred in our Baptism. Moreover, the tongues of fire were not a Sacrament for that reason, because they lacked institution for sanctifying the sanctifying thing. Furthermore, they were not signs of grace that would always endure: but were to remain only for a time. Because of the defect of this condition, Manna also and the bronze serpent are excluded from the proper definition of a Sacrament, because these themselves also were not to endure for a period equal to the Mosaic law.

And let this suffice to have said concerning the nature and the, as it were, proper affection of Sacramental signs: It remains that it become plain how its correlative, namely the Signified, behaves.

Latin:

SIgnorum appellatione Sacramenta omnibus temporibus fuisse indigitata, nemo nescit, nisi qui S. Patrum disputationes, quin & recentiore nostri seculi, de hoc Articulo Controversiam, nunquam, ne quidem per transennam inspexit aut cognovit. Beatus certè Lutherus noster ab hoc termino minimè abhorruit, qui Articulo XIII. Confessionis Augustanae, Sacramenta definire voluit, quòd sint Signa & testimonia voluntatis DEI erganos, ad excitandam & confirmandam fidem, in his, qui utuntur, proposita. Caeterùm quo sensu atque respectu Sacramenta sint & dicantur Signa: quid etiam signent, sive quodnam eorum proprium atq; adaequatum sit Signatum: id verò est, de quo potissimùm hodiè controvertitur. Hinc etiam quid sit Signum, & quotuplex illud sit, non una omnium est sententia. D. Augustinus, lib. 2. de doct. Christ. cap. 1. Signum est, inquit, quod praeter speciem, quam infert sensibus, facit aliquid aliud in cognitionem venire. Constituit autem ipse Augustinus Signa hujusmodi duplicia: ibid. cap. 1. & 2. Alia naturalia, quae suapte natura aliquid repraesentant, ut fumus ignem, vestigium pedem.: Alia verò Signa data, qualia sunt, voces ad aliquid significandum ab hominibus editae, sonus tubarum, clangor campanarum & similia. Haec divisio si attendatur, Sacramenta certè referri nullo modo possunt aut debent ad signa naturalia: sed ad signa data, siquidem divinitùs sunt promulgata, ad signandum sive significandum aliquid. Verùm haec Augustini de signis Sacramentalibus doctrina, adhuc generalior est, licèt erroris nihil contineat. Ergo ut ad specialiora pedetentim descendamus, distinguimus utraque haec ab Augustino definita signa, rursus in duo genera: quorum alia habent similitudinem cum re significata, ut imago hominis cum ipso homine: alia verò nullam habent similitudinem. Haec distinctio, si accommodetur ad Sacramenta propriè sic dicta, statuimus ea referri posse & debere ad speciem Signorum datorum, & quidem eorum, quæ cum re signata similitudinem habent. Quod agnovit Augustinus quoque Epist. 23. ad Bonifacium; Si inquiens, Sacramenta similitudinem quandam earum rerum, quarum sunt Sacramenta, non haberent, omninò Sacramenta non essent. Et Hugo de S. Victore libr. 1. de Sacramentis, part. 9. cap. 1. Sacramentum est, quod ex similitudine repræsentat. Habent autem Sacramenta vim hanc signandi, non ex insita quapiam vi naturali, sed tantùm ex institutione divinâ. Quare licèt Baptismi aqua, quâ fit ablutio externa corporis, videatur naturâ suâ habere aptitudinem quandam, ad significandam ablutionem internam animæ: actu tamen eam non significat, nisi postquàm ordinatione divinâ sancitum fuit, ut ablutio baptistica externa, internam animæ mundationem significaret.

Cæterùm ut tota hæc de Signo & Signato disputatio à Sacramentariorum strophis vindicetur, tria potissimùm observationem merentur: 1. nùm Signu & Signaculum hac in materia pro synonymis haberi possint: ubi nos negativam simpliciter tenemus. Etsi enim Chrysostomus & alij, σημεῖον καὶ σφραγῖδα, Signum & Signaculum, synonyma esse, ac eandem prorsus significationem obtinere contenderunt: tamen sic edocti ab Apostolo Rom. 4, 11. statuimus, duo hæc vocabula differre, ut Rem sive substantiam Sacramenti, & usum sive fructum Sacramenti: ita quidem, ut vox σημεῖε sive Signi, totam Sacramenti essentiam complectatur: vox verò σφραγῖδος sive signaculi, usum ac fructum Sacramenti notet. Nam disertè Apostolus Circumcisionem, quatenùs erat Sacramentum, nominat σημεῖον: ejus verò usum sive effectum nominat σφραγῖδα signaculum justitiæ fidei.

Hinc altera jam emergit observatio, quæ est: Quemadmodum non uni partium essentialium, sive terrenæ sive cœlesti, sed utrique simul sumtæ & in unum compositæ five unitæ, Sacramenti nomen ac definitio competit: ita rursus non uni parti seorsim, sed utrique simul, & quoad totum compositum, Signi appellatio, & Signandi officium competit. Exempli gratia, Panis & Vinum in Eucharistia: Aqua elementaris in Baptismo sunt quidem forma visibilis, invisibilis gratiæ: sed non sunt tota Sacramenti sive signi materia, verùm una tantùm ejus pars: ac proindè etiam non sunt Sacramentum, quia non sunt signum integrum: sed pars tantùm signi Sacramentalis: quæ tamen respectu alterius partis, suam quoque peculiarem Signandi rationem obtinet. Undè gemina Signandi ratio sive facultas in quolibet Sacramento oboritur. Quæ ut à Sacramentariorum Sophisticationibus asseratur, notanda initiò venit æquivocatio vocis Sacramenti, quæ in Patrum scriptis frequentissimè occurrit. Interdum enim illi Sacramenti appellationem uni tantùm parti essentiali, sive terrenæ sive cœlesti tribuunt: id quòd tamen impropriè fieri, ex jam dictis manifestum evadit: siquidem Sacramentum non est, nisi quod ex utraque parte est compositum. Neque tamen hinc quicquam præsidij ad Sacramentarios redundat. Patres enim non sensu Calvinistico sic locuti sunt quasi hæc Elementa sive Symbola omnem Sacramenti rationem, sive totam ejus naturam atq; essentiam absolvant. Sed respexerunt illi ad partē alterā cœlestem, quam suo etiam modo, res terrena sive Elementaris signat. Neq; n. Sacramenta tantùm integra, ratione utriusq; partis essentialis, obtinent vim signandi aliquid extra se: sed etiam una pars, ut terrena, signat alteram, nempè cœlestem, cum qua Sacramentaliter est unita. Et profectò nisi duplex hæc Signandi ratio cuilibet Sacramento concedatur: & gemina indè resultans Signi & Signati distinctio probè attendatur, quisquam vel in Patrum scriptis evolvendis feliciter versabitur, vel Sacramentariorum tricas ac Sophisticationes ritè evitabit. Alia ergò est Signandi ratio totius Sacramenti: Ubi Signatum est usus & fructus Sacramenti, & sic aliquid extra ipsam Sacramenti substantiam positum. Sic totum Sacramentum circumcisionis ratione utriusque partis essentialis, signabat circumcisionem illam spiritualem, sive adoptionem in foed9, quam Apostolus nominat circumcisionem ἀχειροποίητον Coloss. 2, 11. Sic Sacramentum totum Agni Paschalis, ratione utriusq́ partis essentialis, signabat escam Spiritualem Carnis Christi. Sic totum Sacramentum Baptismi ratione utriusque partis essentialis signat Regenerationem sive Renovationem Spiritus Sancti, Tit. 3, 5. Sic totum Sacramentum Eucharistiæ ratione utriusque partis essentialis, signat spiritualem coalitionem omnium ipsius beneficiorum. Ubi semper signatum est aliquid extra Sacramenti essentiam positum.

Deinde verò alia est signatio Sacramentalis ratione unius duntaxat partis ad alteram. Quia enim usus & fructus Sacramentorum, non per externa tantùm & caduca elementa: sed & per res cœlestes, ceu pignora quædam obsignatur: Res verò hæ cœlestes non sunt visibiles, ideò alterâ etiam hac signatione opus fuit, quâ funguntur externa & visibilia elementa: quæ ideò à Patribus dicuntur Symbola, Typi, figuræ, tesseræ, non quòd eâ sola signent usum seu fructum Sacramenti, uti Calviniani autumant. Nam ad hoc signandi munus nimis infirma forent sola externa elementa: sed quòd signent alteram partem essentialem Sacramenti, cœlestem videlicet & invisibilem; non quidem (uti rursus Calviniani impiè contendunt) planè remotam & absentem, vel ut Beza in Colloquio Possiaceno effutijt, tam procul ab externis illis Symbolis distantem, quàm procul distat supremum cœlum ab ima terra: sed præsentissimam, & externis illis Symbolis unitissimam,

Ex his quæ jam diximus, resultat Tertia observatio, quæ est de Signandi modo, qui pro diversa Signandi ratione, non est unus & idem, sed plurimùm variat. Quando enim una pars essentialis Sacramenti signat alteram, tùm fignandi modus non est nudè σημαντικὸς significativus aut adumbrativus: sed simul est προσφερόμενος καὶ διαδοτικὸς collativus sive exhibitivus. Quia enim externis elementis cum re cœlesti, intercedit intima & arctissima unio Sacramentalis, hinc adeò fit, ut externa Symbola non modò fignent rem cœlestem, sed eandem simul verè conferant & exhibeant. Quando verò totum Sacramentum ratione utriusque partis essentialis fignat aliquid extrà suam essentiam positum, nempè usum sive fructum Sacramenti: tùm semper quidem est signum fignificativum: sed non semper προσφερόμενον. Quia enim salutaris iste Sacramenti usus, ratione actus sive perfruitionis, non simpliciter dependet à Sacramenti essentia: Sic enim omnes quotquot Sacramento participant, salutari etiam ipsius usu participarent: id quod manifestè falsum: sed quia ille dependet vi divinæ ordinationis à fide usurpantium: hinc fit, ut Sacramenta respectu infidelium non semper sint προσφερόμενα quoad usum salutarem, licèt ex intentione DEI talia semper esse possent & deberent, nisi utentium infidelitas salutarem hanc διάδοσιν καὶ ἐνέργειαν, impediret, imò tolleret.

Dependet ab hac observatione & illud, quod pro diversa hac Signandi ratione, diversimodè etiam Signatum definiri potest & debet. Si enim totum Sacramentum, ratione utriusque partis essentialis, est Signum, hoc est, fignat usum seu fructum Sacramenti: tùm Signatum non est pars aliqua essentialis Sacramenti: Sic enim pars & totum: Signum & Signatum forent idem: quod absurdum. Sed fignatum est, & dicitur aliquid extra Sacramenti Substantiam positum: nempè usus seu fructus Sacramenti.

Vice versa, si Sacramenti pars una essentialis dicitur Signum, hoc est, fignat alteram partem essentialem: tùm Signatum est aliquid intra ipsam Sacramenti substantiam constitutum: imò ad ejusdem integritatem necessariò pertinens: nempè altera pars essentialis: Res cœlestis & invisibilis. Diversitas hæc Signi & Signati, nisi probè attendatur, nunquàm ex tricis Calvinianorum, quas sub vocabulorum istorum indiscreto & confuso usu nectere solent, feliciter quis se expediet.

Exemplo res fiet illustrior: Si Sacramentum cœnæ Dominicæ totum, prout constat & consideratur ex utraque parte essentiali terrenâ & cœlesti, nempè pane & vino, corpore & sangvine Christi, est & dicitur Signum: tùm Signatum est spiritualis usus seu fructus Sacramenti, qui ad essentialem Sacramenti integritatem non pertinet. Et sic verum est, quòd indigni participantes Sacramento, accipiant Signum non autem Signatum. Sin autem una tantùm Sacramenti hujus pars, nempè res terrena, panis & vinum, dicitur Signum: uti Patribus & alijs Scriptoribus est usitatissimum: tùm Signatum non est aliquid extra Sacramenti essentiam positum, uti subdolè fingunt

Calviniani: sed Signatum est, altera essentialis pars Sacramenti, Res videlicet cœlestis, Corpus & Sangvis CHRISTI: quæ cum parte terrena sive elementari, semper Sacramentaliter est unita, & unitissimè præsens. Et hoc sensu falsissimum jam est, quòd indigni utentes Sacramento accipiant quidem Signum, sed non Signatum, uti Sacramentarij volunt. Fieri enim nequit, ut aliquis utens Sacramento unam tantùm partem essentialem, nempè elementarem: non autem alteram quoque, cœlestem videlicet, accipiat: propterea quod neutra pars seorsim aut sine altera, sed semper utraque junctim essentialem integritatem Sacramenti constituit. Proindè Calviniani vel fateantur indignos, planè non Sacramento potiri: vel Sacramenti essentiam unâ tantùm ejus parte, nempè terrenâ, perfici & absolvi: Quod utrumque cum stupenda absurditate foret conjunctum.

Et hæc quidem de gemina Signandi ratione, ut & de diversa Signi & Signati usurpatione, propter nostri seculi controversias, & Calvinianorum cumprimis Sophisticationes, paulò accuratiùs annotare libuit: aliàs extra istum cum Sacrnmentarijs conflictum, paulò aliter informata fuit Theologorum puriorum doctrina, de Signis sacramentalibus: quæ tamen usque adeò superiorem nostram disputationem non everrit aut labefactat, ut potiùs mirificè eam stabiliat.

Nonnulli ergò Signorum naturam in genere considerantes, tria Signorum genera ex sacris elicuerunt: quorum alia sunt Signa fœderalia, Bundszeichen; ut Circumcisio & Baptismus: & cum hæc signa sint testimonia Divinæ voluntatis erga nos, juxta promissionem Evangelij, meritò Sacramenta nominari statuerunt. Alia sint Signa veritatis, rerumquè vel gestarum vel gerendarum, Warzeichen: qualia erant: vellus Gedeonis, item ignis sacrificia consumens: Sudaria in sepulchro post resurrectionem CHRISTI. Et talibus quidem Signis rectè statuerunt definitionem Sacramentorum propriè sic dictorum non competere. Aliæ denique sint Signa memoralia sive μνημονευτικά Gedenckzeichen: qualia sunt Pascha, & Cœna Domini: quibus quoque Sacramentorum nomen verè ac propriè tribui posse, rectè statuerunt.

Alij Theologi paulò pressiùs doctrinam hanc de Signis Sacramentalibus pertractarunt, illud potissimùm pensi habentes, quòd in definitione Sacramentorum, Genus quòdSigni termino exprimitur, non ad rem quamlibet extenditur (quo sanè generico significatu in LegeMosaica quamplurima signa dari possunt) sed restringitur, quasi, ita ut Sacramentum non sit, nisi rei sacræ signum. Theologorum proindè istorum vestigia secuti,illud potissimùm notandum esse statuimus,quod modus signandi,quoSacramenta signare dicuntur,non est unus atq; idem: sed triplex potissimùm. NamSacramentum omne signat pro diversitate partium temporis; tùm præteriti, tùm præsentis, tùm futuri. Ratione temporis præteriti, Sacramenta sunt signa commemorativa: ratione temporis præsentis, sunt signa exhibitiva & προσφερόμενα: ratione temporis futuri sunt Sacramenta, signa quasi prognostica. De tribus istis Signandi respectibus, prolixè admòdùm differunt, Dionysius in Hiarchia Ecclesiastica. Ambrosius libro de Sacramentis: & libro de iis qui mysteriis initiantur: Damascenus lib. 4. Orth. fid. cap. 10. Sed & scriptura sacra, hos ipsos diversos signandi respectus in aliquibus Sacramentis haud obscurè expressit. De Baptismo, quod sit Signum commemorativum, habetur Rom. 6, 3. Quicunque baptizati sumus in Christo Jesu, in morte ipsius baptizati sumus.

Deinde quod sit Signum demonstrativum præsentis gratiæ, patet ibidem, versu 7. Qui mortuus est, justificatus à peccato est. Tandem quòd sit prognosticon partim futuræ Sanctitatis, partim futuræ etiam gloriæ, docetur ibidem vers. 11. Existimate vos mortuos quidem esse peccato: Vivere autem DEO, in CHRISTO JESU: & vers. 5 Si complantati facti sumus similitudini mortis ejus, simul & resurrectionis erimus.

De Cœnâ Domini, quod sit primum signum commemorativum mortis Christi, testis est Apostolus, 1. Cor. 11, 26. Quotiescunq; de calice isto biberitis, mortem Domini annunciabitis, donec veniat: Item, facite hoc in mei commemorationem. Quod sit signum demonstrativum & προσφερόμενον præsentis gratiæ collatæ, ostenditur his Verbis: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur: Hic est sangvis meus, qui pro vobis funditur, in remissionem peccatorum. Matth. 26, 28. Quod denique sit signum prognosticum futuræ gloriæ, ratione salutaris usus & fructus, prolixè admodùm docet Johannes cap. 6. Qui manducat me, vivet propter me.

Sic circumcisio 1. significabat reatum peccati originalis, propter quem excisione dignum humanum genus fuerat. 2. præsentem gratiam fœderis & adoptionem in populo DEI. 3. futuram abstinentiam à peccatis.

Sic Agnus paschalis notabat. 1. liberationem ex servitute Ægyptiaca 2. præsentem peccatorum expiationem. 3. futuram agni benedicti mactationem.

Jam quamvis Sacramenta omnia tam vario respectu sint significantia: κατ̓ έξοχὴν tamen, ratione temporis præsentis, quatenùs nimirùm sunt Signa προσφερόμενα exhibitiva, sunt & dicuntur Signa: quia nimirùm conferunt gratiam Sanctificationis, aut rem Sanctificantem. Consistit autem Sacramentorum efsentia sive natura non in eo, ut sint Signa rei sanctificantis simpliciter, aut quocunque modo: sed in eo potiùs, ut signent gratiam & rem sanctificantem in legitimè utente, seu Sacramentum recipiente. Si enim ad essentiam Sacramenti satis esset, signare rem sanctificantem: tùm omnia sacrificia Veteris Testamenti forent Sacramenta, quia mortem Christi significarunt: quæ fuit utique res sanctificans. Atqui in Veteri Testamento tria fuerunt distincta: Sacra: Sacrificia: Sacramenta. Sacra fuerunt, Vasa, templum, Vestes & similia. Sacrificia oblationibus animalium, aliarumq; rerum constabant. Sacramenta fuerunt duo tantùm; Circumcisio & Agnus paschalis.

Porrò & illud hoc loco notandum, ut invifibilis gratiæ fignum verè Sacramentale fit, non fatis efse, ut ad fignandam gratiam aliquid fit adhibitum : fed fic adhibitum, ut inftitutum fit à DEO, ad fignificandum femper, & ad efficiendum gratiam & fanctificationem. Neque enim quicquid quoquo modo fignat, ftatim eft Sacramentum: ut exempli gratia, verba illa Matth. 9, 2. Luc. 7, 48. Remittuntur tibi peccata: erant fignum gratiæ per Chriftum collatæ: non tamen erant Sacramentum. Ratio hæc eft, quia verba illa erant quidem Signum ex præfenti voluntate ad fignificandum mifericordem affectum Chrifti: fed non erant inftituta à Chrifto pro figno, ad fignificandum femper, & ad conferendam gratiam.

Tandem Sacramentorum propria eft fignatio Græciæ, fed non cujusvis: verùm Evangelicæ folius, & quidem internè ac immediatè fanctificantis. Exempli gratiâ: Manna in deferto, & ferpens æneus, erant figna rerum facratiffimarum: illud quidem CHRISTI, in Euchariftiâ : hic verò ejufdem in cruce. Atqui nihil horum fuit Sacramentum. Ratio eft hæc, quia fignis iftis ex inftitutione divinâ non fignificabatur res internè atque immediatè fanctificans: fed figuræ potiùs erant rerum facrarum, extrinfecam fanctificationis caufam atque mediatam notantes. Sic columba in Baptifmo CHRISTI, Matth. 3, 16. & lingvæ igneæ apparentes fuper Apoftolis in die Pentecoftes, Actor. 2, 3. erant quidem figna gratiæ invifibilis Spiritus Sancti: nec tamen Sacramenta erant. Ratio manifefta hæc fuit, quia ifta Signa non fignificabant Sanctificationem gratiæ Evangelicæ propriam. Chriftus enim fuperventu columbæ non eft factus fanctior: neque hoc pro Signo rei fanctificantis tum inftitutum fuit: fed præfentiæ Spiritus Sancti peculiaris illud documentum fuit, & figura fanctificationis in noftro Baptifmo conferendæ. Lingvæ autem igneæ eo nomine non erant Sacramentum, quia carebant inftitutione ad fanctificandam rem fanctificantem. Præteréa non erant Signa gratiæ femper duratura: fed ad tempus duntaxat permanfura. Ob cujus conditionis defectum, Manna etiam & ferpens æneus à propriâ Sacramenti ratione excluduntur, quia hæc ipfa quoque non pari cum lege Mofaicâ periodo duratura erant.

Et hæc quidem de naturâ & propriâ quafi affectione Signorum Sacramentalium dixiffe fufficiat: Reftat ut quomodo ejus correlativum nempè Signatum fe habeat, planum fiat.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: On the Thing Signified

IN the beginning, however, it is to be noted that in the writings both of the Sacramentarians and of certain of our own theologians, the signatum and the Res Sacramenti are taken as equivalent. And although there seems to be little difference between these two, since both the Signatum and the Res Sacramenti are in this place taken for the use and fruit of the Sacrament, yet if the proper nature of each be examined a little more accurately with regard to the very sealing of the Sacraments, it will readily appear that some difference exists between these two. For the Res Sacramenti, which for us in this place is nothing else than the virtue of the merit of Christ, or as the Apostle speaks Rom. 4, 11. The seal of the righteousness of faith, is common to all Sacraments of both the Old and New Testament. For what the Apostle pronounces in the place just cited concerning the Sacrament of Circumcision, that it is a seal of the righteousness of faith: that can be pronounced concerning all Sacraments in general: meanwhile, however, if the nature and institution of any Sacrament be weighed more accurately, it appears that every Sacrament has its own, and adequate or appropriated signified thing, bearing a certain ἀναλογίαν or likeness with its sign: and therefore incommunicable to the remaining Sacraments: through which finally, and thus mediately and δευτέρως, that Thing of the Sacrament, namely the seal of the righteousness of faith, comes to those using the Sacrament: so indeed that the Thing of the Sacrament is more correctly called a seal, than a signified thing. For example: In Circumcision the proper and appropriated signified thing, as the Apostle defines, Coloss 2, 11. is the spiritual Circumcision ἀχειροποίητος. With this signified thing finally mediating, the Thing of the Sacrament was obtained, which is the seal or sealing of the righteousness of faith. Thus in the Paschal Lamb, the proper and adequate signified thing was the spiritual food of the Typical Body of Christ: by which finally mediating, the Thing of the Sacrament was obtained, namely the seal of the righteousness of faith. Thus in Baptism the signified thing ἀνάλογον and appropriated is the Regeneration or Renewal of the Holy Spirit. Tit. 3, 5. By this finally mediating is obtained the Thing of the Sacrament, namely the seal of the righteousness of faith. Thus in the Supper of the Lord the proper and adequate signified thing is, the spiritual coalition, or as some of the Fathers have spoken, the co-uniting with CHRIST: or that spiritual eating and drinking of the Body and Blood of Christ, of which John 6. By which spiritual eating finally mediating is obtained the Thing of the Sacrament, namely the seal of faith.

Nor does it stand in the way, that this spiritual eating and drinking of the Body and Blood of Christ, of which John 6 treats, can also take place outside the Sacrament of the Eucharist. For it is not of simple and absolute necessity that signified things should uniquely cohere with their signs, and be unable to have their operation outside the use of the Sacrament. That the signified thing of Circumcision was certainly the circumcision ἀχειροποίητος, we have just now learned from the Apostle: But yet the same Apostle requires this very spiritual circumcision from his Colossians, who certainly were not observing that sacramental sign, namely the external circumcision of the foreskin. Thus in this place, spiritual eating, which takes place through faith, also has a place in the faithful outside this Sacrament: nor yet does anything stand in the way, so that it may not be the proper and adequate signified thing of the Eucharist.

They indeed scourge this purer doctrine of ours concerning the nature of the signified thing, having used this argument: It is necessary that the sign and the signified thing be together: otherwise the nature of the Sacraments will not be whole. But yet spiritual eating is not joined to the

Substance of the Sacrament: since it ought rather to be referred to its fruit or salutary use. Therefore this spiritual eating cannot be called the signified thing of the Sacrament of the Eucharist.

I answer that both of the premises suffer from childish sophisms. In the Major, an error of ἀμφιβολίας is committed. For things are said to be together in two ways. For in one way those things are together which exist together in the nature of things: in another way, those which are truly and really joined, if not always in act, at least δυνάμει. If the Major proposition be taken in the former sense, we concede it willingly. For because the sign and the signified thing follow the nature of relative things, of which one being posited, the other is posited: one being destroyed, the other is also destroyed: therefore the sign and the signified thing must be together. Thus in this very sense we willingly concede also the Adversative, so that if the sign and the signified thing are not together, then the nature of the signs is not even whole: Or to speak more clearly, then in the Sacraments every reason for a sign expires: for the reason that no sign can be the signified thing of itself: nor can a part of a sign be the signified thing. And thus in this former sense and respect these Critics fight without an adversary.

But if the major proposition be understood in the latter sense: then it is not universally true, and thus the argumentation proceeds only in part.

For it is not the property of all signs that they have signified things joined to themselves: but this is only the property of that certain species of signs, namely those which are and are called παραφερόμενα. For the rest of the signs, which are σημαντικὰ, removal is more proper than conjunction, at least as far as sense is concerned.

For the sake of greater clarity, I am pleased to illustrate this response with the example of the Eucharist.

If you understand the major in the former sense, certainly in the Sacrament of the Eucharist the sign and the signified thing are most joined, when by the sign you understand only one essential part, namely the earthly, Bread and Wine: but by the signified thing, the other essential part, namely the Body and Blood of Christ. For because these two parts exist together in the use of the Sacrament, and indeed from the very nature of the Sacrament: certainly also the signified thing without the sign, in this sense and respect, can in no way exist. But if indeed by the word Sign you understand the whole Sacrament composed of both things, the earthly and the heavenly: and if the signified is then taken as the salutary use and fruit of the Sacrament: then no reason or necessity compels that the Sign and the Signified must always be present together in act: but it is enough if the Sacrament performs the duty of signifying, and signifies that salutary use, even if it does not confer it with the act, or have it present to itself: which is most clearly evident from the eating of the unworthy.

The cause therefore of the error is that those Critics dream of only one manner of signifying, which nevertheless was shown above to be twofold.

And this indeed is the first thing which concerning the thing signified deserves observation: It remains, secondly, that it be shown in a few words by what marks of difference the Sign can and ought to be distinguished from the Signified (if it be taken for the use or fruit of the Sacrament).

A fourfold distinction, however, can be made between them. And first, they differ in dispensation: for Signs, or Sacraments, by reason of their substance, are dispensed by ministers; but the Signified has its power and operation principally from the Holy Spirit alone.

Then they differ in the mode or organ of perception: for Signs, or Sacraments, by reason of both essential parts, are perceived by that mode or organ which GOD himself destined for each Sacrament in its institution: as for example: the whole Baptism is perceived by means of immersion into water; the whole Sacrament of the Supper is perceived by the mouth of the body, by eating bread and drinking wine. But the Signified in any Sacrament is perceived by faith alone.

Thirdly, they differ in end and efficacy: for Signs, or Sacraments, even the whole, although in themselves and by their nature they are most sacred, indeed clearly divine, can nevertheless harm and injure those who treat them unworthily or use them badly. But the Signified, once bestowed, can never fail to be beneficial.

Finally, they differ in scope. For Signs, or Sacraments, and indeed the whole, both by reason of the part or heavenly thing and by reason of the earthly thing, are common to all who use them, and are perceived as much by the unworthy as by the worthy; but the Signified in the use of any Sacrament is perceived only by the faithful.

Latin:

INitiò autem notandum, in fcriptis tùm Sacramentariorum, tùm quorundam noftratium Theologorum, pro æquipollentibus accipi fignatum & Rem Sacramenti. Et quanquàm parùm difcrminis inter hæc duo effe videtur: fiquidem & Signatum & Res Sacramenti hoc loco pro ufu & fructu Sacramenti accipitur: quod fi tamen paulò accuratiùs propria cujuslibet natura, ad ipfam Sacramentorum fignationem examinetur, ultrò patebit, duobus iftis aliquid difcriminis intercedere. Res enim Sacramenti, quæ nobis hoc loco nihil est aliud, quàm virtus meriti Christi, vel ut Apostolus loquitur Rom. 4, 11. Obsignatio justitiæ fidei, communis est omnibus Sacramentis tàm Veteris quàm Novi Testamenti. Quod enim Apostolus loco jam citato de Sacramento Circumcisionis pronunciat, quòd sit Signaculum justitiæ fidei: illud de omnibus Sacramentis in genere pronunciari potest: interim verò, si Sacramenti cujuslibet natura & institutio accuratiùs expendatur, apparet quodlibet Sacramentum habere proprium, & adæquatum sive appropriatum signatum, gerens ἀναλογίαν sive similitudinem quandam, cum suo signo: ac proindè reliquis Sacramentis incommunicabile: per quod demùm, & sic mediarè ac δευτέρως, Res illa Sacramenti, nempè obsignatio justitiæ fidei, Sacramento utentibus obtingit: ita quidem ut Res Sacramenti rectiùs Signaculum, quàm Signatum dicatur. Exempli gratiâ: In Circumcisione Signatum proprium & appropriatum, definiente Apostolo, Coloss 2, 11. est spiritualis Circumcisio ἀχειροποίητος. Hoc Signato demùm mediante, obtinebatur Res Sacramenti, quæ est Signaculum sive obsignatio justitiæ fidei. Sic in Agno Paschali, Signatum proprium & adæquatum fuit esca Spiritualis Corporis Christi Typici: quâ demùm mediante, obtinebatur Res Sacramenti, nempè obsignatio justitiæ fidei. Sic in Baptismo Signatum ἀνάλογον & appropriatum est Regeneratio sive Renovatio Spiritus S. Tit. 3, 5. Hâc demùm mediante obtinetur Res Sacramenti, nempè obsignatio justitiæ fidei. Sic in Cœnâ Domini Signatum proprium & adæquatum est, spiritualis coalitio, sive ut nonnulli ex Patribus locuti, coadunatio cum CHRISTO: vel spiritualis illa manducatio & bibitio Corporis ac Sanguinis Christi, de qua Johan 6. Quâ spirituali manducatione demùm mediante obtinetur Res Sacramenti, nempè signaculum fidei.

Neque obstat, quòd spiritualis hæc manducatio & bibitio Corporis & Sangvinis Christi, de quâ Joh 6. agitur, fieri etiam potest extra Sacramentum Eucharistiæ. Non enim de necessitate simplici & absolutâ est, ut Signata suis signis unicè cohæreant, & extra usum Sacramenti suam operationem habere nequeant. Circumcisionis certè Signatum fuisse circumcisionem ἀχειροποίητον, jam modò ex Apostolo didicimus: Atqui hanc ipsam spiritualem circumcisionem requirit idem Apostolus à suis Colossensibus, qui certè Signum illud Sacramentale, nempè externam præputii circumcisionem non observabant. Sic hoc loco, spiritualis manducatio, quæ fit per fidem, etiam extra Sacramentum istud in fidelibus locum habet: neque tamen quicquam obstat, quò minus sit signatum Eucharistiæ proprium ac adæquatum.

Puriorem hanc nostram doctrinam de naturâ Signati flagellant quidem, hoc usi argumento: Signum & Signatum simul esse necessum est: alioqui non integra erit Sacramentorum natura. Atqui spiritualis manducatio, non est conjuncta ipsi

Sacramenti Substantia: siquidem ad fructum sive usum ejus salutarem ea potiùs referri debet. Ergò spiritualis haec manducatio non potest dici signatum Sacramenti Eucharistiae.

Respondeo utramque praemissarum puerilibus laborare Sophismatis. In Majore committitur error ἀμφιβολογίας. Duobus enim modis quaedam dicuntur esse simul. Alio enim modo simul sunt, quae simul in rerum naturâ existunt:alio modo, quae verè ac realiter sunt conjuncta, si non semper actu, saltem δυνάμει. Priore sensu si accipiatur Major propositio ultrò eam concedimus. Quia enim Signum & Signatum sequuntur naturam τῶν πρός τι, quorum uno posito, ponitur alterum: destructo uno, destruitur etiam alterum: ideoque Signum & Signatum simul esse debent. Sic hoc ipso sensu libenter concedimus etiam Adversativam, ita ut Signum & Signatum simul non sint, tùm ne quidem integra etiam sit signorum natura: Vel ut dilucidiùs loquar, tùm in Sacramentis omnis Signi ratio expiret: propterea, quod nullum signum sui ipsius signatum: neque etiam pars signi signatum esse potest. Et sic priore hoc sensu ac respectu sine adversario pugnant isti Critici.

Posteriore autem sensu si intelligatur major propositio: tùm ea non est universaliter vera, & sic ex parte procedit argumentatio.

Neq; enim omnium signorum hoc est proprium, ut sibi signata conjuncta habeant: sed tantùm proprium hoc est, certae illius speciei signorum, eorum videlicet, quae sunt & dicuntur παραφερόμενα. Caeterorum signorum, quae σημαντικὰ sunt, magis propria est remotio, quàm conjunctio saltem quoad sensum.

Responsionem hanc majoris perspicuitatis gratiâ, exemplo Eucharistiae illustrare libet.

Si priore sensu majorem intelligas, certè in Sacramento Eucharistiae signum & signatum sunt conjunctissima, quando per signum intelligis, unam tantùm partem essentialem, nempè terrenam, Panem & Vinum: per signatum verò, alteram partem essentialem, nempè Corpus & Sangvinem Christi. Quia enim duae hae partes in usu Sacramenti, & quidem ex ipsâ naturâ Sacramenti, simul existunt: utique etiam signatum sine signo, hoc sensu & respectu, nullatenùs esse potest. Quod si verò Signi voce intelligas totum Sacramentum ex utraque re, terrenâ & caelesti compositum: & signatum tùm accipiatur de salutari usu & fructu Sacramenti: tùm nulla cogit ratio aut necessitas, ut Signum & Signatum semper actu simul sint: sed satis est, si Sacramentum signandi munere fungatur, & signet usum illum salutarem, licèt cum actu non conferat, sive sibi praesentem habeat: id quod ex manducatione indignorum, liquidissimè patet.

Causa ergò erroris est quod Critici isti, unam tantùm signandi rationem somniant, quam tamen geminam esse, supra ostensum fuit.

Et hoc quidem primum est, quod de signato observationem meretur: Restat alterum, ut quibus differentiarum notis Signum à Signato (si pro usu sive fructu Sacramenti accipiatur) distingvi possit & debeat, paucis ostendatur.

Quadruplex autem dari potest inter ea discrimen. Ac Primùm quidem differunt dispensatione: Signa enim, sive Sacramenta, ratione suæ substantiæ, dispensantur à ministris: Signatum verò vim suam atque operationem principaliter habet à solo Spiritu Sancto.

Deindè differunt perceptionis modo sive organo: Signa enim sive Sacramenta, ratione utriusque partis essentialis, percipiuntur eo modo sive organo, quod cuilibet Sacramento DEUS ipse in institutione destinavit: ut Exempli gratiâ: Baptismus integer percipitur mediante immersione in aquam: Sacramentum cœnæ integrum percipitur ore corporis, manducando panem, & bibendo vinum. Signatum verò in quolibet Sacramento non nisi solâ fide percipitur.

Tertiò differunt fine & efficaciâ: Signa enim sive Sacramenta integra, licèt in se & suâ naturâ, sint sacratissima, imò planè divina: indignè tamen ea tractantibus, aut malè utentibus, obesse ac nocere possunt. Signatum verò præceptum nunquàm non prodesse potest.

Tandem differunt latitudine. Signa enim sive Sacramenta, & quidem integra, tàm ratione partis sive rei cœlestis, quam ratione rei terrenæ omnibus utentibus sunt communia, & percipiuntur tàm ab indignis, quàm à dignis: Signatum verò in cujuslibet Sacramenti usu non nisi à fidelibus percipitur.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: III. Question. On the Sacramental Union of the earthly and heavenly things in any Sacrament

The Calvinist race, because of the remarkable lust for slandering with which it labors, accuses our Churches of maintaining that the sacramental preaching of words and the union of things with signs are one and the same. But the very benches and walls of our temples and schools clearly testify to the contrary, namely, that while the united things are indeed announced through preaching, the preaching or announcement itself, which declares something about the thing, is one thing, but the thing itself announced—namely, the union of the earthly and heavenly thing in the use of the Sacrament—is another. Furthermore, regarding this whole dispute about the Sacramental Union, they sell smoke, and by various clouds and tricks cast upon the subject, they entangle the very matter being questioned more than they explain it. For in these words they betray their opinion: The sacramental union of things with signs is properly the power and grace of the Sacrament, and it comes to pass and happens in the true and legitimate use, by the power and operation of the Holy Spirit. Consens. Orthod. page 319 of the 1588 edition. And after a few words: This union is the reason why the names of things are exchanged with the symbols: but it is not, as is thought by many in an opinion of error, an absolute, physical, and essential coupling of things with signs in the same subject and place: but a mystical and relative conjunction, by which the whole nature of the Sacrament consists and is perfected, to effect this truly in the believers and the elect: that which is figured. Therefore, this sacramental union of things with signs ought to be understood as such, as is that of the Sacrament with grace, which certainly is not bound or affixed to the Sacrament by any essential coupling: But as Bernard says, it is divinely dispensed by some visible sign, as if by a mode of investiture, just as if a ring were given for the investiture of some inheritance. So far the Calvinists: whose opinion consists of almost more falsehoods than words.

For first, there presents itself a malicious perversion of the state, and a sophistic confusion of very diverse questions. There is a question and controversy concerning the union of the essential parts constituting the entire essence of the Sacrament: namely, how do they concur and unite with one another to constitute a composite that is one in number and species? Here the Calvinists respond concerning the effect and fruit of the Sacrament in believers, namely how that relates to the sacramental signs themselves: namely, being asked about onions, they answer about garlic. Then they play sophistically under the sophism of the equivocation of the term (the Thing of the Sacrament), because although it sometimes denotes the substance itself, and indeed the entire Sacrament, composed of both the earthly and heavenly part: yet sometimes it is taken for the use and fruit of the Sacrament: they nowhere in this place explain in which meaning they wish this term to be accepted in the present dispute: but with mere verbal tricks, they cast mists before the more imprudent reader, so that he may less perceive what the matter is and what is being said.

Thirdly, they entangle both themselves and the matter at hand with mere absurdities and petitions of the principle. For if by the Thing of the Sacrament they understand the entire essence of the Sacrament: it would follow that they establish that a Sacramental Union intervenes between the Substance of the Sacrament, or the Sacramental Signs, and the effect or fruit of the Sacrament, which is manifestly false and absurd: since that effect subsists outside the substance of the Sacrament. And indeed their own words seem to hint at this very thing, writing that the Sacramental Union of things with signs is properly the power and grace of the Sacrament, etc. But this power and grace of the Sacrament is never sacramentally united with the elementary part, nor with the heavenly thing, in any Sacrament whatsoever, nor does it constitute one thing: but it exists outside the essence of the sacrament, and does not befall, every bus, the Sacrament, however much it is complete in terms of its essence, for those who use it. Now, such is the proper nature and quality of the Sacramental union, that the united things, in the use of the Sacrament, both with regard to unbelievers and with regard to believers, are always most presentially united to one another, and neither can be obtained by those using the Sacrament without the other.

Furthermore, it is clearly absurd to establish that any real union intervenes between an efficient and instrumental cause and the effect itself; since it is established from all sciences and disciplines that these two differ in their principles, subjects, forms, ends, and matter. But if, by the Thing of the Sacrament, they understand the fruit of the Sacrament, then they are shamefully talking nonsense and begging the question. This is the very thing that is in dispute: whether the Sacramental Union of the Thing with the signs is the grace and power of the Sacrament itself, which is obtained by believers through the power and operation of the Holy Spirit? This is what we deny.

Fourthly, they deceive and are deceived by the fallacy παρα το ἐλλιπὲς διαιρέσεως, an insufficient division. For although we willingly concede that the Sacramental Union is not an absolute, essential, or physical coupling of the sign and the signified, or, as the Adversaries say, of things with signs; and much less that it consists in any local inclusion or presence of the heavenly thing; since we have long known that all these modes can have no place in this mystery: nevertheless, it does not immediately follow: Therefore, no other mode of this union can be given than that which is σχετικός or Relative, where the Sacrament is said to obtain a σχέσιν or relation to the heavenly thing. For another mode is given, which the Calvinists are accustomed to hate worse than a dog or a snake, and which we call Sacramental, Real, and Mystical: what kind of thing this is will be shown a little later.

Fifthly, the Adversaries labor under a zeal for slandering, while in this place they argue at length that Sacramental Grace is not essentially coupled to the Sacraments: as if such a thing had ever been either said or written by us. We have certainly defended the contrary against the Papist Doctors strenuously up to this point, as will be clearly evident from the following chapter 2, where we will expressly argue about the effect of the Sacrament. But there is also something treacherous underlying this false accusation, while again, under this ambiguous phrase, they strive to persuade their own people that the heavenly thing, that is, the Body and Blood of Christ, is not truly and really coupled to the Sacramental signs, namely, to the bread and wine.

Sixthly, they utterly undermine and overturn every union of the Sign and the Signified: for they grant no other mode of Union except the Relative or σχετικόν, the nature and proper quality of which is that, without any true and real union or coupling of the essential parts, the name and appellation of the heavenly thing is attributed to the elemental thing or external symbols, not as if it were present, but as absent and remote by as great an interval as the highest heaven is distant from the lowest earth: and that thus, by means of this verbal permutation of names, the heavenly thing is signified and figured through external symbols. But what is this other than to neither believe nor admit any true and real Union of the Sign and the Signified at all? And indeed, if the Sacramental Union can be perfected and completed by this naked σχέσει or Relation: what, I ask, prevents me from thinking, in any feast or banquet, while eating bread and drinking wine, of that spiritual κοινωνίᾳ or participation of the Body of Christ, which happens through faith σχέτικως?

Seventhly, they commit the crime of forgery while they strive to distort the simile of Bernard to their own purpose, by hook or by crook. For if this simile is considered in its proper place, and both the preceding and following context are weighed more accurately, it would shine forth more clearly than the midday sun that Bernard is not dealing at all in that place with the Union of the Sign and the Signified, that is, with the Sacramental Union of the earthly and heavenly thing, that is, of the Bread with the body: of the Wine with the Blood of Christ: But only with the use and fruit, for the sake of which the Sacrament was instituted by Christ. For his words sound thus in the Sermon on the Lord's Supper: A ring is given to invest someone with an inheritance: and it is a sign: so that he who receives the ring can say: The ring is worth nothing, but it is the inheritance that I was seeking. Item: Just as a Canon is invested by a book: an Abbot by a staff: a Bishop by a staff and a ring: Just as, I say, it is in such things: so also are the distributions of graces handed down in the various Sacraments.

Whoever does not see that Bernard is discussing the distribution of graces or spiritual gifts, that is, the effect of the Sacrament, certainly sees nothing. But what is this to the Sacramental union about which the question is asked? Again, the same Bernard, when he expressly deals with the very substance of the Sacrament, and with the Sacramental union of the two essential parts to each other: there he shapes his style in a far different, and clearly Lutheran sense: Three things (he says in the same Sermon) are proposed as distinct in the Sacrament, namely, 1. the visible species. 2. The truth of the Body: 3. and the power of spiritual grace.

And after a few words: Sacramental eating, as far as the visible species and the truth of the Body of Christ are concerned, belongs to the good and the bad in common: even if not all who take the Body of the Lord are filled spiritually with that heavenly blessing and grace. Which single assertion of Bernard clearly overturns the cause of the Calvinists.

Finally, under the term of mystical union, from which our own Churches are otherwise not at all averse, the snares of errors they

Latin:

GENS Calviniana pro insigni, quâ laborat calumniandi libidine, nostras insimulat Ecclesias, quòd statuant unum idemquè esse, tùm Sacramentalem verborum prædicationem: tùm unionem rerum cum signis. Sed vel templorum ac Scholarum nostrarum subsellia & parietes contrarium liquidò testantur, quòd nimirùm per prædicationem quidem enuncientur res unitæ: sed interim aliud sit prædicatio sive enunciatio ipsa, quæ aliquid de re prædicat: aliud verò sit res ipsa enunciata, unio videlicet rei terrenæ & cœlestis in usu Sacramenti. Deindè circa totam hanc disputationem, de Unione Sacramentali, fumos venditant, & variis objectis nebulis ac præstigiis, rem ipsam, de quâ quæritur, magis implicant, quàm explicant. His enim verbis suam produnt sententiam: Sacramentalis unio rerum cum signis, est propriè virtus & gratia Sacramenti, & sit ac contingit, in vero & legitimo usu, virtute & operatione Spiritus Sancti. Consens. Orthod. pag. 319. editionis anni 1588. Et post pauca: Hæc unio causa est, cur nomina rerum cu Symbolis commutentur: non autem ea est, ut à multis, erroris opinione putatur, absoluta, physica & essentialis quædam copulatio rerum cum signis, in eodem subjecto & loco: sed mystica & relativa conjunctio, quâ integra Sacramenti ratio constat & perficitur, ad efficiendum hoc verè in credentibus & electis: quod figuratur. Sacramentalis igitur hæc unio reru cu signis, talis intelligi debet, qualis est Sacramenti cum gratia, quæ certè non essentiali aliquâ copulatione alligata seu affixa est Sacramento: Sed ut Bernhardus ait, visibili aliquo signo, quasi per investitura cujusdam modum, divinitus dispensatur, sicut si annulus ob hæreditatis alicujus investituram daretur. Hactenùs Calviniani: quorum sententia pluribus fermè falsitatibus, quàm verbis constat.

Primùm enim se offert malitiosa status perversio, & Sophistica diversissimarũ quæstionum confusio. Quæstio est & Controversia, de unione partium essentialium, constituentium integram Sacramenti essentiam: Quomodo nimirùm invicem concurrant & uniantur ad unum numero & specie constituendum compositum? Hic respondent Calviniani, de effectu & fructu Sacramenti in credentibus, quomodo nimirùm ille se habeat ad ipsa signa Sacramentalia: nimirùm de cepis interrogati, respondet de alliis. Deindè Sophisticè ludunt sub Sophismate æquivocationis vocabuli (Res Sacramenti) quòd cùm interdum ipsam substantiam, & quidem integram Sacramenti, ex utraque parte terrenâ & cœlesti compositam, notet: interdum verò pro usu & fructuSacramenti accipiatur: illi nuspiam hoc loco explicant, quo in significatu vocabulu hoc, in præsenti disputatione velint acceptum: sed meris verborum præstigiis, lectori imprudentiori nebulas offundunt, ut quâ de re, & quid dicatur minùs percipere queat.

Tertiò meris absurditatibus, principiique petitionibus, & seipsos, & rem de quâ agitur, implicant. Si enim per Rem Sacramenti, intelligunt integram Sacramenti essentiam: consequens fuerit, ipsos statuere, Substantiæ Sacramenti, sive Signis Sacramentalibus, intercedere Unionem Sacramentalem, cum effectu sive fructu Sacramenti, id quod manifestè falsum & absurdum: siquidem effectus iste extra substantiam Sacramenti subsistit. Et profectò hoc ipsum innuere videntur ipsorummet verba, scribentium, Sacramentalem Unionem rerum cum signis, esse propriè virtutem & gratiam Sacramenti &c. Atqui virtus & gratia hæc Sacramenti, neq; cum parte elementari, neq; cum re cœlesti, in ullo aliquo Sacramento, unquàm Sacramentaliter unitur, aut unum quid constituit: sed versatur extra sacramenti essentiam, neque obtingit, omnibus, Sacramento quantumvis ratione essentiæ integro, utentibus. Jam verò ea est unionis Sacramentalis propria natura & affectio, ut res unitæ, in usu Sacramenti tàm quoad infideles, quàm quoad fideles, semper sibi sint præsentissimè unitæ, & neutra sine alterâ Sacramento utentibus obtingere possit.

Præterea absurdum planè est statuere, Causæ efficienti & instrumentali, cum ipso effectu intercedere realem aliquam unionem : cùm ex omnibus scientiis ac disciplinis constet, differre hæc duo principiis, subjectis, formis, finibus & materiâ. Quod si verò per Rem Sacramenti intelligunt fructum Sacramenti, tùm turpiter nugantur & petunt principium. Hoc ipsum est, de quo controvertitur, an Unio Sacramentalis, Rei cum signis, sit ipsa gratia & virtus Sacramenti quæ virtute & operatione Spiritus Sancti obtingit credentibus? id quod negamus.

Quartò fallunt & falluntur Sophismate παρα το ἐλλιπὲς διαιρέσεως, insufficienti divisione. Etsi enim libenter concedimus, Unionem Sacramentalem non esse absolutam, essentialem, aut physicam copulationem signi & signati, sive, uti Adversarii loquuntur, rerum cum signis : multò verò minùs eam consistere in locali aliquâ, sive inclusione, sive præsentiâ rei cœlestis : siquidem hos modos omnes hoc in mysterio, locum nullatenùs habere posse, jampridem novimus : interim tamen non statim sequitur: Ergò nullus alius dari potest unionis hujus modus, quàm qui est σχετικός sive Relativus, ubi Sacramentum σχέσιν sive relationem ad rem cœlestem obtinere dicitur. Datur enim modus alius, quem Calviniani cane & angve pejus odisse solent, quemque nos vocamus Sacramentalem, Realem, & Mysticum: qui qualis sit, paulò post ostendetur.

Quintò calumniandi studio laborant Adversarii, dùm hoc loco multis disputant, Gratiam Sacramentalem Sacramentis non esse essentialiter copulatam: quasi verò tale quid à nobis unquàm vel dictum vel scriptum fuerit. Contrarium certè contra Doctores Pontificios strenuè hactenùs defendimus, uti luculenter patebit, ex subsequente cap. 2. ubi de effectu Sacramenti ex professo disputabimus. Sed & falsæ huic accusationi ὕπουλόν τι subest, dùm rursus sub ambiguâ hac phrasi, suis hominibus persuadere satagunt, Rem cœlestem, hoc est, Corpus & Sangvinem Christi, non esse verè ac realiter copulatam signis Sacramentalibus, nempè pani & vino.

Sextò, omnem unionem Signi & Signati penitùs subruunt & evertunt: Nullum enim alium Unionis modum largiuntur, præter Relativum sive σχετικόν, cujus hæc sit natura & propria affectio, ut, sine ullâ verâ ac reali partium essentialium unione sive copulatione, rei Elementari, sive Symbolis externis, nomen duntaxat & appellatio tribuatur rei cœlestis, non præsentis, sed tanto intervallo absentis & remotæ, quantum summum cœlum distat ab infimâ terrâ: & ut sic mediante hac verbali nominum permutatione, res cœlestis significetur & figuretur per externa Symbola. Quid verò hoc est aliud, quàm nullam prorsus veram ac realem Unionem Signi & Signati vel credere, vel admittere? Et profectò, si nudâ hâc σχέσει sive Relatione, Unio Sacramentalis perfici & absolvi queat: quid quæso prohibet, quo minùs in quovis epulo aut convivio, comedens panem & bibens vinum, cogitem de spirituali illâ κοινωνίᾳ sive participatione Corporis Christi, quæ fit per fidem σχέτικως.

Septimò crimen falsi committunt, dùm Bernhardi similitudinem, ad suum institutum per fas & nefas detorquere student. Si enim in propriâ suâ sede similitudo hæc consideretur, & tùm antecedentia, tùm consequentia accuratiùs expendantur, sole meridiano clariùs elucescat, Bernhardũ nihil quiequam eò loci agere, de Unione Signi & Signati, hoc est, de Unione Sacramentali rei terrenæ & cœlestis, hoc est, Panis cum corpore: Vini cum Sangvine Christi: Sed tantùm de usu & fructu, propter quem Sacramentum à Christo sit institutum. Sic enim verba ipsius sonant in Sermone de Cœnâ Domini: Datur annulus ad investiendum aliquem de hæreditate: & signum est: ita ut dicere possit, qui annulum accipit: Annulus non valet quicquam, sed hæreditas est, quam quærebam. Item: Quemadmodum investitur Canonicus per librum: Abbas per baculum: Episcopus per baculum & annulum: Sicut, inquam, in ejusmodi rebus est: sic & divisiones gratiarum diversis in Sacramentis sunt traditæ.

Ubi de distributione gratiarum sive donorum spiritualium, hoc est, de effectu Sacramenti differere Bernhardum, qui non videt, certè nihil videt. Sed quid hoc ad unionem Sacramentalem de quâ quæritur? Rursus idem Bernhardus, quando ex professo agit de ipsâ Sacramenti substantiâ, deque unione Sacramentali duarum partium essentialium ad se mutuò: ibi longè alio, & planè Lutherano sensu stylum informat: Tria (inquiens eodem in Sermone) in Sacramento discreta proponuntur, scilicet, 1. species visibilis. 2. Veritas Corporis: 3. & virtus gratiæ spiritualis.

Et post pauca: Comestio Sacramentalis, quantum ad visibilem speciem, & quantum ad veritatem Corporis Christi attinet, convenit bonis & malis communiter: etsi non omnes, qui Corpus Domini sumunt, spiritualiter illâ benedictione cœlesti, & gratiâ replentur. Quæ vel una Bernhardi assertio, causam Calvinianorum planè evertit.

Tandem sub termino mysticæ unionis, à quo nostræ etiam Ecclesiæ aliàs minimè abhorrent, errorum insidias satis Sophisticè


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: The true opinion concerning the Sacramental Union

are accustomed to construct quite sophistically. To the Orthodox Fathers, as also to us, the Sacramental Union of the earthly and heavenly thing is and is called mystical, on account of that tremendous and ineffable mystery which, by reason of that Sacramental Union, intercedes between those two things, the earthly and the heavenly: by the virtue of which it comes to pass that the heavenly thing is or coupled to the elementary or earthly thing, and together with it is truly perceived in the use of the Sacrament by all, as well the unworthy as the worthy.

But to the Calvinists this is a mystical union of the Sign and the Signified, when the names of things are exchanged with the Symbols (as they speak): that is, when to the earthly and elementary thing, as for example, to the Bread and Wine of the Eucharist, the name and appellation of the heavenly thing, namely the Body and Blood of Christ, is attributed: without any true and real union or coupling of those two things to each other. Let the whole Christian World judge whether this is not to mock the Church, and under empty wrappings of words, to overturn, nay, clearly to take away, the entire substance of the Sacraments?

Away, therefore, with this crafty sophistry of disputing. In order that we may at last set forth the Orthodox doctrine of our Churches concerning the Sacramental Union: we remove at the beginning from this mystery an Essential or Physical mode of union, for the reason that these two things, the Sign and the Signified, that is, the earthly and the heavenly thing, even in the very use of the Sacrament, remain distinct as to their essences, and are neither mixed with each other, nor confounded, nor exchanged, nor in any way transubstantiated, as the Romanists trifle. And although it is not rarely asserted by our theologians that the Body of Christ is received with the bread, in the use of the Eucharist, Essentially and Substantially: yet only the Subject, and not indeed the mode of the Union, is expressed by these phrases: that is, it is shown What and what kind of Body of Christ is eaten with the bread: namely, not tropical or metonymical, or most remotely absent: But the very true essential or Substantial Body of Christ, that very same which was delivered to death for us. Meanwhile, the mode by which this Body of Christ is united with the element of bread in the use of the Sacrament is in no way noted or expressed by these terms.

Next, we remove from this mystery also a Personal or Hypostatic mode of union, since that properly belongs only to the Person of Christ: and is not communicable to any other thing or mystery. For although our Blessed Luther, as also other Orthodox theologians, have not rarely borrowed arguments from the personal union of the two natures in CHRIST against the Sacramentarians, to define the Sacramental Union of the Sign and the Signified: just as the same is read to have been done long ago by Justin the Philosopher and Martyr: yet they never and nowhere established that one and the same mode of union obtains in both cases: But rather they wished to demonstrate one and the same truth of most diverse modes of union: So that, just as through the Hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ, truly and really, not merely verbally, or at least σχετικῶς or ἀλλοιωτικῶς, Man is predicated of GOD: GOD of Man: so also in the use of the Sacrament, not only in name, or σχετικῶς; but truly and really, the heavenly thing is united or coupled with the earthly or elementary thing: So that when the one is perceived, the other cannot but be perceived at the same time.

Thirdly, we remove also that mode of Union which results from a certain arcane and Magical power of the recitation of the words of institution, such as the Romanists invent and defend. For although we establish that the recitation of the words of institution, concerning the use of any Sacrament, is by no means to be omitted, for other reasons, which partly recall to the mind of the communicants the institution of Christ and its end, and partly separate those external Symbols or Elements from the common census of other creatures of the same species, and destine them for a certain sacred use: yet no power results from thence for constituting the union of the Sign and the Signified: but this whole depends upon the promise and power of Christ the institutor, and indeed in the sole external use of the Sacrament: so that if the words of Institution were recited or sung even a thousand times: but the use of the Sacrament did not follow: no Sacramental union of the Sign and the Signified would emerge at all.

Fourthly, we remove also that mode of Sacramental Union which is feigned to depend either upon the dignity of the administrator: or upon the faith of the user.

For the former was already thrashed out above, where we disputed concerning the efficient cause of the Sacraments.

But the latter is likewise easily refuted. For just as, by the testimony of the Apostle, the incredulity of men does not evacuate the promise, faith, and ordination of GOD, in respect to the substance of the Sacramental Signs: Rom. 3, 3. & 4. So neither does the Faith of men constitute the same promise and Ordination of Christ, in respect to the Substance of the Sacramental Signs. For it depends entirely upon the very promise and power of GOD ordaining and instituting: nor does it matter whether the Quality of the user be good or bad: provided the external use of the Sacrament follows.

Finally, we remove from this place all other modes of Union which Aristotle recounts in his Metaphysics. For neither do the Sign and the Signified become one Sacramentally by nature τῇ φύσει. For those things which are one in such a way have continuity in themselves, either by reason of essence or by reason of inherence: a thing which does not fit this mystery. Thus, those things which are one by Art cohere through the continuity of another: just as bundles are said to be one certain thing by reason of the bond συνδεσμῷ: if a table, one thing by reason of glue. But God forbid that we should even in a dream imagine any such συνάφειαν or coherence or conglutination of the essential parts of the Sacrament. Thus, things which are one in species have one and a common definition. But every essential part, even in the Sacramental Union itself, just as it obtains its own proper definition, so also it obtains its own being, distinct from the other. Thus, things which are one in number have also one matter. But in any Sacrament there is a double matter: namely, earthly and heavenly, as was shown above. Thus, we proscribe all other individual and universal modes which introduce either a physical mixture, or a verbal ἀλλοίωσιν τῶν ὀνομάτων, or merely a naked παράθεσιν or apposition of united things.

These and other false modes of this kind having been utterly banished from this mystery, we finally establish the Mode of the union of the Sign and the Signified, in the use of the Holy Eucharist, as clearly supernatural and Mystical, yet true and real, which, since it is proper to the Sacraments, has been accustomed to be called Sacramental. Moreover, it depends solely upon the will of the promising and the power of the instituting Christ; who, just as He is the creator of all things that are, and calls those things which are not that they might be (Rom. 4:17), so He also knows how to powerfully perform, nay, by the force of His promise, He wills to perform, and indeed performs most effectively: that (not indeed outside of use, but always in the external use of any Sacrament) those two things, otherwise differing in their entire genus, namely the Earthly as the Sign, and the Heavenly or invisible thing as the Signified, become one, not σχετικῶς, not φυσικῶς, not τροπικῶς, but Sacramentally: so that by the force of this Sacramental Union, the heavenly thing, namely the Body and Blood of Christ, is most excellently united to the earthly thing, namely the Bread and Wine, and both are perceived together by those using them, whether he who uses the Sacrament believes or does not believe, in a mode clearly mystical and hyperphysical.

Looking to this most intimate union, the Holy Fathers and other Orthodox Theologians very frequently call the Sacraments Mysteries, and indeed miraculous mysteries: which certainly would no longer be such if, in the Sacramental sense, according to the nature and condition of common signs, they had merely some naked σχέσιν or Relation, consisting in a naked permutation of names, and did not contain the very presence of the heavenly thing.

The Adversaries carp at this point, especially at the term (Really), which they wish to denote the same thing as physically or Essentially. But it is known even to boys that in this meaning, where Real denotes physical mixture or confusion, this term was never used by our side in explaining this mystery: But that the Real or Really is for us the same as truly, not fictitiously, not simulatedly, not figuratively, not significatively, but truly and in the thing itself. For not even among philosophers are Real and

Physical terms that are simply ἀντιςρέφοντες or convertible on both sides, as the Calvinists dream: but these two terms stand in relation to each other, as ἀντιςρέφοντες, reciprocal from only one side of themselves: so that while every Physical thing is also real, not however conversely is every real thing also physical. For real extends more widely than physical: which is abundantly clear from the distinction of the three persons of the Divinity. For the Calvinists themselves admit that these differ really, which nevertheless they will never grant differ essentially and τῇ φύσει. Let them remember, therefore, that something can be Real which is nevertheless not Essential or Physical.

Latin:

struere solent. Orthodoxis Patribus, ut & nobis Unio Sacramentalis rei terrenæ & cœlestis, est & dicitur mystica, propter tremendum illud & ineffabile mysterium, quod ex Unione Sacramentali duabus istis rebus, terrenæ & cœlesti, invicem intercedit: cujus virtute fit, ut res cœlestis, sit rei elementari sive terrenæ præsentissimè unita sive copulata, & unà cum hac verè in usu Sacramenti ab omnibus, tàm indignis, quàm dignis percipiatur.

Calvinianis verò hæc est mystica unio Signi & Signati, quando nomina rerum cum Symbolis (ut loquuntur) commutantur: hoc est, quando rei terrenæ & elementari, ut exempli gratiâ, Pani & Vino Eucharistiæ, nomen & appellatio rei cœlestis, nempè Corporis & Sangvinis Christi tribuitur: sine ullâ verâ ac reali duarum istarum rerum ad se mutuò unione sive copulatione. Judicet totus Orbis Christianus, an hoc non sit Ecclesiæ illudere, & sub inanibus verborum involucris, universam Sacramentorum substantiam evertere, imò planè tollere?

Facessat proindè veteratoria isthæc disputandi Sophisticatio. Nos ut Orthodoxam nostrarum Ecclesiarum doctrinam, de Unione Sacramentali, vel tandem proferamus: removemus initiò ex hoc mysterio, modum unionis Essentialem vel Physicum, propterea quòd duæ hæ res, Signum & Signatum, hoc est, res terrena & cœlestis, in ipso etiam usu Sacramenti, manent quoad essentias distinctæ, neque invicem vel commiscentur, vel confunduntur, vel commutantur, vel ullo pacto transsubstantiantur, uti Romanenses nugantur. Et quanquàm à nostratibus Theologis haud rarò asseritur, quòd Corpus Christi cum pane, in usu Eucharistiæ, accipiatur Essentialiter & Substantialiter: tamen Subjectum tantùm, non verò modus Unionis his phrasibus exprimitur: hoc est, ostenditur, Quod & quale Corpus Christi cum pane manducetur: nempè non tropicum aut metonymicum, aut remotissimè absens: Sed ipsum verum essentiale sive Substantiale Corpus Christi, illud ipsum, quod pro nobis in mortem traditum. Interim modus, quo Corpus hoc Christi, cum elemento panis, in usu Sacramenti est unitum, hisce terminis nullatenùs notatur aut exprimitur.

Deindè removemus ex hoc etiam mysterio modum Unionis Personalem, sive Hypostaticum, quippè qui soli Personæ Christi propriè competit: neque ulli alii rei sive mysterio est communicabilis. Etsi enim B. Lutherus noster, ut & alii Orthodoxi Theologi, ex unione personali duarum naturarum in CHRISTO, haud rarò contra Sacramentarios argumenta mutuati sunt, ad definiendam Unionem Sacramentalem Signi & Signati: quemadmodum idem jam olim etiam, Justinus Philosophus & Martyr fecisse legitur: minimè tamen unum eundemque Unionis modum, utrobique obtinere, unquàm uspiam statuerunt: Sed potiùs diversissimorum Unionis modorum, unam eandemque veritatem demonstrare voluerunt: Ita, ut quemadmodum per unionem Hypostaticam duarum naturarum in Christo, verè ac realiter, non verbaliter tatùm, vel σχετικῶς saltem aut ἀλλοιωτικῶς Homo de DEO: DEUS de Homine prædicatur: ita in usu etiam Sacramenti non nominétenus duntaxat, aut σχετικῶς; sed verè ac realiter, res cœlestis, unita sit sive copulata sit cum re terrenâ sive elementari: Ita ut hâc perceptâ, non possit non simul percipi & altera.

Tertiò removemus illum etiam Unionis modum, qui ex arcanâ quadam & Magicâ vi recitationis verborum institutionis resultat, qualem Romanenses fingunt & defendunt. Etsi enim recitationem verborum institutionis, circa usum cujuslibet Sacramenti, minimè omittendam esse, statuimus, ob causas alias, quæ communicantib9 partim institutionem Christi, ejusdemque finem ad animum revocant, partim verò externa illa Symbola sive Elementa, ex communi reliquarum ejusdem speciei creaturarum censu separent, & certo usui sacro destinant: tamen nihil inde virtutis ad unionem Signi & Signati constituendam resultat: sed hæc tota dependet ab instituentis Christi promissione & virtute, & quidem in solo externo usu Sacramenti: ita ut si vel millies verba Institutionis vel recitarentur vel canerentur: usus autem Sacramenti non accederet: nulla prorsus unio Sacramentalis Signi & Signati emergeret.

Quartò removemus eum etiam Unionis Sacramentalis modum, qui pendere fingitur, vel à dignitate administrantis: vel à fide utentis.

Prius enim istud suprà protritum fuit, ubi de causâ efficiente Sacramentorum disputavimus.

Posterius verò hoc itidem facilè eliditur. Quemadmodum enim, Apostolo teste, incredulitas hominum, DEI promissionem, fidem ac ordinationem, ratione substantiæ Signorum Sacramentalium non evacuat: Rom. 3, 3. & 4. Ita neque Fides hominum eandem promissionem & Ordinationem Christi, quoad Substantiam Signorum Sacramentalium constituit. Dependet enim ea in solidum, ab ipsâ promissione & potentiâ DEI ordinantis ac instituentis: neque refert, nùm Qualitas utentis vel bona sit vel mala: modò usus Sacramenti externus accedat.

Tandem removemus hinc omnes alios Unionis modos, quos in Metaphysicis recenset Aristoteles. Neque enim Signum & Signatum fiunt unum Sacramentale Naturâ τῇ φύσει. Quæ enim sic unum sunt, ea continuitatem in se habent, vel ratione essentiæ, vel ratione inhærentiæ: id quod huic mysterio non quadrat. Sic quæ Arte sunt unum, ea cohærent per continuitatem alterius: quemadmodum fasces unum quiddam esse dicuntur, ratione συνδεσμᾶ vinculi: Si mensa, unum quid ratione glutinis. Absit verò, ut talem aliquam συνάφειαν sive cohærentiam aut conglutinationem, partium essentialium Sacramenti, vel per somnium fingamus. Sic quæ specie sunt unum, ea unam & communem habent definitionem. At verò pars quælibet essentialis, in ipsâ etiam Unione Sacramentali, uti suum proprium, & ab alterâ distinctum esse, ita propriam etiam definitionem obtinet. Sic quæ unum sunt numero, eorum una etiam est materia. Atqui in Sacramento quolibet duplex est materia: terrena nimirùm & cœlestis: uti suprà ostensum. Sic reliquos singulos ac universos proscribimus modos, qui vel physicam mixtionem, vel verbalem ἀλλοίωσιν τῶν ὀνομάτων, vel nudam duntaxat παράθεσιν aut rerum unitarum appositionem inferunt.

His & id genus aliis modis falsis ex hoc mysterio prorsus relegatis, constituimus tandem Modum unionis Signi & Signati, in usu S. Eucharistiæ, planè supernaturalem & Mysticum, verum tamen ac realem, qui cùm Sacramentorum sit proprius, Sacramentalis appellari consuevit. Dependet autem ille ex solâ voluntate promittentis, & potentiâ instituentis Christi; qui, quemadmodum rerum omnium, quæ sunt, est conditor: & ea, quæ non sunt, vocat ut sint: Rom. 14, 17. ita novit etiam potenter præstare, imò vi promissionis suæ, vult præstare, quin & præstat efficacissimè: ut (non quidem extra usum, sed semper in usu externo cujuslibet Sacramenti) res illæ duæ, toto alioqui genere discrepantes, Terrena nimirùm, tanquàm Signum, & Res Cœlestis sive invisibilis, tanquàm Signatum, unum fiant, non σχετικῶς, non φυσικῶς, non τροπικῶς, sed Sacramentaliter: ita ut vi hujus Unionis Sacramentalis, Res cœlestis, nempè Corpus & Sangvis Christi, rei terrenæ, nempè Pani & Vino, sit præstantiffimè unita, & utraque simul ab utentibus percipiatur, sive credat, sive non credat, qui Sacramento utitur, modo planè mystico & hyperphysico.

Ad arctissimam hanc unionem respicientes Sancti Patres, & alij Orthodoxi Theologi, frequenter admodum Sacramenta appellant Mysteria & quidem mysteria miraculosa: qualia profectò non ampliùs forent, si sensu Sacramentario, secundum naturam & conditionem vulgarium signorum, nudam duntaxat aliquam σχέσιν sive Relationem, nudâ nominum permutatione constantem, haberent: non verò ipsam rei cœlestis præsentiam continerent.

Vellicant Adversarij hoc loco, cumprimis Terminum (Realiter) quem idem notare volunt, atque physicè sive Essentialiter. Verùm vel pueris notum est, hoc in fignificatu, quo Reale Physicam mixtionem aut confusionem notat, à nostris hunc terminum, hoc in mysterio explicando nunquàm usurpatum fuisse: Verùm τὸ Reale sive Realiter idem nobis esse, ac verè, non fictè, non simulatè, non figuratè, non significativè, sed verè ac in reipsâ. Neque enim apud Philosophos etiam, Reale ac

Physicum, sunt termini simpliciter ἀντιςρέφοντες sive ex utraque sui parte convertibiles, uti Calvi-viani somniant: sed habent ad se mutuò duo isti termini, tanquàm ἀντιςρέφοντες, ex unâ duntaxat sui parte reciproca: ita ut quidem omne Physicum sit etiam reale: non tamen vice versa, omne reale sit etiam physicum. Nam reale latiùs patet physico: id quod ex distinctione trium personarum Divinitatis, abundè liquet. Has enim realiter differre, vel ipsi fatentur Calviniani, quas tamen propterea essentialiter & τῇ φύσει differre nunquàm largientur. Meminerint ergò Reale aliquid esse posse, quod tamen non sit Essentiale aut Physicum.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: IV. Question. What mode of Predication obtains in the Sacraments?

According to the diverse signification of the Sign and the Signified, a diverse mode of Predicating also obtains in the Sacraments. For when the word of the Sign denotes the whole substance of the Sacrament, composed of both essential parts, earthly and heavenly: so that the Signified is something placed outside the substance of the Sacrament, namely the use and fruit, or effect of the Sacrament: and indeed such a proposition is given, in which this Signified is predicated of the Sign, that is, the fruit of the Sacrament is predicated of the substance of the Sacrament itself: as when I say, Circumcision is the Covenant, Baptism is Regeneration: the Supper of the Lord is a Spiritual Coalition with Christ: then anyone easily understands what the sense of these predications is.

But when the word of the Sign denotes only one essential or συςατικὴν part of the Sacrament, namely the earthly: so that the Signified is now the other essential or constitutive part of the Sacrament: and thus one essential part is predicated of the other essential part: and when Blessed Luther says: The blessed Bread is the Body of Christ: The blessed Wine is the Blood of Christ: and thus it is not a simple λέξις, but a predication: then neither metonymy, nor any other figure can have a place: But this Predication is called and is unusual, that is, mystical and singular, the entire nature and affection of which depends entirely upon the Sacramental union, which is wholly singular, arcane, mystical, hyperphysical. In which part there exists the greatest diversity between these propositions and those former ones. For in these, not only is a disparate thing predicated of a disparate thing: but also one essential part is predicated of the other, and indeed truly and really, not only τῇ λέξει καὶ φράσει, but through a true and real mode of union. Where even a beginner in Theology understands that a clearly unusual manner of predicating obtains: Since not even a single similar example occurs in the whole universe of things: except for the predications of the two natures in Christ to each other: which likewise transcend every order and reason of nature by infinite parasangs.

But this unusual or singular the mode of predication is so constituted that the individual words of the Institution retain their own proper sense and admit nothing figurative: meanwhile, however, the whole predication cannot be referred to any mode of regular or customary predication, neither simple or proper, nor improper or figurative.

The Sacramentarian party objects to us at this point an implication of contradiction, because we contend that the individual words of the Institution are to be understood κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν & properly: and yet, nevertheless, the mode of predication is not only not proper, but not even improper: but clearly singular and unusual. But every reason for ἀντίφασις expires of its own accord if it is noted that both are affirmed by us not ὡσαύτως, but in a different sense and respect. For τὸ ῥητὸν or the proper or literal sense of the words is urged by us regarding the individual words of the institution considered separately. Again, the unusual predication is urged by us regarding the entire manner of predicating. Whence no ἀντίφασις or contradiction follows. What?
