That an unusual predication cannot have a place except in the simple and proper signification of individual words: so that if one of those words is bent toward some impropriety and figurative sense, immediately the whole reason for the unusual predication expires, and a figurative or tropical one succeeds. The truth of this assertion can be demonstrated by an illustrious example taken from the Article concerning the Person of CHRIST. The predication by which GOD is predicated of Man, and Man of GOD, is not regular and proper: a fact which both we and our Adversaries confess. It would therefore follow that it is either improper or figurative: or singular or unusual. But it is not figurative. For a trope would be present either in the particle (Man) and for a true man a specter or Φάντασμα of a man would have to be understood: in which way a secession would be made into the camp of the Manichaeans: or a trope would be present in the word (GOD) and not true GOD, but some creature would have to be understood: in which way the Arian heresy would be established: or finally a trope would be present in the substantive verb (IS) and it would denote the same as if the human nature were changed into GOD: in which way the Eutychian impiety would be confirmed. It remains, therefore, that that predication, GOD is Man, or Man is GOD, while the proper, native, and literal signification of the individual words is still retained, is not Tropical or figurative: nor is it regular and customary: since a similar example cannot be given in the whole of nature: but it is unusual or singular: because the thing itself, namely the union of two natures in Christ, which the mode of predication imitates, is singular and unusual.

And indeed, even the Sacramentarians themselves, though unwittingly, establish this very mode of predicating, as often as they boast quite splendidly and magnificently that they understand the words of the institution not carnally, but Sacramentally and mystically. Now, however, there is nothing of mystery, nothing Sacramental in Tropes and figures: but their nature is so common and vulgar that it is known even to children. Furthermore, all figurative propositions, as all Logicians attest, can be reduced to regular and proper propositions: a thing which cannot be affirmed of Sacramental propositions.

Latin:

PRo diversâ Signi & Signati significatione, diversus etiam Prædicandi modus in Sacramentis obtinet. Quando enim vox Signi notat totam Sacramenti substantiam, ex utrâquè parte essentiali, terrenâ & cœlesti compositam: ita ut Signatum sit aliquid extra Sacramenti substantiam positum, nempè usus & fructus, sive effectus Sacramenti: & verò talis detur propositio, in quâ Signatum hoc, de Signo, hoc est, fructus Sacramenti, de ipsâ substantiâ Sacramenti prædicatur: ut quando dico, Circumcisio est Fœdus, Baptismus est Regeneratio: Cœna Domini est Spiritualis Coalitio cum Christo: tùm quis sit harum prædicationum sensus, quivis facilè intelligit.

Quando verò Signi vox notat unam tantùm partem essentialem sive συςατικὴν Sacramenti, nempè terrenam: ita ut Signatum jam sit altera pars essentialis sive constitutiva Sacramenti: & sic pars una essentialis, de alterâ essentiali prædicatur: & cùm B. Lutherus dicit: Panis benedictus est Corpus Christi: Vinum benedictum est Sangvis Christi: & sic non simplex λέξις, sed prædicatio est: tùm neque metonymia, neque figura ulla alia locum habere potest: Sed Prædicatio hæc dicitur & est inusitata, hoc est, mystica & singularis, cujus universa natura & affectio, ex unione Sacramentali in solidum dependet, quæ tota est singularis, arcana, mystica, hyperphysica. Quâ in parte propositionibus hisce maxima intercedit diversitas, cum prioribus illis. In his enim non tantùm disparatum de disparato: sed & pars una essentialis, de alterâ, & quidem verè ac realiter, non tantùm τῇ λέξει καὶ φράσει, sed per verum ac realem unionis modum prædicatur. Ubi inusitatam planè prædicandi rationem obtinere, vel tyro Theologiæ intelligit: Siquidem exemplum aliquod simile, in rerum universitate totâ, ne unicum quidem occurrit: exceptis prædicationibus de duabus naturis in Christo ad se mutuò: quæ itidem omnem naturæ ordinem & rationem infinitis parafangis trascendunt.

Est verò inusitatus sive singularis iste prædicationis modus ita comparatus, ut singula Institutionis verba proprium suum sensum retineant, neque quicquam figurati admittant: interim verò tota prædicatio ad nullum regularis sive usitatæ prædicationis modum, neque simplicem sive proprium, neque improprium sive figuratum referri possit.

Contradictionis implicationem hoc loco nobis objicit gens Sacramentaria, propterea quòd contendamus, singula Institutionis verba κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν & propriè intelligenda esse: & tamen nihilominus prædicationis modum non modò non esse proprium: sed ne quidem improprium: quin planè singularem & inusitatum. Verum omnis ἀντιφάσεως ratio ultrò expirat, si non ὡσαύτως, sed diverso sensu ac respectu, utrumque à nobis affirmari attendatur. Nam τὸ ῥητὸν sive proprius aut literalis verborum sensus, urgetur à nobis, quoad singula institutionis verba, seorsim considerata. Rursus inusitata prædicatio urgetur à nobis, quoad integram prædicandi rationem. Undè nulla sequitur ἀντίφασις sive contradictio. Quid? quòd inusitata prædicatio locum habere nequit, nisi in simplice ac propriâ singularum vocum significatione: ita, ut si una istarum vocum, ad improprietatem aliquam, & figuratum sensum inflectatur, statim omnis inusitatæ prædicationis ratio expiret, & figurata sive tropica succedat. Assertionis hujus veritas illustri exemplo, ex Articulo de Personâ CHRISTI petito demonstrari potest. Prædicatio illâ quâ DEUS de Homine, Homo de DEO prædicatur, regularis & propria non est: id quod & nos & Adversarij fatentur. Consequens igitur fuerit, eam esse vel impropriam sive figuratam: vel singularem sive inusitatam. Atqui figurata non est. Nam tropus inesset vel particulæ (Homo) & pro vero homine, spectrum sive Φάντασμα hominis intelligendum esset: quo pacto in Manichæorum castra fieret secessio: vel tropus inesset voci (DEUS) & non verus DEUS, sed creatura aliqua intelligi deberet: quo pacto Ariana hæresis stabiliretur: vel denique tropus inesset verbo substantivo (EST) & idem notaret, ac si humana natura esset mutata in DEUM: quo pacto Eutychiana impietas confirmaretur. Relinquitur ergò Prædicationem istam, DEUS est Homo, vel Homo est DEUS, retentâ etiam singularum vocum propriâ, nativâ ac literali significatione, non esse Tropicam aut figuratam: non etiam regularem & usitatam: siquidem simile exemplum in universâ naturâ dari non potest: sed esse inusitatam sive singularem: quia res ipsa, nempè unio duarum naturarum in Christo, quàm prædicationis modus imitatur, est singularis & inusitata.

Et profectò hunc ipsum prædicandi modum, vel ipsi Sacramentarij, licèt inscij stabiliunt, quoties satis splendidè & magnificè gloriantur, se verba institutionis non carnaliter, sed Sacramentaliter & mysticè intelligere. Jam verò in Tropis & figuris nihil inest mysterij, nihil Sacramentale: sed ita communis & vulgaris est eorum natura, ut vel pueris ea innotescat. Præterea omnes figuratæ propositiones, attestantibus omnibus Logicis, ad regulares & proprias propositiones reduci possunt: id quod de propositionibus Sacramentalibus affirmari nequit.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: On the final cause of Sacraments

That there can be several ends for one thing, but yet one principal or primary one, and all the rest subordinate: the very nature of the Sacraments also proves this quite clearly to be most true. But from where that primary end is rightly elicited, there could hardly be any more convenient method than that we should descend through ἀφαίρεσιν to θέσιν: that is, having rejected the partly manifestly false and partly improper ends of the Sacraments, we may finally investigate and define the truer one.

I. Carlstadt granted no other use to the Sacraments in the Church than that they are marks and tokens of confession, by which the Church of CHRIST is distinguished from the peoples of other religions. For, as Calvin himself also testifies, book 4, chapter 14, § 13, he maintained that a Sacrament has only one signification, which agrees with signs: namely, as it signifies that solemn oath which a soldier renders to the Emperor when he is initiated into military service. For just as new soldiers bind their faith to the Emperor by that military Sacrament, and profess military service: so by our signs we profess CHRIST the Emperor, and testify that we serve under his standards. He added similarities by which he might make the matter clearer: Just as the toga distinguished Romans from the pallium-wearing Greeks: just as also the orders themselves at Rome were distinguished among themselves by their Symbols: the Senatorial from the equestrian by purple and crescent-shaped shoes: the Equestrian from the plebeian by a ring: so we wear our Symbols, which distinguish us from the profane. But Calvin rightly objects that this argument is not at all firm. For although all the Orthodox freely confess that the Sacraments are marks or tokens distinguishing the Christian people from any peoples of other religions: and by a symbol of which, as it were, those who communicate in the same profession of faith coalesce into one society of the Church: yet they judge this end to be neither the only nor the primary one, thus dissenting greatly from Carlstadt. Scripture certainly assigns a far different and more noble end to Baptism: namely, the remission of sins. Acts 2:38, the washing away of sins: Acts 22:16, the laver of spiritual regeneration: John 3:6, Titus 3:5, salvation, 1 Peter 3:21. Then, all participate equally in one and the same Sacrament, namely the Baptismal one, who nevertheless, regarding the profession of Religion, differ from one another in every possible way.

How then shall the whole nature of the Sacraments consist in this (as Carolostadius feigns), that they should, forsooth, distinguish men of different religions from one another?

II. The Anabaptists pretend that the Sacraments were instituted by GOD for this reason: that they might be allegories of profession and good works: For example: that circumcision was nothing else than an allegory or a certain likeness of the subduing of desires and lusts: that Baptism is a sign of the afflictions and calamities in which Christians are immersed. That the Lord's Supper is a symbol of mutual benevolence, concord, and charity. But although this opinion is not to be rejected entirely—since it can in no way be denied that very illustrious types and figures concerning external discipline of morals are contained in the Sacraments, just as Dionysius the Areopagite is sufficiently prolix and accurate in explaining them in his Ecclesiastical Hierarchy—yet this is neither the only nor the principal end for which the Sacraments were instituted. For there would have been no need for Sacraments on account of such allegories, because such rules or admonitions are proposed much more clearly through the Word: whereas, conversely, there is great obscurity inherent in sacramental allegories. Furthermore, those who use the Sacraments already have the doctrine of morals known and understood beforehand: therefore, for them, the use of the Sacraments would be clearly null if they did not contain another and more noble end. And even if one using a Sacrament were not skilled in the doctrine of morals, he would never learn it from the Sacraments on account of their remarkable obscurity: and thus, in this respect also, the use of the Sacraments will be futile, nay, null. Thirdly, what of the fact that, while this opinion stands, no excellence at all is left to the Sacraments of the New Testament over the Sacraments of the Old Testament? Finally, Scripture itself expressly assigns another end to Baptism, as was shown a little earlier.

III. There are and are found many for whom the end of the Sacraments seems to consist solely and principally in this: that they are, forsooth, signs of that grace which is conferred upon the faithful outside the use of the Sacrament: through which signs our faith is merely excited and confirmed, so that we may believe all the more confidently that our sins have been forgiven, and that we are in the grace and friendship of GOD. Our author does not seem to differ much from this opinion, defining a Sacrament as a sign of grace, or of gratuitous reconciliation, which is given on account of Christ and is preached in the Gospel. Corp. doctr. p. 504. But although it can in no way be denied that the Sacraments obtain this end—whence the Apostle, Rom. 4:11, calls them seals of the righteousness of faith—yet this opinion does not complete or exhaust the primary end of the Sacraments. For if the Sacraments are signs of divine grace only insofar as they excite faith and recall to our memory the proper promise of the Gospel, certainly the Sacraments will have no other use than that of some image or painting, which can perform the same thing in us. But this is absurd: therefore that will also be absurd. 2. This end does not apply to every Sacrament. Therefore it is not the proper end. The antecedent is clear, because when infants are baptized, then faith is certainly not excited or confirmed: but is finally conferred: and consequently, if this sole end is to be admitted, then no infants should be baptized, but only adults, as those in whom this end can have a place. 3. The end of salvation is attributed to Baptism, 1 Pet. 3:21. Therefore.

Perhaps the authority of Blessed Luther, as well as Article XIII of the Augsburg Confession, could be objected to us in this place. For Luther writes in his book On the Babylonian Captivity: Baptism justifies no one, nor does it profit anyone: but faith in the word of promise, to which Baptism is added. And in the assertion of certain articles, art. 1: The Sacrament does not justify, but faith in the Sacrament. The same Luther, in his book against the armed man Cochlaeus, asserts that no part of justification can be attributed to Baptism: and that the Apostle Peter, in the passage already alleged, means this: that through Baptism as an external sign, faith is provoked and exercised, which saves. But Article XIII of the Augsburg Confession is as follows: Concerning the use of the Sacraments, they teach that the Sacraments were instituted not only to be marks of profession among men, but rather that they should be signs and testimonies of the will of GOD toward us, proposed to excite and confirm faith in those who use them. But no inconvenience redounds to our doctrine from this. For first, the exclusive particle (only, or solely) is read neither in Luther nor in the Augsburg Confession: therefore it is concluded firmly enough that it cannot be inferred from the produced passages that the Sacraments were instituted only or solely for exciting and confirming faith. Then, the produced passages deal with the use of the Sacraments taken not actively, but passively—that is, not the use which the Sacraments confer upon those who use them, but that by which they themselves are received by those who use them. Finally, all these passages are directed against the abomination of the work performed, not against the proper use or efficacy or virtue of the Sacraments.

IV. Huldricus Zwingli, in his book On True and False Religion, chapter on the Sacraments, p. 201, says: The Sacraments are signs or ceremonies by which a man proves to the Church that he is either a candidate or a soldier of Christ: and they render the whole Church more certain of your faith than they do you. Martin Bucer supports Zwingli, writing (on the words of chapter 3 of Matthew: And they were baptized by him) that nothing at all is conferred upon the souls of men through the Sacraments, whether you look at the conferring of grace or the confirmation of faith: indeed, he said that through our doctrine, men were led away from the admiration of Christ to respect the signs more than is right. And so that they might in some way cloak the error, they distinguished between men using the Sacrament, so as to establish that if these sacramental signs are exhibited to those already justified, then they are not naked tokens, but are professions and initiations of a life worthy of CHRIST. But if they are exhibited to others, then they are only naked signs, by which they are received into the Church not by GOD, but by men. And Bucer concludes finally, since Baptism is an external sign, signifying that we put on CHRIST and are in the

Latin:

UNius rei plures posse esse fines, sed unum tamen principalem sive primarium, reliquos omnes subordinatos: ipsa quoque Sacramentorum natura, longè verissimum esse, satis luculenter comprobat. Undè verò finis ille primarius ritè eliciatur, vix commodior ulla fuerit ratio, quàm ut per ἀφαίρεσιν ad θέσιν descendamus: hoc est, partim manifestè falsis, partim impropriis Sacramentorum finibus rejectis, veriorem tandem investigemus & definiamus.

I. Carolostadius Sacramentis nullum alium in Ecclesia concessit usum, quàm quòd sint notæ & tesseræ confessionis, quibus ab aliarum religionum populis CHRISTI Ecclesia discernitur. Nam, ipso quoque Calvino teste, lib. 4. cap. 14. § 13. statuebat, Sacramentum unam tantùm habere significationem, quæ signis conveniat: nempè quà solenne illud juramentum significat quod miles Imperatori præstat, cùm militia initiatur. Sicut enim militari illo Sacramento fidem suam obstringunt Imperatori novi milites, & militiam profitentur: ita nostris signis CHRISTUM Imperatorem profitemur, & sub ejus signis nos militare testamur. Addebat similitudines, quibus rem magis dilucidam reddat: Quemadmodum toga Romanos, à palliatis Græcis discernebat: sicut etiam ipsi inter se ordines Romæ suis Symbolis distingvebantur: Senatorius ab equestri, purpurâ & lunatis calceis: Equester à plebejo, annulo: ita nos Symbola nostra gestamus, quæ nos à prophanis discernunt. Sed rectè subjicit Calvinus, argumentum hoc minimè firmum esse. Etsi enim Orthodoxi quique ultrò fatentur, Sacramenta esse notas sive tesseras, discernentes populum Christianũ, à quibusvis aliarum religionum populis: & quarum quasi Symbolo quodam, in unam Ecclesiæ societatem coalescunt, qui eâdem fidei professione communicant: tamen finem hunc neque unicum, neque primarium esse judicant, sic à Carolostadio plurimùm dissentientes. Scriptura certè Baptismo longè alium & nobiliorem finem assignat: nempè remissionem peccatorum. Actor. 2, 38. ablutionem peccatorum: Actor. 22, 16. regenerationis spiritualis lavacrum: Joh. 3, 6. Tit. 3, 5. salvationem, 1. Petr. 3, 21. Deindè uno eodemque Sacramento, nempè Baptistico, participant ex æquo omnes, qui tamen, quoad Religionis professionem, δις διὰ πασω̂ν à se invicem discrepant.

Quomodo ergò Sacramentorum natura tota in eo (uti Carolostadius fingit) consistet, ut nimirùm diversarum religionum homines invicem discernat.

II. Anabaptistae Sacramenta ideò à DEO instituta esse fingunt, ut essent professionis atque bonorum operum allegoriae: Exempli gratiâ: circumcisionem fuisse nihil aliud, quam allegoriam sive similitudinem quadam coërcendarum cupiditatum & libidinum: Baptismum esse signum afflictionum & calamitatum, quibus immergantur Christiani. Caenam Domini esse Symbolum mutuae benevolentiae, concordiae & charitatis. Quanquàm verò & haec opinio non prorsus est rejicienda: siquidem in Sacramentis illustres admodùm typos & figuras contineri de externâ morum disciplinâ, negari nullo modo potest: quemadmodum in illis explicandis satis prolixus & accuratus est Dionysius Areopagita de Hierarchiâ Ecclesiasticâ: tamen neque unus iste, neque praecipuus est finis, cujus gratiâ Sacramenta sint instituta. Nam propter allegorias hujusmodi non opus fuiffet Sacramentis, propterea quòd per Verbum multò dilucidiùs tales regulae sive commonefactiones proponuntur: cùm vice versâ allegoriis Sacramentalibus, magna insit obscuritas. Accedit, quòd qui Sacramentis utuntur, jam ante doctrinam morum habent cognitam & perspectam: His ergò Sacramentorum usus planè esser nullus, si non alium & nobiliorem finem continerent. Et si vel maximè utens Sacramento, doctrinam morum non calleat: tamen hanc ex Sacramentis propter insignem obscuritatem, nunquàm addiscet: & sic horum etiam respectu, Sacramentorum usus erit frustraneus, imò nullus. Tertiò Quid? quòd stante hâc sententiâ, nulla prorsus excellentia Sacramentis Novi Testamenti, prae Sacramentis Veteris Testamenti relinquitur. Tandem Scriptura ipsa Baptismo alium finem expressè adsignat: uti paulò antè ostensum.

III. Sunt & reperiuntur multi, quibus Finis Sacramentorum in eo unicè & praecipuè consistere videtur: ut nimirùm sint signa illius gratiae, quae extra usum Sacramenti fidelibus est collata: per quae signa tantùm excitetur & confirmetur fides nostra, ut tantò confidentiùs credamus, peccata nobis esse remissa, nosque esse in gratiâ & amicitiâ DEI. A quâ sententiâ Autor noster non multùm abhorrere videtur, definiens Sacramentum, quod sit signum gratiae, sive reconciliationis gratuitae, quae propter Christum donatur, & in Evangelio praedicatur. Corp. doctr. pag. 504. Quanquàm verò negari nullo modo potest, quin Sacramenta finem istum obtineant: undè Apostolus Rom. 4, 11. ea nominat Sigilla justitiae fidei: tamen neque haec sententia primarium Sacramentorum finem perficit aut absolvit. Si enim Sacramenta sunt signa divinae gratiae, tantùm quatenùs fidem excitant, & promissionem Evangelii propriam, in memoriam nobis revocant: certè Sacramenta non alium usum habebunt, quàm imaginis aut picturae alicujus: quae idem in nobis praestare possunt. Atqui hoc absurdum: Ergò absurdum erit & illud. 2. Finis iste non competit omni Sacramento. Ergò non est finis proprius. Antecedens patet, quia quando Infantes baptizātur, tùm fides certè non excitatur aut confirmatur: sed demùm confertur: & per consequens, si finis hic unicus admitti debeat, tùm nullus infantum baptizari deberet, sed tantùm adulti, ut in quibus finis iste locum habere potest. 3. Baptismo 1. Petr. 3, 2. tribuitur Salvationis finis. Ergò.

Objici fortassis hoc loco nobis posset, tùm autoritas B. Lutheri, tùm Articulus XIII. Confessionis Augustanæ Lutherus enim in lib de Captivit. Babyl. scribit: Baptismus neminem justificat, nec ulli prodest: sed fides in verbum promissionis, cui additur Baptismus. Et in assertione articulorum quorundam, art. 1. Sacramentum non justificat, sed fides Sacramenti. Idem Lutherus in libro adversus armatum virum Cochlæum asserit, non posse ullam partem justificationis tribui Baptismo: & Apostolum Petrum dicto jam allegato hoc velle, per Baptismum ceu signum externum, fidem provocari & exerceri, quæ salvet. Articulus autem XIII. Confessionis Augustanæ sic habet: De usu Sacramentorum docent, quòd Sacramenta instituta sint, non modò ut sint notæ professionis inter homines: sed magis, ut sint signa & testimonia voluntatis DEI erga nos ad excitandam & confirmandam fidem in his, qui utuntur, proposita. Verùm nihil indè incommodi ad nostram doctrinam redundat. Nam primò particula exclusiva (tantùm, sive unicè) neq; apud Lutherum, neque in Confessione Augustanâ legitur: Ergò satis firmiter colligitur, ex locis productis concludi non posse, quòd Sacramenta tantùm sive unicè pro fide excitandâ & confirmandâ sint instituta. Deindè loca producta agunt de usu Sacramentorum, non activè, sed passivè sumto, eo nimirùm, non quem Sacramenta conferunt utentibus: sed quo ipsa ab utentibus suscipiuntur. Tandem contra operis operati abominationem loca ista omnia sunt directa: non contra usum sive efficaciam aut virtutem Sacramentorum propriam.

IV. Huldricus Zvvinglius lib. de verâ & falsâ religione, cap. de Sacramentis, pag. 201. Sacramenta, inquit, sunt signa vel ceremoniæ, quibus homo Ecclesiæ probat, se aut candidatum, aut militem esse Christi: redduntquè Ecclesiam totam potiùs certiorem de tuâ fide, quàm te. Suffragatur Zvvinglio Martinus Bucerus, scribens (sup. capitis 3. Matthæi verba hæc: Et baptizabantur ab illo) per Sacramenta nihil prorsus hominum animis conferri, sive spectes collationem gratiæ, sive confirmationem fidei: quin per nostram doctrinam, homines abduci dicebat ab admiratione Christi, ad signa plus æquo suspicienda. Et ut errorem quodammodo palliarent, ita distingvebant inter homines utentes Sacramento, ut statuerent, signa isthæc Sacramentalia si jam justificatis exhibeantur, tùm non esse nudas tesseras, sed esse professiones & initiationes vitæ CHRISTO dignæ. Sin aliis exhibeantur, tùm tantùm esse nuda signa, quibus non à DEO, sed ab hominibus recipiuntur in Ecclesiam. Et concludit tandem Bucerus, cùm Baptismus sit externum signum, significans nos induere CHRISTUM: & esse in-


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: Opinion of the Scholastics

Church, that it then only truly signifies if those who are baptized are predestined to eternal life. Whence the Pious, he says, do not intend to baptize, except the predestined.

Moreover, this opinion labors under horrendous errors and absurdities. For 1. it arises from a false hypothesis, which posits that a man, even not yet baptized, is in the grace of God and has the remission of sins, of which in the reception of Baptism only a protestation is made. But Scripture expressly denies this, asserting that Baptism is that medium through which a man is regenerated, is received into the covenant of the grace of God, is washed from sins, is sanctified, is saved, John 3:5, Tit. 3:5, 1 Pet. 3:21. Whence Acts 2:38, men are read to have been baptized into the remission of sins; not finally after the remission of the same. 2. If it is true, as the Apostle affirms, that we in Baptism die together with Christ, rise again with the same, put on Christ, become one with Christ, become the seed of Abraham, and heirs according to the promise: and indeed that this spiritual effect redounds to all baptized believers, not to the elect alone: Rom. 6:4, Gal. 3:27, then it must necessarily be false that Baptism signifies only external reception into the Church. 3. What he discourses concerning the predestined, as if they alone ought to be baptized, and they alone, if they are baptized, put on Christ, that is too trifling, as will be demonstrated in the exodus of the Article on Baptism.

V. Johannes Calvinus, in defining the proper and adequate end of the Sacraments, is not sufficiently consistent with himself. For book 4, Inst. chap. 14, § 1. 'It seems,' he says, 'that this definition of the Sacraments would be simple and proper, if we should say that they are an external symbol by which the Lord seals to our consciences the promises of his benevolence toward us, for the sustaining of the weakness of our faith: and we in turn testify our piety toward him, as much before him and the Angels as among men.' Although it is also possible to define the Sacraments more briefly in another way: that it be called a testimony of divine grace toward us, confirmed by an external sign, with a mutual testimony of our piety toward him.

Then, when he discourses concerning the principal end and office of the Sacraments, book 4, chap. 14, § 12. 'The sole office of the Sacraments,' he says, 'is to subject his promises to our eyes to be looked upon, nay, to be pledges of them to us.' And § 17. 'Let it remain fixed that there are no other parts of the Sacraments than of the Word of God: which are to offer and propose Christ to us, and in him the treasures of heavenly grace.' This is the opinion of Calvin: that the Sacraments are true, certain, and efficacious signs only to those predestined to eternal life, since they alone receive the Thing of the Sacrament. Which indeed flows from that false principle of his, in the establishing of which he labors: book 3, Inst. chap. 2, § 10. Namely, that only the predestined have true faith. From these, therefore, it is concluded that Calvin feels that the Sacraments are not signs of present grace, which is conferred in the very act or use of the Sacraments: but that they are only signs of grace and the remission of sins indefinitely, namely, that which is either already given in the present: or was given long ago: or is finally to be conferred in the future. Hence it is that in chap. 15, § 15, he writes that the remission of sins sometimes precedes the Sacrament, as in Acts 9 and 10 in the Baptism of Paul and Cornelius: sometimes follows, as in baptized children, as he has in chap. 16, § 20 and 21. Which very thing, however, he does not concede except in the predestined, and those who are to live until the use of reason: who, however, if they die sooner, regeneration happens to them in some way unknown to us. Hence in his antidote against Sess. 7. of the Council of Trent he expressly asserts: Many baptized infants are damned, and unbaptized ones are saved, namely, according to the absolute decree of predestination.

But this opinion of Calvin is in many ways impious and erroneous. For 1. The Sacraments, by reason of their use or primary end, are not signs of a past thing, but of a present one. For it is not attributed to Baptism in the sacred writings that it is a sign of preceding regeneration: but that it is itself the medium through which regeneration is now conferred in the present. Tit. 3:5, Acts 22:16, Eph. 5:26. Therefore it is false that the Sacraments by reason of their primary use are signs of past grace. 2. Since the Sacraments, according to the defining Sacred Scriptures, are not signs of past grace in their primary use, but of present, it will certainly be false that the Sacraments are principally signs of predestination, which is a past thing. 3. All who receive the Sacraments with true faith obtain their effect: for example: all the baptized, regeneration. But not all who are thus baptized either persevere in faith or are predestined. Therefore Baptism is not principally a sign of predestination. The major premise is evident from Scripture.

For Rom. 6:3, the Apostle says: Do you not know that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?

And Gal. 3:26. As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. The Apostle confirms the minor premise likewise in Gal. 4:9, 10, 11. Now when you have known God, or rather are known by God: how do you turn again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you desire to be in bondage again, etc.

VI. The Scholastic Doctors under the papacy likewise contend with one another concerning the proper end of the Sacraments: namely, whether the Sacraments are to be called the efficient cause of grace?

Hugh of St. Victor, book 1, On the Sacraments, part 9, chapter 2, looking to the elements and to the external things of the Sacraments, teaches that the Sacraments were instituted for a threefold reason: 1. On account of humiliation: For when man is commanded to seek salvation in those things to which he is superior by condition, what else is this than that the superior is subjected to his inferior. 2. On account of instruction, so that through that which is perceived outwardly in the Sacrament in visible form, the mind may be instructed. 3. For the sake of excitement, so that the faithful mind, while it is led outwardly to various holy exercises of study, may be renewed inwardly more and more by its very devotion unto holiness. This is the view of that Hugo, whose opinion, however, is too obscure to be able to be determined as to what proper and principal end he ascribed to the Sacraments. For it is not about subordinate ends, but about the proper and primary one, that there is controversy in this place.

Durandus, however, explains his mind a little more clearly, lib. 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 4. Almost all say that the Sacraments are not efficient causes of grace, except improperly: but that they are properly causes without which not: so that GOD immediately and alone produces grace: but the use of the Sacraments is this, that they are present only to the divine action.

Later Papists contend that the use of the Sacraments is such that they are not improperly, but properly and truly, a cause of divine grace: Furthermore, they struggle here again. Namely, how the Sacraments are a cause of divine grace: Alexander of Hales, part 4. q. 8. memb. 3. art. 5. §. 3. Thomas, lib. 4. sent. dist. 1. admit that there is a supernatural virtue in the Sacraments, through which, however, the Sacraments do not immediately produce grace: but only a certain disposition, to which grace follows infallibly.

Scotus and those who follow him, in lib. 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 5. assert that the use of the Sacraments is such that they can not only truly be called causes of such a disposition as the preceding ones posited: but also of grace itself, and that in two ways: 1. Because every disposition which certainly and necessarily disposes to the introduction of a form actively, not passively, can be called an instrumental effective cause of that form, as labor is of a reward, or motion of a terminus. Such, however, is the reception of a Sacrament, whence it can be called an instrumental cause of grace. 2. Now just as no artificial instrument concurs actively to the work of the artisan: but only by disposing formally: For example, only the smith acts by moving the saw: but the saw, by formally occupying the place, extrudes another body from that same place: and thus it is said to dispose formally so that the agent may effect something: so in a similar way Scotus thinks that the Sacraments dispose to grace and thus are truly called instrumental causes.

Gabriel Biel in lib. 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 1. art. 3. dubio 3. similarly denies any such virtue in the Sacraments, and contends that their use is to be causes without which grace is not conferred, and nevertheless he maintains that the Sacraments no less truly and properly effect and attain grace, as he puts it, than any natural cause attains its effect.

The mind of Gabriel, therefore, was that no secondary cause immediately produces an effect, so that not even fire produces heat: but that GOD alone produces the effect at the presence of the secondary cause. Henry of Ghent, quodlibeto 4. q. 37., thought that a similar thing happens in the Sacraments, denying that any such virtue should be posited in the Sacraments: and yet he asserts that by their use they are properly causes of grace. He says, however, that GOD is in the Sacraments by a certain peculiar influx, and in them and through them produces grace.

There are finally others who wish the Sacraments of the New Testament not only to be truly and properly instrumental causes of grace: but in such a way that there is truly in them a certain virtue, through which grace itself is produced, and not just some disposition. This virtue, they say, is not some permanent quality, different from the Sacrament and its use, but is the very use and motion by which GOD uses the Sacraments to this end, so that ex opere operato, through them He confers grace. Which opinion was common not only among the ancient writers under the Papacy: but not so long ago was also approved by the authority of the Council of Trent, Sess. 6. can. 8. in these words: If anyone shall say that grace is not conferred by the Sacraments of the new law themselves ex opere operato, etc., let him be anathema.

VII. And finally, the Orthodox hold the middle ground between these extremes of various errors, maintaining that the Sacraments, by reason of the primary or principal end for which they were especially instituted, are means or organs through which divine grace is partly conferred, and partly also confirmed and sealed in the minds of the faithful: yet in a different respect. For as regards us, the Sacraments are means confirming faith: but as regards GOD, they are organs conferring and sealing the grace of the Evangelical promise. This purer doctrine holds the middle between two extremes, one of which, on the side of excess, is proper to the Papists, who imagine that the Sacraments confer grace ex opere operato: the other, on the side of defect, is proper to the Sacramentarians or Zwinglians, who partly deny the efficacy of justifying simply to the Sacraments: and partly maintain that the Sacraments excite faith only by way of admonition, by which faith, however, outside the use of the Sacraments, it apprehends the righteousness of the Gospel as its own. Which opinion, although it has something of truth, nevertheless in no way confirms the error of the Zwinglians. For although it is true, and has never been denied by us, that faith is excited, the remission of sins is offered, and the benefits acquired by the death of Christ are proposed to us even through the Word of the Gospel: (in which respect both the Word and the Sacraments could be called the object of justifying faith: because both, in respect of Evangelical grace, act as an instrumental cause:) it does not therefore follow that the Sacraments do not confer grace otherwise, or are not causes of grace otherwise, than as the Word of the Gospel is. For just as it may be said of him who points out a physician to some sick person, and of the physician himself, and finally even of the medicine, that each was an instrumental cause and a means of health, while nevertheless a certain power of acting, proper to each and distinct from the rest, remains with every one of them: so the Sacraments, although they no less propose and show CHRIST and his benefits than the word of the Gospel, do not, however, to both one and the same power and efficacy of acting, one and the same use can or ought to be attributed.

Moreover, the Apostle expressed this primary and principal end of the Sacraments, naming them with clearly sharp brevity σφραγῖδας δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίσεως, seals of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4, 11. Whence it is evidently gathered, Whatever is destitute of this end, that is, whatever does not contain the power of sealing or confirming the righteousness of faith; that cannot obtain the name and definition of a Sacrament properly so called: as we shall expressly show below against the Romanists in chapter 4.

There are those to whom this doctrine of ours is not a little distasteful, arguing thus: Whatever does not seal salvation and the righteousness of faith, that cannot be a Sacrament properly so called.

But the Sacrament of the Eucharist, taken by the unworthy, does not seal salvation and the righteousness of faith. Therefore the Sacrament of the Eucharist, taken by the unworthy, will not be a Sacrament properly so called: or, if it is, it will follow that the primary and only principal end of the Sacraments is not that they always confirm and seal salvation and the righteousness of faith.

I answer that this argument proceeds from the negation of the second act to the negation of the first act or power. Whence a base fallacy of four terms emerges, just as if someone were to conclude thus: A sleeping man does not use reason in the second act. Therefore it is not proper to man that he is always endowed with reason. It is to be noted therefore that in definitions of things, by verbs of the indicative mood, the second act is not always denoted, but the first act or power.

Wherefore, although the Sacrament of the Eucharist taken by infidels does not in the second act seal salvation and the righteousness of faith: yet it always has in itself in the first act that power or potentiality, so that it could perform this, unless the infidelity of the unworthy stood in the way. And this indeed necessarily depends on the nature of any Sacrament, so that by the will of God the institutor, it can and ought always to seal the righteousness of faith: but it does not always effect it, because of the infidelity of the one using the Sacrament: which infidelity does not cause the Sacrament, as regards its nature, as regards even the gift and the intention of God, to not always be and remain a true Sacrament, and whole in respect of its essence: but it only causes the Sacrament in the second act not to exert a salutary use upon the person using the Sacrament unworthily.

Latin:

Ecclesia: tunc solum verè significare, si illi, qui baptizantur, sint prædestinati ad vitam æternam. Undè Pii, inquit, non intendunt baptisare, nisi prædestinatos.

Cæterùm horrendis erroribus & absurditatibus hæc laborat sententia. Nam 1. ex falsâ oritur hypothefi, quæ statuit, Hominem etiam nondum baptisatum esse in gratia DEI, & habere remissionem peccatorum, cujus in Baptismi acceptione duntaxat fiat protestatio. Negat verò hoc disertè Scriptura, asserens, Baptismum esse illud mediu, per quod homo regeneretur, in fœdus gratiæ DEI recipiatur, à peccatis abluatur, sanctificetur, salvetur, Joh. 3, 5. Tit. 3, 5. 1. Pet. 3, 21. Undè Actor. 2, 38. leguntur homines baptizati esse in remissionem peccatorum; non demùm post eorundem remissionem. 2. Si verum est, quòd Apostolus assirmat, nos in Baptismo commori cum Christo, consurgere cum eodem, induere Christum, unum fieri cum Christo, fieri semen Abrahæ, & hæredes secundum promissionem: & quidem spiritualem hunc effectum ad omnes fideles baptisatos redundare, non ad solos electos: Rom 6, 4. Galat. 3, 27. utique falsum sit necesse est, Baptismum significare tantùm externam receptionem in Ecclesiam. 3. Quæ de prædestinatis disserit, quasi illi tantùm baptizari debeant, & hi soli, si baptizentur, Christum induant, id nimis nugatorium est, uti in diexodo Articuli de Baptismo demonstrabitur.

V. Johannes Calvinus in definiendo Sacramentorum fine proprio & adæquato, sibipsi non satis constat. Nam lib. 4. instit. cap. 14, §. 1. Videtur, inquit, hæc Sacramentorum definitio simplex fore & propria, si dixerimus, ea externum esse Symbolum, quo benevolentiæ erga nos suæ promissiones conscientiis nostris Dominus obsignat, ad sustinendam fidei nostræ imbecillitatem: & nos vicissim pietatem erga eum nostram, tàm coram eo & Angelis, quàm apud homines testamur. Licèt etiam majore compendio Sacramenta aliter definire: ut vocetur divinæ in nos gratiæ testimonium, externo signo confirmatum, cum mutuâ nostræ ergaipsum pietatis testificatione.

Deindè ubi de præcipuo Sacramentorum fine atque officio disserit, lib. 4. cap. 14. §. 12. Sacramentorum, inquit, unicum officium est, ejus promissiones oculis nostris spectandes subjicere, imò earum nobis esse pignora. Et §. 17. Fixum maneat, non esse alias Sacramentorum, quam Verbi DEI partes: quæ sunt, offerre nobis, ac proponere Christum, & in eo cœlestis gratiæ thesauros. Sententia Calvini hæc est: solis ad vitam æternam prædestinatis, Sacramenta esse vera, certa atq; efficacia signa quippè qui soli Rem Sacramenti accipiunt. Quod quidem ex falso illo ejusdem principio scaturit, in quo astruendo ille laborat: lib. 3. instit. cap. 2. §. 10. Solos nempè prædestinatos veram fidem habere. Ex his ergò illud efficitur, Calvinum sentire, quòd Sacramenta non sint signa gratiæ præsentis, quæ in ipso Sacramentorum actu five usu conferatur: sed esse tantùm signa gratiæ & remissionis peccatorum indefinitè, nimirum ejus, quæ vel jam in præsenti detur: vel jampridem data sit: vel in futuro demùm conferenda. Hinc est, quòd cap. 15. §. 15. scribit, Remissionem peccatorum aliquando præcedere Sacramentum, ut Actor. 9. & 10. in Baptismo Pauli & Cornelii: aliquando subsequi, ut in pueris baptizatis,uti habet cap. 16. §. 20. & 21. Quod ipsum tamen non concedit, nisi in prædestinatis, & ad rationis usum usque victuris: Qui tamen, si citiùs moriantur, regenerationem ipsis obtingere modo quopiam nobis incognito. Hinc in suo antidoto contra Sess. 7. Concilii Tridentini disertè asserit: Multos infantes baptizatos damnari, & non baptizatos salvari,nempè secundum decretum prædestinationis absolutum.

Est verò sententia hæc Calvini multis modis impia & erronea. Nam 1. Sacramenta, ratione usûs sive finis primarii, non sunt signa rei præteritæ, sed præsentis. Baptismo enim in sacris non tribuitur,quòd sit signum antegressæ regenerationis: sed quòd ipse sit medium, per quod jam in præsenti conferatur regeneratio. Tit. 3, 5.Actor. 22, 16.Ephes. 5, 26. Ergò falsum, quòd Sacramenta ratione usûs primarii sint signa gratiæ præteritæ. 2. Cum Sacramenta ne definientibus Scripturis Sacris non sint signa gratiæ præteritæ in primario usu, sed præsentis, utique falsum erit, Sacramenta præcipuè esse signa prædestinationis, quæ est res præterita. 3. Omnes qui verâ fide Sacramenta suscipiunt, effectum eorum consequuntur: Verbi gratiâ: Baptizati omnes, regenerationem. Atqui non omnes, qui sic baptizantur, vel in fide perseverat,vel sunt prædestinati. Ergò Baptismus principaliter non est signum prædestinationis. Major patet ex Scripturâ.

Nam Rom. 6, 3. inquit Apostolus: An ignoratis, quia quicunq́; baptizati sumus in CHRISTO JESU, in mortem ipsius baptizati sumus.

Et Gal. 3, 26. Quicunque in CHRISTO baptizati estis, CHISTUM induistis. Minorem confirmat itidem Apostolus Gal. 3, 9. 10. 11. Nunc cùm cognoveritis DEUM, imò cogniti sitis à DEO: quomodo convertimini iterum ad infirma & egena elementa, quibus denuò servire vultis &c.

VI. Scholastici Doctores sub pontificatu itidem de fine Sacramentorum proprio invicem digladiantur: An nimirùm Sacramenta sint causa efficiens Gratiæ dicenda?

Hugo de S.Victore lib. 1. de Sacr. parte 9. cap. 2. respiciens ad elementa, & ad res externas Sacramentorum,triplici de causâ Sacramenta instituta esse docet 1. propter humiliationem: Nam cùm homo in his salutem quærere jubetur, quibus conditione superior existit, quid aliud quàm suo inferiori superior subjicitur. 2. Propter eruditionem, ut per id,quod foris in Sacramento, in specie visibili cernitur, ad visibilem virtutem, quæ intùs in re Sacramenti constat, agnoscendam, mens humana erudiatur. 3. Propter excitationem, ut fidelis animus, dum foris ad varia sancta exercitationis studia ducitur, magis semper & magis intus ex ipsa sua devotione ad sanctitatem innovetur. Haec Hugo iste, cujus tamen sententia obscurior est, quam ut constare possit, quemnam proprium ac principalem finem Sacramentis adscripserit. Neque enim de subordinatis finibus, sed de proprio ac primario, hoc loco controvertitur.

Durandus vero paulo clarius mentem suam explicat, lib. 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 4. Plerique omnes dicunt, Sacramenta non esse causas efficientes gratiae, nisi improprie: proprie vero esse causas, sine quibus non: ita ut DEUS immediate & solus gratiam producat: Sacramentorum autem usus sit hic, ut non nisi actioni divinae adfint.

Pontificii posteriores pugnant, Sacramentorum eum esse usum, ut non improprie: sed proprie & vere sint causa gratiae divinae: Caeterum & hic rursum dimicant. Quomodo nimirum Sacramenta sint causa gratiae divinae: Alexander ab Ales. part. 4. q. 8. memb. 3. art. 5. §. 3. Thomas lib. 4. sent. dist. 1. fatentur, in Sacramentis esse virtutem supernaturalem, per quam tamen Sacramenta non immediate producant gratiam: verum duntaxat dispositionem quandam, ad quam infallibiliter sequatur gratia.

Scotus & qui ipsum sequuntur, in lib. 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 5. Sacramentorum usum perhibent esse eum, ut non tantum vere possint dici causae dispositionis ejusmodi, qualem praecedentes posuerunt: verum etiam ipsius gratiae idque bifariam: 1. Quia omnis dispositio, quae certo & necessario disponit ad introductionem formae active, non passive possit dici causa instrumentalis effectiva ipsius formae, ut labor praemii, motus termini. Talem autem esse susceptionem Sacramenti, unde possit dici causa instrumentalis gratiae. 2. Jam sicut nullum instrumentum artificiale, active concurrat ad opus artificis: sed tantum formaliter disponendo: Exempli gratia, solus faber agit movendo serram: serra autem formaliter occupando locum extrudit aliud corpus ex eodem loco: & sic dicitur formaliter disponere ut agens efficiat aliquid: ita simili modo existimat Scotus, Sacramenta disponere ad gratiam & sic vere, dici causas instrumentales.

Gabriel Biel in lib. 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 1. art. 3. dubio 3. similiter negat, omnem talem virtutem in Sacramentis, & contendit, usum eorum esse, ut sint cau sae sine quibus non conferatur gratia, & nihilominus tamen statuit, Sacramenta non minus vere & proprie efficere & attingere gratia, ut ipse loquitur, quam quacunque causa naturalis suum effectum attingit.

Mens ergo fuit Gabrieli, quod nulla causa secunda immediate producat effectum, adeo ut ne ignis quidem calorem: sed quod DEUS solus ad praesentiam causae secundae producat effectum. Cujus simile in Sacramentis fieri putabat, Henricus de Gandano, quodlibeto 4. q. 37. negans ponendam esse ullam ejusmodi virtutem in Sacramentis: & tamen usu suo illa perhibet esse proprie causas gratiae. Dicit autem, quod DEUS peculiari quodam illapsu sit in Sacramentis, atque in tis & per illa producat gratiam.

Sunt tandem alii, qui volunt Sacramenta Novi Testamenti, non tantùm esse verè ac propriè causas instrumentales gratiæ: sed ita, ut in ipsis reverà sit virtus quædam, per quam producatur ipsa gratia, & non tantùm dispositio aliqua. Hanc tamen virtutem, dicunt, non esse aliquam qualitatem permanentem, à Sacramento & ejus usu diversam, sed esse ipsum usum & motum, quo DEUS Sacramentis utatur ad hunc finem, ut ex opere operato, per ista Gratiam conferat. Quæ opinio non veterum tantùm Scriptorum sub Papatu communis fuit: Sed haud ita pridem Concilii etiam Tridentini autoritate comprobata Sess. 6. can. 8. his verbis: Si quis dixerit, per ipsa novæ legis Sacramenta ex opere operato non conferri gratiam, &c. anathema sit.

VII. Et postremò Orthodoxi inter extrema isthæc variorum errorum medium tenent, statentes, Sacramenta ratione finis primarii sive principalis, ob quē potissimùm sunt instituta, esse mediata sive organa, per quæ in mentibus fidelium, partim conferatur, partim etiam confirmetur, & obsignetur divina gratia: diverso tamen respectu. Quoad nos enim, Sacramenta sunt media, confirmantia fidem: Quoad DEUM verò, sunt organa conferentia & obsignantia Gratiam promissionis Evangelicæ. Tenet purior hæc doctrina medium inter duo extrema, quorum unum ex parte ὑπερβολῆς sive excessus, Pontificiorũ est proprium, fingentium Sacramenta conferre gratiam ex opere operato: alterum verò ex parte ἐλλείψεως, defectû, Sacramentariorum sive Zvvinglianorum proprium, qui partim Sacramentis efficaciam justificandi simpliciter negant: partim verò statuunt, per modum commonefactionis tantùm Sacramenta excitare fidem, qua tamen extra usum Sacramentorum, justitiam Evangelii propriam apprehendat. Quæ opinio licèt veri aliquid habeat, minimè tamen Zvvinglianorum errorem confirmat. Etsi enim verùm est, & à nobis nunquàm negatum fuit, quòd per Verbum etiam Evangelii excitetur fides, offeratur remissio peccatorum, & proponantur nobis beneficia morte Christi acquisita: (quod respectu tùm Verbum, tùm Sacramenta dici possent objectum fidei justificantis: quia utrumque respectu gratiæ Evangelicæ, habet se instar causæ instrumentalis:) non tamen propterea est consequens, Sacramenta non aliter conferre gratiam, aut non aliter causas esse gratiæ, quàm prout est Verbum Evangelii. Quemadmodum enim tùm de eo, qui ægroto cuipiam monstrat medicum: tùm de medico ipso: tùm denique de medicamento etiam dici potest, quòd sanitatis causa instrumentalis, & medium fuerit: interim tamen singulis certa sua, & à reliquis distincta constat agendi facultas: ita Sacramenta, licèt, non minùs proponant & ostendant CHRISTUM, ejusque beneficia, quàm verbum Evangelii: non tamen utrique una atque eadem vis & efficacia agendi, unus idemque usus attribui potest aut debet.

Cæterùm finem hunc primarium ac principalem Sacramentorum expressit Apostolus, argutâ planè brevitate nominans ea σφραγῖδας δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίσεως, signacula justitiæ fidei, Rom. 4, 11. Undè evidenter colligitur, Quicquid hoc fine destituitur, hoc est, quicquid non continet vim obsignandæ sive confirmandæ justitiæ fidei; illud Sacramenti propriè sic dicti, nomen ac definitionem sortiri non posse: uti infra contra Romanenses capite 4. ex professo ostendemus.

Sunt, quibus doctrina hæc nostra haud parùm sordet, sic argumentantes: Quicquid salutem & justitiam fidei non obsignat, illud Sacramentum propriè sic dictum esse nequit.

Atqui Sacramentum Eucharistiæ, ab indignis sumtum, non obsignat salutem & justitiam fidei. Ergò Sacramentum Eucharistiæ ab indignis sumtum, non erit Sacramentum propriè sic dictum: vel, si erit, consequetur, Sacramentorum finem primarium atque unicum principalem non esse, ut semper confirment & obsignent salutem & justitiam fidei.

Respondeo, procedere hoc argumentum à negatione actûs secundi, ad negationem actûs primi sive potentiæ. Undè turpis ἀσυλλογισία quatuor terminorum emergit, haud secus ac si quis ita colligeret: Homo dormiens actu secundo non utitur ratione. Ergò Hominis proprium non est, ut sit semper ratione præditus. Notandum proindè in definitionibus rerum, per verba indicandi, non semper notari actum secundum, sed actum primum sive potentiam.

Quapropter etsi Sacramentum Eucharistiæ ab infidelibus sumtum, actu secundo non obsignat salutem & justitiam fidei: semper tamen illud actu primo in se habet illam vim sive potentiam, ut posset hoc præstare, nisi indignorum obstaret infidelitas. Et hæc quidem necessariò dependet à naturâ cujuslibet Sacramenti, ita ut ex voluntate instituentis DEI, possit & debeat semper obsignare justitiam fidei: non autem semper id efficiat, propter infidelitatem utentis Sacramento: quæ infidelitas non facit, ut Sacramentum, quoad suam naturam, quoad δώρημα etiam, & intentionem DEI, sit semper & maneat Sacramentum verum, & ratione essentiæ integrum: sed facit tantùm, ut Sacramentum actu secundo usum salutarem non exerat ad personam, indignè Sacramento utentem.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacraments: Chapter II

CHAPTER II.

Latin:

CAPUT II.


### Chapter II. On the Effect of the Sacraments

We wished to assign a special place to this question, because of that difficult controversy which exists today in our churches with the Jesuit faction concerning Sacramental Grace.

For although it is sufficiently agreed upon in general, and the Jesuit Bellarmine himself does not deny, that the Sacraments confer grace upon those using them legitimately, and that especially in the Baptism of infants: and that they confirm and seal grace already conferred; and that principally in the Sacrament of the Eucharist, as also in the Baptism of adults, who have just received the firstfruits of the Spirit, and in the very conversion to the Christian faith, have obtained the Grace of God and the remission of sins: yet it is keenly disputed today, both how the Sacraments effect this, and in whom they effect it, and finally how this Sacramental grace ought to be defined? Now this whole dispute can, for the sake of method and memory, be most correctly expedited by a complex of four questions: the first of which asks, Whether the Sacraments effect Grace and Salvation? the second, what is Sacramental grace? the third, What is the mode of operation by which the Sacraments truly confer Grace? the fourth and last, Whether that Effect reaches all who participate in the Sacrament?

Latin:

PEculiarem Quæstioni huic locum assignare voluimus, propter difficilem illam controversiam, quæ de Gratiâ Sacramentali nostris hodiè Ecclesiis, cum gente Jesuiticâ intercedit.

Etsi enim de eo in genere satis constat, & Jesuvvita Bellarminus ipse non inficiatur, quòd Sacramenta legitimè iis utentibus conferant gratiam, idque præcipuè in Baptismo infantium: collatam etiam confirment & obsignent; idque principaliter in Sacramento Eucharistiæ, ut & in Baptismo adultorum, qui primitias Spiritûs modò acceperunt, & in conversione ipsâ ad fidem Christianam, Gratiam DEI & remissionem peccatorum sunt consecuti: acriter tamen disputatur hodiè, tùm quomodo Sacramenta hoc operentur, tùm in quibus operentur, tùm denique quomodo Sacramentalis hæc gratia definiri debeat? Potest autem universa hæc disputatio, methodi & memoriæ gratiâ, quatuor quæstionum complexu rectissimè expediri: quarum prima quærit, An Sacramenta Gratiam & Salutem operentur? altera, quid sit Sacramentalis gratia? tertia, Quis operationis modus, quo Sacramenta Gratiam verè conferant? quarta & postrema, An Effectus iste omnibus Sacramento participantibus obtingat?


### Chapter II. On the Effect of the Sacraments: I. Do the sacraments operate grace and salvation?

St. Augustine rightly advises in book 3 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 9: Just as it is a mark of servile weakness to follow only the letter and to take signs for the things which are signified by them, so it is a mark of a wandering error to interpret signs uselessly. Now, however, the question is what kind of grace or utility specifically emerges from the Sacraments. Following the footsteps of the Scriptures, we maintain that the Sacraments work salvation in their own way. For thus Paul says in Titus 3:5: GOD saved us through the washing of regeneration; and St. Peter, 1 Peter 3:21: Baptism saves us. The very words of the Eucharist also intimate this: This is my body, which is given for you for the remission of sins. This is my blood, which is poured out for you for the remission of sins. For since the remission of sins is obtained from the eating of the body and the drinking of the blood of Christ, it can be doubtful to no one that salvation is also obtained by them. Therefore, we establish the effect of the Sacraments to be the operation of salvation, both as regards the excitation and as regards the confirmation and sealing of faith, by which one believes unto righteousness and confession is made unto salvation. Nor do our Churches establish anything new in this part, but they hold and follow the unanimous consent of Orthodox Antiquity, which the Nicene Council, book 3 on Baptism, expressed in these words: We do not consider our Baptism with the eyes of the body, but with the eyes of the mind: Do you see water? Consider the power of GOD hidden in the waters. For the Gospel teaches us that we are baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire: Therefore, he who is to be baptized descends guilty of sins and subject to the servitude of corruption; and he ascends liberated from this servitude and sin, having been made a son of GOD and his heir by grace, and a co-heir of CHRIST, having put on CHRIST himself: as it is written: As many of you as have been baptized into CHRIST have put on CHRIST: Gal. 3:27.

Chrysostom, Homily 45 on John: Let us therefore arise from that table like lions breathing fire, terrible to the Devil: This mystical blood drives demons far away; it attracts to us the Angels and the Lord of Angels: demons, when they see the Lord's blood in us, are put to flight: but the Angels gather round. This blood poured out washes the whole world: it is the salvation of our souls.

Ambrose, on those who are initiated into the mysteries, chapter 8. This food which you receive, this living bread, which descended from heaven, provides the substance of eternal life, and whoever, being a man, shall have eaten this bread, shall not die forever.

Augustine, book 1 on the merits of sins, chapter 24. The Punic Christians very aptly call baptism itself nothing other than salvation; and the Sacrament of the body of CHRIST, nothing other than life. Whence they hold from ancient and Apostolic tradition, that besides Baptism and participation in the Lord's table, not only can no man attain to the kingdom of GOD, but not even to salvation and eternal life.

Hence the pious Sedulius sings in book 4 of his Paschal work: —— for after he established the two gifts of his own body and blood, and gave food and drink, by which faithful souls without stain may never hunger or thirst forever, etc. And concerning Baptism: Reborn in the font, we feed on the members and blood of CHRIST: and therefore we are held to be the temple of the DEITY.

Latin:

REctè monet D. Augustinus l. 3. de doct. Christ. cap. 9. Quemadmodum servilis est infirmitatis, literam tantùm sequi, & signa pro rebus, quæ his significantur, accipere: ita malè vagantis erroris est, signa inutiliter interpretari. Jam verò, quænám in specie Gratia sive utilitas ex Sacramentis emergat, quæritur. Nos Scripturarum secuti vestigia statuimus. Sacramenta suo modo operari salutem. Sic enim Paulus Tit. 3, 5. Salvos nos fecit DEUS per lavacrum regenerationis: Et D. Petrus, 1. cap. 3, 21. Baptismus salvat nos. Quod ipsum innuunt etiam verba Eucharistiæ, Hoc est, corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur in Remissionem peccatorum. Hic est sangvis meus, qui pro vobis effunditur, in Remissionem peccatorum. Quibus enim ex manducatione corporis, & bibitione sangvinis Christi obtingit Remissio peccatorum, quin illi etiam salus obtingat, nemini potest esse dubium. Effectum ergò Sacramentorum constituimus operationem salutis, tùm quoad excitationem, tùm quoad confirmationem & obsignationem fidei, quâ creditur ad justitiam, & fit confessio ad salutem. Neque novi quicquam hâc in parte nostræ statuunt Ecclesiæ, quin unaninem tenent ac sequuntur consensum Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, quem Concilium Nicænum, lib. 3. de Baptismo his verbis expressit: Baptisma nostrum non oculis corporis consideramus: sed oculis mentis: Aquam vides? considera virtutem DEI, in aquis absconditam. In Sancto enim Spiritu & igni baptizári nos docet Evangelium: Descendit itaquè qui baptizari debet reus peccatorum, & obnoxius servituti corruptionis: & ascendit liberatus ab hac servitute & peccato, factus filius DEI, & hæres ejus gratia, cohæres autem CHRISTI, indutus ipsum CHRISTUM: sicut scriptum est: Quicunquè in CHRISTUM baptizati estis, CHRISTUM induistis: Gal. 3, 27.

Chrysost. Homil. 45. in Johannem: Ab illâ igitur mensâ, tanquàm leones ignem spirantes surgamus Diabolo formidolosi: Hic mysticus sangvis dæmones procul pellit; Angelos & Angelorum dominum ad nos allicit: dæmones, cum in nobis Dominicum sangvinem vident, in fugam vertuntur: Angeli autem concurrunt. Hic sangvis effusus abluit universum terrarum orbem: hic nostrarum animarum salus est.

Ambrosius, de iis, qui initiantur mysteriis, cap. 8. Ista esca quam accipis, iste panis vivus, qui descendit de cælo, vitæ æternæ substantiam subministrat, & quicunq; hunc panem manducaverit homo, non morietur in æternum.

Augustinus lib. 1. de peccatorum meritis, cap. 24. Optimè Punici Christiani baptismum ipsum nihil aliud, quàm salutem; & Sacramentum corpus CHRISTI, nihil aliud, quàm vitam vocant. Undè ex antiquâ & Apostolicâ traditione tenent, præter Baptismum & participationem mensæ Dominicæ, non solùm non ad regnum DEI, sed nec ad salutem & vitam æternam posse quenquam hominum pervenire.

Hinc piè Sedulius lib. 4. Paschali canit: —— nam corporis atq; Sangvis ipse sui postquam duo munera sanxit Atquè cibum potumquè dedit, quo perpete nunquam Esuriant, sitiantquè animæ sine labe fideles &c. Et de Baptismo: Fonte renascentes, membris & sangvine CHRISTI Vescimur: atquè ideò templum DEITATIS habemur.


### Chapter II. On the Effect of the Sacraments: II. What sacramental grace is?

The Scholastic Doctors name the effect of the Sacraments that grace for the sake of which the Sacrament exists: as the Master of the Sentences holds. They understand this Sacramental grace, however, as the gratuitous gifts of GOD, or as gratuitous effects, not as the clemency and favor of GOD, in such a way that some inherent habit of gratuitous gifts accrues to us from the use of the Sacraments. Whence Thomas, part 3, question 62, article 1, says: Grace is nothing other than a certain participated likeness of the divine nature.

We, making a divorce from this dogma of the Scholastics, determine that by the name of Sacramental grace there ought to be understood, either generally, all that which a man receives when he undertakes a Sacrament: namely, a certain aggregate of many things: such as, First, the Grace of justification, which is called by the Scholastics grace making one pleasing: Then the grace of gifts and virtues, which cannot be absent where the grace of justification has a place: and it is named by the Scholastics, Grace freely given. This contains, however, Faith, Hope, Love, and not only the Cardinal virtues: but also any others, which are the fruits, gifts, and works of the indwelling Holy Spirit: finally, the grace of special divine aid, by which a man is peculiarly instructed to attain the end proper to each Sacrament. Or by Sacramental grace, specially and strictly in another way, is understood only this last grace of special divine aid. For through the Sacraments there is conferred upon the faithful not only a certain peculiar grace of divine assistance, which provides aid to those taking the Sacraments more effectively, more frequently, and more swiftly than to other faithful: but a peculiar gift is also bestowed, to attain the end proper to each Sacrament, much more effectively than from common grace alone, without the Sacrament. And indeed this grace is distinguished in species from the grace of other gifts, which is conferred otherwise without the Sacraments and outside of them. For as the Sacraments differ in species, so also do the effects they have differ in species: The reason for this is: because causes are distinguished by their effects. A man is therefore indeed justified and saved through the Sacraments: from which it is a consequence that all those things are also conferred through the Sacraments which are given in every justification: But besides these gifts, Sacramental grace adds something more: otherwise those who are already justified and instructed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit would receive the Sacraments in vain: as Sacramental grace in Baptism, besides the fact that it makes one pleasing and reconciled to GOD: opens in addition the door to the renewal of the Spirit and to regeneration, by which the inner man is peculiarly strengthened, and his will is animated to rightly receive another Sacrament as well. Thus in the Sacrament of the Eucharist, Sacramental grace generates a certain spiritual sweetness, by which the spiritual life in a man is refreshed and animated, which had contracted a certain languor in this part either through sloth, or through the guilt of sins, or through the assaults of temptations.

Latin:

DOctores Scholastici Sacramentorum effectum, nominant gratiam illam, cujus causa Sacramentum existit: uti habet Magister sent. Intelligunt autem gratiam hanc Sacramentalem de donis DEI gratuitis, sive de effectibus gratuitis, non de DEI clementiâ & favore, ita ut ex usu Sacramentorum nobis obtingat inhærens aliquis donorum gratuitorum habitus. Undè Thomas part. 3. quæst. 62. art. 1. Gratia, inquit, nihil est aliud, quam quædam participata similitudo divinæ naturæ.

Nos à dogmate hoc Scholasticorum divortium facientes statuimus, nomine Sacramentalis gratiæ intelligi debere vel generaliter totum illud, quod homo accipit, quando Sacramentum suscipit: nempè aggregatum quoddam ex multis: qualia sunt, Primùm, Gratia justificationis, quæ à Scholasticis vocatur gratia gratum faciens: Deindè gratia donorum & virtutum, quæ non potest abesse, ubi gratia justificationis locum habet: & nominatur à Scholasticis, Gratia gratis data. Continet autem hæc, Fidem, Spem, Dilectionem, & virtutes non Cardinales tantùm: sed alias etiam quasvis, quæ sunt fructus, dona & opera inhabitantis Spiritus Sancti: tandem gratia specialis auxilii divini, quo homo peculiariter instruitur ad finem Sacramenti cujusque proprium consequendum. Vel per gratiam Sacramentalem specialiter & strictè altero modo intelligitur tantùm postrema hæc gratia specialis auxilii divini. Nam per Sacramenta fidelibus non tantùm confertur gratia quædam peculiaris assistentiæ divinæ, quæ Sacramenta sumentibus, efficaciùs, frequentiùs & celeriùs auxilium præstat, quàm aliis fidelibus: sed donum etiam peculiare tribuitur, ad finem Sacramenti cujusque proprium, multò efficaciùs, quàm ex solâ gratiâ communi, sine Sacramento consequendum. Et sanè gratia hæc specie distingvitur à gratiâ donorum aliorum, quæ sine Sacramentis, & extra eadem aliàs confertur. Nam ut Sacramenta specie differentes, ita effectus & jam habent specie differentes: Ratio hæc est: quoniam causæ per effectus distingvuntur. Justificatur ergò quidem & salvatur homo per Sacramenta: ex quo consequens est, ea etiam omnia conferri per Sacramêta, quæ dantur in omni justificatione: Verùm præter hæc dona, Gratia Sacramentalis quiddam superaddit: alioquin frustrà acciperent Sacramenta, qui jam antè sunt justificati, & donis Spiritus Sancti instructi: ut Gratia Sacramentalis in Baptismo, præterquàm quod gratum & reconciliatum facit DEO: insuper renovationi Spiritus & regenerationi januam aperit, quâ peculiariter roboratur internus homo, & voluntas ejus animatur, ad rectè suscipiendum alterum etiam Sacramentum. Sic in Sacramento Eucharistiæ gratia Sacramentalis gignit spiritualem aliquam dulcedinem, quâ reficitur & animatur quasi vita spiritualis in homine, qui langvorem quendam hac parte vel per desidiam, vel per peccatorum reatus, vel per tentationum insultus contraxerat.


### Chapter II. On the Effect of the Sacraments: III. In what manner the sacraments operate grace?

THIS is the primary question which is agitated today concerning the effect of the Sacraments: and which has not been explained in one and the same way by Theologians, especially the Pontifical ones. There are some among the Scholastic Doctors who determine that the Sacraments, with respect to grace making one pleasing, are like a cause without which it is not: with respect to the character and adornment, which are grace freely given, they are like an efficient cause: with respect, however, to the weakening of the incentive or the strengthening of the faculties, they are a disposing cause for grace: and this through a power which is spiritual in the Sacrament, and bestowed upon it by GOD.

Others from the same crowd of Scholastics think a little more correctly that divine power attends the Sacraments, which is the cause of grace, and of faith and devotion sufficient, by which it disposes to grace: and therefore according to the common mode of speaking, the Sacraments are said to have 1. Power, and 2. to be a cause, and 3. to effect something on account of the assistance of divine power. that indeed the name of power is extended to some ordination, so that when something has an efficacious ordination to something, it is said to have power, so that the power of the Sacrament is an efficacious ordination. Thus also they extend the name of cause, because it sometimes signifies the reason for ordaining something. They illuminate these shadows with such a simile: Just as royal letters, sealed with the royal ring, are of great dignity, power and value, and are said to be able to do great things, yet in them there is no absolute power, but only an ordination to the assistance of royal power: so it is in the Sacraments. Whence the Causality of the Sacraments to them is nothing else than a certain efficacious ordination for receiving grace from a divine pact.

Augustine seems to have refuted this doctrine of the Scholastics long ago: The Sacraments, he says, are not to be joined to the merit of CHRIST, the grace of GOD, and the efficacy of the Spirit, as helping or partial causes: For this would be the crime of Idolatry, and a servitude of signs, or a servile infirmity: But the Sacraments are Instrumental Causes, or Organs, through which GOD wills to exhibit, bestow, and apply His Grace, that is, His Clemency and Mercy. Faith therefore should not seek any power or efficacy inherent in the external elements of the Sacraments themselves: but only in the promise, which is annexed to the Sacraments, should it seek, apprehend, and receive the Grace of the Father, the merit of the Son, and the efficacy of the Holy Spirit. Similarly, that the Sacraments are said to confirm faith; it is not to be established that there is a secret force in external things, by which they are able to promote or confirm faith by themselves: but because they were instituted by GOD to that end, that they might serve for establishing and increasing faith. Nor does Thomas seem to have abhorred this opinion of ours, part 3, question 62, article 1. There is, he says, a twofold Agent Cause, Principal and Instrumental. The Principal acts through the power of its form: and in this way nothing can cause grace, except GOD. The Instrumental, however, does not act through the power of its form: but only through the motion by which it is moved by the principal agent. And in this way the Sacraments of the new law cause grace: for they are applied by divine ordination to cause grace in them: as: The water of Baptism cleanses the body according to its own power: it cleanses the soul, insofar as it is an instrument of divine power. So far Thomas: following whose opinion in this place, we bid all and singular the opinions of the Scholastics to depart, by which the Sacraments are feigned to be either efficient causes of the Grace of GOD, but improperly: or causes without which not, and at whose presence alone GOD immediately confers grace, just as if someone should receive a thousand gold pieces upon the presentation of a promissory note which he received from a prince: or only moral causes of divine grace, as Ledesma trifles, part 1, q. 3, art. 1, indeed in that way by which money is the cause of the liberation of a captive.

Which opinion is the more intolerable for this reason, that a moral cause is not a cause in such a way that it produces an effect: but it only moves another, so that he may perform the effect, just as money moves a captor to release a captive. But GOD is not moved by the Sacraments themselves to confer His grace. For GOD is moved to this matter principally by His mere goodness and promise: Secondarily, however, He is moved by the repentance and faith of the recipient: which, however, like other dispositions, can in no way be called causes of grace. What? That the Sacraments are not instituted to move GOD to confer grace: but for this, that through these GOD might work by conferring grace.

Finally, the doctrine of the Jesuits, and in general of almost all Romanists, is clearly erroneous, by which they feign that the Sacraments confer grace from the work worked; that is, from the dignity and merit of the work of him who either celebrates the Sacrament or receives it. Concerning the stupendous impiety of which dogma, before we deal expressly against the Jesuits, it must be demonstrated: How are the Sacraments instruments according to our opinion? Or how do they contain Grace as instruments? Is this Grace bound to the Sacraments, and how?

But it has just now been shown that the Sacraments are truly and properly causes of grace, and have in themselves the power of effecting grace: But not except Instrumentally: indeed in such a way that that power is not something physically inherent in the Sacrament: or any permanent quality in the same: but it is the ordination itself, and that supernatural motion, which GOD uses in the Sacraments to produce this end and effect. But how this may be done can be declared by certain hypotheses.

I. Grace is not in the Sacraments according to the likeness of species: so that the Sacraments and Grace are of the same species, just as otherwise a natural effect is in a homogeneous and univocal cause: For example: Fire kindled in kindling fire: nor is it in them according to any inherent and permanent form: in which way generated things are in the Sun: but only according to an organic and non-permanent power: as will be demonstrated more fully a little later.

II. The Sacraments can be said to contain grace in two ways: 1. Just as the signified is contained or is in its Sign. For the Sacraments are Signs of grace. Nor should it seem absurd that an instrumental cause, if it is exposed to the senses, be said to be a Sign and a cause at the same time. 2. Just as a caused thing is said to be in its cause, which is said to that extent, insofar as the cause has the power of producing the effect.

III. Sacraments are and are called vessels of grace and causes, not indeed in a physical sense, by which vessels signify a containing place: for grace is not substantially contained in the sacraments, nor is it causally effected by them: but in the sense that they signify an organ of some thing, or an instrument for doing something. In which sense this word is used in Ezekiel 9:1, "Each one has a vessel of destruction in his hand." In which sense

Thomas also writes not ineptly, part 3, q. 62, art. 3: Grace is not said to be in a Sacrament as in a subject, nor as in a vessel, insofar as a vessel is a certain place: but insofar as a vessel is called an instrument for doing some work. And Hugo, lib. 1, de Sacr., part 9, cap. 2: The spiritual gifts of grace are certain invisible antidotes, which are offered to man in the sacraments, as if in certain visible vessels. Which words of Hugo, Bonaventura explains thus, lib. 4, dist. 1, quest. 3: Just as what is in a vessel is not of it, nor from it, but is drawn with it: so grace is not from the sacraments, nor of the sacraments: but it arises from the eternal fountain, and is drawn from that, by the soul itself in the sacraments.

IV. And the final hypothesis is: When grace is said to be conferred by GOD through the sacraments, it is not to be understood as if an accident identical in number migrates from subject to subject: but that it is in all of these simultaneously: yet in different ways: namely in GOD, as in the principal cause: in the Sacrament, as in the instrumental cause: in the soul of the faithful man, as in the subject.

Moreover, that the name and office of an instrumental cause truly and properly belong to the sacraments is evident from this twofold reason: 1. An instrument is properly called that by which someone works. But GOD works the salvation of men through the sacraments. Tit. 3, 5. Therefore. 2. If that which is accustomed to be done properly in instruments is in the sacraments: then an instrument will most correctly be predicated of the sacraments. But the former is true. For just as instruments do not act unless moved: so the sacraments also do not act, except insofar as they are moved by GOD as the principal cause. Therefore this latter is also true.

It is evident from what has already been said that the sacraments are and are called causes of Grace: but only instrumentally. In order that this instrumental action may be correctly defined, so that it does not err either with the Papists in excess, or with the Sacramentarians in defect, two things especially come under observation, and indeed more accurate observation. For first, one must properly distinguish between the twofold action which the sacraments have when they are said to effect Grace instrumentally. One is Natural, which, when the whole action of the instrument is considered, can be called proper to the Sacrament in that part where it touches the body: since it can effect this action from its own properties, that is, not from some special divine power. The other is Instrumental, with respect to divine power, which reaches even to the soul. The latter of these actions always presupposes the former. For example: The natural action of Baptism is to wash the body: the instrumental action is, with respect to divine power, to wash and cleanse the heart, that is, the whole exterior and unregenerate man: nor is the soul ordinarily washed by instrumental action unless the body is washed at the same time by natural action. Which is that very thing which Augustine skillfully expressed, tractate 80 on John: Such is the power of the water, that it touches the body and cleanses the heart.

Then one must also properly distinguish between the actions which GOD himself performs.
