For first, he acts immediately by himself without any creature: in which way he certainly has the power to do what he wills: Ps. 135, 6. For there is as much power of will in GOD as there is the will of power itself: because for him to whom it is always present, when he wills, to be able: to will in him is nothing other than to be able, as Fulgentius has it, ad Monimum, lib. 1, cap. 12. Then GOD acts through creatures and instruments. And in this way also GOD can do whatever he wills: because he is no less powerful when he uses creatures than when he does not use them. For God does not act through instruments as man does: but in far different respects: and indeed placed in a threefold difference especially with respect to human instrumental actions.

Latin:

EST hæc primaria quæstio, quæ de effectu Sacramentorum hodiè agitatur: quæque non uno eodemque modo à Theologis, præsertim Pontificiis explicata fuit. Sunt ex Doctoribus Scholasticis, qui statuant, quòd Sacramenta respectu gratiæ gratum facientis, sint sicut causa sine quâ non:respectu characteris & ornatus, quæ sunt gratia gratis data, sint sicut causa efficiens: respectu verò debilitationis fomitis sive roboris potentiarum sint causa disponens ad gratiam: & hæc per virtutem, quæ est in Sacramento spiritualem, & à DEO sibi collatam.

Alii ex eâdem Scholasticorum turbâ paulò rectiùs sentiunt, quod Sacramentis assistat divina virtus, quæ sit causa gratiæ, & fidem atq; devotionem sufficientis, qua disponat ad gratiam: ac proinde secundum communem loquendi modum, Sacramenta dicantur habere 1. Virtutem, & 2. esse causam, & 3. efficere aliquid propter assistentiam divinæ virtutis. Virtutem & causam hoc modo declarant: quod nimirùm nomen virtutis extendatur ad aliquam ordinationem, ut quando aliquid habet efficacem ordinationem ad aliquid, dicatur habere virtutem, ita ut virtus Sacramenti sit efficax ordinatio. Sic quoq; extendunt nomen causæ, quòd interdum significet rationem ordinandi aliquid. Has tenebras illustrant tali similitudine: Sicut literæ regiæ, annulo regio sigillatæ, magnæ sunt dignitatis, virtutis & valoris, & magnadicuntur posse & facere, tamen in eis nulla est virtus absoluta, sed sola ordinatio ad assistentiam virtutis regiæ: ita in Sacramentis. Undè Causalitas Sacramentorum ipsis nihil est aliud, quàm quædam efficax ordinatio, ad recipiendam gratiam ex pactione divina.

Hanc Scholasticorum doctrinam jam olim refutasse videtur Augustinus: Sacramenta, inquiens, non sunt adjungenda merito CHRISTI, gratiæ DEI, & efficaciæ Spiritus, tanquàm causæ adjuvantes sive partiales: Hoc enim esset crimen Idololatriæ, & servitus signorum, sive servilis infirmitas: Sed Sacramenta sunt Causæ Instrumentales, sive Organa, per quæ DEUS vult Gratiam suam, hoc est, Clementiam & Misericordiam exhibere, dona re & applicare. Fides proindè non quærat aliquam virtutem sive efficaciam inhærentem ipsis externis Sacramentorum elementis: sed tantùm in promissione, quæ annexa est Sacramentis, quærat, apprehendat & accipiat Gratiam Patris, meritum Filii & efficaciam Spiritus Sancti. Consimiliter quòd Sacramenta dicuntur confirmare fidem; non statuendum est, externis rebus arcanam vim inesse, quâ fidem per se promovere aut confirmare valeant: sed quia eum in finem à DEO sunt instituta, ut stabilienddæ augendæq; fidei serviant. Neq; ab hâc nostrâ sententiâ abhorruisse videtur Thomas, part. 3. quæst. 62. art. 1. Duplex, inquiens, est Causa Agens, Principalis & Instrumentalis. Principalis agit per virtutem suæ formæ: & hoc modo nihil potest causare gratiam, nisi DEUS. Instrumentalis verò non agit per virtutem suæ formæ: sed solū per motū, quo movetur à principali agente. Et hoc modo Sacramenta novæ legis gratiam causant: adhibentur enim ex divinâ ordinatione ad gratiam in eis causandā: ut: Aqua Baptismi abluit corpus secundum propriam virtutē: abluit animā, in quatenus est instrumentū virtutis divinæ. Hactenus Thomas: cujus sententiā hoc loco secuti, jubemq facessere singulas & universas opiniones Scholasticorū, quibq Sacramenta finguntur esse vel causæ efficientes Gratiæ DEI, sed impropriè: vel causæ sine quibus non, & ad quarum præsentia duntaxat, DEUS solus immediatè gratiā conferat, veluti, si quis ad oblationē Cheirographi, quod à principe accepit, mille aureos capiat: vel causæ tantùm morales gratiæ divinæ, uti Ledesma nugatur, part. 1. q. 3. art. 1. adeū nimirùm modum, quo pecunia est causa liberationis captivi.

Quæ sententia vel ideò intolerabilior est, quòd moralis causa, non est ita causa, ut producat effectum: sed tantùm movet alterum, ut effectum præstet, sicut captivatorem movet pecunia, ut captivum dimittat. Atqui Sacramentis ipsis non movetur DEUS, ut gratiam suam conferat. Principaliter enim movetur DEUS hanc ad rem, merâ suâ bonitate & promissione: Secundariò autem movetur pœnitentiâ & fide suscipientis: quæ tamen, ut & aliæ dispositiones nullo modo dici possunt causæ gratiæ. Quid? quod Sacramenta non sunt instituta, ut moveant DEUM ad conferendam gratiam: sed ad hoc, ut per ista DEUS gratiam conferendo operetur.

Tandem erronea planè est Jesuvvitarum, & in genere omnium fermè Romanensium doctrina, quâ fingunt, Sacramenta conferre gratiam ex opere operato; hoc est ex dignitate & merito operis ejus, qui vel celebrat Sacramentum, vel accipit. De cujus dogmatis stupenda impietate priusquàm contra Jesuvvitas ex professo agamus, illud demonstrandum fuerit: Quomodo ex nostrâ sententiâ Sacramenta sint instrumenta? vel quomodo ut instrumenta Gratiam contineant? num Gratia hæc Sacramentis, & quomodo sit alligata?

Cæterùm jam modò ostensum, Sacramenta esse verè ac propriè causas gratiæ, & in se habere virtutem efficiendi gratiam: Verùm non nisi Instrumentaliter: ita nimirùm, ut virtus illa non sit quiddam physicè inhærens Sacramento: aut qualitas aliqua permanens in eodem: sed sit ipsa ordinatio, & motus ille supernaturalis, quo DEUS ad finem istum & effectum producendū, in Sacramentis utitur. Quomodo autem hoc fiat, certis hypothesibus declarari potest.

I. Gratia non est in Sacramentis secundum similitudinem speciei: ita ut Sacramenta & Gratia sint ejusdem speciei, sicut aliàs effectus naturalis est in causâ ὁμογενεῖ & univocâ: Exempli gratiâ: Ignis accensus in igne accendente: neq; etiam in illis est secundum aliquam formam inhærentem & permanentem: quo modo res generatæ sunt in Sole: sed duntaxat secundum virtutem organicam & non permanentem: uti paulò pòst uberiùs demonstrabitur.

II. Sacramenta possunt dici continere gratiam dupliciter: 1. Sicut signatum continetur aut est in suo Signo. Sunt enim Sacramenta Signa gratiæ. Neq; absurdum videri debet, ut causa instrumentalis, si sit sensibus exposita, dicatur esse Signum simul & causa. 2. Sicut causatum dicitur esse in suâ causâ, quod eatenùs dicitur, quatenùs causa virtutem habet producendi effectum.

III. Sacramenta sunt & dicuntur vasa Gratiæ & causæ, non quidem sensu physico, quo vasa significant locum continentem: neq; enim in Sacramentis gratia substantialiter continetur, vel causaliter efficitur: Sed prout significant organum rei cujuspiam, aut instrumentum faciendi aliquid. Quo sensu habetur hoc vocabulum Ezech. 9, 1. Unusquisque vas interfectionis habet in manu suâ. Quam in sententiam

Thomas etiam haud ineptè scribit, part. 3. q. 62. art. 3. Gratia non dicitur esse in Sacramento sicut in subjecto, neq; sicut in Vase, prout Vas est locus quidam: Sed prout Vas dicitur instrumentum alicujus operis faciendi. Et Hugo lib. 1. de Sacr. part. 9. cap. 2. Dona gratiæ spiritualia sunt quædam antidota invisibilia, quæ in Sacramentis, visibilibus quasi quibusdam vasculis homini porriguntur. Quæ verba Hugonis sic explicat Bonaventura lib. 4. dist. 1. quæst. 3. Sicut quod est in Vase, non est de ipso, nec ex ipso, sed cum ipso hauritur: Sic gratia non est à Sacramentis, nec de Sacramentis: sed oritur à fonte æterno, & ab illo hauritur, ab ipsâ animâ in Sacramentis.

IV. Et postrema hypothesis est: Cùm gratia à DEO per Sacramenta conferri dicitur, non id ita est accipiendum, quasi accidens idem numero è subjecto migret in subjectum: sed quòd sit in omnibus istis simul: verùm diversimodè: nimirùm in DEO, ut in causâ principali: in Sacramento, ut in causâ instrumentali: in animâ hominis fidelis, ut in subjecto.

Cæterùm Sacramentis causæ instrumentalis nomen & officium verè ac propriè competere, duplici hac ratione constat: 1. Instrumentum propriè vocatur, per quod aliquis operatur. Atqui DEUS per Sacramenta operatur salutem hominū. Tit 3, 5. Ergò. 2. Si sit in Sacramentis, quod in Instrumentis propriè fieri consuevit: utiq; Instrumentum de Sacramentis rectissimè prædicabitur. Atqui priq illud verum. Quemadmodum enim instrumenta non nisi mota agunt: ita Sacramenta etiam non agunt, nisi quatenùs à DEO causâ principali moventur. Ergò verum & hoc posterius.

Constat ex jam dictis, Sacramenta esse & dici causas Gratiæ: sed tantum instrumentaliter. Quæ instrumentalis actio ut rectè definiatur, neque vel cum Pontificijs in excessu, vel cum Sacramentarijs indefectu peccet, duo potissimùm sub observationem, & quidem accuratiorem veniunt. Primùm enim probè distingvendum inter duplicem actionem, quam Sacramenta habent, quando Gratiam instrumentaliter efficere dicuntur. Una est Naturalis, quæ considerata totâ actione instrumenti, eâ parte, quâ corpus tangit, potest dici Sacramenti propria: siquidem ex proprijs, hoc est, non ex virtute quadam divinâ speciali, actionem hanc potest efficere. Altera Instrumentalis est, respectu divinæ virtutis, quæ ad animam etiam usq; pertingit. Harum actionum posterior, semper præsupponit priorem. Exempli gratiâ: Naturalis actio Baptismi est, abluere corpus: Instrumentalis est, respectu divinæ virtutis, abluere & mundare cor, hoc est, totum exteriorem & non renatum hominem: neq; abluitur ordinariè anima actione instrumentali, nisi abluatur simul corpus actione naturali. Quod illud ipsum est, quòd scitè expressit Augustinus, tractatu 80. in Johannem: Tanta virtus est aquæ, ut corpus tangat, & cor abluat.

Deindè probè etiam distingvendum inter actiones, quas DEUS ipse operatur. Nam primò immediatè agit per seipsum sine ullâ creaturâ: Quo certè modo potestas facere quæ vult: Psal. 135,7. Tanta enim est in DEO virtus voluntatis, quanta est voluntas ipsa virtutis: quia cui semper subest, cùm voluerit, posse: non aliud est in ipso velle, quàm posse, ut habet Fulgentius ad Monimum, lib. 1. cap. 12. Deinde per creaturas & instrumenta agit DEUS. Et hoc etiam modo potest DEUS facere, quicquid vult: quia non minus potens est, quando utitur creaturis, quam quando non utitur. Neq; enim Deus ita agit per instrumenta, sicut homo: sed longè alijs respectibus: & quidem in triplici potissimùm differentiâ respectu humanarum actionum instrumentalium positis.


### Chapter II. On the Effect of the Sacraments: III. In what manner the sacraments operate grace? (continued)

For first, when man uses an instrument, there is need of a twofold motion: one, by which he joins himself to the instrument: the other, by which he moves the instrument. The former motion is in the craftsman: the latter in the instrument. But now, when GOD uses an instrument, there is no need of the former motion: since the nature and power of GOD is most present to all things.

Then: Man cannot use an instrument unless it has by its nature some aptitude for such a work. The reason is because man is helped by instruments. GOD has no need of such an aptitude of instruments, since he is helped by nothing from them, nor does he need them. Whence it is that he sometimes uses most inept instruments: as when in John 9 CHRIST heals the eyes of the blind man with clay: and through the Apostles, fishermen and simple men, he converts the whole world. And this is the reason why the instruments of GOD can produce effects far more excellent than themselves, and to which they have absolutely no proportion. For these effects are neither in part, nor in whole, from the natural power of the instrument: but from the instrument through supernatural power, namely divine motion.

Thirdly and finally: Men cannot perform any work with any instrument whatsoever: but according to the variety of works, a variety of instruments is also required. The opposite happens in GOD.

With these differences observed, it can be understood without difficulty how the matter stands when GOD is said to confer grace through the instruments of the sacraments. For from the first difference it is clear that the motion which is attributed to GOD is not an application to the instrument: but is to be understood concerning the pleasure of his will, by which GOD willed to use the sacraments for conferring grace.

From the two final differences it is clear that one should not seek a quality, or a permanent power, or a disposition and aptitude in the sacraments before the use of the Sacrament: But that it is solely the ordination and pleasure of GOD from which the whole power depends which the sacraments have for conferring grace: nor is there any other power or form through which the sacraments act, except through this motion of GOD,

Hence it follows that, however much water may wash someone, nothing is nevertheless accomplished in Baptism unless GOD also washes within: And yet when the Minister celebrates the Baptismal action, this action is at once GOD's and the Minister's. As it is the Minister's, it is a visible sign, and sometimes a cause without which it would not be: As it is from GOD, it is truly effective of grace. Therefore the minister washes outwardly: GOD inwardly: and yet by the same action, by which the minister washes outwardly, GOD washes inwardly. Hence it is that it is taught in the Church that the action of the minister is to be accepted as the action of GOD. Concerning which matter Augustine treats at length, tract. 3 on John: and Ambrose Epist. 84 to Demetrias, in these words: It is one thing that is done invisibly: another that is celebrated visibly: nor is the form and the power the same in a Sacrament. For the form is applied with the service of human ministry: But the power is provided through the effect of the divine work, to whose power it is certainly to be referred that, while the exterior man is washed, the interior is cleansed. From this very foundation Augustine argues against the Donatists, book 4, chapter 12, that this action is always holy, because of Him whose it is, whether the minister be evil or upright.

Opposed to this purer doctrine are both those various opinions of the Scholastics, noted above: and indeed, and especially, that horrible dogma which the Jesuits still hold today, contending that the Sacraments confer grace ex opere operato. Where, at the beginning, it must be examined what they understand by opus operatum. Bellarmine explains this, Tom. 2, book 2, on the effect of the Sacraments, chapter 1, page 143 in my edition, in these words: That the Sacraments confer grace ex opere operato is the same as saying they confer grace by the force of the Sacramental action itself instituted by GOD for this purpose, not from the merit of the agent or the recipient. Bellarmine certainly thinks the same as the Scholastics also thought long ago: namely, that the Sacraments confer grace by the force of the Sacramental action itself: and therefore that grace is essentially bound to the Sacraments: and that the Sacraments confer salvation by the virtue of the action itself which strikes the eyes. For as Gabr. Biel in book 4, Sent. d. 1, q. 3, says that then there is an opus operatum in the Sacraments, when an interior movement is not required in the recipient. And Petrus de Palude, book 4, Sent. d. 1, q. 1: It is not required in the Sacraments that a man dispose himself: but the disposition is effected by the Sacrament itself, and this is to cause grace ex opere operato. To these Marsilius subscribes in 4, Sent. q. 2, art. 2, and Mensingerus in chapter 6 of John, who expressly distinguish opus operatum against the internal devotion of the one operating. Added to this is the determination of the Council of Trent, which in Sess. 7, Can. 8, brandishes the thunderbolt of anathema against those who say that grace is not conferred by the Sacraments of the new law themselves ex opere operato.

The Jesuits are ashamed today of so insipid and absurd a dogma, and therefore Bellarmine, in the place already cited, tries to excuse the Scholastics, as if they had thought nothing other than that the truth of the Sacraments does not depend on the dignity of the minister, or on the faith of the recipient, so that the Sacraments would be any less true, however much men might have labored under malice or perfidy. In which part, however, he both does manifest violence to the words and opinion of the Scholastics: and also, even unwittingly, falls into that very opinion which he seems to want to avoid. For if the Sacraments confer grace to those who use the Sacraments ex opere operato, that is, however much the very men who receive the Sacraments lack faith, how, I ask, shall we understand this very grace to be derived to them, unless you attribute the grace entirely to the external action itself, that is, to the opus operatum? For not to speak of Infants, whose case is different: So certainly, both in the Baptism of adults and in the Sacrament of the Supper, faith is required, so that he who approaches without faith not only acquires no grace, but suffers the greatest loss of grace and salvation. Whence the Apostle warns, Let a man examine himself (namely, whether he is in the faith:) and then let him eat of this bread, and drink of this cup, 1 Cor. 11:28 and 29. And the same Apostle, Rom. 4:11, calls the Sacraments Seals of the righteousness of faith. He therefore who is devoid of faith receives harm from the Sacraments, let alone obtaining grace and salvation. But the Romanists maintain the opposite, so that, provided you are not a murderer or an adulterer, or a thief, or desire to admit some crime conceived in your mind, then the Sacraments ex opere operato make you pious and full of manifold grace.

And indeed, if we wish to examine a little more accurately the mysteries of iniquity which are hidden under this Papal dogma, we shall notice that the entire abomination of the Papal religion consists in this opus operatum alone. Therefore it will not be irrelevant for us to examine more accurately the individual points of this whole dispute.

And at the beginning, indeed, it must be well noted by those who desire to stand successfully in the arena of debate against the Jesuits in this place, what primarily comes into question when one discourses about the opus operatum. However, the question here is not about the very power and efficacy of the Sacraments in themselves and absolutely, whether they confer grace to those who use them or not: nor is it even disputed from what principle that power depends, which, that it proceeds from nowhere else but from the author Christ himself, is established beyond controversy in the Church. But it is primarily disputed about the use of the Sacraments: By whom and by what kind of users do the Sacraments, by exerting their power, confer grace? Concerning which question it must immediately be observed that there are many and various things that concur when the pious and legitimate dispensation and use of a Sacrament must take place. For 1. the will itself and the ordinance of Christ, by which He willed to sanction the Sacrament, is attended to. 2. The predestination or eternal election of God, by which He chose the one rightly receiving the Sacraments to eternal life: 3. the action or the dispensation of the Sacrament itself: 4. the quality of the minister dispensing: 5. finally, faith and the previous disposition, with the devotion of pious movements in the recipient.

Here the question now arises, from which of these five members the virtue and efficacy of the Sacrament depends, so that it may confer grace upon those who use it? The Orthodox, proceeding in the most direct order from ἄγω to θέσιν, thus maintain: 1. that for grace to be conferred upon one using a Sacrament, this does not proceed from the simple and absolute will and ordination of Christ who instituted the Sacrament: for otherwise the Sacraments would confer grace upon everyone, since the Savior intended them to be common to all: 2. nor from the grace of election: for in this way no one of the elect would ever receive a Sacrament without fruit: and no one not elect would ever participate in a Sacrament usefully: that both of which are false, experience itself sufficiently proves: 3. nor from the action or dispensation of the Sacrament itself simply and in itself: For by this reasoning again, it would confer grace upon everyone using the Sacrament: 4. nor from the quality of the minister dispensing it: For that was the specific error of the Donatists: It remains therefore at last, that for the Sacraments to confer grace, it depends solely upon the faith of the recipient: which in the use of the Sacraments, as being extremely necessary, is required, is manifest from the very form of the institution of the Sacraments: since they must be performed on the part of the recipients with a commemoration or proclamation of the Lord's death, likewise with a clear examination of whether or not one is about to use the Sacrament in faith? Of this faith the Papists teach nothing; nay, they oppose doubt to it, and plainly invert everything: They pretend that the incredulous, through the external use of the Sacraments, receive and have grace without faith. But in believers, they command them to doubt, in the use of the Sacraments, whether they receive and have grace. Some even among the Scholastics notice the futility of this dogma of theirs, who write that the efficacy of the Sacraments has its impediments: and therefore that they indeed always have the sanctification of truth, but not always the efficacy of healing, not because of a defect on their own part: but on the part of the recipient, who does not place an obstacle, that is, as they themselves interpret it, who does not have mortal sin: As if, indeed, to be without faith were not a mortal sin? It is truly a great obstacle, not to believe the divine promise. Incredulity is the wood from which all obstacles are manufactured: since incredulity is the fountain and origin of all mortal sins. And this is the one thing that comes under observation regarding the Papist dogma of opus operatum.

The other thing is that it should be carefully attended to how the Papist Doctors attempt to cloak this dogma of theirs. They assert, therefore, that it happens in two ways that some action has its force: One, when it receives its efficacy from the one who operates: in which way the good works of a justified man are valid for the increase of grace and eternal life; which kind of works are said to be valid from the work of the worker (ex opere operantis), inasmuch as they have value and efficacy from the worker himself; The other way, when an action or work does not have its virtue from the worker: but from itself, namely when that action always has its force, by whomever it is exercised: such an action is the application of fire to burn a house, which has its force from the work worked (ex opere operato): likewise the exhibition of medicine. For thus, whether the Physician be a good man or a bad one, the medicine exhibited works health. In this latter way they contend that the Sacraments have the power of conferring grace ex opere operato, although this power is not naturally inherent in the Sacraments, as it is in the examples already given, yet it is inherent by virtue of divine institution.

Since this dogma is too absurd and atrocious to be defended, the more recent ones therefore seek various hiding places to cloak it. And 1. indeed they do not deny the literal statement of that dogma, as is sufficiently evident from Bellarmine. For it would be too crude, nay, they would bring darkness to the Sun, as it is said, if they dared to deny this. 2. They flee therefore to an ignorance of the saying, and by a new invention of interpretation they attempt to save its impiety, saying that the words of the Catholics are less skillfully understood by our people, by which it is not noted as if the Sacraments are valid from the work worked of the person receiving: but from the work worked of the person instituting the Sacraments, and conferring grace through them, namely CHRIST, so that the sense of that dogma here is that the Sacraments have their efficacy, not from the dignity of either the administrator or the recipient: but from the will and virtue of CHRIST who instituted them. But it has just now been shown above that this interpretation diametrically opposes the opinion of the Scholastics: nay, even the opinion of those Doctors who, not yet a hundred years ago, opposed the Evangelical Reformation with great effort. For this was, among other things, almost the primary head, on the occasion of which the Evangelical Church departed from the Roman Babylon, because the Papacy did not want the impiety of this dogma of theirs to be condemned in itself: which if it had then testified was alien to itself, certainly neither to Blessed Luther, nor to any Orthodox person would there have been any cause for which he would have moved any controversy about this dogma against the Papacy: since regarding the phrase itself or the manner of speaking, none of us would ever have contended more odiously. But as I said, the doctrine of the ancient Papists plainly opposes the more recent ones. For they established the distinction between the old and the new law in this, that the former indeed justified by reason of the work of the worker, not the work worked: but the latter justify by reason of the work worked. And they called the work of the worker the faith of the user: but they named the work worked the external Sacrament, that is, the naked action of the recipient, as is to be seen in Bonaventure, in 4. Sent. dist. 1. q. 3. & 5. Furthermore, the ancient Romanists explained their mind in such a way as to say that grace is conferred through the Sacraments ex opere operato, in such a way that by the very fact that that work, or Sacrament, is exhibited, grace is conferred, so that besides the exhibition of the sign exhibited outwardly, no good motion is required in the recipient: but it suffices if he does not place an obstacle, as the manifest words of Biel have it, already cited above from l. 4. Sent. dist. 1. q. 3.

As for the more recent Papists, the Council of Trent, in the cited canon 8 of Session 7, certainly expressly excludes faith and every good movement of the recipient by means of the opus operatum: and it simply approves that phrase of opus operatum, with no explanation added, and least of all with the addition of the commentary of Jesuit interpretation. Therefore, it either simply approved the impiety of the ancient dogma, or, having tacitly acknowledged it in a better sense, it insidiously reserved for itself, under an obscure phrase, a return to the impiety of the original dogma.

If they are sufficiently conscious of neither of these, let them either cast away the impious phrase entirely, or, having retained it, at least correct their understanding: and when they repeatedly assert that grace is conferred by the Sacraments ex opere operato, and that too with faith and the disposition of the one receiving or using them excluded: let them confess that nothing else is understood than that the Sacrament does not have its efficacy from the faith and dignity of the user, as if that depended upon this as its primary and first cause: but rather from the Will and Ordination of the author, namely CHRIST, who instituted the Sacraments themselves: Thus at length this controversy will find its end.

Finally, as if in the place of a finishing touch, from those things which we have disputed concerning the effect of the Sacraments, it is permitted to gather what and how stupendous is the vanity and futility of that dogma by which they contend that the power of certain Sacraments is to imprint a Character. Concerning which matter Canon 9, Session 7 of the Council of Trent holds thus: If anyone shall say that in three Sacraments, namely Baptism, Confirmation, and Order, a Character is not imprinted in the soul, that is, a certain spiritual and indelible sign, whence they cannot be repeated, let him be anathema. They wish, indeed, and decree that it be believed under peril of salvation, that which is not in the nature of things. For the Scholastics themselves doubted: Is there any such Character, and what is it, and where is it? Alexander, Thomas, and Bonaventure hold that the Character is an absolute thing and a quality. Scotus and others establish that it is a real relation. Thus they never agree among themselves concerning the Subject of the Character: whether it should be placed in the essence of the soul, or indeed in a power: Likewise, whether in a knowing power, or indeed in a willing power. Then they define this Character thus: A Character is a spiritual sign, imprinted on the soul by GOD alone in the reception of an unrepeatable Sacrament, remaining indelibly by common law, that is, according to the ordained power of GOD. Hence Gabriel Biel produced wonderful and marvelous emblems concerning this Character: I. That a Character is to be posited in the way it is defined, neither reason nor essence demonstrates, nor does evident authority prove. And others say that the necessity of positing a Character is for the sake of the authority of the Church alone: because one must think about the Sacraments of the Church as the Roman Church thinks. II. A Sacramental Character is not a relation of reason or a real one, but an absolute form of the genus of quality. III. There are only three Sacraments unrepeatable regarding the same person: Baptism, Confirmation, and Order, because only through these three Sacraments is a man placed into a certain state: through Baptism, into the state of the faithful: through Confirmation, into the state of those warring: through Order, into the state of those ministering in the temple of the Lord. IV. It is from divine institution alone, not from the impression of a Character, that those three Sacraments cannot be repeated, and that the Character is not deleted after impression.

But this whole fiction can borrow no support at all from universal Scripture, or from orthodox antiquity, or even from reason. For it is not yet proven that this Character is in the nature of things: How then can they define it, what it is, whether it is an absolute or relative thing... Be silent: therefore, this delirium with the brute thunderbolt of the Council of Trent.

Latin:

Nam primò quando homo utitur Instrumento, duplici motione opus est: Unâ, quâ se conjungit instrumento: Alterâ, quâ movet Instrumentum. Prior motio est in artifice: posterior in Instrumento. Jam verò cùm DEUS Instrumento utitur, priore motione non est opus: siquidem natura & potentia DEI rebus omnibus est præsentissima.

Deinde: Homo non potest Instrumento, uti, nisi illud natura sua habeat aptitudinem aliquam ad tale opus. Ratio est, quia homo ab instrumentis juvatur. Tali aptitudine instrumentorum DEO non est opus, quippè qui ab istis nihil juvatur, neq; indiget istis. Undè est, ut ineptissimis instrumentis interdum utatur: ut quando Johan. 9. CHRISTUS luto curat oculos cæci: & per Apostolos piscatores & homines simplices, totum convertit mundum. Et hæc est causa, cur Instrumenta DEI possint facere effectus, seipsis longè præstantiores, & ad quos planè nullam habent proportionem. Nam hi effectus neq; ex parte, neq; ex toto sunt à virtute naturali instrumenti: sed ab instrumento per virtutem supernaturalem nempè motionem divinam.

Tertiò & postremò: Homines non possunt quodvis opus quocunq; instrumento perficere: sed pro operum varietate, etiam instrumentorum varietas requiritur. Contrarium fit in DEO.

His differentijs observatis, haud difficulter intelligi potest, quonam modo se res habeat, cùm per instrumenta Sacramentorum DEUS conferre gratiam dicitur. Nam ex primâ differentiâ patet, motionem quæ DEO tribuitur, non esse applicationem ad instrumentum: sed intelligendam esse de placito voluntatis, quâ DEUS Sacramentis ad conferendam gratiam uti voluit.

Ex duabus postremis differentijs patet, in Sacramentis non esse quærendam qualitatem, aut virtutem permanentem, vel dispositionem & aptitudinem in Sacramentis ante usum Sacramenti: Sed Solâ ordinationem & placitum DEI esse, ex quo virtus tota dependeat, quam habent Sacramenta ad conferendam gratiam: neq; aliam esse virtutem aut formam, per quam agant Sacramenta, nisi per hanc motionem DEI,

Hinc illud consequens est, quantumvis aqua aliquis abluat, nihil tamen fieri in Baptismo, nisi & DEUS intus abluat: Et tamen quando Minister actionem Baptisticam celebrat, actio haec eâdem tùm DEI est, tùm Ministri. Prout Ministri est, signum est visibile, & aliquando causa sine quâ non: Prout est à DEO verè est effectiva gratiae. Lavat ergò minister exteriùs: DEUS interiùs: & tamen eâdem actione, quâ minister lavat foris, DEUS intùs abluit. Hinc est, quod in Ecclesiâ docetur, Actionem ministri esse accipiendam tanquàm Actionem DEI. Quâ de re fusè agit Augustinus, tract. 3. in Johannem: & Ambrof. Epist. 84. ad Demetriadem, his verbis: Aliud est, quòd invisibiliter agitur: aliud quòd visibiliter celebratur: nec est idem in Sacramento forma & virtus. Nam forma cum humani ministerij adhibetur obsequio: Virtus autem praestatur per divini operis effectum, ad cujus utiq; potentiam referendum est, quòd dùm homo abluitur exterior, mundatur interior. Ex hoc ipso fundamento Augustinus contra Donatistas lib. 4. cap. 12. disputat, Semper sanctam esse actionem istam, propter illum cujus est, sive malus sit minister, sive probus.

Puriori huic doctrinae adversantur tùm variae illae Scholasticorum sententiae, suprà notatae: tùm verò & imprimis horrendũ illud dogma, quod hodièquè tenent Jesuvvitae, contendentes, Sacramenta conferre gratiam ex opere operato. Ubi initiò quid per opus operatum intelligant, dispiciendum est. Id verò explicat Bellarminus, Tom. 2. lib. 2. de effectu Sacram. cap. 1. pag. mihi 143. his verbis: Sacramenta conferre gratiam ex opere operato, idem est, quod conferre gratiam ex virpsius actionis Sacramentalis à DEO ad hoc institutae, non ex merito agentis vel suscipientis. Idem nimirùm sentit Bellarminus, quod jam olim senserunt etiam Scholastici: nempè, Sacramenta conferre gratiam ex vi ipsius actionis Sacramentalis: ac proindè Gratiam Sacramentis essentialiter esse alligatam: & Sacramenta virtute ipsius actionis in oculos incurrentis, conferre salutem. Nam ut scribit Gabr. Biel in l. 4. Sent. d. 1. q. 3. tunc est opus operatum in Sacramentis, cùm non requiritur motus interior in suscipiente. Et Petrus de palude, lib. 4. Sent. d. 1. q. 1. Non requiritur in Sacramentis, ut homo se disponat: sed dispositio efficitur ab ipso Sacramento, & hoc est causare gratiam ex opere operato. Quibus subscribit Marsilius in 4. Sent. q. 2. art. 2. & Mensingerus in cap. 6. Johannis, qui disertè distingvunt opus operatum contra devotionem internam operantis. Accedit Concilij Tridentini determinatio, quod Sess. 7. Can. 8. anathematis fulmen vibrat in eos, qui dixerint, per ipsa novae legis Sacramenta non conferri gratiam ex opere operato.

Pudet hodiè Jesuvvitas tàm insulsi & absurdi dogmatis, ac proindè Bellarminus loco jam citato conatur Scholasticos excusare, quasi nihil aliud senserint, quàm Sacramentorum veritatem nõ pendere ex dignitate ministri, aut ex fide suscipientis, quò minùs Sacramenta vera sint, utcunq; homines vel malitiâ vel perfidiâ laborarint. Quâ tamen in parte tùm vim manifestam infert verbis & sententiae Scholasticorum : tùm vel inscius in eam ipsam opinionem incidit, quam declinare velle videtur. Etenim si Sacramenta conferunt Gratiam ijs, qui Sacramentis utuntur ex opere operato, hoc est, quantumvis ipsi homines, qui Sacramenta percipiunt, fide careant, quomodo quæso hanc ipsam gratiam ad illos derivari intelligemus, nisi gratiam ipsi actioni externæ, hoc est, operi operato in solidum acceptum referas? Nam ut de Infantibus non loquar, quorum dispar est ratio: Sic certè tùm in Baptismo adultorum, tùm in Sacramento Cœnæ fides requiritur, ut qui sine fide accesserit, non modò nullam gratiam acquirat, sed maximam gratiæ ac salutis jacturam faciat. Undè Apostolus monet, Probet seipsum homo (nempè utrum in fide sit:) & tunc edat de pane hoc, & bibat de calice hoc 1. Cor. 11, 28. & 29. Et idem Apostolus Rom. 4, 11. Sacramenta vocat Sigilla justitiæ fidei. Qui ergò fidei expers est, damnum accipit ex Sacramentis, nedum gratiam & salutem impetrat. Sed diversum planè statuunt Romanenses, ita ut, si modò non sis homicida aut adulter, aut latro, aut flagitium aliquod animo conceptum admittere cupias, tùm Sacramenta ex opere operato, te pium & gratiâ multiplice plenum efficiant.

Et profectò si paulò accuratiùs iniquitatis mysteria, quæ sub hoc dogmate Pontificio occultantur, rimari volumus, universam religionis Pontificiæ abominationem, in solo hoc opere operato consistere animadvertemus. Proindè haud abs re fuerit, ut totius hujus disputationis momenta singula accuratiùs excutiamus.

Ac initiò quidem ijs, qui in arenâ disputatoriâ contra Jesuvvitas hoc loco feliciter stare cupiunt, notandum probè fuerit, quid potissimùm in quæstionem veniat, quando de opere operato disseritur. Non est autem hic quæstio de ipsâ virtute & efficaciâ Sacramentorum perse, & absolutè, conferantné illa gratiam utentibus nec ne? neq́; illud etiam controvertitur, è quo principio virtus ista dependeat, quam non aliundè, nisi ab autore ipso Christo provenire, extra controversiam in Ecclesiâ est positum. Sed de usu Sacramentorum potissimùm controvertitur: Quibusnám & quomodo utentibus, Sacramenta vim suam exerendo, gratiam conferant? Circa quam quæstionem statim observandum, benè multa & varia esse, quæ concurrunt, quando fieri debet pia & legitima Sacramenti tùm dispensatio, tùm usurpatio. Nam 1. voluntas ipsa atq́; ordinatio Christi, quâ Sacramentum sancire voluit, attenditur. 2. Prædestinatio sive electio Dei æterna, quâ ritè suscipientem Sacramenta, ad vitam æternam elegit: 3. actio sive dispensatio ipsa Sacramenti: 4. Ministri dispensantis qualitas: 5. fides denique ac dispositio prævia, cum devotione piorum motuum in suscipiente.

Hîc jam quæritur, ex quo inter isthæc quinq́, membra, dependeat virtus & efficacia Sacramenti, ut gratiam utentibus conferat? Orthodoxi per ἄγω ad θέσιν rectissimo ordine progredientes sic Fff 2 statuunt: 1. ut utenti Sacramento conferatur gratia, hoc non proficisci â simplici & absolutâ voluntate & ordinatione Christi instituentis Sacramentum: aliàs enim nemini non Sacramenta conferrent gratiam, quippè quæ Servator communia voluit esse omnibus: 2. nec à gratiâ electionis: hoc enim modo nemo electorum unquàm sine fructu Sacramentum perciperet: & nemo non electus Sacramento utiliter unquàm participaret: quod utrumq́; falsum esse, experientia ipsa satis comprobat: 3. nec ab ipsâ Sacramenti actione sive dispensatione simpliciter & per se: Hâc enim rursus ratione nemini non Sacramento utenti, illud conferret gratiam: 4. nec à qualitate ministri dispensantis: Donatistarum enim iste proprius error fuit: Relinquitur ergò tandem, ut Sacramenta conferant gratiâ, id unicè pendere à fide suscipientis: quam in usu Sacramentorum, tanquàm extremè necessariam requiri, ex formâ ipsâ institutionis Sacramentorum manifestè constat: quippè quæ ex parte suscipientium, peragi debent, cum commemoratione sive annunciatione mortis Dominicæ, item cum luculentâ probatione, an usurus Sacramento in fide sit, nec ne? De hâc fide Pontificij nihil docent, imò opponunt ei dubitationem, & planè invertunt omnia: Incredulos fingunt, per externum Sacramentorum usum accipere & habere gratiam sine fide. In credentibq verò ipsam fidem, in usu Sacramentorum jubent dubitare, an accipiat & habeat gratiam. Animadvertunt dogmatis hujꝰ sui futilitatem nonnulli etiam ex Scholasticis, qui scriptitant, Sacramentorum efficaciam habere sua impedimenta: ac proindè ea semper quidem habere sanctificationem veritatis, non verò semper efficaciam curationis, nõ propter defectum ex parte sui: sed ex parte suscipientis, non ponentis obicem, hoc est, ut ipsimet interpretantur, non habentis peccatum mortale: Quasi verò sine fide esse, non sit peccatum mortale? Magnus profectò obex est, non credere promissioni divinæ. Incredulitas lignum est, ex quo omnes obices fabricantur: siquidem incredulitas fons est & origo omnium peccatorum mortalium. Et hoc unum est, quod circa dogma Pontificium de opere operato sub observationem venit.

Alterum est illud, ut quomodo Doctores Pontificij dogma hoc suum palliare conentur, probè attendatur Asserunt ergò duobus modis fieri, ut actio aliqua vim suam habeat: Uno, quando suam efficaciam accipit ab eo, qui operatur: quo modo valeant opera bona hominis justificati ad augmentum gratiæ & vitam æternam; cujusmodi opera valere dicuntur, ex opere operantis, utpote quæ ab ipso operante valorem & efficaciam habeant; Altero modo, quando actio vel opus virtutem suam non habet ab operante: sed ex se, nempè quando actio illa semper vim suam habet, à quocunque exerceatur: cujusmodi actio est applicatio ignis ad comburendam domum, quæ ex opere operato vim suam habet: item exhibitio medicamenti. Sic enim Medicus sit vir bonus, sive malus, medicamentum exhibitum sanitatem operatur. Hoc posteriore modo Sacramenta ex opere operato vim conferendi gratiam habere contendunt, quævis licèt non naturaliter in sit Sacramentis, quemadmodum est in exemplis jam datis, insit tamen ex virtute & institutione divina.

Hoc dogma cùm absurdius & atrocius sit, quàm ut defendi queat, ideò recentiores ad illud palliandum, varia quærunt κρησφύγετα. Ac 1. quidem τὸ ῥητὸν istius dogmatis non negant, uti ex Bellarmino satis constat. Nam nimis crassum foret, imò Soli, quòd dicitur, tenebras inferrent, hoc si negare auderent. 2. confugiunt ergò ad ἄγνοιαν dicti, & novo interpretationis commento impietatem ejs salvare conantur, dicentes, verba Catholicorū minùs dextrè à nostris intelligi, quibus non hoc notetur, quasi Sacramenta valeant ex opere operato personæ suscipientis: sed ex opere operato personæ instituentis Sacramenta, & gratiam per eadem conferentis CHRISTI nimirum, ut sensus dogmatis istius hic sit, Sacramenta habere suam efficaciam, non ex dignitate vel administrantis, vel suscipientis: sed ex voluntate & virtute CHRISTI eadem instituentis. Verùm jam modò suprà ostensum, interpretationem hanc cum sententia Scholasticorum è diametro pugnare: imò cùm eorum etiam Doctorum opinione, qui ante annos nondum centum Reformationi Evangelicæ magno conatu se opposuerunt. Fuit enim hoc inter alia fermè primarium caput, cujus occafione à Romana Babylone Ecclesia Evangelica discessum fecit, quod Papatus dogmatis hujus sui impietatem in se damnari noluit: quam si à se alienam esse tùm testatum fuisset, certè neq; B. Luthero, neq; ulli Orthodoxo causa ulla fuisset, ob quam de hoc dogmate controversiam aliquam Papatui movisset: siquidem de phrasi ipsâ sive modo loquendi nemo nostrûm unquam odiosiùs dimicasset. Sed uti dixi priscorum Pontificiorum doctrina planè recentioribus adversatur. Illi enim discrimen veteris & novæ legis in eo constituebant, quòd illa quidem justificarent ratione operis operantis, non operati: hæc autem justificent ratione operis operati. Opus autem operans appellarunt illi fidem utentis: Opus verò operatum nominârunt exterius Sacramentum, hoc est, nudam actionem suscipientis, uti est videre apud Bonaventuram, in 4. Sent. dist. 1. q. 3. & 5. Præterea veteres Romanenses mentem suam ita explicarunt, ut dicerent, per Sacramenta gratiam conferri ex opere operato, ita, quod eo ipso, quod opus illud, seu Sacramentum exhibetur, gratia conferatur, sic quòd præter exhibitionem signi foris exhibiti, non requiratur bonus motus in suscipiente: sed sufficere si non ponat obicem, ut habent manifesta verba Bielis, jam suprà citata ex l. 4. Sent. dist. 1. q. 3.

Quoad recentiores Pontificios, certè Concilium Tridentinum citato can. 8. Sessionis 7. per opus operatum disertè excludit fidem, & omnem bonum motum suscipientis: & simpliciter phrasin istam operis operati approbat, nullâ additâ explicatione, minimè omnium adjecto commento interpretationis Jesuiticæ. Aut ergò impietatem prisci dogmatis simpliciter approbavit: aut sensu meliore tacitè agnito, sub obscurâ phrasi regressum ad pristini dogmatis impietatem sibi insidiosè reservavit.

Quorum neutrius si satis sibi conscij sunt, aut impiam phrasin prorsus abjiciant, aut retentâ illâ mentem saltem corrigant: & cùm Sacramêtis ex opere operato gratiam conferri dictitant, idq́; exclusis fide & dispositione suscipientis sive utentis: nihil aliud intelligi fateantur, quàm quòd Sacramentum efficaciam suam non habeat ex fide & dignitate utentis, quasi illa ex hâc tanquàm præcipuâ & primâ causâ dependeat: sed potiùs à Voluntate & Ordinatione autoris, CHRISTI nimirùm, Sacramenta ipsa instituentis: Sic tandem controversia isthæc finem sortietur.

Tandem coronidis quasi vice, ex his quæ de effectu Sacramentorum disputavimus, colligere licet, quæ & quàm stupenda sit vanitas ac futilitas illius dogmatis, quo contendunt, Sacramentorum quorundam vim esse, ut imprimant Characterem. Quâ de re sic habet Can. 9. Sess. 7. Concilij Tridentini: Si quis dixerit, in tribus Sacramentis, Baptismo scilicet, Confirmatione & Ordine, non imprimi Characterem in animâ, hoc est, signũ quoddam spirituale & indelebile, undè ea iterari nõ possunt, anathema sit. Volunt nimirùm & decernunt, ut sub salutis periculo credatur id, quod non est in rerum naturâ. Nam Scholastici ipsi dubitarunt, An sit talis aliquis Character, & quid sit, & ubi sit? Alexander, Thomas, Bonaventura volunt, quòd Character sit res absoluta, & qualitas. Scotus & alij statuunt esse relationem realẽ. Sic de Subjecto Characteris nuspiam ipsis convenit: an ponendus sit in essentiâ animæ, an verò in potentiâ: Item, an in potentiâ cognoscente, an verò in potentiâ volente. Tùm Characterem hunc sic definiunt: Character est signum spirituale, à solo DEO animæ impressum in susceptione Sacramenti initerabilis, manens indelebiliter de lege communi, hoc est, secundum ordinatam DEI potentiam. Hinc Gabriel Biel de Charactere hoc mira ac miranda prodidit emblemata: I. Characterem esse ponendum eo modo, quo definitus est, nec ratio, nec essentia demonstrat, nec evidens autoritas probat. Et alij dicunt, necessitatem ponendi Characterem esse propter solam Ecclesiæ autoritatem: quia sentiendum sit de Sacramentis Ecclesiæ, sicut Romana sentit Ecclesia. II. Character Sacramentalis non est relatio rationis vel realis, sed forma absoluta de genere qualitatis. III. Tantùm tria sunt Sacramenta, circa eandem personam irreiterabilia, Baptismus, Confirmatio & Ordo, propterea quòd tantùm per hæc tria Sacramenta homo ad certum statum ponatur: per Baptismum, in statu fidelium: per Confirmationem, in statum bellantiũ: per Ordinem, in statum ministrantium in templo Domini. IV. Ex solâ institutione divinâ est, non ex impressione Characteris, quòd tria illa Sacramenta iterari non possunt, & quòd Character post impressionem non deleatur.

Cæterùm totum hoc commentum, nihil quicquam præsidij vel ex universâ Scripturâ vel ex orthodoxâ antiquitate, vel ex ratione etiam mutuari potest. Nondum enim probatum, Characterem istum esse in rerum naturâ: Quomodo ergò definire illum queant, quid sit, ut nùm sit res absoluta an relativa... Fa-te: ergò hoc delirium cùm bruto Concilij Tridentini fulmine.


### Chapter II. On the Effect of the Sacraments: Whether the effect of the Sacraments obtains for all participants?

That effect of the Sacraments, indeed, about which we have disputed until now, is common to all the Sacraments of both the Old and the New Testament: Since those are no less than these σφραγίδες δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίςεως [seals of the righteousness of faith] Rom. 4, 11: yet it is not for that reason also common to all using the Sacrament: But it happens only to those who use the Sacraments with faith: so much so that he who is destitute of this, is so far from obtaining this effect, that it rather turns into judgment for him. Whence it is that the Apostle, in a man about to participate in the Sacraments, requires not only use, but especially dignity and self-probation: 1 Cor. 11, 28. 2 Cor. 13, 5.

Then the Sacraments are added to the promise of the Gospel as seals. By what means or organ, therefore, the promise itself is apprehended, namely by faith alone: it is a necessary consequence that the same use or salutary effect of the Sacraments is also apprehended. Whence that saying of Augustine: Not the Sacrament, but the faith of the Sacrament justifies: not because it is done, but because it is believed. Tract. 80 in John. Concerning which matter see also B. Luther against the obelisks of Eck, Tom. 1. lat. Jen. p. 26 & 33. But this is not the sense of the things just said, which the Calvinists are accustomed to hide in this place, as if faith must necessarily precede the use of any Sacrament, so indeed that the infants of faithful parents bring faith with them from the mother's womb, and are in the grace of GOD even before the use of Baptism. Which opinion will be expressly refuted in the following next Article. But the Orthodox wish and establish this, that faith is indeed necessarily required for the salutary use of any Sacrament: but not that faith must precede every use of a Sacrament in time. For example: In order for the Sacrament of Baptism to exert its salutary use or effect in a baptized infant, it is necessary that faith be present, without which regeneration and adoption can happen to no one: John 1, 12. This faith, however, does not precede in time, nor do infants bring it to the Sacrament: but by the operation of the Holy Spirit, through baptism, it is conferred upon infants in, with, and through the very sprinkling of water, in the act itself: Whence it happens that they thus obtain the salutary effect. It is to be established otherwise, however, concerning the salutary use of the Eucharist, as also concerning the Baptism of adults: as will be shown more fully in its own place.

And let it suffice to have disputed these things concerning the Effect of the Sacraments. But that other question, which is moved concerning the Necessity of the Sacraments, depends upon this very dispute. Where, however, it is not asked, Are the Sacraments, after they have been instituted by GOD, necessary for the salvation of men? For it would be too impious to deny this. Nor is it also controverted, Was it of absolute necessity to institute these Sacraments, so that without these GOD could save no one. For all easily concede regarding the denier, as Hugo of St. Victor rightly wrote, book 1, part 9, chapter 4. GOD could have saved man, even if He had not instituted these: but man could in no way be saved, if he were to despise these: Item: the power of GOD is not subject to the elements by necessity, even if the grace of GOD is given by dispensation through the Sacraments. Item. Those who received the Sacraments after their institution had in them signs of their righteousness rather than a cause from them. Therefore, let no one so institute a law of divine righteousness in the elements as to say that a man can neither be justified without these, even if he has justifying grace: nor be saved without these, even if he has been righteous, when either an article of necessity excludes him from receiving these, or the consideration of time does not bind him to receive these. Therefore, let it not be ascribed to these, what is ministered to us through these: nor let us so venerate the visible appearance in them that we are convinced to subject the invisible truth to them.

But that is properly disputed, whether it was necessary by a necessity of convenience that GOD should institute the Sacraments, namely for this reason, that thus men might be able to attain to salvation all the more conveniently? Which necessity of convenience 1. regards the end of the Sacraments most of all: 2. regards not what could have been more convenient or advantageous for GOD, but only what could have been more convenient or advantageous for men in this regard? Now, this ζήτημα can be answered most correctly by a distinction between the state of innocence before the fall: and the state of corruption after the fall. For in the state of integrity and innocence, the Sacraments were not necessary in any way at that time: whether they are considered insofar as they are remedies for sins: or insofar as they are ordained for the consolation of the soul and for preserving health. Not the latter: Because those who are well had no need of a physician, Matt. 9, 12. Not this latter: For man then had much nobler gifts, and those internal and concreated, by which he could easily be preserved from sin, if only he had willed it. But now after the fall in the state of corruption, the Sacraments are most necessary on the part and use of men, for the greatest part of this life. I say the greatest, not every part of this life. For that part of human life is excluded which preceded both the promulgation of the law and the sanction of the covenant expressed with Abraham. For this, because it was strong also in the rarity of men, which it was less necessary to bind together into one body, as it were, by the fellowship of the Sacraments: and was distinguished by longevity: and was especially adorned by those aids divinely, to which human life in later centuries did not pertain: it could easily do without the use of the Sacraments. But those principal aids or Privileges were these: private conversation with GOD, the appearances of Angels, the sign of fire fallen from heaven upon the sacrifices, all of which could very easily compensate for the use of the Sacraments by a certain analogical reason. But after these aids ceased, in order that men might arrive at salvation more conveniently, it was certainly necessary that the Sacraments be instituted, namely by a necessity of convenience. The truth of this assertion can be evidently demonstrated from the twofold end or use of the individual Sacraments: in this manner:

I. Man is led to spiritual things more conveniently and advantageously through those signs which have some analogy or similarity with human nature itself. But human nature is corporeal and sensible. Therefore, through corporeal and sensible signs he can be led to spiritual things more easily and conveniently. The Apostle himself seems to have hinted at the connection of the Major premise in Rom. 1, 20, asserting that the nations knew the invisible things of GOD, namely His eternal power and divinity, through the visible things of this world. Then the same is clear from the consideration of divine providence. For since GOD disposes all things sweetly, Wis. 8, 1, and provides for all things according to the mode of their nature: it pleased Him to declare that power, by which He sanctifies us, through signs falling under the senses, for the sake of His goodness toward us. For as Chrysostom elegantly discusses, Hom. 83 on Matthew & hom. 60 to the People of Antioch. If man had lacked the concretion of a body, the heavenly goods would have been offered to him naked, and not wrapped in any coverings. But because the soul is joined to the body, it was altogether necessary that it should use the aid of things which are perceived, in order to understand those things.

II. It is necessary, partly so that the true people of GOD may be distinguished from other peoples, even under a visible form: partly so that the very assembly of the faithful may coalesce by certain symbols and a visible bond. But both are done through the use of the Sacraments: For men cannot be gathered into any name of religion, whether true or false, unless they are collected by some fellowship of signs or visible Sacraments: as Augustine himself also judges, book 19 against Faustus, chapter 11. Therefore.

But furthermore, in this place, the question is about the Quality of this Necessity: how it stands. Now it must be established thus, that the Sacraments are so necessary that they are not either arbitrary: or superfluous: or necessary only in the way in which the preaching of the word is, which the pious and faithful have need of, so that faith may be stirred up in them from time to time on account of infirmity: but they are necessary as effective instruments of GOD, by whose power, through these, with the faith of men mediating in part, the grace of justification and the very salvation of men is effected: and they are so necessary that without them, either in reality, or at least received by desire and vow of the soul, men cannot obtain grace. 1. Therefore, profane and fanatical men err gravely in this part who establish that the use of the Sacraments is superfluous. 2. Similarly, the presumptuous err, who are persuaded that the same is arbitrary, or necessary only for those weak in faith. 3. Nor is that temptation without danger and error, by which the minds of even the pious are sometimes infested; Because GOD in His word offers and exhibits all things which are necessary for salvation, and in the same word faith finds and apprehends all things: to what end is there need of Sacraments, the use of which might seem able to be neglected without loss of salvation. 4. Most atrocious of all is the calumny of the Papists, who clamor that Sacraments are excluded by Evangelicals, who teach justification by faith alone. Concil. Trid. Sess. 7. can. 4.

To this first error, besides that axiom of Christ, John 3:5, 'Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of GOD,' may be opposed the most weighty opinion of Augustine, which exists in book 19 against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 11: 'The power of the sacraments is ineffably great; and therefore contempt makes them sacrilegious. For it is impiously despised, without which piety cannot be perfected.' To the second error must be opposed the fact that God, by the words of an express command in the institution of the individual sacraments, did not leave their use free or arbitrary to us, but clearly necessary: for the reason that our judgment concerning the firmness or infirmity of faith can deceive us, and it is most clearly perceived by God alone, who is the καρδιογνώστης [knower of hearts]. To the third class of men, and indeed to the pious as well, it must be inculcated: 1. That the nature of our condition is human, not angelic. 2. That nature, or to speak as a Christian, GOD the maker of nature, does nothing in vain: 3. That such is the condition of the Word, that it contains only general promises, to which, through the use of the sacraments, an effective subsumption and individual application is made. 4. That those things are for the most part proposed in the Word which, surpassing all sense, are joined with the greatest difficulty of believing: for they are placed both as invisible and under hope, and indeed against hope: Rom. 4:18. In the apprehension of which things, through the aids of the senses, God willed to support human faith in some way in the use of the sacraments. From which very fact, however, it does not follow, as some infer, that the sacraments are only necessary for weaker Christians who acknowledge their own infirmity, but that they are not necessary for those who have faith confirmed by the Word. There is indeed no other promise or grace which is exhibited in the Word of promise or the Gospel, and another which is exhibited in the sacraments, but one and the same: yet the mode of exhibition is different, according to the diversity of the instrument by which the same grace is conferred: for there, God willed that the external hearing, but here, the judgment of the eyes also, be proposed to us as a medium. In which way it happens that the sacraments, as far as we are concerned, are signs confirming the faith of the Evangelical promise; but as far as God is concerned, they are organs through which God offers, exhibits, applies, seals, confirms, increases, and preserves His grace. On which account Augustine, in 'On Baptism against the Donatists,' book 4, chapter 22, proves by the example of Cornelius and his friends that the use of the sacraments is necessary even for the most perfect, and that no one, in any progress of the inner man, ought to despise the sacrament. Finally, the Papists wrongly and entirely oppose the necessity of the sacraments to justification by faith alone. For although the genus of the cause is one and the same on both sides, namely, organic, yet in species it differs on both sides. For the sacraments have the power of an organ on the part of God; faith is an instrument on the part of man, by which the application of salvation and righteousness is made. That conclusion is therefore false: 'The sacraments are necessary for salvation. Therefore, the grace of justification is not received by faith alone.'

Latin:

ESt quidem effectus iste Sacramentorum de quo hactenus disputavimus, communis omnibus tùm Veteris, tùm Novi Testamenti Sacramentis: Siquidem non minus illa, quàm hæc sunt σφραγίδες δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίςεως Rom. 4, 11: non tamen propterea communis etiam est ille omnibus Sacramento utentibus: Verùm ijs duntaxat obtingit, qui fide Sacramētis utuntur: adeò ut qui hâc destituitur, ille hoc effectu usq́; adeò non potiatur, ut potiùs ipsi cedant in judicium. Undè est, quòd Apostolus in homine Sacramentis participaturo, non usum duntaxat, sed dignitatem præcipuè, & sui probationem requirit: 1. Cor. 11, 28. 2. Cor. 13. 5.

Deindè Sacramenta promissioni Evangelij sunt addita, tanquàm sigilla. Quo ergò medio sive organo promissio ipsa apprehenditur, nempè solâ fide: eundem usum quoque sive effectum salutarem Sacramentorum apprehendi, necessarium est consequens. Undè illud Augustini: Non Sacramentum, sed fides Sacramenti justificat: non quia fit, sed quia creditur. Tract. 80. in Joh. Quâ de re videatur etiam B. Lutherus contra obeliscos Eccij, Tom. 1. lat. Jen. p. 26. & 33. Est verò non iste sensus jam dictorum, quem Calviniani hoc loco occultare solent, quasi ante usum cujuslibet Sacramenti Fides necessariò præcedere debeat, ita quidem, ut infantes fidelium parentum, fidem ex utero materno secum adferant, & sint in gratiâ DEI, etiam ante usum Baptismi. Quæ sanè sententia subsequente Articulo proximo ex professo refutabitur. Verùm hoc volunt & statuunt Orthodoxi, quòd fides necessariò quidem requiratur, ad salutarem usum cujuslibet Sacramenti: non verò quòd fides omnem usum Sacramenti tempore debeat præcedere. Exempli gratiâ: Ut Sacramentum Baptismi salutarem suum usum sive effectum in infante baptizato exerat, necessum est, ut adsit fides, sine quâ regeneratio & adoptio nemini obtingere potest: Joh. 1, 12. Hæc autem fides tempore non præcedit, neq́; infantes eam ad Sacramentum afferunt: sed operatione Spiritus Sancti, per baptismum infantibus in, cum & per ipsam aspersionem aquæ, ipso actu confertur: Quo fit, ut & sic salutari effectu potiantur. Secus tamen statuendum de usu salutari Eucharistiæ, ut & de Baptismo adultorum: uti suo loco fusiùs ostendetur.

Et hæc quidem de Effectu Sacramentorum disputasse sufficiat. Dependet autem ab hac ipsâ disputatione quæstio illa altera, quæ de Necessitate Sacramentorum movetur. Ubi tamen non illud quæritur, An Sacramenta postquàm à DEO instituta sunt, ad salutem hominum sint necessaria? Nimis enim impium foret, hoc negare. Neq́; etiam illud controvertitur, An absolutæ fuerit necessitatis Sacramenta hæc instituere, ita ut fine his DEUS neminem salvare potuerit. Nam in negantem omnes facilè concedũt, ut rectè scripferit Hugo de S.Victore, lib.1.part.9.cap.4. Potuit DEUS hominē salvare, etsi ista non instituisset: sed homo nullatenus servari posset, si ista contemneret: Item: virtus DEI ex necessitate elementis non subditur, etiamsi gratia DEI ex dispensatione per Sacramenta donetur. Item. Qui Sacramenta post institutionem susceperunt, signa magis justitiæ suæ habuerunt in istis, quàm causam ex istis. Nemo ergò in elementis sic legem justitiæ divinæ instituat, ut dicat, Hominem nec justificari posse sine his, etiamsi gratiam justificantem habuerit: nec salvari posse sine his, etiamsi justus fuerit, cùm ab his percipiendis vel articulus necessitatis excludit, vel ad hac percipienda ratio temporis nõ adstringit. Non itaq́, istis adscribatur, quod per ista nobis ministratur: neq́, in illis visibilem itavenèremur speciem ut invisibilem eis subjicere convincamur veritatem.

Verùm illud propriè controvertitur, Annecessitate convenientiæ necessarium fuerit, ut DEUS Sacramenta institueret, ideò nimirùm, ut sic homines tantò commodiùs ad salutem pertingere possent? Quæ necessitas convenientiæ 1. respicit finem maximè Sacramentorum: 2. respicit non quid DEO, sed tantùm quid hominibus convenientiùs aut commodiùs hâc in parte obtingere potuerit? Responderi autem ad hoc ζήτημα rectissimè potest, per distinctionem inter statum innocentiæ ante lapsum: & inter statum corruptionis post lapsum. In statu enim integritatis & innocentiæ, non erant Sacramenta tùm ullo modo necessaria: sive considerentur ea, quatenùs peccatorum sunt remedia: sive, quatenùs ad animæ consolationem, & conservandam sanitatem ordinata sunt. Non illud: Quia valentibus non opus erat medico, Matth. 9, 12. Non hoc posterius: Habuit enim homo tùm multò nobiliora dona, eaq́; interna & concreata, quibus à peccato, si modò voluisset, facilè præservari poterat. Cæterùm jam post lapsum in statu corruptionis, Sacramenta ex parte & usu hominum, maximè sunt necessaria, quod maximam vitæ hujus partem. Maximam dico, non omnem vitæ hujus partem. Excluditur enim pars ea vitæ humanæ, quæ tùm promulgationem legis, tùm fœderis cum Abrahamo expressi sanctionem antecessit. Hæc enim, quia & raritate hominum valebat, quam Sacramentorum consortio in unũ quasi corpus colligari, minùs necessum fuit:& longævitate insignis erat: & præcipuè ijs adminiculis divinitùs ornata erat, ad quæ posterioribus seculis vita humana non pertinebat: usu Sacramentorum facilè carere potuit. Adminicula autem sive Privilegia illa præcipua erant isthæc: privatum cum DEO colloquium, Angelorum apparitiones, ignis super sacrificia cælitùs delapsi indicium, quæ omnia analogicâ quadam ratione usum Sacramentorũ pensare perfacilè potuerant. Postquàm verò hæc adminicula defierunt, ut commodiùs homines ad salutem pervenirent, necessum utiq; erat Sacramenta institui, necessitate nimirùm convenientiæ. Assertionis hujus veritas ex gemino fine sive usu singulorum Sacramentorum, evidenter demonstrari potest: in hunc modum:

I. Convenientius atq́, commodius homo ad spiritualia deducitur per ea signa, quæ cum ipsâ naturâ humanâ aliquâ analogiâ sive similitudinẽ habent. Atqui Natura humana est corporea & sensibilis. Ergò per corporea etiam & sensibilia signa faciliùs & commodiùs deduci potest ad spiritualia. Connexum Majoris vel ipse Apostolus innuisse videtur Rom. 1, 20. asserens Invisibilia DEI, nempè æternam ipsius potentiam & divinitatem, cognovisse gentes per visibilia hujus mundi. Deindè patet idem ex consideratione divinæ providentiæ. Cùm enim DEUS omnia disponat svaviter, Sap. 8, 1. & provideat rebus omnibus secundum modum naturæ suæ: placuit ipsi eam virtutem, quâ nos sanctificat, signis sub sensum cadentibus, pro suâ in nos bonitate declarare. Nam ut eleganter Chrysostomus disserit, Hom. 83. in Matth. & hom. 60. ad Pop. Antioch. Si homo corporis concretione caruisset, nuda ipsi bona cælestia, neq́, ullis integumentis involuta, essent oblata. Quia verò anima corpori conjuncta est, omninò opus fuit, ut rerum, quæ sentiuntur, adminiculo ad ea intelligenda uteretur.

II. Necessarium est, partim ut verus populus DEI, ab alijs populis, sub visibili etiam formâ distingvatur: partim ipse etiam fidelium cætus certis quibusdam Symbolis & vinculo visibili coalescat. Atqui utrumq́, fit per usum Sacramentorum: In nullum enim religionis nomen, sive verum, sive falsum, coagulari homines possunt, nisi aliquo signaculorum, vel Sacramentorum visibilium consortio colligentur: sic ipso etiam censente Augustino, lib. 19. cont. Faust. cap. 11. Ergò.

Cæterùm porrò hoc loco quæritur de Necessitatis hujus Qualitate: quomodo ea se habeat. Sic autem statuendum est, Sacramenta ita esse necessaria, ut non sint vel arbitraria: vel superflua: vel necessaria tantùm eo modo, quo prædicatio verbi, quo opus habent pij & fideles, ut propter infirmitatem subindè in ipsis excitetur fides: sed sunt necessaria, ut instrumenta efficacia DEI, cujus virtute, per ista, mediante ex parte hominũ fide, gratia justificationis, & salus ipsa hominum efficitur: suntq́; adeò necessaria, ut sine ipfis vel reipsâ, vel desiderio saltem votoq́; animo susceptis, non possint homines adipisci gratiam. 1. Errant ergò hac parte graviter prophani & fanatici homines qui statuunt, Superfluum esse Sacramentorum usum. 2. Errant similiter præsumtuosi, qui eundem arbitrarium, aut non nisi infirmis in fide, necessarium esse, persuasum habent. 3. Nec caret periculo & errore illa tentatio, quâ piorum etiam animi quandoq́, infestantur; Quia verbo suo DEUS omnia, quæ sunt ad salutem necessaria, offert atq́; exhibet, & in eodem verbo fides omnia invenit atq́; apprehendit: quorsum sit opus Sacramentis, quorum usus sine dispendio salutis negligi posse videatur. 4. Maximè omnium atrox est calumnia Pontificiorum, qui ab Evangelicis, justificationem solius fidei docentibus, Sacramenta excludi clamitant. Concil. Trid. Sess. 7. can. 4.

Primo isti errori, præter illud Christi axioma, Joh. 3, 5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum DEI : opponi potest gravissima Augustini sententia, quæ extat lib. 19. contr. Faust. Manich. cap. 11. Sacramentorum vis inenarrabiliter valet plurimùm: & ideò contemta sacrilegos facit. Impiè quippè contemnitur, sine quâ non potest perfici pietas. Secundo errori opponendum illud, quòd Deus expressi mandati verbis, in singulorum Sacramentorum institutione, usum eorundem nobis non reliquit liberum aut arbitrarium: sed planè necessarium : ideò quòd nostrum judicium de firmitate aut infirmitate fidei, nos fallere potest: & soli Deo καρδιογνώστης est perspectissimum. Tertio hominum generi, imò pijs quoq́; inculcandum est, 1. Humanam, non Angelicam esse conditionis nostræ naturam. 2. Naturam, vel ut Christianè loquamur, DEUM naturæ opificem nihil facere frustrà: 3. Eam esse Verbi conditionem, ut promissiones duntaxat generales contineat, ad quas per Sacramentorum usum efficax fit subsumtio, & individualis applicatio. 4. Ea plerumq́; in Verbo proponuntur, quæ omnem sensum superantia, maxima cum difficultate credendi sunt conjuncta:quippè tùm invisibilia, tùm sub spe, & quidem contra spem posita: Rom. 4, 18. In quarum rerum apprehensione, per adminicula sensuum, Deus in Sacramentorum usu fidem humanam suffulcire quodammodo voluit. Ex quo tamen ipso etiam non sequitur, quod inferunt aliqui, Sacramenta esse tantùm necessaria Christianis imbecillioribus, & infirmitatem suam agnoscentibus : ijs autem, qui fidem ex verbo confirmatam habent, nõ esse necessaria. Non est quidem alia vel promissio, vel gratia, quæ in Verbo promissionis sive Evangelij, & alia, quæ in Sacramentis exhibetur: sed una prorsus atq; eadem: Verùm modus tamen exhibitionis est diversus, pro diversitate instrumenti, quo gratia eadem confertur: Ibi enim Auditum externum, hic verò oculorum etiam κρίσιν, tanquàm medium nobis DE9 voluit esse propositum. Quo modo fit, ut Sacramenta quoad nos, sint signa confirmantia fidem promissionis Evangelicæ: quoad Deum verò sint organa, per quæ Deus gratiam suam offert, exhibet, applicat, obsignat, confirmat, auget, conservat. Quo nomine Augustinus de Bapt. cont. Donat. lib. 4. cap. 22. exemplo Cornelij & amicorum ejus evincit, perfectissimis etiam necessarium esse Sacramentorum usum, & neminem in quolibet etiam profectu hominis interioris, contemnere debere Sacramentum. Tandem Pontificij perperam omninò justificationi per solam fidem Sacramentorum necessitatem opponunt. Nam etsi genus quidem causæ utrobiq; unum est atq; idem organicum, scilicet: specie tamen utrobiq; illud differt. Nam Sacramenta vim organi habent ex parte DEI: fides ex parte hominis instrumentum est, quo fit salutis & justititiæ applicatio. Falsa est ergò collectio illa, Sacramenta sunt ad salutem necessaria. Ergò, Gratia justificationis per solam fidem non accipitur


### Chapter III. On the mutual agreement and difference of the Sacraments of the two Testaments

What the mutual affection of the two Testaments toward each other is, and what the discrepancy is, was shown above in a special Article. Now, how the sacraments of these two Testaments also relate to each other, and in what they differ, must be repeated in this place in a few words.

They agree, therefore, among themselves: 1. In Author, who is one in both, namely GOD. 2. In Number, which is completed by the binary in both. 3. In essential parts, or principal causes, which are required to constitute the condition of a sacrament, which in all sacraments are two: the earthly thing and the heavenly thing. 4. In signification. For in both, the sacraments have a mutual respect between the Sign and the Signified, as was shown above in chapter 1. 5. In end: for both are seals of the righteousness of faith. 6. In latitude, for both extend themselves to all members of the Church, so that just as in the Old Testament no stranger, so today no one is admitted to the use of the sacraments unless he is a member and citizen of the Church. 7. In office. For just as Circumcision was there, so Baptism is with us the sacrament of initiation: and just as the Paschal Lamb was for them, so the Eucharist serves for us for the confirmation of faith. 8. In necessity: for in both, the use of the sacraments is not arbitrary, but necessary for salvation. 9. In fruit or Effect: for both, through faith in those participating in them, are means of conferring grace.

Then, however, they also differ greatly from each other: as 1. In time: those are proper to the Old, these to the New Testament. 2. In external and visible symbols, which GOD willed to be peculiar to each sacrament. 3. In the rites of dispensation: for there the mode was bloody; here, however, it is bloodless. 4. In duration: those met their end with the polity of the Jewish people; these, however, will endure until the LORD comes to judgment. 5. In latitude: those were included within the limits of one people, namely the Jewish; these, however, extend as widely as the Christian world spreads itself. 6. In the mode of signifying and in perspicuity. For although those also signified the body and blood of CHRIST, yet they did this only typically and figuratively through the flesh and blood of animals and men. These, however, do not have and exhibit CHRIST in types and figures, but present in his very flesh. With respect to this final difference, the Sacraments of the Old Testament are compared to shadows, but ours to the body: Col. 2:17, Heb. 10:1; and St. Augustine says that those had promises of things to be fulfilled, while these are indications that they have been fulfilled: the former were pre-annunciative of Christ to come, the latter are annunciative of Christ exhibited, lib. 19. cont. Faust. Manich. c. 14. And in Ps. 73.

It can also be evidently gathered from this last difference that our Sacraments are in many ways more excellent than the old ones: 1. In ease: for they are not so laborious as those were. 2. In the evidence of signifying: for there was not such great light, or such great power in the Sacraments of the Old Testament as in ours, since they have the very body and blood of CHRIST, no longer typical but essential, in place of signs, most present. Therefore, by how much greater the perspicuity is in that which is exhibited than in that which is promised, and likewise by how much greater the power is in the body itself than in the shadow or type, by so much do our Sacraments obtain greater perspicuity and power of signifying than those old ones; so that Augustine wrote most truly that our Sacraments are greater in virtue, better in utility, and easier in act: lib. 19. contr. Faust. cap. 13.

This purer doctrine concerning the distinction between the Sacraments of both Testaments was already contradicted long ago by the Scholastics, who contended that in the Sacrament of the new law, grace follows from the work worked (ex opere operato): but in the Sacraments of the old law, grace was conferred from the work of the worker (ex opere operantis), or of the one receiving, if he was an adult, or of the parent, or of the one circumcising the child. For it was necessary for them to have faith in CHRIST who was to come. But in the Sacraments of the new law, grace is conferred from the work worked, and it is not necessary that the worker believe: but it suffices that he works, and intends to do what the Church of Christians does, even if he does not believe that this is valid. Whence Thomas did not shudder to write, part. 3. quæst. 62. art. 6. that the Sacraments of the old law did not have in themselves any virtue by which they might work to confer justifying grace: but only signified the faith by which they were justified. And the Master of the Sentences, lib. 4. dist. 1., from Augustine on Psalm 73, assigns this difference of the Sacraments, that those only promised and signified: but these give salvation. Where, however, the Master committed the crime of falsehood, adding to the words of Augustine the word 'signifying,' which does not exist in Augustine: for his words are thus: 'Some are the Sacraments, giving salvation: others promising the Savior: the Sacraments of the New Testament give salvation: the Sacraments of the Old Testament promised the Savior.' Therefore, Augustine has nothing about the work worked, but only intimates this, that the Sacraments of the Old Testament were Sacraments of the Savior who was to come: but those of the New are Sacraments of the Savior already exhibited and present. Bonaventura subscribes to the Master in 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 5. The causality, he says, of the Sacraments is nothing other than a certain efficacious ordination for receiving grace from a divine covenant: but this was only in the Sacraments of the new law, and not the old, except in circumcision, which was a covenant there.

But concerning this impiety of the Scholastics, more than enough has been said above, which is further increased by that paradox which they establish, that faith was necessary for those who used the old Sacraments: but to us who are baptized and celebrate the Supper of the Lord, it is not necessary: and because they oppose that work of theirs, the work worked, to faith, and through it they utterly evacuate faith, which apprehends the promise of the Gospel.

These things having been thus premised in general concerning the nature and affection of the Sacraments of the Old Testament, it will be worth the effort to contemplate the nature of each one in particular more accurately. But there are only two Sacraments of the Old Testament. For although many Sacraments are named in the writings of the Fathers which were in use among the old people: yet it is sufficiently clear that this is done improperly, and that the word 'Sacrament' is taken there either for a mystery, or for a rite and ceremony proper to divine worship. Meanwhile, speaking properly, it is clear by the consensus of all theologians that there were only two Sacraments of the old people, namely, Circumcision and the Paschal Lamb.

Latin:
