QUæ sit mutua ad se invicem duorum Testamentorum affectio, quæque discrepantia, suprà peculiari Articulo fuit ostensum. Jam quomodo Sacramenta etiam duorum istorum Testamentorum, ad se mutuò habeant, quidq́; discrepent, paucis hoc loco repetendum fuerit.

Conveniunt ergò inter se. 1. Autore, qui unus utrobiq; est, nempè DEUS. 2. Numero, qui utrobiq; binario absolvitur. 3. Partibus essentialibus, sive causis præcipuis, quæ ad constituendam Sacramenti conditionem requiruntur, quæ in omnibus Sacramentis duæ sunt: Res terrena, & Res cælestis. 4. Signatione. Utrobiq; enim Sacramenta mutuum habent respectum, inter Signum & Signatum: uti suprà cap. 1. ostensum. 5. Fine: utraq; enim sunt signacula justitiæ fidei. 6. Latitudine, utraq; enim ad omnia Ecclesiæ membra se extendunt, ita ut quemadmodum in Veteri Testamento nullus extraneus; ita hodieq; nemo ad usum Sacramentorum admittatur, nisi qui sit membrum & civis Ecclesiæ. 7. Officio. Quemadmodum enim ibi Circumcisio, sic apud nos Baptismus est Sacramentum initiationis: & quemadmodum illis Agnus Paschalis, sic nobis Evcharistia cedit in confirmationem fidei. 8. Necessitate: utrobiq; enim Sacramentorum usus non est arbitrarius, sed ad salutem necessarius. 9. Fructu sive Effectu: utraq; enim per fidem illis participantibus, sunt media conferendæ gratiæ.

Deindè verò plurimùm etiam à se invicem differunt: ut 1. Tempore, illa Veteris: hæc Novi Testamenti sunt propria. 2. Symbolis externis ac visibilibus, quæ cuilibet Sacramento DEUS peculiaria esse voluit. 3. Ritibus dispensationis: illic enim modus cruentus erat: hîc verò incruentus. 4. Duratione: illa cum populi Judaici politiâ finem sunt sortita; Hæc verò durabunt, usq; dum DOMINUS venerit ad judicium. 5. Latitudine: illa unius populi, Judaici nimirùm terminis includebantur: Hæc verò tàm latè patent, quàm latè se diffundit orbis Christianus. 6. Signandi modo & perspicuitate. Etsi enim illa signabant etiam corpus & sangvinem CHRISTI; tamen hoc tantùm faciebant typicè & figuratè per carnem & sangvinem pecuinum ac humanum. Hæc verò non in typis & figuris: sed in ipsâ carne CHRISTUM habent & exhibent præsentem. Cujus ultimæ differentiæ respectu, Sacramenta Veteris Testamenti comparantur umbris: nostra verò corpori: Col. 2, 17. Hebr. 10, 1. & D. Augustinus, illas ait promissiones habuisse rerum complendarum: hæc indicia esse completarum: Illa prænunciativa venturi: hæc annunciativa exhibiti Christi, lib. 19. cont. Faust. Manich. c. 14. Et in Pf. 73.

Potest etiam ex postrema hac differentia evidenter colligi, nostra Sacramenta multis modis præstantiora esse Veteribus: Ut 1. Facilitate: neq; enim adeo laboriosa sunt, sicut illa. 2. Signandi evidentia: Neq; enim tanta fuit Lux, vel vis tanta Sacramentis Veteris Testamenti, quanta nostris, quippe quæ ipsum corpus & sangvinem CHRISTI, non amplius typicum, sed essentialem, signorum loco habent præsentissimum. Quanto ergo major perspicuitas est in exhibito, quam in promisso: quanto item major vis in ipso corpore, quam in umbra sive typo: tanto majorem etiam perspicuitatem ac vim signandi nostra Sacramenta præ veteribus illis obtinent: adeo ut verissime Augustinus scripserit, Sacramenta nostra, virtute esse majora, utilitate meliora, actu faciliora: lib. 19. contr. Faust. cap. 13.

Puriori huic doctrinæ de discrimine utriusq; Testamenti Sacramentorum, contradictum fuit jam olim a Scholasticis contendentibus, In Sacramento novæ legis, sequi gratiam ad opus operatum: In Sacramentis vero Veteris legis collatam fuisse gratiam, ex opere operantis, vel suscipientis, si erat adultus, vel parentis, vel circumcidentis Puerum. Oportebat enim ipsos habere fidem in CHRISTUM venturum. Sed in Sacramentis novæ legis, ex opere operato conferri gratiam, nec necessum esse, ut operans credat: sed sufficere ut operetur, & intendat facere quod facit Ecclesia Christianorum, licet non credat hoc valere. Unde Thomas scribere non exhorruit, part. 3. quæst. 62. art. 6. Sacramenta Veteris legis non habuisse in se aliquam virtutem, qua operentur, ad conferenda gratiam justificantem: sed solum significasse fidem, per quam justificabantur. Et Magister sententiarum lib. 4. dist. 1. ex Augustino in Psalmum 73. hanc Sacramentorum assignat differentiam, quod illa promiserint tantum, & significaverint: hæc autem dent Salutem. Ubi tamen Magister crimen falsi commisit, defuo verbis Augustini affuens Verbum significandi, quod apud Augustinum non extat: Sic enim ejus habent verba: Alia sunt Sacramenta, dantia salutem: alia promittentia Salvatorem: Sacramenta Novi Testamenti dant Salutem: Sacramenta Veteris Testamenti promiserunt Salvatorem. Nihil igitur habet Augustinus de Opere operato, sed hoc tantum innuit, Sacramenta Veteris Testamenti, fuisse Sacramenta venturi Salvatoris: Novi vero esse Sacramenta Salvatoris jam exhibiti & præsentis. Magistro subscribit Bonaventura in 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 5. Causalitas, inquiens, Sacramentorum, non est aliud, quam efficax quædam ordinatio ad recipiendam gratiam ex pactione divina: Hoc autem fuit solum in Sacramentis novæ legis, & non Veteris, nisi in circumcisione, quæ ibi fuit compactio.

Verum de hac Scholasticorum impietate jam supra plus satis dictum, quam auget illud etiam paradoxon, quod statuunt, Fidem necessariam fuisse illis, qui usi sunt Veteribus Sacramentis: nobis autem qui baptizamur, & Cœnam Domini celebramus, non esse necessariam: & quod opus illud suum operatum opponunt fidei & per illud fidem apprehendentem promissionem Evangelij propriam, prorsus evacuant.

His ita præmissis in genere de naturâ & affectione Sacramentorum Veteris Testamenti: operæ pretium fuerit in specie singulorum naturam accuratiùs contemplari. Sunt autem duo tantùm Veteris Testamenti Sacramenta. Etsi enim in scriptis Patrum multa nominantur Sacramenta, quæ Veteri populo in usu fuerunt: tamen impropriè illud fieri, & vocabulum Sacramenti vel pro mysterio, vel pro ritu & ceremoniâ cultûs divini propriâ ibi accipi, satis constat. Interim propriè loquendo duo tantùm fuisse Veteris populi Sacramenta, Circumcisionem nimirùm, & Agnum Paschalem, omnium Theologorum consensu liquet.


### Chapter III. On the mutual agreement and difference of the Sacraments of the…: I. On Circumcision

Various questions are moved concerning this Sacrament: and at the beginning, indeed, there is a controversy about the time when it was promulgated. A more accurate calculation produces the year of the world 2047, although others, among the more recent ones indeed Augustine, Torniellus lib. 1. of the annals, place it in A. M. 2138, concerning which see the chronologists. That certainly is clear from sacred history, that the promulgation of this Sacrament falls in the 99th year of Abraham, and the 13th of Ishmael. But why this Sacrament was finally given to Abraham, these reasons are assigned primarily by theologians: because Abraham was the first who, having been called forth by divine vocation from Ur of the Chaldeans, segregated himself from infidels and from the worship of idols: because also Abraham was the first who received the promise accommodated to his seed. But perhaps this reason is more pregnant, that no cause seems able to be given for which it was necessary that circumcision should be instituted immediately after the fall, or certainly before the age of Abraham. For in all that preceding century, reason and faith were more vigorous, and the immediate colloquies of GOD with men were more frequent. But with the passage of time, faith decreased more and more through the sins of men, and God himself withdrew mutual conversations from the human race. Therefore, at the time of Abraham, GOD wished to promulgate the Sacrament of Circumcision, so that thus, in the defect of divine colloquies, there might be material for the faithful to exercise, nourish, and increase their faith. Furthermore, with respect also to the subsequent century, it was convenient for Circumcision to be instituted before the promulgation of the written law, both because the people of GOD had to be segregated from other peoples before the law was delivered: and also because the people were then still in some small number, and thus could be more easily persuaded to receive Circumcision.

Then the question is raised concerning the Object, namely, who or what persons were required to be circumcised? If we consult the commandment of GOD, or the institution of this Sacrament, it is clear that all males in the house and family of Abraham were to be circumcised, whether adults, or infants, or servants, and those either born in the house, or bought, whether they were free. Nor was this done without a certain reason. For although the institution of this Sacrament, since it was opposed to the disease of original sin, to which all, as well Jews as Gentiles, were subject, could seem to pertain to all: yet because this Sacrament was the sealing of that covenant which GOD made with Abraham concerning CHRIST who was most certainly to be born, and also concerning the land of promise, with which He was about to endow his posterity: therefore only those were bound to the observation of this Sacrament to whom this covenant pertained, namely all the sons of Israel, not indeed simply all who in any way descended from the seed of Abraham: but those especially who traced the origin of their lineage from Abraham through Isaac and Jacob. For to Isaac, as it were, the promise of the seed to come was properly dedicated, the Lord saying in Gen. 17, 19: I will establish my covenant with him, and with his seed after him. Nor yet was Ishmael with his posterity excluded from this Sacrament on that account, nay, even in his own house the true and genuine Sacrament was administered, as long as they observed the federal formula of this Sacrament, I will be thy GOD, and of thy seed after thee, together with the amputation of the foreskin, and thus the substantial parts of this Sacrament entire. But after they had neglected the federal promise, and retained only the external rite of Circumcision: then also the true Sacrament ceased to be among them. And indeed Scripture looks to this, asserting that Ishmael was cast out of the house of Abraham, Gen. 17, 25, and that he would not be heir with the son: likewise that Esau was held in hatred, but Jacob loved: Gen. 25, 21, Malach. 1, 2, Rom. 9, 13. Which ejection, however, did not prevent access to the society of faith and salvation from being open to them, just as much as to the Gentiles. It is believed that Job was of the seed of Abraham, namely that Jobab, of whom mention is made in Genesis 36, 33. And yet Gregory writes in the prologue that it is not read that Job was circumcised, the cause of which thing is thought to be that he traced his origin from Abraham, not through the line of Jacob, but through Esau, as is evident from the already cited 36th chapter of Genesis. Although there are not wanting those who think he descended from the stock of Nahor.

These things being thus established, there were excluded from the Sacrament of Circumcision.

1. The Gentiles, who were not of the seed of Abraham: They could nevertheless be circumcised, if they wished to keep the law, Exod. 12, 44, Judith 14, 6. And such were called Proselytes, as is had in Matthew 23, 15.

2. Females were also excluded, however much they were sprung from the stock of Abraham. For because of the mystery of Circumcision, which had to be done in the foreskin of the male genital member, women could not be capable of this Sacrament. Because, however, they traced their origin from circumcised Fathers, they were nevertheless reckoned in the grace of the covenant by GOD, as will be demonstrated a little later, when the Effect of this Sacrament is treated.

Finally, although the sons of Israel are commanded to circumcise servants both bought and home-born: they are nevertheless forbidden to circumcise stranger servants, whether free or hired. Exod. 12, 45.

Thirdly, the question is concerning the Subject. Namely, in what part of the body Circumcision had to be performed? Scripture defines the male genital member, the foreskin of which had to be amputated. Which very thing we shall judge not to have been done without a grave cause. For because the Sacrament of Circumcision had to be a remedy against original sin: it certainly had to be performed in that member through which the propagation of original sin is chiefly made. Then because the chief fuel of original sin is Concupiscence, which dominates most of all in the genital member: certainly for this reason also, this member could be the most convenient Subject of this Sacrament. Finally, because Circumcision was the sealing of the covenant initiated with Abraham concerning the blessed seed, certainly the marking of this member also could warn the Jews concerning Christ who was to be born from the seed of Abraham. Because also the foreskin of the member had to be amputated, it was a sign that Christ was to be born, not from male seed: For which very reason also not women, but men were circumcised, so that it might be hinted that Christ was to be born from a woman, not from a man. There is added, however, the analogy between regeneration and generation. For in what part of the body infants were generated from parents, it was convenient that they should also receive the Sacrament of regeneration from the same.

Fourthly, it is asked, why did GOD will that males be circumcised only on the eighth day, and not immediately when they were brought into the light? Where the constant opinion of all is that this was done by the singular providence of GOD, which did not wish infants to be exposed to the pains of circumcision before they had become somewhat more confirmed in body and strength. Moreover, this eighth day was of the necessity of the precept, which it was not permitted to anticipate or even to defer, however much it might fall on the Sabbath itself, as is clear from John 7:22; meanwhile, however, this day was not of the necessity of the Sacrament itself: otherwise they could not or should not have been circumcised after the eighth day: or certainly such an administration would have been ineffective: which is manifestly false. Since the contrary is clear from the son of Moses, Exod. 4:25, and in the infants whom the Israelites had brought with them from the desert into Palestine, Josh. 5:7. But it was not permitted to anticipate or precede the eighth day, even if the infant were in the greatest danger of death and in agony. The various reasons for this matter may be read in Ambrose, On Abraham, book 2, last chapter; Chrysostom, Homily 39 on Genesis; Augustine, Sermon 15 on the words of the Apostle, and Sermon 141 on the season, and Against Pelagius and Caelestius, book 2, chapter 11.

Fifthly, it is also asked about the instrument with which the amputation of the foreskin had to be performed, which sacred history testifies was a knife, although it does not express the material from which that knife had to be made. It is likely, however, that an iron knife was used, although there are those who interpret the Hebrew words צר and Josh. 5 חרבות צרים as stone or flint knives, which sacred history itself also confirms were in use, Exod. 4:25 and Josh. 5:2. There are, however, others, and indeed more recent ones, who think these knives were also iron: but that they are called stone because they had been made sharper against a rock or stone or whetstone: who nevertheless seem to depart from the property of the Hebrew word. Let this controversy rest with the grammarians. That certainly is confessed, that even today the Jews use iron knives in circumcising their males.

Finally, the question is raised concerning the effect of this sacrament, which we, with the Apostle, assert to have been the seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4:11. For through this sacrament, faith in Christ who was to come was conferred upon infants: and by means of this faith, an effective remedy against original sin was established: so that circumcision formerly provided the same thing that baptism provides today, regarding this effect of the remission of sins. However, a remedy was provided in circumcision not only against original sin, but also against actual sin, if there was any, both in children and in adults. For the full grace of justification was conferred upon the circumcised: and it would be impious to hope for half a pardon from GOD: as Augustine speaks, book 4, on true and false repentance, chapter 9. But it has also been shown above that the individual sacraments, and therefore circumcision as well, are not merely a cause without which not, or merely a moral cause: but are truly and properly a cause of grace and justification, and that instrumentally, not by the work performed.

Moreover, a doubt arises at this point: whether females, who were not capable of circumcision, just as male infants who were snatched away by death before the eighth day, had no remedy against original sin, or what that was or of what kind? But it is answered both briefly and sufficiently that while females indeed lacked this sealing of the covenant, which was done through the sacrament of circumcision, they nevertheless did not lack the federal promise itself, which in its scope contained females as well as males: I will be your GOD, and of your seed after you: Which promise alone could be for them a most effective remedy against all sins: provided they rested with firm faith in that seed who was to come, and who would crush the head of the serpent: indeed, in whom eternal blessing, that is, the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life, was to be obtained by all who embraced this promise with true faith. And certainly, since GOD himself instituted no external remedy or sacrament for females, it could not be to their detriment that they did not use such an external remedy. Thus, regarding the remaining male infants whom premature death snatched away before the eighth day, they were certainly in the grace of GOD by the power of the federal promise: since it is not the deprivation, but the contempt of the sacrament that damns. Let the horrendous theology of the Jesuits therefore perish, who maintain that infants who died without the use of this sacrament are damned: and likewise that females could not be saved except through some external remedy against original sin: which, however, is not made explicit in the sacred scriptures. The Sophists dream, of course, that GOD does not cleanse men from original sin otherwise than through some external sacrament: a thing which is asserted beyond and against the authority of Scripture. That GOD, certainly, who could endow John the Baptist in his mother's womb with the Holy Spirit and faith, without any external means or remedy at all: can also sanctify females, without the intervention of an external remedy, through faith alone in the federal promise: just as He also sanctified those male infants who, snatched away by premature death, could not obtain the sacrament of initiation. For that divine threat, The male whose foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people, is to be understood as concerning contempt and the reckless transgression of this commandment. And this concerns adults most of all. But infants who were deprived of the sacrament not by their own fault, but by that of their parents, we commit to divine judgment, and we maintain that the parents themselves are most guilty: For the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. Ezek. 18:20.

Latin:

VAriæ de hoc Sacramento moventur quæstiones: ac initiò quidem de Tempore controvertitur, quo illud promulgatum fuit. Accuratior autem calculus producit Annum Mundi 2047. licet alij ex recentioribus quidem Augustinus, Torniellus lib. 1. annalium ponat A. M. 2138. de quo videant Chronologi. Illud certè ex historiâ sacrâ patet, promulgationem Sacramenti hujus incidere in annum 99. Abrahami, & 13. Ismaëlis. Cur autem Abrahamo demum hoc Sacramentum fuerit datum, hæ potissimùm à Theologis assignantur rationes, quia Abrahamus primus fuerit, qui se ab infidelibus, & à cultu idolorum, divinâ Vocatione ex Ur Chaldæorum excitus, segregaverit: quia etiam Abrahamus primus promissionem, semini suo accommodatam, acceperit. Sed fortè hæc ratio est prægnantior, quòd nulla videtur dari posse caussa, ob quam necessum fuerit, ut statim post lapsum, vel certè ante Abrahami ætatem circumcisio institueretur. Nam omni illo præcedente seculo magis vigebat ratio & fides, & crebriora erant DEI immediata cum hominib9 colloquia. Atqui successu temporis fides magis magisq; per peccata hominum decrefcebat, & Deus ipse mutuos sermones hominum generi subtrahebat. Ergò Abrahami tempore Circumcisionis Sacramentum DEUS promulgare voluit, ut sic in defectu colloquiorum divinorum, fidelibus materia esset, fidem suam exercendi, alendi augendique. Præterea respectu etiam subsequentis seculi, conveniens fuit Circumcisionem institui ante legis scriptæ promulgationem, tùm quia populus DEI ab alijs populis priùs erat segregandus, quàm lex traderetur: tùm etiam, quia populus tunc erat adhuc in paucitate aliquâ, & sic faciliùs ad suscipiendam Circumcisionem persuaderi poterat.

Deindè quæritur de Objecto, Quisnám sive quæ personæ circumcidi debuerint? Si præceptum DEI, sive institutionem hujus Sacramenti consulamus, patet circumcidendos fuisse omnes masculos in domo & familiâ Abrahæ, sive adulti, sive infantes, sive servi, ijq; vel domi nati, vel emti, sive liberi fuerint. Neq; hoc sine certâ ratione factum. Etsi enim institutio hujus Sacramenti, quoniam erat opposita morbo peccati originalis, cui omnes tàm Judæi, quàm gentes erant obnoxij, ad omnes etiam pertinere videri poterat: quia tamen Sacramentum hoc erat obsignatio pacti illius, quod DEUS cum Abrahamo de CHRISTO certissimè nascituro, nec non de terrâ promissionis, quâ posteritate ejus donaturus erat, pepigit: ideò ad observatione Sacramenti hujus obligati duntaxat erant ij, ad quos pactum hoc pertinuit, filij nimirum Israel omnes, non quidé simpliciter omnes, qui quovis modo ex semine Abrahæ descendebant:sed ij præcipuè, qui ab Abrahamo per Isaaco & Jacobum ortum generis sui ducebant. Isaaco n. propriè quasi dicata fuit venturi seminis promissio, dicente Domino Gen. 17, 19. Cum ipso æternũ meum fœdus erigã, & cum semine illius post ipsum. Neq; tamen propterea Ismael cũ sua posteritate, ab hoc Sacramento erat exclusus, quin & in ipsius domo verum ac genuinum Sacramentum administratī fuit, quamdiu fœderale Sacramenti hujus formula, ego ero DEUS tuus, & seminis tui post te, unà cum amputatione præputij, & sic Sacramenti hujus substantialia integra observârunt. Postquàm verò posthabitâ promissione fœderali, externum saltem Circumcisionis ritum retinuerunt: tum etiam verum Sacramentum apud illos esse desijt. Et sanè huc respicit Scriptura afferens, Ismaëlemejectum fuisse de domo Abrahæ, Gen 17, 25. nec fore ipsum hærede eum filio: item Esavum odio fuisse habitum, Jacobī verò dilectum: Gen. 25, 21. Malach. 1, 2. Rom. 9, 13. Quæ tamen ejectio non obstitit, quo minùs aditus ipsis ad societatem fidei & salutis pateret, æquè atq; gentilibus. Creditur Job de semine Abrahæ fuisse, ille nimirùm Jobab, cujus fit mentio Genes. 36, 33. Et tamen Gregorius in prologo scribit, non legi, quòd Job fuerit circumcisus, cujus rei ea fuisse causa putatur, quod áb Abraham ortum duxerit, non per lineam Jacobi, sed per Esavum, ut ex citato jam capite 36. Geneseos patet. Quanquàm non desunt, qui ex stirpe Nahor ipsum descendisse existiment.

Quibus ita constitutis, excludebantur à Sacramento Circumcisionis.

1. Gentes, quæ non erant ex semine Abrahæ: Poterant tamen circumcidi, si vellent servare legem, Exod. 12, 44. Judith. 14, 6. Et tales vocabantur Proselytæ, ut habetur Matth 23, 15.

2. Excludebantur etiam fœmellæ, quantumvis ex stirpe Abrahæ oriundæ. Nam propter mysterium Circumcisionis, quæ in præputio membri genitalis virilis fieri debuit, fœminæ Sacramenti hujus capaces esse non poterant. Quia tamen illæ ex Patribus circumcisis ortum ducebant, nihilominus in gratiâ fœderis à DEO reputatæ fuerunt uti paulò pòst demonstrabitur, cùm de Effectu hujus Sacramenti agetur.

Tandem licèt filij Israel circumcidere jubeantur servos tùm emtitios, tú vernaculos sive dominatos: prohibeantur tamen circumcidere servos advenas sive liberos, sive mercenarios. Exo. 12. 45.

Tertiò quæritur de Subjecto. Quâ nimirúm corporis parte Circumcisio fieri debuerit? Definit Scriptura membrum genitale virile, cujus præputium amputari debuerit. Quod ipsum non sine gravi causâ factum fuisse arbitrabimur. Quia enim Sacramentum Circumcisionis debuit esse remedium contra peccatum originale: utiq; in eo membro illud peragi debuit, per quod præcipuè originalis peccati sit propagatio. Deinde quia peccati originalis fomes præcipuus est Concupiscentia, quę in membro genitali vel maximè dominatur: utiq; vel hanc etiam ob causam, membrum hoc convenientissimum Sacramenti hujus Subjectum esse potuit. Tandem quia Circumcisio erat obsignatio fœderis cum Abrahamo de semine benedicto initi, utiq; membri etiam hujus notatio, Judæos de Christo ex semine Abrahæ nascituro, monere poterat. Quia etiam præputium membri amputandum fuerat, signum erat Christum nasciturum, non ex virili semine: Quam ipsam ob causam etiam non fœminæ, sed viri sunt circumcisi, ut è fœminâ, non ex viro Christus nasciturus innueretur. Accedit tamen analogia inter regenerationem & generationem. Quâ enim parte corporis, ex parentibus generabantur infantes, ex eadem etiam Sacramentum regenerationis ut acciperent, erat conveniens.

Quartò quæritur, Cur die demùm octavo, & non statim, cùm in lucem fuerunt editi, masculos circūcidi DEUS voluerit? Ubi constans omnium est sententia, singulari DEI providentiâ hoc factū esse, quæ haud prius Circumcisionis doloribus objici voluit infantes, quàm corpore & viribus jam aliquantum confirmantiores essent facti. Fuit autem dies iste octavus de necessitate præcepti, quem antevertere, aut differre etiam non licebat, quantumvis in Sabbatum ipsum ille incideret, uti patet Joh. 7, 22. interim tamen dies iste non fuit de necessitate ipsius Sacramenti: alioqui non potuissent vel debuissent circumcidi post diem octavum: vel certè talis administratio fuisset inefficax: id quod manifestè falsum. Siquidem contrarium patet, ex filio Mosis, Exod. 4, 25. & in infantibg: quos Israëlitæ è deserto in Palæstinā secū adduxerant. Jos. 5. 7. Prævenire a. sive antevertere diem octavum non licebat, si vel maximè infans in mortis periculo & agone esset constitutus. Cujus rei causas varias legere licet apud Ambrosiu de Abrahamo lib. 2. c. ult. Chrysostomum homil 39. in Genes. Augustinum serm. 15 de verbis Apostoli: & serm. 141. de tempore, & contra Pelagium & Cœlestium lib. 2. cap. 11.

Quintò quæritur etiam de Instrumento, quo amputatio præputij fieri debuit, quod cultrū fuisse historia sacra testatur, licet non exprimat materiam, ex quâ culter ille fieri debuerit. Verisimile tamen est, fuisse adhibitum cultellū ferreum, licèt sint, quæ vocabula Hebræa צר & Jos. 5. חרבות צרים de saxeis sive petrinis cultris interpretentur, quos in usu fuisse ipsa quoq; historia sacra confirmat, Exod. 4, 25. & Jos. 5, 2. Sunt tamen alij, & quidem recentiores, qui existimant hos quoq; cultros fuisse ferreos: dici autē saxeos, quia ad petram sive lapidem aut cotem acutiores essent facti: qui tamen â proprietate vocabuli Hebræi recedere videntur. Quæ controversia sit penes Grammaticos. Illud certè in confesso est, quod hodieq; Judæi in circumcidendis suis masculis adhibeant cultros ferreos.

Tandem quæritur de Effectu hujus Sacramenti, quem nos cum Apostolo fuisse asserimus σφραγίδα τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίςεως Rom. 4, 11. Conferebatur n. per hoc Sacramentum infantibus fides in Christum venturum: & mediante hâc fide efficax constituebatur remedium contra peccatum originale: ut sic Circumcisio idem olim præstiterit, quod hodiè præstat Baptismus, quoad effectum istum remissionis peccatorum. Non autem duntaxat contra peccatum originale in Circumcisione præstabatur remedium: sed & contra peccatum actuale, si quod erat tùm in pueris, tùm in adultis. Plena enim justificationis gratia conferebatur circumcisis: & impium foret à DEO dimidiam sperare veniam: uti loquitur Augustinus, lib. 4. de verâ & falsâ pœnitentiâ. cap. 9. Sed jam supra quoq; ostensum, Sacramenta singula, ac proindè Circumcisionem etiam esse non tantùm causam sine quâ non, vel moralem duntaxat causam: sed verè ac propriè esse causam gratiæ & justificationis, idq; instrumentaliter, non ex opere operato.

Cæterùm oritur hoc loco dubium, Num fœmellæ quæ Circumcisionis non erant capaces, ut & infantes masculi, qui ante octavum diem, morte abripiebantur, nullum habuerint remedium contra peccatum originis, vel quod aut quale illud fuerit? Sed respondetur & breviter & sufficienter, caruisse quidem fœmellas hâc obsignatione fœderis, quæ fiebat per Sacramentum Circumcisionis: interim tamen eas non caruisse ipsâ promissione fœderali, quæ sub suo complexu cùm fœmellas quàm masculos continebat: Ero DEus tuus, & seminis tui post te: Quæ sola promissio potuit illis esse efficacissimum remedium adversus omnia peccata: Siquidem firmâ fide acquiescebant in semine illo venturo, & contrituro caput serpentis: imò in quo benedictio æterna, hoc est, remissio peccatorum, justitia & vita æterna obtingere debebat, omnibus verâ fide promissionem hanc amplectentibus. Et sanè cùm DEUS ipse nullum externum remedium, sive Sacramentum pro fœmellis instituerit: utiq; fraudi ipsis esse non potuit, quod tali externo remedio non sunt usæ. Sic quoad reliquos infantes masculos, quos mors præmatura ante diem octavum abripuit, illi certè vi promissionis fœderalis erant in gratiâ DEI: Siquidem non privatio, sed contemptus Sacramenti damnat. Facesfat proindè horrenda Jesuvvitarum Theologia, statuentium, Infantes, qui sine Sacramenti hujus usu decesserunt, damnatos esse: fœmellas item salvari non potuisse, nisi per externum aliquod remedium contra Peccatum originis: quod tamen in sacris non fit expressum. Somniant nimirùm Sophistæ, DEUM non mundare homines à peccato Originis aliter, quàm per aliquod Sacramentum externum: id quod tamen præter & contra Scripturæ autoritatem asseritur. Ille certè DEUS, qui Johannem Baptistam in utero matris donare potuit Spiritu Sancto & fide, sine ullo prorsus externo medio aut remedio: idem potest etiam sanctificare fœmellas, absq; interventu externi remedij, per solam fidem in promissionem fœderalem: quemadmodum sanctificavit ipsos quoque infantes masculos, qui præmaturâ morte abrepti, Sacramento initiationis potiri non potuerunt. Divina enim illa interminatio, Masculus cujus præputium circumcisum non fuerit, delebitur anima illa de populo suo; Intelligenda est de contemtu, & temerariâ transgressione præcepti hujus. Et hoc quidem adultos potissimùm concernit. Infantes autem qui non suâ, sed parentum culpâ Sacramento privati sunt, divino judicio committimus, ipsosq́; parentes maximè reos esse statuimus: Filius enim non portabit iniquitatem patris. Ezech. 18, 20.


### Chapter III. On the mutual agreement and difference of the Sacraments of the…: II. On the Paschal Lamb

At what time this sacrament was instituted, and by what rites it was to be celebrated, one may see from chapter 12 of Exodus. We, having now passed over these things as having nothing to do with our present purpose, have only this task: whether the celebration of the Paschal Lamb should be called truly and properly a sacrament, or rather a sacrifice? For theologians do not hold one and the same opinion on this point. And indeed, these circumstances seem to suggest that the nature of a sacrifice might apply here: 1. that this rite was instituted in commemoration of that benefit by which GOD led the people of Israel out of Egypt: by which name it might seem to be more like a peace offering than a sacrament. 2. This rite seems to have borne primarily the type of Christ slaughtered and sacrificed on the cross: in which respect it might again be thought to be alien to the nature of a sacrament. 3. The very immolation or slaughtering of the Lamb approaches the nature of a sacrifice more than that of a sacrament. But these reasons are not of such weight or moment that we should allow ourselves to be moved from the received opinion of the Church: rather, we are most persuaded that this rite of the Paschal Lamb was truly and properly a sacrament: and this for the following reasons. I. The universal consensus of the Church explicitly testifies to this. II. In Exod. 12, the commandment was given not about sacrificing, but about slaughtering the Lamb. III. This slaughtering was done not by a priest, but by the whole multitude: which conflicts with a sacrifice properly so called. IV. Not every slaughtering presupposes a sacrifice, but only that which was joined with burning. Now, the end of the slaughtering of the Paschal Lamb was not burning, but eating. V. There were indeed two different things in the rite of the Paschal Lamb, namely 1. Slaughtering, 2. Eating: both of which we perhaps not unwillingly concede to have been typical of the sacrifice of Christ: but with this clear restriction, that we maintain the type of the slaughtering was fulfilled on the altar of the cross: but the type of the eating in the Eucharist: so that just as the commemoration of the sacrifice of the death of CHRIST, which is done today in the use of the Eucharist, does not take away the nature of a Sacrament properly so called: so neither could that type of the slaughter of the paschal lamb subvert the nature of a Sacrament, which consisted in the reason of its end in eating, not in sacrificing: for the lamb was not slaughtered by the Israelites so that it might be offered to God: but so that it might be eaten. VI. The Israelites slaughtered the lamb in Egypt: But yet in Egypt a Sacrifice ought not to have been offered, as Moses testifies: Exod. 8, 26. VII. Just as the eating of the first lamb provided bodily strength to the people for completing the flight from Egypt: so in later times, it provided to the faithful an increase of grace, and strength of faith, as an ἐφόδιον or viaticum on the way of pilgrimage: just as the proper effect of the Eucharist in the New Testament is not to sanctify anew: which is the property of Baptism: But to increase grace and to add strength and increment to faith. Whence the nature of a Sacrament properly so called, as much concerning the Paschal Lamb as concerning the Eucharist, evidently shines forth. VIII. Finally, unless this Israelitic rite had been a Sacrament, it would follow that in the Old Testament there was absolutely no Sacrament which had prefigured the Sacrament of the Eucharist: When yet these things correspond to each other mutually in every way or even most greatly. For this duty cannot or ought not to be assigned to the Levitical Sacrifices, because among heterogeneous species such an analogical prefiguration cannot have a place: but all the power of figuring, which the Sacrifices of the Old Testament had, was completed in prefiguring the unique Sacrifice of CHRIST, performed on the altar of the cross.

And although the Paschal Lamb, in that part in which it contained the memory of the liberation from Egypt and from the striking Angel, was not a Sacrament, no more than our Eucharist also has not from that the appellation of a Sacrament, by which it comprehends the memory of our redemption, which was made by the precious Blood of the immaculate Lamb: yet in that reason it was a Sacrament, in which it was a sign of the confirmation of present faith, from which same fruit the Eucharist also received the appellation of a Sacrament.

The essential parts of this Sacrament were two: Earthly and Heavenly. The Earthly was the eating of the flesh of the Paschal Lamb: as also the distribution of the lamb's blood, which indeed did not yield to eating or drinking: but was applied to the smearing of the doorposts. The Heavenly was the typical Flesh of CHRIST, and the typical Blood of the same: as was shown above in the first chapter.

Latin:

QUlo tempore institutum fuerit hoc Sacramentum, quibus item ritibus celebrari debuerit, ex cap. 12. Exodi videre licet. Nos his jam prætermissis, tanquàm ad præsens institutum nostrum nihil attinentibus, id duntaxat pensi habemus, Utrum celebratio Agni Paschalis verè ac propriè Sacramentum, an verò sacrificium potius dici debeat? Neq́; enim unam eandemq́; sententiam hâc in parte tenent Doctores Theologi. Et sanè Sacrificij rationem hîc militare, fortè hæ Circumstantiæ innuere videntur: 1. quòd ritus iste institutus fuit in commemorationem illius beneficij, quo DEUS populum Israëliticum ex Aegypto eduxit: Quo sanè nomine magis instar hostiæ pacificæ, quàm Sacramentum fuisse videri queat. 2. Christi in cruce mactati immolatiq́; typum potissimùm ritus iste gessisse videtur: quo respectu iterum à Sacramenti naturâ putari queat esse alienus. 3. Ipsa immolatio sive mactatio Agni, ad Sacrificij magis, quàm Sacramenti naturam accedit. Verùm rationes hæ tanti non sunt ponderis aut momenti, ut à receptâ Ecclesiæ sententiâ dimoveri nos patiamur: quin ritum istum Agni Paschalis, verè ac propriè fuisse Sacramentum, habemus persuasissimum: idq́; ob sequentes rationes. I. Universalis Ecclesiæ consensus hoc disertè contestatur. II. Exod. 12. non de sacrificando, sed de mactando Agno datum fuit præceptum. III. Mactatio hæc fiebat non à Sacerdote, sed ab universâ multitudine: id quod cùm Sacrificio propriè sic dicto pugnat. IV. Non omnis mactatio præsupponit Sacrificium, sed ea demùm, quæ cum combustione erat conjuncta. Jam verò finis mactationis Agni Paschalis non erat combustio, sed manducatio. V. Duo quidem fuerint diversa in ritu Agni Paschalis, nempe 1. Mactatio, 2. Manducatio: quod utrumq́; fortè haud illibenter concedimus, typicum fuisse ad Sacrificium Christi: sed cum luculentâ hac restrictione, ut Mactationis typum in arâ crucis: Manducationis verò typum in Eucharistiâ adimpletum esse statuamus: ita ut quemadmodum commemoratio Sacrificij mortis CHRISTI, quæ fit hodiè in usu Evcharistiæ, non tollit naturam Sacramenti propriè sic dicti: ita neq; typus ille mactationis agni paschalis, potuerit subvertere naturam Sacramenti, quæ consistebat ratione finis in manducando, non in sacrificando: neq; enim ab Israëlitis mactabatur agnus, ut offerretur Deo: sed ut manducaretur. VI. Agnum mactarunt Israëlitæ in Ægypto: Atqui in Ægypto Sacrificium offerri non debuit, teste Moyse: Exod. 8, 26. VII. Sicut primi agni manducatio corporale robur præstabat populo ad fugam ex Ægypto perficiendam: ita posteris temporibus, augmentum gratiæ, & robur fidei, tanquam ἐφόδιον sive viaticum in viâ peregrinationis, fidelibus præstitit: quemadmodum Eucharistiæ in Novo Testamento proprius effectus est, non de novo sanctificare: id quod Baptismi proprium est: Sed augere gratiam & fidei robur atq; incrementum addere. Undè natura Sacramenti propriè sic dicti, tam circà Agnum Paschalem, quàm circà Eucharistiam evidenter elucescit. VIII. Tandem nisi ritus iste Israëliticus Sacramentum fuisset, consequens foret, in Veteri Testamento nullum prorsus fuisse Sacramentum, quod Sacramentum Eucharistiæ præfigurasset: Cùm tamen sibi ista invicem undequaque vel maximè respondeant. Neq; enim hoc munus adsignari potest aut debet Sacrificiis Leviticis, propterea quod inter species Heterogeneas talis analogica præfiguratio locum habere nequit: sed omnis figurandi potestas, quam Sacrificia Veteris Testamenti habebant, absolvebatur in præfigurando unico CHRISTI Sacrificio, in arâ crucis peracto.

Et quamvis Agnus Paschalis eâ parte, quâ memoriam liberationis ex Ægypto & ab Angelo percussore continebat, Sacramentum non fuit, nihilo magis, quâm nostra etiam Eucharistiæ non ab eo Sacramenti appellationem habet, quo memoriam redemtionis nostræ comprehendit, quæ præcioso Sanguine Agni immaculati facta est: eâ tamen ratione Sacramentum fuit, quâ præsentis fidei confirmationis signum fuit, à quo eodem fructu Eucharistia etiam Sacramenti appellationem accepit.

Partes essentiales hujus Sacramenti fuerunt duæ: Terrena & Cœlestis. Terrena erat manducatio carnium Agni Paschalis: ut & Sanguinis agnini dispensatio, qui quidé in esum aut potum non cedebat: sed ad postium infectionem adhibebatur. Cœlestis erat Caro CHRISTI typica, & Sanguis ejusdem typicus: uti suprà capite primo ostensum.


### Chapter IV. and Last. On the Number of the Sacraments of the New Testament

The controversy concerning the Number of the Sacraments of the New Testament exists between us and the Romanists alone, who constitute seven Sacraments, and those most properly so called. For thus Canon 1, Session 7 of the Council of Trent has this: If anyone shall say that the Sacraments of the new law were not all instituted by JESUS CHRIST: or that there are more or fewer than seven, namely Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, Order and Matrimony: or also that any one of these seven is not truly and properly a Sacrament, let him be anathema. We determine that this Canon is true only concerning Baptism and the Eucharist. The Romanists, however, labor anxiously to this very day for confirming and establishing the remaining five also of the feigned Sacraments: but with a clearly vain effort: as will be shown a little later specifically concerning each one. The Jesuits, noticing the vanity of their cause, presuppose three hypotheses, which being granted, they are finally to descend into the arena with us.

The first is: For the confirmation of the septenary number, a place of Scripture is not to be demanded from them, in which it is said that there are seven Sacraments: but it is enough if all seven are gathered from different places of Scripture.

The second: It is not to be demanded that it be proved that these seven are expressly called Sacraments in the Scriptures: but it is enough if the thing itself is shown in the Scriptures.

Tertia: It is not to be required of them that they prove this certain number precisely from the Fathers: but it is enough if it is proved that the notion and reason of a Sacrament properly so called, and sometimes even the appellation itself of a Sacrament, has been attributed by the Fathers to these seven signs.

Concerning which hypotheses, although we do not greatly move a dispute with them: yet we hold this as most clearly perceived: that neither can seven Sacraments properly so called be gathered from different places of Scripture: nor is the thing itself shown in the Scriptures: nor can this Septenary be confirmed by any pact from the Fathers.

Let us therefore banish this rancid fiction from the field and boundaries of the Church, and we conclude irrefragably from the Scriptures themselves, from the analogy of faith, from the unanimous consent of Orthodox Antiquity, and of the Catholic Church, in this manner, that there are neither more nor fewer Sacraments of the New Testament besides these two, Baptism and the Supper of the Lord.

I. Argument: The Sacraments of the New Testament, since they agree with the Sacraments of the Old Testament in Author, Essential Parts, Ends, and Efficacy, ought also to agree in Number. But the binary number of Sacraments, as even the Jesuits themselves admit, obtained in the Old Testament: Therefore, the same binary number of Sacraments will also agree entirely with the New Testament. The connection of the major premise is necessarily proven to be most true by the very nature of type and antitype, so much so that if on either side more Sacraments are given, it is necessary that just as many be given on the other: unless one wishes to posit shadows without bodies, or bodies without shadows: which is absurd and repugnant to the analogy of faith.

II. From the nature of Baptism and the Lord's Supper, which both sides confess to be truly and properly two Sacraments, a most certain judgment can and ought to be made as to

Latin:

Controversia de Numero Sacramentorũ Novi Testamenti, cùm solis Romanensibus nobis intercedit, qui septem constituunt Sacramenta, eaque propriíssimè sic dicta. Sic enim hoc habet Canon 1. Sess. 7. Concilij Tridentini: Si quis dixerit, Sacramenta novæ legis no fuisse omnia à JESU CHRISTO instituta: aut vel plura vel pauciora, quàm septem, videlicet Baptismum, Confirmationem, Eucharistiam, Pœnitentiam, Extrema Unctionem, Ordinem & Matrimonium: aut etiam aliquod horum septem, non esse verè & proprie Sacramentum, anathema sit. Nos Canonem istum non nisi de Baptismo & Eucharistiâ verum esse statuimus. Romanenses autem pro confirmandis stabiliendísq; reliquis etiam quinq; commentitijs Sacramentis in hunc usq; diem anxiè laborant: sed irrito planè conatu: uti paulò pòst in specie de singulis ostendetur. Jesuvitæ causæ suæ vanitatem animadvertentes, tres præsupponunt hypotheses, quibus concessis, in arenam demum nobiscum descensuri.

Prima est Pro Confirmatione numeri septenarij non esse ab ipsis exigendum Scripturæ locum, in quo dicatur, septem esse Sacramenta: sed satis esse, si ex diversis Scripturæ locis omnia septem colligantur.

Altera: Non esse postulandum, ut probetur, septem ista in Scripturis expressè vocari Sacramenta: sed satis esse, si res ipsa in Scripturis monstretur.

Tertia: Non requirendum ab ipsis, ut probent hunc certum numerum præcisè ex Patribus: sed satis esse, si probetur, à Patribus notionem & rationem Sacramenti propriè sic dicti, septem istis signis, interdum etiam appellationem ipsam, Sacramenti esse tributam.

De quibus hypothesibus tametsi litem ipsis magnoperè non movemus: illud tamen habemus perspectissimum: neq; ex diversis Scripturæ locis septem Sacramenta propriè sic dicta colligi: neq; rem ipsam in Scripturis monstrari: neq; ex Patribus Septenarium istum ullo pacto confirmari posse.

Relegamus proindè ex agro & finibus Ecclesiæ rancidum hoc commentum, & neq; plura, neq; pauciora esse Sacramenta Novi Testamenti præter duo hæc, Baptismum & Cœnam Domini, ex Scripturis ipsis, ex analogiâ fidei, ex unanimi consensu Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, & Catholicæ Ecclesiæ irrefragabiliter colligimus, in hunc modum.

I. Argumentu: Sacramenta Novi Testamenti, cum Sacramentis Veteris Testamenti, uti Autore, Partibus Essentialibus, Finibus & Efficaciâ conveniunt: ita Numero quoq; convenire debent. Atqui binarius Sacramentorum numerus ipsis etiam fatentibus Jesuvitis, in Veteri Testamento obtinuit: Ergò idem binarius Sacramentorum numerus Novi etiam Testamento ex asse conveniet. Connexum Majoris ipsa Typi & antitypi ratio necessariò evincit esse verissimum, usq; adeò, ut si alterutra ex parte, plura dentur Sacramenta, ex alterâ totidem dari, necesse sit: nisi vel umbras sine corporibus; vel corpora sine umbris statuere quis velit: id quod absurdum, & analogiæ fidei repugnans.

II. Ex naturâ Baptismi & Cœnæ Dominicæ, quæ duo verè ac propriè esse Sacramenta, utrinq; in confesso est, judicium certissimum fieri potest ac debet,


### Chapter IV. and Last. On the Number of the Sacraments of the New Testament: Requisites of a true Sacrament

whether more Sacraments properly so called can be admitted. Yet those requirements, which are found in Baptism and the Lord's Supper, and necessarily pertain to the constitution of a Sacrament properly so called: cannot be accommodated to the remaining five Sacraments of the Papists. Therefore they are not Sacraments properly so called.

The major premise is in itself most certain: For those things which ought to share in a definition, it is necessary that they also be of the same nature and essence.

The minor premise contains the principal κρινόμενον [point of judgment], namely, do those essential and inevitably necessary requirements of a Sacrament properly so called belong to the five fictitious Sacraments of the Papists? We deny it: they affirm it. We confirm our negative, however, by an enumeration of those six requirements which necessarily pertain to constituting the definition of a Sacrament properly so called.

I. It is: that some sacramental rite be instituted by Christ himself, and indeed immediately: since to institute true and proper Sacraments belongs to none but Christ alone: a fact which even the Scholastic Doctors have acknowledged, and indeed Bellarmine himself does not deny, writing thus: True Sacraments could be instituted by Christ alone: by which reasoning he proves that holy water, the Sign of the cross, Exorcism, and similar ceremonies are not Sacraments, because it is not established whether they were instituted by Christ, or indeed by the Apostles.

The antecedent, however, is most evidently proved 1. thence: Because Sacraments are a part of divine worship that is by no means the least: Yet no divine worship, either in whole or in part, proceeds from any human institution, Therefore. 2. Then: Sacraments are the means and organs by which the sealing of the grace of GOD, and of the merit of Christ, is effected in the faithful for salvation. Yet no human force or power can bestow this efficacy upon its own inventions. Therefore.

II. That it be instituted by Christ himself, in the time of the New Testament, and indeed at the very time of the consummation. For since the administration of the Sacraments pertains to the perfect form of the Church, and indeed not of the Jewish, but of the Evangelical Church: certainly their institution also ought not to have taken place before the consummation of this saving work had been made by Christ.

III. That the sacramental rite have a visible and external Element joined to it: a fact which the very definition of a Sacrament evinces, which names a Sacrament a visible Sign: and according to Augustine, it becomes a Sacrament only then, when the word comes to the element.

IV. That some sacramental rite have a certain word of command, by which men are ordered at all times to do what Christ, instituting the Sacrament, either did himself, or willed to be done by us: such as are the words of command: Baptize, Eat, Drink.

V. That it also have an annexed word of promise, not indeed of just any kind: but one proper to Evangelical grace, or grace that makes one pleasing [to God].

VI. That some sacramental rite be common to all the faithful, no less than the grace of the Gospel itself pertains to all believers. Bellarmine also seems to affirm this very thing, writing in book 2 de Sacr. cap. 25. Sacraments, and the knowledge of them, pertain to the practice of individual men.

Now if the subsumption be made, that is, the accommodation of those six κριτηρίων [criteria] to the septenary number of the Romanists, it will be most clearly evident without any difficulty that the name and definition of a Sacrament properly so called belong to at least two, namely Baptism and the Eucharist: but that the remaining five are to be simply expunged from the class of Sacraments of the New Testament: as will be demonstrated a little later in detail concerning each one.

The third and final argument of our proof can be sought from the unanimous consent of antiquity and the whole Catholic Church. For if that Papal dogma had ever been received in the Church, certainly even one of the Orthodox Fathers would have betrayed it. But in truth, there is absolutely no one among so many who would confirm this number of seven sacraments. Therefore. What? That before Hugh of St. Victor and Peter Lombard this opinion was never heard: so that Lombard himself, who nevertheless most diligently collected the testimonies of the Fathers, brings forward absolutely nothing in this place, and expressly confesses with Hugh that not all those seven sacraments were immediately instituted by CHRIST. Nay rather, Hugh, book 1 de Sacramentis, part 9, chapter 6, defines no certain number of sacraments at all, but recounts the consecration of water, oil, salt, and some other things among the sacraments.

As regards the Councils, none exists except the Florentine and the Tridentine, in which this number of sacraments is approved and sanctioned.

Thus the entire ancient Church of Christ acknowledged no more than two Sacraments of the New Testament: as Clement of Rome in book 1 of the Recognitions; Justin the Philosopher and Martyr in Apology 2; Tertullian in books 1 and 4 against Marcion, and in De Corona Militis. Cyprian in book 2, Epistle 1, says: Then at last they can be fully sanctified and be sons of God, if they participate in both Sacraments. Cyril of Jerusalem in his Catecheses mentions only two Sacraments. Ambrose wrote a book expressly on the Ecclesiastical Sacraments, but he commemorates only two Sacraments, Baptism and the Lord’s Supper: Augustine in book 3 of De Doctrina Christiana, chapter 9, says: The Lord himself and apostolic discipline have handed down a few, and those most easy to perform, most august to understand, and most chaste to observe, such as the Sacrament of Baptism and the celebration of the Body and Blood of the Lord. Augustine again in De Symbolo ad Catechumenos. These are, he says, the twin sacraments of the Church. Dionysius the Areopagite de Hierarchia Ecclesiastica recognizes neither Penance nor Matrimony as sacraments: and he celebrates the anointing not of the sick, but of the dead. Gregory the Great established no more than three sacraments: Baptism, Chrism, and the Body and Blood of the Lord. He referred Chrism, however, to Baptism. And what need is there of many words, when the entire Orthodox antiquity agrees in this, that the sacraments of the New Testament flowed from the side of Christ: namely, the water of Baptism and the Eucharistic Blood. But the five falsely-named sacraments can in no way be derived from the side of Christ.

But to return to the Romanists, it must first be observed in this place how they are accustomed to establish the septenary number in general. They proceed in this way.

I. The argument is this: There ought to be as many Sacraments, properly so called, as are required and suffice for a man to be perfected in every way regarding the Christian religion or the spiritual life. But these are seven: Therefore, there are also seven Sacraments. They prove the major premise from the cause for which the Sacraments were instituted in part, namely, that man might be perfected in worship and religion: and they are accustomed to demonstrate this from a comparison of the spiritual life with the bodily life. They strive to confirm the minor premise by an enumeration of the seven ways by which a man is perfected in the bodily life: which are: 1. Generation: 2. Growth. 3. Nutrition: 4. Remedy against diseases. 5. Remedy against remnants and Purgation: 6. Propagation: 7. Governance. They maintain that individual Sacraments are ordained for each of these in the spiritual life, so that by Baptism a man is regenerated and receives spiritual being: by Confirmation he is strengthened: by the Eucharist he is nourished: by Penance the fallen is repaired: by external Unction he is prepared for the final departure: by Matrimony he is multiplied: by Order the number of the ministers of the Church is increased for the governance of the whole body.

II. Argument. As many as are the mortal sins: and likewise as many as are the defects or penalties: so many also ought to be the remedies against them: and consequently, so many also the Sacraments. But there are seven mortal sins. Therefore. They corroborate the connection of the whole argument from the fact that Baptism is a remedy primarily against original sin: Penance against actual sin: Extreme Unction against the remnants of sins: The remaining four against the penalties, as they call them: for example: Confirmation against weakness in power: the Eucharist against malice in the will: Matrimony against concupiscence in the appetite: Order against ignorance in the intellect. As for venial sins, they say that other remedies are directly established for removing them: namely, holy water, the blessings of Bishops, the beating of the breast, and the like.

III. Argument. There are seven Sacraments because they dispose us to the seven virtues, namely, the three Theological and the four Cardinal. For Baptism is the Sacrament of faith: Confirmation, of hope: (according to others, and of fortitude) the Eucharist, of charity: Penance, of justice: Extreme Unction, of perseverance (according to others, of hope): Order, of prudence: Matrimony, of temperance.

IV. There are seven Sacraments because there are seven diversities of men in the Church of GOD: the first is of those entering, for whom Baptism is ordained: the second is of those fighting, for whom Confirmation is suitable: the third is of those recovering strength, for whom the Eucharist is ordained: the fourth is of those rising again, for whom Penance is instituted: the fifth is of those ministering, for whom Order is given: the sixth is of those introducing new soldiers, for whom Matrimony is instituted: the seventh is of those departing from the militia, for whom Extreme Unction is suitable.

V. And the final argument is sought from the dignity and perfection of the number seven. The world was created in seven days. Therefore, in order for the Recreation to correspond in number to the creation, there had to be seven Sacraments. Whence they are commanded in expiations either to offer seven animals, or to perform the sprinkling of blood seven days or times, or to celebrate festivals: Exod. 29. Levit. 4. 8. 13. 14. 15. Num. 19. Deut. 15: Thus Naaman the Syrian was commanded to wash seven times in the Jordan to cleanse his leprosy. 2 Kings 5. But these arguments are too futile to need refutation. For by the same arguments the septenary number of Sacraments ought to have obtained in the Old Testament as well: since the same virtues, the same sins and defects, and the same mysteries had a place there. Furthermore, if the convenience of a number ought to be looked at in this part, a ternary, or a quinary, or some other could be elicited with no trouble and with equal firmness of collection.

But someone might ask in this place, if there are only two Sacraments properly so called, how both Philip and Luther dared to refer Absolution and Order among the Sacraments: so that the Apology of the Augsburg Confession approves this opinion of Luther and Philip in express words. But it is most correctly answered that this was done by them improperly, and because of some analogy or similarity which they are represented as having with the Sacraments properly so called. For in Absolution the promise of the Gospel is denounced specifically to individuals: and in some Churches the external ceremony of the Imposition of hands is also used: Which very ceremony is also accustomed to be used in Ordination. Because of this analogy and similarity, therefore, the Apology of the Augsburg Confession and other Orthodox Doctors did not hesitate at all to refer Absolution and Ordination among the Sacraments: but with the word Sacrament taken in a loose and improper, or analogical, signification. For if this word is used in its proper signification, the Analogy itself expressly denies that all those things which have a command of GOD, and to which promises are added, can be called Sacraments: otherwise, it says, prayers also, alms, afflictions, and many other things would have to be numbered in the place of Sacraments. Thus Luther writes in the book on the Babylonian Captivity: We call those Sacraments properly which have signs annexed to them: the others, because they are not bound to signs, are bare promises. Whence it happens that, if we wish to speak properly (rigidly), there are only two Sacraments in the Church of GOD, Baptism and the Bread, since in these alone do we have both the divinely instituted sign and the promise of the remission of sins.

These things having been premised in general, let us now see specifically and briefly concerning each of the so-called Sacraments of the Papists.

Latin:

nùm plura Sacramenta propriè sic dicta admitti possint. Atqui requisita illa, quæ in Baptismo & Cænâ Domini reperiuntur, & ad constitutionem Sacramenti propriè sic dicti, necessariò pertinent: reliquis quinque Pontificiorum Sacramentis, accommodari non possunt. Ergò non sunt Sacramenta propriè sic dicta.

Major per se est certissima: Quæ enim definitione communicare debent, ea ejusdem etiam sint naturæ & essentiæ necesse est.

Minor continet principale κρινόμενον, An nimirùm essentialia illa & inevitabilitèr necessaria requisita Sacramenti propriè sic dicti, competant quinq; fictitiis Pontificiorum Sacramentis? Nos negamus: illi ajunt. Negativam autem confirmamus nostram, enumeratione sex illorum requisitorum, quæ ad constituendam definitionem Sacramenti propriè sic dicti, necessariò pertinent.

I. Est: ut ab ipso Christo, & quidem immediatè, ritus aliquis Sacramentalis sit institutus: Siquidem Sacramenta vera & propria instituere, non est, nisi solius Christi: id quod Scholastici etiam Doctores agnoverunt, imò bellarminus ipse non diffitetur, sic scribens: Vera Sacramenta à solo Christo institui potuerunt: quâ ipsiratione probat, aquam benedictam, Signum crucis, Exorcismum, & similes ceremonias non esse Sacramenta, quia non constat, Num à Christo institutæ sint, an verò ab Apostolis.

Antecedens autem evidentissimè probatur 1. indè: Quia Sacramenta sunt pars minimè postremacultûs divini: Atqui nullus cultus divinus vel ex toto vel ex parte, ab ullâ institutione humanâ proficiscitur, Ergò. 2. Deindè: Sacramenta sunt media atq; organa, quibus gratiâ DEI, & meriti Christi, in fidelibus ad salutem fit obsignatio. Atqui nulla vis aut potestas humana suis inventis hanc vim potest largiri. Ergò.

II. Ut ab ipso Christo sit institutum, tempore Novi Testamenti, & quidem ipso consummationis tempore. Cùm enim Sacramentorum administratio ad perfectam Ecclesiæ formam pertineat, & Ecclesiæ quidem non Judaicæ, sed Evangelicæ: utiq; eorundem etiam institutio non priùs fieri debuit, quàm à Christo salutaris hujus operis facta esset consummatio.

III. Ut ritus Sacramentalis habeat conjunctum Elementum visibile & externum: id quod ipsa Sacramenti definitio evincit, quæ Sacramentum nominat visibile Signum: & secundum Augustinum, tùm demum fit Sacramentum, quando verbum accedit ad elementum.

IV. Ut ritus aliquis Sacramentalis habeat certum verbum mandati, quo jubeantur homines omnibus temporibus facere, quod Christus instituens Sacramentum, vel ipse fecit, vel à nobis fieri voluit: qualia verba mandati sunt: Baptizate, Comedite, Bibite.

V. Ut habeat etiam annexum verbum promissionis, non quidem cujusvis: sed gratiæ Evangelicæ, seu gratum facientis proprium.

VI. Ut ritus aliquis Sacramentalis communis sit omnium fidelium, haud minùs, quàm ipsa gratia Evangelij ad omnes credentes pertinet. Videtur hoc ipsum Bellarminus quoq; affirmare, scribens lib. 2. de Sacr. cap. 25. Sacramenta, & eorundem cognitio, ad singulorum hominum praxin pertinet.

Jam si fiat subsumtio, hoc est, sex istorum κριτηρίων accommodatio, ad septenarium numerum Romanensium, nullo negotio patebit clarissimè, duobus saltem, Baptismo nimirùm & Eucharistia, nomen ac definitionem Sacramenti propriè sic dicti competere: reliqua verò quinq; ex classe Sacramentorum Novi Testamenti simpliciter expungenda esse: uti paulò pòst in specie de singulis demonstrabitur.

Tertium & postremum Probationis nostrae argumentum ex Unanimi consensu Antiquitatis, & totius Ecclesiae Catholicae peti potest. Si enim unquàm dogma istud Pontificium in Ecclesia receptum fuisset, certè vel unus ex Orthodoxis Patribus illud prodidisset. At verò nullus omninò est ex tam multis, qui hunc septenarium Sacramentorum numeru confirmaret. Ergò. Quid? quod ante Hugonem de S. Victore, & Petrum Lombardum haec opinio nunquàm audita fuit: Ita ut Lombardus ipse, qui tamen Patrum testimonia diligentissimè collegit, hoc loco nulla prorsus in medium adferat, & expressè cum Hugone fateatur, non omnia illa septem Sacramenta à CHRISTO immediatè esse instituta. Quin imò Hugo lib. 1. de Sacramentis, part. 9. cap. 6. nullum prorsus certum definit Sacramentorum numerum, sed consecrationem aquae, olei, salis, & nonnulla alia inter Sacramenta recenset.

Quoad Concilia, nullum extat praeter Florentinum & Tridentinum, in quibus hic numerus Sacramentorum approbetur, & sanciatur.

Sic universa vetus Christi Ecclesia, non nisi duo agnovit Sacramenta Novi Testamenti: ut Clemens Romanus lib. 1. recognitionum: Justinus Philosophus & Martyr in Apolog. 2. Tertull. lib. 1. & 4. contra Marcionem, & de Corona militis. Cyprianus lib. 2. Epist. 1. Tunc demùm, inquit, planè sanctificari, & filij DEI esse possunt, si utroq; Sacramento participent. Cyrillus Hierosolymitano in Catechismis suis, duorum tantùm Sacramentoru meminit. Ambrosius ex professo librum scripsit de Sacramentis Ecclesiasticis, sed duo tantùm Sacramenta commemorat, Baptismum & Cœnam Domini: August. lib. 3. de doctr. Christ. cap. 9. Pauca, inquit, eaq; factu facillima, intellectu augustissima, & observatione castissima, ipse Dominus & Apostolica tradidit disciplina, sicuti est Baptismi Sacramentum, & celebratio Corporis ac Sangvinis Dominici. Augustino iterum de Symbolo ac Catech. Haec sunt, inquit, Ecclesia gemina Sacramenta. Dionysius Areopagita de Hierach. Eccl. neq; Poenitentia, neq; Matrimonii pro Sacramentis agnoscit: & unctione non Infirmorum, sed Mortuorum celebrat. Gregorius M. non nisi tria Sacramenta statuit, Baptismum, Chrisma, Corpus & Sangvine Domini. Chrisma autem ad Baptismum referebat. Et quid multis opus, cùm universa Antiquitas Orthodoxa in eo consentiat, quòd Sacramenta Novi Testamenti ex Christi latere fluxerint: Aqua nimirú Baptismi, & Sangvis Eucharisticus. Quinq; auté ψευδώνυμα Sacramenta, ex Christi latere nullo modo deduci possunt.

Sed ut ad Romanenses redeamus, cumprimis hoc loco observandum fuerit, quo pacto in genere septenarium numerum stabilire soleant. Sic autem illi progrediuntur.

I. Ratio est hæc: Tot debent esse Sacramenta propriè sic dicta, quot requiruntur, & sufficiunt, ut homo omnibus modis perficiatur, quoad Religionem Christianam, sive vitam Spiritualem. Atqui hæc sunt septem: Ergò septem etiam sunt Sacramenta. Majorem probant ex causâ, propter quàm sunt instituta Sacramenta ex parte, nempè ut homo perficiatur in cultu & religione: idque demonstrare solent ex comparatione vitæ Spiritualis cum corporali. Minorem confirmare student enumeratione septem modorum, quibus homo in vitâ corporali perficitur: qui sunt: 1. Generatio: 2. Argumentatio. 3. Nutritio: 4. Remedium contra morbos. 5. Remedium contra reliquias & Expurgatio: 6. Propagatio: 7. Gubernatio. Singulis istis in vitâ spirituali singula Sacramenta esse ordinata dictitant, ita ut per Baptismum homo regeneretur, & accipiat esse spirituale: per Confirmationem roboretur: per Eucharistiam nutriatur: per Pœnitentiam lapsus reparetur: per Unctionem externam, ad finalem exitum præparetur: per Matrimonium multiplicetur: per Ordinem augeatur numerus ministrorū Ecclesiæ ad toti9 corporis regimen.

II. Ratio. Quot sunt peccata mortalia: quot item defectus, sive pœnalitates: tot etiam debent esse remedia contra illa: & per consequens, tot etiam Sacramenta. Atqui septem sunt peccata mortalia. Ergò. Connexum totius argumenti indè corroborant, quia Baptismus sit remedium contra peccatum originale præcipuè: Pœnitentia contra actuale: Unctio extrema contra reliquias peccatorum: Reliqua quatuor contra pœnalitates, quas vocant: verbi gratiâ: Confirmatio contra imbecillitatem in potentiâ: Eucharistia contra malitiam in voluntate: Matrimonium contra concupiscentiam in appetitu: Ordo, contra ignorantiam in intellectu. Quoad peccata venialia, illis tollendis alia constituta esse directè remedia: nempè aquam benedictam, benedictiones Episcoporum, tunsionē pectoris, & similia.

III. Ratio. Ideò septem sunt Sacramenta, quia disponunt nos ad septem virtutes, nempè tres Theologicas, & quatuor Cardinales. Nam Baptismus est Sacramentum fidei: Confirmatio, spei: (secundum alios, & fortitudinis) Eucharistia, charitatis: Pœnitentia justitiæ: Extrema Unctio, perseverantiæ (secundum alios, spei:) Ordo prudentiæ: Matrimonium temperantiæ.

IV. Ideò septem sunt Sacramenta, quia septem sunt diversitates hominum, in Ecclesiâ DEI: prima est intrantium, quibus ordinatur Baptismus: secunda est pugnantium, quibus convenit Confirmatio: tertia est vires refumentium, quibus ordinatur Eucharistia: quarta resurgentium, quibus instituta est Pœnitentia: quinta ministrantium, quibus datur Ordo: Sexta novos milites introducentium, quibus institutum est Matrimonium: septima, ex militiâ discedentium, quibus convenit Extrema Unctio.

V. Et postrema ratio petitur ex dignitate & perfectione numeri septenarij. Septem diebus mundus creatus fuit. Ergò ut Recreatio respondeat numero creationi, utique septem Sacramenta esse oportuit. Undè in expiationibus vel septem animalia offerri, vel septem diebus aut vicibus aspersio sangvinis fieri, aut festivitates celebrari jubentur: Exod. 29. Levit. 4. 8. 13. 14. 15. Num. 19. Deut. 15: Sic Naaman Syrus septies in Jordane lavari ad purgandam lepram jussus fuit. 2 Reg. 5. Verùm futiliores hæ sunt rationes, quàm ut refutatione opus habeant. Iisdem enim rationibus septenarius Sacramentorum numerus in Veteri etiam Testamento obtinere debuisset: siquidem eædem virtutes, eadem peccata & defectus eadem mysteria ibidem locum habuerunt. Deindè si numeri convenientia hâc in parte spectari debeat, nullo negotio ternarius, aut quinarius, vel alius aliquis, pari collectionis firmitudine elici posset.

Sed quærat hoc loco aliquis, si duo tantùm sint Sacramenta propriè sic dicta, quomodo tùm Philippus, tùm Lutherus, Absolutionem quoque &amp; Ordinem inter Sacramenta referre ausi fuerint: ita ut Apologia Confessionis Augustanæ disertis verbis hanc Lutheri &amp; Philippi sententiam approbet. Sed rectissimè respondetur, impropriè hoc ab ipsis factum esse, &amp; propter aliquam analogiam sive similitudinem, quam cum Sacramentis propriè sic dictis habere reprehenduntur. Nam in Absolutione promissio Evangelii propria singulis sigillatim denunciatur: ac in quibusdam Ecclesijs externa quoque ceremonia Impositionis manuum adhibetur: Quæ ipsa ceremonia in Ordinatione quoque usurpari consuevit. Propter hanc ergò analogiam &amp; similitudinem Apologia Confessionis Augustanæ, &amp; alij Doctores Orthodoxi Absolutionem &amp; Ordinationem inter Sacramenta referre minimè dubitarunt: sed Sacramēti vocabulo in laxâ &amp; impropriâ, sivè analogicâ significatione accepto. Nam si in propriâ significatione hæc vox usurpetur, ipsa Analogia difertè negat, omnes illas res, quæ mandatum DEI habent, &amp; quibus promissiones sunt additæ: Sacramenta dici posse: alias, inquit, preces quoque, Eleemosynæ, afflictiones, &amp; res complures aliæ Sacramentorum loco numerandæ essent. Sic Lutherus scribit in libro de Captiv. Babyl. Propriè ea vocamus Sacramenta, quæ annexis signis promissa sunt: cætera, quia signis alligata non sunt, nuda promissa sunt. Quo fit, ut si propriè (rigidè) loqui velimus, tantùm duo sint in Ecclesia DEI Sacramenta, Baptism9 &amp; Panis, cùm in his solis, &amp; institutum divinitùs signū, &amp; promissionē remissionis peccatorum habeam9.

His in genere præmissis, nunc in specie de singulis ψευδωνύμοις Pontificiorum Sacramentis seorsim &amp; breviter videamus.


### Chapter IV. and Last. On the Number of the Sacraments of the New Testament: I. On Confirmation

The definition of Papal Confirmation is handed down by Gabriel Biel in 4 sent. dist. 7, comprising everything that pertains to the description and explanation of Confirmation: Confirmation, he says, is the anointing of a baptized wayfaring man, consenting in some measure, or not having the use of reason before reception, performed on the forehead, in the figure of the Cross, with sanctified Chrism, by a suitable minister, together with due intention, uttering certain words, from divine institution, effectively signifying the anointing of the soul, through grace strengthening, for confessing confidently the faith of Christ. The same Gabriel explains this definition in these words: 1. It is said that it is the anointing of a baptized person, because one who is not baptized cannot be confirmed, nor receive another Sacrament, since Baptism is the door and foundation of the other Sacraments. 2. It is also said that it is of a person consenting in some way, either by themselves, as adults, and having the use of reason: or through godparents, as infants. 3. It is said to be done on the forehead, where a determined part of the body is noted, in which if it were not done, there would be no confirmation. 4. It is said in the figure of the cross, so that it may accord with the form in which it is said: I sign you with the sign of the cross: otherwise, if it were not done thus, the form would not be true. 5. It is said, with sanctified Chrism. For if it were done with holy oil, or the oil of the sick, it would not be a Sacrament. And for Chrism to be the matter of confirmation, it is not sufficient that it be made from oil and balsam, but it is necessary that it be consecrated by a Bishop. 6. It is said, by a suitable minister, that is, by a Bishop, if the Episcopate has always been distinct from the Priesthood. 7. It is said, together with due intention, because without the intention of the minister there is no Sacrament. 8. It is said, uttering certain words, where the form of the Sacrament is touched upon, which is: I sign you with the sign of the cross: I confirm you with the Chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. 9. It is said, from divine institution, where the author and institutor of this Sacrament is touched upon, 10. and finally it is added, effectively signifying the anointing of the soul etc., where the reality of this Sacrament is touched upon, which is, Grace conferred upon the soul for constantly believing, and for confessing with the mouth intrepidly without shame the faith of the crucified etc.

The Council of Trent also approved and sanctioned this confirmation, in three distinct Canons: the first of which is: If anyone shall say that the confirmation of the baptized is an idle ceremony, and not rather a true and proper Sacrament: or that it was once nothing other than a certain catechesis, by which those approaching adolescence gave an account of their faith before the Church, let him be anathema. The second: If anyone shall say that those who attribute some virtue to the sacred Chrism of confirmation are injurious to the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema. The third, If anyone shall say that the ordinary minister of holy confirmation is not the Bishop alone: but any simple Priest, let him be anathema.

The action or administration of this Sacrament is performed thus: that several short prayers are recited in set words, and peace be with you is said. But while the form of words is pronounced, the Bishop, with his thumb dipped into the Chrism or oil previously exorcised, anoints the one to be confirmed on the forehead in the figure of the cross: then with his whole hand he strikes a blow on his face: 3. he binds the forehead smeared with ointment with a white linen cloth: 4. he commands that the head of the confirmed not be washed before the seventh day, lest any of the Chrism be taken away or perish at the same time: and finally he commends the one thus confirmed to the godparents or sponsors.

They attribute a much more excellent and effective end or Effect to this Sacrament than to Baptism: 1. on the part of the minister dispensing it, while they write that confirmation can be conferred only by a Bishop; but Baptism by any simple Priest. 2. on the part of the effect: while they contend that in Baptism ordinary grace is conferred, but in confirmation the sevenfold Grace of the Holy Spirit, which in Isaiah 11:2 would be named the Spirit of 1. Wisdom, 2. Understanding: 3. Counsel: 4. Fortitude: 5. Knowledge: 6. Piety: 7. Fear of the Lord.

The origin of this ceremony seems to depend on that custom which anciently obtained in the Church regarding the baptized. For it was the custom that those baptized in infancy, when they had grown up a little, and had progressed in catechetical instruction, before they were admitted to the use of the Holy Communion, were brought to the Pastors, and were admonished concerning Baptism, and the covenant entered into there between GOD and themselves: then, having given a confession of faith, they were finally reminded of constancy in doctrine, faith, and piety of life. When these things were finished, prayers were made over them, to which, without any superstition, the laying on of hands and generally in some places and at some times the anointing of oil was also applied. If any Church wished to use such a rite even in our own age for the sake of children, who are sprinkled with Baptism in infancy, and indeed without the opinion of necessity and merit: and thus used without superstition, there is no intelligent person who would condemn it; But that a Sacrament properly so called is feigned by the Papists from this rite, that indeed labors under impiety: that is also not lacking in sacrilege, that they not only equate this rite, proper to human tradition, with the Sacrament of Baptism itself in dignity and efficacy; but even prefer it by far. Finally, it is blasphemous that they dare to constitute CHRIST himself the Author of this Sacrament: although in this part they do not even agree among themselves. Some of the Scholastics not only expressly taught that only he can institute a Sacrament who can attribute spiritual efficacy to a Sacrament: but they also admitted that the Sacrament of Confirmation was neither established nor dispensed by CHRIST or by the Apostles, because nothing of this is read in Scripture; but that it was finally instituted by the Church in the Council of Meaux: as Alexander of Hales testifies in part 4 dist. 24. memb. 1. and Bonaventure in book 4 of the sentences dist. 7. q. 2. Others said that it was instituted not indeed by CHRIST, but by the Apostles. Thomas, observing what kind of impiety it is to foist upon the Church, under the guise and name of a true and proper Sacrament, that which lacks institution, command, and divine promise, attributes this whole Sacrament to divine institution: yet in such a way that he says its matter and form were used neither by CHRIST nor by the Apostles; but that both were so instituted by Him, that when the visible gifts and signs of the Holy Spirit ceased, only then were both to be used in the Church, for which assertion, however, he has no other proof than from that passage in John 20:30, that CHRIST surely did many signs which are not written. Andradius, having spoken rhetorically in various ways for the assertion of this Sacrament, finally bursts out into these words: What if CHRIST instituted this Sacrament? The Jesuit Bellarmine seeks a defense for his cause from chapter 8:17 and chapter 19:6 of the Acts of the Apostles, where both the external ceremony of the laying on of hands and the effect of this Sacrament, namely the bestowal of the Holy Spirit, are expressed in explicit words.

But this has nothing at all to do with the fictitious Sacrament of Confirmation. For there is no word about it in the Acts of the Apostles. The Apostles laid hands on believers so that they might receive the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, which does nothing to establish this Sacrament. For this ceremony is common also to Ordination, Absolution, and other things, which, however, it will be demonstrated a little later are not Sacraments. What of the fact that the Ancients, in the more solemn blessings of their children, had this very sign of the laying on of hands in custom and practice: as is clearly evident from the history of the Patriarch Jacob.
