Furthermore, those extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit were proper to those times: nor was it necessary for that wonderful outpouring of divine grace upon the faithful to last longer than the preaching of the Gospel had already been diffused throughout the whole world, and sufficiently and more than sufficiently confirmed by signs and miracles. 3. What of this laying on of hands in relation to Chrismal anointing? Has it perhaps already been transformed by the power of the Roman Pontiff into Chrism or anointing? Certainly, the Apostles are nowhere read in the Scriptures to have anointed those upon whom they laid hands, so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. 4. In the Acts, no perpetual rite of the Church is described (such as any sacramental action ought to be), but one that is durable only for a short time. 5. Nor did that rite of the laying on of hands, used by the Apostles, confer the grace proper to the Gospel: which is what must necessarily happen in every Sacrament, since they are seals of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4:11. The truth of the antecedent is evident from the fact that that laying on of hands and the conferring of miraculous gifts happened even to some hypocrites and infidels, as the same history of the Acts of the Apostles clearly proves: 6. The Sacrament of Confirmation can and ought to be administered by none but Bishops. Yet the laying on of hands was common to all, so that the whole multitude laid hands on the chosen Deacons, Acts 6:5 and 6. Therefore. 7. This laying on of hands in the Acts happened not to children, but to adults and those destined for a certain office. 8. There is the deepest silence in the Acts concerning that form of confirmation, 'I sign thee with the sign of the cross, and I confirm thee with the Chrism of salvation.' 9. Likewise, there is no word in the sacred texts about the slap. We therefore willingly leave this rite, which is done by the infliction of slaps, to the Papists, as they are most worthy of it. Finally, not even a single requirement of the Sacraments, properly so called, can be truly and properly accommodated to this fictitious rite.

Bellarmino proceeds and strives to overwhelm us with a great many gathered testimonies of the Fathers. But with a vain effort. For 1. Even if such a method of anointing were used in the ancient Church, it does not follow from that that Christ commanded it and commended it to the Church as a Sacrament. 2. Tertullian and Cyprian—the former indeed in his discourse on Baptism, the latter in his book on Chrism and in book 2, epistle 1—expressly testify that that ceremony of Chrism was taken from the discipline of the Old Testament, not from the command of Christ. 3. That book of Cyprian on Chrism is supposititious: just as Eusebius and Pope Gelasius, dist. 15, are witnesses that the writings of Clement of Rome have always been held to be adulterated. 4. It cannot be denied that some of the Fathers, especially Tertullian and Cyprian, suffered something human in this regard: the former of whom, from the school of the heretic Montanus, introduced some error and tares into the Church; the latter, namely Cyprian, followed the tenets of his teacher Tertullian in this regard. But in the Church, one must not attend to what this or that person has said, but to what He who was before all has commanded, Christ the Savior, who alone is the way, and the truth, and the life. Finally, what some of the Fathers relate concerning that adiaphorous rite, by which in the ancient Church children were anointed with oil after making some confession of faith, the Jesuitical party most viciously distorts to establish this Chrismal Sacrament: concerning which nothing at all was established by them. Indeed, even if the Fathers were to call that ancient rite a Sacrament, it is irrefragably evident from the fact that all the Fathers with one mouth acknowledged and believed in no more than two Sacraments properly so called, as was shown above, that it is done in a loose sense.

Latin:

DEfinitio Confirmationis Pontificiæ traditur à Gabriele Biel. in 4 sent. dist. 7. comprehendens omnia, quæ ad Confirmationis descriptionē &amp; explicationem pertinent: Confirmatio inquiens, est Unctio hominis viatoris baptizati, aliqualiter consentietis, vel ante susceptionem, usum rationis non habentis, facta in fronte, in figurâ Crucis, cum Chrismate sanctificato, à ministro idoneo, simul cum debitâ intētione, certa verba proferēte, ex institutione divinâ, efficaciter fignificans unčtionem animæ, per gratiam roborantem, ad confitendum fiducialiter Christi fidem. Definitionem hanc his verbis idem Gabriel explicat: 1. Dicitur,quod fit unčtio hominis baptizati quia non baptizatǫ confirmari non potest, nec aliud Sacramentum suscipere, cum Baptismus sit janua & fundamentum cæterorumSacramentorum. 2. Dicitur etiam, quòd sit hominis aliqualiter consentientis, vel per se, ut adulti, & usum rationis habentis:vel per patrinos,ut infates.3.Dicitur fačta in fronte, ubi notatur determinata pars corporis,in quâ si non fieret, non esset confirmatio. 4. Dicitur in figurâ crucis,ut cōcorder formæ in quâ dicitur: Signo te signo crucis: alioquin nisi sic fieret, forma non esset vera. 5. Dicitur, cum Chrismate sančtificato.Nam si fieret cum oleo sančto, aut oleo infirmorum,non esset Sacramentū. Et ut Chrisma sit materia confirmationis non sufficit,quod sit confečtum ex oleo & balsamo,sed necesse est,ut sit consecratum ab Episcopo. 6. Dicitur,à ministro idoneo, hoc est, ab Episcopo, si Episcopatus à Sacerdotio semper fuit distinčtus.7.Dicitur,simul cum debità intentione, quia sine intentione ministri non est Sacramentum. 8. Dicitur, certæ verba proferente, ubi tangitur forma Sacramenti, quæ est: Signo te signo crucis: confirmo te Chrismate salutis, in nomine Patris,& Filij,& Spiritus Sancti.9. Dicitur, ex divinâ institutione,ubi tangitur autor & institutor hujus Sacramenti, 10. & postremò additur, efficaciter significans unčtionem animæ &c.ubi tangitur res Sacramenti hujus,quæ est, Gratia animæ collatæ ad constanter credendum, & ore intrepidè sine verecundiâ confitendum fidem crucifixi &c.

Confirmationem hanc approbavit & sancivit etiam Concilium Tridentinum, tribus distinčtis Canonib9: quorum primus est: Si quis dixerit, confirmationem baptizatorum otiosam ceremoniam esse,& non potiùs verum & propriumSacramentum: aut olim nihil aliud fuisse quàm catechesin quandã, quâ adolescentiæ proximi: fidei suæ rationẽ coramEcclesiâ edebant,anathema sit. Secundus: Si quis dixerit injurios esse Spiritui Sancto eos,qui sacro confirmationis Chrismati virtutem aliquam tribuūt, anathema sit. Tertius, Si quis dixerit, sančtæ confirmationis ordinarium ministrum, non esse solum Episcopum:sed quemvis simplicẽ Sacerdotem,anathema sit.

Sacramenti hujus ačtio sive administratio sic peragitur: ut complures precatiunculæ conceptis verbis recitentur, dicaturque pax tecum. Dum autem forma verborum pronunciatur, Episcopus confirmandum pollice in Chrisma, sive oleum priùs exorcisatum intinčto, inungit in fronte figurâ crucis: deindè totâ manu alapam faciei ejus impingit: 3. frontem ungvento delibutam, linteo albo cingit: 4. mandat, ut confirmati caput ante diem septimum non lavetur,neChrismatis quicquam simul auferatur aut pereat: tandemque sic confirmatum,patrinis sive susceptoribus commendat.

Finem aut Effečtum multò præstantiorem efficacioremq́; Sacramento huic affingunt, quàm Baptismo: 1. ex parte ministri dispensantis, dùm nimirùm confirmationem non nisi ab Episcopo; Baptismum verò à quolibet simplice Sacerdote conferri posse scriptitant.2. ex parte effečtus:dùm contendunt, in Baptismo conferri vulgarem gratiam, in confirmatione verò Gratiam septiformem Spiritus Sancti, quæ Jes. 11, 2. nominaretur Spiritus 1. Sapientiæ, 2. Intellectus: 3. Consilij: 4. Fortitudinis: 5. Scientiæ: 6. Pietatis: 7. Timoris Domini.

Origo hujus ceremoniæ videtur dependere ab eâ consuetudine, quæ antiquitùs circa baptizatos in Ecclesiâ obtinuit. Moris enim fuit, ut in infantiâ baptisati, ubi paululùm adolevissent, & in doctrinâ catecheticâ profecissent, priusquàm ad usum S. Synaxeos admitterentur, ad Pastores adducti, de Baptismo, & fœdere isthic inter DEUM & ipsos inito admonerentur: tùm editâ fidei confessione, tandem ad constantiam in doctrinâ, fide & pietate vitæ commonefierent. Quibus peractis, preces super istis fiebant, quibus sine omni superstitione, manus impositio plerumque alicubi & aliquando olei etiam inunctio adhibebatur. Qualem ritum si nostro etiam seculo Ecclesia aliqua usurpare vellet propter pueros, qui in infantiâ Baptismo tinguntur, & quidem sine opinione necessitatis ac meriti: & sic sine superstitione usurpatum, nemo est intelligens, qui damnaret; Verùm quod ex isto ritu Sacramentum propriè dictum à Pontificijs fingitur, id verò impietate laborat: illud sacrilegio etiam non caret, quòd Baptismi ipsius Sacramento, ritum istum humanæ traditionis proprium, dignitate & efficaciâ non æquiparant tantùm; sed etiam longè anteferunt. Blasphemum denique illud est, quòd ipsum CHRISTUM Sacramenti hujus Autorem constituere audent: quanquàm hâc in parte ipsimet invicem non consentiunt. Scholasticorum nonnulli, expressè non modò docuerunt, solum illum posse Sacramentum instituere, qui potest Sacramento spiritualem efficaciam tribuere: sed & fassi sunt, Sacramentum Confirmationis, neque conditum, neque dispensatum esse, vel à CHRISTO, vel ab Apostolis, quia hujus nihil in Scripturâ legatur; sed in Concilio Meldensi demùm id ab Ecclesiâ institutum esse: sic testantibus Alexandro ab Ales part. 4 dist. 24. memb. 1. & Bonaventurâ in lib. 4. sent. dist. 7. q. 2. Alij non quidem à CHRISTO, sed ab Apostolis institutum illud esse dicebant. Thomas animadvertens, cujus sit impietatis, sub specie & nomine Sacramenti veri ac proprij, Ecclesiæ obtrudere id, quod & institutione & mandato, & promissione divinâ careat: totum Sacramentum istud divinæ institutioni tribuit: sic tamen ut hujus materiam & formam, neque à CHRISTO, neque ab Apostolis usurpatam esse dicat; verùm utramque sic ab eodem institutam, ut cessantibus visibilibus Spiritus Sancti donis & signis, tunc demùm utrâque in Ecclesiâ usurpareturn, cujus assertionis tamen non aliam habet probationem, quàm ex loco illo Johannis 20. 30. Multa nimirùm signa fecisse CHRISTUM, quæ non sint scripta. Andradius varia pro hujus Sacramenti assertione rhetoricatus, tandem in hæc verba erumpit, Quid si CHRISTUS hoc Sacramentum instituit? Jesuvita Bellarminus præsidium causæ quærit, ex cap. 8. 17. & cap. 19, 6. Actorum Apostolicorum, ubi tùm ceremonia externa impositionis manuum, tùm effectus hujus Sacramenti, nempè Spiritus Sancti collatio disertis verbis exprimatur.

Verùm nihil quicquam hoc ad Confirmationis Sacramentum fictitium. Verbum enim de eo in Actis Apostolicis nullum. Manus Apostoli credentibus imponebãt, ut dona Spiritus Sancti extraordinaria acciperent, quòd nihil ad hoc Sacramentum astruendum facit. Nam hæc ceremonia communis est etiam Ordini, Absolutioni & rebus aliis, quæ tamen Sacramenta esse paulò pôst negatè demonstrabitur. Quid quod Veteres in solennioribus benedictionibus filiorum, hoc ipsum signum Impositionis manuum, in more ac consuetudine habuerunt positum: uti ex historiâ Patriarchæ Jacobi luculenter patet. Porrò dona illa extraordinaria Spiritus Sancti erant temporum illorum propria : neque istam mirificam divinæ gratiæ in fideles effusionem, diutiùs durare oportebat, quàm prædicatio Evangelij per universum terrarum orbem jam esset diffusa, & Signis atque miraculis satis superque confirmata. 3. Quòd hæc impositio manuum, ad unctionem Chrismaticam? Nùm fortè illa jam virtute Pontificis Romani, in Chrisma sive unctionem transformata est? Nuspiam certè in Scripturis Apostoli leguntur unxisse illos, quibus manus imponebant, ut Spiritum Sanctum acciperent. 4. In Actis non describitur ritus aliquis Ecclesiæ perpetuus (qualis debet esse quævis Sacramentalis actio) sed ad tempus duntaxat breve durabilis. 5. Neque ritus iste impositionis manuum, Apostolis usitatus, conferebat gratiam Evangelij propriam : id quod in omni Sacramento necessariò fieri debet: siquidem sunt Sigilla justitiæ fidei, Rom. 4, 11. Antecedentis veritas indè patet, quod impositio illa manuum, & collatio donorum miraculosorum obtingebat etiam nonnullis hypocritis, & infidelibus, uti eadem historia Actorum Apostolicorum luculenter comprobat : 6. Confirmationis Sacramentum non nisi à solis Episcopis administrari potest & debet. Atqui impositio manuum, communis erat omnibus, ita ut universa multitudo, electis Diaconis Actor. 6, 5. & 6. manus imponeret. Ergò. 7. Impositio hæc manuum, non pueris, sed adultis, & certo cuidam muneri destinatis, in Actis obtingebat. 8. Altissimum in Actis silentium de formâ illâ confirmationis, Signo te signo crucis, & confirmo te Chrismate salutis. 9. De alapâ itidem in Sacris nullum verbum. Hunc ergò ritum, qui fit per inflictiohem alaparum, Pontificijs libenter relinquimus, quippè quo sunt dignissimi. Tandem ne quidem unicum requisitum Sacramentorum propriè sic dictorum, fictitio huic ritui verè & propriè accommodari potest.

Pergit Bellarminus & benè multis conquæsitis Patrum testimonijs nos obruere studet. Sed irrito conatu. Nam 1. Si vel maximè in antiquâ Ecclesiâ, talis inungendi ratio fuit usitata, non tamen indè sequitur, quod Christus eam præceperit, & Ecclesiæ pro Sacramento commendarit. 2. Tertullianus & Cyprianus, ille quidem sermone de Baptismo: hic verò in libro de Chrismate, & lib.2. epist. 1. disertè testantur ceremoniam illam Chrismatis ex disciplinâ Veteris Testamenti, non ex Christi mandato sumtam esse. 3. Liber ille Cypriani de Chrismate est suppositius: quemadmodum etiam Clementis Romani scripta pro adulterinis semper fuisse habita, testis est Eusebius & Gelasius Papa dist. 15. 4. Negari non potest, quin quidam ex Patribus, Tertullianus præsertim & Cyprianus hâc in parte humani quid passi sint: quorum ille ex scholâ Montani hæretici, aliquid erroris ac lolij in Ecclesiam invexit: hic verò, Cyprianus nempè præceptoris Tertulliani placita, hâc in parte secutus est. Non autem in Ecclesiâ attendendum est, quid hic vel ille dixerit, sed quid præceperit ille, qui ante omnes fuit, Christus Servator, qui solus est via, & veritas & vita. Tandem quæ Patrum nonnulli differunt, de ritu illo adiaphoro, quo in antiquâ Ecclesiâ, pueri editâ aliquâ confessione fidei, oleo inungebantur: vitiosissimè detorquet Jesuvitica ad stabiliendum Sacramentum hoc Chrismaticum: de quo nihil quicquam ipsis constitit. Quin si vel maximè ritum istum antiquum Patres nominarent Sacramentum: in laxâ tamen significatione illud fieri, vel indè irrefragabiliter constat, quòd Patres omnes uno ore non nisi duo Sacramenta propriè sic dicta agnoverunt & crediderunt, uti suprà ostensum.


### Chapter IV. and Last. On the Number of the Sacraments of the New Testament: On the Sacrament of Penance

That Penance, whether defined in our sense or the Papal sense, is not a Sacrament properly so called, is evident from those requirements which constitute and complete such a Sacrament, and indeed one proper to the New Testament. For it does not, 1. have CHRIST immediately as its author: but depends on a general divine, and indeed mediated, will and command: for it was commanded through the Prophets and Apostles. 2. Nor is it proper to the New Testament, but is common to all times and men indifferently. 3. Nor does it consist of a visible external element defined by the Savior himself. For the fact that some substitute the recitation of words in place of an Element, 'I absolve thee, penitent, from all thy sins, etc.,' is too absurd. For in no Sacrament does the rite of the action itself and the word itself, whether of command or of promise, take the place of an external Element: just as in the Eucharist, those words, 'Take, eat, this is my body,' cannot be substituted in place of the Element. More absurd is that which makes the voice of the absolving minister an essential part of the Sacrament in this way. 4. It is the nature and property of the Sacraments properly so called that GOD acts with us in them, and through this action confers spiritual grace upon us. But those who perform penance act with GOD: and penance itself, by reason of only one part, namely Faith, can be called a medium through which the remission of sins comes to us: but not by reason of both parts: which is contrary to the nature

it clearly conflicts with the sacraments. 5. All people, even unbelievers, enjoy the sacraments, and indeed those that are integral according to their essence, although not all obtain the saving fruit: But Penance is never performed without fruit: nor can it ever be performed without faith, so that if it is destitute of this, it is not Penance, but rather hypocrisy. Therefore, in this part also, it degenerates from the nature of a sacrament properly so called.

Moreover, the Jesuit Bellarmino, in order to give credence to his dogma, brings forward two testimonies of Scripture, from chapter 18, 18 of Matthew: and chapter 20, 23 of John: Where the Savior says to the disciples: Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them: whose you shall retain, they are retained. Where, in place of a response, we note at the beginning that the Jesuit, producing the passage from Matthew, fixes an obelisk to the Council of Trent, which established that the sacrament of Penance was instituted by CHRIST only after the Resurrection. But the discourse of Matthew 18 preceded the Passion and Resurrection. Therefore that passage is nothing to the point. 2. But as far as the matter itself is concerned, the Jesuit trifles rather than argues. For let him show from these words of the Savior even a single indication of any instituted sacrament. No element, no heavenly sacramental thing, no form proper to a sacrament appears anywhere. The Apostles are indeed commanded both to retain and to forgive sins: which is done in the very ministry of the word, while the remission of sins is announced to believers, and condemnation to the stubborn and impenitent. Now if this constituted some sacrament, certainly it should be called a sacrament not of penance, but rather of the ministry of the word: especially since in the ministry, not only general promises are proposed; but they are also privately accommodated to any faithful penitent individually.

Finally, regarding the imposition of hands, which some of the Romanists wish to be held in the place of an external sign, it has just now been shown that this is done quite absurdly and ineptly. It is added that this rite of the imposition of hands is, properly speaking, a human action, and not any elemental thing: moreover, it lacks a divine mandate, and was received by men arbitrarily and indifferently in the Church. Nor does it stand in the way that Augustine, book 5 against the Donatists, chapter 20, puts the imposition of hands simply for penance itself, and under the title of sacrament counts it among the sacraments themselves. For we showed above that this is done partly improperly and loosely, and partly analogically.

There are also some among the Jesuits who object to us the heresy of Novatus in this part: but without any merit. For that man was condemned for heresy, not because he denied that penance was a sacrament, but because he left no place for penance for those who had fallen once. Which heresy we detest from our heart.

Latin:

POEnitentiam sive nostro, sive Pontificio sensu definiatur, Sacramentum propriè sic dictum non esse, constat ex illis requisitis, quæ Sacramentum tale, & quidem Novi Testamenti proprium constituunt & absolvunt. Neque enim ea, 1. immediatè CHRISTUM autorem habet: sed à generali divinâ, & quidem mediatâ voluntate & mandato dependet: quippè per Prophetas & Apostolos mandata. 2. Neque Novi Testamenti propria, sed omnibus temporibus, & hominibus indifferenter est communis. 3. Neque visibili, & à Servatore ipso definito externo elemento ea constat. Nam quòd nonnulli Elementi loco substituunt recitationem verborum, Absolvo te pœnitentem ab omnibus peccatis tuis &c. nimis absurdum est. In nullo enim Sacramento ritus ipse actionis & verbum ipsum sive mandati, sive promissionis, Elementi externi vicem sustinet: quemadmodum nec in Eucharistiâ, Verbâ, illa, Accipite, Comedite, Hoc est corpus meum, Elementi loco substitui possunt. Absurdius est illud, quod vocem ministri absolventis, partem essentialem Sacramenti hoc pacto constituunt. 4. Ea est natura & affectio Sacramentorum propriè sic dictorum, ut DEUS in illis nobiscum agat, & mediante hac actione, gratiam spiritualem nobis conferat. Atqui pœnitentiam agentes cum DEO agunt: & pœnitentia ipsa, ratione unius tantùm partis, Fidei nimirùm, potest dici medium, per quod nobis obtingat Remissio peccatorum: non verò ratione partis utriusque: id quod cum naturâ

Sacramentorum manifestè pugnat. 5. Sacramentis & quidem secundum essentiam integris fruuntur omnes, etiam infideles, licèt salutari fructu non omnes potiantur: Atqui Pœnitentia sine fructu nunquàm agitur: neque sine fide peragi unquàm potest, ita ut si hâc destituatur, Pœnitentia non sit, sed potiùs hypocrisis. Ergò & hâc in parte à naturâ Sacramenti propriè sic dicti degenerat.

Cæterùm Jesuitavita Bellarminus fidem dogmati suo facturus duo profert Scripturæ testimonia, ex c. 18. 18. Matthæi: & cap. 20, 23. Johannis: Ubi Servator ad discipulos: Si quorum peccata remiseritis, remittuntur eis: si quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt. Ubi responsionis loco initiò illud notamus, quòd Jesuitavita producens locum ex Matthæo, obeliscum figit Concilio Tridentino, quod statuit, Sacramentum Pœnitentiæ à CHRISTO post Resurrectionem demùm institutum esse. Atqui concio Matthæi. 18. præcessit Passionem & Resurrectionem. Ergò locus ille nihil ad rem. 2. Sed ad rem ipsam quod attinet, veriùs nugatur, quàm disputat Jesuitavita. Monstret enim ex verbis hisce Servatoris vel unicum instituti Sacramenti alicujus indicium. Nullum elementum, nulla res cœlestis Sacramentalis, nulla forma Sacramenti propria uspiam apparet. Jubentur nimirùm Apostoli & retinere & remittere peccata: quod in ipso quidem verbi ministerio fit, dùm credentibus remissio peccatorum, præfractis & impœnitentibus condemnatio denunciatur. Jam si hoc constitueret aliquod Sacramentum, certè non pœnitentia, sed verbi magis ministerium dici deberet Sacramentum: præsertim cùm in ministerio, non generales tantùm promissiones proponantur; sed eæ etiam privatim ad quemvis fidelem pœnitentem in individuo accommodentur.

Tandem quoad Impositionem manuum, quam externi signi loco haberi volunt Romanensium aliqui, jam modò ostensum est, absurdè planè & ineptè hoc fieri. Accedit, quod ritus iste impositionis manuum, est propriè loquendo actio humana, non verò res aliqua elementaris: insuper divino etiam mandato carens, & ab hominibus arbitrariè atque indifferenter in Ecclesiâ recepta. Neque obstat, quòd Augustinus lib. 5. contra Donatistas cap. 20. Impositionem manuum simpliciter pro ipsâ pœnitentia ponit, & sub Sacramenti titulo Sacramentis ipsis annumerat. Nam impropriè partim & laxè, partim analogicè hoc fieri, suprà ostendimus.

Sunt etiam ex Jesuitavitis, qui hæresin Novati nobis hâc in parte objiciunt: sed præter omne meritum. Hærefeos enim damnato ille fuit, non quòd pœnitentiam negarit esse Sacramentum, sed quod semel lapsis nullum pœnitentiæ locum reliquerit. Quam hæresin nos ex animo detestamur.


### Chapter IV. and Last. On the Number of the Sacraments of the New Testament: III. On Extreme Unction

Anointing in the primitive, or rather the even older prophetic Church, was nothing other than medical treatment. For GOD, in order to surround the Fathers and Prophets with some authority, adorned them from the very beginning with the gift of healing. CHRIST renewed this ancient custom, sending out the Apostles, and giving them the power to heal the sick miraculously. This gift, with the other miracles, ceased to be in use once the doctrine of the Gospel had been spread and confirmed throughout the whole world: although there is no doubt that even today, through the prayers of the Church, health is recovered by many. The Romanists, with shameful zeal, have recalled the rite of anointing, but a thoroughly superstitious one, into the Church: which is performed in this manner. 1. An ointment is made from oil, but not just any oil, but such as has first been consecrated and exorcised by a Bishop. 2. With this oil the organs of the senses are anointed, and especially those members by whose ministry more serious sins are perpetrated: such as the ears, eyes, nostrils, lips, hands, feet, and all but the genital members themselves. 3. A certain form of prayer is used, for imparting heavenly virtue to this oil: and indeed according to the Venetian Pontifical, such as this: Send forth, I beseech Thee, O Lord, the Holy Spirit the Paraclete from heaven into this fatness of olive, which Thou hast deigned to produce from the green wood; for the refreshment of mind and body: that by Thy holy blessing, this ointment may be to everyone anointed with it a heavenly medicine, a protection of mind and body, for the evacuation of all pains, all infirmities, and all sickness of mind and body, etc. 4. They claim its use is to wipe away the offenses that are still to be expiated by those about to die, and the remnants of sin, to alleviate the soul of the sick person, and to confer grace and the remission of sins. 5. They confer this sacrament on no one, unless he is placed in danger of life and in the agony of death.

The Council of Trent, for the asserting of this Sacrament, produced the following Canons, sess. can. 1. If any one shall say that extreme unction is not truly and properly instituted by CHRIST, and promulgated by the Blessed Apostle James: but is only a rite received from the Fathers, or a human figment, let him be anathema. Can. 2. If any one shall say that the sacred unction of the sick does not confer grace, nor remit sins, nor alleviate the sick: but has already ceased, as if it were formerly only a grace of healings, let him be anathema. Canon 3. If any one shall say that the rite and use of extreme unction, which the holy Roman Church observes, is repugnant to the opinion of the Apostle James: and therefore that it ought to be changed, and can be despised by Christians without sin, let him be anathema.

But the arguments by which the Romanists desire this fictitious Sacrament to be asserted, they bring forward chiefly two, one sought from Mark, chap. 6. 13. where they insist that this Sacrament is insinuated in these words: They cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them.

The other from James chap. 5, 14. where they write that the whole matter and form of this Sacrament is expressed, in these words: Is any one sick among you? let him call for the Presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil, in the name of the Lord: and the prayer of faith shall save the one laboring, and the Lord shall raise him up: and if he has committed, they shall be forgiven him. By these words they claim is contained: 1. An element, namely oil. 2. A form, which consists in prayers over the sick person. 3. A promise of grace: inasmuch as through this Sacrament GOD preserves the sufferer, and forgives his sins. 4. A mandate: for he commands that the Elders of the Church be summoned, and that they pray. Now, that the mandate of the Apostle is the mandate of CHRIST himself. For unless the Apostle had received this mandate from CHRIST, he himself would never have commanded such a thing: because it is not of human authority to promise grace.

I answer that this argument is sophistically constructed from true and false premises, and deceives under some appearance of truth. It is indeed true, and never denied by our side: 1. That the Apostles used oil in healing the sick as a medium or a certain instrument. For we do not side in this part with Beza, who maintains that this oil was merely a symbol of health already recovered. 2. It is also true that such Apostolic anointing then had some miraculous power. But that the Romanists gather from thence to establish their own anointing, can be demonstrated without difficulty and irrefragably to be partly impious and blasphemous, partly manifestly false, and finally partly absurd, provided one attends a little more accurately to what difference exists between the Apostolic anointing and the Pontifical anointing.

For 1. they differ in kind. For the Apostolic was miraculous: as is evident from Mark chapter 16, 18, where this healing of the sick is expressly referred to among the σημεῖα or miracles, no less than the gift of tongues and the casting out of demons, and 1 Cor. 12, 9 it is counted in express words among the χαρίσματα of the Holy Spirit: and therefore it ought not to have lasted longer than the gifts of healing themselves lasted. But the Pontifical anointing is feigned to be Sacramental, and therefore always to endure even to the end of the age.

2. They differ in the very form, so to speak, of the oil. The Apostles used common and ordinary oil, the use of which was daily in the families of the sick: but the Pontificalists reject such entirely, unless it has first been freed and purged from unclean spirits, and from every incursion of Satan, and from every phantom, by exorcism: and that both by a certain person and at a certain time.

3. A simple anointing was clearly customary for the Apostles: but for the Pontificalists it is, through a certain gross superstition, directed to certain organs of the senses and certain members of the body: as if indeed the Heart were not rather the source and root of all sins, to which this oil cannot reach.

4. In the object. For the Apostles anointed the sick, but only those in whom there was hope of recovery: but the Pontificalists anoint only those whose life is already despaired of.

5. In the end and effect: the Apostles anointed for the purpose of recovering health: but the Pontificalists for the cleansing of sins and the remnants of the same.

6. The Apostles assigned the power of healing not to the anointing itself, but to prayer, as is clearly evident from the words of James.

Two other things also are added, which eliminate this rancid Sacrament. For first, whatever Sacraments CHRIST instituted, He instituted them publicly, with a certain prescribed form of action: but the Romanists feign that this Sacrament was instituted privately: which, however, they have not yet proven. For grant that CHRIST gave a mandate privately concerning the anointing of the sick, yet this was special, and ought by no means to be distorted to the general nature of Sacraments. Observing which, Bonaventura in book 4, sent. dist. 23, art. 1, q. 2, preferred to maintain that extreme unction was finally instituted by the Apostle James. Furthermore, Sacraments ought not to be celebrated ordinarily except by legitimate ministers: but the Church once permitted this anointing and its administration to all Christians, as Sigebert testifies in his chronicle. As for the authorities of certain Fathers, whom the Romanists object to us in this place, we do not greatly concern ourselves with them. For it cannot be denied that this superstitious rite or custom of anointing in the Church also broke out into a nerve among the ancients, on account of the κακοζηλία of the Apostolic anointing: meanwhile, however, neither Chrysostom, nor Prosper, nor others call this anointing a Sacrament.

Latin:

UNctio in primitivâ, imò antiquiore etiam propheticâ Ecclesiâ, nihil fuit aliud quàm curatio medica. Nam DEUS ut autoritatem aliquam Patribus & Prophetis circumdaret, indè usque ab initio ornavit eos dono sanandi. Hunc veterem morem renovavit CHRISTUS, emittens Apostolos, & potestatem eis faciens miraculosè sanandi ægros. Hoc donum cum reliquis miraculis, diffusâ jam & confirmatâ doctrinâ Evangelij per universum terrarum orbem, in usu esse desijt: licèt dubium sit nullum, quin hodièque Ecclesiæ precibus, sanitas multis recuperetur. Romanenses turpi κακοζηλίᾳ unctionis, sed prorsus superstitiosæ ritum denuò in Ecclesiam revocarũt: qui hunc in modum peragitur. 1. Fit ungventum ex oleo, sed non quovis, verùm tali, quod priùs non nisi ab Episcopo sit consecratum & exorcisatum. 2. Hoc oleo inunguntur organa sensuum, & ea præcipuè membra, quorum ministerio graviora peccata perpetrantur: ut aures, oculi, nares, labia, manus, pedes, & tantùm non ipsa membra genitalia. 3. Certa quædam precationis forma adhibetur; pro impertiendâ cœlesti virtute huic oleo: & quidem secundum Pontificale Venetianum, talis: Emitte quæso Domine Spiritum Sanctum paracletum de cælis, in hanc pingvedinem olivæ, quam de viridi ligno producere dignatus es; ad refectionem mentis & corporis: ut tuâ sanctâ benedictione, sit omni hoc ungvento cælestis medicina peruncto, tutamen mentis & corporis, ad evacuandos omnes dolores, omnes infirmitates, omnemquè ægritudinem mentis & corporis &c. 4. Usum ejus eum esse perhibent, ut delicta, quæ morituris adhuc sunt expianda, & peccati reliquias abstergat, ægroti animam alleviet, & gratiam ac remissionem peccatorum conferat. 5. Nemini Sacramentum hoc conferunt, nisi qui in vitæ periculo, mortisque agone sit constitutus.

Concilium Tridentinum pro asserendo hoc Sacramento, sequentes Canones prodidit sess. can. 1. Si quis dixerit, extremam unctionem, non esse verè & propriè institutum à CHRISTO, & à B. Jacobo Apostolo promulgatum: Sed ritum tantùm acceptum à Patribus, aut figmentum humanum anathema sit. Can. 2. Si quis dixerit, sacram infirmorum unctionem non conferre gratiam, nec remittere peccata, nec alleviare infirmos: sed jam cessasse quasi olim tantùm fuerit gratia curationum, anathema sit. Canon. 3. Si quis dixerit, extremæ unctionis ritum & usum, quem observat sancta Romana Ecclesia, repugnare sententiæ Jacobi Apostoli: ideoqué eum mutandum, possequé à Christianis absqué peccato contemni, anathema sit.

Argumenta verò, quibus Romanenses fictitium hoc Sacramentum assertum cupiunt, præcipuè duo proferunt, unum ex Marco petitum, cap. 6. 13. ubi Sacramentum hoc his verbis insinuatũ esse dictitant Dæmonia multa ejiciebant, ungebantqué oleo multos ægrotos, & sanabant eos.

Alterum ex Jacobo cap. 5, 14. ubi totam Sacramenti hujus materiam & formam expressam esse scriptitant, his verbis: Infirmatur quis inter vos? accersat Presbyteros Ecclesiæ, & orent pro eo, ungentes eum oleo, in nomine Domini: & oratio fidei servabit laborantem, erigetqué eũ Dominus: quod si peccommiserit, remittentur ei. His verbis ajunt contineri. 1. Elementum, nempe oleum. 2. Formam, quæ consistat in precibus super ægrotum. 3. Promissionem gratiæ: siquidem per hoc Sacramentum DEUS servet laborantem, & peccata ei remittat. 4. Mandatum: jubet enim, ut accersantur Seniores Ecclesiæ, & orent. Jam mandatum Apostoli, esse mandatum ipsius CHRISTI. Nisi enim à CHRISTO mandatum hoc accepisset Apostolus, nunquàm ipse tale quid præcepisset: proptereà quòd humanæ auctoritatis non est, promittere gratiam.

Respondeo, argumentum hoc ex veris & falsis sophistice esse conflatum, & sub specie aliquâ veri decipere. Verùm quidem est, & à nostris nunquàm negatum. 1. Apostolos in curandis ægrotis, oleo, tanquàm medio sive organo quodam usos fuisse. Neque enim hâc in parte cum Beza facimus, qui statuit, oleum hoc tantùm fuisse Symbolum valetudinis jam recuperatæ. 2. Verùm etiam est vim aliquam miraculosam, ejusmodi unctionem Apostolicam tùm habuisse. Cæterùm quæ indè ad stabiliendam suam unctionem colligunt Romanenses, partim impia & blasphema, partim manifestè falsa, partim denique absurda esse, nullo negotio irrefragabiliter demonstrari potest, dummodò paulò accuratius attendatur, quid discriminis unctioni Apostolicæ, cum unctione Pontificiâ intercedat.

Nam 1. differunt Genere. Apostolica enim fuit miraculosa: uti patet ex cap. 16, 18. Marci, ubi hæc sanatio ægrotorum, disertè inter σημεῖα sive miracula refertur, haud minùs, atque donum lingvarum, & dæmonum ejectio, Et 1. Cor. 12, 9. expressis verbis numeratur inter χαρίσματα Spiritus Sancti: ac proindè diutiùs durare non debuit, quam ipsa durarent dona sanationum. Pontificia verò unctio fingitur esse Sacramentalis, ac proindè semper duratura ad finem usque seculi.

2. Differunt ipsâ, ut sic loquar, olei formâ, Apostoli utebantur oleo communi & vulgari, cujus usus erat in ægrotorum familijs quotidianus: Pontificij verò tale prorsus repudiant, nisi priùs à spiritibus immundis, & ab omni incursione Sathanæ, & ab omni phantasmate, per exorcismum sit liberatum & purgatum: idque tùm à certâ personâ, tùm certo tempore.

3. Apostolis simplex planè unctio erat usitata: Pontificijs verò ea per crassam quandam superstitionem, ad certa sensuum organa, certaque corporis membra directa: quasi verò non Cor potiùs sit fons & radix peccatorum omnium, ad quod oleum istud pertingere non potest.

4. Objecto. Apostoli enim inungebant ægrotos, sed non nisi eos, in quibus convalescendi spes erat: Pontificij verò inungunt non nisi eos, de quorum vitâ jam conclamatum est.

5. Fine & Effectu: Apostoli ungebant in finem recuperandæ sanitatis: Pontificij verò in abstersionem peccatorum, eorundemque reliquiarum.

6. Apostoli vim sanationis non per se unctioni, sed orationi assignabant, uti ex verbis Jacobi luculenter patet.

Accedunt & duo alia, quæ rancidum hoc Sacramentum eliminant. Nam primò quæcunque Sacramenta CHRISTUS instituit, ea publicè, certâ præscriptâ actionis formâ instituit: atqui hoc Sacramentum privatim sanctum fuisse, fingunt Romanenses: id quod tamen nondum probarunt. Esto enim, quod CHRISTUS privatim mandatum dederit de ungendis ægrotis, tamen speciale hoc fuit, & ad generalem Sacramentorum naturam detorqueri minimè debet. Quod animadvertens Bonaventura in lib. 4. sent. dist. 23. artic. 1. q. 2. maluit statuere, unctionem extremam ab Apostolo Jacobo demùm fuisse institutam. Deindè Sacramenta non nisi à legitimis ministris ordinariè celebrari debent: Atqui unctionem hanc, ejusdemque administrationem omnibus Christianis permisit olim Ecclesia teste Sigeberto in chronico. Quoad autoritates Patrum quorundam, quos hoc loco nobis objiciunt Romanenses, eas non magnoperè moramur. Negari enim non potest, superstitiosum hunc unctionis in Ecclesiâ ritum sive morem apud antiquos etiam in nervum erupisse, propter κακοζηλίαν unctionis Apostolicæ: Interim tamen neque Chrysostomus, neque Prosper, neque alij unctionem hanc vocant Sacramentum.


### Chapter IV. and Last. On the Number of the Sacraments of the New Testament: Of the Sacrament of Matrimony

By almost the same reasons or arguments, this fictitious Sacrament is also overturned, as were the preceding ones. For 1. CHRIST himself nowhere instituted Matrimony as a Sacrament. 2. It lacks an external element. 3. It is destitute of a certain form of celebration. Some among the Papists pretend that, in the Sacrament of matrimony, the place of the element or sensible sign is held by the mutual consent of the contracting parties, and the words, and the pledges by which the contract is expressed. That the mandate and institution are contained in the words of CHRIST, Matt. 19, 6: What GOD has joined, let not man separate. Finally, that the promise of grace lies in it, in that it signifies the conjunction of CHRIST and the Church. Which signification can have no place, unless the spouses are also spiritually united. Which grace of spiritual union is conferred through this Sacrament, so that the signification may be perfect. But all these things are said ἄπερ γραφῆς, and are refuted by the following reasons. Therefore 4. Matrimony is common to the Old Testament with the New, since it was instituted in Paradise itself, immediately after the creation of man. 5. It is read that CHRIST added nothing at all to this first institution: Therefore it is not a Sacrament proper to the New Testament. 6. The marriages of the ancient people were no less symbols of that spiritual marriage of CHRIST and the Church, than ours. Therefore if on account of this signification our marriages will have the status of a Sacrament: then certainly those ancient ones will by no means be of an inferior condition. 7. Sacraments from CHRIST are common to all: and are participated in by the Priests themselves. And yet marriage, according to the doctrine of the Romanists, is denied to Clerics and Priests: Therefore. Nor indeed must it be established that through the Sacrament of Order he excludes the Mass-priests from the perception of this Sacrament: For thus it would follow that CHRIST himself instituted Sacraments conflicting with one another, and mutually excluding each other with respect to a certain species of men: which is absurd, nay even impious to think. 8. If Marriage is a Sacrament, it is necessary that the Pontiff Syricius, who condemned marriage as a workshop of impurity and filth, was clearly impious and a blasphemer. 9. Marriage is not a matter of simple command, but partly of choice, partly of natural necessity. 10. it is destitute of the promise of Evangelical grace, which is by no means conferred through marriage. For it is ridiculous that some of the Jesuits maintain that Grace is also promised in Marriage: Grace, namely, for procreating children. As if indeed the question in this place were about any grace whatsoever, and not rather about the grace proper to the Gospel alone. Otherwise, certainly, as many Sacraments would have to be instituted as there are orders or offices of men, to each of which GOD has promised his own certain and adequate grace. 11. Sacraments are rites proper to Christians. And yet Marriage is common to them with the Gentiles. 12. A Sacrament is not dispensed except by the work of a minister or Priest. And yet marriages are contracted even without the work of any minister. For it is not the blessing of the Priest, but the consent of the contracting parties, that constitutes a true and legitimate marriage. 13. Sacramental elements ought to contain a likeness or image of that sanctification of which they are said to be signs and causes: as Augustine testifies, Epist. 23 to Boniface. And yet marriage neither bears the image of sanctification, nor is it used for sanctifying: Therefore.

But what need is there of many words, when the Romanists themselves, for confirming this Sacrament, cannot bring forward even a single testimony of Scripture, except that one at Eph. 5:32, where the Apostle calls marriage a Sacrament. But not even this has anything to do with the matter. For the Apostle does not there call marriage a Sacrament, but rather our spiritual conjunction with CHRIST: where, however, in the Greek it is μυστήριον, which the Latin version improperly rendered as Sacrament. That which convinces this assertion is the fact that the Apostle himself explains his own mind, immediately adding: But I speak concerning CHRIST, and the Church. Although this spiritual marriage may in some way shadow forth civil marriage: it does not therefore follow that the latter is a Sacrament. For otherwise as many Sacraments would have to be established as there are parables, types, and figures in the Scriptures.

As for the Fathers, they, intending to assert the holiness of marriage among Christians, wished to designate it by the word Sacrament, though taken loosely and improperly. Whence no help at all redounds to the Romanists.

Latin:

TIsdem fermè rationibus sive argumentis, hoc etiam fictitium Sacramentum evertitur, quibus præcedentia. Nam 1. CHRISTUS ipse Matrimonium nuspiam tanquàm Sacramentum instituit. 2. caret illud externo elemento. 3. destituitur certâ celebrationis formâ. Fingunt nonnulli ex Pontificijs, in Sacramento matrimonij, Elementi sive signi sensibilis loco esse, mutuum contrahentium consensum, & verba, atq; arrhas, quibus contractus exprimitur. Mandatum & institutionem contineri Verbis CHRISTI, Matth. 19, 16. Quod DEUS conjunxit, homo ne separet. Tandem Gratiæ promissionem in eo latére, quòd conjunctionem CHRISTI & Ecclesiæ significat. Quæ significatio locum non habeat, nisi conjuges etiam spiritualiter sint uniti. Quæ unionis spiritualis gratia, per Sacramentum istud conferatur, ut significatio sit perfecta. Sed omnia hæc ἄπερ γραφῆς dicuntur, & rationibus subsequentibus refutantur. Ergò 4. Matrimonium commune est Veteri Testamento cum Novo, quippè in ipso Paradiso, statim post hominis creationem, institutum. 5. Primæ huic institutioni CHRISTUS nihil quicquam addidisse legitur: Ergò non est Sacramentum Novi Testamenti proprium. 6. Veteris populi matrimonia non minùs erant Symbola spiritualis illius conjugij CHRISTI & Ecclefiæ, quàm nostra. Ergò si propter hanc significationem nostra matrimonia habebunt rationem Sacramenti: utique deterioris conditionis minimè erunt illa vetera. 7. Sacramenta à CHRISTO communia sunt omnibus: & participantur ab ipsis Sacerdotibus. Atqui matrimonium ex doctrinâ Pontificiorum, negatur Clericis & Sacerdotibus: Ergò. Neque verò statuendum est, per Ordinis Sacramentum excludit Sacrificulos à perceptione hujus Sacramenti: Sic enim CHRISTUM ipsum Sacramenta inter se pugnantia, & respectu certæ cujusdam speciei hominum se mutuò excludentia, instituisse, foret consequens: id quod absurdum, imò vel cogitatu impium. 8. Si Matrimonium est Sacramentum, impio planè & blasphemus Pontifex Syricius fuerit, necesse est, qui Conjugium tanquàm impuritatis & turpitudinis officinam, condemnavit. 9. Matrimonium non est res mandati simplicis, sed partim arbitrii, partim naturalis necessitatis. 10. destituitur promissione gratiæ Evangelicæ, quæ per matrimonium minimè confertur. Ridiculum enim est, quod nonnulli Jesuvvitarum Matrimonio etiam Gratiã promissam esse dictitant: Gratiam nimirùm procreandi liberos. Quasi verò de quâvis gratiâ hoc loco sit quæstio, & non potiùs de solâ gratiâ Evangelij propriâ. Aliàs certè tot erunt Sacramenta instituenda, quot sunt hominum ordines sive munera, quibus singulis DEUS suam certam & adæquatam gratiam promisit. 11. Sacramenta sunt ritus Christianorum proprij. Atqui Matrimonium his commune est cum gentilibus. 12. Sacramentum non dispensatur nisi operâ ministri sive Sacerdotis. Atqui matrimonia contrahuntur, etiam sine ullius ministri operâ. Neque enim benedictio Sacerdotis, sed consensus partium contrahentium, verum ac legitimum constituit matrimonium. 13. Elementa Sacramentalia debent continere similitudinem sive imaginem illius sanctificationis cujus signa & causæ esse dicuntur: teste Augustino, Epist. 23. ad Bonifacium. Atqui matrimonium neque sanctificationis imaginem gerit, neque ad sanctificandum adhibetur: Ergò.

Sed quid multis opus, cum ipsi Romanenses pro confirmando hoc Sacramento, ne quidem unicum proferre possint Scripturæ testimonium, excepto unico illo ad Ephes. 5. 32. ubi Apostolus conjugium nominat Sacramentum. Verùm ne hoc quidem quicquam ad rem facit. Neque enim ibi Apostolus conjugium, sed nostram potiùs cum CHRISTO spiritualem conjunctionem nominat Sacramentum: ubi tamen in Græco est μυστήριον, quod impropriè versio Latina reddidit Sacramentum. Fidem assertioni huic facit id, quod Apostolus ipse mentem suam explicat, statim subjiciens: Loquor autem de CHRISTO, & de Ecclesiâ. Spirituale hoc matrimonium licèt adumbret quodammodo matrimonium civile: non tamen propterea illud fuerit Sacramentum. Aliàs enim tot essent constituenda Sacramenta, quot sunt in Scripturis parabolæ, typi, figuræ.

Quoad Patres, illi asserturi sanctitatem matrimonij inter Christianos, vocabulo Sacramenti, laxè tamen & impropriè accepto, illud indigitare voluerunt. Undè ad Romanenses nihil quicquam redundat præsidij.


### Chapter IV. and Last. On the Number of the Sacraments of the New Testament: V. On the Sacrament of Order, § On Ordination

Just as it was shown above that the Rite of Absolution has been accustomed to be called a Sacrament analogically and improperly even by some Orthodox Theologians: so there are not wanting those who establish that the same denomination, but likewise in a loose and improper signification, belongs to the Order or Ordination of ecclesiastical men to the Ministry: with whom we have no controversy. But the Romanists contend that Ordination to the Priesthood of the New Testament is a Sacrament truly and properly so called. For thus the Council of Trent, Sess. 7, Can. 3: If anyone shall say that Order or holy Ordination is not truly and properly a Sacrament instituted by CHRIST: or that it is a certain human figment, devised by men unskilled in ecclesiastical matters: or that it is only a certain rite of choosing ministers of the Word of GOD and the Sacraments: let him be anathema.

However, not having delayed over this brute thunderbolt, we hold the negative simply in this place also, for the following reasons.

1. In every Sacrament properly so called, a certain external, visible, corporeal matter or element is necessary, as we perceive in Baptism and the Supper. And yet there is no element of Order, therefore it is not a Sacrament. The minor premise is evident, because not even the Romanists themselves can show, to this very day, a certain element commanded and defined by CHRIST. The Imposition of hands is not such, as was shown above: nor is Insufflation such an element. For although it is read that CHRIST used the rite of Insufflation once on the very day of the Resurrection, John 20:22, yet it is nowhere read that he gave any command about retaining this rite in the Church, so that it might be an external Symbol in the ordination of ministers at all times. What? That the same Savior elsewhere, sending out the Apostles, as also those seventy disciples, to teach the Gospel, is read to have used neither Imposition of hands nor Insufflation, but to have destined them to the ministry without any rite or element or external Symbol: Matt. 10, Mark 3, Luke 9 and 10. Thus also in that final inauguration of the disciples, and their sending away into the whole world, CHRIST employed nothing at all of any rite or external Symbol, Matt. 28, Mark 16.

2. Sacraments pertain to all Christians, because they are seals of the righteousness of faith in all believers, and they apply the promise of the Gospel, which is not proper to one order of men, but common to all men. But Order belongs to a few men: only to those who offer their service to the ecclesiastical ministry: nay, not even to all of these: since hands are not easily to be laid upon anyone, 1 Tim. 5:22. Therefore.

3. Ordination is not an instrument or medium through which the application and sealing of the remission of sins occurs: a fact which is evident from the example of Judas. of the traitor Apostle, and of other most wicked men, especially in the Papacy ordained for the Ministry of Sacrificing. And although Christ the Savior, when sending away his disciples, is read to have added the promise of grace, saying, Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age; yet this grace is not the grace of reconciliation or of the remission of sins, but it is the grace of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which afterwards in a certain miraculous way, through the laying on of hands, was obtained by the faithful in the primitive Church: Which grace of the collation of peculiar gifts, however, has ceased today. For GOD no longer bestows through such an external ceremony the χαρίσματα of the Holy Spirit, such as are the gifts of various languages, the gifts of healings, the gift of prophecy, and others of this kind: But he acts through legitimately ordained means: so that unless someone has previously acquired these gifts for himself in Schools, whether private or public, he will never obtain them from ordination, even if hands were laid upon him a thousand times. But the prayers used in the rite of ordination can effect this, that GOD may confirm those gifts of Theological erudition more and more: so indeed, that Ordination, speaking truly and properly, is nothing other than a public testimony of a legitimate calling and of aptitude for teaching.

The Papists are in an uproar at this point, and they contend that from the collation of orders, as they speak, a certain peculiar and latent grace is conferred upon the ordained, relying especially upon these testimonies of Scripture: 1 Timothy 4:14. Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. 2 Timothy 1:6. I admonish you, that you stir up the grace of GOD, which is in you, through the laying on of my hands.

I answer from what has already been said, that not every collation of grace is proper to the Sacraments: but only that which is proper to the Gospel, and consists in the gratuitous remission of sins, through and on account of CHRIST, apprehended by faith. For that this is conferred through the rite of ordination is simply false: otherwise it ought to be conferred not only upon ministers of the Church, but upon all men whatsoever, so that all might receive the remission of sins. But by the name of grace, through an enallage, are understood all the gifts granted to Timothy for usefully discharging an Ecclesiastical office. But the Apostle does not say that these gifts were conferred upon him through the laying on of hands, but διὰ προφητείας, through prophecy, which what kind it was, interpreters today hardly agree upon. Most, however, are of the opinion that it was signified through the Holy Spirit, either to the parents of Timothy or to some other person, how great an excellent servant of GOD and chosen instrument of GOD he would be. Even if the collation of this grace were referred most strongly to the rite of the laying on of hands, yet this was a singular gift proper to the primitive Church, and it ceased with the gift of miracles. Finally, even the single Greek word χαρίσματος, which the Apostle uses, can refute the Papists, which is nowhere in the whole New Testament applied to the grace proper to the Gospel. By way of a conclusion, it is to be noted that the whole doctrine which the Romanists cherish concerning Order overturns every respect for the Sacraments. For first, they do not want the Office of the ordained to be called a Ministry: But they maintain it must be called a Priesthood, inasmuch as it is occupied in Sacrificing. And yet the duty of offering sacrifices was not even in the Old Testament commended to anyone through any Sacrament. What of the fact that a Sacrament and a Sacrifice are disparate species, and there is no progression from one to the other. Then, concerning the Substance of the Priesthood of the New Testament, they fight that there are seven orders, which are mockeries rather than offices proper to the Ecclesiastical ministry; indeed, they lie that Christ the Savior himself passed through these orders: and that 1. he was a Doorkeeper, when with a scourge made of cords, he cast out those buying and selling from the temple. 2. A Reader, when in Luke 4 he read the passage from Isaiah in the Nazarene Synagogue. 3. An Exorcist, when in Mark 8 he touched the ears and tongue of the deaf and mute man with spittle; likewise as often as he is read to have cast out demons. 4. An Acolyte, or as others speak, a Candle-bearer, when in John 8:12 he said: I am the light of the world. 5. A Subdeacon, when after the last supper he girded himself with a linen cloth, and washed the feet of the disciples. 6. A Deacon, when in the same supper, he distributed the Body and Blood to the Apostles, whom they then pretend were created Bishops. 7. A Priest or Presbyter, when before he distributed the Sacrament, he made and consecrated it with his own mouth and his own hands: and when afterwards on the altar of the cross he sacrificed himself. But what do those fables contain that could move even a suspicion, I do not say faith, of an instituted Sacrament of order? Let the Romanists enjoy these orders: We give immortal thanks to CHRIST the Savior, that through the Blessed Luther he freed us even from this yoke of Roman captivity: to him be glory for infinite ages. AMEN.

Latin:

QUemadmodum suprà ostensum, Ritum Absolutionis, analogicè & impropriè à nonnullis Orthodoxis etiam Theologis, Sacramentum nominari consuevisse: ita non desunt, qui Ordini sive Ordinationi hominum Ecclesiasticorum ad Ministerium, eandem denominationem, sed itidem in laxâ & impropriâ significatione, competere statuunt: cum quibus nobis nulla est controversia. Verùm Romanenses Ordinationem ad Sacerdotium Novi Testamenti, contendunt esse Sacramentum verè ac propriè sic dictum. Sic enim Concilium Tridentinum. Sess. 7. Can. 3. Siquis dixerit, Ordinem sive sacram Ordinationem, non esse verè & propriè Sacramentum à CHRISTO institutum: vel esse figmentum quoddam humanum, excogitatum à Viris rerum Ecclesiasticarum imperitis: aut esse tantum ritum quendam eligendi ministros Verbi DEI, & Sacramentorum: Anathema sit.

Cæterùm non morati fulmen hoc brutum, Negativam simpliciter hoc etiam loco tenemus, ob rationes subsequentes.

1. In omni Sacramento propriè sic dicto, necessaria est certa quædam externa, visibilis, corporea materia sive elementum, quemadmodum in Baptismo & Cœnâ perspicimus. Atqui Ordinis nullum est elementum, Ergò non est Sacramentum. Minor constat, quòd nec ipsi Romanenses certum elementum, à CHRISTO mandatum & definitum, in hunc usque diem monstrare possunt. Tale non est Impositio manuum, uti suprà ostensum: Tale etiam elementum non est Insufflatio. Etsi enim CHRISTUS Insufflationis ritu, semel in ipso Resurrectionis die, usus fuisse legitur, Joh. 20, 22. nuspiam tamen legitur mandatum aliquod dedisse, de ritu hoc retinendo in Ecclesiâ, ut omnibus temporibus esset Symbolum externum in ordinatione ministrorum. Quid? quod idem Servator alibi emittens Apostolos, ut & septuaginta illos discipulos, ad docendum Evangelium, neque Impositione manuum, neque Insufflatione usus fuisse, sed sine omni ritu aut elemento sive Symbolo externo, ad ministerium illos destinasse legitur: Matth. 10. Marc. 3. Luc. 9. & 10. Sic in postremâ etiam illâ discipulorum inauguratione, & ablegatione in universum terrarum orbem, nihil quicquam ritus vel Symboli externi CHRISTUS adhibuit, Matt. 28. Marci 16.

2. Sacramenta pertinent ad omnes Christianos, quia sunt sigilla justitiæ fidei in omnibus credentibus, & applicant promissionem Evangelij, non uni hominum ordini propriam, sed omnibus hominibus communem. Ordo verò est paucorum hominum: eorum tantùm qui ministerio Ecclesiastico suam offerunt operam: imò ne istorum quidem omnium: siquidem non facilè cuivis manus imponendæ 1. Tim. 5, 22. Ergò.

3. Ordo non est organum sive medium, per quod sit applicatio & obsignatio remissionis peccatorum: id quod patet exemplo Judæ Apostoli proditoris, & aliorum nequissimorum hominum, in Papatu præsertim ad Ministerium Sacrificandi ordinatorum. Et quanquàm Christus Servator ablegans discipulos, promifsionem Gratiæ addidisse legitur, Ecce, inquiens, ego sum vobiscum omnibus diebus, usq́; ad consummationem seculi; Gratia tamen hæc non est gratia reconciliationis aut remissionis peccatorum, sed est gratia donorum Spiritus Sancti, quæ postmodùm modo quodam miraculoso, per impositionem manuum, in primitivâ Ecclesiâ fidelibus obtingebat: Quæ ipsa tamen gratia collationis peculiarium donorum, hodiè cessavit. Neque enim DEUS amplius per talem externam ceremoniam largitur χαρίσματα Spiritus Sancti, qualia sunt, dona lingvarum variarum, dona Sanationum, donum Prophetiæ, & hujus generis alia: Sed agit per media legitimè ordinata: ita ut nisi quis prius in Scholis, sive privatis sive publicis hæc dona sibi comparaverit, ex ordinatione nunquàm, si vel millies ipsi manus imponatur, ea consequatur. Preces autem in ritu ordinationis adhibitæ, id efficere possunt, ut DEUS dona illa eruditionis Theologicæ magis magisque confirmet: ita quidem, ut Ordinatio, verè ac propriè loquendo, nihil sit aliud, quàm publicum legitimæ vocationis, & aptitudinis ad docendum testimonium.

Tumultuantur hoc loco Pontificij, & ex collatione ordinum, uti loquuntur, peculiarem & latentem quandam Gratiam ordinatis conferri contendunt, his potissimum freti Scripturæ testimonijs: 1. Timoth. 4, 14. Noli negligere gratiam, quæ in te est, quæ data est tibi per prophetiam, cum impositione manuum, presbyterij. 2. Timoth. 1, 6. Admoneo te, ut resuscites gratiam DEI, quæ est in te, per impositionem manuum mearum.

Respondeo ex jam dictis, non quamlibet collationem gratiæ, esse Sacramentorum propriam: sed eam tantùm, quæ Evangelij est propria, & consistit in gratuitâ peccatorum remissione, per & propter CHRISTUM, fide apprehensum. Hanc enim per ordinationis ritum conferri, simpliciter falsum est: aliàs ille non solis Ecclesiæ ministris, sed omnibus omninò hominibus conferri deberet, ut omnes remissionem peccatorum acciperent. Sed Gratiæ nomine per Enallagen intelliguntur dona omnia ad munus Ecclesiasticum utiliter obeundum, Timotheo concessa. Non autem dicit Apostolus, quòd hæc dona in ipsum collata sint per impositionem manuum, sed διὰ προφητείας per prophetiam, quæ qualis fuerit, vix hodie inter interpretes convenit. Plerique tamen in eâ sunt opinione, quasi vel parentibus Timothei, vel alicui alteri per Spiritum Sanctum significatum sit, quàm ille sit futurus eximius DEI servus, & organum electum DEI. Quin si maximè ad ritum impositionis manuum Gratiæ hujus collatio referatur, tamen singulare hoc erat donum primitivæ Ecclesiæ proprium, & cum dono miraculorum desijt. Tandem Pontificios vel una Græca vox χαρίσματος, quo utitur Apostolus, refutare potest, quæ ad Gratiam Evangelij propriam in toto Novo Testamento nuspiàm accommodatur. Coronidis vice notandum, quod tota doctrina, quam de Ordine fovent Romanenses, omnem Sacramentorum respectum evertit. Nam primò Officium Ordinatorum, nolunt nominari Ministerium : Sed Sacerdotium vocandum esse autumant, quippè quod in Sacrificando sit occupatum. Atqui Sacrificiorum offerendorum munus, ne quidem in Veteri Testamento, cuipiam per Sacramentum aliquod commendabatur. Quid quòd Sacramentum & Sacrificium sunt disparatæ species, & ab unâ ad alteram non datur progressio. Deindè de Substantiâ Sacerdotij Novi Testamenti, septem ordines esse pugnant, qui ludibria potiùs sunt, quàm officia ministerij Ecclesiastici propria; imò mentiuntur ipsum Christum Servatorem per ordines istos transiisse: & 1. quidem Janitorem fuisse, quando flagello ex funiculis facto, ementes & vendentes templo ejecit. 2. Lectorem, cùm Luc. 4. in Synagogâ Nazarethanâ locum ex Esaiâ prælegit. 3. Exorcistam cùm Marci 8. sputo tetigit aures & lingvam surdi & muti ; item quoties ejecisse legitur dæmonia. 4. Acoluthum, vel ut alij loquuntur Ceroferarium, cùm Joh. 8, 12. dixit : Ego sum lux mundi. 5. Subdiaconum, cùm post ultimam cænam linteo sese præcinxit, & discipulorum pedes lavit. 6. Diaconum, cùm in eâdem cænâ, Corpus & Sangvinem Apostolis, quos tùm Episcopos creatos esse fingunt, distribuit. 7. Sacerdotem sive Presbyterum, cùm antequàm distribueret Sacramentum, illud suo ore & suis manibus confecit & consecravit : & cùm postmodùm in arâ crucis seipsum sacrificavit. Quid verò fabellæ illæ continent, quod aliquam instituti Sacramenti ordinis suspicionem saltem, non dico fidem movere possit? Fruantur istis ordinibus Romanenses: Nos CHRISTO Servatori agimus gratias immortales, quod per B. Lutherum ab isto etiam jugo captivitatis Romanæ nos libravit: ipsi sit gloria seculis infinitis. AMEN.


## 20 On Baptism

The Economy of the Future Treatment.

IF the state of the Church of GOD today were that which it was in the times of our Author Philip Melanchthon: certainly it would be a matter of conscience for us to depart even a little from that Method of treatment which he himself wished to observe concerning the exposition of this Article. For that fourfold Philippean Treatment, which we find to have been woven together in a style partly disputatious, partly exegetical, at the beginning concerning the end and the perpetual practical use of this Sacrament, then indeed concerning its various significations; then concerning the Baptism of John and of the Apostles; and finally concerning the Baptism of infants; could suffice for the Church of GOD today, if it were enjoying its former peace and tranquility. Now since in the last few years, and especially after the instituted Colloquy of Montbéliard, the horrible dogmas of the Calvinists, which utterly undermine and overturn the orthodoxy of this Article, have clearly erupted into strength: certainly even the very salvation of the Church, as also the purity of Religion, demands,

Latin:

Οἰκονομία Futuræ Tractationis.

SI ea hodiè Ecclesiæ DEI facies, quæ Autoris nostri Philippi Melanchthonis fuit temporibus: certè religio nobis esset, ab eâ tractationis Methodo, quam ipse observare voluit, circa Articuli bujus diexodon, vel tantillum recedere. Quadripartita enim illa Tractatio Philippea, quàm initio, de fine, & perpetuo usu practico hujus Sacramenti, deindè verò de varijs ejus fignificationibus ; tùm de Baptismo Johannis ac Apostolorum; ac tandem de Baptismo infantium, disputatorio partim, partim exegetico stylo pertextam esse deprehendimus; Ecclesiæ DEI hodieque sufficere posset, si pristinâ pace atq; tranquillitate eâ frueretur. Jam cùm annis superioribus proximis, ac cumprimis post institutum Colloquium Mompelgartense, in nervum planè eruperint, horrenda Calvinianorum dogmata, quæ Articuli hujus ὀρθοδοξίαν penitùs subruunt & evertūt: certè vel ipsa Ecclesiæ salus, ut & Religionis puritas exigit,


### When and by whom Baptism was instituted

so that we may serve the time, and hold in high regard those controversies especially which are proper to our own age. Therefore, making a short departure from the Philippian Method, we divide the entire exposition of this Article into four distinct special controversies, included in as many chapters: the FIRST of which will be concerning the Definition and essential parts of Baptism: the SECOND concerning the number or multitude of Baptism: namely, whether this Sacrament admits of division, and can be dispersed into several, differing in time and species? The THIRD concerning the Object: the FOURTH finally concerning the Effect or operation of this Sacrament. Where at the same time a dissertation will be instituted concerning its necessity as well as its practical use.

These things having been dispatched both positively and antithetically, we append as a kind of conclusion a certain Theological discourse concerning the rites still used today around the action of Baptism: and specifically concerning the Place, Time, Godparents, Exorcism, the Sign of the Cross: and concerning other questions both theoretical and practical, which are agitated today among Theologians concerning the persons to whom the power of dispensing this Sacrament has been granted, likewise concerning the Baptism of heretics and women, and concerning the reiteration of Baptism.

But before we make an approach to the treatment itself, it pleases us in place of a prologue to examine that one question, concerning which there does not seem to be one and the same opinion for everyone: namely, when and by whom the Sacrament of Baptism was instituted? Where at the beginning we establish that these two things are placed beyond controversy: 1. That John the Baptist did not institute the rite of baptizing by his own daring or judgment: 2. That only GOD and indeed Christ the Savior is its sole Author. For Scripture quite evidently supports both, as in Luke 3:2 and 3: The word of the LORD came upon John the son of Zacharias in the desert: and he came into all the region of the Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. And John the Baptist himself says, John 1:33: He who sent me to baptize in water, said to me. Hence Luke 7:30: Baptism is called the counsel of GOD, which the Pharisees and Lawyers rejected against themselves. What of the fact that the Savior himself asserts that the Baptism of John was from heaven? Matt. 21:25, Mark 11:30, Luke 20:4. But that is the thing concerning which various opinions of Doctors exist; namely, at what time was Baptism instituted by CHRIST? Whether before or after the passion? And if before: in what year was it done? And where does its institution appear in the sacred writings? Most interpreters are of the opinion that CHRIST ordained and instituted his baptism only after the Resurrection, when he was already sending the Apostles into the whole world, with this mandate: Going, teach all nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Matt. 28:19. But John the Evangelist protests against this opinion, saying: After this, Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea, and there he stayed with them, and baptized. And John was also baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there, and they came and were baptized, chap. 3:22 and 23. The sense of which words is this: That namely the Savior, having finished the festival at Jerusalem, departed into the territory of Judea properly so called: and having stayed there for some time with his disciples, he did not however lie hidden in idleness: but by both teaching and baptizing he strenuously fulfilled the parts of his ministry. Now indeed, how it was that baptism was performed by Christ, that correction or declaration shows, which is had in chapter 4:2 of John, that namely Christ himself did not administer baptism with his own hands: but that he executed this through the ministry of his disciples. Although some interpreters explain it thus: that Christ commanded the ministry of baptizing to the Apostles, not that he baptized absolutely no one: but just as Paul says that he was not sent to Baptize, but to Evangelize, who nevertheless baptized some, 1 Cor. 1:14, so Christ was occupied for the most part with doctrine. And Nicephorus is a witness, lib. 2, cap. 3, that Christ conferred the Baptism of water with his own hands upon Peter: who then baptized his brother Andrew, and the sons of Zebedee: but that the rest of the Apostles were baptized by them. But whatever the case may be, it is certainly evident from the cited chapter 3:22, that Christ was already administering baptism through his disciples in the land of Judea, when John the Baptist was staying in Galilee, and was baptizing in Aenon near Salim—not that Jerusalem one, but that other one, of which there is mention in Gen. 33:18, situated not far from Shechem—thus separated from Christ by an interval of at least twenty miles. All of which happened soon after that conversation of Christ held with Nicodemus, and indeed, as the 24th verse of this third chapter testifies, before John the Baptist had been cast into prison: which falls in the first years of Christ's ministry, and indeed in that year in which Christ first came to his temple in Jerusalem, according to the prophecy of Malachi 3:3. When the ruler shall come to his temple, he shall sit and purge the sons of Levi, and shall refine them like gold and silver, as is clear from John chapter 2:13 seqq. Therefore, at that time the disciples of Christ were already baptizing: Where a question immediately emerges: Whether they perhaps received the power of baptizing from John the Baptist, and administered that same baptism of John? Where it must be answered in the negative, that murmur of John's disciples implies, complaining about Christ and his disciples, that they also baptize, and everyone flocks to him. John 3:26. Which they certainly would not have done if they had baptized with the baptism of John. It is asked therefore further, whether the disciples of Christ took this authority upon themselves by their own daring? But John the Baptist denies this, ascribing this act of the disciples of Christ to divine ordination: A man, he says, cannot take anything upon himself, unless it has been given to him from heaven. John 3:27. It remains therefore, and from this it is gathered by necessity, that the disciples of Christ baptized at the command and ordination of the Savior himself, and consequently that Baptism was instituted by Christ, many years before the passion. But here a question immediately pushes another question: In what year, therefore, precisely was this done by Christ? Here indeed some difficulty arises, and since Scripture itself is silent, it would not be at all easy to define anything certain. this Sacrament had to be instituted with some solemnity, that it was instituted then, when Christ was baptized by John in the Jordan. For it is evidently gathered from the sacred writings that it was nowhere else done before the passion, nor could it have been done with equal majesty. And hence it is that the Fathers commonly feel that in the Baptism of Christ, the water received the power of sanctifying from the touch of the most pure and most holy flesh of Christ. But this cannot be understood otherwise than that Baptism was instituted at that time. For water does not otherwise have the power of sanctifying, except because it is the matter of Baptism, and indeed not of itself, or by itself, nor even simply from the Baptism of Christ: but from the singular ordination or destination of the Element of Water as a medium or instrument for conferring sanctification. Nor, however, is this to be understood as if Christ then expressly and in particular set forth what the matter and form of Baptism ought to be: for this was done afterwards: nor as if Christ was then baptized in the Jordan with his own baptism: for by this reasoning, baptism could be said to have been received by Christ rather than instituted by him: But because by that act of his, Christ determined, or as it were delineated, both the matter and the form of this Sacrament. The matter, indeed, when by the touch of his flesh he sanctified the water, not otherwise than by so ordaining it that it would henceforth be the matter of Baptism. The form, however, when by the visible appearance of the three persons of the Trinity, it was thus shown to be the will of GOD that in conferring Baptism, the three Persons of the divinity should be expressed. Which determination at that time was sufficient for the condition of the land of Judea and its people. Furthermore, this very institution of Baptism was, after the Resurrection of Christ, more plainly declared to the Apostles, and a wider power was even granted to them by Christ, because, namely, this Sacrament had to be propagated to all nations and peoples dispersed throughout the whole world.

Latin:

ut tempori serviamus, & eas potissimùm pensi habeamus Controversias, quæ nostri seculi sunt propriæ. Proindè à Methodo Philippéâ paulisper secessione facientes, partimur universam Articuli hujus diexodon in quatuor distinctas controversias speciales, totidem capitibus inclusas: quarum quidem PRIMA erit de Definitione, & partibus essentialibus Baptismi: ALTERA de numero sive multitudine Baptismi: Utrum nimirùm Sacramentum hoc divisionem admittat, & in plures, tempore ac specie differentes dispesci possit? TERTIA de Objecto: QUARTA denique de Effectu sive operatione Sacramenti hujus. Ubi simul de ejusdem tùm necessitate, tùm usu practico dissertatio instituetur.

Quibus tùm θετικῶς tùm ἀντιθετικῶς expeditis, coronidis quasi vice subjicimus discursum quendam Theologicum, de ritibus circa actionem Baptistieam hodieque usitatis: ac in specie quidem de Loco, Tempore, Patrinis, Exorcifmo, Signo Crucis: deque quæstionibus aliis tùm theoreticis tùm practicis, quæ de personis, quibus Sacramentum hoc dispensandi concessa potestas, de Baptismo item hæreticorum, & mulierum, deque reiteratione Baptismi hodiè inter Theologos agitantur.

Priusquàm verò ad ipsam tractationem accessum faciamus, placet προλεγομένων loco unam illam excutere quæstionem, de quâ non unum idemque videtur omnibus: Quando nimirùm & à quo Sacramentum Baptismi sit institutum? Ubi initiò duo isthæc extra controversiam posita esse statuimus: 1. Johannem Baptistam non proprio ausu sive arbitratu instituisse ritū baptizandi: 2. Solum DEUM & quidem Christum servatorem, ejus esse Autorem unicum. Utrumque enim scriptura satis evidenter adstruit, ut Luc. 3, 2. & 3. Factum est verbum DOMINI, super Johannem Zachariæ filium in deserto: & venit in omnem regionem Jordanis, prædicans baptismum pœnitentiæ, in Remissionem Peccatorum. Et ipse Johannes Baptista, inquit Joh. 1, 33. Qui misit me baptizare in aquâ, dixit mihi. Hinc Luc. 7, 30. Baptismus vocatur consilium DEI, quod Pharisæi & Legisperiti contra seipsos spreverint. Quid quòd Servator ipse, Baptismum Johannis è cælo fuisse asserit. Matth. 21, 25. Marci. 11, 30. Luc. 20, 4. Illud verò est, de quo variæ Doctorum extant opiniones; Quonám videlicet tempore Baptismus à CHRISTO sit institutus? Num ante vel post passionem? Et si ante: quonám anno id factum? & ubinám ejus institutio in sacris extet? Plerique interpretes in eâ sunt sententiâ, quòd CHRISTUS suum baptismum ordinârit & instituerit demùm post Resurrectionem, cum jam Apostolos ablegaret in universum terrarum orbem, cum hoc mandato: Euntes docete omnes gentes, & baptisate eos in nomine Patris, Filij, & Spirit9 S. Matth. 28, 19. Verùm sententiæ huic reclamat Johannes Evāgelista, Posthæc, inquiens, venit Jesus & discipuli ejus in terram Judæam, & illic morabatur cū eis, & baptisabat. Baptisabat a. etiam Johannes in Ænon propè Salem, quia multæ aquæ erant ibi, & veniebant, & baptizabantur cap. 3, 22. & 23. Quorum verborum iste est sensus : Quod nimirùm Servator exactâ Hierosolymis festivitate, digressus sit territorium Judææ propriè sic dictæ: ibique aliquamdiu cum discipulis commoratus, non tamen otiosus latuerit : sed & docendo & baptisando ministerij sui partes strenuè expleverit. Jam verò quomodo à Christo baptizatum fuerit, ostendit ea sive correctio, sive declaratio, quæ habetur cap. 4, 2. Johannis, quod videlicet non suis manibus ipsemet Christus baptismum administraverit : sed quòd discipulorum ministerio hoc executus sit. Quanquam nonnulli interpretes id sic explicant : Christum baptizandi ministerium Apostolis mandasse, non quod prorsus neminem baptizârit: sed sicut Paulus dicit, sed non missum esse ad Baptizandum, sed ad Evangelizandum, qui nihilominus tamen quosdam baptizavit 1, Cor. 1, 14. ita Christum maximam partem occupatam fuisse circa doctrinam. Et testis est Nicephorus lib. 2. cap. 3. Christum suis manibus Baptismum aquæ contulisse Petro : qui deindè fratrem suum Andream, & filios Zebedæi baptisârit : ab illis verò reliquos Apostolos baptizatos esse. Sed quicquid sit, illud certè ex citato capite 3, 22. constat, quòd Christus per discipulos suos jam tùm in terrâ Judææ baptismum administraverit, cùm Johannes Baptista in Galilæâ versaretur, & in Ænon propè Salem, non illam Hierosolymitanam, sed alteram illam, cujus sit mentio Gen. 33, 18. haud procul à Sichem sitam, baptifaret, sic ad minimum intervallo viginti milliarium à Christo sejunctus. Quæ omnia evenerunt mox post colloquium illud Christi cum Nicodemo habitum, & quidem utiversus 24. capitis hujus tertij testatur, priusquàm Johannes Baptista conjectus fuisset in carcerem: id quod incidit in primos annos ministerij Christi, & quidem in eum annum, quo Christus primùm Hierosolymis venit ad templum suum, secundum vaticinium Malach. 3, 3. Quando dominator veniet ad templum suum, sedebit & purgabir filios Levi, & colabit eos quasi aurum & argentum, uti patet ex cap. 2, 13. seqq. Johannis. Illo ergô modò tempore jam baptizabant discipuli Christi: Ubi statim emergit quæstio: An potestatem baptizandi fortè acceperint à Johanne Baptistâ, & eundem baptismum Johannis administraverint? Ubi negatè respondendum esse, innuit murmur illud discipulorum Johannis, conquerentium de Christo & discipulis ejus, quòd & illi baptizent, & omnes confluant ad eum.
