Joh. 3, 26. quod non fecissent utique, si baptismo Johannis baptisafsent. Quæritur ergò porrò, num discipuli Christi hanc autoritatem sibi proprio ausu sumserint? Verùm hoc negat Johannes Baptista, divinæ ordinationi factum hoc discipulorum Christi adscribens: Non potest, inquiens, sibi homo sumere quicquam, nisi datum ipsi sit è cælo. Joh. 3, 27. Relinquitur ergò, & ἐξ ἀνάγκης hinc colligitur, Baptisasse discipulos Christi, ad mandatum & ordinationem ipsius Servatoris, & per consequens Baptismum à Christo institutum fuiffe, annis benè multis ante passionem. Sed hic statim Quæstio quæstionem trudit, Quonám igitur anno præcisè hoc à Christo sit factitatum? Hic sanè difficultas aliqua oritur, & cum Scriptura ipsa taceat, certi quid definire, haud usq́; adeò facilè fuerit. Est autem verò maximè consentaneum, quia sine omni dubio, cum solennitate aliquâ, Sacramentum hoc institui debuit, fuisse id institutum tùm, quando à Johanne in Jordane Christus baptisatus fuit. Alibi enim ante passionem nuspiam id pari majestate factum fuisse, vel fieri etiam potuisse ex sacris evidenter colligitur. Et hinc est, quod Patres communiter sentiunt, in Baptismo Christi, aquam accepisse virtutem sanctificandi ex tactu mundissimæ sanctissimæquè carnis Christi. Atqui hoc aliter intelligi nequit, nisi quia tunc Baptismus institutus fuit. Non enim aqua aliter vim habet sanctificandi, nisi quia Baptismi est materia, & quidem non ex se, aut per se, neque etiam simpliciter ex Baptismo Christi: sed ex singulari ordinatione sive destinatione Elementi Aquæ ad sanctificationis conferendæ medium sive instrumentum. Neque tamen hoc ita intelligendum est, quasi tunc expressè & in particulari Christus exposuerit, quænám Baptismi materia & forma esse debeat: Hoc enim posteà factum est: neque etiam quasi Christus tùm in Jordane suo baptismo baptizatus fuerit: Hâc enim ratione, susceptus magis, quàm institutus a Christo baptismus fuisse, dici poterat: Sed quoniam facto illo suo Christus & materiam & formam Sacramenti hujus determinavit, vel quasi delineavit. Materiam quidem, dùm tactu suæ carnis aquam sanctificavit, non aliter, quàm sic ordinando ipsam, ut deinceps esset materia Baptismi. Formam verò, dùm factâ visibili apparitione trium personarum Trinitatis, sic ostensum fuit, esse voluntatem DEI, ut in conferendo Baptismo, tres divinitatis Personæ exprimerentur. Quæ determinatio tùm temporis, pro terræ Judææ & populi conditione sufficiens fuit. Cæterùm hæc ipsa Baptismi institutio, post Resurrectionem Christi, planiùs Apostolis declarata, & amplior etiam ipsis potestas à Christo concessa fuit, quia nimirùm Sacramentum hoc, jam ad omnes gentes & populos, per universum terrarum orbem dispersos, propagari debuit.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacrament of Baptism

Baptism, as regards its essence, just like the other individual Sacraments, consists of two things: the Earthly, namely, or Elemental: and the Heavenly or Invisible. But concerning each part, because of the differing opinions of Theologians, we must look into them separately. And at the beginning, indeed, as regards the part or Elemental Thing, today it is agreed among

Theologians, insofar as all admit that Elemental Water was named by Christ in general; insofar as most also concede that some analogy intervenes between the effect of Baptism and this Elemental water: as, just as water wipes away the filth of the body: so the stains of souls are washed away by Baptism. But various questions are raised concerning the nature and quality of this Water.

And first indeed it is asked, Whether only Elemental water was so defined and ordained by Christ, that if it is clearly lacking, no other liquid can be substituted? And indeed D. Augustine reports, in his book on heresies, chapter 46, that the Manichaeans simply relegated Water from Baptism, because not GOD, but the devil had created it. And chapter 59, that the Seleucians and Hermians around the year of the Lord 180 maintained that water is not simply necessary in Baptism. Nay, Philastrius is a witness that the same heretics rejected the Baptism of Water for the reason that it was written in Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, 'He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire,' saying that the Soul is composed of Spirit and fire. Thus around the year of the Lord 590 there were Jacobites, who conferred Baptism by a cautery, with the sign of the Cross impressed on the forehead of the person to be baptized. A custom which certain Ethiopians, called Abazini, who live under Prester John, are written to observe even today, with the sole exception that instead of the sign of the cross, they are said to impress a character like a certain star. What of the fact that in our age Theodore Beza was not horrified to write: 'If water is lacking, and yet the Baptism of someone cannot and ought not to be deferred with edification: I certainly would baptize with any other liquid, no less rightly than with water.' Nor did the most superstitious Scholastic Writers themselves judge otherwise concerning these matters. In Volume 1 of his Letters, Epistle 2, to Thomas Tilius. Orthodox Theologians hold the negative in all respects, and defend that Elemental Water, without prejudice to the substance of Baptism, cannot be exchanged with any other liquid of a different species: moved by this chief and indeed irrefutable reason.

That is called essential which is so required for constituting the essence of something, that if its form is abolished, and changed through its essence, its essence—which it constitutes—immediately also collapses and is changed:

Now, however, water is an essential and ουσιωτικὴ part of Baptism, even by the admission of the Calvinists themselves. Therefore its form cannot be changed with another species of any liquid, unless the essence of this Sacrament itself is also changed.

And this other reason is added. The Sacramental union of the earthly thing with the heavenly thing depends solely on the word of promise expressed in the institution itself. It would therefore be a sin, nay, blasphemous, to imagine a Sacramental union of the heavenly thing with such an element, about which the word of promise defines nothing at all: so that he is no less impious who maintains that Milk, Beer, or Lye, or some other similar liquid, different in species from natural water, is sacramentally united with the Holy Spirit, or the blood of CHRIST in Baptism: than he who contends that, in the Sacrament of the Eucharist, in place of bread can be substituted either marchpane, or another cake differing in species from bread: or in place of wine can be substituted water, milk, honey, or beer. Strictly, therefore, must be observed the Theological axiom: Whatever differs in species from elemental water cannot be an element of Baptism. Hence Christ himself willed to be baptized with nothing but water: and says to Nicodemus:… Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, etc. John 3, 3. and Acts 10, 47. Peter, Who can forbid that these be baptized with water, who have received the Holy Spirit. And this very opinion was held also by the Scholastic Doctors, so that Beza, not without manifest crime of falsehood, strives to draw them into his own opinion. For this axiom is commonly accepted among them: Whatever differs in species from Elemental water cannot be the matter of Baptism: Hence the same [authors] contend that it would have been fitting that Baptism be made in that humor which is cold, fluid, clear, and ready for repressing the fervor of concupiscence, for bending the rigor of disobedience, for illuminating the sharpness of the intelligence, and for obliging all, as well the poor as the rich, so that no one might excuse poverty and the difficulty of preparation. Hence also Canon 2, Session 7, concerning Baptism of the Council of Trent: if anyone shall say that true and natural water is not of the necessity of Baptism: and therefore has distorted those words of our Lord Jesus Christ; Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, to some metaphor, let him be anathema. We certainly, subscribing in this part to this council, say Anathema to John Calvin, who in his commentary on the 3rd chapter of John, contends that Spirit and Water are put by Christ for the same thing: so that he may not be forced to confess that Christ ascribes to the external element of Water the power of regenerating in Baptism.

Moreover, some doubts are moved in this place: such as 1. that in Matthew 3, 11 and Luke 3, 16 no mention is made of water: But of Baptism, Spirit, and fire. 2. That the washing away of sins can be done by other liquids just as well as by Water. 3. That water and blood flowed from the side of Christ, and therefore Baptism can be performed in blood. 4.

That Blessed Luther in his table talks, when asked whether in the absence of water it is permitted to baptize in milk or beer: first answered that it should be committed to divine judgment: but afterwards added, Whatever can be called by the name of a bath, that is apt for baptizing, whether it be wine, or milk, or beer.

But the answer to each is easy: For as regards 1, an ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꙋ is committed. For by the word fire, Sacramental Baptism is not there denoted, but that miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit, which happened on the day of Pentecost in tongues of fire, and is metaphorically called Baptism. Which very thing Jerome also acknowledged on this same passage of Matthew.

As regards II, it has already been shown above to be manifestly false, which is taken as confessed: that is, that both the essence of Baptism and the Sacramental promise, made to the Element of Water, in no way admit the substitution of any other liquid differing in species from natural water. And in this question, one must not look so much at that analogical reason of washing, which other species of liquids might sustain just as well as water: but this alone must be attended to, to which Element in species the promise of Sacramental Union with the heavenly thing was made. As regards III, I answer 1. that an allegory proves nothing unless it is supported by testimonies of Scripture. 2. We will more correctly accommodate this allegory if we say that water and blood flowed from the side of Christ for this reason, that thus the Sacramental Union of the Water and Blood of Christ in Baptism might be hinted at. 3. The Fathers understand Baptism by Water: but by blood, the Sacrament of the Eucharist. As regards IV, we note at the beginning that it is taken from such a book of Luther that was never even seen or read by him, let alone approved: but was compiled only after his death, quite tumultuously, and without due judgment and circumspection, by various people who perhaps have not always sufficiently grasped the mind of Luther. Therefore, one should not stand by the authority of this book in deciding questions or doubtful and controversial cases: unless in his other writings, whether polemical or didactic, the same Luther holds and defends the same opinion. Now, however, as we answer in the second place, Blessed Luther, writing professedly on this question, clearly stands on our side. For thus he says in a Sermon held in the year 41, four years before his death: You shall not care whether he who administers baptism is good and has faith, or whether he does not. For even if he is impious and without faith, if he at least keeps the institution and does not take wine, beer, lye, or anything else for baptizing: But uses water with the word of GOD, his Baptism is called, and is, Holy Baptism: Because here are all things which pertain to the essence or integrity of baptism: namely natural water, with the word of GOD, from divine ordination and institution: [German text follows: Let the person be godless and unbelieving, if he only keeps the institution of Christ and does not take wine, beer, lye, or another thing, but water with the added word of GOD, so it is called and is a Holy Baptism, for here is everything that belongs to the essence of holy baptism, namely, natural water, with the word from God's ordinance and command, etc.]

But furthermore it is asked, whether any elemental water can be the matter of this Sacrament? Eusebius indeed reports, in book 4 of the life of Constantine, ch. 62, that Constantine the Great did not wish Baptism to be conferred upon him from any other water than from the Jordan, in which CHRIST himself was baptized, for the sake of which thing we read that he even went there for that very purpose. Hence some also of the Ancients contended that Christ, by the touch of his most pure flesh, had therefore conferred power upon the waters of the Jordan: so that it alone was suitable for baptism. But neither the deed of Constantine, nor this little argument of some, deserves any approval. For that [deed] is not entirely devoid of all superstition.

What? That Constantine himself, in that very preparation for his journey to Palestine to the Jordan, seized by a lethal disease, obtained Baptism in Nicomedia in Bithynia. To the little argument brought forward, we respond with Bonaventure, that that power is not some property or absolute essence added to the water: but only its ordination to this end, that it may be for man a washing of regeneration. Wherefore this virtue is derived to all water, not because of the continuity of place, as Thomas says, but because of the similarity of species. Thus, therefore, it must be established that Water is the matter of Baptism, and that it is elemental and simple, Eph. 5, 26, such as indeed was the water of the Jordan, which Christ for that reason sanctified by the contact of his most pure flesh, so that not it alone, but because of the similarity of species, all other waters are likewise considered sanctified and suitable for this saving washing of regeneration, as the Fathers commonly speak: Greg. Naz. homily on the Epiphany. Jerome on chapter 3 of Matthew, Augustine Sermon 29 and 36 on the Season.

Thirdly, it is asked, Can and should water exorcised by the Papists be recognized as elemental water in the action of Baptism? We respond that that exorcism, although in and of itself it is impious and superstitious, nevertheless does not change the species of the water itself: and therefore that water can be held as elemental water. It is added that the Scholastic Doctors themselves commonly teach that that exorcism or blessing is not of the necessity of Baptism, but pertains only to a certain solemnity of it.

Finally, it is asked, Is only simple, or purely natural, or elemental water the matter of Baptism: or indeed, especially in a case of necessity, can even artificial water be used: or water changed to some extent by nature: such as sea water, rain water, cooking water, lye, thermal water, rose water, dew, snow, hail, sweat, ice, and others of this kind. We respond by a distinction. For either it is a case of necessity, where a supply of simple water cannot be had: Or the question is general, namely, which water is to be preferred to another: Where, from what has already been said, we establish that that water is most suitable for this Sacramental act which is simpler than the rest: not indeed because any power resides in the simplicity or purity of water in itself; but because we read that such was ordained by Christ. Moreover, in a case of necessity, if the simplest water cannot be had, we judge that even that water can be used which has undergone some change either by a natural cause or by art, but such a change as has not destroyed the species and substance of the water itself, so that the washing can take place. For example, in sea water, there is not such a great transmutation as to take away the species of the water itself and convert it into some disparate one. Nor does impurity prevent it from being baptismal water, provided it does not hinder it from being suitable for washing; the matter is otherwise with lye, which, although it is suitable for washing, nevertheless constitutes a disparate species of water; and therefore it serves the Baptismal action not at all. Moreover, thermal waters, although they suffer some alteration by nature, nevertheless do not take away the species of the water itself, and therefore in a case of necessity they can be used. Thus water from dew, snow, hail, and ice, once melted, can be used for baptism: for they are natural waters. But as long as they are frozen, they cannot be used: For although snow and ice not yet melted are water by substance: they are not, however, by species. Thus rain and cooking water share the same condition, that they do not vary or take away the species of the water itself. Moreover, sweat, tears, and waters distilled either from roses or from other plants are not substantially elemental water: and therefore they are not at all suitable for the administration of this Sacrament. We conclude therefore with Arnobius on Psalm 74 that one Baptism can be administered in all natural waters, whether of rivers or of the sea, or of fountains, or of torrents, or of stagnant pools, provided that it has received nothing of change regarding its natural substance.

Latin:

Baptismus quoad essentiam suam, prout reliqua Sacramenta singula, duabus constat rebus: Terrenâ nimirùm sive Elementari: & Cælesti sive Invisibili. Verùm de utraque parte, propter discrepantes Theologorum opiniones, seorsim nobis fuerit dispiciendum. Ac initiò quidem, quoad partem sive Rem Elementarem hodiè eatenùs convenit inter

Theologos, quatenùs in genere Aquam Elementarem à Christo nominatam esse, fatentur omnes; quatenùs etiam effectui Baptismi, cum aquâ hac Elementari analogiam aliquam intercedere plerique concedunt: ut, quemadmodum corporis sordes abstergit aqua: sic animarum maculæ Baptismo abluantur. Verùm de naturâ & qualitate Aquæ hujus variæ moventur quæstiones.

Ac primùm quidem quæritur, Num à Christo sola aqua Elementaris ita sit definita & ordinata, ut eâ planè deficiente, non alius aliquis liquor substitui possit? Et sanè refert D. Augustinus, lib. de hæresibus cap. 46. Manichæos ex Baptismo Aquam simpliciter relegasse, eò quòd non DEUS, sed diabolus eam creasset. Et c. 59. Seleucianos & Hermianos circa annum D. 180. statuisse, aquam in Baptismo non simpliciter esse necessariam. Quin imò testis est Philastrius, eosdem hæreticos, ideò rejecisse Baptismum Aquæ, quòd scriptum esset Matth. 3, 11. & Luc. 3, 16. ipse Baptisabit vos Spiritu Sancto & igni, dicentes Animam esse compositam ex Spiritu & igni. Sic circa annum D. 590. fuerunt Jacobitæ, qui conferebant Baptismum per cauterium, hominis baptizandi fronti impresso signo Crucis. Quem morem etiamnùm hodiè observare scribuntur Æthiopes quidam, Abazini dicti, qui vivunt sub Presbytero Johanne, eo duntaxat excepto, quòd pro signo crucis, characterem instar stellæ cujusdam imprimere perhibentur. Quid? quod nostrâ ætate Theodorus Beza scribere non exhorruit: Si desit aqua, & tamen Baptismus alicujus differri cum ædificatione non possit, nec debeat: ego certè quovis alio liquore, non minus ritè, quam aquâ baptizârim. Nec aliter de his rebus ipsi etiam superstitiosissimè Scholastici Scriptores censuerunt. Tomo 1. Epistolarum, Epist. 2. ad Thomam Tilium. Orthodoxi Theologi negativam per omnia tenent, ac defendunt, Aquam Elementarem, salvâ substantiâ Baptismi, cum alio quocunque diversæ speciei liquore, permutari non posse: hâc potissimùm & quidem irrefragabili moti ratione.

Essentiale est ac dicitur, quod ita ad constituendam rei alicujus essentiam requiritur, ut si forma ejus aboleatur, ac per essentiam mutetur, mox ipsa etiam corruat, & mutetur essentia illius rei, quam constituit:

Jam verò aqua pars est essentialis & ουσιωτικὴ Baptismi, ipsis quoꝙ fatentibus Calvinianis. Ergò forma ejus cum aliâ specie cujusvis liquoris, mutari non potest, nisi ipsa etiam mutetur Sacramenti hujus essentia.

Accedit & ratio hæc altera. Unio Sacramentalis rei terrenæ cum re cælesti, unicè dependet ex verbo promissionis in ipsâ institutione expresso. Nefas ergò fuerit, imò blasphemum, fingere unionem Sacramentalem rei cælestis, cum tali elemento, de quo verbum promissionis nihil quicquam definit: ita ut haud minùs impius sit, qui statuat, Lac, Cerevisiam, aut Lixivium, vel similem liquorem alium, specie differentem ab aquâ naturali Sacramentaliter uniri cum Spiritu Sancto, aut sangvine CHRISTI in Baptismo: quàm qui contendit, in Sacramento Eucharistiæ, loco panis posse substitui, vel panem martium, vel placentam aliam specie à pane differentem: vel loco vini posse substitui aquam, lac, mel, aut cerevisiam. Strictè ergò observandum axioma Theologicum: Quicquid specie differt ab aquâ elementari, non potest esse elementum Baptismi. Hinc Christus ipse non nisi aquâ baptizari voluit: & ad Nicodemum inquit: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aquâ & Spiritu &c. Joh. 3, 3. & Actor. 10, 47. Petrus, Quis prohibere potest, quò minùs aquâ baptizentur hi, qui acceperunt Spiritum Sanctum. Et hanc ipsam sententiam tenuerunt etiam Doctores Scholastici, ita ut Beza, non sine manifesto crimine falsi ipsos in suam sententiam pertrahere studeat. Hoc enim apud ipsos communiter receptum est axioma: Quicquid specie differt ab aquâ Elementari, non potest esse materia Baptismi: Hinc contendunt iidem, congruum fuissent, Baptismus fieret in illo humore, qui est frigidus, fluidus, lucidus & obvius ad reprimendum fervorem concupiscentiae, ad flectendum rigorem inobedientiae, ad illustrandam aciem intelligentiae, & ad obligandum omnes tam pauperes, quàm divites, ne quis inopiam & apparatus difficultatem excuset. Hinc etiam Canon. 2. Sess. 7. de Bapt: Concilij Tridentini: si quis dixerit, Aquam veram & naturalem, non esse de necessitate Baptismi: atq; ideò verba illa Domini nostri Jesu Christi; Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aquâ & Spiritu Sancto, ad metaphoram aliquam detorserit, anathema sit. Nos certè hâc in parte concilio huic subscribentes, Anathema dicimus Johanni Calvino, qui in commentario super caput 3. Johannis, contendit, Spiritum & Aquam à Christo pro eodemponi: ne videlicet fateri cogatur, Christum externo Aquaelemento regenerandi vim in Baptismo adscribere.

Caterùm moventur hoc loco nonnulla dubia: ut 1. quòd Matth. 3, 11. & Luc. 3, 16. nulla aquae fiat mentio: Sed Baptismi, Spiritus & ignis. 2. Quòd per alios liquores æquè fieri possit peccatorum ablutio, atque per Aquam. 3. Quòd ex latere Christi fluxerit aqua & sangvis, ac proindè in sangvine fieri possit Baptismus. 4.

Quòd B. Lutherus in colloquiis convivialibus, interrogatus, nùm deficiente aquâ liceat baptizare in lacte aut cerevisia: primùm responderit, judicio divino esse id committendum: deindè verò addiderit, Quicquid balnei nomine nuncupari potest, illud esse aptum ad baptizandum sive sit vinum, sive lac, sive Cerevisia.

Sed facilis est ad singula responsio: Nam quoad I. committitur ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꙋ. Nam vocabulo ignis ibi non notatur Baptismus Sacramentalis, sed miraculosa illa effusio Spiritus Sancti, quæ facta est in die Pentecostes in lingvis igneis, & Metaphoricè Baptismus nominatur. Quod ipsum agnovit etiam Hieronymus super hunc ipsum locum Matthæi.

Quoad II. jam suprà ostensum manifestè falsum esse, quod pro confesso sumitur: quòd nimirùm tùm essentia Baptismi, tùm promissio Sacramentalis, Elemento Aquæ facta, nullatenùs admittat ullius alicujus liquoris, specie cum aquâ naturali differentis, substitutionem. Et hac in quæstione non tam spectanda est analogica illa ratio ablutionis, quam aliæ liquorum species itidem atque aqua sustinere queant: sed id unicè attendendum, cuinám Elemento in specie facta sit promissio de Unione Sacramentali cum re cælesti. Quoad III. respondeo 1. allegoriam nihil probare, nisi Scripturæ suffulciatur testimoniis. 2. rectiùs accommodabimus hanc allegoriam, si dixerimus, ideò aquam & sangvinem effluxisse è latere Christi, ut sic innueretur Sacramentalis Unio, Aquæ & Sangvinis Christi in Baptismo. 3. Patres per Aquam intelligunt Baptismum: per sangvinem verò, Sacramentum Eucharistiæ. Qubad IV. initiò notamus, illud desumtum esse ex tali Lutheri libro, qui ipsi nunquàm vel visus vel lectus, nedùm approbatus: sed post obitum demùm ipsius, satis & tumultuariè, & sine judicio ac circumspectione debitâ, à diversis compilatus est, qui fortè mentem Lutheri non semper satis sunt assecuti. Haud proindè Libri hujus autoritate standum fuerit, in decidendis quæstionibus sive casibus dubijs & controversis: nisi in reliquis suis scriptis sive elencticis sive didacticis, idemLutherus eandem sententiam teneat ac defendat. Jam verò, quod secundò loco respondemus, B. Lutherus ex professo de hâc quæstione scribens, à nostris planè stat partibus. Sic enim ille in Sermone habito anno 41. quadriennio ante obitum: Non curabis, nùm ille, qui baptismum administrat, bonus sit, & fidem habeat, an verò non. Etsi enim impius & sine fide est, si saltem institutionem servat & ad baptizandum non accipit vinum, cerevisiam, lixivium, vel aliud quiddam: Sed aquam adhibito DEI verbo, Baptismus ejus vocatur, & est Sanctus Baptismus: Quia hic omnia sunt, quæ ad essentiam sive integritatem baptismi pertinent: videlicet naturalis aqua, cum verbo DEI, ex ordinatione ac institutione divinâ: Laß gleich die Person Gottloß und Ungläubig sein/ So er nur die Einsetzung Christi hält/ und nimpt darzu nicht Wein/ Bier/ Laugen/oder ein ander Ding/ Sondern Wasser mit zugethanen GOTTES Wort/ So heist und ist es ein Heilige Tausse/ denn hie ist alles/ was zu dem Wesen der heiligen Tauffe gehöret/ nehmlich / natürlich Wasser/mit dem Wort aus Gottes Stifft und Befehl/ etc.

Sed porrò quæritur An quævis aqua elementaris Sacramenti hujus materia esse possit? Refert quidem Eusebius, lib. 4. de vita Constantini, c. 62. Constantinum Magnum noluisse ex ullâ aliâ aquâ, quàm ex Jordane, in quo CHRISTUS ipse baptizatus fuit, Baptismum sibi conferri, cujus rei gratiâ eò etiam inter ipsum ingressum fuisse legimus. Hinc nonnulli etiam ex Veteribus contendebant, Christum ideò tactu mundissimæ suæ carnis, vim contulisse aquis Jordanis: ut ea sola idonea esset ad baptismum. Verùm neque factum Constantini, neque ratiuncula hæc quorundam approbationem ullam meretur. Illud enim superstitione non planè omni caret.

Quid? quòd ipse Constantinus, in illo ipso itineris apparatu in Palæstinam ad Jordanem, lethali morbo correptus, Nicomediæ in Bithyniâ Baptismum consecutus est. Ad ratiunculam allatam respondemus cum Bonaventurâ, Vim illam, non esse aliquam proprietatem, vel essentiam absolutam, additam aquæ: sed solùm ordinationem ejus ad hoc, ut homini sit lavacrum regenerationis. Quare virtus hæc derivata est ad omnem aquam, non propter continuitatem loci, ut inquit Thomas, sed propter similitudinem speciei. Sic ergò statuendum, Aquam esse materiam Baptismi, eamquè elementarem simplicem, Eph. 5, 26. qualis nempè fuit aqua Jordanis, quam Christus contactu mundissimæ suæ carnis ideò sanctificavit, ut non ea sola, sed propter similitudinem speciei, omnes aliæ aquæ itidem sanctificatæ, & ad salutare hoc regenerationis lavacrum idoneæ censeantur, uti communiter Patres loquuntur: Greg. Naz. homil. de Epiphan. Hieron. in cap. 3. Matthæi, August. Serm. 29. & 36. de Tempore.

Tertiò quæritur, An aqua per Pontificios exorcisata, pro aquâ elementari in actione Baptisticâ agnosci possit & debeat? Respondemus exorcisationem illam, licèt in & per se sit impia & superstitiosa, ipsam tamen aquæ speciem non mutare: ac proindè illam aquam, pro aquâ elementari haberi posse. Accedit quòd ipsi Doctores Scholastici communiter docét, exorcisationem illam, vel benedictionem non esse de necessitate Baptismi, sed pertinere tantùm ad quandam ejus solennitatem.

Tandem quæritur, An tantùm simplex sive purè naturalis sive elementaris aqua, sit materia Baptismi: an verò, præsertim in casu necessitatis, adhiberi possit aqua etiam artificialis: vel per naturam aliquatenùs mutata: qualis est aqua maritima, pluvialis, coquinaria, lixivium, therma, aqua rosacea, ros, nix, grando, sudor, glacies, & hujus generis aliæ. Respondemus per distinctionem. Vel enim agitur de casu necessitatis, ubi simplicis aquæ copia haberi nequit: Vel quæstio est generalis, Quænam videlicet aqua alteri sit præferenda: Ubi ex jam dictis statuimus, Aquam eam actui huic Sacramentali maximè convenire, quæ reliquis est simplicior: non quidem quòd simplicitati sive puritati aquæ per se vis aliqua insit; sed quia talem à Christo ordinatam esse legimus. Cæterùm in casu necessitatis, si simplicissima aqua haberi non possit, arbitramur eam etiam aquam adhiberi posse, quæ vel per causam naturalem, vel per artem mutationem aliquam passa est, sed talem mutationem, quæ ipsam speciem & substantiam aquæ non destruxerit, uti fieri possit ablutio. Exempli gratiâ, in aquâ maritimâ, non est tanta transmutatio, quæ ipsam aquæ speciem tollat, & in disparatam aliquam convertat. Neque etiam impuritas prohibet, quin possit esse aqua baptismi, modò non impediat, quin ad abluendum sit conveniens, secus res habet cum lixivio, quod licèt ad abluendum sit conveniens, disparatam tamen aquæ speciem constituit; ac proindè Baptistica actioni minimè servit. Cæterùm aquæ thermales, licèt naturâ alterationis aliquid patiantur, speciem tamé ipsam aquæ non tollunt, ac proindè in casu necessitatis usurpari possunt. Sic aqua ex rore, nive, grandine, glacie, jam resolutis, ad baptismum adhiberi possunt: sunt enim aquæ naturales. Verùm quamdiu sunt congelatæ, non possunt adhiberi: Nam licet nix, & glacies nondùm resolutæ per substantiam sunt aqua: non tamen sunt per speciem. Sic pluvialis & coquinaria aqua eandem conditionem fortiuntur, ut speciem ipsam aquæ non varient aut tollant. Cæterùm sudor, lachrymæ, & aquæ vel ex rosis, vel ex alijs plantis distillatæ non sunt substantialiter aqua elementaris: ac proindè Sacramenti huj9 dispensationi minimè conveniens. Concludimus proindè cum Arnobio in Psalmum 74. Unum Baptisma in aquis naturalibus omnibus sive fluminum sive maris, sive fontium, sive torrentum, sive stagnorum administrari posse, modò mutationis nihil quoad naturalem substantiam ea acceperit.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacrament of Baptism: Of the Other Essential Part of Baptism: which is the Celestial and invisible Thing

Just as in the immediately preceding Article, from the analogy partly of all the Sacraments, but partly from the unanimous consent of Orthodox Antiquity, it was demonstrated that each Sacrament consists of two things, differing in their whole genus: so it must entirely be established that of Baptism also, there is not only one substantial part, namely the Element of Water, expressed by the Word of institution: but that a second, heavenly one must be granted: concerning which, however, it does not seem the same to all: but Theologians depart into four differing opinions.

I. There are those who substitute the Word in place of the heavenly thing, urging that saying of Augustine: Let the Word be added to the Element and it becomes a Sacrament. Likewise that saying of Blessed Luther in the smaller Catechism asserting that Baptism is not simply water, but water included and comprehended by the Word of GOD. But these men do not notice that the discourse of Augustine and Luther is not about the causes or constitutive principles, which constitute and complete the very essence of the Sacrament in itself, and by itself, and as it were absolutely considered: but about the productive principles, which complete the whole action of the Sacrament, and not its substance alone. Where indeed this Theological axiom is most true, that no Sacrament properly so called can exist unless the express Word is present, both of command, and of the promise: neither of which, however, can be or be called a substantial part of the Sacrament. For if the Word of the promise were such a constitutive or essential part of the Sacrament, it would follow that hypocrites and infidels, as well as the faithful, would obtain the saving fruit of Regeneration. The reason is that hypocrites, like the unworthy, obtain the whole Sacrament in the Eucharist, according to both essential parts, entire; as was shown more fully above in chapter 1, in the doctrine concerning the Sacraments in general. But this latter is manifestly false. Therefore, the former is also false.

II. There are those who maintain that the Holy Spirit concurs in the action of the Baptismal Sacrament, not only as the original cause, or as the instituting cause, just as the other two persons of the Trinity also concur; nor even only as a pledge or seal, by reason of the saving fruit and effect which He confirms and seals in the faithful; but also as a constitutive cause, that is, as a cause entering into the very substance of this Sacrament and constituting its other, heavenly and invisible part. And indeed, the opinion of these men is not destitute of manifest testimonies of Scripture: both of Christ Himself, John 3:5, "Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven"; and of the Apostle, asserting that GOD sends the Spirit in and through Baptism as a pledge into our hearts: 2 Cor. 1:22. Eph. 1:14, which they understand not only concerning the saving effect of Baptism, but concerning its very substantial part. And lest any absurdity follow from this opinion of theirs regarding hypocrites, they explain their mind more fully in this way: Just as, they say, in the Holy Supper the unworthy eat the very body and blood of Christ, and yet do not become partakers of the vivifying virtue of the Flesh of Christ, their unbelief standing in the way; so also hypocrites are washed in Baptism not only with water, but with the Holy Spirit Himself; yet they are not made partakers of the saving fruit or operation of the Holy Spirit: since the Holy Spirit thus conferred upon them indeed intends that saving operation, but does not perfect or exert it in the act itself, because of their unbelief. Nor is it a necessary consequence that where the Holy Spirit is substantially, there He must also be according to the saving effect of Regeneration. For He is present substantially, by the condition of His nature and essence, whose property it is to be substantially present to all things and creatures, Ps. 139:7, Wis. 1:7. But that He is present by a special energy of grace, that depends upon His most free will, which is efficacious in believers, but not so in hypocrites.

We are so far from rejecting or simply disapproving of their opinion that we rather pronounce it to contain nothing inconsistent with the analogy of faith, leaving it free to anyone whether he prefers to subscribe to this or to the subsequent opinions.

III. There are those who judge the heavenly part of this Sacrament to be the Blood of Christ: led to this chiefly by these reasons: I. All cleansing from sin does not occur, nor can it occur, except through the blood of CHRIST, 1 John 1:7, "The blood of the Son of GOD cleanses us from all sin," Heb. 9:22, "All things are cleansed in blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission." But indeed, in baptism, cleansing from sin happens to the baptized, Eph. 5:26. Therefore, it is necessary that the Blood of Christ intervene.

But perhaps someone might object that the Blood of Christ does indeed intervene, but that it does not follow from this that the Blood is constituted as the other essential part of this Sacrament; because we are cleansed daily and incessantly from sin by the blood of Christ, as often as we look upon Him with faith; where, however, no perception of the Blood of Christ occurs, as regards its substance. But it can be answered that this argument is deceived and deceives by the sophism of disparate questions, which are confused; since one must accurately distinguish between the Sacramental cleansing, which occurs in Baptism, and that Spiritual cleansing, which is performed daily and incessantly by faith. For although by reason of the saving effect, the cleansing is one and the same in both cases, it cannot be denied that in the Sacrament it is conferred by a certain sign, as a medium or organ. But this Sacramental Sign in Baptism is not naked and mere water; but it is established beyond controversy that a heavenly thing also is added. This heavenly thing, according to its essence, must be Sacramentally united and coupled with the earthly and elemental thing; otherwise there would be no Sacrament. If, therefore, the Blood of Christ, together with the Water, constitutes that Sacramental Sign, it follows of necessity that the Blood of Christ, as the other substantial part, is substantially conferred in Baptism to all the baptized. II. The reason is sought from the nature of the Sacraments. For such is the nature of Sacramental signs that there always intervenes some similarity of the Elemental thing with the heavenly thing. For if, as Augustine speaks in Epist. 23 to Boniface, the Sacraments did not have a certain similarity to those things of which they are Sacraments, they would not be Sacraments at all. Now, a sufficiently exquisite similarity of the elemental water with the Blood of Christ is evident; which that fact also seems to have hinted at, that both water and Blood flowed out simultaneously from the side of Christ. Therefore. III. The reason is sought from the analogy which, regarding the essential parts of the Sacraments, intervenes between the Old Testament and the New: For just as the paschal lamb bore the type of the Sacrament of the Eucharist, so that the flesh of the slaughtered lamb shadowed forth the flesh of the crucified Christ, and its blood, the blood of Christ; so in the Sacrament of Circumcision, which was a type of Baptism, the amputation of the foreskin, consisting in the shedding of blood, seems to have expressed the sprinkling of water in Baptism, mixed with the Blood of Christ. IV. And the last is taken from the authority of Augustine, Luther, and other Orthodox Theologians. Augustine certainly, tract. 11 in John, says that Baptism is reddened by the blood of CHRIST. Luther, however, says that the Water of Baptism is mixed with the blood of Christ: relying on the Apostolic authority of John, who affirms that CHRIST came by Water and blood: not by Water only, but also by blood. 1 John 5:6. The words of Blessed Luther sound thus:

Therefore St. John the Evangelist is accustomed to speak gladly of dear Baptism in this way, that it is a water mingled with the blood of CHRIST. As in John 19, when Christ was crucified and had died, and one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, there came out (he says) immediately blood and water, and he confirms this with great words, and says: And he who has seen it bears witness to it, and his witness is true, and he knows that he speaks the truth, so that you also may believe. Likewise in his Epistle in the last chapter he speaks of Christ, this is he who comes with water and blood, JESUS Christ, Not with water only, But with water and blood. Thus he always wishes to mingle the blood into Baptism, so that the rose-colored innocent blood of Christ may shine and be seen therein. To human eyes nothing appears there, neither clear white water, that is true. But St. John wishes to open for us the inner and spiritual eyes of faith, so that we may see with them not only water, But also the blood of our LORD JESUS CHRIST etc.

IV. And finally, there is no lack of Theologians who make the Heavenly Thing of this Sacrament combined, and constitute it as the Holy Spirit and the Blood of CHRIST, together, yet with a distinction of subalternation: having followed in this part the footsteps of certain Fathers. Cyprian certainly, comparing the passage of the Israelites through the Red Sea, writes: The Hebrews were baptized in the cloud and in the sea: but now the people of GOD are cleansed from sins by the Holy Spirit and the Blood of CHRIST. Thus Ambrose in his book on those who are initiated into the mysteries, chapter 2. You have read, he says, that the three witnesses in Baptism are one: Water, Blood, and Spirit: because if you take away one of these, the Sacrament of Baptism does not stand.

This last opinion, as also the two preceding, although they obtain some diversity, are nevertheless not contradictory, much less do they fight against the analogy of faith: but without any

danger of error or of conscience can be approved, provided that it be left free to anyone whether he wishes to follow this or that of these three latter ones.

These things being thus established, we define Baptism as being a Sacrament of the New Testament, divinely instituted, in which through water and the Spirit in the Blood of CHRIST, all who are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, being gifted with true faith, are truly reborn, are adopted as children of GOD, and are sealed for an eternal inheritance: so that they may henceforth walk in newness of life, John 3:5. Rom. 6:4. Acts 2:38. Eph. 5:26. Tit. 3:5. 1 Pet. 3:21.

Moreover, two things especially are moved concerning this definition. I. What and of what kind is the Union of these two essential parts, constituting the substance of this Sacrament. II. What and of what kind is the form that ought to be observed concerning the administration of Baptism?

Latin:

QUemadmodum Articulo præcedente proximo, ex analogiâ partim omnium Sacramentorum, partim verò ex unanimi consensu Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, demonstratum fuit, unumquodque Sacramentum constare duabus rebus, toto genere discrepantibus: ita omninò statuendum, Baptismi etiam, non unam tantùm esse partem substantialem, Aquæ videlicet Elementum, Verbo institutionis expressum: sed & alteram cœlestem concedendam esse: de quâ tamen non unum videtur omnibus: sed in quatuor discrepantes sententias abeunt Theologi.

I. Sunt, qui loco rei cœlestis substituunt Verbum, urgentes illud Augustini; Accedat Verbum ad Elementum & fit Sacramentum. Item illud B. Lutheri in minore Catechismo asserentis, Baptismum non esse simpliciter aquam, sed aquam, verbo DEI inclusam, & comprehensam. Sed non animadvertunt isti, sermonem esse Augustino & Luthero non de causis sive principijs συστατικοῖς, quæ constituunt & absolvunt ipsam essentiam Sacramenti in se, & per se, & quasi absolutè consideratam: sed de principijs ποιητικοῖς, quæ totam actionem Sacramenti, & non solam ejus substantiam absolvunt. Ubi sanè verissimum est hoc axioma Theologicum, quòd nullum fieri possit Sacramentum propriè sic dictum, nisi adsit expressum Verbum, tùm mandati, tùm promissionis: quorum tamen neutrum potest esse aut dici pars substantialis Sacramenti. Si enim Verbum promissionis esset talis pars συςατικὴ sive essentialis Sacramenti: consequens foret, tàm hypocritas & infideles, quàm fideles potiri salutari fructu Regenerationis: Ratio est, quia hypocritæ, ut & indigni, in Eucharistiâ toto potiuntur Sacramento, secundùm utráque partem essentialem integro; uti fusiùs ostensum suprà cap. 1. in doctrinâ de Sacramentis in genere. Atqui hoc posterius manifestè falsum. Ergò falsum etiam prius illud.

II. Sunt qui statuunt, Spiritum Sanctum concurrere ad actionem Sacramenti Baptistici, non tantùm ut ἄιτιον ἀρχίγονον, sive ut causam instituentem, prout reliquæ etiam duæ Trinitatis personæ concurrunt: neq́ue etiam tantùm ut arrhabonem sive σφραγῖδα obsignaculum, ratione salutaris fructus & effectus, quem in fidelibus confirmat & obsignat: sed & ut ἄιτιον σύςατικὸν, hoc est, ut causam ingredientem ipsam substantiam hujus Sacramenti, & constituentem partem ejus alteram cœlestem & invisibilem. Et sanè istorum sententia non destituitur manifestis Scripturæ testimonijs: tùm ipsius Christi, Joh. 3, 5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aquâ & Spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum cœlorum: tùm D. Apostoli asserentis, DEUM in & per Baptismum Spiritum tanquàm arrhabonem mittere in corda nostra: 2. Cor. 1, 22. Eph. 1, 14. id quod non tantùm de effectu salutari Baptismi, sed de ipsâ ejus substantiali parte intelligunt. Et né ex hâc ipsorum sententiâ quoad Hypocritas, absurdi aliquid sequatur, mentem suam hunc in modum latiùs explicant: Quemadmodum inquiunt in S. Cœnâ indigni manducant ipsum corpus & sangvinem Christi, neque tamen virtutis vivificæ Carnis Christi evadunt participes, obstante ipsorum incredulitate: ita Hypocritæ quoquè perfunduntur in Baptismo non solâ aquâ, sed ipso Spiritu sancto: nequê tamen fructus salutaris, sive operationis Spiritus Sancti reddūtur compotes: Siquidem Spiritus Sanctus sic ipsis collatus intendit quidem operationem illam salutiferam: sed ipso actu non perficit aut exerit, propter infidelitatem ipsorum. Nequè etiam necessarium est consequens, ut ubi substantialiter est Spiritus Sanctus, ibi etiam esse debeat secundum salutarem Regenerationis effectum: Adest enim ille substantialiter, ex conditione suæ naturæ & essentiæ cujus proprium est, omnibus rebus & creaturis substantialiter adesse, Psal. 139, 7. Sap. 1, 7. Sed ut adsit per specialem ἐνέργειαν χάριτος, id dependet à liberrimâ ipsius voluntate, quæ in credentibus est efficax, in hypocritis verò non item.

Quorum sententiam tantùm abest ut nos rejiciamus, aut simpliciter improbemus, ut potiùs nihil analogiæ fidei dissentaneum eam continere pronunciemus: liberum cuilibet relinquentes, num huic, an subsequentibus sententijs subscribere malit.

III. Sunt qui partem cœlestem Sacramenti hujus judicant esse Sangvinem Christi: his potissimùm adducti rationibus: I. Omnis mundatio à peccato non sit, nec fieri potest, nisi per sangvinem CHRISTI, 1. Joh. 1, 7. Sangvis filij DEI mundant nos ab omni peccato, Hebr 9, 22. Omnia in sangvine mudantur, & sine sangvinis effusione non fit remissio. Atqui verò in baptismo obtingit baptizatis mundatio a peccato. Ephes. 5, 26. Ergò ut Sangvis Christi interveniat necesse est.

Sed excipiat fortasse aliquis, intervenire quidem Sangvinem Christi, sed nullum propterea esse consequens, ut Sangvis constituatur pars altera essentialis Sacramenti hujus: eò quòd indies ac indefinêter mundemur sangvine Christi à peccato, quoties fide illum intuemur: ubi tamen nulla fiat perceptio Sangvinis Christi, quoad ejus substantiam. Verùm responderi potest, falli & fallere hanc argumentationem Sophismate disparatarum quæstionum, quæ confunduntur: Cùm potiùs interSacramentalem mundationem, quæ fit in Baptismo, & inter Spiritualem illam, quæ indies ac indefinenter fide peragitur, accuratè sit distingvendum. Etsi enim ratione salutaris effectus, una utrobique est mundatio: negari tamen non potest, in Sacramento, eam certo quodam signo, tanquàm medio sive organo, conferri. Hoc verò Signum Sacramentale in Baptismo, non est nuda & sola aqua: sed rem etiam insuper cælestem accedere, extra controversiam est positum. Hæc verò res cœlestis, secundum suam essentiam cùm re terrenâ & elementari, Sacramentaliter unita & copulata sit necesse est: alioquin enim nullum foret Sacramentum. Quod si ergò jam Sangvis Christi, unà cùm Aquâ constituit Signum illud Sacramentale, ἐξ ἀνάγκης consequitur, Sangvinem Christi, tanquàm alteram partem substantialem, in Baptismo substantialiter conferri omnibus baptizatis. II. Ratio petitur ex naturâ Sacramentorum. Ea enim est signorum Sacramentalium ratio, ut semper intercedat similitudo aliqua rei Elementari cum re cœlesti. Si enim, ut Augustinus loquitur Epist. 23. ad Bonifacium, Sacramenta similitudinem quandam earum rerum, quarum sunt Sacramenta, non haberent, omninò Sacramenta non essent. Jam verò satis exquisita constat similitudo aquæ Elementari, cum Sangvine Christi: quàm innuisse etiam videtur illud, quod ex latere Christi simul effluxit & aqua & Sangvis. Ergò. III. Ratio petitur ex analogiâ, quæ quoad partes essentiales Sacramentorum, Veteri Testamento cum Novo intercedit: Quemadmodum enim agnus paschalis typum gessit Sacramenti Eucharistiæ, ita quidem ut caro agni mactati, adumbraret carnem Christi crucifixi: ejusdem sangvis, sangvinem Christi; Ita in Sacramento Circumcisionis, quod fuit Baptismi typus, amputatio præputij constans sangvinis effusione, expressisse videtur aspersionem aquæ in Baptismo, permixtam Sangvine Christi. IV. & postrema sumitur ab autoritate Augustini, Lutheri, & aliorum Orthodoxorum Theologorum. Augustinus certè tractat. 11. in Johan. Baptismum inquit, rubere sangvine CHRISTI. Lutherus verò Aquam Baptismi, sangvine Christi permixtam esse esse statuit: fretus autoritate Apostolicâ Johannis, qui affirmat CHRISTUM venisse per Aquam & sangvinem: non solùm autem per Aquam: sed & per sangvinem. 1. Joh. 5, 6. Verba B. Lutheri sic sonant:

Daher pfleget S. Johannes der Evangelist gerne also von der lieben Tauffe zu reden/ daß sie sey ein Wasser mit dem Blut CHRISTI gemenget. Als Johan. 19. Da Christus gecreutziget und gestorben war/ und der Kriegsknecht einer mit einem Speer/ seine Seiten öffnet/ da gieng (spricht er) alsbalde Blut und Wasser heraus/ und bekräfftiget solches mit grossen Worten/ und spricht: Und der das gesehen hat/ bezeuget es/ und sein Zeügnis ist war/ und er weis/ daß er war saget/ auff daß auch ihr glaubet. Desgleichen in seiner Epistel am letzten Capitel spricht er von Christo/ dieser ists/ der da kompt mit Wasser und Blut/ JESUS Christus/ Nicht mit Wasser alleine/ Sondern mit Wasser und Blut. Also wil er allezeit das Blut in die Tauffe mengen/ das darinnen scheine und ersehen werde/ das Rosinfarbe unschuldige Blut Christi. Nach Menschlichen Augen scheinet da nichts/ weder lauter weis Wasser/ daß ist wahr/ Aber S. Johannes wil uns die innerlichen und geistlichen Augen des Glaubens auffthun/ daß wir damit sehen/ nicht allein Wasser/ Sondern auch das Blut unsers HERREN JESU CHRISTI etc.

IV. Et postremò non desunt Theologi, qui Rem Cœlestem hujus Sacramenti faciunt combinatam, eamq; constituunt, Spiritum Sanctum & Sangvinem CHRISTI, simul, cum discrimine tamen subalternationis: secuti hâc in parte Patrum quorundam vestigia. Cyprianus certè conferens transitum Israëlitarum per mare rubrum scribit: Hebræi baptizabantur in nube & mari: at jam populus DEI mundatur à peccatis Spiritu Sancto & Sangvine CHRISTI. Sic Ambrosius lib. de his qui mysteriis initiantur, cap. 2. Legisti, inquit, quòd tres testes in Baptismate unum sint: Aqua, Sangvis, & Spiritus: quia si unum horum detrahas, non stat Baptifmatis Sacramentum.

Postrema hæc sententia, ut & præcedentes duæ, licèt diversitatis aliquid obtineant, non tamen sunt contradictoriæ, multò minùs cum analogiâ fidei pugnant: sed sine ullo vel

'erroris, vel conscientiæ periculo approbari possunt, modò liberum cuivis relinquatur, sive 'hanc sive illam ex tribus hisce postremis sequi 'velit.

'Quibus ita constitutis, definimus Baptismum, 'quòd sit Sacramentum Novi Te- 'stamenti, divinitùs institutum, in 'quo per aquam & Spiritum in 'Sanguine CHRISTI, omnes in 'nomine Patris, Filij & Spirit˥ San- 'cti baptizati, verâέ fide donati, 'verè renascuntur, in filios DEI 'adoptantur, & ad æternam hære- 'ditatem obsignantur: ut deinceps 'in novitate vitæ ambulent, Joh. 3, '5. Rom. 6, 4. Act. 2, 38. Eph. 5, 26. Tit. '3, 5. 1. Petr 3, 21.

Cæterùm duo potissimùm circa definitionem istam moventur. I. Quæ & qualis sit Unio 'duarum istarum partium essentialium, constituen- 'tium Sacramenti hujus substantiam. II. Quæ & qualis forma circà administrationem Baptismi observari debeat?


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacrament of Baptism: I. Concerning the Union of the essential parts of this Sacrament

I. Concerning the Union of the essential parts of this Sacrament.

Regarding that first point, it is evident from those things which we discussed in the first chapter concerning the Sacraments in general, that the Union of these two essential parts, in the very use of Baptism, is sacramental, that is, supernatural and unusual, yet true and real: which causes the heavenly thing to be really, nay most really and most presently, conjoined with the earthly or elementary thing: so indeed that Water without the Holy Spirit, or without the Blood of Christ, is not Baptism: nor does either the Holy Spirit, or the Blood of Christ, without water, constitute this Sacrament: but water, united and coupled sacramentally with either one of these, makes one and an entire Baptism: as will be demonstrated more fully in the following chapter.

II. Concerning the Form of this Sacrament.

What and of what kind the form is that ought to be observed concerning the administration of this Sacrament, has both long since been variously disputed, and even today there is not one opinion among all. And the ancient heretics indeed, just as each one impugned the article of the Trinity, so also did they either bend, or change, or utterly remove the very form of the words promulgated by Christ. There were those who baptized in three principles, likewise in three sons, likewise in three paracletes, as can be seen in the canons of the Apostles, Canon 49. Thus Irenaeus recounts the various forms which, in his own time, heretics used regarding baptism, in this manner: in the name of the unknown Father of all, in the truth of the mother of all, and in the name of the descending Jesus, for the union and redemption and communion of the mighty works, I baptize you. Others, however, used certain Hebrew names, in this way: Basema, Chancoßè, Baeanora mistadia, Ruada: Kusta, Babophor, Calachthi: and thus they would strike a kind of terror into the baptized: of which words they rendered this meaning: I invoke upon every mighty work of the Father that which is called light, and the good Spirit and life, because you have reigned in the body. Others again would utter the redemption in this way: The name which is hidden from every Deity, and denomination, and truth which Jesus of Nazareth put on, in the life of the light of the living CHRIST through the Holy Spirit for the redemption of the Angelic name of the restitution of the Messiah, Meßia llphareg, Namempsemam, Chaldean, Mosomedaëa, Acphrane, Psaova Jesus Nazaria: Of which words they rendered this meaning: I do not divide the Spirit, the heart, the supercelestial merciful mighty work, would that I might enjoy your name, O Savior of truth. And these words indeed are uttered by those who initiate. But he who is initiated responds: I have been confirmed and redeemed: and my soul is redeemed from this age, and from all things that are from it, in the name of Jao, who redeemed his own soul into redemption in the living CHRIST. Then all who are present utter: Peace to all upon whom this name rests. Then they anoint the initiated with the juice of balsam. For they say this ointment is above all things a type of good odor. Some of them, however, consider it superfluous to lead to water, but with oil and water mixed together, with the addition of the pronunciation of words of the same kind, which we mentioned before, they pour it upon the head of the initiated, and they wish this to be the redemption. They also anoint with balsam themselves. Others, however, who reject all these things, say that it is not fitting for the mystery of the ineffable and invisible mighty work to be performed through visible and corruptible creatures; and that things which cannot be comprehended by the mind, and lack a body, should not be performed through those things which are corporeal and sensible. Thus far Irenaeus, book 1, against heresies, chapter 18, section 4. A certain pious old man complains in Eusebius, book 7, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 8, that he had been baptized by heretics with a form full of blasphemies. The Arians, as Augustine testifies in On Heresies, chapter 49, baptized in the name of the greater Father and the lesser Son: and they rebaptized those baptized otherwise. The Eunomians, as Socrates reports in the Tripartite History, book 5, chapter 13, baptized not into the Trinity, but into the death of CHRIST.

The Scholastic Doctors are solicitous even to the point of superstition regarding the correct pronunciation of the words: I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Amen; and at the beginning they distinguish between these words: some of which they name principal, as in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: some less principal, as I baptize you: by which words the minister conferring, the person receiving, and the act itself are comprehended. Then they command that the form of Baptism is not to be changed: Because from a change of form, another baptism also emerges, different from the baptism of CHRIST. In which part we willingly agree with them. Thirdly, they teach that a change of form happens in four ways.

1. When entirely different voices are put in place of the words of CHRIST, which are either synonyms according to the idioms of languages: or disparate, as in the name of Paul, of Peter, of Mary: or not signifying in the same way, as in the name of the begetter, the begotten, and the one proceeding from both. Synonyms do not change the form: but equipollents, that is, those not signifying in the same way, as well as the disparate, do change the form.

2. When other words are added to the words of CHRIST, which either are repugnant, as in the name of the greater Father and the lesser Son: or in the name of the Father through the Son, in the Holy Spirit: Or are not repugnant: as, I baptize you in the name of the Almighty Father, and of the Only-begotten Son, and of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete: Or are entirely impertinent, which discontinue the form, as if someone were to say: I baptize you in the name of the Father (and here he were to stop, and have words about another matter, and afterwards proceed to say) and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Here they teach that the Baptism is true, if that addition does not vary the true sense of the form. But null and entirely useless, if the things which are interposed are repugnant to the form, or introduce another sense. Similarly, it is not a Sacrament if what is so added takes away the truth of the form even through the slightest interruption. Theodorus Lector, book 2, of the Collectanea, reports that Deuterius, the Arian Bishop of Constantinople, when he was baptizing a certain Barbas so called, having rejected and corrupted the Dominical tradition, dared to say while baptizing: Let Barbas be baptized in the name of the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. Upon which saying, the water in the font vanished: but Barbas took to flight and left, and made this miracle public.

3. They teach that a change of form happens when some word or syllable is subtracted from the words of CHRIST: and they say, in the words less principal, such as I baptize you, the subtraction of the pronoun I does not change or hinder the effect of Baptism: but in the principal ones, no subtraction ought to be made: Likewise, that the form is not destroyed on account of a syllable pronounced by syncope. They warn, however, that such a pronunciation ought to be avoided in Sacramental words.

4. And finally, they assert that a change of form occurs when the words of CHRIST are transposed: and therefore they determine that it is not baptism if the sense is varied by transposition: as if it were said: I baptize thee in the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: But if by transposition it does not

may be varied, but the same sense remains, then the baptism is true, as if it were said: I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: or I baptize you in the name of the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit. Although they warn that the order of the Persons according to their origin ought to be observed.

1. Furthermore, the Scholastics are also concerned about the individual words: and concerning the pronoun (I) they say that it is not of the substance of the form, but is placed for the expression of greater intention: wherefore the subtraction of this pronoun does not change the form of Baptism: and that the Greeks, who say: Let the servant of Christ be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, baptize correctly.

2. Concerning the active verb itself (I baptize) they teach that it expresses the act of Baptism: which if it were not expressed, there would be no Baptism: and they cite that of Pope Alexander: If anyone should immerse a boy three times in water, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. amen: and should not say, I baptize you in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, then the boy is not baptized. Here indeed the Scholastics say something with which we subscribe to them: but that they add: if it be said, I wash, or I cleanse you, it would not be a true baptism, because of the change of form: that we do not approve. For it is not true, what they say, that the verb I wash, or I cleanse, is not a synonym with the verb, I baptize: Also that I baptize does not signify any washing whatsoever, but only this one, which is done in Baptism.

3. Concerning the pronoun YOU they determine thus, that its subtraction changes the form of Baptism: which we easily grant: but the reason which they assign, that forsooth the words which are uttered are pronounced not only for the sake of signifying, but also for the sake of effecting, we simply disapprove. For thus they strive either tacitly to confirm their work performed: We determine that this pronoun obtains the force of application.

4. But they proceed, and they contend that in the phrase (in the name) if the preposition IN is omitted, it is not Baptism, because of the change of form through subtraction. They add, however, a mitigation of their opinion, that it may piously be believed, forsooth, that it is Baptism, if by reason of language or idiom, the ablative without a preposition would signify the same as with the preposition. They also warn that it should not be said in the plural, In the names, but in the singular, in the name: because the divine power, which operates in baptism, pertains to the divine essence, just as every operation ad extra. Whence it becomes plain that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three baptizers, but One.

5. Here the Scholastics are caught not understanding this phrase: What it is to baptize in the name of someone. For instead of what is said, In the name, they think it is done viciously if it is said, to baptize in the name of Christ, or in the name of Christ. Furthermore, they contend that one ought not to be baptized in the name of the begetter and the begotten, and the one proceeding from both: because these words designate notional

Latin:

I. De Unione partium essentialium hujus Sacramenti.

QUoad prius illud, constat ex ijs, quæ capite primo de Sacramentis in genere disputavimus, Unionem duarum istarum partium essentialium, in ipso usu Baptismi, esse Sacramentalem, hoc est, supernaturalem, & inusitatam, veram tamen & realem: quæ facit ut res cœlestis, cum re terrenâ sive elementari, realiter, imò realiffimè & præsentissimè sit conjuncta: ita quidem ut Aqua sine Spiritu Sancto, vel sine Sangvine Christi, non sit Baptismus: neq; etiam vel Spiritus Sanctus, vel Sangvis Christi, sine aquâ, constituat Sacramentum hoc: sed aqua, cum alterutro istorum Sacramentaliter unita ac copulata; Baptismum unum atque integrum efficiat: uti capite subsequente fusiùs demonstrabitur.

II. De Formâ hujus Sacramenti.

QUæ & qualis forma circa Sacramenti hujus administrationem observari debeat, & jam olim variè disputatum fuit, ac etiamnum hodiè non una omnium est sententia. Et Veteres quidem hæretici, prout quisq; articulum Trinitatis impugnabat, ita formam etiam verborum à Christo promulgatam, vel inflectebat, vel mutabat, vel penitùs tollebat. Fuerunt qui baptizarent in tribus principijs, item in tribus filijs, item in tribus paracletis, uti videre est in canonibus Apostolorum, Canone 49. Sic recenset Irenæus varias formas, quibus suo jam tempore, hæretici circa baptismum sint usi, in hunc modum: in nomine ignoti Patris omnium, in veritate matris omnium, & in nomine descendentis Jesu, ad unitionem & redemptionem & communionem virtutum, te baptizo. Alij verò Hebraica quædam nomina usurpabant, hoc modo: Basema, Chancoßè, Baeanora mistadia, Ruada: Kusta, Babophor, Calachthi: & sic terrorem quasi incuterent baptizatis: Quorum verborū hunc reddebant sensum: Super omnem virtutem Patris invoco id quod lux nominasur, & bonus Spiritus & vita quoniam in corpore regnasti. Alij rursus redemptionem effabantur hoc modo: Nomen quod absconditum est ab omni Deitate, & denominatione, & veritate quod induit Jesus Nazarenus, in vita lucis CHRISTI viventis per Spiritum Sanctum ad redemptionem Angelicum nomen restitutionis Meßia llphareg, Namempsemam, Chaldean, Mosomedaëa, Acphrane, Psaova Jesu Nazaria: Quorum verborum hunc reddebant sensum; Non divido Spiritum, cor, supercælestem virtutem misericordem, utinam fruar nomine tuo Salvator veritatis. Et hæc quidem verba effantur illi, qui initiant. Qui verò initiatur respondet: confirmatus sum & redemptus: & redimor anima mea ab hoc seculo, & omnibus quæ ab ipso sunt in nomine Jao, qui redemit animam sua in redemtionem in CHRISTO vivente. Deindè effantur omnes qui adsunt; Pax omnibus super quos hoc nomen requiescit. Deindè succo balsami initiatum perungunt. Nam unguentum hoc dicunt supra omnia esse typum boni odoris. Nonnulli verò ipsorum ad aquam ducere supervacaneum esse ducunt, verùm oleo & aqua simul permixtis, addita ejusdem generis verborum pronunciatione, quæ priùs diximus, capiti initiati infundunt, ac volunt hanc esse redemtionem. Ungunt autem & ipsi balsamo. Alij verò, qui hæc omnia aversantur, dicunt non oportere mysterium ineffabilis & invisibilis virtutis, per visibiles & corruptibiles creaturas; & quæ mente comprehendi nequeunt, & corpore carent, per eas, quæ corporea & sensibilia sunt, perfici. Hactenus Irenæus lib. 1. adversus hæreses, cap. 18. sect. 4. Conqueritur apud Eusebium lib. 7. Hist. Eccl. cap. 8. pius quidam senex, se ab hæreticis formâ blasphemijs plenâ baptizatum fuisse. Arriani teste Augustino de hæref. cap. 49. baptizabant in nomine Patris majoris, & Filii minoris: & secus baptizatos rebaptizabant. Eunomiani, referente Socrate in histor. tripart. lib. 5. cap. 13. non in Trinitatem, sed in mortem CHRISTI baptisabant.

Scholastici Doctores circa rectam pronunciationem verborum: Ego te baptizo in nomine Patris, Filij, & Spiritus Sancti, Amen; ad superstitionem usq; sunt solliciti: ac initio quidem distingvunt inter hæc verba: quorum quædam nominant principalia, ut in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti: quædam minùs principalia, ut ego te baptizo: quibus verbis comprehendatur minister conferens, persona suspiciens, & actus ipse. Deindè præcipiunt, Formam Baptismi non esse mutandam: Quia ex mutatione formæ alius etiam emergat baptismus, à CHRISTI baptismate diversus. Quâ in parte nos illis libenter assentimur. Tertiò docent mutationem formæ fieri quatuor modis.

1. Quando prorsus aliæ voces loco verborum CHRISTI ponuntur, quæ sint aut Synonyma juxta idiomata lingvarum: aut disparata, ut in nomine Pauli, Petri, Mariæ: aut non eodem modo significantia, ut in nomine genitoris, geniti & procedentis ab utroq́;. Synonyma non mutare formam: æquipollentia verò, hoc est, non eodem modo significantia, ut & disparata mutare formam.

2. Quando alia vocabula Verbis CHRISTI adduntur, quæ aut repugnent, ut in nomine Patris majoris, & filij minoris: sive in nomine Patris per Filium, in Spiritu Sancto: Aut non repugnent: ut, baptizo te in nomine Patris Omnipotentis, & Filij Unigeniti, & Spiritus Sancti Paracleti: Aut omninò impertinentia, quæ formam discontinuant, ut si quis diceret: Ego te baptizo in nomine Patris (& hîc subsisteret, & haberet verba de aliâ re, & posteà pergeret dicere) & Filij & Spiritus Sancti. Hîc docent verum esse Baptismum, si additio illa verum sensum formæ non variet. Nullum verò & prorsus inutilem, si, quæ interposita sunt, formæ repugnent, aut alium sensum inducant. Similiter non esse Sacramentum, si quod ita additum est, Veritatem formæ per interruptionem etiam minimam tollit. Theodorus Lector, lib. 2. Collectaneorum refert, Devterium Arrianorum Episcopum Constantinopolitanum, cùm Barbam quendam sic dictum baptizaret, reprobatâ & corruptâ Dominicâ traditione, ausum fuisse inter baptizandum dicere: Baptizetur Barbas in nomine Patris, per filium, in Spiritu Sancto. Quo dicto, aqua in colymbethrâ evanuerit: Barbas verò arreptâ fugâ exiverit, & hoc miraculum evulgaverit.

3. Mutationem formæ fieri docent, quando de verbis CHRISTI verbum aliquod vel syllaba detrahitur: & dicunt, in verbis minus principaliter, ut Ego te baptizo, subtractionem pronominis EGO, non mutare, aut impedire effectum Baptismi: in principalibus verò nullam subtractionem fieri debere: Item, propter syllabam per Syncopen prolatam, non destrui formam. Monent tamen, quòd talis prolatio caveri debeat in verbis Sacramentalibus.

4. Et postremò mutationem formæ fieri asserunt, quando verba CHRISTI transponuntur: atquè ideò statuunt, non esse baptismum, si per transpositionem varietur sensus: ut si dicatur: Ego Patris baptizo te in nomine, Filij & Spiritus Sancti: Si verò per transpositionem non

varietur, sed maneat idem sensus, tùm verum esse baptismum, ut si dicatur: Ego in nomine Patris, Filij & Spiritus Sancti te baptizo: vel ego te baptizo in nomine Filij, Patris & Spiritus Sancti. Quanquàm ordinem Personarum juxta originem earum observandum esse monent.

1. Porrò de singulis etiam vocabulis solliciti sunt Scholastici: & de pronomine (EGO) dicunt, quod non sit de substantiâ formæ, sed ponatur ad majoris intentionis expressionem: quare subtractionem hujus pronominis non mutare formam Baptismi: & Græcos rectè baptizare, qui dicunt: Baptizetur servus Christi in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti.

2. De ipso verbo activo (Baptizo) docent, quod exprimat actum Baptismi: Qui si non exprimeretur, non esset Baptismus: & citant illud Papæ Alexandri: Si quis puerum ter in aquam merserit, in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti. amen: & non diceret, Ego te baptizo in nomine Patris, Fi lij, & Spiritus Sancti, tùm puer non est baptizatus. Hîc quidem aliquid dicunt Scholastici, in quo illis subscribimus: sed quòd addunt: si dicatur, Ego lavo, vel abluo te, non esset verus baptismus, propter mutationem formæ : id non approbamus. Neq; enim verum est, quod dicunt, Verbum lavo, vel abluo, non esse Synonymum cum verbo, Baptizo: Item quòd Baptizo non significet quamlibet ablutionem, sed tantùm hanc, quæ fiat in Baptismo.

3. De pronomine TE sic statuunt, quòd ejus subtractio mutet formam Baptismi: id quod facilè largimur: sed rationem quam assignant, quòd nimirùm verba, quæ proferuntur, non tantùm significandi causâ, sed etiam efficiendi gratia, pronuncientur, simpliciter improbamus. Sic enim illi vel tacitè opus suum operatum confirmare student: Nos applicandi vim hoc pronomen obtinere statuimus.

4. Sed pergunt, & in phrasi (in nomine) si præpositio IN omittatur, non esse Baptismum contendunt, propter mutationem formæ per subtractionem. Addunt tamen sententiæ suæ mitigationem, piè scilicet credi posse, quod sit Baptismus, sit lingvæ aut idiomatis ratione, ablativus absq; præpositione idem significaret, quod cum præpositione. Monent etiam non esse pluraliter dicendum, In nominibus, sed singulariter, in nomine: proptereà quod virtus divina, quæ operatur in baptismo, ad essentiam divinam pertineat, sicut omnis operatio ad extra. Undè planum fiat, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum non tres baptizatores esse, sed Unum.

5. Hîc deprehenduntur Scholastici non intelligere phrasin hanc: Quid sit in nomine alicujus baptizare. Pro eo enim, quod dicitur, In nomine, putant vitiosè fieri, si dicatur, in nomen Christi, vel in nomine Christi baptizare. Porrò contendunt, non esse baptizandum in nomine genitoris & geniti, & procedentis ab utroq;: proptereà quod hæc vocabula designent notio-


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacrament of Baptism: I. Concerning the Union of the essential parts of this Sacrament (continued)

nal acts and not hypostases, nor are they synonyms, since they are of different categories, and therefore the form of the change is made by him who baptizes in this way. Then they say: If anyone today were baptized only in the name of JESUS CHRIST, that he would not be baptized: because, they say, by special revelation of Christ, the Apostles in the primitive Church baptized in the name of Christ, so that the name of CHRIST, which was hateful to the Jews and honorable to the Gentiles, might be rendered honorable, through the fact that at its invocation the Holy Spirit was given in Baptism: but this reason ceasing, and the name of CHRIST being divulged, the Church returned to the former form promulgated by CHRIST. Which shadow of the Scholastics we leave for them to defend.

Furthermore the Scholastics contend: If anyone were baptized in the name of the Trinity, that he would not be baptized: because Sacramental words are effective not so much from their signification as from their institution: but Christ, in handing down the form of Baptism, gave such a one and wished it to be observed, in which an express profession of faith in the Trinity is explained under the proper names of the divine persons.

Moreover, they maintain that it also brings about a change of form if anyone in pronouncing should omit the conjunction AND, because a copulative conjunction is required to denote the personal distinction between the Father and the Son. They add, however, because of synonymy, that the conjunction (que) can be placed without a change of form.

Concerning the pronunciation of the words of Baptism they determine generally thus: Although those words in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, might be corrupted somewhat through inexperience, or a defect of speech, as is that of those who stutter, or a slip of the tongue, provided that the bystanders could grasp the full sense, nevertheless, provided the intention is truly present, the Baptism is true, because these corrupted words are synonyms to the integral words. Otherwise, if the corruption of the words were so great that their sense was not grasped by the hearers. To this pertains the decretal letter of Pope Zachary, which he wrote to Bishop Boniface, concerning a Priest who through ignorance of the Latin language would err in the invocation of the Trinity: part 3 of the decrees, dist. 4, de consecratione. which has it thus: Your messengers reported that there was in the same province a Priest, who was entirely ignorant of the Latin language: and while he was baptizing, not knowing how to speak Latin, breaking the language he said: I baptize you in the name of the Fatherland and the Daughter, and the Holy Spirit. And through this your reverend Holiness considered rebaptizing them: But most holy brother, if he who baptized, not introducing error or heresy, but for the sake of ignorance of the Roman speech breaking the language (as we said above) had said this while baptizing, we cannot consent that he be baptized again.

They maintain that it is not permitted to pronounce these words, except in Greek words in the Greek Church, and in Latin in the Latin Church. Of this opinion they have this reason, although it is permitted because of synonymy to deliver Baptism in every language; they hold that a Latin priest baptizing in another language sins against the statutes of the Roman Church, which has ordained that ecclesiastical offices be said in the Latin or at least the Greek language, etc. But this reasoning is too futile: for if every language and every spirit ought to praise GOD, why should it not also be permitted to administer Baptism in every language?

10. Concerning the word AMEN, they determine thus: since it is not part of the completion of the form, but a matter of the custom of certain baptizers, it therefore makes no difference whether it is added or omitted. Concerning which we also do not contend in the least.

Thus, therefore, there has always been varied contention in the Church of GOD concerning the Form of Baptism: but in such a way that you can scarcely find where you might firmly plant your foot. We, having followed the theoretical and partly practical counsels of Orthodox theologians, shall include a purer opinion on this matter within certain hypotheses.

I. Hypothesis: In order for the truth and perfection of the Sacrament of Baptism to remain inviolate, it is necessary that a certain form be observed, in which mention is made of both the baptismal action itself and the Most Holy Trinity. The unanimous consensus of orthodox antiquity confirms this hypothesis: such as Augustine, book 6 against the Donatists, chapter 25, and book 3 against the Donatist Fulgentius, chapter 15; Basil against Eunomius, book 3, chapter 5; Ambrose, book 2 on the Sacraments, chapter 5; Chrysostom on chapter 5 of Ephesians; Athanasius, sermon 4 against Arius. And although Bernard, in Epistle 340, seems to assert that a Baptism administered under such a form as 'I baptize you in the name of GOD and of the Holy and true Cross' is true: because, however, Epistle 310 was written shortly before Bernard's death, and is therefore not undeservedly believed to be his last epistle, the remaining ones after the author's death were added by someone else, and for this reason alone they ought to be suspect to us. What is more? The author of this epistle himself speaks of such a case: if, namely, this is done not of set purpose, but out of mere simplicity. For if it is done of set purpose, he himself confesses that a grave sin is committed. Nay, he even adds that he wrote that without prejudice to those who judge more correctly.

II. Hypothesis. The form which ought to be holily observed regarding the action of this Sacrament has been most fully and correctly handed down by Christ, Matthew 28:19. For if the author of this Sacrament, according to his infinite wisdom, instituted the element, which is the humbler part of the Sacrament, he certainly also established the form of words, which concern the whole action of this Sacrament, and are both better known and more effective for demonstrating the use of the Sacrament. In which part no more is to be conceded to the judgment of men than to divine authority.

III. Unless this very form of words instituted by Christ is observed, the truth of the Sacrament can in no way remain. The reason for this assertion is manifest: for if it is certain that the substance of Baptism suffers when the material element is changed, it is far more certain that when the formal elements of this Sacrament are changed, its truth can in no way remain. Augustine also subscribes to this assertion, book 6 against the Donatists, chapter 25: 'Who,' he asks, 'does not know that it is not the Baptism of CHRIST if the evangelical words, of which the Symbol consists, are missing there? And it is easier to find heretics who do not baptize at all than those who do not baptize with those words.'

IV. This certain observation of the words of CHRIST contains nothing in itself that is either magical or superstitious: no more than the strict observation of a certain element implies anything magical or superstitious.

V. This certain observation of the words of CHRIST does not concern any certain external sound of syllables or characters, or the exact number of words, all of which it is agreed are mutable according to the variety of languages: but it concerns the sense of the words which Christ intended to denote, in whatever words that sense may truly and properly be expressed.

VI.
