And the last: Although a change, if any were to be made in the form of words, and which were made while the true and proper sense remained, could indeed be made without violating the truth of the Sacrament: nevertheless, no one is permitted to attempt anything in this regard by private authority, not only because of the danger of schism, which easily arises in this way, but also because of heresy and errors. For according to Jerome, heresy arises from words uttered improperly. This danger would be at hand if anyone were permitted to change the form of words, even if their proper sense were preserved. Concerning which matter, the judgment of that great theologian, Johannes Brentius, is worthy of note, who in his Catechism speaks thus concerning the form of baptizing: 'There are those who think that Christ instituted Baptism in such a way that it must be distributed with these words (I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit), and unless we use these words, they think it is not true Baptism.' It must therefore be observed: Although in Baptism these customary words are entirely to be retained, nor is it permitted to anyone to change these words according to his own whim and rashness, and to use other words at his own discretion in Baptism: yet this usage is to be rightly understood. For Christ did not place the foundation of His Baptism upon certain letters, syllables, or expressions, nor did He bind us to certain words: for He did not institute magic, which is bound to a certain form of words and rites: but He instituted heavenly Sacraments, which consist in His own meaning and will, signified to us by these or those words. And a little later: Therefore, if anyone after the recitation of the Apostles' Creed, in Baptism, were to say these words to the one being baptized: I have now heard from you the confession of your faith, that you believe in GOD THE FATHER almighty, Creator of heaven and earth: And in His only-begotten Son our Lord JESUS CHRIST, and in the HOLY SPIRIT. Into this confession and faith, therefore, I dip you in water, or pour water over you, so that by this sign you may be made certain that you have been inserted into JESUS CHRIST,

& the communion of all his goods. Go therefore in peace. This certainly would be a true baptism, because it contains those things which are necessary for baptism: and the sentence of the words of CHRIST has been recited, even if the sound of the words themselves seems slightly changed. This was seen fit to be added, not because a change of the customary words of Christ should be permitted to anyone: But so that the words of Christ may be rightly understood, and so that we may learn to distinguish magic far from the true consecration of the heavenly Sacraments. Thus Brentius.

Moreover, there are not wanting those who take up a censorious rod against this opinion of ours, saying that we are by no means bound to any certain form of conferring Baptism, because no such form was prescribed by CHRIST in the last chapter of Matthew: but that only this was shown, that those who are to give their name to the Christian faith ought to be initiated into the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: Then, however, they seek confirmation of this opinion of theirs from Acts chapter 19, verse 5, where some are said to have been baptized by Paul in the name of CHRIST.

But the answer is easy: For the former reason is manifestly false, as is evident from what has already been said. The latter reason, taken from chapter 19 of Acts, confuses the literal sense and the interpretation of the words of Luke, in which the interpretation is to be regarded more than the literal sense. For the Evangelist wishes to show in this place, not by what form of words Paul baptized, or what he changed in the same: But he wishes only to teach this, by what norm of doctrine he used while conferring Baptism: namely this, that all the virtue of Baptism consists in CHRIST, and depends solely upon the ransom of this redemption of his: so that the argument of Paul's doctrine concerning the action of Baptism was clearly the same as that which he himself later expressed in his Epistle to the Romans, chapter 6, verse 3: As many of us as were baptized into CHRIST JESUS were baptized into his death. Ambrose also supports this answer of ours from pious antiquity, writing in book 1, de Spiritu Sancto, chapter 3: If the Apostle had baptized even with that form which is written by the Evangelist, it would nevertheless have been valid, because in that one name of Christ, the whole most holy Trinity is included, namely the Father, by whom Christ was anointed: and he himself who was anointed: and the Holy Spirit, through whom he was anointed. Which answer other Fathers also hold, especially Basil and Augustine. But more fully and precisely on this statement below.

These things having been thus settled, one thing remains still to be examined concerning the consideration of the form: Namely, whether in the act of Baptism one should use sprinkling at least, or rather immersion, and that either triple or single? To the first part of the question I answer, that for Baptism to be true and salutary, immersion into water is not necessary: but that either sprinkling or pouring is sufficient. We offer these reasons for this affirmation: 1. CHRIST himself commanded nothing concerning the mode of washing, whether the whole body or only some part ought to be immersed? 2. The Greek word βαπτίζειν signifies both: immersion into water and the sprinkling of water: Whence they are read to have baptized hands and face, that is, to have washed them, Mark 7:4 & Luke 11:38. 3. The power and efficacy of Baptism does not depend on the rite of washing, but on the virtue of the instituting CHRIST, who promised that he would be efficacious through water in whatever way one to be baptized is washed with water, whether by immersion or by sprinkling. 4. This seems to be able to be gathered from the deed of Peter, Acts 2:41, where three thousand men are read to have been converted in one day, and baptized on the same day: Which, since it could hardly have been done by the immersion of each one, it is gathered quite probably that it was done at least by sprinkling. 5. Baptism was instituted for the washing away of sins, both to be conferred and to be signified: which can be conveniently done by the pouring or sprinkling of water. Whence the Epistle to the Hebrews several times with express words inculcates ῥαντισμὸν, sprinkling: chapter 9:13, chapter 10:22, chapter 12:24. 6. Orthodox Antiquity was of the same opinion. For although in the time of Cyprian, it was disputed by some whether the Clinici, sprinkled only with water, had been rightly baptized: yet it was rightly answered by Cyprian, book 4, Epistle 7, that it is in the power of the Church to use Baptism done by sprinkling alone and to have the same use for it as for Baptism performed by immersion: which both rites the same Father thinks the Apostles also used in the Acts. Thus Augustine, de Eccl. dogmatibus, chapter 74: The one to be baptized, he says, confesses his faith before the Priest, and when asked, answers: and after the confession of faith, he is either sprinkled with water or immersed. And although Blessed Luther, in a Sermon on Baptism held in the year 19, praises immersion: yet he does not disapprove or reject sprinkling. By some Scholastics indeed, as also by Peter Lombard, the rite of immersion is urged, because, forsooth, the burial of Christ is thus better represented: Which Chrysostom also seems to think, homily 24 on John & Gregory, book 1, Epistle 41, to Leander the Bishop. But however this may be: the reason of the washing to be signified seems to be more important in Baptism than that of the burial of Christ, which seems to have a place in the signification of this Sacrament only secondarily. Hence Thomas himself also, part 3, q. 66, art. 7, says: Washing can be done with water, not only by way of immersion, but also by way of sprinkling or pouring. And therefore, although it is safer to baptize by way of immersion: yet baptism can be done by way of sprinkling, or even pouring. We conclude therefore, although concerning the baptism of adults the rite of immersion into water was both observed long ago, and can still be freely observed today concerning the same: yet there are not light causes for which the Church, having used the rite of immersion for a very long time in the Church, finally exchanged it with sprinkling in previous centuries.

Latin:

nales actus & non hypostases, nec sint Synonyma, cum sint diversorum prædicamentorum, ideoq; formæ mutationem fieri ab eo, qui hoc modo baptizet. Deindè dicunt: Siquis hodiè baptizaretur tantùm in nomine JESU CHRISTI, quòd non esset baptizatus: quia, inquiunt, ex speciali Christi revelatione, Apostoli in primitiva Ecclesiâ, in nomine Christi baptizarunt, ut nomen CHRISTI, quod fuerit odiosum Judæis & gentibus honorabile redderetur, per hoc, quòd ad ejus invo cationem Spiritus S. dabatur in Baptismo: sed ratione hac cessante, & nomine CHRISTI divulgato, Ecclesiam rediisse ad priorem formam à CHRISTO promulgatam. Quam Scholasticorum σκίαν ipsis defendendam relinquimus.

Præterea contendunt Scholastici: Si quis baptizaretur in nomine Trinitatis, quod non esse baptizatus: proptereà quod verba Sacramentalia non tàm ex Significatione, quàm institutione sint efficacia: Christum verò tradendo formam Baptismi, talem dedisse & observari voluisse, in quâ expressa fidei Trinitatis professio, sub proprijs divinarum personarum nominibus explicetur.

Insuper volunt, illud quoq; mutationem formæ inferre, si quis in pronunciando omitteret conjunctionem ET, propterea quod ad denotandam, personalem discretionem inter Patrem & Filium requiritur conjunctio copulativa. Addunt tamen propter συνωνυμίαν, conjunctionem, (que) sine mutatione formæ, poni posse.

De pronunciatione verborum Baptismi generaliter ita statuunt: Licèt verba illa in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti, ex imperitiâ, vel vitio linguæ, ut est traulorum, vel lapsu linguæ, aliquantulum corrumperentur, dùm tamen circumstantes plenum capere possent sensum, nihilominùs modò verè adsit intentio, verum esse Baptisma, proptereà quòd verba hæc corrupta, sint verbis integris Synonyma. Secus, si tanta esset corruptio verborū, ut sensus eorum non caperetur ab audientibus. Huc pertinet Epistola decretalis Zachariæ Papæ, quam scripsit Bonifacio Episcopo, de Sacerdote, qui per ignorantiam lingvæ latinæ, in invocatione Trinitatis delinqueret: part. 3. decretorum, dist. 4. de conser. quæ sic habet: Retulerunt nuncij tui, quòd fuit in eâdem provinciâ Sacerdos, qui latinâ lingvam penitùs ignorabat: & dùm baptizaret, nesciens loqui latinè, infringens lingvam diceret: Baptizate in nomine Patria & Filia, & Spiritua Sancta. Et per hoc tua reverenda Sanctitas consideravit eos rebaptizare: Sed Sanctissime frater, si ille qui baptizavit, non errorem introducens aut hæresin, sed pro solâ ignorantiâ Romanæ locutionis infringendo lingvam (ut supra diximus) hoc baptizans dixisset, non possumus consentire, ut denuò baptisetur.

Volunt non licere verba hæc pronunciare, nisi verbis Græcis in Græciâ, & Latinis! in Latinâ Ecclesiâ. Hujus sententiæ hanc habent rationem, quamvis liceat propter συνωνυμίαν in omni lingvâ Baptismum tradere: Latinum tamen Sacerdotem baptizantem in aliâ lingvâ, peccare contra statuta Ecclesiae Romanae, quae ordinaverit, ut officia Ecclesiastica dicantur in Latinâ saltem & Graecâ lingvâ &c. Sed nimis futilis haec est ratio: Nam si omnis lingva & omnis Spiritus laudare debet DEUM; quidnî etiam in omni lingvâ Baptismum administrare liceat?

10. De vocabulo AMEN sic statuunt, cùm non sit de complemento formae, sed de usu quorundam baptizantium, ideò nihil referre, sive addatur, sive omittatur. De quo nos quoq; minimè pugnamus.

Sic ergò de Formâ Baptismi in Ecclesiâ DEI variè semper pugnatum fuit: sed ita, ut vix ubi pedem certò figere queas, invenias. Nos Orthodoxorum Theologorum theoretica partim, partim practica consilia secuti, puriorem hâc de re sententiam, certis hypothesibus includemus.

I. Hypothesis: Ut Sacramento Baptismi sua inviolata constet veritas & perfectio; necesse est, ut certa forma observetur, in quâ tùm ipsius actionis baptisticae, tùm Sacrosanctae Trinitatis expressa fiat mentio. Confirmat hanc hypothesin unanimis Orthodoxae antiquitatis consensus: ut Augustini lib. 6. cont. Donat cap. 25. & lib. 3. contra Fulgent. Donat. cap. 15. Basilij contra Eunomium lib. 3. cap. 5. Ambrosij lib. 2. de Sacramentis, cap. 5. Chrysostomi super cap. 5. Ephes. Athanasij serm. 4. contra Arium. Et quanquàm Bernhardus, Epist. 340. asserere videtur: verum esse Baptismum, qui sub tali formâ administraretur: Ego baptizo te in nomine DEI & Sanctae ac verae Crucis: quia tamen Epistola 310. paulò ante mortem Bernhardi scripta fuit, ac proindè haud immeritò ultima etiam ejus epistola esse creditur: ideò reliquae post mortem autoris ab alio aliquo adjectae sunt, & vel hanc ob causam suspectae nobis esse debent. Quid? quòd hujus etiam epistolae autor de tali casu loquitur: si nimirùm hoc fiat non ex proposito: sed ex merâ simplicitate. Nam si ex proposito fiat, graviter peccari ipsemet fatetur. Quin imò subjicit, se sine praejudicio rectiùs sapientis illud scripsisse.

II. Hypothesis. Forma, quae circa actionem hujus Sacramenti sanctè observari debet, plenissimè rectissiméq; tradita est à Christo, Matth. 28, 19. Sienim autor Sacramenti hujus, pro infinitâ suâ sapientiâ, elementum instituit, quae est pars Sacramenti humilior: utíq; formam etiam verborum constituit, quae totam Sacramenti hujus actionem respiciunt, & sunt tùm notiora, tùm ad usum Sacramenti monstrandum efficaciora. Quâ in parte hominum arbitrio non est plus concedendum, quàm autoritati divinae.

III. Forma haec ipsa Verborum à Christo instituta nisi servetur, Sacramento sua veritas constare neutiquam potest. Ratio assertionis manifesta est: Si enim mutatâ materiâ elementi, substantiam Baptismi laborare certum est: certius longè est illud, formalibus Sacramenti hujus mutatis, veritatem ipsi constare nullo modo posse. Subscribit & huic assertioni Augustinus lib. 6. contra Donat. cap. 25. Quis inquiens nesciat, non esse Baptismum CHRISTI, si verba Evangelica, quibus Symbolum constat, illic defuerint. Et facilius inveniuntur hæretici, qui non omninò baptisent, quàm qui illis verbis no baptisent.

IV. Certa hæc verborum CHRISTI observatio, nihil in se continet vel magicum, vel superstitiosum: haud magis, atq; certi Elementi observatio stricta nihil magicum aut superstitiosum innuit.

V. Certa hæc verborum CHRISTI observatio, non respicit certum aliquem exteriorem sonum syllabarum aut characterum, vel exactu verborum numerum: quæ sanè omnia pro varietate lingvarum mutabilia esse constat: Sed respicit verborum sensum, quem Christus notare voluit, quibuscunq; tandem verbis, sensus ille verè ac propriè exprimatur.

VI. Et postrema: Etsi mutatio, si quæ fieri deberet in formâ verborum, quæq; fieret manente vero ac proprio sensu, fieri sanè posset illæsâ veritate Sacramenti: privatâ tamen autoritate nihil hâc in parte attentare cuiquam permittitur, non tantùm propter Schismatis, quod hoc modo facilè emergit, periculum: sed & propter hæresin atq; errores. Nam ex verbis impropriè prolatis, teste Hieronymo, hæresis oritur. In promptu autem hoc esset periculum, si cuilibet formam verborum, salvo licet eorum sensu proprio, mutare permitteretur. Quâ de re notatu dignum judicium magni illius Theologi, Johannis Brentij, qui de formâ baptizandi fic in suo Catechismo: Sunt qui sentiunt, quòd Christus sic instituerit Baptismum, ut etiam his verbis (Ego baptizo te in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti) distribuendus sit, & nisi his verbis utamur, existimant non esse verum Baptismum. Observandum igitur: Etsi in Baptismo hæc usitata verba omnino retinenda sunt, nec cuiquam permittendum est, ut hæc verba pro suâ libidine & temeritate mutet, ac alijs verbis pro suo arbitrio in Baptismo utatur: tamen hic usus rectè est intelligendus. Nam Christus non collocavit fundamentum Baptismi sui, super certis literis, syllabis aut dictionibus, nec alligavit nos ad certa verba: Non enim instituit Magiam, quæ ad certam verborum formam & ritus alligata est: sed instituit cælestia Sacramenta, quæ constant suâ ipsius sententiâ & voluntate, his vel illis verbis nobis significata. Et paulò pòst: Itaq; si quis post recitationem Symboli Apostolici, in Baptismo diceret ad baptizandum hæc verba: Audivi jam ex te confessionem fidei tuæ, quòd credas in DEUM PATREM omnipotentem, Creatorem, cæli & terræ: Et in unigenitum filium ejus Dominum nostrum JESUM CHRISTUM, & in SPIRITUM SANCTUM. In hanc igitur confessionem & fidem intingo te in aquam, seu perfundo te aquâ, ut hoc signaculo certus fias, te insertum esse in JESUM CHRISTUM,

& communionem omnium bonorum ejus. Vade ergo in pace. Hic certè Baptismus esset verus baptismus, quia continet ea quæ ad baptismum necessaria sunt: & recitata est sententia verborum CHRISTI, et si sonus ipse verborum paululum immutatus videtur. Hoc ideo visum est addere, non quod cuivis permittenda sit mutatio usitatorum verborum Christi: Sed ut verba Christi rectè intelligantur, & ut magiam à vera cælestium Sacramentorum confecratione, longè discernere discamus. Hæc Brentius.

Cæterùm non desunt, qui in hanc nostram sententiam virgulam sibi sumunt censoriam, dictitantes, ad certam aliquam Baptismi conferendi formam nos minimè esse alligatos, proptereà quod talis aliqua Matthæi ultimo à CHRISTO non sit præscripta: sed illud duntaxat monstratum, ut qui fidei Christianæ nomen sunt daturi, Patri, Filio, & Spiritui Sancto initiari debeant: Deinde verò hujus suæ sententiæ confirmationem petunt, ex Actis cap. 19. 5. Ubi à Paulo aliqui baptizati esse perhibentur in nomine CHRISTI.

Sed facilis est responsio: Nam prior ratio manifestè falsa est, uti ex jam dictis constat. Posterior ratio, ex cap. 19. Actor. petita, confundit τό ῥητὸν, & ἐξήγησιν verborum Lucæ, in quibus ἐξήγησις magis, quàm τὸ ῥητὸν est spectandum. Vult enim Evangelista hoc loco ostendere, non quâ formâ verborum Paulus baptizârit, aut quid in eâdem mutârit: Sed hoc duntaxat vult docere, quâ doctrinæ normâ sub Baptismo conferendo usus sit: nempè hâc, quòd omnis virtus Baptismi consistat in CHRISTO, & ab hujus redemtionis λύτρῳ unicè dependeat: ita, ut idem planè doctrinæ Pauli circa actionem Baptismi fuerit argumentum, quod postmodum ipsemet in suâ ad Romanos Epistolâ cap. 6, 3. expressit: Quotquot baptizati sumus in CHRISTUM JESUM, in mortem ipsius baptizati sumus. Suffragatur responsioni huic nostræ, ex piâ antiquitate Ambrosius etiam, lib. 1. de Spiritu Sancto, cap. 3. scribens: Si maximè formâ illâ baptisasset Apostolus, quâ ab Evangelistâ scribitur, illa tamen fuiffet valida, quia in uno illo Christi nomine, tota sanctissima Trinitas includitur, nempè Pater, à quo unctus est Christus: & ipse qui unctus est: & Spiritus Sanctus, per quem unctus est. Quam responsionem alij quoq; Patres tenent, præsertim Basilius & Augustinus. Verùm de hoc dicto fusius & pressiùs infrà.

His ita expeditis, Unum circà formæ confiderationem restat adhuc excutiendum: Nùm videlicet in actu Baptismi vel aspersione saltem: vel immersione potiùs, eâq; vel trinâ, vel unâ sit utendum? Ad priùs quæsiti membrum respondemọ, Ut verus & salutaris sit Baptismus non esse necessariam immersionem in aquam: sed sufficere vel adsperfionem vel superfusionem. Rationes affirmati hujus, proferimus has: 1. CHRISTUS ipse de modo ablutionis nihil præcepit, an totum corpus, vel pars tantùm aliqua immergi debeat? 2. Græcum βαπτίζειν utrumque significat: mersionem in aquam & aspersionem aquæ: Undè manus & faciem baptizasse leguntur, hoc est, abluisse, Marc. 7, 4 & Luc. 11, 38. 3. Vis & efficaeia Baptismi, non dependet ex ablutionis ritu, sed ex virtute instituentis CHRISTI, qui per aquam promisit se fore efficacem quocunq; etiam modo baptizandus aquâ abluatur, sive per immersionem, sive per aspersionem. 4. Videtur hoc colligi posse ex facto Petri, Act. 2, 41. ubi tria millia hominum uno die conversa, eodemque die baptizata esse leguntur : Quod cum per immersionem singulorum fieri vix potuerit: aspersione saltem factum id esse, satis probabiliter colligitur. 5. Baptismus institutus est ad ablutionem peccatorum tum conferendam, tum significandam: id quod superfusione vel aspersione aquæ commodè fieri potest. Unde Epistola ad Hebræos aliquoties expressis verbis ῥαντισμὸν aspersionem inculcat: cap. 9, 13. cap. 10, 22. cap. 12, 24. 6. Eâdem in sententia fuit Orthodoxa Antiquitas. Etsi enim tempore Cypriani, à quibusdam disceptatum fuit, An Clinici, aquâ tantum aspersi, rectè baptizati essent: rectè tamen responsum fuit à Cypriano lib. 4. Epist. 7. in potestate Ecclesiæ esse, uti Baptismo per solam aspersionem facto eumq; parem habere usum cum Baptismo, immersione peracto: quo utroq; ritu Apostolos etiam in Actis usos fuisse, idem Pater existimat. Sic August. de Eccl. dogmatibus cap. 74. Baptizandus, inquit confitetur fidem suam coram Sacerdote, & interrogatus respondet: & post confessionem fidei, vel aspergitur aquâ, vel intringitur. Et quanquam B. Lutherus in Sermone de Baptismo, Anno 19. habito, immersionem laudat: aspersionem tamen non improbat aut rejicit. A Scholasticis quidem nonnullis, ut & à Petro Lombardo ritus immersionis urgetur, quia nimirum sic melius repræsentetur sepultura Christi: Quod ipsum sentire etiam videtur Chrysost. homil. 24. in Joh. & Greg. lib. 1. Ep. 41. ad Leandrum Episcopum. Verum utut hoc sese habeat: ablutionis significandæ potior videtur esse in Baptismo ratio, quam sepulturæ Christi, quæ secundariò demum in significatione hujus Sacramenti locum habere videtur. Hinc ipse quoq; Thomas part. 3. q. 66 art. 7. inquit: Ablutio aquâ fieri potest, non solum per modum immersionis, sed etiam per modum aspersionis vel effusionis. Et ideò quamvis tutius sit baptizare per modum immersionis: potest tamen fieri baptismus per modum aspersionis, vel etiam effusionis. Concludimus proindè, licèt circa adultorum baptismum ritus immersionis in aquam & jam olim observatus fuerit, & adhuc hodiè circa eundem observari liberè possit: causas tamen non leves subesse, ob quas Ecclesia, immersionis ritum diutissimè in Ecclesia usurpatum, cum aspersione tandem superioribus seculis permutaverit.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacrament of Baptism: Whether triple immersion or sprinkling is required

The causes, moreover, seem to have been chiefly these: 1. The multitude of those to be baptized. 2. The scarcity of much water, especially in eastern places. 3. The inconvenience of the administration regarding the rite of immersion. 4. The weakness and danger of the infants to be baptized, especially, whose immersion, particularly in the winter season, could hardly be done without some risk.

Regarding the latter part of the question, whether one who is to be baptized ought to be immersed or sprinkled three times or only once, the Church has likewise observed either rite out of Christian liberty: so that Bonaventure writes not ineptly: If it is asked, how many times one should be immersed? one must answer according to the custom of the Church: but he who changes it by his own authority sins. And Thomas, part 3, q. 66, art. 8: Just as for baptism, in itself, the washing of water is required, which is of the necessity of baptism: but the mode of washing relates to baptism accidentally: So, as far as it is in itself, either can be done lawfully, both to immerse once and three times; but for different reasons, according to the ordinance of the Church, one mode was sometimes instituted, sometimes another. For when in the beginning of the nascent Church certain people thought wrongly about the Trinity, like Praxeas and Sabellius, considering CHRIST a mere man, and that He was neither to be called the Son of GOD, nor GOD except by His merit, which was chiefly in His death; therefore they did not baptize in the name of the Trinity: But in commemoration of the passion of CHRIST, and with one immersion. Which was reprobated in the primitive Church. Hence the canons of the Apostles define: If any Presbyter or Bishop does not celebrate the triple immersion of one mystery: but immerses once in baptism, which is ordered by some to be given in the death of the LORD, let him be deposed. For the Lord did not say to us, baptize in my death: But in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But afterwards the error of certain Schismatics grew, who baptized men, as Augustine narrates concerning the Donatists in his commentary on John, and therefore in detestation of their errors it was decreed, in the Council of Toledo, that one single immersion should be performed; but with such a cause ceasing, triple immersion is commonly observed in baptism. Therefore they sin gravely who baptize otherwise, as if not observing the rite of the Church; nevertheless, it would still be baptism. Thus far Thomas. That he makes mention of the IV Council of Toledo, that is clearly evident from the fifth Canon of the Council, whose words are these: Concerning the Sacrament of Baptism, because in Spain some priests perform a triple, some a simple (one) immersion, it is seen by some to be a schism, and the unity of the faith seems to be rent. For while different parties act in a seemingly contrary way in baptizing, they contend that others are not baptized. Therefore, what is to be done by us in the diversity of the Sacrament, let us be informed by the precepts of the Apostolic see, following not our own, but the paternal institution. Therefore, Gregory of blessed memory, Pontiff of the Roman Church, who not only enlightened parts of Italy, but also instructed far-distant Churches with his doctrine, at the urgent request of the most holy Bishop Leander concerning this diversity of Spain, what was rather to be followed, writing back to him among other things, said thus: Concerning the triple immersion of Baptism, nothing truer can be answered than what you yourselves have felt, that in one faith a diverse custom of the holy Church does no harm.

But it is not that by immersing three times we signify the sacraments of the three-day burial, so that while the infant is brought up from the waters for the third time, the resurrection of the three-day period is expressed. But if anyone perhaps thinks it is done for the veneration of the supreme Trinity, neither does anything stand in the way of this, to immerse the one to be baptized once in the waters: because while there is one substance in three subsistences, it is in no way reprehensible to immerse an infant in water in baptism either three times or once, when both the Trinity of Persons can be designated in three immersions, and the singularity of the divinity in one. But if until now an infant was immersed three times in baptism by heretics, I do not think it should be done among you, lest while they count the immersions, they divide the divinity: and while they do what they were doing, they glory that they have overcome your custom. Wherefore, because a reason has been rendered by so great a man concerning both sacraments which are done in Holy Baptism, that both are right, both are irreprehensible in the Holy Church of GOD: but for the sake of avoiding the scandal of schism, or the use of heretical dogma, let us hold to the simple immersion of baptism, lest we seem to those who immerse three times to approve the assertion of the heretics, while they follow our custom as well. Thus far the words of the Toletan Canon, which was later repeated almost word for word in the Synod of Worms, around the year 868. In the time of Jerome, triple immersion was in use: as appears from those things which he wrote upon the words of the Apostle, who in the Epistle to the Ephesians 4 says: One Baptism: Three times, says Jerome, we are immersed, so that the one Sacrament of the Trinity may appear. And a little later: One Baptism can also be said to be so, because although we are baptized three times, on account of the mystery of the Trinity, it is nevertheless reckoned as one Baptism. The reason for the assertion depends on the unity of the Form, which, applied to three immersions, made individually for individual persons of the Divinity, does not in the least cease to be one. We conclude finally from these things, which have already been variously disputed in the Church, that there is no absolute necessity that either a triple or a single immersion, or sprinkling of water, be done: but that it is free to immerse or sprinkle either once or three times: and that this detracts nothing at all from the truth of this Sacrament. Meanwhile, however, whether this or that custom has been received by the Church in use: it certainly would not be in anyone's judgment or power to change it of his own motion, or to neglect it rashly. Finally, we note also this, that whether Baptism is performed by one, or three immersions, or by aspersion, the utterance of the words must nevertheless take place at the same time as the aspersion itself, since it is this which thoroughly constitutes and completes the form of this Sacrament: yet so that it is sufficient if they are together, morally speaking: that is, if the word and the act of the baptizer are so together that one is begun before the other is entirely finished, whether the one or the other be prior in the meantime. And thus far we have seen the purer doctrine of our Churches concerning the definition of Baptism, and its essential parts, as also concerning its Form, explained: it remains now in the conclusion of this first chapter to do nothing else than to touch briefly upon certain errors, both of the Romanists and of the Calvinists, which impinge upon the purity of this doctrine.

Latin:

Causæ a. præcipuè hæ fuisse videntur. 1. Multitudo baptisandorũ. 2. inopia aquæ multæ, in locis cumprimis orientalib9. 3. Administrationis incommoditas circà immersionis ritū. 4. Debilitas & periculū baptisandorũ infantum præcipuè, quorum immersio fieri, hyberno præcipuè tempore, vix sine aliquo discrimine poterat.

Quoad posterius quæsiti membrum, Utrum ter vel semel tantùm baptizandus immergi aut aspergi debeat, item Ecclesia ex libertate Christianâ, utrũq̃ ritum, pro arbitrio observavit: ita ut Bonaventura haud ineptè scribat: Si quæritur, quoties sit mergendum? respondendum est secundum morem Ecclesiæ: Qui autem propriâ autoritate mutat peccat. Et Thomas part 3 q.66. art 8. Sicut ad baptismum per se requiritur ablutio aquæ, quæ est de baptismi necessitate: modus autem ablutionis per accidens se habet ad baptismum: Ita quantum est de se, utrumq̃ licitè fieri potest, & semel & ter immergere; sed ex diversis causis, secundum ordinationem Ecclesiæ quandoq̃ institutus est unus mod9, quandoque alius. Cùm enim in principio nascentis Ecclesiæ quidam de Trinitate, ut Praxeas & Sabellius malè sentiebant, CHRISTUM purum hominem æstimantes, nec dici filium DEI, nec DEŨ nisi per meritum ejus, quod præcipuè fuit in morte ejus; ideò non baptizabant in nomine Trinitatis: Sed in commemoratione passionis CHRISTI, & unâ immersione. Quod reprobatum fuit in primitivâ Ecclesiâ. Hinc canones Apostolorum definiunt: Si quis Presbyter aut Episcopus non trinam immersionem unius mysterij celebrat: sed semel immergit in baptismate, quod dari à quibusdam jubetur in morte DOMINI, deponatur. Non enim nobis dixit Dominus, in morte meâ baptizate: Sed in nomine Patris, & Filij & Spiritus Sancti. Postmodum verò inolevit quorundam Schismaticorum error, homines baptizantiū, sicut de Donatistis Augustinus narrat super Johannem, & ideò in detestationem errorum eorum fuit statutum, in Concilio Toletano, ut fieret una sola immersio sed cessante tali causa, communiter observatur in baptismo trina immersio. Ideò graviter peccant aliter baptizantes, quasi ritū Ecclesiæ non observantes; nihilo minus tamen esset baptismus. Hactenus Thomas. Quòd autem Concilij Toletani IV. mentionem facit, id ex quinto Concilij Canone liquidò patet, cujus hæc sunt verba: De Baptismi Sacramento propter quodin Hispaniis quidam Sacerdotes trinam, quidam simplicem (unam) immersionem faciunt,à nonnullis Schisma esse conspicitur, & unitas fidei scindi videtur. Nam dùm partes diversæ in baptizandis quasi contrario modo agunt, alij alios non baptizatos es se contendunt. Proindè quid à nobis in Sacramenti diversitate faciendum sit, Apostolicæ sedis informemur præceptis, non nostram, sed paternam institutionem sequentes. Beatæ ergò memoriæ Gregorius, Romanæ Ecclesiæ Pontifex qui non solùm partes Italiæ illustravit,sed & longè existentes Ecclesias sua doctrina perdocuit, efflagitante Sanctissimo Leandro Episcopo, de hac Hispaniæ diversitate, quidpotius esset sequendū, inter cætera rescribens ei,sic ait: De trinâ verò mersione Baptismatis, nihil respon deri veriùs potest, quàm ipsi sensistis, quiain unâ fide nihil officit sanctæ Ecclesiæ consuetudo diversa.

Non autem quòd tertiò mergimus, triduana sepulturæ Sacramenta signamus, ut dùm tertiò infans ab aquis educitur, resurrectio triduani temporis exprimatur. Quòd si quis fortè etiam pro summæ Trinitatis veneratione existimet fieri, neq́; ad hoc aliquid obstitit, baptizandum semel in aquis mergere: quia dum in tribus subsistentiis una substantia est, reprehensibile esse nullatenùs est, infantem in baptismate in aquam vel ter vel semel mergere, quando & in tribus mersionibus Personarum Trinitas, & in unâ potest divinitatis singularitas designari. Sed si nunc usq́; ab hæreticis infans in baptismate tertiò merge batur, faciendum apud vos esse non censeo, nedum mersiones numerant, divinitatem dividant: dumq́; quod faciebant, faciunt, morem vestrum se vicisse glorientur. Quapropter quia de utroq́; Sacramento, quod fit in Sancto Baptismo à tanto viro reddita est ratio, quod utrumq́; rectum, utrumq́; irreprehensibile in Sanctâ DEI Ecclesiâ habeatur: propter vitandum autem Schismatis scandalum, vel hæretici dogmatis usum, simplam teneamus baptismi mersionem, ne videamur apud eos, quid tertiò mergunt hæreticorum approbare assertionem, dum sequuntur & morem nostrum. Hactenus verba Canonis Toletani, qui postea in Synodo Wormatiensi, circa A. 868. ferè de verbo ad verbum repetitus est. Tempore Hieronymi trina immersio in usu fuit: sicut apparet ex ijs, quæ scripsit super verba Apostoli, qui in Epistolâ ad Ephes. 4. dicit: Unum Baptisma: Ter, inquit, Hieronmergimur, ut Trinitatis unum appareat Sacramentum. Et Paulò pòst: Potest unum Baptisma & ita dici, quòd licet ter baptizemur, propter mysterium Trinitatis, unum tamen Baptisma reputetur. Ratio assertionis pendet ab unitate Formæ, quæ tribus immersionibus applicata, singulis ad singulas Divinitatis personas factis, una esse minimè desinit. Colligimus tandem ex his, quæ jam olim in Ecclesiâ variè disputata sunt, nulliǵ absolutæ esse necessitatis, ut vel trina vel una fiat immersio, vel aspersio aquæ: sed liberum esse vel semel, vel ter immergere aut aspergere: idq́; veritati Sacramenti hujus nihil quicquam dettahere. Interim tamen sive hæc, sive illa consuetudo ab Ecclesiâ usu sit recepta: non profectò in cujusvis arbitrio aut potestate fuerit positum, proprio motu illam vel mutare, vel temerè negligere. Tandem notamus & illud, sive unâ, sive trinâ immersione, vel aspersione fiat Baptismus, prolationem tamen verborum cum ipsâ aspersione simul fieri debere, quippè quæ formam hujus Sacramenti penitùs constituit & absolvit: ita tamen, ut satis sit, si sint simul moraliter loquendo: hoc est, si verbum & factum baptizantis sic sint simul, ut unum inchoëtur, priusquam alterum ex toto finiatur, sive unum interim prius sit, sive alterum. Et hactenùs quidem puriorem Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctrinam de definitione Baptismi, deǵ; partibus essentialibus, ut & de Formâ ejus, expedi vimus: Restat jam in diexodo capitis hujus primi nihil aliud, quàm ut errores quosdam tùm Romanensium, tùm Calvinianorum, in puritatem doctrinæ hujus impingentes, paucis perstringamus.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Essence of the Sacrament of Baptism: Things to be observed regarding Baptism

And at the beginning, indeed, the Sacramentarians define baptism viciously and imperfectly, as being a sign of initiation, by which we are co-opted into the society of the Church, so that, engrafted into CHRIST, we may be reckoned among the children of GOD Calvin. lib. 4. Institut. cap. 15. §. 1. Which definition recalls, as it were, from hell the error of Zwingli, and confirms it, who raved that the Sacraments are nothing else than signs by which we are received into the Church, and thus give us assurance more proximately than they do to us, that we are inserted into Christ, and are children of GOD. What is more, this definition does not express any essential part of Baptism, nay, not even its proper effect. Indeed, it can be accommodated in all respects to the Sacrament of Circumcision as well. Therefore, it is neither essential, nor does it belong to Baptism καθʼ ἁυτὸ (in itself).

Of the same flour is also that Definition of Baptism which the Heidelberg Catechism, question 69, has produced, asserting that Baptism is a Sacrament by which we are admonished (Erinnert werden) that we are as certainly cleansed from sins by the Holy Spirit and the Blood of Christ, as we are certainly washed from the filth of the flesh by Water. This remarkable Catechesis maintains, forsooth, that Baptism is not a medium through which Regeneration is truly and effectively conferred upon us: but that it is only an admonition (eine Erinnerung) of that which, even before the sprinkling of water, had already happened to them, partly from the faith of their parents, partly from the covenant of GOD, into which infants are inserted from their carnal birth from faithful parents. 2. That the water of Baptism does no more than wash away the filth of the body. Concerning which two errors we shall have to treat expressly in the following chapters.

Another error of the Calvinists is that they dare to constitute the Celestial Thing of this Sacrament as the Promise of the remission of sins and of Regeneration. For thus writes Daniel Tossanus, the Heidelberg Sacramentarian, in his disputation on Baptism against the articles of the Meissen Visitation, thesis 2: Although there is but one Baptism: it consists, however, no less than the Supper of the Lord, of two most distinct things, the earthly, elemental, and visible, namely Water: and the celestial and invisible thing, namely the promise of the remission of sins through the blood of CHRIST, and of regeneration through the Spirit of the same. But we have already just now, in the preceding article concerning the Sacraments in general, chapter 1, refuted this error, showing that the Word, neither of command nor of promise, enters into the Substance of the Sacrament, and therefore never constitutes an essential part of the Sacrament.

As for the Romanists, they do not even to this day sufficiently agree upon a certain definition of Baptism. The Scholastics commonly define Baptism as being a Sacrament of the washing of the soul from sin, consisting in the washing of the body of a man consenting in some way, performed by another in water with certain words, pronounced at the same time by the same person washing with due intention.

This definition is distasteful to Gregory of Valencia, who approves more of that one of Thomas, part 3, q. 66, art. 1: Baptism is the exterior washing of the body, performed under the prescribed form of words. Bellarmine, book 1, on Baptism, chapter 1, setting aside the definition of Thomas, embraces that which is of the Roman Catechism, and it is thus: Baptism is the Sacrament of regeneration by water in the word of life. Which definition is certainly more perfect than the other two: but in the meantime, it does not express all the essential parts of this Sacrament, and therefore it is not causal: which is easily possible to estimate if a comparison of it is made with our definition.

That other error of the Romanists is fouler, by which they contend that, for the essence and truth of this Sacrament, besides those parts which we defined above, there are also required as necessary: the blessing of the font, salt, spittle, the sign of the cross, exsufflation, exorcism, and other things of that kind; concerning which there will be a dispute by us expressly at the end of this treatise. Let Lombard alone suffice in this place, who in book 4, Sent. dist. 3, argues that this doctrine of the Romanists is false, saying: The Sacrament of Baptism consists in two things: namely, in the word and the element: Therefore, even if other things are lacking, which were instituted for the adornment of the Sacrament, it is not for that reason any less a true and holy Sacrament, if the word and the element are there. For in this Sacrament, as in others, certain things are wont to be done for the adornment and seemliness of the Sacrament: and certain things pertaining to the substance and cause of the Sacrament. Of the substance of this Sacrament are the Word and the Element: the rest pertain to its solemnity.

Moreover, someone might not undeservedly ask in this place, Since under the Papacy Baptism has been so foully defiled for many centuries now, and is defiled today, whether those who were baptized in the Papacy received a true and efficacious Baptism. We answer simply in the affirmative. The firmest reason is that, although Baptism was foully contaminated by various corruptions and abuses, the element of the matter nevertheless remained intact, and the form of the words of institution also remained unblemished. Therefore, the truth of this Sacrament indeed labored, but it was not yet completely taken away, in such a way that, through the multitude of abuses, the substance of its use was by no means destroyed. For which reason there is no need for those to whom this Sacrament was administered in the Papacy to be rebaptized.

But if anyone concludes from this: Therefore it is still lawful today for Evangelicals or Lutherans to seek and use either this very Sacrament or the other, the Sacrament of the Eucharist, among the Papists: he concludes most viciously. For that would be nothing other than to bear a foreign yoke with unbelievers, as the Apostle speaks, 2 Cor. 6:14. But this would be joined with the very denial of the faith, because those things which pertain to the substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament are neither found nor retained among the Romanists, neither in the material nor in the formal aspects.

Finally, it does not follow from our decision that the truth of religion or of the Church therefore stands on the side of the Papists because the truth of the Sacrament of Baptism is efficacious among them: which can be taught by a manifest example. For just as the Sacrament of Circumcision was indeed effective in the time of Christ in the assembly of the Jews, since it was celebrated according to the institution of Christ: meanwhile, however, Christ warned his hearers to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees: so nothing prevents the Sacrament of Baptism from being true and effective among the Papists: yet meanwhile their very Religion and Church labors under abominable falsehood.

Latin:

Ac initio quidem Sacramentarij baptismum vitiosè & imperfectè definiunt, quòd sit signum initiationis, quo cooptamur in Ecclesia societatem, ut CHRISTO insiti, inter filios DEI censeamur Calvin. lib. 4. Institut. cap. 15. §. 1. Quæ definitio errorem Zvvinglij ab orco quasi revocat, & confirmat, qui deliravit, Sacramenta nihil esse aliud, quàm Signa quibus recipiamur in Ecclesiam, & sic proxime magis, quàm nobis fidem faciant, nos esse Christo insertos, & filios DEI. Quid quòd definitio hæc ullam partem essentialem Baptismi, imò ne quidem proprium ejus effectum exprimit. Quin Circumcisionis etiam Sacramento per omnia accommodari potest. Ergò neq; essentialis est, neq; καθʼ ἁυτὸ Baptismo convenit.

Ejusdem farinæ est & Definitio illa Baptismi, quam Catechismus Heidelbergensis quæst. 69. prodidit, asserens Baptismum esse Sacramentum, quo admoneamur (Erinnert werden) nos tam certò per Spiritum Sanctum, & Sanguinem Christi mundari à peccatis: quàm certò per Aquam à sor dibus carnis abluimur. Statuit nimirum egregia hæc Catechesis, Baptismum non esse medium, per quod nobis verè & efficaciter conferatur Regeneratio: sed commonefactionem tantùm esse (eine Erinnerung) illius, quod jam ante asperfionem aquæ partim ex fide parentum, partim ex fœdere DEI, cui infantes ex carnali nativitate, ex fidelibus parentibus sint inserti, illis obtigerit. 2. Aquam Baptismi plus non operari, quàm abluere sordes corporis. De quibus duobus erroribus in subseqq. capitibus nobis ex professo dispiciendum fuerit.

Alter error Calvinianorum est, quod Rem Cœlestem Sacramenti hujus constituere audent Promissionem Remissionis peccatorum & Regenerationis. Sic enim scribit Daniel Tossanus Sacramentarius Heidelbergensis, in disputatione de Bapt. contra articulos Visitationis Misnicæ, thesi 2. Ut maximè unum sit Baptisma: constat tamen non minus ac Cœna Domini duabus rebus maximè distinctis, terrena, elementari & aspectabili, nempè Aquâ: & Re cœlesti ac invisibili, videlicet promissione remissionis peccatorum per sangvinē CHRISTI, & regenerationis per Spiritum ejusdem. Verùm jam modò præcedente articulo proximo de Sacramentis in genere, capite 1. errorem istum protrivimus, ostendentes, Verbum neq; mandati, neq; promissionis ingredi Substantiam Sacramenti, ac proindè partem essentialem Sacramenti nunquam constituere.

Quoad Romanenses, illi de certâ definitione Baptismi ne quidem in hunc usq; diem satis conveniunt. Scholastici communiter Baptismum definiunt, quòd sit Sacramentum ablutionis animæ à peccato, consistens in ablutione corporis hominis aliqualiter consentientis, facta ab alio in aquâ cum verbis certis, simul ab eodem abluente cum debita intentione prolatis.

Sordet hæc definitio Gregorio de Valentia, qui magis probat illam Thomæ part 3. q 66. art. 1. Baptismus est ablutio corporis exterior, facta sub præscriptâ formâ verborũ Bellarminus l. 1. de Bapt. cap. 1. posthabitâ definitione, Thomæ, amplectitur eam quæ est Catechismi Romani, & sic habet: Baptismus est Sacramentum regenerationis per aquam in verbo vitæ. Quæ sanè definitio reliquis duabus est perfectior: sed interim essentialia omnia Sacramenti hujus non exprimit, ac proindè causalis non est: id quod facilè licèt æstimare, si ejus cum nostrâ definitione fiat collatio.

Fœdior ille alter Romanensium est error, quo contendunt, ad Essentiam & veritatem Sacramenti hujus, præter partes eas, quas nos suprà definivimus, requiri etiam tanquam necessaria: Benedictionem fontis, Sal, Salivam, Signum Crucis, Ex sufflationem, Exorcismum, & id genus alia: de quibus sub finé hujus Tractatus ex professo nobis futura disputatio. Sufficiat hoc loco un9 Lombardus, qui l. 4. Sent.dist. 3.doctrinã hanc Romanensiu falsitatis arguit: In duob9, inquiens, consistit Sacramentum Baptismi: scilicet in verbo & elemento: Ergò etsi alia desint, quæ ad decorem Sacramenti instituta sunt, non ideò minùs verum est Sacramentum, & sanctum, si verbum sit ibi & clementum. Nam & in hoc Sacramento, & in alijs quædam solent fieri ad decorem & honestatem Sacramenti: quædam ad substantiam & causam Sacramenti pertinentia. De substantiâ hujus Sacramenti sunt Verbum & Elementum: cætera ad solennitatem ejus pertinent.

Cæterùm quærat haud immeritò hoc loco aliquis, Cum sub Papatu tàm fœdè Baptismus multis jam seculis conspurcatus fuerit, hodièq́ conspurcetur, an verum & efficacem Baptismum acceperint, qui in Papatu baptizati sunt. Respondemus nos simpliciter affirmatè. Ratio firmissima est, quia licèt corruptelis & abusibus varijs Baptismus fœdè contaminatus fuit: remansit tamen elementum materię integrum, remansit etiam forma verborum institutionis illibata. Laboravit ergò quidem, sed non tamen penitùs est sublata Sacramenti hujus veritas, ita quidem, ut per abusuum multitudinem, substantia usus minimè deperierit. Quo nomine non est opus, ut rebaptizentur, quibus in Papatu Sacramentum hoc collatum fuit.

Verùm si quis indè colligat: Ergò etiamnum hodiè Evangelicis sive Lutheranis æq́ licitum esse, vel hoc ipsum, vel alterum etiam Evcharistiæ Sacramentum, apud Pontificios requirere atque usurpare: ille vitiosissimè colligit: Nam illud nihil aliud foret, quàm cum infidelibus peregrinum jugum trahere, uti loquitur Apostolus, 2. Cor. 6, 14. Hoc verò cum ipsâ fidei abnegatione esset conjunctum, propterea quòd quæ substantiam Sacramenti Evcharistici pertinent, neq́ in materialibus, neq́ in formalibus, apud Romanenses reperiantur aut retineantur.

Tandem neq́ ex decisione nostrâ illud sequitur, quòd veritas Religionis aut Ecclesiæ ideò stet à partibus Pontificiorum, quia Sacramenti Baptismi efficax apud ipsos sit veritas: id quod ex exemplo manifesto doceri potest. Nam quemadmodum Sacramentum quidem Circumcisionis efficax fuit tempore Christi in cœtu Judæorum, quippe secundum institutionem Christi celebratum: interim tamen a fermento Pharisæorum sibi cavere auditores suos Christus monuit: ita nihil prohibet, quo minus verum atq; efficax apud Pontificios sit Sacramentum Baptismi: ipsa tamen interim Religio eorum & Ecclesia, abominabili falsitate laboret.


### Chapter Two on the Number of Baptism


### Chapter Two on the Number of Baptism: CAN this Sacrament be or ought it to be divided into several Baptisms, and those different in species?

The true Church of GOD believes and confesses one Baptism in number and kind, being so taught by the Apostle, who, just as he declares that there is one GOD in number, and one faith in number; so he also declares that there is one Baptism, Eph. 4:5. Moved by this Apostolic authority, the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea wished to add this Article also to their Creed: ὁμολογῶ ἓν βάπτισμα εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν: I confess One Baptism for the remission of sins.

Nothing detracts from this unity at the beginning, that ancient doctrine, both of the Holy Fathers and of the Scholastics, concerning the threefold Baptism of the Church, one of which they called of the Spirit: another of the Spirit: the third of Blood: as can be seen in Origen, Volume VIII on John; and homily 7 on the book of Judges: in Augustine, book 13 on the City of GOD, chapter 7. Likewise in the ordinary gloss, on chapter 6 of the Epistle to the Hebrews. For even the definitions themselves, regarding the baptism of blood and of the spirit, show clearly enough that the name of Baptism is applied to those two kinds improperly and in a metaphorical sense. For by the Baptism of the Spirit, they understood that miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit, which happened first to the Apostles immediately, and then indeed to the faithful in the primitive Church through the laying on of hands. But by the Baptism of Blood, they understood the martyrdom of the faithful shedding their blood for the profession of the truth: so named by CHRIST himself, Mark 10:38 and 39, Luke 12:50. In a similar metaphorical sense, the Cloud also accompanying the Israelites through the desert, and the crossing of the Red Sea, are designated by the Apostle with the name of Baptism, 1 Cor. 10:2. From which, however, the collection does not militate for establishing several kinds of the Baptismal Sacrament: since argumentation does not proceed from the figurative to the proper. It remains therefore, although several baptisms may be given, so called equivocally and figuratively: that only the Baptism of water is truly and properly a Sacrament. But that which is to be noted παραδιαφωνητικω̃ς as it were in this place, concerning the dogma of the Scholastics, is that, not without notable blasphemy, they ascribe the first place to the baptism of blood or martyrdom, and prefer it in all ways to the baptism of water, nay, they trifle splendidly that through it all sins whatsoever, as much regarding the penalty as regarding the guilt, are washed away: and that grace is conferred ex opere operato: as can be seen in Thomas: and especially in Biel in book 4 of the sentences, dist. 4. This opinion is indeed insulting to that most perfect λύτρον of the precious blood of CHRIST: nay, and injurious to the very martyrdoms of the Saints; of whom Antiquity truly said: The martyrs received crowns, they did not give them.

Then: Those two diverse species or Essential parts of this Sacrament, about which we dealt in the immediately preceding chapter, do not divide the unity of the Sacrament of Baptism into two diverse species. For even if those parts differ in their whole genus: yet the Sacramental Union of those two parts prevents a double Baptism from arising thence, which causes them to coalesce into one composite Sacrament in number: so that neither water separately or separated from the heavenly thing: nor the heavenly thing separately or separated from the elemental thing, constitutes a peculiar Baptism, or has any peculiar operation: but water with the heavenly thing: and the heavenly thing with water, constitutes this Sacrament. Hence it is that the Savior himself, John 3:5, ascribes one operation in number, namely Regeneration, not to water alone, or to the spirit alone or separately, but to both things together and jointly. Nor is it to be considered here what GOD can do: but what He wills. For there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit can regenerate a man even without the water of Baptism: which we ourselves admit happens entirely in the infants of the faithful, who have died in the mother's womb, or who have been prevented from the reception of Baptism by some inevitable case of necessity: but this is the question, Does the Holy Spirit ordinarily wish to confer and work Regeneration in this Sacramental Baptismal action without the Element of water? Where we hold the negative; which we will also confirm quite vigorously in chapter 4 against the clamors of the Calvinists.

Thirdly: The diversity of the dispensing persons does not tear apart the unity of this Sacrament: of whom one is the minister, sprinkling water in baptizing: the other indeed is CHRIST, working the effect of regeneration inwardly through the Holy Spirit. For just as the two essential parts of this Sacrament, the earthly and the heavenly, do not constitute and complete two diverse, but One Sacrament in number: So each part, and thus this whole Sacrament, is dispensed by one and the same Ministry. Hence the gross error of the Calvinists, who constitute two baptizing Ministers: One, Man, who sprinkles at least the water: the other, GOD who confers the Holy Spirit immediately, and not through water in Baptism: of which interior dispensation, the element of water dispensed by man is merely an external sign, but not indeed a medium. This is, to be sure, to delete and erase with one stroke everything that is found in sacred writings concerning the virtue and efficacy of the Ecclesiastical Ministry: as that which is called by the Apostle in 2 Cor. 3:8, the ministry of the Spirit.

The authority of John the Baptist is objected to in this place, who seems to distinguish his own ministry and that of Christ in such a way that he ascribes to himself only the sprinkling of water, but to Christ the internal operation of grace: saying, I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he who is to come after me, he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. Matt. 3:11. And indeed this Johannine passage is not without every difficulty, on account of the manifold discrepancy of both recent and ancient theologians, which offers itself even today in the writings of our own theologians; therefore, so that we may be able to extricate ourselves more correctly and easily, it will not be irrelevant to relate the opinions of the theologians in this place, so that from their comparison something certain may finally be defined.

And at the beginning, indeed, the Fathers themselves did not agree with one another concerning the Baptism of John. Cyprian, in his Sermon on the Baptism of Christ and the manifestation of the Trinity, has it thus: Although it does not have full virtue, Christ nevertheless received the baptism of John: John was preparing the way for the Lord, by washing bodies outwardly, so that the external washing might precede the baptism that was to follow, in which the cleansing of souls and the remission of sins would be conferred. That which was in part preceded, so that the consummation might follow. Chrysostom, weighing those words of John, Matt. 3:11, I baptize you with water unto repentance, writes that the baptism of John had nothing more than that it led the people to repentance, for he did not say, I baptize you with the water of remission, but of repentance. And a little later: The baptism of John did not have the remission of sins: for this was the gift of that Baptism which Christ instituted. Augustine is not sufficiently consistent with himself concerning the Baptism of John. For he often holds the same opinion as Cyprian and Chrysostom: but sometimes, weighing more diligently this, which John preached concerning his own baptism, that it was a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, he does not dare simply to deny the remission of sins to the baptism of John: and yet he does not simply attribute it to him: but he finally embraced a middle opinion, writing thus in book 1 against the Donatists, chapter 10. I believe that John baptized in the water of repentance for the remission of sins in such a way that sins were remitted to those baptized by him in hope: but in reality, it was done in the Lord's Baptism. And chapter 11. Lest anyone contend that sins were also forgiven in the Baptism of John: but according to some broader meaning; I do not argue contentiously that remission was conferred by the Baptism of CHRIST upon those whom Paul ordered to be baptized again in Acts 19. That, however, is manifest, he submits, in book 2, chapter 37, against the letters of Petilian, that the baptism of John was one thing, and that of Christ another. The ordinary gloss upon that passage in Mark 1, John was in the desert, baptizing and preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, has it thus: He gave the baptism of repentance, he preached the baptism for the remission of sins, he did not give it.

The Scholastic Doctors likewise do not agree in all things. The Master of the Sentences, book 4, dist. 2, letter D, says: John washed only bodies, but he did not cleanse from sins: The baptism of John was unto repentance, not unto remission: but the Baptism of Christ was unto remission. Afterwards he asks: To what end, therefore, was the baptism of John? And he answers, So that men might be prepared by the use of baptizing for the Baptism of Christ. Again he asks, Why was it called the baptism of John? And he answers, because there the operation of John was only visible, of one washing outwardly, not the invisible grace of GOD working inwardly. And a little later: But if it is asked: Whether it was a Sacrament, it can be sufficiently conceded in that sense in which legal signs are called Sacraments. For the baptism of John signified a sacred thing, namely, the baptism of Christ. But to the question, Whether those baptized by John were baptized again with the Baptism of Christ? he answers: Those who were baptized by John, not knowing that there is a Holy Spirit, and placing their hope in his baptism, were afterwards baptized with the Baptism of Christ: but those who did not place their hope in the baptism of John, and believed in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, were not baptized afterwards: but by the laying on of hands done upon them by the Apostles, they received the Holy Spirit. These are the words of Lombard: Where, however, the marginal gloss has: The Master is not held here. Gabriel Biel follows the ordinary gloss noted above, explaining the text of Mark thus: John was baptizing and preaching a baptism; namely, not his own, but the future one of Christ, which would be a Baptism of repentance and of the remission of sins. Thomas, Bonaventura, Scotus, and others commonly hold that all who were baptized with the baptism of John were to be rebaptized with the baptism of Christ, for the reason that the Baptism of John did not confer grace, but was only a preparation and habituation for the Baptism of Christ, and a figure of it. They seek the foundation of this opinion of theirs from chapter 19 of the Acts, where it is read that Paul found disciples at Ephesus and, although they were baptized with the baptism of John, baptized them in the name of Christ.

The opinion of the Pontiffs is defined by canon 1 of the Council of Trent concerning Baptism: If anyone shall have said that the Baptism of John had the same power as the Baptism of Christ, let him be anathema.

Thus, therefore, both ancient and most recent writers have established that the Baptism of John is distinct in kind from the baptism of Christ, and that it differed from it altogether, not so much regarding the ceremony of the external ministry as regarding the salutary effect: so that the Baptism of John did not confer the grace of the remission of sins.

And indeed there are not lacking among the Theologians of our century who

Latin:

UNum numero & specie Baptismum credit & confitetur vera DEI Ecclesia, sic edocta ab Apostolo, qui uti unicum numero DEUM, & unam numero fidem; sic unum etiam Baptismum esse pronunciat, Ephes. 4, 5. Autoritate hac Apostolica moti Patres Concilij Niceni, Symbolo suo hunc etiam adjicere voluerunt Articulum: ὁμολογῶ ἓν βάπτισμα εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν: confiteor Unum Baptisma in remissionem peccatorum.

Unitati huic initio nihil derogat, Vetus illa, tum S. Patrum, tum Scholasticorum doctrina, de triplici Ecclesiæ Baptismo, quorum unum nominabant Flaminis: alterum Flaminis: tertium Sangvinis: uti videre est apud Originem, Tomo VIII. super Johannem; & homil. 7. in librum Judicum: apud Augustin. lib. 13. de Civit. DEI, cap. 7. Item in glossa ordinaria, ad c. 6. Epistolæ ad Hebræos. Nam vel definitiones ipsæ, quoad Baptismum sangvinis & flaminis, satis dilucidè ostendunt, Baptismi nomen impropriè, & sensu metaphorico, duabus istis speciebus accommodari. Per Baptismum enim Flaminis, intelligebant miraculosam illam effusionem Spiritus Sancti, quæ primum Apostolis immediate, deinde vero fidelibus in primitivi Ecclesiâ per impositionem manuum obtigit. Per Baptismum verò Sangvinis, intelligebant Martyrium fidelium ob professionem veritatis sangvinem profundentium: sic a CHRISTO ipso nominatum, Marc. 10, 38, & 39. Luc. 12, 50. Pari sensu metaphorico Nubes etiam concomitans Israelitas per desertum, & transitus maris rubri, ab Apostolo Baptismatis appellatione indigitantur, 1. Cor. 10, 2. Unde tamen ad plures constituendas Sacramenti Baptistici species, non militat collectio: siquidem à figurato ad proprium non procedit argumentatio. Relinquitur ergo proindè, licèt plura dari possint baptismata, æquivoce ac figuratè sic dicta: Solum tamen Baptismum aquæ, verè ac propriè Sacramentum esse. Illud verò παραδιαφωνητικω̃ς quasi hoc loco, de Scholasticorum dogmate est notandum, quòd nimirum non sine insigni blasphem iâ, Baptismati sangvinis sive martyrio, primas adscribunt, & aquæ baptismo modis omnibus præferunt, imò per illum omnia prorsus peccata, tam quoad pœnam, quàm quoad culpam ablui: & gratiam ex opere operato conferri, splendidè nugantur: uti videre est, apud Thomam: & cumprimis apud Bielem in lib. 4. sent. dist. 4. Est nimirùm opinio hæc contumeliosa in perfectissimum illud λύτρον pretiosi sangvinis CHRISTI: quin & injuriosum in ipsa Sanctorum martyria; de quibus Antiquitas verè dixit: Martyres acceperunt coronas, non dederunt.

Deindè: Unitatem Sacramenti Baptismi non in duas diversas species dirimunt duæ illæ diversæ species sive partes Essentiales Sacramenti hujus: de quibus cap. præcedente proximo egimus. Etiamsi enim partes illæ toto genere discrepant: quò minùs tamen geminus indè oriatur Baptismus, obstat Sacramentalis Unio duarum istarum partium, quæ facit, ut in unum numero Sacramentum compositum coalescant: ita ut neq; aqua seorsim aut separata à re cœlesti: neq; res cælestis seorsim aut separata à re elementari, peculiarem Baptismum constituat, vel peculiarem aliquam operationem habeat: sed aqua cum re cælesti: & res cælestis cum aquâ, Sacramentum hoc constituat. Hinc est, quod Servator ipse Johan. 3. 5. non vel aquæ soli, vel spiritui soli aut seorsim, sed utriq; rei simul & junctim, unam numero operationem, nempè Regenerationem adscribit. Neq; etiam hîcc attendendum, quid DEUS possit facere: sed quid velit. Neq; enim dubium est ullum, quin Spiritus Sanctus etiam sine aquâ Baptismi possit regenerare hominem: id quod in infantibus fidelium, in utero matris extinctis, vel à perceptione Baptismi, inevitabili quodam necessitatis casu prohibitis, omninò fieri, nos ipsi fatemur: sed hoc quæstionis est, An Spiritus Sanctus ordinariè in actione hâc Sacramentali Baptisticâ, Regenerationem sine Elemento aquæ conferre & operari velit? Ubi negativam tenemus; quam etiam cap. 4. contra Calvinianorum clamores satis nervosè confirmabimus.

Tertiò: Unitatem Scramenti hujus non divellit, personarum dispensantium diversitas: quarum una est ministri, aquam baptizando aspergentis: altera verò est CHRISTI, intus per Spiritum Sanctum regenerationis effectum operantis. Nam quemadmodum duæ partes essentiales Sacramenti hujus, terrena & cælestis, non duo diversa, sed Unum numero constituunt & absolvunt Sacramentum: Ita utraque etiam pars, & sic totum hoc Sacramentum, uno eodemq; Ministerio dispensatur. Crassus proindè error Calvinianorum, duos constituen tium Ministros baptizantes: Unum, Hominem, qui Aquam saltem aspergat: alterum, DEUM qui Spiritum Sanctum immediatè, & non per Aquam in Baptismo, conferat: cujus interioris dispensationis, externum duntaxat signum, non verò medium sit, Elementum Aquæ ab homine dispensatum. Hoc nimirùm est unâ liturâ delere & expungere omnia, quæ in sacris de virtute & efficaciâ Ministerij Ecclesiastici reperiuntur: ut quod ab Apostolo 2. Cor. 3, 8. Διακονία πνεύματος ministerium Spiritus Sancti nominatur.

Objicitur hoc loco autoritas Johannis Baptistæ, qui suum & Christi ministerium ita distingvere videtur, ut sibi tantùm Aquæ aspersionem: Christo autem internam Gratiæ operâtionem adscribat: Ego, inquiens, aquâ quidem vos baptizo in pœnitentiam: qui autem post me venturus est, ipse vos baptizabit in Spiritu Sancto & igni. Matth. 3, 11. Et profectò nõ omni difficultate locus iste Johanniticus caret, propter multiplicem tàm recentiorum quàm priscorum Theologorum discrepantiam, quæ hodiéq; in nostratium Theologorum scriptis se offert, proindè ut rectiùs ac faciliùs nos extricare queamus, non abs re fuerit ordine Theologorum sententias hoc loco referre, ut ex earum collatione tandem certi quid definiri possit.

Ac initiò quidem Patres ipsi de Baptismo Johannis invicem non consenserunt. Cyprianus in Serm. de Baptismo Christi, & manifestatione Trinitatis sic habet: Licèt plenam non habeat virtutem, suscepit tamen Christus baptisma Iohannis: præparabat viam Domino Iohannes, lavando exteriùs corpora, ut præcederet exteriùs lavacrum, secuturum baptismum, in quo conferretur animarum ablutio, & peccatorum remissio. Præcessit quod erat ex parte, ut consummatio sequeretur. Chrysostomus expendens illa verba Johannis, Matth. 3, 11. Ego baptizo vos aquâ in pœnitentiam: scribit, baptisma Iohannis non habuisse quicquam ampliùs, quàm ut populum ad pœnitentiam duceret, non enim dixit; Ego baptizo vos aqua remissionis, sed pœnitentiæ. Et paulò pòst: Baptisma Iohannis non habebat remissionem peccatorum: hoc enim munus illius Baptismatis erat, quod Christus instituit. Augustinus sibiipsi satis non constat de Baptismo Johannis. Nam sæpiùs eandem cum Cypriano & Chrysostomo tenet sententiam: interdum verò diligentiùs expendens hoc, quod Johannes de Baptismo suo prædicavit, quòd esset Baptismus pœnitentiæ in remissionem peccatorum, non audet simpliciter Baptismo Johannis derogare remissionem peccatorum: & tamen eam non simpliciter illi tribuit: sed mediam sententiam tandem amplex9 est, sic scribens lib. 1. contra Donatistas, cap. 10. Credo Iohannem ita baptizare in aqua pœnitentiæ in remissionem peccatorum, ut ab eo baptizatis in spe remitterentur peccata: reipsa verò in Domini Baptismo id fieret. Et cap. 11. Ne quisquam contendat, etiam in Baptismo Iohannis dimissa esse peccata: sed secundum aliquam ampliorem significationem; eis quos Paulus denuò jussit baptizari Actor. 19. per Baptismum CHRISTI remissionem esse collatam, non ago pugnaciter. Illud tamen manifestum est, subjicit, lib 2. cap. 37. contra literas Petiliani, alium fuisse Baptismum Johannis, & alium Christi. Glossa ordinaria super illud Marc. 1. Fuit Johannes in deserto, baptizans & praedicans Baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem peccatorum, sic habet: Baptismum poenitentiae dedit, baptismum in remissionem peccatorum praedicavit, non dedit.

Scholastici Doctores itidem non per omnia conveniunt. Magister sententiarum lib. 4. dist. 2. lit. D. Johannes, inquit, sola corpora abluebat, à peccatis verò non mundabat: Baptismus Johannis erat in poenitentiam, non in remissionem: Baptismo verò Christi in remissionem. Postea quaerit: Ad quid ergò Baptismus Johannis? & respondet, Ut homines usu baptizandi praeparentur ad Baptismum Christi. Rursum quaerit, Quare dictus est baptismus Johannis? & respondet, quia ibi Johannis operatio tantùm visibilis erat, exterius lavantis, non invisibilis gratia DEI interiùs operantis. Et paulò post: Si verò quaeritur: An Sacramentum fuerit, satis potest concedi ex eo sensu, quo legalia signa dicuntur Sacramenta. Significabat enim Baptismus Iohannis rem sacram, scilicet baptismum Christi. Ad quaestionem verò, Utrum baptizati à Johanne, iterum baptizati sint Baptismo Christi? respondet: Illi qui baptizati sunt à Johanne, nescientes Spiritum Sanctum esse, ac spem ponentes in illius baptismo, postea baptizati sunt Baptismo Christi: illi verò qui spem non posuerunt in baptismo Iohannis, & Patrem, & Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum credebant, non postea baptizati fuerunt: sed impositione manuum ab Apostolis super eos facta, Spiritum Sanctum acceperunt. Haec Lombardus: Ubi tamen glossa marginalis habet: Hic non tenetur Magister. Gabriel Biel sequitur glossam ordinariam supra notatam, textum Marci ita exponens: Iohannes erat baptizans & praedicans baptismum; scilicet non suum, sed futurum Christi, qui esset Baptismus poenitentiae & remissionis peccatorum. Thomas, Bonaventura, Scotus & alij communiter sentiunt, quod omnes baptizati Johannis baptismate, iterum rebaptizandi erant baptismo Christi, ideò quòd Baptismus Johannis non contulerit gratiam, sed fuerit tantùm praeparatio & assuefactio ad Baptismum Christi, & figura ejus. Sententiae hujus suae fundamentum petunt ex cap. 19. Actorum, ubi legitur Paulus invenisse Ephesi discipulos eosq́, licet baptizatos baptismo Iohannis, baptizasse in nomine Christi.

Pontificiorum sententiam definit canon. 1. Concilij Tridentini de Baptismo: Si quis dixerit, Baptismum Iohannis habuisse eandem vim cum Baptismo Christi, anathema sit.

Sic ergò tùm prisci tùm recentiores Scriptores pleriq́; statuerunt Baptismum Iohannis, specie esse distinctum à baptismo Christi, quin ab eodem, non tam quoad externi ministerij ceremoniam, quàm quoad salutarem effectum omninò discrepassse: ita ut Baptismus Johannis Gratiam Remissionis peccatorum non contulerit.

Et profectò non desunt ex nostri seculi Doctoribus Theologis, qui ab eâdem sententiâ


### Chapter Two on the Number of Baptism: On the Baptism of John

from the same opinion seem to differ not far. But in this manner they are accustomed to explain their mind. The Evangelical history relates that John, the forerunner of Christ, before the revelation or manifestation of Christ, for almost a year and a half, used a religious rite of baptizing in Judea, from the use of which he was called the Baptist. However, this rite was accustomed to be called the Baptism of John, not as if he himself were its author and founder: (for that it was instituted by GOD is argued by the fact that he asserts he was sent by GOD to baptize, John 1:35) but because he was its first dispenser. The form of this Baptism was that he baptized men in the name of the CHRIST who was to come: Acts 19:4. For although CHRIST had already come into the flesh, which was not unknown to John: yet he had not yet come to his manifestation and to the carrying out of the parts of his office. For this being finally done, that is, CHRIST being manifested and executing the parts of his ministry, the Baptism of John had to cease. Which was done when John, consigned to prison, sent his disciples to Christ to ask whether he was the one who was to come, etc. By which question John wished to testify that his ministry was fulfilled, and at the same time to show that his Baptism had been sanctioned only for a certain time: the end of which had now effectively arrived in the presence of Christ himself. Hence it is that those theologians determine that the Baptism of John is to be entirely excluded from the explanation of the present passage, which is about the Baptism of CHRIST, as being in species another and different thing. Now as to the principal question, concerning the kinship and difference of the Baptism of John and of Christ, they wish to appear to hold a certain middle opinion. For they do not subscribe to those who determine that both baptisms were one in number and species: nor do they simply approve the opinion of those who so separate both baptisms that they strip the baptism of John of the grace of the remission of sins. But they teach that a manifold distinction is to be established between both baptisms: and they explain this chiefly in these words: 1. The Baptism of John was in water: but that of Christ in the Holy Spirit. Luke 3:16, John 1:33. Which distinction is not infringed (they say) by that explanation by which it is said that John attributes to himself the external ministry, but to Christ the internal effect. For John does not say, I baptize you in water, and Christ baptizes in the Spirit under the common termination of the present tense: but under the termination of different tenses, past and future: Mark 1:8. I indeed have baptized you with water: but he will baptize with the Holy Spirit. Therefore a greater power is attributed to the baptism of Christ than to the baptism of John. 2. Those baptized by John afterwards received the baptism of Christ. Acts 19:5. But the baptism of Christ is neither repeated: nor does it admit the addition of another baptism, which indeed is done by water. 3. The baptism of John was of repentance, Matthew 3:11, by which it came about that it was received only by adults. But the baptism of Christ is conferred even on infants, who cannot repent. 4. With CHRIST arriving and entering upon his office, the baptism of John ceased: but the baptism of CHRIST is perennial, that is, it lasts until the end of the age. 5. The baptism of John was only in the name of the Christ who was to come, as clearly something preparatory to the imminent kingdom of Christ: but the baptism of CHRIST is given in the name of the Holy Trinity: which distinction is noted also by Ambrose, book 1 on the Holy Spirit, chapter 3, and Jerome on chapter 2 of Joel. 6. The baptism of Christ is a true Sacrament: which cannot be pronounced of the Baptism of John even for this reason alone: Because the Sacraments of the New Testament were instituted immediately by Christ while he was already performing the parts of his ministry in act. But it is certain that the Baptism of John was not instituted by Christ while he was already performing the parts of his ministry, since it was in use at least a year and a half before the preaching and manifestation of CHRIST. Which distinctions are for the most part noted by Luther in a certain disputation, Tom. 1 Lat. Jen. fol. 524 b for me. Thus therefore at length those theologians conclude that the Baptism of John and of Christ were not entirely one and the same; nor yet that both are to be so separated that the former is entirely emptied of the remission of sins, although the Baptism of CHRIST confers it much more effectively.

Moreover, there are others among the Orthodox theologians who determine differently, and contend that the Baptism of John, with the Baptism of Christ, was one in respect of ministry and effect, relying chiefly on these arguments.

I. It is placed beyond controversy that the Baptism of John was a Sacrament not of the Old but of the New Testament. Therefore it would be as absurd to determine that John baptized only unto repentance; as it is absurd to affirm that the New Testament, properly so called, is concerned only with the doctrine of the Law arguing sins. Nor does it stand in the way that John seems only to have been the forerunner of Christ, and to have at least prepared the way for him: for this very preparation is inserted, which is proper to the New Testament: otherwise John could be considered a minister of the Old Testament more than of the New, which is clearly absurd.

II. The ministry of John, as much regarding preaching as the rite of baptizing, is so described in the Scriptures as having GOD for its author, that it was joined with the efficacy of the remission of sins and of salvation, indeed with the HOLY SPIRIT itself. It is false, therefore, that he baptized only unto repentance, without the HOLY SPIRIT and without the remission of sins, and that it did not have the same power as the Baptism of CHRIST. The antecedent is clear from the Scriptures. For John was sent by GOD to perform both these duties: Joh. 1, 33. Thus John baptized in the desert, and preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. Marc. 1, 4. Hence Zacharias the father, describing the ministry of his son, Luc. 1, 76, says: And thou, child, shalt be called the Prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways; to give knowledge of salvation unto his people, which is in the remission of sins. Thus he preach-

he cautioned concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. John 3, v. 34, 35, 36. He who believes in the Son has eternal life. John 1, 32. I beheld the Holy Spirit descending like a dove. He pointed out Christ the Savior with his index finger, saying: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. John 1, 36. Furthermore, the end of John's baptism, with Paul himself as witness, Acts 19, 4, was that those baptized should believe in Christ. From this, therefore, they conclude that the doctrine of both John and Christ was the same, the same Spirit, the same faith, the same baptism, the same remission of sins.

III. CHRIST our head was not baptized with a different baptism than that with which we, who are his members, are now baptized, because we are all baptized into one body, and we put on Christ through baptism. But Christ was baptized with the baptism of John. It is necessary, therefore, that the baptism of John be one and the same with ours, that is, with the Baptism of Christ and the Apostles. The reason for the consequence is evidently apparent from the absurdities that follow from a different opinion. For if the baptism of John differs in species and number from our baptism, then there is no longer any analogy and agreement between the baptism with which Christ was dipped and that with which we are dipped. 2. That baptism which was conferred upon Christ will contribute nothing at all to our sanctification or confirmation. For those things which differ in species are also accustomed to differ in definition, causes, and effect. 3.
