The communion of Saints and the society of the faithful, which we confess in the Creed, will be taken away. But all these things are manifestly false and absurd. Therefore.

IV. And the Apostle provides the final argument, Ephesians 4, 5, who, about to describe the Unity of the Church and of all the faithful of the times of the New Testament, also takes his argument from the Unity of Baptism, by which, indeed, all the faithful alike, even those baptized by John, have coalesced into the unity of the mystical Body, which is Christ. Which method of arguing would certainly not hold up if the baptism of John differed from the baptism of CHRIST, either in whole or in degree.

And indeed these arguments are of such weight and moment that they easily deserve our applause and approval. For the differences which we reviewed above from the opinion of other Theologians do not seem to be of such evidence that they prove the contrary. For first, although John is read to have baptized with water, yet it is not read that he baptized in water alone, and that his baptism lacked the Holy Spirit: for our third argument has already proven the contrary. Nor can the diversity of past and future time stand in the way of our assertion, as will be clear a little later, when we shall treat of the true sense of the words of John, which are in dispute in this place. 2. That those baptized by John were later dipped with the baptism of Christ was not yet demonstrated clearly enough from the text of Acts 19, as we shall soon show. 3. John's Baptism was indeed one of repentance, but not of that alone: but also of the remission of sins, as was just shown. 4. The end of John's ministry no more strips his Baptism of its salutary effect than the end of the Apostles' ministry could take away the effect of Christ's baptism. 5. The distinction between Christ about to come and Christ exhibited no more takes away the effect of baptism than this very distinction makes the faith of the Old and New Testaments different in species. 6. That hypothesis seems clearly groundless, that a Sacrament is not instituted by Christ unless he is already fully performing the parts of the ministry by his own act. Certainly, since baptism enjoys divine authority, we do not doubt at all to call it a Sacrament.

Furthermore, what the meaning of the words of John the Baptist is, attributing the baptism of Water to himself, but the baptism of the Spirit to Christ, must now be shown. He does not, however, speak simply of the power and efficacy of his own ministry and that of Christ: but in a certain respect, namely, with regard to the principal efficient cause, and the one working that spiritual effect of Baptism by itself. This, therefore, the Baptist intends: Although in that one action of Baptism, virtue and salutary grace are dispensed both by himself and by the other ministers, yet it is not to be ascribed to the minister as the principal efficient cause: since it is not placed in the power of any man to confer the Holy Spirit and the grace of the remission of sins by his own virtue: but this is to be attributed entirely to Christ, who, as the author of the Sacrament, alone as the principal agent, grants this power to the external action of the minister dispensing it as an instrumental or organic efficient cause. Which distinction of John the Baptist is to be well noted even today in the baptismal action: For in that one and the same action, a twofold action concurs: One of the minister dispensing, namely the sprinkling of elemental water: the other action is of CHRIST, namely the conferring of the Holy Spirit. Now if you trace any action back to its first principles: the sprinkling of water will be the minister's: the conferring of the Holy Spirit will be Christ's. These two actions, however, always concur together in the baptism of the faithful, toward a certain result: and indeed not dividedly, but unitedly: yet with this distinction, that Christ is the principal efficient cause: the minister, the less principal or organic efficient cause.

But that John the Baptist, speaking words about Christ, uses a verb of the future tense (he will baptize), it was not done because he wished to imply that the baptism of CHRIST would be distinct from his own both in number and in species: but he looked partly to the end of his ministry, which was already imminent: partly to the perpetuity and continuation of the office of Christ, who, not for a small space of time, but thereafter always until the end of the age, would be about to confer the Spirit upon the faithful through baptism: partly, finally, to that visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit

Latin:

haud procul distare videntur. Hunc autem in modum illi suam mentem explicare solent. Refert Evangelica historia, Johannem præcursorem Christi ante revelationẽ sive manfestationem Christi, anno ferè sesquialtero, ritum baptizandi religiosum in Judæâ usurpâsse, à cujus usu Baptista nuncupatus fuit. Consuevit autem ritus iste, Johannis Baptismus appellari, non quasi ipse autor illius & conditor fuerit: (à DEO enim illum institutum fuisse illud arguit, quòd se à DEO ad baptizandum missum esse, asserit Joh. 1, 35.) sed, quia primus illius dispensator fuit. Forma hujus Baptismi ea fuit, quòd in nomine venturi CHRISTI homines baptizavit: Act. 19, 4. Etsi enim jam tùm in carnem CHRISTUS venerat, quod Johanni non ignotum fuit: nondùm tamen venerat ad manifestationem, & ad partes officij peragendas. Nam hoc demùm facto, hoc est, CHRISTO manifestato, & ministerij sui partes exequente, Baptismus Johannis cessare debuit. Quod factum est, cum Johannes carceri mancipatus ad Christum misit discipulos suos, quæsitum, Nùm is esset, qui venturus esset &c. Quâ quæstione id Johannes testari voluit, impletum esse suum ministerium, simulque ostendere, Baptismum suum non nisi ad certum tempus sancitum fuisse: cujus finis jam in præsentia ipsius Christi efficaciter appulerit. Hinc est quòd à præsentis loci, qui est de Baptismo CHRISTI, explicatione, Baptismum Johannis prorsus secludendum esse, tanquàm specie alium ac diversum, isti Theologi statuunt. Jam quoad quæstionem principalem, de cognatione & differentiâ Baptismi Johannis & Christi, mediam quandam sententiam tenere, videri volunt. Neque enim illis subscribunt, qui statuuut, utrumq́; baptismum fuisse unum numero & specie: neque etiam eorum simpliciter approbant sententiam, qui utrumq́; baptismum ita disjungunt, ut Johannis baptismum gratiâ remissionis peccatorum spolient. Sed multiplex discrimen inter utrumq́; baptismum constituendum esse tradunt: idque his potissimùm verbis explicant: 1. Baptismus Johannis erat in aquâ: Christi autem in Spiritu Sancto. Luc. 3, 16. Johann. 1, 33. Quod discrimen non infringitur (ajunt) eâ explicatione, quâ dicitur, Johannem sibi tribuere externum ministerium, Christo autem internum Effectum. Non enim dicit Johannes, Ego baptizo vos in aquâ, & Christus baptizat in Spiritu sub terminatione Communi præsentis temporis: sed sub terminatione diversorum temporum, præteriti & futuri: Marc. 1, 8. Ego quidem baptizavi vos aquâ: ille verò baptizabit Spiritu Sancto. Major ergò virtus baptismo Christi, quàm baptismo Johannis tribuitur. 2. Baptisati à Johanne, posteà baptismum Christi susceperunt. Actor. 19, 5. At Baptismus Christi neque iteratur: neque alterius baptismi accessionem, quæ quidem fiat per aquam, admittit. 3. Johannis baptismus erat pœnitentiæ, Matth. 3, 11. quo fiebat, ut ab adultis tantùm susciperetur. Christi autem baptismus etiam infantibus, qui pœnitere non possunt, confertur. 4. Christus sto adveniente, & officium suum ingresso, baptismus Johannis cessavit: Christi autem baptisma est perenne, hoc est, durat ad finem usq́; seculi. 5. Johannis baptismus tantùm fuit in nomine venturi Christi, tanquàm planè quiddam præparatorium ad instans regnum Christi: CHRISTI autem baptisma datur in nomine S. Trinitatis: quod discrimen annotatur etiam ab Ambrosio, lib 1. de Spiritu Sancto, cap. 3. & Hieronymo in cap. 2. Joëlis. 6. Baptismus Christi verum est Sacramentum: quod de Baptismo Johannis pronunciari non potest vel ob hanc solam rationem; Quia Sacramenta Novi Testamenti immediatè à Christo partibus ministerij sui jam ipso actu fungente, instituta sunt. Atqui constat, Baptismam Johannis non à Christo, partes ministerij sui jam obeunte, institutum esse, quippè qui ante predicationem & manifestationem CHRISTI, ut mimmùm sesquiennio, in usu fuit. Quæ discrimina pleraque notantur à Luthero in disputatione quadam, Tom. 1. Lat. Jen. fol. mihi 524. b. Sic ergò tandem concludunt Theologi isti, Baptismum Johannis & Christi non fuisse prorsus unum eundemque; neq́; tamen utrumq́; sic disjungendum, ut prior ille Remissione peccatorum penitùs evacuetur, licèt Baptismus CHRISTI multò efficaciùs eam conferat.

Cæterùm sunt alij ex Orthodoxis Theologis, qui diversum statuunt, & Baptismum Johannis, cum Baptismo Christi, ratione ministerij & effectus Unum fuisse contendunt, his potissimùm freti argumentis.

I. Extra controversiam est positum, Baptismum Johannis fuisse Sacramentum non Veteris sed Novi Testamenti. Ergò tàm absurdum fuerit statuere, Johannem baptizasse duntaxat in pœnitentiam; quàm absurdum est, affirmare Novum Testamentum propriè sic dictum, versari tantùm circa doctrinam Legis arguentis peccata. Neq́; obstat, quòd Johannes videtur tantùm fuisse præcursor Christi, & viam ipsi saltem præparasse: nam hæc ipsa præparatio subinsertid, quod Novi Testamenti proprium est: aliàs Veteris magis, quàm Novi Testamenti minister Johannes censeri posset, id quod palàm absurdum.

II. Ministerium Johannis, tàm quoad prædicationem, quàm quoad ritum baptizandi, ita in Sacris describitur, quod DEUM autorem habeat, ut cum efficaciâ remissionis peccatorum & salutis, imò cum ipso Spiritu Sancto fuerit conjunctum. Falsum ergò quòd tantùm baptizarit in pœnitentiam, sine Spiritu Sancto, & sine remissione peccatorum: & quòd eandem vim cum Baptismo CHRISTI non habuerit. Antecedens ex Scripturis liquet. Nam à DEO missus est Johannes ad utrumq́; hoc munus peragendum: Joh. 1, 33. Sic baptizabat Johannes in deserto, & prædicabat baptismum pœnitentiæ ad remissionem peccatorum. Marc. 1, 4. Hinc Zacharias pater describens ministerium filij sui, Luc. 1, 76. Tu puer, inquit, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis: præibis enim ante faciem Domini, præparare vias ejus, ad dandam scientiam salutis plebi ejus, quæ est in remissione peccatorum. Sic prædi-

cavit de Patre, Filio & Spiritu Sancto. Joh. 3, v. 34. 35. 36. Qui credit in filium, habet vitam æternam. Joh. 1. 32. Conspexi Spiritum Sanctum descendentem quasi columbam. Monstravit Christum Salvatorem digito indice: Ecce inquiens agnus DEI, qui tollit peccata mundi. Joh. 1, 36. Prætereà finis baptismi Johannis ipso Paulo teste, Actor. 19, 4. fuit, ut baptizati crederent in Christum. Hinc ergò colligunt, eandem fuisse & Johannis & Christi doctrinam, eundem Spiritum, eandem fidem, eundem baptismum, eandem remissionem peccatorum.

III. CHRISTUS caput nostrum non inalio baptismate baptizatus fuit, quàm quo nos, qui membra ipsius sumus, nunc baptizamur, quia omnes in unum corpus baptizamur, & Christum induimus per baptismum. Atqui Christus baptizatus est, baptismate Johannis. Necesse est ergò, ut baptismus Johannis sit unus & idem cum nostro, hoc est, cum Baptismo Christi & Apostolorum. Ratio consecutionis evidenter patet ex absurdis, quæ diversam sententiam consequuntur. Nam si baptismus Johannis specie ac numero differt à baptismo nostro, utique nulla ampliùs est analogia & convenientia, inter baptismum, quo Christus tinctus fuit, & quo nos tingimur. 2. Baptismus iste qui Christo collatus, nihil quicquam ad nostri sanctificationem aut confirmationem faciet. Quæ enim specie differunt, ea definitione etiam, causis & effectu differre solent. 3. Tolletur communio Sanctorum & societas fidelium, quam in Symbolo confitemur. Sed hæc omnia manifestè sunt falsa & absurda. Ergò.

IV. Et postremum argumentum subministrat Apostolus, Ephes. 4, 5. qui Unitatem Ecclesiæ & fidelium omnium temporum Novi Testamenti descripturus, argumentum etiam sumit ab Unitate Baptismi, quo nimirùm pariter omnes fideles, etiam à Johanne baptizati, in unitatem Corporis mystici, quod est Christus, coaluerint. Quæ sanè argumentandi ratio non subsisteret, si baptismus Johannis à baptismo CHRISTI, vel secundum totum, vel secundum magis & minus discreparer.

Et sanè argumenta hæc illius sunt ponderis & momenti, ut nostrum quoque applausum & calculum facilè mereantur. Nam discrimina quæ suprà ex sententiâ aliorum Theologorum recensuimus, non tantæ videntur esse evidentiæ, ut contrarium evincant. Primum enim licèt Johannes baptisasse legitur aquâ: tamen non legitur, quòd in solâ aquâ baptizarit, & baptismus ejus Spiritu Sancto caruerit: Diversum enim jam argumentum nostrum tertium evicit. Neque etiam diversitas temporis præteriti & futuri assertioni nostræ obstare potest: uti paulò post patebit, ubi de vero sensu verborum Johannis, de quibus hoc loco controvertitur, agemus. 2. quod baptizati à Johanne posteà baptismo Christi tincti fuerint, nondum satis liquidò ex textu Actor. 19. demonstratum fuit, uti mox ostendemus. 3. Johannis Baptismus erat quidem pœnitentiæ, sed non solius: verùm etiam remissionis peccatorum, uti modò ostensum. 4. Finis ministerij Johannis haud magis Baptismum ipsius effectu suo salutari spoliat: atquè finis ministerij Apostolorum effectum baprismi Christi tollere potuit. 5. Distinctio in Christum venturum, & exhibitum, haud magis tollit effectum baptismi, atq; hæc ipsa distinctio non facit fidem specie diversam Veteris & Novi Testamenti. 6. Hypothesis illa videtur planè ἀνυπόθετος, quòd Sacramentum à Christo non institutum sit, nisi jam partes ministerij plenè ipso actu obeunte. Certè cum divinâ autoritate gaudeat baptismus, Sacramentum ipsum nominare, nihil quicquam dubitamus.

Cæterùm quænam sit sententia verborum Johannis Baptistæ, sibi baptismum Aquæ, Christo verò baptismum Spiritus tribuentis, jam ostendendum fuerit. Non autem de vi & efficaciâ Ministerij sui & Christi simpliciter loquitur: sed κατά τι, nempè respectu principalis causæ efficientis, & per se operantis spiritualem illum Baptismi effectum. Hoc igitur intendit Baptista, Licèt in unâ illâ actione Baprismi, virtus & salutaris gratia, & à se, & à reliquis ministris dispensetur: eam tamen non esse adscribendam ministro, tanquam causæ efficienti principali: siquidem in nullius hominis potestate sit positum, propriâ suâ virtute conferre Spiritum Sanctum & Remissionis peccatorum gratiam: sed in solidum hoc esse acceptum ferendum Christo, qui tanquàm autor Sacramenti, solus tanquàm agens principale, vim hanc largiatur externæ actioni ministri dispensantis, tanquàm causæ efficienti instrumentali sive Organicæ. Quæ distinctio Johannis Baptistæ hodièquè in actione baptisticâ, probè notanda venit: Nam in unâ eâdemq; actione illâ, gemina concurrit actio: Una Ministri dispensantis, nempè aquæ elementaris aspersio: altera actio est CHRISTI, nempè collatio Spiritus Sancti. Jam si quamlibet actionem ad sua prima principia revoces: Aquæ aspersio erit Ministri: Spiritus Sancti collatio erit Christi. Concurrunt autem duæ hæ actiones semper simul in baptismo fidelium, ad unum quòddam ἀποτέλεσμα: & quidem non διῃρημένως divisè: sed ἡνωμένως unitè: hâc tamen distinctione, ut Christus sit causa efficiens principalis: Minister, causa efficiens minus principalis sive organica.

Quòd verò Johannes baptista de Christo verba faciens, utitur verbo futuri temporis (baptizabit) non ideo factum, quod innuere voluerit, CHRISTI baptismum à suo, & numero & specie fore distinctum: sed respexit partim ad finem sui ministerij, qui jam jam ingrueret: partim ad perennitatem & continuationem officij Christi, qui non exiguo temporis spatio, sed deinceps semper ad finem usque seculi, fidelibus per baptismum collaturus sit Spiritum: partim denique ad visibilem illam effusionem Spiritus Sancti,


### Chapter Two on the Number of Baptism: 2. Of the Pontificians. Whether Baptism ought to be repeated?

which was to happen from Christ to the Apostles, on the day of Pentecost.

But it remains that we should disclose what is to be thought concerning the passage Acts 19:4 & 5. That passage, however, rendered from the Greek text, reads thus: When Paul had found certain disciples at Ephesus, he said to them: Have you received the Holy Spirit after you believed? But they said to him: We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit. Then he said to them: Into what then were you baptized? But they said: Into John's baptism. But Paul said: John indeed (μὲν) baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Christ Jesus: But those who (δὲ) heard him were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Some attach this meaning to these words, as if Paul rebaptized those Ephesians, who had previously been dipped with the baptism of John. But since the whole continuity of the text fights against this diametrically, and the error arises from a faulty division of the members or periods, as well as from the more obscure Vulgate version. For they think that these words (But those who heard him were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus) belong to the Evangelist Luke, and that their meaning is that Paul rebaptized those twelve Ephesians because they had previously been baptized only with the baptism of John. But as I said, the coherence of the text protests and proves that these words are not to be torn away from the words of Paul immediately preceding: which is shown by the adversative particles, δὲ and μὲν, which are read in all Greek codices with the highest consensus. Therefore, this is the true and genuine sense of the words of the Apostle Paul, which Luke recites as a historian: Those who approached the baptism of John, they indeed were baptized with the baptism of repentance, and taught by John to believe in him who was to come, that is, in Christ Jesus: But those who heard him (thus indeed preaching about Christ), they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And this speech of Paul was directed not so much to those twelve Ephesians as to the whole standing crowd: so that it might be clear to them what the parts of the Baptist's ministry were: namely, that he preached repentance, that he urged faith in the Christ who was to come, and finally that he thus baptized those who heard and professed faith in the name of Christ. Thus, therefore, what John did, not what Paul did, is expressed in these two verses. Now, however, the subsequent text finally shows what happened to those twelve Ephesians: namely, that while they were ignorant of whether the Holy Spirit had been visibly poured out, Paul laid hands on them: and by this act, the Holy Spirit was also miraculously conferred upon them. And this is the plain and clear explanation of Luke's words, which all the sounder theologians approve: and among these especially also Chemnitius, part 2 of the Examination of the Council of Trent, pages 38, 39.

Thus, therefore, we have so far demonstrated in the thesis that there is one baptism in number and in kind, which can neither be nor ought to be torn into several differing either in time or in effect.

But the Sacramentarians sharply contradict our purer doctrine, who invent a twofold Baptism: one external, the other internal: the former conferred in infancy, the latter in more adult age, often finally in old age: the former washes away the filth of the body only, the latter indeed of the soul: the former consists of water alone, the latter indeed of the virtue and efficacy of the Holy Spirit, which, however, is conferred not through the sprinkling of water, but without this singular action of CHRIST, even outside the baptism of water; the former comes to all baptized infants equally, the latter indeed only to those who are in the catalog of those absolutely predestined to eternal life: the former is a naked sign of this interior Baptism, to be conferred many years later without water. But we shall have to discuss this error expressly in the following fourth chapter.

The Romanists also err enormously concerning this part of Christian doctrine, while they have fashioned a new species of Baptism, and have established it in holy or lustral water: concerning which they teach first in general that its sprinkling is like a saving bath: but in particular they assign to it a twofold spiritual effect. The former is that it repels the snares of the Devil, and in this part obtains a common power with all consecrated things, such as salt, wine, bread, wax, herbs, etc. The latter is that it remits venial sins, as Thomas has it, part 3, q. 87, art. 3, and Clement in the Apostolic Constitutions, book 8, chapter 35, and that not only from the work of the worker, that is, because of the merit and devotion of the user (although this also ought to be present), but also from the work performed. To this figment can be added the cowl-baptism, which we can name thus. For the Pontificians babble that the assumption of the monastic habit has the same grace that Baptism has. To have enumerated these impieties is the same as to have refuted them. For us, resting in the unity of GOD, of faith, and of Baptism, there is safe and firm security.

Moreover, another question emerges at this point, one that is highly relevant to both theological practice and theory, and most necessary to explain. For since it has been demonstrated thus far that Baptism is one in number and in species, it is not without reason asked, Is Baptism also one in terms of its use, such that once conferred it ought not to be reiterated? Here, indeed, there have not been lacking in times past those who consented not obscurely to the reiteration of Baptism. The Marcionites certainly, as Epiphanius testifies in heresy 42, contended that Baptism must be received three times: first in childhood, on account of original sin; then in more mature age, twice, in imitation of Christ, who, when he had been baptized first by John, then also willed to be baptized by the baptism of blood on the cross. The falsity of this opinion collapses by its own futility. Thus there were in times past those whom they called ἡμεροβαπτιστὰς, who contended that Baptism should be repeated daily, since we sin daily.

But Cyprian also ought to be referred to here, who at one time held this error and endeavored to defend it, namely, that those baptized by heretics should be rebaptized. Which same error the Anabaptists cherish even today. For although they never rebaptize those baptized by their own people, nor do they concede that true baptism can be repeated, yet this consensus is deceptive, because it rests upon a most false hypothesis. For they deny that baptism conferred by ministers of a different religion is true: and thus they rebaptize them, not as if they had been baptized once before, but as if they had never been baptized at all. In reality, therefore, they commit Anabaptism: and while they depart from our Churches and allow themselves to be rebaptized by men of their own flour, they design a horrendous profanation of the Sacrament: and while they presume to do this, in reality, however, they do not confer Baptism. For even if the things pertaining to the form of this Sacrament are applied, there is nevertheless lacking a capable and legitimate Subject: which is none other than a man not already baptized before.

All the Orthodox hold the negative with us, and establish that baptism once legitimately conferred must never be reiterated, even if it was conferred by a heretic, or any other minister, whether impious in his life or impure in his doctrine, or even if it was received by a hypocrite: so that not undeservedly, by Civil Law, the penalty of death has been established, as much for those who rebaptize as for those who are rebaptized: l. 2. C. let not holy Baptism be repeated. The principal reasons for this negative of ours are these.

I. Concerning the reiteration of Baptism, we have no command at all in the sacred writings, as we do concerning the reiteration of the Sacrament of the Eucharist. Therefore.

II. Baptism succeeded into the place of Circumcision. Therefore, it ought no more to be repeated than it was lawful to repeat Circumcision in the past.

III. No example at all of a reiterated Baptism, once legitimately conferred, occurs either in Holy Scripture or in the entire Ecclesiastical history. Therefore.

IV. If the reiteration of Baptism were to be conceded, then no other end could be given for it than that the covenant, which is entered into with GOD in the act of Baptism, as if evacuated and destroyed by our sins, might be restored anew. But in truth, such an evacuation of the divine covenant, as far as GOD is concerned, never happens. Therefore. The minor premise is sufficiently evident from this: Because the covenant that intercedes with GOD, even if it has been violated on the human side, is not, however, abolished in such a way that there is need for a new covenant to be sanctioned: for thus the perfidy of men could abolish the faithfulness of GOD, which the Apostle expressly denies: Rom. 3, 3. and chap. 11, 29. 2 Cor. 1, 20. 2 Tim. 2, 13. But there is need only for a return, so that man may return to GOD through true repentance. For as soon as he returns, and is seriously grieved for the sins he has committed, and raises and consoles himself by faith in Christ, the doors of divine grace immediately open of their own accord, and the original right of the federal action remains inviolate for him. The same thing must be established entirely concerning the baptism of Hypocrites: as will be shown more accurately in chapter 4.

V. The reason is that of Augustine, in tractate 11 on John: Just as carnal generation is,

so also must spiritual regeneration be, as regards the act of conferral. But that carnal generation happens only once. Therefore.

VI. It is of the same Augustine: We are baptized into the death of Christ: Therefore, just as Christ died once, so baptism is not to be repeated: For by His one death He redeemed all in such a way that death no longer has dominion over Him, Rom. 6. book on true and false repentance, chap. 3.

The story which Socrates recounts concerning a certain Jewish impostor, book 7 of Ecclesiastical history, chapter 7, can also be referred to here. For this man, by feigning Christianity, received Baptism quite often in different places, especially among heretics, so that he might collect money. But when he asked to be baptized by the Orthodox as well, and was led to the place destined for this action, and the font of the baptistery was filled with water twice, the water immediately vanished while everyone was watching. Upon this happening, the deceit of the Jew was detected, which he himself also openly confessed.

And we wish this decision of ours to be understood concerning all, even those legitimately baptized by heretics according to the institution of Christ. We except, however, those who have been baptized by heretics who do not believe in the Trinity, nor baptize in the name of the Trinity: provided, however, that it is certain to that Church concerning this error of the baptizer: and indeed not without some approval of this heresy. For these, because they have not received true baptism conferred in the name of the Most Holy Trinity, are certainly to be baptized: Which baptism cannot or ought not to be called a reiteration of baptism: since such persons have received no prior baptism: But that former action ought to be held rather as a vain game, or more truly as a horrendous profanation of this Sacrament, than as baptism. The nineteenth Canon of the Council of Nicaea pertains here, written against the Photinians, Arians, and Antitrinitarians, in which it is defined that if those baptized by such heretics who deny the ὁμοούσιον of the three persons of the Divinity take refuge in the Catholic Church, they are to be baptized entirely in the name of the Trinity. Which canon was later repeated in the Second Council of Arles, chapter 16, in these words: It is necessary that Photinians or Paulianists be baptized, according to the statutes of the Fathers.

Latin:

quæ à Christo eventura esset Apostolis, in die Pentecostes.

Sed superest, ut quid de loco Actor. 19, 4. & 5. sentiendum sit, aperiamus. Ille verò ex Græco textu redditus sic habet: Cum Paulus discipulos, quosdam invenisset, Ephesi, dixit ad eos: Nùm Spiritum Sanctum accepistis, posteaquàm credidistis? illi verò dixerunt ei: Imò sitnè Spiritus Sanctus, ne audivimus quidem. Tunc dixit eis: In quid ergò baptizati estis; Ipsi verò dixerunt: In Johannis baptisma. Dixit autem Paulus: Johannes quidem (μὲν) baptizavit baptismo pœnitentiæ, dicens populo, ut in eum, qui venturus post ipsum, crederent, hoc est, in Christum Jesum: Qui verò (δὲ) illum audierunt, baptizati sunt in nomen Domini Jesu. Verbis hisce hunc sensum affingunt nonnulli, quasi Paulus Ephesios illos, priùs baptismo Johannis tinctos, rebaptizarit. Verum cum tota textus συνεχεία id è diametro pugnat, & error oritur ex vitiosâ divisione membrorũ sive periodorum, ut & ex obscuriore versione vulgatâ. Existimant enim illi, verba isthæc, (Audientes verò baptizati sunt in nomen Domini Jesu) esse Evangelistæ Lucæ, & hunc eorum sensum esse, quòd Paulus duodecim illos Ephesios rebaptizarit, quia prius tantùm baptizati fuissent baptismo Johannis. Verùm uti dixi, textus cohærentia reclamat & evincit, verba hæc non esse divellenda à verbis Pauli immediatè præcedentibus: id quod ostendunt particulæ adversativæ, δὲ, & μὲν, quæ in omnibus Græcis codicibus summo consensu leguntur. Iste proindè verus ac genuinus est sensus verborum Apostoli Pauli, quæ recitat Lucas tanquàm historicus: Qui accesserunt ad baptismum Johannis, illi quidem baptismo pœnitentiæ baptizati sunt, & edocti à Johanne, ut in eum crederent, qui venturus esset, hoc est, in Christum Jesum: Qui verò illum (sic nimirùm de Christo concionantem) audiverunt, illi baptizati sunt in nomine Domini Jesu. Et hæc oratio Pauli, non tàm ad duodecim illos Ephesios, quàm ad universum astantem populum erat directa: ut ipsi constaret, quæ fuerint partes ministerij Baptistæ: nempè quòd prædicaverit pœnitentiã quòd urserit fidẽ in Christum venturum, quòd deniq; sic audientes & fidem profitentes baptizarit in nomine Christi. Sic ergò quid Johannes, non quid Paulus fecerit, duobus istis versibus exprimitur. Jam verò subsequens demùm textus ostendit, quid duodecim istis Ephesijs obtigerit: nempè, quòd ipsis ignorantibus, an Spiritus Sanctus visibiliter esset effusus, Paulus manus imposuerit: & hoc facto, Spiritus Sanctus ipsis quoq; miraculosè collatus sit. Et hæc est plana ac perspicua verborum Lucæ explicatio, quam saniores quiq; Theologi approbant: & inter hos cumprimis etiam Chemnitius, part. 2. Examinis Concil. Trid. pag. 38. 39.

Sic ergò hactenùs demonstravimus in thesi, Unum numero ac specie esse baptismum, qui in plures vel tempore, vel effectu differentes divelli neq; possit, neq; debeat.

Puriori autem doctrinæ nostræ acriter contradicunt Sacramentarij, qui geminum comminiscuntur Baptismum: Externum unum: Internum alterum: quorum ille in infantia: hic in adultiore ætate sæpiùs in senectute demùm conferatur: ille abluat sordes corporis tantùm: hîc verò animi: ille solâ constet aquâ: hic verò virtute & efficaciâ Spiritus Sancti, quæ tamen non per aspersionem aquæ, verùm sine hâc singulari actione CHRISTI, etiam extra baptismum aquæ conferatur, ille omnibus baptizatis infantibus ex æquo obveniat: hic verò tantùm ijs, qui sunt in catalogo absolutè ad vitam æternam prædestinatorum: ille nudum sit signum hujus interioris Baptismi: multis annis demùm pòst conferendi sine aquâ. Verùm de hoc errore ex professo dispiciendum nobis fuerit, capite subsequente quarto.

Romanenses quoq; circa hanc partem doctrinæ Christianæ enormiter errant, dùm novam Baptismi speciem confinxerunt, eamque constituerunt in aqua benedicta sive lustrali: de quâ primùm in genere docent, quòd ejus aspersio, sit instar salutaris lavacri: in specie autem duplicem ei effectum spiritualem assignant. Prior est, quòd repellat insidias Diaboli, & hac in parte communem vim obtineat cum omnibus rebus consecratis, ut sale, vino, pane, cerâ, herbis &c. Posterior est, quòd remittat peccata venialia, ut habet Thomas part 3. q 87. art. 3. & Clemens Apostol. constitut. l 8 c. 35. idq; non tantùm ex opere operantis, hoc est, ob meritum & devotionem utentis (quanquàm hæc etiam adesse debeat) sed etiam ex opere operato. Figmento huic addi potest Baptismus cucullaris, quem sic nominare possumus. Nam assumtionem habitus Monastici eandem gratiam Pontificij habere nugantur, quàm habeat Baptismus. Quas impietates enumerasse perindè est, atq; refutasse. Nobis in unitate DEI, fidei, & Baptismi acquiescendi, tuta firmaq; est securitas.

Cæterùm alia hoc loco emergit quæstio, tàm praxi, quàm theoriæ theologicæ plurimùm inserviens, & explicatu maximè necessaria. Cùm enim hactenùs demonstratum, unum numero ac specie esse Baptismum, haud immeritò quæritur, An Baptismus etiam ratione usûs ita sit unus, ut reiterari semel collatus non debeat? Ubi sanè non defuerunt jam olim, qui in Baptismi reiterationem haud obscurè consenserunt. Marcionitæ certè, teste Epiphanio hæresi 42. contenderunt, ter suscipiendum esse Baptismum, primùm in ætate puerili, propter peccatum Originis: deindè in adultiore ætate, bis tidq; ad imitationem quandam Christi, qui cum esset primùm baptisatus à Johanne; deindè etiam baptismo Sangvinis in cruce baptisari voluit. Cujus sententiæ falsitas propriâ futilitate corruit. Sic fuerunt olim quos ἡμεροβαπτιστὰς vocabant, qui contendebant Baptismum quotidiè iterandum, cùm quotidiè peccemus.

Sed referri huc etiam debet Cyprianus, qui aliquando hunc errorem tenuit, ac defendere studuit, nempè ab hæreticis baptizatos, rebaptizandos esse. Quem eundem errorem etiamnum hodie fovent Anabaptistae. Etiamsi enim a suis baptisatos nunquam rebaptisant: neque verum baptisma iterari posse concedunt, tamen fucatus iste est consensus, quia falsissimae hypothesi innititur. Nam baptismum a diversae religionis ministris collatum, verum esse negant: & sic eos rebaptisant, non tanquam prius semel baptisatos: sed quasi nunquam omnino baptisatos. Revera ergo Anabaptismum committunt: & dum ex nostris Ecclesiis egressi, a suae farinae hominibus se rebaptisari sinunt; horrendam Sacramenti prophanationem designant: & dum facere hoc praesumunt, revera tamen Baptismum non conferunt. Nam si maxime adhibeantur res, ad formam hujus Sacramenti pertinentes: deest tamen Subjectum capax ac legitimum: quod non est aliud, nisi homo jam antea non baptisatus.

Orthodoxi omnes nobiscum negativam tenent, & baptismum semel legitime collatum nunquam reiterandum esse statuunt, licet ille vel ab haeretico, aut ministro quovis alio, sive ratione vitae impio, sive ratione doctrinae impuro, ille collatus: vel ab hypocrita etiam suscepto sit: ut haud immerito de Jure civili poena capitis constituta sit, tam in eos, qui rebaptizant, quam qui rebaptizantur: l. 2. C. non sanctum Baptisma iteretur. Rationes autem negativae hujus nostrae, hae sunt praecipuae.

I. De reiterando Baptismo nullum prorsus mandatum, sicut de reiterando Eucharistiae Sacramento, in sacris habemus. Ergo.

II. Baptismus successit in locum Circumcisionis. Ergo haud magis ille repeti debet, atque olim Circumcisionem repetere fas fuit.

III. Nullum prorsus vel in Scriptura Sacra, vel in universa historia Ecclesiastica, reiterati Baptismi, semel legitime collati, exemplum occurrit. E.

IV. Si reiteratio Baptismi concedenda esset, tum ejus finis nullus dari posset alius, quam ut foedus, quod cum DEO in actione Baptistica initur, tanquam per peccata nostra evacuatum & destructum, denuo restauraretur. Atqui vero talis evacuatio foederis divini, quoad DEUM nulla unquam fit. Ergo. Minor inde satis constat: Quia foedus, quod cum DEO intercedit, si maxime ex parte humana violatum sit, non ita tamen aboletur, ut novo sanciendo foedere opus sit: Sic enim perfidia hominum, fidem DEI abolere posset, quod diserte negat Apostolus: Rom. 3, 3. & cap. 11, 29. 2. Cor. 1, 20. 2. Tim. 2, 13. Sed reditu tantum opus est, ita ut homo per veram poenitentiam redeat ad DEUM. Quamprimum enim redit, & de admissis peccatis serio dolet, seque fide in Christum erigit & consolatur, protinus gratiae divinae fores ultro patent, & pristinum foederalis actionis jus ipsi constat inviolatum. Quod ipsum de Hypocritarum etiam baptismo omnino statuendum: uti cap. 4. accuratius ostendetur.

V. Ratio est Augustini, tractatu 11. in Johannem: Quemadmodum se habet carnalis generatio,

sic se habere etiam debet, quoad collationis actum, Spiritualis regeneratio. Atqui carnalis illa semel tantum fit. Ergo.

VI. Ejusdem est Augustini: Baptizamur in mortem Christi: Sicut ergo semel Christus mortuus fuit: sic baptismus iterandus non est: Una enim morte sua sic omnes redemit, ut amplius ipsi mors non dominetur, Rom. 6. lib. de vera & falsa pœnitentia. cap. 3.

Potest huc referri etiam historia, quam recitat Socrates de Judæo quodam impostore, lib. 7. hist. Eccl. cap. 7. Hic enim Christianismum simulando, sæpius in diversis locis Baptismum suscepit, apud hæreticos cumprimis, ut sic pecunias colligeret. Sed cum ab Orthodoxis etiam baptizari peteret: & ad locum actioni huic destinatum adduceretur, & fons baptisterij bis aquâ impleretur: semper aspectantibus omnibus, aqua protinus evanuit. Quo facto Judæi dolus deprehensus fuit, quem ipse quoque palàm confitebatur.

Et hanc quidem decisionem nostram de omnibus, etiam ab hæreticis legitimè secundum institutionem Christi baptizatis, intellectam volumus. Excipimus autem eos, qui ab hæreticis, Trinitatem non credentibus, nec in nomine Trinitatis baptizantibus, baptizati sunt: si tamen Ecclesiæ illi de hoc errore baptizantis constet: & quidem non sine aliquâ hæresews hujus approbatione. Hi enim, quia verum baptismum in nomine Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis collatum non susceperunt, utique baptizandi sunt: Qui baptismus non reiteratio baptismi dici potest aut debet: siquidem nullum prius baptismum tales perceperunt: Sed actio illa prior pro inani ludo potiùs, imò verius pro horrendâ Sacramenti hujus prophanatione, quàm pro baptismo haberi debet. Pertinet huc Canon decimus nonus Concilij Niceni, contra Photinianos, Arianos & Antitrinitarios conscriptus, in quo definitum est, si ab ejusmodi hæreticis ὁμοούσιον trium personarum Divinitatis negantibus baptisati, ad Catholicam Ecclesiam confugiant, ut omninò baptizentur in nomine Trinitatis. Qui canon postea repetitus est in Concilio Arelatensi Secundo cap. 16. his verbis: Photinianos sive Paulianistas, secundum Patrum statuta, baptizari oportet.


### Chapter Three, On the Object of Baptism: and in particular concerning Paedobaptism against the Anabaptists

On the Object of Baptism: and specifically on Infant Baptism against the Anabaptists.

ON the Object of Baptism, when it is disputed, that especially comes under question: To what things, according to the institution of CHRIST the Savior, ought this Sacrament to be conferred? What ought to be answered to this inquiry will then finally be more exactly established, when by ἀφαίρεσιν to Having progressed to the thesis, we shall remove those things which are incapable of being recipients of this Sacrament.

And at the beginning, indeed, we simply exclude all irrational creatures, by whatever name they may come, and whether destined for sacred or profane use, from this Sacrament: because this, by the institution of Christ, is the proper Sacrament of humans alone, not of other creatures. Hence, it is easy to gather what ought to be judged concerning the baptism of bells, which is customary among the Papists. That began, according to Bale, under the Roman Pontiff John XIV, not without a horrendous profanation of the divine name and of this Sacrament. For they teach 1. that this baptism can be conferred upon bells by suffragans alone.

2. That bells thus baptized have the power of driving away demons and storms. 3. They employ godparents, holding the rope of the bell to be baptized, and answering for it, and repeating its name. 4. The suffragan receives and keeps for himself the money given by the godparents, as if in place of the baptized bell. 5. Finally, sumptuous and rich banquets are instituted. But these βδελύγματα (abominations) of Papal abomination are too foul to need a more lengthy refutation.

Then, from the reception of this Sacrament, there are also excluded from the number of rational creatures those who have not yet been fully and perfectly brought forth into this world. Infants, therefore, who are still entirely in the maternal womb cannot be baptized with the mother, as the words of Augustine and Isidore hold, which are cited in De Consecratione, dist. 4, can. In maternis. The same judgment must be passed concerning those infants who, while having indeed put forth their head, are still in the maternal womb regarding the rest of the body. For in order for someone to be a suitable candidate to be baptized, it is necessary that he be born. For he cannot be reborn unless he is first born. Scholastic Doctors also support this decision, such as the Master of the Sentences, book 4, dist. 8. And the opinion of Isidore is evident, which holds as follows: Those who are in the maternal wombs cannot be baptized for this reason, because he who has not yet been born according to Adam cannot be reborn according to CHRIST: nor can regeneration be spoken of for him whom generation has not preceded. In the same manner, our blessed Luther also responded in the year 42, saying: If it happens with a woman in labor that she cannot bring forth the infant entirely, but shows only a hand or another limb, then that appearing limb ought not to be baptized by the women present in this necessity. Much less should an infant still placed entirely in the mother's womb, or one who cannot be born, be baptized by pouring water over the mother's belly. For that this is wrong and contrary to divine Scripture is manifest from the words of Christ, John 3: Unless one is born again, etc. For which reason, in order for an infant to be rightly baptized and thus born again, it is necessary that he first be born once into the world, which does not happen if only one limb emerges from the mother's womb.

Furthermore, a question is raised in this place, iii concerning Monsters born into the light, whether they ought to be baptized? I answer by a distinction: if that monster does not have the figure of a perfect and rational human, it is by no means to be baptized, for the reasons which we have just now assigned. But if the monstrosity appears only from the less noble parts of the body, and does not take away the figure of a perfect and rational human, then we determine that such a human is to be baptized entirely.

But a more difficult question arises here: If a monster were born that presented the appearance of a doubled human, whether it should be baptized only once, or twice, and whether it should be held as one or two humans? Although the decision of this question is left by some theologians, not undeservedly, partly to be ventilated by the speculation of idle men, and partly to be estimated by the judgment of the thing born and present: yet this knot also seems to be able to be untied by a distinction. For if it cannot be exactly detected whether they are two humans corporally glued together, yet having certain things in common regarding the body, or whether it is one human having one intellectual soul, then it would be most advisable that it be baptized once, with water sprinkled on the more principal parts, and with the words of baptism directed to one individual in the singular number: I baptize thee, etc. But if it can be exactly established that the subject about which the question is asked has two souls in distinct and, as it were, separate bodies, yet in such a way that they cohere around the lower parts of the body, then baptism can be conferred separately for two persons or individuals, not by one, but by two distinct and successively following acts, notwithstanding the fact that the fusion of the feet represents only one individual.

Thirdly, others are deservedly kept from the reception of Baptism, who are mentally disturbed and insane. Where, however, this assertion of ours must be accepted with a distinction, and as it were with a grain of salt. For some are demented, foolish, and insane from the very beginning of their birth, so that this madness of theirs could not be detected when they were brought into the light. These, therefore, just like other infants who are destitute of the use of reason, are rightly baptized. But if neither in the progress of time, in their more adult age, nor indeed throughout their whole life does any act of reason manifest itself in them, then we determine that the same judgment is to be made concerning the baptism of such persons as is made concerning the baptism of infants, and that there is no reason to doubt concerning their salvation: especially since the use of reason contributes nothing at all to the conferring of regeneration, although in adults it is entirely required regarding the act of making a confession. Which profession of faith, however, does not seem so necessary in those adults who can be equated with boys and infants. Others, however, are not such from childhood, but sometimes possess the use of reason, and indeed at certain intervals. If the question is asked concerning the baptism of such persons, it would be safest that the judgment be made according to

Latin:

De Objecto Baptismi: & in specie de Pædobaptismo contra Anabaptistas.

DE Objecto Baptismi quando controvertitur, illud potissimùm sub quæstionem venit: Quibus rebus ex institutione CHRISTI Servatoris, Sacramentum hoc conferri debeat? Ad quod quæsitum quid responderi debeat, tùm demùm exactius constabit, quando per ἀφαίρεσιν ad θέσιν progressi removebimus ea, quæ Sacramenti hujus capaces esse nequeunt.

Ac initiò quidem omnes creaturas irrationales, quocunque veniant nomine, & tam usui sacro, quàm prophano destinatas, ab hoc Sacramento simpliciter excludimus: propterea quòd hoc, ex institutione Christi, solorum hominum, non aliarum creaturarum est proprium Sacramentum. Hinc quid de Campanarum baptismo, Pontificiis usitato, judicari debeat, promptum est colligere. Cœpit ille teste Balæo, sub Pontifice Romano XIV. non sine horrendâ nominis divini & Sacramenti hujus prophanatione. Docent enim 1. hunc baptismum Campanis conferri posse, à solis suffraganeis.

2. Campanas sic baptizatas habere vim propulsandi dæmones, & tempestates. 3. adhibent patrinos, fune tenentes Campanam baptizandam, & pro eâ spondentes, ejusdemq; nomen ingeminantes. 4. Pecuniam à patrinis testeræ quasi loco campanæ baptizatæ donatam, accipit, sibique servat suffraganeus. 5. Tandem sumtuosa & opipara instituuntur convivia. Sed tetriora sunt hæc abominationis Pontificiæ βδελύγματα, quàm ut refutatione prolixiore opus sit.

Deinde excluduntur à perceptione hujus Sacramenti, ex numero etiam creaturarum rationalium ij, qui plenè & perfectè in hunc mundum non sunt prognati. Infantes ergò qui ex toto adhuc sunt in utero materno, cum matre baptisari nequeunt, ut habent verba Augustini Isidori, quæ citantur, de Consecr. dist. 4. can. In maternis. Idem judicium ferendum est, de ijs infantibus, qui exerto quidem capite, sed quoad reliquam corporis partem adhuc sunt in utero materno. Nam ut idoneus sit aliquis, qui baptisetur, necesse est ut sit natus. Renafci enim non potest, nisi prius nascatur. Decisioni huic suffragantur etiam Scholastici Doctores, ut Magister sentent. lib. 4. dist. 8. Et evidens est sententia Isidori, quæ sic habet: Qui in maternis uteris sunt, ideò baptizari non possunt, quia qui natus adhuc secundum Adam non est, secundum CHRISTUM non potest renasci: neque regeneratio in eum dici potest, quem generatio non præcessit. Quem ipsum in modum respondit etiam B. Lutherus noster, anno 42. Si accidit, inquiens, de fæmina parturiente, ut infantem non possit totum parere: sed tantùm vel manum, vel aliud membrum ostendat, tunc membrum illud apparens non debet baptizari à mulierculis in hâc necessitate præsentibus. Multò minùs infans adhuc totus in utero matris posit9, aut qui nasci non potest, baptizari debet, infundendo aquam super ventrem matris. Hoc enim iniquum esse, & Scripturæ divinæ dissentaneum, manifestum est ex verbis Christi, Johan. 3: Nisi quis natus fuerit denuò &c. Quam ob rem ut infans rectè baptizari, & ita denuò nasci possit, necesse est ut semel prius sit natus in mundum, quod non fit, si unum tantùm membrum matris uterum egreditur.

Cæterùm movetur hoc loco quæstio, iii de Monstris, in lucem prognatis, an ea baptizari debeant? Respondeo per distinctionem, si monstrum illud figuram perfecti & rationalis hominis non habeat, illud nequaquàm esse baptizandum: ijs de causis, quas jam modò assignavimus. Si verò monstrositas ex ignobilioribus saltem partibus corporis appareat, neque figuram perfecti & rationalis hominis tollat: tùm talem hominem omninò baptizandum esse statuimus.

Sed difficilior hîc oritur quæstio: Si nasceretur monstrum, quod geminati hominis speciem referret, an semel tantùm, an verò bis sit baptizandum, & num pro uno, an verò duobus hominibus habendum? Cujus quæstionis decisio licèt partim otiosorum hominum speculationi ventilanda, partim verò rei natæ & præsentis judicio æstimanda, haud immeritò à nonnullis Theologis relinquatur: tamen & iste nodus per distinctionem tolli posse videtur. Si enim non exactè deprehendi potest, an sint duo homines corporaliter sibi conglutinati, habentes tamen quædam quoad corpus communia: vel an sit unus homo, unam habens animam intellectualem: tùm consultissimum fuerit, ut semel baptizetur, aquâ principalioribus partibus aspersâ: & verbis baptismi ad unum individuum, in singulari numero directis: Ego te baptizo &c. Sin autem exactè constare queat, subjectum de quo quæritur, duas habere animas, in distinctis, & quasi separatis corporibus: ita tamen ut circa inferiores partes corporis cohæreant: tùm pro duabus personis sive individuis, seorsim baptismus conferri potest, non uno, sed duobus distinctis, & se invicem subsequentibus actibus: non obstante eo, quod pedum concretio, unum duntaxat individuum repræsentat.

Tertiò à Baptismi perceptione arcentur mertiò & alij, qui sunt mente moti, & furiosi. Ubi tamen assertio hæc nostra per distinctionem, & quasi cum grano salis est accipienda. Quidam enim sunt amentes, stulti, & furiosi ab ipso nativitatis exordio, ita ut hæc ipsorum amentia tùm, cùm in lucem ederentur, deprehendi non potuerit. Hi ergò æquè ac alij infantes, qui rationis usu destituuntur, rectè baptizantur. Quod si nec progressu temporis, in ipsâ adultiore ætate, imò per omnem vitam nullus prorsus rationis actus in ipsis se exerat, tùm de talium baptismo idem fermè, quod de infantium baptismo judicandum, nec de ipsorum salute dubitandum esse statuimus: præsertim cùm rationis usus nihil prorsus ad regenerationem conferendam faciat, licèt in adultis quoad confessionis edendæ actum omninò requiratur. Quæ tamen fidei professio in istis adultis, qui pueris ac infantibus æquiparari possunt, haud ita necessaria videtur. Alij verò à pueritiâ tales non sunt, sed aliquando rationis usu, & quidem per certa intervalla potiuntur. De talium baptismo si quæratur, tutissimum fuerit, ut judicium fiat secundum


### Chapter Three, On the Object of Baptism: Who ought to be baptized

their own will, which they have had, or have, while they exercise the use of a sounder mind. If, therefore, in this state they seek baptism and make a profession of faith, then certainly baptism should by no means be denied to them. But it must be decided otherwise if such persons, not even being of sound mind, have any will to receive baptism: since will.

It is evident from this what should be thought concerning the baptism of those who are asleep, namely, as regards infants, it matters not at all whether they are asleep or awake when they are baptized: but as regards adults, in them both the will to receive baptism and the profession of faith are entirely required: neither of which can apply to those who are asleep.

It is also evident from this what can and should be judged concerning the deaf and the mute: namely, that they are to be baptized for the same reasons for which infants are baptized: provided only that they show by act and gesture that they seek baptism and approve the doctrine of the Church.

Fourthly, baptism should not be conferred on anyone against their will. For he who is baptized against his will sins most gravely: but one who sins in this way is not to be baptized. Therefore. Hence, in dist. 45, can. Qui sincera, and Can. de Judæis, express prohibitions are contained, by which it is most severely forbidden that any Jew be baptized against his will. But it is asked, if parents do not want their children to be baptized, what then is to be done. It can be answered most correctly by a twofold distinction: one regarding the children of such parents, who are either still infants or are adults: the other regarding the parents themselves, who are either in our power or enjoy free jurisdiction themselves. Hence, therefore, the truest decision of the question is sought: for if those children are adults and they themselves seek baptism, they certainly can and should be baptized even against the will of their parents. The reason is that in divine matters they are not subject to the authority of their parents: but if they are still infants and do not yet have the use of reason, then they are not to be baptized against the will of parents who are under free jurisdiction: first, because this conflicts with the law of nature: for such children do not yet have the use of free will, and therefore, according to natural law, they are under the care of their parents as long as they cannot provide for themselves. Then, indeed, for this reason especially, because there is a certain danger that such infants might afterwards be perverted and corrupted by their parents. But if the parents are subject to civil servitude and have been made slaves by the right of war, then their children or offspring can be baptized even against their will.

The decision of that question also depends on this: Should the children of infidels, such as Turks, Jews, and other peoples living outside the Church, be baptized? To the question as asked, we indeed answer in the affirmative: but under a twofold caution, or in two cases. 1. When the children have been taken away to foreign parts while the parents are absent. 2. When such infants are in certain danger and in a case of extreme necessity: because then there is no longer any danger of subsequent perversion to be feared, as that is removed by the death of the baptized.

But for the explanation and confirmation of this decision of ours, certain hypotheses must be observed.

1. By the will and institution of Christ the Savior, all who are born of the flesh and have need of regeneration are to be baptized and regenerated by water and the Spirit. John 3:5. But not only those who are born within the boundaries of the Church and, as it were, at home are born of the flesh: but also those who are born outside the Church, begotten by infidel parents. Therefore, the Sacrament of Baptism should not be absolutely and simply denied to them either.

2. The object of baptism extends as widely as the object of circumcision once did: indeed, according to the nature of the New Testament, the object of baptism extends much more widely: since the Church of the New Testament extends not to one certain people, much less to one certain land, but to all nations. Matthew 28:19. But by divine institution and command, not only the home-born, who was born at home, that is, in the Church, was to be circumcised in the families of the Patriarchs: but also the purchased one, indeed, as the words of the institution clearly sound, everyone, whoever was not even of that lineage of the faithful: Genesis 17:12. Therefore, the object of baptism will spread itself much more to all men whatsoever, both those who are born outside and those who are born inside the Church: although in a different manner and process, as will be demonstrated shortly. The history of Abraham provides the practice of the minor proposition, who, obeying the divine command in Genesis 17:23, circumcised not only all the home-born of his house, and each and every one whom he had bought, all the males of his house, of whom he is read to have had three hundred and eighteen: Genesis 14:14. Now, hardly any sane person would deny that in such a multitude of servants, there were very many infants, whom Abraham also circumcised by virtue of the command received from God. It would therefore be absurd to deny the same right today to the Church of GOD concerning the infants of the Gentiles to be baptized, if they are in our power.

3. If the promise pertains even to those who are far off, then the sealing of the promise will certainly pertain to the same: namely, the participation in the Sacraments. But the former is true: therefore the latter is also. I prove the minor with the words of the Apostle Peter, thus addressing the faithful, converted both from Gentilism and from Judaism, Acts 2:39: The promise is made to you, and to your children, and to all who are far off, whomsoever the Lord your GOD shall call. But for a better understanding of this proof, two things especially deserve explanation. 1. Who those are whom the Apostle calls μακρὰν ὄντες, those existing far off. 2. What the Apostle affirms concerning them. As regards the first, the very context of the text clearly shows that those born at home, or Jews, are not meant by μακρὰν ὄντες, for it speaks clearly of two distinct peoples:

Noting the Jews with the pronoun (TO YOU and your children), but naming the Gentiles and all infidels, still constituted outside the Church, as those who are far off. Scripture itself explains the cause of this denomination sufficiently. Eph. 2:12, 13. Naming the Gentiles atheists and strangers to the covenants, guests of the covenants, impious in this world, strangers to Christ, strangers to the commonwealth of Israel, not having the hope of the promise (formerly in the Old Testament first). What? That it expressly names those Gentiles walking in the vanity of their mind: Eph. 4:17. Nay, more, does it not clearly accommodate the words of Peter, which are treated here, to the Ephesians, still constituted in Gentilism? You, saying, who were sometimes afar off, those who were once afar off, now in Christ Jesus you have been made near by his blood. Eph. 2:13. Now, indeed, regarding the latter member of the Petrine saying, which the Apostle pronounced concerning the Ephesians once constituted in Gentilism: the same, according to Peter, ought to be accommodated to all Gentiles and infidels whatsoever, because the promise pertains to them also, and consequently the sealing of the promise as well.

Nor does that Apostolic passage in 1 Cor. 5:12 & 13 stand in the way: What does it matter to judge those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? But God judges those who are outside. For the Apostle is not dealing with ecclesiastical law, or the promises of the New Testament and their breadth, or even a whit of that; but he is entirely concerned with showing the correct form and quality of ecclesiastical discipline. The Apostle had exhorted that the Corinthians should not be mixed with fornicators. The Corinthians were taking this admonition so universally and simply that they thought the company of any wicked persons whatsoever was to be avoided by them according to Paul's prescription: which was impossible to do, since the Corinthians lived in a city the greater part of which was still devoted to Gentilism and was entirely teeming with promiscuous lusts and other vices. Therefore, the Apostle corrects this inconvenient sense and shows that he understood his admonition concerning associates and brothers of the same religion, so that if such a person is given over to such manifest crimes and wickedness, he should be avoided, and one should not even eat with him, nor should a bond of closer familiarity be cultivated. But as for the rest who are strangers and given over to such crimes, he does not care much, nor should the Corinthians be much concerned about the censure of those wicked people, but rather, as the situation requires and according to the common necessity of men, they should converse with them freely and leave them to the judgment of God. Which scope of the Apostolic admonition, as it is clearly evident from the text itself, so it firmly proves that this passage is impertinently accommodated by some to that hypothesis, as if Baptism did not pertain to the infants of the faithful by any right, manner, or respect.

4. The practice of the Church of all times

establishes that infidels, both adults and infants, are to be admitted to the use of Baptism, provided that other things, as they say, are equal. Therefore, it is deservedly retained in vigorous observance even today. The antecedent is clearly evident from universal ecclesiastical history, which deals with the conversion of the Gentiles, so that St. Augustine writes fearlessly: This grace (namely, that they be baptized) is granted even to the children of infidels when, by the hidden providence of God, they come in any way into the hands of the pious: lib. de Grat. & lib. arbitr. cap. 21. And elsewhere: Sometimes offspring born of religious parents are overtaken by death at a tender age and in the most recent womb before they are washed in the laver of regeneration: sometimes, however, an infant born of the enemies of Christ is baptized by the mercy of Christians. Prosper also holds this same opinion in lib. 2 de vocat. Gent. cap. 8.

(Our Church also wished to observe the same practice when, not many years ago, by the counsel of our theologians, a female Turkish infant, who had come into the power of the Most Illustrious Pro-Elector of Saxony, Frederick William, of blessed memory, was to be baptized at Torgau: who, however, because the infant was snatched away by an unexpected death, or as there was suspicion, was suffocated by the mother herself, was not conferred in the act itself.)

5. The infants of infidels are either still in the power of their parents, who live and rejoice in their own laws, customs, institutions, and rites: or they have come into our power, and thus have become some part of our family: and this either by right of war, or by purchase, or by surrender, or by some other legitimate way. Considered in the former way, they ought not to be baptized against the will of their parents, for the reason already alleged above: because it is most certain that this Sacrament is thus prostituted and thrown to be, as it were, torn and defiled by dogs, while the parents subsequently accustom such an infant to embrace their own worship. The guilt of which horrible profanation would reside not least with those who would baptize the infant against the parents' will. It is evident from this also that the opinion of those who establish that such infants are to be snatched from their parents by some violence, whether secretly or manifestly, and once snatched are to be baptized, and once baptized are to be either restored to the parents or retained under our rule, can by no means be approved. For 1. such a kidnapping has no command at all in the scriptures. 2. no example. 3. no promise. 4. not even a probable reason: but rather it fights against the law of nature, and against sacred and civil laws, which most severely prohibit us from snatching goods or property, much less infants, by force from those over whom we have no right: and which constitute such a kidnapping as a species of theft. Nor can that intention and end, which is feigned to be good, have any place, while, namely, spiritual regeneration is truly conferred upon such an infant. For an intention is not, and ought not to be called, good which relies on means prohibited by God, whatever the end may be considered.

Latin:

ipsorum voluntatem, quam habuerunt, aut habent, dùm sanioris mentis usum exerunt. Si ergò hoc statu expetant baptismum & professionem fidei edant, tum sanè baptismus ipsis minimè negari debet. Secus verò statuendum, si tales ne quidem sani, baptismi suscipiendi voluntatem ullam habeant: Siquidem baptismus nemini invito conferendus est.

Constat hinc quid de dormientium Baptismo sit sentiendum, nempe quoad infantes, nihil prorsus referre, sive dormiant, sive vigilent, quando baptizantur: Quoad adultos verò, in illis & voluntatem suscipiendi baptismi, & professionem fidei omninò requiri: quorum neutrum in dormientes cadere potest.

Constat etiam hinc, quid judicari possit & debeat, de surdis & de mutis: eos videlicet baptizandos esse ijsdem de causis, quibus infantes baptizantur: dùm modò actu & gestu ostendant, se expetere baptismum, & approbare doctrinam Ecclesiæ.

Quartò nemini etiam invito Baptismus conferri debet. Qui enim baptisatur invitus, gravissimè peccat: Atqui sic peccans baptizandus non est. Ergò. Hinc dist. 45. can. Qui sincera, & Can. de Judæis, expressa continentur interdicta, quibus severissime prohibetur, ne Judæus aliquis invitus baptizetur. Sed quæritur, si parentes nolint filios suos baptizari, quid tùm faciendum. Responderi rectissimè potest per distinctionem geminam: Unam quoad filios ejusmodi parentum: qui vel adhuc sunt infantes: vel sunt adulti: Alteram quoad parentes ipsos, qui vel in nostrâ sunt potestate: vel ipsimet liberâ Jurisdictione fruuntur. Hinc ergò quæstionis decisio verissima petitur: Si enim filij illi sunt adulti, & Baptismum ipsi expetunt: utique invitis etiam parentibus baptizari possunt & debent. Ratio est, Quia in rebus divinis, parentum imperio non subsunt: Si verò adhuc sint infantes, & usum rationis nondùm habeant: tùm invitis parentibus, sub liberâ Jurisdictione versantibus, non sunt baptizandi: primùm, quia cùm jure naturæ hoc pugnat: Tales enim pueri nondum habent usum liberi arbitrij, & idcirco secundum jus naturale, sub curâ parentum sunt, quamdiu sibiipsis providere non possunt. Deindè verò eam præcipuè ob causam, quia certum subest periculum, tales infantes à parentibus postmodùm perverti & corrumpi. Quod si verò parentes civili servituti sint subjecti, & jure belli mancipia facti: tùm ipsis etiam invitis baptizari filij sive liberi ipsorum possunt.

Dependet hinc decisio illius etiam quæstionis: An infidelium, ut Turcarum, Judæorum, aliorumque populorum extra Ecclesiam versantium liberi baptizari debeant? An quod quæsitum affirmatè quidem respondemus: sed sub geminâ cautione, sive in duobus casibus. 1. Quando parentibus absentibus filij peregrè sunt abducti. 2. Quando versantur tales infantes in periculo certo, & extremæ necessitatis casu: Quia tunc non est subsecurutæ perversionis periculum amplius metuendum, ut quod morte baptizati tollitur.

Sed pro explicatione & confirmatione decifionis hujus nostræ, certæ quædam sunt observandæ hypotheses.

1. Ex voluntate & institutione Christi Servatoris baptizandi, & ex aquâ & Spiritu regenerandi, quotquot ex carne nati sunt, & renascentiâ opus habent. Joh. 3, 5. Atqui ex carne nati sunt, non ij tantùm, qui intra Ecclesiæ pomœria & domi quasi nati sunt: sed & qui foris extra Ecclesiam, ab infidelibus procreati sunt parentibus. Ergò his quoque Baptismi Sacramentum non absolutè & simpliciter fuerit negandum.

2. Tàm latè patet Objectum Baptismi, quàm latè olim patuit Objectum Circumcisionis: imò secundum naturam Novi Testamenti Objectum Baptismi multò latiùs se extendit: Siquidem Ecclesia Novi Testamenti, non ad unum certum populum, multò minùs ad unam certam terram: sed ad omnes gentes se extendit. Matth. 28, 19. Atqui ex institutione & mandato divino circumcidendus erat in familijs Patriarcharum, non vernaculus duntaxat, qui domi, hoc est, in Ecclesiâ natus erat: sed & emtitius, imò, uti verba institutionis clarè sonant, Omnis, quicunque etiam non fuerit de stirpe illâ fidelium: Gen. 17, 12. Ergò multò magis Objectum Baptismi sese diffundet ad omnes omninò homines, tàm eos qui extrâ, quàm qui intra Ecclesiam sunt nati: licèt dispari modo & processu, uti mox demonstrabitur. Praxin minoris propositionis subministrat historia Abrahami, qui mandato divino morem gerens Gen. 17, 23. circumcidit non modò omnes vernaculos domus suæ: & singulos ac universos, quos emerat, omnes mares domus suæ, quorum trecentos decem & octo habuisse legitur: Gen. 14, 14. Jam vix quisquam sanus inficias iverit, quin in tantâ multitudine servorum, plurimi fuerint infantes, quos & ipsos Abrahamo circumcidit, vi mandati divinitùs accepti. Ἀθεόλογον proindè fuerit idem jus hodiè negare Ecclesiæ DEI, circa infantes gentilium baptizandos, si in nostrâ sint potestate.

3. Si ad eos etiam, qui sunt à longè, pertinet promissio: utique ad eosdem pertinebit etiam promissionis obsignatio: nempè Sacramentorum participatio. Atqui prius verum: Ergò & posterius. Minorem probo verbis Apostoli Petri, sic alloquentis fideles, tàm ex gentilitate, quàm ex Judaismo conversos, Actor. 2, 39. Vobis facta est promissio, & liberis vestris, & omnibus qui sunt à longè, quoscunque advocaverit Dominus DEUS vester. Sed pro majore intelligentiâ hujus probationis duo potissimùm explicationem merentur. 1. Quinam sint illi, quos Apostolus vocat μακρὰν ὄντες, à longè existentes. 2. Quid de his affirmet Apostolus. Quoad prius, per μακρὰν ὄντες non domi natos, sive Judæos intelligi, ipsa textus συνάφεια clarè evincit, qui de duobus distinctis populis perspicuè loquitur:

Judæos notans, pronomine, (VOBIS & liberis vestris) Gentes verò & infideles quosque, extra Ecclesiam adhuc constitutos, nominans μακρὰν ὄντας. Cujus denominationis causam Scriptura ipsa satis explicat. Ephes. 2, 12, 13. Gentiles nominans ἀθέες καὶ ξένες τῶν διαθηκῶν hospites testamentorum, impios in hoc mundo, alienos à Christo, alienos à conversatione Israël, spem promissionis (olim in veteri Testamento primò (non habentes, alienos à Vitâ DEI &c. Quid? quòd istos expressè nominat Gentes ambulantes in vanitate sensus sui: Ephes. 4, 17. Quin imò haud obscurè verba Petri, de quibus hîc agitur, accommodat ad Ephesios, in Gentilismo adhuc constitutos? Vos, inquiens, qui aliquando eratis à longè, οἱ ποτὲ ὄντες μακρὰν, nunc in Christo Jesu propè facti estis in sangvine ipsius. Ephes. 2, 13. Jam verò quoad posterius membrum dicti Petrini, quod de Ephesijs olim in Gentilismo constitutis pronunciavit Apostolus: idem secundum Petrum ad omnes omninò gentes ac infideles accommodari debet, quòd ad eos quoque pertineat promissio, & consequenter promissionis etiam obsignatio.

Neque obstat illud Apostolicum, in 1. Cor. 5, 12. & 13. Quid attinet de his, qui foris sunt judicare? Nonné de his, qui intus sunt, judicatis? Eos verò, qui foris sunt, DEUS judicat. Neque enim vel de jure Ecclesiastico, vel de promissionibus Novi Testamenti, earumque latitudine, vel γρὺ quidem agit Apostolus: sed in eo totus est, ut monstret rectam formam & qualitatem disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ. Hortatus fuerat Apostolus, ne commiscerentur Corinthij scortatoribus. Hanc admonitionem ita pro universali simpliciter accipiebant Corinthij, ut quorumvis flagitiosorum consortia sibi ex præscripto Paulino vitanda esse putarent: quod factu erat impossibile: siquidem Corinthij in eâ vivebant civitate, cujus major pars gentilisino adhuc dedita, promiscuis libidinibus, alijsque vitijs tota scatebat. Corrigit ergò incommodum hunc sensum Apostolus, ac ostendit, de ejusdem religionis socijs & fratribus se admonitionem suam intellexisse, ita ut, talis si ejusmodi manifestis sceleribus & flagitijs sit deditus, vitetur, & ne quidem cum eo cibus capiatur, aut arctioris familiaritatis consortium colatur. Reliquos verò qui sunt extranei, & hujusmodi sceleribus dediti, se non admodùm curare, neque Corinthios quoque de censurâ istorum sceleratorum debere multum sollicitos esse, quin potius pro re natâ & communi hominum necessitate liberè cum ipsis conversari, ipsosque DEI judicio relinquere. Qui sanè scopus admonitionis Apostolicæ, uti ex textu ipso luculéter patet, ita firmiter evincit, impertinenter hunc locum accommodari à nonnullis, ad eam hypothesin, quasi Baptismus ad infantes fidelium nullo jure, modo aut respectu pertineat.

4. Praxis Ecclesiæ omnium temporum

statuit, infideles tùm adultos, tùm infantes, adusum Baptismi, cæteris tamen, uti loquuntur, paribus admittendos esse. Ergò in viridi observatia meritò ea hodiequè retinetur. Antecedens ex universâ historiâ Ecclesiasticâ, quæ agit de conversione gentium, liquidò patet, ita ut D. Augustinus intrepidè scribat: Filijs infidelium etiam præstatur hæc gratia (ut nimirùm baptizentur) cùm occultâ DEI providentiâ in manus piorum quomodocunq; perveniunt: lib. de Grat. & lib. arbitr. cap. 21. & alibi: Nonnunquàm de religiosis orta proles in tenerâ ætate, atque in utero recentissimo prævenitur morte, antequàm lavacro regenerationis abluatur: nonnunquàm verò infans, ex inimicis Christi natus, misericordiâ Christianorum baptizatur. Quam eandem sententiam tenet etiam Prosper lib. 2. de vocat. Gent. cap. 8.

(Praxin eandem observare voluit Ecclesia etiam nostra, cum ante annos haud ita multos, de consilio nostrorum Theologorum, infans fœmina Turcica, quæ in potestatem Illustrissimi pro-Electoris Saxoniæ, Friderici VVilhelmi, τῶν ἐν ἁγίοις, devenerat. Torgæ baptizari debuit: Qui tamen morte inopinatâ infante abrepto, vel uti suspicio erat, ab ipsâ matre suffocato, ipso actu collatus non fuit.)

5. Infantes infidelium, vel in parentum adhuc sunt potestate, qui suis propriis vivunt gaudéntque legibus, moribus, institutis, sacris: vel in nostram venerunt potestatem, & sic pars aliqua nostræ familiæ facti: idque vel jure belli, vel emtione, vel deditione, vel modo alio legitimo. Priore modo considerati, baptizari invitis parentibus non debent, ob causam jam suprà alligatam: quia certissimum est sic prostitui Sacramentum hoc, & canibus quasi lacerandum & conspurcandum projici, dùm nimirùm parentes talem infantem postmodùm ad suum cultum amplectendum assuefaciunt. Cui horrendæ prophanationis culpa minimè postrema resideret penes eos, qui infantem parentibus invitis, baptizarent. Patet hinc etiam minimè approbari posse eorum sententiam, qui statuunt, ejusmodi infantes, per violentiam quandam, sive clam, sive manifestè parentibus raptendos, raptos baptizandos, baptizatos vel parentibus restituendos, vel sub nostro imperio retinendos. Nam 1. talis raptus nullum prorsus in sacris mandatum. 2. nullum exemplum. 3. nullam promissionem. 4. nullam vel probabilem saltem rationem habet: quin potiùs pugnat cum jure naturæ, cum legibus sacris ac civilibus, quæ severissimè prohibent, ne bona aut facultates, multò minùs infantes vi rapiamus ijs, in quos nullum nobis jus competit: quæque hujusmodi raptum, speciem furti constituunt. Neque locum habere potest intentio, illa, & finis, qui fingitur bonus, dùm nimirùm spiritualis regeneratio, in talem infantem verè conferatur. Non enim bona est, aut dici debet intentio, quæ nititur medijs à Deo prohibitis, qualiscunque etiam spectetur finis.


### Chapter Three, On the Object of Baptism: Of the mode of baptizing adults

GOD certainly knows, according to His immense and inscrutable wisdom, various and infinite ways by which He can gather into the society of the Church those infants whom, also according to His infinite mercy, He would most certainly lead to Himself in act, if He knew that they would embrace the grace of regeneration offered to them and would preserve it with true faith.

Considered in the latter case and manner, the infants of infidel peoples can and truly ought to be baptized: for those reasons which we have just brought forward from the Scriptures: because the promise pertains to these also, and consequently the sealing of the promise. As for adult infidels, they indeed ought not to be baptized against their will. But if they have perceived the heads of the Christian Religion and have uttered a profession of faith with their mouth, then nothing stands in the way of their being baptized: a thing which was observed everywhere in the primitive Church, as the Acts of the Apostles report; and today it is also observed in our Churches regarding the baptism of Jews.

These things being thus firmly confirmed, the theology of the Calvinists must be clearly crude, who, regarding the present question, concede in the negative simply and in all respects, establishing that the children of infidels, even if they have legitimately come into our power, can or ought in no way or respect to be baptized, as Theodore Beza teaches in the second part of his Questions and Answers, Quest. 120 and 118. Who at the same time also argues that if it should happen by chance that Turkish parents were captured by Christian Hungarians, and the infidel mother were to give birth to an infant, whom the master of those captives would offer for baptism: then such an infant is not to be admitted by the minister to the reception of Baptism, because, forsooth, he cannot show the tablets of the covenant; that is, because he is not in the census and number of those absolutely predestined to life. But enough and more than enough on this question.

Now, that we may return to our subject, it is asked in the fifth place, whether exposed infants, about whom it is not certain whether they have been baptized, ought to be baptized? Gregory answers not badly in book 12, Epist. 31: As often as there is doubt about the baptism of some, and there is no certain account by writings or witnesses whether they have been baptized, such persons should certainly be baptized, lest the doubt become a ruin to the faithful, since that which is not shown by certain evidence to have been duly performed is not shown to be repeated. And indeed, a sufficiently probable reason underlies this response: For because such infants are for the most part conceived and born from impure concubinage and are exposed by men of profligate modesty and conscience, there is certainly a great presumption that such exposed infants have not yet been baptized; and therefore it would be safest to baptize such persons immediately, since in these cases there is no legitimate cause for doubting. However, we cannot approve the Papist custom, which baptizes such infants with a condition in this manner: If you have been baptized, I do not baptize you: But if you have not yet been baptized, I baptize you in the name of the Father, etc. For such conditional baptism is of no moment, because it is always doubted whether an infant conditionally baptized has been truly baptized or not.

These things having been thus explained regarding certain doubtful questions concerning the Object of Baptism, we conclude finally that all Christians, or those descending from Christian parents, are to be baptized, both adults and infants, yet in a different manner.

And indeed as regards adults, because they too are born of flesh, and therefore are flesh, they certainly cannot attain eternal life unless they are first regenerated of water and the Spirit: John 3:5. And this is what that universal command of Christ wills, Matthew 28:19: Baptize all nations. As for the thing itself, the Apostolic practice also hints at it everywhere: so that there has been less doubt in the Church about the baptism of adults. Moreover, we have already warned that the baptism of adults must first be preceded by Instruction regarding the knowledge of Catechetical doctrine and the Articles of faith: and then by a public confession of the mouth.
