That instruction is necessary so that from hearing the law he may recognize his sins and seriously grieve for them: and from the articles of the Apostolic Creed, he may conceive true faith in CHRIST the Savior. For baptism is not to be conferred upon the impenitent: but according to that of Peter, Acts 2:38: Let each one repent, and thus be baptized. Thus the grace of regeneration is not conferred except to the believer: For he who shall have believed and shall have been baptized, shall be saved: Mark 16:16. Therefore it is necessary that faith should approach.

Finally, lest the Church communicate in the sins of others, it therefore demands a public confession of faith from the adult being baptized, so that if by chance he fosters hypocrisy in his mind, the Church itself does not have to pay for this guilt. And the primitive Church also observed this practice: as is evident from the baptism of the eunuch of Queen Candace, Acts 8:29, and following. It is worth noting in this place that the truth of our doctrine concerning true Repentance is so great that even the Papists themselves tacitly approve it in their doctrine concerning the baptism of adults. For although they require Repentance from the adult being baptized, they do not require its principal part, which they otherwise demand most of all, namely, the satisfaction of works. Hence Thomas, part 3, quest. 28, art. 5, driven by the force of truth, wrote: To him who is baptized, no Satisfaction is to be enjoined for any sins whatsoever. For this would be to do injury to the passion and death of Christ, as if it were not sufficient for plenary satisfaction for the sins of those being baptized.

But it is further asked in this place: Whether adults are to be compelled to receive the Sacrament of Baptism. But the answer is sought from those things which we have demonstrated above, that Baptism is to be conferred upon no one against his will. And there exists on this matter a Decree of the Fourth Council of Toledo, Canon 56, which holds as follows: concerning the Jews, the Holy Synod commands that henceforth force be brought to bear upon no one to believe, for whom GOD wills He has mercy, and whom He wills, He hardens. For such persons are not to be saved against their will, but willingly, so that

Latin:

Novit certè DEUS pro immensâ suâ ac imperscrutabili sapientiâ varios & infinitos modos, quibus infantes illos Ecclesiæ societati aggregare potest, quos etiam pro infinitâ suâ misericordiâ ipsos actu certo certius adduceret, si collatæ regenerationis gratiam ipso amplexuros, & verâ fide conservaturos sciret.

Posterióre casu ac modo considerati infantes infidelium populorum, omninò baptizari & possunt & verè debent: eas ob causas, quas ex Scripturis modò adduximus: quia ad hos quoque pertinet promissio, & consequenter promissionis obsignatio. Quoad adultos infideles, illi quidem inviti baptizari non debent. Sin autem capita Religionis Christianæ perceperint, & fidei professionem ore ediderint, tùm nihil obstat, quò minus baptizentur: id quod in primitivâ Ecclesiâ passim fuit observatum, sic referentibus Actis Apostolicis; hodieque in nostris etiam Ecclesiis circa baptismum Judæorum observatur.

Quibus ita firmiter confirmatis, cruda planè Calvinianorum Theologia sit necesse est, qui circa præsentem quæstionem, in negantem simpliciter & per omnia concedunt, statuentes, Infidelium liberos, etiamsi in nostram potestatem legitimè devenerint, nullo modo aut respectu baptizari vel posse vel debere, sic docente Theodoro Beza, parte alterâ Quæstionum & Responsionum, Quæst. 120, & 118. Qui simul etiam suadet, si fortè contingat, ut parentes Turciti ab Hungaris Christianis caperentur, mater verò infidelis adhuc infantem eniteretur, quem captivorum illorum Dominus, ad baptizandum offerret: tùm infantem talem ad Baptismi perceptionem à ministro non esse admittendum, quia nimirùm tabulas fœderis monstrare nequeat; hoc est, quia non sit in censu numeroq; absolutè prædestinatorum ad vitam. Sed de hâc quæstione plus satis.

Jam ut ad institutum nostrum redeamus, Quæritur quinto loco, An infantes exposititij, de quibus non constat, an baptisati sint, baptisari debeant? Respondet haud malè Gregorius lib. 12. Epist. 31. Quoties de baptismo aliquorum dubitatio habetur, & nec scriptis, nec testibus ratio certa habetur, utrùm baptizati sint, utiq; baptizentur tales, ne dubitatio fiat ruina fidelibus, quoniam non monstratur iteratum, quod non certis indicijs ostenditur ritè peractum. Et sanè Responsioni huic subest ratio satis probabilis: Quia enim plerumque ejusmodi infantes ex impuro concubinatu sunt concepti & nati, ac à profligatæ pudicitiæ & conscientiæ hominibus exponuntur: certè magna præsumtio est, sic exposititios nondù esse baptizatos: ac proinde tutissimum etiam fuerit, illitò tales baptizare, cùm in his casibus legitima non sit causa dubitandi. Non autem probare possumus morem Pontificium, qui tales infantes cum conditione baptizant in hunc modum: Si baptizatus es ant eà, ego te non baptizo: Si autem nondùm es baptizatus, ego te baptizo in nomine Patris &c. Talis enim baptismus conditionalis nullius est momenti, quia semper dubitatur, an infans conditionaliter baptizatus, verè baptizatus sit, nec nè.

His ita de dubijs quibusdam quæstionibus, circa Baptismi Objectum explicatis, colligimus tandem Omnes Christianos, vel ex Christianis parentibus descendentes esse baptizandos, tum adultos, tum infantes, modo tamen dispari.

Et quidem quoad adultos, quia & ipsi ex carne nati, ac proindè caro sunt, utique vitam æternam consequi non possunt, nisi prius regenerentur ex aquâ & Spiritu: Johan. 3. 5. Et hoc vult mandatum illud universale Christi, Matthæi 28, 19. Baptizate omnes gentes. Quoad ipsum innuit etiam praxis Apostolica passim: ita ut de baptismo adultorum minùs dubitatum fuerit in Ecclesiâ. Cæterùm jam admonuimus Baptismum adultorum primùm præcedere debere Informationem, quoad notitiam doctrinæ Catecheticæ, & Articulorum fidei: deindè verò publicam oris confessionem. Ideò autem informatio illa est necessaria, ut ex auditu legis agnoscat peccata, deœue ijsdem seriò doleat: ex articulis verò Symboli Apostolici, fidem veram concipiat in CHRISTUM Servatorem. Neque enim Impœnitentibus est baptismus conferendus: sed secundum illud Petri, Actor. 2, 38. Agat unusquisque pœnitentiam, & sic baptizetur. Sic regenerationis gratia non confertur nisi credenti: Nam qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur: Marc. 16, 16. Ergò fides ut accedat necesse est.

Tandem ne Ecclesia peccatis alienis communicet, ideò publicam fidei confessionem ab adulto baptizando exigit, ut si fortè hypocrisin animo foveat, culpam hanc ipsa luere non necesse habeat. Et hanc praxin observavit etiam Ecclesia primitiva: uti patet ex baptismo ubi cubicularij Reginæ Candazes Actor. 8, 29. & seqq. Observationem autem hoc loco meretur, quòd tanta est veritas doctrinæ nostræ de Pœnitentiâ verâ, ut in doctrinâ circa Baptismum adultorum, vel tacitè eam approbent ipsi Pontificij. Nam licèt ab adulto baptizando requirant Pœnitentiam: præcipuam tamen ejus partem, quam aliàs vel maximè exigunt, nempè satisfactionem operis non requirunt. Hinc Thomas part. 3. quæst. 28. art. 5. vi veritatis adactus scripsit: Ei qui baptizatur, non est aliqua Satisfactio injungenda, pro quibuscunque peccatis. Hoc enim esset injuriam facere passioni & morti Christi, quasi ipsa non esset sufficiens, ad plenariam satisfactionem pro peccatis baptizandorum.

Sed ampliùs hoc loco quæritur: An adulti sint cogendi ad percipiendum Sacramentum Baptismi. Sed Responsio petitur ex ijs, quibus suprà demonstravimus, Nemini invito Baptismum conferendum esse. Et extat hac de re Decretum Concilij Toletani IV. Canone 56. qui sic habet: de Judæis præcipit Sancta Synodus nemini deinceps ad credendum vim inferri, cujus enim vult DEUS miseretur: & quem vult, indurat. Non enim tales inviti salvandi sunt: Sed volentes, ut


### Chapter Three, On the Object of Baptism: Padobaptism is proved by various arguments

the form of justice may be whole. For just as man perished by the proper will of his own judgment obeying the Serpent: so, when the grace of GOD calls him, everyone is saved by the conversion of his own mind through believing. Therefore, they are to be persuaded rather than compelled, so that they may be converted, not by force, but by the free will and faculty of their own judgment. this canon insofar as it prohibits coercion: but insofar as it asserts the faculty of free will in the conversion of man, we simply disapprove of it.

But for the sake of obtaining coercion, some urge that saying of Christ, Luke 14:23, 'Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in.' But a gross ignorance of the point at issue is committed. For it is more manifest than to require laborious proof that Christ is not speaking of some violent impulse or of coercion: but of constant and accurate information and exhortation, which is done through the Word.

As for the infants of Christians, it can be obtained by most evident arguments that they ought to be baptized without any doubt.

I. Wherever there is sin, and the punishment of sin: there the remedy for sin is also necessarily established. In infants there is both sin and the punishment of sin. Therefore. The major is evidently clear from the immutable law of divine mercy, by which GOD does not will that anyone should perish, 1 Pet. 3:9, but that all should be saved, 1 Tim. 2:4, and especially He does not will that any of the infants should perish, Matt. 18:14. But there is no other remedy given by which regeneration may be obtained than Baptism, John 3:5, Tit. 3:5. The minor is clear from Ps. 51:7, 'I was born in sins, and in iniquities my mother conceived me,' Eph. 2:3, 'By nature we are children of wrath,' Rom. 5:12, 'As by one man sin entered into this world, and by sin death: so death passed into all men because all have sinned,' and as verse 14 has it, 'death passed even into those who have not sinned in the likeness of the transgression of Adam.' Hence it is that infants are subject to pains, diseases, and death itself, no less than adults.

II. To whomever the thing signified by the Sacrament pertains: to them also pertains the sign itself, namely the Sacrament: which is clear even from the Old Testament, where the covenant of GOD pertained to infants: according to that saying in Gen. 17:7, 'I will be your GOD, and of your seed after you.' Therefore, the sign of the covenant, namely Circumcision, also pertained to them. Now, however, the condition of the New Testament ought least of all to be considered worse regarding infants and the whole business of salvation.

But the Grace of the heavenly kingdom, as the thing signified by the Sacrament, pertains to infants. Therefore. The minor consists in the assertion of Christ: Matt. 19:14, Mark 10:14, 'Suffer the little children to come unto me, and do not forbid them: for of such is the kingdom of heaven,' which same thing is repeated also in Luke 18:16.

III. Whoever are born of the flesh, and are flesh, they, unless they are regenerated of water and the spirit, cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. But infants are born of the flesh, and are flesh. Therefore. The major has Christ himself as its author, John 3:5 and 6. The minor is clear in itself. But regarding the declaration of the major, that is most especially to be observed, that the Savior speaks so universally that no exception of sex, or age, or any other condition can have a place.

IV. Whoever come into the census and number of the nations, they ought to be baptized: according to the command of the Savior, Matt. 28:19, 'Going, teach all nations, baptizing them, etc.' But that infants ought to be included under the census and number of the nations: no one except one who is extremely stupid or insane will deny. Therefore.

V. Whatever is received and confirmed by Apostolic practice regarding the baptism of infants in the primitive Church, that it rests upon divine authority, no pious person can doubt. But Infant baptism was received and confirmed by Apostolic practice in the primitive Church. Therefore. The history of the Acts of the Apostles corroborates the minor, reporting that whole families were frequently baptized by the Apostles: Acts 16:15 and 33, 1 Cor. 1:16. Now, that infants also constituted a part, and by no means the least, of those families is asserted much more probably than it is denied.

VI. Whatever GOD pursues with certain immense gifts of His grace: that He certainly approves. But He pursues Infant baptism with certain and immense gifts of His grace. Therefore. The major is evidently clear from the fact that GOD, as the most just avenger of all crimes, by no means pursues with singular gifts and benefits those who are transgressors of His will. The minor is sufficiently manifest. For 1. it cannot be denied that GOD for many centuries, indeed even from the first institution of baptism, has gathered a Church for Himself from infants baptized in early childhood, and gathers it today. 2. Thus He endows those baptized in infancy with His Holy Spirit, protects and preserves them against the furies of the Devil, and uses their ministry afterwards, both in the preservation of the Church and in asserting the remaining hierarchical orders. Therefore, that He approves of the baptism of infants: no pious person can doubt.

VII. That graphic prophetic description may be referred here, depicting to the life almost the entire act of Baptism of the New Testament, Isaiah 49:22. For thus Jehovah says there: Behold, I will lift up my hand to the Gentiles, and will exalt my standard (Baptism) to the peoples: and they shall bring thy sons in their arms, and thy daughters shall be carried upon their shoulders. The Anabaptists, and those who side with them, had already explained, is there any other sign, besides Baptism alone, erected in the New Testament, to which sons in arms and little daughters on shoulders are to be brought?

VIII. Finally, there is added the unanimous consensus of Orthodox antiquity, which although the Anabaptist sect may treat with contempt, yet it wonderfully confirms us in the doctrine of Infant Baptism.

Irenaeus, book 2 against heresies, chapter 39. All are saved who are reborn in Christ, infants, children, youths, old men.

Cyprian, in his Epistle to Fidus concerning the baptizing of infants: This was the opinion of our council, that no one should be prohibited by us from Baptism and from the grace of God: which, as it is to be observed and maintained regarding all, we think it is to be observed even more regarding infants themselves, and those newly born, who by this very fact deserve our help and divine mercy, in that

Latin:

integra sit forma justitiæ. Sicut enim homo propria arbitrij voluntate Serpēti obediens perijt: Sic vocāte se gratia DEI propria mentis conversione quisq; credendo salvatur. Ergò non vi, sed liberâ arbitrij sui voluntate & facultate, ut convertantur, suadendi potiùs sunt, quàm impellendi. Quem canonem eatenùs nos approbamus, quatenùs coactionem prohibet: quatenùs verò arbitrij liberi facultatem in conversione hominis astruit, simpliciter improbamus.

Verùm pro obtinendâ coactione nonnulli urgent illud Christi, Luc 14. 23. Exi in vias, & circa sepes, & compelle eos intrare. Sed crassa committitur elenchi ignoratio. Neque enim de violentâ quadam impulsione, sive de coactione: sed de jugi & accuratâ informatione ac exhortatione, quæ fit per Verbum, agere Christum, manifestiùs est, quàm ut operosam probationem requirat.

Quoad infantes Christianorum, eos citra omnem dubitationem baptizari debere, eventissimis argumentis obtineri potest.

I. Ubicunque peccatum est, & peccati pœna: ibi necessario statutum est etiam peccati remedium. In Infantibus est & peccatum, & peccati pœna. E. Major evidenter patet ex immutabili divinæ misericordiæ lege, quâ non vult DEUS perire quenquam, 1. Petr. 3, 9. sed salvari omnes, 1. Tim. 2, 4. præcipuè autem ex infantibus neminem vult perire. Matth. 18, 14. Remedium autem, quo regeneratio obtingat, datum aliud nullum est, quàm Baptismus, Johan. 3, 5. Tit. 3, 5. Minor liquet ex psal. 51, 7. In peccatis sum natus, & in iniquitatibus concepit me mater mea Ephes. 2, 3. Natura sumus filij iræ. Rom. 5, 12. Sicut per unum hominem peccatum in hunc mundum intravit, & per peccatum mors : ita in omnes homines mors pertransiit quia omnes peccaverunt: & uti versus habet 14. mors pertransijt: etiam in eos, qui non peccaverunt in similitudinem prævaricationis Adami. Hinc est, quòd infantes doloribus, mo bis, morti ipsi, non minùs quàm adulti sunt obnoxij.

II. Ad quoscunque pertinet Sacramenti signatum: ad eosdem pertinet etiam signum ipsum, nempè Sacramentum: id quod vel ex veteri etam Testamento liquet, ubi ad Infantes pertinuit fœdus DEI: secundum illud Genes 17, 7. Erò DEUS tuus, & seminis tui post te. Ergò ad eosdem etiam pertinuit Signum fœderis nempè Circumcisio. Jam verò Novi Testamenti conditio minimè omnium quo ad infantes, & universum salutis negotium, censeri debet deterior.

Atqui Gratia regni cœlestis, tanquàm Signatum Sacramenti ad infantes pertinet. Ergò. Minor constat assertione Christi: Matth. 19, 14. Marc. 10, 14 Sinite parvulos ad me venire, & nolite prohibere ipsos: talium enim est regnum cælorum, Quod ipsum repetitur etiam, Luc. 18. 16.

III. Quicunq; ex carne nati, & caro sunt, illi, nisi ex aquâ & spiritu regenerentur, regnum cælorū ingredi non possunt. Atqui Infantes ex carne nati, & caro sunt. Ergò. Major autorem habet ipsum Christum, Joh. 3, 5. & 6. Minor per se liquet. Circa majoris declarationem verò illud vel maximè observandum, quod Servator usque adeò universaliter loquitur, ut nulla vel sexus, vel ætatis, vel alius alicujus conditionis exceptio locum habere possit.

IV. Quicunq́; in censum numerumq́; Gentium veniunt, illi baptizari debent: secundum mandatum Servatoris Matth. 28, 19. Euntes docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos &c. Atqui infantes sub censum numerumq́; Gentium referri debere: nemo nisi extremè stupidus aut amens negaverit. Ergò.

V. Quicquid praxi Apostolicâ, circa baptismum infantum, in primitivâ Ecclesiâ usu est receptum, & confirmatum, quin illud divinâ autoritate nitatur, nemini pio potest esse dubium. Atqui Pædobaptismus praxi Apostolicâ primitivâ Ecclesia usu fuit receptus & confirmatus. E. Minorem corroborat historia Actorum Apostolorum, integras sæpiùs familias ab Apostolis baptizatos fuisse, referens: Actor. 16, 15. & 33. 1. Cor. 1, 16. Jam infantes quoque partem minimè postremam illarum familiarum constituisse, multò probabiliùs asseritur, quèm negatur.

VI. Quicquid DEUS certis immensis gratiæ suæ donis prosequitur: illud certè approbat. Atqui Pædobaptismum certis & immensis gratiæ suæ donis prosequitur. Ergò. Major evidenter patet vel indè, quòd DEUS tanquàm justissimus scelerum omnium vindex, nullo pacto singularibus donis & beneficiis prosequitur eos, qui sunt voluntatis suæ transgressores. Minor satis manifesta est. Nam 1. negari non potest, quin DEUS multis seculis, imò jam indè à primâ baptismi institutione, ex infantibus in primâ pueritiâ baptizatis Ecclesiam sibi collegerit, hodieque colligat. 2. Sic in infantiâ baptizatos Spiritu suo Sancto donat, contra furores Diaboli protegit & conservat, eorundemque ministerio postmodùm, tùm in conservatione Ecclesiæ, tùm in reliquis asserendis ordinibus hierarchicis utitur. Quin ergò Baptismum infantum approbet: nemini pio potest esse dubium.

VII. Referri huc potest graphica illa descriptio prophetica, depingens ad vivum integrum fermè actum Baptismi Novi Testamenti, Jesaiæ 49, 22. Sic enim ibi Jehovah: Ecce levabo ad Gentes manum meam, & ad populos exaltabo signum meum (Baptismum:) & afferent filios tuos in ulnis, & filias tuas super humeros portabunt. Edisserant jam Anabaptistæ, & qui cum ijs faciunt, an ullum aliud signum, præter solum Baptismum, in Novo Testamento sit erectum, ad quod filij in ulnis, & filiolæ in humeris adportentur?

VIII. Tandem accedit unanimis consensus Orthodoxæ antiquitatis, quem licèt adunco naso suspendat sex Anabaptistica: nos tamen illa in doctrinâ de Pædobaptismo mirificè confirmat.

Irenæus lib. 2. adversus hæreses cap. 39. Salvantur omnes, qui renati sunt in Christo, infantes, pueri, juvenes, senes.

Cyprianus Epistolâ ad Fidem de baptizandis infantibus: Hæc fuit consilij nostri sententia, neminem à Baptismo, atq́; à gratiâ DEI per nos debere prohiberi: Quod cùm circa universos observadũ sit atq́; retinendũ, tùm magis circa infantes ipsos, & recens natos observandũ putamus, qui hoc ipso de ope nostrâ, ac divinâ misericordiâ plg merētur, quòd


### Chapter Three, On the Object of Baptism: Various errors concerning the legitimate object of Baptism

in the very first moment of their birth, wailing and weeping, they do nothing else but pray.

Augustine, in his book On the Merits and Remission of Sins, chapter 26: 'Since they concede that infants must be baptized, they must also concede that they stand in need of those benefits of the Mediator, so that, being offered through the Sacrament and the charity of the faithful, and thus reconciled to GOD in the bodily body of Christ which is the Church, they may be made alive in Him, saved, liberated, redeemed, and enlightened.'

The Council of Milevis, at which Lord Augustine was also present and subscribed, chapter 2, decrees as follows: 'It has been resolved that whoever denies that infants fresh from their mothers' wombs should be baptized, let him be anathema.' Tom. 1. Concil. p. 482. b. de consecr. dist. 4. c. placuit.

With Infant Baptism thus clearly demonstrated and established from the Holy Scriptures, it may not undeservedly seem a wonder to anyone what the reason is that both the Jesuits and the Calvinists are much more favorable to the Anabaptists than they wish to be to our doctrine. The Jesuits certainly clamor everywhere in their writings that Infant Baptism cannot be proven from the Holy Scriptures. John Calvin, however, petulantly interprets that illustrious passage in John 3:5, 'Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven,' not of Baptism, but of new obedience; and 'Water,' not of the element of water, but of the Spirit itself. Both of which impieties we leave to be judged by GOD, the most just judge.

Now, to make an approach to the antithesis of this chapter, grave errors have long since been committed by various people concerning the true and legitimate object of Baptism.

And in the beginning, indeed, the Cataphrygians, according to Augustine in his work On Heresies, heresy 26, besides the fact that they made the Sacraments of the New Testament bloody—when they were about to administer the Eucharist, they pierced a one-year-old infant all over its body with tiny puncture wounds and mixed the extracted blood with flour, and from that made the Eucharistic bread—furthermore, they also decreed that not only the living but also the dead should be baptized, thus impiously thinking that even after this life there are means of salvation left; which is in conflict with the entire Scripture: 'For where the tree falls, there it shall be,' Ecclesiastes 11:3.

Following them, the Marcionites baptized those who had died without baptism, but with a different and diverse rite. For they would hide some living man under the bed or the place of the deceased; afterwards, they would ask the dead man: 'Do you wish to be baptized?' Then he who was hiding under the bed would answer that he did wish it; and thus that living man was baptized for the dead. To cloak this impiety of theirs, they accommodated that somewhat obscure Apostolic passage which exists in 1 Cor. 15:29, and it sounds thus: 'What shall they do who are baptized for or over the dead (οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν) if the dead do not rise at all? Why, I say, are they baptized over the dead?'

In which Apostolic passage, interpreters certainly disagree greatly in their explanation. Ambrose replies that the Apostle approves not the act itself, but only the end, which was that such baptism of the dead was, as it were, a symbol of the future Resurrection. But the Apostle could not have approved even that end, since that symbolic end of our Resurrection is represented more in the baptism of the living than of the dead. For we living ones are baptized into the death of Christ, and, as the Apostle says, we are buried with Him, so that just as death no longer has dominion over Him, so we too in Christ are to pass through death into life. Other Fathers maintain that it deals with the baptism of the Clinici, with a somewhat twisted sense, so that to be baptized over the dead or for the dead was nothing else in this place than to baptize those lying lethally ill as if they were dead, being indeed near to death. But this explanation also seems forced and less suited to the Greek text, although it establishes nothing contrary to the analogy of faith. Our blessed Luther, following the older Greek interpreters, maintains that the Apostle looked to that rite or rather custom which was accustomed to be observed at that time in conferring baptism. For because the resurrection of the flesh was absurd to the Greeks and Gentiles, the faithful, to confirm this Article, brought those to be baptized to the tombs of the dead; and there, in testimony of the resurrection of the flesh (which, according to Theophylact, those to be baptized ought to confess publicly), they conferred baptism upon them. The Apostle therefore concludes that this rite would be clearly frivolous unless there is a resurrection. Now, indeed, this rite was introduced into the Church with a clearly salutary purpose and for the greatest use. Therefore, even from that, the certainty of the Resurrection is confirmed quite evidently. And this interpretation of Luther, being consonant with the analogy of faith and agreeable to ecclesiastical history, we follow most of all; and we constantly oppose it to the delirium of the Marcionites and Cataphrygians. But there is, besides this, another explanation of this passage, likewise quite probable. It was customary for the Jews to purify and wash the bodies of the deceased with water before they were committed to the earth. Which custom was also accustomed to be observed among Christians in the primitive Church, as is evident from Acts 9:37, where it is read that the deceased Tabitha was washed before she was placed in the coffin. Nor is there any doubt that this custom also was a symbol of the future Resurrection for the pious and faithful, although afterwards it fell partly into superstition and partly into contempt among the Gentiles: so that Lucian mocks it, and Ennius in Virgil seems in a way to criticize it, saying: A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquin.

Therefore they wish the sense of the Apostle's words to be this: if there is no resurrection of bodies, why are the bodies of the dead washed and cleansed before they are committed to the earth? So that the word βαπτίζεσθαι in this place is not taken specifically concerning the Sacrament of Baptism, but generally concerning that washing of corpses: in the same sense clearly as in Mark 7:4 and Hebrews 9:10, where mention is made of the baptism of cups and various other baptisms. We leave this interpretation in the middle, since it is not entirely alien to the present Apostolic scope: but meanwhile we most embrace the opinion of Blessed Luther, who was himself also instructed by the spirit of prophecy.

The Anabaptists, who today lead the column in the class of those erring in this chapter, simply disapprove of infant baptism, chiefly with these arguments.

I. Infant baptism according to the letter is nowhere expressed or commanded in the holy scriptures. For it is not written, baptize infants, therefore.

I answer, that this argument alone betrays the vertigo of the fanatical spirit in the Anabaptists. For by this argument, the use of this Sacrament will be denied not only to infants, but also to adults, youths, men, women, and the aged, and to any sex whatsoever. For it is not written in the scriptures: Baptize adults, youths, men, women, etc. Now since CHRIST has commanded all nations and peoples to be baptized, with absolutely no notation made of sex, or rank, or age: it would certainly be a sin to wish to restrict the universality of Christ's command, and to sequester the order of infants from it: as was shown above in the construction.

II. Christ willed that the preaching of the Gospel and doctrine be placed before Baptism, Mark 16:15, Matt. 28:19. But infants are not capable of doctrine. Therefore.

I answer with Augustine: Distinguish the times and the Scripture will agree. The Savior looked in this precept to the state of that time, in which the Church had finally to be gathered. Here, therefore, account had to be taken of adults first and foremost in propagating the doctrine concerning Christ, rather than of infants. But after the Church has now been gathered, that order certainly ought not to be observed with regard to infants. Furthermore, there also occurs a sophistication of equivocation in the word μαθητεύσατε, which is general, and signifies the same as to assert into the school or discipline of Christ: which is done no less by the collation of Baptism than by the preaching of the Gospel.

III. Michael Servetus the Spaniard brings forward these reasons especially for the Anabaptists: I. The Symbols of Christ are perfect, therefore they admit none but the perfect, or at least those capable of perfection, to their enjoyment. II. The Symbols of Christ are to be for a memory, so that each may recall that he is buried with Christ: But such a recollection does not fall to infants. Therefore. III. Spiritual things square with spiritual things. But infants are carnal: Baptism, however, is spiritual. Therefore. IV. Through regeneration we become like to GOD. But this is proper to those to whom the word of GOD has been made: of which infants are not capable, therefore. V. They are new men, who are begotten through the word of GOD. But infants cannot hear this. Therefore. VI. In the Old Testament, infants and little ones of the New Testament were signified by sheep and goats. But it was forbidden in the Old Testament to offer goats and sheep immediately from their mothers' womb. Therefore, neither should infants immediately from their mothers' womb be offered to GOD in the New Testament through Baptism. VII. If it is permitted to baptize infants understanding nothing at all. Therefore, Baptism could also be administered by children playing in mimicry and in jest. IIX. And finally, he calls to his aid Trismegistus and the prophecies of the Sibyls, by which it is asserted that sacred ablutions are not appropriate except for adults.

But these reasons are so frivolous that they scarcely deserve any censure. For

The first reason confuses the Sacrament considered in itself and by reason of its essence, which is certainly most perfect, with the person using the Sacrament, whom Servetus dreams ought to be of the same perfection; but without reason. Nay, rather, it is inverted. For if men were perfect, they would certainly have no need of a Sacrament: since it is the property of it to relieve our imperfection, and to preserve us from destruction as if by some antidote. Which same reason also militates concerning infants.

The second reason likewise confuses the ends of the Sacraments of the New Testament; the end of the Eucharist is indeed ἀνάμνησις, a remembrance of the death of Christ: and therefore none are admitted to its use except those who are capable of this ἀνάμνησις. But the proper end of Baptism is Regeneration, which does not require such a commemoration in infants. Therefore.

The third reason wanders off the mark. For the Apostle does not deal with the proper and adequate object of the Sacraments, but with doctrine and the understanding of spiritual things, which does not fall to profane men. 2. Baptism was instituted for this reason, that they might become spiritual from carnal: but infants are carnal. Therefore, they are to be baptized for that very reason. 3. The spirituality which the Anabaptist flock attributes to the men of its own order is fictitious, neither commanded in the Scriptures, nor conformable to the law of GOD: nor does it fall to any mortal in this life: as we have shown elsewhere.

The fourth reason rests upon a false hypothesis. For it is false that the benefit of Regeneration, namely υἱοθεσίαν (adoption), does not reach any but adults and those hearing the Word of GOD. For if it is true, as Christ asserts concerning infants, that of such is the kingdom of heaven, with what face, I ask, nay, with what conscience will the Anabaptists deprive them of the benefit of regeneration, or υἱοθεσίας (adoption)?

The fifth argument suffers from the same futility: For they are new men, not only who are regenerated by the word, but also who are regenerated by water and the Spirit, John 3:5, Titus 3:5. For therefore are the baptized buried with Christ, that they may walk in newness of life, Rom. 6:4.

The sixth argument is allegorical, which by itself proves nothing at all, unless the thing itself, for the proving of which it is applied, can first be clearly confirmed from the Scriptures. 2. It is manifestly false: For in the Old Testament, all the firstborn, as soon as they opened the womb, were holy to the LORD. Exod. 12:13. 3. Christ himself calls children to himself, and specifically τὰ βρέφη infants: as shown above.

The seventh argument plays upon the παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον in two ways. For 1. understanding contributes nothing at all to the perception of saving Baptism: which depends solely upon the promise and ordinance of Christ. 2. Hence it is wrongly inferred for establishing mimic or jocular baptism, about which there was also once an inquiry in the Church. And indeed Augustine pronounces almost nothing certain about such a baptism. For he himself says thus, book 7 on baptism against the Donatists, chapter 53: If the whole thing were done playfully and mimicly and jocularly, whether a baptism that was given in such a way should be approved, I would judge that the divine judgment must be implored by the oracle of some revelation with concordant prayer and with sighs offered with suppliant devotion (in a council, that is), in such a way indeed that I would humbly await the opinions of those who were to speak after me. But the Scholastics rightly answer: Since the institution and intention, and the will of giving the baptism of CHRIST, and of receiving it, are not observed in a jocular baptism, it is not the baptism of CHRIST, which is administered by thus playing and joking. For the institution of baptism does not intend that it be some common washing, much less a mimic action or a profanation of the institution; but that it be a sacrosanct action, which ordinarily is not administered except by persons established in the ecclesiastical ministry as a sacred thing proper to the Church. But what Rufinus wrote about Athanasius as a boy, book 1 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 14, is peculiar, and is not to be drawn into imitation.

Latin:

in primo statim nativitatis suæ ortu, plorantes ac flentes, nihil aliud faciunt, quàm deprecantur.

Augustinus lib. de peccatorum meritis & remissione, cap. 26. Quia parvulos baptizandos esse concedunt: concedant etiam oportet, eos egere illis beneficiis Mediatoris, ut oblati per Sacramentum, charitatemquè fidelium, ac sic in corporali Christi corpore quod est Ecclesia, reconcilientur DEO, ut in eo vivi, ut salvi, ut liberati, ut redemti, ut illuminati fiant.

Concilium Milevitanum, cui interfuit etiam & subscripsit D. Augustinus, cap. 2. sic decernit: Placuit, ut quicunq; parvulos recentes ab uteris matrum baptizandos esse negat, anathema sit. Tom. 1. Concil. p. 482. b. de consecr. dist. 4. c. placuit.

His ita stabiliendo Pædobaptismo ex Scripturis sacris evidenter demonstratis, mirum cuipiam haud immeritò videri possit, Quid causæ sit, quòd tum Jesuvitæ, tum Calviniani, Anabaptistis multò æquiores, quàm nostræ doctrinæ esse volunt. Jesuvitæ certè passim suis in scriptis clamitant, Pædobaptismum ex Scripturis sacris probari non posse. Johannes Calvinus verò, illustrem illum locum Johan. 3, 5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non poterit ingredi in regnum cœlorum, non de Baptismo, sed de Novâ obedientia: & Aquam, non de Elemento Aquæ, sed de ipso Spiritu petulanter interpretatur. Quam utramque impietatem nos DEO justissimo judici vindicandam relinquimus.

Jam ut ad Antithefin hujus capitis accessum faciamus, jam olim graviter à diversis circa verum ac legitimum Baptismi objectum, peccatum fuit.

Ac initiò quidem Cataphryges testè Augustino de hæresibus, hæresi 26. præterquàm quòd cruenta fecerunt Sacramenta Novi Testamenti, dum administraturi Eucharistiam, infantem anniculum toto corpore minutis punctionum vulneribus perfoderunt, & sangvinem extortum farinæ miscuerunt, indeque panem Eucharisticum confecerunt: insuper etiam statuerunt, non vivos tantùm, sed & mortuos baptizandos esse: sic impiè sentientes, post hanc etiam vitam salutis media esse relicta: id quod cum universa Scripturâ pugnat: Ubi enim ceciderit arbor, ibi erit, Ecclesiasta 11, 3.

Hos secuti Marcionitæ, eos, qui sine baptismo decesserant, baptizabant: sed ritu alio ac diverso. Nam vivum aliquem hominem, infrà lectum, sive locutum defuncti occultabant: postmodùm interrogabant mortuum: An vellet baptizari: tùm ille, qui infrà lectum latitabat, velle se, respondit: atque ita vivus ille pro mortuo baptizabatur. Impietati huic suæ palliandæ accommodabant locum illum Apostolicum, paulò obscuriorem, qui extat in 1. Cor. 15, 29. & sic sonat: Quid facient, qui baptizantur pro vel super mortuis (οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν) si mortui omninò non resurgent? quid inquam baptizantur super mortuis.

In quo sanè loco Apostolico explicando valdè dissentiunt interpretes. Ambrosius, non factum ipsum, sed finem duntaxat, ab Apostolo probari respondet, qui fuerit, ut baptismus ille mortuorum, symbolum quasi esset futuræ Resurrectionis. Verùm ne finem quidem istum probare potuisset Apostolus: siquidem finis iste Symbolicus Resurrectionis nostræ, magis in vivorum, quàm mortuorum baptismo repræsentatur. Ideò enim in mortem Christi, nos viventes baptisamur, & ut Apostolus loquitur, consepelimur, ut quemadmodum ipsis mors non ampliùs dominatur: ita & nos in Christo transituri simus per mortem in vitam. Alij ex Patribus de baptismo Clinicorum agere autumant, sensu nonnihil inflexo, ita ut super mortuis, sive pro mortuis baptizari, ipsius nihil hoc loco fuerit aliud, quàm lethaliter decumbentes baptizare quasi mortuos, quippè morti vicinos. Sed & hæc explicatio videtur contorta, & Græco textui minùs quadrare, licèt nihil analogiæ fidei contrarium statuat. B. Lutherus noster, Græcos antiquiores interpretes secutus, statuit, Apostolum respexisse ad ritum illum sive potius morem, qui tum temporis in conferendo baptismo, observari consuevit. Quia enim Græcis & Gentibus absurdum erat carnis Resurrectio: ideo fideles ad confirmandum hunc Articulum, baptizandos adducebant ad sepulchra mortuorum: atq; ibi in testimonium Resurrectionis carnis (quàm Theophylacto teste baptizandi publicè confiteri debeant) baptismum illis conferebant. Colligit proindè Apostolus, ritum istum planè frivolum fore, nisi sit Resurrectio. Jam verò salutari planè consilio, & usu maximo ritus iste in Ecclesiam est invectus. Ergò vel indè Resurrectionis certitudo satis evidenter confirmatur. Et hanc interpretationem Lutheri, quippè analogiæ fidei consonam, & historiæ Ecclefiasticæ congruam nos vel maximè sequimur: eamque Marcionitarum ac Cataphrygum delirio constanter opponimus. Sed est præterea & alia loci hujus explicatio, itidem admodum probabilis. Usitatum fuit Judæis, ut demortuorum corpora, priusquam terræ mandarentur, aquâ purgarent & abluerent. Qui mos apud Christianos etiam in primitivâ Ecclesiâ observari consuevit, uti patet ex cap. 9, 37. Actor. ubi demortua illa Tabitha prius lota fuisse legitur, quàm loculo inclusa. Neque dubium est ullum, quin hæc etiam consuetudo, pijs ac fidelibus futuræ Resurrectionis fuerit Symbolum, licèt postmodùm ea partim in superstitionem, partim in contemtum apud Gentiles abierit: ita ut Lucianus eam rideat, & Ennius apud Virgilium perstringere quodammodò videatur, inquiens: Tarquinij corpus bona fæmina lavit & unxit.

Sensum ergò verborum Apostoli volunt esse istum: si nulla est corporum Resurrectio, cur abluuntur & purgantur corpora mortuorum, priusquam terræ mandantur? ita ut verbum βαπτίζεσθαι hoc loco nõ specificè de Sacramento Baptismi: sed generaliter de ablutione illâ cadaverum, accipiatur: eodem planè sensu, quo Marci 7, 4. & Hebr. 9, 10. ubi baptismatis poculorum, & diversorum aliorum baptismatum fit mentio. Nos hanc interpretationem in medio relinquimus, quippè à præsenti scopo Apostolico non prorsus alienam: sed interim B. Lutheri sententiam, qui & ipse spiritu prophetiæ instructus fuit, nos maximè amplectimur.

Anabaptistæ, qui in classe errantium hoc in capite agmen hodiè ducũt, Pædobaptismũ simpliciter improbant, his potissimùm argumentis.

I. Pædobaptismus secundum literam in scripturis sacris nuspiam est expressus aut mandatus. Neg. enim scriptum est, baptizate infantes, Ergò.

Respondeo, vel solum hoc argumentum, Spiritus fanatici vertiginem in Anabaptistis prodere. Hoc enim argumento non infantibus modò, sed & adultis, juvenibus, viris, mulieribus, & anui, sexuiq; cuivis Sacramenti hujus usus negabitur. Neque enim in sacris scriptum legitur: Baptizate adultos, juvenes, viros, fœminas &c. Jam cum omnes gentes & populos baptizari CHRISTUS jusserit, nullâ prorsus vel sexûs, vel ordinis, vel ætatis factâ notatione: nefas utique fuerit, universalitate mandati Christi velle restringere, & infantum ordinem indè sequestrare: uti suprà in κατασκευῇ fuit ostensum.

II. Christus prædicationem Evangelij & doctrinam voluit præmitti Baptismo, Marci 16, 15. Matth. 28, 19. Atqui infantes doctrinæ non sunt capaces. Ergò.

Respondeo cum Augustino: Distingue tempora & concordabit Scriptura. Respexit Servator hoc præcepto ad statum illius temporis, quo Ecclesia demùm colligi debuit. Hîc ergò adultorum prior fuit habenda ratio & potior, in propagandâ doctrinâ de Christo, quàm infantum. Postquàm verò jam Ecclesia est collecta, utique ordo ille, quoad infantes observari haud debet. Deindè occurrit etiam Sophisticatio æquivocationis in verbo μαθητεύσατε, quod generale est, & idem significat, ac in Scholam sive disciplinam Christi asserere: id quod non minùs fit, per collationem Baptismi, quàm per prædicationem Evangelij.

III. Profert Michael Servetus Hispanus has potissimùm rationes pro Anabaptistis: I. Christi Symbola sunt perfecta, Ergò non nisi perfectos, vel saltem perfectionis capaces, ad sui perfruitionem admittunt. II. Christi Symbola sunt futura ad memoriam, ut quisq; recolat, se Christo esse consepultum: Atqui talis recordatio non cadit in Infantes. Ergò. III. Spiritualibus quadrant spiritualia. Atqui infantes sunt carnales: Baptismus verò Spiritualis. Ergò. IV. Per regenerationem DEO similes evadimus. Atqui hoc proprium est eorum, ad quos sermo DEI factus est: cujus capaces non sunt infantes, Ergò. V. Novi homines sunt, qui gignuntur per verbum DEI. Atqui infantes hoc audire non possunt. Ergò. VI. In Veteri Testamento per oves & capras notati fuerunt infantes & parvuli Novi Testamenti. Atqui prohibitum erat in Veteri Testamento, statim ab utero matrum offerre capras & oves. Ergò neque infantes statim ab utero matrum in Novo Testamento offerri debent DEO per Baptismum. VII. Si Infantes nihil quicquam intelligentes licet baptizare. Ergò poterit etiam Baptismus à pueris ludentibus mimicè & per jocum administrari. IIX. & postremò in subsidium vocat Trismegistu, & vaticinia Sibyllarum, quibus asseratur, sacras ablutiones non convenire, nisi adultis.

Verùm usque adeò frivolæ sunt rationes istæ, ut vix ullam censuram mereantur. Nam

Prima ratio, confundit Sacramentum in se & ratione suæ essentiæ consideratum, certè longè perfectissimum, cum persona utente Sacramento, quam ejusdem perfectionis esse debere, somniat Servetus; sed sine ratione. Quin imò invertitur ea. Si enim homines essent perfecti; utique non opus haberent Sacramento: quippe cujus proprium est, imperfectionem nostram sublevare, & tanquam alexipharmaco quopiam ab interitu asserere. Quæ ipsa ratio de infantibus quoque militat.

Altera ratio itidem confundit fines Sacramentorum Novi Testamenti, Eucharistiæ quidem finis est ἀνάμνησις recordatio mortis Christi: ac proindè ad hujus etiam usum non admittuntur, nisi qui hujus ἀναμνήσεως sunt capaces. Atqui Baptismi finis proprius est Regeneratio, quæ talem commemorationem in infantibus non requirit. Ergò.

Tertia ratio extra oleas vagatur. Nihil enim Apostolus de Sacramentorum objecto proprio & adæquato, sed de doctrinâ, & rerum spiritualium intelligentiâ agit, quæ in homines prophanos non cadit. 2. Baptismus ideò institutus, ut ex carnalibus fiant spirituales: Atqui infantes sunt carnales. Ergò vel ideò baptizandi. 3. Fictitia est spiritualitas, quam grex Anabaptistica sui ordinis hominibus affingit, neque in Scripturis præcepta, neque legi DEI conformis: neque hâc in vitâ in mortalium quemquam cadit: ut alibi à nobis ostensum.

Quarta ratio, falsâ nititur hypothesi. Falsum enim Regenerationis beneficium, nempè υἱοθεσίαν non obtingere, nisi adultis & Verbum DEI audientibus. Nam si verum est, quod Christus de infantibus asserit, quòd talium sit regnum cælorum, quâ quæso fronte, imò quâ conscientiâ ipsos Anabaptistæ privabunt regenerationis, sive υἱοθεσίας beneficio?

Quinta ratio eâdem futilitate laborat: Nam novi homines sunt, non tantùm qui per verbum, sed & qui per aquam & Spiritum regenerantur, Johan. 3, 5. Tit. 3, 5. Ideò enim consepeliantur baptizati cum Christo, ut in novitate vitæ ambulent Rom. 6, 4.

Sexta ratio allegorica est, quæ per se nihil quicquam probat, nisi res ipsa priùs, cui probandæ adhibetur, ex Scripturis liquidò confirmari queat. 2. manifestè falsa est: Nam in Veteri Testamento, primogenita omnia, simul ac vulvam aperiebant, sacra erant DOMINO. Exod. 12, 13. 3. Christus ipse ad se vocat pueros, & in specie τὰ βρέφη infantes: uti suprà ostensum.

Septima ratio ludit παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον dupliciter. Nam 1. intelligentia nihil quicquam facit, ad perceptionem salutaris Baptismi: qui ex promissione & ordinatione Christi unicè dependet. 2. Hinc malè colligitur ad stabiliendum mimicum sive jocularem baptismum de quo olim quoque in Ecclesia quæsitum fuit. Et sanè Augustinus nihil fermè certi de tali baptismo pronunciat. Sic enim ipse, lib. 7. de baptismo contra Donatistas, cap. 53. Si totum ludicrè & mimicè & joculariter ageretur, utrùm approbandus esset baptismus, qui sic daretur, divinum judicium, per alicujus revelationis oraculum concordi oratione, & impensis supplici devotione gemitibus implorandum esse censerem (in concilio videlicet) ita sanè ut post me dicturos sententias, humiliter expectarem. Verùm Scholastici rectè respondent: Cùm institutio & intentio, voluntasque dandi baptismum CHRISTI, & accipiendi, in joculari Baptismate non servetur, non esse baptismum CHRISTI, qui ita ludendo & jocando administratur. Institutio enim baptismi non hoc vult, ut sit vulgaris aliqua lotio, multò minùs mimica actio aut profanatio institutionis; sed ut sacrosancta actio, quæ ordinariè non nisi à personis in ministerio Ecclesiastico constitutis tanquàm sacrum Ecclesiæ proprium, administretur. Quod autem Ruffinus scripsit de Athanasio puero lib. 1. Hist. Ecclesiast. c. 14. peculiare est, & ad imitationem non trahendu.


### Chapter Three, On the Object of Baptism: The history itself in Rufinus is as follows

The history itself in Rufinus is as follows:

At the time when Bishop Alexander was celebrating the day of Peter the Martyr at Alexandria, when after the solemnities were completed he was expecting the clergy to come to his banquet, in a place near the sea he sees from afar a game of boys at the seashore, imitating, as is wont to happen, the Bishop and those things which it is the custom to perform in the churches. But when he watched the boys more intently and for a longer time, he sees that certain things even more secret and mystical were being performed by them. Disturbed, he immediately orders the clergy to be called to him, and shows them what he himself was seeing from afar. Then, having dismissed them, he orders all the boys to be seized and brought to him. And when they were present, he asks what their game was, and what they had done or how. They, as such an age has it, were at first afraid to deny it: then they reveal the deed in order, and confess that certain catechumens had been baptized by them through Athanasius, who had been the one who simulated the Bishop in that game. Then he, diligently inquiring from those who were said to be baptized what they had been asked and what they had answered, and at the same time from him who had asked, when he sees that everything was consistent according to the rite of our religion, it is handed down that, having conferred with the council of the clergy, he decided that for those upon whom water had been poured with the interrogations and responses intact, the baptism ought not to be repeated: but that those things which are the custom of the priests should be fulfilled: but Athanasius and those who had seemed to be either presbyters or ministers in that game, having called their parents, he hands over under the adjuration of GOD to be nurtured by his Church. This is what Rufinus says about Athanasius.

The eighth and final reason is not worth a penny. For to the law and to the testimony: not to Trismegistus or the oracles of the Sibyls: which we willingly leave to the Anabaptists, so that it may happen to them according to that trite saying: Such lips, such lettuces.

IV. And finally there are some among the Anabaptists who attempt to elude by a double devised sophism that primary foundation of infant baptism, taken from chapter 19, 14 of Matthew, where the Savior says: Suffer the little children to come to me: For of such is the kingdom of heaven. For first they urge the pronoun τοιούτων: Since the Savior did not say τούτων: Of these: but τοιούτων of such: So that Christ by this pronoun does not denote the infants themselves: but rather the adults, those who are humble, simple, and innocent in the manner of infants: or as the Apostle speaks, who are children and little ones in malice: 1 Cor. 14, 20. Then from the word or phrase (suffer them to come) they gather that the discourse of CHRIST is not about infants, but about children already possessing some use of reason: because he did not say: Suffer that the little children be carried to me; but, that they come to me. Now those who are more adult come: But infants are carried.

But both sophistications are overturned from the foundation by the text itself. For as regards the former, the whole evangelical history proves the contrary: The little children had been brought to CHRIST, so that he might lay his hands upon them. The Apostles were taking this ill. Therefore CHRIST rebukes them, saying: Suffer the little children to come to me. With this reason added: Because of such is the kingdom of heaven. Now if anyone should imagine in the Anabaptist sense that this latter member of the speech of CHRIST was not directed to those children, a most inept structure and meaning of the words of CHRIST would emerge, which nowhere coheres: namely this: You Apostles do not forbid that these children come to me: Because of the adults, who are simple as children, is the kingdom of heaven. Then as regards the pronoun τοιούτων, it is to be noted that the causal particle γὰρ, For, has been added: which again necessarily adapts these words of CHRIST to those children: as those who for that reason are not to be forbidden, Because of such is the kingdom of heaven. Finally, CHRIST did not simply say τοιούτων, but τῶν τοιούτων, of these such. Where the article again points the finger to the children, and binds the pronoun τοιούτων to them.

The latter sophistication is easily refuted from the Greek text. For Luke, chapter 18, 15, calls those children τὰ βρέφη: Which designation is proper to infants. Thus the text has προσέφερον αὐτῷ, they brought (and not they led) to him: and as Matthew speaks more clearly, προσηνέχθη αὐτῷ, they were brought to him. Therefore those children did not themselves come to CHRIST, but were brought, and according to the prophecy of Isaiah 49, 22, were carried to Christ either in arms or upon shoulders. Finally, as regards the word (To come), it is general, and is predicated in a broader sense of those who approach in any way, whether they are carried, or are conveyed, or walk themselves.

Latin:

Historia ipsa apud Ruffinum sic habet:

TEmpore, quo apud Alexandriam, Petri Martyris diem Alexander Episcopus agebat, cùm post completa solemnia, conventuros ad convivium suum Clericos expectaret, in loco mari vicino, videt eminùs ludum puerorũ ad littus maris, imitancium, ut fieri solet, Episcopum, atq́; ea quæ in Ecclesijs geri mos est. Sed cùm intentiùs diutiusvè pueros inspectaret, videt ab his geri quædam etiam secretiora & mystica. Perturbatus illicò ad se vocari jubet Clericos, atquè eis, quid eminùs ipse videret, ostẽdit. Tùm his dimissis, jubet pueros omnes comprehensos, ad se perducere. Cumq́; adessent, quis eis ludus, & quid egissent vel quomodo, percunctatur. Illi, ut talis habet ætas, pavidi negare primò: deindè rem gestam per ordinem pandunt, & baptizatos à se esse quosdam catechumenos confitentur per Athanasium, qui ludi illius simulatus fuerat Episcopus. Tum ille diligenter inquirens ab his qui baptizari dicebantur, quid interrogati fuerint, quidve responderint: simul & ab eo, qui interrogaverat: ubi videt, secũdum religionis nostræ ritum cuncta constare, collocutus cum Concilio Clericorum statuisse traditur, illis, quibus integris interrogationibus & responsionibus aqua fuerat infusa, iterari baptismum non debere: sed adimpleri ea, quæ à Sacerdotibus mos est: Athanasium verò atquè eos, quos ludus ille vel Presbyteros habere visus fuerat vel ministros, convocatis parentibus, sub DEI obtestatione tradit Ecclesiæ suæ nutriendos. Hæc Ruffinus de Athanasio.

Octava & postrema ratio non unus est teruntij. Ad legem enim & ad testimonium: non ad Trismegistum aut oracula Sibyllarum: quæ Anabaptistis ultrò relinquimus, ut eveniat illis secundum tritum illud: Qualia labra, tales lactucæ.

IV. Ac postremò sunt ex Anabaptistis, qui gemino excogitato sophismate eludere conantur primarium illud Pædobaptismi fundamentum, petitum ex cap. 19, 14. Matthæi, ubi Servator inquit: Sinite parvulos ad me venire: Talium enim est regnum cœlorum. Primùm enim urgent pronomen τοιούτων : Siquidem Servator non dixerit, τούτων: Horum: sed τοιούτων talium: Ita ut Christus hoc pronomine non notaril infantes ipsos: sed adultos potiùs eos, qui infantum more sint humiles, simplices & innocentes: vel ut Apostolus loquitur, qui pueri & parvuli sunt malitiâ: 1. Cor. 14, 20. Deindè ex verbo sive phrasi (sinite eos venire) colligunt, non de infantibus, sed de pueris, jam aliquo rationis usu pollentib9, sermonem esse CHRISTO: propterea quòd non dixerit: Sinite ut parvuli ad me portentur; sed, ut ad me veniant. Jam adultiores veniunt: Infantes verò portantur.

Sed utraque sophisticatio ex textu ipso funditùs evertitur. Nam quoad priorem, tota historia Evangelica contrarium evincit: Adducti erant parvuli ad CHRISTUM, ut manus ipsis imponeret. Hoc ægrè ferebant Apostoli. Objurgat ergò ipsos CHRISTUS, dicens: Sinite parvulos ad me venire. Hâc adjectâ ratione: Quia talium sit regnum cœlorum. Jam si quis fingat sensu Anabaptistico, posterius hoc membrum orationis CHRISTI non ad pueros illos directum fuisse, ineptissima, & nuspiam cohærens emerget verborum CHRISTI structura & sententia: nempè talis: Vos Apostoli nolite prohibere, quo minùs pueri isti ad me veniant: Quia adultorum, qui sunt simplices ut pueri, est regnum cœlorum. Deindè quoad pronomen πώτων, notandum est, adjectam esse particulam causalem γδ, Enim: quæ rursus necessariò verba hæc CHRISTI ad pueros illos accommodat: ut qui ideò non sint prohibendi, Quia talium sit regnum cœlorum. Tandem non simpliciter dixit CHRISTUS τοιούτων, sed τῶν τοιούτων, horum talium. Ubi Articulus rursus digitum intendit ad pueros, & pronomen τοιούτων ad eos adstringit.

Posterior Sophisticatio ex textu Græco facilè eliditur. Lucas enim cap. 18, 15. pueros illos vocat τὰ βρέφη: Quæ notatio Infantum propria est. Sic textus habet προσέφερον αὐτῷ, attulerunt (non verò adduxerunt) ad ipsum: & ut Matthæus clariùs loquitur, προσηνέχθη αὐτῷ, allati sunt ad ipsum. Non ergò ipsimet pueri illi venerunt ad CHRISTUM, sed allati, & secundum vaticinium Jesaiæ 49, 22. vel in ulnis, vel super humeris portati fuerunt ad Christum. Tandem quoad Verbum (Venire) id generale est, & latiore sensu prædicatur de ijs, qui quovis modo appropinquant, sive gestentur, sive vehantur, sive ipsi incedant.


### Chapter Four

On the Effect of Baptism: and its Necessity, and Practical Use.

Just as it is the nature and quality of any Sacrament whatsoever, both of the Old and of the New Testament, regarding its use and fruit: that it partly has a seal in common with the remaining Sacraments: but partly indeed a proper one,

and a signatum adequate to itself, nay, incommunicable to the remaining Sacraments: as has been shown with sufficient accuracy in the doctrine concerning the Sacraments in general: so also a twofold effect of Baptism is given: one common: the other proper: but each again divisible into its own species.

It is common, in that it is σφραγὶς, a seal of the promise, annexed to the Word, for the sake of strengthening our weakness. This, subdivided again, is twofold, Internal and External.

The internal consists in this, that Baptism is a Seal of the righteousness of faith, and of our salvation, Rom. 4:11. For we see that it is also arranged among men in such a way that that which has been confirmed between contracting parties by words, writing, and Seal, is held as ratified and inviolable. In the same manner, GOD also wished to provide for his paternal affection toward us, not only by a bare word, but also by this sacramental seal, so that our faith might have that in which it can be more safely and firmly rooted. Whence Baptism to St. Peter is ἐπερώτημα, a stipulation, or as Oecumenius rendered it, an earnest and pledge of a good conscience with GOD, 1 Pet. 3:21. For just as for the Jurisconsults a stipulation is such a conception of words, by which he who is questioned answers that he will give or do that which he was asked: l. stipulationum alia, § stipulatio ff. de verb. obligationibus: So in Baptism, GOD, being about to enter into a covenant with us, under the condition of faith and obedience, concerning which we are questioned and answer affirmatively, receives us into grace.

The external end or effect of Baptism, and that a common one, consists in the external marking: for just as the other Sacraments, so Baptism also, regarding external ecclesiastical profession, acts as a token or some mark, by which the people of GOD are distinguished from the peoples of other religions. But concerning this common use or fruit of Baptism, theologians easily agree: nor is it properly controverted today. We therefore judge that a fuller explanation of both pertains rather to the ecclesiastical pulpit than to the Academic Chair.

The proper use or effect of Baptism is that which Scripture assigns to it as its specific property, distinguished from all other Sacraments, both of the Old and New Testament, as if by a certain specific characteristic. The Holy Spirit Himself has established four primary and distinct species of this proper effect, through the mediation of which that final and more remote end, which consists in salvation and eternal blessedness, may at last be obtained by us, Tit. 3, 5. 1. Petr. 3, 21. The first species is the washing or cleansing from sins through the water of baptism: the second is the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, while as many of us as are baptized, put on CHRIST. The third is regeneration or renewal in the Holy Spirit: the fourth is adoption as sons of GOD. Concerning each of which we must examine more accurately on account of the controversies of our age.

Latin:

De Effectu Baptismi: ejusdemque Necessitate, & Usu Practico.

QUemadmodum cujuslibet Sacramenti, tàm Veteris tàm Novi Testamenti, ea est, quoad usum & fructum, natura & affectio: ut partim commune cum reliquis Sacramentis habeat signaculum: partim verò proprium,

& sibi adæquatum, imò reliquis Sacramentis incommunicabile signatum obtineat: uti in doctrinâ de Sacramentis in genere accuratè satis est ostensum: ita Baptismi quoque geminus datur effectus: unus communis: alter proprius: sed uterque rursus in suas species divisibilis.

Communis est, ut sit σφραγὶς signaculum promissionis, verbo annexum, infirmitatis nostræ corroborandæ gratiâ. Hic subdivisus iterum geminus est, Internus & Externus.

Internus in eo consistit, ut Baptismus sit Signaculum sive Sigillum justitiæ fidei, & salutis nostræ, Rom. 4, 11. Sic enim humanitùs etiam comparatum esse videmus, ut id quod inter contrahentes, verbis, scripto & Sigillo firmatum est, illud pro rato & inviolato habeatur. Quem eundem in modum DEUS quoque non nudo tantùm verbo, sed & sigillo hoc Sacramentali, de paterno suo in nos affectu, cavere voluit, ut sic haberet fides nostra, in quo tutiùs ac firmiùs radicari queat. Undè Baptismus D. Petro est ἐπερώτημα stipulatio, vel ut Oecumenius reddidit, arrha & pignus bonæ conscientiæ cum DEO, 1. cap. 3, 21. Quemadmodum enim Jureconsultis stipulatio est talis verborum conceptio, quibus is, qui interrogatur, sed daturum facturumve id, quod interrogatus est, respondet: l. stipulationum alia, § stipulatio ff. de verb. obligationibus: Ita in Baptismo DEUS fœdus nobiscum initurus, sub conditione fidei & obedientiæ, de quâ interrogati, respondemus affirmatè, nos in gratiam recipit.

Externus Baptismi finis sive effectus, isque communis, in externâ signatione consistit: sicut enim cætera Sacramenta, ita Baptismus quoque quoad externam professionem Ecclesiasticam, habet se instar tesseræ sive notæ alicujus, quâ populus DEI, à reliquarum religionum populis discernitur. Verùm de utroque hoc communi usu sive fructu Baptismi, facilè inter Theologos convenit: neque propriè de eo hodiè controvertitur. Pleniorem proindè utriusque explicationem, ad suggestum potiùs Ecclesiasticum quàm ad Cathedram Academicam pertinere arbitramur.

Proprius Usus sive Effectus Baptismi est ille, quem Scriptura tanquàm specificum ipsi assignat, à reliquis omnibus Sacramentis tàm Veteris, quàm Novi Testamenti, tanquàm per proprietatem quandam specificam, distinctum. Ipse verò Spiritus Sanctus quatuor potissimùm distinctas species, Effectûs hujus proprij constituit: quibus demùm mediantibus, nobis ultimus ille & remotior finis, qui in salute & beatitudine æterna consistit, Tit. 3, 5. 1. Petr. 3, 21. obtingere possit. Prima species est Ablutio sive Mundatio à peccatis per aquam baptismi: altera Imputatio justitiæ Christi, dum quotquot baptizamur, CHRISTUM induimus. Tertia; Regeneratio sive Renovatio in Spiritu Sancto: Quarta: Adoptio in filios DEI. De quibus singulis propter nostri seculi controversias accuratiùs nobis dispiciendum fuerit.


### Chapter Four: I. On the Ablution or Cleansing from sins, which by the water of Baptism befals us

Concerning this first special Effect of Baptism, which is in the Ablution or Cleansing from sins, which is in the remission of sins, and is both conferred and prefigured through the external rite of washing or sprinkling, the Scripture of both Testaments discourses quite clearly in various places: as Ezek. 36:25, I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your filthiness. Zech. 13:1, In that day there shall be a fountain opened to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for the ablution of sins. Acts 2:38, Let every one be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of sins. Acts 22:16, Ananias to Paul: Arise, be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of CHRIST. Eph. 5:26, Christ sanctifies the Church, cleansing it with the washing of water by the Word. 1 Cor. 6:11, you are washed, you are sanctified, in the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, and in the Spirit of our GOD.

The subject of this Ablution or Cleansing is not either the soul alone, or the body alone: but the whole man, as he consists of soul and body: not indeed in the Calvinian sense, which imagines that the Water of Baptism washes away the filth of the body: but that the Holy Spirit within, without water, washes away the filth of the soul: but in the Orthodox sense. For because sin has passed into man in such a way that he is infected with sin according to both parts: certainly the whole man also is in need of this Sacrament of ablution: not to purge external and visible filth, the deposition of which is not Baptism: 1 Pet. 3:21. But those spiritual ones, which adhere most tenaciously to both body and soul, so that they cannot be washed away and removed except through this washing.

But the question is raised in this place concerning the Object of this cleansing, whether all sins, or only certain ones, are washed away and taken away in Baptism. We, instructed by the oracles of the Scriptures, firmly maintain that through the water of Baptism, by the power and operation of the Holy Spirit, the cleansing not of this or that sin, considered specifically, but generally of every sin whatsoever, namely both Original and Actual, and of this as much mortal as venial, as much past as future, truly comes to us.

This assertion of ours can be demonstrated chiefly by these reasons.

1. Without the Blood of Christ no remission of sins can take place: Hebr. 9, 22. If therefore in baptism we obtain remission of sins, as certainly we do obtain it, it is necessary that through the blood of Christ the water of baptism should exert this power. Whence more prudent theologians, among whom our blessed Luther holds the first place, establish that the blood of Christ, as an essential part, enters into the very substance of this sacrament. Now, however, the blood of Jesus Christ does not cleanse us from this or that sin, from this or that species of sin: but simply from all sin: John 1, 7. Therefore.

II. The power of the divine covenant extends to everything which in any way, or in any respect, can strip us of the grace of God: for which very reason this covenant of God is called an eternal covenant: as in Genesis 17, 13. This my covenant shall be an eternal covenant. And Hosea 2, 19. I will betroth you to me forever. Now, however, this eternal power of the divine covenant would falter if it were destined only for original sin, and not for all actual sins: or conversely, if it were destined only for these, and not also for the cleansing of that. Therefore.

But this our opinion is not to be snatched away according to the mind of the Calvinists, as if the grace of baptism could by no means be shaken off or lost through sins against conscience: which impiety we shall elsewhere, God willing, refute: but it is to be accepted in this way, that the covenant, once entered into with God in baptism, is never so evacuated by sins committed, on the part of God, that he who falls into sins after receiving baptism has no further use of it: but, if such a baptized sinner should afterwards repent, then he has no need of a new baptism, or a new plank, as the Romanists say, by which he might sail back and reach the port of divine grace: no more than he who has fallen into the sea needs a new ship, for whom it is enough if he returns to the original one in which he was: but if he performs penance for the sins committed, he may feel the fruit and benefit of the covenant entered into in baptism.

With these things thus established, they have erred gravely, not only the Pelagians and Clinici of old, of whom the former feigned that only actual sins were washed away by baptism: while the latter trifled that only past sins were removed, and therefore dreamed that the reception of baptism was to be deferred until the end of life, indeed until the very last breath: But even today the Romanists foster a clearly gross error, who contend that the use of baptism does not extend further than to infants and the newborn: and therefore that it expiates only past sins, which were committed in infantile age: and not subsequent ones. Which is the reason that they fashion two planks of salvation, one for infants, which is baptism, and which afterwards, if the infant reaching the age of reason sins, is utterly broken and is clearly useless: the other proper to adults, which is penance, by which alone, without any regard to the former plank, the washing or expiation of sins can afterwards be obtained by adults. St. Peter, 1 Peter 3, 20, compares baptism not to some broken plank of a ship: but to such an entire and firm ship, which acts like the ark of Noah: so that those who are in it do not need another plank or ship, but rather can boast of the stipulation of a good conscience with God. And if for the faithful of the Old Testament circumcision was the firmest plank of salvation throughout their whole life, by which, relying on it, they fought most successfully against the insults of all, indeed of the devil himself: why, I ask, or how would baptism be of a worse condition? which we have already shown to have the power of an eternal covenant. But we shall expressly, God willing, refute the prodigious impiety of this error below in the Article on Penance.

Now rather that controversy should be more accurately weighed by us, which has been variously agitated long ago concerning the mode of washing or cleansing from sin which is in baptism, and is today also being agitated quite sharply between us and the Romanists. Gregory is the author that in his time there were those who taught that sins in baptism are only superficially washed away and forgiven: concerning which error he says thus: What, I ask, is more unfaithful than this preaching? Since through the sacrament of faith, the soul, absolved from sins at the root, adheres to God alone: which he proves from those words of Christ, John 13, 10. He who is washed does not need except to wash his feet: but is clean all over. Thus Augustine complains in book 1 to Boniface, ch. 13. That it is falsely imputed to him and to all Catholics by Julian the Pelagian, as if they taught that in baptism full indulgence of sins is not given, nor are crimes taken away: but that they are only shaved, so that the roots of all sins are held in the evil flesh. But Augustine answers: Who, unless an infidel, would affirm this against the Pelagians? For we say that the indulgence of all sins is given, and crimes are taken away, not shaved.

The Synod of Trent vibrates the thunderbolt of anathema against those who say that not all that which has the true and proper nature of sin is taken away: but is only shaved or not imputed. Sess. 5, decr. 1, of June 17, 1546. Which decree is indeed entirely directed toward deceiving. For they so bend their style as if the Romanists felt the same as the orthodox: but meanwhile they betray themselves by their own evidence like mice, while through calumny they join these two things (to be shaved and not to be imputed) as if we established both of these, as if also the latter, namely, the non-imputation, were the same as being shaved: whereas we disapprove of the latter as heretical: but embrace the former as orthodox. To that end, indeed, these snares of theirs tend, that they may utterly deny that concupiscence, which remains in man after baptism, possesses the nature and definition of sin properly so called. Although, therefore, the Romanists feel with us to this extent, that 1. They concede that in baptism every sin is remitted, both original and actual, especially that which precedes baptism: 2. that they confess, although a full remission is made, yet not every evil of original sin is immediately taken away from the flesh of the reborn: but concupiscence remains, and other remnants of original sin, with which the reborn must be assiduously in conflict: yet in that which is the hinge of the matter, they dissent very much from us, in that the remission of sins, which we obtain in baptism,

Latin:

DE primo hoc speciali Effectu Baptismi, qui in Ablutione sive Mundatione a peccatis, quae est in remissione peccatorum, & per externum lotionis sive aspersionis ritum tam confertur, quam praefiguratur, Scriptura utriusque Testamenti satis perspicue passim disserit: ut Ezech. 36, 25. Effundam super vos aquam mundam, & mundabimini ab omnibus inquinamentis vestris. Zachar. 13, 1. In die illa, erit fons patens domui David, & habitantibus Hierosolymae in ablutionem peccatorum. Actor. 2, 38. Baptizetur unusquisq;, in nomine Jesu Christi, in remissionem peccatorum. Actor. 22, 16. Ananias ad Paulum: Surge baptizare, & ablue peccata tua, invocato nomine CHRISTI. Ephes. 5, 26. Christus sanctificat Ecclesiam, mundans eam lavacro aquae in Verbo. 1. Cor. 6, 11. abluti estis, sanctificati estis, in nomine Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI, & in Spiritu DEI nostri.

Ablutionis sive Mundationis hujus subjectum non est vel anima sola, vel corpus solum: sed totus homo, prout constat anima & corpore: non quidem sensu Calviniano, qui fingit, Aquam Baptismi abluere sordes corporis: Spiritum Sanctum vero intus sine aqua abluere sordes animae: sed sensu Orthodoxo. Quia enim peccatum ita in hominem pertransijt, ut secundum utramque partem peccato sit infectus: utique totus etiam homo ablutionis hujus Sacramento indiget: non ad expurgandas externas & aspectabiles sordes, quarum depositio non est Baptismus: 1. Petr. 3, 21. Sed spirituales illas, quae & corpori & animae tenacissime inhaerent, ut non nisi per hoc lavacrum ablui & tolli queant.

Quaeritur autem hoc loco de Objecto mundationis hujus, An omnia peccata, vel quaedam tantum in Baptismo abluantur & tollantur. Nos Scripturarum edocti oraculis firmiter statuimus, per aquam Baptismi, virtute & operatione Spiritus Sancti, non hujus vel illius peccati, in specie considerati: sed generatim omnis omnino peccati, nempe & Originalis & Actualis, & hujus tam mortalis, quam venialis, tam praeteriti, quam futuri, ablutionem nobis vere obtingere.

Assertio haec nostra hisce potissimum demonstrari potest rationibus.

1. Sine Sangvine Christi nulla potest fieri remissio peccatorum: Hebr. 9, 22. Si ergo in Baptismo nobis obtingit Remissio peccatorum, uti certè obtingit, necessum est, ut per sangvinem Christi virtutem hanc Aqua Baptismi exerat. Undè cordatiores Theologi, inter quos primas tenet B. Lutherus noster, statuunt, Sangvinem Christi, tanquàm partem essentialem ingredi ipsam substantiam Sacramenti hujus. Jam verò Sangvis JESU CHRISTI non emundat nos ab hoc vel ab illo peccato, ab hâc vel ab illâ specie peccati: sed simpliciter ab omni peccato: Joh. 1, 7. Ergò.

II. Fœderis divini vis se extendit ad omne id, quod quovis modo, aut respectu, Gratiâ DEI nos exuere potest: Quam ipsam ob causam fœdus hoc DEI nominatur fœdus æternum: ut Genes. 17, 13. Erit fœdus hoc meum in fœdus æternum. Et Hos. 2, 19. Desponsabo te mihi in sempiternum. Jam verò æterna hæc vis fœderis divini labasceret, si originali tantùm peccato, non verò actualibus omnibus expiandis: vel vice versa, si his tantùm, non verò illi etiam abluendo, esset destinatum. Ergò.

Est verò hæc nostra sententia, non secundum mentem Calvinianorum eò rapienda, quasi Baptismi gratia per peccata contra conscientiam, nullo prorsus pacto excuti aut amitti possit: Quam impietatem alibi σὺν θεῶ proteremus: Sed sic est accipienda, quòd fœdus, cum DEO semel in Baptismo initum, per admissa peccata, ex parte DEI, nunquàm ita evacuctur, ut nullum ejus usum ampliùs habeat, qui post perceptum baptismum, in peccata prolabitur: sed, si talis peccator baptizatus postmodùm resipiscat, tùm non novo baptismo, aut novâ tabulâ, uti Romanenses loquuntur, opus habeat, quâ ad portum gratiæ divinæ rursus enavigare & appellere possit: haud magis, ac qui in mare est prolapsus, non novâ navi indiget, cui satis est, si ad pristinam, in quâ erat, redeat: Sed si pœnitentiam de peccatis admissis agat, ut fœderis in baptismo initi fructum & beneficium sentiat.

Quibus ita constitutis graviter errarunt non modò jam olim Pelagiani & Clinici, quorum illi actualia tantùm peccata per baptismum ablui fingebant: hi verò, præterita tantùm peccata tolli nugabantur, ac proindè baptismi perceptionem ad finem usq; vitæ, imò ad extremum usq; halitum differendam esse somniabãt: Sed & hodiè crassum planè errorem fovent Romanenses, qui usum Baptismi contendunt, non latiùs se extendere, quàm ad infantes & recens natos: ac proindè præterita tantùm peccata, quæ in infantili ætate sunt admissa, expiare: non verò sequentia. Quæ causa est, quòd duas tabulas salutis effingunt, Unam pro infantibus, quæ sit Baptismus, quæque postmodùm si infans ad usum rationis discretum perveniens peccet, penitùs frangatur, ac planè inutilis sit: alteram adulterorum propriam, quæ est Pœnitentia, quâ solâ, sine ullo intuitu ad priorem tabulam, postmodùm adultis peccatorum ablutio sive expiatio, obtingere possit. D. Petrus 1. cap. 3, 20. Baptismum comparat non tabulæ alicui fractæ navis: sed tali integræ & firmæ navi, quæ se habeat instar arcæ Novæ: ut qui in ea sunt, usque adeò aliâ tabulâ aut navi non indigeant, ut potiùs gloriari possint de stipulatione bonæ conscientiæ cum DEO. Et si fidelibus Veteris Testamenti Circumcisio per omnem vitam fuit firmissima tabula salutis, quâ nixi adversus omnium, imò ipsius Diaboli insultus felicissimè pugnarunt : cur quæso, aut quomodo Baptismus deterioris esset conditionis? quem æterni fœderis vim habere, jam ostendimus. Sed hujus erroris prodigiosam impietatem ex professo συν̀ Θεῷ refutabimus, infrà Articulo de Pœnitentiâ.

Jam potiùs illa controversia nobis accuratiùs expendenda fuerit, quæ de Modo ablutionis sive Mundationis à peccato, quæ sit in Baptismo, variè & jam olim agitata fuit, & hodie quoque inter nos & Romanenses satis acriter agitatur. Autore est Gregorius, suo tempore fuisse, qui docerent, peccata in baptismo superficietenus tantùm ablui & dimitti: de quo errore sic ille: Quid quæso hac prædicatione infidelius? cum per fidei Sacramentum, animæ peccatis radicitùs absoluta, soli DEO inhæreat : id quod probat ex iis Christi verbis, Joh. 13, 10. Qui lotus est, non indiget, nisi ut pedes lavet : sed est mundus totus. Sic Augustinus conqueritur lib. 1. ad Bonifacium, c. 13. Sibi & Catholicis omnibus falsò imponi à Juliano Pelagiano, quasi docerent, in Baptismo non dari plenam peccatorum indulgentiam, nec auferri crimina: sed radi duntaxat, ut omnium peccatorum radices in malâ carne teneantur. Sed respondet Augustinus : Quis hoc adversus Pelagianos, nisi infidelis, affirmet ? Dicimus enim dari omnium peccatorum indulgentiam, & auferri crimina, non radi.

Synodus Tridētina anathematis fulmen vibrat in eos, qui non totum id, quod veram & propriam peccati rationem habet, tolli : sed radi tantùm aut non imputari dicunt. Sess. 5. decr. 1, d. 17. Junij, an. 1546. Quod sanè decretum totum ad decipiendum est directum.
