Nam ita inflectunt stylum, ac si cum orthodoxis sentirent Romanenses: sed interim suo se indicio soricum instar produnt, dum per calumniam, duo isthæc conjungunt (Radi & non imputari) quasi utrumque istud nos statuamus, quasi etiam posterius hoc nempè, τὸ non imputari, idem sit quod radi: cum nos hoc, tanquàm hæreticum improbemus : illud autem ut orthodoxum amplectamur. Eò nimirùm tendunt hæ ipsorum insidiæ, ut concupiscentiam, quæ in homine post Baptismum est reliqua, naturam & rationem peccati propriè sic dicti obtinere prorsus negent. Quanquam ergò eatenùs nobiscum sentiunt Romanenses, quod 1. Concedunt, in baptismo remitti peccatum omnè tùm Originale, tùm Actuale, maximè id, quod Baptismum antecedit: 2. quòd fatentur, licèt plena fiat remissio, non tamen ex carne renatorum mox tollatur omne malum peccati Originalis: sed remaneat concupiscentia, aliæque peccati Originalis reliquiæ, cum quibus sit renatis assiduè conflictandum: tamen in eo, quod cardo est negotij, plurimùm à nobis dissident, quòd remissionem peccatorum, quæ nobis in Baptismo obtingit,


### Chapter Four: Quaestio: Whether through Baptism likewise all punishments of sins are washed away and taken away?

they do not understand in the Apostolic sense, concerning not imputing: but concerning the real removal or abolition of all sin, so that there is nothing more in the regenerate which obtains the character of sin and properly so called. Whence the same Synod in the same canon establishes that those regenerate through baptism are innocent, immaculate, pure, and concerning Imputation, the preceding Anathema prohibits. Thus, therefore, they slay themselves with the sword of contradiction while they attack our opinion or doctrine concerning Imputation. For what else is it to remit sins than not to impute them.

But they object to us that Christ is preached in the Scriptures not as such a Redeemer who at least does not impute, but who takes away the sins of the world, and who blots out our iniquities. Which predicates would not suit Christ, would be false in truth, or merely apparent and deceptive, if sin were merely remitted, but not thoroughly abolished in the regenerate. For if He did not truly take away sins, certainly He did not need to truly die: nor did He truly free us from the power of the devil: but only imputatively: and thus we shall be members of Christ only imputatively, not in reality.

I answer, that this argument savors of Pelagianism. Furthermore, it is shamefully mistaken under a false definition of the word Imputing: which the sophists take for a merely human λογισμῷ [reasoning], which often consists in opinion, and is accustomed to be verbal rather than real. Now, however, we establish the seat or subject of this Imputation not as our own, but as the mind of GOD Himself: and therefore we define the word Imputation not through human, but through the very λογισμὸν [reasoning] of GOD, which is simply infallible. For what, I pray, can be truer than that which is thus established to be by GOD, who is truth itself? Since there is no essence of any things, except insofar as GOD considers them in His conscious mind, and in His conforming will wills and commands them to be? Therefore our doctrine stands firm and immovable, namely that sin is most truly and most really removed and abolished, insofar as it is removed from the eyes of GOD the avenger and judge, that is, remitted and pardoned through grace, even if it were still visible and obvious in the eyes of all men. Therefore, as far as the present question pertains, original sin is indeed taken away and abolished in baptism: But it is taken away by remitting, and that by not imputing: that is, it is not the act and nature of sin itself considered in itself that is taken away: but only the guilt of sin, so that it cannot be for our destruction. For as Augustine speaks, sin passes away in guilt: but remains in act: and as the same explains himself more clearly, sin is remitted in baptism, not so that it does not exist: but so that it is not imputed: lib. 1. de nupt. & concupisc. ad Valerium, cap. 27. But concerning this controversy, and specifically, How concupiscence is taken away through baptism in the regenerate: it was expressly disputed in the Article concerning original sin.

Furthermore, in this place the question is moved concerning the Punishment of sin, Whether all punishments of sins are similarly washed away and taken away through baptism, just as all guilt? Among the Scholastics, Thomas would define this question quite orthodoxly, if only he did not afterwards viciously refer those things which he wrote correctly to the opus operatum. Thus, however, he [writes] part. 3. quaest. 69. art. 2. Through Baptism we are incorporated into the passion and death of Christ, according to that in Rom. 6. If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with Christ. From which it is clear that the passion of Christ is communicated to the baptized man as a remedy, as if he himself had suffered and died. But the passion of Christ is a sufficient satisfaction for all the sins of all men, and therefore he who is baptized is freed from the guilt of all punishment owed to him for sins, as if he himself had sufficiently satisfied for all his sins. But that we may unfold this question more accurately, two distinctions are especially to be premised: one of Punishments: the other of Objects. For first, one punishment is eternal, another temporal. Each of these again is twofold, either contracted, which the Scholastic doctors call penalty: or attracted. Contracted: such as that which inheres in us from original sin. Attracted: which each one attracts to himself by a peculiar offense, as thieves, murderers, adulterers, and other criminals of that kind, attract to themselves punishments sanctioned by civil laws, and indeed even by divine ones. Then, however, regarding objects: The remission of punishment is one thing regarding GOD: another regarding men. These things being premised, the question is answered thus: 1. Regarding GOD, there is in Baptism a washing away from every punishment owed to sins, both eternal and any temporal one whatsoever. For because the Apostle is a witness, Rom. 6, 8, that we are baptized into the death of Christ, and therefore that we, having thus died to sin, live with Christ: it is a consequence that the merit of the passion and death of Christ is communicated to the baptized just as if they themselves had made expiation for their sins by suffering and dying in their own person: Which having been truly done, no punishment remains before GOD which would need another expiation. 2. Then, however, regarding men, temporal or civil punishment is not taken away through Baptism, which each one has attracted to himself by a peculiar offense. For example: If anyone had committed homicide before receiving Baptism, the capital punishment is not taken away through Baptism. The reason for the assertion is taken from the common rule: The Gospel and the kingdom of Christ does not abrogate polities. If, however, the Magistrate were to remit something from the rigor of the law in honor of the Sacrament and the Christian faith, he would not sin: provided that it were done 1. without scandal: 2. without fear and danger of a more serious evil. 3. As regards those kinds of punishments which are contracted from original sin, Baptism indeed has the power of taking them away: for the Apostle is a witness, Rom. 6, 5, that through baptism we have been made partakers not only of the death of Christ, but also of His Resurrection. But baptism does not take these away in this life: rather, it leaves them to be taken away only in the life to come. The reason for this is commonly assigned as threefold: 1. Because we are to be conformed to Christ through Baptism: yet we ought not to be in a better condition than He was. But He was made subject to those sufferings resulting from sin. Therefore it could not be that we should be immune from the same. 2. Augustine, book 1, On the Baptism of Infants, chapter 39, determined that this very thing was entirely useful to us for the sake of spiritual exercise, namely, that under these, man, struggling from time to time against concupiscence, might have material for acquiring a crown. A type of this matter preceded in the fact that the Lord left some nations in the land of Canaan, in order to instruct the Israelite people in them, and that their sons might learn to contend with enemies and have the habit of warring. Judg. 3, 1 and 2. The use of this exercise, however, is for learning humility, for conciliating the fear of GOD, for acquiring knowledge of oneself, for conceiving a stimulus in the pursuit of good and the flight from evil, and similar things. 3. Because, if it were done otherwise, many would have taken up Baptism not so much for the sake of CHRIST and the glory of the future life, as for the convenience of this life. There can be added in the fourth place also that which these remnants do toward manifesting the equity of the divine judgment, which was pronounced in the sentence of death against Adam; a certain particle of which sentence had to redound to all the descendants of Adam. Finally, as regards concupiscence, which has joined to it difficulty toward the good and a propensity toward evil; that very thing also is indeed not taken away in Baptism: but yet its right is greatly infringed, both because its motions, for the most part, are not so vehement and unbridled as they are in the unregenerate: nor even as frequent as in them: and because in Baptism that grace is conferred by which these can be resisted, and by which the assaults of these motions can be weakened and repelled.

But enough and more than enough concerning this first species of the Effect of Baptism.

Latin:

non intelligunt sensu Apostolico, de non imputando: sed de reali ablatione sive abolitione peccati omnis, ita, ut nihil ampliùs sit in renatis, quod rationem peccati ac propriè sic dicti obtineat. Unde eadem Synodus eodem canone, renatos per baptismum statuit innocentes, immaculatos, puros & innoxios: quod ne de Imputatione intelligere videantur, prohibet præcedens Anathema. Sic ergò semetipsos contradistionis gladio jugulant, dùm nostram impugnant sententiam sive doctrinam de Imputatione. Quid enim est aliud remittere peccata, quàm non imputare illa.

Sed objiciunt nobis id, quòd Christus prædicetur in Scripturis non talis Redemtor, qui saltem non imputet, sed qui tollat peccata mundi, & qui iniquitates nostras deleat. Quæ prædicata Christo non convenirent, in rei veritate forent falsa, aut apparentia duntaxat & deceptoria, si remitteretur duntaxat, non autem penitùs aboleretur in renatis peccatum. Si enim non verè sustulit peccata, certè nec verè mori debuit: nec nos verè liberavit à potestate diaboli: sed imputativè duntaxat: & sic imputativè tantùm nos erimus mēbra Christi, non reverâ.

Respondeo, Pelagianismum 1. resipere argumentum hoc. Deindè verò turpiter illud fallit, sub falsâ definitione verbi Imputandi: quod pro humano tantùm λογισμῷ, qui in opinando sæpiùs consistit, & verbalis magis, quàm realis esse consuevit, sophistæ accipiunt. Jam verò nos Imputationis hujus sedem sive subjectum non nostram, sed ipsius DEI mentem constituimus: ac proindè Imputationis verbum, non per humanum, sed per ipsius DEI λογισμὸν, qui simpliciter est infallibilis, definimus. Quid enim obsecro potest esse veriùs, quàm quod à DEO, qui est ipsissima veritas, sic statuitur esse? cùm nihil sit quarumvis rerum essentia, nisi quatenùs DEUS in mente suâ conscia reputat, & in conformi voluntate vult & jubet eas esse? Ergò firma & immota stat nostra doctrina, nempè verifsimè & realissimè ablatum & abolitum esse peccatum, quatenùs illud ex oculis DEI vindicis & judicis est amotum, hoc est, per gratiam remifsum & condonatu, licèt id omnium in hominum oculis adhuc esset adspectabile atque obvium. Quod ergò ad præsentem quæstionem attinet, tollitur sanè atque aboletur in baptismo peccatum originale: Sed remittendo tollitur, atque id non imputando: hoc est, tollitur non ipse peccati actus & natura in se considerata: sed peccati reatus duntaxat, ut ad salutem nobis esse haud possit. Nam ut Augustinus loquitur, peccatum transit reatu: manet autem actu: & ut idem clariùs se explicat peccatum in baptismo remittitur, non ut non sit: sed ut non imputetur: lib. 1. de nupt. & concupisc. ad Valerium, cap. 27. Verùm de hâc controversiâ, & in specie, Quomodo concupiscentia per baptismum in renatis tollatur: Articulo de peccato originis, ex professo disputatum fuit.

Porrò autem hoc loco de Pœnâ peccati movetur quæstio, An per baptismum similiter omnes pœnæ peccatorum abluantur & tollantur, sicut omnis culpa? Inter Scholasticos Thomas satis orthodoxe quaestionem hanc definiret, si modo ea, quae recte scripsit, postmodum non vitiose ad opus operatum referret. Sic autem ille part. 3. quaest. 69. art. 2. Per Baptismum incorporamur passioni & morti Christi, juxta illud Rom. 6. Si mortui sumus cum Christo, credimus, quod etiam simul vivemus cum Christo. Ex quo patet, quod homini baptizato communicatur passio Christi ad remedium, ac si ipse passus & mortuus esset. Passio autem Christi est sufficiens satisfactio pro omnibo peccatis omnium hominum, & ideo ille qui baptizatur, liberatur a reatu omnis poenae sibi debitae pro peccatis, ac si ipse sufficienter satisfecisset pro omnibus peccatis suis. Sed ut accuratius hanc quaestionem evolvamus, duae potissimum distinctiones sunt praemittendae: una Poenarum: altera Objectorum. Primum enim poena alia est aeterna, alia temporalis. Haec utraque rursus duplex est, vel contracta, quam Scholastici doctores poenalitatem vocant: vel attracta. Contracta: ut quae ex originali peccato nobis inhaeret. Attracta: quam quisque peculiari delicto sibi attrahit, ut fures, homicidae, adulteri, id genus facinorosi alij, poenas legibus civilibus, imo divinis etiam sancitas, sibi attrahunt. Deinde vero quoad objecta: Remissio poenae alia est quoad DEUM: alia quoad homines. His praemissis ad propositum ζητημα sic respondetur: 1. Quoad DEUM, fit in Baptismo ablutio ab omni poena peccatis debita, tum aeterna, tum temporali qualibet. Quia enim testis est Apostolus, Rom. 6, 8. nos in mortem Christi baptizari, ac proinde nos sic peccato mortuos, cum Christo vivere: consequens est, baptizatis meritum passionis & mortis Christi communicari perinde, ac si ipsi patiendo moriendoque in persona propria peccatorum expiationem fecissent: Qua sane facta, nulla manet poena reliqua apud DEUM, quae alia expiatione indigeret. 2. Deinde vero quoad homines, per Baptismum non tollitur poena temporalis sive civilis, quam peculiari delicto sibi quisque attraxit. Exempli gratia: Si quis ante perceptum Baptismum homicidium commisisset, per Baptismum capitalis poena non tollitur. Ratio assertionis ex vulgari regula sumitur: Evangelium & regnum Christi politias non abrogat. Si quid tamen in honorem Sacramenti & fidei Christianae Magistratus a rigore legis remitteret, non peccaret: dummodo id 1. sine scandalo: 2. sine gravioris mali metu atque periculo fieret. 3. Quoad ea poenarum genera, quae ex peccato primitivo sunt contracta, Baptismus vim quidem habet ista auferendi: Testis est enim Apostolus, Rom. 6, 5, nos per baptismum, uti mortis Christi, sic etiam Resurrectionis ejusdem consortes factos esse. Verum non tollit ista baptismus hac in vita: sed relinquit ea demum in futura vita auferenda. Causa hujus rei vulgo triplex assignatur: 1. Quia conformandi sumus Christo per Baptismum: non autem melioris conditionis esse debemus, quam ipse fuit. Ipse autem passionibus istis ex peccato redundantibus, factus est obnoxius. Fieri ergo non potuit, ut nos ab ijsdem essemus immunes. 2. Augustinus lib. 1. de Baptismo parvulorum cap. 39. statuit, hoc ipsum omninò nobis utile fuisse, propter exercitium spirituale, nempè ut sub istis, homo subinde contra concupiscentiam depugnans, acquirendæ coronæ materiam haberet. Cujus rei typus in eo præcessit, quod Dominus gentes aliquas in terrâ Canaan reliquit, ut in eis Israëliticum populum erudiret, & discerent filij eorum certare cum hostibus, & habere consuetudinem præliandi. Judic. 3, 1. & 2. Usus autem istius exercitij est ad humilitatem discendam, ad timorem DEI conciliandum, suiipsius cognitionem comparandam, ad concipiendum stimulum in studio boni, & fugâ mali, & similibus. 3. Quia, si secus fieret, Baptismum non tam propter CHRISTUM, & futuræ vitæ gloriam, quàm propter commoditatem hujus vitæ multi fuissent assumturi. Addi potest quarto loco & illud, quod reliquiæ hæ faciant ad manifestandam judicij divini æquitatem, quod est in sententiâ mortis pronunciatum contra Adamum; cujus sententiæ particula aliqua, ad universos Adæ posteros redundare debuit. Tandem quod ad concupiscentiam attinet, quæ habet sibi conjunctam difficultatem ad bonum, pronitatem ad malum; ea ipsa quoq; non aufertur quidem in Baptismo: sed tamen jus ejus plurimùm infringitur, tùm quia motus ejus, ut plurimùm non sunt ita vehementes & effrænes, quemadmodum sunt in non renatis: neq; etiam tam frequentes, quàm in istis: tùm quia in Baptismo ea confertur gratia, quâ resisti istis, quâq; debilitari & repelli insultus istorum motuum possunt.

Sed de primâ hâc specie Effectus Baptismi plus satis.


### Chapter Four: II. Imputation of the righteousness of Christ

II. Imputation of the righteousness of CHRIST.

The other species of the proper Effect of Baptism consists in the Imputation of the righteousness of CHRIST: concerning which Holy Scripture discourses quite magnificently, as often as it shows that we are inserted into CHRIST through Baptism, that we put on CHRIST, that we put on the garments of salvation and the vestments of righteousness. To which these passages of Scripture pertain: Isa. 61, 10. I will rejoice with joy in the LORD, and my soul shall exult in my GOD: because He has clothed me with the garments of salvation: and has surrounded me with the vestment of righteousness. Gal. 3, 27. Whoever of you have been baptized into CHRIST, have put on CHRIST. This truly happens in Baptism, because the righteousness and innocence of CHRIST is truly imputed to each and all regenerated believers, so that in the sight of GOD they are glorious, not having spot or wrinkle, or anything of this kind; but that they may be holy and immaculate. Eph. 5, 27. But of what members this imputation consists, and what its true and genuine form is, was shown more fully above in the Article concerning the justification of a sinful man before GOD.

III. Regeneration or Renewal.

The third species of the proper Effect which Baptism obtains is Renewal or Regeneration, taken more strictly, by which it comes about that man, who had been a slave to sin, having been freed from sin, is asserted into the service of GOD. For thus Scripture, Rom. 6, 4, 20, 21. We have been buried together with CHRIST through Baptism into death, that just as He rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life. As therefore you have presented your members into the service of uncleanness and iniquity, unto iniquity: so now present your members into the service of righteousness, unto sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were made free from righteousness. Gal. 6, 15. In CHRIST JESUS you are a new creature, so that according to that Rom. 7, 22, the regenerated man delights in the law of GOD according to the inner man. This more special effect arises, however, from the two prior ones preceding. For in Baptism, through the washing away of sin and of the eternal punishment of sin, the purpose of sinning is simultaneously taken away from the baptized; and through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, the pursuit of new obedience is conferred. Nor is it to be determined that Infants after Baptism are therefore destitute of this Effect, because they are unable for the acts of good works. For one must distinguish here between the habit or first act, and the second act. The inability to perform good by the second act does not happen to Infants from a defect of this spiritual Gift: but from a bodily impediment: concerning which the physicists speak. Indeed, even regarding the second Act, this Effect cannot or ought not to be simply denied to them. For if infants through Baptism, by means of the power of the Holy Spirit, conceive such faith, although how they believe is entirely unknown to us: then the same Holy Spirit will work the Effect of faith, namely the Act of good works, in them, although the manner of these does not fall under our senses.

Latin:

II Imputatio justitiæ CHRISTI.

ALtera species proprij Effectus Baptismi consistit in Imputatione justitiæ CHRISTI: de quâ Scriptura Sacra satis magnificè disserit, quoties ostendit, nos per Baptismum CHRISTO inseri, CHRISTUM induere, induere vestimenta salutis ac indumenta justitiæ. Quò pertinent hæc Scripturæ loca: Esa. 61, 10. Gaudens gaudebo in DOMINO, & exultabit anima mea in DEO meo: quia induit me vestimentis salutis: & indumento justitiæ circumdedit me. Galat. 3, 27. Quicunq; in CHRISTUM baptizati estis, CHRISTUM induistis. Fit verò hoc in Baptismo, quia singulis ac universis regeneratis fidelibus, verè imputatur justitia ac innocentia CHRISTI ita ut in conspectu DEI sint gloriosi, non habentes maculam aut rugam, aut aliquid hujusmodi; sed ut sint sancti & immaculati. Eph. 5, 27. Quibus verò membris hæc imputatio constet, & quæ vera ac genuina ejus sit forma, suprà in Articulo de justificatione hominis peccatoris coram DEO fusiùs fuit ostensum.

III. Regeneratio sive Renovatio.

TErtia species Effectus proprij, quem Baptismus obtinet, est Renovatio sive Regeneratio, strictiùs accepta, quâ fit, ut homo, qui peccato servus fuerat, peccato liberatus, in servitutem DEI asseratur. Sic enim Scriptura, Rom. 6, 4, 20. 21. Conseputti sumus cum CHRISTO per Baptismum in mortem, ut quemadmodum ipse surrexit à mortuis per gloriam Patris, ita & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus. Sicut ergò exhibuistis membra vestra in servitutem immundiciæ & iniquitati, ad iniquitatem : ita nunc exhibite membra vestra in servitutem justitiæ, in sanctificationem. Cum enim servi esfetis peccati, liberi facti estis justitiæ. Galat. 6, 15. In CHRISTO JESU nova estis creatura, ita ut secundum illud Rom. 7, 22. homo regeneratus condelectetur legi DEI secundum interiorem hominem. Exurgit verò specialior iste effectus, ex duobus prioribus præcedentibus. In Baptismo enim per ablutionem à peccato & ab æternâ peccati pœnâ, simul aufertur à baptisatis propositum peccandi; & per sanctificationem Spiritus Sancti, confertur studium novæ obedientiæ. Neq; statuendum est, Infantes post Baptismum Effectu hoc ideò destitui, quia inhabiles sunt ad actus bonorum operum. Distingvendum enim hîc est, inter habitum sive actum primùm, & actum secundum. Impotentia operandi bonum actu secundo, non accidit Infantibus ex defectu Doni hujus spiritualis: sed ex impedimento corporali: de quo Physici. Quin quoad Actum etiam secundum, non simpliciter illis Effectus iste negari potest aut debet. Si enim infantes per Baptismum mediante virtute Spiritus Sancti, talem concipiunt fidem, licèt quomodo credant, nobis planè sit incognitum: Sic idem Spiritus Sanctus Effectum fidei, nempè Actum bonorum operum in ijsdem operabitur, licèt istorum ratio sub sensus nostros non cadat.


### Chapter Four: IV. Adoption as sons of GOD

IV. Adoption as sons of GOD.

The fourth species of the proper effect of Baptism is not undeservedly established as Adoption into the sons of GOD. For the baptized, from being sons of wrath, Eph. 2, 3, of death, 1 Sam. 26, 16, of perdition, Luke 15, 32, become sons of grace and adoption, Rom. 8, 15, Ephes. 1, 5, of light, Luke 16, 8, and heirs of eternal life, Tit. 3, 7. Whence Bernard not unskillfully wrote, In Baptism there occurs the investiture and induction of the sons into the goods of CHRIST.

And let it suffice to have said this much concerning the proper Effect of Baptism and its four distinct species. But because at all times various things have come into question or controversy concerning this very matter, and do so today, it is pleasing to expedite them in order by Questions.

Latin:

IV. Adoptio in filios DEI.

QUarta species proprij effectus Baptismi haud immeritò constituitur, Adoptio in filios DEI. Nam baptizati ex filijs iræ, Eph. 2, 3. mortis, 1. Sam. 26, 16. perditionis, Luc. 15, 32. evadunt filij gratiæ & adoptionis. Rom. 8, 15. Ephes. 1, 5. Lucis, Luc. 16, 8. & hæredes vitæ æternæ. Tit. 3, 7. Undè haud inscitè scripsit Bernhardus, In Baptismo fieri investituram & immissionem filiorum in bona CHRISTI.

Et hæc hactenùs de Effectu Baptismi proprio, ejusdemque quatuor speciebus distinctis dixisse sufficiat. Quia verò nullis non temporibus circa hanc ipsam materiam varia in quæstionem sive controversiam venerunt, hodieq; veniunt: placet per Quæstiones ea ordine expedire.


### Chapter Four: II. Is the grace of regeneration affixed to the element of water?

Therefore, it is asked at the beginning: Does this effect of Baptism apply also to that Baptism with which Christ was baptized? We answer in the negative. Nor does it follow from this that the Baptism of Christ lacked its own certain use and fruit. For He Himself, in Matthew 3:15, assigns another end, saying to John: Thus it becomes us to fulfill all righteousness. Scholastic Doctors assign four principal causes for this propriety. 1. That Christ wished not only to be circumcised, but also to be baptized, was done to show that He is the Savior of both Jews and Gentiles. 2. To approve of Baptism, or rather to sanctify it. 3. That there might be a closer union and connection between Him as the head of the Church and the members of the same, even in the external ceremony of the covenant. 4. That He might render the beginning of His ministry more auspicious, while indeed in Baptism He was proclaimed and declared by a heavenly oracle and divine inauguration as the Teacher who is to be heard. See regarding these reasons Damascene, book 4 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 5, on faith and baptism.

Next, it is asked: Does the water of Baptism obtain such power that the grace of regeneration is affixed to the element? This question invites manifest calumny. Hence John Calvin, in his commentary on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, does not shrink from writing that a certain idol is set up by some who attribute to the element of water the power of cleansing souls: a thing which should be ascribed entirely either to the Blood of Christ or to the Holy Spirit. We answer, however, that this idol does not arise from our doctrine, but was conceived in the brain of Calvin under an unhappy star. For who among us has ever said or written that the elemental water of Baptism has the status of an efficient cause of Baptism, which of itself and by its own virtue confers the grace of regeneration upon the baptized? Perhaps in this way that idol could be imputed to us. But we establish nothing of the sort; rather, we readily admit that nothing more than the office of an instrumental or organic cause belongs to the element of water in regeneration: so that it is the medium and organ which the Holy Spirit uses in regenerating men through this Sacrament. Hence it is that St. Peter declares that we are saved by the waters of Baptism, 1 Peter 3:20-21, and the Apostle writes that the Church is cleansed by God through the washing of water in the Word, Eph. 5:26. It is not, therefore, idolatry when the power of renewing the heart is ascribed to baptismal waters: not as an efficient cause, but only as an organic or instrumental cause. Let the Calvinists see, however, how they might wish to repel from themselves the charge not indeed of idolatry, but of sacrilege, while they constitute the water of Baptism as a bare and empty sign, by which the internal Baptism is shadowed forth, by which the soul of man is cleansed from sin by the Holy Spirit, without water. Christ the Savior expressly ascribes the effect of regeneration to water and the Spirit together, although under a different kind of cause, John 3:5. Yet the Calvinists sacrilegiously strip the water of Baptism of this effect. Therefore.

I said, however, under different kinds of causes, that one and the same effect of regeneration is to be ascribed to both water and the Holy Spirit together. For water concurs to produce this ἀποτελεσμα (result), organically by divine ordination: but the Holy Spirit κυρίως καὶ ἐνεργητικῶς (properly and energetically), as the primary efficient cause. Therefore, water does not provide this spiritual virtue and operation by itself, in itself, or separately: for this is the work proper to the Holy Spirit alone. Meanwhile, because the same Holy Spirit, in this Sacrament, does not produce and effect this result ἀμέσως (immediately)—for thus there would have been no need for the ordination of a Sacrament, but it could have been effected by the preaching of the Word alone—but rather ἐμμέσως (mediately), with water and through water, as through an organ destined for this end: therefore it is undoubtedly certain that water also concurs to produce this one and same spiritual effect: not separately, or διῃρημένως (dividedly), but ἡνωμένως (unitedly), as was shown above, where we disputed concerning the essential parts of this Sacrament. Nor does it follow from this that we teach that the grace of the Holy Spirit is affixed to the element of water: or (as the adversaries understand it) that it physically inheres in the water as in a subject, or is naturally infused or bound to it: but we establish that by the sacramental mystery, by divine ordination, that power is conferred upon us through water as through an organ.

Thirdly, it is asked, Does the grace of regeneration depend upon Baptism as upon an opus operatum? We answer simply in the negative. For how can an opus operatum be established on the part of the infant, when such a one is constituted in mere terms of passivity, as it were? How likewise can such an opus operatum be admitted on the part of adults, when the entire spiritual power depends entirely upon the ordination and power of Christ the Savior, and the operation of the Holy Spirit: as was accurately shown in the doctrine concerning the Sacraments in general, chapter 2.

Fourthly, it is asked: At what time does this spiritual effect befall the baptized person? The orthodox respond that this happens immediately in the very act of baptism, as regards infants, when the one to be baptized is sprinkled with water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The Calvinists, however, dissenting from us in this part, maintain that this effect sometimes occurs a long time before baptism; sometimes, indeed, a long time after.

Before baptism, indeed, because they openly teach that children are neither all, nor any (therefore none at all) actually regenerated in the very moment of baptism; nor are they baptized for that reason, that they may receive adoption: but rather, that the adoption, which they already possess beforehand by virtue of the federal promise, 'Therefore I am thy GOD, and of thy seed after thee,' may be sealed: as Beza writes in the acts of the Colloquy of Montbéliard, page 24. After baptism, however, they teach that its effect is conferred upon those who do not have faith, but who will have it only in their own time, namely, infants constituted in the number of the elect,

Latin:

Initiò ergò quæritur: Nùm Effectus iste Baptismi competat illi etiam Baptismo, quo CHRISTUS baptizatus fuit? Respondemus negatè. Neq; tamen indè sequitur, Baptismum CHRISTI suo certo usu ac fructu caruisse. Ipsemet enim Matth. 3, 15. finem alium assignat, inquiens ad Johannem: Sic decet nos omnē implere justitiam. Decentiæ verò hujus quatuor potissimùm causas assignant Doctores Scholastici. 1. Quod CHRISTUS voluerit non tantùm circumcidi, sed & baptizari, factum esse, ut ostenderet, se Salvatorem esse & Judæorum & gentium. 2. Ut approbaret Baptismum, imò potiùs sanctificaret. 3. Ut sibi tanquàm capiti Ecclesiæ, cum membris ejusdem etiam in externâ fœderis ceremoniâ, arctior aliqua Unio ac copulatio intercederet. 4. Ut ministerij sui initium auspicatius redderet, dùm nimirùm in Baptismo cœlesti oraculo, ac divinâ inauguratione Doctor proclamatus & declaratus fuit, qui sit audiendus. Videatur autem de hisce rationibus Damascenus lib. 4. Orth. fidei cap 5. de fide & baptismate.

Deindè quæritur. An aqua Baptismi tantum vim obtineat, ut Regenerationis gratia; Elemento sit affixa? Quæ quæstio calumniam manifestam resipit. Hinc Johannes Calvinus, in suo ad caput. 5. Epistolæ ad Ephesios commentario, scribere non exhorrescit, Idolum quoddā à nonnullis constitui, qui Elemento Aquæ vim purgandi animas attribuant: Id quod vel Sanguini CHRISTI vel Spiritui Sancto in solidum sit adscribendum. Respondemus autem, hoc Idolum non ex nostrâ doctrinâ enasci, sed in cerebello Calvini esse infelici sidere conceptum. Quis enim unquàm nostrûm vel dixit, vel scripsit, Aquam Elementarem Baptismi, habere se ut causam efficientem Baptismi, quæ ex se, suaq; virtute Regenerationis gratiam conferat baptizatis. Hoc fortassis pacto idolum istud nobis imputari posset. Verùm nihil tale statuimus, quin ultrò fatemur, Elemento Aquæ in Regeneratione, nihil magis, quàm causæ instrumentalis sive organicæ officium competere: ita ut illud sit medium atq; organū, quo Spiritus Sanctus in regenerandis per hoc Sacramentum hominibus utitur. Hinc est, quòd aquis Baptismi nos salvari perhibet D. Petrus, 1. cap. 5, 20. & 21. & Apostolus Ecclesiam à DEO purgari scribit per lavacrum Aquæ in Verbo. Eph. 5, 26. Non igitur Idololatria est, quando aquæ baptisticæ adscribitur vis renovandi cor: non tanquàm causæ efficienti, sed duntaxat ut causæ organicæ sive instrumentali. Viderint autem Calviniani, quo pacto non quidem Idololatriæ, sed Sacrilegij crimen à se propulsare velint, dùm Aquam Baptismi nudum ac morum signum constituunt, quo adumbretur internus Baptismus, quo à Spiritu Sancto, sine aquâ, anima hominis purgetur à peccato. CHRISTUS Servator Aquæ & Spiritui simul, licèt sub diverso causarum genere, Regenerationis Effectum disertè adscribit, Johan. 3, 5. Atqui Calviniani hoc Effectu Aquam Baptismi sacrilegè spoliant. Ergò.

Dixi autem sub diversis causarum generibus, unum eundemq́; Regenerationis Effectum, & Aquæ & Spiritui Sancto simul esse adscribendum. Aqua enim concurrit ad hoc producendum ἀποτελεσμα, ὀργανικῶς ex ordinatione divinâ: Spiritus Sanctus verò κυρίως καὶ ἐνεργητικῶς, tanquàm causa efficiens primaria. Non igitur Aqua per se, in se, aut seorsim, virtutem hanc & operationem Spiritualem præstat: Hoc enim solius Spiritûs Sancti proprium est opus. Interim quia idem Spiritus Sanctus, in Sacramento hoc, non ἀμέσως immediatè: (Sic enim Sacramenti Ordinatione opus non fuisset, sed solâ prædicatione Verbi id effici potuisset) verùm ἐμμέσως mediatè, cum aquâ & per aquam, tanquàm per organum ad hunc finem destinatum, Effectum istum præstat & efficit: ideò indubitatò constat, Aquam quoq; ad unum eundemq́; Effectum hunc Spiritualem producendum concurrere: non separatim, sive διῃρημένως: sed ἡνωμένως, uti suprà ostensum, ubi de partibus essentialibus hujus Sacramenti disputavimus. Neq; tamen indè sequitur, doceri à nobis, Gratiam Spiritus Sancti Elemento Aquæ esse affixam: sive, (uti Adversarij intelligunt) Aquæ tanquàm subjecto physicè inhærere, aut naturali quâpiam ratione inditam, vel alligatam esse: sed Sacramentali mysterio vim illam, ex ordinatione divinâ, per Aquam tanquàm per organum, nobis conferri statuimus.

Tertiò quæritur, An Gratia regenerationis dependeat à Baptismo, tanquàm ab opere operato? Respondemus simpliciter negatè. Quomodo enim op9 operatum ex parte Infantis statui queat, cùm talis in meris quasi terminis patiendi sit constitutus? Quòmodo item ex parte adultorum tale opus operatum admitti possit, cùm universa vis Spiritualis in solidum dependeat ex ordinatione & potentiâ CHRISTI Servatoris: atq; operatione Spiritus Sancti: uti in doctrinâ de Sacramentis in genere, cap. 2. accuratè fuit ostensum.

Quartò quæritur: Quo tempore Effectus iste Spiritualis Baptizato obtingat? Respondent Orthodoxi, Fieri hoc mox in ipso actu Baptismi, quoad Infantes, quando baptizandus aspergitur aquâ in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti. Calviniani verò hâc in parte à nobis dissentientes, statuunt, Effectum istum interdum obtingere multo tempore ante Baptismum: interdum verò longo tempore pòst.

Ante Baptismum quidem, quia apertè docent, Pueros neq́; omnes, neq́; aliquos (ergò nullos prorsus) reipsâ in ipso Baptismi momento regenerari: neq́; etiam ideò illos baptizari, ut adoptionẽ accipiant: sed potiùs, ut adoptio, quam jam antè, vi fœderalis promissionis, Ergò DEUS tu9, & seminis tui post te, possideant, obsignetur: uti scribit Beza ad acta Colloquij Mompelgart. pag. 24. Post Baptismum verò ejus effectum conferri docent, ijs, qui fidẽ non habeant, sed suo demùm tempore habituri sint, nempè Infantibus in numero electorum constitutis,


### Chapter Four: V. Are the children of faithful parents born in the covenant?

who receive the benefit of regeneration at its own time divinely ordained: as Beza has it again, in the place already cited: as also in the Colloquy itself, page 434. If Beza had determined such a thing concerning adults, he would certainly deserve pardon. For concerning these it can be affirmed that the grace of Regeneration sometimes precedes Baptism, sometimes follows it. Certainly it preceded the Baptism of Cornelius, Acts 10, and of others who are read in the Acts of the Apostles to have been converted to CHRIST through the Word of the Gospel, and to have believed in Him, before they were baptized. Thus, regarding future time, if any adult is a hypocrite and does not bring faith to Baptism, who nevertheless, after having performed penance, is seriously converted: it is certain that there the grace of Regeneration, or the efficacy of Baptism, follows the act of Baptism itself at last. But both of these are far from the truth regarding baptized Infants: for in these the benefit of Regeneration does not precede Baptism: since all are before baptism, by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2:2, and unless they are regenerated of water and the Spirit, they cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven, John 3:5. But neither does it follow it at last: rather, in the federal action itself, from children of wrath they become children of grace: they receive the Spirit of adoption, and, truly liberated from the power of darkness, they are transferred into the kingdom of the Son of GOD.

But this doctrine of the Calvinists is taken from the school of Zwingli and Karlstadt. For the former writes in his 'Ratio Fidei' to Charles: Baptism does not take away Original sin, nor does it confer grace, nor is anything else done in Baptism than the sealing of those who are numbered among the Church.

And in the book against the Confession of Luther: Baptism does not make children of GOD, but those who are already children of GOD receive the testimony, sign, or token of the children of GOD.

The foundation, however, of this Calvinistic error is that they posit that the children of faithful parents, before Baptism, are in the covenant and in the grace of GOD. Whence now arises the fifth question: Are the children of such faithful parents indeed in the covenant and grace of GOD in such a way that Baptism does not at last confer this grace upon them? To which question the Calvinists answer affirmatively, writing expressly that the children of the faithful, before they draw vital Spirit, indeed even while still enclosed in the maternal womb, are contained in the covenant by hereditary right: and that even unto a thousand generations, who, if they do not have a father or mother, or their own parents joined to GOD, perhaps have had some among their ancestors: whence it happens that the formal aspect of sin, which is guilt, is not in these Infants. Calvin, lib. 4, Institut. cap. 16, § 24. Beza in 'Summa Christ.', pages 140 and 225. Hemming in 'Syntag.', page 23.

The Orthodox hold the negative simply, for such reasons as we assigned a little earlier from John 3:6 and Eph. 2:2. But it pleases us to press the Adversaries more strongly, whom we lovingly ask to answer us categorically. I. If the Infants of faithful parents, before

Baptism, are in the covenant and grace of GOD: did this grace reach them mediately or immediately? Not immediately: for GOD is never read anywhere, either in the Old or in the New Testament, to have conferred His grace upon the faithful immediately, so that He even willed that Paul, although converted in a violent manner, should learn what he must do only mediately through the information of Ananias. Therefore, if the Adversaries wish to posit an immediate operation, it is necessary that they be concerned about evident proof before they persuade the Church of GOD of this Enthusiastic delirium of theirs. Now if they assert that this is done mediately, it would certainly be their task to define that very medium in express words. We are most persuaded that, besides Baptism, no other can be given: and we demonstrate this through the removal of those media which perhaps could be given by the Adversaries. For.

1. Such a medium cannot be the Word of GOD: since the Calvinists themselves otherwise argue that Infants cannot hear the Word of GOD, as those who are still destitute of the use of reason.

2. Such a medium cannot be the faith of the Church, or of the Parents, or of the Ancestors. For the just man lives not by another's, but by his own faith, Habakkuk 2:4, Rom. 1:17. And that very much-discussed aphorism of the New Testament is: He who believes will not perish, but will have eternal life: but not, If parents believe, their children will not perish, but will have eternal life. What? Since it is as absurd that Infants believe through another's faith, and by means of this alien faith are in the covenant and grace of GOD, as it can be absurd that someone understands by another's reason, or feels or lives by another's soul. Furthermore, if another's faith profits Infants: either they will lack their own faith, or they will have their own: But they cannot have their own before Baptism: for they would have it either mediately or immediately: neither of which can be affirmed of Infants, as has already been shown. Therefore it is necessary that they have another's. But this profits no one, therefore it cannot provide that Infants, destitute of their own faith, are in the covenant and grace of GOD.

3. Such a medium cannot be carnal generation from faithful parents. For thus the clear Johannine decision holds, chapter 1:12 & 13. GOD gave the power to become children of GOD, not who are born of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man: but who are born of GOD: but to those who believe in his name.

II. Of things disparate and differing in their whole kind, there cannot be one matter, nor one medium of propagation. But original sin and the grace of GOD are things disparate and differing in their whole kind. Therefore, there cannot be one matter for both, nor one medium through which both are transmitted into children. Now indeed, the Scripture defining it, the seed of parents is that ὄχημα or vehicle through which we are conceived in sins, in iniquities we are born, and finally the sin of origin, with all its powers, is transfused and propagated into children: Ps. 51:7, Rom. 5:12. Therefore the same seed, through which the natural propagation of children occurs, cannot at the same time be the medium through which, before Baptism, regeneration, the covenant, grace, and adoption can befall the children of faithful parents.

III. Those universal assertions of the Scriptures: Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, John 3:5; we are all by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2:2; we are all born in sins, Ps. 51:7; the heart of man is only evil from his youth, Gen. 6:5, ch. 8:21; and many others of this kind, simply remove this privilege of carnal generation from faithful parents: so that it can be universally affirmed with Job: Who will bring a clean thing out of an unclean seed? Job 14:4.

IV. If this carnal generation from faithful parents ensures that children are in the covenant and grace of God before Baptism, are regenerated, and are adopted as sons, it would follow that this benefit should befall not one or another, but all who descend from faithful parents. The reason is: because in the very seed of the parents, no ground for diversity can be shown. But this is manifestly false, according to the very doctrine of the Calvinists: for thus, in the covenant and grace of God before the received Sacrament of either Circumcision or Baptism, there would have been as much Cain as Abel, as much Ishmael as Isaac, as much Esau as Jacob, as much Absalom as Solomon: whom, however, the adversaries count in the class of the absolutely, and indeed eternally, reprobate. We therefore conclude irrefragably that from carnal generation from faithful parents, the covenant and grace of God cannot be propagated into children. Hence it is that St. Augustine also long ago laughed at and refuted this dream of the Pelagians. If, he says, sinners are from a sinner, why are righteous ones not born from a baptized believer, to whom all sins have been remitted? Therefore, a righteous person is not born from a baptized one, because he does not beget him from where he is regenerated, but from where he is generated.

4. Such a medium cannot be the breadth of the federal promise, which extends even to infants. For although in Gen. 17:7, God is read to have used this formula of federal promise to Abraham and his entire posterity: I will be your God, and of your seed after you; it cannot and ought not to be understood so simply and absolutely that its fruit must redound to the descendants of Abraham, however they may conduct themselves, and whether they keep or neglect the covenant of God. Such an absolute breadth certainly never even entered the mind of God himself: but He willed it to be limited or rather determined, saying: You, therefore, shall keep my covenant, and your seed after you in their generations: And this is my covenant: Let every male among you be circumcised, etc. The breadth of the federal promise must therefore be defined not absolutely, but by the reciprocal condition of the covenant. For just as in every covenant, two contracting persons concur: one promising something, but under a certain condition; the other to whom the enjoyment of the promised thing is granted, also under the condition of the kept federal pact. Thus in this spiritual covenant, God is the person promising His grace with these words: I will be your God, and of your seed after you; but under the condition, If you keep my covenant, and are circumcised. The faithful, however, are those to whom the power of enjoying this federal grace is given, but under the condition of the kept federal pact, if indeed they are circumcised. And thus God Himself expressly bound the benefits of this covenant to the Sacrament of Circumcision: indeed, so that he who has not been circumcised, his soul must be cut off from the number of the faithful: and therefore he will not be in the covenant itself, unless he is first circumcised. The same must be established entirely regarding the Sacrament of Baptism as an antitype: so that no one among infants should be considered to be in the covenant and grace of God, unless he who has believed in Him and has been baptized.

With these reasons duly weighed, it is most evidently clear that the grace of God and the divine covenant cannot befall the infants of the faithful before Baptism, neither mediately nor immediately, and therefore clearly not at all: but through Baptism alone, and indeed in the very act or moment of Baptism, it is truly conferred upon each and every baptized infant: which was to be demonstrated.

Latin:

qui regenerationis beneficium suo demùm tempore divinitùs ordinato accipiant: uti rursus habet Beza, loco jam citato: ut & in Colloquio ipso pag. 434. Si de adultis tale quid statuisset Beza, veniam utiq; mereretur. De his enim affirmari potest, quòd Regenerationis gratia interdum præcedat Baptismum, interdum subsequatur. Certè præcessit Baptismum Cornelij Actor. 10. & aliorum, qui in Actis Apostolicis, priùs leguntur per Verbum Evangelij ad CHRISTUM conversi fuisse, inq; ipsum credidisse, quàm baptisarentur. Sic quoad futurum tempus, si adultorum aliquis sit hypocrita, & fidem ad Baptismum non afferat: qui tamen postmodùm actâ pœnitentiâ, seriò convertatur: certum est, ibi Regenerationis gratiam, sive efficaciam Baptismi, ipsum actum Baptismi demùm subsequi. Verùm utrumq; hoc longè est falsissimum, quoad Infantes baptizatos: in his enim Regenerationis beneficium, Baptismum non præcedit: Siquidem omnes sunt ante baptismum, naturâ filij iræ: Ephes. 2, 2. & nisi regenerentur ex aquâ & Spiritu, non possunt ingredi in regnum cœlorum, Joh. 3, 5. Sed neq; eundem demùm sequitur: quin in ipsâ actione fœderali, ex filijs iræ, fiunt filij gratiæ: Spiritum adoptionis accipiunt, & reverà ex potestate tenebrarum liberati, in regnum Filij DEI transferuntur.

Est verò doctrina hæc Calvinianorum ex Zvinglij & Carolostadij scholâ petita. Ille enim in ratione fidei ad Carolum scribit: Baptismus peccatum Originis non tollit, neq; gratiam confert, neq; quicquam in Baptismo aliud fit, quam confignatio eorum, qui Ecclesiæ connumerantur.

Et in libro contra Confess. Lutheri: Baptifmus filios DEI non facit, sed qui jam antè filij DEI sunt, filiorum DEI testimonium, signum vel tefferam recipiunt.

Fundamentum autem erroris hujus Calvinistici est, quod statuunt, Fidelium parentum liberos, ante Baptismum, esse in fœdere, & in gratiâ DEI. Undè Quinta jam exurgit quæstio: Verùm ejusmodi fidelium parentum liberi ita sint in fœdere & gratiâ DEI, ut Baptismus ipsis non demum hanc gratiam conferat? Ad quam quæstionem Calviniani affirmatè respondent, expressè scriptitantes, Fidelium liberos, antequàm vitalem Spiritum hauriant, imò adhuc utero materno inclusos, hæreditario jure in fœdere contineri: idq; in mille etiam generationes, qui, si patrem aut matrem, vel proprios parentes non habuerint DEO conjunctos, fortassè habuerint aliquos ex suis majoribus: undè fiat, ut peccati formale, quod est reatus, non sit in istis Infantibus. Calvin. lib. 4. Institut. cap. 16. §. 24. Beza in summâ Christ. pag. 140. & 225. Hemming in Syntag. pag. 23.

Orthodoxi Negativam simpliciter tenent, eismodi rationibus, quas paulò antè, ex Johan. 3, 6. Eph. 2, 2. assignavimus. Sed placet fortiùs premere Adversarios, quos ut categoricè nobis respondeant, peramanter rogamus. I. Si fidelium parentum Infantes, ante

Baptismum sunt in foedere & gratia DEI: utrùm hæc gratia ipsis obtingerit mediatè an immediatè? Non immediatè: Neq; enim DEUS unquàm uspiam vel in Veteri, vel in Novo Testamento fidelibus gratiam suam Immediatè contulisse legitur, ita ut Paulum quoque, licèt violento modo conversum, non nisi Mediatè ex informatione Ananiæ addiscere voluerit, quid ipsi faciendum. Proindè, si Immediatam operationem statuere velint Adversarij, priùs de evidenti probatione solliciti sint necesse est, quàm suum hoc delirium Enthusiasticum Ecclesiæ DEI persuadeant. Jam si Mediatè hoc fieri asserant, ipsorum utiq; fuerit, illud ipsum medium expressis verbis definire. Nos præter Baptismum, nullum aliud dari posse, habemus persuasissimum: idq; per remotionem eorum mediorum demonstramus, quæ fortassis ab Adversarijs dari possent. Nam.

1. Medium tale esse nequit Verbum DEI: siquidem ipsimet Calviniani alioquin pugnant, Infantes non posse audire Verbum DEI: ut qui rationis usu adhuc destituantur.

2. Tale medium esse nequit, fides vel Ecclesiæ, vel Parentum, vel Majorum. Neque enim alienâ, sed suâ fide vivit justus, Habacuc 2, 4. Rom. 1, 17. Et ipse πολυθρύλλητος, est Aphorismus Novi Testamenti: Qui crediderit, non peribit, sed habebit vitam æternam: non autem, Si crediderint parentes, illorum filij non peribunt, sed habebunt vitam æternam. Quid? quòd tàm absurdum est, Infantes per alienam fidem credere, & mediante hac fide aliena esse in foedere atque gratia DEI, quàm absurdum esse potest, quòd aliquis aliena ratione intelligat, aliena animâ sentiat aut vivat. Porrò si aliena fides Infantibus prodest: vel ipsi carebunt propriâ fide, vel habebunt propriam: Atqui propriam ante Baptismum habere non possunt: haberent enim eam vel mediatè, vel immediatè: Quorum neutrum de Infantibus affirmari potest, uti jam ostensum. Alienam ergò habeant necesse est. Atqui hæc nemini prodest, Ergò nec præstare potest, ut Infantes propriâ fide destituti, sint in foedere & gratia DEI.

3. Tale medium esse nequit, carnalis generatio ex fidelibus parentibus. Sic enim habet dilucida decisio Johannitica, cap. 1, 12. & 13. DEUS dedit potestatem filios DEI fieri, non qui ex sangvinibus, non qui ex voluntate carnis, non qui ex voluntate viri: sed qui ex DEO nati sunt: sed his qui credunt in nomine ejus.

II. Rerum disparatarum & toto genere discrepantium, una non potest esse materia, neque unum propagationis medium. Atqui peccatum Originis, & gratia DEI, sunt res disparatæ, & toto genere discrepantes. Ergò una utriusque nequit esse materia, vel unum medium, per quod utrumq; in filios transmittatur. Jam verò, definiente Scripturâ, semen parentum est ὄχημα sive vehiculum illud, per quod in peccatis concipimur, in iniquitatibus nascimur, peccatum denique originis, cum omnibus suis viribus, in liberos transfunditur & propagatur: Psal. 51, 7. Rom. 5, 12. Ergò idem semen, per quod naturalis liberorum fit propagatio, non potest esse simul medium, per quod ante Baptismum fidelium parentum liberis ob tingere possit Regeneratio, fœdus, gratia, adoptio.

III. Universales illæ assertiones Scripturærum: Quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est, Joh. 3, 5. omnes naturâ sumus filij iræ, Ephes. 2, 2. omnes in peccatis nascimur. Psal. 51, 7. cor hominis tantùm malum est ab adolescentiâ, Gen. 6, 5. c. 8. 21. & hujus generis complures aliæ, privilegium hoc carnalis generationis ex fidelibus parentibus, simpliciter tollunt: ita ut universaliter cum Jobo affirmari queat: Quis dabit mundum, de immundo conceptum semine. Job. 14, 4.

IV. Si carnalis hæc generatio ex fidelibus parentibus, præstat, ut ante Baptismum liberi sint in fœdere & gratiâ DEI, sint regenerati, sint adoptati in filios: consequens fuerit, hoc beneficium, non uni aut alteri: sed omnibus ex fidelibus parentibus descendentibus, obtingere. Ratio est: Quia in ipso semine parentum, nulla diversitatis ratio monstrari potest. Atqui hoc manifestè falsum, ex ipsâ doctrinâ Calvinianorum: Sic enim in fœdere & gratiâ DEI ante perceptum Sacramentum vel Circumcisionis vel Baptismi, fuisset tàm Cain, quàm Abel: tàm Ismaël, quàm Isaac: tàm Esavus quàm Jacob, tàm Absolon quàm Salomon: Quos tamen in classem absolutè, & quidem ab æterno reprobatorum numerant Adversarij. Colligimus proindè irrefragabiliter, ex carnali generatione, ex fidelibus parentibus, fœdus & gratiam DEI, in liberos non posse propagari. Hinc est, quòd D. Augustinus etiam jam olim in Pelagianos somnium hoc risit & elisit. Si, inquiens, de peccatore peccatores sunt: quare non de baptizato jam fideli, cui remissa sunt omnia peccata, justi nascuntur? Idcò de baptizato non nascitur justus, quia non eum generat, undè regeneratus est, sed undè generatus.

4. Tale medium esse nequit Fœderalis promissionis latitudo, quæ ad Infantes etiam se extendit. Etsi enim Genes. 17, 7. DEus ad Abrahamum, ejusdemq; posteritatem universam hâc usus fuisse legitur Fœderalis promissionis formulâ: Ego ero DEUS tuus, & seminis tui post te: non tamen ita simpliciter & absolutè ea vel potest vel debet intelligi, ut ejus fructus ad posteros Abrahæ, quomodocunque etiam illi se habeant, & pactum DEI vel custodiant, vel negligant, redundare debeat. Qualis certè latitudo absoluta, ne quidem DEO ipsi unquàm in mentem venit: sed eam limitatam vel potiùs determinatam esse voluit: Tu ergò, inquiens, custodies pactum meum, & semen tuum post te in generationibus suis: Hoc est autē pactum meum: Circumcidatur ex vobis omne masculinum &c. Fœderalis ergò promissionis latitudo definienda est non absolutè, sed per reciprocam conditionem fœderis. Quemadmodum enim in omni fœdere, duæ concurrunt personæ paciscentes: una promittens aliquid, sed sub certâ conditione; altera cui rei promissæ perfruitio conceditur, item sub conditione servati pacti fœderalis. Sic in fœdere hoc spirituali, DEUS est persona promittens gratiam suam, his verbis: Ego ero DEUS tuus, & seminis tui post te: sed sub conditione, Si tu custodieris pactum meum, & circumcisus fueris. Fideles verò sunt, quibus facta est potestas perfruendi gratiâ hâc fœderali sed sub conditione servati pacti fœderalis, si nimirùm circumcisi fuerint. Et sic DEUS ipse Fœderis hujus beneficia disertè alligavit ad Sacramentum Circumcisionis: ita quidem, ut qui circumcisus non fuerit, illius anima eradicari debeat ex numero fidelium: ac proindè neq; in fœdere ipso futura, nisi priùs circumcidatur. Quod ipsum de Sacramento etiam Baptismi tanquàm antitypo omninò est statuendum: ita ut in fœdere & gratiâ DEI ex infantibus nullus censeri debeat, nisi qui crediderit ipsi & baptizatus fuerit.

Quibus rationibus ritè expensis, evidentissimè liquet, Infantibus fidelium gratiam DEI & fœderis divini, ante Baptismum, neq; mediatè neq; immediatè, ac proindè planè non obtingere posse: sed per solum Baptismum, & quidem in ipso Baptismi actu sive momento, eam verè singulis ac universis baptizatis infantibus conferri: id quod erat demonstrandum.


### Chapter Four: V. Are the children of faithful parents born in the covenant? (continued)

The Calvinists make two exceptions at this point: First, they keep saying that by this pact, no prerogative at all is granted by us to the children of faithful parents over the infants of Turks and other infidel peoples.

Then, however, they object with two passages of Scripture: one from Rom. 11:16: If the root is holy, the branches are also holy; the other from 1 Cor. 7:14: Your children are holy.

I reply that both objections suffer from the fallacy of 'in a certain respect' and 'simply'. For we do not immediately strip the children of faithful parents of every prerogative if we deny with Scripture that a hereditary holiness is engendered and as it were co-created in them from the mother's womb. We certainly leave and assign to them that prerogative which regards the very right to the kingdom of God, or access to the covenant and grace: so that the covenant pertains to such infants born of Christian parents, even before Baptism, although they are finally inserted into this covenant through Baptism.

These things are distinct, nor does the consequence hold affirmatively from the prior to the posterior. It is one thing to pertain to the covenant of God; it is another thing, however, to be already in the covenant of God. For the former bestows nothing more than a right to the thing; the latter, however, delivers the possession of the thing itself. The former they have from the privilege of carnal generation, because they are descended from the seed of believing parents; the latter, however, they obtain from the reception of Baptism. The former does not sanctify; the latter, however, sanctifies and cleanses from all sin.

Regarding the two Apostolic passages, the former does not at all admit the ἄγνοιαν ἀνέλεγχον (unrefuted ignorance) craftily concealed by the Adversaries. For the Apostle is not dealing with any natural and hereditary holiness that might accrue to children from the womb of their parents, or γεῦ (taste): but he is occupied with other and clearly different terms. For he raises the question there: Whether reprobation has so entirely befallen Israel, that is, the Israelite people, that clearly no hope of returning into favor with GOD is left to them: or whether at least certain individuals of the Jews can be converted to GOD. Here the Apostle answers by a simple negation: that reprobation has not befallen Israel entirely, but in part: since until the end of the world, there will always be branches who, imitating the faith of the Root, that is, of Abraham and the remaining holy Patriarchs, will return into favor with GOD. But what is this to the Calvinist hypothesis concerning the holiness of children born of believers. Furthermore, that also deserves observation, that the Apostle in this place is occupied solely with that possibility by which those branches, however much cut off, can nevertheless be grafted into the olive tree again, if indeed they seek election by faith; that which again utterly undermines and overturns the Calvinist dogma, and especially their figment concerning absolute Election and reprobation.

The latter passage, taken from 1 Cor. 7:14, convicts the Calvinists of a shameful fallacy of four terms (ἀσυλλογισίας). For the Apostle expressly discusses the political or civil holiness of children: which consists in this, that the infidelity of one spouse cannot prevent the children conceived from such a marriage from being considered not as spurious, but as pure and legitimate. But now the Calvinists make a subsumption concerning the spiritual holiness of children. Therefore, even a beginner in Theology notices that they are wickedly playing with a Sophism of four terms. Wolfgang Musculus Dusanus himself also supports this response of ours from among the Calvinist doctors, being driven by the force of truth to argue thus in his Commentary on 1 Cor. ch. 7, pp. 202, 203: The term holiness is taken here for the purity of the marriage bed, which it has from the tradition of GOD. Therefore he says: Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy. He ought to have said, but now they are clean, unless to be holy and to be clean were the same thing in this place. Therefore, the simplest understanding of this passage is, first, that we should not understand the term holiness of that holiness which is either from the covenant of GOD, or from the spirit of faith, by which believers are sanctified into the people of GOD: but of the purity of the marriage bed. Otherwise, it will cause a troublesome dispute as to how an unbelieving husband can be said to be sanctified. Secondly, that we attribute this sanctification, that is, purity, not to the faith of the believing spouse, but to the marriage because of the tradition of GOD, with Jerome, who says that marriages are holy because of the tradition of GOD: and Ambrose, who holds it thus: The children are holy because they are born from legitimate marriages.

And p. 104. I once abused the present passage against the error of the Anabaptists, who keep the infants of Christians from Baptism, thinking that (But now they are holy) is the same as saying they are of the people of GOD, because of a believing parent. But the present passage has nothing to do with this case, in which the subject is not the holiness of the covenant and the people of GOD, but the purity of legitimate marriage, even of unbelievers. For that holiness is ascribed not only to children, to whom perhaps the holiness of a believing parent might so pertain that they are participants of the covenant of GOD because of it: but also to unbelieving husbands and wives, even though they oppose the faith of CHRIST. Nor is there any other holiness and purity of children in question than that which also belongs to unbelieving parents: but to them, no other belongs than that which is from legitimate marriage.

But enough and more than enough concerning that error of the Calvinists regarding this Fifth Question. There are, however, Scholastic Doctors also who are not entirely immune from all error regarding the same. The Master of the Sentences, book 4, dist. 4, near the end, and the remaining sounder Scholastics incline to the opinion that in baptized infants, the habits of the theological virtues—Faith, Charity, and Hope—are infused, but not their acts. For since infused habits, such as the theological virtues, have their origin from GOD, not from nature, as innate habits: nor from free will, as acquired habits: they conclude that infused habits can exist in baptized infants before the use of free will. And by this reasoning, faith exists in infants, namely habitually, although they do not have the act of faith. They also add that the theological virtues are not therefore entirely idle in infants; but that they adorn and dispose their souls, or render them capable, upon the arrival of the use of reason, for the acts of the virtues: as Thomas argues, part 3, q. 69, art. 6. The cause and foundation of the error is that they have distinguished less correctly between habit and act in this place. For the second act of faith, which consists in doing good, does not depend on the natural power or will of the baptized themselves: but entirely on the grace and virtue of GOD, working within through these virtues in His own way, and indeed by a second act, although it cannot be perceived by us. Therefore, let this error also depart, which gives some patronage to the fury of the Anabaptists concerning the ἀναισθησίᾳ (insensibility) of infants.

Sixthly, regarding the Effect of Baptism, it is asked: Whether the mode of efficacy which Baptism has and confers is exhibitive, or merely significative? The Sacramentarians again admit only a significative mode. For as shown above, they invent a twofold Baptism: one external, the other internal. The external, they say, is performed by the sprinkling of Water, and is conferred in Infancy, which however cleanses not the soul, but only the body from filth: which consists only of the element of water: which, finally, only analogically signifies and figures that internal Baptism, which happens without water, consists only of the Holy Spirit, and occurs only in more adult age, often in old age. But what is this other than to strip the baptism of water of all efficacy and virtue whatsoever, and as someone not ineptly wrote: to invent the bath of the comic Menander out of Baptism. For once the exhibitive power and efficacy of cleansing is denied, a naked, empty, and clearly inefficacious Baptism is left. How this agrees with the Scriptures, which assert that by Baptism it is not only signified, but also exhibited: not merely shadowed forth, but also effected, namely regeneration, and indeed through the washing of water in the Spirit, John 3:5, Titus 3:5, let the Adversaries see. We assign to the baptism of water the mode of exhibitive efficacy with these very Scriptures, in the way which has already been shown above. To this point tends the fact that St. Peter, 1 Pet. 3:20, calls Baptism not a type, but an antitype, not which itself signifies merely its own proper power, but in which is fulfilled that which had been prefigured by the old type of the waters of the flood. Just as therefore in the Eucharistic Supper, bread and wine are not merely bare symbols, but are organs and media exhibitive of the body and blood of CHRIST: so also to the Elemental Water in Baptism, its efficacy and the grace of regeneration is most closely joined. Although Water does not have this efficacy inherently in itself, nor does it have it of itself separated from the Holy Spirit: but only by the accident of divine ordination: because, however, this very Water is an organ of the Holy Spirit, it certainly has it in reality, and the Holy Spirit works regeneration through the same in baptized Infants.

Seventhly, it is asked: Does the Effect of regeneration, in the very act or moment of Baptism, befall all baptized adults equally as it does infants? For the solid decision of this question, it must be observed that the Effect of baptism, by reason of order, can be posited as twofold: One ordinary and proper, for the sake of which this Sacrament was chiefly instituted: which is Regeneration.

The other extraordinary and improper, such as was that of Constantine, who is read to have been freed from leprosy by the Water of Baptism: such as is also reported by Augustine, book 22 de Civ. DEI, ch. 8, concerning a certain physician, who at that time was healed of gout through baptism: and also concerning another, who similarly received relief from paralysis through this means. This Effect, just as it is not ordinary and proper, so it does not exert itself equally in adults or in infants: but it befalls these according to the good pleasure of the divine will, and not those.

Then it must be distinguished in this place between the genuine sense which this question sustains. For the effect itself about which it is asked seems to receive some inequality, when it is considered either in itself or by accident. If it is considered by accident, then it is certain that among adults receiving it, he receives more grace in whom there is a greater and better disposition: not indeed from the meritorious virtue of the disposition itself, but from the gratuitous and remunerative goodness of GOD. To which opinion Cyprian wrote in book 2, Epist. 2 to Donatus: As much of capable faith as we bring to it, so much of inundating grace we receive. And Augustine on John, Tract. 32: As much faith as a man has brought to the font of Baptism, so much is he filled. But in itself and ordinarily, Baptism does not have an unequal effect: but to those equally disposed, such as infants, it confers equal grace to all. And although in Baptism more sins are remitted to one than to another: it does not follow from that, however, that an inequality of grace is produced from this. The reason is because even the least grace suffices to blot out the sins of infants: nor is grace itself increased or diminished in itself, according to the multitude or paucity of sins which are remitted. Finally, if one asks specifically about Adults, they also admit a diversity: for they either truly believe in their heart, as they utter confession with their mouth: or they are hypocrites, and receive Baptism with a feigned mind, such as was Simon Magus, Acts 8:13. The former truly receive the sealing of Regeneration even in the very act or moment of Baptism. But concerning these latter it is asked, What grace is conferred upon them. We answer, that none at all in the act itself. The Donatists formerly opined that even in the very act of Baptism all sins were remitted to hypocrites: yet in such a way that they would return soon after Baptism. And there are those who maintain that Augustine also, book 1 against the Donatists, ch. 12, approved this opinion. But the Master of the Sentences rightly answers that Augustine speaks thus partly for the sake of disputation: partly that the opinion of others is reported by him: not that these things are asserted by him as his own opinion. Therefore, the hypocrite does not receive the Thing of Baptism, i.e., the salutary use or grace: but only the Sacrament itself. The reasons for the affirmation are these: 1. Where there is no faith, there is no regeneration. In hypocrites there is no faith. Therefore. 2. Where there is regeneration, there is also the renewal of the mind: whence the Apostle calls Baptism the washing of both regeneration and renewal, Tit. 3:5. In hypocrites there is no renewal of the mind. Therefore. 3. For hypocrites, as long as they are such, there is no part nor lot in the word of the Gospel: as Peter said to Simon Magus: Acts 8:20 & 21. Therefore, no part of regeneration.

But here a new and Eighth question immediately arises: Should such a Hypocrite, if he should repent afterwards, be baptized again, or does the grace of Baptism then at last begin to be salutary to him? The former, concerning the reiteration of Baptism, we simply deny: but the latter we altogether Affirm with Augustine, who in the place cited a little before has it thus: Baptism begins to be of value for salvation when that hypocrisy, or feigning, has departed through a truthful confession. Just as therefore every permanent form, when the impediment is removed, attains its end, for example, gravity remaining in a stone, the stone is carried downward: if the impediment is removed, it exhales upward: so likewise it is to be thought that it happens here. The Huberians object to that Apostolic assertion, which seems to extend itself as much to adults as to Infants: Gal. 3:27, As many of you as have been baptized, have put on CHRIST: And Rom. 6:3. Whoever of us have been baptized have been baptized into the death of CHRIST. But I answer that the Apostle’s assertion is not to be extended more broadly than the text itself permits. For the Apostle himself added a manifest and clear restriction in the immediately preceding words: saying, All of you are children of GOD, because you have believed in CHRIST JESUS. Therefore, concerning these he immediately subjoins: Whoever of you (namely, you who have believed in Christ Jesus) have been baptized, have put on Christ. Where anyone easily understands that the mark of universality is not to be extended promiscuously to all baptized adults, but to all baptized believers. As for the latter passage, it is again clear in itself that it must be understood according to the condition

Latin:

Duo excipiunt hoc loco Calviniani: Primùm enim dictitant, hoc pacto nullam prorsus prærogativam, fidelium parentum liberis, præ Turcarum, aliorumŕ; infidelium populorum infantibus à nobis concedi.

Deindè verò objiciunt, duo Scripturarum loca: unum ex cap. 11, 16. ad Romanos: Si radix sancta, sancti & rami: Alterum ex 1. Cor. 7, 14. Filij vestri sancti sunt.

Respondeo utrumque objectum laborare Sophismate ἀπὸ τῶ πῇ και ἁπλῶς. Neque enim omni statim prærogativâ spoliamus fidelium parentum liberos, si hæreditariam sanctitatem ex utero matris ipsis ingeneratam & quasi concreatam illis cum Scripturâ negemus. Relinquimus certè & assignamus ipsis eam prærogativam, quæ respicit ipsum jus ad regnum DEI, sive aditum ad fœdus & gratiam: ita ut ad ejusmodi infantes ex Christianis parentibus prognatos pertineat fœdus, etiam ante Baptismum, licèt fœderi huic demùm per Baptismum inserantur.

Distincta autem sunt ista, neque à priore ad posterius affirmatè valet consequentia. Aliud est, pertinere ad fœdus DEI: aliud verò est, Esse jam in fœdere DEI. Illud enim plus non largitur, quàm jus ad rem: hoc verò, ipsam rei possessionem tradit. Prius illud habent ex carnalis generationis privilegio, quia nimirùm descendunt ex semine fidelium parentum: Posterius verò hoc consequuntur ex perceptione Baptismi. Prius illud non sanctificat: Posterius verò hoc sanctificat & emundat ab omni peccato.

Quoad duo loca Apostolica, Prior ἄγνοιαν ἀνέλεγχον ab Adversarijs subdolè occultatam, minimè admittit. Neq; enim de naturali aliquâ & hæreditaria sanctitate, quæ ex utero parentum liberis obveniat, vel γεῦ agit Apostolus: sed in alijs ac diversis planè terminis versatur. Movet enim ibi quæstionem, An Israëli, hoc est populo Israëlitico ita ex toto obrigerit reprobatio, ut planè nulla spes redeundi in gratiam cum DEO ipsis sit relicta: vel quædam saltem Judæorum individua, ad DEUM converti queant. Hic respondet Apostolus per simplicem negationem: non ex toto: sed ex parte Israëli obtigisse reprobationem: Siquidem ad finem usq; mundi, semper futuri sint ramuli, qui Radicis, hoc est, Abrahæ & reliquorum Sanctorum Patriarcharum fidem imitaturi, & in gratiam cum DEO redituri sint. Sed quid hoc ad Calvinianorum hypothesin de sanctitate liberorum ex fidelibus prognatorum. Porrò illud quoq; observationem meretur, quòd Apostolus hoc loco unicè versatur circa possibilitatem illam, quâ rami illi quantumvis excisi, oleæ tamen rursus inseri queant, si nimirùm ex fide quærant electionem; id quod rursus Calvinianorum dogma, & cumprimis figmentum de absolutâ Electione & reprobatione funditùs subruit & evertit.

Posterior locus ex 1. Cor. 7, 14. petitus Calvinianos arguit turpis ἀσυλλογισίας quatuor terminorum. Ex professo enim disserit Apostolus de politicâ sive civili sanctitate liberorum: quæ in eo consistat, ut alterius conjugis infidelitas obstare non possit, quò minus liberi, ex tali conjugio concepti, non pro spuriis, sed pro puris & legitimis censeantur. Jam verò Calviniani subsumtionem faciunt de spirituali sanctitate liberorum. Ergò sub Sophismate quatuor terminorum ipsos improbè ludere, vel Tyro Theologiæ animadvertit. Suffragatur responsioni huic nostræ ex doctoribus Calvinianis, ipse quoque Wolfgangus Musculus Dusanus, vi veritatis adactus sic differens in Commentario in 1. Cor. cap. 7. pag. 202. 203. Sumitur hîc sanctitatis dictio, pro mundiciâ conjugalis thori, quam ille habet ex traditione DEI. Ideo dicit: Alioqui filij vestri immundi essent, nunc autem sancti sunt. Debebat dicere, nunc autem mundi sunt, nisi idem hoc loco esset, sanctum esse, & mundum esse. Est itaq; simplicissimus hujus loci intellectus primùm in eo, ut sanctitatis dictionem non intelligamus de eâ sanctitate quæ est vel ex fædere DEI, vel ex spiritu fidei, quo credentes in populum DEI sanctificantur: sed de mundiciâ conjugalis thori. Alioqui molestam pariet disputationem, quomodo vir infidelis sanctificatus dici possit. Deindè ut hanc sanctificationem, id est, mundiciam tribuamus non fidei conjugis fidelis, sed conjugio propter traditionem DEI, cum Hieronymo, qui dicit, quia ex traditione DEI sanctæ sunt nuptiæ: & Ambrosio, qui ita habet: Sancti sunt liberi, quia ex legitimis conjugijs nati sunt.

Et pag. 104. Abusus sum aliquando præsenti loco contra errorem Anabaptistarum, infantes Christianorum Baptismo arcentium, putans illud: (Nunc autem sancti sunt) idem esse atq; de populo DEI sunt, propter fidelem parentem. Nihil aute ad hanc causam facit præsens locus, in quo non de fœderis & populi DEI sanctimoniâ, sed de conjugij legitimi, etiam infidelium, puritate, agitur. Non enim liberis tantùm, ad quos forsan poterie ita pertinere fidelis parentis sanctimonia, ut fœderis DEI sint propter illam participes: sed & maritis ac uxoribus infidelibus eadem sanctimonia adscribitur, ut ut fidei CHRISTI repugnent. Nec de aliâ agitur sanctitate ac puritate liberorum, quàm quæ & infidelibus parentibus competit: Illis autem non competit alia, quàm quæ est ex conjugio legitimo.

Sed de errore isto Calvinianorum circa Quintam hanc Quæstionem plus satis. Sunt verò Doctores etiam Scholastici circa eandem, non ab omni planè errore immunes. Magister Sententiarum lib. 4. dist. 4. sub finem, & reliqui saniores Scholastici in eam inclinant sententiam, Infantibus baptizatis, virtutum Theologicarum, Fidei, Charitatis & Spei infundi habitus, non verò actus illarum. Nam cùm habitus infusi, ut sunt Theologicæ virtutes, ortum habeant à DEO, non à naturâ, ut habitus innati: nec à libero arbitrio, ut habitus acquisiti: Colligunt illi, habitus infusos esse posse in infantibus baptizatis ante usum liberi arbitrij. Et hâc ratione fidem esse in Infantibus, nempè habitualiter, licèt actum fidei non habeant. Addunt quoq;, virtutes Theologicas non propterea planè otiosas esse in Infantibus; sed animas ipsorum ornare atq; disponere, sive habiles reddere, adveniente usu rationis, ad actus virtutum: uti disputat Thomas part. 3. q. 69. art. 6. Causa & fundamentum erroris est, quòd inter habitum & actum hoc loco minùs rectè distinxerunt. Actus enim secundus fidei, qui consistit in benè operando, non dependet ex ipsâ vel naturali potentiâ, vel voluntate baptizatorum: sed in solidum ex gratiâ & virtute DEI, intus per istas virtutes suo modo utiq; operantis, & quidem actu secundo, licèt ille à nobis percipi non possit. Facessat proindè & iste error, Anabaptistarum furori de ἀναισθησίᾳ infantum, nonnihil patrocinium faciens.
