Sexto circa Effectum Baptismi quæritur: An modus efficaciæ, quam habet & confert Baptismus, sit exhibitivus, an verò duntaxat significativus? Sacramentarij rursum admittunt modùm tantùm significativum. Nam uti suprà ostensum, geminum comminifcuntur Baptismum: Unum externum, alterum internum. Externum verò peragi aspersione Aquæ, & conferri in Infantiâ, qui tamen non animam, sed corpus tantùm à sordibus purget: quiq; solo aquæ elemento constet: qui deniq; analogicè tantùm signet & figuret internum illum Baptismum, qui sine aquâ fiat, solo constet Spiritu Sancto, & in adultiore demùm ætate, sæpiùs in senectute obtingat. Quid verò hoc est aliud, quàm Baptismum aquæ omni prorsus efficaciâ ac virtute spoliare, & ut quidam haud ineptè scripsit: Comici Menandri balneum ex Baptismo comminisci. Negatâ enim vi & efficaciâ mundationis exhibitivâ, nudus, vacuus, atq; planè inefficax Baptismus relinquitur. Quod quomodo conveniat Scripturis, asserentibus per Baptismum non significari tantùm, sed & exhiberi: non adumbrari duntaxat, sed & effici regenerationem, & quidem per lavacrum aquæ in Spiritu, Johan. 3,5. Tit. 3,5. viderint Adversarij. Nos modum efficaciæ exhibitivum cum his ipsis Scripturis, Aquæ baptismo adsignamus, eo modo, quo jam supra ostensum. Huc facit, quod D. Petrus 1. cap. 3,20. Baptismum non typum nominat, sed ἀντίτυπον, non qui ipse vim suam propriam duntaxat significet: sed in quo impleatur id, quod typo veteri aquarum diluvij præfiguratum fuerit. Quemadmodum ergò in Cœnâ Eucharisticâ, panis & vinum non nuda tantùm Symbola : Sed organa & media sunt exhibitiva corporis & sangvinis CHRISTI : Ita quoq; Aquæ Elementari in Baptismo, efficacia sua & gratia regenerationis est junctissima. Quam efficaciam tametsi non habet Aqua in se inhærenter, neq; etiam per se habet à Spiritu S. separatam: sed ex accidente duntaxat ordinationis divinæ: quia tamen hæc ipsa Aqua est organon Spiritus S. utiq; reverà habet, & Spiritus S. per eandem operatur regenerationem in Infantibus baptisatis.

Septimò quæritur: An Effectus regenerationis, in ipso Baptismi actu sive momento æquè obtingat omnibus adultis baptizatis, ac infantibus ? Pro solida quæstionis hujus decisione, illud observandum fuerit, Effectum baptismi, ratione ordinis, posse statui duplicem: Unum ordinarium & proprium, cujus potissimum gratia hoc Sacramentum est institutum : qui est Regeneratio.

Alterum extraordinarium & improprium, qualis fuit ille Constantini, qui per Aquam Baptismi a leprâ liberatus fuisse legitur: qualis item refertur ab Augustino, lib. 22. de Civ. DEI, cap. 8. de quodam medico, qui illo tempore per baptismum à podagra sanatus fuerit : nec non de altero, qui similiter à paralysi per hoc medium levationem acceperit. Hic Effectus, uti non est ordinariq & proprio: ita neq; in adultis, neq; in parvulis æqualiter se exerit: sed pro beneplacito voluntatis divinæ his obtingit, illis non ité.

Deinde distinguendum hoc loco inter genuinum sensum, quem quæstio hæc sustinet. Nam effectus ipse de quo quæritur, inæqualitatem aliquam sortiri videtur, quando ille consideratur vel per se, vel ex accidente. Si ex accidente consideretur, tum certum est inter suscipientes adultos, eum plus gratiæ accipere, in quo major ac melior est dispositio : non quidem ex virtute ipsius dispositionis meritoriâ, sed ex bonitate DEI gratuita & remuneratoriâ. In quam sententiam Cyprianus scripsit lib. 2. Epist. 2. ad Donatum: Quantum illuc fidei capacis afferimus, tantum gratiæ inundantis accipimus. Et Augustin. in Johannem Tract. 32. Quantũ vos fidei attulerit homo ad fontem Baptismi, tantũ impletur. Per se autem atq; ordinarie, inæqualem Baptismus effectum non habet: sed æqualiter dispositis, utpote infantibus, æqualem gratiam omnibus confert. Et quamvis in Baptismo plura peccata remittantur uni quàm alteri : inde tamen non efficitur, inæqualitatem gratiæ hinc produci. Ratio est, quia minima etiam gratia sufficit ad peccata infantum delenda: nec augetur, vel minuitur ipsa gratia in sese, pro multitudine vel paucitate peccatorum, quæ remittuntur. Tandem in specie de Adultis si quæratur, illi etiam diversitatem admittunt: vel enim corde reverà credunt, uti ore confessionē edunt: vel sunt hypocritæ, & ficto animo Baptismum suscipiunt, qualis fuit Simon Magus Act. 8. 13. Priores illi in ipso etiam Baptismi actu sive momento, Regenerationis obsignationem reverà accipiunt. De his verò posterioribus quæritur, Quid gratiæ in ipsos conferatur. Respondemus, quod nulla prorsọ ipso actu. Donatistæ olim, hypocritisetiā in ipso actu Baptismi omnia peccata remitti, opinabantur: ita tamen, ut postBaptismum mox redeant. Et sunt, qui Augustinum quoq́, lib. 1. contra Donatistas c 12. hanc sententiam approbasse statuant. Rectè a. respondet Magister sententiarum, partim disputandi causa sic Augustinũ loqui: partim aliorum opinionem ab ipso referri: non a ex propriâ sententia hæc ab ipso asseverari. Hypocrita ergò non Rem Baptismi, h.e.salutarem usum sive gratiam: sed tantùm Sacramentum ipsum accipit. Rationes affirmati sunt hæ: 1. Ubi nō est fides, ibi neq́; est regeneratio. In hypocritis nulla est fides E. 2. Ubi regeneratio, ibi est & renovatio mentis: unde Apostolus Baptismum nominat lavacrum & regenerationis & renovationis Tit. 3. 5. In hypocritis nulla est mentis renovatio. E. 3. Hypocritis, quamdiu tales, non est pars, neq́ fors in sermone Evangelij: uti Petrus ad Simonem Magum: Act. 8. 20. & 21. E. neq́ pars regenerationis.

Verùm hîc nova statim & Octava oritur quæstio: An talis Hypocrita, postmodum si pœniteat, denuò baptizari debeat, an verò tùm demùm Baptismi gratia ipsi incipiat esse salutaris? Prius illud, de reiteratione Baptismi simpliciter negamus: Posterius verò hoc cũ Augustino omninò Affirmamˠ, qui loco paulò ante citato sic habet: Tunc valere incipit ad salutē Baptismus cùm illa hypocrisis, sive fictio veraci confessione recesserit. Quemadmodũ ergò omnis forma permanens, remoto impedimento, consequitur finem suum, verbi gratiâ, gravitate manente in lapide, lapis deorsum fertur: si impedimentum amoveatur, sursum exhalat: Ita pariter hîc fieri existimandum est. Objiciunt Huberiani assertionem illam Apostolicā, quæ tàm ad adultos, quàm ad Infantes se extendere videtur: Gal. 3. 27. Quotquot vestrûm baptizati estis, CHRISTUM induistis: Et Rom. 6. 3. Quicunq́, baptizati sumus in mortem CHRISTI baptizati sumus. Sed Respondeo, latiùs non esse extendendam assertionem Apostoli, quàm ipse textọ permittit. Adjecit autem Apostolus ipse manifestam & luculentam restrictionem in immediatè præcedentibọ: Omnes, inquiens, filij DEI estis, eò quòd credidistis CHRISTO JESU. De his ergò subjicit statim: Quicunq́, (nempè qui credidistis Christo Jesu) baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Ubi quivis facilè intelligit, universalitatis notam nō promiscuè ad omnes baptizatos adultos, sed ad omnes baptizatos credētes extendendā esse. Quoad locum posteriorem rursus per se liquet, illum intelligendum esse pro conditione sub-


### Chapter Four: Whether faith in Infants is prepared, or whether by Baptism itself it is conferred?

of the subject matter. But now, in that passage, the Apostle is not dealing with hypocrites and those not yet converted, but with the reborn and those believing in CHRIST, or as the Apostle speaks in the immediately preceding verse 2, with those who were already dead to sin: indeed, as chapter 1, 8 has it, whose faith was being announced in the whole world. It remains, therefore, firm and fixed that adult hypocrites, if they are baptized, do indeed receive the very substance of this Sacrament, but not its salutary use or fruit. Now if such persons are to be converted and saved, it is necessary that true repentance intervene. If this is present, then for such a converted hypocrite, by the Baptism itself, the covenant of grace and the stipulation of a good conscience with GOD is ACTUALLY made: which, when Baptism was conferred upon him, was not ACTUALLY the case, although by reason of the divine intention and ordination, that salutary Effect was offered to him. For Baptism is and remains, by reason of the intention of GOD, whose will is ἀμεταμέλητος, always a washing of regeneration, whether the person to be baptized has faith and a good purpose or does not have it. Although, therefore, he who does not have faith does not ACTUALLY aspire to the grace of Regeneration, yet, being baptized into CHRIST and his death, he was not only sprinkled with water, but was, as to substance, bathed in the entire Sacrament: and consequently, the grace of the Sacrament, with respect to the divine intention, was indeed offered to him, but was not ACTUALLY conferred, because of the obstacle of unbelief.

With these things standing thus, Huber's paradox must be most absurd, when in his writing on the children of Turks and Jews, page 48, he has it thus: All who are baptized, whether children or adults, are baptized into the name of GOD: and although they do not believe, nor acknowledge the benefit and grace which accrues and is conferred upon them through Baptism: nevertheless they are baptized into the name of GOD, adopted as children of GOD, and grafted into CHRIST. But that they do not acknowledge this immense goodness of GOD, and persevere in unbelief, this will result for them in a heavier judgment, and on that day they will again be cut off from the tree of life, and like dead members and withered vines, will be cast into eternal fire. Thus far the schismatic Huber: whose opinion certainly consists of more absurdities and falsehoods than words: as is partly clear from those things which have just been said about this Question; but partly it will be demonstrated more fully and expressly in the Article of Predestination.

Ninthly and lastly, it is asked: Since the salutary Effect of Baptism necessarily presupposes faith, is it also required in Infants, and is it conferred upon them through Baptism? We answer affirmatively to both parts of the question. For the true use of this Sacrament consists in nothing but faith, which is so necessarily required for receiving the fruit of Baptism that without it, it not only does not profit, but also harms greatly. A witness greater than any exception is CHRIST himself, saying: He who believes and is baptized shall be saved: he who does not believe shall be condemned. The foundation of this dogma consists in that Aphorism which is expressed somewhere in Canon law: No one can obtain the virtue of the Sacrament without faith. Whence was born that common rule, most well-known to the Schools of Theologians: Not the Sacrament, but the faith of the Sacrament justifies. This being thus presupposed, it follows ἐξ ἀνάγκης that all baptized infants believe in Christ. For unless they believed, they would not be reborn through Baptism, they would not have put on Christ, they would not have been baptized into the death of Christ, they would not please GOD: finally, none of them dying in such a state would be saved. Since all these things are diametrically opposed to the sacred Scriptures, that all baptized infants truly believe in Christ can no longer be a matter of doubt for anyone.

But whence this faith for them? Certainly, just as we deny that they have faith before Baptism, being by nature children of wrath, so we fearlessly affirm that in the very act and moment of Baptism, by the virtue of the Holy Spirit, true faith is given to them. In which part there exists an excellent analogy between Baptism and the circumcision of the Old Testament: that just as Circumcision in infants was σφραγὶς δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίστεως, a seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4, 11, so Baptism is of the same virtue and efficacy. And indeed, if the Holy Spirit works regeneration in infants through Baptism, he will necessarily work faith as well. For where there is regeneration, there also is faith: since neither can exist without the other.

The purity of this doctrine of ours first refutes the twofold error of the Papists concerning the Effect of Baptism in infants. For first, they imagine that Baptism profits infants without any faith of their own, partly ex opere operato, partly from the faith of the Church and those standing by. The former part of this absurdity we have expressly refuted in the Article on the Sacraments in general, chapter 2. But Scripture overturns this latter paradox, asserting that the just man lives by HIS OWN, not another's faith, Hab. 2, 4. For just as one cannot be baptized for another, so also one cannot believe for another. Indeed, by praying, others can obtain faith for others: but no believer can communicate his own faith to others.

Then, however, the Romanists dream that through Baptism a character is imprinted upon the souls of baptized infants: Which Gregorius de Valentia, Tom. 4, comment. Theol. disp. 3, quæst. 4, on the character of the Sacraments, point 3, p. 693, l. A. & B., defines as a certain spiritual power for doing or receiving something, for doing indeed in the Sacrament of Order and Confirmation, and for receiving indeed in Baptism. To prove this character, Thomas twists that of the Apostle 2 Cor. 1: GOD has sealed us, and given the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. But too ignorantly: For he does not understand by pledge and sealing some imprinted character, but the Holy Spirit himself, who is the earnest and pledge of our inheritance: that is, with the Apostle himself as interpreter, Rom. 8: Who gives testimony to our spirit that we are children of GOD, etc. D. Augustine indeed also names, lib. 2, contra Parmenianum cap. 13, Baptism a character, but in another meaning, for a mark or token of the Church and of the profession of Christians, the word character being used.

Furthermore, the fury of the Anabaptists and Sacramentarians also fights against the purity of this doctrine of ours, agreeing in this, that both deny that faith is possessed by baptized infants: yet under this distinction, that the Calvinists do indeed bestow Baptism upon infants: but [claim it] will not profit them except through the faith of another, namely, of the Church, of parents, and of godparents: an error they borrowed from the Pontificians, from whom, however, they otherwise wish to appear most alien: but we have just now crushed the vanity of this error. The Anabaptists, however, simply deny Baptism to infants, because it would greatly harm them, since they are destitute of faith, the foundation of which error is that they dream that faith does not fall to infants. To which only that one thing must be opposed, that the Savior himself expressly asserts that infants are endowed with faith in τǿ ἀγεσ̔ιν, Matt. 18:6, Luke 18:15, Mark 10:13.

They object: The use of reason does not fall to infants: Therefore, neither does faith. But I answer that loose brooms are being objected, which fall apart of their own accord. For no nerve of consequence fights here. Since faith does not depend on the use of reason, not even in adults: but solely on the power and operation of the Holy Spirit. Thus, indeed, the fanatics heap error upon error.

They object further: Infants cannot hear the word of GOD. Therefore, they cannot believe. The argument proceeds from the denied organ of faith to the denial of the habit of faith: where a sophistry is committed of non-cause as cause. For the hearing of the word is destined as an organ for conceiving faith, at least for adults: but not for infants, for whom the Sacramental Baptismal operation provides what they cannot attain through the defect of an external organ. But whence will these fanatics dream that faith came to John the Baptist, who, still constituted in his mother's womb, could not hear the word about CHRIST being born: and yet he brought forth manifest signs of his faith? Luke 1:41. What of the fact that the Apostle John, 1 Ep. 2:14, attributes to infants the knowledge of the heavenly Father. If this is found in them: why not also faith? Hence not ineptly St. Augustine, or whoever else wrote that book, De Spiritu et Anima, chapter 42. It does not excuse little ones from guilt, because they do not know it: nor does it exclude grace from them, because they do not know it. You seek guilt in them, you find it transmitted from the flesh: you seek grace in them, you find it bestowed by GOD.

Latin:

jectæ materiæ. Jam verò eo loco non agit Apostolus cum hypocritis & nondum conversis: sed cum renatis, & in CHRISTUM credentib9, vel ut Apostolus versu immediatè præcedente 2. loquitur, cum ijs, qui peccato jam mortui erant: imò ut habet cap. 1, 8. quorum fides annunciabatur in universo mundo. Manet ergò firmum & fixum, Hypocritas adultos, si baptizentur, percipere quidem ipsam substantiam Sacramenti hujus, non verò usum sive fructum ejus salutarem. Jam si tales converti & salvari debeant, Pœnitentia vera interveniat, necessum est. Hæc si adsit, tum tali Hypocritæ converso, Baptismo ipso ACTU fit fœdus gratiæ, & stipulatio bonæ conscientiæ cum DEO : Quod, cum conferretur illi Baptismus, ACTU non erat, licèt ratione intentionis ac ordinationis divinæ, salutaris iste Effectus ipsi offerretur. Est enim & manet Baptismus ratione intentionis DEI, cujus voluntas est ἀμεταμέλητος, semper lavacrum regenerationis, sive fidem & bonum propositum baptizandus habeat, sive non habeat. Etsi igitur, qui fidem non habet, ad Regenerationis gratiam, ipso ACTU non aspirat: in CHRISTUM tamen & mortem ejus baptizat9, non tantum aquâ aspersus est, sed integro, quoad substantiam, Sacramento tinctus fuit: ac proindè Sacramenti gratiâ, respectu intentionis divinæ, ipsi quidem oblata: sed ACTU non collata fuit, propter incredulitatis obstaculum.

Quibus ita stantibus, absurdissimum Huberi paradoxon sit necesse est, quando in scripto de Turcarum & Judæorum liberis, pag. 48. sic habet: Omnes qui baptizantur, sive pueri sive adulti, in nomen DEI baptizantur: & licèt non credant, nec beneficium & gratiam, quæ per Baptismum illis obtingit & confertur, agnoscant: nihilominus tamē in DEI nomen sunt baptizati, in filios DEI adoptati, & CHRISTO inferti. Quòd verò immensam hanc DEI bonitatem non agnoscunt, inq; incredulitate perseverant, hoc ipsis cedet ad gravius judicium, & in die illo ex arbore vitæ rursus excidentur, & tanquàm membra mortua, & vites aridæ, in ignem æternum conjicientur. Hactenus Schismaticus Huberus: cujus sanè sententia pluribus constat absurditatibus & falsitatibus, quàm verbis: uti partim liquet ex ijs, quæ de Quæstione hâc modò sunt dicta: partim verò in Articulo Prædestinationis uberiùs & ex professo demonstrabitur.

Nono & postremò quæritur: Cum Effectus salutaris Baptismi necessariò præsupponat fidem; An ea in Infantibus quoq; requiratur, & per Baptismum ijsdem conferatur? Respondemus affirmatè ad utrumque quæstionis membrum. Consistit enim verus hujus Sacramenti usus non nisi in fide, quæ ad fructum Baptismi percipiendum ita necessariò requiritur, ut sine hâc non tantùm non prosit, sed & obsit quamplurimùm. Testis omni exceptione major est CHRISTUS ipse, inquiens: Qui credit, & baptizatur, salvabitur: qui non credit, condemnabitur. Cujus dogmatis fundamentum consistit in eo Aphorismo, qui alicubi in jure Canonico est expressus: Virtutem Sacramenti sine fide nemo potest consequi. Undè nata est vulgaris illa regula, Scholis Theologorum notissima: Non Sacramentum: sed fides Sacramenti justificat. Hoc ita præsupposito, sequitur ἐξ ἀνάγκης, Infantes baptizatos omnes credere in Christum. Nisi enim crederent, non essent per Baptismum renati, non Christum induissent, non in mortem Christi baptizati essent, non placerent DEO: nullus deniq; ipsorum sic decedentium salvaretur. Quæ omnia cùm Scripturis sacris è diametro repugnent, quin utiq; omnes Infantes baptizati verè credant in Christum, nemini ampliùs potest esse dubium.

Sed undénam ipsis hæc fides? Certè uti ante Baptismum ipsos, quippè naturâ filios iræ, fidem habere negamus: ita in ipso Baptismi actu & momento, virtute Spiritus Sancti, Fidem veram ipsis donari intrepidè affirmamus. Quâ in parte Baptismo cum circumcisione Veteris Testamenti egregia intercedit analogia: ut quemadmodum Circumcisio in infantibus fuit σφραγὶς δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίστεως, signaculum justitiæ fidei, Rom. 4, 11. Ita Baptismus ejusdem sit virtutis & efficaciæ. Et profectò si Spiritus Sanctus per Baptismum regenerationem in infantibus operatur, necessariò operabitur & fidem. Nam ubi regeneratio, ibi etiam fides: siquidem neutra sine alterâ esse potest.

Puritas doctrinæ hujus nostræ, primùm refellit geminum Pontificiorum errorem de Effectu Baptismi in infantibus. Nam primum fingunt, Baptismum infantibus prodesse sine ullâ fide propriâ, partim ex opere operato: partim ex fide Ecclesiæ & astantium. Cujus absurditatis partem priorem, ex professo refutavimus, Articulo de Sacramentis in genere, cap. 2. Posterius verò hoc παράδοξον Scriptura evertit, asserens, Justum SUA non alienâ fide vivere Hab. 2, 4. Quàm enim alius pro alio baptisari non potest: tam etiam credere pro alio alius nequit. Fidem quidem precando alij alijs impetrare possunt: sed fidem suam alij communicare nemo fidelis potest.

Deindè verò somniant Romanenses, per Baptismum imprimi animabus baptizatorum infantũ characterem: Quem Gregorius de Valentia Tom. 4. comment. Theol. disp. 3. quæst. 4. de Sacramentorum charactere, puncto 3. p. 693. l. A. & B. definit, quod sit potentia quædam spiritualis ad aliquid agendum vel recipiendum, ad agendum quidem in Sacramento Ordinis & Confirmationis e ad recipiendum verò in Baptismo. Ad probandum hunc characterem Thomas detorquet illud Apostoli 2, Cor 1. DEUS signavit nos, & dedit pignus Spiritus in cordibus nostris. Sed nimis inscitè: Neq; enim per pignus & signationem intelligit impressum aliquem characterem, sed ipsum Spiritum Sanctum, qui sit arrhabo, & pignus hæreditatis nostræ: hoc est, interprete ipso Apostolo, Rom. 8. Qui dat testimonium Spiritui nostro, quod simus filij DEI &c. Nominat quidem D. Augustinus quoq; lib. 2. contra Parmenianum cap. 13. Baptismum characterem, sed in alio significatu, pro notâ sive tesserâ Ecclesiæ, & profeffionis Christianorum, characteris vocabulo usurpato.

Porrò cum puritate doctrinæ hujus nostræ pugnat etiam Anabaptistarum & Sacramentariorum furor, in eo convenientium, quod utriq; negant, ab infantibus baptisatis haberi fidem : sub eo tamen discrimine, quod Calviniani infantibus Baptismum quidem largiuntur: verùm non nisi alienâ Ecclesiæ scilicet, parentum & patrinorum fide profuturum : errorem hunc à Pontificijs mutuati, à quibus tamen aliàs videri volunt alienissimi : sed hujus erroris vanitatem jam modò protrivimus. Anabaptistæ verò Baptismum infantibus simpliciter negant, proptereà, quod ille ipsis, quippè fide destitutis, magnoperè sit obfuturus, cujus erroris fundamentum est, quod somniant, Non cadere in infantes fidem. Cui vel unicum illud opponendum, quod Servator ipse infantes τǿ ἀγεσ̔ιν fide instructos esse disertè asserit Matth. 18, 6. Luc. 18, 15. Marc. 10, 13.

Objiciunt: Usum rationis non cadere in infantes: Ergò nec, fidem. Sed respondeo, scopas objici dissolutas, quæ sponte suâ diffluunt. Nullus enim consequentiæ nervus militat. Siquidem fides non pendet ab usu rationis, ne quidem in adultis: sed à solâ virtute & operatione Spiritus Sancti. Sic nimirùm errorem errore cumulant fanatici.

Objiciunt porrò : Infantes non possunt audire verbum DEI. Ergò nec possunt credere. Procedit argumentum à negato fidei organo, ad negandum fidei habitum : ubi Sophisticatio committitur non causæ ut causæ. Auditus enim verbi adultis saltem, fidei concipiendæ organon est destinatus : non verò infantibus, quibus operatio Sacramentalis Baptistica præstat, quod per defectum externi organi consequi non possunt. Undè verò isti fanatici fidem Johanni Baptistæ obtigisse somniabunt, qui in utero materno adhuc constitutus, audire verbum de CHRISTO edendo non potuit: & tamen fidei suæ signa manifesta edidit? Luc. 1, 41. Quid quod Johannes Apostolus 1. cap. 2, 14. infantibus tribuit cognitionem patris cœlestis. Si hæc ipsis comperit: cur non & fides? Hinc haud ineptè D. Augustinus, vel quisquis alius illum librum scripsit, de Spiritu & animâ cap. 42. Non excusat parvulos à culpâ, quia eam non norunt: nec excludit gratiam ab eis, quia eam nesciunt. Quæris in eis culpam, invenis ex carne traductam: quæris in eis gratiam, invenis à DEO collatam.


### Chapter Four: On the Necessity of Baptism

Thus far we have disputed more than enough about the Effect, which, since it looks to the prow and stern, as it were, of our regeneration and salvation: certainly there is hardly anyone, unless he be impious or insane, whose mind would not immediately be struck by some thought concerning the supreme necessity of Baptism: Whether, namely, it is so absolutely necessary that its defect or lack is joined with the loss and expense of salvation? Concerning which question some have erred in excess, others in defect, and still err today.

On the side of ἐλλείψεως or defect, both the Schwenkfeldians and the Sacramentarians err, who opine that it does not matter much whether an infant is baptized or not: whether he obtains the effect of Baptism or not. Therefore, if an abundance of some minister constituted in a legitimate ministry cannot be had, however much the infant may be in danger of life, they think that one should not labor much so that the infant is baptized before he dies: nay, they think it happens without the loss of salvation, even if the infant dies unbaptized, although he could have been baptized by some other believer. To which opinion Whitaker writes too profanely, book 8 against John Durie the Scot, Vol. 1 of his works, p. 195. Although we say that infants obtain salvation without Baptism, whom the Lord has indeed predestined to life, it does not follow that Baptism is useless. For it is the final pledge of adoption, which no pious person would willingly want to lack. But if he does lack it, provided he looks to the eternal election of GOD, he cannot perish.

The Romanists, sinning on the side of ὑπερβολῆς, contend that Baptism is so necessary for salvation that they contend that infants, in whatever case they are snatched away by death before they have received Baptism, are simply damned. Hence it is that they despoil such infants of the customary place and honor of burial. And indeed, the importunity of the Pelagians long ago, who condemned the baptism of little ones and denied Original sin in infants, drove Augustine to such a point that he determined that infants who died without Baptism are damned with the eternal punishment of hell, as he speaks in ch. 27 of the book De Fide ad Petrum: although in the Enchiridion, ch. 93, he states that their punishment is most mild.

But both errors are easily refuted from the Scriptures: And the former indeed from the words of Christ, John 3:5, Amen, amen I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven. Whence he who does not see that Baptism is necessary for salvation sees nothing. For it is not true, as Whitaker dreams in the place just now cited, that this aphorism of CHRIST is to be understood only of adults, not likewise of infants. The Augsburg Confession, Article Nine, determines much more rightly: as also its Apology: We confess, it says, that Baptism is necessary for salvation, and that children are to be baptized: and that the baptism of children is not void: but necessary and efficacious for salvation. Whence the Fathers of the Council of Trent, Canon 4 on Baptism, did not pronounce badly: If anyone shall say that Baptism is free, that is, not necessary for salvation, let him be Anathema. What? That in a case of confession, we have a necessity, even at the peril of our life, to offer children for our Baptism. Just as we read that those mothers circumcised their children against the command of the tyrant Antiochus, 2 Maccabees 6:10. The latter error is refuted by the customary rule of the Church: Not the lack or defect; but the contempt of the Sacraments damns.

Therefore, that the Orthodox Church may rightly guard itself against both of these precipices of error, it determines that Baptism is least of all to be referred to the category of things indifferent: but that it is necessary for salvation, yet not by a simple or absolute necessity, as the hyperbole of the Papists holds: but by a necessity of order, of command, and of divine institution: which necessity indeed does not bind GOD to this medium, or take away His power, so that He could not also in an extraordinary way work regeneration and salvation in an infant: but it prescribes a law to men only, so that, the ordinary media not being neglected, they may neither despise the ordinance of God, nor rashly trust in extraordinary media. Therefore, some case of inevitable necessity can arise, where not will or some set purpose, but impossibility excludes either us or our own from the reception of this Sacrament: as when some adult eagerly desires the use of Baptism, but is situated in a prison or some other place where he cannot have the means of Baptism: or some infant is extinguished in the very maternal womb, or even having been brought into this light, ceases to be among the living before Baptism could in any way be conferred upon him. In such a case, indeed, that Ecclesiastical rule has a place, and he who is thus excluded from this Sacrament is not damned: which is most rightly demonstrated from the analogy of Circumcision and Baptism.

For just as infants who had died before the eighth day, and thus uncircumcised, were not subject to the curse: For they did not make the covenant of GOD void, having been snatched away by such a premature death: since they could not reach the just time defined by GOD Himself: So today the deprivation of Baptism, which happens by no fault or negligence of ours: but either through some violent and unexpected accident: or through manifest impossibility: can be a loss to no one. The reason is: Because GOD neither wills, nor ought, nor can be bound to the use of the Sacraments: and the Sacraments ought not to serve the order, but the order the Sacraments. Thus the thief on the cross was saved without the Baptism of water, being indeed excluded from its reception by a case of necessity. Thus very many Catechumens in the primitive Church were snatched to martyrdom before they were baptized. There are some among the Scholastics who themselves also subscribe to this doctrine: Thomas especially, who holds thus: The Sacrament of Baptism can be lacking to someone in two ways: In one way, in reality and in desire: in another, in reality but not in desire. To those to whom Baptism is lacking in the first way, there is no salvation in any way: for it pertains to the contempt of the Sacrament not to wish to be baptized. But if Baptism is lacking in reality only, but not in desire, as when someone desires to be baptized but is prevented by death, such a one can obtain salvation because of the desire for Baptism, which proceeds from faith working through love, through which GOD sanctifies the man inwardly: whose power is not bound to visible Sacraments. In which opinion Ambrose writes piously and elegantly concerning Valentinian, who died as a Catechumen before receiving Baptism: I have lost him whom I was about to regenerate, nevertheless he did not lose the grace which he asked for, for GOD looks at the heart. Let the cruelty of the rest of the Romanists therefore depart, who simply consign infants dying without Baptism to the Devil and hell. Christ certainly says indeed in Mark 16:16: He who believes and is baptized shall be saved: but He does not say in the antithesis similarly: He who does not believe and is not baptized shall be damned: but only: He who does not believe shall be condemned: thus implying that he indeed is damned who does not believe: but not likewise he who is not baptized, namely, being excluded from this Sacrament by an inevitable accident. There is no reason, therefore, why Christian parents should doubt even in the slightest about the salvation of their little ones dying without Baptism in such an inevitable case. For here that federal promise has a place most of all: I will be your GOD, and of your seed after you, Genesis 17:7. Which promise indeed GOD fulfills most of all when He grants faith and imparts salvation to infants situated in such a case of necessity, even in an extraordinary way. Relying therefore on this federal promise, let pious parents commend their children to the mercy of GOD with pious prayers, being most certain of being heard, according to that: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give you. John 16:23.

Latin:

HActenus de Effectu plus satis disputavim9, qui cum regenerationis & salutis nostræ proram quasi ac puppim respiciat : certè vix quisquam, nisi vel impius, vel amens fuerit, cujus animum non statim subeat cogitatio aliqua, de summâ necessitate Baptismi : An videlicet ita absolutè ille sit necessarius, ut ejus defectus sive carentia, cum salutis jacturâ ac dispendio sit conjuncta? Circa quam quæstionem alij in excessu, alij in defectu errarunt, hodiéq; errant.

Ex parte ἐλλείψεως sive defectus errant tùm Schvvenckfeldiani, tùm Sacramentarij, qui non multum referre opinantur, sive infans baptisetur, sive non: sive potiatur Baptismi effectu, sive non. Proindè si ministri alicujus in legitimo ministerio constituti copia non haberi, queat, quantumvis etiam de vitâ periclitetur infans, non tamen multum laborandum esse existimant, ut infans antequam moriatur, baptizetur: quin imò citra jacturam salutis fieri opinantur, si vel maximè infans non baptizatus moriatur, licèt baptizari ab alio aliquo fideli potuisset. Quam in sententiam nimis prophanè scribit Withakerus l. 8. contra Johannem Duræum Scotum Tom. 1. operum p. 195. Quanquàm dicimus, sine Baptismo infantes salutem consequi, quos nempè Dominus ad vitam prædestinavit, non tamen inutilem Baptismum esse sequitur. Est enim extremum adoptionis pignus, quo nullus pius carere lubens velit. Si vero careat, modò ad DEi æternam electionem spectet, perire non potest.

Romanenses ex parte ὑπερβολῆς peccantes, usq; adeò Baptismum ad salutem necessarium esse contendunt, ut infantes, quocunq; etiam casu, prius per mortem, quàm Baptismum perceperint, abreptos, simpliciter damnatos esse contendant. Hinc est, quod consueto sepulturæ loco & honore ejusmodi infantes spoliant. Et sanè jam olim Pelagianorum importunitas, baptismum parvulorum damnantium, & peccatum Originale in infantibus negantium, eò adegit Augustinum, ut statueret, Infantes sine Baptismo defunctos damnari æternaliter supplicio gehennæ, uti loquitur c. 27. libri de fide ad Petrum: licet in Enchiridio cap. 93. statuat, eorum pœnam esse mitissimam.

Cæterùm uterq; error ex Scripturis facilè refellitur: Et prior quidem ille ex verbis Christi Joh. 3, 5. Amen, amen dico vobis, nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aquâ & Spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum cælorum. Undè Baptismum ad salutem necessarium esse, qui non videt, nihil videt. Neque enim verum est, quod Withakerus loco jam nuper citato somniat, hunc aphorismum CHRISTI tantùm de adultis, non item de infantibus esse intelligendum. Rectiùs multò statuit Confessio Augustana Articulo nono: ut & ejusdem Apologia: Confitemur, inquiens, quòd Baptismus ad salutem sit necessarius, & quod pueri sint baptizandi: & quòd Baptismus puerorum non sit irritus: sed necessarius, & efficax ad salutem. Undè haud malè pronunciârunt Patres Concilij Tridentini Canon. 4. de Baptismo: Si quis dixerit, Baptismum liberum esse hoc est, non necessarium ad salutem, Anathema sit. Quid? quòd in casu confessionis, necesse habemus etiam vitæ nostræ periculo, pueros nostro Baptismo offerre. Sicut matres illas contra mandatum Antiochi tyranni pueros suos circumcidisse legimus 2. Macchab. 6, 10. Posteriorem errorem refellit usitata Ecclesiæ regula: Non carentia sive defectus; sed contemtus Sacramentorum damnat.

Proindè ut ab utroque errorum istorum præcipitio sibi rectè caveat Ecclesia Orthodoxa, statuit Baptismum minimè omnium referre posse aut debere inter adiaphora: sed ad salutem esse necessarium, non tamen necessitate simplici, aut soluta, uti Pontificiorum habet hyperbole: sed necessitate ordinis, mandati, & institutionis divinae: quae quidem necessitas DEUM non adstringit ad hoc medium, aut potentiam ei adimit, quin modo etiam extraordinario, regenerationem & salutem in infante operari possit: sed hominibus tantùm legem praescribit, ut ne medijs ordinarijs neglectis, vel Dei ordinationem contemnant, vel extraordinarijs medijs temerè confidant. Potest ergò casus aliquis necessitatis inevitabilis evenire, ubi à Sacramenti hujus perceptione vel nos, vel nostros, non voluntas, aut destinatum aliquod consilium, sed impossibilitas excludit: ut cum adultorum aliquis Baptismi usum avidè desideret: sed in carcere, vel loco alio sit constitutus, ubi Baptismi copia habere nequeat: vel infantum aliquis in ipso utero materno extinguatur, aut etiam in lucem hanc editus, prius tamen in vivis esse desinat, quàm Baptismus ipfi quoquo modo conferri potuerit. In tali sanè casu regula illa Ecclesiastica locum habet, & qui sic à Sacramento hoc excluditur, non damnatur: id quod ex analogiâ Circumcisionis & Baptismi rectissimè demonstratur.

Quemadmodum enim infantes, qui ante diem octavum, & sic incircumcisi decesserant, maledictioni non subjacebant: Neqs enim pactum DEI, sic praematurâ morte abrepti, faciebant irritum: siquidem ad justum à DEO ipso definitum tempus, pertingere non potuerunt: Ita hodièque Privatio Baptismi, quae nullâ nostrâ culpâ, vel negligentiâ: sed vel per casum quendam violentum & inopinatum: vel per manifestam impossibilitatem evenit: fraudi nemini esse potest. Ratio est: Quia DEUS negs vult, neq; debet, neqs potest alligari ad usum Sacramentorum: & Sacramenta non ordini: sed ordo Sacramentis inservire debent. Sic latro in cruce, absq; Baptismo aquae, salvatus fuit, quippè casu necessitatis ab ejus perceptione exclusus. Sic Catechumenorum plurimi in primitivâ Ecclesiâ, prius rapti sunt ad martyrium, quàm essent baptizati. Sunt ex Scholasticis nonnulli, qui & ipsi doctrinae huic subscribunt: Thomas praesertim, qui sic habet: Sacramentum Baptismi potest alicui duobus modis deesse: Uno modo, Re & Voto: altero verò, re sed non voto. Quibq primo modo deest Baptismus, illis nullo modo est salus: pertinet enim hoc ad contemtū Sacramenti, non velle baptizari. Si verò deficiat Baptismus, re tantum, non autem voto, ut cum quis baptizari desiderat, morte tamen praevenitur, talis propter desiderium Baptismi salutem consequi potest, quod procedit ex fide, per dilectionem operante, per quam DEUS interius hominem sanctificat: cujus potentia Sacramentis visibilibus non alligatur. Quam in sententiam Ambrosius de Valentiniano, qui Catechumenus ante perceptum Baptismum mortuus fuit, piè & eleganter scribit: Quem regeneraturus eram, amisi, Veruntamen ille gratiam, quam poposcit, non amisit, DEUS enim cor intuetur. Facessat ergò reliquorum Romanensium crudelitas, qui infantes sine Baptismo decedentes, simpliciter Diabolo & gehennæ mancipant. Christus certè Marc. 16, 16. dicit quidem: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur: non verò in antitheto similiter dicit: Qui non crediderit, nec baptizatus fuerit, damnabitur: sed tantùm: Qui non crediderit, condemnabitur: sic innuens, illum quidem damnari, qui non credat: non verò itidem, qui non sit baptizatus, nempè casu inevitabili ab hoc Sacramento exclusus. Non est igitur ut Christiani parentes, de parvulorum suorum sic inevitabili casu sine Baptismo decedentium salute, vel tantillum dubitent. Hîc enim locum vel maximè habet promissio illa fœderalis: Ero DEUS tuus, & seminis tui post te Genes. 17, 7. Quam sanè promissionem DEUS tùm maximè adimplet, quando infantibus in tali necessitatis casu constitutis, fidem modo etiam extraordinario donat, & salutem impertit. Hâc ergò promissione fœderali freti pij parentes liberos suos pijs precibus DEI miserationi commendent, de exauditione certissimi, secundum illud: Quicquid rogaveritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Joh. 16, 23.


### Chapter Four: On the Practical Use of Baptism

The practical use of Baptism is twofold: One παραμυθητικὸς Consolatory: the other νυθετικὸς ὴ παραινετικὸς Exhortatory.

Regarding the former: since Baptism is a sign of the covenant, is a seal of the righteousness of faith, is an ἐπερώτημα, a stipulation of a good conscience with GOD: truly the most ample matter of consolation is proposed to us in this Sacrament: so that just as David, about to fight with Goliath the Philistine, an uncircumcised man, was both confirming and sustaining himself by circumcision alone, 1 Sam. 17. So any baptized person, against any temptations whatsoever of both soul and body, can raise and sustain himself from Baptism alone: so that he can say: GOD promised this to me, wherefore He will perform the promise, because He cannot lie. I enjoy therefore a good and joyful conscience, bearing the sign of the covenant in my body: knowing that no calamity, however such, however great it may be, can snatch me from the hand of my Savior, whom I put on in Baptism, etc. Thus the little martyr Agatha, when she was being led out to punishment, kept repeating: I am a Christian, I am baptized, I fear nothing. Hence parents also can be most certain concerning the regeneration and salvation of their infants dying after Baptism: establishing that they in Baptism put on Christ, were baptized into the death of CHRIST, and were buried together with Him.

As to the latter use, Baptism admonishes us concerning the conflict of the Spirit and the flesh, concerning the death of the old man, and the resurrection of the new, as is taught in Rom. 6. fication of the flesh, of the vivification of the Spirit, of the newness of life. The Apostle himself inculcates this use in Rom. 6. 4. & 6. We are buried, he says, with CHRIST by Baptism into death: that as he himself rose again by the glory of the father, so we also should walk in newness of life: Knowing this, that our old man is crucified together with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we should no longer serve sin. This very thing is declared partly by the rites used around Baptism, such as are, washing, immersion, and emersion, a white and mystical garment: partly by the nature itself, and the force of the covenant entered into in Baptism, which always contains a reciprocal obligation.

CHAPTER FIVE OR APPENDIX explaining certain miscellaneous questions, both concerning the persons both baptizing and to be baptized: and concerning certain rites and Ceremonies used around Baptism, both as to practice and as to theory.

There is hardly any other article of the Christian religion which produces more scruples of theological practice than that which is about Baptism. But that we may resolve these one and all, neither the consideration of time nor of Method allows. We shall, however, recall the principal and more frequent ones to the censure of truth: those, namely, from the decision of which a right judgment may be made concerning the remaining easier ones.

In the beginning, therefore, it is asked concerning the persons baptizing: Can a vicious quality, or any defect from which the baptizing Minister suffers, render the salutary effect of Baptism void? Now this question cannot be explained more correctly than if it is distinctly shown through a certain analysis: What and how various defects can occur in baptizing Ministers: and whether in particular any defect can derogate anything from the salutary effect of Baptism? Three defects, or vicious qualities, are especially noted in Ministers: The first is: Lack of legitimate calling. The second: Manifest defense of heresy. The third: Corruption of life and morals.

Regarding the first defect, it is asked, Do those who have been called to the ministry by the enemies of our religion, for example, by the Papists, administer a true and salutary Baptism? The decision of which question is subordinate to that other principal question: Are those to be considered legitimately called who, with the ordinary ministers ejected, are substituted by Papist persecutors? Which question seems for this reason more difficult to explain; 1. because to such persecutors, no right and power at all seems to belong to call Evangelical ministers. 2. because if such ministers substituted by Papist persecutors are not received by the Evangelical Church, there is a danger that the preaching of the Gospel might entirely perish, or at least be removed by public edict: and consequently such a Church might be exposed to be torn apart and devastated by wolves. And thus this Question constrains us on both sides. But that we may candidly open what seems to us concerning this question, we establish in the beginning that it is beyond all controversy that such Papist persecutors not only sin by ejecting pious and faithful ministers: but also that they do not at all desire the good of the Evangelical Church: and that no pious person can or even ought to approve of this institution of theirs. But here the foot must by no means be fixed, lest while it is permitted to seek an argument from thence, that the ministry of ministers thus called by Papists is a void and ineffective ministry. For 1. one must distinguish between the state of the Church when free, and when pressed by servitude or tyranny. In the former case, certainly, the Church will not admit those thus called by Papists: but in this latter case, it is compelled to admit them, unless it wishes to suffer the loss of the whole Gospel. Although therefore the calling of those substituted by the Papists is not in all respects legitimate; but suffers from a vicious quality: it is not however on that account a calling that is entirely nothing: and therefore it is not to be established that it lacks the salutary effect and operation of the Holy Spirit. For immediately at the threshold regarding this question, those err gravely who think that a calling made by those who seize for themselves the right of calling through a certain tyranny is not only vicious in quality; but also in its very substance is entirely nothing. This is indeed truly asserted of those who, without any calling, clandestinely thrust themselves into Churches, and secretly creep into the fold of Christ. Even if these were immune from every error in doctrine, yet they are to be established as not sent by GOD, and therefore are by no means to be heard: according to that of Jeremiah 23, 21. I did not send them, and they ran; I did not speak to them, and they prophesied: And Rom. 10, 15. How shall they preach, if they have not been sent? But this can by no means be extended, nor ought it to be, to those who do not thrust and obtrude themselves upon the Church without any calling, but are called by others, and indeed by those who either entirely or alone do not have the right of calling, or under some title of Right falsely claim it for themselves. For those thus called, if they are pure in the doctrine of faith, and administer the Sacraments according to the institution of Christ, are not to be numbered among those of whom both the Prophet and the Apostle complain gravely in the places already cited. For by the very fact that they are divinely instructed with the gifts of teaching, that likewise they undertook the Ministry not by private will, but by the authority of others: they are to be considered as sent by GOD himself: so that that of the Apostle truly fits them: Woe to me, if I do not preach the Gospel 1. Corinth. 9, 16. And, Woe to those who have hidden the talent entrusted to them by GOD, Matth. 25, 24 Such therefore, when

Churches, in proportion to their gifts, perform the public Ministry rightly and sincerely: they can, and indeed must, be heard with a clear conscience for as long as the controversy that has arisen concerning the right of vocation between the litigating parties is not settled, and for as long as the ministers themselves, so called, maintain the purity of Christian doctrine intact. And even if it should happen that this controversy is never resolved to the satisfaction of the Evangelical Church, but the Pontifical magistrate finally obtains dominion in this matter by force, yet not even then should one abstain from the ministry of such ministers called by the Pontificials, and much less should one doubt even in the slightest about its salutary efficacy, for the following most evident reasons. For 1. when the question is raised concerning the virtue and efficacy of the Ministry: it is certainly not considered whether the ministers arrived at the Ministry legitimately or illegitimately, whether by flattery, bribery, gifts, or other evil arts, or by force or tyranny; but it is properly looked at whether those who perform the Ministry teach the uncorrupted Word of God and administer the Sacraments legitimately. If this is done, it is not for the hearers, because of the vicious quality of the vocation, to drag the ministry itself into contempt, much less to abstain from it petulantly; but rather to embrace this care of God with a thankful heart, and to commend the vice of the vocation and the struggle concerning the right of calling entirely to His providence with pious prayers. 2. The efficacy of the Word and Sacraments does not depend either on the person of the minister or on the quality of the vocation, but on the divine institution and promise. Where, therefore, the institution of the Ministry is kept inviolate, that is, the Word of God and the Sacraments, as well as the power of the keys, are rightly handled, there the grace of the Holy Spirit is present and works effectively for salvation in all who do not morosely oppose or petulantly neglect this ministry. 3. Innumerable absurdities would follow if the efficacy of the Word and Sacraments depended on the quality of the vocation of the ministers. For thus the error of the Donatists, long since condemned, would be established concerning the inefficacy of the ministry of those who are not rightly called: as Augustine has it in Epistle 5 to Boniface. Thus under the Papacy for many centuries there would have been no power and efficacy of the Sacraments: since it is certain that the vocation of most of the sacrificers was vicious even for the reason that it lacked the suffrage of the people or the laity; thus today there would be no Church in many places throughout Franconia, Silesia, Lusatia, and elsewhere, where the right of patronage is in the hands of Bishops or Pontifical nobles: thus no pious person could be certain of his own regeneration: for who would give you, or me, assurance that the vocation of that minister by whom we were baptized was in every respect legitimate? 4. Christ Himself partook of the sacred rites of those priests who were not called according to the law of God, but according to the will of men against the ordination of God: nay, He teaches that the doctrine of the law is to be heard from them: according to that in Matthew 23:2: The Scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat: whatsoever they tell you, do. The truth of this decision is evident from Phil. 1:15 and following, where the Apostle affirms that some preach Christ out of envy and contention, but others out of good will: And he defines those who announce Christ out of contention, not purely, in that they think that by preaching the Gospel they add affliction to Paul's bonds: but those who do so out of charity, because they know that he is set for the defense of the Gospel. What then? Because those others announced Christ out of envy and contention, and indeed οὐχ ἁγνῶς, not purely, and out of hatred for Paul, what does the Apostle pronounce about them? Does he forbid anyone to hear them or use their ministry? Not at all: What then? Nevertheless, he says, in every way, whether by envy or by truth, Christ is announced: In this I rejoice, and in this I will rejoice. 6. & finally, the authority of the Holy Fathers is added, and especially that of the Blessed Luther, who in his book against the private Mass and the ordination of sacrificers, confirms this definitive position of ours at great length: writing thus among other things: The office and the Sacraments are not ours, but Christ's. Therefore our faith and the Sacrament must not stand upon the person, whether he be pious or evil, consecrated or unconsecrated, called or having entered in secretly, the devil or his mother, but upon Christ, upon His Word, upon His office, upon His command and order: where these go, there it must go and stand rightly, let the person be who and how he will or can.

And after a few words: Look to it, that the preacher holds the pastoral office, which is not his, but Christ's office: do not let yourself be misled either, whether he is duly called, or has bought his way in, or forced his way in, however he has come in, over the head or over the foot, be it Judas or St. Peter, let that be of no concern to you, separate the office from the person, and the holy thing from the abomination.

We conclude, therefore, that vicious qualities of vocation do not render the ministry itself void, much less infringe upon the power and efficacy of the Sacraments in any way: but that the faithful can and ought to use the work of such ministers rightly and salutarily in all parts of the ecclesiastical ministry.

The other defect of ministers, which comes under consideration in this place, is the defense of heresy: Namely, does a heretical minister administer a true and salutary Baptism? To which question a simple affirmative answer can neither be given, nor ought it to be. For although the power and efficacy of Baptism does not depend (as has already been demonstrated) on the vocation of the minister to the ministry, or on his intention, or on other external qualities: yet with regard to faith and doctrine, the reason for all is not the same: just as the reason for the errors and heresies themselves, with regard to the object, is not one and the same.

Latin:

USus Baptismi practicus est geminus: Unus παραμυθητικὸς Consolatorius: alter νυθετικὸς ὴ παραινετικὸς Hortatorius.

Quoad priorem: cùm Baptismus sit signum fœderis, sit signaculum justitiæ fidei, sit ἐπερώτημα stipulatio bonæ conscientiæ cum DEO: amplissima profectò consolationis materia in hoc Sacramento nobis est proposita: ut quemadmodum David pugnaturus cum Goliatho Philistæo, homine incircumciso, se solâ circumcisione & confirmabat, & sustentabat 1. Sam. 17. Ita baptizatus quilibet adversus quasvis tàm animæ, quàm corporis tentationes, ex solo Baptismo se erigere, & sustentare queat: ut dicere possit: Hoc mihi promisit DEUS, quare promissum præstabit, quia mentiri non potest. Bonâ ergò & lætâ fruor conscientiâ, signum fœderis in corpore meo gerens: sciens, quòd nulla calamitas, qualis qualis, quanta quanta sit, me possit eripere ex manu Servatoris mei, quem in Baptismo indui &c. Sic martyrilla Agatha, cùm ad supplicium educeretur, subindè ingeminabat: Christiana sum, baptizata sum nihil extimesco. Hinc parentes quoque de infantum suorum, post Baptismum decedentium, regeneratione, & salute possunt esse certissimi: statuentes ipsos in Baptismo Christum induisse, in mortem CHRISTI baptizatos, & cum ipso consepultos esse.

Quoad posteriorem usum, admonet nos Baptismus de pugnâ Spiritus & carnis, de mortificatione carnis, de vivificatione Spiritus, de novitate vitæ. Inculcat usum istum ipse Apostolus Rom. 6. 4. & 6. Consepulti sumus, inquiens, cum CHRISTO per Baptismum in mortem : ut quemadmodum ipse resurrexit per gloriam patris, ita & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus: Hoc scientes, quod vetus noster homo simul crucifixus est, ut destruatur corpus peccati, ut non ampliùs serviamus peccato. Declarant hoc ipsum partim ritus circa Baptismũ usitati, quales sunt, ablutio, immersio, & emersio, vestis alba & mystica: partim natura ipsa, & vis fœderis in Baptismo initi, quod reciprocam semper obligationem continet.

CAPUT QUINTUM SIVE APPENDIX MISCELLAneas quasdam quæstiones, tùm de personis & baptizantibus, & baptizandis : tum de ritibus ac Ceremonijs quibusdam, circa Baptismum usitatis, quâ πράξιν, quâ θεωρίαν, explicans.

VIx quisquam alius est articulus religionis Christianæ, qui plures πράξεως Theologicæ scrupulos pariat, quàm qui est de Baptismo. Hoc verò singulos & universos ut enodemus, neq; temporis, neq; Methodi ratio patitur. Præcipuos tamen, & frequentiores, sub veritatis censuram revocabimus: eos nimirùm, ex quorum decisione, de reliquis facilioribus, rectum possit fieri judicium.

Initiò igitur de Personis baptizantibus quæritur: An qualitas vitiosa, vel defectus aliquis, quo laborat Minister baptizans, salutarem Baptismi effectum possit reddere irritum? Potest autem quæstio hæc rectiùs non explicari, quàm si per ἀνάλυσιν quandam distinctè ostendatur: Qui & quàm varij defectus in Ministris baptizantibus oc currere possint: & num in specie quilibet defectus, effectui salutari Baptismi aliquid derogare possit? Tres autem potissimum defectus, sive vitiosæ qualitates in Ministris attenduntur: Prima est: Legitimæ vocationis carentia. Altera: Hæreseos manifesta defensio. Tertia: Vitæ morumque consceleratio.

Quoad primum defectum, quæritur, An illi, qui vocati sunt ab hostibus nostræ religionis ad ministerium, exempli gratiâ, à Pontificijs, verum & salutarem administrent Baptismum? Cujus quæstionis decisio subordinata est principali illi alteri quæstioni: An ij legitimè vocati sint censendi, qui ejectis ordinarijs ministris à persecutoribq Ponttificijs substituuntur? Quæ quæstio ideò videtur explicatu difficilior; 1. quod ejusmodi persecutoribus, nullum planè jus ac potestas competere videtur vocandi ministros Evangelicos. 2. quòd si tales ministri à persecutoribus Pontificijs substituti non recipiantur ab Ecclesia Evangelica, periculum subest, ne planè intercidat, vel certè edicto publico tollatur prædicatio Evangelij: ac consequenter talis Ecclesia lupis dilanianda, ac vastanda objiciatur. Atq; sic utrinq; nobis hæc Quæstio constringit. Sed ut quid nobis videatur de hoc quæsito candidè aperiamus, statuimus initiò, extra omnem controversiam esse, quòd persecutores hujusmodi Pontificij, non modò ejiciendo pios & fideles ministros peccent: sed & Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ minimè consultum cupiant: quodq; hoc ipsorum institutum nemo pius probare vel possit, vel etiam debeat. Verùm hîc pes minimè figendus est, ne dùm indè argumentum petere licebit, quod ministrorum sic à Pontificijs vocatorum ministerium, ministerium sit irritum, & in efficax. Nam 1. distingvendum inter statum Ecclesiæ liberum, & servitute, sive tyrannide quasi pressum. Illo certè casu Ecclesia sic vocatos à Pontificijs non admittet: Hoc verò posteriore admittere cogitur, nisi totius Evangelij jacturam facere velit. Quanquàm ergò istorum à Pontificijs substitutorum vocatio, non per omnia est legitima; sed qualitate vitiosa laborat: non tamen proptereà planè nulla est vocatio: ac proindè non etiam salutari effectu & operatione Spiritus Sancti carere statuendum est. Nam statim in limine cica hanc quæstionem graviter errant, qui autumant, vocationem factam ab ijs, qui jus vocandi per tyrannidem quandam ad se rapiunt, non modò qualitate vitiosam; sed & substantia ipsa planè nullam esse. Verè quidem hoc afferitur de ijs, qui absq; omni vocatione, clandestinè se Ecclesijs ingerunt, & ovile Christi clàm irrepunt. Hi si vel maximè ab errore omni in doctrina sint immunes, tamen non à DEO missi esse, statuendi, ac proindè minimè audiendi sunt: secundum illud Jeremiæ 23, 21. Non mittebam eos, & currebant; non loquebar ad eos, & prophetabant: Et Rom. 10, 15. Quomodo prædicabunt, si missi non fuerint? Verùm hoc extendi nullo pacto vel potest, vel debet ad eos, qui non sine omni vocatione sese ingerunt, & obtrudunt Ecclesiæ, sed ab alijs vocantur, & quidem ab ijs, qui vel omninò, vel soli jus vocandi non habent, vel sub titulo aliquo Juris falsò illud sibi vendicant. Sic enim vocati, si in doctrina fidei sint puri, & Sacramenta secundum institutionem Christi administrent, non numerandi sunt inter eos, de quibus & Propheta & Apostolus locis jam citatis graviter conqueruntur. Nam eo ipso, quòd donis docendi divinitus sunt instructi, quòd item non privata voluntate, sed aliorum autoritate Ministerium susceperunt: à DEO ipso missi censendi sunt: ita ut verè in illos quadret illud Apostoli: Væ mihi, si non Evangelizavero 1. Corinth. 9, 16. Et, Væ illis, qui talentum sibi à DEO creditum absconderint, Matth. 25, 24 Tales proindè, quando

Ecclesiæ pro ratione donorum suorum publico Ministerio ritè & sincerè funguntur: tàm diu non modò salvâ conscientiâ audiri possunt, sed & debent, donec Controversia de Vocationis jure exorta inter partes litigantes componatur, & quamdiu ipsi etiam ministri sic vocati, puritatem doctrinæ Christianæ sartam tectam asserant. Et si vel maximè eveniat, ut Controversia hæc nunquàm ad placitum Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ dirimatur: sed Magistratus Pontificius tandem per vim dominium hac in parte obtineat; tamen ne sic quidem ab ejusmodi ministrorum à Pontificijs vocatorum Ministerio fuerit abstinendum, multò verò minùs de ejus salutari efficaciâ, vel tantillum dubitandum, ob sequentes rationes longè evidentissimas. Nam 1. quando de virtute & efficaciâ Ministerij quæstio movetur: non certè illud attenditur, an Ministri legitimè, vel illegitimè, nùm blanditiis, largitione, muneribus, vel alijs malis artibus, vel per vim aut tyrannidem, ad Ministerium pervenerint? sed illud propriè spectatur, nùm qui Ministerio funguntur, Verbum DEI incorruptum doceant, & Sacramenta legitimè administrent. Hoc si fiat, non competit Auditoribus, ob vocationis vitiosam qualitatem, Ministerium ipsum in contemptum rapere, nedum ab eo petulantius abstinere: sed grato animo hanc DEI curam amplecti, ipsiusque providentiæ, Vocationis Vitium, & certamen de jure Vocandi, in totum pijs precibus commendare. 2. Verbi & Sacramentorum efficacia non pendet vel à personâ Ministri, vel à vocationis qualitate, sed ab institutione & promissione divinâ. Ubi ergò institutio Ministerij inviolata servatur, hoc est, Verbum DEI & Sacramenta, ut & potestas clavium ritè tractantur, ibi gratia Spiritus Sancti præstò adest, & ad salutem efficaciter operatur in omnibus, quotquot hoc Ministerium non morosiùs aversantur, aut petulantiùs negligunt. 3. Innumera sequerentur absurda, si efficacia Verbi & Sacramentorum penderet à qualitate vocationis Ministrorum. Sic enim stabiliretur error Donatistarum, jam pridem damnatus, de inefficaci ministerio eorum, qui non ritè sunt vocati: ut habet Augustinus Epist. 5. ad Bonifacium. Sic sub Papatu multis seculis nulla fuisset vis & efficacia Sacramentorum: Siquidem constat, plerorumque Sacrificulorum vocationem vel eo nomine fuisse vitiosam, quod caruit plebis sive Laicorum suffragio; Sic hodiè nulla esset Ecclesia in multis locis per Franconiam, Silesiam, Lusatiam & alibi, ubi jus patronatus est penes Episcopos, aut Nobiles Pontificios: Sic nemo pius de suâ regeneratione certus esse posset: Quis enim vel tibi, vel mihi fidem certò faceret, Ministri illius, à quo baptizati sumus vocationem ex omni parte fuisse legitimam? 4. CHRISTUS ipse communicabat sacris eorum sacerdotum, qui non juxta legem DEI, sed voluntatem hominum contra DEI ordinationem vocati erant: quin imò doctrinam legis ex illis audiendam esse docet: secundum illud Matth. 23, 2. In cathedrâ Mosis sedent Scribæ & Pharisæi: quodcunq́; dixerint vobis, facite. 5. Patet decisionis hujus veritas ex cap. 1. Phil. v. 15. & seqq. ubi Apostolus alios quidem per invidiam, & contentionem: alios verò per bonam voluntatem Christum prædicare affirmat: Et eos quidem, qui ex contentione Christum annunciant, non purè, sic definit, quod existiment, se prædicando Evangelium, afflictionem addere vinculis Pauli: Eos verò, qui ex charitate, quòd sciant, ipsum in defensionem Evangelij constitutum esse. Quid igitur? Quia illi alteri ex invidiâ & contentione Christum annunciabant, & quidem ἐκ' ἁγνῶς, non purè, & ex odio Pauli, Quid de his pronunciat Apostolus? Prohibet né, ut nemo illos audiat, vel illorum ministerio utatur? Minimè: Quid ergò? Attamen quovis modo inquit, sive per invidiam, sive per veritatem, Christus tamen annunciatur: In hoc gaudeo, & in hoc gaudebo. 6. & postremò accedit autoritas S. Patrum, & cumprimis B. Lutheri, qui in libro contra Missam privatam & Sacrificatorum ordinationem, prolixè admodùm definitivam hanc nostram confirmat: sic scribens inter reliqua: Daß Ampt und Sacramenta sind nicht unser/ sondern Christi. Darumb muß unser Glaube und Sacrament nicht auff der Person stehen/ sie sey fromm oder boͤse/ geweihet/ oder ungeweihet/ beruffen oder heimlich hierein kommen/ der Teuffel/ oder seine Mutter/ Sondern auff CHRISTO/ auff seinem Wort/ auff seinem Ampt/ auff seinem Befehl und Ordnung: wo dieselben gehen/ da mus es recht gehn und stehn/ die Person sey/ wer und wie sie wolle oder koͤnne.

Et post pauca: Da schawe auff/ daß der Prediger dz Pfarrampt innen hat/ welches nicht sein/ sondern Christi Ampt ist: laß dich auch nicht irren/ ob er sey ordentlich beruffen/ oder habe sich hineingekaufft/ oder gedrungen/ wie er hinein kommen ist/ uͤber Haupt/ oder uͤber Fuß/ es sey Judas/ oder S. Peter/ da las dir nichts an liegen/ scheide du das Ampt von der Person/ und das Heiligthumb vom Grewel.

Concludimus ergò Vocationis qualitates vitiosas, non reddere ministerium ipsum irritum, nedùm Sacramentorum vim & efficaciam ullo pacto infringere: sed fideles talium Ministrorum opera, in omnibus partibus ministerij Ecclesiastici, rectè & salubriter uti posse ac debere.

Alter defectus Ministrorum, qui sub considerationem hoc loco venit, est hæreseos defensio: An nimirùm Minister hæreticus verum & salutarem Baptismum administret? Ad quam quæstionem simplex Affirmativa responsio dari nec potest, nec debet. Etsi enim vis & efficacia Baptismi non pendet (uti jam demonstratum) à vocatione Ministri ad ministerium: vel ab ejusdem intentione: vel ab alijs qualitatibus externis: tamen ratione fidei & doctrinæ, non par est omnium ratio: prout ipsorum quoque errorum atque hæreseων ratione objecti, non una eademque est ratio.


### Chapter Four: II. Question: Whether in a case of necessity any faithful layperson, or a woman, can confer a true and salutary Baptism?

For whoever retains the institution of the Savior inviolate in substantial matters, and thinks rightly concerning the Most Holy Trinity, in whose name Baptism is performed: although they may cherish some error in other chapters of Christian doctrine, and indeed one that impinges upon the foundation of the faith: they administer a true and salutary Baptism. For which reason we determine that those baptized by Papists and Calvinists are truly and duly baptized. Nor is it an obstacle that some of the Calvinists decline not obscurely toward the camp of the Arians: a fact which is sufficiently evident both from the examples of many and from the very type of doctrine which they cherish especially concerning the person of CHRIST. For since Baptism is not some private good, proper to Ministers, but a public one, entrusted to the whole Church: hence it follows that as long as the Calvinist Church publicly holds sound doctrine concerning the mystery of the adorable Trinity—a thing of which we are most persuaded regarding the churches of the Calvinists, in which the hearts of the hearers are purer than the mouths of the priests—and as long as it changes nothing in substantial matters: we determine that a true and salutary Baptism is administered by it. Nor can the error of the Calvinists concerning the Effect of Baptism, which we noted in the preceding chapter, stand in the way of this assertion of ours: since the effect depends not upon the doctrine of the baptizing Minister, but upon the authority and will of GOD who institutes it, as it depends entirely upon the faith of the one baptized.

But as for those heretics who deny the mystery of the Trinity, either in whole or in part, or who infect the ὁμοεσίαν of the persons, and therefore administer Baptism in the name of the Most Holy and undivided Trinity either not at all or with a perverse sense, and indeed the whole Church approves such heresy: then it is so far from the case that we determine a true and salutary Baptism to be conferred by them, that we rather judge there to be no Sacrament of Baptism there at all. If, however, the Church thinks rightly both concerning the substance of baptism and the mystery of the Trinity, and keeps the form of Baptism prescribed by the Savior inviolate, but the baptizing Minister is secretly addicted to the Arian, or Photinian, or some other similar heresy: then this can in no way harm the one baptized. The reason is: Because Baptism is not the good of one or another private person, but of the whole Church, which offers and commends the one to be baptized not to the Minister, but to CHRIST.

The third defect of baptizing Ministers is the corruption of life and morals. For it often happens that such are adulterers, usurers, drunkards, etc. If, therefore, one asks about the ministry of these, we follow the decision of Article VIII of the Augsburg Confession, which holds as follows: Although the Church is properly the congregation of Saints and true believers, yet since in this life many hypocrites and evil men are mixed in, it is permitted to use the Sacraments which are administered by evil men, according to the voice of CHRIST: The Scribes and Pharisees sit in the chair of Moses. And the Sacraments and the Word of GOD are effective on account of the ordination and command of Christ, even if they are exhibited by evil men. We therefore condemn the Donatists and those like them, who denied that it was lawful for the people to use the ministry of evil men in the Church, and felt that the ministry of evil men was useless and ineffective. The Scholastic Doctors themselves also support this opinion of ours, among whom Gabriel Biel recounts five reasons. 1. Because the Sacraments have their efficacy from CHRIST who institutes them and assists with his practical sign, to cause the signified thing from the determination of his own will. 2. Because if Baptism depended upon the goodness of the minister, no one could ever be certain that he had received true Baptism. For since no one can be certain of his own goodness, much less of the goodness of another. 3. Because it would be entirely unjust for one to be punished for the iniquity of another, which would certainly happen if the one to be baptized did not receive the grace of Baptism on account of the malice of the minister. 4. Because Baptism is a Sacrament of the greatest necessity, especially regarding infants, who have no other remedy for their salvation, which would be rendered entirely ineffective for them if evil ministers did not truly baptize. 5. Because the Fathers also approve this opinion, especially Augustine, who writes in Tractate 5 on John: It is one thing to baptize through a ministry, another to baptize through power. For such is the Baptism as is he in whose power it is given, not as is he through whose ministry it is given. And toward the end: Those whom Judas baptized, Christ baptized: thus therefore those whom a murderer baptized, those whom an adulterer baptized, if it was the Baptism of Christ, Christ baptized. I do not fear the adulterer, I do not fear the drunkard, I do not fear the murderer, because I attend to the Dove, through whom it is said to me, This is he who baptizes. See more testimonies in Lombard, book 4, distinction 5.

Further, Gabriel Biel asks in this place: Can a drunkard who is using his reason baptize? And he answers quite appropriately that neither the Sacramental virtue nor his ministry is hindered by the fault or sin of the minister. But what if the baptizing minister were so drunk that those standing around could not perceive the sense of the words, and thus he gave a sound without a mind? Gabriel answers that such a one clearly does not baptize, nor is this action of his to be held as baptism. To which decision we subscribe thus far: if the drunkenness of the minister is such that not only does he not know what he is doing, but he also cannot pronounce the words, 'I baptize thee, etc.,' which constitute the very Form of Baptism, so that they cannot be understood. It would be better, however, to carry the infant to be baptized back home from the temple, if an abundance of some other minister cannot be had, and to defer the Baptism until the drunkenness subsides, if only the strength of the infants permits it, than to prostitute this Sacrament to be defiled by such a drunkard.

II. Question: Whether in a case of necessity any faithful layman, or a woman, can confer a true and saving Baptism? The Sacramentarians concede to the negative, such that Calvin writes in Epist. 326: That no private person can be a legitimate minister of Baptism. And after a few words: Therefore we deem that baptism to be adulterous which has been administered by a private person.

vire: and in a rightly constituted Church, this rashness would not be tolerable. And again after some words: It was a monstrous audacity that women should thrust themselves into this office contrary to the law of nature. The same, Epist. 51. To permit baptism to midwives is an impious and sacrilegious profanation of Baptism. Theodore Beza, Epist. 12. The question is asked whether we approve of baptism administered by midwives? We answer, that it is not only disapproved by us, but also seems utterly intolerable.

But we, even in this place, making a divorce from the Calvinists, hold entirely to the Affirmative, but under this law and condition, that it be understood that baptism administered by women is approved by us only in a case of extreme necessity, where there is absolutely no supply of a minister or any other man to be had: our main reasons for the Affirmative are these:

1. Women also are created in the image of GOD: they are redeemed by the blood of Christ: they are regenerated in Baptism through the Holy Spirit: they are adopted as daughters of GOD: they are a royal Priesthood: they are co-heirs of grace: they are a part of the Church, and united to CHRIST through faith: so that the Apostle does not hesitate to affirm: In Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female: Gal. 3, 28.

2. The virtue and efficacy of this Sacrament does not depend upon the quality of the one baptizing, whether man or woman: but upon the virtue, power, and promise of GOD who institutes it. Therefore, the quality of the person neither perfects nor takes away the virtue of the Sacrament.

3. An argument is drawn, not at all invalid, from the place of equals. If the Sacrament of Circumcision could be administered by a woman: Why not also Baptism? But the former was permitted: by the example of Zipporah, conferring the Sacrament of Circumcision upon her son. Exod. 4, 25. Also by the example of certain Maccabean women, circumcising their sons, 1 Maccab. 1, 63. 2 Maccab. 6, 10.

4. The preaching of the word is permitted to both laymen and the female sex in a case of necessity: Why not therefore the administration of this Sacrament as well? The antecedent is clear from the example of Deborah, Judg. 4, 4. Huldah, 2 Kings 22, 14. Anna, Luke 2, 36. Priscilla, Acts 18, 26, whom the Apostle names his fellow-worker in the Lord, Rom. 16, 3. Nor does it stand in the way that the same Apostle commands silence to women in the Church, 1 Cor. 14, 34; for he does not command this absolutely, but because of the presence of men. By which very thing the Apostle wished to imply that in a different case, and in the absence of men, especially in a case of necessity, it is by no means forbidden for women to perform the duties of teaching. To which the Emperor Licinius undoubtedly had regard, when by law he prohibited men and women from gathering in one place of the Church, but that men should be separate and apart: and women likewise, separated from the men, should attend to divine worship: as witnessed by Eusebius, book on the life of Constantine, ch. 48.

5. The practice of the Church, concerning which Augustine, book 2 against the epistle of Parmenianus, ch. 13: If a layman, compelled by some necessity of a dying person, gives baptism: I do not know if anyone could piously say that it must be repeated. For if it is done when no necessity compels it, it is a usurpation of another's office:

‘But if necessity should urge, it is either no sin or a venial one.’

In this place the Sacramentarians object to the Decree of the Fourth Council of Carthage, by which women were prohibited from the office of baptizing. I answer 1. that this is forbidden to women only in part, and not absolutely: if, namely, Clerics or other faithful Men are present. In this case, that Council, over which St. Augustine presided, forbids women to speak. For the ninety-eighth chapter of that Council holds thus: Let a layman not dare to teach in the presence of Clerics, unless they themselves order it. And ch. 99. Let a woman, however learned and holy, not presume to teach men in a meeting. And ch. 100. Let a woman not presume to baptize.

Others object to the authority of Tertullian, who disapproved of γυναικοβαπτισμὸν (baptism by women). But it is sufficiently manifest that he speaks of the public and ordinary Ecclesiastical Ministry, and not of a case of necessity. He writes indeed in his book on Baptism: The right to give Baptism belongs to the high Priest, who is the Bishop: then to presbyters and Deacons, yet not without the authority of the Bishop: Nevertheless, when necessity presses, the same Tertullian asserts in the same place that the same right belongs also to Laymen.

III. Question: Whether an infant baptized either by a layman, or by a woman, ought to be rebaptized by a minister, and be carried to the church: and what process is to be observed there? It is answered from the practice of the Church hitherto received in use: That, namely, an infant so baptized ought by no means to be rebaptized. Just as also the ceremonies and prayers, which are afterwards wont to be publicly employed by the minister of the Church over such infants carried to the church, are not to be considered as a repetition of Baptism: but are nothing else than a public confirmation of the Baptism previously received, performed indeed with the solemnity of rites: but yet without a sacramental essence, which is neither instituted as new, nor as another, through that action.

But in this place that also is to be observed, which perhaps may easily happen: If, namely, women, when afterwards questioned by the minister of the Church as to what they did, whether they sprinkled the infant with water, with the pronunciation of the words, 'I baptize thee, etc.', should answer that it is not so exactly clear to them what they did in such a state of perturbation and anxiety? What is to be done in such a case? Here, indeed, it would be most advisable, without delay and further hesitation, to baptize the child publicly and solemnly: for the reason that the women could testify nothing certain concerning the baptism of this infant.

IV. Question: Whether any unbaptized infidel, such as a Jew or some Turk, can confer baptism? Augustine, in book 2 against the epistle of Parmenianus, chapter 13, answers that nothing is to be rashly affirmed concerning this question without the authority of such a Council as is sufficient for so great a matter. In Volume 3 of the Councils, such a rescript of Pope Nicholas exists: by a certain Jew, whether Christian or pagan is unknown,

Latin:
