Where at the same time he establishes that it is the duty of pastors to examine the doctrine and faith of individuals among the people; and of the hearers to profess their faith and show what they think about doctrine, according to that Petrine saying: Be ready always to give an account of your faith to everyone who asks. 1 Pet. 3:15. Fourth and finally, he discourses on the abuses and profanations of this Sacrament, especially those which are practiced even today in the Pseudo-Catholic Church of the Romans: such as are primarily the carrying about of the Host of this Sacrament, and its wicked transmutation into the Mass Sacrifice.

And such indeed is the entire Philippian treatment regarding this Article, which, as it may have perhaps sufficed in those times in which our author lived, so it does not satisfy our present century in any part: a fact which he easily understands who conceives in his mind even a superficial thought of the controversies of our century. But two things in this treatment especially smack of Ὀρθοδοξίαν [orthodoxy]. 1. That Philip expressly asserts that CHRIST is truly present in this Sacrament, and through this gives His Body and Blood to the one eating and drinking. 2. That it may not be distorted by degenerate disciples, who call themselves Philippists, to a spiritual eating and drinking of the Body and Blood of CHRIST, which happens by faith alone, not by the mouth of the body, that other point stands in the way, that he attributes this Sacramental eating and drinking to the unworthy as well, asserting that they therefore heap divine punishments upon themselves because, by eating the body of the Lord unworthily, they treat the body of the Lord with contumely. And would that Philip had subsequently maintained the same ὀρθοδοξίαν [orthodoxy] in this Article, as also in others, safe and sound: certainly the Church of GOD would labor less today. But what sort of person he showed himself to be in this arena in the last years of his life and in his other writings, and how he passed over not obscurely to the camp of the Calvinists, has been pointed out by us elsewhere.

Therefore, these things being dismissed for the present, we must rather labor on the correct method of treating this controversy. But if we examine more accurately the controversies of our century, which today intervene between us and the Calvinists, partly, and partly with the Romanists, regarding this Article, if we also examine other questions which are agitated among the learned today, partly regarding the definition of this Sacrament, partly regarding the nature of Sacramental predications, the entire exposition of it can most conveniently be divided into five chapters, or rather special controversies: The FIRST of which will be concerning the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament, expressly directed against the Calvinists: Where at the same time the question concerning the definition of this Sacrament and the nature of Sacramental predications must be examined against certain Critics.

The SECOND will be concerning the True and Real Presence of the body and blood of CHRIST in the Holy Supper.

The THIRD concerning the Triple Eating and Drinking, which occurs in the Sacrament of the Eucharist: likewise directly opposed to the Sacramentarians.

The FOURTH concerning the use of this Sacrament, both internal and external, and concerning various practical questions which can be raised regarding the administration of this Sacrament, as much regarding the ministers themselves as regarding the communicating persons.

The FIFTH and last will recall to a more accurate censure, and indeed will solidly refute, the errors of the Romanists impinging upon both the Substance and the Use of this Sacrament.

But before we make an approach to the exposition of the Controversies itself, the very purity of the Christian Religion seems to demand that we speak briefly, as if in the place of προλεγομένων [prolegomena], concerning four chapters in particular. First, indeed, concerning the origins, or the first cradles or beginnings of the Sacramentarian dogma, concerning the absence of the Body and Blood of Christ from the external elements in the use of the Holy Supper of the Lord. Then, indeed, concerning the clearly ill-omened progress, or propagation, of this very dogma. Then concerning the remarkable variety, uncertainty, and fluctuation of the sentiments and opinions with which the Sacramentarians have hitherto endeavored to cloak this dogma of theirs. Finally, concerning the far most sad Effects of this dogma. Moreover, we establish this primary end for this entire narrative: that thus it may be able to be established to us beyond doubt, partly concerning the immovable certainty and true antiquity of the doctrine which, by the benefit of GOD, the genuine Lutheran Churches hold and defend even today concerning the Sacrament of the Supper: partly, indeed, concerning the prodigious lust for slandering and lying with which the Sacramentarian race, seething, makes our B. LUTHER, both the Author and the primary Restorer, that is, the torch and trumpet, of this ill-fated Sacramentarian war, both first moved and hitherto continued.

Latin:

TRactatio Articuli hujus universa, qualis quidem in libello locorum Theologicorum D. Philippi Melanchthonis se offert, duarum est partium: quarum prior προλεγόμενα quædam; posterior ipsam diexodon continet. Προλεγόμενα rursus sunt tripartita. Primùm n. differit Autor partim de Patefactionibus divinis, quibus ceu illustribus testimoniis, DEUS humano generi agnoscendum se præbuit: partim verò de Promissionibus, quibus voluntatem suam de salute hominum revelavit: sed ita, ut semper addiderit ritus incurrētes in oculos, tanquàm certa ac indubitata sigilla promissionis Evangelicæ. Deindè verò facti hujus causas recēset tres: quarum prima est, ut signis istis commonefierent utentes de promissione, & voluntate DEI erga nos, atque ita fides per ista in nobis erga DEUM excitaretur & confirmaretur. Secunda, Ut memoria publicè durabilior esset, & promissio ad omnem posteritatem certiùs propagari posset: siquidem alspectabilia quæ sunt, memoriæ refricandæ, & propagandæ rectiùs conducunt, quàm quæ in animo sine adminiculis istis externis tantùm hærent. Tertia, Ut ritus illi sint nervi publicorum congressuum, in quibus DEUS sonare vult vocem Evangelij, vultque celebrari & invocari, & populi sui, ab aliarum religionum cætibus & sectis manifestam sejunctionem fieri. Tandem de excellentiâ Sacramenti Eucharistiæ verba facit, ostendens inter omnes ritus alios, ne quidem eo excepto signo, quod in paradiso proto-parentibus in arbore vitæ constituit DEUS, ullum alium vel dignitate præstantiorem; vel usu commodiorem: vel efficaciâ salubriorem esse eo, quem in Sacramento hoc Servator ante mortem suam sancitum nobis esse voluit, ut esset mortis suæ μνημόσυνον, nec ullo alio gratiæ suæ pignore abrogaretur, sed ad mundi usque hujus finem permaneret. Et talia sunt προλεγόμενα Philippæa.

Quoad diexodon ipsam Articuli hujus quadripartitam eam esse voluit ipse Philippus. Primum enim ostendit, Quomodo Cœna Doni sit instituta, non ut inane aliquod sit spe ct aculum: sed tale sacrum, in quo CHRISTUS reverà adsit, dans per hoc ministerium, su um corpus & sangvinem manducanti & bibenti, eo fine, ut & nos in CHRISTO, & CHRISTUS in nobis sit. Deinde verò monstrat, quibus prosit hæc manducatio: non ijs, qui ab e jus usu abstinent: non etiam indignis: sed ijs, qui ad hoc Sacramentum fidem & pœnitenti am adferunt, quibus etiam per hoc medium confirmatur fides in remissionem peccatorum. Ubi simul in dogma Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum de opere operato Autor justo zelo invehitur. Tertio admonet, qui sint ad usum hujus Sacramenti admittendi: non ij, qui manifestâ vitæ morumque consceleratione laborant: sed verè resipiscentes: secundum illud: Nolite sanctum dare canibus! Ubi simul Pastorum officium esse statuit, explorare doctrinam & fidem singulorum in populo: Auditorum verò, profiteri fidem, & ostendere quid sentiant de doctrinâ: secundum illud Petrinum: Estote parati semper, rationem reddere de fide vestrâ omni petenti. 1. Pet: 3, 15. Quarto ac postremo disserit de abusibus & profanationibus hujus Sacramenti, ijs præcipuè, quæ in Pseudo-Catholicâ Romanensium Ecclesia hôdieque exercentur: quales cumprimis sunt circumgestatio Comicæ Sacramenti hujus, & ejus nefaria transmutatio in Sacrificium Missaticum.

Et talis quidem est universa tractatio Philippéa, quoad Articulum istum, quæ uti temporibus illis, quibus vixit autor noster, fortassis sufficere potuit: ita nostro huic seculo nulla ex parte satisfacit: id quod facilè intelligit, qui vel superficiariâ tantùm controversiarum nostri seculi cogitationem animo concipit. Ὀρθοδοξίαν autem duo cumprimis hâc in tractatione sapiunt. 1. Quod Philippus disertè asserit, CHRISTUM in hoc Sacramento reverà adesse, & per hoc Corpus ac Sangvinem suum dare manducanti & bibenti. 2. Quod ne à discipulis degeneribus, qui se Philippistas nominant, ad spiritualem manducationem & bibitionem Corporis ac Sangvinis CHRISTI, quæ fit solâ fide, non ore corporis detorqueri possit, obstat illud alterum, quòd indignis quoque hanc manducationem & bibitionem Sacramentalem tribuit, asserens, ideò eos sibi cumulare pœnas divinas, quia indignè manducando corpus Domini, contumelia afficiant corpus Domini. Atque utinam eandem ὀρθοδοξίαν hoc in Articulo, ut & in alijs, deinceps quoque sartam tectam asseruisset Philippus: certè minùs hodiè laboraret Ecclesia DEI. Sed qualem se hac in Palæstrâ postremis vitæ annis & in scriptis ejo alijs præstiterit, & quomodo ad castra Calvinianorum haud obscure transierit, alibi à nobis offensum fuit.

Proinde his in præsentiarum missis, de rectâ potiùs pertractandæ hujus controversiæ methodo, laborandum nobis fuerit. Quod si verò nostri seculi controversias, quæ cum Calvinianis partim, partim verò cum Romanensibus, de hoc Articulo nobis hodiè intercedunt, si etiam quæstiones alias, quæ inter literatos hodiè partim de definitione Sacramenti hujus, partim de naturâ prædicationum Sacramentalium, agitantur, accuratiùs expendamus, commodissimè universa ejus diexodo, in quinque capita, vel potiùs controversias speciales, dispesci poterit: Quarum PRIMA erit de Substantiâ Sacramenti Eucharistici, contra Calvinianos ex professo directa: Ubi simul quæstio de definitione Sacramenti hujus & naturâ prædicationum Sacramentalium contra quosdam Criticos expendenda fuerit.

ALTERA erit de Verâ ac Reali Præscientiâ corporis & sangvinis CHRISTI in S. Cœnâ.

TERTIA de Triplici Manducatione & Bibitione, quæ Sacramento Eucharistiæ obtingit: itidem Sacramentarijs directè opposita.

QUARTA de Usu Sacramenti hujus tùm interno & externo, deque quæstionibus varijs practicis, quæ circa dispensationem hujus Sacramenti, tàm quoad ministros ipsos, quàm quoad personas communicantes moveri possunt.

QUINTA & postrema Romanensium errores tàm in Substantiam, quàm in Usum Sacramenti hujus impingentes, sub censuram accuratiorem revocabit, imò solidè refutabit.

Priusquàm verò ad ipsam Controversiarum diexodon accessum faciamus, vel ipsa Religionis Christianæ puritas flagitare videtur, ut de quatuor potissimùm capitibus, προλεγομείων quasi loco, breviter verba faciamus. Primum quidem de primordijs, sive primis incunabilis aut initijs dogmatis Sacramentarij, de absentia Corporis & Sangvinis Christi, ab externis elementis in usu S. Coenæ Dominicæ. Deinde verò de inauspicato planè progressu, sive propagatione hujus ipsius dogmatis. Tum de insigni varietate, incertitudine & fluctuatione sententiarum ac opinionum, quibus dogma hoc suum palliare hactenus studuerunt Sacramentarij. Tandem de Effectibus dogmatis hujus longè tristissimis. Finem autem universæ hujus narrationis constituimus hunc primarium : ut sic indubitato constare nobis possit, partim de immota certitudine, & vera antiquitate doctrinæ, quam DEI beneficio Ecclesiæ γνήσιος Lutheranæ, de Sacramento Cœnæ hodieque tenent ac defendunt : partim verò de prodigiosa calumniandi, mentiendique libidine, quâ gens Sacramentaria æstuans, B. LUTHERUM nostrum, tùm Autorem, tùm Instauratorem primarium, hoc est, facem & tubam, tam primùm moti, quàm hactenùs continuati, infausti belli Sacramentarij constituit.


### On the Lord's Supper: I

I.

IF one must come to the first principles, or the κύριον ἄιτιον [principal cause], we attribute whatever dissension has ever arisen anywhere concerning the tables of the Testament of Christ to the most hostile enemy of the human race, the Devil, as the first and supreme Author. For he himself is that Angel, concerning whom it was doubted whether he was black or white, who appeared as a monitor, ἀπὸ μηχανῆς [from the machine], in sleep to the primary leaders of the Sacramentarian heresy, who were established in the highest anguish and difficulty of defending their opinion, and supplied them with weapons. Now, indeed, it is manifest that the Devil has many times plotted the mystery of Sacramentarian impiety in the ancient Church of the Holy Fathers: but with an unhappy attempt, and indeed with a clearly vain success. For as soon as anything of this impious opinion began to grow in the course of all the preceding centuries, it was immediately refuted and crushed both by individual lights of the Church and also by plenary councils.

This is manifest enough even from the fact that, as often as the Calvinists have sought from the writings of the Fathers at least some color for their opinion, they have brought forward the testimonies of the same only truncated, twisted, distorted, and contorted, with that very same good faith that could not be worse in the case of open forgers. Nor did the dogma concerning the absence of the body and blood of Christ from the elements of the Eucharist ever become publicly known until Berengarius, around the year of our Lord one thousand, was almost the first not so much to scatter the seeds of this opinion as to undertake its public defense for some time by voice and in writing: which, however, was immediately by learned men and orthodox theologians refuted, nay, even abjured by the author himself. But what the Berengarian Controversy properly was, must be judged from the monuments of history, not from the false narratives of the Calvinists. This controversy, however, was not principally about Transubstantiation, although this too was moved afterwards, but incidentally: but rather about the real presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist. For when two writings on the Lord's Supper were then proposed, one of which was by Scotus, whom others call Erigena, the other by Paschasius, Berengarius professed that he had learned what he thought about the Eucharist from Scotus. Scotus, however, as the Calvinists themselves admit, simply denied the true and real presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Supper: nay, he contended that the properties of Christ's body could not even be taken away by divine power, so that it could be in many places at once: On account of the stupendous impiety of which dogma, it is written that he was pierced by his disciples with iron styli, or writing knives.

Paschasius, however, detesting the impiety of this dogma, did not assert that impious dogma of Transubstantiation, nor even the dream of any Consubstantiation, as the Calvinists trifle: but he constantly asserted the true and real presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper, without any opinion of μετουσίᾳ, or συνουσίᾳ, or any other physical transmutation or Union, so that in the ninth chapter of his book on the Sacrament, he burst forth into these words: by the power of the Holy Spirit we are daily fed with the body of CHRIST, and given to drink of his blood, not only by faith: but insofar as he (namely the Holy Spirit) works the substance of Bread and Wine, the flesh and blood of CHRIST by an invisible power, through the sanctification of his Sacrament, although they are comprehended neither by sight externally, nor by the taste of flavor. Making a divorce from this purer doctrine of Paschasius, and embracing the opinion of Johannes Scotus, Berengarius, as Lanfranc reports, expressed his confession in these words: Through the consecration of the Altar, the Bread and Wine become the Sacrament of religion, not so that they cease to be what they were: but so that they are changed into something else, and become what they were not: just as Blessed Ambrose writes: And the sacrifice of the Church consists of two things, one visible, the other invisible, that is, the Sacrament and the reality, or the substance of the Sacrament: Which substance, however, that is, the body of CHRIST, if it were before our eyes, would be visible. But since it has been taken up into the heavens, and sits at the right hand of GOD the Father: until all things are restored, according to the words of the Apostle Peter, it cannot be called down from there. Hidden in this Berengarian confession are almost all the κενοφύγετα of the Sacramentarians: so that it is clear from the open tenor of the words that he himself did not have a controversy then with the Church about the dogma of Transubstantiation, which the Sacramentarians are not ashamed to wickedly feign today: but about the true and real presence of the Lord's body and blood in the Holy Supper: But Berengarius revoked this impiety of error in the Council celebrated at Rome, in these words through a public palinode; which stands written in de consecr. dist. 2. c. Ego Berengarius: I Berengarius, unworthy Deacon of the Church of St. Maurice of Angers, anathematize every heresy, especially that for which I have hitherto been defamed, which attempts to assert that the Bread and Wine, which are placed on the Altar, after consecration are only a Sacrament, and not the true body and blood of our Lord JESUS CHRIST. I profess, however, with mouth and heart, concerning the Sacraments of the Lord's table, that I hold the same faith which the Lord and venerable Pope Nicholas, and this holy Synod holds, namely, that the Bread and Wine, which are placed on the altar, after consecration, are not only a Sacrament: but also the true body and blood of our Lord JESUS CHRIST: and are sensibly not only a Sacrament: but in truth are handled by the hands of Priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful.

The Gloss rightly warns in this place that the words of Berengarius must be understood soundly: because unless this is done, one falls into a more serious heresy than Berengarius himself held. Of the sounder understanding, it says, the sum is this: that all the later words should be referred to the species themselves, so that we do not make parts of the body of CHRIST. For these things belong to the species properly and in the truth of their nature and substance; but they are by no means ascribed to the body of CHRIST properly in itself and by itself; but only on account of the Sacramental Union with the external things, to which this properly happens. With this soundness of understanding, this recantation, having been accepted, is deservedly approved by both Luther and the entire purer Church, caring not a straw how the Papists labor in explaining this recantation for the sake of asserting Transubstantiation.

But Berengarius, having changed his mind a little later, returned to his former error like a dog to its vomit: nevertheless, he was more cautious in criticizing the true and real presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Supper with his words, while speaking splendidly and magnificently meanwhile about the power and efficacy of the body of CHRIST. In this very part again, he expressed to the life the mind and affection of the clandestine Calvinists, who even today determine that one should dispute and preach more about the salutary use and efficacy of this Sacrament than about its substance: with a truly cunning plan, so that, of course, even by this means, the doctrine concerning the true and real presence of the body and blood of CHRIST in the Holy Supper, and their Sacramental eating and drinking, might gradually expire in the minds of the faithful. Sabellicus is indeed a witness in his Enneads that Berengarius sang a second recantation in this manner: I believe with my heart and profess with my mouth that the Bread and Wine in the Eucharist are the true body of CHRIST, which hung on the cross and sits at the right hand of the Father: and the true blood, which was poured out from his side, not only through the sign and power of the Sacrament: But in the property of nature and the truth of substance. But not even thus did he cast off his error, but by pretending, dissembling, affirming, and denying, he strove to serve the stage in such a way that he imposed upon the Church of GOD several times most shamefully.

In the Synod of Tours, certainly, by the Fathers he was ordered to give an account of his faith, since he distrusted his own cause, he protested that he embraced the common faith of the Church: but he played with ambiguous and evasive wrappings of words all the while.

Although even in the Lateran Council, in the presence of 113 bishops, he consecrated the books of his dogma to Vulcan and handed them over to be burned, and indeed even swore holily by GOD that he would never again scatter such a kind of doctrine among the common people, but would constantly rest in the opinion of the Fathers: yet afterwards, having returned to his own genius and disposition, he strove to propagate far and wide the poison of his dogma concerning the absence of the Body of CHRIST from the Supper, partly through certain disciples, and partly indeed through little books scattered secretly here and there.

At length, dying on the very day of the Epiphany, having poured forth many groans and sighs, remembering too late in his mind how many miserable adolescents he had infected with his unhappy dogma, he is read to have burst forth into these words, most full of despair: Today, on the day of His manifestation, our Lord JESUS CHRIST will appear to me, for penance, as I hope, unto glory: or for others, as I fear, unto punishment: witnesses being Vincentius, book 25, chapter 30; William of Malmesbury, book 3, chapters 58 and 59, concerning the deeds of the English. Thus, therefore, the Devil cast the first seeds and foundations of this unhappy Sacramentarian dogma concerning the Holy Supper through that Berengarius; although, once he had finished his course, it was always so repressed by the zeal of the pious Fathers that it could not resume its strength, until in the memory of our Fathers it was, as it were, resurrected from the infernal regions by Carlstadt, Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Calvin, and others, and brought back onto the stage of the Church after a long absence. By what means this was done, the second chapter of the prolegomena will now explain.

Latin:

I.

SI ad prima principia, vel κύριον ἄιτιον sit veniendum, infensissimo generis humani hosti Diabolo, tanquàm Autori primo ac summo, quicquid unquàm uspiam dissensionis de Testamenti Christi tabulis obortum fuit, acceptum referimus. Ipse enim Angelus ille, de quo dubitatum fuit, ater an albus fuerit, qui primarijs hærefeos Sacramentariæ antefignanis, in summo angore & difficultate defendendæ opinionis suæ constitutis, in somno ceu monitor, ἀπὸ μηχανῆς apparuit, & arma subministravit. Jam verò manifestum est, Diabolum in antiquâ S. Patrum Ecclesiâ multoties impietatis Sacramentariæ mysterium, molitum esse: sed infelici conatu, imò successu planè irrito. Quamprimùm enim seculorum superiorum omnium decursu, impiæ hujus opinionis gliscere aliquid cœpit, confestim tùm à singulis Ecclesiæ luminibus: tùm à plenarijs etiam concilijs refutatum & protritum fuit.

Patet hoc vel indè satis manifestè, quod quoties Calviniani ex Patrum scriptis, aliquid saltem coloris opinioni suæ quæfiverunt, testimonia eorundem non nisi detruncata, obtorta, detorta, contorta adduxerunt, eâ planè fide, quâ in apertos falsarios pejor cadere nulla possit. Neque dogma de absentia corporis & sangvinis Christi ab Elementis Eucharistiæ, vix priùs unquàm publicè innotuit, quam Berengarius circa Annum Domini millesimum, primus fermè, non tàm semina spargeret opinionis hujus, quàm publicam ejus defensionem aliquandiu voce scriptisque susciperet: quæ tamen statim à viris eruditis, & Theologis Orthodoxis refutata, quin ab ipso autore abjurata fuit. Quæ autem propriè fuerit Berengariana Controversia, ex historiarum monumentis, non ex falsis Calvinianorum narrationibus, judicandum est. Fuit autem hæc controversia non principaliter de Transubstantiatione, licèt postea hæc quoque, sed incidenter, mota fuerit: Verum de reali præsentia corporis & sangvinis Christi in Eucharistia. Propositis enim tùm duobus de Cœnâ Domini scriptis, quorum unum erat Scoti, quem alij Erigenam appellant: alterum Passchasij, professus est Berengarius, se id, quod de Eucharistia sentiret, ex Scoto didicisse. Scotus autem, fatentibus ipsis Calvinianis, veram ac realem præsentiam corporis & sangvinis Christi in Cœnâ simpliciter negavit: quin contendit, ne quidem per potentiam divinam proprietates corpori Christi adimi posse, ut in pluribus locis simul esse queat: Ob cujus dogmatis stupendam impietatem, à discipulis suis, ferreis gryphis, sive cultellis scriptorijs confossus esse scribitur.

Paschasius verò impietatem dogmatis hujus detestatus, non impium illud Transsubstantiationis dogma, neq; etiam Consubstantiationis alicujus somnium, uti Calviniani nugantur: sed veram ac realem præsentiam corporis & sangvinis Christi in S. Cœnâ, sine ullâ vel μετουσίᾳ, vel συνουσίᾳ, aut alius alicujus physicæ transmutationis aut Unionis opinione constanter asseruit, ita ut capite nono libri de Sacramento editi, in hæc verba erumperet: virtute Spiritus Sancti corpore CHRISTI quotidiè pascimur, & potamur sangvine, non solùm fide: sed quatenùs ipse (scilicet Spiritus Sanctus) Panis & Vini substantiam, carnem & sangvinem CHRISTI invisibili potentiâ, per Sacramenti sui sanctificationem operatur, quamvis nec visu exteriùs, nec gustu saporis comprehendantur. Ab hâc puriore doctrinâ Paschasij, divortium faciens Berengarius, & Johannis Scoti sententiam amplexus, confessionem suam, referente Lanfranco, his verbis expressit: Per consecrationem Altaris, Panis & Vinum fiunt Sacramentum religionis, non ut desinant esse, quæ erant: sed ut in aliud mutentur, & fiant, quæ non erant: quemadmodum B. Ambrosius scribit: Et sacrificium Ecclesiæ ex duabus rebus constat, alterâ visibili, alterâ invisibili, hoc est, Sacramento & re, sive substantiâ Sacramenti: Quæ tamen substantia, hoc est, corpus CHRISTI, si præ oculis esset, visibile esset. Cùm verò in cælos sublatum sit, atq; ad DEI Patris dextram sedeat: donec omnia restituantur, secundum Apostoli Petri verba, non potest inde devocari. Latent in hâc Berengarianâ confessione pleraq; ferè omnia Sacramentariorum κενοφύγετα: ita ut ex aperto Verborum tenore pateat, non ipsi fuisse tunc cum Ecclesiâ de Transubstantiationis dogmate controversiam, quod improbè fingere non pudet hodiè Sacramentarios: sed de verâ ac reali præsentiâ corporis & sangvinis Dominici in S. Cœnâ: Hanc autem erroris impietatem in Concilio Romæ celebrato, his verbis Berengarius per publicam palinodiam revocavit; quæ descripta extat de consecr. dist. 2. c. Ego Berengarius: Ego Berengarius, Andegavensis Ecclesiæ S. Mauritij " indignus Diaconus, anathematizo omnem hæresin, " præcipuè eam, de quâ hačtenus infamatus sum, quæ " astruere conatur, Panem & Vinum, quæ in Altari " ponuntur, post consecrationem solummodò Sacra- " mentum, & non verum corpus & sangvinem Do- " mini nostri JESU CHRISTI esse. Profiteor autem ore & corde, de Sacramentis Dominicæ mensæ, eandem fidem me tenere, quam Dominus & venerabilis Papa Nicolaus, & hæc sancta Synodus tenet, scilicet, Panem & Vinum, quæ in altari ponuntur, post consecrationem, non solùm Sacramentum : sed etiam verum corpus & sangvinem Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI esse : & sensualiter non solum Sacramentum : sed in veritate manibus Sacerdotum tractari, frangi, & fidelium dentibus atteri.

Rectè autem hoc loco monet Glossa, verba Berengarij sanè intelligenda esse: quòd nisi fiat, in graviorem incidi hæresin, quam Berengarius ipse tenuerit. Sanioris autem intellectus, hanc esse summam, inquit, ut verba posteriora omnia ad species ipsas referantur, quin de corpore " CHRISTI partes non faciamus. Speciebus enim " ista propriè & in veritate naturæ atǫ substantiæ suæ " competunt; corpori autem CHRISTI propriè in " se, & per se nequaquàm adscribuntur; sed tantùm " propter Unionem Sacramentalem cum rebus externis, quibus hoc propriè accidit. Quâ sanitate intellectus acceptam hanc Palinodiam, & Lutherus & omnis purior Ecclesia meritò approbat, flocci interimpendens, quomodo in hâc palinodia explicanda Pontificij pro asserendâ Transsubstantiatione laborent.

Cæterùm Berengarius paulò pôst mutato animo, ad pristinum errorem, tanquàm canis ad vomitum redijt : misiùs tamen veram ac realem præsentiam corporis & sangvinis Christi in Cœnâ, verbis perstringens : Splendidè interim & magnificè de virtute & efficaciâ corporis CHRISTI verba faciens. Quâ ipsâ rursus in parte, clanculariorum Calvinistarum animum & affectum ad vivum expressit, qui & ipsi, de usu magis salutari, & efficaciâ hujus Sacramenti, quàm de ejus substantiâ disputandum ac concionandum esse, hodiéque statuunt: astuto sanè consilio, ut nimirùm vel hoc pacto, doctrina de verâ ac reali præsentiâ corporis & sangvinis CHRISTI in S. Cœnâ, eorundemque manducatione ac bibitione Sacramentali, paulatim in animis fidelium expiret. Testis verò est Sabellicus in suis Enneadibus, Berengarium secundùm etiam palinodiam cecinisse, in hunc modum : Corde credo & ore profiteor, Panem & Vinum in Eucharistiâ esse verum corpus CHRISTI, quod in cruce pependit, sederǫ́ ad dextram Patris: & verum sangvinem, qui de latere ejus effusus est, non tantùm per signum & virtutem Sacramenti: Sed in proprietate naturæ, & veritate substantiæ. Sed neque sic errorem abjecit, quin simulando, dissimulando, affirmando, negando, ita Scenæ inservire studuit, ut Ecclesiæ DEI aliquoties turpissimè imponeret.

In Synodo certè Turonensi, à Patribus fidei fidei suæ rationem reddere jussus, cùm causæ suæ diffideret, communem Ecclesiæ fidem se amplecti protestatus est: sed ambiguis & flexiloquis verborum involucris subindè ludens.

Quanquam etiam in Lateranensi Concilio præsentibus 113. Episcopis, libros sui dogmatis Vulcano consecravit, & comburendos tradidit, quin per DEUM etiam sanctè juravit, se ejusmodi doctrinæ genus deinceps nunquàm in vulgus sparsurum: sed in Patrum sententiâ constanter acquieturum: postea tamen ad genium & ingenium reversus, virus dogmatis sui, de absentiâ Corporis CHRISTI à Cœnâ per discipulos partim quosdam, partim verò per libellos, clam hinc indè sparsos, longè latéque propagare studuit.

Tandem moribundus ipso die Epiphaniæ, multis gemitibus ac suspirijs fusis, nimis serò apud animum recordatus, quot miseros adolescentes infelici suo dogmate infecerit, in hæc verba desperationis plenissima erupisse legitur: Hodie in die apparitionis suæ, apparebit mihi Dominus noster JESUS CHRISTUS, propter pœnitentiam, ut spero ad gloriam: vel propter alios, ut timeo, ad pœnam: testibus Vincentio lib. 25. cap. 30. VVilhelmo Malmesburiense lib. 3. cap. 58. & 59. de gestis Anglorum. Sic ergò Diabolus prima semina & fundamenta jecit per Berengarium istum infausti dogmatis Sacramentarij, de S. Cœnâ; quanquam satis ipso functo, piorum Patrum studio, ita illud repressum semper fuit, ut vires resumere haud potuerit, usque dùm Patrum nostrorum memoriâ per Carolostadium, Zvvinglium, Oecolampadium, Calvinum & alios, illud ab inferis quasi resuscitatum, & postliminiò in proscenium Ecclesiæ revocatum fuit. Quod quibus medijs factum; secundum προλεγομένων caput jam expediet.


### On the Lord's Supper: II

II.

When in the year 1521 the Evangelical Reformation, undertaken by the blessed Luther, was in great peril, and the tender salvation of the barely reformed Evangelical Church seemed to be placed ἐπὶ ξυρῦ ἀκμῆς on the razor's edge: with Luther himself having been proscribed by the Emperor and stationed in Patmos near Eisenach in Thuringia: there Andreas Bodenstein Carlstadt judged that he too must emerge: and therefore, by private daring, without consulting the Church, and with his colleagues unaware—nay, even protesting—he seized an axe, demolished the statues and images in our parish church, and abrogated the customary ceremonies: he scattered Anabaptist and Schwenckfeldian seeds not obscurely: he contended that there was no need for the study of letters, dreaming that divine revelations were rather to be expected: and in order to undermine the authority of the blessed Luther, who was then absent, he did not hesitate to gnaw at the very sounder doctrine concerning the Supper of the Lord.

Confirmed by imperial authority, he discusses in book 3, page 45 of the Geneva edition: Andreas Carlstadt, meanwhile while Luther was away, proposed diverse dogmas and had tumultuously ejected statues from the temples, having stirred up the populace. And in book 5, page 82: Carlstadt, dissenting from Luther, having left Wittenberg, was very familiar with those clandestine teachers who feigned visions and conversations with GOD. For this reason, the prince of Saxony had interdicted him from his borders: he himself, however, by published pamphlets, attacked Luther and his colleagues as if they were new flatterers of the Roman Pontiff. He also interpreted those words of CHRIST, 'This is my Body,' in this way: 'Here sits my Body.'

Philip supports Sleidan in the preface of his little book concerning the opinions of the ancients on the Lord's Supper, establishing Carlstadt as the first author of the Sacramentarian struggle, writing thus: Carlstadt first stirred up this tumult, a wild man, without talent, without learning, without common sense: and he moved the controversy concerning the Lord's Supper only out of hatred for Luther, not from any opinion of piety. But from where Carlstadt drew this dogma of his, he himself confesses, but that he did not receive it from the Holy Scriptures, not from the words of the Institution, not from the analogy of faith, or the nature of the Sacraments: but that a certain man appeared to him in a vision, who revealed that opinion concerning the Supper to him, whom he himself thinks to have been the heavenly Father.

Following Carlstadt was Huldrych Zwingli, who, according to Lavater, even long before Carlstadt had begun to stir up this dispute concerning the Lord's Supper, cherished and brought forth in his mind a new dogma against Luther, writing here and there to the principal learned men of Germany and France that he was about to bring forth a certain new and singular opinion concerning the Lord's Supper.

The opinion, however, finally brought forth by him was this: Christ, he says, 'This is my body': that is, 'Bread signifies my body'.

It is most worthy of observation, however, from where Zwingli also drew this explanation of the words of the Supper. For although he confesses that he had cherished that opinion concerning the Eucharist in his mind for many years, indicating that time in which he lived under the Papacy, in which 'no one of us,' says Zwingli, 'ever truly believed that he was eating in that bread such a thing as we dreamed' (thus indeed establishing mere infidelity as the beginning of his error): yet he writes that he did not find or understand how he might reconcile this opinion with the words of the Institution until he found in the baggage of a certain Dutchman, whom he calls Hoen, a letter [showing] that these words, 'This is my body,' could be explained thus: 'This signifies my body'.

Which letter was published to the public by Zwingli himself in the year of our Lord 1525. Furthermore, when a controversy arose over this very interpretation between him and a certain Senatorial Scribe at Zurich, who contended that it was not consistent with the words of the Institution; and when, thinking over everything in his mind and revolving everything, he found nothing to answer those Scribes: there On the thirteenth day of April, as the time approached which had been set for the litigating parties to plead their case, it seemed to me in a dream that I was contending again with the scribe, and had become so dumb that, when my tongue refused its service, I could not speak out what I knew to be true. When I seemed to be vehemently troubled by this anguish, there appeared a monitor ἀπὸ μηχανῆς (so his words sound) (whether he was black or white, I do not remember: for I am telling a dream), who said: Why do you answer him sluggishly, regarding what is written in Exodus 12: For it is the Lord's Passover. As soon as this phantom was seen, I woke up at once, and leaping from my bed, I first looked everywhere for the passage in the Septuagint, and I discoursed upon it before the whole assembly to the best of my ability.

Oecolampadius, intending to bring aid to Zwingli in almost the same year, contends that there is no miracle in the mystical bread above the grasp of man: and that those words, This is my Body, cannot stand without a trope, so that many absurdities may be avoided. In eliciting, defining, and glossing this trope, those who followed Zwingli and Oecolampadius labored so much that they could scarcely find where to set their foot: until at length John Calvin attached a Metonymy to the words of CHRIST: in defending which the Sacramentarian sect labors with great effort to this day. And these were the clearly ill-omened beginnings of the Calvinian dogma concerning the absence of the Body of CHRIST in the Supper: these were its advances: which the unhappy end of those Authors whom we have just named also followed, and not of them only, but of most who were the leaders of this dogma. The ecclesiastics or ministers of Basel report that Carlstadt was a most poisonous plague to their Church: and that he was killed by the Devil. For they write that, while he was preaching, a tall man appeared to him, whom he thought to be the Consul standing there: and that he went out again, and immediately entered the house of Carlstadt, and there found his son alone, and lifted him up with his hands, as if to dash him to the ground: but let him go unharmed: and ordered him to tell his father that he would return after three days, and take him away: Which also happened. For Carlstadt, after the sermon was finished, asked the Consul who that tall man was: to whom the Consul replied that he had seen no one. But having returned home, Carlstadt, learning of this sad message from his son, began to be saddened, and seized by immense terrors, he reclined on his bed, and on the third day, amidst horrible gusts of wind, he breathed out his impious soul.

Zwingli, voluntarily involving himself in civil and intestine war, when he had even advanced into the middle of the battle line, was killed by the enemies, his body was dismembered, his skin cut into thongs, and the fat of his abdomen was used by the cavalry for the greasing of their boots.

Oecolampadius, having received this sad news of the miserable death of Zwingli, drank in such sorrow and consternation of mind that not long after, in the morning, he was found dead and lifeless in his bed.

In which way the prophecy of Blessed Luther was fulfilled, who said at Marburg: Not three whole years will pass before these two men, Zwingli and Oecolampadius, will miserably perish.

Latin:

II.

CUm Anno 1521. Reformatio Evangelica, per B. LUTHERUM suscepta, plurimum periclitaretur, & salus tenella, vix reformatæ Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ, ἐπὶ ξυρῦ ἀκμῆς in acie novaculæ posita videretur: ipso nimirùm Luthero ab Imperatore proscripto, inque pathmo propè Jesenacum Thuringiæ constituto: ibi Andreas Bodenstein Carolostadius sibi quoque emergendum esse arbitratus est: ac proindè ausu privato, inconsultâ Ecclesiâ, insciis, imò reclamantibus Collegis, arreptâ bipenni, statuas & imagines in templo nostro parochiali demolitur, ceremonias usitatas abrogat: seminalecta Anabaptistica & Schvenckfeldiana haud obscurè spargit: studijs literarum nihil opus esse contendit: divinas potius revelationes expectandas esse somnians: Et ut B. Lutheri, tùm absentis autoritatem covelleret, ipsam quoque saniorem doctrinam de Cœnâ Domini arrodere non dubitavit.

Imperiali autoritate confirmatus, lib. 3. pag. 45. editionis Genevensis, disserit: Andreas Carolostadius, interea dum Lutherus abest, diversa dogmata proposuit, & tumultuosè statuas è templis ejecerat, concitatâ plebe. Et lib. 5. pag. 82. Carolostadius à Luthero dissentiens, VVittebergâ relictâ, clandestinis illis doctoribus, qui visiones & colloquia cum DEO simulabant, multum erat familiaris. Hâc de causâ Saxoniæ princeps finibus illi suis interdixerat: Ipse verò libellis editis, Lutherum & Collegas insectabatur, tanquàm novos Romani Pontificis adulatores. Illa etiam CHRISTI verba: Hoc est Corpus meum: sic interpretabatur: Hic sedet Corpus meum.

Sleidano suffragatur Philippus, in præfatione libelli de sententijs veterum de Cœnâ Domini, Carolostadium constituit primùm autorem certaminis Sacramentarij, sic scribens: Carolostadius primùm excitavit hunc tumultum homo ferus, sine ingenio, sine doctrinâ, sine sensu communi: & controversiam de Cœnâ Domini tantùm odio Lutheri, non aliquâ pietatis opinione movit. Sed undè dogma hoc suum hauserit Carolostadius, ipsemet fatetur, sed illud non ex Scripturis Sacris, non ex verbis Institutionis, non ex analogiâ fidei, aut naturâ Sacramentorum accepiffe: sed sibi in visione virum quendam apparuisse, qui opinionem illam de Cœnâ sibi revelaverit, quem ipse cœlestem Patrem fuisse existimet.

Carolostadium insecutus Huldricus Zvvinglius, qui teste Lavatero, multò antè etiam, quàm Carolostadius disputationem hanc de Cœnâ Domi movere cœpisset, dogma novum contra Lutherum animo fovit ac parturijt, passim ad præcipuos Germaniæ & Galliæ viros doctos scribens, se novam quandam ac singularem de Cœnâ Domini sententiam producturum.

Sententiâ autem tandem ab ipso prodita, hæc fuit: Christus inquit, Hoc est Corpus meum: id est, Panis significat Corpus meum.

Observatu autem dignissimum, undénam Zvvinglius quoque hanc verborum Cœnæ explicationem hauserit. Etsi enim fatetur, se ante plures annos opinionem illam de Eucharistiâ animo fovisse, tempus illud innuens, quo sub Papatu vixit, quo nemo nostrûm (inquit Zvvinglius) unquàm verè credidit, se in isto pane tale quiddam edere, quod somniavimus (sic nimirùm meram infidelitatem principium erroris sui statuens:) tamen quomodo hanc opinionem cum verbis Institutionis conciliaret, se non priùs invenisse aut intellexisse scribit, quàm in sarcina Batavi cujusdam, quem ille Honium appellat, epistolam repererit, verba isthæc, Hoc est corpus meum, sic explicari posse, Hoc significat Corpus meum.

Quæ epistola ab ipso Zvvinglio, Anno Domini 1525. typis evulgata in publicum prodijt. Cæterùm cùm super hac ipsâ interpretatione controversia ipsi cum Scribâ quodam Senatorio Tiguri intercederet, qui cōtendebant, eam verbis Institutionis non esse consentaneam; cúmq; omnia apud animum cogitans, omnia revolvens nihil inveniret, quod Scribæ isti responderet: ibi decimâ tertiâ die Aprilis appetente, quæ causæ dicendæ partibus litigantibus dicta fuerat, in somnio se visum sibi esse, denuò cum scribâ contendere, sicq; obmutuisse, ut quod verum sciret, negante lingvâ beneficium suum, proloqui non posset. Quo angore cùm vehementer perturbatus videretur, ibi ἀπὸ μηχανῆς (sic sonant ejus verba) visus est monitor ad esse, (ater fuerit, an albus, nihil memini: somnium enim narro) qui diceret: Quin ignavè respondes ei, quod Exod. 12. scribitur: Est enim Phase Domini. Protinùs ut hoc phasma visum est, simul expergiscor, & e lecto exsilio, locum apud septuaginta primùm undique circumspicio, ac de eo coram totâ concione pro virili dissero.

Zvvinglio eodem fermè anno suppetias laturus Oecolampadius, cõtendit, Nullum miraculum esse in pane mystico suprà captum hominis: Et verba illa: Hoc est Corpus meum, absquè tropo constare non posse, ut multa absurda caveantur. In quo tropo eliciendo, definiendo, palliando ita laborarunt, qui Zvvinglium & Oecolampadium sequebantur, ut ubi pedem figerent, vix invenirent: donec tandem Johannes Calvinus Metonymiam verbis CHRISTI affixit: in quâ defendenda hodieque magno conatu laborat gens Sacramentaria. Et hæc fuerunt infausta planè dogmatis Calviniani de absentiâ Corporis CHRISTI, in Cœnâ, primordia: hi progressus: quos infelix etiam exitus istorum, quo nominavimus modò, Autorum, subsecutus est, nec istorum tantùm, sed plerorumque, qui dogmatis hujus Antesignani fuerunt. Referunt Ecclesiastæ sive ministri Basilienses, Carolostadium fuisse pestem suæ Ecclesiæ venenosissimam: & occisum ipsum esse à Diabolo. Scribunt enim, ipsi concionanti apparuisse virum grandem Consulem stetisse: rursúsque egressum, statim in ædes Carolostadij intrasse, ibique filium ipsius solum invenisse, ac ipsum manibus elevasse, quasi in terram collisurum: sed illæsum dimisisse: ac jussisse, ut patri diceret, se reversurum post triduum, ipsumque ablaturum: Quod etiam factum est. Carolostadius enim finitâ concione interrogavit Consulem, quis ille grandis vir fuerit: cui Consul, se neminem vidisse, respondit. Domum autem reversus Carolostadius, nuntio hoc tristi ex filio cognito contristari cœpit, & immensis terroribus correptus, lecto se reclinavit, dieque tertiâ inter horrendos ventorum turbines impiam exhalavit animam.

Zvvinglius bello civili & intestino se ultrò immiscens, cum in aciem etiam mediam prodijsset, ab hostibus occisus, corpus ejus difsectum, cutis in lora concissa, & abdominis pingvedo, ab equitibus ad ocrearum inunctionem adhibita fuit.

Oecolampadius tristi hoc nuntio de miserabili interitu Zvvinglij accepto, eum animi mœrorem & consternationem hausit, ut non multò pòst manè in lecto mortuus & exanimis inventus sit.

Quò pacto impletum B. Lutheri vaticinium, Marpurgi dicentis: Non triennium integrum abibit, quo duo ipsi Viri, Zvvinglius &amp; Oecolampadius miserabiliter interibunt.


### On the Lord's Supper: III

III.

But we make our approach to the third chapter of the prolegomena, intending to show in a few words how much polycephaly, variety, uncertainty, and fluctuation underlies this Sacramentarian dogma: so much, indeed, that the minds of the faithful can rest in no part of full assurance. There are those from their own class who remove from their sight the proper seat of this matter, namely the Words of Institution, nay, they plainly mock them. To which sense Zwingli writes explicitly in his letter to the Princes of Germany, letter D. 2. That Christians desiring to know the truth in this contest ought not to look to the Words of CHRIST, This is my Body. And in his book on true and false religion, pages 244 and 291, he writes: The words, This cup is my blood, are too dry for the grasp of some: Nay, he calls our doctrine a clever fiction, because it consists only of the words of CHRIST.

The Tigurines in the consensus, which they call Orthodox, page 48, explicitly warn: That one ought not to look simply at the words of CHRIST: for this is to understand carnally: but one must, they say, think of something else, and look with interior eyes.

Marcus Beumler, likewise a Tigurine, in the plucked falcon, page 63, says that the Words of Institution ought not to be assumed as an argument: because, forsooth, there is controversy about these very words and their meaning: as Bullinger holds, in his assertion of the Testament against Jacob Andreae.

Peter Martyr ironically called the words of Institution a five-word proof.

The Consul of Bremen, in a public assembly held at Bremen in the year 1560, said that the Lutherans had nothing else besides, except only three impotent words: This is my Body.

The Neostadians mock those words in such a way that they ironically call them, Words, Words, Words.

Then, to prove their dogma, they seek foundations or principles that are plainly foreign and alien, from the Article of the Ascension of CHRIST to the heavens, his return for judgment, likewise from the words concerning the departure of CHRIST from this world, from the condition of the Sacraments of the Old Testament, and especially from the sixth chapter of John.

Thirdly, they derive a common and primary principle from philosophy and the dictates of reason. This is that which Schwenckfeld said: Remove from your eyes those words: Hoc est corpus meum; and furthermore consider what is the nature of a human body, of eating, etc.

These are the words of the Neostadians in the Admonition, pages 98, 99: We certainly do not hesitate to confess that we apply the judgment of right reason, as much in understanding divine matters as in human ones.

Victorinus Strigelius wrote in a certain letter in the year 1567: that he had his right eye directed toward the religion of all times, and toward the natures of Christ and the writings of antiquity: but his left toward the words of the Institution.

Zwingli writes in the letter cited a little earlier: that every Christian ought to consult and examine his own faith, his own heart, and his own mind, and that he will say to each one that it is the Spirit that satisfies us in the Supper of the Lord. Which principle Servetus also clearly held, denying the Trinity of Persons in the Unity of the Divine Essence, repeatedly insisting: That which comes into my sense does not come into my intellect.

Fourthly, there are others who indeed wish to appear to admit the words of the Institution and to seek from them the decision of this Sacramentarian struggle: but they depart into such various and discrepant opinions that they can scarcely all be enumerated.

Some refer the demonstrative pronoun THIS absolutely to the Body of Christ: others wish it to denote the same thing as This action: others suppose it is placed for spiritual food.

Which Zwingli himself also, as Lavater testifies, marked with a black stone as speσολόγητα, writing that the same thing had happened in this regard to Carlstadt as to a recruit, who does not lack the spirit and weapons for fighting, but lacks skill in arms. Who, not knowing which part of the body should be protected by which weapons, places a helmet on his chest in place of a breastplate, covers his legs with bracelets, his temples with greaves, makes a shield out of a breastplate, etc. Thus Carlstadt indeed recognizes the truth: but because he does not have the force of tropes perceived, he does not arrange the words in the right order. Zwingli therefore betook himself to the word IS, which was the same to him as signifies. To others, the gloss of representing pleased them more: to some, that of reminding of an absent thing. There followed those who established a trope in the name of Body: so that to some it denoted the same as Figure of the Body: to others the same as Symbolic Body: to others the same as the efficacy and merit of the Body. There were others who fixed their foot on the Relative Pronoun (Which): and that again in diverse ways: For some explained it by 'of what kind': others by 'insofar as',

Now as to the state of the controversy of this struggle, it has been from time to time by those people either plainly changed or sophistically entangled, with some asserting that the controversy is about Transubstantiation: others about Consubstantiation: others about a durable presence outside of use: others about adoration: others about local inclusion: others about physical commixture: others about Capernaitic eating: others about Spiritual eating, which is in John 6: others about the Spiritual indwelling of CHRIST in us through grace: others sometimes affirming that, in reality, there is the greatest consensus regarding the presence of the Lord's Body: that it is disputed only about the mode of eating: others, from a dizziness of spirit, sometimes asserting that the whole dispute is in truth more a λογομαχίαν, a contention of words, than of the thing itself: others finally sometimes establishing that this controversy is not of such moment that our salvation depends upon it: nor that this dissension is of such a kind that we ought to be divided on account of it, and that sport should be provided for our common enemies.

Fifthly and lastly, it is also to be observed with how wavering and seared a conscience the Sacramentarians have always conducted this cause. For some said that it was only for the sake of exercise that they had disputed about this matter: as Carlstadt wrote to Luther in the year 1525. Oecolampadius wished that his right hand had been cut off at the time when he first began to write anything against Luther concerning the business of the Lord's Supper. Thus, therefore, the Sacramentarians have hitherto shown themselves in this struggle such that it has been most truly fulfilled in them what St. Peter wrote concerning those who do not suffer themselves to be taught by the Holy Spirit, and who are wavering in faith, 2 Pet. 3:16, ὅ τι στρεβλοῦσι τὰς γραφὰς.

Latin:

III.

SEd ad tertium προλεγομένων caput accessum facimus, paucis ostensuri, quanta dogmati huic Sacramentario subsit πολυκεφαλία, varietas, incertitudo, fluctuatio: tanta nimirùm, ut fidelium animi in nullâ πληροφορίας parte consistere queant. Sunt ex ipsorum classe, qui sedem hujus materiæ propriam, Verba nimirùm Institutionis, ex oculis removent, imò planè eludunt. Quem in sensum disertè scribit Zvvinglius in epistolâ ad Principes Germaniæ lit. D. 2. Christianos veritatem in hoc certamine scire cupientes, non debere in Verba CHRISTI, Hoc est Corpus meum, respicere. Et in lib. de verâ ac falsâ religione. pag. 244. &amp; 291. scribit: Sicca nimis pro quorundam captu sunt verba, Hoc poculum est sangvis meus: Quin doctrinam nostram, commentum argutum vocat, quod solis verbis CHRISTI constet.

Tigurini in consensu, quem Orthodoxum vocant, pag. 48. disertè monent: Non oportere simpliciter intueri verba CHRISTI: Hoc enim esse carnaliter intelligere: sed oportet, inquiunt, aliud cogitare, &amp; interioribus oculis aspicere.

Marcus Beumlerus itidem Tigurinus in falcone deplumato, pag. 63. ait, Verba Institutionis non debere pro argumento assumi: quia nimirùm de his ipsis, ipsorumque sensu controvertatur: uti habet Bullingerus, in assertione Testamenti contra Jacobum Andreæ.

Petrus Martyr ironicè verba Institutionis, Quinqueverbiam probationem appellavit.

Bremensis Consul, in conventu publico, Anno 1560. Bremæ habito, Lutheranos nihil præterea habere dixit, nisi tria tantùm impotentia verba: Hoc est Corpus.

Neostadiani sic istis verbis illudunt, ut ironicè vocent, Verba, Verba, Verba.

Deinde dogmati suo probando peregrina planè &amp; aliena fundamenta sive principia quærunt, ex Articulo Ascensus CHRISTI ad cælos, reditus ad judicium, item ex verbis de transitu CHRISTI ex hoc mundo, ex conditione Sacramentorum Veteris Testamenti, præcipuè ex capite sexto Johannis.

Tertiò, commune &amp; primarium principium ex Philosophiâ &amp; rationis dictatu translumunt. Hoc illud est, Schvvenckfeldius dixit, Remove ex oculis ista verba: Hoc est corpus meum; & porrò considera, quæ sit natura corporis humani, comestionis &amp; c.

Neostadianorum in Admonitione pag 98. 99. hæc sunt verba: Non sanè dubitamus fateri, nos rectæ rationis judicium, tàm in divinis, quàm in humanis rebus intelligendis adhibere.

Victorinus Strigelius Anno 67. supra sesquimillesimum scripsit in quâdam epistolâ : se dextrum habere oculum directum ad omnium temporum religionem, & in naturas Christi scriptaque antiquitatis : sinistrum verò ad verba Institutionis.

Zvvinglius in epistolâ paulò antè allegatâ scribit: Quemlibet Christianum debere suam propriam fidem, suum proprium cor, & suum ipsius animum consulere, & explorare, illum singulis dicturum esse, spiritum esse, qui nos in Cœna Domini satiet. Quod planè principium tenuit etiam Servetus negans Trinitatem Personarum in Unitate Essentiæ divinæ, subindè ingeminans ; Non venit in meum intellectum, quod venit in meum sensum.

Quartò sunt alij, qui quidem Institutionis Verba admittere, & ex ijs decisionem certaminis hujus Sacramentarij petere videri volunt : sed usque adeò in varias ac discrepantes sententias abeunt, ut vix enumerari omnes queant.

Alij pronomen demonstrativum HOC ad Corpus CHRISTI absolutè referunt : alij illud idem notare volunt, atque Hæc actio : alij pro cibo spirituali positum esse autumant.

Quam speσολόγητα ipse quoque Zvvinglius, teste Lavatero, atro notavit calculo, scribens idem hac in parte accidisse Carolostadio, quod Tyroni, cui animus & arma ad pugnandum non desunt: sed armorum peritia. Qui nescit, quæ corporis pars, quibus armis munienda sit, galeam pectori thoracis loco præfigit armillis crura tegit, ocreis tem pora, ex thorace clypeum facit, &c. Ita Carolostadium veritatem quidem agnoscere: sed quia troporum vim non habeat perspectam, verba non recto ordine collocare. Zvvinglius ergò ad Verbum EST se recepit, quod idem illi fuit, ac significat. Alijs Repræsentandi : quibusdam de absente re commonefaciendi glossa magis placuit. Subsecuti sunt, qui in nomine Corporis tropum constituerunt : ita ut nonnullis corpus idem notaret, quod Figura Corporis : alijs idem quod Symbolicum Corpus : alijs idem quod efficacia & meritum Corporis. Fuerunt alij, qui in Pronomine Relativo (Quod) pedem fixerunt: idque iterum diversimode: Alij enim illud explicarunt, per Quale: alij per Quatenus,

Jam quoad statum controversiæ certaminis hujus, ille subindè ab istis vel planè mutatus : vel Sophisticè involutus fuit, alijs asserentibus, Controversiam esse de Transsubstantiatione : alijs de Consubstantiatione : alijs de durabili præsentia extrâ usum : alijs de adoratione : alijs de locali inclusione: alijs de physica commixtione : alijs de Capernaiticâ manducatione : alijs de Spirituali manducatione, quæ est Joh. 6. alijs de Spirituali CHRISTI in nobis per gratiam inhabitatione: alijs interdum affirmantibus, in reipsâ, quoad præsentiam Corporis Dominici summum esse consensum: disputari tantùm de modo manducationis: alijs ex vertigine Spiritus interdum asserentibus, totam disputationem reverâ magis esse λογομαχίαν verborum contentionem ; quàm rei : alijs denique interdum statuentibus, controversiam hanc non tanti esse momenti, ut indè pendeat nostra salus: nec hoc dissidium esse ejusmodi, ut propterea scindi nos oporteat, & ludos communibus hostibus præberi.

Quintò & postremò observandum etiam, quàm titubante & cauteriatâ conscientiâ, causam istam Sacramentarij semper egerint. Nam alij tantùm exercitij gratiâ à se de hâc materiâ disputatum fuisse dixerunt: ut Carolostadius scripsit ad Lutherum Anno 1525. Oecolampadius dextram sibi tùm abscissam fuisse optavit, cùm primùm inciperet de negocio Cœnæ Dominicæ contra Lutherum quicquam scribere. Sic ergò Sacramentarij in certamine hoc tales hactenus se præstiterunt, ut verissimè in ipsis completum sit, quod de illis, qui à Spiritu Sancto doceri se non patiuntur, inque fide fluctuabundi sunt, D. Petrus scripsit 2. Petr. 3, 16. ὅ τι στρεβλοῦσι τὰς γραφὰς.


### On the Lord's Supper: IV

IV.

It remains that we show in a few words what excellent fruits the Sacramentarian dogma produces. If, however, any heresy has existed at any time that is a most fertile mother of very many absurdities and blasphemies: this one certainly, if only this one, easily snatches the palm from the rest. For as soon as the patrons of this dogma began to impugn the Testament of the Son of GOD, they did not shrink from either denying or interpreting at their own pleasure most of the articles of faith, however manifest they were.

Hence they simply deny the Article concerning the descent of CHRIST into hell, interpreting it partly by the torments of his soul, partly by the very death of CHRIST. Hence they draw arguments from the article of the Ascension of CHRIST into heaven, and his sitting at the right hand of GOD the Father, against the presence of the Lord's Body in the Supper: that is: they pervert the double sense and scope of both articles, they change the right hand of GOD into a certain and finite place: nay, they soon even cast shackles upon the divine omnipotence itself: if indeed GOD cannot effect all things by His power, so that a human body can be in several places at once: nor can it be brought about by any force that a created thing should be everywhere. Departing from this, and having set upon the doctrine of the Sacraments, they transformed the Sacraments into mere external signs and such ceremonies by which a man might prove himself to the Church, as a candidate and soldier of Christ, not by which a man himself might be made more certain of the grace of GOD; but rather the Church might be made more certain of the faith of men, that is, they denied the primary use of the Sacraments, which consists in this, that they are salutary organs of divine grace, and instruments not only for confirming faith, but also for conferring it. Hence, having emptied Baptism, they did not concede that which the Apostle attributes to it, that it is the washing of regeneration, by which men are saved: but salvation and regeneration, either already conferred in the mother's womb, or to be conferred in its own proper time to be sealed. Here, having restored Anabaptism, and having as it were denied original sin in its entirety, they asserted that the children of the faithful, according to the formula of the covenant, are holy before GOD from the mother's womb. Furthermore, they also attacked the very citadel of the Christian faith, and promised salvation and participation in eternal life to the Gentiles who were established outside the faith of Christ. When at length this impiety acquired strength in various kingdoms and provinces, it began to rage and rave against CHRIST the Savior, having brandished the sword of slander especially against the Majesty of the flesh and human nature, which, through the assumption of τοῦ λόγου, was not only personally united to the Son of GOD, but, as Ambrose speaks, raised to the very fellowship of the most blessed Trinity. Therefore, they did not shrink from gnawing at the bond of the union of these two natures in CHRIST, from infesting the real communication of idioms, from hostilely attacking the glory of the assumed flesh, especially from accusing the adoration of the flesh—which no one eats unless he has first adored it, and which by adoring, one not only does not sin, but by not adoring, one does sin, as Augustine speaks—of the foulest idolatry: from eluding the benefit and merit of universal redemption accomplished through the death of CHRIST: from devoting the greatest part of the human race to an absolute decree of reprobation: and finally from disturbing the Churches of all places in the benefit obtained by CHRIST, and from tearing down and overturning all things that are tranquil, with their affairs having been clearly reduced to the state of the Arians, concerning whom it was written to the Emperor Constantius, by the Synod of Rimini, that what is brought forward by the Arians brings incredulity to the faithful and credulity to the unfaithful, so that that oracle might be fulfilled which was uttered by Adam Neuser, who, having fallen from Calvinism into Arianism, and again from this into Mahometanism, is written to have said: He who fears for himself, lest he fall into Arianism, let him beware of Calvinism.

Latin:

IV.

SUperest, ut quàm egregios fructus pariat dogma Sacramentarium, paucis ostendamus. Si quâ tamen hæresis ullis temporibus extitit, mater fœcundissima plurimarum absurditatum & blasphemiarum: hæc certè vel sola palmam facilè reliquis præripit. Quamprimùm enim Testamentum Filij DEI semel impugnare cœperunt dogmatis hujus patroni: mox plerosque fidei articulos, quantumvis manifestos pro suo arbitrio vel negare, vel interpretari non exhorruerunt.

Hinc Articulum de descensu CHRISTI ad inferos simpliciter negant, partim per animi cruciatus, partim per ipsam mortem CHRISTI eum accipientes. Hinc ex articulo Ascensionis CHRISTI ad cælos, & sessionis ad dextram DEI Patris, contra presentiam Corporis Domini in Cœnâ, argumenta ducunt: hoc est: geminum sensum & scopum utriusque articuli pervertunt, dextram DEI in certum ac finitum locum commutant: quin mox ipsi etiam omnipotentiæ divinæ compedes injiciunt: siquidem DEUS omnia suâ potentiâ efficere nequeat, ut corpus humanum possit esse in pluribus locis simul: neque nullâ vi fieri possit, ut res creata sit ubique. Hinc digressi, & Sacramentorum doctrinam adorti, Sacramenta in signa tantùm externa & ceremonias tales transformarunt, quibus se homo Ecclesiæ probet, ut Candidatus & miles Christi, non quibus homo ipse de gratiâ DEI; sed Ecclesia potiùs de fide hominum certior fiat, hoc est, usum Sacramentorum primarium abnegarunt, qui in eo consistit, ut sint divinæ gratiæ salutaria organa, & fidei non confirmandæ tantùm: sed & conferendæ instrumenta. Hinc Baptismo evacuato non illud concesserunt, quod Apostolus tribuit, quod sit lavacrum regenerationis, quo salventur homines: sed salus & regeneratio, aut jam collata in utero matris, aut conferenda suo demùm tempore obsignetur. Hic instaurato Anabaptismo, & peccato originali in universum quasi abnegato, fidelium liberos, ex fœderis formulâ, ab utero matris coram DEO sanctos esse asseruerunt. Prætereà ipsam quoq́; fidei Christianæ acropolin impugnarunt, & gentilibus extra fidem Christi constitutis, salutem & æternæ vitæ participationem promiserunt. Ubi vires tandem impietas ista in diversis regnis & provincijs acquisivit, tota in CHRISTUM Servatorem sævire ac furere cœpit, maledicentiæ gladio præcipuè vibrato in Majestatem carnis & naturæ humanæ, per assumtionem τοῦ λόγου, non tantùm Filio DEI personaliter unitam, sed in ipsum beatissimæ Trinitatis consortium evectæ, ut Ambros. loquitur. Harum ergò duarum in CHRISTO naturarum Unionis vinculum arrodere, communicationem idiomatum realem infestare gloriam assumtæ carnis hostiliter impetere, præcipuè adorationem carnis, quam nemo manducat, nisi prius adoraverit, & quam adorando, non solùm non peccatur; sed peccatur non adorando ut August. loquitur, idololatriæ fœdissimæ insimulare: beneficium & meritum universalis redemtionis per mortem CHRISTI factæ eludere: absoluto reprobationis decreto maximam humani generis partem devovere: tandem Ecclesias omnium locorum, in liberatis à CHRISTO partæ beneficio turbare, & tranquilla omnia convellere & evertere non cohorruerint, rebus suis ad Arianorum statum planè redactis, de quibus Constantio Imp. à Synodo Ariminensi scriptum fuit, quòd quæ ab Arianis adferantur, fidelibus incredulitatem: infidelibus credulitatem afferant, ut impleatur oraculum illud, quod ab Adamo Neusero est proditum, qui ex Calvinismo in Arianismum, rursus ex hoc in Mahometismum prolapsus dixisse scribitur. Qui timet sibi, ne incidat in Arianismum, caveat Calvinianismum.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Of the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament

The substantials, or τὰ περὶ τὴν ὀυσίαν of any Sacrament, cannot be defined more correctly than if the words of the Institution are weighed more accurately. Here, however, from the very threshold, it is disputed between us and the Calvinists: Where and what is the proper seat of the words of the Institution of the Eucharistic Sacrament? For they contend that the sixth chapter of John, or that sermon of CHRIST to the Capernaites, held partly concerning spiritual eating and drinking, which is performed by faith alone, and partly concerning the crass and carnal eating and drinking of his body and blood, is the proper seat and, as it were, the matrix of the Institution of the Eucharist. We, however, uniquely in this part urge that action which, after the last Paschal Supper was finished, was celebrated by CHRIST the Savior on that very night on which he was handed over to death, in Jerusalem, and which is described in Matt. 26, 26. 27. 28. Mark 14,

22. 23. 24. Luke 22, 19. 20. 1 Cor. 11, 24. 25. Now it is asked and disputed, To which party, to us or to the Calvinists, should the palm of Truth be awarded? We, therefore, about to fight for our opinion, premise this general Syllogism.

The proper seat of the Eucharistic Sacrament must be established either in that sermon of CHRIST, held in the sixth chapter of John to the Capernaites: or in that description which is held in the three earlier Evangelists and the Apostle Paul: or in both at once.

But the first and the third can be demonstrated to be established on no foundation of truth. It remains, therefore, that the seat of the Eucharistic Sacrament must be established uniquely in the description of the Supper celebrated by CHRIST with the disciples: just as it is described by the three Evangelists and the Apostle Paul with great consensus of words.

As for the major premise, it is established by a sufficient enumeration. For a fourth cannot be given, nor has it ever been given, even by any most absurd disputant from the Calvinist sect.

The negative of the minor premise can be demonstrated invincibly to the eye by many most weighty reasons. And first, indeed, that the sermon of CHRIST held in John chapter six to the Capernaites is not the proper seat of the Eucharistic Sacrament, however much mention is made in it of eating the flesh of CHRIST and drinking his blood: this is evident from these arguments.

I. The sermon of CHRIST held in John chapter six was held at least a full year before CHRIST was handed over to death. But as the Gospel history teaches, the Sacrament of the Supper was sanctified on the night that CHRIST was handed over to death. Hence, therefore, it is thus evidently gathered: Either the Eucharistic Sacrament was founded before it was instituted by CHRIST: or the seat of this doctrine is to be placed in its very institution. But the former is by far most absurd: 1. Because it implies a contradiction if something is said to be founded before it is instituted, since the foundation of every thing necessarily presupposes an institution, because every foundation is nothing other than the confirmation of a preceding institution. 2. Because the Apostle would have lied, who clearly asserts that this Sacrament was instituted on the night that He was handed over, 1 Cor. 11, 23. Therefore this latter point is ratified: and it is so much the more evident, the more certainly it is established that the genuine seat of any instituted thing can be sought only from the institution itself.

II. Reason. Different things in different, and disparate things in disparate, cannot be the proper seat. But the nature of the Eucharistic Sacrament is clearly disparate from that action which is described in John chapter six. Therefore the proper seat of the Eucharistic Sacrament cannot be in that sixth chapter of John. The assumption is proven most evidently by these reasons.

1. The three earlier Evangelists and the Apostle describe such an eating of the body of CHRIST, and a drinking of his blood, with which eternal damnation can stand, namely among those who eat and drink unworthily, and thus to judgment 1 Cor. 11, 29. But the sermon of CHRIST in John speaks of such an eating and drinking which cannot be unworthy, and is thus always salutary: John 6, 54. & 56. He who eats my flesh, and drinks my blood, has eternal life: And he who eats my flesh, and drinks my blood, remains in me, and I in him. Therefore, Sacramental eating and drinking is not treated in this sixth chapter.

2. The sermon of CHRIST in John chapter six deals with such an eating as is necessary for all who are to be saved, that is, without which no one ever was or will be saved: for it is performed by faith alone. But Sacramental eating is not necessary, except for those who can examine themselves, namely adults 1 Cor. 11, 28. Therefore.

3. Sacramental eating requires an external Element for its truth and essence. But that which is described in John chapter six has absolutely nothing to do with any external sign or visible element, since the bread there is understood not as elemental, but as metaphorical. Therefore.

4. In the sermon of CHRIST in John, by the diversity of the predicates, not a different thing, but clearly the same is denoted. For to eat the flesh of CHRIST there is the same as to drink his blood. For by both is denoted the same communion of the benefits of CHRIST, which is done through faith. But in the Eucharistic Supper, as the distribution of the body and blood of CHRIST is distinct: so also by both predicates a very different action is denoted. Therefore.

5. The diversity of the organ also implies a diversity of the matter. Now in that sermon of CHRIST, the organ of faith is expressed, by which that eating and drinking of the body and blood of CHRIST is done, in verses 47 and 64. But in the Eucharistic Sacrament, by the words of eating and drinking, the instrument of the Mouth is denoted: since bread and wine can be perceived by no other organ. Therefore.

6. That which is prior to the Sacramental action cannot be the same as that which is proper to it in species. Now indeed, all the pious bring with them the spiritual eating, which is treated in John chapter six, to that communication which finally takes place in the Eucharist. Therefore.

7. The nature of the signed and the sign is different. For although they have a certain mutual σχέσιν and respect, they nevertheless differ greatly in the meantime in species, or even in genus. Now indeed, Eucharistic eating is a seal of that eating, as of the thing signed, which is done through faith alone. Therefore.

With these seven reasons thus premised, we shall argue invincibly against the Sacramentarians: Con-

I. If CHRIST in John chapter six instituted clearly no sacrament: it certainly cannot happen that the proper seat of the Eucharistic Sacrament is established in it. The reason for the connection is this most evident one: Because the proper seat of any thing cannot be except in matter that is συγγενεῖ or ὁμογενεῖ to it: and not in disparate matter. Now indeed, the former is most clearly evident from the reasons already produced. Therefore.

I I. The seat of that action, whose words are proper and native, cannot be in that matter which consists of merely figurative and metaphorical words and phrases. Now indeed, the words of the Eucharistic action consist of a proper and literal sense: Con-

but the words of the Johannine sermon are to be taken in a figurative or metaphorical sense: so that to eat the flesh and drink the blood of CHRIST is nothing other than to believe in CHRIST. Therefore, the proper seat of the Eucharistic action cannot be established in this.

There is added at last the consensus of certain Calvinist Doctors, who, compelled by the force of truth, found it necessary to admit that the sixth chapter of John treats of nothing at all concerning the Sacrament of the Supper. Zwingli certainly, in his Commentary on this chapter of John, enumerates five notes by which the distinction between spiritual and sacramental eating may be recognized: and of the fifth he says: By this we detect that CHRIST is here in no way speaking of the Sacrament.

Calvin writes thus on the same chapter of John: Here there is no discourse held concerning the Supper, but concerning that perpetual communication which exists for us outside the use of the Supper. And at verse 54 of the chapter, he adds these things: This whole passage is wrongly expounded concerning the Supper. For it would have been inept and untimely to discourse then about the Supper, which he had not yet instituted. Therefore it is certain that he is treating of the perpetual eating of faith. Peter Martyr in his Commentary on chapter 10 of the first to the Corinthians: The sixth chapter of John treats of that spiritual eating in which the symbols are not had, and which every believer exercises by himself, wherever he may be, by believing.

Stupendous, therefore, is the rashness of the authors of the Calvinistic consensus, who have not shuddered to write that the very same eating is commanded both in the Sacrament of the Supper and in the sixth chapter of John.

With these things thus established, we conclude irrefragably at last that the proper seat of this Article is to be established only in the words of institution. But now, since there is a dispute today among many concerning the quality and sense of those words, not so much sharply as confusedly, it will be worth the effort, for the sake of method, to comprehend the whole matter in certain questions: of which

I. the first is: Does any dissonance at all intervene between the three Evangelists and the Apostle Paul concerning the description of this Sacrament?

II. In what sense are the words of Institution to be understood: whether κτ' τὸ ῥητὸν or according to the letter: or rather κτ' τὴν διάνοιαν, that is, according to some such meaning which carries with it something other than the letter itself implies?

III. What is the substance of this Sacrament: or, what are the essential parts constituting the entire nature and substance of this Sacrament?

IV. In what way are these two essential parts, otherwise differing in their whole kind, united so that they constitute one Sacrament in number and species?

V. What mode of predication holds place when one of these two essential parts is predicated of the other? Which questions being duly explained, it will spontaneously be evident what the true and essential definition of this Sacrament ought to be established as.

Latin:

SUbstantialia, sive τὰ περὶ τὴν ὀυσίαν cujuslibet Sacramenti rectiùs definiri non possunt, quàm si Institutionis verba accuratiùs ponderentur. Hîc verò à primo statim limine inter nos & Calvinianos controvertitur, Ubi & quænam sit propria sedes verborum Institutionis Sacramenti Eucharistici? Illi enim caput sextum Johannis, sive concionem illam CHRISTI ad Capernaitas, partim de Spirituali, quæq́; solâ fide peragitur, partim de crassâ & carnali manducatione ac bibitione corporis & sangvinis sui habitam, contendunt propriam esse sedem, & ipsam quasi matricem Institutionis Eucharistiæ. Nos verò unicè hâc in parte urgemus actionem illam, quæ peractâ Cœnâ ultimâ Paschali, à CHRISTO Servatore, illâ ipsâ nocte, quâ in mortem traditus fuit, Hierosolymis celebrata est, quæq́; describitur Matt. 26, 26. 27. 28. Marc. 14,

22. 23. 24. Luc. 22, 19. 20. 1. Cor. 11, 24. 25. Jam quæritur & controvertitur, Utri parti, nobiśne an Calvinianis Veritatis palma decerni debeat? Nos ergò pro nostrâ sententiâ pugnaturi, generalem hunc præmittimus Syllogismum.

Sedes propria Sacramenti Evcharistici, aut constituenda est in concione illâ CHRISTI, Johannis sexto capite, ad Capernaitas habita: aut in descriptione illâ, quæ apud tres priores Evangelistas & Apostolum Paulum habetur: aut in utrâg, simul.

Atqui primum & tertium nullo veritatis fundamento statui, demonstrarivè potest. Relinquitur ergò, quod sedes Sacramenti Evcharistici unicè constituenda sit in descriptione Cœnæ cum discipulis à CHRISTO celebratæ: prout ea à tribus Evangelistis & Apostolo Paulo, magno verborum consensu describitur.

Quoad majorem, constat ea sufficienti enumeratione. Quartum enim dari nequit, neque datum est unquàm, etiam à quovis absurdissimo disputatore ex gente Calvinianâ.

Minoris negativa multis gravissimis rationibus ad oculum invictè demonstrari potest. Et primum quidem, quòd concio CHRISTI Johannis sexto ad Capernaitas habita, non sit sedes propria Sacramenti Evcharistici, quantumvis in eâ, carnis CHRISTI manducandæ, & sangvinis bibendi fiat mentio: his patet argumentis.

I. Concio CHRISTI Johannis sexto habita, integro ut minimùm anno prius est habita, quàm CHRISTUS in mortem fuit traditus.
