Atqui docente historiâ Evangelicâ, Sacramentum Cœnæ, eâ nocte est sanctitū, quâ CHRISTUS in mortem fuit traditus. Hinc ergò sic evidenter colligitur: Aut prius fuit fundatum Sacramentum Evcharisticum, quàm à CHRISTO institueretur: aut sedes hujus doctrinæ est in ipsâ ejus institutione collocanda. Atqui prius illud longè est absurdissimum: 1. Quia contradictionem implicat, si fundari aliquid prius dicatur, quàm institutum sit cùm omnis rei fundatio necessariò præsupponat institutionem, proptereà quòd omnis fundatio nihil est aliud, quàm antegressæ institutionis confirmatio. 2. Quia mentitus esset Apostolus, qui nocte eâ, quâ traditus fuit, Sacramentum hoc institutum fuisse, liquidò asserit 1. Cor. 11, 23. Ratum ergò hoc posterius: idq; tantò evidentiùs, quantò certiùs constat, cujuslibet rei institutæ sedem germanam, non nisi ex institutione ipsâ peti posse.

II. Ratio. Diversi in diverso, & disparati in disparato sedes esse propria non potest. At Sacramenti Evcharistici disparata planè est ratio, ab eâ actione, quæ Johannis sexto describitur. Ergò Sacramēti Evcharistici sedes propria in capite illo sexto Johannis esse nequit. Assumtio his rationibus probatur evidentissimè.

1. Evangelistæ tres priores & Apostolus talem describunt manducationem corporis CHRISTI, & bibitionem sangvinis ejus, cum quâ stare potest æterna damnatio, apud eos nimirùm, qui manducant & bibunt indignè, & sic ad judicium 1. Corinth. 11, 29. Atqui concio CHRISTI apud Johannem de tali manducatione & bibitione loquitur, quæ indigna esse non potest, & fic semper salutaris est : Johan. 6, 54. & 56. Qui manducat meam carnem, & bibit meum sangvinem, habet vitam æternam: Et qui manducat meam carnem, & bibit meum sangvinem, in me manet, & ego in illo. Ergò Sacramentalis manducatio & bibitio, capite hoc sexto non traditur.

2. Concio CHRISTI Johannis sexto, de tali agit manducatione, quæ salvandis omnibus est necessaria, hoc est, sine quâ nemo unquàm vel salvatus fuit, vel salvabitur: quippè quæ solâ fide peragitur. Atqui Sacramentalis manducatio non est necessaria, nisi ijs, qui seipsos probare possunt, adultis scilicet 1. Cor. 11, 28. Ergò.

3. Manducatio Sacramentalis requirit ad sui veritatem & essentiam externum Elementum. Atqui ea, quæ Johannis sexto describitur, nihil prorsus cum ullo externo signo, sive visibili elemento habet negocij, siquidem panis non elemetaris, sed metaphoricus ibi intelligitur. Ergò.

4. In concione CHRISTI apud Johannem, per diversitatem prædicatorum, non res diversa; sed eadem planè notatur. Nam carnem CHRISTI edere istic idem est, quod sangvinem, ejus bibere. Utroq; enim notatur beneficiorum CHRISTI communio eadé, quæ per fidem fiat. Atqui in Cœnâ Evcharisticâ, uti distincta est distributio corporis & sangvinis CHRISTI: sic utroq; etiam prædicato diversissima notatur actio. Ergò.

5. Organi diversitas diversitatem materiæ etiam importat. Jam in concione illâ CHRISTI, fidei organon exprimitur, quo fiat manducatio & bibitio illa corporis & sangvinis CHRISTI, versu 47. & 64. Atqui in Sacramento Evcharistico, verbis edendi & bibendi instrumentum Oris notatur: siquidem nullo alio organo Panis & vinum percipi possunt. E.

6. Id, quod actione Sacramentali prius est, non potest esse idem cum eo, quod est ipsius in specie proprium. Jam verò Spiritualem manducationem, de quâ Johannis sexto agitur, omnes pij secum adferunt ad eam, quæ in Evcharistiâ tandem fit, communicationem. Ergò.

7. Signati à signo ratio est diversa. Nam quamvis mutuam quandam σχέσιν & respectum habeant, specie tamen, aut genere etiam, plurimùm interim discrepant. Jam verò manducatio Evcharistica est sigillum illius manducationis, tanquàm rei signatæ, quæ fit per solam fidem. Ergò.

Rationibus hisce septé ita præmissis, sic contra Sacramentarios invictè argumentabimur: Con-

I. Si CHRISTUS Johannis sexto sacramentum planè nullu instituit : fieri certè nequit, ut in eo Sacramenti Evcharistici sedes propria constituatur. Ratio connexi est evidentissima hæc: Quia cujusq; rei sedes propria esse non potest, nisi in materiâ sibi συγγενεῖ aut ὁμογενεῖ: non autem in disparatâ. Jam verò prius illud ex jam productis rationibus liquidissimè patet. Ergò.

I I. Illius actionis, cujus verba sunt propria & nativa, non potest esse sedes in eâ materiâ, quæ verbis & phrasibus constat merè figuratis & metaphoricis. Jam verò Evcharisticæ actionis verba constant proprio & literali sensu : Con-

cionis verò Johanneæ verba, sensu figurato sive metaphorico sunt accipienda: ita ut manducare carnem, & bibere sangvinem CHRISTI, nihil sit aliud, quàm credere in CHRISTUM. Ergò in hâc non potest constitui sedes propria actionis Eucharisticæ.

Accedit tandem consensus quorundam Doctorum Calvinianorum, qui vi veritatis coacti fateri necesse habuerunt, de Sacramento Cœnæ nihil quicquam agi, capite sexto Johannis. Zvvinglius certè in Commentario ad hoc caput Johannis, quinq; notas recenset, ex quibus discrimen Spiritualis & Sacramentalis manducationis agnosci queat: & de quintâ inquit: Hâc deprehendimus, CHRISTUM hîc nullo pacto de Sacramento loqui.

Calvinus ad idem caput Johannis sic scribit: Hîc non de Cœnâ habetur concio: sed de perpetuâ communicatione, quæ extra Cœnæ usum nobis constat. Et ad versum 54. capitis, hæc adjicit: Perperã de Cœnâ exponitur totus hic locus. Ineptum enim fuisset ac intempestivum, de Cœnâ tunc disserere, quam nondum instituerat. Ideò de perpetuâ fidei manducatione eum tractare certum est. Petrus Martyr in Commentario ad cap. 10. prioris ad Corinthios: Agitur in capite sexto Johannis de Spirituali illâ manducatione, in quâ non habentur Symbola quamq; fidelis quisq; per seipsum, ubicunq; fuerit, credendo exercet.

Stupenda ergò temeritas Autorum consensus Calvinistici, qui eandem planè manducationé, & in Sacramento Cœnæ, & in capite sexto Johãnis præceptam esse, scribere non exhorruerunt.

His ita constitutis irrefragabiliter concludimus tandem, sedem Articuli hujus propriam non nisi in verbis institutionis esse constituendam. Jam verò cùm de Qualitate & Sensu istorum verborum, non tàm acriter, quàm confusè à multis hodiè disputetur: operæ pretium fuerit, Methodi gratiâ, rem omnem certis quibusdam quæstionibus comprehendere: quarum

I. est: An ulla aliqua dissonantia tribus Evangelistis, & Apostolo Paulo circa descriptionem hujus Sacramenti invicem intercedat?

II. Quo sensu sint intelligenda verba Institutionis: nùm κτ' τὸ ῥητὸν sive secundum literam: an verò κτ' τὴν διάνοιαν, h. e. secundu talem aliquã sententiã quæ aliud præ se ferat, quàm litera ipsa innuit?

III. Quænam sit Sacramenti hujus substantia: vel, quæ partes essentiales, integrum Sacramenti hujus naturam & substantiam constituentes?

IV. Quo pacto duæ hæ partes Essentiales, toto alioqui genere discrepantes uniantur, ut unum numero ac specie constituant Sacramentum?

V. Quis prædicandi modus locũ obtineat, quando duarum istarum partium Essentialium una prædicatur de alterâ? Quibus quæstionibus ritè explicatis, ultrò patebit, quænam vera & Essentialis Definitio Sacramenti hujus constitui debeat?


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Question On the consonance of the words of the Institution, among the three earlier Evangelists and the Apostle Paul

If there is anywhere among the Evangelists and Apostles, concerning the description of both the Words and the Deeds of CHRIST, any agreement and harmony: certainly in the description of the Eucharistic Sacrament, there exists between them the greatest and most elegant consensus: a fact which can be demonstrated to the eye by the two following tables, according to the two parts of this Sacrament.

Latin:

SI ulla uspiam Evangelistis & Apostolis, circa descriptionem tum Verborum, tum Factorum CHRISTI, intercedit Consonantia, & Harmonia: certè in descriptione Sacramenti Evcharistici, illis consensus intercedit maximus & elegantissimus: id quod subsequentibus duabus tabellis, secundum duas Sacramenti hujus partes, ad oculum demonstrari potest.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Concerning the Eucharistic Bread

In the beginning, therefore, what Matthew said in the form of a participle: Jesus λαβὼν τὸν ἄρτον, taking bread: the other two Evangelists, Mark and Luke, repeated in the same words and syllables. Paul, however, having changed the participle into a verb, while the sense remained the same, said: Jesus ἔλαβε ἄρτον, he took bread.

2. What Matthew and Mark have, εὐλογήσας, having made a blessing: that Luke and Paul again rendered with the sense in no way varied: εὐχαριστήσας, having given thanks.

3. All unanimously have, ἔκλασε, he broke.

4. What the three Evangelists said: ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς: he gave to them, namely to the disciples: that the Apostle wished to be understood as lying hidden within the following action, that is, the eating of the bread, and especially in the word 'Taking,' which necessarily presupposes the giving of the bread.

5. What Matthew, Mark, and Paul have: he said, Take, eat: that Luke omitted: meanwhile differing in nothing from the others, as will be shown a little later.

6. What the three Evangelists assert that CHRIST said: τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά μου: This is my body: that the Apostle wished to be repeated, changed only by the transposition of the pronoun, saying: τοῦτό μου ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμα: This my is body.

7. Luke and the Apostle added two other members to these six already noted, which were omitted by the other two Evangelists: the former of which is the predicate of the Body: that that body is certainly to be understood which (according to Luke) is given for you: but according to Paul, Which is broken for you. The latter is the word of the command: Do this in remembrance of me: which Luke and Paul expressed. This first table shows that all those members by which the essence of the Eucharistic Sacrament, regarding the first part, is described, have been defined and expressed by the three Evangelists and the Apostle with such a consonance of words that it could not have been greater. For although in the remaining members some dissimilarity or dissonance of words presents itself: yet it is neither of any moment, nor does it render the sense of the words of the Institution more obscure, a fact which again can be invincibly demonstrated.

For first, it is clearly evident from a comparison of the scriptures that an equivalence, or some synonymy, exists between the words εὐλογίας and εὐχαριστίας, as when CHRIST is read to have blessed the few loaves and fishes: the Holy Spirit himself explains this blessing through εὐχαριστία: as in Matt. 14:19 and ch. 15:36, Mark 6:41 and

ch. 8:6, Luke 9:16, John 6:11. For this was very frequent and solemn for the Savior, that as often as he wished to produce some singular and excellent specimen of divine omnipotence while using the elementary bread, he would for the most part, with eyes lifted to heaven and having given thanks to GOD the Father, bless it: not indeed doing that by this rite which is otherwise accustomed to be done by us at the table, namely, that he might profess with a grateful mind that our daily bread is provided to us by GOD, and at the same time pray that its use might be salutary: but he had this rather, and indeed primarily, in mind concerning the institution of the Eucharistic bread, that having as it were taken counsel with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit concerning the establishing of the most holy mystery of his Testament, he would both give thanks for the admirable decree of redemption: and indeed invoke the heavenly Father for the confirmation of this institution, and its perennial propagation to all posterity.

Then, although the Apostle omitted the word (GAVE), and Luke does not have these words (TAKE, EAT), nevertheless no dissonance arises from that, either regarding the matter or the sense. For it is always expressed unanimously by the three witnesses, which is omitted by the fourth either because it is included in the following members: or because that matter seemed to be so arranged that all could understand of their own accord, without any interpreter, that the bread was not given to the disciples in vain, nor with any other intention, except to take and eat: And again, that it could not have been taken and eaten before it was given.

Finally, regarding that designation of the body of CHRIST which Luke and Paul added, it must indeed be confessed that it is a useful and excellent declaration: but it was not so simply necessary, for even without it the mind of CHRIST could have been understood quite evidently from the preceding words: since it is sufficiently certain that besides the One Body, which could be eaten and which could be delivered into death and broken, there was no other for CHRIST. Thus, regarding the word of command annexed by Luke and Paul, it indeed has its own force, which is by no means small: but it is one that concerns at least the use, and not the substance, of this Sacrament.

Thus, therefore, the greatest possible concordance is found to exist everywhere in the Words of Institution regarding this first part: and especially regarding those things which concern the substance of this first part.

With these things thus established, it is spontaneously clear how foul is the corruption of the Words of Institution, by which the Sacramentarians, fighting among themselves like blind gladiators, have depraved almost every single word with wondrous sophistries.

Carlstadt, having seized upon the demonstrative pronoun (THIS), contending that it was not the bread held out by CHRIST, but his own body then sitting at the table, that was demonstrated by that same pronoun.

Zwingli referred this demonstrative pronoun δεικτικὸν to the bread indeed, thus openly contradicting Carlstadt: but he sought a refuge for his error in the substantive verb (IS), which he interpreted as SIGNIFIES.

Oecolampadius, speaking in direct opposition to Zwingli, contends that the substantive verb (εστ) must be taken not significatively, but existentially: but meanwhile he seized upon the word body, and argued that it must be taken not for the true body of CHRIST, but for a figure of the body.

Calvin, making a divorce from all these, contends that the whole complex of CHRIST'S words must be interpreted metonymically concerning the benefits of the body of CHRIST.

To which opinions, individually and collectively, the unanimous consensus or concordance of the three Evangelists and the Apostle Paul is most rightly opposed: with which they diametrically conflict: For if you wish to accommodate Carolostadius's τῶτο demonstratively to the body of CHRIST sitting nearby: Mark protests, accommodating the same pronoun also to the blood of CHRIST, saying: This is my blood: τῶτό εστι τὸ ἅιμά με: Where that visible pointing out of the blood of CHRIST sitting nearby has clearly no place. Thus, if you wish to render the substantive verb is as signifies with Zwingli, the consensus of the Evangelists protests, bringing forward unanimously that that which CHRIST offered to the disciples to be eaten and drunk is the body of CHRIST: and lest you understand it as a figure with Oecolampadius, or only as the benefits of the body of CHRIST with the Calvinists, Luke and Paul protest, bringing forward that that very body is given to be eaten which is delivered unto death for us: that that very blood is given to be drunk which is shed for us for the remission of sins. And indeed such is the force and evidence of the truth that Theodore Beza, whether unknowingly or unwillingly, broke forth into this excellent confession, epist. 5. to Alemannus: It would be too absurd to interpret the names of body and blood as the fruit and efficacy of the death of the LORD: or to restrict them to His Spirit alone: Which, that you may understand most clearly, come, let us substitute that interpretation for these words (BODY and BLOOD), and let us say: This is the efficacy of my death which is delivered for you: and this is my Spirit, which is poured out for you. What is more inept than this speech? For certainly those words (Which is delivered for you, and which is poured out for you) necessarily drive you to this, that you are compelled to understand this concerning the very substance of the body and blood.

Latin:

INitio igitur, quod Matthæus Participij formâ dixit: Jesus λαβὼν τὸν ἄρτον, accipiens panem: id reliqui duo Evangelistæ Marcus & Lucas ijsdem verbis ac syllabis repetiverunt. Paulus verò mutato Participio in Verbum, sensu manente eodem dixit: Jesus ἔλαβε ἄρτον, accepit panem.

2. Quod Matthæus & Marcus habet, εὐλογήσας benedictione facta: id Lucas & Paulus rursus sensu minimè variato reddiderunt: εὐχαρισήσας, gratiis actis.

3. Omnes unanimiter habent, ἔκλασε fregit.

4. Quod tres Evangelistæ dixerunt: ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς: dedit illis, nempè discipulis: id Apostolus sequenti actioni, hoc est, manducationi panis, & cumprimis verbo Accipiendi, quod panis dationem necessariò præsupponit, inclusum latére voluit.

5. Quod Matthæus, Marcus & Paulus habent: dixit, Accipite, edite: id Lucas omisit: nihil interim à reliquis discrepans, uti Paulò pòst ostendetur.

6. Quod tres Evangelistæ asserunt, CHRISTUM dixisse: τῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά με: Hoc est meum corpus: id Apostolus non nisi cum trajectione pronominis mutatum ac repetitum voluit, inquiens: τῦτό με ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμα: Hoc meum est corpus.

7. Lucas & Apostolus, membris hisce sex jam notatis duo addiderunt alia, à reliquis duobus Evangelistis omissa: quorum Prius est προσκατηγορούμενον Corporis: illud nimirum corpus intelligendum esse, quod (secundum Lucam) pro vobis datur: secundum Paulum verò Quod pro vobis frangitur. Posterius est, Verbum mandati: Facite hoc ad mei commemorationem: quod Lucas & Paulus expresserunt. Monstrat prior hæc tabella, omnia ea membra, quibus essentia Sacramenti Evcharistici, quoad priorem partem describitur, tantâ verborum consonantiâ à tribus Evangelistis, & Apostolo esse definita & expressa, ut majori non potuerit. Etsi enim in reliquis membris aliqua dissimilitudo, sive dissonantia verborum se offert: neq; tamen ea alicujus est momenti, neq; etiam verborum Institutionis sensum gignit obscuriorem, id quod rursum invictè demonstrari potest.

Nam primò vocabulis εὐλογίας καὶ εὐχαρισίας æquipollentiam, sive συνωνυμίαν aliquam intercedere, ex scripturarum collatione liquidò constat, ut quando CHRISTUS legitur benedixisse paucis panibus & piscibus: hanc verò benedictionem ipse Spiritus S. per εὐχαρισίαν explicat: ut Matth.14,19.& c.15,36.Marc.6,41.&

cap. 8, 6. Luc. 9. 16. Joh. 6, 11. Hoc enim frequens admodum & solenne fuit Servatori, ut quoties usurpato pane elementari singulare aliquod & eximium divinæ omnipotentiæ specimen edere vellet, plerumq́; in cœlum sublatis oculis, actis DEO Patri gratijs, illi benediceret: non illud quidem hoc ritu agens, quod alioquin ad mensam à nobis fieri consuevit, nempè ut gratâ mente profiteatur, Panem quotidianum nobis à DEO præberi, simulq́; precetur, ut usus ipsius salutaris sit: sed id potiùs, & quidem cumprimis, circa institutionem panis Evcharistici pensi habuit, ut cú æterno Patre & Spiritu S. de Sacrofancto Testamenti sui mysterio condendo collatis quasi consilijs, tùm pro admirando redemtionis decreto gratias ageret: tùm verò Patrem Cœlestem pro hujus instituti confirmatione, & perenni ad omnem posteritatem propagatione invocaret.

Deindè licèt Apostolus verbum (DEDIT) omiserit: Lucas etiam verba hæc (ACCIPITE, MANDUCATE) non habeat: nihil tamen indè dissonantiæ, vel quoad rem, vel quoad sensum, emergit. Nam semper à tribus testibus unanimiter exprimitur, quod à quarto vel ideò est omissum, quia sequentibus membris id est inclusum: vel quia sic comparatum illud esse videbatur, ut omnes suâ sponte, nemine etiam interprete, intelligere possent; nó frustrà, nec aliâ intentione, panem datum fuisse discipulis, nisi ad accipiendum & manducandum: Et rursus non priùs illum accipi & manducari potuisse, quàm datus esset.

Tandem quoad illam προσηγορίαν corporis CHRISTI, quam Lucas & Paulus addiderunt, fatendum quidem est, utilem & præclaram eam esse declarationem: sed non ita simpliciter eam fuisse necessariam, quin etiam absque illâ mens CHRISTI ex verbis præcedentibus satis evidenter potuisset intelligi: Siquidem præter Unum Corpus, quod manducari, quodq́; in mortem tradi ac frangi potuerit, CHRISTO nullum aliud fuisse satis constat. Sic quoad annexum à Lucâ & Paulo Verbum Mandati, habet quidem illud suam quoq́; vim minimè exiguam: sed quæ usum saltem, non verò substantiam hujus Sacramenti concernat.

Sic ergò concordantia longè maxima, undequaq; Verbis Institutionis, quoad priorem hanc partem intercedere deprehenditur: & cumprimis quoad ea, quæ substantiam primæ hujus partis respiciunt.

Quibus ita constitutis, ultrò liquet, quàm fœda sit corruptio Verborum Institutionis, quâ Sacramentarij Andabatarum more invicem digladiantes, singula penè vocabula miris strophis depravârunt.

Carolstadius pronomine demonstrativo (HOC) arrepto, non panem à CHRISTO porrectum: sed corpus suum mensæ tùm assidens, eodé pronomine demonstratú fuisse contendens.

Zvvinglius pronomen hoc δεικτικὸν, ad Pané quidem retulit, sic Carolostadio apertè contradicens: sed erroris subsidium quæsivit in verbo substantivo (EST) quod per SIGNIFICAT interpretatus est.

Oecolampadius Zvvinglio adversâ fronte obloquens verbum quidem substantivum (εστ) no σημαντικῶς sed, ὑπαρκτικῶς accipiendum esse contendit: sed interim vocabulum corporis arripuit, idœ; no pro vero CHRISTI corpore, sed pro figurâ corporis accipiendum esse litigavit.

Calvinus ab his omnibus divortium faciens, totum verborum CHRISTI complexum, μετωνυμικῶς de beneficijs corporis CHRISTI interpretandum esse, contendit.

Quibus opinionibus singulis & universis rectissimè unanimis consensus sive concordantia trium Evangelistaru & Apostoli Pauli opponitur: cum quâ illæ diametraliter pugnant: Nam si Carolostadij τῶτο δεικτικῶν ad assidens CHRISTI corpus accommodare velis: reclamat Marcus, idem pronomen ad sangvinem CHRISTI etiam accommodans, inquiens: Hoc est sangvis meus: τῶτό εστι τὸ ἅιμά με: Ubi visibilis illa ostensio assidentis sangvinis CHRISTI locum planè nullum habet. Sic si cum Zvvinglio verbum substantivum est per significat reddere velis, reclamat consensus Evangelistarum, όμοθυμαδὸν afferentium, id quod CHRISTUS manducandum & bibendum porrexit discipulis, esse corpus CHRISTI: & ne cum Oecolampadio figuram, vel cum Calvinianis beneficia tantùm corporis CHRISTI intelligas, reclamant Lucas & Paulus afferentes, illud ipsum corpus dari manducandum, quod pro nobis in mortem est traditum: illum ipsum sangvinem dari bibendum, qui pro nobis effusus in Remissionem peccatorum. Et profectò tanta est vis ac evidentia veritatis, ut Theodorus Beza sive infcius, sive invitus in hanc egregiam confessionem eruperit, epist. 5. ad Alemannum: Nimis absurdum foret, corporis & sangvinis nomina de fructu & efficacia mortis DOMINI interpretari: vel ad solum ipsius Spiritum restringere: Quod ut planissimè intelligas, age pro his vocibus, (CORPUS & SANGVIS) substituamus, illam interpretationem, & dicamus: Hoc est efficacia mortis meæ qua pro vobis traditur: & hoc est Spiritus meus, qui pro vobis effunditur. Quid ineptius est hâc oratione? Nam certè verba illa, (Quod pro vobis traditur, & qui pro vobis effunditur) necessariò huc te adigunt, ut de ipsamet corporis & sangvinis substantiâ hoc intelligere cogaris.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: II. Table concerning the Eucharistic Cup

II. Table concerning the Eucharistic Cup.

No less a consensus of words and phrases is discovered concerning the other part of this Sacrament also. For because Matthew and Mark report that the Saviour

1. Took the cup:

2. To have given thanks:

3. To have given to the disciples: that [phrase] Luke and Paul, κατ᾽ αυτου ωξιν, insinuate with two words, saying: Likewise also the cup. Where, by the adverb of comparison, it is quite evidently hinted that Christ did the same thing concerning the cup as he did concerning the bread, namely, that he took it, gave thanks, and gave it to the disciples. Where even a boy understands that there can be no discrepancy at all between the evangelists.

4. Luke and the Apostle add a particular notation of time, asserting that Christ took the cup μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι, after they had supped. The sense of this notation is not as if from the beginning of that Supper [he gave] the Eucharistic bread: and only afterwards, the Supper now being finished, after some interval of time, the Savior gave the cup

to the disciples. For it would be absurd for one and the same mystery not only to be broken by intervals of time, but also to be clearly subverted by the intervention of dissimilar actions, so that its essential parts could appear to have been instituted at interrupted turns and actions: just as, indeed, the compilers of the Calvinistic consensus were not ashamed to feign, that a quite large interval of time had intervened between the dispensation of the Bread and the Cup. But this scope was set before Luke and Paul, that they might distinguish the Eucharistic Cup from the cup of the Paschal lamb. For as Luke reports in chapter 22, 17, CHRIST, being about to put an end to that Old Sacrament of the Paschal lamb, took the cup or fruit of the vine, drank, and offered it to the disciples to be divided among themselves. Therefore, in order to distinguish the Eucharistic cup from this cup, they added that this was done after that Paschal Supper had been completed: where at the same time, and at one and the same moment of time, the bread separately, and the cup separately, was administered by CHRIST: who also calls this cup not the fruit of the vine, but his blood, or the blood of the New Testament. Calvin himself acknowledged this, writing in the Harmony of the Evangelists: It would have been absurd for one and the same mystery to be broken by a distance of time: therefore I do not doubt that he added the cup in continuous time, after he had distributed the bread.

5. That which Matthew asserts CHRIST said by way of command: Drink from this all of you: that Mark, describing the historical act, expresses thus: And they all drank from it. Which both Luke and Paul nevertheless omit: with no scruple of discrepancy or doubt remaining in the meantime. For any sane person easily gathers that the cup was offered by Christ to the disciples for no other end than that they should drink from it: and that this was done by them in the very act.

Moreover, the fact that Mark records that the disciples drank from the cup before CHRIST said: This is my blood: that does nothing at all to establish the craftiness of the Sacramentarians toward the method of error, by which they do not fear to distort the order of this Sacramental action, as if after those words: Take, Eat: likewise Drink etc., the disciples had immediately eaten the bread blessed by CHRIST: and had immediately also drunk from the cup, before it had been said concerning the bread and the cup: This is my body, This is my blood. He refutes this insolence 1. Because Mark, acting as a historian in this part, did not have as much concern for the order in which each thing was either said or done, as for what was done in the very truth of the matter. 2. Because the narrative of the remaining Evangelists makes these members (Eat, This is my body: Drink, This is my blood) into a continuous discourse. In which part the authority of Luke is especially valid, who says that this was the principal cause for his writing the Gospel, that since many had undertaken to weave the Evangelical history, it seemed good also to him, having repeated everything from the high beginning, to describe and follow it in order, καθεξῆς πάντα ἀκριβῶς γράψαι Lu. 1, 3.

6. Because the first two Evangelists said: THIS is that blood of mine of the New Testament, which is shed for many, and indeed according to Mark, for the Remission of sins: this Luke and Paul state thus: This cup is the New Testament in my blood.

Where Luke adds, Which is shed for you: but Paul repeats that: Do this in remembrance of me. It seems to some that in this place a certain ἐναντιοφανὲς, or apparent contradiction, has been committed: because it is one thing for the Wine to be the very blood of CHRIST, but another for the Wine to be the New Testament in the blood of CHRIST. But the matter is safe. For although between these two statements, as far as the phraseology is concerned, there intervenes some diversity, which the very transposition of the words designates: yet in the sentence itself, and even in the sense of the words themselves, there is clearly no dissonance. Now the former phrase is proper to the Greek language: the latter especially to the Hebrew. For what the Greeks say in a uniform manner of speech: This is my blood of the New Testament: that the Hebrews express in an inflected mode: This cup is the New Testament in my blood. Our theologians demonstrate the solidity of this explanation most correctly in this manner: Just as when a promise has been made about giving silver to a creditor as a mortgage, if by offering a silver cup they say: This is that silver for the promised mortgage: Or if I express it thus: This cup is the promised mortgage in silver: in either way I shall certainly have said one and the same thing, not only in sense: but also in words, although through the transposition of the words, I shall have enunciated that by the propriety of the Greek idiom, this by that of the Hebrew. In exactly the same manner, when CHRIST, by exhibiting the Cup, in the Greek manner, according to Matthew and Mark, said: This is my blood of the New Testament, and when in the Hebrew manner according to Luke and Paul he said: This cup is the New Testament in my blood: he certainly said nothing dissonant in the reality, but indicated one and the same thing clearly both in words and in meaning, namely this, that what he himself distributes in this cup is that blood of his of the New Testament: or the New Testament in his blood. The reason is: Because the cup itself, not by reason of its matter or external form, is the New Testament: but in the blood, and with the blood, or on account of the blood of CHRIST, which CHRIST distributes in mystery present from this cup.

Moreover, there are not lacking very pregnant reasons, on account of which this change or transposition of words was in a way necessary. For two things are contained in the predicate of each statement, of which one pertains to the substance of the Sacrament; the other to its use or fruit, of which the former is expressed by the word Blood: the latter by the word Testament. It pleased the Evangelists and the Apostle to explain both of these in this other part of the Sacrament for this reason especially, because the Blood of CHRIST, which is the substance of the New Testament, has a certain analogy to the blood of cattle, which constituted the substance of the Old Testament. Therefore, according to the diversity of the subject, the predicate itself also had to be varied and changed. For since an absolute pronoun, or a complex word, This, is placed in the subject, which implies the notation of a double thing, visible and invisible: the thing itself does not allow that in the predicate that which is only the fruit

“should be placed first: but since in that complex word one thing lies hidden, another is seen: certainly in the predicate, the notation of the invisible thing and that which pertains to the substance of the Sacrament ought to precede: but the mention of the fruit to follow. Whence it is, that by Matthew and Mark, seeing that they used the complex word this, the predicate could not or ought not to be formed otherwise than that they should say, This is the blood of the New Testament, by the preceding word, namely Blood, noting the substantial part of this Sacrament: but by the subsequent word: New Testament, declaring the fruit of this Sacrament. Now indeed when Luke and Paul, conversely, instead of the complex word, wished to place one determined species, and that entirely visible and external: the thing itself, and the truth of the thing, necessarily demanded that, with the subject changed, the form of the predicate itself also be immediately changed, the sense of the proposition meanwhile not being changed: so that they most correctly named the Cup not the blood of Christ, but the New Testament in his blood: as also regarding the former part of this Sacrament, in 1 Cor. 10:16, they named the Bread not the body of CHRIST; but κοινωνίαν the communication of the body of Christ: and thus, concerning one essential part, that is, external and visible, they predicated not simply the other, namely the heavenly and invisible: but the fruit with the notation of the other part. For although in a Sacramental mode of preaching, CHRIST could also truly say: That the bread is his body, that the wine is his blood: yet lest that be understood in a Capernaitic sense, he wished deliberately to abstain from this phrase: as will be shown more accurately below in question 5 of this first chapter: where there will be a discussion expressly for us concerning these Sacramental Predications.

7. And finally, it is a peculiar thing that Luke, in the Greek language, refers these words, 'Which is poured out for you,' not to the blood of CHRIST, but to the cup. Whence Beza writes in the glosses of his larger Testament that a certain solecism was committed by Luke. For Luke says, τοῦτο ἐστὶ τὸ ποτήριον ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου, (not τῷ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχευομένῳ) but τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχευόμενον: a thing which we are fully persuaded was done by singular design and divine instinct. For Luke wished to demonstrate that that which is exhibited in or under the cup of blessing, and which is drawn and drunk from it, is that very thing which was poured out for us for the remission of sins, namely, the very blood of CHRIST itself. For as to the fact that the Holy Spirit not only places the article (τὸ) in the nominative case, which, according to Beza's opinion, ought to have been placed in the dative case to avoid a solecism, but did not even place the relative pronoun (ὃ) in its stead: who, I ask, would doubt that this was done for the sake of emphasis, so that, namely, by the prepositive article (τὸ) it might be expressly noted that it is not some symbolic, or typical, or figurative blood that is to be understood: nor even the virtue or efficacy of the blood: but that very essential blood of CHRIST which was poured out for our sins.

Latin:

II. Tabula de Poculo Eucharistio.

HAud minor consensus verborum ac phrasium, circa alteram etiam Sacramenti hujus partem deprehenditur. Nam quòd Matthæus & Marcus afferunt, Servatorem

1. Accepisse poculum:

2. Gratias egisse:

3. Dedisse discipulis: illud Lucas & Paulus κατ᾽ αυτου ωξιν, duobus verbis insinuant dicentes: Similiter & poculum. Ubi per adverbium comparandi satis evidenter innuitur, de Poculo idé fecisse Christũ, quod de Pane, nempè accepisse illud, gratias egisse, & dedisse discipulis. Ubi nihil prorsῳ, discrepãtiēgelici posse, vel puer intelligit.

4. Lucas & Apostolus peculiarem temporis notationem adjiciunt, asserentes, poculum accepisse Christum μῶ τὸ δειπνῆσαι, postquam cœnassent. Cujus notationis non is sensus est, quasi à principio Cœnæ illius panem Evcharisticum: & post demùm, peractâ jam Cœnâ, post aliquod temporis intervallum, Calicem Servator dederit

discipulis. Absurdum enim foret, unum & idem mysterium non modò temporis intervallis abrumpi: sed & actionum dissimilium interventu, planè interverti, ut partes ejus essentiales, interruptis vicibus & actionibus institutæ esse, videri possint: quemadmodum sanè compilatores consensus Calvinistici fingere non depuduit, inter dispensationem Panis & Calicis benè magnum temporis intervallum intercessisse. Verum is scopus Lucæ & Paulo fuit præfixus, ut distingverent Poculum Evcharisticum à poculo agni Paschalis. Nam referente Luca c. 22, 17. CHRISTUS impositurus jam finem Veteri illi Sacramento agni Paschalis, poculum sive genimen vitis accepit, bibit, & discipulis inter se dividendum porrexit. Ab hoc ergò poculo ut distingverent poculum Evcharisticum, addiderunt factum hoc esse, post peractam illam Cœnam paschalem: ubi simul etiam, & uno eodemq; temporis momento, seorsim panis, seorsim poculum Evcharisticum, à CHRISTO fuit administratum: qui etiam poculum hoc non genimen vitis, sed sangvinem suum, sive sangvinem Novi Test. appellitat. Agnovit hoc ipsum Calvinus, scribens in Harmonia Evangelistarum: Absurdum fuisset, unum & idem mysterium Temporis distantiâ abrumpi: proindè non dubito, quin continuo tempore, postquam panem distribuerat, calicem addiderit.

5. Quod Matthæus per modum imperandi CHRISTUM dixisse asserit: Bibite ex hoc omnes: id Marcus historicum actum describens, sic exprimit: Et biberunt ex eo omnes. Quod utrumq; tamen & Lucas & Paulus omittunt: nullo interim discrepantiæ vel dubitationis scrupulo relicto. Neq; enim alio fine poculum à Christo discipulis porrectum fuisse, quivis sanus facilè colligit, quàm ut ex eo biberent: idq; actu ipso ab ijsdem factum esse.

Cæterùm quod Marcus habet discipulos prius ex poculo bibisse, quàm CHRISTUS dixerit: Hoc est sangvis meq: nihil quicquam illud facit pro stabiliendâ Sacramentariorum πανεργίᾳ πρὸς τὴν μεθοδείαν τῆς πλάνης, quâ Ordinem actionis hujus Sacramentalis ita distorquere non verentur, ac si post illa verba: Accipite, Edite: item Bibite &c. discipuli panem à CHRISTO benedictum, statim ederint: & continuò ex poculo etiã biberint, priùsquàm de pane & poculo dictum fuisset: Hoc est corpus meũ, Hoc est sangvis meus. Redarguit hanc petulantiam 1. Quod Marcus historicum hâc in parte agens, no tam pensi habuit, Quo ordine quidq; vel dictum, vel gestum sit, quàm quid in ipsâ rei veritate factum sit. 2. Quod reliquorum Evangelistarum narratio ex membris istis (Edite, Hoc est corpus meũ: Bibite, Hic est sangvis meus) continuâ oratione faciunt. Quâ in parte Lucæ potissimũ valet autoritas, qui scribendi evangelij sui hanc præcipuè causã fuisse inquit, quod cùm multi historiã Evangelicã texere aggressi sint, visum etiã sit sibi, omnia repetito altè principio, ordine describere atq; persequi, καθεξῆς πάντα ἀκριβῶς γράψαι Lu. 1, 3.

6. Quod priores duo Evangelistæ dixerunt: HOC est sangvis ille meus Novi Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur, & quidé secundũ Marcũ, in Remissionẽ peccatorũ: id Lucas & Paul9 sic enunciant: Hoc poculũ est Testamentũ Novum in meo sangvine.

Ubi Lucas addit, Quod pro vobis funditur: Paulus verò repetit illud: Facite hoc in mei commemorationem. Videtur nonnullis hoc loco : ἐναντιοφανὲς quoddam, sive apparens contradictio esse commissa : proptereà quod aliud est Vinum esse ipsum sangvinem CHRISTI, aliud verò, Vinum esse Novum Testamentum in sangvine CHRISTI. Verùm salva res est. Etsi enim duabus istis enunciationibus, quoad Φρασιολογίαν aliqua intercedit diversitas, quam ipsa vocabulorum trajectio designat: In sententiâ tamen ipsâ, adeoque sensu etiam ipsorum vocabulorum planè nulla est dissonantia. Est autem prior ista phrasis, Lingvæ Græcæ: posterior Hebrææ potissimûm propria. Quod enim Græci æquabili oratione dicunt : Hoc est sangvis meus Novi Testamenti: id Hebræi inflexo modo efferunt : Hoc poculum est Novum Testamentum in meo sangvine. Explicationis hujus soliditatem nostrates Theologi hunc in modum rectissimè demonstrant: Quemadmodum promissione factâ de argento in hypothecam creditori dando, si poculum argenteum offerendo dicant: Hoc est argentum illud in promissam hypothecam: Vel sic id efferam : Hoc poculum est promissa hypotheca in argento: utrovis certè modo unum atq; idem dixero, non sensu tantùm : sed verbis etiam, licèt per trajectionem vocabulorum, illud Græci, hoc Hebræi idiomatis proprietate, enunciaverim. Eundem planè in modum, quando CHRISTUS Calicem exhibendo, more Græco, secundum Matthæum & Marcum dixit: Hoc est sangvis meus Novi Testamenti, & quando more Hebræo secundum Lucam & Paulum dixit : Hoc poculum est Novum Testamentum in meo sangvine : certè reipsâ nihil dissonans, sed idem planè tùm in verbis, tùm in sententiâ innuens dixit, videlicet hoc, quod ipse in hoc poculo distribuit, esse sangvinem illum suum Novi Testamenti: seu Novum Testamentum in sangvine suo. Ratio est : Quia poculum ipsum non ratione suæ materiæ aut externæ formæ, est Novum Testamentum: sed in sangvine, & cum sangvine, sive propter sangvinem CHRISTI, quem ex hoc poculo in mysterio præsentem CHRISTUS distribuit.

Cæterùm neq; rationes prægnatissimæ desunt, propter quas hæc verborum mutatio sive trajectio quodammodo fuerit necessaria. Nam duo insunt prædicato utriusq; enunciationis, quorũ unum ad substantiam Sacramenti; alterum ad ejusdem usum sive fructum pertinet, quorum illud Sangvinis: hoc Testamenti vocabulo exprimitur. Utrumq; istud placuit Evangelistis & Apostolo in hac alterâ Sacramenti parte explicare hanc potissimùm ob causam, quia Sangvis CHRISTI, qui est Novi Testamenti substantia, analogiam quandam habet ad sangvinem pecuinum, qui constituebat substantiam Veteris Testamenti. Pro diversitate ergò subjecti, ipsum quoque prædicatum variari & mutari debuit. Cum enim in subjecto ponitur Pronomen absolutum, sive vox complexa, Hoc, quæ rei geminæ, visibilis & invisibilis notationem implicat : res ipsa non patitur, ut in prædicato id, quod fructus tantùm

“indicationem habet præmittatur: sed quoni- “am in voce illâ complexâ aliud latet, aliud vi- “detur: utique in prædicato, rei invisibilis & “ad substantiam Sacramenti pertinentis, nota- “tio præcedere debuit: fructus verò mentio sub- “sequi. Undè est, quod à Matthæo & Marco, “quippè qui vocabulo complexo hoc sunt usi, “prædicatum aliter formari non potuit, aut de- “buit, quàm ut dicerent, Hoc esse sangvinem “Novi Testamenti, per vocem præcedentem, “nempè Sangvinem, partem Sacramenti hujus “substantialem notantes: per vocem verò subse- “quentem: Testamenti Novi, fructum Sacramenti hujus declarantes. Jam verò quando Lucas & Paulus, vice versâ, pro voce complexâ, unam speciem determinatam, eamq; ex integro visibilem & externam ponere voluerunt: res ipsa, reiq; veritas necessariò efflagitavit, ut mutato subjecto, statim ipsius etiam prædicati forma mutetur, sensu propositionis interim non mutato: ita ut Poculum non sangvinem Christi, sed Novum Testamentum in ipsius sangvine: ut & quoad priorem partem hujus Sacramenti, in 1. Cor. 10, 16. Panem non corpus CHRISTI; sed κοινωνίαν communicationem corporis Christi rectissimè nominaverint: & sic, de unâ parte essentiali, hoc est, externâ ac visibili, non simpliciter alteram, nempè cœlestem & invisibilem: sed fructum cum notatione alterius partis prædicaverint. Etsi enim Sacramentali modo prædicandi, CHRISTUS verè etiam dicere po- “tuit: Panem esse corpus suum, Vinum esse sangvi- “nem suum: tamen ne sensu Capernaitico illud “intelligeretur, ab hac phrasi consultò abstinere “voluit: uti infrà quæst. 5. hujus capitis primi accuratiùs ostendetur: ubi de Prædicationibus istis Sacramentalibus nobis ex professo futura disputatio.

7. Et postremò, peculiare illud est, quod Lucas in Græco sermone, verba hæc, Quod pro vobis effunditur, non ad sangvinem CHRISTI, sed ad poculum refert. Undè Beza σολοικοφανὲς quoddam à Lucâ commissum esse scriptitat in glossis majoris Testamenti. Dicit enim Lucas, τῦτο ἐςί τ᾿ ποτήριον ἐν τῷ ἁιματί μγ, (non τῷ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχευομένῳ) sed τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχευόμενον: id quod singulari consilio, & instinctu divino factum fuisse, habemus persuasissimum. Voluit enim demonstrare Lucas, Id, quod in, vel sub poculo benedictionis exhibetur, quodq; ex eo hauritur ac bibitur, esse illud ipsum, quod pro nobis effusum est in remissionem peccatorum, nempè ipsissimum sangvinem CHRISTI. Nam quod Spiritus S. non modò Articulum (τὸ) in nominativo casu ponit, qui ad vitandum σολοικοφανὲς, juxta Bezæ opinionem, in tertio casu ponendus erat: sed nequidem ejus loco postpositivum Articulum (ὃ) collocavit: quis quæso dubitet, quin id emphaseως causa factum sit, ut nimirùm per articulum præpositivum (τὸ) expressè notetur non symbolicum, aut typicum, sive figuratum aliquem sangvinem: non etiam virtutem aut efficaciam sangvinis: sed ipsum illum Essentialem CHRISTI sangvinem, qui pro peccatis nostris effusus est, intelligi debere.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Question II. Are the words of the Institution to be understood according to the letter (κτ τὸ ῥητὸν)?

QUESTION II. Are the words of the Institution to be understood according to the letter (κτ τὸ ῥητὸν)?

The words of the Institution are of two different kinds: the former of which describes τὰ πραχθέντα, that is, those things which CHRIST himself did regarding both the condition and the administration of this Sacrament: the latter, however, contains τὰ λεχθέντα, those things which CHRIST spoke concerning this Sacrament.

To that former kind we refer what the Savior 1. took bread: 2. gave thanks 3. broke 4. gave to the disciples: Thus, regarding the other part of this Sacrament, that 1. he took the cup. 2. he blessed. 3. he distributed. Concerning these individual members, and all of them, at the beginning between B. Luther and the Zwinglians, as also later between us and the Calvinists, no controversy was stirred: until some innovators, or rather disturbers of the reformed Churches, arose from the Calvinist people, who, according to their own critical arrogance, 1. simply disapproved of the use of smaller breads, which they commonly call hosts, and rejected them as impious and idolatrous. 2. They contended, however, that such a breaking must necessarily be used in the Eucharistic action as the Savior used, so that, namely, bread of a certain size is broken into smaller pieces, and is put into the mouth of the communicants by the minister, or is even given into the hand of the communicant, who afterwards eats that morsel at pleasure. Concerning the former member, we shall discourse expressly in Question 3, and we shall assert the use of smaller breads, or hosts. The latter question, however, concerning the breaking of bread, is proper to this place, although it is curious, and serves more to disturb the Churches than to edify.

Latin:

QVAESTIO II. An verba Institutionis κτ τὸ ῥητὸν secundum literam sint intelligenda?

VErba Institutionis duorum diversorum sunt generum: quorum prius τὰ πραχθέντα, h. e. ea, quæ CHRISTUS ipse circa Sacramenti hujus & conditionem, & administrationem fecit, describit: posterius verò continet τὰ λεχθέντα ea, quæ CHRISTUS de hoc Sacramento locutus est.

Ad genus prius illud referimus, quod Servator 1. pane accepit: 2. gratias egit 3. fregit 4. dedit discipulis: Sic quoad altera Sacramenti hujus partem, quod 1. poculu accepit. 2 benedixit. 3. distribuit. De his membris singulis, & universis, initio inter B. Lutheru & Zuvinglianos, ut & postea inter nos & Calvinianos, nulla mota fuit Controversia: usq; dum Novatores nonnulli, vel turbatores potiùs Ecclesiarum reformataru, ex gente Calviniana prodierunt, qui pro critico suo supercilio, 1. usum panu minutioru, quos vulgò hostias appellant, simpliciter improbarunt, & tanquã impiu ac idololatricu rejecerunt. 2. verò contenderunt, necessario tale fractione in actione Eucharistica esse usurpandam, quali Servator usus est, ut nimirum panis justa alicujus magnitudinis, in frusta minutiora frangatur, & communicantiu ori à ministro ingeratur, vel etiam in manus communicanti detur, qui postmodu frustulum illud manducet ad placitu. De priore membro Quæst 3. ex professo differemus, & usum panum minutiorum, sive hostiaru asseremus. Posterior verò Quæstio, de fractione panis, hujus loci est propria, licèt sit curiosa, & ad turbandum magis Ecclesias, quàm ad ædificandum faciat.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: I. On the Breaking of the Eucharistic Bread

This whole controversy can be explained most conveniently if, by observing four main questions, it is shown in the beginning: What mode of breaking regarding the Eucharistic bread has been observed in the Church, both Eastern and Western, ever since the times of the Apostles: indeed, even in the Church which they call that of the Lutherans, it has been retained, used, and accepted for almost an entire century, with no one contradicting? Then, what exactly comes into controversy when the Calvinist innovators bring a suit against our Churches concerning the breaking of the Eucharistic bread? Then, whether the breaking of bread, such as the Calvinists introduced into the Church not many years ago under the opinion of absolute necessity, agrees more with the deed of CHRIST, or with the analogy of faith, than the breaking of the Lutherans? Finally, how one ought to respond solidly to the arguments of the Calvinists, with which they fight tooth and nail to defend their rite?

Regarding I. The word for breaking פָּרַס in sacred writings takes on an equivocal meaning. Sometimes it signifies the same as to destroy, to slay, to devastate: sometimes, however, it denotes distribution: and indeed any kind, whether it happens through some cutting into pieces, or through the division or distribution of some thing, as Isa. 58:7, Break your bread to the hungry. Hence, regarding the breaking of the Eucharistic bread, a clearly different rite was observed in the Church. Certain Eastern Churches used a whole cake, and some divided it into certain particles with a knife, others by hand: some used only one bread, others several, others placed parts already cut or dissected upon the altar. Thus, the Greeks are read to this day to use a large bread for the number of communicants, and one which can suffice for all. But when the use of smaller breads, or hosts, or oblations, which Gregory the Great calls 'nummular' breads in his Register, prevailed in the Latin Church, it is perhaps not so exactly clear: some referring it to the times of Alexander I, around the year of Christ 119, others to the year of Christ 607, and indeed to the times of the Emperor Phocas. But whatever the case, that certainly cannot be denied in any way, that already in the times of Epiphanius, who lived and flourished around the year 380, bread of this kind, round and circular, was accepted in use, which Epiphanius also names στρογγυλοειδῆ bread: which word does not denote an oblong and wide bread, as some of the Calvinists trifle; but a smaller and orbicular one, which is clearly evident from the unanimous consent of Greek lexicographers. For στρογγύλος sounds the same to all as round: and is opposed to μάκρῳ, long or oblong. Hence in Thucydides, book 2, σώματα στρογγύλα were called, not tall and slender bodies; but shorter or smaller, and as it were compact. That this custom and usage also obtained in the times of Augustine can perhaps be easily demonstrated. For what else is that comminution for distribution, which Augustine mentions in epistle 59 to Paulinus, than the breaking of oblations into the Eucharist, as he himself explains in the heresy of the Ophites to Quodvultdeus. This breaking is used in our Churches to this day, when from the finest and purest wheat or rye flour, with the intervention of water, some whole mass is made, which is afterwards baked to the proper consistency in smaller and round parts, whether broken or divided. Although this breaking does not happen publicly in the temple, it is nevertheless seen to have been done publicly: just as the infusion of wine, although it does not happen publicly, is nevertheless seen to have been done. Furthermore, it is also rightly said among us that the Bread is broken when it is distributed among the communicants. And indeed this very ancient custom of breaking bread does not lack its own evident reason, which is not undeservedly heeded in more populous churches. Because, namely, a public breaking, on account of the multitude of communicants, would have caused some delay for the whole assembly: therefore, some shortcut was thought of, by which everything in the Church might be done not only εὐσχημόνως (decently), but also εὐτάκτως (in order). Therefore, the Lutheran Churches can neither be accused of, nor ought they to be accused of, a violated divine institution, even if they do not publicly break a whole cake by hand in the Eucharistic action itself in the manner of the Calvinists, and place the torn-off parts into the hands of the communicants. For it has not been proven even by them to this day that Christ broke bread and distributed it to the Apostles in the way they themselves are accustomed to. For what Hospinian writes, that it is credible that the Lord broke the bread into two parts, and gave one of them to him who was reclining next to him on the right: and the other to him who was on the left, so that they might pass them on to those reclining next to them in turn, until each had taken a piece for himself: is partly rash, and partly built upon mere conjectures: so that that 'Credible' can easily be refuted by 'Incredible'. Which he himself noticing, immediately adds by way of a correction as it were: It is for the Church, he says, provided the foundation in it

Latin:

POtest a. tota hæc controversia commodissime explicari, si quatuor potissimum observatis quæstionibus, in tio ostendatur, Quis fractionis modus circa pane Eucharisticu, jam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus, in Ecclesia tum Orientali, tum Occidentali sit observatus: imò in Ecclesia etia, quam vocant Lutheranorum per integru ferme seculu, nemine contradicente, retentus, usug, receptg? Deinde, quid potissimum in controversiam veniat, quando nostris Ecclesiis Novatores Calviniani, de fractione panis Eucharisticilitem intendunt? Tum, Anne fractio panis, qualem Calviniani ante annos haud ita multos in Ecclesiam, sub necessitatis absolutæ opinione invexerunt, vel cum facto CHRISTI, vel cum analogia fidei magis conveniat, quam fractio Lutheranorum? Tandem qui ad Calvinianorum argumenta, quibus pro suo defendendo ritu mordicus pugnant, solide responderi debeat?

Quoad I. Verbu Frangendi פָּרַס in sacris æquivocatione sortitur. Interdum ide significat, ac perdere, interimere, vastare: interdu verò distributione nota: & quidem quamlibet, sive ea fiat per quanda in frusta sectione, sive perdivisionem aut distributione rei alicujus, ut Esa. 58, 7. Frange esurienti pane tuu. Hinc circa fractione panis Eucharistici diversus plane ritus in Ecclesia observatus fuit. Orientales quædam Ecclesiæ integram placenta usurpabant, eamq; aliæ cultro, aliæ manu in certas particulas dividebant: aliæ unu tantum pane, aliæ plures, aliæ partes ja abscissas sive dissectas altari imponebant. Sic Græci hodieq; pro numero communicantiũ panem magnũ, & qui omnibus sufficere possit, usurpare leguntur. Quando verò in Latinâ Ecclesiâ usus panũ minorum, sive hostiarũ, aut oblatarũ, quas Gregorius Magno in Registro panes nummularios vocat, invaluerit, fortè haud ita exactè liquet: alijs ad tempora Alexandri I. circa an. Christi 119. alijs ad an. Christi 607. & quidem ad Tempora Phocæ Imperatoris, id referentibus. Sed quicquid sit, illud certè negari nullo modo potest, jam modò temporibus Epiphanij, qui vixit ac floruit circa A. 380. panẽ hujusmodi terete ac rotundum usu fuisse receptũ, quem Epiphanius etiam nominat panem στρογγυλοειδῆ: quæ vox non panẽ oblongũ, & latũ, uti quidam ex Calvinianis nugantur; sed minorẽ & orbiculare notat, id quod unanimis Græcorũ Lexicographorũ consensu liquidò constat. Nam στρογγύλος omnibq idẽ sonat ac rotundus: & opponitur τῷ μάκρῳ longo vel oblongo. Hinc Thucydidi lib. 2. σώματα στρογγύλα dicebantur, non procera ac gracilia corpora; sed breviora sive minutiora, & quasi compacta. Quem more ac consuetudinẽ Augustini etiam temporibo obtinuisse, facilè fortassis demonstrari potest. Quid n. aliud est illa ad distribuendũ comminutio, cujus August. meminit epist. 59. ad Paulinũ: quàm oblationũ in Eucharistiam confractio, ut ipse explicat in hæresi Ophisarũ ad Quodvultdeũ. Hæc fractio hodieq; nostris Ecclesiis est usitata, quando ex farinâ de tritico vel siligine, optima & purissima, interveniente aquâ, integra aliqua fit massa, quæ postmodùm in partes minutiores ac rotundas, sive fracta sive divisa igni ad justam consistentiam pinsitur. Hæc fractio licèt publicè in templo non fiat, publicè tamẽ facta esse conspicitur: perindè atq; vini infusio, licèt publicè non fiat, facta tamẽ esse videtur. Prætereà rectè etiam apud nos Panis frangi dicitur, quando inter communicantes distribuitur. Et sanè hæc ipsa vetustissima consuetudo frangẽdi panẽ, non caret evidenti suâ ratione, quæ in Ecclesiis populosioribus haud immeritò attenditur. Quia n. fractio publica, propter multitudinẽ communicantiũ, universo cœtui remoram aliquam paritura erat: ideò de compendio aliquo cogitatũ fuit, quo non εὐσχημόνως tantùm: sed & εὐτάκτως omnia in Ecclesiâ fierent. Haud igitur violatæ institutionis divinæ insimulari vel possunt, vel debent Ecclesiæ Lutheranæ, licet non Calvinianorũ more integram placẽtam in actione ipsâ Eucharisticâ publicè manu frangant, & partes avulsas in communicantiũ manq collocent. Nam neq; ab ipsis in hunc usq; diem probatũ est, Christum hoc modo fregisse panẽ, & distribuisse Apostolis, quo ipsi consueverunt. Nam quod Hospinianus scribit, credibile esse, Dominum in duas partes panẽ confregisse, earumq alterã dedisse illi, qui proximus illi ad dextrã accũbebat: alterã vero illi, qui ad sinistrã, ut isti deinceps proximè accũbentibus porrigerẽt, donec singuli particulã sibi decerpsissent: partim temerariũ est, partim meris conjecturis superstructum: ita ut illud Credibile per Non-Credibile facilè elidi possit. Quod ipsemet animadvertens, per correctionem quasi quandam statim subjicit: Ecclesiæ est, inquiens, modò fundamentum in eâ ma-


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Status Controversy about the Breaking of Bread, what it properly is?

remains safe: and much more is the Supper there, where the principal things, and truly the substance, are preserved, even if there be error in some rites used by Christ himself. This very thing Beza also acknowledged, establishing that the breaking of bread does not pertain to the substance itself, or to the confession of the Sacrament: I think, he says, that its omission, since it pertains not to the confession of the Sacrament itself, but only to the form of its true and altogether legitimate use, does not vitiate the act itself: just as a mole on a beautiful face indeed harms its charm, but does not abolish the form itself. Therefore, it is not without the guilt of extreme rashness that certain innovators of the Calvinian sect, in this part making a secession from their teacher Beza, contend that the breaking of bread, such as they observe, is essential to the Lord's Supper, nay, is simply commanded by Christ in these words: DO THIS. Which rashness, that it may be brought more into the light, which will be the second member of the present dispute, it must be more accurately examined, what properly comes into controversy in this place, and what does not?

II.

But in the beginning, it is not primarily controverted whether Christ, instituting this Sacrament, broke the bread before He gave it to His disciples? For we hold the affirmative, moved not so much by the clarity of the words of institution themselves, as by the condition or rite of the Paschal feast itself, by which larger unleavened breads were prepared, of such breadth and thickness that either one, or at least a few, would suffice for the whole family. From which rite, however, it is not right that anyone should slander us, as if we had departed from the institution of CHRIST by our observation, as will be shown more accurately a little later.

Then, neither is the question properly about this: Whether a similar mode of Eucharistic bread was observed in the primitive Church? For we have already shown before that this cannot be denied, so that even today in the Churches of the Greeks, some one bread, baked in that size, is placed upon the altar, which can suffice for all.

Thirdly, neither is that contested by us: Whether, for certain and evident causes, the Church could, if it wished, recall that ancient custom into use after a long interval? For just as we establish that it was done out of Christian liberty that the use of smaller breads or wafers was introduced into the Church for the sake of order and decency, so we judge it to be of the same liberty, having abrogated this use, to restore the custom and habit of the ancient Oriental Church; provided that this is not done for the sake of the innovators, who under this pretext or mask, go about to corrupt, nay, to overturn the sacrosanct deposit of the purer Lutheran doctrine itself. In which case, concerning the use or change of indifferent things, such as we establish the form of bread to be, considered in the category of both quantity and quality, etc., we altogether establish that not even a nail's breadth is to be yielded to innovators of that kind. But if there be in the Church either many, or even the best, who otherwise think rightly about Religion, who suffer scandal over such a rite as is observed in our Churches, and wish that ancient custom to be brought back: in this case, surely, we are not at all ignorant of what Christian Charity demands of us. Although such weak ones have not been found in our Churches to this very day, nor pointed out by the innovators.

Fourthly, neither do we urge it as if the rite used in our Churches, by which very thin and circular cakes are made, like a small coin, as Durandus speaks, is simply and absolutely necessary, so that it could or should by no means, and for no reason, be changed?

But that is what is properly controverted between us and the Calvinists: Whether that rite of breaking, which certain innovators have very recently introduced into the reformed Churches, is so necessary in the administration of the Supper, nay, so commanded by CHRIST, that it ought by no means to be omitted or changed: nay, that without it the Sacrament of the Supper cannot be administered legitimately at all. Where the Calvinists hold the affirmative stubbornly: but we descend into the negative.

Moreover, so that it may be more certainly established whether the palm of truth should be awarded to us or to them, first of all the rite which those innovators are accustomed to observe regarding the Eucharistic bread comes under consideration.

In the beginning, therefore, they take care that the loaves are baked not unleavened, as Christ used, but leavened: and for the most part of such size that one can suffice for four communicants.

Then, indeed, when they are about to celebrate the Eucharist, they order several such loaves or cakes to be placed upon a wooden table destined for this action.

Third, the Calvinist minister approaches that public table, and in the sight of the Church, breaks such bread into four parts.

Fourth, he hands one particle into the hand of each communicant: so that these may afterwards put the received particles into their own mouths.

Regarding this rite, in the second place now, it must be examined: whether it expresses the very act of Christ, or contributes anything to the essence of this Sacrament, or finally is so necessary that on account of its defect, the very purity of the Evangelical religion is endangered? Wherein we maintain the negative throughout, and demonstrate it invincibly by these reasons.

1. It is uncertain in what form or in what manner the Savior broke the bread. Therefore it would be rash to attribute this or that manner to the breaking of Christ. The antecedent is evident 1. from the fact that none of all those who were spectators of the first Supper ever described this form anywhere. 2. The Evangelical history is a witness that Christ did not break the bread in any common and customary way: but in a clearly singular one, so that in Luke 24:35, the disciples at Emmaus recognized Christ even from the breaking of bread alone: they would certainly not have recognized him if he had broken the bread in the common and customary manner of men.

2. It is uncertain, and not yet proven, that Christ distributed the broken bread among the Apostles in such a way that he gave a particle into the hands of each one, just as under the law of necessity, the Calvinist innovators urge this rite.

3. This rite of breaking, either is simply necessary, or it is not: If it is simply necessary, it must be expressly commanded by the Word of GOD: But such a word or command nowhere exists in the Sacred Scriptures. Therefore, it will not be simply necessary, and consequently it is forced upon peaceful and reformed Churches by force and tyranny, and under the law of necessity. The truth of the assumption is clearly evident, 1. because in the entire sacred history, nothing at all can be found concerning leavened, or concerning four-part bread, regarding the action of this Sacrament. 2. We read that Christ indeed broke bread, and therefore we determine that the same must be done by us also: but since the manner of this breaking is nowhere expressed or defined in the sacred writings: who would be so impudent and rash as to dare to invent any manner whatsoever, as simply necessary and commanded by Christ, and to force it even upon an unwilling Church?

4. The very leaders of the Calvinist dogma are not sufficiently consistent with themselves in this part. Theodore Beza certainly refers the breaking of bread among those things which, although they cannot be changed, much less abolished, without just reproach: yet they are not of such moment that one should think that no Supper is celebrated there because of it. Thus the Marburg Calvinists, distinguishing the words of the Institution into words of circumstances and of command: expressly refer the word (BROKE) to the class of circumstances, and pronounce clearly concerning these, that they are not to be equated with the words of the command. For these have the force of obligation and necessity (Rightly binding and compelling words): but those are only πειστατικα [circumstantial], and therefore of a different kind, and possess neither the force of obligation nor of necessity. In the German booklet printed at Kassel: A iiij. B. & C. f. whose title is: A short simple report on the Holy Supper of the LORD. Moreover, they add in the same place, that in the manner and form of the bread taken and distributed, broken or not broken, taken by hand or by mouth, the Church of CHRIST enjoys its own peculiar liberty: nor does it matter whether unleavened or leavened: black or white: round or angular: large or small is used.

5. If the opinion of the innovators prevails, it follows that the Orthodox Churches, ever since the times of Epiphanius, through the course of so many centuries, through so many ages of the faithful, have not administered the true and legitimate Sacrament of the Eucharist. Which would be highly insulting even to think: and insulting indeed to CHRIST himself, the head of the Church: as if he had granted to his Church the purity of the Word in every way, but in the meantime had not granted it the grace to be able to have and administer a legitimate Sacrament.

6. And finally: The breaking is not indeed considered in itself: but such a manner of breaking is a thing which has entirely free observance, and which must be referred solely to the class of indifferent things, which theologians call Adiaphora. Therefore, under the law of obligation and necessity, it can neither be nor ought to be forced upon anyone to observe. The reason for the consequence is by far most firm and evident 1. from this: because under this pretext the depravation of the most holy deposit of Lutheran doctrine is sought: 2. because bonds and snares are cast upon the consciences of men. 3. Because Christian Liberty, into which we have been asserted by CHRIST, is dangerously undermined, nay, clearly taken away: 4. Because a part of divine worship is established in a free and external thing. 5. Because finally, a new tyranny is exercised in the Church by this pact. Just as therefore it was done piously and rightly by the Orthodox Churches, that at the time of the Interimistic confusion [συῤῥάξεως], when under the pretext of adiaphorous things the idolomania of the whole Papacy was being hidden, it was manfully resisted: so regarding the state of the present Calvinist innovation also, the same faith, the same liberty, the same constancy must be intrepidly preserved.

Nor is there any reason for them to object to us even Blessed Luther, whom they pretend once thought that the bread of the Eucharist must necessarily be broken: or to impute to us a desire for contention, by which alone (as they keep writing) we are moved to refer the breaking of bread among the adiaphora. For both of these objections are nothing other than a rancid quibble. Blessed Luther certainly wrote that the breaking of bread is necessary: which we ourselves also admit: but he did not write that this or that form, this or that manner of breaking bread is necessary, as the Calvinists wish. For Luther never used such a Calvinistic breaking of bread. Thus Luther does not contradict himself when he writes elsewhere that the Eucharist was not instituted by CHRIST to be received in a private mass by some one sacrifice: but to be broken among many, that is, as he explains himself, to be distributed. To which end Luther generally joins these two words, To break and To distribute, in an exegetical sense, so that it may be more correctly understood what he understands by the word of breaking. Now, to oppose to the Evangelicals or Lutherans those things which fight against the Papists, and to twist into a simple sense against the same person those things which were said by Luther in a transferred sense, is a most certain indication of bad faith. The latter quibble strikes not so much us as the leaders of the Calvinists themselves, who themselves also refer the rite of breaking, in terms of manner and form, among the adiaphora: as was shown above.

Latin:

neat salvum: ac multò magis ibi Cœna est, ubi præcipua, & verè substantia conservantur, etiamsi in aliquibus ritibus ab ipso Christo usurpatis erretur. Quod ipsum Beza quoq; agnovit, statuens fractionem panis ad substantiam ipsam, vel confessionẽ Sacramenti non pertinere: Sentio, inquiens, ejus præteritionem, quoniam non ad ipsam Sacramenti confessionem: sed tantùm ad veri, & prorsus legitimi ejus usus formam pertinet, actum ipsum non vitiare: sicuti nævus in facie formosâ venustatem quidem lædit, sed formam tamen ipsam non abolet. Proindè extremæ temeritatis culpâ non caret, quòd quidam ex Gente Calvinianâ Novatores, hâc in parte secessionem à præceptore suo Bezâ facientes, contendunt, Fractionem panis, qualem illi observant, esse Essentialem Cœnæ Dominicæ, imò à Christo simpliciter præceptam his verbis: HOC FACITE. Quæ temeritas, ut in lucem magis protrahatur, quod alterum erit præsentis disputationis membrum, accuratiùs dispiciendum fuerit, quid proprie hoc loco in controversiam veniat, quid non?

II.

Initiò autem non illud principaliter controvertitur, an Christus instituens hoc Sacramentum, panem priùs fregerit, quàm discipulis suis dederit? Affirmativam enim ipsi tenemus, non tam moti ipsorum verborum institutionis claritate, quàm ipsius epuli Paschalis conditione sive ritu, quo panes azymi grandiores apparabantur, ea & amplitudine & crassitie, ut vel unus, vel pauci saltem toti familiæ sufficerent. Ex quo tamen ritu, fas non esse, ut aliquis calumnietur, quasi ab institutione CHRISTI, nostrâ observatione discesserimus, paulò pòst accuratiùs ostendetur.

Deindè neq; de eo propriè est quæstio: An in primitivâ Ecclesiâ similis fermè panis Eucharističi modus sit observatus? Jam enim antè ostendimus, negari id non posse, ita ut hodieq; Græcorum Ecclesiis unus aliquis panis, eâ magnitudine pistus altari imponatur, qui omnibus sufficere possit.

Tertiò neq; illud à nobis pugnatur: Annon propter certas & evidentes causas possit Ecclesia, si velit, veterem illum morem postliminio in usum revocare? Quemadmodum enim ex libertate Christianâ factum esse statuimus, ut minutiorum panum sive hostiarum usus, propter ἐυταξίαν καὶ ἐυσχημοσύνην, in Ecclesiam sit introductus: ita ejusdem libertalis esse censemus, abrogato hoc usu, veteris Ecclesiæ Orientalis morem ac consvetudinem restituere; dummodò hoc non fiat in gratiam Novatorum, qui sub hoc prætextu sive fuco, ipsius purioris doctrinæ Lutheranæ sacrosanctum depositum, depravatum, imò eversum eunt. Quo casu circa usum aut mutationem rerum indifferentium, qualem statuimus esse etiam formam panis, in prædicamento tùm quantitatis, tùm qualitatis consideratam &c. Novatoribus ejusmodi ne quidem latum ungvem cedendum esse, omninò statuimus. Si verò sint in Ecclesiâ vel plurimi, vel etiam optimi, rectè alioqui de Religione sentientes, qui super tali ritu, qui in nostris Ecclesiis observatur, scandalum patiantur, & veterem illum morem reductum velint: hoc sane casu, quid Charitas Christiana a nobis flagitet, minime ignoramus. Quanquam tales infirmi in nostris Ecclesijs in hunc usq; diem non sunt reperti: neq; a Novatoribus monstrati.

Quarto neq; id urgemus, ac si ritus, nostris usitatus Ecclesijs, quo placentæ tenuissimæ & orbiculares fiunt, instar denarioli, ut Durandus loquitur, simpliciter & absolute sit necessarius, ut mutari nullo pacto, nullamq; ob causam vel possit, vel debeat?

Verum illud proprie inter nos & Calvinianos controvertitur, An illius fractionis ritus, que nuper admodum, in Ecclesias reformatas Novatores quidam invexerunt, in administratione Cænæ ita sit necessarius, imo ita a CHRISTO mandatus, ut omitti aut mutari nullo modo d. beat: imo sine eo Sacramentum Cœnæ legitime administrari omnino nequeat. Ubi affirmantem mordicus tenent Calviniani: Nos vero in negantem descendimus.

Cæterum, ut certius constare possit, Num nobis, an illis veritatis palma decerni debeat, primum omnium ritus, quem circa panem Evcharisticum Novatores isti observare solent, sub considerationem venit.

Initio igitur illi Panes pinsi curant non azymos, quali CHRISTUS usus est, sed fermentatos: & plerumq; tantæ magnitudinis, ut unus quatuor communicantibus sufficere possit.

Deinde vero Evcharistiam celebraturi, aliquot ejusmodi panes sive placentas mensæ ligneæ, huic actioni destinatæ, imponi jubent.

Tertio minister Calvinianus accedit ad mensam illam publicam, & in conspectu Ecclesiæ, in quatuor partes Panem talem frangit.

Quarto singulis communicantibus unam particulam in manu porrigit: ut hi postmodum acceptas particulas ori suo ingérant.

De hoc ritu, secundo jam loco, dispiciendum fuerit, An vel ipsius Christi factum exprimat, vel ad Essentiam Sacramenti hujus quicquam faciot, vel deniq; ita sit necessarius, ut propter ejus defectum, ipsa Religionis Evangelicæ puritas periclitetur? Ubi per omnia nos negantem tenemus, eamque hisce rationibus invicte demonstramus.

1. Incertum est, qua forma, quove modo Servator panem fregerit. Ergo temerarium fuerit, hunc vel illum modum CHRISTI fractioni affingere. Antecedens patet 1. inde, quod nemo eorum omnium, qui spectatores primæ Cænæ fuerunt, formam hanc unquam uspiam descripsit. 2. Testis est historia Evangelica, Christumnon vulgari aliquo ac usitato modo panem fregisse: sed plane singulari, ita ut Luc. 24, 35. vel ex sola fractione panis, discipuli Emauntici CHRISTUM agnoverint: haud certe agnituri, si vulgari & consueto hominum more panem fregisset.

2. Incertum, ac nondum probatum est, CHRISTUM panem fractum ita distribuisse inter Apostolos, ut cuilibet particulam in manus dederit, quemadmodum sub necessitatis lege, hunc ritum urgent Novatores Calviniani.

3. Hujusmodi fractionis ritus, aut est simpliciter necessarius, aut non est: Si simpliciter est necessarius, Verbo DEI expresse sit mandatus, oportet: Atqui tale verbum aut mandatum nuspiam in Sacris extat. Ergo non erit simpliciter necessarius, ac per consequens Ecclesiis pacatis & reformatis, per vim ac tyrannidem, & sub necessitatis lege ille obtruditur. Assumti veritas liquido patet, 1. quod in universa historia sacra, nihil quicquam de fermentato, deq; quadripartito pane, circa actionem Sacramenti hujus reperire licet. 2. Christum fregisse quidem panem, legimus, ac proinde idem nobis quoque faciendum esse statuimus: sed cum modus fractionis hujus nuspiam in sacris sit expressus, aut definitus: quis adeo impudens ac temerarius fuerit, qui ullum aliquem modum, tanquam simpliciter necessarium, & a Christo mandatum, comminisci, & Ecclesiae etiam invitae obtrudere ausit?

4. Ipsi antesignani dogmatis Calviniani, non satis sibi constant hac in parte. Theodorus certe Beza, Fractionem Panis refert inter ea, quae licet mutari, nedum tolli, sine justa reprehensione non possint: tamen non tanti sint momenti, ut propterea existimandum sit, Coenam ibi nullam celebrari. Sic Calviniani Marpurgenfes distingventes verba Institutionis, in verba Circumstantiarum & Mandati: expresse verbum (FREGIT) ad classem circumstantiarum referunt, ac diferte de his pronunciant, quod verbis mandati non sint aequiparanda. Haec enim habere vim obligationis & necessitatis (Rechte verbuͤndtliche und zwingliche Wort): illa vero esse πειστατικα tantum, ac proinde diversi generis, neque obligationis, neq; necessitatis vim obtinere. In libello Germanico Casellis impresso: A iiij. B. & C. f. cui titulus: Kurtzer einfaͤltiger Bericht vom H. Abendmahl des HERRN. Quin ibidem subjiciunt, In modo & forma sumti & distributi panis, fracti, vel non fracti, manu vel ore sumti, Ecclesiam CHRISTI sua frui peculiari libertate: neq; referre, sive azymus, sive fermentatus: ater an albus: rotundus an angularis: magnus aut minutus adhibeatur.

5. Si Novatorum sententia obtineat, consequens est, Ecclesias Orthodoxas jam inde a temporibus Epiphanij, per tot seculorum decursus, per tot fidelium aetates, non administrasse verum ac legitimum Eucharistiae Sacramentum. Quod vel cogitatu summe contumeliosum foret: & contumeliosum quidem in ipsum CHRISTUM caput Ecclesiae: ut qui Ecclesiae suae omnimodam quidem Verbi puritatem, at interim non eam gratiam largitus sit, ut legitimum habere & administrare posset Sacramentum.

6. Et postremo: Fractio non quidem ipsa in se considerata: sed fractionis modus talis est res, quae liberam prorsus observationem habet, quaeque ad classem rerum indifferentium, quas Adiaphora vocant Theologi, unice est referenda. Ergò sub obligationis ac necessitatis lege, nemini ad observandum obtrudi vel potest vel debet. Ratio consecutionis longè firmissima patet 1. indè: quia sub hoc prætextu sanctissimi depositi doctrinæ Lutheranæ depravatio quæritur: 2. quia Conscientijs hominum vincula & laquei injiciuntur. 3. Quia Libertas Christiana, in quam per CHRISTUM asserti sumus, periculosè labefactatur, imò planè tollitur: 4. Quia pars cultus divini in re liberâ & externâ constituitur. 5. Quia deniq; nova Tyrannis in Ecclesiâ hoc pacto exercetur. Quemadmodum ergò piè rectéq; factum ab Ecclesijs Orthodoxis, quòd tempore συῤῥάξεως Interimisticæ, cùm sub prætextu rerum adiaphorarum, totius Papatus Idolomania occultaretur, masculè fuit repugnatum: ita circa præsentis etiam Novationis Calvinianæ statum, eadem fides, eadem libertas, eadem constantia intrepidè est conservanda.

Neque est, ut vel B. Lutherum nobis objiciant, quem fingunt aliquando sensisse, Panem Eucharistiæ necessariò esse frangendum: vel φιλονεικίας studium nobis imputent, quo solo (uti scriptitant) nos moti, Fractionem Panis, inter adiaphora referamus. Utrumque enim istud objectum nihil est aliud, quàm rancidum cavillum. Scripsit sanè B. Lutherus, Fractionem Panis esse necessariam: Quod ipsum fatemur & nos: sed non scripsit, quod hæc vel illa forma, hic vel ille modus fractionis panis sit necessarius, uti Calviniani volunt. Nam talem fractionem panis Calvinisticam Lutherus nunquàm usurpavit.
