Sic non sibi adversatur Lutherus, quando alibi scribit, Eucharistiam nō esse à CHRISTO institutam, ut in missâ angulari ab uno aliquo sacrificio accipiatur: sed ut inter multos frangatur, hoc est, ut ipsemet se explicat, distribuatur. Quem in finem Lutherus duo hæc verba, Frangere & Distribuere, sensu ἐξηγητικῷ plerumque conjungit, ut rectiùs constare possit, quid per Frangendi verbum intelligat. Jam ea, quæ contra Pontificios militant, Evangelicis sive Lutheranis opponere, quæque translato sensu à Luthero dicta sunt, in simplicem sensum, contra eundem intorquere, malæ fidei certissimum est indicium. Posterius cavillum non tâm nos, quàm ipsos Calvinianorum antesignanos ferit, quos ipsos quoque ritum fractionis ratione modi & formæ, inter adiaphora referunt: uti suprà ostensum.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Status Controversy about the Breaking of Bread, what it properly is? (continued)

But it remains that we now respond to the principal arguments of the innovators.

THE FIRST is such: Every action of CHRIST is our instruction. But CHRIST in the first Supper broke bread. Therefore.

I answer that both premises are destitute of a true ἐλέγχῳ [proof/refutation], for proving that which is at issue in the question. For the major premise is indeed true, namely by reason of its genus: so that there is nothing done or performed by CHRIST which does not serve to instruct us: but it is false if it be applied to any particular species of the deed.

For thus it would follow that every action of CHRIST must also be expressed by us in the very act: and consequently that we must fast in the desert for forty days and nights: that we must likewise receive baptism only at a more mature age: that we must go out into the desert if we wish to invoke GOD more ardently: and so on. Therefore the adversaries themselves understand that the complex of the medium is not universal, and therefore that there is a weak, or rather no connection of the extremes. The minor premise is indeed true regarding the fact, which is so far from being denied that we ourselves assert simply that this Sacrament cannot be legitimately celebrated without the breaking and distribution of bread: But it is false if it is adapted by the Calvinists to define the mode of breaking itself; Where 1. there is no reason for the consequence: CHRIST broke bread. Therefore he broke it thus or thus. 2. The fallacy of the non-cause. Christ did not break bread for the reason that he might propose an example to us of how some large bread ought to be broken into parts: but for the reason that the bread, which was then at hand, could not be distributed into parts otherwise than through breaking. 3. The fallacy of ignoring the refutation is committed. For the Calvinists argue that CHRIST took whole bread into his hands and broke it into pieces. And yet this very thing is placed in doubt: indeed the opposite seems more probable: namely, that the Paschal meal having already been completed, Christ, about to institute the Supper, distributed from the fragments which had remained from the loaves, broken into certain parts, as much as could suffice for the twelve disciples for this act. Why therefore do our Innovators not also celebrate their Supper from the fragments of bread, the leftovers from other feasts: if they wish to be and to appear such rigid observers of the fact and example of CHRIST.

II. The argument of the Calvinists. CHRIST spoke not only of eating, but also of the breaking of bread: Do this. Therefore the breaking of bread is of divine command, and therefore absolutely necessary.

I answer out of superabundance by concession of the whole argument. For we ourselves willingly maintain that the bread to be broken, that is to be distributed, depends on a divine command.

But if this command of CHRIST is adapted to the mode of Calvinist breaking as if it were simply necessary that in the very act of the Eucharist, with the people watching, a certain whole bread must be broken into parts: then we simply deny the Antecedent. For the word of the command, Do this, does not refer to the act of breaking: but to the eating, which is evident from these reasons. 1. Christ did not simply say: Do this, which I have done: but, Do this in remembrance of me. Now when, and by what act this remembrance of death is made, whether by breaking, or indeed by eating and drinking, we have a clear interpreter in the Apostle, who restricts this remembrance to eating and drinking alone: saying, As often as you eat this bread, and drink of this cup, you shall announce the death of the LORD 1 Cor. 11:26. 2. Whatever uniquely and properly belongs to the Sacrament, that ought not to be referred to its external rite and circumstance. But to do this in remembrance of the death of Christ uniquely and properly belongs to the Sacrament. Therefore it is wrongly referred by the Innovators to the external circumstance or rite of breaking. 3. What will become of the chalice or wine? since the words of institution, Do this, apply to it equally as to the bread. Must therefore the wine also be divided into certain draughts, in the very action, publicly and with the people watching? 4. If that, Do this, ought to be referred to all those things which Christ himself is read to have done then: Why, I ask, do the Innovators not use unleavened bread? why not at night? why not only in Jerusalem? why not in a private house? why not only at the time of the Passover? why not after other foods? why do they celebrate the Lord's Supper not by reclining, but by standing?

III. Argument: The Apostles without doubt did nothing unless they had an express command from CHRIST. But they observed the breaking of bread: Acts 2:42 and 46 and ch. 20:7 and ch. 27:35.

I answer that the major premise is not simply true if they understand it of some express command of CHRIST. For where, I ask, did the Savior give the disciples a command that they should cast lots in the election of some Apostle who would succeed into the place of Judas the traitor? Acts 1:26. or that they should choose Deacons who would preside over alms-giving? Acts 6. or that they should pass a law concerning abstinence from things strangled and blood, Acts 15:20. If they except that the Apostles received the command concerning these matters not through Scripture, but through tradition, the Innovators had better look to themselves, 1. whence do they wish to prove this very thing which they say? 2. lest they incautiously fall into the snares of the Jesuits, who are accustomed to appeal from Scripture to secret commands made through tradition. We approve that of Augustine, tract. 96 in John: When the LORD has been silent, who will say, this or that is the case; or if he dares to say it, whence will he prove it?

The minor premise is true, let the 'still' be attended to: For we read, hear, and believe that the disciples broke bread. But what kind of breaking this was, the Innovators have not yet demonstrated: and it is not so clearly evident from the cited texts. The breaking of bread in the Scriptures sometimes denotes the distribution of alms: as Isa. 58:7. sometimes any taking of food. And indeed, that the breaking of bread in the cited passages is to be understood in this latter sense is evidently demonstrated by the fact that in Acts 2:46 the disciples are read to have broken bread from house to house, which cannot be taken concerning the Lord's Supper. 2. In the same verse this is explained more specifically and clearly in these words: they took food with exultation and simplicity of heart. Therefore this breaking of bread is to be understood concerning ordinary food, not indeed taken simply, but distributed out of pious liberality: just as indeed

Calvin himself interprets the passage of Acts 2, 42 and 46 regarding the distribution of alms. 3. The common consensus of interpreters supports this interpretation, as can be seen in Theophylact, Chrysostom, Jerome, Oecumenius, Bede, and others, on chapters 2 and 20 of Acts. Indeed, they even explain the passage of Acts 27, 35 in such a way that the Apostle broke common and ordinary bread, and ate it in the sight of the Gentiles. Which method of breaking was then very common, because the form of bread common to the Hebrews was not thick or dense, but broad and thinner, such as our festive cakes usually are, which are broken more correctly and conveniently than they are cut. "But even if the cited texts are taken as referring to the Lord's Supper, nothing more can be elicited from them than that the disciples broke bread: but in what manner this was done by them is not perceived from there.

IV. Argument: The breaking of bread was seen as so necessary to the primitive Church that they designated the Sacrament itself by it, calling it the breaking of bread. E.

I respond, not only do we readily grant this, but we also maintain that those who eliminate the breaking of bread from the use of the Holy Supper sin against the Apostle, who said: The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? But this is nothing against us, who also urge the breaking itself, although we do not hold to that manner which the Calvinists observe. But that remarkable disputatious acumen which the adversaries display in this place deserves observation. For they conclude thus: The primitive Church named this Sacrament the breaking of bread. Therefore, bread must be broken in this manner and at that time which the Calvinists desire. By equal and firmer logic, it could be concluded thus: The Eucharist, according to the Evangelists, was instituted after the completion of the paschal supper: whence it also deserved to be called the Lord's Supper. Therefore, this Sacrament ought to be celebrated not in the morning, but in the evening after the completion of the supper. By which one instance the vanity of this argument is plain to the eye.

V. Argument: The breaking of bread represents and foreshadows the Lord's passion: so that the Apostle himself seems to allude to this, stating that the Body of Christ was broken for us: and Christ himself in John 2, 19, saying, Break this temple, etc., which he said concerning his Body. Furthermore, the same breaking foreshadows the Unity of the Ecclesiastical Body, or of the members of CHRIST. Whence the Apostle in 1 Cor. 10, 17: We being many are one bread, one body. Therefore, say the Innovators, we ought to partake of one bread, not of many breads. Now, however, among the Lutherans, as many hosts as are offered, so many breads are also given. Therefore, the unity of bread ceases among them, and consequently, the Unity of the Ecclesiastical Body, or of the members of Christ, also expires.

I respond: 1. That types have absolutely no place in the New Testament, as they were proper to the Old Testament. 2. To invent types without Scripture would be bold and rash. Let the adversaries first show where, and in what words, the foreshadowing of the passion of Christ, in the act of the Lord's Supper, is either expressed or prescribed. A remembrance of the death of CHRIST, which is done by eating his body and drinking his blood, is indeed mentioned in the words of Institution: but of any typical foreshadowing, not even a jot. 3. Scripture itself manifestly explodes the former foreshadowing and analogy, asserting that not even a bone of Christ is to be broken and crushed: so that the analogy between that typical Paschal Lamb of the Old Testament and CHRIST may remain inviolate: Exod. 12, 46; John 19, 33 and 36. If the Innovators object that the bones of CHRIST were not indeed properly broken, but yet analogically, since his hands and feet were pierced with iron nails, his side opened with a spear, and finally his soul was torn from his body, they certainly make their case much worse. For if the breaking of the body of CHRIST was analogical, then certainly the Sacramental bread also ought not to be broken properly and simply, but only analogically, so that the certainty and integrity of this foreshadowing may stand. Now there is no analogy between that which is done properly and that which is done analogically, or only through a certain similarity. 4. The Holy Spirit willed the type of Christ's passion to be foreshadowed in the Non-breaking: but these Innovators devise a type that consists in breaking. In which manner they contradict the Holy Spirit with a hostile front. 5. The type of the New Testament would be more obscure than that of the Old: which is absurd. For the Paschal lamb, and its slaughter, represented the passion of CHRIST far more exactly and clearly than any breaking of Eucharistic bread could represent. 6. The Apostle, naming the passion of Christ a breaking, speaks not properly, but metaphorically: which metaphorical locution has been properly rendered and explained by the remaining Evangelists through the word of being delivered to death. Thus, the Scripture of the Old Testament also wished to express the atrocity of the passion of Christ with similar figurative words, as often as it says that he was bruised: from which surely no one gathers a bruising of bones, unless he dares to contradict the Holy Spirit openly. 7. Christ nowhere in John, or in the remaining Evangelists, Matthew and Mark, said: κλᾶτε, Break: but λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον, Destroy this Temple, John 2, 19. Therefore, this has nothing to do with breaking. The Jerusalemite ass was loosed by the disciples and brought to Christ; was it therefore broken?

Regarding the latter foreshadowing, which the Innovators bring forward from Paul concerning the Unity of the mystical Body, which is represented by the Unity of bread: not even that has anything to do with the matter. For this is not the question: Ought we all to partake of one bread? Which we ourselves affirm, and declare to be constantly done in our churches, as will soon be clear: But this is the specific κρινόμενον (point of judgment): Must that one bread, which foreshadows this mystical unity of the members of the Church, necessarily be broken in public in the manner of the Calvinists? When therefore and how often

Innovators argue from the unity of the bread to the mode of public breaking: so often do they confuse the thing itself with the mode of the thing. 2. If we examine the Apostolic comparison more accurately, it is evident that he regards not the breaking, but rather the kneading and baking of it: so that just as from much flour one bread is made, and from many grapes pressed together one wine is made, so from the pious, participating in one and the same bread and wine, one Body is made in CHRIST. Therefore, the Innovators must henceforth necessarily perform not only the breaking of the bread, but also its kneading and baking in public, provided they wish there to be any firmness in this argument of theirs.

3. Regarding the thing itself: Certainly in our Eucharist, we being many are one bread and one Body. For the bread, which we all eat, is one and the same in respect of mass and substance. But that this Bread is not broken into many parts publicly and in the very act of the Supper, but privately and before the Communion: that does not any more take away the unity of the bread than the Calvinistic breaking constitutes this unity. 4. The Calvinists themselves, in the administration of the Supper, do not always use one bread, but two, three, or more, according to the number of communicants. If, therefore, this spiritual unity consists in the unity of the bread that is broken, then certainly among them this unity will clearly expire; or at least it will not be among more people than among three or four communicants, as many, indeed, as have eaten of that one bread. But if they reply that the unity of the bread is to be defined by the mass and substance from which individual breads are baked, and that although they are many in number, they nevertheless constitute one bread by reason of the mass; let them remember that this very thing also militates for our opinion. 5. Let the Innovators explain whether they believe in the communion of saints and the true unity of the Spirit even among those who, separated by a very long interval of places, cannot participate in one mass of bread? They will answer, I suppose, in the affirmative, unless they wish to deny the communion of saints outright. Let them learn, therefore, henceforth to define more correctly that mystical unity of the members of CHRIST, and not to bind it, quite theologically and irrationally, either to one bread in number or to that public breaking of bread, as they have been accustomed to do until now. Finally, let the Innovators hear Wolfgang Musculus Dusanus himself, discoursing on this Apostolic passage as follows: Nor is it for the unskilled to say, how can a numerous Church, in which several thousands communicate, participate in one bread? The unity of this bread is not to be referred to the unity of one round loaf, but rather to the unity of the institution of the Sacrament and of the communication. Just as the family of one house is rightly said to eat one and the same bread, even if it consumes several loaves at one meal, so at the table of CHRIST all communicants are rightly said to participate in one and the same bread, even if one loaf does not suffice because of the multitude of communicants.

And thus far we have explained the thing done, that is, that which

CHRIST, instituting this Sacrament, is read to have done. There follow the things said, those which CHRIST said concerning this Sacrament.

Latin:

Sed super est, ut ad præcipua Novatorum argumenta jam respondeamus.

PRIMUM tale est: Omnis CHRISTI actio est nostra institutio. Atqui CHRISTUS in primâ Cænâ fregit panem. Ergò.

Respondeo, utramque præmissarum destitui verò ἐλέγχῳ, ad probandum id, quod in quæstione versatur. Major enim κ̄ τὶ vera est, nempè ratione generis: ita ut nihil à CHRISTO gestum actumque sit, quod non nobis erudiendis inserviat: falsa autem est, si ad quamlibet facti speciem accommodetur.

Sic enim sequeretur, Omnem CHRISTI actionem, nobis quoq; actu ipso esse exprimendam: ac per consequens nobis jejunandum in deserto quadraginta diebus ac noctibus : nobis item baptismum percipiendum, non nisi in adultiore ætate: exeundum nobis in desertum, si ardentiùs DEUM invocare velimus: & sic deinceps. Intelligunt ergò ipsi adversarij, complexum medij non esse universale, ac proindè extremorum langvidam, imò nullam esse connexionem. Minor ratione facti vera quidem est, quod tantùm abest, ut negemus, ut nos ipsi quoque Sacramentum hoc sine fractione & distributione panis legitimè celebrari non posse, simpliciter asseramus: Falsa verò est, si à Calvinianis ad modum ipsum fractionis definiendum, accommodetur; Ubi 1. nulla est ratio consequentiæ: CHRISTUS fregit panem. Ergòsic vel sic fregit. 2. Sophisma tō mē aitiō. Neq; n. Christus ideò fregit panem, ut nobis exemplum proponeret, quomodo panis aliquis magnus in partes frangi debeat: sed ideò, quia panis, qui tùm in promtu erat, aliter non, quàm per fractionem in partes distribui poterat. 3. Committitur ágnoia eléngxō. Pugnant enim Calviniani CHRISTUM sumpsisse in manus panem integrum, eumque in frusta comminuisse. Atqui hoc ipsum in dubio est positum: imò diversum videtur probabilius: videlicet, quòd peracto jam epulo Paschali, Christus instituturus Cœnam, ex fragmentis, quæ de panibus remanserant, in certas partes comminutis tantum distribuerit, quantum duodecim discipulis ad hunc actum sufficere poterat. Cur ergò Novatores nostri suam quoque Cœnam non celebrant ex fragmentis panum, ex alijs convivijs residuorum: si usque adeò rigidi observatores facti & exempli CHRISTI esse & videri velint.

II. Ratio Calvinianorum. CHRISTUS non modo de manducatione, sed & de fractione panis dixit: Facite hoc. Ergo fractio panis est mandati divini, ac proindè absolutè necessaria.

Respondeo ek perissoia ex superabundanti per syngchōrēsin concessionem totius argumenti. Panem enim frangendum, hoc est distribuendum esse, ipsi ultrò à mandato divino dependere statuimus.

Verùm si ad modum fractionis Calvinianæ ita accommodetur hoc mandatum CHRISTI, ac si simpliciter sit necessarium, ut in ipso actu Evcharistiæ, adspectante populo, integer quidam panis, in partes frangi debeat: tunc negamus simpliciter Antecedens. Neque enim verbum mandati, Hoc facite, respicit fractionis actum: sed manducationem, id quod his patet rationibus. 1. Christus non simpliciter dixit: Hoc facite, quod ego feci: sed, Hoc facite in mei commemorationem. Jam quando, & quo actu fiat hæc mortis commemoratio, Nùm per fractionem, an verò per manducationem & bibitionem, luculentum habemus interpretem Apostolum, qui ad solam manducationem & bibitionem hanc commemorationem restringit: Quotiescunq;, inquiens, panem hunc ederitis, & de poculo hoc biberitis, mortem DOMINI annunciabitis 1. Cor. 11, 26. 2. Quicquid unicè ac propriè competit Sacramento, id ad externum ejus ritum, & περίστασιν referri non debet. Atqui facere hoc ad commemorationem mortis Christi, unicè & propriè competit Sacramento. Ergò perperàm à Novatoribus ad περίστασιν externam sive circumstantiam, aut ritum fractionis refertur. 3. Quid fiet de calice sive vino? siquidem de eodem æquè ac de pane habent verba institutionis, Hoc facite. Nùm quid ergò & vinum in certos haustus, in ipsâ actione, publicè & aspectante populo, erit dividendum? 4. Si illud, Hoc facite, ad omnia ea referri debet, quæ Christus ipse fecisse tùm legitur: Cur obsecro Novatores non utuntur pane azymo? cur non noctu? cur non Hierosolymis tantùm? cur non in privatâ domo? cur non Paschali tantùm tempore? cur non post cibos alios? cur non recumbendo, sed stando Cœnam Dominicam celebrant?

III. Ratio: Apostoli sine dubio nihil fecerunt, nisi cujus expressum mandatum à CHRISTO habuerunt. Atqui fractionem panis observarunt: Act. 2, 42. & 46. & cap 20. 7. & cap. 27, 35.

Respondeo, Majorem non simpliciter veram esse, si de expresso aliquo CHRISTI mandato eam intelligant. Ubi enim obsecrò discipulis mandatum dedit Servator, ut sortem mitterent in electione Apostoli alicujus, qui succederet in locum Judæ proditoris? Actor. 1, 26. vel ut Diaconos eligerent, qui rei eleemosynariæ præessent? Actor. 5. vel ut legem ferrent de abstinentia à suffocato & sanguine, Act. 15, 20. Sin excipiant, non per Scripturam, sed per traditionẽ, mandatum de rebus istis accepisse Apostolos, probè viderint Novatores, 1. undè hoc ipsum, quod dicunt, probare velint? 2. ne incauti incidant in casses Jesuitanarum, qui à Scripturâ, ad occulta mandata, per traditionem facta, provocare solent. Nobis probatur illud Augustini tract. 96. in Joh. Cùm DOMINUS tacuerit, quis dicet, illud vel illud esse; aut si dicere audeat, undè probabit?

Minor vera est, τὸ ἔτι attendatur: Panem enim discipulos fregisse legimus, audimus, credimus. Verùm qualis hæc fuerit fractio, nondum Novatores demonstrarunt: & neque ex allegatis textibus usque adeò perspicuè liquet. Fractio panis in Scripturis interdum notat eleemosynæ distributionem: ut Jes. 58, 7. interdum quamlibet sumtionem cibi. Et sanè locis allegatis in posteriore hoc sensu, fractionem panis intelligendum esse, illud evidenter demonstrat, quod Actor. 2, 46. discipuli leguntur fregisse panem κατ̓ οἶκον quasi ostiatim, id quod de Cœnâ Domini accipi non potest. 2. Eodem versu specialiùs ac dilucidiùs hoc explicatur, his verbis: μετελάμβανον τροφῆς ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει καὶ ἀφελότητι καρδίας, capiebant cibum cum exultatione, & simplicitate cordis. De cibo ergò vulgari, non simpliciter quidem sumto, sed ex piâ liberalitate distributo, fractio hæc panis intelligenda est: quemadmodum sanè

Calvinus ipse de Eleemosynarum distributione, locum Actor. 2, 42. & 46. interpretatur. 3. Communis interpretum consensus interpretationi huic suffragatur, uti videre est apud Theophilactum, Chrysostomum, Hieronymum, Oecumenium, Bedam & alios, super caput 2. & 20. Actorum. Quin locum etiam Actor. 27, 35. ita explicant, quòd Apostolus usitatum & vulgarem panem fregerit, inq; conspectu gentilium manducaverit. Quæ frangi ratio tùm erat usitatissima, propterea quod Hebræis forma panis usitata erat non crassa aut densa: sed lata & tenuior, quales esse solent placenta nostræ festales, quæ rectiùs ac commodiùs franguntur, quàm scinduntur. " Cæterùm si maximè de Cœnâ Domini textus " allegati accipiantur, plus tamen indè erui non " potest, quam discipulos fregisse panem: quo ve- " rò modo hoc ab ipsis factum sit, indè non perspicitur.

IV. Ratio: Fractio panis primitiva Ecclesia usq; adeò fuit visa necessaria, ut Sacramentū ipsū ab eâ indigitaverint, nominantes eam fractionē panis.E.

Respondeo, Non hoc tantùm nos ultrò largiri, sed & statuere eos, qui fractionem panis ex usu Sacræ Cœnæ eliminant, peccare contra Apostolum, qui dixit: Panis, quem frangimus, nonne est communicatio corporis Christi? Verùm nihil hoc contra nos, qui & fractionem ipsi urgemus: licèt non eum modum teneamus, quem observant Calviniant. Sed observationem meretur egregium illud acumen disputatorium, quod hoc loco produnt Adversarij. Sic autem illi colligunt: Primitiva Ecclesia Sacramentum hoc nominavit Fractionem panis. Ergò panis hoc modo & eo tempore est frangendus, quo volunt Calviniani. Pari & firmiori logicâ sic colligi posset: Eucharistia referentibus Evangelistis instituta fuit, post peractam cœnam paschalem: Undè etiam Cœna Domini dici meruit. Ergò Sacramentū hoc non manè, sed vesperè post peractam cœnam celebrari debet. Quâ unâ instantiâ argumenti hujus vanitas ad oculum patet.

V. Ratio: Fractio panis repræsentat & adumbrat passionem Dominicam: ut Apostolus ipse huc alludere videatur, afferens, Corpus Christi pro nobis fractum esse: & Christus ipse Joh. 2, 19. Frangite, inquiens, templum hoc &c. quod de Corpore suo dicebat. Porro eadem fractio adumbrat Unitatem Corporis Ecclesiastici, sive membrorum CHRISTI. Unde Apostolus 1. Cor. 10. 17. Unus panis, unum corpus multi sumus. Ergò, inquiunt Novatores, de Uno pane, non de multis panibus participare debemus. Jam verò apud Lutheranos, quot proferuntur hostiæ, tot etiam dantur panes. Ergò unitas panis apud illos cessat, & per consequens, expirat etiam Unitas Corporis Ecclesiastici, sive membrorum Christi.

Respondeo: 1. Typos in Novo Testamento nullos prorsus obtinere locum, ut qui Veteris Testamenti fuerunt proprij. 2. Typos sine Scripturâ fingere, audaculum & temerarium fuerit. Monstrent priùs adversarij, ubinám, & quibus verbis adumbratio passionis Christi, in actu Cœnæ Dominicæ, sit vel expreffa, vel præscripta. Recordationis quidem mortis CHRISTI, quæ fit manducando corpus & bibendo sangvinem ipsius, fit mentio in verbis Institutionis: sed de adumbratione aliquâ typicâ, ne γρῦ quidem. 3. Adumbrationem & analogiam priorem Scriptura ipsa manifestè explodit, asserens, Christo ne os quidem ullum frangendum & comminuendum esse: ut sic analogia inter Agnum illum Paschalem typicum Veteris Testamenti,& inter CHRISTUM inviolata subsistat: Exod.12,46. Joh.19,33. & 36. Si objiciant Novatores, Non quidem propriè fracta esse Ossa CHRISTO,sed tamen analogicè, dùm nimirùm manus & pedes ipsius clavis ferreis perforati: latus lancea apertum: anima tandem à corpore avulsa fuit: certè causam suam multò deteriorem reddunt. Nam si analogica fuit fractio corporis CHRISTI, utiq; panis quoq; Sacramentalis non propriè & simplicitèr, sed analogicè tantùm frangi debet, ut sic adumbrationi huic sua constet certitudo & integritas. Jam nulla est analogia inter id,quod fit propriè, & quod sit analogicè, sive per quandam tantùm similitudinem. 4. Spiritus Sanctus passionis Christi typum adumbrari voluit, in Non-fragendo: Atqui Novatores isti typum excogitant, qui consistat in frangendo. Quo pacto Spiritui Sancto adversâ fronte obloquuntur. 5. Obscurior esset typus Novi, quàm Veteris Testamenti: id quod absurdum. Longè enim exactiùs & dilucidiùs repræsentavit passionem CHRISTI,agnus Paschalis, ejusdemq; mactatio: quàm ulla panis Evcharistici fractio repræsentare possit. 6. D. Apostolus nominans passionem Christi fractionem, non propriè,sed metaphoricè loquitur: quæ metaphorica locutio, à reliquis Evangelistis per verbum Tradendi in mortem, propriè est redditum & explicatum. Sic Scriptura Veteris etiam Testamenti,consimilibus verbis figuratis, atrocitatem passionis Christi exprimere voluit, quoties dicit, ipsum attritum esse: Ubi sanè ossium attritionem nemo indè colligit, nisi qui Spiritui Sancto apertè contradicere ausit. 7. Christus nuspiam apud Johannem, vel apud reliquos Evangelistas, Matthæum & Marcum dixit: κλᾶτε, Frangite: sed λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον, Solvite Templum hoc Joh.2,19. Nihil ergò hoc ad fractionem. Asinus Hierosolymitanus à discipulis fuit solutus, & Christo adductus; Ergoné fuit fractus?

Quoad posteriorem adumbrationem, quam ex Paulo de Unitate Corporis mystici, quæ Unitate panis repræsentetur, proferunt Novatores: ne illa quidem quicquam ad rem facit. Nam non hoc quæstionis est, An de uno pane participare debeamus omnes? Quod ipsum & nos affirmamus, & nostris in Ecclesijs constanter fieri,pronunciamus: uti mox patebit: Sed hoc proprium est κρινόμενον: An panis ille unus, qui unitatem hanc mysticam membrorum Ecclesiæ adumbrat, necessariò more Calvinianorum in publico frangi debeat? Quando ergò & quoties

Novatores ab Unitate panis ad modum fractionis publicæ argumentantur: toties rem ipsam cum modo rei confundunt. 2. Si Apostolicam comparationem accuratiùs evolvamus, constat eum non ad fractionem, sed ad subactionem potiùs, & pistionem ejus respicere: ita ut sicut ex farinâ multâ unus fit panis: ex acinis uvarum expressarum multis unum fit vinum: ita ex „ pijs, uno eodemq́; pane & vino participantib9, „ unum in CHRISTO fiat Corpus. Ergò non ad „ fractionem tantùm panis, sed & subactionem „ ac pistionem ejus necessariò in publico deinceps peragere debent Novatores: dummodò quicquam firmitudinis argumento huic suo inesse velint.

3. Quoad rem ipsam: Certè in nostrâ Eucharistia, Unus panis, & Unum Corpus sumus multi. Nam panis, quo vescimur omnes, ratione massæ & substantiæ unus idemque est. Quòd verò Panis iste non publicè, & in ipso actu Cœnæ, sed privatim, & antè Communionem, in partes plures scinditur: id haud magis Unitatem panis tollit, at́que fractio Calvinistica Unitatem hanc constituit. 4. Ipsi Calviniani in administratione Cœnæ pro numero Communicantium, non unum semper, sed duos, tres, pluresve panes usurpant. Quod si ergò unitas hæc Spiritualis consistit in unitate Panis, qui frangitur: certè apud ipsos Unitas hæc planè expirabit: vel certè inter plures ea non erit, quàm inter tres, vel quatuor communicantes, quotquot nimirùm de Uno illo comederunt. Sin respondeant, Unitatem panis ratione massæ & substantiæ definiendam esse, ex quâ singuli Panis sint pisti: & licet numero plures sint, ratione massæ tamen unum Panem constituant; meminerint hoc ipsum pro nostrâ etiam militare sententiâ. 5. Edisserant Novatores, anné credant Communionem sanctorum, & veram Unitatem Spiritus, inter eos etiam, qui longissimo locorum intervallo dissiti, de unâ panis massâ participare non possunt? Respondebunt opinor affirmatè: nisi Communionem Sanctorum perfrictè negare velint. Discant ergò deinceps rectiùs definire Unitatem illam mysticam membrorum CHRISTI, neq́; illam vel ad Unum numero panem: vel ad publicam illam fractionem panis, ἀθεολόγως planè, καὶ ἀλογως alligare: uti hactenùs consueverunt. Tandem audiant Novatores ipsum Wolffgangum Musculum Dusanum, de loco hoc Apostolico sic disserentem: Nec est, ut dicat imperitus, quomodo numerosa Ecclesia, in quâ aliquot millia communicant, de uno pane participare poterit? Unitas panis hujus, non est ad unitatem Unius orbiculati panis: sed magis ad Unitatem institutionis Sacramenti, & communicationis referenda. Quemadmodum unius domus familia, rectè unum & eundem panem manducare dicitur: etiamsi plures orbes uno prandio absumat: sic in mensâ CHRISTI rectè omnes communicantes de uno & eodem pane participare dicuntur: licet propter communicantium multitudinem unus orbis non sufficiat.

Et hactenùs τὸ πραχθὲν, hoc est, id quod

CHRISTUS instituens Sacramentum hoc, fecisse legitur, expedivimus. Sequuntur τὰ λεχθέντα, ea quæ CHRISTUS de Sacramento hoc dixit.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: II. On the sense of the words of Christ

II. On the sense of the words of CHRIST.

The Evangelists and the Apostle report that CHRIST said concerning the bread offered to the disciples: Take, eat, This is my Body, which is given for you: And concerning the blessed Cup: Take, drink: This is that blood of mine of the New Testament: which is shed for many for the remission of sins. Concerning the sense of those words, there has been a dispute for many years now: whether they are to be taken according to the letter, as they sound, or according to some figurative exposition. Having repudiated this latter opinion, we embrace the former, establishing that in the words of institution that sense is to be accepted and retained which is simple and native to the letters themselves, or to the literal sense, that is, to the proper sense of the words. Where, however, no one should consider us so dull as if, fighting for the ῥητῷ [literal word], we were to strip the words of the institution of all ἄλνοια [other-mindedness] or sense: but this at least we deny, and we contend: that such an ἄλνοια is not to be attributed to these words, which departs from the proper, simple, and native signification of the individual words, and attributes to them an alien sense, which conflicts with the letter: and which removes the Body and Blood of CHRIST by as great an interval from the external Symbols of bread and wine as the highest Heaven is distant from the lowest earth. Meanwhile, we admit and approve such an ἄλνοια which, κατὰ γράμμα [according to the letter] or τὸ ῥητὸν [the literal word], firmly establishes that, in the beginning, the demonstrative pronoun THIS refers to the preceding command of CHRIST, Take, Eat, Drink: so that it comprehends the Bread and Wine, as media προσφερόμένα [offered things], and as containing the principal good, under its sense. Then we take the word (IS) ὑπαρκτικῶς [existentially] or substantively, for that which truly is and exists. Thirdly, we understand the noun (BODY) as the true and natural, indeed the very Body of CHRIST, which was delivered to death for us. Similarly, the noun (BLOOD) as the true and natural, indeed that very Blood of CHRIST, which was shed for us on the altar of the cross. Finally, we establish that the pronoun MY denotes the person of CHRIST himself, who is speaking and promising.

The principal foundations of this opinion of ours are:

THE FIRST is such: If no new dogma, and no new article of faith can be founded in those places whose words are ambiguous and improper: it follows irrefragably, certainly, that those words also, by which the proper seat of new dogmas is contained, must be accepted only in a proper and simple, or, as they say, literal sense.

And yet the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, when it was instituted, was clearly a new dogma, and a new head or article of the Christian Religion:

whose proper seat is contained nowhere else than in the words of the Institution: as demonstrated in question 1. Therefore, the words of this Institution must be accepted in no other than their proper, simple, and native sense.

The antecedent of the major proposition must be partly proven: but the reason for the connection, or the evidence of the consequence, must be demonstrated.

The proof of the antecedent can be expedited through a sufficient induction. For although certain dogmas and articles of faith, handed down elsewhere in a simple context of words and known to the Church, are sometimes explained and illustrated in the most elegant metaphors or translations and figures in the sermons of the Prophets and of CHRIST: yet where any doctrine is first revealed, or some rite and dogma is introduced anew, the reason of the divine Word does not allow that it be done by ambiguous and improper phrases and terms of words. This reason is most evident: Because the foundation of the whole Christian religion, and the only Canon and immovable rule and norm of all truth and certainty in Theological doctrine, is the WORD OF GOD, by which GOD willed His will to be revealed to the human race. Now, unless GOD had done this in founding new dogmas and establishing articles of faith with clear and proper speech, which could be easily understood by all: He certainly would not have proposed the revelations or manifestations of His will, but would have cast illusions and deceits, apples of discord, and the riddles of the Sphinx upon miserable men. But to think even that of GOD would be impious and blasphemous. Yet such an induction itself can be given. When a command was proposed by GOD to our first parents concerning not eating the fruit of the forbidden tree: when to Noah concerning building the ark: when to Abraham concerning circumcising every male: concerning sacrificing his son: when to Moses concerning the Sacrament of the Paschal Lamb, concerning the various and almost innumerable rites of sacrifices to be established: when to the Apostles concerning propagating the Gospel through the whole world, concerning baptizing all nations: GOD always used such a form of speech as consisted in the proper, simple, literal, and native sense of the individual words. Thus in the Old Testament, the history or article of creation: the article concerning the fall of our first parents, the article concerning the extreme corruption of human nature: the article concerning the law: but in the Evangelical history, the articles of the Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension of CHRIST into heaven: likewise the article of the Redemption of the human race, of Justification, of the Gospel, of Good Works, of Repentance, and if there are many other such articles, they are proposed and described in such words as cannot be accepted and understood otherwise than as they sound, in their native and proper sense. Nor can a contrary example of any article of faith be given from the whole Scripture. Therefore, this induction maintains its immovable certainty and truth.

The connection of the major proposition, or the reason for the consequence, is most evidently apparent from the fact that words are the symbols of the things themselves, and indices for forming a correct sense. If, therefore, GOD willed the words of dogmas and articles, in their proper seats, by a certain and salutary counsel, to be promulgated in no other way than properly, simply, and plainly

GOD: it would certainly be rash, nay, impious, if anyone should dare to attach another, improper, figurative, and ambiguous sense to them.

The minor is invincibly asserted and corroborated by the preceding first question. Therefore, the conclusion also maintains its firm and settled truth.

SECOND Argument. Whatever part of heavenly doctrine does not have a different interpretation in Scripture itself: the words of its description cannot, and ought not, be accepted in any other than a simple and proper or literal sense of the words.

But the words of the Institution, by which the Sacrament of the Supper is described, nowhere in Scripture have a different interpretation from that sense which the simple words produce. Therefore, here too the sense must be uniquely retained.

For the explanation of the Major premise, it is to be noted. 1. That there is indeed a different mode of speech and writing in Scripture. For some things are explained in a literal manner of speech, which are to be accepted no otherwise than the words sound. Others are interwoven with the wrappings of figures, which manner of speech requires a peculiar interpretation of tropes or figures. 2. It is to be noted regarding the articles of faith and principal dogmas, that Scripture never uses only the latter, namely the figurative manner of speech: but then at last uses it, when in other places those things have first been set forth properly and clearly. Which St. Augustine also observed in lib. 2 de Doctr. Christ. cap. 6. From those obscurities nothing is to be elicited which is not found stated most plainly elsewhere. 3. Whatever Scripture has proposed figuratively in any place, it does not permit its judgment and interpretation to others: but claims it for itself. These things being premised, the evident certainty of the Major proposition is confirmed by that which the Apostle Peter, 2 cap. 1, 20, expressly denies, that Scripture is of private, that is, human interpretation. Therefore, in this kind of matter, Scripture is always its own interpreter, so that those things which have been said by it tropically and figuratively are most clearly explained and expounded by itself in other places.

Regarding the Minor proposition, the Words of Institution exist repeated in four different places of Scripture, described by different Evangelists and one Apostle, in different places, and also at a different time, and what is most worthy of observation, consigned by the Apostle, when he had received them not from tradition or the report of the remaining Apostles: but from the living παραδώσει (tradition) of CHRIST Himself, now sitting at the right hand of GOD the Father, and he had inserted the same into his Epistle not for the sake of weaving a history, as the Evangelists: but for the sake of correcting errors that had arisen in the Corinthian Church. And yet from none of those places can it be taught or proven that, in those things which pertain to the substance of this Sacrament, one must depart from the simple, proper, and native signification of the Words: but rather that sense which the literal meaning of the words produces is, in those different repetitions, more and more declared and confirmed.

Matthew was present at the first Institution of this Sacrament, who saw and heard all that was said and done in his presence. This witness, both ear and eye, recounted the words of CHRIST with such fidelity that he leaves no one any just cause for doubting. Moreover, he wrote his Gospel in the Hebrew language, in Judea, as Jerome testifies, and carried it, written out by his own hand, into India, which Pantaenus is finally written to have brought back to Alexandria. Regarding the reason for the writing, Nicephorus relates in book 2, chapter 45, that he departed from Judea to India and compensated for his absence with the present writing: a fact which Theophylactus notes was done in the eighth year, and Nicephorus in the fifteenth year, after the Resurrection of CHRIST.

Mark was not an eyewitness, but only an earwitness: yet he was so worthy of belief that he wrote at a time when he deserved to be approved not only by the primitive Church of CHRIST, but also by the Apostles themselves still remaining in the flesh, as Augustine speaks: nay, as Jerome testifies, the commentary of this Gospel was heard and approved by Peter himself, and by his authority was commended to the Church to be read: which Eusebius and Nicephorus note was compiled in the West at the request of those who were seized with a singular desire for the doctrine of Peter. Paul is thought to have written his epistle in the twentieth year after the Ascension of CHRIST, and to have sent it from Ephesus to Corinth by Timothy, during the most serious dissipation of the Church which had arisen from the profanation of this Sacrament. The Apostle, however, recalls his hearers not only to the primitive origin of the Institution, but also to that singular and stupendous revelation of the same Institution made to him by CHRIST, who was already dwelling in glory and sitting at the right hand of the Father.

Latin:

II. De Sensu Verborum CHRISTI.

REferunt Evangelistæ & Apostolus, CHRISTUM de pane discipulis porrecto dixisse: Accipite, manducate, Hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur: Et de Calice benedicto: Accipite, bibite: Hoc est sangvis ille meus Novi Testamenti: qui pro multis effunditur in Remissionem peccatorum. De Verborum istorum sensu, annis jam plurimis disceptatum fuit: num κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν secundum literam, prout sonant: an verò κατὰ τὴν ἄλνοιαν, secundum figuratam aliquam expositionem sint accipienda. Posteriore hâc sententiâ repudiata, prius illud amplectimur, statuentes, In verbis institutionis eum sensum acceptandum & retinendum esse, qui est ipsis γράμμασι, sive ῥητῷ, hoc est verborum proprio, simplex, & nativus. Ubi tamen nemo nos ita bardos existimaverit, quasi pro ῥητῷ pugnantes, omni prorsus ἄλνοια sive sensu verba institutionis spoliemus: sed id saltem negamus, & pugnamus: Verbis hisce non talem ἄλνοιαν affingendam esse, quæ à propriâ, simplici, & nativâ singulorum verborum significatione recedat, ijsdemq́; alienum sensum affingat, quæ pugnet cum literâ: quæq́; Corpus & Sangvinem CHRISTI tanto intervallo ab externis Symbolis Panis & vini removeat, quanto summum Cœlum distat ab imâ terrâ. Interim ἄλνοιαν talein admittimus, & approbamus, quæ κατὰ γράμμα sive τὸ ῥητὸν, firmiter statuit, Initiò pronomen δεικτικὸν HOC, respicere præcedens mandatum CHRISTI, Accipite, Edite, Bibite: ita ut Panem & Vinum, tanquàm media προσφερόμένα, & complectentia principale bonum, sub suo sensu comprehendat. Deindè verbum (EST) accipimus ὑπαρκτικῶς sive substantivè, pro eo, quod reverâ est & existit. Tertiò, nomen (CORPUS) intelligimus de vero ac naturali, imò ipso Corpore CHRISTI, quod pro nobis est in mortem traditum. Consimiliter nomen (SANGVIS) de vero ac naturali, imò illo ipso Sangvine CHRISTI, qui pro nobis in arâ crucis effusus est. Tandem pronomen MEUM statuimus notare personam ipsius loquentis ac promittentis CHRISTI.

Sententiæ hujus nostræ fundamenta præcipua sunt:

PRIMUM tale est: Si nullum dogma novum, nullusq́; novus fidei articulus fundari potest ijs in locis, quorum verba sunt ambigua, & impropria: irrefragabiliter utiq́; sequitur, ea quoq́; verba, quibus propria novorum dogmatum sedes continetur, non nisi proprio ac simplice, sive, ut loquuntur, literali sensu accipienda esse.

Atqui Sacramentum Cœnæ Dominicæ, cùm instrueretur, novum planè fuit dogma, & novum caput sive articulus Religionis Christianæ:

cujus sedes propria nuspiam alibi, quàm in verbis Institutionis continetur: uti quæst. 1. demonstratum. Ergò Verba Institutionis hujus, non nisi proprio, simplice, ac nativo sensu sunt accipienda.

Propositionis majoris Antecedens partim est probandum: partim verò connexi ratio, sive consequentiæ evidentia demonstranda.:

Probatio Antecedentis per ἐπαγωγὴν sufficientem expediri potest. Etsi enim dogmata quædam & articuli fidei, simplici verborum contextu alibi traditi, & Ecclesiæ noti interdum in concionibus Prophetarum & CHRISTI elegantissimis Metaphoris, sive translationibus & figuris suavissimis explicantur, & illustrantur: tamen ubi doctrina aliqua primùm revelatur, aut ritus aliquis atque dogma de novo demùm introducitur, Verbi divini ratio non fert, ut id ambiguis atq; improprijs verborum phrasibus atq; terminis fiat. Ratio evidentissima est hæc: Quia totius Religionis Christianæ fundamentum, & veritatis atq; certitudinis omnis in doctrinâ Theologicâ, unicus Canon atq; immota regula & norma est VERBUM DEI, quo voluntatem suam hominum generi DEUS revelatam voluit. Jam nisi hoc in fundandis novis dogmatibus, & condendis articulis fidei, perspicuâ & propriâ oratione fecisset DEUS, quæ ab omnibus facilè posset intelligi: non certè revelationes aut patefactiones suæ voluntatis proposuisset: sed offucias & præstigias, poma ἔριδος & Sphingis ænigmata miseris hominibus offudisset. Atqui de DEO istud vel cogitare, impium ac blasphemum fuerit. Ipsa verò ἐπαγωγὴ sive inductio talis dari potest. Quando DEUS primis parentibus de non vescendo prohibitæ arboris fructu: quando Noaho de fabricandâ arcâ: quando Abrahæ de circumcidendo omni masculo: de mactando filio: quando Moysi de Sacramento Agni Paschalis, de varijs & penè innumeris constituendis Sacrificiorum ritibus: quando Apostolis de propagando Evangelio per universum terrarum orbē, de baptizandis omnibus gentibus, mandatum fuit propositum: DEUS semper tali orationis formâ usus est, quæ proprio simplici, literali, ac nativo singulorum verborum sensu constaret. Sic in Veteri Testamento historia sive articulus creationis: articulus de lapsu primorum parentum, articulus de extremâ corruptione naturæ humanæ: articulus de lege: In historiâ verò Evangelicâ, Passionis, Mortis, Resurrectionis & Ascensionis CHRISTI in cœlum articuli: Articulus item Redemtionis generis humani, Justificationis, Evangelij, Bonorum Operum, Pœnitentiæ, & si qui sunt complures articuli alij, ejusmodi verbis sunt propositi & descripti, quæ non possunt aliter, quàm sicut sonant, nativo & proprio sensu accipi & intelligi. Neǵ contrarium exemplū ullius articuli fidei, ex universâ Scripturâ dari potest. Ergò Inductioni huic sua immota constat certitudo & veritas.

Connexum Majoris propositionis, sive Consequentiæ ratio vel indè evidentissimè patet, quòd Verba sunt Symbola ipsarum rerum, & recti sensus informandi indices. Si ergò dogmatum & articulorum verba, in proprijs suis sedibus, certo & salutari consilio, non nisi propriè, simpliciter, & planè promulgata voluit

DEUS: certè temerarium, imò impium fuerit, si quis alium, improprium, figuratum atq; ambiguum sensum ijsdem affingere ausit.

Minor invictè asserta & corroborata est, quæstione præcedente primâ. Constat ergò Conclusioni sua quoq; firma & rata veritas.

SECUNDUM Argumentum. Quæcunq; pars doctrinæ cælestis, diversam interpretationẽ in ipsâ Scripturâ non habet: ejus descriptionis verba, non possunt, neq; debent alio, quàm simplice verborum, proprioq; sive literali sensu accipi.

Atqui verba Institutionis, quibus Sacramentum Cænæ est descriptum, nuspiam in Scripturâ diversam interpretationem habent ab eo sensu, quem verba simplicia gignunt. Ergò hîc etiam sensus unicè est retinendus.

Pro Majoris explicatione notandum est. 1. Diversum sanè esse in Scripturâ dictionis scriptionisq; modum. Quædam enim proprio sermonis genere explicantur, quæ non aliter, quàm verba sonant, accipienda sunt. Alia figurarum involucris intexuntur, cujus sermonis tropi sive figuræ peculiarem interpretationem requirunt. 2. Notandum quoad articulos fidei, & dogmata principalia, nunquàm scripturam uti solo posteriore, nempè figurato sermonis genere: sed tùm demùm eo uti, quando alijs in locis priùs propriè illa, & perspicuè sunt exposita. Quod observavit etiam D. Augustinus lib. 2. de Doctr. Christ. cap. 6. De obscuritibus illis nihil eruendum est, quod non planissimè alibi dictũ reperiatur. 3. Quicquid figuratè Scriptura alicubi proposuit, ejus judicium & interpretationem, non alijs permittit: sed sibi ipsi vendicat. His prænotatis, Majoris propositionis evidentem certitudinem confirmat id, quod Apostol9 Petrus 2. cap. 1, 20. ἐξαρρήδην negat, Scripturam esse ἰδίας, hoc est, ἀνθρωπίνης ἐπιλύσεως propriæ, sive humanæ interpretationis. Scriptura ergò in hoc genere materiæ, semper sui ipsius est interpres, ita ut quæ tropicè & figuratè ab eadem dicta sunt, ab ipsamet alijs in locis clarissimè explicentur, explanenturque.

Quoad Minorem propositionem, Verba Institutionis in quatuor diversis Scripturæ locis repetita extant, à diversis Evangelistis, & uno Apostolo, diversis in locis, diverso etiam tempore descripta, quodque observatu est dignissimum, ab Apostolo tum consignata, cùm non ex traditione, aut relatu reliquorum Apostolorum: sed ex ipsius CHRISTI, jam ad dextram DEI Patris confidentis, vivâ παραδώσει ea accepisset, & non historiæ texendæ causa, uti Evangelistæ: sed errores in Corinthiacâ Ecclesiâ obortos corrigendi gratia, Epistolæ suæ eadem inseruisset. Atqui ex nullo istorum locorum doceri aut evinci potest, in his, quæ ad substantiam hujus Sacramenti pertinent, à simplici, propriâ, & nativâ Verborum significatione discedendum esse: sed potiùs sensus ille, quem τὸ ῥητὸν verborum gignit, in diversis illis repetitionibus, magis magisq; declaratur, & confirmatur.

Interfuit Matthæus primæ Institutioni hujus Sacramenti, qui dicta, actaque omnia coram vidit & audivit. Hic tum auritus, tum oculatus testis, verba CHRISTI ea fide recensuit, quae justam dubitandi causam nemini relinquit. Descripsit autem hic suum Evangelium Hebræo sermone, in Judaea, teste Hieronymo, idq; sua manu exaratum in Indiam deportavit, quod Pantænus tandem Alexandriam retulisse scribitur. De causa scriptionis id refert Nicephorus lib. 2. c. 45. eum ex Judaea profectum in Indiam, præsenti scripto absentiam suam, compensasse: id quod Theophylactus octavo, Nicephorus decimo quinto post Resurrectionem CHRISTI anno factum fuissue annotat.

Marcus non αὐτόπτης, sed ἀκουστὸς tantùm testis: sed ita fide dignus fuit, ut eo tempore scripserit, quo non solùm ab Ecclesia CHRISTI primitiva: sed etiam ab ipsis adhuc in carne manentibus Apostolis probari meruit, ut Augustinus loquitur: imo teste Hieronymo, à Petro ipso auditus probatus, ejusque autoritate ad legendum Ecclesiæ commendatus fuit hujus Evangelij commentarius: quem Eusebius & Nicephorus rogatu eorum, qui doctrinæ Petri singulari desiderio capti erant, in Occidente congestum fuisse annotant. Paulus epistolam suam vicesimo anno post Ascensum CHRISTI scripsisse putatur, eamque Epheso Corinthum misisse per Timotheum, in dissipatione Ecclesiæ gravissima, quæ ex prophanatione Sacramenti hujus exorta fuerat. Revocat autem Apostolus suos Auditores, non tantùm ad primævam Institutionis originem: sed ad singularem etiam illam, ac stupendam revelationem, ejusdem Institutionis, sibi à CHRISTO in gloria jam versante, & ad dextram Patris sedente, factam.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: II. On the sense of the words of Christ (continued)

Luke, however, the companion of the travels and associate of the labors of Paul, almost enumerates the words of the Apostle, and joins to them that most evident declaration, 'Which is given for you,' the same as his Master the Apostle, just as if both had been appointed interpreters of those words, 'THIS IS MY BODY.' And although each of these witnesses describes the latter part of the Sacrament with words somewhat varied and transposed, as is customary in sacred letters and common speech, so that the same sense repeated in different forms of words may be inculcated for the more certain perception of the mind of the speaker: yet by that very fact he more firmly fortifies the proper and native meaning of the words, so much so that if anyone had wished to interpret the word 'Blood' in Matthew and Mark figuratively, it could not have been permitted at all through the description of Luke and Paul: since the covenant of the New Testament was sanctioned and completed not in type and figure, but in the truth of the Blood of CHRIST. From what has been said, therefore, the truth of the Conclusion is firmly evident.

The third argument of proof is given as follows: The testaments of prudent and sane men are described in such proper words, lacking all ambiguity, that it is a sin to depart even from the points of the letters, let alone the simple sense of the words, unless for the most serious and full reasons. But the description of the Eucharistic institution contains the testament and declaration of the last will not of a mere man, but of the Son of GOD Himself, described in words so plain that there can be no reason why one should depart from their literal and proper sense. Therefore, with much greater faith and religion, the simple and native sense of his words must be retained.

The proof of the major proposition depends on the public and solemn law of testaments. Here, indeed, public laws teach that if the mind of the testator is manifest from elsewhere, it is better to embrace the mind than to follow the words. But if the matter of the testament has not been disposed of previously and elsewhere, and nothing is known for certain about the mind of the testator from elsewhere, but the disputes are controversial and doubtful: they expressly pronounce that in doubt it is safest not to depart from the words, nay, from the rigor of the words, but to adhere tenaciously to them. The reason for the decision is plain, namely, because it is not to be believed that the testator intended anything other than what he expressed in words. For if he had intended something else or the contrary, there was certainly no difficulty in expressing that very thing in words. When there is no ambiguity in the words (they have the words of a certain law), a question of intent should not be admitted. Likewise, one should not depart from the meaning of words otherwise than when it is most manifest that the testator intended something else. And there are others of this kind, described and pronounced in the tables of political laws.

Civil laws do indeed permit some reasons for speaking against the rigor or the literal sense of testamentary words: but only if they are most serious and most plain, such as: If something plain has been disposed of elsewhere regarding the mind of the testator: If it is certain that after the testament he repented of his will: if the words have perchance taken on a different sense than that which was known to the testator, etc. But apart from such causes, testaments obtain the sense which the simple, proper, native, common, and literal meaning of the words provides.

The lesser is supported by the very attestation of CHRIST the testator, who in the description of the tables of the Instrument, asserts in plain words that nothing else is being done: but that a testament is being established by Him, and that not in the manner or mode of the Old Testament, which was typical and figurative: but a NEW one, that is, one proper to fulfillment and the antitype.

2. Now this testator himself was not only prudent and of sound mind: but he was heavenly and divine wisdom itself, that teacher and orator to whom the LORD gave a learned tongue, Isa. 50, 4, the master of all eloquence, and he was omniscient, from whom could not be hidden the stratagems through which, in times to come, this instrument of his would be reviled by fanatical men and sciolists, to whose lust he wished to provide absolutely no handle by any ambiguity of speech.

3. What, seeing that he was then very near to death, which he was even then approaching, with affections, words, and groans most serious, and with singular gesture, he established this testament of his, which, until the consummation of the age, in the Church should be religiously observed, a perpetual monument of the punishment and death undergone for our salvation; and a clear pledge of all benefits, and a seal of grace and the divine covenant.

4. Moreover, this testament was made κεκυρωμένη καὶ βεβαία by the death of the testator himself.

5. No reason, either weighty or plain, can be given why one should depart from the tenor, or the proper and literal sense of the words. The judgment of reason is indeed objected, with which this sense does not agree. The law of nature is opposed, with which it conflicts: But both objections are destitute of the nerve of a conclusion: since in the mysteries of faith, one must attend not to what is consistent with reason or the law of nature, but to what GOD himself commands. The Article of the Ascension into Heaven is objected, which might take away this same literal sense. But even here no argument of consequence holds: because this Testament was established before He ascended into the Heavens. 2. The fallacy of non-cause is committed. For this Ascension is so far from standing in the way of the literal and proper sense of the words, that it rather wonderfully confirms the same. Since for this reason CHRIST ascended into Heaven, that sitting at the right hand of the Father, He might, being omnipotent and filling all things, most powerfully perform what He sanctioned and established in this His testament. Thus it cannot be objected that anything was revealed more plainly elsewhere concerning the mind of the testator: since the Savior established nothing at all concerning this testament before He instituted it itself.

These things being thus proven, there emerges a Conclusion more certain than any exception, that one must not depart even a hair's breadth from the proper, native, and literal sense of the words of Institution. Which very conclusion the Apostle has handed down to us, fortified by divine authority, reasoning for this theme thus briefly indeed, but sufficiently vigorously, from the dictation of the Holy Spirit himself, Gal. 3, 15. No one abrogates or adds to a man's testament, if it has received confirmation. Much more, therefore, is it a crime to attempt anything similar in a divine testament.

I wish to set forth the FOURTH argument of proof thus: No mystery maintains its truth unless in a simple sense of the words, and one not at all bent to the grasp of human reason. But the Sacrament of the Supper is a true and mere mystery: Therefore.

The major proposition has as its author from orthodox antiquity Cyril, saying, in mysteries one must simply believe what is said, because they are mysteries for that reason. The reason can be given from Chrysostom as follows: Because it is a mystery, and is so called, when one thing is seen, another is believed. For this is the nature of divine mysteries. There is therefore always in mysteries something conflicting with human reason, conflicting with the senses themselves: indeed, even something as it were miraculous. But such things cease to be so if they are subjected to natural intelligence and the examination of our reason: if they are reduced to the order of common signs and the class of relative relations; and

finally, the words which are proposed in them are so bent that the understanding of the things may agree with the grasp of human reason.

As for the minor premise, it is indeed common to the Sacraments, especially those of the New Testament, that they are called mysteries: To which also pertains the fact that Ministers are called by the Apostle Dispensers of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. 4, 1. In which sense Chrysostom, Homily 83 on Matthew, called Baptism and the Lord's Supper mysteries. But antiquity attributed this to the Sacrament of the Eucharist specifically, and as it were by way of eminence, so that it named it that Mystery, as can be seen in Chrysostom, Homily 24 on the 1st Epistle to the Corinthians: nay, the same man called it a Tremendous mystery, μυςήριον φοβερὸν καὶ Φρικωδέστατον. However, this appellation is not attributed to it in such a sense that the absence of the heavenly thing (the Body and Blood of Christ) or a bare, or merely sole, signification of the same is implied: In which sense the eminence of the Mystery would utterly perish for this Sacrament: but because it is not comprehended by reason and sense, and is to be embraced by faith alone, which, lying hidden under visible elements, CHRIST willed to be dispensed to His Church. For it is a mystery that one and the same body is at once in Heaven and in the Supper. Concerning which matter Chrysostom, book 3 on the Priesthood: O miracle, O the goodness of GOD, who sits above with the Father, and at that very moment of time is handled by the hands of all. It is a mystery that the flesh of CHRIST is distributed in all Suppers, yet devoid of partition. For it is, as Cyril speaks in book 12 on John, chapter 32, indivisibly in all, since He is one everywhere, in no way divided. Finally, it is a mystery, as Chrysostom speaks in Homily 83 on Matthew, because not only those things which are subject to the senses are to be looked upon: but especially those things which are delivered by the word are to be believed. And although it was formerly proclaimed to the communicants: LIFT UP YOUR HEARTS: yet by this phrase antiquity did not intend to signify that the absence of the Lord's Body from the Supper should be established: or as if faith ought to turn itself away from the action of the Supper, and travel upward to Heaven, but, as the Nicene Canon explains, it warned that the mind only should be lifted up, so that faith might recognize that the Lamb of GOD, who takes away the sins of the world, is placed upon the sacred table. Chrysostom explains that sacred command thus, Homily 24 on 1 Corinthians: That we may not with our mind adhere to this world, or the earth, and those things which are in it: but that we may seek those things which pertain to the kingdom of GOD and eternal life. This is what these words of the same man show, which exist in the same place: It is necessary that he who is about to approach this body should strive toward the heights.

The FIFTH argument of proof is as follows: Whichever sense so generates one and a certain meaning, that it uniquely establishes faith in an immovable certainty, or πληροφορίᾳ: that one deservedly prevails. But the literal sense, or the proper and simple sense of the words, accomplishes this very thing more than the intellectual sense. Therefore, the literal sense ought also deservedly to prevail over the intellectual, or figurative, sense.

Latin:

Lucas verò, comes peregrinationum, & socius laborum Pauli, verba Apostoli penè annumerat, idemque cum Magistro suo Apostolo, perindè ac si ambo interpretes constituti essent eorum verborum HOC EST CORPUS MEUM, evidentissimam illam declarationem adjungit, Quod pro vobis datur. Et quamvis testis hic uterque verbis nonnihil variatis & trajectis, posteriorem Sacramenti partem describit, prout in sacris literis, & vulgari sermone usitatum est, ut idem sensus diversis verborum formis repetitus inculcetur, ad mentem dicentis certiùs percipiendam: tamen eo ipso propriam & nativam verborum significationem firmiùs munit, adeò, ut si quis vocabulum Sanguinis in Matthæo & Marco figuratè interpretari voluisset: id per Lucæ & Pauli descriptionem minimè licere potuisset: siquidem foedus Novi Testamenti non in typo & figura: sed in veritate Sanguinis CHRISTI sancitum & confectum est. Ex dictis ergo Conclusionis veritas firmiter pates scit.

TERTIUM probationis argumentum tale datur: Testamenta prudentum & sanorum hominum, verbis proprijs, & ambiguitate omni carentibus ita describuntur, ut nefas sit, etiam ab apicibus literarum, nedum simplice verborum sensu, nisi gravissimas & plenissimas ob causas discedere. Atqui descriptio institutionis Eucharisticæ non nudi hominis, sed ipsius Filii DEI, testamentum, & voluntatis ultimæ declarationem continet, verbis ita planis descriptam, ut causa nulla esse possit, cur à literali, & proprio eorum sensu discedendum sit. Ergò multò majori fide & religione sensus verborum ejus simplex ac nativus retinendus est.

Majoris propositionis probatio, ex jure Testamentorum publico & solenni dependet. Hic tradunt quidem jura publica, si mens testatoris aliundè sit manifesta, melius esse, amplecti mentem, quàm verba sequi. Sin autem res testamenti anteà & alibi non sit disposita, & de mente testatoris aliundè nihil certò constet, sed disputationes controversæ sint & ancipites: disertè pronunciant, in dubio tutissimum esse, à verbis, imò à rigore verborum non recedere: sed tenaciter illis inhærere. Ratio decisionis plana est, nempè, quia non credendum est, testatorem aliud voluisse, quàm quod verbis expressit. Si enim aliud, aut contrarium voluisset: nulla certè erat difficultas, illud ipsum verbis exprimere. Cùm in verbis nulla est ambiguitas, (habent verba legis cujusdam) non debet admitti voluntatis quæstio. Item, Non aliter à significatione verborum recedi oportet, quàm cùm manifestissimum est, aliud sensisse testatorem. Et quæ sunt hujus generis alia, in legum politicarum tabulis descripta & pronunciata,

Permittunt quidem jura civilia causas aliquas dicendi à rigore, sive à literali sensu verborum testamentalium: sed non nisi & gravissimas & planissimas, Quales sunt: Si alibi de mente testatoris, aliquid plani sit dispositum: Si post testationem pœnituisse eum suæ voluntatis constet: si verba alium sensum fortè quàm qui testatori notus fuit, induerint &c. Verùm citra istiusmodi causas, sensum testamenta eum obtinent, quem simplex, propria, nativa, trita & literalis verborum significatio præbet.

Minori patrocinatur ipsa CHRISTI testatoris attestatio, qui in descriptione tabularum Instrumenti, verbis planis asserit, non aliud agi: sed testamentum à se condi, idque non in morem aut modum Veteris Testamenti, quod erat typicum atque figuratum: sed NOVUM, hoc est, complementi, & antitypi proprium.

2. Jam testator hic ipse non prudens tantùm erat, sanæque mentis: sed ipsa cœlestis ac divina sapientia, doctor atque orator is, cui DOMINUS dedit eruditam lingvam Jes. 50, 4. magister omnis eloqvij, isque omniscius, quem latere non potuerunt Strophæ, per quas temporibus venturis, instrumentum hoc suum, fanatici homines, & scioli sugillaturi, quorum libidini ipse nihil prorsus ansæ, ullâ aliquâ sermonis ambiguitate præbere voluit.

3. Quid, quòd morti tùm erat vicinissimus, quam ille jamjam adiens, affectibus, verbis & gemitibus maximè seriis, & singulari gestu testamentum hoc suum condidit, quod usque ad consummationem seculi in Ecclesiâ religiosè servatum, perpetuum supplicij & mortis pro nostra salute subitae monimentum; & beneficiorum omnium luculentum pignus, gratiaeque & foederis divini sigillum esset.

4. Quin testatio haec morte ipsius testatoris κεκυρωμένη καὶ βεβαία facta est.

5. Non dari causa ulla vel gravis, vel plana potest, cur à tenore, sive proprio ac literali verborum sensu recedendum sit. Objicitur quidem judicium rationis, cum quo sensus iste non congruat. Lex naturae opponitur, cum quâ iste pugnet: Sed concludendi nervo utrumque objectum destituitur: Siquidem in mysteriis fidei, non quid rationi aut legi naturae sit consentaneum: sed quid DEUS ipse jubeat, attendendum est. Objicitur Articulus Ascensionis in Caelum, qui sensum eundem literarum tollat. Atqui & hîc consequentiae nulla militat ratio: propterea quòd Testamentum hoc conditum est, priusquam in Coelos afcendit. 2. Fallacia non causae committitur. Ascensio enim haec usque adeò non obstat literali & proprio verborum sensui: ut eundem potiùs mirificè confirmet. Siquidem ideò ascendit CHRISTUS in Coelum, ut consedens ad dextram Patris omnipotens, omnia implens, & potentissimè praestet, quod in testamento hoc suo sancivit & constituit. Sic objici non potest, quod alibi de mente testatoris aliquid planiùs sit proditum: Siquidem nihil quicquam priùs de hoc testamento constituit Servator, quàm illud ipsum instituit.

His ita probatis, emergit Conclusio omni exceptione certior, quod à proprio, nativo, & literali verborum Institutionis sensu, ne latum quidem ungvem sit recedendum. Quam ipsam conclusionem divinâ autoritate munitam nobis tradidit Apostolus, sic breviter quidem, sed satis nervosè ex dictatu ipsius Spiritus Sancti, pro hoc themate ratiocinans, Gal. 3, 15. Hominis saltem testamentum, si confirmatio accefferit, nemo abrogat, aut superordinat. Multò ergò magis nefas est, in divino testamento simile quippiam attentare.

QUARTUM probationis argumentum sic libet informare: Nulli mysterio sua constat veritas, nisi in simplice, & ad rationis humanae captum minimè inflexo verborum sensu. Atqui Sacramentum Coenae verum & merum est mysterium: Ergò.

Major propositio ex orthodoxâ antiquitate autorem habet Cyrillum, dicentem, in mysteriis simpliciter credendum est, quod dicitur, quia ideò sunt mysteria. Ratio ex Chrysostomo dari potest haec: Quia mysterium est, & appellatur, quando aliud videtur, aliud creditur. Haec enim mysteriorum divinorum est natura. Est ergò semper in mysteriis aliquid pugnans cum humanâ ratione, pugnans cum ipsis sensibus: imò etiam quasi miraculosum quiddam. Talia autem jam esse desinunt, si naturali intelligentiae, & rationis nostrae examini subjiciantur: si in ordinem signorum vulgarium, & classem relationum σχετικῶν rediguntur; &

denique verba, quæ in istis proponuntur, ita inflectuntur, ut intellectus rerum, captui humanæ rationis congruat.

Quoad minorem, commune quidem est Sacramentis, Novi Testamenti præcipuè, ut mysteria appellentur: Quo illud pertinet etiam, quòd Ministri vocantur ab Apostolo Dispensatores mysteriorum Divinorum 1. Cor. 4, 1. Quo sensu Chrysostomus Homil. 83. in Matth. Baptismum & Cœnam Dominicam, Mysteria appellavit. Verùm Sacramento Eucharistiæ sigillatim, & κατ' ἐξοχήν quasi quandam, id tribuit antiquitas, ut Mysterium illud nominarit, uti videre est apud Chrysostomum, Homil. 24. in ep. 1. ad Corinthios: imò Tremendum mysterium, μυςήριον φοβερὸν καὶ Φρικωδέστατον idem nuncupavit. Non autem eo sensu hæc appellatio illi attributa est, ut absentia rei cœlestis (Corporis & Sangvinis Christi) aut nuda, sive sola ejusdem significatio duntaxat innuatur: Quo sensu Mysterij ἐξοχή huic Sacramento prorsus deperiret: sed quia ratione & sensu non comprehenditur, & fide solâ amplexandum est, quod sub visibilibus elementis latens, CHRISTUS Ecclesiæ suæ dispensatum voluit. Mysterium enim est, quod Unum & idem corpus simul in Cœlo est, & in Cœnâ. Quâ de re Chrysostomus lib. 3. de Sacerdotio: O miraculum, ô DEI bonitatem, qui cum Patre sursum sedet, & in illo ipso temporis articulo omnium manibus tractatur. Mysterium est, quod caro CHRISTI in omnibus Cœnis, expers tamen partitionis distribuitur. Estenim ut Cyrillus loquitur lib. 12. in Johannem, cap. 32. impartibiliter in omnibus, cum unus sit ubique, nullo modo divisus. Mysterium est denique ut Chrysostomus Homil. 83. in Matth. loquitur, quia non ea tantùm, quæ sensibus subjacent aspicienda sunt: sed præcipuè credenda ea, quæ traduntur verbo. Et quamvis olim acclamatum sit communicantibus: SURSUM CORDA: tamen hâc phrasi non id significatum voluit antiquitas, absentiam Corporis Dominici à Cœnâ statuendam esse: aut quasi fides se avertere debeat ab actione Cœnæ, & sursum ad Cœlum peregrinari, sed, uti Canon Nicenus explicat, mentem duntaxat elevandam esse monuit, ut fides agnoscat, in sacrâ mensâ positum esse Agnum DEI, qui tollit peccata mundi. Chrysostomus sacrum illud κέλευσμα sic explicat, Homil. 24. in 1. ad Corinth. Ne mente nostrâ huic mundo, seu terræ, & ijs, quæ in ea sunt, adhæreamus: sed ea, quæ ad regnum DEI & vitam æternam pertinent, quæramus. Id quod verba hæc ejusdem ostendunt, quæ ibidem extant: Ad alta contendat oportet, qui ad corpus hoc accessurus est.

QUINTUM probationis argumentum sic habet: Quicunque sensus ita unam ac certam gignit sententiam, ut fidem in immotâ certitudine, sive πληροφορίᾳ unicè stabiliat: is meritò prævalet. Atqui τὸ ρητὸν sive proprius ac simplex verborum sensus præ sensu διανοητικῷ hoc ipsum præstat Ergò τὸ ρητὸν etiam meritò τῇ διανοίᾳ sive sensui figurato prævalere debet.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Hence

Hence:

The text does not deceive: a specious Gloss has deceived many: rely on the word of GOD, you will be safe. And: A single point of the word is stronger than every argument: and than a thousand decrees, and than the prior Councils.

The Major premise is clear by its own light, and stands in need of no proof. Therefore, as regards the Minor, the very confusion of any adversaries whatsoever provides its firmest confirmation, who, having neglected the literal sense, have devised such a manifold Allegory that they themselves did not perceive that they could safely rest in any one of them: and consequently they were constantly seeking new opinions. For from the beginning some taught that the eating of the Eucharistic bread is to be understood as a mere figure and reminder, the sign of which was given by CHRIST to the Church, just as if a Bridegroom, setting out on a journey, should leave a ring for his bride. 2. Others said that a communication of the divine nature of CHRIST takes place, which, because it is united to the human, is as it were secondarily offered as a body. 3. Others referred that communication, which takes place in the Supper, to the Holy Spirit, who is the same in CHRIST and in believers. 4. Others interpreted the words of the same as being about the benefits of CHRIST. 5. Others invented an intelligible Body: of which a participation might take place in the Supper. 6. To others, to eat the body of CHRIST was the same thing as to believe in CHRIST. 7. Others fought indeed gravely for the substance of the Lord's Body itself: but in order that men might participate in it, they banished them to the furthest Heaven. Finally, others rendered and explained the words of CHRIST differently, but in such a way that when the end is reached, piety and faith falter, and they do not find in what the full assurance of faith consists, so that not even to this day is it settled, since they have changed their explanations so many times, in which Allegory or gloss they are finally to fix their foot. But if the writings of the Sacramentarians are examined a little more accurately, it will be clear that they have changed their opinion thirty times over. On which matter see the Sacramentarian Theology of Cunrad Schlüffelburg, Art. 22, page 100.

Conversely, the literal sense observed in the words of CHRIST produces one and the same meaning, and one that is consistent with itself in every part, which provides peace of Conscience and the most solid strength of faith, namely this: That "in this mystery with the blessed bread, the Body: "with the blessed wine, the very Blood of CHRIST, is truly and essentially: "yet in a manner by no means natural: but clearly heavenly, and altogether unsearchable to human reason, offered, and received by all who communicate.

We have Martin LUTHER, who writes that he will use such an apology before the tribunal of the Son of GOD: LORD JESUS CHRIST, a controversy was agitated in the world over the words of your Testament, with some departing into an opinion different from the tenor of your words, and it being distracted into various opinions, to which I could not, nor would I, commit my faith and my conscience. But I, who considered those words to be of your Testament and last will, and found nowhere in Scripture that you wished the same to be received from you in a sense different than they sounded, to which declaration you would undoubtedly not have spared in so grave a matter if you had wished the words to be understood otherwise than they simply sound: I have rested in the native and simple sense of the same: Judge you LORD, whether I have erred: and if I have erred, by whose fault it has primarily come to pass that I have erred.

PHILIP MELANCHTHON also produced a similar example of full assurance, while he was still like himself, to Friedrich Myconius, thus writing out his opinion: I find no sufficiently firm reason why we should depart from this opinion (he understands that which is proper to Luther and the Lutheran Church). It may be that another opinion (he thinks of the Zwinglian) flatters an idle mind, which is more agreeable to human judgment, especially when thus instructed and adorned with learnedly devised arguments. But what will happen in temptation, when the conscience will dispute, what cause it had for dissenting from the opinion received in the Church? Then those words, This is my body, will be thunderbolts. What will a terrified mind oppose here? with what scriptures, with what voice of GOD will it fortify itself, and persuade itself that a metaphor necessarily had to be interpreted here? Those seem not sufficiently experienced in these struggles who so easily bear new dogmas, who are so delighted by wit that they admire craftily thought-out arguments more than the words of scripture. I know how lightly those arguments dissenting from the scriptures are shaken from our hands in temptation, however plausible they may have seemed before.
