But if the adversaries are not moved by these examples: at least they ought to be terrified by that thunderbolt with which the Apostle denounces judgment to those who do not discern the Body of the LORD 1 Cor. 11, 29. which is to be thought to happen not only by eating unworthily: but also by not discerning that which CHRIST pronounced concerning his body, in establishing this his testament: i.e., by attacking the literal sense, which is to be believed to have been used by CHRIST with a most deliberate mind and a clearly divine counsel. For it is certain that all the disputes which are agitated by the opposing side here draw their origin solely from the fact that the literal sense of the words is wickedly attacked: and again, that they aim solely at this, that the simple and native sense of the literal meaning be nefariously torn asunder and overturned: with the most diverse and, to this mystery, most alien places and materials from Scripture and Theology, and indeed even from all Philosophy, sought out for this purpose, and twisted and mixed in. And indeed we cannot deny that disputes of this kind are ventilated in the treatment of this mystery even by our own people, indeed were even agitated by Luther himself, such as those concerning the article of the Ascension of CHRIST to the heavens, concerning the Session of the same at the Right hand of the Father, concerning the Personal Union of the two natures in CHRIST, concerning the Communication of the Idioms, concerning the human Majesty in CHRIST, concerning the Omnipotence of GOD, concerning the essential properties of a true human body, and those which are similar. But the condition of our theologians is one thing: that of the Sacramentarian theologians is another, amidst the agitations of these disputes. For the latter move about in these matters as if in their own forum: we as if in another's: they offensively: we defensively: they arbitrarily: we under compulsion. For after the Calvinists have forced these disputes upon this subject, our men have been compelled by necessity to provide true explanations of these articles, and to show that it is so far from the case that the τὸ ῥητὸν is overturned by them, that it is even more confirmed. Otherwise, our men would easily contain themselves within the proper boundaries of this mystery.

The sixth argument of proof can be such: That interpretation, or that sense of the words of CHRIST, is the best and to be preferred to the others, which most agrees with the mind and will of CHRIST himself. But the τὸ ῥητὸν, or the proper and literal sense of the words of CHRIST, most agrees with the very mind and will of the Savior. Therefore.

The minor premise, which contains the κρινόμενον, is confirmed by that explicit designation of the Body and Blood of CHRIST, which rejects every figurative and tropical sense: as when the Savior says: This is my Body, which is given for you: This is my Blood, which is poured out for many. Which words, indeed, admit no other διάνοιαν than that which is proper to the τὸ ῥητὸν: unless they wish to dream that Christ gave and poured out some figurative or tropical Body and Blood.

The seventh argument of proof is such: If the Eucharistic Cup is the New Testament in the blood of CHRIST: then certainly no figurative or metonymical διάνοια can have a place in the words of Christ. But the former is true; therefore the latter is also valid.

The first member of the major premise has the Apostle Paul himself as its author, in 1 Cor. 11:24, saying τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον, ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐστὶν ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου: This cup is the new Testament in my blood. The latter member, namely the connection of the major premise, is proved thus: For if, in the Sacramentarian διανοητικῷ sense, the Eucharistic Cup is a figure of the New Testament in the Blood of CHRIST: it would follow: 1. That the Blood of CHRIST differs in no way from the blood of the Paschal Lamb and of the sacrifices. 2. That the New Testament consists of shadows and figures. 3. That the New Testament is a figure of itself. 4. If the cup is a figure of the New Testament in the blood of CHRIST: it will be this either in respect of the matter: or by reason of the form: or in respect of the content, namely the Wine. The Calvinists themselves do not even admit the first two respects. Therefore, the third remains. Now if the Eucharistic cup is the New Testament in the blood of CHRIST, in respect of the wine, let the Calvinists explain to us what reason there is why, between the cup and the wine, which are certainly disparate species, such a Union can be granted that one may indeed be put for the other, but one cannot be predicated of the other.

The eighth and final argument of proof can be sought from the unanimous consent of Orthodox Antiquity: concerning which, let the blessed Chemnitius be consulted in the book whose title is: Fundamenta Cœnæ: let the Refutatio Consensus Calvinistici also be consulted, and whatever other books of our theologians have been published on this matter.

The Sacramentarian race has opposed this purer doctrine of ours with great effort for almost an entire century, seeking such an ἀξιοποιίαν of the words of CHRIST as consists of mere figures, types, tropes, and relations: and which snatches away from us the very Body and Blood of CHRIST as the principal Good from this Sacrament. And so that we may perceive at least some taste of this impiety, we shall not go further, but we shall examine in a few words how Carolstadius, Zwinglius, Oecolampadius, and Calvin have shown themselves in this contest.

1. Andreas Bodenstein Carolstadius, in the year 1525, brought forth this sense of the words of CHRIST: This is my Body: that is: My Body is that which you see sitting here. In his Dialogue: Where this blasphemy also is found, which must be avenged by heavenly lightning: That I believe that CHRIST can be essentially in several places with his body as easily as I believe that St. Anne had five heads: or that one of the innocent children had a beard twelve ells long: That Christ can at the same time be essentially in many places, that I believe as easily as I believe that St. Anne had five heads: and that one of the innocent children had a beard twelve ells long.

Latin:

Hinc:

Non fallit textus: multos speciosa fefellit Glossa: DEI verbo nitere, tutus eris. Et: Unus apex verbi ratione valentior omni est: Millequè decretis, Concilijsquè prior.

Major suâ luce patet, neque probatione ullâ indiget. Ergò quoad Minorem, firmissimam ejus confirmationem suppeditat ipsa ςρεφλὴ adversariorum quorumvis, qui neglecto τῷ ῥητῷ ejusmodi Ἀλληγορίας multiplicem excogitarunt, ut ne ipsi quidem in ullâ aliquâ tutò acquiescerese posse animadverterent: ac proinde subindè novas sententias inquirerent. Nam ab initio aliqui docuerunt, manducationem panis Eucharistici intelligendam esse de nudâ figurâ & commonefactione, cujus signum à CHRISTO datum sit Ecclesiæ, perindè ac si Sponsus peregrè proficiscens, annulum sponsæ relinquat. 2. Alij divinæ naturæ CHRISTI communicationem fieri dixerunt, quæ quia humanæ sit unita, secundariò quasi præberi corpus. 3. Alij communicationem illam, quæ fit in Cœnâ, ad Spiritum Sanctum retulerunt, qui idem sit in CHRISTO & credentibus. 4. Alij de beneficijs CHRISTI verba ejusdem sunt interpretati. 5. Alij Corpus νοητὸν confinxerunt: cujus in Cœnâ fieret participatio. 6. Alijs corpus CHRISTI edere, idem fuit, quod in CHRISTUM credere. 7. Alij pro substantia Corporis Dominici ipsâ graviter quidem pugnarunt: sed utea participare homines possint, ablegaverunt eos ad extremum Cœlum. Alij denique aliter verba CHRISTI reddiderunt, & explicarunt, sed ita, ut cum ventum ad finem est, pietasque fidesque labascant, & non inveniant, in quo fidei πληροφορία constistat, ut ne in hunc usque diem constet, cum toties explicationes suas mutaverint, in quâ tandem Ἀλληγορίᾳ sive glossâ pedem fixuri sint. Quod si paulò accuratiùs scripta Sacramentariorum evolvantur, patebit tricies ampliùs eos mutasse sententiam. Quâ de re videatur Theologia Sacramentaria Cunradi Schlüffelburgij Art. 22. pag. 100.

Vice autem versâ, τὸ ῥητὸν in verbis CHRISTI observatum, sensum gignit unum, eundemque, atque illum ex omni parte sibi constantem, qui Conscientiæ pacem, fidei robur solidissimum suppeditat, hunc nimirùm: Quod „ in hoc mysterio cum pane benedicto, Corpus: „ cum vino benedicto, Sangvis CHRISTI i- „ psissimus, verè quidem atque essentialiter: mo- „ do tamen minimè naturali: sed planè cœlesti, ac rationi humanæ prorsus impervestigabili præbeatur, & à communicantibus quibus libet sumatur.

landro LUTHERO habemus, qui tali apologiâ se apud tribunal Filij DEI usurum scribit: DOMINEJESU CHRISTE, Controversia in mundo agitata fuit, super verbis Testamenti tui, aliquibus in sententiam à verborum tuorum tenore diversam abeuntibus, eamq́; in varias opiniones distractam, quibus ego fidem & conscientiam meam committere nec potui, nec volui. Ego verò, qui Testamenti tui & voluntatis ultimæ verba ista esse consideravi, neǵ; diverso, quàm sonarent, sensu, eadem abs te accipi velle, uspiam in Scripturâ comperi, cui declarationi faciendæ haud dubiè non pepercisses in re tàm gravi, si aliter voluisses verba, quàm simpliciter sonant, intelligi: in nativo & simplice eorundem sensu acquievi: Judica tu DOMINE, an erraverim: & si erravi, cujus culpâ potissimùm factum sit, ut erraverim.

Simile πληροφορίας exemplum edidit etiam PHILIPPUS MELANCHTHON, dùm adhuc sui esset similis, ad Fridericum Myconium, sic suam perscribens sententiam: Ego nullam satis firmam rationem invenio, cur ab hâc sententiâ, (intelligit eam, quæ est Lutheri & Ecclesiæ Lutheranæ propria) discedamus. Fieri potest, ut alia sententia (Zvinglianam putat) blandiatur otioso animo, quæ est magis consentanea humano judicio, præsertim sic instructa & ornata argumentis eruditè excogitatis. Sed quid fiet in tentatione, cùm disputabit conscientia, quam habuerit causam dissentiendi à receptâ sententiâ in Ecclesiâ? Tunc ista verba, Hoc est corpus meum, fulmina erunt. Quid hic opponet mens perterrefacta? quibus scripturis, quâ voce DEI se muniet, ac sibi persuadebit, necessariò hîc fuisse interpretandam metaphoram? Non satis periti videntur horum certaminum isti, qui tàm facilè ferunt nova dogmata, qui sic delectantur ingenio, ut magis admirentur vasrè cogitatas rationes quàm verba scripturæ. Ego scio, quàm leviter in tentatione excutiantur nobis è manibus rationes illæ dissentientes à scripturis, quantùvis antea visa plausibiles.

Quod si exemplis istis non moventur adversarij: saltem fulmine eo terreri deberent, quo Apostolus judicium denunciat ijs, qui Corpus DOMINI non dijudicant 1. Cor. 11, 29. id quod non tantùm indignè manducando fieri putandum est: sed etiam non judicando illud, quod de corpore suo, in condendo hoc testamento suo, CHRISTUS pronunciavit: h. e. τὸ ῥητὸν impugnando, quod à CHRISTO deliberatissimâ mente, & consilio planè divino usurpatum esse, credendum est. Certum est enim, disputationes omnes, quæ ab adversâ parte agitantur hîc unicè originem trahere, quod τὸ ῥητὸν verborum improbè impugnantur: rursus eò unicè collimare, ut sensus τοῦ ῥητοῦ simplex & nativus nefariè convellatur, & evertatur: conquisitis hunc in finem, & eodem detortis, atque immixtis ex Scripturâ & Theologiâ, imò Philosophiâ etiam universâ locis & materijs diversissimis, & ab hoc mysterio alienissimis. Et quidem inficias ire non possumus, istiusmodi disputationes, in hujus mysterij tractatione etiam à nostratibus ventilari, imò ab ipso etiam Luthero agitatas esse, quales sunt de articulo Ascensionis CHRISTI ad cælos, de Sessione ejusdẽ ad Dextram Patris, de Unione Personali duarum naturarũ in CHRISTO, de Communicatione Idiomatum, de Majestate humana in CHRISTO natura, de Omnipotentia DEI, de proprietatibus essentialibus veri corporis humani, & quae sunt similes. Verùm alia est nostratium: alia Sacramentariorum Theologorum, inter istarum disputationum agitationes, conditio. Hi enim in istis tanquàm in proprio suo foro versantur: nos tanquàm in alieno: illi offensivè: nos defensivè: illi arbitrariè: nos coactè. Postquàm enim istas disputationes huic materiae Calviniani ingesserunt: necessitate sunt compulsi nostrates, veras explicationes istorum articulorum tradere, & ostendere, tantùm abesse, ut per istos τὸ ῥητὸν evertatur: ut etiam magis confirmetur. Alioquin intra metas mysterij hujus proprias facilè se nostrates continerent.

SEXTUM probationis argumentum tale esse potest: Illa interpretatio, sive ille sensus verborum CHRISTI est optimus, & caeteris praeferendus qui cum mente & voluntate ipsius CHRISTI maximè congruit. Atqui τὸ ῥητὸν, sive proprius ac literalis sensus verborum CHRISTI, cum ipsa mente atq; voluntate Servatoris maximè consentit. Ergò.

Minorem, τὸ quæ continet κρινόμενον, confirmat diserta illa notatio Corporis & Sangvinis CHRISTI, quæ figuratum omnem ac tropicum sensum respuit: ut cum dicit Servator: Hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur: Hoc est Sangvis meus, qui pro multis effunditur. Quæ sanè verba nullam aliam διάνοιαν, quàm quæ τῷ ῥητῷ est propria, admittunt: nisi figuratum aliquod, aut tropicum Corpus ac Sangvinem, Christum tradidisse & effudisse, somniare velint.

SEPTIMUM probationis argumentum tale est: Si Poculum Eucharisticum est Novum Testamentum in sangvine CHRISTI: nullæ profectò διάνοια figurata, aut metonymica in verbis Christi locum habere potest. Atqui prius verum; Ratum ergò & posterius.

Majoris membrum prius habet autorem ipsum Apostolum Paulum, in 1. Cor. 11, 24. dicentem τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον, ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐστὶν ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου: Hoc poculum, novum Testamentum est in meo sangvine. Membrum posterius, nempè connexum majoris, sic probatur: Si enim sensu διανοητικῷ Sacramentario, Poculum Eucharisticum est figura Novi Testamenti in Sangvine CHRISTI: Consequens fuerit: 1. Sangvinem CHRISTI à sangvine Agni Paschalis & Sacrificiorū nihil differre. 2. Novum Testamentum constare umbris & figuris. 3. Novum Testamentum sui ipsius esse figuram. 4. Si poculum est figura Novi Testamenti in sangvine CHRISTI: erit hoc aut respectu materiæ: aut ratione formæ: aut respectu contenti, nempè Vini. Priores duos respectus ne ipsi quidem admittunt Calviniani. Remanet ergò tertius. Jam si poculum Eucharisticum est Novum Testamentum in sangvine CHRISTI, respectu vini, edisserant nobis Calviniani, Quid causæ sit, quod inter poculum & vinum, species certè disparatas, talis concedi potest Unio, ut una quidem pro altera poni: non verò una de altera prædicari queat.

OCTAVUM & postremum probationis argumentum peti potest ex unanimi consensu Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis: de quo videatur B. Chemnitius in libro, cui titulus est: Fundamenta Cœnæ: Videatur item Refutatio Consensus Calvinistici, & si qui sunt alij nostratium Theologorum libri, hâc de re editi.

Puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ magno conatu, per integrum fermè seculum se opposuit Gens Sacramentaria, talem quærens verborum CHRISTI ἀξιοποιίαν, quæ meris constet figuris, typis, tropis, relationibus: & ipsum Corpus ac Sangvinem CHRISTI, tanquàm principale Bonum ex hoc Sacramento nobis eripiat. Et ut gustum impietatis hujus aliquem saltem percipiamus, non longiùs abibimus, sed quales se hoc in certamine præbuerint Carolstadius, Zvvinglius, Oecolampadius, Calvinus, paucis dispiciemus.

1. Andreas Bodenstein Carolstadius, Anno 1525. hunc protulit verborum CHRISTI sensum: Hoc est Corpus meum: id est: Corpus meum est id, quod hîc sedere cernitis. In Dialogo: Ubi hæc etiam blasphemia, fulmine cœlesti vindicanda reperitur: Quòd CHRISTUS corpore suo pluribus in locis essentialiter esse possit, tàm facilè credo, quàm credo, B. Annam habuisse quinque capita: vel infantum innocentium aliquem habuisse barbam duodecim ulnas longam: Daß Christus zugleich an vielen orthen Wesentlich sein könne/ daß gläube ich so leichtlich/ als ich gläube/ das S. Anna habe fünff köpffe gehabt: und hat der Unschuldigen kindlein eins/einen Bart gehabt/zwölff Ellen lang.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Hence (continued)

The arguments with which he fought were these principal ones:

I. This sentence: (This is my body, which is given for you) is enclosed by points: it has points at the beginning and at the end, by which it is indicated that this verse: This is my body, is not connected with the preceding words, but is a distinct statement in itself: therefore I must needs confess that CHRIST, by saying, (This is my Body) pointed to his body, not to bread.

I reply: from the undistributed to the distributed the consequence is not valid. For the reason of the connection is not completely universal: since new points do not immediately produce or imply a new and different meaning of the sentence. I say nothing now of the λεπτολογίᾳ which is feigned to be in the words of Christ. For it would scarcely be the speech of a sane man: Take, eat this Bread: For here you see my body: And take, drink from this cup: For here sits my blood. Nay, rather, the argument of Carlstadt concerning the blood of Christ being pointed out is most false: a thing which even a boy understands.

II. The argument of Carlstadt consisted in these words: This sentence: (This is my Body, which is given for you) is a full and perfect sentence. For the pronoun THIS, has a large (H.) But a capital letter indicates the beginning of a new sentence. Therefore this verse is inserted into the discourse concerning the Lord's Supper, as something is wont to be interposed which serves the present discourse, and yet is a perfect discourse in itself.

It would be good if the interpreters had left the Greek pronoun τοῦτο and mixed it into the Latin language: and if it were read thus: τοῦτο is this my body: and in German: τοῦτο Ist der Leib Mein / welcher für euch gegeben wirdt. Then certainly men would have thought about what the little word τοῦτο might mean.

I answer that Carlstadt is shamefully hallucinating with the fallacy of the non-cause as a cause. For the use of the masculine form of the letters is not merely a single use, but a double one. For sometimes we are accustomed to use it for the sake of noting some new speech or sentence: sometimes, indeed, for the sake of signifying the dignity of things. The rest, which he has subjoined, betray the fanatical spirit of that man. Carlstadt therefore babbles, he does not dispute.

III. Carlstadt's argument. Grammarians teach that an adjective and a substantive should be joined not only in the same number and case, but also in the same gender. Now, however, since the pronoun τοῦτο, being neuter, does not agree in gender with the masculine noun τῷ ἄρτῳ or Bread: it follows that the pronoun τοῦτο cannot or ought not to be referred to the preceding discourse of CHRIST, in which He treats of eating bread. For neither in the Greek nor in the Latin language is it correctly said: Istud panis est corpus meum: nor even in German: Der Brodt ist mein Leib.

I answer that Carlstadt is deceived and deceives with the fallacy of the figure of speech. For the pronoun τοῦτο, THIS, is not always, even in the daily use of speech, referred to the gender of the preceding noun or substantive: but it is mostly adapted to denote the entire complex of the present matter of which we are speaking: as when I say: Take this purse, THIS is a hundred florins, etc. But what need is there of many words, when even Calvin himself, in his Commentary on the 11th chapter of the first to the Corinthians, calls this babbling of Carlstadt an insipid invention: and Beza, in his Dialogue against Illyricus, condemns and rejects this very dogma as inept.

II. Huldrych Zwingli followed Carlstadt, who gave this sense to the words of Christ: This is my Body: that is: This signifies my Body. The principal arguments with which he fought for his 'This signifies' were these:

FIRST, he borrowed from certain places of the Scriptures, in which the word IS seems to be put for 'signifies': as 1 Cor. 10:4, The Rock was CHRIST; Exod. 12:11, You shall eat it in haste: for it is the Lord's Passover; Matt. 11:14, John is Elijah; John 15:1, CHRIST is the vine.

The response to this argument must be weighed and dispatched with all the more accuracy, the greater the effort with which the Sacramentarian sect strives to place the defense of its cause in it. For both the ancient and the more recent Zwinglians, whom we are otherwise accustomed to call Calvinists, heap up a great number of testimonies of Scripture in which the substantive verb IS seems to sustain some trope, and especially a metonymy of the sign: such as those already enumerated: as also these following: The seed is the word:

The field is the world: The harvest is the end of the age: The reapers are the Angels: The seven golden lampstands are the seven Churches: The seven stars are the seven Bishops: My Father is the Vinedresser: You are the branches: I am the good shepherd: Circumcision is the covenant: Baptism is the covenant, and many others of this kind. To all these places and propositions the adversaries attach such a metonymy, which changes the existential signification of the copula IS into a significative one: in this sense, that the Rock is not CHRIST, but signifies CHRIST, the Seed is not the Word of GOD, but signifies it, etc. Therefore, they attach the same sense to the words of the Supper, so that, namely, that which is exhibited and eaten with the Bread is not, but at least signifies, the Body of CHRIST.

In order to overthrow this engine of the Calvinists solidly and from the foundations, we premise these general hypotheses.

I. In every proposition, the Substantive Verb, or copula IS, admits of no trope or figure at all. For in every perfect predication where the Predicate is expressly stated, the Copula IS is always συγκατηγορούμενον, that is, it is never predicated alone, but is always συνκατηγορεῖται. Therefore, it can never sustain a Trope by itself alone: but it must necessarily have a Trope together with the predicate, if indeed it should be granted to have one at all. The reason is: Because the Copula does not sustain the office of predicating alone, but together with the predicate.

II. If any trope lies hidden in the words of the Supper, it must necessarily lie hidden either in the subject or in the predicate. For the Copula IS cannot sustain it, as has already been shown. But no trope lies hidden in the predicate. For who would be so senseless, or absurd even to the point of prodigy, as to dare to affirm that a tropical Body was delivered to death for us: or that tropical blood was shed for us. Which Beza himself also understood, writing to Alamannus, a minister of the Church of Lyons: Those words: (Which is delivered for you, and which is shed for you) necessarily drive you to this, that you are forced to understand this concerning the very substance of the Body and Blood.

III. The subject of the words of the Institution is twofold: One in the words of the Apostle saying: The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the Body of CHRIST? The cup which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of CHRIST? Where in the former member the Subject is BREAD, which no one but a madman would deny to be free from every trope. In the latter member it is the Cup, where we ourselves readily admit that the container is taken for the contained, but at the same time we also add that this Synecdoche, δὶς διὰ πασῶν, differs from that Calvinian Metonymy. For the latter, by changing the proper and native sense of the words of the Institution, completely removes the substance of this Sacrament, namely the very Body and Blood of CHRIST, from the midst. But that Synecdoche posits and asserts this very substance, in this sense, that the cup, that is, the wine, is the communion of the Blood of CHRIST. For thus he himself

The Apostle explains himself in the eleventh chapter immediately following of the first to the Corinthians, v. 24, saying: τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον, ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐστὶν ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου: This cup is the New Testament in my blood.

For imagine at least, as the Sacramentarians contend, that the Cup is metonymically a figure of the New Testament in the Blood of CHRIST: it would follow: 1. That the Blood of CHRIST differs in nothing from the Blood of the Paschal Lamb and the sacrifices: since here too it was nothing else than a type, shadow, and signification of the New Testament. 2. That the New Testament does not differ in substance from the Old Testament. 3. That the New Testament bears a type and figure of itself. Since all these things are more absurd than the most absurd things, it is plain that the Cup is not metonymically, but in a proper and native sense, the New Testament in the Blood of CHRIST: because, indeed, the Eucharistic wine does not signify, does not figure, or shadow: but exhibits and confers the present Blood of CHRIST, that very Blood which constitutes and completes the substance of the New Testament.

IV. Another subject offers itself in the words of Matthew and Mark: and that expressed by the demonstrative pronoun THIS: Which, with blessed Luther, we determine to contain a Synecdoche as a figure: but not that rhetorical one which, just as the Calvinian metonymy, changes its proper signification into a figurative and alien one, but a Grammatical Synecdoche, which under one word and its complex comprehends two distinct things, with the proper and native sense of the words clearly left whole and inviolate.

"Therefore this Grammatical Synecdoche wills and implies that two disparate things, namely Bread and Body: Wine and Blood, are present together and are exhibited at the same time."

With these four hypotheses premised, we conclude irrefragably that in the words of the Institution, This is my body, there is, neither regarding the subject nor regarding the predicate, nor regarding the copula, any metonymy or other rhetorical figure that overturns the literal sense and supports the signification of the Calvinists or Zwinglians.

Now, in order to answer the proposed argument, we determine with blessed Luther in the Greater Confession: In each and every phrase or proposition of Scripture in which there is something figurative, there is never a trope or figure in the copula IS, but either in the subject or the predicate: But that figure is not a metonymy: but only a metaphor, which leaves the copula IS in its own proper and native sense and signification.

The truth of the statement is evident from those very examples which the adversaries produce in great number: among which these propositions maintain a trope of metaphor in the subject.

I. The Rock was CHRIST 1 Cor. 10, 4. Where there is a metaphor in the word Rock, which denoted not a corporeal or earthly, but a spiritual Rock, namely CHRIST. For that corporeal rock, from which they drank

Latin:

Argumenta, quibus pugnavit, hæc fuerunt præcipua:

I. Hæc oratio: (Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur) est conclusa punctis: habet puncta in initio & in fine, quibus indicatur, hunc versum: Hoc est corpus meum, non esse connexum cum præcedentibus, sed per se esse distinctum sermonem: ideò necessum habeo fateri, CHRISTUM dicendo, (Hoc est Corpus meum) corpus suum, non panem demonstrasse.

Respondeo: à non distributo ad distributum non valet Consequentia. Ratio enim connexi non est completè universalis: Siquidem Puncta nova, non statim novam etiam & diversam pariunt aut innuunt orationis sententiam. Nihil jam dico de λεπτολογίᾳ quæ verbis Christi ineffe fingitur. Vix enim sani hominis hæc esset Oratio: Accipite, manducate Panem hunc: Hîc enim cernitis corpus meum: Et accipite, bibite ex hoc poculo: Hîc enim sedet sangvis meus. Quin imò de ostenso Sangvine Christi argumentatio Carolstadij est falsissima: id quod vel puer intelligit.

II. Argumentum Carolstadij his verbis constabat: Oratio hæc: (Hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur) plena & perfecta est sententia. Nam pronomen HOC, habet magnum(H.) Majuscula autem litera indicat initiū novæ sentētiæ. Est itaq; hic versus insertus Sermoni de Cœna Domini, ut aliquid solet interponi, quod præsenti Sermoni inservit, & tamen per se sermo est perfectus.

Bonum esset, si interpretes Graecum pronomen τοῦτο reliquissent, & Latino sermoni permiscvissent: & si ita legeretur: τοῦτο est hoc corpus meum: & Germanice: τοῦτο Ist der Leib Mein / welcher für euch gegeben wirdt. Tum utique cogitassent homines, quid vocula τοῦτο sibi vellet.

Respondeo, turpiter hallucinari Carolstadium Sophismate τοῦ μὴ αἰτίου, ὡς αἰτίου. Usus enim formae literarum masculae non usus duntaxat est, sed geminus. Interdum enim novae alicujus orationis, aut sententiae notandae gratia: interdum vero dignitatis rerum significandae causa, ea uti solemus. Reliqua, quae subjunxit, produnt Spiritum fanaticum hominis istius. Blaterat ergo, non disputat Carolstadius.

III. Carolstadii argumentum. Grammatici praecipiunt, ut Adjectivum & Substantivum, non modo in eodem numero & casu, sed & genere eodem conjungantur. Jam vero cum pronomen τοῦτο Neutrum, Masculino nomini τῷ ἄρτῳ sive Pani in genere non conveniat: Sequitur pronomen τοῦτο, ad praecedentem CHRISTI sermonem, in quo de manducando pane agit, minime referri posse aut debere. Nam neq;, in Graeca, neque in Latina lingua recte dicitur: Istud panis est corpus meum: neque etiam in Germanica: Der Brodt ist mein Leib.

Respondeo, falli & fallere Carolstadium Sophismate παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως. Pronomen enim τοῦτο HOC, non semper, in quotidiano etiam sermonis usu, ad praecedentis nominis sive Substantivi genus refertur: sed plerumque ad notandum praesentis, de quo loquimur, materiae complexum integrum accommodatur: ut quando dico: Accipe hanc crumenam, Hoc sunt centum floreni &c. Sed quid multis opus, cum vel Calvinus ipse, in Commentario ad cap. 11. prioris ad Corinthios, hanc Carolstadii Φλυαρίαν nominet insulsum commentum: Beza vero in Dialogo adversus Illyricum, hoc ipsum dogma, ceu ineptum damnet, & rejiciat.

II. Carolstadium infecutus est Huldricus Zvvinglius, qui verborum Christi sensum dedit istum: Hoc est Corpus meum: id est: Hoc significat Corpus meum. Argumenta praecipua, quibus pro suo Hoc Significat pugnabat, fuerunt isthaec:

PRIMVM mutuabatur a certis Scripturarum locis, in quibus verbum EST, pro Significat, positum esse videtur: ut 1. Cor. 10, 4. Petra erat CHRISTVS: Exod. 12, 11. Festinanter comedetis: Est enim Pascha Domini. Matth. 11, 14. Johannes est Elias. Joh. 15, 1. CHRISTUS est vitis.

Responsio argumenti hujus tanto accuratius fuerit expendenda, & expedienda, quanto majore conatu gens Sacramentaria causae suae praesidium in eo collocare studet. Nam tum veteres, tum recentiores Zvvingliani, quos alias Calvinistas appellitare solemus, magno numero coacervant Scripturae testimonia, in quibus verbum Substantivum EST, Tropum aliquem, & cumprimis Metonymiam signi sustinere videtur: Qualia sunt jam enumerata: ut & haec sequentia: Semen est verbum:

Ager est mundus: Messis est consummatio seculi: Messores sunt Angeli: Septem candelabra aurea sunt septem Ecclesiæ: Septem stellæ sunt septem Episcopi: Pater meus est Agricola: Vos estis palmites: Ego sum pastor bonus: Circumcisio est fœdus: Baptismus est fœdus, & hujus generis complura alia. His locis & propositionibus universis talem Metonymiam affingunt Adversarij, quæ significationem ὑπαρκτικὴν copulæ EST, mutet in σημαντικὴν significativam: hoc sensu, ut Petra non sit CHRISTVS, sed significet CHRISTUM, Semen non sit Verbum DEI, sed significet illud, &c. Proindè verbis Cœnæ eundem sensum affingunt, ut, nimirùm id, quod cum Pane exhibetur, & manducatur, non sit, sed saltem significet Corpus CHRISTI.

Hanc Calvinianorum machinam, ut solidè & funditùs evertamus, generales hasce præmittimus hypotheses.

I. In omni propositione, Verbum Substantivum, sive copula EST, tropum sive figuram planè nullam admittit. In omni enim perfectâ prædicatione ubi Prædicatum desertè exprimitur, Copula EST, semper est συγκατηγορούμενον, hoc est, nunquàm sola κατηγορεῖται, sed semper συνκατηγορεῖται. Ergò Tropum etiã ea sola sustinere nunquàm potest: sed unà cum prædicato Tropum habeat necesse est, si modò aliquem habere concedi debeat. Ratio est: Quia Copula non sola, sed unà cum prædicato sustinet officium prædicandi.

II. Si in verbis Cœnæ latet tropus aliquis, vel in subjecto, vel in prædicato lateat necesse est. Copula enim EST cum sustinere nequit, uti jam ostensum. Atqui in prædicato non latet ullus tropus. Quis enim ita vecors, aut ad prodigium usquè absurdus fuerit, qui Corpus tropicum pro nobis in mortem traditum esse: vel sangvinem tropicum pro nobis effusum esse, affirmare ausit. Quod ipsum Beza etiam intellexit, scribens ad Alamannū, Lugdunensis Ecclesiæ ministrum: Verba illa: (Quod pro vobis traditur, & qui pro vobis effunditur) necessariò buc te adigunt, de ipsamet Corporis & Sangvinis substantia hoc intelligere cogaris.

III. Subjectum verborum Institutionis est geminum: Aliud in verbis Apostoli dicentis: Panis, quem frangimus, nonné communicatio Corporis CHRISTI est? Poculum, cui benedicimus, nonné communicatio sangvinis CHRISTI est? Ubi in priore membro Subjectum est PANIS, quod ab omni tropo esse liberum, nemo nisi amens negaverit. In posteriore membro est Poculum, ubi continens pro contento accipi, nos ipsi ultrò fatemur, sed simul illud quoque addimus, hanc Synechdochen, δὶς διὰ πασῶν discrepare à Metonymiâ illâ Calvinianâ. Hæc enim mutato proprio & nativo verborum Institutionis sensu, substantiam Sacramenti hujus, nempè ipsum Corpus & Sangvinem CHRISTI prorsus è medio tollit. Synechdoche verò illa hanc ipsam ponit & asserit substantiam, hoc sensu, ut poculum, hoc est, vinum, sit κοινωνία Sangvinis CHRISTI. Sic enim ipse

Apostolus se explicat capite mox insequente undecimo prioris ad Corinthios, v. 24. inquiens: τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον, ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐστὶν ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου: Hoc poculum Novum Testamentum est in meo sangvine.

Finge enim saltem, quod Sacramentarij contendunt, Calicem μετωνυμικῶς esse figuram Novi Testamenti in Sangvine CHRISTI: consequens fuerit: 1. Sangvinem CHRISTI à Sangvine Agni Paschalis, & Sacrificiorum nihil differre: siquidem hîc quoque nihil fuit aliud, quàm typus, umbra, & Significatio Novi Testamenti. 2. Novum Testamentum substantiâ non differre à Vetere Testamento. 3. Novum Testamentum sui ipsius gerere typum & figuram. Quæ omnia cùm absurdissimis quibusque sint absurdiora, planum est, non Metonymicè, sed proprio ac nativo sensu, Poculum esse Testamentum novum in Sangvine CHRISTI: quia nimirùm vinum Eucharisticum, non significat, non figurat, aut umbrat: sed præsentem exhibet ac confert Sangvinem CHRISTI, illum ipsum Sangvinem, qui substantiam Novi Testamenti constituit & absolvit.

IV. Aliud Subjectum sese offert in verbis Matthæi & Marci: idque per pronomen demonstrativū HOC expressum: Qui cum B. Luthero figuram Synecdochen, inesse statuimus: non autem illam Rhetoricam, quæ æquè ac Metonymia Calviniana, mutat propriam ejus significationem, in figuratam & alienam Sed Synechdochen Grammaticam, quæ sub uno vocabulo, ejusque complexu duo distincta comprehendit, proprio ac nativo verborum sensu planè relicto integro & inviolato.

"Vult proindè, & innuit hæc Synechdo- "che Grammatica, duas disparatas res, Panem ni- "mirùm & Corpus: Vinum & Sangvinem simul ad- "esse præsentes, & unà exhiberi.

Præmissis quatuor hisce hypothesibus, irrefragabiliter concludimus, Verbis Institutionis, Hoc est Corpus meum, neque quoad Subjectum neque quoad prædicatum, neq; quoad Copulam, ullam inesse vel Metonymiam, vel figuram Rhetoricam aliam, quæ τὸ ῥητὸν evertat, & Calvinianorum, aut Zvvinglianorum significationi patrocinetur.

Jam ut ad propositum argumentum respondeamus, statuimus cum B. Luthero in Confessione Majore; In singulis & universis Scripturæ phrasibus sive propositionibus, quibus figurati aliquid inest, nunquàm Tropum sive figuram inesse copulæ EST, sed vel Subjecto, vel Prædicato: Eam verò figuram non esse Metonymiam: sed tantùm Metaphoram, quæ Copulam EST, in suo proprio & nativo sensu ac significatu relinquit.

Patet dicti veritas ex illis ipsis Exemplis, quæ magno numero producunt Adversarij: inter quæ Tropum Metaphoræ in Subjecto, sustinent hæ propositiones.

I. Petra erat CHRISTUS 1. Cor. 10, 4. Ubi Metaphora inest vocabulo Petræ, quæ non Corporalem aut terrenam: sed Spiritualem Petram, nempè CHRISTUM notabat. Siquidem Petra illa corporalis, ex quâ biberunt


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Hence (continued)

the Fathers, bore a type of that spiritual Rock which accompanied the Fathers in the desert: This spiritual Rock accompanying the Israelites did not signify, as Zwingli raves, CHRIST: but was CHRIST himself. Therefore the copula IS remains in its signification entirely intact and inviolate.

2. The seed is the word. Matth. 13, 38. Luke 8. Likewise: The field is the World v. 39. Matth. 13. The harvest is the end of the age: ibid. The reapers are the Angels. In all these predications we readily concede that the subject is tinged with the trope of metaphor: but we deny again and again that the copula (IS) is to be taken metonymically. For by seed is not denoted something earthly: but spiritual: which is likewise sown, not in an earthly field: but in a spiritual field. Thus harvest denotes to the Savior not some external and earthly harvest: but metaphorically denotes the heavenly harvest, which does not signify, but is the very end of the age: Thus reapers by some similarity do not signify the Angels: but are the Angels themselves. For as the harvest, so also are the reapers.

3. The seven lampstands are the seven Churches, Apoc. 1. Now they are not understood as earthly lampstands, but spiritual ones: which do not signify, but are those seven Churches, which by similitude, and in a transferred sense, on account of the brilliant radiance of the Gospel in them, are designated by the Holy Spirit with the epithet of lampstands.

4. The seven stars, which the Son of man holds in his right hand while walking in the midst of those lampstands, do not signify, but are the seven Angels or Bishops of the Churches: so called in a transferred sense, on account of the radiance of their doctrine and evangelical preaching.

The principal examples, where the same trope of Metaphor is present, are these:

1. I am the vine. 2. My Father is the husbandman. 3. You are the branches. 4. John is Elias. Where by metaphor, or a certain similitude, is understood: the heavenly or Spiritual vine and husbandman: likewise the spiritual branches, which are grafted into CHRIST through faith. Thus John is not simply Elias: but (as the words of Christ have it in Matth. 11, 14.) he is THAT Elias, who is to come in the Spirit and power of Elias: Luc. 1, 17. Matth. 17, 12, & 13. The sense therefore is not that John is Elias the Thesbite himself: but that he is the one who was predicted by Malachi in chapter 4, 5. and who was endowed with the Spirit and power of that Elias. Now if someone should imagine with the Zwinglians that a Metonymy is present in these propositions: this excellent sense will emerge: 1. That CHRIST is not that vine into which the faithful are grafted: but that he signifies another, who is this Vine. 2. That the heavenly Father is not the Husbandman: but that another heavenly husbandman must be sought, outside of GOD the Father: and so on: which is most absurd.

But there remain also other phrases, which are vehemently urged by our adversaries: such as these two: Circumcision or Baptism is the covenant: and the Lamb is the passover. But neither do these support their cause even in the least degree. For as regards the former, it is nowhere found ἀυτολεξεὶ in the Scriptures.

2. Orthodox theologians, if any use this phrase, by the Subject, namely the word Circumcision, do not understand only the external act, which is the amputation of the foreskin: but the entire federal action, consisting both of that external rite and of the federal promise itself, or the salutary use and fruit of this Sacrament. In which sense and broader complex the word Circumcision and Baptism does not signify the covenant, but is the very covenant itself entered into between GOD and the circumcised of the Old Testament, and the baptized faithful of the New Testament.

3. Even if the word Circumcision and Baptism were taken for the external rite alone, or the Sacramental act, which consists in the amputation of the foreskin and immersion in water: and indeed the word covenant, as the thing signified or fruit, were predicated of the Sign or Sacrament: yet no advantage redounds from that to the adversaries. For although we willingly concede that such a predication is Tropical, nay Metonymical: when the Effect is put for the Sign: just as when the toga is put for peace, or the fasces are put for authority: yet by no right can or should this be twisted to the words of the Institution. For it is not in question here between us and the Adversaries, in what mode of predication the fruit of the Sacrament is put for the Substance of the Sacrament itself: which no learned man would deny to be done by a Metonymy of Sign and Effect: But this is the question, How one essential part, that is, the body and blood of CHRIST, is predicated of the other Essential part, namely of the bread and wine? Where nothing figurative has any place: but the proper and native sense of each word being left, a singular and unusual predication emerges, yet a most true and most real one: as will be expressly demonstrated under the following fifth question.

As regards the latter proposition: The Lamb is the Passover, which the Adversaries explain thus by Metonymy: The Lamb is not, but signifies the Passover, or the passing over of the Lord: at the beginning the very words of Moses are to be noted, which exist in Exod. 12, 11, and are thus: You shall eat it in haste: It is the Passover of Jehovah. In which words two things are contained: 1. The command of Moses, concerning eating the Lamb in haste. 2. The reason on account of which the Lamb is to be eaten in haste, because namely on that very night the LORD is about to pass through Egypt, and to strike all the firstborn. Now anyone not entirely stupid or dull understands that not one, but two distinct propositions and predications, and both proper and regular, are noted in this place: One is: The Lamb is to be eaten in haste: The other: Today is the Passover of the Lord: or which is the same: Today the Lord will pass through Egypt. Whence now the remarkable insolence of the Sacramentarians becomes clear, who from two different predications construct one, and such a one indeed, as is nowhere found in the Scriptures. As if Moses had said:

The Lamb is the Passover of the LORD. Next, it well deserves observation that Moses himself, as if about to go against that insolence, so instructs his Israelites, that if by chance their children should ask, What does this work or Religion mean? then, they should not answer in the Calvinistic manner, The Lamb is the Passover of the LORD: but this is the Sacrifice or victim of the transition, or the passing over of the Lord: verse 26. Or if we render the Hebrew words as they sound: it is the Sacrifice of the transition itself to the LORD הוּא לַיהוָה זֶבַח פֶּסַח Where the word Transition is not of the Nominative, but of the Genitive case, in this sense: it is the Victim of the Transition or of the passing over, or of the passover. In which manner indeed Moses himself most clearly distinguishes between the passing over of the Lord, and the Lamb, so that neither is the other, or is said to be, whether Tropically or properly: but they are and remain distinct things, nay distracted and separated, because just as the Lamb is one thing, and the passing over of the Lord is another: so the one is also not said or predicated of the other. These things being so, we rightly detest the rashness of the Sacramentarians, who bring manifest force to the words of Moses: and as we explode every Metonymy, so also we explode every Metaphor from the words of the Supper. For neither is any parable here, or any dream proposed: such as was that concerning the seven cows, denoting seven years: or even any vision: but the Testament of the Son of GOD conceived in proper and clear words: so that even if parables, dreams, or visions could be given, in which a Metonymy might have a place: yet the consequence would not hold from there to the words of the Institution. And this indeed was the first argument of Zwingli, by which he wished to obtain that, in the words of the Supper, the Substantive verb IS is to be explained by SIGNIFIES.

Another argument of the same man was such: If the words of the Institution are to be taken literally, it would follow that in the Supper the body of CHRIST is present visibly: But this latter is false: Therefore also the former. He proved the connection of the major thus: That body is received in the Supper, which was delivered for you on the cross. But it was delivered visibly, Therefore it is also received visibly.

I answer that a fallacy is committed ϖᾱρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως (according to the figure of speech). For in the major premise, the word 'body' is taken not insofar as it is in the category of substance, as a true and natural human body endowed with a rational soul, but insofar as it is considered in the category of quality from the mere accident of visibility. Now, however, no reason for the consequence holds at all if, from the negation of an accident, an inference is made to the negation of the substance itself: as if actual visibility were of the necessity of presence, or indeed of the substance of the body of CHRIST: which is most false, as is evident even by the example of those who rose again together with CHRIST and, having entered the city of Jerusalem, could not be seen except by those to whom they voluntarily manifested themselves, Matt. 27. 53.

An accident is commonly defined as that which can be present or absent without the corruption of the subject. Zwingli therefore produces a notable ἀρρωsίαν διανόιας (sickness of mind), contending that an accident, namely visibility, cannot be absent without the corruption of the subject. For although it happens to physical bodies, and those not yet glorified, because of ὕνητὴν δυσχέρειαν (material difficulty), as the Philosopher speaks, lib. 2. de cœlo cap. 1, that they are always actually visible wherever they are: meanwhile, however, this visibility is not their property susatikὴ (essential): since it does not enter into the definition of a true natural body: nor, and indeed much less, can it be distorted to glorified bodies and their essence: since they can be somewhere, even if they are not seen: but least of all in the body of CHRIST is this Accident of any necessity, so that in Luke 24:31, with the two Apostles sitting by in the inn at Emmaus, that ἄφαν- τω (invisible) state could have come to pass. The connection of the major premise labors under the same futility. For he confuses the Accident with the subject, or the Thing with the mode of the thing. What? Because the delivery unto death was an act of the deepest humiliation: therefore an act of power and majesty, such as also obtains in this Sacrament, the consequence is not valid.

Latin:

Patres, Typum gessit Spiritualis illius Petræ, quæ Patres in deserto fuit comitata: Hæc Spiritualis Petra Israelitas concomitans, non significabat, uti Zvvinglius delirat, CHRISTUM: sed erat ipse CHRISTUS. Manet proindè Copula EST significatio ἰδιαρτικὴ omninò sarta & inviolata.

2. Semen est verbum. Matth. 13, 38. Luc. 8. Item: Ager est Mundus v. 39. Matth. 13. Messis est consummatio seculi: ibid. Messores sunt Angeli. In his prædicationibus omnibus Subjectum Metaphoræ tropo tinctum esse, ultrò concedimus: Copulam verò (EST) Metonymicè accipiendam esse, iterum atque iterum negamus. Semen enim non notatur aliquod terrenum: sed spirituale: quod mittitur itidem, non in agrum terrenum: sed in agrum Spiritualem. Sic messis notat Servatori non messem aliquam externam & terrenam: sed Metaphoricè notat messem Cœlestem, quæ non significat, sed est ipsa consummatio seculi: Sic Messores per similitudinem aliquam non significant Angelos: sed sunt ipsi Angeli. Nam qualis messis, tales etiam sunt messores.

3. Septem candelabra sunt septem Ecclesiæ, Apoc. 1. Jam non intelliguntur Candelabra terrena, sed spiritualia: quæ non significant, sed sunt septem illæ Ecclesiæ, quæ per similitudinem, & sensu translatitio, propter luculentem in eis Evangelij fulgorem, à Spiritu Sancto, Candelabrorum epitheto indigetantur.

4. Septem stellæ, quas tenet Filius hominis in medio candelabrorum illorum obambulans, in manu suâ dextrâ, non significant, sed sunt septem Angeli sive Episcopi Ecclesiæ, rum: sensu translatitio sic dicti, propter fulgorem doctrinæ, & prædicationis Evangelicæ.

Exempla, ubi idem tropus Metaphoræ Prædicatio inest, præcipua sunt hæc:

1. Ego sum vitis. 2. Pater meus est agricula. 3. Vos estis palmites. 4. Johannes est Elias. Ubi per metaphoram, sive similitudinem quandam intelligitur: vitis & agricola cœlestis, sive Spiritualis: Spirituales item palmites, quæ per fidem CHRISTO inseruntur. Sic Johannes non simpliciter est Elias: sed (uti verba Christi habent Matth. 11, 14.) est Elias ILLE, qui venturus est in Spiritu, & virtute Eliæ: Luc. 1, 17. Matth. 17, 12, & 13. Sensus ergò non est, Johannem esse ipsum Eliam Thesbitem: sed esse illum, qui prædictus erat à Malachiâ cap. 4, 5. quique qui Spiritu & virtute Eliæ illius fuit præditus. Jam si fingat aliquis cum Zvvinglianis, propositionibus istis inesse Metonymiam: sensus egregius evadet iste: 1. CHRISTUM non esse vitem illam, cui inseruntur fideles: sed significare alium, qui sit hæc Vitis. 2. Patrem cœlestem non esse Agricolam: sed alium, extra DEUM patrem, quærendum esse cœlestem agricolam: & sic deinceps: id quod absurdissimum.

Sed supersunt & aliæ phrasæs, quæ ab adversarijs vehementer urgentur: quales sunt hæ duæ: Circumcisio vel Baptismus est fœdus: & Agnus est pascha. Sed neque hæ ipsorum causæ vel tantillum patrocinantur. Nam quoad priorē, ea nuspiam ἀυτολεξεὶ in Scripturis reperitur.

2. Orthodoxi Theologi, si qui hâc phrasi utuntur, per Subjectum, nempè vocem Circumcisionis, non intelligunt solum actum externum, qui est amputatio præputij: sed integram actionem fœderalem, constantem tùm externo illo ritu, tùm ipsâ promissione fœderali, sive salutari usu & fructu Sacramenti hujus. Quo sanè sensu & complexu latiorê accepta vox Circumcisionis & Baptismi non significat fœdus, sed est ipsissimus fœdus inter DEUM ac circumcisos Veteris Testamenti, & baptizatos Novi Testamenti fideles initum.

3. Si vel maximè Circumcisionis & Baptismi vox, accipiantur pro solo externo ritu, sive actu Sacramentali, qui in amputatione præputij, & immersione in aquam consistit: & verò vox fœderis, tanquàm signatum sive fructus, prædicetur de Signo sive Sacramento: nihil tamen indè præsidij ad adversarios redundat. Etsi enim libenter concedimus, talem prædicationem esse Tropicam, imò Metonymicam: quando Effectus pro Signo ponitur: haud secus, ac quando pro pace ponitur toga, vel pro imperio ponuntur fasces: nullo tamen jure hoc ad verba Institutionis detorqueri vel potest, vel debet. Non enim hoc loco inter nos & Adversarios controvertitur, quo prædicationis modo fructus Sacramenti, pro ipsâ Substantiâ Sacramenti ponatur: id quod per Metonymiam Signi & Effectus fieri, eruditorum nemo negaverit: Sed hoc quæstionis est, Quomodo pars una essentialis, hocest, corpus & sangvis CHRISTI, prædicetur de alterà parte Essentiali, nempè de pane & vino? Ubi nihil quicquam figurati locum obtinet: sed relicto proprio ac nativo singulorum verborum sensu, prædicatio emergit singularis & inusitata, verissima tamen & realissima: uti sub sequente quæstione quintâ ex professo demonstrabitur.

Quoad posteriorem propositionem: Agnus est Pascha, quam Adversarij per Metonymiam sic explicant: Agnus non est, sed significat Pascha, sive transitum Domini: initiò ipsa verba Mosis notanda veniunt, quæ extant Exod. 12, 11. & sic habent: Comedetis festinantes: Est enim Pascha Jehovæ. Quibus verbis duo continentur: 1. Mandatum Mosis, de comedendo Agno festinanter. 2. Ratio propter quam Agnus festinanter sit comedendus, quia nimirùm eâ ipsâ nocte DOMINUS transiturus sit per Ægyptum, & percussurus omnia primogenita. Jam quisq́; non planè stupidus aut bardus intelligit, non unam, sed duas distinctas propositiones & prædicationes, & utraq́; proprias ac regulares, hoc loco notari: Una est: Agnus festinanter est comedendus: Altera: Hodiè est Pascha Domini: vel quod idem est: Hodie transibit Dominus per Ægyptū. Undè jam insignis petulantia Sacramentariorū elucescit, qui ex duabǫ diversis prædicationibǫ unā extruunt, & talem quidem, quæ in Sacris nuspiam reperitur. Quasi Moses dixisset:

Agnus est Pascha DOMINI. Deindè observationem probè meretur, quod Moses ipse, quasi petulantiæ isti obviam iturus, sic instruit suos Israëlitas, ut si fortè filij ipsorum quæsiverint, Quid sibi velit opus hoc sive Religio? tum, non respondeant more Calvinistico, Agnus est Pascha DOMINI: sed hoc est Sacrificium sive victima transitionis, sive transitus Domini: versu 26. Vel si verba Hebræa reddamus prout sonant: est Sacrificium transitionis ipsum DOMINO הוּא לַיהוָה זֶבַח פֶּסַח Ubi vox Transitus non est Nominativi, sed Genitivi casus, hoc sensu: est Victima Transitus sive Transitionis, sive paschatis. Quo sanè pacto Moses ipse luculentissimè distingvit, inter Transitum Domini, & inter Agnum, ita, ut neutrum sit alterum, aut esse dicatur, sive Tropicè, sive propriè: sed sint & maneant res distinctæ, imò distractæ & separatæ, quòd sicut aliud est Agnus, & aliud Transitus Domini: sic alterum quoque de altero non dicatur, aut prædicetur. Quibus ita se habentibus meritò detestamur Sacramentariorum temeritatem, vim manifestam inferentium verbis Mosis: & uti Metonymiam omnem, sic etiam Metaphoram omnem ex verbis Cœnæ explodimus. Neque enim hîc vel parabola aliqua, vel somnium aliquod proponitur: quale fuit illud de septem vaccis, notantibus septem annos: vel etiam visio aliqua: sed Testamentum Filij DEI proprijs ac perspicuis verbis conceptum: ita ut si maximè dari possent parabolæ, somnia, visiones, in quibus Metonymia locum haberet: tamen indè ad verba Institutionis non valeret consequentia. Et hoc quidem primum fuit argumentum Zvvinglij, quo obtinere voluit, in verbis Cœnæ, verbum Substantivum EST, esse exponendum per SIGNIFICAT.

Alterum ejusdem argumentum tale erat: Si κʹ το ρητὸν verba Institutionis sunt accipienda, consequens fuerit, ut in Cœnâ corpus CHRISTI adsit visibiliter: Atqui hoc posterius falsum: Ergò & prius illud. Majoris connexum sic probabat: Illud corpus accipitur in Cœnâ, quòd pro vobis traditum est in cruce. Atqui traditum est visibiliter, Ergò visibile etiam accipitur.

Respondeo, committi Sophisma ϖᾱρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως. Nam in Majore vox corporis accipitur, non quatenùs illud in categoriâ Substantiæ, pro vero & naturali corpore humano, animâ rationali præditum, sed quatenùs in Categoriâ Qualitatis ex nudo Visibilitatis accidente consideratur. Jam verònulla prorfus militat ratio consequentiæ, si ex negatione accidentis, fiat collectio ad negationem ipsius substantiæ: ac si visibilitas actualis sit de necessitate præsentiæ, imò de substantiâ corporis CHRISTI: Quod falsissimum esse, vel illorum exemplo patet, qui cum CHRISTO simul resurrexerunt, inque urbem Hierosolymorum ingressi non videri potuerunt, nisi ab illis, quibus se ultrò manifestarunt, Matth. 27. 53.

Vulgò definitur accidens, quòd possit adesse, vel abesse, subjecti corruptionem. Prodit ergò Zvvinglius insignem ἀρρωsίαν διανόιας contendens, accidens, nempè visibilitatem non posse abesse citra subjecti corruptionem. Etsi enim corporibus Physicis, ac nondum clarificatis, propter ὕνητὴν δυσχέρειαν, ut loquitur Philosophus, lib. 2. de cœlo cap. 1. usu venit, ut semper actu sint visiblia, ubi, ubi sunt: interim tamen visibilitas isthæc, neque est illorum proprietas susatikὴ: siquidem definitionem veri naturalis corporis non ingreditur: neque, & quidem multò minùs ad corpora clarificata, eorundemque essentiam detorqueri potest: quippè quæ alicubi esse possunt, licèt non videantur: minimè verò omnium in corpore CHRISTI Accidens hoc ullius est necessitatis, ita, ut Luc. 24, 31. assidentibus duobus Apostolis, in diversorio Emauntico, ἄφαντω inconspicuum illud fieri potuerit. Connexum Majoris eadem futilitate laborat. Confundit enim Accidens cum subjecto, sive Rem cum modo rei, Quid? quòd traditio in mortem, actus fuit exinanitionis profundissimæ: Undè actum potentiæ & majestatis. qualis etiam in hoc Sacramento obtinet, non valet consequentia.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Hence (continued)

But enough of Zwingli: Oecolampadius followed him, who, intending to correct Zwingli's error as being too harsh, judged that the words of CHRIST should be interpreted thus: THIS IS MY BODY, that is, the bread is a figure, or sign of my body: thus constituting the Trope not in the substantive verb IS, but in the word body, namely in the Predicate: Which he contends is to be understood not for the true body of CHRIST, but for a figure of it.

But this error is too gross to need refutation by many words. For

1. he opposes even the grammatical precepts themselves. For in every Trope, by which the proper meaning of any word is transferred to a new one, the method of signifying and figuring is such: that the proper meaning always signifies or figures the new one: but not vice versa, that the new meaning figures the proper one. As for example, when CHRIST is called a vine: there the proper and old meaning remains for the word Vine, which however figures the new meaning, by reason of which CHRIST is said to be the Vine: indeed so that CHRIST does not signify the vine, or is a figure of the vine: but rather that the vine figures CHRIST. Now, however, in the Oecolampadian Trope or figuration, the exact opposite happens. For he places the figure, or sign of the body, in a new and transferred sense, for the body itself: where the new meaning, in a clearly inverted order, figures the proper one: which is absurd.

2. It has already been demonstrated before that the Savior speaks of that body which was delivered unto death for us: which cannot be predicated of any figure or image of the body of CHRIST except by horrible blasphemy.

3. It is established by the confession of the Adversaries themselves: that the bread in the Holy Supper is a Sign or Symbol of the body of CHRIST: Now if in the Oecolampadian sense,

the word body will denote the same thing as Figure, or Sign of the body: It would follow: that the Sign is no longer a Sign of the Signified: But a Sign of a Sign: nor is the shadow any longer a shadow of the body: but is a shadow of a shadow: and consequently both the bread of the Holy Supper is a Sign and figure: and the body likewise is a Sign and figure. What then will finally be given as the Signified or figured? Thus therefore the Adversaries become fools in the thinking of their mind, wishing to seem wise. Rom. 2:28.

But Oecolampadius also repeatedly urged the authority of Tertullian against B. LUTHER, who writes thus in lib. 4. against Marcion: CHRIST, having taken the bread and distributed it to the disciples, made it his body: by saying This is my body: that is, a Figure of the body. But it would not have been a Figure, unless it were a body of truth: Moreover, an empty thing, which is a phantom, could not take a figure. Or if he feigned the Bread to be a body for himself because he lacked the truth of a body: Therefore he ought to have delivered the Bread for us.

But not even in this way does Oecolampadius obtain anything. For

1. Clear is the assertion of Tertullian saying: that CHRIST made the bread he received his Body, by saying: This is my body: which is what utterly undermines and overturns the gloss of Oecolampadius. For these two things can in no way stand together: CHRIST by saying, This is my Body, makes the Bread his body: which is what Tertullian asserts: And CHRIST by saying, This is my body: made the body a figure of his body: which is what Oecolampadius foolishly raves.

2. A fallacy is committed παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως, in these words of Tertullian: that is, figure of the body. For to be a figure is understood in two ways: Sometimes it signifies the same as to sustain the shadow, image, or type of some thing, just as the Sacrifices and Ceremonies of the Old Testament were such figures of a thing absent, and at some time to be exhibited. But sometimes this phrase is taken in a stricter sense, so that Figure does not denote the shadow or image of an absent thing, but designates a Mathematical Form, which consists of its own certain dimensions: In which sense the word Figure is equivalent to the word species. Having rejected the former, Tertullian has embraced this latter. For because he himself had a controversy with the heretic Marcion, who contended that CHRIST did not have a true and natural body: but only a phantom and semblance of a true body: therefore Tertullian, intending to go against this impiety, seeks an argument from the figure of the visible species, and from this, for the sake of asserting the truth of the Body of CHRIST, he concludes most firmly in this manner:

" If the Body of CHRIST was only a phantom, " and a semblance: it certainly could not have been represented by a visible figure and species. But he did represent his Body by a visible figure and " species. Therefore it was not that phantom " or semblance.

And again the same Tertullian, regarding the present business, infers thus: CHRIST says; This is my Body, which is given for you: Now if CHRIST, as Marcion contends, does not have a true body, but only a phantom: it follows that Bread was given for us unto death, since a phantom cannot be delivered up. But this latter is absurd and impious. Therefore, the former will also be impious: namely, that CHRIST did not have a true Body. Both of which arguments of Oecolampadius are so far from establish and corroborate it.

But, setting aside Oecolampadius, I make an approach to the school of Calvin, which, intending to impugn the literal sense of the words of CHRIST, repeats from the beginning from the school of Zwingli all those places of the Scriptures which, either by reason of the subject or by reason of the predicate, sustain a trope of metaphor: and from there they are accustomed to collect [arguments] to establish metonymy. Since the vanity of this collection was demonstrated quite evidently a little while ago, it is of no use to deal with it at greater length in this place.

But the Calvinists also have other arguments, which we shall examine in a few words:

I. It stands thus: Those things which are to be understood sacramentally cannot be taken literally. But the words of CHRIST: This is my Body, are words proper to a sacrament: Therefore they are to be understood sacramentally: and consequently they cannot be taken in the literal sense.

Calvin valued this argument so highly that in his last admonition to Westphal he exclaimed: Let this be a wall of bronze.

But I reply that this argument is hardly worth a straw. For the major premise labors under a manifest begging of the question: For no evident nerve of consequence has yet been given in this assertion: Whatever words are proper to a sacrament, they ought not to be taken in their native sense. Let them therefore first demonstrate the truth of this hypothesis. If they bark: Words proper to a sacrament are not to be understood except sacramentally. If sacramentally: Therefore also tropically or figuratively. We reply again that the antecedent is not completely true. So that this may appear more clearly, we correct the false hypothesis of the Calvinists through a more accurate explanation of the equivocation. For something is said to be sacramental or sacramentally in two ways: First, in the Lutheran and Orthodox sense: then, in the Calvinistic and heterodox sense. For to Luther and all the Orthodox, sacramentally is the same as mystically: so that the sacramental is opposed to that which behaves according to a royal, proper, customary, and essential mode of predicating. In which sense, to the Orthodox, the sacraments are and are called mysteries, because, forsooth, they transcend every order of nature and surpass every human intellect. But to the Calvinists, sacramental and sacramentally, in a new and fictitious sense unknown to all antiquity, is the same as tropical or figurative. When, therefore, they contend that the words of CHRIST are to be taken sacramentally, they mean nothing else than that they are to be understood tropically, so that the Bread and Wine are not media exhibiting the very Body and Blood of Christ: but are only signs, and by metonymy represent the Body and Blood of CHRIST significatively.

Where a memorable trickery and craftiness toward the method of deceit, a crafty Sophistry, is detected in the Calvinists. They contend that the words of the Supper are to be taken figuratively. If you ask the reason, they reply, Because they are words proper to a sacrament: Therefore they are to be understood sacramentally. If you press by asking: What is sacramentally? He replies that it is the same as figuratively. Thus, therefore, they most shamefully prove the same by the same, and wickedly trifle, not otherwise than if they were to say: The words of the Supper are to be understood figuratively, because they are to be understood figuratively. Such, forsooth, is the candor the adversaries display in disputing. Which same dishonesty they also display as often as they contend that the words of CHRIST are words of a mystery. Therefore they are to be understood mystically. Where again, mystery to them is the same as a trope: and mystical the same as figurative: which is most rightly denied by the Orthodox. For that is and is called mystical which is singular and unusual. But in figures there is nothing of mystery, nothing unusual: since all figurative locutions can be reduced to proper or regular ones. But this proposition (This is my body) can never be reduced to any proper or regular predication! Therefore it is not figurative.

II. The argument of the Calvinists is as follows: The words of the Institution are to be accepted according to CHRIST'S interpretation. But CHRIST interprets them thus: Do this in remembrance of me. Therefore they are to be accepted tropically.

I answer that this argument consists of as many terms as it is almost completed in words: therefore it collapses by its own ἀσυλλογισίᾳ (non-syllogism). 2. It suffers from the fallacy of ἑτεροζητήσεως (irrelevant conclusion): and it confuses the substance of the Sacrament with the fruit of the Sacrament. The question between us and our Adversaries is concerning the very substance of this Sacrament, which ought to be elicited from these words, This is my body: whether they ought to be understood properly or tropically? They themselves answer, tropically: but why indeed? Because CHRIST afterwards said: Do this in remembrance of me: which words designate the use and fruit of this Sacrament. Let every pious person judge here again what candor these men use in disputing. Calvin certainly is more candid than his disciples, for he expressly writes that these words, Do this in remembrance of me, do not pertain to the substance of this Sacrament, but to the Action. 3. Let them at last demonstrate to us the nerve of the connection in this inference. The Sacrament of the Supper is to be performed in remembrance of the death of CHRIST. Therefore the words of CHRIST, This is my body, are to be accepted tropically. If they show us this nerve, then we shall respond more fully to this cavil.

III. The argument of the Calvinists, drawn from the authority of the Fathers, is likewise liable to many weaknesses and charges of falsehood: concerning which, let the Refutation of the Calvinist Consensus be seen first of all: and the booklet of D. Chemnitz, whose title is, Foundations of the Supper. That one thing is to be observed, that the Fathers have many times called bread and wine a Symbol, Sign, Figure, Type, Image of the Body of CHRIST, not in a metonymic sense: but in that sense in which they rightly disputed against heretics, that Bread is not essentially changed into the Body of CHRIST, but is a Type, Symbol, Sign, not indeed merely σχετικὸν, as the Calvinists wish, but προσφερόμενον καὶ διαδοτικὸν. For because the Body of CHRIST is not seen, but as if covered under the figure of bread, it is truly received with the bread; therefore they most rightly and most truly called the Bread a Symbol and Type, nay even a Figure of the Body of CHRIST, in the sense already explained.

Latin:

Sed satis de Zvvinglio: Hunc insecutus est Oecolampadius, qui Zvvinglij errorem, tanquam duriorem correcturus, verba CHRISTI sic interpretanda esse censuit: HOC EST CORPUS MEUM, id est, Panis est figura, sive signum corporis mei:sic Tropũ constituens non in verbo substantivo EST, sed in voce corporis, nempè in Prædicato: Quod non pro vero CHRISTI corpore: sed pro figurâ ejus intelligendum esse contendit.

Verùm crassior est error iste, quàm ut pluribus refutari debeat. Nam

1. ipsis quoque præceptis Grammaticis ille adversatur. In omni enim Tropo, quo propria vocabuli alicujus significatio ad novam transfertur, ea est signandi & figurandi ratio: ut propria significatio, semper signet aut figuret novam: non verò vice versâ, nova significatio figuret propriam. Ut exempli gratia, cùm CHRISTUS appellatur vitis: ibi vocabulo, Viti, propria sua & vetus manet significatio, quæ ramen novam figurat significationem, ratione cujus CHRISTUS dicitur esse Vitis: ita quidem, ut CHRISTUS non significet vitem, aut sit figura vitis: sed ut vitis potiùs figuret CHRISTUM. Jam verò in Tropo, sive figuratione Oecolampadianâ prorsus fit contrarium. Ponit enim ille figuram, sive signum corporis, novo & translatitio sensu, pro ipso corpore: ubi nova significatio, inverso planè ordine, figurat propriam: id quod absurdum.

2. Jam antè demonstratum, Servatorem de eo loqui corpore, quod pro nobis in mortem est traditum: id quod de figurâ aliquâ aut imagine corporis CHRISTI, non nisi per horrendam blasphemiam prædicari potest.

3. Constat ipsorum etiam Adversariorum confessione: Panem in S. Cœnâ esse Signum sive Symbolum corporis CHRISTI: Jam si sensu Oe-

colampadiano, vox corporis idem notabit, quod Figura, sive Signum corporis: Consequens fuerit: Signum non ampliùs esse Signum Signati: Sed Signum Signi: neque umbram ampliùs esse umbram corporis: sed esse umbram umbræ: ac proindè & Panem S. Cænæ esse Signum ac figuram: & corpus itidem esse Signum & figuram. Quodnám ergò dabitur tandem Signatum aut figuratum? Sic ergò stulti evadunt in cogitatione mentis suæ Adversarij, volentes videri sapientes. Rom. 2, 28.

Sed & autoritatem Tertulliani subindè contra B. LUTHERUM urgebat Oecolampadius, qui lib. 4. adversus Marcionem sic scribit: CHRISTUS acceptum panem, & distributum discipulis, fecit illum corpus suum: Hoc est corpus meum dicendo: id est, Figura corporis. Figura autem non fuisset, nisi veritatis esset corpus: Cæterùm vacua res, quod est phantasma, figuram capere non posset. Aut si proptereà Panem corpus sibi finxit, quia corporis carebat veritate: Ergò Panem debuit tradere pro nobis.

Verùm ne sic quidem aliquid obtinet Oecolampadius. Nam

1. Luculenta est assertio Tertulliani dicentis: CHRISTUM panem acceptum fecisse Corpus suum, dicendo: Hoc est corpus meum: id quod Oecolampadij glossam funditus subruit, & evertit. Duo enim hæc simul stare nullo modo possunt: CHRISTUS dicendo, Hoc est Corpus meum, efficit Panem corpus suum: id quod Tertullianus asserit: Et CHRISTUS dicendo, Hoc est corpus meum: effecit corpus figuram corporis sui: id quod Oecolampadius ineptè delirat.

2. Committitur Sophisma παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως, in verbis hisce Tertulliani: id est, figura corporis. Figuram enim esse duobus modis accipitur: Interdum enim idem signat, ac umbram, imaginem, aut typum alicujus rei sustinere, quemadmodum Sacrificia ac Ceremoniæ Veteris Testamenti, tales erant figuræ rei absentis, & aliquando exhibendæ. Interdum verò phrasis hæc in strictiore sensu accipitur, ita ut Figura non umbram aut imaginem rei absentis notet, sed designet Formam Mathematicam, quæ certis suis constat demensionibus: Quo sensu Figuræ vocabulum æquipollet vocabulo speciei. Priore illa repudiatâ, posteriorem hanc amplexus est Tertullianus. Quia enim ipsi Controversia erat, cum Marcione hæretico, qui contendebat, CHRISTUM non habuisse verum & naturale corpus: sed phantasma tantùm ac simulachrum veri corporis: ideò Tertullianus, impietati huic obviam iturus argumentum petit à figurâ visibilis speciei, & ex hâc firmissimè pro asserendâ veritate Corporis CHRISTI, colligit in hunc modum:

" Si Corpus CHRISTI phantasma tantùm, " & simulachrum fuit: utique visibili figurâ ac specie " repræsentari non potuit. Atqui visibili figurâ ac " specie Corpus suum repræsentavit. Ergò Phantaf- " ma illud aut simulachrum non fuit.

Et rursus idem Tertullianus, quoad præsens negocium sic infert: CHRISTUS dicit; Hoc est Corpus, quod pro vobis traditur: Jam si CHRISTUS, uti Marcion contendit, verum corpus non habet; sed phantasma tantùm: sequitur, Panem pro nobis traditum esse in mortem: Phantasma siquidem tradi non potest. At posterius hoc absurdum & impium. Ergò impium erit etiam prius illud: nempè CHRISTUM verum Corpus non habuisse. Quæ utraque argumentatio Oecolampadij tantum abest, ut τὸ ῥητὸν verborum CHRISTI evertat, ut mirificè potiùs id stabiliat & corroboret.

Sed misso Oecolampadio, ad Calvini scholam accessum facio, quæ τὸ ῥητὸν verborum CHRISTI impugnatura, initiò ex scholâ Zvvinglij repetit universa illa scripturarum loca, quæ vel ratione subjecti, vel ratione prædicati Tropum Metaphoræ sustinent: & indè ad stabiliendam metonymiam colligere solent. Cujus collectionis vanitas cùm paulò antè satis evidenter sit demonstrata, nihil attinet, pluribus hoc loco de eâ agere.

Sed habent & alia argumenta Calviniani, quæ paucis examinabimus:

I. Sic habet: Quæ Sacramentaliter sunt intelligenda, ea propriè accipi non possunt Atqui verba CHRISTI: Hoc est Corpus meum, sunt verba Sacramenti propria: Ergò Sacramentaliter sunt intelligenda: & per consequens τὸ ῥητὸν accipi non possunt.

Hoc argumentum tanti fecit Calvinus, ut in ultimâ admonitione ad VVestphalum exclamaret: Hic murus aheneus esto.

Sed respondeo, vix stramineum hoc esse argumentum. Major enim manifestâ laborat petitione principij: Nondùm enim datus est evidens aliquis consequentiæ nervus, in hâc assertione: Quæcunque verba sunt Sacramenti propria, ea in nativo sensu accipi non debent. Demonstrent ergò priùs hypotheseos hujus veritatem. Si ogganniant: Verba Sacramenti propria, non sunt, nisi Sacramentaliter intelligenda. Si Sacramentaliter: Ergò & tropicè sive figuratè. Respondemus rursus, Antecedens non esse completè verùm. Quod ut dilucidiùs pateat, corrigimus falsam Calvinianorum hypothesin per æquivocationis accuratiorem enodationem. Duobus enim modis aliquid dicitur esse Sacramentale, vel Sacramentaliter: Primùm sensu Lutherano & Orthodoxo: deindè sensu Calvinistico, & heterodoxo. Luthero enim & Orthodoxis omnibus Sacramentaliter idem est, quod Mysticè: ita, ut τὸ Sacramentale opponatur ei, quod se habet secundum regalem, proprium, usitatum ac essentialem prædicandi modū. Quo sensu Orthodoxis Sacramenta sunt, & dicuntur Mysteria, quia nimirùm omnem naturæ ordinem transcendunt, omnemq; intellectum humanum superant. Calvinianis verò Sacramentale & Sacramentaliter, novo & fictitio, totique antiquitati ignoto sensu, idem est, quod Tropicum sive figuratum. Quando ergò contendunt, verba CHRISTI esse Sacramentaliter accipienda, nihil volunt aliud, quàm Tropicè ea esse intelligenda, ita ut Panis & Vinum non sint media exhibentia ipsum Corpus & Sangvinem Christi: sed sint Signa tantùm, & per metonymiam significativè repræsentent Corpus & Sangvinem CHRISTI.

Ubi memorabilis κυβεία καὶ πανεργία πρὸς τὴν μεθοδείαν τῆς, veteratoria Sophisticatio in Calvinianis deprehenditur. Contendunt illi, Verba Cœnæ esse figuratè accipienda. Si causam rogites, respondent, Quia sunt verba Sacramenti propria: Ergò Sacramentaliter sunt intelligenda. Si quærendo instes: Quid Sacramentaliter? Respondet esse idem, quod figuratè. Sic ergò turpissimè probant idem per idem, & improbè nugantur, non aliter, ac si dicerent: Verba Cœnæ sunt figuratè intelligenda, quia sunt figuratè intelligenda. Talem nimirùm candorem in disputando produnt Adversarij. Quam eandem improbitatem produnt etiam, quoties contendunt, verba CHRISTI esse verba Mysterij. Ergò mysticè esse intelligenda. Ubi rursus Mysterium ipsis idem est, quod Tropus: & mysticum idem, quod figuratum: id quod ab Orthodoxis rectissimè negatur. Mysticum enim est ac dicitur, quod est singulare atque inusitatum. Atqui in figuris nihil inest mysterij, nihil inusitati: Siquidem omnes figuratæ locutiones, reduci possunt ad proprias, sive regulares. Hæc verò propositio (Hoc est corpus meum) ad ullam propriam aut regularem prædicationem in æternum reduci nequit! Ergò figurata non est.

II. Argumentum Calvinianorum tale est: Verba Institutionis sunt accipienda juxta CHRISTI interpretationem. Atqui CHRISTUS ea sic interpretatur: Hoc facite, in mei commemorationem. Ergò Tropicè sunt accipienda.

Respondeo, tot terminis constare hoc argumentum, quot ferimè verbis absolvitur: Ergò propriâ ἀσυλλογισίᾳ corruit. 2. Laborat illud Sophismate ἑτεροζητήσεως: & confundit substantiam Sacramenti cum fructu Sacramenti. Quæstio est inter nos & Adversarios, de ipsâ substantiâ Sacramenti hujus, quæ ex verbis hisce, Hoc est corpus meum, erui debet: Utrum propriè, an Tropicè ea intelligi debeant? Respondent ipsi, Tropicè: Quare verò? Quia CHRISTUS postmodum dixerit: Hoc facite in mei commemorationem: Quæ verba usum & fructum Sacramenti hujus designant. Judicet hic rursus pių quisque, quod candore in disputando utantur isti homines. Calvinus certè candidior suis discipulis verba isthæc, Facite hoc in mei commemorationem, non ad substantiam hujus Sacramenti, sed ad Actionem pertinere disertè scribit. 3. Demonstrent nobis vel tandem nervum connexi, in hâc collectione. Sacramentum Cœnæ est peragendum in commemorationem mortis CHRISTI. Ergò verba CHRISTI, Hoc est corpus meum, sunt accipienda Tropicè. Quem nervum si nobis ostenderint, tum uberiùs ad hoc cavillum respondebimus.

III. Calvinianorum argumentum petitum ab autoritate Patrum, multis itidem infirmitatibus, & criminibus falsi est obnoxium: de quo cuprimis videatur Refutatio Consensus Calvinistici: & Libellus D. Chemnitij, cui titulus, Fundamenta Cœnæ. Unum illud observandum, quodPatres panem & vinum nominârint multoties Symbolum, Signum, Figuram, Typum, Imaginem Corporis CHRISTI, non sensu metonymico: sed eo sensu, quo contra hæreticos rectè disputârunt, Panem non essentialiter mutari in Corpus CHRISTI, sed esse Typum, Symbolum, Signum, non quidem σχετικὸν tantùm, ut Calviniani volunt, sed προσφερόμενον καὶ διαδοτικὸν. Quia enim Corpus CHRISTI non videtur, sed sub figurâ panis quasi opertum, verè accipitur cum pane; ideò Panem rectissimè ac verissimè nominarunt Symbolum ac Typum, imò Figuram etiam Corporis CHRISTI, sensu jam explicato.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: What are the essential parts, constituting the substance of this Sacrament
