Just as all the other Sacraments, both of the Old and of the New Testament, have a twofold constituting matter: Elementary and Heavenly: So the Sacrament of the Eucharist also consists of, and is completed by, two parts, as regards substance: not however existing in any way whatsoever, but as things, or essences, or substances, existing in reality.

This is proved 1. from the words of the Institution, which pertain to describing the substance of this Sacrament, by all of which nothing νοητὸν, or λογικὸν, ἢ τυπικὸν is signified: but mere things and matters existing in the nature of things.

2. From the analogical nature of the Sacraments of the Old and New Testament, to the former of which the Apostle attributes a shadow: but to the latter he assigns ἀυτὸ τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἀυτὴν τὴν ἐικόνα τῶν πραγμάτων to denote the real existence of the matter.

3. From the Use of this Sacrament. For this Sacrament is joined to the Evangelical promise, so that it may provide the use of a pledge. Now it is the nature and property of pledges that they be something material, or Essential. The Sacramentarians indeed pretend that the Sacraments were instituted for this end, that through visible and external things we might be led to the contemplation of heavenly things: but by this arrangement they constitute only one thing, or matter of one kind in the Sacrament: and thus new loaves of proposition, as it were, are introduced into the Church of the New Testament. Which is clearly ἀσύστατον.

Moreover, these two things or matters, proper to the substance itself in this Sacrament, are meanwhile of a most diverse kind, and of most dissimilar nature: one Elementary; and therefore visible: the other heavenly, and therefore invisible, not indeed in every way, and simply: but to the nature of men still corrupt, and still joined with the concretion of mortal matter.

Now both these parts, as well the invisible as the visible, are not of one, but of a twofold species: according to the very diversity of the act, which the Savior willed to be proper to this Sacramental action, and indeed twofold.

For because CHRIST willed to institute in this Sacrament not a half-full, but an entire and perfect feeding, which would consist of both eating and drinking together: therefore for eating, from the elementary kind, He destined Bread: but from the heavenly, His Body: for drinking, however, again from the elementary kind, He destined Wine: but from the heavenly, His Blood. To these two, therefore, although most diverse, and differing in their whole kind, the name of Sacrament properly belongs not to one or the other separately: but to both together: and the office of Signifying belongs to the same, not to one, but to both together.

These things which have already been said concerning the nature of these two parts can be demonstrated by certain reasons: And first indeed from the very τῷ ῥητῷ (literal wording) of the words of CHRIST, their tenor, vigor, and rigor. For each elementary part is expressed by the name of Bread and Cup, or wine: each heavenly part is expressly noted by the name of the Body delivered for us and the Blood poured out for us.

Furthermore, the same is evident from the primary use of the Sacraments. For Sacraments are σφραγῖδες or seals of the righteousness of faith: Rom. 4, 11. And yet, external or elementary things alone, namely Bread and Wine, cannot seal the righteousness of faith; indeed, they ought not to. The reason is: Because they would be much humbler means than what could suffice for strengthening faith in the souls of men. Because the Savior himself wished this Sacrament to be joined to the Evangelical Promise, the dignity of which was to be greater than that of the word itself; for the account of the Word and the divine promise is truly more potent in this kind than that of bare Bread and Wine. It follows that the perspicuity of this Sacrament in sealing the grace of righteousness ought to have been greater than that of the Paschal Lamb. And yet, there exists a greater analogy between the flesh and blood of a lamb and the flesh and blood of CHRIST than between Bread and Wine. It is therefore plain and clear that the external or elementary thing alone cannot seal the righteousness of faith.

Antiquity also supports this purer doctrine of ours, the Orthodox one: As Irenaeus, book 4 against heresies, chapter 34. The bread which is from the earth, receiving the calling of GOD, is no longer common bread: but the Eucharist, consisting of two things, earthly and heavenly.

Hence the Nicene Canon pronounces that not only Bread and Wine, but also the Body and Blood of CHRIST, are τὰ προκείμενα (the things set before us) on the sacred table.

Augustine in the sentences of Prosper, which are cited in De Consecr. dist. 2. This is what we say, what we strive to approve by all means, that this Sacrament is composed of two things, consists of two things, the visible species of the elements, and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord JESUS CHRIST.

The same in his work on catechizing the uninstructed: Sacraments are visible signs of divine things: but the things themselves are honored invisibly in them. The same to the Neophytes: What you see is Bread and a Cup, which even our eyes report to us. But what our faith demands to be instructed in is that the Bread is the Body of CHRIST, the Wine is the Blood of CHRIST. The same, cited by Bede in 1 Cor. 10: In the Sacrament one thing is seen, another is understood: what is seen has a bodily appearance: what is understood has a spiritual fruit. To this pertain the disputations of Theodoret, Dial. 1 & 2, and other Orthodox Fathers, by which, from the article concerning the Person of CHRIST, the truth of this mystery is illustrated: and just as that Person of CHRIST consists of two natures, divine and human: so this mystery of the Eucharist is declared to consist of bread and body, wine and blood of CHRIST. Concerning which matter that most ancient Justin Martyr and Philosopher, who as a young man was able to hear and see the aged Apostles, wrote thus in Apology 2: We do not receive these as common Bread, nor as common drink: but just as through the Word of GOD JESUS CHRIST became incarnate and had both flesh and blood for our salvation: so we have been taught that this food, blessed by the word of prayer from Him, from which our blood and flesh are nourished by alteration, is the flesh and blood of that incarnate CHRIST. Chrysostom to the monk Caesarius during the time of his second exile against Apollinaris: Just as before the bread is sanctified, we name it bread: but when the divine grace sanctifies it through the mediation of the Priest, it is indeed freed from the appellation of bread: but it is deemed worthy of the appellation of the Lord's Body, even though the nature of bread remained in it and there are not two bodies, but one Body of the Son: So also this divine nature residing in the body, made both one Son, one person. Cyprian, Sermon on the Lord's Supper: This bread, which the LORD offered to the disciples, changed not in appearance, but in nature, was made flesh by the omnipotence of the word. And just as in the Person of CHRIST the Humanity was seen and the Divinity lay hidden: so in the visible Sacrament, the divine essence transfuses itself ineffably, so that there might be devotion to religion concerning the Sacraments. Euthymius on Matthew 26. Just as the Son of GOD deified the flesh He assumed supernaturally (if one may speak so), so He ineffably transforms this into His own life-giving Body and precious blood.

To these things, which have been brought forward by way of proof, there can also be added an argument taken from the analogy of the Sacrament of the Paschal Lamb and the Eucharistic one, in this manner: If the Sacrament, which bore the type of the Eucharistic Sacrament, and therefore was complete in this very thing, was bipartite: then it is necessary that the Eucharistic Sacrament also be of the same condition. But the former was entirely such. Therefore. The connection of the major premise is evident from this: For if the Eucharistic Sacrament is determined to lack either part, whether the elemental or the heavenly: a monstrous absurdity will follow. For if it lacks the elemental, it will no longer be a Sacrament: If it is destitute of the heavenly part, the analogy between the type and the archetype will cease entirely. The major premise therefore has its certainty. The minor is sufficiently manifest in itself. For concerning the external and elemental thing, the flesh and blood of the lamb, the matter does not need proof. Now it is also agreed on both sides that the flesh and blood of the lamb bore the type of the flesh and blood of CHRIST: which typical ratio constituted the other part in that old Sacrament. For besides this, no other can be given. But it is necessary that this type and shadow be completed by its archetype and body in this Sacrament. Therefore, the conclusion also has its truth and proof.

But it is asked at this point, whether from the combination of these two different parts, two Sacraments also follow: One, which is completed by an earthly and a heavenly thing, namely Bread and the Body of Christ: The other, which likewise consists and is perfected by an earthly and a heavenly thing, namely Wine and the Blood of CHRIST? The reason for doubting is this, because it seems impossible that when the genus is multiplied, the species is not also multiplied: Now, the Sign is the Genus of the Sacrament: Therefore, since there are two signs in the Eucharist, namely Bread and wine: it seems indeed to follow that two distinct species of Sacraments, and thus two Sacraments distinct in species, emerge.

The Master of Sentences, lib. 4, dist. 11, answers this question: They should not for that reason be called two Sacraments: but One: because under each species the same thing is taken. This response ought not to be conceded, as it solves a doubt by an equally doubtful thing, and not obscurely supports the figment of Papal Transubstantiation, from which our Confession abhors, and thus also believes and maintains, that the same thing is not taken under each species: but that under the Bread, nothing but the Body of CHRIST is received: under the wine, nothing but the blood of CHRIST. Therefore, the response of those seems more convenient to us who maintain that this Sacrament is indeed multiplied materially; but yet is One formally and perfectively, in so much as it is perfected by them as one refreshment. And just as bodily refreshment is one, even though two things are required for it, namely food and drink: so spiritual refreshment, which is conformed to the bodily, is also one, and requires spiritual food and drink.

Latin:

QUemadmodum reliqua Sacramenta omnia, tùm Veteris, tùm Novi Testamenti, geminam habent materiam constituentem: Elementarem & Cœlestem: Sic Eucharistiæ etiam Sacramentum duabus constat, & absolvitur partibus, quoad substantiam: non tamen illis quoquo modo se habentibus, sed rebus, sive essentiis, aut substantiis, reipsâ existentibus.

Probatur hoc 1. ex verbis Institutionis, quæ ad substantiam hujus Sacramenti describendam pertinent, quibus omnibus nihil νοητὸν, vel λογικὸν, ἢ τυπικὸν: sed meræ res & materiæ in naturâ rerum existentes significantur.

2. Ex naturâ analogicâ Sacramentorum Veteris & Novi Testamenti, quorum illis Apostolus umbram tribuit: his verò ἀυτὸ τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἀυτὴν τὴν ἐικόνα τῶν πραγμάτων ad notandam realem materiæ existentiam assignat.

3. Ex Usu Sacramenti hujus. Est enim Sacramentum hoc promissioni Evangelicæ, adjunctum, ut arrhæ usum præstet. Arrharum autem natura est & proprietas, ut sint materiatum quiddam, seu Essentiale. Fingunt quidem Sacramentarij, Sacrament a eo fine esse instituta, ut per res aspectabiles & externas ad rerum cælestium contemplationem perduceremur: sed hoc pacto unam tantùm rem, seu unius generis materiam in Sacramento constituunt: & sic novi quasi panes propositionis in Ecclesiam Novi Testamenti invehuntur. Quod est planè ἀσύστατον.

Cæterùm res istæ duæ sive materiæ, ipsius substantiæ hoc in Sacramento propriæ, diversissimi interim generis sunt, & naturæ dissimillimæ: Elementaris una; ac proindè visibilis: altera cælestis, ac proindè invisibilis non quidem omni modo, ac simpliciter: sed naturæ hominum adhuc corruptæ, & cum concretione materiæ mortalis adhuc conjunctæ.

Est verò utraque hæc pars, tàm invisibilis, quàm visibilis, non unius, sed geminæ speciei: secundum ipsam actus diversitatem, quem Sacramentalis hujus actionis proprium, & quidem geminum esse, Servator voluit.

Quia enim non semiplenam, sed integram & perfectam cibationem, hoc in Sacramento CHRISTUS instituere voluit, quæ constaret, & manducatione, & bibitione conjunctim: ergò manducationi, ex genere elementari, Panem: ex cœlesti verò, Corpus suum: bibitioni autem rursus ex genere elementari, Vinum: ex cœlesti verò, Sangvinem suum destinavit. Harum ergò duarum, licèt diversissimarum, & toto genere differentium rerum, non uni, aut alteri seorsim: sed utrique simul, Sacramenti nomen propriè competit: earundemque non uni: sed utrique simul, Signandi officium convenit.

Possunt hæc quæ de naturâ duarum istarum partium jam dicta sunt, certis rationibus demonstrari: Et primò quidem ex ipso τῷ ῥητῷ verborum CHRISTI, tenore, vigore, rigore. Nam elementaris pars utraque, nomine Panis, & Poculi, sive vini, exprimitur: Cœlestis utraque, nomine Corporis pro nobis traditi: & Sangvinis pro nobis effusi disertè notatur.

Deindè verò idem constat ex usu Sacramentariorum primario. Sacramenta enim sunt σφραγῖδες sive signacula justitiæ fidei: Rom. 4, 11. Atqui solæ res externæ sive elementares, Panis nempè & Vinum, justitiam fidei obsignare non possunt: imò ne quidem debent. Ratio est: Quia multò humiliora essent media, quàm quæ fidei in animis hominum roborandæ sufficere possent. Quia Servator ipse Sacramentum hoc Promissioni Evangelicæ adjungi voluit, cujus major esset, quàm ipsius verbi dignitas, Já verè potior est in hoc genere Verbi & promissionis divinæ ratio, quàm nudi Panis & Vini. Accidit, quòd major in obsignandâ gratiâ justitiæ debuit esse hujus Sacramenti perspicuitas, quàm Agni Paschalis. Atqui carni & sangvini agnino, major cum carne & sangvine CHRISTI, quàm Pani & Vino analogia intercedit. Planum ergò & perspicuum, quòd sola res externa sive Elementaris justitiam fidei obsignare non possit.

Adstipulatur puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ Orthodoxæ etiam Antiquitas: Ut Irenæus lib. 4. adversus hæreses cap. 34. Qui est à terrâ panis, percipiens vocationem DEI, jam non communis panis est: sed Eucharistia, & duabus rebus constans, terrenâ & cœlesti.

Hinc Canon Nicenus non tantùm Panem & Vinum: sed etiam Corpus & Sangvinem CHRISTI, τὰ προκείμενα in sacrâ mensâ esse pronunciat.

Augustinus in sententijs Prosperi, quæ allegantur de Conseer. dist. 2. Hoc est, quod dicimus, quod modis omnibus approbare contendimus, Sacramentum hoc duobus confici, duobus constare, Visibili Elementorum specie, & invisibili Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI carne & sangvine.

Idem de catechifandis rudibus: Sacramenta menta sunt visibilia rerum divinarum signacula: sed res ipsæ invisibiles in eis honorantur. Idem ad Neophytos: Quod videtis, Panis est, & Calix, quod nobis etiam oculi renunciant. Quod autem fides nostra postulat instruenda, Panis est Corpus CHRISTI, Vinum est Sanguis CHRISTI. Idem, citante Bedâ in 1. Cor. 10. In Sacramento aliud videtur, aliud intelligitur: quod videtur, habet speciem corporalem: quod intelligitur, habet fructum spiritualem. Quò pertinent Theodoreti, Dial. 1. & 2. & aliorum Patrum Orthodoxorum disputationes, quibus ex articulo de Personâ CHRISTI, veritas hujus mysterij illustratur: & quemadmodum personâ illâ CHRISTI naturis duabus, divinâ & humanâ: ita hoc Eucharistiæ mysterium, pane & corpore, vino & sanguine CHRISTI constare perhibetur. Quâ de re antiquissimus ille Justinus Martyr & Philosophus, qui juvenis Apostolos senes audire & videre potuit, Apolog. 2. sic scripsit: Non ut communem Panem, neque ut communem potum hæc accipimus: sed quemadmodum per Verbum DEI incarnatus JESUS CHRISTUS, & carnem & sanguinem pro salute nostrâ habuit: ita & hunc per precationis verbum ab ipso benedictum cibum, ex quo sanguis & carnes nostræ per alterationem nutriuntur, illius incarnati CHRISTI, carnem & sanguinem esse edocti sumus. Chrysostomus ad Cæsarium Monachum tempore secundi sui exilij contra Apollinarium: Sicut antequàm sanctificetur panis, panem nominamus: divinâ autem illu sanctificante gratiâ, mediante Sacerdote, liberatus est quidem ab appellatione panis: dignus autem habitus est Dominici Corporis appellatione, etsi natura panis in ipso permansit & non duo corpora, sed unum Filij Corpus: Sic & hæc divina in corpore residente natura, unum Filium, unam personam utraque fecerunt. Cyprianus Sermon. de Cœnâ Domini: Panis iste, quem DOMINUS discipulis porrigebat, non effigie, sed naturâ mutatus, omnipotentiâ verbi factus est caro. Et sicut in Persona CHRISTI Humanitas videbatur, & latebat Divinitas: ita in Sacramento visibili, ineffabiliter divina se transfundit essentia, ut esset religioni circa Sacramenta devotio. Euthymius in Matth. 26. Quemadmodum Filius DEI supernaturaliter assumtam carnem Deificavit (si ita loqui liceat) ita hoc ineffabiliter transmutat in ipsum vivificum Corpus, & pretiosum sanguinem suum.

Potest his, quæ probationis loco adducta sunt, addi etiam argumentum petitum ex analogiâ Sacramenti Agni Paschalis, & Eucharistici, in hunc modum: Si Sacramentum, quod typum Sacramenti Eucharisti ci gessit, ac proindè in hoc ipso completum erat, bipartitum fuit: utique ejusdem conditionis Eucharisticum etiam Sacramentum sit, necesse est. At prius illud tale omninò fuit. Ergò. Majoris connexum patet indè: Si enim Sacramentum Eucharisticum alterutrâ parte, sive elementari, sive cœlesti carere statuatur: prodigiosa sequetur absurditas. Si enim elementari tò careat, Sacramentum jam non ampliùs erit: Si parte cœlesti destituatur, analogia inter typum & archetypum penitùs cessabit. Constat ergò majori sua certitudo. Minor per se satis est manifesta. Nam de re externâ, & elementari, carne & sangvine agnino, res probatione non indiget. Jam & carnem & sangvinem agninum, typum gessisse carnis & sangvinis CHRISTI itidem utrinque constat: Quæ typica ratio constituebat partem alteram in veteri illo Sacramento. Dari enim præter hanc alia nulla potest. Typum autem & umbram istam, suo archetypo & corpore in hoc Sacramento completam esse, necessum est. Stat ergò conclusioni sua etiam veritas & probatio.

Quæritur autem hoc loco, Annon ex duarum istarum diversarum partium combinatione, duo etiam sequantur Sacramenta: Unum, quod absolvatur re terrena & cœlesti, Pane nimirùm & Corpore Christi: Alterum verò, quod itidem constet & perficiatur Re terrenâ & cœlesti, Vino nimirùm & Sangvine CHRISTI? Ratio dubitandi est hæc, quia impossibile videtur, ut multiplicato genere, non multiplicetur etiam species: Jam verò Signum est Genus Sacramenti: Ergò cum in Eucharistiâ sint duo signa, Panis scilicet & vinum: videtur utique consequens, duas etiam distinctas Sacramentorum species, & sic duo Sacramenta specie distincta emergere.

Respondet ad hanc quæstionem Magister Sententiarum, lib. 4. dist. 11. Non ideò debent dici duo Sacramenta : sed Unum: quia sub utraque specie idem sumitur. Quæ responsio concedi non debet, ut quæ dubium per æquè dubium solvit, & Transsubstantiationis Pontificiæ figmento haud obscurè patrocinatur, à quo vis nostra abhorret Confessio, ita credit etiam, & statuit, non sub utraque specie idem sumi: sed sub Pane, non nisi Corpus CHRISTI: sub vino, non nisi sangvinem CHRISTI accipi. Commodior proindè eorum nobis videtur responsio, qui statuunt, Sacramentum hoc materialiter quidem multiplicari; sed tamen Unum esse formaliter & perfectivè, in quantum perficitur ex eis una refectio. Sicut autem corporalis refectio una est quamvis ad eam duo requirantur cibus nimirùm & potus: sic spiritualis refectio, quæ corporali conformatur, etiam una est, & requirit spiritualem cibum & potum.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: What are the essential parts, constituting the substance of this Sacrament (continued)

Wherefore, although there are two elements in the Lord's Supper, and also two heavenly things: yet it is one Sacrament, by reason of the institution, which ordains these several things to one Sacramental refreshment.

Various heretics have long since brought a dispute against this purer doctrine concerning the essential parts of this Sacrament: such as the Messalians, who, rejecting the entire substance of this Sacrament, assigned the power of sealing the righteousness of faith to prayers alone.

2. The Ophites, who, when about to celebrate the Lord's Supper, would summon a serpent or snake with their incantations. Where St. Augustine reports that this serpent used to hide in some cave not far from the Altar, and, having been charmed, would ascend the Altar, and touch the Eucharistic bread and wine with its poisonous tongue, and soon would return into the cave (heresy 17; Irenaeus, book 1: Against Heresies, chapter 34; Epiphanius, Tome 3, book 1, heresy 37).

3. Artotyritae, who in the celebration of this Sacrament, not content with bread, added cheese as well, saying that the offerings of the first men were celebrated from the fruits of the earth and of sheep. Augustine, heresy 28.

4. Cataphrygians and Pepuzians, who, as Augustine holds in heresy 26, celebrated a truly deadly Sacrament. For they made their Eucharist from the blood of a one-year-old infant (whom, as Damascenus testifies in his book on heresies, page 579, they killed), which they extracted from his whole body with tiny puncture wounds, mixing that blood with flour and making bread from it for the Eucharist. If that boy died from the wounds, he was held to be some distinguished martyr; if he survived, he was held to be a great priest. Epiphanius attributes this same cruel error also to the Tascodrugites, Quintilians, and Priscillianists.

5. Gnostics, who, as Epiphanius reports in Tome 2, book 1, heresy 26, defiled the Synaxis and communion with the filth of manifold intercourse. For after they were mingled among themselves in wicked fornications, finally some little woman (O wickedness, O blasphemy!), just as some one of the men, would receive the flow of male semen into their own hands, and they would stand looking up to heaven, and holding those impurities in their hands, they would pray to the Father of all, and offer that very thing which they had in their hands, saying: "We offer to you this gift, the body of CHRIST," and thus they would eat it, taking their own filth. In like manner, they would collect blood from a woman suffering from her period and drink it in common, saying: "This is the blood of CHRIST." Augustine also assigns this most foul error to the Manichaeans in heresy 46, namely that they too received the Eucharist sprinkled with human semen.

" 6. Barsanians or Semidalitae, who, neglecting bread, took only as much fine flour or meal as they could hold with their fingertips, and tasted it only with their outermost lips. Damascenus, book on heresies, pages 584 and 585.

7. Aquarians, who substituted water in place of wine. Augustine, heresy 64. The Severians, Encratites, Tatianists, and Manichaeans did this same thing, as testified by Epiphanius in Tome 1, book 2, heresy 47, and Augustine in heresies 24, 25, 26, and Cyprian, book 2, Epistle 3.

8. Marcosians, who mixed a little white wine with water: but in such a way that they first made the water red through magical incantation, and thus corresponding to the Eucharistic blood by a certain similarity of color: Irenaeus, book 1, against heresies, chapter 9. Epiphanius, Tome 3, book 1, heresy 34.

9. And finally: certain of the Armenians contended that unleavened bread must necessarily be used: they also used milk in place of wine: nay, they even used pressed clusters of grapes without juice for wine: as is evident from the preface of the Council of Braga.

Thus, therefore, the Devil, soon after the age of the Apostles, went about defiling this most holy Testament of JESUS CHRIST with various and horrible errors and superstitions: so that in almost no part did the institution of CHRIST remain safe and inviolate.

From which impiety the Sacramentarian sect is not entirely averse even today, which discourses thus concerning both elemental parts of this Sacrament, through Theodore Beza, their leader, in epistle 2: "Bread and Wine are signs of the Supper by the institution of CHRIST. Where, therefore, there is either no use of bread or wine, or no supply at a certain time, will the Supper of the Lord not be celebrated? Nay, it will be rightly celebrated if that which takes the place of bread or wine, either from common use or according to the necessity of the time, is used in place of bread or wine. For this was the mind of CHRIST when He chose bread and wine for these mysteries, that by proposing the signs of those things by which our body is nourished, He might represent, as if before our eyes, true spiritual nourishment. Therefore, he does not stray at all from the opinion of CHRIST who, with no desire for innovation, substitutes for bread and wine things which, even if they do not have an equal analogy of nourishment, yet have a similar one, etc." Thus far Beza, to whom we cannot subscribe until he has proven: 1. That CHRIST left it free for the Church, should some case of necessity so demand, to exchange the elementary part for another of a different species. 2. That Christ directed the promise concerning the sacramental union of the heavenly thing with the earthly thing to any other element analogous to it, other than bread and wine. Since neither of these has yet been proven, but rather directly conflicts with the manifest institution of this Sacrament, and indeed with the analogy of the Sacraments of the Old Testament: it will certainly not be more lawful today to change the sacramental elements than it was once lawful to change the circumcision of the foreskin, or the paschal lamb with some other animal, however similar and analogous.

Finally, from the absurdity which necessarily follows from Beza's opinion, we conclude thus: Whatever can be removed, or exchanged for a different species, while the essential integrity of the Eucharistic Sacrament remains, that is not an essential part of it. For every whole is composed of whatever exists from the presence and nature of its essential parts. But according to Beza's opinion, bread and wine can be removed, and exchanged for a different, yet analogous, species while the essential integrity of the Eucharistic Sacrament remains. Therefore, according to Beza's opinion, bread and wine are not essential parts of the Eucharistic Sacrament: since, in Beza's view, it obtains its essential integrity even without them.

But the Sacramentarian sect also stirs up another controversy today concerning the Eucharistic bread, which, so that it may be dispatched in very few words, we enclose the whole matter within these hypotheses.

1. That the Eucharistic bread should be made from wheat alone, and not from other purer grain, such as rye, emmer, spelt, maize, or the like, is not a matter of necessity: because neither the authority of Scripture, nor the determination of the Church, nor any peculiar revelation, nor any reason confirms it. Therefore, from whatever kind of grain the bread is made, it is suitable for the Eucharistic sacramental action.

2. It is also of no necessity that this bread be either leavened or unleavened: but this is placed in the liberty of the Church: yet the Church has almost always labored to retain unleavened bread, for this reason especially, that it may be shown that there is nothing corrupt, or corrupting, in this Sacrament, but that it is all sincere and making sincere: as the words of Innocent, book 4, on mysteries, chapter 4, have it. To which the constitution of the Sixth Council of Constantinople gives its support, which holds as follows: The oblation, which is offered in the Sacrifice of the Altar, ought to have no mixture of leaven: since indeed the Body of CHRIST was born without corruption. The Greeks attempted a change of this rite, around A.D. 1054, at the instigation of Michael, Bishop of Constantinople, with whom a sharp controversy concerning unleavened bread took place with Humbert. But the example of CHRIST prevailed, and the reason of greater antiquity, so that the controversy being settled, unleavened bread was retained in the Church, as has been handed down to memory by Rupert of Deutz, and Peter the Venerable, and other writers. Thus, therefore, the use of unleavened bread prevailed for some time in the Church, without any discord of contradiction, until at length a new contention arose between the Greeks and the Latins concerning unleavened bread: for the sake of settling which a Council was summoned at Ferrara, to which the Patriarch of Constantinople came, along with the Emperor John Palaiologos. Which Council the Greeks name and count as the eighth Oecumenical or universal. Therefore, this Council was begun at Ferrara, around A.C. 1438, and finally completed at Florence in the time of Eugenius IV, Roman Pontiff. It was disputed, among other things, concerning unleavened and leavened bread: and at length, in the letters which they called of Union, this decree was inserted: In unleavened, as also in leavened wheaten bread, the body of CHRIST is truly fashioned, and priests ought to fashion the same Body of the LORD in either, each one, that is, according to the custom of his own Church, whether Eastern or Western. In which opinion is also Beza himself, Epist. 12. 3. The Lutheran Churches, in the action of this Sacrament, employ unleavened bread: to the example of CHRIST, whom ecclesiastical Doctors (excepting Euthymius on Matthew and Nicephorus, book 1, chapter 18) testify with great consensus to have used such bread as was common and customary among the Jews, not indeed at all times, but especially at that Paschal time. 4. Although the bread which is customary for us in the Eucharistic action, namely, diminished from an entire mass into many particles or small rounds, and distributed among those eating, is not common bread, if you look at daily sustenance: yet it is common, if you consider the most ancient custom and use of the Church. And because this feast itself is not vulgar, the Church rightly uses not vulgar, but true bread in its action: so that in this way also the part may correspond to the condition of the whole. 5. These smaller breads we are accustomed to name Hosts and Oblations, not in the Pontifical sense: but in the Ecclesiastical, and that by far the most ancient, and free from all superstition and Idolatry.

For with Irenaeus and Justin as witnesses, in the celebration of the Lord's Supper, in ancient times bread was brought by the faithful to the altar of the Lord as a free-will offering. From the oblation of which, because some part was destined for consecration for the use of the Supper, the custom prevailed that they were called Oblations, which were afterwards used in place of blessed bread. Since Scripture itself calls these free-will offerings Hosts, Philippians 4:18, Hebrews 13:16, we certainly do not at all shrink from such an appellation, provided its sense is correct.

6. Therefore, our breads, or Hosts, do not support the Pontifical figment of Transubstantiation, as the Sacramentarians cavil, writing that for that reason, around A.C. 1220, at the instigation of Pope Honorius, the image or idol of the crucified CHRIST began to be imprinted on those little hosts, so that they might in some way represent the transubstantiation of Bread into the Body of CHRIST. For this is a manifest calumny: since the use of these smaller breads prevailed in the Church before anything of the figment of μετουσίας became known to the Church: as that which in the time of Peter Lombard was not yet defined, as he himself writes in book 4, Sent. dist. 11.

Then there was a far different reason for the smallness of these breads, namely, that those about to participate in this Sacrament might be admonished that this bread is not destined for filling the belly or nourishing the body: and as the words of the Nicene Council have it, that we do not take much, but a little, so that we may recognize that these are taken not for satiety, but for sanctification. 2. That they might also be more safely preserved for ecclesiastical use: 3. And that they could be more conveniently distributed among many. Moreover, the image of the crucified CHRIST offends no one, unless he is either an open or a secret enemy of the Cross of CHRIST.

7. The definition of true and natural bread applies to these smaller breads. For it consists of flour, whether wheaten or siligineous, which, when kneaded with bread, is baked in the manner of other breads. With what face and conscience, therefore, do the Sacramentarians dare to call them, through calumny, the foam of bread?

8. The roundness of the form likewise rests on the most ancient practice of the Church, which prevailed even in the time of Epiphanius, who reports that in his own age breads of a round form were in use, which is called by him στρογγυλοειδης. The calumny, by which the Sacramentarians call these round breads of ours 'coin-breads' and harass them with other taunts, we leave to be avenged by GOD.

9. The use of four-part breads never obtained in the ancient Orthodox Church, so that it is evident from Gregory that formerly a large bread, such as was accustomed to be placed on common tables, was used. Hence Paulinus writes thus to Augustine: We ask that you bless by receiving the one bread which we have sent to your charity as a sign of unanimity: ep. 31. of Aug. Hence Basil to the patrician Caesaria: It is the same in virtue, whether one receives one part from the Priest: or several parts at the same time.

Latin:

Quare quamvis in Cœnâ Domini duo sint elementa, & duæ etiam res cœlestes: Unum tamen est Sacramentum, ratione institutionis, quæ ista plura ad unam refectionem Sacramentalem ordinat.

Puriori huic doctrinæ de patribus Essentialibus hujus Sacramenti litem intenderunt jam olim varij hæretici: ut Messaliani, qui integram Sacramenti hujus substantiam repudiantes, vim obsignandi justitiam fidei, solis precibus adsignabãt.

2. Ophitæ, qui Cœnam Domini celebraturi, Serpentem sive Colubrum incantationibus suis evocabant. Ubi refert D. Augustinus, Serpentem istum in speluncâ quapiam haud procul ab Altari latitasse, & incantatum Altare conscendisse, panemque ac vinum Eucharisticum venenosâ lingvâ contrectasse, & mox in speluncam redijsse hæresi 17. Iren. lib. 1: adversus hæreses, cap. 34. Epiphan. Tom. 3 libri. 1. hæres. 37.

3. Artotrytæ, qui in Sacramenti hujus celebratione, non pane contenti, caseum etiam addebant, dicentes, à primis hominibus oblationes de fructibus terræ & ovium fuisse celebratas. Augustin. hæresi 28.

4. Cataphryges, & Pepuziani, qui ut Augustinus habet hæresi 26. funestum planè celebrabant Sacramentum. Nam de infantis anniculi, (quem teste Damasceno lib de hæresibus pag 579. cædebant) Sangvine, quem de toto ejus corpore, minutis punctionum vulneribus extorquebant, Eucharistiam suam conficiebant, miscentes sangvinem illum farinæ, panemque indè Eucharistiam facientes. Qui puer, si ex vulneribus moreretur, pro insigni aliquo martyre: sin superviveret, pro magno Sacerdote habebatur. Quem ipsum etiam crudelem errorem Epiphanius tribuit Tascodrugitis, Quintilianis, & Priscillianis.

5. Gnostici, qui referente Epiphanio, Tom. 2. libri 1. hæresi 26. Synaxin ac communionem multiplicis coitus turpitudine conspurcabant. Nam postquam inter se nefandis scortationibus permixti fuerunt, tandem muliercula quæpiam (o scelus, ô blasphemiam!) ut & virorum aliquis excipiebant fluxum seminis virilis in proprias manus, & stabant cœlum intuentes, ac sordes istas in manibus habentes, precabantur Patrem " universorum, offerebantque illud ipsum, quod " in manibus habebant, dicentes: Offerimus tibi " hoc donum corpus CHRISTI, & sic ipsum ede- " bant, assumentes suam ipsorum immunditiem. " Pari ratione de fœmina, laborante menstruo, " sangvinem colligebant, eumque in communi " bibebant, dicentes: Hic est sangvis CHRISTI. " Quem fœdissimum errorem Manichæis etiam " assignat Augustinus, hæresi 46. quòd nimirùm " & hi Eucharistiam conspersam semine huma- " no acceperint.

" 6. Barsaniani sive Semidalitæ, qui ne- " glecto pane, tantum simila sive farinæ, quantum " summis digitis tenere poterant, capiebant, idque " summis duntaxat labris degustabant. Damasc. " lib. de hæresibus, pag. 584. & 585.

7. Aquarij, qui in locum vini substituebant Aquam. August. hæresi 64. Quod ipsum fecerunt etiam Severiani, Encratitæ, Tatiani, Manichæi, teste Epiphanio Tom. 1. libri 2. hæresi 47. & Augustino hæresi 24. 25. 26. Cypriano lib. 2. Epist. 3.

8. Marcosij, qui Aquæ pauxillum Vini albi admiscebant: sed ita, ut aquam prius per incantationem magicam efficerent rubram, & sic sangvini Eucharistico similitudine quadam coloris respondentem: Iren: lib 1. adversus hæreses cap. 9. Epiph. Tom 3. libri 1. hæresi 34.

9. Et postremo: quidam ex Armenijs contendebant, Pane azymo necessario esse utendum: vini etiam loco, Lacte utebantur: quin uvarum botros compressos, etiam sine succo pro vino adhibebant: uti patet ex præfatione Concilij Bracarensis.

Sic ergo Diabolus, mox post Apostolorum ætatem Sacrosanctum hoc JESU CHRISTI Testamento varijs & horrendis erroribus ac superstitionibus conspurcatum ivit: ut sic ex nullâ ferè parte institutio CHRISTI maneret salva & inviolata.

A' quâ impietate non planè abhorret hodiéque Gens Sacramentaria, quæ de parte Elementari utrâquè Sacramenti hujus, per Theodorum Bezam Antesignanum suum, epist. 2. sic disserit: Panis & Vinum sunt Cœnæ Signa ex CHRISTI institutione. Ubi igitur panis aut vini vel nullus est usus vel nulla certo tempore copia nùm Cœna Domini nulla celebrabitur: Imò ritè celebrabitur si quod panis aut vini vicem, vel ex usu communi, vel pro temporis ratione supplet, panis aut vini loco adhibeatur. Hæc enim mens fuit CHRISTI cùm panem & vinum ad hæc mysteria deligeret ut propositis earum rerum signis quibq corpus nostrum alitur, veram alimoniam spiritualem, velut ob oculos repræsentaret. Itaq; à CHRISTI sententiâ nihil aberrat, qui nullo prorsus novandi studio, pro pane & vino substituat, quæ etsi non parem, similem tamen alimoniæ analogiam habeant, &c. Hactenus Beza, cui haud prius subscribere possumus, quàm probaverit, 1. CHRISTUM liberum reliquisse Ecclesiæ, partem Elementarem sic aliquo necessitatis casu flagitante, cum aliâ diversa specie commutare. 2. Christum promissionem de Unione Sacramentali rei cœlestis cum re terrenâ tam ad quodvis Elementum analogon aliud, quàm ad panem & vinum direxisse. Quod utrumque cum nondum probatum sit, quin cum manifestâ institutione Sacramenti hujus, imò cum analogiâ Sacramentorum Veteris Testamenti directè pugnet: haud profectò magis hodiè licitum erit, mutare Elementa Sacramentalia: atque olim licitum fuit, mutare amputationem præputij: vel agnum paschalem cum alio aliquo animali, quantumvis simili & analogo.

Tandem ex absurdo, quod ex sententiâ Bezæ necessariò sequitur, sic colligimus: Quicquid salvâ manente Essentiali integritate Sacramenti Eucharistici, tolli, aut cum diversâ specie mutari potest: illud non est pars ejus Essentialis. Omne enim totum συνῶδες quicquid est ex partium Essentialium præsentiâ & naturâ. Atqui ex sententia Bezæ, panis & vinum tolli, & cum diversâ, analogâ tamen specie salvâ Essentiali integritate Sacramenti Eucharistici mutari possunt. Ergò ex sententia Bezæ, Panis & Vinum, non sunt partes Essentiales Sacramenti Eucharistici: Siquidem hoc etiam sine illis, suam Essentialem integritatem obtinet: censente Bezâ.

Sed & aliam Controversiam movet hodiè Gens Sacramentaria, de Pane Eucharistico, quæ ut paucissimis expediatur, his hypothesibus rem universam includimus.

1. Ut ex solo tritico panis Eucharisticus, & non ex alio puriore frumento, ut siligine, farre, spelta, zeâ vel consimili conficiatur, non est necessitatis: quia id neque Scripturæ autoritas, neque determinatio Ecclesiæ, neque peculiaris quæpiam revelatio, neque ratio aliqua confirmat. Ex quocunque ergo frumenti genere panis sit confectus, ille actioni Sacramentali Eucharisticæ est conveniens.

2. Nullius etiam est necessitatis, ut panis iste sit vel fermentatus, vel azymus: sed in libertate Ecclesiæ hoc est positum: pro azymo tamen pane retinendo Ecclesia fermè semper laboravit, eam præcipuè ob causam, ut nihil corrupti, sive corrumpens, sed totum sincerum atq; sincerans, in hoc Sacramento esse monstretur: uti habent verba Innocentij lib. 4. myster. cap. 4. Cui suffragatur constitutio Concilij Constantinopolitani VI. quæ sic habet: Oblatio, quæ in Sacrificium Altaris offertur, nullam commixtionem fermenti habere debet: siquidem CHRISTI Corpus fuit sine corruptione genitum. Attentarunt Græci mutationem hujus ritus, circa A. D. 1054. autore Michaële episcopo Constantinopolitano, cui cum Humberto de pane azymo acris controversia intercessit. Sed vicit exemplum CHRISTI, & majoris antiquitatis ratio, ut sopitâ controversiâ azymus panis in Ecclesiâ fuerit retentus, uti est à Ruperto Tuicensi, & Petro Cluniacensi, alijsque Scriptoribus memoriæ proditum. Sic ergò obtinuit aliquandiu usus panis azymi in Ecclesiâ, sine ullo contradictionis dissidio, donec tandem nova oborta contentio inter Græcos & Latinos, de pane azymo: cujus componendæ gratiâ Concilium indictum fuit Ferrariæ, cui intereant Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus, cum Imperatore Johanne Palæologo. Quod Concilium Græci nominant, & numerant octavum Oecumenicum sive universale. Ferrariæ ergò hoc Concilium inchoatum est, circa A. C. 1438. & Florentiæ demùm peractum tempore Eugenij IV. Pontif. Romani. Disputatum fuit inter alia de pane azymo & fermentato: & tandem literis, quas vocarunt, Unionis, hoc decretum est insertum: In azymo, ut & in fermentato pane triticeo, corpus CHRISTI veraciter conficitur, Sacerdotesque in alterutro ipsum DOMINI Corpus conficere debent, unusquisque scilicet, juxta suæ Ecclesiæ sive Orientalis, sive Occidentalis consvetudinem. Quâ in sententiâ est etiam ipse Beza Epist. 12. 3. Ecclesiæ Lutheranæ, in actione Sacramenti hujus adhibent panem ἄζυμον: ad exemplum CHRISTI, quem tali etiam pane, qualis apud Judæos, non quidem omni: at inprimis Paschali illo tempore, fuerat communis & usitatus, usum fuisse, magno consensu Doctores Ecclesiastici (exceptis Euthymio in Matt. & Nicephoro lib. 1. cap. 18.) testantur. 4. Etsi panis, qui in actione Evcharisticâ nobis est usitatus, nempè ex integrâ massâ in plures particulas sive orbiculos diminutus, & inter vescentes distributus, non est panis communis, si victum quotidianum respicias: communis, tamen est, si vetustissimam Ecclesiæ consvetudinem ac usum consideres. Et quia epulum hoc ipsum non est vulgare, rectè Ecclesia non vulgari, vero tamen pane in ejus actione utitur: ut sic hoc etiam pacto pars respondeat conditioni totius. 5. Hosce panes minutiores, nominare solemus Hostias & Oblata, non sensu Pontificio: sed Ecclesiastico, eoque longè antiquissimo, & ab omni superstitione, ac Idololatriâ libero.

Nam Irenæo & Justino testibus, in celebratione Cœnæ Dominicæ, antiquitus à fidelibus ad altare Domini afferebatur panis liberalis. Ex cujus oblatione, quia in usum Cœnæ pars aliqua consecrationi destinabatur, mos obtinuit, ut Oblatæ nuncuparentur, quæ postmodum loco panis benedicti usurpabantur. Quas liberales oblationes cùm Scriptura ipsa Hostias vocet Philipp. 4, 18. Hebr. 13, 16. nos sanè à tali etiam appellatione minimè abhorremus, modò sensus ejus rectè habeat.

6. Non ergò Pontificiæ Transsubstantiationis commento Panes nostrates, sive Hostiæ patrocinantur, uti cavillantur Sacramentarij, scriptitantes, ideò circa A. C. 1220. autore Papa Honorio, imaginem sive idolum crucifixi CHRISTI, hostiolis illis imprimi cœptum fuisse, ut transsubstantiationem Panis in Corporis CHRISTI aliquatenùs repræsentarent. Calumnia enim hæc est manifesta : Siquidem usus panum istorum minutiorum in Ecclesiâ obtinuit, priusquàm aliquid de μετουσίας figmento Ecclesiæ innotesceret: ut quod Petri Lombardi tempore nondum fuit definitum, sic ipsomet scribente lib. 4. Sent. dist. 11.

Deindè longè alia parvitatis panum istorum causa fuit, ea nimirùm ut sic Sacramento hoc participaturi admonerentur, non ventri alendo, aut corpori nutriendo, panem istum esse destinatum: & ut habent Concilij Niceni verba, non multum nos sumere, sed parùm, ut agnoscamus, non ad saturitatem, sed ad sanctificationem hæc sumi. 2. ut etiam in usum Ecclesiasticum tutiùs asservari: 3. utque inter plures commodiùs distribui possent. Imago autem crucifixi CHRISTI neminem offendit, nisi qui Crucis CHRISTI sive manifestus, sive occultus est hostis.

7. Competit minutioribus istis panibq definitio veri & naturalis panis. Farinâ enim sive triticeâ, sive siligineâ constat, quæ cum pane subacta, more aliorum panum pinsuntur. Quâ ergò fronte & conscientiâ Sacramentarij per calumniam spumam panis appellitare audent?

8. Formæ rotunditas itidem nititur antiquissimâ Ecclesiæ praxi, quæ tempore etiam Epiphanij obtinuit, qui refert, suâ jam ætate in usu fuisse panes rotundæ formæ, quæ ab ipso στρογγυλοειδης vocatur. Calumniam, quâ Sacramentarij panes istos nostros rotundos, nominant panes Nummularios, alijsque dicterijs exagitant, DEO vindicandam relinquimus.

9. Usus panum quadripartibilium in Ecclesiâ antiquâ Orthodoxâ nunquàm obtinuit, ita, ut ex Gregorio constet, olim panem magnum, qualis in mensis communibus apponi consuevit, fuisse adhibitum. Hinc sic Paulinus ad Augustinum scribit: Panem unum, quem unanimitatis indicio misimus charitati tuæ, rogamus, ut accipiendo benedicat: epist. 31. August. Hinc Basilius ad Cæsariam patriciam: Idem est virtute, sive unam partem quis accipiat à Sacerdote: sive plures partes simul.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Question IV. On the Union of the two essential parts into one Sacrament

Since every Union receives its name from the term to which it tends, or from that which is constituted by the Union: it must certainly be seen which and what kind of Union holds a place in this mystery. Moreover, that some union intervenes between the essential parts of this Sacrament, hardly anyone would deny who has weighed the matter itself, which is being discussed, a little more accurately. For since this is the nature of the Sacraments, that they are not simple things, but something composite, and that mystical, in which there is something visible: but another thing, which does not strike the senses, but is apprehended by faith: certainly, just as the natures of other composite things come under a certain unity, expressed by one name, under which, however, the parts from which the composition is made are comprised: so in the use of the Sacraments it is necessary that they themselves, although they consist of diverse things, nevertheless come under a Union, and are assigned one name, under which the essential parts are comprised.

Moreover, it happens in various ways that from the conjunction of two or more distinct things, one thing is constituted. For it becomes one κτ' μῖξιν by mixture, which for the Philosopher is the union of alterable things capable of being mixed: it becomes one κτ' μεταβολὴν by Conversion, as when a little water is mixed with wine: it becomes one κτ' σῶρον, by heaping together, when from diverse seeds, grains, or corn, one pile is made: it becomes one κτ' συνάφειαν ἤ παϱάθεσιν, by apposition or contact, as when the gluing of two boards occurs, either in whole or in part: it becomes one relatively or κατ' ἀξίαν, ὁμοτιμίαν, ἐυδοκίαν, ὁμωνυμίαν, when they are said to be one by a mutual respect of relation, which are joined to each other by dignity, order, power, or some similarity: it becomes one when from two or more humors κτ' κϱᾶσιν: or from moist and dry things κτ' Φύϱσιν: or from two or more dry things κτ' συναλοιΦὴν one thing arises by confusion: it becomes one καθ' ἁρμονίαν ἤ ταυτοβυλίαν, when two or more are one by consent and will: it becomes one κτ' μετοχὴν ἤ χάϱιν, as when believers are one Spirit: it becomes one formally κατ' ὀσίαν, as when body and soul are essentially and naturally united to each other: it becomes one κατὰ σάρκα, as when spouses are joined by the bond of matrimony: Thus the Union of the three persons of the Divinity, communicating in one and the same most simple essence, is believed to be καθ' ὁμοοσίαν, ὀσιώδης: but the Union of the Divine and human natures in CHRIST is established as being καθ' ὑπόστασιν, Personal. The Sacramental Union differs from all these forms and modes of unions. For from bread and the Body of CHRIST, there does not become one nature, or one essence or substance, nor one person, not one pile, not one mass, there does not occur any consubstantiation or local inclusion, not transubstantiation or conversion, not in number, not in nature, not by art, not by contact, not by relation, least of all hypostatically or substantially does it become one thing: But it becomes one Sacramentally or mystically. This Sacramental Union is indeed a conjunction of two most diverse things, differing in their whole genus, by which, through the virtue and will of the institutor, the external elements of bread and wine are united with the heavenly thing expressed by the word of institution, namely the Body and Blood of CHRIST, into one Sacrament, so that because of this Union, in the very use of this Sacrament, but not outside of it, the Body and Blood of CHRIST are exhibited with the bread and wine, to be eaten and drunk orally by all communicants whatsoever in commemoration of the death of CHRIST.

This definition shows what is the medium, and as it were the bond, by which it comes about that bread and the Body of CHRIST are joined to constitute one Sacrament: not, namely, the dignity or intention of the administrator: not the faith of the communicant himself: but the Word and Ordinance of the one instituting this Sacrament. For as far as the ministers are concerned, they do not have power over the Sacraments: but are only dispensers of the Sacraments. Whence it was aptly said by Augustine: What does a bad minister do to you where the LORD is good? Tract. 5 on John. Now as regards the faith of the communicants, does not he who eats unworthily eat the Body of CHRIST: but he causes that he eats it unto judgment: 1 Cor. 11:29, just as he who has not believed, by the testimony of CHRIST, does not cause that he is not baptized: but that he is not saved.

With these things thus established, it is clearer than the midday sun itself that, beyond all merit, out of a mere lust for slandering, there is attributed to the doctrine of our Churches either the figment of Papal μετουσίας, which, if nothing else, at least the very word Union, which is at minimum between two, excludes: Or the delirium of Impanation or συνουσίας, or the commixtion of substances: for we constantly assert that the substances of both things remain safe on both sides: Or the dogma of local and durable affixion, by which it is feigned that the Body of CHRIST, outside the use of the Sacrament, is affixed to the bread, or is included lurking under the bread: Or if there are any others similar to these, they are not the dogmas of our Churches, but the figments and dreams of fanatics: to explode which, this single dogma of Sacramental Union suffices. But concerning this purer doctrine of ours, it is also to be observed that that Union has a place on both sides, and on the part of each species. Therefore, what has been said concerning the Bread and the Lord's Body being united, the same is also to be understood concerning the Wine and the Lord's Blood being united. By which twofold act of Union, however, the unity of the Sacrament is not dissolved: just as neither is the plurality of this Sacrament constituted by the multiplication of the signs themselves: as was shown in the immediately preceding question.

Nor, however, does it follow from this, as the Calvinists object against us by a quibble, namely that we maintain that Bread and Body constitute one substance. Consent. Orth. p. 354. For it is one thing to confess the Sacrament to be one in number: but quite another to affirm that the substance of this Sacrament is one, or as the compilers of the Calvinist Consensus speak, to teach such a real coupling of things with signs, which emerges into the unity of the same mass or substance. The former we teach and fight for against the concomitance of the Papists. The latter, however, we abhor with our whole heart, as is clearly evident from what has just been said. For we believe and confess such a union, by which disparate things, Bread and Body, Wine and Blood of CHRIST, in the very use of this Sacrament, without any conversion or mutation, are truly and really so united that they indeed constitute one Sacrament in number: but each of them retains its own εἶναι or its own substance, safe, integral, and simply unchanged, even in the use itself.

Nor does the blessed LUTHER oppose these things, writing in the greater Confession: when the bread is shown, the Body of CHRIST is shown: when the bread is touched, the Body of CHRIST is touched: when the bread is chewed, the Body of CHRIST is chewed. For he refers to the most intimate bond of Sacramental Union, which intervenes between the bread and the Body of CHRIST, and causes that, in the use of this Sacrament, the Bread can neither be eaten nor handled by the mouth of the Body, without the Body of CHRIST itself being simultaneously eaten and handled: not indeed in a natural or Capernaitic manner, but in a mystical and Sacramental one. Which very thing Luther felt and believes, when he immediately explains himself thus: 'But nevertheless, in the meantime, that remains ratified, that no one sees, touches, or grinds with their teeth the Body of CHRIST: even though it is most certain that what is done to the Bread is rightly and truly attributed to the Body of CHRIST on account of the Sacramental Union.' An impudent, therefore, and malicious reproach is made against us by the Sacramentarians, when they write that it is taught by us that the Body of CHRIST is eaten and ground by teeth IN ITSELF and properly. Luther indeed writes that it is truly and directly said that, when the bread is eaten, the Body of CHRIST is eaten: but he never said that this is done in itself and properly. Thus, therefore, these men wickedly pervert the words of Luther, so that by whatever means possible, even through manifest crimes of falsehood, they may bring odium upon our doctrine.

They themselves, however, in the meantime so involve their own opinion concerning Sacramental Union, that even an attentive reader can scarcely grasp what they are saying or wish to say: as when they write thus in their Consensus: 'Sacramental Union of things with signs is properly the virtue and grace of the Sacrament: which is the cause why the names of the things are exchanged with the symbols.' Likewise in the margin: 'Sacramental Union is the communication of things with signs in the word of grace and promise.' Or, 'Sacramental Union is mystical and relative, by the institution and ordination of GOD in the word.'

That these definitions consist of almost more faults than words, we have shown at great length and with sufficient vigor in the Article concerning

Sacraments in general, chap. 1, quest. 3. The sum of all returns to this, that they attribute to the bread merely a bare respect, or σχέσιν, or relation, on account of these words: This is my body: and they teach that the bread is the true and essential body of CHRIST, by respect, that is, and by σχέσις to the true body of CHRIST, which it represents, and whose place it takes; when that is removed from the Supper by as great an interval as the highest heaven is distant from the lowest earth. Not otherwise than when rustics set up a stone at the boundaries of fields, and attribute to it the name of a boundary, because it marks off fields and meadows. Thus they say that CHRIST took bread, and attributed to it the name of his true Body, delivered for us: so that in this way in the breaking, distribution, and eating, it represents the absent Body of CHRIST, and takes its place: and that the breaking, distribution, and eating of the true and essential Body of CHRIST, but σχετικῶς, because it sustains and bears the name of the absent Body of CHRIST, and one enclosed in a certain place of heaven: Such a σχέσιν or respect they call a Sacramental Union: that is, they wickedly and craftily strive to sell to their own people shells for kernels, and mustard for pepper.

Latin:

CUm omnis Unio nomen accipiat à termino Ad quem, sive ab eo, quod ex Unione constitutum est : videndum utique, quæ & qualis Unio hoc in mysterio locum obtineat. Intercedere autem partibus essentialibus Sacramenti hujus aliquam unionem, vix quisquam iverit inficias, qui rem modò ipsam, de quâ agitur, paulò accuratiùs expenderit. Cum enim hæc sit Sacramentorum natura, ut non sint res simplices, sed quiddam compositum, idq; mysticum, in quo quiddam est visibile : aliud verò, quod sensus non incurrit, sed fide apprehenditur : certè, quemadmodum aliarum rerum compositarum naturæ diversæ sub unitatem quandam veniunt, nomine uno expressam, sub quo tamen partes, undè compositio fit, sunt comprehensæ : ita in Sacramentis usu venire necessum est, ut & ipsa, licèt ex diversis rebus constent, sub Unionem tamen veniant, atq; unum nomen sortiantur, sub quo partes essentiales comprehenduntur.

Cæterùm varijs fit modis, ut ex conjunctione duarum vel plurium distinctarum rerum, Unum quiddam constituatur. Fit enim Unum κτ' μῖξιν mixtione, quæ Philosopho est miscibilium alteratorum Unio : fit Unum κτ' μεταβολὴν per Conversionem, ut quando modicum aquæ vino miscetur : fit Unum κτ' σῶρϱν, per coacervationem, quando ex diversis seminibus, granis, frumentis unus fit cumulus : fit Unum κτ' συνάφειαν ἤ παϱάθεσιν, per appositionem, vel attingentiam, ut cum duorum asserum fit conglutinatio, vel ex toto, vel ex parte : fit Unum σχετικῶς sive κατ' ἀξίαν, ὁμοτιμίαν, ἐυδοκίαν, ὁμωνυμίαν, quando mutuo relationis respectu Unum dicuntur, quæ dignitate, ordine, potestate, aut similitudine quapiam sibi invicem sunt conjuncta : fit Unum quando ex duobus aut pluribus humoribus κτ' κϱᾶσιν : aut ex humidis & siccis κτ' Φύϱσιν : aut duobus vel pluribus siccis κτ' συναλοιΦὴν Unum quiddam oritur per confusionem : fit Unum καθ' ἁρμονίαν ἤ ταυτοβυλίαν, quando duo vel plures Unum sunt, consensu & voluntate: fit Unum κτ' μετοχὴν ἤ χάϱιν, ut quando credentes Unus sunt Spiritus : fit Unum formaliter κατ' ὀσίαν, ut quando Corpus & anima essentialiter & naturaliter sibi invicem uniuntur : fit Unum κατὰ σάρκα, ut quando Conjuges vinculo matrimoniali conjunguntur: Sic Trium Divinitatis personarum, unâ eâdemq; simplicissimâ essentiâ communicantium, Unio καθ' ὁμοοσίαν, ὀσιώδης esse creditur : Divinæ verò & humanæ in CHRISTO naturarum Unio καθ' ὑπόστασιν Personalis esse statuitur. Ab his omnibus Unionum formis & modis differt Unio Sacramentalis. Nam ex pane & Corpore CHRISTI, non sit una natura, aut una essentia sive substantia, neq; una persona, non unus cumulus, non una massa, no fit consubstantiatio aliqua aut localis inclusio, non transubstantiatio aut conversio, non numero, non naturâ, non arte, non contactu, non σχέσει minimè omnium hypostaticè aut substantialiter unum quiddam sit: Sed sit Unum Sacramentaliter sive mysticè. Est verò Unio hæc Sacramentalis duarum diversissimarum, totóq; genere discrepantium rerum conjunctio, quâ ex virtute & voluntate instituentis, externa elementa panis & vinum, cum re cœlesti verbo institutionis expressa, Corpore videlicet & Sangvine CHRISTI, ad Unu Sacramentum, uniuntur, ut propter hanc Unionem, in ipso Sacramenti hujus usu, non verò extra illum, Corpus & Sangvis CHRISTI, cum pane & vino, oraliter manducanda & bibenda exhibeantur, omnibus omninò communicantibus in commemorationem mortis CHRISTI.

Monstrat hæc definitio, quodnám sit medium, & quasi vinculũ, quo fiat, ut panis & Corpus CHRISTI jungantur ad Unum constituendum Sacramentum: non videlicet administrantis dignitas, aut intentio: non fides ipsius communicantis: sed Verbum & Ordinatio instituentis hoc Sacramentum. Nam quod ad ministros attinet, non habent illi potestatem in Sacramenta: sed sunt tantùm dispensatores Sacramentorum. Undè scitè dictum est ab Augustino: Quid faciat tibi malus minister ubi bonus est DOMINUS Tract. 5. in Johannem. Jam quoad fidem communicantium, indignè manducans nonné Corpus CHRISTI edat: sed ut illud in judicium comedat, efficit: Cor. 11, 29. perindè, ut qui non crediderit, ille CHRISTO teste, non hoc efficit, ut non baptisetur: sed ut non salvetur.

Quibus ita constitutis, ipso Sole meridiano clariùs liquet, præter omne meritum, ex merâ calumniandi libidine, nostrarum Ecclesiarum doctrinæ affingi vel Pontificiæ μετουσίας commentum, quam si nihil aliud, saltē ipsum Unionis vocabulum, quæ ut minimum est inter duo, excludit: Vel Impanationis sive συνουσίας, sive substantiarum commixtionis delirium: nam salvas utrinq; utrarúƊ; rerum substantias manere, constanter asserimus: Vel localis & durabilis affixionis dogma, quo Corpus CHRISTI extra usum Sacramenti ad panem affixum esse, vel sub pane delitescens inclusum esse fingitur: Vel si quæ sunt alia his similia, non nostrarum Ecclesiarum dogmata: sed fanaticorum figmenta atq; somnia: ad quæ displodenda unicum hoc Sacramentalis Unionis dogma sufficit. Est verò circa puriorem hanc nostram doctrinam & illud observandum, Unionem istam utrinq; locum habere, & ex parte speciei utriusque. Quod ergò de Pane & Corpore Dominico unitis dictum est: idem de Vino & Sangvine Dominico unitis etiam sentiendum est. Quo tamen utroq; Unionis actu, Sacramenti unitas non solvitur: quemadmodum nec signorum ipsorum multiplicatione, pluralitas Sacramenti hujus constituitur: uti quæstione præcedente proximâ fuit ostensum.

Neq; tamen indè sequitur, quod per cavillum nobis objectant Calviniani, nempe statuere nos, quòd Panis & Corpus unam constituant substantiam. Consent. Orth. pag. 354. Aliud enim est, " Unum numero fateri Sacramentum : aliud ve- " rò, unam affirmare, Sacramenti hujus substan- " tiam, vel ut Compilatores Consensus Calvini- " stici loquuntur, talem docere realem copula- " tionem rerum cum signis, quæ in ejusdem mas- " sæ, sive substantiæ unitatem emergat. Prius illud docemus & pugnamus contra Pontificiorum concomicantiam. Posterius verò hoc toto " pectore abominamur, uti ex jam dictis luculen- " ter patet. Talem enim unionem credimus ac confi- " temur, quâ res disparatæ, Panis & Corpus, Vinum & Sanguis CHRISTI, in ipso usu Sacramenti hujus, sine ulla conversione, aut mutatione, verè & realiter ita uniuntur, ut Unum quidem numero constituant Sacramentum : sed qualibet ipsarum suum εἶναι sive substantiam suam, salvam, integram, & simpliciter immutatam, in ipso etiam usu retineant.

Neq; his adversatur B. LUTHERUS, scribens in majore Confessione: monstrato pane, monstrari Corpus CHRISTI : tacto pane tangi corpus CHRISTI : masticato pane, masticari Corpus CHRISTI. Respicit enim ille ad arctissimum Unionis Sacramentalis vinculum, quod pani cum Corpore CHRISTI intercedit, & facit, ut in usu Sacramenti hujus, Panis neq; manducari, neq; ore Corporis attrectari queat, quin simul manducetur & contrectetur ipsum Corpus CHRISTI: non quidem modo naturali, aut " Capernaitico: sed mystico, & Sacramentali. Quod " ipsum sensit, & credit Lutherus, cum statim " sic se explicat: Verum tamen interim, ratumq; il- " lud manet, quòd nemo Corpus CHRISTI cernat, " tangat, dentibus conterat: tametsi quod Panis fit, rectè vereq; Corpori CHRISTI propter Unionem Sacramentalem tribui sit certissimum. Impudens, ergò & malitiosum convitium nobis faciunt Sacramentarij, quando scribunt, doceri à nobis, PER SE ac propriè Corpus CHRISTI manducari, & conteri dentibus. Scribit quidem Lutherus, verè & directè dici, manducato pane, manducari Corpus CHRISTI: nuspiam verò dixit, per se ac propriè hoc fieri. Sic ergò improbè pervertunt verba Lutheri isti homines, ut quâ fieri queat ratione, etiam per manifesta crimina falsi, nostræ doctrinæ invidiam concilient.

Ipsi verò interim sententiam suam de Unione Sacramentali ita involvunt, ut quid dicant, aut dicere velint, Lector etiam attentus vix assequi possit: ut quando in Consensu suo sic scriptitant: Sacramentalis Unio rerum cum signis, est propriè virtus & gratia Sacramenti: quæ causa est, cur nomina rerum cum Symbolis commutentur. Item in margine: Unio Sacramentalis est communicatio rerum cum signis in verbo gratiæ & promissionis. Vel, Unio Sacramentalis est mystica & relativa, ex instituto, & ordinatione DEI in verbo.

Quas sanè definitiones pluribus fermè constare vitijs, quàm verbis, prolixè admodùm, & satis nervosè ostendimus, in Articulo de

Sacramentis in genere cap. 1. quæst. 3. Summa omnium eò redit, quòd nudum duntaxat respectum, sive σχέσιν aut relationem pani tribuant, propter hæc verba: Hoc est corpus meum: & docent, Panem esse verum & Essentiale CHRISTI corpus, respectu scilicet & σχέσει ad verum CHRISTI corpus, quod repræsentet, & cujus vicem gerat; cùm illud à Cœnâ tanto intervallo sit remotum, quanto summum cælum distat ab imâ terrâ. Non aliter, ac cùm Rustici lapidem in finibus agrorum erigunt, & tribuunt illi nomen limitis, proptereà, quòd agros & prata limitet. Sic CHRISTUM panem accepisse, & tribuisse ei nomen veri sui Corporis, pro nobis traditi: ut hoc modo in fractione, distributione, & manducatione, absens Corpus CHRISTI repræsentet, atq; vicem ejus gerat: & ut fractio, distributio, & manducatio Corporis CHRISTI veri & essentialis, sed σχετικῶς, proptereà, quod absentis Corporis CHRISTI, & certo cuidam cœli loco inclusi, nomen sustineat, & gerat: Talem σχέσιν sive respectum nominant Unionem Sacramentalem: hoc est, pro nucleo putamina, & pro pipere mufcerdam improbè & veteratoriè suis venditare student.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Question V. On Sacramental Predication

Concerning the doctrine of Sacramental Predications, we hold at the beginning, as the firmest anchor of faith, this Theological axiom: As is the Union, such also is the predication. For because the mode of predicating results from the Union of things, it must certainly be judged solely from this. Now, if we examine more accurately the phrases or propositions proper to this Article: a twofold mode of predicating will also emerge.

But two Sacramental propositions occur most especially, of which the former is this: This is my body: the latter: The bread is the body of CHRIST. For the orthodox Church acknowledges that both of these are true, and consistent with the words of the Institution, when a correct explanation is applied, and it has almost never in any age shrunk from the use of either.

There is, however, a clear distinction between the two, both as to authority and as to emphasis, or the evidence of the predication. The former is ἔγγραφος, and has CHRIST himself as its author: the latter has prevailed through ecclesiastical use: the former is proper to the primitive institution: necessity brought in the latter, which corruptions that arose in the Church gave birth to. The former is plain and perspicuous, which does not greatly require further explanation among those who show themselves teachable to the Holy Spirit. For it produces this manifest sense, that CHRIST that which he commands to eat, to be his body. The latter stands in need of a certain explanation of its own.

Concerning both these propositions, judgment is most correctly taken from the doctrine of Sacramental Union. In the former proposition, therefore, the demonstrative pronoun THIS does not point to one thing; but it contains a complex of two things. For it exhibits to the sense that which is less principal: but to the mind it points out the more principal thing, namely that which is expressly placed in the predicate immediately, and which, by means of that former thing as a symbol of exhibition, is offered in the Sacrament. In the subject, therefore, of this proposition, a complex of those two things, elemental and heavenly, is always held to be involved: of which, however, the dignity or condition of each is not equal and the same. For one is more, the other less principal: One provides the use of symbol and medium: The other is the Signified, or the treasure itself: to both of which it is necessary to turn the mind to the thing at the same time, when we are engaged in this confused consideration of the subject concerning the former proposition. But if an approach ought to be made to resolve and unfold that complex, and the bread is considered separately, then it must be well observed that the Body of CHRIST is predicated of it, not essentially (for the bread and the Body of CHRIST remain, even in the Union itself, or the use of this Sacrament, things differing in essence) but Sacramentally, or by and because of that mystical Union, and therefore that the Body is predicated of the bread by a predication that is neither proper or regular, nor identical, nor figurative; but clearly unusual, and unknown to all human reason. Now, however, when the other part is considered in unfolding this subject, namely the Body of CHRIST itself: in this respect indeed, because that which the subject has complexly, and that which the predicate then expressly enunciates, are something one and the same: it is by no means to be denied that something of an identical predication occurs.

Moreover, in the other proposition, when the Body of CHRIST is enunciated of the Bread individually and expressly: it must be well held that the predication is again neither customary, that is, neither proper, nor figurative: but clearly singular and unusual: of which this is the genuine explanation: that the Bread is not properly, not essentially, not tropically the Body of CHRIST: but by the force and mode of Sacramental Union, just as was shown in the immediately preceding question.

With these things thus explained, it is clearly evident that both these propositions, although they differ somewhat from each other in mode of expression and perspicuity: nevertheless agree most correctly in the sense itself in every way.

Furthermore, it is evident from this and that, why we do not tolerate or admit any trope or figure in the words of either proposition. For as soon as such a thing is conceded, the mystery of the Sacramental Union, or rather the rationale of every mystery, would immediately perish completely. For that which is feigned to be a Union in a bare signification and in respect of Relation or σχέσεως: that is not Sacramental or mystical; but merely a common relation, as was shown above. Nor does the authority of Luther oppose us in this place, whose writings testify that he did not abhor the trope of Synecdoche. For Luther understands a Grammatical Synecdoche, which is placed in the whole sentence: not a Rhetorical one, which is a trope of a Diction and consists in individual words, which can be admitted without difficulty in the former proposition (This is my Body): as was explained more fully above in Question 2.

Nor is any ἀντίφασις or Contradiction implied when we establish that the individual words of those propositions are to be taken κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν: and yet that each proposition is unusual. This reason is manifest, because each is not asserted according to the same thing, to the same thing. For when we urge τὸ ῥητὸν, then we look at the individual words of those propositions: but when we urge an unusual predication, then we consider the whole proposition. What? That an unusual predication cannot have a place except in the simple, proper, and literal signification of the individual words, so much so that if you bend a single little word toward impropriety and a figurative sense: immediately the unusual predication would perish completely: and a figurative or tropical one would succeed. For example: In each of those propositions: This is my Body: or Bread is the body of CHRIST, the predication is either regular, or figurative, or singular or unusual. It cannot be regular, even by the confession of the Adversaries themselves: since it fights against every rule of nature. Now if it is figurative: a Trope will be present either in the subject, and thus it is not to be understood as true bread: or in the predicate, and thus it is to be understood as a Tropical body: Or in the Copula IS: which, however, can by no means happen, because it is never predicated alone, but is always a συγκατηγορούμενον, as was shown above in question 2. There remains, therefore, a singular and unusual predication, which strictly retains and observes the proper, simple, and native sense of the individual words.

Nor does it stand in the way of this opinion of ours that the Blessed Luther never and nowhere made mention of an unusual predication. For the cause is at hand: Because, namely, the Blessed Luther had a controversy with those who established a trope either in the subject, like Carlstadt: or in the Copula, like Zwingli: or in the predicate, like Oecolampadius. But after the Calvinists, after the death of the Blessed Luther, began to dispute no longer about individual words, but about the whole proposition, This is my Body, and to contend that it is figurative and metonymical: here at last the necessity also fell upon us to insert the doctrine concerning the unusual manner of predicating into this Article.

Regarding Identical Predication, it has just now been shown when it can have a place in Sacramental propositions. That alone deserves observation, what struggle was agitated concerning this controversy in the time of Luther: and indeed between the Scholastic Doctors and Wycliffe. For to both it seemed absurd that diverse and disparate things or substances should be identical to one another and can be predicated: because the species of things are so distinct that each one, by the very fact that it is, cannot be another. And indeed both parties of the dissenters struck heavily against this rock, while the Scholastics contended that by the demonstrative pronoun THIS, the Body of CHRIST alone is uniquely denoted: and thus they removed the bread from the complex of this Pronoun: Wycliffe, however, understood only and solely the bread: meanwhile, both the Sacramental Union and the presence of the body of Christ being not obscurely denied.

Blessed LUTHER, therefore, entering upon a middle path, subscribed to neither party: and demonstrated with excellent reasons and examples that there is absolutely no danger or inconvenience if it be established that things or disparate species are predicated of one another, not indeed by identical, but by Sacramental predication.

This purer doctrine of ours contains the foundation of those assertions, or formulas of speaking, by which the Body and Blood of CHRIST are said to be and to be exhibited IN, WITH, UNDER bread and wine. For by these phrases, there is no departure whatsoever from the native, proper, and literal meaning of the words.

The reason is this: because the predication is not customary, but uncustomary, for the explanation of which these formulas of speaking are employed. Therefore, just as Scripture itself explains similar kinds of predications, such as, CHRIST is GOD, The Word was made Flesh, John 14, in this manner: GOD is in CHRIST: 2 Cor. 5:19, GOD was manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3:16: with the sense of those propositions not differing in the least: So similarly, that proposition, Bread is the Body of CHRIST, with those particles of the propositions applied, receives that explanation which produces no variation whatsoever in the sense.

And it is frivolous if a figment of local inclusion or of some hiding place is imputed to these particles. If these particles were applied to physical things, then perhaps some local inclusion or hiding would have a place: But in divine matters, it is so far from the case that this quibble can stand, that the explanation of even the highest mysteries does not admit it: For example: When CHRIST declares that He is in the Father, and the Father in Him: John 14:10, the Apostle asserts that CHRIST dwells in our hearts: Eph. 3:17.

Furthermore, it is not without weighty reason that the Orthodox Church has judged that it must use these formulas of speaking.

1. For if, in the first place, it most conveniently expressed its mind concerning the mystery of the Sacramental Union: likewise concerning the true and real presence, and the distribution of the Body and Blood of CHRIST in the Supper.

Latin:

Circa doctrinam de Prædicationibus Sacramentalibus initiò ceu firmissimam fidei anchoram tenemus axioma hoc Theologicum: Qualis est Unio, talis etiam est prædicatio. Quia enim prædicandi modus ex Unione rerum resultat, utiq; ex hâc de eo unicè judicandum fuerit. Jam verò si phrases sive propositiones Articuli hujus proprias accuratiùs expendamus: geminus etiam emerget prædicandi modus.

Duæ autem potissimùm occurrunt propositiones Sacramentales, quarum prior hæc est: Hoc est Corpus meum: posterior: Panis est corpus CHRISTI. Utramq; enim harum veram esse, & verbis Institutionis, dextrâ adhibitâ explicatione, convenientem, Ecclesia orthodoxa agnoscit, quæ ab usu utriusq; nullis ferè unquam seculis abhorruit.

Est tamen inter utrasque luculentum discrimen, tùm quoad autoritatem, tùm quoad emphasin, sive prædicandi evidentiam. Prior illa ἔγγραφος est, & autorem habet ipsum CHRISTUM: posterior usu Ecclesiastico invaluit: prior institutionis primitivæ propria: posteriorem necessitas invexit, quam obortæ in Ecclesiâ corruptelæ pepererunt. Prior plana atq; perspicua est, quæ ulteriorem explicationem magnoperè non requirit apud eos, qui se Spiritui Sancto dociles præbent. Gignit enim hunc manifestum sensum, quod CHRISTUS id, quod edere jubet, corpus suum esse pronunciet. Posterior suâ quâdam explicatione indiget.

De utraque hâc propositione, ex doctrinâ de Unione Sacramentali, judicium quàm rectissimè sumitur. In priori ergò propositione, pronomen δεικτικὸν HOC, rem non unam monstrat; sed complexum duarum rerum continet. Nam sensui, id quod minùs principale est, exhibet: menti verò rem principaliorem monstrat, eam scilicet, quæ statim in prædicato exprefsè ponitur, quæque mediante priore illâ, ceu symbolo exhibitionis, in Sacramento offertur. In subjecto ergò propositionis hujus, se mper complexus duarum istarum rerum elementaris & cœlestis, involutus habetur : cujus tamen utriusq; non est par & æqualis vel dignitas, vel conditio. Altera enim magis, altera minùs principalis est : Una symboli & medij usum præstat: Altera est Signatum, sive thesaurꝙ ipse: ad quam utramq; rem simul animum advertere necessum est, cum in confusâ hac quasi subjecti consideratione, circa priorem propositionem versamur. Quod si ad complexum istud dirimendum, & evolvendum accessus fieri debeat, & seorsim panis consideretur, tùm probè observandum, Corpus CHRISTI de eo prædicari, non essentialiter, (manent enim panis & corpus CHRISTI, in ipsâ etiam Unione, sive usu Sacramenti hujus, res essentiis differentes) sed Sacramentaliter, sive per & propter Unionem istam mysticam, ac proindè prædicatione neq; propriâ sive regulari, neque identicâ, neq; figuratâ; sed inusitatâ planè, & omni rationi humanæ ignotâ, Corpus de pane prædicari.
