Jam verò quando pars altera consideratur in evolvendo hoc subjecto, nempè ipsum Corpus CHRISTI: hoc sanè respectu, quia id, quod subjectum complexè habet, & quod prædicatum deindè exprefsè enunciat, quiddam unum atq; idem sunt: identicæ prædicationis quiddam fieri, minimè negandum est.

Cæterùm in alterâ propositione, cum de Pane Corpus CHRISTI sigillatim atq; exprefsè enunciatur: probè tenendum est, prædicationem rursus neq; usitatam hoc est, neq; propriam, neq; figuratam esse : sed planè singularem & inusitatam: cujus hæc est genuina explicatio: Panem non propriè, non essentialiter, non tropicè esse Corpus CHRISTI : sed vi & modo Sacramentalis Unionis, prout quæstione præcedente proximâ est ostensum.

His ita explicatis liquidò patet, ambas istas propositiones, quamvis modo locutionis, & perspicuitate inter sese nonnihil differant: sensu tamen ipso undequaque rectissimè congruere.

Deindè constat hinc & illud, cur nullum tropũ aut figuram, in verbis utriusq; propositionis, toleremus vel admittamus. Quamprimùm enim talis conceditur, statim Unionis Sacramentalis mysterium, imò omnis mysterij ratio penitùs exolesceret. Nam quæ in nudâ significatione, & Relationis sive σχέσεως respectu fingitur esse Unio: ea Sacramentalis aut mystica non est; sed vulgaris duntaxat relatio, uti supra ostensum. Neq; adversatur nobis hoc loco Lutheri autoritas, quem à tropo Synecdoches non abhorruisse, scripta ejus testantur. Nam Grammaticam Synecdochen, quæ in oratione integrâ ponitur : non Rhetoricam, quæ Dictionis tropus est, & in singulis verbis consistit, Lutherus intelligit, quæ in priore propositione (Hoc est Corpus meum) admitti haud difficulter potest: uti supra Quæst. 2. fusiùs explicatum fuit.

Neq; ulla etiam ἀντίφασις sive Contradictio implicatur, quando propositionum istarum verba singula, κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν accipienda esse: & inusitatam tamen utramq; propositionem esse statuimus. Ratio hæc est manifesta, quia non secundum idem, ad idem utrumq; asseritur. Quando enim τὸ ῥητὸν urgemus, tum singula propositionum istarum verba respicimus: Quando verò inusitatam prædicationem urgemus, tum integram propositionem consideramus. Quid? quòd inusitata prædicatio locum habere nequit, nisi in simplice, propriâ, ac literali singulorum vocabulorum significatione, adeò, ut si unicam voculam ad improprietatem, & sensum figuratum inflectas: mox inusitata prædicatio penitùs expiret: & succedat figurata, sive tropica. Exempli gratia: In utrâque propositione istâ: Hoc est Corpus meum : vel Panis est corpus CHRISTI, prædicatio vel regularis, vel figurata, vel singularis sive inusitata locum habet. Regularis esse nequit, ipsa etiam Adversariorum confessione: cum omni enim naturæ regula ea pugnat. Jam figurata si est: Tropus inerit vel subjecto, & sic non verus panis intelligendus: vel prædicato, & sic Tropicum corpus intelligendum: Vel Copulæ EST: id quod tamen fieri nullâ ratione potest, propterea, quòd ea nunquàm sola κατηγορεῖται, sed semper est συγκατηγορούμενον, uti supra ostensum quæst. 2. Relinquitur ergò prædicatio singularis & inusitata, quæ proprium, simplicem ac nativum singulorum vocabulorum sensum strictè retinet, & observat.

Neq; sententiæ huic nostræ quicquam obstat, quòd B. Lutherus nunquàm & nuspiam Inusitatæ prædicationis mentionem fecit. In promptu enim causa est: Quia nimirùm B. Luthero controversia fuit cum illis, qui tropum constituebant vel in subjecto, ut Carolostadius: vel in Copulâ, ut Zvvinglius: vel in prædicato, ut Oecolampadius, constituerunt. Postquàm verò non ampliùs de vocabulis singulis: sed de integrâ propositione, Hoc est Corpus meum, Calviniani post obitum B. Lutheri disputare, eamq; figuratam, & metonymicam esse contendere cœperunt: hîc demùm nostris etiam incumbebat necessitas, doctrinam de inusitatâ prædicandi ratione, Articulo huic inserere.

Quoad Prædicationem Identicam jam modò ostensum, quando ea in propositionibus Sacramentalibus locum habere possit. Illud tantùm observationem meretur, quid certaminis de hâc controversiâ tempore Lutheri agitatum fuerit: & quidem inter Doctores Scholasticos, & inter Wiclephum. Utrisque enim videbatur absurdum, ut diversæ ac disparatæ res sive substantiæ de se invicem identicæ prædicari possint: proptereà quòd species rerum ita sint distinctæ, ut quælibet eo ipso, quod est, aliud esse nequeat. Et sanè utraq; pars dissidentium ad hunc scopulum graviter impegit, dùm Scholastici per pronomen δεικτικὸν HOC, solum Corpus CHRISTI unicè notari contenderent: & sic panem è complexu hujus Pronominis tollerent: Wiclefus verò solum ac unum panem intelligeret: ipsâ interim & Unione Sacramentali, & præsentia corporis Christi haud obscurè negatâ.

B. ergò LUTERUS mediâ viâ ingressus, neutri parti subscripsit: & præclaris rationibus atque exemplis demonstravit, nihil prorsus subesse vel periculi, vel incommodi, si res sive species disparatæ, non quidem per prædicationem identicam, sed Sacramentalem, de se invicem prædicari, statuatur.

Continet purior hæc doctrina nostra fundamentum earum assertionum, sive formularum loquendi, quibus Corpus & Sangvinem CHRISTI, IN, CUM, SUB pane & vino esse, ac exhiberi dicitur. Neq; enim istis phrasibus, à nativâ, propriâ & literali verborum significatione quicquam receditur.

Ratio hæc est: quia non usitata, sed inusitata est prædicatio, ad cujus explicationem hæ loquendi formulæ adhibentur. Proindè, sicut scriptura ipsa, similis generis prædicationes, quales sunt, CHRISTUS est DEUS, Verbum Caro factum est, Johann. 14. in hunc modum explicat: DEUS est in CHRISTO: 2. Cor. 5, 19. DEUS manifestatus est in carne, 1. Tim. 3, 16: sensu propositionum istarum nihil quicquam differente: Ita consimiliter, propositio ista, Panis est Corpus CHRISTI, particulis istis propositionum adhibitis eam explicationem recipit, quæ in sensu nullam prorsus variationem gignit.

Et frivolum est, si localis inclusionis, aut latitationis cujuspiam figmentū particulis istis impingatur. Si rebus physicis particulæ istæ adhiberentur, tùm fortassis localis aliqua inclusio aut latitatio locum haberet: Verùm in divinis tantùm abest, ut hæc argutatio subsistere possit, ut summorum etiam mysteriorum explicatio eam non admittat: Verbi gratia: Cùm CHRISTUS se in Patre, & Patrem in se esse prædicat: Johann. 14, 10. Apostolus CHRISTUM in cordibus nostris habitare asserit: Ephes. 3, 17.

Porrò non sine gravi ratione fit, quòd formulis istis loquendi Ecclesia Orthodoxa sibi utendum esse censuit.

1. Si enim primùm commodissimè illa mentem suam expressit de mysterio Sacramentalis Unionis: item de verâ & reali præsentiâ, ac distributione Corporis & Sangvinis CHRISTI in Cœnâ.


### Chapter I. On the Substance of the Eucharistic Sacrament: Question V. On Sacramental Predication (continued)

3. Then, by these very words, it was testified that it has nothing in common with the Papal figment of transubstantiation.

4. Finally, in this very way he wished to insist upon the footsteps of Orthodox antiquity: from which St. Augustine writes thus to the Neophytes: Receive this IN the bread, which hung on the cross: and receive this IN the chalice, which was poured out from the side of CHRIST, The same in the Sentences of Prosper: The blood of CHRI-

STI under the appearance and taste of wine we drink. Chrysostom, book 3 on the Priesthood: With those things which are seen, the Body and Blood of CHRIST is believed to be present at the same time. Gregory of Nyssa: This is my blood, which is poured out: It is not this blood that is one thing, and that another; but one and the same, both this and that: Therefore, tomorrow it will be poured out from this side of mine, which you now drink, and see IN the chalice.

This is also what the adverbs Substantially, essentially, corporally mean for themselves: which do not define the mode of Union, or the quality of the predication, or even the mode of the presence itself of the Body of CHRIST: but only determine the Truth of the subject, that is, the true and real presence of the Body of CHRIST, and distinguish it against the σχετικὴν absence of the Calvinists.

The Sacramentarian party opposes itself with great effort to this purer doctrine, fighting for a figurative predication, and indeed such a one as, in this proposition, This is my body, through the pronoun THIS, defines nothing beyond mere and naked bread, and which attributes to external symbols only a naked appellation without the thing: or a naked σχέσιν or relation: but not any real Union with the heavenly thing. Hence such a definition has long since prevailed among them: Sacramental predication is a mode of speaking, by which the Sacrament of the thing is called by the name of the thing. Consensus Calv. page 319. The principal arguments, however, with which they fight are these:

I. As often as two or more things joined together are contained in a subject, it is by no means fitting that only one of them be predicated of it: because there ought never to be less in the predicate than is contained in the subject. Therefore, neither in the proposition of CHRIST, This is my body, will the pronoun THIS denote both bread and body at the same time.

I answer that the antecedent is true concerning those things which are coupled in the subject by some physical or essential Union. But now, such a Union has no place in this mystery. Therefore. It is added that the antecedent cannot even subsist in other mysteries of the faith, otherwise the argumentation of the Arians could be such.

There ought never to be less in the predicate than in the subject. But in those propositions by which the Savior calls himself the Son of Man, the predicate has no more than that CHRIST is the Son of man, that is, a true man. Therefore the subject also, namely the name of CHRIST, will not involve more in its complex than that CHRIST is a true man: and consequently he will not be GOD. Whence it is clear with what excellent reasons the Calvinist strives to palliate his ὀξεῖᾳ.

II. Every proposition in which there is a contradiction in the subject and predicate, as when I say: Man is a bird, is impossible in its proper and literal sense. But in this proposition: Bread is the Body of CHRIST, there is a contradiction in the subject and predicate: Because the subject (Bread) by its own definition contradicts or is repugnant to being that which is the predicate, and vice versa. Therefore, such a proposition, in its proper and literal sense, is simply impossible: and consequently, the predication will have to be established not as unusual, but as figurative: by which Bread is said to signify the Body of CHRIST σχετικῶς.

I answer that the major premise is true κατὰ τί (in a certain respect), but not absolutely. For it is true when things are disparate, in themselves, by themselves, and separated from each other, without regard to any intervening true and real Union, are understood and considered. Where it is impossible that the subject and predicate, contradictorily opposed to each other, should either be predicated of one another or be true. In which manner, indeed, we readily concede that bread, considered in itself, by itself, and outside the Sacramental Union, can never be called the Body of CHRIST.

But now, regarding the minor premise, in this proposition, 'Bread is the Body of CHRIST,' neither bread nor the Body of CHRIST is considered in itself, by itself, and outside the Sacramental Union: nor is one predicated of the other with respect to some simple and regular predication, as when I say, 'Man is an animal': but with respect to a third intervening thing, which is the Sacramental Union, which, just as it depends entirely upon the power and will of the institutor, so it causes things, however diverse and disparate, to concur to constitute one Third thing, not indeed in any physical way, but in a mystical, Sacramental, and unusual way.

Furthermore, it is also to be noted that in this mystery, the predication does not follow the nature and property of either the subject or the predicate, but the Union itself, which depends entirely upon the words of CHRIST, 'This is my body.' The argument therefore suffers from the fallacy of Division to Composition, and at the same time from ἐπερωτήσεως (begging the question).

I pass over the fact that this very argument does not sufficiently fit the rules of Logic. For which of the logicians has ever said or established that disparate things are contradictory, since by the consensus of all who philosophize correctly, disparate things must be held as diverse, but not as contradictory? But that diverse things can be united and joined to constitute some third thing, and with respect to this Union, can be predicated of one another, is clear from the example of the hypostatic union of two natures in CHRIST: from the example of the union of the Dove and the Holy Spirit: likewise of flame and Angels.

III. The mode of predication must be such as are the extremes: namely, the Subject and the Predicate. But these two extremes, Bread and Body, are συσιαστικὰ (essential). Therefore, the mode of predication itself will also be essential.

I answer that the major premise is again true only in a certain respect, namely concerning those things which are joined by a natural or Essential mode of Union: but it is most false concerning these mysteries of faith. This major premise is therefore corrected in this way: As is the mutual Union of the extremes, namely of the subject and predicate, such is also the resulting Predication. But in this mystery, the mode of Union is not essential; therefore, neither will the predication be such. However, this Sacramental Union differs from the Essential in its entire species. For those things which are united essentially constitute one Essence, as if composed of matter and form. But the Sacramental union leaves the essence of each of the united things entirely intact, safe, and simply unchanged.

IV. By the same mode of predication that Wine is the Blood of CHRIST, the Bread is also the Body of CHRIST. But Wine is the Blood of CHRIST just as the cup is the New Testament in the Blood of CHRIST, namely by Metonymical predication, insofar as the Cup is the pledge and seal of the New Testament. Therefore, by the same Metonymical predication, Bread is said to be the Body of CHRIST, insofar as it relates σχετικῶς (relatively) to the Body of CHRIST.

I answer that the minor premise is most false and suffers from a begging of the question. For this very thing must be proved, that just as the Cup is said μετωνυμικῶς (metonymically), or rather συνεκδοχικῶς (synecdochically), to be the New Testament in the Blood of CHRIST, in the same way Wine is said to be the Blood of CHRIST. But whether that phrase of Luke and Paul, 'The cup is the New Testament in the Blood of CHRIST,' supports a trope, and whether anything is thereby taken away from the literal sense of the words of the Supper, was shown expressly above in Question 2.

V. A Metonymy is whenever a Sign is put for the thing signified, and vice versa. But in the Sacraments, the thing signified is for the most part predicated of the Sign. Therefore, Metonymical predication has a place in them.

I answer, first, that a fallacy of faulty Definition is committed: for a Metonymy is said to be whenever the name of the signified thing is attributed only to the sign, without the intervention of any true and real Union between the Sign and the Signified: as when I call the toga 'peace,' or call the fasces 'power.' But now, in this mystery, between the Sign and the Signified, there intervenes not only a verbal predication, but a true and real Union with each other. Therefore, Metonymical predication has absolutely no place here.

Then the fallacy of equivocation is committed in the terms of Sign and Signified. For sometimes by the term Sign, the elementary part is understood; but by the appellation of Signified, the heavenly thing is understood: as when the Body and Blood of CHRIST are predicated of the bread and wine. That a metonymical predication can by no means have a place here has been demonstrated invincibly thus far: for not only does a mere permutation of names obtain here, but also the closest Union of Sign and Signified, which causes the sign to be no longer predicated merely in word, but to be in reality that Signified thing with which it is united: not indeed physically, but singularly, mystically, Sacramentally. Sometimes, however, by the term Signified, the fruit of the Sacrament is denoted, and then by the word Sign comes not some part, but the whole substance of the Sacrament: as when I say, Baptism is regeneration: that a metonymy might perhaps be conceded here was already shown above.

VI. The Testaments of the Patriarchs and Kings of the Old Testament consist of figurative words. Therefore, so does the Testament of CHRIST.

I answer 1. This argument proceeds from a part to the whole: where the consequence is not valid. 2. The fallacy of non-cause is committed. Those Testaments of the Old Testament consisted of figurative words, for the reason that they were for the most part nothing else than predictions and prophecies concerning the person and kingdom of CHRIST. Which respect is clearly excluded from the present Sacrament. Otherwise, where those testaments deal with the distribution of goods and assets among heirs: there they certainly consist of proper and most clear words, so that it is a sin to depart from their literal sense, according to the rules of the jurists:

1. One must not depart from the words of the testator, because such is presumed to have been the intention as the propriety of the words implies: nor is it to be believed that the testator intended what he did not say.

2. It is not presumed that the testator intended anything other than what he expressed in words: for if he had intended the contrary, there was certainly no difficulty in writing it.

Latin:

3. Deindè his ipsis verbis testatum fuit, nihil sibi commune esse cum figmento μετουσίας Pontificiæ.

4. Tandem hoc ipso modo Orthodoxæ antiquitatis vestigiis insistere voluit: ex quâ D. Augustinus ad Neophytos sic scribit: Hoc accipite IN pane, quod pependit in cruce: & hoc accipite IN calice, quod est effusum ex CHRISTI latere, Idem in Sent. Prosperi: Sangvinem CHRI-

STI SUB Vini specie & sapore potamus. Chrysost. lib. 3. de Sacerdotio: CUM illis rebus, quæ videntur, simuladesse creditur Corpus & Sanguis CHRISTI. Gregor. Nyssenus: Hic est sanguis meus, qui effunditur: Non est alius iste sanguis, & alius ille; sed unus idemq́; & iste, & ille: Cras igitur fundetur ex hoc meo latere, quem vos modò bibitis, & videtis IN calice.

Quod ipsum sibi quoq́; volunt Adverbia, Substantialiter, essentialiter, Corporaliter: quæ non vel modum Unionis, vel prædicationis qualitatem, vel ipsius etiam præsentiæ Corporis CHRISTI modum definiunt: sed tantùm Veritatem subjecti, hoc est, veram ac realem præsentiam Corporis CHRISTI determinant, & contra σχετικὴν absentiam Calvinianorum contra distingvunt.

Puriori hinc doctrinæ magno conatu se opponit Gens Sacramentaria, pugnans pro prædicatione figuratâ, & tali quidem, quæ in propositione hâc, Hoc est corpus meum, per pronomen HOC, nihil præter merum ac nudum panem definiat, quæq́; externis symbolis, nudam duntaxat appellationem sine re: sive nudam σχέσιν sive relationem: non verò ullam realem Unionem cum re cœlesti tribuat. Hinc talis definitio jam pridem apud ipsos obtinuit: Prædicatio Sacramentalis est modus loquendi, quo Sacramentum rei, nomine rei appellatur. Consens. Calv. pag. 319. Argumenta autem, quibus pugnant, præcipua sunt hæc:

I. Quoties duo aut plura simul conjuncta continentur in subjecto, minimè convenit alterum duntaxat de eo prædicari: quia in prædicato nunquàm minus debet esse, quàm in subjecto continetur. Ergò neq́; in propositione CHRISTI, Hoc est Corpus meum, pronomen HOC, & panem & corpus simul notabit.

Respondeo, antecedens verum esse de ijs, quæ in subjecto per Physicam quandam, aut essentialem Unionem sunt copulata. Jam verò talis Unio hoc in mysterio locum non habet. Ergò. Accedit, quòd Antecedens ne quidem in alijs fidei mysterijs potest subsistere, alioquin Arianorum argumentatio talis esse posset.

Nunquàm minùs debet esse in prædicato, quàm in subjecto. Atqui propositionibus illis, quibus Servator se Filium Hominis appellitat, prædicatum plus non habet, quàm quòd CHRISTUS sit Filius hominis, hoc est, verus homo. Ergò subjectum etiam, nempè nomen CHRISTI, plus suo complexo non involvet, quàm quòd CHRISTUS sit verus homo: & per Consequens non erit DEUS. Unde patet, quam egregijs rationibus Calviniani suâ ὀξεῖᾳ palliare studeat.

II. Omnis propositio, in quâ Contradictio est in Subjecto & Prædicato: ut quando dico: Homo est avis, in suo proprio & literali sensu est impossibilis. Atqui in hac propositione: Panis est Corpus CHRISTI, contradictio est in subjecto & prædicato: Quia subjectum (Panis) propriâ suâ definitione contradicit sive repugnat esse id, quod est prædicatum, & contrà. Ergò talis propositio, in suo proprio & literali sensu, simpliciter est impossibilis: ac per consequens, Prædicatio non inusitata: sed figurata erit constituenda: quâ Panis σχετικῶς Corpus CHRISTI significare dicatur.

Respondeo, Majorem veram esse κατὰ τί, non verò ἀπλω̃ς. Vera enim est, quando res disparatæ, in se, per se, & à se invicem separatæ, sine respectu intervenientis veræ ac realis alicujus Unionis, intelliguntur & considerantur. Ubi impossibile est, ut subjectum & prædicatum, Contradictoriè sibi opposita, de se mutuò vel prædicentur, vel vera esse queant. Quo sanè pacto ultrò concedimus, Panem in se, per se, &- extra Unionem Sacramentalem consideratum, nunquàm posse dici Corpus CHRISTI.

Jam verò, quoad Minorem, in propositione hâc, Panis est Corpus CHRISTI, neq; Panis, neq; Corpus CHRISTI, in se, per se, & extra Unionem Sacramentalem consideratur: vel unum de altero, respectu simplicis & regularis alicujus prædicationis, prædicatur, ut quando dico, Homo est animal: sed respectu tertij intervenientis, quod est Unio Sacramentalis, quæ ut in solidum dependet à virtute, & voluntate instituentis: ita facit, ut res, quantumvis diversæ ac disparatæ, ad unum constituendum Tertium concurrant, non quidem modo aliquo physico, sed mystico, Sacramentali, & inusitato.

Porrò & illud notandum, quòd hoc in mysterio, Prædicatio non sequitur naturam & proprietatem vel subjecti, vel prædicati: sed ipsam Unionem, quæ in solidum dependet à verbis CHRISTI, Hoc est Corpus meum. Laborat ergò argumentum Sophismate à Divisis ad Conjuncta: & simul ἐπερωτήσεως.

Mitto illud, quod ad præcepta Logica hoc ipsum argumentum non satis quadrat. Quis enim Logicorum unquàm dixit aut statuit: Disparata esse contradictoria: cùm omnium rectè philosophantium consensu disparata sint habenda pro diversis: non verò pro contradictorijs. Diversa autem ad unum quoddam tertium constituendum uniri ac conjungi, & Unionis hujus respectu, de se mutuò prædicari posse, patet exemplo Unionis hypostaticæ duarum naturarum in CHRISTO: exemplo Unionis Columbæ, & Spiritus Sancti: Item flammæ & Angelorum.

III. Talis debet esse prædicationis modus, qualia sunt extrema: Subjectum nimirùm & Prædicatum. Atqui duo isthæc extrema, Panis & Corpus sunt συσιαστικὰ essentialia. Ergò ipse quoq; prædicationis modus erit essentialis.

Respondeo, Majorem rursus veram esse tantùm secundum quid, nempè de ijs, quæ junguntur Unionis modo naturali sive Essentiali: Falsissimam verò de ijs mysteris fidei. Corrigitur ergò Major hæc in hunc modum: Qualis est Unio mutua extremorum, nempè subjecti & prædicati: talis etiam est indè resultans Prædicatio. At verò hoc in mysterio modus Unionis non est essentialis, Ergò neq; talis erit Prædicatio. Differt autem Sacramentalis hæc Unio ab Essentiali totâ specie. Quæ enim Essentialiter uniuntur, unam Essentiam, tanquàm ex materiâ & formâ compositâ constituunt. Sacramentalis verò unio cuilibet rerum unitarum, suam essentiam planè relinquit sartam, tectam, ac simpliciter immutatam.

IV. Quo Prædicationis modo Vinum est Sanguis CHRISTI, eodem etiam Panis est Corpus CHRISTI. Atqui Vinum ita est Sangvis CHRISTI, sicut calix est Novum Testamentum in Sanguine CHRISTI, nempè per prædicationẽ Metonymicam, quatenùs nimirùm Calix est pignus & sigillum Novi Testamenti. Ergò per eandem prædicationem Metonymicam Panis dicitur esse Corpus CHRISTI, quatenùs nimirùm σχετικῶς se habet ad Corpus CHRISTI.

Respondeo, Minorem esse falsissimam, & laborare petitione Principij. Hoc ipsum enim probandum est, quod quemadmodum Calix μετωνυμικῶς, vel potiùs συνεκδοχικῶς dicitur esse Novum Testamentum in sangvine CHRISTI, eodem etiam modo Vinum dicatur esse Sangvis CHRISTI. An verò phrasis illa Lucæ & Pauli, Calix est Novum Testamentum in Sangvine CHRISTI, tropum sustineat, & num indè τῷ ῥητῷ verborum Cœnæ quicquam decedat: supra Quæst. 2. ex professo ostensum fuit.

V. Metonymia est, quoties Signum ponitur pro signato, & contra. Atqui in Sacramentis plerumǫ signatum prædicatur de Signo. Ergò prædi- ... Metonymica in illis locum habet.

Respondeo, primùm committi ἀσφισμα vitiosæ Definitionis: Metonymia enim est àc dicitur, quoties figno tantùm nomen tribuitur rei signatæ: sine interventu veræ ac realis alicujus Unionis inter Signum & Signatum: ut quando togam nomino pacem: fasces nomino imperium. Jam verò hoc in mysterio, Signo & Signato, non verbalis tantùm prædicatio: sed vera ac realis invicem intercedit Unio. Ergò Metonymica prædicatio hîc locum planè nullum obtinet.

Deindè committitur Sophisma æquivocationis, in vocabulis Signi & Signati. Nam interdum Signi termino pars Elementaris: Signati verò appellatione, res cœlestis intelligitur: Ut quando Corpus & Sangvis CHRISTI de pane & vino prædicantur. Hîc metonymicam prædicationem locum nullo pacto habere posse, hactenùs invictè demonstratum: Neq; enim nuda tantùm permutatio nominum hîc obtinet: Verum etiam arctissima Unio Signi & Signati, quæ facit, ut signum jam non verbótenus prædicetur: sed reverà sit Signatum illud, cum quo unitum est: non quidem physicè, sed singulariter, mysticè, Sacramentaliter. Interdum verò Signati termino notatur fructus Sacramenti, & tùm Signi voce venit non pars aliqua, sed tota substantia Sacramenti: ut quando di co, Baptismus est regeneratio: hîc fortassis metonymiam concedi posse, jam suprà ostensum fuit.

VI. Testamenta Patriarcharum & Regum Veteris Testamenti constant verbis figuratis. Ergò & Testamentum CHRISTI.

Respondeo 1. argumentum hoc ex parte ad totum progredi: Ubi non valet consequentia. 2. Fallacia committitur non causæ. Testamenta illa Veteris Testamenti constabant verbis figuratis, ideò, quia plerumque nihil erant aliud, quàm prædictiones & vaticinia de personâ & regno CHRISTI. Qui respectus in præsenti Sacramento planè exulat. Aliàs ubi de distribuendis bonis & facultatibus inter hæredes agunt illa Testamenta : ibi certè constant verbis proprijs, maximeq; perspicuis , ita ut ab eorum literali sensu recedere nefas sit: secundum regulas Jureconsultorum :

1. Non recedendum à verbis Testatoris,quia talis præsumitur fuisse intentio , qualem verborum proprietas importat : Neq; credendum est,Testatorem id voluisse, quod non dixit.

2. Non præsumitur,Testatorem aliud voluisse, quàm verbis expressit : Nam si contrarium voluisset,nulla certè erat difficultas scribere.


### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Holy

On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of CHRIST in the Holy Supper.

The end and scope of all those things which have been discussed thus far aims solely at this, that it may be established upon certain and clearly immovable foundations, upon which the Orthodox most firmly build their doctrine concerning the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of CHRIST in the Holy Supper, and concerning the eating and drinking of the same. That this may be understood more clearly, in this second chapter, we contend for the παρουσίᾳ of the Body and Blood of the Lord with these arguments.

1. If everyone is the best interpreter of his own words: then certainly faith beyond all exception must be accorded to the Savior also, who explains himself quite clearly as to what he intends in this testament of his. But the Savior explains it in such a way that no pious person can have any doubt about the true and real presence of his Body and Blood in this Sacrament. Therefore, faith beyond all exception is deservedly accorded to him.

I prove the assumption thus: 1. CHRIST acts δεικτικῶς (demonstratively) concerning a present thing, namely that which he holds in his hands and offers to the disciples: he does not, however, act concerning a thing which is removed by very long intervals from the present action. 2. What the Savior wishes to be understood by that which he offers as present, he expresses lucidly when he explicitly names it his Body and his Blood: he does not, however, call it the virtue, the efficacy, the merits, or the benefits of his Body. 3. So that there may be no doubt concerning either the truth or the substance of the Body: he asserts that it is that very body which is now to be delivered; that very blood which is soon to be poured out for a saving ransom, which προκατηγορέμενα (predicates) apply to no absent thing, to no abstract thing. 4. The word IS expresses a manifest ὕπαρξιν (existence), to which neither the evidence of the mystery nor the clarity of the predicates permits one to attach a σημασίαν (signification).

II. The entire Sacrament of the Eucharist consists and is completed as to its substance, not by one thing or another, whether earthly or heavenly: but by both together, and thus by a presence that is far more intimate: so that with one of them removed,

and separated by very long intervals from the other, it must be determined that it is not an entire Sacrament, but only a part, and indeed a less noble one, that is present.

And yet the Savior instituted the Sacrament not for some part, but by reason of the whole Substance, and thus by reason of both essential parts most present, and exhibited it to the disciples. Therefore, it is necessary that not only the earthly, but also the heavenly thing, namely the Body and Blood of CHRIST, be most truly present in the Sacrament.

Alluding to this argument, St. Augustine in the sentences of Prosper says: Just as the person of CHRIST consists and is composed of GOD and man, since Christ is true GOD and man: So the Sacrifice of the Church consists of two things, the Sacrament and the reality of the Sacrament, that is, the Body of CHRIST.

III. There is added the consent of Orthodox antiquity, which (as shown above) 1. asserts that this Sacrament is made and consists of two things: namely, the earthly and the heavenly. 2. It warns, however, that we should not allow ourselves to be moved in any way from the simplicity of the words of institution: as Chrysostom, Homily 38 on Matthew: Let us believe GOD, and not contradict Him, even if what He says seems absurd to our sense and thought, and His word surpasses both our sense and our reason. Let us do this in all things, and especially in the mysteries, not looking only at those things which are placed before our eyes: but also holding to His words. For we cannot be deceived by His words: but our sense is very easily deceived. Since, therefore, He said, THIS is my Body, let us be held by no ambiguity, but let us believe, and perceive it with the eyes of the intellect.

IV. The foundations which blessed LUTHER used in this cause are these:

I. CHRIST JESUS is true GOD and man, in one indissoluble person.

II. The right hand of GOD is everywhere.

III. The Word of GOD is true, nor can it lie.

IV. GOD has various modes by which something can be somewhere. Commonly three modes are enumerated: 1. Local and Circumscriptive, which is proper to natural bodies, by which they have places equal to themselves. 2. Definitive, in which mode Angels and Spirits are somewhere, who are not however measured by the capacity of a place. Christ used this mode when going out through the sepulchral stone, and entering through closed doors. 3. Repletive, proper to GOD alone, who so fills all places that He is concluded by none. Jeremiah 23, 24.

Indeed, the Body of CHRIST, considered according to its different states, is clearly perceived to be somewhere in a triple mode.

THE FIRST mode is physical, which he mostly used at the time of his emptying, and not rarely even after the resurrection, in which mode he can also use even now, when he wishes. He will, however, use it on the last day 1 Tim. 6, 15. In which mode, indeed, he is neither with GOD, nor with the Father, nor in Heaven. For the spaces of places do not reach here.

THE SECOND is spiritual or glorious, which is the same as the definitive, by which CHRIST was able to penetrate even the most solid bodies in a moment: In which way CHRIST is now in his Body in the Heavens with the Angels and the blessed heavenly inhabitants, not occupying the spaces of places abut like spirits, anything in a moment. How we also await bodies, conformed to the body of CHRIST in the resurrection of the just: Phil. 3, 21.

The THIRD mode is singular and divine, by which, indeed, the Body is one person with GOD. If therefore, (says Blessed LUTHER) we wish to think piously and rightly, one must think of CHRIST in such a way that his divinity is outside and above all creatures. Then, because the humanity of CHRIST alone (although by itself it is a creature) is so joined to the Divinity that it constitutes one hypostasis with it: it cannot be otherwise, but that this very thing also must be placed above and outside all other creatures, and nowhere but below GOD alone. In this respect, we are about to undergo a consideration of this mystery, as if we are snatched outside this world and into a certain new orb. Here, therefore, let the judgment rest with faith. Outside creatures, there is nothing besides GOD. But the humanity of CHRIST alone reaches to GOD, so that it is personally one with him. Thus, therefore, it is necessary that it be raised above all creatures, so that where GOD is, there also is this humanity. Now, however, because the Word is not incarnate in part, but wholly, and is never separated in eternity from the humanity assumed personally: nay rather, outside this Man, who is united hypostatically with GOD, no GOD is known at all: it is absolutely brought about that this Man is nowhere absent where GOD is: and thus all things are most thoroughly full of CHRIST, even according to his humanity; not indeed in that mode of being somewhere first, which is corporeal: but in that last mode, which is singular and divine. For this must be held with undoubted firmness, that in whatever place you establish the Divinity of the Son of GOD, or the Word, to be, there you must establish the incarnate one, and hypostatically undivided. But if he is personally wherever he is: it is necessary that the man also be there. For there are not two divided persons, but CHRIST is one: and wherever you can say, Here is GOD, you must say that the Man CHRIST is there also. But if you wished to grant any place where GOD would be, but the man would not be there at the same time, then a dissolution of the person would occur: for you could say, GOD is there who is not at the same time man. But far be it that we should have such a CHRIST. For if it followed that the spaces and intervals of places could separate those natures united personally: when, however, neither death nor the Devil could tear them apart. And thus a miserable CHRIST would be made, who would reign joined to the Divinity in only one place, but in all other places, separated from the same, would have to act. Far, far be such a separation of natures. Now it must be observed how Blessed Luther adapts this to the business of the Supper. From the second mode of being somewhere, therefore, it has now been shown that if the Body of CHRIST is somewhere, it is not necessary that it be in a physical mode, according to dimensions. For it is certain that his Body penetrated through the sepulchral stone and closed doors in an uncircumscribed and supernatural manner. But if at least in that mode, which will be common to our bodies in glory, he could be outside the conditions of dimensions and places, in the stone and doors: what prevents him from being able to be in the same way also in the bread of the Supper? Nay, if Christ, using that mode, was not subject to the condition of natural things, and was thus in creatures, so that they did not measure or comprehend him: how much more according to this third singular and divine mode, if he will be able to penetrate all creatures, so that while he himself is most present to all, he is nevertheless comprehended by none. For you will place this mode, by which this man has been made one person with GOD, very far outside every condition of creatures, by an interval as great as GOD himself is removed from them. Again, you will place the same as closely and deeply within all creatures as GOD is most thoroughly within them.

These things which Blessed LUTHER argued with great spirit against Zwingli in his Greater Confession, the Sacramentarians variously agitate as alien and having nothing to do with the matter, shouting that by this pact two Articles are confused, concerning the Person of CHRIST and the Supper of the LORD: and that it is not right that foundations be sought from the former for the confirmation of the latter.

But this cavil is spineless. For if they fear so greatly that some confusion of the Articles of faith might arise, why, I ask, did they not impose this law upon themselves: but, having transgressed it many times, they sought arguments even from the single article concerning the Person of CHRIST for asserting the absence of the Body and Blood in the Supper: because the presence of these fights against the properties of a true and natural human body: with the ascension, with the session at the right hand of the Father, with the return for judgment. Here, therefore, Luther, provoked by his adversaries, wished, nay indeed ought, to seek the foundations of purer doctrine from the same article. But this also must be noted in this place, that in this Eucharistic Controversy not one, but two diverse Questions are agitated: of which one is concerning the will and intention of CHRIST, whether, indeed, he wishes to exhibit his body to be eaten and his blood to be drunk in the Supper, and thus to be most present with his Body and Blood to the Eucharistic bread and wine? Where, indeed, Luther determined that the decision of this question must be sought from nowhere else than from the Article of the Lord's Supper alone, and we with him determine the same. The other question is concerning the power of Christ: whether, indeed, he can be present with his body and blood in all places where this Sacrament is dispensed? Whether the flesh of Christ so eaten can provide life for us? Where, indeed, he would be a fool who determined that the decision of these questions must be sought from anywhere other than from the Article concerning the Person of CHRIST. Blessed Luther is therefore free from all reproach, who wished to explain, illustrate, and assert against the babblings of the Sacramentarians these two questions from their own proper seats.

Latin:

De verâ ac reali præsentiâ Corporis & Sanguinis CHRISTI in S. Cœnâ.

FInis & scopus eorum omnium, quæ hactenùs disputata sunt, eò unicè collineat, ut de certis ac planè immotis constet fundamentis,quibus Orthodoxi doctrinam de verâ ac reali præsentiâ Corporis & Sanguinis CHRISTI in S. Cœnâ, deq; eorundem manducatione & bibitione firmissimè superstruunt. Quod ut planiùs intelligatur, hoc quidem capite secundo, pro παρουσίᾳ Corporis & Sanguinis Dominici his rationibus pugnamus.

1. Si unusquisq; verborum suorum optimus est interpres : utiq; Servatori etiam seipsum , quid in Testamento hoc suo velit, satis perspicuè explicanti, fides omni exceptione major fuerit adhibenda. Atqui ita Servator ipsum explicat, ut nemini pio de verâ ac reali præsentiâ Corporis & Sanguinis ipsig in Sacramento hoc possit esse dubium. Ergò fides omni exceptione major ipsi meritò adhibetur.

Assumtionem sic probo: 1. CHRISTUS δεικτικῶς de re præsenti agit, eâ nimirùm, quam manibus acceptam discipulis porrigit: non autem agit de re, quæ à præsente actione longissimis intervallis sit remota. 2. Quid Servator intelligi velit per id, quod præsens porrigit, dilucidè exprimit, quando illud disertè nominat Corpo suum, & Sangvinem suum: non autem virtutem, non efficaciam, non merita, non beneficia Corporis sui appellat. 3. Ne dubium ullum esse possit vel de Veritate, vel de Substantiâ Corporis: illud ipsum corpus esse asserit, quod jamjam sit tradendum; eum ipsum Sangvinem, qui mox sit pro λύτρῳ salutari effundendus, quæ προκατηγορέμενα nulli rei absenti, nulli abstractæ competunt. 4. ὕπαρξιν manifestam exprimit Verbum EST, cui σημασίαν affingere, neq; mysterij evidentia, neq; prædicatorum perspicuitas permittit.

II. Integrum Eucharistiæ Sacramentum quoad Substantiā,non re unâ, aut alterutrâ,vel terrenâ, vel cœlesti: sed utraq; junctim, & sic longè præsentiâximâ constat & absolvitur:adeò, ut unâ carū remo-

tà, & longissimis intervallis ab alterà separatà, jã sentissime non Sacramentum integrum: sed pars duntaxat, & quidem ignobilior praesens adesse, statuendum sit.

Atqui Servator non partem aliquam, sed integriū ratione Substantia Sacramentum, & sic ratione utriusq́ partis essentialis praesentissimum instituit, & discipulis exhibuit. Ergò, non terrena duntaxat, sed & res cœlestis, Corpus nimirùm & Sangvis CHRISTI, relatissimè sit praesens Sacramento necesse est.

Alludens ad hoc argumentum D. Augusting in sententijs Prosperi, Sicut, inquit, persona CHRISTI constat & consistitur ex DEO & homine, cùm Christus sit verus DEUS & homo: Ita Sacrificium Ecclesiae duobus consistitur Sacramento, & re Sacramenti, hoc est, Corpore CHRISTI.

III. Accedit Orthodoxae antiquitatis consensus, quae (uti suprà ostensum) 1.asserit, Sacramentum hoc duabus confici & constare rebus: terrenâ nimirum & cœlesti. 2. verò monet, ne ulla pacto à simplicitate verborum institutionis nos dimoveri patiamur: ut Chrysost. Homil. 38. in Matthaeum: Credamus DEO, neq́, contradicamus ei etiamsi sensui & cogitationi nostrae videatur absurdum esse, quod dicit, superetq́, & sensum, & rationem nostrã verbum ipsius. Quod in omnibus, & praecipuè in mystarijs faciamus, non illa solummodò, qua prae oculis posita sunt, adspicientes: sed verba quoq́, ejus tenentes. Nam verbis ejus defraudari non possumus: sensus verò noster deceptu facillimus est. Quoniam ergò ille dixit, HOC est Corpus meum, nulla teneamur ambiguitate, sed credamus, & oculis intellectus id perspiciamus.

IV. Fundamenta, quibus in hâc causâ B. LUTHERUS usus est, haec sunt:

I. CHRISTUS JESUS verus est DEUS & homo, in unâ insolubili personâ.

II. Dextera DEI est ubiquè.

III. Verbum DEI verum est, nec mentiri potest.

IV. DEUS varios habet modos, quibus alicubi possit esse aliquid. Vulgò tres modi recensentur: 1. Localis & Circumscriptivus, qui est corporú naturalium proprius, quâ loca sibi habent ἐσόμετρα. 2. Definitivus, quo modo alicubi sunt Angeli & Spiritus, qui loci capedine non tamen mensurantur. Hoc modo Christus usus est per lapidem sepulchralem egrediens, per clausas fores intrans. 3. Repletivus, solius DEI proprius, qui sic loca omnia replet, ut nullò concludatur. Jerem. 23, 24.

Imò CHRISTI Corpus secundum diversos status consideratum, triplici modo alicubi esse, manifestè deprehenditur.

PRIMUS modus est Physicus, quo tempore exinanitionis plerumq́; usus est, & non rarò etiam post resurrectionem, Quo modo etiam nùcn uti potest, quando vult. Utetur autem in die novissimo 1. Tim. 6, 15. Quo sanè modo neq́; cum DEO, neq́; cum Patre, neq́; in Coelo est. Huc enim locorum spatia non pertingunt.

SECUNDUS spiritualis sive gloriosus est, qui idem est cum definitivo, quo ipsa etiam corpora solidissima in momento penetrare CHRISTUS potuit: Quomodo CHRISTUS Corpore suo nunc in Cœlis est cum Angelis, & beatis cœlitibus, non spacia locorum occupans ased Spirituum more quidvis in momento penetrans. Quomodo nos etiam expectamus Corpora, Corpori CHRISTI in resurrectione justorum σύμμορφα: Phil. 3, 21.

TERTIUS modus singularis ac divinus est, quo nimirùm Corpus cum DEO una persona est. Si ergò, (inquit B. LUTHERUS) piè rectèq́; sentire volumus, sic de CHRISTO cogitandum est, quod divinitas ejus sit extra & supra omnes creaturas. ,, Deindè, quia humanitas CHRISTI sola, (quamvis ,, per se est creatura) sic est conjuncta Divinitati, ut ,, unum cum eâ ὑπόστασιν constituat: fieri aliter ,, nequit, quin hæc ipsa quoq́;, supra & extra omnes ,, alias creaturas, nec nisi infra solum DEUM collo- ,, canda sit. Hoc respectu considerationem hujus my- ,, sterij subituri, qua si extra hunc mundum, & in no- ,, vum quendam orbem rapimur. Hic ergò judicium ,, penes fidem eﬅo. Extra creaturas præter DEUM ,, nihil est. Ad DEUM autem sola CHRISTI pertin- ,, git humanitas, ita ut unum cum ipso personaliter si- ,, at. Sic igitur supra creaturas omnes evehatur ne- ,, cesse eﬅ, ut ubi DEUS eﬅ, ibi etiam sit iﬅa humani- ,, tas. Jam verò quia λόγος non ex parte, sed totus ,, incarnatus eﬅ, incarnatus autem ab assumtâ perso- ,, naliter Humanitate in æternum nunquàm sejungi- ,, tur: Quin imò extra iﬅum Hominem, qui cum DEO ,, ὑποστατικῶς unitus eﬅ, nullus plane DEUS notus ,, eﬅ: prorsus efficitur, ut Homo iﬅe nusquàm absit, ,, ubi DEUS eﬅ: & sic omnia penitißimè plena sint ,, CHRISTO, etiam secundum Humanitatem; non ,, quidem modo illo eﬀendi alicubi primo, qui Corpo- ,, reus eﬅ: sed modo illo ultimo, qui singularis ac di- ,, vinus eﬅ. Hoc enim indubitatâ firmitate tenen- ,, dum eﬅ, ut quocunq́; loco statuis esse Divinitatem ,, Filij DEI, sive λόγον, ibi incarnatum statuas, & ,, ὑποστατικῶς indivisum. Quod si personaliter eﬅ, ,, ubicunq́; eﬅ: homo etiam iﬅic sit, necesse eﬅ. Non ,, enim duæ divisæ sunt personæ, sed unus eﬅ CHRI- ,, STUS: & ubicunq́; dicere potes, Hic eﬅ DEUS, di- ,, cendum tibi eﬅ, ibidem esse etiam Hominem ,, CHRISTUM. Quod si ullum locum dare velles, quo ,, DEUS esset, non autem ibi simul esset homo, jam so- ,, lutio personæ fieret: Posses enim dicere, ibi DEUM ,, esse qui non simul homo esset. Absit verò talem ut ,, CHRISTUM habeamus. Nam si sequeretur, quòd ,, spacia, & διασήματα locorum, naturas illas per- ,, sonaliter unitas separare possent: cùm tamen neq́; ,, mors, neq́; Diabolus divellere eas potuerit. Et sic mi- ,, ser CHRISTUS fieret, qui uno tantùm loco Divini- ,, tati junctus regnaret, reliquis verò locis omnibus, ,, ab eadem separatus, agere necessum haberet. Absit, ,, absit procul talis naturarum separatio. Jam quo- ,, modo ad negotium Cœnæ B. Lutherus hoc accommo- ,, det, observandum eﬅ. Ex secundo igitur modo essen- ,, di alicubi, jam monstratum eﬅ, si Corpus CHRISTI ,, sit alicubi, non esse necesse, ut sit modo physico, se- ,, cundum dimensiones. ,, Nam ἀπεριγράπτως, ὑπερφυσικῶς Corpus ,, ipsius per lapidem sepulchralem, & fores clausas pe- ,, netrasse, certum eﬅ. Quòd si iﬅo saltem modo, qui ,, corporibus nostris in gloriâ communis erit, potuit ,, esse extra dimensionum & locorum conditiones, in ,, lapide & foribus: quid prohibeat, quo minus eodem ,, modo poßit esse etiam in pane Cœnæ? Imò si Chri- ,, stus isto modo usus, conditioni rerum naturalium nõ subjacuit, & sic in creaturis fuit, ut nõ mensurarent ipsum aut comprehenderent : quantò magis secundum tertium istum singularem ac divinum modum, si penetrare creaturas omnes poterit, ut cum ipse omnibus sit præsentissimus, à nullâ tamen comprehendatur. Hunc enim modum, quo homo iste cum DEO una persona factus est, longissimè extra omnem creaturarum conditionem collocabis, tanto nimirùm intervallo, quantò DEUS ipse ab istis remotus est. Rursus ita propinquè & profundè eundem intra omnes creaturas collocabis, quàm penitissimè inest DEUS.

Hæc quæ in Majore suâ, Confessione, magno Spiritu contrà Zvvinglium disputavit B. LUTHERUS, tanquàm ἀλλότρια, nihilq́; ad rem facientia, variè exagitant Sacramentarij, clamitantes, hoc pacto confundi duos Articulos, de Personâ CHRISTI, & de Cœnâ DOMINI: neq́; fas esse, ut ex illo fundamenta petantur, pro hujus confirmatione.

Sed elumbe est hoc cavillum. Quod si enim tantoperè metuunt, ne aliqua oriatur Articulorum fidei confusio, cur quæso ipsi met hanc legem sibi non indixerunt: sed eam multiplicetur transgressi, vel ex solo articulo de Personâ CHRISTI argumenta petierunt, pro asserendâ ἀπουσίᾳ Corporis & Sangvinis in Cœnâ : propterea quod horum præsentia pugnet cùm proprietatibus veri & naturalis corporis humani: cum ascensione, cum sessione ad dextram Patris, cùm reditu ad judicium. Hîc ergò Lutherus ab adversarijs provocatus, ex eodem articulo purioris doctrinæ firmamenta petere voluit, imò vero debuit. Sed & illud hoc loco animadvertendum est, quòd in Controversiâ hâc Evcharisticâ non una, sed duæ diversæ agitantur Quæstiones: quarum una est, de voluntate & intentione CHRISTI, An nimirùm corpus suum in Cœnâ manducandum, & sangvinem bibendum exhibere, & sic Corpore & Sangvine suo, pani & vino Evcharistico præsentissimè adesse velit? Ubi sanè quæstionis hujus decisionem non aliundè, quàm ex solo Articulo Cœnæ Dominicæ, petendam esse, statuit Lutherus, statuimus & nos cum ipso. Altera quæstio est de potentiâ Christi: An nimirùm possit corpore suo & sangvine præsens adesse in omnibus locis, quibus Sacramentum hoc dispensatur? An caro Christi sic manducata, vitam nobis præstare possit? Ubi sanè bardus fuerit, qui abunde, quàm ex Articulo de Personâ CHRISTI, quæstionum istarum decisionem petendam esse statuerit. Reprehensione ergò omni vacat B. Lutherus, qui duas istas quæstiones, ex proprijs suis sedibus explicare, illustrare, & contra Sacramentariorum Φλυαρίας asserere voluit.


### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Holy (continued)

This doctrine, however, concerning the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of CHRIST in the Holy Supper is a thorn in the eyes of the Sacramentarians; therefore, they strive to destroy and weaken it with various cavils and sophistications.

And at the BEGINNING, indeed, they clamor that Christ sat with his disciples in his Body at the first Supper: therefore, it could not have happened that he offered his Body to be eaten by the disciples through another mode of presence.

I answer, however, from that theological rule: One must not depart from the words of Scripture when an absurdity impinges only upon the judgment of reason. For the impossibility which the adversaries dream of arises only from the judgment of reason, to which, if the mystery of faith is opposed, every absurdity vanishes. Therefore, the presence of the Body of CHRIST in the Holy Supper, which we call Sacramental, differs in its entire genus from the local presence of the Body of CHRIST, by which He then sat with His disciples. Just as, therefore, the local presence, by which He visibly stood by Nicodemus, could not prevent Him from being truly in Heaven at the same time in another invisible mode of presence: as He Himself said: The Son of Man, who is in Heaven: so also this local sitting of the Body of CHRIST could not prevent Him from being truly present to the bread according to another mode of the presence of His Body, and with it, exhibiting that Body of His to be eaten. For that local mode depended upon the natural condition of a human body: but this Sacramental one depends upon the truth and omnipotence of the promising CHRIST, nay, upon the personal condition of the Body of CHRIST: as was evidently demonstrated a little before from Luther. Because, therefore, these two modes of presence depend upon different causes, and neither is predicated of the Body of CHRIST by reason of the same principle: certainly neither can hinder the other.

THEN, if the adversaries argue: No such sense is to be affixed to the words of the Lord's Supper in which those words cannot always and immutably be true, as often as the Lord's Supper is celebrated according to the institution of CHRIST. But if the Apostles had celebrated the Holy Supper immediately after the institution during those three days of the death of CHRIST: certainly the words of institution could not have been understood, nay, they could not even have been true, concerning the true and real presence of the Body of CHRIST. For thus they would have distributed a Body that was simultaneously living and dead. Therefore, such a sense of the words of institution, which implies a real presence, cannot be true.

I answer that the connection of the minor premise is most false. For since the presence of the Body of CHRIST in the Supper depends not upon the property of the Body, but upon the will of CHRIST: certainly nothing is detracted from the Real presence, which He provides through the use of divine Majesty, even if CHRIST most especially abdicated the use of that Majesty for a time: which is what happened during the three days of His death.

Furthermore, with remarkable temerity this argument assumes authority for itself over the power of CHRIST, namely, how He Himself could have really distributed His Body and Blood as present during those three days of death and the sepulcher, if this Sacrament had been celebrated at that time. The Council of Ephesus refutes this petulance, which holily defined that in the Eucharist the flesh of Christ is not received as that of some common man, or of some saint through the indwelling of GOD: but as the flesh proper to the Word. What petulance, therefore, this is, to wish to prejudice the divine power as to what it wills or can provide in this part. Finally, the Savior, in instituting this Sacrament, looked principally not to the three days of His death, but to the whole time that the world would endure.

FINALLY, the adversaries bring forward various arguments, taken from the Ascension, from the Session at the right hand of the Father: from the return to judgment: and others of this kind: concerning which, since they were discussed quite prolixly in the Article on the Person of CHRIST, it does not behoove us to deal with them at greater length in this place. By way of a conclusion, we invert that principal one, which is taken from the Session at the right hand of the Father, with the blessed LUTHER as follows:

If the right hand of GOD and the Deity itself are nowhere separated by reason of place: it follows that whatever is at the right hand of GOD is nowhere divisible from the divinity by reason of place. But CHRIST according to His Body sits at the right hand of GOD. Therefore, by reason of place, even this Body of His is nowhere separable from the divinity.

And again a ὑποσυλλογισμὸς [sub-syllogism]: Whatever is inseparable from the Divinity by reason of place, that must necessarily be everywhere. The human nature of Christ, and consequently the Body of the same, is inseparable from the essence of the Divinity by reason of place. Therefore the human nature of CHRIST, and consequently the Body also, is everywhere.

Or thus more briefly: Whatever is inseparable from the right hand of GOD by reason of place, that is everywhere and thus can be really present to the Eucharistic Bread. But the Body of Christ, by reason of place, is inseparable from the right hand of GOD. Therefore.

The minor premise is clear in itself: For how can Locality anywhere separate from the Right hand of GOD that which, in the Right hand of GOD, transcends all locality by infinite parasangs? 2. The Right hand of GOD is not some place, but the very infinite power of GOD itself, included in no place, excluded from no place. Psalm 139:10. Isaiah 48:13. Luke 22:69. 3. To sit at the right hand of GOD does not denote any local φορὰν [motion] or position: unless one wishes to invent, through a manifest contradiction, that which has been raised to the illocal right hand is nonetheless in the right hand of GOD itself, as if in a place, and is circumscribed by a place. Scripture expressly denies this, asserting that Christ sits at the right hand of GOD in the highest, and in the heavenly places. Heb. 1:3. Eph. 1:20. And the Apostle defines sitting by reigning. 1 Cor. 15:25.

By way of a conclusion, the λογοδαιδαλία [word-labyrinth] of John Calvin deserves special observation, by which he complains that a great injury is done to him, being accused of the opinion as if he denies the true presence and communication of the very Substance of the Lord's Body and Blood in the Holy Supper: Far be it, he says, from us, that we should think the Body and Blood of Christ to be absent from the Supper. For having been accused by the Swiss on this writing of defection from the consensus of the Helvetic Confession, in the defense of the Confession he produces such a declaration of his words: The Body of Christ is given to us, and feeds us, only insofar as, remaining in Heaven, it descends to us by its power. Likewise, it infuses the vivifying vigor of its flesh into us, not otherwise than as we are enlivened by the vital heat of the Sun through its rays. And elsewhere: I said that the Body of Christ is effectively exhibited, not naturally, according to power, not according to substance. And elsewhere: That power and faculty of vivifying could not inconveniently be called something abstracted from the substance. From all of which it is clear that, in this, the opinions of the fanatics at last coalesce, or rather that their opinions coalesce, so that they deny in general both the presence and the very participation of the Body and Blood of the Lord, especially that which occurs by eating and drinking: as will become clear from the following third chapter.

Beza uses the same πύθελα, writing thus in his Creophagia: We do not deny it: but we posit the presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Supper: not that the flesh of CHRIST is now on earth: but that, remaining in the Heavens, it is nevertheless truly communicated to us through the omnipotence of the Spirit, we having been raised up to Heaven by faith. And Epist. 5. In truth, the Body of Christ is now as far removed from our eyes, and consequently from the place in which we celebrate the Supper of the Lord, as Heaven is from the earth: yet insofar as this action is heavenly, and our faith is raised up to Heaven so that it may apprehend Christ most effectively: unless you confess that the flesh of CHRIST is most present in this respect, you empty the Supper of the Lord.

Joh. Jacobus Grynæus, part 2 of his Theorems, page 112, twists himself thus: We judge that it is placed beyond all risk of controversy: That in the Holy Supper the Body and Blood of Christ πρόκεισθαι, ϰαι πάρειναι, ϰαι insofar as that was delivered for the faithful: here it is shed for the same, is present, and is exhibited. II Really, and furthermore that the Body and Blood of CHRIST are present in the Sacraments, if you do not understand the adverb of the things of the Body themselves: but take it transcendentally, so that it signifies everything which in any way pertains to the Body and Blood of CHRIST.

From which flowers of the Sacramentarians even a dullard might gather: that they leave present in the Sacrament administered here on earth only bare symbols, that is, nothing at all besides bread and wine.

Which nudity we can name nudity ἐϰ προσθέσεως, and ἐξ ἀφαιρέσεως. Nudity ἐϰ προσθέσεως is when the followers of Calvin contend that the Sacramental symbols obtain no other function or office than to testify what is given to us, that is, to show, to signify, to signify.

Nudity ἐξ ἀφαιρέσεως is when the Body and Blood of CHRIST are so separated from the external and visible symbols that they are clearly nowhere except in Heaven before the last day.

Latin:

Est verò doctrina hæc de verâ & reali præsentiâ Corporis & Sangvinis CHRISTI in S. Cœnâ, fudes præusta in oculis Sacramentariorum, proindè varijs cavillis & Sophisticationibus eam elidere, ac labefactare student.

Ac INITIO quidem Christum Corpore suo in primâ Cœnâ discipulis suis assedisse clamitant: Fieri ergò haud potuisse, ut per alium præsentiæ modum, Corpus suum manducandum præberet discipulis.

Respondeo autem ex regulà illâ Theologicâ: Non discedendum est à verbis Scripturæ, cùm absurditas tantùm in judicium rationis impingit. Impossibilitas enim, quam somniant adversarij, oritur tantùm ex judicio rationis, cui si opponatur mysterium fidei, absurditas omnis evanescit. Differt ergò præsentia Corporis CHRISTI in S. Cœnâ, quam Sacramentalem vocamus, toto genere, à præsentiâ Corporis CHRISTI locali, quâ tùm assedit discipulis. Quemadmodum ergò præsentia localis, quâ Nicodemo visibiliter astitit, non potuit impedire, quò minùs simul alio invisibili præsentiæ modo, Corpore suo verè esset in Cœlo: uti ipsemet dixit: Filius Hominis, qui est in Cœlo: ita localis etiam hæc assidentia Corporis CHRISTI, impedire non potuit, quò minùs verè secundum alium Corporis sui præsentiæ modum, adesset pani, & cum eo, Corpus illud suum manducandum exhiberet. Localis enim ille modus pendebat ex conditione naturali Corporis humani: Sacramentalis verò iste, pendet ex veritate & omnipotentiâ promittentis CHRISTI, imò ex conditione personali Corporis CHRISTI: uti ex Luthero paulò ante evidenter demonstratum fuit. Quia ergò duo isti præsentiæ modi, dependent ex causis alijs atq; alijs, neq; uterq; ratione unius principij de CHRISTI Corpore prædicatur: utiq; neuter alterum impedire potest.

DEINDE, si argumentantur Adversarij. Verbis Cœnæ Dominicæ non est talis aliquis affingendus sensus, in quo verba illa non semper, & incommutabiliter possunt esse vera, quotiescunq; ex instituto CHRISTI Cœna Dominica celebratur. Atqui si Apostoli mox post institutionem per triduum illud mortis CHRISTI, S. Cœnam celebrassent: certè verba institutionis non intelligi potuissent, imò ne vera quidem esse potuissent, de verâ ac reali Corporis CHRISTI præsentia. Sic enim simul vivum & mortuum Corpus distribuissent. Ergò talis verborum institutionis sensus, qui realem inferat præsentiam, verus esse nequit.

Respondeo, Minoris connexum esse falsissimum. Cùm enim præsentia Corporis CHRISTI in Cœnâ, non à proprietate Corporis, sed à voluntate CHRISTI dependeat: nihil certè Reali præsentiæ detrahitur, quam per usum Majestatis divinæ præstat, si vel maximè ad tempus illi9 Majestatis usu realiter CHRISTUS se abdicavit: id quod triduo mortis factum est.

Deindè insigni temeritate argumentum hoc magisterium sibi sumit, in potentiam CHRISTI, quòmodo nimirùm ipse triduo illo mortis & sepulcri, Corpus ac Sangvinem suum realiter præsentia distribuere potuisset, si maximè illo tempore Sacramentum hoc celebratum fuisset. Petulantiam hanc redarguit Concilium Ephesinum quod sanctè definivit, in Eucharistia carnem Christi non accipi, tanquàm communis alicujus hominis, aut sancti alicujus per inhabitationem DEI: sed tanquàm Verbi propriam carnem. Quæ ergò hæc petulantia fuerit, potentiæ divinæ præjudicare velle, quid hâc in parte velit aut possit præstare. Tandẽ Servator instituens hoc Sacrament tum, non ad triduum mortis suae, sed ad universum tempus mundi duraturi, principaliter respexit.

TANDEM proferunt Adversarij varij argumenta, petita ab Ascensione, à Seßione ad dextram Patris: à reditu ad judicium: & quae hujus generis sunt alia: de quibus, cum in Articulo de Persona CHRISTI, prolixe admodum disputatum sit, hoc loco pluribus de ijs agere haud attinet. Coronidis vice illud praecipuum, quod a Sessione ad dextram Patris est petitum, cum B. LUTHERO sic invertimus:

Si Dextra DEI & Deitas ipsa, ratione loci nuspiam separantur: sequitur, ut quicquid ad dextram DEI est, ratione loci, a divinitate nuspiam sit dividuum. Atqui CHRISTUS secundum Corpus suum sedet ad dextram DEI. Ergo ratione loci, etiam Corpore hoc suo nuspiam a divinitate est separabilis.

Et rursus ὑποσυλλογισμὸς: Quicquid ratione loci a Divinitate est inseparabile, id ubiq; sit necesse est. Humana Christi natura, & consequenter Corpus ejusdem, est ab essentia Divinitatis, ratione loci, inseparabilis. Ergo Humana CHRISTI natura, & consequenter Corpus etiam est Ubiq;.

Vel sic brevius: Quicquid ratione loci a dextra DEI est inseparabile, illud est ubiq; & sic Pani Eucharistico realiter adesse potest. Atqui Corpus Christi, ratione loci, est a dextra DEI inseparabile. Ergo.

Minor per se liquet: Quomodo enim Localitas ullibipoffit a Dextra DEI separare id, quod in Dextera DEI omnem localitate infinitis parasangis transcendit ? 2. Dextra DEI non est locus aliquis, sed ipsamet infinita DEI potentia, loco nulli inclusa, a loco nullo exclusa. Psalm. 139,10. Jes. 48,13. Luc. 22, 69. 3. Sedere ad dextram DEI non notat localem aliquam φορὰν sive situm: nisi per manifestam contradictionem fingere quis velit, id quod ad illocalem dexteram est evectum, nihilo minus in ipsa dextera DEI, tanquam in loco esse, & loco circumscribi. Hoc diserte negat Scriptura asserens, Christum sedere ad dextram DEI in excelsis, & in cœlestibus. Heb. 1, 3. Eph. 1, 20. Et Apostolus sedere definit per Regnare. 1. Cor. 15,25.

Coronidis vice observatione vel maxime meretur λογοδαιδαλία Johannis Calvini, qua magna sibi injuriam fieri quiritatur, insimulatus ejus sententia, quasi veram praesentiam & communicationem neget ipsius Substantiae Corporis & Sangvinis Dominici in Coena Sacra: Absit, inquiens, a nobis, ut existimemus Corpus & Sangvine Christi abesse a Cœna. Nam super hac scriptione ab Helvetijs accusatus defectionis a consensu Confessionis Helveticae, in defensione Confessionis talem declarationem producit suorum verborum: Eatenus Corpus Christi nobis datur, nosq; pascit, quatenus in Cœlo manens, virtute sua ad nos descendit. Item, vivificu carnis suae vigore in nos transfundit, non secus ac vitali Solis calore per radios vegetamur. Et alibi: Efficaciter dixi exhiberi Corpus Christi non naturaliter, secundu virtute, non secundum substantiam. Et alibi: Vis & facultas illa vivificandi non incommode abstractum aliquid a substantia dici posset. Ex quibus omnibus patet, in eo tandem fanaticorum sententias sive opiniones potiùs coalescere, ut & præsentiam, & ipsam etiam participationem Corporis & Sangvinis Dominici, præcipuè quæ manducando & bibendo fiat, in universum abnegent: uti ex subseq. cap. tertio perspicuum evadet.

Beza eadem πύθελα utitur, sic scribens in Creophagiâ: Non negamus: sed ponimus Corporis & Sangvinis Christi præsentiam in Cœna: non quòd nunc sit in terris CHRISTI caro: sed quod manens in Cœlis, nobis tamen per fidem, in Cœlum usq́; evectis, verè per Spiritus omnipotentiam communicetur. Et Epist. 5. Reverà à nostris oculis, ac proindè à loco, in quo Cœnam Domini celebramus, tàm procul nunc abest Christi Corpus, quàm abest Cœlum à terrâ: tamen quatenus hæc actio cælestis est, & fides nostra in Cœlum usq́; subvehitur, ut Christum quàm efficacissimè apprehendat: hoc sanè respectu præsentissimam esse CHRISTI carnem nisi fatearis, Cœnam Domini evacuas.

Joh. Jacobus Grynæus, part. 2. Theorematum pag. 112. sic se torquet: Extra omnem controversiæ aleam posita esse censemus: In S. Cœna Corpus & Sangvinem Christi πρόκεισθαι, ϰαι πάρειναι, ϰαι quatenus illud pro fidelibus traditum: hic pro ijsdem fusus est, adesse, & exhiberi. II Realiter, quin etiam Corpus & Sangvinem CHRISTI adesse Sacramentis, si non de ipsis rebus Corporis adverbium intelligas: sed trascendente illud sumas, sic, ut id omne significet, quod ad Corpus & Sangvinem CHRISTI quovis modo spectat.

Ex quibus Sacramentariorum flosculis vel bardus quispiam colligere queat: nuda tantùm symbola, hoc est, præter panem & vinum nihil prorsus ampliùs, in Sacramento hisce in terris administrato, præsens relinquere.

Quam nuditatem nominare possumus, nuditatem ἐϰ προσθέσεως, & ἐξ ἀφαιρέσεως. Nuditas ἐϰ προσθέσεως est, quando contendunt Calvini ani, Symbola Sacramentalia nullum alind obtinere munus sive officium, quàm ut testentur, quid nobis detur, hoc est, ut ostendant, ut significent, ut significent.

Nuditas ἐξ ἀφαιρέσεως est, quando Corpus & Sangvis CHRISTI ab externis & visibilibus Symbolis ita sejunguntur, ut nisi in Cœlo ante diem novissimum planè sint nullibi.


### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in…: On the Eating and Drinking of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Holy Supper

A sharp controversy is agitated among theologians concerning Sacramental Eating: some fighting for oral eating alone: others for spiritual eating alone: others finally banishing physical eating simply from this mystery: perhaps none weighing the nature of this mystery sufficiently exactly: or certainly treating the matter indistinctly and confusedly. Therefore, in order that this controversy may be examined more accurately, a few things must be repeated from the doctrine concerning the Sacraments considered in general, and especially those which deserve observation concerning the nature and the equivocal affection of the words Sign, Signified, and Thing of the Sacrament. There are, however, three supreme principles, as it were, to which the whole consideration of this question must be referred: namely 1. The Elemental Thing, 2. The Heavenly Thing: which are ουσιατικα in this Sacrament and 3. The matter of the Sacrament, which is τὸ τελικὸν, namely that for the sake of which we chiefly use this Sacrament: which is not for this reason, that we may feed upon the Body and Blood of the Lord, much less that we may enjoy bread and wine, bare elements: but that by using this Sacrament, we may be spiritually refreshed, and may obtain eternal life, which is to be drawn from CHRIST, that true and only bread of life, and fountain. Commonly, however, both in disputations and in writings, we denote and express the Elemental Matter by the term Sign: the Heavenly Matter by the term Signified, or the thing signified: but the spiritual Use by the Matter of the Sacrament. Of which terms, however, there is great variety and perplexity among Ecclesiastical writers: which, if it be more accurately unfolded, great clarity is added to this whole disputation. The term Sign, therefore, is accepted in two ways, either as it embraces a part, or as it embraces the whole substance of this Sacrament. As to the part, indeed, when only the external Symbol, or the elemental and visible thing, is denoted by this word. As to the whole, when the substance of the whole Sacrament, consisting of both things, as well heavenly as earthly, is expressed by the word Sign, as it is accepted by the Apostle in Rom. 4:11, naming the whole Sacrament of Circumcision, a Sign. This diversity observed in this relative word immediately argues that the same diversity happens to the Correlative also, namely the word Signified. The Signified, therefore, or the thing Signified, is likewise constituted in every way as twofold.

For if the word Sign is taken partially, namely for the elemental thing only, or the external Symbol: then its Signified is the heavenly thing, namely the other essential part of the Sacrament, for the sake of the signifying of which invisible thing, that visible or external thing was employed by CHRIST. But if the word Sign is placed for the whole Sacrament, namely so that the entire substance of the Sacrament is explained by this general term: the Signified, or the thing signified, is the fruit of the Sacrament, which is otherwise more conveniently called the Matter of the Sacrament. Whence it is that the Master of the Sentences rightly warns that there is a twofold matter of the Sacrament of the Supper; one contained and signified, the other signified and not contained: that the former is the Flesh of CHRIST: but that the latter is heavenly grace.

This observation serves, first, to understand and explain the sayings of the Fathers more conveniently. For example: It is written by Augustine, tract. 26 in John, that the Sacraments of the Jews were different from ours: but in the things signified they were equal. In the former part of this saying, because the word Sign is used for the whole Sacrament: the Thing signified is to be taken for the fruit of the Sacrament, or for the thing of the Sacrament, which is called by us in this way in respect of species. Again, a saying of the same Augustine is cited from De Cons 2. c. Hoc est: The Sacrifice of the Church is made up of the Sacrament, and the Thing of the Sacrament, that is, the Body of CHRIST: just as the person of Christ consists and is made up of GOD and man. In which place, because the Thing of the Sacrament is called the other essential part of the Sacrament: the word Sacrament is certainly perceived to have been used by Augustine partially for the Sign, so that it signifies only the Symbol, or Element, to which its opposite, the Signified, is named the Thing of the Sacrament. Thus, what was written by the same Augustine, Epist. 50: That the unworthy receive the Sacrament, not the Thing of the Sacrament: likewise what the same Augustine noted in book 19 against the same, chapter 16, that it was a raving error of Faustus the Manichaean, that he thought that by the changing of Signs and Sacraments, the very things of the Sacraments were also changed: how this is to be understood from the present observation is most rightly understood.

Then, the same observation contributes greatly to refuting the error of the Sacramentarians, who in the Lord's Supper simply constitute the Thing of the Sacrament in the Body itself and the Blood of the Lord, that is, in the other essential part of the Sacrament. This could indeed be tolerated if they took the Thing of the Sacrament for the signified thing of the Sacrament, partially so called. But understood as the fruit of the Sacrament, it is wrongly so called. For a part of a thing cannot in any way be the fruit of the same, and vice versa. And against this abuse of the term, it is rightly written by Augustine, tract. 26 in John: The Sacrament is taken from the Lord's table by some to life, by some to destruction: but the thing itself, of which it is the Sacrament, is taken by every man to life, by none to destruction.

From this ternary of sacramental principles, a threefold Eating and Drinking emerges: which must be properly observed in this mystery, and each one must be cautiously circumscribed by its own terms.

The FIRST is Physical, and proper to the Symbols or merely external Elements, namely Bread and Wine, which remains such even in the very use of this Sacrament, nor does it extend itself beyond this Physical property.

The remaining two are mystical, indeed in such a way that each is proper to the Body and Blood of the Lord himself, not to the elementary things: but yet in the meantime each differs from the other as much as possible in species.

The SECOND therefore is called Sacramental, namely from the species of that Sacrament, to which it alone is proper. Now it consists of those things which were said a little before, that this Sacrament consists of two things, as essential parts, Heavenly and earthly: Sign and Signified, both particularly so called. Because therefore neither the Sign is a Sacrament without the signified thing, nor the signified thing without the Sign: but for the integrity of the Sacrament both things are required, which are also sacramentally united: on account of which Union that which is proper to the Signified is attributed to the Sign, and conversely: hence it comes about that this eating and drinking is called Sacramental. This happens in the very external use of this Sacrament, and is common to the pious with the impious, and can be done not only to life, but also to judgment.

The THIRD is called and is Spiritual, which also has a place outside the use of the Sacrament, and which is done by faith alone, and is so profitable to salvation that it can never be done to destruction. But that is done when it is believed that the flesh of CHRIST was delivered to death for us, and his blood shed for us for the remission of sins. Concerning which eating Christ speaks expressly in John 6.

Besides those two later modes of eating the flesh of Christ, namely the Sacramental and the Spiritual, the Orthodox Church acknowledges absolutely no other or third mode, which might take place properly by the Mouth in the substance of the FLESH of CHRIST (by which nothing is understood but Capernaitic butchery). Moreover, this twofold eating of the flesh of CHRIST, Sacramental and Spiritual, considered in relation to each other, arises chiefly from a triple principle: 1. from the diverse disposition of communicants, of whom some are good, others evil. 2. from the diverse organ of reception, which in Sacramental eating is the Mouth of the body: but in Spiritual, the Mouth of the heart, that is, faith. 3. from the condition of the Sacrament itself, which has a double thing, one of which can exist without the other, as was shown a little before. But because those who approach the Holy σύναξιν worthily join both modes of eating, it has come about that the sixth chapter of John, in which nothing is treated but spiritual eating, is read to have been not rarely employed by Ecclesiastical Writers for the doctrine concerning the Supper of the Lord: meanwhile, however, that other Sacramental eating is by no means denied. Augustine writes elegantly concerning both modes of eating joined together: What is it to eat Christ? It is not this alone, to receive His Body in the Sacrament, (for many receive unworthily) but to remain in Him, and to have Him remaining in oneself. For he eats spiritually who remains in the unity of Christ and the Church, which the Sacrament signifies. Therefore, while both differ from each other, they differ in such a way that neither excludes or overturns the other: but one conveniently subordinates itself to the other. This is to be well observed in the reading of the Fathers, lest when they urge one more sharply, the other be thought to be immediately denied by them. For example: Augustine writes in book 21 of the City of GOD, chapter 25. Those are not to be said to eat the Body of Christ who are not to be counted among the members of Christ. Under the pretext of this saying, the Sacramentarians wish the Sacramental eating, which is common to the unworthy with the worthy, to be utterly destroyed and excluded. But it must be attended to what Augustine is arguing in that place. For there were those who promised themselves liberation from eternal fire, precisely because they participated in the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Eucharistic Supper. They persuaded themselves that this hope was valid, however they might live in the meantime, or with whatever heresy or impiety they might be imbued, relying on the foundation of their opinion in that because it was written in John 6: He who eats my flesh, and drinks my blood, abides in me, and I in him. To refute this impiety and error, Augustine teaches who are to be said to truly eat the Body of CHRIST, in the sense that is proper to these words of CHRIST in John: namely, not those who eat the Body of CHRIST only sacramentally, or merely as far as the Sacrament goes: a thing which even the impious can perform, though to their own certain destruction: but those who abide in CHRIST, and who persevere in the faith of CHRIST. The same Augustine, about to strike down the impiety of the Capernaitic madness, writes in Tract. 25 on John: Why do you prepare your teeth and belly? Believe, and you have eaten. Likewise, from the words of the Lord in Luke, Homily 33: Do not prepare your jaws, but your heart. Similarly, Cyprian in his Sermon on the Supper of the Lord has it thus: As often as we do these things, we do not sharpen our teeth for eating: but with sincere faith we break and share the holy bread.
