These things, which make most of all for urging spiritual eating (which it would be a sin to neglect), the Adversaries distort, as if they were noted by the Fathers simply to deny and remove from the midst sacramental eating: although, however, in compared degrees, from that which is principally urged, that which is less principal is in no way excluded.

Finally, from that triad of Sacramental Principles which has been posited, two corollaries evidently result: the former of which is concerning the organ by which sacramental eating and drinking is done: which is none other than the Mouth of the Body: The other concerning the reception of the unworthy, what kind it is, and of what things it is proper. Concerning each separately.

Latin:

DE Manducatione Sacramentali acris omninò inter Theologos agitatur Controversia: nonnullis pro solâ Orali: alijs pro solâ spirituali Manducatione pugnantibus: alijs deniq́; physicam Manducationem simpliciter ex hoc mysterio relegantibus: nullis fortassè satis exactè mysterij hujus naturam expendentibus : vel certè indistinctè ac confusè rem tractantibus. Proindè ut hæc Controversia accuratiùs excutiatur, pauca quædam ex doctrinâ de Sacramentis in genere consideratis, & cumprimis ea, quæ de naturâ & affectione æquivocâ vocabulorum Signi, Signati, & Res Sacramenti, observationem merentur, repetenda sunt. Tria autem sunt summa quasi principia, ad quæ tota quæstionis hujus consideratio referenda est : nempè 1. Res Elementaris, 2. Res Cœlestis : quæ sunt ουσιατικα in hoc Sacramento & 3. Res Sacramenti quæ est τὸ τελικὸν, nimirùm id, cujus gratiâ potissimum Sacramento isto utimur : quod non sit eam ob causam, ut Corpore & Sangvine Dominico vescamur, multò minùs, ut pane & vino, elementis nudis fruamur : sed & Sacramento isto uti, spiritualiter reficiamur, & vitâ æternâ potiamur, quæ ex CHRISTO, vero illo atq; unico pane vitæ, ac fonte est haurienda. Vulgò autem tùm in disputationibus, tùm in scriptionibus, Rem Elementarem vocabulo Signi : Rem Cœlestem termino Signati, sive rei signatæ : Usum verò spiritualem per Rem Sacramenti notamus & exprimimus. Quorum tamen vocabulorum magna est apud scriptores Ecclesiasticos varietas & perplexitas : quæ si accuratiùs evolvatur, magna toti huic disputationi accedit perspicuitas. Signi ergò vocabulum dupliciter accipitur, vel prout partem, vel ut totam Sacramenti hujus substantiam complectitur. Pro parte quidem, cùm externum duntaxat Symbolum, vel res elementaris, & adspectabilis, per hanc vocem notatur. Pro toto, cùm totius Sacramenti substantia, ex utrâquè re, tàm cœlesti, quàm terrenâ constans, voce Signi exprimitur, prout accipitur ab Apostolo Rom. 4, 11. nominans totum Circumcisionis Sacramentum, Signum. Diversitas hæc in vocabulo hoc relato observata, statim arguit, Correlato etiam, nempè vocabulo Signati, eandem diversitatem accidere. Signatum ergò sive res Signata, duplex omninò itidem constituitur.

Si enim Vox Signi partialiter accipiatur, nempè pro re tantùm elementari, sive externo Symbolo : tùm Signatum ejus est res cœlestis, pars nempè Sacramenti essentialis altera, cujus quippè invisibilis signandæ gratia, res illa visibilis seu externa à CHRISTO est adhibita. Sin pro toto Sacramento Signi vox ponatur, nempè ut universa Sacramenti substantia generali isto vocabulo explicetur : Signatum, vel Res signata est fructus Sacramenti, qui alias Res Sacramenti commodiùs appellatur. Unde est, quod rectè monet Magister sententiarum, Sacramenti Cænæ geminam esse rem; Unam contentam & significatam alteram significatam, & non contentam : priorem istam esse Carnem CHRISTI : hanc verò esse gratiam cœlestem.

Servit hæc observatio, primò ad dicta Patrum commodiùs intelligenda, & explicanda. Verbi gratia : Scriptum est ab Augustino tractat. 26. in Joh. Sacramenta Judæorum in signis diversa fuisse a nostris: in rebus autem significatis paria. In hujus dicti parte priori, quia Signi vox pro toto Sacramento ponitur: Res significata pro fructu Sacramenti esse accipienda, sive pro re Sacramenti, quæ à nobis in specie sic appellatur. Rursus citatur ejusdem Augustini dictum de Consecr. dist. 2. c. Hoc est: Sacrificium Ecclesiæ conficitur ex Sacramento, & Re Sacramenti, hoc est, Corpore CHRISTI: sicut persona Christi constat & conficitur ex DEO & homine. Quo loco, quia Res Sacramenti vocatur pars Sacramenti essentialis altera: utiq; Sacramenti vox partialiter pro Signo, ab Augustino posita esse deprehenditur, ut Symbolum, sive Elementum duntaxat significet, cui Signatum suum oppositum, Res Sacramenti nominatur. Sic quod ab eodem Augustino, Epist. 50. scriptum est: Indignos Sacramentum, non Rem Sacramenti percipere: item quod crasso errore à Fausto Manichæo deliratum esse, annotavit idem Augustinus lib. 19. contra eundem, cap. 16. quod Signis, Sacramentisq; mutatis, res etiam ipsas Sacramentorum mutatas esse senserit: id ex præsenti observatione quomodo sit accipiendum, rectissimè intelligitur.

Deindè ad Sacramentariorum errorem arguendum, eadem observatio plurimùm conducit, qui in Cœnâ Dominicâ, Rem Sacramenti, in Corpore ipso, & Sanguine Dominico, hoc est, parte Sacramenti essentiali alterâ simpliciter constituunt. Quod tolerari quidem posset, si Rem Sacramenti, pro Re signatâ Sacramenti, partialiter sic dictâ, acciperent. De fructu autem Sacramenti intellecta, perperàm sic appellatur. Pars enim rei, fructus esse ejusdem, & vice versâ, nullo modo potest. Et contra hunc abusum vocabuli, rectè scriptum est ab Augustino, tract. 26. in Joh. Sacramentum de mensâ Dominicâ sumitur à quibusdam ad vitam, à quibusdam ad exitium: Res verò ipsa, cujus Sacramentum est, omni homini ad vitam, nulli ad exitium sumitur.

Ex ternario hoc principiorum Sacramentàlium, triplex emergit Manducatio & Bibitio: quæ hoc in mysterio probè est observanda, & suis unaquæque terminis cautè circumscribenda.

PRIMA Physica est, & Symbolorum sive externorum duntaxat Elementorum, nempè Panis & Vini, propria, quæ etiam in ipso usu Sacramenti hujus talis permanet, neq; ultra Physicam hanc proprietatem se extendit.

Reliquæ duæ sunt mysticæ, ita quidem, ut utraque ipsius Corporis & Sangvinis Dominici, non rerum elementarium sit propria: sed specie tamen interim inter se utraq; quàm maximè differt.

ALTERA ergò Sacramentalis appellatur, nempè à specie ejus Sacramenti, cujus illa unicè est propria. Constat autem ex his, quæ paulò antè sunt dicta, Sacramentum hoc duabus rebus, tanquàm partibus essentialibus constare, Cœlesti & terrenâ: Signo & Signato, particulariter utroque sic appellato. Quia igitur neque Signum sine re signatâ, neque res Signata sine Signo, Sacramentum est: sed ad Sacramenti integritatem utraq; res requiritur, quæ etiam Sacramentaliter sunt unitæ: propter quam Unionem Signo tribuitur, quod Signati propriũ est, & contrà: hinc adeò fit, ut manducatio & bibitio hæc appelletur Sacramentalis. Fit autem hæc in ipso externo Sacramenti hujus usu, & est pijs cum impijs communis, & non solùm ad vitam, sed ad judicium etiã fieri potest.

TERTIA dicitur & est Spiritualis, quæ etiam locum habet extra usum Sacramenti, quæq; fit per fidem tantùm, & ad salutem ita prodest, ut ad exitium fieri nunquàm possit. Ea verò fit, cùm caro CHRISTI in mortem pro nobis tradita, & sangvis ejusdem pro nobis in remissionem peccatorum fusus esse creditur. De quâ manducatione Christo ex professo sermo est Joh. 6.

Præter duos istos posteriores modos manducandæ carnis Christi, Sacramentalẽ nimirùm & Spiritualem, alium aut tertium, qui propriè fiat Ore in substantiâ Carnis CHRISTI (quo nil nisi Capernaitica laniena intelligitur) Ecclesia Orthodoxa planè nullũ agnoscit. Cæterùm gemina hæc manducatio carnis CHRISTI, Sacramentalis & Spiritualis, ad se mutuò considerata, à triplici potissimùm principio oritur: 1. à diversâ dispositione communicantiũ, quorum alij boni sunt, alij mali. 2. à diverso sumtionis organo, quod in Sacramentali manducatione, est Os Corporis: in Spirituali verò, Os cordis, hoc est, fides. 3. ab ipsius Sacramenti conditione, quod rem habet duplicem, quarum una potest esse sine alterâ, uti paulò antè ostensum. Utramq; auté manducationem quia conjungunt illi, qui dignè ad S. σύναξιν accedunt: hinc factũ est, ut caput sextũ Johannis, quo non nisi de spirituali manducatione agitur, ad doctrinam de Cœnâ Domini à Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis non rarò adhibitũ esse legatur: interim tamen Sacramentali illâ alterâ minimè negata. De Utraq; manducatione conjunctâ, eleganter scribit Augustinus: Quid est Christum manducare? Non est hoc solùm, in Sacramento Corpus ejus accipere, (multi enim indignè accipiunt) sed in ipso manere, & habere ipsum in se manentem. Spiritualiter enim manducat, qui in unitate Christi & Ecclesiæ, quam Sacramentum significat, manet. Differt ergò quidem inter se utraq;: sed ita differt, ut neutra alteram excludat, aut evertat: Sed una alteri sese commodè subordinet. Quod est in Patrum lectione probè observandum, ne cùm acriùs urgent unam, altera ab illis statim negari putetur. Exempli gratia: Scribit Augustinus lib. 21. de Civit. DEI, cap. 25. Non sunt dicendi manducare Corpus Christi, qui non in membris Christi computandi sunt. Hujus dicti prætextu manducationem Sacramentalem, quæ est indignis communis cum dignis, Sacramentarij elisam prorsus & exclusam volunt. Atqui attendendum est, quid isto loco Augustinus pugnet. Erant enim, qui sibi promittebant liberationem ab æterno igni, indè adeò, quia Corpore & Sangvine Dominico in Cœnâ Evcharisticâ participabant. Hanc autem spem persuadebant sibi esse ratam, quomodo libet interim viverent, aut quacunq; hæresi vel impietate imbuti essent opinionis suæ fundamento nixi eo, quia Joh 6. scriptum esset: Qui manducat carnem, & bibit sangvinem meum, in me manet, & ego in ipso. Pro hac impietate, & errore refutando, Augustinus docet, qui sint dicendi revera manducare Corpus CHRISTI, eo sensu, qui est verborum istorum CHRISTI apud Johannem proprius: nempe, non ij, qui Sacramentaliter duntaxat, aut Sacramento tenus tantum Corpus CHRISTI manducant: id quod possint praestare etiam impij, cum suo tamen certo exitio: sed qui in CHRISTO maneant, & qui in fide CHRISTI perseverent. Idem Augustinus Capernaitici furoris impietatem perstricturus, Tract. 25. in Joh. scribit: Ut quid paras dentes & ventrem? Crede & manducasti. Item de verbis Domini in Lucam, Homil. 33. Nolite parare fauces, sed Cor. Consimiliter Cyprianus Serm. de Coena Domini sic habet: Haec quoties agimus, non dentes ad manducandum acuimus: sed fide sincera panem sanctum frangimus & partimur. Haec quae pro urgenda spirituali manducatione potissimum faciunt (quam negligere nefas fuerit) eo detorquent Adversarij, quasi ad negandam, tollendamq; e medio manducationem Sacramentalem simpliciter a Patribus annotata sint: cum tamen in gradibus comparatis, ab eo, quod principaliter urgetur, id quod minus principale est, nullo modo excludatur.

Tandem ex eo, qui positus est Principiorum Sacramentalium, ternario, evidenter duo resultant πορίσματα: quorum prius est de organo, quo fit manducatio & bibitio Sacramentalis: quod nullum est aliud, praeter Os Corporis: Alterum de indignorum perceptione, qualis ea, & quarum rerum sit propria. De utroq; seorsim.


### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in…: Concerning Oral Manducation and the Drinking of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Holy Supper

Just as individual Sacraments do not lack an appropriate organ by which they are perceived: and indeed one of which mention is expressly made in the individual institutions: So by the tenor of the words of CHRIST, in the institution of this Sacrament also, it is expressed clearly enough: by what organ this Sacrament is perceived. Mention is made, however, of Eating and Drinking: Both of which, since they are done by no other organ than the Mouth, hence it is clearer than the light of day that this Sacrament is perceived by nothing other than the Mouth. Nor does it stand in the way that the fruit of heavenly things, namely of the Body and Blood of CHRIST, is established to redound also to the soul, and indeed principally. In which respect Cyprian called this food not of the belly, but of the mind. For that this very thing is also done by the corporeal organ of the mouth is not as absurd (provided the figments of profane thoughts are absent) as it is not inconvenient that the instrument of the ears, through the word, which by means of the sprinkling of the water of Baptism the Holy Spirit works in us Faith, Conversion, and salvation. In which sense it was written by Augustine in Epistle 118 to Januarius: It pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a Sacrament, the Lord's Body should enter into the mouth of a Christian before other foods.

Leo the Great, Sermon 6 on Fasting: You ought to communicate at the Holy table in such a way that you doubt nothing at all concerning the truth of the Body and Blood of CHRIST: For this is taken by the MOUTH, which is believed by faith, and it is answered in vain with Amen by those by whom it is disputed against that which is received.

And it is worthy of memory that, when Valentinus and Marcion, and their followers, were pretending that the flesh would not rise again, but that only the soul is capable of eternal life: Irenaeus and Tertullian, and other Fathers, sought arguments to refute this impiety, both from the Article of the Incarnation of Christ: and from the present mystery, in which the Body of Christ is eaten by the Mouth. The flesh, says Tertullian in his book on the resurrection of the flesh, is fed with the Body and Blood of CHRIST, so that the soul also may be fattened from GOD. Flesh and soul cannot be separated in the reward, which GOD joined in the work.

The reasons and arguments, however, by which we evidently establish this doctrine of ours concerning the Oral eating and drinking of the Body and Blood of CHRIST in the Holy Supper, are these principal ones:

I. Just as the Sacraments differ from the Word in nature and essence, so they also differ in their instrument. For the Word, which is ἀκουστὸν (audible), is apprehended by faith alone, whereas the Sacraments, being the visible Word, are something αἰσθητόν (sensible). Therefore, they also have their own appropriate δεικτικόν (demonstrative) or instrument.

Nor is it an objection that the external senses do not apprehend a spiritual thing, either by sensing or by understanding; much less does the mouth itself feel in the Supper that it is partaking of the Lord's Body: but faith recognizes the promise from the words of CHRIST and believes it. For it does not follow in any way if someone should argue thus: Every promise is received by faith alone: Therefore, every promised thing is also received by faith alone. For one must distinguish between the promise in itself and considered absolutely, and the promise weighed with its certain object. In the former way, this proposition is true: Every promise is received by faith alone; but in the latter way, it is false, and only particularly true according to the quality of the object, whether external or internal. For example: A promise is given to us concerning daily bread, concerning the health of the body. This promise, considered absolutely, is received by faith alone; but the promised thing or object is apprehended not by faith, but by a bodily instrument: which even a child understands. Thus, in this place, the instrument of the promise to be accepted is one thing, namely faith, but the other, by which the promised thing itself is apprehended, is namely the mouth of the body. And it is worthy of note that the Savior, in defining the instrument of perception, does not use the word for believing: for thus He would have had to exclude Judas from this communion: but the words for eating and

Latin:

QUemadmodum singula Sacramenta non carent appropriato organo, quo percipiuntur: & quidem eo, cujus in singulis institutionibus expressa sit mentio: Ita tenore verborum CHRISTI, in hujus etiam Sacramenti institutione deserte satis est expressum: quo organo Sacramentum hoc percipiatur. Fit autem mentio Manducationis & Bibitionis: Quae utraq;, cum nullo alio, nisi Oris fiat organo, hinc utique, non nisi Ore etiam Sacramentum hoc percipi, luce meridiana clarius patet. Neque obstat, quod rerum Coelestium, Corporis nimirum & Sangvinis CHRISTI fructus, ad animam etiam, & quidem praecipue redundare statuitur. Quo respectu Cyprianus non ventris: sed mentis cibum istum appellavit. Nam hoc ipsum quoque organo oris corporeo fieri, tam non est absurdum, (modo figmenta prophanarum cogitationum absint) quam non est inconveniens, quod aurium insiup strumento, per verbum, quod mediante aspersione aquæ Baptismi in nobis, Fidem, Conversionem & salutem Spiritus Sanctus operatur. In quem sensum scriptum est ab Augustino Epist. 118. ad Januarium: Placuit Spiritui Sancto, ut in honorem tanti Sacramenti, in Os Christiani, priùs Dominicum Corpus intraret, quàm exteri cibi.

Leo M. Serm. 6. de Jejunio: Sic Sanctæ mensæ communicare debetis, ut nihil prorsus de veritate Corporis & Sangvinis CHRISTI ambigatis: Hoc enim ORE sumitur, quod fide creditur & frustrà ab illis Amen respondetur, à quibus contra id, quod accipitur, disputatur.

Et memoratu dignum est, quòd cùm Valentinus & Marcion, horumque gregales fingerent, carnem non resurrecturam, sed solam animam vitæ æternæ capacem esse: Irenæus & Tertullianus, Patresque alij argumenta hujus impietatis refutandæ, tùm ex Articulo Incarnationis Christi: tùm ex præsenti mysterio, in quo Ore Corpus Christi manducatur, petiverunt. Caro, inquit Tertull. lib. de resurrectione carnis, Corpore & Sangvine CHRISTI vescitur, ut & anima de DEO saginetur. Caro & anima non possunt separari in mercede, quas DEUS conjunxit in opere.

Rationes autem & argumenta, quibus doctrinam hanc nostram de Orali manducatione ac bibitione Corporis & Sangvinis CHRISTI, in S. Cœnâ evidenter astruimus, præcipua sunt: hæc:

I. Sacramenta sicut naturâ & essentiâ à verbo differunt: ita etiam organo. Verbum quippe ἀκουστὸν solâ fide apprehenditur, Sacramenta quippe verbum visibile, sunt quiddam αἰσθητόν. Ergò habent etiam suum appropriatum δεικτικόν sive organum.

Neque obstat, quòd sensus externi rem spiritualem non apprehendat, vel sentiendo, vel intelligendo: multò minus os ipsum sentit in Cœnâ, se Corpus Dominicum percipere: sed fides ex verbis CHRISTI promissionem cognoscit, eique credit. Nullo enim modo sequitur, si quis ita colligat: Omnis promissio solâ fide accipitur: Ergò etiam omnis res promissa solâ fide accipitur. Distingvendum enim inter promissionem in se, & absolutè consideratam: & inter promissionem cum suo certo objecto pensitatam. Priore modo vera est propositio hæc: Omnis promissio solâ fide accipitur: posteriore verò modo falsa, & particulariter tantùm vera pro qualitate Objecti vel externi, vel interni. Exempli gratia: Promissio nobis data est de Pane quotidiano, de Sanitate Corporis. Hæc promissio absolutè considerata solâ fide accipitur: atqui res promissa vel objectum non fide, sed organo corporeo apprehenditur: id quod vel puer intelligit. Sic hoc loco Promissionis acceptandæ organum est aliud, nempè fides, aliud verò, quo res ipsa promissa apprehenditur, nempè Os Corporis. Et memoratu dignum, quod Servator organon perceptionis definiturus, non credendi vocabulo utitur: Sic enim Judam ab hâc communicatione excludere debuisset: sed edendi & bi-


### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in…: Difference between Sacramental and Spiritual manducation

drinking, which would leave Judas's shared participation in this Sacrament with the remaining disciples, from which another argument of proof emerges, and such a one as this:

II. The Elemental Bread is received only by the Mouth of the Body, as all admit. Now, however, concerning that very thing which is taken and eaten by the mouth, the Savior declares that it is his body. It is impossible, however, for one and the same word, in one and the same proposition, to obtain at the same time both a proper signification of eating and a figurative one of believing. Therefore, that the Body of Christ itself is received and eaten together with the bread only by the Mouth of the Body, a most firm conclusion is inferred.

III. Whatever things are united Sacramentally in the same Sacrament and in the same action: they are also received by the same organ: unless perhaps someone, by establishing a difference, wishes to dissolve the Sacramental Union itself in the very use of the Sacrament: when, however, this Union consists only in the external use of this Sacrament: and with that ceasing, the Union itself also ceases. But the Bread and the Body, the Wine and the Blood of CHRIST, are united Sacramentally in the same Sacrament and in the same action: For unless they were united in this way, there would be no Sacrament at all. Therefore, both are perceived together by one and the same organ of the body in the use of this Sacrament.

IV. Unless it be granted that Sacramental eating is done by the Mouth of the Body, no distinction will be left between Sacramental and Spiritual eating. But this is absurd. Therefore. For the explanation of the Major premise, it should be well noted by what marks of difference these two eatings are mutually distinguished from each other in the holy Scriptures.

1. In the beginning, therefore, they differ in the Organ of perception. For the eating of the Body of Christ in the Sacrament takes place, as Christ defines, by no other means than by eating the Bread: which is done by the Mouth of the Body. Spiritual eating, however, which is described in John 6, does not take place except by faith.

2. Then they differ in Object. For Sacramental eating regards only the substance of the Body and Blood of the Lord. Spiritual eating, however, regards not so much the substance as the benefits acquired by the merit of Christ.

3. Thirdly, in Subject. For Sacramental eating has no place except in this one Eucharistic Sacrament. Spiritual eating, however, takes place in any Sacrament by the faithful: indeed, it takes place even outside the use of the Sacraments, in the daily application of the benefits of the death of Christ.

4. Fourthly: In the Quality of the persons. For Sacramental eating is common to the pious and the impious, to the worthy and the unworthy. Spiritual eating, however, is proper only to believers.

5. Fifthly, in Efficacy. For Sacramental eating does not always profit, but results in judgment for those who eat unworthily. Spiritual eating, however, always and for all profits, even if Sacramental eating does not concur.

6. Sixthly, Sacramental eating is not absolutely necessary for salvation: which is evident from the example of infants, and of the pious, who are prevented from the use of this Sacrament by some immutable circumstance. To whose salvation, however, nothing is lacking, provided they believe in Christ the Savior. For here that saying of Augustine has place: Believe and

you have eaten. Spiritual eating, however, is always and absolutely necessary for salvation: For it is impossible to please GOD without faith. The Sacramentarians object against these things, and accuse us of both crudeness and absurdity. Of crudeness: when we contradict the pious Antiquity with a full mouth, as one which explicitly calls Sacramental eating spiritual, and grants that it is done spiritually. Of absurdity, however, because we strip Sacramental eating of all spirituality, and define it in a crass manner. But this cavil of theirs vanishes of its own accord, if it be observed more accurately in what ways something is said to be Spiritual, and to be done Spiritually, and what also comes into controversy between us and the Adversaries in this place.

But first, the word Spiritual or Spiritually is opposed to that which is Physical or Natural, and which behaves according to the laws and rules of nature. If the adversaries were to call sacramental eating Spiritual in this way, certainly none of us would object. For although we contend that it is done by the mouth of the body, we nevertheless readily grant that it is done not in a physical way, but in a hyperphysical way, and only through the mediation of divine power, as has already been shown before.

“Furthermore, the word spiritual is taken in special senses, and in this sacramental business it is opposed: not contradictorily, but subordinately: in such a way, indeed, that sacramental and spiritual eating are two different species, differing from each other in many ways: meanwhile, however, if sacramental eating is to be profitable, it must necessarily subordinate spiritual eating, which nevertheless is done by another means.

Finally, the word Spiritual, through a notable abuse, is opposed by the adversaries to the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Holy Supper: so that while they contend that the Body of Christ is eaten Spiritually in the Sacrament, they do not mean by this that it is not eaten in a physical and Capernaitic way: nor that it cannot be profitable unless spiritual eating, which is done by faith, is added: in both of which parts we would not in the least object: but they fight solely for this, that the Body of Christ is as far removed from the Eucharistic bread as the highest heaven is distant from the lowest earth: and therefore that the Body of Christ is eaten only Spiritually, when faith flies upward and apprehends the Body of Christ sitting in the heavens. We simply banish this meaning of the word Spiritual from this mystery: and this is the very thing about which there is the greatest struggle between us and the adversaries in this place.

V. And the final argument of proof can be sought from the unanimous consent of Orthodox Antiquity: concerning which, see the refutation of the Calvinistic Consensus. We shall be content with these few points for this time.

Augustine, Sermon 215 de tempore: See, dearest brothers, whether it is just that from the mouth of Christians, where the Body of CHRIST enters, a lewd song, or something similar like the poison of the Devil, should be brought forth.

Theodoret, in the explanation of the first to the Corinthians: Thus they treat him with ignominy and disgrace, who receive his most holy Body with unclean hands, and put it into a polluted and incestuous mouth. Chrysost. Homil. 29. on 2 Corinthians. Our mouth has attained no common honor, receiving the Lord's Body.

This doctrine also has suffered sharp contradiction, even from the very first beginnings of the Sacramentarian struggle: indeed, even today it suffers no less from the Calvinian race, which attacks oral eating with wondrous quibbles.

The arguments, however, upon which both the ancient and the more recent Sacramentarians rely, are chiefly these:

I. To teach an expiation of sins other than that which was made on the cross of Christ is nothing else than to overturn the faith of Christ. But if a real presence of the Body of Christ in the Holy Supper is posited, and the oral eating of the same: nothing else is taught than that the remission of sins is to be sought from oral eating. Therefore, the dogma concerning the oral eating of the Body of Christ overturns the faith of Christ.

I answer, the minor premise suffers 1. from the crime of falsehood. For neither blessed Luther, nor any of the Orthodox, ever posited that the remission of sins is to be sought from oral eating, which we teach, if it happens without faith and the Spirit, not only does not profit for the remission of sins, but also brings eternal death itself. 2. It suffers from the fallacy παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον [non sequitur]. For let it be granted that the Body of Christ is not eaten in the Supper for the sake of the remission of sins; it does not follow from that, however, that the Body of Christ is absent from the Supper, or that it is not eaten by the mouth in this Sacrament.

3. In this argument, a gross ἀγνοια ἐλέγχου [ignorance of the refutation] reveals itself: For they differ among themselves: the merit of Christ, and the distribution of the merit: the deed itself differs, and the application or use of the deed: the passion of CHRIST itself differs, or the expiation of sins, and the use of the passion, or appropriation. The passion or expiation was made once on the cross. But the distribution of this merit happens daily and everywhere through the ministry of the Word and Sacraments. It is said, therefore, that there is remission of sins in the Supper, not by a new expiation, or by a new merit of Christ: nor is it said to be from oral eating alone: but the distribution of the merit, and the application of the remission of sins, once obtained on the cross, is taught to happen there by the power of the divine promise to believers. What is said, therefore, about application is maliciously adapted to expiation, and the use of the deed is confused with the deed itself. Finally, this collection suffers from absurdities: For if therefore in the Holy Supper the Body of Christ is not present, nor is it eaten orally there, because the expiation of sins was not made in the Supper, it will follow: that the Body of Christ is neither in Heaven, nor was born of Mary: because in neither was the expiation made.

II. John 6:63, the Savior says: The flesh profits nothing. Therefore the Body of Christ is not eaten orally.

I answer: 1. That there is no strength in the consequence. 2. That the fallacy παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως [figure of speech] is committed. For the Savior does not discourse about His own Flesh, as Zwingli raved, but according to the subject matter at hand, He understands carnal thoughts, which, in the manner of Capernaitic profanity, without faith and the Spirit, break into divine mysteries and judge them according to their own whim.

Therefore, the rule of B. LUTHER must also be observed in this place: Wherever in the Scriptures Flesh and Spirit are opposed, there it is not the flesh of Christ, but the corruption which is from Adam, that is understood. 3. An ἄγονοια ἐλέγχυ (ignorance of the refutation) is committed. For to be profitable, and to be present, do not have one and the same ἔλεγχον (refutation). For thus God would not be everywhere, because He does not profit everywhere. 4. The inference suffers from an absurdity: For if CHRIST is therefore not present in the Supper with His Flesh, because the flesh does not profit: it would follow that it is nowhere, and consequently clearly does not exist, because these words, 'The flesh profiteth nothing,' are true as much outside the Supper as in the Supper, since they are stated indefinitely. 5. It will follow that bread and wine profit more than the flesh of CHRIST: since they are present in the Supper. 6. A charge of falsehood: For CHRIST, speaking of His own flesh, does not say: 'My flesh can do nothing': But: 'My flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed': [2] 'He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him.' John 6:55.

III. Whatever things differ in their entire genus cannot be perceived in one and the same way. But Bread and Wine: the Body and Blood of CHRIST, differ in their entire genus. Therefore.

I answer: 1. A σόφισμα προ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς (sophism of the relative and the absolute) is committed. For the major premise is true in a relative sense concerning those things between which no union intervenes that makes some third thing out of two disparate things. Now as for the minor premise, although the heavenly thing differs in its entire genus from the elemental thing: nevertheless, a true and real union intervenes between them in the use of this Sacrament. Therefore the consequence collapses. 2. A sophism of ἑτεροζητήσεως (asking about a different matter). For, as the premises hold, the controversy in this place is not about the mode of eating: but about the medium, or organ, by which those disparate things, united sacramentally, are perceived in the very use. We ourselves freely admit that the mode is hyperphysical, indeed clearly ἄῤῥητον (ineffable). But since the Savior Himself defined the medium, or organ of perception, as the mouth of the body: it would be an act of impiety to invent something different and contrary. Where, however, we also freely grant that to our adversaries: [5] those disparate things are perceived by one organ, namely the mouth of the body, but not in one and the same way: For bread is eaten by the mouth physically, πρώτως καὶ ἀμέσως (primarily and immediately): but the Body of CHRIST sacramentally and hyperphysically, δευτέρως καὶ ἐμμέσως (secondarily and mediately). Which is also the reason why the same predicates cannot be uttered concerning the Body of CHRIST as concerning the Eucharistic bread: such as that it is converted into chyle, etc.

IV. In the same way that Christ dwells in us, in that same way He is eaten by us. But Christ dwells in us only through faith. Therefore.

I answer: The major premise is most false, and proceeds from a false hypothesis, which we correct by establishing that the foundation of the eating of the flesh of CHRIST is one thing, but the foundation of the Union of the same with us is another; and that neither depends upon one and the same principle. The former rests upon the words of institution; the latter, however, upon the words of the Evangelical promise, John 6:56: He who eats my flesh (that is, he who believes in me) abides in me, and I in him. With these diverse principles standing thus, the diverse organs of perception also stand unmoved: so that the Body of CHRIST is eaten by the mouth, but the Spiritual Union with CHRIST is accomplished by faith.

V. CHRIST himself took into his hands, and ate and drank with his mouth, what the Apostles took. Now, however, it must not be established that Christ ate his own proper Body Orally. Therefore, neither did the disciples eat it Orally.

I reply that we seek a proof of the Major premise, rather than simply denying it as false: being so taught by Christ himself, who, about to put an end to the Paschal feast, protests in express words that he would no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until he drinks it new in the kingdom of his Father, which thing Peter testifies was done only after the Resurrection, Acts 10:41, so that it can be irrefragably proven from this that after the Paschal feast was finished, Christ did not drink from the Eucharistic cup. Now, there is no doubt that what the Savior affirms concerning the fruit of the vine, he understood the same also concerning the bread: unless perhaps the Sacramentarians wish to dream that Christ participated in the Holy Supper under one species only.

VI. The authority of Dr. Augustine is objected, who says thus in chapter 6 of John, among other things: You are not to eat this Body which you see, and drink that blood which they who crucify me are about to shed. I have commended a certain Sacrament to you, which, understood Spiritually, will give you life.

I reply, consider the sole scope which Augustine had proposed to himself in this place, to refute our Adversaries evidently. Augustine argues in that place expressly against the Capernaites, who were seeking here only the work of the belly and teeth: or, as Augustine himself speaks in the preceding parts, they were thinking Carnally, that the Lord was about to cut off certain particles from his Body and give them to them. Augustine therefore opposes his argument to these, but not to our doctrine, which has nothing to do with the dreams of the Capernaites, but has Augustine himself as an ally.

Latin:

bendi vocibus, quæ promiscuam Judæ cum reliquis discipulis, Sacramenti hujus participationem relinquerent, undè alterum probationis argumentum emergit, idque tale:

II. Panis Elementaris non nisi Ore Corporis accipitur, omnibus fatentibus. Jam verò de eo ipso, quod ore sumitur & manducatur, pronunciat Servator, quòd sit corpus suum. Impossibile est autem unum & idem verbum, in unâ & eadem propositione, simul & propriam edendi, & figuratam credendi significationem obtinere. Quòdergò non nisi Ore Corporis, ipsum Corpus Christi unà pane accipiatur, & manducetur firmissima infertur conclusio.

III. Quæcunq́, eodem in Sacramento, eademq́, in actione unita sunt Sacramentaliter: ea eodem quoquè organo accipiuntur: nisi fortassis diversum quis statuendo, ipsam Unionem Sacramentalem, in ipso usu Sacramenti dirimere velit: cùm tamen Unio hæc non nisi in externo usu hujus Sacramenti constat: & eo cessante, cesset ipsa quoq́, Unio. Atqui Panis & Corpus Vinum & Sangvis CHRISTI, in eodem Sacramento, eademq́, actione unita sunt Sacramentaliter: Nisi enim hoc modo unita essent, Sacramentum planè nullum esset. Ergò uno eodemquè Organo corporis simul utraquè in usu Sacramenti hujus percipiuntur.

IV. Nisi Sacramentalis manducatio, Ore Corporis fieri concedatur, nihil relinquetur discriminis inter Sacramentalem & Spiritualem manducationem. Atqui hoc absurdum. Ergò. Pro explicatione Majoris probè notandum fuerit, quibus differentiarum notis duæ hæ manducationes in Scripturis sacris, à se mutuò discernantur.

1. Initiò ergò differunt Organo perceptionis. Manducatio enim Corporis Christi in Sacramento sit, definiente Christo, nullo alio medio: quàm manducando Panem: id quod sit Ore Corporis. Manducatio autem spiritualis, quæ describitur Joh. 6. non sit, nisi fide.

2. Deindè differunt Objecto. Sacramentalis enim respicit solam substantiam Corporis & Sangvinis Dominici. Spiritualis verò non tàm substantiam, quàm beneficia Christi merito acquisita.

3. Tertiò, Subjecto. Sacramentalis enim manducatio locum non habet, nisi in hoc uno Sacramento Eucharistico. Spiritualis verò sit in quolibet Sacramento per fideles: imò sit etiam extra Sacramentorum usum, in quotidianâ applicatione beneficiorum mortis Christi.

4. Quartò: Qualitate personarum. Sacramentalis enim pijs ac impijs, dignis ac indignis communis est. Spiritualis verò solorum credentium propria.

5. Quintò, Efficaciâ Sacramentalis enim non semper prodest, sed indignè manducantibus cedit ad judicium. Spiritualis verò semper & omnibus prodest, etiamsi Sacramentalis manducatio non concurrat.

6. Sextò, Sacramentalis manducatio ad salutem absolutè non est necessaria: id quod patet exemplo infantum, & piorum, qui ab usu Sacramenti hujus, immutabili quodam casuarcentur. Quorum tamen saluti nihil decedit, modò credant in Christum Servatorem. Hîc enim locum habet illud Augustini: Crede &

manducasti. Spiritualis verò semper & absolutè ad salutem est necessaria: Impossibile enim est, sine fide placere DEO. Excipiunt adversus haec Sacramentarij, & tùm ruditatis, tùm absurditatis nos insimulant. Ruditatis: dùm nimirùm piae Antiquitati pleno ore contradicamus, ut quae Sacramentalem manducationem disertè spiritualem nominet, & spiritualiter fieri concedat. Absurditatis verò, quòd Sacramentalem manducationem omni spiritualitate spoliemus, & crasso quodam modo definiamus. Sed utrumque hoc cavillum sponte suâ evanescit, si quibus modis aliquid Spirituale sit, & Spiritualiter fieri dicatur, quid etiam hoc loco inter nos & Adversarios in controversiam propriè veniat, accuratiùs observetur.

Primùm autem vox Spiritualis sive Spiritualiter, opponitur ei, quod est Physicum sive Naturale, & secundum naturae leges ac regulas se habet. Hoc modo si Adversarij Sacramentalem manducationem nominarent Spiritualem: nemo profectò nostrum repugnaret. Etsi enim Ore Corporis eam fieri contendimus: non tamen modo physico, sed hyperphysico, & non nisi divinâ mediante virtute, fieri ultrò largimur: uti jam antè ostensum.

“ Deindè verò vox spiritualis specialibus ac- “ cipitur, & hoc in negocio Sacramentali opponi- “ tur: non Contradictoriè, sed subordinatè: ita quidé, “ ut Sacramentalis & Spiritualis manducatio sint “ duae diversae species, multis modis invicé differé- “ tes: interim tamen Sacramentalis si prodesse de- “ beat, necessariò subordinet Spiritualem, quae tamen alio fiat medio.

Tandem vox Spiritualis, per insignem abusum, ab adversarijs opponitur verae acreali praesentiae Corporis & Sangvinis Christi in S. Coenâ: ita, ut dùm contendunt, Corpus Christi in Sacramento Spiritualiter manducari, non hoc velint, quòd non manducetur modo physico & Capernaitico: quòd item non prodesse possit, nisi accedat Spiritualis manducatio, quae fit fide: Quâ utrâquè in parte minimè reluctaremur: sed id unicè pugnent, Corpus Christi tanto intervallo à pane Eucharistico esse remotum, quanto summum Caelum distat ab imâ terrâ: ac proindè Spiritualiter tantùm manducari Corpus Christi, tùm quando fides sursum evolat, & in Caelis sedens Corpus Christi apprehendat. Hanc significationem vocabuli Spiritualis ex hoc mysterio simpliciter relegamus: Et hoc ipsum est, de quo hoc loco inter nos & Adversarios maximè pugnatur.

V. Et postremum probationis argumentum peti potest ab unanimi consensu Orthodoxae Antiquitatis: de quo videatur refutatio Consensus Calvinistici. Nos paucis istis hac vice contenti erimus.

Augustinus Serm. 215. de tempore: Videte fratres charissimi, an justum sit, ut ex ore Christianorum, ubi Corpus CHRISTI ingreditur, luxuriosum carmen, aut simile quoddam quasi venenum Diaboli proferatur.

Theodoretus in explicatione prioris ad Corinth. Ita eum ignominia & dedecore afficiunt, qui sanctissimum ejus Corpus immundis manibus accipiunt, & in pollutum atque incestum os immittunt. Chrysost. Homil. 29. in 2. ad Corinth. Non vulgarem honorem consecutum est Os nostrum, accipiens Corpus Dominicum.

Passa est hæc quoque doctrina acrem planè contradictionem, jam indè à primis initijs certaminis Sacramentarij: imò hodieque haud leviorem patitur à gente Calvinianâ, quæ Oralem manducationem miris cavillis exagitat.

Argumenta autem, quibus tùm veteres, tùm recentiores Sacramentarij nituntur, præcipua sunt hæc:

I. Aliam, quàm quæ in cruce Christi facta est, expiationem peccatorum docere, nihil est aliud, quàm fidem Christi evertere. Atqui si realis statuatur præsentia Corporis Christi in S. Cœnâ, ejusdemque oralis manducatio: nihil docetur aliud quàm Remissionem peccatorum ex orali manducatione requirendam esse. Ergò dogma de orali manducatione Corporis Christi, evertit fidem Christi.

Respondeo, Minorem laborare 1. crimine falsi. Neque enim vel B. Lutherus, vel Orthodoxorum quisquam statuit unquàm, ex Orali manducatione remissionem peccatorum esse requirendam, quam docemus, si sine fide & Spiritu fiat, non tantùm non prodesse ad remifsionem peccatorum, sed ipsam quoque æternam mortem adferre. 2. Laborat Sophismate παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Esto enim, propter remissionem peccatorum Corpus Christi in Cœnâ non comedatur; non tamen indè sequitur, vel abesse Corpus Christi à Cœnâ, vel Ore Corporis illud in hoc Sacramento non manducari.

3. Prodit sese in hoc argumento crassa ἀγνοια ἐλέγχγ: Differunt enim inter se: meritum Christi, & distributio meriti: differt factum ipsum, & applicatio sive usus facti: differt passio ipsa CHRISTI, sive expiatio peccatorum, & usus passionis, sive appropriatio. Passio sive expiatio facta est semel in cruce. Hujus autem meriti distributio quotidiè & ubique fit per ministerium Verbi & Sacramentorum. Dicitur ergò in Cœnâ esse remissio peccatorum, non expiatione novâ, aut merito Christi novo: neque esse dicitur illa ex solâ orali manducatione: sed distributio meriti, & applicatio remissionis peccatorum, semel in cruce impetratæ, isthic ex vi divinæ promissionis fieri credentib9 docetur. Quod igitur de applicatione dicitur, malitiosè ad expiationem accommodatur, & usus facti cum facto ipso confunditur. Tandem abfurditatibus laborat hæc collectio: Si enim ideò in S. Cœnâ non est Corpus Christi, neque ibi oraliter manducatur, quia in Cœnâ non est facta expiatio peccatorum, sequetur: Corpus Christi neque in Cœlo esse, neque ex Maria natum esse: quia in neutro facta est expiatio.

II. Johan. 6, 63. inquit Servator: Caro non prodest quicquam. Ergò non oraliter manducatur Corpus Christi.

Respondeo: 1. Nullum nervum inesse Consequentiæ. 2. Committi Sophisma παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως. Neque enim Servator de Carne suâ disserit, uti deliravit Zvvinglius, sed pro subjectâ rei materiâ, intelligit carnales cogitationes, quæ in morem prophanitatis Capernaiticæ, sine fide ac Spiritu, irrumpit in mysteria divina, eaque pro lubitu dijudicat.

Observanda ergò hoc etiam in loco regula B. LUTHERI: Ubicunque in scripturis Caro & Spiritus opponantur, ibi non caro Christi, sed corruptio, quæ est ex Adamo, intelligitur. 3. Committitur ἄγονοια ἐλέγχυ. Prodesse enim, & præsentem adesse, non unum habent ἔλεγχον. Sic enim nec DEUS ubique esset, quia non ubique prodest. 4. Absurditate laborat collectio: Si enim CHRISTUS ideò non adest in Cœnâ Carne suâ, quia caro non prodest: consequens fuerit, eam nullibi esse, ac proindè planè non esse, quia verba hæc, Caro non prodest, tàm extra Cœnam, quàm in Cœnâ vera sunt quippè indefinitè enunciata. 5. Consequens erit, Panem & vinum plus prodesse, carne CHRISTI: siquidem ea in Cœnâ sunt præsentia. 6. Crimen falsi: CHRISTUS enim de suâ carne verba faciens, non dicit: Caro mea non potest quicquam: Sed: Caro mea verè est cibus, & Sanguis meus verè est potus: qui manducat meam carnem, & bibit meum sangvinem, in me manet, & ego in illo. Johan. 6, 55.

III. Quæcunque toto genere differunt, eauno eodemque modo percipi non possunt. Atqui Panis & Vinum: Corpus & Sangvis CHRISTI, toto genere differunt. Ergò.

Respondeo: Committitur 1. σόφισμα προ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Major enim vera est secundum quid de ijs, quibus nulla invicem intercedit Unio, quæ ex duobus disparatis efficiat aliquod tertium. Jam quoad Minorem, licèt res Cœlestis toto genere differat à re Elementari: vera tamen ac realis in usu Sacramenti hujus, ipsis intercedit Unio, Corruit ergò Consequentia. 2. Sophisma ἑτεροζητήσεως. Non enim, uti præmissæ habent, hoc loco de modo manducationis controvertitur: sed de medio, sive organo, quo res illæ disparatæ, Sacramē taliter unitæ, in usu ipso percipiantur. Modum nos ipsi ultrò fatemur esse hyperphysicum, imò planè ἄῤῥητον. Medium autem, sive organon perceptionis cùm Servator ipse definiverit os Corporis: impietatis fuerit, diversum ac contrarium quid comminisci. Ubi tamen Adversarijs illud quoque ultrò largimur: res istas disparatas, uno quidem organo, nempè Ore Corporis percipi, sed non uno, eodemque modo: Panis enim ore manducatur physicè, πρώτως καὶ ἀμέσως: Corpus verò CHRISTI Sacramentaliter hyperphysicè, δευτέρως καὶ ἐμμέσως. Quæ causa etiam est, quod de Corpore CHRISTI non eadem prædicata efferri possint, quæ de pane Eucharistico: ut quod in chylum convertatur &c.

IV. Quo modo Christus in nobis manet, eodem etiam modo à nobis manducatur. Atqui Christus per fidem tantùm in nobis manet. Ergò.

Respondeo: Major est falsissima, & ex falsâ procedit hypothesi, quam corrigimus, statuentes, aliud esse fundamentum manducationis carnis CHRISTI: aliud verò fundamentum Unionis ejusdem nobiscum: nequè ab uno, eodemquè principio utramquè pendere. Illa nititur verbis institutionis: Hæc verò verbis promissionis Evangelicæ, Joh. 6, 56. Qui edit meam carnem, (hoc est, qui credit in me) is in me manet, & ego in ipso. Quibus diversis principijs ita stantibus, stant etiam immota diversa perceptionis organa: ita ut Corpus CHRISTI ore manducetur: Spiritualis verò Unio cum CHRISTO fide peragatur.

V. CHRISTUS idem sumsit in manus suas, & ore suo manducavit & bibit, quod Apostoli sumserunt. Jam verò statuendum non est, Christum proprium suum Corpus manducasse Omiliter. Ergò nec discipuli illud manducarunt Oraliter.

Respondeo, nos petere probationem Majoris, quàm ut simpliciter falsani negamus: sic edocti ab ipso Christo, qui epulo Paschali finem impositurus disertis verbis protestatur, sed non ampliùs bibiturum de genimine vitis, donec novum bibat in regno patris sui, id quòd post Resurrectionem demùm factum esse, Petrus testatur Actor. 10, 41. ita ut post peractum epulum paschale, Christum de calice Eucharistico non bibisse, irrefragabiliter indè evinci queat. Jam verò quod de genimine vitis affirmat Servator, quin idem de pane quoque intellexerit, dubium est nullum: nisi fortè Sacramentarij Christum sub unâ tantùm specie, de S. Cœnâ participasse, somniare velint.

VI. Objicitur autoritas D. Augustini, qui in caput 6. Johannis sic inter reliqua: Non hoc Corpus, quod videtis, manducaturi estis, & bibituri sangvinem illum, quem fusuri sunt, qui me crucifigunt. Sacramentum aliquod vobis commendavi, Spiritualiter intellectum vivificabit vos.

Respondeo, vel solum scopum, quem Augustinus hoc loco sibi habuit propositum, Adversarios nostros evidenter refellere. Disputat autem Augustinus eo loci ex professo adversus Capernaitas, qui ventris tantum, & dentium opus hic quærebant: vel, ut Augustinus ipse in præcedentibus loquitur, Carnaliter cogitabant, quòd Dominus quasdam particulas de suo Corpore præcisurus, illissque daturus sit. His ergò opponit suam illam disputationem Augustinus, non verò nostræ doctrinæ, quæ cum Capernaitarum somnijs nihil habet negocij, sed ipsum etiam Augustinum habet ὁμόψηφον.


### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in…: On the Eating of the Unworthy

The other corollary which results from the ternary of Sacramental principles is concerning the Eating of the Unworthy. Where, at the beginning, it comes under observation, who the unworthy are. We reject, however, that distinction which some invent between hypocrites, lacking true faith and repentance, and Epicureans and Empačlas, who are still nevertheless involved in the external communion of the Church: concerning which distinction we have spoken at length in our Commentary on the Book of Concord.

Furthermore, we do not count as Unworthy those who lack their own sufficient preparation, even that which they proposed to themselves: much less those who are weak in faith. For these, above others, are invited by the Savior to the enjoyment of this heavenly feast, Matt. 11:28 and ch. 9:12. But since, as the Apostle himself also agrees in 1 Cor. 11, there are not in general more than two kinds of guests found in this mystical banquet, the Worthy and the Unworthy: unworthiness is not to be measured by the standard of one's own preparation, but is to be defined partly in general by the lack of faith, and partly in particular by that which the Apostle hints at, ἀδιακρισίαν: so that, indeed, they are unworthy who do not communicate in this most holy feast with legitimate discernment. These, therefore, whoever they may be, using—or rather abusing—this supper, participate not in some part of the Sacrament, but in the whole Sacrament itself, that is, in both essential parts of the Sacrament, as much the Heavenly as the earthly Elemental.

The chief foundations of this assertion of ours are these:

I. The Apostle Paul himself 1 Cor. 11:27 & 29 thus discourses on this matter: If anyone shall eat this bread, or drink of the cup of the LORD unworthily, he shall be guilty of the Body and Blood of the LORD. And he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Body of the LORD. Where the emphasis of the Apostle's words deserves notice: For he does not simply say, whoever shall eat the bread, or whoever shall drink of the cup: but he expressly adds: He who shall eat of THIS bread, namely that which is the κοινωνία of the Body of Christ: And, whoever shall drink of the cup of the LORD, which is the κοινωνία of His Blood: thus irrefragably implying that the unworthy not only enjoy the bread, but with the bread, the very Body of CHRIST also in the use of the Holy Supper.

II. If those eating unworthily involve themselves in the guilt of eternal death and damnation: this will happen either because the unworthy eating of those things is directed only at the bread: or because it strikes at the Body of CHRIST itself. A third option cannot be given. But that former respect cannot subsist. For thus, not only in the use of this Sacrament, but in the daily use of bread, and its unworthy treatment, that guilt would be contracted: nor would there have been need for the Apostle to accommodate it with such zeal to the Eucharistic bread. Furthermore, the Apostle would not have had to say that the cause of this crime and punishment results from the fact that those eating thus do not discern the Body of the LORD: but that they do not discern the Eucharistic bread. But since the Apostle expressly says that the unworthy involve themselves in the guilt of eternal death because they do not discern the Body of the Lord: it follows that the unworthy contract guilt only by eating the Body of the Lord: since in no other way, than by the manner of eating, can they become partakers of the Body of the Lord in the Sacrament. Therefore the unworthy do not discern, because, forsooth, the Body

the Lord, which they pollute and treat with ignominy, both by infidelity and by other crimes and wickednesses, when they eat it with bread in the Sacrament.

Some of the Sacramentarians object that the cause of the guilt which the unworthy incur is that which pertains to violated royal charters or seals. For just as he who treats such letters and insignia contumeliously is considered to be injurious not to the paper, not to the parchment, not to the red wax, but is held guilty of the royal Majesty itself being injured: so, they say, the crime of those who eat unworthily redounds not to the bread and wine, but to the Body of the Lord itself; although they have eaten not the Body, but only bread. But the Apostle himself long ago refuted this weak and truly dissimilar analogy, for he does not hold those who eat unworthily guilty of injuring the majesty, virtue, or merit of Christ, which is offered to them through the tablets or letters of the Apostles: which is what he would have had to say if this analogy held; but he expressly asserts that they become guilty of the Body and Blood of the Lord itself. Furthermore, the Apostle does not say, Those who eat unworthily bring judgment upon themselves because they do not discern the external Element of Bread: but because they do not discern the Body of CHRIST itself.

III. The unworthy receive the Sacrament of the Eucharist. But this Sacrament consists of and is completed by not one part, namely the Elemental, but also the Heavenly, that is, the Body of Christ. Therefore, if they receive the Sacrament, it is necessary that they receive both things, as much the heavenly as the earthly. The Adversaries themselves do not deny the major premise, using this phrase everywhere: That the unworthy have communion of the Sacraments. They likewise concede the minor premise to be most true. Therefore, it is necessary that they also concede that the unworthy partake of the whole Sacrament, as much of the Heavenly thing as of the Elemental: or that the Sacrament consists and is perfected by only one part, and that the more ignoble one, namely the earthly, which is absurd: or finally that the Eucharist is not a Sacrament for the unworthy: which is equally absurd.

IV. It is sought from the consensus of Orthodox Antiquity, from which Augustine says thus in book 5 against the Donatists, chapter 8: Anyone taking the Lord's Sacrament unworthily does not cause, because he himself is evil, that what he receives is evil, or that because he does not receive it for salvation, he has received nothing. For the Body of the LORD and the Blood of the LORD was nonetheless also for those to whom the Apostle was saying: He who eats unworthily, eats judgment to himself.

The reason for this Augustinian affirmation is most firm: Because the integrity of the Sacrament depends not on the faith of men, but on the virtue and ordination of the divine institution. Therefore, the infidelity of those using it causes not that the Sacraments cease to be, but that they are not useful, at least: and just as outside of use they cease to be Sacraments, so outside of legitimate use they cease to be useful. Which reason Augustine himself also confirms with his own calculation, saying in book 3 against the Donatists, chapter 14: It does not matter, when one is treating of the integrity and holiness of the Sacrament, what he believes, and with what kind of faith he is imbued, who receives the Sacrament. It matters indeed very much for the way of salvation: But for the question of the Sacrament it matters nothing. For it can happen that a man has the whole Sacrament and a perverse faith. And lest an example be lacking for this assertion, such a one is produced by Augustine, book 9 against Fulgentius: Judas the traitor received the good Body of CHRIST, and Simon Magus the good baptism of CHRIST: But because they did not use the good well, they were destroyed by using the evil badly. The same Augustine, book 5 against the Donatists, chapter 8: Judas, to whom the LORD handed the morsel, did not by receiving evil, but by receiving badly, provide a place for the Devil in himself. For it was nonetheless the Body of the LORD and the Blood of the LORD even for those to whom the Apostle was saying: He who eats unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself. Bernard: He who receives the Body of the LORD with Judas the traitor is condemned: He who with Peter and the other faithful receives it devoutly and faithfully, without doubt is sanctified in the Body of CHRIST with Peter and the other Apostles.

But our Adversaries oppose Augustine to Augustine, who they say is not sufficiently consistent with himself in this question, and writes elsewhere: They are not to be said to eat the Body of Christ who are not to be counted among the members of Christ: for even an evil person can receive the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of Christ: but he who is not in the Body of Christ is not to be said to truly eat the Body of Christ.

But I answer that an ignorance of the refutation is being committed. For it must be examined of what eating Augustine is speaking. He is arguing in that place expressly against those who, according to the whim and pleasure of their flesh, thought that any crime was permitted to them with impunity: nay, they promised themselves eternal life solely from the fact that they had participated in the Body and Blood of the Lord. Augustine therefore shows that it is not sufficient for the possession of eternal life that one receives the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of CHRIST: but that it is required above all that one truly eats and drinks: which is done by those who truly believe in CHRIST, that is, who also spiritually eat the Body of Christ. For these remain in CHRIST, and CHRIST in them, John 6.

But the Adversaries have another argument, which is as follows: Nothing has the nature of a Sacrament outside the use instituted by Christ. But without faith there is no other legitimate use of the Supper. Therefore the unworthy, being destitute of faith, perceive only the external Sacrament without the body of Christ.

I answer: The argument fails under the Sophism of Ignorance of the Refutation. For this rule, Nothing has the nature of a Sacrament outside the use instituted by Christ, was opposed by the Blessed LUTHER to the dogma of the Papists and Scholastics, who dreamed that sacramental signs obtain the nature and definition of a Sacrament even outside of use. Therefore, the sense of the rule is not that which the Calvinists invent, as if the Body of Christ could not be perceived in the Sacrament outside of faith: But, that the Sacramental signs do not have the nature of a Sacrament properly so called, unless the legitimate use, instituted by CHRIST himself, which consists only in eating and drinking, is added.

Finally, the Sacramentarians also object to this: If the entire Sacrament is to be received by the unworthy, it must be established that CHRIST instituted this Sacrament for the unworthy also: which seems absurd.

But to this cavil also one must respond distinctly, and that must be explained first of all, Whether the Sacrament of the Supper was instituted by CHRIST for the unworthy?

First, therefore, if one asks about the Substance of the Holy Supper, it is the same instituted by CHRIST for the worthy and the unworthy, since the integrity of the Sacraments depends not on the faith or the belief of those using them, but on the truth and power of the one instituting them.

2. If one asks about the fruit, it is certain that the Savior never willed that the unworthy, insofar as and as long as they are such, should perceive the saving power and efficacy of the Sacrament. Where, however, the guilt of subsequent perdition does not depend on this will of Christ, who seriously seeks the conversion of the unworthy, and for this end permits the use of the Sacraments to be common to all equally: but it depends on the very guilt of the unworthy, who eat judgment to themselves against the will of GOD.

3. If one asks about the intention and purpose of CHRIST the institutor, we answer first concerning the general will of GOD, according to which, just as salvation itself, so also the means of salvation, the Word and the Sacraments, have been prepared for all, yet to be used legitimately in their own certain order, determined by CHRIST in the Word. Then, if one asks about the Right, Whether CHRIST instituted the supper for the unworthy, that is, whether He willed that the impenitent, insofar as they are such and remain so, should approach the Holy Supper; we answer simply in the negative, since they eat judgment to themselves, since they do not examine themselves, since they are cast out by the LORD as impure guests lacking the wedding garment, since finally no absolution, no remission of sins or consolation is proposed to them in the Gospel. Whence the Church deservedly denies the use of the Lord's Supper to those whom it finds to be unworthy and impenitent: which it could by no right do, if this sacred feast had been instituted by CHRIST for such persons.

4. If finally one asks about the fact, by which the unworthy approach the table of the LORD beyond the institution and will of CHRIST: then indeed they receive in it the Body and Blood of Christ, and that not without the institution of Christ: nevertheless, by the unworthy taking of this Treasure they bring judgment upon themselves, and by Accident Christ, who is present in the Supper as a life-giver, is to those eating unworthily a judge and avenger of impiety: just as the Gospel, which is the word of life John 6, 68, is to the unbelieving a savor of death unto death, 2 Cor. 2, 16, not from the institution of GOD, but from the unspeakable and obstinate malice of those using it.

Latin:

ALterum, quod ex ternario principiorum Sacramentalium resultat πόρισμα, est de Manducatione Indignorum. Ubi initiò sub observationem venit, Quinám sint indigni. Rejicimus autem discrimen illud, quod inter hypocritas, fide verâ & pœnitentiâ carentes, & inter Epicuræos atque Empačlas, adhuc tamen in externâ Ecclesiæ communione versantes, nonnulli fingunt: de quo discrimine in Commentario nostro ad Librum Concordiæ prolixè egimus.

Prætereà pro Indignis etiam non censemus eos, qui propriâ & sufficiente præparatione carent, etiam quam ipsimet sibi proposuerunt: nedùm qui sunt infirmi in fide. Hi enim præ cæteris ad cœlestis hujus epuli perfruitionem invitantur à Servatore Matth. 11, 28. & cap. 9, 12. Sed cùm in universum non sint, ipso etiam Apostolo astipulante 1. Cor. 11. nisi duo genera convivarum, qui in hoc mystico convivio reperiuntur, Digni & Indigni: Indignitas non propriæ præparationis modulo metienda: sed partim definienda est in genere per carentiam fidei: partim in specie, per illam, quam Apostolus innuit, ἀδιακρισίαν: ut nimirùm indigni sint, qui non cum legitimâ discretione, sanctissimo hoc epulo communicant. Hi igitur, quales quales sunt, cœnâ hac utentes, imò abutentes potiùs, Sacramenti non parte aliquâ: sed toto ipso Sacramento, hoc est, utrâque Sacramenti parte essentiali, tàm Cœlesti, quàm terrenâ Elementari participant.

Assertionis hujus nostræ fundamenta præcipua sunt hæc:

I. Ipse Apostolus Paulus 1. Cor. 11, 27. & 29. sic hâc de re disserit: Si quis ederit panem hunc, aut biberit de poculo DOMINI indignè, reus erit Corporis & Sangvinis DOMINI. Et qui edit ac bibit indignè, judicium sibi ipsi edit & bibit, non dijudicans Corpus DOMINI. Ubi emphasis verborum Apostoli notationem meretur: Non enim simpliciter dicit, quisquis ederit panem, aut quisquis biberit de poculo: sed disertè addit: Qui ederit de pane HOC, eo videlicet, qui est κοινωνία Corporis Christi: Et, quisquis biberit de calice DOMINI, qui est κοινωνία Sangvinis ipsius: sic irrefragabiliter innuens, Indignos non modò pane, sed cum pane, ipso etiam Corpore CHRISTI in usu S. Cœnæ perfrui.

II. Si indignè manducantes æternæ mortis ac damnationis reatu se implicant: fiet hoc vel ideò, quòd manducatio istorum indigna fertur in solum panem: vel quòd in ipsum CHRISTI Corpus impingit, Tertium dari nequit. Atqui prior ille respectus non potest subsistere. Nam sic non in usu tantùm Sacramenti hujus, sed in quotidiano usu panis, ejusque indignâ tractatione, reatus iste contraheretur: neque opus fuisset, ut ad panem Eucharisticum tanto studio eam accommodaret Apostolus. Deindè non dicendum fuisset Apostolo, causam criminis & pœnæ hujus ex eo resultare, quòd sic manducantes non discernant Corpus DOMINI: sed quòd non discernant panem Eucharisticum. Verùm cùm disertè dicat Apostolus, Indignos æternæ mortis reatu se implicare, quia non discernant Corpus Domini: Consequens est, Indignos non nisi manducando Corpus Domini reatum contrahere: Siquidem nullo alio pacto, quàm per manducationis modum, Corporis Domini participes evadere possunt in Sacramento. Ideò autem indigni non discernunt, quia nimirùm Corpus

Domini, quod cum pane in Sacramento manducant, tum infidelitate, tum alijs sceleribus ac flagitijs quasi polluunt, & ignominia afficiunt.

Excipiunt nonnulli Sacramentariorum, Causam reatus, quem subeunt indigni, esse eam, quæ sit violatorum diplomatum, aut Sigillorum regiorum. Quemadmodum enim, qui hujusmodi literas & insignia contumeliosius tractat, non in chartam, non in tabulam, non in ceram rubram injurius esse censetur; sed ipsius læsæ Majestatis regiæ reus peragitur: ita, inquiunt, non in panem & vinum, sed in ipsum Corpus Domini crimen indignè manducantium redundat: licèt non Corpus, sed panem dunt axat comederint. Verum elumbem hanc, & vere dissimilem similitudinem jampridem elisit ipse Apostolus, qui indignè manducantes non reos peragit læsæ majestatis, virtutis aut meriti Christi, quod per tabulas sive literas Apostolorum ipsis offertur: id quod omnia dicere debuisset, si Similitudo isthæc quadraret: sed disertè asserit, reos ipsos fieri ipsius Corporis & Sangvinis Dominici. Deindè Apostolus non dicit, Indignè manducantes judicium sibi sumere, propterea, quòd non discernant externum Elementum Panis: sed quod non discernant ipsum Corpus CHRISTI.

III. Indigni accipiunt Sacramentum Eucharistiæ. Atqui Sacramentum hoc non una parte, nempè Elementari, sed & Cælesti, hoc est, Corpore Christi constat & absolvitur. Ergò si Sacramentum accipiunt, utramq; rem, tam cælestem, quam terrenam accipiant necesse est. Majorem ne ipsi quidem negant Adversarij, passim hac utentes phrasi; Indignos Sacramentorum communionem habere. Minorem itidem concedunt esse verissimam. Ergò concedant etiam necesse est, Indignos toto Sacramento, tam re Cælesti, quam Elementari potiri: vel Sacramentum constare & perfici una tantum parte, & quidem ignobiliore, nempe terrena, id quod absurdum: vel denique Eucharistiam Indignis non esse Sacramentum: id quod æque absurdum.

IV. Petitur a consensu Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, ex qua sic Augustinus lib. 5. contra Donatistas cap. 8. Indignè quisque sumens Dominicum Sacramentum, non efficit, ut quia ipse malus est, malum sit, quod accipit, aut quia non ad salutem accipit, nihil acceperit. Corpus enim DOMINI, & sangvis DOMINI, nihilo minus etiam erat ijs, quibus dicebat Apostolus: Qui manducat indignè, judicium sibi manducat.

Ratio autem affirmati hujus Augustiniani firmissima est hæc: Quia integritas Sacramenti non ab hominum fide: sed a virtute & ordinatione divinæ institutionis dependet. Infidelitas ergo utentium, non ut Sacramenta esse desinant: sed ne utilia sint, saltem efficit: & quemadmodum extra usum, Sacramenta esse: sic extra legitimum usum utilia esse desinunt. Quam rationem ipse quoque Augustinus calculo suo comprobat, inquiens lib. 3. cont. Donat. cap. 14. Non interest, cum de Sacramenti integritate, & sanctitate tractatur, quid credat, & quali fide imbutus sit ille, qui Sacramentum accipit. Interest quidem plurimùm ad salutis viam: Sed ad Sacramenti quæstionem nihil interest. Fieri enim potest, ut homo integrum habeat Sacramentum, & perversam fidem. Et ne assertioni huic desit exemplum, ab Augustino tale producitur, lib. 9. contra Fulgentium: Judas proditor bonum CHRISTI Corpus, & Simon Magus bonum CHRISTI baptisma percepit: Sed quia bono benè usi non sunt: mali malè utendo deleti sunt. Idem Augustinus lib. 5. contra Donat. c. 8. Judas, cui bucellam tradidit DOMINUS, non malum accipiendo, sed malè accipiendo, locum in se Diabolo præbuit. Corpus enim DOMINI, & Sangvis DOMINI nihilominus erat etiam illis, quibus dicebat Apostolus: Qui manducat indignè, judicium sibi manducat & bibit. Bernhardus: Ille, qui cum Juda proditore Corpus DOMINI accipit, condemnatur: Qui cum Petro & cæteris fidelibus, devotè & fideliter illud sumit, sine dubio cum Petro & cæteris Apostolis in Corpore CHRISTI sanctificatur.

Cæterùm Adversarij nostri Augustinum opponunt Augustino, qui sibi non satis constet in hâc quæstione, & alibi scribat: Non sunt dicendi manducare Corpus Christi, qui non in membris Christi computandi sunt: Sacramentum enim Corporis & Sangvinis Christi accipere etiam malus potest: Corpus autem Christi reverâ manducare dicendus non est, qui in Christi Corpore non est.

Sed respondeo, committi ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχꙋ. De quâ enim manducatione agat Augustinus, dispiciendum est. Disputat autem ille eo loci ex professo contra eos, qui pro carnis libitu & arbitrio, sibi quidvis sceleris impunè licere autumabant: imò Vitam sibi æternam ex eo unicè promittebant, quòd Corpore & Sangvine Domini participassent. Ostendit ergò Augustinus, non hoc sufficere ad æternæ vitæ possessionē, ut quis Sacramentum Corporis & Sangvinis CHRISTI accipiat: sed id præcipuè requiri, ut aliquis reverâ manducet & bibat: id quod fiat ab ijs, qui verè in CHRISTUM credunt, hoc est, Spiritualiter etiam manducant Corpus Christi. Hi enim manent in CHRISTO, & CHRISTUS in ipsis Joh. 6.

Sed habent Adversarij & aliud argumentum, quod sic habet: Nihil habet rationem Sacramenti extra usum à Christo institutum. Atqui sine fide non est ullus alius legitimus Cœnæ usus. Ergò indigni, quippè fide destituti, externum tantùm Sacramentum sine corpore Christi percipiunt.

Respondeo: Fallit argumentum sub Sophismate Ignorationis Elenchi. Regula enim isthæc; Nihil habet rationem Sacramenti extra usum à Christo institutum, opposita est à B. LUTHERO, Pontificiorum & Scholasticorum dogmati qui signa Sacramentalia extra usum etiam, Sacramenti rationem ac definitionem obtinere somnia bant. Sensus proindè regulæ non est ille, quem Calviniani fingunt, ac si extra fidem Corpus Christi in Sacramento percipi non possit: Sed, quòd signa Sacramentalia non habeant rationem Sacramenti propriè sic dicti, nisi accedat usus legitimus, à CHRISTO ipso institutus, qui tantùm in manducando & bibendo consistit.

Tandem & istud objiciunt Sacramentarij: Si indignis Sacramentum integrum percipiendum: statuendum fuerit, CHRISTUM pro indignis etiam instituisse Sacramentum hoc: id quod videtur absurdum.

Sed ad hoc etiam cavillum distinctè respondendum, & illud cumprimis explicandum, An Sacramentum Coenæ à CHRISTO pro indignis sit institutum?

Primùm ergò, si de Substantiâ S. Cœnæ quæritur, eadem est dignis & indignis à CHRISTO instituta, cùm Sacramentorum integritas non à fide, vel in credulitate utentium, sed à veritate & potentiâ instituentis dependeat.

2. Si de fructu quæratur, certum est, Servatorem nunquàm voluisse, ut indigni, quatenùs, & quamdiu tales sunt, salutarem vim & efficaciam Sacramenti percipiant. Ubi tamen culpa subsequentis perditionis non pendet ab hac voluntate Christi, qui Indignorum conversionem seriò expetit, & hoc fine Sacramentorum usum omnibus ex æquo communem esse permittit: sed pendet ex ipsâ Indignorum culpâ, qui præter DEI voluntatem judicium sibi manducant.

3. Si de intentione & proposito CHRISTI instituentis quæratur, respondemus primò de voluntate DEI generali, secundum quam, ut salus ipsa, sic media quoque salutis, Verbum & Sacramenta præparata sunt omnibus, suo tamen certo, & à CHRISTO in verbo determinato ordine legitimè usurpanda. Deindè si de Jure quæritur, Utrum CHRISTUS cœnam instituerit indignis, hoc est, voluerit impœnitentes, quatenùs tales sunt, & manent, ad S. Cœnam accedere; Respondemus simpliciter negativè, cùm illi sibi judicium manducent, cùm seipsos non probent, cùm à DOMINO, tanquàm convivæ impuri, carentes veste nuptiali ejiciantur, cùm denique nulla ipsis absolutio, nulla peccatorum remissio aut consolatio in Evangelio sit proposita. Undè meritò Ecclesia his, quos indignos & impœnitentes deprehendit, Cœnæ Dominicæ usum denegat: quod facere nullo jure posset, si talibus à CHRISTO sacrum hoc epulum esset institutum.

4. Si denique de facto quæratur, quo Indigni præter CHRISTI institutum & voluntatem ad mensam DOMINI accedunt: tùm sanè in eâ accipiunt Corpus & Sangvinem Christi, idque non sine instituto Christi: veruntamen indignâ Thesauri hujus sumtione judicium sibi accersunt, & per Accidens Christus, qui in Cœnâ adest ut fivicator, indignè manducantibo sit judex & vindex impietatis: perindè ut Evangelium, quod est verbum vitæ Joh. 6, 68. incredulis sit odor mortis ad mortem, 2. Cor. 2, 16. non ex DEI instituto, sed ex utentium infanabili & obstinatâ malitiâ.


### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in…: On the Use of the Eucharistic Sacrament

The use of this Sacrament is twofold: one internal, the other external. The internal is that which, done in true faith and joined with true repentance, is profitable for the salvation of the faithful. This is evident from the sentiment of Christ, saying: Do this in my remembrance. Therefore, the Papist figment concerning the Work performed is excluded. For if this had a place, the Savior would have had to say: Do this for the remission of sins. Hence Origen writes excellently in chapter 15 of Matthew: That which is sanctified by the Word of GOD, and by observance, does not sanctify the user by its own nature. For if that were so, it would also sanctify him who eats unworthily. And tract. 25 on Matthew: Assiduity of communication and other similar things are not justice itself: but are held to be the seasoning of justices: But spiritual things, which are justices in themselves, are called Judgment, Mercy, Faith. And Augustine in tractate 80 on John: The Savior does not say, You are clean because of the Baptism with which you have been washed, but because of the word which I have spoken to you. Therefore, to attribute salvation, and the grace of GOD, and the remission of sins, which are spiritual goods and internal actions, to some external office, is of a certain error that is clearly superstitious, inept, and Jewish. Therefore, the horrible voice of Cardinal Cajetan, saying to Luther: Faith is not necessary for one about to approach the Eucharist.

But there is also another error, no lighter than the former, which Canon 5 of the Session of the Council of Trent put forth concerning the internal use and the true efficacy of this Sacrament, which consists in the remission of sins, in these words: If anyone shall say that the principal fruit of the most holy Eucharist is the remission of sins, or that other effects do not proceed from it, let him be anathema. Those little fathers forged this Canon for this reason, that they might save the doctrine of the Scholastics concerning the effects of the Eucharist. For they teach that the Eucharist blots out certain light and minor sins, and sometimes even certain grave ones, namely those whose memory has escaped us when we confess: for then the virtue of the Sacrament supplies what ignorance lacked. But that mortal sins are not blotted out by the use of the Eucharist, but that one is only preserved from them: As if indeed the Blood of Christ received in the Eucharist did not have the power of blotting out mortal and graver sins, but that that dignity and virtue must be attributed to our satisfactions, papal indulgences, the sacrifice of the Mass, and the remaining peddling. Furthermore, they also condemn the sealing of the remission of sins, which takes place in the Eucharist, so that they may cloak their dogma concerning doubt: and they teach that the effects of the Eucharist are obtained only by those who, by their own preparations, have rendered themselves immune, free, pure, and holy from graver sins. All of which doctrine is impious and blasphemous; against the most holy Blood of Christ, and his most precious blood, which, with John as witness, cleanses us

Latin:

USus Sacramenti hujus est geminus: Unus internus, alter externus. Internus, est ille, qui in fide verâ factus & cum verâ pœnitentiâ conjunctus, fidelium saluti expedit. Patet hoc ex Christi sententiâ, dicentis: Facite hoc in meam commemorationem. Excluditur ergò figmentum Pontificium de Operê operato. Hoc enim si locum haberet, dicendum fuiffet Servatori: Facite hoc in remiffionem peccatorum. Hinc præclarè Origines scribit in cap. 15. Matthæi: Quod sanctificatur per Verbum DEI, & per observationem, non suapte naturâ sanctificat utentem. Nam si id esset, sanctificaret etiam illum, qui comedit indignè. Et tract. 25. in Matthæum: Affiduitas communicationis & alia similia, non ipsa sunt justitia: sed conditura habentur justitiarum: Res autem spirituales, quæ ex seipsis justitiæ sunt, dicuntur Judicium, Misericordia, Fides. Et Augustinus tractatu 80. in Johannem: Non ait Servator, Mundi estis propter Baptisma, quo loti estis, sed propter verbum, quod locutus sum vobis. Salutem ergò, & gratiam DEI, ac remissionem peccatorum, quæ sunt spiritualia bona, & internæ actiones, externo cuipiam officio acceptam referre, erroris est cujusdam planè superstitiosi, inepti, Judaici. Horrenda ergò vox Cardinalis Cajetani, dicentis ad Lutheru: Fides non est necessaria accessuro ad Eucharistia.

Sed est & alius error, priore nihil levior, quem de Usu interno, verâquè efficaciâ Sacramenti hujus, quæ in remissione peccatorum consistit, prodidit Canon 5. Sess. Concilium Tridetinum his verbis: Si quis dixerit, vel præcipuum fructum sanctissimæ Eucharistiæ esse remissionem peccatorum, vel ex eâ non alios effectus provenire, anathema sit. Hunc Canonem ideò cuderunt Paterculi illi, ut doctrinam Scholasticorum de Effectibus Eucharistiæ salvarent. Docent enim illi, levia quædam & minora peccata delere Eucharistiam, aliquando etiam gravia quædam, illa scilicet quorum memoria confitentibus nobis exciderit: Tunc enim Sacramenti virtutem supplere, quod ignorantia desiderabat. Mortalia autem peccata usu Eucharistiæ non deleri: sed tantùm ab ijs præservari: Quasi verò Sangvis Christi in Eucharistiâ perceptus, non habeat vim delendi peccata mortalia & graviora: sed illa dignitas & virtus tribuenda sit nostris satisfactionibus, indulgentijs papalibus, Missæ sacrificio, & reliquis nundinationibus. Prætereà damnant etiam Obsignationem remissionis peccatorum, quæ fit in Eucharistiâ, ut dogma suum de dubitatione palliare queant: & tradunt Eucharistiæ effectus illis tantùm obtingere, qui suis præparationibus à peccatis gravioribus immunes, liberos, puros & sanctos se reddiderunt. Quæ universa doctrina impia & blasphema est; in sanctissimum Christi, ejusque pretiosissimum sangvinem, qui Johanne teste, emundat nos
