### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in…: Whether the minister is bound to communicate?

from all sin 1 John 1. and cleanses our consciences from dead works. Heb. 9.

The external use of this Sacrament, and its external form, consists in eating and drinking: as Christ himself asserts: Eat, Drink, Do this, etc. For which use the condition of this Sacrament is so destined, that outside of it, that which is called, i.e., the Sacrament, does not exist. Which condition is common to this Sacrament with the Sacrament of Baptism: For just as baptismal water, outside the use and act of baptizing, is not sacramental water: so in this Sacrament, when eating and drinking cease, the Sacrament itself ceases to be.

Moreover, concerning this external use of the Sacrament, various practical questions are raised, which are very necessary for a minister of the Church to know.

And at the beginning, the question is asked concerning the Consecration, as they call it, of the elements, Bread and Wine: For what thanks is it employed, and what is its end? The Romanists, both ancient and more recent, write that a certain hidden magical power underlies the pronunciation of those four words, This is my Body, by whose power the bread is essentially changed into the Body, and the wine into the Blood of Christ. Thus, there were even those addicted to our own religion who, once the recitation of the words of Institution was performed, dreamed of a certain lasting Sacramental Union of the bread and the body, and of the wine and the Blood of Christ: and deceived by this false principle, they brought forth opinions partly impious, partly absurd, and partly ridiculous, concerning the consecrated hosts which remained after the communion had already been completed. Both errors result from that false principle by which it is imagined that the Sacramental Union depends on the power and virtue of the recited words of Institution. The purer Church, correcting this, determines that the Sacramental Union does not occur until the external use itself, which consists in eating and drinking, approaches: so that if the words of Institution were recited even a thousand times, but that use, that is, eating and drinking, did not approach, then no Sacramental Union at all would intervene between the Bread and the Body, or the Wine and the Blood of Christ. Therefore, there is no need to inquire more curiously: In what place are the consecrated hosts to be held, if the use does not approach? Or what is to be done if there are fewer communicants than there are consecrated hosts? Namely, they are to be put back and kept for the next subsequent action: and they are not to be held in any other place than the remaining unconsecrated hosts, for the reasons already alleged.

The same thing must be determined concerning the Wine, if by chance some drops of it fall to the ground: which can very easily happen. Anciently under the Papacy, and indeed in the Canon Law, part 3 of the Decrees concerning Consecration, chapter 2. If through negligence: such a decree was established by the Pontiff: If through negligence anything of the blood has dripped onto the ground, it shall be licked up with the tongue, the board shall be scraped: If there are no boards, so that it may not be trampled, the place shall be scraped up, and consumed by fire, and the ash shall be buried within the altar, and the priest shall do penance for forty days: if the chalice has dripped onto the altar, the minister shall suck up the drop, and do penance for three days: If it has reached the linen of the altar, and the drop has reached it, he shall do penance for four days: If as far as the third, he shall do penance for nine days: If as far as the fourth, he shall do penance for twenty days, and the minister shall wash the linens which the drop has touched three times, with a chalice placed underneath: and the water of the washing shall be taken, and buried next to the altar. Thus the Pontiff. But the counsel of a certain theologian does not differ much from this superstition, which was as follows: If by chance anything from the cup of the LORD has been spilled after the consecration, it pleases me that the earth, into which it was spilled from the cup of blessing, (if it can be done) be dug up and burned: But where anything has flowed onto a stone, which cannot be dug up, that a small fire be kindled on that stone, and the ash be collected, and thrown into a flowing stream. Thus he. But what need is there for these superstitions? The cup of blessing ought indeed to be handled reverently and with due circumspection: but if by any chance anything falls, it is not to be determined that anything of the Blood of Christ has flowed away: For the Wine is neither changed into Blood, nor is it Sacramentally united with the Blood, before the act of drinking approaches. Therefore it is and remains wine, whatever has flowed away either by chance or by negligence, and it ought not to be treated more superstitiously. The same thing must also be held concerning wine that has indeed been swallowed by a man, but due to the violence of a disease, or some other accident occurring, is spat back into the chalice. For if such wine can no longer serve for the use of drinking, due to nausea, it may be poured out freely, and without any bite of conscience, onto the ground or into a flowing stream. For it remains irrefragably true that no insult redounds from it to the Blood of Christ: since outside the use of complete drinking, it is not a Sacrament.

But to what end, someone might say, are the words of the Institution recited? What is its purpose and effect? I answer, although this recitation contains in itself no power of effecting a sacramental Union, it is nevertheless not to be rashly neglected. For it performs the office of a Blessing: 1. indeed ἀξιακριτικῶς, distinctively: while through this recitation, the bread and wine are distinguished from the rest of the creatures of the same kind, and are destined for the Sacramental action: 2. but εὐκτικῶς, precatorily: while, namely, this recitation of the words of Christ not only recalls the history of the first institution to the mind of the communicants, but at the same time obtains the force of prayers, so that the Savior, mindful of this institution of His, may will that that very thing be ratified also now in the present Eucharistic action, and may make us worthy guests and fellow-diners of this Heavenly table.

Then it is asked, Whether the consecrating minister is always bound to communicate himself? There exist canons of Councils concerning this question, and Thomas cites the XII Council of Toledo, chapter 15, which holds as follows: It is to be held by all means, that as often as the one sacrificing immolates the Body and Blood of our Lord JESUS CHRIST on the altar, so often he should show himself a participant in the reception of the Body and Blood of our Lord JESUS CHRIST. But since we have no business or dealings with the Popish Sacrifice, that Canon cannot bind us. Therefore I judge it to be placed in the liberty of the minister, whether, after the Consecration has been performed,

Latin:

ab omni peccato 1. Joh. 1. & purgat conscientias nostras ab operibus mortuis. Hebr. 9.

Usus Externus Sacramenti hujus, ejusque forma externa consistit in manducando & bibendo : sic ipso asserente Christo: Edite, Bibite, Facite hoc &c. Ad quem usum ita destinata est Sacramenti hujus conditio, ut extra eum, id quod dicitur, h. e. Sacramentum non sit. Quæ conditio communis est huic Sacramento, cum Sacramento Baptismi : Quemadmodum enim aqua baptistica extra usum & actum baptizandi, Sacramentalis aqua non est: ita in hoc Sacramento, cessante manducatione & bibitione, Sacramentum ipsum esse desinit.

Cæterùm de usu hoc externo Sacramenti variæ moventur Quæstiones practicæ, ministro Ecclesiæ scitu perquàm necessariæ.

Ac initiò quæritur de Consecratione, ut vocant, Elementorum, Panis & Vini: Cujus gratia ea adhibeatur, & quis ejus sit finis? Romanenses tùm veteres, tùm recensiores, pronunciationi quatuor istorum verborum, Hoc est Corpus meum, latentem quandam vim magicam subesse scripitant, cujus vi panis essentialiter mutetur in Corpus, Vinum in Sangvinem Christi. Sic reperti fuerunt nostræ etiam religioni addicti, qui factâ recitatione verborum Institutionis, durantem quandam Unionem Sacramentalem panis & corporis, vini & Sangvinis Christi somnia bant: & falso hoc decepti principio, partim impias, partim absurdas, partim ridiculas tulerunt sententias, de hostijs consecratis, quæ peractâ jam communione remanserant. Error uterque resultat ex falso illo principio, quo fingitur, quòd Unio Sacramentalis pendeat ex vi & virtute recitationis verborum Institutionis. Quem Ecclesia purior corrigens, Unionem Sacramentalem non prius fieri statuit, quàm accedat ipse externus usus, qui in manducando & bibendo consistit: ut si vel millies recitarentur verba Institutionis : Usus autem iste, hoc est, manducatio & bibitio non accederet: tùm nulla prorsus Unio Sacramentalis intercederet Pani cum Corpore, Vino cum Sangvine Christi. Proindè non est, ut curiosiùs inquiratur, Quo loco sint habendæ hostiæ consecratæ, non accedente usu: vel quid faciendum, si pauciores sint communicantes, quàm sit hostiæ consecratæ? Nempè reponendæ, & in subsequentem actionem proximam afservandæ : neque alio loco, quàm reliquæ non consecratæ hostiæ habendæ sunt: ex causis jam allegatis.

Quod ipsum statuendum est de Vino, si fortè guttulæ ejus aliquæ in terram cadant: id quod facillimè fieri potest. Antiquitùs sub Papatu, & quidem in Jure Canonico, part. 3. Decretorum de Consecratione, cap. 2. Si per negligentiam: à Pontifice decretum tale erat conditum: Si per negligentiam aliquid de sangvine stillaverit in terram, lingvâ lambetur, tabula radetur : Si non fuerint tabulæ, ut non conculcetur, locus corradatur, & igne consumatur, & cinis intra altare cõdatur & sacerdos quadraginta dieb9 pœniteat: si super altare stillaverit calix, sorbeat minister stillam, & trib9 diebus pœniteat: Si super linteum altaris, & ad illud stilla pervenerit, quatuor diebus pœniteat : Si usq́; ad tertium, novem diebus pœniteat : Si usq́; ad quartum, viginti diebus pœniteat, & linteamina, quæ tetigerit stilla, tribus vicibus minister abluat, calice supposito: & aqua ablutionis sumatur, & juxta altare recondatur. Hæc Pontifex. Sed adhâc superstitione non multùm abhorret Concilium cujusdam Theologi, quod tale erat: Si fortè aliquid ex populo DOMINI post consecrationem effusum est, placet mihi, ut terra, in quam illud effusum est ex poculo benedictionis, (si fieri potest) effodiatur & comburatur: Ubi verò aliquid in lapidem defluxit, qui non potest erui, ut ignis parvus in illo lapide incendatur, & cinis colligatur, atq́; in profluentem conjiciatur. Hæc ille. Sed quorsum opus est istis superstitionibus? Reverenter quidem, & cum debitâ circumspectione tractari debet poculum benedictionis: sed si casu aliquo quicquam decidat, non statuendum est, aliquid defluxisse de Sangvine Christi: Neque enim Vinum vel mutatur in Sangvinem, vel Sacramentaliter est unitum cum Sangvine, priusquàm bibitionis actus accedat. Ergò vinum est & manet, quicquid sive per casum, sive per negligentiam defluxit, neque superstitiosiùs curari debet. Quod ipsum tenendum est etiam de vino, ab homine quidem hausto, sed ob morbi vehementiam, vel alio quodam casu accidente, rursus in calicem exputo. Quod si enim tale vinum, in usum bibitionis, ob nauseam, cedere ampliùs non possit, liberè, & sine ullo conscientiæ morsu, profundatur in terram aut profluentem. Manet enim irrefragabiliter verum, quod indè nihil contumeliæ redundet ad sangvinem Christi: siquidem extra usum integræ bibitionis, non est Sacramentum.

Sed quorsum, dicat aliquis, recitantur verba Institutionis? Quis ejus finis, ac effectus? Respondeo, licet nullam vim Unionis sacramentalis efficiendæ recitatio hæc in se contineat, non tamen temerè eam esse negligendam. Fungitur enim ea Benedictionis officio: 1. quidem ἀξιακριτικῶς, distinctivè: dum per hanc recitationem, panis & vinum, à reliquis ejusdem generis creaturis discernuntur, & actioni Sacramentali destinantur: 2. verò εὐκτικῶς precatoriè: dum nimirum recitatio hæc verborum Christi, non solùm historiam primæ institutionis ad animum communicantibus revocat, sed simul precum vim obtinet, ut Servator institutionis hujus suæ memor, illud ipsum jam quoq́; in instante actione Eucharisticâ, ratũ esse velit, & dignos nos hospites atq́; cõvivas Cœlestis huj9 mensæ efficiat.

Deindè quæritur, An minister consecrans semper teneatur sibiipsi communicare? Extant de hâc mquæstione canones Conciliorum, & Thomas citat Concilium Toletanum XII. cap. 15. quod sic habet: Modis omnibus tenendum est, ut quotiescunquè sacrificans, Corpus & Sangvinem Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI in altari immolat, toties perceptionis Corporis & Sangvinis Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI participem se præbeat. Cæterùm cum nobis nihil rei aut commercij sit cum Sacrificio Papistico, Canon iste nos obligare nequit. Proindè in libertate ministri positum esse arbitror, utrum peractâ Consecratione,


### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in…: VII. Whether all who have in some manner been baptized, and live within the external society of the Church of Jesus, are to be admitted to…

he himself also wishes to communicate or not. Meanwhile, however, it must be well observed what is received by custom in any given Church, without superstition. If indeed custom so prevails, I would never advise that the consecrating minister should rashly change it or neglect it: not because it is necessarily and absolutely required that it be done, and unnecessary disturbances may not be stirred up in a peaceful and tranquil Church.

Thirdly, it is asked: Can a layman, in a case of necessity, consecrate and administer the Lord's Supper, or rather, ought he to? We answer in the negative. For although a layman can administer Baptism in a case of necessity, the same right is not granted to him regarding the action of the Eucharistic Sacrament. The reason for the difference is this: because the necessity of the Lord's Supper is not the same as that of Baptism, which, as the washing of regeneration, must necessarily be conferred upon infants. But indeed, even in a case of necessity, or in the lack of the elemental matter, we can be without the Lord's Supper without danger to salvation. For here that saying of Augustine has place: Believe and you have eaten. Baptism confers faith, without which no one can be saved; the Lord's Supper does not confer faith, but confirms and seals that which is already conferred. Which confirmation or sealing, even in such a case of necessity, can be done through the Evangelical promises: so that from its lack, no danger to salvation is to be feared.

Fourthly, it is asked: Can someone who thinks rightly about the Lord's Supper, in a time of necessity, communicate among Calvinists or Papists? I answer in the negative: 1. lest we participate in the sins of others and in another's heresy: 2. Sacraments are public symbols of our confession, by which the true Church distinguishes itself from the church of the wicked and heretics: so that each person is presumed to be devoted to that confession whose sacraments he participates in. But what if? If such a person is held by such a desire to receive this Sacrament that, without it, he would scarcely wish to admit any consolation? I answer again in the negative: not even in this case should one participate in the sacraments of heretics. For such a person, about whom it is asked, either has knowledge and clear understanding of what and how abominable impieties and blasphemies the heresy of both the Papists and the Calvinists teems with, or he does not have it: if he has knowledge, and nevertheless desires to participate in their sacraments, it would be the most evident sign that he is a hypocrite and not entirely devoted to our confession. If he does not have knowledge, then he must be well informed. Where, once he is taught about those βδελύγμασι (abominations) of the heretics, he will abhor such communion with his whole heart. To him, therefore, it must be inculcated again and again: Believe and you have eaten, and that passage 1 Thess. 5:22: Abstain from every form of evil. It is added that scandals must not be given to the weaker ones; indeed, no scruple should be injected into any consciences.

Fifthly, it is asked: How often should one communicate? I answer that the use of the Lord's Supper is not left to men as an arbitrary matter, but that we are bound to it under the condition of necessity. An effective proof of which is sought first from the formula of the divine command. For concerning the use of this mystery, the Savior did not say: If you wish, you may eat; but He said: Take, Eat, Drink, Do this.

2. To this command is added a most urgent reason concerning recalling the memory of CHRIST to the mind: Do this in remembrance of me: the parts of which duty the Apostle recalls more pressingly to the commemoration of the Lord's death. From which reason it is elicited by good consequence: As much as the forgetting of the Lord's death cannot or ought not to happen in a Christian man, so much is it a sin if the use of this mystery is omitted by him.

3. There is added the highest utility, which is proposed by CHRIST for the infirmities of our souls in this very Sacrament. But when it is asked discreetly, How often should one communicate: a discreet answer can scarcely be given. In the times of Augustine, some thought that one should communicate daily: to others it seemed that this should be done more rarely, for the sake of greater reverence. Where Augustine, in the book De Ecclesiasticis Dogmatibus, chapter 53, answers thus: To receive the communion of the Eucharist daily, I neither praise nor blame: yet I advise and exhort that one should communicate on all Lord's days, provided that the mind is without the desire to sin. For I say that one who still has the will to sin is burdened more by the reception of the Eucharist than purified. Thomas Aquinas, part 3, q. 80, art. 10, explains the opinion of the Romans on this question thus: According to the diverse state of the Church, diverse statutes have emanated regarding this. For in the primitive Church, when the devotion of the Christian faith was more vigorous, it was decreed that the faithful should communicate daily. Whence Pope Anacletus says: After the consecration is finished, let all communicate who do not wish to lack the Eucharistic lights: for if the Apostles decreed it, and the holy Roman Church holds it. But afterwards, when the fervor of faith had diminished, Pope Fabian allowed that, if not more frequently, at least three times a year all should communicate, namely at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord. Pope Soter also says that one should communicate on the day of the Lord's Supper, as is held in the decrees De Consecratione, dist. 2. But afterwards, because of the abundance of iniquity, with the charity of many growing cold, Innocent III decreed that the faithful should communicate at least once a year, namely at Easter. This is Thomas. The Council of Trent confirmed the decree of Innocent, in the Canon concerning the Sacrament of the Eucharist. Unde consequens fuit sub Papatu, ut populus sibi persuaderet, nihil prorsus peccari, si non sæpius in anno communicet. Nos sic statuimus: Etsi neque Christus neque Apostoli definiverunt, quoties sumenda sit Eucharistia; sed id reliquerunt liberum in cujusque Ecclesiæ arbitrio: tamen cavendum esse maxime, ne libertate ad licentiam malam usurpemus. Proinde quo majore timore, ac tremore quisque salutis suæ negocium curaverit: quo ferventiore etiam Spiritu, Diaboli & carnis nostræ suggestionibus pravis reluctari studuerit: quo denique majore studio apud animum reputaverit: mortem quidem esse certissimam, nihil vero incertius hora: is sua etiam sponte dabit operam, ut frequenter admodum, & ad minimum quotannis quater, sacrosancto, & efficacissimo alexipharmaco se instruat, quo roboratus in fide Christi perseveret. Hence it followed under the Papacy that the people persuaded themselves that there was no sin at all if one did not communicate more than once a year. We determine as follows: Although neither Christ nor the Apostles defined how often the Eucharist should be taken, but left that free to the judgment of each Church, yet we must take the greatest care not to use liberty for evil license. Therefore, with whatever greater fear and trembling each person shall have attended to the business of his own salvation, with whatever more fervent Spirit he shall have striven to resist the depraved suggestions of the Devil and our flesh, and finally with whatever greater zeal he shall have pondered in his mind that death is indeed most certain, but nothing is more uncertain than the hour: he will also of his own accord take pains to provide himself very frequently, and at the very least four times a year, with the most holy and most efficacious antidote, by which, strengthened, he may be able to persevere in the faith of Christ, and against any temptations and assaults, stand strong and undaunted.

Sixthly, it is asked for whom this Sacrament was instituted and destined by CHRIST? I answer: It was ordained not for Angels, but for men. CHRIST is indeed commonly called the Bread of Angels, from Psalm 78:25, and the food of Angels, from Wisdom 16:20, because that which is our daily Bread for the sustenance of this fleeting life is to the Angels a mutual vision, by which they enjoy CHRIST in heaven. But just as CHRIST assumed not the seed of Angels, but of men (Hebrews 2:16), so He founded the Sacrament of the Supper, the casket of His Body and Blood, to be used not by Angels, but by men.

The use of this Sacrament pertains, however, not to just any men, but only to those whom that assembly represented in whose presence this mystery was first established and celebrated. That was the Apostolic flock, which bore the type and person, as it were, of the Christian assembly, just as in the Old Testament the whole body of the Israelite people was represented by the twelve tribes and their names. And so, the use of this mystery is open not to Jews, nor to Gentiles or Turks, but only to those who have been called into use and, as it were, gathered into the bosom of the Church of CHRIST by the voice and ministry of Apostolic preaching.

Seventhly, it is asked: Are all men whatsoever, as many as are baptized and live in the external society of the Church, to be admitted to the participation of this Sacrament? I answer in the negative: For in this very assembly of the baptized and the called, the condition of all is not equal and the same. Therefore, they are excluded from the use of this Sacrament.

1. Infants. For although in the time of Pope Innocent, Cyprian, and Augustine, this Sacrament was given and granted to infants in Europe as well as in Africa, yet an evident reason militates against this, for which this custom has most rightly become obsolete and should not be recalled into use. For since, according to the admonition of the Apostle (1 Cor. 11:28), infants cannot examine themselves as to whether they are in the faith, nor proclaim the death of the LORD, they are certainly not to be considered suitable guests for this table.

2. The Flagitious, the Manifest, and the Excommunicated are excluded. I say the Excommunicated and the Manifest, because in this place one must accurately distinguish between the flagitious and the wicked. For either the flagitious act is still hidden—that is, known only to the guilty party and the minister of the Church—or it is manifest, or publicly notorious. If it is hidden, then the sinner shall be restrained by private admonition so that he may refrain from the use of the Supper until he has brought forth fruits worthy of true repentance. But if, having spurned this admonition, he nevertheless thrusts himself into the assembly of communicants, he is not to be publicly barred. For any Christian, by the very fact that he is baptized, has a right to the blessed table, which cannot be denied to him except in a manifest and public case.

But if the sin is still hidden, however great it may be, certainly such a sinner should not be publicly barred from the use of the Sacrament, even if he approaches against the minister's admonition. For if the minister were to do this, he would constitute himself a revealer of confession and a betrayer of the crime, from which crime he ought to be most alien. But neither is the Supper to be offered to such a sinner in secret, unless in danger of death, provided that a clear promise of repentance precedes. If, however, the flagitious acts are manifest, then either the sinners are excommunicated or they are not. If they are excommunicated, it is obvious to any minister that the way to this Sacrament is not open to such persons unless a public reconciliation with the Church precedes. Hence it was decreed in antiquity that a Priest who gives the Eucharist to an excommunicated person, whom he knows to be such, is to be deposed.

Latin:

semper & ipse communicare velit, nec ne. Interim tamen probè observandum fuerit, quid in quâlibet Ecclesia, sine superstitione, usu sit receptum. Si sanè consuetudo ita obtineat, nunquàm suaserim, ut minister consecrans temerè eam mutet, aut negligat: non quòd necessariò, & absolutè illud fieri necesse sit: sed ne offendantur infirmiores, & turbæ non necessariæ moveantur in Ecclesia pacatâ, & tranquillâ.

Tertiò quæritur: An Laicus in casu necessitatis consecrare, & Cœnam Domini administrare possit, imò debeat? Respondemus negatè. Etsi enim Laicus in casu necessitatis, Baptismum administrare potest: non tamen circa Sacramenti Eucharistici actionem, idem jus ipsi est concessum. Ratio diversitatis est hæc: quia non eadem est necessitas Cœnæ Dominicæ, quæ est Baptismi, qui tanquàm lavacrum regenerationis, infantibus necessariò conferri debet. At verò vel in casu necessitatis, vel in defectu res Elementaris, sine periculo salutis, Cœnâ Domini carere possumus. Hîc enim locum habet illud Augustini: Crede & manducasti. Baptismus confert fidem, sine quâ nemo salvari potest; Cœna DOMINI fidem non confert: sed jam collatam confirmat, & obsignat. Quæ sive confirmatio, sive obsignatio, in ejusmodi etiam casu necessitatis, fieri potest per promissiones Evangelicas: ut ex ejus defectu, nullum sit extimescendum salutis periculum.

Quartò quæritur, An aliquis rectè sentiens de Cœnâ Domini, tempore necessitatis, possit communicare apud Calvinianos vel Pontificios? Respondeo negatè: 1. ne peccatis alienis, & alienâ hæresi participemus: 2. Sunt Sacramenta symbola publica confessionis nostræ, quibus Ecclesia vera se à malignantium & hæreticorum Ecclesia discernit: ita ut quisque illi confessioni addictus esse præsumatur, cujus sacris participat. Sed quid? Si talis aliquis tanto desiderio teneatur Sacramenti hujus percipiendi, ut absque eo, vix ullam consolationem admittere velit? Respondeo rursus negatè: ne hoc quidem casu hæreticorum sacris participandum. Nam talis, de quo quæritur, aut cognitum, perspectumque habet, quibus & quam abominandis impietatibus atq; blasphemijs utraque tùm Pontificiorum, tùm Calvinianorum hæresis scateat, vel non habet: si habet cognitum, & nihilominus sacris ipsorum participare desiderat, evidentissimum Signum fuerit, ipsum esse hypocritam, & nostræ confessioni nō ex asse addictum. Si non habeat cognitum: tùm probè informandus fuerit. Ubi mox ipsimet, de istis hæreticorum βδελύγμασι edoctus, à tali cómunione toto pectore abhorrebit. Huic ergò iterum atq; iterum inculcandum: Crede & manducasti, & illud 1. Thess. 5.22. Ab omni specie mali abstinete. Accedit, quòd non danda sunt scandala infirmioribus: imò nullus etiam conscientijs scrupulus injiciendus.

Quintò quæritur: Quoties sit Communicandum? Respondeo, Usum Cœnæ Dominicæ non esse hominibus relictum arbitrarium: sed sub necessitatis conditione nos ad eum esse adstrictos. Cujus probatio efficax primùm petitur è formulâ mandati divini. Nam de usu hujus mysterij non dixit Servator: Si volueritis, poteritis edere sed dixit: Accipite, Edite, Bibite, Facite hoc.

2. Mandato huic urgentissima apposita est ratio de recolendâ animo memoriâ CHRISTI: Facite hoc ad mei commemorationem: Cujus officij partes Apostolus ad mortis Dominicæ commemorationem pressiùs revocat. Ex quâ ratione illud per bonam consequentiam elicitur: Quàm non fieri potest, aut debet in homine Christiano mortis Dominicæ oblivio: tàm nefas est, si mysterij hujus usus ab eodem omittatur.

3. Accedit summa utilitas, quæ est à CHRISTO animarum nostrarū infirmitatibus in hoc ipso Sacramento proposita. Cæterùm quando discretè quæritur, Quoties sit communicandum: Vix discreta dari potest responsio. Augustini temporibus existimabant nonnulli, quotidiè esse cōmunicandum: Alijs videbatur hoc rariùs esse faciendum, majoris reverentiæ gratia. Ubi Augustinus in libro de Ecclesiasticis dogmat. cap. 53. sic respondet: Quotidiè Eucharistiæ communionem percipere, nec laudo, nec reprehendo: Omnibus tamen diebus Dominicis communicandum suadeo & hortor, si tamen mens sine affectu peccandi sit. Nam habentem adhuc voluntatem peccandi, gravari magis dico Eucharistiæ perceptione, quàm purificari. Thomas Aquinas part. 3 q. 80. art. 10, Romanensium sententiam de hâc quæstione sic explicat: Secundum statum Ecclesiæ diversum, diversa circa hoc statuta emanarūt. Nam in primitivâ Ecclesiâ, quando magis vigebat devotio fidei Christianæ, statutū fuit, ut quotidiè fideles communicarent. Undè Anaclerus Papa dicit: Peractâ consecratione omnes communicent, qui nolunt Eucharisticis carere luminibus: Si enim Apostoli statuerunt, & sancta Romana tenet Ecclesia. Postmodùm verò diminuto fidei fervore, Fabianus Papa indulsit, ut si non frequentiùs, saltem ter in anno communicent omnes, scilicet in Paschate, Pentecoste, & Nativitate Domini. Soterus etiam Papa dicit, in die Cœnæ Dominicæ esse communicandum, ut habetur in decretis de consecr. dist. 2. Postmodùm verò propter iniquitatis abūndantiam, refrigefcente charitate multorum, statuit Innocentius III. ut saltē semel in anno, scilicetin Paschate fideles communicent. Hæc Thomas. Concilium Tridentinum Innocentij decretum confirmavit, Canone enim de Sacramento Eucharistiæ. Undè consequens fuit sub Papatu, ut populus sibi persuaderet, nihil prors9 peccari, si nō sæpiùs in anno cōmunicet. Nos sic statuimus: Etsi neq; Christus neq; Apostoli definiverunt, quoties sumenda sit Eucharistia; sed id reliquerunt liberum in cujusque Ecclesiæ arbitrio: tamen cavendum esse maximè, ne libertate ad licentiam malā usurpemus. Proindè quo majore timore, ac tremore quisq; salutis suæ negocium curaverit: quô ferventiore etiam Spiritu, Diaboli & carnis nostrę suggestionib9 pravis reluctari studuerit: quô deniq; majore studio apud animum reputaverit: mortem quidē esse certissimam, nihil verò incertiùs horâ: is suâ etiam sponte dabit operam, ut frequenter admodùm, & ad minimùm quotānis quater, sacrosancto, & efficacissimo alexipharmaco se instruat, quo roboratus in fide Christi perseverare, & contra quasvis tentationes ac insultus, fortis & imperterritus stare possit.

Sextò quæritur Quibusnam hoc Sacramentum à CHRISTO sit institutum, & destinatum? Respondeo: Non Angelis, sed hominibus illud esse ordinatum. Vulgò quidem CHRISTUS appellatur Panis Angelorum, ex Psal. 78, 25. & esca Angelorum, ex Sap. 16, 20. ideò, quia quod nobis Panis quotidianus est ad vitæ caducæ sustentationem: id Angelis mutuus est conspectus, quo ex CHRISTO, in cælis fruuntur. Verùm uti non Angelorum, sed hominum semen assumsit CHRISTUS Hebr. 2, 16. Ita Cœnæ quoque Sacramentum Corporis & Sangvinis sui myrothecium, non Angelis, verùm hominibus usurpandum unicè condidit.

Pertinet verò Sacramenti hujus usus ad homines non quoslibet: sed eos duntaxat, quos cœtus ille repræsentavit, in cujus præsentiâ mysterium hoc primitùs conditum & celebratum fuit. Fuit is autem grex Apostolicus, qui typum & personam quasi cœtus Christiani gessit, perindè atque in Testamento Veteri, per tribus duodecim, earumque nomina totum populi Israëliti ci corpus repræsentatum fuit. Itaque neque Judæis, neque gentilibus aut Turcis: sed ijs duntaxat patet mysterij hujus usus, qui ad Ecclesiæ CHRISTI gremium, voce & ministerio Apostolicæ prædicationis sunt in usum convocati, & quasi aggregati.

Septimò quæritur: An omnes omninò homines quotquot quidem sunt baptizati, & in externâ societate Ecclesiæ versantur, ad Sacramenti hujus participationem sint admittendi? Respondeo negatè: Nam in hoc ipso cœtu baptisatorum & vocatorum, non est par, & æqualis omnium conditio. Excluduntur ergò ab usu Sacramenti hujus.

1. Infantes. Etsi enim tempore Innocentij Papæ, Cypriani & Augustini, cùm in Europâ, quàm in Africâ Sacramentum hoc infantibus quoque datum & concessum fuit: ratio tamen evidens militat, propter quam consuetudo hæc rectissimè & antiquata, & in usum revocari non debet. Quia enim secundum admonitionem Apostoli 1. Cor. 11, 28. Infantes seipsos probare non possunt, an sint in fide: neque annunciare mortem DOMINI: utique convivæ hujus mensæ, haud idonei sunt censendi.

2. Excluduntur Flagitiosi, Manifesti, & Excommunicati. Excommunicati dico, & Manifesti, quia hoc loco inter flagitiosos & sceleratos accuratè est distingvendum. Vel enim flagitium adhuc est occultum, hoc est, soli reo & ministro Ecclesiæ notum: vel est manifestum, sive publicè notorium. Si occultum tùm admonitione privatâ peccator coërcebitur, ut ab usu cœnæ sibi temperet, donec fructus verâ pœnitentiâ dignos ediderit. Quod si spretâ hâc admonitione, communicantium cœtui nihilominus sese ille ingesserit: publicè non est arcendus. Nam Christianus quilibet, eo ipso, quod est baptizatus, jus habet mensæ benedictæ, quod negari ipsi, nisi in causâ manifestâ & publicâ, non potest.

Quod si peccatum occultum adhuc est, quantum quantum illud sit: certè talis peccator publicè ab usu Sacramenti, si etiam contra admonitionem ministri accedat, arceri non debet: Hoc enim si faceret minister, tùm Confessionis revelatorem, & proditorem criminis se constitueret, à quo crimine alienissimum ipsum esse oportet. Sed neque tali peccatori Cœna in occulto est præbenda, nisi in periculo mortis, præcedente tamen luculentâ resipiscentiæ promissione. Sin manifesta sint flagitia, tùm aut peccatores sunt excommunicati, aut non sunt. Si sunt excommunicati, cuivis ministro ultrò liquet, ejusmodi non patere aditum ad hoc Sacramentum, nisi præcedat reconciliatio publica cum Ecclesiâ. Hinc antiquitùs est decretum, Quòd Sacerdos, dans excommunicato Eucharistiam, quem scit esse talem, sit deponendus.


### Chapter II. On the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in…: VII. Whether all who have in some manner been baptized, and live within the external society of the Church of Jesus, are to be admitted to……

It is to be noted, however, that such persons also, in danger of death, if they desire to be received, are not to be repelled, as is clear from the example of Serapion in Eusebius, Book 6, Chapter 44. If they are not excommunicated, and the Church in this part neglects its duty, then the Minister will have regard for his own conscience, imitating the example of Chrysostom, who writes thus in Homily 83 on Matthew: 'But if you yourself do not dare to drive them away, tell me; I will not permit these things to happen. I will rather surrender my own soul than allow the LORD'S Body to be given to anyone unworthily, and I will rather suffer my own blood to be shed than grant that most sacred Blood to an unworthy person.'

3. Idiots and fools are excluded, but with this condition: if they are such by nature or by accident that they have no use of right reason at all. For since these can neither examine themselves nor conceive in their minds the devotion of this mystery, they are to be entirely barred from the use of the Supper. A different judgment is to be made concerning those who suffer only from some infirmity of reason.

Concerning actors, however, who are masters of affected foolishness, Cyprian answers thus in Book 1, Epistle 10, to Everatius: 'Out of your affection and mutual respect, you thought it right to consult me, dearest brother, as to what I think about a certain actor who, living among you, still persists in the disgrace of his art, and as a Master and Teacher of boys—not to be educated but to be corrupted—insinuates to others what he has learned so badly: whether such a one ought to communicate with us. I think that it is consistent with neither the divine majesty nor the Evangelical discipline that the honor and modesty of the Church should be defiled by such a shameful and infamous association.'

4. Phrenetics, energumens, those seized by spirits, the obsessed, the furious, and the like are excluded, but likewise with this clear exception: namely, if they are destitute of that faculty so that they cannot distinguish this food from others with right discretion, and cannot examine or judge themselves as to whether they are in the faith. Otherwise, in those for whom the force of the evil is not continuous, but who have lucid intervals, and where other impediments or dangers do not stand in the way, such as vomiting, or ejections through sputum, or the like: then to these the Sacrament is safely, and indeed sometimes even usefully, administered.

5. Infamous persons are also excluded, such as those who devote their efforts to exercises or arts of such a kind that they cannot be practiced without mortal sin and cannot stand with the grace of God: such as magicians, pimps, public prostitutes or harlots, usurers, and those fighters or athletes who contend for life and blood. As long as they do not renounce these illicit things, they are not to be admitted to the use of the Eucharist: and even after renunciation, they are not to be admitted otherwise, unless they have either performed public penance beforehand, or some public indication of this renunciation has first become known to the Church of the faithful. It is to be noted, however, that lictors and executioners, because of the very nature of their life, if personal crimes do not supervene, are in no way to be held as infamous persons in this case and respect.

6. Abstemious persons are also excluded, but not simply all of them: this is what Blessed Luther declared in this manner: If there are any who so abhor wine that they cannot taste even a drop or endure the very smell of wine without danger of vomiting or of their health: it is safer that they abstain entirely from the use of this Sacrament, than that the Sacrament be administered to them under one species at least. The reason alleged is that the mutilation of the Sacrament does not take place without the guilt of sacrilege: and a natural defect sufficiently excuses from the fault of contempt. For it is not the deprivation, but only the contempt of the Sacrament, that is damnable. Therefore, partly that saying of Augustine, Believe and you have eaten: that is, that spiritual eating which exists in John 6, will be more firmly inculcated: and partly it will be enjoined that more frequent spectators at least be present at the celebration of this mystery, so that the public vows of the same, joined with prayers and sighs, may provide greater efficacy for the strengthening of faith.

Eighthly, it is asked: Whether those are to be admitted who have not first made their confession before the Minister? The Romanists hold the negative in all respects, so that they may in some way bolster the dogma concerning auricular confession: which will have to be dealt with in its own place, in the article on Penance. We answer by a distinction: Where the rite of public confession is received by use in any Church, it ought not to be rashly neglected or despised: since according to the precept of the Apostle: many things are sometimes lawful, but not all things edify. Therefore, so that the weaker may not be offended, it is better to strictly observe the rite of the Church, so that you do not approach the Holy Supper before you have made confession before the Minister. Although if for certain and evident causes, and without any scandal, that is omitted, no one ought to be barred from the use of the Holy Supper on that account. Just as Blessed Luther testifies concerning himself, that he sometimes used the Holy Supper without having confessed (as they say), so that even by this means he might demonstrate that that public confession is not of absolute necessity. But where that rite is not in use, there this question also has no place.

Ninthly, it is asked concerning the Mute, whether they are to be admitted or not? To which question Blessed Luther answers thus, Tom. 1. G. p. 339, in the Sermon on the New Testament, held in the year 1520: Some think that the mute are to be deceived blandly by the offering of an unconsecrated host. This joke is not good: nor will it please GOD, who made them Christians just as He did us, and they have the same right that we have. Wherefore if they are of sound mind, and it can be observed from certain signs that they desire the Sacrament with true and pious devotion, as I have often seen, let us allow the Holy Spirit His office and work, and let us not deny to the mute what he asks. It may be that he has greater knowledge and faith within than we do, to whom no one should rashly oppose himself.

Tenthly, it is asked, Whether the Holy Supper is to be given to those who are to be subjected to capital punishment? Under and in the Papacy this was simply denied. But the Church protested against this impiety in the Council of Mainz, chapter 27, in these words: If Communion is to be given at the end, according to the Canonical command, to all who make a pure confession of their sins and are worthily penitent: Why not to those who pay the extreme penalty for their sins. Hence it was decreed and permitted in the same place that thieves could be brought from the gallows to the churches, that offerings could be made for them, and Masses celebrated; if they had confessed beforehand and received absolution. Therefore, in the Evangelical Churches it is by no means considered a sin if the Sacrament of the Eucharist is dispensed to those destined for capital punishment, provided they are truly penitent and demand it.

Eleventhly, it is asked, whether it is permitted to administer the Holy Supper to the infirm and sick in private houses? We answer affirmatively from Canon 12 of the Council of Nicaea, with this admonition, that the minister should act circumspectly in this matter, and have regard for the infirm or sick person. For if, when he enjoyed firm health, he neglected the use of this Sacrament, it is certainly not to be given to him even when he asks for it, unless, broken and dismayed by legal sermons, he has brought forth signs of true repentance. Furthermore, the Holy Supper is not to be offered to such an infirm person who has put off the use of this sacred feast for so long that, now deprived of the benefit of both tongue and senses, he can neither confess his sins, nor discern the Lord's Body, nor examine himself. Meanwhile, we detest that custom and practice by which, under the Papacy, the host, long since consecrated and kept in the sanctuary of the temple, is carried through the streets to the house of the sick person with lights and a bell: dreaming that they cannot consecrate the Eucharist except in a place already consecrated, and that the Body of CHRIST is contained even outside of use, under the Bread, or in the Bread. We also detest the μωροσoφiαν of the Sacramentarians, who condemn this private communion simply, but without any evident cause.

Twelfthly and lastly, it is asked, what is to be determined concerning silver and gilded vessels, stone altars, mass vestments, and other things used in the Eucharistic action? I answer, that all these things are steadfastly retained in our churches, not out of any necessity, much less any worship, but out of Christian liberty, which, so that everything might be performed around the Eucharistic action not only εὐτάκτως, but also ευσχημόνως, introduced the use of these vessels and vestments, and still retains it even now without any superstition.

nor does he see any evident cause for which those things ought to be changed in favor of the Sacramentarians. For if it is therefore a sin to administer the Sacrament at an altar, because this seems to Judaize and Papalize; certainly it will no longer be permitted to use temples, or bells, or books, which likewise served the idolatrous Papacy. What of the fact that CHRIST is not read to have sat at a table and distributed the Supper, but to have reclined according to the custom of the Jewish nation. Therefore, the Sacramental tables will also have to be removed, and the Holy Supper will have to be celebrated only by those reclining on the ground: Furthermore, it is frivolous and trifling that they write that Altars were destined for nothing but sacrifices. Abraham is certainly read to have built an altar to GOD, Gen. 12, 7, not for sacrificing, but as a monument and sign of a divine apparition. Thus the sons of Reuben erected an altar, not for sacrificing, but in memory of a miraculous liberation and crossing. Thus for us Christians there are altars, not indeed Levitical, not for immolating external sacrifices: but for offering the Evangelical and Spiritual sacrifices of lips confessing the name of the Lord, and in memory of the Sacrifice of CHRIST performed on the altar of the cross. Nor do we move a dispute with anyone here concerning either the material or the external form. For whether they be wooden or stone, it will be the same to us, establishing no law of necessity in either: nor do we reject the name of table, especially if it is called sacred: nay, we even call this an Altar with pious Antiquity.

We conclude finally with the words of Augustine from Epist. 118 to Januarius: That whole class of things has free observances, nor is there any discipline better for a serious and prudent Christian in these matters than to act in the way he has seen the Church act, to which he may happen to have come. For what is enjoined neither against faith nor against good morals is to be held indifferently, and is to be observed for the sake of the society of those among whom one lives.

Latin:

Notandum tamen, tales quoque in periculo mortis, si recipi cupiant, non esse repellendos, ut patet exemplo Serapionis, apud Eusebium lib. 6. cap. 44. Si non sunt excommunicati, & Ecclesia hâc in parte officium suum negligat: tùm Minister suæ conscientiæ habebit rationem, imitatus exemplum Chrysostomi, qui Homil. 83. in Matth. sic scribit: Quod si ipse pellere non audes, mihi dicas, non permittam ista fieri: animam potiùs tradam meam, quàm Dominicum Corpus alicui dari indignè: & Sanguinem meum effundi potiùs patiar, quàm sacratissimum illum Sanguinem indigno concedam.

3. Excluduntur moriones & stulti, sed cum hâc conditione, si vel naturâ, vel casu tales sint, ut nullum prorsus rectæ rationis usum habeant. Hi enim cùm neque probare sese neque mysterij hujus devotionem animo concipere possint: à Cœnæ usu omninò sunt arcendi. Secus statuendum est de ijs, qui infirmitate tantùm aliquâ rationis laborant.

De histrionibus autem, qui affectatæ stultitiæ sunt magistri, sic respondet Cyprianus lib. 1. Epist. 10. ad Everatium: Pro dilectione tuâ, & verecundiâ mutuâ consulendum me existimasti, frater charissime, quid mihi videatur de histrione quodam, qui apud vos constitutus, in ejusdem adhuc artis suæ dedecore perseverat, & Magister & Doctor non erudiendorum sed perdendorum puerorum, id quod malè didicit, cæteris quoque insinuat: an talis debeat communicare nobiscum: quod puto ego, nec majestati divinæ, nec Evangelicæ disciplinæ congruere, ut honor & pudor Ecclesiæ, tam turpi & infami cogitatione fœdetur.

4. Excluduntur phrenetici, energumeni, arreptitij, obsessi, furiosi & similes, sed itidem cum luculentâ hâc exceptione: si nimirùm eâ facultate destituuntur, ut rectâ discretione inter hunc & alios cibos se cernere, & seipsos etiam probare, aut dijudicare non possint, an in fide sint. Cæterùm in quibus vis mali non est continua: sed lucida habet intervalla, & non obstant impedimenta aut pericula alia, ut vomitus, vel ejectiones per sputum, vel similia: tùm his turò, imò utiliter etiam quandoque Sacramentum hoc exhibetur.

5. Excluduntur etiam persona infames, quales sunt, quæ ejusmodi exercitijs sive artibus suam navant operam, quæ sine mortali peccato exerceri, & cum gratiâ DEI stare non possunt: quales sunt Magi, lenones, publica scorta, sive meretrices, usurarij, pugiles, sive athletæ illi, qui de vitâ & sangvine certant. Hi quamdiu illicitis istis rebus se non abdicant, ad usum Eucharistiæ non sunt admittendi: & post abdicationem etiam aliter non sunt admittendi, nisi vel publicam priùs egerint pœnitentiam, vel abdicationis hujus publica aliqua significatio, Ecclesiæ fidelium priùs innotuerit. Notandum verò est, lictores & carnifices, propter ipsum vitæ genus, si personalia delicta non superveniant, pro personis infamibus hoc casu & respectu nullatenùs esse habendos.

6. Excluduntur etiam abstemij, sed non simpliciter omnes: id quod B. Lutherus hunc in modū declaravit: Si qui ita à vino abhorreant, ut sine periculo, vomitus aut valetudinis, ne guttulam quidem gustare, aut odorem ipsum viniferre possint: tutius est, ut ab hujus Sacramenti usu penitùs abstineant, quàm sub unâ saltem specie Sacramentum ipsis administretur. Ratio allegatur ea, quia & mutilatio Sacramenti, sine reatu Sacrilegij locum non habeat: & defectus naturalis, à culpâ contemtus, sufficienter excuset. Non enim privatio, sed contemtus duntaxat Sacramenti, est damnabilis. His ergò partim Augustini illud, Crede & mãducasti: hoc est, spiritualis illa, quæ Joh. 6. extat, manducatio firmiùs inculcabitur: partim illud injungetur, ut celebrationi hujus mysterij saltem spectatores adsint frequentiores, quo precibǫ & suspirijs eorundem vota publica conjuncta, confirmandæ fidei efficaciam majorem præstent.

Octavò quæritur: An admittendi sint, qui non prius confessionem suam coram Ministro ediderunt? Romanenses negativam per omnia tenent, ut sic aliquo modo suffulciant dogma de auriculari confessione: de quâ suo loco, in articulo de Pœnitentiâ, agendum fuerit. Nos respondemus per distinctionem: Ubi in Ecclesiâ aliquâ publicæ confessionis ritus usu est receptǫ, non temerè ille negligi aut contemni debet: Siquidem secundum præceptum Apostoli: multa interdum licent, sed non omnia ædificant. Ne ergò offendantur infirmiores, satiùs est, strictè observare ritum Ecclesiæ, ut priùs S. Cœnam non accedas, quàm coram Ministro confessionem edideris. Quanquam si certas & evidentes ob causas, & sine ullo scandalo, illud intermittatur, non proptereà aliquis ab usu S. Cœnæ arceri debet. Quemadmodum B. Lutherus de seipso testatur, quòd aliquoties non confessus, (ut loquuntur) S. Cœnâ usus sit, ut vel hoc pacto demonstraret, confessionem illam publicam non esse absolutæ necessitatis. Ubi verò ritus iste non est in usu, ibi quæstio etiam hæc locum non habet.

Nonò quæritur de Mutis, An hi admittendi sint, nec ne? Ad quam quæstionem sic B. Lutherus, Tom. 1. G. p. 339. in Serm. de Novo Testamēto, Anno 1520. habito, respondet: Quidam putant, blandè decipiendos esse mutos porrectione hostiæ non consecratæ. Hic jocus non est bonus: nequè placebit DEO, qui illos æquè atquè nos, Christianos fecit, & habent idèm jus, quod nos habemus. Quamobrem si mentis sunt compotes, & ex certis signis observari potest, quòd verâ & piâ devotione desiderent Sacramentum, sicut sæpè vidi sinamus Spiritui Sancto suum officium, & opus, & non denegemus muto, quod postulat. Potest fieri, ut intus majorem scientiam, & fidem habeat, quàm nos, cui nemo temerè se opponat.

Decimò quæritur, An S. Cœna danda illis, qui capitali supplicio sunt afficiendi? Sub & in Papatu hoc simpliciter negatum fuit. Reclamavit autem Ecclesia impietati huic in Concilio Moguntinensi cap. 27. his verbis: Si omnibus depeccatis suis puram confessionem agentibus & dignè pœnitentibus, Communio in fine, secundum Canonicum jussum, danda est: Cur non eis, qui pro peccatis suis pœnam extremam persolvunt. Hinc ibidem decretum & permissum est, posse fures à patibulo ad templa deferri, oblationes pro eis offerri, & Missas celebrari; si antè confessi sint, & absolutionem acceperint. In Ecclesiis ergò Evangelicis pro piaculo minimè habetur, si supplicatio capitali destinatis, verè tamen pœnitentibus, & id flagitantibus, Sacramentum Eucharistiæ dispensetur.

Undecimò quæritur, An infirmis & ægrotantibus S. Cœnam in privatis ædibus administrare liceat? Respondemus affirmatè ex Canone 12. Concilij Niceni, cum hâc admonitione, ut nimirùm minister circumspectè hâc in parte agat, & infirmi sive ægri rationem habeat. Nam sic cum firmâ uteretur valetudine, Sacramenti hujus usum talis neglexit: utiq; etiam petenti non dandum illud est, nisi concionibus legalibus fractus & consternatus, veræ pœnitentiæ signa ediderit. Deindè neque tali infirmo porrigenda est S. Cœna, qui usum sacri hujus epuli tàm diu distulit, ut jam & linguæ & sensuum beneficio destitutus, neque peccata sua confiteri, neque Corpus Domini dijudicare, neque seipsum probare possit. Interim detestamur eum morem atque consuetudinem, quâ sub Papatu defertur hostia jampridem consecrata, & in templi sacrario conservata, cum luminib9 & tintinnabulo per plateas ad ædes ægroti: somniantes, se non posse consecrare Eucharistiam, nisi in alteri consecrato: & CHRISTI Corpus etiam extra usum, sub Pane, vel in Pane contineri. Detestamur etiam μωροσoφiαν Sacramentariorum, Privatam hanc communionem simpliciter, sed sine ullâ evidenti causâ damnantium.

Duodecimò ac postremò quæritur, Quid statuendum de vasis argenteis & inauratis, de aris lapideis, de vestibus missalibus, dequè rebus alijs circa actionem Eucharisticam usitatis? Respondeo, Hæc omnia constanter retineri in nostris Ecclesijs, non ex aliquâ necessitate nedùm cultu aliquo: sed ex libertate Christianâ, quæ, ut circa actionem Eucharisticam omni non modò εὐτάκτως, sed & ευσχημόνως peragerentur, usum vasorum istorum, & vestium introduxit, eumque sine ullâ superstitione etiamnum retinet:

neque videt causam ullam evidentem, propter quam in gratiam Sacramentariorum illa mutari debeant. Si enim in altari ideò nefas est Sacramentum administrare, quia Judaizare, ac papizare hoc videtur; certè neque templis ampliùs uti licebit, aut campanis, aut libris, qui itidem Papatui idololatrico inservierunt. Quid, quòd CHRISTUS non legitur ad mensam assedisse, & Cœnam distribuisse, sed discubuisse pro more gentis Judææ. Ergò removendæ etiam erunt mensæ Sacramentariæ, & ab humi tantùm discumbentibus S. Cœna fuerit celebranda: Deindè frivolum & nugatorium est, quòd scriptitant, Altaria non nisi sacrificiis esse destinata. Abrahamus certè DEO altare extruxisse legitur, Gen. 12, 7. non ad sacrificandum, sed ad monimentum & signum divinæ apparitionis. Sic Filii Ruben altare erexerunt, non ad sacrificandum, sed in memoriam miraculosæ liberationis, & traductionis. Sic nobis Christianis sunt altaria, non quidem Levitica, non ad externa Sacrificia immolanda: sed ad offerenda sacrificia Evangelica & Spiritualia labiorum confitentium nomini Domini, & in memoriam Sacrificij CHRISTI in arâ crucis peracti. Neque hîc vel de materiâ, vel formâ externâ, cuiquam litem movemus. Sive enim lignea sint, sive lapidea, perindè nobis fuerit, nullam in neutro necessitatis legem statuentes: quin nec mensæ nomen, præcipuè si sacra vocetur, repudiantes: quin & hanc cum piâ Antiquitate Altare nominantes.

Concludimus tandem verbis Augustini ex Epist. 118. ad Januarium: Totum illud genus rerum liberas habet observationes, nec disciplina ulla est in his melior gravi prudentique Christiano, quàm ut eo modo agat, quo agere viderit Ecclesiam, ad quamcunque fortè devenerit. Quod enim neque contra fidem, neque contra bonos mores injungitur, indifferenter est habendum, & pro eorum, inter quos vivitur, societate servandum est.


### Chapter Five and Last. On the Horrible Errors of the Pontiffs concerning the Sacrament of the Eucharist

The errors of the Papists partly strike at the very substance of this Sacrament: but partly at its proper use, sanctioned by CHRIST himself in express words.

Regarding the errors of the former kind, first there presents itself the MUTILATION OF THE SACRAMENT, which they call COMMUNION UNDER ONE

KIND. This was introduced by the Romanists in the Year of our Lord 1415, in the Council of Constance, where a decree was made concerning keeping the Laity from the use of the Chalice in this manner, Sess. 13. Although CHRIST after the Supper instituted, and administered to his disciples, this venerable Sacrament under both kinds, of Bread and Wine: and although in the primitive Church this kind of Sacrament was received by the faithful under both kinds: afterwards it is received by those consecrating under both, and by the Laity under the kind of bread only: NEVERTHELESS, NOTWITHSTANDING THIS, the authority of the sacred Canons, and the approved custom of the Church, has kept and keeps that this kind of Sacrament be dispensed under one kind only, to avoid certain dangers and scandals. We command therefore under pain of excommunication, that no Priest communicate the people under both kinds of bread and wine. But those dangers which underlie the distribution of the chalice, Johannes Gerson, not the least part of that Council, recounts as such in his treatise on the Communion of the Laity: 1. Of spilling. 2. Of the soiling of vessels. 3. Of carrying from place to place: 4. Of adhesion in the beards of the Laity. 5. Of preservation for the sick, especially in summer time, because of drinkers and flies. 6. Of costliness, at least in those places where wine is bought dearly. 7. Of freezing. 8. Of false belief, and that in many ways. 1. that the dignity of the Laity, regarding the reception of the Sacrament, would be as great as that of Priests: 2. that the Roman Church would not think rightly about the Sacrament: and that the Council of Constance erred in faith, and good morals, and the like.

Moreover, these individual reasons are worthy of explosion rather than refutation: since they are derived partly from the fictitious figment of Transmutation, as if wine by the force of the recitation of the words of consecration is essentially changed into the very blood of CHRIST: but partly from that absurd delirium of concomitance, by which they pretend that the Body is not the Blood: so that just as the Body of CHRIST is not naturally without Blood: so also Sacramentally the same Body cannot be perceived, unless the Blood of CHRIST is perceived at the same time. But from the mode of natural presence, the consequence does not hold for the mode of Sacramental perception, since that depends not on the condition of human nature in CHRIST: but on a singular ordination and disposition, which promises and destines the Sacramental perception of the blood of CHRIST not to Bread: but only to Wine.

We therefore overwhelm this sacrilegious decree of the Romanists with these reasons, nay, we thoroughly undermine and overturn it.

I. CHRIST did not institute two, but One Sacrament, and that common to all, and not halved, but entire, and absolute and perfect in its essential parts. The evidence of this reasoning is demonstrated, according to all its parts, from the words of the Institution. For when one Sacrament was abrogated, namely the Paschal Lamb, the Saviour willed that not Sacraments or Testaments in the plural, but a Testament in the singular be substituted. Then concerning the cup He expressed this specifically: Drink from this all of you, so that he might show that from the use of the Cup especially, no one is to be excluded. But in order to show that the condition of the Cup under this mystery is not different from the prior species, namely, the Bread: it is read that after the distribution of the blessed bread, he took the cup IN LIKE MANNER, and offered the same under an equal condition: it would therefore be a crime to attribute to one and the same mystery a plurality, or to its integrity a mutilation, or to the Communicant a segregation.

II. The use of the entire Sacrament, commonly employed by all, after the ascension of CHRIST to the heavens, throughout the entire course of fourteen centuries or centuries, was religiously and conveniently observed either in all, or at least in many places of the whole Christian world. From this it is inferred that the same rite could have been, and indeed even ought to have been, observed in the times of all the remaining centuries as well. The antecedent is proven by an induction of examples. Paul refers the Corinthian Church, consisting for the most part of Laity, to the original institution of the Supper. From the subsequent antiquity closest to Cyprian, he writes in book 2, epistle 3: If it is not permitted to loosen even the least of the Lord's commands: how much more is it not right to infringe upon such great, such grand things, which pertain to the very Sacrament of the Lord's passion and our redemption, or to change them by human tradition into something other than what was divinely instituted. And Chrysost. Homily 18 on 2 Corinthians: There is a time when the Priest differs nothing from the Layman, as when the sacred mysteries are to be used: For we are all held worthy to participate in these things in like manner. And not as in the time of the Old Testament, where the Priest ate some things, and the people others: but now one Body and one cup is set before all. Pope Gelasius writes thus to Bishops Majoricus and John, in part 3 of the decree, dist. 2: We have discovered that some, having taken only a portion of the body, abstain from the Cup of the sacred blood: who without doubt (I know not by what superstition they are taught to be constrained) should either receive the entire Sacraments, or be kept away from the entire ones: Because the division of one and the same mystery cannot come about without great sacrilege. What? That this use prevailed even in the times of Thomas Aquinas, that question shows, by which part 3, quest. 8, art. 12, he asks, Whether it is permitted to take the Body of the Lord without the blood: He answers affirmatively with this added reason: If this were not permitted, it would be against the use of many Churches, in which the Body of CHRIST is given to the communicating people to be taken: but not the blood. And soon he says: In some Churches it is observed that the blood is not given to the people to be taken. From which it is clear that the contrary rite still prevailed in most Churches at that time as well.

III. CHRIST did not permit the Church the freedom to distribute either one or both species of the Sacrament to the Laity: but he bound this by a mandate of necessity, so that the distribution of the entire Sacrament might take place. Not only that which the Evangelist noted pertains here, Drink from this all of you: but also that which the Apostle expressed, Do this, as often as you drink, in remembrance of me. But if the Papists were to maintain most strongly that the use of the Cup promised by CHRIST was a matter of indifference: they would nevertheless not escape the mark of impiety, who decree that what CHRIST willed to be free and indifferent is absolutely necessary, and indeed under the threat of anathema.

IV. The thing itself does not permit that it should be in any way lawful to inflict this mutilation upon this mystery. For 1. whose power it is to establish the Sacraments themselves, his alone it is to change and mutilate them in their essentials. But that is not the power of any but the divine. Therefore human power, whatever it may be, can in no way claim this for itself. But the species of the Blood of CHRIST pertains to the essentials of the Sacrament of the Eucharist. 2. If the laws of human testaments are inviolable, as Paul testifies, Gal. 3:15, much more will this right apply to a divine Testament, such as this Eucharistic Sacrament is. 3. The public goods of the Church are indifferently common to all, whom a peculiar inability does not exclude. For in Christ there is no slave or free, male or female, or any distinction of any order whatsoever: but we are all one in CHRIST JESUS, Gal. 3:28. But the Sacraments are in that class of goods in which the holy communion of the Church intervenes. It is therefore a crime to invent some distinction of men regarding the communion of these Sacramental goods: or to attribute some singular prerogative to one order of men.

V. And the final reason: The promise which the Savior willed to be annexed to the Communion of the Cup is universal, in these words: This Cup is the New Testament in my Blood, which is poured out for you for the remission of sins. It would therefore be sacrilege to despoil the Laity of the communion of the Blood of CHRIST, whom nevertheless no one, unless prodigiously absurd and impious, would have dared to keep away from the communion of the New Testament, and the sealing of the remission of sins: and consequently, If the promise of the New Testament pertains to the Laity, the sealing of the same, which is through the participation of the Blood of CHRIST, will also pertain to them.

Latin:

ERrores Pontificiorum partim impingunt in ipsam Sacramenti hujus substantiam: partim verò in proprium ejus, & à CHRISTO ipso expressis verbis sancitum usum.

Quoad prioris generis errores, primùm se offert MUTILATIO SACRAMENTI, quam vocant COMMUNIONEM SUB UNA

SPECIE. Introducta est haec à Romanensibus Anno Domini 1415. in Concilio Constantiensi, ubi decretum factum est, de Laicis ab usu Calicis arcendis in hunc modum Sess. 13. Licet CHRISTUS post Cœnam instituerit, & suis discipulis administraverit, sub utrâq; specie, Panis & Vini, hoc venerabile Sacramentum: & licet in primitivâ Ecclesia hujusmodi Sacramentum reciperetur à fidelibus sub utrâquè specie: posteà à conscientibus sub utrâquè, & à Laicis sub specie panis tantummodò suscipitur: TAMEN HOC NON OBSTANTE, sacrorum Canonum autoritas laudabilis, & approbata consuetudo Ecclesia servavit, & servat, quòd hujusmodi Sacramentum sub unâ tantum specie dispensetur, ad evitanda aliqua pericula & scandala. Præcipimus ergò sub pœnâ excommunicationis, quod nullus Presbyter communicet populum sub utrâquè specie panis & vini. Pericula autē illa, quæ subsunt distributioni calicis, Johannes Gerson, pars illius Concilij nõ postrema, in tractatu de Communione Laicorum talia recenset: 1. Effusionis. 2. Vasorum sordidationis, 3. Deportationis de loco ad locum: 4. Adhæsionis in barbis Laicorum. 5. Asservationis pro infirmis, præcipuè tempore æstivo, propter bibiones & muscas. 6. Sumtuositatis, saltem in illis locis, ubi vinum carè comparatur. 7. Congelationis. 8. Falsæ credulitatis, idq; multipliciter. 1. quod tanta esset dignitas Laicorum, circa sumtionem Sacramenti, quanta est Sacerdotum: 2. quòd Ecclesia Romana non ritè sentiret de Sacramento: & quòd Concilium Constantiense erraverit in fide, & bonis moribus, & similia.

Cæterùm explosione magis, quàm refutatione dignæ sunt hæ rationes singulæ: quippè petitæ partim ex fictitio Transmutationis commento, quasi vinum vi recitationis verborum consecrationis essentialiter mutetur in ipsum sangvinem CHRISTI: partim verò ex absurdo illo concomitantiæ delirio, quo fingunt, Corpus non esse Sangvinem: ita ut quemadmodum Corpus CHRISTI naturaliter non est sine Sangvine: ita Sacramentaliter quoque idem Corpus non possit percipi, nisi simul percipiatur Sangvis CHRISTI. Atqui ex modo præsentiæ naturali, non valet consequentia ad modum perceptionis Sacramentalis, quippè qui nõ à conditione humanæ naturæ in CHRISTO: sed à singulari ordinatione & dispositione dependet, quæ perceptionem sangvinis CHRISTI Sacramentalem non Pani: sed tantum Vino promittit & destinat.

Nos proindè Sacrilegium hoc decretum Romanensium his rationibus obruimus, imò penitùs subruimus, & evertimus.

I. CHRISTUS non duo, sed Unum, idque commune omnibus, neque dimidiatum, sed integrum, & partibus suis essentialibus absolutum & perfectum Sacramentum instituit. Demonstratur rationis hujus evidentia, secundum omnes partes, ex verbis Institutionis. Nam Uni Sacramento abrogato, Agno Paschali scilicet, non Sacramenta aut Testamenta pluraliter: sed Testamentum singulariter surrogatum voluit Servator. Deindè de calice speciatim hoc expressit: Bibite ex hoc omnes, ut fic à Calicis præcipuè usu, neminem excludendum esse, ostenderet. Ut autem Calicis sub hoc mysterio conditionem, à priori specie, Panis, videlicet, non esse dissimilem monstraret: post benedicti panis dispensationem CONSIMILITER calicem sumsisse, & pari conditione eundem porrexisse, legitur: Nefas proindè fuerit, vel uni & eidem mysterio pluralitatem: vel integritati mutilationem: vel Communicati segregationem affingere.

II. Integri Sacramenti usus, ab omnibus communiter adhibitus, post ascensionem CHRISTI ad cœlos, toto quatuordecim seculorum sive centuriarum decursu, aut in omnibus, aut pluribus saltem locis totius orbis Christiani religiosè & commodè observatus fuit. Hinc infertur potuisse, imò verò debuisse etiam, eundem ritum reliquorum etiam seculorum temporibus omnibus observari. Antecedens probatur inductione exemplorum. Paulus Ecclesiâ Corinthiacam parte maximâ ex Laicis constantem, ad primam Cœnæ institutionem remittit. Ex subsequente antiquitate proximâ Cypriano scrib. l. 2. epist 3. Si nec minima de mandatis Domini licet solvere: quantò magis tàm magna, tam grandia, tam ad ipsum Dominicæ passionis, & nostræ redemtionis Sacramentum pertinentia, fas non est infringere, aut in aliud, quàm quod divinitùs institutum est, humanâ traditione mutare. Et Chrysost. Homil. 18. in 2. ad Corinthios: Est ubi nihil differt Sacerdos à Laico, ut quando sacris utendum est mysteriis: Similiter enim omnes, ut ista participemus digni habemur. Et non sicut tempore Veteris Testamenti, quædam Sacerdos, quædam verò populus comedebat: sed nunc omnibus unum Corpus proponitur & unum poculum. Gelasius Papa Majorico & Johanni Episcopis, in parte 3. decreti dist. 2. sic scribit: Comperimus, quòd quidam sumtâ tantummodò corporis portione, à Calice sacrati cruoris abstineant: qui procul dubio (nescio qua superstitione doceatur adstringi) aut integra Sacramenta percipiant, aut ab integris arceantur: Quia divisio unius ejusdemq́; mysterij, sine grandi sacrilegio non potest provenire. Quid? quod temporibus etiam Thomæ Aquinatis, usus iste obtinuerit, quæstio illa ostendit, quâ part. 3. quæst. 8. art. 12. quærit, An liceat Corpus Domini sumere sine sangvine: Respondet autem affirmatè hâc additâ ratione: Si hoc non liceret, fore hoc contra multarum Ecclesiarum usum, in quibus populo communicanti datur Corpus CHRISTI sumendum: non autem sangvis. Et mox inquit: In quibusdam Ecclesijs observari, ut populo sangvis sumendus non detur. Ex quo patet, contrarium in plerisque Ecclesijs ritum, isto etiam tempore adhuc obtinuisse.

III. CHRISTUS liberum Ecclesiæ non permisit, ut vel unam, vel utramque Sacramenti speciem Laicis distribueret: sed necessitatis mandato hoc adstrinxit, ut integri Sacramenti fieret dispensatio. Pertinet huc non illud tantum, quod Evangelista annotavit, Bibite ex hoc omnes: sed & illud, quod Apostolus expressit, Facite hoc, quotiescunque biberitis, ad mei commemorationem. Quod si jam maximè Pontificij obtinerent, usum Calicis à CHRISTO promissum fuisse adiaphorum: notam tamen impietatis non effungerent, qui id, quod CHRISTUS liberum ac indifferens esse voluit, statuunt absolutè esse necessarium, & quidem sub anathematis interminatione.

IV. Res ipsa non permittit, ut mutilationem istam mysterio huic inferre ullo modo liceat. Nam 1. cujus potestatis est Sacramenta ipsa condere, ejus est solius, in essentialibus eadem mutare & mutilare. At non est illud, nisi divinæ. Ergò humana potestas, qualis qualis ea sit, sibi hoc vendicare nullo modo potest. Pertinet autem species Sangvinis CHRISTI ad essentialia Sacramenti Eucharistiæ. 2. Si jura testamentorum humanorum sunt inviolabilia, teste Paulo, Gal. 3, 15. Multò magis jus hoc divino Testamento conveniet, quale est Sacramentum hoc Eucharisticum. 3. Bona Ecclesiæ publica, indifferenter omnium sunt communia, quos peculiaris inhabilitas nõ excludit. Nam in Christo non est servus aut liber, mas aut fœmina, aut ullu cujuscunq; ordinis discrimen: sed omnes sumus unum in CHRISTO JESU, Gal. 3, 28. Atqui Sacramenta sunt in isto bonorum genere, in quo Ecclesiæ sancta communio intercedit. Nefas est ergò, discrimen aliquod hominum, quoad communionem istorum bonorum Sacramentalium comminisci: vel uni hominum ordini singularem aliquam prærogativam tribuere.

V. Et postrema ratio: Universalis est promissio, quam Communioni Calicis Servator annexam esse voluit, his verbis: Hic Calix Novum Testamentum est in meo Sangvine, qui pro vobis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Sacrilegium ergò fuerit, Laicos spoliare communione Sangvinis CHRISTI, quos tamen à communione Novi Testamenti, & obsignatione remissionis peccatorum, nemo, nisi prodigiosè abfurdus ac impius arcere ausus fuerit: & per consequens, Si ad Laicos pertinet promissio Novi Testamenti, ad eosdem etiam pertinebit obsignatio ejusdem, quæ sit per participationem Sangvinis CHRISTI.


### Chapter Five and Last. On the Horrible Errors of the Pontiffs concerning the…: On Transubstantiation

The other error of the Romanists, which strikes at the very substance of this Sacrament, is μετουσία, or Transubstantiation, a little older than the former error: but in impiety not inferior. For it was devised originally in that Lateran Council, which was celebrated more than four hundred years ago, under Innocent III, in which it is read to have been defined thus in the Decretals, lib. 1, cap. Firmiter credimus, that the Body and Blood of CHRIST are truly contained in the Sacrament of the Altar, under the species of bread and wine, the bread being transubstantiated into the Body, and the wine into the Blood of CHRIST, by divine power. Which words indeed seem to sound as if, for the sake of retaining and defending the sounder doctrine concerning the true and real presence, exhibition, and taking of the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Sacrament of the Supper, the figment of this dogma was introduced, or rather, as it were, brought in by necessity.

But the writings of the Papists testify to the contrary, especially those in which they themselves more freely open and explain this mystery of iniquity: having brought forward these causes in particular: 1. Lest any substance other than the Flesh of CHRIST be adored in the Sacrament of the altar. 2. Lest anything other than the same substance of the Flesh of Christ be offered to GOD the Father in the Sacrament. 3. That the durable presence of the Body of Christ in the Sacrament of the altar may be obtained even outside of its use. This, therefore, is that Delilah, for the painting and coloring of whom allurements had to be drawn from the fiction of this dogma. From this mystery alone it is clear how much impiety is contained in this dogma. To the increase of which, no small moment is added by the circumstance of time. For the time when this dogma was introduced into the Church was that time when, with the decline of purer Theology, a flood of all superstition and idolatry overwhelmed the Christian World in the Western Church.

Against this error, it must be held FIRST that the true and real presence of the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Supper can be retained and defended without this figment of Transubstantiation: and this most rightly from that which was treated above in chapters 1 and 2, the foundation of Sacramental Union. Therefore, just as Eutyches once viciously wished to infer the transmutation of the human nature into the divine from those words of Peter, 'You are CHRIST the son of the living GOD,' when rather the pronoun YOU and the name of CHRIST stand for the person, which consists of two natures: so the Papists falsely infer Transubstantiation from the words of CHRIST, 'This is my body.' For that THIS stands for two things, earthly and heavenly, which, being Sacramentally united, without substantial conversion, cause it to be said of the other, placed complexly, because of the most intimate Union, 'It is the Body of CHRIST.'

FURTHERMORE, it must also be noted and confessed that the Fathers of the Ancient Church did not indeed abhor the words of mutation and conversion, which they familiarly asserted to happen concerning the matter of the elements. But both their mind and their language were far more correct than those of the Papists. For they understood a Sacramental, not a substantial, mutation, by which it comes to pass that after consecration, the Bread and Wine, although they do not lose their nature and substance, are nevertheless no longer, as before, common elements: but are (in the very use itself) Sacramentally united with the heavenly thing, and are a tremendous mystery, that is, the Sacrament of the Eucharist. Moreover, they had such a regard for their own manner of speaking that, although they used the somewhat unusual words of conversion and mutation, they nevertheless abstained from the horrible word Transubstantiation: and at the same time they also explained the terms of their words in such a way that it was sufficiently clear that those senses were alien to impiety. I am pleased to make this attested by the example of that Gelasius, who was mentioned a little earlier. He writes in his book on the two natures in CHRIST against Eutyches and Nestorius, that the Bread and Wine of the Eucharist pass into the divine substance of the Body and

Blood of the Lord. Any Romanist dances and rejoices when these words are heard. But the same author is immediately the interpreter of his own words, saying that those elements pass into the divine substance in such a way that, 1. the bread and wine nevertheless remain in their own property of nature. 2. the substance or nature of the bread and wine does not cease. 3. with the addition, moreover, of the example of the natures in the person of CHRIST, which meanwhile both remain, although they come together to constitute one person. Similarly, Ambrose writes in his book on the Sacraments, book 4, chapter 4: 'If there is such power in the Word of the Lord Jesus that things began to be which were not: how much more operative is it that they should be what they were, and be changed into something else.' Here also Ambrose is the interpreter, because he says distinctly that they are indeed changed into something else, but yet in such a way that they are meanwhile what they were.

THIRD. It must also be observed that Scotus, Andradius, and some other Romanists expressly confess that no one can be compelled by the words of Scripture, nor by the symbols of faith, nor by the authority of the ancients, to embrace that dogma. Indeed, Scripture inclines to the completely opposite side. For CHRIST did not say: 'This shall be,' or 'Let this become my Body,' to imply transmutation: but to indicate the mystery of the Union, He said: 'This is my Body.' But the divine Apostle, 1 Cor. 10:16 and 1 Cor. 11:26, 27, 28, at least five times, even after Consecration, calls the Elements what they are, namely Bread and Wine. Nor is there any reason for the Papists to growl about the rod of Aaron in Exodus 7 and the Wine made from water in John 2, which rod and water are said to be such even after conversion, so that it is signified not what they are now, but what they were before conversion.
