For Scripture expressly testifies that a conversion took place in these examples. Which cannot be shown in the same way for the Elements in the Supper.

FOURTH, the writers of purer antiquity unanimously fight for the truth of our opinion. For that well-worn saying of Augustine holds thus: 'The word comes to the Element, and it becomes a Sacrament.' From which saying we argue thus: If the word comes to the Element, then certainly the abolition of the Element has no place: But the former is true. Therefore, the latter is also. Now Irenaeus, Augustine, and the whole of purer antiquity assert that this Sacrament consists of two things, the earthly and the heavenly, the visible species of the Elements, and the invisible flesh and Blood of CHRIST: indeed, by the most efficacious example of this mystery, they defended against the fury of Eutyches the τὸ ἄτρεπτον, τὸ ἀσύγχυτον, καὶ τὸ ἀμετάβλητον of the two natures in CHRIST, which Theodoret calls it in his Dialogues. From which we conclude thus: Either there will no longer be a Sacrament here, and it will be conceded that Eutyches was undeservedly condemned for heresy: or a substantial conversion of the elements is not to be posited. The former is impious: therefore, the latter must deservedly be eliminated.

Finally, Augustine again holds thus: 'If Sacraments did not have a likeness of those things of which they are Sacraments, they would not be Sacraments.' From this it is inferred thus: Either the analogy, which is sought in the Sacraments from the signification of the Elements, will cease, and consequently in Baptism also the water will be a transmuted element: or the conversion which is asserted in the Sacrament will be frivolous. Piety does not allow either of these to be felt. It remains, therefore, that this should rather be felt.

By way of a conclusion, that also must be noted, which the heretics, called Marcitae, according to the testimony of Augustine in his work on heresies, heresy 14, formerly maintained: that by words and incantations they change the wine, which is in the chalice, into the blood of Christ, and draw the grace of God into that very chalice. Epiphanius also mentions this heresy in book 1, tome 3, heresy 34, where he uses the word μετεσίας and rejects it as shameful. The Papists therefore have an argument from antiquity for cloaking this dogma, if they wish to use it.

Latin:

ALter Romanensium error, qui in ipsam Sacramenti hujus substantiam impingit, est μετουσία, sive Transubstantiationis, priore errore paulò antiquior: sed impietate haud inferior. Excogitatus enim ille primitùs in Concilio illo Lateranensi, quod ante annos quadringentos ampliùs est celebratum, sub Innocentio III. in quo sic definitum esse legitur in Decretalibus, lib. 1. cap. Firmiter credimus, Corpus, & Sangvinem CHRISTI, in Sacramento vel Alaris, sub speciebus panis, & vini veraciter contineri, Transsubstantiatis pane in Corpus, & vino in Sangvinem CHRISTI, potestate divina. Quæ quidem verba sic sonare videntur, quasi pro retinendâ & tuendâ saniori doctrinâ, de verâ & reali præsentiâ, exhibitione & sumtione Corporis & Sangvinis Dominici in Sacramento Cœnæ, figmentum hujus dogmatis introductum, imò necessitate quasi quandam invectum sit.

Verùm diversum testantur scripta Pontificiorum, ea præcipuè, in quibus liberiùs mysterium hoc iniquitatis ipsimet aperiunt, & explicant: his potissimùm causis in medium adductis: 1. Ne alia substantia, quàm Carnis CHRISTI, in Sacramento altaris adoretur. 2. ne aliud, quàm eadem substantia Carnis Christi, DEO Patri in Sacramento offeratur. 3. ut durabilis præsentia Corporis Christi in Sacramento altaris, etiam extra usum obtineatur. Hæc igitur est illa Dalila, cui pingendæ fucandæq; ex hujus dogmatis commento lenocinia fuerunt depromenda. Ex quo vel solo mysterio liquet, quantum in hoc dogmate impietatis insit. Cui augendæ ex circumstantiâ temporis non parum momenti accedit. Fuit autem dogmatis hujus in Ecclesiam invecti tempus illud, quo inclinatione purioris Theologiæ factâ, diluvium omnis superstitionis, & idololatriæ Orbem Christianum in Ecclesiâ Occidentali adobruit.

Contra hunc errorem tenendum PRIMO illud est, veram & realem præsentiam Corporis & Sangvinis Dominici in Cœnâ retineri & defendi posse, citra hoc Transubstantiationis figmentum: idque rectissimè ex eo, de quo suprà cap. 1. & 2. actum est, Sacramentalis Unionis fundamento. Quàm ergò vitiosè olim Eutyches humanæ naturæ transmutationem in divinam, ex illis verbis Petri, Tu es CHRISTUS filius DEI vivi, colligere voluit: cùm potiùs pronomen TU, & nomen CHRISTI pro personâ supponant, quæ duabus constat naturis: ita falsò colligunt Pontificij Transubstantiationem ex verbis CHRISTI, Hoc est Corpus meum. Nam illud HOC, pro duabus rebus supponit, terrenâ & cœlesti, quæ Sacramentaliter unitæ, sine conversione substantiali faciunt, ut de altero complexè posito, propter Unionem arctissimam dicatur, Esse Corpus CHRISTI.

DEINDE illud etiam notandum, & fatendum est, non abhorruisse quidem Veteris Ecclesiæ Patres, à mutationis & conversionis vocabulis, quam circa elementorum materiam fieri illi familiariter asseruerunt. Verùm & mens fuit ipsis, & lingva etiam, quàm Pontificijs, longè correctior. Nam Sacramentalem, non substantialem mutationem illi intellexerunt, quâ fiat, ut post consecrationem, Panis & Vinum, licèt naturam & substantiam suam non amittant, non tamen ampliùs, ut anteà sint vulgaria elementa: sed sint (in ipso tamen usu) cum re cœlesti Sacramentaliter unita, sint tremendum mysterium, hoc est, Eucharistiæ Sacramentum. Locutionis autem suæ eam rationem habuerunt, ut quamvis uterentur conversionis & mutationis, paulò insolentioribus vocibus: tamen ab horrido Transubstantiationis vocabulo abstinerent: & simul etiam terminos suorum verborum ita explicarent, ut ab impietate sensus illos fuisse alienos satis constaret. Libet hoc ipsum Gelasij illius, cujus paulò antè mentio est facta, exemplo testatum facere. Scribit ille lib. de duabus naturis in CHRISTO contra Eutychen & Nestorium, Panem & Vinum Eucharistiæ in divinam transire, Spiritu Sancto perficiente, substantiam Corporis &

Sanguinis Dominici. Tripudiat & gestit auditis hisce verbis Romanista quilibet. Sed idem autor statim ita suorum verborum est interpres, ut dicat, Sic elementa illa transire in divinam substantiam, 1. ut permaneat tamen panis & vinum in sua proprietate naturæ. 2. ut non desinat substantia vel natura panis & vini. 3 addito insuper exemplo naturarum in persona CHRISTI, quæ duæ interim permaneanr, licèt ad personam unam constituendam coëant. Similiter Ambrosius de Sacramentis lib. 4. c. 4. scribit: Si tanta est vis in Sermone Domini Jesu, ut inciperent esse, quæ non erant: quantò magis operatorius est, ut sint, quæ erant, & in aliud commutentur. Hîc etiam Ambrosius est interpres, quia distinctè dicit, commutari quidem in aliud, sed tamen sic, ut sint interim, quæ erant.

TERTIO. Illud etiam observandum est, quod Scotus, Andradius, & alij nonnulli Romanenses disertè fatentur, Nec verbis Scripturæ, nec symbolis fidei, nec veterum autoritate cogi quenquam posse, ut dogma istud amplectetur. Imò Scriptura in diversam planè partem inclinat. Non enim dixit CHRISTUS: Hoc erit, vel Hoc fiat Corpus meum, pro innuenda transmutatione: sed pro mysterio Unionis indicando dixit: Hoc est Corpus meum. Divus autem Apostolus 1. Cor. 10, 16. & 1. Cor. 11, 26. 27. 28. ut minimum quinquies, etiam post Consecrationem, Elementa id, quod sunt, Panem scilicet & Vinum appellat. Neq; est, quod de virga Aaronis Exod. 7. & de Vino ex aqua facto Johan. 2. ogganniant Pontificij, quæ virga & aqua dicantur etiam post conversionem, ut significetur, non quid jam sint, sed quid ante conversionem fuerint. Nam in his exemplis conversionem factam esse, Scriptura disertè testatur. Quod Elementis in Cœna non itidem monstrari potest.

QUARTO purioris antiquitatis Scriptores, pro nostræ sententiæ veritate unanimiter militant. Sic enim habet tritum illud Augustini: Accedit verbum ad Elementum, & fit Sacramentum. Ex quo dicto sic argumentamur: Si verbi fit accessus ad Elementum, utique Elementi abolitio non habet locum: At verum prius. Ergò & posterius. Jam Irenæus, Augustinus, totaque purior antiquitas asserit, Sacramentum hoc duabus rebus constare, terrena & cœlesti, visibili Elementorum specie, & invisibili CHRISTI carne & Sanguine: imò hujus mysterij efficacissimo exemplo, contra Eutychetis furorem, duarum in CHRISTO naturarum τὸ ἄτρεπτον, τὸ ἀσύγχυτον, καὶ τὸ ἀμετάβλητον, quod appellat in suis Dialogis Theodoretes, propugnarunt. Ex quo sic colligimus: Aut Sacramentum hic non erit amplius, & Eutychetem immeritò hæreje s fuisse damnatum concedetur: aut non est statuenda elementorum substantialis conversio. Illud impium est: Hæc igitur meritò eliminan da est.

Tandem iterum Augustinus ita habet: Si Sacramenta earum rerum, quarum sunt Sacramenta similitudinem non haberent, Sacramenta non essent. Indè sic infertur: Aut desinet analogia, quæ in Sacramentis ex Elementorum significatione petitur, & consequenter in Baptismo etiam aqua elementum transmutabitur: aut frivola erit, quæ in Sacramento cõversio asseritur. Istorum neutrum sentire pietas permittit. Hoc ergo potius sentiendum esse relinquitur.

Coronidis vice illud etiam notandum, quod haeretici, Marcitae dicti, teste Augustino de haeresibus, haeresi 14. olim statuebant, Verbis & incantationibus Vinum, quod est in calice, se mutare in Sangvinem CHRISTI, & gratiam DEI in illum Ipsum Calicem deducere. Cujus haeresis meminit etiam Epiphanius lib. 1. Tom. 3. haeresi 34. Ubi μετεσίας voce utitur, eamq; ceu turpem rejicit. Habent ergo Pontificij Antiquitatis argumentum, pro hoc dogmate palliendo, si eo uti velint.


### Chapter Five and Last. On the Horrible Errors of the Pontiffs concerning the…: On the Mixing of Wine with Water

A third error can be established, in that they insist that Eucharistic wine must be mixed with water: and they do not leave this to the freedom of the Church, but wish it to be observed under a law of necessity: although they add some limitation, namely that this mixing must be done in such a way that the species of wine is not dissolved. Thus, the water with which the wine is mixed must not be artificial water, but simple and elemental. And the Council of Trent did not hesitate to fortify this rite even with an anathema: Sess. 6, cap. 7, can. 9, which reads as follows: If anyone shall say that water is not to be mixed with wine in the chalice to be offered, let him be anathema. However, Epiphanius reports, Tome 1, book 2, heresy 47, that there were heretics called Encratites, who, having utterly condemned the use of wine in the Sacrament of the Eucharist, substituted the element of water: whence they were called Aquarians by the Church. Whether the Romanist Semiaquarians are any better than these is not without reason doubted. For it is the same sacrilege either to abolish an element entirely or to mix it with another, and indeed under a law of absolute necessity. Both strike enormously at the very substance of this Sacrament. For the promise of sacramental union with the blood of Christ was made by Christ not to pure water, nor to water mixed with wine, but to pure and simple wine, or as Luke has it, the fruit of the vine.

The Romanists object: 1. That Christ himself used diluted wine in the institution of the Supper. 2. That this custom was always observed in the primitive Church. 3. That by this rite the union of the faithful people themselves with their head, Christ, is represented. But these individual reasons are destitute of a certain proof, and therefore they conclude nothing certain either. For as regards the first, although it may perhaps be conceded that in Eastern regions, where very strong wines were produced, this mixing or tempering was accepted by custom: yet the Romanists have not yet demonstrated that the Savior either mixed it with water himself, or used it for this Sacrament having been mixed by another beforehand. The authority of Luke is stronger for us, who expressly testifies that He used the fruit of the vine. 2. Even if Christ had used such wine to the greatest extent, it is nowhere read, however, that He gave any commandment, either that wine so tempered must necessarily always be used; or that this mixing must be done by the ministers or priests in the Consecration itself.

As regards the second reason, we by no means deny that in the primitive Church, in certain places, the Lord's Supper was dispensed with wine tempered somewhat with water: but that this was observed under any law of necessity, or under the rationale of a divine commandment, that we most steadfastly deny. They had other far more serious causes and reasons for this act of theirs, of which this was perhaps not the last, that they might thus meet the outcries and calumnies of the Gentiles by the very act, for whom it was customary to harass Christians all the more odiously for the very reason that they celebrated the Lord's Supper merely for the sake of satisfying gluttony or drunkenness. Which calumny seemed of such importance to many of the faithful that, sinning in excess, they would use pure and mere water in the Eucharist: whom, however, Cyprian rightly rebuked, and recalled to the form of the primitive institution of the Lord. But whatever the case may be, it is certainly manifest that this custom of mixing wine with water was not Catholic and Universal. The Greek Church, certainly, which is most Eastern, never wished to observe this rite, as is evident from the Council of Florence, and from Durandus, book 4, cap. 42. Indeed, also from Scotus, dist. 9, quest. 1, art. 6.

As regards the third reason, we are certainly not ignorant that Cyprian, book 3, Epistle 2, and Emissenus following him, wished to construct a certain allegory from this tempering of wine: using this argument above all, that blood and water flowed from the side of Christ: but water, according to John in the Apocalypse, denotes peoples: and therefore the mixing of water and wine figures the union of the faithful people with Christ. But those good Fathers were too liberal in inventing allegories. 2. An allegory by itself proves nothing, unless the thing itself is first demonstrated by the Scriptures. 3. To seek allegories and types in a matter manifest in itself: and, having neglected the most perspicuous words of institution, to wish to make a judgment concerning the substantials of the Sacrament from obscure, uncertain, and far-fetched allegories, is a sign of a great sickness of the Truth. 4. Scripture, when about to express the spiritual union of the faithful with Christ, knows nothing at all of this allegory: but illustrates it by a certain similitude, taken from the matrimonial union of one man and one woman: Eph. 5:28, etc. 5. The Romanists make themselves guilty of a double sacrilege: 1. That they despoil the laity of the use of the wine or chalice. 2. That they thus simultaneously despoil them of that means, or organ, by which they could be made more certain of that spiritual union of the people with Christ. 6. The water and blood, which flowed from the side of Christ, did not shadow forth this mixing, but, as pious antiquity attests, they shadowed forth the two Sacraments of the New Testament, Baptism and the Lord's Supper. 7. There is no nerve, no connection in this whole argument, which proceeds thus: The waters which were seen by John in Apocalypse 17:1 and 15 denoted many peoples. Therefore, Eucharistic wine must be diluted with water so that the union of the faithful with Christ may be prefigured. 8. Finally because in allegories the Romanists delight, we propose to them the sermon of Isaiah chapter 1, 21, 22, which is as follows: Your silver is turned into dross: Your wine is mixed with water: How is the faithful city become a harlot? Now because an excellent analogy exists between the now Roman Church and the Babylonian harlot, it will not be difficult for the Romanists to construct an excellent allegory also from the comparison of diluted wine with the harlot, of whom the Prophet speaks. Thus far we have briefly touched upon the errors of the Romanists, which strike at the very substance of the Sacrament. Two others remain, which however concern not the substance, but rather the use of this Sacrament: the former of which is Adoration: the latter indeed Reservation and Circumgestation. Concerning both errors the Council of Trent is as follows: If any one shall say that, after the Consecration in the admirable Sacrament of the Eucharist, the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are not present, but only in use, while it is being received, or not before, or after, and that in the consecrated hosts or particles, which are preserved or remain after Communion, the true Body of the LORD does not remain, let him be anathema. Likewise: If any one has said that, in the Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist, CHRIST the only-begotten Son of God is not to be adored with the worship of latria, even external, to be venerated, and in processions according to the laudable and universal rite and custom of the Holy Church, and to be solemnly carried about: or not to be publicly proposed to the people to be adored, and that his adorers are Idolaters, let him be anathema. Item: If any one shall say that it is not lawful for the Holy Eucharist to be reserved in a shrine, but that it must necessarily be distributed to those standing by immediately after consecration: or that it is not lawful for it to be carried honorably to the sick, let him be anathema. We shall treat of both separately. And indeed regarding the former, we by no means deny that CHRIST, not only as GOD and Man, is to be affected with one true worship of adoration: but also that the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of CHRIST is to be followed with due veneration: and what Augustine said concerning Baptism, that the Baptism of CHRIST, wherever it is, is to be venerated; that we ingenuously profess concerning this Sacrament also. Nay, we also honor the word of GOD, and as Anastasius advises, we faithfully adore it. Finally, we venerate other things which in a similar way pertain to the religion of Christ. But just as we honor these things as sacred and instituted by CHRIST for our salvation, yet do not exhibit divine honor to them, as if to CHRIST himself, according to that which Ambrose wrote concerning the Magi: They knew this was the star which signified the man and GOD: but they adored the little child: So likewise we determine concerning this Sacrament. Nor can any precept of CHRIST be given, or example of the Apostles, nor even any opinion of the purer Antiquity, by which the adoration of the Sacrament is proven. And it was finally introduced in the Year of our Lord 1226 under Pope Honorius: but afterwards under Urban in the Year of our Lord 1264, strengthened by the addition of a new feast: at length under Clement V in the Year of our Lord 1310, in the Council of Vienne, this Idolatry was finally confirmed, which however the Asian and Greek Churches have not received to this very day. And the ineptitude is too childish, by which they conclude thus: The Body of CHRIST ought to be honored with divine honor. In the Sacrament is

The Body of Christ. Therefore the Sacrament ought to be affected with divine worship. For there are four terms in the argument: that which can be demonstrated by such an attempted collection: The Body of CHRIST is to be adored: but the Body of CHRIST is in Heaven. Therefore Heaven is to be adored. When rather the conclusion in both cases can only be inferred thus: Therefore the Body of CHRIST is to be adored even in the Sacrament, but not the Sacrament itself: And, the Body of CHRIST is to be adored even in Heaven, but not Heaven itself.

Some Fathers are indeed read, with a burning affection of devotion, to have addressed sacred mysteries in a figurative mode of speech more devoutly, as can be seen in Dionysius, who exclaims thus: O divine, deeply holy mystery: Which words Pachymeres the Greek Scholiast interprets thus: ὡς ἐμψύχω αὐτῇ διαλέγεται. Just as Gregory also exclaims: O great and holy Passover. Ambrose addresses the water of Baptism in this manner: O water which hast deserved to be the Sacrament of CHRIST. The Apostle Andrew is also read to have greeted the Cross, by whose martyrdom he was about to end his life, thus: Hail, O Cross, which standest here, having awaited me for so long: I approach gladly: For I know thy secret, I know thy mystery. I see in thee those things which are promised to me by my Lord. Receive me, O chosen cross, who am so wretched for the sake of GOD, and restore the miserable little servant to his Lord. But whoever wishes to elicit invocation and adoration from this, he will surely have denied reason along with piety altogether. Therefore, just as Theophilus once, when asked why he would not deem the Emperor worthy of divine honor according to the custom of that time, replied: Because he is not appointed for this, that he should be adored: but that he should be honored with legitimate honor. So, if we are asked about the Sacrament, we will reply that divine honor is not paid to it for this reason: Because it was not instituted that it should be adored: but that it should be received by holy and religious eating and drinking.

See the booklet of B. LUTHER written to the Waldensian brethren in Bohemia and Moravia: In the year 1523.

See also Peter Martyr, in the fourth class of Common Places, place 10, section 50. Where he concedes the adoration of this Sacrament in such a way that it is directed not to the Symbols themselves, which ought not to be adored: but to Him who is signified through the symbols: dissenting in this part from the remaining Calvinists, who do not deem this Sacrament worthy of even external genuflection.

The later error of the Romanists concerning the use of the Sacrament is Reservation in a canopy, and theatrical carrying about. Now, indeed, it cannot be denied at the beginning that in some places, and by some men, the Sacrament was formerly kept according to custom. Cyprian writes in Sermon 5 on the lapsed that women were accustomed to keep the Sacrament at home in caskets. Tertullian testifies that the faithful were accustomed to keep the Sacrament in private houses, and to taste it before other foods. Jerome reports that Exuperius of Toulouse was accustomed to carry the Eucharist in a wicker basket. Basil is the authority that in Egypt, especially around Alexandria, almost every individual had the Sacrament in his own home. Eusebius writes that a priest kept it in his bedchamber. Ambrose relates that men carried the Sacrament with them not only on land: but also at sea in handkerchiefs.

All these were abuses of the most sacred mysteries, introduced partly by the injury of time, partly by the private authority of men, which were later both corrected and removed from the Church by public authority. For thus Cyprian writes: This bread is received, not enclosed. Clement, whom some falsely claim to have been a companion of the Apostles, writes thus: As many burnt offerings are offered on the altar as ought to suffice for the people, and if any remain, they are not to be reserved for the morrow. Origen or Cyril (for the same book is inscribed with the name of each) says: The Lord did not delay the bread which He was giving to His disciples, nor did He order it to be kept until the morrow. Jerome says: After the Communion, whatever remained of the Sacrifices, they consumed together there in the Church, eating the common Supper. Augustine also seems to say the same: Bread made for this purpose is consumed in receiving the Sacrament. Hesychius testifies that the remains of the Sacrament were accustomed to be consumed by fire immediately. Nicephorus notes that those remains were in some places given to boys learning in schools, which they would eat immediately in the church. Almost the same thing was also decreed in the Council of Mâcon. Gabriel Biel also wrote thus: He did not give it to the disciples so that they might honorably preserve it, but He gave it for their use, saying: Take and eat. And although it is read that something of reservation was also done in public, the end and condition were very different. The witness is the letter of Chrysostom to Innocent, that the Sacrament was indeed reserved even at that time, but that it was reserved first in both kinds, and then so that it might be received in communion by the people immediately on the following day, or shortly after. And in Greece the custom prevailed that during Lent, consecration should take place only on Sundays and Saturdays, and the people would use the Sacrament thus consecrated on the remaining days, especially the excommunicated, if they were suddenly seized by illness and were in danger of life. But if there is nothing else, these are the dangers which ought to have rightly moved all pious men to abolish this rite of superstition. Formerly, when the Sacrament was kept in small boxes, napkins, or baskets in private homes, there was no danger of adoration. Now everything is so arranged to persuade the minds of superstitious men to this impiety, that the primary part of worship seems to be placed in this head. King Hezekiah therefore took away and crushed the bronze serpent, although GOD had explicitly commanded Moses to raise it up, because he saw that some were abusing it for idolatry. And yet a greater consideration of piety militates here against that abomination. I pass over external dangers, rust, mold, worm-eatenness, which are utterly unworthy of this most sacred mystery: but that they can not only happen, but have also frequently occurred, the Papists themselves do not deny. Alphonsus, King of Aragon, in order to protect his dignity and safety, is said to have carried the Sacrament with him for so long that it rotted and produced worms, which, as they devoured one another, at last only one larger worm remained, which had consumed all the others. The Lateran Council under Innocent III.

celebrated, Can. 20, admits that, with the Sacrament kept in this manner, some have sometimes abused it for detestable and wicked crimes. And because of some similar abuses, in the Third Council of Braga, the Reservation itself was in some part abolished. We give eternal thanks to the eternal and merciful GOD, that He has restored to our Churches the purity of this Article also, asserted both against these and any other profanations and errors: which, that He may preserve it unblemished until the end of the age, we supplicate and venerate His immense mercy with the most ardent prayer of our vows, through CHRIST JESUS: To whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be praise, glory, and adoration, for ages never to be ended. AMEN.

Latin:

Tertius error constitui potest, quod Vinum Eucharisticum Aqua permiscendum esse dictitant: idq; non liberum Ecclesiae relinquunt, sed sub necessitatis lege observari volunt: quanquam limitationem aliquam adjiciunt, nempe ita fieri debere mixtionem hanc, ut non folvatur vini species. Sic aquam, qua vinum miscetur, non debere esse aquam artificialem: sed simplicem & elementarem. Et hunc ritum Concilium Tridentinum anathemate etiam munire non dubitavit: Sess. 6 cap. 7. can. 9. qui sic habet: Si quis dixerit, aquam non miscendam esse vino in Calice offerendo, anathema sit. Refert autem Epiphanius, Tom. 1. lib. 2. haeresi 47. fuisse haereticos Encratitas, qui vini usu in Sacramento Evcharistiae penitus damnato, Aquae elementum substituerint: Unde ab Ecclesia Aquarij dicti sunt. His utrum meliores sint Semiaquarij Romanenses, haud immerito dubitatur. Ejusdem enim est Sacrilegij, Elementum vel integrum abolere, vel cum alio permiscere, & quidem sub absolutae necessitatis lege. Utrumq; in ipsam substantiam Sacramenti hujus enormiter impingit. Neq; enim vel Aquae purae vel Aquae vino permixtae, sed Vino puro ac simplici, sive uti Lucas habet, Genimini vitis facta est a CHRISTO promissio, de Sacramentali Unione cum sangvine CHRISTI.

Excipiunt Romanenses 1. CHRISTUM ipsum usum fuisse in institutione Coenae vino diluto. 2. In primitiva Ecclesia semper hunc morem fuisse observatum. 3. hoc ritu repraesentari, ipsius fidelis populi cum capite CHRISTO unionem. Sed destituuntur rationes hae singulae certo ελεγχω, ac proinde nihil etiam certi concludunt. Nam quoad primam, etsi fortassis concedi potest, in regionibus Orientalibus, ubi fortissima nascebantur vina, mixtionem hanc sive temperaturam usu fuisse receptam: nondum tamen Romanenses demonstratum dederunt, Servatorem vel ipsum unum aqua miscuisse, vel ab alio prius mixtum, ad Sacramentum hoc adhibuisse. Potior nobis est Lucae autoritas, qui ipsum Genimine vitis usum fuisse, diserte testatur. 2. Si vel maxime tali vino CHRISTUS usus fuisset, nuspiam tamen legitur, praeceptum aliquod dedisse, vel ut necessario vinum sic temperatum semper adhibeatur; vel ut haec mixtio fiat a ministris, sive Sacerdotibus in ipsa Consecratione.

Quoad alteram rationem, inficias minimè imus, in primitivâ Ecclesiâ quibusdam in locis, Cœnam Dominicam sub vino, aquâ nonnihil temperato, dispensatam fuisse: Verùm quòd hoc sub aliquâ necessitatis lege, aut sub ratione præcepti divini observatum fuerit, id constantissimè negamus. Habuerunt illi facti hujus sui causas & rationes alias longè gravissimas, quarum hæc fortè non fuit postrema, ut sic Gentilium clamoribus ac calumniis ipso facto obviam irent, quibus solenne erat, vel ideò odiosiùs exagitare Christianos, quod Cœnam Domini celebrent duntaxat gulæ sive ebrietatis explendæ gratia. Quæ calumnia tanti momenti visa fuit multis fidelium, ut in excessu peccantes, purâ ac merâ aquâ in Eucharistia uterentur: quos tamen Cyprianus rectè reprehendit, & ad formam primævæ institutionis Dominicæ revocavit. Sed quicquid sit, illud certè propalam constat, hunc etiam morem, miscendi aqua vinum, non fuisse Catholicum & Universalem. Græca certè Ecclesia, quæ maximè Orientalis est, nunquàm ritum hunc observare voluit, uti patet ex Concilio Florentino, & ex Durando lib. 4. cap. 42. Imò ex Scoto quoq; dict. 9. quæst. 1. art. 6.

Quoad tertiam rationem, haud sanè ignoramus, quòd Cyprianus lib. 3. Epist 2. & hunc secutus Emissenus, allegoriam quandam ex hâc vini temperaturâ extruere voluerint: hoc potissimùm usi argumento, quòd ex latere Christi profluxerit Sangvis & Aqua: Aqua verò secundum Johannem in Apocalypsi, denotet populos: ac proindè mixtio aquæ & vini, figuret Unionem populi fidelis cum Christo. Sed boni isti Patres in fingendis allegorijs nimis liberales fuerunt. 2. Allegoria per se nihil probat, nisi res ipsa Scripturis priùs demonstretur. 3. Allegorias & typos quærere in re per se manifestâ: & neglectis verbis institutionis maximè perspicuis, de Substantialibus Sacramenti, ex obscuris, incertis, & longius petitis allegorijs, judicium velle facere, signum est magnæ ἀῤῥωστίας τῆς Ἀληθείας. 4. Scriptura expressura Spiritualem Unionem fidelium cum Christo, nihil quicquam novit de hâc allegoriâ: sed similitudine quadam eam illustrat, petitâ ab Unione matrimonialis unius viri, & unius fœminæ: Eph. 5, 28. &c. 5. gemini Sacrilegij reos seipsos faciunt Romanenses: 1. quòd Laicos spoliant usu vini sive calicis. 2. quòd eosdem sic simul spoliant eo medio, sive organo, quo certiores reddi queant de Spirituali illâ Unione populi cum Christo. 6. Aqua & Sangvis, quæ fluxerunt ex latere Christi, non mixtionem hanc, sed attestante piâ Antiquitate, adumbrarunt duo Sacramenta Novi Testamenti, Baptismum & Cœnam Domini. 7. Nullus nervus, nullus nexus inest toti huic rationi, quæ sic procedit: Aquæ quæ fuerunt conspectæ à Johanne in Apocal. 17, 1. & 15. denotabant populos multos. Ergò vinum Eucharisticum ideò aquâ diluendum est, ut præfiguretur unio fidelium cum Christo. 8. Tandem quia allegorijs delectantur Romanenses, proponimus ipsis cocionem Jesaiæ cap. 1, 21, 22. quæ sic habet: Argentu tuum versum est in scoriam: Vinum tuum mixtum est aquâ: Quomodo facta est meretrix civitas fidelis? Jam quia Ecclesiæ nunc Romanæ egregia analogia intercedit cum meretrice Babylonicâ, haud difficile fuerit Romanensibus, egregiam etiam allegoriam extruere ex comparatione vini diluti, cum meretrice, de quâ agit Propheta. Hactenùs perstrinximus brevitèr errores Romanensium, impingentes in ipsam Sacramenti Substantiam. Supersunt duo alij, qui tamen non substantiam, sed Usum potiùs Sacramenti hujus concernunt: quorum prior est Adorationis: posterior verò Reservationis & Circumgestationis. De utroq; errore Concilium Tridentinũ sic habet: Si quis dixerit, peractâ Consecratione in admirabili Eucharistiæ Sacramento, non esse Corpus & Sangvinem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, sed tantùm in usu, dùm sumitur, aut non antè, vel post, & in hostijs seu particulis consecratis, quæ post Communicationem servantur, vel supersunt, non remanere verum Corpus DOMINI, anathema sit. Itè: Si quis dixit, In Sancto Eucharistiæ Sacramento, CHRISTUM unigenitũ Dei filiũ, non esse cultu latriæ etiã externo adorandũ, venerandũ, atq; in procesionibg secundum laudabilem & universalẽ Ecclesiæ Sanctæ ritum & consuetudinem & solenniter circumgestãdum: vel non publicè, ut adoretur populo proponendum, & ejus adoratores esse Idololatras, anathema sit. Item: Si quis dixerit, non licere Sacram Eucharistiam in Sacrario reservari, sed statim post consecrationem astantibus necessariò distribuendam: aut non licere, ut illa ad infirmos honorificè deferâtur, anathema sit. Nos de utroq; seorsim agem9. Et quidem quoad Priorem, minimè negamus, CHRISTUM non ut DEUM tantùm & Hominem, vero atq; uno adorationis cultu afficiendum esse: sed & Sacramentum Corporis atq; Sangvinis CHRISTI, veneratione debitâ prosequendum: & quod de Baptismo Augustinus dixit Baptismum CHRISTI, ubicunq; est, venerandum; id de hoc etiam Sacramento ingenuè profitemur. Quin & verbum DEI colimus, & ut Anastasius monet, fideliter adoramus. Deniq; res alias veneramur, quæ consimili ratione ad religionem Christi pertinent. Verùm quemadmodum res has ita colimus, ut sacras & à CHRISTO ad salutem nostram institutas, divinum autem illis, tanquàm CHRISTO ipsi, honorem non exhibemus, juxta illud, quod de Magis scripsit Ambrosius: Cognoverunt hanc stellam esse, quæ hominem DEUMq; signabat: sed adoraverunt parvulum: Ita pariter de hoc Sacramento nos statuimus. Neq; dari præceptum CHRISTI ullum, aut exemplum Apostolorum, neq; etiam purioris Antiquitatis sententia ulla potest, quâ Sacramenti adoratio probetur. Et est ea demùm Anno Domini 1226. sub Honorio Papa invecta: postea verò sub Urbano Anno Domini 1264. Novi festi accesfione roborata: tandem sub Clemente V. Anno D. 1310. in Concilio Viennensi demùm confirmata est hæc Idololatria, quam tamen Asianæ & Græcæ Ecclesiæ in hunc usq; diem non receperunt. Et nimis puerilis est ineptia, quâ sic colligunt: Corpus CHRISTI divino honore coli debet. In Sacramento est

Corpus Christi. Ergò Sacramentum divino cultu affici debet. Sunt enim quatuor termini in argumento : id quod tali inceptâ collectione demonstrari potest: CHRISTI Corpus est adorandum : atqui Corpus CHRISTI est in Cœlo. Ergò Cœlum est adorandum. Cum potiùs conclusio utrobiq; talis tantùm inferri possit : Ergò Corpus CHRISTI etiam in Sacramento, non verò Sacramentum ipsum : Et, Corpus CHRISTI etiam in Cœlo, non verò Cœlum ipsum est adorandum.

Leguntur quidem Patres aliqui, flagrante devotionis affectu, figuratò sermonis modo mysteria sacra compellasse devotiùs, ut videre est apud Dionysium, qui sic exclamat : O divinum penitùs sanctumq; mysterium: Quæ verba Pachymeres Scholiastes Græcus sic interpretatur. ὡς ἐμψύχω αὐτῇ διαλέγεται. Quomodo & Gregorius exclamat : O magnum & sanctum Pascha. Ambrosius aquam Baptismi ad hunc modum affatur: O aqua quæ Sacramentum esse CHRISTI meruisti. Andreas Apostolus Crucem etiam, cujus martyrio vitam finiturus erat, sic salutasse legitur: Salve crux quæ hic stas, tam diu me expectans: Lætus accedo: Novi enim tuum secretum, novi mysterium. Video in te, quæ mihi à Domino meo promittuntur. Recipe me, ô electa crux, qui tam sum milis propter DEUM, & redde miserum servulum suo Domino. Verùm hinc invocationem & adorationem elicere qui voluerit, næ ille rationem cum pietate, omnem prorsus abnegaverit. Proindè quemadmodum Theophilus olim rogato, cur Imperatorem pro more temporis illius, divino honore dignari nollet, respondit : Quia ad hoc non est constitutus, ut adoretur: sed ut legitimo honore honoretur. Ita Sacramento à nobis si rogemur, divinum honorem ideò non deferri respondebimus : Quia non sit institutum ut adoretur: sed ut sanctâ ac religiosâ manducatione & bibitione accipiatur.

Vide libellum B. LUTHERI ad fratres Waldenses in Bohemiâ, & Moraviâ scriptum: An. 1523.

Vide etiam Petrum Martyrem, classe quartâ Locor. Comm. loco 10. §. 50. Ubi adorationem Sacramenti hujus ita concedit, ut ea dirigatur non ad Symbola ipsa, quæ adorari non debeant : sed ad eum, qui per symbola significatur : dissentiens hac in parte à reliquis Calvinistis, qui Sacramentum hoc ne quidem externâ genuflexione dignantur.

Posterior Romanensiu circa usum Sacramenti error est Reservationis in Canopeo, & theatricæ circumgestationis. Jam verò initiò negari nõ potest, olim quibusdam in locis, & à quibusdam hominibus, Sacramentum ex more fuisse affervatum. Scribit Cyprianus Serm. 5. de lapsis, Mulieres domi in cistis servare Sacramentũ consuevisse. Tertullianus fideles in ædibus privatis custodire, atq; ante alios cibos gustare Sacramentũ solitos fuisse testatur. Hieronymus Exuperium Tolosanum in vimineo canistro Eucharistiã gestare consuevisse refert. Basilius autor est, in Ægypto, maximè circà Alexandriam, singulos ferè homines Sacramentum domi suæ habuisse. Eusebius Sacerdotem in cubiculo suo custodijsse scribit. Ambrosio homines Sacramentum unà secum non terrâ modò : sed mari etiam in sudarijs circumtulisse tradit.

Hi omnes sacratissimorum mysteriorum abusus fuerunt, temporum injuria partim, partim privatâ hominum autoritate invecti, qui & correcti postea & publica autoritate ex Ecclesia sublati fuerunt. Sic enim Cyprianus scribit: Panis iste recipitur, non includitur. Clemens, quem aliqui Apostolorum comitem fuisse mentiuntur, sic scribit: Tanta in altari holocausta offeruntur, quanta populo sufficere debeant, quo si remanserint, in crastinum non reserventur. Origenes seu Cyrillus (idem enim liber utriusq; nomine inscribitur) inquit: Dominus panem, quem discipulis suis dabat, non distulit, nec servari jussit in crastinum. Hieronymus ait: Post Communionem, quæcunq; de Sacrificijs superfuissent, illic in Ecclesia, communem Cœnam comedentes, pariter consumebant. Idem etiam dicere videtur Augustinus, Panis ad hoc factus, in accipiendo Sacramento consumitur. Hesychius Sacramenti reliquias igni statim consumi solitas fuisse testatur. Nicephorus eas reliquias quibusdam in locis, pueris in scholis discētibus datas fuisse, quas statim in Ecclesia comederent, annotat. Idem ferè etiam in Concilio Matisconensi sancitum fuit. Gabriel Biel sic etiam scripsit: Non dedit discipulis, ut ipsum honorificè conservarent: sed dedit in sui usum, dicens: Accipite & manducate. Et quamvis reservationis etiam in publico nonnihil esse factum legitur: finis tamen, & conditio fuit diversissima. Testis est Chrysostomi ad Innocentium epistola, reservatum quidem fuisse Sacramentum illo etiam tempore: sed utraq; specie primum reservatum esse: deinde, ut in communione à populo statim sequenti die, aut paulò post perciperetur. Et in Græcia mos obtinuit, ut durante Quadragesimâ, diebus duntaxat Dominicis & Sabbatis fieret consecratio, & Sacramento sic consecrato reliquis diebus populo uteretur, præcipuè excommunicati, si quando improviso morbo correpti, de vita periclitarentur. Quod si nihil aliud sit, pericula sunt, quæ ad hunc superstitionis ritum antiquandum, promovere pios quosq; meritò debebat. Olim cum in cistulis, sudorijs, canistris, privatis ædibus asservaretur Sacramentum, nullum fuit ab adoratione periculum. Nunc omnia ita sunt comparata ad impietatem hanc animis superstitiosorum hominum persuadendam, ut cultus pars primaria in hoc capite posita esse videatur. Serpentem æneum ideò sustulit & comminuit Rex Ezechias, licèt eundem erigere Moysi DEUS disertè manducaverat, quòd eo nonnullos abuti ad idololatriam videret. Atqui major hîc pietatis ratio contra abominationem istam militat. Taceo externa pericula, rubiginem, mucorem, vermiculationem, quæ sunt sacratissimo hoc mysterio planè indignissima: accidere autem non modò posse: sed & sæpenumerò contigisse, Pontificij ipsi non diffitentur. Alphonsus Arragonum Rex, ut dignitatem & incolumitatem suam tueretur, Sacramentum tamdiu secum circumtulisse perhibetur, donec id putresceret, vermesq; gigneret, quibus semutuò depascentibus, unus duntaxat ad extremum superfuit grandior vermis, qui cæteros omnes affumserat. Concilium Lateranense sub Innocentio III.

celebratum, Can. 20. fatetur, Sacramento ad hunc modum servato, nonnullos aliquando ad detectanda & nefaria facinora abusos esse. Et propter consimiles aliquos abusus in Concilio Braccarensi III. Reservatio ipsa quâdam ex parte sublata fuit. Nos æternas æterno & misericordi DEO gratias agimus, quòd hujus etiam Articuli puritatem tùm ab istis, tùm quibusvis alijs prophanationibus & erroribus assertam, nostris Ecclesiis restituit: quam ut ad finem usque seculi illibatam conservet, ardentissima votorum precatione, immensam ejus misericordiam, per CHRISTUM JESUM veneramur supplices: Cui cum Patre, & Spiritu Sancto, sit laus, gloria, & adoratio, seculis nunquam finiendis. AMEN.


## 22 On Sacrifices

Intending to dispute professionally concerning Sacrifices, I clearly maintain that not only useful, but also absolutely necessary labor can be expended in elucidating this Article of Christian doctrine by one who has spent some study and time on this subject. For since the people of GOD in the Old Testament placed the prow and stern, as it were, of divine worship, nay, of their own salvation, most especially in the rite of Sacrifices: and indeed most Nations established outside the Church have determined that their GODS are uniquely appeased by the offering of Sacrifices: And for this very end have been accustomed to offer Hecatombs, that is, one hundred oxen and sheep solemnly: Nay, even among the people of GOD themselves, many of the Jews long ago fostered clearly various and discrepant opinions concerning the use and effect of Sacrifices: and today in the New Testament not a few foster them; while some still urge the use of Sacrifices, and contend that the power of sanctifying and justifying resides in them ex opere operato: while others strenuously and constantly deny that very thing: Who, I beseech you, unless extremely dull and foolish, would neglect the knowledge of these controversies as superfluous and useless? Therefore, I will propose in order the doubts that may seem capable of being raised concerning the Nature of Sacrifices, but in such a way that, according to the reason of our method, I shall first examine the purer doctrine of our Churches, and then weigh the contrary opinions, which have ever existed anywhere concerning Sacrifices in the Church of CHRIST, in the balance of the divine Word.

And at the beginning, indeed, the word for sacrificing is accepted in this dispute in the sense which the etymon of the word itself reveals, so that, namely, to Sacrifice is the same as to perform sacred rites, or to be occupied with divine worship through the offering of victims and Sacrifices. In which very sense also, the verb 'to do' (facere) is accepted by the profane, by ecclesiastics, and even by sacred writers: but in such a way that, never placed separately and absolutely, but always joined with the things that are offered, and thus understood Transitively, it obtains the sense of Sacrificing: as can be seen in the Poet: Eclogue 3. 'When I shall perform [sacrifice] with a heifer, for the crops, come yourself.' And in Moses, Leviticus 23:18.

23, 19. You shall make a goat for a sin offering, and two yearling lambs as sacrifices of peace offerings. And in David: Ps. 66, 15. (according to the Hebrew text) I will offer you oxen with goats. And this is indeed the proper meaning of the word sacrificing. Furthermore, by metaphor and transferred sense, this word, when applied to any divine worship, whether internal or external, can be adapted to prayers, to thanksgivings, to confessions, and to other spiritual exercises of that kind: just as it is taken in this sense in Ps. 50, 14. Sacrifice to GOD a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High. Ps. 51, 19. A sacrifice to GOD is a broken spirit. Rom. 12, 1. Present your bodies as a θυσίαν, a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to GOD, etc. Heb. 13, 15. through him let us offer a sacrifice of praise always to GOD, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. 1. Pet. 2, 5. You are a holy priesthood, offer spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to GOD through CHRIST. See the excellent enumeration of all things to which the name of sacrifice is attributed in the New Testament in Chemnitz, part 2, Exam. page 138.

Προσκόμψα, what is required for a true sacrifice pleasing to God, St. Augustine, in his book to the thanks to GOD, in the resolution of the third question, writes that two things are necessarily required in a true sacrifice. 1. That it be offered not to fictitious gods, but to the true GOD. 2. That it be offered not from our own invention or figment, but from the doctrine of Holy Scripture. Which two things, indeed, although they concur in any true sacrifice, do not yet constitute the very substance of a true sacrifice. For if we look deeply into the sacrifices instituted by God himself through Moses, it becomes manifest that five things especially pertain to constituting the substance of a true sacrifice pleasing to God: I. The very substance of the sacrifice, or the thing to be offered to God, and not just any thing, but that defined by God himself in his word. II. A certain rite and action of offering, again not devised by men, but described by God himself. III. A certain person ordained by God for this duty of offering. IV. Also a certain place, divinely destined for this rite. And finally V. a just intention, or a certain end, which, of course, GOD himself sanctioned as the one to be regarded in these works.

Wherefore it is not placed in the power of man, out of some good intention, from his own ingenuity, to offer either new victims, or even in a manner and place other than what was defined by God. Whence both the Gentiles and some of their κακόζηλοι (misguided) Jews sinned most gravely, who were accustomed to offer human victims to God. Abraham, certainly, about to immolate his son by the very command of GOD, is prohibited by an Angel, lest perhaps through foolish κακοζηλία (misguided zeal) his descendants might think the same was permitted to them. Which very thing the Lord also sharply rebukes in the Gentiles, saying to Moses: Beware, lest you imitate the nations, etc., and seek their ceremonies, saying: As these nations worshipped their GODS, so I will worship: You shall not do likewise to the Lord your GOD. For all the abominations which the Lord hates, they have done to their gods, offering their sons and their daughters, and burning them with fire. What I command you, this ONLY do to the Lord, neither add anything, nor diminish. Deut. 12, 30. 31. 32. To which our Savior also looked, promulgating a general aphorism concerning this question: In vain, he says, they worship me with the doctrines of men. Matt. 15, 9.

Although it is certain that Jephthah offered his daughter as a result of a vow, nevertheless the dispute is still under judgment as to whether Jephthah offered his daughter or not: or whether he devoted her to perpetual virginity: For no fewer interpreters, and no less weighty reasons, fight for this latter opinion than for the former. But however that may be, whether he fulfilled this or that by a vow in his daughter, he certainly did not entangle himself in a light guilt. For if he offered her as a burnt offering to the Lord: it is clear that both the vow was impious, and the fulfillment of the vow was as impious as it was cruel. For it is not lawful to vow anything against the law of GOD, much less to fulfill such a vow. But if the father devoted her to perpetual virginity, again he certainly erred not lightly: while, of course, he vowed that which was not in his power. For to marry, or not to marry, and to sanctify a daughter to the LORD in perpetual celibacy, is not in the power of the father, but is placed primarily in the consent of the daughter. But since the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11, 32, places him in the catalog of the saints and those justified by faith, it should in no way be doubted that he performed serious repentance concerning this illicit vow and its fulfillment, and was subsequently justified by faith in the coming Messiah.

Nor does it stand in the way of GOD being the author of sacrifices that he says he turns away from and detests offerings and sacrifices: For the cause of this matter proceeds primarily from the vice of the accident, which resides not in GOD, but solely in hypocritical men. For soon in that original church of the first parents, Cain and his posterity, who constituted a hypocritical and spurious church, straying from the true end and use of sacrifices, attributed to them the power of merit, and that indeed ex opere operato (by the work performed), so much so that they determined that GOD was placated by the mere external offering of victims, even without faith and repentance performed, and thence promised themselves remission of sins and eternal life. Therefore, GOD, about to correct this abuse of sacrifices, most severely decreed both that these sacrifices did not please him, and that grace was hoped for from them in vain, in the same sense exactly as the Savior in Matt. 6, 16. He rejects the fasts of hypocrites: namely, of those who, trusting in that work, almost dared to expostulate with GOD, saying: Wherefore have we fasted, and thou hast not regarded? we have humbled our souls, and thou hast not taken knowledge? Jes. 58. 3. Then GOD speaks comparatively, a comparison having been made, namely, between the external rite of Sacrifices and the internal worships of the mind, such as Faith, Contrition, Prayers, Obedience, and thanksgiving. For if these two are compared with one another, GOD testifies that He prefers those internal worships to the external rites of Sacrifices: since even without that external offering of victims those internal ones are pleasing and acceptable to Him: whereas, on the contrary, external Sacrifices, destitute of these internal ones, are held in no value: according to that saying of the Saviour, In vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men. Matt. 15, 9.

But if it should be further objected: If GOD alone is the author of Sacrifices, it would follow that a certain commandment concerning the offering of them was given by GOD before Cain & Abel offered their gifts to GOD. But since such an express mandate nowhere exists in Genesis, it follows that God is not the first author of Sacrifices. The response is plain: The argument commits the fallacy of non-cause as cause, and of that which does not follow. Nor is the inference firm: The express Institution of this or that thing does not exist before Moses. Therefore, GOD is not the author of those things either: but they were devised by men solely with good intention. The invocation of the divine Being in the history of our first parents certainly rests upon no express mandate: therefore, was GOD not the author of that Invocation, by which the protoplasts worshipped their GOD, nor did He give them a mandate for this thing. Certainly no one will be of such a dull nose that he does not smell the weakness of this inference. Wherefore I maintain entirely by firm & evident reasons that the first parents, immediately after the fall and their restoration to integrity, received an express mandate from GOD, and one indeed given immediately, concerning the offering of Sacrifices. Which mandate, as it was propagated to the sons of Adam, so consequently through the families of the Patriarchs, up to Moses, and was handed down as if from hand to hand, until afterwards GOD, through Moses, wished to arrange the worship of Sacrifices into its distinct species and a certain order, as it were, and, having without doubt cast off and repudiated many things which the vain and curious superstition of men was mixing in, to restore it to its pristine brightness and purity.

Latin:

DE Sacrificijs ex professo disputaturus, planè statuo, non utilem modò, sed prorsus etiam necessariam operam, in hoc doctrinæ Christianæ Articulo enucleando, navari posse ab eo, qui hâc in materiâ studij aliquid, & temporis impenderit. Cum enim & populus DEI in Veteri Testamento, proram quasi ac puppim cultus divini, imò salutis suæ, in Sacrificiorum ritu vel maximè posuerit: & verò pleræq; Gentes extra Ecclesiam constitutæ, Sacrificiorum oblatione DEOS suos unicè placari statuerint: Et hunc i psum in finem Hecatombas, hoc est centum boves & oves solenniter offerre consueverint: Quin imò in ipso populo DEI, Judæorum plurimi jam olim varias planè ac discrepantes sententias de Sacrificiorum usu & effectu foverint: hodieq; in Novo Testamento haud pauci foveant; dùm alij Sacrificiorum usum etiamnùm urgent, ijsq; sanctificandi justificandiq; vim ex opere operato inesse contendunt: alij verò illud ipsum strenuè & constanter negant: Quis obsecrò nisi extremè bardus & stultus harum controversiarum cognitionem ceu supervacaneam & inutilem, negligeret? Proindè quæ de Sacrificiorum Naturâ, moveri dubia posse videbuntur, ordine proponam, sed ita, ut pro ratione methodi nostræ, initiò puriorem Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctrinam examinem, deindè verò contrarias opiniones, quæ unquàm uspiam de Sacrificijs in Ecclesia CHRISTI extiterunt, ad trutinam Verbi divini appendam.

Ac initiò quidem, accipitur hâc in disputatione vox sacrificandi eo sensu, quem ipsum vocabuli ἔτυμον prodit, ut nimirùm Sacrificare, idem sit ac sacra facere, sive cultui divino vacare per oblationem victimarum & Sacrificiorum. Quo ipso etiam sensu, verbum Facere, tùm à prophanis, tùm ab Ecclesiasticis, imò etiam sacris scriptoribus accipitur: sed ita, ut nunquàm seorsim & absolutè positum, sed semper cum rebus, quæ offeruntur junctum, & sic Transitivè intellectum, Sacrificandi sensum obtineat: ut videre est apud Poëtam: Ecloga 3. Cum faciam vitulâ, pro frugibus, ipse venito. Et apud Mosen Levit. 23, 18.

23, 19. Facietis hircũ pro peccato, duosq́; agnos anniculos hostias pacificorũ. Et apud Davidem : Pf. 66, 15. (seecundum Hebræũ textum)Faciam tibi boves cum hircis. Et hæc quidem propria est vocis Sacrificandi significatio. Cæterùm per Metaphorā & sensu translatitio vox hæc accepta ad quévis sermè cultum divinum, tàm internũ, quàm externũ: ut ad preces,ad gratiarum actiones,ad confessiones, & id genus alia spiritualia exercitia accommodari potest : Quemadmodum hoc sensu accipitur Pf. 50, 14. Immola DEO Sacrificiũ laudis, & redde Altissimo votatua Pf. 51, 19. Sacrificium DEO Spiritus contribulatus. Rom. 12, 1. Exhibete corpora vestra θυσίαν hostiam viventem, sanctam, DEO placentem &c. Hebr. 13, 15. per ipsum offeramus hostiam laudis semper DEO, id est fructum labiorum confitentium nomini ejus. 1. Petr. 2, 5. Estis Sacerdotium sanctum, offerte spirituales hostias, acceptabiles DEO per CHRISTUM. Vide egregiam enumerationem omnium rerum, quibus in Novo Testamento Sacrificij nomen tribuitur apud Chemnitium part. 2. Exam. pag. 138.

Προσκόμψα, quæ ad verum, Deóq; gratum Sacrificium requiruntur, D. Augustinus, in libro ad DEO gratias, in dissolutione quæstionis tertiæ; duo in vero Sacrificio necessariò exigi scribit. 1. ut non fictitiis, sed DEO vero offeratur. 2. ut non ex nostro invento aut figmento, sed ex Sacra Scripturæ doctrinâ offeratur. Quæ sanè duo, etsi in quovis Sacrificio vero concurrunt, nondùm tamen ipsam substantiam veri Sacrificij constituunt. Nam si Sacrificia à Deo ipso per Mosen instituta penitùs intueamur, manifestum evadit, ad constituendam substantiam veri, Deóq; grati Sacrificij, quinq́, potissimùm requisita pertinere: I. Ipsam Substantiam Sacrificij, sive Rem offerendam Deo, & eam non quamvis, sed à Deo ipso in verbo definitam. II, Certum offerendi ritum, & actionem, rursus non ab hominibus excogitatam, sed ab ipso Deo descriptam. III. Certam personam ad hoc offerendi munus à Deo ordinatam. IV. Certum etiam locum,divinitùs huic ritui destinatum. Et Tandem V. justam intentionem, sive finem certum, quem nimirùm DEUS ipse in hisce operibus respiciendum esse, sancivit.

Quapropter in hominis potestate positum non est, ex bonâ quadam intentione, de proprio ingenio, vel novas victimas, vel etiam alio quàm à Deo definitum fuit, & modo & loco, offerre. Undè gravissimè peccarunt & gentes, & harum κακόζηλοι Judæi nonnulli, qui victimas humanas Deo offerre fuerunt soliti. Abraham certè filium ex ipso mandato DEI, immolaturus, per Angelum prohibetur, ne fortè per stultam κακοζηλίαν posteri idem sibi licere, arbitrentur. Quod ipsum in Gentibus etiam acriter reprehendit Dominus, dicens ad Mosen: Cave, ne imiteris gentes &c. & requiras ceremonias earũ dicens:Sicut coluerunt Gentes istæ DEOS suos, ita & ego colam: Non facies similiter Domino DEO tuo. Omnes n. abominationes quas aversatur Domin9, fecerũt Diis suis, offerentes filios suos, & filias suas, & cōburentes igni. Quod præcipio tibi, hoc TANTũ facito Domino, nec addas quicquā, nec minuas. Dev. 12, 30. 31. 32. Quò respexit Servator etiam noster, generalem Aphorismum de hac Quæstione promulgans : Frustrà, inquiens, colunt me doctrinis hominum. Matth. 15, 9.

Quàmvis autem Jephtah filiam suam ex voto obtulisse constat, attamen primùm adhuc sub Judice lis est, an Jephtah filiã suã obtulerit, nec ne: an verò perpetuæ virginitati eam devoverit: Haud enim pauciores interpretes, haud leviores etiam rationes, pro posteriore hac, quàm priore illâ sententiâ militant. Sed utut sit, sive hoc, sive illud ex voto in filiâ suâ expleverit, haud certè levi reatu sese obstrinxit. Quod si enim eam obtulit in Holocaustum Domino: perspicuum est, quod & votum fuerit impium, & impletio voti fuerit tàm impia, quàm crudelis. Haud enim fas est, adversus legem DEI quicquam vovere, nedùm votum implere. Quòd si verò eam perpetuæ virginitati devovit Pater, rursus profectò haud leviter erravit : dùm nimirùm vovit id, quod in potestate suâ non habebat. Nam nubere, aut non nubere, ac DoMiNo sanctificare perpetuo cœlibatu Filiam, non in Patris potestate, sed in filiæ potissimum consensu est positum. Verùm cum Epistola ad Hebræos cap. 11, 32. in catalogum sanctorum & fide justificatorum illum reponat, nullatenùs fuerit dubitandum, quin de illicito hoc voto, ejusque impletione seriam egerit pœnitentiam, & Fide postmodùm in venturum Messiam justificatus fuerit.

Nec obstat, quo minùs DEUS autor sit Sacrificiorum, quòd oblationes & Sacrificia se aversari, & detestari dicit: Causa enim hujus rei, primùm ex accidentis vitio, quod non in DEo, sed in hominibus hypocritis unicè residet, promanat. Nam mox in originali illâ primorum parentum Ecclesiâ, Cain & ipsius posteritas, quæ Hypocriticã & Spuriã Ecclesiam constituebat, à vero Sacrificiorum fine & usu aberrantes, vim meriti illis affingebant, & eam quidem ex opere operato, adeò ut DEUM solâ externâ Victimarum oblatione, etiam sine fide, & pœnitentiâ peractâ placari statuerent, & indè peccatorum Remissionem, vitamq; æternam sibi promitterent. Hunc ergò Sacrificiorum abusum DEUS correcturus, utrumq; severissimè edixit, & Sacrificia isthæc sibi non placere, & frustrà ex illis sperari gratiam, eodem planè sensu, quo Servator Matth. 6, 16. Hypocritarum jejunia repudiat: eorum nimirùm, qui in opere isto confidentes, cum DEo expostulare quasi audebant, dicentes: Quare jejunavimus, & non aspexisti, humiliavimus animas nostras, & nescivisti. Jes. 58. 3. Deindè comparatè DEUS loquitur, facta nimirùm collatione inter externum Sacrificiorum ritum : & internos mentis cultus, quales sunt Fides, Contritio, Preces, Obedientia, Gratiarũ actio. Hæc enim duo, si invicem comparentur, testatur DEUS, se internos illos cultus præferre externis Sacrificiorum ritibus: siquidem etiam sine externâ illâ victimarum oblatione interni illi sibi sint grati & accepti: Cùm contrà externa Sacrificia, internis hisce destituta, in nullo precio habeantur: secundum illud Servatoris, Frustrà colunt me, docentes doctrinas hominum. Matt. 15, 9.

Qud si porrò objiciatur: Si DEUS solus est autor Sacrificiorum, consequens fore, certum quoddam præceptum de illis offerendis à DEO esse datum, priusquàm Cain & Abel sua munera obtulerunt DEO. Cùm verò tale expressum mandatum in Genesi nuspiam extat, sequi Deú primum Sacrificiorum autorem haud esse. Responsio est plana: Committi in argumento sσ́φισμα τη̃ς μὴ αἰτίας ὠς αἰτίας, & ω̗ δὲ το̃ μὴ ἐπό- μενον. Neq́; est firma collectio: Hujus vel illius rei expressa Institutio ante Mosen non extat. Ergò neq́; illarum rerum DEUS est autor: sed ab hominibus duntaxat illæ bonà intentione fuerunt excogitatæ. Invocatio certè divini Numinis in primorum parentum historiâ, nullo expresso nititur mandato: ergóne Invocationis illius, quâ DEUM suum venerabantur protoplasti, DEUS non fuit autor, neq́; hujus rei dedit illis mandatum. Haud sanè quisquam tàm obesæ erit naris, qui infirmitatem collectionis hujus non olfaciat. Quare firmis & evidentibus rationibus omninò statuo, Accepisse à DEO primos parentes mox post lapsum & restitutionem eorum in integrum expressum mandatum, & quidem immediatè datum de Sacrificiorum oblatione. Quod mandatum, uti in filios Adami, ita consequenter per Patriarcharum familias, usq́; ad Mosen fuit propagatum, & tanquàm per manus traditum, donec postmodùm DEUS per Mosen Sacrificiorum cultum, in suas distinctas species, & certum quasi ordinem digerere, & abjectis ac repudiatis sine dubio multis, quæ vana & curiosa hominum superstitio admiscuebat, pristino candori & puritati restituere voluit.


### On Sacrifices (continued)

And certainly the reasons are sufficiently pregnant by which it can be proved against the Papists that the first parents had a divine mandate concerning the offering of Sacrifices. But the first of these is that of B. Luther, who in his commentary on the Fourth Chapter of Genesis responds to the proposed question thus: They (the first parents & their sons) had the word or mandate of sacrificing. For all sacred Histories prove this, that the merciful GOD, through His superabundant grace, has always established some external and visible sign of His grace alongside the word, so that men, admonished by an external work and sign, as by a Sacrament, might more certainly believe that GOD favors them and is merciful.

A second Reason can be sought from the consequent Effect which the Sacrifices obtained with respect to GOD Himself. From which I argue thus: Whatever Sacrifices GOD approves and regards as an odor of sweetness, they must necessarily have GOD Himself as their author and institutor. But GOD approved the Sacrifices of Abel and Noah and regarded them as an odor of sweetness. Therefore, it must be that GOD Himself was their first author. The connection of the Major is evident from Deut. 12:32, where GOD says to Moses: What I command you, that ONLY do, nor add anything, nor diminish. And from that Aphorism of the Savior in Matthew 15:9: In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men. If therefore only that is to be done which GOD has commanded: If only that pleases God which He Himself has mandated: If also GOD is worshipped in vain by the inventions of men: then certainly from the contrary sense it necessarily follows that whatever it is, and is done with the approval of GOD, that is done not without His word and mandate; it also follows that those things by which GOD is not worshipped in vain have not men, but GOD alone, as their author.

The truth of the Minor is evident from the Scriptures: For Gen. 4:4, concerning the Sacrifice of Abel, it is said that GOD regarded it: and by some external sign testified that both the person and the Sacrifice of Abel were approved by Him: Which B. Luther, and before him D. Jerome, maintain was done by a flame sent from heaven, consuming the victims, no differently than in the Sacrifices of Abraham Gen. 15:17, Aaron Lev. 9:24, Solomon 2 Chron. 7:1, Elijah 1 Kings 18:38. Thus we read of Noah, that he himself after the flood built an altar, and offered Burnt offerings from clean cattle and birds, of which thing, that he had a certain mandate, it is evident even from this, that the Holy Spirit immediately adds: And the Lord smelled the odor of sweetness, and gave a promise of not cursing the Earth anymore because of men, Gen. 8:20, 21.

The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 11:4, provides a third foundation. Abel by Faith offered a sacrifice of greater value to GOD than Cain, by which he was adorned with the testimony that he was righteous, GOD bearing witness to his gifts. Whence I argue thus:

Whatever Sacrifices obtain their dignity from faith: And likewise those Sacrifices to which GOD Himself bears witness: it is a consequence that they are not offered without the mandate of GOD.

But the Sacrifice of Abel obtained its dignity from faith, and GOD Himself bore witness to it.

Therefore it is a consequence that it was not offered without the mandate of GOD.

The truth of the Major shines forth from this: Because faith always regards the word, according to that of the Apostle Rom. 10: Faith comes from hearing: And indeed not just any word, but as they say, an appropriated one. Now, Abel is said to have offered by faith: Therefore, that Faith must have had a certain word upon which it could firmly rely. Otherwise, it would follow that that Faith, which the Holy Spirit commends in the Sacrifices of Abel, had no certain object or word. Nor is it for anyone to object that Abel, as a faithful and Reborn man, devised the Sacrifices through some good intention, and in this way, insofar as he was reborn and faithful, the Holy Spirit affirms that he offered by faith. For every reborn and faithful person considers it a sin for himself to devise a certain worship not prescribed by GOD, much less to fulfill it by the act itself. And as impossible as it is that Man, however much he may be regenerate, can know outside the word and command of GOD, what manner of worship is pleasing and acceptable to GOD, so impossible is it also for Faith to coexist with ἐθελοθρησκίαις [will-worship], or forms of worship devised by human intention.

As for the minor proposition, it is ἔγγραφος [scriptural], and cited simply from the Epistle to the Hebrews.

Therefore, the conclusion of the argument itself will also be valid and firm.

The fourth foundation is provided by that indefinite and universal aphorism of Samuel: 'Obedience is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams,' 1 Sam. 15:22. Since this aphorism was most true not merely from the age of Samuel, but from the beginning, it is manifest that the first parents offered their sacrifices either with some obedience toward GOD or without it: if without obedience, they certainly could not have pleased GOD; if with obedience, it is necessary that that obedience had a certain word and command, without which there can be no true obedience.

Fifthly: since GOD always is and remains like unto Himself, it is certainly not to be concluded that He was ever delighted by carnal and external worship. But GOD was indeed delighted by the sacrifices of the first men. It follows, therefore, that they did not offer them to GOD carnally, but spiritually; that is, those Fathers did not play with human or empty ceremonies, but grasped something higher and more recondite, which they could not have done without the Word. For only the interior truth of GOD, leaning upon His Word, distinguished true worship of GOD from false and superstitious worship in signs or external ceremonies. Finally, the very Religion and Salvation of those first men most urgently required that their worship should rest upon a certain word and command of GOD. For first, while they professed themselves to be GOD's, it was necessary for them to have known what God in turn demanded of them. Then it was of the greatest importance to them to learn from the offering of victims that there was a need for some Expiation for their reconciliation with GOD. Which expiation, although it was not placed in the act of the sacrifices themselves, always pointed the finger toward that promised seed of the woman, of whom they had heard soon after the fall, that he would crush the head of the serpent, Gen. 3:15.

As regards the place of sacrifices, it is established from the Scriptures that it is required that they be offered in no other place than that which GOD Himself has defined. This is clear from chapter 12 of Deuteronomy, v. 4, 5, 6, where GOD says to Moses: 'Ye shall not do so (as the Gentiles do) unto the Lord your GOD: but unto the place which the Lord your GOD shall choose out of all your tribes, to put his name there, and to dwell in it, shall ye come: and ye shall offer in that place your burnt offerings, and your sacrifices, your tithes, and heave offerings of your hand, and your vows, and your freewill offerings, the firstlings of your herds and of your flocks, etc.'

That place, indeed, was none other than the door of the Tabernacle, in which was the ark of the mercy seat: just as GOD Himself had defined in Leviticus 17:8-9, saying: 'Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among you, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice, and does not bring it to the door of the Tabernacle of the Testimony, to offer it to the Lord, shall be cut off from his people.'

Whence it also came to pass that the Israelite people, in the passage of time, having neglected this command of GOD, and offering sacrifices in high places, under trees and in groves, were held guilty of idolatry by the Prophets for the mere change of place, however much they may have offered those things which GOD had otherwise commanded in His Word. Jer. 2:28, ch. 11:13.

It should be noted in this place, however, that the reason was different regarding the Place in the sacrifices of the Patriarchs before Moses: for at that time this command concerning the observation of a certain place had not yet been promulgated by GOD; whence we also read that the Patriarchs offered in various places.

If you ask for what reasons GOD willed the worship of sacrifices to be restricted to a certain place? One truly does not have to go far, nor are the causes of this matter to be inquired into too solicitously, most of which, however they may be covered with paint, nevertheless rest upon uncertain conjectures, and leave the reader more in suspense than they instruct him. The highest and chief cause is the very will and good pleasure of GOD, who, just as He willed to be worshipped not by any sacrifices, but by certain ones, out of His free will: so He willed to be worshipped by the same not in any place, but in a certain place. Then this cause also can be given, that this fact and others of this kind were so, that the people of GOD might have certain objects, around which they could exercise and prove their obedience owed to GOD. To which cause GOD Himself seems to have alluded in Deut. 12, 25, saying: that it may be well with you and your children after you, when you have done what is pleasing in the sight of GOD. Thus, therefore, the strict observation of Place was like some matter, around which the Jews might prove their obedience to GOD.

That finally not any persons, but certain ones were ordained by GOD to sacrifice; the distinction of Time must be observed at the beginning, by which the Church of GOD is considered, either before Moses, or after Moses. Before Moses indeed, just as no precept had yet been given to the Patriarchs concerning a certain place, in which alone they should offer their sacrifices to GOD: so the ministry of sacrifices was not yet restricted to certain persons: but it was permitted to individual Patriarchs, when and where each wished to sacrifice. But after Moses, when GOD now wished to reduce the state of the Church into a certain form, and to remove all ἀναρχίαν or confusion, which had crept into the Church: and to found and establish an ecclesiastical hierarchy with certain laws and precepts: there, just as He defined a certain place for His worship, so He willed there to be certain persons, in whose power alone the authority to sacrifice would reside.

GOD therefore at the beginning set Aaron, the brother of Moses, over the Tabernacle, and commanded him to be held in the title and place of high priest. Exod. 28, 1. 29, 6. Moreover, He willed him to be clothed in certain garments, and

Latin:

Et certè rationes sunt satis prægnantes, quibus primos parentes divinum habuisse mandatum de offerendis Sacrificijs, contra Pontificios probari potest. Earum verò prima est B. Lutheri, qui in enarratione Capitis Quarti Geneseωs, ad propositum ζήτημα sic respondet. Habuerunt illi (primi parentes & horum filij) verbum sive mandatum sacrificandi. Hoc enim omnes sacræ Historiæ comprobant, quod misericors DEUS per superabundantem suam gratiam semper juxta verbum constituerit aliquod externum & visibile signum gratiæ suæ, ut homines externo opere & signo, ceu Sacramento admoniti, certiùs crederent, DEUM sibi favere & misericordem esse.

Altera Ratio peti potest ex consequente Effectu, quem sortita sunt Sacrificia, respectu ipsi9 DEI. Ex quo sic arguo: Quæcunq́; Sacrificia DEUS probat, & respicit seu odorem suavitatis illa ipsum DEUM autorem & institutorem habeant necessum est. At verò Sacrificia Abelis, & Noahi DEUS probavit, & ceu odorem suavitatis respexit. Ergo DEUS ipse eorum autor primus fuerit necessum est. Connexum Majoris patet ex cap. Deuter. 12, 32. ubi DEUS ad Mosen dicit: Quod præcipio tibi, hoc TANTUM facito, nec addas quicquam, nec minuas. Et ex Aphorismo illo Servatoris Matthœi thæi 15, 9. Frustrà colunt me docentes doctrinas hominum. Quod si ergò Tantùm faciendum, quod DEUS præcepit: Quod si id solum Deo placet, quod ipse mandavit: Quod si etiam frustrà colitur DEUS inventis hominum: certè ex contrario sensu necessariò consequitur, quòd quicquid sit, & sit approbante DEO, illud fiat non sine ejusdem verbo ac mandato, consequitur & illud, ut quibus rebus DEUS non frustrà colitur, eæ non homines, sed DEUM solum authorem habeant.

Minoris veritas patet ex Scripturis: Nam Gen. 4, 4. de Sacrificio Abelis dicitur, quòd DEUS illud respexerit: & externo quopiam signo testatus fuerit, sibi probari & personam & Sacrificium Abelis: Id quod B. Lutherus, & ante hunc D. Hieronymus, per flammam cœlitùs de missam, & victimas absumentem, haud secus ac in Sacrificijs Abrahæ Gen. 15, 27. Aaronis Levit. 9, 24. Salomonis 2. Paral. 7, 1. Eliæ 1. Reg. 18, 38. factum fuisse statuunt. Sic de Noaho legimus, quod & ipse post diluvium ædificaverit altare, & de pecoribus & volucribus mundis obtulerit Holocausta, cujus rei, quin certum habuerit mandatum vel indè patet, Quod mox Spiritus Sanctus subjicit: Et odoratus est Dominus odorem suavitatis, & promissionem dedit de non maledicendo ampliùs Terræ propter homines, Gen. 8, 20. 21.

Tertium fundamentum subministrat autor Epistolæ ad Hebr. cap. 11, 4. Abel per Fidem majoris pretij Sacrificium obtulit DEO, quàm Cain, per quam testimonio fuit ornatus, quòd esset justus, Testimonium perhibente DEO de donis ejus. Undè sic arguo:

Quæcunq; Sacrificia suam dignitatem ex fide obtinere: Quibus item Sacrificijs, DEUS ipse Testimonium perhibet: ea non absq; DEI mandato offerri consequens est.

At verò Abelis Sacrificium suam dignitatē ex fide obtinuit, illiq; DEUS ipse Testimonium perhibuit.

Ergò non absq; mandato DEI illud fuisse oblatū, consequens est.

Majoris veritas indè elucet: Quia fides semper respicit verbum, secundum illud Apostoli Rom. 10. Fides ex auditu: Et verbum quidem non quodvis, sed uti loquuntur, appropriatum. Jam verò ex fide obtulisse dicitur Abel: Ergò Fides illa, certum habuerit verbum, quo firmiter inniti potuerit, necesseum est. Alioqui sequeretur, Fidem illam, quam Spiritus Sanctus in Sacrificijs Abelis commendat, nullum habuisse certum objectum, sive verbum. Neq; est, ut quisquam objiciat, Abelem tanquàm fidelem & Renatum excogitasse per bonam quandam intentionem Sacrificiorum, & hoc pacto, quatenùs nimirùm renatus & fidelis erat, Spiritum Sanctum affirmare, ipsum ex fide obtulisse. Nam quisque renatus & fidelis piaculo sibi ducit, certum quendam cultum à DEO non præscriptum excogitare, nedùm actu ipso implere. Et quàm impossibile est, ut Homo, quantumvis etiam renatus extra verbum & mandatum DEI scire possit, quinam cultus DEO gratus & acceptus: tàm impossibile etiam est, Fidem cum ἐθελοθρησκίαις sive cultibus ab humanâ intentione excogitatis, stare posse.

Quoad Minorem propositionem, ea est ἔγγραφος, & ex Epistolâ ad Hebræos, simpliciter citata.

Rata proindè & firma erit etiam ipsa argumenti conclusio.

Quartum fundamentum suppeditat indefinitus ille & universalis Aphorismus Samuelis, Melior est obedientia, quàm victima: & auscultare magis, quàm offerre adipem arietum, 1. Sam. 15, 22. Qui sanè Aphorismus, cùm non à Samuelis demùm ætate, sed ab initio fuerit longè verissimus, manifestum est, vel ex quapiam obedientiâ erga DEUM, vel absq; eâ, primos parentes sua Sacrificia obtulisse: si sine obedientiâ: placere utiq; DEO non potuerunt: Si cum obedientiâ: necessum est, ut obedientia illa certum habuerit verbum & mandatum: sine quo obedientia vera nulla esse potest.

Quintò: cùm DEUS semper sit maneatq; sui similis, haud certè statuendum, unquàm fuisse ipsum delectatum carnali & externo cultu. At verò delectatus fuit DEUS primorum hominum Sacrificijs. Consequens ergò non carnaliter, sed spiritualiter DEO illos obtulisse, hoc est, non humanis aut inanibus ceremonijs lusisse Patres illos, sed aliquid comprehendisse altius & magis reconditum, quod absq; verbo non poterant. Sola enim interior veritas DEI Verbo innitens, in signis sive ceremonijs externis verum DEI cultum à falso & superstitioso distingvit. Tandem ipsa primorum istorum hominum Religio & Salus maximè efflagitabat, ut cultus ipsorum certo DEI verbo & mandato niteretur. Primùm enim dum se DEI esse profitebantur, necessum utiq; erat novisse, quid Deus vicissim ab ipsis flagitet. Deindè ipsorum maximè intererat, ex victimarum oblatione addiscere, Expiatione aliquâ, ad sui reconciliationem cum DEO, opus esse. Quæ expiatio licèt non in ipso Sacrificiorum opere erat posita, digitum tamen semper intendebat ad promissum illud semen mulieris, de quo mox post lapsum inaudiverant, illud contriturum caput serpentis Genes. 3, 15.

Locum Sacrificiorum quod attinet, requiri, ut ea non alio loco, quam eo, quàm DEUS ipse definivit offerantur, ex Scripturis constat. Quod patet ex cap. 12. Devteronomij, v. 4. 5. 6. ubi DEUS ad Mosen inquit: Non facietis ita (quemadmodum Gentes) Domino DEO vestro: sed ad locum, quem elegerit Dominus DEUS vester de cunctis tribubus vestris, ut ponat nomen suum ibi, & habitet in eo, venietis: & offeretis in loco illo holocausta, & victimas vestras, decimas & primitias manuum vestrarum, & vota atq; donaria, primogenita boum & ovium & c.

Erat verò Locus ille, non alius, quàm ostium Tabernaculi, in quo erat arca propitiatorij: Quemadmodum DEUS ipse Levit. 17, 8. & 9. definiverat, dicens: Homo de domo Israel, & de advenis, qui peregrinantur apud vos, qui obtulerit holocaustum sive victimam, & ad ostium Tabernaculi Testimonij non adduxerit eam, ut offeratur Domino, interibit de populo suo.
