Undè etiam factum fuit, ut populus Israëliticus progressu temporis, neglecto hoc mandato DEI, in excelsis, sub arboribus & lucis Sacrificia offerens, Idololatriæ reus à Prophetis perageretur ob solam loci mutationem, quantumvis obtulerint ea, quę DEUS alioqui in Verbo suo præcepisset. Jer. 2, 28. cap. 11, 13.

Observandum verò hoc loco fuerit: diversam fuisse rationem respectu Loci in Sacrificijs Patriarcharum ante Mosen: Tùm enim præceptum istud de certi loci observatione nondùm à DEO fuerat promulgatum: Undè etiam diversis in locis Patriarchas obtulisse legimus.

Si quæras, quibus de causis ad certum locum voluerit DEUS Sacrificiorum cultum esse adstrictum? haud sanè longè est abeundum, neq́; nimis sollicitè inquirendæ rei hujus causæ, quarum pleræq́; quocunq́; etiam fuco tegantur, incertis tamen nituntur conjecturis, & Lectorem magis in suspenso relinquunt, quàm erudiunt. Summa & princeps causa est, ipsa DEI voluntas & beneplacitum, qui uti ex liberâ voluntate per Sacrificia non quævis, sed certa coli: Ita non quovis etiam, sed certo loco per eadem coli voluit. Deindè causa dari potest & isthæc, Factum nimirùm hoc & id genus alia esse, ut populus DEI certa haberet objecta, circa quæ suam DEO debitam obedientiam exercere & probare posset. Ad quam causam allusisse videtur DEUS ipse Devt. 12, 25. dicens: ut benè sit tibi & filijs tuis post te, cum feceris, quod placet in conspectu DEI. Sic ergò stricta Loci observatio initar materiæ alicujus fuit, circa quam Judæi suam DEO probarent obedientiam.

Quòd deniq́; personæ non quævis, sed certæ nonnullæ à DEO ad sacrificandum fuerunt ordinatæ; observanda initiò venit distinctio Temporis, quâ Ecclesia DEI consideratur, vel ante Mosen, vel post Mosen. Ante Mosen quidem, uti nullum adhuc præceptum Patriarchis datum fuerat de certo quodam loco, in quo solo sua DEO offerrent Sacrificia: Ita Sacrificiorum ministerium nondùm ad certas quasdam personas erat restrictum: sed singulis Patriarchis, quando & ubi quisq́; volebat Sacrificare fuerit licitum. Post Mosen verò, cum DEUS jam Ecclesiæ statum in certam quandam formam redigere, & omnem ἀναρχίαν sive confusionem, quæ in Ecclesiam irrepserat, tollere: certisq́; legibus & præceptis hierarchiam Ecclesiasticam fundare ac stabilire vellet: ibi uti certum quendam locum cultui suo definivit, ita certas voluit esse personas, penes quas solùm sacrificandi esset potestas.

Præfecit Ergò DEUS initiò TabernaculoAaronem, fratrem Mosis, eumque summi Sacerdotis titulo & loco haberi præcepit. Exod. 28, 1.29, 6. Quin & certis quibusdam vestibus indui, & o-


### On Sacrifices (continued)

to be publicly anointed with the oil of anointing as high priest, as can be seen, Exod. 28, 29. 39.

Whence he alone also, but only once in any given year, namely on the day of atonement, had to enter the Holy of Holies. Levit. 16, 2. 17. 29. & 30.

Then, however, GOD appointed the sons of Aaron as priests, so that under Aaron the High Priest, their father, they might offer sacrifices and perform other public sacred rites, according to the prescriptions of GOD, in the second part of the Tabernacle, adorned indeed with priestly clothing, but not as excellent as that which Aaron the High Priest was required to wear by the institution of GOD. Exod. 28, 1. Num. 3, 4. & 10.

Thirdly: Lest the sons of Aaron, now priests, be weakened by the burdens of their labors, GOD added to them colleagues and fellow tribesmen, namely the Levites, not indeed to sacrifice or to enter the second part of the Tabernacle, which was called the Holy Place, to burn incense: but to keep watch before the Tabernacle and to carry out other duties assigned to them by the priests.

Moreover, since the tribe of Levi alone was destined for the sacred mystery and distributed into three families, of which one was that of Gershon, another of Kohath, the third of Merari: lest again any confusion should arise in carrying out tasks, GOD assigned through Moses to each family its own specific labors, especially in transporting the sacred vessels and instruments of the Tabernacle: and in managing those wagons, consecrated to the Tabernacle by the princes of Israel, upon which were placed those things that could not be conveniently carried: as can be seen, Num. 3, 6. 17. & cap. 4, 15. cap. 7, 2. & seqq. up to v. 11. cap. 8, 24. & cap. 18, 2. & seqq. up to v. 8.

Finally, just as GOD added to each of these families of the Levites a specific inspector, who as an ἐργοδιώκτης (taskmaster) would observe their operations: so also over the three inspectors of the Levites, he set Eleazar the priest: but over the priests, Aaron himself the High Priest. Num. 3, 24. 30. & seqq. to 38.

And indeed this ecclesiastical polity or hierarchy, prescribed to the Israelite people by GOD himself, had to be observed so holily and religiously in all its parts that he who took upon himself the duty and office of sacrificing would be implicated in the guilt of death, so much so that even those who arrogated to themselves only the parts of ministering, outside the tribe of Levi, would bring upon themselves the vengeance of divine wrath, as is clear from Num. 3, 10. An outsider (that is, who was not of the tribe of Levi) who approaches to minister shall be put to death.

But the priests could by no means offer at will whatever pleased them: but GOD himself prescribed many and various, yet certain and mutually distinct, kinds of sacrifices, which alone, and no others, he willed to be offered to him.

Since, however, they possess a huge variety and diversity, it would be most prudent, and indeed by the law of Method, that above all, each and every sacrifice be divided into its own certain and distinct kinds: afterwards, any species of sacrifice should be referred back to its certain kind and, as it were, its certain seat.

And, so that one may descend from the genus to the species; at the beginning it must be shown in what way sacrifices considered in general can be conveniently distinguished. For thus, by one and the same effort, the discrepancy between the sacrifice of the New and the Old Testament may be more easily known. Suidas, a writer by no means to be despised, allows for each and every sacrifice. 1. into δωροφορικά, which offer some gift to GOD: 2. into απολυτρωτικά, which redeem: 3. into διαλλακτικά, which appease or reconcile: 4. Finally into αποπληρικά, which fulfill or pay vows. Suid. p. 453. in the more recent Basel edition. Which distinction, in my judgment, is of such breadth and propriety that no species of all sacrifices, both of the Old and New Testament, can be given that cannot be most conveniently referred to one of these four kinds.

But lest by bringing in new distinctions we seem to depart from the received doctrine of the Church, let us retain those common distinctions of sacrifices, which, however, for the sake of aiding the memory, we shall propose with a slightly more accurate Method.

A sacrifice considered in general is either ἱλαστικὸν, propitiatory, or it is ἐυχαριστικὸν, eucharistic. Each again is twofold: for a propitiatory sacrifice is either Mosaic or Evangelical. A Mosaic propitiatory sacrifice, as will be shown below, redeemed the righteousness of the Law, not indeed by itself or from itself, but in the type of that true propitiatory sacrifice, to be performed at some time by the Messiah, apprehended by firm faith: an Evangelical propitiatory sacrifice is the unique death of CHRIST the Savior, taking away the sins of the whole world.

A eucharistic sacrifice, again considered in general, is likewise either Mosaic or Evangelical. The Mosaic was that by which the Israelite people proved their obedience to GOD, whether in offerings, or in first fruits, or in tithes. But an Evangelical eucharistic sacrifice is that by which the reborn and the faithful in spirit and in truth offer to GOD the calves of lips confessing his name: or also declare works of charity toward their neighbor.

Orthodox theologians recount twelve principal species of Levitical sacrifices in this order: 1. Burnt offering. 2. Sin offering. 3. Guilt offering. 4. Minha, or food offering, or drink offering.

5. Sacrifice of purification. 6. Sacrifice of peace offerings. 7. Sacrifice of praise: which approaches the sacrifice of peace offerings most closely. 8. Offering of firstfruits & firstborn, & tithes. 9. Sacrifice of the ram in the consecration of priests. 10. Offering of the calf & goat. 11. Sacrifice of the red heifer. 12. Paschal lamb.

Which species all together are again recalled to certain & distinct genera. For it is an old, and not so (as it seems to some) inconvenient distribution, by which these individual species are divided into two genera: namely, into most holy things; and into common holy things. Now those were called most holy which were slaughtered on the northern side of the altar, and were either entirely consumed by fire, either on the altar or outside the camp or city: or although they were not entirely burned, it was nevertheless not lawful for anyone to eat of the remains, except for the priests alone, and indeed in a holy place.

Common holy things were called those which were slaughtered in any place of the court: and of whose remains it was permitted to eat not only for the priests, but also for their family, and indeed for others cleansed or purified according to the law.

Most holy sacrifices, as they are called, not inconveniently, according to the matter of the sacrifices, can again be subdivided into two classes: The former of which comprises in itself those sacrifices which were offered from brute animals: Such as were, 1. Burnt offering. 2. Offering for sin. 3. Offering for trespass. 4. Sacrifice of the consecration of priests. 5. Red heifer. 6. Sacrifice of expiation. The latter class, however, embraces those sacrifices which were made from grain: as is the Minha sacrifice, of which there are three species, fine flour, bread, ears of corn.

To common holy things belongs 1. Sacrifice of peace offerings, or of salvation: which comprises under itself the sacrifice of confession or praise, and the spontaneous vow: 2. Offering of firstfruits. 3. Offering of firstborn. 4. Offering of tithes. 5. Offering of the Paschal lamb.

Concerning each of these Levitical sacrifices in particular it must be shown what each one is, and by what rite it was to be offered: for this is the fourth παρακολούθημα of sacrifices, that they should be offered not only from a certain matter: but also by a certain rite. I shall proceed in order.

I. Therefore a BURNT OFFERING, in Hebrew Olah, from Alah, to ascend, because it indeed ascends entirely on the altar, or is consumed. 1. A burnt offering was a sacrifice in which, according to the opinion of Philo, for the sake of honoring and even propitiating GOD, the whole victim which was offered was consumed by fire on the altar, and was sent up as it were from the earth to heaven with smoke as a sweet-smelling savor to GOD: and nothing of it was left there, except the skin, which was the priest's. Now this sacrifice was made either from herds, as are the ox and the calf: both, however, unblemished, male, whole. Levit. 1, 3. Or from the flock of sheep or goats, as are the ram, the goat, the kid, whole, male, Levit. 1, 3. Or from birds, as are turtledoves, young pigeons. Lev. 1, 14.

2. A species of burnt offering is the CONTINUAL SACRIFICE ὁλοκαύτωμα ἐνδελεχὲς, Hebr: Olath Thamid, which had to be repeated daily. For on each day, it was necessary that one lamb be offered to GOD in the morning, and one lamb in the evening. Num. 28, 2.

II. Offering for sin, namely for that which had been committed through ignorance Lev. 4, 1, and following, chap. 5, 1. and following. Hebr. Chataah from Chatah, he sinned, and Chatta, he expiated sin.

There were, however, two kinds of sin offerings. For the blood of certain animals offered for sins was not brought into the Tabernacle of the Testimony, and it was permitted for the priests to eat of their flesh. Lev. 6, 26. c. 10, 17. But the blood of others was brought into the Holy Place, and their flesh, skins, head, etc., were burned outside the camp, nor was it permitted for the priests to eat anything of them. Lev. 4, 4. 11.

It was offered for sin either 1. of the High Priest, or 2. of the whole people, or 3. of a prince, or 4. of a private person. For the sins of the High Priest and the people, a calf was offered at the door of the Tabernacle, Lev. 4, 1. & 13. But for the sin of a prince, a goat was offered. Lev. 4, 22. & 23. For the sins of a private person, if he had been rich, a female goat, a sheep, without blemish was to be offered: Lev. 4, 27. & seqq. If he had been of moderate fortune, either two turtledoves or two young pigeons were offered. Lev. 5, 7. If he was poor, he was obliged to offer a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour. Lev. 5, 11.

Philo Judaeus left this written concerning that sacrifice: The sacrifice called for sin varies both in persons and in victims: in persons, such as the High Priest, the people, the prince, the private individual: but in victims, a calf, a goat, a female goat or a lamb. A cow was also offered by those who sinned through ignorance, or indeed knowingly, but having changed their will, they condemn their deed and institute a better life.

III. Offering for a trespass, namely ἐκ προαιρέσεως committed by set purpose and will. Heb. אָשָׁם Ascham: Trespass, or sacrifice for a trespass, or expiatory offering.

For the expiation of this sin, the Law demanded not only a victim, but also a fine in money, or another penalty. Moreover, a ram was to be offered at the same time. Lev. 5, 15. & 16. chap. 6, 1. to 8. chap. 7, 1. to 10.

Latin:

leo unctionis in summum Sacerdotem publicè ipsum inungi voluit, uti videre est, Exod. 28, 29. 39.

Undè solus etiam, sed semel duntaxat quovis anno, videlicet in festo expiationis, Sanctum Sanctorum ingredi debuit. Levit. 16, 2. 17. 29. & 30.

Deindè verò DEUS filios Aaronis constituit Sacerdotes, ut sub Aarone Summo Sacerdote, patre suo offerrent Sacrificia, aliaq́; sacra publica, juxta præscripta DEI, in secundâ parte Tabernaculi peragerent, ornati quidem Sacerdotali quoq́;, sed non adeò præstanti vestitu, qualem Aaron summus Sacerdos ex DEI instituto gestare debuit. Exod. 28, 1. Num. 3, 4. & 10.

Tertiò: Ne Filij Aaronis jam Sacerdotes laborum oneribus nimirùm debilitarentur, adjunxit eis DEUS collegas, & contribules, Levitas videlicet, non quidem ut sacrificarent, aut ingrederentur secundam Tabernaculi partem, quæ vocabatur Sanctum, adolentes incensum: sed ut ante Tabernaculum excubarent, & expedirent alia sibi à Sacerdotibus demandata officia.

Cæterùm cum Tribus Levi sola Sacro mysterio esset destinata, & in tres familias distributa, quarum Una erat Gersonis, altera Caathi, tertia Merari: ne rursus aliqua confusio in expediendis negocijs oriretur, assignavit DEUS per Mosen singulis familijs certis suos labores, præsertim in transportandis Sacris Tabernaculi vasis & instrumentis: & in regendis illis curribus, à principibus Israëlitis Tabernaculo consecratis, quibus ea imponebantur, quæ commodè portari non poterant: uti videre est, Num. 3, 6. 17. & cap. 4, 15. cap. 7, 2. & seqq. usq́; ad v. 11. cap. 8, 24. & cap. 18, 2. & seqq. usq́; ad v. 8.

Tandem, Quemadmodum DEUS singulis hisce Levitarum familijs certum adjunxit inspectorem, qui ceu ἐργοδιώκτης illarum expeditiones observaret: Ita tribus etiam Levitarum inspectoribus, præfecit Eleazarum Sacerdotem: Sacerdotibus verò ipsum Aaronem summum Pontificem. Num. 3, 24. 30. & seqq. ad 38.

Et sanè Ecclesiastica hæc sive politia, sive hierarchia, populo Israëlitico à DEO ipso præscripta, tam sanctè & religiosè in omnibus ejus partibus observari debuit, ut mortis reatu implicaretur, qui sacrificandi munus & officium sibi sumeret, adeò, ut etiam illi, qui ministrãdi duntaxat partes, extra Levitarum tribum, sibi arrogarent, iræ divinæ ultionem sibi accerserent, uti patet ex Num. 3, 10. Externus (hoc est, qui non fuerit de tribu Levi) qni ad ministrandum accesserit, morte morietur.

Minimè verò Sacerdotes pro libitu offerre potuerunt, quicquid illis arridebat: sed DEUS ipse multa quidem & varia, certa tamen, & ab invicem distincta Sacrificiorum genera, quæ sola, & non alia sibi offerri voluit, præscripsit.

Cum verò ingentem ea varietatem ac diversitatem obtineant, consultissimum fuerit, & quidem ex lege Methodi, ut ante omnia, singula & universa Sacrificia in certa sua ac distincta genera dispescantur: postmodum quælibet Sacrificiorum species, ad certum suum genus, & certam quasi sedem revocetur.

Et, ut à genere ad speciem descendantur; initiò ostendendum, quó pacto Sacrificia in genere considerata commodè distingvi possint. Sic enim unâ eâdemque operâ, Sacrificium tàm Novi, quàm Veteris Testamenti discrepantia faciliùs innotescat. Suidas Scriptor minimè contemnendus, singula & universa Sacrificia patitur. 1. in δωροφορικά, quæ munus aliquod offerunt DEO: 2. in απολυτρωτικά, quæ redimunt: 3. in διαλλακτικά quæ placant, sive reconciliant: 4. Tandem in αποπληρικά, quæ explent, sive vota exsolvunt. Suid. p. 453. Edit. recentiore Basiliensi. Quæ distinctio, meo quidem judicio, ejus est & latitudinis & proprietatis, ut nulla dari queat Sacrificiorum omnium, tàm Veteris, quàm Novi Testamenti species, quæ non ad unum quoddam istorum quatuor generum, commodissimè referri possit.

Verùm ne novis allatis distinctionibus, à receptâ Ecclesiæ doctrinâ recedere videamur, retineamus vulgatas illas Sacrificiorum distinctiones, quas tamen memoriæ juvandæ gratia, paulò accuratiore Methodo, proponemus.

Sacrificium in genere consideratum, aut est ἱλαστικὸν Propitiatorium: aut est ἐυχαριστικὸν. Utrumque rursus geminum: Propiiatorium enim aut est Mosaïcum, aut Evangelicum. Mosaïcum Propitiatorium, uti infrà ostendetur, redimebat Justitiam Legis, non quidem per se, aut ex se: sed in Typo veri illius Propitiatorij, per Messiam aliquando peragendi, firmâ fide apprehensi: Evangelicum Propitiatorium Sacrificium est Unica Mors CHRISTI Servatoris, tollens peccata totius Mundi.

Evcharisticum Sacrificium rursus in genere consideratum, itidem est vel Mosaïcum, vel Evangelicum. Mosaïcum erat illud, quo populus Israëliticus, vel in Oblationibus, vel in Primitis, vel in Decimis, suam obedientiam DEO probabat. Evangelicum verò Evcharisticum Sacrificium est, quo renati & fideles in Spiritu & veritate DEO offerunt vitulos labiorum confitentium nomini ipsius: vel etiam opera charitatis erga proximum declarant.

Leviticorum Sacrificiorum duodecim potissimum species Orthodoxi Theologi recensent hoc ordine: 1. Holocaustum. 2. Oblatio pro peccato. 3. Hostia pro Delicto. 4. Minha, sive Sacrificium cibarium, aut Libamen.

5. Sacrificium mundationis. 6. Sacrificium Pacificorum. 7. Sacrificium Laudis: quod ad Sacrificium Pacificorum quam proximè accedit. 8. Oblatio Primitiarum & primogenitorum,& Decimarum. 9. Sacrificium Arietis in Consecratione Sacerdotum. 10. Oblatio Vituli & Hirci. 11. Sacrificium vaccæ rufæ. 12. Agnus Paschalis.

Quæ species simul omnes rursum ad certa & distincta genera revocantur. Vetus namq; est, & non usq; adeò (uti aliquibus videtur) incommoda Distributio, quâ singulæ istæ species in duo genera dispescuntur: nempè ad Sanctissima; & ad sancta vulgaria. Sanctissima autem dicebantur ea, quæ in latere Altaris Aquilonari mactabantur, & aut totâ igni absumebantur, vel in Altari, vel extra castra, sive urbem: aut licèt non tota cremarentur, nemini tamen de reliquis vesci fas erat, exceptis solis Sacerdotibus, & quidem in loco sancto.

Sancta vulgaria appellabantur, quæ in quovis loco atrij mactabantur: & de quorum reliquijs vesci licebat non tantùm Sacerdotibus, sed & familiæ eorum, imò & alijs juxta legem mundatis sive purificatis.

Sanctissima Sacrificia, uti appellantur, haud incommodè, secundum Sacrificiorum materiam, rursus in duas classes possunt subdividi: Quarum prior ea in se comprehendit Sacrificia, quæ ex Animantibus brutis offerebantur: Qualia erant, 1. Holocaustum. 2. Oblatio pro peccato. 3. Oblatio pro delicto. 4. Sacrificium Consecrationis Sacerdotum. 5. Vacca ruffa. 6. Sacrificium expiationis. Posterior vero classis ea complectitur Sacrificia, quæ fiebant ex Adoreo: ut est Sacrificium Minha, cuj9 tres sunt species, simila, panis, spicæ.

Ad sancta vulgaria pertinet 1. Sacrificium Pacificorum, vel salutis: quod sub se comprehendit Sacrificium Confessionis sive laudis, & Votum spontaneum: 2. Oblatio primitiarum. 3. Oblatio Primogenitorum. 4. Oblatio Decimarum. 5. Oblatio Agni Paschalis.

De singulis hisce Sacrificijs Leviticis in specie monstrandum, quidnám quodlibet sit, & quo ritu fuerit offerendum: nam hoc Quartum Sacrificiorum est παρακολούθημα, ut nimirùm non ex certâ duntaxat materiâ: sed etiam certo quodam ritu offerantur. Ordine autem progrediar.

I. Igitur HOLOCAUSTUM, Hebraicè Olah, ab Alah afcendit, Quod nimirùm totum in altari afcendit, seu absumitur. 1. Holocaustum fuit Sacrificium, in quo, ex sententiâ Philonis, honorandi, atque adeò etiam propitiandi DEI gratia, tota hostia, quæ offerebatur, igne in Altari consumebatur, & veluti à terris in cœlum cum fumo admandabatur in odorem suavitatis DEO: neque quicquam de ea eo relinquebatur, praeter pellem, quae erat Sacerdotis. Fiebat autem hoc Sacrificium vel ex Armentis, ut sunt Bos & Vitulus: Uterq; autem immaculatus, masculus, integer. Levit. 1, 3. Vel ex Ovium aut Caprarum grege, ut sunt Aries, Caper, Hircus, Integer, masculus, Levit. 1, 3. Vel ex Avibus, ut sunt Turtures, pulli Columbarum. Lev. 1, 14.

2. Holocausti species est JUGE SACRIFICIUM ὁλοκαύτωμα ἐνδελεχὲς, Hebr: Olath Thamid, quod quotidiè erat repetendum. Singulis enim diebus, unum agnum manè, & unum agnum vesperi DEO offerri oportebat. Num. 28, 2.

II. Oblatio pro peccato, eo videlicet, quod per ignorantiam erat admissum Lev. 4, 1, & seqq. cap. 5, 1. & seqq. Hebr. Chataah à Chatah peccavit, & Chatta, expiavit peccatum.

Fuerunt autem duae species Hostiarum pro peccato. Quorundam enim animalium pro peccatis oblatorum sangvis non inferebatur in Tabernaculum Testimonij: & horum carnibus vesci licebat Sacerdotibus. Levit. 6, 26. c. 10, 17. Quorundam autem Sangvis inferebatur in Sancta: & horum carnes, pelles, caput &c. extra castra cremabantur, nec licebat Sacerdotibus de illis edere quicquam. Lev. 4, 4. 11.

Offerebatur pro peccato vel 1. Pontificis, vel 2. Totius populi, vel 3. Principis, vel 4. Privati hominis. Pro Pontificis & populi peccatis offerebatur Vitulus ad ostium Tabernaculi, Levit. 4, 1. & 13. Pro peccato verò Principis offerebatur Hircus. Levit. 4, 22. & 23. Pro peccatis privati hominis, si dives fuerat, offerenda erat Capra, Ovis, Foemella integra: Levit. 4, 27. & seqq. Sin mediocris fortunae fuerat, offerebantur vel duo Turtures, vel duo pulli columbarum. Levit. 5, 7. Sin pauper erat, offerre debebat similae partem Ephae decimam. Levit. 5, 11.

Philo Judaeus de Sacrificio isto sic scriptum reliquit: Sacrificium pro peccato nuncupatum variatur & personis & hostijs: personis, ut Pontificis, populi, principis, privati: Hostijs verò, vitulo, hirco, capra vel agna. Vacca quoq; offerebatur ab ijs, qui per Ignorantiam peccarunt, vel scientes quidem, sed mutatâ voluntate factum suum damnant, & vitam meliùs instituunt.

III. Oblatio pro delicto, scilicet ἐκ προαιρέσεως destinato consilio & voluntate admisso. Hebr. אָשָׁם Ascham: Delictum, sive Hostia pro delicto, seu piaculum.

Pro peccati hujus expiatione Lex non tantùm Hostiam, verùm etiam mulctaritiam pecuniam, aut aliam poenam exigebat. Erat autem hic simul offerendus Aries. Levit. 5, 15. & 16. cap. 6, 1. ad 8. cap. 7, 1. ad 10.


### On Sacrifices: IV. Sacrifice of Consecration, or Perfection-

IV. Sacrifice of Consecration, or Perfection-

fection, by which Sacrifice priests were consecrated. Of this there were three Sacrifices: 1. A calf for sin, by which the Altar of Burnt Offering was purged and sanctified. Exod. 29, 10. Levit. 8, 14. 2. A ram for a burnt offering. Exod. 29, 15. Levit. 8, 18. 3. A ram of fillings, which was called a Sacrifice of thanksgiving, or of peace offerings, because it had almost similar ceremonies to the Sacrifice of peace offerings, or of the sacrificed. Lev. 8, 22. Exod. 29, 31.

V. Sacrifice of Purification, which concerned the defilement of a woman in childbirth, a leper, a man with an issue of seed, and a menstruating woman. Concerning the purification of a woman in childbirth. Levit. 12, throughout the whole chapter. Concerning purification, it is treated in chapters 13 and 14 of Leviticus. Concerning a man with an issue of seed, Lev. 15, from v. 2 to 16. Concerning a woman suffering from a menstrual flow of blood, Levit. 15, from v. 19 to the very end.

VI. Sacrifice of the red heifer, which was to be burned outside the camp, and its ashes were to be kept for the use of the water of purification, by which they were to be cleansed and purified, if any were unclean according to the Levitical rite. Num. 19, 7.

VII. Sacrifice of Expiation, in which was expiated 1. The High Priest with his house, where a calf was offered. 2. The Tabernacle of the testimony. 3. The Altar of Incense. 4. The whole Israelite Church. And in these three cases two goats were offered. Levit. 16, throughout the whole chapter.

VIII. Sacrifice Minhah, or food sacrifice, or meal offering, or libation, from a cake. Of which there were three species:

1. Fine flour, or most clean meal, not yet baked, the rite of which is described in Lev. 2, 1. In the Minhah not only flour and bread were offered, but a measure of oil, wine, salt, and incense was also added. Lev. 2, 1. and following. Num. 15, 4. and 5.

2. Bread or a cake baked from clean flour without leaven, Lev. 2, 4. To this also pertains the Sacrifice of Jealousy, concerning which Num. 5, 14.

3. Ears of corn, or grains of the firstfruits, which had not yet been ground into flour: These were offered roasted with fire with oil and frankincense. Lev. 2, 14. & 15.

To the sacrifices of living creatures also, their legitimate Minhah had to be added. Num. 14, 8. & 9. & ch. 28, 9. & ch. 29, 3.

IX. Sacrifice of Peace-offerings or Eucharistic, which, as Luther translates, Danckopffer. Levit. 3, 7. 10. In Hebrew Zebah Schalomin. Gr. ϑυσία σωτηρία : also ἐιρηνικὴ. [A species of this, I. Thodah. תוֹדָה, ϑυσία ἀινέσεως, Sacrifice of Confession and Praise: Which was as it were a Minhah or food sacrifice, always to be joined to the peace-offering: in which was to be offered, either of the oxen male or female, or of the sheep, or of the goats. Lev. 3, 1.

II. Spontaneous vow: which was offered with the same rite as the former, Lev. 3. through chapter 7, 16.

Origen, Homily V, proves that this was a twofold sacrifice, from ch. 3 of Leviticus: One of Confession, or Praise: The other of a spontaneous vow. From which it is elicited that this sacrifice was offered when they either prayed to GOD for peace or salvation, or, having obtained it, praised Him and gave Him thanks. But in both, there was to be offered either a male or a female, whether of the oxen, or of the sheep, or of the goats: But so that the fat only was burned for a sweet-smelling savor to God: the breast, however, and the shoulder were the priest's: the remaining flesh, however, was to be eaten by private individuals. The manner of offering is described through the entire chapter 3 of Leviticus. Also chapter 7, from v. 11 to 34. And chapter 10, 14. & 15.

X. Offering of firstfruits. Now those were called firstfruits which first arose for anyone, whether from men, or from animals, or from the seed of the earth. But the firstfruits can conveniently be divided into two species, of which the former was offered by Law, the latter by Vow: but both fell to the use of the Priests. Concerning the firstfruits of the law, God Himself commanded Exod. 22, 29. & 30. Num. 5, 9. & 10.

Concerning the Votive firstfruits, God, speaking to Aaron and the Levites, prescribed certain precepts. Num. 18, 11. to 15.

But those Precepts concerning the offering of firstfruits can conveniently be divided into General and Special. The General ones may be seen in Exod. 13, 1. 22, 29. 23. 19. The Special ones, however, regard those certain species of firstfruits to be offered defined by God: of which six especially present themselves.

1. The firstborn of men and animals, which how they were to be redeemed for a certain price, is evident from ch. 18 of Num. from v. 15 to 19.

2. Novalia, or the first-fruits of new crops, just born from the earth. Concerning which see Deut. 26, from v. 2 to 12.

3. Sheaves of ears of corn: which were to be offered on the second day of the Passover, Levit. 23, from v. 10 to 15.

4. Grains beaten out of ears still green, which had not yet been ground into flour. Lev. 2, 14 & 15.

5. Two leavened loaves. Concerning the two tenths of fine flour leavened, at the feast of Pentecost. Levit. 23, from v. 16 to 19.

6. Cakes, or pottages and foods. Num. 16, 19, 20, 21.

XI. The Offering of Tithes. Tithes were the tenth part of all the fruits which the Israelite people counted out from the land and from their cattle every year. These Tithes, however, were partly offered to God, and partly pertained to the use of the Priests. Exod. 22, 29. Lev. 27, 30, 31, 32.

But St. Jerome in his Commentary on Ezekiel established four kinds of Tithes from the law of Moses: One, which the people gave to the Levites, for the preservation and sustenance of the Ministers. Num. 18, 21 to 25. Deut. 14, 22 to 28.

A second, which the Levites gave to the Priests from their own tithes. Num. 18, 26, 27, 28.

A third, which every one of the people of Israel set aside in his own barns, so that he might eat it, traveling every year to the Temple in its vestibule, and might invite the Priests and Levites to a feast. Deut. 12, 11, 12 & 17. chap. 14, 22 to 28. It is to be noted, however, that there are some who disagree with St. Jerome in this part, and contend that this third tithe is the same as the first: who also assert that it was lawful to take something from the first tithes and to feast with the Levites in the temple. We certainly do not disapprove of their opinion in all respects: but so that, in the meantime, we rather praise and follow the accuracy of Jerome in distinguishing the tithes. The fourth tithe was that which was stored up, not every year, but every third year, for the sustenance of the poor. Deut. 14, 28 & 29.

XII. The Sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb: concerning the rite of which see Exodus 12, from verse 2 to 15. At what time of the year it was celebrated by the Jews is indeed a grave question, its decision difficult, and not so much because of God's command as because of the immense discrepancy among interpreters. But nevertheless, from approved authors I shall repeat in few words those things which seem to contain the truer opinion. In the beginning, therefore, you will observe that the year before Moses began from the autumn equinox, in the month of September, with the Sun being in Libra: just as Joseph Scaliger confirms this with many most evident reasons in book 3 of De emendatione temporum, page 152, edition of Frankfurt, A.D. 1593. But that God himself later gave the command to Moses, Exodus 12:2. This month shall be for you the beginning of months: it shall be the first in the months of the year, so that they might begin the year from that month in which the people had gone out from Egypt: which was then the first month, but afterwards was called Nisan, and corresponds to the March of the Romans, and contained the vernal equinox. Whence the same month is called in Exodus 13:4 the month of new fruits: And Deuteronomy 16:1, the Lord himself says: observe the month of new fruits, and of the first of the spring time, so that you may perform the Passover. Now this month was called so for this reason, because in Egypt and Syria the crops began to ripen in the month of March: as Philo testifies, book 3 of The Life of Moses.

The Passover, therefore, was to be celebrated on the fourteenth moon, or day of the month of March, in the evening, when individual families would kill a lamb for themselves and eat it roasted with unleavened bread.

The following day, namely the fifteenth, was called both the Passover and the first of the Unleavened Bread: Then the seventh day from that, namely the twenty-first, was the seventh of the unleavened bread, which they named the Assembly, because they were reaping and gathering the fruits of the earth. But since a feast day among the Jews began from the evening, therefore they began to celebrate the Passover on the fourteenth day, and finished on the fifteenth: which we have just said is called both the Passover and the first of the unleavened bread: as Luke teaches in chapter 22:1 and 7, Mark chapter 14:1 and 12. See more in Sigonius, De Republica Hebraeorum, pp. 631 and 632.

The fifth and final result of the sacrifices instituted by God as an end, which can be given in many ways; such as, that they were a kind of material around which the Israelite people might declare both their obedience and gratitude to God: that by this arrangement the ministry of the Priests and Levites had to be sustained: that they distinguished the Jewish Church from the gatherings and worship of the infidel Gentiles: that they were a kind of bond of public gatherings: That they bore the type of that unique sacrifice truly Propitiatory, offered by Christ for the sin of the whole world on the Altar of the Cross: Concerning which end the Psalmist discourses in Psalm 40:7, 8, 9. [Thus in the person of Christ, speaking words to God the Heavenly Father: Sacrifice

& offering you did not desire: But you have fashioned ears for me: Burnt offering and sin offering you did not ask for: Then I said: Behold I come, in the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will, my God, I have willed, and your law is in the midst of my heart.]

Moreover, the first and principal end was the confirmation of faith in the coming Messiah, who alone is the propitiation for sins: Just as the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11:4, affirms concerning Abel, that by his sacrifice he raised up his faith, through which he obtained testimony of righteousness.

A double scruple arises here: The former, whether those Levitical uncleannesses, which were to be expiated through sacrifices, were in themselves and by their own nature sins and uncleannesses: the latter, whether the Levitical sacrifices truly expiated those uncleannesses? To both of which I answer distinctly: And indeed, regarding the former, I state thus, that those uncleannesses were not in themselves and by their own nature sins: nor was anyone before God in conscience polluted for that reason, because he had touched a dead body, or a woman in childbirth, or a menstruating woman: or because he had entered a house in which there was a corpse of a dead man, etc. Just as today nothing contaminates a man that enters into the mouth, as the Savior testifies in Matthew 15:11. But these were sins by reason of disobedience and transgression of the divine law. For because God prescribed not only a moral but also a ceremonial law to his people, and willed that both be observed holily, and indeed in the Ceremonial law defined that those were to be held as unclean who had touched a thing unclean according to this Ceremonial law: and therefore, violating this law, he involved himself in the guilt of sin, not indeed through the contact of those things, but through disobedience and transgression of the divine command.

Latin:

IV. Sacrificium Consecrationis, sive Perfectio-

fectionis, quo Sacrificio Sacerdotes consecrabantur. Hujus tria erant Sacrificia: 1. Vitulus pro peccato, quo Altare Holocausti purgbatur, & sanctificabatur. Exod, 29, 10. Levit. 8, 14. 2. Aries in holocaustum. Exod. 29, 15 Levit. 8, 18. 3. Aries impletionū, quod vocabatur Sacrificiū Gratiarum actionis, sive pacificorum, proptereà, quòd similes fermè ceremonias habebat Sacrificio pacificorum, vel sacrificatorum Lev. 8, 22. Exod. 29, 31.

V. Sacrificium Mundationis, quod spectabat labem puerperæ, leprosi, viri scminiflui & mulieris menstruatæ. De Mundatione puerperæ. Levit. 12. per totum caput. De mundatione agitur capitibus Levitici 13 & 14. De viro seminifluo, Lev. 15. à v. 2. ad 16. De muliere menstruum sangvinis fluxum patiente Levit. 15, à v. 19. ad finem usq́;.

VI. Sacrificium vaccæ rufæ, quæ extra castra fuit comburenda, ejusq́; cineres servandi in usum aquæ mundationis, quâ lustrarentur, & immundarentur, si qui juxta Leviticum ritum erant immundi. Num. 19, 7.

VII. Sacrificium Expiationis, in quo expiabatur 1. Summus Pontifex cum suâ domo, ubi offerebatur Vitulus. 2. Tabernaculum testimonij. 3. Altare Thymiamatis. 4. Tota Ecclesia Israëlitica. Et in his tribus casibus offerebantur Duo Hirci. Levit. 16. per totum caput.

VIII. Sacrificium Minhah, sive Sacrificium cibarium, vel mola, vel libatio, à libo. Cujus tres erant species:

1. Simila, sive farina mundissima, nondùm coacta, cujus ritus describitur Lev. 2, 1. In Minhah non offerebatur tantùm farina & panis, sed addebatur etiam mensura olei, vini, salis, & thuris. Lev. 2, 1. & seqq. Num. 15, 4. & 5.

2. Panis sive placenta ex farinâ mundâ sine fermento coacta, Lev. 2, 4. Huc pertinet etiam Sacrificium Zelotypiæ, de quo Num. 5, 14.

3. Spicæ, sive grana primitiarum, quæ nondum in farinam contrita erant: Hæc igne tosta cum oleo & thure offerebantur. Lev. 2, 14. & 15.

Sacrificijs quoq́; animantium sua legitima Minhah addenda erat. Num. 14, 8. & 9. & cap. 28, 9. & cap. 29, 3.

IX. Sacrificium Pacificorum sive Evcharisticum, Quod, ut Lutherus vertit Danckopffer. Levit, 3, 7. 10. Hebraicè Zebah Schalomin. Gr. ϑυσία σωτηρία : item ἐιρηνικὴ. [Hujus species, I. Thodah. תוֹדָה, ϑυσία ἀινέσεως, Sacrificium Confessionis & Laudationis: Quod fuit velut Minhah seu cibarium Sacrificium, semper jungendum Sacrificio pacificorũ: in quo offerendus erat, vel de bobus mas vel fœmina, vel de ovibus, vel de capris. Lev. 3, 1.

II. Votum spontaneum: quod eodem ritu offerebatur, quo prius, Lev. 3. per caput 7, 16.

Origenes Homilia V. duplex hoc fuisse Sacrificium, ex c. 3. Levitici comprobat: Unum Confessionis, sive Laudis: Alterum voti spōtanei. Ex quo elicitur, Sacrificium hoc oblatũ fuisse, cùm aut DEUM pro pace aut salute orarunt, aut eâ impetrata laudarunt, & gratias ei egerunt. In utroq́; verò offerendus erat sive masculus, sive fœmina, vel de bobus, vel de ovibus, vel de capris: Sed ita ut adeps solùm cremaretur in odorem suavitatis Deo : pectus autem & armus essent Sacerdotis: reliquæ verò carnes ederentur à privatis. Modus offerendi describitur per integrum caput 3. Levit. Item cap. 7. à v. 11. ad 34. Et cap. 10, 14. & 15.

X. Oblatio primitiarum. Dicebantur autem primitiæ, quæ cuiq; primùm, sive ex hominib9, sive ex animalibus, sive ex semine terræ orta sunt. Possunt verò Primitiæ commodè in duas species dispesci, quarum prior offerebatur ex Lege, posterior ex Voto : utraq; autem in usum Sacerdotum cedebat. De primitijs legis præcepit ipse Deus Exod. 22, 29. & 30. Num. 5, 9. & 10.

De primitijs Votivis ad Aaronem & Levitas loquens Deus, certa præcepta præscripsit. Num. 18, 11. ad 15.

Possunt autem Præcepta illa de offerendis primitijs commodè dispesci in Generalia & Specialia. Generalia videre licet Exod. 13, 1. 22, 29. 23. 19. Specialia verò respiciunt certas illas à Deo definitas Primitiarum offerendarum species: quarum sex potissimùm sese offerunt.

1. Primogenita hominum & animalium, quæ quomodo certo pretio redimenda fuerint, patet ex cap. 18. Num. à v. 15. ad 19.

2. Novalia, sive primitiæ novarum frugũ, terrâ modò natarum. De quibus Deut. 26. à v. 2. ad 12.

3. Manipuli Spicarum: qui erant offerendi die altero Paschæ Levit. 23. à v. 10. ad 15.

4. Grana de spicis adhuc virentib9 expulsa, quæ nondũ in farinam erant contrita. Lev. 2, 14. & 15.

5. Duo panes fermentati. De duabus decimis similæ fermentatæ, in festo Pentecostes. Levit. 23. à v. 16. ad 19.

6. Placentæ, sive pulmenta & cibi. Num. 16, 19. 20. 21.

XI. Oblatio Decimarum. Decimæ erant pars decima omnium fructuum, quos singulis annis populus Israëliticus è terrâ & pecudibus numerabat. Hæ autem Decimæ partim offerebantur Deo, partim ad usum Sacerdotum pertinebant. Exod. 22, 29. Lev. 27, 30, 31. 32.

Constituit verò D. Hieronymus in Commentario super Ezechielem quatuor species Decimarum ex lege Mosis: Unam, quam populus Levitis dabat, ad conservationem & sustentationem Ministrorum. Num. 18, 21. ad 25. Deut. 14, 22. ad 28.

Alteram, quam ex suis decimis Levitæ dabant Sacerdotibus. Num. 18, 26, 27. 28.

Tertiam, quam unusquisq; de populo Israel in suis horreis separabat, ut comederet eam, proficiscens quotannis ad Templum in vestibulo ejus, & Sacerdotes ac Levitas invitaret ad convivium Deut. 12, 11. 12. & 17. cap. 14, 22. ad 28. Notandum verò esse quosdam, qui à D. Hieronymo hac in parte dissentiunt, & tertiam hanc decimam eandem esse cum primâ contendunt: qui & licitum fuisse asserunt, ex primis decimis aliquid sumere, & cum Levitis in templo epulari. Quorum sanè sententiam non per omnia improbamus: sed ita, ut interim Hieronymi in distinguendis decimis ἀκρίβειαν magis & laudemus, & sequamur. Quarta decima fuit, quæ non singulis annis, sed tertio quoq; recondebatur, ad sustentationem pauperum. Deut. 14, 28. & 29.

XII. Sacrificium Agni paschalis: de cujus ritu Exod. 12. à v. 2. ad 15. Qui, quo anni tempore à Judæis celebratus fuerit, gravis sanè est quæstio, difficilis ejus decisio, & non tam propter DEI mandatum, quàm propter ingentem interpretum discrepantiam. Sed tamen ex autoribus probatis ea paucis repetam, quæ veriorem sententiam continere videntur. Initiò igitur observabis, Annum antè Moysen incepisse, ab æquinoctio autumni, mense Septembri, Sole existente in Librâ: quemadmodum multis evidentissimis rationibus hoc confirmat Josephus Scaliger lib. 3. de emendat. temporum pag. 152. Edit: Francofurt. A. 1593. Ipsum verò DEUM postmodùm mandasse Moysi, Exod. 12, 2. Mensis iste vobis erit principium mensium: primus erit in mensibus anni, ut Annum ordirentur ab eo mense, quo ex Ægypto egressus esset populus: qui tùm primus mensis, posteà autem Nisan appellatus fuit, & Romanorum Martio respondet, Vernumq; æquinoctium continuit. Undè idem mensis Exod. 13, 4. Mensis novarum frugum est dictus: Et Devter. 16, 1. ipse dicit Dominus: observa mensem novarum frugum, & Verni primum temporis, ut facias Phase. Sic autem mensis iste ideò appellabatur, quoniam in Ægypto & Syriâ mense Martio segetes mature-scere incipiebant: uti testantur Philo, lib. 3. de vitâ Moysis.

Pascha igitur celebrandum fuit quartâ decimâ Lunâ, sive die mensis Martij ad vesperam, cum singulæ familiæ sibi agnum occiderent, & assatum cum azymis comederent.

Dies autem sequens, nempè decimâ quintâ, & Pascha, & prima Azymorum vocabatur: Indè dies septima ab illâ, nempè vicesimâ primâ, erat septima azymorum, quam Collectam nominabant, quia fruges terræ metebant, & colligebant. Quoniam autem dies festus apud Judæos incipiebat à Vespere, ideò die decimâ quartâ Pascha celebrare incipiebant, & in quintâ decimâ desinebant: Quam & Pascha, & primam azymorum appellari modò diximus: sic docente Lucâ cap. 22, 1. & 7. Marco cap. 14, 1 & 12. Plura vide apud Sigonium de Repub. Hebr. p. 631. & 632.

Quitum, & postremum Sacrificiorum ἀποτέλεσμα est Sacrificiorum à DEO institutorum ut finis, qui multiplex dari potest; ut, quòd fuerunt materia quasi quædam, circa quam populus Israëliticus suam DEO & obedientiam & gratitudinem declararet: quòd hoc pacto ministerium Sacerdotum & Levitarum sustentari debuit: quòd distinxerunt Ecclesiam Judaicam ab infidelium Gentium congressibus, & cultu: quòd fuerunt vinculum quasi quoddam publicorum congressuum: Quòd gesserunt typum unici illius Sacrificij verè Propitiatorij, â CHRISTO, pro peccati totius mundi, in Altari Crucis oblati: De quo fine disserit Psaltes Psal. 40, 7. 8. 9. [Sic in personâ CHRISTI, ad DEUM patrem Cœlestem verba faciens: Sacrificium

& oblationem noluisti : Aures autem perfecisti mihi : Holocaustum & pro peccato non postulasti : Tunc dixi: Ecce venio, in capite libri de me est scriptum, ut facerem voluntatem tuam, Deus meus, volui, & legem tuam in medio cordis mei.]

Cæterùm primus & principalis finis fuit confirmatio fidei in venturum Messiam, qui solus sit propitiatio pro peccatis : Quemadmodum Epistola ad Hebr. cap. 11, 4. de Abele affirmat, quòd Sacrificio suo fidem suam erexerit, per quam testimonium justitiæ sortitus sit.

Geminus hîc oritur scrupulus : Prior. An immundicies istæ Leviticæ, quæ per Sacrificia expiandæ erant, per se & suâ naturâ fuerint peccata & immundiciæ : posterior, An Sacrificia Levitica verè istas immundicias expiaverint? ad quemutrumq; distinctè respondeo : Et quidem, Quoad priorem, sic statuo, Immundicies istas per se, & suâ naturâ non fuisse peccata : neq; quenquam coram Deo in conscientiâ ideò fuisse pollutum, quia attigisset mortuum, aut puerperam, aut menstruatam : aut quia ingressus esset domum, in quâ erat cadaver hominis mortui &c. Quemadmodum hodiéq; nihil contaminat hominem, quòd intrat in os, teste Servatore Matth. 15, 11. Verùm peccata isthæc fuerunt ratione inobedientiæ, & transgressionis legis divinæ. Quiâ enim Deus non moralem duntaxat, sed & ceremonialem legem populo suo præscripsit, & utramq; sanctè observari voluit, & verò in Ceremoniali lege definivit, pro immundis habendos esse, qui rem, secundum legem hanc Ceremonialem immundam, attigerit : ideoq; legem hanc violans, peccati reatu sese implicabat, non quidem per attactum istarum rerum, sed per inobedientiam & transgressionem mandati divini.


### On Sacrifices: IV. Sacrifice of Consecration, or Perfection- (continued)

Regarding the latter scruple, it must likewise be stated that neither to the High Priests nor to their sacrifices is the power of expiating sins attributed in themselves, or from the dignity of the person sacrificing, or from the work performed by the victims: as the Hypocrites falsely persuaded themselves, whose opinion the Lord refutes everywhere through the Prophets, Isaiah 1:11 and following, Hosea 6:6, Micah 6:7, Psalm 50:13 and 14. But that power is attributed to the High Priests and their victims only typically, under the aspect of Type and shadow, insofar as they indeed foreshadowed that true and unique High Priest and mediator Christ Jesus, and his most holy victim, by which he offered himself to God for an odor of sweet fragrance, and by this his one sacrifice makes perfect those who are sanctified. And thus the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews teaches, chapter 10:4: It is impossible, he says, for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. And verse 1. The Law had a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things. Likewise ch. 8, 5. The priests served the copy and shadow of heavenly things. Moreover, ch. 9, 13 & 14 expressly teaches that the Levitical victims, and the blood of bulls and of goats, were effective only for the purifying of the flesh, not for sanctification, or the sprinkling of the consciences themselves: which is that which is proper to the Sacrifice of CHRIST. And certainly there is no doubt that the pious and those studious of the divine law truly understood that the Sacrifices did not take away sins except τυπικῶς, that is, by reason of the Sacrifice of Christ to be performed at some time. For they knew that GOD himself had testified that he wished to be appeased by the blood of victims. But they also knew that other thing, that GOD again expressly affirms that he is not delighted by Sacrifices. These two passages, since they seemed to conflict with each other in appearance, had to be reconciled in such a way that the people were taught that by the latter assertion it is noted that the Sacrifices, neither by their own power and nature, nor by the work performed, have any value for appeasing GOD: but by the former proposition, that GOD testifies that in those victims and the offering of the same, the promised Messiah himself is proposed to be looked upon, and his Sacrifice, in which alone, apprehended by faith, the Remission of sins comes to the pious and the faithful. As many, therefore, as seriously considered this doctrine, they certainly believed that GOD could be appeased not by the victims, but by Christ, shadowed forth through the victims. And although it may seem to stand in the way of what has been said, that the Jews are never read to have expressly invoked Christ in the Sacrifices, that they never prayed for the Remission of sins through and on account of the Messiah: yet it is not an obstacle at all, because it is clear even from this that they did this: As often as they prayed: Remember O Lord the covenant which you struck with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and also with David: so often they recalled to their memory the promises made to those Fathers, concerning the seed in whom all nations would be blessed, that is, concerning Christ, just as Paul interprets in Galatians 3:16. Thus Solomon certainly prayed in 2 Chronicles 6:42: Lord GOD, remember the mercies of David your servant. Thus David in Psalm 105:8 & 9: GOD mindful of his covenant for ever, which he arranged to Abraham, and of his oath to Isaac. Thus the Jews prayed, 2 Maccabees 4:10: Now we cry to heaven, and the Lord will have mercy on us, and will be mindful of the Testament of our Fathers. And since these Levitical Sacrifices served as a type of the future Sacrifice of Christ, it is most rightly concluded that they are now abolished, that having been accomplished. And this very thing can be most evidently proven not only from the New Testament, but also from the Old, against the impious opinion of the Jews, both ancient and more recent, who dreamed that the Levitical Priesthood and its Sacrifices would last forever. For thus in Jeremiah 3:15 & 16, the Lord says: I will give you Pastors according to my heart, who will feed you with knowledge and doctrine: And when you have multiplied in the land, they will no longer speak of the ark of the Testament of the covenant, nor will it ascend upon the heart, nor will they remember it, nor will it be visited, nor will it be sacrificed any more. Whence Daniel also predicted, chapter 9:27, that the covenant having been confirmed by the Messiah, the Sacrifice and the offering would be abrogated. What of the fact that when the Jews, Christ having already been exhibited, nonetheless continued to sacrifice, GOD in reality put an end to the Sacrifices, while he allowed that place to be utterly overturned, to which alone it was permitted to sacrifice according to the prescription of the law.

Those reasons and arguments which are constructed from the very nature of the Sacrifices confirm this further and quite invincibly. Let this therefore be the first argument: If the Levitical Priesthood and its Sacrifices had been destined to last forever, and consequently could have rendered men perfected, that is, just and holy before GOD, and conferred perfection: then there would have been no need for another Priesthood to be promised, different in kind from that Levitical one. But GOD promised both a new High Priest and another Priesthood, which would not be according to the order of Aaron, but the order of Melchizedek, Psalm 110:4: The Lord has sworn, and it will not repent him: You are a Priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek. Therefore that Levitical or Aaronic Priesthood, as imperfect and invalid for conferring justice, had to be abolished.

A second argument: If the Levitical Priesthood had been destined to last forever: then certainly it could not have been transferred from the tribe of Levi to another, just as Jeroboam is indeed most gravely rebuked on this account, appointing priests not from the tribe of Levi, but from the tribes of Israel, 1 Kings 12:31. But in truth GOD himself willed that a translation of the Priesthood be made from the tribe of Levi to the tribe of Judah. Therefore that Levitical Priesthood with its entire worship had to be abrogated. All those testimonies of the Prophets and Psalms confirm the assumption, which indeed predicted that the Messiah, that new High Priest and true Priest, would arise not from the tribe of Levi, but from the tribe of Judah: and that to this new Priest finally, born from the tribe of Judah, an eternal Priesthood was decreed and promised by GOD, even through an oath. Genesis 49:10. 2 Samuel 7:12 and following. Psalm 89 through almost the entire Psalm. Isaiah 11:1, 2 & 10. Ezekiel 34:23, 24. Psalm 110:4. Zechariah 6:13.

This abrogation of the Levitical Sacrifices demonstrates that the Priesthood and Sacrifice of CHRIST are more excellent than those Levitical ones. For that by which something is abolished is always more excellent than that which is abolished. Now the first argument is such:

Whatever demands more priests through succession, on account of their fragility, being subject to death: that is more imperfect than that which has one priest, and such a one indeed who lives forever, and who also offers a Unique Sacrifice, but such a one that is of eternal efficacy, and renders perfect all who are sanctified. But in truth Christ is an eternal High Priest, and from him there is no passage open to another successor. For although he died once for the propitiation of sin, not his own, but ours: yet now raised from the dead he does not die, nor does death have dominion over him any longer, Romans 6:9. But he lives and remains forever, exercising his Priesthood at the right hand of GOD the Father, and that indeed not an imperfect one, but a most perfect one: since, as the Epistle to the Hebrews testifies, he is able to save to the full those who believe, for whom he intercedes: Hebrews 7:25. Therefore Christ has a far more perfect, nay, a most perfect Priesthood and Sacrifice.

A second argument can be given as follows: Whoever is a High Priest so holy that he is plainly innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners: he is more perfect than one who is not holy in this way; indeed, he possesses both a more perfect Priesthood and Sacrifice. But CHRIST is such that no guile was ever found in his mouth, Isa. 53, 9, and he was undefiled and separated from sinners, Heb. 7, v. 26. Therefore CHRIST is more perfect than the priests of the Old Testament; indeed, he possesses a more perfect Priesthood than they, as they were indeed pious, holy, and even just, but only in an incipient way, and partly even by imputed justice and holiness, while they themselves, in their own persons and by reason of their nature, were not free from the stain of sin.

1. A third can be added, which is sought from the attributes of the priests of the Old Testament. For first, those priests were constituted by the law, which, as the Epistle to the Hebrews ch. 10, 1 teaches, had only a shadow of the good things to come: whence they are said to have served only the copy and shadow of heavenly things, Heb. 8, 5. But CHRIST was not constituted by the law of Moses, but by the Word of the Evangelical promise, Gen. 3, 15, ch. 12, 3, Deut. 18, 3, Jer. 3, 15 & 16. Which word is the fulfillment of the whole law, and therefore more excellent than the law itself.

2. Then the law constituted its priests without an oath. But Christ was constituted High Priest by an oath. Psalm 89, 4 & 36 & 110, 4.

3. Then the Law constituted as priests mortal men, subject to human infirmities, both of sin and of death. But the Word of the Gospel decrees the Priesthood to him who is not merely a man, but the Son of GOD himself, who, although he performed his Priesthood on the cross, still existing as mortal by his own free will, yet after the purification of sins was thus made by him, having laid aside that infirmity which he had taken upon himself for our sake, sin excepted, he sat down at the right hand of GOD.

4. Fourthly: The priests of the Old Testament served in a tabernacle made by hand, and afterwards destroyed again; into whose Holy of Holies the High Priest alone entered only once a year, namely on the feast of Atonement, but not without the blood of animals. But CHRIST has entered into the eternal tabernacle, namely into the heavens, and indeed with his own blood.

5. Fifthly: Whoever is the intercessor of a more excellent Testament, he also possesses a more excellent Priesthood. But Christ is the intercessor of a more excellent Testament than those Levitical High Priests were. Therefore, Christ's Sacrifice is also more excellent than the Levitical one. The Epistle to the Hebrews ch. 8, 6 proves the assumption from the fact that the New Testament was sanctioned by more distinguished promises: namely, no longer by shadows or figures, but by the open proclamation of the Gospel.

6. Sixthly: Whatever is eternal is more excellent than that which vanishes. But Christ's priest-

hood in the New Testament is eternal. Psalm 89, 5, 29 & 38. Heb. 7, 24. Finally: Whatever Priesthood has need of frequent reiteration, that is more imperfect than that which, once performed, ought not to be offered again, but obtains eternal efficacy. But such was the Levitical Priesthood, since its sacrifices had to be repeated every year at set times; on the contrary, however, CHRIST by his one Sacrifice has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. Heb. 10, v. 14. E.

These things having been thus explained, and it having been shown that Christ offered his Sacrifice once, and that it is eternal, it follows spontaneously: If one asks about a Propitiatory Sacrifice, whether a Propitiatory Sacrifice can or ought to be offered by Christian believers of the New Testament: that whoever presumes to do this confuses the Old Testament with the New, and annihilates the Sacrifice of CHRIST, since it is so perfect and absolute in every part that it can bear no addition: just as this is shown more fully in the Article of Justification.

But indeed, if the question is instituted concerning Eucharistic sacrifices; and the term of sacrifices is taken in this part with Scripture μεταφορικῶς, or in a transferred sense; then certainly the believers of the New Testament also have their sacrifices: such as are: 1. The ministry of the Gospel, Rom. 15, 16. 2. The conversion of the Gentiles, who embrace the Gospel through faith. Rom. ibid. Phil. 2, 17. 3. Prayers or orations. Heb. 5, 7. Apoc. 5, 8 & ch. 8, 3 & 4. 4. Praise and thanksgiving. Heb. 13, 15. 5. Beneficence toward the poor and toward the ministers of the word; Heb. 13, 16. Phil. 4, 18. 6. The mortification of the old man: indeed the whole man, when he is consecrated and devoted to GOD, so that he may die to the world and live to GOD, is called a sacrifice. Rom. 12, 1. Finally, generally, St. Peter calls all the worship of Christians spiritual sacrifices 1 Pet. 2, 5. And indeed these Eucharistic sacrifices of the New Testament are more pleasing to GOD than those Levitical ones were: as is evident from Psalm 50, from v. 8 to 16. And Psalm 69, 31 & 32.

Latin:

Quoad posteriorem scrupulum itidem statuendum est, neq; Pontificibus, neq; Sacrificijs illorum vim expiandi peccata tribui per se, vel ex dignitate personæ sacrificantis ; vel ex operi operato victimarum : uti falsò sibi persuadebant Hypocritæ, quorum opinionem passim per Prophetas redarguit Dominus Jes. 1, 11. & seqq. Hos. 6, 6. Mich. 6, 7. Psal. 50. 13. & 14. Verùm tribuitur vis illa & Pontificibus & eorum victimis non nisi τυπικῶς, sub ratione Typi & umbræ, quatenùs nimirùm adumbrabant verum illum & unicum Pontificem, ac mediatorem CHRISTUM JESUM, ejusq; Sacrosanctam victimam, quâ seipsum Deo obtulit in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ, suoq; hoc unico sacrificio perfectos efficit eos, qui sanctificantur. Atq; sic docet Autor Epistolæ ad Hebræos, cap. 10, 4: Impossibile, inquiens, est sangvine taurorum & hircorum auferri peccata. Et v. 1. Lex Umbram habuit futurorum bonorum, non ipsam rerum imaginem. Item cap. 8, 5. Sacerdotes deservierunt Exemplari & Umbræ rerum cœlestium. Quin & cap. 9, 13. & 14. disertè tradit, victimas Leviticas, & sangvinem taurorum & hircorum tantum ad carnis purificationem valuisse, non ad sanctificationem, aut asperfionem ipsarum conscientiarum: id quod proprium sit Sacrificij CHRISTI. Et certè nullum est dubium, quin pij, & studiosi legis divinæ verè intellexerint, Sacrificia non nisi τυπικῶς, hoc est, ratione Sacrificij Christi aliquando peragendi, delere peccata. Noverunt enim DEUM ipsum testatum esse, se placari velle sangvine victimarum. Noverunt autem & illud, DEUM rursus disertè affirmare, se Sacrificijs non delectari. Hæc duo loca, cùm specietenus inter se pugnarent, sic certè conciliari debuerunt, ut populus doceretur, posteriore assertione illud notari, quòd Sacrificia neq; suâ vi, & naturâ, neq; ex opere operato, ad placandum DEUM quicquam valeant: Priore vero propositione illud testari DEUM, in victimis illis, earundemq; oblatione conspiciendum proponi ipsum promissum Messiam, ejusdemq; Sacrificium, in quo solo, fide apprehenso, obveniat Remissio peccatorum pijs, & fidelibus. Quotquot igitur hanc doctrinam seriò considerabant, ij certè non ex victimis, sed ex Christo, per victimas adumbrato, placari posse DEUM crediderunt. Et licèt dictis obstare videatur, quòd Judæi Christum in Sacrificijs nunquàm expressè invocasse, quòd nunquàm Remissionem peccatorum per & propter Messiam orasse leguntur: Obstat tamen minimè, quod ipsos hoc fecisse, vel hinc sit perspicuum: Quoties orarunt: Memento Domine fœderis, quod cum Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo pepigisti, nec non cum Davide: toties in memoriam sibi revocabant promissiones Patribus illis factas, de semine, in quo benedicerentur omnes gentes, hoc est, de Christo, quemadmodum Paulus interpretatur Gal. 3, 16. Sic Salomon certè oravit 2. Paral. 6, 42. Domine DEUS, memento misericordiarum David servi tui. Sic David Psal. 105, 8. & 9. Memor DEUS testamenti sui in seculum, quod disposuit ad Abraham, & juramenti sui ad Isaac. Sic Judæi orabant, Maccab. 4, 10: Nunc clamamus in cœlum, & miserebitur nostri Dominus, & memor erit Testamenti Patrum nostrorum. Cumq; Sacrificia isthæc Levitica typum futuri Sacrificij Christi, gesserint, eadem nunc illo peracto antiquata, rectissimè colligitur. Et hoc ipsum non modò ex Novo Testamento: sed etiam ex Veteri, adversus impiam Judæorum tùm veterum, tùm recentiorum opinionem, qui Sacerdotium Leviticum, ejusdemq; Sacrificia perpetuò duratura somniabant, evidentissimè comprobari potest. Sic enim Jer. 3, 15. & 16. dicit Dominus: Dabo vobis Pastores juxta cor meum, qui pascant vos scientiâ & doctrinâ: Cumq; multiplicati fueritis in terrâ, non dicent ampliùs de arcâ Testimonij fœderis, neq; ascendet super cor, neq; recordabuntur illius, nec visitabitur, nec sacrificabitur ultrà. Undè Daniel quoq; prædixit, c. 9, 27. Confirmato per Messiam fœdere, abrogatum iri Sacrificium & hostiam. Quid, quòd cum Judæi, exhibito jam Christo, nihilo minus pergerent sacrificare, DEUS reipsâ finem Sacrificijs imposuit, dùm eú locum funditùs everti passus est, ad quem solum ex legis præscripto sacrificare licuit.

Confirmant id ulteriùs invictè prorsus eæ rationes & argumenta, quæ ex ipsâ naturâ Sacrificiorum extruuntur. Sit ergò hoc primum argumentum: Si Sacerdotium Leviticum, ejúsdemq; Sacrificia debuissent perpetuò durare, ac proindè potuissent consummatos reddere homines, hoc est, justos & sanctos coram DEO, & conferre perfectionem: tùm non opus fuisset, ut promitteretur Sacerdotium aliud, specie à Levitico illo diversum. Atqui DEUS promisit & Pontificem novum, & Sacerdotium aliud, quod non secundum ordinem Aaronis, sed Melchisedeci ordinem esset, Pf. 110, 4. Juravit Dominus, & non pœnitebit eum: Tu es Sacerdos in æternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Ergò Sacerdotium illud Leviticum, sive Aaronicum, velut imperfectum, & ad conferendam justitiam invalidum, fuit antiquandum.

Argumentum alterum: Si Sacerdotium Leviticum perpetuò durare debuit: tùm certè non potuisset transferri, ex tribu Levi in aliam, Quemadmodum sanè hoc nomine gravissimè reprehenditur Jeroboamus, constituens Sacerdotes non ex tribu Levi, sed ex tribubus Israelis, 1.Reg.12,31. Atqui verò DEUS ipse voluit fieri translationem Sacerdotij ex tribu Levi, in tribum Juda. Ergò Leviticum illud Sacerdotium cum cultu suo universo abrogari debuit. Assumtionem confirmant universa illa Prophetarum & Psalmorum testimonia, quæ quidem prædixerunt, Messiam novum illum Pontificem, & verum Sacerdotem oriturum non de tribu Levi: sed de tribu Judâ: & huic demùm novo Sacerdoti ex tribu Judâ prognato, æternum Sacerdotium à DEO, mediante etiam juramento, decretum ac promissum esse. Gen. 49. 10. 2. Sam. 7, 12. & seqq. Psalmo 89. per integrum fermè Psalmum. Esaiæ, 11, 1.2. & 10. Ezech. 34, 23. 24. Psal. 110, 4. Zach. 6, 13.

Demonstrat hæc Sacrificiorum Leviticorum abrogatio, CHRISTI Sacerdotium & Sacrificium Leviticis illis esse præstantius. Semper enim illud, per quod aliquid aboletur, præstantius est abolito. Argumentum autem primum tale est:

Quicquid plures per successionem Sacerdotes, propter fragilitatem ipsorum, quippè morti obnoxiorum, flagitat: illud imperfectius est eo, quod unum habet Sacerdotem, & talem quidem, qui æternùm vivit, quiq; Unicum etiam offert Sacrificium, sed tale, quod æternæ est efficaciæ, & perfectos reddit omnes, qui sanctificantur. At verò Christus Pontifex est æternus, & ab hoc non ullus transitus ad alium succesiorem patet. Quamvis enim semel sit mortuus ad propitiationem peccati non sui, sed nostri: nunc tamen à mortuis suscitatus non moritur, nec mors illi ampliùs dominatur, Rom. 6, 9. Sed vivit & manet in æternum, fungens ad dextram DEI Patris Sacerdotio suo, & eo quidem non imperfecto, sed longè perfectissimo: fiquidem, teste Epistolâ ad Hebræos, ad plenum salvos facere potest credentes, pro quibus interpellat: Heb. 7, 25. Ergò Christus longè perfectius, îmò perfectissimum habet & Sacerdotium, & Sacrificium.

(Alterum argumentum tale dari potest: Quicunq; Pontifex ita est sanctus, ut planè sit innocens, impollutus, & à peccatoribus segregatus: ille perfectior est eo, qui hoc modo sanctus non est: imò perfectius habet & Sacerdotium & Sacrificium. Atqui CHRISTUS talis est, ut nullus unquàm dolus in ore ejus fuerit repertus, Esa. 53, 9. ut fuerit impollutus, & à peccatoribus segregatus. Hebr. 7. v. 26. Ergò CHRISTUS perfectior est Sacerdotibus veteris Testamenti: imò perfectius habet Sacerdotium, quàm illi: ut qui pij quidem, sancti & justi etiam fuerunt; sed inchoata duntaxat, partim etiam imputatâ justitiâ & sanctitate: ipsi interim per se, & ratione suæ naturæ peccati labe non carentes.

1. Tertium addi potest, quod ex attributis Sacerdotum Veteris Testamenti petitur. Primùm enim Sacerdotes illi constituti sunt per legem, quæ docente Epistolâ ad Hebræos cap. 10, 1. umbram duntaxat habuit futurorum bonorum: Undè Exemplari etiam duntaxat, & umbræ rerum cœlestium inservijsse dicuntur. Hebr. 8, 5. CHRISTUS autem non per legem Moysis: sed per Sermonem promissionis Evangelicæ, Gen. 3, 15. c. 12. 3. Deut. 18, 3. Jer. 3, 15. & 16. Qui sermo est totius legis complementum, ac proindè lege ipsâ præstantior.

2. Deindè lex sine Juramento suos constituit Sacerdotes. At Christus per Jusjurandum est constitutus Pontifex. Psalm. 89, 4. & 36. & 110, 4.

3. Tùm Lex Sacerdotes constituit homines mortales, & humanis infirmitatibus, tùm peccati, tùm mortis subjectis. At Sermo Evangelij ei decernit Sacerdotium, qui est non nudus duntaxat homo, sed ipsius DEI Filius, qui etsi Sacerdotium suum præstitit in cruce, mortalis adhùc ex liberâ voluntate existens: tamen postquàm sic purgatio peccatorum per ipsum facta est, depositâ infirmitate illâ, quam in se, excepto peccato, nostri causâ receperat, consedit ad dextram DEI.

4. Quartò: Sacerdotes Veteris Testamenti serviebant in tabernaculo manu facto, & postea rursum destructo: in cujus etiam Sancta Sanctorum solus Pontifex summus in anno semel duntaxat, nempè in festo Propitiationis, sed non absq; pecudum sangvine ingrediebatur. At CHRISTUS ingressus est in æternum tabernaculum, nempè in cœlos, & quidem proprio suo sangvine.

5. Quintò: Quicunq; Pontifex præstantioris Testamenti est intercessor, ille præstantiq quoq; habet Sacerdotium. Atqui Christus præstantioris Testamenti intercessor est, quàm fuerunt Levitici illi Pontifices. Ergò præstantius etiam Christi Sacrificium Levitico. Assumtionem probat epistola ad Hebr. cap. 8, 6. indè, quia Novum Testamentum sancitum fuit insignioribus promissionibus: non umbris videlicet ampliùs aut figuris, sed apertâ Evangelij annunciatione constantibus.

6. Sextò: Quicquid est æternum, præstantius est eo, quod evanescit. At Christi sacer-

dotium in Novo Testamento est æternum. Psal. 89, 5. 29. & 38. Hebr. 7, 24. Tandem: Quodcunq; Sacerdotium crebrâ reiteratione opus habet, illud imperfectius est eo, quod semel peractum offerri non ampliùs debet, sed æternam efficaciam obtinet. Atqui tale fuit Sacerdotium Leviticum, quippè cujus Sacrificia singulis annis statis temporibus debuerunt repeti: Contrà verò CHRISTUS unico suo Sacrificio in æternum perfecit sanctificandos. Hebr. 10. v. 14. E.

His ita explicatis, & ostenso, quod Christus Sacrificium suum semel obtulerit, idq; æternum; spontè sequitur; Si de Sacrificio Propitiatorio quæratur, tàm à Christianis fidelibus Novi Testamenti Sacrificium Propitiatorium offerri vel non posse, vel debere: ut qui hoc facere præsumat, is Vetus Testamentum cum Novo confundat: & Sacrificium CHRISTI annihilet, quippè quod ita ex omni parte est perfectum & absolutum, ut nullam additionem ferre possit: Quemadmodum in Articulo Justificationis fusiùs illud ostenditur.

At verò, si de Sacrificijs Eucharisticis instituatur quæstio; & Sacrificiorum terminus hâc in parte cum Scripturâ μεταφορικῶς, sive sensu translatitio accipiatur; tùm sanè fideles etiam Novi Testamenti sua habent Sacrificia: qualia sunt: 1. Ministerium Evangelij, Rom. 15, 16. 2. Conversio Gentium, per fidem amplectentium Evangelium. Rom. ibid. Phil. 2, 17. 3. Preces sive orationes. Hebr. 5, 7. Apoc. 5, 8. & cap. 8, 3. & 4. 4. Laus & gratiarum actio. Hebr. 13, 15. 5. Beneficentia in pauperes, & in Ministros verbi; Hebr. 13, 16. Phil. 4, 18. 6. Mortificatio veteris hominis: imò totus homo, quando DEO consecratur, & devovetur, ut mundo moriatur, & DEO vivat, vocatur Sacrificium. Rom. 12, 1. Tandem generaliter D. Petrus omnem cultum Christianorum nominat hostias spirituales 1. Pet. 2, 5. Et sanè hæc Eucharistica Novi Testamenti Sacrificia gratiora sunt DEO, quàm Levitica illa fuerunt: uti patet ex Psalmo 50, à v. 8. ad 16. Et Psal. 69, 31. & 32.


### Part Two of the Article concerning Sacrifices

Furthermore: there have always been very many, and today there are, who scatter various and erroneous opinions concerning this doctrine of Sacrifices. And at the beginning indeed there occur the Gentiles or Heathens, who, hearing of the Sacrifices of the Jews, through a certain impious κακοζηλίαν, devised various Sacrifices, which nevertheless, as Suidas warns, were divided by the Gentiles themselves into perfect and imperfect Sacrifices.

And indeed they called those Sacrifices perfect, in which they offered animals, nay (O the crime) even living men themselves and their own children, as can be seen in 2 Kings 3:27 concerning the king of the Moabites, who, being placed in straits, offered his own son as a burnt offering upon the wall. Which impiety later spread to the Jews themselves. Deut. 12:31, 2 Kings 16:3, chap. 21:6, where Achaz and Manasseh are read to have burned their sons in the fire.

They called those sacrifices imperfect which were offered from any vile and abject material: nay, even from parts of living creatures. Such sacrifices were those of the Phaselites, who sacrificed salted fish to Calabrus, as Callimachus testifies in his Barbaric Institutions, as is found in Suidas, page 950. Likewise the Nephalia sacrifices, θυσίας νηφάλιοι, in which wine was not drunk, but honeyed water, as Suidas again reports, p. 621.

But these sacrifices of the Gentiles had their mockers, not only that impious Lucian in the Dialogue of Prometheus and Jupiter, where he introduces Jupiter expostulating with Prometheus because he had unfairly divided the sacrifice with his god Jupiter, having placed the bones on one side, but covered with the skin of the victim, and on the other side the meat, which he himself had devoured alone, leaving to Jupiter his god only the bones. But they also had those who were civilly wise, who denied that God could be appeased by sacrifices: as Cato: Since you yourself are guilty, why does the victim die for you?

And Ovid, Epist. 19, Heroid.: The heavenly deities do not rejoice when a bull is slaughtered, but [in that which] is to be performed, and without a witness, by faith.

But omitting the Gentiles, since they were placed outside the Church, we shall make an approach to those false dogmas which were scattered in the very bosom of the Church.

And the Pharisees indeed occupy the first class of those who err, who, however much the Messiah was exhibited, nonetheless established the rite of sacrifices as so necessary that they determined it to be profitable by the work performed, nay, they preferred them to all virtues and works of charity, and thus consequently to the moral Law of God itself, saying that worship is far more pleasing if the people offer sacrifices than if they were to help their needy parents with those expenses of the sacrifices. Matt. 15:5 and 6. The Jews occupy the second class, who even today urge the rite of Levitical sacrifices: whose great impiety has already been refuted just now.

After the Pharisees, it is not permitted to find any other heretics who likewise moved [questions] publicly in the Church concerning sacrifices, unless perhaps you decide that those should be called here who entirely repudiated the Old Testament, and thus the entire worship of sacrifices as well: such as, with Augustine and Epiphanius as witnesses, were the Simonians, Cainites, Archontics, Cerdonians, Marcionites, Apellites, Severians, Tatianists, Manichaeans, etc.

But in these later centuries, Antichrist, that son of perdition, from the cave and smoke-hole of hell itself, produced a new dogma concerning a certain Propitiatory Sacrifice, truly and properly so called: which he and his little sacrificers are accustomed to call the Mass-offering.

If they were to accept this term of sacrifice even in the most general sense of the term sacrifice, and broadly as a certain worship, and affirm that the Mass is generally called a sacrifice: yet not even so could they save that idol. For that saying of the Savior remains firm and unmoved, Matt. 15:9: In vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments of men. For that entire Mass-worship enjoys no word of God, no command, no promise, no example of the Orthodox Church. But it is helpful to know from their own monuments what kind of Mass-sacrifice they understand, whether taken in a metaphorical or a proper sense. Thus therefore the Council of Trent: If anyone shall say that the sacrifice of the Mass is only one of praise and thanksgiving, or a bare commemoration of the sacrifice performed on the cross, but not propitiatory: or that it profits only the one who receives it, and ought not to be offered for the living and the dead, for sins, punishments, satisfactions, and other necessities, let him be anathema. Sess. 22, Can. 3. Which impiety Bellarmine increases with a certain new paradox, book 2, on the Mass, chap. 2, asserting that the Mass is a sacrifice applying the promises of the New Testament concerning the remission of sins. And chap. 4, affirming that the sacrifice of the Mass does not have force only from the work of the worker, but also from the work performed.

But, since we must speak elsewhere expressly against this Mass-idol, we shall now only resolve this: Can or ought the Holy Eucharist to be called a sacrifice properly so called?

Why most of the Ancients called the holy supper a Sacrifice will be clear from the unfolding of that homonymy or equivocation which presents itself in the writings of the Fathers concerning the use of the word Sacrifice: For sometimes by Sacrifice they understand the offering of gifts, or ἀγαπῶν, among which bread and wine held the chief place, which were offered in the name of the whole Church for the sake of gratitude, as can be seen in Irenaeus, book 4, chapters 32 and 34. But sometimes by Sacrifice they denote nothing else than the memorial of that true and unique Sacrifice, which ought to be instituted by the faithful in the use of the Eucharistic Sacrament. Concerning which matter Augustine speaks thus in book 10 against Faustus, chapter 18: The Hebrews in the victims of cattle, which they offered to GOD, celebrated a prophecy of the future victim, which CHRIST offered: Christians now celebrate the memorial of the completed Sacrifice, by the most holy oblation and participation of the body of CHRIST. The same person explains this very thing in more words in the book on faith to Peter the Deacon (although it is doubted whether this book is by Augustine), the same in book 4 on the Trinity, chapter 24.

Therefore there is no support from these expressions of the Fathers that can redound to establishing the Romanists' fictitious sacrifice: for it is certain that by the term of sacrifices they partly looked to the agapae, or the distribution of alms, which was anciently joined with the celebration of the Holy Eucharist; but partly indeed to the memory of the sacrifice of Christ, which in the distribution of the sacramental symbols same way as the Apostle affirms that CHRIST had been crucified before the eyes of the Galatians, when the preaching of the cross had been set before them and nearly inculcated.

In the meantime, however, we by no means deny that in the progress of time some of the Fathers deviated too much toward the Jewish manner of sacrificing, and inclined more closely to the shadow of the Law than either the ordinance of CHRIST or the reason of the Gospel allowed. Where, however, not even in this way will the Romanists find any foundation for confirming the Mass-sacrifice: since neither in the monuments of those Fathers is the Eucharist ever called a sacrifice properly so called, much less a propitiatory sacrifice for sins, punishments, and faults, of the dead as well as the living: But only a sacrifice of praise, of thanksgiving, and of memory, as can be seen in Eusebius, book 1, De Demonstratione, and in Augustine, book 20, against Faustus, chapter 13.

And the differences are at hand which intervene between the Church of the Fathers and the Pontifical Synagogue concerning the use of the word sacrifice: For if we weigh the matter more accurately, the sacrifices of that ancient Church seem to differ from the Mass-sacrifice in four ways especially.

The first mark of difference can be sought from the form and manner of each sacrifice. For in the primitive Church the sacrifice was called the very common and general κοινωνία or dispensation of the Supper: Whence the Eucharist is also called by Ambrose, Chrysostom, and Augustine an example, a figure, a sign, an image of that one true sacrifice of CHRIST. And Cyril, in his 11th Synodical Epistle: If, he says, Christ had not been crucified, we would not be eating the sacrifice of His own Body.

The second is derived from the end of the sacrifice: For to that primitive Church the Eucharist was not some ἱλαστικὸν, or propitiatory sacrifice, which was to be applied to others by the very virtue of the work. But to the Romanists the Mass-sacrifice is ἱλαστικὸν for the sin, punishments, and faults of the living and the dead.

Concerning which difference Irenaeus speaks excellently in book 4, chapter 34: Sacrifices do not sanctify a man.
