For the action of the one absolving, or absolution, cannot be such a heavenly thing: because the Romanists themselves refer it to the form of the sacrament; but the form cannot be a part of the sacramental matter consisting of an earthly and heavenly thing; rather, the form consists in the external action. 2. In every sacrament, the earthly and heavenly things are sacramentally united in the use of the sacrament, whether the one who participates in the sacrament believes or does not believe. Therefore, by the Esauvite hypothesis, its sacramental union will consist for the act of the one confessing and the act of the one absolving, even if the penitent is a hypocrite and does not believe in the evangelical promises. By which means even unbelievers and hypocrites would obtain absolution from sins by the force of this sacramental union. Absurd and impious.

Finally, from the entire orthodox antiquity, not even one Doctor of the Church can be brought forward who ever wrote about penance as a sacrament of the New Testament properly so called. But a collation of ecclesiastical history shows that the Latin Church, which otherwise indulged too much in superstitious traditions, drew this opinion, or rather this error, about the sacrament of penance from the spectacles of public penance, which the old Church maintained with great severity in manifest and atrocious crimes. Concerning which matter there will be a place to speak below in chapter 3, where we shall make remarks about Pontifical satisfaction.

Bellarmine is in a tumult in this place, and in chapter 10 of book 1 on Penance, intending to confirm his opinion quite prolixly, he finds that one thing in which he may in some way plant his foot, namely that in John 20:23, the Savior after the resurrection said to the disciples: Whose sins you shall remit, they are remitted to them; and whose you shall retain, they are retained. But this is too diluted and weak a kind of arguing, destitute of every legitimate nerve of conclusion. For 1. no reason of consequence is fighting here: Christ uttered these words after the resurrection. Therefore he instituted a sacrament properly so called. 2. Christ, always instituting a sacrament, defined an external visible element: but here there is none. Therefore 3. an ἄγνοια ἐλέγχου (ignorance of the refutation) is committed. For no sacrament was sanctioned here; but an ecclesiastical ministry was solemnly entrusted to the Apostles and their successors, with the power of the keys granted. Therefore, if any Sacrament had been instituted by Christ in this place, certainly it would not be the repentance of men, but the Ecclesiastical ministry that would be that Sacrament. By which arrangement an octonary number of Sacraments would emerge among the Papists. 4. The Savior spoke the same words also before the resurrection, and indeed with a religious attestation, which is not read in John 20: Amen I say to you, whatsoever you shall bind upon earth, shall be bound also in heaven: and whatsoever you shall loose upon earth, shall be loosed also in heaven. Matth. 18, 18. And yet in this place the Savior instituted no Sacrament, as the Council of Trent defines. What reason, therefore, will be given by which it can be demonstrated that, by the same words, by the same letter, and by the same meaning

Latin:

de carne nostra, & donat cor carneum, Ezech. 36. 26. Sic non est habitus animi infusus. Etsi enim Spiritus Sanctus movet cor hominis ad agnoscendum peccata: haec ipsa tamen peccatorum agnitio, non provenit ex inhaerentibus qualitatibus arbitrij: sed ex Lege DEI, Rom. 3, 20. Rom. 7, 7. Sic, & quidem multo minus respectu Fidei, ut quae donum DEI est, Poenitentia est habitus virtutis infusus: Siquidem Fides uti in Articulo Justificationis, sic in praesenti etiam, non consideratur ut virtus aut qualitas inhaerens subjective: sed tantum ut medium sive ὄργανον apprehendens meritum CHRISTI. Quid? quod Nova obedientia, sive Sanctificatio aut renovatio mentis nostrae, quam per infusam aliquam a DEO qualitatem, definiri posse, haud fortasse inficias iverimus, non est pars constituens veram poenitentiam: sed ejus tantum effectus sive consequens. Animadverterunt ipsi quoque Scholastici assertionis hujus Pontificiae vanitatem, ac proinde argumentorum nostrorum vim, quoquo modo enervaturi, stolide finxerunt, Poenitentiam esse virtutem quiescentem, ac interdum tantum sese exerentem. Quae sane quiescentia, licet, quoad virtutum moralium actum secundum, non negetur: siquidem saepius ille interrumpitur, ut vere scripserit Philosophus: Tempore quo dormimus, licet simus felices, non distamus tamen a miseris: nullo tamen pacto ad poenitentiam, quiescentia haec accommodari vel potest, vel debet. Nam lapsi & convertendi ad DEUM, tam non ex virtutis alicujus habitu, sive quiescente sive ἐνεργητικῷ poenitentiam agere possunt, sive dormiant, sive vigilent, ut nisi Spiritu DEI, moveantur, talis actus poenitendi nunquam in ipsos cadere possit: id quod de virtutum habitibus affirmari nequit, quorum actus, secundum rectam rationem libere se exerit, tam in non renatis, quam in renatis. Quid quod perpetua etiam illa renatorum poenitentia, sive mortificatio carnis, ex singulari gratia Spiritus Sancti proficiscitur, secundum illud Joh. 15, 5. Sine me nihil potestis facere: Et talem quiescentiam non admittit: siquidem Apostolo teste 2. Cor. 3, 18. Renati transformantur in imaginem Christi, ex claritate in claritatem. Et ne hoc quis ex habitu Virtutis quiescentis, ac interdum tantum se exerentis fieri existimet, mox additur: Sed a Spiritu DOMINI.

Et quidem tanta vis est veritatis, ut tum Scholastici, tum Scriptores Pontificij recentiores etiam non invicem conveniant quomodo virtus poenitentiae definiri debeat. Thomas in 4. sent dist. 14. q. 1. refert, quosdam statuere, Poenitentiam non esse Specialem Virtutem, differentem ab alijs Virtutum habitibus: sed sub illis omnibus contineri, quatenus nimirum quaelibet virtus detestatur vitium sibi oppositum. Verum Thomas ab his dissentiens contendit, Poenitentia Virtute esse in voluntate, tanquam in subjecto, parte 3. q. 84. art. 4. eandemq́, divinitus infundi, art. 5. & 6. Gui tamen rursus contradicit Scotus, in 4. Sent. dist. 14. q. 3. & Durandus ead. dist q. 2. qui contendit, Poenitentia virtutem esse ipsam justitiam commutativam moralem. Cajetanus art. 2. lib 4. sent. dist. 14. Poenitentia virtutem dicit esse ipsam Religionem, Scotus denique in 4. Sent. dist. 14 q. 2. quatuor virtutis hujus actus constituit: 1. velle punire peccatum. 2. nolle peccasse. 3. velle acceptare punitionem pro peccato. 4. pœnam susceptam patienter ferre. Quæ sanè Andabatarum istorum celpitatio, futilitatem hujus dogmatis luculenter arguit.

ALTER error gentis Esavviticæ planè intolerabilis est, quòd aliam comminiscitur definitionem pœnitentiæ Veteris, aliam Novi Testamenti; quin & Novi Testamenti aliam ante perceptum Baptismum : aliam verò post Baptismum. Quæ sanè distinctio, 1. ne unico quidem apice ex Scripturis demonstrari potest. 2. Scripturis & analogiæ fidei è diametro repugnat: quippè quæ expressè testantur, utriusque Testamenti Pœnitentiam constare eadem materiâ, eâdemque formâ, nempè Contritione & Fide: Exemplo Davidis, qui ad concionem legalem Prophetæ Nathanis toto pectore, ob commissum adulterium & homicidium exhorrescens, Peccavi, inquiens; mox audit lætam absolutionis vocem, Dominus transtulit peccatum tuum, non morieris. 2. Sam. 12, 13. Et splendidè mentitur Esavvita, asserens, in Veteri Testamento non fuisse potestatem remittendi peccata cum autoritate: nequê Nathanem, aut ullum alium ut DEI ministrum, peccatores absolvisse, quia nondùm auditum erat illud: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis. lib. de Pœnit. cap. 11. Nam ne quidem in Novo Testamento uslibi commissa est ministris Ecclesiæ, judiciaria aliqua potestas in lapsos sive pœnitentes, qualem Bellarminus tacitè hoc loco subinnuit, tanquàm Novi Testamenti propriam. Sed uti in veteri Testamento alligati erant Sacerdotes ad legem & ad testimonium, sive Evangelium: ex illâ peccata arguere: ex hoc verò Contritos sanare jussi fuerant: ita hodieque in Novo Testamento plus sive potestatis, sive autoritatis circa Absolutionem ministris non est concessum. Neque obstat, quod nondùm auditum erat illud: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis. Nam non nova Absolutionis ratio aut forma his verbis promulgabatur: Sed publica tantùm ac solennis hæc erat Ministerij Ecclesiastici commendatio: & simul, pro ratione Novi Testamenti dilucidior doctrinæ Evangelicæ explicatio, quæ in Veteri Testamento typis ac umbris involuta erat: ejusdemque in universum terrarum orbem propagatio, quæ priùs angustis populi Judaici finibus inclusa erat. Neque unius etiam teruncij alterum illud est κηνοφύγετον Bellarmini, asserentis, Exemplum Nathanis prophetæ nihil ad rem facere, propterea quod Nathan non dixerit, Ego te absolvo: vel, Ego tibi peccata remitto: sed solum: Dominus transtulit peccatum tuum à te. Ibid. Nam ubi quæso Christus Servator hanc formulam præscripsit ministris Novi Testamenti? vel ubi ad hanc eos unquàm adstrinxit? vel ubi formulæ huic certam quandam vim aut potestatem occultam, vel etiam illam judiciariam, quam somniat

Esauvita, unquam uspiam adscripsit. Gerris Siculis vaniora sunt haec, & nimis manifeste morbidam Esauvitarum Theologiam hac in parte arguunt. Unum est, quod in tota hac disputatione vel maxime probamus, nempe quod Esauvita eodem capite diserte fatetur: Pœnitentiam, quam Christus, & Johannes Baptista predicarunt, Sacramentum non fuisse, & exemplum pœnitentiae Sacramenti in Sacris ante resurrectionem Christi non haberi. Sufficiat nobis fundamenti loco pro veritate nostrae doctrinae haec assertio: imo sufficiat nobis Pœnitentia a Johanne Baptista, & Christo Servatore monstrata: facessat vero ea, quae non Christum, non Apostolos: sed filium perditionis, Antichristum Romanum, autorem habet.

TERTIUS error est, quod Esauvitae contendunt, Pœnitentiam, quae externis constat signis, hoc est, Contritione cordis, confessione oris, satisfactione operis, quaeque annexam habet vocem Absolutionis, sub hac forma: Ego te absolvo &c. esse Sacramentum Novi Testamenti proprie sic dictum. Pluribus scateter roriste falsitatibus & absurditatibus, quam ut omnes enumerari possint. Nam I. Pœnitentiae non convenit definitio Sacramenti. Ergo. Antecedens patet: 1. quia ritus iste, qui requiritur a Romanensibus, in poenitentia, non est institutus ab ipso Christo: id quod fatetur Bellarminus ipse, lib. 2. de Effectu Sacramenti, cap. 24. Jam vero vera Sacramenta a Christo solo instituta sint oportet. 2. Quia poenitentia est ritus veteri Testamento cum Novo communis. 3. Quia destituitur elemento externo, sive re terrena. Absurdus enim est Bellarminus, qui actum confitentis pro elemento externo substituere audet: id quod cum natura & annalogia omnium Sacramentorum utriusque Testamenti e diametro pugnat: quorum nullum dari potest, ubi actio hominis constituat partem elementarem Sacramenti: sed haec semper sit aliquid extra actionem hominis subsistens. Sic absurdus est Bellarminus, qui scriptitat: ritum Sacerdotis, dicentis: Absolvo te, concurrere ad constitutionem hujus Sacramenti: Quasi vero verba Ministri partem essentialem Sacramenti constituant. Quae sane absurdissima Theologia si subsisteret, utique verba Ministri dicentis: Ego te baptizo, pro elemento externo habenda forent: id quod prodigiose absurdum. II. Per Sacramenta DEUS nobiscum agit: atque id agit, cum similitudinem analogam actio humana habet. Atqui talis actio non est poenitentia: sed est actio potius humana, qua ab homine erga DEUM praecipue agitur: Ergo. III. Sacramenta omnia sic sunt comparata, ut integra quidem sine fide percipi possint, sed non sint salutaria. At poenitentia sine fide usque adeo stare nequit, ut hac absente, non amplius sit poenitentia, haud magis atque homo sine anima esse potest. Ergo. IV. Omne Sacramentum proprie dictum, constat re terrena, & re coelesti, Sacramentaliter unitis. Atqui poenitentia non constat re terrena & re coelesti Sacramentaliter unitis. Ergo. Assumtio patet 1. licet pro materia & re terrena sensu Esauvitico habeatur actus confitentis (id quod tamen falsum est) nulla tamen dari potest res cœlestis, quæ cum terrenâ hâc Sacramentaliter uniatur. Nam actio absolventis, sive Absolutio, non potest esse talis res cœlestis: quia ipsi Romanenses eam referunt ad formam Sacramenti: Forma autem non potest esse pars materiæ Sacramentalis constantis ex re terrenâ & cœlesti: sed forma in externâ actione consistit. 2. In omni Sacramento res terrena & cœlestis sunt in usu Sacramenti Sacramentaliter unitæ, sive credat, sive non credat, qui Sacramento participat. Ergò ex hypothesi Esavviticâ, actui confitentis, & actui absolventis constabit sua unio Sacramentalis, licèt pœnitens sit hypocrita, & promissionibus Evangelicis non credat. Quo pacto absolutionem à peccatis consequentur, vi unionis hujus Sacramentalis, etiam increduli & hypocritæ. Absurdum & impium.

Tandem ex universâ orthodoxâ Antiquitate, ne unus quidem proferri potest Ecclesiæ Doctor, qui de Pœnitentiâ, tanquàm de Sacramento Novi testamenti propriè sic dicto, unquàm scripserit. Sed collatio historiæ Ecclesiasticæ monstrat, Ecclesiam latinam, quæ aliàs superstitiosis traditionibus nimiùm indulgebat, opinionem vel errorem potiùs hunc de Sacramento Pœnitentiæ hausisse, ex spectaculis publicæ pœnitentiæ, quam magnâ severitate vetus Ecclesia, in manifestis & atrocibus criminibus servabat. Quâ de re infra cap. 3. dicendi locus erit, ubi de Satisfactione Pontificiâ verba faciemus.

Tumultuatur hoc loco Bellarminus, & cap. 10. libri 1. de Pœnitentiâ, prolixè satis suam confirmaturus sententiam, unicum illud, in quo pedem quodammodo figat, reperit, nempè quòd Joh. 20, 23. Servator post resurrectionem ad discipulos dixit: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: & quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt. Sed nimis dilutum ac elumbe hoc est argumentandi genus, omni legitimo concludendi nervo destitutum. Nam 1. nulla militat consequentiæ ratio: Christus hæc verba protulit post resurrectionem. Ergò Sacramentum propriè sic dictum instituit. 2. Christus semper Sacramentum instituens, externum Elementum visibile definivit: Atqui hic nullum. Ergò 3. ἄγνοια ἐλέγχου committitur. Non enim Sacramentum aliquod hîc sancitum: Sed Ministerium Ecclesiasticum Apostolis, ipsorumq; successoribus solenniter demandatum fuit: concessâ potestate clavium. Ergò si Sacramentum aliquod hoc loco fuisset à Christo institutum: certè non pœnitentia hominum, sed ministerium Ecclesiasticum esset illud Sacramentum. Quo pacto octonarius Sacramentorum numerus apud Pontificios emergeret. 4. Eadem verba prolocutus est etiam Servator ante resurrectionem, & quidem cum religiosâ attestatione, quæ Johannis 20. non legitur: Amen dico vobis, quæcunq; ligaveritis super terram, erunt ligata & in cælis: & quæcunq; solveritis super terram, erunt soluta in cælis. Matth. 18, 18. Atqui hoc loco Servator Sacramentum nullum instituit, sic definiente Concilio Tridentino. Quæ ergò dabitur ratio, quâ demonstrari queat, ijsdem verbis, quâ literâ, quâ sensum idé significantibus


### Opinion of the Libertines about Penance: Whether to the state with GOD begun in baptism, if it is violated by sins, a return is open and how?

the Sacrament was instituted after the resurrection? 5. Penance and Absolution are most distinct acts: not only in their very genus, but also differing entirely in their subjects. The former indeed in the penitent sinner: the latter, however, in the Minister of the Church. This therefore can in no way be subalternated to that: and consequently, what the Savior said concerning absolution cannot be accommodated to penance. But Bellarmine further objects in the same chapter 10, the definition of a Sacrament, and indeed such a one: A Sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing: and a sign indeed practical and efficacious: but that sacred thing is the grace of Justification. But the most vain disputer mixes true things with false, and weaves false consequences from ambiguous presuppositions. For 1. A Sacrament is a practical sign, only in a certain respect, not in its entirety: namely, by reason of its form, which consists in action: but not by reason of its matter, which in any Sacrament is in the category of substance. 2. That the Sacred Thing is the Grace of Justification is indeed true in itself: but by reason of the Sacrament, it is most false. For the grace of Justification pertains to the fruit or use of the Sacrament, which is considered outside the thing or substance of the Sacrament: and it is not called the Sacred Thing of the Sacrament except in a most general signification. But speaking properly, the Sacred Thing of the Sacrament is another substantial thing, which together with the external element constitutes the essence of the Sacrament: namely, the heavenly or invisible thing. Since such a thing cannot be demonstrated in penance, it is plain that not even this general definition of a Sacrament applies to it: and that is also plain which the Sophist asserts in the following chapter 11: that the nature and essence of a Sacrament does not consist properly in substance, but in action. But this is true only concerning the form of the Sacrament, which requires an external action: but it is most false concerning the matter of the Sacrament, which, as it consists in any Sacrament of an earthly thing and a heavenly thing, so it must always be referred to the predicament of substance.

On the occasion of this controversy concerning the Sacrament of Penance, it began to be disputed, and is still disputed quite sharply today by the Romanists, concerning the difference between Baptism and Penance: as can be seen in Bellarmine, lib. 1. de Pœnit. cap. 12. where, however, the Esauvite at the very threshold commits a manifest crime of falsehood. For he writes that B. LUTHER and most orthodox Lutheran theologians teach that those who have fallen after Baptism are reconciled through the MEMORY of Baptism, not however by the thing itself: thus intending to persuade the simpler folk that we posit such a perpetuity of the covenant once initiated with GOD in baptism, by which men who have fallen after Baptism are reconciled with GOD, if at least they remember or recall that they were once baptized. But that our Churches are afflicted with a signal injury in this part also, will soon be evident, if we first have explained what properly comes into controversy in this place. The Romanists, therefore, who transformed Penance into a Sacrament of the New Testament properly so called, in order that they might in some way put a gloss upon this error of theirs, devised a clever remedy, and that a double one: but both of them manifestly impious: THE FORMER was: That those who have fallen after Baptism cannot be reconciled with GOD except through some Sacrament. THE LATTER, however: That the virtue and efficacy of Baptism is so entirely evacuated by mortal sins that there can be no further use of it: consequently, that a second plank must be sought by which we may be able to escape from the flood of divine wrath: and that this is the Sacrament of Penance. Hence in the schools and Churches of the Papists was born that impious doctrine, by which it was contended that the Sacrament of Penance is of the same virtue and efficacy as Baptism once was: so that Thomas in 4. sent. dist. 17. q. 3. art. 5. did not shudder to write: that in the Sacrament of Penance grace is infused, through which the remission of sins is obtained, just as in Baptism. Nay, there have been found among the Papist Doctors those who assigned to Penance a greater force and efficacy in express words, writing: That while we are indeed freed from the guilt of sin by the grace of Baptism: we are freed from the punishment of sin by the Sacrament of penance: as one may read in the Compendium Theolog. verit. lib. 6. cap. 22.

Openly contradicting this impiety, our orthodox Church has always taught and teaches today: That the covenant once initiated with GOD in baptism, if it be afterwards violated on the part of man through sins, is not so abolished or made void on the part of GOD, that there is now need of either a new Sacrament or a new covenant, but that there is need only of a new return to that very covenant, which on the part of GOD always remains irrevocable; which is done, not through a bare memory or recollection of the Baptism previously received: but only through FAITH, apprehending again CHRIST, in whom alone every covenant is founded, and every promise is Yes and Amen. 2 Cor. 1:20.

Hence, therefore, this true state of the controversy emerges: Whether the covenant once initiated and sanctioned with GOD in Baptism is on the part of GOD always so remaining, irrevocable, firm, stable, and perpetual: that, although those who have fallen after Baptism have lost its salutary use through mortal sins, a return to it is nevertheless always open to them through penance, so that as often as they return to Christ through true faith, the substance, virtue, and efficacy of this covenant always exerts itself for the reconciliation of man with GOD: and there is no need of a new Sacrament? Where we hold the affirmative in all respects, while the Esauvites on the contrary fight clearly for the Negative.

But the principal arguments for this our Affirmative are these:

THE FIRST is such: If GOD in Baptism decreed to enter into such a covenant with baptized men, nay, in very deed entered into and ratified it with all the baptized, which on His part should be ἀμεταμέλητον: by the force of which the door of grace and mercy should perpetually stand open to all fallen penitents, and those returning through Faith: then it must necessarily be false, impious, and erroneous, that by mortal sins that covenant of Baptism is so evacuated and taken away, that no use of it at all can any longer exist. But the former is true. Therefore the latter is also.

Latin:

post resurrectionem, institutum fuisse Sacramentum? 5. Pœnitentia & Absolutio sunt diparatissimi actus: non genere tantùm ipso: sed Subjectis etiam prorsus discrepantes. Illa quidem in peccatore pœnitente: hæc autem in Ministro Ecclesiæ. Hæc ergò isti subalternari nullo modo potest: ac proindè, quæ de absolutione dixit Servator, ad pœnitentiam accommodari nequeunt. Sed objicit porrò Bellarminus eodem cap. 10. Definitionem Sacramenti, & quidem talem: Sacramentum est rei sacræ signum: & Signum quidem practicum atque efficax: Res verò illa sacra est gratia Justificationis. Sed vera falsis miscet vanissimus disputator, & ex ambiguis præsuppositis falsas nectit consequetias. Nam 1. Sacramentum est signum practicum, tantùm secundum quid, non ex toto: nempè ratione formæ, quæ in actione consistit: non verò ratione materiæ, quæ in quovis Sacramento est in Categoria substantiæ. 2. Rem Sacram esse Gratiam Justificationis, per se quidem verum est: sed ratione Sacramenti, falsissimum est. Gratia enim Justificationis pertinet ad fructum sive usum Sacramenti, qui extra rem sive Substantiam Sacramenti consideratur: & non nisi in generalissima significatione dicitur Res Sacramenti. Propriè autem loquendo Res Sacramenti est res altera substantialis, unà cum elemento externo constituens Sacramenti essentiam: Res nimirùm cœlestis sive invisibilis. Qualis res cùm in pœnitentia demonstrari non possit, planum est, ne quidem generalem hanc Sacramenti definitionem illi competere: planum est & illud, quod capite subsequente 11. asserit Sophista: Sacramenti naturam atque essentiam propriè non in substantia: sed in actione consistere. Verùm enim hoc est tantùm de formâ Sacramenti, quæ externam actionem requirit: falsissimum verò de materiâ Sacramenti, quæ uti in quolibet Sacramento re terrenâ, & re cœlesti constat: ita ad prædicamentum substantiæ semper referri debet.

Occasione hujus controversiæ de Sacramento Pœnitentiæ, disputari cœptum fuit, hodieque satis acriter disputatur à Romanensibus, de differentia Baptismi & Pœnitentiæ: uti videre est apud Bellarminum, lib. 1. de Pœnit. cap. 12. ubi tamen Esauvita in primo statim limine, manifestum crimen falsi committit. Scribit enim B. LUTHERUM & orthodoxos Theologos Lutheranos plerosque docere, Lapsos post Baptismum reconciliari per Baptismi MEMORIA, non autem reipsâ reperitum: sic persuasurus simplicioribus nos talem perpetuitatem fœderis semel cum DEO in baptismo initi statuere, quâ homines post Baptismum lapsi cum DEO reconcilientur, si saltem meminerint, aut recordentur, se aliquando baptizatos esse. Insigni autem injuriâ hâc etiam in parte nostras affici Ecclesias, mox patebit, si priùs, quid propriè hoc loco in controversia veniat, expeditum dederimus. Romanenses igitur, qui Pœnitentiam in Sacramentum Novi Testamenti propriè dictum transformarunt, ut errori huic suo quoquo modo fucum facere possent, excogitârunt σοφὸν Φάρμακον, id geminum: utrúmque autem manifestè impium: PRIUS erat: Lapsos post Baptismum, non nisi per Sacramentum aliquod reconciliari cum DEO posse. POSTERIUS verò: Baptismi virtutem atque efficaciam, per peccata mortalia, ita ex toto evacuari, ut nullus ejus usus ampliùs esse possit: proindè querendam esse secundam tabulam quâ ex diluvio iræ divinæ eluctari queamus: hanc verò esse Sacramentum Pœnitentiæ. Hinc in scholis & Ecclesijs Pontificiorum nata est impia illa doctrina, quâ contendebatur, Pœnitentiæ Sacramentum ejusdem esse virtutis atque efficaciæ, cujus olim fuerit Baptismus: ita ut Thomas in 4. sent. dist. 17. q. 3. art. 5. scribere nõ exhorruerit: in Sacramento Pœnitentiæ infundi gratiam, per quam obtingat remissio peccatorum, sicut in Baptismo. Imò reperti sunt ex Doctoribus Pontificijs, qui Pœnitentiæ majorem vim atq; efficaciam expressis verbis assignarunt, scriptitantes: Quod per gratiam quidem Baptismi liberemur à reatu peccati: per Sacramentum autem pœnitentiæ à pœnâ peccati: uti legere licet in Compendio Theolog. verit. lib. 6. cap. 22.

Impietati huic orthodoxa nostra Ecclesia apertè contradicens semper docuit hodieque docet: Quod fœdus semel cum DEO in baptismo initum, si postmodùm ex parte hominis, per peccata violatum sit, non ita ex parte etiam DEI aboleátur, aut irritum fiat, ut jam vel novo Sacramento, vel novo fœdere opus sit, sed, quòd tantùm novo reditu ad illum ipsum fœdus, ex parte DEI semper manens ἀμεταμέλητον, opus sit: id quod fiat, non per nudam memoriam sive ἀνάμνησιν aut recordationem Baptismi priùs percepti: sed tantùm per FIDEM, apprehendentem iterum CHRISTUM, in quo solo omne fœdus est fundatum, omnisq́ue promissio est Etiam & Amen. 2. Cor. 1, 20.

Hinc ergò verus emergit status controversiæ iste: An fœdus in Baptismo semel cum DEO initum sancitumq́;, ex parte DEI ita semper sit maneatq́;, ἁμεταμέλητον, firmum, stabile, perpetuum: ut, licèt lapsi post Baptismum, per peccata mortalia, salutarem ejus usum amiserint, semper tamen ipsis ad illud pateat reditus per pœnitentiam, ita, ut quotiescunq́; per veram fidem ad Christum redeunt semper fœderis hujus substantia, virtus & efficacia, ad reconciliationem hominis cum DEO, se exerat: nequè novo Sacramento opus sit? Ubi nos affirmativam per omnia tenemus, Esavvitis contrà pro Negativâ planè pugnantibus.

Sunt autem Affirmativæ hujus nostræ argumenta præcipua isthæc:

PRIMUM tale est: Si DEUS in Baptismo cum hominibus baptizatis, tale fœdus inire decrevit, imò reverà cum omnibus baptizatis inijt & sancivit, quod ex suâ parte esset ἀμεταμέλητον: cujus vigore Janua gratiæ & misericordiæ perpetuò omnibus lapsis pœnitentibus, & per Fidem redeuntibus pateret: utíq; falsum, impium & erroneum sit necesse est, quòd per peccata mortalia fœdus illud Baptismi ita evacuetur & tollatur, ut nullus prorsus ejus usus ampliùs esse possit. Atqui prius verum. Ergò & posterius.


### Opinion of the Libertines about Penance: On the Difference between Baptism and Penance

The assumption contains the point at issue: It is therefore proved by these reasons: 1. Because in Baptism there occurs a washing away of sin, not, as the compendium of theological truth raves, of original sin only, but also of actual sin: and of this, as much mortal as venial, as much future as past: For the blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1:7. 2. Because the virtue and efficacy of the divine covenant, on the part of the will and intention of God, is valid forever: Genesis 17:13. This my covenant shall be for an everlasting covenant. Hosea 2:19. I will betroth you to me forever. Romans 3:3. Shall the unbelief of men make the faith of God of no effect? God forbid: For God is true: but every man a liar. Romans 11:29. The gifts of God are without repentance. 2 Timothy 2:13. If we are unfaithful, we are faithless, yet he remains faithful, he cannot deny himself. Of which sayings indeed there is such evidence that they irrefragably demonstrate that the substance of Baptism, which by reason of its end is a federal pact, always remains inviolate with respect to God: for otherwise God would not be true: he would not be faithful: but he would repent of this his covenant, nay, as the Apostle speaks, he would deny himself: which to even think of God would be supremely blasphemous. Whence emerges that other point, namely that on the part of the fallen all the guilt resides: so that as long as they persevere in unbelief, so long also this covenant initiated in Baptism does not exert its efficacy. The reason is: because this covenant is not absolute: but conditional, under the determination of faith. When, however, one so fallen is afterwards renewed to faith through true repentance: then the original covenant begins again to be useful and salutary to him. By which arrangement repentance in the fallen is not a new Sacrament, or a new method of obtaining the remission of sins, as the Council of Trent dreams: Sess. 14, chap. 2, but is only a return to that gratuitous federal promise concerning the remission of sins, given and sealed to us in Baptism on account of the satisfaction of Christ the Mediator.

A second argument can be formulated thus: Baptism saves us, which is not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the stipulation of a good conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. 1 Peter 3:21. Now indeed the end of true repentance is none other than that the stipulation, the ἐπερώτημα, of a good conscience with God may again be established for us. But that end, as Peter testifies, is obtained by us for salvation only from Baptism. Therefore the fruit and salutary effect of Baptism for the penitent always is and remains valid and effective.

Third. By the same arrangement or means by which St. Peter, after his most sad fall, returned into favor with God and obtained the remission of his most atrocious sin: by the same also, and no other, can and ought all penitents to be reconciled with God. But Peter, having fallen most gravely by his defection from Christ, denying his Lord and Master for the third time: yet afterwards performing repentance, consoled himself most effectively by nothing other than his Baptism: which he himself testifies concerning himself, 1 Peter 3:20 and 21. Whose (the ark of Noah) figure, Baptism, now also saves us: thus including himself through the figure of communication. Therefore.

Fourth: the same Apostle Peter in the place already cited, approves of Baptism not as some broken plank of a ship, as the Papists are accustomed to do: but as an entire and most firm ship, namely the ark of Noah: outside of which salvation can be obtained by no one.

Fifth, that Apostolic passage pertains here, Ephesians 5:25 and 26. Christ loved the Church, and gave himself for it, that he might sanctify it, cleansing it with the washing of water by the Word, that he might present it to himself glorious, not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing, but that it should be holy and without blemish. Which passage Blessed Augustine, according to our opinion, explains against the Romanists thus: book 1 de nupt. & concup. chap. 33. That the Apostle says: Christ loved the Church, cleansing it with the washing of water by the word, etc. is to be understood thus, that by the same washing of regeneration, and the word of sanctification, all the evils of regenerated men are thoroughly cleansed and healed, not only sins, which are all now remitted in Baptism, but also those which are contracted LATER by human ignorance or infirmity: not that Baptism is repeated as often as one sins: but because by it, which is given once, it comes to pass that not only before, but also afterwards, the pardon of any sins whatsoever is obtained by the faithful. For what would repentance profit even before Baptism, unless Baptism followed? Or what would it profit afterwards, unless Baptism preceded?

In which opinion the same Augustine writes vigorously and elegantly, book 4 de Bapt. Cont. Donatist. chap. 15. It is manifest that Baptism remains inseparably in the baptized: because into whatever depth of evils, and into whatever horrible abyss of sins the baptized may fall, even to apostolic ruin: he does not however lack Baptism: and therefore it is not returned to him who returns through repentance, because it is judged that he could not have lacked it.

And book 7, chap. 36. So there is one Baptism in the Catholic Church, that when some have gone out from it, in those who go out, there are not made two, but the same one remains. What therefore is recognized in those who return, this is also in those who received it from those who were departing, which they did not lose while they were departing.

The Efavvitic sect opposes itself to this purer doctrine with great effort, feigning that in Baptism the remission of sins is indeed conferred freely without our works, on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith: but that in those who have fallen after Baptism, Repentance obtains pardon, not by faith, not freely, not without works: but through and on account of the works of Sacramental Repentance.

But this is a sink of the grossest errors: nay, it is an atrocious sacrilege against that eternal and immutable covenant of GOD: as if GOD had promulgated one method of reconciliation and salvation in Baptism, but another and clearly different one through penance, which utterly annihilates and abolishes that former one. By which arrangement contradictory wills would be attributed to GOD. Furthermore, through this Efavvitic ματαιολογίαν, a shameful confusion of consequences with effects is committed: nay, manifest blasphemy is designated in this, that an equal and equivalent efficacy is ascribed to a human work, along with the sacramental action of GOD.

The arguments with which Bellarmine fights for his painted impiety are not worth a farthing. For first, we have never said, written, or thought that the memory of Baptism is a means or remedy for obtaining the remission of sins. Nor do we define Faith by the memory or recollection of Baptism: as the Esauvites themselves know.

Furthermore, it is manifestly false that the Sacrifices, expiations, and justifications of the Old Testament conferred the remission of sins upon men of themselves, and as works, or by the work performed. For as the epistle to the Hebrews clearly teaches, those Sacrifices obtained this power of expiation not of themselves: but in type, that is, in Christ, whom they prefigured from afar. For they served only as a likeness, an exemplar, and a shadow, or they foreshadowed that most full and most perfect victim, namely Christ, who alone of himself, and by the work performed, is to merit and confer the remission of sins upon the faithful.

Thirdly, Bellarmine displays remarkable insolence by objecting to us that passage, Heb. 6:1, where the Apostle warns the Hebrews not to look back again to the beginnings of Baptism, and of faith, and of that repentance which precedes Baptism. From which the Esauvite tacitly implies that there can be no further use of Baptism for those who have fallen after baptism. But no such thing entered the Apostle's mind, nor does the text even imply it: but a manifest crime of forgery is being attached to the text. But let it be, let that be the sense of the Apostle's words; what infinite absurdities, I ask, would follow from that? For from this egregious Esauvitic explanation it would follow: that those who have fallen after Baptism must no longer look back to the Decalogue, nor must repentance be formed according to its precepts: Because in the same place, verse 1, the Apostle says: The foundation of repentance is no longer to be laid: That by these words the finger is pointed at the Decalogue is too well known to need proof. Thus it would follow: that for those who have fallen after baptism there can no longer be any use for the Apostles' Creed, and consequently, that one must no longer even believe in Christ: since the Apostle immediately adds: the foundation of faith in God is no longer to be laid: That the Apostles' Creed is indicated by these words, there is no one who would deny. From this is evident the desultory insolence of the Esauvite race in corrupting the testimonies of the Scriptures. We correct this error by opening up the genuine sense of the Apostle's words, which is not that the Hebrews should no longer look back to Baptism, or to repentance, or to faith: but that they should not always cling to those first elements of Catechetical doctrine like children: but should instruct and prepare their minds to perceive the more sublime mysteries of the Christian Religion. What of the fact that it completely undermines and overturns every attack of the Esauvite, that the Apostle immediately enumerates three heads of Catechetical doctrine, and also includes the Resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment, where, by the Esauvite's interpretation, it would follow that those who have fallen after Baptism, just as they should no longer look back to or care for Baptism, so also they should no longer look back to or care for the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment: which is absurd and impious.

Fourthly and lastly, it is frivolous and utterly feeble that the Esauvite repeatedly cites from the Fathers that Repentance is called the second plank after shipwreck because there can no longer be any use for Baptism, as a broken plank. For we learned a little earlier from Augustine that such a thing never entered the minds of the Fathers. Furthermore, as for the phrases about the second plank, which Jerome and others frequently use, we do not deny that Repentance can analogically be called the second plank: but not in the Esauvitic sense, as if the plank of Baptism had already been broken in every part and rendered void and useless: but in the orthodox sense: because Repentance is that other plank by which we may return to the former, as if from a shipwreck, and aspire to the original shore of Baptism or the divine covenant.

Latin:

Assumtio continet τὸ κρινόμενον: Ea ergò his rationibus probatur: 1. Quia in Baptismo fit ablutio peccati, non uti compendium Theologicæ veritatis delirat, originalis tantùm, sed & Actualis: & hujus tàm mortalis, quàm venialis, tàm futuri, quàm præteriti: Sangvis enim Jesu Christi Filij DEI emundat nos ab omni peccato 1. Johan. 1, 7. 2. Quia fœderis divini virtus & efficacia, ex parte, voluntate & intentione DEI, valet in perpetuum: Genes. 17, 13. Erit hoc pactum meum in fœdus æternum. Hoseæ 2, 19. Desponsabo te mihi in sempiternum. Rom. 3, 3. Numquid incredulitas hominum, DEI fidem evacuat? Absit: Est enim Deus verax: Omnis autem homo mendax. Rom. 11, 29. Dona DEI sunt ἀμεταμέλητα. 2. Tim. 2, 13. Si nos infideles erimus, ἀπιστῶμεν, ille tamen fidelis manet, negare seipsum non potest. Quorum sanè dictorum ea est evidentia, ut irrefragabiliter demonstrent, Substantiam Baptismi, quæ ratione finis, est fœderalis pactio, semper manere respectu DEI inviolatam: aliàs enim DEUS non esset verax: non esset fidelis: sed pœniteret ipsum sui hujus fœderis, imò ut Apostolus loquitur, negaret seipsum: id quod de DEO vel cogitare, summe blasphemum foret. Undè emergit illud alterum, nempè ex parte lapsorum omnem culpam residere: ut quamdiu in incredulitate perseverant, tamdiu etiam fœdus hoc in Baptismo initium, efficaciam suam non exerat. Ratio est: quia fœdus hoc non est absolutum: sed conditionatum, sub determinatione fidei. Quando verò sic lapsus, postmodùm per veram pœnitentiam ad fidem renovatur: tùm fœdus pristinum denuò ipsi incipit esse utile ac salutare. Quo pacto pœnitentia in lapsis non est novum Sacramentum, vel nova ratio promerendæ remissionis peccatorum, uti Concilium Tridentinum somniat: Sess. 14. cap. 2. sed tantùm est reditus ad gratuitam illam promissionem fœderalem de remissione peccatorum, propter satisfactionem Christi Mediatoris, in Baptismo nobis donatam & obsignatam.

ALTERUM argumentum sic informari potest: Baptismus salvos nos facit, qui non est abjectio sordium carnis, sed stipulatio bonæ conscientiæ in DEUM per resurrectionem Jesu Christi. 1. Pet. 3. 21. Jam verò finis veræ pœnitentiæ non est alius, quàm ut nobis constare rursus possit stipulatio ἐπερώτημα bonæ conscientiæ cum DEO. Atqui finis iste, teste Petro, nobis ad salutem obtingit, non nisi ex Baptismo. Ergò Baptismi fructus & effectus salutaris pænitentibus semper est & manet ratus atquè efficax.

TERTIUM. Quo pacto sive medio D. Petrus post tristissimum suum lapsum, rediit cum DEO in gratiam, & remissionem peccati, atrocissimi impetravit: eodem quoq́; & non alio, pœnitentes quiq́; cum DEO reconciliari possunt ac debent. Atqui Petrus, defectione à Christo gravissimè prolapsus, tertia vice Dominum ac Magistrum suum abnegans: pœnitentiam verò postmodùm agens, non nisi suo se Baptismo efficacissimè consolatus est: id quod ipse de se testatur, 1. cap. 3, 20 & 21. Cujus (arcæ Noæ) figuræ nunc res spondens Baptismus, nos quoque salvos reddit: sic per figuram Communicationis seipsum includens. E.

QUARTO: idem Apostolus Petrus loco jam citato, Baptismum comprobat non tabulæ alicui fractæ navis, uti Pontificij solent: sed integræ & firmissimæ navi, arcæ videlicet Noæ: extra quam salus nemini obtingere possit.

QUINTO pertinet huc locus ille Apostolicus, Ephes. 5, 25. & 26. Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, & seipsum tradidit pro eâ, ut illam sanctificaret, mundans eam lavacro aquæ in Verbo, ut exhiberet eamsibi gloriosam, non habentem maculam aut rugam, aut aliquid hujusmodi, sed ut esset sancta & immaculata. Quem locum B. Augustinus ex nostrâ sententiâ, contra Romanenses sic explicat: lib. 1. de nupt. & concup. cap 33. Quòd ait Apostolus: Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, mundans eam lavacro aquæ in verbo &c. sic accipiendum est, ut eodem lavacro regenerationis, & verbo sanctificationis omnia prorsus mala hominum regeneratorum mundentur atque sanentur, non solùm peccata, quæ omnia nunc remittuntur in Baptismo, sed etiam quæ POSTERIUS humana ignorantia vel infirmitate contrahantur: non ut Baptisma, quoties peccatur, toties repetatur: sed quia ipso, quod semel da- " tur, fit, ut non solùm anteà, verùm etiam postea, " quorumlibet peccatorum venia fidelibus impetre- " tur. Quid enim prodesse vel ante Baptismum pœ- " nitentia, nisi Baptismus sequeretur? Vel quid prodes- " set postea, nisi præcederet Baptismus? "

Quam in sententiam idem Augustinus nervosè & eleganter scribit, lib. 4. de Bapt. Cont. Donatist. cap. 15. In baptizato inseparabiliter Baptismum permanere manifestum est: quia in quodlibet profundum malorum, & in quamlibet horribilem peccatorum voraginem irruat baptizatus, usq; ad apostolicam ruinam: non tamen caret Baptismo: & ideò per pœnitentiam redeunti non redditur, quia eo non carere potuisse, judicatur.

Et lib. 7. cap. 36. Sic est unum Baptisma in Ecclesiâ Catholicâ, ut cum exindè aliqui exierint, in ijs, qui exeunt, non fiant duo, sed idem unum maneat. Quod ergò in redeuntibus agnoscitur, hoc & in eis, qui à recedentibus acceperunt, quod illicùm recederent non amiserunt.

Puriori huic doctrinæ magno conatu se opponit gens Efavvitica fingens, in Baptismo conferri quidem remissionem peccatorum gratis sine nostris operibus, propter meritum Christi, fide apprehensum: verùm in lapsis post Baptismum, Pœnitentiam impetrare veniam, non fide, non gratis, non sine operibus: sed per & propter opera Pœnitentiæ Sacramentalis.

Sed sentina hæc est crassissimorum errorum: imò atrox sacrilegium, est in æternum illud & immutabile fœdus DEI: quasi aliam reconciliationis & salvationis rationem in Baptismo promulgarit DEUS, aliam verò ac planè diversam per pœnitentiam, quæ priorem illam prorsus annihilet & aboleat. Quo pacto contradictoriæ DEO affingerentur voluntates. Præterea per Efavviticam hanc ματαιολογίαν, consequentium cùm effectis turpis committitur confusio: imò blasphemia manifesta designatur in eo, quòd humano operi, cum actione DEI Sacramentali, par & æqualis efficacia adscribitur.

Argumenta, quibus Bellarminus pro suâ fucandâ impietate pugnat, non unius sunt teruntij. Nam primùm memoriam Baptismi esfe medium aut remedium pro peccatorum remissione impetrandâ, nunquàm diximus, scripsimus, aut cogitavimus. Neq; enim Fidem, per memoriam aut recordationem Baptismi definimus: uti ipsimet noverunt Esavvitæ.

Deindè manifestè falsum est, quòd Sacrificia, expiationes & justificationes Veteris Testamenti, contulerint hominibus remissionem peccatorum, ex se, & tanquàm opera, vel ex opere operato. Nam ut epistola ad Hebræos evidenter docet, obtinebant Sacrificia illa hanc vim expiandi non ex se: sed in typo, hoc est, in Christo, quem eminùs præfigurabant. Inserviebant enim tantùm similitudini, exemplari & umbræ, sive adumbrabant, plenissimam illam perfectissimamque victimam, Christum nimirùm, qui solus ex se, & ex opere operato fidelibus & promeriturus, & collaturus sit remissionem peccatorum.

Tertiò insignem petulantiam prodit Bellarminus, objiciens nobis locum illum, Hebr. 6, 1. ubi Apostolus monet Hebræos, ne iterum respiciant ad primordia Baptismi, & fidei, & illi9 pœnitentiæ, quæ Baptismum præcedit. Undè tacitè innuit Esavvita nullum ampliùs Baptismi usum esse posse, apud lapsos post baptismum. Atqui nihil tale in mentem venit Apostolo, neque textus etiam innuit: sed manifestum crimen falsi textui affingitur. Sed esto, sit iste sensus verborum Apostoli, quæ obsecrò infinita absurda indè consequerentur. Nam ex egregiâ hâc explicatione Esavviticâ sequeretur: lapsis post Baptismum non ampliùs respiciendum esse ad Decalogum, neque secundum ejus præcepta informandam esse pœnitentiam: Quia ibidem, versu 1. dicit Apostolus: Non ampliùs jaciendum esse fundamentum pænitentiæ: Quibus verbis ad Decalogum digitum intendi, notius est, quàm ut probatione indigeat. Sic sequeretur: lapsis post baptismum nullum posse ampliùs esse usum Symboli Apostolici, & per consequens, ne quidem ampliùs credendum in Christum: qui statim subjicit Apostolus: non ampliùs, jaciendum esse fundamentum fidei in Deum: Quibus verbis Symbolum Apostolicum notari, nemo est, qui eat inficias. Patet hinc desultoria petulantia gentis Esavviticæ, in depravandis Scripturarum testimoniis. Nos errorem istum corrigimus, genuinum verborum Apostoli sensum aperiendo, qui non est iste, quasi Hebræi non ampliùs respicere debeant, vel ad Baptismum, vel ad pœnitentiam, vel ad fidem: sed quòd non semper in primis illis elementis doctrinæ Catecheticæ, tanquàm pueri, inhærere: sed ad sublimiora Religionis Christianæ mysteria percipienda, animos suos instruere, & præparare debeant. Quid? quod omnem Esavvitæ impetum prorsus subruit & evertit, quòd Apostolus statim tribus jam enumerat Capitibus doctrinæ Catecheticæ, annumerat etiam Resurrectionem mortuorum, & judicium æternum, ubi ex Esavvitæ interpretatione sequeretur, Lapsos post Baptismum uti Baptismum, sic etiam resurrectionem mortuorum, & judicium æternum respicere aut curare ampliùs non debere: id quod absurdum & impium.

Quartò ac postremò frivolum ac elumbe planè est, quòd Esauvita subindè ex Patribus repetit, Pænitentiam ideò nominari secundam post naufragium tabulam, quia Baptismi, tanquàm fractæ tabulæ, usus nullus ampliùs esse possit. Nam Patribus tale quid in mentem nunquàm venisse, paulò antè ex Augustino cognovimus. Cæterùm, quo ad phrases de tabulâ secundâ, quibus Hieronymus, & alij frequenter utuntur, non negamus, Pœnitentiam analogicè dici posse tabulam secundam: non autem sensu Esauvitico, quasi Baptismi tabula jam ex omni parte fracta, & irrita ac inutilis facta sit: sed sensu orthodoxo: quia Pœnitentia est altera illa tabula, quâ ad priorem redire, ex naufragio quasi, ad pristinum Baptismi sive fœderis divini littus adspirare queamus.


### Chapter Second. On the Parts of Penitence

It is the constant and perpetual doctrine of the orthodox Church that there are only two parts of true repentance: namely, Contrition and Faith. The chief foundations of this doctrine are these:

I. The essential parts of true repentance can and must be sought only from those requirements which are necessarily required in a penitent man, provided that he ought to return to favor with GOD. But there are only two such requirements: namely, contrition and Faith. Therefore.

The proposition has as its supporter Bellarmine himself, lib. 1, de Pænit., Cap. 18. The assumption is evident from the Scriptures, which always join these two, namely repentance, strictly and specifically placed for Contrition, and Faith: as in Mark 1:15. Repent, and believe in the Gospel. Luke 24:47. It behooves repentance and remission of sins to be preached in the name of Christ. Acts 5:31. to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins. Acts 20:21. I have announced to you repentance and faith, which is toward our Lord Jesus Christ.

II. The entire Scripture consists of two, and no more, kinds of doctrines: namely, the Law and the Gospel: But both of these doctrines perform their own certain and proper function in approaching true and saving repentance: the Law indeed by working wrath and leading to the acknowledgment of sin: but the Gospel by effecting faith in Christ, by raising up, and by comforting. Therefore there will also be only two parts of repentance: Contrition, and Faith.

III. The entire practice of the Apostles: as also

The Scripture of the Old Testament describes the repentance of the fallen in such a way that it reduces it to only these two parts, as 1. By the example of Adam, who, struck by the terror of the law, flees from the face of GOD, and hides himself and is afraid: but, raised up by the voice of the Gospel concerning the seed of the woman, who will crush the head of the serpent, he breathes again. Gen. 3, 8, and 10, and 15. 2. Of David, who, terrified by the legal threat, 'You are that man of death,' exclaims: I have sinned against the Lord: but soon, having heard the voice of the Gospel: 'The Lord has taken away your sin, you shall not die,' he is refreshed and finds rest. 2 Sam. 12, 7, and 13. 3. Of the thief, who, contrite because of the guilt of sin acknowledged, confesses that he is suffering things worthy of his deeds: but groaning from faith toward CHRIST, 'Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom': having heard the most joyful voice of absolution: 'Today you will be with me in paradise': he dies with a quiet mind. Luke 23, 41, and following. 4. Of the sinful woman, Luke 7, 37. who, struck under the sense of sin, wept, but trusting in the salvation of CHRIST alone, hears the most joyful voice of the Gospel: Your sins are forgiven you: Your faith has made you safe: go in peace, verses 49 and 50. 5. Of the Apostle Peter, who, having denied CHRIST three times, struck by the atrocity of this sin, wept most bitterly: but raised up by the look of CHRIST, he breathed again, Luke 22, 60 and 62. Nor can a dissimilar example of saving repentance be shown. Therefore.

IV. Every change has a term from Which and to Which. The repentance of the fallen is a change. Therefore it will also consist of both these terms. Now, indeed, contrition sustains the office of the term from Which: for sorrow over committed sin shows from what one must depart. Faith, however, has the nature of the term to Which, showing to whom one must approach, namely to CHRIST, and in his merit alone one must find rest.

Finally, from Augustine's book on true and false repentance, chapter 2, we repeat this: If faith is the foundation of repentance, apart from which there is nothing that is good, that repentance must be sought which is established to be founded in faith. For repentance which does not proceed from faith is not useful. It is necessary, however, to believe that the remedy of repentance is granted by the Savior.

But we shall examine these individual parts, and their proper nature and affection, separately.

I. Concerning Contrition.

The term contrition is ἔγγραφον [written/scriptural], and very familiar to the Holy Spirit himself in the matter of repentance; as when David, struck by the atrocity of the sin committed, exclaims: A contrite and humbled heart, O GOD, you will not despise. Ps. 51, 19. And King Hezekiah, As a lion he has crushed all my bones, Isa. 38, 13. Therefore, no controversy exists between us and the Efavvites regarding the use of this term: but it is mainly regarding its definition and nature that we are fighting today. We establish, however, that the subject of true and serious contrition is not the external sad and tragic gestures of the body, which can also fall to hypocrites, but rather the very fountain and root of all sins, namely the heart, or the conscience of man, which is at once the infallible Witness and Judge of the deeds committed by him. Such contrition ensures that, as the Prophet Joel has it, garments are not torn—a thing which hypocrites can also perform—but that hearts are torn. How this tearing of hearts can be detected, the Apostle shows, Rom. 2, 15, saying: The work of the law is written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness together, and their thoughts mutually accusing or even excusing one another. Then, therefore, at last, the heart is truly contrite when it feels within itself the judicial seat of divine justice, pronouncing the man cursed and guilty of eternal damnation because of sins committed: and when the thoughts themselves accuse, convict, and condemn the man.

2. The προκαταρκτικὴ (preliminary) cause of this contrition is the Law of GOD, and whatever in any way performs the office of the law. In which part, great use is also had, not only by the consideration of the most sorrowful examples, of Adam, David, Solomon, and the like, whose falls drew with them huge ruins, not only of private evils but also of public ones: Such as are, the most sorrowful tearing away of the whole human race from GOD: the primeval flood: the Sodomitic conflagration: the Israelitic destruction: civil wars: pestilent contagion: the tearing apart of the Israelitic kingdom: the dissipation of religion: and other innumerable calamities: But also the frequent meditation of those things by which the foulness and atrocity of sin is partly argued, partly punished: such as are: The severity of the precepts of the Decalogue, and the immutable rigor, pronouncing a curse upon him who does not do those things which are written in the book of the law: Likewise, the wrath and fury of the heavenly avenger, who is a consuming fire: The invariable rule of divine judgment and justice, the loss of the grace of GOD, and of the Holy Spirit: the loss of reputation, poverty, diseases, confusion of counsels, errors, the torment of conscience, the unhappiness of studies, of children, and the degeneration of posterity, scandals, the tyranny of the devil, death, and finally the horror of eternal damnation: But especially the passion and death of Christ, if you regard the consideration of it not as primary and proper: but as secondary and accidental: which sets before the eyes the clearest and most polished mirror of divine wrath, and performs the office of the law excellently. Scripture confirms this very thing, pronouncing concerning the Law, that from it comes the knowledge of sin: Rom. 3, 20. that it works wrath, Rom. 4, 15. that it shows what sin is, Rom. 7, 7. Moreover, that effect of the Law, namely serious contrition for committed sins, arises from the Law, not by means of the virtue or quality of free will, and of our own powers: but from the operation of the Holy Spirit: for it is GOD who effects the compunction of the heart and repentance. Acts 2, 37. 1 Tim. 2, 25.

3. The end and effect of contrition is not in any part of itself meritorious, such as the Romanists imagine: but it is required as a part of that order which GOD observes in converting men: while He determines to raise up and convert none but those who are contrite, and prostrated by the sense of divine wrath: so that just as from the hearing of the divine word, saving faith indeed arises: but the hearing itself is by no means or respect the merit of our justification: since if God had not ordained to work faith through this medium, man would never conceive faith, even if he were to hear the word for a thousand years with the utmost study and attention: Thus contrition does not merit reconciliation with God: but is only a part of the order which God has ordained to use in converting man.

4. The manner also, the quantity and quality of contrition come under observation. Concerning which matter a sharp controversy exists today between us and the Romanists: as we shall show in the third chapter. But following the Scriptures, we define the manner and quality and require that from it all pharisaical hypocrisy be absent. Regarding the quantity, however, we maintain that no certain measure of sorrow and dread can or ought to be established or defined: nor do we think it should be measured or weighed by a certain time: For with God the measure of time does not avail as much as the measure of sorrow, as Jerome writes somewhere. These members having been duly observed, we define contrition as the serious compunction of a dismayed and groaning mind, kindled by the voice of the law, from the recognition of admitted sin and the remembrance of the offenses against God, by which the penitent man both seriously grieves for the sins admitted, and from the inmost heart dreads the wrath of God and the punishments deserved for sins.

To this orthodox doctrine, besides the Papists, of whom we shall treat in the third chapter, the opinion of Philip and the Philippists is most opposed, who maintain that contrition is sought and arises not from the Law alone, but also from the Gospel, because not only the Law, but also the Gospel convicts of sins. Which error was indeed rightly exploded and rejected by the Book of Christian Concord, because it confuses the Law and the Gospel, and utterly undermines and overturns the essential distinction between these two kinds of doctrine: as we showed above in the prolegomena: and in the exegesis of the Book of Concord we have expressly disputed concerning this error.

Latin:

COnstans est & perpetua orthodoxæ Ecclesiæ doctrina, Duas tantùm esse partes veræ pœnitentiæ: nempè Contritionem & Fidem. Doctrinæ autem hujus fundamenta præcipua sunt hæc:

I. Partes veræ Pœnitentiæ essentiales, non nisi ex illis requisitis peti possunt & debent, quæ in homine pœnitente necessariò requiruntur, dumm odò cum DEO in gratiam redire debeat. Atqui duo tantùm sunt hujusmodi requisita: nempè contritio & Fides. Ergò.

Propositio adstipulatorem habet ipsum quoque Bellarminum lib. 1. de Pænit. Cap. 18. Assumtio patet ex Scripturis, quæ duo hæc, pœnitentiam nimirùm, strictè & μερικῶς pro Contritione positam, & Fidem semper conjungit: ut Marci 1,15. Agite pœnitentiam, & credite Evangelio. Luc. 24, 47. Oportet prædicari in nomine Christi pœnitentiam & Remissionem peccatorum. Actor. 5, 31. ad dandam Israëli pœnitentiam, & remissionem peccatorum. Actor. 20, 21. Annunciavi vobis pœnitentiam & fidem, quæ est erga Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum.

II. Scriptura universa duobus, & non pluribus constat doctrinarum generibus: Lege nimirùm & Evangelio: Atqui utraque hæc doctrina, in accêdendâ verâ ac salutari pœnitentiâ, certum suum ac proprium munus exequitur: Lex quidem iram operando, & ad agnitionem peccati adducendo: Evangelium verò, fidem in Christum efficiendo, erigendo, consolando. Ergò duæ etiam tantùm erunt partes pœnitentiæ: Contritio, & Fides.

III. Praxis Apostolorum universa: ut &

Scriptura Veteris Testamenti, sic describit pœnitentiam lapsorum, ut ad has duas tantùm partes eam revocet, ut 1. Exemplo Adami, qui terrore legis perculsus, fugit à facie DEI, sequè abscondit & timuit: sed voce Evangelij de semine mulieris, contrituro caput serpentis, erectus respirat. Gen.3,8. & 10, & 15. 2. Davidis, qui comminatione legali, Tu es vir ille mortis, perterrefactus exclamat: peccavi in Dominum: sed mox auditâ voce Evangelij: Abstulit Dominus peccatum tuum, non morieris, recreatus acquievit. 2.Sam.12,7. & 13. 3. Latronis, qui reatu peccati agniti contritus, confitetur se digna factis perpeti: sed ad CHRISTUM ex fide ingemiscens, Domine, memento mei cùm veneris in regnum tuum: auditâ absolutionis voce jucundissimâ: Hodiè mecum eris in paradiso: quieto animo moritur. Luc. 23, 41. & seqq. 4. Mulieris peccatricis, Luc. 7,37. quæ sub sensu peccati perculsa illachrymatus, sed in unius CHRISTI salute confidens, audit lætissimam Evangelij vocem: Remissa sunt tibi peccata: Fides tua te salvam fecit: vade in pace, versu 49. & 50. 5. Petri Apostoli, qui ter abnegato CHRISTO, atrocitate peccati hujus perculsus flevit amarissimè: sed CHRISTI intuitu erectus, respiravit, Luc. 22, 60. & 62. Neq; dissimile exemplum pœnitentiæ salutaris monstrari potest. Ergò.

IV. Omnis mutatio terminum habet à Quo & ad Quem. Pœnitentia lapsorum est mutatio. Ergò constabit etiam utroq; isto termino. Jam verò contritio sustinet officium termini, à Quo: Dolor enim de admisso peccato, monstrat à quo sit recendendum. Fides verò habet rationem termini ad Quem, monstrans ad quem sit accedendum, nempè ad CHRISTUM, inq; ipsius merito unicè acquiescendum.

Tandem ex Augustini libro de verâ & falsâ pœnit cap. 2. repetimus illud: Si Fides fundamentum est pœnitentiæ, præter quam nihil est, quod bonum sit, appetenda est ea pœnitentia, quam constat in fide esse fundatam. Pœnitentia enim quæ ex fide non procedit, utilis non est. Oportet autem credi, remedium pœnitentiæ à Salvatore concedi.

Verùm de singulis istis partibus, earumq; propriâ naturâ atque affectione seorsim dispiciemus.

I. De Contritione.

COntritionis Vocabulum ἔγγραφον est, & ipsi Spiritui Sancto in materiâ de Pœnitentiâ admodùm familiare; ut cum David peccati admissi atrocitate perculsus exclamat: Cor contritum & humiliatum DEUS non despicies. Ps. 51, 19. Et Rex Ezechias, Sicut Leo contrivit omnia ossa mea, Jes.38, 13. De usu ergò vocabuli hujus controversia nulla nobis cum Efavvitis intercedit: sed de definitione & naturâ ejus præcipuè inter nos hodiè pugnatur. Constituimus autem contritionis veræ ac seriæ subjectum, non externos corporis gestus tristes ac tragicos: qui in hypocritas quoq; cadere possunt: sed potiùs ipsum fontem ac radicem peccatorum omnium, nempè cor, sive conscientiam hominis, quæ factorum à se commissorum, infallibilis simul & Testis & Judex est. Talis contritio præstat, ut quod Joël Propheta habet, non scindantur vestimenta: id quod hypocritæ etiam præstare possunt, sed ut scindantur corda. Quæ cordium scissio quomodo deprehendi queat, monstrat Apostolus, Rom. 2, 15. Opus legis, inquiens, scriptum est in cordibus ipsorum, unà testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientiâ, & cogitationibus sese mutuò accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus. Tum ergò demum cor verè est contritum, quando intra se sentit sedem judicialem justitiæ divinæ, maledictum pronunciantis hominem, & æternæ damnationis reum ob peccata admissa: & quando ipsæ cogitationes hominem accusant, convincunt, damnant.

2. Causa προκαταρκτικὴ contritionis hujus est Lex DEI, & quicquid quoquo modo legis officio fungitur. Quâ in parte usum magnũ etiam habet, non modò consideratio tristissimorum exemplorum, Adami, Davidis, Salomonis, & similium, quorum lapsus secum ingentes traxerunt ruinas, non privatorum tantùm malorum sed & publicorum: Qualia sunt, universi generis humani tristissima à DEO avulsio: diluvium primævum: incendium Sodomiticum: excidium Israëlïticum: bella civilia: pestilens contagio: divulsio regni Israëlïtici: religionis dissipatio: & calamitates aliæ innumeræ: Verùm etiam meditatio frequens earum rerum, quibus peccati fœditas & atrocitas arguitur partim, partim punitur: quales sunt: Præceptorum Decalogi severitas, & rigor immutabilis, maledictũ pronuncians non facientem ea, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis: Item, ira & furor vindicis cœlestis, qui ignis consumens est: Judicij justitiæque divinæ regula invariabilis, amissio gratiæ DEI, & Spiritus Sancti: jactura famæ, inopia morbi, vertigo consiliorum, errores, carnificina conscientiæ, infelicitas studiorũ, liberorũ, & posteritatis degeneratio, scandala, diaboli tyrannis, mors, tandemq́; æternæ damnationis horror: Cumprimis autem passio & mors Christi, si considerationem ejus non primam atq; propriam: sed secundariam & accidentalem respicias: quæ limpidissimum politissimumq́; speculum iræ divinæ: ob oculos constituit, & legis officio præclarè fungitur. Confirmat hoc ipsum Scriptura, de Lege pronuncians, quòd ex eâ fit agnitio peccati: Rom. 3, 20. quòd iram operetur, Rom. 4, 15. quòd ostendat, quid sit peccatum, Rom. 7, 7. Cæterùm effectus iste Legis, nempè seria contritio de admissis peccatis ex Lege oritur, non mediante virtute aut qualitate liberi arbitrij, nostrarumq́; virium: sed ex operatione Spiritus Sancti: DEUS enim est, qui efficit compunctionem cordis & pœnitentiam. Act. 2, 37. 1. Tim. 2, 25.

3. Finis & Effectus contritionis non est ullâ sui parte meritorius, qualem fingunt Romanenses: sed requiritur, ut pars ordinis illius, quẽ DEus in convertendis hominib9 observat: dùm non nisi contritos, & sensu iræ divinæ prostratos, erigere & convertere constituit: ita ut quemadmodum ex auditu verbi divini, fides quidem salvifica oritur: auditus autem ipse nullo prorsus pacto aut respectu est meritum justificationis nostrae: siquidem nisi Deus per hoc medium fidem operari constituisset homo nunquam fidem conciperet, si vel mille annis, studio & attentione summa verbum audiret: Ita contritio non mereatur reconciliationem cum Deo: sed tantum sit pars ordinis, qua Deus in convertendo homine uti constituit.

4. Modus etiam, quantitas & qualitas contritionis sub observationem venit. Qua de re acris hodie cum Romanensibus nobis intercedit cotroversia: uti capite tertio ostendemus. Verum Scripturas secuti, modum & qualitatem definimus & requirimus eam, a qua absit omnis pharisaīca hypocrisis. Quoad Quantitatem vero nullum certum doloris & pavoris modum statui aut definiri vel posse vel debere statuimus: quin nec certo tempore eam vel metiendam vel ponderandam esse arbitramur: Nam apud Deum nō tam valet mensura temporis, quam doloris, uti Hieronymus alicubi scribit. Membris istis rite observatis, definimus contritionem, quod sit seria animi consternati & gemebundi compunctio, per vocem legis, ex peccati admissi agnitione, offensisq́; Dei recordatione accensa, qua & de admissis peccatis, homo pœnitens serio dolet, & ad iram Dei, pœnasq́; ob peccata promeritas, ex intimo pectore expavescit.

Orthodoxae huic doctrinae praeter Pontificios, de quibus capite tertio agetur, maxime adversatur Philippi & Philippistarum opinio, statuentium, non ex sola Lege, sed & ex Evangelio peti ac oriri contritionem, propterea quod non tantum Lex, sed & Evangelium arguat peccata. Qui sanè error per librum Christianae Concordiae rectè explosus & rejectus fuit, propterea quod Legem & Evangelium confundit, & essentiale discrimen inter haec duo doctrinarum genera, penitus subruit & evertit: uti suprà in prolegomenis ostendimus: & in diexodo libri Concordiae ex professo, de hoc errore disputavimus.


### Chapter Second. On the Parts of Penitence: II. Of Faith

We constitute the other part of repentance as faith in Christ the Savior, by which a man, prostrated by the Law of God, raises himself up, believes certainly in the promises concerning the free remission of sins, and safely rests in the mercy of God. The reasons for our assertion, besides those general ones which we noted above, are these more special ones: 1. Because faith alone completes our conversion and renders it perfect: because that former part, contrition, sustains only the nature of a term from which, showing from what the penitent man must turn away and flee: where this change has attained only its beginning, not however its end. Now, however, faith alone provides this complement, which shows the term to which one must flee in such great dismay of heart and conscience, where we may safely rest and be certain of the remission of sins. 2. Because faith alone ensures that contrition is true and useful, or, as the Apostle speaks, that contrition is sorrow according to God, and does not drive us to separation: which is evident from the difference between the Contrition or Repentance of Judas and Peter: of Cain and David, etc. 3. Because faith alone works in man the fear of GOD, not servile, but filial, so that now the penitent does not flee from GOD but raises himself up amidst the terrors, and seeks and receives effective consolation from GOD. 4. Because faith alone receives the remission of sins, acquires peace with GOD, and produces tranquility in the conscience, according to that Rom. 5, 1: justified by faith, we have peace toward GOD, through our Lord JESUS CHRIST. Eph. 6, 16: above all take up the shield of faith, by which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one. Eph. 3, 12: In CHRIST we have confidence and access in confidence, through his faith. 5. Because faith alone can apply in species and in the individual the promise concerning the free remission of sins, through and on account of Christ: which no other virtue can provide.

Furthermore, we understand faith not as historical at least, which consists of a bare knowledge and assent to the history concerning Christ: and which falls even to the Devils themselves: but that which is a firm trust of the heart, apprehending the promises of saving grace in Christ, and opening access to GOD, and which, believing the promises, is no less certain of things not even appearing, but future, than if it were contemplating them as present in the very act: Whence it is defined by the Apostle as ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων, καὶ ἔλεγχος πραγμάτων οὐ βλεπομένων, Hebr. 11, 1. To this purer doctrine concerning faith, the Romanists, the Calvinists, and certain Philippists oppose themselves. The Romanists indeed in this, 1. that, although they concede that faith is necessary in penitents: yet they contend that it is a property of some condition at least, but not of the essence itself: that is, they contend that faith is only a certain requirement in the penitent man, but not an essential and, as it were, formal part of repentance.

2. They do not define this faith by a firm πεποίθησιν or trust in the promise of the Gospel, concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, through and for the sake of Christ apprehended by faith: such as we require. For Bellarmine writes expressly in lib. 1 de poen. c. 19: That what we said, that repentance cannot be had without faith: we understood of true and Catholic faith: not of that figment of the Lutherans, which they call justifying faith, and is the principal part of repentance. And the Council of Trent more clearly, Sess. 6. c. 12: If anyone shall say that justifying faith is trust in the mercy of God, who remits sins for Christ's sake, let him be anathema. It is asked therefore now, What then is the faith of the Jesuits today, that is true and Catholic faith? That indeed from the decrees of the Council of Trent it is permitted to gather: where among other things they will that a penitent man ought to conceive such trust concerning divine mercy, if he of his own accord and voluntarily out of love for God assumes sorrow for sins, and presents it to be seen by external gestures and motions: and has the purpose that he wishes to confess to a priest each and every sin, and all circumstances which could in any way vary the species of the sin: nay, that he will also with a willing and patient mind take upon himself and execute the satisfactions enjoined by the Priest in the act of confession: If, I say, he does these things, it will be that by this compact he satisfies for his sins, obtains the remission of the same and reconciliation with God. Hence such a definition of Jesuit-Catholic faith emerges, that it is a trust by which one believes and determines that the actions of repentance, voluntarily undertaken and performed by man, have by the merit of Christ the power that they can merit the remission of sins and reconciliation with GOD. Concerning this faith Bellarmine writes, that it is not indeed a part of repentance, yet it is necessarily required for effecting it. And the Council of Trent, Sess. 6, cap. 6, that this faith is to be placed in the first rank among those things which dispose to justification: and yet it ought to be clearly distinguished from repentance, which holds the fifth place among those dispositions.

But concerning this faith, which certainly believes and maintains that in our works, by the merit of CHRIST, there is inherent the power of meriting the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life, the whole Holy Scripture knows not even γρὺ (a whit). Therefore we deservedly abhor and execrate it as a βδέλυγμα (abomination) of Esauvitic impiety.

Moreover, the arguments by which the Esauvites are moved to deny that Faith is a part of Repentance are chiefly these:

I. In the Holy Scriptures faith is distinguished from Repentance: as in Mark 1:15, the Lord does not say: Repent believing the Gospel: but Repent and believe the Gospel. Therefore Faith is not a part of Repentance.

Or according to others: Just as the Law and the Gospel are joined together: so also are Repentance and Faith. But that is done in such a way that the Gospel is by no means constituted a part of the law. Therefore it is necessary that it be done here also, that Faith and Repentance are indeed joined together in the scriptures: yet faith is not a part of Repentance.

I ANSWER: This whole structure rests upon the sophism of homonymy. For in Mark, and elsewhere in the Scriptures, where Faith and Repentance are mutually distinguished from each other: the word Repentance is not used in its proper meaning, for the whole conversion to GOD: but in a less proper sense for contrition alone. In which sense we readily grant that faith is not a part of Repentance, that is, of Contrition: but a thing clearly distinct from it. But when the word Repentance is taken in its proper sense, for the whole conversion to GOD: certainly the truth of the Gospel does not allow us to exclude faith from repentance as something distinct: both because of the causes and reasons explained a little before: and because of these two: 1. Because the remission of sins, and reconciliation with GOD, is the proper and highest end of repentance: which, however, neither is apprehended otherwise than by faith alone. 2. Because conversion and despair differ insofar as in conversion the conscience of man is not left in doubt. But faith alone is the conqueror of doubts. Therefore, so that conversion may not degenerate into despair, it is necessary that it consist of Faith.

II. Faith precedes Repentance, and begets it, therefore it is indeed a cause, but it can in no way be a part. Bellarmine confirms the antecedent, 1. by the example of the Ninevites, who believed in GOD, and only afterwards proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, Jonah 3:5. 2. By reason: Because it cannot be understood that anyone seriously begins to perform repentance unless he first believes that those things are true which GOD both threatens to sinners and promises to the penitent.

I ANSWER the Antecedent by a distinction between the repentance of those who, having fallen from the grace of GOD, are to be converted anew: and the repentance of those who stand, or that constant and daily repentance of the reborn, who persevere in the exercise of piety, and having mortified the old Adam, proceed from faith to faith, through daily increments. Regarding that former species of repentance, the Antecedent is false. For faith does not there precede repentance, but exists at the same time with it in time: indeed, in order of reason, it is posterior to contrition. But regarding the repentance of those who stand or the daily repentance of the Reborn: we willingly concede that faith precedes that constant mortification of the flesh, just as a cause precedes an effect. But this is not the dispute in this place regarding this species of repentance.

Furthermore, it must be well noted that, although faith, regarding the repentance of those who stand, is a cause of the mortification of the flesh, nevertheless it is also a part of this repentance: so that faith sustains the character of both cause and part, but in a different respect. For insofar as the Reborn is moved by true faith in CHRIST and love of GOD to undergo that perpetual crucifixion of the flesh; faith deservedly obtains the respect of a cause. But insofar as the Reborn certainly believes and maintains that in the same work, whatever remains of the flesh and the dross of the old Adam is forgiven him, not otherwise than on account of the merit of CHRIST by grace: it is manifest that faith, in this species of repentance also, sustains the respect of a part. Nor can or ought this to seem absurd to anyone: since even in natural things, the same thing can obtain the respect of both a part and a cause, but in a different respect. The soul certainly, which is the entelechy informing man, is at once both the cause and a part of man: a thing which no sane person will deny.

The example of the Ninevites is nothing to the point: for when they proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, they did not only then begin to do penance; but they declared the penance which they had conceived in their mind—both by serious sorrow for the sins committed and by true trust in GOD—in this manner, as if by certain external signs. These signs of penance, we willingly grant, are subsequent to faith, nay, are the effects of preceding faith.

The Esavvitic argument added likewise deals only with the external signs of penance, from which it can be understood that someone is doing penance seriously. But just as these signs or external works are not penance itself, nor even a part of it, but only its effect or consequence: so we readily concede that they are also subsequent to faith; nor does our doctrine suffer anything from that.

III. Those actions which flow from the virtue of Penance are to be considered parts of Penance. But to believe is an action not of Penance, which is a moral virtue, but of the virtue of faith, which is Theological. Therefore.

I ANSWER: The proposition fails under a false hypothesis: for the Esavvitic feigns that there are no parts of actions, except those which emanate from some inherent habit of moral virtue: which is most false. Therefore, that error is corrected by the contrary hypothesis,

Latin:

ALteram Poenitentiae partem constituimus fidem in Christum Servatorem, quà homo Lege Dei prostratus, sese erigit, promissionibus de gratuità peccatorum remissione certo credit, inquè Dei misericordia tutò acquiescit. Rationes assertionis nostrae, praeter generales illas, quas suprà notavimus, sunt specialiores istae 1.
