Quia sola fides conversionem nostram absolvit, & perfectam reddit: proptereà quod prior illa pars contritio, sustinet tantum rationem termini, à Quo; ostendens à quo homini poenitenti declinandum fugiendumq́; sit: ubi mutatio haec tantum initium, non autem finem suum assecuta est. Jam verò complementum hoc praestat sola fides, quȩ monstrat terminum ad Quem in tanta cordis & conscientiae consternatione sit confugiendum, ubi tutò acquiescere, & de remissione peccatorum certi esse queamus. 2. Quia sola fides praestat, ut contritio sit vera atq́; utilis, vel, ut Apostolus loquitur, contritio sit dolor secundum Deum, neq́; ad separationem nos adigat: id quod patet ex differentià Contritionis sive Poenitentiae Judae & Petri: Caini & Davidis &c. 3. Quia sola fides operatur in homine timorem DEI, non servilem, sed filialem, ut jam pœnitens non fugiat à DEO sed inter medios pavores sese erigat, & à DEO consolationem efficacem quærat & accipiat. 4. Quia sola fides remissionem peccatorum accipit, pacem cum DEO acquirit, tranquillitatem in conscientiâ parit, secundum illud Rom. 5, 1. justificati fide, pacem habemus erga DEUM, per Dominum nostrum JESUM CHRISTUM. Eph. 6, 16. ante omnia assumite scutum fidei, quo possitis omnia tela nequissimi ignea extinguere. Eph. 3, 12. In CHRISTO habemus fiduciam & accessum in confidentiâ, per fidem ejus. 5. Quia sola fides potest in specie atq; in individuo applicare promissionem de gratuita peccatorum remissione, per & propter Christum: id quod nulla virtus alia præstare potest.

Cæterùm intelligimus fidem non historicam saltem, quæ nudâ constet notitiâ & assensu historiæ de Christo: & in ipsos etiam Diabolos cadit: sed eam, quæ est firma cordis fiducia, promissiones gratiæ salutaris in Christo apprehendens, & accessum ad DEUM patefaciens, quæq; promissionibus credens, de rebus etiam nō apparentibus, sed futuris haud minùs certa est, quàm si actu ipso præsentia contemplaretur : Undè ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων, καὶ ἔλεγχος πραγμάτων ὀ βλεπομένων ab Apostolo definitur, Hebr. 11, 1. Puriori huic doctrinæ de fide sese opponunt tùm Romanenses, tùm Calviniani, tùm quidam Philippistæ. Romanenses quidem in eo, 1. quòd, licèt concedant, fidem in pœnitentibus esse necessariam : Conditionis tamen saltem alicujus, non verò ipsius essentiæ propriam: h. e. requisitum tantùm quoddam in homine pœnitente, non verò partem essentialem, & quasi formalem pœnitentiæ fidem esse contendunt.

2. Fidem hanc non definiunt per firmam πεποίθησιν sive fiduciam in promissionem Evangelij, de gratuitâ peccatorum remissione, per & propter Christum fide apprehensum : qualem nos requirimus. Disertè enim scribit Bellarminus lib. 1. de pœn. c. 19. Quòd nos dixim9, sine fide pœnitentiam haberi non posse: de fide verâ & Catholicâ intelleximus: non de illo Lutheranorum figmento, quod ipsis fides justificans, & pars est præcipua pœnitentiæ. Et Concilium Trident. clariùs, Sess. 6. c. 12. Si quis dixerit, fidem justificantem esse fiduciam in DEI misericordiam, peccata remittentis propter Christum, anathema sit. Quæritur ergò jam, Quænam igitur fides Esavvitis hodie, sit fides Vera & Catholica? id verò ex decretis Concil. Trident. colligere licet: ubi inter reliqua volunt, Hominem pœnitentem debere de divinâ misericordiâ talem concipere fiduciā, si sponte suâ & voluntariè ex amore DEI assumat dolorem pro peccatis, eumq́; externis gestibus ac motibus conspiciendū præbeat: & propositu habeat, se velle sacrificulo confiteri singula & universa peccata, omnesq́; circumstantias, quæ peccati specie quoquo modo variare poterant: quin se quoq́; lubenti patientiq́; animo in se suscepturū ac executurū satisfactiones à Sacerdote in confessionis actu injunctas: Si inqua hæc faciat, fore, ut hoc pacto satisfaciat pro peccatis suis, impetret remissionē eorundē & reconciliationē cum DEO. Hinc talis emergit definitio fidei Esavvitico-Catholicæ, quod sit fiducia, quâ quis credit ac statuit, actiones pœnitētiæ, ab homine spōte susceptas ac præstitas, ex merito Christi ea habere vim, ut remissionē peccatorum & reconciliatione cum DEO promereri possint. De hac fide scribit Bellarminus, quod non quidem sit pars poenitentiae, ad eam tamen efficiendam necessario requiratur. Et Concilium Trid. Sess. 6. cap. 6. quod haec fides primo loco ponenda sit inter ea, quae ad justificationem disponunt: & tamen a poenitentia, quae inter dispositiones illas quintum locum obtinet, plane distingvi debeat.

Verum de hac fide, quae certo credat ac statuat nostris operibus, ex merito CHRISTI, inesse vim promerendi remissionem peccatorum, justitiam, & vitam aeternam, universa Scriptura Sacra ne γρὺ quidem novit. Proinde eam merito, ceu βδέλυγμα impietatis Esavviticae abominamur & execramur.

Caeterum argumenta, quibus Esavvitae moti, Fidem negant esse partem Poenitentiae, praecipua sunt haec:

I. In Scripturis Sacris distingvitur fides a Poenitentia: ut Marci 1, 15. non dicit Dominus: Poenitentiam agite credentes Evangelio: sed Poenitentiam agite & credite Evangelio. Ergo Fides non est pars Poenitentiae.

Vel secundum alios: Sicut Lex & Evangelium conjunguntur: ita Poenitentia etiam & Fides. Atqui illud sic fit, ut Evangelium neutiquam pars legis constituatur. Perinde ergo hic etiam fieri necessum est, ut Fides & Poenitentia in sacris quidem conjungantur: neq; tamen fides sit pars Poenitentiae.

RESPONDEO: Sophismate ὁμωνυμίας tota haec structura nititur. Nam apud Marcum, & alibi in Scripturis, ubi Fides & Poenitentia a se mutuo distingvuntur: Vox Poenitentiae non proprio significatu, pro tota ad DEUM conversione: sed sensu minus proprio pro sola contritione ponitur. In quo sensu ultro largimur, fidem non esse partem Poenitentiae, hoc est, Contritionis: sed rem eidem plane contradistinctam. Quando vero vox Poenitentiae proprio sensu, pro tota ad DEUM conversione accipitur: Certe veritas Evangelij non patitur, ut a poenitentia fidem, tanquam contradistinctum quid fecludamus: tum ob causas & rationes paulo ante expeditas: tum ob duas hasce: 1. Quia remissio peccatorum, & reconciliatio cum DEO, finis est proprius & summus poenitentiae: quae tamen neutra aliter, quam sola fide apprehenditur. 2. Quia conversio & desperatio eatenus differunt, quatenus in conversione conscientia hominis in dubitatione non relinquitur. Atqui sola fides est victrix dubitationum. Ut ergo conversio non degeneret in desperationem, Fide constet necesse est.

II. Fides Poenitentiam praecedit, eamq; gignit, Ergo causa quidem, pars vero esse nullo modo potest. Antecedens confirmat Bellarminus, 1. exemplo Ninivitarum, qui crediderunt in DEUM, & post demum pradicaverunt jejunium, & induti sunt saccis, Jonae 3, 5. 2. Ratione: Quia intelligi non potest, quod serio aliquis poenitentiam agere incipiat nisi prius credat vera esse, quae DEUS tum peccatoribus comminatur, tum poenitentibus pollicetur.

RESPONDEO ad Antecedens per distinctionem inter poenitentiam eorum, qui ex gratia DEI prolapsi, denuo sunt convertendi: & inter poenitentiam stantium, sive jugem illam ac quotidianam renatorum poenitentiam, qui in exercitio pietatis perseverant, & mortificato vetere Adamo, de fide in fidem, per quotidiana incrementa progrediuntur. De priore illa poenitentiae specie, falsum est Antecedens. Neq; enim fides ibi praecedit poenitentiam, sed simul cum ea existit tempore: Imo ratione ordinis posterior est contritione. Verum quoad poenitentiam stantium sive Renatorum quotidianam: libenter concedimus, fidem praecedere jugem illam mortificationem carnis, quemadmodum causa praecedit effectum. Verum de hac poenitentiae specie, hoc loco non est disputatio.

Deinde vero probe notandum, licet fides, quoad poenitentiam stantium, sit causa mortificationis carnis, nihilominus tamen eam quoque esse partem hujus poenitentiae: ita ut fides, causae & partis rationem sustineat, sed diverso respectu. Nam quatenus Renatus vera in CHRISTUM fide, & amore DEI movetur ad illam carnis perpetuam crucifixionem subeundam; causae utiq; respectum fides merito obtinet. Quatenus vero in eodem opere, quicquid reliquiarum est ex carne & scorijs Adami veteris, id sibi, non nisi propter meritum CHRISTI ex gratia condonari, Renatus certo credit ac statuit: eatenus fidem in hac etiam poenitentiae specie, partis respectum sustinere, manifestum est. Neq; absurdum hoc cuipiam videri potest aut debet: siquidem in naturalibus etiam, idem & partis, & causae respectum sortiri potest, sed diverso respectu. Anima certe, quae est εντελεχεια informans hominem, simul est & causa, & pars hominis: id quod nemo sanus inficiabitur.

Exemplum Ninivitarum nihil ad rem facit: Nam cum praedicaverunt jejunium, & induti sunt saccis, non demum inceperunt agere poenitentiam: sed tantum poenitentiam, quam animo conceperant, tum serio dolore de admissis peccatis, tum vera in DEUM fiducia, hoc pacto tanquam externis quibusdam signis declararunt. Quae sane signa poenitentiae, fide posteriora, imo praecedentis fidei effecta esse libenter largimur.

Ratio adjuncta Esavvitica itidem tantum agit de externis signis poenitentiae, ex quibus intelligi potest, quod serio aliquis agat poenitentiam. Quemadmodum vero signa haec sive opera externa non sunt ipsa poenitentia, neq; ejus etiam pars, sed ejusdem tantum effectum sive consequens: ita posteriora etiam ea esse fide ultro concedimus: neq; inde doctrinae nostrae quicquam decedit.

III. Partes Poenitentiae censenda sunt illa actiones, quae a virtute Poenitentia manant. Atqui credere, est actio non Poenitentia, quae virtus moralis est, sed fidei virtutis Theologica. Ergo.

RESPONDEO: Propositio fallit sub falsa hypothesi: Fingit enim Esavvita, Partes actiones no esse, nisi quae ex inhaerente aliquo virtutis moralis habitu emanant: id quod falsissimu. Corrigitur ergo error iste per contraria hypothesin,


### Chapter Second. On the Parts of Penitence: Whether these three are the genuine parts of penitence, Contrition, Faith, and New Obedience

that according to the Scriptures, there are parts of repentance, which are kindled in the mind of the penitent by the Holy Spirit through the ministry of the law and the Gospel by divine power. Furthermore, although believing is an action of faith, a theological virtue: yet in this Article, as also in that which is concerning Justification, Faith is not considered insofar as it is a theological virtue in the category of quality: or insofar as it is also in the predicament of Action, it is our work: but only insofar as it relates to the merit of CHRIST, and apprehends that with firm confidence.

And such indeed is the structure of the Esauvitic sect, opposed to our purer doctrine concerning Faith, the other part of Repentance, with an altogether vain attempt.

It remains that we examine in a few words what the opinion of the Calvinists is concerning the parts of Repentance.

But if we examine the writings of Calvin, of Theodore Beza, and of the principal Calvinist Doctors, their doctrine can be comprehended in these three hypotheses:

1. The parts of Repentance are the Mortification of the flesh, and the vivification of the Spirit: or the withdrawal from evil, and the approach to good.

2. Neither contrition, nor Faith, ought to be established as parts of repentance.

3. True repentance is nothing other than the change of the whole life for the better.

The sum tends to this: that repentance consists solely in the amendment or change of life: that is, in the perpetual sanctification of the heart and of all affections: or the mortification of the flesh, and the vivification of the Spirit.

Concerning which doctrine, in the beginning, the Terms themselves which the Calvinists use must be explained. For our theologians also use them in this very matter: but in a sense and respect far other and different. For in our churches, the mortification of the flesh, when it is posited as a part of repentance, is nothing other than the serious sorrow of the heart and conscience for sins committed, kindled from the legal threats by the power of the Holy Spirit. Vivification, however, in this article for us is that true confidence in the grace of GOD forgiving all sins on account of Christ. But to Calvin and his associates, mortification is the denial of self, that is, the putting off of the vicious affections of the flesh, or of the whole old man: Vivification, however, is the renewal of life, and the pursuit of justice and piety. Therefore, our theologians and the Calvinists differ greatly regarding the sense and use of these terms. Furthermore, we can in no way subscribe to the doctrine of the Calvinists concerning the parts of repentance. For 1. This repentance, which in the Calvinist sense consists of the mortification of the flesh and the vivification of the Spirit, does not at all apply to those who are merely reborn or standing, but not yet converted: For these neither withdraw from evil, nor approach to good: unless a true conversion to GOD precedes: which finally existing, man learns more and more from the doctrine of the law to hate sin: but from the doctrine of faith, to love GOD. Thus, therefore, the amendment of life, which consists of withdrawal from evil and approach to good, is not the conversion to GOD of a fallen man itself: concerning which it is properly disputed in this place: but it is an effect of Conversion: which we are accustomed to call by another name, New Obedience. 2. All true repentance, or conversion to GOD, precedes justification. And yet the mortification of the flesh and the vivification of the Spirit, which consists in a withdrawal from evil and an approach to good, finally follows justification. Therefore. The proposition is evident from the Scriptures: Ezek. 18:21. If the wicked man shall repent of all his sins, he shall live by life and shall not die. Luke 24:27. It behooves repentance and remission of sins to be preached. Acts 3:19. Repent and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out. The truth of the assumption is built upon those foundations by which we shall now show against certain Philippists that New Obedience is not a part, but at least a consequent or effect of true repentance.

III. Some Philippists oppose our purer doctrine concerning the parts of repentance, ἀλλ̓ οὐ κατ̓ ἐπίγνωσιν [but not according to knowledge], establishing three parts of repentance: Contrition, Faith, and New Obedience. But they betake themselves in vain to the authority of Philip. For although Philip in his Examination of those to be ordained enumerates these three parts in this order, yet he immediately adds, as if by way of a correction: that this partition was handed down by him for the sake of teaching, with good counsel, and he asks that it be understood to that end, free from calumnies. Philip himself surely notices that if this partition is examined according to the ἀκρίβειαν [precision] of Evangelical doctrine, it cannot stand; but that it holds a place only in a looser and confused homiletic method of teaching, where a minister of the Church, speaking about the parts of repentance, ought always to add an admonition toward the pursuit of New Obedience, or Good Works. At other times, Philip certainly established only two parts of repentance: Contrition and Faith, as in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, art. 12, and in his Loci, under the title 'On Repentance.' Therefore, those who even today are accustomed to include New Obedience among the parts of repentance abuse Philip's authority. We break and subvert their ματαιολογίαν [vain talk] with these reasons.

1. Good Works do not enter into the act of repentance, but follow it; since they are not present in the act of converting, but follow only after one is already converted. But whatever does not enter into the act of repentance cannot be a part of it.

2. The fruit and effect of a thing is never a part of the thing itself; otherwise, something would be prior to itself, which is absurd. But Scripture itself calls Good Works the fruits of repentance. Matt. 3:8; Luke 3:8; Acts 26:20. Therefore.

3. Constituent parts are distinguished from the whole, and from each other, not by time, but only by order. But Good Works are separated from conversion itself by an interval of time, as it were. Therefore.

4. This opinion provides a handle and occasion for doubt and despair. For doubt, insofar as every pious person must always doubt whether he has enough good works, which ought to effect his conversion. For despair, indeed, when in more serious temptations no good works appear: Now if from these

judgment must be sought from the presence of the certainty of conversion, as they wish, so that from their absence one necessarily infers the nullity of one's own conversion. Whence nothing else emerges but an abyss of despair.

3. This opinion provided an opportunity for the Majorists to teach that Good Works are necessary for salvation.

Although therefore Philip in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession writes, among other things, that he would by no means object if someone wished to call New Obedience a part of repentance: namely, in a loose, confused, and homiletic manner of teaching, and outside the case of danger and scandal: yet we can by no means approve of the theology of those who, lest they even appear ungrateful to their teacher, or recede a hair's breadth from his doctrine, observe that τριχοτομίαν (trichotomy) so strictly that they are accustomed to fight for it no less than for hearth and home. Their zeal we certainly cannot approve, and we hold that they are rightly rebuked by Bellarmine, book 1, On Repentance, chapter 18. For here too that saying holds: Philip is a friend, Socrates is a friend: but truth is a greater friend.

Therefore, that petulance of Pezelius is by no means to be endured, who in his explanation of the Philippic Examination did not shudder to write that whatever is brought forward against this third part of Repentance is a mere λογομαχίαν (war of words): page 227. For would it be a λογομαχία (war of words) if one were to argue that Good Works contribute nothing to our conversion to GOD? Or if it were shown that one should not judge the certainty of our reconciliation with God from the presence, nor from the quantity, nor from the quality of good works.

But Pezelius objects: Just as in the Sun there are these three: the Body of the Sun, the Rays, and the Solar or vivifying heat: And heat is indeed an effect of the rays of the Sun, yet it is usually mentioned in the description of the Sun. So, although New Obedience is the fruit or effect of true obedience, nothing prevents it from being mentioned in the definition of repentance.

I ANSWER, the foolish disputant wanders off the track: For this is not the question: Whether the definition of repentance can also consist of a notation of the effect or fruit, which is New Obedience: For philosophy does not even entirely reject or disapprove of such descriptions. But this is the question: Whether Good Works enter into the act of true repentance, or reconciliation with GOD: or in any way constitute it? To which we answer negatively in all respects: nor does the analogy brought forward prove or demonstrate anything to the contrary.

Pezelius continues, and argues thus: New Obedience or Good Works cannot be torn away or separated from justifying faith, and they exist at the same time as Faith: Therefore New Obedience does not follow repentance in such a way as fruit follows a tree: but is always with it at the same time in Time.

I ANSWER 1. The state of the controversy is again changed. It had to be proved by the Adversary that New Obedience acts as a constituent part of the Essential whole: which this argument does not accomplish. 2. A manifest πλεονεξία (excess) of the Consequent arises, which springs from a false presupposition. For it is false, and not yet proved by the Adversary: That whatever things are at the same time, they likewise also act as an essential whole. For that distinction always remains valid, which is between cause and effect: as also between the constituent parts themselves, and that which follows the whole already constituted. For example: The Sun and Heat cannot be torn away and separated in the act itself: but they are at the same time in time: yet heat cannot be called either the cause or an essential part of the Solar body. 3. Just as in physics there are Accidents παρεπόμενα τῇ Φύσει (concomitant to nature), which arise and perish at the same time as the subject: yet they do not constitute the subject itself as any part: but rather follow it once it is already constituted: So Good works indeed always accompany Faith: yet they cannot and ought not for that reason be called a part of Repentance.

Moreover, this New Obedience, which we constitute as the fruit or effect of true repentance, is not merely a bare induction of the mind, or a bare purpose, or vow, to retain the justice of a good conscience, and to render obedience to GOD: but it is a serious and ardent intensity of the powers of mind and body toward that very thing, from that faculty which the Holy Spirit grants to those who repent, so that they may become fruits worthy of repentance. And although this new obedience, in this life, never becomes perfect or consummated: yet it is to be begun, and to be labored for with all one's might: according to that of the Apostle: Let not sin REIGN in your mortal body. Rom. 6, 12.

But let this suffice to have disputed here concerning the parts of repentance.

Latin:

quòd secundum Scripturas, partes pœnitentiæ sint, quæ à Spiritu Sancto ministerio legis & Evangelij, in animo pœnitentis divinâ virtute accenduntur. Porrò etsi credere actio est fidei, virtutis Theologicæ: hoc tamen in Articulo, ut & in eo, qui est de Justificatione, Fides non attenditur, quatenùs in Categoriâ qualitatis est virtus Theologica: vel quatenùs etiam in prædicamento Actionis, est opus nostrum: sed tantùm quatenùs relatè se habet ad meritum CHRISTI, illudq́; firmâ fiduciâ apprehendit.

Et talis quidem est Esauviticæ gentis structura, puriori nostræ doctrinæ de Fide, alterâ parte Pœnitentiæ, irrito prorsus conatu opposita.

Restat, ut quæ Calvinianorum de partibus Pœnitentiæ sit sententia, paucis dispiciamus.

Quod si verò tùm Calvini, tùm Theodori Bezæ, tùm præcipuorum Doctorum Calvinianorum scripta evolvamus, tribus istis hypothesibus ipsorum doctrina comprehendi potest:

1. Partes Pœnitentiæ sunt Mortificatio carnis, & vivificatio Spiritus: sive recessus à malo, & accessus ad bonum.

2. Neq́; contritio, neq́; Fides, partes pœnitentiæ statui debent.

3. Vera pœnitentia nihil aliud est, quam totius vitæ commutatio in melius.

Summa eò tendit: quod pœnitentia unicè consistat in emendatione sive mutatione vitæ: hoc est, in perpetuâ sanctificatione cordis & omnium affectuum: sive mortificatione carnis, & vivificatione Spiritus.

Circa quam doctrinam initiò Termini ipsi, quibus utuntur Calviniani, explicandi veniunt. Nam illis nostri quoq́; Theologi hâc ipsâ in materiâ utuntur: sed sensu ac respectu longè alio ac diverso. Nam nostris Ecclesiis, mortificatio carnis, quando pro parte pœnitentiæ ponitur, nihil ea est aliud, quàm serius dolor cordis ac conscientiæ de peccatis admissis, accensus ex comminationibus legalibus, virtute Spiritus Sancti. Vivificatio autem hoc in articulo nobis est, Vera illa fiducia in gratiam DEI propter Christum remittētis omnia peccata. Calvino autem & socijs mortificatio est abnegatio sui, hoc est, depositio vitiosorū affectuum carnis, sive totius veteris hominis: Vivificatio autem est vitæ innovatio, & studium justitiæ & pietatis. Plurimùm ergò nostrates Theologi & Calviniani, quoad sensum & usum istorum terminorum, dissentiunt. Deindè verò doctrinæ Calvinianorum de partibus pœnitentiæ subscribere nullo modo possumus. Nam 1. Pœnitentia isthæc, quæ sensu Calviniano constat mortificatione carnis & vivificatione Spiritus, tantùm renatis sive stantibus, nondū verò conversis planè non competit: Hi n. neq́; à malo recedunt, neq́; ad bonum accedunt: nisi præcedat vera conversio ad DEUM: quâ demùm existente, homo ex doctrinâ legis magis magisq́; discit odisse peccatum: ex doctrinâ verò fidei, amare DEUM. Sic ergò vitæ emendatio, quæ constat recessu à malo, & accessu ad bonum, non est ipsa conversio ad DEUM hominis lapsi: de quo hoc loco propriè controvertitur : sed est effectus Conversionis : quem nos aliàs nominare solemus Novam Obedientiam. 2. Omnis vera pœnitentia, sive conversio ad DEUM, justificationem præcedit. Atqui mortificatio carnis, & vivificatio Spiritus, quæ constat recessu à malo, & accessu ad bonum, justificationem demùm insequitur. Ergò. Propositio patet ex Scripturis: Ezech. 18, 21. Si impius egerit pœnitentiam ab omnibus peccatis suis, vitâ vivet & non morietur. Luc, 24, 27. Oportet prædicari pœnitentiam, & remissionem peccatorum. Act. 3, 19. pœnitemini & convertimini, ut deleantur peccata vestra. Assumtionis veritas superstruitur illis fundamentis, quibus jam contra quosdam Philippistas ostendemus, Novam obedientiam non esse partem, sed consequens saltem sive effectum veræ pœnitentiæ.

III. Puriori nostræ doctrinæ de partibus pœnitentiæ adversantur nonnulli Φιλιππίζοντες ἀλλ̓ οὐ κατ̓ ἐπίγνωσιν: tres constituentes pœnitentiæ partes, Contritionem, Fidem, Novam Obedientiam. Frustrà autem ad autoritatem Philippi se recipiunt. Etsi enim Philippus in Examine ordinandorũ tres istas partes hoc ordine recenset: statim tamen per quandam quasi correctionem subjicit: Hanc partitionem, docendi causa, bono consilio sic à se traditam esse, sequè petere, ut ea fine calumnijs intelligatur. Animadvertit nimirùm ipse Philippus si ad ἀκρίβειαν doctrinæ Evangelicæ partitio hæc exigatur, eam non posse subsistere: sed in laxiori tantùm & confusâ docendi ratione homiliticâ, locum obtinere: Ubi minister Ecclesiæ verba faciens de partibus pœnitentiæ, semper subjicere debet commonefactionem ad studium Novæ Obedientiæ, sive Bonorum Operum. Aliàs certè Philippus duas tantùm pœnitentiæ partes constituit: Contritionem & Fidem, ut in Apologiâ Confessionis August. art. 12. & in Locis tit. de Pœnit. Abutuntur ergò Philippi autoritate, qui hodiéque Novam Obedientiam inter partes pœnitentiæ referre solent. Quorum ματαιολογίαν his rationibus infringimus & subvertimus.

1. Bona Opera pœnitentiæ actum non ingrediuntur: sed consequuntur: Siquidem convertendo non adsunt: sed jam conversum demùm sequuntur. Quicquid verò pœnitentiæ actum non ingreditur, illud pars ejus esse nequit.

2. Fructus & effectus rei nunquàm est pars ipsius rei: Alioqui seipso quiddam prius esset: id quod absurdum. At Scriptura ipsa vocat Bona opera fructus pœnitentiæ. Matth. 3, 8. Luc 3, 8. Actor. 26, 20. Ergò.

3. Partes constituentes non tempore, sed ordine duntaxat à toto, ut & à se invicem distingvuntur. At bona opera temporis quasi intervallo à conversione ipsâ sejunguntur. Ergò.

4. Ansam & occasionem opinio isthæc præbet dubitationi, & desperationi. Dubitationi quidem, quatenùs pius quisque semper dubitare necessum habet, nùm satis habeat bonorum operum, quæ conversionem suam efficere debeant. Desperationi verò quando in gravioribus tentationibus, nulla apparent bona opera: Jam si ex horum

præsentiâ de conversionis certitudine petendum est judicium, ut illi volunt, utiq; ex eorundem absentiâ conversionis suæ nullitatem colligat, necesse est. Undè nihil aliud quàm abyssů desperationis emergit.

3. Opinio hæc Majoristis ansam præbuit, ut docerent, Bona Opera necessaria esse ad salutem.

Etsi proindè Philippus in Apologiâ Confessionis Augustanæ, inter alia scribit, se minimè repugnaturum, si quis Novam Obedientiam, partem pœnitentiæ appellare velit: nempè in laxo, confusiore & homilitico docendi genere, & extra casum periculi atq; scandali: minimè tamen probare possumus eorum Theologiam, qui ne vel ingrati in Præceptorem videantur, vel latum ungvem ab ipsius doctrinâ recedant, τριχοτομίαν istam ita strictè observant, ut pro eâ, haud minus atq; pro aris & focis pugnare soleant. Quorum sanè studium probare non possumus, & jure ipsos à Bellarmino lib. 1. de Pœnit. cap. 18. reprehendi statuimus. Nam & hîc valeat illud: Amicus Philippus, amicus Socrates: sed magis amica veritas.

Minimè ergò ferenda est petulantia illa Pezelij, qui in explicatione Examinis Philippici scribere non exhorruit, meram λογομαχίαν esse, quicquid contra tertiam hanc Pœnitentiæ partem in medium proferatur: pag. 227. Anné enim λογομαχία fuerit, si pugnetur, Bona Opera nihil conferre ad nostram ad DEUM conversionem? Vel si ostendatur, de certitudine nostræ reconciliationis cum Deo, neq; ex præsentiâ, neq; ex quantitate, neq; ex qualitate bonorum operum, judicandum esse.

Sed objicit Pezelius: Quemadmodum in Sole sunt hæc tria: Corpus Solis, Radij, & calor Solaris sive vivificus: Et calor quidem est effectus radiorum Solis usitatè tamen in Solis descriptione ejus fit mentio. Ita licèt Nova Obedientia sit fructus sive effectů veræ obedientiæ, nihil tamen prohibet, quò minùs in definitione pœnitentiæ ejus fiat mentio.

RESPONDEO, extra oleas vagatur ineptus Disputator: Non enim hoc quæritur: An pœnitentiæ definitio possit etiam constare Notatione effectus sive fructus, qui est Nova Obedientia: Nam tales descriptiones ne quidem Philosophia omninò rejicit aut improbat. Sed hoc quæstionis est: An actum veræ pœnitentiæ, sive reconciliationis cum DEO ingrediantur: aut quovis modo constituant Bona Opera? ubi negatè per omnia respondemus: neq; similitudo allata quicquam in contrarium probat aut demonstrat.

Pergit Pezelius, & sic arguit: Nova Obedientia sive Bona Opera à fide justificante non possunt divelli aut separari, & simul tempore cum Fide existunt: Ergò Nova Obedientia non ita sequitur pœnitentiam, ceu fructus arborem: sed cum eâ semper simul est Tempore.

RESPONDEO 1. rursus mutatur status controversiæ. Probandum erat Adversario, Novam Obedientiam habere se ut partem constituentem ad totum Essentiale: id quod hæc argutatio non efficit. 2. Manifesta oritur πλεονεξία Consequentis, quæ ex falso præsupposito oritur. Falsum enim est, nondùm ab Adversario probatum: Quod quacunq́; tempore simul sunt, ea pariter etiam sese ad totum essentiale habeant. Manet enim discrimen illud semper ratum, quod est inter causam & effectum: ut & inter partes ipsas constituentes, atq́; id, quod totum jam constitutum subsequitur. Exempli gratia: Sol, & Calor non possunt divelli, & separari ipso actu: sed tempore simul sunt: neq́; tamen calor vel causa vel pars essentialis corporis Solaris dici potest. 3. Quemadmodum in physicis dantur Accidentia παρεπόμενα τῇ Φύσει, quæ simul cum subjecto oriuntur & occidunt: neq́; tamen ut pars aliqua, subjectum ipsum constituunt: sed illud potiùs jam constitutum, subsequuntur: Ita Fidem semper quidem concomitantur Bona opera: pars tamen propterea Pœnitentiæ dici nec possunt, nec debent.

Cæterùm Nova hæc Obedientia, quam veræ pœnitentiæ fructum sive effectum constituim9, non est nuda duntaxat inductio animi, vel nudú propositum, sive votum, de justitiâ bonę conscientiæ retinenda, deq́; præstanda DEO obedientia: sed est seria & ardens virium animi corporisq́; in idipsum intensio, ex eâ facultate, quam Spiritus S. resipiscentibus præstat, ut fiant fructus digni pœnitentia. Et quanquàm nova hæc obedientia, hâc in vitâ, nunquàm evadit perfecta aut consummata: inchoanda tamen, & pro virili elaboranda est: secundum illud Apostoli: Non REGNET peccatum in mortali vestro corpore. Rom. 6, 12.

Verùm hæc de partibus pœnitentiæ hoc loco disputasse sufficiat.


### Chapter Three

Of the Parts of Papal Penance.

The Romanists divide penance into three parts: namely, Contrition, Confession, and Satisfaction. Where Bellarmine stumbles shamefully right at the very threshold, when in book 1 of Penance, chapter 19, as if forgetful of himself, instead of bringing forward these three parts, he produces reasons, testimonies, and examples from the Old Testament. For the Council of Trent expressly denies that Penance was a sacrament in the Old Testament. Now, indeed, according to the opinion of the Esauvites: the matter of the Sacrament of Penance consists of and is completed by these three parts: And yet these parts, and consequently the very Sacramental Essence of penance, according to Bellarmine, existed equally in the Old Testament, just as it exists today in the New. Therefore, it must necessarily follow that either Bellarmine's proofs taken from the Old Testament are worth nothing, or that we must conclude that the Fathers of the Council lied. But each of these parts must be examined separately.

Latin:

De Partibus Pœnitentiæ Pontificiæ.

Pœnitentiam dispescunt Romanenses in tres partes: nempè Contritionem, Confessionem, & Satisfactionem. Ubi mox in limine primo turpiter impingit Bellarminus, cum lib. 1. de Pœnit. cap. 19. sui quasi oblitus, pro tribus istis partibus afferendis, rationes, testimonia & exempla, ex Veteri Testamento profert. Nam Concilium Tridentinum disertè negat, in Veteri Testamento Pœnitentiam fuisse Sacramentum. Jam verò ex sententiâ Esavvitarum: Sacramenti Pœnitentiæ materia, constat & absolvitur tribus istis partibus: Atqui partes hæ, ac proindè ipsa Essentia Sacramentalis pœnitentiæ, teste Bellarmino, fuit æquè in Veteri Testamento, æq́; atq́; hodiè est in Novo. Ergò alterutrum sequatur necesse est, vel ut probationes Bellarmini petitæ ex Veteri Testamento, sint de nihilo: vel ut Patres Concilij mentitos fuisse statuamus. Sed de singulis istis partibus seorsim dispiciendum fuerit.


### Chapter Three: On Contrition (Pontifical)

The doctrine of the Romanists concerning Contrition consists of these heads.

1. They teach that Contrition is a disagreement, a sorrow, and a displeasure regarding a sin committed, by which such a detestation of sin is made by man, that he vehemently wishes that it had not been committed by him, and has a purpose of not sinning henceforth. Council of Trent, Session 14, on Penance, chapter 4, Canon 5.

2. They establish a twofold sorrow in Contrition: one of the will, which is an act; the other proper to the senses, which is a passion: the former of which they claim is of necessity, the latter of the perfection of contrition.

3. They make a distinction between Contrition and Attrition, of which the latter is an imperfect contrition, not formed from the love of GOD, but undertaken out of fear of punishment.

4. They deny that Contrition is a work of the Holy Spirit, but contend that it is an act of the human will, elicited by the power of free choice: and this for the sake of a difference from natural sorrow, which is not meritorious. Roman Catechism, part 2, on Penance, question 23. Hence the Compendium of Theological Truth, book 6, chapter 24, defines Contrition as sorrow VOLUNTARILY assumed for sins with the purpose of confessing and making satisfaction. Which definition they call Magisterial.

5. They argue that its power is such that it blots out sins, and obtains from GOD the forgiveness of all sins. Roman Catechism, page 447.

6. They deny that Contrition is necessary for a man regarding venial sins, Scotus in 4, distinction 17, article 3.

7. They teach that a man cannot be certain when he is sufficiently contrite: for which reason he is bound to confess and make satisfaction. Thomas in 4, distinction 2, article 5.

8. That Contrition in a man can be so great that the bitterness of the sorrow corresponds to the magnitude of the sin: or certainly that the sorrow of contrition for sins ought to be so great that a greater cannot be conceived. Roman Catechism, part 2, on Penance, question 26, page 219.

9. That Contrition can be intensified to such a degree that not only the guilt, but the entire punishment is diminished. Compendium of Theological Truth, book 6, chapter 24. Thomas in distinction 17, question 2.

Bellarmine is so far from disapproving or correcting this very absurd and impious theology that he rather pours cold water on it and heaps errors upon errors. Hence he argues in book 2, On Penance, ch. 2 and following, that contrition is a free action; that it is not an error conceived from legal threats, but that it pertains to the Gospel, is a good work, frees one from sins, and brings about good works and blessing; that it is necessary for justification and the remission of sins by the necessity of a means; that sorrow for sins must be supreme, at least appreciatively, that is, so that the penitent values the detestation of some evil more than the attainment of any good: likewise, that it is most useful to weep bitterly and for a long time over individual sins, so that contrition can be called supreme not only appreciatively, but also intensively and extensively. Furthermore, he argues that contrition redeems sins and is the cause of the remission of sins: nay, that even servile fear, conceived only from the fear of punishment, is good, useful, and avails for obtaining the remission of sins.

Moreover, this theology of the Romanists teems with many most absurd errors and impieties, which we shall recount in order. FIRST, therefore, contrition is most viciously defined by a displeasure of the mind rather than by a sense of sorrow. For Scripture, in describing the affections of the contrite and therefore accurately expressing the nature of true and genuine contrition, explicitly notes not only a displeasure of the mind but also supreme sorrow. Isa. 38:13, 'As a lion, so he broke all my bones.' And verse 14, 'Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me.'

2. That distinction between voluntary and sensual, active and passive sorrow is to be held in no account. For to posit sorrow without passion, what else is it than to assert an opposite in an adjunct?

3. The distinction between contrition and attrition is for the most part trifling. For we judge that in the regenerate and baptized who are truly repenting, both occur; nay, we maintain that they ought to occur, so that they may both tremble at the fear of punishment from a sense of the wrath and judgment of God, and grieve, out of love for virtue, that God has been offended by them. Furthermore, that sorrow for committed sin, conceived merely from the fear of punishment, is neither contrition nor attrition, but rather sin, because it is not of faith, Rom. 14, last verse.

4. It recalls Pelagianism, that which they maintain, that contrition is not a work of the Holy Spirit, but rather an act of the human will, elicited by the power of free choice.

5. They commit a twofold blasphemy, asserting that the power of contrition is such that it deletes sins and obtains the pardon of all sins from God.

The former of these, that they sacrilegiously take away grace and the remission of sins from the Gospel and faith, nay, from the gratuitous mercy of God and the merit of Christ, and assign them to the merits of human works.

The latter, that they invent such a mercy in God as does not freely remit sins to the penitent for Christ's sake, but merely bestows a reward upon our works. Which indeed should no longer be called mercy, but rather justice. Scripture most strongly refutes both blasphemies, as often as it asserts that Christ by His obedience, and Christ ALONE indeed, has borne, expiated, and even now freely remits sins to believers, without our merits: because He ALONE has trodden the winepress, and of the people there was no man with Him. Isa. 63:3.

6. That they deny that contrition for venial sins is necessary, they manifestly betray their own astounding ignorance in theological matters: dreaming that there are certain sins that are venial by their own nature, and therefore stand in need of neither contrition, nor satisfaction, nor any remission. Job, certainly, being far more correctly versed in the forum of divine justice, asserts that not even the innocent is innocent in the sight of God: and that before Him not even the heavens are clean, and that He found wickedness in His angels, chap. 4, 18. and chap. 15, 15.

7. That a man cannot be certain when he is sufficiently contrite follows entirely from the Papal doctrine: and for this very reason we rightly abhor it as a gateway to despair. The Orthodox Church, however, pronouncing anathema upon this impiety, maintains that contrition is not to be estimated by its own force or magnitude, much less is salvation to be hoped for from it: but rather that one must take refuge in the contrition and sorrows of Christ, who, as is evident from the sacred writings, was most perfectly and absolutely contrite for our sins, and suffered even to the sweating of blood. Isa. 53, 4. and 5. As regards our own contrition, we know that it is in every way too imperfect to correspond to the magnitude and atrocity of even the smallest sin, let alone to be able in any way to remove or expiate it: For who understands his errors? Ps. 19, 13.

8. That they write that contrition in man can be so great that it corresponds to the magnitude of sin: that stands in direct contradiction to the immediately preceding assertion. For if no one can be certain of sufficient contrition, how can it be so great that it corresponds to the magnitude of sin? And conversely: How can a man know that his contrition corresponds to the magnitude of sin, if he can never be certain of sufficient contrition? Furthermore, this eighth assertion arises from that false figment concerning perfect contrition and that which is entirely sufficient for meriting the remission of sins. By which dream men are driven at last either to Pharisaism or to despair. For in the serious exercises of repentance, contrition ought indeed always to grow: but it grows in such a way that it never becomes perfect and sufficient, at least for this reason, because it is written too truly, Who understands his errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults? Ps. 19, 13. And, Who knows the gravity of your wrath? Ps. 90, 11. What is more, in true contrition, we must grieve most of all about this very thing, that we cannot grieve sufficiently for our sins. Meanwhile, however, one must not despair, but that very thing must be firmly held, that the remission of sins does not depend either upon the magnitude, or the sufficiency and perfection, or the merit of our contrition: but solely and entirely upon the obedience, contrition, and satisfaction of Christ the Mediator.

9. The prodigious vanity of the ninth assertion is evident from what has already been said. For if contrition, whether appreciatively or intensively, can be so great that it merits the remission not only of guilt but also of punishment: then surely, through a detestable sacrilege, that which is owed entirely to the merit of Christ is attributed to our own work, and it is feigned that our work, even without faith, is meritorious: which, however, the Apostle pronounces in express words to be both sin and impossible to please God, Rom. 14, 23. Heb. 11, 6.

The theology of Bellarmine labors entirely under the same impieties which we have already noted.

For as to what he contends first, that contrition ought to be free, that is, to proceed from the freedom of the will, it partly smacks of Pelagianism: and partly it burdens our churches with a certain sinister suspicion, as if they taught that there is a certain extorted and forced contrition: such as certainly none of us ever dreamed of, even in a fever. Nor does any logic of consequence hold: If contrition is not extorted and forced: Therefore it will be free, that is, elicited from the will of the choice: or conversely: If it is not free: Therefore it will be forced and extorted. For free and forced are not opposed, nor should they even be opposed, as immediate contraries: which is manifest from the article of our conversion: which is certainly not a work of our own powers, nor yet for that reason is it extorted, violent, or forced: But just as there the Holy Spirit makes those who are unwilling willing, and those who are resistant obedient: so in this place He moves, excites, and impels the will of man, by the ministry of the law, so that now, not forcedly, but with a ready will, he detests sins: but not from the faculty of his own powers: but from the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Then, that he argues that contrition pertains to the Gospel properly so called, expressly contradicts the Apostle, Rom. 3, 20. through the law is the knowledge of sin. And Rom. 7, 7. I would not have known sin, except the Law had said: You shall not covet.

Thirdly, that contrition is necessary for justification, by the necessity of a means, is simply false and erroneous. For with the blessed Luther we do indeed believe that contrition is necessary, by reason of the divine command: and because the Holy Spirit through it as it were prepares us for salutary conversion: but that contrition is therefore the cause of obtaining the remission of sins or justification, and indeed by the necessity of a means: that we utterly deny. For justification after the fall can be obtained by no one from the law: so that the Apostle in Rom. 3, 21. brings in this general aphorism: But now apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been manifested: and in verse 28. We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law. And Gal. 3, 11. No one is justified before God by the law: This is manifest, because the just shall live by faith: And in verse 21. If a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly have been by the Law: But the Scripture has concluded all things under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.

Finally, concerning the quantity of contrition, as also concerning the utility of attrition, Bellarmine argues in vain clearly until the end of the second book: and with perpetual trifles and principles he strives to deceive the reader with petitions. For he ought to have proved that first, namely, that the conversion of man and the remission of sins depend upon the quantity and quality of our Contrition or Attrition, as if upon a Cause, whether primary, or organic, or in any way meritorious. Which we have already shown to be contrary to the Holy Scriptures.

Latin:

DOctrina Romanensium de Contritione his constat capitibus.

1. Docent Contritionem esse dissensum, dolorem & displicentiam de peccato commisso, quâ talis ab homine fiat peccati detestatio, ut id à se commissum esse vehementer nolit, & propositum non peccandi de cætero habeat. Concil. Trid. Sess. 14. de Pænit. cap. 4. Can. 5.

2. Duplicem in Contritione dolorem statuunt: Unum voluntatis, qui sit actus: Alterum sensus proprium, qui sit passio: quorum priorem de necessitate; posteriorem de perfectione contritionis esse perhibent.

3. Faciunt discrimen inter Contritionem & Attritionem, quarum hæc imperfecta sit contritio, non formata ex charitate DEI, sed ex formidine pœnæ suscepta.

4. Contritionem negant esse opus Spiritus Sancti, sed contendunt esse actum voluntatis humanæ, vi liberi arbitrij elicitum: idq; ad differentiam doloris naturalis, qui non est meritorius. Catech. Rom. part. 2. de Pænit. q 23. Hinc compendium veritatis Theologicæ, lib. 6. cap. 24. Contritionem definit, quod sit dolor VOLUNTARIE pro peccatis assumtus cum proposito confitendi & satisfaciendi. Quam definitionem vocant Magistralem.

5. Eam ejus vim esse disputant, ut peccata deleat, & omnium peccatorum veniam à DEO impetret Catech. Rom. pag. 447.

6. De venialibus peccatis Contritionem homini negant esse necessariam, Scotus in 4. dist. 17. art. 3.

7. Docent, Hominem non posse esse certum, quando satis sit contritus: Quam ob causam teneatur confiteri & satisfacere Thom. in 4. dist. 2. art. 5.

8. Contritionem in homine tantam esse posse, ut doloris acerbitas, magnitudini peccati respondeat: vel certè tantum esse debere contritionis dolorem de peccatis, ut major cogitari non possit. Catech. Rom. part. 2. de Pænit. quæst. 26. pag. 219.

9. Contritionem in tantum posse intendi, ut non solùm culpa, sed tota pœna diminuatur. Compend. Theol. verit. lib. 6. cap. 24. Thomas in dist. 17. q. 2.

Hanc ipsam absurdam & impiam Theologiam, tantum abest, ut Bellarminus, vel improbet, vel corrigat, ut frigidam potiùs suffundat, ac errores erroribus cumulet. Hinc disputat lib. 2. de Pœnitentiâ c. 2. & seqq. Contritionem esse actionem liberam.neq; esse errorem ex comminationibus legalibq conceptũ, sed pertinere eam ad Evangelium, esse opus bonũ, à peccatis liberare, bona opera ac benedictionẽ adducere: esse necessariam ad justificationem & remissionem peccatorũ, necessitate medij: dolorem de peccatis debere esse summum, saltem appreciativè, hoc est, ut pænitens pluris æstimet detestationem alicujus mali, quàm cujuscunq boni consecutionem : Item utilissimum esse, peccata singula amarissimè & longo tempore deflere, ita ut contritio non solùm appreciativè, sed etiam intensivè & extensivè, summa dici possit. Porrò disputat, contritionem peccata redimere, esse causam remissionis peccatorum : Quin timorem etiam servilem, tantùm metu pœnæ conceptum, esse bonum, utilem, ac ad remissionem peccatorum consequendam prodesse.

Cæterùm scatent Theologia isthæc Romanensium, multis absurdissimis erroribus ac impietatibus, quas ordinè recensebimus. PRIMUM igitur contritio vitiosissimè definitur, per displicentiam magis animi, quàm per sensum doloris. Scriptura enim describens affectus contritorum, ac proindè naturam veræ ac feriæ contritionis accuratè exprimens, non displicentiam tantùm animi, sed & summum dolorem disertè notat. Esa. 38, 13. Quasi Leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Et versu 14. Sicut grus & hirundo garriebam, ingemiscebam ut columba: attenuati sunt oculi mei, DOMINE, violenter opprimor, parce mihi.

2. Discrimen illud doloris voluntarij & sensualis, activi & passivi, nullo loco est habendũ. Nam dolorem statuere sine passione, quid aliud est, quàm oppositum in adjecto astruere ?

3. Nugatorium maximâ ex parte est discrimen contritionis & attritionis. Nam in renatis & baptizatis verè resipiscentibus utrumq; fieri judicamus, imò fieri debere statuimus, ut & formidine pœnæ expavescant ex sensu iræ & judicij divini : & amore virtutis, doleant à se offensum esse DEUM. Deindè dolor ille de admisso peccato, tantummodò metu pœnæ conceptus, neq; contritio est, neq; attritio : sed peccatum potiùs, quia non est ex fide, Rom. 14, ult.

4. Pelagianismum revocat id, quod statuunt, Contritionem non esse opus Spiritus Sancti, sed actum potiùs voluntatis humanæ, vi liberi arbitrij elicitum.

5. Geminam committunt blasphemiam, asserentes, contritionis eam esse vim, ut peccata deleat, & omnium peccatorum veniam à DEO impetret.

Prior hæc, Quòd gratiam & remissionem peccatorum, Evangelio ac fidei, imò gratuitæ DEI misericordiæ, & merito CHRISTI sacrilegè adimunt, & meritis humanorum operum adsignant.

Posterior, Quod talem in DEO misericordiam comminiscuntur, quæ non gratis propter CHRISTUM peccata pœnitentibus remittat: sed operibus nostris mercedem duntaxat tribuat. Quæ quidem non misericordia ampliùs, sed justitia potiùs nominanda foret. Utramque blasphemiam Scriptura fortissimè retundit, quoties asserit, CHRISTUM suâ obedientiâ, & CHRISTUM quidem SOLUM portasse, expiasse, ac etiamnùm credentibus gratis, fine nostris meritis, remittere peccata : quia ipse SOLUS torcular calcavit, & de gentibus non fuit vir cum ipso. Esa. 63, 3.

6. Quod negant Contritionem de venialibus peccatis esse necessariam, stupendam suam inscitiam in rebus Theologicis manifestè produnt: somniantes, esse quædam peccata naturâ suâ venialia, ac proindè neq́, Contritione, neq́, Satisfactione, aut Remissione ullâ indigere. Jobus certè in foro justitiæ divinæ longè rectiùs versatus, asserit, quòd ne quidem innocens, in conspectu DEI sit innocens: & coram ipso ne cæli quidem mundi sint, quin in Angelis suis invenerit pravitatem, cap. 4, 18. & cap. 15, 15.

7. Quòd homo non possit esse certus, quando satis sit contritus, ex doctrinâ quidem Pontificiâ omninò sequitur: ac vel ideò eam, tanquâm desperationis januam meritò abominamur. Orthodoxa verò Ecclesia impietati huic anathema dicens, statuit Contritionem non ex suâ vi, aut magnitudine æstimandam, nedùm ex eâ salutem sperandam: sed ad CHRISTI potiùs contritionem & dolores confugiendum esse, quem perfectissimè & absolutissimè pro peccatis nostris contritum fuisse, & ad sanguinis usq́, sudorem doluisse, ex sacris constat. Esa. 53, 4. & 5. Nostram contritionem quod attinet, novimus, modis omnib9 eam imperfectiorem esse, quàm ut vel minimi peccati magnitudini & atrocitati, respondeat, nedùm eam quovis modo tollere aut expiare possit: Delicta enim quis intelligit: Ps. 19, 13.

8. Quòd scriptitant, Contritionem in homine tantam esse posse, ut magnitudini peccati respondeat: illud è diametro pugnat, cum assertione præcedente proximâ. Si enim de sufficiente contritione certus esse nemo potest, quinam tanta ea esse queat, ut magnitudini peccati respondeat? & vice versâ: Quomodo Homo scire possit contritionem suam respondere magnitudini peccati, si de sufficienti contritione nunquàm potest esse certus? Cæterùm oritur hæc octava assertio ex falso illo figmento de contritione perfectâ & omninò sufficiente ad remissionem peccatorum promerendam. Quo somnio vel ad Pharisaismum, vel ad desperationem tandem homines adiguntur. Nam in serijs pœnitentiæ exercitijs, crescere quidem semper debet contritio: sed sic tamen crescit, ut perfecta & sufficiens nunquàm evadat, saltem eam ob causam, quia nimis verè scriptum est, Delicta quis intelligit, ab occultis meis munda me? Ps. 19, 13. Et, Quis cognoscit gravitatem iræ tuæ? Ps. 90, 11. Quid quòd in verâ contritione, de hoc ipso nobis vel maximè est dolendum, quod de peccatis sufficienter dolere non possumus. Interim tamen non desperandum, sed illud ipsum probè tenendum, quod remissio peccatorum non pendeat, vel ex magnitudine, vel sufficientiâ & perfectione, vel merito nostræ contritionis: sed unicè & in totum, ex Obedientiâ, Contritione & Satisfactione CHRISTI Mediatoris.

9. Nonæ assertionis prodigiosa vanitas patet ex jam dictis. Si enim contritio, sive appreciativè, sive intensivè, tanta esse potest, ut non solùm culpæ, sed & pœnæ remissionem mereatur: utiq; rursus per detestandum sacrilegium, nostro operi tribuitur, quod merito CHRISTI in solidum debetur, & fingitur opus nostrum, etiam absq; fide esse meritorium: quod tamen Apostolus & peccatum esse, & DEO placere non posse, disertis verbis pronunciat, Rom. 14, 23. Hebr. 11, 6.

Theologia Bellarmini ijsdem impietatibus, quas jam notavimus, omninò laborat.

Nam quod primùm contendit, Contritione debere esse libera, hoc est, ex voluntatis libertate proficisci, partim Pelagianismum resipit: partim verò Ecclesias nostras finistrâ quapiam suspicione onerat, ac si doceant, contritionem quandam extortam & coactam: qualem certè nemo nostrûm unquàm vel per febrim somniavit. Neqt verò ulla militat consequentiæ ratio: Si contritio non est extorta & coacta: Ergò erit libera, hoc est, ex voluntate arbitrij elicita: vel vice versa: Si non est libera: Ergò erit coacta & extorta. Nam liberum & coactum non opponuntur, neq; opponi etiam debent, ut contraria immediata: id quod ex articulo Conversionis nostræ manifestum est: quæ sanè non est opus nostrarum virium, neq; tamen propterea est extorta, violenta aut coacta: Sed quemadmodum ibi Spiritus Sanctus ex nolentibus facit volentes, ex repugnantibus obedientes: ità hoc loco voluntatem hominis, ministerio legis movet, excitat & impellit, ut jam non coactè, sed promptâ voluntate sua detestetur peccata: sed non ex facultate virium propriarum: sed ex gratiâ Spiritus Sancti.

Deindè quòd disputat, Contritionem pertinere ad Evangelium propriè dictum, Διαρ́ρήδην pugnat cum Apostolo, Rom. 3, 20. per legem agnitio peccati. Et Rom. 7, 7. Peccatum non novissem, nisi Lex dixisset: Non concupisces.

Tertiò, Contritionem ad Justificationem esse necessariam, necessitate medij, simpliciter falsum atq; erroneum est. Nam cum B. Luthero credimus quidem contritionem necessariam esse, ratione mandati divini: & quia Spiritus Sanctus per eam nos quasi præparat ad salutarem conversionem: verùm ideò contritionem causam esse remissionis peccatorum vel justificationis impetrandæ, & quidem necessitate medij: id verò pernegamus. Justificatio enim nemini post lapsum potest obtingere ex lege: ita ut Apostolus Rom. 3, 21. generalem hunc inferat Aphorifmum: Nunc autem sine lege, Justitia DEI manifestata est: & versu 28. Colligimus ergò Justificari hominem per fidem, sine operibus legis. Et Gal. 3, 11. Nemo in lege justificatur apud DEUM: Manifestum hoc est, quia justus ex fide vivit: Et versu 21. Si data esset Lex, quæ posset vivificare, verè ex Lege esset justitia: Sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccatum, ut promissio ex fide JESU CHRISTI daretur Credentibus.

Tandem de quantitate Contritionis, ut & de utilitate Attritionis, frustrà planè ad finem usque libri secundi disputat Bellarminus: & perpetuis nugationibus principijsƣ; petitionibus Lectorem decipere studet. Illud enim priùs probare debebat, nempè conversionem hominis, & remissionem peccatorum dependere à quantitate & qualitate nostræ vel Contritionis vel Attritionis, tanquàm à Causâ sive efficiente primariâ, sive organicâ, sive quovis modo meritoriâ. Quod Scripturis Sacris adversari, jam ostendimus.


### Chapter Three: On Confession both Orthodox and Heretical

The word for confession is ἔγγεαφω, and in the Scriptures it admits of various meanings; and according to the diversity of the subject matter, it denotes either most generally any attestation, or more specifically the doctrine and profession of faith, or the acknowledgment, invocation, and celebration of GOD: or finally, most specifically, the Acknowledgment and Confession of sins. In which latter sense it is taken in this article: but in such a way that, because of the diversity of objects, causes, and times, this Confession can be divided into many species: so that one is Political, another Ecclesiastical. Political, again, is either to the Magistrate, by the example of Achan, Josh. 7:19, or to a brother or neighbor offended: James 5:16. Ecclesiastical is to GOD alone, and that either immediately, by the example of David, Ps. 32:5, or the Publican, Luke 18:13, or mediately: and that again either publicly before the whole Church, or privately before the Minister of the Church alone. That public confession, again, is either ordinary, when the confession of sins is issued by the whole gathered Church: Lev. 16, Neh. 9. Such as is observed today in our Churches. Or extraordinary, which was proper to the primitive Church, where those caught in public enormous crimes confessed their offenses publicly both in words and deeds, and endured the imposed penalties, so that they might satisfy not GOD, but the Church. Private confession likewise is either General, when in general, before the minister of the Church, we confess ourselves guilty of divine wrath and eternal damnation because of sins committed: or Special, when the mind, prostrate with the sense of the law, exposes one or another more serious sin committed by itself in particular, and seeks for it also comfort and the remission of sins, separately and in particular.

And concerning this private confession, both general and special, a dispute and controversy exists for us today with the Romanists and Calvinists. And our truly purer doctrine can be explained in the following Aphorisms.

1. This confession is not Sacramental, and it is neither a Sacrament in itself complete, nor does it constitute the matter of a Sacrament, or any part of it: as was shown above in chapter 1.

2. Nor is it of simple or absolute necessity: and therefore it can be omitted without guilt.

For it is nowhere commanded in the Scriptures. It is therefore arbitrary and left to the conscience of each person. Yet it is not to be rashly neglected by anyone in Churches that observe it: both so that we may not appear to oppose ourselves too insolently to Ecclesiastical constitutions; and because such confession is adjacent and conformable to that examination which the Apostle requires of the guests of the Lord's Supper in 1 Cor. 11:28. Whence Article XI of the Augsburg Confession rightly declares: That private absolution is to be retained in the Churches, although in Confession the enumeration of all offenses is not necessary.

3. This confession should be observed diligently especially by those who are either more ignorant in the doctrine of piety, or colder in acknowledging sins and in the pursuit of New Obedience: or who have troubled and afflicted consciences: or finally, who cannot sufficiently examine themselves whether they are in the faith.

4. This confession, if it is to be legitimate, should consist of: 1. A serious acknowledgment and detestation of sins committed, both those whose memory cannot be held and those which are known and perceived by us. 2. An acknowledgment and profession of the guilt of eternal punishments. 3. A petition for Evangelical Absolution. 4. A serious and not at all hypocritical purpose of amending one's life. And all these things can and ought to be performed by penitents without the snares of consciences and a scrupulous inquiry or discussion into individual sins.

5. The reasons for which this confession is retained in our churches are chiefly these:

I. As much utility as private absolution has in the consolation of consciences terrified by the sense of the wrath of GOD, just so much does private confession itself provide, since it is that upon which the whole weight of absolution depends.

II. The examination of the worthiness and unworthiness of communicants is especially necessary for a Minister of the Church, provided he wishes to recognize and distinguish his sheep, and not exercise the power of the keys in the Church without judgment. But from confession this examination is most rightly informed. Therefore.

III. For the mutual acquaintance of sheep and pastors, for the examination of progress in religion, for correcting ignorance, for shaking off the sluggishness of hearers, for the amendment of private vices, private confession, and the observation sought from it, generally has more weight on the part of the hearers than any other ministry work and instruction which is expended publicly among the more unlearned.

IV. And finally: In more serious disturbances of mind and conscience, arising from the acknowledgment of sin and the sense of the wrath of GOD, no remedy seems to be more convenient by which the mind of the penitent may be raised and confirmed than if, in this private confession, he understands that absolution is announced to him through the special proclamation of the Evangelical promises. Whence more effective consolation is most rightly sought.

To this private ecclesiastical confession is correlative, or subordinate Absolution: and these two things behave as correlates, mutually positing and removing one another. Moreover, Absolution is nothing other than the very voice of the evangelical ministry applying the promise concerning the remission of sins to be granted to individual believers; according to the institution of Christ. Matt. 16:19. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. And John 20:23. Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them: and whose you retain, they are retained.

Furthermore, concerning the act of absolution, on the part of both the Minister absolving and the person being absolved, certain axioms come to be noted.

I. The action of absolution, with respect to the Minister, is entirely ministerial, but not judicial. Therefore, the grace of the remission of sins does not depend upon the person absolving, or his intention, or his will, or his affection: But this is proper to the office. Whence it is that no minister of the Church absolves a penitent sinner in his own name, but only in the name of CHRIST, or of the most Holy Trinity, nor does he simply say, or ought he to say: I absolve you: But: I, by the authority, command, and power of CHRIST, absolve you from all your sins.

Whence it is that Ministers sin gravely who sometimes in the act of private absolution, letting loose the reins to private affections or enmities, show themselves more difficult in announcing the voice of absolution. By which course, indeed, through an atrocious sacrilege, they invade another's work, and no longer constitute themselves ministers, but lords and judges of consciences: more solicitous about private revenge and the assertion of their own authority than about the edification and salvation of the one confessing. Which preposterous method, although it can do nothing to harm the Salvation of the one Confessing: nevertheless constitutes the Minister himself guilty of the foulest abuse of the keys before GOD.

II. The action and power of Absolution relies uniquely and entirely upon the merit of CHRIST. From which follows this: Although nothing prevents us from using a certain formula in absolving, especially one that contains an express mention of this merit: it does not happen by the force of the words pronounced that we obtain the remission of sins: but this power depends upon the merit of CHRIST alone.

III. This Absolution has its dependence upon Confession. Therefore the key never errs, nor are words scattered in vain. For because Absolution always presupposes the condition of confession, either tacitly or expressly: hence it happens that while Absolution can be void or ineffectual: it is nevertheless never false, provided it is pronounced by a Minister: only under the condition of a Confession rightly and seriously made.

IV. Absolution, with regard to those truly confessing and believing in Christ, does not merely signify, or offer or promise that it is to be conferred only after a long time, namely when works of satisfaction have been performed: but it confers it immediately and at the same time, and in the very act exhibits the remission of sins, by the force and power of the promise of CHRIST: Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them.

V. Although without a legitimate calling no Christian ought to take or usurp for himself the ministerial parts of teaching the Word, exercising the power of the keys, and administering the Sacraments: Yet just as in a case of necessity any Christian can administer the Sacrament of Baptism: So also concerning Absolution the Blessed LUTHER rightly pronounced: Where a Priest is not present, in a case of necessity any Christian can announce it.

Both the Calvinists and the Papists have made a divorce from this purer doctrine. The Calvinists indeed in this, that they approve only of public Confession and Absolution: but they reject and disapprove of private; so that Calvin, in his 2nd defense against Westphal, did not shrink from writing that this private Confession and Absolution has its origin from the foul pits of the Roman Anti-Christ, and was introduced into the Church by the Devil himself. Which assertion, although it is most true concerning the auricular confession of the Romanists, yet he makes a bad inference for the extermination of any private confession whatsoever from the Church. For indeed, because of an abuse, the thing itself is by no means to be abolished, the great and manifold use of which was shown a little before. It is to be noted, however, that the Sacramentarians do not in this part agree with Calvin in all things: so that Beza also disagrees with him, book 1, epist. writing: that oral and private Confession has always been observed in well-constituted Churches, and that for the sake both of the Pastor himself administering the sacrament of the supper, and of the sheep receiving it. Which same thing Peter Martyr also establishes, part 1 of the Commonplaces, title on penance, § 28, page 1123 in my edition.

But the Romanists attempt to establish a horrendous idolomania under the act of confession. For because the Sacrament of Penance is said by them to be a judgment of the Church, in the forum of the soul or conscience, where the sinner accuses himself before a Priest, who is a judge knowing the offense of the one confessing, and imposing satisfaction upon him: therefore they define Sacramental and Auricular Confession thus: That it is a secret and full accusation of his sins by the delinquent before a Priest, having jurisdiction over him, undertaken with the hope of obtaining pardon.

2. They posit the formal cause of this action as the enumeration of all and singular sins, especially mortal ones, even the most hidden, of which the penitent can have consciousness after a diligent examination of himself: in which enumeration, the penitent is bound to explain also all the circumstances which could change the nature of the deed: which the Compendium of Theological Truth enumerates in book 6, chapters 25 and 26.

3. They constitute the final cause as the hope of obtaining pardon through the merit of Contrition, Confession, and Satisfaction, Compend. Theol. verit. cap. 26.

4. They pretend that this is so necessary by divine law,

Latin:

COnfessionis vox est ἔγγεαφω, & in Scripturis varias admittit significationes, & pro diversitate materiæ vel generalissimè notat quamlibet attestationem, vel specialiùs doctrinâ & professionem fidei, vel agnitionem, invocationem, celebrationem DEI: vel deniƣ; specialissimè pro Agnitione & Confessione pecatorum. Quâ in postremâ significatione hoc in articulo accipitur: sed ita, ut pro objectorum, causarum ac temporum diversitate, Confessio hæc in multas species dispesci possit: ita ut alia sit Politica, alia Ecclesiastica. Politica rursus sit vel Magistratui, exemplo Achan, Jos. 7, 19. vel fratri aut proximo offenso: Jacob. 5, 16. Ecclesiastica sit soli DEO, eaq́; vel immediatè exemplo Davidis, Ps. 32, 5. Publicani Luc. 18, 13. vel Mediatè: idque rursus vel publicè coram universâ Ecclesiâ: vel privatim coram solo Ecclesiæ Ministro. Publica illa rursus vel est ordinaria, quando à totâ Ecclesiâ congregata editur peccatorum confessio: Levit. 16. Nehem. 9. Qualis hodieƣ; in nostris observatur Ecclesijs. Vel extraordinaria, quæ fuit primitivæ Ecclesiæ propria, ubi in publicis enormibus criminibus deprehensi, publicè & verbis & factis confitebantur sua delicta, & pœnas impositas sustinebant, ut satisfacerent non DEO, sed Ecclesiæ. Privata itidem vel est Generalis, quando in genere, coram ministro Ecclesiæ nos propter commissa peccata reos iræ divinæ & æternæ damnationis confitemur: vel Specialis, quando mens sensu legis prostrata, unum aut alterum peccatum gravius à se commissum, in specie exponit, & de eo quoque solatium & remissionem peccatorum, seorsim ac in specie expetit.

Et de privatâ hac confessione, tàm generali, quàm speciali, nobis lis hodiè & controversia cum Romanensibus & Calvinianis intercedit. Et nostra sanè purior doctrina subsequentibus Aphorismis expediri potest.

1. Confessio hæc non est Sacramentalis, & neƣ; Sacramentum per se integrum, neƣ; materiam Sacramenti, sive partem ej9 aliquam constituit: uti supra cap. 1. ostensum.

2. Neque simplicis aut absolutæ est necessitatis: ac proindè sine reatu piacuari inter-

mitti potest. Nuspiam enim in Scripturis est præcepta. Arbitraria proindè & Conscientiæ cujusq́; libera relinquitur. Neq́; tamen in Ecclesijs, quæ eam observant, temerè cuivis est negligenda : tùm ne constitutionibus Ecclesiasticis nos petulantiùs opponere videamur : tùm quia talis confessio, probationi illi, quam in 1. Cor. 11, 28. à convivis cœnæ Dominicæ Apostolus exigit, finitima & conformis est. Undè Articulus XI. Confessionis Augustanæ rectè pronunciat : Absolutionem privatam in Ecclesijs retinendam esse, licèt in Confessione non sit necessaria omnium delictorum enumeratio.

3. Confessio hæc illis cumprimis observanda sedulò fuerit, qui vel in doctrinâ pietatis rudiores, vel in agnoscendis peccatis, & studio Novæ Obedientiæ frigidiores sunt: vel qui turbatas & afflictas habent conscientias : vel deniq́; seipsos satis probare non possunt, an in fide sint.

4. Confessio hæc, si legitima sit, constet. 1. seriâ agnitione & detestatione peccatorum commissorum, tàm eorum, quorum memoria haberi nequit quàm quæ nobis sunt cognita & perspecta. 2. agnitione & professione reatus æternarum pœnarum. 3. petitione Absolutionis Evangelicæ. 4. Serio miniméǵ; hypocritico emendandi vitam proposito. Et hæc omnia sine Conscientiarum laqueis & scrupulosâ in singula peccata inquisitione sive discussione à pœnitentibus præstari & possunt & debent.

5. Causæ, propter quas hæc confessio in Ecclesijs nostris retinetur, præcipuè sunt hæ :

I. Quantum absolutio privata utilitatis habet, in consolatione conscientiarum sensu iræ DEI territarum : tantundem confessio ipsa privata præstat, quippè à quâ omne absolutionis momentum depender.

II. Dignitatis & Indignitatis, communicantium exploratio apprimè est necessaria Ministro Ecclesiæ, dummodo oves suas agnoscere & dignoscere, neq́; sine judicio clavium potestatem in Ecclesiâ exercere velit. Atqui ex confessione exploratio hæc rectissimè informatur. Ergò.

III. Ad mutuam ovium & pastorum notitiam, ad profectuũ in religione examinationem, ad corrigendam ruditatem, ad torporem auditorum excutiendum, ad privatorum vitiorum emendationem, privata confessio, & indè petita observatio, plus plerumq́; ex parte Auditorum momenti habet, quàm quævis alia, quæ publicè apud rudiores impenditur Ministerij opera & informatio.

IV. Et postremò : In gravioribus animi & conscientiæ perturbationibus, ex agnitione peccati, & sensu iræ DEI obortis, nullū commodius videtur esse remedium, quo animus pœnitentis erigi & confirmari queat, quàm si in privatâ hac confessione, ex speciali annunciatione promissionum Evangelicarum, absolutionem sibi annunciari intelligat. Undè efficacior consolatio rectissimè petitur.

Confessioni huic privatæ Ecclesiasticæ coradλληλo est, sive subordinata Absolutio: & habent se duo haec tanquàm correlata, se mutuò ponentia & tollentia. Est autem Absolutio nihil aliud, quàm ipsa vox ministerij Evangelici promissionem de Remissione peccatorum credentibus donandâ singulis applicans; juxta institutionem Christi. Matth. 16, 19. Quicquid ligaveris super terram, erit ligatum & in caelis: & quicquid solveris super terram, erit solutum & in caelis. Et Joh. 20, 23. Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: & quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt.

Caeterùm circa actum absolutionis, ex parte tùm Ministri absolventis, tùm hominis absolvendi, certa quaedam notanda veniunt axiomata.

I. Actio absolutionis, respectu Ministri, tota Ministerialis est, non verò judiciaria. Ergò non à personae absolventis, vel intentione, vel voluntate, vel affectu dependet Remissionis peccatorum gratia: Sed hoc officij est proprium. Undè est, quod ministrorum Ecclesiae nullus, in suo, sed tantùm in CHRISTI, sive in Sacrosanctae Trinitatis nomine, peccatorem poenitentem absolvit, neq; simpliciter dicit, aut dicere debet: Ego te absolvo: Sed: Ego te autoritate, mandato & virtute CHRISTI, absolvo ab omnib9 peccatis tuis.

Undè est, quòd graviter peccant Ministri, qui interdum in actu privatae absolutionis, privatis vel affectibus, vel inimicitiis frena nimirùm laxantes, in absolutionis voce annuncianda, difficiliores se praebent. Quo sanè pacto, per atrox sacrilegium, alienum opus invadunt, neq; ampliùs se ministros, sed dominos & judices conscientiarum constituunt: de privatâ magis vindictâ, ac propriae autoritatis assertione, quàm de aedificatione & salute confitentis solliciti. Quae sanè praepostera ratio, licet Confitentis Saluti nihil officere possit: ipsum tamen Ministrum foedissimi abusus clavium reum coram DEO constituit.

II. Actio & vis Absolutionis, unicè & in solidu innititur merito CHRISTI. Ex quo illud consequitur: Licet nihil prohibeat, quin certâ utamur formulâ in absolvendo, eâ praecipuè, quae expressam meriti hujus mentionem contineat: non tamen fieri vi verborum pronunciatorum, ut remissione peccatorum potiamur: sed vim hanc dependere ex solo merito CHRISTI.

III. Absolutio haec suam habet dependentiam à Confessione. Ergò nunquàm errat clavis, aut inventum verba sparguntur. Quia enim Absolutio semper vel tacitè, vel expressè praesupponit conditionem confessionis: hinc fit, ut Absolutio quidem esse possit irrita aut inefficax: nunquàm tamen falsa, siquidem à Ministro: non nisi sub conditione Confessionis ritè & seriò factae, ea pronunciatur.

IV. Absolutio, quoad verè confitentes & credentes in Christum, non tantùm significat, aut longo demùm tempore pòst, peractis videlicet satisfactionis operibus, conferendam offert aut promittit: sed statim ac simul confert, atque ipso actu exhibet remissionem peccatorum, vi ac virtute promiffionis CHRISTI: Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis.

V. Etsi sine legitimâ vocatione nemo Christianus sibi partes ministeriales docendi Verbum, exercendi potestatem clavium, & administrandi Sacramenta sumere aut usurpare debet: Quemadmodum tamen in casu necessitatis, quivis Christianus Sacramentum Baptismi administrare potest: Ita de Absolutione etiam rectè pronunciavit B. LUTHERUS: Ubi non adest Sacerdos, in casu necessitatis eam quivis Christianus annunciare potest.

A puriore hac doctrinâ divortium fecerunt, tùm Calviniani, tùm Pontificij. Calviniani quidem in eo, quòd publicam tantùm Confessionem & Absolutionem probant: privatam verò rejiciunt & improbant: ita ut Calvinus defens. 2. contra Westphalum scribere non exhorruerit, Confessionem hanc & Absolutionem privatam à fœtidis Anti-Christi Romani lacunis originem suam habere, & à Diabolo ipso invectam esse in Ecclesiam. Quæ assertio licèt de confessione auriculari Romanensium sit verissima: malè tamen ad quamlibet privatam confessionem ex Ecclesiâ exterminandam, collectionem facit. Siquidem propter abusum res ipsa minimè est tollenda, cujus magnum & multiplicem esse usum, paulò antè ostensum. Notandum tamen, Sacramentarios hac in parte non per omnia consentire Calvino: ita ut Beza quoque ab ipso dissentiat, lib 1, epist. scribens: Confessionem oris & privatam Absolutionem, semper in Ecclesiis benè constitutis observatam esse, idq́; tùm ipsius Pastoris Sacramentum cœnæ administrantis, tùm ovis illud recipientis causâ. Quod ipsum statuit etiam Petrus Martyr. part. 1. Locorum, tit. de pœnit. §. 28. pag. mihi 1123.

Romanenses verò horrendam idolomaniam sub confessionis actu stabilire conantur. Quia enim Pœnitentiæ Sacramentum ab illis dicitur esse judicium Ecclesiæ, in foro animæ sive conscientiæ, ubi peccator seipsum accuset coram Sacerdote, qui sit judex cognoscens delictum confitentis, & imponens ei satisfactionem: ideò Confessionem etiam Sacramentalem & Auricularem sic definiunt, Quod sit secreta & plena delinquentis accusatio suorum peccatorum coram Sacerdote, jurisdictionem in eum habente, spe veniæ consequendæ susceptam.

2. Formale hujus actionis ponunt, Enumerationem omnium & singulorum peccatorum, præcipuè mortalium, etiam occultissimorum, quorum post diligentem sui discussionem pœnitens conscientiam habere potest: in quâ enumeratione, circumstantias etiam omnes quæ facti speciem mutare poterant, confessor explicare teneatur: quas enumerat Compendium Theologicæ Veritatis lib. 6. cap. 25. & 26.

3. Finalem causam constituunt, spem veniæ consequendæ per meritum Contritionis, Confessionis & Satisfactionis, Compend. Theol. verit. cap. 26.

4. Hanc jure divino ita necessariam esse fingunt,


### Chapter Three: Examination of the dogma of private Confession

they feign, that without it, there can be absolutely no hope of the remission of sins for the sinner. They hold, however, that it is necessary either in reality or in act, or by purpose or by vow. In reality and in act, when the opportunity is had: but by vow or purpose, when a moment of necessity excludes it, and not a contempt of religion.

5. Concerning the matter of Confession they determine: 1. That original sin is not to be confessed, because, having been remitted in Baptism, it does not return again.
