Thus, that the confession of actual sins, which are and are called venial, is not commanded: yet that it is not ill-advised for the penitent to confess those as well, because the remission of venial fault, which is done by the Priest, is a temporal solution or remission, which otherwise would have to be endured either here or in purgatory, unless it were remitted by the Priest in this life.

6. Concerning Time they dispute: That it is not of the necessity of salvation that one should immediately grieve for sins committed and confess them: but that it suffices if such confession is made at least once a year.

Now, concerning Absolution, they likewise produce a monstrous and impious Theology. For they do not define it by the sole Ministry of announcing the Gospel to those who have confessed in particular: but by a judicial act, by which sins are judged by the Minister himself, and a sentence is passed according to their quality and quantity, for either aggravating or mitigating the punishment. M. S. lib. 4. dist. 18 lit. B. & G.

2. They feign that Absolution cannot be performed except by that Priest who has ordinary or at least sub-delegated jurisdiction. Concil. Trident. c. 7.

3. They all commonly teach that this Absolution can be pronounced to the Laity even in the Latin and unknown tongue.

4. They generally observe this form of Absolution: May the merit of the Passion of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, and of the Blessed Mary ever virgin, and of all the Saints: the merit of the order, and the burden of religion, the humility of confession, the contrition of the heart, the good works which you have done, and which you will do for the love of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, yield to you for the remission of sins, for the increase of merit and grace, and for the reward of eternal life. Amen.

5. That there are certain more atrocious crimes which can be absolved only by the highest Priests, or Bishops: Furthermore, that the Roman Pontiff has cases reserved above other Bishops, which not even Bishops can remit. Concil. Trident. Sess. 14. cap. 7.

Moreover, as to who and what those reserved cases are, there is not sufficient agreement even among the Pontifical writers themselves: a fact which Antoninus himself admits in part 3 of his Summa: tit. 17. cap. 11. But the sins commonly reserved to the supreme Pontiff are enumerated as follows: Enormous mutilation of a Cleric: burning of temples: falsification of Apostolic instruments: a sacred act performed during the time of major excommunication, or of an interdict from divine things.

And such indeed is the Theology of the Romanists concerning Confession, Absolution, and the Reservation of Cases, which we shall demonstrate in a few words with what impieties, falsehoods, and blasphemies it is truly filled.

At the beginning, therefore, concerning such Confession, not one little letter is found in the whole Holy Scripture: It lacks every divine command itself: it lacks every promise of grace: it lacks, finally, every example of the sacred writings. And although, regarding the simple term of the word, the Romanists scrape together various things from the Scriptures which have been said about Confession: nevertheless, those things are said either only figuratively: or they pertain to that confession which is poured out either privately and secretly into the bosom of GOD alone, or is accustomed to be made publicly before the Church, or for the sake of reconciliation before a neighbor. What is more, very many examples from the sacred writings can be brought forward to the contrary. CHRIST certainly said in Matthew 9:2 and Luke 7:48, 'Take heart, son (daughter), your sins are forgiven': But concerning auricular Confession, or a special enumeration of sins, there is clearly no word at all. That which, therefore, does not have authority from Canonical Scripture is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted, according to the judgment of the Blessed Jerome. This is the reason why the gloss of the Canon Law, de Pœnit. dist. 5. cap. Tenere, preferred to refer the origin of this confession to the tradition of the Church rather than to divine institution. Hence, even in the ancient Church, private Confession was indeed in use, but not under the opinion of divine law and necessity: this is what both the example of Nectarius and the sermons of Chrysostom show; who writes thus on Psalm 51: 'If you are ashamed or blush to tell anyone that you have sinned, say them daily in your soul: I do not say that you should confess to your fellow servant, so that he may reproach you: Say them to GOD, who heals them.'

Furthermore, this Papal confession abounds on all sides with absurdity, danger, and impossibility. For 1. Who will be found, even from the assembly of the pious, who will reveal his sins, at the remembrance of which he himself blushes within himself, to another through a full and open confession with a free and ready will? 2. Many, because of such confession, have subsequently been endangered not only regarding their bodies and fortunes: but also regarding their reputation, and finally, the very salvation of their soul. 3. Such a special enumeration, and according to all circumstances, is impossible: For who can understand his errors? Psalm 19:13.

Finally, such confession is highly blasphemous against the merit of CHRIST and the entire doctrine of the Gospel. For as much efficacy as is attributed to this by reason of either quantity or quality in expiating sins, so much is detracted from the merit of Christ, as well as from the power of the Gospel and the Sacraments, and indeed even from faith. For no πληροφορία of faith is left where doubt reigns: but this cannot fail to afflict consciences, where the mind can never be certain whether it has enumerated all its sins. Thus, it fights against Christian liberty to bind the act of confessing to a certain time in such a way that it is not permitted to transgress or anticipate it: as if indeed a confession made in the Lenten season were far more pleasing to GOD than one made at other times? To this also pertains that impiety, that they dream that Original sin is not to be confessed. As if indeed it were so taken away through Baptism, that the depraved concupiscences no longer have the nature of sin, as the Romanists otherwise rave; that this is false is evident from the example of David, who confesses Original sin most especially in Psalm 51:7. Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins did my mother conceive me.

Now regarding Absolution and the Reservation of cases, a certain bilge of errors arises again from the Theology of the Romanists. For first, they dream that the Ministers of the Church, or Priests, have been appointed by Christ as Judges, who possess the key of discerning and the key of the power of judging: that is, according to the quality and quantity of sins, to impose, diminish, or increase works of satisfaction, etc. But Scripture hints at nothing of the sort: nor does the remission of sins depend upon the quality or quantity of confession, such as the Pseudo-Catholics define it: but only upon the merit of Christ: whose blood cleanses us from all sin. 1 John 1:7. Furthermore, it is vain and false what they invent, that in Ordination a character is imprinted upon Priests, by the virtue of which he can absolve those confessing, and without which all Absolution is inefficacious. Thirdly, they transform the true and legitimate use of the keys, granted by Christ to the Ministry, into an act that is clearly different and specifically distinct: when they define the binding key through the imposition of Satisfaction: and the loosing key, through the remission or mitigation of the imposed Satisfaction. Finally, the figment concerning the Reservation of cases is in many ways blasphemous against the doctrine of the Gospel. For this gives to any minister the power of absolving the penitent and believing from all sins, of whatever kind and of whatever magnitude. It is a sacrilege against Christ the Savior, who alone, by judicial power, as the καρδιογνώστης, judges men: nor does he need in this regard that wicked Roman chest of the breast.

Latin:

fingunt, ut sine eâ, Remissionis peccatorum spes planè nulla peccatori esse possit. Necessariam autem esse vel re sive actu, vel proposito sive voto. In re quidem & actu, quando habetur opportunitas: In voto autem sive proposito, quando necessitatis articulus eam excludit, & non religionis contemtus.

5. De materiâ Confessionis statuunt, 1. Originale peccatum non esse confitendum, propterea quòd in Baptismo remissum, non ampliùs redeat. Sic peccatum actualium, quæ sunt & dicuntur venialia, confessionem non esse præceptam: haud tamen inconsultum esse, ut pœnitens illa quoq́; confiteatur, propterea quod culpæ venialis remissio, quæ fit à Sacerdote, sit solutio sive remissio temporalis, quæ aliàs vel hîc, vel in purgatorio sustinenda esset, nisi hâc in vitâ à Sacerdote remitteretur.

6. De Tempore disputant: De Necessitate salutis non esse, ut statim quis de peccatis admissis doleat, & ea confiteatur: sed sufficere, si ad minimum semel in anno fiat talis confessio.

Jam de Absolutione itidem monstrosam & impiam produnt Theologiam. Neq; enim eam definiunt, per solum Ministerium annunciandi Evangelium confessis in specie: sed per actum judicialem, quo à Ministro ipso peccata dijudicentur, & pro eorum qualitate & quantitate sententia, de pœnâ vel aggravandâ, vel mitigandâ feratur. M. S. lib. 4. dist. 18 lit. B. & G.

2. Fingunt Absolutionem fieri non posse, nisi ab eo Sacerdote, qui ordinariam vel subdelegatam saltem habeat jurisdictionem. Concil. Trident. c. 7.

3. Absolutionem hanc Laicis etiam, Latinâ atq́; ignotâ linguâ, pronunciari posse communiter omnes docent.

4. Formam Absolutionis passim observant hanc: Meritum Passionis Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI, & B. Mariæ semper virginis, & omnium Sanctorum: Meritum ordinis, & gravamen religionis, humilitas confessionis, contritio cordis, bona opera quæ fecisti, & quæ facies pro amore Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI, cedant tibi in remissionem peccatorum, in augmentum meriti, & gratiæ, & in præmium vitæ æternæ Amen.

5. Esse quædam atrociora crimina, quæ à summis tantùm Sacerdotibus, sive Episcopis absolvi queant: Quin Pontificem Romanum supra Episcopos alios habere casus reservatos, quos ne Episcopi quidem possint remittere. Concil. Trident. Sess. 14. cap. 7.

Cæterùm quinam & quales sint casus isti reservati, ne quidem inter ipsos Scriptores Pontificios satis convenit: id quod fatetur ipse Antoninus part. 3. Summæ: tit. 17. cap. 11. Communiter autem peccata summo Pontifici reservata, hæc recensentur: Enormis mutilatio Clerici: combustio templorum: instrumentorum Apostolicorum falsificatio: Sacrum factum tempore excommunicationis majoris, aut interdicti à rebus divinis.

Et talis quidem est Theologia Romanensium, de Confessione, Absolutione, & Reservatione Casuum, quæ quibus impietatibus, falsitatibus, blasphemijs sit revera, paucis demonstrabimus.

Initiò igitur, de Confessione tali, in totâ Scripturâ Sacrâ, non literula una invenitur : Caret ipsa omni mandato divino : caret omni promissione gratiæ : caret deniq; omni exemplo sacrarum literarum. Et licèt, quoad simplicem vocabuli terminum, varia corradant ex Scripturis Romanenses, quæ de Confessione dicta sunt : tamen vel figuratè ea duntaxat dicta sunt: vel ad eam confessionem pertinent, quæ vel privatim & secretò in solius DEI sinum effunditur, vel publicè coram Ecclesiâ, aut reconciliationis causa coram proximo fieri solet. Quid quòd Exempla ex sacris in contrarium proferri possunt plurima. CHRISTUS certè Matth. 9, 2. & Luc. 7, 48. dixit Confide fili, (filia) remissa sunt tibi peccata : Verum de auriculari Confessione, vel speciali enumeratione peccatorum, verbum planè nullum. Quod ergò de Canonicâ Scripturâ autoritatem non habet, eâdem facilitate contemnitur, quâ asseritur, judice B. Hieronymo. Quæ causa est, quod glossa Juris Canonici, de Pœnit. dist. 5. cap. Tenere : maluit, confessionis hujus originem, ad traditionem Ecclesiæ, quàm ad institutionem divinam referre. Hinc in antiquâ etiam Ecclesiâ, Confessio privata in usu quidem fuit, sed non sub opinione juris divini ac necessitatis: id quod & Nectarij Exemplum, & Chrysostomi conciones ostendunt: qui in Psalmum 51. sic scribit: Si confunderis aut erubescis alicui dicere, quod peccasti, dicito ea quotidiè in animâ tuâ: Non dico; ut confitearis Conservo tuo, ut exprobret : Dicito DEO, qui curat ea.

Deindè confessio hæc Pontificia absurditate, periculo & impossibilitate undiquâquè scatet. Nam 1. Quis dabitur ex piorum etiam cœtu, qui peccata sua, ad quorum recordationem ipsemet apud seipsum erubescit, liberâ & promptâ voluntate, alteri per confessionem plenam & apertam revelet? 2. Multi ex tali confessione postmodùm non de corporibus tantùm & fortunis : sed & de existimatione, ipsâ deniq; animæ salute sunt periclitati. 3. Talis enumeratio specialis, & secundum omnes circumstantias est impossibilis : Delicta enim quis intelligit Psal. 19, 13.

Tandem confessio talis in meritum CHRISTI, & universam doctrinam Evangelij summè blasphema est. Quantùm enim efficaciæ huic ratione vel quantitatis, vel qualitatis in expiandis peccatis tribuitur, tantum merito Christi, ut & virtuti Evangelij & Sacramentorum, imò fidei etiam derogatur. Nulla enim relinquitur fidei πληροφορία, ubi dubitatio regnat: hæc autem non potest non conscientias affligere, ubi animus nunquàm potest esse certus, utrum peccata omnia enumerârit. Sic cum libertate Christianâ pugnat, confitendi actum ad certum tempus ita adstringere, ut illud transgredi vel anticipare non liceat: Quasi vero confessio tempore Quadragesimali edita, DEO longe sit gratior, quam que alijs temporibus? Quo pertinet illa quoque impietas, quod somniant, Originale peccatum non esse confitendum. Quasi vero per Baptismum illud ita tollatur, ut pravae concupiscentiae peccati rationem non amplius habeant, uti alias delirant Romanenses; id quod falsum esse, patet Exemplo Davidis, qui peccatum Originale vel maxime confitetur Psal. 51,7. Ecce in iniquitatibus sum conceptus, & in peccatis concepit me mater mea.

Jam quoad Absolutionem & Reservationem casuum rursus sentina quaedam errorum, ex Romanensium Theologia oritur. Nam primo somniant, Ministros Ecclesiae, sive Sacerdotes, a Christo constitutos esse Judices, qui habeant clavem discernendi, & clavem potentiae judicandi: hoc est, secundum qualitatem & quantitatem peccatorum, satisfactionis opera imponendi, minuendi, augendi &c. Atqui Scriptura nihil tale innuit: neque remissio peccatorum dependet ex qualitate aut quantitate confessionis, qualem quidem definiunt Pseudo-Catholici: sed tantum ex merito Christi: cujus sangvis nos emundat ab omni peccato. 1. Johan. 1, 7. Deinde vanum & falsum est, quod fingunt, in Ordinatione imprimi Sacerdotibus characterem, cujus virtute confitentes absolvere possit, & sine quo omnis Absolutio sit inefficax. Tertio, verum ac legitimum usum clavium, a Christo Ministerio concessarum, in actum plane diversum, & specie differentem transformant: quando clavem ligantem per impositionem Satisfactionis: clavem vero solventem, per Satisfactionis impositae sive remissionem, sive mitigationem definiunt. Tandem figmentum de Reservatione casuum multis modis in doctrinam Evangelij blasphemum est. Haec enim cuilibet ministro potestatem facit absolvendi poenitentem ac credentem ab omnibus peccatis, qualibus qualibus, quantis quantis. 2. Sacrilegium est in Christum Servatorem, qui solus ex potestate judiciaria, quippe καρδιογνώστης judicat homines: neque indiget hac in parte scelerato illo scrinio pectoris Romani.


### Chapter Three: III. On the Satisfaction of Works

CONCERNING Satisfaction, which the Romanists constitute as the third part of Penance, they have hitherto produced these emblems especially.

1. That the guilt of sins is indeed remitted by GOD to the penitent through absolution: but that the penalty remains, for which man himself must make satisfaction: Council of Trent, Session 14, Canon 12.

2. That temporal penalties inflicted upon us by GOD, if they are patiently endured, are Satisfactions for sins. Ibid., chapter 9.

3. That such is the power of divine mercy and the merit of Christ, that not only through temporal scourges inflicted by God and patiently tolerated by us: but through penalties even voluntarily undertaken by us for the sake of avenging sins;

or imposed by a Priest, we can make satisfaction before GOD the Father. Ibid.

4. By suffering and making satisfaction for our sins, we are made conformable to Christ, who made satisfaction for sins. Ibid., chapter 8.

5. That it is altogether fitting for the divine clemency that sins should not be remitted to us without our satisfaction: Ibid.

6. That the merit of Christ is so far from being obscured by our satisfactions, that it is thereby the more illustrated and commended. Catech. Rom. part. 2. p. 242. q. 57. tit. de pœnit.

7. That by works of satisfaction, which are prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, sins are redeemed, the stains of the soul are washed away, and GOD is rendered propitious. Catech. Rom. ibid. q. 59.

This doctrine, as if with a single blow, utterly undermines and overturns the entire merit of Christ and the whole doctrine of the Gospel concerning the promises of grace and faith. For the whole Holy Scripture of both Testaments knows no other satisfaction for our sins than that which is in the blood of Jesus Christ, shed for our sins, 1 John 1:7, 1 John 2:2.

Furthermore, Christ did not institute such a ministry of the keys as would remit sins only by half, or in part; or remit them on account of our works, whatever they may be, whether they precede or follow repentance: but GOD saved us according to his mercy, Tit. 3:5.

Finally, from the whole of Holy Scripture, not a single testimony can be brought forth by which such a distinction between penalty and guilt is established regarding the remission of sins: that the latter is indeed remitted in absolution, but the former is not. For the fact that Adam, David, and other saints were subject to various afflictions even after receiving the remission of sins, was not done to the end that they could or ought to satisfy for the penalties of sins in this way: but partly for their chastisement and discipline, and partly as an example to others, so that both they and others might henceforth avoid with greater zeal the sins which they perceive to be so highly displeasing to GOD. For just as the afflictions of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us, Rom. 8:18, so they are not worthy to satisfy for the least sin. The chastisement of our peace is upon Christ: Isa. 53:5. But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world, 1 Cor. 11:32.

Moreover, this impiety of the Romanists drew its origin from the abuse and depravation of that ecclesiastical censure, the traces of which are found partly in Scripture, especially in 1 Cor. 5 and 6, and partly in the writings of the Fathers and the decrees of the sounder Councils. And it must indeed be confessed that the word 'satisfaction' is found in these latter writings, but in a sense far different from that which has been fabricated by the Papacy. For they understood that by the severity of that ecclesiastical censure and discipline, satisfaction was made not to GOD, but to the offended Church, and that reconciliation was made with the same, as can be seen in Augustine, Epist. 108 to Seleucianus; in Enchir. ad Laurent. cap. 64; and in Jerome on Matt. 16. Examples are likewise recounted of Sidonius and Celerinus, of the Novatians in Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. lib. 6, cap. 43, and of Natalis, ibid. lib. 5, cap. 28, and in

Sozomen in the Tripartite History, book 9, chapter 35. And although the Fathers eventually established certain works of penance and fasts, to which the name of Canonical Satisfactions was given—and they even observed certain degrees in the order in which penitents were to be received into the Church, as can be seen in Canon 11 of the Council of Nicaea and Canon 4 of the Council of Ancyra—yet every Papal opinion concerning a Satisfaction that is made to GOD was entirely absent; and that custom, introduced into the Church by human judgment, was tolerable for this reason alone, because there was absent then the servitude of auricular confession, of coercion, and of Satisfactions accumulated in both number and severity, which might drive men to hypocrisy or despair sooner than it would win them for CHRIST. And indeed, if in this age of ours the severity of that same ecclesiastical discipline (all other things being equal) were recalled into use, no Orthodox person would easily object; for it does not take away that liberty into which we have been asserted through CHRIST, provided that the Papal tyranny is absent, to which, out of the πληροφορίᾳ (full assurance) of faith in CHRIST, we deservedly say Anathema. AMEN.

Latin:

DE Satisfactione, quam tertiam Poenitentiae partem, Romanenses constituunt, haec potissimum prodiderunt hactenus emblemata.

1. Culpam quidem peccatorum a DEO poenitentibus per absolutionem remitti: verum remanere poenam, pro qua homini ipsi sit satisfaciendum: Concil. Trid Sess 14. Can. 12.

2. Temporales poenas a DEO nobis inflictas, si patienter sustineantur, esse Satisfactiones pro peccatis Ibid. cap. 9.

3. Eam esse divina misericordiae & meriti Christi vim, ut non solum per tẽporalia flagella a Deo inflicta, & a nobis patienter tolerata: sed per poenas sponte etia a nobis pro vindicãdis peccatis susceptas;

vel à Sacerdote impositas, apud DEUM Patrem satisfacere possimus. Ibid.

4. Patiendo & satisfaciendo pro peccatis nostris, nos Christo, qui pro peccatis satisfecit, conformes effici. Ibid. cap. 8.

5. Divinam clementiam omninò decere, ne nobis absq; nostra satisfactione peccata remittantur: Ibid.

6. Nostris satisfactionibus meritum Christi usq́ adeò non obscurari, ut illud indè magis illustretur & commendetur. Catech. Rom. part. 2. p. 242. q. 57. tit. de pœnit.

7. Operibus Satisfactionis, quæ sunt, Oratio, Jejunium, Eleemosyna, redimi delicta, ablui sordes animæ, DEUM reddi propitium. Catech. Rom. ibid. q. 59.

Hæc doctrina uno quasi impetu universum meritum Christi, totamque doctrinam Evangelij de promissionibus gratiæ, & fide, funditùs subruit & evertit. Nam tota Scriptura Sacra utriusque Testamenti, nullam aliam novit pro peccatis nostris Satisfactionem, quàm quæ est in Sanguine Jesu Christi, pro peccatis nostris effuso, 1. Joh. 1. 7. 1. Johan. 2, 2.

Deindè Christus non tale instituit ministerium clavium, quod ex semisse, sive ex parte duntáxat, peccata remittat: aut propter opera nostra remittat, qualia qualia illa sint, sive pœnitentiam præcedant, sive consequantur: sed secundum misericordiam salvos nos fecit DEUS, Tit. 3, 5.

Tandem ex universâ Scripturâ Sacrâ non potest unicum proferri testimonium, quo circa remissionem peccatorum tale constituatur discrimen pœnæ & culpæ: ut hæc quidem in absolutione remittatur: illa non item. Nam quod Adam, David, alijque Sancti etiam post acceptam remissionem peccatorum, afflictionibus varijs obnoxij fuerunt: id non eo fine factum est, quasi hoc pacto pro peccatorum pœnis satisfacere vel possent, vel deberent: sed partim in castigationem & disciplinam eorum, partim in exemplum aliorum, ut & ipsi & alij majori deinceps studio vitarent peccata, quæ DEO tantoperé displicere animadvertunt. Sicut enim præsentis temporis afflictiones, non sunt pares ad gloriam, quæ in nobis aliquando revelabitur, Rom 8, 18. ita non sunt pares ad satisfaciendum pro minimo peccato. Omnis disciplina pacis nostræ super Christo est: Esa. 53. 5. At nos cùm judicamur, à Domino corripimur, ne cum mundo pereamus 1. Cor. 11, 32.

Cæterùm impietas isthæc Romanensium originem traxit, ex abusu & depravatione censuræ illius Ecclesiasticæ, cujus vestigia partim in Scripturâ: præcipuè in 1. Cor. 5. & 6. partim in Scriptis Patrum, & decretis Conciliorum saniorum reperiuntur. Et fatendum est sanè, Satisfactionis vocabulum in his postremis Scriptis haberi: sed longè alio sensu, quàm qui à Papatu est confictus. Nam censuræ & disciplinæ illius Ecclesiasticæ severitate, non DEO: sed Ecclesiæ offensæ satisfieri, & cùm eâdem reconciliationem fieri senserunt, uti videre est apud Augustinum, epist. 108. ad Seleucianum: in Enchir. ad Laurent. cap 64 apud Hieronymum super c. 16. Matth. Exempla itidem recensentur, Sidonij & Celerini. Novatianorum apud Eusebium lib. 6. hist. Eccl. cap. 43. Natalis, ibid. lib. 5. cap. 28. & apud

Sozomenum in trip. hist. l. 9. c. 35. Et quamvis Patres tandem certa quædam pœnitentiæ opera & jejunia constituerunt, quibus inditum fuit nomen Satisfactionum Canonicarum. Quin & certos gradus observârunt, quo ordine pœnitentes recipiendi essent in Ecclesiam, quemadmodum videre est, in Concilij Nicenij Can. 11. & Ancyrani Can 4. tamen omnis prorsus tùm abfuit opinio Pontificia de Satisfactione, quæ fiat DEO: & mos ille humano arbitrio in Ecclesiam invectus, solam eam ob causam fuit tolerabilis, quia abfuit tùm Confessionis auricularis, tùm coactionis, tùm Satisfactionum & numero & gravitate accumulatarum servitus, quæ vel ad hypocrisin, vel desperationem citiùs homines adigat, quàm CHRISTO lucrifaciat. Et sanè si nostro hoc seculo, ejusdem disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ (cæteris tamen paribus) severitas, in usum revocaretur: nemo Orthodoxorum facilè repugnaret: quippè quæ libertatem eam non tollit, in quam per CHRISTUM asserti sumus: modò Tyrannis absit Pontificia, cui ex πληροφορίᾳ fidei in CHRISTUM, meritò Anathema dicimus. AMEN.


## 24 Of Eternal Predestination, or the Election of the sons of God to Salvation

EXPOSITION of the Article concerning the eternal PREDESTINATION, or Election of the children of GOD to Salvation.

The Apostle, in that golden epistle of his to the Romans, having treated the matter of divine Predestination at sufficient length and with accuracy, finally, as if turned to astonishment, and examining the inexhaustible abyss of divine mysteries concerning this article a little more deeply, breaks out into an almost unusual exclamation: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of GOD, how incomprehensible are his judgments, and his ways past finding out, Rom. 11:33. This exclamation caused most of the Orthodox Fathers to discourse upon the article of Predestination rather timidly and sparingly; indeed, even today there are not lacking those who judge its treatment to be rash and useless, nay, thorny and bitter, and who maintain that it cannot be proposed in an assembly of learners without significant danger: adapting to this that trite saying: Touch me not. But just as we judge the modesty and circumspection of the ancient Fathers to deserve all the greater praise, the sadder the form and face of the Church of GOD and of the Christian Religion was then under the dominion of the Roman Antichrist: so we can in no way approve, nor ought we to approve, the overly haughty censure of certain later writers. For if the treatment of this Article ought to seem rash, certainly CHRIST and the Apostles could scarcely be vindicated from the suspicion of rashness, who frequently, and indeed exactly and expressly, proposed and explained the matter of Predestination to their hearers: so much so that, if you except the one article of Justification, there can scarcely be any other theological topic that the Holy Spirit has given to be explained more accurately in the Scriptures of the New Testament. Matt. 24:22 and 31. Mark 13:20, 22 and 27. Luke 18:7. John 13:18 and ch. 15:16. Rom. 8:30 and chapters 9, 10. and 11, almost in their entirety, 1 Cor. 1:27 and 28. Eph. 1:4 and 5. Col. 3:12. 2 Thess. 2:13. 2 Tim. 1:9. 2 Tim. 2:10. Tit. 1:1. 1 Pet. 1:2. Rev. 17:14. Therefore, just as those things which GOD willed to be hidden are not to be scrutinized, so those which He has made manifest are not to be denied or dissembled, lest we be found illicitly curious in the former, but damnably ungrateful in the latter: as already long ago Ambrose rightly pronounced in book 1 of On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 7, and Damascene in book 1 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 2.

Furthermore, that treatment cannot and ought not to seem useless, from which alone the most effective comfort in any adversities whatsoever flows. Since, besides the doctrine of the Gospel, it proposes no other: which no one would doubt to be most full of consolation, unless he does not have the nature of the Gospel, and of the Predestination that depends upon it, and its own proper affection, as it were, known and perceived. CHRIST, the Savior, certainly, when about to console and confirm His own against any calamities that might happen, seeks a remedy from the article of Predestination, Matt. 11:27, John 10:28, 29. The Apostle also observed this same practice in Rom. 8 and Eph. 1, so that Chrysostom truly concludes from it, homily 19 on the epistle to the Ephesians, that that stupendous and otherwise unsearchable care and providence of the heavenly Father for His elect, none of whom He allows to perish, shines forth most especially from this article.

Nor can this very subject be thorny or bitter. For even if the abyss of divine judgments offers itself in it, and many things here are hidden: yet we ought not even so to be broken in spirit, which would be an argument of sloth and pusillanimity, clearly unworthy of a Christian man. For just as we do not scrutinize hidden things, so we are certain that in those things which are revealed in the Scriptures concerning our Election, the entire cause of our salvation is contained, which GOD has taken care to propose as manifest, so that we may use an undoubted confidence toward GOD, and we ought not to fear that we are entirely to commit ourselves to the revealed divine will: and to exclaim with David: How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O LORD, which thou hast hidden for them that fear thee? Ps. 31, 20. Which very confidence, however, ought to be absent from all presumption and security, lest, having cast aside all care for divine Predestination, we seek from it an argument for carnal license. in this mystery should lie hidden from men, lest there be an opportunity for wantonness or for living more securely: but that we should work out our salvation with fear and trembling, Phil. 2, 12. and make our calling and election sure, walking in the stadium of piety, and progressing more and more in the study of good works, for which we were created in Christ Jesus, and which God prepared, that we should walk in them. 2 Pet. 1, 10. Eph. 2, 10.

These things having been thus considered, we are most fully persuaded that we can usefully and with a good conscience occupy ourselves in explaining the mystery of eternal Predestination, yet so that we keep ourselves within the bounds and limits of the divine word, and do not sin either in excess or in defect. Here, however, this caution must be observed by us above all, that we pay close attention to where the judgment concerning this article can and ought to be sought and informed. The book of Christian Concord rightly admonishes that no place is to be left for human Reason, outside and beyond the Word of God, when it weighs this mystery. For just as all human reason is blind in judging and knowing the nature and essence of God: of which thing the Apostle proposes a sad example among the Gentiles, Rom. 1, so the human mind cannot, nay, much less can it, succeed in the investigation of this article, without that saying of Solomon, Prov. 25, 27, happening to it. He that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory.

But neither should judgment concerning the mystery of Predestination be sought from any external appearance of men or from the experiment of the senses, since it is more certain than certainty itself that this is too fallacious in divine matters.

Furthermore, Predestination is not to be sought immediately in God himself, whom no man has ever seen. But the word of God alone is that from which the entire treatment of this mystery is uniquely to be sought: as that in which nothing has been omitted which indeed concerns the business of our Salvation and Election: but rather, as the Apostle testifies, all the counsel of God has been revealed to us in it, Acts 20, 27. But neither will it be permitted to learn this mystery from every word of God:

For the Law of Moses is indeed the Word of God: but it has nothing in common with this doctrine. It remains, therefore, that our faith concerning this mystery must be informed from that Word alone which has been made manifest through the appearance of our Savior Jesus Christ, declared to all nations for the obedience of faith. Rom. 16, 25. Eph. 1, 9. and ch. 3, 9. Col. 1, 26. 2 Tim. 1, 10. Which Word is none other than the Gospel concerning CHRIST. Therefore, we assert that the will of God which we have revealed in the Word of the Gospel is to be established as the eternal and immutable decree, counsel, and good pleasure of GOD, concerning our eternal Election and Salvation. The reason is: Because there are no contradictory wills in GOD. Following this Word of the Gospel, therefore, as an infallible Cynosure, we prepare ourselves for the exposition of this Article, having first premised a few things concerning the doctrine or opinion of Philip. Johannes Calvin had already published, around the year of our Lord 1536, the Institutes of the Christian Religion, by which he attempted to establish that horrendous decree of absolute Predestination and Reprobation with a new artifice. For although before him Zwingli also had disputed quite a lot in his Treatise on Providence, in the Helvetian style and Spirit, in favor of a fatal and Stoic necessity of all things, actions, and events, both evil and good: yet those things seemed too crude, and too absurd even to the followers of Zwingli themselves, to easily merit applause. Calvin, therefore, noticing this, attacked the matter by another and more sublime way, and by using wonderful enticements of words, and flexible formulas of phrases, and finally exquisite Sophistries, he strove to palliate the absurdities of Zwingli, his teacher, in any way possible, and to render them more plausible to the Reader: by publishing and insidiously thrusting upon the Church of God a dogma which would constitute GOD as both the author of sin and the primary cause of the damnation of men. Although indeed Philip, in other Articles, especially in the Eucharistic doctrine, was, though rightly, yet seriously, of the same mind as Calvin, which we have demonstrated elsewhere: yet he never wished to agree with Calvin on this Article. For which reason Calvin also expostulated with Melanchthon several times by letter: intending to extort his assent even by this means: as can be seen in the Epistle written on the 6th of the Kalends of September, in the year 1554, written by Calvin to Philip, where it is permitted to read thus among other things: Your silence, as I judge it to be harmful to the Church of GOD, so it ought deservedly to be sad and troublesome to me. I was writing recently about that head of doctrine (namely, about Predestination) in which you dissemble your sense more than you dissent from us. For what else am I to think of a man of the sharpest judgment (he means Philip himself) and most expert in heavenly doctrine: Since it escapes no one who is moderately versed in sacred matters, what you cover as if it were unknown? And yet the knowledge of the gratuitous mercy of God perishes at the root, unless we hold this, that the faithful are distinguished from the reprobate by the mere good pleasure of God, whom he willed to choose for Salvation: unless this also is then established, that faith flows from the secret election of God: because he illuminates with his Spirit those whom it seemed good to him to choose before they were born, and inserts them into his family by the grace of adoption. Consider, with your usual prudence, how absurd it is for this doctrine to be torn down by a supreme theologian. You see that a manifest disagreement noted in our writings is certainly of the worst example. Nor do I prescribe this rule for removing the discrepancy so that you may agree with me: but so that we may not be ashamed to subscribe to the sacred oracles of God. Whatever method of seeking reconciliation you may please, I will gladly embrace it, etc. Volume of Calvin's Letters: page 133.

And the same Calvin to Johannes Sleidanus, in the same year and on the same day, in this manner. How much I ought to congratulate myself regarding Philip's consensus in one matter, I do not know: since in the highest heads [of doctrine], either he who sells himself as a philosopher openly opposes sound doctrine: or, lest he stir up the hatreds of certain people against himself, he cunningly, or at least not very ingenuously, conceals his meaning. May the Lord instruct him with a stronger spirit, lest posterity suffer a grave loss from his timidity. ibid. p. 138.

And in the year immediately following, 55, 3rd of the Nones of March, the same Calvin to Melanchthon: This was lacking in your letter, which I had wished to be fuller. Nor, however, do I urge it importunately: but as far as with all respect to you it is permitted, I would wish to ask you again and again, that you would at least silently weigh with yourself the things about which I have written. For I trust that you will take such pains that a form of teaching concerning the gratuitous election of the pious, more sincere than heretofore, may be mutually agreed upon between us. Ibid. page 157.

Although Calvin could not draw Philip, even after being so often warned and asked, over to his own opinion: he did, however, obtain this, that Philip would never explicitly attack Calvin for the impiety of his dogma, unless perhaps under the guise of the Stoics, whose fatal and absolute tablets Philip rejects and condemns in this place; who would wish to affirm that Calvin was also noted there?

But as for the Philippic treatment itself of this Article, it is established and completed in two general Chapters: the FIRST of which demonstrates the supreme necessity of this article from the fact that if Predestination is denied, the certainty and perpetuity of the Holy Catholic Church is also denied: indeed, it is denied that there is any certain number of men who are particularly the care of God, to whom GOD is truly present by His grace and benefits, in whom He also does many things beyond the manner and order of secondary Causes. The LATTER contains the dogmata proper to this article, included in a complex of three Questions: the FIRST of which is concerning the Cause of Election, from where it ought to be sought: the SECOND concerning the immovable certainty of our Election in Christ, and concerning the kinds of Consolations by which we may be able to sustain ourselves in any adversities whatsoever. The THIRD and last deals with the cause of Reprobation; and it establishes it as Pertinacity against Christ, or Unbelief: and therefore it determines that the fatal and absolute tablets of the Stoics are to be execrated. And this indeed is the general economy or arrangement of the Philippic treatment, regarding this Article.

Now since not only Philip's son-in-law Caspar Peucer, but also other Crypto-Calvinists, under the authority of the Philippic Body of Doctrine, strive to seek and build a hiding place and a kind of fortress for their abominable dogma concerning absolute Predestination: it will be worth the effort to have in sight and memory the hypotheses and principles of Philip Melanchthon, by which he so built up his doctrine and faith concerning Predestination, that it would be easier to transform the Devil into an Angel of light than to build up or in any way palliate the Calvinian abominations from them. The following table will exhibit them.

1. One must not judge concerning Election from reason, nor from the law, but from the Gospel.

2. The whole number of those to be saved is elected on account of Christ. Wherefore, unless we embrace the knowledge of Christ, it cannot be spoken of concerning election.

3. Let us not seek one cause of justification and another of election. Peter is elected for this reason, because he is a member of Christ, just as he is righteous for this reason, that is, pleasing to God, because by faith he has been made a member of Christ.

4. Let us therefore seek the promise in which God has expressed His will, and let us know that no other will is to be sought concerning grace outside the Word: but that the command of God is immutable, that we should hear the Son: that we should believe the promise of grace, which is the sum of the Gospel.

5. As the preaching of repentance is universal; and convicts all, as is clearly stated in Rom. 3: So also the promise of grace is universal.

6. It is rightly said that the cause of election is mercy in the will of God, who does not wish the whole human race to perish, but for the sake of the Son gathers and preserves the Church. This is what Paul means when, in chapter 9 to the Romans, he cites the saying, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy.

7. We judge of election a posteriori, namely that those are undoubtedly elect who apprehend by faith the mercy promised for Christ's sake, and do not cast away that confidence to the end.

8. In Eph. 1 it is said: He chose us in Christ, to teach us that the cause of election is not our worthiness, but Christ: so that we may not think of election with Christ and the Gospel removed, but seek the cause of election in the promise of Christ.

9. Let students know that the Hebrew phrase in those words, I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, signifies permission. I will allow it to be hardened: As in the daily prayer, Lead us not into temptation.

10. It is certain that the cause of reprobation is this, namely sin in men who do not hear or receive the Gospel at all, or who cast away faith before they depart from here. In these it is certain that the cause of reprobation is their own sin and human will. And Paul says openly (Rom. 9) that the cause of reprobation is stubbornness against the Son.

11. Men for the most part have either Epicurean or Stoic imaginations: that is, a great part imagine that men are not cared for by God. Others imagine God sitting in Heaven, and writing fatal laws, as if on the tablets of the Fates, according to which He wishes to distribute virtues and vices: Just as the Stoics felt about their fate, and they think Paris and the like are driven by a fatal motion. But let us, having cast aside these ravings of human darkness, turn our eyes and mind to the testimonies set forth concerning God, and let us know that God is a truly free agent, and only wills good things, and does not will sins, and has bound us to His Gospel, in which Christ says: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

12. Let us therefore remove from Paul the Stoic disputations, which overturn faith and invocation. For how can Saul believe or invoke, when he doubts that the promise pertains to him, or when that tablet of the Fates creeps in? It is already decreed that you are to be rejected, you are not written in the number of the Elect, etc. Against these imaginations let us learn the will of GOD from the Gospel, let us acknowledge that the promise is universal, so that faith and invocation may be kindled.

On these foundations and principles, therefore, sought solely from Scripture, Philip rightly and solidly built up the orthodoxy of this Article, and excellently obtained the palm of sincerity against the clandestine, and indeed sufficiently insidious, machinations of the Calvinists.

Latin:

DIEXODOS Articuli de æternâ PRÆDESTINATIONE, sive Electione filiorum DEI ad Salutem.

DApostolus in aureâ illâ suâ ad Romanos epistolâ Prædestinationis divinæ materiâ prolixè & accuratè satis pertractatâ, tandem in stuporem quasi versus, inexhaustâ mysteriorum divinorum abyssum circa hunc articulum paulò altiùs expendens, in exclamationem penè insolitam erumpit: O profunditas divitiarum sapientiæ & scientiæ DEI, quàm incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, & investigabiles viæ ejus, Rom. 11 33. Fecit hæc exclamatio, ut pleriquè Orthodoxorum Patrum timidiufculè & parcè admodum, de Prædestinationis articulo dissererent: imò, hodieque non desint, qui Tractationem ejus temerariam, & inutilem, imò spinosam & acerbam judicant, inq; cœtu discentium non sine insigni periculo proponi posse statuunt: huc accommodantes tritum illud: Noli me tangere. Quemadmodum verò Patrum antiquorum modestiam ac circumspectionem, laudem tantò majorem mereri arbitramur, quantò tristior tùm sub Antichristi Romani dominio Ecclesiæ DEI, ac Religionis Christianæ erat forma ac facies: Ita posteriorum quorundam superciliosam nimis censuram probare nullo modo vel possumus vel debemus. Quod si enim temeraria videri debet Articuli hujus Tractatio, certè à temeritatis suspicione vix vindicari poterunt CHRISTUS & Apostoli, qui sæpenumerò, & quidem exactè atque ex professo Prædestinationis materiam suis proposuerunt & explicarunt auditoribus: adeò ut si unum Justificationis articulum excipias, vix locus ullus Theologicus alius dari possit, quem accuratiùs in Scripturis Novi Testamenti, Spiritus Sanctus explicatum dederit. Matth. 24, 22. & 31. Marc. 13, 20 22. & 27. Luc. 18, 7. Joh. 13, 18. & c. 15, 16. Rom. 8, 30. & capitibus 9. 10. & 11. fermè integris, 1. Cor. 1, 27. & 28. Eph. 1, 4. & 5. Col. 3, 12. 2. Theß. 2 13. 2. Tim. 1, 9. 2. Tim. 2. 10. Tit. 1, 1. 1. Pet. 1, 2. Apoc. 17, 14. Quemadmodum ergò ea, quæ DEUS occulta esse voluit, non sunt scrutanda: ita quæ manifesta fecit, non sunt neganda, aut dissimulanda: ne in illis illicitè curiosi, in istis verò damnabiliter inveniamur ingrati: ut jam olim rectè pronunciarunt Ambrosius lib. 1. de vocat. gent. cap. 7. & Damasceno lib. 1. Orth. fidei cap. 2.

Porrò inutilis ea tractatio videri nec potest, nec debet, ex quâ vel solâ efficacissimum ad nos solatium inquibusvis adversitatibus promanat. Siquidem præter Evangelij doctrinam, nullam aliam proponit: quam consolationis esse plenissimam, nemo dubitaverit, nisi qui & Evangelij, & indè dependentis Prædestinationis naturam, & propriam quasi affectionem non habet cognitam & perspectam. CHRISTUS certè Servator suos adversus eventuras quasvis calamitates & consolaturus & confirmaturus, ex Prædestinationis articulo remedium petit, Matth. 11, 27. Joh. 10, 28. 29. Quam eandem praxin observavit etiam Apostolus Rom. 8. & Eph. 1. ita ut verè indè colligat Chrysostomus, homil. 19. in epistolam ad Ephesios, stupendam illam & aliàs imperscrutabilem curam & providentiam Patris cœlestis de suis electis, quorum nullum perire sinit, ex hoc articulo vel maximè elucescere.

Neque spinosa aut acerba esse potest hæc ipsa materia. Etsi enim abyssus judiciorum divinorum in eâ se offert, & multa hîc occulta sunt: tamen ne sic quidem animis frangi debemus, id quod socordiæ & pusillanimitatis, homine Christiano planè indignæ, argumentum esset. Nam uti occulta non scrutamur: ita certi sumus in illis, quæ de Electione nostrâ in Scripturis sunt revelata, causam salutis nostræ universam contineri, quam ita manifestam DEUS proponi curavit, ut fiducia indubitata erga DEUM uti possimus, nec timere debeamus, nos totos voluntati divinæ revelatæ in folidum committere: & exclamare cum Davide: Quam magna est multitudo dulcedinis tuæ DOMINE, quam abscondisti timentibus te? Psal. 31, 20. Quæ ipsa tamen fiducia abesse debet ab omni præsumtione & securitate, ne omni curâ in Prædestinationem divinam rejectâ, licentiæ carnalis argumentum indè petamus. Nam hoc ipso nomine DEUS multa in hoc mysterio latere homines voluit, ne lasciviendi aut securiùs vivendi ansa esset: sed ut cum timore ac tremore salutem nostram operaremur Phil. 2, 12. & firmam faceremus vocationem & electionem nostram, ambulantes in stadio pietatis, & magis magisque proficientes in studio bonorum operum, ad quæ creati sumus in Christo Jesu, quæquè præparavit Deus, ut in istis ambularemus. 2. Petr. 1, 10. Eph. 2, 10.

His ita consideratis, utiliter & bonâ conscientiâ in explicando æternæ Prædestinationis mysterio versari nos posse, habemus persuasissimum, ita tamen, ut intra cancellos atque limites verbi divini nos contineamus, neque vel in excessu, vel in defectu peccemus. Hîc verò ea cumprimis cautio nobis observanda fuerit, ut undenam judicium de hoc articulo peti ac informari possit & debeat, probè attendamus. Rectè autem admonet liber Christianæ Concordiæ Rationi humanæ, extra & citra Verbum Dei, mysterium hoc pensitanti locum nullum esse relinquendum. Quàm enim de naturâ & essentiâ Dei judicandâ cognoscendâque omnis humana cæcutit ratio: cujus rei triste exemplum Apostolus in gentibus proponit, Rom. 1. tàm non potest, imò multò minus potest in hujus articuli investigatione præstare mens humana, quin illi usuveniat illud Salomonis Proverb. 25, 27. Scrutator majestatis opprimetur à gloriâ.

Sed neque ex ullâ aliquâ externâ vel hominum specie, vel experimento sensuum, de Prædestinationis mysterio judicium peti debet, quippè quod in divinis nimis fallax esse, certo ipso certius est.

Porrò neque in Deo ipso immediatè quærenda est Prædestinatio, quem nemo vidit unquam. Sed verbū Dei solum est, ex quo universa mysterij hujus tractatio unicè est petenda: ut in quo nihil est prætermissum, quod quidem Salutis & Electionis nostræ negotium spectet: quin potiùs Apostolo teste, revelatum sit nobis in eo omne consilium Dei, Act. 20. 27. Sed neque ex omni verbo Dei mysterium istud addiscere licebit:

Lex enim Mosis Verbum quidem Dei est: sed cum hâc doctrinâ nihil commune habet. Relinquitur ergò, ex eo tantùm Verbo, quod per apparitionem Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi manifestum est, in obedientiam fidei, omnibus gentibus declaratum. Rom. 16, 25. Eph. 1, 9. & cap. 3. 9. Coloss. 1, 26. 2. Timoth. 1, 10. fidem nostram de hoc mysterio informandam esse. Quod Verbum nullum est aliud, præter Evangelium de CHRISTO. Quam ergò in Verbo Evangelij revelatam habemus voluntatem Dei, eam ipsam statuendam esse asserimus æternum & immutabile decretum, consilium ac beneplacitum DEI, & æternâ Electione & Salute nostrâ. Ratio est: Quia in DEO non sunt voluntates contradictoriæ. Hoc ergò Verbum Evangelij tanquàm infallibilem Cynosuram secuti, ad ipsam Articuli hujus diexodon nos accingimus, pauca quædam de doctrinâ sive sententiâ Philippi præmissuri. Ediderat jam cùm circa annum Domini 36. supra sesquimillesimum, Johannes Calvinus, Institutiones Religionis Christianæ, quibus horrendum illud absolutæ Prædestinationis & Reprobationis decretum, novo artificio stabilire conatus fuit. Etsi enim ante ipsum Zvvinglius quoque in Tractatu de Providentiâ, pro fatali & Stoicâ, rerum, actionum, ac eventuum, tàm malorum quàm bonorum omnium necessitate, stylo, & Spiritu Helvetico benè multâ disputaverat: crassiora tamen illa, & ipsis quoque Zvvinglij asseclis absurdiora videbantur, quàm ut applausum facilè mererentur. Calvinus ergò animadvertens, aliâ & sublimiore viâ rem aggressus, mirisque tùm verborum lenocinijs, tùm flexiloquis phrasewn formulis, tùm denique exquisitis Sophisticationibus usus Zvvinglij Præceptoris sui absurda quoquo modo palliare, & Lectori plausibiliora reddere studuit: eo prodito, & Ecclesiæ Dei per insidias obtruso dogmate, quod DEUM & peccati autorem, & damnationis hominum causam primam constitueret. Quanquàm verò Philippus, in alijs Articulis, præsertim in doctrinâ Eucharisticâ, Calvino licèt rectè, seriò tamen esset ὁμόψηφος, id quod alibi à nobis demonstratum: nunquàm tamen Calvino hoc in Articulo adstipulari voluit. Quam etiam ob causam Calvinus aliquoties cum Melanchthone per literas expostulavit: assensum ipsius vel hoc pacto extorsurus: uti videre est in Epistolâ VI. Calend. Septembr. anno 54. suprà sesquimillesimum à Calvino ad Philippum scriptâ, ubi sic inter reliqua legere licet: Silentium tuum, uti Ecclesiæ DEI noxium esse judico, ita meritò triste molestumquè mihi esse debet. Scribebam nuper de illo doctrinæ capite (nempè de Prædestinatione) in quo magis sensum tuum dissimulas, quàm à nobis dissentis. Quid enim aliud de homine acerrimi judicij (Philippum ipsum intelligit) cælestisquè doctrinæ peritissimo arbitrer: Cùm neminem mediocriter in sacris versatum lateat, quod ipse quasi ignotum tegis? Et tamen funditùs perit gratuita Dei misericordiæ cognitio, nisi hoc tenemus, merò Dei beneplacito à reprobis discerni fideles, quos in Salutem eligere voluit: nisi & hoc deindè constat, fidem ab arcanâ Dei electione manare: quia Spiritu suo illuminat, quos eligere, antequàm nascerentur, ei visum est, & adoptionis gratiâ in familiam suam inserit. Hanc doctrinam à summo Theologo convelli, quàm absurdum sit, pro tuâ prudentiâ expende. Manifestum certè dissidium in scriptis nostris notari pessimi exempli esse vides. Nec verò hanc tollendæ discrepantiæ legem præscribo, ut tu mihi assentiaris: sed ne pudeat nos sacris Dei oraculis subscribere. Quærendæ verò reconciliationis quæcunquè tibi placuerit ratio, eam libenter amplectar.&c. Volum. Epistolarum Calvini: pag. 133.

Et idem Calvinus ad Johannem Sleidanum, anno & die ijsdem in hunc modum. De Philippi consensu quantopere unâ in re mihi gratulari debeam, nescio: quando in summis Capitibus, vel Philosophus se venditans, sanam doctrinam apertè oppugnat: vel ne in se quorundam irritet odia, sensum astutè, saltem parum ingenuè tegit. Dominus eum fortiore spiritu instruat, ne gravem ex ejus timiditate jacturam sentiat posteritas. ibid. p. 138.

Et anno statim subseq. 55. 3. Non. Martij idem Calvinus ad Melanchthonem: Hoc literis tuis defuit, quod pleniores esse optassem. Neq; tamen importuniùs urgeo: sed quoad pace tuâ licet, etiam atq; etiam te rogatum velim, ut tecum, de quibus scripsi, tacitus saltem expendas. Sic enim te operam daturum confido, ut de gratuitâ piorum electione, sincerior, quàm ante hac docendi forma inter nos mutuò conveniat. Ibid pag. 157.

Quanquàm verò Calvinus Philippum, toties etiam monitum rogatumque in suam sententiam pertrahere non potuit: illud tamen obtinuit, ut Philippus Calvinum ob impietatem dogmatis nominatim nunquàm perstringeret, nisi fortè sub Stoicorum turbâ, quorum fatales & absolutas tabulas, Philippus hoc loco rejicit & damnat, Calvinum quoque notatum fuisse quis affirmare velit.

Cæterùm quoad ipsam Tractationem Philippeam hujus Articuli, constat ea & absolvitur duobus Capitibus generalibus: quorum PRIUS summam articuli hujus necessitatem ex eo demonstrat, quod negatâ Prædestinatione, negetur etiam certitudo & perennitas Ecclesiæ Sanctæ Catholicæ: imò negetur esse certus aliquis hominum, qui peculiariter Deo curæ sit, cui DEUS verè adsit suâ gratiâ & beneficijs, in quo etiam multa agat præter modum & ordinem Causarum secundarum. POSTERIUS continet τὰ δογματικὰ, articuli hujus propria, trium Quæstionum complexu inclusa: quarum PRIMA est de Causâ Electionis, undè ea peti debeat: ALTERA de immotâ Electionis nostræ in Christo certitudine, dequè Consolationum generibus, quibus nos in adversis quibusvis sustentare queamus. TERTIA & postrema agit de causâ Reprobationis; eamque constituit Pertinaciam adversus Christum, sive Incredulitatem: ac proindè Stoicorum tabulas fatales & absolutas execrandas esse statuit. Et hæc quidem generalis est ὀικονομία sive dispositio Tractationis Philippicæ, quoad hunc Articulum.

Jam cùm non modò Philippi Gener Casparus Peucerus, sed & alij Crypto-Calvinistæ sub autoritate Corporis Doctrinæ Philippici, abominando suo de Prædestinatione absolutâ dogmati, latibulum & præsidium quasi quoddam quærere & extruere studeant: operæ precium fuerit in conspectu & memoriâ habere hypotheses & principia Philippi Melanchthonis, quibus doctrinam fidemque suam de Prædestinatione ita superstruxit, ut citiùs Diabolum in Angelum lucis transformare, quam Calviniana βδελύγματα indè extruere, vel quovis modo palliare fas sit. Eas verò subsequens tabella exhibebit.

1. Nec ex ratione, nec ex lege judicandum est de Electione, sed ex Evangelio.

2. Totus numerus salvãdorum propter Christum electus est. Quare nisi complectamur agnitionem Christi, non potest de electione dici.

3. Non aliam justificationis, aliam electionis causam quæramus. Ideò Petrus est electus, quia est membrum Christi, sicut ideò justus est, id est, Deo placens, quia fide factus est membrum Christi.

4. Quæramus ergò promissionem, in quâ voluntatem suam expressit Deus, & sciamus non aliam esse voluntatem quærendam de gratiâ extra Verbum: sed mandatum Dei immutabile esse, ut audiamus Filium : ut promissioni gratiæ credamus, quæ est summa Evangelij.

5. Ut prædicatio pœnitentiæ universalis est; & omnes arguit, ut Rom. 3. clarè dicitur : Ita & Promissio gratiæ est universalis.

6. Rectè dicitur, Causam electionis esse misericordiam in voluntate Dei, qui non vult perire totum genus humanum, sed propter Filium colligit & servat Ecclesiam. Hoc vult Paulus, cum 9. capite ad Romanos citat dictum, Misereor cujus misereor.

7. De Electione à posteriore judicamus, videlicet haud dubiè electos esse eos qui misericordiam propter Christum promissam fide apprehendunt, nec abjiciunt eam fiduciam ad extremum.

8. Ad Ephes. 1. dicitur : Elegit nos in Christo, ut doceat nos, Causam Electionis esse, nõ nostram dignitatem, sed Christum : ne remoto Christo & Evangelio, de Electione cogitemus, sed Causam electionis in promissione Christi quæramus.

9. Sciant Studiosi phrasin Hebraicam in illis verbis: Ego indurabo Cor Pharaonis, significare permissionem. Ego sinam indurari : Ut in quotidianâ precatione, Ne nos inducas in tentationem.

10. Causam Reprobationis certum est, esse hanc, videlicet peccatum in hominibus, qui prorfus non audiunt nec accipiunt Evangelium, aut qui abjiciunt fidem, antequàm hinc descedunt. In his certum est, Causam esse Reprobationis peccatum ipsorum & humanam voluntatem. Et Paulus apertè dicit (Rom. 9.) Causam Reprobationis esse pertinaciam adversus filium.

11. Homines plerumquè aut habent Epicureas imaginationes aut Stoicas: idest magna pars imaginatur homines non curari à DEO. Alij fingunt Deum sedere in Cælo, & scribere fatales leges, quasi in tabulis Parcarum, secundum quas velit distribuere Virtutes & Vitia: Sicut Stoici de fato suo sentiebant, & cogitant fatali motu impelli Paridem & similes. Sed nos abjectis his deliramentis humanæ caliginis, referamus oculos & mentem ad testimonia de Deo proposita, sciamus Deum esse agens verè liberum, & tantùm velle bona, nec velle peccata, & alligasse nos ad Evangelium suum, in quo dicit Christus : Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, ego reficiam vos.

12. Removeamus igitur à Paulo Stoicas disputationes, quæ fidem & invocationem evertunt. Quomodo enim potest Saul credere aut invocare, cum dubitat promissionem ad se pertinere, aut cùm obrepit illa tabula Parcarum? Jam decretum est, te rejiciendum esse, non es scriptus in numero Electorum &c. Adversus has imaginationes discamus voluntatem DEI ex Evangelio, agnoscamus promissionem esse universalem, ut fides & invocatio accendi possit.

His ergò fundamentis ac principijs, ex Scripturâ unicè petitis, Articuli hujus ὀρθοδοξίαν Philippus rectè ac solidè superstruxit, & sinceritatis palmam contra Calviniani clancularias, & satis pol insidiosas machinationes egregiè obtinuit.


### I. Special Controversy, on the Vocabularies both of the Latins and of the Greeks, whose use in this matter is wont to be, their proper…

We, therefore, following in the same footsteps, will henceforth discuss the mystery of Predestination σὺν θεῶ, but in such a way that, having taken careful account of our present age and the controversies which are agitated today, we shall divide the entire exposition into two parts: the former of which will treat the διδασκαλία proper to this topic θετικῶς ἠ δογματικῶς; the latter, however, will be entirely πολεμικὴ, and by pointing out, or rather refuting, the precipices of four principal erroneous opinions—namely, those of the Calvinists, the Esavvites, the Huberians, and the more recent Photinians—it will show how much each of them departs and dissents from the Scriptures and the analogy of faith.

THE FIRST PART, Dogmatic or Positive.

They commit themselves to a very deep sea of most difficult questions and controversies who undertake in their minds a more accurate meditation on the mystery of Predestination, from which they will scarcely ever emerge conveniently or with an unoffending foot, unless they keep their course within certain bounds and set certain limits for themselves. Therefore, we divide the first part of our treatise, namely the positive part, into eight distinct special controversies.

THE FIRST will be concerning the proper nature and affection of the terms, both Latin and Greek, which are wont to be in frequent use in the present dispute, and concerning the mutual difference of the same.

THE SECOND concerning the proper and adequate object of Predestination.

THE THIRD concerning the causes, parts, and members constituting the whole complex of our Election.

THE FOURTH concerning the will of GOD, and the distinction of the same into Antecedent and Consequent.

THE FIFTH, concerning the parts or degrees of the Antecedent will in GOD, by which He willed to render it attested to us.

THE SIXTH concerning the conditions and attributes of the same will.

THE SEVENTH concerning the consequent will of GOD, and the difference of this from the Antecedent.

THE EIGHTH concerning the eternal decree of Predestination itself, and the other eternal decree of Reprobation opposed to it; and concerning the more abstruse questions which are agitated regarding the quality of both decrees.

THE NINTH and last concerning the true and perfect definition of Predestination: and other vicious definitions opposed to it.

I. Special Controversy, ON THE proper meaning and mutual difference OF THE TERMS, both Latin and Greek, which are accustomed to be used in this subject matter.

Regarding the subject of Predestination, several terms offer themselves, which, although they may have some relation to one another in thought, nevertheless differ greatly from each other: such as the Knowledge of GOD, Foreknowledge, Providence, Will, Decree, the Counsel of GOD, and whatever is similar to these. Thomas Aquinas correctly discusses the mutual relationship and difference of these terms in 1 Sent. dist. 40. q. 1. art. 2. And in the treatise on Foreknowledge and Predestination, chapter 1, that they stand in relation κατὰ τὸ πρότερον καὶ ὕστερον, according to prior and posterior: so that the posterior always includes the prior, and adds something to it. For the Knowledge of GOD is of all things: Foreknowledge is only of future things, which adds to the Knowledge of GOD τὸ μέλλον, by reason of us, and of the work not yet existing in act. Providence includes both of the preceding: but adds to them an ordering toward an end, suitable to the nature of each thing. Predestination includes the three preceding: but adds to them an end, which is above the nature of the thing destined, namely eternal salvation. Most of the more recent theologians constitute Predestination as a part of Providence, so that these two differ as genus and species: and Providence as a genus takes care of all created things, both individual and collective: but Predestination as a species is occupied only with the blessedness or eternal salvation of men. Which difference Gabriel long ago in 1 Sent. dist. 40 explained thus: Predestination is as it were a species of Providence. For the Providence of God is of all things to be governed: but Predestination is only with respect to those to be saved: the former is with respect to any end whatsoever, both natural and supernatural: the latter only with respect to the ultimate and supernatural end, that is, eternal life. Looking to this mutual relation of these terms to one another, some have not hesitated to affirm that their relation is almost the same as that which those signifying terms obtain, which are called by philosophers πρὸς ἕν καὶ ἀφ' ἑνὸς, and which, as the Philosopher advises, lib. 2. de Ortu & Interitu, are considered according to prior and posterior. To whose opinion we subscribe, if the explanation is made in that manner and sense in which it has already been shown: so that the more special is always referred to that which is more general and as it were more principal.

But that we may say something about each one in particular: the Knowledge of GOD is either simple and sole awareness: or awareness with approval. The former is of all things indefinitely, as well evil as good: The latter is only of good things which GOD wills, effects, and approves: just as, on the contrary, he hates, turns away from, and punishes all evils. This knowledge, with respect to things and acts in time, and finally with regard to us, the future ones, is called foreknowledge κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν (according to human feeling). For in God, because there is nothing either past or future, therefore foreknowledge, strictly speaking, does not apply to him: but knowledge, which knows all things in one most simple and most perfect act: and sees, knows, and understands all things in one perpetual and infallible intuition: so that this knowledge is rightly called in the Schools of the Theologians the Omniscience of GOD, which admits of nothing either earlier or later, by reason of time, any more than eternity itself does.

This knowledge, or omniscience, or foreknowledge of GOD, although it is by far the most certain and clearly infallible, nevertheless brings no necessity to the things foreknown, and therefore cannot or ought not to be called the cause of any events, whether good or evil: so that the assertion of Beza, contending that the foreknowledge of GOD constitutes the cause of foreknown things, is not without notable impiety: Respons. 2. to the acts of the Colloquy of Montbéliard, page 152 and following. Augustine skillfully refutes this error in book 3 of On Free Choice, chapter 3. If the foreknowledge of GOD imposed necessity on future things, it would do so either because it is foreknowledge, or because it is GOD's. But neither can be truly said. For if the foreknowledge of GOD, insofar as it is foreknowledge, imposed necessity on things, not only the foreknowledge of GOD, but also the foreknowledge of men would impose necessity on things. But that is false. For the foreknowledge of men is not the cause of things, nor does it posit anything in things: just as the foreknowledge of a mathematician or astronomer is not the cause that an eclipse of either the sun or the moon occurs. Thus, neither does the foreknowledge of GOD, insofar as it is GOD's, impose necessity on foreknown things: because an act cannot be the cause of its own object: but on the contrary, the object is rather the cause of the act: that is, interpreting Justin the Philosopher and Martyr: Foreknowledge is not the cause of that which is to be: but that which was otherwise to be from its own principles is the cause of the foreknowledge. Respons. 58 to the Orthodox. GOD therefore foreknows, or rather knows, both good and evil: he knows even the individual species and circumstances of deeds: and yet he does not dispose them in that way. And although according to the rule of the Hebrews: Words of knowledge sometimes connote the affection which follows knowledge: yet that affection does not immediately posit the effect of the thing itself: but it ought to be referred to the Providence of GOD, in that manner and respect which will be shown presently. Therefore, by no means and by no artifice can or ought the foreknowledge of GOD be constituted as the cause of the Adamic fall or of any other sin: although he foreknows the fall and all sins from eternity. For, says Augustine, you would not immediately compel someone to sin whom you foreknew would sin: nor would your foreknowledge itself compel him to sin, although without doubt he would sin: for you would not foreknow that it would happen otherwise: and just as you by your memory do not compel things to have happened which have passed: so GOD by his foreknowledge does not compel things to be done which are to be. And just as you have remembered certain things which you have done: and yet you have not done all things which you have remembered: so God foreknows all things of which he himself is the author: and yet he is not the author of all things which he foreknows: But of those things of which he is not the evil author, he is the just avenger. l. 3 de l. arb. c. 4.

Nor do these things imply an ἀντίφασιν or contradiction, when we assert that those things which are foreknown by GOD happen certainly and infallibly: and yet happen freely and contingently, and through this cannot not happen. For the cause of each statement is very different. For GOD, who foreknows the future, by his eternal wisdom or knowledge, or if I may so speak, intelligence, from eternity runs ahead of the effect of the thing, such as it is to be in time, and beholds the thing already done before it is done: and through this, the foreknowledge is not deceived: For if the thing were to happen otherwise, GOD would have foreknown that very thing as well. Now indeed, that very thing which has been done cannot not have been done: and through this, with regard to the foreknowledge of God, it is rightly asserted that it has necessarily been done, namely by a necessity ἐξ ὑποθέσεως (from hypothesis), or of consequence. Again, what has been done, with respect to its own principles, whether natural or artificial, has been done freely and contingently: and could have been done otherwise, which God himself would have also foreseen. Those who explain this question more accurately constitute a twofold knowledge in God: One of simple intelligence, by which God knows all things which can in any way be: The other of vision, by which he knows things as they are in reality, or will be, or have been: because vision is terminated at the existence of the thing, not at mere possibility.

And such indeed is the Foreknowledge of God generally, indefinitely, and loosely accepted, concerning the simple knowledge of all future things: according to that of Job 28:24. He beholds the ends of the earth, and sees all things which are under heaven. Truly, there are not lacking in the Scriptures certain testimonies in which the word Foreknowledge is taken restrictedly and determinately to the subject matter: as Rom 8:30. Whom he foreknew, them he also predestined: that is, with D. Augustine as interpreter, Whom he foreknew would believe in his son, them he predestined to salvation. Which Foreknowledge is never without Predestination: so much so that in the Scriptures we are said to be chosen κατὰ πρόγνωσιν θεῶ (according to the foreknowledge of God), 1 Pet 1:1 & 2. In which sense and respect the word Foreknowledge is expressly accommodated by the Holy Spirit strictly only to the good, or the children of God, and not indeed to all men, even the unbelievers. Concerning which matter there will be a place to speak below in the eighth special digression of the controversy.

Latin:

Nos proindè ijsdem infistêtes vestigijs, de Prædestinationis mysterio deinceps σὺν θεῶ disputabimus, sed ita, ut nostri hujꝰ seculi, & controversiarum, quæ hodiè agitantur, accuratâ habitâ ratione, universam diexodon in duas partes dispescamus: quarum quidem priore διδασκαλία loci hujus propria, θετικῶς ἠ δογματικῶς tractabitur: Posterior verò tota πολεμικὴ erit, & quatuor potissimùm erronearum opinionum præcipitijs monstratis, imò refutatis, Calvinianorum videlicet, Esavvitarum, Huberianorum, & recentiorum Photinianorum, ostendet, quantum earum quælibet à Scripturis & analogiâ fidei recedat ac dissentiat.

PARS PRIOR Δογματικὴ ἠ θετικὴ.

ALtissimo diffiscillimarum Quæstionum & Controversiarum pelago se committunt, qui de Prædestinationis mysterio accuratiorem meditationem animo suscipiunt, ex quo vix unquàm satis commodè aut inoffenso pede emergent, nisi intra certas metas cursum teneant, certosque limites sibi præfigant. Proindè partem Tractationis nostræ priorem, θετικὴν nimirùm, in octo distinctas controversias speciales patimur.

PRIMA erit de vocabulorum, tùm Latinorum, tùm Græcorum, quorum in præsenti disputatione usus frequens esse solet, propriâ naturâ & affectione, deque mutuâ eorundem differentiâ.

ALTERA de Prædestinationis objecto proprio & adæquato.

TERTIA de causis, partibus & membris constituentibus totum complexum Electionis nostræ.

QVARTA de voluntate DEI, ejusdemque in Antecedentem & Consequentem distinctionem.

QVINTA, de voluntatis Antecedentis in DEO partibus sive gradibus, quibus eam, quoad nos, testatam reddere voluit.

SEXTA de ejusdem voluntatis conditionibus & attributis.

SEPTIMA de voluntate DEI consequente, & hujus ab Antecedente differentiâ.

OCTAVA de ipso æterno Prædestinationis decreto, & huic opposito itidem æterno Reprobationis decreto altero: deque abstrusioribus quæstionibus, quæ circa utriusque decreti qualitatem agitantur.

NONA & postrema de verâ & perfectâ Prædestinationis definitione: & huic oppositis vitiosis definitionibus alijs.

I. Controversia Specialis, DE VOCABULORUM tùm Latinorum, tùm Græcorum, quorum hâc in materiâ usus esse solet, propriâ affectione, & mutuâ differentiâ.

CIrca Prædestinationis materiam plura sese offerunt vocabula, quæ licet cogitationis aliquid ad se mutuò habeant, plurimùm tamen ab invicem differunt: qualia sunt, Scientia DEI, Præscientia, Providentia, Voluntas, Decretum, Consilium DEI, & si quæ his sunt similia. Rectè autem de istorum vocabulorum mutuâ & cognatione & differentiâ disserit Thomas Aq. 1. Sent. dist. 40. q. 1. art. 2. Et in tractatu de Præsc. & Prædest. cap. 1. quod sese habeant κατὰ τὸ πρότερον καὶ ὕστερον, secundum prius & posterius: ita ut posterius semper includat prius, eidemque aliquid superaddat. Nam Scientia DEI est omnium: Præscientia tantùm futurorum, quæ supra Scientiam DEI addit τὸ μέλλον, ratione nostri, & operis nondùm actu existentis. Providentia includit utrumque præcedens: sed superaddit ordinationem ad finem, naturæ cujusque rei convenientem. Prædestinatio includit præcedentia tria: sed superaddit finem, qui est supra naturam destinati, nempè salutem æternam. Recentiorum Theologorum plerique Prædestinationem, constituunt partem Providentiæ, ita ut hæc duo differant ut genus & species: & Providentia tanquàm genus curam agat rerum creatarum omnium & singularum: Prædestinatio verò ceu species occupetur tantùm circa beatitudinem sive æternam salutem hominum. Quam differentiam jam olim Gabriel in 1. Sent. dist. 40. sic explicavit: Prædestinatio est quasi species Providentiæ. Nam Providentia Dei est omnium gubernandorum: Prædestinatio verò est solùm respectu salvandorum: illa est respectu cujuslibet finis, tam naturalis, quàm supernaturalis: hæc tantùm respectu finis ultimi & supernaturalis, hoc est, vitæ æternæ. Ad hanc mutuam vocabulorum istorum ad se affectionem respicientes aliqui, non dubitarunt affirmare, eundem fermè eorum respectum esse, quem ea obtinent vocabula significantia, quæ Philosophis dicuntur πρὸς ἕν καὶ ἀφ' ἑνὸς, quæque, ut Philosophus monet, lib. 2. de Ortu & Interitu, considerantur secundum prius & posterius. Quorum sententiæ subscribimus, si explicatio fiat eo modo ac sensu, quo jam ostensum: ut semper specialius referratur ad id, quod est generaliùs & quasi principalius.

Sed ut de singulis in specie aliquid dicamus: Scientia DEI vel est simplex & sola notitia: vel notitia cum approbatione. Illa est rerum indefinitè omnium, tàm malarum, quam bonarum: Hæc tantùm rerum bonarum quas DEUS vult, efficit, approbat: uti contra mala omnia odit, aversatur, punit. Hæc scientia respectu rerum & actuum in tempore demùm ratione nostri, futurorum, κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν dicitur Præscientia. Deo enim, quia nihil est vel præteritum vel futurum, ideoque Præscientia etiam ipsi propriè loquendo non convenit: sed scientia, quæ uno simplicissimo perfectissimoque actu novit omnia: & uno perpetuo ac infallibili intuitu omnia videt, scit & intelligit: ita ut scientia hæc in Scholis Theologorum rectè dicatur Omniscientia DEI, quæ haud magis, atque æternitas ipsa, quicquam vel priùs, vel posterius, ratione temporis admittit.

Hæc sive Scientia, sive Omniscientia, sive Præscientia DEI, licèt longè sit certissima, & planè infallibilis: nullam tamen rebus præscitis affert necessitatem, ac proindè nullorum eventuum, sive bonorum, sive malorum causa propriè dici potest vel debet: ita ut insigni impietate non careat assertio Bezæ contendentis, Præscientiam DEI constituere causam rerum præscitarum: Respons. 2. ad acta Colloq. Mompelg. pag. 152. & seqq. Errorem hunc scitè refutat Augustinus lib. 3. de lib. arb. cap. 3. Si Præscientia DEI rebus futuris necessitatem imponeret, vel id faceret, quia Præscientia est: vel quia DEI est. Neutrum autem verè dici potest. Nam si Præscientia DEI, quatenùs præscientia est, imponeret rebus necessitatem, non solùm Præscientia DEI, sed & Præscientia hominum imponeret rebus necessitatem. Id autem falsum est. Nam Præscientia hominum non est causa rerum, neque aliquid ponit in rebus: quemadmodum Præscientia Mathematici Astronomi non est causa, ut eveniat Ecclipsis vel Solis, vel Lunæ. Sic neque Præscientia DEI, quatenùs DEI est, imponit rebus præscitis necessitatem: quia actus non potest esse causa sui objecti: sed contrà potiùs objectum est causa actus: hoc est, interprete Justino Philosopho & Martyre: Præscientia non est causa ejus quod futurum est: sed id quod alioqui ex suis proprijs principijs futurum erat, causa est præscientiæ. Respons. 58 ad Orthodoxos. Præscit ergò DEUS, vel scit potiùs, tàm bona quàm mala: novit singulas etiam factorum species & circumstantias: neque tamen eas ita disponit. Et quanquàm secundum Hebræorum regulam: Verba notitiæ interdum connotant affectum, qui sequitur notitiam: tamen affectus iste non statim ponit ipsum quoque rei effectum: sed ad Providentiam DEI referri ille debet, eo modo ac respectu, quo mox ostendetur. Nullo ergò pacto, nulloque artificio Præscientia DEI, vel causa lapsus Adamici, vel ullius alicujus peccati causa constitui potest aut debet: licèt lapsum & peccata omnia ab æterno præsciat. Non enim inquit Augustinus, tu continuò peccare cogeres, quem peccaturum esse, præscires: neq́; ipsa præscientia tua peccare eum cogeret, quamvis sine dubio peccaturꝫ esset: non enim aliter id futurum præscires: & sicut tumemoria tua non cogis facta esse quæ præterierunt: sic DEUS præscientiâ suâ non cogit facienda, quæ futura sunt. Et sicut tu quædam, quæ fecisti, meminii sti: nec tamen quae meministi, omnia fecisti: ita Deus omnia, quorum ipse autor est praescit: nec tamen omnium, quae praescit, ipse autor est: Quorum autem non est malus autor, justus est ultor. l. 3 de l. arb. c. 4.

Neque ἀντίφασιν sive contradictionem haec implicant, quando asserimus ea, quae praesciuntur a DEO certo ac infallibiliter evenire: & tamen libere ac contingenter evenire, ac per hoc fieri non posse. Causa enim utriusque pronunciati diversissima est. Nam DEUS, qui futurum praescit, aeterna sua sapientia sive scientia, aut ut sic loquar intelligentia, ab aeterno praecurrit effectum rei, qualis ille in tempore futurus est, & intuetur rem jam factam antequam fiat: ac per hoc non fallitur praescientia: Nam si res aliter eveniret, DEUS illud ipsum quoque praescivisset. Jam vero illud ipsum quod factum est, non potest factum non esse: ac per hoc quoad praescientiam Dei, necessario illud factum esse recte asseritur, necessitate nimirum ἐξ ὑποθέσεως, sive consequentiae.
