Rursus quod factum est, respectu suorum principiorum vel naturalium, vel artificialium, libere & contingenter factum est: & aliter fieri potuisset, quod ipsum tamen Deus etiam praevidisset. Qui accuratius hanc quaestionem explicant, duplicem in Deo constituunt scientiam: Unam simplicis intelligentiae, qua Deus cognoscit res omnes, quae quoquo modo esse possunt: Alteram visionis, qua cognoscit res prout reipsa sunt, vel erunt, vel fuerunt: propterea quod visio terminatur ad existentiam rei, non ad solam possibilitatem.

Et talis quidem est Praescientia Dei generaliter indefinite & laxe accepta, de notitia simplici rerum futurarum omnium: secundum illud Jobi 28, 24. Ipse fines mundi intuetur, & omnia, quae sub caelo sunt, respicit. Verum non desunt in Scripturis certa testimonia, in quibus Praescientiae vocabulum restricte & determinate ad subjectam materiam accipitur: ut Rom 8, 30. Quos praescivit, hos & praedestinavit: hoc est, D. Augustino interprete, Quos credituros in filium suum praescivit, hos ad salutem praedestinavit. Quae Praescientia nunquam est sine Praedestinatione: usque adeo, ut in Scripturis κατὰ πρόγνωσιν θεῶ electi dicamur, 1. Petr. 1, 1. & 2. Quo sensu ac respectu Praescientiae vox stricte tantum ad bonos, sive filios Dei, non vero ad omnes homines, etiam incredulos, a Spiritu Sancto expresse accommodatur. Qua de re infra in diexodo controversiae specialis octavae, dicendi locus erit.


### I. Special Controversy, on the Vocabularies both of the Latins and of the Greeks, whose use in this matter is wont to be, their proper… (continued)

And this is indeed the first difference, which deserves observation regarding the terms Prescience and Predestination: and it is twofold. For I. That general Prescience denotes a simple knowledge of all things, not a cause: but Predestination is at once the cause of the salvation of the elect, or the children of God, Eph. 1:5. Next, the general prescience of God extends at once to the wicked and the good, to the unbelieving and the believing: 2 Kings 19:27, Exod. 3:19, Isa. 37:28, Ecclus. 23:28, Heb. 4:13. But Predestination pertains only to the children of GOD:

OF GOD: For those whom He predestined, these He also justified, and glorified, a thing which is no more common to the evil with the good, to the unbelieving with the believing, than heaven and hell can be assigned to both at the same time.

II. A second difference, which is to be noted in this place concerning the terms, intervenes between the Providence of GOD and His Predestination. For the Providence of GOD, just as the foreknowledge of GOD, extends most widely, reaching itself to all creatures, but in such a way that, beyond an exact knowledge of all things, it adds also an efficacious care, disposition, and determination of the same: yet with a most diverse respect. For it governs the good wills and actions of the pious in such a way that He wills, commands, and perfects them: according to that of the Savior, John 15:5, Without me you can do nothing: And Philippians 2:13, GOD works in us both to will and to perform for His good pleasure. But it governs the evil actions of men by detesting, punishing, and directing them to a certain end, as much supernatural as natural, for His own glory and the edification of the Church, even serving against the intention of the impious. Deut. 32:19. Psalm 5:5. Ezekiel 18:32. 1 John 2:16. Concerning which matter we have expressly argued in the digression of the article on Providence. Predestination, however, pertains only to the good, and directs and governs the eternal salvation of the elect or children of GOD, a clearly supernatural end: as will be shown hereafter.

III. A third difference consists in this, that the Purpose and Counsel of GOD, of which very frequent mention is made in this article, is not the eternal predestination of GOD itself: but something distinct from it: Which is evident even from this, that in the Scriptures Predestination is asserted to have been made κατα προθεσιν, according to purpose, and κατα βυλην, according to the counsel of GOD: How this stands, the following Treatise will show.

Furthermore, the use of these differences between the terms already explained can and ought to be twofold. The first, that it may be established that the consequence from Foreknowledge and Providence to Predestination is not valid: if anyone should infer in the Calvinian sense: GOD foreknew and provided for the fall of Adam. Therefore He also predestined or ordained Adam to that fall. Or in the Huberian sense: The foreknowledge of GOD extends to all men: Therefore all are predestined to life. For a confusion of genus and species occurs: and the argumentation proceeds from the affirmation of the genus to the affirmation of a certain species: in almost the same way as if one were to infer: This is an animal: Therefore it is a horse. The other use consists in this, that the consequence from Providence to the decree of GOD is not always valid: For example: Evil actions or sins are indeed an object of divine Providence: meanwhile, however, they are not thus decreed or ordained by GOD. But a distinction must be held in this place, and strenuously urged against the attacks of the Calvinists, between the Decree itself, and those things which are subject to the decree. Evils, insofar as they are evils, are never decreed: but they are subject to the decree: not indeed as regards this or that species of evil action considered in itself: but only as regards the event, or determination, or even as regards its punishment. And from this can be understood that Petrine passage, Acts 4:28, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, did what thy hand and thy counsel decreed to be done. For this evil action of Herod, Pontius Pilate, and the Jews was not decreed by GOD; but it was subject to the decree of GOD, by which He determined from eternity to use this evil action of the Jews and Gentiles for the redemption of the fallen human race. But if they had refrained themselves from that wickedness: then GOD would have also decreed otherwise from eternity to redeem the human race. But concerning these things we have argued more fully in the Article of Providence.

These more general matters having been thus premised, there now offers itself the Question which is agitated today concerning the term Predestination and Election: Namely, whether they stand toward each other as Genus and species. And indeed the Calvinists hold the affirmative, contending that the Predestination of GOD, as a genus, contains under its scope two species, namely Election and Reprobation. Or as others speak, it contains two decrees: One of Election: the other of Reprobation. Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, page 523, and Response 2 to the acts of the colloquy, page 232. Grynæus in the Thesaurus, class 2, locus 5, page 92, and others. From whom, however, Keckermann dissents, System of Theology, book 3, chapter 1, page 296, and refutes his teachers from philosophical principles. Indeed, not even Calvin himself subscribes to these, but rather constitutes two decrees of one Election: One to salvation: the other to damnation: so that in the School of Calvin, Election to death, Predestination to damnation, Reprobation, Rejection, etc., are synonyms and equipollent, book 3 of the Institutes, chapter 23, dist. 4. Furthermore, these things are invented without scriptural authority, and collapse by their own impiety. We, having followed the oracles of the sacred scriptures, establish that a synonymy intervenes between Predestination and Election. For although there are those who, by examining these things more subtly, keep saying that Election is prior to Predestination: and that the former is presupposed by the latter, nay, that Election is the cause of Predestination at least according to logic or reason, that is, according to our mode of understanding: and they accommodate that Apostolic passage, Ephesians 1:4 and 5, in place of confirmation, GOD chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid, predestining us, etc. because, however, it is indubitably evident from the Scriptures that the breadth of both Election and Predestination is equal and that they are convertible; and the Apostle has used both terms indiscriminately throughout: and therefore, imitating the Formula of Concord, we use these two terms as synonyms, promiscuously and indiscriminately. For this very reason, we also reject the position of a certain innovator, who did not hesitate to write that Election occurs in time and pertains to some, but that Predestination is eternal and pertains to all men.

Furthermore, that neither the term Predestination nor Election properly contains Reprobation under itself as a species is evident, first, from the fact that this phrase is nowhere to be found in the entire Scripture: GOD predestined or elected certain ones to damnation. Therefore, whatever does not have authority from Scripture is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted, as the blessed Jerome declares in some place.

Furthermore, every end ordained by GOD is some good and the perfection of a thing: But damnation is by its own nature evil, and the destruction of a thing. How then can the end of Predestination be or be called damnation? Finally, the Greek word προορίζειν under its scope comprehends not only the end, but also the means leading to the end. Therefore, if Predestination or προορισμὸς regards Reprobations as a species: it will follow that GOD predestines men not only to the end, namely damnation: but also to sins and unbelief, as means leading to that end: which is manifestly absurd and blasphemous.

But that we may speak something specifically about the term Election, it is accepted in the Scriptures either generally, and according to the propriety of its etymology, it always denotes segregation to some certain end, or use, or office, and is converted with the verb ἀφορίζειν to segregate, as Deut. 10, 15. and ch. 32, 8. Acts 13, 2. Job 15, 19. Or it is taken specifically, for the very prayer or predestination of the children of GOD to salvation, Eph. 1, 4. Rom. 11, 5. And in this special signification the word Election is accommodated only to the children of GOD, so much so that the Holy Spirit does not hesitate to use metonymically the term ἐκλογῆς or Election, for the appellation of τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν the Elect.

But a new Question or controversy arises here: Whether ἐκλεκτοὶ nominally and ἐκλελεγμένοι participially differ in such a way that all men are indeed ἐκλελεγμενοι participially: but not all are ἐκλεκτοὶ nominally, such as are only those who apply that participial Election to themselves through faith, and thus turn out to be ἐκλεκτοὶ: just as Huber dreams: Or as some other fanatic raves: Whether οἱ ἐκλελεγμένοι perpetually bear the title of τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν, so that just as all men whatsoever are from eternity ἐκλελεγμένοι, so also they may be said from eternity to be all ἐκλεκτοὶ? where the same person answers in this manner: I assert that the name ἐκλεκτὸς, in the present matter, used of men, is attributed to no one except a believer, just and holy, and who through faith has Election applied to himself: But the title of ἐκλελεγμένων, to belong to all men at all times, whether they are already converted and believers: or are not yet converted, and do not yet believe. But this distinction labors under manifest absurdities and falsehoods. For 1. it is novel, recently devised in the brain of those who have studied to offer auxiliary hands, as it were, to the most lost cause of Huber. 2. It is unknown to all orthodox antiquity and the Church. 3. It sophistically perverts the proper and legitimate state of the controversy. For it is not being controverted, whether among grammarians, nouns from participles, by reason of signification, really differ? which perhaps none of us will easily deny: although in this part the grammatical propriety of languages can or ought to prejudice the analogy of faith and the Holy Scriptures not at all. Thus it is also not fought over: Whether ἐκλεκτοὶ are truly believers, just, holy: which that fanatic disputer went to demonstrate with many testimonies brought from Scripture: but without an adversary. For this is not only conceded by us, but defended by the firmest arguments. Finally, neither does that come into question, whether ἐκλεκτοὶ are also ἐκλελεγμένοι participially. For this we likewise willingly grant, and we have confirmed it thus far from ch. 13, 20 where Christ predicts that the days of the Lord's coming will be shortened, on account of the ἐκλεκτοὺς, οὓς θεὸς ἐξελέξατο, whom GOD chose: or as the Apostle has it, οὓς εἵλετο, whom he chose, 2 Thess. 2, 13. οὓς προώρισε whom he predestined. But this is the question, whether besides ἐκλεκτοὺς nominally, there are others ἐκλελεγμένοι participially, namely those whom GOD indeed chose from eternity to eternal life without intuition of faith: and who afterwards in time do not apply Election to themselves through faith: but fall away by the grace of Election. Here is Rhodes, here is the leap, and around this question the followers of Huber ought to leap, and demonstrate its affirmative from the Scriptures, which, however, they will not demonstrate any sooner than they have given proof that GOD from eternity chose all men whatsoever, without intuition of faith, to salvation? In which part all proof of the Scriptures fails them, as will be shown below in its place expressly: where a future dispute awaits us concerning particular Election. 4. The participle ἐκλελεγμένος is not found in the whole New Testament: By which one reason alone this distinction in the present matter collapses. 5. The Holy Spirit does not attend to this grammatical distinction so much, that he rather calls κλητοὺς nominally those who do not obey the calling: as Matt. 22, 14. and vice versa calls κεκλημένους participially those who leave room for the calling: as Apocal. 19, 9. Blessed are the κεκλημένοι called to the marriage supper of the Lamb: and Hebr. 9, 15. that they may receive the promise of eternal inheritance, the οἱ κεκλημένοι called. Let it be therefore, let there be and remain among grammarians a real distinction between a verbal and a participial noun, and indeed in things placed outside the mystery of faith: yet to the present article it can or ought to be distorted by no right. Least of all, however, can the opinion of those fanatics be saved from this distinction, who with respect and consideration of both time and application, constitute a double Election: One which was made from eternity, and is of all men, without respect of faith: Another, which is made in time, namely then, if men through faith join themselves to the assembly of Believers and Elect. Certainly, we have already shown that no help can redound to this vain talk from that fictitious distinction of words. Furthermore, it wanders clearly outside the olive trees. For if a man through faith joins himself to the assembly of the Elect, a new species of Election is not constituted: but rather the execution of the Election made from eternity is done: and is brought into act: which GOD foresaw from eternity would be, and by whose intuition also GOD from eternity chose the man who would believe: as will be demonstrated in its place.

It remains that we should offer some remarks concerning the term Predestination, which was not introduced by the usage of the Church, but is proper to Scripture itself: Rom. 8:30, derived by a sufficiently convenient translation from the Greek word προορισμὸς, which has its origin ἀπὸ τοῦ προορίζειν, from predefining, determining, or predestinating. Moreover, this appellation, as Dionysius the Areopagite testifies in On the Divine Names, ch. 5, has a double sense in itself: one of Destination or Deputation and Ordination; the other of Precession. Now, to destine is to ordain to a certain end, according to that 2 Cor. 9:7: Each one, as he has destined in his heart. But because man is ordained by God to his end in a singular way and with special care, he is said to be destined κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of eminence), especially since this destination is directed to a most excellent end, and one higher than human nature. But the sense of precession or antegression denotes priority, not primarily that which is of dignity and excellence, by which the predestined are loved and exalted in a singular way above others; nor does it denote that which is on the part of the divine mind, in which predestination, as a cause, precedes all those things which are on the part of man; but it denotes primarily that which is in respect of eternity, in order to time. For this order in the mind of GOD preceded all things that happen, and that have been done in time, even the calling, justification, and glorification of the Elect. Which the Apostle expressed, asserting that we were chosen by GOD in Christ before the very foundations of the world were laid, Eph. 1:4, and before times eternal, 2 Tim. 1:9.

Latin:

Et haec quidem prima est differentia, quae de vocabulis Praescientiae & Praedestinationis observationem meretur: eaque gemina. Nam I. Praescientia illa generalis simplicem rerum omnium notitiam denotat, non causam: Praedestinatio vero, simul est causa salutis electorum, sive filiorum Dei Ephes. 1, 5. Deinde praescientia Dei generalis simul ad malos & bonos, ad incredulos & credentes se extendit: 2. Reg. 19, 27. Exod. 3, 19. Esa. 37, 28. Eccles. 23, 28. Hebr. 4, 13. Praedestinatio vero tantum pertinet ad Filios DEI:

DEI : Nam quos prædestinavit, hos & justificavit, & glorificavit, id quod malis cum bonis, incredulis cum credentibus, haud magis commune est, atque cœlum & infernus utrisque simul adsignari potest.

II. Altera differentia, quæ de vocabulis hoc loco notanda, intercedit Providentiæ DEI, cum ejusdem Prædestinatione. Nam Providentia DEI æquè ac præscientia DEI latissimè patet, extendens se ad omnes creaturas, sed ita, ut præter exactam rerum omnium notitiam, superaddat efficacem quoque curam, dispositionem & determinationem earundem: diversissimo tamen respectu. Bonas enim piorum voluntates & actiones ita gubernat, ut eas velit, mandet, perficiat: juxta illud Servatoris, Johan. 15, 5. Sive me nihil potestis facere: Et Philipp. 2, 13. DEUS operatur in nobis velle & perficere pro beneplacito. Malas verò hominum actiones detestando, puniendo, & ad finem certum tàm supernaturalem, quàm naturalem gloriæ suæ Ecclesiæque ædificationi, etiam contra impiorum intentionem subservientem dirigendo. Deut. 32, 19. Psal. 5, 5. Ezech. 18, 32. 1. Joh. 2, 16. Quâ de re ex professo disputavimus in diexodo articuli de Providentiâ. Prædestinatio autem tantùm ad bonos pertinet, & æternam salutem electorum sive filiorum DEI finem planè supernaturalem dirigit & gubernat: uti deinceps ostendetur.

III. Tertia differentia in eo consistit, quòd Propositu & Consilium DEI, cujus hoc in articulo creberrima fit mentio, non est ipsamet æterna DEI prædestinatio: sed quiddam ab eâ distinctum: Id quod vel indè patet, quod in Scripturis Prædestinatio facta esse asseritur κατα προθεσιν, secundum propositum, & κατα βυλην secundum consilium DEI: Quod quomodo sese habeat, insequens Tractatio ostendet.

Cæterùm usus istarum differentiarum inter vocabula jam explicata, potest & debet esse geminus. Prior, ut constet, non valere consequentiam à Præscientiâ, & Providentia ad Prædestinationem: si quis inferat sensu Calviniano: DEUS præscivit & providit lapsum Adami. Ergò Adamum etiam ad lapsum istum prædestinavit sive ordinavit. Vel sensu Huberiano: Præscientia DEI ad omnes homines se extendit: Ergò omnes sunt prædestinati ad vitam. Fit enim confusio Generis & speciei: ac procedit argumentatio ab affirmatione generis, ad affirmationem certæ speciei: eodem penè modo, ac si quis inferat: Hoc est animal: Ergò est equus. Alter usus in eo consistit, quod à Providentiâ ad decretum DEI non semper valet consequentia: Exempli gratia: Malæ actiones sive peccata sunt quidem objectum Providentiæ divinæ: interim tamen à DEO non sic sunt decreta, sive ordinata. Sed tenenda hoc loco, & contra Calvinianorum impetus strenuè est urgenda distinctio, inter Decretum ipsum, & inter ea, quæ subjacent decreto. Mala, quatenùs mala, nunquàm sunt decreta: sed subjacent decreto: non quidem quoad hanc vel illam speciem malæ actionis in se consideratæ: sed tantùm quoad eventum, sive determinationem, vel etiam, quoad ejus pœnam. Et hinc intelligi potest, illud Petrinum, Actor. 4, 28. Fecerunt Herodes & Pontius Pilatus, cum gentibus & populis Israël, quæ manus tua, & consilium tuum fieri decreverunt. Nam actio hæc mala Herodis, Pontij Pilati, & Judæorum, non erat decreta à DEO; sed subjacebat decreto DEI, quo ab æterno constituit hac malâ actione Judæorum & Gentium uti ad redemtionem lapsi generis humani. Quod si verò ab istâ nequitiâ sibi illi temperassent: tùm DEUS aliter etiam ab æterno decrevisset redimere genus humanum. Verùm de his in Articulo Providentiæ fusiùs à nobis disputatum fuit.

His generalioribus ita præmissis, ea jam se offert Quæstio, quæ de vocabulo Prædestinationis & Electionis hodiè agitatur: Utrum nimirum ea ad se mutuò se habent, ut Genus & species. Et sanè Calviniani affirmativam tenent contendentes, Prædestinationem DEI tanquàm genus, sub suo ambitu duas continere species, Electionem videlicet & Reprobationem. Vel ut alij loquuntur, duo continere decreta: Unum Electionis: alterum Reprobationis. Beza in Colloquio Mompelgart. pag. 523. & Respons. 2. ad acta colloquij pag. 232. Grynæus in Thesauro classe 2. loco 5. pag. 92. & alij. A quibus tamen dissentit Keckermannus Syst. Theol. lib. 3. cap. 1. pag. 296. & ex principijs philosophicis Præceptores suos refutat. Quin nec Calvino ipse istis subscribit, sed potiùs unius Electionis duo decreta constituit: Unum ad salutem: alterum ad damnationem: ita ut in Scholâ Calvini Synonyma & æquipollentia sint, Electio ad mortem, Prædestinatio ad damnationem, Reprobatio, Rejectio &c. lib. 3. Instit. cap. 23. dist. 4. Cæterùm ἀνεξγράφως hæc sic finguntur, & propriâ impietate concidunt. Nos sacrarum literarum oracula secuti, Prædestinationi cum Electione συνωνυμίαν intercedere statuimus Etsi enim sunt, qui subtiliùs ista excutiendo, Electionem Prædestinatione priorem esse: & illam ab hac præsupponi, imò Electionem Prædestinationis causam esse saltem secundum λόγον sive rationem, hoc est, secundùm nostrum intelligendi modum, dictitant: illudque Apostolicum Ephes. 1, 4. & 5. confirmationis loco accommodant, DEUS elegit nos in Christo ante jacta mundi fundamenta, prædestinans nos &c. quia tamen parem & Electionis & Prædestinationis latitudinem, eamque convertibilem esse, ex Scripturis indubitatò constat: & Apostolus indifferenter utroque vocabulo passim usus est: ideoque Formulam Concordiæ imitati vocabulis istis duob9 tàquàm Synonymis, promifcuè & indifferenter utimur. Quam ipsam etiam ob causam rejicimus Summum cujusdam Novatoris, qui scribere non dubitavit, Electionem fieri in tempore, & esse aliquorum: Prædestinationem verò esse æternam, & esse omnium hominum.

Cæterùm quòd neque Prædestinationis, neque Electionis vocabulum, propriè sub se contineat Reprobationem tanquàm speciem: primùm indè patet, quòd hæc phrasi in universâ Scripturâ nuspiam reperitur: DEUS prædestinavit sive elegit quosdam ad damnationem. Quicquid ergò de Scripturâ autoritatem non habet, pari facilitate rejicitur, quâ asseritur: uti alicubi pronunciat B. Hieronymus.

Deindè omnis finis à DEO ordinatus est bonum quid & rei perfectio : At damnatio sua natura mala est, & destructio rei. Quomodo ergò Prædestinationis finis esse aut dici queat damnatio? Tandem verbum græcum προορίζειν sub suo complexu non finem tantùm, sed & media perducentia ad finem comprehendit. Ergò si Prædestinatio sive προορισμὸς respicit tanquàm speciem Reprobationum: consequens fuerit, DEUM prædestinare homines non modò ad finem, nempè damnationem: sed & ad peccata, & incredulitatem, tanquàm media ad finem illum perducentia: id quod manifestè absurdum & blasphemum.

Sed ut in specie de Electionis vocabulo aliquid dicamus, illud in Scripturis vel generatim accipitur, & secundum proprietatem etymi sui, semper segregationem ad certum aliquem finem, sive usum, sive officium notat, & cum verbo ἀφορίζειν segregare convertitur, ut Deut. 10, 15. & cap. 32, 8. Actor. 13, 2. Job. 15, 19. Vel sumitur speciatim, pro ipsâ oratione sive prædestinatione filiorum DEI ad salutem, Ephes. 1, 4. Rom. 11, 5. Et hoc speciali significatu Electionis vox tantùm filijs DEI accommodatur, usque adeò, ut Spiritus Sanctus, non dubitet μετωνυμικῶς ἐκλογῆς sive Electionis termino uti, pro appellatione τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν Electorum.

Sed nova hîc oritur Quæstio sive controversia: An ἐκλεκτοὶ nominaliter: & ἐκλελεγμένοι participialiter ita differant, ut omnes quidem homines sint ἐκλελεγμενοι participialiter: non verò omnes sint ἐκλεκτοὶ nominaliter, quales illi tantùm sint, qui Electionem participialem illam sibi per fidē applicant, & evadunt sic ἐκλεκτοὶ: quemadmodum Huberus somniat: Vel ut alius quidam fanatic9 delirat: An titulum τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν perpetuò gerant οἱ ἐκλελεγμένοι, ita ut quemadmodum omnes omninò homines ab æterno sunt ἐκλελεγμένοι, ita etiam ab æterno dici possint omnes esse ἐκλεκτοὶ? ubi idem respondet in hunc modum: Assero nomen ἐκλεκτὸς, in præsenti materiâ, de hominibus usurpatum, nemini nisi credenti, justo ac sancto, quique per fidem Electionem sibi applicatam habet tribui: Titulum verò ἐκλελεγμένων, omnibus hominib9 omni tempore convenire, sive jam sint conversi & credentes: sive nondùm conversi sint, nondùm credant. Verùm manifestis & absurditatibus & falsitatibus distinctio hæc laborat. Nam 1. novella est, in eorum nuper cerebro excogitata, qui Huberi causæ perditissimæ auxiliares quasi manus præbere studuerunt. 2. Toti orthodoxæ antiquitati & Ecclesiæ est ignota. 3. Sophisticè pervertit statum controversiæ proprium ac legitimum. Nam non illud controvertitur, An apud Grammaticos, nomina à participijs, ratione significationis, realiter differant? id quod fortè nemo nostrûm facilè negaverit: quanquàm hac in parte lingvarum proprietas Grammatica, analogiæ fidei, & Scripturis Sacris nihil quicquam præjudicare vel potest vel debet. Sic de eo etiam non pugnatur: An ἐκλεκτοὶ sint verè credentes, justi, sancti: id quod fanaticus ille disputator multis ex Scripturâ allatis testimoniis demonstratum ivit: sed sine adversario. Nam hoc à nobis non modò conceditur, sed firmissimis argumentis propugnatur. Tandem neque illud in quæstionem venit, An ἐκλεκτοὶ sint etiam ἐκλελεγμένοι participialiter. Nam hoc itidem ultrò largimur, idque hactenùs confirmavimus ex cap. 13, 20 ubi Christus prædicit, abbreviatum iri dies adventus Dominici, propter ἐκλεκτοὺς, οὓς θεὸς ἐξελέξατο, quos DEUS elegit: vel ut Apostolus habet, οὓς εἵλετο, quos elegit, 2. Thess. 2, 13. οὓς προώρισε quos prædestinavit. Verùm hoc quæstionis est, An præter ἐκλεκτοὺς nominaliter, sint alij ἐκλελεγμένοι participialiter, illi videlicet, quos ab æterno quidem DEUS elegit ad vitam æternam sine intuitu fidei: quique postmodùm in tempore per fidem sibi Electionem non applicant: sed Electionis gratiâ excidunt. Hîc Rhodus, hîc saltus est, & circa hanc quæstionem saltare debebant Huberi asseclæ, ejusque affirmativam ex Scripturis demonstrare, quam tamen haud citiùs demonstrabunt, quàm probatum dederint, DEUM ab æterno omnes omninò homines, sine intuitu fidei, ad salutem elegisse? Quâ in parte omnis Scripturarum probatio ipsos deficit, uti infrà suo loco ex professo ostendetur: ubi de Electione particulari nobis futura disputatio. 4. Participium ἐκλελεγμένος non reperitur in toto Novo Testamento: Quâ vel unâ ratione distinctio hæc in præsenti materiâ corruit. 5. Spiritus Sanctus discrimen hoc Grammaticum usque adeò non attendit, ut potiùs κλητοὺς nominaliter vocatos nomineteos etiam, qui vocationi non obtemperant: ut Matth. 22, 14. & vice versâ κεκλημένους participialiter nominet eos, qui vocationi locum relinquunt: ut Apocal. 19, 9. Beati κεκλημένοι vocati ad cænam nuptiarum Agni: & Hebr. 9, 15. ut promissionem æternæ hæreditatis accipiant οἱ κεκλημένοι vocati. Esto igitur, sit maneatque apud Grammaticos discrimen reale, inter nomen verbale & participiale, & quidem in rebus, extra mysterium fidei positis: ad præsentem tamen articulum illud detorqueri nullo jure vel potest, vel debet. Minimè omnium autem ex hoc discrimine salvari potest eorum fanaticorum opinio, qui respectu & consideratione tùm temporis, tùm applicationis, Electionem geminam constituunt: Unam quæ sit facta ab æterno, & sit omnium hominum, sine respectu fidei: Alteram, quæ in tempore fiat, tùm nimirùm, si homines per fidem se adjungant cætui Credentium & Electorum. Certè ad hanc matæologiam nihil quicquam ræsidij ex fictitio illo vocabulorum discrimine redundare posse, jam ostendimus. Præterea extra oleas planè ea vagatur. Nam si homo per fidem cætui Electorum se adjungit, non nova Electionis species constituitur: sed Electionis ab æterno factæ executio potiùs fit: & in actum deducitur: quod DEUS ab æterno futurum præscivit, & cujus intuitu etiam DEUS ab æterno hominem crediturum elegit: uti suo loco demonstrabitur.

Superest, ut de Prædestinationis vocabulo aliquid moneamus, quod non usu Ecclesiæ est introductum: sed Scripturæ ipsius proprium: Rom. 8, 30, ex voce Græcâ προορισμὸς translatione satis commodâ deductum, quæ originem habet ἀπὸ τοῦ προορίζειν, à præfiniendo, determinando, seu prædestinando. Habet autem teste Dionys. Areopag. de Divi. nom. cap. 5. appellatio ista duplicem in se sensum: Unum Destinationis sive Deputationis atquê Ordinationis: alterum Præcessionis. Destinare autem est ad finem certum ordinare, juxta illud 2. Cor. 9, 7. Unusquisquê, prout in corde suo destinavit. Quia verò homo singulari quodam modo & curâ ordinatur à Deo in finem suum, κατ' ἐξοχὴν destinari dicitur, maximè cum destinatio ista ad finem excellentissimum, & naturâ humanâ altiorem, directa sit. Præcessionis verò sive antegressionis sensus, prioritatem notat, non eam præcipuè, quæ est dignitatis atquê excellentiæ, quâ prædestinati singulari quodam modo, præ alijs diliguntur atque evehuntur: Neque eam etiam notat, quæ est ex parte mentis divinæ, in quâ prædestinatio tanquàm causa, præcedit ea, quæ sunt ex parte hominis, omnia: Sed eam potissimùm, quæ est respectu æternitatis, in ordine ad tempus. Nam iste ordo in mente DEI præcessit omnia, quæ fiunt, quæque facta sunt in tempore, etiam vocationem, justificationem, glorificationem Electorum. Quod Apostolus expressit, asserens, nos in Christo à DEO esse electos ante jacta ipsa fundamenta seculi, Ephes. 1, 4. & ante tempora secularia. 2. Tim. 1, 9.


### II. Special Controversy, On the Subject & Object of Predestination

We constitute GOD himself as the Subject of Predestination, not indeed that any accident falls into GOD, but only for the sake of teaching, as far as we are concerned: because, clearly, the matter of Predestination from which no other can be given, besides the one and only GOD, who is the fountain, author, and origin, as of every good, so also of our Election to salvation. Concerning which matter Thomas argues not ineptly in Part 1, Question 23, Article 1. For he asks, Does Predestination belong to GOD? And he answers that it does, because partly eternal life exceeds the faculty of man; and partly because Predestination is a part of Providence, which places nothing in the predestined. Now, it is the nature of Providence to ordain a thing to a certain end; but the end is twofold: one, which exceeds the proportion and faculty of nature, such as eternal life, the supernatural end of man; the other, which is proportionate to nature, which indeed a caused thing can attain by the virtue of its own nature. Now because Man could not attain that former end by the powers of nature, Thomas concludes that it was necessary for him to obtain it from elsewhere. But outside of GOD no creature could provide this. Therefore, it remained that this supernatural end, eternal life, should be transmitted to man by GOD alone: which was done by GOD through gratuitous predestination, calling, justification, and glorification.

Furthermore, we leave in the middle the questions which the Scholastics debate in this place, whether predestination pertains more to the intellect or to the will of GOD, as they obtain no use at all; establishing that, by reason of divine providence, the act of Predestination is most correctly referred to the intellect or rather the infinite wisdom of GOD; but by reason of the foundation and the προκαταρκτικὴν (pre-initiating) cause, it is referred to the will of God. But no controversy is being conducted on this matter in this place. Therefore, we must look more accurately into the OBJECT of Predestination, concerning which it does not seem to be one and the same for everyone today. And indeed there are among Orthodox Theologians some who constitute a twofold Object of Predestination: one of Angels, the other of Men. And indeed they prove that predestination also belongs to the Angels, because the Angels also share in the destination of an end which exceeds their own nature. For the Angels do not participate in eternal blessedness by nature, but by grace, and consequently from predestination. For grace is an effect of Predestination.

Again, there are others who contradict these, and write expressly: That only men are elect, not also Angels; and they demonstrate this with this argument: Those are elect to eternal life who were immersed in misery on account of sin: for the redeeming of whom Christ was given, and the Gospel is preached, and the Sacraments are administered, and through them, by the virtue and grace of the Holy Spirit, they themselves believe in Christ, and thus, with sins forgiven, they are saved. But nothing of the sort can be said of the blessed Angels. Therefore, the blessed Angels are not said to be elect to eternal life, but only miserable sinful men believing in Christ.

Moreover, all this variety of opinions is found to consist more in words than in the thing itself and its meaning. For those later writers only mean this, that the mode of Predestination which is defined in the Scriptures by the reason of men, and consists of certain external means, such as the preaching of the Word and the use of the Sacraments, does not apply to the Angels: a thing which even those former writers never and nowhere affirmed. On the other hand, those former writers, in contending for the Election of the Angels, consider only the supernatural end, which is eternal life, and which befalls the Angels also not by nature, but by mere grace: a thing which even those later writers do not deny; insomuch that they expressly write that, in that the Angels are called elect, it has another meaning.

This disagreement among theologians is therefore most rightly reconciled if it is first established that the proper and adequate object of the predestination which is treated in this article is nothing other than miserable sinners alone, who believe in Christ through the Word of the Gospel. Then, indeed, if it is not simply and in all respects denied that mention is also made in the Scriptures of the election of angels, the reason for which, however, is entirely different and distinct from the election of men: so that both can neither be, nor ought to be, referred under one and the same definition of election. And hence it is that not only the orthodox Fathers, but also certain more recent theologians, establish a twofold species of predestination: one of angels, the other of men: as can be seen in Augustine, De correptione et gratia, chapters 10, 11, 12. We have no evident causes to reject this distinction.

For in the beginning the Apostle mentions the election of angels, 1 Tim. 5:21: 'I charge you before God, and Christ Jesus, and in the sight of the elect angels,' etc. Then, that angels also were not elected to eternal life on account of either the excellence and holiness of their nature or the foresight of good works is placed beyond all risk of controversy. But whether this election of angels was brought about through mere confirmation in good, or also through other means, we freely confess that we are ignorant: asserting meanwhile, however, that the opinion of those who define this election of angels through the preservation and confirmation of their first state and origin seems more probable to us, so that it is said that absolutely nothing was restored to them through this election, since nothing had previously been either lost or taken away from them. Therefore, they were preserved and confirmed later just as and in the state in which they were first created by God. Nor, however, do we establish that quality and that state in which they were first created as the cause of this election. For thus all angels whatsoever, even those who fell, would have to be called elect, as they were all created in the same happy state in the beginning: but we establish as the cause that singular grace of confirmation, which differs in species from the grace of creation. Whether, however, that grace of confirmation, by which angels are said to be elect, also presupposes the merit of Christ as the meritorious cause of election is not expressed in the Scriptures. We concede to the negative, moved chiefly by this reason: because the redemption and merit of Christ presupposes the fall, which never befell the elect angels. We therefore establish that the angels were elected by God out of mere grace, and indeed not outside the Son, but in the Son: but not in respect of his merit. For the Son of God did not take hold of angels, but the seed of Abraham: therefore he did not redeem the angels either: but in a general respect, insofar as every good pleasure of God is founded only in the only-begotten Son. There are those who therefore deny the predestination of angels because they were never miserable. But the consequence is rightly denied: for, as Thomas rightly argues, part 1, q. 23, art. 1, a motion does not receive its species from the term from which, but from the term to which. It matters nothing, therefore, to the definition of predestination whether someone is predestined from a state of misery or not: but it matters that he is predestined to eternal life as the ultimate term to which. Others urge the sayings of Scripture asserting that Christ restored all things which are in heaven and on earth. Therefore they conclude that the angels also were elected by the power of the merit of Christ. But a manifest ignorance of the refutation is committed. For those things which are in heaven are restored by Christ in this respect, insofar as that discord which had existed between the angels and the fallen human race was removed through the merit of Christ: but not in respect of the redemption of the angels. But because the mode of this angelic election is not expressed in the Scriptures, we certainly will not inquire into it too curiously, and we establish that this former species of election pertains nothing to the present article.

There remains, therefore, that question still to be decided: what is the proper and adequate object of the predestination defined and explained in the Scriptures. Here we first remove all irrational creatures whatsoever. The reason is this: for these are not ordained to an end which exceeds their own nature: they are indeed subject to the providence of God, but not to predestination, which ordains its object only to a supernatural end.

Then, indeed, following the Scriptures, we establish the proper object of predestination as only and solely man, but not in the Huberian sense, every man whatsoever, as much the unbeliever as the believer, but only man believing in Christ to the very end.

But in this place another question arises: namely, whether in respect of this object, that is, believing men, one predestination is to be established, or a varied and manifold one? To which question we, with all the orthodox, respond that there is only one and the same predestination of all who are to be saved, made from eternity. For just as the hope of the calling in which we have been called is but one (Ephesians 4:4), and the mode of salvation is but one (Acts 15:11), so the principle from which all these things depend is but one in God, and that eternal: since before the foundation of the world, which the Apostle asserts that election preceded (Ephesians 1:4), there was nothing besides eternity itself. From this purity of our thesis, some of the fathers have already departed long ago, who made a twofold predestination even in respect of men: one of men before the fall, another of the same after the fall: as can be seen in Augustine, De correptione et gratia, chapter 10 and the two following: and in the book De bono perseverantiae, chapter 7. But these things were asserted without the Scriptures. For to our first parents before the fall, the reason of creation more according to the image of God than of election is assigned in the Scriptures. What is more, the term of election does not properly apply to them before the fall, seeing that they by nature bring about a separation of their own: Such a separation did not take place then. It would therefore be better to abstain entirely from that term, as far as the first parents considered before the fall are concerned.

Furthermore, the Romanists foster an error in the Church of God that is by no means to be tolerated, concerning the object of Predestination, in that they make one kind of Predestination peculiar to some men and consisting of a certain singular Privilege: and another kind common to the rest of those to be saved. Of that former kind they again establish various degrees and orders, and those seven in number, below that degree which pertains to Christ the Savior. For they say that He was predestined in the highest and most excellent way, so that He neither sinned nor could sin: and they most viciously accommodate to this that passage in Rom. 1:4, where the Latin version reads viciously, that Christ was chosen or predestined by GOD the Father to be the Son of GOD: when, however, in the Greek neither the word προωρίσθη nor ἐκλέγη is read, but only the simple ὁρισθεὶς, which denotes nothing other than that Christ was declared, defined, and known to be the Son of God. Therefore, those things which Bellarmine argues in Book 2 de grat. & lib. arb. cap. 12 concerning the Predestination of Christ, and that it was done freely, without the foresight of his works, are false and clearly discordant with the orthodox faith. After Christ, they place the Blessed Virgin Mary in the first degree, predestined in such a way that she was free from all sin, whether venial, mortal, or original. In the second order or degree, they place those who were never subject to actual sin, but only to Original sin, such as Jeremiah the Prophet and John the Baptist. In the third, they count those who were indeed not free from venial sin, nor even from Original sin, but were nevertheless immune from mortal sin: such as Abraham, many Prophets, and the Apostles after they received the Holy Spirit. In the fourth, they refer those who are effectively predestined to salvation: yet in such a way that they were permitted to fall into mortal sin: such as David. In the fifth, they place those who, though initially destitute of the gift of perseverance, nevertheless obtained it before death through works and prayers, so that they would not finally fall away from the grace of GOD. In the sixth, they place Infants who received that efficacy of Predestination by the virtue of Justification itself, because by reason of their age they could not sin mortally. In the last or seventh order, they refer those who, while they lived and were in health, were subject to mortal sin, but finally at the end of life, and in the very agony of death, received the gift of perseverance: such as the thief on the right at the Crucifixion of Christ. And indeed, they are accustomed to prove the diversity of these seven degrees partly from the conformity and adornment of the Church: concerning which see Psalm 45 and Canticles 6; and partly from the distinction of the gifts which the Apostles and Prophets exercised. Ephes. 2:20. But these things are manifestly false, and they fight diametrically against the analogy of faith, both in this article and in those which concern the sin of Origin and the Justification of a sinful man before GOD: a fact which even a beginner in Theology understands, to such an extent that Bellarmine, although he fights strenuously enough for the absolute holiness of the Virgin Mary and her being clearly immune from the sin of Origin, nevertheless does not wish to undertake the defense of the remaining degrees in this article. But the proof itself is entirely foreign to this business, and the cited passages deal with that dispensation by which GOD governs His Church in this world and adorns it through the divisions of gifts. Concerning which matter, Matthew 25 deals with the parable of the talents; and 1 Cor. 12 with the distinction of gifts; and 2 Tim. 2 with the likeness of household vessels.

Latin:

Subjectum Prædestinationis constituimus DEUM ipsum, non quidem quòd accidens aliquod cadat in DEUM: sed tantùm docendi gratiâ, quoad nos: quia nimirùm Prædestinationis materia ex quâ non potest dari alia, præter unum ac solum DEUM, qui est fons, autor & origo, uti omnis boni, sic etiam Electionis nostræ ad salutem. Quâ de re haud ineptè disputat Thomas part. 1. quæst. 23. art. 1. Quærit enim, Nùm DEO conveniat Prædestinatio? Et respondet, quòd sic, quia partim æterna vita excedat hominis facultatem: Partim verò Prædestinatio sit pars Providentiæ, quæ nihil ponat in Prædestinatis. Jam verò Providentiæ esse, rem ad certum finem ordinare: Finem autem esse geminum: Unum, qui excedat proportionẽ & facultatem naturæ, qualis sit vita æterna, Finis hominis supernaturalis: Alterũ, qui sit naturæ proportionat9, quẽ scilicet res caufata ex naturæ suæ virtute potest assequi. Jam quia priorem illum finem Homo ex naturæ viribus attingere non potuit, hinc necessarium fuisse, colligit Thomas, ut aliundè eum consequeretur. Atqui extra DEUM nulla creatura hoc præstare poterat. Ergò ut à solo DEO finis iste supernaturalis, vita æterna ad hominem transmitteretur, relinquebatur: id quod à DEO factum per gratuitam prædestinationem, vocationem, justificationem, glorificationem.

Cæterùm quæ hoc loco disputant Scholastici, utrùm prædestinatio magis ad intelligentiam, quàm ad voluntatem DEI pertineat? in medio relinquimus, ut quæ usum planè nullum obtinent: statuentes, ratione providentiæ divinæ ad intelligentiam vel potiùs sapientiam DEI infinitam: ratione verò fundamenti & causæ προκαταρκτικῆς, ad voluntatem Dei, Prædestinationis actum rectissimè referri. Sed hâc de re nulla hoc loco agitur controversia. Ergò de OBJECTO Prædestinationis, de quo non unum idemque hodiè videtur omnibus, nobis accuratiùs dispiciendum fuerit. Et sanè sunt inter Orthodoxos etiam Theologos nonnulli, qui geminũ Prædestinationis Objectum constituunt: Unum Angelorum: Alterum Hominum. Et sanè Angelis quoque prædestinationem convenire, vel indè probant, quia Angeli etiam in destinatione finis, qui naturam ipsorum excedit, communicat. Nam Angeli non per naturam æternâ beatitudine participant: sed per gratiam, & consequenter ex prædestinatione. Gratia enim est effectus Prædestinationis.

Rursum sunt alij, qui his contradicunt, & disertè scriptitant: Solos homines esse electos, non etiam Angelos: idq́; hoc argumento demonstrant: Illi sunt electi ad vitam æternam, qui fuêre propter peccatum immersi miseriæ: quibus redimendis datus est Christus, & Evangelium prædicatur & Sacramenta administrantur, & per illa, virtute & gratiâ Spiritus Sancti ipsi credunt in Christum, & ita remissis peccatis salvi fiunt. Atqui nihil tale potest dici de beatis Angelis. Ergò beati Angeli non dicuntur electi ad vitam æternam, sed soli homines miseri peccatores in Christum credentes.

Cæterùm omnis hæc sententiarum varietas, in verbis magis, quàm in reipsâ atq́ue sensu consistere deprehenditur. Nam posteriores isti hoc tantùm volunt, eam Prædestinationis rationem, quæ in Scripturis ratione hominum definitur, & constat certis medijs externis, ut prædicatione Verbi, & usu Sacramentorum, Angelis non competere: id quod priores etiam illi nunquàm ac nuspiam affirmârunt. Rursus priores illi pugnantes pro Electione Angelorum, finem tantùm supernaturalem, qui est vita æterna, quique Angelis etiam non ex naturâ, sed ex merâ gratiâ obtingit, considerant: id quod posteriores etiam isti non negant: usque adeò, ut disertè scribant, Quòd Angeli dicantur electi, illud alium sensum habere.

Rectissimè ergò hæc Theologorum dissonantia conciliatur, si primùm statuatur, Prædestinationis, de quâ hoc in articulo agitur, Objectum proprium & adæquatum non esse aliud, præter solos homines miseros peccatores, per Verbum Evangelij in Christum credentes. Deindè verò si non simpliciter & per omnia negetur, in Sacris mentionem etiam fieri Electionis Angelorum, cujus tamen ab Electione hominum, alia prorsus & dispar sit ratio: Ita ut sub unam eandemque Electionis definitionem utraque referri nec possit, nec debeat. Et hinc est, quòd non Patres modò Orthodoxi, sed & recentiores quidam Theologi, duplicem Prædestinationis speciem constituunt: Unam Angelorum: Alteram Hominum: uti videre est apud Augustin. de corrept. & grat. Capp. 10. 11. 12. Quam distinctionem ut nos rejiciamus, causas evidentes habemus nullas.

Nam initiò Electionis Angelicæ meminit Apostolus, 1. Tim. 5, 21. Testor coram DEO, & Christo Jesu, & in conspectu τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν ἀγγέλων electorum Angelorum &c. Deindè quin Angeli quoque, non propter vel naturæ excellentiam & sanctitatem, vel bonorum operum prævisionem ad vitam æternam sint electi, extra omnem controversiæ aleam est positum. Verùm nùm Electio hæc Angelorum, per solam confirmationem in bono, an per alia etiam media, facta sit, id nos ignorare libenter fatemur: asserentes tamen interim probabiliorem nobis videri eorum sententiam, qui Electionem hanc Angelorum, per conservationem & confirmationem primi eorum status & originis definiunt, adeò ut nihil prorsus illis per hanc Electionem restitutum fuisse dicatur, quoniam nihil priùs ab illis fuerat vel amissum, vel ablatum. Ergò ipsi, quatenùs & quales à DEO primùm conditi fuerunt, tales postmodùm conservati & confirmati fuerunt. Neque tamen Electionis hujus causam constituimus Qualitatem & statum illum, in quo primum creati sunt. Sic enim omnes omninò Angeli, etiam illi, qui lapsi sunt, dicendi essent electi, ut qui in eodem statu felici omnes initiò conditi sunt: sed causam statuimus singularem illam confirmationis gratiam, quæ à Gratiâ creationis specie differt. Utrum verò Gratia illa confirmationis, quâ Angeli electi esse dicuntur, præsupponat etiam meritum Christi, tanquàm Electionis causam meritoriam: in Scripturis expressum non est. Nos in negantem concedimus, hac potissimùm ratione moti: quia Redemtio & meritum Christi, præsupponit lapsum, qui in Angelos electos nunquàm cecidit. Statuimus ergò Angelos ex merâ gratiâ à DEO electos esse, & quidem non extra Filium, sed in Filio: verùm non respectu meriti hujus. Nam Filius DEI non Angelos, sed semen Abrahæ assumssit: Ergò neque Angelos etiam redemit: sed generali respectu, quatenùs omne beneplacitum DEI non nisi in Filio unigenito est fundatum. Sunt qui ideò negant Prædestinationem Angelorum, quia hi nunquàm fuerint miseri. Sed rectè negatur consequentia: Nam, uti Thomas rectè disputat part. 1. q. 23. Art. 1. Motus non accipit speciem à termino à Quo: sed à termino, Ad Quem. Nihil ergò refert ad rationem Prædestinationis, utrum aliquis prædestinetur à statu miseriæ vel non: sed illud refert, ut prædestinetur ad vitam æternam tanquàm terminum ultimum ad quem. Urgent alij dicta Scripturæ asserentia, Christum restituisse omnia, quæ in Cœlis & in terrâ sunt. Ergò Angelos etiam vi meriti Christi electos esse colligunt. Sed manifesta committitur ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꙋ. Nam restituuntur à Christo, quæ in cœlis, eo respectu, quatenùs per meritum Christi sublata est illa discordia, quæ inter Angelos & lapsum genus humanum intercesserat: non verò respectu redemtionis Angelorum. Sed quia in Scripturis Electionis hujus Angelicæ modꝰ non est expressus, utiq́; nos quoque curiosiùs eam non inquiremus, & priorem hanc Electionis speciem, ad præsentem Articulum nihil pertinere statuimus.

Relinquitur ergò Quæstio illa adhuc decidenda, Quodnám sit Prædestinationis, in Scripturis definitæ & explicatæ, objectum proprium & adæquatum. Ubi nos initiò removemus creaturas irrationales quascunque. Ratio hæc est: Nam hæ non ordinantur ad finé, qui excedit ipsarum naturam: Providentiæ ergò DEI subjacent quidem: sed non Prædestinationi, quæ tantùm ad finem supernaturalem Objectum ordinat.

Deindè verò Scripturas secuti, Prædestinationis objectum proprium constituimus solum atque unum Hominem, sed non sensu Huberiano, omnem omninò hominem, tàm incredulum, quàm credentem, verùm tantùm Hominem in CHRISTUM ad finem usque credentem.

Verùm hoc loco alia exurgit Quæstio: An videlicet respectu hujus Objecti, nempè Hominum credentium, una numero, an varia ac multiplex constituenda sit Prædestinatio? Ad quod ζήτημα nos cum orthodoxis omnibus respondemus, unam esse tantùm atque eandem, illam quidem ab æterno factam salvandorum omnium Prædestinationem. Quemadmodum enim spes vocationis, in quâ vocati sumus, non est nisi una: Ephes. 4, 4. & modus salutis non est nisi unus: Actor. 15, 11. ita principium, à quo hæc omnia dependent, non est nisi unum in DEO, idque æternum: siquidem ante constitutionem mundi, quam Electio antecessisse Apostolus perhibet, Ephes. 1, 4. præter æternitatem ipsam nihil fuit. Ab hac puritate thesews nostræ defecerunt jam olim aliqui ex patribus, qui respectu etiam hominum geminam Prædestinationem fecerunt: Unam Hominum ante lapsum: aliam eorundem post lapsum: uti videre est apud Augustinum lib. de corrept. & gratiâ, cap. 10. & seqq. duobus: Et in lib. de Bono Perseverantiæ cap. 7. Verùm sine scripturis hæc fuerunt asserta. Nam proto-parentibus ante lapsum creationis magis ad imaginem DEI, quam Electionis ratio in Scripturis assignatur. Quid quod illis ante lapsum Electionis terminus propriè non competit, quippè qui naturâ suâ segregationem infert: Qualis segregatio tùm locum non habuit. Satius ergò fuerit ab isto termino, quoad primos parentes ante lapsum consideratos, penitùs abstinere.

Porrò errorem in Ecclesiâ Dei minimè ferendum, circa Prædestinationis objectum fovent Romanenses, qui aliquam nonnullorum hominum peculiarem, & singulari quodam Privilegio constantem faciunt Prædestinationem: aliam reliquorum salvandorum communem. Prioris illius diversos iterum gradus & ordines constituunt, eosque septem potissimùm, infra eum gradum, qui Christo Servatori competit. Hunc enim summo & præstantissimo modo prædestinatum esse inquiunt, ita ut nec peccaret, nec peccare posset: & huc vitiosissimè accommodant illud Rom. 1, 4. ubi versio latina vitiosè legit, quod Christus sit à DEO patre electus sive prædestinatus in filium DEI: cùm tamen in Græco neque verbum προωρίσθη, neque ἐκλέγη: sed tantùm simplex ὁρισθεὶς legatur, quod nihil aliud notat, quàm quod Christus declaratus, definitus & cognitus sit, esse Filius Dei. Falsa proindè, & à fide orthodoxâ planè sunt absona: quæ de Prædestinatione Christi, eâquè gratis, sine prævisione operum ipsius factâ, disserit Bellarminus lib. 2 de grat. & lib arb. cap. 12. Post Christum in primo gradu collocant B. Mariam virginem, sic prædestinatam, ut omni peccato vacaret, tùm veniali, tùm mortali, tùm orignali. In secundo ordine sive gradu collocant eos, qui nunquàm actuali, sed tantum Originali peccato fuerunt obnoxij, quales fuerint, Jeremias Propheta, & Johannes Baptista. In tertio numerant eos, qui non quidem à veniali, neque etiam ab Originali, sed à mortali tamen peccato immunes fuerunt: Ut Abrahamus, Prophetæ multi, & Apostoli post acceptum Spiritum Sanctum. In quartum referunt eos, qui efficaciter ad salutem sint prædestinati: sic tamé, ut permissi sint ruere in peccatum mortale: Ut David. In quinto ponunt eos, qui dono perseverantiæ destituti primùm, ante obitum tamen operibus & precibus id impetrarunt, ne finaliter gratiâ DEI excidant. In sexto collocant Infantes, qui efficaciam istam Prædestinationis, virtute ipsius Justificationis acceperunt, proptereâ quia per ætatem peccare mortaliter non potuerint. In postremum sive septimum ordinem eos referunt, qui dùm viverent, & valerent, mortali peccato obnoxij, demùm in fine vitæ, & in ipso agone mortis, donum perseverantiæ acceperunt: qualis fuerit Latro dexter in Crucifixione Christi. Et sanè septem istorum graduum diversitatem probare solent partim à conformitate & ornatu Ecclesiæ: de quo Psalm. 45. & Cant. 6. partim à discrimine munerum, quibus Apostoli & Prophetæ functi sunt. Ephes. 2, 20. Verùm manifestò falsa hæc sunt, & cum analogiâ fidei, tùm in hoc articulo, tùm in illis, qui sunt de peccato Originis, deque Justificatione hominis peccatoris coram DEO, è diametro pugnant: id quod vel Tyro Theologiæ intelligit, usque adeò ut Bellarminus, licet pro Sanctitate absolutâ, & à peccato Originis planè immuni Mariæ Virginis strenuè satis pugnet: reliquorum tamen graduum patrocinium, hoc in articulo suscipere nolit. Ipsa verò probatio prorsus aliena est ab hoc negotio, & agunt citata loca de illâ dispensatione, quâ DEUS Ecclesiam suam hoc in mundo gubernat, & per divisiones donorum exornat. Quâ de re Matth. 25. in parabolâ talentorum: & in 1. Cor. 12. sub distinctione donorum: & in 2. Timoth. 2. sub similitudine vasorum domesticorum agitur.


### III. Special Controversy, Concerning the Causes, Members, and parts which together constitute the whole complex of Predestination or of our…

Before this controversy is explained positively, various errors of both ancient and certain recent Writers must be repudiated.

And the first error indeed was that of Origen, who opined that the souls of men, before they were sent into bodies, had merited the grace of Election in another life: lib. 1. περι αρχων cap. 6 & 7, and lib. 2. cap. 9. Augustine mentions this opinion in lib. 11. de Civit. Dei, Cap. 23, and Serm. 7 de verbis Apostoli; and Jerome on those words of the Apostle, Ephes. 1:4. Epiphanius argues at length against this error in heresy 64, and Thomas, part 1, q. 23, art. 5, rightly opposes the words of the Apostle in Rom. 9, 'when they had done nothing good or evil,' and 2 Tim. 1, 'he called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose.' This error was also condemned in the Council of Braga 1, Can. 8.

Another error, bordering on that first one, was that of those who opined that Predestination, regarding the will to save, did not arise from the will of God alone, but from foreseen works. In which error stuck Irenaeus, book 4, Against Heresies, chapter 76. Justin Martyr, responses to the Orthodox, question 9. Clement of Alexandria, book 4, Στρωματων, chapter 7, end. Tertullian, against Marcion, book 2. Chrysostom, homily 16, on chapter 9 of Romans and on chapter 1 of Ephesians. Theodore, Theophylact, Oecumenius in the same places. Ambrose on chapters 8 and 9 of Romans and on chapter 1 of Ephesians and in two books on the calling of the Gentiles. Jerome, Epistle to Hedibia, question 10. Damascene, on the Orthodox faith, book 2, chapter 29 and book 4, chapter 20. Cyril on chapter 21 of John. Prosper and Hilary in their letters to Augustine testify that before Augustine all the Fathers were of this opinion.

The third error was that of the Pelagians, who, while they taught that justifying grace is from the merits of works, also added this: that predestination is from good works preceding justification, or that the cause of predestination is merits pre-existing in this life, as witnessed by Augustine, heresy 88, and epistle 105 to Sixtus, and in 'On the Predestination of the Saints', chapter 2. Augustine opposed various treatises to this heresy, which are contained in volume 7 of his works. And Thomas disputes quite learnedly against these men, part 1, question 23, article 5. He says the Pelagians posited that the beginning of doing good is from us, but the completion is from God. And thus they determined that it happens from this that the effect of predestination is given to one and not to another: because one gave the beginning by preparing himself, and the other did not. But Thomas rightly answers against this error, which is what the Apostle says in 2 Cor. 3, that we are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves. Moreover, no prior principle can be found than thought. Whence it cannot be said that any beginning exists in us which is the cause of the effect of predestination. This error was condemned in many councils: Carthaginian, Milevitan, Palestinian, Arausican: Canons 3 and 6.

The fourth error is that of the Scholastics, who constitute works as the cause of predestination, but under a notable variety of opinions. For most of those who are called Nominalists think that predestination arises from moral works preceding justification, and that these merit predestination, not indeed by condignity, but by congruity. The reason for this matter is: because to him who does what is in him, God does not deny aids, so that he may be able to prepare himself for the infusion of grace by the power of free will. Most commentators on book 1 of the Sentences, distinction 41, hold this opinion. Others constitute good works following justification, and those foreseen by God, as the cause of predestination, not indeed properly meritorious, but in some way motive, as Alexander of Hales speaks and thinks, part 1, question 28, member 3, article 3; Bonaventure and Albert the Great in book 1 of the Sentences, distinction 41, article 1, question 2.

The fifth error is that of almost all Pontificians today, who argue that for the whole of predestination, which includes both grace and glory, no cause can be posited on the part of men in the foreknowledge of good works, whether preceding, accompanying, or following justification; nevertheless, that a truly meritorious cause of some part of predestination can be given, namely of glorification and the increase of grace in the present journey, of both of which the good works themselves are the meritorious cause. Bellarmine himself is not at all averse to this opinion, although he truly holds the wolf by the ears regarding the present question. For in book 2 'On Grace and Free Will', chapter 13

thus among other things: Since God has so predestined men that He wills them to arrive at glory through good works, it is a sign of predestination to diligently avoid sins. And after a few words: It is not absurd that men become vessels unto honor both by predestination and by their own actions. For God predestined those whom He willed to be vessels unto honor, but He brings it about afterwards that they are such both by His grace and by their own works; and predestination does not therefore depend on works, but works depend on

predestination. Therefore, good works are the effect of predestination, although God justifies us with free will concurring and His grace cooperating. Bellarmine and his associates drew this theology from Thomas Aquinas, part 1 of the Summa, question 23, article 5. Gregory of Valencia explains his opinion in volume 1 of his Theological Commentaries, Disp. 1, Question 23, point 4, with two assertions in this manner.

Assertion FIRST: If predestination is referred to all its effects, there is no reason or cause in any way meritorious of it in the predestined, neither for which, nor without which not; but it ought to be referred solely to the gratuitous will of God.

SECOND assertion: Although neither the cooperation of the predestined, nor any work of his at all, is the reason, is the condition, or is the cause in any way meritorious of the whole of predestination: nevertheless GOD does not predestine any adult in the ordinary way, except with a certain respect of His divine foreknowledge to the persevering cooperation of the predestined person himself, as it is from the aid of grace, and from free will, as if to one certain effect as a means of predestination, with which all the remaining effects of predestination are connected: so indeed, that although it is not true that GOD therefore predestines some, BECAUSE He foreknows from eternity that they will cooperate with divine grace with final perseverance, as if this cooperation were the reason or condition or cause of the whole of predestination; it is nevertheless most true that God ordinarily predestines all and only those adults whom He foreknows from eternity will cooperate with divine grace with final perseverance.

The sum of Esauvitic impiety is this, that God from eternity indeed found nothing in man, on account of which He ought to have predestined him, and conferred any effect of predestination upon him: and therefore that He confers even that Grace, by which a man might afterwards merit eternal life by his own works, entirely freely upon man: but meanwhile that GOD from eternity foreknew who would cooperate through the Grace of free will, freely received, unto the end of divine Grace: and therefore that GOD did not predestine without respect to works from future Grace, according to divine Foreknowledge.

Which cooperation, however, says Gregory of Valencia, is not the cause of the WHOLE of Predestination, as regards all its effects: because this very cooperation is an effect of Predestination. Now nothing can be the cause of itself. Indeed, it is not even the cause of Predestination, as regards its first effect, which is efficacious calling: since that cooperation is an effect not of free will alone; but also of efficacious calling, and of assisting Grace: But it is the cause of Predestination only as regards ONE of its effects in particular, namely the last, which is eternal salvation and beatitude.

In order that this may be understood more clearly, it is pleasing to hear Gregory of Valencia again, distinguishing thus according to the sense of Thomas in the place cited above: point 4. page 501: Just as the effects of Predestination themselves, in a different kind of cause, are causes to one another: So also one effect can be called the cause of predestination related to another effect: and conversely also in another kind of cause. As, for example, the merits of St. Peter were the meritorious and moral cause of that predestination, related to that other effect, which is the glory of St. Peter. And conversely in another kind of cause, namely the final, the glory of St. Peter was the cause of that predestination related to his merits. Inasmuch as, of course, for that reason GOD, by the benefit of His grace, bestowed merits upon St. Peter, so that through them, as through means, he might attain glory. Thus also the movements of faith, hope, and charity, and of repentance, by which the predestined person is disposed to obtain the grace of justification, are in some way a cause, as it were material and disposing, of predestination related to grace. And conversely, grace in another kind of cause, namely the efficient, is the cause of the predestination related to those same motions, inasmuch as they effectively proceed from that same grace of justification.

The sixth error is that of those who establish that the meritorious cause of predestination is FAITH, so that we ought to be said to be chosen by GOD because of or on account of foreseen faith, which they were persuaded was of their own powers. There were in this opinion certain Pelagians, whom Prosper and Hilary of Arles mention in their letters to Augustine, which are prefixed to the seventh volume of his works in the book on the Predestination of the Saints. Augustine himself was also of this opinion for some time, as he himself testifies in the book on the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 3, so that certain Papist writers, and especially Alexander Pesantius, are gravely impudent, who dare to deny this. But he retracted this error, book 1 of the Retractations. chapter 25, where he says that he would never have said this if he had understood that election without any preceding merits is from grace alone: and that faith itself is found among the gifts of GOD, which are given through the Holy Spirit. And the same Augustine argues very excellently and sufficiently at length against this error in the whole cited book, especially from chapter 1 up to the tenth. 'I had not yet,' he says, 'inquired more diligently, nor had I yet found what kind of election of grace it is, of which the Apostle says in Romans 11, The remnant have been made safe by the election of grace.' But our doctrine concerning foreseen faith, with respect to which GOD from eternity chose believers, has nothing in common with that error. For we have never taught, nor do we teach, that we are chosen because of or on account of foreseen faith, or on account of precognized or foreknown faith: just as Huberus, according to his custom, most impudently accuses us. But this is our doctrine, that we are chosen ἐν πίσει ἀληθείας in the faith of truth, that is, in true faith, or through true faith. 2 Thessalonians 2:13. But what and how much difference exists between these two phrases, 'We are chosen on account of faith' and 'We are chosen through faith or in faith,' even a beginner in theology notices. For the former establishes that faith as the meritorious cause of predestination: but the latter notes the τάξιν or order of the means, with respect to which GOD chose believers. The former we abhor with our whole heart, and with Augustine we willingly confess and believe that we are not chosen because we have believed:

Latin:

PRiusquàm controversia hæc θετικῶς expediatur, varij errores tùm veterum, tùm recentiorum Scriptorum quorundam repudiandi veniunt.

Ac primus quidem error fuit Origenis, opinantis, Animas hominum, priusquàm in Corpora immitterentur, in alia vitâ meruisse Electionis gratiam: lib. 1. περι αρχων cap. 6. & 7. & lib. 2. cap. 9. Meminit hujus opinionis Augustinus lib. 11. de Civit. Dei, Cap. 23. Et Serm. 7. de verbis Apostoli: & Hieronymus super verba illa Apostoli, Ephes. 1, 4. Prolixè autem adversus istum errorem disputat Epiphanius hæresi 64. & Thomas part. 1. q. 23. art. 5. rectè opponit verba Apostoli Rom. 9. cum nihil boni vel mali egissent: & 2. Tim. 1. vocavit nos vocatione sanctâ, non secundum opera nostra: sed secundum propositum suum. Damnatus etiam fuit error iste, in Concilio Bracar. 1. Can. 8.

Alter error primo isti finitimus, eorum fuit, qui Prædestinationem, quoad Salvandi voluntatem non ex solâ Dei voluntate: sed operibus prævisis nasci opinati sunt. In quo errore hæsit Irenæus lib. 4. Contra hæreses, cap. 76. Justinus Martyr. respons. ad Orthod. q. 9. Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 4. Στρωματων cap. 7. fin. Tertull. contra Marcio: lib. 2. Chrysost. hom. 16. in cap. 9. Rom. & super cap. 1. Ephes. Theodorus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius ijsdem locis. Ambrosius super cap. 8. & 9. Rom. & super cap. 1. Eph. & duobus libris de vocatione gentium. Hieron. Epist ad Hedibiam. q. 10. Damascenus de fide Orthodoxâ lib. 2. cap. 29. & lib. 4. cap. 20. Cyrill. super cap. 21. Johannis. Prosper & Hilarius in Epistolis suis ad Augu stinum testantur, ante Augustinum Patres omnes fuïsse in hac sententiâ.

Tertius error fuit Pelagianorum, qui cum docerent, Gratiam justificantem esse ex meritis operum, etiam illud addiderunt, Prædestinationem esse ex bonis operibus, justificationem antegressis: vel, causam Prædestinationis esse merita præexistentia in hac vita: teste Augustino hæres. 88. & epist. 105. ad Sixtum, & de prædestinat. Sanctorum, cap. 2. Hæresi huic varios tractat9 opposuit Augusting, qui continentur Tomo. 7. operum ipsius. Et Thomas satis eruditè disputat contra istos, part. 1. q. 23. art. 5. Posuerunt inquiens Pelagiani, quod initium benefaciendi sit ex nobis: Consummatio autem à Deo. Et sic ex hoc contingere statuerunt, quod alicui datur Prædestinationis effectus, & non alteri: quia unus initium dedit, se præparando, & non alius. Sed rectè respondet Thomas, contra errorem istume est, quod dicit Apostolus 2. Cor. 3. quod non simus idonei, cogitare aliquid à nobis ipsis, quasi ex nobis. Nullum autem prius principium inveniri potest, quam cogitatio. Undè non potest dici, quod aliquod initium in nobis existat, quod sit causa effectus Prædestinationis. Damnatus est autem error iste in multis Concilijs, Carthaginensi, Milevitano, Palæstino, Arausicano: Can. 3. & 6.

Quartus error est Scholasticorum, qui opera causam Prædestinationis constituunt: sed sub insigni sententiarum varietate. Nám qui Nominales vocantur, plerique omnes sentiunt, quod Prædestinatio nascatur ex operibus moralibus, justificationem antecedentibus: & quod hæc mereantur Prædestinationem, non quidem ex condigno: sed ex congruo. Cujus rei ea sit ratio: quia facienti quod in se est, DEUS auxilia non denegat, ut ad gratiam infundendam vi liberi arbitrij se præparare possit. Quam sententiam plerique tenent Commentatores super librum 1. Sent. dist. 41. Alij bona opera justificationem sequentia, eaque à DEO prævisa, Prædestinationis causam constituunt, non quidem propriè meritoriam: sed aliquâ ratione motivam: ut loquuntur & sentiunt Alex. ab Alex part. 1. quæst. 28. memb. 3. art. 3. Bonaventura & Albertus M. in lib. 1. Sent. dist. 41. art. 1. q. 2.

Quintus error est Pontificiorum hodiè fermè omnium, qui disputant, Totius Prædestinationis, quæ simul gratiam & gloriam includat, non posse quidem ex parte hominum, causam ullam poni in præscientia bonorum operum vel præcedentium, vel concomitantium, vel sequentium justificationem: tamen partis alicujus in prædestinatione dari posse causam verè meritoriam, nimirùm glorificationis & augmenti gratiæ in præsenti viâ, cujus utriusque causa meritoria sint ipsa bona opera. A quâ sententiâ ipse quoq; Bellarmino minimè abhorret, licet vere lupum teneat auribus circa præsentem quæstionem. Nam lib. 2. de gratiâ & lib. arb. cap. 13.

sic inter reliqua: Cum DEUS ita prædestinaverit homines, ut per bona opera eos pervenire velit ad gloriam signum est Prædestinationis, diligenter vitare peccata. Et post pauca: Non est absurdum, Homines & Prædestinatione, & proprijs actionibus fieri vasa in honorem. Deus enim prædestinavit, quos voluit, ut essent vasa in honorem: sed efficit postea, ut sint tales & gratia sua & operibus ipsorum: & non ideò, pendet Prædestinatio ab operibus, sed opera à

Prædestinatione. Itaque sunt opera bona effectus Prædestinationis, licet Deus nos justificet concurrente libero arbitrio, & cooperante Gratia ejus. Quam Theologiam Bellarminus & socij hauserunt ex Thom. Aq. part. 1. Summæ, quæst. 23. art. 5. Cujus sententiam Gregorius de Valentia Tomo 1. Commentariorum Theologicorum Disp. 1. Quæst. 23. puncto 4. duabus assertionibus explicat in hunc modum.

Assertio PRIMA: Si Prædestinatio referatur ad omnes ipsius effectus, nulla est ratio seu causa ullo modo meritoria ipsius in prædestinato, neque propter quam, neque sine qua non: sed in solam gratuitam voluntatem DEI referri debet.

SECUNDA assertio: Quamvis neq; cooperatio prædestinati, neque aliquod omnino opus ipsius, sit ratio, sit conditio, seu causa ullo modo meritoria totius prædestinationis: tamen DEUS neminem adultum ordinario modo prædestinat, nisi cum respectu quodam divinæ suæ præscientiæ ad cooperationem perseverantem ipsius prædestinati, ut est ex gratiæ auxilio, & ex libero arbitrio, tanquàm ad unum quendam effectum ut medium prædestinationis, cum quo reliqui omnes Prædestinationis effectus sunt connexi: ita quidem, ut quamvis verum non sit, DEUM ideò prædestinare aliquos, QUIA præscit ab æterno eos divinæ gratiæ cum perseverantiâ finali cooperaturos, quasi hæc cooperatio sit totius prædestinationis ratio seu conditio seu causa; verissimum tamen sit, Deum eos adultos omnes & solos ordinariè prædestinare, quos ab æterno præscit divinæ gratiæ cooperaturos cum perseverantiâ finali.

Summa impietatis Esavviticæ hæc est, Deum ab æterno quidem nihil invenisse in homine, propter quod ipsum prædestinare, & ullum prædestinationis effectum in ipsum conferre debuerit: ac proindè Gratiam etiam illam, quâ homo postmodùm æternam vitam proprijs operibus promereri possit Gratis omninò in hominem conferre: sed interim DEUM ab æterno præscivisse, quinàm per Gratiam Liberi arbitrij, gratis acceptam, cooperaturi essent ad finem usque Gratiæ divinæ: ac proindè DEUM non prædestinasse sine respectu ad opera ex Gratiâ futurâ, secundum divinam Præscientiam.

Quæ tamen cooperatio, inquit Gregorius de Valentia, non est causa TOTIUS Prædestinationis, quo ad omnes ejus effectus: quia hæc ipsa cooperatio est effectus Prædestinationis. Jam nihil potest esse causa sui ipsius. Imò non etiam est causa Prædestinationis, quoad primum ejus effectum, qui est vocatio efficax: quandoquidem cooperatio illa est effectus non solius liberi arbitrij; sed vocationis quoque efficacis, & Gratiæ adjuvantis: Sed est causa Prædestinationis tantùm quoad UNUM ejus effectum in particulari, nempè ultimum, qui est æterna salus & beatitudo.

Quod ut clariùs intelligatur, placet rursum audire Gregorium de Valentia, ex sensu Thomæ sic differentem loco suprà citato: puncto 4. pag. 501: Sicut ipsi effectus Prædestinationis, in diverso genere causæ sunt sibi invicem causæ: Ita etiam unus effectus potest dici causa Prædestinationis relatæ ad alium effectum: & vicissim etiam in alio causæ genere. Vt, Verbi gratia, Merita D. Petri fuerunt causa Prædestinationis illius meritoria & moralis, relatæ ad illum alium effectum, qui est D. Petri Gloria. Et vicissim in alio genere causæ, puta finalis, Gloria D. Petri fuit causa Prædestinationis illius relatæ ad ejusdem merita. Quatenus nimirùm ideò DEUS gratiæ suæ beneficio contulit D. Petro merita, ut per illa, tanquàm per media assequeretur gloriam. Sic etiam motus fidei, spei & charitatis, & Pœnitentiæ, quibus prædestinatus disponitur ad obtinendam gratiam Justificationis, sunt aliquo modo causa qualis materialis & disponens prædestinationis relatæ ad gratiam. Et vicissim Gratia in alio genere causæ, nempè efficientis est causa Prædestinationis relatæ ad eosdem illos motus, quatenus scilicet illi effectivè procedunt ab eâdem etiam gratiâ Justificationis.

Sextus error est eorum, qui statuunt, causam Prædestinationis meritoriam esse FIDEM, ita ut electi esse à DEO dici debeamus ob sive propter prævisam fidem, quam propriarum virium esse, persuasum habuerunt. Fuerunt in hâc sententiâ quidam πελαγιανίζοντες, quorum meminerunt Prosper & Hilarius Arelatensis in Epistolis ad Augustinum, quæ Tomo 7. operum ipsius, præmissæ sunt libro de Prædestinatione Sanctorum. Fuit in eâdem sententiâ etiam aliquandiu ipse Augustinus, ut testatur ipsemet libro de Prædest Sanctorum, cap. 3. ut graviter impudentes sint, Scriptores quidam Pontificij, & cumprimis Alexander Pesantius, qui hoc negare audent. Sed retractavit hunc errorem, lib. 1. Retract. cap. 25. ubi dicit, se nunquàm hoc fuisse dicturum, si intellexiffet Electionem sine ullis præcedentibus meritis esse ex solâ gratiâ: & Fidem ipsam inter DEI munera, quæ dantur per Spiritum Sanctum reperiri. Et præclarè admodùm ac prolixè satis contra errorem hunc idem Augustinus toto libro citato disputat, præcipuè à Cap. 1. usquè ad Decimum. Nondùm, inquit, diligentiùs quæsiveram, nec adhuc inveneram, qualis sit Electio Gratiæ, de quâ Apostolus Rom. 11. dicit, Reliquiæ per Electionem gratiæ salvæ factæ sunt. Cæterùm cum errore isto nihil quicquàm commune obtinet nostra doctrina de prævisâ fide respectu cujus DEUS ab æterno credentes elegerit.
