Neque enim unquàm vel docuimus vel docemus, nos ob vel propter prævisam fidem, sive propter præcognitam sive præscitam fidem electos esse: quemadmodum Huberus pro more suo impudentissimè nos infimulat. Sed hæc est doctrina nostra, quod electi sumus ἐν πίσει ἀληθείας in fide veritatis, hoc est, in fide verâ, sive per fidem veram. 2. Thess. 2, 13. Quid verò & quantum discriminis duabus istis phrasibus, Electi sumus propter fidem: & Electi sumus per fidem sive in fide, invicem intercedat, vel Tyro Theologiæ animadvertit. Prior enim illam Fidem constituit causam meritoriam Prædestinationis : Posterior verò hæc notat τάξιν sive ordinem mediorum, respectu quorum DEUS credentes elegit. Priorem abominamur toto pectore, & cum Augustino ultrò fatemur & credimus, Electos nos non esse, quia crediderimus:


### III. Special Controversy, Concerning the Causes, Members, and parts which together constitute the whole complex of Predestination or of our… (continued)

but rather so that we may believe. The latter we embrace, and with the same Augustine from tractate 46 on John we assert that GOD foreknew who would believe (not from their own powers, as the Pelagians affirmed, but from the grace of GOD, through the word of the Gospel) and that Christ said of these that they are from GOD. But more accurately on this matter below in its own place.

The SEVENTH error is that of the Calvinists, who eliminate every meritorious cause from the decree of predestination to such an extent that they do not even leave a place in it for the merit of Christ: but contend that it precedes all causes, and is simply absolute: concerning which dogma there will be a place for discussion below in part 2, in the antithetical section.

The EIGHTH and last error is that of Huberus, who seeks and establishes election in the antecedent will of GOD alone, which is universal and regards all equally: utterly removing and excluding every prevision and intuition of faith in Christ from that eternal decree of election: as will be shown below.

Having therefore rejected these errors and others of this kind, we respond to the question concerning the cause of Predestination both ἀποφατικῶς negatively and καταφατικῶς affirmatively. Negatively first, because for the whole of Predestination, and for all its parts and effects, whether considered particularly or universally, absolutely no cause can be assigned on the part of man, whether efficient, or meritorious, or sine qua non, or cooperating, or any other whatsoever, on account of which we might be predestined, or even one single effect of Predestination might or ought to befall us, whether it be the first, or intermediate, or final.

We oppose this negative thesis of ours to each and every error which in any way assigns Predestination, either in whole or in part, or by any effect of Predestination at least, or with respect to the final end, to our works or to the merit of our cooperation. We prove it, moreover, initially from the Holy Scriptures: as:

John 15:16. You have not chosen me: but I have chosen you, and have appointed you, that you should go, and should bring forth fruit. From which passage St. Augustine, in his book On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 17, constructs such an argument: The effect of Predestination is not the cause of the same. All our fruit is an effect of Predestination: Therefore it is not the cause.

Rom. 9:11, 16, 18. Three arguments are set forth, from which Augustine contends for our affirmative position. I. The example of the infants Jacob and Esau: verse 11, not yet born, and having done neither good nor evil, so that there was no refuge in preceding works. Augustine, Epistle 106, and to Simplicianus, q. 2. II. What the Apostle says, It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth: but of GOD that showeth mercy, verse 16. Where Augustine infers thus: Our willing and running is not the cause of GOD's mercy: but this makes us will and run. Therefore III. Verse 18, the Apostle adds: He hath mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardeneth. He hardeneth, however

GOD, says Augustine in epist. 105, not by imparting malice, but by not imparting grace. Rom. 11, 5. The remnant according to the election of grace are made safe: But if by grace, then it is no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace: If it be of works, then it is no more of grace: otherwise work is no more work. Ephes. 1, 4. He chose us, that we should be holy. Hence Augustine gathers in De Prædest. Sanctorum, cap. 17. Therefore not because we were to be holy, were we chosen. 2. Timoth. 1, 9. GOD made us safe, and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works: but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us before the secular times. Whence this part of the lot is called grace, Coloss. 1, 12. But just as a lot does not regard persons or works: So neither does Predestination: as Chrysostom skillfully infers in the explanation of that passage. Where then, says Augustine, are now the merits? where are works either past, or future as if fulfilled by the powers of free will, or to be fulfilled? Epist. 105. to Sixtus the Presbyter.

Finally, the authority of the Holy Fathers approaches, especially the Latins, who lived after the times of Augustine: such as, Prosper in the book on Free Will and Grace to Ruffinus: Fulgentius book 1 to Monimus: Primasius, Anselm and other interpreters in the Explanation of chapter 8 of the Epistle to the Romans: But especially Augustine when he was already mature, and raised to the Episcopacy: epist. 105. 106. Tom. 2. Also book 1 to Simplicianus, q. 2. Tom. 4. but most especially in those four books on Predestination and Grace: on the Predestination of the Saints, on the Gift of Perseverance: on Rebuke and Grace Tom. 7. Whence the same Augustine in book 6 of the Hypognosticon finally breaks out into these words: Let human language be silent, and let it not be extolled at all in Predestination concerning merits: this is a gift of the divine will, not a merit of human frailty.

Finally, if anyone should also desire the weight of Reasons for the confirmation of this opinion, let him consult Augustine on the Predestination of the Saints, cap. 12. 13. & 15. Also on the Gift of Perseverance, cap. 9. 12. 13. & the last.

And thus far indeed we have shown that there is or was never any cause in us for Predestination, on account of which GOD chose us for salvation. Now the very Method of the Treatise demands that we demonstrate affirmatively that the cause of Predestination is to be sought solely and entirely in GOD. But that this may be rightly investigated, and fully and plainly explained, it must indeed be confessed that we are carried away to a deep abyss, and to the unsearchable ways of the Lord. But if we keep ourselves within the bounds of the revealed Word, and properly attend to those things which the Scriptures report to have happened concerning the fall and restoration of the human race: we shall certainly be able to gather and pronounce something about this mystery, but as in a figure.

GOD therefore, since he was in himself both most perfect and most blessed, undertook the counsel of creating the human race for no other reason than to take it into the fellowship of his blessedness: and by this pact, both to give an evident testimony of his ineffable love for mankind; and to be affected by the same with worship and celebration forever. When GOD had proposed this end from eternity, he thus finally decided to approach the creation of man, so that he would not suffer anything to be lacking in perfect goodness to him who was created in his own image: and in the granted liberty of will, he would leave more than enough capacity for rendering spontaneous worship. But when GOD, who from eternity sees and knows all things, had foreseen that he would not remain in that state of perfection: but having abused his liberty, would shamefully fall: he did not so cast his love for mankind out of his heart, that he rather, having pity on it, took counsel about saving the human race by another way, and being rich in his mercy, thought thoughts of peace, and not of affliction upon us. Wherefore in that same eternal counsel of his, he conceived the purpose and good pleasure of sending his only-begotten Son into the flesh, who, by his death having made a plenary expiation for the sins of the whole human race, and at the same time having performed perfect obedience to the law, would again assert the human race into grace with GOD, to be accepted by faith through the preaching of the Gospel in the whole world. But because, having already considered and foreseen the difference of men, he had known what would happen, with how disparate an outcome the greatest part of men would accept or despise this doctrine of salvation preached even to nausea: he immediately made a decree of Judgment, and that a twofold one; namely such: 1. Whoever would embrace the Word of salvation with true faith (which he himself most deeply knew from eternity who they would be) and would persevere in that faith to the end, they were certainly to be saved: who indeed have obtained the name of Elect from this in Scripture. 2. But those who would either entirely reject faith, or having once accepted it would finally cast it away again, they were to be consigned to eternal damnation. And these Scripture names the Reprobate.

With this typical description premised, it will be permitted from here to make a judgment concerning the two primary members of Predestination: First indeed concerning the terms or parts, within the scope of which the business of the whole Predestination turns. But then concerning the causes constituting and completing the decree of Election.

Regarding that PRIOR point, three terms can, nay must, be given, within the complex of which the business of the whole Predestination turns. The FIRST is of the Principle, from which this divine work emanates, in which Election principally has its seat: namely that beneficial WILL in GOD, and love for mankind, by which the most benevolent Father deigned to have mercy upon the lost human race from eternity. The SECOND term is the Medium, through which, or in which, Predestination was made, which is the GRACE OF FAITH, not only of that which begins, or lasts for some time: but of that which perseveres even to the end. The THIRD is the End, toward which Election tends, namely SALVATION & ETERNAL LIFE its name, so that the Election of those to be saved is named.

Now these three parts exist in GOD, just as they exist outside of GOD in relation to man. For it is certain among all Orthodox that GOD from eternity so proposed to save men, as they are now saved in time: nor are they saved in time otherwise than as He had proposed to save them from eternity. For otherwise either the purpose of GOD would differ from the execution: or it would follow that the purpose had been changed by GOD. Whence it was sagely said by Gregory, Moral. 28, ch. 9: What is done outwardly in things, was previously done inwardly through Predestination. Therefore, just as on the part of the external thing the first is that Man is loved by GOD, that grace is offered to him, and that sufficient means for salvation are given to him: the second, however, is that, having been converted to GOD, he is inserted into CHRIST by faith, and perseveres in the same even to the end: according to that: He who believes is not judged: He who does not believe is already judged: John 3. The last is that, thus persevering, he is crowned and saved: In the same way, from eternity in the mind and will of the one predestinating, that First thing was the purpose, by drawing forth the bowels of His mercy, to destine means sufficient and most efficacious for salvation, and to omit nothing of all things on His part that could be done to deliver man from sin and damnation.

And thus far in this purpose of GOD no man has been passed over by any decree. Now, however, just as GOD in act, or in execution, saves no one except believers alone: so in His eternal counsel He made a decree to save no one except those who truly believe: who these were, and how many of them there would be, could no more be hidden from His foreknowledge than it is hidden from it in the least.

Finally, just as those persevering in faith are certainly saved: so for these GOD has sanctioned and destined coronation and glorification by an immutable decree.

The older Fathers named these three parts the Purpose or will to crown, in which is included the ordination of means. 2. The collation of grace. 3. The glory of the Crown. And first indeed, that the Will to crown or the purpose to save is of the essence of Predestination, they proved from the Scriptures: Fear not, little flock: for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom, Luke 12:32. Possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: Matt. 25:34. Then from reason: For Predestination, just as Providence, cannot even be imagined without including in itself the will of the end; just as Augustine also admits, Epist. 105 to Sixtus and in the book On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 13. But in that will is also included the ordination of means to that end. But because these divine acts are not distinguished except with respect to the effects on the part of the thing, which is outside, two effects must be posited in order, according to which these acts are distinguished. One is Glorification: which corresponds to the purpose of saving or the will to crown, which is the BEGINNING of predestination in the mind of GOD. And indeed, Fathers have been found who, by the name of Predestination, understood on the part of GOD, that Beginning of Predestination: but on the part of the thing, the End, that is, glory: which are the two principal parts. But because Augustine, acting against the Pelagian adversaries and enemies of the grace of GOD, noticed that grace and faith, which is given in time, were being insidiously elided, and that in this elision the primary defense of the Pelagian cause was constituted: he referred also the means of Grace, in which Faith is principal, to the complex of Predestination with grave counsel: so that Predestination must be defined not only with respect to the Will in GOD, and Glory: but also with respect to Grace and the means. And he sought the proof of this his opinion from ch. 1, 4, and 5 of Ephesians: He chose us, that we might be holy, and predestinated us into the adoption of the sons of GOD. But that adoption made by faith has a place in the present life, and precedes glory. Likewise Acts 13:48: As many as were ordained to life believed. And in that golden chain, which is linked by the Apostle, Rom. 8:30. Between predestination and glorification, calling and justification, which take place in the present life, are interposed.

Those who wish the whole complex of this mystery reduced into a certain articulated Synopsis, they distribute the whole business of Predestination and our Salvation into eight distinct members from the Scriptures already cited: which not only Thomas observed, part 1, q. 23: but the Book of Concord also, in the consideration of this mystery and its causes, warns should be well observed.

1. And 1. indeed he shows that GOD in His eternal counsel decreed, That He wills to redeem the whole human race, and to reconcile it to Himself through CHRIST, by the merit of the obedience and death of the Son.

2. That He wills to offer the merit and benefits of CHRIST to men, individually and collectively, through the Word and Sacraments.

3. That He wills to be effective through the ministry of the Word and Sacraments by His Holy Spirit in the hearts of those hearing and participating in the sacred rites.

4. That He wills to justify all who are truly penitent and believe in CHRIST, having received them into favor and adopted them as sons.

5. That He wills to sanctify those justified by faith in true charity.

6. That he wills to protect the justified, and to console them in any temptations whatsoever and under the cross.

7. That he wills to promote the good work begun by himself, to bestow the gift of perseverance, and to preserve them in faith and grace even unto the end.

8. Finally, That he wills to crown the same, that is, to endow them in that other life with the eternal glory of blessedness.

All these things are comprehended according to Scripture in the article of divine Predestination and Election, which must always be revolved and thought upon in the mind as a whole, not piecemeal, but all at once, with none of these members excluded or omitted, as often as thought is undertaken concerning the mystery of eternal Predestination. But there is no discord whatsoever between this eight-membered partition and our three-membered one. For the first three, the Redemption of CHRIST, the offering of benefits, and efficacy, are subject to the ordination of means, which is included in the most benign divine purpose and will concerning our salvation. The four following, Justification, Sanctification, Preservation, and Perseverance, pertain to the Grace of faith, which holds the place of a middle term. Glorification is the proper End, which terminates and finishes Predestination itself, so that the whole complex of Predestination is contained in that ternary of parts.

And thus indeed do the Terms or parts of our Predestination stand: whence it is evident, clearer than the midday sun, that on the part of men no cause of Election can be given at all. 2. What the true and only cause of Predestination ought to be constituted: that which the later member of our thesis will now explain.

As regards therefore the LATTER member, since it is irrefragably established from what has already been said that the cause of Predestination must be sought not in ourselves, but entirely outside of us: and yet no creature, whether in heaven or on earth, can claim for itself any work in this part: it remains that it must be sought and found in GOD alone. Now if we most accurately search the whole Scripture, if we also weigh those things which have been argued hitherto concerning the parts or members of Predestination from the analogy of faith: it will become plain that the sole and only merciful Will of GOD must be constituted the cause of Election. For this is the root and foundation of our entire predestination, as the Apostle himself also testifies, Rom. 9. 18. He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. But how this will of GOD stands in the present mystery, on account of the controversies of our age, must be examined more deeply: that which the exodus of the following special controversies will most plainly explain.

Latin:

sed potiùs ut credamus. Posteriorem amplectimur, & cum eodem Augustino ex tractatu 46. in Johannem asserimus, DEUM præscivisse, qui fuerint credituri (non ex suis viribus, quod affirmabant Pelagiani, sed ex gratiâ DEI, per verbum Evangelij) & de his dixisse Christum, quòd sint ex DEO. Sed hâc de re infrà suo loco accuratiùs.

SEPTIMUS error est Calvinianorum, qui usque adeò omnem causam meritoriam ex decreto Prædestinationis eliminant, ut ne quidem Merito Christi in eo locum relinquant: sed contendant, illud omnes causas antegredi, simpliciter esse absolutum: de quo dogmate infra part. 2. ἀντιθετικῇ erit differendi locus.

OCTAVUS & postremus error est Huberi, qui Electionem quærit & constituit, in solâ Antecedenti DEI voluntate, quæ universalis est, & ex æquo omnes respicit : Omnem fidei in Christum prævisionem & intuitum, ex decreto illo Electionis æterno, penitùs removens & excludens: uti infra ostendetur.

His ergò erroribus, & hujus generis alijs repudiatis, ad quæstionem de causâ Prædestinationis, respondemus & ἀποφατικῶς negatè, & καταφατικῶς affirmatè. Negatè primùm quòd totius Prædestinationis, omniumque ejus partium & effectuum, tàm in particulari quàm universaliter consideratorũ, ex parte hominis causa planè nulla adsignari possit, sive efficiens, sive meritoria, sive sine quâ non, sive Cooperans, sive quæcunque alia. propter quam vel prædestinati simus, vel unus saltem aliquis Prædestinationis effectus, nobis obtingere possit aut debeat, sive primus ille sit, sive intermedius, sive ultimus.

Thesin hanc nostram Negativam opponimus singulis & universis erroribus, qui quoquo modo operibus nostris, vel cooperationis nostræ merito, Prædestinationem vel ex toto, vel ex parte, vel ex aliquo saltē Prædestinationis effectu, vel respectu finis ultimi adsignant. Probamus autem eam initiò ex Scripturis Sacris: ut:

Johan. 15, 16. Non vos me elegistis: sed ego elegi vos, & posui, ut eatis, & fructum feratis. Ex quo loco D. Augustinus lib. de Prædestinatione Sanctorum, cap. 17. tale argumentum extruit: Effectus Prædestinationis non est causa ejusdem. Omnis fructus noster est effectus Prædestinationis: Ergò non causa.

Rom. 9, 11. 16, 18. tria ponuntur argumenta, ex quibus pro affirmatâ nostrâ pugnat Augustinus. I. Exemplum parvulorum Jacobi & Esavi: versu 11. nondûm genitorum, & nihil vel boni vel mali operatorum, ut nullum esset refugium ad præcedentia opera. Augustinus Epist 106. & ad Simplicianum, q. 2. II. Quod dicit Apostolus, Non esse volentis, neque currentis: sed miserentis DEI, versu 16. Ubi sic infert Augustinus: Nostrum velle & currere, non est causa misericordiæ DEI: sed hæc facit nos velle & currere. Ergò III. Versu 18. subjicit Apostolus: Cujus vult, miseretur, quē vult, indurat. Indurat autem

DEUS, inquit Augustinus epist. 105. non impertiendo malitiam, sed non impertiendo gratiam. Rom. 11, 5. Reliquiæ secundum Electionem gratiæ, salvæ factæ sunt: Si autem ex gratiâ, jam non ex operibus: alioqui gratia jam non est gratia: Si ex operibus, jam non ex gratiâ: alioquin opera jam non sunt opera. Ephes. 1, 4. Elegit nos, ut essemus sancti. Hinc colligit Augustinus de Prædest. Sanctorum, cap. 17. Ergò non quia futuri eramus sancti, electi sumus. 2. Timoth. 1, 9. DEUS salvos nos fecit, & vocavit vocatione sanctâ, non secundum opera nostra: sed secundum suum propositum & gratiam, quæ data est nobis ante tempora secularia. Undè pars sortis hæc gratia vocatur, Coloss. 1, 12. Sicut autem fors non respicit personas aut opera: Ita nec Prædestinatio: uti scitè infert Chrysostomus in explicatione loci istius. Ubi ergò, inquit Augustinus, nunc sunt merita? ubi opera vel præterita, vel futura tanquàm liberi arbitrij viribus adimpleta, vel adimplenda? Epist. 105. ad Sixtum Presbyterum.

Accedit tandem autoritas Sanctorum Patrum, Latinorum præcipuè, qui post Augustini tempora vixerunt: ut, Prosperi in lib. de Libero Arbitrio & Gratiâ ad Ruffinum: Fulgentij lib. 1. ad Monimum: Primasij, Anshelmi & aliorum interpretum in Explicatione capitis 8. Epistolæ ad Romanos: Imprimis autem Augustini jam adulti, & ad Episcopatum evecti: epist. 105. 106. Tom. 2. Item lib. 1. ad Simplicianum, q. 2. Tom. 4. maximè verò in quatuor istis libris de Prædest. & Gratiâ: de Prædestin. Sanctorum, de Bono Perseverantiæ: de Correptione & Gratiâ Tom. 7. Undè idem Augustinus lib. 6. Hypognosticon tandem erumpit in hæc verba: Taceat humana lingva, & prorsus in Prædestinatione de meritis non extollatur: divinæ voluntatis est hoc donum, non humanæ fragilitatis meritum.

Tandem si quis pro sententiæ hujus confirmatione Rationum etiam momenta desideret, is consulat Augustinum de Prædest. Sanctorum, cap. 12. 13. & 15. Item de Bono Perseverantiæ, cap. 9. 12. 13. & ultimo.

Et hactenùs quidem ostendimus, Prædestinationis causam prorsus nullam in nobis esse aut fuisse nunquam, propter quam DEUS ad salutem nos elegerit. Jam ipsa Tractationis Methodus flagitat, ut καταφατικῶς demonstremus, causam Prædestinationis unicè & in solidum in DEO esse quærendam. Hæc verò sit ritè investigari, & plenè ac planè explicari debeat, fatendum profectò est, nos ad abyssum profundam, & vias Domini impervestigabiles abripi. Verùm si intra metas Verbi revelati nos contineamus, & ea quæ circa lapsum & restitutionem generis humani evenisse Scripturæ referunt, probè attendamus: utique de hoc mysterio aliquid, sed ὡς ἐν τύπῳ colligere & pronunciare licebit.

DEUS igitur, cum in seipso esset & perfectissimus, & beatissimus, non aliâ ratione consilium de creando genere humano suscepit, quàm ut in consortium beatitudinis illud ascisceret: & hoc pacto, tùm ineffabilis suæ Φιλανθρωπίας testimonium evidens ederet; tùm cultu & celebratione in æternum ab eodem afficeretur. Hunc finem cùm ab æterno DEUS habuisset propositum, sic tandem ad creationem hominis accedere decrevit, ut ipsi ad imaginem suam condito, nihil ad bonitatem perfectam deesse pateretur: & in concessâ arbitrij libertate, ad spontaneum cultum præstandum facultatis plus satis relinqueret. Cum autem prævidisset DEUS, qui ab æterno videt, novítque omnia, in statu isto perfectionis non permansurum: sed libertate suâ abusum, turpiter prolapsurum esse: Φιλανθρωπίαν suam erga genus humanum adeò ex animo suo non abjecit, ut ejus potiùs misertus, de salvando per aliam viam genere humano consilium ceperit, & dives in misericordiâ suâ cogitârit cogitationes pacis, & non afflictionis super nos. Quapropter in eodem æterno consilio suo, propositum & ἐυδοκίαν concepit de mittendo in carnem Filio unigenito, qui pro peccatis totius generis humani, per mortem suam plenariâ factâ expiatione, simul etiam legi perfectâ præstita obedientia, genus humanum, per prædicationem Evangelij, in universo terrarum orbe fide acceptandam, in gratiam cum DEO rursus assereret. Quia verò, considerato jam tùm, prævisoque hominum discrimine, futurum noverat, quàm dispari eventu, doctrinam hanc salutis ad nauseam usque prædicatam, maxima hominum pars acceptura, & contemtura esset: statim decretum Judicij fecit, idque geminum; nempè tale: 1. Quicunque Verbum salutis fide verâ amplexuri essent (quiqui futuri essent, ipse penitissimè ab æterno noverat) in eâquè fide ad finem usque perseveraturi, eos certò salvandos esse: Qui quidem nomen Electorum hinc in Scripturâ sunt sortiti. 2. Qui verò fidem aut repudiaturi prorsus, aut semel acceptam rursus finaliter projecturi essent, eos æternæ damnationi esse mancipandos. Et hos Reprobatos Scriptura nominat.

Præmissâ typicâ hâc περιγραφῇ licebit hinc de duobus, Primarijs Prædestinationis membris facere judicium: Primùm quidem de terminis sive partibus, intra quarum ambitum totius Prædestinationis negotium vertitur. Deindè verò de causis constituentibus & absolventibus Electionis decretum.

Quoad PRIUS illud, tres potissimùm dari possunt, imò debent Termini, intra quorum complexum, totius Prædestinationis negotium vertitur. PRIMUS est Principij, à quo opus hoc divinum emanat, in quo principaliter Electio sedem suam habet: nempè VOLUNTAS illa in DEO benefica, & Φιλανθρωπία, quâ perditi generis humani, ab æterno Pater benignissimus misereri dignatus est. SECUNDUS terminus est Medij, per quod, vel in quo Prædestinatio facta est, quod est, GRATIA FIDEI, non inchoantis tantùm, vel aliquandiu durantis: sed ad finem perseverantis etiam. TERTIUS est Finis, ad quem Electio tendit, SALUS nempè & VITA ÆTERNA, Undè etiam Prædestinatio nomen est fortita, ut Electio salvandorum nominetur.

Habent autem se tres istæ partes in DEO, quemadmodum se habent extra DEUM ad hominem. Nam apud omnes Orthodoxos certum est, quòd DEUS ab æterno sic proposuerit salvare homines, uti jam in tempore servantur: neq; aliter jam servantur in tempore, quàm sicut salvare eos ab æterno proposuerat. Alias enim vel propositum DEI ab executione differret: vel sequeretur, à DEO mutatum esse propositum. Undè scitè dictum est à Gregorio 28. Moral. cap. 9. Quod foris in rebus geritur, anteà intus per Prædestinationem factum est. Sicut ergò ex parte rei externæ primum est, Hominem à DEO diligi, gratiam ipsi offerri, eidemq; sufficientia ad salutem media dari: alterum verò, ut ad DEUM conversus fide CHRISTO inseratur, & in eadem ad finem usq; perseveret: secundum illud: Qui credit, non judicatur: Qui non credit, jam judicatus est: Joh. 3. ultimum, ut sic perseverans coronetur, salveturque: Eodem modo ab æterno in mente & voluntate prædestinantis, Primum illud fuit propositum, viscera misericordiæ suæ depromendo, media ad salutem sufficientia atq; efficacissima destinare, rerum omnium ex suâ parte nihil omittere, quod ad liberandum ex peccato & damnatione hominem facere possit.

Atq; hactenùs in isto proposito DEI nemo hominum ullo decreto est præteritus. Jam verò sicut DEUS neminem actu, sive in executione salvat, præter solos credentes: ita in consilio suo æterno decretum fecit, præter eos, qui verè credunt, salvum facere neminem: qui qui essent, & quot ipsorum futuri, tàm non præscientiam ipsius latere potuit, quàm non latet eam vel minimum.

Tandem, quemadmodum in fide perseverantes certò servantur: ita his coronationem & glorificationem immutabili decreto sancivit DEUS & destinavit.

Tres istas partes Patres antiquiores Propositum sive voluntatem coronandi nominârunt, cui inclusa sit ordinatio mediorum. 2. Collationem gratiæ. 3. Gloriam Coronæ. Ac primùm quidem, quòd Voluntas coronandi seu propositum salvandi sit de ratione Prædestinationis, probarunt ex Scripturis: Noli timere pusille grex: quoniam complacuit Patri vestro dare vobis regnum, Luc. 12, 32. Possidete regnum paratum vobis à constitutione mundi: Matth. 25, 34. Deindè ex ratione: Nam Prædestinatio, sicut & Providentia, ne fingi potest quidem, quin includat in se voluntatem finis; Quemadmodum fatetur Augustinus etiam, epist. 105. ad Sixtum & lib. de corrept. & grat. cap. 13. Verùm voluntati isti est etiam inclusa ordinatio mediorum ad finem illum. Quia verò hi actus divini non distingvuntur, nisi respectu affectuum ex parte rei, quæ est extra duo ponendi sunt effect9 in ordine, ad quos, sive secundum quos hi actus distingvuntur. Unus est Glorificatio: qui respondet proposito salvandi sive voluntati coronandi, quæ est PRINCIPIUM prædestinationis in mente DEI. Et quidem reperti sunt Patres, qui nomine Prædestinationis intellexerunt ex parte DEI, Principium illud Prædestinationis: ex parte verò rei, Finem, hoc est, gloriam: Quæ sunt duæ partes præcipuæ. Verùm quia Augustinus contra Pelagianos adversarios & hostes gratiæ DEI agens, animadvertit, gratiam & fidem, quæ datur in tempore, insidiosè elidi, & in hac elisione primarium præsidium causæ Pelagianæ constitui: ad complexum Prædestinationis gravi consilio retulit etiam media Gratiæ, in quibus est Fides præcipuè: ita, ut non tantùm respectu Voluntatis in DEO, & Gloriæ: sed etiam respectu Gratiæ & mediorum Prædestinatio definienda sit. Et hujus suæ sententiæ probationem petijt, ex cap. 1, 4. & 5. Ephes. Elegit nos, ut essemus sancti, & prædestinavit nos in adoptionem filiorum DEI. At ista adoptio fide facta, in præsenti vitâ locum habet, & gloriam antecedit. Item Actor. 13, 48. Crediderunt, quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam. Et in Catenâ illâ aureâ, quæ nectitur ab Apostolo. Rom. 8. 30. Prædestinationi & glorificationi medio loco vocatio & justificatio, quæ in præsenti vitâ fiunt, interferitur.

Qui totum complexum hujus mysterij in Synopsin quandam articulatam redactum volunt, illi ex Scripturis jam citatis, in octo distincta membra totum Prædestinationis & Salutis nostræ negotium dispescunt: id quod non Thomas modò part. 1. q. 23. observavit: sed Liber etiam Concordiæ, in mysterij hujus, ejusque causarum consideratione, probè observandum esse admonet.

1. Et 1. quidem DEUM in æterno suo consilio detrevisse ostendit, Quod totum genus humanum redimere, & per CHRISTUM reconciliare sibiipsi velit, merito obedientiæ & mortis Filij.

2. Quod CHRISTI meritum & beneficia per Verbum & Sacramenta hominibus offerre singulis & universis velit.

3. Quod per Verbi & Sacramentorum ministerium velit efficax esse Spiritu suo Sancto in cordibus audientium, & sacris participantium.

4. Quod omnes verè pœnitentes & in CHRISTUM credentes, in gratiam receptos, & in filios cooptatos justificare velit.

5. Quod fide justificatos, in verâ charitate sanctificare velit.

6. Quòd justificatos tueri, & in quibusvis tentationibus ac sub cruce consolari velit.

7. Quòd bonum opus à se cœptum promovere, perseverantiæ donum largiri, & in fide ac gratiâ ad finem usq́; velit conservare.

8. Tandem, Quòd eosdem coronare, hoc est, in alterâ illâ vitâ æterna beatitudinis gloriâ donare velit.

Hæc omnia secundum Scripturam in articulo Prædestinationis & Electionis divinæ comprehenduntur, quæ universa semper, non particulatim, sed simul animo volvenda & cogitanda sunt, nullo istorum membrorum excluso aut omisso, quoties de æternæ Prædestinationis mysterio cogitatio suscipitnr. Verùm octimembri huic partitioni, cum nostrâ trimembri nihil quicquam discordiæ intercedit. Nam tria priora, Redemtio CHRISTI, beneficiorum oblatio, & efficacia, subsunt ordinationi mediorum, quæ proposito & voluntati divinæ circa salutem nostram benignissimæ est inclusa. Quatuor sequentia, Justificatio, Sanctificatio, Conservatio & Perseverantia, ad Gratiam fidei pertinent, quæ medij termini vicem obtinet. Glorificatio, Finis est propria, qui Prædestinationem ipsam terminat ac finit, ita ut ternario isto partium totum Prædestinationis complexum contineatur.

Et sic quidem se habent Termini sive partes Prædestinationis nostræ: undè patescit Sole meridiano clariùs, ex parte hominum nullam prorsus Electionis causam dari posse. 2. Quænam vera atq́; unica Prædestinationis causa constitui debeat: id quod posterius θέσεως nostræ membrum jam expediet.

Quoad POSTERIUS ergò membrum, cùm ex jam dictis irrefragabiliter constet, Prædestinationis causam, non in nobis ipsis, sed extra nos omninò quærendam esse: at verò Creatura nulla vel in cœlo, vel in terrâ, hâc in parte, operæ quicquam sibi vendicare possit: relinquitur utiq́; in solo DEO eam & quærendam & inveniendam esse. Jam si universam Scripturam accuratissimè scrutemur, si expendamus etiam ea, quæ hactenùs de partibus sive membris Prædestinationis, ex analogiâ fidei disputata sunt: planum evadet, solam atq́; unam misericordem DEI Voluntatem, Electionis causam constituendam esse. Hæc enim est radix & fundamentum totius prædestinationis nostræ, sic attestante ipso quoq́; Apostolo, Rom. 9. 18. Cujus vult, miseretur: quem vult, indurat. Cæterùm hæc voluntas DEI, quomodo in præsenti mysterio se habeat, propter nostri seculi controversias, altiùs dispiciendum fuerit: id quod sequentium controversiarum specialium diexodus planissimè explicabit.


### IV. Special Controversy, On the Will of GOD, and its distinction into Antecedent and Consequent

The Will of GOD in this mystery is not considered through his most simple essence, by which he is distinguished from the essence of GOD himself only according to our intellect, and to which there is no access for our mind: but by reason of the act, insofar as GOD goes forth outside his essence toward created things. In that former mode of consideration, and respect, the Will in GOD is no more divisible than the essence of GOD itself can be divided into many. And just as the Mercy of GOD, by which GOD is affected toward our salvation, is in number one and most simple: So also the Will of GOD, by which he wills the salvation of the human race, cannot be but one. But in the latter respect of consideration, namely, insofar as the Will of GOD goes forth outside the Essence toward creatures: it stands in a twofold manner.

For whatever God wills to be done in created things, He wills it either simply or with a certain mode and condition. That former Will is commonly called in the Schools of the Theologians Absolute, and it is joined with an immutable necessity of the event: by which He calls those things which are not, that they may be: Romans 4:17. And all things whatsoever He wills, He does in heaven and in earth: Psalm 115:3, Psalm 135:6. Concerning which Will the Apostle says in Romans 9:19, Who shall resist His will? The reason for this Will is sought from the sole omnipotence of God. The latter Will is that which is not fulfilled unless the prefixed mode or the condition itself is fulfilled: which not being fulfilled, it also comes to pass that what God nevertheless greatly willed to be done, does not happen. That former one is to be thoroughly excluded from this mystery and relegated to the Schools of the Stoics and Calvinists, who, walking on air outside the revealed Word of God, invent some absolute Will of God concerning the salvation of men, and from thence construct fatal lists of both the Elect and the Reprobate, joined with an immutable necessity of the event. But this latter one, namely the modified or determined Will of God, enters into the act of the present mystery.

Moreover, this same conditional Will of God is customarily distinguished by ancient and recent Theologians into Antecedent and Consequent: or as others speak, and it amounts to the same thing, into General and Special: not that the Will of God is twofold by Essence and as it were composite: but that God has so revealed Himself in His Word, that He has shown not only by what favor He is led toward the human race, but has also explained what He has specifically and particularly decreed concerning those who either accommodate themselves to, or oppose, His general or universal purpose. Indeed, this distinction is the Church on account of those places in Scripture which testify that the Will of God is not always done or fulfilled. For example: Matt. 23:37. How often would I have gathered thy children, as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not. And 1 Tim. 2:4. God will have all men to be saved. Yet the contrary of this seems to happen, and indeed to happen with some contradiction of the sayings of Scripture concerning the Will of God already produced. And indeed the Scholastic Doctors noticed here that their much-discussed axiom was struggling: A particular cause never fails from a universal one: and therefore they attempted to save this axiom with such a distinction: that it is to be understood contrarily, not negatively: in such a way, indeed, that by sinning a man is said to act against the will of God negatively, because he does that which He forbids, and God does not will; but not contrarily: Because God nevertheless permits this very thing, and by so permitting, in His own way God may also be said to will it. And certainly Augustine does not seem to differ greatly from this explanation of the Scholastics, when in the book On the Spirit and the Letter, ch. 33, and on that Psalm 111:3. Great are the works of God sought out in all his wills, he writes: That sinners indeed act against the Will of God: but do not overcome it: Because those who do not wish to have God appeased, will not escape Him angered, experiencing in punishments His Power, whose mercy they despised in His gifts. But these responses do not yet remove the difficulty in the alleged passages, and the contradiction. For that scruple still remains, How God can be said to will that, namely the salvation of all, from which that which Scripture clearly asserts God also wills, namely the damnation of the impious, is most different. Where indeed interpreters have formerly tortured themselves variously and anxiously. For some said that the saying of the Apostle should be read and understood in a composite sense: namely, that God wills all to be saved who are saved: as Augustine in the book On Nature and Grace, ch. 41, in the Enchiridion, ch. 103, and On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 8. Who Augustine himself explains other places of Scripture in a similar way, book 6 against Julian, ch. 12, and On the Merits and Remission of Sins, ch. 15, with these examples brought forward: When there is only one teacher in a city, we say of him that he teaches everyone, by supplying, of course, those who come to school; thus we say everyone enters the house through the doors, namely those who enter the house. Thus Rom. 5:18 it is said that all are justified in Christ, namely by way of repetition, those who are justified.

Others have interpreted the particle ALL distributively, referring it not to individuals of the kinds, but to the kinds of individuals: As if the Apostle were saying: God from every nation, sex, and condition of men wills some of them to be saved: just as it is said that every animal was in Noah's ark: namely, by animals of every species of living things. But these explanations are too twisted, and manifestly conflict with other places of Scripture, in which neither that repetition nor this distributive sense deserves a place, as when God protests that He does not even will the death of the one who dies: that He willed to gather, and thus to save even those who perish: nay, that He does not will that ANY should perish: but that all should come to the knowledge of the truth.

Finally, others are found who take refuge in that old distinction of the Scholastics between the will of the Sign and the will of Good Pleasure: contending that God indeed wills all to be saved, by the Will of the Sign, as regards the external appearance and form of Baptism and the preaching of the Gospel: but by reason of the Will of Good Pleasure, which is secret and hidden, He does not will that all be converted and saved through the hearing of the Word and the use of the Sacraments: but rather that through these very means most are more and more blinded and hardened: and thus accumulate for themselves the wrath of God in the day of wrath. Which opinion most Calvinists hold today. But this distinction of the Will of God so accepted and explained is manifestly blasphemous: and diametrically conflicts with the explanation of the Scholastics and other theologians who have used this very distinction. But what the proper meaning of this distinction was, our blessed Luther explains clearly in his Commentary on the sixth chapter of Genesis, in these words: page 98b. The Will of the Sign is the Effect of God, when He Himself proceeds outwardly to us, dealing with us through some covering, or through external things which we can apprehend: such as the Word of God, and the Ceremonies (Sacraments) instituted by Him. The Will of Good Pleasure is the Substantial will of God, or the naked majesty, which is God Himself. From this, eyes must be removed: for it cannot be apprehended. Thus far Luther.

From whose words it appears that the Scholastics understood by the Will of the Sign that Will of God which is revealed in the Word of God concerning the business of our salvation: but by the Will of Good Pleasure they noted those secret judgments of God, which do not come under consideration or explanation concerning our salvation and its means, but concerning other wonderful and inscrutable ways and works of God, only under admiration, as when it is asked: Why did God appoint Moses, and not rather Korah, or Dathan, or Abiram, as leader of His people? Why did He will Nimrod to be the first author of the first Babylonian Monarchy? Why did He undertake the work of the Evangelical Reformation through Luther, and not through another? Why did He send His Son into this world to accomplish the work of Redemption finally in the fullness of time, and not immediately after the fall of our first parents? And things that are similar to these, which do not pertain at all to the business of our salvation. Now, however, the Calvinists seize and explain this Will of Good Pleasure as concerning a certain hidden will that is plainly and contradictorily opposed to the revealed Will of GOD concerning our salvation; a thing which never entered the mind of the Scholastic Doctors.

B. LUTHER rightly admonishes in this place that it is plainly improper, and beside the sense of Scripture, for the Will of Good Pleasure to be applied by the Scholastics to those hidden judgments of GOD, and his unsearchable ways: for the reason that even the revealed Will, or the will of the Sign, is named in the Scriptures the Will of Good Pleasure, or the εὐδοκία of GOD: as 1 Cor. 1:21, εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς, it pleased GOD through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. And Col. 1:19 & 20, εὐδόκησε, it pleased him through the blood of the Cross of CHRIST to reconcile all things. These things being thus weighed, it is manifest that this distinction, even when accepted in the sense of the Scholastics, does nothing to the matter, nor does it remove or explain the difficulty of the proposed Question.

Most rightly, therefore, is the proposed question answered by the distinction of the Will in GOD into Antecedent and Consequent: namely, that GOD wills all to be saved by an Antecedent Will, but not by a consequent one. How this stands, and how it agrees with the Scriptures, we shall show presently, if we first explain that this very distinction has not been accepted and explained by all in the same manner and sense: and is not even today explained correctly by the Esavites.

Thomas Aquinas, therefore, in lib. 1. Sent. says: Something is said to be willed in two ways: In one way by precisely considering the thing in itself, naked, which we will. 2. By considering it with its circumstances. But we will many things in the former way which we do not will in the latter, and vice versa. For example: Someone wishes to buy the works of Augustine, considering the thing in itself: Yet again, considering how certainly it is sold, he does not wish to buy. Thomas says the former will is called Antecedent: the latter, Consequent. And the same Thomas, part 1, q. 19, art. 11 & 12, as Gregorio de Valentia explains it, Tom. 1. of Commentaries on Aquinas, Disp. 1, q. 19, point 2, page 424, establishes that GOD wills by an antecedent will that which, when it is first considered absolutely according to its nature, appears good and desirable. But that [he wills] by a Consequent Will, which, if it is then considered not only according to its nature, but also according to all its attached circumstances, appears good and desirable: and thus, all things being considered, it falls simply into the divine will. And in this way, according to the opinion of Thomas, GOD also wills by an antecedent will that all men be saved, their nature being looked at, according to which it appears good. But by a consequent will, because of the attached circumstance of sin, he wills some to be damned. But this explanation does not square with the present mystery according to the Scriptures. For 1. that in the antecedent will only the nature of the thing or of men is looked at by GOD is simply false. For if he had looked at this, he would never have willed our salvation according to this will: but when we were his enemies, he reconciled us to himself through the death of his Son, Rom. 5:10. And although according to our nature it appeared good that all should be saved: yet not even in this respect can or ought the Antecedent Will, by which he wills the salvation of all men, be defined: For it was not the indigence of our nature, but the sole mercy of GOD that impelled him to think thoughts of peace and salvation concerning us: as is clear from the above. Furthermore, under the consequent will, through attached circumstances, they do not understand the order or that arrangement of means in which Faith in CHRIST the Savior is included: But the disposition of one's own merits. Whence the Valentian Esavite immediately adds from the opinion of Thomas, page 425: that GOD by a consequent will wills to justify a man disposed to that: which again fights against the analogy of faith, as was demonstrated in the preceding special proximate controversy concerning the causes of Election. Finally, that also is abhorrent to the truth which Thomas adds, that only that falls simply into the Will of GOD which falls into the consequent will. For the Antecedent Will, he says, is a certain Velleity, that is, a certain conditional will: by which, indeed, someone would will that which, considered absolutely, appears desirable, unless particular circumstances stood in the way. Which opinion inclines to this, that GOD by an antecedent will does not seriously will the salvation of all men, much less of those whom he knows will be impious and will perish eternally because of their sins. To which opinion Bellarmine writes blasphemously enough in lib. 2. de Grat. & lib. arbitrio, cap. 3, page 586 A in my edition: Just as it is true that not all are saved, because they themselves do not will it: so also it is true that not all are saved, because GOD does not will it by that will of good pleasure, etc. But this also cannot stand with the universal love of GOD, and that most serious: as the following fifth and sixth controversy will expressly show.

More convenient is the other explanation of this Distinction, which Bonaventure has in 1. d. 47. art. unico, q. 1. Likewise Scotus, Gabriel, Durandus, and others: who teach: that by an Antecedent Will GOD wills all men to be saved, and to live rightly, insofar as he offers sufficient means to all, so that they may perform and attain that: but by a Consequent Will GOD wills that which he wills not now only in its cause, but also immediately, and according to itself: When, namely, nothing is either lacking or standing in the way to prevent it from being brought into existence at some time. In which manner GOD wills every good already actually existing by a consequent will.

But most convenient is the explanation of this Distinction which Damascenus has in his book against the Manichaeans: where he defines the Antecedent will by the will of the Love and Mercy of GOD: but the Consequent by the will of justice. The Antecedent Will, therefore, is born or proceeds from the sole goodness and mercy of GOD: and is so called because it precedes every other consideration and respect not only in man, but even in GOD himself. According to this will, therefore, GOD, moved by mercy alone, wills that all men without exception be saved: he sends the Son to all men equally: he has redeemed all through the same: he calls all to the kingdom of his Son through the word, etc., as the following fifth controversy will expressly show. The consequent will is that which is born not from the mercy of GOD alone, but from the consideration of the appointed means, by which, according to the requirement of the order, life was destined for believers, and damnation for unbelievers. For because the merciful GOD foresaw that the offered grace would be rejected by a large, indeed a very large, part of the human race, he so determined his will with respect to men that he destined those who would believe to the end for salvation, and those who would not believe for damnation, by both decrees being far most just.

Nor is there any reason for Huberus to be in an uproar at this point, and to clamor that this distinction, and its explanation, was recently born in the brain of certain Theologians. Certainly, before us, Damascenus held it long ago, lib. 2. Orth. fidei cap. 19. It is necessary, he says, to know that GOD antecedently wills all to be saved, and to attain his kingdom. For he did not fashion us to punish us, but so that we might be made partakers of his goodness, as he is good: but he wills that those who sin be punished, as he is just. Therefore the first is called ἡγεμένη Antecedent Will, and the Will of Good Pleasure existing from himself. The other, however, is ἑπομένη consequent will, and συγχώρησις concession for our sake: And this again is twofold: One οἰκονομικὴ καὶ παιδευτικὴ Disputatory and eruditive for salvation: the other, however, ἀπογνωσικὴ constitutive for final punishment.

And Chrysostom, Homil. 1. on those words of the first chapter to the Ephesians: According to the purpose of his will. There is, he says, another will of GOD, such as that first one, by which he does not will those who had sinned to perish. But the second, by which those who have become evil are destroyed. For it is not some necessity (namely, absolute) that punishes them, but Will.

Similar things may be seen in Theophylact and Ambrose on the same words of Paul: and in Augustine de sp. & lit. cap. 33. and in Lyra on Rom 9.

But if we were entirely destitute of all support from the Fathers, yet the authority of CHRIST himself would not be lacking to us, who so clearly and evidently illustrates and confirms this distinction with two parables concerning the royal wedding and the great supper, Matt. 22 and Luke 14, that hardly anything could be said more clearly. For that King, who is GOD the heavenly Father, prepares a great supper, and prepares a wedding for his son; he wills, invites, and commands that all should come: he cries out; Behold, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready, Come to the wedding. Behold for you the Antecedent will of GOD, breathing nothing other than an abyss of mercy. Now, however, since the greatest part of those invited have held this merciful will of GOD in mockery, have despised it, and have repudiated it: the same King wills (by a consequent will) not all, but only those who appeared at the invitation, having left their place, to taste that supper: but concerning the rest (by the same consequent will) he brings forth this sentence: I say to you, that none of those men who were called shall taste my supper: Indeed, inflamed with a just fury of indignation, having sent out his army, he destroyed them, and burned their city with fire. From which it becomes clear that the King, however much he may have invited all to his wedding and supper by his Antecedent Will, and may have willed all to come: yet he never willed that all should taste that supper of his, whether they leave a place for the invitation or not: whether they come or not. But concerning both wills and the proper affection of each, it will have to be discussed separately.

Latin:

VOluntas DEI hoc in mysterio non consideratur, per simplicissimam sui essentiam, quâ ab ipsâ DEI essentiâ, non nisi secundum nostrum intellectum distingvitur, & menti nostræ ad eam non patet accessus: sed ratione actus, quoad res creatas, extra suam essentiam DEus egreditur. Priore illo considerationis modo, & respectu, Voluntas in DEo haud magis est dividua, atque ipsa DEI essentia in plures dividi nequit. Et quemadmodum Misericordia DEI, quâ DEus erga salutem nostram afficitur, numero una ac simplicissima est: Ita Voluntas etiam DEI, quâ salutem generis humani vult, non potest esse, nisi una. Posteriore verò considerationis respectu, quatenùs videlicet Voluntas DEI extra Essentiam ad creaturas egreditur: bifariam se habet.

Quicquid enim in rebus creatis fieri vult DEus, id vel simpliciter vult: vel cum certo modo ac conditione. Prior illa Voluntas vulgò in Scholis Theologorum Absoluta dicitur, estque ea cum immutabili eventus necessitate conjuncta: quâ quæ non sunt, vocat ut sint: Roman. 4, 17. & omnia quæcunque vult, facit in cœlo & in terrâ: Psal. 115, 3. Psal. 135, 6. De quâ Voluntate Apostolus Rom. 9, 19. Voluntati ejus quis resistet? Hujus Voluntatis ratio ex solâ DEI omnipotentiâ petitur. Posterior Voluntas ea est, quæ non impletur, nisi cum modus præfixus, vel conditio ipsa impletur: quâ non impletâ, fit etiam, ut non eveniat, quòd DEus tamen maximè factum voluit. Prior illa ab hoc mysterio penitùs secludenda, & ad Stoicorum ac Calvinianorum Scholas releganda, qui extra Verbum DEI revelatum ἀεροβατοῦντες, absolutam quampiam Voluntatem DEI de salute hominum comminiscuntur, ac exindè fatales tùm Electorum, tùm Reproborum tabulas conficiunt, cum immutabili eventus necessitate conjunctas. Posterior verò hæc, nempè modificata sive determinata Voluntas DEI, præsentis mysterij actum ingreditur.

Distingvitur autem hæc ipsa conditionata DEI Voluntas usitatè à Veteribus & recentioribus Theologis in Antecedentem & Consequentem: vel ut alij loquuntur, & eôdem recidit in Generalem & Specialem: non quòd Voluntas DEI per Essentiam gemina sit & quasi composita: sed quod in Verbo suo sic se Deus revelârit, ut non tantùm quo favore erga genus humanum ducatur, ostenderit: sed quid speciatim ac peculiariter de ijs decreverit etiam, qui proposito ipsius generali sive universali, sese vel attemperant, vel opponunt, explicârit. Est verò Distinctio hæc Voluntatis DEI in Antecedentem & Consequentem introducta in Ecclesiam, propter ea Scripturæ loca, quæ Voluntatem DEI non semper fieri aut impleri testantur. Exempli gratiâ: Matth. 23, 37. Quoties volui congregare filios tuos, sicut gallina pullos suos sub alis, & noluistis. Et 1. Tim. 2, 4. DEUS vult omnes homines salvari. Cujus tamen contrarium fieri, & quidem fieri cum contradictione aliquâ dictorum Scripturæ de Voluntate DEI jam productorum, videtur. Et profectò Doctores Scholastici hîc animadverterunt laborare axioma illud suum πολυθρύλλητον: Particularis causa nunquàm deficit ab universali: ac proindè tali distinctione axioma hoc salvare conati fuerunt: intelligendum id esse contrariè, non negativè: ita quidem, ut peccando homo dicatur facere contra voluntatem DEI negativè, quia facit id, quod prohibet, & non vult DEUS: sed non contrariè: Quia hoc ipsum tamen permittat DEUS, & sic permittendo, suo quodam modo DEUS velle etiam dici possit. Et sanè Augustinus ab hâc Scholasticorum explicatione non magnoperè abludere videtur, quando in lib. de Spiritu & literâ, cap. 33. & in illud Psalmi, 111, 3. Magna sunt opera DEI exquisita in omnes voluntates ejus, scribit: Peccatores facere quidem contra Voluntatem DEI: sed non vincere eam: Quia qui non volunt habere DEUM placatū, non evadent ipsum iratum, expereuri in suppliciis Potentiam ejus, cujus in donis misericordiam contempserunt. Verùm hæc responsa difficultatem in locis allegatis, & contradictionem nondùm omnem tollunt. Manet enim adhuc scrupulus iste, Quomodo velle Deus dici possit id, salutem nempè omnium, à quo sit diversissimum id, quod itidem DEUM velle Scriptura liquidò asserit, Damnationem scilicet impiorum. Ubi sanè variè & anxiè sese olim torserunt interpretes. Aliqui enim dictum Apostoli sensu composito legendum & intelligendum esse dixerunt: nempè, Velle DEUM omnes salvari, qui salvantur: ut Augustinus lib. de Nat. & Grat. cap. 41. in Enchiridio cap, 103. & de Prædest. Sanctorum, cap. 8. Qui ipse Augustinus alia etiam Scripturæ loca simili modo explicat, lib. 6. contra Julianum cap. 12. & de peccat. meritis & remiss. cap. 15. his allatis exemplis: Quando unus tantùm est Magister in civitate, de eo dicimus, quòd omnes doceat, supplendo eos scilicet, qui ad Scholam veniunt; sic dicimus omnes ingredi domum per portas, eos scilicet, qui domum ingrediuntur. Sic Rom. 5, 18. dicitur, omnes in CHRISTO justificari, nempè κατ' ἀναδίπλωσιν, Qui justificantur.

Alij particulam OMNES distributivè interpretati sunt referendo eam non ad singulos generum: sed ad genera singulorum: Quasi dicat Apostolus: Deus ex omni natione, sexu & conditione hominum vult alios eos quos salvos: sicut dicitur, omne animal fuisse in arcâ Noë: nempè per animalium de qualibet animantium specie. Verùm nimis contortæ sunt hæ explicationes, & cum alijs Scripturæ locis manifestè pugnant, in quibus & ἀναδίπλωσις illa, & sensus iste distributivus locum non meretur, ut quando DEUS protestatur, se ne quidem morientis velle mortem: se voluisse congregare, & sic salvare eos etiam, qui pereunt: imò se non velle, ut ULLUS pereat: sed omnes ad agnitionem veritatis perveniant.

Alij denique reperiuntur, qui confugiunt ad veterem illam Scholasticorum distinctionem inter voluntatem Signi, & voluntatem Beneplaciti: contendentes, DEUM quidem velle omnes salvos, Voluntate Signi, quoad externam speciem & formam Baptismi & prædicationis Evangelicæ: verùm ratione Voluntatis Beneplaciti, quæ arcana & occulta sit, eum non velle, ut per auditum Verbi & usum Sacramentorum omnes convertantur & salvi fiant: sed ut potiùs per hæc ipsa media plurimi magis magisque excæcentur & indurentur: sibique sic accumulent iram DEI in die iræ. Quam sententiam hodiè plerique tenent Calviniani. Verùm Distinctio hæc Voluntatis DEI sic accepta & explicata, manifestè blasphema est: & cum explicatione Scholasticorum aliorumque Theologorum, qui hâc ipsâ distinctione usi fuerunt, diametraliter pugnat. Quæ autem propria fuerit Distinctionis hujus sententia, perspicuè explicat B. LUTHERUS noster in Commentario ad caput sextum Geneseos, his verbis: pag. 98. b. Voluntas Signi est Effectus DEI, quando ipse foràs procedit ad nos, nobiscum agens, per aliquod involucrum, vel per res externas, quas possumus apprehendere: sicut sunt Verbum DEI, & Ceremoniæ (Sacramenta) ab ipso institutæ. Voluntas Beneplaciti est Substantialis voluntas DEI, sive nuda majestas, quæ est DEUS ipse. Ab hâc removendi oculi sunt: Non enim potest apprehendi. Hactenus Lutherus.

Ex cujus Verbis apparet, Scholasticos per Voluntatem Signi intellexisse eam Voluntatem DEI, quæ de salutis nostræ negotio, in Verbo DEI est revelata: per Voluntatem autem Beneplaciti notasse arcana illa DEI judicia, quæ non de salute nostrâ, ejusq; medijs: sed de alijs mirandis & imperscrutabilibus DEI vijs ac operibus, sub admirationem tantùm, non verò sub considerationem sive explicationem veniunt, ut quando quæritur: Cur DEUS Mosen, & non potiùs vel Core, vel Dathan, vel Abiramum constituerit Ducem populi sui? cur Nimrothum voluerit esse primum autorem primæ Monarchiæ Babylonicæ: Cur per Lutherum, non per alium opus Reformationis Evangelicæ molitus sit? Cur Filium suum demùm in plenitudine temporis, non verò statim à lapsu proto-parentum nostrorum, hunc in mundum miserit, ad expediendum Redemtionis opus? Et quæ his sunt similia, quæ salutis nostræ negotium nihil quicquam attinent. Jam verò Calviniani rapiunt & explicant hanc Voluntatem Beneplaciti, de arcanâ quadam, & revelatæ DEI Voluntati de salute nostra, planè contradictoriè oppositâ voluntate; id quod Scholasticis Doctoribus nunquam in mentem venit.

Rectè autem admonet hoc loco B. LUTHERUS, impropriè planè, & præter Scripturæ sensum, Voluntatem Beneplaciti à Scholasticis accommodari ad arcana illa DEI judicia, & vias ejus impervestigabiles: propterea quòd Voluntas etiam revelata, sive voluntas Signi in Scripturis nominetur Voluntas Beneplaciti, sive εὐδοκία DEI: ut 1. Cor. 1, 21 εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς Beneplacuit DEO per stultitiam prædicationis salvos facere credentes. Et Coloss. 1, 19. & 20. εὐδόκησε per sangvinem Crucis CHRISTI reconciliare omnia. Quibus ita expensis manifestum est, Distinctionem hanc, Scholasticorum etiam sensu acceptam nihil ad rem facere, neq; propositæ Quæstionis difficultatem tollere aut explicare.

Rectissimè ergò ad propositam quæstionem respondetur per distinctionem Voluntatis in DEO, in Antecedentem & Consequentem: nempè DEUM velle omnes salvos fieri; Voluntate Antecedente: non autem consequente. Quod quomodo se habeat, & cum Scripturis conveniat, mox ostendemus, si priùs explicaverimus; Distinctionem hanc ipsam non pari modo ac sensu ab omnibus acceptam & explicatam esse: & ne quidem hodie ab Esavytis dextrè explicari.

Thomas ergò Aquinas in lib. 1. Sent. inquit: Dupliciter dicitur aliquid velle: Uno modo precisè cōsiderando rem per se nudam, quam volumus. 2. Considerando eam cum suis circumstantijs. Multa autem volumus priore modo, quæ non volumus posteriore, & vice versa. Verbi gratia: Opera Augustini vult aliquis emere, considerando rem in se: Tamen rursò considerando, quàm certè vendatur, non vult emere. Priorem voluntatem dicit Thomas vocari Antecedentem: Consequentem alteram. Et idem Thomas part. 1. q. 19. art. 11. & 12. sic explicante Gregorio de Valentia, Tom. 1. Commentariorum in Aquinatem Disp. 1. q 19. puncto 2. pag. 424. statuit, DEUM velle voluntate antecedente id quod cùm primò secundum suam naturam absolutè consideratur, apparet bonum & expetendum. Illud autem Voluntate Consequente, quod si deindè consideretur non modò secundum suam naturam, sed etiam secundum omnes adjunctas circumstantias bonum & expetendum apparet: atq; ita consideratis omnibus simpliciter in divinam voluntatem cadit. Atque isto modo ex sententiâ Thomæ, DEUS etiam antecedente voluntate vult omnes homines salvos fieri, spectatâ eorum naturâ, secundum quam id apparet bonum. Consequenti verò voluntate, propter adjunctam peccati circumstantiam; vult aliquos damnari. Verùm hæc explicatio ad præsens mysterium secundum Scripturas non quadrat. Nam 1. in voluntate antecedente à DEO tantùm naturam rei sive hominum spectari, simpliciter falsum est. Nam si hanc spectasset, nunquàm secundumhanc voluntatem, nostram voluisset salutem:sed cùm inimici ipsius essemus, reconciliavit nos sibi per mortem Filij, Rom 5, 10. Et quanquàm secundum naturam nostram apparebat bonum, ut omnes salvarentur: tamen ne hoc quidem respectu Voluntas Antecedens, quâ omnium hominum vult salutem, definiri potest aut debet: Neq; enim naturæ nostræ indigentia; sed sola DEI misericordia impulit ipsum, ut cogitaret super nos cogitationes pacis & salutis: ut ex superioribus patet. Deindè sub voluntate consequente per circumstantias adjunctas, non intelligunt τάξιν sive ordinê illum mediorum, cui inclusa sit Fides in CHRISTUM Servatorem: Sed dispositionem propriorum meritorum. Undè Esavvita Valentianus statim ex sententia Thomæ pag. 425. subjicit: DEUM consequente voluntate velle justificare hominem ad id dispositum: id quod rursus cum analogiâ fidei pugnat, uti præcedente controversiâ speciali proximâ, de causis Electionis fuit demonstratum. Tandem & illud à vero abhorret, quod Thomas addit, illud solùm simpliciter cadere in Voluntatem DEI, quod cadit in voluntatem consequentem. Nam Voluntas Antecedens, inquit, est quædam Velleitas, id est, Conditionata quædam voluntas: quâ nimirùm aliquis vellet id, quod absolutè consideratum apparet expetendum, nisi particulares circumstantiæ obstarent. Quæ sententia eò inclinat, DEUM voluntate antecedente non seriò velle omnium hominum salutem, nedùm eorum etiam, quos novit impios futuros, & propter peccata æternùm perituros. Quam in sententiam blasphemè satis scribit Bellarminus lib. 2. de Grat. & lib. arbitrio, cap. 3. pag. mihi 586. A. Sicut verum est, non omnes salvos fieri, quia ipsi non volunt: sic etiam verum est, non omnes salvos fieri, quia DEUS non vult voluntate illa beneplaciti &c. Sed & hoc cum dilectione DEI universali, eáq; maximè seriâ stare nequit: uti insequens controversia quinta & sexta ex professo ostendet.

Commodior est explicatio Distinctionis hujus altera, quam habet Bonaventura in 1. d. 47. art. unico, q. 1. Item Scotus Gabriel, Durandus & alij: qui docent: Voluntate Antecedente velle DEUM omnes homines salvos fieri, & rectè vivere: quatenùs omnibus media sufficientia offert, ut id præstare & consequi possint: Voluntate verò consequente velle DEUM id, quod non jam in sua causâ solùm: sed immediatè etiam, & secundum se vult: Quando nimirùm nihil vel deest vel obstat, quo minùs id aliquando in esse ponatur. Quo pacto DEũ omnem bonum jam actu existens, velit voluntate consequente.

Commodissima autem est Distinctionis hujus explicatio, quam habet Damascenus in lib. contra Manichæos: ubi Antecedentem voluntatem definit per voluntatem Amoris & Misericordiæ DEI: Consequentem verò per voluntatem justitiæ. Antecedens ergò Voluntas nascitur sive provenit ex solâ bonitate & misericordiâ DEI: ideò sic dicta, quia antecedit omnẽ aliâ confiderationem & respectum non in homine tantùm, sed in ipso etiam DEO. Secundum hanc ergò voluntatem DEUS solâ misericordiâ motus,vult omnes omninò homines salvos : omnibus hominibus ex æquo mittit Filium : omnes per eundem redemit : omnes ad regnum Filij sui per verbum vocat &c. uti subsequens controversia quinta ex professo ostendet. Consequens voluntas ea est, quæ nascitur non ex solâ misericordiâ DEI: sed ex consideratione destinati medij, quâ secundum exigentiam ordinis, credentibus vita, incredulis damnatio destinata fuit. Quia enim misericors DEUS oblatam gratiam à magnâ, imò maximâ generis humani parte repudiatum iri prævidit : sic voluntatem suam respectu hominum determinavit, ut qui ad finem usq; crederent,saluti: qui non crederent,damnationi destinaret decreto utroq; longè justissimo.

Neq; est, ut hoc loco tumultuetur Huberus, & distinctionem hanc, ejusq; explicationem, in cerebro quorundam Theologorum nuper natam esse, clamitet. Certè ante nos eam jam olim tenuit Damascenus, lib. 2. Orth. fidei cap. 19. Oportet, inquiens, scire, quod DEUS antecedenter vult omnes salvari, & regnum suum consequi. Neq; enim ad puniendos nos finxit, sed ut efficiamur bonitatis ipsius participes, ut bonus: peccantes autem vult puniri, ut justus. Dicitur igitur prima ἡγεμένη Antecedens Voluntas, & Beneplaciti ex ipso existens. Altera verò ἑπομένη consequens voluntas, & συγχώρησις concessio ex nostri causâ : Et hec rursum gemina : Una οἰκονομικὴ καὶ παιδευτικὴ Disputatoria & eruditiva ad salutem : altera verò ἀπογνωσικὴ constitutoria ad finalem pœnam.

Et Chrysostomus Homil. 1. super illa verba capitis primi ad Ephesios : Secundum propositum voluntatis suæ. Alia, inquit, voluntas est DEI, qualis est prima illa, quâ eos perire non vult, qui peccaverant. Secunda verò, quâ perduntur,qui mali facti sunt. Nam non necessitas quædam ( scilicet absoluta ) illos punit, sed Voluntas.

Similia videantur apud Theophylactum & Ambrosium in eadem Pauli verba : & apud Augustinum de sp. & lit. cap. 33. & apud Lyram ad Rom 9.

Sed si maximè omni Patrum præsidio destitueremur:ipsius tamen CHRISTI nobis non deesset autoritas, qui distinctionem hanc duabus parabolis de nuptijs regijs & cœnâ magnâ Matth. 22. & Luc. 14. ita perspicuè & evidenter illustrat & confirmat, ut vix quicquam dilucidiùs dici possit. Rex enim ille, qui est DEUS Pater cœlestis, cœnam magnam instruit, & nuptias parat filio; vult, invitat, mandat, ut omnes veniant : clamat; Ecce, prandium meum paravi, tauri mei, &altilia mea mactata, &omnia parata, Venite ad nuptias. En tibi Antecedentem DEI voluntatem, nihil aliud præter misericordiæ abyssum spirantem. Jam verò cùm hanc misericordem DEI voluntatem maxima pars invitatorum ludibrio habuerit, contemserit, pserit, repudiarit: Vult idem Rex (voluntate consequente) non omnes, sed illos tantùm gustare cœnam illam, qui invitationi loco relicto comparuerunt: de reliquis verò (eadem voluntate consequente) hanc profert sententiam: Dico vobis, quod nemo virorum illorum, qui vocati sunt, gustabit, cœnam meam: Imò justo indignationis furore accensus, emisso exercitu perdidit illos, & civitatem illorum igni exussit. Undè perspicuum evadit, Regem illum quantumvis Voluntate Antecedente omnes ad nuptias & cœnam suam invitaverit, & voluerit omnes venire: nunquàm tamen voluisse, omnes gustare cœnam illam suam, sive invitationi locum relinquant, sive non: sive veniant, sive non. Verùm de utrâq; voluntate & propriâ cujuslibet affectione seorsim dispiciendum fuerit.


### V. Special Controversy, On the parts, or members, of the Antecedent Will in GOD, by which he makes it testified to the whole world

It is evident from the premises that the antecedent will in GOD is and is called nothing else to us than the purpose, Counsel, and Good Pleasure of GOD eternal, concerning saving the whole human race, and liberating the same from sin through CHRIST the Redeemer, and always offering to the same the means necessary for salvation. There are therefore three members, or Parts, which are to be considered properly and accurately in this will of GOD. I. The immense mercy of GOD, by which, having embraced the whole human race, he passed over no mortal in that eternal counsel of his concerning our salvation in this world. II. The merit of CHRIST, by which a most sufficient expiation and satisfaction was rendered to GOD the Father for the sins of the whole world. III. The Ministry of the Word and Sacraments, in which the preceding benefit of both is seriously offered to the whole world, and as it were held out by a divine hand. In these three primary foundations, since the hinge of our salvation for the most part turns, it will be worth the effort that we discuss each one separately and more accurately.

Latin:

COnstat ex præmissis, quod voluntas antecedens in DEO nihil sit & dicatur nobis aliud, quàm propositum, Consilium & Beneplacitum DEI æternum, de salvando universo genere humano, eodemque ex peccato per CHRISTUM Redemptorem liberando, & medijs ad salutem necessarijs eidem semper offerendis. Tria ergò potissimùm sunt membra, sive Partes, quæ in hâc voluntate DEI, probè & accuratè sunt considerandæ. I. Immensa DEI misericordia, quâ totum genus humanum complexus, neminem mortalium, in consilio illo suo de salute nostrâ æterno, hoc in mundo præterijt. II. Meritum CHRISTI, quo pro totius mundi peccatis, sufficientissima DEO Patri expiatio & satisfactio præstita est. III. Ministerium Verbi & Sacramentorum, in quo præcedens utrumque beneficium toti mundo seriò offertur, & quasi divinâ manu porrigitur. In istis tribus primarijs fundamentis, cùm salutis nostræ cardo maximam partem versetur, operæ precium fuerit, ut de singulis seorsim accuratiùs dispiciamus.


### I. The Member of the Antecedent Will is the immense Mercy of GOD

What affection the FATHER GOD has had from all eternity towards the whole human race, and how immense the Φιhumanity burned, he made it manifest in time in two principal ways. FIRST, indeed, by the form of CREATION. For he did not endow man, as he did the rest of living creatures, with only a certain bodily form and some sort of soul: but he also endowed him with REASON, nay, what is most excellent, he fashioned him in his own image: and he fashioned him in such a way that not only did the first man possess this Image for himself: but also that he would propagate the same to all his posterity in a natural way through generation, if he had persisted in innocence. Now, however, these two things, the Image of GOD and eternal salvation, cohere in such an undivided bond that, with one lost, the other is also forfeited.

Therefore, since one and the same thing cannot be destined for contrary ends at the same time: certainly, even from the creation of Man, an undoubted and infallible argument is drawn that GOD, even then in that eternal counsel of his, looked to no other primary end of creation than the temporal and eternal salvation of the whole human race. And this was the first document of divine pity, sufficiently illustrious indeed, and to be celebrated with eternal praises.

But Scripture shows a second one, not inferior to the former. For although GOD had foreseen from eternity that Man, by his own fault, would lose the most noble Image of GOD through detestable ingratitude and disobedience, not only for himself but also for all his posterity, and would bring upon himself eternal destruction: yet not even then, and though so enormously offended, did he loosen the reins of his wrath and justice, and will that Man should perish eternally: but being rich in his mercy, he again thought thoughts of peace, and not of affliction, concerning us, having made a decree to send into the world his only-begotten Son, who would himself become Man, and would restore the whole fallen and lost human race, and redeem it from sin, death, and hell. And in celebrating this species of divine mercy, the whole of Scripture is occupied throughout, but most especially,

Ezek. 18:23. Is it my will that the wicked should die, says the Lord GOD, and not that he should turn from his ways, and live?

And in verse 32. I do not desire the death of him who dies, says the Lord GOD, return and live.

Ezek. 33:11. As I live, says GOD, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked should turn from his evil way, and live.

John 3:16. For GOD so loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

Rom. 8:32. GOD did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all: how will he not with him also give us all things?

Eph. 1:4 & 5. GOD chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight, in love: Who predestined us to the adoption of sons through JESUS CHRIST, in himself.

And in verses 9 & 10. According to the riches of the grace of GOD, which abounded in us, that he might make known the mystery of his Will according to his good pleasure, which he proposed in him, that in the fullness of time he might restore all things in Christ, both those which are in heaven, and those which are on earth, in him. Eph. 2:4. GOD, who is rich in mercy, because of his abundant love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together in Christ. Col. 1:19 & 20. It pleased GOD the Father through his Son to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, both those things which are on earth and those which are in heaven. 1 Tim. 2:4. GOD wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the Truth. 2 Pet. 3:9. GOD does not will that any should perish, but that all should return to repentance.

Latin:

QUis jam indè ab omni æternitate DEI Patris erga totum genus humanum affectus fuerit, & quàm immensa Φιλανθρωπία flagrârit, duobus potissimùm modis in tempore testatum fecit. PRIMUM quidem CREATIONIS formâ. Nam non ut reliqua animantia, certâ tantùm corporis specie; & animâ qualicunq; hominem donavit: sed & RATIONE ipsum prædidit, imò quod præstantissimum est, ad imaginem suam illum condidit: & ita quidem condidit, ut non solùm primus homo Imaginem hanc pro se possideret: sed & ut eandem in omnem posteritatem naturali modo per generationem propagaret, si in innocentiâ ille perstitisset. Jam verò duo isthæc, Imago DEI & salus æterna, indiviso nexu ita cohærent, ut uno perdito, amissum sit alterum.

Proindè cum una eademq; res finibus contrarijs simul destinari non possit: certè vel ex creatione Hominis indubium atq; infallibile argumentum petitur, DEUM jam tùm in æterno illo suo consilio Finem primarium creationis respexisse nullum alium, quàm temporalem & æternam totius generis humani salutem. Et hoc primum erat miserationis divinæ documentum, satis profectò illustre, & æternis laudibus celebrandum.

Sed Scriptura monstrat & alterum, priore haud inferius. Nam licèt DEUS ab æterno prævidisset, Hominem propriâ suâ culpâ, nobilissimam Imaginem DEI, per detestandam ingratitudinem & inobedientiam, non sibi modò, sed & toti posteritati perditurum, æternumq; exitium attracturum: tamen ne sic quidem, & tam enormiter offensus, iræ atq; justitiæ suæ fræna laxavit, Hominemq; æternùm perire voluit: sed dives in misericordiâ suâ, iterum cogitationes pacis, & non afflictionis super nos cogitavit, facto decreto, de mittendo in mundum Filio suo unigenito, qui & ipse Homo fieret, & lapsum perditumq; genus humanum universum restauraret, & à peccato, morte ac inferno redimeret. Et in hac misericordiæ divinæ specie celebranda, universa Scriptura passim occupatur, maximè verò,

Ezech. 18, 23. Nunquid Voluntatis meæ est mors impij, dicit Dominus DEUS, & non ut convertatur à viis suis, & vivat.

Et Versu 32. Nolo mortem morientis, dicit Dominus DEUS, revertimini & vivite.

Ezech. 33, 11. Vivo ego DEUS, nolo mortem impij, sed ut convertatur impius à viâ suâ malâ, & vivat.

Johan. 3, 16. Sic DEUS dilexit mundum, ut Filiu suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis, qui credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam.

Rom. 8, 32. DEUS proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum: quomodo non cum illo donavit nobis omnia?

Ephes. 1, 4. & 5. DEUS elegit nos in Christo ante jacta mundi fundamenta, ut essemus Sancti & irreprehensibiles in conspectu ejus, in charitate: Qui prædestinavit nos in adoptionem filiorum per JESUM CHRISTUM, in ipsum.

Et versibus 9. & 10. Secundum divitias gratiæ DEI, quæ superabundavit in nobis, ut notum faceret mysterium Voluntatis suæ secundum beneplacitu ejus, quod proposuit in eo, ut in plenitudine temporis instauraret omnia in Christo, quæ in cœlis, & quæ in terrâ sunt, in ipso.
