But he is looking for a knot in a bulrush. For to what purpose does it tend to call into the hazard of doubt that which Scripture expressly asserts, as has been demonstrated thus far? But so that this part of this dispute may also be clearer, it is pleasing to explain it, as it were, by its parts and certain members.

And at the beginning, indeed, it is sufficiently clear from what has already been said that the condition and presence of FAITH must be referred to that part of the divine order, in which GOD willed the eternal decree of Election to be included. Nor does this, however, prevent one from being allowed in the meantime to establish Faith in its own way as also the cause of Election. For that common rule is true: The causes of Election are the same as those of Justification. And it is established by irrefragable Truth that by the same causes by which GOD saves men in time in the execution of that eternal purpose of His, by those same causes He also decreed from eternity to save men. Now, indeed, men are saved in time by the mercy of GOD on account of Christ the Mediator apprehended by Faith. Therefore, by the same causes (in the number of which is also faith) their Salvation decreed from eternity, or what amounts to the same thing, the Election itself of the same, will be considered to have been made.

But this smacks of Pelagianism, says Huberus, if faith is said to enter into Election in this sense, as a cause. But a fallacy of non-cause and of a vicious consequent is committed. For, besides the fact that we readily grant that faith is a purely gratuitous gift of God: faith is furthermore established as a cause of Election, not a meritorious one, on account of which, and by whose dignity eternal Election was made: but merely an organic or instrumental one, by whose dignity or merit Election was not made, but only by its order: so that, just as in the work of Justification: so also in the mystery of Election, faith relates only to Christ the Mediator. If therefore faith cannot enter into the decree of Election because it is gratuitous: by the same reasoning it would have to be excluded from Justification: which the reason of Truth by no means allows. Similarly, this phrase (Faith is a cause of Election by reason of order) does not have the sense which is falsely attributed to our doctrine by calumny, as if men themselves ordain themselves to eternal Life: which would be Pelagian: but that men follow the order established by God himself; so that men are ordained by God, not by themselves: they are ordained, however, partly by reason of Vocation, through the Gospel, by which God anticipates every human effort: and partly by reason of faith itself, which the Holy Spirit kindles in man through the heard Word.

It is further objected that faith is a consequent and effect of Election: and therefore cannot be called either its instrumental cause or any part of it. The antecedent is confirmed, not only by the authority of the Fathers, and especially of Augustine and blessed Luther: but also of Scripture itself, as that which affirms in Acts 13:48 that only those believed who had been ordained to eternal Life.

Latin:

Quæstio III. An Electio sit absoluta, an verò ordinata?

QUæstioni huic accuratiùs explicandæ ansam occasionemque præbet, non Calvinianorum modò figmentum, de absoluto uti Reprobationis, sic & Electionis decreto: Verùm etiam Huberi somnium, quo semiabsolutam fingit Electionem, quæ Christi quidem meritum includat, sed sine respectu fidei. Nos ergò utrique isti fanaticorum gregi nuncio remisso, Scripturarum oracula secuti statuim9, Nullam cujusquam hominis vel Electionem vel Reprobationem esse absolutam: sed utramquè ordinatam. Nam quemadmodum DEUS ab æterno proposuit eligere homines ad vitam æternam, eosdemque salvare: ita ordinem etiam ac media sanxit, & in consilio suo æterno decrevit, quo mediante Electorum Salus constitueretur, & qui ab Electionis decreto definiendo nunquàm sejungeretur. Ordo autem iste, qui & qualis sit paulò accuratiùs ex Scripturis dispiciendum fuerit.

Primum igitur locum in eo obtinet Christus Servator cum suo merito. Affirmat hoc Scriptura, quando testatur, 1. Quòd in Christo electi simus. Ephes. 1, 4. Hinc sic licet argumentari: Quicunque eliguntur in certo aliquo objecto, sive per aut propter illud, vel etiam respectu illius, illi non absolutè, sed ordinatè eliguntur. Absolutum enim non est, quod certo alterius respectu fit. Atqui electi omnes, in Christo sunt electi. Ergò non absolutè, sed ordinatè sunt electi.

Deindè Scriptura loco citato asserit, quod benedixerit nos DEUS in benedictionibus spiritualibus in Christo, in quo etiam nos elegit ante constitutionem mundi. Ephes. 1, 3. & 4. Hinc sic colligitur: Cujus generis est benedictio spiritualis, quæ fit in tempore: ejusdem generis est etiam æterna electio. Atqui illa non est absoluta, sed in Christo ordinata: Ergò neque hæc erit absoluta.

Tertiò, Ephes. 1, 5. dicitur, Quod DEUS prædestinârit nos in adoptionem filiorum per Christum Jesum in seipsum, secundum beneplacitum voluntatis suæ: id quod Apostolus 2. Timoth. 1, 9. explicat, asserens, Gratiam nobis esse datam in Christo Jesu ante tempora secularia. Quæ duo testimonia haud levius, pro ordinatâ Electione: atque priora duo pugnant. Et cumprimis observanda venit in singulis istis locis, expressa æternitatis notatio, quæ minimè permittit, ut de temporali executione verba Apostoli interpretemur. Et quidem quoad Huberum, planior est res de primâ hac parte ordinis, quàm quæ operosam probationem requirat.

ALTERA pars ordinis hujus est FIDES, apprehendens meritum Christi: de quâ acrior hodiè agitatur disceptatio. Cæterùm Fidem hanc ingredi τάξιν sive ordinem Decreti Electionis, evidentissimè his rationibus ex Scripturâ demonstratur.

I. Christus cum omnibus suis beneficiis & merito suo etiam abundantissimo, absque fide nemini quicquam prodest. Ergò Fides ad τάξιν prædestinationis divinæ accedat necesse est: ita ut in quibus ordo iste, non modò ratione meriti CHRISTI, sed & ratione fidei meritum illud apprehendentis, completur, hi sint in in numero electorum: reliqui verò ex eo sint seclusi, non aliquo absoluto divinæ Voluntatis beneplacito: sed propriæ incredulitatis & finalis impœnitentiæ culpâ ac vitio.

II. Fidem decretum Electionis æternæ ingredi, Scriptura ipsa luculenter comprobat.

Ephes. 1, 1. & 12. Electio propria dicitur esse FIDELIUM sive credentium in JESU: qui ipsi paulò post, usitatâ in Scripturis phrasi, nominantur SPERANTES in Christo.

2. Thess. 2, 13. Elegit nos DEUS ab initio ad salutem, in fide Veritatis.

Tit. 1, 1. Fides Jesu Christi vocatur fides Electorum.

Jacobi 2, 5. Elegit pauperes mundi hujus, divites in fide.

Et ut in pauca res redigatur: si impossibile est placere DEO sine fide Hebr. 11, 6. Si vitam æternam habere, nisi qui credit, non potest. Johan. 6. 39. Si extra Christum nulla facta est Electio, Ephes. 1, 4. extra Christum autem sunt, quotquot non credunt in ipsum: utique ab electionis: decreto Fides excludi nullâ ratione vel potest vel debet.

III. Quo modo se habet Gratia DEI ad peccatorum remissionem, eodem etiam modo illa se habet, ad nostram Electionem. Atqui Gratia DEI nunquàm peccata remittit, nisi Credentibus, Ergò neq; Electionis Gratia obtinget cuipiam sine fide. Connexum

Majoris patet inde 1. quia utrobique una eademque est gratia. Rom. 11, 5. & 6. & 22. Ephes. 1, 5. 6. & 7. 2. Tim. 1, 9. & 20. 2. quia non sunt electi, nisi quibus remissa sunt peccata.

IV. DEUS nos eligendo adoptavit in filios. Ephes. 1, 5. Atqui υἱοθεσία sive adoptio in filios, non est nisi Credentium: Joh. 1, 12. Gal. 3, 26. Ergo Electio etiam est non nisi Credentium.

V. Electio tendit ad vitam & salutem æternam: ita ut quicunque sunt prædestinati, illi etiam justificentur & glorificentur, Rom. 8, 30. Atqui justus non nisi Fide vivit. Rom. 1, 17. Hebr. 2, 4. nec glorificantur nisi soli credentes.

VI. Quomodo se habet æterni decreti Electionis executio, quæ fit in tempore, eodem etiam modo se habet ipsa electio: Atqui Executio decreti æterni sic se habet, ut non salvetur, nisi qui credit in Christum. Ergo ipsum quoque æternum Electionis decretum, non nisi credentes complectatur necesse est.

VII. Tandem accedit Consensus Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis, & Libri Christianæ Concordiæ decisio luculentissima, Huberi delirium de prædestinatione sine intuitu fidei ab æterno facta, simpliciter, explodens.

Theophylactus certe super cap. 1. Ephes. sic commentatur: Eligi in Christo nihil est aliud, quam eligi in fide Jesu Christi.

Theophylacto in explicatione hujus ipsius capitis primi ad Ephesios suffragantur, Hieronymus, Chrysostomus, Ambrosius & alij.

Epitome vero libri Concordiæ sic habet: In Christo Electio æterna DEI patris est quærenda: is in æterno suo Consilio decrevit, quod præter eos, qui Filium ejus JESUM CHRISTUM agnoscunt, & in eum vere credunt, neminem salvare velit.

Et jam supra recensuimus octo illa requisita, quæ liber Concordiæ semper conjungenda esse statuit in doctrina Prædestinationis: Quorum in numero FIDES est vel maxime, eaque ut mihimu ter inculcata ac repetita: Quare subjicit idem liber Symbolicus: Hæc omnia in articulo Prædestinationis comprehenduntur: universa illa sub hoc articulo complecti debemus, nec quicquam horum excludendum aut omittendum est.

His de Fide, tanquam parte altera Decreti Electionis sic constitutis, emergit tandem plenum ordinis hujus complementum istud: nempe quod Christus cum suo merito, non nisi fide apprehensus, Electionis ordinem constituit: & sic pars hæc ordinis posterior, priori parti addita, Universalitatem & efficaciam meriti Christi, ratione fructus salutaris, adstringit ad solos credentes.

Tumultuatur hoc loco Huberus, & quo modo, quove titulo Fides æternum Electionis decretum ingredi possit, & num Fides Electionis causa dici debeat, anxie disputat. Sed nodum in Scirpo quærit. Quorsum enim attinet sub dubitationis aleam vocare id, quod Scriptura expresse asserit, uti hactenus demonstratum. Verum ut hæc etiam pars disputationis hujus sit planior, per partes quasi suas, & certa membra eam explicare placet.

Ac initiò quidem, FIDEI conditionem & præsentiam, ad partem τάξεως illius divinæ, cui DEUS æternum Electionis decretum inclufum voluit, referendam esse, ex jam dictis satis liquet. Neque hoc obstat tamen, quò minùs Fidem liceat interim suo quodam modo statuere etiam Electionis causam. Est enim vera regula illa usitata: Eadem sunt causæ Electionis, quæ sunt Justificationis. Et irrefragabili Veritate constat, quibus causis in executione æterni illius sui propositi, DEUS homines in tempore salvat: ijsdem etiam decrevisse illum ab æterno salvare homines. Jam verò salvantur homines in tempore, ex misericordiâ DEI propter Christum Mediatorem Fide apprehensum. Ijsdem ergò etiam causis (in quarum numero est & fides) Salus eorum ab æterno decreta, vel quod eodem recidit, Electio ipsa eorundem facta esse existimabitur.

Sed Pelagianismum hoc sapit, inquit Huberus, si hoc sensu Fides dicatur ingredi Electionem, ut causa. Verùm committitur Elenchus non causæ & vitiosi Consequentis. Nam, præterquàm quòd Fidem donum DEI merè gratuitum esse; ultrò largimur: Fides insuper statuitur esse causa Electionis, non meritoria, propter quàm, & ob cujus dignitatem æterna Electio facta sit: sed organica duntaxat sive instrumentalis, cujus non dignitate aut merito: sed ordine solummodò Electio sit facta: ita ut, quemadmodum in opere Justificationis: sic etiam in mysterio Electionis, RELATE duntaxat se habeat Fides ad Christum Mediatorem. Quod si ergò Fides ideò non possit ingredi Electionis decretum, quia illa est gratuita: pari utique ratione à Justificatione eadem excludenda foret: quod Veritatis ratio minimè patitur. Consimiliter phrasis hæc (Fides est causa Electionis ratione ordinis) non eum sensum habet, qui nostræ doctrinæ per Calumniam affingitur, Quasi homines ipsi sese ordinent ad Vitam æternam: id quod Pelagianum foret:sed quòd homines ordinem à DEO ipso constitutum sequantur; ita ut homines à DEO, non à seipsis ordinentur: Ordinentur autem partim ratione Vocationis, per Evangelium, quâ DEUS omnè studium humanum antevertit: partim verò ipsius ratione Fidei, quam per Verbum auditum Spiritus Sanctus in homine accendit.

Objicitur porrò, Quòd Fides sit consequens & effectum Electionis: ac proindè non dici possit ejusdem sive causa instrumentalis, sive pars aliqua. Antecedens confirmatur, non modò autoritate Patrum, & cumprimis Augustini, & B. Lutheri: sed & ipsius Scripturæ, ut quæ Actor. 13, 48. affirmat, eos tantùm credidisse, quotquot ordinati fuerant ad Vitam æternam.


### VII. Special Controversy, Concerning the Consequent Will of GOD: and the difference of this from the Antecedent: Question III. Whether Election is absolute, or indeed ordered? (continued)

I answer that the presupposition upon which this whole argument is built is false. For it is imagined that nothing can have the respect of both cause and effect, however much in a different sense and respect, both are affirmed of the same thing: that which even sounder Philosophy shows to be false. This is indeed a true axiom, in things placed under the same genus of cause, and opposed to one another in one and the same respect. For in this way, nothing can be the cause and effect of the same thing. But because Relata are commonly said to be causes of one another, in a different genus of cause and a dissimilar respect, certainly nothing prevents the same thing from being said to be both the cause and effect of the same thing. That this also has a place in Election and faith, which are related to each other, contains no absurdity. Otherwise, speaking properly, eternal Election is neither the Efficient cause, nor the form, nor the matter of Faith. In which respect, Faith also cannot properly be called the Effect of Election. But if Faith is most strongly said to be the effect of Election, it is not absurd, under another genus of cause, to constitute Faith as the cause of Election, as its relative. Whence Nicolaus Lyranus, on those words of Rom. 9, 'He has mercy on whom he wills,' etc., not ineptly writes: 'In the Effects of divine Predestination, the prior is always the cause of the posterior, by way of disposing: And the posterior is always the cause of the prior, by way of an end.'

We respond the same also to that other point: Faith is a Consequence of Election: Therefore it is not its part. For some things are enunciated of the whole, as it is a whole: but some things are enunciated of the whole on account of some part of it. As a hypocaust is an Effect of the whole house, insofar as the remaining structure was undertaken on account of the hypocaust: And at the same time it is a part of the house, if you look at the whole itself as constituted. Thus, if Election is considered as a certain whole, Faith is rightly said to be its part, or instrumental cause. But if, in the same decree of Election, you look at the grace of GOD, then indeed Faith depends upon it, as an Effect from its cause. Which same thing can also be demonstrated concerning the Merit of Christ. For if you consider the whole decree of Election, then the Merit of Christ is said to be a part and the meritorious cause of Election: But if, in the same decree of Election, you attend to the grace of GOD, then the Merit of Christ behaves as an Effect of Election. For that grace of GOD is the fountain and origin, both of the merit of Christ and of our faith.

The passage Acts 13:48 neither helps Huber's cause in the slightest, nor hinders ours. For if it is taken in the Huberian sense, namely that all were ordained to eternal Life without regard to faith, it would follow that all men also believed in Christ: Since the text expressly asserts: 'As many as were ordained to eternal life believed.' But this is manifestly false. Therefore, another and indeed Orthodox sense emerges, namely, that they believed, as many as followed that order sanctioned in the eternal Counsel, by diligently hearing the sermons of the Apostles, learning and glorifying the Word of the Lord: as the words immediately preceding clearly intimate.

Furthermore, Huber clamors that it is absurd to introduce into an eternal act, such as Election is, that which happens in time. Now, however, Faith only reaches us in time, when, namely, we begin to believe by the act itself. Therefore, it would be absurd to include it in the eternal decree of Election.

I respond that this is clearly no absurdity at all: which I prove by these arguments. 1. By the example of human counsels and decrees. For the ends of actions, although they are the last in the act itself, nevertheless occupy the first place in the mind of those deliberating. And just as an artisan conceives the form of a future artifact in his mind first, by whose intuition and consideration he is moved to the structure, which is far later than that mental concept: So what prevents GOD, in electing, from having had regard to faith (which is far later than the election itself, if you consider it by the act in time), who willed that no one be elected except by the condition and order of faith? 2. By the example of the Passion and death of Christ, the same absurdity is dispelled. For no pious and orthodox person will deny that the merit of this was included in that eternal counsel and decree of Predestination: Which same thing we also confirmed above quite evidently. But that death of the Son of GOD followed only in time. Thus, therefore, Election, whose meritorious cause is piously established to have been the Death of Christ, preceded its cause, which is placed in an act, by the very embrace of eternity. Therefore, it is devoid of all absurdity if it is established that GOD, from all eternity, in the Election of those to be saved, had regard to the faith of those who believe, which was to be in time. 3. This whole absurdity vanishes into smoke if one attends properly to the difference between concepts in human minds and that knowledge, or vision, which is in GOD. For the ends of things differ from human counsels by an interval of time, because human actions are subject to the motions and measure of time, in which, also, frustrations not rarely happen to the intention and Counsels of men, from the outcome of the proposed ends, for various reasons. In GOD, however, there is infallible Foreknowledge, or rather Knowledge, or Omniscience. For, speaking properly, GOD foreknows nothing: but He has viewed all future things as most present, from the very last eternity. He therefore foreknew, or rather as it were saw before Him, that some men, by faith in Christ—by the order of which it pleased Him from eternity to elect men—would attune themselves to the divine order, that is, would truly believe: not as if the faith itself of the Elect of GOD were to be future, as He who, outside and above the intervals of time, has all things most perfectly and most presently: but because the faith of the Elect did not yet exist by the very fact, when those who were to believe were not yet in the nature of things: But GOD did not merely foreknow in a confused way that some would believe: but He had most exactly foreknown who those individuals would be, and when they would believe. Considered therefore in this business of eternal Election is Faith, not as in act or in the very deed it already exists kindled in the heart of man through the Holy Spirit: that it finally comes to pass in time is certain enough: but it falls partly under the order and decree of Predestination and of GOD choosing from eternity; partly under His eternal foreknowledge and notice. Nor does this doctrine of ours have anything in common with the Scholastic figment concerning foreseen works, by the intuition of which GOD chose us from eternity. For in both cases there is the greatest disparity. For first, we do not consider Faith in this place as it is a virtue, quality, or some work: but only insofar as it relates to the merit of Christ. Then, Faith apprehending the merit of Christ is not opposed to the grace of GOD: but is subordinated to it. But works are so far from being able to stand with the grace of GOD, either in this or in the article of Justification, that they rather mutually exclude each other: as the Apostle teaches, Rom. 11:6, 'If we are chosen by grace, it is no longer of works, otherwise grace is no longer grace: But if of works, it is no longer of grace: otherwise work is no longer work.' Looking to which, Orthodox Theologians rightly abhor this phrase, which is falsely imputed to us, 'That we are chosen BECAUSE OF faith': Which phrase tacitly presupposes some merit of ours: but they speak thus with Scripture, 'That we are chosen THROUGH Faith,' or in the faith of JESUS CHRIST: in the same sense exactly as we are accustomed to use this phrase in the article of Justification also. 2 Thess. 2:13, ἐν πίςει ἀληθείας.

But a new and sharper Disputation emerges here concerning the Foreknowledge or prevision of faith, namely, whether the decree of Election can and ought to be defined with respect to divine Foreknowledge? Where we indeed hold the affirmative with the Scriptures, while Huber and others fight for the Negative, stubbornly indeed, but in vain. We establish these as the foundations of our affirmative, sufficiently firm and immovable.

1. The entire matter of Predestination is subject to the article of divine Providence: which no one but a prodigiously impious and stupid person would deny. But it is proper to divine Providence that it has knowledge of all things and actions, both good and evil, not finally acquired in time: but conceived from eternity. Therefore, they must necessarily be agitated by a Spirit of Giddiness who would assert that the Faith of the elect was not well known to GOD, who chooses and predestines us in eternity, and subject to His divine foreknowledge, or rather Omniscience: but was unknown.

2. The infallible certainty of our Election is placed solely in this, that we believe GOD is not deceived in choosing, or that Election itself cannot be frustrated of its end, because GOD from eternity had a most perfect view of who would receive grace and who would persevere in it, and who would not. Therefore, Faith will certainly be included in that eternal decree, under the aspect of προγνώσεως: the intuition of which is attributed to GOD, not indeed as it is considered in its own dignity: but as it apprehends Christ the Mediator.

3. The Holy Spirit in the Scriptures clearly asserts and confirms this very thing. For, being expressly occupied with this very matter of Predestination, He speaks thus: 'Whom He foreknew, them He also predestined,' Rom. 8:29, and again: 'God has not cast away His people whom He foreknew,' Rom. 9:2. Thus Peter calls the predestined believers Elect κατὰ πρόγνωσιν Θεῦ πατρὸς, according to the foreknowledge or precognition of GOD the Father, 1 Pet. 1:2.

4. Although in the Book of Concord it is diligently cautioned that we should not think as if Election comprises nothing else, or that nothing else is required for it, or that nothing else should be spent in meditating upon it, except this, that GOD foresaw who and how many men would attain salvation, etc.: yet it so far from simply and entirely excluding or proscribing Foreknowledge from this article, that it is certain that by these very words, when rightly weighed, it is asserted and established. The preceding paragraph teaches this very thing more plainly, in which the eternal Election of GOD is said not only to foresee and foreknow: but also to procure, effect, and promote the salvation of the Elect.

These things being thus confirmed, how this Foreknowledge of GOD stands in the mystery of Election will have to be considered further: which we shall provide explained in the following Aphorisms.

I. The word Foreknowledge in this place is not taken generally, indefinitely, and loosely, concerning the knowledge of all future things: in which sense the Foreknowledge of things both evil and good belongs to GOD: and does not presuppose predestination. But it is taken restrictively and determinately to a certain matter and a certain subject: namely, to the Foreknowledge of faith in Christ, which is proper to the Elect. Which determinate notation of Foreknowledge always presupposes predestination, according to that of Romans 8:29: 'Whom He foreknew,' namely, even with Augustine as interpreter, 'as going to believe in His Son, them He also predestined': and He predestined them indeed to be conformed to the image of His Son. Where Huber is vain and false, barking that GOD wills that all men should be conformed to the image of His Son. For in this place the Apostle does not treat of the antecedent Will of GOD, by reason of which He wills all men to be conformed to the image of His Son: but he treats of those who are already in the very decree of GOD conformed to this image. Whence the Apostle does not say in the Huberine sense that GOD foreknows, that they may be conformed, ἵνα ὦσι σύμμορφοι: but προώρισε συμμόρφες, he predestined them to be conformed to the image of His Son: that which pertains to believers alone.

II. This foreknowledge is not the very predestination of GOD, or the decree of Election, as Calvin asserts, lib. 3. Instit. cap. 23. §. 7. & Marloratus in cap. 9. Rom. vers. 27. For the Apostle in the words just cited Rom. 8, 29. expressly considers two distinct things: Foreknowledge and Predestination: 'Whom,' he says, 'he foreknew, them he also predestinated.' Otherwise, this most absurd sense would emerge: 'Whom he predestinated, them he also predestinated.' And in Peter, 1st chapter, 1, 2: 'He chose us according to the foreknowledge of GOD the Father': this sense would emerge: 'He chose us according to Election.' May such βαττολογία (babbling) be far from being attributed to the Holy Spirit. Rightly, therefore, it is established that the word 'Foreknowledge' in this place denotes, according to the idiom of the Hebrews, the knowledge of GOD, not simple, but with approval and delight: indeed, terminated upon an object pleasing to GOD: namely, upon Christ apprehended by faith: or, which comes to the same thing, upon faith apprehending the merit of Christ.

III. This foreknowledge, which we have said enters into the decree of Election, is not therefore established as a cause for which, or on account of which, election is made, or salvation itself is conferred upon the elect. Nor is it an essential part constituting Election itself: but it is asserted merely as an adjunct of Predestination, and indeed an inseparable one. For Foreknowledge, being placed in an inferior degree, although it can sometimes be separated from Predestination, which happens in sins and the depraved actions of men: yet, Predestination being posited, as the superior degree, it is necessary that the inferior is always included. Hence the Apostle says, 'The foundation of GOD stands firm, having this seal, THE LORD KNOWETH them that are his.' 2 Tim. 2:19. But he does not know them only in time: but he foreknew them from all eternity. This knowledge or πρόγνωσις (foreknowledge) is, therefore, a kind of eye, as it were, of that eternal Election: which, whoever wishes to pluck out, will produce and foist upon us a blind Election.

IV. When the word γνώσεως (knowledge) or προγνώσεως (foreknowledge) is applied to the Elect, as in Rom. 8:29, 1 Peter 1:2, and elsewhere: the sense of a general and indefinite Foreknowledge is not to be understood: as we showed in the first aphorism, but that which is more special, and proper only to the elect, who are προεγνωσμένοι ἐν τῷ προεγνωσμέ- νῳ (foreknown in the foreknown) 1 Pet. 1:20, namely, that which is accommodated to men, not promiscuously and indifferently to all, but limited by a certain respect to Christ: namely, those who will believe in Christ unto eternal life, just as Scripture defines the Elect. 1 Tim. 1:16. According to this πρόγνωσις (foreknowledge), therefore, we are chosen, 1 Pet. 1:2, and in this way, those who are foreknown are also predestinated by GOD. Rom. 8:29. And these very ones, already known to GOD from eternity and inscribed in the book of Life, are declared by Scripture to be Elect.

V. This doctrine concerning the foreknowledge of faith, entering into the decree of Election, does not patronize the madness of the Pelagians, as if anything were established in man by whose merit and dignity he is chosen. For (as was said several times above) these are said to be chosen by GOD not by the merit of faith, but by the order of believing. And Faith, although it is effected in us, does not, however, arise from us. Just as this foreknowledge also

Latin:

Respondeo falsum esse præsuppositum, cui tota hæc ratio superstituitur. Fingitur enim nihil posse, & causæ, & effectus, respectum sortiri, quantumvis diverso sensu ac respectu utrumque de eodem affirmetur: id quod falsum esse, ipsa quoque sanior Philosophia monstrat. Verùm quidem hoc est axioma, in rebus, sub eodem causæ genere positis, & uno eodemque respectu sibi oppositis. Hoc enim pacto nihil potest esse causa & effectum ejusdem. Quia verò Relata vulgò sibi mutuò causæ esse dicuntur, indiverso causæ genenere, dissimilique respectu: nihil certè prohibet, quò minus idem ejusdem & causa, & effectus esse dicatur. Id quod in Electione & fide, relatè se invicem habentibus, locum itidem habere, nihil absurditatis continet. Alioqui propriè loquendo æterna Electio, neque Efficiens causa, neque forma, neque materia Fidei est. Quo respectu neque Fides etiam Effectum Electionis propriè dici potest. Verùm si Fides maximè dicatur Electionis effectum, absurdum non est, sub alio genere causæ, Fidem Electionis, tanquàm sui relati causam constituere. Undè Nicolaus Lyranus super Verba illa Rom. 9. Miseretur cujus vult &c. haud ineptè scribit: In Effectibus divinæ Prædestinationis, Prius semper est causa posterioris, per modum disponentis: Et posterius semper est causa prioris, per modum finis.

Idem Respondemus etiam ad illud alterum: Fides est Consequens Electionis: Ergò non est ejus pars. Nam quædam enunciantur de toto, quà totum est: quædam verò enunciantur de toto propter aliquam ejus partem. Ut Hypocaustum est Effectum domus totius: quatenùs reliqua structura propter hypocaustum est suscepta: Et simul est pars domus: si totum ipsum constitutum spectes. Sic si Electio consideretur, ut quiddam totum, rectè Fides dicitur esse ejus pars, sive causa instrumentalis. Si verò in eodem decreto Electionis, Gratiam DEI spectes, tùm sanè Fides ab eâ dependet, tanquàm Effectum à suâ causâ. Quod ipsum de Merito etiam Christi demonstrari potest. Si enim totum Electionis decretum consideres: tùm Meritum Christi dicitur esse pars, & causa meritoria Electionis: Sin autem in eodem Electionis decreto Gratiam DEI attendas, tùm Meritum Christi habet se ut Effectum Electionis. Nam Gratia illa DEI est fons & origo, tùm meriti Christi, tùm nostræ fidei.

Locus Actor. 13, 48. Neque Huberi causam vel tantillum juvat, neque nostræ officit. Nam si sensu Huberiano ille accipiatur, nempè ordinatos fuisse omnes ad Vitam æternam sine intuitu fidei, sequetur, omnes etiam homines credidisse in Christum: Siquidem textus expressè asserit: Credidisse, quotquot ordinati fuerant ad vitam æternam: Atqui hoc manifestè falsum. Ergò sensus alius & quidem Orthodoxus emergit iste, Quòd crediderint, quotquot ordinem illum in æterno Consilio sancitum sunt secuti, diligenter audiendo Conciones Apostolorum, discendo & glorificando Verbum Domini: uti verba immediatè præcedentia dilucidè innuunt.

Porrò absurdum esse clamitat Huberus, id quod in tempore fit, actui æterno, qualis est Electio, inferere. Jam verò Fides in tempore demùm nobis obtingit, quando nimirùm ipso actu credere incipimus. Ergò absurdum fuerit, eam æterno Electionis decreto includere.

Respondeo absurdum hoc planè nullum esse : idquod his argumentis probo. 1. Humanorum Consiliorum & decretorum exemplo. Nam fines actionum, cùm actu ipso sint postremum : in mente tamen deliberantium primas occupant. Et quemadmodum artifex formam artificij futuri mente concipit primùm, cujus intuitu & consideratione, ad structuram, conceptu illo mentis longè posteriorem movetur : Ita quid obstet, quò minùs ad fidem (electione ipsâ longè posteriorem, si actu in tempore consideres) respectum habere potuerit DEUS in eligendo, qui non nisi conditione & ordine fidei electum esse quenquam voluit? 2. Exemplo Passionis & mortis Christi eadem absurditas dipellitur. Nam meritum hujus, consilio illi & decreto Prædestinationis æterno inclusum fuisse, nemo pius & orthodoxus inficiabitur : Quod ipsum & nos suprà satis evidenter confirmavimus. Atqui mors illa Filij DEI in tempore demùm secuta fuit. Sic ergò Electio, cujus causa meritoria Mors Christi fuisse piè statuitur, causam suam in actu positam æternitatis ipsius complexu antecessit. Omni proindè absurditate caret, si DEUS ab omni æternitate in Electione salvandorum ad fidem credentium quæ in tempore futura erat, respectum habuisse statuatur. 3. In fumum abit universa hæc absurditas, si ad discrimen inter conceptus in humanis mentibus, & inter notitiam, seu visionem illam, quæ est in DEO, probè attendatur. Nam fines rerum à consilijs humanis temporum intervallo ideò discrepant, quia motibus & mensuræ temporis actiones humanæ subjacent, in quibus etiam intentioni & Consilijs hominum, ab eventu finium propositorum, varijs de causis non rarò frustrationes contingunt. In DEO autem Præscientia est infallibilis, imò Scientia potiùs, aut Omniscientia. Nam propriè loquendo DEUS nihil præscit: sed futura omnia ceu præsentissima, indè ab ultimâ usque æternitate coràm est intuitus. Prænovit ergò, imò quasi coràm vidit, aliquos ex hominibus, fide in Christum, cujus ordine eligere homines ipsi ab æterno placuit, sese ordini divino attemperaturos, hoc est, verè credituros esse: non quasi fides ipsa Electorum DEI fuerit futura, ut qui extra & supra temporum intervalla, omnia habet & perfectissima & præsentissima : sed quòd fides Electorum facto ipso tùm nondùm fuerit, cum nondùm in rerum naturâ essent, qui erant credituri: Non autem confusè tantùm credituros aliquos præscivit DEUS: sed quinám illi in individuo futuri essent, & quandò credituri, exactissimè præcognitum habuit. Consideratur ergò in hoc Electionis æternæ negotio Fides, non ut eaactu sive facto ipso, jam in corde hominis, per Spiritum Sanctum accensa existit: quod in tempore demùm fieri, satis certum est: sed ut illa partim sub Praedestinationis, atque ab aeterno eligentis DEI ordinem & decretum; partim sub ejusdem praescientiam & notitiam aeternam cadit. Neque quicquam commune nostra haec habet doctrina cum figmento Scholasticorum de operibus praevisis, quorum intuitu DEUS ab aeterno nos elegerit. Nam utrobique maxima est disparitas. Primùm enim Fidem hoc loco etiam non consideramus, prout est Virtus, qualitas aut opus aliquod: sed tantùm, quatenùs relatè se habet ad meritum Christi. Deindè Fides apprehendens meritum Christi, non opponitur Gratiae DEI: sed ei subordinatur. Opera verò tàm non cum Gratiâ DEI, vel in hoc, vel in Justificationis articulo stare possunt, ut potiùs se mutuò excludant: sic docente Apostolo, Rom, 11, 6 Quod si per gratiam electi sumus, non jam ex operibus, alioquin gratia jam non est gratia: Sin ex operibus, jam non ex gratiâ: alioquin opus jam non est opus. Quò respicientes Orthodoxi Theologi, rectè abhorrent ab hac phrasi, quae per calumniam nobis affingitur, Quod electi simus PROPTER fidem: Quae phrasis aliquod nostrum meritum tacitè praesupponit: sed sic loquuntur cum Scripturâ, Quod electi simus PER Fidem, sive in fide JESU CHRISTI: eodem planè sensu, quo in articulo etiam Justificationis hac phrasi uti solemus. 2. Thess. 2, 13. ἐν πίςει ἀληθείας.

Sed nova hîc & acrior emergit Disputatio de Praescientiâ sive praevisione fidei, An nimirùm Praescientiae divinae respectu Electionis decretum definiri possit & debeat? ubi nos sanè affirmantem cum Scripturis tenemus Hubero, & alijs pro Negativâ mordicùs quidem, sed frustrà pugnantibus. Nos affirmativae nostrae fundamenta haec potissimùm constituimus, satis firma & immota.

1. Providentiae divinae articulo subjacet universa Praedestinationis materia: id quod nemo nisi prodigiosè impius & stupidus negaverit. Atqui providentiae divinae proprium est, ut rerum & actionum omnium tùm bonarum, tùm malarum notitiam habeat, non in tempore demùm acquisitam: sed ab aeterno conceptam, Ergò Vertiginis Spiritu agitentur necesse est, qui Fidem electorum DEO in aeternitate nos eligenti ac praedestinanti, non probè notam, & divinae ipsius praescientiae, vel Omniscientiae potiùs subjectam: sed incognitam fuisse afferere velint.

2. In eo unicè infallibilis certitudo Electionis nostrae est posita, quod ideò DEUM in eligendo non falli, aut Electionem ipsam fine suo frustrari non posse credimus, quia DEUS ab aeterno perspectissimum habuerit, qui sint recepturi gratiam, inque ea perseveraturi, qui minùs. Erit ergò utique aeterno illi decreto inclusa Fides, sub ratione προγνώσεως : cujus intuitus DEO tribuitur, non quidem ut in propriâ dignitate illa consideratur: sed ut Christum Mediatorem apprehendit.

3. Spiritus Sanctus in Scripturis hoc ipsum liquidò asserit & confirmat. Nam in hâc ipsâ Prædestinationis materiâ ex professo occupatus sic loquitur: Quos præscivit, hos prædestinavit, Rom. 8, 29. & rursus: Non abjecit Deus populum suum, quem præscivit Rom. 9, 2. Sic Petrus fideles prædestinatos appellat Electos κατὰ πρόγνωσιν Θεῦ πατρὸς secundum præscientiam sive præcognitionem DEI patris, 1. Petr. 1, 2.

4. Quamvis in libro Concordiæ sedulò cavetur, ne putemus, quasi nihil prætereà complectatur Electio, aut ad eam requiratur, aut in eâ meditanda expendendum sit, nisi hoc, quod præviderit DEUS, quinám & quot homines salutem sint consecuti &c: tamen Præscientiam ex hoc articulo, adeò non simpliciter & omninò excludit aut proscribit, ut verbis his ipsis rectè ponderatis, asseri eam & stabiliri certum sit. Quod ipsum planiùs docet præcedens paragraphus, quo æterna DEI Electio, non tantùm prævidere & præscire: sed & procurare, efficere & promovere Electorum salutem dicitur.

His ita confirmatis, Quomodo Præscientia hæc DEI in Electionis mysterio se habeat, porrò considerandum fuerit: id quod sequentibus Aphorismis expeditum dabimus.

I. Præscientiæ vox hoc loco non accipitur generaliter, indefinitè & laxè, de notitiâ rerum futurarum omnium: Quo sensu rerum tàm malarum, quàm bonarum Præscientia DEO competit: & prædestinationem non præsupponit. Sed restrictè ac determinatè ad certam materiam, certumque subjectum: nempè ad Præscientiam fidei in Christum, quæ est Electorum propria. Quæ determinata Præscientiæ notatio, semper Prædestinationem præsupponit, secundum illud Romanor. 8, 29. Quos præscivit, nempè Augustino etiam interprete, credituros in Filium suum, hos & prædestinavit: & prædestinavit quidem conformes imagini Filij sui. Ubi vanus & falsus Huberus est, ogganniens, DEUM velle, ut omnes homines sint conformes imagini Filij sui. Nam hoc loco Apostolus non agit de Voluntate DEI antecedente, ratione cujus vult omnes homines esse conformes imagini Filij sui: sed agit de ijs, qui jam in ipso DEI decreto sunt conformes imagini huic. Undè Apostolus non dicit sensu Huberiano DEUM præscire, ut sint conformes, ἵνα ὦσι σύμμορφοι: sed προώρισε συμμόρφες, prædestinavit conformes imagini Filij sui: id quod solis credentibus competit.

II. Præscientia hæc non est ipsa DEI prædestinatio, sive decretum Electionis, uti Calvinus autumat, lib. 3. Instit. cap. 23. §. 7. & Marloratus in cap. 9. Rom. vers. 27. Nam Apostolus in verbis modò citatis Rom. 8, 29. expressè tanquàm duo distincta considerat Præscientiam & Prædestinationem: Quos, inquiens, præscivit, hos & prædestinavit. Alioquin ineptissimus iste sensus prodiret: Quos prædestinavit, hos & prædestinavit: Et apud Petrum 1. cap. 1, 2. Elegit nos secundum præcognitionem DEI patris: sensus emergeret iste: Elegit nos secundum Electionem. Quæ βαττολογία absit, ut Spiritui Sancto tribuatur. Rectè ergò statuitur, quod Præscientiæ vox hoc loco notet juxta Hebræorum idiotismum notitiam DEI, non simplicem, sed cum approbatione & delectatione: quippè terminatam ad objectum DEI placens: videlicet ad Christum fide apprehensum: vel quod eodem recidit, ad fidem apprehendentem Christi meritum.

III. Præscientia hæc, quam diximus ingredi decretum Electionis non ideò statuitur esse causa, ob vel propter quam fiat electio, aut salus ipsa electis conferatur. Quin neque pars essentialis est constituens ipsam Electionem: sed pro adjuncto duntaxat Prædestinationis, & quidem inseparabili astruitur. Nam Præscientia, quippè inferiori gradu posita, tametsi à Prædestinatione aliquando possit esse seclusa, quod fit in peccatis, & pravis hominum actionibus: Posita tamen prædestinatione, quippè gradu superiore, inferiorem semper includi necessum est. Hinc Apostolus, Firmum, inquit, stat fundamentum DEI, habens hoc signaculum, NOVIT DEUS, qui sunt ejus. 2. Tim. 2, 19. Non novit autem in tempore demùm: sed præcognovit indè ab omni æternitate. Est proindè notitia sive πρόγνωσις isthæc, quidam quasi oculus Electionis illius æternæ: quem qui eruere voluerit, cæcam nobis pariet & obtrudet Electionem.

IV. Quando ad Electos accommodatur vocabulum γνώσεως aut προγνώσεως, ut Rom. 8, 29. 1. Petri 1, 2. & alibi: non generalis duntaxat & indefinitæ Præscientiæ sensus intelligendus est: uti in primo aphorismo ostendimus, sed is, qui est specialior, & electorum duntaxat proprius, qui sunt προεγνωσμένοι ἐν τῷ προεγνωσμένῳ 1. Petr. 1, 20. nempè qui est accommodatus ad homines, non promiscuè & indifferenter omnes, sed certo quodam respectu ad Christum limitatos: credituros nimirùm in Christum ad vitam æternam, quemadmodum Scriptura Electos definit. 1. Tim. 1, 16. Secundum hanc ergò πρόγνωσιν electi sumus, 1. Petr. 1, 2. & hoc modo præsciti qui sunt, ij à DEO prædestinati etiam sunt. Rom. 8, 29. Et hi ipsi DEO jam indè ab æterno noti, & in libro Vitæ consignati, hoc est, Electi esse à Scripturâ perhibentur.

V. Doctrina hæc de Præscientiâ fidei, ingrediente Electionis decretum, non patrocinatur furiori Pelagianorum, quasi quicquam statuatur in homine, cujus merito, & dignitate eligatur. Nam (uti suprà aliquoties dictum) non merito fidei: sed ordine credendi, præsciti isti dicuntur à DEO eligi. Et Fides, quamvis in nobis efficitur: non tamen ex nobis oritur. Quemadmodum præcognitio etiam hæc


### VII. Special Controversy, Concerning the Consequent Will of GOD: and the difference of this from the Antecedent: Becomes absolute

becomes absolute,

is not the cause of our Election: but rather that foreknown CHRIST JESUS, whom GOD the Father beholds in that πρόγνωσις (foreknowledge) of His under the order of faith, and on account of Him chooses those believing, or who will believe in Him, unto life.

These things having been established in this manner for the confirmation of our thesis, it may be clear what must be answered when it is asked: If Election is ordered under the condition of persevering faith, does Election therefore depend on the faith of men, or does faith depend on election? For both can be said not inconveniently in their own way, but under a different respect. For because Election is ordered, therefore, insofar as there is a mutual connection between those things which mutually respect each other in order: to that extent, Faith also depends on Election: and conversely, faith depends on Election: since they are not chosen by GOD unless they believe unto the end, and vice versa, they do not believe unto the end unless they are chosen. Therefore, faith depends on Election, just as its determination or condition depends on its determined: or as its subordinate depends on its ordered: Conversely, election depends on faith, not indeed as on an impulsive or meritorious cause: since, as has been shown, we are not chosen on account of faith: but as the determined from its determination.

Latin:

fit absoluta,

fidei non est causa nostræ Electionis: sed præcognitus potiùs ille CHRISTUS JESUS, quem sub ordine fidei, in suâ illâ προγνώσει aspicit DEUS Pater, & propter hunc credentes, sive credituros in ipsum, ad vitam eligit.

His in hunc modum pro confirmatione theseos nostræ constitutis, perspicuum sit, quid respondendum, quando quæritur: Si Electio est ordinata sub conditione fidei perseverantis, Anné igitur Electio pendeat à fide hominum an verò fides ab electione? Utrumque enim suo modo haud incommodè dici potest, sed sub diverso respectu. Quia enim ordinata est Electio, ergò quatenùs inter ea, quæ mutuo ordine respiciunt, mutuus quidam nexus est: eatenùs & ab Electione Fides: & rursum: fides ab Electione pendet: siquidem non sunt electi à DEO, nisi credentes, ad finem usque & vice versa, credunt ad finem, non nisi electi. Pendet ergò ab Electione fides, quemadmodum à determinato sua pendet determinatio sive conditio: vel sicut ab ordinato suum subordinatum: Rurso pendet à fide electio, non quidem ut à causâ impulsivâ, aut meritoriâ: siquidem, ut ostensum, non propter fidem electi sumus: verùm ut determinatum à suâ determinatione.


### Question IV. Whether Election be Universal or rather Particular

On the occasion of the Huberian controversy, this Question also began to be agitated: and indeed in a far different sense and respect than that in which it was previously disputed against the Calvinists concerning the Universality of Election, and it was asked: If Election is particular, is the cause of that particularity in GOD who chooses, or in men? However, a confused and indistinct signification of terms caused some among the Orthodox, even before the Huberian controversy was stirred up, to establish a Universal, others a Particular Election: yet without any contradiction: since both were asserted not in one and the same sense and respect: but in a very different one. For first, a certain limited Universality is also granted, under the condition of faith. And this Universality is defined and completed by the inclusion and universality of all who believe in Christ and persevere in faith. In this sense, no Orthodox person will deny that Election is determinately universal, namely in that way in which, in their own kind, the Evangelical Promises truly are and are called Universal. Such a universal proposition is this: All who believe in Christ unto the end are elect. And this universality is opposed to that absolute Particularity which simply excludes every respect and consideration of order, and thus of faith: such a particularity as the Sacramentarians impiously and blasphemously invent.

Furthermore, the term election is sometimes used loosely and improperly in the disputes of theologians for the love of God, or for that universal benevolence of the antecedent will in God toward the whole human race. This meaning of the word election is indeed improper and clearly abusive, both because it is destitute of the support of Scripture and because it lacks the consensus of the Orthodox Church; but it was borrowed from the Sacramentarians, for whom love in God is just as broad as election, or rather they are clearly synonyms and equivalent. The impropriety and misuse of this word is also evident from the fact that the word election, taken in this way, does not express the whole nature and essence of the thing, but only a part; namely, at least the first cause or part of our election. Now, no learned man will ever deny that a part is improperly and figuratively put for the whole. Some other Orthodox theologians, when placed in the arena of debate, and even in homiletic sermons expressly opposed to the impiety of the Sacramentarians, followed this impropriety of the word election, which was born in the schools of the Sacramentarians, and by using the word election for the general love of God, they asserted a universal election of God; intending thus to oppose that horrible figment of the Calvinist race concerning the absolute reprobation of the damned. However, since the charge of defection, or at least of most shameful contradiction, is today leveled against these theologians by Huber, on the grounds that universal and particular election cannot be asserted without a manifest implication of contradiction, we must look a little more accurately at how this charge ought to be repelled by our side. We maintain, however, that before the Huberian controversy was stirred up, both, that is, universal and particular election, were defended by Orthodox theologians without any charge of true contradiction: and it pleases us to set this forth in their own words. For 1. They asserted universal election in a different subject matter, as it were, namely in the question of divine love and the merciful will in God; but particular election in the proper place of predestination. 2. The former was brought against the Sacramentarians: the latter is constructed against other schismatics: for because for the Sacramentarians election and love are one and the same thing, and yet love is granted by them to be only particular, for the very reason that election, which is just as broad as love and is one and the same thing, is likewise particular: certainly nothing prevented universal election from being asserted against them at that time, with the term election being used for the word love. 3. The former was done and granted by hypothesis: but the latter was asserted in a categorical sense. One may seek a very illustrious example from the Scriptures by which all suspicion of contradiction is removed in such phrases. The Apostle says in Rom. 14:8, Whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. Now, however, Christ says in Matt. 22:32, God is not the God of the dead. Where it is certainly rightly denied that a contradiction is implied in these statements. For the opposition was not made according to the same thing, nor in respect to the same thing. The former statement uses the word dead in its proper and genuine sense; but the latter in an improper sense, namely that which the Sadducees attributed to this word, who called the dead those who were reduced entirely to nothing and were alienated from all hope of resurrection. Christ, therefore, using this word hypothetically, and in that sense which held weight among his adversaries, when he denied that God is the God of the dead, did not contradict by even a jot the Apostle, who asserted that the dead are also the Lord's. But let these things suffice for the defense of those theologians who, before the new controversy of Huber, asserted universal election against the Sacramentarians.

But after Huber, twenty years ago, brought a lawsuit against Orthodox theologians under the guise of universal election, and contended that election properly so called is universal, of those who do not believe as well as those who do believe; and this fanatical opinion gave the Sacramentarians an opportunity to write publicly that such a universal election is taught in our churches, by which dogs, wolves, swine, and all the impious and reprobate enjoy the benefit of Christ's death, and all men without distinction are cleansed from sins and sanctified into the temple of God: here, certainly, our theologians realized that one must speak more cautiously and circumspectly in this matter. Therefore, just as they always rejected the fatal and absolute particularity of the Calvinists, so now they also relegated the Huberian universality to hell; and at the same time they proscribed from the Church the impropriety of the word election, which had hitherto been as it were accepted by usage: yet in such a way that they left it free for Huber, abounding in his own sense, to assert a universal election, provided he publicly confessed that he was speaking improperly and catachrestically, with the word election being used for the love of God. Since this could not be obtained from him, but rather he contended that election according to the Scriptures, and in its most proper sense, is universal and consists of the inclusion of both unbelievers and believers: there at last the controversy erupted into an open schism, and the Orthodox, making a divorce from Huber, contended that election properly so called must be defined as nothing other than particular and consisting of the inclusion of believers alone, and those who persevere in faith to the end. To whose opinion we also willingly subscribe, relying not only on the authority of the Book of Concord, which contradicts the Huberian dogma expressly, but especially on the oracles of the Scriptures and other reasons and arguments, taken from the analogy of faith, which are clearly invincible.

For first, that classic saying of the Savior is inculcated here: Matt. 20:16 and ch. 22:14, Many are called, but few are chosen. From which saying a universal election will not be built up until it has been demonstrated that it is so, that white is black. For as for the fact that Huber distinguishes between the elect and those elected, that is, between those elected nominally and those so called participially, it is clearly frivolous and trifling, as was abundantly demonstrated above in special Controversy 1. And this one testimony alone is so clear and evident that it could suffice even by itself in this question. But more remain. 2. Scripture everywhere accurately distinguishes between the elect and the non-elect, between believers and unbelievers. But if the Universality of Election is posited, the distinction between the Elect and the Non-Elect has no place. Therefore. The major premise is proved by these sayings: Matt. 24:24, "So as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect." John 15:19, "I chose you out of the world." John 17:6, "I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world." And verse 9, "I am not praying for the world, but for those whom you have given me." 1 Cor. 1:27, Those who are held to be chosen by GOD are, by antithesis, opposed to the wise of this world. Rom. 9:5, The remnant of the Elect are separated from the rest of the multitude. 3. Scripture calls only those who are to be saved and those who believe the elect. But not all believe to the end, nor are all saved. Therefore. The Apostle shows a sufficiently evident proof of the major premise in the passage, Rom. 8:30. Whom He foreknew, He also predestined. But not all are foreknown, having regard to faith. Therefore, neither are all predestined. Thus, Whom He predestined, these He also called: Therefore, Election is not to be extended outside the company of the called. Furthermore, whom He called, these He also justified: But none are justified except those who believe. Therefore. Finally, Whom He justified, these He also glorified: But glorification or salvation is not for all: Therefore. 4. The elect are distinguished in the Scriptures by such marks as in no way belong to the universality of men: Therefore, Universal Election does not exist. The antecedent is proved by these sayings: Matt. 24:24. The elect do not perish in errors. John 6:37. They come to Christ, inasmuch as they are given by the Father, not merely under the rationale of redemption, which is general to all, but under the peculiar mode of Election. Johan. 10, 28. they are not snatched from the hands of the shepherd: but they know him, follow him, and hear his voice. Act. 13, 48. They believe most certainly. Rom. 8, 33. 35. they are not accused, they are not separated from the love of Christ. Ephes. 1, 5. They are adopted as sons of God, Jacob. 2, 5. They are rich in faith. Apocal. 13, 8. they adore Christ, and their names are written in the book of life. Apoc. 17, 14. they fight under the banner of Christ. Now, truly, all these things do not belong to the universality of the human race: therefore, neither does Election belong to it. 5. Election is not made except in Christ. Ephes. 1, 4. And yet not all are in Christ, but only those who through faith are grafted into Christ. Therefore, Election is also proper only to these, and not indeed to all. 6. True and constant faith belongs only to the elect of God, Tit. 1, 1. But that faith is not of all, 2. Thess. 3, 2. Therefore, neither is Election of all. 7. To whom the definition of Election does not apply, to him the thing defined does not apply either. But the definition of Election does not apply to the greatest part of men. Therefore, neither does the thing defined: and consequently Election will be particular, not universal. The assumption is proved by an induction of all the forms which, according to the Scriptures, constitute the definition of Election: as that Election is defined only by the implication of a saving end and outcome, which is faith, persevering to the end, salvation, and eternal blessedness.

8. Eternal Reprobation does not at all admit of universal Election. For neither can stand together with respect to all men. But Eternal Reprobation cannot be denied: as was demonstrated in the preceding question 2. Therefore.

9. The consensus of the Church is added: In the Council of Constance, that article of John Hus was condemned, that the Church of Christ is the university of the predestined. Regarding this condemnation, B. Luther said at the Diet of Worms that this article of the Apostles' Creed had been condemned: I believe in the Holy Catholic Church. For the defense of which article, Luther said that he did not refuse to expend both his life and his blood. Hence it is gathered with invincible truth: If the Church of Christ is the university of the predestined, it can in no way come to pass that the predestination of the sons of GOD extends outside the Church of Christ and to the universality of the whole human race. See the history of the life and acts of Luther written by Phil. Mel. fol. D. 4. And Luther’s commentary on chapter 17 of John, Vol. 6 of the German works, Jena, page 169.

10. The decision of the Book of Concord pertains to this matter, the formal words of which are these: Predestination, or the eternal election of God, pertains only to the good and beloved children of God. Item: All those who attain eternal salvation are inscribed in the book of life. Epitome, art. 11, on predestination, § 4 & 6. Item: The eternal election, or predestination of God to salvation, does not pertain to the good and the bad alike, but only to the children of God, who were chosen and ordained to attain eternal life before the foundations of the world were laid: page 770. Item: It must by no means be thought that those who despise the Word of God are to be held in the number of the elect: whence the Book of Concord concludes that, according to these reasons, it must be understood what Scripture says: that many are called, but few are chosen. Item: The eternal election of God the Father is to be sought in Christ. He indeed in his eternal counsel decreed that, besides those who acknowledge his Son Jesus Christ and truly believe in him, he wills to save no one.

11. If the eternal Election of God regards both those who do not believe and those who do believe, it would follow that God, in that eternal decree and counsel of His, made no distinction between those who were to believe and those who were not to believe: but without any respect to either faith or incredulity, He absolutely elected and ordained to eternal life as well those whom He knew would either never believe in Christ, or certainly would not believe unto the end, as those whom He knew would believe in Him. But this is prodigiously blasphemous, both against the eternal providence of GOD and against His supreme justice: which is evident from those things which we have argued a little before, both concerning the twofold decree of the Consequent Will in GOD, and indeed both made from all eternity, and also concerning eternal Reprobation.

12. While the Universal Election of all men indifferently stands without regard to faith in CHRIST: contrary wills emerge in GOD: The one, that eternal will, which according to Huber is such: I, GOD, will that all men whatsoever, whether they believe or do not believe, be elected to eternal life. The other, a temporal one, and it is such: I will

GOD, that only believers are elected to eternal life: but that unbelievers fall away by the grace of Election. How absurd a Theology this is, and how Huberus wishes to reconcile it with the Scriptures and the analogy of faith, let him see to it himself.

Moved by these reasons, we have determined that Election is nothing but Particular, and determined by the inclusion of only those who believe to the end: the reason for which Particularity can be demonstrated by four hypotheses:

I. The particularity of Election detracts nothing at all from the Universality of the merciful will in GOD: nor is it ἀντιφατικῶς (contradictorily) opposed to Universal Love: but this particular Election is most rightly placed under, or subordinated to, that Universal will and good pleasure in GOD, by its own certain and legitimate reason, just as the Consequent will is subordinated to the Antecedent will, without any contradiction. For because GOD wills all to be saved, but under the condition of faith in Christ: it results that those who do not believe fall away from salvation, not by the fault of the divine will, but by the fault of their own infidelity. An example of this matter can be seen in every will, even a human one, that is Universal but ordered: as was shown more fully above, where we discussed the mutual affection of the Antecedent and Consequent will.

II. The particularity of Election does not shut the door of salvation to any mortal by any decree of GOD. The reason is most manifest: for that GOD chose a few, and not all, did not happen because He simply did not wish to choose all, or did not wish, or does not now wish, all to be saved from eternity: which indeed to think of GOD is more impious than impiety itself. But because He foreknew that a few, not all, would be converted by His Word, that is, would receive the offered grace, and thus would be saved. For the will of GOD concerning the salvation of all is not absolute, but ordered. Since the greatest part of men neglects this order, the particularity of those who are saved emerges, certainly by their own will, not by the fault of GOD.

III. The particularity of Election, such as it is asserted and defended in our Churches, has nothing in common with the Calvinian dogma. For although particularity is taught in both places and in general: yet the reason, nature, and affection of each is most diverse, and differs from the other as much as heaven from earth. For the Calvinists make their Particularity an absolute and fatal decree, as if GOD never wished all men to be saved. But we assert such a particularity that is subordinated to the Universal divine will concerning the salvation of all: as has been shown many times hitherto.

IV. The cause of this particularity is in no way to be sought or established in GOD, and least of all is it to be referred to the simple and absolute decree of His good pleasure, as if GOD from eternity, by some absolute and simple will that preceded all causes, had established such a distinction among men to be created, that He immutably decreed to save some, and those very few, without any respect to faith: but to consign others, and those very many, to eternal damnation, without any intuition of infidelity. But this Particularity emerges solely from the incredulity and final impenitence of men, by which the offered grace is wickedly spurned by them, and the word of salvation and faith in Christ—by the acceptance of which the damned and reprobate themselves could have been co-opted among the elect—is stubbornly repudiated. Scripture expresses this cause of Particularity everywhere, when it asserts that most people impiously despise the riches of divine goodness, Rom. 2:4; that they do not receive the true light coming into this world, John 1:11; that they love darkness more than light, John 3:19; that they refuse to hear the Son of GOD, whom the heavenly Father commanded to be heard, and refuse to know the time of their visitation and the things that make for their peace, Luke 19:44; indeed, that they do not wish to be gathered by Christ, Matt. 23:37; that some even crucify Christ to themselves again, and after receiving the knowledge of the truth, sin voluntarily, Heb. 6:6 and ch. 10:26; and deny Him who redeemed them, 2 Pet. 2:1, etc. And what need is there of many words, when GOD Himself expressly removes every cause of this particularity from Himself and transfers it to men alone: saying, Your destruction, O Israel, is from yourself: salvation is from me, Hosea 13:9.

Latin:

Occafione certaminis Huberiani hæc etiam Quæstio agitari cœpta fuit: & quidem longè alio sensu ac respectu, quàm quo contra Calvinianos de Electionis Universalitate disputatum anteà fuit, & quæsitum: Si particularis est Electio, nùm particularitatis illius causa sit in DEO eligente, an in hominibus? Fecit autem confusa & in distincta terminorum significatio, ut inter Orthodoxos, & quidem ante motum certamen Huberianum, aliqui Universalem: alij Particularem Electionem statuerent: sine ullâ tamen contradictione: siquidem non uno eodemque sensu ac respectu utrumque asserebatur: sed longè diversissimo. Nam primùm datur Universalitas etiam quædam limitata, sub conditione fidei. Et hæc Universalitas definitur & absolvitur, omnium in Christum credentium, inque fide perseverantium, complexu & universalitate. Hoc sensu Electionem determinatè universalem esse, nemo Orthodoxus negaverit, eo nempè modo, quo in suo genere, Promissiones Evangelicæ, verè sunt & dicuntur Universales. Talis universalis propositio est hæc: Omnes ad finem usquè in Christum credentes, sunt electi. Et opponitur hæc universalitas illi Particularitati absolutæ, quæ omnem ordinis, & sic fidei respectum & confiderationem simpliciter excludit: qualem particularitatem Sacramentarij impiè & blasphemè fingunt.

Deindè Electionis terminus interdum in Theologorum disputationibus laxè & impropriè sumitur, pro dilectione DEI, sive pro universali illâ antecedentis in DEO voluntatis benevolentiâ erga totùm genus humanum. Est verò hæc significatio vocabuli Electionis impropria & planè abusiva, tùm quia Scripturæ destituitur præsidio, tùm Ecclesiæ Orthodoxæ caret consensu: sed transsumta à Sacramentarijs, quibus æquè latè patet dilectio in DEO, atque electio, imò planè sunt συνώνυμα καὶ ἰσοδυναμῶντα. Improprietas autem & κατάχρησις vocabuli hujus vel indè etiam elutescit, quòd hoc modo sumtum vocabulum Electionis, non totam rei naturam & essentiam exprimit: sed partem tantùm: nempè primam saltem Electionis nostræ causam sive partem. Jam verò partem pro toto impropriè & figuratè poni, nemo doctus unquam inficiabitur. Improprietatem hanc vocabuli Electionis, in Scholis Sacramentariorum natam, nonnulli Orthodoxi aliàs Theologi, in foro disputatorio constituti, quin & pro concionibus homiliticis, Sacramentariorum impietati ex professo oppositis, secuti sunt; & Electionis vocabulo, pro dilectione DEI generali usurpato, Universalem DEI electionem statuerunt: sic horrendum illud Calvinianæ gentis figmentum, de absolutâ damnatorum reprobatione oppugnaturi. Cæterùm cùm ab Hubero hodiè defectionis, vel certè turpissimæ contradictionis crimen istis Theologis impingatur, eò quòd Universalis & Particularis Electio, sine manifestâ ἀντιφάσεως implicatione statui non possit: dispiciendum paulò accuratiùs, quomodo & istud crimen à nostris propulsari debeat. Sic autem statuimus, ante motam controversiam Huberianam, utrumque, hoc est, Universalem & Particularem Electionem, ab Orthodoxis Theologis, sive ullo veræ ἀντιφάσεως crimine defensam fuisse: id quod ipsorummet verbis expeditum dare placet. Nam 1. Universalem Electionem statuerunt in alienâ quasi materiâ, nempè in Quæstione dilectionis divinæ, & misericordis in DEO voluntatis: Particularem verò in loco Prædestinationis proprio. 2. Illud contra Sacramentarios affertum fuit: hoc contra alios Schismaticos astruictur: Quia enim Sacramentarijs electio & dilectio unum quiddam sunt: Dilectio autem ab ijsdem tantùm particularis conceditur, eam scilicet ob causam, quia Electio quoque, quæ cum dilectione æquè latè pateat, & unum quiddam sit, itidem est particularis: nihil certè obstitit, quò minùs tùm adversus istos Electio Universalis afferi potuerit: Electionis termino pro Dilectionis vocabulo usurpato. 3. Illud ex hypothesi factum & concessum fuit: Hoc verò sensu categorico assertum fuit. Ex Scripturis illustre admodùm exemplum petere licet, quo contradictionis omnis suspicio in ejusmodi phrasibus tollitur. Apostolus dicit Rom. 14, 8. Sive vivamus, sive moriamur, DEI sumus. Jam verò CHRISTUS Matth. 22, 32. dicit: DEUS non est DEUS mortuorum. Ubi sanè rectè negatur dictis istis ἀντίφασις implicari. Nam non secundum idem, neque respectu ejusdem facta est oppositio. Prius illud dictum proprio & germano sensu vocabulum mortuorum usurpat: Posteriùs verò sensu improprio, eo nimirùm, quem vocabulo huic Sadducæi affingebant, qui mortuos appellabant prorsus in nihilum redactos, & à spe omni resurrectionis alienos. Christus ergò hypotheticè usus isto vocabulo, idque sensu eo, qui valebat apud adversarios suos, cùm DEUM negavit esse DEUM mortuorum, ne γρῦ quidem contradixit Apostolo, qui mortuos etiam DEI esse asseveraverit. Sed hæc sufficiant pro defensione eorum Theologorum, qui ante novam Huberi controversiam, Universalem Electionem contra Sacramentarios statuerunt.

Postquàm verò annis ab hinc viginti Huberus sub Universali Electione Orthodoxis Theologis litem intendit, & Electionem propriè sic dictam contendit esse Universalem, tam eorum qui non credunt, quàm qui credunt: & hæc fanatica opinio ansam præbuit Sacramentarijs, ut publicè Scriptitarent, talem Universalem Electionem nostris in Ecclesiis doceri, quâ canes, lupi, porci & impij ac reprobi omnes, mortis Christi beneficio fruantur, & omnes indifferenter homines à peccatis mundentur, & in templum DEI sanctificentur: hîc certè nostrates Theologi cautiùs, ac circumspectiùs hac in materiâ loquendum esse animadverterunt. Quemadmodum ergò Calvinianorum particularitatem fatalem, atque absolutam semper reprobarunt: ita jam quoque Huberianam universalitatem ad orcum relegarunt: simulque improprietatem vocabuli Electionis hactenùs usu quasi receptam, ex Ecclesiâ proscripserunt: ita tamen, ut Hubero liberum quasi relinquerent, ut suo ipse sensu abundans, Electionem statueret Universalem, modò publicè fateretur, se impropriè & καταχρηστικῶς loqui, Electionis vocabulo pro Dilectione Dei usurpato. Quòd cùm ab ipso obtineri non posset, quin potiùs ille contenderet, Electionem secundum scripturas, & in propriissimo suo sensu esse Universalem, & tàm incredulorum, quàm credentium complexu constare: ibi demùm Controversia in apertum Schisma erupit, & Orthodoxi ab Hubero divortium facientes, Electionem propriè sic dictam, non nisi particularem & solorum credentium, inquè fide ad finem usque perseverantium complexu definiendam esse, contenderunt. Quorum sententiæ & nos ultrò subscribimus: freti non modò autoritate libri Concordiæ, qui Huberiano dogmati διαρρήδην contradicit: Sed cumprimis Scripturarum oraculis, alijsque rationibus & argumentis, ex analogiâ fidei petitis, planè invictis.

Primùm enim classica est illa Servatoris gnome his inculcata: Matth. 20, 16. & cap. 22, 14. Multi sunt vocati: pauci electi. Ex quo dicto Universalis electionis non priùs extruetur, quàm demonstratum fuerit, ita esse quatuor, album esse nigrum. Nam quod Huberus inter ἐκλεκτοὺς καὶ ἐκλελεγμένους, hoc est, inter electos nominaliter, & participialiter sic dictos, distingvit, plane frivolum & nugatorium est, uti suprà Controversiâ 1. speciali abundè demonstratum fuit. Et vel hoc unum testimonium ita clarum & evidens est, ut vel solum sufficere in hac quæstione possit. Sed supersunt plura. 2. Scriptura passim inter electos & non electos, inter fideles & infideles accuratè discernit. Atqui positâ Universalitate Electionis, discrimen Electorum & Non-Electorum locum non habet. Ergò. Major probatur his dictis : Matth. 24, 24. Ut in errorem inducātur, si possibile sit, etiam electi. Johan. 15, 19. Elegi vos ex mundo. Johan. 17, 6. Manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus, quos dedisti mihi de mundo. Et versu 9. Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his, quos dedisti mihi. 1. Cor. 1, 27. Illi qui electi à DEO esse perhibentur, per antithesin sapientibus hujus mundi opponuntur. Rom. 9, 5. ReliquiæElectorum à reliquâ multitudine separantur. 3. Scriptura solos salvandos & credentes vocat electos. At neque credunt ad finem usquè, neque salvantur omnes. Ergò. Majoris probationem satis evidentem monstrat loco Apostolicus, Rom. 8, 30. Quos præscivit, hos prædestinavit. At præsciti non sunt omnes, habito respectu ad fidem. Ergò neque omnes prædestinati. Sic, Quos prædestinavit, hos & vocavit : Ergò extra vocatorum cœtum Electio non est extendenda. Porrò, quos vocavit, hos & justificavit : At non justificantur, nisi soli credentes. Ergò. Tandem, Quos justificavit, hos glorificavit : At glorificatio seu salvatio non est omnium: Ergò. 4. Electi in Scripturis ejusmodi notis insigniuntur, quæUniversitati hominum nullo modo competunt : Ergò Electio Universalis non est. Antecedens his dictis probatur : Matth. 24, 24. Non pereunt electi in erroribus. Johan. 6, 37. Veniunt ad Christum, quippè ipsi à Patre dati, non sub ratione redemtionis solummodò quod generale est omnium : sed sub peculiari Electionis modo. Johan. 10, 28. non rapiuntur ex manibus pastoris : sed cognoscunt eum, sequuntur ipsum, & audiunt vocem ejus. Act. 13, 48. Credunt certissimè. Rom. 8, 33. 35. non accusantur, non separantur à dilectione Christi Ephes. 1, 5. Sunt adoptati in filios Dei, Jacob. 2, 5. Sunt divites in fide. Apocal. 13, 8. adorant Christum, & sunt nomina ipsorum scripta in libro vitæ. Apoc. 17, 14. militant sub vexillo Christi. Jam verò hæc omnia Universalitati generis humani non competunt: Ergò neque Electio ei competit. 5. Electio non est facta nisi in Christo. Ephes. 1, 4. Atqui in Christo non sunt omnes, sed ij tantùm, qui per fidem Christo sunt insiti. Ergò Electio etiam istorum tantùm est propria, nō verò omniũ. 6. Fides vera & constans, non est nisi electorum Dei, Tit. 1, 1. Atqui fides ista non est omnium. 2. Thess. 3, 2. Ergò neque Electio est omnium. 7. Cui non competit Electionis definitio, eidem nec definitum. At maxima hominum parti definitio Electionis non competit. Ergò nec definitum : & per consequens Electio erit particularis, non Universalis Assumtio probatur inductione formarum omnium, quæ secundum Scripturas Electionis definitionem constituunt : ut quòd Electio non nisi finis atque eventus salutaris implicatione definitur, qui est fides, ad finem perseverans, salus ac beatitudo æterna.

8. Reprobatio æterna Electionem universalem prorsus non admittit. Neutra enim respectu omnium hominum simul stare potest. Atqui Reprobatio æterna negari non potest: uti quæst. præcedente 2. demonstratum. Ergò.

9. Accedit consensus Ecclesiæ: In Concilio Constantiensi damnatus fuit articulus iste Johannis Hussi, Ecclesiam Christi esse Universitatem Prædestinatorum. Hac damnatione B. Lutherus in Comitiis VVormatiensibus dixit, damnatum esse articulum hunc Symboli Apostolici: Credo Ecclesiam Sanctam Catholicam. Pro cujus articuli defensione, dicebat Lutherus, se non recusare, & vitam, & sangvinem impendere. Hinc invictâ veritate colligitur: Si Ecclesia Christi est universitas prædestinatorum: fieri nullo modo potest, ut extra Ecclesiam Christi, & ad totius generis humani universalitatem, Prædestinatio filiorum DEI extendatur. Videatur historia de vitâ & actis Lutheri à Phil. Mel. scripta fol. D. 4. Et commentarius Lutheri in c. 17. Johannis Tom. 6. operum Germ. Jen. pag. 169.

10. Pertinet huc decisio Libri Concordiæ: cujus hæc sunt verba formalia: Prædestinatio sive æterna DEI electio, tantùm ad bonos, & dilectos DEI filios pertinet. Item: in libro vitæ inscripti sunt omnes & electi, qui salutem æternam consequuntur. Epitome art. 11. de prædest. §. 4. & 6. Item: Æterna electio, seu prædestinatio DEI ad salutem, non simul ad bonos & malos pertinet: sed tantùm ad filios DEI, qui ad æternam vitam consequendam electi & ordinati sunt, priusquam mundi fundamenta jacerentur: pag. 770. Item: Nequaquàm sentiendum est, eos etiam in electorum numero habendos, qui Verbum DEI contemnunt: Undè concludit liber Concordiæ, secundum has rationes intelligendum esse, quod Scriptura dicit: Multos vocatos, paucos verò electos esse. Item: In Christo æterna Electio Dei Patris est quærenda. Is verò in æterno suo consilio decrevit, quòd præter eos, qui Filium ejus Jesum Christum agnoscunt, & in eum verè credunt, neminem salvare velit.

11. Si æterna Dei Electio respicit cùm non credentes, quàm credentes, Consequens fuerit, Deum in illo suo æterno decreto & concilio, nihil distinxisse inter credituros, & non credituros: sed sine ullo respectu vel fidei, vel incredulitatis, absolutè ad vitam æternam elegisse & ordinasse, cùm eos, quos siciebat in Christum, vel nunquàm, vel certè non ad finem usquè credituros: quam quos in eundem credituros noverat. Atqui hoc tùm in æternam DEI providentiam, tùm in summam ejus justitiam prodigiosè est blasphemum: id quod patet ex ijs, quæ tùm de gemino decreto Voluntatis Consequentis in DEO, & quidem utroque ab omni æternitate facto: tùm verò de æternâ Reprobatione paulò ante disputavimus.

12. Stante Universali Electione omnium indifferenter hominum sine intuitu fidei in CHRISTUM: contrariæ emergent in DEO voluntates: Una æterna illa, quæ secundum Huberum talis est: Volo ego DEUS, ut omnes omninò homines, sive credant, sive non credant, ad vitam æternam sint electi. Altera temporalis, eaque talis: Volo ego

DEUS, ut tantùm credentes, ad vitam æternam sint electi: increduli verò Electionis gratiâ excidant. Quam absurdam Theologiam, quomodo cum Scripturis, & analogiâ fidei conciliare velit Huberus, ipsemet viderit.

His rationibus adducti, Electionem non nisi Particularem, & solorum ad finem usque credentium complexu, determinatam esse statuimus: Cujus Particularitatis quænam sit ratio, quatuor hypothesibus demonstrari potest:

I. Electionis particularitas, Universalitati misericordis in DEO voluntatis nihil quicquam detrahit: neque Dilectioni Universali ἀντιφατικῶς opponitur: sed Universali illi voluntati, & beneplacito in DEO, particularis hæc Electio certâ suâ & legitimâ ratione, perindè ut voluntati Antecedenti, Consequens rectissimè sine ullâ contradictione substernitur, sive subordinatur. Quia enim vult DEUS omnes salvos, sed sub conditione fidei in Christum: efficitur, ut qui non credunt, non divinæ voluntatis, sed propriæ infidelitatis culpâ salute excidant. Cujus rei in omni voluntate, etiam humanâ, Universali; sed ordinatâ, Exemplum videre licet: uti suprà copiosiùs ostensum, Ubi de mutuâ voluntatis Antecedentis & Consequentis affectione disseruimus.

II. Electionis particularitas nemini mortalium salutis januam, ex aliquo DEI decreto intercludit. Ratio manifestissima hæc est: Quòd enim paucos, & non omnes DEUS elegit, non indè factum est, quasi omnes eligere simpliciter noluerit, aut vel ab æterno, vel nunc etiam salvari omnes noluerit, sive nolit: quod quidem de DEO sentire impietate ipsâ magis impium est. Verùm quia paucos, non omnes, Verbo suo convertendos, hoc est, oblatam gratiam recepturos, sicque salvandos esse præscivit. Voluntas enim DEI de salvandis omnibus, non absoluta, sed ordinata est. Quem ordinem cùm maxima hominum pars negligat, utique suâ sponte non DEI culpâ, particularitas salvandorum emergit.

III. Electionis particularitas, qualis quidem in nostris asseritur & defenditur Ecclesiis, cum dogmate Calviniano nihil quicquam habet commercij. Nam tametsi particularitas utrobique, & in genere docetur: diversissima tamen, & toto cœlo à se mutuò dissidens, utriusque est ratio, natura & affectio.
