Nam Calviniani Particularitatis suæ absolutum & fatale decretum faciunt, quasi nunquàm DEUS voluerit omnes homines salvari. Nos vero particularitatem talem asserimus, quæ Universali voluntati divinæ de salvandis omnibus, est subordinata: uti hactenùs multoties ostensum.

IV. Causa particularitatis istius, non est ullo modo quærenda aut statuenda in DEO, minimè omnium ad simplex & absolutum beneplaciti ipsius decretum referenda, quasi ab æterno DEUS voluntate quâdam absolutâ, simplice, & causas omnes antegressa, tale quoddam inter homines condendos discrimen constituerit, ut immutabiliter decreverit, alios quidem, eosque paucissimos, nullo fidei respectu salvare: alios autem, eosque plurimos, nullo infidelitatis intuitu, æternæ damnationi mancipare. Verùm ex solâ hominum incredulitate, & finali impœnitentiâ, Particularitas isthæc unicè emergit, quâ oblata gratia ab istis improbè spernitur, & verbum salutis, fidesque in Christum, cujus acceptatione electis, ipsi quoque damnati & reprobi cooptari poterant, pervicaciter repudiatur. Causam hanc Particularitatis Scriptura passim exprimit, quando asserit, quòd divitias bonitatis divinæ plerique impiè contemnant, Rom. 2, 4. quòd veram lucem in hunc mundum venientem non recipiant, Johan. 1, 11. quòd tenebras magis, quàm lucem diligant, Johan. 3. 19. quòd Filium DEI audire, quem audiendum Pater cœlestis præcepit, recusent, & tempus visitationis suæ, atque ea, quæ ad pacem suam faciunt, cognoscere, Luc. 19, 44. imò ut à Christo congregentur, permittere nolint, Matth. 23, 37. quòd nonnulli etiam rursum sibi crucifigentes Christum, & post acceptam veritatis notitiam, voluntariè peccent, Hebr. 6, 6. & cap. 10, 26. & eum, qui redemit ipsos rursus, abnegent: 2. Petr. 2, 1. &c. Et quid multis opus, cum DEUS ipse expressè omnem particularitatis istius causam à se amoveat, inque solos homines transferat: Perditio, inquiens, tua Israël ex te: salus ex me, Hosea 13, 9.


### Question V. Whether the number of the Elect is certain and infallible: or whether it can be increased or diminished?

This Question implies a twofold sense: The former is, whether the number of the elect is so certain and infallible that those who are saved are necessarily saved, and those who are damned are likewise necessarily damned: or if both of these do not happen to men necessarily, whether something fortuitous and casual ought to be established concerning the salvation and damnation of men? The latter sense of the question is, Whether the number of the elect is so certain and definite that it can neither be increased nor diminished? Concerning both separately.

As to the former sense, the Sacramentarians have long since accused our Churches, as if they taught that both the salvation and the damnation of men were placed in such uncertainty that both befall men by chance and accident. The cause of this calumny arises from the fact that our Churches deny that men are either saved or damned by any absolute decree. From this they infer: If not by an absolute decree, therefore they are saved and damned by chance, and GOD has determined nothing certain concerning the human race in either direction. But we respond by a distinction, if the fortuitous is opposed in the Sacramentarian sense to the absolute: certainly the unbelievers are condemned by the fortuitous, because they are not condemned by absolute necessity, and they could not have been condemned, but they perish by their own fault. Thus in this respect the faithful are saved by the fortuitous, because they are not saved by absolute necessity, and they could not have been saved if they had not believed to the very end. But if you oppose the Fortuitous to the divine Ordination, revealed in the scriptures concerning the salvation and damnation of men: then we most simply deny that either believers are saved or unbelievers are condemned by the fortuitous: but that both these events befall both parties necessarily, yet not by an absolute necessity: but by the necessity of the divine order, of the decree both of Election and of Reprobation, already included from the furthest eternity: according to this authentic word of the Savior: Whoever shall have believed and been baptized shall be saved; whoever shall not have believed shall be condemned. Mark 16, 16. Since this decree was established from eternity and holds itself immutably: that calumny falls of its own accord, that it follows from our doctrine that GOD has decreed nothing certain from eternity concerning the salvation and condemnation of men.

Regarding the latter sense of the proposed question, concerning the certain and infallible number of the Elect, whether it can be increased or diminished? The entire difficulty can be most deeply removed and most solidly explained by the distinctions and propositions employed here.

I. The number of the Elect is entirely certain, nay most certain, so much so that it can neither be increased nor diminished. We assert the same thing also concerning the certain number of those to be damned. For as Augustine writes piously in book 14 of The City of God, chapter 26: To the omnipotent GOD, the highest and supremely good, the creator of all natures, but the helper and rewarder of good wills; the abandoner and punisher of evil ones; the ordainer of both, there was certainly no lack of a plan by which he might fill the certain number of his city, predestined by his wisdom, even from the damned human race. And in the book On Rebuke and Grace, chapter 13, among other things he applies to this point that from the Apocalypse, chapter 3, 11: Hold what you have, lest another receive your crown. For if another is not going to receive it unless this one has lost it, the number is certain, says Augustine. But Holy Scripture also confirms the same: For if the hairs of the Elect are numbered even with GOD, Matt. 10, 30, how much less doubt will there be that the number of the elect themselves is most certain to GOD.

II. However, the number of the Predestined is certain and infallible, not in respect of any absolute decree: but only by reason of divine foreknowledge, or rather Omniscience: which knows not only formally but materially, as the Scholastics say, that is, it knows not only confusedly and in general how many the Elect are: but also in the singular and individual, and it knows this a priori, who the elect are. The Apostle confirms this in 2 Timothy 2, 19: The foundation of GOD stands firm, having this seal, GOD knows who are his. But this very foreknowledge of GOD

does not wander in uncertainty: but is defined by the act of persevering faith: insofar as GOD from eternity foreknew who and how many would believe in Christ to the very end, and who would not. III. This number is neither increased nor diminished by reason of divine foreknowledge. For in either way the Omniscience of GOD would labor: Since if there were to have been more or fewer in the number of either the elect or the damned: GOD would certainly have had that very thing also known and perceived from eternity. Although this number is neither increased nor diminished: it is not, however, so constituted by fate that it could not, or never could, be increased or diminished by the pleasure of some absolute decree: as the Calvinists impiously teach.

For because GOD seriously wills all men to be saved, it is most false that the number of the Elect is immutably fixed by fate. Because the assertion of CHRIST the Savior in Matt. 11, 21, issued concerning the Tyrians and Sidonians, would also be false, that they would have done penance in sackcloth and ashes if those miracles had been performed there which were performed among the Galileans. What of the fact that the Apostle is a witness, Rom. 11, 23, that the Jews already cast off by GOD can be grafted back into the true olive tree, if indeed they do not remain in unbelief? But that the number of the Elect is said to be unable to be increased or diminished, that is only affirmed in respect of divine foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived, and sees and knows all things with a most present intuition, just as they are at some time to be in act. Certainly more could have believed in Christ: since they were not prohibited from the perception of faith by an absolute decree. If this power were transferred into act, that is, if more than those who believe and are saved were to be about to believe and be saved; GOD would have foreseen this very thing, and nothing else: and thus that very number, either increased or diminished, would have been infallibly known to GOD.

IV. This number of the Elect is so constituted that those who are already saved and blessed could nevertheless have been damned at some time: which the Apostle hints at by his own example, 1 Cor. 9, 27, saying: I bring my body into servitude, lest perhaps when I have preached to others, I myself should become a reprobate. If that had happened, they could never have been called Elect, because they would have lacked perseverance in faith. Conversely, those who are already in the number of the damned could likewise have been saved: since they were excluded from the number of the Elect by no fatal or absolute decree, if only they had done penance and believed in Christ.

With these things thus posited, we infer that the number of the Elect is certain and infallible, but not fatal. 2. That the same could have been increased and diminished, insofar as no one is either absolutely saved or damned: but the means of salvation are offered equally to all. 3. That the same number could not have been increased and diminished, regarding the infallible foreknowledge of GOD, which knows most exactly each thing as it is and as it is to be.

Latin:

GEminum sensum Quæstio hæc implicat: Prior est, utrum Electorum numerus ita sit certus & infallibilis, ut, qui salvantur, necessariò salventur: qui damnantur, itidem necessariò damnentur: vel si non necessariò utrumque hoc hominibus obtingit, an fortuitum aliquid & casuale, circa hominum & salutem, & damnationem statui debeat? Posterior sensus quæstionis est, An ita Electorum numerus sit certus ac definitus, ut neque augeri ille, neque minui possit? De utroque seorsim.

Quoad priorem sensum, jam pridem nostras Ecclesias Sacramentarij insimularunt, ac si docerent, tùm salutem, tùm damnationem hominum ita in incerto, esse positam, ut utraq; fortuitò, & casu inter hominibus obtingat. Causa calumniæ indè resultat, quia nimirùm negant nostræ Ecclesiæ, Homines absoluto aliquo decreto vel salvari, vel damnari. Hinc inferunt, Sinon absoluto decreto, Ergò fortuitò &, salvantur & damnantur, nequè in utramquè partem de genere humano DEUS certi quicquam constituit. Sed respondemus per distinctionem, si fortuitum sensu Sacramentario opponatur absoluto: utique fortuito damnantur increduli, quia non absoluta necessitate damnantur, & damnari non potuissent, sed suapte culpa pereunt. Sic hoc respectu fortuito salvantur fideles, quia non absoluta necessitate salvantur, & salvari non potuissent, si non credidissent ad finem usque. Verùm si Fortuitum opponas Ordinationi divinæ, de salute & damnatione hominum in scripturis revelatæ: tùm simplicissimè negamus, fortuito vel salvari credentes, vel damnari incredulos: sed utrumque istum eventum, utrisque necessario obtingere, necessitate verò non absoluta: sed necessitate ordinis divini, decreto & Electionis, & Reprobationis, jam indè ab ultima æternitate inclusi: secundum hanc authenticam Servatoris: Quicunque crediderit, & baptisatus fuerit, salvabitur; qui non crediderit, condemnabitur. Marc. 16, 16. Quod decretum, cùm ab æterno constitutum sit, idque immutabiliter se habeat: suâ sponte corruit calumnia illa, Quòd ex nostrâ doctrinâ sequatur, DEUM nihil certi de salute & condemnatione hominum ab æterno decrevisse.

Quoad posteriorem propositæ quæstionis sensum, de numero Electorum certo & infallibili, an augeri ille, vel minui possit? Difficultas omnis his propositionibus, distinctionibusque adhibitis penitissimè tolli, & solidissimè explicari potest.

I. Numerus Electorum omninò certus est, imò certissimus, adeò, ut neque augendus, neque minuendus sit. Quod ipsum de certo etiam damnandorum numero asserimus. Nam ut Augustinus lib. 14. de Civit. DEI cap. 26. piè scribit: Omnipotenti DEO, summo, ac summè bono, creatori omnium naturarum, voluntatum autem bonarum adjutori, & remuneratori: malarum relictori ac damnatori: utrarumque ordinatori, non defuit utique consilium, quo certum numerum civitatis suâ sapientiâ prædestinatum, etiam ex damnato genere humano suæ civitatis impleret. Et in lib. de corrept. & grat. cap. 13. inter cætera huc accommodat illud Apocalypsœas cap. 3, 11. Tene quod habes, ne alius accipiat coronam tuam. Si enim alius non est accepturus, nisi iste perdiderit, certus est numerus, inquit Augustinus. Sed & Scriptura sacra idem confirmat: Quòd si enim Electorum capilli etiam apud DEUM sunt in numerato, Matth. 10, 30. quantò minùs dubium erit, quin ipsorum electorum numerus DEO sit certissimus.

II. Est autem numerus Prædestinatorum certus & infallibilis, non respectu absoluti alicujus decreti: sed tantùm ratione præscientiæ, vel potiùs Omniscientiæ divinæ: quæ non formaliter tantùm: sed materialiter, ut Scholastici loquuntur, hoc est, non tantùm confusè, & in communi novit, Quot sint Electi: sed etiam in singulari atque individuo, idéque à priori cognoscit, quinam sint electi. Confirmat hoc Apostolus 2. Timoth. 2, 19. Firmum stat fundamentum DEI, habens signaculum hoc, Novit DEUS, qui sunt ejus. Hæc ipsa verò DEI præscien-

tia non in incerto vagatur: sed fidei perseverantis actu definitur: quatenus DEUS ab æterno præscivit, Qui & quot in Christum ad finem usque essent credituri, qui non. III. Numerus iste ratione præscientiæ divinæ neque augetur, neque minuitur. Utroque enim modo laboraret DEI Omniscientia: Quin si plures futuri fuissent, vel pauciores, in numero sive Electorum, sive damnatorum: DEUS utique illud ipsum quoque ab æterno cognitum perspectumque habuisset. Quanquam verò Numerus iste neque augetur, neque minuitur: non tamen fataliter sic est comparatus, ut per absoluti cujusdam decreti beneplacitum augeri vel minui non possit, aut nunquàm potuerit: uti Calviniani impiè docent.

Quia enim DEUS seriò vult omnes homines salvos fieri, utique falsissimum est, quòd Electorum numerus fataliter sit immutabilis. Quia falsa etiam esset assertio CHRISTI Servatoris Matth. 11, 21. de Tyris & Sidonijs edita, quòd pœnitentiam in cinere & sacco egissent, si patrata fuissent isthic ea miracula, quæ apud Galilæos fuerunt edita. Quid quòd Apostolus testis est, Rom. 11, 23. Judæos à DEO jam projectos, rursus posse veræ oleæ implantari, si videlicet incredulitate non permaneant? Verùm quòd numerus Electorum dicitur neque augeri, neque minui posse, illud tantum affirmatur, respectu præscientiæ divinæ, quæ falli nequit, & omnia præsentissimo intuitu videt novitque, prout ipso actu aliquando sunt futura. Potuissent utique plures credere in Christum: siquidem absoluto decreto à fidei perceptione non fuerunt prohibiti. Hæc potentia, si in actum transferretur, hoc est, si plures quàm credunt & salvantur, credituri & salvandi essent; hoc ipsum, & non aliud, prævidisset DEUS: & sic numerus ille ipse vel auctus, vel minutus, DEO infallibiliter cognitus fuisset.

IV. Sic est numerus iste Electorum comparatus, ut qui jam salvi & beati sunt, damnari tamen aliquando potuerint: id quod suo exemplo Apostolus innuit, 1. Cor. 9, 27. In servitutem, inquiens, redigo corpus meum, ne fortè cum aliis prædicaverim, ipse reprobus fiam. Quod si factum fuisset, nunquàm isti dici potuissent Electi, quia perseverantia in fide caruissent. Vice versâ, qui jam in numero damnatorum sunt, falvari itidem potuissent: siquidem nullo fatali aut absoluto decreto è numero Electorum sunt exclusi, si modò acta pœnitentia in Christum credidissent.

His ita positis, inferimus, Electorum numerum esse certum ac infallibilem, non verò fatalem. 2 Eundem augeri & minui potuisse, quatenùs nemo vel absolutè salvatur, vel damnatur: sed omnibus media salutis ex æquo offeruntur. 3. Eundem numerum augeri & minui non potuisse, quoad infallibilem DEI præscientiam, quæ singula prout sunt, & futura sunt, exactissimè novit,


### Question VI. Concerning the book of life, and concerning the double inscription therein

Of the book of life, and of the double inscription into it.

Since Scripture everywhere makes mention of the inscription of the Elect into the book of life, and according to the analogy of faith the Elect and those Inscribed into the book of life are clearly convertible: It is asked, Who is, or What is the Book of Life: How does the Inscription of men into the same stand: and Can they, once inscribed, be erased from it any more?

But at the beginning it is beyond controversy that, according to an anthropopathy and in a transferred sense, a Book is assigned to GOD in the Scriptures: thus defining His eternal, certain, and infallible knowledge and care of all human things and actions: which, each and every one, according to all circumstances, He has no less perceived than if they were Inscribed in some book. In which metaphorical sense Writing is assigned to GOD, and denotes the same as to decree, to ordain, to confirm. Moreover, many books are attributed to GOD in the Scriptures: as Apoc. 20, 12. I saw the dead, small and great, standing before GOD, and the BOOKS were opened: and ANOTHER Book was opened, which is the book of life. All these books, for the sake of teaching, can not inconveniently be divided into three distinct books: Of which ONE is of universal providence, or the Government of all creatures in heaven and on earth, of which David, Psalm 139, 16. Your eyes saw my unformed substance (me still an embryo), and in Your Book were written all the days that were to be, and not one of them yet existed. The SECOND book, and as it were subordinate to the former, is of the Universal Judgment: of which Daniel chap. 7, 9. and 10. I watched until the thrones were placed, and the ancient of days sat, and the books were opened. Moreover, this book is expressed in the plural number, because not one and the same, but a different, and indeed one sentence concerning the Elect, and another concerning the reprobate, will then be promulgated. The THIRD book is and is called the Book of life, which itself, however, is various in the Scriptures. For Ecclesiasticus 24, 32. the sacred Scripture itself is called the Book of life, for that reason, because it contains the record of those things by the study of which men can aspire to eternal life. Then mention is also made in Apoc. 20, 12. of the book of life, which Augustine lib. 20. de Civit. DEI chap. 14. defines by that divine power, by which it will come to pass in the last judgment, that all his works, whether good or evil, are recalled to the memory of each one: among which, since those things which the elect have performed for the blessed life will be especially future: hence he maintains that this book is named the Book of life. In which part we allow Augustine to abound in his own sense: although the following verse 15. hints that it is a matter there of the book of eternal life: For whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire. Finally, both in this place already cited, and elsewhere in the Scriptures, mention is made of the Book of Life, in which are described those who are elected to eternal life: not otherwise than as a book of the military is said, either which contains the described military art: or which narrates the deeds of soldiers: or in which soldiers are enrolled: as Thomas notes somewhere. And this is indeed the proper signification of the present place and matter, taken in a transferred sense, from the record of those who are of some value above the rest, whose names and histories are recorded in certain books: Such as are Counselors and Senators especially, who from this rite are called Conscript Fathers. Concerning this Book of Life, Who and what sort it is, it will have to be examined more deeply.

Therefore, in the beginning, this Book of Life is nothing other than the certain and infallible knowledge of GOD, by which from eternity He knows those whom He chose in His Son to eternal life. Moreover, those inscribed into the book of life are and are called the Elect alone, whose Election GOD infallibly knows in His own mind, and retains in firm memory according to a peculiar habit of knowledge.

Then this Book of Life differs from predestination itself, only by the word or by reason. For beyond Predestination it contains and adds the acknowledgment of GOD.

Thirdly, because this Book of Life, by reason of the inscrutable knowledge in GOD, is indeed a sealed book: but CHRIST has been made the mediator and intercessor of our Election, in whom, and on account of whom, the Election was made from eternity: hence CHRIST, insofar as He has declared the will concerning our salvation from the secret bosom of the Father in the Gospel, is and is called the Book of Life explained.

Fourthly: Although the Book of Life, which is CHRIST, is one in number: yet a twofold inscription into the same is given in the Scriptures: One is Temporal, which takes place in Baptism, through which we are inserted and implanted into CHRIST the Vine, as branches: according to that of the Apostle. Gal. 3, 27. As many of you as have been baptized into Christ, have put on Christ: Or as the Apostle explains the same in Rom. 5, 6.: As many as have been baptized into His death have been united, being planted together with Christ.

The Church calls this Implantation an Inscription into the book of Life, thus metaphorically expressing that insertion into the Church, whose head is Christ, Ephes. 5, 23. This inscription, although it is joined with the Grace of GOD: is nevertheless liable to erasure again, so that it is not only possible for it to happen: but it happens also most frequently, that those inscribed in this way are erased again from this book of life: and that not only by those who believe and are reborn in a common way, both totally and finally: but even by the elect themselves, truly only totally, but not finally, as is to be seen in David, Peter, and similar saints. The truth of this erasure Christ expressed, Mark 16, 16: He who shall have believed, and shall have been baptized, shall be saved: He who shall not have believed, shall be condemned.

THE OTHER Inscription is eternal, which is nothing else than Predestination itself, or the Election of the children of GOD to salvation, and which was made before the foundation of the world: and it respects not only Grace: but also eternal Glory. To which end also this Election or Inscription is never frustrated, Rom. 11, 7. It happens therefore, that many in time have Grace, but on account of a defect of perseverance in faith do not arrive at glory, and consequently are not of the number of the Elect: or of those from eternity inscribed in the book of life. This Inscription is indelible, by reason of the end and glory: not indeed by any fatal decree thus bringing it about: for by reason of his own person, both Peter, and Paul, and any Elect person whatsoever, could have become reprobate, as was shown above: but by fact and event. For he who is elected, and from eternity inscribed in the book of life, he perseveres in faith even to the end. For unless GOD had foreseen that he himself would persevere, He would never have inscribed him from eternity in the book of life, that is, would have elected him to life. But he who does not persevere in faith, he truly and therefore speaking could never be called Elect, and therefore neither inscribed from eternity in the book of life: since these are convertible terms; To be elected to life, and to persevere even to the end. Therefore Judas the traitor, because he deserted Christ the book of life both by nefarious betrayal, and by final despair: we rightly assert that he was neither Elect, nor ever from eternity inscribed in the book of life: however much he may have been Temporally inscribed in the Book of Life through the Sacrament of initiation. And indeed, since GOD most exactly knows, who are his, 2. Tim. 2, 19. but to these, who on the last day shall be placed on the left, it will be said by the Lord: Depart from me, I never knew you: It is a consequence of that, that the names of those who are damned were not inscribed in the book of life from the foundation of the world, Apoc. 17, 8. It shines forth from this, what discrepancy intervenes between each Inscription: For first, the eternal Inscription is of the Elect alone, or of those to be saved: but the Temporal is of all the reborn or baptized. Then, that eternal inscription is never rendered void: but always attains its end: Rom. 11, 7. But the Temporal can be so evacuated by the vice and fault of men, that those who had been grafted into the olive tree of the people of GOD in this way, may again be utterly cut off. Rom. 11, 17. & seqq. Then that eternal Inscription always (if you look at the Ordinary manner) includes the Temporal: But this one does not include or presuppose that eternal one, to be sure. Finally, the eternal inscription asserts those inscribed as members of the Church Triumphant: but the Temporal as members of the Church militant.

Fifthly and lastly; Whether they can be blotted out again from the book of life, in which the Elect are inscribed from eternity, we have answered only negatively. But it is asked, What those testimonies of scripture mean, which declare that those inscribed are blotted out from the book of the living: as Ps. 69, 28. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the just. Which likewise Moses Exod. 32, 32. desires to be blotted out of the book, which GOD wrote, if He should wish to forgive the sins of the Israelites otherwise: That finally the Apostle Rom. 9, 3. wishes to be anathema from Christ for his brothers &c. But it is most rightly answered, that this blotting out does not signify a change on the part of the knowledge of GOD, as if GOD first knows this, and afterwards knows the contrary: but only on the part of men. For according to the opinion of men, which now becomes known to them concerning the book of life, insofar as they think all the just and believers ought to be saved, those are blotted out of the book of life, concerning whom it becomes known, that they were never written with the just, Which in respect to the place also of Ps. 69, 29. ought to be understood and explained not privatively, but negatively: that which the Holy Spirit Himself immediately declared ἐξηγητικῶς, when He added, The impious are thus blotted out from the book of the living, when they are not written with the just. On which place D. Augustine writes excellently: Were they ever written there? Brothers, we ought not to accept it in such a way, that GOD writes anyone in the book of life, and blots him out. If a man said: What I have written, I have written concerning the title, where it was written, King of the Jews: does GOD write anyone and blot him out? He is foreknowing, He predestined before the foundation of the world those who were to reign with His Son in eternal life. The book of life contains those whom He has written down. Finally, in the Apocalypse what does the Spirit of GOD say, when the same Scripture was speaking about the pressures to come from the Antichrist? They will consent to him, he says, all who are not written in the book of life. Therefore without doubt those who are written will not be going to consent. How then are those blotted out from there, where they were never written? This was said according to their hope (opinion), because they thought themselves written there. Which is Let them be blotted out of the book of life: And it is established to them, that they are not there.

And after a few words: So also here, those who hoped themselves to be written in the book of GOD as if by the merit of their own justice: when their damnation shall have been brought, even to their own knowledge, they will be blotted out of the book of the living, that is, they will know that they are not there. For the verse, which follows, explains what was said: And let them not be written with the just. Tom. 8. pag. 738. & 739. The Scripture itself confirms this explanation: as Isa. 44, 5. according to the sentiment and opinion of the impious it is read thus: This one will say: I am the Lord's: and that one will call himself by the name of Jacob: and that one will write with his hand to the Lord, and will name himself by the name of Israel. But to these the Lord answers in Ezekiel 13, 9.: They shall not be in the assembly of my people, and they shall not be written in the Scripture of the house of Israel: that is, they shall not be recounted in the Catalogue of true Israelites.

As far as the example of Moses concerns, both ancient and recent interpreters torture themselves wonderfully, so that they may be able to reconcile that in such a way, that it may not strike against the Scriptures anywhere. The ancient Rabbis of the Jews, understood the words of Moses concerning the book of the Law, which is therefore called the book of life, because it contains the precepts of life: As if Moses had said:

If you do not wish to spare that people: I do not wish to be named any longer in this law of yours, much less to promulgate it any longer to your people: For thus, by the promulgation of this law of yours, I constitute myself as it were the author and cause of the destruction of your people. But this explanation is too inept to deserve an elaborate refutation.

Others suppose that Moses understood not the book of eternal life, but the book of this temporal life: As if he had said: I prefer to die, rather than to see such a slaughter of your people. But this interpretation also, although it contains nothing inconvenient or false, is too inferior to express sufficiently the zeal and affection of Moses toward his people.

Others interpret the words of Moses not concerning the book of life, but concerning the catalogue of the people of GOD, or concerning that covenant which GOD had struck with the Israelites. Which interpretation is admitted only insofar as that covenant implies at the same time a regard for the book of eternal life: but in the meantime, it does not solve the proposed knot.

Others think that Moses indeed desired this, but in the meantime knew well that on the part of GOD it could never happen. Which interpretation is impious, and makes Moses a hypocrite, as if he had feigned one thing with his words, but had thought another thing in his heart.

The truest interpretation of all, finally, is this, which establishes that Moses indeed understood the book of eternal life, and asked to be blotted out from it, but not ἁπλῶς (simply), but κατὰ τι (in a certain respect), if indeed it could be done by any reason, that he was ready and prepared, even at the loss and expense of his own salvation, to redeem the damnation of the Jews. Which petition of Moses was certainly not feigned or hypocritical, but most serious, yet conditional. The fulfillment of which condition Moses also uniquely willed to be placed in the will of GOD. And although this condition is not read as expressed by Moses: it is nevertheless most rightly understood: since such vows always presuppose what must be presupposed, if indeed it can be done with piety intact and the will of GOD unharmed. Which very thing we answer also to the example of the Apostle Paul, who pronounces nothing categorically: but uses the potential mode, which presupposes the will of GOD. Moreover, such vows express that incredible affection of the Saints toward the impious, whom they likewise desire to be saved: which sometimes in the Saints also blazes up so that it is carried even to impossibilities.

Latin:

De libro vitæ, dequè duplici inscriptione in illum.

CUm Scriptura passim inscriptionis Electorum in librum vitæ meminerit, & secundum analogiam fidei Electorum & Inscriptorum in librum vitæ planè sint convertibiles : Quæritur, Quis sit, vel Quid sit Liber Vitæ: Quomodo se habeat Inscriptio hominum in eundem: & Nùm semel inscripti, deleri ampliùs ex eo possint?

Initiò autem extrà controversiam est, DEO κατ᾽ ἀνθρωποπάθειαν, & sensu translatitio in Scripturis assignari Librum: sic definiens æternam ipsius certam, infallibilemque notitiam, curamque rerum & actionum humanarum omnium: quas singulas & universas secundùm omnes circumstantias, haud minùs habet perspecta, ac si libro cuipiam essent Inscripta. Quo sensu metaphorico Scribere DEO assignatur, & idem notat, ac decernere, ordinare, confirmare. Plures autem libri in Scripturis DEO tribuuntur: ut Apoc. 20, 12. Vidi mortuos parvos & magnos, stantes in conspectu DEI, & LIBRI aperti sunt: & ALIUS Liber apertus est, qui est vitæ. Possunt autem omnes isti libri, docendi causâ, haud incommodè in tres distinctos libros dispesci: Quorum UNUS est providentiæ Universalis, sive Gubernationis omnium creaturarum in cœlo & in terrâ de quo David, Psalm. 139, 16. Informe meũ (me adhuc embryonem) viderunt oculi tui, & in Libro tuo scripti erant omnes dies, qui futuri erant, & nondùm unus extabat ex illis. ALTER liber, & priori quasi subordinatus, est Universalis Judicij: de quo Daniel cap: 7, 9. & 10. Adspiciebã, donec throni positi sunt, & antiquus dierum sedit, & libri aperti sunt. Exprimitur autem liber iste in plurali numero, quia non una atque eadem; sed diversa planè, & alia quidem de Electis, alia de reprobis tùm promulgabitur sententia. TERTIUS liber est & dicitur Liber vitæ, qui ipse tamen in Scripturis varius est. Nam Ecclesiastici 24, 32. Scriptura ipsa sacra Liber vitæ appellatur, eam ob causam, quia consignationem earum rerum continet, quarum studio ad vitam æternam homines adspirare possunt. Fit deindè etiam Apoc. 20, 12. mentio libri vitæ, quem Augustinus lib. 20. de Civit. DEI cap. 14. definit per vim illam divinam, quâ fiet in novissimo judicio, ut unicuique sua opera omnia in memoriam revocentur, sive bona, sive mala: inter quæ cùm præcipuè sint futura ea, quibus electi ad beatam vitam sunt perfuncti: hinc librum istum, Librum vitæ nominari autumat. Quâ in parte Augustinum suo quidem sensu abundare patimur: quanquàm versus insequens 15. Innuit, agi ibi de libro vitæ æternæ: Quicunque enim non inventus est in libro vitæ scriptus, is conjectus est in stagnum ignis. Tandem & hoc loco jam citato, & alibi in Scripturis fit mentio Libri Vitæ, in quo descripti sunt, qui ad vitam æternam sunt electi: haud secus, atque liber milititæ dicitur, vel qui descriptam continet artem militarem: vel qui narrat gesta militum: vel in quo conscripti sunt milites: uti alicubi Thomas annotat. Et hæc quidem propria est præsentis loci & materiæ significatio, translato sensu sumta, ab eorum consignatione, qui præ reliquis in aliquo sunt pretio, quorum nomina & historiæ certis libris confignantur: Quales sunt Consiliarij & Senatores præcipuè, qui ab hoc ritu Patres conscripti nuncupantur, De hoc Libro Vitæ, Qui & qualis ille sit, altius dispiciendum fuerit.

Initiò igitur Liber iste Vitæ nihil est aliud, quàm certa ac infallibilis DEI notitia, quâ ab æterno novit eos quos in Filio suo ad vitam æternam elegit. Inscripti autem in librum vitæ sunt & dicuntur soli Electi, quorum Electionem DEUS in mente suâ infallibiliter novit, & secundum peculiarem notitiæ habitum in firmâ memoriâ retinet.

Deindè differt Liber istæ Vitæ à prædestinatione ipsâ, non nisi τῷ λόγῳ sive ratione. Nam supra Prædestinationem continet & addit agnitionem DEI.

Tertiò, quia Liber iste Vitæ ratione imperscrutabilis in DEO cognitionis, liber quidem signatus est: CHRISTUS autem Electionis nostræ μέσιτης καὶ ἱκέτης factus est, in quo, & propter quem Electio ab æterno facta est: hinc CHRISTUS quatenùs ex arcano sinu Patris voluntatem de salute nostrâ in Evangelio enarravit, est & dicitur Liber Vitæ explicatus.

Quartò: Etsi unus est numero Liber Vitæ, qui est CHRISTUS: Gemina tamen in Scripturis datur inscriptio in eundem: Una Temporalis est, quæ fit in Baptismo, per quem CHRISTO Viti, tanquàm palmites inserimur & inplantamur: secundum illud Apostoli. Gal. 3, 27. Quotquot in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis: Vel ut Rom. 5, 6. idem explicat Apostolus: Cum Christo complantati coaluerunt, quotquot in mortem ipsius baptizati sunt.

Hanc Implantationem Ecclesia nominat Inscriptionem in librum Vitæ, sic metaphoricè exprimens insertionem illam in Ecclesiam, cujus caput Christus est, Ephes. 5, 23. Hæc inscriptio etsi cum Gratiâ DEI est conjuncta: Deletioni tamen rursus est obnoxia, ut non fieri tantùm possit: sed fiat etiam frequentissimè, ut hoc modo inscripti, è libro isto vitæ rursus deleantur: idque non vulgariter tantùm credentes & renati, tùm totaliter, tùm finaliter: sed ipsi etiam electi, verùm totaliter duntaxat, non autem finaliter, ut in Davide, Petro & similibus sanctis est videre. Deletionis hujus veritatem expressit Christus, Marci 16, 16. Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur: Qui non crediderit, condemnabitur.

ALTERA Inscriptio est æterna, quæ nihil est aliud, quàm ipsa Prædestinatio, sive Electio filiorum DEI ad salutem, quæque facta est ante constitutionem seculi : & respicit non modò Gratiam : sed & æternam Gloriam. Quo fine etiam Electio sive Inscriptio hæc nunquàm frustratur, Rom. 11, 7. Fit ergò, ut multi in tempore habeant Gratiam, sed propter defectum perseverantiæ in fide non perveniant ad gloriam, & per Consequens nõ sint ex numero Electorum: sive ab æterno inscriptorum in librum vitæ. Hæc Inscriptio indelebilis est, ratione finis & gloriæ: non fatali quidem aliquo sic ferente decreto : potuisset enim ratione personæ suæ, & Petrus, & Paulus, & Electus quilibet, fieri reprobus, uti suprà ostensum : sed facto & eventu. Qui enim electus est, & ab æterno inscriptus in librum vitæ, is in fide ad finem usque perseverat. Nisi enim perseveraturum ipsum prævidisset DEUS, nunquàm ipsum ab æterno in librum vitæ inscripsisset, hoc est, ad vitam elegisset. Qui verò in fide non perseverat, is verè ac proindè loquendo Electus dici nunquàm potuit, ac proindè neque ab æterno inscriptus in librum vitæ : siquidem hi sunt termini convertibiles ; Ad vitam electum esse, & ad finem usque perseverare. Judam ergò proditorem, quia & nefariâ proditione, & desperatione finali Christum librum vitæ deseruit: meritò ipsum neque Electum, neque ab æterno nunquàm in librum vitæ inscriptum fuisse asserimus : quantumvis etiam per Sacramentum initiationis Temporaliter in librum Vitæ inscriptus fuerit. Et sanè, cùm DEUS exactissimè noverit, qui sunt ejus, 2. Tim. 2, 19. his autem, qui in novissimo die à sinistris collocabuntur, dicetur à Domino: Discedite à me, nunquàm novi vos : Consequens illud est eorum, qui damnantur, nomina, in libro vitæ à condito mundo inscripta non fuisse Apoc. 17, 8. Elucet hinc, quid discrepantiæ utrique Inscriptioni invicem intercedat: Primùm enim æterna Inscriptio est solorum Electorum, sive salvandorum: Temporalis verò est omnium renatorum sive baptizatorum. Deindè æterna illa inscriptio nunquàm redditur irrita: sed finem suum semper assequitur: Rom. 11, 7. Temporalis verò vitio & culpâ hominum ita evacuari potest, ut qui oleæ populi DEI insiti hoc modo fuerant, rursus penitùs exscindantur. Rom. 11, 17. & seqq. Tùm Inscriptio illa æterna semper (Ordinariam rationem si spectes) includit Temporalem: Hæc verò non includit aut præsupponit illam æternam scilicet. Tandem æterna inscriptio asserit inscriptos in membra Ecclesiæ Triumphantis: Temporalis verò in membra Ecclesiæ militantis.

Quintò & postremò; An ex libro vitæ, in quem ab æterno Electi sunt inscripti, deleri rursum possint, negativè modò respondimus. Sed Quæritur, Quid sibi velint ea scripturæ testimonia, quæ inscriptos de libro viventium deleri perhibent: ut Psal. 69, 28. Deleantur de libro viventium, & cum justis non scribantur. Quod item Moses Exod. 32, 32. cupit deleri de libro, quem DEUS scripsit, si aliter condonare velit peccata Israëlitis: Quòd denique Apostolus Rom. 9, 3. optat anathema esse à Christo pro fratribus suis &c. Sed rectifsimè respondetur, quòd deletio isthæc non significet mutationem ex parte notitiæ DEI, quasi DEUS primùm sciat hoc, & posteà norit contrarium: sed tantùm ex parte hominum. Secundum opinionem enim hominum, quæ jam innotescit ipsis de libro vitæ, quatenùs putant omnes justos & credentes debere salvari, delentur de libro vitæ illi, de quibus innotescit, quòd cum justis scripti nunquàm fuerint, Quod respectu locus etiam Psalmi 69, 29. non privativè, sed negativè intelligi & explicari debet: id quod Spiritus Sanctus ipse ἐξηγητικῶς statim declaravit, quando subjecit, Impios sic deleri ex libro viventium, quando cum justis non scribuntur. Quem in locum D. Augustinus præclarè scribit: Anné aliquando illic scripti erant? Fratres, non sic accipere debemus, quòd quemquam DEUS scribat in librum vitæ, & deleat illum. Si homo dixit: Quod scripsi, scripsi de titulo, ubi scriptum erat, Rex Judæorum: DEUS quenquamné scribit & delet? Præscius est, prædestinavit ante constitutionem mundi regnaturos cum Filio suo in vitâ æternâ. Hos, quos conscripsit, ipsos continet liber vitæ. Denique in Apocalypsi quid ait Spiritus DEI, cum de pressuris ab Antichristo futuris loqueretur eadem Scriptura? Consentient illi, inquit, omnes qui non sunt scripti in libro vitæ. Proindè sine dubitatione non erunt consensuri, qui scripti sunt. Isti ergò quomodo indè delentur, ubi nunquàm scripti sunt? Hoc dictum est secundum spem (opinionem) ipsorum, quia ibi se scriptos putabant. Quod est Deleantur de libro vitæ: Et ipsis constat, non illos ibi esse.

Et post pauca: Sic & hîc, qui se sperabant tanquàm merito justitiæ suæ in libro DEI scriptos esse: cum perducta fuerit damnatio ipsorum, etiam ad cognitionem eorum, delebuntur de libro viventium, id est non ibi se esse cognoscent. Nam versus, qui sequitur, exponit quod dictum est: Et cum justis non scribantur. Tom. 8. pag. 738. & 739. Explicationem hanc confirmat ipsa Scriptura: ut Esa. 44, 5. ex sententiâ & opinione impij sic legitur: Iste dicet: Domini ego sum: & ille se vocabit nomine Jacob: & ille scribet manu suâ Domino, atque in nomine Israël nominabit se. Sed his apud Ezechielem 13, 9. respondet Dominus: In cœtu populi mei non erunt, & in Scripturâ domus Israël non scribentur: hoc est, non recensebuntur in Catalogo verorum Israëlitarum.

Exemplum Mosis quòd attinet, mirè se torquent, tùm veteres tùm recentiores interpretes, ut illud ita conciliare queant, ne uspiam in Scripturas impingat. Veteres Rabbini Judæorum, intellexerunt verba Mosis de libro Legis, qui ideò dicatur liber vitæ, quia præcepta vitæ continet: Quasi dixisset Moses:

Si tu non vis parcere populo illi: nolo ego ampliùs nominari in lege hac tuâ, nedùm illam ampliùs promulgare populo tuo: Sic enim ego promulgatione legis hujus tuæ, Autorem me quasi & causam constituo interitus populi tui. Verùm ineptior est hæc explicatio, quàm ut operosam refutationem mereatur.

Alij autumant, Mosen intellexisse non librum vitæ æternæ, sed librum vitæ hujus temporalis: Quasi dixisset: Mori malo, quàm videre tantam populi tui stragem. Sed & hæc interpretatio, licèt incommodi aut falsi nihil contineat, inferior est, quàm ut Zelum & affectum Mosis erga populum suum satis exprimat.

Alij interpretantur verba Mosis non de libro vitæ, sed de Catalogo populi DEI, sive de fœdere illo, quod DEUS cum Israëlltis pepigerat. Quæ interpretatio eatenùs quidem admittitur, quatenùs illud fœdus respectum simul implicat ad librum vitæ æternæ: sed interim nodum propositum non solvit.

Alij Mosen quidem hoc optasse existimant, sed interim probè novisse, ex parte DEI id nunquàm fieri posse. Quæ interpretatio impia est, & Mosen facit hypocritam, quasi aliud verbis simulavefit, aliud verò sub corde cogitaverit.

Verissima tandem omnium interpretatio est hæc, quæ statuit, Mosen intellexisse quidem librum vitæ æternæ, & petijsse ex eo deleri, Verùm non ἁπλῶς, sed κατὰ τι, si nimirùm id ullâ ratione fieri posset, se promtum ac paratum esse, vel propriæ suæ salutis jacturâ ac dispendio, damnationem Judæorum redimere. Quæ sanè petitio Mosis non simulata, aut hypocritica, sed maximè seria fuit, conditionata tamen. Cujus conditionis impletionem Moses etiam in voluntate DEI unicè voluit positam. Et quanquàm conditio hæc à Mose non expreffa legitur: rectissimè tamen subintelligitur: Siquidem ejusmodi vota semper præsupponunt præsupponenda, si nimirùm id salvâ pietate, & illæsâ DEI voluntate fieri possit. Quod ipsum respondemus ad exemplum etiam Apostoli Pauli, qui nihil Categoricè pronunciat: sed utitur modo potentiali, qui præsupponit DEI voluntatem. Exprimunt autem ejusmodi vota incredibilem illum Sanctorum affectum erga impios, quos itidem salvatos cupiunt: qui interdum in Sanctis etiam ita exardescit, ut feratur etiam ad impossibilia.


### Question VII. Whether and whence can the Elect be infallibly certain of their Election and perseverance?

Among the other most foul errors of the Papists, this is not the last: That no man can know with the certainty of faith, since it could not be subject to falsehood, that he has obtained the grace of GOD: and that those who are truly justified ought not to establish without any doubt at all that they are justified. For they say that faith in general indeed establishes that the divine promises concerning the mercy of GOD, concerning the merit of Christ, concerning the efficacy of the Sacraments, and others of that kind are true: but concerning the application to the individual, faith ought always to be held in suspense in doubt, unless a special revelation intervenes. Especially in the doctrine of Predestination, it cannot be done from the Word of GOD, unless a special revelation is added beyond and outside the Word, so that anyone of the truly believing and justified can also certainly establish that he is in the number of the Elect. For even if some certainty were established for someone concerning present grace, justice, and the remission of sins, (which they nevertheless deny is established), yet concerning predestination, certainty would not yet be established for him. They bring forward this reason, Because for present grace to yield to salvation, perseverance is needed, according to that Matt. 10:22: He who has persevered to the end, this one shall be saved: and Matt. 24:13. And John 15:7: If you have remained in me, and my words have remained in you: whatever you wish, you shall ask, and it shall be done for you. Rom. 11:22: If you have remained in goodness, you shall not be cut off. Gal. 6:9: If we do not fail while doing good. Col. 1:23: If you remain in the faith, founded, stable, and immovable. Heb. 3:6: If we have retained the confidence and glory of hope firm until the end.

But that no one can be certain concerning perseverance, not even a believer and one truly justified: since not every justified person is predestined, and indeed a truly justified person could be not predestined. Hence it is that they indeed concede to believers some certainty of HOPE in this matter: but such that is always joined with doubt: (By which pact they establish an opposite in an adjective) but they condemn an indubitable certainty as extreme presumption and impiety, because Scripture itself commands us fear, dread, and trembling: 1 Cor. 10:12: He who thinks he stands, let him see that he does not fall. Rom. 11:20: Do not be high-minded; but fear. Phil. 2:12: With fear and trembling work out your salvation. 1 Pet. 1:17: Conduct yourselves in fear, during the time of your sojourn. These things the Papists, as can be seen in Sess. 6 of the Council of Trent, ch. 12 & 13. Bellarmine, book 3 de Justificat., ch. 12 & 13.

The Sacramentarians suppose that the certainty of Election is to be sought from the sense of true faith, and from some internal motion.

Latin:

Pontificiorum inter cæteros errores fœdissimos hic non est postremus: Neminem hominum scire posse certitudine fidei, cùm non posset subesse falsum, se gratiam DEI esse consecutum: & verè etiam justificatos non debere absquè ullâ omninò dubitatione statuere, se esse justicatos. Nam fidem ingenere quidem statuere promissiones divinas de misericordiâ DEI, de merito Christi, de Sacramentorum efficaciâ, & id genus alias esse veras: sed de applicatione ad individuum, fidem semper in dubitatione suspensam esse debere, nisi peculiaris revelatio interveniat. Præcipuè in doctrinâ Prædestinationis non fieri posse ex Verbo DEI, nisi præter & extra Verbum specialis revelatio accedat, ut quisquam verè credentium & justificatorum etiam certò possit statuere, se esse in numero Electorum. Etsiamsi enim de præsenti gratiâ, justitiâ & remissione peccatorum cuipiam certitudo aliqua constaret, (quam constare tamen negant) tamen de prædestinatione nondùm ipsi constare certitudinem. Rationem proferunt hanc, Quia ut præsens gratia ad salutem cedat, perseverantia sit opus, juxta illud Matth. 10, 22. Qui perseveravit usque ad finem, hic salvus erit: & Matth. 24, 13. Et Johan. 15, 7. Si manseritis in me, & verba mea in vobis manserint: quodcunque volueritis, petetis, & fiet vobis. Rom. 11, 22. Si in bonitate permanseris, non excinderis. Gal. 6, 9. Si bonum facientes, non deficiamus. Coloss. 1, 23. Si permanetis in fide fundati stabiles & immobiles. Hebr. 3, 6. Si fiduciam & gloriam spei usquè ad finem firmam retinuerimus.

De Perseverantiâ autem certum neminem esse posse, ne quidem credentem, & verè justificatum: siquidem non omnis justificatus sit prædestinatus, quin verè etiam justificatus posset esse non prædestinatus. Hinc est, quod concedunt quidem, credentibus aliquam certitudinem SPEI in hoc negocio: sed talem, quæ semper cum dubitatione sit conjuncta: (Quo pacto oppositum in adjecto statuunt) certitudinem autem indubitatam, extremæ præsumtionis & impietatis damnant, quia Scriptura ipsa timorem, metum & tremorem, nobis præcipiat: 1. Cor. 10, 12. Qui sibi videtur stare, videat ne cadat. Rom. 11, 20. Noli altum sapere; sed time. Phil. 2, 12. Cum timore & tremore operamini salutem vestram. 1. Petr. 1, 17 In timore conversamini, tempore incolatus vestri. Hæc Pontificij, uti videre est Sess. 6. Concilij Trid. cap. 12 & 13. Bellarminum lib. 3. de Justificat. cap. 12. & 13.

Sacramentarij Electionis certitudinem ex veræ fidei sensu, & interno quodam motu petendam esse autumant.


### On the Certainty of Election

Huberus, in his work on the Certainty of Election, dreams that it can be known to no one except from the Universality of Election, meanwhile simply condemning our doctrine concerning the particularity of Election as being full of Despair.

This threefold error imposes upon us the necessity of examining more accurately this question concerning the certainty of Election and the Perseverance of the Elect.

At the beginning, however, in this place, the controversy is not properly about that head of certainty which concerns the present grace of GOD: but about that which deals specifically with the certainty of Predestination. Moreover, our dispute in this part is not about the faith of heretics, who foster and defend false opinions that fight against the foundation of faith: nor about the persuasion of Epicureans, who, in the height of license for crimes, promise themselves salvation and impunity for their crimes: the certainty of whose salvation and election is not only doubtful, if they continue in this way: but their damnation is also rather just and certain. But neither must it be denied that the true faith of the Elect is not perfect: furthermore, also, because of the wondrous counsel of GOD, it is sometimes subject to temptations. In both of which cases one must flee to the anchor of prayers, and one must pray, I believe Lord; but help my unbelief. Mark 9:24. Likewise, Lord increase our faith. Luke 17:5. But also this must be observed in this place, that we are not fighting for some absolute certainty, which believers and the Elect could possess in such a way that, whatever they might do, and however they might conduct themselves in life, they could nevertheless be certain of salvation and Election. Such a certainty, indeed, would patronize carnal security. Therefore, all these things must be properly removed from the present state of the Controversy, and we must see what is affirmed or established on our part.

Our thesis, however, is this: All the pious and truly believing, if only they themselves wish, not only can be, but are, nay rather ought to be, most certain in their own mind, not only of the present grace of GOD: but also of future salvation, and thus of their own eternal Election. Indeed, if the passages of Scripture which deal with Predestination are weighed more accurately; it will be manifested clearly that the doctrine of Predestination was revealed to us in Scripture for no other end or purpose than that, with doubt concerning the grace of GOD and the salvation of believers being driven from their minds, this very doctrine might be proposed to us as a kind of basis and foundation of certainty. The conclusion of the eighth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, from verse 28 to the end of the chapter, shows this. The words of the Apostle in Romans 11:29, inserted into the doctrine of Election, teach this very thing: The gifts and calling of GOD are ἀμεταμέλητα, without repentance. Other sayings of Scripture will prove this: Eph. 1:4. He chose us, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love. 2 Tim. 2:19. The solid foundation of GOD stands, having this seal: The Lord knows who are his.

The proof of this thesis of ours consists 1. of the certainty and infallibility of predestination itself. For it is certain and infallible, and therefore it always attains the end which it seeks. Rom. 11:7. Moreover, it is certain first on the part of GOD who chooses, and of that whole order which must be considered on the part of GOD. For the life which GOD promised to his sheep, he bestows upon them: they do not perish forever: no one snatches them from his hands, John 10:28. Now when the elect fall, they are not crushed, because the Lord supports them with his hand, Psalm 37:24, so that, with him providing, they are sufficiently fortified against any hostile cases of misfortune. Nay, the very power of GOD has provided for them in such a way that there is no creature that can separate them from the love of GOD, which is in Christ Jesus: Rom. 8:39. Then, Election is also infallible by reason of the foreknowledge in GOD, which cannot be deceived or err: as was shown in the preceding, nearest question.

Moreover, so that we may not sin in excess or in defect concerning this very certainty and infallibility of Election, it must be diligently examined. Therefore, at the beginning, it is extended beyond its limits if a fatal and absolute necessity of being saved is asserted, by which they could in no way not be saved: and conversely, the Elect could in no way be damned, whatever they might do, or however they might live. Such a fatal and absolute certainty is handed down in the Schools of the Calvinists: but quite impiously and abundantly. For although on the part of GOD and all creatures, nay even of the gates of hell, there is nothing that can intercept the salvation of the Elect: yet it must by no means be denied that the guilt of perdition can emerge from the Elect themselves. For if (which they can certainly do by the powers of their own will) they cease to obey the voice of their shepherd, if, having cast aside faith and a good conscience, they degenerate from the flock of sheep into goats: since they are not separated from the love of GOD, which is in CHRIST JESUS, either by GOD or by any creature; they separate themselves from it. Provided, therefore, that we do not separate ourselves, provided that we persevere to the end, Matt. 24:13, provided that we remain founded and stable in the faith, and are not moved from the hope of the Gospel, Col. 1:23, provided that we persist in good, Rom. 11:22, provided that we are found faithful even unto death, Rev. 2:10, nothing at all will detract from the certainty of Election.

Then, the certainty and infallibility of Election is not asserted by us to be such that it imposes a necessity on men in being saved: just as neither the will of GOD, nor the certainty of providence, brings such a necessity to anyone. For just as GOD so wills and provides that their own freedom of acting is not meanwhile taken away from secondary causes: so also he chooses men so that they may nevertheless be saved freely and contingently in the meantime. Moreover, although according to itself in order to secondary causes it is possible for the predestined to die in mortal sin: yet in order to the Predestination of GOD, the salvation of the predestined is not contingent, but most certain. And although, speaking absolutely, GOD could not predestine anyone: yet in the composite sense, the predestined cannot not be predestined: since this has necessity from the hypothesis. It is commonly said, however, that a thing has certainty in two ways, as Thomas teaches in q. 6. de Verit. art. 3. In one way, from itself alone, such as the heavens, and similar necessary things, the Resurrection of the dead, and what other things are contained in the articles of faith. In the second way, from the concurrence of many things, just as, although any single thing may fail: yet the whole species is always preserved, because GOD provides in such a way that new individuals always succeed. Predestination has this second certainty. For although the predestined can of himself sin mortally, and fall away finally (which having happened, he would not properly have been called elect or predestined), yet GOD applies so many aids that he either does not sin mortally: or if he should fall greatly, and fall away entirely from the grace of GOD, he may nevertheless rise again, and in the harbor of repentance betake himself to the sacred anchor of faith, and thus never finally fall away. Therefore, although in relation to secondary causes and the will of the judgment he is saved freely and contingently: yet in relation to the providence of GOD and predestination, he is saved most certainly and infallibly. And this is what has the greatest use, not only for comforting the minds of the pious against every doubt in the matter of salvation: but also for exhortation, namely, that they may never cease to beseech GOD with assiduous prayers for the gift of perseverance, to make their calling and election firm, and to work out their salvation in fear and trembling. And this is the first proof of our thesis.

The second must be sought from the nature and property of faith. For true and justifying faith is such a confidence in the mind of the believer, concerning the promises and mercy of GOD through and on account of Christ, which makes him certain not only of the remission of sins: but also of his own election and eternal adoption, so that he who doubts about this, can hardly ever be sufficiently certain about that. For very little confidence of salvation is left to us, if we know that we are in grace only for the present moment: but doubt what is to happen tomorrow: and divine mercy is terminated by too narrow limits, if it is so restricted that the mind, relying on gratuitous promises, cannot conceive an undoubted expectation of salvation. Therefore, true faith is that which, with the terror of conscience set aside, and the fear of losing salvation repelled, effectively provides the firmest confidence and certainty of eternal Election and salvation, so that he who does not believe with the same certainty of faith that Christ is the Son of GOD, and that he will have eternal life, that is, that he is in the number of the Elect: he does not yet have true and integral faith.

Thirdly, there are examples of the Saints at hand, which clearly prove our Thesis: The Apostle testifies concerning Abraham, that he believed in hope against hope, not being weak in faith, nor hesitating in unbelief regarding the promise of GOD, knowing most fully that GOD is able to keep whatever He has promised, Rom. 4, 18. and the three following verses. 2. The example of David is illustrious, Psal. 23, 4. If I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: and Psal. 31, 1. In thee O Lord have I hoped, I shall not be confounded forever. 3. The fearless confidence of the Apostles concerning themselves and other believers from Rom. 8, 39. and following, 1 Tim. 4, 8. is sufficiently known. 4. The same could be seen in the Martyrs, who, how undoubted, nay, most certain confidence they had concerning their own salvation and predestination, is evident even from the fact that they underwent even the most atrocious martyrdoms with a most willing and most prepared mind.

Nor is it for the Papists to object that these things were done by some singular privilege and peculiar revelation of GOD: as the Council of Trent has it, Sess. 6. cap. 12. It was indeed said to Abraham, Thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace. Gen. 15, 15. It was said to Moses, I will show thee all good, Exod. 33, 19. To the Blessed Virgin Mary, when it had been said, Blessed art thou among women, she herself said: All generations shall call me blessed: Luc. 1, 28. & 48. It was said to the Apostles by Christ: I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever: John 14, 16. But what was said to them in this part, will be thought to have been said to all who are instructed with the same faith: Mark 13, 37. Since, apart from the personal gift of miracles, there was nothing in that mission of the Holy Spirit which was not common to all believers.

Latin:

Huberus de CertitudineElectionis, non nifi ex Univerfalitate Electionis constare cuiquam posse somniat, nostram interim doctrinâ de particularitate Electionis, tanquàm Desperationis plenam, simpliciter damnans.

Triplex iste error necessitatem nobis imponit, Quæstionem hanc de Electionis certitudine, & Perseverantiâ Electorum accuratiùs evolvendi.

Initiò autem hoc loco non propriè controvertitur de eo capite certitudinis, quo de præsente gratiâ DEI quæritur: sed de eo, quod in specie de Prædestinationis certitudine agit. Non est autem in hac parte nobis disputatio vel de hæreticorum fide, qui falsas, & cum fidei fundamento pugnantes opiniones fovent, & tuentur: vel de Epicuræorum persuasione, in summâ scelerum licentiâ, salutem sibi, & impunitatem scelerum pollicente: Quorum utrorumque salutis & electionis certitudo non est tantùm dubia, si sic pergant: sed damnatio etiam justa potiùs ac certa. Sed nec illud diffitendum est, veram etiam fidem Electorum non esse perfectam: insuper etiam pro mirando DEI consilio, tentationibus quandoque obnoxiam. Quo utroque casu ad precum anchoram confugiendum, orandumque est, Credo Domine; sed opem tufer incredulit ati meæ. Marc. 9, 24. Item, Dominè adauge nobis fidem. Luc. 17, 5. Sed & illud hoc loco observandum est, pugnari à nobis, non pro absolutâ aliquâ certitudine, quam credentes & Electi ita habere possint, ut quicquid etiam agant, & quales quales se in vitâ gerant, certi tamen de salute & Electione esse possint. Qualis sanè certitudo carnali securitati patrocinaretur. Hæc ergò omnia à præsenti Controversiæ statu probè removenda sunt, & videndum, quid ex nostrâ parte affirmetur, aut statuatur.

Thesis verò nostra hæc est: Pij omnes, & verè credentes, si modò ipsi velint, non tantum esse possunt, sed & sunt, quin imò esse debent in animo suo certissimi, non de præsente tantum DEI gratiâ: sed futurâ etiã salute, & sic de suâ æternâ Electione. Imò si Scripturæ loca, quæ de Prædestinatione agunt accuratiùs expendantur; patebit manifestè, non alio fine aut nomine magis, doctrinam Prædestinationis in Scripturâ patefactam nobis esse, quàm ut dubitatione degratiâ DEI & salute credentium, ex animis profligatâ, in hac ipsâ doctrinâ, basis quasi quædam & fundamentum certitudinis nobis proponeretur. Monstrat hoc conclusio capitis octavi Epistolæ ad Romanos versu 28. ad finem usque capitis. Quod ipsum docent etiam verba Apostoli Rom. 11, 29. Electionis doctrinæ inserta; Dona & vocatio DEI sunt ἀμεταμέλητα sine pœnitentiâ. Evincent hoc alia Scripturæ dicta: Ephf. 1, 4. Elegit nos, ut simus sancti & irreprehensibiles coram eo in charitate. 2. Tim. 2, 19. Solidum stat fundamentum DEI, habens signaculum hoc: Novit Dominus, qui sunt ejus.

Thesews hujus nostrae probatio constat 1. ex certitudine & infallibilitate ipsius praedestinationis. Certa enim ea est, atque infallibilis, ac proinde finem, quem quaerit, semper affequitur. Rom. 11, 7. Certa autem est primum ex parte DEI eligentis, & totius illius ordinis, qui ex parte DEI considerandus est. Vitam enim, quam promisit DEUS ovibus suis, eam largitur: non pereunt in aeternum: nemo rapit eas de manibus ipsius, Johan. 10, 28. Jam cum cadunt electi, non colliduntur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam Psal. 37, 24. ut providente ipso, adversus quosvis infestos infortuniorum casus satis sint muniti. Quin ipsa quoque DEI potentia ita ipsis prospexit, ut nulla creatura sit, quae ipsos separare possit a dilectione DEI, quae est in Christo Jesu: Rom. 8, 39. Deinde est & infallibilis Electio ratione praevisionis in DEO, quae falli, aut errare non potest: uti praecedente quaestione proxima ostensum.

Caeterum ut circa hanc ipsam Electionis certitudinem ac infallibilitatem neque in excessu neque in defectu peccemus, sedulo dispiciendum fuerit. Initio ergo extra limites ea extenditur, si fatalis & absoluta salvandi necessitas astruatur, qua non possint ullo modo non salvari: & ex adverso, non possint ullo modo damnari Electi, quicquid etiam faciant, aut quomodocunque vivant. Qualis fatalis & absoluta certitudo in Scholis Calvinianorum traditur: sed satis impie & abunde. Nam licet ex parte DEI & creaturaru omnium, imo portarum etiam infernalium nihil est, quod salutem Electorum intervertere possit: quin tamen ex ipsis Electis perditionis culpa emergere possit, negari minime debet. Si enim (quod viribus suae voluntatis facere utique possunt) voci pastoris sui obedire desinant, si fide & bona conscientia abjecta, ex ovium grege, in haedos degenerent: cum neque per DEUM, neque per creaturam ullam segregentur a dilectione DEI, quae est in CHRISTO JESU; ipsi sese inde segregant. Dummodo ergo ipso nos non segregemus, dum ad finem modo perseveremus Matth. 24, 13. dummodo permaneamus in fide fundati, & stabiles, nec a spe Evangelij dimoveamur, Coloss. 1, 23. dummodo in bono persistamus, Rom. 11, 22. dummodo fideles ad mortem usque reperiamur, Apoc. 2, 10. Certitudini Electionis nihil quicquam decidet.

Deinde certitudo & infallibilitas Electionis, non talis a nobis asseritur, quae necessitatem hominibus in salvando imponat: quemadmodum neque voluntas DEI, neque providentiae certitudo talem necessitatem cuiquam affert. Sicut enim ita vult, & providet DEUS, ut causis secundis sua interim libertas agendi non adimatur: ita etiam eligit homines, ut libere tamen interim, & contingenter salventur. Caeterum quamvis secundum se in ordine ad causas secundas possibile sit praedestinatum mori in peccato mortali: in ordine tamen ad Praedestinationem DEI, salus Praedestinati non est contingens, sed certissima. Et quamvis, absolutè loquendo, possit DEUS quemcunque non prædestinare: tamen in sensu composito prædestinatum non potest non prædestinare: siquidem hoc necessitatem habet ex hypothesi. Dicitur autem vulgò res habere certitudinem dupliciter, sic docente Thomâ q. 6. de Verit. art. 3. Uno modo, ex seipsâ solâ, sicut cœlum, & similia necessaria, Resurrectio mortuorum, & quæ in articulis fidei alia continentur. Secundo modo ex concursu multarum rerum, Sicut, quamvis singulare quodlibet deficiat: tamen tota species semper conservatur, quia ita providet DEUS, ut semper succedant nova singularia. Hanc secundam certitudinem habet prædestinatio. Nam quamvis prædestinatus ex se possit peccare mortaliter, & excidere finaliter (quo tamen facto propriè electus aut prædestinatus dicendus non fuisset) tamen tot adminicula adhibet DEUS, ut aut non peccet mortaliter: aut si ruat maximè, & gratiâ DEI totaliter excidat, resurgat tamen, & in portu pœnitentiæ ad sacram fidei anchoram se recipiat, & fic finaliter nunquàm excidat. Proindè quamvis in ordine ad causas secundas, & arbitrij voluntatem liberè & contingenter salvetur: in ordine tamen ad providentiam DEI & prædestinationem, certissimè & infallibiliter salvetur. Et hoc est, quod non ad confolandas tantùm piorum mentes adversus omnem dubitationem in negocio salutis: sed ad exhortationem etiam usum maximum habet, nempè ut DEUM pro perseverantiæ dono assiduis precibus interpellare, vocationem & electionem suam firmam facere, & salutem suam in timore & tremore operari nunquam desinant. Et hæc est prima thesews nostræ probatio.

Altera peti debet ex naturâ fidei & proprietate. Est enim fides vera & justifica, talis in animo credentis fiducia, de promissionibus & misericordiâ DEI per & propter Christum, quæ ipsum non de remissione tantùm peccatorum: sed electione etiam suâ, & adoptione æternâ certum efficit, adeò, ut qui de hac dubitat, de illâ satis certus esse vix unquàm possit. Exigua enim perquàm salutis fiducia nobis relinquitur, si ad præsens duntaxat momentum sciamus, nos esse in gratiâ: dubitemus autem, quid in crastinum sit futurum: & nimis angustis finibus terminatur divina misericordia, si ita restringitur, ut non indubitatam salutis expectationem, animus promissionibus gratuitis fretus possit concipere. Fides ergò vera est, quæ terrore conscientiæ secluso, & metu amittendæ salutis propulsato, firmissimam æternæ Electionis, & salutis fiduciam & certitudinem efficaciter præstat, adeò, ut qui non eâdem fidei certitudine credit, Christum esse Filium DEI, & se habiturum vitam æternam, hoc est, se esse in numero Electorum: is veram & integram fidem nondùm habeat.

Tertiò, sunt in promtu exempla Sanctorum, quæ Thesin nostram luculenter comprobant: De Abrahamo Apostolus perhibet, quòd crediderit in spem contra spem, non infirmatus fide, neque diffidentiâ hæfitans in promissione DEI, plenissimè sciens, DEUM, quæcunque promiserit, posse servare Rom. 4, 18. & sequentibus tribus. 2. Davidis illustre est exemplum, Psal. 23, 4. Si ambulem in mediâ umbrá mortis, non timebo mala: & Psal. 31, 1. In te Domine speravi, non confundar in æternum. 3. Apostoli de se, & alijs fidelibus intrepida fiducia ex Rom. 8,39. & sequ. 1. Tim 4, 8. satis nota est. 4. In Matyribus idem videre licuit, qui quàm indubitatam, imò certissimam de suâ salute & prædestinatione fiduciam habuerint, vel indè patet, quod libentissimo, paratissimoque animo martyria etiam atrocissima subierunt.

Neque est, ut ex singulari aliquo privilegio, & revelatione DEI peculiari ista facta esse, Pontificij objiciant: uti habet Concil. Trid. Sess. 6. cap 12. Dictum quidem fuit Abrahæ, Tu ibis ad partes tuos in pace. Genes. 15, 15. Mosi dictum fuit, ego ostendam tibi omne bonum Exod.33, 19. B. Virgini Mariæ, cùm dictum esset, Benedicta tu inter mulieres, ipsa dixit; Beatam me dicent omnes generationes: Luc. 1. 28. & 48. Apostolis dictum fuit à Christo : Rogabo Patrem, & alium Paracletum dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in æternum: Johan. 14, 16. Verûm quod hac inparte istis dictum fuit, omnibus eâdem fide instructis dictum putabitur: Marc. 13, 37. Siquidem extra personale miraculorum donum, nihil fuit in istâ missione Spiritus Sancti, quod non credentibus omnibus fuerit commune.


### On the Certainty of Election (continued)

Fourthly, the Apostle is witness, that we have not received the Spirit of fear, but of love: not the Spirit of bondage again to fear: but the Spirit of adoption, by which we cry, Abba Father: Rom. 8, 15. that we may know what things have been given to us by GOD: 1 Cor. 2, 12. nay, that we may know that we have eternal life, 1 John 5, 13. Now, indeed, he who doubts about his own Election, what does he do other than make the testimony of the Spirit clearly void. There is therefore no place for doubt.

Finally, Peace of Conscience, and peace with GOD, and the testimony concerning Christ is a certain necessary good, which is proper to believers: Rom. 5, 1. Being justified by faith we have peace with GOD. John 5, 10. He who believes in the Son, has the testimony in himself. But doubt concerning salvation and Election takes away the peace of conscience, and the testimony concerning Christ. Therefore it has no place in believers.

And by these reasons indeed the certainty of our Election is most rightly built up against the Papist doubt. But since it is wont to happen not rarely, that in more serious temptations of faith no sense or motion of it appears at all: this will be the work, this the labor, that we have most thoroughly explored upon what foundations the certainty of our Election rests. Huberus, as has already been said above, lays down the Universality of Election as a foundation: Which is nothing else than to build a bridge out of spider webs, and in affliction especially, and when one is constituted in temptation, to offer wormwood for consolation, and to hand over a rope of despair, even a doubled one, into the hands. For what kind of certainty is this, if an afflicted mind concludes thus: GOD has chosen all men, whether they believe or not. I am a man: I am chosen. The Devil will immediately object: Very well: but Jews, Turks, and infidels are also men. Therefore they are equally chosen. But now they perish eternally with their Election; therefore no privilege is left to you from this Election of yours: If Huber here seeks protection and comfort from the application of Election, which ought to take place in time through faith: he will render the afflicted and tempted man even more dismayed, as one who perceives in himself no sense or movement of faith, and has learned from Huber's doctrine that the Election of the children of GOD was made without any regard to faith.

The Calvinists seek the certainty of Election in the hidden, they creep into the very vaults of the Heavens, they pry into the secret counsel of GOD, and they inquire a priori, as the saying goes; whether they are in the number of the Elect? Where they refer everything to an absolute decree in GOD concerning the salvation and damnation of men. But this is nothing else than to point out a precipice to one traveling along the royal and military road, and to pave the way for men either to security or to despair. For as the Book of Concord rightly warns, from that absolute decree of both Election and damnation, men are taught to conclude thus: If I am elected to eternal life, nothing will be lacking to my salvation, even if without any repentance, I have committed crimes and outrages of every kind, and have despised the Word and the Sacraments etc.: For I shall necessarily be saved, because the Election of GOD must come to pass by absolute necessity. But if I am not predestined: it will profit me nothing at all, even if I have repented, because I shall be able neither to hinder nor to change the Predestination of GOD. Augustine reports, in his book on the Good of Perseverance, chapter 15, that there was a monk in his monastery who, when the brothers rebuked him for not doing what should be done, and doing what should not be done, replied: Whatever I am now, it does not matter: for I shall be such as GOD foresaw I would be. This is, to be sure, to grasp the mysteries of faith a priori, and as Chrysostom said somewhere, to handle glowing iron not with tongs, but with one's fingers: which is the characteristic of all fanatics.

Our churches, taking great care to avoid both these precipices, judge that the certainty of Election is to be defined a posteriori, and from what is plain or manifest. Holy Scripture shows that plain and manifest foundation, directing us to the revealed decree of Election, and one that has been sufficiently explained thus far. If we examine this decree a little more accurately, a twofold principle can be given, upon which the unshaken certainty of our Election depends. ONE is of the order in Election: THE OTHER is of the ordered. As far as the order is concerned, the doctrine of Predestination with the whole complex of causes, of the manner, and of the order in saving, is fully contained and plainly revealed in the Gospel. For 1. out of mere mercy and love toward the human race, GOD decreed to send His Son, by whose death and obedience the redemption of the whole human race might come to pass. 2. He decreed through the preaching of

the Word, to call all to the fellowship of the kingdom of His Son, especially the Elect, of whom no one would be one outside the assembly of the called. 3. He decreed that He wishes to be effective in the Word and Sacraments through the Holy Spirit to work repentance, faith, righteousness, and sanctification in His Elect. 4. He decreed that He would defend His elect against the world and the devil, and would so perfect the good work begun in them, that no one would snatch them from His hand. Therefore, with that fatherly heart of the loving GOD regarded: with the wounds of Christ the redeemer inspected: with the promises of the Gospel considered: with the faith and truth weighed, which GOD has already abundantly provided and confirmed to us in protecting and defending us ever since the first breath of vital air: nothing at all, not even the least bit, is left on the part of GOD that could detract from or diminish anything concerning the certainty of the salvation and election of the pious. Thus therefore, as regards the former Principle, our Election and Salvation, placed in the hand of GOD, is most certain. And this is what the Blessed Luther writes, that in his temptation and affliction concerning his Election, he was excellently answered by Staupitz: Look upon the wounds of Christ, and His blood shed for you, and thence Predestination will shine forth. And Luther himself writes in a certain sermon: If an afflicted mind wishes to dispute about Predestination, then the beginning must be made from the wounds of Christ. And elsewhere he writes to one who was tempted: Christ is the true mirror of Predestination, in which the immense love of GOD is discerned: concerning whom this highest command exists: Hear Him. Similar things are read in Luther, Tom. 8. Jen. fol. 263. And such indeed is the former Principle, upon which the certainty and foundation of our Election depends.

As regards the latter principle: namely, the men who are ordered: it is indeed true that explicit mention of singular and individual persons is not had in the Scriptures. For Election was not made in this manner, as if GOD had said: Let John, Peter, Paul, or this or that person, be in the number of the Elect: let Cain, Saul, Judas, or this or that person, be in the number of the Reprobate. Indeed, Election ought not to have been made in this manner. For thus the universality of the promises would have been rendered vain: thus the faith of the pious would also have been languid. But it is true that, under the universal condition of the order, all singular ordered persons are contained. Therefore, where individuals and singular persons are found to be duly subordinated to the Order of Election: it is to be believed and known with no less certainty of faith that they are of the number of the Elect, than if their Election had been expressed by name in the Word of GOD: Which indeed is entirely contained therein: but implicitly: namely, included in the most certain Universality of believers. However, the pious and truly believing find this subordination, as it were written and inscribed:
