1. In their profession, which is proper to Christianity. Hence St. Blandina, to the Devil afflicting her, answered nothing other than I am a Christian. Now this profession includes

my very Vocation, and thus subordinates the believing man to the second part of the divine Order.

2. Every pious person also finds this very thing inscribed upon his own name, while he remembers his Baptism, which is a character imprinted, as Augustine holds in Psalm 59. By which are marked those who, through Baptism, begin to be sheep of Christ: Indeed, it is that Sign of the covenant, and Seal of righteousness Rom. 4, 11. For through Baptism the elect have been buried together into the death of Christ, and have put on Christ Rom. 6, 4. In which is again a great part of the order, to which GOD willed the business of salvation to be bound.

3. Every pious person finds this subordination ascribed to his ears and mouth, as it were, in an excellent way, when he recalls to memory with what Zeal and eagerness he heard the Word of salvation: with what faith he received the message of Absolution from the Ministry of the Church, in the name of the Most Holy Trinity: with what end and fruit he strengthened his faith with the pledge of the Lord's Body and Blood: Where he recognizes himself to be ascribed to the third part of the divine Order.

4. When a pious and faithful person certainly believes or determines that he is inscribed in the hand of GOD, Isa. 49, 16, he now understands himself to be subordinated to the first part of the divine Order. On which matter let Luther be seen in the explanation of the Gospel of John 3, on the second day of Pentecost.

5. Yet every pious faithful person finds and acknowledges the chief Scripture of this matter in his own mind, For while every pious person is a faithful witness to himself of the righteousness accepted from GOD through faith freely; while of adoption given through the Spirit and internal testimony; while of the desire and ardent purpose, clinging in the pious mind and heart, of persevering in the grace of GOD: it cannot be but that from this part also, an immovable certainty concerning Predestination arises. On which matter Luther writes excellently in Tom. 6, page 181, on chapter 17 of John: If anyone desires to know whether he is elect, let him observe the mouth of Christ. For he who, being called, hears the Word of Christ, and embraces it seriously, he is of those who are given to Christ by the Father. And a little later on page 148: If you adhere to Christ the Lord, you are certainly of the company of those whom GOD chose from the beginning, so that they might be peculiarly His. And in the enarratio of the Gospel of the Good Shepherd, he writes thus: Whoever recognizes Christ in this way, as I have said, is certainly of his sheep, and elected into a sheep: nor is there need for him to torture himself further with empty thoughts, whether he is predestined: but let him comfort himself confidently, and be certain that he has GOD propitious. And on chapter 26 of Genesis: If you adhere with firm faith to the revealed Word, so that your heart feels that you will not lose Christ, even if you were despoiled of everything: then you are most certainly predestined. Again in ch. 17 of John, fol. 182: Do not esteem it lightly, but let it be a certain and safe comfort to you, if you feel that you love Christ and His Word, and desire from the heart to persevere in the same, that you are of that company who are Christ's, and are not to perish. Luther made the practice of this certainty testified by his own example, Tom. 3, fol. 513, in the Confession Minor: If I, out of temptation or the agonies of death (which GOD forbid), were to say something else, then it should be nothing,

And I wish hereby to have publicly confessed that it is wrong, and inspired by the Devil. Moreover, in the exploration of these things, everyone can be the best witness to himself. Whence the Apostle warns that everyone should test himself, 1 Cor. 11, 28; indeed, he even commands that the pious should explore themselves, whether they are in the faith, whether they feel Christ dwelling in them, 2 Cor. 13, 5. Now the same Apostle is a witness that the Holy Spirit Himself bears witness together with our spirit that we are Children of GOD, Rom. 8, 16. And Peter warns that we should make our Election firm, 2 Pet. 1, 10. Which is most rightly accomplished both by other exercises of piety frequented, and by this exploration frequently and diligently repeated. But whatever exceeds these limits, especially if the mind torments itself concerning PERSEVERANCE, the pious will be certainly persuaded that it proceeds from the author the Devil. Here, therefore, it must be cautiously observed that neither ear nor any place at all be given in the mind to the Devil's disputations. For nowhere does any command exist by which we are ordered to be anxious and tormented about our Perseverance in the future: Indeed, Christ is witness that each day has its own care: but the same prohibits us from being anxious for the morrow, Matt. 6, 34.

Furthermore, the testimonies which are brought forth from the Scriptures concerning the gift of Perseverance and fear and trembling have no weight at all for weakening the certainty of our Election. Perseverance is indeed necessary, but not more necessary than that which is confirmed by illustrious promises to those believing in God, 1 Cor. 1, 8 and 9. Faithful is GOD, by whom you were called into the fellowship of His Son, who will confirm you even to the end without blame to the day of our Lord JESUS CHRIST. And Phil. 1, 6. He who began a good work in you will perfect it even to the day of JESUS CHRIST. 1 Cor. 10, 13. Faithful is GOD, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you can bear: but will even with the temptation give the outcome, that you may be able to bear it. Heb. 13, 5. I will not desert you, nor will I leave you: so that we may say confidently: The Lord is my helper, I will not fear what man may do to me.

Therefore the sum of the matter turns on this: Either believers are held by a true ardor and desire for the gift of perseverance: or, not being anxious about it, they sleep securely on both ears. If the former, notwithstanding any of their own infirmity, they are sufficiently provided for regarding this gift through the divine promises. But if the latter, such are not even to be held as elect.

The remaining sayings of Scripture, which commend and demand fear from believers, do not treat of servile fear, such as is altogether that which suffocates and extinguishes faith by doubting: But of filial fear, Rom. 8, 15. Nor are those sayings discourses about the doubting of faith: but about carnal security and insolence from the confidence of received gifts, which the pious are commanded to drive away, since by it true Faith itself is shaken out and extinguished.

Latin:

Quartò, testis est Apostolus, Nos non accepisse Spiritum timoris, sed dilectionis : non Spiritum servitutis rursus ad timorem : sed Spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus, Abba Pater: Rom. 8, 15. ut sciamus, quæ sint nobis à DEO donata : 1. Cor. 2, 12. imò ut sciamus, quòd vitam æternam habeamus, 1. Joh. 5, 13. Jam verò qui dubitat de suâ Electione, quid facit aliud, quàm quod testimonium Spiritus planè facit irritum. Non est ergò dubitationi locus.

Tandem, Pax Conscientiæ, & pax cum DEO, ac testimonium de Christo est necessarium quoddam bonum, quod est credentium proprium : Rom. 5, 1. Justificati fide pacem habemus ad DEUM Johan. 5, 10. Qui credit in Filium, habet testimonium in seipso. At dubitatio de salute & Electione tollit pacem conscientiæ, & testimonium de Christo. Non ergò locum habet in credentibus.

Et his quidem rationibus Electionis nostræ certitudo contra Pontificiam dubitationem rectissimè astruitur. Cæterùm cùm haud rarò fieri soleat, uti in gravioribus tentationibus fidei sensus aut motus planè nullus appareat : hoc opus, hic labor fuerit, ut quibus fundamentis certitudo Electionis nostræ nitatur, exploratissimů habeamus. Huberus, uti jam suprà dictum, pro fundamento substernit Electionis Universalitatem : Quod nihil est aliud, quàm ex texturis aranearum pontem cõstruere, & in afflictione præsertim, tentationeq; constituto absynthium pro solatio propinare, & desperationis funem vel duplicatum in manus porrigere. Ecquæ enim hæc est certitudo, si mens afflicta sic colligat: DEUS omnes homines elegit, sive credant, sive non. Ego sum homo: sum electus. Excipiet statim Diabolus: Benè quidem: sed & Judæi, Turcæ, & infideles, quique sunt homines. Ergò æquè sunt electi. Jam verò illi cum Electione suâ æternùm pereunt; nihil proindè tibi privilegij ex hâc Electione tuâ est relictum: Hîc si Huberus ex applicatione Electionis, quæ in tempore per fidem fieri debeat, præsidium & solatium quærat: rursus afflictum & tentatum hominem magis consternatum reddet, ut qui nullum fidei vel sensum, vel motum in se deprehendit, & ex Huberi doctrinâ didicit, Electionem filiorum DEI factam esse sine ullo respectu ad fidem.

Calviniani Electionis certitudinem in abscondito quærunt, ipsa Cælorum claustra perreptant, arcanum DEI consilium rimantur, & à Priori, quod dici solet, inquirunt; nùm sint in numero Electorum? Ubi ad absolutum in DEO decretum de salute & damnatione hominum omnia referunt. Sed hoc nihil est aliud, quàm pro viâ regiâ & militari iter facienti præcipitium monstrare, & vel ad securitatem, vel ad desperationem hominibus viam sternere. Nam ut liber Concordiæ rectè admonet, ex absoluto illo & Electionis, & damnationis decreto, homines sic colligere docentur: Si electus sum ad vitam æternam, nihil saluti meæ decedet, etiamsi absque omni pœnitentiâ, omnis generis scelera & flagitia designavero, Verbum & Sacramenta contempsero &c: Necessariò enim salvabor, quia Electionem DEI absolutâ necessitate fieri oportet. Sin autem prædestinatus non sum: nihil prorsus mihi profuerit, etiam si pœnitentiam egero, quia Prædestinationem DEI neque impedire, neque mutare potero. Refert Augustinus, lib. de bono Perseverantiæ cap. 15. fuisse in suo monasterio Monachum, qui fratribus corripientibus, cur facienda non faceret, & non facienda faceret, responderit: Qualiscunque nunc sum, nihil refert: talis enim ero, qualem me DEUS futurum esse præscivit. Hoc nimirum est à priori mysteria fidei capessere, & quod Chrysostomus alicubi dixit, candens ferrum non forcipe, sed digitis contrectare: id quod fanaticorum omnium est proprium.

Ab utroque isto præcipitio Ecclesiæ nostræ sibi apprimè caventes, certitudinem Electionis à posteriori, & ex plano, sive manifesto, definiendam esse censent. Illud verò planum & manifestum fundamentum monstrat Scriptura Sacra, ablegans nos ad decretum Electionis revelatum, & hactenùs satis fufficienter explicatum. Hoc decretum, si paulò accuratiùs expendamus, geminum dari potest principium, ex quo immota Electionis nostræ certitudo dependet. UNUM est ordinis in Electione: ALTERUM est Ordinati. Quod ad Ordinem attinet, doctrina Prædestinationis cum toto complexu causarum, modi, ordinis in salvando, in Evangelio plenè comprehensa, & planè revelata est. Nam 1. ex merâ misericordiâ & dilectione erga genus humanum, decrevit DEUS, mittere Filium suum, cuj9 morte & obedientiâ totius generis humani fieret redemtio. 2. Decrevit per prædicationem

Verbi, ad societatem regni Filij sui vocare omnes, Electos præcipuè, quorum extra cœtum vocatorum nemo quisquam futurus esset. 3. Decrevit, quòd in Verbo & Sacramentis velit esse efficax per Spiritum Sanctum ad operandam in Electis suis pœnitentiam, fidem, justitiam, sanctificationem. 4. Decrevit, se electos suos adversus mundum & diabolum defensurum, & ita bonum opus, in ipsis cœptum, perfecturum esse, ut de manu suâ nemo eos sit rapturus. Ergò paterno isto corde diligentis DEI spectato: vulneribus Christi redimentis inspectis: promissionibus Evangelij consideratis: expensâ fide & veritate eâ, quam in nobis protegendis tuendisque jam indè à primo Vitalis auræ Spiritu DEUS nobis abundè præstitit, & confirmavit: nihil profectò, ne minimum quidem ex parte DEI relinquitur, quod de certitudine salutis & electionis piorum, quicquam detrahere, aut diminuere possit. Sic ergò, quoad prius Principium, Electio & Salus nostra in manu DEI reposita, est certissima. Et hoc est, quod B. Lutherus scribit, in tentatione & afflictione de suâ Electione sibi constituto, à Staupitio egregiè responsum esse: Inspice vulnera Christi, & sangvinem ejus pro te effusum, & indè fulgebit Prædestinatio. Et Lutherus ipse in sermone quodam scribit: Si animus afflictus de Prædestinatione disputare velit, tùm initium à vulneribus Christi faciendum est. Et alibi scribit ad quendam tentatum: Christus est verum Prædestinationis speculum, in quo cernitur dilectio DEI immensa: de quo præceptum hoc summum extat: Hunc audite. Similia leguntur apud Lutherum, Tom. 8. Jen. fol. 263. Et tale quidem prius est Principium, ex quo Electionis nostræ certitudo ac fundamentum dependet.

Quoad posterius principium: Homines nimirùm ordinatos: verum quidem est, de singularibus & individuis explicitam mentionem in Scripturis non haberi. Neque enim in hunc modum Electio facta est, quasi dixisset DEUS: Johannes, Petrus, Paulus, vel hic, aut ille, sit in numero Electorum: Cain, Saul, Judas, vel hic, aut ille, sit in numero Reproborum. Imò ne quidem hunc in modum Electio fieri debuit. Sic enim inanis promissionum Universalitas reddita: sic piorum quoque fides langvida futura esset. Sed enim verum est illud, sub universali conditione ordinis, singularia ordinata omnia contineri. Proindè ubi individua & singularia Ordini Electionis ritè subordinata esse deprehenduntur: non minori fidei certitudine credendum & sciendum est, esse illa ex numero Electorum, quàm si nominatim Electio illorum, in Verbo DEI expressa esset: Quæ quidem omninò comprehensa ibidé extat: sed implicitè: nempè Universalitati credentium certissimæ inclusa. Inveniunt autem pij & verè credentes subordinationem istam, scriptam quasi & insculptam:

1. In professione suâ, quæ est Christianismi propria. Hinc S. Blandina, Diabolo affligenti nihil aliud respondit, quàm Christiana sum. Includit autem professio hæc Christianis-

mi ipsam Vocationem, & sic hominem credentem secundæ parti Ordinis divini subordinat.

2. Hoc ipsum quoque nomini suo inscriptum pius quisque invenit, dùm Baptismi sui recordatur, qui est character infixus, ut habet Augustin. in Psalm 59. Quo notantur, qui per Baptismum oves Christi esse incipiunt: Imò est Signum illud fœderis, & Signaculum justitiæ Rom. 4, 11. Per Baptismum enim in mortem Christi consepulti sunt electi, & induerunt Christump Rom. 6, 4. In quo est rursus pars magna ordinis, ad quem salutis negotium adstrictum esse DEUS voluit.

3. Auribus atque ori quasi suo, subordinationem istam adscriptam pius quisque peregregiè invenit, quando recolit memoriâ, quo Zelo & studio Verbum salutis audiverit: quâ fide à Ministerio Ecclesiæ, in nomine Sacro-Sanctæ Trinitatis, Absolutionis nuncium acceperit: quo fine & fructu, Dominici Corporis & Sangvinis arrhâ fidem suam roboraverit: Ubi tertiæ parti Ordinis divini se adscriptum esse cognoscit.

4. Cùm pius ac fidelis certò credit aut ststuit, in manu DEI se esse adsignatum, Jes 49, 16. jam primæ Ordinis divini parti se subordinatum esse intelligit. Quâ de re videatur Lutherus in explicatione Evangelij Johan. 3. Feria secundâ Pentecostes.

5. Præcipuam tamen hujus rei Scripturam in animo suo piè fidelis quisque invenit & agnoscit, Nam dùm justitiæ per fidem à DEO acceptæ gratuitæ; dùm adoptionis per Spiritum & testimonium internum donatæ; dùm desiderij & propositi ardentis, in animo & corde pio hærentis, de perseverando in gratiâ DEI, ipse sibi pius quisque fidus testis est: non potest non hac etiam parte, de Prædestinatione immota certitudo exoriri. Quâ de re Lutherus, Tom. 6. pag. 181. super caput 17. Johannis egregiè scribit: Si quis scire cupit, sitné electus, is observet os Christi. Qui enim vocatus Verbum Christi audit, idque seriò amplectitur, hic ex ijs est, qui sunt Christo dati à Patre. Et paulò pòst pag. 148. Si adhæres Christo Domino, certè es ex eorum cœtu, quos DEUS ab initio elegit eò, ut sint peculiariter sui. Et in enarrat. Evangelij de Bono Pastore, sic scribit: Quicunq; Christum hoc modo, quo dixi, agnoscit, certò ex ovibus ejus, & in ovem electus: neq; opus est ei, ulteriùs se torquere inanibus cogitationibus, Sitné prædestinatus: sed confidentur se soletur, & certus sit, quod habeat DEUM propitium, Et ad cap. 26. Genes. Si firmâ fide revelato Verbo adhæres, ita ut cor tuum sic sentiat, te non amissurum Christum, etiamsi omnibus spoliatus fueris: tùm certissimè es prædestinatus. Rursus in c. 17. Joh. fol. 182. Ne leviter æstimes, sed sit tibi certum ac tutum solatium, si sentis, quòd Christum, Verbumq; ejus ames, & ex corde cupias in eodem perseverare, quòd sis ex eo cœtu, qui sunt Christi, nec sunt perituri. Praxin hujus certitudinis suo exemplo testatam fecit Lutherus, Tom. 3. fol. 513. in Conf. Minore: Ob ich aus Anfechtung oder Todesnöthen (da GOTT für sey) etwas anders würde sagen/ so solle es doch nichts seyn/

Und wil hiermit offentlich bekennet haben/ daß es unrecht/und vom Teuffel eingegeben seye. Potest autem in harum rerum exploratione sibiipsi quisque optimus esse testis. Unde Apostolus monet, ut seipsum quisque probet, 1. Cor. 11, 28. imò præcipit etiam, ut pij explorent seipsos, utrum in fide sint, utrum in se habitantem Christum sentiant. 2. Cor. 13, 5. Jam idem Apostolus testis est, ipsum Spiritum Sanctum unà cum Spiritu nostro perhibere nobis testimonium, quòd simus Filij DEI, Rom. 8, 16. Et Petrus monet, ut firmam faciamus Electionem nostram 2. Petr. 1, 10. Quod tùm alijs pietatis exercitijs frequentatis: tum exploratione istâ crebrò & sedulò iteratâ rectissimè perficitur. Quicquid autem limites istos excedit, præcipuè si de PERSEVERANTIA animus se excruciet, id ab autore Diabolo proficisci, certò persuasum pij habebunt. Hîc ergò cautè observandum illud est, ne Diaboli disputationibus vel auris, vel locus saltem ullus in animo præbeatur. Nuspiam enim ullum extat præceptum, quo de Perseverantiâ nostrâ in futurum angi & discruciari jubeamur: Imò cuilibet diei suam curam esse, Christus testis est: nos autem in crastinum solicitos esse, idem prohibet, Matth. 6, 34.

Porrò quæ de dono Perseverantiæ & timore ac tremore ex Scripturis proferuntur testimonia, ea ad infirmandam certitudinem Electionis nostræ nihil prorsus momenti habent. Necessaria quidem est perseverantia, sed non necessaria magis, quàm illustribus promissionibus â Deo credētibus confirmata, 1. Cor. 1, 8. & 9. Fidelis est DEUS, per quem vocati estis in societatem Filij ejus, qui confirmabit vos usq́ ad finem sine crimine ad diem Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI. Et Phil. 1, 6. Qui cœpit in vobis opus bonum, perficiet usquè ad diem JESU CHRISTI. 1. Cor. 10, 13. Fidelis DEUS est, qui non patietur vos tentari super id, quod ferre potestis: sed etiam cum tentatione dabit eventum, ut sufferre possitis. Hebr. 13, 5. Non te deseram, nequè te relinquam: ita ut confidentes dicamus: Dominus mihi adjutor, non timebo, qui faciat mihi homo.

Ergò in eo summa rei vertitur: Aut vero ardore, & desiderio doni perseverantiæ tenentur credentes: aut de eo non solliciti, securi in utramque aurem dormiunt. Si prius illud, quacunque suâ non obstante infirmitate, satis ipsis de dono isto per promissiones divinas cautum est. Sin hoc posterius, tales ne quidem pro electis habendi erunt.

Reliqua dicta Scripturæ, quæ Timorem commendant, & exigunt à credentibus, non de servili timore agunt, qualis omninò est, qui fidem dubitando suffocat & extingvit: Sed de filiali, Rom. 8, 15. Neque illa dicta conciones sunt de dubitatione fidei: sed de carnali securitate & insolentiâ ex fiduciâ acceptorum donorum, quam pellere pij jubentur, quippe quâ Fides ipsa vera excutitur & extingvitur.


### Can someone be certain of another's election?

Since these things are so, the use of this doctrine is to be well noted, which does not consist in this, that where the certainty of election is not felt: but rather either languor or trepidation is detected, there the danger of salvation is immediately judged to be present. But here it ought rather to be: 1. That whatever trepidation or doubt is felt, we determine it not to be of the nature of faith: but to pertain to the infirmity of the flesh. 2. That we diligently resist such trepidations and doubts, and whatever is prepared for us from the divine promises, from the love of God, from the merit of Christ, from the πληροφορία of faith, as a place of remedy, to overcome those things: that we diligently seek, use, and strenuously urge against the insults of the Devil and the infirmities of our flesh.

These things being thus established, it is clear what must be answered when it is asked, Whether anyone can be certain of his own election? Where we hold the affirmative: Since the Spirit of adoption received in the elect bears witness to their spirit, that they are the children of God. Rom. 8, 16. But if it is asked, Whether anyone can be certain of another's election? We answer, Although charity, which hopes all things, 1 Cor. 13, 7, promises itself nothing but good concerning a neighbor who also lives piously and honestly: yet by the certainty of faith, into which error cannot fall, no one can know a priori, and before the end of life, concerning others, who belong to the number of the predestined, or not.

Latin:

Quæ cùm ita sefe habeant, Usus Doctrinæ istius probè est notandus, qui non in eo consistit, ut ubi certitudo Electionis non sentitur: sed vel langvor potiùs, vel trepidatio deprehenditur, ibi statim salutis periculum esse judicetur. Sed hîc potiùs esse debet: 1. Ut quicquid trepidationis aut dubitationis sentitur, statuamus non esse de naturâ fidei:sed ad carnis infirmitatē pertinere. 2. Ut ejusmodi trepidationibus, & dubitationibus sedulò resistamus, & quicquid ex promissionibus divinis, ex dilectione DEI, ex merito Christi, ex fidei πληροφορίᾳ, remedij quasi loco, ad istas expugnandas nobis est paratum: illud sedulò requiramus, usurpemus, & contra Diaboli insultus, & carnis nostræ infirmitates strenuè urgeamus.

His ita constitutis, liquet,quid respondendum sit, quando quæritur, An de suâ Electione aliquis possit esse certus? Ubi affirmativam tenemus: Siquidem in Electis acceptus adoptionis Spiritus,testimonium perhibetSpiritui ipsorum, quod sint Filij DEI. Rom. 8, 16. Quod si verò quæratur, An aliquis de alterius Electione certus esse possit? Respondemus, Licèt charitas, quæ sperat omnia, 1. Cor. 13, 7. de proximo quoque piè ac honestè vivente, nihil non boni sibi polliceatur: tamen certitudine fidei, in quam non cadat error, scire à priori, & ante finem vitæ de alijs nemo potest, quinám ad prædestinatorum numerum pertineant, necne?


### Question VIII. Can the Elect fall away from the Grace of God?

Concerning this question we hold the affirmative, but under this clear distinction, that we determine that the elect can indeed fall away totally, but not finally. For because the elect are never defined except by the implication of the end and the saving event, which is faith persevering to the end, salvation and blessedness: hence it certainly follows that those who fall away finally cannot be held as elect. Therefore the terms and propositions are clearly convertible: Every elect person perseveres to the end: And: Everyone who perseveres in faith to the end is elect. Which ἀντιστροφὴ does not apply to all the regenerate, many of whom believe for a time, but afterwards fail, and persevere in incredulity to the end, and perish eternally: which is manifest by the example of Judas the traitor. Whence it is rightly said: that every elect person is indeed regenerate: but not conversely, that every regenerate person is elect, but only he who perseveres in faith to the end.

This perseverance of the elect in faith is defined, not in the Sacramentarian sense by a continuous and never-interrupted act of believing, or a perpetual duration of faith: so that whatever the elect do, even if they commit the most atrocious crimes, they nevertheless retain the Holy Spirit, the grace of God, and faith: for such perseverance falls to no mortal: since even the just man falls seven times a day, and rises again, Proverbs 24, 16. But it is defined by the reason of the end and the saving event, insofar as the elect person, however much he may have fallen into grave sins, even those committed against conscience, nevertheless, having performed true and serious repentance, perseveres in the faith of Christ to the end, and thus dies in faith. Nor was this distinction between the regenerate and the elect: likewise between the twofold fall, one total, which can happen even to the elect, the other final, which never falls upon the elect, but only upon the regenerate, born or devised in our brain, as Huberus grunts: but it has Christ himself as its author, who expressly distinguishes between προσκαίρους, or temporary ones, who believe at least for a time: and between those who persevere in faith to the end. Matt. 13, 21, and 23. Luke 8, 13, and 15. Matt. 10, 22. But it is also to be noted that the term (TOTALLY), when the question is about the elect, is not to be understood by reason of time, as some are accustomed to agitate this term through childish sophistication: but by reason of the subject matter, that is, the grace of God, the Holy Spirit, and faith, that the elect, falling into mortal sins, do not merely lose some particle of the grace of God, the Holy Spirit, and faith, and faith in them lies hidden like fire under ashes: but that they lose these good things entirely: so that they no longer have God propitious: they expel the Holy Spirit, as one who never dwells in an unclean soul κατ᾿ ἐνέργειαν τῆς χάριτος: finally, they cast off faith entirely, as that which cannot stand with mortal sins in one and the same subject at once. Away then with the cavil of the Sacramentarians, writing that the elect lose faith, at least as regards sense and use: Beza in Respon. 2. ad acta colloq. Mompel. page 68. Furthermore, that the elect can lose both the sense and use, and the movement of faith, and faith itself entirely, and the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit, we demonstrate to the eye with the following arguments:

I. Express testimonies of Scripture contend for this thesis, Ezek. 18:24. If the righteous man turns away from his righteousness, and commits iniquity according to all the abominations that the wicked man has done, shall he live? ALL his righteousness that he has done shall not be remembered, etc.

Matt. 12:44 & 45. When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he walks through dry places, and seeks rest, and finds none: Therefore he says: I will return to my house from whence I came out: And coming he finds it swept with brooms, and adorned: Then he goes, and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there: and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first. Which same thing is repeated also in Luke 11:24 & 25.

Rom. 8:13. If you live according to the flesh, you shall die.

1 Cor. 10:12. Let him who thinks he stands, take heed lest he fall.

1 Tim. 1:19. Hold faith and a good conscience: which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck.

2 Pet. 2:20, 21, & 22. For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning. For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them. But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.

1 John 3:15. Whosoever is a murderer hath not eternal life abiding in him.

Rev. 2:5. Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.

In these and similar places of Scripture, certain things are to be observed, and must be strenuously urged against the sophistries of the Calvinists. 1. The subject, of whom it is predicated that he can overthrow himself, that he can slip, die, and be damned, is established by the Holy Spirit Himself as any truly regenerate and believing person: this is proven partly by the description of the Just man in Ezek. ch. 18, 5 and the following four verses; partly by the opposition of the Wicked, who because of impenitence is to perish eternally; and finally, partly by the periphrasis of that just man who had been such that the Lord no longer remembered all his former injustice, that is, to whom He had forgiven sins: indeed, those who are led by the Spirit of Christ, who are not in the flesh but in the Spirit; who ought to mortify the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit. 2. That not only temporal punishments, but also eternal death are denounced to those who have thus fallen, is manifest from 1 John 3:15. Where eternal life is denied to them: furthermore, that Scripture treats of that death which can be averted through conversion and faith: which cannot be said of temporal death. 3. That not just any, or hypocritical faith is understood, but that which produces all righteousness, Ezek. 18:24, which produces a good conscience, 1 Tim. 1:19, and which ought to be retained, ibid., indeed, the shipwreck of which happens in such a way that it delivers a man to Satan and his empire, by the example of Hymenaeus and Alexander, 1 Tim. 1:20, 2 Tim. 2:18. 4. And lastly, that such threats in the Scriptures are not empty flashes from a chamber pot, much less are they to be understood κατὰ δόξαν only, or according to the opinion of men, or according to the judgment of charity, and not according to the very truth of the matter and fact. For the very sound of the words and the emphasis of the phrases clearly prove the contrary: and far be it that we should attribute such a game to the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scriptures.

II. The argument shows by the example of the Saints and the Elect, who having fallen into mortal sins, lost the grace of God, the Holy Spirit, and faith: such as our first parents, Gen. 2:17 and ch. 3:17, Rom. 5:12 and following. A clear sign of which matter was that servile fear and flight from the face of God the just judge, Gen. 3:8, 9, 10. Likewise the example of Aaron, for whom

the calf-making and idolatry God had been so angry that He wished to cut him off: Deut. 9:20. Likewise the example of Saul, 1 Sam. 15:26, of Judas the traitor, John 17:12, of David the murderer and adulterer, 2 Sam. 11:4 & 15 and ch. 12:5 & 7 & 13, of Peter the denier, Matt. 26:69 and following, of Thomas denying the article of faith concerning the Resurrection of Christ, John 20:25, of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who made shipwreck of the faith: 1 Tim. 1:19, 2 Tim. 2:18, of the incestuous Corinthian, whom the Apostle delivered to Satan, and later received back into the Church, 1 Cor. 5:5, 2 Cor. 2:8. Which examples, each and all, irrefutably show that the Elect can fall from the grace of God and totally lose faith. For the immovable definitive sentence of the Apostle stands, Gal. 5:19: The works of the flesh are manifest, which are these: Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, idolatry, etc. They which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. And Eph. 5:5. For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ. Matt. 10:33, Luke 9:16: Whosoever shall deny me before this world, him will Christ also deny before the heavenly Father. Now indeed, where there is the loss of eternal life, there also is the loss and deprivation, and indeed the total loss, of justifying faith. For they mutually exclude each other: eternal damnation, and faith lurking as it were under the ashes, as Beza dreams.

And that we may pass over a thousand examples which could be brought forward for the confirmation of our thesis, it is pleasing to inquire of one from the Sacramentarians: Were the first parents holy and elect before the fall? They will answer affirmatively: and their creation to the image of God proves this, that is, in holiness and righteousness before God, Gen. 1:27, Eph. 4:24. But I ask further: Did the same persons, having admitted that most sad fall, commit mortal sin and fall from the grace of God? If the Sacramentarians wish to deny this as much as possible, they nevertheless dare not: since one may read the contrary in the whole of Scripture, Rom. 5:12 and following. What madness, therefore, it would be to wish to ascribe to the Elect, even after such a fall, such a perfection that, having once received the grace of God, they could not simply fall from faith and sanctification.

III. Reasons and arguments taken from the analogy of faith clearly demonstrate our thesis. 1. Christ and Belial, the Holy Spirit and the Devil cannot dwell in the same subject at the same time: but one being admitted, the other is expelled. 2 Cor. 6:15, Wisd. 1:5: Wisdom (namely Christ, Luke 7:35) does not dwell in a body subject to sins. And yet the Saints and the Regenerate, indeed even the Elect falling into sins against conscience, provide a lodging for the Devil: whence Eve exclaims, the serpent beguiled me, Gen. 3:13, and it is read concerning David that Satan provoked him to number the people, 1 Chron. 21:1. 2. Where there are mortal sins, there faith has no place. The reason is: Because he who sins mortally, he is subject to death and eternal damnation. And yet, where there is damnation, there is no faith: just as conversely, where there is true faith in Christ, there is no condemnation, Rom. 5:1. And yet the Regenerate and The elect can sin mortally: as has been demonstrated thus far. Therefore.

3. Whoever is overcome by sin, he is enslaved to sin: Now whoever serves sin, does not perform the works of righteousness: and consequently is destitute of true faith. And yet the elect are very often overcome by sin, however much the struggle of the flesh and Spirit may have preceded, by the example of Peter, denying the Lord. Therefore. The proposition has as its author the Apostle Peter himself, 2 Pet. 2:19. The minor is manifest in itself from the preceding.

And what need is there for many words in a manifest matter, when even Beza himself, driven by the force of truth, found it necessary to write, in Resp. 2 to the acts of the Colloquy of Montbéliard, page 74, that David (certainly an elect person) would have perished, had he not repented. But truly, whoever is so constituted that he can perish, he certainly must have totally lost faith: For where a little spark of faith remains, there damnation has no place, according to the sweetest promises: GOD will not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking flax: Isa. 42:3, Matt. 12:20. And CHRIST himself calls such as are weary and heavy-laden to himself, Matt. 11:28.

Latin:

Circa hanc quæstionem Affirmativam tenemus, sed sub luculentâ hac distinctione, ut Electos totaliter quidem, non autem finaliter excidere posse statuamus. Quia enim Electi nunquàm, nisi finis atque eventus salutaris implicatione definiuntur, qui est, fides ad finem perseverans, salus atque beatitudo: hinc utique fit, ut qui finaliter excidunt, pro Electis haberi non possint. Sunt ergò termini ac propositiones planè convertibiles: Omnis Electus ad finem usquè perseverat: Et: Omnis ad finem usquè in fide perseverans, est Electus. Quæ ἀντιστροφὴ in renatos quosvis non cadit, quorum plurimi ad tempus credunt, posteà verò deficiunt, & in incredulitate ad finem usque perseverant, æternumque pereunt: id quod exemplo Judæ proditoris, manifestum est. Undè rectè dicitur: quòd Omnis quidem electus sit renatus: non verò vice versâ, Omnis renatus sit Electus, sed ille tantùm, qui ad finem usque in fide perseverat.

Definitur autem hæc Electorum in fide perseverantia, non sensu Sacramentario per continuum, & nunquàm interruptum actum credendi, sive perpetuam fidei durationem: ita ut quicquid agunt Electi, & si maximè atrocissima scelera definent, tamen Spiritum Sanctum, Gratiam DEI & fidem retineant: Talis enim perseverantia in mortalium neminem cadit: siquidem Justus etiam in die cadit septies, & resurgit, Proverb. 24, 16. Sed definitur ratione finis & eventus salutaris, quatenùs nimirum Electus, quantumvis in gravia peccata, etiam contra conscientiam commissa, prolapsus sit, acta tamen vera ac seria poenitentia, in fide Christi ad finem usque perseverat, & sic in fide moritur. Neque haec distinctio inter Renatos & Electos: item inter geminum lapsum, Totalem unum, qui Electis etiam obtingere potest, Finalem alterum, qui in Electos nunquam, sed tantum in Renatos cadit, in cerebro nostro nata, aut excogitata est, uti Huberus grunnit: sed ipsum Christum autorem habet, qui disertè distingvit inter προσκαίρους, sive temporaneos, qui ad tempus saltem credunt: & inter eos qui ad finem usque in fide perseverant. Matth. 13, 21, & 23. Luc. 8, 13. & 15. Matth. 10, 22. Est verò & illud notandum, Terminum (TOTALITER) quando de Electis est quaestio, non ratione temporis intelligendum esse, uti quidam per puerilem Sophisticationem hunc terminum exagitare solent: sed ratione subjectae materiae, hoc est, Gratiae DEI, Spiritus Sancti, & Fidei, quòd nimirùm Electi in peccata mortalia ruentes, non tantùm particulam aliquam Gratiae DEI, Spiritus Sancti & fidei amittant, & fides in ipsis quasi ignis sub cineribus sopitus delitescat: sed quòd bona haec ex toto amittant: ut DEUM non ampliùs habeant propitium: Spiritum Sanctum expellant, ut qui in immundâ animâ κατ᾿ ἐνέργειαν τῆς χάριτος nunquàm habitat: Fidem denique prorsus excutiant, ut quæ cum peccatis mortalibus in uno eodemque subjecto simul ac semel stare nequit. Facessat ergò Sacramentariorum cavillatio, scriptitantium, Electos amittere fidem, saltem quoad sensum & usum: Beza in Respon. 2. ad acta colloq. Mompel. pag. 68. Cæterùm Electos posse & sensum, & usum, motumque fidei, & fidem ipsam totam, ac gratiosã Spiritus Sancti inhabitationem amittere, sequentibus argumentis ad oculum demonstramus:

I. Militant pro hac thesi expressa Scripturæ testimonia Ezech. 18, 24. Si averterit se Justus à justitia sua, & fecerit iniquitatem secundum omnes abominationes quas fecit impius, numquid vivet? OMNES justitiæ ejus, quas fecerat, non recordabuntur &c.

Matth. 12, 44. & 45. Cum immundus Spiritus exierit ab homine, ambulat per loca arida, & quærit requiem, nec tamen invenit: Dicit ergò: Revertar in domum meam, undè exivi: Et veniens invenit eam scopis mundatam, & ornatam: Tunc vadit, & assumit septem alios Spiritus secum, nequiores se, & intrantes habitant ibi: & fiunt novissima hominis illius deteriora prioribus. Quod ipsum repetitur etiam Luc. 11, 24. & 25.

Rom. 8, 13. Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini.

1. Cor. 10, 12. Qui se existimat stare, videat, ne cadat.

1. Tim. 1, 19. Retine fidem & bonam consciensiam : quâ repulsâ nonnulli fidei naufragium fecerunt.

2, Pet. 2. 20. 21. & 22. Postquàm effugerunt coinquinationes mundi, in cognitione Domini, & Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, his rursus implicati, superantur, facta sunt eis posteriora deteriora prioribus. Melius enim erat illis, non cognovisse viam justitiæ, quàm post cognitionem retrorsum converti ab eo, quod illis traditum est, sancto mandato. Contingit enim eis illud veri proverbij : Canis reversus ad suum vomitum, & sus lota in volutabro luti.

1. Johan. 3, 15. Omnis homicida non habet vitam æternam in se manentem.

Apoc. 2, 5. Memor esto, undè excideris, & age pœnitenciam : & prima opera fac : Si minus, venio tibi citò, & movebo candelabrum tuum de loco suo, nisi pœnitentiam egeris.

In his & similibus Scripturæ locis, observanda quædam, & contra Calvinianorum strophis strenuè urgenda veniunt. 1. Subjectum, de quo prædicatur, quòd evertere se, quòd labi, mori, ac damnari possit, ab ipso Spiritu Sancto constitui quemlibet verè renatum & credentem: id quod evincit partim descriptio Justi apud Ezech. c. 18, 5. & sequentibus quatuor : partim oppositio Impij, qui propter impœnitentiam sit æternùm periturus : partim deniq; periphrasis justi illius, qui talis fuerit, ut Dominus omnis prioris injustitiæ ipsius non ampliùs recordatus fuerit, hoc est, cui peccata remiserit : imò, qui Christi Spiritu ducuntur, qui non in carne, sed in Spiritu sunt : qui Spiritu actiones carnis mortificare debent. 2. Non pœnas tantùm temporales, sed & æternam mortem his sic prolapsis denunciari, liquet manifestè ex 1. Joh. 3, 15. Ubi vita æterna illis negatur : deindè verò quòd de eâ morte agit Scriptura, quæ per Conversionem & fidem averti potest : id quod de temporali morte dici nequit. 3. Non quamlibet, vel hypocriticam fidem intelligi, sed eam, quæ omnem justitiam gignit. Ezech. 18, 24. quæ bonam conscientiam gignit. 1. Tim. 1, 19. quæq; retineri debet, ibtd. imò cujus naufragium ita fiat, ut hominem Satanæ, ejusq; imperio tradat, exemplo Hymenæi & Alexandri, 1. Tim. 1, 20. 2. Tim 2, 18. 4. & postremò, hujusmodi comminationes in Scripturis non esse inania fulgura è pelvi, nedùm eas κατὰ δόξαν tantùm, sive secundum opinionem hominum, vel juxta judicium charitatis, non de ipsâ rei & facti veritate intelligendas esse. Ipse enim sonus verborum, & emphasis phraseων contrarium luculenter evincit: & absit, ut Spiritui Sancto, in Scripturis loquenti, talem lusum affingamus.

II. Argumentum monstrat exemplo Sanctorum, & Electorum, qui in peccata mortalia prolapsi, Gratiam DEI, Spiritum Sanctum, & fidem amiserunt: ut Primorum parentum, Genes. 2, 17. & cap. 3, 17. Rom. 5, 12. & seqq. Cujus rei signum luculentum erat Metus ille servilis, & fuga à facie DEI justi judicis Gen. 3, 8. 9. 10. Exemplum item Aaronis, cusob

μοσχοποιίαν & Idololatriam ita iratus fuerat DEUS, ut voluerit ipsum excindere: Deut. 9, 20. Exemplum item Saulis 1. Sam. 15, 26. Judæ proditoris Joh. 17, 12. Davidis homicidæ & adulteri 2. Sam. 11, 4 & 15. & c. 12, 5 & 7. & 13. Petri abnegatoris Matth. 26, 69. & seqq. Thomæ articulum fidei negantis de Resurrectione CHRISTI Joh. 20, 25. Hymenæi & Phileti, qui naufragium fidei fecerunt: 1. Tim. 1, 19. 2. Tim. 2, 18. incestuosi Corinthiaci, quem Satanæ traditum Apostolus, postmodùm in Ecclesiam recipit, 1. Cor. 5, 5. 2. Cor. 2, 8. Quæ sanè exempla singula & universa irrefragabiliter ostendunt, Electos gratia DEI excidere, & fidem totaliter amittere posse. Stat enim immota sententia definitiva Apostoli, Gal. 5, 19. Manifest a sunt opera carnis, Scortatio, immundicia, luxuria, homicidia, Idololatria & c. Qui talia agunt, regnum DEI non consequentur. Et Eph. 5, 5. Hoc scitote, quòd omnis fornicator, aut immundus, aut avarus, non habet hæreditatem in regno Christi. Matt. 10, 33. Luc. 9, 16. Qui negaverit me coram hoc mundo, hunc & negabit Christus coram Patre cœlesti. Jam verò ubi est jactura æternæ vitæ, ibi etiam est jactura, & amissio, & quidem totalis fidei justificantis. Se enim mutuò excludunt: Damnatio æterna, & fides sub cineribus quasi delitescens, uti Beza somniat.

Et ut mille exempla, quæ pro confirmatione theseωs nostræ in medium proferri possent prætereamus, unum illud ex Sacramentarijs sciscitari lubet: Nùm primi parentes ante lapsum fuerint sancti & electi? Affirmatè respondebunt: idq; evincit Creatio ipsorum ad imaginem DEI, hoc est, in sanctitate & justitiâ coram DEO, Gen. 1, 27. Eph. 4, 24. Sed porrò quæro: An ijdem lapsu illo longè tristissimo admisso, peccatum mortale admiserint, & gratiâ DEI exciderint? Negare hoc si maximè velint, non tamen audent Sacramentarij: siquidem Scriptura universa contrarium benè longum legere licet, Rom. 5, 12. & seqq. Quæ ergò vesania fuerit, Electis jam post lapsum talem perfectionem velle adscribere, quâ simpliciter gratiâ DEI semel acceptâ, fide & sanctificatione excidere non possint.

III. Rationes & argumenta ex analogiâ fidei petita thesin nostrã liquidò demonstrant. 1. Christus & Belial, Spiritus Sanctus & Diabolus simul & semel in eodem subjecto habitare nequit: sed unò admisso expellitur alter. 2. Cor. 6, 15. Sap. 1, 5. Sapientia (Christus videlicet, Luc. 7, 35. non habitat in corpore peccatis subdito. Atqui Sancti & Renati, imò Electi quoq; ruentes in peccata contra conscientiam Diabolo hospitium præbent: Undè Heva exclamat, serpens seduxit me, Gen. 3, 13. & de Davide legitur, quòd Satanas ipsum concitârit, ad numerandum populum 1. Paral. 21, 1. 2. Ubi sunt peccata mortalia, ibi fides locum non habet. Ratio est: Quia qui peccat mortaliter, ille subjacet morti, & æternæ damnationi. Atqui, ubi est damnatio: ibi nulla est fides: Quemadmodum vice versâ ubi est fides vera in CHRISTUM, ibi nulla est condemnatio, Roman, 5, 1. Atqui Renati & Electi possunt peccare mortaliter : uti hactenus demonstratum. Ergo.

3. Quicunq; se superatur a peccato, is peccato in servitum est addictus : Jam quicunq; peccato servit, justitiae opera non facit: ac proinde fide vera destituitur. Atqui Electi saepius superantur a peccato, quantumvis etiam lucta carnis & Spiritus praecesserit, exemplo Petri, abnegantis Dominum. Ergo. Propositio autorem habet Apostolum ipsum Petrum, 2. cap. 2, 19. Minor perse manifesta ex praecedentibus.

Et quid multis in re manifesta opus, cum vel Beza ipse, vi veritatis adactus, scribere necessum habuerit, in Resp. 2 ad acta Colloq. Momp. pag. 74. Davidem (certe Electum) periturum fuisse, nisi resipuisset. At vero, quicunq; ita comparatus est, ut perire possit, is certe fidem totaliter amiserit, necessum est : Nam ubi scintillula fidei reliqua est, ibi damnatio locum non habet, secundum dulcissimas promisiones : Calamum conquassatum non confringet DEUS, nec linum fumigans extinguet : Esa. 42, 3. Matth. 12, 20. Et CHRISTUS ipse tales laborantes & oneratos ad se vocat, Matth. 11, 28.


### Special Controversy Ninth and Last

Concerning the true and perfect definition of Predestination.

Various definitions of Predestination are read among the Ancients and the moderns: but partly vicious and imperfect: and partly concise and obscure. Some have defined Predestination as the purpose of GOD to crown the just, from the foreknowledge of their good end.

Although these made mention of Grace and a good end, that is, of faith in CHRIST and perseverance: yet they determined that both were not comprised by Predestination: but were merely presupposed by it: and what was worst, they constituted the cause of Election in the foreknowledge of a good end: meanwhile referring only the will to crown, that is, the purpose of saving, to Predestination. Of this opinion were Faustus, Bishop of the Gauls, lib. 1 de lib. arbit. cap. 4, Damascene in a certain book against the Manichaeans, and that whole crowd of bishops, whom Prosper of Aquitaine mentions, and Hilary, Bishop of Arles, in his letters to Augustine, which are extant in Tom. VII of his Works, prefixed to the book on the Predestination of the Saints.

But Lord Augustine himself produced various definitions. For sometimes he defines it by the Preparation of Grace: in the book on the Predestination of the Saints, cap. 10. Sometimes he says it is nothing other than the Foreknowledge and preparation of the benefits of GOD, by which those who are delivered are most certainly delivered. lib. de bono perseverantiae c. 14. But the most accepted definition, both to Augustine and to other older writers, is that Election is an Efficacious ordination of the elect to eternal life through efficacious means. And this definition approaches most closely to the truth, and most correctly constitutes more parts of Predestination than those former ones.

We, more fully and more plainly, define Predestination from those things which have been argued thus far in this manner: Election or Predestination is the divine purpose and decree of the will made from eternity, by which GOD, out of mere mercy, in CHRIST, chose to eternal life, and certainly determined to save all those who truly believe in CHRIST, and persevere in that faith unto the end: the rest of the company of men being destined to eternal damnation solely on account of unbelief and final impenitence.

Some carp at the Genus of this Definition, and prefer to define Predestination by Action, rather than by the decree of GOD, chiefly for these reasons: 1. Because Election is noted in the Scriptures as being a certain divine action. 2. Because synonyms such as, to inscribe in the book of life, to consign into the hand of GOD, show the same. 3. Because according to the ancients, predestination is the eternal preparation and disposition of future works. 4. Because Scripture constitutes that purpose of GOD as the rule of Predestination. 5. And lastly, because by the word action all things are ascribed entirely to GOD, and nothing at all is left to human merits. But, which I would say with all respect to those theologians, these reasons do not seem to be of such weight and moment that they can persuade us that the word action, by reason of Genus, is more convenient than the word decree or purpose.

For as regards the first reason, certainly every decree of GOD presupposes his action, and shows according to what rule that action behaves itself, namely according to the purpose or decree: which is what the fourth reason demands.

Then those phrases, to inscribe in the book of life, to seal in the hand of GOD, are improper, and in a metaphorical sense signify nothing other than to decree or determine certainly: so that thus the second reason militates more for our opinion.

The third reason coincides with the first; nor does it oppose us. For the word Decree, which we use in place of Genus, shows as if by a closer proximity that that preparation consists in its own certain decree: and it is the same, whether I express this decree in the genus itself, or show it afterwards by parts. That that preparation was made according to some decree.

The fourth and final reason supports our cause. For all things pertaining to our salvation and Election are much more evidently ascribed to GOD alone, and derogated from human merits and powers, by the word Decree than by the word Action: which even the very emphasis of the word Decree manifestly implies.

Latin:

De Praedestinationis definitione vera & perfecta.

VAriae apud Veteres & recentiores leguntur Praedestinationis definitiones : sed partim vitiosae & imperfectae : partim vero concisae & obscurae. Quidam Praedestinationem definierunt. Quod sit propositum DEI coronandi justos, ex praescientia boni exitus eorundem.

Hi licet Gratiae & boni exitus, hoc est, fidei in CHRISTUM & perseverantiae mentionem fecerint: utramq; tamen Praedestinatione non comprehendi : sed ab eadem duntaxat praesupponi statuerunt : quodq; pessimum fuit, in boni exitus praescientia causam Electionis constituerunt : interim solam coronandi voluntatem, hoc est, salvandi propositum ad Praedestinationem referentes. Fuerunt in hac sententia Faustus Galliarum Episcopus, lib 1. de lib. arbit. cap. 4. Damascenus in libro quodam contra Manichaos, & tota illa Episcoporum turba, cujus meminit Prosper Massiliensis, & Hilarius Arelatensis Episcopus in Epistolis suis ad Augustinum, quae Tom. VII. Operum ejus extant, lib. de Praedestinat. Sanctorum praefixae.

Ipse vero D. Augustinus varias prodidit definitiones. Interdum enim eam definit per Praeparationem Gratiae : in lib. de Praedest. Sanct. cap. 10. Quandoq; nihil aliud eam esse dicit, quam Praescientiam, & praeparationem beneficiorum DEI, quibus certissime liberentur, quicunq; liberantur. lib. de bono perseverantiae c. 14. Receptissima autem tum Augustino, tum alijs vetustioribus, Electio est Efficax, quaedam ordinatio electorum ad vitam aeternam per media efficacia. Et haec definitio quam proxime ad veritatem accedit, & plures Praedestinationis partes, quam priores illae, rectissime constituit.

Nos pleniùs & planiùs Prædestinationem ex ijs, quæ hactenùs disputata sunt, hunc in modum definimus: Electio sive Prædestinatio est divina voluntatis propositum & decretum ab æterno factum, quo DEUS ex merâ misericordiâ, in CHRISTO ad vitam æternam elegit, ac certò salvare constituit omnes eos, qui in CHRISTUM verè credunt, & in eâ fide ad finem usq́; perseverant: reliquo hominum cœtu duntaxat propter incredulitatem, ac finalē impœnitentiā æternæ damnationi destinato.

Vellicant nonnulli Definitionis hujus Genus, & malunt Prædestinationem definire per Actionem, quàm per decretum DEI, eas potissimùm ob causas 1. Quòd Electio in Scripturis ita notetur, ut sit quædam actio divina. 2. Quòd Synonyma qualia sunt, inscribere in librum vitæ, in manu DEI consignare, idem ostendant. 3. Quia secundum veteres prædestinatio sit futurorum operum æterna præparatio & dispositio. 4. Quòd Scriptura Propositum illud DEI constituat Prædestinationis regulam. 5. & postremò. Quia per vocabulum actionis omnia in solidum DEO adscribantur, & humanis meritis nihil prorsus relinquatur. Verùm, quod pace bonâ istorum Theologorum dixerim, rationes hæ tanti non videntur esse ponderis atq́; momenti, ut persuadere nobis possint Vocabulum actionis, ratione Generis, commodius esse vocabulo Decreti aut Propositi.

Nam quoad primam rationem, certè omne decretum DEI præsupponit actionem ejusdem, & ostendit secundum quàm regulam illa actio sese habeat, nempè juxta propositum sive decretum: id quod quarta ratio exigit.

Deindè phrases illæ, inscribere in librum vitæ, in manu DEI consignare, sunt impropriæ, & sensu translatitio nihil aliud, quàm certò decernere, sive constituere significant: ut sic secunda ratio magis pro nostrâ militet sententiâ.

Tertiæ ratio cum primâ coincidit: neq́; nobis adversatur. Nam Decreti vox, quâ nos loco Generis utimur, tanquam per propinquius ostendit, præparationem illam certo suo constare decreto: & perindè est, sive decretum hoc in ipso genere exprimam, sive postmodùm per partes ostendam. Quòd præparatio illa facta sit secundum aliquod decretum.

Quarta & postrema ratio nostræ causæ patrocinium facit. Nam multò evidentiùs omnia ad salutem & Electionem nostram pertinentia soli DEO adscribuntur, & humanis meritis ac viribus derogantur, per vocem Decreti, quàm per vocem Actionis: id quod vel ipsa emphasis vocabuli Decreti manifestè innuit.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic)

Heretics of all times have opposed the purer doctrine of Predestination with great zeal, ever since the first cradles of the New Testament Church. And indeed, while the Apostle Paul was still alive, the Israelites or Jews constituted the cause of Predestination and salvation partly in the external prerogative of the Fathers, but partly in the works of the law. Whom the Apostle refutes sufficiently at length, both here and there elsewhere, and especially in the whole ninth chapter to the Romans.

After the times of the Apostles, the Pelagians and Caelestians repudiated the doctrine of Predestination as useless, nay, clearly harmful to the Church; indeed, they openly denied all Predestination, contending that the salvation of every single man depends entirely upon the free will of his own volition. Whence they deserved to be called enemies of the Grace of GOD.

Others attributed Predestination not to the Grace of GOD, but to Works, such as the Basilidians, the Cainites, and certain of the Pelagians. Their error, long since condemned by the Church, was resurrected from the depths of hell under the reign of the Roman Anti-Christ by the Scholastic Doctors and the Romanists, who teach that preparation for grace—when, namely, a man does what is in him, that is, what he can perform by the powers of free will—can merit predestination, or be the cause of it by reason of merit of congruity.

Others ascribed the predestination and salvation of men to some fate and to the stars and the influences of the heavenly bodies: such as the Bardesanists, who, as Augustine testifies, subjected the evil and good morals, acts, counsels, and the whole manner of human life, and eternal salvation, to fate. They named fate that connection of inferior causes with superior ones which imposes an inevitable necessity upon all things, so that not even GOD himself is free or exempt from that Law and yoke. This was a flower of the most absurd dogma of the Stoic Philosophers concerning Fate, which even the heathens themselves mocked: whence that saying: You would not believe in fate, unless your heart were fatuous. And that of Juvenal: Fates rule men: fate is in those parts, which the fold hides.

To these must be added the Priscillianists, who, pouring cold water on the matter, attributed the course and event of all human life to the twelve signs of the Zodiac, in such a way that they assigned a certain member of the body to each sign. To Aries the head: to Taurus the neck: to Gemini the humors: to Cancer the chest, and so on, down to the soles of the feet, which they attributed to Pisces, because astrologers teach that this is the last sign of the Zodiac. Which truly most foul heresy not only deprives man of all freedom of will in natural and civil matters, but also wickedly removes from GOD all providence, and in particular all predestination, and every decree concerning the salvation of men. Whence in the Council of Braga this heresy was publicly condemned, with such a Canon promulgated: chap. 9. If anyone believes that the souls and bodies of men are bound by a fatal sign, as the Pagans and Priscillian said, let him be anathema. And chap. 10. If any believe that the twelve signs which mathematicians are accustomed to observe are distributed through the individual members of the soul or body, let them be anathema. But let some astrologers see how far they are from this impiety, who in the very same way assign not only the members of the body, but also entire provinces, regions, kingdoms, and cities to certain signs of the Zodiac, and from thence strive to construct fatal predictions. Concerning which matter we have disputed elsewhere.

Following these were others, who, from the height of their heresy, were called Predestinarians; they established that for those living piously, the pursuit of piety and good works is of no profit whatsoever if they have been ordained by GOD to death: and conversely, for the impious and sinners, even the most atrocious crimes and outrages committed against the Law of GOD are of no harm whatsoever, if GOD has predestined them to eternal life.

The Libertines of the previous century strove to interpolate the heresy of these men, and they themselves taught that neither are evil works to be avoided by men elected by GOD, nor do they harm them: nor are the reprobate to pursue good works: because the Predestination of GOD can in no way be changed.

That the Sacramentarians of today are not far from this most foul error will be evident from what follows.

Finally, in the ancient Church of the Fathers, there were heretics who, through predestination, as they spoke, praised and worshipped the reprobate as the most excellent organs and instruments of GOD: so much so that they adored Judas the Traitor, thinking him to be something divine, and his detestable crime to be a huge benefit, and that he himself had foreseen how much the passion of CHRIST would profit the human race, and therefore that he himself, by the impulse of GOD, had handed over CHRIST to be killed by the Jews. Furthermore, they pursued with divine honor the Sodomites consumed by heavenly fire: likewise Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, because they had attained the end of predestination in a singular way. They established, moreover, that all these had attained salvation because they had descended to CHRIST in the underworld: whereas, on the contrary, Abel, Enoch, Noah, the Patriarchs, the Prophets, and the remaining Saints and Elect remain in the underworld because they did not descend to CHRIST. The Cainites, Corinthians, Marcionites, and Pepuzians held this foul heresy.

But these, and other heresies of that kind, are by their nature too foul to deserve a more accurate refutation: so that to have enumerated them is to have refuted them: we therefore approach those who, in this our century, scatter false, erroneous, and horrible dogmas concerning the eternal Predestination of the Sons of GOD, and strive to fix their foot in the Church of GOD. They can, however, be not inconveniently divided into four distinct bands: so that the first is that of the Calvinists, or Sacramentarians: the second that of the Esauvites, or modern Papists. The third that of Franciscus Buccius, Dr. Samuel Huber, and a few followers. The fourth and last is that of the recent Photinians, who, just as they impiously deny and tear down the entire doctrine concerning the satisfaction of CHRIST, so also do they bark at and defile with blasphemous mouth and pen the decree of Predestination made in CHRIST the Mediator. Of each separately.

Latin:

PUriori de Prædestinatione doctrinæ, jam indè à primis Ecclesiæ Novi Testam. incunábulis, omnium temporum hæretici magno studio se opposuerunt. Et quidem in vivis adhuc existente Apostolo Paulo, Israëlitæ sive Judæi, Prædestinationis & salutis causam constituebant partim in externâ Patrum prærogativâ, partim verò in operibus legis. Quos prolixè satis refutat Apostolus, tùm passim alibi, tùm in primis toto capite nono ad Romanos.

Post Apostolorum tempora Prædestinationis doctrinam, tanquàm inutilem, imò planè noxiam Ecclesiæ repudiarunt, quin Prædestinationem omnem palàm negarunt Pelagiani & Cælestiani, contendentes, uniuscujuslibet hominis salutem ex voluntatis libero arbitrio in solidum dependere. Undè hostes etiam Gratiæ DEI dici meruerunt.

Alij Prædestinationem non DEI Gratiæ, sed Operib9 tribuerunt, ut Basilidiani, Cajani & quidam ex Pelagianis. Quorum errorem jam pridem ab Ecclesiâ damnatum, sub regno Anti-Christi Romani, resuscitarunt ab inferis quasi Doctores Scholastici, & Romanenses docentes, præparationem ad gratiam, quando scilicet homo facit, quod in se est, hoc est, quod ex viribus liberi arbitrij præstare potest promereri prædestinationem, sive causam ejus esse ratione meriti de congruo.

Alij Prædestinationem & salutem hominum fato cuipiam, & astris, siderumą; influentijs adscripserunt: ut Bardesanistæ, qui Augustino teste hominum malos, bonosą, mores, actus, consilia, & totam vitæ humanæ rationem, æternamą salutem fato subjecerunt. Fatum autem nominarunt eam causarum inferiorum cum superioribus connexionem, quæ necessitatem imponat reb9 omnibus inevitabilem, adeò, ut ne DEUS quidem ipse ab eâ Lege & jugo liber sit aut immunis. Flosculus hic fuit absurdissimi dogmatis Stoicorum Philosophorum de Fato: quod ipsi quoą; Ethnici irriserunt: Undè illud: Non crederes fatum, nisi cor tuum esset fatuum. Et illud Juvenalis: Fata regunt homines: fatum est in partibus illis, Quas sinus abscondit,

His annumerandi sunt Priscillianistæ, qui frigidam suffundentes, universæ vitæ humanæ cursum & eventum duodecim signis Zodiaci attribuerunt, ita ut cuilibet signo, certú corporis membrum adsignarent. Arieti Caput: Tauro Cervitem: Geminis humores: Cancro pectus, & sic deinceps, usą; ad plantas pedum, quas Piscibus tribuerunt, eò quòd hoc postremum Zodiaci signum esse, doceant Astrologi. Quæ sanè teterrima hæresis non modò homini omnem libertatem voluntatis in naturalibus & civilibus adimit: sed & DEO omnem providentiam, & in specie Prædestinationem omnem, omneą; decretum de salute hominum nefariè tollit. Undè in Concilio Braccarensi hæresis hæc publicè damnata fuit, tali promulgato Canone: cap. 9. Si quis animas & corpora hominum fatali signo credit adstringi, sicut Pagani & Priscillianus dixerunt, anathema sit. Et cap. 10. Si qui duodecim signa quæ Mathematici observare solent, per singula animæ vel corporis membra dissipata credunt, anathema sit. Viderint autem nonnulli Astrologi, quàm procul ab hàc impietate absint, qui eodem planè modo, non membra tantùm corporis, sed & integras provincias, regiones, regna, urbes, certis Zodiaci signis assignant, & indè fatales prædictiones extruere student. Quâ de re alibi à nobis disputatum.

Hos secuti alij, qui ab hæresews summâ Prædestinati dicti statuerunt, piè viventibus nihil quicquam prodesse pietatis ac bonorum operum studium, si à DEO ad mortem ordinati sint: & rursus impijs ac peccatoribus nihil quicquam obesse atrocissima etiam scelera atq; flagitia contra Legem DEI commissa, si DEUS ad vitam æternam eos prædestinârit.

Istorum hominum hæresin superiore seculo interpolare studuerunt Libertini, qui & ipsi docuerunt, neq; mala opera hominibus à DEO electis fugienda vel obesse : neq; reprobis bonis operibus studendum: quia nullo modo Prædestinatio DEI immutari queat.

A quo fœdissimo errore haud procul abesse Sacramentarios hodiè, ex sequentibus patêbit.

Tandem in antiquâ Patrum Ecclesiâ fuerunt hæretici, qui per Prædestinationem, uti loquebantur, reprobatos laudarunt & coluerunt, tanquam DEI organa & instrumenta præstantissima: adeò, ut Judam Proditorem adorarent, arbitrantes eum aliquid divinum esse, ejusq; detestandum scelus, ingens beneficium esse, ipsumq; præscivisse, quantum esset generi humano passio CHRISTI profutura, ac proindè ipsum DEI impulsu CHRISTUM Judæis occidendum tradidisse, Insuper divino honore prosecuti sunt Sodomitas igni cœlesti absumtos: Item Core, Dathan, & Abironem, eò quòd Prædestinationis finem, singulari modo essent assecuti. Statuerunt insuper, hos omnes salutem consecutos esse, eò quòd ad CHRISTUM ad inferos descenderint: Contrà verò Abelem, Enochü, Noahum, Patriarchas, Prophetas, & reliquos Sanctos & Electos, apud inferos manere, eò quòd ad CHRISTUM non descenderint. Fœdam hanc hæresin tenuerunt Cajani, Corinthiani, Marcionitæ, Pepuziani.

Verùm hæ, & id genus aliæ hæreses, suâ naturâ fœdiores sunt, quàm ut accuratiorem refutationem mereantur: ita ut eas enumerasse sit refutasse: ad eos proindè accedimus, qui nostro hoc seculo, circa æternam Prædestinationem Filiorum DEI, falsa, erronea, & horrenda dogmata spargunt, inq; Ecclesiâ DEI pedem figere satagunt. Possunt verò illi in quatuor distincta agmina haud incommodè dispesci: ita ut primum sit Calvinianorum, sive Sacramentariorum: Alterum Esavvitarum, sive modernorum Pontificiorum. Tertium Francisci Buccij: D. Samuelis Huberi, & paucorum asseclarum. Quartum & postremum sit Photinianorum recentiorum, qui uti universam doctrinam de satisfactione CHRISTI impiè negant & convellunt: Ita Prædestinationis etiam decretum in CHRISTO Mediatore factum, blasphemo ore ac stylo allatrant, & conspurcant. De singulis seorsim.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic): I. Calvinian error. concerning Predestination

I. Calvinian error. concerning Predestination.

The root and foundation of all errors, as many as the Calvinists cherish in this Article, is that they teach in general: that GOD, by an eternal and immutable counsel—that is, for no other cause than the free purpose of His will—destined the greatest part of the human race, without any regard for unworthiness or any sin, or as Piscator says, by a simple and absolute Decree of GOD, depending on nothing else but the pleasure of GOD Himself, to eternal damnation, and from this very thing, to declare His justice, created them for eternal destruction: and on the contrary, that He chose and ordained a few to grace and salvation likewise by a simple and absolute decree, without regard for either the merit of Christ or faith. One may read the express profession of this blasphemous opinion in Calvin, lib. 3. Inst. c. 21. 22. 23.

Nor do Calvin's disciples differ from it even in the slightest: Beza certainly, in his book of questions and answers, Volum. 1. Tractat. Theol. p. 683, defines predestination as an eternal and immutable decree, preceding in order all causes of salvation and damnation, by which GOD determined to be glorified in some, who are to be saved in Christ out of mere grace, but in others, who are to be damned in Adam and in themselves by His just judgment. And in Colloq. Mompel. page 517, he writes: That it is false that unbelief is the cause of this divine decree concerning the just perdition of some. And Vol. 1. page 417, upon chapter 9 of Romans, he does not shudder to affirm that GOD has predestined not only to damnation, but also to the causes of damnation, whomsoever He pleased. And that the reprobate are held in hatred by GOD before they are even born, and are destined for destruction without any regard for unworthiness. And in his second response to the Colloq. Momp. he writes: That the merit of Christ is not the cause, but the effect of Election.

Paræus, in Neostad. Apolog. page 46, writes that the damnation of the reprobate was not only foreseen by GOD: but he asserts that they, as vessels of wrath, were ordained to it and prepared for destruction.

Hermannus Rennecherus, in his golden chain of salvation, pages 36, 37, 38, repeatedly states that GOD looked at nothing outside Himself: but that He chose those whom He chose solely on account of Himself, and in Himself, not on account of any other cause. That sin can by no means be the cause of Reprobation: And that the cause of Reprobation is by no means to be sought in man, but in the supreme and primary cause, namely, the very free will of GOD. And on page 135, he asserts that, just as with Election, so also with Reprobation, no merit intervened: but that both proceed from and depend upon the good pleasure of GOD.

Boquinus, in the Heidelberg disputation, writes expressly that the reprobate were rejected not on account of foreseen infidelity or other sins: but solely according to the purpose of the will of GOD.

P. Martyr, in chapter 9 to the Romans, says: We deny, he says, that CHRIST, as far as His humanity and death are concerned, is the cause of our Predestination. Which same thing Ursinus also asserts in Explicat. Catech.

From this blasphemous dogma, as from the most bitter root of despair, many other errors, no less foul and impious, have sprouted like shoots and offshoots: which we shall enumerate in order:

I. That GOD created the vast majority of the world for damnation, in order to have material to declare

His justice. Calvin in the place already cited. Zanchius, lib. 5. de naturâ DEI cap. 2. page 690. b. 691. a., saying: That GOD, according to His will, determined to hate so many thousands of men, even before He had been affected by any injury from them: and afterwards also to create them as vessels of His wrath, and to prepare them for destruction. See more, and more horrible things, in the same author, in the same book, page 692, in response to Object. 13 from Hosea 13:9. To which Piscator subscribes in disp. de prædest. th. 24: GOD created and fashioned certain men for destruction: and th. 27 and 33: He created men with this intent, that they might fall in reality.

II. That there never was, is, or will be a time when GOD willed, wills, or will will to have mercy on individuals. Beza, resp. 2. ad acta Coll. Mōmp. p. 194.

III. That GOD predestined not only to damnation, but also to the causes of damnation: For man fell because GOD so decreed, and by His providence so ordained. Beza Vol. 1. p. 417.

IV. That GOD never loved the whole human race: but held the greatest part in hatred, and therefore destined them to eternal destruction. Colloq. Momp. p. 529.

V. That the Son was not sent by GOD to suffer for the whole human race, and to satisfy the Father: but only for the elect. Indeed Beza writes, part 2. Resp. ad acta Colloq. Momp. p. 221. I say again, and I profess before the whole Church, that it is false, blasphemous, and impious to say that Christ, whether it concerns the counsel of GOD, or whether it concerns the effect, did not suffer, was not crucified, did not die, and did not make satisfaction for the sins of those who are to be damned and are adjudged to eternal judgment, no less than for the sins of Peter, Paul, and all the Saints. And in the antitheses on the passage 1 John 2. To us and our associates your statement seemed intolerable, that CHRIST died for the damned. ibid. pag. 514.

V. That the promises of the Gospel, although they may seem to be universal, nevertheless pertain only to the Elect alone: Nor does GOD wish to give grace to all so that they may believe: And although the Gospel may be preached to them, and in it, and through it, the grace of GOD may be offered, yet GOD does not do this with the intention of communicating it: but rather, so that through it they may be more hardened, and rendered more inexcusable. Wherefore Piscator writes, GOD does indeed call the reprobate, but He does not wish them to come, by a holy simulation, of course: Nor does He wish them to be saved, but He blinds and hardens them, so that they do not believe, for the reason that they are reprobated. For the principal cause of unbelief is Reprobation: Because. Whatever is the cause of an inferior cause, that is also the cause of the common effect, that is, that which is born from both causes, both the superior and the inferior. Now the superior causes are: destination to destruction, reprobation, deprivation of calling, or at least deprivation of the efficacy of the Holy Spirit while calling. Piscator th. 16. 75. 76. 84. 92. 94. 103.

VII. That the elect, by no crimes, however atrocious, lose the faith once given, or cast off the Holy Spirit, and least of all can they fall from eternal salvation, to which they were once elected from eternity, or sin unto death. Nay, that the elect, even if they lead the worst life, nevertheless have greater perseverance in their infirmity than Adam had in his perfection. Beza Vol. 1. tract. Theol. p. 207. Zanch. in Miscel. p. 72. & 242. Rennech. in cat. p. 157. & 261.

VIII. That it is to be judged only from the internal motions of the Holy Spirit, which the elect feel, whether we are elect.

IX. By the power of Election it comes to pass that salvation and blessedness are obtained even by some Gentiles who were never called or brought into the fellowship of the Church. Cingl. in the book on true and false religion.

Moreover, that point well deserves observation, that although all Calvinists agree in this, that both the Election and Reprobation of men depend upon an absolute decree of GOD, preceding all causes, or upon His mere good pleasure and will: yet in glossing over and palliating this, they diverge into such different opinions that even from this a judgment can be formed regarding the stupendous impiety and vanity of this dogma. For example: most constitute the subject of Reprobation as men not yet created, and thus considered absolutely and without respect to sin: others, making a divorce from these, make the subject men already fallen into sin: as the Herborn theologians in Method. Theol. lib. 2, cap. 12; Perkins on Predestination, page 11 and following. Again, regarding the decree of Reprobation, others, and especially the more recent ones, such as Keckermann in Syst. Theol. page 208, constitute two acts of it: One, which is purely absolute, and contains in itself the purpose of GOD to pass over certain ones and leave them to themselves; which act they commonly call the Negative: The other, the ordained, which contains the decree of condemning on account of sins: which they otherwise name the Positive or Affirmative act. But Zanchius, lib. 5, cap. 2, part 4, on the Nature of GOD simply denies this, and contends that both acts are absolute, writing among other things as follows: Nothing is clearer, nothing more certain, than that the will of GOD ALONE is the cause not only of negative, but also of affirmative Reprobation: and therefore that nothing is accomplished by this distinction against that which we concluded from the Apostle; that no cause of Reprobation can be assigned simply, except the will of GOD: And that it makes no difference whether Reprobation is taken negatively or affirmatively: Since the same effect follows both, namely eternal damnation; although one immediately, the other indeed mediately.

Again, others contend that not only Reprobation, but the impiety and unbelief of men is the cause of their damnation: as Beza, Resp. 2 to Coll. Momp. p. 161. The cause of the execution of this decree, that is, of the damnation of those who perish, is not the decree of GOD. But others deny that sins are the total cause of damnation: for thus all men would have to be adjudged to eternal fire, since all have sinned: but that the hatred and will or decree of GOD preceded, and that a most just one, by which He destined the impious to eternal death: since the Apostle says that they are vessels of wrath fitted or CREATED and destined, namely by GOD, for destruction, so that in them He might show His wrath and power: as Zanchius expressly writes on the Nature of GOD, lib. 5, cap. 2, part 4, to Obj. 4, page 686 a. Piscator subscribes to Zanchius in disp. de Prædest. th. 92. We assert that the principal cause of faith is election itself: and likewise that the principal cause of unbelief is reprobation. And in thesis 94: Truly it happens from unbelief that not all are saved, but not as from a solitary cause: but as from a secondary and proximate cause. Meanwhile, however, the superior causes are not to be denied or dissembled, such as destination to destruction, Reprobation, deprivation of calling, or at least deprivation of the efficacy of the Holy Spirit during the calling.

Latin:

I. Error Calviniano. rum de Prædestinatione.

Radix & fundamentum errorum omnium, quotquot quidem hoc in Articulo fovent Calviniani, est, quòd docent in genere: DEUM æterno & immutabili consilio, hoc est, non alia quâ quam de causâ, nisi ex libero voluntatis proposito, maximam humani generis partem, nullo indignitatis, aut peccati cujusquam intuitu, vel ut piscator loquitur, Decreto DEI simplici atq; absoluto, non aliundè, nisi ab ipso DEI placito pendente, æternæ damnationi destinârit, atq; ex hoc ipso, pro declaranda sua justitia, ad æternum exitium creaverit: paucos contrà ad gratiam & salutem itidem simplici & absoluto decreto, sine intuitu vel meriti Christi, vel fidei, elegerit, & ordinârit. Disertam blasphemæ hujus opinionis professione legere licet apud Calvinum lib. 3. Inst. c. 21. 22. 23.

Neq; vel tantillum ab eâ abhorrent Calvini discipuli: Beza certè in lib. quæst. & responsionum, Volum. 1. Tractat. Theol. p. 683. Prædestinationem definit, quòd sit æternum & immutabile decretum, ordine antegrediens omnes salutis & damnationis causas, quo DEUS constituit, in aliis quidem in Christo, ex merâ gratiâ servandis, in aliis verò in Adamo & semet ipsis justo suo judicio damnandis, glorificari. Et in Colloq. Mompel. pag. 517. scribit: Falsum esse, quòd incredulitas sit causa divini hujus decreti, de justè perdendis aliquibus. Et Vol. 1. pag. 417. sup. cap. 9. Rom. affirmare non exhorrescit, DEUM non tantùm ad damnationem, sed etiam ad causas damnationis prædestinasse, quoscunq; libuerit. Et Reprobos odio haberi à DEO nondùm natos, & nullo indignitatis respectu exitio destinari. Et resp. 2. ad Colloq. Momp. scribit: Meritum Christi non esse causam, sed effectum Electionis.

Paræus in Neostad. Apolog. pag. 46. Reproborum damnationem à DEO non tantùm prævisam esse scribit: sed eos tanquàm vasa iræ ad eam ordinatos, & ad exitium præparatos esse, asserit.

Hermannus Rennecherus in aureâ salutis catenâ, pag. 36. 37. 38. subindè repetit, DEUM nihilextra se respexisse: sed solùm propter sese, & in sese, nõ propter ullam aliam causam elegisse, quos elegerit. Peccatum Reprobationis causam nequaquàm esse posse: Et causam Reprobationis nequaquàm in homine, sed in supremâ & primâ causâ, ipsa nimirùm liberâ DEI voluntate quærendam esse.
