Et pag. 135. asserit, uti Electionis, sic etiam Reprobationis nullum meritum intervenisse: sed utramq; ex DEI beneplacito provenire, & dependere.

Boquinus in disputatione Heidelbergensi, Reprobos non propter prævisam infidelitatem, aut alia peccata: sed tantùm secundum voluntatis DEI propositum rejectos esse, disertè scribit.

P. Martyr in cap. 9. ad Romanos, Negamus, inquit, CHRISTUM quoad ejus humanitatem & mortem attinet, esse causam Prædestinationis nostræ. Quod ipsum asserit etiam Ursinus in Explicat. Catech.

Ex hoc blasphemo dogmate, tanquàm ex amarissimâ desperationis radice, errores complures alij, fœditate ac impietate nihilò leviores, quasi surculi & propagines pullulârunt: quos ordine enumerabimus:

I. DEUM multò maximam mundi partem ad damnationem condidisse, ut haberet materiam decla-

randa sua justitia. Calvinus loco jam citato. Zanchius lib. 5. de naturâ DEI cap. 2. pag. 690. b. 691. a. DEUS, inquiens, pro suâ voluntate tot hominum millia, & antequàm ab ipsis ullâ affectus fuisset injuriâ, odisse: & postea etiã vasa iræ suæ creare, & ad interitũ apparare constituit. Vide plura, & magis horrenda apud eundem, libro eodem pag. 692. resp. ad Object. 13 ex Oseæ 13, 9. Cui subscribit Piscator in disp. de prædest. th. 24. DEus homines quosdam creavit, & coagmentavit ad interitũ: & th. 27. & 33. hoc consilio homines cōdidit, ut reipsâ laberētur.

II. Nunquam tempus fuisse, vel esse, vel futurũ esse, quo DEUS voluerit, velit, aut voliturῥ sit singulorū misereri. Beza resp. 2. ad acta Coll. Mōmp. p. 194.

III. DEUM non tantùm ad damnationem, sed etiã ad causas damnationis prædestinasse: Ideò enim lapsum esse hominem, quià DEUS ita censuerit, & providentia suâ sic ordinârit. Beza Vol. 1. p. 417.

IV. DEUM nunquàm totum genus humanum dilexisse: sed maximam partem odio habuisse, ideoῥ æterno exitio destinasse. Colloq. Momp. p. 529.

V. Non esse missum à DEO Filium ut pro toto genere humano pateretur, & Patri satisfaceret: sed tantùm pro electis. Imò scribit Beza, part. 2. Resp. ad acta Colloq. Momp. p. 221. Iterū dico, & coram totâ Ecclesia profiteor, falsum, blasphemū, impiũ esse dicere, Christum, sive quoad Concilium DEI attinet, sive quod ad effectū, non minus pro damnandorū, & æterno judicio adjudicandorum peccatis passum, crucifixum, mortuum esse, & satisfecisse, quàm pro peccatis Petri, Pauli, & omnium Sanctorum. Et in antithes. de loco 1. Joh. 2. Nobis cum socijs intolerabilis vox vestra visa est, CHRISTUM esse mortuum pro damnatis. ibid. pag. 514.

V. Promissiones Evangelij licet videantur universales esse, tamen ad solos duntaxat Electos spectare: Neῥ, DEUM velle omnibus dare gratiã ut credant: Et ut maximè Evangelium illis prædicetur, & in eo, & per illud gratia DEI offeratur, tamen hoc facere DEUM non animo communicandi: sed potiùs, ut per illud magis indurentur, magisῥ reddantur inexcusabiles. Quare scribit Piscator, DEus vocat quidem reprobos, sed non vult eos venire, sanctâ nimirùm simulatione: Neῥ, vult eos salvari, sed excæcat, & indurat eos, ut non credant, ideò, quia sunt reprobati. Nam princeps incredulitatis causa est Reprobatio: Quia. Quicquid est causa causæ inferioris, id etiam est causa effecti communis, hoc est, quod ex utrâῥ causâ tùm superiore, tùm inferiore nascitur. Jam causæ superiores sunt: destinatio ad exitium, reprobatio, privatio vocationis, aut saltem privatio efficaciæ Spiritus Sancti inter vocandum. Piscator th. 16. 75. 76. 84. 92. 94. 103.

VII. Electos nullis flagitiis, quantumvis atrocibus, fidem semel datam amittere, aut Spiritum Sanctum excutere, minimè omnium salute æternâ, ad quam semel ab æterno sint electi, excidere, aut ad mortem peccare posse. Quin Electos, si vel vitam pessimam agant: tamen in suâ infirmitate majorem perseverantiam habere, quàm Adam in suâ perfectione habuit. Beza Vol. 1. tract. Theol. p. 207. Zanch. in Miscel. p. 72. & 242. Rennech. in cat. p. 157. & 261.

VIII. Tantùm ex motibus internis Spiritus Sancti, quos electi sentiant, judicandum esse, an simus electi.

IX. Vi Electionis fieri, ut gentilibus etiam nonnullis, ad consortium Ecclesiæ nunquàm vocatis aut adductis, salus obtingat & beatitudo. Cingl. in lib. de verâ & falsâ relig.

Cæterùm observationem probè meretur illud, quòd licèt Calviniani in eo consentiant omnes, & Electionem, & Reprobationem hominum dependere ab absoluto, omnesq́; causas antegrediente DEI decreto, sive mero ipsius beneplacito ac voluntate: in eo tamen sucando & palliando sic in diversas abeant sententias, ut vel indè de dogmatis hujus stupendâ & impietate & vanitate judicium fieri possit. Exempli gratia: Subjectum Reprobationis plerique constituunt homines nondùm conditos, & sic absolutè, ac sine respectu peccati consideratos: alij ab his divortium facientes, Subjectum faciunt, Homines jam in peccatum prolapsos: ut Herbonenses in Method.Theol.l. 2. c. 12. Perkinsius de Prædest. pag. 11. & seqq. Rursus quoad Reprobationis decretum, alij & præsertim recentiores, ut Keckermannus in Syst.Theol.pag. 208. duos ejus actus constituunt: Unum, qui sit planè absolutus, & contineat in se propositum DEI deferendi quosdam, & sibi relinquendi; Quem actum vulgò Negativum appellant: Alterum ordinatum, qui contineat decretum damnandi propter peccata: Quem aliàs nominant actum Positivum sive Affirmativum. Atqui Zanchius lib. 5. cap. 2. part. 4. de Nat. DEI simpliciter hoc negat, & utrumque actum contendit esse absolutum, inter reliqua sic scribens: Nihil clarius est, nihilvé certius, quàm voluntatem DEI SOLAM, non tantùm negativæ, sed etiam affirmativæ Reprobationis causam esse: ac proindè hâc distinctione nihil effici contra id, quod ex Apostolo conclusimus; causam Reprobationis simpliciter nullam, præter DEI voluntatem assignari posse: Et nihil referre, utrùm negativè, an affirmativè accipiatur Reprobatio: Quando utramq́; idem sequitur effectus, nempè æterna damnatio; quanquàm unam immediatè, alteram verò mediatè.

Rursus alij contendunt, non solam Reprobationem: sed impietatem & incredulitatem hominũ esse causam damnationis ipsorum: ut Beza Resp. 2. ad Coll. Momp. p. 161. Hujus decreti executionis, id est, damnationis, qui pereunt, causa non est DEI decretum. Alij verò negant, peccata esse totalem causam damnationis: sic enim omnes homines æterno igni adjudicandos esse, quoniam omnes peccaverunt: sed præcessisse odium ac voluntatem sive decretum DEI, illudq́; justissimum, quo impios æternæ morti destinavit: quoniam Apostolus ait, eos vasa esse iræ aptata sive CREATA & destinata, nempè à DEO, ad interitum, ut in eis suam ostendat iram & potentiam: uti expressè scribit Zanchius de Nat. DEI lib. 5. cap. 2. part. 4. ad Obj. 4. pag. 686. a. Subscribit Zanchio Piscator in disp. de Prædest. th. 92. Asserimus, principem fidei causam esse ipsam electionem: itemq́; principem incredulitatis causam esse reprobationem. Et thesi 94. Sanè ex incredulitate fit, quòd non omnes salvantur, sed non tanquàm ex causâ solitariâ: sed tanquàm ex causâ secundâ & proximâ. Interim verò non sunt negandæ, aut dißimulandæ causæ superiores, ut destinatio ad exitium, Reprobatio, privatio vocationis, aut saltem privatio efficaciæ Spiritus Sancti inter vocandum.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic): I. Calvinian error. concerning Predestination (continued)

But let us dismiss these blindfolded gladiators, who, however much they may twist themselves, will never prove themselves immune from that horrible crime of impiety, that GOD is the cause and author of both sin and human destruction, although they do not wish to admit this, with the exception of Pezel, who in his treatise on Predestination published in the year 1604, p. 148, did not shudder to write: If you understand him as an author who persuades something, exhorts, incites, impels: or in any way provides an occasion for doing something, you will certainly be able to call GOD the author of sin. And although Pezel adds that GOD wills sin, not as the author of evil, but as the avenger and punisher: yet this distinction is too weak, and can in no way be accommodated to the fall of our first parents: since in willing that, GOD could not be avenging or punishing anything at all: because no other sin had preceded which could be avenged through the fall.

But what need is there of many words, when they are accustomed to fight for their opinion with arguments which prove more clearly than the midday sun that, according to their own opinion, GOD is the author and principal cause of both sin and damnation. So that this may be more clearly established, it is my pleasure to recall their individual and universal arguments to certain classes: and to append to each a brief Epikrisis or censure and refutation.

To the FIRST class we refer those testimonies of Scripture by which the Calvinists strive to confirm that GOD wills, commands, and incites men to do evil: as for example: 1 Sam. 2:25. The sons of Eli are read to have therefore not listened to the voice of their father, Because the LORD willed to kill them. 2 Sam. 16:10. GOD commanded Shimei to curse David. Exod. 4:21. Pharaoh is hardened by GOD: and Exod. 9:16, he is read to have been incited by the same for this very purpose. Isa. 19:14. GOD mixes a spirit of error: Isa. 63:17, He causes them to err: Ezek. 14:9, He seduces: Isa. 6:9, John 12:40, He blinds the eyes and hardens the hearts of men: Rom. 1:18, He gives them up to a reprobate mind: 2 Thess. 2:11, He sends an efficacy of error, that they may believe a lie.

Moreover, in these and other such places of Scripture, when they are accommodated to the absolute decree of Reprobation, a gross sophistry is committed against the figure of speech. For the very letter of the words, the literal sense, is urged: when yet not only the idiom of the language, but even the manifest analogy of faith, commands that the Dianoia, that is, such a sense as does not conflict with Scripture, should be given and followed. Which if, in the Calvinistic sense, phrases of this kind, which are harsher, κατά το ρητὸν, according to the letter, are understood concerning an efficacious operation: Scripture will fight against itself: which is impious even to think. Eccles. 15:21 reads: GOD has commanded no one to act impiously. Psalm 5:5: You are not a GOD who wills iniquity. James 1:13: GOD tempts no one. Ecclesiasticus 15:11: Do not say, GOD has supplanted me: it was done by GOD that I should fail. Wisdom 14:10: Similarly, the impious man and his impiety are hateful to GOD. Furthermore, if the τώ ρητώ stands, the justice, mercy, and truth of the law once established by GOD will suffer. Therefore, having abandoned the τω ρητω, we give that διάνοιαν, or 7πήλυσιν, as Peter speaks in chapter 1, verse 23, that is, such an explanation of the produced testimonies of Scripture as the analogy of faith shows: so that we may establish that in some sayings, divine permission is to be understood; in others, desertion; in others, merely a general action which is occupied with the preservation of created things; in others, probation; and in others, finally, punishment. It is indeed the condition of men that by nature they are and remain blind, hard, in error and seduction. But if GOD leaves us at least as such, certainly nothing more is lacking for our extreme misery. Now, GOD indeed wills to illuminate all: but by the medium of His Word. Those who spurn this medium are at length, by the just judgment of GOD, left by GOD in their own blindness, which takes increments daily in the impious: which Scripture calls hardening by a Hebrew idiom. In this very sense GOD is also said to deceive, not by performing deception: but by permitting it to happen. Furthermore, in the Scriptures, the same works are sometimes referred both to GOD and to Satan, yet with a different respect, and considering in one and the same motion both action and passion, things which are clearly most diverse. As for example, in the plundering of Job's goods, it was both a fault and a punishment: and an action and a passion. Insofar, therefore, as this calamity was a punishment and a passion, to that extent it is referred to GOD: but insofar as it was a fault and a wicked action, to that extent the same plundering is referred to Satan, the history of Job itself attesting to this in chapter 1. Moreover, it is read in the Scriptures that GOD often punishes sins with sins, so that in actions of this kind, neither the action nor the passion is honest. But here too, the phrases of Scripture must be noted. For such things are predicated of GOD improperly, for three reasons primarily: as 1. When GOD, by just judgment and as a punishment for preceding inexpugnable contumacy, withdraws, or rather completely takes away, His grace and the Spirit of illumination. For by this act, error, darkness, and most atrocious sins soon rush in of their own accord. When, therefore, men are thus destitute of all grace of GOD and rush into crimes with full force: there Scripture says that they have been hardened, blinded, led into error, and deceived by GOD. 2. When GOD uses the minister of Satan to execute His judgments: then it is said in the Scriptures that GOD Himself has done what is perpetrated by Satan. For example, 1 Chronicles 21:1 reads that Satan incited David to number the people. Now this very deed 2. Samuel 24 is attributed to the fury of the LORD: but under a most diverse respect, insofar as GOD, as a just judge, passes a judicial sentence concerning the inflicting of a certain punishment upon the people for their sins: and thus permits Satan, the executor of His judgments, to incite David to that sin. 3. When one and the same Word of the Gospel is to some an odor of death unto death: it happens that the contumacious are blinded occidentally and by occasion, by which the minds of the pious are illuminated. Thus, therefore, GOD is and remains always free and immune from every evil of fault: so much so that Augustine rightly pronounced long ago: Those are to be held unworthy of the name of Christians who establish GOD, who is good by nature, as the cause of evil, or the author of any wicked will, or action, whether inciting, or persuading, or impelling.

THE SECOND class of arguments of the Sacramentarian sect contains those sayings of Scripture by which the cause of human perdition seems to be referred to an external and divine principle, and the means of salvation are claimed to have been denied to men by God. As Acts 1:16, Judas the traitor is said to have perished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled. And Matthew 11:25, GOD is read to have hidden the Word of salvation from the wise, and it is added that this was so pleasing to Him. Thus Matthew 3:11, it is said that it is not given to all to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. What is more, the Epistle of Jude, verse 4, claims that certain impious men were written down beforehand for this judgment, προγεγραμμένως. Nay, even Luke 12:32, it is said to be the good pleasure of GOD to give the kingdom of heaven to the little flock.

But it is most rightly answered that in these and similar testimonies of Scripture, a sophistry is for the most part committed, either of the vicious consequent, or of the saying in a certain respect to the saying simply. It is indeed the good pleasure of GOD that the kingdom of heaven be given to the little flock. But from this it does not follow that GOD never willed, or that it never pleased Him, that the same should be given also to the great flock. Thus it is not given to all to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven: but from this it does not follow that GOD never willed that this very thing should be given also to all. For there is a great difference between the Act and the Will: and then between the Antecedent and the Consequent Will. For by an antecedent will it pleases GOD to give what by a consequent will it pleases Him to deny: just as it pleases a Magistrate that it be well with all subjects by an antecedent will: to whom, however, by a consequent will, it also pleases that, on account of preceding crimes or sedition, punishments be inflicted upon them, or even that they be utterly cut off.

Furthermore, the distinction between the Simple, or Absolute, will and the Hypothetical will is also to be noted well in this place: which distinction the adversaries shamefully confuse, and what GOD wills conditionally, they take as being willed simply. Examples of another sophistry, ὠδὴ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς, occur in the passage of Matthew 11:25 and the Epistle of Jude. GOD hides His Word from the wise: and the ungodly were described long ago for destruction: but neither by the absolute will of GOD; but rather relatively, with respect to preceding impiety and contumacy. Concerning the perdition, or destruction, of Judas the traitor, it is rightly affirmed that that prediction most viciously constitutes the cause of this destruction. For Judas did not perish because it had been predicted in the Scriptures: but rather it was predicted because he was otherwise going to perish by his own fault and malice.

The third class of arguments, by which the Calvinists fight for the absolute dogma of both Election and Reprobation, is occupied by those sayings which are wont to be brought forward from chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Romans: As in verse 13, Jacob was loved, Esau was held in hatred by GOD, before they were born, or had done anything good or evil. Therefore, the reason for Election and Reprobation before GOD is absolute. Then from verse 15, and from Exodus 33:19, that is cited: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion. By which saying again, the absolute counsel of GOD, and the will of showing mercy in particular, seems to be established entirely. Thirdly, from verse 22 of this very ninth chapter, as also from 2 Timothy 2:10, that which is read in both places is urged, that GOD has the power, from the same lump, to make one vessel indeed for honor, and another for ignominy: or to prepare vessels of wrath for destruction. Finally, from the same ninth chapter they bring forward that GOD, from this very fact that He prepared vessels of wrath for destruction, took the material for showing His justice, which otherwise He could scarcely have declared by any other reason, verse 22.

Latin:

Sed mittamus Andabatas, qui utcunq; se torqueant, nunquàm tamen immunes se præstabunt, ab horrendo illo impietatis crimine, quòd DEUS sit & peccati, & exitij humani causa atq; autor, quamvis hoc fateri nolint uno excepto Pezelio qui in tractatu de Prædestinatione Lichædito Anno 1604 p.148. scribere non exhorruit: Si eum intelligis autorem, qui suadet aliquid, hortatur, incitat, impellit: aut quocunq; modo occasionem ad aliquid faciendum præbet, DEUM sanè autorem peccati dicere poteris. Et quanquàm subjicit Pezelius, DEUM velle peccatum, non tanquàm auctorem mali, sed tanquàm ultorem & vindicem: nimis tamen elumbis hæc est distinctio, & ad lapsum primorum parentum accommodari nullo modo potest: quippè in quo volendo, DEUS nihil quicquam ulcisci, aut vindicare poterat: proptereà quòd nullum peccatum aliud antecesserat, quod per lapsum vindicaretur.

Sed quid multis opus, cùm ejusmodi argumentis pro suâ sententiâ, pugnare soleant, quæ Sole meridiano clarius evincant, DEUM ex ipsorum sententiâ & peccati, & damnationis autorem, causamq; principem esse. Quod ut dilucidius constet, placet singula & universa illorum argumenta, ad certas quasdam classes revocare: & cuilibet brevem quandam Ἐπίκρισιν sive censuram ac refutationem subjicere.

Ad PRIMAM classem ea referimus Scripturæ testimonia, quibus Calviniani confirmare student, DEUM velle, præcipere, excitare homines, ad malè agendum: ut Exempli gratiâ: 1.Sam. 2,25. Filij Eli leguntur ideò non audivisse vocem Patris sui, Quia DOMINUS voluerit eos occidere. 2.Sam 16,10. DEUS præcepit Semei, ut Davidi malediceret. Exod. 4, 21. Pharao à DEO induratur: & Exod. 9, 16. in hoc ipsum ab eodem excitatus fuisse legitur. Esa.19,14. DEUS miscet Spiritum erroris: Esa. 63,17. errare facit: Ezech. 14,9. seducit: Esa. 6, 9. Johann. 12, 40. excæcat oculos, & indurat corda hominum: Rom.1,18. Tradit in sensum reprobum: 2.Thess.2,11. mittit efficaciam erroris, ut credatur mendacio.

Cæterùm in his, & id genus alijs Scripturæ locis, ad absolutum Reprobationis decretum accommodandis, committitur crassa Sophisticatio παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως. Urgetur enim ipsa verborum litera, τὸ ῥητὸν: cùm tamen non modò lingvæ ἰδιωτισμὸς: sed ipsa etiam manifesta fidei analogia, τὴν Διάνοιαν, hoc est, talem sensum, qui cum Scripturâ non pugnet, dandum & sequendum esse, præcipiat. Quod si enim sensu Calvinistico, phrases ejusmodi duriores, κατά το ρητὸν, secundum literam, de efficaci operatione intelligantur: Scriptura secum ipsa pugnabit: id quod vel cogitatu impium. Eccles. 15, 21. legitur: Nemini mandavit DEUS impiè agere Psal. 5, 5. Non DEUS, volens iniquitatem, tu es. Jacob. 1. 13. DEUS neminem tentat. Ecclesiastici 15, 11. Ne dixeris, DEUS me supplantavit: per DEUM factum est, ut deficerem. Sap. 14, 10. Similiter DEO sunt odio impius, & impietas ipsius. Deindè stante τώ ρητώ. Justitia, misericordia, & legis à DEO semel latæ veritas laborabit. Ergò relicto τω ρητω eam διάνοιαν, sive 7πήλυσιν, uti Petrus 2. cap 1, 23. loquitur, hoc est, talem explicationem productorum Scripturæ testimoniorum damus, quam analogia fidei monstrat: ut in quibusdam dictis, Permissionem divinam; in alijs desertionem; in alijs generalem duntaxat actionem, quæ circa conservationem rerum creatarum occupatur; in alijs probationem, in alijs deniq; pœnam intelligendam esse, statuamus. Est profectò ea hominum conditio, ut naturâ cæci, duri, in errore & seductione sint & hæreant. Quod si tales saltem nos DEUS relinquit, certè nihil ampliùs ad extremam miseriam nobis deest. Jam vult quidem DEUS illuminare omnes: sed medio Verbi sui. Hoc medium qui spernunt, illi tandem justo DEI judicio, in suâ cæcitate, quæ in impijs quotidiè incrementa sumit, à DEO relinquuntur: id quod Scriptura idiotismo Hebræo excæcationem appellat. Quo ipso sensu DEUS etiam decipere dicitur, non deceptionem faciendo: sed ut fiat; permittendo. Porrò in Scripturis opera eadem & ad DEUM, & ad Satanam interdum referuntur, diverso tamen respectu, & considerata in uno eodemq; motu, tùm actione, tùm passione, rebus planè diversissimis. Ut Exempli gratia in direptione facultatum Jobi, & culpa erat, & pœna: & actio, & passio. Quatenùs igitur hæc calamitas & pœna, & passio fuit, eatenùs ad DEUM: quatenùs verò culpa & actio prava, eatenùs ad Satanam refertur eadem direptio, ipsâ historiâ Jobi attestante cap. 1. Prætereà in Scripturis legitur DEUS sæpiùs peccata peccatis punire, ita, ut in hujusmodi actionibus neque actio, neque passio honesta sit. Verùm & hîc scripturæ phrases notandæ veniunt. Nam impropriè talia de DEO prædicantur, tribus potissimùm respectibus: ut 1. Quando DEUS justo judicio, & in pœnam antegressæ inexpugnabilis contumaciæ, Gratiam suam, & Spiritum illuminationis subtrahit, imò planè aufert. Hoc enim facto, mox suâ sponte error, tenebræ, & atrocissima peccata ingruunt. Quando ergò sic homines omni gratiâ DEI destituuntur, & pleno impetu in scelera proruunt: ibi Scriptura dicit, eos à DEO esse induratos, excæcatos, in errorem inductos, deceptos esse. 2. Quando DEUS ad judicia sua exequenda utitur ministro Satanæ: tùm in Scripturis dicitur DEUS ipse fecisse, quæ à Satanâ patrantur. Exempli gratia, 1. Paral. 21, 1. legitur, Quòd Satanas incitaverit Davidem ad numerandum populum. Jàm hoc ipsum factum 2. Sam. 24. tribuitur furori DOMINI: sed sub diversissimo respectu, quatenùs nimirùm DEUS ut justus judex fert sententiam judicialem de infligendâ certâ pœnâ populo ob peccata: & sic permittit Satanæ judiciorum suorum executori, ut ad peccatum illud instiget Davidem. 3. Quando unum idemque Verbum Evangelij nonnullis est odor mortis ad mortem: fit utiq; jam occidentaliter, & per occasionem excæcentur contumaces, quâ piorum animi illuminantur. Sic ergò DEUS est & manet ab omni malo culpæ semper liber & immunis: adeò, ut rectè pronunciaverit jam olim Augustinus: Christianorum nomine indigni sunt habendi, qui DEUM naturâ bonum, mali causam, vel pravæ cujusquam aut voluntatis, aut actionis autorem statuunt sive excitantem, sive suadentem, sive impellentem.

ALTERA classis argumentorum gentis Sacramentariæ, ea continet Scripturæ dicta, quibus perditionis humanæ causa ad externum, idq; divinum principium referri videtur, & salutis media hominibus divinitùs negata esse perhibentur. Ut Act. 1, 16. Judas proditor perijsse dicitur, ut impleretur Scriptura. Et Matth. 11, 25. DEUS Verbum salutis legitur à sapientibus abscondisse, & hoc quidem ita complacitum ipsi fuisse additur. Sic Matth. 3, 11. Non omnibus datum esse dicitur, nosse mysteria regni cœlorum. Quid quòd Epistola Judæ v. 4. Impios quosdam homines in hoc judicium jam antea descriptos esse προγεγραμμένως perhibet. Quin imò Luc. 12, 32. Beneplacitum DEI esse dicitur, parvo gregi dare regnum cœlorum.

Sed rectissimè respondetur, in his & similibus Scripturæ testimonijs plerumq; committi Sophisticationem vel vitiosi Consequentis, vel dicti secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter. Beneplacitum est quidem apud DEUM, parvo gregi dari regnum cœlorum. Sed hinc non est consequens, nunquàm voluisse DEUM, vel nunquàm ipsi placuisse, ut idem daretur etiam magno gregi. Sic non omnibus datur nosse mysteria regni cœlorum: Verùm hinc non est consequens, nunquàm voluisse DEUM, ut hoc ipsum daretur etiam omnibus. Est enim inter Actum & Voluntatem: Deindè inter Voluntatem Antecedentem & Consequentem, magna differentia. Nam antecedente voluntate dare placet DEO, quod consequente negare eidem complacet: Sicut Magistratui placet omnibus subditis benè esse voluntate antecedente: cui tamen consequente voluntate etiam placet, ut propter antegressa flagitia aut seditionem, pœnæ ijsdem irrogentur, imò penitùs illi exscindantur.

Deindè probè etiam hoc loco est notanda distinctio inter voluntatem Simplicem, sive Absolutam, & Hypotheficam : quam distinctionem turpiter confundunt adversarij,&quod DEUS vult conditionatè, id ipsi accipiunt simpliciter. Alterius Sophisticationis ὠδὴ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς exempla occurrunt in loco Matth. 11, 25. & Epistolæ Judæ. Abscondit DEUS Verbum suum à Sapientibus : & descripti sunt impij jampridem ad exitium: sed neutrum absolutâ DEI voluntate : verùm secundum quid, respectu antegressæ impietatis & contumaciæ. De perditione, sive interitu Judæ proditoris rectè affirmatur, Prædictionem illam vitiosissimè constituit causam hujus interitus. Nam non ideò interiit Judas, quia in Scripturis prædictum fuerat : sed ideò potiùs prædictum fuit, quia aliàs interiturus erat propriâ suâ culpâ, & malitiâ.

TERTIAM classem argumentorum, quibus Calviniani pro absoluto & Electionis & Reprobationis dogmate pugnant, occupant ea dicta, quæ ex cap. 9. Epistolæ ad Romanos proferri solent : Ut versu 13. Jacob dilectus, Esau odio fuit habitus à DEO, antequàm nati, vel boni, vel mali quicquam operati fuissent. Ergò absolutâ est Electionis & Reprobationis apud DEUM ratio. Deindè ex versu 15. & ex Exod. 33, 19. citatur illud : Miserebor,cujus misereor, commiserabor quẽ commiseror. Quo rursus dicto absolutum DEI consilium, & voluntas miserendi particularis, omninò stabiliri videtur. Tertiò ex versu 22.hujus ipsius noni capitis, ut & ex 2. Tim. 2. 10. urgetur illud, quod, utrobique legitur DEUM habere potestatem, ex eâdem massâ aliud quidem vas in honorem, aliud in ignominiam facere : aut vasa iræ ad interitum præparare. Tandem ex eodem capite nono proferunt, quòd DEUS ex hoc ipso,quòd vasa iræ præparavit ad interitum, materiam sumserit ostendendæ suæ justitiæ, quam alioqui vix ullâ ratione aliâ declarare potuerit, versu 22.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic): I. Calvinian error. concerning Predestination (continued)

I answer regarding the first argument, that the genuine and proper meaning of the Apostle's words must be accurately weighed: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated. In order that we may infallibly elicit this meaning, 1. it must be considered of whom the Apostle's alleged words are to be understood. Now if one recurs to the proper seat of this oracle, which exists in Malachi 1:2, it is most plain that the Prophet is not dealing with the person of either brother: For then both had long since ceased to be among the living, but that the Prophet's discourse is about the posterity of both. Which very thing is also confirmed by the history of Genesis 25:23, where the heavenly oracle gave such a response to Rebecca: Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly, and one people shall overcome the other, and the greater shall serve the lesser. The first error, therefore, in the argument of the Calvinists emerges from the fact that what is to be understood concerning the posterity of Jacob and Esau is wrongly applied to the very persons of those two brothers. Then it must be considered what is being dealt with expressly, or properly, which again shines forth most clearly from the cited 25th chapter of Genesis and chapter 1 of Malachi. For that oracle: The greater shall serve the lesser, is soon explained concerning the external prerogative of the birthright, which Jacob had bought from his brother Esau for bread and lentil pottage, and thus had transmitted to his posterity. Where indeed, by right of birthright, the right of dominion over his brother Esau pertained to Jacob and his posterity: But according to the oracle issued to Rebecca, Esau arrogated to himself dominion over his brother Jacob: Where the greater ought to have served the lesser, so that in Genesis 33, Jacob calls Esau his brother, his Lord: and himself his servant. verses 5, 8, 13, 14, 15. With this foundation standing again as clearly invincible, a second error shines forth in the Calvinistic argument, which wrongly accommodates this passage to the figment of absolute Election and Reprobation.

Thirdly, from the opinion of the adversaries it would necessarily follow that not only Jacob, but his entire posterity had been absolutely predestined by GOD to eternal life: But conversely, that Esau, with all his progeny, had been absolutely reprobated and damned. But that both labor under manifest absurdity and falsehood is sufficiently evident in itself. Certainly in Isaiah 11:14, the Edomites or Idumeans, who descend from Esau, are called to the kingdom of the Messiah. And in Mark 3:8, the Idumeans follow Christ: What of the fact that a comparison of the history of Job and the thirty-sixth chapter of Genesis shows quite evidently that the most holy Job was descended from the posterity of Esau? For in verse 10 of Genesis 36, mention is made of Eliphaz the son of Adah, the wife of Esau: that he was a kinsman of Job is clear from chapter 2:11 of Job. Nay, even in Genesis 36:33, mention is made of a certain Jobab, whom most interpreters not without reason think to have been Job himself. Nor does Calvin himself dare to deny this, who in his Commentary on verse 1 of the first chapter of Job, notes in express words: Mention, he says, is made of the region of Uz, in which Job lived: Which region is indeed placed by some rather in the East: but in chapter 4:21 of the Lamentations of Jeremiah, a part of Idumea is designated by this same name. We know, however, that the Idumeans are descended from Esau. Therefore, if we say that Job was from the region of Uz, he was an Idumean, that is, from the posterity of Esau. Although he was from the posterity of Esau, we see, however, how uprightly he lived, and worshipped GOD, not only by keeping righteousness and equity toward men: but also by retaining pure religion, and being guarded from the idolatry and superstition of the infidels. This is Calvin in the cited place, page 2b. Thus, regarding the posterity of Jacob, no one would affirm that all of them without exception were elected and eternally saved, unless he is a complete stranger and foreigner to sacred history and the sermons of the Prophets.

Fourthly, it is most evidently gathered from the premises that the Apostle in this place did not, as the Sacramentarians pretend, propose an example of absolute Predestination in Jacob, and of likewise absolute Reprobation in Esau: but only a type,

and to have accommodated to the antitype of eternal life: so that just as for those two persons, the privilege of the flesh availed or was worth nothing, because Esau was born before Jacob: So in the antitype, carnal birth from Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, or other works or prerogatives do nothing at all toward the possession of eternal life.

Fifthly, let us grant to our adversaries that this passage, if it is treated soberly, can be accommodated to the business of election: just as indeed the Apostle, having taken the occasion from here, institutes a transition to explain the matter of Predestination: yet the application is not to be made according to all the parts of the adduced type: but only in those which the Apostle himself urges above all: such as are: the firmness of the divine covenant, even in the diverse outcome of those in covenant: the exclusion of carnal privileges in the business of salvation: finally, the gratuitous purpose of divine goodness in the Election of those to be saved. Thus, regarding the Reprobation of Esau, the Apostle hints at nothing at all that in any way presents the appearance of absolute Reprobation: Rather, the contrary is most clearly evident from the same chapter: as when the Apostle transfers all blame for reprobation onto unbelief, in verses 31 and 32. Israel, he says, who was looking for the Law of righteousness, did not arrive at the Law of righteousness. Why? Because not by faith, but as if by the works of the Law. And in the preceding verses 7 and 8. Not all who are the seed of Abraham are children: but in Isaac shall your seed be called: That is, not those who are children of the flesh, these are children of GOD: but those who are children of the promise are counted in the seed: that is, as the Apostle interprets in Gal. 3, 9. Those who are of faith will be blessed with faithful Abraham: And in verse 29. If you are Christ's, you are also Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise. Whence the Apostle infers a general aphorism of both Election and Reprobation, neither of which is absolute, but both are ordered, Rom. 11, 20. Through unbelief they were cut off: But you stand by faith. Far be it, therefore, that we should affix the dogma of absolute Reprobation to the words of the Apostle in the Sacramentarian sense. For although in the Reprobation of Esau, that is, in the abrogation of the birthright (which could be done without prejudice to his salvation), we easily grant that the primary cause is to be sought in nothing but the will of GOD: yet we by no means concede that in the Reprobation or Damnation of men the same primary cause must be given. Nor in this part is the reason for the primary and highest cause the same for Predestination as it is for reprobation. For indeed it is a sin to seek the primary and highest cause of Election outside the merciful will of GOD, yet not an absolute one, but an ordered one: but to refer the Principle of Reprobation to the same is more impious than impiety itself: as was expressly shown above in the first part. Nor do these words of the Apostle in Rom. 9, 11 have any strength or support for the opinion of our adversaries. (For when the children were not yet born, when they had done nothing either good or evil.) For these words do not define the mode or the cause of either Election or Reprobation: but they define only the time at which this oracle was delivered to the mother Rebecca: which is what happened, when these little boys had not yet been brought into the light.

Sixthly and lastly: one must also note the equivocation in the word To Hate (I have hated Esau) which does not always signify a hostile affection of an alienated mind: much less some most atrocious hatred of absolute Reprobation, such as the Adversaries imagine: but it signifies either neglect, or setting aside, or passing over: Just as also in this place the antithesis, namely To Love, is the same as preferring one to another in an external matter. We have the Holy Spirit Himself as the author of this interpretation. For what Christ is read to have said in Luke 14, 26, that those coming to Him should hate father and mother, wife and children, etc., Matthew explains comparatively, reporting that it was said by Christ: He who loves father and mother more than me is not worthy of me, and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. Matt. 10, 37. In which sense both words are also taken, Ps. 87, 2. The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tabernacles of Jacob: not that He does not also love these: but that He prefers the gates of Zion to them. Thus Christ, No one, he says, can serve two masters, he will love the one, and hate the other. Matt. 6, 24. Luke 16, 13. To which pertains that dispute of Augustine, book 1, to Simplician, question 2. Since it is written in Wis. 11, 25 that GOD loves all things that are, and hates nothing of those which He has made, how does this have a place regarding Esau? But distinguish between the creature of GOD and the work of the Devil: GOD does not hate the man Esau, but He hates the sinner Esau. Therefore, this hatred is not of the person, but of the cause: Thus the cause. Therefore, it is not an absolute hatred: For although the person is noted: yet it is not understood without a cause: whether foreseen, or actually existing: according to that in John 3, 18. He who does not believe is already judged. But let it suffice to have spoken a little more lengthily on this first argument taken from chapter 9 of the epistle to the Romans, in which the Sacramentarians place the chief support of their cause.

THE OTHER argument of the third class urges that oracle of GOD asserting, Rom. 9, 15. Exod. 33, 19. I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy: and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion. Which words, according to the surface of the letter, seem to generate this sense, as if GOD Himself distinguishes among men to be pitied: and shows that He does not deem all men worthy of His mercy. But this is a most vicious interpretation, and blasphemous against GOD Himself. For that these words do not militate for a particular will of showing mercy, nor for an absolute affection or decree of divine mercy, is proven from the fact that Scripture everywhere most clearly explains on whom GOD wishes to have mercy: especially Ezech. 33, 11. As I live, says the LORD, I do not desire the death of the sinner: but that the wicked may turn from his evil way, and live. Rom. 11, 23. GOD has shut up all under unbelief, that He might have mercy on all. 1 Tim. 2, 4. GOD desires all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Unless, therefore, the Holy Spirit is to be accused of a shameful contradiction, certainly the Mosaic passage can in no way, nor ought it to be, opposed to these testimonies: but an interpretation consonant with the analogy of faith must be sought and held. Now, if the passage, both Mosaic and Apostolic, be weighed in its own proper seat and from the whole coherence of the matter, the sense of both clearly emerges as this: that GOD is kind and merciful, and that any benefits whatsoever proceed from Him, not from human dignity, merits, or works: but flow from the sole grace of the merciful GOD and from favor that is clearly unmerited. Moses himself shows himself to be the interpreter of this sense in that discourse which he held in the chapter immediately following, Exodus 34:6: Lord GOD, merciful and gracious, long-suffering and of great mercy, who keepest mercy for thousands, etc. But the Apostle likewise confirms this interpretation: inasmuch as by the allegation of these words from Moses, he wished to go to meet the tacit objection of the Jews, who maintained that the justice of GOD would labor, unless GOD conferred salvation and eternal life upon their course and labor as a wage due. The Apostle therefore answers negatively, showing that election and salvation are owed to the mercy of GOD alone: Wherefore he immediately and directly adds, in verse 16: It is not therefore of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of GOD that showeth mercy.

The THIRD argument of this class is concerning the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction: concerning which Beza, in his commentary on these words, sings a triumph, as it were: Again, he says, let it be permitted to say with Paul, that certain men were created by GOD the artificer for destruction. But this is a boast of victory. For 1. we concede willingly both of these things: both that there are in the Church vessels of honor and of dishonor: and that both are fitted or prepared, or joined together. But this is in controversy: Whether GOD makes or prepares both of those vessels? Where, since the Calvinists answer affirmatively, they commit a notable greed and blasphemy. For the Apostle indeed affirms concerning the vessels of Glory, that GOD prepared them, which He had afore prepared unto glory: verse 23. And concerning these, there is no controversy between us and the Adversaries. But that the Apostle also affirms the same concerning vessels made for disgrace or dishonor: that, indeed, we simply deny: inasmuch as he says only absolutely that they are prepared: but by whom they are prepared, he does not expressly add. Now if other sayings of Scripture and the analogy of faith are consulted, it is manifest that they are prepared not by GOD, insofar as they are such: but partly by themselves, partly by the Devil. Furthermore, the Apostolic text itself convicts the sense of the adversary party of manifest falsehood. For he says that those vessels of wrath are endured by GOD in much patience. But that GOD endures in patience works of His own, made and ordained by His most free will, can no more be affirmed than

it is said of some architect that he endures in great patience a work finished and completed by himself. Therefore, this tolerance evidently argues that those vessels of wrath are the effect not of GOD, but of an alien work, not at all pleasing to GOD. Moreover, GOD hates nothing of those things which He has made: Wis. 11:25. But He hates the vessels of wrath: inasmuch as in punishing them He shows His wrath: as the Apostle has in verse 22 of this ninth chapter. Therefore, GOD did not make the vessels of wrath, insofar as they are such.

Nor does the Apostle's similitude of the potter, forming from one and the same lump of clay one vessel unto honor and another unto dishonor, stand in the way of this response. For Chrysostom long ago rightly answered concerning this very similitude: that examples are not to be taken in a general sense, but if that for which they have been taken is understood, the rest is to be left alone: that in similitudes individual words are not to be urged, nor are they to be dragged outside the purpose for which they were employed, nor are peculiar dogmas to be built from them. But the purpose of the Apostle is this: That it is right and lawful for GOD, who owes nothing to anyone, if He has had mercy on those who accept the offered grace, to allow the remaining stubborn and clamorous ones, that is, vessels of substance created by GOD, to become vessels of dishonor, that is, to be more and more hardened by the Devil.

Nor does that which is alleged from verse 22 concerning the declaration of divine justice obtain any weight or importance. For a manifest refutation is not committed to the cause. For although it is true that GOD declares His justice against the vessels of wrath: yet this very showing of wrath and of justice itself is not the cause or origin of the reprobation of some: But rather the end of Reprobation, to which the damnation or destruction of the vessels of wrath is recalled and reduced. Scripture clearly confirms this, saying: Impious men are not necessary to GOD: Ecclesiasticus 15:12, nor are evils to be done that good may come, Rom. 3:8. Indeed, as Fulgentius says in book 1 to Monimus, chapter 22: Justice will not be just, if it be said not to have found a guilty person to punish, but to have made one. Furthermore, that most absolute self-sufficiency in GOD does not admit that necessity of declaring justice: since without it nothing would have been lacking to His eternal justice: no more than nothing would have been lacking to His omnipotence, if He had not created this Universe at all. Finally, in the punished Adamic fall, in the damnation of the fallen Angels, and finally in the death of His Son, He abundantly enough declared His justice, so that there is no need at all for that Calvinistic figment concerning the absolute [predestination] of some to damnation or destruction, to assert the justice of GOD. Nor does the particle (willing, in the same verse 22) hint at any such thing. For not any absolute will is noted: but the will of judgment, or a consequent one: which finally punishes the contumacy of the impious eternally.

The third and final class of arguments, by which the Calvinists fight, contains the defenses of certain reasons: Of which kind these are the chief: I. If God were to reprobate men on account of sins: all would have to be reprobated, because all are sinners. But this does not happen. Therefore. II. Some only are chosen: Matt. 20:16 and ch. 22:14. Few are adopted as sons: Rom. 8:29. Few are called: Acts 14:16. Few believe: John 6:36 and ch. 10:26. Few are justified and glorified, Rom. 8:30. But if God truly willed it, He could certainly grant this to all. For God can do whatever He wills: Wis. 12:18. And, whatever He willed, He did, Ps. 35:6. But because He does not do this, it is certainly gathered from that very fact that He never willed this. III. The matter stands in the same way regarding the redemption of the human race. For Christ came to save His people from their sins, Matt. 1:21. To give His life for the sheep, John 10:15: to acquire the Church of God with His own blood, Acts 20:28. To die for the elect, Rom. 8:33. But not all are such. Therefore, He did not redeem all either. To which also pertains this collection of Piscator: He gave His soul as a price for many: Matt. 20:28, Mark 10:45. He poured out His blood for the remission of sins for many, Matt. 26:28. But many are not all. Therefore, He did not redeem all either.

I answer: The first reason labors in the proposition with the fallacy παρὰ τὸ πὴ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For sins are not the cause of reprobation simply, but with respect to final unbelief and impenitence. Now not all sinners persevere to the end in unbelief, therefore not all are reprobated either.

The second reason fails first by a shameful confusion of the absolute and the ordained. For some absolute election, adoption, calling, justification, and glorification of a few is imagined: which excludes the rest by some fatal and absolute decree. But such a calling, or adoption, or election, etc., is nowhere taught in the Scriptures. Therefore, a shameful πλεονεξία and begging of the question is committed in the conclusion. Then, the same paralogism is committed in the reasoning of the consequent: while the absolute will is wrongly confused with the ordained. For God truly does everything that He absolutely wills: but not what He wills by a certain τάξει or order of means, which is very often overturned by men, and therefore it does not happen, even by the fault of men, what God indeed wills to happen, but with the order observed.

The third reason labors under the same vice of πλεονεξία. For to give life for the sheep, to die for the elect, and similar things, means as much to the Calvinists as if this were done ONLY for the sheep and the elect: which contradicts the other sayings of Scripture, which assert that Christ died for the whole world, that is, for all, and indeed specifically for the reprobate as well. Then, this reason labors with the fallacy τῆς λέξεως καὶ ὁμωνυμίας. For the word (MANY) sometimes denotes the entire multitude of the human race: just as Augustine shows, De Civit. Dei, lib. 20, cap. 23. Indeed, Scripture itself: Rom. 5:19, Dan. 12:2, Gen. 17:4, Gen. 22:18.

Latin:

Respondeo quoad argumentum primum, accuratè expendendum esse, quænam sit germana & propria verborum Apostoli sententia: Jacob dilexi, Esau verò odio habui. Quam sententiam ut infallibiliter eruamus, 1. considerandum, de quonám allegata verba Apostoli sint intelligenda. Jam si ad propriam sedem hujus oraculi, quæ extat Malach. 1, 2. recurratur, planiffimum sit, de personâ fratris utriusque apud Prophetam non agi: Tùm enim jam pridem uterque in vivis esse defiderat, Sed de posteritate utriusque sermonem esse prophetæ. Quod ipsum confirmat etiam historia Geneseos 25, 23. ubi cœleste Oraculum Rebeccæ tale responsum dedit: Dua gentes sunt in utero tuo, & duo populi ex ventre tuo dividentur, populusquè populum superabit, & major serviet minori. Primùm ergò vitium in argumento Calvinianorum emergit indè, quòd quæ de posteritate Jacobi & Esau intelligenda sunt, ea ad ipsas personas duorum istorum fratrum malè accommodentur. Deindè considerandum, Quâ de re ex professo, sive propriè agatur, id quod rurfus ex citato capite 25. Geneseos: & c. 1. Malachia clarissimè elucescit. Nam oraculum illud: Major serviet minori, mox de externâ prærogativâ primogenituræ explicatur, quàm Jacob â fratre Esau pro pane & lentis edulio emerat, & sic ad posteritatem suam transmiserat. Ubi sanè ad Jacobum & posteritatem ipsius, jure primogenituræ pertinebat Jus etiam dominij in fratrem Esau: Verùm secundum Oraculum Rebeccæ editum, Esau dominium sibi arrogabat in fratrem Jacob: Ubi major servire debuit minori, ita ut Genes. 33. Jacob appellat Esau fratrem, suum Dominum: Se verò ipsius Servum. versu 5. 8. 13. 14. 15. Stante hoc rurfum fundamento planè invicto, alterum elucescit vitium in argumento Calvinistico, quod locum istum ad Electionis & Reprobationis absolutæ figmentum perperàm accommodat.

Tertiò ex sententiâ Adversariorum necefsariò sequeretur, non solùm Jacobum, sed universam ejus posteritatem absolutè à DEO ad vitam æternam prædestinatam fuisse: Vice autem versâ, Esavum, cum totâ suâ progenie absolutè reprobatum & damnatum esse. Atqui utrumque manifestâ & absurditate, & falsitate laborare, per se satis constat. Certè Esaiæ 11, 14, Edòmitæ sive Idumæi, qui descendunt ab Esavo, vocantur ad regnum Messiæ. Et Marci 3, 8. Idumæi sequuntur Christum: Quid quod collatio historiæ Jobi, & capitis tricesimi sexti Geneseos, satis evidenter ostendit, Sanctissimum Jobum fuisse oriundum ex posteritate Esau. Nam versu 10. Genes. 36. mentio fit Eliphazi filij Hadad uxoris Esau: quem Jobi consangvineum fuisse, patet ex cap. 2, 11. Jobi. Quin imò Gen. 36, 33. mentio fit cujusdam Jobab, quem Jobum ipsum fuisse plerique interpretes haud sine causâ arbitrantur. Neque id negare audet Calvinus ipse, qui in Commentario ad versum 1. capitis primi Job, disertis verbis annotat: Mentio, inquiens, fit regionis Hus, in quâ Jobus habitaverit: Quæ quidem regio à nonnullis in Oriente poriùs collocatur: verùm cap. 4, 21. Threnorum Jeremiæ, hoc eodem nomine designatur pars Idumææ. Scimus autem, Idumæos oriundos esse ex Esavo. Itaquè si Jobum dicamus fuisse ex regione Hus, erat Idumæus, id est, ex posteris Esavi. Quamvis verò esset ex Esavi posteris, videmus tamen, quàm integrè vixerit, DEUMQUE coluerit, non tantùm rectitudine & æquitate erga homines servatâ: sed etiam purâ religione retentâ, & ab Idololatriâ & superstitione infidelium custoditâ. Hæc Calvinus loco citato pag. 2. b. Sic quoad posteros Jacobi, omnes in universum electos, & æternum salvatos fuisse, nemo affirmaverit, nisi qui in historiâ sacrâ, & concionibus Prophetarum hospes planè & peregrinus est.

Quartò ex præmissis evidentissimè colligitur, D. Apostolum hoc loco, non, uti Sacramentarij fingunt, Exemplum Prædestinationis absolutæ in Jacobo, & Reprobationis itidẽ absolutæ in Esavo: sed Typum duntaxat proposuisse,

& accommodasse ad antitypum vitæ æternæ: ut quemadmodum duabus istis personis, nihil profuit, aut valuit carnaleprivilegium, quòd Esavv prior natus Jacobo : Ita in antitypo carnalis nativitas ex Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo, vel opera aut prærogativæ aliæ nihil quicquam faciant ad possessionem vitæ æternæ.

Quintò largiamur adversarijs, posse locum istum, in sobriè tractetur, ad electionis negocium accommodari: quemadmodum sanè Apostolus hinc sumtâ occasione, transitum instituit ad Prædestinationis materiam explicandam: tamen applicatio non facienda est, secundum omnes allati typi partes: sed in ijs duntaxat, quas ipse Apostolus cumprimis urget: quales sunt: fœderis divini firmitas, in diverso etiam confœderatorum exitu: exclusio carnalium privilegiorum in salutis negocio: tandem gratuitum divinæ bonitatis propositum in Electione salvandorum. Sic quoad Reprobationem Esavi, nihil quicquam innuit Apostolus, quod absolutæ Reprobationis speciem quoquo modo præ se ferat: Quin diversum potiùs liquidissimè patet ex eodem capite: ut quando Apostolus omnem culpam reprobationis transfert in incredulitate, versibus 31. & 32. Israël, inquiens, qui spectabatur Legem justitiæ, ad Legem justitiæ non pervenit: Quare? Quianon ex fide, sed velut ex operibus Legis. Et versibus præcedentibus 7. & 8. Non qui semen sunt Abrahæ, omnes sunt filij: sed in Isaac vocabitur tibi semen: Hoc est, non qui filij carnis sunt, ij sunt Filij DEI: sed qui sunt filij promissionis, censentur in semine: hoc est, interprete Apostolo Gal. 3, 9. Qui ex fide sunt, benedicentur cum fideli Abraham: Et versu 29. Si estis Christi, estis etiam semen Abrahæ, & secundum promissionem hæredes. Undè generalem & Electionis, & Reprobationis aphorismum, neutrum verò absolutum, sed utrumque ordinatum, infert Apostolus, Rom. 11, 20. Per incredulitatem excisi sunt: Tu verò fide stas. Absit ergò, ut absolutæ Reprobationis dogma, verbis Apostoli, sensu Sacramentario affingamus. Nam licèt in Reprobatione Esavi, hoc est in abrogatione primogenituræ (quæ salvâ salute ipsius fieri poterat) causam primam non nisi in voluntate DEI quærendam esse facilè largimur: tamen in Reprobatione, sive Damnatione hominum eandem causam primam dari debere, minimè concedimus. Neque hac in parte ratione causæ primæ ac summæ eadem est ratio Prædestinationis, quæ est reprobationis. Nam Electionis quidem causam primam atque summam, extra misericordem DEI voluntatem, non tamen absolutam, sed ordinatam, quærere nefas est: at Reprobationis Principium ad eandem referre, impietate ipsâ magis impium est: uti suprà parte priore ex professo ostensum. Neque pro sententiâ adversariorum quicquam roboris aut præsidij habent hæc verba Apostoli Rom. 9, 11. (Nondum natis pueris, cum nihil fecissent vel boni vel mali.) Nam hæc verba non definiunt modum aut causam, vel Electionis vel Reprobationis: sed definiunt tantùm tempus, quo oraculum hoc editum fuerit matri Rebeccæ: id quod factum est, puerulis istis nondùm in lucem editis.

Sextò & postremò: notanda etiam venit æquivocatio in verbo Odisse (Esau odio habui) quod non semper hostilem animi alienati affectum: nedùm odium aliquod atrocissimum absolutæ Reprobationis, quale fingunt Adversarij: sed vel neglectum, vel posthabitionem, aut præteritionem significat: Quemadmodum etiam hoc loco antithetori, nempè τὸ Diligere idem est, quod in re externâ alterum alteri anteferre. Cujus interpretationis autorem habemus ipsum Spiritum Sanctum. Nam quod Luc. 14, 26. Christus dixisse legitur, ut ad ipsum venientes, odio habeant patrem & matrem, uxorem & liberos suos &c. illud Matthæus comparativè explicat, à Christo dictum fuisse referens: Qui patrem & matrem super me diligit, non est me dignus, & qui amat filium aut filiam plus, quàm me, non est me dignus. Matth. 10, 37. Quo sensu utraque etiam vox accipitur, Psal. 87, 2. Diligit Dominus portas Sion, super omnia tabernacula Jacobi: non quòd hæc non etiam diligat: sed quòd portas Sion his præferat. Sic Christus, Nemo, inquit, potest duobus Dominis servire, alterum diliget. alterum odio habebit Matth. 6, 24. Luc. 16, 13. Quo pertinet disputatio illa Augustini lib. 1. ad Simplic. quæst. 2. Cùm scriptum sit Sap. 11, 25. DEUM diligere omnia, quæ sunt, & nihil odisse eorum quæ fecerit, quomodo hoc de Esavo locum habet? Sed distingue inter creaturam DEI & opus Diaboli: DEUS non odit hominem Esavv, sed peccatorem Esavv odit. Est ergò odium hoc non personæ, sed causæ: Sic causa. Ergò non absolutum odium: Tametsi enim persona notatur: non tamen intelligitur sine causâ: sive prævisâ, sive actu existente: secundum illud Joban. 3, 18. Qui non credit, jam judicatus est. Sed hæc de primo argumento ex cap. 9. epistolæ ad Romanos petitio, in quo præcipuum causæ suæ præsidium collocant Sacramentarij, paulò prolixiùs dixisse sufficiat.

ALTERUM tertiæ classis argumentum, urget oraculum illud DEI asseverantis, Rom. 9, 15. Exod. 33, 19. Misereor, cujus misereor: & commiseror, quem commiseror. Quæ verba secundum superficiem literæ hunc sensum gignere videntur, Quasi DEUS ipse inter homines miserandos distingvat:seq; non omnes homines suâ misericordiâ dignari, ostendat. Verùm vitiosissima hæc, & in DEUM ipsum blasphema est interpretatio. Nam hæc verba neque pro particulari miserendi voluntate, neque pro absoluto misericordiæ divinæ affectu aut decreto militare, vel indè evincitur, quòd quorum DEUS velit misereri, Scriptura passim clarissimè explicat: præcipuè Ezech. 33, 11. Vivo ego DEUS, nolo mortem peccatoris: sed ut convertatur impius à vitâ suâ malâ, & vivat. Rom. 11, 23. Conclusit DEUS omnes sub incredulitate, ut omnium misereretur. 1. Tim. 2, 4. DEUS vult omnes homines salvos fieri, ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Nisi ergò Spiritus Sanctus turpis contradictionis arguatur, certè locus Mosaicus his testimoniis opponi nullo modo vel potest, vel debet: sed interpretatio analogiæ fidei consona quærenda & tenenda est. Jam si in propriâ suâ sede, & ex totâ materiæ cohærentiâ, Locus & Mosaic9, & Apostolicus expendatur: sensus utriusq; idem planè emergit iste: Benignum & misericordem esse DEUM, & beneficia quævis ab ipso profecta, non ab humanâ dignitate, meritis, aut operibus: sed ab unicâ miserentis DEI gratiâ & favore planè indebito promanare. Cujus sensus interpretem Moses ipse se exhibet in eâ concione, quam habuit capite statim insequente 34, 6. Exodi: Domine DEUS misericors & clemens: patiens & multæ misericordiæ, qui custodis misericordiam in millia &c. Apostolus verò itidem interpretationem hanc confirmat: Siquidem allegatione verborum istorum ex Mose, obviam ire voluit Judæorum tacitæ objectioni, qui justitiam DEI laborare statuebant, nisi DEus ipsorum cursui & labori, Salutem & vitam æternam, tanquàm mercedem conferret ex debito. Respondet ergò Apostolus negatè, ostendens, Soli DEI misericordiæ deberi electionem & salutem: Quare statim & immediatè subjicit, versu 16. Non est igitur volentis, neq; currentis, sed miserentis DEI.

TERTIUM hujus classis argumentum est de vasis iræ ad interitum aptatis: de quo Beza in suo adhæc verba commentario triumphum quasi canit: Iterum, inquiens, liceat cum Paulo dicere, quosdam homines à DEO opifice conditos esse ad interitum. Verùm περὶ νίκης hoc est ἐγκώμιον. Nam 1. concedimus ultrò utrumque istud: & quòd sint in Ecclesiâ vasa honoris atq; ignominiæ: & quòd utraq; sint κατηρτισμένα sive præparata, aut coagmentata. Verùm id in controversiâ est: An DEUS utraq; illa vasa faciat, vel præparet? Ubi cùm Affirmatè respondeant Calviniani, insignem πλεονεξίαν & blasphemiam committunt. Apostolus enim de vasis quidem Gloriæ affirmat, quòd DEUS ea præparaverit, ἅ προητοίμασεν εἰς δόξαν: versu 23. Et de his inter nos & Adversarios nulla est controversia. Verùm quòd de vasis ad dedecus, sive ignominiam factis, idem etiam affirmet Apostolus: id verò simpliciter negamus: Siquidem absolutè duntaxat dicit, ea apparari: sed à quo apparentur, non expressè adjicit. Jam si alia Scripturæ dicta, & analogia fidei consulantur, manifestum est, apparari ea non à DEO, quatenùs talia sunt: sed partim à seipsis, partim à Diabolo. Deindè adversariæ partis sensum textus ipse Apostolicus falsitatis manifestæ convincit. Nam vasa illa iræ, à DEO tolerari inquit in multâ patientiâ. Atqui DEUS opera propria ex liberrimâ suâ voluntate facta & ordinata in patientiâ tolerare, haud magis affirmari potest, atq; de

Architecto aliquo dicitur, quòd opus à se perfectum & absolutum in magnâ patientiâ toleret. Ergò tolerantia hæc evidenter arguit, vasa illa iræ, non DEI, sed alieni operis, DEOƉ; minimè placiti, effectum esse. Tùm DEUS nihil odit eorum, quæ fecit: Sap. 11, 25. At vasa iræ odit: Siquidem in illis puniendis ostendit iram suam: uti habet versus Apostoli 22. hujus capitis noni. Ergò DEUS vasa iræ non fecit, quatenùs talia.

Neq; responsioni huic obstat Similitudo Apostoli de figulo, formante ex unà eademq; luti massâ vas aliud in honorem, aliud in dedecus. Nam rectè jam olim Chrysostomus de hoc ipso simili respondit: δεῖ τὰ ὑποδείγματα ᾀ καθόλε λαμβάνειν; ἀλλ' εἰ ὅπερ παρειλήπται; τὸ λοιπὸν ἅπαν ἐᾶν: In similitudinibus non esse urgenda singula verba, neq; illas extra institutum, ad quod adhibitæ sunt, trahendas, neqs peculiaria dogmata indidem extruenda esse. Est autem institutum Apostoli hoc: Fas ac licitum esse DEO, qui nemini quicquam debeat, si misertus eorum, qui gratiam oblatam acceptant, reliquos pervicaces & obstreperos, hoc est, vasam tione substantia à DEO condita, vasa ignominia fieri, hoc est, à Diabolo magis, magisq; indurari patiatur.

Neque illud etiam ponderis, momentique quicquam obtinet, quod ex versu 22. de declaratione justitiæ divinæ obtenditur. Manifestus enim ἔλεγχὸς non causæ committitur. Etsi enim verum est, DEUM suam justitiam declarare adversus vasa iræ: tamen hæc ipsa ostensio iræ & justitiæ ipsius, non est causa, vel origo reprobationis quorundam: Sed Reprobationis potius finis, ad quem damnatio, sive interitus vasorum iræ revocatur, ac reducitur. Confirmat hoc dilucidè Scriptura: Non, inquiens, necessarij sunt DEO homines impij: Ecclesiastici 15, 12. nec facienda mala, ut eveniant bona, Rom. 3, 8. Imò, quòd Fulgentius inquit lib. 1. ad Monimum. cap. 22. Justitia justa non erit, si puniendum reum non invenisse: sed fecisse dicatur. Deindè absolutissima illa in DEO αὐτάρχεια, necessitatem istam declarandæ justitiæ non admittit: quippè sine quâ justitia ipsius æternæ nihil decessisset: haud magis, atque omnipotentiæ ipsius nihil decessisset, si maximè hoc Universum non creasset. Tandem in punito lapsu Adamico, in damnatione lapsorum Angelorum, in morte deniq; Filij sui, abundè satis Justitiam suam declaravit, ut figmento isto Calvinistico de absolutâ quorundam ad damnationem, sive interitum, ad asserendam DEI justitiam, nihil quicquam opus sit. Neque tale quid innuit particula (volens eod. versu 22.) Nam non voluntas aliqua absoluta: sed voluntas judicij, &ve consequens notatur: quæ contumaciam impiorum tandem æternùm punit.

TERTIA & postrema classis argumentorum, quibus pugnant Calviniani , continet Rationum quarundam præsidia : Cujus generis hæc sunt præcipua : I. Si propter peccata DEUS homines reprobaret : omnes reprobandi essent , quia omnes sunt peccatores. At hoc non fit. Ergò. II. Aliqui tantùm eliguntur : Matth.20, 16. & cap. 22, 14. pauci adoptantur in filios : Rom. 8, 29. pauci vocantur : Act. 14, 16. pauci credunt : Joh. 6, 36. & cap. 10, 26. pauci justificantur, & glorificantur, Rom. 8, 30. Quod si verò seriò Deus vellet, posset utiq́, omnibus hoc præstare. DEUS enim quicquid vult etiam potest : Sap. 12, 18. Et, quæcunq́, voluit, fecit, Psal. 35, 6. Quia verò hoc non facit, utiq́, vel indè ipsum hoc nunquàm voluisse colligitur. III. Res eodem modo circa Redemtionem humani generis se habet. CHRISTUS enim venit salvare populum suum à peccatis, Matth. 1, 21. Vitam dare pro ovibg, Joh 10, 15 : acquirere sanguine suo Ecclesiam DEI, Act. 20, 28. mori pro electis, Rom. 8, 33. At tales non sunt omnes. Ergò neq́, omnes redemit. Quò pertinet etiam hæc collectio Piscatoris : Animam suam dedit pretium pro multis : Matth. 20, 28. Marci 10, 45. fudit sanguinem suum in remissionem peccatorum pro multis, Matth. 26, 28. At multi non sunt omnes. Ergò neq́, omnes redemit.

Respondeo : Primam rationem in propositione laborare Sophismate παρὰ τὸ πὴ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Peccata enim non simpliciter, sed respectu finalis incredulitatis & impœnitentiæ sunt causa reprobationis. Jam non omnes peccatores perseverant ad finem usq; in incredulitate, Ergò non omnes etiam reprobantur.

Altera ratio fallit primùm turpi Confusione Absoluti & Ordinati. Fingitur enim paucorum absoluta aliqua electio, adoptio, vocatio, justificatio, & glorificatio : quæ reliquos fatali quopiam, & absoluto decreto excludat. Atqui talis in Scripturis nuspiam traditur vel vocatio, vel adoptio, vel electio &c. Ergò turpis πλεονεξία & Principij petitio in Conclusione committitur. Deindè idem paralogismus committitur in Consequentis ratione : dùm absoluta voluntas cum ordinatâ perperàm confunditur. Verè enim facit DEUS omne, quicquid absolutè vult : non verò, quod vult certâ mediorum τάξει sive ordine, qui ab hominibus sæpiùs intervertitur, ac proindè non fit etiam culpâ hominum, quod quidem DEUS fieri vult , sed observato ordine.

Tertia ratio eodem πλεονεξίας vitio laborat. Nam vitam dare pro ovibus, mori pro electis, & similia, tantundem valet Calvinianis, ac si TANTUM pro ovibus & electis hoc factum sit : id quod reliquis Scripturæ dictis , Christum pro toto mundo, hoc est, pro omnibus , imò in specie pro reprobis quoq; mortuum esse asserentibus, Contradictoriè repugnat. Deindè laborat hæc ratio Sophismate τῆς λέξεως καὶ ὁμωνυμίας, Nam vox (MULTI) interdum universam generis humani multitudinem notat : quemadmodum oftendit Augustinus, de Civit. DEI, lib. 20. cap. 23. Imò Scriptura ipsa: Rom. 5, 19. Dan. 12, 2. Gen. 17, 4. Gen. 22, 18.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic): II. The error of the Papists and especially of the Esau-vites

II. The error of the Papists and especially of the ESAU-VITES.

The Church of the Romans is not sufficiently consistent with itself regarding the doctrine of Predestination: but is split into diverse opinions: so that the Roman Papacy can most correctly be divided into two specifically different ones, the Old and the New: so far is it from being able to boast of perpetual consensus in doctrine. For the more recent Papacy, which the Esauvite crowd claims for itself, has defected from the older one, and having committed a foul schism, has passed not obscurely to the camp of the Calvinists.

In ancient times under the Papacy, this doctrine was taught concerning the eternal Predestination of God, not indeed sufficiently Orthodox, yet more tolerable than that of the modern Esauvites: namely: That men were chosen by God to eternal life on account of foreseen good works and the good use of free will. Which very opinion many even of the Fathers held before the times of Augustine, as was shown above in part 1 of this treatise: in special controversy 3. However, those who defended this doctrine under the Papacy were Bonaventure, Albert the Great, Alexander of Hales, Biel lect. 79, Roffensis in his assertion on free will against Luther. Erasmus in his Diatribe on free will and his Hyperaspistes against Luther: Pighius on the use of free will, lib. 8, cap. 2, p. 137.

This opinion (in itself indeed not at all to be approved) the Esauvite race today repudiates and condemns, as can be seen in Bellarmine, lib. 2, De grat. & lib. arbit., cap. 9, in these words: Although sufficient grace is given to all: yet no reason for divine predestination can be assigned on our part. And after a few words: God, in those whom He chose for glory, [sees] nothing but the merit of death: and therefore He mercifully frees them, not rendering to them the due punishment, but bestowing undue grace. Column 608 A, 609 C, and cap. 10, p. 611 D. Men are chosen, he says, not only freely: but also without any foresight of works. And indeed, thus far we do not intend any quarrel with Bellarmine, although it does not escape us at all that he harbors some ὕπυλόν τι under this very assertion. But we note this most of all in this place, that Bellarmine not only rejects the opinion of the Scholastics and the ancient Pontifical Doctors: but also embraces an opinion on Predestination that is entirely new, and never before publicly received and approved in the Roman Church: namely, that which has much kinship and affinity with the blasphemous opinion of the Sacramentarians.

For in the already cited ninth chapter he establishes such an order of Predestination in the divine mind: First, he says, GOD foresaw, if He should create man, that he would fall with all his posterity, and at the same time He saw that He could in various ways liberate either all or some according to His own will. Secondly, He willed to create man, and to permit him to fall, and to mercifully liberate some from the number of the fallen, while others were justly left in the mass of perdition. Thirdly, he devised remedies suitable for the elect to be saved, in which the incarnation and passion of the Savior held the first place. Fourthly, he approved those remedies, and then chose Christ, and us in him before the foundation of the world. Fifthly, he disposed, ordained, and in a certain way commanded that it should be done so. pag. 610. B.

And on page 607. B. or in chapter 8, he writes: We have believed that GOD by an absolute will wills to save many, both infants and adults: and by an absolute will does not will to save others, both infants and adults.

And in chapter 16, he writes: We say that Reprobation comprises two acts, the one negative, the other positive; since the reprobate are opposed to the elect contradictorily and contrarily. For first, GOD does not have the will to save them; then, he has the will to damn them; and indeed, as regards the former act, no cause for it is given on the part of men, just as neither is there for Predestination. But for the latter, a cause is given, the Forevision of sin. pag. 639.

Which opinion is read to have been defended formerly also by some Scholastic Theologians, namely Scotus, Durandus, Gregory of Rimini in book 2 of the Sentences, dist. 40 and 41, and by Thomas, lecture 4 on chapter 9 to the Romans.

Although Bellarmine protests in many places that this doctrine of his is different from the opinion of the Calvinists, who contend that men were predestined to sin and eternal death before the forevision of sin: yet this protestation is null and void in fact. For the Calvinists themselves would never concede that they teach that men were predestined to sin itself: since it is permitted to read in Calvin and others that very many were indeed not reprobated by GOD on account of foreseen sin, yet not before the forevision of sin. That these two differ from each other, everyone understands. I pass over the fact that this very opinion overturns itself. For to imagine predestination to sin, prior to the forevision of sin, what is it but to manifestly separate things that cohere, and to posit an opposite in the adjunct?

The Esauvite indeed cloaks his opinion with the authority of Augustine, who taught that Predestination did not precede, but followed the forevision of original sin, on account of which the entire human race was made as it were a mass commonly damned, from which GOD, having chosen certain men, justly left the rest in the mass of perdition. But how truly he attributes this to Augustine, and what strength there is in the opinion of Augustine, has been demonstrated above: contr. spec. 8. quæst. 2. Whatever, however, it may be, because he posits that no cause for the negative Reprobation, as he calls it, can be given on the part of man, and contends that those left in the common mass of perdition were reprobated by the absolute will of GOD: an egg is no more like an egg, or milk like milk, than this doctrine of the Esauvite is in part Calvinism.

Nor does it relieve the Esauvite that they posit this reprobation of theirs not as prior to the forevision of sin, but as posterior. For in eternity there is nothing prior or posterior by reason of time. But the priority and posteriority of order, not even the Sacramentarians themselves will deny.

There is added the express consensus of the Calvinists, especially the more recent ones, who, intending to palliate the absurdity of their dogma in any way, imagine that this Decree of Reprobation is not simply and in every respect absolute: but only by reason of the first act. How this is to be understood is evident from nowhere else than from the doctrine of the Esauvites, who constitute a twofold act of Reprobation: one Affirmative, or Positive: the other Negative: as we learned a little before from Bellarmine. To this distinction Perkins adds his suffrage and calculation, who in his book on Predestination, page 25, discourses thus: The act of Reprobation is twofold: The former is the purpose of forsaking certain men and declaring justice in them. This arises from the mere good pleasure of GOD, with no regard had to either good or evil in the creature. For the will of GOD is the cause of causes. And therefore GOD, by his supreme right, makes vessels for wrath, he does not find them. The second act is the ordination to punishment, or just destruction.

In which opinion Keckermann also writes in System. Theol. page 208. The first act is the purpose of GOD to forsake certain men, and to leave them to themselves. This act is absolute, depending on the sole and absolute will of GOD. The other act is the decree to damn on account of sins. This act is not absolute, but contains a respect to the condition of sin.

Moreover, these two different acts of Reprobation were not devised by the more recent Calvinists at last: but were drawn from the doctrine of the Scholastics, who themselves also feigned a twin act of preterition: one Passive and Negative, and that indeed plainly absolute: the other Affirmative and Active, which is the preparation of punishment, or pre-damnation from eternity, and has respect to sin. Which doctrine of the Scholastics, although it later suffered an obelisk under the Papacy: today, however, it is openly recalled to the stage of the Church by the Esauvites and Calvinists. Whence it is no longer permitted to doubt about their syncretism in this article also.

Latin:

II. Error Pontificiorum & cumprimis ESAVVITARUM.

ECclesia Romanensium circa doctrinam de Prædestinatione sibi non satis constat: sed in diversas scissa est sententias: ita ut Papatus Romanus in duos specie differentes rectissimè dispesci possit, Veterem & Novum: tantum abest, ut de perpetuo consensu in doctrinâ gloriari possit. Nam recentior Papatus, quem turba Esavvitica sibi vendicat, ab antiquiore defecit, & fœdo commisso schismate ad castra Calvinianorum haud obscurè transijt.

Antiquitùs sub Papatu de Prædestinatione DEI æternâ, hæc tradebatur doctrina, non quidem satis Orthodoxa, tolerabilior tamen, quàm modernorum est Esavvitarum: nempè: Homines ob prævisa bona opera, & bonum liberi arbitrij usum, ad vitam æternam à DEO electos esse. Quam ipsam sententjam multi etiam ex Patribus ante tempora Augustini tenuerunt, uti suprà part. 1. hujus Tractationis ostensum fuit: Controversiâ speciali 3. Propugnarunt autem sub Papatu hanc doctrinam, Bonaventura, Albertus M. Alexander ab Ales, Biel lect. 79. Roffensis in assert. de lib. arb. contra Lutherum. Erasmus in suâ Diatribe de lib. arb. ejusq́; Hyperaspiste contra Lutherum: Pighius de usu liberi arbitrij, lib. 8. cap. 2. pag. 137.

Hanc opinionem, (in se quidem minimè probandam) gens Esavvitica hodiè repudiat & damnat, uti videre est apud Bellarminum lib. 2. de grat. & lib. arbit. cap. 9. his verbis: Quamvis gratia sufficiens omnibus datur: tamen prædestinationis divinæ nulla ratio ex parte nostri adsignari potest. Et post pauca: DEUS in ijs, quos elegit ad gloriam, nisi meritum mortis: & propterea misericorditer eos liberat, non reddens eis debitam pœnã, sed donans indebitam gratiam. Columnâ 608. A. 609. C. & cap. 10. pag. 611. D. Eliguntur, inquit, homines, non solùm gratis: sed etiam absq́; ullâ prævisione operum. Et sanè hactenùs Bellarmino litem nullam intendimus, quanquàm sub hâc ipsâ assertione, ὕπυλόν τι ipsum fovere, nos minimè latet. Sed illud hoc loco maximè notamus, quòd Bellarminus non modò Scholasticorum, & Veterum Doctorum Pontificiorum sententiam rejicit: sed & novam planè, ac prius in Ecclesiâ Romanâ nunquàm publicè receptam ac approbatam de Prædestinatione opinionem, amplectitur: eam videlicet, quæ cum blasphemâ Sacramentariorum sententiâ plurimum cognationis & affinitatis habet.

Nam capite jam citato nono talem Prædestinationis ordinem, in divinâ mente constituit: Primùm, inquit, prævidit DEUS, si hominem conderet, eum lapsurum cum omni posteritate, & simul vidit, posse se varijs modis liberare vel omnes, vel aliquos pro arbitratu suo. Deindè voluit hominem condere, ac ut laberetur permittere, & quosdam ex numero lapsorum misericorditer liberare, alijs in massâ perditionis justè relictis. Tertiò excogitavit remedia, salvandis electis idonea, in quibus primum locum habuit incarnatio & passio Salvatoris Quartò approbavit ea remedia, & tunc elegit Christum, & nos in ipso ante mundi constitutionem. Quintò disposuit, ordinavit, & quodammodò imperavit, ut ita fieret. pag. 610. B.

Et pag. 607. B. sive capite 8. scribit: Credidimus, DEUM absolutâ voluntate velle salvare multos, tùm parvulos, tùm adultos: & absolutâ voluntate alios non velle salvare, tùm parvulos, tùm adultos.

Et cap. 16. scribit: Dicimus, Reprobationem duos actu comprehendere, alterum negativum: alterum positivum; siquidem reprobi opponuntur electis contradictoriè, & contrariè. Primùm enim non habet DEUS voluntatem illos salvandi; Deindè habet voluntatem eos damnandi; Et quidem, quod attinet ad priorem actum, nulla datur ejus causa ex parte hominum sicut neq; Prædestinattonis. Posterioris autem datur causa, Prævisio peccati. pag. 639.

Quæ sententia à Scholasticis nonnullis Theologis olim etiam defensa fuisse legitur, Scoto nimirùm, Durando, Gregorio Ariminensi lib. 2. Sent. dist. 40. & 41. & à Thomâ lect. 4. in cap. 9. ad Romanos.

Quanquàm verò Bellarminus multis protestatur passim, suam hanc doctrinam, à Calvinianorum opinione diversam esse, quippè qui homines ante prævisionem peccati, ad peccatum, & mortem æternam prædestinatos esse contendant: tamen protestatio hæc ipso facto nulla est. Nam ipsi quoq; Calviniani nunquàm concesserint, se docere, homines prædestinatos esse ad ipsum peccatum: Siquidem apud Calvinum & alios legere licet, plurimos quidem non ob prævisum peccatum: non tamen ante prævisionem peccati à DEO reprobatos esse. Quæ duo inter se discrepare, nemo non intelligit. Taceo, quòd ipsa hæc sententia sese evertit. Nam prædestinationem ad peccatum fingere, prævisione peccati priorem, quid est, nisi manifestè cohærentia segregare, & oppositum in adjecto statuere?

Prætexit quidem opinioni suæ Esauvita Augustini autoritatem, qui docuerit, quòd Prædestinatio non præcesserit, sed secuta sit prævisionem peccati originalis, ob quod universum genus humanum factum sit quasi massa quædam communiter damnata, ex quâ DEUS certis hominibus electis, reliquos justè in massâ perditionis reliquerit. Sed quàm verè hoc Augustino tribuat, quidq; sententiæ Augustini roboris insit, supra est demonstratum: contr. spec. 8. quæst. 2. Quicquid tamen omninò sit, quia Reprobationis negativæ, quam vocat, nullam ex parte hominis causam dari posse statuit, & in communi perditionis massâ relictos, absolutâ DEI voluntate reprobatos esse contendit: non ovum ovo magis est simile, aut lac lacti, quàm Esavvitæ doctrina hæc in parte est Calvinismo.
