We assert the contrary, and indeed from the context itself. For

The Apostle calls the elect not those προσκαίρους [temporary ones], who fail in the time of persecution: but those who 1. accepted the Word of God not only ἐν λόγῳ [in word], that is, in speech or external preaching: but in power, and in the Holy Spirit. ver. 5. then those who retained that very word ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ [in much assurance], which clearly denotes the perseverance of faith. 3. who received the word ἐν θλίψει πολλῇ [in much affliction] in much affliction, and with the joy of the Holy Spirit, ver. 5. & 6. Therefore the Apostle excludes from this the προσκαίρους [temporary ones], who fail in the time of persecution. 4. He understands under the designation of the Elect those who bear examples to all believers in Macedonia, and in Achaia: v. 7. which cannot or ought not to be accommodated to the προσκαίρους [temporary ones]. 5. whose faith in God has spread into every place, so that the Apostles have had no need to say anything. 6. finally, having left idols, they served the true and living God: and WAITED FOR His Son from the heavens: that is, those who Persevered, which the Greek word ἀναμένειν [to wait for] irrefragably proves. Whence the name ἀναμονὴ [waiting/expectation], Perseverance, tolerance. These things having been weighed in this way, it becomes plain that the term Election neither admits any generality in this place: nor includes the προσκαίρους [temporary ones], about whom the question is, under its scope: that many of whom could have been, indeed were, in the Church of the Thessalonians, the very treatment of this Epistle clearly proves. Whence, however, it does not follow that the title of Elect is attributed by the Apostle to these also in a general signification.

Who called us, with a holy calling according to His purpose and Grace, 2. Pet. 1. v. 10. Be diligent to make your calling and election sure: For doing these things, you will never stumble: not that the Elect can make their Election infirm: which the Apostle denies, asserting that Election always attains its end, Rom. 11. v. 7. but that they can fall into grave crimes and wickedness. Apoc. 17. v. 14. Those who are with the Lamb are called, and elect, and faithful. And what need is there of many words, when the text itself implies that a Special calling, which is convertible with Election, must necessarily be understood. For the Apostle does not treat of that calling by which all men, and thus many wise according to the flesh, many powerful and noble are called: just as indeed according to the general calling the whole world is called: but of that by which, the many wise, powerful, and noble of this world having been passed over, the ignoble, weak, and foolish of this age have been called.

THE SECOND assertion, about the truth of which there is doubt, is this: That the Antecedent will of God, and the Universal Counsel of God, can also be called Election: but in the broadest and most general signification.

They seek another proof from the words of the Apostle, 1. Cor. 1. v. 26. You see your calling, Brethren, that not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble, but God chose the foolish things of the world, that He might confound the strong &c. Where the Apostle bids the Corinthians to judge of their own Election from the calling, to which they had been obedient.

I answer 1. If this most general signification is ἄγραφος [unwritten]: then if it is established as καταχρηστικὴ [catachrestic] or abusive. 3. If it is urged in the disputatious forum against the Calvinists: then it can be tolerated in some way. Just as we showed above in the eighth special controversy, quest. 4, that before the Huberian struggle was set in motion, many Orthodox Theologians established Election as Universal, against the absolute particularity of the Calvinists, but with the term of Election used καταχρηστικῶς [catachrestically] for the Universal Love of God. In which sense also Universal Election was defended by many, the Tubingen Acts testify, pages 53, 54, 118, 127, & following. But after the Huberian struggle was set in motion, any Orthodox very rightly abstain from that improper use of the word Election, for causes and reasons already explained above in the cited place: among which this easily holds the chief place: That the Universal holy Scripture nowhere designates the Antecedent will of GOD, or that Universal Counsel of GOD concerning all men to be saved through Christ to be apprehended by faith, by the term of Election. Let us speak therefore with the Holy Spirit, and let us not attend to what our Reason might plausibly devise in any way for this broadest and most general signification. For even these, when weighed in the balance of the Scriptures, fall away of their own accord. Such are:

I answer, neither does this proof establish that general signification of the word Election, as if that, besides those who persevere in faith to the end, also applies to all believers, when they believe, and as long as they believe: but in a broader signification. For the Apostle in this place does not understand that external calling, considered from the bare intention of God, which is general: but that Special one, which is joined with saving effect, and which is of the same breadth as predestination, and these two terms are convertible, according to that of the Apostle Rom. 8. ver. 30. Whom He called, these He also elected: And Whom He elected, these He also called. Concerning which Special calling other testimonies of Scripture are to be understood, which are wrongly distorted by some to a general calling: Such as: 2. Timoth. 1. vers. 9.

I. RATIO : No counsel can be without Election: But the Antecedent Universal will of GOD, concerning all men whatsoever, to be saved through Christ to be apprehended by faith, is a Counsel: Luc. 7. v. 30. Therefore that counsel cannot be understood without election.

I answer 1. The major proposition in the present mystery is false. For the damnation even of the reprobate falls under the counsel, decree, and will of God: yet it does not fall under election. Therefore, there is in divine matters counsel without election. 2. Not even in ethical doctrine is the major simply true. For according to the philosopher, will and election differ in object, nor are they of the same breadth. For the will is concerned with all things, even those which do not actually come to pass: but election is only of those things which can be brought to the destined end through certain means. 3. In the Holy Scriptures, election is nowhere defined as being the very βουλὴ or counsel of God, or the will of God, but it informs the style in such a way as to assert that election was made κατ᾿ πρόθεσιν according to purpose, and κατ᾿ βουλὴν ̇& θελήματος θεῦ: according to the counsel of the will of God Rom. 8. v. 28. Ephes. 1. v. 11. Therefore, election always includes the counsel and will of God: but not every counsel and will of God presupposes election itself. As for the minor, it is a clearly inconvenient phrase when it is said: that God wills all men whatsoever to be saved through Christ to be apprehended by faith. For if we consult the Scriptures, it is nowhere read that God wills him to be saved who ought to apprehend Christ by faith: but that He wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth, all actually to believe, and thus all to be saved through Christ (not to be apprehended: which denotes a mere δύναμιν, and τὸ δυνατὸν) but actually apprehended: so that the antecedent will also requires not potential faith, but actual faith entirely.

mon, on the part of men does not presuppose universal election: but universal love: so that the terms of the opposition may be legitimate, not preterition, or neglect of the fallen angels, and election of men: but preterition of the demons, and reception, or love of men. And this is what that passage in Heb. 2. v. 16 means. He did not take hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham.

III. ARGUMENT: If we consider the human race not by comparison with the angels, but in itself, and with respect to either destruction or reparation, death or life; the word election cannot possibly have a place. For God, in that fatherly counsel, whether He willed to leave the human race in destruction and death, or indeed to restore it to life, certainly chose man to be restored, not to be abandoned.

I answer. This argument again confuses election with the decree of reparation or redemption: which two things, however, must be most accurately distinguished. For Scripture nowhere affirms that God, in that fatherly counsel, whether He willed to leave the human race in destruction and death, CHOSE man to be restored: but it speaks thus, that God so LOVED the world in that fatherly counsel of His, that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life. John 3. v. 16. Which very thing, and nothing more, other sayings of Scripture mean: Ezek. 33. v. 11. As I live, says the Lord God, I do not take pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live: And 2. Pet. 3. v. 9. God does not will any to perish, but all to return to repentance. Where not even a jot is hinted about election: but the truly fatherly affection of God's love toward the human race is expressed: which pertains to the antecedent will of God.

II. ARGUMENT In whatever counsel, where different things are proposed, one of which is accepted and the other rejected, there the word election has a place in its proper and grammatical signification. But God decreed, from the fallen angels as well as from men, to redeem the latter and to leave the former. Rightly, therefore, can this decree be called election.

IV. ARGUMENT taken from chapter 1 to the Ephesians, sounds thus: Whomever God 1. wills to be holy and blameless: 2. Whom He wills to be adopted as sons through Jesus Christ from curse and wrath. 3. Whom He wills to be saved by grace in the beloved: 4. Whom He wills to be redeemed through His blood: 5. To whom He wills to remit sins by grace: 6. To whom He wills the mystery of His will to be known: 7. Whom, finally, He wills to be gathered under one head in Christ: THEM He chose before the foundation of the world. But He wills all men whatsoever to be such. Therefore He chose all men whatsoever.

I answer: 1. The major is again most false, for 1. Election properly and according to grammatical signification is not made from heterogeneous species, such as angels and men: but from objects of the same species: as if I consider men among themselves: there, that some are ordained to salvation, but the rest are reprobated. The word election finds a place. Furthermore, the major proposition also does not sufficiently attain the mind and intention of the author. For intending to prove that the word election obtains a very general signification in the Scriptures, he produces an argument which asserts its PROPER signification. As for the minor, even if the opposition of heterogeneous species were admitted, yet according to the Scriptures and the analogy of faith, it ought not to be affirmed that with respect to the fallen angels men are elect: that they are loved. For the preterition of the demons I answer, that this argument repeats in a sort of compendium those six arguments by which we showed a little earlier that Huber was accustomed to fight for the assertion of universal election, from the first chapter to the Ephesians, but with vain effort. The chief foundations of the error, however, are these: I. That each and every one of those seven heads already enumerated are considered only insofar as they are turned nakedly within the intention and sole will of God, but are hindered by the perversity of men: whereas, nevertheless, the Apostle does not consider those things in chapter 1 to the Ephesians so generally, but rather insofar as Election by its very act attains that end in each of these members: 2. That the universal Love of GOD is basely confounded with the Special love, which is proper to the Elect. 3. That the Redemption of the human race, and the Remission of sins, is wrongly attended to in this place, not insofar as it is already defined in the Elect by the very saving event, but nakedly and generally, insofar as it is common to all men by reason of that merit: 4. That the mystery of the will of GOD, revealed in the Gospel, is poorly considered, outside the τάξιν and order containing the complex of our salvation, 5. And lastly, the reconciliation of the human race, which was made through that ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν, of which the Apostle makes mention in Eph. 1:10, is confounded with Predestination itself. Where again that ἀντιστροφὴ, and the reciprocal collection from both sides, does not hold. For all the elect are indeed restored, or reconciled: but not all who are restored are elect: as has been shown more fully and vigorously above.

Latin:

RATIO V. Huberi: Nisi electio statuatur Universalis esse: omnis solidæ consolationis materia tollitur.

Respondeo, Huberum mutuatum esse hoc argumentum à Puccio, qui & ipse hoc fuco dogma suum palliare conabatur: somnians cum Hubero omnis veræ ac solidæ consolationis nervum in eo esse positum, si sine discrimine omnibus hominibus uti salutem & vitam æternam, ita etiam Electionem ad salutem ex æquo communem esse: & quidem ex æterna DEI ordinatione, quæ omnes homines elegerit. Sed turpissimè fallunt, & falluntur, solatium omne in amarissimum absinthium, & immotam spei, fideíque πληροφορίαν omnem in desperationis laqueos commutantes. Ecquæ enim consolatio hæc fuerit, si tentatus & afflictus, se æqvè ac Judæorum & Turcarum aliquem ab æterno esse electum: Ubi nihil præter angores, & desperationis cruciatus oboriri necessum est. Jam verò qui statuunt, electionis certitudine excidere nunquàm posse, qui unicè in Christi merito acquieseunt; & in hac fide ad finem usque perseverant: illis amplissima consolationis materia in doctrina de Electione credentium est proposita: uti supra parte priore circa finem prolixè fuit ostensum.

Et hæ quidem sunt præcipuæ Huberi rationes, quibus nostris, sed irrito conatu, molestus esse voluit.

Cæterùm præter Huberum sunt & reperiuntur alii, & quidem Orthodoxi Theologi, qui, licèt cum futili & fanatico Huberi dogmate nihil commune habeant, nedùm ejus patrocinium suscipiant; nonnullis tamen hoc in articulo loquendi formulis, sive assertionibus uti consueverunt: de quibus haud immeritò dubitatur, nùm analogiæ fidei & Scripturæ Sacræ sint conformes: quas ut paucis examinemus, haud fuerit inconveniens.

PRIMA assertio est, Quòd illis, qui à Servatore nominantur πρόσκαιροι, hoc est, ad tempus credentes, postmodùm verò deficiunt, Titulus Electionis in latiori & generalior significatione tribui possit. Probationem hujus rei petunt ex 1. Thes. 14. Ubi Paulus, Silvanus & Timotheus ad Ecclesiam Thessalonicensium hunc in modũ scribunt: Scientes fratres dilecti à DEO electionem vestram. Jam scire hoc non poterant, nisi ex confessione fidei, & obedientia erga Evangelium, quam Ecclesia Thessalonicensium tota præ se ferebant, quanquam multi in ea πρόσκαιροι esse poterant, qui nihilominus Electionis titulo exornantur.

Sed respondeo, Probationem hanc non apodicticè, sed in speciem saltem probabiliter ad propositum ζήτημα accommodari posse. Nam 1. hoc loco Thessalonicensibus tribui Electionis titulum in latiori & generaliori significatione, simpliciter negamus: Etsi enim inscriptio hæc ad totam Thessalonicensium Ecclesiam est directa: tamen interprete & Doctore B. Luthero nostro, semper ea est intelligenda συνεκδοχικῶς, ita ut nominetur quidem totum; sed intelligatur tantùm nobilior ejus pars quæ est Electorum. Nam impossibile est, ut in cœtu vocatorum, ubi sonat pura Evangelii doctrina, & legitima Sacramentorum administratio: ibi non sint etiam aliqvi verè pii & Electi. Horum ergò respectu toti Ecclesiæ, sed συνεκδοχικῶς, & ratione potioris partis, Electorum titulus accommodatur. Ubi non fas est, generalem aliquam, & laxiorem significationem vocabulo Electionis affingere: sed determinatè potiùs & restrictè ad potiorem illam Ecclesiæ partem, accipiendum illud est. 2. allatæ probationis Consequentia valdè infirma est; & petit principium. Nam propter solam illam externam confessionem fidei, & obedientiam erga Evangelium, toti Ecclesiæ Thessalonicensium tribui titulum Electorum, nondùm probatum est. Nos contrarium asserimus, & quidem ex ipso contextu. Nam

Electos appellat Apostolus non προσκαίρους illos, qui tempore persecutionis deficiunt : sed eos, qui 1. Verbum Dei non tantum ἐν λόγῳ, hoc est, in Sermone sive externâ prædicatione : sed in virtute, & in Spiritu Sancto acceptârunt. vers. 5. deindè qui illud ipsum verbum retinuerunt ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ, id quod fidei perseverantiam disertè notat. 3. qui receperunt verbum ἐν θλίψει πολλῇ in afflictione multâ, & cum gaudio Spiritus Sancti, vers. 5. & 6. Ergò excludit Apostolus hinc προσκαίρους, tempore persecutionis deficientes. 4. Eos sub Electorum notatione intelligit, qui ferunt exemplaria omnibus credentibus in Macedoniâ, & in Achaiâ : v. 7. id quod ad προσκαίρους accommodari non potest aut debet. 5. quorum fides in Deum dimonavit in omnem locum, ut non necesse habuerint Apostoli quicquam loqui. 6. denique relictis idolis servierunt Deo verò & vivo: & EXPECTARUNT Filium ejus è cœlis : hoc est, qui Perseverunt, id quod irrefragabiliter evincit verbum græcum ἀναμένειν. Undè nomen ἀναμονὴ, Perseverantia, tolerantia. Quibus ita expensis planum fit, Electionis vocabulum neque generalitatem aliquam hoc loco admittere: neqs προσκαίρους, de quibus quæstio est, sub suo ambitu complecti : quorum multos in Ecclesiâ Theffalonicensium effe potuisse, imò fuisse, ipsa Epistolæ hujus tractatio luculenter evincit. Undè tamen Electorum titulum, his quoqve in generali fignificatu ab Apostolo tribui, non est consequens.

Qui vocavit nos, vocatione sancta secundum suum propositum & Gratiam, 2. Petr. 1. v. 10. Studete vocationem & electionem vestram firmam facere : Hæc enim facientes, nunquàm impingetis : non quòd Electionem suam Electi infirmare possint : id quod negat Apostolus, afferens, Electionem semper affequi finem, Rom. 11. v. 7. sed quòd in gravia scelera & flagitia incidere possint. Apoc. 17. v. 14. Qui cum agno sunt vocati, & electi, & fideles. Et quid multis opus, cum textus ipse innuat, Specialem vocationem, quæ cum Electione convertitur, necessariò intelligendam effe. Nam Apostolus non de eâ vocatione agit, quâ omnes homines, & sic multi sapientes secundum carnem, multi potentes & nobiles sunt vocati : quemadmodum sanè secundum generalem vocationem totus mundus est vocatus: sed de eâ, quâ sapientibus, potentibus, & nobilibus multis hujus mundi præteritis, ignobiles, infirmi & stulti hujus seculi vocati sunt.

ALTERA assertio, de cujus veritate dubitatur, est hæc: Quod Antecedens Dei voluntas, & Consilium Dei Universale, dici etiam possit Electio: sed in latissimâ & generalissimâ significatione.

Alteram probationem petunt ex verbis Apostoli, 1. Cor. 1. v. 26. Videtes vocationem vestram, Fratres, quia non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles, sed quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit, Deus, ut confunderet fortia &c. Ubi Apostolus Corinthios de sua ipsorum Electione jubet judicare ex vocatione, cui obediverant.

Respondeo 1. Si hæc generalissima significatio ἄγραφος : deindè si καταχρηστικὴ sive abusiva constituitur. 3. Si in foro disputatorio contra Calvinianos urgeatur: tùm utcunqve eam tolerari posse. Quemadmodum suprà controversiâ speciali octavâ, quæst. 4. ostendimus, ante motum certamen Huberianum, multos Orthodoxos Theologos Electionem statuisse Universalem, contra absolutam Calvinianorum particularitatem, sed Electionis termino καταχρηστικῶς pro Universali Dilectione Dei usurpato. Quo sensu etiam Universalem Electionem à multis defenfam fuisse, testantur Acta Tubingensia pag. 53. 54. 118. 127. & feqq. Verùm post motum certamen Huberianum, rectissimè ab isto usu improprio vocabuli Electionis, Orthodoxi quivis abstinent, ob causas & rationes jam suprà loco citato expeditas: inter quas locum facilè principem obtinet hæc : Quod Universa Scriptura sacra nuspiam Antecedentem DEI voluntatem, sive Consilium illud DEI Universale de omnibus hominibus per Christum fide apprehendendum salvandis, Electionis termino insigniat. Loquamur ergò cum Spiritu Sancto, neque attendamus, quid quovis modo pro latissimâ & generalissimâ hac fignificatione, Ratio nostra plausibiliter excogitare possit. Nam & hæ ad Scripturarum trutinam appensæ, ultrò concidunt. Quales sunt:

Respondeo, neque hanc probationem asstruere generalem illam significationem vocabuli Electionis, quasi istud præter eos, qui ad finem usque in fide perseverant, conveniat etiam omnibus credentibus, quando credunt, & quamdiu credunt : sed in latiori significatione. Nam Apostolus hoc loco non intelligit vocationem illam externam, ex nudâ Dei intentione consideratam, quæ generalis est : sed Specialem illam, quæ cum effectu salutari est conjuncta, quæqve ejusdem est latitudinis cum prædestinatione, & hi duo termini sint convertibiles, secundum illud Apostoli Roman. 8. verf. 30. Quos vocavit, hos & elegit: Et Quos elegit, hos & vocavit. Dequâ Speciali vocatione intelligenda sunt & alia Scripturæ testimonia, quæ perperàm à nonnullis ad generalem vocationem detorquentur : Qualia sunt: 2. Timoth. 1. vers. 9.

I. RATIO : Nullum consilium fine Electione esse potest: Voluntas autem DEI antecedens Universalis, de omnibus omninò hominibus, per Christum fide apprehendendum salvandis, est Consilium: Luc. 7. v. 30. Ergò consilium illud non fine electione potest intelligi.

Respondeo 1. Propositio Major in præfenti mysterio falsa est. Nam reproborum etiam damnatio cadit sub Consilium, Decretum, & voluntatem DEI: non tamen cadit sub Electionem. Ergò datur in divinis Consilium sine Electione. 2. Ne quidem in doctrinâ Ethicâ Major simpliciter vera est Nam secundum Philosophum Voluntas & Electio differunt objectu, neqve ejusdem sunt latitudinis. Nam voluntas versatur circa res omnes, etiam eas, quæ actu non eveniunt: At Electio earum rerum tantùm est, quæ per certa media, ad finem destinatum perduci possunt. 3. In Scripturis Sacris Electio nuspiam definitur, quòd sit ipsa βουλὴ sive Consilium DEI, aut voluntas DEI, sed sic informat stylum, ut asserat, Electionem factam esse κατ᾿ πρόθεσιν secundum propositum, & κατ᾿ βουλὴν ̇& θελήματος θεῦ: secundum Consilium voluntatis DEI Rom. 8. v. 28. Ephes. 1. v. 11. Includit ergò Electio semper Consilium & Voluntatem DEI: non verò omne Consilium & voluntas DEI præsupponit ipsam quoqve Electionem. Quoad Minorem, incommoda planè phrasis est, quando dicitur: DEUM velle omnes omninò homines, per Christum fide APPREHENDENDUM salvari. Nam si Scripturas consulamus, nuspiam legitur, quòd Deus velit salvari eum, qui Christum Fide apprehendere debeat: sed quòd velit omnes ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire, omnes actu credere & sic omnes per Christum (non apprehendendum: id quod nudam δύναμιν, & τὸ δυνατὸν notat) sed actu APPREHENSUM salvari: ita ut voluntas etiam Antecedens, non Fidem Potentialem, sed actualem omninò requirat.

monum, ex parte Hominum non præsupponit Universalem Electionem: sed Universalem Dilectionem: ita ut termini oppositionis legitimi sint, non Præteritio, sive Neglectio lapsorum Angelorum, & Electio hominum: sed Præteritio Cacodaemonum, & Receptio, sive Dilectio hominum. Et hoc ipsum sibi vult illud Hebr. 2. v. 16. Non Angelos assumsit, sed semen Abrahæ.

III. RATIO: Si humanum genus non collatione Angelorum, sed in se, & respectu vel interitus vel reparationis, Mortis vel vitæ consideremus; Vox Electionis non ming potest locum obtinere. Deus enim in paterno illo consilio, utrù relinquere vellet genus humanum in interitu & morte, an vero reparare illud ad vitam, utiq́; reparandum hominem, non derelinquendum elegit.

Respondeo. Confundit rursus hæc ratio Electionem cum Decreto Reparationis sive redemtionis: quæ duo tamen accuratissimè distinguenda sunt. Scriptura enim nuspiam affirmat, quod DEUS in paterno illo Consilio, utrum relinquere vellet genus humanum in interitu & morte, reparandum hominem ELEGERIT: sed sic loquitur, quod Deus mundum in paterno illo suo consilio DILEXERIT, ita ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis, qui credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Joh. 3. v. 16. Quod ipsum etiam, & nihil ampliùs volunt dicta Scripturæ alia: Ezech. 33. v. 11. Vivo ego, dicit DOMINUS DEUS, non delector Morte impii, sed ut convertatur impius à viâ suâ & vivat: Et 2. Petr. 3. v. 9. Non vult DEUS ullos perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam reverti. Ubi ne γρῦ quidem de electione innuitur: sed dilectionis DEI erga genus humanum verè paternus affectus exprimitur: qui ad voluntatem DEI Antecedentem pertinet.

II. RATIO In quocunq́; consilio, diversis rebus propositis, altera illarum acceptatur, altera repudiatur, ibi propriâ & Grammaticâ significatione locum habet vox Electionis. Atqui Deus ex lapsis tùm Angelis, tùm Hominibus, hos redimere, illos relinquere decrevit. Rectè igitur hoc decretum Electionis vocari potest.

IV. RATIO petita ex cap. 1. ad Ephesios, sic sonat: Quoscunq́; DEUS 1. vult esse Sanctos & irreprehensibiles: 2. Quos ex maledicto & ira vult adoptatos in filios per Jesum Christum. 3. Quos servatos per gratiam in dilecto: 4. Quos redemtos per sanguinem ejus: 5. Quibus remittere peccata ex gratiâ: 6. Quibus notum esse vult mysterium voluntatis suæ: 7. Quos deniq́; Reductos esse vult sub unum caput in Christo: EOS elegit ante constitutionem mundi. Sed omnes omninò homines vult tales esse. Ergò omnes omninò homines elegit.

Respondeo: 1. Major rursus falsissima est, nam 1. Electio propriè & secundum Grammaticam significationem, non fit ex speciebus heterogeneis, quales sunt Angeli & Homines: sed ex ejusdem speciei objectis: ut si Homines inter se considero: ibi quòd quidam ad salutem sunt ordinati, reliqui verò reprobati. Electionis vocabulum locum sortitur. Deindè Major etiam propositio mentem & intentionem Autoris non satis assequitur. Nam probaturus Electionis vocabulum in Scripturis generalissimam quandam obtinere significationem, producit rationem, quæ PROPRIAM ejus significationem astruat. Quoâd Minorem, si maximè oppositio specierum heterogenearum admittatur, tamèn secundum Scripturas, & fidei analogiam non affirmari debet, quòd respectu lapsorum Angelorum Homines sint Electi: quòd sint dilecti. Nam præteritio CacodaRespondeo, Rationem hanc in Compendio quasi quodam repetere Sex illa argumenta, quibus Huberum pro asserenda Universali Electione, excapite primo ad Ephesios, sed irrito conatu, pugnare consvevisse, paulò antè ostendimus. Erroris autem fundamenta præcipua sunt hæc: I. Quod singula & universa illa jam enumerata capita septem, considerantur tantùm, quatenùs illa nudè intra DEI intentionem & solam voluntatem vertuntur, per hominum autem perversitatem impediuntur: cùm tamen Apostolus ea cap. 1 ad Ephesios non sic generaliter consideret, sed potiùs quatenùs ipso actu Electio finem istum in singulis his membris assequitur : 2. Quòd Dilectio DEI universalis, cum Speciali, quæ est Electorum propria, turpiter confunditur. 3. Quòd Redemtio generis humani, & Remissio peccatorum, non quatenùs jam in Electis ipso salutari eventu definitur, sed nudè & generaliter, quatenùs ea ratione meriti, omnibus hominibus communis est, perperàm hoc loco attenditur: 3. Quòd mysterium voluntatis DEI, in Evangelio revelatum, malè consideratur, extra τάξιν & ordinem salutis nostræ complexum continentem, 5. Et postremò, Confunditur reconciliatio generis humani, quæ facta est per illam ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν, cujus meminit Apostolus Ephes.1,10. cum ipsâ Prædestinatione. Ubi rursus ἀντιστροφὴ illa, & ex utraque parte reciproca collectio non valet. Nam omnes quidem electi, sunt illi restaurati, sive reconciliati: non verò omnes restaurati, sunt electi: uti suprà pleniùs & nervosiùs ostensum.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic): A Synoptic Table setting before the eyes an illustrious antithesis and delineation or ὑποτύπωσιν of the doctrine of the Orthodox, the…

A Synoptic Table setting before the eyes an illustrious antithesis and delineation or ὑποτύπωσιν of the doctrine of the Orthodox, the Calvinists, and the Huberians concerning the mystery of Predestination.

Since, according to the common rule of the Schools, truth shines forth more brightly when contraries are placed side by side, it would certainly not be inappropriate to inform our own judgment, as well as that of others, by the ἀντίθεσις of three most diverse opinions concerning the eternal predestination of God, so as to determine to which of them the palm of truth and ὀρθοδοξία ought to be awarded. And this will be all the more worth the effort, since the corrupters of truth today, when caught in manifest absurdity, more insidiously peddle a semblance of agreement with the truth; for in this way the stupendous vanity of these men will shine forth more clearly. Furthermore, by this method the falsehood of those calumnies which are leveled with great clamor against the orthodox assertors of evangelical truth, both by the Calvinists and by the Huberians, can be more rightly and more firmly repelled and refuted. For just as virtue, like a mean, stands between two extremes of vice: so Truth, between two precipices of error, of which the one in excess, the other in defect, deviates enormously from the mean, is held as if pressed: so that from both extremes envy is for the most part stirred up against it. Which very thing, if in any other, happens to the Truth most especially in this article. For if there is a controversy between the Orthodox doctors of our Churches and the Sacramentarians or Calvinists, who sin gravely in the defect or on the side of ἐλλείψεως, they immediately strive to bring odium upon the truth by means of the absurd and truly fanatic dogma of Huberianism: again, if the Orthodox have business concerning the same matter with Huber and the few followers he has, there is nothing he has more frequently in his mouth than to weigh down the cause and defense of the truth with the accusation of Calvinism, and with a less than sound clamor to summon both the East and the West to his aid against this apostasy, as he himself slanders it. Therefore, that this synoptic ἀντίθεσις of opinions will certainly provide a singular use, so that the vanity and falsity of the calumny of both sides may be able to be not so much seen by the eyes as most manifestly felt by the hands themselves.

These things being thus established, we conclude according to the Scriptures that the term Election, in the present mystery, admits of only one signification, determined solely to the children of GOD, and to those actually persevering in the faith unto the end. As for the other two significations, of which the one is looser and, in place of an object, regards the ordained themselves as well, while the other is most loose and most general, regarding in place of an object, according to the nature of the antecedent counsel and will of God, all men whatsoever: these, as being unwritten and sufficiently suited for causing disturbances, and in some way—not indeed entirely, but at least in part—establishing the dogma of Huber, and finally as being in no way conformable to the genuine Symbolical books of the Lutheran Churches, we simply reject and repudiate from the present article and the mystery of Election, meanwhile suggesting in a friendly manner to those who contend with these arguments that saying of the Apostle: All things are lawful for me, but not all things edify. 1. Cor. 6. v. 12.

Latin:

Tabella Synoptica ob oculos constituens illustrem ἀντίθεσιν & delineationem sive ὑποτύπωσιν doctrinæ Orthodoxorum, Calvinistarum, Huberianorum de Prædestinationis mysterio.

CUm secundum vulgatam Scholarum regulam, Contrariis juxta se positis, veritas magis elucescat: utíque inconveniens haud fuerit, ex trium diversissimarum, de æternâ Dei Prędestinatione sententiarum ἀντιθέσει, judicium tùm nostrum, tùm aliorum solidè informare:cuinam illarum veritatis & ὀρθοδοξίας palma decerni debeat. Et hoc tantò magis operæ pretium fuerit,quando insidiosius hodiè veritatis depravatores, in manifesta absurditate deprehensi, speciem consensûs cum veritate, interdum venditant Sic enim stupenda istorum vanitas clariùs elucesces. Quid, quòd hoc etiam pacto, & rectiùs, & firmiùs retundi, & convinci potest falsitas earum calumniarum, quæ tùm à Calvinianis, tùm ab Huberianis, Orthodoxis veritatis Evangelicæ assertoribus, magno hiatu intentantur. Quemadmodum enim virtus, tanquàm medium, inter duo vitiorum extrema, se habet: ita Veritas, inter duo errorum præcipitia, quorum illud in excessu, hoc in defectu, à medio enormiter declinat, ita quasi pressa hæret: ut ei ab utroq;extremo invidia utplurimùm concilietur. Quod ipsum, si in ullo alio, hoc cumprimis articulo, Veritati obtingit. Nam si Orthodoxis Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctoribus controversia sit, de Prædestinationis negotio cum Sacramentariis sive Calvinianis, qui in defectu, sive ex parte ἐλλείψεως graviter peccant: statim ex absurdo, & verè fanatico Huberianismi dogmate, invidiam veritati constare student: Rursus, si cum Hubero, & paucis, quos habet, asseclis, de eodem negotio Orthodoxis sit negocium, nihil ille frequentius in ore habet, quàm ut Calvinismi insimulatione, veritatis causam, defensionemque prægravet, & minùs sano clamore, & Orientem, & Occidente contra hanc, uti ipse calumniatur, Apostasia, in subsidium evocet. Utriusq; ergò calumniæ vanitas & falsitas, ut non tàm oculis videri, quàm manibus ipsis palpari manifestissimè queat: singularem usum Synoptica hæc sententiarum ἀντίθεσις certè præstabit.

Quibus ita constitutis, colligimus secundum Scripturas, in præsenti mysterio Electionis vocabulum, non nisi unam admittere significationem, tantùm ad filios DEI, & actu in fide ad finem usque perseverantes, determinatam. Reliquas verò duas significationes, quarum altera sit laxior, & objecti loco ipsos quoque τεταγμένους respiciat: altera verò sit laxissima, & generalissima, Objecti loco, secundum naturam Consilii & voluntatis DEI antecedentis, omnes omninò homines respiciens: tanquam ἀγραφους, & turbis dandis satis idoneas, & aliquo modo, non quidem ex toto, sed ex parte saltem, Huberi dogma stabilientes: ac tandem libris Ecclesiarum γνησίως Lutheranarum Symbolicis, minimè conformes, ex præsenti articulo, & Electionis mysterio simpliciter rejicimus, & repudiamus: illis interim, qui Rationibus istis militant, amicè suggerentes illud Apostoli: Omnia mihi licent: sed non omnia ædificant. 1. Cor. 6. v. 12.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic): Against Antithesis I

AGAINST

ANTITHESIS I.

THE ORTHODOX, or LUTHERANS, believe, teach, and confess that Election or Predestination does not pertain to all, as well the evil as the good, as well the unbelieving as the believing: but to a few, and indeed only to those believing, and persevering in faith even to the end.

THE CALVINISTS teach that Election does indeed pertain to a few, but that they are predestined to salvation and eternal life without respect to faith.

HUBER teaches that Election, properly so called, pertains to all men, as well the unbelieving as the believing: and that it was made from eternity without respect to faith.

ANTITHESIS II.

THE ORTHODOX, with Holy Scripture, establish that Election or Predestination is indeed of a few: but that it is ordered, and defined by its own certain τάξει (order).

THE CALVINISTS contend that Election is indeed also of a few: but that it is entirely ἄτακτον (disordered), and nakedly absolute.

HUBER invents a semi-absolute Election of all men.

ANTITHESIS III.

THE ORTHODOX, from the Holy Scriptures, teach that God has always from eternity willed seriously, and still wills, and will continue to will until the end of the world, that no one should perish: but rather that all should be saved: And they believe that this Universal will does indeed differ from Election itself: but that it can most rightly stand ἀναλλήλως (inconsistently/without contradiction) with the particularity of Election.

THE CALVINISTS impiously and without the Scriptures contend that there never was a time, nor will there ever be one, in which God has willed, wills, or will will, that all should be saved, or that some should not perish: since this would entirely conflict with particular Election.

HUBER concedes that will: but he denies that it is different from Election itself: and he contends that particular Election made from eternity is excluded by that same will and is καὶ δὶς ὀξὺ πασῶν ἀνάρμοστον (and twice sharply inconsistent with all things).

ANTITHESIS IV.

THE ORTHODOX believe that the whole world was loved by God, John 3:16, but was not elected: so that that general love of God extends more widely than Election.

THE CALVINISTS contend that none are loved, or are loved by God, unless they are elected: so that according to them the scope of love and election in God is the same.

HUBER trifles, that the whole world has been loved and elected by God from all eternity: so that in his opinion the breadth of divine Love and Election is the same.

ANTITHESIS V.

THE ORTHODOX profess that the Antecedent Will in GOD is as it were the foundation and principle of Election, nay, even its cause and a certain part of it.

THE CALVINISTS do not admit that Will, because they simply deny the Consequent [Will].

HUBER feigns that the Antecedent Will is absolutely the same and one thing with Election itself; and thus he also completely rejects the distinction of both Wills in God.

Latin:

ANTI-

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ I.

ORTHODOXI, sive LUTHERANI credunt, docent, ac confitentur, Electionem sive Prædestinationem non ad omnes, tam malos, quàm bonos, tam incredulos, quàm credentes: sed ad paucos, & quidem tantùm ad credentes, & in fide ad finem usq́; perseverantes, pertinere.

CALVINIANI docent, Electionem pertinere quidem ad paucos, sed sine respectu fidei ad salutem, & vitam æternam prædestinatos.

HUBERUS docet, Electionem propriè sic dictam, pertinere ad omnes homines, tàm non credentes quam credentes: eamq́; ab æterno sine fidei respectu factam esse.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ II.

ORTHODOXI cum Scripturâ Sacrâ Electionem sive Prædestinatione paucorum quidem: sed eam ordinatam, & suâ certâ τάξει definitam statuunt.

CALVINIANI, Electionem quidem etiam paucorum: sed eam prorfus ἄτακτον, ac nudè absolutam esse, contendunt.

HUBERUS Semiabsolutam omnium hominum Electionem comminiscitur.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ III.

ORTHODOXI ex Scripturis Sacris docent, Deum semper ab æterno voluisse seriò, & adhuc velle, & voliturum esse ad finem usq́; mundi, ut pereat nemo: sed potius salventur omnes: Et hanc voluntatem Universalem, ab Electione quidem ipsâ discrepare: sed cum Electionis particularitate ἀναλλήλως rectissimè stare posse, credunt.

CALVINIANI impiè & sine Scripturis contendunt, nunquam fuisse tempus, neq́; futurum unquam quo voluerit, velit, aut voliturus sit Deus, ut salventur omnes, aut ut aliqui non pereant: siquidem hoc cum particulari Electione prorfus pugnet.

HUBERUS Voluntatem istam concedit: sed eam ab Electione ipsâ diversam esse pernegat: ab eadem autem Electionem particularem ab æterno factam excludi καὶ δὶς ὀξὺ πασῶν ἀνάρμοστον esse contendit.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ IV.

ORTHODOXI credunt, totum mundum à Deo dilectum esse, Johan. 3. v. 16. non autem electum esse: ita ut dilectio illa Dei generalis Electione latiùs pateat.

CALVINIANI pugnant, non dilectos esse, aut diligi à Deo, nisi electos: ita ut secundum istos dilectionis & electionis in Deo eadem sit angustia.

HUBERUS nugatur, Dilectum atq́; Electum esse à Deo jam inde ab æterno universum mundum: ita ut ex hujus opinione eadem sit Dilectionis & Electionis divinæ latitudo.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ V.

ORTHODOXI Voluntatem Antecedentem in DEO Electionis fundamentum quasi & principium, imò causam etiam, & partem quandam esse profitentur.

CALVINIANI Voluntatem istam non admittunt, quia Consequentem simplicitèr negant.

HUBERUS Voluntatem Antecedentem cum Electione ipsâ, idem prorfus atq́; unum esse fingit; & sic discrimen Voluntatis utriusq́; in Deo prorfus etiam rejicit.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic): Antithesis VI

ANTITHESIS VI.

THE ORTHODOX place Election not merely in the Antecedent, but in the Consequent will of God.

THE CALVINISTS seek Election in a merely absolute and simple will of God, which precedes all causes.

HUBER establishes Election in a semi-absolute will of God, which has made all those elected, as many as are redeemed through Christ.

ANTITHESIS VII.

THE ORTHODOX teach that, by the benefit of the antecedent will in God, the Son was sent to the whole world for salvation: and that the same satisfied for all men: and that He has seriously called the whole world to the kingdom of grace through the preaching of the Gospel, and calls it today, and will call it until the end of the world. That by the decree of the consequent will, the same Son was sent to many for judgment.

THE CALVINISTS write repeatedly that, by an absolute and purely simple decree of the will, the Son was sent to very few for salvation: but to all the rest for judgment.

HUBER argues that Christ was sent to no one for judgment by either will: but was sent absolutely to all for salvation.

ANTITHESIS X.

THE ORTHODOX maintain that the decree of judgment pertains to the consequent will in God, which God has had from eternity, which includes the act of faith, or of unbelief, at least as something future.

THE CALVINISTS contend that the judgment or decree of salvation and reprobation was conceived in the mind of God with no respect to either repentance and faith, or impenitence and infidelity.

HUBER fights for the view that there was no eternal decree of judgment, except that which emerges only at the event of application, whether made or omitted.

ANTITHESIS VIII.

THE ORTHODOX place the reprobation of many men in the consequent will of God: since in that alone do those two unsearchable decrees finally present themselves: one of election to life: the other of judgment to condemnation: and that not from an absolute good pleasure: but on account of the infidelity and impiety of the reprobate.

THE CALVINISTS attribute the reprobation of by far the greatest part of the human race to the absolute good pleasure of God.

HUBER admits no reprobation of any man from eternity in any will of God.

ANTITHESIS XI.

The ORTHODOX affirm that the universality of the redemption accomplished through Christ, as well as of the calling which occurs in the Word, and finally of the evangelical promises, stands correctly and without any contradiction with particular election.

The CALVINISTS write that just as election is absolutely particular, so redemption, calling, and the evangelical promises are absolutely particular, and pertain only to the absolutely elect.

HUBERUS contends that the universality of redemption, calling, and the evangelical promises can in no way stand unless it also extends to the same breadth of election.

Latin:

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ VI.

ORTHODOXI Electionem non nudè in Antecedente, sed in Consequente Dei voluntate collocant.

CALVINIANI Electionem inmerè absolutâ atque simplici, omnesq́; causas antegrediente Dei voluntate quærunt.

HUBERUS, Electionem in Semiabsoluta Dei voluntate constituit, quæ Electos fecerit omnes, quotquot per Christum sunt redemti.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ VII.

ORTHODOXI docent, Ex beneficio Antecedentis in Deo voluntatis, missum esse Filium toti mundo ad salutem: eundemq́; pro omnibus hominibus satisfecisse:totumq́; mundum ad regnũ Gratiæ per Prædicationem Evangelii seriò vocasse, hodieq́; vocare, ac vocaturum ad finem usq́; mundi. Ex consequentis a: voluntatis decreto missum esse eundem Filium multis ad judicium.

CALVINIANI ex absoluto puræq́; simplicis voluntatis decreto, Filium paucis admodùm ad salutem: reliquis verò omnibus ad judicium missum esse, scriptitant.

HUBERUS neutrâ voluntate cuiquam Christum ad judicium: sed absolutè omnibus ad salutem missum esse litigat.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ X.

ORTHODOXI statunt, Decretum judicii pertinere ad Voluntatem Consequentem in DEO, quèm ab æterno DEUS habuerit, quæ actum fidei, vel incredulitatis, saltem futurum, includat.

CALVINIANI nullo vel pœnitentiæ ac fidei, vel impœnitentiæ atque infidelitatis respectu, judiciã sive decretum salutis & reprobationis in mente Dei conceptum fuisse pugnant.

HUBERUS decretum judicii æternum nullum fuisse dimicat, nisi quòd e: ventu demùm applicationis vel factæ, vel omissæ, emergat.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ IIX.

ORTHODOXI in Voluntate Dei Consequente, plurimorũ hominũ Reprobationẽ ponunt: quippe in quâ solâ demùm duo illa ανυποδηγημέρια decreta sese offerunt:Unum Electionis ad vitam: alterum Judicii ad Condemnationẽ: idq́ non ex absoluto beneplacito:sed propter infidelitatem & impietatem reproborũ.

CALVINIANI reprobationem multò maximæ generis humani partis, absoluto DEI beneplàcito tribuunt.

HUBERUS nullam cujusquam hominis reprobationem ab æterno in ulla voluntate DEI admittit.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ XI.

ORTHODOXI affirmant, cum particulari Electione rectè, & sine ullâ contradictione stare Universalitatem Redemtionis per Christum factæ, ut & Vocationis, quæ in verbo fit: & denique promissionum Evangelicarum.

CALVINIANI scribunt, Quemadmodum Electio absolutè sit particularis: ita Redemtionem, Vocationem, & Promissiones Evangelicas, absolutè esse particulares: & solos absolutè Electos attinere.

HUBERUS Redemtionis, Vocationis, Promissionum Evangelicarum Universalitatem stare nullo modo posse contendit, nisi ad eandem latitudinẽ Electionis etiam complexus se extendat.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic): Antithesis IX

ANTITHESIS IX.

The ORTHODOX assert that no one is damned except in respect of final impenitence, foreseen by GOD from eternity.

The CALVINISTS furiously affirm that the greatest part of the human race is damned, not in respect of impenitence or unbelief, but by a simple, absolute decree of reprobation that precedes all causes.

HUBERUS prattles that very many are damned because they do not embrace for themselves the election made universally by GOD.

ANTITHESIS XII.

The ORTHODOX hold the view that the elect, although they are not damned, could nevertheless have been damned; likewise, that the reprobate, although they are not saved, could nevertheless have been saved.

The CALVINISTS openly profess that neither could the elect ever be damned in any way, nor could the reprobate ever be saved; so that there is an immutable necessity of predestinatory fate on both sides.

HUBERUS asserts that it is not only possible for very many of the elect to become damned, but that they actually do become so in the very act:

ANTITHESIS XIII.

THE ORTHODOX teach from the word of GOD that Election does not fail, that is, is not deceived or rendered void, by reason of infallible foreknowledge.

THE CALVINISTS expressly write that Election does not fail because it depends upon the immutable necessity of an absolute divine decree.

HUBERUS asserts that Election can fail, that is, is variable by the contrariety of the event.

ANTITHESIS XIV.

THE ORTHODOX include faith in Christ in the decree of Election: inasmuch as in the mind of God electing, regard was had to faith, although it was to be in the future only in time, on account of eternity.

THE CALVINISTS simply sequester faith in Christ from the eternal decree of Election, and subordinate it only to the Execution of Predestination.

HUBERUS dreams that faith in Christ, being entirely excluded from eternal Election, is required only for the event of application.

ANTITHESIS XV.

THE ORTHODOX admit Christ the Mediator, both as author and as finisher of salvation, into the counsel of eternal Predestination.

THE CALVINISTS simply exclude Christ, as much as author as finisher of salvation, from the decree of Predestination.

HUBERUS admits Christ into the decree of Predestination as the author of salvation, by reason of acquired righteousness: but not as the finisher, by reason of righteousness imputed through faith.

ANTITHESIS XVI.

THE ORTHODOX affirm that all baptized infants are regenerated, but only on the condition of perseverance in the faith, and that they are the Elect.

THE CALVINISTS write with a horrendous pen that infants who are not inscribed in the fatal tablets of absolute Election, even if they are baptized a thousand times, are nevertheless never regenerated; and that nothing certain can be pronounced concerning the salvation of infants, even those who are baptized.

HUBERUS declares that all infants who are baptized and regenerated, even if they subsequently fall away from the grace of God in the highest degree and are damned, are nevertheless the Elect.

Latin:

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ IX.

ORTHODOXI asserunt, Neminem damnari nisi respectu finalis impœnitentiæ, à DEO ab æterno prævisæ.

CALVINIANI furenter affirmant, damnari maximam generis humani partem, non respectu impœnitentiæ, sive incredulitatis:sed simplici, absoluto, omnesq́; causas antegrediente Reprobationis decreto.

HUBERUS garrit, damnari plùrimos, quia Electionem Universaliter à DEO factam, sibi non amplicent.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ XII.

ORTHODOXI sentiunt; Electos, licet non damnentur, damnari tamen potuisse: Reprobos itidem, licet non salventur, salvari tamen potuisse.

CALVINIANI apertè profitentur, neq́; Electos ullo modo damnari: neq́; reprobos salvari unquam potuisse; ita ut immutabilis utring; Fati Prædestinatorii sit necessitas.

HUBERUS asserit, ex Electis non tantùm fieri posse: sed & ipso actu fieri damnatos quamplurimos:

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ XIII.

ORTHODOXI ex verbo DEI docent, Electionem non excidere, h.e. non falli, aut evacuari, ratione infallibilis præscientiæ.

CALVINIANI disertè scribunt, Electionem ideò non excidere, quia ex immutabili necessitate absoluti decreti divini dependeat.

HUBERUS asserit, Electionem posse excidere, hoc est, contrarietate eventus esse variabilem.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ XIV.

ORTHODOXI Fidem in Christu, Electionis decreto includunt: siquidem in mente Dei eligentis, ad fidem, licèt in tempore demùm futuram, ob æterna respectus fuit habitus.

CALVINIANI Fidem in Christum ab Electionis decreto æterno simpliciter sequestratam, Executioni Prædestinationis duntaxat, substernunt.

HUBERUS Fidem in Christum, ab Electione æternâ omninò seclusam, tantùm ad applicationis eventum requiri somniat.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ XV.

ORTHODOXI Christum Mediatorem, tùm ut autorem, tùm consummatorem salutis, in consilium Prædestinationis æternæ admittunt.

CALVINIANI Christum, tàm quà autorem, quàm quà consumatorem salutis, ex Prædestinationis decreto simpliciter excludunt.

HUBERUS Christum, ut autorem quidem salutis, ratione acquisitæ justitiæ: non autem ut consummatorem, ratione imputatæ per fidem justitiæ, in Prædestinationis decretum admittit.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ XVI.

ORTHODOXI infantes omnes baptizatos regenerari, sed non nisi sub conditione perseverantiæ in fide, Electos esse affirmat.

CALVINIANI infantes qui fatalibus absolutæ Electionis tabulis non sunt adscripti, etiamsi millies baptisentur, nunquam tamen regenerari: neq, de salute infantium, etiam baptisatorum, quicquam certi pronunciari posse, horrendo calamo scriptitant.

HUBERUS infantes omnes baptisatos, regeneratosq́, si postmodum gratiâ Dei maximè excidant, & damnentur, Electos tamen esse pronunciat.


### Part II. Πολεμικη (Polemic): IV. Error: Which is that of the recent Photinians

IV. Error: Which is that of the recent Photinians.

Although the recent Photinians seem in this Article to declare war primarily against the dogma of the Calvinists, and to be more favorable to our doctrine, as is especially evident from chapter 35 of the German Institutions of Christoph Ostorodt of Goslar: yet, when the reasons and arguments with which they are accustomed to fight against that absolute dogma of Calvinistic Predestination are weighed a little more accurately, it becomes clearer than the midday sun that they also set up an obelisk against our purer doctrine, and indeed, as far as in them lies, fundamentally undermine and overturn the entire mystery of Predestination or Election. This is demonstrated by those most evident hypotheses by which they attempt to prove that God from eternity made no decree at all concerning the saving or damning of certain men. Those hypotheses are indeed partly taken from other Articles of the Christian Religion, and partly proper to this place and Article.

Of the FORMER kind are: that 1. they deny Original sin in all respects. 2. They contend that the image of God in man was not lost through the fall. 3. That the freedom of the Will remained even in Spiritual matters after the fall. 4. That man can satisfy the law of God. 5. That God, because of the sin of our first parents, was not so angry with the human race that it could not be appeased except through satisfaction. 6. Indeed, that neither did Christ satisfy the divine anger or justice for the human race, nor did He fulfill the law for us. 7. But that we are justified by that faith which consists of obedience toward the precepts of the Decalogue, as God promulgated it, and as Christ also rendered it more complete. 8. That Baptism is not a medium or instrument of regeneration and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, but is an indifferent matter, and can be fully abrogated without any loss of salvation. 9. That the Lord's Supper is not a medium through which we can spiritually coalesce with Christ and confirm our faith, but only a certain external work pertaining to the Ceremonial law.

Therefore, with these and other such horrible Paradoxes standing, it should seem strange to no one that the entire business of Predestination is denied by these heretics, since it cannot stand with them in any part or in any way. Nor is it our intention in this place to bring each of those Paradoxes back to the anvil of refutation; that is more conveniently accomplished in their own distinct and proper places. But this must be our task in this place, that we examine in a few words upon what hypotheses, properly pertaining to the present article, these heretics rely.

Therefore, the hypotheses of the LATTER kind are these.

I. No reason can be given, nor any place of Scripture, from which it can be openly gathered that God foresees and foreknows the future actions of men, especially evil ones: Nor (contends Ostorodt) does anything depart from divine omniscience thereby; no more than

nothing at all is detracted from divine Omnipotence, even if He cannot render a done deed undone. Indeed, it is enough for asserting divine Omniscience if it is said that God knows all past good and evil things: that He knows all present things, good and evil, in the hearts of men: and finally that He knows future things too, but only those which He Himself has decreed to do, whether they be good or the evil of punishment. To palliate this impiety, they put forward that passage in Gen. 6:6 and 7: It repented God that He had made man on the earth: and being touched with sorrow of heart, He said, I will destroy man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth: for it repenteth me that I have made him. But it cannot be said that God repents of that which He foreknew would be such. Thus Gen. 22:12, concerning Abraham about to sacrifice his son Isaac, God says: NOW I know that thou fearest the LORD: Therefore He did not foreknow it. Thus Num. 14:23, concerning the Israelites in the desert, God says: They shall not see the land, for which I SWORE to their Fathers: nor shall any of those who have blasphemed me behold it. Now, if God had foreknown the crimes of the Israelites, He certainly would not have sworn to their Fathers that He wished to lead them into the land of blessing. Faustus Socinus the Italian, chapters 8, 9, 10, 11 of his Theological Lectures.

II. It is false, they write, that God from eternity made a decree concerning all and individual men, and determined which ones ought to be saved, and which ones indeed ought to be damned. Ostorodus brings forward two reasons chiefly for this hypothesis or assertion, c. 35. Instit. Germ. p. 287. Schmaltz. in Catech. p. 296.

THE PRIOR reason is that from the doctrine of Predestination it necessarily follows that all things whatsoever that pertain to the duties of piety and the worship of GOD are done not freely, but necessarily: Which being posited, every endeavor, and every study and desire for piety is taken away, since in those things which are done necessarily, and cannot be otherwise, all work and all labor is useless and vain: Wherever, moreover, all labor and all study of piety ceases, there necessarily all religion and all worship of God is overturned. pag. 288.

THE LATTER reason is that, the decree of Predestination and Reprobation standing, it must necessarily follow that God is to be accused of 1. Injustice, 2. Hypocrisy and fraud, 3. Ignorance and imprudence, 4. Malice, which thing is horrible and blasphemous even to think of.

Of injustice indeed, because nothing more iniquitous could be devised than that someone should be punished for the reason that he did not do, so as to perform, that which he was nevertheless in no way able to perform and do, because the Decree, as of Election, so also of Reprobation, is immutable, pag. 288. & 289. Schmal. Catech. c. 10. p. 292. Socinus in praelectionibus c. 6.

Of hypocrisy and fraud, because God, although He has immutably decreed that the greatest part of those to whom the Word of GOD is announced should perish, nevertheless offers them remission of sins and eternal life under the condition of repentance: the grace to perform which, however, He withdraws from them. p. 289. Schmal. p. 292. Socinus ibid.

Of ignorance and imprudence, because God through the preaching of the Gospel attempts to lead all those who hear it to eternal life: but because the eternal and immutable decree of Reprobation stands in the way of this, it cannot effect it, nor bring it into act, p. 290. Schmaltz. p. 293. Socinus ibid.

Finally, the malice, because it follows necessarily from the doctrine of Predestination that God is the author of sin: For since He condemns no one except a sinner, and on account of sin: therefore He decreed not only who should be condemned, but also who should sin, p. 290. & Schmaltz. p. 293. Socinus ibid.

III. The hypothesis of the Photinians is: The word Election, when there is talk of our salvation, has a twofold meaning: general and special. For sometimes it is said of all who consent to the preaching of the Gospel that they are Elect of God: But sometimes the title of Election is attributed only to those who not only admit the preaching of the Gospel, but also shape their lives according to it. The former meaning of Election is the same as that of the word calling, according to that 1 Cor. 1. v. 26. & 27. See your calling, brethren, not many are wise according to the flesh, not many are mighty, not many are noble who are called: But God has chosen the foolish things of this world. Where to call and to choose are the same. The latter meaning is expressed in Matt. 22, 14. Many are called, few are chosen. Both meanings, however, are confirmed by that of Peter, 2. c. 1. Strive to make your calling and election sure through good works. Schmaltz cap. 10. of the Catechism, page 296.

IV. Election to salvation includes the foresight of good works. Therefore, those are the elect who love God, which they are able to perform by their own powers. Schmaltz. ibid. pages 297 & 298.

V. The Apostolic passage Rom. 8. v. 28. & seqq. We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to his purpose: For whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, that He might be the firstborn among many brothers. And whom He predestined, these He also called: whom He called, these He also justified: whom He justified, these He also glorified, etc. This truly noble and classic Apostolic passage, expressly discussing the matter of Predestination, Schmaltz explains thus in cap. 10 of the Catechism, page 298: The simple understanding of this place is that the Apostle affirms that for those people who love God and have believed in the Gospel of Christ, all manner of tribulation helps for the best: Which the Apostle demonstrates in such a way that he determines them in the things which happened to the Lord Christ himself. Just as tribulation did not hinder the Lord Christ from immortality, so it can do no harm to his believers. When the Apostle has demonstrated this, he describes several stages through which people attain immortality, in that he proves that God, through the preaching of the Gospel, has gathered those whom He has determined should be like the Lord Christ both in tribulation and in glory into the community of His believers: and thereafter has freed them from all sins, and accounted them as righteous: and finally has provided for them through a perfect way for immortality and for eternal life. And page 304, that St. Luke says, Acts 13. v. 48: As many as were ordained to eternal life believed. This can be understood of the people themselves, that they were ordained, that is, prepared, to accept the teaching of the Lord Christ, and thus to attain eternal life.

The sum returns to this, that he contends that in the Scriptures such a Predestination, or Election of God to salvation, is described, which is to be defined by the holiness and perfection of those who, by the powers of free will, have made themselves worthy and fit, both for the preaching of the Gospel and for the attainment of eternal life itself.

Although the vanity and impiety of each of these hypotheses is so stupendous that any pious person can detect and refute it, nothing prevents us from submitting a brief critique of each.

The FIRST hypothesis labors from the beginning with manifest falsehood. For Scripture explicitly asserts that God knows not only the past, the present, and those future things alone which He Himself has at some time decreed to work in men, whether good or evil of punishment: but also the individual and universal thoughts, counsels, actions, and events of all things of men, both evil and good: as 2 Kings 19. v. 27. God Himself says thus concerning the impiety of the king of the Assyrians: I have foreknown your dwelling place, and your going out, and your way, and your fury against me: Which same thing is repeated in Isaiah 37. 27. Exod. 3. 19. But I know that the King of Egypt will not let you go, so that you may go, unless by a mighty hand. Eccles. 23. v. 28. The eyes of the Lord are much brighter than the sun, looking round upon all the ways of men, and the depth of the abyss, and looking into the hearts of men into hidden parts. For to the Lord God, before they were created, all things are known: thus also after they are perfected he looks upon all things. Heb. 4. 13. There is no creature invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes.

Thence God foreknew and foresaw from eternity the fall of our first parents, and the death of his Son: and he foreknew it not under a condition, or confusedly, if indeed men should sin, but according to a distinct knowledge he foreknew and foresaw both the fall of the human race, and its redemption, nay, he took care that it be so graphically described and predicted some centuries before, Ps. 22 and Isaiah 53, that it might seem to be a history already enacted, rather than a matter described as yet to come.

The reasons by which they strive to confirm this first hypothesis are not worth a farthing. For God is said to repent, not because he was ignorant of the future malice of men: or because any change of counsel can befall him: but ανθρωποπαθω̃ς, to express his supreme indignation against the malice and sins of men. Whence Lyra rightly notes:

That repentance and similar affections are in GOD, neither in reality nor by way of likeness: but are said of GOD by way of likeness to effects: namely, that effects are produced by GOD similar to the effects produced by repentance. Just as indeed the punishment of the Universal Flood, by our reasoning, seems to argue that it repented GOD that He had created man. Thus, that which GOD says in Genesis 22:12 must be understood κατ' ἄνθρωποπάθειαν (according to human feeling): NOW I know that you fear the Lord. Not that GOD did not know that before: but that now the piety of Abraham has been truly manifested.

Finally, regarding the passage in Numbers 14:23, GOD truly performed what He swore to the Fathers. For in Genesis 12:7 the promise sounds thus: To your seed I will give this land. Therefore, what was not fulfilled in the Israelites who were struck down in the desert, was nevertheless fulfilled in reality in their posterity and in the Seed of Abraham.

Furthermore, that oath did not apply absolutely to each and every one of Abraham's descendants, as if they were to possess that land of blessing, however and whatever they might conduct themselves toward the commandments: but it was limited under the condition of obedience and piety: Genesis 17:8 and 9: I will give to you and to your seed the land of your pilgrimage, and all the land of Canaan for an eternal possession, and I will be their GOD: But you shall keep my covenant, and your seed after you, in their generations. Which very condition is also read in Leviticus 20:24 and 25, and Deuteronomy 9:5 and 6.

The SECOND Hypothesis of the Photinians does not attack our doctrine, but the doctrine of the Calvinists concerning Election. For regarding the former argument, it militates quite strongly against a decree of Election and Reprobation that is absolute and precedes all causes. For with that standing, every effort and every pursuit of piety is removed. But now, when Election is established as ordered and determined to certain means, then indeed, even by this arrangement, the pursuit of piety and devotion to divine worship is wonderfully kindled and fostered. Since, in the order of Election, this very pursuit of piety is subordinated by reason of Faith: not indeed as a cause, or as a medium apprehending, but as an effect of justifying faith. The latter argument is of the same stamp. For with our doctrine standing, GOD is clearly freed from every suspicion of injustice, hypocrisy, ignorance, and malice.

For He is not unjust, because what He wills to be done by man, that very thing He provides so that man can perform it, with certain and legitimate means shown: that is, He Himself works in us both to will and to perform. Philippians 2:13.

For this very reason GOD is not a Hypocrite, because those who perish do not perish from an immutable absolute decree: but He seriously offered the means of salvation to them, just as much as to the elect, and wished to gather them as a hen gathers her chicks: but they themselves did not wish it.

Thirdly, GOD cannot be argued to have any ignorance or imprudence. For GOD did not wish the decree of either Election or Reprobation to be confused: but so distinguished that each might consist and be completed in its own certain order. Nor should such immutability be attributed to these decrees, which is absolute and simply devoid of all mutability, so that necessarily, and indeed by absolute necessity, some are saved and others perish. Such immutability the Calvinists imagine. Concerning which matter we have argued expressly above in the first part. Finally, how could GOD be accused of any malice, who does not will the death of the one who dies, but that he should be converted and live, and therefore much less does He will the cause of condemnation, namely sin: But He hates, detests, and punishes it. Moreover, the error of this second hypothesis arises solely from the fact that the Photinians dream that, given and granted a certain decree of Election and Reprobation, and therefore also a certain and infallible number of both the Elect and the Reprobate, there follows a fatal and simply immutable damnation for the latter and salvation for the former. In which part they are most shamefully mistaken and deceived. For the number of the Elect is indeed certain and immutable: but not in respect of an absolute decree. The THIRD hypothesis of the Photinians reveals the stupendous ignorance of these men in sacred matters. For it is so far from the case that a twofold meaning of the word Election is brought forward in the Scriptures, that that very Apostolic passage 1 Corinthians 1:26 and 27, and that other one, which Socinus cites in chapter 13 of his Prelections from 1 Thessalonians 1:4. They define only one Election: namely, of those among whom the Gospel was, not only by word: but by power and the Holy Spirit: as the Apostle expressly has it, in the cited chapter 1 of the first to the Thessalonians, verse 5. Therefore, when they conclude from these passages, as from 2 Peter 1, that Calling and Election are of the same meaning and breadth: that is only true of that singular species of calling which the Apostle calls κλῆσιν κατ' πρόθεσιν (calling according to purpose), which indeed is always joined with Election and stands in reciprocal relation with it. Concerning which special calling the cited passages of Scripture from the Photinians also deal. But it is false if it is taken concerning general calling: since not even one passage of Scripture can be given where general calling is named Election, or those generally called are said to be Elect: unless it is done synecdochically by reason of the nobler part. Therefore, a twofold meaning of calling, but not of Election, can be proven and obtained from the Scriptures. The FOURTH and FIFTH Hypotheses are simply false, bringing forward such a predestination, namely, that which is made in respect of holiness and perfection, or of our works, or as they speak, in respect of obedience to the commandments of GOD performed by us. In which part they are so destitute of all support from the Scriptures that they cannot bring forward even one testimony by which they might confirm their opinion, even probably in appearance. We [have argued] above in part 1, Special Controversy 3, in [the section on] Repentance. tifics and Pelagians, we thoroughly undermine and overturn this error, so that there is no need for a more lengthy refutation. May GOD, the author of all truth, at long last confound these stubborn heretics: but may He preserve us in the truth: whose magnificent name be blessed for infinite ages. AMEN.

Latin:

IV. Error : Qui est recentiorum Photinianorum.

QUanquàm recentiores Photiniani hoc in Articulo Calvinianorum potissimùm dogmati bellum indicere : nostræ verò doctrinæ benigniores esse videntur : uti cumprimis patet ex c. 35. Institutionum Germanicarum Christophori Ostorodi Goslariensis: tamen paulò accuratiùs expensis rationibus & argumentis, quibus contra absolutum illud Prędestinationis Calvinisticæ dogma pugnare solent : Sole meridiano clàriùs patescit, ipsos puriori quoque nostræ doctrinæ obeliscum figere, imò quantum in ipsis universum Prædestinationis sive Electionis mysterium funditus subruere & evertere. Demonstrat hoc evidentissimæ illæ hypotheses, quibus evincere conantur, Deum ab æterno nullum prorsus fecisse decretum, de hominibus quibusdam vel salvandis, vel damnandis. Sunt verò hypotheses illæ partim ex aliis Religionis Christianæ Articulis petitæ : partim verò hujus loci & Articuli propriæ.

PRIORIS Generis sunt: quòd 1. negant per omnia peccatum Originale. 2. Contendunt, imaginem Dei in homine per lapsum non fuisse amissam. 3. Libertatem Voluntatis etiam in Spiritualibus post lapsum mansisse reliquam. 4. Hominem posse legi Dei satisfacere. 5. Deum propter peccatũ primorum parentum, non ita fuisse iratum generi humano, ut non nisi per satisfactionem placari potuerit. 6. Imò neq; Christum pro genere humano, iræ aut justitiæ divinæ satisfecisse : neq; legem pro nobis implevisse. 7. Sed justificari nos ea fide, quæ constet obædientiâ erga præcepta Decalogi, prout eum promulgavit Deus, prout etiam Christus eum completiorem reddidit. 8. Baptismum non esse medium sive organon regenerationis & sanctificationis Spiritus Sancti: sed rem esse adiaphoram, & plenè sine ullâ salutis iacturâ abrogari posse. 9. Cœnam Domini non esse medium, per quod cum Christo Spiritualiter coalescere, & fidem nostram confirmare poßimus: sed externum tantùm opus quoddam, ad legem Ceremonialem pertinens.

His ergô & id genus aliis horrendis stantibus Paradoxis, mirum nemini videri debet, negari ab istis hæreticis universum Prædestinationis negotium : quippè quod cum illis nullâ ex parte, nulloq; modo stare potest. Neque verò nostri est instituti, hoc loco singula illa Paradoxa sub refutationis incudem revocare: id quod suis distinctis & propriis locis convenientiùs peragitur. Illud autem hoc loco pensi habendum, ut quibus hypothesibus ad præsentem articulum propiè pertinentibq, hæretici isti nitantur, paucis dispiciamus.

POSTERIORIS ergo generis hypotheses sunt hæ.

I. Nulla dari potest ratio, nullúsque Scripturæ locus, ex quo apertè colligi possit, Deum futuras hominum actiones, præsertim malas prævidere & præscire: Neq; inde (contendit Ostorodus) quicquam decedere omniscientiæ divinæ: haud magis, atq; Omnipo-

tentia divinæ nihil quicquam derogatur, licet factum non possit reddere infectum. Quin imò ad asserendam Omniscientiam divinam satis esse, si dicatur Deus scire omnia præterita bona & mala: scire præsentia omnia, bona & mala; in cordibus hominum : scire deniq; futura etiam, sed ea tantùm, quæ ipse facere decreverit sive bona, sive mala pœnæ. Cui impietati palliandę obtendunt illud Gen. 6, 6. & 7. Pœnituit Deum, quòd fecisset hominem in terra: & tactus dolore cordis, Delebo, inquit, hominem, quem creavi, à facie terræ: pœnitet enim me, fecisse eum. non potest autem dici Deus pœnitere de eo, quod præscivit tale futurum. Sic Gen. 22, 12. de Abrahamo immolaturo filium Isaac, dicit Deus NVNC cognovi, quod timeas DOMINUM: Ergo non præscivit. Sic Num. 14, 23. de Israelitis in diserto dicit Deus: Non videbunt terram, pro quâ JVRAVI Patribus eorum: nec quisquam ex illis, qui blasphemarunt me, intuebitur eam. Jam verò si præscivisset Deus scelera Israelitarum, utiq; non jurasset Patribus ipsorum, quòd velit eos inducere in terram benedictionis. Faustus Socinus Italus, cap. 8. 9. 10. 11. prælectionum Theologicarum.

II. Falsum est, scribunt, Deum ab æterno fecisse decretum de omnibus & singulis hominibus, & constituisse, quinam salvari, qui verò damnari debeant. Hypotheseos sive assertionis hujus rationes profert Ostorodus duas potissimùm, c. 35. Instit. Germ. p. 287. Schmaltz. in Catech. p. 296.

PRIOR Ratio est, quòd ex doctrinâ de Prædestinatione necessariò sequatur, omnia quæcunq; ad pietatis officia, & cultum DEI faciunt, non liberè, sed necessariò fieri: Quo posito, omnis conatus, omneque studium ac desiderium pietatis tollatur, quoniam in iis, quæ necessariò fiunt, nec aliter se habere possunt, omnis opera, omnisq; labor inutilis sit ac frustraneus: Ubicúq; a. omnis labor, omneque studiu pietatis cessat, ibi necessariò omnis religio, omnisq; cultus Dei evertitur. pag. 288.

POSTERIOR ratio est, quòd stante Prædestinationis & Reprobationis decreto, sequi necessum sit, Deum 1. Injustitiæ, 2. Hypocriseos ac fraudis, 3. Inscitiæ ac imprudentiæ, 4. Malitiæ insimulandum esse, id quod vel cogitatu horrendum & blasphemum sit.

Injustitiæ quidem ideò, quia nihil iniquius excogitari possit, quàm aliquem ideò puniri, quòd non fecerit, ut præstiterit id, quod tamen præstare ac facere minimè potuerit, proptereà quòd Decretum, uti Electionis, sic & Reprobationis sit immutabile, pag. 288. & 289. Schmal. Catech. c. 10. p. 292. Socinus in prælectionibus c. 6.

Hypocriseos ac fraudis ideò, quia Deus, licèt immutabiliter decreverit, ut maxima pars eorum, quibus Verbum DEI annunciatur, pereat, nihilominùs tamen illis remissionem peccatorum, & vitam æternam sub condicione pœnitentiæ offerat: cujus tamen agendæ gratiam illis subtrahat. p. 289. Schmal. p. 292. Socinus ibid.

Inscitiæ ac imprudentiæ ideò, quia Deus per Evangelii prædicationem omnes, qui illud audiunt ad vitam æternam perducere conetur: verùm id obstante æterno ac immutabili Reprobationis decreto, efficere, inq; actum deducere non possit, p. 290. Schmaltz. pag. 293. Socinus ibid.

Malitia denique, quòd ex Prædestinationis doctrina necessariò sequatur, Deum peccati autorem esse: Cùm enim ille neminem, nisi peccatorem, & ob peccatum condemnet: ideo ipsum, non tantùm, quinàm condemnari, sed etiam, quinàm peccare debeant, decrevisse p. 290. & Schmaltz. p. 293. Socinus ibid.

III. Hypothesis Photinianorum est: Vocabulum Electionis, quando de salute nostra sermo est, geminam habet significationem: generalem & specialem. Nam interdum de omnib9, qui in Evangelii prædicationem consentiunt, dicitur, quòd à Deo Electi sint: Interdum autem illis tantùm Electionis titulus tribuitur, qui non modò prædicationem Evangelii admittunt, sed etiam secundum eam vitam suam informant. Prior significatio Electionis eadem est, quæ vocabuli vocationis, secundum illud 1. Cor. 1. v. 26. & 27. Videte fratres vocationem vestram, non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles sunt vocati: Verùm quæ stulta sunt mundi hujus, elegit DEUS. Ubi vocare & eligere idem sunt. Posterior significatio exprimitur Matth. 22, 14. Multi vocati, pauci electi. Utraq; autem significatio confirmatur ex illo Petri, 2. c. 1. Studete vocationem & electionem vestram firmam facere per bona opera. Schmaltz cap. 10. Catechismi pag. 296.

IV. Electio ad salutem includit prævisionem bonorum operum. Electi ergo sunt, qui Deum diligunt, id quod ex viribus suis præstare possunt. Schmaltz. ibid. pag. 297. & 298.

V. Locum Apostolicum Rom. 8. v. 28. & seqq. Scimus, quòd diligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum, iis, qui juxta propositum vocati sunt: Quos enim præscivit, eos etiam prædestinavit, ut conformes essent imagini filii sui, ut ipse esset primogenitus inter multos fratres. Quos autem prædestinavit, hos etiam vocavit: Quos vocavit, hos & justificavit: quos justificavit, hos & glorificavit &c. hunc verè nobilem & classicum locum Apostolicum, de Prædestinationis negotio ex professo disserentem, Schmalrz. cap. 10. Catechismi pag. 298. sic explicat, Dieses Orts schlechter Verstandt ist der / daß der Apostel affirmirt, daß denen Menschen / die Gott lieben / vnnd dem Evangelio Christi gegleubet haben / allerley Trübsal zum besten helffen: Welches der Apostel auff solche weise darthut / daß sie in den dingen bestimmet/welche dem HErrn Christo selbst begegnet sind. Wie nun die Trübsal dem HERRN Christo zur Vnsterbligkeit nichts gehindert / also können sie auch seinen gleubigen nichts nicht schaden. Da solches der Apostel dargethan / beschreibet er etliche Stuffen /durch welche die Menschen die Vnsterbligkeit erlangen / in dem er beweiset / daß Gott die / welche er darzu bestimmet/ daß sie beydes in Trübsal vnd in der Herrligkeit dem HERREN Christo sollen gleich seyn/ durch die verkündigung des E-vangelij/ zur Gemeine seiner Gleubigen ver-samlet: vnd darnach von allen Sünden be-freyet/ vnd für gerecht geachtet: vnd endlich durch eine volkommene weise zur Vnsterb-ligkeit / vnd zum ewigen Leben versehen hat. Et pag. 304. das S. Lucas sagt / Actor. 13. v. 48: Es wurden gleubig/ wie viel jhr zum e-wigen Leben verordnet waren / Solches kan von den Menschen selbst verstanden werden/ daß sie verordnet / das ist / geschickt gewesen/ die Lehr des HErrn Christi anzunemen/ vnd also das ewige Leben zuerlangen.

Summa huc redit, quòd contendit, in Scri-pturis talem describi Prædestinationem, sive Electio nem Dei ad salutem, quæ definienda sit, per san-ctitatem & perfectionem eorum, qui ex viribus liberi arbitrii dignos & idoneos sese fecerunt, tùm prædicationis Evangelicæ, tùm ipsius vi-tæ æternæ consequendæ.
