Quanquàm verò singularum istarum hy-pothesewn ea est stupenda, tùm vanitas, tùm impietas, ut pius quisq́; eam deprehendere & refutare possit, nihil tamen obstat, quô minus de singulis brevem subjiciamus έπίκρισιν.

PRIMA hypothesis initiò manifestâ falsitate laborat. Scriptura enim disertè asserit, Deum scire non tantùm præterita, præsentia, & ea dunta xat futura, quæ ipsemet aliquando operari decreve-rit in hominibus sive bona, sive mala pœnæ: sed etiā singula & universa hominum cogitata, consilia, a-ctiones, eventus rerum omnium tàm malarum,quàm bonarum: ut 2. Reg. 19. v. 27. de impietate regis Assyriorum sic Deus ipse. Habitaculum tuum & egressum tuum, & viam tuam, & furorem tuum contra me ego præscivi: Quod ipsum repetitur Esai. 37. 27. Exod. 3. 19. Sed ego scio, quòd non dimit-tet vos Pharao Rex Ægypti, ut eatis, nisi per manum validam. Eccles. 23. v. 28. Oculi Domini multò plus lucidiores sunt super Solem, circumspicientes omnes vias hominum, & profundum abyssi, & homi-num corda intuentes in absconditas partes. Domino enim Deo, antequam crearentur, omnia sunt cogni-ta: sic & post perfectum respicit omnia. Hebr. 4. 13. Non est ulla creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus, o-mnia autem nuda & aperta sunt oculis ejus.

Deindè præscivit & prævidit Deus ab æter-no lapsum primorum parentum, & mortem Filii sui: eamq́; præscivit non sub conditione, vel confusè, si nimirùm peccarent homines, sed secundum discretam notitiam utrumque & lapsum generis humani, & redemtionem ejus præscivit ac prævidit, imò seculis aliquot antè ita graphicè describi & prædici curavit, Psal. 22. & Esaiæ 53. ut historia magis jam gesta, quàm res futura demum descripta esse, videri possit.

Rationes, quibus primam hanc hypothesin confirmare student, non unius sunt teruntii. Nam pœnitere dicitur DEUS, non quòd i-gnorârit futuram hominum malitiam: vel quòd ulla consilii mutatio in ipsum cadat: sed ανθρωποπαθω̃ς, ad exprimendam summā ipsius indignationem contra malitiam & pec-cata hominum. Undè rectè Lyra annotat:

Pœnitentiam, & similes affectus esse in DEO, neque secundum rem, neque secundum similitudinem : sed dici de DEO secundum similitudinem effectuum: scilicet, quòd producantur à DEO effectus, similes effectibus à pœnitentiâ productis. Quemadmodum sanè Diluvij Universalis pœna, ratione nostri videtur arguere, quòd DEUM pœnituerit creasse hominem. Sic κατ' ἄνθρωποπάθειαν accipiendum est & illud, quòd DEUS dicit Genes. 22. 12. NUNC cognovi, quòd timeas Dominum. Non quòd DEUS antea illud nesciverit: sed quòd jam verè pietas Abrahami manifestata sit.

Tandem quoad locum Num. 14. 23. verè præstitit DEUS, quod juravit Patribus. Nam Genes. 12. 7. sic sonat promissio: Semini tuo dabo terram hanc. Quod ergo non in Israë转变 in deserto prostratis impletú fuit, reipsa tamen impletum est in illorum posteritate, & Semine Abrahæ.

Deindè Juramentum illud non absolutè se habebat ad singulos & universos Abrahæ posteros, quasi terram illam benedictionis possessuri sint, quomodocunque etiam, & qualescunque erga mandata sese gerant: sed erat limitatum sub conditione obedientiæ, & pietatis: Genes. 17 8 & 9 Dabo tibi, & semini tuo terram peregrinationis tuæ, omnéǵ; terram Chanaan in possessionem æternam, eroǵ; DEUS eorum: Sed tu custodies pactum meum, & semen tuum post te, in generationibus suis. Quæ ipsa conditio legitur etiam Levitici 20. 24. & 25. Deut. 9. 5. & 6.

ALTERA Hypothesis Photinianorum non nostram, sed Calvinianorum doctrinam de Electione impugnat. Nam quoâd priorem rationem, militat illa satis fortiter, contra absolutum, omnesque causas antegrediens, tùm Electionis, tùm Reprobationis decretum. Eo enim stante, omnis conatus, omneǵ; studiú pietatis tollitur. Jam verò quando Electio statuitur ordinata, & ad certa media determinata, utique etiam vel hoc pacto pietatis studium, & cultus divini devotio mirificè accenditur & fovetur. Siquidem Electionis τάξει hoc ipsum pietatis studium, ratione Fidei est subordinatum: non quidem ut causa, vel ut medium apprehendens: sed ut effectum fidei justificantis. Ejusdem farinæ est & posterior ratio. Nam nostra stante doctrina, DEUS ab omni injustitiæ, hypocrisews, inscitiæ, malitiæ suspicione planè liberatur.

Injustus enim non est, quia quod ab homine vult fieri, illud ipsum ut homo præstare possit, certis ac legitimis monstratis mediis, procurat: hoc est, operatur ipse in nobis & velle, & perficere. Phillip. 2. 13.

Quam ipsam ob causam Hypocrita DEUS non est, quia non ex immutabili absoluto decreto pereunt, qui pereunt: sed & his, æquè ac electis media salutis seriò obtulit, & ceu gallina pullos suos congregare evos voluit: sed ipsimet noluerunt.

Tertiò Inscitiæ atq; imprudentiæ nullilius potest DEUS argui. Neque enim vel Electionis, vel Reprobationis decretum confusum DEUS esse voluit: sed ita discretum, ut utrumque suo certo constaret, & absolveretur ordine. Neque talis immutabilitas decretis istis affingi debet, quæ absoluta sit, & simpliciter omnis mutabilitatis expers, ut necessariò, & necessitate quidem absolutâ alij salventur, alii pereant. Qualem immutabilitatem Calviniani fingunt. Quâ de re suprà parte primâ ex professo disputavimus. Tandem quî ullius malitiæ insimulari possit DEUS, qui non vult mortem morientis, sed ut convertatur & vivat ac proindè multò minus vult causam condemnationis, nempè peccatum: Sed illud odit, detestatur, punit. Cæterùm error secundæ hujus hypothesews, ex eo unicè emergit, quòd somniant Photiniani, dato & concesso certo Electionis & Reprobationis decreto, ac proindè certo etiam ac infallibili tùm Electorum, tùm Reproborum numero, sequi fatalem, & simpliciter immutabilem tùm istorum damnationem, tùm illorum salutem. Quâ in parte turpissimè fallunt & falluntur. Nam Electorum numerus est quidem certus & immutabilis: sed non respectu absoluti decreti. TERTIA Photinianorum hypothesis stupendam hominum istorum inscitiam in sacris prodit. Tantum enim abest, ut gemina significatio vocabuli Electionis in Scripturis afferatur, ut ille ipse locus Apostolicus 1. Cor. 1, 26. & 27, & ille alter, quem citat Socinus cap. 13. prælectionum ex 1. Thess. 1. 4. Unam tantùm Electionem definiant: eorum nimirum, apud quos Evangelium fuit, non tantùm per sermonem: sed per virtutem & Spiritum Sanctum: uti expressè habet Apostolus, citato cap. 1. prioris ad Thess. vers. 5. Proindè quando colligunt ex istis locis, ut ex 2 Petr. 1. Vocationem & Electionem ejusdem esse significationis, & latitudinis: id tantùm verum est de singulari illâ vocationis specie, quam Apostolus vocat κλῆσιν κατ' πρόθεσιν vocationem secundum propositum, quæ nimirùm semper cum Electione est conjuncta & cum ea se habet reciprocè. De quâ speciali etiam vocatione agunt dicta Scripturæ à Photinianis citata. Falsum verò id est, si de generali vocatione accipiatur: Siquidem ne unus quidem Scripturæ locus dari potest, ubi generalis vocatio nominetur Electio, vel generaliter vocati, dicantur Electi: nisi id fiat συνεκδοχικῶς ratione partis nobilioris. Ergo vocationis quidem, non verò Electionis gemina significatio ex Scripturis evinci & obtineri potest. QUARTA ET QUINTA Hypotheses simpliciter sunt falsæ, talem nimirùm prædestinationem afferentes, quæ facta sit respectu sanctitatis & perfectionis, sive operum nostrorũ, vel ut illi loquuntur, respectu obedientiæ mandatis DEI â nobis præstitæ. Quâ in parte usque adeò omni Scripturarum destituuntur præsidio, ut ne unum quidem in medium proferre possint testimonium, quo vel in speciem probabiliter saltem suam confirment sententiam. Nos suprà parte 1. Controv. special. 3. in Pontificiis & Pelagianis errorem istum funditùs subruimus & evertimus, ut prolixiore refutatione nulla opus sit. DEUS omnis veritatis autor, vel tandem præfractos istos hæreticos confundat: Nos verò in veritate conservet: Cujus nomen magnificum sit benedictum seculis infinitis. AMEN.


## 25 On the Kingdom of Christ


### Disposition of the Philippic Treatise on the Kingdom of Christ

That CHRIST, that promised Messiah and Savior of the World, would be King, is acknowledged among Jews and any heretics whatsoever, as well as Christians, from the plainest Scriptures of both Testaments; so much so that the Jews, in the hope of this Kingdom, endure the harshest servitude and an exile of more than fifteen hundred years with a certain foolish alacrity of spirit; blinded by the most just judgment of God, because they refuse to acknowledge JESUS of Nazareth, the Son of Mary, as the Messiah and promised King. But what the quality and condition of that Kingdom is to be—or rather, not that it is to be, but that it already exists in actual fact—has always been disputed quite sharply, and is disputed today, while not a few dream that it was one thing at one time, and is another even to this day. This is, of course, the cause that brought to our Author the necessity of treating this place as well. It is, however, dispatched by the inclusion of two parts: one of which is didactic, consisting of the explanation of sounder doctrine; the other polemical, which unfolds and refutes the shifts of various errors. The didactics or thesis of this Article is completed primarily by three Aphorisms. The first is: The Kingdom of Christ is spiritual, and not of this world. The second: This same Kingdom will always suffer persecution in this world and will never have firm peace or tranquility. The third: In the Kingdom of Christ, in this life, the wicked will always be mixed with the good; nor, once these are removed, will the pious alone ever reign in this world. The other, the polemical part, at the beginning recounts the errors of the Jews, the Chiliasts, and the Anabaptists; then, however, it responds to the principal arguments of the Anabaptists and other fanatics. And such indeed is the Philippic Treatise: whose footsteps we also shall follow: but in such a way that we prefix an accurate treatment of that controversy which today exists between Christians and Jews concerning Christ or the Messiah: Whether He has already come into this world: and Who He is. We therefore establish two principal parts of this our treatise: the former of which will be concerning the King Himself, or the Messiah: the latter, however, concerning the Form, Quality, and Condition of the Kingdom itself. We are pleased to dispatch both of these parts in such a way that at the beginning we demonstrate the thesis or purer doctrine solidly from the Scripture of both Testaments: then, however, we subject the antithesis, and accurately refute and overthrow both the errors themselves and their foundations.

Part One. CONCERNING THE KING CHRIST OR THE MESSIAH.

That CHRIST, or the Messiah, promised long ago by GOD through Moses and the Prophets to the Fathers, that is, to the Jews, would be King, the Jews believed, and today still believe: nor do Christians disagree with them in this part. For the Scriptures of both Testaments confirm this clearly: as Psalm 2:2 and 6. The princes and kings of the earth gathered together against the Lord, and His Messiah or anointed one: But I have set my King upon my holy hill. Jeremiah 23:5 and chapter 33:17. I will raise up a righteous branch unto David, a king shall reign, and shall be wise, etc. Daniel 2:44. The GOD of heaven will set up a kingdom, which shall not be destroyed for ever, and his kingdom shall not be delivered to another people. Zechariah 9:9. Rejoice, O daughter of Zion, shout, O daughter of Jerusalem, Behold THY KING cometh unto thee, just and a savior, etc. Luke 1:33. The Son of Mary, JESUS of Nazareth, shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end. Revelation 17:14 and chapter 19:16. Christ or the Lamb is Lord of lords, and King of kings.

There are, however, two other things which come into controversy in this place, and about which it is disputed quite sharply between us and the Jews today.

FIRST, Whether that promised King and Messiah has already come into this world, and administers His kingdom according to the prophecies of the Prophets?

THE SECOND, whether Jesus of Nazareth, the Son of Mary, be that very promised King of the World and Messiah? Concerning both questions, the Jews even today tenaciously hold the negative and strive to defend it: but we, for our part, entirely concede to the affirmative, relying upon those reasons and arguments which it is our pleasure to set forth separately according to these two questions.

Latin:

CHRISTUM, promissum illum Mundi Messiam ac Salvatorem Regem fore, cùm apud Judæos, & hæreticos quosvis, quàm Christianos, ex planiffimis utriusque Testamenti Scripturis, in confesso est: adeò ut Judæi, spe Regni hujus durissimam servitutem, & exilium mille quingentorum ampliùs annorum, stolidâ quâdam animi alacritate sustineant; justissimo Dei judicio excæcati, proptereà quòd JESUM Nazarenum Mariæ Filium, pro Messia, & Rege promisso agnoscere nolunt. Verùm quæ nám Regni istius futura sit, imò non futura ampliùs, sed ipso actu jam existat Qualitas & conditio, satis acriter semper controversum fuit, hodieq; controvertitur, dùm aliam atque aliam tùm olim fuisse, tùm in hunc etiam diem usque esse, non parum multi somniant. Hæc nimirùm causa est quæ Autori nostro, hujus etiam loci pertractandi necessitatem attulit. Expeditur verò ea duarum partium complexu: quarum una est διδασκαλικὴ, sanioris doctrinæ explicatione constans: altera πολεμικὴ, quæ variorum errorum strophas evolvit, & refutat. Διδασκαλία sive θέσις Articuli hujus, tribus potissimùm Aphorismis absolvitur. Primus est: Regnum Christi est spirituale, & non de hoc mudo. Alter: Idem Regnum hoc in mundo semper patietur persecutionem neque firmam habebit unquam pacem aut tranquillitatem. Tertius: In Regno Christi semper hac in vita, bonis admixti erunt mali: neque his deletis, pii soli hoc in mundo unquam regnabunt. Pars πολεμικὴ altera, initio recitat errores Judæorum, Chiliastarum, & Anabaptistarum: Deindè verò ad præcipua Anabaptistarum aliorumque fanaticorum argumenta respondet. Et talis quidem est Tractatio Philippea: cujus vestigia nos quoque sequemur: sed ita, ut præmittamus accuratam Tractationem Controverssiæ illius, quæ hodièque Christianis cum Judæis, de Christo sive Messia intercedit: An ille hunc in mundum modò venerit : & Quis ille sit. Constituimus ergò Tractationis hujus nostræ partes principales duas : quarum Prior erit de Rege ipso, sive Messiah : Posterior verò de Regni ipsius Forma, Qualitate, & Conditione. Quam utramque partem ita expedire placet, ut initid θέσιν sive puriorem doctrinam, ex Scriptura utriusque Testamenti solidè demonstrem9: deindè verò subjiciamus ἀντίθεσιν, & tùm errores ipsos, tùm eorum fundamenta accuratè refutemus & profligamus.

Pars Prior. DE REGE CHRISTO SIVE MESSIAH.

CHRISTUM, sive Messiam, jam olim à DEO per Mosen & Prophetas Patribus, hoc est Judæis promissum, Regem fore crediderunt, hodieq́; credunt Judæi : neque Christiani hac in parte ab ipsis dissentiunt. Hoc enim liquidò confirmant utriusque Testamenti Scripturæ: ut Psal. 2. 2. & 6. Principes & Reges terræ convenerunt in unum adversus Dominum, & משיחו Messiam sive unctum ejus : Ego verò constitui ipsum Regem meum, super montem sanctitatis meæ. Jerem 23. 5. & cap. 33. 17. Suscitabo Davidi germen justum, regnabit rex, & sapiens erit &c. Daniel. 2. 44. Suscitabit DEUS cæli regnum, quod in æternum non dissipabitur, & regnum ejus alteri non tradetur. Zachar. 9. 9. Exulta filia Sion, jubila filia Jerusalem, Ecce REX TVUS veniet tibi justus & salvator &c. Luc. 1. 33. Filius Mariæ, JESUS Nazarenus, regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum, & regni ejus non erit finis. Apocal. 17. 14. & cap. 19. 16. Christus sive Agnus est Dominus dominorum, & Rex regum.

Sunt autem duo alia, quæ hoc loco in controversiam veniunt, & de quibus satis acriter inter nos, & Judæos hodiè controvertitur.

PRIMUM, An promissus ille Rex & Messias modò in hunc mundum venerit, & regnum suum secundum vaticinia Prophetarum administret ?

ALTERUM, an JESUS Nazarenus, Mariæ Filius, sit ille ipse promissus Mundi Rex & Messias ? Circa utrumque quæsitum Judęi hodièquę Negativam mordicùs tenent, & propugnare student : Nos verò in Affirmantem omninò concedimus freti illis rationibus & argumentis, quę seorsim secundum duas hasce quæstiones expedire placet.


### On King Christ or Messiah


### On King Christ or Messiah: Whether the promised Messiah of the world, King and Saviour, hath long since come into this world, or no?

Among Christians, who place undoubted faith not only in the oracles of the Prophets but also in the books of the New Testament, the affirmative of this question is placed beyond all risk of doubt. For from the historical account of the Evangelists they have learned that he who was promised to the Fathers has already been brought forth: Luke 1. 55. that just now, through the Nativity of Jesus of Nazareth, that horn of salvation had been raised up in the house of David, of which GOD had spoken by the mouth of all His Prophets, who have been from the beginning: that He might be mindful of His holy covenant, and the oath which He swore to Abraham our Father. Luke 1. 69. 70. and following. that just now the SALVATION has been exhibited, prepared by GOD in the sight of all peoples, and a LIGHT, to enlighten the Gentiles, for the glory of the people of Israel: Luke 1. 30. and following. and that Christ of Nazareth is that very Messiah, of whom it is written that, when He comes, He will announce all things. John 4. 25. and 26. that He is that Son of GOD, who was to come into the world: John 11. 27. that He has been made Lord and Christ: Acts 2. 36. etc.

But on the part of the Jews, who hold the oracles of the New Testament in contempt, and with seared brow and conscience utterly deny that the promised Messiah of the World has yet come into the world; the affirmative of the proposed question must be asserted all the more solidly and evidently, the more certainly the shipwreck of our faith and salvation results from the negative of the Jews. The arguments, however, by which we irrefragably demonstrate our affirmative, are these principal ones:

I. The time prefixed for the nativity of the Messiah in the oracles of the Prophets has passed by more than sixteen hundred years ago. Therefore, it follows necessarily that the Messiah has long since come into the world.

The reason for the connection is clearly evident from this: 1. Because GOD is truthful in His promises, and knows not how to deceive. 2. Because from the notation of the defined time, GOD Himself wished a certain and infallible judgment to be sought concerning the truth and certainty of the exhibited Messiah, whether he has come into the world or not? For no other end can be shown for which GOD Himself would have wished the time certain for the Nativity of the Messiah to be so solicitously and accurately prefixed.

The truth of the antecedent is evident from the Scriptures in two ways: For 1. The Messiah had to be born when the scepter of Judah was removed. 2. When the seventy weeks defined by the Prophet Daniel were completed. The former notation was expressed by the Patriarch Jacob, Gen. 49. 10, in these words according to the Hebrew truth: The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples, or, as the Vulgate has it: to him shall be the gathering of the peoples.

The Rabbis of the Jews have striven to corrupt this illustrious prophecy about Christ in many wicked ways, and still study to do so today. Some have contended that it should be understood of David: Others of Saul, who is noted by an allusion to the word Shiloh: Others refer this prophecy to the place of Shiloh, in which the ark was for some time: Others to the times of Jeroboam, who was anointed in Shiloh, and who weakened the kingdom of Judah. But these interpretations are all twisted and utterly alien to the evidence of this prophecy. For 1. regarding David, it is false that he then ordinarily reigned over the tribe of Judah: since only after the times of David was the Jewish kingdom split and divided into two distinct kingdoms, of Judah and Israel: as can be seen in the history of Jeroboam, 1 Kings 12. 16. But Jacob speaks in this place of the Kingdom of Judah, insofar as it is considered distinctly and separately from the remaining tribes: and insofar as it, with the kingdom of Israel now destroyed, was to endure long after until the arrival of Shiloh: which the context of the text clearly proves. Thus it is also false that the Scepter was removed from Judah when David was raised to royal dignity: nay rather, by this very pact it was confirmed and stabilized.

Then the Place of Shiloh does nothing for the matter. For although the ark of the Lord was later moved from Shiloh into the tribe of Judah: yet the Scepter, or empire, was not therefore removed from Judah: but rather it was confirmed by this very means. What? That the text itself utterly overturns this gloss. For Jacob is not dealing with any place, but with a certain person, under whose arrival the Scepter is to be taken away from Judah. Who therefore could patiently bear this insolence of the Jews, that a place should be substituted for a person?

The remaining two glosses of the Jews obtain some plausibility. For the Scepter or empire seems to have been taken away from Judah then, when Saul and Jeroboam came, the former of whom was sprung from the tribe of Benjamin, the latter indeed from the tribe of Ephraim: but each (as the gloss of the Jews has it) anointed in Shiloh, transferred the royal dignity from the tribe of Judah to the other two tribes already named.

But the vanity of this interpretation is also sufficiently manifest. For 1. the Jews cannot prove from the Scriptures that before the coming of Saul the Scepter or empire was in the possession of the tribe of Judah. Moses certainly was the leader of the Israelite people from the tribe of Levi: Joshua from the tribe of Ephraim: most of the Judges from other tribes, with at least two excepted, Othniel and Ibzan: Judg. 1. 13. and chap. 12. 8. Eli from the tribe of Levi: Samuel from the tribe of Ephraim. how then could the kingdom be taken away from Judah through Saul, which until now had never been in the possession of the tribe of Judah? Furthermore, sacred history is a witness that when GOD transferred the kingdom of Saul to the family and tribe of David, then at last the kingdom arrived through this very means to the tribe of Judah, from which David was descended. Regarding which matter has it thus in Psalm 78. 67. & 68. The LORD rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim: but He chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which He loved. Thirdly, it is manifestly false that Saul was anointed in Shiloh. For 1 Sam. 10. 17 it is read that Samuel had gathered the people to the Lord in Mizpah, and had caused the whole people to stand there according to the order of tribes and families, and that lots having been cast, it fell upon the tribe of Benjamin, and the family of Matri, even to Saul the son of Kish. And the following chapters. n. 15. it is expressly held that after Saul brought back victory over the King of the Ammonites, the whole people gathered in Gilgal, and made Saul King there before the Lord.

Fourthly, the Jewish Gloss also fails in this, that a gathering of the nations was never made to King Saul: concerning which Jacob prophesied. Finally, manifest violence is done to the text when it is feigned, in the words of Jacob, that this phrase (Until Shiloh comes) denotes the same as (Until he comes, who was anointed in Shiloh). Where a malicious substitution of the name of a person with the name of a Place appears, affixing a meaning to the text that is entirely foreign.

Regarding Jeroboam, it is clearly false what the Rabbis of the Jews feign in this place. For his entire history testifies that under his rule, the Kingdom of Judah was indeed weakened, but that it was taken away, or clearly overturned, that truly cannot be proven from the sacred writings; rather, the opposite is evident from there, that the Kingdom of Judah endured for more than four hundred years even after Jeroboam, until the Babylonian captivity. Thus it is false that Jeroboam was anointed king in Shiloh: since a comparison of the first and twenty-first verses of chapter 12 of the 1st book of Kings proves that it was done in Shechem. Moved by the irrefragable evidence of those reasons, not a few of the Jewish Rabbis seized upon that as a kind of stronghold, so that, having abandoned the glosses refuted thus far, they might contend that the prophecy of Jacob was fulfilled in Nebuchadnezzar, who clearly overturned both the kingdom and the Jewish polity, and led the people captive into Babylon. 2 Kings 25, or the last: verse 9 and following. Hence, therefore, they express the meaning of the Jacobite prophecy with such an argument: The Scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, until Shiloh comes; that is, until he comes who is to be sent, Nebuchadnezzar. Now, however, the kingdom of Judah was so taken away by Nebuchadnezzar that no one from that tribe ever reigned afterwards: so much so that Jeremiah in his Lamentations complains repeatedly that a King from the house of Judah no longer survives. Moreover, a gathering of the nations was made to this very Babylonian king: since his dominion extended itself to all nations. Therefore the Rabbis infer that the prophecy of the Patriarch Jacob is to be understood not of the Messiah, but of Nebuchadnezzar.

Latin:

APud Christianos, qui oraculis non modò Prophetarum; sed & libris Novi Testamenti fidem indubitatam adhibent, Quaestionis hujus Affirmativa, extra omnem dubitationis aleam est posita. Nam ex relatione historicâ Evangelistaru didicerunt, jam editum esse illum, qui promissus erat Patribus: Luc. 1. 55. jam modò per Nativitatem Jesu Nazareni, erectum fuisse cornu illud salutis, in domo Davidis, de quod locuto fuerat DEUS per os omnium suorum Prophetarum, qui à seculo fuerunt: ut memor esset foederis sui sancti, & juramenti, quod juravit Abrahamo Patri nostro. Luc. 1. 69. 70. & seqq. jam modò exhibitum esse SALUTARE, à DEO paratum in oculis omnium populorum, & LUMEN, ad illuminandum Gentes, in gloriam populi Israelis: Luc. 1. 30. & seqq. & Christum Nazarenum esse illum ipsum Messiam, de quo scriptum, quòd, cum venerit, anunciaturus sit omnia. Johan. 4. 25. & 26. esse Filium illum DEI, qui in mundum venturus erat: Johan. 11. 27. esse factum Dominum & Christum: Actor. 2. 36. &c.

Verùm ex Judaeorum parte, qui Novi Testamenti oracula floccipendunt, & promissum Mundi Messiam nondum in mundum venisse, cauteriatâ fronte ac conscientia pernegant; Affirmativa propositae quaestionis tantò solidiùs ac evidentiùs astruenda fuerit, quantò certiùs fidei ac salutis nostrae naufragium, ex negativa Judaeorum, redundat. Argumenta autem, quibus Affirmativum nostram irrefragabiliter demonstramus, praecipua sunt isthaec:

I. Tempus nativitati Messiae in oraculis Prophetarum praefixum, ante annos mille sexcentos ampliùs praeterfluxit. Ergo quin Messias jam pridem in mundum venerit, necessariò consequitur.

Ratio connexi indè evidenter patet: 1. Quia DEUS in promissionibus suis verax est, & fallere nescit. 2. Quia ex notatione temporis definiti, DEUS ipse certum ac infallibile judicium peti voluit, de veritate ac certitudine exhibiti Messiae, an ille in mundum venerit, nec ne? Neque enim finis alius monstrari potest, propter quem usque adeò solicitè & accuratè Tempus certum Nativitati Messiae DEUS ipse praefinitum voluerit.

Antecedentis veritas patet ex Scripturis dupliciter: Nam 1. Messias nasci debuit ablato sceptro Juda. 2. completis septuaginta hebdomadibus, per Prophetam Danielem definita. Priorem notationem expressit Patriarcha Jacob. Genef. 49. 10. his verbis secundum Hebream veritatem: Non recedet virga ex Jehudah, & legislator de pedibus ejus, usquequò veniat Schiloh, & ei erit obedientia populorum, vel, ut vulgata habet: ad ipsum erit congregatio populorum.

Judæorum Rabbini illustre hoc vaticinium de Christo, multis modis nefariè corrumpere struerunt, hodieq́; student. Nonnulli de Davide illud intelligendū esse contenderunt: Alij de Saule, qui notetur per allusionem vocis Schilo: Alij ad locum Siloh, in quo aliquandiu fuit arca, vaticinium hoc referunt: Alij ad tempora Jeroboami, qui fuerit unctus in Siloh, quiq; regnum Juda debilitaverit. Verùm contortæ sunt, & ab evidentiâ vaticinij hujus prorsus alienæ, singulæ hæ interpretationes. Nam 1. quoad Davidem, falsum est, quod tùm ordinariè regnârit tribus Juda: siquidem post tempora Davidis demùm regnū Judaicum in duo distincta regna, Judæ & Israelis scissum ac divisum fuit: uti videre est in historiâ Jeroboami, 1. Reg. 12. 16. Loquitur autem hoc loco Jacobus de Regno Judæ, quatenus illud à reliquis tribubus distinctè & separatim consideratur: & quatenùs illud, exciso jam regno Israelis, multò post usque ad adventum Siloh duraturum erat: id quòd textus συνέπεια luculenter evincit. Sic falsum etiam est, quòd Sceptrum de Judâ sit ablatum, quando David ad regiam dignitatem evectus fuit: quin imò hoc ipso potiùs pacto illud confirmatum ac stabilitum fuit.

Deindè Locus Siloh nihil facit ad rem. Nam licèt arca Domini ex Siloh postmodùm translata fuerit in tribum Juda: non tamen ideò ablatum est de Juda Sceptrum, sive imperium: sed potiùs per hoc ipsum medium illud confirmatum. Quid? quòd textus ipse hanc glossam funditùs evertit. Neque enim de loco aliquo, sed de persona certa agit Jacobus, sub cujus adventum Sceptrum de Judâ sit auferendum. Quis ergò patienter ferat hanc Judæorum proterviam, ut pro personâ substituatur locus?

Reliquæ duæ Judæorum glossę plausibilitatis aliquid obtinent. Nam Sceptrum sive imperium de Juda videtur ablatum fuisse tùm, quando venerunt Saul & Jeroboam, quorum ille ex tribu Benjamiticâ, hic verò de tribu Ephraim oriundus: uterque autem (uti habet Judæorum glossa) in Siloh unctus, regiam dignitatem à tribu Juda, ad reliquas jam nominatas duas tribus transtulit.

Verùm & hujus interpretationis vanitas satis est manifesta. Nam 1. ex Sacris probare nō possunt Judæi, ante adventum Saulis Sceptrū sive imperium fuisse penes tribū Juda. Moses certè dux populi Israëlitici erat de tribu Levi: Josua de tribu Ephraim: Judices plerique ex aliis tribubus, duob9 saltē exceptis, Othoniele & Abesamo: Judic. 1. 13. & cap. 12. 8. Eli ex tribu Levi: Samuel ex tribu Ephraim. Quomodo ergò per Saulom auferri potuit regnum de Juda, quod penes tribum Juda hactenus nunquàm fuerat? Deinde testis est historia sacra, quòd cùm DEUS transtulit regnum Saulis ad familiam ac tribum Davidis, tùm demù regnū pervenerit per hoc ipsum medium ad tribum Juda, de qua oriundus erat David. Quâ de re sic habet Asaphus Psalmo 78. 67. & 68. Repulit DOMINUS tabernaculum Joseph, & tribum Ephraim non elegit: sed elegit tribum Juda, monte Sion, quem dilexit. Tertiò manifeste falsum est, quòd Saul unctus fuerit in Siloh. Nam 1. Sam. 10. 17. legitur, quòd Samuel convocâverit populum ad Dominum in Mispba, & curârit ibidem stare universum populum secundum ordinem tribuum & familiarum, & quòd jacta forte, ceciderit ea super tribum Benjamin, & cognationem Metri, usque ad Saulum filium Kis. Et cap. subseqq. n. 15. expressè habetur, quòd postquam Saul victoriam reportavit de Rege Ammonitarum, universus populus convenerit in Galgala, & fecerit ibi Regem Saul coram Domino.

Quartò, deficit in eo quoq; Glossa Judæorum, quòd ad Saulem regem nunquàm facta est congregatio gentium: de qua vaticinato est Jacobus. Tandê manifesta vis infertur textui, quando fingitur, in verbis Jacobi, phrasin hâc, (Donec veniat Siloh) idem notare ac (Donec veniat, qui unctus est in Siloh) Ubi malitiosa apparet nominis personæ, cum nomine Loci permutatio, alienum planè sensum textui affingens.

Quoad Jeroboamum, falsum planè est, quòd Judæorum Rabbini hoc loco fingunt. Testatur enim universa ipsius historia, quòd sub ejus imperio, Regnum Juda debilitatū quidem fuerit, sed quòd illud sublatum, aut planè ever sum fuerit, id verò ex sacris probari nequit; quin diversum potiùs indè patet, quòd Regnū Juda etiam post Jeroboamum, usquad captivitatem Babylonicam, per annos quadringentos ampliùs duraverit. Sic falsum est, quòd in Siloh rex unctus fuerit Jeroboam: cum in Si chem illud factum esse, evincat collatio versus primi & vicesimi capitis 12. l. 1. Regum. Rationum istarum irrefragabili evidentia moti nō nulli Judæorum Rabbini, præsidij quasi loco arripuerunt illud, ut relictis glossis hactenus solidè refutatis contenderent, impletum fuisse vaticinium Jacobi in Nebucadnezare, qui & regnū, & politiam ludaicam planè everterit, & populum captivum abduxerit in Babylonem. 2. Reg: 25. sive ultimo: vers. 9. & seqq. Hinc ergo vaticinii Iacobæi sensum tali argumento exprimunt: Non auferetur Sceptrum de Juda, donec veniat Siloh; id est, donec veniat, qui mittendus est, Nebucadnezar. Jam verò per Nebucadnezarem regnum Juda ita ablatum fuit, ut ex eâ tribu nullus unquam postea regnaverit: usq; adeò, ut Jeremias in threnis subindè conqueratur, Regem de domo Juda non superesse ampliùs. Quin etiam ad hunc ipsum regem Babylonicum facta est congregatio gentium: siquidem ipsius dominium ad omnes gentes se extendit. Ergò inferunt Rabbini, non de Messia, sed de Nebucadnezare accipiendum est vaticinium Patriarchæ Jacobi.


### On King Christ or Messiah: Just now in

just now in.

This argument has not entirely no difficulty, which, however, if it be examined a little more accurately according to the standard of the scriptures, can easily be removed. Therefore, regarding the major proposition, the Hebrew word שילה Shiloh comes under consideration, which, as P. Galatinus notes, book 4 of the Mysteries of the Catholic Truth, chapter 4, is equivocal, and admits various meanings: which, however, can easily be reduced to a ternary number. For there were first, not only among the Jews, but also among Christian interpreters, not a few, among whom is also Jerome, who for שילו Shiloh read שילוח Shiloah, which word takes its origin from the root שלח to send. Hence the Vulgate version renders it, until he comes who is to be sent. Whether this interpretation can stand in this place, and whether שילוח Shiloah assumes the form of a participle or a noun, and can be derived from the root שלח, let the Grammarians or the interpreters of the Hebrew language see. We insist upon the Hebrew sources, which do not read שילוח, but שילה. And although this interpretation, or derivation, produces no support for the cause of the Jews, nor does it hinder ours: since we ourselves readily grant that the Messiah can rightly be called שילוח, that is, one to be sent, yet we do not at all concede that it is founded in the Hebrew text regarding that prophecy. What? That even with this granted, by no right can the subsumption be instituted or ought it to be for Nebuchadnezzar, or for any other besides the Messiah, as will be most solidly demonstrated a little later in the response to the minor proposition of the Jewish argument.

The other interpretation of the word Shiloh is of those who explain Shiloh by שליה Silya, which is the membrane or covering in which the fetus is wrapped in the maternal womb: and by physicians it is called the afterbirth. Galatinus, in the place already cited before, greatly approves this reading: he says that Shiloh is derived from the word Silya, which is a certain little sac in which the infant remains in the mother's womb, which is sometimes taken in Scripture for an embryo in the womb: so that Shiloh signifies the son of a woman: and thus it is shown that the Messiah was to be born of a mother without a father. Some derive the Hebrew word שליה from שיל: which word the Rabbis signify as son, but without any authority of the Scriptures: others from שלה Shalah, which signifies the same as peaceful, tranquil, happy, Savior, for the reason that the fetus rests peacefully in the maternal womb. Although both of these derivations are sufficiently pious and tolerable: since the former denotes the admirable birth of the Messiah from the Virgin Mary: and the latter expresses his saving office: we nevertheless leave it in the middle, not insisting upon it stubbornly: especially since in those derivations there seems to be a sin not only against the vowel points, but also against the grammatical doctrine concerning affixes: about which let the Grammarians see.

The third, therefore, and the simplest, is the opinion which, without any inflection or more far-fetched derivation, reads שילה Shiloh from the root שלה, that is, he rested, brought peace, was happy and auspicious. That the propriety of this etymology belongs to the Messiah alone is gathered not only from the fact that this word is found only once in the Scriptures, but rather because the office of the Messiah had to be directed solely to the end that he might obtain salvation and rest for the world from GOD the Father in spiritual matters. Regarding this matter, since it required great labor and sweat, B. LUTHER not inappropriately rendered the word Siloh by the German term der Heldt. Although these three meanings vary in a certain sense, they nevertheless agree in this, that they designate the Messiah and his person and office: a thing which even the sounder Jews do not deny, although more recent ones dare to deny it against the testimony of their own heart and conscience, but without reason and Scripture, as has just been demonstrated and will soon be demonstrated more fully.

For as regards the minor proposition of the Jewish argument, it is simply false that by שִׁילֹה Siloh, Nebuchadnezzar is denoted: a thing which is irrefragably shown and confirmed by the following reasons. For first, the prophecy of Jacob by no means has this as its proposed goal, to show at least that the kingdom of Judah was at some time to be abolished, or even who the destroyers of this kingdom were to be: but rather, to teach expressly who the Savior or deliverer was to be, at the time when the royal majesty was completely taken away from the tribe of Judah: that he was certainly not Nebuchadnezzar, the Jews themselves, however obstinate, are forced to admit. Therefore, it necessarily follows that this prophecy extends beyond the kingdom of Nebuchadnezzar.

Then P. Galatinus rightly notes in book 4, chapter 4, page 197 for me, and indeed from R. Solomon, that in the devastation of the Jerusalem temple and the abduction of the people into the Babylonian captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, the scepter was not completely taken away from Judah. For then not all the Sanhedrin, who were the leaders and lawgivers of the Jews, were killed: but many of them went down into Babylonia, and there, according to their own laws, by the permission of the King, judged and decided the cases of the Jews. This is confirmed not only by the Jerusalem Targum: but the same is also clearly evident from 2 Kings 25:27 and Jeremiah 52:31. Where it is read that Jechonias, King of Judah, survived in the very Babylonian captivity, and Evil-Merodach, King of Babylon, released him from prison and endowed him with royal honor and office. Furthermore, this very thing is confirmed by the fact that although in the Babylonian captivity the Kingdom of Judah was vehemently weakened, it was not yet completely extinguished or abolished: so much so that, those seventy years of captivity now completed, the Jewish people not only returned home, restored Jerusalem and the temple, but also appointed leaders and princes of the people from the tribe of Judah, as is clearly evident from the book of Ezra and Nehemiah. Certainly, Zerubbabel, who was appointed Prince of the people upon the return from captivity, was of the tribe of Judah, Haggai 1:1. And this rule of the tribe of Judah lasted until the year

160 before the birth of Christ, in which the last leader from the tribe of Judah, namely John Hyrcanus, was killed. Nay, even in later times, although the Maccabees, in whose hands was the supreme Sanhedrin or judgment, were descended from the tribe of Levi, they nevertheless wished the Priesthood to be established through Levites and Princes who were of the tribe of Judah. What is more, these very Maccabees, as regards their maternal line, were descended from the tribe of Judah. And not only do the Talmudists report this: but sacred history also testifies that the royal and priestly stock or tribe were then mixed by marriages, as can be gathered from the fourth chapter of the second book of Kings. Furthermore, it cannot be denied by any reason, not even by the Jews themselves, that after Nebuchadnezzar there remained in the Jewish people elders, lawgivers, or rather interpreters of the divine law, Priests, and Pontiffs, who presided over the government and prescribed laws, and indeed from the tribe of Judah, until Herod the Great, who finally abolished the Maccabees and the Sanhedrin, and, having killed the experts in the law and the elders, attempted to cut off the entire posterity of David. Now, the Patriarch Jacob deals with such an ablation of the Jewish Scepter as would be future and joined with the total abolition of the Sanhedrin itself. For he joins expressly the Scepter, שֵׁבֶט Schevet, and מְחֹקֵק Mehokek, the lawgiver, so that Shiloh was not to come before both the Scepter or political rule, and the order of Doctors or experts in the law, which consisted of 72 Elders and was called the Sanhedrin—a word corrupted from the Greek συνέδριον—had been completely abolished. Since this was not done by Nebuchadnezzar, the minor proposition of the Jewish argument is discovered to be most false.

Finally, Jacob deals with such a Shiloh, to whom the gathering of all peoples and nations shall be: and indeed not by the external force and power of arms, by which Nebuchadnezzar, relying on it, subjugated peoples and nations to himself: but by spontaneous obedience, through the mediation of the preaching of the Word. The Hebrew word which Jacob wished to use, יִקְהַת likkehath, hints at this, which, derived from the unused root יָקַהּ Iakah, that is, he heard, he obeyed, denotes obedience or hearing: Although others derive it from קָוָה, that is, he gathered and aggregated: so that this word denotes the congregation of all nations, made through the preaching of the Word: but that former derivation denotes the effect of this congregation, namely the hearing of the Word and obedience.

These things having been thus weighed, it becomes manifest that the prophecy of Jacob deals directly with the advent of the Messiah, who was to be at that time when the government, both political and ecclesiastical, had been so completely taken away from the tribe of Judah that it could never be restored. How this was fulfilled under the advent of Christ Jesus of Nazareth will be shown a little later.

And indeed so great is the force and evidence of these reasons that the modern Jews are held constrained and convicted, nor is any refuge left to them any longer. This is the reason why they wickedly corrupt this whole illustrious prophecy, contending that it treats not at all of the scepter or dominion of the kingdom of Judah: but that the Hebrew word שֵׁבֶט Schebet denotes a cross or tribulation in this sense: The cross and calamity shall not be taken away from Judah until Shiloh comes, that is, the Messiah. Now, since the cross and calamity of the Jews have not been taken away from Judah to this very day, they presume it follows that the Messiah has not yet come into this world. But I answer 1. that we readily embrace that which they concede, that by Shiloh the Messiah is denoted. 2. But, that it is simply false that the Hebrew word שֵׁבֶט signifies a cross or calamity: For they cannot bring forward even a single proof from the entire Hebrew code; rather, wherever this word is found, it always signifies a kingdom, a principality, or even a tyrannical dominion, expressed by the Hebrews with the word for a rod: as in Psalm 2:9, 'You shall break them (namely the nations) בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל beschebet Barzel, with a rod of iron': And Isaiah 10, 'Assyria the rod of my fury, or of my anger, שֵׁבֶט אַפִּי Schebet Appi.' Jacob, however, does not treat of a rod or tyrannical dominion which Judah was to suffer from others: but of his own, which he himself was to have until the coming of the Messiah. Which being taken away and cut off, the Messiah would truly be about to come into the world.

Latin:

jam modò in.

Habet hoc argumentum non planè nihil difficultatis, quæ tamen si ad scripturarum amussim paulò accuratius exigatur, facilè tolli potest. Ergo, quoad majorem propositionem, sub considerationem venit vox Hebræa שילה Schiloh, quæ annotante P. Galatino, l. 4. de arcanis Catholicæ veritatis, cap. 4. æquivoca est, & varias admittit significationes: quæ tamen ad numerum ternarium facilè reduci potest. Fuerunt enim primò, non inter Judæos tantùm, sed & Christianos interpretes haud pauci, inter quos est etiam Hieronymus, qui pro שילו Siloh שילוח Schiloah legūt, quæ vox trahit originem à radice שלח misit. Hinc vulgata versio reddit, donec veniat, qui mittendus est. Quæ interpretatio, nùm subsistere hoc loco possit, & num שילוח Schiloah sive participii, sive nominis formam induat, à radice שלח derivari possit, viderint Grammatici, sive Hebrææ linguæ interpretes. Nos fontibus Hebræis insistimus, qui non legunt שילוח, sed שילה. Et quanquam interpretatio hæc, sive derivatio, Judæorum causæ nihil parit præsidij, neque nostræ officit: Siquidem Messiam rectè nominari posse שילוח hoc est, mittendum, ipsi ultrò largimur tamen in Hebræo textu, quoad istud vaticinium, fundata eam esse, minimè concedimo. Quid? quod etiam hoc concesso, nullo tamen jure subsumtio vel pro Nebucadnezare, vel pro alio aliquo, præter Messiam, institui potest, aut debet, uti paulò pòst, in responsione ad Minorem propositionem argumenti Judaici, solidissimè demonstrabitur.

Altera interpretatio vocabuli Siloh est eorum qui Siloh explicant per שליה Silea, quod membranam, sive involucrum, cui fœtus in utero materno involutus est: & Medicis Secudina dicitur. Quam lectione maximè probat Galatinus loco jam antè citato: derivatur inquiens, Siloh à vocabulo Silya, quod est sacculus quidam, in quo manet infans in utero matris, qui aliquando in Scripturâ pro embryone in matrice sumitur: ita ut Siloh significet filium mulieris: & sic ostedatur Messiam de matre absq; patre nasciturum fuisse. Derivant autem vocem Hebræam שליה nonnulli à שיל: quæ vox Rabbini filium significat sed sine omni Scripturarum autoritate: alii à שלה Schalah, quod idem significat, ac pacificum, tranquillum, felicem, Salvatorem, eò quod fœtus in alvo maternâ placidè quiescat. Etsi autraque hæc derivatio satis pia est, & tolerabilis: siquidem illa notat admirandam Messiæ nativitatem ex Mariâ virgine: hæc verò officium ipsius salutare exprimit: nos tamen eam in medio relinquimus, mordicùs eam non urgentes: præsertim cùm in derivationibus istis non tantùm in puncta vocalia, sed etiam in doctrinam Grammaticam de affixis peccati videatur: de quo viderint Grammatici.

Tertia ergò, eaque simplicissima est sententia, quæ sine ullâ inflexione, sive longiùs petita derivatione legit שילה Siloh à radice שלה hoc est, quievit, pace attulit, fœlix ac auspicatus fuit. Cuj9 etymi proprietatem soli Meffiæ competere, non modò indè colligitur, quòd vox hæc semel tantùm in facris reperitur, sed potiùs quod officium Mefsiæ eò unicè debuit effe dire tum, ut salutem & quietem mundo à DEO Patre in spiritualibus impetraret. Quam ad rem, cùm magno labore ac sudore opus fuerit, haud incommòdè B. LUTHERUS vocem Siloh reddidit per vocabulum Germanicum der Heldt. Quanquàm verò tres hæ fignificationes sensu quodammodo variant, in eo tamen conveniunt, quod Messiam, ejusque personam, & officiũ designant: id quod ne quidem saniores Judæi inficiantur, licèt recentiores contra proprium cordis ac conscientiæ testimonium id, sed præter rationem & Scripturam negare ausint, ut modò demonstratum, & mox fusius demonstrabitur.

Nam quoad Minorem propositionem argumenti Judaici, simpliciter falsum est, per שִׁילֹה Siloh notari Nebucadnezare: id quod sequentibus rationibus irrefragabiliter ostenditur & confirmatur. Primum enim vaticinium Jacobi nequaquam hunc sibi scopum habet propositum, ut ostendat saltem, regnum Juda aliquando esse abolendum, vel etiam, quinam futuri sint eversores regni hujus: sed potius, ut disertè doceat, quisnam venturus sit Salvator sive liberator, tum, quando regia majestas à tribu Juda penitus est ablata: Quem profectò Nebucadnezarem non fuiffe, ipsi Judæi, quantumvis obstinati, fateri necesse habent. Ergo ultra Nebucadnezaris regnum, vaticinium hoc se extendat, necessariò consequitur.

Deindè rectè annotat P. Galatinus lib. 4. cap.4. pag. mihi 197. & quidem ex R. Solomo, in devastatione templi Hierosolymitani, & abductione populi in captivitatem Babylonicam, per Nebucadnezarem sceptrum de Judâ non fuisse penitus ablatu. Tunc n. non omnes Sanhedrin, qui duces, & legumlatores Judæorum erant, fuerunt interfecti: sed multi eorum, in Babyloniam descenderunt, ibiq; juxta leges suas, ex permissu Regis, Judæorum causas judicarunt ac definiverunt. Confirmat hoc non modò Targum Hierosolymitanum: sed & idem luculenter patet ex 2. Reg. 25. 27. & Jerem. 52, 31. Ubi legitur, quod Jechonias Rex Judæ, in ipsâ captivitate Babylonicâ superstes fuerit, & Evilmerodach Rex Babylonis ipsum è carcere dimissum, regio honore & officio donaverit.3. Porrò confirmat hoc ipsum & illud, quòd licet in captivitate Babylonicâ, Regnum Juda vehementer debilitatum; non tamen planè extinctum aut abolitum fuit: ita quidem, ut septuaginta illis captivitatis annis jam completis, populus Judaicus non modò domũ redierit, Jerosolymam & templũ restaurarit, sed & ex tribu Juda duces ac principes populi constituerit, uti ex libro Esdræ & Nehemiæ luculenter patet. Certè Zorobabel qui in reditu ex captivitate Princeps populi constitutus fuit, erat de tribu Juda, Haggai 1. 1. Et duravit hoc regimen tribus Juda usq; ad annum

160. ante natum Christum, quo ultimus dux ex tribu Juda, nempè Iohannam Hircanus, fuit interfectus. Quin imò posteris etiam temporibus, licet Macchabæi, penes quos supremum erat Sanhedrin, sive judicium, oriundi essent ex tribu Levi, Sacerdotium tamen constitutu voluerunt per Levitas ac Principes, qui essent ex tribu Juda. Quid quod hi ipsi Macchabæi, quoad lineam maternam oriundi erant ex tribu Iuda. Et non modò Thalmudistæ referunt: sed & historia sacra testatur, stirpem, sive tribum regiam & sacerdotalem connubiis tum fuisse mixtas, uti ex capite quarto libri secundi Regum colligere licet. 4. Præterea negari ullâ ratione, ne quidem ab ipsis Judæis potest, post Nebucadnezarem mansisse in populo Juda seniores, legislatores, vel potiùs legis divinæ interpretes, Sacerdotes, Pontifices, qui præerant gubernationi, & leges præscribebant, & quidem ex tribu Iuda, usque ad Herodem Magnum, qui demùm Macchabæos & Sanhedrin sustulit, & interfectis legisperitis ac fenioribus, omnem Davidis posteritatem excindere conatus fuit. Iam verò Iacobus Patriarcha de tali ablatione Sceptri Iudaici agit, quæ futura sit conjuncta cum ipsius etiam Sanhedrin totali abolitione. Conjungit enim expressè, Sceptrũ שֵׁבֶט Schevet, & מְחֹקֵק Mehokek legislatorem, ita ut Schiloh non prius sit venturus, quàm & Sceptrum sive regimen politicum, & Doctorum, sive legisperitorum ordo, qui constabat 72. Senioribus, & Sanhedrin vocabatur: corruptâ voce ex Græco συνέδριον penitus sit abolitus. Quod cùm per Nebucadnezarem factum non sit, Minor propositio argumenti Iudaici deprehenditur esse falsissima.

Tandem de tali Siloh agit Iacobus, ad quem futura sit aggregatio omnium populorum, atque gentium: & quidem non per externam armorum vim atque potentiam, quâ fretus Nebucadnezar populos ac gentes sibi subjugavit: sed per spontaneam obœdientiam, mediante prædicatione verbi. Innuit hoc vox Hebræa, qua Jacobus uti voluit, יִקְהַת likkehath, quæ ab inusitata radice יָקַהּ Iakah, id est, audivit, obœdivit, deducta, notat obœdientiam sive auditum: Quanquam alii eam derivant à קָוָה hoc est, congregavit, & aggregavit: ita ut vox hæc notet congregationem omnium gentium, factam per prædicationem Verbi: Prior autem illa derivatio notet congregationis hujus effectum, nempè auditum Verbi & obedientiam.

Quibus ita expensis, manifestum evadit, vaticinium Jacobi directè agere de adventu Messie, qui tum futurus, quando regimen & politicum & Ecclesiasticum de tribu Iuda ita pœnitus fuerit ablatum, ut restaurari illud nunquàm potuerit. Quod quomodo sub adventum Christi Iesu Nazareni impletum fuerit, paulò post ostendetur.

Et profectò tanta est vis, atque evidentia istarú rationum, ut moderni Iudæi constricti ac convicti teneantur, neque ullum ampliùs præsidium ipsis sit relictum. Quæ causa est, quòd totum hoc illustre vaticinium sceleratè corrumpunt, contendentes, nihil in eo agi de sceptro, sive dominio regni Iuda: sed você Hebræam שֵׁבֶט Schebet, notare crucem sive tribulationem hoc sensu: Non auferetur crux & calamitas de Juda, donec veniat Siloh, hoc est, Messias. Iam verò cùm crux & calamitas Iudeorum in hunc usque diem non sit ablata de Juda, consequens esse autumant, Messiam nondum etiam hunc in mundum venisse. Sed respondeo 1. ultrò nos amplecti illud, quod concedunt isti, per Siloh notari Messiam. 2. verò, simpliciter falsum esse, quòd Hebræa vox שֵׁבֶט significet cruce aut calamitatem: Neque enim ex universo codice Hebræo vel unicam probationem proferre possunt; quin ubi ubi vox hæc reperitur, ibi semper significat regnum, principatum, dominatum etiam Tyrannicum, Hebræis virgæ vocabulo expressum: ut Psal. 2. 9. Conteres eas (videlicet gentes) בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל beschebet Barzel, in virga ferrea: Et Esa: 10. Assur virga furoris, sive nasi mei, שֵׁבֶט אַפִּי Schebet Appi. Jacob9 autem non agit de virgâ sive dominatu Tyrannico quem Juda ab aliis sit perpessurus: sed de proprio, quem ipse habiturus sit usque ad adventum Messiæ. Quo ablato & exciso, verè in mundum venturus sit Messias.


### On King Christ or Messiah: Just now in (continued)

Furthermore, this Jewish gloss manifestly conflicts with the whole context of the text: which shows that Jacob in this place is not treating of the diminution or excision of the tribe of Judah, much less prophesying ill omens for it: but is prophesying of its magnificence and excellence, namely that the dominion was to remain with this tribe of Judah until the coming of the Messiah. For which reason he attributed to it in the preceding verses and assigned a lion-like strength, by which it exerted its power over the remaining tribes. And although afterwards, by the defection of the ten tribes, this tribe was greatly diminished: yet the authority of the Kings of Judah always remained greater than that of the kings of Israel: both because of the seat of the Davidic kingdom, and because of the religion and the promises concerning the Messiah made to the descendants of David, and finally because of the college of Elders instituted by Moses: Whence the vanity of the Jewish quibble is readily apparent.

Of the same sort is also that, that they interpret those two particles עַד כִּי as 'after' in this sense: After Shiloh, or the Messiah, shall have come, the kingdom shall no longer be taken away from Judah. But that has been taken away from Judah to this very day. Therefore Shiloh or the Messiah has not yet come into the world.

I answer that the major premise is most false. For it rests upon a manifest depravation of the proper and genuine meaning of those two words עַד כִּי which, as all the sounder Hebrews attest, nowhere signify 'after' or 'when': but always denote the same as 'until' or 'up to the point that' etc., as infinite testimonies of Scripture prove, and the Rabbis of the Jews themselves admit.

Moreover, it might not undeservedly seem strange to anyone what spirit impelled John Calvin to not hesitate to side with the Jews in part regarding this very prophecy of the Patriarch Jacob, in these words: 'That they explain from Judah that the right of reigning was given to the tribe of Judah, because it would have been a crime for it to be transferred elsewhere, but not that it was necessary for the glory of the crown once erected to be perpetuated, I judge it necessary to side with this opinion in some part.' But Calvin maliciously perverts the state of the controversy, nay, he attaches a meaning to the prophecy of Jacob that is clearly foreign to it. For Jacob does not mean this, that the kingdom of the tribe of Judah was to be in a perpetual flower of dignity and eminence until the coming of the Messiah: and that one and the same form of that government was always to remain. For we ourselves also grant that this kingdom suffered various mutations and, as it were, eclipses, especially when the Jews were tributary to foreign kings for five hundred years: when under Antiochus the dignity of the royal line was extinguished: when the Hasmoneans usurped for themselves the title and royal honors. Nay, we even readily grant that these various mutations of the form of the Jewish kingdom were predicted by the prophets themselves, as when Ezekiel in Chapter 21:26 predicted that it would come to pass that the crown, which was the badge of royal majesty, would be changed into a miter, which was a priestly badge: Exodus 28:4, Leviticus 16:4, and afterwards was also the badge of Princes. Isaiah 22:18. Whence it is called the Miter of the kingdom, Isaiah 62:3. By which arrangement it was indeed quite clearly predicted that the royal power of the tribe of Judah would degenerate after Zedekiah into a Ducal power: and that instead of Kings, Princes would rule. Nay, we are not even ignorant of, much less do we deny, that it was predicted that it would come to pass that the Miter also, that is, the ducal power, would be taken away from the house of David, and thus from the tribe of Judah, and would be exchanged with another form of government: that this was done by Antiochus, the Maccabees, the high priests, and Herod, and lasted for 160 years before the birth of Christ, is certain from sacred history. Although indeed the persons who held the principality at this time were not all of the tribe of Judah: nevertheless, the right of the Kingdom itself and the royal dignity remained with the tribe of Judah: not otherwise than as today the Roman Empire is and is called Roman, although the Emperor himself is by nation either Greek, or Spaniard, or Gaul. Therefore, Calvin's gloss contributes nothing to the matter, because Jacob least of all intended that to be noted, as if the form, appearance, fortune, and condition of the kingdom of the tribe of Judah were always to be one and the same until the coming of the Messiah.

But he intended to signify this, that the Empire or kingdom of the tribe of Judah, even under diverse forms of government, was to be continued until the coming of Shiloh or the Messiah: not otherwise than if Jacob had said: The royal power shall not utterly fail from the tribe of Judah, in such a way that it is never again recovered.

Although, therefore, the principate did not remain among men of the tribe of Judah perpetually and in continuous succession, but passed also to others of other tribes, yet until the times of the Messiah it always returned several times to the descendants of Judah: as when, after Othoniel, who was of the tribe of Judah, the government indeed passed to other princes, but in such a way that it returned to the tribe of Judah shortly after, when Abesan was constituted supreme Judge of the whole people: and again, when David and Solomon began to reign first over Judah, then over the remaining tribes of Israel as well, and his descendants over the two tribes, until the Babylonian transmigration: when finally, after the return from the Babylonian captivity, although for many centuries of years the principate was in the hands of the High Priests, who originated from other tribes, as it was also in the hands of the Maccabees; yet from them the principate returned again, and the scepter of the whole kingdom of Israel, to a man of the tribe of Judah, namely to Herod, under the end of whose reign was born Christ, the true Messiah who was then expected. That this Herod was indeed an Idumean or Ascalonite by upbringing, or as the Fathers say, a foreigner, but in blood and lineage a Jew, Augustinus Torniellus confirms quite extensively and forcefully in his Sacred Annals under the Year of the World 4018, Sect. 7 and 8, against those who maintain the contrary, using Nicolaus of Damascus, a most weighty author, Suidas, and other approved authors, and indeed even sufficiently evident reasons. We agree with him in this part all the more willingly, the more strength and weight this opinion seems to contribute to establishing the prophecy of Jacob. For if, according to the common and inveterate opinion, Herod was not a Jew by blood, but a foreigner, it will follow that, upon his being raised to the kingdom, and indeed before the Messiah was born, the Scepter had been completely taken away from Judah: a thing which simply conflicts with the Jacobite prophecy, since it clearly implies that this Scepter was not to be taken away from Judah before the Messiah, but only after the Messiah had already been brought into the light. We maintain, therefore, that the kingdom at the time of Christ's birth was in the hands of Herod, and that he was indeed a Jew by blood, and consequently that the Scepter still remained with the tribe of Judah under his rule. But when and how the Scepter was gradually taken away from Judah under the reign of Herod, and with the Messiah already brought into the light, so that it could never again recover its strength, but was plainly and fully subjected to the dominion of the Roman Emperors, that must be explained in a few words.

gradually, and by various degrees, it can be demonstrated to the eye. For shortly after the death of Herod, although Archelaus is said to have reigned in place of his father, having been constituted Ethnarch of the Jews by Caesar Augustus: he was nevertheless never able to obtain royal dignity from Caesar: as Josephus testifies in Book 17 of the Antiquities, chapter 13, and Book 2 of the Jewish War, chapter 4. But rather, in the end, the same Archelaus was relegated to Gaul by the same Augustus, and Judea came under the empire and government of the Romans: under which it also remained throughout the whole time of Christ's life spent in these lands, and subsequently even up to Claudius Caesar, having no king but Caesar. Nor does it stand in the way that later the same Claudius (as Josephus testifies, Book 19 of the Antiquities, chapter 4) gave the kingdom of Judea, among other things, to Herod Agrippa, the grandson of Herod the Ascalonite; yet this government had scarcely begun when it again met its end according to the truth of the prophecy of Jacob: for after the third year from when he had obtained this kingdom, he died (as Josephus reports not far from the end of Book 19 of the Antiquities and Book 2 of the Jewish War, chapter 10), struck by divine vengeance by an Angel, because he had not attributed to God himself the divine honors shown to him by the people: Acts 12:23. And from this time Judea always had Roman governors, so that a King and Leader from the seed of David was truly taken away from it, nor did it ever afterwards aspire in any way, or under any form of government, to its former dignity of ruling: just as the Jews themselves confessed in express words before Pilate, that they had no king but Caesar. For neither the son of Herod Agrippa, who was called Agrippa the younger to distinguish him from his father, and of whom there is mention several times in Acts chapters 25 and 26, nor any other Jew afterwards reigned absolutely in Judea. And although Claudius Caesar, after the death of Agrippa the elder, granted to Herod his brother and Dynast, or king of Chalcis, a certain power over the temple and the sacred treasury, and the right of electing High Priests, which remained to his descendants even until the end of the Jewish war, as Josephus testifies in Book 20 of the Antiquities, at the end of the first chapter: yet he granted him no rights of any Kingdom. What is more, in the progress of time, when the Jews attempted to shake off the Roman dominion through various seditions and rebellions, not only was Jerusalem (which from the time of David had begun to belong to the tribe of Judah, and had been the head, metropolis, and seat of the Jewish kingdom) captured and overturned by Titus: but the kingdom itself was likewise utterly lost to the region of the Jews, and royal power and the principate utterly perished from the seed or descendants of Judah: with the Jews themselves being partly killed in various ways, partly dispersed most miserably through various regions of the world, and thus reduced to perpetual servitude, and the tribes so intermingled and confused with one another, that today it is not even certain to the Jews themselves which is, or where properly, the tribe of Judah, or if it can be found. And these things indeed concerning the prophecy of the Patriarch Jacob,

Latin:

Deindè manifestè pugnat glossa hæc Judaica cum tota textus συντελείᾳ: quæ ostendit, Iacobum hoc loco non agere de imminutione, sive excisione tribus Iuda, nedùm infausta ei ominari: sed vaticinari de ipsius magnificētia & excelsitate, quòd nimirùm penes hanc tribum Iuda sit mansurum dominium usq; ad adventum Messiæ. Quam ob causam eidem tribuit in præcedentibus assignavit robur leoninum, quo potentiam suam exeruit in reliquas tribus. Et quanquàm postmodùm defectione decem tribuum, tribus hæc valdè imminuta fuit: semper tamen Regum Iuda autoritas major mansit, quàm regū Israel: tùm propter sedem regni Davidici, tùm propter religionem & promissiones de Messia posteris Davidis factas, tùm denique propter collegium Seniorum à Mose institutum: Undè vanitas cavilli Iudaici ultrò patet.

Cujus farinæ est & illud, quòd duas illas particulas עַד כִּי exponūt per postquam hoc sensu: Postquàm venerit Siloh, sive Messias, regnum de Juda non amplius auferetur. Atqui illud in hunc usque diem est ablatum de Iuda. Ergo Siloh sive Messias nondùm venit in mundum.

Respondeo, Majorem esse falsissimam. Nititur n. manifestâ de pravatione significationis propriæ ac genuinæ duarum illarum vocum עַד כִּי quæ attestantibus omnibus sanioribus Hebræis nuspiam significant Postquam, vel quando: sed semper notant idem, ac, Donec vel usque quò &c. uti infinita Scripturæ testimonia comprobant, & ipsorum Judeorum Rabini fatentur.

Mirum autem cuipiam haud immeritò videri possit, quis Spiritus impulerit Iohannem Calvinum, ut super hoc ipsum vaticinium Jacobi Patriarchæ Judeis ex parte suffragari non dubitaverit, his verbis: Quòd ex Judau quide expōnunt, jus regnandi datum esse tribui Juda, quia nefas fuerit aliò transferri, non autem quòd gloriā coronæ semel erectā perpetuari necesse fuerit, aliqua ex parte huic sententiæ suffragari necesse arbitror. Sed malitiosè pervertit statū controversiæ Calvinus, imò vaticinio Jacobi alienum planè sensum affingit. Neque enim hoc vult Jacobus, quòd regnū tribus Juda in perpetuo dignitatis atque eminentiæ flore sit futurum, usque ad adventum Meffiæ: quodque una eademque semper illius regiminis forma sit mansura. Largimur enim ipsi quoque, varias mutationes & eclipses quasi, hoc regnum perpessum esse, tùm potissimùm, quando Judæi quingentis annis fuerunt alienis regibus tributarii: quando sub Antiocho regii generis dignitas fuit extincta: quando Asmonæi titulum & honores regios sibi usurparunt. Quin imò largimur ultrò, varias hasce mutationes formæ regni Judaici, ab ipsis quoque prophetis prædictas fuisse, ut quando Jezechiel Cap. 21. 26. prædixit fore, ut corona, quæ erat infigne regiæ majestatis, mutaretur in cidarin, quæ erat insigne sacerdotale: Exod. 28. 4. Levit. 16. 4. & postmodum fuit etiam insigne Principum. Esa. 22. 18. Unde vocatur Cidaris regni Esa. 62. 3. Quo sanè pacto fatis perspicuè prædictum Regiam potestatem tribus Juda post Sedechiam degeneraturam in Ducalem: & loco Regum, Principes dominaturos. Quin imò neque illud etiam ignoramus, nedùm negamus, prædictum esse, fore, ut Cidaris quoq;, hoc est, ducalis potestas auferatur de domo David, & sic de tribu Juda, & cū alia regiminis forma commutetur: id quod per Antiochum, Machabæos, Sacerdotes summos, & Herodem factū esse, & per annos 160. ante natum Christum durasse, ex historia sacra certum est. Quanquam verò personæ, quæ hoc tempore principatum gesserunt, non omnes fuerunt de tribu Juda: niholominus tamen ipsum jus Regni, & dignitas regalis penes tribum Juda mansit: haud secus, atq; hodiè imperium Romanum est & dicitur Romanum, licet Imperator ipse sit natione vel Græcus, vel Hispanus, vel Gallus. Proindè Calvini gloffa nihil facit ad rem, propterea, quòd Jacobus minimè omnium id notatum voluit, ac si una eademque semper, usque ad adventum Meffiæ futura sit regni tribus Juda, forma, facies, fortuna, conditio.

Verùm hoc significare voluit, Imperium sive regnum tribus Juda, sub diversis etiam gubernationum formis, continuandum esse usque ad adventum Siloh sive Meffiæ: haud secus, ac si dixisset Jacobus; Non penitùs deficiet regia potestas de tribu Juda, ita, ut nunquàm ampliùs recuperetur.

Quanquam ergo non perpetuo, & continuata successione, principatus in viris de tribu Juda remansit: sed ad alios quoque aliarum tribuum pertransiit : tamen usque ad Messiae tempora semper aliquoties ad Judae posteros rediit: ut quando post Othonielem qui erat, de tribu Juda, ad alios principes regimen quidem pertransiit, sed ita, ut ad tribum Judam paulo post redierit, quando Abesan constitutus est totius populi supremus Iudex: & rursus, quando super Judam primo, deinde super reliquas quoque tribus Israel regnare ceperunt David & Salomo, & posteri ejus super duas tribus, usque ad transmigrationem Babylonicam: quando denique post reditum ex captivitate Babylonica, licet per plures annorum centurias principatus penes summos Sacerdotes, de aliis tribubus oriundos, ut & penes Machabaeos fuerit; attamen ab ipsis denuo rediit principatus, sceptrumq; totius regni Israel, ad virum de tribu Juda, nempe ad Herodem, sub cujus regni finem natus est Christus, verus, qui tunc expectabatur, Messias. Herodem autem istum educatione quidem Idumaeum, aut Ascalonitam, vel ut Patres loquuntur, alienigenam, sanguine vero, ac genere Judaeum fuisse, contra diversum statuentes, prolixe satis ac nervose exNicolao Damas ceno, autore gravissimo, ex Suida & aliis probatis autoribus, quin etiam rationibus satis evidentibus confirmat Augustinus Torniellus in Annalibus sacris sub Anno Mundi 4018. Sect. 7. & 8. Cui hac in parte tanto lubentius suffragamur; quanto plus roboris ac momenti ad stabiliendum vaticinium Iacobi ex hac sententia redundare videtur. Si enim secundum communem, & inveteratam opinionem Herodes sanguine non fuit Iudaeus: sed alienigena: sequetur, ipso ad regnum evecto, & quidem ante natum Messiam, Sceptrum de Iuda penitus fuisse ablatum: id quod cum vaticinio Iacobeo simpliciter pugnat, quippe quod diserte innuit, Sceptrum hoc de Juda, non ante Messiam; sed in lucem jam edito Messia demum auferendum esse. Satuimus ergo regnum tempore nati Christi fuisse penes Herodem, & quidem sanguine Iudaeu, ac proinde Sceptru penes tribum Iuda sub hujus regimine adhuc mansisse. Quando vero & quomodo palatim sub regno Herodis, & Messiah jam in lucem edito, Sceptrum de Iuda penitus sit ablatum, ita ut vires nunquam amplius refumere potuerit, sed Romanorum Imperatorum dominatui plane ac plene subjectum fuerit, id vero paucis explicandum est.

paulatim, & diversis gradibus, ad oculum demonstrari potest. Nam paulo post Herodis mortem, quamvis pro ejus patre regnasse dicatur Archelaus, a Cæsare Augusto constitutus Judeorum Ethmarcha: nunquam tamen regiam dignitatem a Cæsare impetrare potuit: teste Josepho lib. 17. Antiquit. cap. 13. & lib. 2. de bello Jud. cap. 4. Quin potius tandem idem Archelaus, ab eodem Augusto in Galliam relegatus fuit, & Judæa sub Romanorum imperium ac regimen pervenit: sub quo etiam toto vitae Christi, in terris hisce peractae, tempore, & deinceps usq; quoq; ad Claudii Caesarem ita permansit, non habens regem, nisi Cæsarem. Neque obstat, quod postea idem Claudius (teste Josepho, lib. 19. antiquit. cap. 4.) Judæae regnum, inter caetera, dedit Herodi Agrippae, Herodis Ascalonitae nepoti; tamen vix dum ceptum erat hoc regimen, rursus secundum veritatem vaticinii Jacobi, finem fortitum est: Siquidem post triennium, ex quo regnum hoc obtinuerat, interiit: (uti refert Josephus non procul a fine lib. 19. antiq & lib. 2. de bello Jud. cap. 10.) divina ultione percussus ab Angelo, eo quod divinos honores sibi a populo exhibitos, in ipsum Deum non retulisset: Act. 12. 23. Et ab hoc tempore Judæa Romanos praesides semper habuit, ut vere ab ea ablatus sit Rex, & Dux de semine David, neque unquam postmodum ad pristinam dominandi dignitatem ullo pacto, sive sub ulla aliqua gubernationis forma adspiraverit: queadmodu ipsimet Judaei coram Pilato disertis verbis fassi sunt, se non habere regem, praeter Cæsarem. Nam neque filius Herodis Agrippae, qui ad differentiam patris Agrippa junior dicebatur, & cujus Act. capp. 25. & 26. aliquoties sit mentio, neque quisquam alius deinceps Judaeus in Judaea absolute regnavit. Et quanquam Claudius Caesar post Agrippae senioris mortem, Herodi ejus fratri ac Dynastae, sive regi Chalcidis, quandam concessit in templum, & sacrum aerarium potestatem, & jus eligendi Pontifices, quod posteris etiam usque ad exitum belli Judaici mansit, teste Josepho lib. 20. antiq. sub finem capitis primi: tamen Regni alicujus jura eidem minime concessit, Quid quod progressu temporis, cum Judaei Romanorum dominatum per seditiones ac rebelliones varias excutere tentarent, non modo Hierosolyma (quae a tempore Davidis ad tribum Juda pertinere ceperat, ac regni Judaici caput, metropolis, sedesque fuerat) a Tito capta atque eversa est: sed & ipsum pariter regnum a regione Judaeorum, & regia potestas ac principatus, a semine, sive posteris, Judae penitus excidit: ipsis Judaeis partim varie interfectis, partim per diversas orbis regiones miserrime dispersis, inque servitutem perpetuam ita redactis, ac tribubus ita invicem permixtis, ac confusis, ut hodie ne ipsis quidem Judaeis constet, quaenam, vel ubinam proprie tribus Juda sit, aut inveniri possit. Et haec quidem de vaticinio Jacobi Patriarchae,


### On King Christ or Messiah: Just now in (continued)

But the first foundations of this matter were laid by Herod himself, who in the penultimate year of his reign killed all the elders who had sprung from the tribe of David, and substituted in their place those learned in the law.

Now, towards the end of the reign of Herod, Christ was born, and the prophecy of Jacob was truly fulfilled, although not in one single moment, but

We seek a SECOND testimony of Scripture, which proves that the time destined in the Scriptures for the Nativity of the Messiah passed many centuries ago, from that place or prophecy of the Angel, which confirms that the Messiah was to be born when the seventy weeks of Daniel were completed, and in Daniel himself according to the Hebrew version it stands thus: Seventy weeks are cut off (determined) upon thy people, and upon thy holy city (or thy holy one) to finish the transgression: and to seal up (end) sins, and to expiate iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the holy of holies. And thou shalt know and understand from the going forth of the word to return, and to build Jerusalem, unto the Messiah the leader, seven weeks, and sixty and two weeks it shall return: and the street and the wall shall be built, and in the straitness of times. And after sixty-two weeks the Messiah shall be cut off, and shall not be: And the people of the leader that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and his end shall be in a flood, and even to the end of the war, desolations are determined. And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week, and in the half of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and upon the extension of abominations he shall make it desolate, and even to the consummation and the end the desolation shall endure. Daniel 9. 24. & seqq.

The sum of this prophecy (insofar as it pertains to the present question) consists solely in this, that the Angel predicts that from the going forth of the mandate concerning the repair of the Temple and the city, until the Messiah the Leader and the confirmation of the new covenant, there would be seventy weeks. Which, since both Jews and Christians confess to be not of days, but of years: such as the Mosaic law also observed in the calculation of the years of the Jubilee. Num. 14. 34. Ezech. 4. 6. But since it is established that they were completed fifteen centuries ago and more, by the very confession of the Jews themselves, it follows by irrefragable necessity that the Messiah has already, and indeed so many centuries ago, truly come into this world, and has duly experienced each and every one of the offices defined by the Angel in this place. But it is too diluted and cold that certain Jews understand by the Messiah in this prophecy either Cyrus, or Nehemiah, or Joshua the high priest, who is mentioned in Hag. 1. 1., or Zerubbabel. For the beginning, perhaps, but not the completion of the 70 weeks, falls into their times. Furthermore, the predicates of the Messiah expressed in this place do not apply to those individuals: namely, to finish transgressions: to expiate sins: to bring in everlasting righteousness: to fulfill every vision and prophecy: to abrogate the Levitical sacrifices: to be the Holy of Holies, etc.

However, the disagreement of chronologers has caused the opinion of all interpreters, even the Orthodox, not to be one concerning the beginning and the end of those seventy weeks. Which dispute we certainly do not make our own in this place: meanwhile, with a certain more recent one, and

with a chronologer more accurate than all the rest, we state thus: that the chief cause of the diversity of these opinions is this, that they did not first count the time itself by itself, and afterwards apply the historical events to it, and that they did not attempt to elicit the mind of the Prophet Daniel from the words of the prophecy themselves: but twisted the words themselves to their own preconceived opinion: although the words, if they are looked at simply, with histories set aside for a little while, would seem obvious and open to anyone. For as far as the end of the same is concerned, it is manifestly shown immediately in the proposition of the prophecy, when the Angel says: Seventy weeks are determined or cut off upon the people and the holy city. If seventy weeks are determined, that is, if seventy weeks are the measure of the time during which the holy city or the Jewish polity is to endure, then those seventy weeks are certainly finished by the destruction of the Jewish people and the city of Jerusalem: otherwise they could not be a measure of time.
