Therefore the Hebrew word עַלְמָה remains in its proper and native signification entirely unblemished: that it signifies a young virgin entirely intact.

But the same people object to the verse immediately following, 20, where Solomon seems to append the reason for which the way of a man with a maiden seems unknown to him: saying thus, such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats, and wipes her mouth, and denies that she has committed iniquity: As if Solomon had said: Just as no trace of corruption and committed fornication remains in a girl already corrupted before, so it happens to an adulterous woman, who is accustomed to brazen it out when she has made herself available to others besides her husband, so that her crime cannot be recognized. Therefore, they say, Almah in this place denotes a corrupted girl, not a virgin. But I answer, 1. that this gloss conflicts with the text itself: For in the preceding verse, 19, he does not say that it seems wonderful to him that an external trace of corruption does not appear in a girl already corrupted: but he says that the way of a man with a maiden is wonderful and inscrutable to him: Where it has already been shown that that natural way of a man with a maiden or girl, being most well-known to Solomon, is not what is meant.

Latin:

Sunt deinde ex Judæis, qui hoc loco ipsi Prophetæ Esaiæ filium promitti fingunt. Sed & istorum vanitas ultrò patescit. Nam duorum filiorum Esaiæ meminit Scriptura : Unius, qui Prophetæ jam modò ante hoc vaticinium natus fuerat : Alterius verò capite octavo fit mentio, qui tamen ipso DEO jubente non Emmanuel, sed aliis nominibus indigitari debuit, ut patet ex versu 3. capitis octavi.

Tertiò cavillantur alii, Nihil quicquam nativitatem Messiæ ad rem præsentem potuisse facere. Qvia enim Achazo Regi Jųda Signum de præsenti dari debuit, qvo certissimus redderetur de liberatione ab hostibus illis duobus, nempè à Rege Israelis, & Rege Syriæ: At verò nativitas Messiæ multis demùm seculis pòst eventura erat. Ergo figni loco ea dari non potuit. Sed ad hoc cavillum respondet textus ipse, perspicuè ostendens, 1. Achazum Signum à DEO petere noluisse, eò quòd tale Signum vel præstari non posse, existimaret, vel si maximè præstaretur, fidem tamen promissionibus de futurâ illâ liberatione adhibere nollet. Deindè verò DEUM, hac partim hypocrisi, partim diffidentiâ Regis Achazi offensum, Signum dedisse, non Achazo, quem indignum judicabat, sed domui David, & toti ejus posteritati: proindè Propheta non ampliùs Achazum, sed domum David compellat, & huic Signum promittit, & tale quidem Signum, quòd non modò in præsente periculo consternatos Judæorum animos erigere posset, sed quod ad ipsam quoque nativitatem Messiæ, in quibuscunque calamitatibus prodesfet credentibus. Ea enim populi Judaici erat natura, ut quotiescunque gravior aliqva ingrueret calamitas, toties metueret stirpis suæ excisionem, ita ut simul irritæ redderentur omnes promissiones, quæ unqvàm uspiam de venturo Messiah essent editæ. Huic ergo metui, & pusillanimitati medicinam adhibiturus Deus, hoc loco non modò jam trepidantes erigere: sed etiam in futuris variis calamitatibus populi, firmam consolationem præstare voluit, non tantùm repetitâ promissione de exhibendo Messiah: sed & eandem novâ promissione illustrando. Prima enim & vetustissima promissio habebat, Semen mulieris contriturum esse caput serpentis. Hæc promissio postea sic illustrata fuerat, ut pro Semine mulieris nominaretur Semen Abrahæ, ex lumbis Davidis. Qvia verò, qui Semen Abrahæ & Davidis nominabatur, existimari poterat, usitatâ generatione, ex commixtione maris & fœminæ oriturus esse: Ideò jam cognitâ familiâ, ad id explicandum redit Dominus, quod in ipsâ primâ promissione nondum fuerat observatum : Messiam scilicet ex semine quidem Abrahæ & Davidis nasciturum, non tamen Semen viri futurum esse, sed Semen mulieris, & quidem puræ ac immaculatæ virginis. Jam ergo, quamdiu virgineus iste partus differebatur, tamdiu Judæi certi esse debebant, non planè sublatum aut excisum iri hunc populum, donec ederetur partus iste virgineus : id quod etiam vaticinium Patriarchæ Jacobi innuebat, uti suprà ostensum. Qvibus consideratis, manifestum est, haud magis ad consolandum appositum signum dari Judæis potuisse, quàm hoc ipsum, quod non ad unam quampiam hujus populi calamitatem esset limitatum : sed ad ipsum usque Messiam benè multis seculis se extenderet. Tandem sunt ex Judæis, qui negant hoc loco, vocem Hebræam עַלְמָה Almah significare virginem, sed notare tantùm conditionem ætatis juvenilis, ita ut exponi possit pro juvenculâ etiam corruptâ sive maritatâ : hoc sensu : Ecce adolescentula concipiet & pariet : Nam si de virginis conceptu locutus esset, non dixisset, Ecce הָעַלְמָה Haalma, id est, adolescentula: sed, Ecce בְּתוּלָה Bethulah, hoc est, virgo concipiet. Verùm stupendam vanitatem objectionis hujus evidenter initiò demonstrat scopus & intentio Prophetæ. Nam ex mandato DEI miraculosum quoddam signum Judæis erigere voluit, ex quo in quibusvis calamitatibus certum ac infallibile argumentum petere possint, se nondum planè excisum aut deletum iri, quia nondum Signum hoc implerum sit, hoc est, quia nondum virgo peperit filium. Nam ut adolescentula sive maritata, sive corrupta filium pariat, Signi instar esse haud potuit. Deinde (annotante etiam Galatino lib. 7. cap. 15.) tria sunt apud Hebræos vocabula, idem ferè significantia ; nempe נַעֲרָה Naarah : בְּתוּלָה bethulah : & עַלְמָה Almah : inter quæ primùm, nempe Naarah, ad ætatem tantùm fœminarum refertur, sive virgines illæ sint, sive à viro cognitæ : Undè quamlibet adhuc puellam sive adolescentulam significat. Alterum verò, nempè Bethulah, virginitatem significat, non modò juvenicularum, sed annis etiam ac ætate provectiorum fœminarum.

Tertium deniq;, nempè Almah, ad utrumque respectum habens, ætatem juvenilem, & virginitatem uno eodemq́; nomine comprehendit & exprimit. Ergo secundum propriam affectionem Hebræam trium istorum vocabulorum, omnis fœmina, sive juvencula sit, sive annosa, quamdiu virgo est, Bethulah appellari potest. Quamdiu autem juvencula est, sive adhuc sit virgo, sive corrupta, Naarah nuncupatur. Almah autem nulla vocari potest, nisi simul sit & juvencula, & virgo intacta : id quod ipsum etiam vocabuli ἔτυμον evincit. Deducitur enim à radice עָלַם quod abscondere, sive celare significat : ita ut nomen עַלְמָה Almah notet adolescentulam aspectibus hominum adhuc quasi absconditam, occultam, atque omninò intactam, de cujus pudicitia atq; integritate nullum sit dubium : maximè cum nomini huic præfigitur articulus, qui apud Hebræos est litera ה He. Nec in totâ Scripturâ Sacrâ invenitur dictio hæc הָעַלְמָה Haalmah, cum articulo He, præterquam in tribus locis, in quibus semper notat virginem juvenculam, puram ac intemeratam : ut Gen. 24:43. Rebeccam, priusquàm Isaaco desponderetur : deinde Exod. 2. 8. Miriam soror Mosis, valde adhuc puellam, ut ex chronologiâ licet conjicere : & tandem matrem Meffiæ, hoc loco, Esa. 7, 14. Quemadmodum ergo Spiritus Sanctus in duobus præcedentibus locis, per vocem הָעַלְמָה Haalmah, non nisi virginem juvenčulam, & planè illibatam notare voluit : dubium certè pio nemini esse potest, quin apud Esaiam quoque per eandem vocem articulatam idem exprimere voluerit. Quam ipsam etiam ob causam, matrem Mesfiæ non Bethulah, sed Haalmah nominare voluit : ut utrumque exprimeret, nempe & adolescentiam, & virginitatem : Nam si dixisset : Ecce Bethulah concipiet, tunc unum tantùm, nempè virginitatem, non verò adolescentiam expressisset. Præter tria isthæc loca, occurrit adhuc unus, Proverb. 30. 19. ubi Salomo inquit : Tria sunt abscondita à me, & quatuor, vel quartum non cognovi : Viam aquilæ in cœlis : viam serpentis super petram : viam navis in corde maris : & viam viri in virgine, בְּעַלְמָה גֶּבֶר וְדֶרֶךְ . De quo loco tumultuantur quidam non Judæi tantùm : sed & Christiani interpretes Hebræi, inter quos est & Pagninus in Lexico, Mercerus super hunc locum, & alij, contendentes, per Almah notari hoc loco juvenculam jam corruptam, ac proindè virginitatem matris Mesfiæ ex vocabuli hujus naturâ & affectione evidenter demonstrari non posse. Verùm ipsa textus evidentia hanc interpretum istorum incogitantiam satis arguit. Quod enim Salomon non intelligat, naturalem illam permixtionem viri cum virgine, vel illud arguit, quod dicit, se hoc planè non cognoscere vel intelligere posse, cùm tamen naturalis illa via viri in virgine plærisque sit cognitissima : Salomoni cum primis, qui naturas hominum, animalium, plantarum, usque ad minima habuit cognitas & perspectas. 1. Reg. 4. 29. & seqq. Ergo de aliâ aliquâ planè supernaturali via viri in virgine loquatur Salomon, omninò necesse est. Illa verò supernaturalis, & Salomoni incognita via, nulla erit alia, quàm de quâ Esaias hoc loco agit, quòd nimirùm virgo paritura sit filium, & de quâ clariùs Propheta Jeremias cap. 31. DEUS creabit novum super terram : Fœmina circumdabit virum, & quidem virum גֶבֶר Ghever, hoc est, fortem, potentem, nempè DEUM ipsum. Via ergo viri fortis & potentis in almah, apud Salomonem nihil est aliud, quàm ipsa Filij DEI ex virgine incarnatio. Et hanc quidem viam plenè atque perfectè Salomon cognoscere non potuit : Quo nimirum pacto, absque humano semine virgo concipere posset, ac perfectum DEUM & hominem in utero concludere, filiumq́; parere, ac virgo post partum etiam remanere, nec Salomonis intellectus plenè capere potuit, nec unquam lingua ulla explicare. Manet proindè vocabulo Hebræo עַלְמָה propria & nativa sua significatio prorsus illibata : quòd nimirùm juvenculam virginem prorsus intactam significet.

Sed objiciunt iidem versum immedietè subsequentem 20. ubi Salomon rationem subjungere videtur, propter quam via viri in virgine sibi incognita videatur: Sic inquiens, est via mulieris adulteræ: concedit, & abstergit os suum, ac negat, se iniquitatem admisisse: Quasi dixerit Salomon: Quemadmodum corruptionis, & stupris commissi nullum superest in puellâ jam antè corrupta vestigium: ita & mulieri adulteræ usu venit, quæ frontem perfricare solet, ubi aliis, extra maritum, sui copiam fecit, ut scelus ejus agnosci non possit. Ergo, inquiunt, Almah hoc loco notat puellam corruptam, non virginem. Sed respondeo, 1. glossam hanc pugnare cum ipso textu: Neque enim versu præcedente 19. illud sibi mirabile videri dicit, quod in virgine jam corrupta non appareat externum corruptionis vestigium: sed viam viri in virgine mirabilem sibi, & imperscrutabilem esse dicit: Ubi naturalem illam viam viri in virgine sive puella, quippe Salomoni perspectissimam, non intelligi, jam ostensum.


### On King Christ or Messiah: Question II. Whether Jesus of Nazareth, son of Mary, is that very promised Messiah of the world? (continued)

Furthermore, as for the following verse, 20, the interpretation of Nicolaus de Lyra does not displease us, who posits that Solomon is bringing in a kind of corollary and gathering from the preceding verse that the malice of the Jewish people is also clearly wonderful to him: so that by the adulterous woman he understands the impregnable malice of the Jewish Synagogue, which, having been betrothed to God on Mount Sinai at the reception of the Law, immediately turned away from God through idolatry, in the adoration of the calf, and afterwards in innumerable idolatries. Nor do we reject the explanation of Galatinus, who, following certain ancient Jews, considers that the prevarication of the first parent is understood in this place by the way of an adulterous woman, because just as the way of an adulterous woman is, so also was the sin of Adam fashioned: for Adam, having committed the fall, did all this to excuse himself for his sin, and to shift all the blame from himself, saying, The woman whom you gave to be with me, gave me of the tree, and I ate: and he acted like a harlot, who eats and wipes her mouth, contending that she has done nothing wrong. P. Galat. book 7, chapter 15, page 534 in my edition. But these responses seem fetched from afar, and do not yet solve the knot. We, saving the sounder judgment of everyone, maintain that the Jewish inference must simply be denied: namely, that verse 20 acts as an ἀποδόσεως συγκριτικῆς (comparative apodosis) to the preceding verse 19, in this sense: that just as no external trace of committed adultery appears in an adulteress, so in a girl deflowered and known by a man, likewise no sign of this matter meets the eyes. For it is not likely that Solomon was concerned in this place with some discrete knowledge of a chaste versus a deflowered maiden: so that he could discern between them accurately and by some evident sign meeting the eyes. For to what end, I ask, would this have profited him, either for the administration of the kingdom, or for the benefit of his own safety, or for the happiness of his subjects, or for the advancement of the truth of divine worship? Certainly, nothing at all. We therefore more correctly maintain that the Holy Spirit in both those verses raised the mind of Solomon to the contemplation of more sublime things: so that one must not stick to the letter, but the spiritual sense must be sought, which, as to what it is regarding verse 19, we showed a little earlier: But as for the twentieth verse, we maintain that by the way of an adulterous woman Solomon understood a certain mystery unknown and clearly hidden to him, whatever that may be. But even if we should urge the literal sense to the utmost, nothing would nevertheless be lost from our opinion. For in two ways things are said to be such or such: either ἀληθῶς (truly) in reality: or δοξαστικῶς, ἢ εἰρωνικῶς (by opinion or ironically): just as sometimes a wicked man is called a good man: not that he is such in reality: but partly ironically: partly by opinion, because he is thought to be such. Thus in this place Solomon calls the harlot woman Haalmah, a virgin: not that she is such, but because she is thought to be such, because she knows how to brazen out her harlot's face so that between her and Almah, that is, an intact virgin, no difference appears. Where indeed the Hebrew word Almah retains its own proper and native meaning entirely safe and sound. And Solomon's own words confirm this explanation. For after he said: That he did not know the way of a man with a maiden: If you ask, with what maiden? he immediately in the following verse explains the kind of maidens: Such, he says, is the way of a woman committing whoredom, she eats, then wipes her mouth: and says, I have not worked iniquity, that is, I am still Almah, a virgin girl, untouched by a man. Whence it shines forth most clearly that Solomon is specifically attacking her who shamelessly affirms herself to be a virgin, and is therefore held to be a virgin by human opinion. Therefore the argument of the Jews concludes nothing, since a figurative manner of speaking does not overturn the proper meaning of this name Almah, which we rightly urge against the Jews both in other places of Scripture cited above: and most especially in this seventh chapter of Isaiah, where the birth of the virgin, the mother of the Messiah, is expressly treated. To which is added also this, that the subsequent words in Isaiah וְקָרָאת שְׁמוֹ עִמָּנוּאֵל And you shall call (namely, you mother) his name Immanuel: evidently establish a virgin birth. For (as Calvin also orthodoxly maintains in this part) the word וְקָרָאת Vekaraah is of the feminine gender, and directly refers to the mother. Where it is certain that something beyond the customary manner is being expressed. For among the Hebrews, not mothers, but fathers imposed names upon their sons, as can be gathered from the entire Sacred history of the Old Testament, and in the New Testament, from the history of the nativity of John the Baptist. For this sign was as it were of the right and power of fathers over their sons: nor did the same authority pertain to women. But here it is transferred to the mother. It follows, therefore, according to this prophecy of Isaiah, that the Messiah had to be conceived and born of a mother in such a way that he lacks a father on earth: otherwise the Prophet would pervert the common usage of Scripture, which ascribes this office only to men. And such is the force and evidence of this argument that even some of the Jewish Rabbis themselves have confessed that in this place is hinted both the virginity of Mary and, in the name Emmanuel, GOD with us, that incomparable mystery concerning the two natures, divine and human, to be personally united in the one person of the Messiah, and already most truly and realistically united in the person of Jesus of Nazareth. On which matter see P. Galatinus, book 3, chapter 18.

Furthermore, they object that Jesus of Nazareth is not that promised Messiah in Isaiah, because he was named not Emmanuel, but Jesus. But the consequence is rightly denied: for one must distinguish between names that designate nature and those that define the office of a person. For it is established that nature itself, which gives form to a thing, also gives a name to that same thing. Just as nature gives a man both humanity and the name that he is, and is called, a man. So also our Messiah, Emmanuel, that is, GOD with us, is rightly named by the Prophet from the consideration of his person, which is both GOD and man, and deserves to be so named by all Christians. Moreover, at his circumcision, the Messiah was named from his office Jesus, that is, Savior, because he was to save his people from their sins: as the Angel testifies in Matthew 1, verse 21. Now this name does not exclude, but includes the name of Immanuel: for he who is the Savior and liberator of the people from their sins, it is fitting that he be not only Man, but also GOD, that is, the true Immanuel. Furthermore, if the Jewish exception held any strength and weight, certainly the Messiah, brought forth into this world, ought to have been designated not only as Immanuel, but also as Wonderful, Mighty GOD, Seed of the woman, Seed of Abraham, Seed of David, Father of the age, Prince of peace, and other names of that kind with which the Prophets adorn him. But now it is manifest that these names were assigned to the Messiah by the Prophets, not because these names must be imposed upon him at his Circumcision, but only so that they might define partly his person and partly his office. Which names, individually and collectively, the single name JESUS embraces under its scope with a certain admirable emphasis.

This having been demonstrated so far, namely that the Messiah was to be born of an intact virgin: there remains the accommodation of this criterion to Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary. To discuss which at length would not be worth the effort. For we have a witness to this matter who is above all exception, the Angel, Matthew 1, verse 20, thus to Joseph: All this was done that it might be fulfilled which the Lord spoke by the Prophet: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son: and you shall call (not he shall call) his name Immanuel: which is, if you interpret it, GOD with us. Which same thing is confirmed in Luke 2, verse 5, and chapter 3, verse 23. Nor have the Jews to this very day been able to bring forward anything that could even plausibly obscure the virginity of Mary or render it suspect. But enough and more than enough about the second criterion of the Messiah.

The THIRD criterion of the exhibited Messiah is most exactly completed in Jesus of Nazareth, because the things which were to happen partly when the Messiah was already born, according to the oracles of the prophets, and partly were to be designated by his own works and miracles: these, individually and collectively, found their fulfillment in no one else but in Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary: such as these principal ones:

1. In Hosea 11, verse 1, it is said of the Messiah: Out of Egypt I have called my son. That this was fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth, Matthew 2, verse 15, is the witness. Jesus, he says, was in Egypt until the death of Herod: that it might be fulfilled which the Lord spoke by the Prophet: Out of Egypt I have called my son.

2. Thus in Jeremiah 31, verse 15: A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and much bitter weeping: Rachel weeps for her children, she would not admit consolation for her children, because none remains. This very thing was fulfilled when the little boy Jesus was already brought into the light, as Matthew chapter 2, verse 18, testifies.

3. Thus the Prophets preached everywhere about the miracles to be performed by the Messiah: Isaiah especially in chapter 35, verses 5 and 6: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped: Then the lame shall leap as a hart, and the tongue of the dumb shall sing. That this was fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth, the entire Evangelical history abundantly testifies: and especially Matthew chapter 15, verses 30 and 31. Then, he says, a great multitude approached him, having with them the lame, the blind, the dumb, the maimed, and many others, whom they cast at the feet of Jesus, and he healed them: so that the multitude marveled. Which same thing even the Jews cannot deny, although they slandered that he performed such signs by the power of Beelzebub.

4. Thus concerning the entry of the Messiah into the city of Jerusalem, Zechariah long ago predicted in chapter 9, verse 9, in these words: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion, shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: Behold, thy King comes to thee, just and a Savior, poor, and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass. That this was fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth, Matthew testifies, describing his entry into the city of Jerusalem, and in verse 8 repeating the prophecy of the prophet: Tell the daughter of Zion, Behold, thy King comes to thee meek, and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of a beast of burden.

5. Thus, those things which in the Psalms and Prophets are predicted at length concerning the passion, death, Resurrection, Ascension into heaven, and Session at the right hand of the Father: Psalm 16, 22, 69, 110, Isaiah 53, Zechariah 11, v. 12 & 13, and chapter 12, v. 10, and elsewhere throughout, that all of them were fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth is manifest in itself from the Evangelical history.

sons of his love. These and similar sayings partly oppose the kingdom of Christ emphatically to the multitude of the kingdoms of the world, under the note of Unity: but partly they exempt it from every human condition and form; so that the Roman Pontiff, who falsely claims to be the vicar of Christ and strives to assert and defend His Kingdom by external and earthly means, is insane with reason.

6. Finally, that which the Prophets predicted, that all nations and peoples would come to the Messiah, and through him would believe in the GOD of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, having abandoned their idols and abominations; that this was also abundantly fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth, both Apostolic and Ecclesiastical history testifies: indeed, experience itself even now testifies sufficiently and more than enough.

Then, just as the head relates to the body, so King Christ relates to his kingdom. Now, indeed, the whole Church relates to Christ as one Body to one head: indeed, the whole human race and all creatures are subject to him as King and Lord of all, Eph. 1, v. 22 & 23. He subjected all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all the Church, which is his Body, the fullness of him who fulfills all things in all. Therefore, the Christian faith teaches us to establish the king himself as One in number, and his Kingdom as Unique in essence.

With these things thus established, we invincibly conclude that Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary, is that true Messiah of the World promised to the Patriarchs and the faithful of the Old Testament, and that no other is to be expected.

Latin:

Deinde verò, quoab subsequentem versum 20. nobis non displicet interpretatio Nicolai Lyrani, qui Salomonem statuit Corollarium quasi quoddam inferre, & ex præcedenti versu colligere, Sic quoque malitiam gentis Judaicæ sibi planè esse mirabilem: ita ut per mulierem adulteram intelligat inexpugnabilem malitiam Synagogæ Judaicæ, quæ Deo desponsata in monte Sinai in legis susceptione statim declinavit à Deo per idololatriam, in adoratione vituli, & posteâ innumerabilibus idololatriis. Neque rejicimus etiam Galatini explicationem, qui priscos quosdam Judæos secutus, per viam mulieris adulteræ, censet hoc loco intelligi primi parentis prævaricationem, quòd sicut se habet via mulieris adulteræ, ita comparatum etiam sit peccatum Adami: Adam enim lapsu commisso totum hoc egit, ut de peccato suo se excusaret, omnemq; culpam à se amoliretur, Mulier inquiens, quam dedisti mihi sociam, dedit mihi de ligno, & comedi: fecitque ut meretrix, quæ comedit, & os abstergit, nihil mali se fecisse contendens. P. Galat. lib. 7. cap. 15. pag. mihi 534. Verùm videntur hæ responsiones longiùs petitæ, & nodum nondum solvere. Nos, salvo saniore cujusque judicio statuimus, simpliciter negandam esse illationem Judaicam: quòd nimirùm versus 20. habeat se instar ἀποδόσεως συγκριτικῆς ad versum præcedentem 19. hoc sensu: ut quemadmodum in adulterâ nullum apparet vestigium externum commissi adulterii: ita in puellâ stupratâ & à viro cognitâ, itidem nullum hujus rei signum incurrat in oculos. Nam verisimile non est, Salomonem sollicitum hoc loco fuisse de discretâ aliquâ notitiâ virginis illibatæ & stupratæ: ut videlicet accuratè, & ex signo aliquo evidenti, in oculos incurrente, inter eas discernere posset. Quorsum enim obsecro hoc ipsi vel ad regni administrationem, vel ad propriæ salutis emolumentum, vel ad subditorum felicitatem, vel ad cultus divini veritatem afferendam profuisset? Nihil certè quicquam. Rectius ergo statuimus, Spiritum Sanctum in utroque isto versu, mentem Salomonis ad contemplationem rerum sublimiorum evexisse: ita, ut literæ non sit inhærendum, sed Spiritualis sensus inquirendus, qui, qualis sit, quoad versum 19. paulò antè ostendimus: Quoad versum autem vicesimum, per viam mulieris adulteræ Salomonem mysterium quoddam sibi incognitum, & planè absconditum intellexisse, quale, quale illud sit, statuimus. Cæterùm si vel maximè literalem sensum urgeamus? nihil tamen nostræ decedet sententiæ. Duobus enim modis aliquid tale, vel tale esse dicuntur: vel ἀληθῶς reverâ: vel δοξαστικῶς, ἢ εἰρωνικῶς: quemadmodum interdum vir nequam dicitur vir Bonus: non quòd talis revera sit: sed partim εἰρωνικῶς: partim δοξαστικῶς, quia talis esse putatur. Sic hoc loco Salomon mulierem meretricem nominat Haalmah, virginem: non quòd talis sit, sed quia talis esse putatur, proptereà quòd frontem meretriciam ita perfricare novit, ut inter eam, & Almah, hoc est, virginem intactam, nihil appareat discriminis. Ubi sane voci Hebrææ Almah, sua propria & nativa significatio prorsus manet sarta & integra. Et explicationem hanc confirmant ipsa verba Salomonis. Nam postquam dixit: Se non novisse viam viri in virgine: Si roges, qua virgine? ipse statim sequente versu genus virginum explicat: Sic est, inquiens, via mulieris scortantis, comedit, deinde absterget os suum: ac dicit, non sum operata iniquitatem, hoc est, sum adhuc Almah, puella virgo, à viro intacta. Unde clarissimè elucescit, Salomonem eam nominatim perstringere, quæ se impudenter affirmat virginem, ac proinde humanâ opinione habetur virgo. Nihil ergo concludit argumentum Judæorum, Siquidem figuratum loquendi genus, non evertit propriam hujus nominis Almah significationem, quam contra Judæos tùm in aliis suprâ citatis Scripturæ locis meritò urgemus: tùm potissimùm capite hoc septimo Esaiæ, ubi de partu virginis, matris Messiæ, ex professo agitur. Quò accedit & illud, quòd verba subsequentia apud Esaiam וְקָרָאת שְׁמוֹ עִמָּנוּאֵל Et vocabis (nempe tu mater) nomen ejus Emmanuel: virgineum partum evidenter astruunt. Nam (uti hac in parte Calvinus etiam orthodoxè statuit) verbum וְקָרָאת Vekaraah est fœminini generis, & directè respicit matrem. Ubi aliquid præter consuetum morem exprimi, certum est. Apud Hebræos enim non matres, sed patres filiis imponebant nomina, quemadmodum ex universâ historiâ Sacrâ Veteris Testamenti, & in Novo Testamento, ex historiâ nativitatis Johannis Baptistæ licet colligere. Hoc enim Signum quasi erat juris & potestatis patrum in filios: nec eadem autoritas ad mulieres pertinet. Hic verò ad matrem transfertur. Sequitur ergò, secundum vaticinium hoc Esaiæ, Messiam sic à matre concipi & nasci debuisse, ut Patre in terris careat: alioqui Propheta communem Scripturæ usum perverteret, quæ viris tantùm hoc officium adscribit. Et tanta est argumenti hujus vis atq; evidentia, ut ipsi quoque Judæorum Rabbini nonnulli fassi sint, hoc loco innui tùm virginitatem Mariæ, tùm in nomine Emmanuel, DEUS nobiscum, incomparabile illud mysterium, de duabus naturis, divina & humana, in unâ personâ Messiæ personaliter uniendis, ac jam in personâ Jesu Nazareni verissimè ac realissimè unitis. Quâ de re videatur P. Galatinus lib. 3. cap. 18.

Porrò objiciunt, quôd Jesus Nazarenus non sit promissus ille apud Esaiam Messias, proptereà quôd non Emanuel, sed Jesus fuerit nominatus. Sed rectè negatur Consequentia: Siquidem distinguendum est inter nomina designantia naturam: & inter ea, quæ officium personæ definiunt. Constat enim, naturam ipsam, quæ dat rei formam, nomen quoque eidem rei dare. Sicut natura dat homini & humanitatem, & nomen, quòd homo est, ac dicitur. Ita quoque Messias noster, Emmanuel, hoc est, nobiscum DEUS, à consideratione personæ ipsius, quæ est & DEUS, & homo, rectè nominatur à Prophetâ, & ab omnibus Christianis sic nominari meritò debet. Cæterum in circumcisione Messias ab officio nominatus fuit Jesus, hoc est, Salvator, quia populum suum salvare debuit à peccatis suis: teste Angelo Matth. 1. v. 21. Jam hoc nomen non excludit, sed includit nomen Immanuelis: Qui enim Salvator est, & liberator populi à peccatis, eum non Hominem tantùm, sed & DEUM, hoc est, verum Emmanuelem esse oportet. Porrô si exceptio Judaica roboris aliquid, momentique obtineret, certè Messias, hunc in mundum editus, non tantùm Immanuel, sed & Admirabilis, DEUS fortis, Semen mulieris, Semen Abrahæ, Semen Davidis, Pater seculi, Princeps pacis, & id genus nominibus aliis, quibus Prophetæ ipsum exornant, indigirari debuisset. Jam verô manifestum est, hæc nomina Messiæ á Prophetis assignata fuisse, non quôd in Circumcisione hæc ipsi nomina imponi debeant, sed tantùm ut partim personam, partim officium ipsius definiant. Quæ nomina singula & universa, unicum nomen JESUS, admirandâ quâdam ἐμφάσει sub suo ambitu complectitur.

Hoc hactenùs demonstrato, nempe Messiam ex virgine intactâ nasciturum fuisse: restat accommodatio hujus κριτηρίε ad Jesum Nazarenum, Mariæ filium. De quo, ut multis agamus, operæ pretium non fuerit. Siquidem hujus rei testem omni exceptione majorem habemus Angelum, Matth. 1. v. 20. sic ad Josephum: Totum hoc factum est, ut impleretur, quod dixit Dominus per Prophetam: Ecce virgo in utero concipiet, & pariet filium: & vocabis (non vocabit) nomen ejus Emmanuelem: quod est, si interpreteris, nobiscum DEUS. Quod ipsum confirmatur Luc. 2. v. 5. & cap. 3. v. 23. Neque Judæi in hunc usque diem proferre quicquam potuerunt, quod vel in Speciem saltem probabiliter virginitatem Mariæ obscurare, aut suspectam reddere queat. Sed plus satis de Secundo Messiæ κριτηρίῳ.

TERTIUM Messiæ exhibiti κριτήριον, in Jesu Nazareno exactissimè completum est, quòd quæ partim nato jam Messiah, secundum prophetarum oracula evenire debuerút, partim verò ab ipsomet designanda erant opera atque miracula: ea singula atque universa in nullo alio, quam in Jesu Nazareno Mariæ filio, complementum suum sunt sortita: Qualia sunt præcipua isthæc:

1. Hoseæ 11. v. 1 de Messia dicitur: Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum. Hoc in Jesu Nazareno impletum esse, testis est Matthæus 2. v. 15. Jesus inquiens, fuit in Ægypto, usque ad obitum Herodis: ut impleretur, quod dixit Dominus per Prophetam: Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum.

2. Sic Jerem. 31. v. 15. Vox in Rama audita est, lamentum & fletus multus amarissimus: Rachel deflet filios suos, noluit consolationem admittere de filiis suis, quia nullus superest. Hoc ipsum impletum fuit, in lucem jam edito puerulo Jesu, teste Matthæo cap. 2. v. 18.

3. Sic de miraculis à Messia edendis passim concionati sunt Prophetæ: Esaias cúprimis cap. 35. v. 5. & 6: Tunc aperient se oculi cæcorum, & aures surdorum patefient: Tunc saliet claudus velut cervus, & cantabit lingua muti. Hoc in Jesu Nazareno impletum esse, universa historia Evangelica abundè testatur: & cumprimis Matthæus cap. 15. v. 30. & 31. Tunc inquiens, adiit ipsum turba multa, habens secum claudos, cæcos, mutos, mancos, & multos alios, quos abjecerunt ad pedes Jesu, & sanavit eos: adeò, ut turba mirata sit. Quod ipsum nec Judæi negare possunt, licet virtute Beelzebub talia signa ipsum edere, calumniarentur.

4. Sic de ingressu Messiæ urbem Hierosolymorum, jam olim prædixit Zacharias cap. 9. v. 9. his verbis: Exulta valde filia Sionus, elange filia Hierusalem: Ecce Rex tuus venit tibi, justus & Salvator, pauper, & insidens asino, & pullo filio asinarum. Hoc in Jesu Nazareno impletum esse, testatur Matthæus, describens ingressum ipsius in urbem Hierosolymam, & vers. 8. repetens vaticinium prophetæ: Dicite filiæ Sion, Ecce, Rex tuus venit tibi mansuetus, & insidens asino, ac pullo filio subjugis (asinæ.)

5. Sic quæ in Psalmis & Prophetis de passione, morte, Resurrectione, Ascensione ad cœlum, Sessione ad dexteram Patris prolixè sunt prædicta: Psalm. 16. 22. 69. 110. Esaiæ 53. Zach. 11. v. 12. & 13. & cap. 12. v. 10 & passim alibi, ea universa in Jesu Nazareno impleta fuisse, per se manifestum est ex historiâ Evangelicâ.

filii dilectionis suæ. Quæ & consimilia dicta regnum Christi partim ἐμφατικῶς multitui-dini regnorum mundanorum, sub Unitas notâ opponunt: partim verò ab omni huma-nâ conditione & formâ eximunt; ita ut cum ratione insaniat Pontifex Romanus, qui se Christi vicarium ementitur, & Regnum ejus externis ac terrenis mediis asserere ac propu-gnare studet.

6. Tandem quòd prædixerunt Prophetæ, Omnes gentes & populos venturos ad Messiam, & per ipsum credituros in DEUM Abraham, Isaac, & Jacob, relictis idolis & abominationibus suis; id in Jesu quoque Nazareno abundè impletum fuisse, tùm Apostolica, tùm Ecclesiastica quoque testatur historia: quin ipsa quoque experientia etiamnum satis superq; testatur.

Deinde quemadmodum se habet caput ad corpus: ita se habet Rex Christus ad suum regnum. Jam verò universa Ecclesia habet se ad Christum, tanquam Corpus unum, ad caput unum: imò universum genus humanum, omnesq; creaturæ ipsi tanquam Regi ac Domino universorum sunt subjectæ, Eph. 1. v. 22. & 23. Omnia subjecit sub pedibus ejus, & ipsum dedit caput super omnem Ecclesiam, quæ est Corpus ipsius, plenitudo ejus, qui omnia in omnibus adimplet. Ergò & regem ipsum numero Unum, & Regnum ipsius essentiâ Unicum statuere, fides Christiana docet.

Quibus ita constitutis, invictè colligimus, Jesum Nazarenum Mariæ filium, esse verum illum, Patriarchis ac fidelibus Veteris Testamenti promissum Messiam Mundi, neq; ullum alium expectandum.


### On the Quality, Form, and Condition of the Kingdom of Christ

THE SECOND THEOREM: Of this one Kingdom of Christ, there are as it were two parts, or, as they were accustomed to speak commonly in the schools, a twofold kingdom of Christ can be constituted regarding the condition and mode of administration: a thing which, however, detracts no more from the essential Unity of the Kingdom of Christ than the plurality of members takes away from the Unity of the Body. One is and is called heavenly, which is circumscribed by the boundary of the Triumphant Church, in which CHRIST sits at the right hand of the Father, on the throne of Majesty, not only interceding for us and bestowing the Holy Spirit, but also ruling in the midst of his enemies, Heb. 8, v. 1, Rom. 8, v. 34, Psalm 110, v. 2. The other is earthly, so called because it is carried out in these lands. Each is again considered in two ways; for that heavenly one is called the Kingdom of justice and the Kingdom of glory. Both of these will especially exert themselves at the resurrection of the dead and the Universal judgment, both of the impious to damnation and of the pious to eternal blessedness: Matt. 25, v. 31, John 5, v. 27 & 28, and chapter 6, v. 39, 1 Thess. 4, v. 16, and in the delivery of this earthly kingdom to GOD the Father: 1 Cor. 15, v. 28. And then GOD will be all in all. The earthly kingdom, which is carried out in this life, is called the Kingdom of Power and the Kingdom of Grace. The kingdom of power is that by which Christ our Savior not only rules within the boundaries of the Church through Grace and the Holy Spirit, but also rules and governs all creatures whatsoever in heaven and on earth by the right hand of omnipotence and divine power, according to the most free will of his own volition: and he most powerfully breaks and overturns the enemies of the Church and all their counsels, pursuits, and endeavors: according to that of the Psalm already cited, 110, v. 2. He will send forth the rod of his power from Zion: Rule in the midst of your enemies. And to the condition of that Kingdom must be referred those things—It has been demonstrated thus far that Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary, is that promised King of the Jews, or rather, the true Messiah of the World and Savior. It will therefore be next to make plain what kind of Kingdom this King has: a thing which we shall provide explained first through a thesis, or purer teaching, and then through an antithesis and refutation of various errors, and we shall forcefully defeat whatever will attempt to infest that kingdom.

Latin:

THEOREMA ALTERUM: Unius hujus Regni Christi, duæ quasi sunt partes, vel, ut vulgò in scholis loqui consueverunt, quoad conditionem, & administrationis modum, geminum Christi regnum constitui potest: id quod tamen Unitati essentiali Regni Christi, haud quicquam magis derogat, atque membrorum pluralitas. Unitatem Corporis tollit. Unum est & dicitur cœleste, quod Triumphantis Ecclesiæ termino circumscribitur, in quo CHRISTUS sedet ad dextram Patris, in throno Majestatis, non tantùm interpellans pro nobis, & donans Spiritum Sanctum: sed & dominans in medio inimicorum suorum, Hebr. 8. v. 1. Rom. 8. v. 34. Psalm. 110. v. 2. Alterum est terrenum, ideò sic dictum, quia in terris hisce peragitur. Utrúmque rursus duobus modis consideratur Cœleste enim illud, dicitur Regnum justitiæ, & Regnum gloriæ. Utrumque istud potissimum se aliquando exeret, in resuscitatione mortuorum, & Universali judicio tùm impiorum ad damnationem, tùm piorum ad æternam beatitudinem: Matth. 25. v. 31. Iohan. 5. v. 27. & 28. & cap. 6. v. 39. 1. Thess. 4. v. 16. & in traditione regni hujus terreni, DEO Patri: 1. Cor 15. v. 28. Ettunc erit DEUS omnia in omnibus. Regnum terrenum, quod in hac vitâ peragitur, dicitur Regnum Potentiæ & Regnum Gratiæ. Regnum potentiæ est illud, quo Christus Servator noster, non tantùm dominatur intra Ecclesiæ pomeria, per Gratiam & Spiritum Sanctum: sed omnes omninò creaturas in cœlo ac in terrâ, regit & gubernat dexterâ omnipotentiæ & virtutis divinæ, pro liberrimo Voluntatis suæ arbitrio: & hostes Ecclesiæ, omniaque ipsorum consilia, studia & conatus potentissimè infringit, & evertit: secundum illud Psalmi jam citati 110. v. 2. Emittet virgam virtutis suæ ex Sion: Dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum. Et ad Regni istius conditionem referri debent eaD Emonstratum hactenus, Jesum Nazarenum Mariæ filium, esse promissum illú Regem Judæorum, imò potiùs verum Mundi Messiam, ac Salvatorem. Proximum ergò fuerit, ut quale Regnum Rex iste habeat, planum faciamus: id quod initiò per θέσιν, sive διδασκαλίαν puriorem: deinde per ἀντίθεσιν καὶ ἔλεγχον variorum errorum explicatum dabimus, & quicquid regnum istud infestare conabitur, fortiter profligabimus.


### On the Quality, Form, and Condition of the Kingdom of Christ: I. ΘΕΣΙΣ OR Orthodox διδασκαλία [teaching], concerning the Kingdom of Christ

We shall include the entire διδασκαλίαν, the Articles concerning the kingdom of Christ, in ten certain specific theorems.

THE FIRST is: The kingdom of Christ is One in substance and number, so that a multitude has no place in this regard. This is demonstrated 1. from Holy Scripture, which, in describing the kingdom of the Messiah, always uses the singular number. Daniel 2, v. 44. In the days of those kingdoms, the GOD of heaven will raise up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed: and his kingdom shall not be delivered to another people: but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms: and it shall stand forever. Luke 1, 33. He shall reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end. John 18, v. 36. My kingdom is not of this world. Colossians 1, v. 13. He has delivered us from the power of darkness, and has translated us into the kingdom of those testimonies of Scripture, which testify that all the works of the hands of God are subject to Christ according to the assumed humanity, and that he himself is constituted Lord over all things which are named either in this or in the future age: Psalm 8. 7. & seqq. Hebr. 2, 8. Ephes. 1. v. 20. & seqq.

The Kingdom of Grace is the special operation of Christ in the Church, consisting of mere goodness and mercy. To which pertain the Mission of the Apostles and Doctors: the Collection of the Church: the preaching of the Word: the Administration of the Sacraments: Regeneration: Justification: Sanctification: the distribution of the various gifts of the Holy Spirit: the protection and preservation of the pious in any troubles and afflictions whatsoever.

Third: Both of this Kingdom, as much that which is of Grace, as that which is of Power, necessarily presupposes in the person of Christ the Divine Majesty and Omnipotence, Essential with respect to his divine nature: truly and really communicated with respect to the human. For if you look at the Kingdom of Grace, that could not be obtained except by crushing the head of the serpent, by expiating sins: by abolishing the dominion of death: by bending the hearts of men to the obedience of faith: by protecting the Church against the furies and assaults of the Devil and the world: and finally by conferring eternal blessing upon the pious and believers. Which ἀποτελέσματα (results), although they are works of Grace: nevertheless necessarily presuppose the κτῆσιν (possession) and χρῆσιν (use) of divine Omnipotence in Christ the King. As regards the Kingdom of Power, it is manifest by itself that it is in no way possible that Christ, according to that nature also according to which he sat down at the right hand of the power and majesty of God the Father, should rule in the midst of his enemies, have known and perceived the most secret counsels of them all, and most powerfully break, repress, and confound the same, unless he be truly and really anointed with the infinite fullness of Omnipotence and divine power according to the same nature.

Fourth. Both this Kingdom belongs to Christ according to both natures, although in a different respect: For in as much as he is God, he has it from eternity with God the Father and the Holy Spirit: in as much as he is Man, he received it in the Union, out of Grace: Which Personal Union itself requires that Christ according to both natures truly and really administers both kingdoms. For if he administered them while absent, he would not be anointed with the infinite fullness of divine Majesty: as was shown in the Article concerning the person of Christ.

Fifth. In this Article, the Kingdom of Grace is chiefly discussed: Where first its Condition is inquired into, which we determine to be not worldly, not secular, not terrestrial: but plainly Spiritual:

and this we prove 1. by the express words of Christ himself asserting that his Kingdom is not of this world, John 18. v. 36. Which is that good Confession which Christ made before Pilate: 1. Tim. 6. v. 13. Then by most firm reasons: the first of which is taken from the Duration. For nothing worldly is eternal: The Kingdom of Christ is eternal: Therefore the Kingdom of Christ is not worldly. The Major premise is plain from the Scriptures: Matth. 24. v. 35. Heaven and earth shall pass away. 1. Corinth. 7. v. 31. The fashion of this world passes away. 2. Pet. 3. v. 10. The heavens shall pass away with a great noise: the elements shall melt with heat: but the earth, and the works that are in it, shall be burned up with fire: The Minor premise is evident from Daniel 2. v. 44. where it is said that all the kingdoms of the world are to be crushed and consumed by this kingdom of the Messiah, but it itself shall remain forever. And Luke 1, 33. He shall reign forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end. Therefore. Nor is there any reason for anyone to cavil at the Hebrew word עולם Olam, or לְעוֹלָם Leolam, which do not always denote absolute eternity, but at least the duration of a longer, yet finite time: as can be seen especially in Moses. For it is rightly answered in this place as well, that such are the predicates as are permitted by the Subjects. Now if the subject itself is capable of absolute eternity, either by reason of essence or by grace: then absolute eternity is certainly predicated of it. For example: GOD the Father by reason of essence is eternal, indeed eternity itself: Therefore when these Hebrew words are predicated of GOD, they denote not only a long-lasting time, but absolute eternity. Thus, because Christ the Savior is eternal by reason of his divine essence: by reason of his human nature he has been made a participant of eternity in such a way that whatever happens to him from the personal union cannot but be, absolutely, eternal: certainly now these words dealing with the kingdom of Christ will also denote absolute eternity. And it is well worth noting that these very Hebrew words are predicated of GOD the Father himself, by reason of eternity. Where, however, no one, either of the Jews or of the heretics, ever dared to deny that absolute eternity is denoted by them: Because, of course, the Subject itself, of which these words are predicated, is eternal. Why, therefore, should we not determine the same concerning Christ and his kingdom, especially when the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures circumscribes this eternity in such a way that it cannot be understood as anything but absolute eternity: as when Dan. 2. v. 44. It is said, not only that the Kingdom of the Messiah shall be eternal, but also that it shall not be corrupted for ever, as the Hebrew text has it; דִּי לְעָלְמִין לָא תִתְחַבַּל & as the Angel explains, Luke 1, 33, of whose kingdom there shall be no end. Whence it is plain; that there is no reason for the consequence in the argument of the Photinians, since it proceeds in part in this manner: The Hebrew words Olam and Leolam do not denote absolute eternity in many places of Scripture: therefore, neither in those places in which the eternity of Christ is treated. The grammarians and rabbis of the Jews have observed this very thing, who teach that the words denoting eternity are twofold: some denote absolute eternity, others determined or conditional. In the first kind they place Sola, and where Scripture has: In the ages of ages. They refer to this first kind also Necali, and where the Psalm in Greek and Latin says: He shall live for eternity: in Hebrew it sounds Necali. In the second kind they place Olam, in Latin Seculum. In this way, in Deuteronomy, concerning a purchased servant, it is said: He shall be your servant Olam, that is, for the age, namely, of your life and his own, not beyond. And Moses uses this word when he treats of the eternity, that is, the long duration of the Sabbath, of the Passover, and of the ceremonies. Nor does that stand in the way, 1. Cor. 15. v. 24. Then also the Son shall be subjected to the Father, when he shall have delivered his Kingdom to GOD the Father. For 1. the Apostle does not treat of the whole Kingdom of Christ considered simply and from every part: but only of the Kingdom of Grace: and 2. nor even of this considered in itself and simply, but only with respect to its administration and external form, which it obtains in this world through the external preaching of the Word and the administration of the Sacraments. This external form will cease. As for the Kingdom itself, the Apostle does not say that it is then to cease: but that Christ is to deliver it to GOD the Father, in that respect, namely, that the Kingdom which has hitherto been the Kingdom of Grace in this world, may then pass into the Kingdom of Glory, where GOD, in those blessed citizens of the kingdom of Christ, after this delivery, will begin to be all in all: as the following verse 28 clearly hints. In which way also the Son himself shall be subjected to God the Father, not that he is to cease to reign over all things that are above and below heaven: or that he is to lay aside that divine majesty with which, even according to the assumed flesh, he was anointed without measure: but only with respect to that external form of administration by which Christ wished to use in gathering the Church in this world: to which he will then put an end on the last day, and thus will return this mode of government to his Father, and as it were resign it. But let us return to the arguments of the proofs.

The second reason, therefore, by which it is demonstrated that the Kingdom of Christ is not earthly but spiritual, is such: As is the throne from which Christ the Savior reigns, such also is the kingdom itself: since the throne or seat of a King expresses the nature of the Kingdom itself sufficiently clearly. But the throne of the King Christ is purely heavenly and spiritual, as that which is and is called by the Holy Spirit in the Holy Scriptures the very right hand of divine Majesty and power; Psalm 110. 1. Sit at my right hand, and rule in the midst of your enemies: Ephes. 1. v. 20. GOD the Father established Christ at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and power. To which also pertains the Scepter, which was delivered to King Messiah as a sign of royal Majesty, which is not external, but spiritual: namely, the rod of power from Zion: that is, the preaching of the Gospel. Ps. 110. v. 2. Isa. 2. v. 3. And David Ps. 45. v. 7. The rod of uprightness or equity is the rod of your kingdom.

The third reason: All the goods and benefits of this kingdom are spiritual: Therefore such will the kingdom itself be. The antecedent is proved Rom. 14 v. 17. The Kingdom of GOD is not food and drink: but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit: the blessing of all nations: the expiation of sins: redemption from the power of the Devil and death: eternal beatitude.

The fourth reason: As is the administration of the kingdom, such is the kingdom itself: But that is entirely spiritual, as will be demonstrated a little later in the seventh theorem.

Therefore.

The fifth reason: From the nature of the end, the judgment concerning the quality of any thing is most correctly made. Now, indeed, the Kingdom of Christ tends toward an end that is merely spiritual, which is the knowledge of Christ and eternal life: John 17. 3.

Therefore.

The sixth and final reason: As are the weapons by which this Kingdom is defended, both by reason of itself and by reason of its subjects, such is the Kingdom itself also: But the weapons are merely spiritual: according to that 2. Cor. 10. v. 4. & 5. The weapons of our warfare are not carnal: but powerful to GOD, for the destruction of fortifications, destroying counsels, and every height exalting itself against the knowledge of GOD, and bringing into captivity every intellect into the obedience of Christ. But concerning these weapons and means also, below in the seventh theorem.

Latin:

UNiversam διδασκαλίαν, Articuli de regno Christi, decem certis quibusdam theorematis includemus.

PRIMVM est: Regnum Christi substantiâ & numero Unum est, ita ut multitudo hac parte locum non habeat. Demonstratur hoc 1. ex Scripturâ Sacrâ, quæ Regnum Messiæ describens, singulari semper numero utitur. Daniel. 2. v. 44. In diebus regnorum illorum, suscitabit DEUS cœli regnum, quod in æternum non dissipabitur: & regnum ejus alteri populo non tradetur: comminuet autem, & consumet universa regna hæc: & ipsum stabit in æternum. Luc. 1, 33. Regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum, & regni ejus non erit finis. Johan. 18. v. 36. Regum meum non est de hoc mundo. Coloff. 1. v. 13. eripuit nos de potestate tenebrarum, & transtulit in regnum ea Scripturæ testimonia, quæ testantur, Christo secundum assumtam humanitatem subjecta esse omnia opera manuum Dei, ipsumque constitutum esse Dominum super omnia, quæ vel in hoc, vel in futuro seculo nominantur: Psalm. 8. 7. & seqq. Hebr. 2, 8. Ephes. 1. v. 20. & seqq.

Regnum Gratiæ est specialis operatio Christi in Ecclesiâ, constans merâ bonitate & misericordiâ. Quò pertinent Missio Apostolorum & Doctorum: Collectio Ecclesiæ: prædicatio Verbi: Administratio Sacramentorum: Regeneratio: Justificatio: Sanctificatio: distributio variorum donorum Spiritus Sancti: protectio, & conservatio piorum in quibusvis ærumnis & afflictionbus.

Tertium: Utriusque hujus Regni, tàm quod est Gratiæ, quàm quod est Potentiæ, præsupponit necessariô in personâ Christi Divinam Majestatem ac Omnipotentiam, respectu divinæ ejus naturæ Essentialem: respectu humanæ, verè ac realiter communicatam. Nam si Regnum Gratiæ spectes, illud obtineri non potuit, nisi conculcando caput serpentis, expiando peccata: abolendo mortis dominium: flectendo corda hominum ad obsequium fidei: protegendo Ecclesiam adversus Diaboli & mundi furores, ac insultus: æternam denique benedictionem piis & credentibus conferendo. Quę ἀποτελέσματα omnia, etsi Gratiæ sunt opera: Omnipotentiæ tamen divinæ κτῆσιν & χρῆσιν, in Rege Christo necessariò, præsupponunt. Quoad Regnum Potentiæ, per se manifestum est, fieri nullâ ratione posse, ut Christus secundum eam quoque naturam, secundum quam consedit ad dextram virtutis, & majestatis Dei Patris, dominetur in medio inimicorum, cognita perspectaque habeat secretissima etiam ipsorum consilia universa, eademque potentissimè infringat, reprimat, confundat, nisi infinitâ plenitudine Omnipotentiæ & virtutis divinæ secundum eandem naturam, verè ac realiter inunctus sit.

Quartum. Utrumque hoc Regnum competit Christo secundum utramque naturam, diverso licet respectu: Nam in quantum Deus est, ab æterno illud habet cum Deo Patre, & Spiritu Sancto: in quantum Homo est, accepit illud in Unione, ex Gratiâ: Quæ ipsa Unio Personalis requirit, ut Christus secundum utramque naturam reverâ præsens Regnum utrumque administret. Si enim absens administraret, non infinitâ plenitudine Majestatis divinæ inunctus esset: uti in Articulo de personâ Christi ostensum.

Quintum. De Regno Gratiæ hoc in Articulo potissimùm disceptatur: Ubi primùm de ejus Conditione quæritur, quam non mundanam, non secularem, non terrestrem: sed planè Spiritualem esse statuimus:

idq́ve probamus 1. expressis verbis ipsius Christi asserentis, Regnum suum non esse de hoc mundo, Joh.18.v.36. Quæ est bona illa Confessio, quam coram Pilato Christus edidit: 1. Tim. 6. v.13. Deinde rationibus firmissimis: quarum prima sumitur à Duratione. Nihil enim mundanum est æternùm: Regnum Christi est æternùm: Ergò Regnum Christi non est mundanum. Major plana est ex Scripturis: Matth. 24. v. 35. Cælum & terra transibunt. 1. Corinth.7. v.31. Figura hujus mundi præteriit. 2. Pet. 3. v.10. Cæli magno impetu transibunt: Elementa calore liquefcent: terra autem, & quæ in ipsâ sunt opera, igni exurentur: Minor patet ex Daniel 2. v.44. ubi dicitur à regno hoc Messiæ comminuenda & confumenda esse universa regna mundi, ipsum autem permanfurum in æternum. Et Luc. 1, 33. Regnabit in æternum, & regni ejus non erit finis. Ergò. Neque est, ut aliquis cavilletur in vocabulo Hebræo עולם Olam, sive לְעוֹלָם Leolam, quæ non absolutam semper æternitatem, sed durationem saltem longioris quidem, finiti tamen temporis notant: uti cumprimis apud Mosen videre est. Nam rectè & hoc loco respondetur, quòd talia sint prædicata, qualia permittuntur à Subjectis. Jam si subjectum ipsum absolutæ æternitatis est capax, vel ratione essentiæ, vel ex gratiâ: de eo utique absoluta etiam æternitas prædicatur. Exempli gratiâ: DEUS Pater ratione effentiæ est æternus, imò ipsissima æternitas: Ergo quando vocabula isthæc Hebræa de DEO prædicantur, non longo tantùm tempore durantem, sed absolutam æternitatem notant. Sic quia Christus Servator ratione divinæ essentiæ est æternus: ratione humanæ naturæ æternitatis ita factus est particeps, ut quicquid ipsi ex unione personali obrigit, non possit non, nisi absolutè, æternum esse: utique jam vocabula hæc de regno Christi agentia, absolutam quoque æternitatem notabunt. Et observationem probè meretur, quòd de ipso DEO Patre, ratione æternitatis, hæc ipsa Hebræa vocabula prædicantur. Ubi tamen nullus unquam vel Judæorum, vel hæreticorum negare ausus fuit, absolutam æternitatem per ea notari: Quia nimirùm Subjectum ipsum, de qvo vocabula hæc prædicantur, æternum est. Qvidnî ergô idem de Christo, ejusdemq; regno statuamus, præsertim, cùm Spiritus Sanctus in Scripturis æternitatem hanc ita circumscribat, ut non nisi de absolutâ æternitate accipi possit: ut quando Dan.2.v.44. dicitur, non modò, quòd Regnum Messiæ futurum sit æternùm, sed &, quòd non sit corrumpendum in æternum, uti textus Hebræus habet; דִּי לְעָלְמִין לָא תִתְחַבַּל & ut Angelus, Luc. 1, 33. explicat, cujus regni non sit futurus finis. Unde planum sit; nullam esse rationem consequentiæ in argumento Photinianorum, quippe quod ex parte procedit in hunc modum: Vocabula Hebræa Olam, & Leolam in multis Scripturæ locis non notant æternitatem absolutam : Ergò neque in illis locis, in quibus de æternitate Christi agitur. Observarunt hoc ipsum Judæorum Grammatici, & Rabini, qui docent, dictiones æternitatem notantes, duplices esse : Alias notare æternitatem absolutam: alias determinatam, sive conditionatam. In primo genere ponunt Sola, & ubi Scriptura habet. In secula seculorum. Referunt ad hoc primum genus etiam Necali, atque ubi Psalmus Græcè & Latinè dicit : Vivet in æternum: Hebraicè sonat Necali. In secundo genere ponunt Olam, Latinè Seculum. Hoc pacto in Deuteronomio de Servo emtitio dicitur : Erit tibi servus Olam, id est, in seculum, scilicet, vitæ tuæ, & ipsius, non ultrà, Et hoc vocabulo utitur Moses, quando de æternitate, hoc est, longâ duratione Sabbati Paschatis & Ceremoniarum agit. Neque obstat illud, 1. Cor. 15. v. 24. Tum & filius subjicietur Patri, cùm tradiderit Regnum suum DEO patri. Nam 1. non de omni Regno Christi simpliciter, & ex omni parte considerato : sed tantùm de Regno Gratiæ : & 2. neque de hoc etiam per se & simpliciter considerato, sed tantùm respectu ejus administrationis & externæ formæ, quam hoc in mundo, per externam prædicationem Verbi, & administrationem Sacramentorum obtinet, agit Apostolus. Hæc externa forma cessabit. Quoad Regnum ipsum non dicit Apostolus, quòd illud tum sit cessaturum: sed quòd Christus illud DEO Patri sit traditurus, eo nimirùm respectu, ut, quod Regnum hactenus hoc in mundo fuit Regnum Gratiæ, tùm transeat in Regnum Gloriæ, ubi DEUS in beatis illis civibus regni Christi, post hanc traditionem, incipiet esse omnia in omnibus : uti versus insequens 28. perspicuè innuit. Quo pacto etiam Filius ipse subjicietur Deo Patri, non quòd cessaturus sit regnare super omnia, quæ sunt supra & infra cælum: vel quòd depositurus sit majestatem illam divinam, quâ etiam secundum assumtam carnem, non ad mensuram inunctus est:sed tantùm quoad externam illam administrationis formam,qvâ Christus in colligendâ Ecclesiâ hoc in mundo uti voluit: cui tùm in novissimo die finem imponet, & sic hunc gubernationis modum Patri suo reddet, & quasi resignabit. Sed ad probationum argumenta redeamus.

Altera ergò ratio, quâ Regnum Christi, non terrenum, sed spirituale esse demonstratur, talis est : Qualis est thronus, ex quo Christus Servator regnat : tale etiam est regnum ipsum: Siquidem thronus vel Solium Regis, naturam Regni ipsius satis perspicuè exprimit. Atqui thronus Regis Christi est purè cælestis & spiritualis, ut qui Spiritus Sancto in Scripturis Sacris, est ac dicitur, ipsa divina Majestatis & potentiæ dextra; Psalm. 110. 1. Sede à dextris meis, & dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum : Ephes. 1. v. 20. DEUS pater constituit Christum ad dexteram suam in cælestibus, supra omnem principatum & potestatem. Quò pertinet etiam Sceptrum,quod Regi Messiæ in Signum regiæ Majestatis est traditum, quod non est externum, sed spirituale: nempe virga virtutis è Sion : hoc est, prædicatio Evangelii. Psal. 110. v. 2. Jesa. 2. v. 3. Et David Psal. 45. v. 7. Virga rectitudinis sive æquitatis est virga regni tui.

Tertia ratio : Bona omnia & beneficia regni hujus sunt spiritualia : Ergo tale erit & ipsum regnum. Antecedens probatur Rom.14 v.17. Regnum DEI non est cibus & potus : sed justitia pax & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto: benedictio omnium gentium : expiatio peccatorum : redemtio ex potestate Diaboli & mortis : æterna beatitudo.

Quarta ratio : Qualis est administratio regni : tale est regnum ipsum : Atqui illa est tota Spiritualis, uti paulò post theoremate septimo demonstrabitur.

Ergo.

Quinta ratio : Ex naturâ finis rectissimè de qualitate rei cujusq; sit judicium. Jam verò Regnum Christi ad finem tendit merè Spiritualem,qui est cognitio Christi, & vita æterna: Joh.17.3.

Ergo.

Sexta & postrema ratio : Qualia sunt arma, quibus defenditur Regnum hoc, tùm ratione sui ipsius, tùm ratione subditorum : tale est Regnum etiam ipsum: Atqui arma sunt merè Spiritualia : secundum illud 2. Cor. 10. v. 4. & 5. Arma militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia : sed potentia DEO, ad destructionem munitionum, consilia destruentes, & omnem altitudinem, extollentem se adversus notitiam DEI, & in captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi. Sed de his quoq; armis & mediis infra theoremate septimo.


### On the Quality, Form, and Condition of the Kingdom of Christ: Theorem Sixth: The fortune of this Kingdom is comprised in four members

THEOREM Sixth: The fortune of this Kingdom is comprised in four members:

I. The glory of the subjects is not of the present age, nor does it strike the eyes of mortals: but it is of the future, and in secret: Whence the Apostle Colossians 3, verse 3: Our life is hidden with Christ in GOD: and John 1, chapter 3, verse 2: Now we are children of GOD: but it has not yet been manifested what we shall be.

II. This Kingdom is subject to perpetual calamities in these lands: Romans 8, verse 17: If indeed we suffer together, we shall also be glorified together. Matthew 16, verse 24: If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross. John 16, verse 33: In the world you will endure afflictions. Acts 14, verse 22: Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven.

III. This Kingdom is always liable to hostile persecution. Psalm 44, verse 22: For your sake we are delivered to death, all the day we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter. 2 Timothy 3, verse 12: All who wish to live godly in Christ will suffer persecution.

IV. Such is the fortune and condition of this Kingdom, that it always has the bad mixed with the good, and will have until the last day. To which pertain those parables of Christ, Matthew 13, concerning the tares and the net: And that discourse of his in Luke 17, concerning

in the times of Noah and Lot, compared with the state of the last times.

THEOREM Seventh: The administra-

tion and propagation of this Kingdom is not political, nor is it done in a worldly manner: For the gathering, as well as the government, of the subjects of this kingdom is effected by the voice and Word of the ministry, not by arms or the sword: as was shown a little earlier from 2 Cor. 10. 4. and 5. Therefore, the preaching of the Word, and the use of the Sacraments, which adheres to it, is the true and effective ministry of the Holy Spirit, by which as a scepter CHRIST directs His people, propagates the boundaries of His kingdom, and dilates it throughout the whole world. Concerning this matter, Christ Himself discourses: Matt. 20. v. 25. and Luke 22. v. 25. The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors: But ye shall not be so: And John 20. v. 21. As my Father hath sent me, even so send I you. Matt. 20. v. 28. The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister. Ps. 2. v. 6. I will declare the decree: the Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son. And the Apostles, sent out by Christ to preach in the whole world, are instructed partly by the gift of tongues, partly by the help of the Holy Spirit: Clothed with which armor, they destroy the counsels of strongholds, and every height exalting itself against the knowledge of GOD. 2 Cor. 10. v. 5. And they had a mouth and wisdom, which all their adversaries could not gainsay nor resist. Luke 21. v. 15. Whence the preaching of the Gospel, proper to this Kingdom, is called by the Apostle the Ministration of the Spirit. 2 Cor. 3. v. 8.

Latin:

THEOREMA Sextum : Fortuna Regni hujus qvatuor membris comprehenditur :

I. Gloria subditorum non est de præsenti seculo, nedum in oculos mortalium incurrit: sed est de futuro, & in abscondito : Unde Apostolus Coloss. 3. v. 3. Vita nostra abscondita est cum Christo, in DEO: & Johannes 1. cap. 3.v.2. Jam silit DEI sumus : sed nondum manifestatum est, quid futuri sumus.

II. Calamitatibus perpetuis Regnum hoc hisce in terris subjacet : Rom. 8. v. 17. Siquidem simul patiemur, simul etiam glorificabimur. Matth. 16. v. 24. Si quis vult me sequi, abneget seipsum, & tollat crucem suam. Joh. 16. v. 33. In mundo afflictiones sustinebitis. Act.14.v.22. Per multas tribulationes ingrediendum est in regnum cælorum.

III. Hostili persecutioni Regnum hoc semper est obnoxium. Psal 44.v.22. Propter te morti tradimur, tota die æstimati sumus sicut oves occisionis. 2. Tim. 3.v.12. Omnes qui pie in Christo volunt vivere, persecutionem patientur.

IV. Regni hujus ea est fortuna & conditio, ut bonis malos mixtos habeat semper, & habiturum sit ad diem usque novissimum. Qvò pertinent illæ Christi similitudines, Matth. 13. de Zizaniis, & sagena : Et Concio illa ejusdem Luc. 17. de

temporibus Noah & Loth, cum novissimorum temporum statu comparatis.

THEOREMA Septimum: Administra-

tio & propagatio Regni hujus non est politica, neque more fit mundano: Voce enim, & Verbo ministerii, non armis, aut gladio subditorum hujus regni fit tum collectio, tum etiam gubernatio: uti paulò antè ex 2. Cor. 10. 4. & 5. fuit ostensum. Est ergo prædicatio Verbi, &, qui huic adhæret, Sacramentorum usus, verum & efficax Spiritus Sancti ministerium, quo ceu sceptro populum suum CHRISTVS dirigit, pomœria regni sui propagat, & per orbem universum dilatat. Qua de re disserit Christus ipse: Matth. 20. v. 25. & Luc. 22. v 25. Reges gentium dominantur, & magnates potestatem exercent: Vos autem non sic: Et Johan. 20. v. 21. Sicut misit me Pater: sic & ego mitto vos. Matth. 20. v. 28. Non venit filius hominis, ut sibi ministraretur: sed ut ipse ministraret. Psal. 2. v. 6. Prædicabo in hunc modum, quod Dominus dixit ad me: Filius meus es tu. Et Apostoli à Christo ad prædicandum in universo mundo emissi, partim linguarum dono, partim Spiritus Sancti ope instruuntur: Quâ panopliâ induti destruunt consilia munitionum, & omnem altitudinem extollentem se adversus scientiam DEI. 2. Cor. 10. v. 5. & os atque sapientiam habuerunt, cui non potuerunt contradicere, aut resistere omnes adversarii. Luc. 21. v. 15. Unde prædicatio Evangelii, Regni hujus propria, ab Apostolo nominatur Ministerium Spiritus. 2. Cor. 3. v. 8.


### On the Quality, Form, and Condition of the Kingdom of Christ: Theorem Eighth. The power and use-

THEOREM Eighth. The power and use-

fulness of the Kingdom of Christ, which is nothing if not Spiritual, consists chiefly in two things. 1. That Christ enriches us with all goods necessary for the eternal salvation of souls. Whatever happiness, therefore, is promised to us in Christ, does not consist in external comforts, so that we might pass our life in this world abounding in goods and carnal delights: but it is all to be referred to the heavenly life. And what would it profit us to be gathered under the rule of a heavenly King, if its fruit did not consist outside the state of earthly life. As therefore one part of external happiness is contained in the abundance of secular goods: so the happiness of the Pious consists in this, that Christ enriches His own with goods necessary for the salvation of souls.

2. Then: That Christ also fortifies His own with strength and power, so that they may be impregnable against any enemies whatsoever. For His royal anointing is not read to have been made from oil and aromatics: but Christ was so called because He was anointed with the oil of gladness above His fellows: Ps. 45. v. 8. namely, because the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, and the fear of GOD rested upon Him: Isa. 11. v. 2. Nor indeed was He enriched privately for Himself, while the Spirit was given to Him not by measure, John 3. v. 34. but He is so suffused with abundance that we all might receive from His fullness grace for grace: John 1. v. 16. Whence we gather that Christ does not reign more for Himself than for us: Whence also we are not undeservedly called Christians. All of which things tend to this, that because we understand that Christ's kingdom is not earthly or carnal, which is subject to corruption, but is Spiritual, which lifts us up to eternal life: hence let us learn first to pass this life patiently under hardships, contempt, reproaches, and troubles, content with this one thing, that our King will not abandon us, but will communicate those things which will be for the use of our salvation: Then, because He strengthens us with His power, let us, animated by true confidence, fight against the Devil, sin, and death. Finally, that being suffused by Him with the oil of grace, and liberally filled with gifts, we may in turn bring forth not the dross of the world or the flesh, but the true fruits of the Spirit to His glory.

THEOREM Ninth. The diversity between the Kingdom of Christ and the kingdoms of this world is greatest. For they differ in substance, and in nature, and in duration of time, and in the kind of benefits, and in the quality of their ends, and in the disparity of Fortune, and in the form and condition of administration, and to speak summarily, they have nothing at all in common with each other, except the Name, and this World, which they sometimes use in common in this age. For duration also, although it is not sempiternal on both sides: Since indeed for both (yet in a different respect, as was shown above in the fifth theorem) abrogation will be incumbent: nevertheless the empires and kingdoms of the world, immediately at the coming of Christ, will be abolished with the world itself: But the Kingdom of Christ, when at last all enemies have been tamed and subjugated, and among these, death itself, which is the last enemy, has been removed, after its most full consummation has finally been made, and all the elect have been asserted to heavenly glory, will finally be delivered to GOD the Father in the very glory of eternity, Christ himself, whose roles in the defense and salvation of his Church will then have been fulfilled, thenceforth to dwell with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the sempiternal and most simple kingdom of Glory, such as he had possessed before the human race was created, from eternity itself, even before.

THEOREM Tenth and last: This Kingdom of Grace extends as widely as the whole globe of the earth spreads itself. For although our Messiah initially began it in Judea, or Palestine, by preaching the Gospel only to the Jews: For he had to be a Minister of the Circumcision, for the sake of the truth of GOD, to confirm the promises of the Fathers: Rom. 15.v.18. yet soon after his ascension, through the Apostles he extended the boundaries of this his Kingdom to all the ends of the earth, while he led all the nations that are under heaven into its fellowship through the preaching of the Gospel, so that there is no race, no nation, no province, no people to whom the sound of the preaching of the Gospel has not gone out. Matt. 28 v. 19. Mark 16 v. 15. Rom. 10 v. 18. Col. 1 v. 13. The truth of this theorem is evident partly from the history of the Acts of the Apostles, and partly from Ecclesiastical history. Certainly, on that first Pentecost of the New Testament, by the single sermon of Peter, more than three thousand were associated with this kingdom of Christ, not only from the Jews, but from every nation of men who are under heaven, so that besides the Jews, the Parthians also and Medes, and Elamites, and the inhabitants of Mesopotamia, and Judea, and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt, and the parts of Libya which is adjacent to Cyrene, and the visiting Romans, both Jews and Proselytes, Cretans and Arabs, and others heard the Apostles speaking in their own language, in which each was born, the mighty works of GOD. Acts 2 v. 5 and following.

In Salamis they preached the Gospel; Acts 13 v. 5, and they traveled through that whole island as far as Paphos, v. 6, and having traveled besides through Pamphylia and Pisidia, and having established churches—the Antiochene, Iconian, Lystran, Derbean, Pergean, and Attalian—they returned to Antioch. Acts 13 v. 13, 14. Acts 14 v. 1, 6, 20, 24, and 25, but in such a way that, having been separated from one another afterwards, Paul indeed traveled through Syria and Cilicia, while Barnabas sailed again to Cyprus. Acts 15 v. 39 and following.

Paul, therefore, having undertaken this journey, revisited the Asian churches, and with Timothy joined to him, converted Phrygia and Galatia to Christ by the preaching of the Gospel. Acts 16 v. 1 and 6. Afterwards, wishing to go into Bithynia, being forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the Word in Asia and Mysia, he descended from Troas into Macedonia: having traveled through Samothrace, and Neapolis, and Philippi, and Amphipolis, and Apollonia, Thessalonica, Beroea, and Athens. Acts 16 v. 7 and 8 and 11. Acts 17 v. 1, 10, and 15. Departing from there, he came to Corinth, Acts 18 v. 1, preaching and disputing in the synagogues about Jesus among the Jews and Greeks, v. 4; but afterwards returning to Asia through Ephesus, having left Aquila there, he revisited the churches of Asia again. Acts 18 v. 19, having greeted the churches of Caesarea and Antioch, v. 22.

Then, a persecution having arisen in Jerusalem, and the Apostles indeed remaining there, many of the faithful, however, who had been dispersed through the regions of Judea and Samaria, announced the Word of GOD, and later passed on as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the LORD JESUS not only to the Jews, but also to the Greeks at Antioch, that is, to the Gentiles. Acts 8 v. 1, 4.

Furthermore, departing from Ephesus again, he returned to Macedonia and Greece, Acts 19 v. 21 and ch. 20 v. 1 and 2. When he had understood that plots had been laid against him, having left Syria, which he had intended, he wished to return through Macedonia, and setting sail from Troas, he sailed to Assos, Mytilene, Samos, and from there to Miletus, where he bade farewell to the Ephesian elders, Acts 20, and from there he arrived at Rhodes, Patara, Tyre, Ptolemais, Caesarea, and again at Jerusalem, where, a sedition having been stirred up against him by the Jews, he was cast into chains by the tribune Lysias, Acts 21; from there he was taken to Rome, and having traveled the whole coast of Asia and Crete, he finally arrived at Malta as a shipwrecked man. Acts 27, and finally he pleaded his case before Nero; and from there, having first greeted the churches of Syria, Asia, and Greece, he returned to the West, and for almost a whole decade traveled through and filled Italy, Gaul, and Spain with the preaching of the Gospel.

At this very time Philip, who is named an Evangelist in Acts 21 v. 8 and was one of the seven Deacons, preached the Gospel in Samaria, converted on the road leading to Gaza the Eunuch, a prefect of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians; from there he set out for Azotus and evangelized all the cities until he came to Samaria. Acts 8 v. 5 and 26 and following and 40.

On the same occasion, Peter and John were also sent by the Apostles to Samaria, so that in preaching the Gospel they might provide, as it were, auxiliary efforts to Philip the Evangelist, Acts 8 v. 14. And Peter, with the first journey then undertaken, announced Christ and traveled through all the churches of Judea, Galilee, and Samaria, which were enumerated earlier; he also arrived at Lydda; from there to Sharon and Joppa; from there, by a special revelation, he was summoned to Caesarea to the Gentiles, and indeed to Cornelius the Centurion. Acts 9 v. 32, 36. Acts 10 v. 10 and following.

It is evident from this brief table not only to what great and various dangers and labors the Apostle exposed himself for the propagation of the Kingdom of Christ, but also how far and wide the Kingdom of Christ was dilated and amplified through this one Apostle, so that he does not write falsely about himself, Rom. 15 v. 17 and following: I have reason to glory through Christ Jesus in those things which pertain to GOD: for I would not dare to speak of any of those things which Christ has not wrought through me, for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Spirit of GOD, so that from Jerusalem and in the surrounding regions, I have fulfilled the Gospel of Christ.

While these things were being done in this way, the Apostle Paul, who was previously named Saul, having been miraculously converted by GOD on the road to Damascus, Acts 9 v. 1 and following, preached the Gospel about Christ to the Gentiles and disputed with the Greeks, Acts 9 v. 29; but afterwards, together with Barnabas, he was set apart by the Holy Spirit through the remaining Apostles for the work to which they were being called: Acts 13 v. 2. When they had gone to Seleucia, they sailed from there to Cyprus: and

But neither did the labor and industry of the remaining Apostles lack its own success and fruit. For when they had been ordered by Christ the Savior before his ascension to teach the Gospel in the whole world, they certainly left nothing undone with all their zeal, so that they might make the boundaries of Christ's Kingdom equal to the breadth of the entire world, not indeed confusedly, but with the work divided distinctly among them.
