Of the same vanity is what the Romanists prattle about a single and visible judge of all controversies in the Church. For if a single and visible judge of controversies is necessary, it would follow that there is not, or has not been, a Church where such a judge did not exist. But he never existed in the Church of Christ before the dominion of the Pope was established. Therefore, it must be that there was no Church then. But this is manifestly false. Therefore, that also from which this follows is false. The judgment concerning ecclesiastical controversies belongs to the ministers of the Church, both individually and collectively: yet in such a way that it is not by their own authority—for this is prevented by the imperfection and weakness of their nature—nor as lords sitting in judgment to decide cases according to their own opinion; but as ambassadors of Christ, according to the received law, they are to judge and condemn heresies not by their own judgment, but by the judgment of GOD expressed in the Scriptures, not by external force, but by the word of the key that binds; committing the rest to Christ, the sole judge of the living and the dead. But this error has been dealt with expressly, both in the article concerning Holy Scripture and in the disputation concerning the head of the Church: where, following the Scriptures, we have established one Head, one Father, one Bridegroom of the Church, Eph. 1. v. 22. & cap. 5. v. 23. Matth. 23. v. 9. 2. Cor. 11. v. 2., namely Christ the Savior: but this vicarious and spurious head we have banished.

V. Error concerning the Kingdom of Christ, of the Calvinists.

The Calvinists also impinge upon the purer doctrine concerning the Kingdom of Christ, as do their associates the Hofmannians: of whom the former perfidiously deny to Christ, according to the human nature assumed, however much it may be exalted to the right hand of the power and divine majesty, both the Kingdom of Grace in the Church and the Kingdom of power; the latter, however, indeed concede to Christ, according to the flesh assumed, the Kingdom of Grace in the Church, but they sufficiently and rashly derogate from the Kingdom of power outside the Church, among all creatures, with respect to universal dominion.

But since both of these errors have been expressly disputed in the digression of the Article concerning the Person of Christ: we do not wish to do over again what has already been done in this place.

Latin:

GRaviter admodùm errant Romanenses, dum monarchicum Ecclesiæ in his terris regimen, & unum visibile ejusdem caput ac judicem fingunt, à qvo tota & universa gubernetur Ecclesia, & controversiæ singulæ de religione ortæ cognoscantur, dijudicentur, & sopiantur. Cujus erroris fundamentum præcipuum petit Bellarminus, & socii ex optima forma regiminis in politia, & conformitate Ecclesiasticæ gubernationis & politicæ, Bellar. Contr. 2. Colloq. Ratisb. Sess. 9. Sed multis modis vanitas commenti hujus patet. Nam 1. non qvicqvid optimum est in politia, statim etiam optimum est in regimine Ecclesiastico. Multa enim sunt in politia optima, quæ ne quidem in Ecclesia sunt licita : Exempli gratia, facinorosum vi externa coercere: Matth. 13. v. 4. & cap. 26. v. 52. 2. Et politiam administrare, id regnare est. Ecclesiam verò administrare, non est regnare, sed servire. 3. Insuper de Ecclesia nunquam rectè dici possunt, quæcunq; de regno dicuntur. 4. Christus ipse Ecclesiam suam hisce in terris monarchicè administrat, quod ab homine fieri alio nemine poterat, ne quidem à Petro Apostolo, cùm unus homo toti administrandæ Ecclesiæ per totum terrarum orbem dispersæ, non sufficiat. 5. Prohibitum est, ut quisquam ministrorum Ecclesiæ aliis dominetur. 6. Apostolus Ephes. 4. & 1. Cor. 12. in descriptione totius hierarchiæ Ecclesiasticæ, nullam fecit mentionem monarchicæ, cùm exprimeret modum nostræ cum Christo conjunctionis. 7. Non uni omnia : sed singulis Ecclesiæ mebris aliqva portio data est. 8. Ministri Ecclesiæ omnes, non dispari, sed uno, eodemqve modo à Christo missi sunt. 9 Ne totus qvidem mundus ab uno externo rege, & visibili capite in secularibus gubernatur : ut id propter perplexitatem & copiam causarum in Ecclesia fieri minimè omnium sit possibile.

Ejusdem vanitatis est, qvod de uno & visibili omnium Controversiarum judice, in Ecclesia, garriunt Romanenses. Nam si necessarius est unus & visibilis Controversiarū judex, conseqvens fuerit, ibi non esse, aut fuisse Ecclesiam, ubi talis judex non fuit. At qvi non fuit in Ecclesia Christi unqvam, ante dominatum Papæ constitutum. Ergò tùm Ecclesia non fuerit, necesse est. Jam verò hoc manifestè falsum. Ergò & illud, ex qvo hoc seqvitur. Competit autem ministris Ecclesiæ singulis & universis judicium de Controversiis Ecclesiasticis: sed ita, ut non propria autoritate : Hoc enim naturæ ipsorum imperfectio & imbecillitas : neq; tanqvam Domini pro tribunali, ex sua sententia causas cognoscant; sed ut, tanqvam legati Christi, juxta acceptam legem, non suo, sed DEI judicio in Scripturis expresso, non vi externa, sed verbo ligantis clavis hæreses dijudicent, ac damnēt: reliqva committentes Christo, soli vivorum & mortuorum judici. Sed de errore isto ex professo actum, tùm in articulo de Scriptura Sacra, tùm in disputatione de capite Ecclesiæ: Ubi unum Caput, unum Patrem, unum Sponsum Ecclesiæ, Scripturas secuti, constituimus, Ephes. 1. v. 22. & cap. 5. v. 23. Matth. 23. v. 9. 2. Cor. 11. v. 2. nempe Christum Servatorem: vicarium autem istud, & spurium caput profligavimus.

V. Error de Regno Christi, Calvinianorum.

IMpingunt in puriorem doctrinam de Regno Christi etiam Calviniani: & horum socii Hofmanniani: quorum illi Christo tàm Regnum Gratiæ in Ecclesia, quàm Regnum potentiæ, secundùm humanam affumtam naturam, qvantumvis ad dextram virtutis ac majeftatis divinæ exaltatam, perfidè negant: Hiverò Christo qvidem secundum affumtam carnem, Regnum Gratiæ in Ecclesia concedunt:Regnum verò potentiæ extra Ecclesiam, apud omnes creaturas,respectu dominii Universalis, satis imprè derogant.

Verùm cùm de utroq; isto errore ex professo disputatum sit in diexodo Articuli de Persona Christi: nolumus hoc loco actum agere.


### On the Quality, Form, and Condition of the Kingdom of Christ: VI. The Error concerning the Kingdom of Christ, of the recent Photinians

Christophorus Ostorrodus of Goslar, in chapter 40 of his Institutions, after having disputed at sufficient length against the heresy of the Chiliasts in the first six paragraphs, finally in §. 7 subjoins a πέρισμα concerning the Kingdom of Christ, comprehending the sum and head of the entire Photinian heresy ὡς ἐν Τύπω̄̄η, and it is as follows: The royal majesty and dignity of Christ is the most important cause of all, on account of which Christ is named in the Scriptures 1. our Savior, 2. God, 3. the Son of God. There are three members of this assertion, which are plainly heretical. The first is that in the Holy Scriptures no other cause is expressed for which Christ is our Savior, than that he procures salvation for us in the kingdom of grace, that is, eternal life, by showing the way of salvation. Thus, therefore, this heretic perfidiously denies the entire merit of Christ, by which he satisfied the Father for our sins and acquired salvation and eternal life. Concerning which matter, because we have expressly treated it in the article on the Justification of a sinful man before GOD: and Ostorrodus himself also does not prove this first member of his Assertion with even a single little word: neither shall we treat of it at greater length in this place.

THE SECOND member is that Christ is called God in the Scriptures primarily for this reason, that is, according to the interpretation of Ostorodt, a divine governor, because royal power over the pious and the impious has been granted to him by GOD. Thus, therefore, this heretic denies that Christ is GOD by nature and essentially, but that he only obtains some likeness to GOD by reason of his royal office. He confirms this member of his with this reasoning: If John in chapter 10, verse 34, named Christ God on account of his Prophetic office, much more, on account of this kingdom of his, which is divine in every respect, ought he to be held as GOD. But it is most rightly answered that the heretic is wandering off the track and is proving that which is placed beyond controversy in this passage. For this is not what is being asked: whether Christ is called God in the Scriptures in a certain way and respect, both on account of his Prophetic and his Royal office, and his divine government from both offices can be elicited according to the Scriptures and confirmed? For this we also willingly grant. But the point at issue here is the κρινόμενον [the matter to be judged], whether the Royal dignity granted to Christ is the principal cause for which Christ is named GOD in the Scriptures? This we simply deny: Ostorrodus, however, does not confirm his affirmative with even one argument. The fanatic man is therefore trifling, not disputing. Moreover, not only for this cause, much less because of it as the principal one: but because of another most principal one, namely because of the eternal generation from the Father, it was clearly demonstrated in the articles concerning GOD and the person of Christ that Christ is GOD by nature and essence. To which this dispute also properly pertains.

not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of GOD they were born, John 1. v. 12. Which Sonship Scripture calls adoptive, as often as it expresses it with the Greek word ὑιοθεσίας [adoption]. We also know, and believe, that men too, both because of that dominion over creatures which was in some way granted to them even after the fall: and because of other spiritual gifts, especially because of that gracious indwelling in the hearts of the pious, are rendered κοινωνὸς θείας Φύσεως, partakers of the divine nature: and for that reason are called Sons of GOD in the Scriptures, Rom. 8. 16. and elsewhere. 2. Pet. 1. 4. Finally, we know that Christ, by that nature according to which He was established in time, and as Peter speaks, was made King and Lord of the Church, is not Son by nature; but that from the union with the λόγῳ [Word], as if by κληρονομίαν [inheritance], He obtained that name by hereditary right, so that He is called Son of GOD: Heb. 1. 4. But concerning all these things there is no controversy properly in this place: But this is the question, Is it true, what Ostorrodus affirms: That the royal Majesty granted to Christ over the Church by GOD is the principal cause for which Christ is, and is called, the Son of GOD? We deny it: He affirms it, but leaning on such an argument that, as has already been shown, it shamefully begs the question, and does not prove that which is placed in controversy.

The third member of the assertion is that Christ is named the Son of God primarily because of his royal majesty. The heretic implies, of course, that Christ is not the Son of GOD by nature, begotten from eternity by the Father: but that He is called the Son of GOD only because of the likeness which He has with GOD on account of his royal office. This opinion of his is evident from two arguments by which he strives to establish this affirmation of his.

The former is such: There is nothing that renders Christ more like to GOD than that He is such a King. And if Likeness between God and men makes men sons of God: If, finally, men also are named sons of God because of the dominion which they have over creatures, whose dominion, however, can in no way be equated with the dominion of Christ: then certainly Christ will be much more like to God because of this dominion, and consequently is called the son of God on that account.

THE LATTER argument, by which Ostorrodus contends that Christ is, and is named, the Son of GOD primarily because of his office and royal dominion, is proposed thus: In Psalm 2, 6, it is read that GOD ordained CHRIST JESUS as king and Lord over the holy mountain of Zion, which Peter explains in these words, Acts 2, v. 25. Let the whole house of Israel know for certain that this one has been made Lord and Christ by God, this Jesus, namely, whom you crucified. But that Christ was made the Son of GOD through this ordination, or coronation, and was then begotten by GOD, can be seen from the same Psalm. For after GOD said that He had constituted Him King over Zion, the Son Himself is immediately introduced speaking in this manner: I will declare the decree or statute of GOD, which He said to me: You are my Son: Today I have begotten you. Whence it appears most clearly that the ordination and coronation of Christ as King over the Church is nothing other than that generation from GOD by which He was made the Son of God. The Apostle confirms this very thing, Acts 13 v. 32. 33. saying, We evangelize to you the promise which was made to the Fathers, that God fulfilled it to their children, that is, to us, by raising up JESUS: as it is written in the second Psalm: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Where it is to be noted, says Ostorrodus, that as in other places, so also in this place, by the resurrection of CHRIST from the dead, all those things which followed the Resurrection, such as immortality, power, kingdom, might, and the like, are to be understood: which can be gathered even from the fact that the Apostle says that GOD fulfilled those things which He promised to the Fathers in their children

I ANSWER, that the heretic is again trifling; not disputing, and is shamefully begging the question regarding the first member of the proof. For this very thing is in question, whether besides the royal office there is nothing else that renders Christ like to God or more like to Him than other creatures. We deny it: he affirms it, and takes it as an αἴτημα πεπωτόθετον [a begged premise] as if it were confessed. By which method it is most clearly evident that the heretic is babbling, and proving a doubtful thing by an equally doubtful thing. Then, regarding the remaining two members of the proofs, the heretic acts the Sophist, and insidiously changes the state of the Controversy. For this is not what is being controverted in this place between us and the Photinians: Whether Likeness between God and men makes men sons of God? Or even: Whether men also, because of their dominion over creatures, have some likeness with God, and therefore can be named sons of GOD in their own certain way and respect? Indeed, neither is it asked properly in this place: Whether Christ can be called the Son of GOD because of the royal, and truly divine, majesty which He exercises in the Church, both over the pious and the impious?

For none of us has ever denied all these things: For we know that the power to become sons of GOD has been given to those men, who then, when he raised Christ from the dead. But he had promised them a King and Savior. A hypothetical syllogism emerges as follows: If Christ, through ordination and coronation as king, was made the Son of GOD: then his Generation and Coronation will be one and the same. But the former is evident: 1. from Psalm 2:6, where GOD constitutes CHRIST King and Lord of Zion with these words in Psalm 2:7: Jehovah said to me: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. For how this was fulfilled is evident from Acts 13:32 & 33, where those same words of the Psalm are explained regarding the royal office of CHRIST. Therefore, the Coronation as King is the very Generation of CHRIST as the Son of GOD.

I reply that the Assumption and its twofold proof are by far most false: That this may be evident, it will have been necessary for us to demonstrate clearly that neither in the second Psalm nor in Acts 13 is the Generation of the Son of GOD defined only by his ordination and coronation to the royal office. First, therefore, regarding the second Psalm, we concede at the beginning that in verse six it is expressly treated of the Anointing of CHRIST as King: an anointing, however, which can never fall upon a mere and simple man, but which necessarily presupposes divine majesty and power, since it is not restricted only to the narrow boundaries of Mount Zion or the Church: but which extends itself to universal dominion over all creatures, as the eighth verse of the Psalm and those following clearly intimate, and the Photinians themselves are forced to admit. Then we also concede to Ostorodt that in the seventh verse of the Psalm the Son is introduced speaking in this manner: I will declare the decree: The Lord said to me: You are my Son: Today I have begotten you. Here, however, that κρινόμενον (point of contention) emerges: Whether the Son of GOD understood these words only concerning that coronation as King, or whether he understood them at the same time also concerning his eternal generation from the Father and his divinity. Where the Photinians affirm the former: but they deny the latter. We affirm that both are intimated, namely both that anointing to the office, both Royal and Priestly: and that eternal Generation from GOD the Father. The former does not need confirmation: the latter we prove first from chapter 1:5 of the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the Apostle cites these words, intending to confirm that CHRIST is above all Angels: not as the most excellent creature of all, as the Photinians wish: but as the Son of GOD by nature and essence, so begotten that it was said to him alone by the Father: You are my Son: and as heir of all things, as the CREATOR of all, even of the Angels: as the ἀπαύγασμα καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆς δόξης καὶ ὑποστάσεως τοῦ πατρὸς (brightness and express image of the glory and substance of the Father). As him who sustains ALL things by his powerful Word, as finally GOD, whom the Angels are commanded to worship, and whose Throne is for ever and ever. Which predicates, each and all, befit none but the true and essential God. But they are predicated of Christ, and indeed in that respect in which JEHOVAH said to him: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Therefore, it is concluded with invincible necessity that CHRIST is GOD, not only in respect of his coronation as King: but also by reason of his eternal generation. To this pertains the fact that if the entire συνέπεια (coherence) of this Psalm is considered, it becomes plain that neither the promise, nor the exhortation, nor the epiphonema, nor the description of the person and office of the King of Zion can befit any creature, however sublime, but only the essential GOD. Nor does it stand in the way that this passage in Acts 13:33 is adapted to confirm the Resurrection of CHRIST. For this was done because then his eternal birth from the Father was most illustriously revealed by miracles. When, however, something is declared: then it is very frequently said in the Scriptures to be done.

In which sense the Apostle also writes in Romans 1:4 that the Son of GOD, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, was declared to be the Son of GOD with power, according to the Spirit of Holiness, from the time when JESUS CHRIST our LORD rose from the dead. With these things thus posited, it is evident that Ostorodt in this argument also begs the question. For this very thing is in question, whether CHRIST, when in his coronation or anointing as king, when likewise in his Priestly office, in his Resurrection, Ascension into heaven, and Session at the right hand of GOD the Father, he declared with power that he was the Son of GOD: whether, I say, this Filiation ought to be defined properly and solely by these acts, as the Photinians wish: or rather by his eternal and infallible generation from GOD the Father? as we teach from the Scriptures: and in the Article of the Trinity we have evidently demonstrated from the Scriptures, and indeed from this very second Psalm. Now when Ostorodt takes the former for granted, and urges it in place of proof, he proves a doubtful thing by an equally doubtful thing. But because the treatment of the eternal generation of the Son of GOD is clearly inappropriate in this place: nor shall we pursue it at greater length: let it suffice to have defined in a few words the vanities of Ostorodt, which indeed pertain to this Article.

To GOD alone and to CHRIST the King, to GOD the eternal Son, and to the ὁμουσίῳ (consubstantial one) be praise, glory, and adoration for infinite ages. AMEN.

Latin:

CHristophorus Ostorrodus Goslariensis, capite 40. suarum Institutionum, postqvam contra Chiliastarum hæresin, primis sex paragraphis, prolixè satis disputavit, tandem §. 7. subjicit πέρισμα de Regno Christi, summam & caput universæ hæreseos Photinianæ ὡς ἐν Τύπω̄̄η comprehendens, idq; tale: Regia Christi majestas & dignitas, est omnium potissima causa, propter quam Christus in Scripturis 1. noster Salvator. 2. Deus. 3. Dei Filius nominatur. Tria sunt assertionis membra, planè hæretica. Primum est, quòd in Scripturis Sacris nulla alia expressa sit causa, ob quam Christus Salvator noster sit, quàm quia in regno Gratiæ nobis salutem, hoc est,vitam æternam procuret, monstrando viam salutis. Sic ergò hæreticus iste universum meritum Christi, qvo Patri pro peccatis nostris satisfecit, & salutem, ac vitam æternam acqvisivit, perfidè negat. Qua de re, quia in articulo de Justificatione hominis peccatoris coram DEO, ex professo egimus: & ipse qvoqve Ostorrodus, primum hoc Assertionis suæ membrum, ne unico qvidem verbulo probet: neq; nos de eo hoc loco pluribus agemus.

ALTERUM membrum est, quòd Christus in Scripturis potissimùm ob hanc causam nominetur Deus, hoc est, interprete Ostorrodo, divinus gubernator, quia regia ipsi potestas in pios & impios à DEO est concessa. Sic ergo hæreticus iste negat, Christum naturâ & essentialiter DEUM esse: sed tantùm ratione officii regii similitudinem aliqvam cum DEO obtinere. Confirmat autem ipse membrum hoc suum hac ratione: Si Johannes cap. 10.v.34. Christum nominavit Deum, propter officium Propheticum:multò magis propter hoc regnum suum, quod ex omni parte divinum est, pro DEO haberi debet. Sed rectissimè respondetur,Hæreticum extra oleas vagari,& probare id,quod extra Controversiam hoc loco est positum. Non enim hoc quæritur: an Christus in Scripturis, certò quodam modo ac respectu, tum propter Propheticum, tum propter Regium officium, Deus appelletur: & divina ipsius gubernatio ex utroque officio, secundum Scripturas elici, & confirmari possit? Nam & hoc ultrò largimur. Verum in eo vertitur hoc loco κρινόμενον an Regia dignitas Christo concessa, præcipua sit causa, propter quam Christus in Scripturis nominetur DEUS? id quod nos simpliciter negamus: Ostorrodus autem affirmativam suam rursus ne uno quidem argumento confirmat. Nugatur ergò, non disputat homo fanaticus. Cæterum non tantùm ob hanc causam, nedum propter eam, tanquàm præcipuam: sed propter aliam maximè principalem, nempe propter æternam generationem à Patre, Christum naturâ & essentiâ DEUM esse, in articulis de DEO, & personâ Christi luculenter demonstratum fuit. Quò etiam hæc disputatio propriè pertinet.

non ex sanguinibus, nec ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex DEO nati sunt, Johan. 1. v. 12. Quam Filiationem Scriptura nominat adoptivam, quoties eam Græco ὑιοθεσίας vocabulo exprimit. Novimus etiam, & credimus, homines etiam,tùm ob dominium illud in creaturas, quod utcunque ipsis etiam post lapsum est concessum : tùm propter alia dona spiritualia, præsertim propter inhabitationem illam gratiosam in cordibus piorum, reddi κοινωνὸς θείας Φύσεως, participes divinæ naturæ: & ob id Filios DEI in Scripturis vocari, Rom. 8. 16. & alibi. 2. Petr. 1. 4. Novimus denique Christum ex ea natura, secundum quam in tempore constitutus, & ut Petrus loquitur, factus est Rex & Dominus Ecclesiæ, non esse naturâ Filium; sed ex unione cum λόγω, tanquam per κληρονομίαν, hæreditario jure consecutum esse illud nomen, ut Filius DEI vocetur: Hebr. 1. 4. Verùm de istis omnibus propriè non controvertitur hoc loco: Sed hoc quæstionis est, An verum sit, quod Ostorrodus affirmat: Quòd Majestas regia Christo in Ecclesiam à DE O concessa, sit præcipua causa, propter quam Christus Filius DEI sit, & appelletur? Nos negamus: Ille affirmat, sed tali nixus argumento, quod, uti jam ostensum, turpiter petit principium, & non probat id, quod in controversia est positum.

Tertium assertionis membrum est, quòd Christus propter regiam potissimùm majestatem nominetur Dei filius. Innuit nimirùm hæreticus, Christum non esse naturâ Filium DEI, ab æterno à Patre genitum: sed tantum propter similitudinem, quam propter regium officium cum DEO habeat, Filium DEI appellari. Patet hæc ipsius sententia ex duobus argumentis, quibus affirmatum hoc suum stabilire studet.

Prius tale est: Nihil est quod Christum DEO similiorem reddat, quàm quod talis Rex est. Et si Similitudo inter Deum & homines, efficit homines Dei filios: Si deniq; homines quoque propter dominium, quod in creaturas habent, quorum tamen dominium cum dominio Christi nullo pacto æquiparari potest, nominantur filii Dei : multò certè magis Christus propter hoc dominium Deo erit similis, ac per consequens ob id filius Dei vocatur.

POSTERIUS argumentum, quo Ostorrodus contendit, Christum præcipuè propter officium ac dominium regium, Filium DEI esse, & nominari, sic proponitur: Psalmo 2, 6. legitur, quòd DEUS CHRISTUM JESVM in regem ac Dominum ordinaverit, super montem Sanctum Sion, id quod Petrus his verbis explicat, Actor. 2, v. 25. Certò sciat tota domus Israel, hunc esse factum à Deo Dominum & Christum, hunc Jesum nimirum, quem vos crucifixistis. Christum autem per hanc ordinationem, sive coronationem factum esse filium DEI, & tùm à DEO ipsum genitum fuisse, ex eodem Psalmo videre licet. Postquam enim DEUS dixit, quòd constituerit ipsum Regem super Sion, mox Filius ipse loquens introducitur, in hunc modum: Enarrabo decretum sive statutum DEI, quòd ipse ad me dixit : Filius meus es tu : Ego hodie genui te. Unde apparet clarissimè, ordinationem & coronationem Christi in Regem super Ecclesiam, nihil esse aliud, quàm generationem illam à DEO, qua Dei Filius factus est. Quod ipsum confirmat Apostolus, Actor. 13 v. 32. 33. Nos inquiens, evangelizamus vobis promissionem eam, quæ Patribus facta est, quod Deus eam explevit filiis illorum, hoc est, nobis, suscitato JESU: sicut in Psalmo secundo scriptum est : Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Ubi notandum est, inquit Ostorrodus, uti in aliis, sic & in hoc loco, per resurrectionem CHRISTI ex mortuis, omnia illa, quæ Resurrectionem consecuta sunt, qualia sunt, immortalitas, potestas, regnum, potentia, & similia intelligenda esse: id quod vel inde colligi potest, quòd dicit Apostolus, DEUM, ea quæ Patribus promisit, explevisse in filiis illorum

RESPONDEO, rursum nugari; non disputare hæreticum, & turpiter petere principium, qvoad prius probationis membrum. Hoc ipsum enim in quæstione est, An præter officium regium nihil sit aliud, quod Christum Deo similem vel similiorem aliis creaturis reddat. Nos negamus: ille affirmat, & tanquam αἴτημα πεπωτόθετον pro confesso sumit. Qvo pacto hæreticum ἀδολεσχεῖν, & probare dubium, per æqvè dubium, clarissimè patet. Deinde qvoad reliqva duo probationum membra, Sophistam agit hæreticus, & insidiosè mutat statum Controversiæ. Non enim hoc controvertitur hoc loco inter nos, & Photinianos : An Similitudo inter Deum & homines, efficiat homines Dei filios? Vel etiam : An homines etiam propter dominium in creaturas, aliquam similitudinem cum Deo habeant, ac proinde suo certo modo atque respectu filii DEI nominari possint? Quin neqve de eo hoc loco qværitur propriè: An Christus propter majestatem regiam, ac verè divinam, quam in Ecclesia exercet, tum in pios, tum in impios, possit Filius DEI vocari?

Nam hæc omnia nemo nostrum negavit unqvam : Novimus enim hominibus illis potestatem filios DEI fieri factam esse, qui tùm, cum Christum excitavit ex mortuis. Promiserat autem ipsis Regem & Salvatorem. Syllogismus hypotheticus emergit talis: Si Christus per ordinationem, ac coronationem in regem, factus est DEI Filius: utique Generatio ac Coronatio ipsius erunt unum & idem. At prius illud patet: 1. ex Psal. 2. 6. ubi DEVS CHRISTVM Regem & Dominum Sionis constituit his verbis Psal. 2. 7. Jehovah dixit ad me: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Nam quomodo hoc impletum sit, patet ex cap. Actor. 13. 32. & 33. ubi eadem illa verba Psalmi de officio CHRISTI regio explicantur. Ergo Coronatio in Regem, est ipsa Generatio CHRISTI in Filium DEI.

Respondeo Assumtionem, ejusque probationem geminam longè esse falsissimam: Quod ut pateat, evidenter demonstrandum nobis fuerit, neque in Psalmo secundo, neque Actor. 13. Generationem Filij DEI, definiri tantùm per ordinationem, ac coronationem ejus ad officium regium. Primùm ergò quoad Psalmum secundum, initiò concedimus, versu sexto ex professo agi de Unctione CHRISTI in Regem: unctione autem tali quæ in nudum ac simplicem hominem nunquam cadere potest, sed quæ divinam majestatem ac potentiam necessariò præsupponit, quippe quæ non ad montis Sionis sive Ecclesiæ angustos tantùm terminos est restricta: sed quæ ad dominium universale super omnes creaturas se extendit, uti versus Psalmi octavus, & sequentes luculenter innuunt, & Photiniani ipsi fateri coguntur Deinde concedimus etiam Ostorrodo, versu Psalmi septimo introduci Filium loquentem in hunc modum: Prædicabo statutum: Dominus dixit ad me: Filius meus es tu: Ego hodie genui te. Hic verò emergit illud κρινόμενον: An Filius DEI hæc verba tantùm de coronatione illa in Regem, an verò simul etiam de æternâ generatione à Patre ac divinitate sua intellexerit. Ubi prius illud affirmant Photiniani: Hoc verò posterius negant. Nos utrumque innui affirmamus, nempe & unctionem illam ad officium tum Regium, tum Sacerdotale: & æternam Generationem illam à DEO Patre Prius illud confirmatione non indiget: Posterius hoc probamus initiò ex cap. 1. 5. Epistolæ ad Hebræos, ubi hæc verba Apostolus citat, confirmaturus CHRISTUM esse supra Angelos omnes: non ut creaturam omnium excellentissimam, uti Photiniani volunt: sed ut naturâ, & essentiâ Filium DEI, ita unigenitum, ut ei soli dictum sit à Patre: Filius meus es tu: & ut hæredem universorum, ut CONDITOREM omnium, etiam Angelorum: ut ἀπαύγασμα καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆς δόξης καὶ ὑποστάσεως τοῦ πατρὸς. ut eum, qui OMNIA Verbo suo potenti sustentat, ut denique DEUM, quem adorare jubentur Angeli, & cujus Thronus est in seculum seculi. Quæ prædicata singula & universa no nisi vero, & essentiali Deo competunt. Atqui de Christo, & quidē eo respectu ea prædicantur, quo JEHOVAH dixit ad eum: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Ergo invicta necessitate concluditur, CHRISTUM esse DEUM, non tantùm respectu coronationis in Regem: sed & ratione æternæ generationis. Quò pertinet, quòd si tota Psalmi hujus συνέπεια consideretur, planum fit, neque promissionem, neque adhortationem, neque Epiphonema, neque descriptionem personæ, & officij Regis Sionis, ulli creaturæ, quantumvis sublimi, sed soli essentiali DEO competere posse. Neque obstat quòd locus iste Actor. 13. 33. ad confirmandam Resurrectionem CHRISTI accommodatur. Hoc enim ideò factum est, quia tùm maximè illustribus miraculis patefacta fuit æterna ipsius ex Patre nativitas. Cùm autem aliquid declaratur: tùm frequenter admodum in Scripturis dicitur, Fieri.

Quo sensu Apostolus etiam scribit Romanorum 1, 4. Filium DEI, qui genitus est ex semine David secundum carnem, declaratum fuisse Filium DEI cum potentia, secundum Spiritum Sanctificationis, ex quo resurrexit à mortuis JESUS CHRISTUS DOMINUS noster. Quibus ita positis, patet, Ostorrodum in hoc etiam argumento petere principium. Hoc ipsum enim in quæstione est, An CHRISTUS, quando in coronatione sua, sive unctione in regem, quando item in officio suo Sacerdotali, in Resurrectione, Ascensione ad cælos, & Sessione ad dextram DEI Patris, declaravit cum potentiâ, se esse Filium DEI: An inquam hæc Filiatio propriè atque unicè per istos actus, uti Photiniani volunt: an verò per æternam ac infallibilem generationem à DEO Patre, definiri debeat? uti nos ex Scripturis docemus: & in Articulo Trinitatis evidenter ex Scripturis, & quidem ex hoc ipso Psalmo secundo demonstravimus. Jam quando Ostorrodus prius illud pro confesso sumit, & probationis loco urget, probat dubium per æquè dubium. Verùm quia de æterna generatione Filij DEI hoc loco planè inconveniens est tractatio: neque nos prolixiùs eam persequemur: Sufficiat Ostorrodi vanitates paucis definivisse, quæ quidem ad hunc Articulum pertinent.

Soli DEO & CHRISTO Regi, DEO Filio æterno, & ὁμουσίῳ sit laus, gloria & adoratio sæculis infinitis. AMEN.


## 26 On the Resurrection of the Dead

Since we are to have a discussion about the resurrection of the dead, it must be known before all else which resurrection of the dead is meant: for Scripture makes mention of a twofold resurrection of the dead: namely, the first and the last or second: of which the former is bodily, but the latter is spiritual and is so called: and it happens then, when the faithful rise from the death of sins in this life: but in the other life, as soon as souls depart from bodies, even before that last or second resuscitation of bodies, they are perfectly freed according to their souls from sins and all evils. But we are not to have a discussion at present about this spiritual resurrection, but about that bodily one, which happens on the last day, when the bodies of all the deceased will be resuscitated and restored to their own souls. What the Christian faith teaches about this resurrection, we shall see at the beginning in the thesis: then we shall proceed to the antithesis and the refutation of various errors.

Latin:

Cùm de Resurrectione mortuorum futura nobis sit disputatio, ante omnia sciendum, quænam Resurrectio mortuorum intelligatur: Meminit enim Scriptura geminæ Resurrectionis mortuorũ: Primæ nimirum & ultimæ sive secundæ: quarum illa corporalis, hæc verò spiritualis est ac dicitur: & fit tùm, quando fideles hoc quidem in seculo à morte peccatorum resurgunt: in altero autem seculo, statim ac animæ excedunt corpora, etiam ante ultimam illam sive secundam corporum resuscitationem, secundum animas perfectè liberantur à peccatis & malis omnibus. De hac verò spirituali Resurrectione nobis in præsentia non est futura disputatio, verùm de corporali illa, quæ fit in die novissimo, quo omnium defunctorum corpora resuscitabuntur, suisquè animabus restituentur. De qua Resurrectione quid fides Christiana doceat, initiò in θέσει videbimus: Deindè ad ἀντίθεσιν & variorum errorum refutationem, accelluri.


### Part I

But before I descend to particulars, I would like you to note the causes for which God has decreed the resurrection of the dead, of which two seem to be able to be given: The first is, that God might render His elect truly and solidly happy. For because, according to that saying of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 13:9 & 10, in this life we know in part, and we prophesy in part: But when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part shall be abolished: therefore He will clearly free them from all these infirmities, and will endow them with true and absolute perfection as much regarding the soul as the body. The latter cause depends upon the very norm of divine justice, which in this life does not always attain its end regarding the lot and fortune of the pious and the impious. For we see the impious for the most part flourishing in power and honors: abounding in wealth and riches, and enjoying the greatest happiness: but the pious being tossed by the perpetual waves of troubles and calamities. Therefore the very immutable norm of divine justice demands that, since this lot is not changed in this life, it should be changed in the other.

The Apostle wished to express this latter reason in 2 Thess. 1:7, saying: It is just with GOD to repay tribulation to those who afflict you: and to you who are afflicted, rest with us, in the revelation of Christ. And indeed the force of this reason is so great that it was impressed even upon the minds of the Gentiles themselves: which is evident from the fact that the poets fashioned various judges, such as Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus, who in the underworld would award to each of the mortals according to how they had conducted themselves in this life. Furthermore, since in this life the soul has had the body as a companion joined to itself in both good and evil actions: therefore the rule of divine justice again demands that the soul not be blessed or afflicted with punishments alone: but together with the body: to which it must be restored in the resurrection of the dead.

The resurrection of the dead, which the Greeks call ἀνάστασιν, the Hebrews Thechiaih Hammehim, that is, the vivification of the dead, Damascenus [calls it] because it is the δεύτερα τῶν νεκρῶν στάσις, the second standing of the dead; Scripture seems to define it by a certain new birth in Matt. 19:28: You who have followed me, in the regeneration ὅτι τῇ παλιγγενεσίᾳ shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. For just as in the first birth, man was created consisting of body and soul. So in the resurrection, a new body and a new soul will not be created: but it will only be repaired. But it can be more fully defined as the action of GOD, by which GOD will vivify the bodies of all the deceased, once again joined to their own souls: and will set them at the final judgment, so that the believers may receive eternal life by inheritance: but the unbelievers may be adjudged to the eternal flames of hell. Which definition indeed demonstrates a clear distinction between the death of men and the death of brute animals, for whom neither is the soul immortal nor is the resuscitation of their bodies to be hoped for: since this resuscitation will happen on account of that final judgment to be instituted concerning each and all mortals.

The action by which the resurrection of the dead is defined, the attached particle (GOD) shows what kind it is. For this excludes every physical action, and all its species, generation, corruption, augmentation, diminution, alteration, and others of this kind, which individually, as they are natural, so they can always be recalled to nature as the first and moving cause. Now, however, the resurrection of the dead is an action transcending all the powers of nature by infinite intervals, and therefore it is hyperphysical, which clearly consists not by nature, but by divine miracle. For it would be a miracle, pertaining solely to divine omniscience, if the earth and the sea will have to pour forth the bodies of the deceased, and indeed of all of them again: if likewise, as Job testifies, the bodies joined to their own souls will revive, and although they will suffer some change of qualities, they will suffer none at all of substance: if indeed each one again in his own skin shall be compassed: and in his flesh he shall see God, the very same who had lived, and not another, Job 19. 25. & seqq.

But if therefore it be asked: is the Resurrection of the dead not to be natural at all? A distinction must be made between the efficient cause or the mode of the resuscitation of the dead, which, as it depends upon the power and omnipotence of God alone, so it is in no way to be called natural: and the very form of the union of body and soul, which will be restored in the resurrection of the dead. For this can and ought to be called natural: since the conjunction of soul and body is to be the same as that which endured in this life before death: with the removal only of the infirmities of both parts, which in this age, because of the original plague, adhered to them to the marrow.

The subject of this Resurrection is Man, who had been extinguished by preceding death. Therefore, the resurrection does not fall upon the soul. For since the Soul is immortal: Man is certainly said, properly and according to the Scriptures, to be about to be resuscitated not according to the soul, but according to the body. For that is said to rise again, which fell, when it had stood: But indeed, souls, however much they may be torn and separated from their body by death, are yet never said to fall or perish: according to that of the Savior: Fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul, Matt. 10. 28. Meanwhile, however, this Resurrection will not take place without the soul: but it will be necessary for it to be present entirely. Furthermore, when we establish Man as the subject of the Resurrection, we rightly exclude from this monsters and inanimate aborted parts, which do not obtain the definition of Man. For concerning these, that they are to rise again, we do not dare to define, especially since there is such deep silence in the sacred writings concerning them: meanwhile committing this very thing to the wisdom and power of God. And indeed, that they are not to rise again is most likely to be true: since the Resurrection presupposes death: Death presupposes life. Now, however, such inanimate and unformed abortions could never die, because they never lived, and therefore they will not rise again. But if the question is concerning aborted fetuses that were once formed and had life: We answer affirmatively, that they are to rise again, but by divine power liberated and purged from every defect and infirmity. Nor does it stand in the way that many of such aborted fetuses are extinguished in the maternal womb. For they are truly dead to themselves: nor does it matter where anyone dies: provided he dies, as D. Augustine aptly concludes, l. 22. cap. 13. de Civit. DEI.

Therefore, speaking properly concerning the soul, that it is to rise again, it is not permitted to affirm: But in a metaphorical and transferred sense, the Resurrection is also attributed to the soul, and thus indeed in two ways. First, insofar as the Soul is the ἐντελέχεια informing and vivifying the body: Which duty, as it had suspended through death: so, insofar as it returns to this its former duty, to that extent it is said to rise again, as it were: but in a figurative and improper sense. Then, however, insofar as the Soul rises from sins, and indeed in this life: to that extent it is also said to rise again: In which sense the Apostle attributes the Resurrection to the faithful as much by reason of the Soul as by reason of the body, which has been done spiritually in this life, saying, If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above. Coloss. 3. 1. And Ephes. 5. 14. the Apostle addresses the whole man, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and CHRIST shall give thee light.

Furthermore: It was asked formerly, by what right the Resurrection, which is nevertheless a singular benefit of CHRIST, is common to the Impious and those cursed by GOD: and it was not so much asked, as even doubted by some concerning the resurrection of these. But taught by the sacred writings, we hold the affirmative in all things: according to that of the Savior, Joh. 5. 28. The hour is coming, in the which ALL that are in the graves shall hear his voice, and shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment. And Matth. 25. 32. ALL nations shall be gathered before the Son of man, and he shall separate them one from another: and he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left. And Acts 24. 15. We have hope in GOD, and expect the resurrection of the just and the unjust. Which the process and final or definitive sentence of the extreme judgment itself, to be pronounced as much concerning the impious as the pious, evidently demonstrates.

To which assertion that fifth verse of the first psalm does not stand in the way: Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in the judgment: For there is a childish fallacy of the figure of speech in this objection, and at the same time an enormous vice of false translation both Greek and Latin. For what is in the Hebrew, The ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, that the Greek interpreter, and the Latins who followed him, viciously rendered, Shall not rise again. But the sense of the Hebrew word יקמ is, That the impious cannot stand in that extreme judgment, that is, prove their cause to GOD, and render just accounts of their deeds: therefore they are to be condemned eternally. Which very punishment of the impious necessarily presupposes their resurrection.

Nor, however, shall all rise again; since not all shall die, but the last day shall find some alive. For which reason Daniel, cap. 12. 2. says, Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake. The universal particle (ALL) is therefore to be taken limitedly concerning all those who have died before the last day. But concerning the rest, who shall then still be living, the Apostle discourses thus: We who live, who are left: we shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air. 1 Thess. 4. 17. And 1 Cor. 15. 51. We shall not all, he says, fall asleep, but we shall all be changed. Whether this change, or ἀλλαγὴ, can or ought to be called death, has been variously questioned. establish that, since this Rapture is to take place while the world is meanwhile burning, through the midst of the flames of this burning universe, men then living on earth, thus caught up through fire, will pass to immortality not by death itself, but by suffering something analogous to death, with wondrous speed, ἐν ἀτόμῳ καὶ ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ.

Latin:

PRiusquam verò ad specialia descendam9, causas velim notes, ob qvas Deus Resurrectionem mortuorum decreverit, qvarum duæ videntur dari posse: Prior est, ut Deus suos Electos verè ac solidè fœlices redderet. Quia enim secundum illud Apostoli, 1. Cor. 13. 9. & 10. hâc in vitâ ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus: Quando verò advenerit, quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur: idcò ab omnibus istis infirmitatibus eos planè liberabit, & tàm quoad animum, quàm quoad corpus verâ & absoluta perfectione donabit. Posterior causa dependet ab ipsâ normâ justitiæ divinæ, quæ hoc in seculo quoad sortem & fortunam piorum ac impiorum non semper finem suum assequitur. Videmus enim impios plerumque florere potentiâ, & honoribus: affluere opibus & divitiis, summaq; frui fœlicitate: pios verò perpetuis agitari ærumnarum & calamitatum fluctibus. Ipsa proindè justitiæ divinæ immutabilis norma exigit, ut, cùm non in hac, in altera tamen vitâ sors hæc immutetur.

Quam posteriorem rationem exprimere voluit Apostolus 2. Thessal 1. 7. justum est inquiens, apud DEUM retribuere tribulationem iis qui vos affligunt: & vobis, qui tribulamini, requiem nobiscum, in revelatione Christi. Et sanè rationis hujus tanta est vis, ut ea ipsorum etiam Gentilium animis impressa fuerit: id quod vel indè patet, quòd Poëtæ varios confinxerint Judices, ut, Minoaem, Radamanthum & Aeacum, qui apud Inferos cuique mortalium tribuerent, prout hæc in vita se gesserant. Porrò, cùm hac in vita, actionum & bonarum & malarum socium sibi adjunctum habuerit Anima corpus nimirùm: ideoque rursus justitiæ divinæ regula flagitat, ut non sola anima vel sit beata, vel pœnis, affligatur: sed unà cum corpore: cui in Resurrectione mortuorum ea est restituenda.

Resurrectio mortuorum, quam Græci ἀνάςασιν, Hebræi Thechiaih Hammehim, hoc est, vivificationem mortuorum nominant, Damascenus, quòd sit δεύτερα τῶν νεκρῶν ςάσις, secunda mortuorum statio; Scriptura definire eam videtur per novam quandam Nativitatem Matth. 19. 28. Vos qui secuti estis me, in regeneratione ὅτι τῆ παλιγγενεσίᾳ sedebitis super sedes duodecim, judicantes duodecim tribus Israël. Quemadmodum enim in priore Nativitate, creatus fuit homo constans corpore & anima. Ita in Resurrectione, non novum corpus & nova anima creabitur: sed duntaxat reparabitur. Pleniùs autem definiri potest, quod sit actio DEI, qua omnium defunctorũ corpora suu denuò conjuncta animabus, DEUS vivificabit: & extremo sistet judicio, ut credentes æternam vitam hæreditario accipiant: Increduli verò æterna infernalium flammis adjudicentur. Quæ sanè definitio luculentum demonstrat discrimen inter mortem hominum: & intermortem brutorum animantium, quorum neque anima immortalis: neque corporum resuscitatio est speranda: Siquidem Resuscitatio hæc fiet propter extremum illud Judicium, de singulis & universis mortalibus instituendum.

Actio, per quam mortuorum resurrectio mortuorum definitur, qualis sit adjuncta particula (DEI) ostendit. Excludit enim hæc omnem actionem physicam, omnesque ejus species, Generationem, Corruptionem, Augmentationem, Diminutionem, Alterationem, & hujus generis alias, quæ singulæ, uti naturales sunt, ita ad naturam, ceu causam primam & moventem, semper revocari possunt. Jam verò Resurrectio mortuorum est actio omnes naturæ vires infinitis intervallis transscendens, ac proindè est hyperphysica, quæ non naturâ, sed miraculo divino planè constat. Miraculum enim, soli divinæ omniscientiæ competens, fuerit, si Terra & mare corpora defunctorum, & quidem omnium rursus effundere necessu habebunt: Si item, Jobo teste, corpora suis juncta animabus reviviscent, & licèt qualitatum aliquam mutationẽ, substantiæ tamen planè nullam, patientur: si quidem sua iterum pelle quisque circundabitur: & in carne sua videbit Dominum idem ipse qui vixerat, & non alius, Job. 19. 25. & seqq.

Quòd si ergò quæratur: etiamne Resurrectio mortuorum planè non sit futura naturalis? Distinguendum est inter causam efficientem sive modum Resuscitationis mortuorū, qui uti à solius Dei dependet virtute & omni potentia: ita naturalis etiam nullo modo est dicendus: & inter ipsam formam Unionis Corporis & Animæ, quæ in Resurrectione mortuorum restaurabitur. Hæc enim Naturalis dici potest & debet: Siquidem eadem futura est conjunctio animæ & corporis, quæ hac in vita ante mortem duravit: sublatis duntaxat utriusque partis infirmitatibus, quæ hoc in seculo, ob luem originalem medullitus ipsis inhærebant.

Subjectum hujus Resurrectionis Homo est, qui per antegressam mortem extinctus fuerat. In animam itaq; resurrectio non cadit. Nam cùm Anima sit immortalis: Homo certe non secundum animam, sed secundum corpus resuscitandus esse, propriè & secundum Scripturas dicitur. Nam id resurgere dicitur, quod cecidit, cùm stetisset: At verò, animæ, quantumvis etiam à corpore suo per mortem divulsæ & separatæ, nunquam tamen cadere aut interire dicuntur: secundum illud Servatoris: Nolite illos timere, qui corpus occidunt, Animā verò non possunt occidere Matt. 10. 28. Interim tamen Resurrectio isthæc sine anima non fiet: sed illam omninò præsentem adesse oportebit. Cæterùm cū Hominem subjectum Resurrectionis constituimus, meritò hinc excludimus monstra, & partꝰ abortivos inanimes, qui Hominis definitionem non sortiuntur. De his enim, quòd Resurrecturi sint, definire non audemus, præsertim cùm tàm altum in sacris de illis sit silentium: divinæ interim & sapientiæ & potentiæ hoc ipsum committentes. Et sanè quòd non sint resurrecturi, vero esse simillimum: siquidem Resurrectio præsupponit mortem: Mors præsupponit vitam. Jam verò abortus hujusmodi inanimes & informati, mori nunquam potuerunt, quia nunquam vixerunt, ac proinde neque resurgent. Verùm si de fœtibus abortivis, qui aliquando formati fuerunt, & vitam habuerunt, sit quæstio: Respondemus affirmatè, quod sint Resurrecturi, sed divinâ virtute ab omni defectu & infirmitate liberati, & purgati. Neque obstat, quod hujusmodi fœtuum abortivorum plurimi in utero materno extinguuntur. Nam & sibi verè sunt mortui: neque interest, ubi aliquis moriatur: modò moriatur, quemadmodum scitè colligit D. Augustinus l. 22. cap. 13. de Civit. DEI.

Ergò propriè loquendo de animâ, quòd illa sit resurrectura, affirmare non licet: Verùm sensu Metaphorico & translalitio Resurrectio etiam tribuitur animæ, & sic quidem duobus modis. Primùm quidem quatenus Anima est ἐντελέχεια informans & vivificans corpus: Quod sanè suum officium, uti per mortem suspenderat: ita, quatenus ad pristinum hoc suum officium redit, eatenus resurgere quasi dicitur: sed sensu figurato & improprio. Deinde verò, quatenus Anima resurgit à peccatis, & quidem hac in vitâ: eatenus etiam Resurgere dicitur: Quo sensu Apostolus fidelibus tàm ratione Animæ, quàm ratione corporis Resurrectionem tribuit, quæ hac in vita, spiritualiter facta sit, Si, inquiens, consurrexistis cùm Christo, quæ sursum sunt, sapite. Coloss. 3. 1. Et Ephes. 5. 14. totum hominem alloquitur Apostolus, Surge à mortuis, Surge & illuminabit te CHRISTUS.

Porrò: Quæsitum fuit olim, quo jure communis sit Impiis & à DEO maledictis, Resurrectio, quæ tamen singulare est CHRISTI beneficium: & non tàm quæsitum, quàm dubitatum etiam fuit à nonnullis de istorum Resurrectione. Sed sacris edocti literis Affirmativam per omnia tenemus: secundum illud Servatoris, Joh. 5. 28. Venit horâ, in quâ OMNES, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus, & prodibunt, qui bona fecerunt, in Resurrectionem vitæ: qui verò mala egerunt, in Resurrectionem Judicii. Et Matth. 25. 32. Congregabuntur ante Filium hominis OMNES gentes, & separabit eas ab invicem: statuetq; oves à dextris suis, hædos autem à sinistris. Et Actor. 24. 15. Spem habemus in DEUM, & expectamus Resurrectionem justorum, & iniquorum. Quod ipsum etiam Judicii extremi processus & sententia finalis sive definitiva, tàm de impiis, quàm piis pronuncianda, evidenter demonstrat.

Cui assertioni non obstat versus iste quintus psalmi primi: Idcò Impii non resurgent in Judicio: Námque puerilis inest objectioni huic fallacia figuræ dictionis, & simul enorme vitium falsæ translationis cùm Græcæ tùm Latinæ. Quod enim in Hebræo est, Impii non stabunt in judicio, illud Græcus interpres, & cum secuti Latini vitiosè reddiderunt, Non Resurgent. Est verò sensus Hebrææ vocis יקמ, Quòd impii in extremo illo judicio non possint stare, hoc est suam causam probare DEO, & justas factorum reddere rationes: proindè æternum damnandi. Quæ ipsa pœna impiorum, necessariò eorundem Resurrectionem præsupponit.

Nec tamen resurgent omnes; siquidê non omnes morientur, sed quosdam dies novissimus vivos deprehendet. Qua de causâ Daniel, cap. 12. 2. Multi, inquit, qui dormiunt in pulvere terræ, evigilabunt. Particula ergò universalis (OMNES) limitatè est accipienda de iis omnibus, qui ante diem novissimum sunt mortui. De reliquis v. qui tùm adhuc victuri sunt, sic disserit Apostolus: Nos qui vivimus, qui relinquimur : simul rapiemur cum illis, in nubibus obviam Christo in aere. 1. Theß. 4. 17. Et 1. Cor. 15.51. Non omne inquit, obdormiemus, sed omnes immutabimur. Quæ immutatio sive ἀλλαγὴ, num mors appellari possit aut debeat, variè quæsitum fuit. Probabilior eorum videtur esse sententia, qui Apostolum secuti, statuunt, cùm Raptus iste, conflagrante interim mundo, per medias ardentis hujus universi flammas sit futurus, Homines tum in terris viventes, sic per ignem raptatos, non mortem quidem ipsam, sed morti quiddam ἀνάλογον passos, mira celeritate, ἐν ἀτόμῳ καὶ ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ, ad immortalitatem transituros.


### Part I (continued)

St. Ambrose, in his book on the faith of the Resurrection, attempts to prove the certainty of this resurrection by various similarities and, as it were, images, taken from plants and seeds, which, though putrefied, yet rise again: taken likewise from the nature of the Phoenix, which, noticing that the end of its life is at hand, builds for itself a nest filled with frankincense, cassia, myrrh, and other perfumes, and sitting upon it dies, and it is written that from its ashes another bird of the same species is born: taken finally from the perpetual vicissitude of night and day, winter and summer, sleep and waking, labor and rest, sorrow and joy. There are others who were accustomed to confirm the Resurrection of the Flesh from the nature of the Pelican, an Egyptian bird, which, if we believe Jerome, mourns for three days over its offspring killed by a serpent: but then, having struck its own breast and sprinkled its blood upon it, is accustomed to restore it to life. There are others who borrow images and similarities from the silkworm, from the swallow, from flies, from bees, from the rabbit: nay, even from the sea urchin, a marine fish, which, when caught and cut into many pieces, but then thrown back into the sea, soon coalesces according to all its parts and revives. Finally, there were those who were accustomed to confirm the same thing even by philosophical arguments: such as these two: 1. An imperfect thing cannot be capable of absolute happiness: But indeed the soul separated from the body is maimed and mutilated. Therefore, to attain that absolute happiness of eternal life, it stands in need of the conjunction of the body most of all. 2. Whatever is against nature cannot be perpetual. But indeed the separation of body and soul, which happens through death, is against nature. Therefore it cannot be perpetual, but the restitution of the whole composite is most required, if only the soul is to be considered immortal. But to speak frankly of the matter, all these similarities and arguments, however customary among the Fathers and Philosophers, cannot stand in spiritual temptations: and, unless other foundations of proof from the Scriptures come to our aid, certainly the hope of our Resurrection would be completely at an end. What of the fact that even the sounder Philosophers would not concede these two arguments in all respects? For the Soul, however separated from the body, is in itself most perfect: nor does it receive any perfection from the body. To the latter argument, the Epicurean Philosophers will respond that it proceeds from a false hypothesis, which is that of immortality. Now, indeed, it is just as doubtful whether the Soul is immortal as it can be doubtful whether there is a Resurrection of the dead, and therefore nothing is concluded. It would therefore be safest not to fix one's foot on those external similarities and natural arguments: but always to keep the oracles of the sacred scriptures in sight and in memory.

Among them, however, that classic passage which is found in Job chapter 19, verses 25, 26, and 27, easily holds the primary place, taken especially from the Old Testament: I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth: And again I shall be surrounded by my skin, and in my flesh I shall see GOD. Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom. But although there are those who deny that Job spoke here of the resurrection of the dead; but contend that he was only anxious about a bodily restoration to wholeness; that, however, inflicts manifest violence upon the text: For first, he had clearly despaired of the health of his body as far as this life is concerned: and therefore he consoles himself with the hope of the Resurrection. This is evident from the preceding tenth verse, where, overcome by impatience, he complains: that God had completely cast down his hope, so that he is like a plant or a certain tree cut down, which does not grow again. Then, if he had been anxious in this place about a temporary or bodily restoration to wholeness, would he surely have wished with such magnificent protestation that these words of his be written in a book, and carved in flint, or in lead for a perpetual memory of the matter? For it cannot seem so new and unusual if bodily calamities come to an end, and the afflicted are brought back to their former state of happiness. Therefore, paying no heed to the Hebrew interpreters, and especially to the babbling of Mercerus, who childishly dreams that Job wished to say nothing else than that he knew his GOD still lived, and that from the atrocity of the afflictions by which he is tormented by GOD. Likewise that he sees GOD in his flesh, that is, he feels His presence, and from those pains recognizes that he himself, and not another, is enduring them: these, I say, and similar trifles we pay no heed to, and we assert that Job expressly discoursed on the Resurrection of the dead, and that he raised and sustained himself in such great troubles by the hope and certainty of it.

That oracle also pertains here, which is found in Isaiah chapter 26, verse 19. Thy dead shall live, and my slain shall rise again. And chapter 66, verse 16. The Lord will judge in fire, and with his sword against all flesh, and the slain of the Lord shall be gathered. Daniel 12. 2. Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, these to eternal life, those to everlasting reproach and ignominy. Hosea 13. 14. I will deliver them from the hand of death, I will redeem them from death: I will be thy plague, O death: thy bite, O hell.

Now if an approach is made to the New Testament, so many demonstrations almost offer themselves

Of the resurrection of the dead, as many sermons of Christ and the Apostles as exist, as may be seen; Matt. 22. 31. & 32. Luke 14. 14. 20. 35. John 5. 21. & 28. 6. 40. 11. 24. Acts 24. 15. 26. 6. & 8. Rom. 8. 11. & 23. 1 Cor. 15. 12. to the end. 2 Cor. 4. 10. & 11. Col. 3. 4. Phil. 3. 11. & 21. 1 Thess. 4. 14. 2 Tim. 2. 11. Rev. 20. 12.

If you desire a type, the history of Jonah certainly shows one that is by far the most illustrious, which the Savior expressly adapts to prefigure his own resurrection, Matt. 12. 40. Next, that same vision offered to the prophet Ezekiel confirms it, who, caught up in the Spirit into a field filled with the dry, withered, and rotten bones of the dead: which, however, at the words of the Prophet, by the power of God are joined to their former sinews, are covered with flesh and skin, and finally receive spirit and life. Ezek. 37. 1 to 11. Finally, the rapture or translation of Enoch and Elijah into heaven gives assurance of the resurrection of the dead, Gen. 5. 24; 2 Kings 2. 9 & 11. Likewise the examples of those who were recalled from the dead to life by the prophets, by Christ, and by the Apostles: such as the son of the widow of Zarephath, 1 Kings 17. 22; the son of the Shunammite, 2 Kings 4. 33. Likewise of him who revived at the touch of the bones of Elisha, 2 Kings 13. 21; the daughter of Jairus: Matt. 9. 25. The son of the widow of Nain, Luke 7. 15. Lazarus, John 11. 43 & 44. Those rising with Christ: Matt. 27. 52 & 53. Tabitha of Joppa raised by Peter, Acts 9. 40. Eutychus awakened by Paul, Acts 20. 10. But above all, the example of Christ the Savior and our head, who became the firstfruits of those who sleep, and likewise of those who rise: just as the Apostle confirms this with many arguments, 1 Cor. 15. 12 & following. And for this reason he calls Christ the firstborn from the dead, Col. 1. 18. Indeed, the Savior himself for this reason designates himself the Resurrection and the Life, John 11. 25.

There remains also that argument for the resurrection of the dead, which the Holy Fathers were accustomed to use most of all, taken from the partaking of the Body and the drinking of the Blood of Christ, which occurs in the Sacrament of the Eucharist. Whence Irenaeus piously writes, book 4, ch. 34: How do they deny that the flesh is capable of Eternal Life, which is nourished by the blood and body of Christ? And after a few words: Just as bread which is from the earth, receiving the calling of God, is no longer common bread: but the Eucharist, consisting of two things, earthly and heavenly: so also our bodies receiving the Eucharist are no longer corruptible, having the hope of the resurrection. And the Synod of Nicaea defined: Since we truly receive the precious Body and Blood of Christ, we ought to believe that these are the symbols of our resurrection.

Enough about the resurrection itself: approaching the bodies of those resurrected, in order to show what properties or qualities they will have, I premise that the bodies of the resurrected will not be of one and the same kind: for the bodies of the wicked will be one thing, those of the pious another. As for the bodies of the pious and blessed, the Apostle describes their quality quite at length, 1 Cor. 15 & following. It is sown in corruption: it will rise in incorruption: It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in

Glory: It is sown in weakness, it will rise in power: It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body. And verse 53: this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. The Scholastic Doctors, and others who followed them, have defined certain species of glorified bodies from these Apostolic words: of which the first is ἀθανασία, immortality. For since both eternal life and the infernal torments themselves will lack an end; it is certainly necessary that the subjects of these also live eternally. What of the fact that Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, nor will death have dominion over him any longer, Rom. 6. 9. Therefore, it is necessary that the members of Christ themselves, once resurrected from the dead, never die again.

The second condition of the blessed resurrected is spirituality. For they will be like the angels of God in heaven: Matt. 22. 30, and therefore will have no need of food, drink, and sexual intercourse: see Rom. 14. 17. The third condition of the blessed and glorified bodies will be clarity. For the Savior will transform the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory, Phil. 3. 21. And according to that of the Savior, Matt. 13. v. 43: The righteous will shine as the sun in the sight of God. The fourth condition of the blessed bodies will be impassibility: concerning which the Apostle, speaking, says: It is sown in corruption: it will rise in incorruption: for this corruptible must put on incorruption. Now, indeed, where there is incorruption or incorruptibility, there also are banished all kinds of affections and passions which can in any way afflict the body. And the Scholastics define these four conditions of the blessed bodies, and indeed not badly: although in the meantime we cannot deny that that glory of the blessed bodies can never be perfectly defined by us: since we know only in part in this life: And eye has not seen, nor ear heard: nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him, 1 Cor. 13. 9 & 12. 1 Cor. 2. 9. Isa. 64. 4.

Latin:

Certitudinem hujus resurrectionis D. Ambrosius lib. de fide Resurrectionis, variis similitudinibus & quasi Imaginibus, probare conatur, petitis à plantis & seminibus, quæ putrefacta, tamen resurgunt: petitis item à natura Phœnicis, quæ vitæ finem adelle animadvertens, nidum sibi de Thure, Casia, Myrrha, aliisque odoribus repletum construit, illique insidens emori, ex ejusq; cinere alia ejusdem speciei avis enasci scribitur: petitis denique à perpetua vicissitudine Noctis & diei, Hyemis & æstatis, Somni & exsurrectionis, Laboris ac quietis, Mœroris ac lætitiæ. Sunt alii, qui Carnis Resurrectione confirmare solebat ex natura Pelicani, avis Ægyptiacæ, quæ, si Hieronymo credimus, fœtum suum à serpente occisum, per triduum luget: deinde verò proprio pectore percusso, & sanguine super eum consperso, vitæ restituere solet. Sunt alii, qui imagines & similitudines mutuantur à Bombyce, ab Hirundine, à muscis, ab apibus, à Cuniculo: imò ab Echino etiam, pisce maritimo, qui captus & in multa frusta discerptꝫ, in mare verò iterum projectus, mox secundùm omnes particulas coalescit & reviviscit. Fuerunt denique, qui rationibus etiam Philosophicis idem confirmare solebant: Quales fuerunt duæ istæ: 1. Res imperfecta non potest esse capax absolutæ felicitatis: At verò anima à corpore separata, manca est ac mutila. Ergò ad absolutam illam vitæ æternæ felicitatem consequendam, corporis conjunctione vel maximè indiget. 2. Quicquid est contra naturam. E. perpetuum esse nequit. At verò separatio corporis & animæ, quæ fit per mortem, est contra naturam. E. perpetua esse nequit, sed restitutio totiꝫ compositi vel maximè requiritur, si mo dò anima immortalis censeri debeat. Verùm ut ingenuè quod res est, dicamus, omnes istæ & similitudines & rationes, quantumvis Patribus & Philosophis usitatæ, in tentationibus sdiritualibus subsistere haud possunt: &, nisi alia exScripturis succurrant probationum funda menta, certè de speResurrectionis nostræ planè fueritactum. Quid quod ipsi quoque Philosophi saniores rationes duas haud per omnia concesserint, Est enim Anima, quantumvis separata à corpore in se perfectissima: neq; à corpore quicquâ perfectionis accipit. Ad posteriore ratione respondesbuntPhilosophi Epicuræi, illam ex falsa hypothesi, quæ est de immortalitate procedere. Jam verò æquè dubium esse, an Anima sit immortalis, quàm dubium esse queat, An sit Resurrectio mortuorum, Proinde nihil concludi. Tutissimum ergò fuerit, in externis illis similitudinibus, & rationibus naturalibus pedem haud figere: Sed sacrarum literarum oracula in conspectu & & memoria semper retinere.

Inter ea verò; cumprimis ex Veteri Testamento petita locum facilè primarium obtinet, classicum illud, quod habetur cap. 19. 25. 26. & 27. Jobi: Scio quod Redemtor meus vivit, & in novissimo die de terra resurrecturus sum: Et rursum circundabor pelle mea, & in carne mea videbo DEUM. Quem visurus sum ego ipse, & oculi mei conspecturi sunt, & non alius. Reposita est hæc spes mea in sinu meo. Etsi autem sint, qui negant Jobum de mortuorum resurrectione hic esse locutum; sed duntaxat de corporali restitutione in integrum, sollicitum fuisse contendunt; Id tamen manifestam vim textui infert: Primùm enim de corporisSalute, quoad hanc vitam planè desperaverat: ac proinde spe Resurrectionis seipsum consolatur. Patet hoc ex Versu præcedente decimo, ubi impatientiâ victus conqueritur: Deum suam spem planè dejecisse, ita ut similis sit plantæ sive arbori cuidam excisæ, quæ non renatestur. Deinde si de temporaria sive corporali restitutione in integrum sollicitus hoc loco fuisset, haud profectò tàto magnificè protestãdo optasset, ut verba hæc sua conscriberentur in libro, & sculperentur in silice, vel in plumbo ad perpe tuam rei memoriam? Neque enim adeò novum & insolens videri potest, si calamitates corporales finem sortiantur, & in pristinum felicitatis statum afferantur afflicti. Proindè nihil morati interpretes Hebræos, & cumpri mis Merceri βαττολογίαs, qui pueriliter somniat. Jobum nihil volusse dicere aliud, quàm se nosse, DEUM suum adhuc vivere, idque saxre ex afflictionum, quibus à DEO excrucietur, atrocitate. Item se carne sua videre DEUM, hoc est, illius præsentiam sentire, & ex illu doloribus agnoscere, quos ipse & non alius, sustineat: has inquam & similes nugas nihil morati, Jobum de Resurrectione mortuorum ex professo disseruisse, seque ejus spe ac certitudine in tantis ærumnis erexisse & sustentasse, asserimus.

Pertinet huc etiam oraculum illud, quod habetur Jesaiæ cap. 26. 19. Vivent mortui tui, & Interfecti mei resurgent. Et cap. 66. 16. In igne Dominus dijudicabit, & in gladio suo ad omnem carnem, & congregabuntur interfecti à Domino. Daniel. 12. 2. Multi dormientium in pulvere terræ expergiscentur, hi ad vitam æternam, illi ad opprobrium & ignominiam sempiternam. Hoseæ. 13. 15. De manu mortis liberabo eos, de morte redimam eos: Ero pestis tua mors: morsus tuus inferne.

Jam si ad Novum Testamentum fiat accessus, tot sermè se offeruntDemonstrationes

Resurrectionis mortuorum, quot extant conciones Christi & Apostolorum, uti videre est; Matth. 22. 31. & 32. Luc. 14. 14. 20. 35. Joh. 5. 21. & 28. 6. 40. 11. 24. Actor. 24. 15. 26. 6. & 8. Rom. 8. 11. & 23. 1. Cor. 15. 12. ad finem usque. 2. Cor. 4. 10. & 11. Coloss. 3. 4. Phil. 3. 11. & 21. 1. Thess. 4. 14. 2. Timoth. 2. 11. Apocal. 20. 12.

Typum si desideres, certè longè praeclarissimum monstrat historia Jona, quam ad suam præfigurandam resurrectionem Servator Matth. 12. 40. disertè accommodat. Deinde idem comprobat Visio illa, oblata Prophetæ Jezechieli, qui in Spiritu abreptus in campu refertum defunctorum ossibus aridis, exuccis & cariosis: quæ tamen ad verba Prophetæ, mediante DEI Virtute pristinis suis colligantur nervis, teguntur carnibus & cute, Spiritum denique & Vitam recipiunt. Jezech. 37. 1. ad 11. usque. Tandem fidem faciunt Resurrectioni mortuorum Raptus sive translatio in Cælum Henochi & Eliæ, Gen. 5; 24. 2. Regum 2. 9. & 11. Item exempla eorum, qui, à Prophetis, à Christo & Apostolis ex mortuis in vitam revocati fuerunt: ut Filij Sareptanæ Viduæ, 1. Reg. 17. 22. Filij Sunamitidis 2. Reg. 4. 33. Item illius, qui ad contactum ossium Elisæi revixit, 2. Reg. 13. 21. Filiæ Jairi: Matth. 9. 25. Filii Viduæ Naimiticæ, Luc. 7. 15. Lazari. Joh. 11. 43. & 44. Resurgentium cum Christo: Matth. 28. 52. & 53. Tabitæ Joppensis à Petro resuscitatæ Act. 9. 40. Eutychi à Paulo excitati Act. 20. 10. Ante omnia verò Exemplum Christi Servatoris & capitis nostri, qui uti dormientium, ita resurgentium factus est primitiæ: Quemadmodum multis argumentis illud confirmat Apostolus 1. Cor. 15. 12. & seqq. Et hoc nomine Christum nominat Primogenitum ex mortuis Col. 1. 18. Imò ipse Servator semetipsum ideò indigitat Resurrectionem atque Vitam. Joh. 11. 25.

Superest & illud argumentum resurrectionis mortuorum, quo Sancti Patres vel maximè uti consueverunt petitum à perceptione Corporis & bibitione Sanguinis Christi, quæ fit in Sacramento Eucharistiæ. Unde Irenæus piè scribit: l. 4. c. 34 Quomodo negant carnem capacem esse Vitæ Æternæ, quæ sanguine & corpore Christi nutritur? Et post pauca: Quemadmodum qui est à terra panis, percipiens Vocationem DEI, jam non communis panis est: Sed Eucharistia ex duabus rebus constans, terrena & cœlesti: Sic & corpora nostra Eucharistiam percipientia, jam non sunt corruptibilia, spem resurrectionis habentia. Et Synodo Nicena definivit. Cum pretiosum Christi Corpus & Sanguinem revera accipiamus, credere nos oportet, hæc esse Resurrectionis nostræ Symbola.

Satis de Resurrectione ipsa: ad corpora resuscitatorum accedens, ut, quasnam proprietates sive qualitates ea habitura sint, ostendam, præmitto, corpora Resuscitatorum non unius ejusdemq; fore generis: Alia enim erunt corpora Impiorum: alia Piorum. Quoad corpora piorum ac beatorum, prolixè satis eorum qualitas describit Apostolus, 1. Cor. 15. & seqq. Seminatur in corruptione: resurget in incorruptiõe: Seminatur in ignobilitate; Resurget in

Gloria: Seminatur in infirmitate, resurget in Virtute: Seminatur corpus animale; resurget corpus spirituale. Et vers. 53. oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitatem:& mortale hoc induere immortalitatem. Doctores Scholastici, & alii hos secuti, certas clarificatorum corporum species ex verbis hisce Apostolicis definiverunt: quarum Prima est ἀθανασία Immortalitas. Quia enim tum Vita æterna, tum ipsi etiam cruciatus infernales carebunt fine; utique ipsa quoque horum subjecta æternùm vivant, necessum est. Quid quod Christus resurgens à mortuis, non amplius moritur, neque mors ei ulterius dominabitur. Rom. 6. 9. Ergo ipsa quoque membra Christi, semel à mortuis resuscitata, nunquam amplius moriantur, necessum est.

Altera beatorum Resurgentium conditio, est spiritualitas. Similes enim erunt Angelis DEI in Cælo: Matth. 22. 30. ac proinde non opus habebunt cibo, potu & venere: ibi d. Rom. 14. 17. Tertia beatorum & clarificatorum corporum conditio erit Claritas. Servator enim transformabit corpus humilitatis nostræ, configuratum corpori claritatis suæ. Philipp. 3. 21. Et secundù illud Servatoris Mat. 13. V. 43. Fulgebunt Justi, ut Sol in conspectu DEI. Quarta beatorum corporum conditio erit Impassibilitas: de qua Apostolus Verba faciens, Seminatur, inquit, Corpus in corruptione: Resurget in incorruptione: oportet enim corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitatem. Jam verò ubi est incorruptio sive incorruptibilitas, ibique exulant omnis generis affectiones, & passiones, quæ quoquo modo corpus affligere possunt. Et has quidem quatuor beatorum corporú conditiones definiunt Scholastici, & profectò haud malè: Ubi tamen interim diffiteri haud possumus, Gloriam illam beatorum corporú perfectè à nobis nunquam definiri posse: Siquidem ex parte duntaxat cognoscimus hac in Vita: Et oculus non vidit, auris non audivit: neque in cor hominis pervenit, quid Deus præparaverit diligentibus se 1. Cor. 13. 9. & 12. 1. Cor. 2. 9. Jesa. 64. 4.


### Part I (continued)

But as for the qualities of the bodies of the wicked and the damned, they will possess only immortality in common with the pious: but they will lack all other things, indeed they will be deformed by clearly contrary qualities: which Scripture, delineating in a certain way, mentions outer darkness: it mentions weeping and gnashing of teeth: it mentions a certain worm, which in the damned will never die: it mentions unquenchable fire: it mentions most ardent affections and desires: it mentions, finally, the execrations of themselves and of their own crimes and wicked deeds. Where, however, again in this life we are not able to acquire any perfect knowledge of the qualities of these bodies either.

With the bodies of the wicked and the damned dismissed, as far as the bodies of the blessed are concerned; all will indeed obtain one and the same blessedness and eternal life in general appointed for the blessed, so that no one will perceive more blessedness than another. But yet, meanwhile, in this one life eternal, which is simply equal for all the blessed, there will be certain and distinct degrees of that glory or brightness with which the bodies of the blessed will be adorned: indeed, in such a way that one will be about to shine more and more splendidly than another: just as the Apostle describes this disparity. 1 Cor. 15. v. 41. There is one brightness of the stars, another of the sun, another brightness of the moon, another brightness of the stars, for star differs from star in brightness: so also is the resurrection of the dead. And Daniel, chap. 12. 3, affirms concerning those who have instructed many unto righteousness, that they will be about to shine like the brightness of the firmament, and like the stars for ever and ever. And just as in hell, which will be common and equal to all the damned: there will nevertheless be degrees of punishments: according to that saying of the Savior, The condition of Sodom will be more tolerable in the day of judgment than yours, Capernaum, etc. Matt. 11, 24. Thus also there will be distinct degrees of brightness, and of the glory resulting from it, in those who are to be saved. Which, however, the merits of human works do not constitute in such a way as the Romanists fable: but the promise of divine mercy, which in this way has promised to reward freely the zeal and labor of those who have placed well and with great interest the talents committed to them.

Since, therefore, the glory of the glorified bodies is to be so great; it is certain that those who in this life were either lame, or one-eyed, or blind, or deaf, will by no means be such in the life eternal. For all these things were not perfections, but defects of human bodies in this life, sent upon them by the just judgment of God on account of sin. Now, however, in the resurrection, corruptibility will put on incorruptibility, infirmity will put on power: ignobility will put on glory. Thus, that excessive bulk of the body, which arises either from excessive fatness or other causes, and which so far from perfecting the very substance of the human body, rather affects it with many great troubles, is most rightly to be reckoned among the defects of nature, which is to be utterly abolished.

It is also asked concerning infants: At what age and at what stature are they to rise again? Which question pertains to those things about which it is better to suspend judgment than to define anything certain. For the Holy Spirit did not wish to define in the Scriptures anything concerning the age or stature of infants at which they are to rise again. Far be it from us, therefore, to have such curiosity.
