There are those who contend that they will have the same age and stature in the resurrection, although devoid of every defect and imperfection. There are others, on the contrary, who affirm that they will rise again in that stature to which they would have attained if they could have enjoyed the use of this light for a longer time. Whose opinion also seems to us more probable. For when God created the first humans, He did not make them either infants, or decrepit, or deformed, or imperfect. Since, therefore, there is no doubt that such will be the restoration and renewal in the resurrection as was the formation and creation in the first creation: it seems to be a most true consequence that the stature and age of the resurrected humans will also be perfect, such as it was of those created in the beginning.

To the question, whether the bodies of the resurrected blessed will be in a place, and indeed in a physical place, in such a way that a physical local motion or displacement ought to be assigned to those glorified bodies by the property of nature? I answer: I hold the negative, against the affirmative of the Sacramentarians, which labors under two far more pernicious errors. For first, that heaven which is in the Scriptures and is called the seat of the blessed, can in no way be or be defined as a physical place. For although the Savior is accustomed to call that seat of the blessed a place, it is nevertheless certain that He spoke according to human accommodation and wished to accommodate Himself to our grasp by words and similitudes taken from the common use of human affairs. And indeed, long ago, the error of Keisersberg, Bullinger, and others was exploded from the schools of the more learned theologians and philosophers, who imagined that heaven or the seat of the blessed is a region of such a kind, long, wide, and deep, in which Christ with the angels and the blessed now sits, now stands, now walks about and wanders, or now conducts Himself in another local manner. Which folly was indeed unknown to the Apostle Paul, who, when he did not dare to define the heaven of the blessed by any physical place, rather affirms: The condition and quality of the heaven in which the blessed are to be did not descend into the body of man. It was also unknown to Christ and all the remaining Apostles, who all with one mouth determined that that heaven of the blessed is to be defined, not by any physical place: but by a heavenly and spiritual condition, a state of glory and blessedness, in which the elect are to be, and are to see God face to face. Furthermore, since in that very heaven God is to be all in all to the pious and the elect, how, I ask, can that heaven ever be defined as a place, and indeed a physical place? St. Augustine once laughed at this insanity of some of his time, saying, If, in heaven, as the higher parts of the world, the place of God is believed to be, birds are of better merit, whose life is nearer to God. Book 1, On the Lord's Sermon on the Mount. What of the fact that the sounder philosophers themselves always taught that no place is to be granted above the last and supreme revolution: as is evident from book 1 of Aristotle's On the Heavens, chap. 9. Now, however, it is manifest that all and each of those revolutions, or celestial spheres, are to perish on the last day; while the seat of the blessed nevertheless remains in the meantime. Therefore, even from the very doctrine of the philosophers, that seat of the blessed, inasmuch as it is to be outside and above that last revolution, or rather already is, can neither be defined by any physical place, nor indeed ought to be.

The latter error, which arises from the affirmative of the Sacramentarians, is that being local is most viciously established as a somatic property of the human body: whereas place happens only to natural bodies, and those still living in this world, and indeed, as the philosopher testifies, on account of that potential passage, book 2 of On the Heavens, chap. 1, to which bodies are subject in this world, which being removed, that accident is also removed, so that now bodies by no means necessarily must be in a place by actual act, or be enclosed by the alien boundary of a place surrounding them from the outside. Philosophers certainly would again confess with one voice that the ultimate Heaven, by which this whole universe is enclosed, is not in any place (Phys. lib. 4, cap. 5). What madness, therefore, would this be, to wish to ascribe to glorified and spiritual bodies that infirmity, by reason of which they must necessarily, and always by actual act, be in some physical place.

It is an essential property of a body that it be a substance long, broad, and deep, that is, that it consist of its three dimensions: or, which is the same thing, that it be finite by the boundaries of its own nature (de Cœlo lib. 1, cap. 1). The consequence of this finiteness is not that a body must always be in a place by actual act, but only that it can be in a place. This δύναμιν (potentiality) we have never denied, nor do we yet deny, even to glorified bodies. But the question is about the act itself: whether it is a natural property of human bodies that they should always, by actual act, be in some physical place? That this is most false is manifestly clear from what has already been said; so much so that, when it is stated ignorantly and ἀφιλοσόφως (unphilosophically) concerning bodies still moving about in this world that it is their property to be always in a place by actual act, it ought to seem like sheer madness and insanity to wish to subject πνευματικὰ (spiritual) and glorified bodies to such local need and infirmity that, even in Heaven itself and the seat of the blessed, they are still exposed to physical places.

Finally, the question is asked: Will the bodies of the resurrected be visible? To which it is answered: Just as 'local' is understood in two ways, either by act or by potentiality, so 'visible' is sometimes understood by potentiality, but sometimes by act. Again: Just as a glorified body is and ought to be called 'local' by reason of δυνάμις (potentiality), but not because it is necessary by the property of its nature that it always be in a place by actual act and be circumscribed by a place, so glorified bodies also have that δύναμιν (potentiality) that they can be seen, although by actual act they are not always necessarily visible to all, and especially not to those who as yet have no proportion to glorified bodies. This can be confirmed from Matthew 27:53, where the Evangelist affirms that with Christ many rose from the tombs and entered the city of Jerusalem, and manifested themselves to many: ἐνεφανίσθησαν πολλοῖς. Whence it is not obscurely clear that those resurrected with Christ were not seen indiscriminately by all whom they encountered, but only by those whose eyes God opened; so that visibility can in no way be counted among the properties of glorified resurrected bodies, although in the meantime they are so constituted that they are visible τῇ δυνάμει (by potentiality). What is more, speaking physically, it cannot even be properly affirmed of bodies still existing naturally in this world that visibility, or τὸ Visibile (the visible), is their

essential property. For 'visible' and 'invisible' are said relatively to the eye, so that the visible is that which can be seen by the eyes or is actually seen; the invisible is that which is not actually seen by the eyes. Now, if no corporeal eye had been created, there would also be no vision; yet natural bodies, by reason of their essential properties, would not cease to be true and natural bodies. This can be demonstrated even by the example of the blind, to whom, although no bodies are ὁρατὰ (visible), nonetheless those same bodies are and remain ἀόρατα (invisible) bodies to the blind; so that the Sacramentarians, who attempt to define the truth of natural bodies by actual visibility, seem to be insane with reason, not to mention that I allow it to remain hidden that such men are found to attribute greater power and efficacy to the Devil and his instruments than to God and our Christ. Certainly the Devil, and magicians, relying on that art of theirs which is magical, or more truly diabolical, achieve this, that they render themselves inconspicuous, although in the meantime they remain true and natural bodies. Is God, therefore, who in the resurrected will be all in all, and who will render their bodies πνευματικὰ (spiritual) by His power—that is, endowed with clearly spiritual qualities—so impotent that He cannot suspend the act of visibility from such bodies?

Yet it does not follow from this that glorified bodies in eternal life cannot be seen by one another. For I have only wished to demonstrate thus far that visibility is not of the essence and property of glorified bodies, in such a way that by the property of nature they are always compelled to be visible by actual act, although they are invisible τῇ δυνάμει (by potentiality). Furthermore, one must distinguish most accurately between those glorified bodies insofar as they are considered in relation to one another, and insofar as they have some respect to us who still live in this mortal life.

Glorified bodies, both those that rose with Christ the Savior and those that were translated there, are always visible to one another by actual act in eternal life, just as also after the Resurrection of the dead, the glorified bodies of the Elect, individually and collectively, will be visible to one another because of that communion of those spiritual qualities, and because of that proportion which those glorified bodies and glorified eyes will have between them. But if the question is whether those glorified bodies are compelled to be visible by actual act to us who are still living in this world, we hold the negative in all respects, since between us and the resurrected, and between our eyes and the eyes of the resurrected, there is no proportion; since our eyes have not yet been brought to that perfection which will be in the other life. And therefore we simply state that those glorified bodies, by no necessity at all, let alone by the property of nature, must be visible to us by actual act, unless our eyes are particularly illuminated and opened by God.

Some Sacramentarian objects here: that the bodies of those resurrected with Christ were therefore not seen by all the citizens of Jerusalem: not because those bodies were not actually visible: but because the eyes of the citizens were restrained, just as the eyes of the disciples at Emmaus were restrained, so that they would not see Christ. Luke 24, v. 16. I answer that a fallacy is committed by treating a non-cause as a cause. For first, the text in Luke does not say that the eyes of the disciples at Emmaus were restrained so that they would not see Christ: for they certainly saw him, walked with him, and indeed conversed with him: but so that they would not recognize Christ. This restraint, therefore, concerned not the eyes of the body, but the eyes of the mind. The Sacramentarian therefore wanders off the path when he calls upon the disciples at Emmaus to support the breaking of our assertion. For even a blind man sees what, and how great, a dissimilarity there is in both examples. For nowhere is it read 1. that the citizens of Jerusalem saw those resurrected with Christ: but rather the contrary is affirmed, that they manifested themselves to many, namely to those to whom they wished. 2. Nowhere is it read that the eyes of those citizens were restrained so that they would not recognize those resurrected. 3. Concerning the disciples at Emmaus, verse 31 of Luke 24, it is read that they did not see Christ any longer, not because their eyes were restrained so that they would not see him: but because Christ, with his glorified body, both became invisible and had withdrawn that visibility which he had wished those disciples to enjoy for a time. Thus, therefore, this Sacramentarian collection labors in many ways, so that it finds no foundation anywhere.

and are children of GOD, since they are children of the Resurrection. Matt. 22, v. 30. Luke 20, v. 34, 35, 36.

To these Sadducees, in the second place, must be added Hymenaeus and Philetus, who, viciously defining the resurrection of the dead through the spiritual regeneration of man, contended that the resurrection of the dead had already taken place: and that no other was to be expected, as the Apostle testifies in 2 Tim. 2, v. 17.

There have been those in more recent centuries who have revived this same error: and, to pass over in silence now the Simonians, Archontics, Hierarchites, and many others, who partly dreamed that the whole man perishes, partly contended that souls would resurrect with bodies, partly opined that new bodies must be created, partly blasphemed that the souls of the wicked or impious are converted into cattle, or even into devils: of all of whom Epiphanius and Augustine make mention: to say nothing now of all these, the delirium of the Manichaeans nevertheless deserves the greatest observation, who establish two principles of all things, or two GODS: one good, the other evil: they also said that he is the creator of the body: and therefore that the soul, after being separated from the body at death, truly becomes happy: and is not to be joined to the body again, since it hinders and disturbs the happiness of the soul more than it promotes or perfects it. Which heresy, indeed, as it is highly insulting and blasphemous against God, the creator not only of the soul but also of the body, so it collapses by its own impiety and futility.

Latin:

Cæterùm quod corporum Impiorum & damnatorum qualitates, solam immortalitatem cum piis communem ea obtinebunt: Cæteris verò omnibus carebunt, imò contrariis planè qualitatibus deformabuntur: Quas scriptura quodammodo delineans, meminit tenebrarum exteriorum: meminit fletus & st侨doris dentium: meminit vermis alicujus, qui in damnatis nunquam moriturus sit: meminit ignis inextinguibilis: meminit ardentissimorum affectuum & desideriorum: meminit denique execrationum suiipsorum, suorumque scelerum ac flagitiorum. Ubi tamen rursus hac in Vita perfectam aliquam istorum etiam corporum qualitatum notitiam nobis comparare haud valemus.

Missis impiorum, & damnatorum corporibus, quantum ad beatorum corpora; Unam quidem, eandemq; beatitudinem & vitam æternam obtinebunt omnes in universum beatis sita, ut nullus plus beatitudinis sit percepturus quàm alter. At verò interim in hac unâ,& omnibus beatis simpliciter æqvali vitâ æterna, certi & distincti erunt Gradus gloriæ sive claritatis illius, qvâ exornabuntur beatorum corpora: ita qvidem, ut unus plus & splendidiùs sit fulsurus altero : Quemadmodum hanc disparitatem describit Apostolus. 1. Cor. 15. v. 41. Alia claritas Stellarum, Solis, alia claritas Lunæ, alia claritas Stellarum, Stella enim à stella differt in claritate: sic & Resurrectio mortuorum Et Daniel. cap. 12. 3. affirmat de his, qui multos erudierunt ad justitiam, quod fulsuri sint sicut splendor firmamenti, & sicut stellæ in perpetuas æternitates. Et quemadmodum in inferno, qvi omnibus damnatis erit communis & æqualis: gradus tamen erunt pœnarum: secundum illud Servatoris, Tolerabilior erit Sodomæ conditio in die judicii, quàm tuæ Capernaum &c. Matth. 11, 24. Sic etiam claritatis, & inde resultantis gloriæ distincti gradus erunt in salvandis. Quos tamen non humanorum operũ merita sic constituunt, uti Romanenses fabulantur: sed divinæ misericordiæ promissio, quæ hoc modo, Gratis remunerari pollicita est, studium & laborem eorum, qui talenta sibi commissa benè & cum fœnore magno collocarunt.

Tanta igitur cùm sit futura corporum clarificatorum gloria; certum est, eos qui hæc in vita vel claudi, vel lusci, vel cæci, vel surdi fuerunt, tales in vita æternâ minimè futuros. Hæc enim omnia non perfectiones, sed defectus erant corporum humanorũ in hac vita, ob peccatum justo DEI judicio illis immissi. Jam verò in Resurrectione corruptibilitas induet incorruptibilitatem, infirmitas induet virtutem: Ignobilitas induet gloriam. Sic nimia illa corporis moles, quæ vel ex pinguedine nimia, vel aliis causis oritur, quæque substantiam ipsam corporis humani adeò non perficit, ut magis multis magnisq; molestiis afficiat, rectissimè inter defectus Naturæ com putanda est, quæ penitùs abolenda.

De Infantibus etiam quæritur: Quâ ætâ se, & quâ statura illi sint resurrecturi? Quæ qvæstio pertinet ad eas, de quibus ἐπέχειν latiùs est, quàm certi aliquid definire. Nihil enim vel de Infantum ætate vel statura, qua sint resurrecturi, Spiritus S. in scripturis definire voluit. Absit ergò à nobis ista curiositas. Sunt qui eandem infantilem & ætatem & staturam ipsos in Resurrectione habituros contendunt, licèt omnis defectus & imperfectionis expertem. Sunt contrà alii, qui in ea staturâ ipsos resurrecturos affirmant, ad quam pervenissent, si diuturniore lucis hujus usura perfrui potuissent. Quorum etiam sententia nobis videtur probabilior. Deus enim cùm primos homines crearet, illos non fecit vel infantes, vel decrepitos, vel deformes, vel imperfectos. Cùm ergò nullum sit dubium, quin talis futura sit in Resurrectione ἀνάπλασις καὶ ἀνακλισις, qualis in prima creatione fuit πλάσις καὶ κτίσις: utique hominum etiam resuscitatorum perfectam fore staturam & ætatem, qualis fuit initiò creatorum, verissimum omninò videtur esse Consequens.

Ad Quæstionem, An corpora beatorum Resuscitatorum futura sint in loco, & loco quidem Physico, ita ut ὥρισις sive motus localis Physicus corporibus illis clarificatis, ex naturæ proprietate, adsignari debeat? respondeo: Negativam teneo, adversus Sacramentariorum affirmativam, quæ duobus longè perniciosissimis erroribus laborat. Primùm enim Cœlum illud, quod in Scripturis est ac dicitur Sedes Beatorum, Locus Physicus esse ac definiri nullo modo potest. Etsi enim Servator Locum appellitare solet Sedesm illam beatorum tamen κατ' ἀνθρωποπά θειαν locutum ipsum esse constat, & ad nostrum captum sese accommodare voluisse vocabulis & similitudinibus ex communi rerum humanarum usu petitis. Et sanè jampridem ex Theologorum & Philosophorum fantiorum Scholis explosus fuit error Keisersbergij, Bullingeri & aliorum, qui finxerunt, Cœlum sive Sedem beatorum esse ejusmodi regionem longam, latam, profundam, in quâ Christus cum Angelis & beatis nunc sedeat, nunc stet, nunc spacietur & inambulet, nunc alio modo locali se habeat. Quæ sanè μωροσοφία ignota fuit Apostolo Paulo, qui Cœlum beatorum cùm non loco aliquo Physico definire ausus fuit, ut potiùs affirmet: In corpus hominis non descendisse conditionem & Qualitatem Cæli, in quo futuri sunt beati. Ignota etiam fuit Christo & reliquis Apostolis omnibus, qui omnes uno ore Cœlum illud beatorum definiendum esse statuerunt, non loco aliquo Physico: sed cœlesti & spirituali conditione, statu gloriæ & beatitudine, in qua futuri sint electi, visurique DEUM à faciè ad faciem. Porrò cùm in illo ipso Cœlo DEUS pijs & electis futurus sit omnia in omnibus, qui quæso Cœlum illud Locus definiri, & quidem Locus Physicus, unquàm poterit? Risit aliquando D. Augustinus, hanc quorundam sui temporis insaniam, Si, inquiens, in Cælo, tanquam superioribus mundi partibus locus DEI esse creditur, melioris meriti sunt aves, quarum vita DEO est vicinior. l. 1. de Serm. Domini in monte. Quid; Quod ipsi saniores Philosophi, supra ultimam & supremam conversionem, nullum locum concedendum esse, semper docuerunt: uti patet ex lib. 1. Aristotelis de Cælo cap. 9. Jam vero manifestum est, quod omnes & singulæ istæ Conversiones, sive Orbes Cœlestes in novissimo die sunt interituræ; manente tamen interim sede beatorum. Ergò vel ex ipsâ Philosophorum doctrinâ, sedes illa beatorum, quippe quæ extra & supra ultimam illam Conversionem est futura, imò jam modò est, nullo loco Physico definiri vel potest, vel etiam debet.

Posterior error, qui ex Sacramentariorum affirmativa oritur, est,quod & Locale vitiosissimè statuitur esse proprietas σωματικὴ corporis humani: cum corporibus etiam naturalibus, & hoc in mundo ad huc degentibus, Locus duntaxat accidat, & quidem Philosopho teste, propter δυνατὸν illam διεξόδειαν l. 2. de Cælo, cap.1.cui corpora subjacet in hoc mundo, qua sublata, tollitur etiam Accidens illud, ut jam corpora nullatenus necessario actu debeant esse in loco, sive loci forinsecus ambientis termino alieno claudi. Philosophi certè rursum ore uno farentur Cœlum ultimum, quo totum hoc universum clauditur, non esse in ullo loco l. 4. Physic. c. 5. Quæ ergo hæc foret insania, corporibus clarificatis & spiritualibus illam adhuc velle adscribere infirmitatem, cujus gratiâ in loco aliquo Physico necessario, & ipso semper actu esse debeant.

Proprietas corporis Essentialis est, ut sit substantia longa, lata, profunda, hoc est tribus suis dimensionibus constet: vel quod idem est, Naturæ suæ terminis sit finita. l. 1. de Cœlo cap. 1. Cujus finitatis consequens est, vel ut corpo ipso actu semper sit in loco: sed duntaxat, ut possit esse in loco. Quam δύναμιν nunquam negavimus, vel adhuc negamus corporibus etiam clarificatis: Verùm de actu ipso est Quæstio, Utrum de proprietate naturali sit corporum humanorum, ut sint semper, ipso actu, in loco aliquo physico? Id quod falsissimum esse, ex jam dictis manifestè patet: adeò cùm de corporibus in hoc mundo adhuc versantibus inscitè planè, & ἀφιλοσόφως statuatur, ipsorum proprietas esse, ut semper actu sint in loco: furor planè & amentia videri debeat, Corpora πνευματικὰ & clarificata Locali indigentiæ & infirmitati ita velle subjicere, ut in ipso Cœlo ac sede beatorum Locis adhuc physicis sint exposita.

Quæritur tandem: An corpora resuscitatorum futura sint visibilia? Ad quam respondetur: Quemadmodum Locale duobus modis intelligitur, vel de actu, vel de potentiâ: Ita Visibile interdum de potentiâ intelligitur, nonnunquam verò de actu. Rursus: Quemadmodum corpus clarificatum est & dici debet Locale, ratione δυνάμεως: non verò quòd ex proprietate suæ naturæ semper ipso actu in loco esse, & loco circumscribi necessum habeat: Ita corpora clarificata etiam eam habent δύναμιν, ut cerni possint, licet ipso actu nó semper necessario omnibus, ac præsertim iis non sint visibilia, qui nullam adhuc ad corpora clarificata habent proportionem. Confirmari hoc potest ex cap. 27. v. 53. Matthæi, ubi Evangelista affirmat, quod cum Christo multi sint egresli è monumentis, urbemque Hierosolymam ingressi, qui sese manifestaverint multis: ἐνεφανίσθησαν πολλοῖς. Unde haud obscurè liquet, quod resuscitati illi cum Christo, non promicuuè ab omnibus, quibus obviam facti sunt, conspecti etiam fuerint: sed ab iis duntaxat, quorum oculos Deus aperuit: adeò, ut visibilitas nullo pacto inter proprietates corporum clarificatorum resuscitatorum numerari vel possit, vel debeat: quanquam interim ita sint comparata, ut τῇ δυνάμει sint visibilia. Quid quod physice loquendo, ne quidem de corporibus in hoc mundo adhuc naturaliter existentibo propriè affirmari potest, quòd visibilitas, vel τὸ Visibile, ipsorum sit

Essentialis proprietas. Nam Visibile & Invisibile Relatè dicuntur ad oculum, ut visibile sit id, quod oculis cerni potest; vel actu cernitur: Invisibile, quod actu & oculis non cernitur. Jam verò si nullus creatus fuisset oculus corporeus, nulla etiam esset visio: neque tamen corpora naturalia ratione proprietatum essentialium definerent esse corpora vera & naturalia: id quod vel exemplo cœcorum demonstrari potest, quibus licet nulla corpora sint ὁρατὰ visibilia, nihilominus tamen illa ipsa cæcis ἀόρατα invisibilia corpora sunt, & manent corpora, adeò, ut cum ratione insanire videantur Sacramentarii, qui ex actuali Visibilitate, corporum naturalium veritatem definire conantur: ut interim illud latere patiar, quòd hujusmodi homines majorem virtutem & efficaciam Diabolo, & Organis ipsius, quàm Deo, & Christo nostro tribuere deprehenduntur. Diabolo certè, & Magi, freti arte illâ suâ Magicâ, veriùs Diabolicâ, illud præstant, ut sese reddant inconspicuos, licèt interim vera & naturalia maneant corpora. Siccinè ergò Deus, qui in resuscitatis futurus est omnia in omnibus, quique corpora illorum suâ virtute reddet πνευματικὰ, hoc est, spiritualibus planè qualitatibus dotata: tàm erit impotens, ut visibilitatis actum ab hujusmodi corporibus suspenderc non possit?

Minimè tamen hinc sequitur: Corpora clarificata in vita æterna à se mutuò non posse conspici? Illud enim duntaxat hactenus demonstrare volui, Visibilitatem non esse de essentia & proprietate corporum clarificatorum, ita quidem ut ex naturæ proprietate semper ipso actu cogantur esse visibilia: licet τῇ δυνάμει sint invisibilia. Deinde accuratissimè distinguendú fuerit inter corpora illa clarificata, quatenus illa ad sese invicem considerantur: & quatenus ad nos, qui in hac adhuc mortali vitâ degimus, respectum aliquem habent.

Corpora clarificata, tùm ea, quæ cum Christo Servatore resurrexerunt, tùm quæ eò translata fuerunt, in vita æterna inter se semper actu sunt conspicua, quemadmodum etiam post Resurrectionem mortuorum Electorum corpora clarificata singula & universa inter se futura sunt aspectabilia, propter communionem illam spiritualium illarum Qualitatum, & ob proportionem illam, quam inter se clarificata illa corpora, & oculi clarificati habebunt. Cæterum, si Quæstio sit, An nobis in hoc mundo adhuc degentibus illa clarificata corpora actu cogantur esse conspicua, Negativam per omnia tenemus: siquidem inter nos, & Resuscitatos, inter nostros, & Resuscitatorum oculos nulla est proportio: Siquidem nostri oculi ad eam perfectionem, quæ in alterâ erit vitâ, nondum sunt reducti. Ac proinde simpliciter statuimus, Corpora illa clarificata, nobis nullâ planè necessitate, nedum ex proprietate naturæ, actu debere esse conspicua, nisi peculiariter à Deo nostri collustrentur, & aperiantur oculi.

Objicit hic Sacramentariorum qvispiam: Corpora resuscitarorum cum Christo ideò non fuisse conspecta ab omnibus civibus Hierosolymitanis: non quòd corpora illa actu non fuerint visibilia: sed quia oculi Civium fuerint retenti, haud secus ac discipulorum Emaunticorum oculi fuerunt retenti, ne viderent Christum. Luc. 24. v. 16. Respondeo, committi aspidua non causæ ut Causæ. Primùm enim textus apud Lucam non habet, retentos fuisse oculos discipulorum Emaunticorum, ne viderent Christum: Nam certè viderunt ipsum, ambulârunt cum ipso, imò collocuti fuerunt cum ipso: Sed ne agnoscerent Christum. Retentio ergò isthæc non oculos corporis sed ocellos mentis attinebat. Extra oleas ergò vagatur Sacramentarius, qvando ad infringendam nostram assertionem in subsidium vocat discipulos Emaunticos. Qvæ enim, & qvanta dissimilitudo in utroqve sit exemplo, vel cæcus videt. Nuspiam enim legitur 1. qvod Cives Hierosolymitani conspexerint illos cum Christo resusciratos: sed contrarium potiùs affirmatur, qvod sese manifestaverint multis, iis nimirùm, quibus voluerunt. 2. nuspiam legitur, qvod civium istorum oculi fuerint retenti, ne agnoscerent illos resuscitatos. 3. De discipulis Emaunticis vers. 31. Luc. 24. legitur, qvod Christum ideò amplius non conspexerint, non qvod oculi ipsorum fuerunt retenti, ne viderent ipsum: sed quia Christus corpore suo clarificato & ἄφαντος ἐγένετο, & visibilitatem illam, quâ aliqvandio frui voluit discipulos illos sustulerat. Sic ergo multis modis Collectio hæc Sacramentaria laborat, ut nihil firmamenti uspiam reperiat.

& filii sunt DEI, cùm sint filii Resurrectionis. Matt. 22. v. 30. Luc. 20. v. 34. 35. 36.

Sadducæis istis secundo loco annumerari debent Hymenæus & Philetus, qui Resurrectionem mortuorum per spiritualem Regenerationem hominis vitiosè definientes, contendebant, Resurrectionem mortuorum jam modo factam:neq; aliam esse expectandum, teste Apostolo 2. Tim. 2. v. 17.

Qvem eundem errorem, fuerunt recentioribus seculis, qui reponerent: & ut silentio nunc involvam Simonianos, Archonticos, Hierarchitas, & plures alios, qui partim totum hominẽ interire somniarunt, partim animas cum corporibus resurrecturas contenderunt, partim nova corpora creanda esse opinati sunt; partim malorum sive impiorum animas in pecora, imo in Diabolos converti blasphemarunt: quorum omnium meminerunt Epiphanius, & Augustinus: ut inqvam de his omnibus nihil nunc dicam, Manichæorum tamen delirium observationem vel maximè meretur, qui rerum omnium duo constituunt principia, sive duos DEOS: Unum bonum: alterum malum: Eum etiam dixerunt esse Creatorem corporis: ac proinde animam post mortẽ à corpore separatam verè evadere felicem: neq; amplius corpori conjungendam: quippe quod felicitatẽ animæ magis impediat, & interturbet, quàm promoveat aut perficiat. Quæ sanè hæresis uti summè contumeliosa & blasphema est in Deum, conditorẽ non animæ modò, sed & corporis: ita propria sua impietate & futilitate concidit.


### Part II

There are those who have impugned the orthodox doctrine concerning the Resurrection, and indeed not a few, arising not so much from the school of theologians as from that of philosophers, who partly denied this article entirely, and partly wickedly corrupted it. And in the beginning, as regards those more ancient heretics of whom Scripture makes mention, the Sadducees hold the first place, who held the resurrection of the dead to be a fable; as is evident from chapter 22, v. 23 of Matthew, and chapter 4, 2, and also chapter 23, v. 8 of the Acts. The Savior shows two sources, as it were, of this error: First, they did not understand the Scriptures: Secondly, they were ignorant of the virtue and power of GOD: foolishly positing that if life is to be expected after the end of the world, it cannot be other than such as it was in this world, where we shall always have need of drink, food, and sexual intercourse: which is sufficiently evident from the cited chapter 22, v. 23 of Matthew, and chapter 20, v. 27 and following of Luke. To this error, in place of a most sufficient refutation, the Savior opposes this aphorism, taken from the very nature of the controversy: You err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of GOD: The children of this world marry, and are given in marriage: but in the resurrection from the dead, they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, nor will they be able to die any more: for they are equal to the Angels,

Nor have there been wanting among the Doctors of the Church those who taught not orthodoxly concerning the truth of this Article. Origen, a writer otherwise most learned, deceived by a false interpretation of the words of the Apostle, who says, It is sown a natural body: It will rise a spiritual body: contended that the flesh which is buried will not resurrect: indeed, that the body, but not the flesh, will resurrect, openly contradicting the most holy Job, who confesses that he will see the Lord in his flesh, and will behold him with his own eyes: Job 19, 26 and 27. As regards the Apostolic passage, it is certain that he does not affirm that the bodies of the resurrected will be πνεύματα spirits: For the Savior himself testifies to the contrary in Luke 24, 39. Handle, he says, and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have: But the Apostle affirms that the bodies will be πνευματικὰ spiritual: which is to be referred to that glory and brightness which our bodies will have, because of that most excellent clarification which will befall them: concerning which much was said above. See more concerning this error in P. Martyr in his Commonplaces.

Pertinent ad hanc qvoqve errantium classem Philosophi & Mathematici, qui Resurrectionem mortuorum tùm fore nugantur, quando post annum magnum, sive post perfectam orbiũ cælestium revolutionem, omnia cum plenè in modum restituentur, quem modum nunc res omnes obtinent, vel aliqvando obtinuerunt: Qvæ Revolutio orbium cælestium perfectissima fiat sem per Anno tricies sexies millesimo. Ut exẽpli gratia, si ab hoc ipso die; qui nunc illuxit, triginta sex millia annorum effluxerint, nos tùm hoc ipso loco, und in hoc ipso Auditorio futuros, & numero, & reipsâ eos- Belonging also to this class of those in error are the Philosophers and Mathematicians, who trifle that the Resurrection of the dead will take place only when, after the great year, or after the perfect revolution of the celestial spheres, all things shall be fully restored to the state which all things now possess, or have at some time possessed: Which most perfect revolution of the celestial spheres is said to occur every thirty-six thousandth year. As for example, if from this very day, which has now dawned, thirty-six thousand years shall have passed, we shall then be in this very place, and in this very lecture hall, both in number and in reality the same: me likewise detaining the parts, and indeed the parts of one lecturing on this very question: while you, however, sustain the roles of the Auditors. They wish the reason for this opinion to be Astronomical. For they contend, following the footsteps of Ptolemy, that that highest sphere of the Heavens contains within itself three hundred and sixty-six degrees: and that each star traverses one degree of those in every hundred years, indeed in such a way that after thirty-six thousand years, each star returns to that point from which it had set out, and had begun its motion. Now since the state or position of the Celestial bodies will then be in the same condition as it was from the beginning, they maintain that it is a consequence that then all things return to their original form and condition. Which Revelation some extend more widely, namely to the fortieth thousandth year. But these are trifles and fables, devised by the petulance of men: whose foundations depend upon principles equally false and erroneous: Such as is: That the pursuits, life, counsels, actions, and death of men depend upon the position of the stars, or upon the degrees of the Celestial spheres. By which one compact, the providence of God, and likewise all promises and threats, are removed and enervated. What of the fact that Scripture expressly affirms that the Resurrection of the pious will not be for the sake of undergoing the former labors in this life: but for eternal life, where they shall live for all eternity, like the Angels of GOD. Which hope is certainly cut off from pious minds by the insanity of these Philosophers and Mathematicians: since they hear that, because of the position of the stars and degrees, they are to be detained again, through this fictitious and fantastic Resurrection, to the former troubles of this life, nay even to mortality. Whence it becomes manifest that Astrologers of this kind, with the ancient heretics, utterly enervate, remove, and overturn the Resurrection of the dead to eternal life.

Added to these is that numerous tribe of Epicureans, to whom the Sermons concerning the Resurrection of the dead, concerning eternal life, and concerning eternal damnation seem to be fables, devised by the heralds of the Word, partly to ensnare the minds of men with the empty hope of eternal life: but partly to terrify the same, and to call them away from vices and sins, by those vain threats concerning Hell. And lest they appear completely atheistic, they say that they are moved to deny the Resurrection of the dead by firm arguments: the chief of which it is pleasing to know.

The first is such: Whatever goes into ashes, and is resolved into the first Elements, or at least returns to the first matter of nature: that it should rise again, and undergo its former species, is utterly impossible. But a body separated from a body by death is reduced to ashes, etc.: Therefore.

Then they say it happens not rarely that a man is torn apart by a wolf, the wolf is devoured by a lion: the lion by birds: the birds in turn are eaten by men, and become a part of the body of the same: indeed in such a way that the flesh of the former man torn by the Wolf has now become the flesh of another man: If therefore the Resurrection of the dead were to be hoped for, it would be impossible in turn for each man to have his own flesh returned to him in species, without the loss of the substance of another man. Which very thing they also try to prove especially from the nature of anthropophagous men, who feed only on human flesh: Where no one denies that a mixture of the most distinct species of flesh occurs.

Thirdly, they argue that God himself willed that perpetual generation and corruption should obtain in the nature of things: so that because one and the same individual in number, once destroyed, cannot be restored: yet there might be the procreation and multiplication of species.

Fourthly: Just as he who falls from health into a more serious disease: loses that former health of his: so if he should even recover afterwards, yet this later health is not one and the same in number with the former: So if the Resurrection of the dead were even to be hoped for: it should not be believed that the same bodies in number would rise again.

And finally, to increase impiety with stupidity, they continue to talk nonsense thus: If bodies are to be restored the same in number, and in the Individual: then they will be restored with all things pertaining to them: and thus all humors, all hairs, all nails will be returned. By which compact the mass of the body will go off into a huge and horrendous monster: But if, however, all these things are not restored, but only some: it will be a consequence that the same thing does not rise again whole in the Individual: nay, that no reason can be given why these things rather than those should be restored?

In order to respond to these; as a foundation I resume that of the Savior, You err, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of GOD, Matt. 20. v. 29. For first, unless the Holy Spirit had proposed to us in the Scriptures the truth and certainty of this Article to be believed: there would truly hardly be anyone who could be certain of it. Then, unless the entire work of the Resurrection of the dead depended upon the sole virtue and power of GOD, and not upon causes either natural or artificial: our faith concerning this Article would again entirely collapse. Now, indeed, relying on the authority of the Scriptures and the infinite omnipotence of GOD, we profess that we firmly believe in our Creed the resurrection of the dead: paying no heed to those rancid and truly foolish quibbles of our reason, which prove nothing more than that it is entirely unknown and uninvestigable to human wit and carnal wisdom, nay, that it cannot even be brought about by any natural causes, that the same body in number, however much torn apart, nay, even as if transposed into the body of another man, should nevertheless rise again perfect and entire, according to all its essential and integral parts. All of which we ourselves also willingly concede and confess, that every work of Nature entirely fails and expires here: But meanwhile we reply that the resurrection of the dead is not to be measured and judged by our wit, nor by the causes of nature, but solely by the Word of GOD and His infinite power. He Himself said in the Creation, and they were made: The same He Himself will say in the resurrection: and they shall rise again. To Him be glory forever, AMEN.

Latin:

SUnt, qui Orthodoxam de Resurrectione doctrinam impugnarunt, & quidem haud pauci, non tam ex Theologorum, quàm Philosophorum schola oriundi, qui Articulum hunc partim planè negarunt, partim verò nefariè corruperunt. Ac initiò quidem, qvoad antiqviores illos hæreticos, quorum scriptura meminit, primum locum obtinent Sadducæi, qui Resurrectionem mortuorum pro fabulâ habebant; uti patet ex cap. 22. v. 23. Matth. & cap. 4, 2. item cap. 23, v. 8. Actorum. Cujus erroris duos quasi fontes ostendit Servator: Primùm enim non intelligebant Scripturas: Deinde ignorabant virtutem ac potentiam DEI: stolidè statuentes, si expectanda sit vita: post finem mundi, non aliam eam esse posse, quàm qualis hoc fuit in mundo, ubi potu, cibo, Venere semper opus simus habituri: id qvod ex citato cap. 22. v. 23. Matthæi, & cap. 20, v. 27. ac seqq. Lucæ satis evidenter liquet. Cui errori Servator Refutationis sufficientissimæ loco hunc opponit Aphorismum, ex ipsa Controversiæ natura petitum: Erratis, nescientes scripturas, & virtutem DEI: Filii hujus seculi ducunt uxores, & nuptui dant: sed in resurrectione ex mortuis, neq; ducunt uxores, neq; nuptui dantur, neq; ultrà mori poterunt: æquales enim Angelis sunt,

Nec defuerunt inter Doctores Ecclesiæ, qui haud orthodoxè de hujus Articuli veritate docerent. Origenes scriptor altoqui eruditissimus, deceptus falsâ interpretatione verborum Apostoli, dicentis, Seminatur Corpus Animale: Resurget Spirituale: contendit, non eam carnem resurrecturam, quæ sepulta est: imò Corpus, non verò carnes resurrecturas, apertè contradicens sanctissimo Jobo, qui in carne sua se visurum, & oculis suis conspecturum Dominum fatetur: Job. 19, 26. & 27. Qvoad Locum Apostolicum, constat ipsum non affirmare, Corpora resuscitatorum fore πνεύματα Spiritus: Contrarium enim Servator ipse testatur Luc. 24. 39. Palpate, inqviens, & videte, Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere: Verùm πνευματικὰ spiritualia fore corpora affirmat Apostolus: id qvod gloriam & claritatem illam referendum est, quã nostra habebunt corpora, propter præstantissimam illam clarificationem, quæ illis obtinget: de quâ suprâ copiosè fuit dictum. Vide plura de hoc errore apud P. Martyrem in locis.

Pertinent ad hanc qvoqve errantium classem Philosophi & Mathematici, qui Resurrectionem mortuorum tùm fore nugantur, quando post annum magnum, sive post perfectam orbiũ cælestium revolutionem, omnia cum plenè in modum restituentur, quem modum nunc res omnes obtinent, vel aliqvando obtinuerunt: Qvæ Revolutio orbium cælestium perfectissima fiat sem per Anno tricies sexies millesimo. Ut exẽpli gratia, si ab hoc ipso die; qui nunc illuxit, triginta sex millia annorum effluxerint, nos tùm hoc ipso loco, und in hoc ipso Auditorio futuros, & numero, & reipsâ eosdem: me itidem detentu partes & quidem hanc ipsam quæstionem prælegentis partes: vobis verò Auditorum vices sustinentibus. Opinionis hujus rationem volunt esse Astronomicam. Contendunt enim secuti vestigia Ptolomæi, orbem illum summum Cælorum continere in se trecentos sexaginta sex gradus: & unumquodque astrum centenis quibusque annis unum gradum ex illis percurrere, ita quidem, ut post triginta sex millia annorum, unumquodque sidus ad illud punctum redeat, unde solverat, & motum suum inceperat. Jam cùm status vel situs corporum Cælestium tunc eâdem ratione, quâ fuit ab initio, sese sit habiturus, hinc consequens esse autumant, ut tum omnia ad pristinam suam formam & conditionem redeant. Quam Revelationem nõnulli latiùs extendunt, ad annum nimirùm quadragies millesimum. Sed nugæ & fabulæ sunt istæ, hominum petulantia excogitatæ: quarũ fundamenta dependent à principiis æquè falsis & erroneis: Qvale est: Hominum studia, vitam, consilia, actiones, mortem dependere ex positu siderum, vel à gradibus orbium Cælestium. Qvo uno pacto Dei providentia promissiones item, & comminationes omnes tolluntur, & enervantur. Qvid qvod scriptura disertè affirmat, Resurrectionem piorum, non ad pristinos hac in vitâ subeundos labores futuram: sed ad vitam æternam, ubi in omnem æternitatem sint victuri, similes Angelis DEI. Qvæ certè spes per Philosophorum & Mathematicorum istorum insaniam, piis mentibus præciditur: siquidem pro positu astrorum & graduum, denuò per fictitiam hanc, & phantasticam Resurrectionem, ad pristinas vitæ hujus molestias, imò ad mortalitatem detendendas sese esse audiunt. Unde manifestum evadit, qvod hujusmodi Astrologi, cum veteribus hæreticis, Resurrectionem mortuorum ad vitam æternam penitùs enervent, tollant, evertant.

Accedit hisce numerosa illa tribus Epicuræorum, quibus Conciones de Resurrectione mortuorum, de vitâ æternâ, de æterna damnatione fabulæ esse videntur, excogitatæ à Verbi præconibus, partim ad inescandos animos hominum inani spe vitæ æternæ: partim verò ad eosdem terrendos, & avocandos à vitiis & peccatis, vanis illis comminationibus, de Inferno. Et ne planè athei videantur, moveri sese dicunt ad negandam Resurrectionem mortuorum, firmis argumentis: qvorũ præcipua lubet cognoscere.

Primum tale est: Quicquid in cineres abit, inque prima Elementa resolvitur, vel certè ad primã naturæ materiam redit: illud iterum resurgere, & pristinam subire speciem, prorsus impossibile. At corpus per mortem separatum à corpore, redigitur in cineres &c: Ergò.

Deindè haud rarò fieri inqviunt, ut homo discerpatur à lupo, lupus devoretur à leone: Leo à volucribus: volucres rursum comeduntur ab hominibus, eorundemqve corporis pars evadant: ita quidem, ut carnes prioris hominis à Lupo discerpti, jam factæ sint carnes alterius hominis: Quod si Ergo speranda esset Resurrectio mortuorum, impossibile rursum sus fuerit, cuilibet homini suam in specie reddi carnem, sine jactura alterius hominis substantia. Quod ipsum cumprimis etiam probare conantur, ex naturâ hominum ἀνθρωποφάγων, qui duntaxat carnibus humanis vescuntur: Ubi carnium distinctissimarum specierum mixtionem fieri, nemo non didet.

Tertiò arguunt, Deum ipsum in rerum natura voluisse perpetuam obtinere generationem & corruptionem: ut quia unum idemq́; numero individuum, semel destructum, restitui nequit: Specierum tamen esset procreatio & multiplicatio.

Qvartò: Quemadmodum, qui ex sanitate incidit in morbum graviorem: pristinam illam suam sanitatem perdit: ita si vel maximè postmodum convalescat, tamen sanitas hæc posterior non sit numero una & eadem cum priore: Ita si vel maximè Resurrectio mortuorum esset speranda: minime tamen eadem numero corpora resurrectura credendum foret.

Et tandem, ut impietatem stoliditate augeant, sic ineptire pergunt, Si eadem numero, & in Individuo restituenda sunt corpora: utiq́; restituentur cum omnibus ad ea pertinentibus: atque sic omnes humores, omnes pili, omnes ungues reddentur. Quo pacto moles corporis in monstrum ingens & horrendum abibit: Quod si verò isthæc omnia non restituentur, sed aliqva duntaxat: Conseqvens erit, non idem in Individuo integrum resurgere: imò rationem dari nullam posse, cur hæc magis, quàm illa sint restituenda?

His ut respondeam; fundamenti loco resumo illud Servatoris, Erratis, nescientes Scripturas, & virtutem DEI, Matth. 20. v. 29. Primùm enim, nisi Spiritus Sanctus in Scripturis Articuli hujus veritatem, & certitudinem nobis credendam proposuisset: vix profectò qvisqvam foret, qui de eâ certus esse posset. Deinde nisi universum Resurrectionis mortuorum opus, à solâ virtute, & potentiâ DEI, non verò ex causis sive naturalibus, sive artificialibus penderet: rursum fides nostra de hoc Articulo tota labasceret. Jam verò nixi Scripturarum autoritate, & DEI infinitâ omnipotentiâ, firmiter in Symbolo nostro, Resurrectionem mortuorum credere nos profitemur: nihil morati rancidas illas, & verè stolidas rationis nostræ argutationes: qvæ nihil magis probant, quàm humano ingenio, & sapientiæ carnali prorsus incognitum, ac impervestigabile esse, imò nullis etiam causis naturalibus fieri posse, ut idem numero corpus, quantumvis discerptum, imò alterius etiam hominis corpus qvasi transpositum, tamen perfectum & integrum, secundum omnes partes Essentiales & integrales resurgat. Qvod omne nos ipsi quoq́; ultrò concedimus, & fatemur, omne prorsus Naturæ opus hîc deficere, & expirare: At interim Resurrectionem mortuorum, non ex nostro ingenio, non ex naturæ causis, sed unicè ex Verbo DEI, & potentiâ ejusdem infinitâ metiendam, judicandamq́; esse, regerimus. Ipse in Creatione dixit, & facta sunt: Idem ipse in resurrectione dicet: & resurgent. Ipsi gloria in ævum, AMEN.


## 27 On Christian Liberty


### Oikonomia Of the Subsequent Treatment

THE ECONOMY of the following Treatise. With God.

That liberty into which all who are subject to the spiritual scepter of Christ—that is, who are citizens and members of the Church of CHRIST militant here on earth—have been asserted through Christ the Savior, is of the same antiquity and duration as the Kingdom of Christ. For such as the Kingdom is, such also is the liberty: namely, the nature and condition of both are spiritual. This is the very reason why it was pleasing not to tear apart or separate these two articles, but to explain them distinctly and separately, though as cause and effect in an uninterrupted order; although Melanchthon, using his own judgment, wished to assign the final or last place to Christian Liberty in the series of Theological Topics. The discussion of Christian Liberty has a most excellent use in the entire system of purer Theology, so that neither the doctrine of the Law nor of the Gospel can be rightly and skillfully proposed and explained unless its purity is left entirely unshaken for Christian Liberty. To which opinion our blessed LUTHER truly established that the integrity of the Christian Religion will endure as long as the Church retains the privileges of Christian Liberty safe and sound. To this is added that errors concerning this Liberty are by far the most dangerous of all, and directly seek the throat of the Christian faith itself. An example can be the sedition of the Peasants, who in the year 1525 took up arms against the political Magistrate throughout almost all of Germany, primarily because, confusing Christian Liberty with political or civil liberty, they thought themselves to be free by divine right itself from all civil burdens and exactions: being persuaded of this principally by Thomas Müntzer, the leader of the Anabaptists, who, speaking grandly before the ignorant peasant mob about divine revelations made to him, lied egregiously that the Sword of Gideon had been divinely granted to him to break the tyranny (as he called it) of the Civil Magistrate: But soon, having been captured with others, he was struck by the sword, and his head was affixed to a spear and erected in the middle of the fields. Moreover, the fury and madness of these men was the more intolerable, the fouler the error is that political liberty is an immunity from the obedience owed to the political Magistrate, or a license from tributes, taxes, or other political burdens: as will be expressly shown below in the topic concerning Civil Magistrates.

Besides the madness of the peasants, even today the innovations, or, as they speak, the reformations of the Sacramentarians, clearly show the abuse of Christian Liberty, having thoroughly infected many illustrious and truly noble churches throughout the Duchy of Anhalt, Hesse, and other provinces with the Sacramentarian poison.

It will therefore be worth the effort to investigate the nature and affection of Christian Liberty, both in emphasis and in practice, in such a way that its true use may be vindicated from every vicious extreme, whether regarding excess or defect: which we shall expressly show both in the present article and in the next following one, which will be on Adiaphora, or ceremonies and human traditions in the Church.

Regarding the Philippean Treatise, it is completed in three parts primarily: the first of which shows, partly that even under these very ruins and confusions of kingdoms and Empires, Christians can nevertheless truly glory in that Liberty into which they have been asserted through Christ: because this does not exclude the cross and calamities, but rather exerts itself and triumphs under these very things; and partly that this Liberty differs greatly from political liberty, especially from that carnal kind which the Jews and fanatics dream of even today.

The second establishes four distinct degrees of Christian Liberty: concerning which we must also discourse below in their proper place.

The third and final part discourses on human traditions, especially Pontifical ones, and shows that they, however specious they may be, lead men away from the Word of GOD, overturn the true consolations revealed in the Scriptures, are idolatrous, and bind consciences to do and believe that which simply fights against the Word of GOD and depends only on human authority.

Not departing much from the footsteps of Melanchthon, we establish two primary chapters of our treatise: the FORMER of which shall treat of the Θέσιν, the LATTER of the ἀντίθεσιν: and may both accurately weigh and explain the controversies of our age, stirred up concerning this matter.

Latin:

ΟΙΚΟΝΟΜΙΑ Subsequentis Tractationis. σὺν θεῷ.

EJusdem cum Regno Christi est & antiquitatis & durationis, Libertas illa, in quam per Christum Servatorem asserti sunt, quotquot sceptro ipsius Spirituali sunt subditi, hoc est, Cives sunt, & membra Ecclesiae CHRISTI, hisce in terris militantis. Qvale enim est Regnum: talis est & libertas: nempe Spiritualis utriusque Natura & Conditio. Quae ipsa causa est, quòd duos istos Articulos neutiquam divellere, aut segregare: sed tanquam causam & effectum interrupto ordine, distinctè tamen ac seorsim explicare libuit: quanquam Melanchthon, suo usus consilio, Libertati Christianae, in serie Locorum Theologicorum, sedem postrema sive ultimam adsignare voluit. Habet verò disputatio de Libertate Christiana praeclarissimum usum in universo Theologiae purioris systemate: ita ut neque Legis, neque Evangelii doctrina ritè ac dextrè proponi & explicari possit, nisi Libertati Christianae sua relinquatur puritas planè inconcussa. Quam in sententiam verè statuit B. LUTHERUS noster, tamdiu Religionis Christianae integritatem duraturam, quamdiu Libertatis Christianae privilegia sarta tecta retinuerit Ecclesia. Hûc accedit, quòd errores circa Libertatem hanc, longè omnium sunt periculosissimi, & ipsius fidei Christianae jugulum directè petunt. Exemplo potest esse seditio Rusticorû, qui anno 25. supra sesquimillesimum, adversus Magistratum politicum, per totam fermè Germaniam arma ideò potissimùm sumserunt, quod Libertatem Christianam cum Politicâ, sive Civili confundentes, ipso jure divino liberos se esse putarent, ab omnibus oneribus ac exactionibus civilibus: sic principaliter persuasi à Thoma Monetario Anabaptistarû coryphaeo, qui de divinis revelationibus sibi factis splendidè coram imperita Rusticorum plebe verba faciens, Gladiu Gedeonis ad infringendam Magistratus Civilis tyrannidem (uti loquebatur) sibi divinitus concessum esse, egregiè mentiebatur: Sed mox cum aliis captus, gladio percussus, ejusque caput hastae affixum, mediis in campis erectum fuit. Erat autem istorum furor & insania tantò intolerabilior, quantò foedior error est, quòd Libertas Politica sit immunitas, ab obedientia Magistratui politico debita, vel licentia à tributis, vectigalibus, vel aliis oneribus politicis: uti infrà loco de Magistratibus Civilibus ex professo oftendetur.

Praeter rusticorum insaniam, hodieque Sacramentariorum Novationes, vel, ut illi loquuntur, Reformationes, perspicuè oftendunt abusum Libertatis Christianae, multas illustres, & verè nobiles Ecclesias, per Ducatum Anhaltinum, Hassiam, aliasq; provincias veneno Sacramentario penitus infectisse.

Operae precium ergo fuerit, naturam & affectionem Libertatis Christianae, quà ἔμφασιν, quà πρᾶξιν ita investigare, ut verus ejus usus, ab omni vitioso extremo, vel quoad excessum, vel quoad defectum vindicetur: id quod tùm praesente articulo, tùm subsequente proximo, qui erit de Adiaphoris, sive Ceremonus & traditionibus humanis in Ecclesia, ex professo ostendemus.

Quoad Tractationem Philippcam, absolvitur ea tribus potissimùm partibus: quarum Prima ostendit, partim sub mediis etiam istis regnorum & Imperiorum ruinis ac confusionibus, Christianos tamen nihilominùs verè gloriari posse de Libertate eâ, in quam per Christum sunt asserti: propterea quòd haec non excludat crucem, & calamitates, sed sub his ipsis potiùs se exerat, & triumphet: partim verò Libertatem hanc à Politica plurimùm differre, cumprimis à carnali illa, qualem Judaei & fanatici hodieque somniant.

Altera quatuor distinctos Gradus Libertatis Christianae constituit: de quibus nobis quoque infrà suo loco erit differendum.

Tertia & postrema de Traditionibus humanis, praesertim Pontificiis, differit, ac ostendit, eas, quantumvis speciosas, abducere homines à Verbo DEI, evertere veras consolationes in Scripturis patefactas, esse idololatricas, obligare conscientias ad faciendum & credendum id, quod cum Verbo DEI simpliciter pugnat, & ab humana autoritate tantùm dependet.

Nos haud multum recedentes à vestigiis Melanchthonis, Tractationis nostrae duo constituimus capita primaria: quorum PRIUS Θέσιν, POSTERIUS ἀντίθεσιν pertractet: Utrumque verò nostri seculi controversias, hac de re motas, accuratiùs expendat & explicet.


### Oikonomia Of the Subsequent Treatment: I. Thesis Or Affirmative

I. THESIS Or Affirmative.

The word liberty is of the number of those which are called τὰ πρός τι [relative terms], and whose nature and proper affection is most rightly understood from the immediately opposed contrary. Therefore, what Christian Liberty is properly and according to the Scriptures will shine forth from there, if we have more accurately known the contrary servitude, by which we were held captive outside of Christ. Now if we search the Scriptures, a threefold Kind of Servitude is shown, into which all mortals individually and collectively were carried away by the envy of the Devil: and from which liberation consists through Christ alone.

THE FIRST kind of Servitude is the Servitude of sin, passing from the most sad fall of our first parents into the whole human race, indeed, as the Apostle speaks, passing also into those who have not sinned in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, Rom. 5. 22. & 14. Concerning which kind of Servitude the Savior treats, John 8.34, saying: He who commits sin is the servant of sin, and the Apostle Rom. 6. 16: Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as servants to obey, you are servants of him whom you obey?

THE OTHER kind, as an effect flowing from the preceding, is the Servitude of vanity, blindness, error, and ignorance of divine things; by which are held constrained as many as in Gentilism outside of Christ changed the truth of GOD, which they recognized from created things, into a lie, and worshipped and served created things, neglecting the Creator, who is blessed forever: thus they became vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened: and while they claim to be wise, they became fools. Rom. 1. 21 & 22. Concerning which kind of Servitude the Apostle discourses expressly Ephes. 4. 17, saying: I testify in the LORD, that you no longer walk, as the rest of the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind: having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of GOD through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart. And at Tit. 3. 3. We were also once foolish, and disobedient, wandering, and serving various desires and pleasures.

THE THIRD kind is the Servitude of the corruption of even our bodies: and the Servitude of death. Concerning which the Apostle Rom. 8. 20. & 21: The creature was subjected to vanity: but it also shall be delivered from the servitude of corruption, into the liberty of the glory of the children of GOD.

According to those three kinds of Servitude, three species also of either Liberty or Liberation are constituted, acquired through Christ the Savior: so that not undeservedly he himself said to the Jews, John 8. 36: You shall be truly free, if the Son of man shall have liberated you.

THE FIRST species is the Liberty of gratuitous justification through faith in Christ, by which, with all sins remitted, we are accepted into grace, and adopted as children of GOD. Concerning which liberty

The Apostle Ephes. 1. 7: In Christ we have ἀπολύτρωσιν [redemption] through his blood, the remission of sins out of his rich grace. And Coloss. 1. 13: He delivered us from the power of darkness, and translated us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through his blood, namely the remission of sins.

THE OTHER species is the liberty of illumination or of the renewal of our mind, by which through the preaching of the Gospel we are more and more liberated from the servitude of vanity, blindness, and error, the Holy Spirit illuminating our minds, and renewing our hearts, that they may serve GOD alone, and put off the former conversation, according to the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error: and put on the new man, who is created according to GOD, in righteousness and holiness of truth: as the Apostle describes this Liberty Ephes. 4. 22. 23. 24.

The third and final species is the Liberty of Glorification, by which we shall be freed from all servitude of corruption, and from death itself, when the Savior shall raise our bodies to glory, and shall assert them into the most perfect and in all respects most absolute liberty. Concerning which species the Apostle says in Rom. 8. 21: We shall be freed from the servitude of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of GOD. And Eph. 1. 14: The Holy Spirit is the earnest of our inheritance, until we are vindicated into liberty, to the praise of his glory.

These three species of liberty depend, however, upon the one and only merit of Christ, as upon the efficient and meritorious cause. For He alone on the cross, by His own blood, obtained for us a perfect redemption, that is, the longed-for liberation from that triple kind of servitude and captivity, and snatched us from the power of sin, vanity, and death. Which liberation Scripture expresses by the terms λυτρώσεως, ἀπολυτρώσεως, of Redemption, and defines this by the remission of sins. Ephes. 1. 7. Coloss. 1. 13. For where there is remission of sins, there the dominion of sin, vanity, death, the Devil, and hell expires entirely.

And this liberation, both because it was accomplished through Christ, and because it is most especially proper to Christians, has obtained the name and appellation of Christian Liberty: the effects of which extend as widely as the scope of all those things which can in any way constrain us or entangle us in any yoke of servitude. Looking to this, Theologians have established four distinct degrees of Christian Liberty: what these are, how they ought to be correctly defined, and how they ought to be vindicated from the sophistries of certain Sacramentarians in particular, it will have been necessary to explain more accurately, because the whole substance and purity of this doctrine consists of and is completed by these four degrees.

The FIRST degree, therefore, is liberation from the curse of the moral Law through the death of Christ. For such an ἀνεκδίκητον (unavenged/unpunished state) was annexed to this Law: Cursed is everyone who has not done all things which are written in the book of this law. Deut. 27. 26. Now since this Law was weakened through the flesh, while no one could provide perfect obedience to it, God, having sent His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin for sin in the flesh, that the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us, Rom. 8. 3. We are therefore no longer under the Law, but under Grace. Rom. 6. 14. And we are now freed from the Law, having died to it (namely, the Law) by which we were held. Rom. 7. 6. The effect of this first degree is this, that with the thought of the moral Law and of all Works removed in the act of our justification, we embrace one and only the mercy of GOD, prepared for us in the Satisfaction of Christ: and with our gaze turned away from us and our own dignity, we look only to Christ: who for us both fulfilled that δικαίωμα of the Law, and rendered to it the most absolute obedience, and underwent and bore its curse and punishments for us. Concerning which matter the Article of Justification treats properly and expressly.

THE SECOND DEGREE is Liberation from the Dominion of sin, so that sin may no longer rule over us: but that, being justified and adopted into the liberty of the Children of GOD, we may live to the righteousness of GOD without any coercion, with a spontaneous Spirit and a ready will. Concerning which matter the Apostle discourses expressly and sufficiently at length in Rom. 6. from verse 6 to the end of the chapter. And Rom. 8. 2. The law of the Spirit of life (the doctrine of the Gospel) in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death. And Galat. 5. 13. You have been called to liberty, brothers: only do not take liberty as an occasion for the flesh: but by love serve one another. 1 Pet. 2. 15 & 16. This is the will of GOD, that by doing good you may silence the ignorance of foolish men: As free, and not as having liberty as a cloak for malice: but as servants of GOD.

But it is asked and disputed in this place, whether the Necessity of a debt, of a divine command, does not conflict with this Liberty, by which we are debtors, not to the flesh, that we should live according to the flesh: Rom. 8. 12. but that we should present our members as weapons of righteousness to GOD according to the law of GOD, for holiness; because, having been freed from sin, we have been enslaved to righteousness: Rom. 6. 13, 18, 19, 22. We answer in the negative, for the following most evident reasons. 1. The words necessity and debt, when the discourse is about the reborn, are not understood as coercion, but only as that due obedience which the faithful, insofar as they are reborn, perform not from coercion or the impulse of the law: but from a free and spontaneous Spirit: although this very liberty of the Spirit is never perfect in this life: but labors under the manifold infirmity of the flesh.

Furthermore, the word Liberty is taken καταχρηστικῶς [improperly] and in a sense not Ecclesiastical, but common, in this question, for that which is completely loosed from every law, and free from every order obligating to certain obedience. Such liberty, speaking properly, is not true liberty, but rather beastly license, wandering like brute animals without law. In which sense there is no liberty not only in the reborn: but even in GOD Himself, and in the Angels. Therefore, an opposition is made most viciously between those things which are not at all opposed to each other: namely, between Liberty, and New Obedience due to the law: Which two, however, are only subordinate. For true liberty is not opposed to Order and Obedience due to the law: but partly to violent coercion, partly to servile necessity. For example: Man in the state of integrity before the fall was most free, and from a most free προαίρεσις [choice] sought the good, fled the evil: nor yet was he meanwhile without law, much less did the law given to him either hinder or take away the liberty of acting: but it was rather the Object, around which he exercised his liberty most of all. For this liberty properly respects the mode of acting ἐκ προαιρέσεως [by choice] with Election: which is occupied about the very Obedience due to the Law, without any coercion. Which itself is evident from the example of the Angels, who whatever they do, they do most freely, nor does any coercion fall upon them: since they are most free Spirits: And yet nevertheless they depend upon the nod and will of GOD, as from the first cause, and thus from an external law. Whence it becomes manifest that this Liberty, and the necessity of debt and divine command, do not mutually destroy each other; but are ὑπαλλήλως [subordinately] subordinate. The Apostle explains this very thing with an excellent simile in Galat. 3. 23 & 25. Before, he says, faith had come, we were kept under the guard of the Law, shut up unto that faith which was to be revealed: Therefore the Law was our schoolmaster unto Christ: But after faith came, we are no longer under a schoolmaster.

THE THIRD Degree is Liberty from the Observation of the Ceremonial Law, and from that manifold yoke of Mosaic burdens, to which the Jews were subject. For since those Ceremonies and Sacrifices were a Type unto Christ: certainly Christ having now been exhibited, those Types, each and all, had expired, so that under the New T. no one is obligated to their observation. Concerning which matter Peter preaches excellently in Acts 15. 10. Now, he says, why do you tempt GOD to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear. And the Apostle Coloss. 2. 16. Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in part of a feast day, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths: which are a shadow of things to come: but the body is in Christ. To which also pertains the Disputation of the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews through two chapters, the ninth and the tenth. And the Savior Himself looked to this, when in Matt. 11. 13 He asserts that the Law and the Prophets prophesied until John.

A Question not entirely lacking in difficulty is moved concerning this degree. For because this degree of liberty is proper to the faithful of the New T., it is asked, Whether and how the virtue of the merit of Christ, and the Promise of the Gospel, pertained to the faithful of the Old T., who it is sufficiently agreed were free from the observation of the Ceremonial laws. The question can be comprised in this Syllogism.

If the promise of the Gospel, and the virtue of the merit of Christ, is common to the faithful of all times: it would follow, either that the observance of Mosaic rites was not necessary for the saints in the Old Testament: or that it did not pertain to them the promise of the Gospel, and the virtue of the merit of Christ. But the former is true. Therefore, it is necessary that one or the other consequence be true. Or in this manner: If the observance of Mosaic rites was not free for the Israelites, it will not be free for us either. The reason is: Because we enjoy the same and equal promise of the Gospel, and the same virtue of the merit of Christ, as the Israelites. But the observance of Mosaic rites was not free for the Israelites. Therefore, it will not be free for us either.

But I reply that a fallacy is committed from a statement in a certain respect to a statement in an unqualified sense. For the truth of the antecedent in the major premise of the prosyllogism is indeed established: but not in a simple and absolute way, but rather determined by the two prior degrees of Christian Liberty, which comprise the chief and highest benefits of the Gospel and the merit of Christ. For in these there is an equal fellowship and communion of the Church of all times: by the force and efficacy of which, this Liberty consisted for the faithful in the Israelite Church, so that in the use of Mosaic rites, neither justification nor the merit of salvation consisted, nor did spiritual newness depend upon their observance. But the matter is otherwise in this third degree of Liberty, where there is a great discrepancy between the two peoples, the Israelite and the Christian. For under the Old Testament, while the two preceding degrees of Christian Liberty, which are common to both and the same, remained safe, it pleased God the Best and Greatest to have the Israelite people constrained in external matters under a peculiar form of polity and the prescription of certain laws. Which polity, having been abolished with the ceremonial and forensic laws themselves, nothing is common to Christians under the New Testament with Mosaic rites, except insofar as they contain something Natural or Moral: that is, they cease to be truly and merely Mosaic.

THE FOURTH Degree is Liberty from the burden of human traditions, by which Christians are free from the observance of human inventions, ceremonies, and similar external things, which, under the guise of piety and religion, are often enough obtruded and imposed upon the Church of God by the enemies of the truth in a tyrannical manner. For things of this kind, if they are indifferent by their nature, and adiaphora, it is certainly permitted to either use or omit them indifferently: If they are impious, superstitious, and are obtruded under the guise of divine worship and by a simple law of necessity, it is better to reject them simply than to be entangled again in a new yoke of servitude and to cast shackles upon the liberty of conscience. Concerning this liberty, the Apostle discourses in 1 Cor. 7. 23: You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. But concerning this degree of Liberty, and the right and free use of adiaphorous and indifferent things, there will be a discussion expressly in the next article following. In this place, let it suffice only to have observed that our Churches have with very good right sent a message of renunciation to the Papal Tyranny; which exercised a foul butchery of consciences, while it proposed to the sheep of Christ traditions devised by the Pope, both very numerous in count, and impious by their nature, and superstitious in observance, to be observed under an absolute law of necessity, and with no less religion of worship than divine commands. To which impiety that saying of the Savior is most rightly opposed, Matt. 15. 9: In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.

The Jesuits cavil at this assertion of ours, and accuse it of impiety, because it follows from it that no Christian is obligated to obey the civil laws of a political Magistrate: because those laws are equally human traditions as those which are prescribed to the Church of God by the Pope and Roman Bishops. But the vanity of this most impudent cavil can be demonstrated in many ways. For 1. a sufficiently gross fallacy of the consequent is committed. For Christians, regarding this fourth degree of Liberty, establish that they are free from the statutes of men, not so that they may obey no laws resting on justice and equity: For such obedience does not take away this liberty: rather it is subordinate to it: but they are said to be free in this sense, that they know their consciences and minds are liberated from the religion of human laws. 2. a fallacy of irrelevant conclusion occurs. For it is one thing to defend Christian liberty: but quite another and clearly different thing to infringe upon the authority of political laws. The former is done by our Churches: the latter is not. But the cause of the Jesuitical error is that they persuade themselves that nothing can be done by a Christian, or even ought to be done, unless it binds a man in conscience: which is most false. Therefore, one must obey political laws, because they are necessary for peace and tranquility, not because they can render our consciences bound before God. Whence soon emerges a clear distinction between human and divine laws. For divine laws must be obeyed simply and without any condition, where no regard is to be had for times, or places, or other circumstances. But human laws must indeed be obeyed, but in that manner which the circumstances of places, times, and things demand and admit. For example: He who is an Italian, and lives in Italy, ought to obey the laws of Italy: The same person, if he has migrated to Germany, is certainly no longer bound by the laws of Italy. Whence it is clearly evident that his conscience was not bound by the laws of Italy: otherwise they would necessarily have to be observed in Germany as well: For those things which bind and constrain the conscience are immutable. 3. The Jesuitical collection wanders off the track. For the obedience owed to a political Magistrate does not depend upon human authority, but upon a divine precept, which binds our consciences so that we render obedience to the Magistrate in those things which are not against God, faith, and good morals. Therefore, as regards the genus itself, one must obey the Magistrate for the sake of Conscience, because God has commanded it: but the particular laws of Magistrates have no dominion over consciences. To this is added that if Christians observe the individual laws of the Magistrate, they do not cling to the laws themselves, as if by performing these or those the conscience is satisfied: but they look to the end, that is, the will of God, which prescribes obedience to honest and just laws. Which being thus observed, it is plain that the conscience is bound by no

Latin:

I. ΘΕΣΙΣ Sive Affirmativa.

LIbertatis vocabulum ex eorum est numero, quæ nominantur τὰ πρός τι, & quorú natura ac propria affectio, ex immediatè opposito contrario rectissimè intelligitur. Ergo, quid Libertas Christiana propriè & secundũ Scripturas sit, inde eluceffet, si contrariam servitutem, qua extra Christum captivi detinebamur, accuratiùs cognoverimus. Jam si Scripturas scrutemur, triplex monstratur Servitutis Genus, in quod invidia Diaboli abrepti fuerunt mortales singuli & universi: & è quo per solum Christum liberatio constat.

PRIMUM Servitutis genus est Servitus peccati, ex tristissimo lapsu proto-parentum nostrorum in universum genus humanum transiens, imò ut Apostolus loquitur, pertransiens in eos quoque, qui non peccaverunt in similitudinem prævaricationis Adam, Rom. 5. 22. & 14. De quo Servitutis genere agit Servator, Johan 8.34. Qui facit peccatum, inquiens, servus est peccati, & Apostolus Rom. 6. 16. An nescitis, quòd cui vos exhibetis servos ad obediendum, servi estis ejus, cui obeditis?

ALTERUM genus, tanquam effectus ex præcedente promanans, est Servitus vanitatis, cæcitatis, erroris & ignorantiæ rerum divinarũ; qua constricti tenentur, quotquot in Gentilismo extra Christum, veritatem DEI, quam ex rebus creatis agnoverunt, mutarunt in medacium, & coluerunt, ac servierunt rebus creatis, neglecto Creatore, qui est benedictus in secula: sic vani facti in ratiocinationibus suis, & obtenebratum est desipiens cor ipsorum: cumque dictitent se sapientes, stulti facti sunt. Rom. 1. 21 & 22. De quo Servitutis genere ex professo disserit Apostolus Ephes. 4. 17. Obtestor, inquiens, DOMINUM, ne ampliùs incedatis, sicut reliquæ Gentes incedunt, in vanitate mentis suæ: obtenebratum habentes intellectum, alienati à vitâ DEI per ignorantiam, quæ est in illis, propter cæcitatem cordis ipsorum. Et ad Tit. 3. 3. Eramus & nos aliquando insipientes, & increduli, errantes, ac servientes desideriis & voluptatibus variis.

TERTIUM genus, est Servitus corru ptionis corporum etiam nostrorum: & Servitus mortis. De qua Apostolus Rom. 8. 20. & 21. Vanitati creatura subjecta est: sed & ipsa liberabitur à servitute corruptionis, in libertatem gloriæ filiorum DEI.

Secundum tria ista Servitutis genera, tres constituuntur etiam sive Libertatis, sive Liberationis species, per Christum Servatorem acquisitæ: ut haud immeritò ipsemet ad Judæos dixerit, Joh. 8. 36. Verè liberi eritis, si Filius hominis vos liberaverit.

PRIMA species est Libertas gratuitæ justificationis per fidem in Christum, qua remissis omnibus peccatis acceptamur in gratiam, & adoptamur in filios DEI. De qua libertate

Apostolus Ephes. 1. 7. In Christo habemus ἀπολύτρωσιν redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum ex divite ipsius gratia. Et Coloss. 1. 13. Eripuit nos ex potestate tenebrarum, ac transtulit in regnum Filii sui dilecti, in quo habemo redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius, nempe remissionem peccatorum.

ALTERA species est libertas illuminationis sive renovationis mentis nostræ, qua per prædicationem Evangelii magis magisque liberamur a servitute vanitatis, cœcitatis, & erroris, Spiritu Sancto illuminante mentes nostras, & renovante corda nostra, ut soli DEO serviant, & deponant pristinam conversationem, secundum veterem hominem, qui corrumpitur secundum desideria erroris: induantque novum hominem, qui secundum DEUM conditus est, injustitia & sanctitate veritatis: uti Libertatem hanc describit Apostolus Ephes. 4. 22. 23. 24.
