TERTIA & postrema species est Libertas Glorificationis qua liberabimur ab omni servitute corruptionis, & a morte ipsa, quando Servator excitabit corpora nostra ad gloriam, & in perfectissimam, omnibusque numeris absolutissimam libertatem asseret. De qua specie Apostolus Rom. 8. 21. Liberabimur a Servitute corruptionis, in libertatem gloriæ filiorum DEI. Et Eph. 1. 14. Spiritus Sanctus est arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ, usq; dum in libertatem vindicemur, ad laudem gloriæ ipsius.

Dependent verò tres hæ libertatis species ab uno ac solo merito Christi, tanquam a causa efficiente, & meritoria. Ipse enim solus in cruce suo sanguine perfectam redemtionem, hoc est, exoptatam liberationem, a triplici illo servitutis, & captivitatis genere, nobis impetravit, & ex potestate peccati, vanitatis & mortis nos eripuit. Quam Liberationem Scriptura exprimit per vocabula λυτρώσεως, ἀπολυτρώσεως, Redemtionis, & hanc per Remissionem peccatorum definit. Ephes. 1. 7. Coloss. 1. 13. Ubi enim est remissio peccatorum, ibi dominium peccati, vanitatis, mortis, Diaboli & inferni omninò expirat.

Et hæc liberatio, tum quia per Christum facta, tum quia Christianorum est maximè propria, Libertatis Christianæ nomen & appellationem sortita est: cujus effectus tam latè se patet, quam latè se extendit omnium earum rerum ambitus, quæ quovis modo nos constringere, aut Servitutis jugo aliquo implicare possunt. Quò respicientes Theologi, Quatuor distinctos gradus Libertatis Christianæ constituerunt: qui quales sint, quomodo rectè definiri, & a quorundam Sacramentariorum cumprimis Sophisticationibus vindicari debeant, vel ideò accuratiùs explicandum fuerit, quia tota doctrinæ hujus substantia & puritas, quatuor istis Gradibus constat, & absolvitur.

PRIMUS igitur gradus est Liberatio a maledictione Legis moralis per mortē Christi. Tale n. ἀνεκδίκητον Legi huic erat annexū: Maledictus omnis, qui nõ fecerit omnia, quæ scrisunt in libro legis hujus. Deuter. 27. 26. Jam cùm Lex hæc infirmaretur per carnem, dum nemo perfectam ipsi obedientiam præstare poterat, Deus suo misso Filio, in similitudine carnis peccati, de peccato damnavit peccatum in carne, ut Jus Legis compleretur in nobis, Rom. 8. 3. Non ergo ampliùs sumus sub Lege, sed sub Gratia. Rom. 6. 14. Et liberati nunc sumus à Lege, mortui ei (scilicet Legi) à quâ detinebamur. Rom. 7. 6. Effectus primi istius gradus est iste, quòd sublata Legis moralis, omniumq; Operum cogitatione, in actu justificationis nostræ, unam ac solam DEI misericordiam, in Christi Satisfactione nobis paratam, amplectimur: ac averso à nobis, nostraque dignitate adspectu, solū Christum intuemur: qui pro nobis tùm illud Legis δικαίωμα complevit, tùm obedientiam absolutissimam ei præstitit, tùm maledictionem, pœnasq; ejus pro nobis subiit & pertulit. Quâ de re in Articulo Justificationis propriè, & ex professo agitur.

ALTER GRADUS est Liberatio à Dominio peccati, ut ne peccatum ampliùs nobis dominetur: sed ut justificati, & adoptati in libertatem Filiorum DEI citra omnem coactionem, Spiritu spontaneo, & promtâ voluntate, justitiæ DEI vivamus. Quâ de re ex professo, & prolixe satis disserit Apostolus Rom. 6. à versu 6. ad finem usq; capitii Et Rom. 8. 2. Lex Spiritus vitæ (doctrina Evangelii) in Christo Jesu liberavit me à lege peccati & mortis. Et Galat. 5. 13. Vos ad libertatem vocati estis fratres:tantùm ne libertatem arripiatis in occasionem carnis:sed ex charitate servite alii aliis. 1. Pet. 2. 15. & 16. Hæc est voluntas DEI, ut benè agendo os obstruatis insipientium hominū ignorantiæ:Ut liberi, ac non veluti malitiæ velamen habentes libertatem: sed ut servi DEI.

Quæritur autem, & disputatur hoc loco, annon cùm Libertate hac pugnet Necessitas debiti, mandati divini,quâ debitores sumus,non carni,ut secundum carnem vivamus: Rom. 8. 12. sed ut secundum legem DEI membra nostra sistamus arma justitiæ DEO,ad sanctimoniam; proptereà quòd liberati à peccato mancipati sumus justitiæ: Rom. 6. 13. 18. 19. 22. Respondemus autem negatè, ob sequentes rationes evidentissimas. 1. Necessitatis & debiti vocabula, quando de renatis sermo est, non intelliguntur de coactione, sed tantùm de debita illa obedientia, quam fideles, quateno renati sunt, non ex coactione aut impulsu legis:sed libero & spontaneo Spiritu præstant: licet hæc ipsa Spiritus libertas, hac in vita nunquàm sit perfecta: sed multiplici infirmitate carnis laboret.

Deinde Libertatis vocabulum καταχρηστικῶς planè, & sensu non Ecclesiastico, sed plebejo sumitur in hac quæstione, pro eo quod est planè solutum omni lege, & liberum ab omni ordine obligante ad certâ obedientiam. Qualis libertas propriè loquendo non vera est libertas, sed belluina potius licentia, brutorum more vagans sine lege. Quo sensu non modò in renatis: sed & in DEO ipso, inque Angelis nulla est libertas. Fit ergo vitiosissimè oppositio inter ea, quæ minimè sibi sunt opposita: nempè inter Libertatem, & inter Novam Obedientiam legi debitam: Quę duo tamen tantùm sunt subordinata. Libertas enim vera non opponitur Ordini & Obedientiæ legi debitæ: sed partim violentæ coactioni, partim servili necessitati. Exempli gratiâ: Homo in statu integritatis ante lapsu erat liberrimus, & ex liberrima προαιρέσει appetebat bonum, fugiebat malum: neque tamen interim erat sine lege, multò minùs lex ipsi data, vel impediebat, vel tollebat libertatem agendi: sed erat potiùs Objectum, circa quod libertatem suam vel maximè exercebat. Libertas enim hæc respicit propriè modum agendi ἐκ προαιρέσεως cum Electione: quæ circa ipsam Obedientiam Legi debitam, sine ulla coactione versatur. Quod ipsum patet Angelorum exemplo, qui quicquid agunt, liberrimè agunt, neque ulla coactio in illos cadit: siquidem Spiritus sunt liberrimi: Et tamen niholominus à DEI nutu, & voluntate, tanquam à causa prima, & sic à lege externa dependent. Unde manifestum fit, Libertatem hanc, & necessitatem debiti ac mandati divini, se mutuò non tollere; sed ὑπαλλήλως esse subordinata. Quod ipsum egregio simili explicat Apostolus Galat. 3 23.& 25. Antequam, inquiens venisset fides, sub Lege præsidio tenebamur conclusi in eam fidem, quæ erat revelanda: Itaque Lex pædagogus noster fuit in Christum: At postquam venit fides, non ampliùs sub pædagogo sumus.

TERTIUS Gradus est Libertas ab Observatione Legis Cæremonialis, & à jugo illo multiplici onerum Mosaicorum, quibus Judæi subjacebant. Quoniam enim Cæremoniæ & Sacrificia illa Typus fuerunt ad Christum: utique Christo jam exhibito, Typi illi singuli & universi expirarant, ut sub Novo T. ad eorum observationem Christianorum nemo sit obligatus. Qua de re Petrus egregiè concionatur Actor. 15. 10. Nunc inquiens, quid tentatis DEUM ad imponendum jugum cervici discipulorum, quod neq; patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus. Et Apostolus Coloss. 2. 16. Nemo vos judicet in cibo aut potu, aut parte diei festi, aut neomenii, aut Sabbatorum: quæ sunt umbra rerum futurarum: at corpus est in Christo. Quò pertinet etiam Disputatio Autoris Epistolæ ad Hebræos per duo capita, nonum & decimum. Et huc respexit Servator ipse, quando Matt. 11. 13. asserit, Legem & Prophetas usque ad Johannem prophetasse.

Movetur circa gradum istum Quæstio non omni planè difficultate carens. Quia enim Gradus iste libertatis proprius est fidelium Novi T. quæritur, An & quomodo virtus meriti Christi, & Promissio Evangelii pertinuerit ad fideles Veteris T.quos ab observatione legu Cæremonialium fuisse liberos satis constat. Quæstio hoc Syllogismo potest comprehendi.

Si Promissio Evangelii, & virtus meriti Christi, communis est omnium temporum fidelibus: Consequens fuerit, aut non neceffariam fuisse Sanctis in Veteri T.rituum Mosaicorum observationem: aut non pertiuuisse adipsos promissionẽ Evangelii, & virtutem meriti Christi. At verum est prius. Alterutrum ergo consequens verum etiam sit necesse est. Vel in hunc modum: Si Israelitis non libera suit rituum Mosaicorum observatio: neq; nobis erit libera. Ratio est: Quia eadem & pari promissione Evangelii, & virtute eâdem meriti Christi fruimur, qua Israelitæ. At Israelitis non fuit libera observatio rituum Mosaicorum. Ergo neq; nobis erit libera.

Sed respondeo committi, Sophisma à Dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter. Constat enim quidem Antecedenti in Majore. Prosyllogismi sua veritas: sed non simplex atque absoluta, verùm gradibus prioribus duobus Libertatis Christianæ determinata, qui præcipua, & summa Evangelii, & meriti Christi beneficia complectuntur. In his enim Ecclesiæ omnium temporum par est societas & communio: ex cujus vi, & efficacia fidelibus in Ecclesia Israelitica, ea constitit Libertas, ut in usu rituum Mosaicorum, neq; justificatio, aut meritum salutis consisteret, neque ab eorundem observatione Spiritualis novitas dependeret. Secus autem res habet in hoc tertio Libertatis gradu, ubi inter utrumq; populum, Israeliticum & Christianum magna est discrepantia. Nam sub veteri T. salvis præcedentibꝙ duobus gradibus Libertatis Christianæ, & utrinq; communibus, atque iisdem: placuit DEO Opt. Max. populum Israeliticum sub peculiari forma politiæ, certarumq́; legum præscripto, in externis rebus constrictum habere. Quæ politia cum legibus ipsis Cæremonialibꝙ, & forensibus sublata, nihil Christianis sub N. T. cõmune est cum ritibus Mosaicis, nisi quatenus Naturale aut Morale quippiam continẽt: hoc est, verè ac merè Mosaicæ esse desinunt.

QUARTUS Gradus est Libertas ab onere traditionum humanarum, quâ Christiani liberi sunt ab observatione humanarũ adinventionum, ceremoniarum, & similium rerum externarum, quæ sub specie pietatis & religionis, Ecclesiæ DEI sæpius satis pro imperio ab hostibus veritatis obtruduntur, & imponuntur. Hujusmodi enim res, si natura sua sint indifferentes, & adiaphoræ, utiq; eas vel usurpare, vel omittere indifferenter licet: Si impiæ sint, superstitiosę, & sub specie cultꝫ divini, ac simplici necessitatis lege obtrudantur, simpliciter eas rejicere præstat, quàm novo servitutis jugo iterum implicari, & conscientiæ libertati compedes injicere. De qua libertate disserit Apostolus 1 Cor. 7. 23. Pretio empti estis, nolite fieri servi hominum. Sed de hoc Libertatis gradu, & recto ac libero usu rerum adiaphorarum ac indifferentium, Articulo subsequẽte proximo, nobis ex professo futura disputatio. Hoc loco illud tantùm sufficiat observasse, jure optimo Ecclesias nostras nuntium remisisse Tyrannidi Pontificię; quæ fœdam conscientiarum carnificinam exercuit, dum ovibus Christi traditiones â Pontifice excogitatas, & numero plurimas, & natura sua impias, & observatione superstitiosas, sub absoluta necessitatis lege, & haud minore cultus religione, quàm divina mandata observandas proposuit. Cui impietati rectissimè opponitur illud Servatoris, Matth. 15. 9. Frustrà colunt me, docentes doctrinas hominum.

Cavillantur hanc nostram assertionem Esavvitæ, & impietatis arguunt, eò quòd inde sequatur, Christianorum neminem obligatum esse ad obtemperandum legibus civilibus Magistratus politici: propterea quòd leges illæ æquè sint traditiones humanæ, ac quæ à Pontifice, & Episcopis Romanis Ecclesiæ DEI præscribantur. Sed vanitas impudentissimi hujus çavilli multis modis demonstrari potest. Nam 1. ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꝫ satis crassa committitur. Christiani enim, quoad quartũ istũ Libertatis gradum statuunt ur esse liberi à statutis hominum, non ut nullis legibus, justitiæ & æquitate nitentibus obtemperent: Talis enim obedientia nõ tollit libertatem hanc: quin ei potiùs est subordinata: sed hoc sensu dicuntur esse liberi, quòd conscientias, mentesq́; suas legum humanarum religione liberatas esse, sciunt. 2. occurrit πόρισμα ἑτεροζητήσεως. Aliud n. est, Christianam libertatẽ defendere: aliud verò, ac diversum planè, legum politicarum autoritatem infringere. Prius illud à nostris fit Ecclesiis: posterius hoc nõ item. Causa autem erroris Esavvitici est, quòd sibi persuadent, nihil posse fieri à Christianu, vel debere etiam fieri, nisi quod hominẽ in conscientiâ constringat: id quod est falsissimum. Obtempetandũ est ergo legibus politicis, quia sunt ad pacem & tranquillitatem necessariæ, nõ quòd conscientias nostras coram DEO patatas reddere queant. Unde mox emergit luculentum discrimen inter humanas & divinas leges. Divinis n. simpliciter & sine omni conditione obsequendũ est, ubi nulla vel temporum, vel locorum, vel aliarum circumstantiarum habenda est ratio. Humanis autem obediendum quidem, sed eo modo, quo circumstantiæ locorum, temporum & rerum postulant ac admittũt. Exempli gratia: Qui Italus est, & in Italiâ degit, Italiæ legibus obedire debet: Idem si migrârit in Germaniam, certè Italiæ legibus non ampliùs tenetur. Unde palàm liquet, Cõscientiam illius legibus Italiæ nõ fuisse adstrictam: aliâs in Germania quoque illæ necessariò servandæ essent: Quæ n conscientiam obligant, & constringunt, ea sunt immutabilia. 3. Extra oleas vagatur collectio Esavvitica. Nã Obedientia Magistratui politico debita nõ de pendet ab autoritate humanâ, sed à præcepto divino, quod Conscientias nostras obstringit, ut Magistratui obedientiam præstemus in iis, quæ non sunt contra Deum, fidem, & bonos mores. Ergo Quoad genus ipsum, parendũ est Magistratui propter Conscientiam, quia Deus præcepit: particulares autem Magistratuum leges, nullum habent in Conscientias dominatum. Huc accedit, quòd si Christiani singulas Magistratus leges observant, non hęrent in ipsis legibus, quasi his aut illis præstandis Conscientiæ satisfiat: sed finem, hoc est, DEI voluntatem spectant, quæ obedientia honestis & justis legibus præscribit. Quibus ita observatis planum sit, Conscientiam nullis legi-


### Use of the doctrine of Christian Liberty

laws, except by divine ones. For it is, as the Prophet has it, Jehovah is our lawgiver: Isa. 32. 22. And as the Apostle James adds: There is one lawgiver, who can save and destroy: James 4. 12. Now, when the Romanists impose their laws and traditions upon consciences, they certainly claim for themselves the power of saving and destroying, and despoil GOD of his right. But what difference would there be any longer between divine and human laws, if the latter bound consciences no less than the former? For thus any edicts of men would be made equal to divine precepts: Which is impious and blasphemous.

With those four degrees of Christian Liberty duly observed, there emerges from it a various and manifold use of this doctrine.

For 1. it shows in what thing the peace and tranquility of conscience consists: namely, in the sole merit of Christ, who redeemed us from the hand of all our enemies, and asserted us into the liberty, relying on which we can exclaim with the Apostle, Rom. 8. 31. to the very end: If GOD is for us, who is against us? To which pertains that Rom. 5. 1. Being justified by faith we have peace with GOD.

Then it is evident from this, that the gifts of GOD are to be used with no scruple of conscience, and with no perturbation or hesitation of mind: provided at least that regard is had for the divine Glory, the edification of one's neighbor, and our own salvation.

Thirdly, it preserves Concord in the Church, where a free use of external rites flourishes.

Fourthly, it brings it about that in the kingdom of Christ we serve GOD willingly, without any coercion or servile fear. Finally, it ensures that, being free from the yoke of Papal servitude, we have a peaceful and tranquil conscience regarding the use of adiaphorous and indifferent things.

With all these things thus established, we elicit this definition of Christian Liberty; that it is a spiritual manumission, acquired by the Blood of Christ, by which those believing in him are free before GOD in conscience from the curse of the law, from the servitude of sin, from the yoke of Mosaic Ceremonies, and finally from the burden of human traditions, so that in the liberty of the Spirit or conscience they may serve GOD all the days of their life.

II. ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ

Or refutation of false opinions concerning Christian Liberty.

Against the purer doctrine of Christian Liberty, the Devil has at no time ceased to lay snares, striving for this one thing: to call and draw men away from Christ to Moses, from the Gospel to the Law, from the grace of God to their own righteousness, and finally from the merit of Christ to the meritorious dignity of their own works.

He attempted this in the time of Christ through the Pharisees, who sought righteousness before God from the works of the moral Law.

Then through the false apostles, who added to the merit of Christ the observance of the ceremonial law, not indeed of the whole, and with respect to all its parts, but at least by reason of the sacrament of initiation, namely circumcision, which they urged as necessary for salvation. Against whom the Apostles disputed expressly in the Council of Jerusalem, Acts 15, from verse 1 up to 30, and especially Paul in his Epistles to the Romans and Galatians.

Thirdly, through the Jews, both ancient and more recent, who promised themselves a certain political and external liberty from the kingdom of the Messiah, by which, according to a certain autonomy and their own laws, without the dominion of any magistrate whatsoever, they were to live in total peace and an abundance of all things. This error the Savior expressly refuted in John chapter 8. Nor is this carnal liberty, as it is something that ends and closes with the term of our life, of such importance that the Son of God should have had to shed his blood for it. What is more, it would not be something proper to Christians, but common with the Gentiles; indeed, this liberty would be that of other nations rather than of Christians, since it is sufficiently established that they have very often served the harshest servitude for very many years, especially under heathen Emperors.

Fourthly, the Devil attempted the same thing in the ancient Church through the Roman Pontiff, who established the worship of God in the works of human traditions, by which God could, or rather must, be served immediately; indeed, they contended that their observance is useful for meriting grace, is valid for making satisfaction for sins, and therefore binds the conscience and is simply necessary.

From which impiety modern Papists are so far from shrinking that Bellarmine did not hesitate to write, Tom. 2, page 260, book 2, on the effects of the Sacraments, chapter 31.

1. That some ceremonies of human traditions have spiritual power: ibid. page 260.

2. That ceremonies instituted by the Church cannot be omitted without sin, even apart from scandal: that is, outside the case of scandal, and that which depends on this, that Ecclesiastical Laws (insofar as he understands human traditions) bind the conscience. Tom. 2, page 263, ibid. same chapter, p. 263, and Tom. 1, p. 1016, book 4, on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 15.

3. Those traditions and ceremonies are not indifferent things: but useful things, meritorious, and a certain part of divine worship: Tom. 2. ibid. pag. 265. 266.

Moreover, this doctrine obscures and corrupts the entire Christian religion concerning the grace of God and the righteousness of faith, or the merit of Christ apprehended by true faith. For where merit is joined to merit, namely human merit is added to the merit of Christ, there certainly as much is detracted from the merit of Christ as is arrogated to human merit.

Furthermore, this Jesuitical doctrine obscures and undermines the true worship of God and the obedience owed to his commandments. For when by human traditions some worship is established as inherent, the human mind can certainly think of nothing other than that, in performing the worship of God, some power has also been granted to itself. By this means the Devil finally drives and impels men to prefer human traditions to divine ones: then, that being occupied with their own traditions, they neglect divine ones, or rather make them completely void: in exactly the same way as Christ once said to the Pharisees: You, leaving the commandment of GOD, hold the tradition of men: you make the commandment of GOD void, that you may keep your tradition. Matt. 15. 6. & Mark 7. 9. Nowhere indeed is it read in the Scriptures that the Scribes and Pharisees prohibited the commandments of GOD from being kept: But because they taught those things which not a little hindered, or certainly suspended, the observance of the commandments of GOD, therefore they are declared by Christ to have made the commandment of GOD itself void. And indeed that this very thing happened under the Papacy is too well known to need lengthy proof. For did not the Invocation of deceased Saints constitute a primary part of divine worship under the Papacy, and thus enormously violate the religion of the first commandment? Were not Vows of perpetual chastity, impossible to be kept by human strength, named under the name and pretext of a divine commandment, and are they not still so named: and is not the destruction and despair of souls excellently promoted even by this means, with the horrible profanation of the divine name: which is what fights directly against the second commandment? Were not divine laws most foully disauthorized, when to vigils, fasts, sleeping on the ground, and austerity of life, not only the merit of congruity and condignity, but also that of supererogation was assigned? Where the true reason for the Sanctification of the Sabbath was turned into sacrilegious abuses. Was not the law of GOD, Thou shalt not kill, enormously violated, when by flagellations, prickings, and other lacerations of the body of that kind, men emaciated themselves even unto death, thus persuaded by the Pope, as if by this means they could satisfy for sins, and promise themselves eternal life? Was not the Law of GOD, Thou shalt not commit adultery, almost completely abrogated, when not only rapes or simple fornications, as they say, but even incests and most foul Sodomies were held as venial sins, so that they could easily obtain remission, provided that the Clergy abstain from the legitimate use of marriage? What shall we say about the commandment concerning honoring parents, which the Pope so defiled with his traditions, and all but completely abolished, that he did not shudder to write that it is better for a Son to trample with his feet the body of his mother who is dissuading him from a monastic Vow; than to obey her, even if she, with disheveled hair and folded hands, prostrated at the threshold of the Monastery, wishes to draw the Son away from entering the cloister: Indeed, that it is a sin for those who have once professed the Monastic religion to be present with dying parents? But not even the seventh commandment was spared, when, namely, those who entered monasteries were compelled to convert all their inheritance to the use of the Clergy, having defrauded and despoiled the legitimate heirs of that part of the inheritance which by divine and human law should have fallen to them. This is indeed to steal and to plunder: but under the specious pretext of Religion. Furthermore, if faith is not to be kept with heretics, even if sworn: if anyone helps and promotes the advantage and revenues of the Church through right or wrong, through frauds and lies, they taught that this is lawful, and they named that lie officious and necessary. Thus therefore the holiness of the eighth commandment concerning not bearing false witness has completely perished among these little saints. Now, there is no need to speak at greater length about the ninth and tenth commandments, which have long since been antiquated among the Romanists, since they expressly deny that concupiscence is a sin, as has been shown in its proper place. Thus, therefore, the truth of our second reason stands unmoved. Finally, the Jesuitical doctrine takes away the Liberty into which we have been asserted through Christ, and in which the Apostle commands us to stand. Gal. 5. 1. And they entangle consciences in an inextricable yoke, from which finally the saddest despair is accustomed to arise: or at least Doubt, by which miserable men are finally accustomed to exhale their unhappy soul without certain hope, without firm consolation. And indeed such is the force and evidence of these three reasons, that Bellarmine himself, as if forgetting himself and driven by the bite of conscience, almost revokes his former hypotheses: while in Tom. 2. page 257. He argues that his fellow confessors are in error, because they place fasts, celibacy, and austerity of life in that category of things which are immediately the worship of GOD. For these, he says, only dispose one to worship GOD. Now indeed, just as motion toward a thing is not motion in the thing: and just as the end of a thing is never one and the same with the thing itself: So these traditions cannot be the worship of GOD, since they only dispose a man to worship GOD. But about this error, more than enough in this place.

Moreover, the Libertines also pertain to the class of those who err, in the fifth place, who most foully abuse Christian Liberty to loosen the reins for the concupiscences of the flesh: and they dream that the Liberty of Christians consists in this, that it is lawful for a man, given over to his own will and license, to perpetrate what he wishes: nor is he in this part bound by any laws, whether human or divine. This most foul error sprouts from that other one, which they cherish concerning Sin, establishing that Nothing is by its nature evil and sin, and hateful to GOD: but only by the opinion of men. Concerning which madness, rather than error, we have disputed several times. There are indeed not a few even among our own people who, under the pretext of Christian Liberty, having broken the barriers of piety and all laws, think that anything is permitted to them. But we most rightly oppose to all these that Apostolic saying: 1. Petr. 2. 16. You are free, but not as having liberty as a cloak of wickedness: but as servants of GOD.

…Sixth, the Anabaptists err enormously, who invent such a Christian Liberty, by which Christians are immune from obedience to the Magistrate, laws, and civil burdens. The fruit and effect of which error was that Sedition of the Peasants, about which in the Prolegomena it was spoken. But indeed, just as the doctrine of the Gospel does not take away those things which are Caesar's, but commands to give to God the things that are God's, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar's: and even by this arrangement does not contradictorily oppose Caesar to God, but only subordinates him: So neither does it take away the Hierarchy of the political Magistrate: nor does it abrogate the Laws legitimately promulgated by the same, but rather establishes and confirms them: and consequently, it also approves the obedience owed to those laws in all things, indeed it demands it as a proper τεκμήριον of Christians: as we shall expressly show, σὺν θεῷ, below in the digression of the Article concerning civil Magistrates.

Seventhly, the Sacramentarians also depart from the path of truth in this Article, who reject as idolatrous certain Ecclesiastical rites, hitherto used freely, without any opinion of absolute necessity, or worship, or merit, and thus clearly immune from all superstition and impiety, used only for the sake of order and decorum in truly Orthodox Churches, and instead introduce into the Church certain new rites, which fight against Christian Liberty, and are indeed necessary by divine command: such as the breaking of bread in the use of the Sacrament: the giving of the same into the hands of communicants: the abrogation of altars, and the substitution of wooden tables: and the like. But since we are to have an express dispute against this μωροσοφίαν of the Calvinists concerning this question in the following next article: it does not pertain to deal with it at greater length in this place.

Finally, in this article we also add to the catalogue of those who err certain Philosophers and Hermits, who feigned such a liberty, by which Christians might possess a mind clearly free from the affections and the care of secular things. Such an ἀναισθησία, or rather μισανθρωπία, besides the fact that it was clearly feigned, is diametrically opposed to the divine Word: for it commands Christians to be affected by the calamities of our neighbor, and to rejoice with those who rejoice, and to weep with those who weep. What is more, this stupor has absolutely nothing in common with Christian liberty, such as it was defined above from the Scriptures according to all its degrees. Rightly, therefore, do we relegate it with its affections to those places of solitude, in which no place at all is left for affections: which, however, they will never and nowhere find in this visible world. We give immortal thanks to Christ our Savior and Liberator with pious veneration of soul, because He has liberated us both from those absurd men, and indeed from the yoke of Levitical Ceremonies, and especially from Pontifical traditions: and has asserted us into the true Liberty of the children of God: in which may He himself grant by his grace that we may persist strong and undaunted.

Latin:

bus adstringi, nisi divinis. Est enim, ut Propheta habet, Jehovah legislator noster: Efa. 32. 22. Et ut Jacobus Apostolus subjicit: Unus est legislator, qui potest servare & perdere: Jacob. 4. 12. Jam, quando Romanenses leges & traditiones suas Conscientiis imponunt, certè servandi & perdendi potestatem sibi vendicant, & DEUM suo jure spoliant. Quid verò inter divinas atq; humanas leges interesset amplius, si hæ non minus quàm illæ conscientias obligarent? Ita enim quævis hominum edicta divinis præceptis æquarentur: Quod impium & blasphemum.

Quatuor istis Gradibus Libertatis Christianę ritè observatis, emergit inde varius & multiplex doctrinæ hujus usus.

Nam. 1. ostendit, quâ in re consistat pax & tranquillitas Conscientiæ: nempe in solo merito Christi, qui nos redemit à manu omnium inimicorum nostrorum, & asseruit in libertatem, quâ freti exclamare possumus cum Apostolo, Rom 8 31. ad finem usque: Si DEUS pronobis, quis contra nos? Quò pertinet illud Rom. 5. 1. Justificati fide pacem habemus apud DEUM.

Deinde patet hinc, DEI donis nullo Conscientiæ scrupulo, nullaque animi perturbatione aut hæsitatione utendum: habitâ saltem ratione Gloriæ divinæ, ædificationis proximi, & nostræ salutis.

Tertiò conservat Concordiam in Ecclesia, ubi liber rituum externorum usus viget.

Quartò efficit, ut in regno Christi DEO sponte serviamus, sine ulla coactione, aut metu servili. Tandem præstat, ut liberi à jugo servitutis Pontificiæ, pacatam ac tranquillam habeamus conscientiam, circa usum rerum adiaphorarum, & indifferentium.

Quibus omnibus ita constitutis, hanc elicimus Libertatis Christianæ definitionem; quòd sit Spiritualis manumissio, acquisita Sanguine Christi, quâ credentes in ipsum a maledictione legis, à servitute peccati, à jugo Ceremoniarum Mosaicarum, & tandem ab onere traditionum humanarum; coram DEO in conscientiâ sunt liberi, ut in libertate Spiritus sive conscientia DEO serviant omnibus diebus vitæ suæ.

II. ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ

Sive ἔλεγχος falsarum opinionum de Libertate Christiana.

PUriori doctrinæ de Libertate Christianâ Diabol9 nullo non tempore insidias struxit, unum illud satagens, ut homi nes à Christo ad Mosen: ab Evangelio ad Legem: Gratia DEI ad justitiam propriam: à merito denique Christi ad propriorum operum dignitatem meritoriam avocaret & abstraheret.

Tentavit hoc tempore Christi per Pharisæos, qui justitiam coram DEO, ex operibus Legis moralis quærebant.

Deinde per Pseuda apostolos, qui Merito Christi addebant observationem legis Ceremonialis, non quidem totius, & respectu omnium partium: sed saltem ratione Sacramenti initiationis, nempe Circumcisionis, quam tanquam ad salutem necessariam urgebant. Contra quos ex professo disputarunt Apostoli, in Concilio Hierosolymitano, Act. 15. a vers. 1. usq; ad 30. & cumprimis Paulus in suis ad Romanos & Galatas Epistolis.

Tertiò per Judaeos tam veteres, quam recentiores, qui Politicam quandam, & externam libertatem, ex regno Messiae sibi pollicebantur, qua secundum αυτονομιαν quandam, & leges proprias, sine ullius alicujus Magistratus dominio, essent victuri, in summa pace, ac rerum omnium abundantia, Quem errorem Servator cap. 8. Johannis. ex professo refutavit. Neque etiam carnalis isthaec libertas, ut quae vitae nostrae termino finitur & clauditur, tanti est momenti, ut propterea Filius DEI sanguinem suum profundere debuerit. Quid? quod non Christianorum propria illa futura esset, sed cum Gentilibus communis: Imo aliarum potiùs Gentium, quàm Christianorum Libertas haec esset: quippe quo durissimam saepius servitutem per annos quàm plurimos, sub Ethnicis potissimùm Imperatoribus deservisse, satis constat.

Quartò, idem tentavit Diabolus in veteri Ecclesia per Pontificem Romanum, qui in Operibus traditionum humanarum cultum constituerunt, quo DEO immediatè serviri possit, imo debeat: imo contenderunt, quod earum observatio utilis sit ad promerendam gratiā: valeat ad satisfaciendum pro peccatis: ac proinde in conscientia obliget, & simpliciter sit necessaria.

A qua impietate usq; adeò non abhorrent moderni Pontificii, ut Bellarminus scribere non dubitaverit, Tom. 2. pag. 260. lib. 2. de effectis Sacrament. cap. 31.

1. Ceremonias aliquas traditionum humanarum, vim habere spiritualem: ibid. pag. 260.

2. Ceremonias institutas ab Ecclesia, non posse omitti sine peccato, etiam citra scandalum: id est, extra casum scandali, & quod ab hoc dependet, Leges Ecclesiasticas (quoad traditiones humanas intelligit) obligare in conscientia. Tom. 2. pag. 263. ibid. cap. eod. p. 263. & Tom. 1. p. 1016. lib. 4. de Rom. Pont. cap. 15.

3. Traditiones istas & Ceremonias, non esse res indifferentes: sed res utiles, meritorias, & partem quandam cultus divini: Tom. 2. ibid. pag. 265. 266.

Cæterùm doctrina hæc obscurat & corrumpit universam Christianam Religionem, de Gratia DEI, & de justitia fidei, sive merito Christi vera fide apprehenso. Nam ubi meritum merito conjungitur, humanum videlicet meritum, merito Christi additur: ibi certè tantùm derogatur merito Christi, quantum arrogatur humano.

Deinde hæc doctrina Esavvitica obscurat, & labefactat verum cultum DEI, & obedientiam præceptis ipsius debitam. Quando enim traditionibus humanis cultus aliquis inesse statuitur: nihil certè aliud mens humana cogitare potest, quàm in faciendo cultu Dei, sibi quoque potestatis aliquid esse concessum. Quo pacto Diabolus eò tandem adigit, & impellit homines, ut traditiones humanas divinis præferant: deinde, ut suis traditionibus occupati, divinas negligant, imò planè irritas faciant: eodem planè modò, quò Christus aliquando ad Pharisæos: Vos relinquentes præceptum DEI, tenetis traditionem hominum: irritum redditis præceptum DEI, ut traditionem vestram servetis. Matt. 15. 6. & Marci. 7. 9. Nuspiam quidem in Scripturis legitur, quòd Scribæ & Pharisæi prohibuerint, quò minùs præcepta DEI servarentur: Sed quia ea docebant, quæ præceptorum DEI observantiam non parùm impediebant, vel certè suspendebant, ideò DEI ipsius præceptum irritum fecisse à Christo perhibentur. Et sanè factum hoc ipsum sub Papatu fuisse, notius est, quàm ut prolixa probatione opus sit. Annon enim Invocatio Sanctorum defunctorum, partem primariam cultus divini sub Papatu constituit, & sic primi præcepti religionem enormiter violavit? Annon Vota castitatis perpetuæ, humanis viribus servatu impossibilia, sub nomine & præcepti divini prætextu nuncupata fuerunt, ac etiamnum nuncupantur: & vel hoc pacto animarum exitium & desperatio egregiè promovetur, cum horrenda nominis divini prophanatione: id quod cum secundo præcepto directè pugnat? Annon leges divinæ sædissimè sunt exautoratæ, quando vigiliis, jejuniis, chameuniis, & asperitati vitæ non modò meritum congrui, & condigni, sed & supererogationis fuit assignatum? Ubi vera ratio Sanctificationis Sabbati, in abusus sacrilegos conversa fuit. Annon lex DEI, Non occides, enormiter violata, quando flagellationibus, compunctionibus, & id genus aliis corporis lacerationibus, homines ad mortem usque se emacerarunt, sic persuasi à Pontifice, ac si hoc pacto pro peccatis satisfacere, & vitam æternã prometeri possent? An non Lex DEI, Non mœchaberis, penitùs fermè abrogata, cùm non stupra modò sive simplices, ut loquuntur, scortationes, sed incestus etiam, & Sodomiæ fœdissimæ pro peccatis venialibus ita sunt habitæ, ut facilè remissionem impetrare possint, dummodò à legitimo conjugii usu Clerici abstineant? Quid de præcepto de honorandis parentibus dicamus, quod traditionibus suis Pontifex adeò conspurcavit, ac tantùm non planè sustulit, ut scribere non exhorresceret, satius esse, Filium corpus matris dissuadentis Votũ monasticum, pedibus calcare; quàm ei obtemperare, si maximè passis crinibus, & manibus plicatis, ad Monasterij limen prostrata, Filium ab ingressu cœnobij abstrahere velit: Imò nefas esse parentibus morituris adesse eos, qui semel religionem Monasticam sunt professi? Sed ne septimo quidem præcepto parsum fuit, quando nimirùm ii, qui monasteria ingressi sunt, coacti fuerunt omnem hæreditatem suam in usum Clericorum convertere, defraudatis ac spoliatis legitimis hæredibus, ea hæreditatis parte, quæ jure divino ac humano ipsis cedere debuisset. Hoc nimirum est furari, & praedari: sed sub specioso Religionis praetextu. Porro si haereticis fides non servetur, etiam jurata: siquis Ecclesiae commodum & reditus per fas nefasque, per fraudes & mendacia juvet ac promoveat, licitum id esse, tradiderunt, illudque mendacium nominarunt officiofum & necessarium. Sic ergo octavi praecepti Sanctitas de non dicendo falso testimonio, penitus apud istos Sanctulos exolevit. Jam de nono ac decimo praeceptis jampridem apud Romanenses antiquatis, nihil attinet prolixius verba facere, cum diserte negent concupiscentiam esse peccatum, uti suo loco ostensum. Sic Ergo secundae nostrae, rationi sua immota constat veritas. Tandem doctrina Esauvitica tollit Libertatem, in quam per Christum asserti sumus, & in qua standum esse, praecipit Apostolus. Gal. 5. 1. & inextricabili jugo conscientias implicati Unde tandem tristissima desperatio oriri solet: vel saltem Dubitatio, qua miseri homines tandem, sine certa spe, sine consolatione firma, infelicem animam exhalare solent. Et profecto tanta est vis, & evidentia trium istarum rationum, ut Bellarminus ipse sui quasi oblitus, & conscientiae morsu adactus, priores suas hypotheses quasi revocet: dum Tom. 2. pag. 257. Confessionis suae socios falsitatis arguit, quod jejunia, coelibatum, vitae asperitatem, in eo rerum genere ponant, quae immediate sunt cultus DEI. Nam haec, inquit, ad colendum DEUM tantum disponunt. Jam vero, sicut motus ad rem, non est motus in re: & sicut finis rei, cum reipsa nunquam unum atque idem est: Ita traditiones istae cultus DEI esse nequeunt, cum ad colendum DEUM duntaxat hominem disponant. Verum de errore isto, hoc loco plus satis.

Pertinent autem ad errantium classem, quinto loco, etiam Libertini, qui Libertate Christiana foedissime abutuntur, ad laxandu frena carnis concupiscentiis: & somniant, Libertatem Christianoru in eo positam esse, ut homini suae voluntati ac licentiae tradito, fas sit perpetrare quae velit: neq, hac in parte ullis legibus sive humanis sive divinis sit adstrictus. Pullulat a foedissimus iste error, ex altero illo, quem de Peccato fovent, statuentes, Nihil natura sua esse malum & peccatum, DEOq exosum: sed tantum opinione hominum. De quo furore magis, quam errore aliquoties disputavimus. Sunt vero ex nostris quoque hominibus haud pauci, qui sub praetextu Libertatis Christianae, ruptis pietatis, & legum omnium repagulis, quidvis sibi licere arbitrantur. Rectissime autem istis omnibus obvertimus illud Apostolicum: 1. Petr. 2. 16. Estis liberi, sed non veluti nequitiae velamen habentes libertatem: sed ut servi DEI.

Sexto enormiter errant Anabaptistae, qui talem Libertatem Christianam commini scuntur, qua Christiani immunes sint ab obedientia Magistratus, legum & onerum civiliu. Cujus erroris fructus & effectus fuit Seditio illa Rusticorum, de qua in Prolegomenis dictum. Atqui verò, sicut doctrina Evangelii non tollit ea, quæ sunt Cæsaris, sed jubet dare Deo, quæ Dei sunt, & Cæsari, quæ Cæsaris sunt: & vel hoc pacto Cæsarem Deo non contradictoriè opponit: sed tantùm subordinat: Ita neque tollit Hierarchiam Magistrat˥ politici: neque Leges ab eodem legitimè promulgatas abrogat, sed stabilit potiùs ac confirmat: & per consequens, obedientiam quoque legibus illis debitam, per omnia approbat, imò tanquam proprium Christianorum τεκμήριον exigit: uti infra in diexodo Articuli de Magistratibus civilibus ex professo, σὺν θεῷ, ostendemus.

Septimò à veritatis tramitte hoc in Articulo recedunt etiam Sacramentarii, qui ritus quosdam Ecclesiasticos, liberè hactenus, sine ullâ vel necessitatis absolutæ, vel cult˥, vel me riti opinione, & sic ab omni superstitione & impietate planè immunes, tantùm ordinis, & decori causâ in Ecclesiis verè Orthodoxis usu receptos, tanquam idolatricos rejiciunt, & contra novos quosdam, cum Libertate Christianâ pugnantes, & quidem mandato divino necessarios ritus, in Ecclesiam invehunt: ut Fractionem panis in usu Sacramenti: porrectionem ejusdem in manus communicantiũ: abrogationem altarium, & substitutionem mensarum lignearum: & similes. Verùm cùm de hac quæstione in subsequéte articulo proximo, ex professò futura nobis sit disputatio, contra istam Calvinianorum μωροσοφίαν: pluribus de eâ hoc loco agere, haud attinet.

Tandem errantium Catalogo, hoc in articulo adscribimus etiam quosdam Philosophos & Eremitas, qui talam libertatem fingebant, quâ Christiani ab affectibus, & curâ rerũ secularium, mentem gerant planè liberam. Qualis certè ἀναισθησία, vel potiùs μισανθρωπία, præterquàm quod simulata planè fuit, Verbo divino è diametro repugnat: quippe quod proximi nostri calamitatibus Christianos affici, eosdemq́; cum gaudentibus gaudere, cum lugentibus autem lugere, jubet. Quid quòd cum Christiana libertate, qualis suprà ex Scripturis secundum omnes suos gradus definita fuit, stupor iste nihil prorsus commune habet. Rectè ergò eum cum suis affectis ad ea solitudinum loca relegamus, in quibus affectibus nullus planè locus relinquitur: qualia tamén in mundo isto adspectabili, nunquàm & nuspiam invenient. Nos Christo Servatori & Liberatori nostro unico gratias piâ animi veneratione agimus immortales, quòd tùm ab absurdis istis hominibus, tùm verò à jugo Ceremoniarum Leviticarum, cumprimis traditionum Pontificiarum liberavit: inq́; veram Libertatem filiorum Dei asseruit: in quâ ut persistamus fortes & imperterriti, faxit ipse suâ gratiâ.


### Use of the doctrine of Christian Liberty: Amen

AMEN.

Latin:

AMEN.


## 28 On Adiaphora or Ceremonies or human Traditions in the Church

Concerning Adiaphora or Ceremonies or human Traditions in the Church.

OIKONOMIA of the future Treatise.

That which a shadow is with respect to a body, that Ceremonies and external rites are with respect to true divine worship, whoever said it among the ancients, did not say it badly. For as a shadow happens to a body from an external light, and is not any part of it: so ceremonies accrue to Religion and worship from the outside, not being inherent by their own nature. Now, just as when the Sun is established on the Horizon, and is very far removed either by rising or setting, the greatest shadows are cast by bodies: so it is accustomed to happen for the most part in the matter of Ceremonies.

But for the most part in newly constituted Churches, where the doctrine of truth has not yet taken root: or even in those same ones deflecting toward the sunset, where the purity of religion begins to languish and totter, the greatest quarrels and dissensions are accustomed to arise and be stirred up concerning Ceremonies. Nay, if we consider the matter a little more carefully, certainly ceremonies and the worship of GOD seem to behave toward each other like certain balances, of which when one is moved upward, the other is necessarily depressed to the bottom; so that for the most part it happens that divine worship is in the greatest danger in those places where the most effort is spent on Ceremonies.

But in truth, although these things are so, there are nevertheless other reasons, both many in number and grave in evidence, which make the Treatise on the Adiaphoric matter very necessary. There is indeed no danger to the body from a shadow: but there is very much to Religion from ceremonies. And although the contentions which arise concerning rites in the Church are, and are called, schisms, not heresies: yet that very thing also is accustomed to do almost as much damage to Churches as heresies themselves: Nay, indeed, they usually degenerate into heresies in the end. The entire history of both the ancient and the more recent Church gives assurance to this assertion. Certainly, that former quarrel and contention between the Eastern and Western Church concerning the time of celebrating Easter provided the handle and occasion for that most sad divorce by which the Eastern Church fell away from the Western, both in ceremonies and in the heads of Christian doctrine; indeed, it erupted to such a point that at length the Western Church degenerated entirely into the Synagogue of the Roman Antichrist. Within the memory of our fathers, in the time of our B. LUTHER, the dissension concerning the Elevation of the Bread in the administration of the Sacrament, the total abrogation of which Carlostadius urged without reason, and thus too impetuously arrogating to himself mastery and dominion over the tender Church, which had scarcely been purged of the Pontifical leaven, finally erupted into heresy.

Latin:

De Adiaphoris sive Ceremoniis aut Traditionibus humanis in Ecclesia.

OIKONOMIA futurae Tractationis.

QUod respectu corporis est umbra, id respectu veri cultus divini esse Ceremonias, & ritus externos, no male dixit, ex veteribus, quisquis dixit. Nam ut corpori ab externo lumine umbra accidit, neq; est ej9 pars aliqua: ita Religioni, & cultui forinsecus accedunt, non ex sua natura insut ceremoniae. Jam, quemadmodum Sole in Horizonte constituto, & vel ortu, vel occasu quam longissime dissito, maximae umbrae a corporibus projiciuntur: ita fieri solet in Ceremoniarum negotio utplurimum.

Plerumq; autem in recens constitutis Ecclesiis, ubi veritatis doctrina nondum radices egit: vel etiam iisdem ad occasum deflectentibus, ubi languescere, & nutare incipit religionis puritas, maximae oriri, & agitari solent de Ceremoniis rixae & dissensiones. Quin imo, si paulo pensiculatius rem considerem9, certe ceremoniae & cultus DEI ad se mutuo, tanqua bilances quaedam sese habere videntur, quarum cum altera sursum agitur, altera ad imum necessario deprimitur; ita ut plerunq; iis in locis cultum divinum maxime periclitari contingat, ubi de Ceremoniis plurimum laboratur.

Verum enim vero, quamvis haec ita se habeant, rationes tamen sunt aliae, & numero multae, & evidentia graves, quae Tractationem materiae Adiaphoricae perquam faciunt necessaria. Corpori quidem ab umbra nihil est periculi: Religioni vero a ceremoniis quamplurimum. Et quamvis Schismata sint, & dicantur, non haereses, quae de ritibus in Ecclesia oriuntur contentiones: illa tamen ipsa quoq; tantunde ferme Ecclesiis damni dare solet: quantu ipsae haereses: Imo vero tandem in haereses pleruq; degenerant. Fidem assertioni facit universa tu veteris, tum recentioris Ecclesiae historia. Olim certe rixa illa & contentio, inter Orientale & Occidentale Ecclesia, de tempore celebrandi Pascha, ansam & occasionem tristissimo illi divortio praebuit, quo Orientalis Ecclesia, ab Occidentali, qua ceremonias, qua doctrinae Christianae capita, defecit: imo eo erupit, ut tandem Ecclesia Occidentalis in Synagogam Antichristi Romani plane degeneraret. Patrum nostrorum memoria, tempore B. LUTHERI nostri, dissensio de Elevatione Panis, in administratione Sacramenti, cujus omnimodam abrogationem Carolostadius sine ratione urgebat, & sic magisterium sibi & dominatum in Ecclesiam tenellam, & vix a fermento Pontificio repurgatam, impetuose nimis sibi arrogans, erupit tandem in haeresin


### Prolegomena to the Article on Adiaphora

Zwinglian and Sacramentarian, which even today disturbs and afflicts the Church of GOD. A little later, the Interimistic σύζηξις degenerated into the most sorrowful errors of the Antinomians, Majorists, Synergists, and others, of whom we have expressly treated in our Commentary on the Formula of Concord. What a tragedy, with what effort and exertion, the Sacramentarian Spirit has stirred up through the Duchy of Anhalt, through Hesse, through our Misnia, concerning Exorcism, concerning the use of images and altars, concerning figured and organ music, concerning priestly vestments, concerning the form of the hosts or Oblations, concerning the breaking of bread, and other things of that kind; and that it is now even striving to stir it up in certain places of the Electoral March, and under the pretext of ἀδιαφορίας to encrust Calvinism itself, even if indirectly, is, alas, better known than that there should be need of a long speech.

Therefore, this Adiaphoristic material will have to be treated the more carefully, the more we notice that the weight for asserting a purer Religion is placed upon it.

There is added another manifold use, which redounds to the faithful from this doctrine, but a purer one. For 1. it obtains much weight for pacifying consciences and removing superstitions: since, on the contrary, where the true nature and true use of adiaphora is ignored, there is no rest of conscience, no end to superstitions: but perpetual doubt whether it is permitted to use these or those rites, while maintaining piety and religion.

Next, Error concerning this matter causes things which are clean in themselves to be unclean to us. Rom. 14. 14. I know, that there is nothing unclean, except to him who considers it to be unclean.

Finally, ignorance of this matter produces contempt of GOD and despair. For whoever is entangled in such doubt concerning the use of adiaphora, wherever they turn, they feel the sting of Conscience present everywhere: and from that, little by little, they are swept away either into the abyss of despair or into contempt of GOD and security, and finally cast off all fear of GOD.

Moreover, the Treatment of this matter, such as it occurs in Philip, is bipartite. For in the beginning he proposes the distinction to be observed between traditions or ceremonies introduced into the Church by human authority: namely, that some make for πρὸς τάξιν καὶ εὐσχημοσύνην: but others were instituted partly by superstition, partly by avarice, partly by tyrannical counsels: which fight diametrically against the precepts of GOD. Through the consideration of the latter traditions, our Author runs off toward the end of this Article to the treatment of the matter of the Mortification of the Flesh, both that Hypocritical and Pharisaical kind, such as is handed down even today in the Papacy; and the true kind, commanded by GOD, which is proper to Christians. The other part of the Philippean treatment proposes and explains three rules to be observed concerning adiaphora. THE FIRST is: It is necessary to obey GOD rather than men. Therefore all sin who obey laws or edicts which command to act against the mandates of GOD, whether those laws have been proposed by Bishops, or by Kings, or by other Magistrates, or by devils. The second rule: One must oppose by teaching those Ceremonies to which pernicious errors are attached: such as are 1. the opinion of merit. 2. the opinion of divine worship. 3. the persuasion of perfection: 4. the opinion of necessity: 5. κακοζηλία: 6. the power of establishing traditions at will: 7. the violent defense of those traditions. The third rule: Ceremonies in reformed Churches which make for order, decorum, and edification are to be kept: but in such a way that the opinion of righteousness, worship, or necessity, or the other errors already enumerated, is not added.

And such indeed is the Philippean Treatment, expressly opposed to the impiety of the Papists, and if you look at the kind itself, sufficiently orthodox: But if you look at the controversies of the present century, too concise and imperfect. For it is manifest that those things which are disputed today concerning the use of certain adiaphorous things in Churches long since purged from the Papal leaven consist of an exposition of very many practical questions.

We therefore divide our future Treatment into three distinct chapters: the first two θετικά: the third: ἀνασκευαστικόν. For the first will show certain and infallible κριτήρια, from which a judgment can and ought to be made concerning the nature and proper affection, both internal and external, of adiaphorous things: how likewise they change their adiaphorous nature from an Accident. The second will explain the Christian practice itself, which ought to be holily observed concerning the right use of adiaphorous things, which is in every way consistent with Christian liberty: and it will declare the same with illustrious examples taken from the present state of affairs and the Church. The third and last will examine errors fighting against the nature and true use of adiaphorous things: and in particular it will touch upon both the μωροσοφίαν and Hypocritical Holiness of the Sacramentarians in this part: and the ἀθεότητα and tyranny of the Romanists. To this tripartite Treatment, following the example of Philip, we shall append, as if in the place of a conclusion, καὶ ἐν προσθήκης μέρει, a certain brief discourse on the Mortification of the flesh. May the Father of lights himself, from whom every good thing descends, according to his accustomed goodness, so illuminate our minds: govern all our affections: direct our meditations, that we may bring forth into the midst, both with heart and mouth, those things which he himself willed that we should learn according to our capacity, to the glory of his name, the peace and benefit of the Church: and finally to our own edification and salvation.

AMEN.

Latin:

Zwinglianam & Sacramentariam, quæ hodieque Ecclesiam DEIturbat, & affligit. Paulò post σύζηξις Interimistica degeneravit in tristissimos errores Antinomorum, Majoristarum, Synergistarum, & aliorum, de quibus in Commentario nostro ad Formulam Concordiæ ex professo egimus. Quàm tragœdiam, quanto conatu & molimine, Spiritus Sacramentarius per ducatum Anhaltinum, per Hafsiam, per Misniam nostram, de Exorcismo, de usu imaginum & altarium, de cantu figurali, & organico, de vestibus Sacerdotalibus, de formâ hostiarum, sive Oblatarum, de fractione panis, deq; id genus rebus aliis excitavit; & jam jam in quibusdam locis Electoralis Marchiæ excitare, & sub ἀδιαφορίας prætextu, ipsissimum Calvinismum, vel per indirectum incrustare studeat, notius prohdolor est, quàm ut longâ oratione opus sit.

Proinde tantò accuratius hæc tractanda erit materia Adiaphorica, quantò plus momenti ad asserendam puriorem Religionem, in eâ positum esse animadvertimus.

Accedit usus multiplex alius, qui ex doctrina hac, sed puriore, ad fideles redundat. Nam 1. ad pacificandas conscientias, & tollendas superstitiones, momenti plurimùm obtinet: cùm ècontra, ubi vera adiaphororum natura, verusq; usus ignoratur, ibi nulla sit conscientiæ quies, nullus superstitionum finis: sed perpetua dubitatio, an his, vel illis ritibus, salva pietate & religione uti liceat.

Deinde Error circa hanc materiam facit, ut quæ per se munda sunt, nobis sint immunda. Rom. 14. 14. Scio, quod nihil immundum sit, nisi illi, qui existimat immundum esse.

Tandem parit materiæ hujus ignoratio contemtum DEI, & desperationem. Nam quicunq; tali dubitatione de usu adiaphororum sunt impliciti, illi quocunq; se vertant, præsentem ubiq; Conscientiæ morsum sentiunt: & ex eo paulatim vel in disperationis abyssum, vel in contemtum DEI, & securitatem abripiuntur, omnemq; tandem DEI timorem abjiciunt.

Cæterùm Tractatio hujus materiæ, qualis quidem apud Philippū occurrit, est bipartita. Initiò enim proponit discrimen, observandum inter traditiones sive ceremonias, humana autoritate in Ecclesiam introductas: quòd nimirùm quædam faciant πρὸς τάξιν καὶ εὐσχημοσύνην: Aliæ verò sint institutæ partim superstitione, partim avaritia, partim consiliis tyrannicis: quæ cum præceptis DEI è diametro pugnent. Quartum posteriorum traditionum consideratione, Autor noster excurrit sub finem Articuli hujus, ad tractationem materiæ de Mortificatione Carnis, tùm Hypocritica illa, & Pharisaica, qualis hodieque in Papatu traditur: tùm vera & à DEO præcepta, quæ Christianorum est propria. Altera tractationis Philippeæ pars, tres proponit, & explicat regulas, circa adiaphora observandas. PRIMA est: Oportet DEO magis obedire, quàm hominibus. Ergo peccant omnes, qui obtemperant legibus, aut edictis, quæ jubent facere contra mandata DEI, sive leges illæ ab Episcopis, sive à Regibus, sive aliis Magistratibus, sive à diabolis propositæ sint. Secunda regula: Adversandum est docendo illis Ceremoniis, quibus perniciosi errores affuuntur: quales sunt 1. opinio meriti. 2. opinio cultus divini. 3. persuasio perfectionis: 4. opinio necessitatis: 5. κακοζηλία: 6. potestas pro lubitu condendi traditiones: 7. violenta traditionum istarum defensio. Tertia regula: Ceremoniæ in Ecclesiis reformatis, quæ faciunt ad ordinem, decorum & ædificationem sunt servandæ: sed ita, ne addatur opinio justitiæ, cultus aut necessitatis, aut cæteri errores jam enumerati.

Et talis quidem est Tractatio Philippéa, Pontificiorum impietati, ex professo opposita, & si genus ipsum spectes, satis orthodoxa: Verùm si præsentis seculi controversias, nimis concisa, & imperfecta. Nam quæ de usu rerum quarundam adiaphorarum in Ecclesiis à fermento Pontificio jampridem repurgatis hactenus observato, hodiè disputantur, ea plurimarum quæstionum practicarum diexodo constare, manifestum est.

Partimur ergò futuram nostram Tractationem in tria distincta capita: duo priora θετικὰ: tertium: ἀνασκευαστικόν. Primum enim certa & infallibilia monstrabit κριτήρια, ex quibus de natura, & propria affectione, tàm interna, & externa rerum adiaphorarum, fieri possit & debeat judicium: quomodo item eæ ex Accidenti suam naturam adiaphoricam mutent. Alterum praxin ipsam Christianam expediet, quæ circa rectum, & libertati Christianæ ex omni parte congruum Rerũ adiaphorarú usum, sanctè observari debeat: eandemque exemplis illustribus è præsenti rerum, & Ecclesiæ statu petitis, declarabit. Tertium ac postremum errores pugnantes cum natura, & vero usu rerum adiaphorarum examinabit: in specie autem tum Sacramentariorum hac in parte μωροσοφίαν, & Hypocriticam Sanctitatem: tum Romanensium ἀθεότητα & tyrannidem perstringet. Cui tripartitæ Tractationi, exemplo Philippi, subjiciemus coronidis quasi loco, καὶ ἐν προσθήκης μέρει, brevem quemdam discursum, de Mortificatione carnis. Ipse pater luminum, à quo descendit omne bonum, pro assueta sua bonitate, ita mentes nostras illustret: affectus omnes regat: meditationes nostras dirigat, ut quæ pro modulo nostro nos addiscere ipse voluit, ea & corde & ore in mediũ proferamus, ad nominis sui gloriam, Ecclesiæ pacem ac emolumentum: nostram denique ædificationem & salutem.

AMEN.
