### Prolegomena to the Article on Adiaphora: On the nature and proper affection of things Adiaphoral

The Church has borrowed the name of Adiaphora from the schools of the philosophers. For just as these, as Suidas testifies, denoted by the term Adiaphora τὰ μέσα, that is, those things whose use is placed in the middle, and which are so constituted that we can use them either well or badly: and as those well used have some importance for adorning, indeed, but not for conferring civil happiness: So the schools of the Theologians have been accustomed to designate with this appellation those rites whose condition is the same in the business of heavenly salvation. The Latins, as Tully testifies in book 3 of De Finibus, rendered the Greek term with the name of Indifferent things: which the schools of the Theologians are also accustomed to use.

Therefore, those businesses, things, and ordinances are called Adiaphora, whose observance or use is neither commanded nor forbidden by God in the New Testament, and therefore is in itself neither good nor bad, nor does it affect the conscience of the user or the abstainer, in the matter of salvation, in the direction of either commendation or hatred before GOD: but for the sake of good order and decorum, it is introduced into the Church, and by the Church itself, in such a way that, excepting the vice of circumstance and external accident, as well as immoderate excess, it is always free to the pious, and in both directions (of observance or omission or abstinence) is arbitrary.

Such indifferent things are given in the common life of men, regarding food, drink, marriage, celibacy, riches, poverty, clothing of this or that color, civil contracts: thus the Apostle himself defining it, Rom. 14. 6. He who eats, eats to the Lord: for he gives thanks to GOD: And he who does not eat, does not eat to the Lord, and gives thanks to GOD. Thus 1 Cor. 7. 24 and 34. The Apostle holds celibacy and marriage as indifferent things; provided that the purity of both remains. And Coloss. 2. 16. he brings in this general aphorism: Let no one judge you in food and drink. But concerning these, there is no controversy in this place: But concerning those whose use has at some time obtained in the Church.

Therefore, what the proper nature and affection of these may be is sought first of all. Now, indeed, from the very etymology and proper signification of the word in general, it is clear that the nature of indifferent things is such that the use of the same is neither commanded to a Christian, nor forbidden; nor is it good, nor bad in itself; nor is it either useful or harmful to the user or the abstainer in the business of salvation: but it is entirely free, indifferent, and middle, and in the cause of salvation, as much as can be said, without quality.

Such indifferent things in Orthodox Churches, and those rightly purged from the Papal leaven, are the principal ones: Holidays, distinctions of times, certain distinctions of garments, foods, times, even of the Ministers of the Church, sacred songs and readings: Figural song: Musical organ: breaking of bread: likewise the use of unleavened and circular bread in the Eucharistic Sacrament: Exorcism: Immersion or sprinkling of the infant to be baptized: The employment of godparents: The ringing of bells: and other similar things.

Concerning this kind of thing, the rule handed down by the Augsburg Confession, article 15, must be held: Those rites are to be observed which can be observed without sin. Which is expressed more explicitly in the Scholias thus: As long as indifferent things are such, that is, are left in middle use and indifferently, they can be observed or neglected without injury to conscience and Christian liberty. By this rule those false opinions are exterminated, by which the nature of true indifferent things is corrupted: Such as are, when 1. either the Law of necessity, 2. or the opinion of worship, 3. or the presumption of merit, is attached to the observance of these things. And indeed, lest one sin from any part of these three excesses, there will be need of great caution and prudence. But then this caution is rightly applied, if the ways in which those three excesses can be committed are diligently observed.

Therefore, first, the Law of necessity is attached to indifferent things in two ways. 1. If they are made necessary from indifferent things. 2. If indifferent things are made from necessary ones. Concerning the former, in the time of Paul, the false brothers who had crept in sinned, who, by defending the necessity of Circumcision, were placing a yoke upon Christian Liberty. To whom the Apostle did not yield in subjection even for an hour, Gal. 2. 5 and 6, and for this very reason did not want Titus to be circumcised. Today, the Papists also sin enormously in this part, attaching necessity to those things of which they can bring forward neither command nor example from the Scriptures: which is sufficiently manifest from the Papal traditions of fasts, the distinction of foods, holidays, and similar things used. Nor do the Sacramentarians suffer any less gross dizziness in this first excess, urging the fermentation of the Eucharistic bread also with an inevitable necessity: of which they can give no evident reason from the Scriptures.

Concerning the latter member of this first excess, those sinned who, in the time of the Apostles, referred many things to the census and number of indifferent things which were in themselves illicit and clearly forbidden by the Word of GOD. In which number was fornication, forbidden by God, Deut. 23. 17, so that this thing provided an opportunity for the Apostles to forbid that wickedness with a new interdict, Acts 15. 20. To which perhaps Polygamy can also be referred, forbidden by GOD in the first institution of marriage: but introduced by the Jews as free: and for this very reason forbidden and abrogated again by Christ the Savior, Gen. 2. 21, Matt. 9. 8. In this very way the Sacramentarians also impinge, establishing that in the defect of the Sacramental elements others can be substituted, which, with the elements sanctioned by Christ, and therefore simply immutable, obtain only a certain analogical conformity. To which fabrications the authority of Scripture must be opposed: Gal. 5, 1. Stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made you free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage. And Ezech. 20, 19. Walk in my statutes, and keep my judgments, and do them.

The second excess, namely the opinion of worship, in the category of indifferent things, is utterly intolerable. For which reason those things are called by the Apostle the elements of the world, Gal. 4.3, Col. 2.8, and indeed weak and beggarly elements, Gal. 4.9, nay even branded with the infamous title of human traditions, ἐθελοθρησκείας Col. 2. 8, 21, & 23, of bondage, Gal. 4.9, of death and destruction, Col. 2. 20 & 22, nay even of doctrines of devils, 1 Tim. 4.1, if they wish to arrogate to themselves any right or authority in divine worship. Nay, in the very terms, as they say, they are repudiated by Christ the Savior, with this authentic proclamation: In vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men, Matt. 15.9. Therefore, to place the matter of divine worship, or any part of such worship, in these things would be too impious.

The third excess, namely the opinion of merit, is the most foul of all: as if by the observance of indifferent and neutral things, men might obtain expiation for both guilt and punishment. Truly, no man is justified before God by the works of any law, however holy and promulgated by God himself, not only forensic or ceremonial, but not even moral: but by faith alone: Gal. 3.16. How great, therefore, is this power of darkness, which can persuade anyone that from the works of some human law and tradition, whether of a Pope, or a Council, or another man, an opinion of merit in the cause of salvation can be had?

And such indeed is the external condition of indifferent things, by which their nature is established to be free 1. from all simple and absolute necessity, 2. from worship that is in itself and immediately pleasing to God, and 3. from any reason of merit.

Furthermore, to the nature of indifferent things also pertains τὸ μέσον καὶ τὸ ἄποιον, that is, the indifferent. But τὸ μέσον is not the ethical, which is proper to virtue, which is a mean between vices reduced on both sides, but the physical, whose nature stands indifferently toward the nature of good or evil. With this mean standing, it follows of its own accord that it is τὸ ἄποιον, indifferent, whereby it happens that he who either uses or does not use these things is affected in no part either of neglect or of amendment.

The Apostle himself confirms this regarding one certain indifferent species, namely food: but in such a way that a judgment can be made from it concerning the whole genus of these things: saying, Food does not commend us: for neither if we eat shall we abound (as if rendered better), nor if we do not eat shall we be worse. 1 Cor. 8.8. Spiridion, Bishop of Cyprus, taught this practice to a certain guest coming to him on a day of fasting. For when, in the lack of other food, he had set before him meat which he had stored away, which the guest denied he could eat on that day because he was a Christian, Spiridion replied that for this very reason it is fitting to eat it, because you are a Christian. Warned by this saying, the guest understood that he was in no way defiled by the use of a middle thing. And this is the second πάθος of indifferent things.

Thirdly, to the nature of indifferent things it is also required that they be ecclesiastical rites, that is, either introduced or at least approved by the Church itself. Therefore, episcopal power has no standing in Evangelical churches to force the form of its own traditions upon them, not even by pretending the Chair in which bishops sit, as our blessed LUTHER rightly judged. Tom. 3. Ien. p. 5. 23. For those mandates of traditions are burdensome, which cannot be kept without sin. In those things, indeed, which are of divine right, consciences must necessarily obey legitimate pastors, according to that: He who hears you, hears me: Luke 10.16. And, The lips of the priest keep knowledge: and they shall seek the law from his mouth: for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts. Mal. 2.7. But this has nothing to do with those masked bishops of the Roman curia in the present matter. Nor is there any reason for anyone to fear that by this pact the authority of the Evangelical Ministry will be diminished, or that public assemblies are to be dissolved, for the retaining of which those solemn rites are as it were a certain bond. For that is finally the true authority of the Ministry, and is asserted as safe and sound, which keeps itself within the limits of divine ordination, and does not invade another's power in burdening consciences and in fixing and unfixing laws. Thus, whatever has God as its author serves to gather assemblies: whatever is forced to be kept by consciences through force and tyranny provides an occasion for dissolving the same. Thus, by equal reason, a conscience sins and sins gravely if it does not obey the laws of the civil Magistrate when rightly constituted: but it does not sin if it rejects and despises the traditions of the Pope and bishops as if they were binding on the conscience. The reason for the diversity is manifest, because God himself has seriously commanded that we be subject to the political order in external matters, not only for wrath, but also for conscience' sake, Rom. 13.5. But in the Church, power is granted to no man to bind consciences with laws of necessity: in indifferent things, Col. 2.16, Gal. 5.1.

Fourthly, regarding this first question, it is also to be observed that indifferent things sometimes change their nature and cease to be what they were: First, at the time of giving a confession, where for the sake of tranquility and asserting liberty, that is tolerated which by its own nature could entirely bear abrogation. Then, with respect to particular churches, just as the nature of middle things is clearly dissimilar because of the diverse opinions of diverse peoples concerning these things. An example of which is had in the epistle to the Corinthians; where he orders men to pray in sacred assemblies with heads uncovered; but women with heads covered, 1 Cor. 11.4. Which rite among other nations is different and otherwise. Finally, with respect to the weak and the enemies of the truth, where the free observance of indifferent things passes into a necessary one: both so that we may not offend the weak, and so that we may not, for the sake of the enemies of the truth, abandon, or rather betray, the Christian liberty into which we have been set free through Christ: concerning which matter we shall dispute expressly in question or chapter 2. Contenting ourselves at this point with the example of Circumcision, we shall illustrate the matter. It had, according to the diversity of times and poand a triple respect of peoples. The first indeed had regard to the reason of absolute necessity, as the Sacrament of the initiation of the old people: Gen. 17. 14. Taken in this respect, it does not fall under the consideration of this Article. But then it is considered according to that nature which it obtained under the abrogation of the Old, and the beginning of the New Testament, Christ the Savior, the end and fulfiller of the Law, having already been brought to light. At this time circumcision obtained for some time an adiaphorous nature, so that it could be freely observed by the weaker and for the sake of the weak brethren, recently brought to the bosom of the Church of the New Testament: and again, it could be freely neglected and omitted by the stronger, and those more correctly informed about the liberty of the New Testament: provided that this were done without offense to the weak. Just as indeed the Apostle, for the sake of the latter, caused Timothy to be circumcised: Acts 16. 3. But finally, after that infirmity of the brethren was removed by the preaching of the Gospel: and the Jews themselves were gathered to the Church of the New Testament, and were more correctly taught concerning Evangelical Liberty: there circumcision took on a third nature, namely, that it no longer had the character of a thing either necessary to be observed, or adiaphorous, or indifferent, but simply prohibited and abrogated, nor was it right for anyone to recall it into use. Looking to which, the Apostle, for the sake of false brethren, simply refused to have Titus circumcised, who were urging circumcision as still necessary to be observed: lest, clearly, by this act, Evangelical Liberty should in any way be endangered. Tit. 2. 3.

it comes to be granted, for whom it is no offense, whether in a cloak, or in a mantle, or in a toga, that the Minister of the Church should come dressed for the proclamation of the word and the dispensation of the Sacraments.

Fifthly and lastly: Although this is the nature of adiaphora, that they are of themselves free to be observed, and neither make him who uses them better, nor him who does not use them worse, much less can they bind the conscience on either side: yet there is an excellent use of them in the business of Religion and for the sake of piety, if only it contains itself within those bounds which that triple end constitutes, for the sake of which adiaphora are introduced and received into the Church. The first is, that they may serve for edification, πρὸς ὀικοδομήν. The second, that they may assist good order, πρὸς τάξιν. The third, that they may preserve the praise of decency, πρὸς εὐσχημοσύνην. Which ends the Apostle himself defined, having established these two rules: I. Let all things be done for edification. II. Let all things be done decently and in order, 1 Cor. 14. 26 & 40.

Moreover, adiaphorous rites attain those three ends only then: 1. If they are lawful and convenient: by which reason edification is served. 2. If they are useful and moderate: by which pact εὐτάξια or good order is aided. 3. If they are elegant and honest: by which way ornament and decorum are most beautifully conducted. Whence three requirements of Adiaphorous rites, if only they are truly such, and ought to be, will now shine forth.

The first of these (namely, that they be lawful) the holiness of Religion itself persuades: in which, because external rites are as it were certain incitements and fuel of piety, by which the minds of men are prepared, instructed, and kindled for the devout hearing of the word and for other exercises of piety: in these, indeed, nothing illicit or inconvenient can find a place. In which part the rusticity of those men is deservedly reproved. The second requirement (namely, that they be useful and moderate) order itself demands. Now indeed ceremonies are useful, says Athanasius; but with the knowledge of truth, and with moderation. Certainly in natural things, for all things πᾶν τὸ πολὺ τῇ Φύσει πολέμιον, as Hippocrates testifies in his Aphorisms: How much more will that have a place in the business of religion, in which it happens not only that ardent devotion, distracted by the delay of impatience, easily fades away: but men, being occupied about τὰ πάρεργα, have less care for τῶν ἔργων themselves. God himself, Augustine is the witness, Epist. 118, has bound [the Church] with sacraments most few in number, most easy in observation, most excellent in signification, by the fellowship of the new people. But the same man complains that in his time the multitude of ceremonies had already so prevailed that the condition of the Jews was more tolerable than that of the Christians: if indeed they, although they did not recognize the time of liberty, were nevertheless subject to legal burdens, not to human presumptions. More correctly, therefore, the Lutheran Churches, having sent a message of dismissal to the immoderate abundance of Papist rites, employ with moderation ceremonies which serve good order and are as it were a certain useful pedagogy of external life. In which part he also disapproves of the barbarism of those who, under the pretext of Christian liberty, by which they define liberation from all human traditions, think it is permitted to them with impunity to violate any rites and ceremonies whatsoever according to their whim. But liberty without the first and second degree is not Christian, but barbaric. And the Apostles themselves wished for order to be consulted in the Church when, with Christian liberty left intact, they instituted rites making for τάξιν.

The third requirement (that namely adiaphorous rites should serve for ornament and decorum) the Apostle himself expressed in 1 Cor. 14. 40. It must be seen, therefore, what becomes persons, what becomes the worship itself, what becomes places, what becomes times, so that one may gather in temples more decently than in a theater or in women's quarters. The reason for which decorum is not to be sought in scenic splendor or Persian pomp: but partly in simplicity and modesty, and partly in that gravity which is proper to divine worship and religion.

Latin:

ADiaphororum nomen Ecclesia ex Philosophorum phrontisteriis mutuata est. Quemadmodum enim hi, teste Suida, Adiaphororum vocabulo notarunt τὰ μέσα, hoc est, eas res, quarum usus in medio est positus, quæq; ita sunt comparatæ, ut vel benè illis uti queamus, vel malè: utque benè usurpatæ ad ornandum quidem; non autem ad conferendam felicitatem civilem, momenti aliquid habeant: Ita Scholæ Theologorũ consueverunt hac appellatione eos ritus insignire, quorum in salutis cœlestis negotio eadem est conditio. Latini, teste Tullio lib. 3. de finibus, Græcum vocabulum reddiderunt nomine Indifferentium: Quo etiam Scholæ Theologorum uti solent.

Adiaphora ergò vocantur negotia, res, & ordinationes eæ, quarum observatio sive usus divinitus in Novo Testamento neq; præceptus, neq; prohibitus, ac proinde in se neq; bonus, neq; malus est, neq; per se conscientiam utentu, vel abstinentu, in partem vel commendationis, vel odij apud DEUM afficit: sed εὐσχημονέσαταν, hoc est, boni ordinis, & decori causa, sic est in Ecclesiam, & ab Ecclesia ipsâ introductus, ut excepto circumstantiæ & accidentis externi, ut & immodici excessus vitio, piis semper liber sit, & in utramque partem (observationis, vel omissionis sive abstinentiæ) arbitrarius.

Talia adiaphora dantur in communi hominum vita, quoad cibum, potum, coniugium, cœlibatum, divitias, paupertatem, vestitum hoc aut illo colore, contractus civiles: fic ipso definiente Apostolo, Rom. 14. 6. Qui manducat, Domino manducat: Gratias enim agit DEO: Et qui non manducat, Domino non manducat, & gratias agit DEO. Sic 1. Cor. 7, 24. & 34. Cœlibatum & conjugium pro rebus indifferentibus habet Apostolus; modò utrique sua constet puritas. Et Coloss. 2. 16. generalem hunc infert Aphorismum: Nemo vos judicet in cibo & potu. Verùm de his hoc loco propriè non controvertitur: Sed de iis, quorum usus in Ecclesiâ aliquando obtinuit.

Horum ergò quænam propria sit Natura & affectio primùm omnium quæritur. Jam verò ex ipso etymo & propria significatione vocabuli in genere patet, Naturam Adiaphoro rum talem esse, ut usus eorundem neq; mandatus sit Christiano, neq; prohibitus; neq; bonus, neq; malus in seipso; neq; utente aut abstinenti in negotio salutis velutilis, vel damnosus: sed sit liber planè, indifferens atq; medius, & in salutis causa, prorsus quod dici queat, αποιος.

Hujusmodi Adiaphora in Ecclesiis Orthodoxis, & à fermento Pontificio ritè repur gatis præcipua sunt: Feriæ, discrimina temporũ, distinctiones quædam vestium, ciborum, temporum, Ministrorum etiam Ecclesiæ, Cantiones & lectiones sacræ: Cantus figuralis: Organon Musicum: fractio panis: usus item panis azymi & orbiculati in Sacramento Eucharistico: Exorcismus: Immersio sive aspersio infantis baptizandi: Patrinorum adhibitio: Campanarum increpatio: & similia alia.

De hoc genere rerum tenenda est regula, à Confessione Augustanâ artic. 15. tradita: Ritus illi sunt servandi, qui sine peccato servari possunt. Quod explicatiùs in Scholiis sic exprimitur: Adiaphora quam diu talia sunt, hoc est, in usu medio atq; indifferenter relinquuntur, sine læsione conscien tiæ, & libertatu Christianæ observari possunt, aut negligi. Hæc regulâ exterminantur opiniones illæ fallæ, quibus natura verorum adiaphoroū rum corrumpitur: Quales sunt, cùm 1. vel Lex necessitatis. 2. vel opinio cultus. 3. vel præsumtio meriti, rerum istarum observationi affingitur. Et profectò, ne ex ullâ trium istorum excessuum parte peccetur, magnâ cautione ac prudentiâ opus fuerit. Tum verò cautio hæc rectè adhibetur, si quibus modis tres isti excessus com­ mitti queant, sedulò observetur.

Primùm igitur Lex necessitatis affingitur rebus adiaphoris dupliciter. 1. Si ex adiaphoris necessaria fiant. 2. Si ex necessariis fiant Adiaphora. Circa prius illud, tempore Pauli, peccabant subintroducti falsi fratres, qui Circumcisionis necessitate propugnatâ, Libertati Christianæ jugum injiciebant. Quibus Apostolus ne ad horam quidem cessit subjectione Gal. 2, 5. & 6. ac hanc ipsam ob causam Titum circumcidi noluit. Hodiè enormiter etiã hac in parte peccant Pontificij, necessitatem iis rebus affingentes, quarū neq; mandatū, neq; exemplum ex Scripturis proferre possunt: id quod extraditionibι9 jejuniorum, discriminis ciborum, feriarum, & similum rerum Pontificiis usitatarum, satis est manifestum. Nec mi­ no crassam omninò vertiginem, in primo hoc excessu, patiuntur Sacramentarii, Fractione panis Euchariftici, fermentationem etiam ejusdē inevirabili necessitate urgentes: cujus evidentem rationem exScripturis nullam dare possunt.

Circa posteriùs primi hujus excessus membrum peccabant illi, qui Apostolorũ tempore, multa in censum, numerumq; rerum adiaphorarū referebant, quæ per se illicita, & manifestoDEIVerbo prohibita erant. Quo in numero fuitScorratio, à Deo prohibita. Deut. 23. 17. ut hæc res ansam præbueritApostolis, novo interdicto flagitium istud prohibendi Act. 15, 20. Quo referri fortassis etiam potest Polygamia, in prima conjugii institutione à DEo prohibita: à Judæis verò tanquam libera introducta: ac hanc ipsam ob causam àChristoServatore rursus prohibita & abrogata, Gen. 2, 21. Matth. 9, 8. Hoc ipso modo impingunt etiam Sacramentarii,statuentes, in defectu elementorū Sacramentalium alia substitui posse, quæ cū elementu à Christo sancitu, ac proinde simpliciter immutabilibƒ, analogicam tantùm cōsirmitatē quandà obtinent. Quibus figmentis autoritas Scripturæ rum opponenda est: Gal. 5, 1. In libertate, in quâ Christƒ vos vocavit,state,& ne rursus jugo servitutis implicemini. Et Ezech. 20, 19. In præceptis meis ambulate, & judicia mea custodite, & facite ea.

ALTER excessus, nempe opinio cultus, in genere rerum adiaphorarum, prorsus est intolerabilis. Quam ob causam res istae ab Apostolo nominantur Elementa mundi, Gal. 4.3. Coloss. 2.8. & quidem Elementa egena, & infirma, Gal. 4.9. quin imò infami quasi titulo traditionum humanarum, ἐθελοθρησκείας Col. 2. 8. 21. & 23. Servitutis, Gal. 4.9. Mortis & exitii, Col. 2. 20. & 22. imò etiam διδασκαλίας δαιμονίων. 1. Tim. 4. 1. perstringuntur, si in cultum divinum aliquid sibi juris, vel autoritatis arrogare velint. Imò, in terminis terminantibus, quod dicitur, à Christo Servatore repudiantur, hac promulgatâ authenticâ: Frustrà me colunt, docentes doctrinas, & mandata hominum, Matth. 15. 9. Cultus ergò divini materiam, aut cultus ejus partem quamcunque, in rebus istis collocare, nimis impium foret.

Tertius excessus Opinio videlicet meriti, omnium est teterrimus: Quasi rerum adiaphorarum & indifferentium observatione, tùm culpae, tùm poenae expiationem homines consequantur. Nullius profectò, quantumvis sanctae, & à DEO ipso promulgatae legis, non forensis tantùm, aut ceremonialis: sed nec Moralis quidem operibus, justificatur ullus homo coram DEO: sed fide duntaxat: Gal. 3. 16. Quanta ergò haec est potestas tenebraru, quae ex humanae alicujus, sive Pontificis, sive Concilii, sive alterius hominis legis & traditionis operibus, meriti opinionem in salutis causâ persuadere cuipiam possit?

Et talis quidem est rerum adiaphorarum externa conditio, quâ Natura earum statuitur esse lib. 1. ab omni necessitate simplici atq; absolutâ 2. à cultu per se, & immediatè DEO placente: & 3. ab omni ratione meriti.

Porrò autem ad naturam Adiaphororum pertinet etiam τὸ μέσον καὶ τὸ ἄποιον, hoc est, indifferens. Τὸ μέσον autem non Ethicum, quod est virtutis proprium; Quae est medium virtiorum utrinque reductum: sed Physicum, cujus ratio se indifferenter habet ad boni, malivé naturam. Quo medio stante ultrò sequitur τὸ ἄποιον, indifferens, quo fit, ut in nullam vel neglectus, vel emendationis partem afficiatur, qui istis vel utitur, vel non utitur.

Confirmat hoc Apostolus ipse, de unâ quâdam specie Adiaphoricâ, nempe de cibis: sed ita, ut inde de genere universo istarum rerum fieri possit judicium: Esca inquiens, nos non commendat: Neque enim si manducaverimus, abundabimus (quasi meliores redditi) neq; si non manducemus, deteriores erimus. 1. Cor. 8. 8. Docuit hanc praxin Spiridion Cypri Episcopus hospitem quendam, die jejunij ad se venientem. Nam cùm in defectu ciborum aliorum, carnes, quas reconditas habebat, illi apposuisset, quas ille à se eâ die comedi negabat, quia Christianus esset: hanc ipsam ob causam, respondit Spiridion, vescite illu decet, quia Christianus es. Quo dicto monitus ille, rei mediae usu, se nullo modo pollui intellexit. Et hoc alterum est rerum adiaphorarum πάθος.

Tertiò, ad naturam rerum Adiaphorarum requiritur etiam, ut ritus sint Ecclesiastici,hoc est, ac Ecclesia ipsa vel introducti, vel saltem approbati. Nihil ergò in Ecclesiis Evangelicis obtinet potestas Episcopalis, traditionum suarum formam istis obtrusura, ne quidem Cathedram prætexendo, in quâ sedeant Episcopi: uti rectè censuit B. LUTHERUS noster. Tom. 3. Ien. p. 5. 23. Nam ea mandata traditionum oggerunt, quæ servari sine peccato non possunt. In illis quidem, quæ divini juris sunt, conscientiæ necessariò parere debent legitimis pastoribus, juxta illud: Qui vos audit, me audit: Luc. 10. 16. Et, Labia Sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam: & legem requirent ex ore ejus: quia Angelus Domini exercituum est. Malach 2. 7. Sed nihil hoc ad larvatos illos curiæ Romanæ Episcopos, in præsenti negotio. Neque est, ut quisquam metuat, hoc pacto imminutum iri Ministerii Evangelici autoritatem, aut congressus publicos dissipandos esse, quorum retinendorum vinculum quasi quoddam sint ritus illi solennes. Nam ea demùm vera est Ministerij autoritas, & sarta tecta asseritur, quæ intra limites ordinationis divinæ se continet, neq; in onerandis conscientiis, & figendis ac refigendis legibus potestatem alienam invadit. Sic colligendis cœtibus servit quicquit DEUM autorem habet: iisdem dissipandis occasionem præbet, quicquid per vim ac tyrannidem Conscientiis servandum obtruditur. Sic pari ratione reavit, & graviter peccat conscientia, si civilis Magistratus legibus ritè constitutis, non obtemperet: Non peccat autem, si Pontificis, & Episcoporum traditiones, quasi obligantes in conscientia, respuat, & contemnat. Ratio diversitatis manifesta est hæc, quia Politico ordini in externis subjectos nos esse, DEUS ipse seriò præcepit, nó propter iram tantùm: sed etiam propter conscientiam, Rom. 13. 5. In Ecclesia autem nemini hominum potestas est concessa, conscientias legibus necessitatis constringendi: in rebus adiaphoris, Coloss. 2. 16. Galat. 5. 1.

Quartò, circa primam hanc quæstionem & illud observandum, Adiaphora interdùm mutare naturam suam, & desinere esse, quod fuerunt: Primùm tempore edendæ confessionis, ubi tranquillitatis, & asserendæ libertatis causa toleratur, quod natura sua abrogationem ferre omninò posset. Deinde respectu particularium Ecclesiarum, uti dissimilis planè est natura rerum mediarum, propter diversorum populorum de rebus istis diversas sententias. Cujus exemplum habetur in epistola ad Corinthios; ubi viros in sacris cœtibus orare jubet retectis capitibus; mulieres verò velatis 1. Cor. 11. 4. Qui ritus apud gétes alias, diverso est, & alius. Tandem respectu infirmorum & hostium veritatis, ubi libera observatio rerum adiaphorarum transit in necessariam: tum ut ne infirmos offendamus, tùm ne in gratiam hostium veritatis deseramus, imò potiùs prodamus libertatē Christianam, in quam per Christum asserti sumus: Quâ de re quæst. sive capite 2. ex professo disputabitur. Exemplo Circumcisionis hoc loco contenti, rem illustrabimus. Habuit ea pro diversitate temporum & po& populorum triplicem respectū. Primum n. absolutæ necessitatis rationē habebat, tanquã Sacramentum initiationis veteris populi: Gen. 17. 14. Hoc respectu accepta, sub Articuli hujõ considerationem non cadit. Deinde verò cōsideratur secundú eam naturam, quam fortita est sub arrogationem Veteris, & initium Novi Testamenti já in luce edito Christo servatore, Legis fine & consummatore. Hoc tempore Adiaphoricâ naturá aliquandiu obtinebat cir cumcisio, ita ut ab infirmiorib9 & in gratiam fratrũ infirmōrū, recens ad gremiũ Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti adductorũ, liberè observari: & rursus à firmiorib9, & de libertate Novi Testamenti rectiùs informatis, liberè negligi & o mitti posset: modò id fieret sine offensione infirmorum. Quemadmodũ sanè Apostol9 in ikorũ gratiam Timotheũ circumcidi curavit: Act. 16. 3. Tandé verò, postquam infirmitas illa fratrũ, prædicatione Evangelij fuit sublata: & Judæi ipsi ad Ecclcsiam Novi Testamēti aggregati, deq; Libertate Evangelicâ rectiùs edocti fuerunt: ibi tertiâ naturam induit crucifixio, nempè ut non ampliùs rei, vel observatu necessarię: vel adiaphorę, sive indifferētis, sed sim pliciter prohibitę, & abrogatę rationē haberet neq; fas esset eâ cuiquá in usum revocare. Quo respiciens Apostol9, in gratiâ falsorum fratrū, circumeisionem, tanquá adhuc observatu necessariã urgentium, Titũ circumcidi simpliciter noluit: ne videlicet hoc facto, Libertas Evangelica ullo pacto periclitaretur. Tit. 2. 3.

denda venit, quibus non est ulli piaculo, sive penula, sive sago, sive toga, ad præconium verbi, & Sacramentorum dispensationem, Minister Ecclesiæ indutus veniat.

Quinto & postremo: Licet hæc sit Adiaphororum natura, ut per se observatu sint libera & neq; qui illis utitur, meliorem: neq; qui non utitur, deterioré reddant, nedú ex alterutrâ parte conscientiam obligare possint: eximius tamen eorundē in Religionis negotio, & pietatis causâ usus est, si modò intrà eas metas ille se contineat, quas triplex ille finis constituit cuj9 gratiâ Adiaphora in Ecclesiam introducū- tur & recipiuntur. Primus est, ut serviant ædificationi, πρὸς ὀικοδομήν. Alter, ut ordinem bonum adjuvent, πρὸς τάξιν. Tertius, ut deco ri laudē servēt, πρὸς εὐσχημοσύνην. Quos fines ipse Apostolus definivit, duabus hisce regulis cõstitutis, I. Omnia ad ædificationē fiant. II. Omnia decorè & ordinatè fiant, 1. Cor. 14. 26. & 40.

Cæterùm tres istos fines, ritus Adiaphorici tum demú assequuntur. 1. Si liciti & convenientes fuerint: quâ ratione ædificationi servitur. 2. Si utiles & moderati: Quo pacto εὐτάξια sive ordo bonus juvatur. 3. Si elegantes & honesti sint: Quo modo ornarii & decoro pulcerrimè conducitur. Unde tria jam requisita rituum Adiaphororum, si modò verè tales sint, & esse debeant, elucescent.

Primum illud, (nempè ut sint liciti) Sanctimonia ipsa Religionis suadet: in qua, quia ritus externi sunt quasi incitamenta & fomēta quædam pietatis, quibus ad devorâ verbi auscultationem, & ad alia pietatis exercitia hominũ animi præparantur, instruuntur, accē- duntur: in his profectò nihil illicitum, aut inconveniens locum fortiri potest. Quâ in parte rusticitas eorum hominum meritò reprehenAlterum requisitum (nempe ut sint utiles & moderati) ordo ipse exigit. Jam verò utiles sūt ceremoniæ, inquit Athanasius; sed cum cognitione veritatis, & cum mediocritate. Certè in rebus naturalibus, quibusvis πᾶν τὸ πολὺ τῇ Φύσει πολέμιον, teste Hippocrate in Aphorismis: Quantò id magis locum habebit in negocio religionis, in qua non tantùm fit, ut devotio ardens sub impatientiæ mora distracta facilè exolescat: sed circa τὰ πάρεργα homines nimirùm occupati, τῶν ἔργων ipsorũ minorem curam habeant Deum ipsum, testis est Augustinus, Epist. 118. Sacramentis numero paucissimis, observatione facillimis, significatione prę stantissimis, societate novi populi colligasse. Atqui idem sua tempestate ita jam invaluisse conqueritur ceremoniarū multitudinē, ut tolerabilior fuerit Judæorũ conditio, quâ Christianorum: siquidem illi, tametsi tempus libertatis non agnoverunt: legalibus tamé farcinis nõ humanis præsumtionibus subjecti fuerint. Rectiùs ergò Ecclesiæ Lutheranæ, immodicæ Pontificiorũ rituū copiæ nuncio remisso, cum mediocritate adhibent ceremonias, quę bono ordini serviant, & sint quasi utilis quædã pædagogia vitæ externæ. Quá in parte improbat eorū etiam barbariē, qui libertatis Christianæ prætextu, quâ liberatione ab omnibus traditionibus humanis definiút, impune sibi esse putant, ritus & ceremonias quasvis pro libidine violare. Atqui libertas sine gradu primo & secundo, Christiana non est, sed batbarica. Et Apostoli ipsi, ordini in Ecclesia consultum volebāt, quando illibata libertatē Christiana, ritus instituebant ad τάξιν facientes.

Tertium requisitum (ut nimirú ritus adiaphorici ornatui & decoro serviant) Apostolus ipse 1. Cor. 14. 40. expressit. Videndũ est ergo, quid personas, quid cultum ipsum, quid loca, quid tempora deceat, ut decentiùs in templis conveniatur, quâm in theatro, vel gynæceis. Cuj9 decori ratio, non splendore scenico, aut pompa Persica, est merieda: sed simplicitate partim, & modestia, partim gravitate ea, quæ est divini cultus, & religionis propria.


### Caput II. On the Right and Legitimate Use of Adiaphorous Things

What things are by their own nature indifferent, both by reason of their internal quality, namely Pious, Useful, Decent, Intermediate: and by reason of their external condition, namely, entirely free from every opinion of the necessity of simple divine worship, and finally of merit, has been shown thus far. It remains that we inquire solicitously concerning the right use of the same. For it is certain that in this class of things there is indeed Liberty for the pious: but such that it prejudices neither the advantage of one's neighbor, nor the honor of GOD. Whence it has come about that the Apostle himself has prescribed certain rules concerning the use of things

Latin:

QUalia sua natura sint adiaphora, tum ratione qualitatis internæ, nempè Pia, Utilia, Decentia, Media: tum ratione conditionis externæ, nimirùm ab omni opinione necessitatis simplicis cultus divini, meriti denique, prorsus libera, hactenus ostensum. Restat, ut de recta eorundem usurpatione sollicitè dis quiramus. Constat enim quidem in isto rerum genere piis Libertas sua: sed talis, quæ neque proximi commodo, neq; honori DEI præjudicet. Unde factum est, ut Apostolus ipse de adiaphororum usu certas regulas præ-


### Caput II. On the Right and Legitimate Use of Adiaphorous Things: The First Apostolic Rule concerning adiaphora

indifferent: which it is my pleasure first to consider in their own sources, and then to illustrate the same with practical examples. The first rule is as follows: Matters of indifference, or Adiaphora, are not to be used indiscreetly, but their use must be measured by the rule of charity; and therefore, concerning their use, one must not dispute with one who is weak in faith and not yet sufficiently informed about Christian liberty. For because the power of religious custom and of conscience is usually great, and not all progress equally in the knowledge of heavenly things, certainly those who have recently come into the society of the Christian profession are not to be offended, but to be borne with, cherished, and with all gentleness more and more instructed. The foundations of this rule exist in Romans 14:1. Receive the weak in faith, not in disputes of thoughts (that is, by interpreting everything sinisterly), provided they admit nothing that might offer a public stumbling block to another, or incur a manifest violation of the faith. And verse 13: Do not place a stumbling block or scandal before a brother. And verse 15: If because of food your brother is grieved, you are no longer walking according to charity. And verse 19: Let us pursue the things of peace, and let us guard those things which are for edification among ourselves. Thus in 1 Corinthians 10:32, the Apostle hands down this general rule: ἀπϱοσκόποι γίνεσθε, be without offense, to the Jews, and to the Gentiles, and to the Church of GOD. Speaking summarily: concerning the use of Adiaphora, regarding this first rule, one must see not what is lawful, but what is expedient: 1 Corinthians 6:12 and chapter 10:23. Christ himself accommodated himself to this rule in paying the tax: Matthew 17:27. And Paul, prohibiting the eating of things sacrificed to idols in a case of scandal, the eating of which he otherwise clearly established to be a matter of indifference: 1 Corinthians 8. Eusebius reports of a certain Alcibiades, who, when he was held in chains for the faith of Christ, had decided to live on bread, water, and salt alone. When Attalus the Martyr, warned by an oracle, had rebuked him on the grounds that he was providing an occasion of scandal to others, Alcibiades, having been taught better, immediately began to eat ordinary foods with thanksgiving. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book. And this is true Ἐπιείκεια (forbearance), the moderation of which, when applied, both contributes to peace and relieves consciences. Therefore, those who are not by nature καὶ ἀκοινώνητοι (unsociable), but understand that they were born for the society of the human race, willingly and studiously accommodate their counsels and actions to the cynosure of this rule. A second rule is handed down in the Scriptures: Stand fast in the liberty with which Christ has freed us, Galatians 5:1, and it must be asserted as safe and sound in such a way that we do not yield, not even for an hour, by any subjection to false brothers who tempt our liberty, which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might reduce us into servitude: Galatians 2:4 and 5. Therefore, just as according to the first rule in a case of scandal, so according to this second, in a case of giving a confession, nothing at all is to be committed or permitted which could in any way prejudice Christian liberty. Thus, in a time of persecution, when a clear and constant confession is required, nothing at all is to be yielded to the enemies of the Gospel in the use of matters of indifference, nor is any gratification to be given in any part regarding the restoration of abrogated things; but for this free use of them, one must fight even to the shedding of blood.

The practice of this rule, besides the Apostle Paul, Galatians 2:4, was excellently observed by the Blessed LUTHER, concerning the controversy about the Elevation of the bread in the Eucharistic action, which he wished to retain in our churches for some time even after the blessed Reformation, for the sake of the weak; and indeed with a pious and prudent counsel. For the Church was then still very tender, and therefore to be nourished with milk rather than with more solid food, lest Luther seem to destroy the Church rather than build it up. Now, from the Papacy, the rite of the Elevation of the bread had indeed remained, in itself clearly a matter of indifference, but obtaining some use of signification. For (as Luther himself writes in the book On the Babylonian Captivity) by this rite the Church imitated the rite of the Mosaic offerings. in which thanksgiving was made; but in part it proposed a certain ocular exposition, as it were, of the words of the Supper, 'This is my body.' For, because the Elevation was accustomed to be made immediately upon these words being pronounced, certainly he who elevated the bread seemed to be saying this: 'Behold, dearest ones, this is that bread with which the Body of Christ is now sacramentally united in the subsequent use.' But when the Blessed LUTHER himself understood that this rite could be drawn toward establishing in part the Consubstantiation of the elemental bread into the body of Christ, and in part the impiety of Transubstantiation and the Mass-sacrifice, he himself thought about abrogating it, provided that the Church had first more correctly perceived the true doctrine concerning the Eucharistic Sacrament, so that it would not be offended in any part by an untimely abrogation of this ceremony. Which very abrogation, in the progress of time, happened by the act itself. Now, however, when Carlstadt, an enemy of the purer doctrine and an assertor of the Sacramentarian dogma, began to rage against this ceremony and to establish the guilt of a most atrocious sin in that in which there was no sin in itself, here Luther did not wish to yield to Carlstadt, not even for an hour, in the use of this matter of indifference. Concerning which matter, let us hear the Blessed LUTHER himself, differing thus in his smaller Confession: 'When it was my intention to abrogate that rite, having changed my counsel, I retained the same in defiance of that Satan (Carlstadt), and I did not wish to suffer that he should use his authority in our churches.' At the same time, I also thought that by this act the peace of consciences should be consulted, to which a scruple could not but be struck, either regarding the past or the future, if I were to acknowledge that there was sin in the rite itself, which was not in it. I therefore judged that this matter was indifferent, indeed in such a way that I would rather have introduced three, seven, or ten elevations than have permitted that this vertiginous and fanatical spirit of the Sacramentarians should impose the burden of necessity upon my conscience. For this reason, the elevation has been retained by us. For in matters of indifference, which are neither commanded nor forbidden by GOD, we rightly wish our liberty to be kept safe and sound: and we think it is placed in our own judgment to decide whatever we wish concerning them. Therefore, we suffer the yoke of servitude in these matters to be imposed upon us by no one. Thus far LUTHER.

Some orthodox and truly Lutheran theologians also held this same Apostolic practice in previous years, who were unwilling to consent to the abrogation of Exorcism at the petition of the Sacramentarians, not because it could not be abrogated, if it was done by the Orthodox Church in a just and legitimate manner: but lest by yielding to adversaries in this part, they should betray the liberty which our Churches have in CHRIST JESUS.

This second rule, and its practice, rests upon firm and immovable foundations, or reasons, which I wish to recount in order.

THE FIRST is sought from the command of the Apostle, 2 Cor. 6. 14. Do not be yoked together with unbelievers: For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? And what communion has light with darkness? What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what part has a believer with an unbeliever? Therefore come out from among them, and be separate, and do not touch the unclean thing, says the LORD. And Eph. 5. 11. Do not have fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them. Now, since in the use of things indifferent one yields to adversaries who are tempting our liberty: certainly the same yoke is being drawn with them, and one participates in their impiety.

THE SECOND cause, or reason, is because one must diligently take care that the truth of Evangelical doctrine, which is as it were the life and soul of Christian Liberty, is not obscured in any way, or defiled by any filth of human traditions: Now, the enemies of the truth, urging that we either receive new traditions or abolish those hitherto observed without any impiety, seek nothing else than to obtrude their errors upon the Church of GOD obliquely and indirectly, and to establish some dominion in the free Church. It was possible to see this both at the time of the Interimistic discussion among the Papists, and at the time of the Exorcistic struggle among the Sacramentarians: the former of whom strove to establish Papist idolomania and the primacy of the Pope, while the latter strove to confirm the Calvinist dogma concerning the holiness of children born of believers, as will be shown more fully below.

THE THIRD reason: Because one must stand in the liberty with which Christ has set us free, and not allow ourselves to be subjected again to a yoke of slavery. Gal. 5. 1. Now, when one yields to the enemies of the truth and persecutors, our Liberty certainly degenerates into a Servitude entirely unworthy of Christians: a thing which the Belgian Churches have experienced, and experience to this day, which, while they did not assert Evangelical liberty intact, but granted the autonomy of religion, perhaps for the sake of some civil advantage, have ended up as a sink of all religions and heresies.

THE FOURTH reason: Because such a concession is joined with manifest scandal and the highest danger: as it does not promote the Glory of GOD, but obscures it: it does not amplify the Kingdom of Christ, but scatters it: it does not promote the course of the Gospel, but delays it: it does not support the weak in faith, but disturbs them, and renders them more doubtful: it does not correct those who err, but confirms them: it does not corroborate the Orthodox in the faith, but splits them into diverse opinions: finally, it does not build up the universal Church, but destroys it, does not gather, but scatters, does not defend, but betrays.

THE FIFTH: Because in this matter a case of Confession is at stake. Now, while the free Confession of the pious ought to shine at all times, it ought especially to spread its beams and rays most widely in a time of persecution, when the Confession of the Truth must be given. But if, for the sake of the enemies of the truth regarding the use of things indifferent, one yields either by abolishing old ones or by usurping new ones: then shackles are already being cast upon the liberty of Confession, so that we appear to collude with those very enemies, if not entirely, yet in some part. How much this is joined with danger and detriment is evident from that Aphorism of the Savior, Matt. 10. 32. Whoever confesses me before men, I will also confess him before my heavenly Father: But whoever denies me before men, I will also deny him before my heavenly Father. To which pertains that of Psalm 116. 10. I believed, therefore I have spoken. And Rom. 10. 10. With the heart one believes unto righteousness: but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

THE SIXTH and last. Because not only is the open and public denial of the Truth itself to be avoided by Christians: but not even any species of denial is to be permitted: by the example of Moses, who, for the sake of bringing liberty to the people, would not leave even a hoof in Egypt at the request of the impious King Pharaoh, Exod. 10. 26. By the example likewise of Daniel, who, for the sake of hypocrites, would not even pray with closed windows, Daniel 6. 10. By the example of Eleazar, who, for the sake of the Tyrant, would not even feign the eating of swine's flesh, 2 Maccabees 6. 24. By the example of Paul, who, for the sake of the false apostles, would not yield to them by circumcising Titus, not even for an hour: Galat. 2. 5. Finally, by the example of Luther and other faithful assertors of the Evangelical truth.

To some today, especially to certain meddlesome fellows from the order of Politicians, this opinion seems too harsh, for the reason that in this question it is not properly and directly a matter of Religion itself, or Articles of faith: but only of one or another miserable thing indifferent, which could easily be abolished without the loss of truth: Furthermore, they try to persuade men of high station that, while this more rigid opinion of the Theologians stands, no firmer Peace can ever coalesce between men of different Religions: which, however, must be sought, fostered, and confirmed in every way in the Roman Empire today.

Truly, this is a political πρόσχημα, not drawn from the apothecary of the Holy Spirit, but from the storehouse of reason, clearly feeble and trifling. For even if (regarding the former exception) it is not directly a matter of an article of faith: yet it is a matter of business concerning the purity and truth of all articles of faith. For once destroyed, or at least

scripserit: quas primùm in suis considerare fontibus: deinde verò easdem exemplis practicis illustrare placet. Prima regula sic habet: Rebus indifferentibus sive Adiaphoris non indiscretè utendum est: sed usus earum ad charitatis regulam exigendus: ac proinde de earũ usu, cum infirmo in fide, & nondum satis de libertateChristiana informato,non est disceptandũ. Quia enim magna solet esse partim religiosae consuetudinis, partim conscientiae vis. & nunquàm pariter in cognitione rerum cœlestium omnes proficiunt:certè nõ offendendi,sed ferendi,fovendi & cü omni mansuetudine magis,magisq́; informandi sunt,qui ad societate professionis Christianae recens accesserunt. Regulae hujus fundamenta extant Rom. 14 1. Infirmũ in fide suscipite: non in disceptationibg cogitationum: (sinistre nimirum interpretando omnia) modò nihil illi admittant, quod vel publicũ praebeat offendiculum alio,vel in manifestam fidei violationẽ incurrat. Et vers.13.Ne ponatis fratri offendiculum, vel scandalum. Et vers. 15. Si propter cibum frater tuus contristatur, jam non secundũ charitatem ambulas: Et vers. 19. Quae pacis sunt, sectemur, & quae edificationis sunt,invicem custodiamus.Sic in 1.Cor. 10 32. generalem tradit regulam hancApostolus ἀπϱοσκόποι γίνεσθε, sine offendiculo estote, Iudaeis, & Gentibus, & Ecclesiae DEI.Summatim loquendo: circa usum Adiaphororum,quoad primam hanc regalam, videndum, non quid liceat: sed quid expediat: 1. Cor 6.12. & cap.10.23. Huic regulae Christus ipse se accommodavit, in exsolvendo censu: Matth. 17.27. Et Paulus, Idolothytis vesci prohibens, in casu scandali, quorum esum alioquin ipse planè adiaphorum esse statuit: 1.Cor. 8. Alcibiadem quendã refert Eusebius,cùm propter fidem Christi in vinculis teneretur,solo pane, aquâ & sale victitare constituisse. Quem cùm Attalus Martyr oraculo admonitus reprehendisset hoc nomine,quòd aliis Scandali occasionem praeberet: Alcibiades meliora edoctus,statim cibis usitatis vesci cum gratiarum actione cepit. Euseb. hist. Eccl. lib. Et haec est vera Ἐπιείκεια, cujus moderatio adhibita, & paci conducit, & levat conscientias. Qui ergo non sunt naturâ fieri καὶ ἀκοινωνικοί, sed ad societatem humani generis se natos esse intelligunt: ad Regulae hujus cynosuram consilia & actiones suas libenter & studiosè accommodant. Altera Regula talis inScripturis traditur: Standum est in libertate,quâ nos Christus liberavit, Gal. 5. 1. eaq́; ita sarta tecta asserenda, ut ne ad horam quidem subjectione aliqua cedamus falsis fratribus tentantibus libertatem nostram, quam habemus in Christo Jesu,ut nos in servitutem redigant: Gal 2.4.& 5. Quemadmodum ergò secundum primam regulam in casu scandali: sic secundum hanc alteram, in casu edendaeConfessionis nihil quicquam committendum, vel permittendum, quod Libertati Christianae quovis modo praejudicare possit. Sic per secutionis tempore, quando perspicua atque constans confessio exigitur,hostibusEvangolii,in rerum adiaphorarum usu,nihil quicquã est cedendum, vel etiam in restitutione abrogatarum, ullâ ex parte gratificandum: sed pro hoc libero earum usu, vel ad sanguinis usque profusionem dimicandum..

Regulæ hujus praxin, præterApostolúPaulum, Gal. 2. 4. egregiè observabat B. LUTHERUS, circa Controversiam de Elevatione panis, in actione Eucharistica, quam aliquandiu post beatam etiam Reformationem, in gratiam infirmorum, in Ecclesiis nostris retinere voluit: & sanè pio ac prudenti consilio. Erat enim tunc adhuc tenella admodumEcclesia, ac proinde lacte potiùs magis, quàm solidiore cibo nutrienda, ne perdere magis, quàm ædificareEcclesiam videreturLutherus. Jam exPapatu quidé remanserat ritus Elevationis panis, in se planè adiaphorus quidem, sed significationis usum aliquem obtinens Nam (utLutherus ipse scribit in libro de Capt. Bab.) hoc ritu imitabaturEcclesia ritum Mosaicarum oblationũ. in quib9 gratiarum actio fiebat: partim verò verborum Cœnæ, Hoc est Corpus meum, quandam quasi expositionem ocularem proponebat Nam, quia statim verbis istis pronunciatis Elevatio fieri consueverat, utiq; ille, qui pané elevabat, hoc dicere videbatur: En charissimi, Hic est panis ille, cü quo jã in usu subsequente Sacramentaliter est unitũ CorpusChristi. Verùm cum B. LUTHERUS ipse intelligeret, Ritum hunc trahi posse ad stabiliendã partim Consubstantiationem Panis Elementaris in corpus Christi, partim Transsubstantiationis & Sacrificii Missatici impietatē: ipsemet de eo abrogando cogitavit, dummodò priùsEcclesia, veram doctrinam de Sacramento Eucharistico rectiùs percepisset, ne nullâ ex parte ea per intempestivam abrogationem huj9 ceremoniæ offenderetur. Quæ ipsa etiam abrogatio, progressu temporis, actu ipso evenit. Jã verò cùm Carolostadius, hostis doctrinæ purioris, & Sacramentarii dogmatis assertor, adversus hanc ceremoniã furere, & peccati atrocissimi reatum statuere cepisset in eo, in quo nullú peccatú per se erat: hîc LUTHERUS ne ad horam quidem in usu hujus adiaphori, Carolostadio cedere voluit. Quâ de re audiamus ipsũ B. LuTHERUM, in Confessione minore sic differentem: Cùm animus mihi esset, abrogare istum ritũ, mutato consilio, in contumeliã istius Satanæ (Carolo stadi) retinui eundem, & ut magisterio in nostras Ecclesias iste uteretur, pati nolui. Simul etiam hoc facto paci conscientiarũ consulendũ esse putavi, cui non poterat non, vel de præterito, vel de futuro scrupul9 impingi, si in ipso simpliciter ritu tantũ agnoscerē inesse peccatũ, quod non inerat. Adiaphoron ergo hoc relinquendum esse censui, ita quidé, ut tres, septem, vel decē elevationes potiùs fuerim introducturus, quã permissurus, ut vertiginos9 iste, & fanatic9 Sacramentariorũ Spirit9, Necessitatis on9 conscientiæ meæ imponeret. Hoc consilio Elevatio à nobis retenta est. In rebus enim Adiaphoris, quæ à DEO neq; præcepta, neq; prohibita sunt, libertatem nostram meritò sartam & tectam esse volumus: & in nostro positum arbitrio putamus, ut de iis statuamus quodlibet. Servitutis ergo jugum in istis imponi nobis à nemine patimur. Hactenus LUTHERUS.

Quâ eandé praxin Apostolicá superiorib9 annis tenuerũt etiá nónulli orthodoxi, & verè Lutherani Theologi, qui ad petitionéSacramétariorũ in Exorcísmi abrogationé consentire noluerũt, non quòd ille abrogari nó posset, si justo ac legitimo modo ab Ecclesia Orthodoxa id fieret: sed ne adversariis hac in parte cedendo, proderent libertatem, quam nostra Ecclesiae habent in CHRISTO JESU.

Nititur autem Secunda haec regula, ejusdemq; praxis, firmis ac immotis fundamentis, sive rationibus, quas ordine recensere libet.

PRIMA petitur ex praecepto Apostoli, 2. Cor. 6. 14. Nolite ducere jugum cum infidelibus: Quae enim participatio justitiae cum injustitia? Quae communicatio luci cu tenebris? qui consensus Christi cum Belial? aut quae pars fidelis cum infideli? Proinde exite de medio illorum, separamini, immundu ne tangite, inquit DOMINUS, Et Eph. 5. 11. Nolite commercium habere cum infrugiferis operibus tenebrarum, sed potius arguite. Jam vero quando in usu rerum adiaphorarum creditur adversariis, tentantibus libertatem nostram: certe idem cum illis jugum ducitur, & de ipsorum impietate participatur.

ALTERA causa, sive ratio est, quia sedulo cavendum, ut ne veritas doctrinae Evangelicae, quae Libertatis Christianae vita quasi est, & anima, ullo pacto obscuretur, vel aliquo humanarum traditionum caeno confpurcetur: Jam vero hostes veritatis, urgentes: ut vel novas traditiones recipiamus: vel hactenus sine ulla impietate observatas, abrogemus, nihil quaerunt aliud, quam ut oblique, & per indirectum, errores suos Ecclesiae DEI obtrudere, & dominatum aliquem in Ecclesia libera constituere possint. Videre hoc licuit, tum tempore συζητήσεως Interimisticae in Pontificiis: tum tempore certaminis Exorcistici in Sacramentariis: quorum illi idolomaniam Pontificiam, & primatum Pontificis stabilire: isti vero dogma Calvinianum de Sanctitate liberorum, ex fidelibus prognatorum, subdole confirmare studebant: uti infra fusius ostendetur.

TERTIA ratio: Quia standum in libertate, qua Christus nos liberavit, neque permittendum, ut servitutis jugo iterum subjiciamur. Gal. 5. 1. Jam vero quando hostibus veritatis & persecutoribus ceditur, certe Libertas nostra in Servitutem, plane indignam Christianis, degenerat: id quod expertae fuerunt, hodieq; experiuntur Ecclesiae Belgicae, quae, dum libertatem Evangelicam sartam tectam non asseruerunt: sed Religionis αυτονομίαν, forte civilis alicujus commodi gratia, concesserunt, evaserunt in sentinam omnium religionum & hereseωn.

QUARTA ratio: Quia talis cessio cum manifesto scandalo, & summo periculo est conjuncta: ut quae Gloriam DEI non pro movet, sed obfuscat: Regnum Christi non amplificat, sed disjicit: cursum Evangelij non promovet, sed remoratur: Infirmos in fide non suscipit, sed turbat, magisq; reddit dubios: errantes non corrigit sed confirmat: Orthodoxas non in fide corroborat, sed in diversas sententias dispescit: Ecclesiam deniq; universam non aedificat, sed destruit, non colligit, sed dispergit, non defendit, sed prodit.

QUINTA: Quia hoc in negotio casus Confessionis agitur. Jam cum omnibus temporibus lucere debeat libera piorum Confessio: tum vero maxime jubar & radios suos latissime spargere debet tempore persecutionis, quo Veritatis edenda est Confessio. Atqui si in gratiam hostium veritatis circa usum rerum adiaphorarum, vel veteres abrogando, vel novas usurpando cedatur: utique Confessionis libertati jam compedes injiciuntur, ut cum illis ipsis hostibus, si non ex toto, ex parte tamen aliqua colludere videamur. Quod quantum cum periculo & detrimento sit conjunctum, constat ex illo Aphorismo Servatoris, Matth. 10. 23. Qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, eundem confitebor & ego coram patre meo calesti: Qui vero me negaverit coram hominibus, eundem negabo & ego coram patre meo calesti. Quo pertinet illud Psalmi. 116. 10. Credidi, propterea locutus sum. Et Rom. 10. 10. Corde creditur ad justitiam: Ore autem fit confessio ad salutem.

SEXTA & postrema. Quia non tantum ipsa Veritatis negatio aperta & publica Christianis est vitanda: sed ne quidem ulla permittenda negationis species: exemplo Mosis, qui pro afferenda libertate populi, ne quidem ungulam in Aegypto, ad petitionem impii regis Pharaonis, relinquere, Exod. 10. 26. Exemplo item Danielis, qui in gratiam Hypocritarum, ne quidem clausis fenestris orare, Danielis 6. 10. exemplo Eleazari, qui in gratiam Tyranni, esum carnium suillarum, ne quidem simulare volebat. 2. Matthab. 6. 24. exemplo Pauli, qui in gratiam Pseudoapostolorum, Titum circumcidere, ac vel ad horam saltem illis cedere nolebat: Galat. 2. 5. Exemplo deniq; Lutheri, & aliorum fidelium veritatis Evangelicae assertorum.

Videtur hodie nonnullis, praesertim ex ordine Politicorum nafutulis quibusdam, nimis dura haec sententia, eo quod in quaestione hac non proprie ac directe agatur de Religione ipsa, sive Articulis fidei: sed tantum de uno atq; altero misello adiaphoro, quod citra jacturam veritatis facile abrogari possit: Deinde persuadere conantur viris principibus, quod stante rigidiore hac Theologorum sententia, nunquam Pax aliqua firmior inter diversarum Religionum homines coalescere possit: Quae tamen hodie in Romano imperio quovis modo quaerenda, fovenda & confirmanda sit.

Verum, Politicum hoc est πρόσχημα, non ex Spiritus Sancti myrothecio, sed ex rationis promptuario petita, plane elumbis & nugatoria. Nam si maxime (quoad priorem exceptionem) non directe agatur de articulo fidei: tamen agitur de negotio concernente puritatem & veritatem omnium articulorum fidei. Destructa enim, vel saltem


### Caput II. On the Right and Legitimate Use of Adiaphorous Things: Fourth rule concerning adiaphora

weakened, the very purity of religion itself must necessarily suffer and be in great peril, a fact easily understood by anyone who has a correct and thorough knowledge of what Christian Liberty is. In this regard, those politicians display astonishing ignorance and crudeness. What is more? It is a matter of no small article of faith that is being contended here, namely, Christian Liberty. Therefore, if this Article is dissolved and broken through errors or abuse, the entire chain and series of the Articles of the Christian Religion must necessarily be broken. We therefore oppose to those conceited fellows that saying of Nazianzen: Let others play in this way: but for us to play in these matters is not safe.

The latter argument is clearly atheological. For even if some public advantage were to be expected from that exception, nevertheless, according to the authoritative word of the Apostle, Rom. 3.8, evils are not to be done so that good may come of them. It must therefore be considered first whether, while preserving heavenly truth, anything in the matter of religion, even regarding the adiaphoric use, can be conceded to the enemies of truth, before some public and carnal good is amplified for many. Furthermore, this very good that is hoped for will last for a short time, and soon it will cause such disturbances that the latter state will become worse than the former. For by yielding, Satan never softens, but having seized this opportunity, he will become more and more ferocious and will rage against our churches, while even by this pact the enemies of truth are made more emboldened, and the weak are most grievously offended. But woe to the man through whom the scandal comes. Matt. 18.7. Finally, if those censors are so very concerned about political peace, why do they not also take more careful thought and concern for the political means by which this end can be legitimately attained? Certainly, for very many years, a most beautiful peace existed for our churches and the Papist churches, following the transaction of Passau, which they commonly call the Religious Pacification, where, however, in the use of adiaphoric matters, our churches used their liberty and did not yield even in the slightest. Let the politicians therefore think today of such a means, and let them leave our churches their liberty whole and inviolate.

But let these things suffice regarding this second rule, which will become clearer from the explanation of certain questions which, having dispatched the remaining rules that survive, we shall shortly subjoin.

The third rule, therefore, to be observed concerning the use of adiaphoric things is this: Outside the case of persecution and the need to issue a Confession, Christians have such a free use of things that are by nature adiaphoric in either direction (observance or abrogation) that they need not fear any scruple of conscience from it. For example: Someone may eat meat, cheese, butter, eggs, and similar things; he may also abstain from them without any injury to his conscience. But if any of the Papists should command abstinence from such foods, then the use of those things ceases to be adiaphoric and becomes necessary, and therefore now binds the conscience, because a Confession must now be issued and our liberty asserted against the Papist dominion, which they wish to arrogate to themselves over our consciences. Never, therefore, will an orthodox person who is and rejoices to be among the Freedmen of Christ consent to Papist laws concerning the celibacy of priests, or abstinence from the eating of meat, cheese, or eggs during the Lenten season. Likewise, he will never consent to Sacramentarian laws concerning the uprooting of images, the destroying of altars, the deauthorizing of figured and organ music, the abrogating of exorcism, the breaking of larger bread in the very act of the Eucharist, and similar things. For even if, outside the case of Confession, the use of these things is most free, and they can be abrogated as freely as they can be observed, nevertheless, because of the clandestine machinations of the enemies, it now begins to be necessary, as has been shown.

The fourth and final rule is as follows: In the use of adiaphoric things, no one should do anything with a wavering mind or a hesitating conscience. The Apostle delivers this rule in Rom. 14.5, saying: Let each one be satisfied in his own mind. For it does not befit us to be led by some superstition or to be carried away by inconsiderate rashness in the use of adiaphoric things, but all things must be directed toward obedience to the divine word and the glory of God, and must be performed with thanksgiving, and indeed from a certain faith, not at all a doubting one.

These rules having been explained, it remains for us to answer certain questions, the use of which pertains most to adiaphoric practice.

First, therefore, it is asked: Is it placed in the power and discretion of any Christian to observe or neglect at will the ecclesiastical laws established concerning adiaphora? The reason for doubting arises from the very nature of adiaphoric things, which consists in this, that they can be observed or neglected without injury to conscience. Hence, there have never been lacking those who, regarding the use of adiaphoric things, notwithstanding ecclesiastical ordinance, have thought that anything was permitted to them. But it is most correctly answered by a distinction of adiaphoric things, which are either considered in themselves and in their own proper nature, or insofar as they have been promulgated for observance by the consent of the whole Church for the sake of order, decorum, and edification. In the former way and respect, they are and remain adiaphora, that is, middle and indifferent things, which can be neglected just as they can be observed. In the latter way, however, it happens by accident that they change this nature and become necessary, not indeed by a simple and absolute necessity, but by a necessity of order and ecclesiastical mandate.

For when the Church, being situated outside the case of either persecution or the need to issue a Confession, out of the liberty which it enjoys in Christ, by a certain and grave counsel, changes or decrees or abrogates something concerning matters that are by their nature indifferent: and that indeed with the foreknowledge and consent of the whole assembly: there it would certainly be lawful for no one by their own daring to resist, and at their own pleasure either to abstain from those things which have been usefully ordained: or to recall into use those things which have been thus antiqued by grave counsel. For example: If the Lutheran Churches, outside the case of persecution or the need to issue a confession, having used their liberty, were to abrogate Exorcism, with the whole people consenting to this matter, having first been rightly and soundly informed about this matter: just as they most rightly determine that the liberty of abrogating this rite pertains to our Church: then certainly it would be lawful for no private person to recall the use of Exorcism into the Church after the fact. Thus, if in the same manner our Churches, in the use or action of the Eucharist, having abrogated the hosts or those smaller breads, were thereafter to employ a larger bread, or even a domestic one, made of wheat and rye, and to break it with their hands; again, it would be lawful for no private person, by their own daring and judgment, to resist these ordinances. But if, however, the Church, out of the liberty which it enjoys, observes the contrary, and retains both the Exorcism and the use of the hosts: then certainly it will again be permitted to no private person by their own motion and judgment to resist this Ecclesiastical observation in any way. The reason for this practice is this: That one must obey the Church when it is in this part legitimately, and for certain causes, ordaining something. But this practice does not have a place indefinitely and universally, in any case and time, but only then, when the Church freely uses its own right, and is situated outside the case of Confession. But when Adversaries demand such a change of indifferent matters, then the clearly contrary practice, both of the public Church and of every private person, is to be observed: as was shown in the exodus of the second Rule. But a new and slightly more difficult question arises here. For since concerning the use of indifferent matters one must always see what the Ecclesiastical Ordinance allows, it is not without merit now asked in particular: Whether the Gregorian Calendar, inasmuch as it was fashioned by the Church and confirmed by certain laws, can and ought to be received and observed with a good conscience? But the answer is in the negative: For the things which have already been answered are not to be extended to any and every church, and thus even to the Church of the Antichrist, which we are most persuaded is a synagogue of the malignant: but they pertain to that which holds the purity of the Gospel unblemished, and claims for itself no dominion over the consciences of men, but only looks into and weighs, and also decides by common counsel, what can contribute to edification, order, and decorum. Now, however, regarding the Gregorian Calendar, it first has as its author not the Roman Emperor, not the Electors,

Princes, Estates, and orders of the Empire, to whom the care of the Calendar principally pertains, and who, with no one easily contradicting, having called into counsel those skilled in history, mathematics, and theology, could undertake and promulgate an accurate correction of the Calendar: But the Roman Pontiff, the Son of perdition, nay, the very Antichrist himself, from whom whatever proceeds, even for this name, deserves to be and ought to be suspected by all pious and good men. And indeed this very Calendar was that ill-fated apple of discord, which, once thrown into the theater of the Church, the Roman Pontiff wickedly violated, nay, clearly destroyed, the public peace between the Pontificians and the Lutherans, which had been holily confirmed by the orders of the Empire: by which he also strove to re-establish in Germany the dominion he had long since lost: by almost the same artifice by which the Greeks once, through the Trojan horse admitted into the city, became the masters of the city itself. Then that wicked one urged the observation of this Calendar under absolute necessity. For thus the words of the Pontifical Bull held: Let it be permitted to no man at all to oppose: But if anyone shall have presumed to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty GOD, and of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul.

Latin:

labefactata libertate Evangelicâ, ipsa quoque religionis puritas male habeat, & vehementer periclitetur necesse est, id quod facilè intelligit, qui, quid sit Libertas Christiana, rectè cognitum, perspectumq; habet. Quâ in parte Politici ististupendam inscitiam & ruditatem produnt. Quid? quod de articulo fidei minimè postremo, hoc loco contenditur, nempe de Libertate Christiana. Hoc ergo Articulo dissoluto, & per errores sive abusum rupto, tota catena & series Articulorum Religionis Christianæ rumpatur, necesse est. Opponimus ergò nasutulis istis illud Nazianzeni: ἄλλοι μὲν ἔτω παιζέτωσαν: ἡμῖν δὲ ταῦτα παίζειν, οὐκ ἀσφαλὲς.

Posterior ratio planè est ἀθεόλογος. Nam si maximè commodum aliquod publicum exceffione istâ esset sperandum: tamen secundum authenticam Apostoli, Rom. 3.8. Non sunt facienda mala, ut eveniant bona. Videndum ergò prius, num salvâ cœlesti veritate aliquid in Religionis negotio, etiam quoad usum adiaphoricum, hostibus veritatis concedi possit: quàm sit bonum aliquod publicum & carnale multis amplificetur. Deinde hoc ipsum bonum, quod speratur, exiguo durabit tempore: & mox eas dabit turbas, ut postrema deteriora fiant prioribus. Cedendo enim nunquam mitesciti Satanas: sed hac arreptâ occasione magis magisq; ferocescet, inq; nostras sæviet Ecclesias: dum vel hoc pacto hostes veritatis redduntur animosiores: infirmi verò gravifsimè offenduntur: Væ autem homini, per quem venerit scandalum. Matth. 18. 7. Tandem si pace politicâ tantopere sunt solliciti censores isti: cur non de mediis etiam politicis, quibus ad hunc finem legitime perveniri queat, curam cogitationemq; suscipiunt accuratiorem? Certè annis quamplurimis nostris & Pontificiis Ecclesiis, ex transactione Passaviensi, quàm vulgò Pacificationem Religionis appellant, pulcerrima Pax constitit: ubi tamen in ulu rerum Adiaphorarum nostræ Ecclesiæ libertate suâ usæ, ne in minimo quidem cesserunt, De tali ergo medio cogitent hodie Politici: & Ecclesiis nostris libertatem suam relinquant integram & inviolatam.

Verùm de regulâ hac secundâ hæc sufficiant, quæ dilucidiora evadent ex quæstionum quarundam explicatione, quàm paulò pòst, expeditis reliquis, quæ supersunt regulis, subjiciemus.

TERTIA ergo regula circa usum rerum adiaphorarum observanda hæc est. Extra Casum persecutionis, & edendæ Confessionis, Christiani in rebus naturâ suâ adiaphoris tam liberum in utramvis partem (observationis & abrogationis) habent usum: ut nullum inde Conscientiæ scrupulum extimescere debeant. Exempli gratia: Potest aliquis vesci carnibus, caseo, butyro, ovis & similibus: potest etiam ab ijsdem abstinere, sine ullâ læsione conscientiæ. Quod si verò Pontificiorum aliquis mandet abstinentiam ab ejusmodi cibis, tum usus istarum rerum cessat esse adiaphorus, & sit necessarius, ac proinde jam obligat in Conscientia: propterea quòd jam edenda Confessio, & asserenda libertas nostra, contra Pontificiorum dominatum, quem sibi in conscientias nostras arrogare volunt. Nunquam ergò orthodoxus qui est & ex Libertis Christi esse gaudet, consentiet, in leges Pontificias, de Cœlibatu Sacerdotum, de abstinentiâ ab esu carnium, casei, ovorum, tempore Quadragesimali: Sic idem nunquam consentiet in leges Sacramentarias, de extirpandis imaginibus, destruendis altaribus, exautorando cantu figurali & organico, abrogando exorcismo: frangendo pane majore in ipsa actione Eucharisticâ, & similibus. Nam etsi extra Confessionis casum, rerum istarum usus est liberrimus, & tàm liberè abrogari, quàm observari potest: tamen propter clandestinas hostium molitiones jam incipit esse necessarius, ut ostensum.

QVARTA & postrema regula sic habet: in usu rerum adiaphorarum, nemo fluctuante animo, sive hæsitante conscientiâ, quicquam agere debet. Regulam hanc tradit Apostolus Rom. 14. 5. Quilibet, inquiens, animo duntaxat suo satisfaciat. Neque enim decet nos vel superstitione quadam duci, vel temeritate inconsideratâ rapi in usu rerum adiaphorarum: sed ad obsequium verbi divini, & ad gloriam DEI dirigenda, cumœ gratiarum actione peragenda sunt omnia, & quidem ex fide certâ, miniméœ dubitante.

Regulis istis explicatis, superest, ut ad Quæstiones quasdam respondeamus, quarum usus ad praxin adiaphoricam maximè pertinet.

Primùm ergò quæritur: An in cujuslibet Christiani potestate, & arbitrio sit positum, leges Ecclesiasticas de adiaphoris sancitas pro lubitu vel observare, vel negligere? Ratio dubitandi emergit ex ipsâ naturâ rerum adiaphorarum, quæ in eo est posita, ut sine læsione conscientiæ, vel observari vel negligi possunt. Unde nunquam defuerunt, qui circa usum rerum adiaphorarum, non obstante ordinatione Ecclesiastica, quidvis sibi licere arbitrari sunt. Verùm rectissimè respondetur per distinctionem rerum adiaphorarum, quæ vel considerantur per se, & in naturâ suâ propriâ: vel quatenus ordinis, decori, & ædificationis causâ consensu totius Ecclesiæ ad observandum sunt promulgatæ. Priore modo ac respectu, sunt & manet adiaphoræ, hoc est, res mediæ & indifferentes, quæ tam negligi, quàm observari possunt. Posteriore autem modo sit ex Accidente ut naturam hanc mutent, & evadant necessariæ, non quidem necessitate simplici & absoluta, sed necessitate Ordinis & mandati Ecclesiastici.

Cùm enim Ecclesia, extra casum vel persecutionis, vel edendæ Confessionis constituta, ex Libertate, quâ in Christo fruitur, certo, graviq; consilio, circa res, naturâ suâ adiaphoras, aliquid mutat vel decernit, vel abrogat: & id quidem præscio ac consentiente universo cœtu: ibi profectò nemini fas fuerit proprio ausu contraniti, & pro libitu vel abstinere ab iis, quæ utiliter sunt ordinata: vel in usum revocare, gravi consilio sic sunt antiquata. Exempli gratia: Si Ecclesiæ Lutheranæ, extra casum persecutionis, aut edendæ confessionis, libertate sua usæ, abrogarent Exorcismum, hanc in rem consentiente universo populo, prius hac de re rectè ac solidè informato: quemadmodum sanè hbertatem abrogandi hunc ritum nostræ Ecclesiæ ad se pertinere rectissimè statuunt: tum sanè nemini privato fas foret, usum Exorcismi postliminiò in Ecclesiam revocare. Sic si eodem pacto Ecclesiæ nostræ in usu sive actione Eucharisticâ, ab rogatis hostiis, sive panibus illis minutioribus, deinceps panem majorem, vel etiam domesticum, triticeum, ac siligineum adhibendum, éumq; manibus frangendum, adhiberent; rursus privato nemini fas foret, proprio ausu ac arbitrio ordinationi hus istis resistere. Quod si verò Ecclesia ex libertate, quâ fruitur, contrarium observet, & tùm Exorcismum, tùm hostiarum usum retineat: tum certè nemini rursus privato licebit proprio motu & arbitrio observationi huic Ecclesiasticæ quovis modo reluctari. Ratio hujus praxeos hæc est: Quòd Ecclesiæ hac in parte legitimo modò, certasq; ob causas aliquid ordinanti est obtemperandum.
