Habet verò hæc praxis non indefinitè ac universaliter, quovis casu ac tempore, sed tùm demùm locum, quando Ecclesia suo jure liberè utitur, & extra Confessionis casum est constituta. Quando autem, Adversarii talem mutationem Adiaphororum exigunt, tum contraria planè praxis, & Ecclesiæ publicæ, & privato cuiq; est observanda: uti in diexodo Regulæ secundæ fuit ostensum. Sed nova hîc, & paulò difficilior oritur quæstio. Cùm enim circa usum rerum adiaphorarum semper videndum, quid ferat Ordinatio Ecclesiastica, haud immeritò in specie jam quæritur: An Calendarium Gregorianum,quippe ab Ecclesia confectum,& certis legibus confirmatum, recipi & observari boná conscientia possit & debeat? Respondetur autem negate: Nam, quæ jam responsa sunt, non ad quamvis, & sic ad Antichristi etiam Ecclesiam sunt extendenda, quam Synagogam malignantium esse, habemus persuasissimum: sed ad eam pertinent, quæ puritatem Evangelij tenet illibatam, nullumq; sibi in conscientias hominum dominatum vendicat? sed tantùm dispicit ac expendit, communicatio etiam consilio decernit, quid ad ædificationem, ordinem, & decorum facere possit. Jam verò quoad Calendarium Gregorianum, illud primùm autorem habet non Imperatorem Romanum, non Electores,

Principes, Status, atque ordines Imperij, ad quos Cura Calendarij principaliter pertinet, quique nemine facilè contradicente in consilium adhibitis peritis & historicis, & Mathematicis, & Theologis accuratam Calendarij correctionem suscipere & promulgare possent: Sed Romanum Pontificem, Filium perditionis, imò ipsissimum Antichristum, à quo, quicquid proficiscitur, vel hoc nomine meritò piis ac bonis quibusq; suspectum esse & videri debet. Et profectò hoc ipsum Calendarium erat infaustum illud pomum ἔριδος, quo in theatrum Ecclesiæ projecto, pacem publicam inter Pontificios & Lutheranos, ab ordinibus Imperii sanctè confirmatam, nefariè violavit, imò planè sustulit Pontifex Romanus: quo item dominatum jampridem amissum, in Germania rursum stabilire studuit: eodem fermè artificio, quo olim Græci per equum Trojanum, intra urbem admissum, ipsius urbis Domini evaserunt. Deinde ursit Calendarij hujus observatio nem Nequam iste, sub absolutâ necessitate. Sic enim habebant verba Bullæ Pontificalis: Nulli omnino hominum liceat contraire: Si quis autem hoc attentare præsumserit, indignationem Omnipotentis DEI, & beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum ejus, se noverit incursurum.


### Caput II. On the Right and Legitimate Use of Adiaphorous Things: Fourth rule concerning adiaphora (continued)

Which necessity certainly snatches away all liberty from Christians, and changes it into the most wretched servitude. Thirdly, the promulgation of this Calendar overturned the rights and privileges of the Transaction of Passau, or the Pragmatic Sanction: which simply took away from the Roman Pontiff all jurisdiction in Ecclesiastical causes toward the Protestant Churches, or those addicted to the Augsburg Confession: or at least suspended it until a general Concord in Religion. Fourthly: It is the common opinion of all wise men that no change is to be instituted in a Republic unless either its evident utility appears, or at least the necessity of an inevitable evil. But neither was to be hoped for from the promulgation of that Calendar; which the event itself, and experience, the Teacher of fools, has, alas, sufficiently proven: while through its violent imposition, very many most flourishing Republics were gravely shaken and troubled: and not a few were even so scattered and distracted that the minds of the citizens will scarcely ever again coalesce into the mutual bond of peace and former love. And from the observation of the old Julian Calendar, there will be no danger at all to be feared. For although it is not lacking in every anomaly or error: which, even with the Pontiff silent, our own theologians and mathematicians have long since observed, yet, as our B. LUTHER speaks, that Astronomical solecism is not of such moment that, without the consent and approval of the whole Empire, some new Calendar should be forged, with the old and commonly received Ephemerides abrogated in all respects, and thrust upon the Church of GOD to be observed under the thunderbolt of an Anathema.

Fifthly, this very Gregorian and novel correction of the Calendar is not without its own gross errors; a fact which has been demonstrated by our mathematicians several times, clearly and visibly. Finally, since according to this Calendar all the feasts and sacred rites proper to the Roman Synagogue, all the worship of fictitious saints, the merits of fasts, the invocations of the dead, and the other Papal idolatrous ἐθελύγματα (will-worships) are performed, surely the mere reception of this Calendar seems to carry with it some approval of this idolatry.

Therefore, someone might further ask, are all those Churches and Republics that follow the Gregorian Calendar to be judged as participating in Papal idolatry?

By no means: For 1. Our decision concerns those Churches which could have used their liberty, but in order to curry favor with the Antichrist, consented to the observation of this Calendar, with no necessity compelling them. These certainly share in the sins of others and participate not lightly in the universal Papal idolatry. Furthermore, we also understand our aforementioned censure to apply to those who flatter the Roman Pontiff to such an extent that they not only use this Calendar in civil matters, but also celebrate according to it idolatrous feasts, such as the Feast of Corpus Christi, the Nativity and Assumption of Mary, the Chair of Peter, the Invention of the Cross, Sebastian, Fabian, Urban, Kilian, Margaret, Anne, the Exaltation of the Cross, Catherine, Cosmas, Damian, and the like, under the plausible pretext that, with idolatrous worships neglected, they are proposing other biblical texts that serve for the edification of the people. With what conscience this can be done, and how it undermines Christian liberty, nay, betrays and prostitutes the truth of the Gospel, has been sufficiently shown thus far. Let some Calvinists, however, see what accounts they will one day have to render to the most just Judge of mortals, because, provided they can make an attack on some Church or obtain some fief, they consent with too loose a liberty both to the reception of this Calendar and to other idolatrous rites.

Just as, therefore, we judge these to sin gravely, so we pass a milder sentence on those Churches to whom, against their will and compelled by a superior Magistrate to whom they are immediately subject, such an observation is forced by manifest violence. In this case, certainly, as the Church cannot use its right and liberty, with external Tyranny standing in the way, so it consults its conscience more rightly when it bears this violence brought by the Magistrate patiently, than if, by stubbornly resisting, it violates the laws of obedience and subjection and incurs the crime of sedition: provided it has established that no change or depravation of the purer Religion is sought under this pretext, but that its free exercise is left by the Magistrate. In this case, it suffices for the purer Church to have testified publicly by protesting: 1. concerning its dissent, 2. that it consented to the reception of the Calendar not for the sake of the Pontiff, but of the Ordinary Magistrate, 3. that it does not wish even a hair's breadth to be changed in the articles of the Christian Religion, but would rather pour out life and blood than permit damage to be inflicted upon religion under this indifferent matter. The Jewish Church under the Babylonian captivity can be an example, which, despoiled of its liberty and right, was forced to accommodate itself to the custom of the Babylonians and to bear and omit many things which it would never have permitted in its free state. But it should be the duty of the Ministers of the Church, above all, not to incite the people to sedition with tribunitian harangues, much less to deny all obedience simply to the political Magistrate in this matter; least of all in this case to desert the sheep committed to their faith and, having formed a column—that is, having drawn others into their society—to break out, to provide the Wolf with an opportunity to invade the flock, and to write a summons publicly against the Magistrate under some pretext of Law; but rather to tolerate this violence patiently and to incite their hearers to the same virtue; and to devote effort so that they may be more rightly informed against Papal idolatry; nay, to be urged to prayers, by which they may obtain a better mind for the Magistrate and greater liberty for themselves, meanwhile committing every outcome to GOD and giving thanks that, under this very external violence, it is still permitted to enjoy a purer exercise of religion.

With these things thus explained, it is clearly evident: 1. What is the true and genuine use of Christian liberty. 2. How one sins in this matter by defect and by excess. Speaking summarily: One sins by defect when indifferent things are used with an opinion of necessity, worship, and merit.

But in excess: 1. By rashness, when Christian liberty is converted into a vague license for all crimes, or the consideration of the weak is not taken. In this way, those who are accustomed to attend the idolatrous rites of the Papists in Spain or Italy today sin gravely, or observe the fasts prescribed by the Pontiff, or in similar things, under the pretext of Christian liberty, associate themselves with the Papists. To whom it usually happens that, later, endowed with the judgment of confirmation, they feel the sting of conscience throughout their whole life; not a few are snatched away into more serious temptations; some even despair entirely. Furthermore, one sins in excess regarding indifferent matters by too much rigor and profanity, after the example of the Sacramentarians, who, being rigid censors of Ecclesiastical Ceremonies, judge that almost all indifferent matters must be eliminated, even with the use of the axe and hatchet, as the Calvinist practice has shown thus far.

Finally, on the side of excess, one also sins by Remissness of spirit, or by excessive pusillanimity, by which one yields to Adversaries either in receiving new adiaphora or in abolishing customary ones. In this way, yielding and sinning occurred more than twenty years ago in this very Saxon Electorate by certain Theologians, who, for the sake of the Crypto-Calvinists, preferred to approve the abolition of Exorcism by their own calculation rather than to suffer the loss of prebends and positions by resisting. For if a defector and traitor to his country is usually considered one who secretly colludes and conspires with the enemy in the camp, certainly he must be considered a much greater traitor to Evangelical truth who, when one ought to stand most firmly in the battle line against the enemies of truth, colludes with them by yielding. A good man would certainly never tolerate such a wife who, while professing in words that she owes faith to her husband, meanwhile prostitutes her body to another. What, therefore, shall we judge of those Vertumni who, in a time of persecution and of making a Confession, do not fear to yield to the enemies of truth regarding the use of Evangelical liberty out of mere pusillanimity.

In this very way, yielding and sinning occurred most gravely at the time of the Interim συμβάζεως, when certain Theologians, for the sake of the Romanist Bishops, permitted those rites to be introduced into the Church of GOD which savored not obscurely of Roman Idolatry. And indeed, this yielding was joined with so much greater inconvenience and danger to the Lutheran Church as the persecution from the Romanists was then more threatening; indeed, as much more vehemently the purity of heavenly doctrine was then in peril. For 1. it was not, as some were then falsely persuaded, a matter of receiving certain adiaphora, truly and properly so called, but of such things as were joined with manifest superstition, as the Synodal Acts published by the counsel and opinion of Philippus and his Colleagues in the year 1559, printed by Georgius Rhavv, testify. Such, indeed, were: Extreme Unction; Salt and Candle in the administration of Baptism; Quatern. Tt. fac. 4. a. The entire form of the Mass: provided that clearly impious things are rejected. Tt. The daily celebration of masses and communion for the people: But if there are none to communicate, nevertheless those things which are wont to be piously sung in the Mass are to be chanted, except for the consecration: Likewise the use of candles, the ringing of bells, the restoration of images: the anointing of those to be ordained: Vigils, and indeed after the burial, provided that superstitious prayers and Ceremonies are omitted, and other songs and prayers are substituted. ibid. The feast of the body of Christ: provided that the theatrical procession with the Sacrament is omitted: Yy. fac. 3. The fast of the fifth and sixth day of every week, and of the whole of Lent. Xx. fac. 3. and similar impious and superstitious rites, which at the time of the Reformation were, by most wholesome counsel, exploded and dismissed from the Church of GOD as idolatry. When Philippus urged that these, therefore, should be received back into the Church for the sake of the Romanists, he was rightly rebuked by Illyricus and others because he did not walk with a straight foot toward the truth of the Gospel and its inseparable companion, the assertion of Christian liberty. Furthermore, the ceremonies already enumerated were not received by the consent of the whole Church, but were thrust upon it by force and fraud by the Roman Antichrist and by those who fawned upon him; in whose footsteps the younger Theologians followed, kissing the tenets of their teacher like mere oracles, in the manner of the Pythagoreans. Thirdly, those ceremonies did nothing πρός εὐταξίαν, but rather disturbed it and drove those who contradicted them into exile. Fourthly, they did not serve Ecclesiastical Decorum. For what, I pray, is that εὐχημοσύνη, when Mass-gesticulations are seen in temples: when banners are carried around in cemeteries like bacchants: when a wooden Cross is laid into a sepulcher: when a statue placed upon a donkey is carried around: and other trifles of this kind, and a theater more histrionic than ecclesiastical, are recalled into use? Finally, they contributed nothing πρός οἰκοδομὴν; but rather destroyed all faith, piety, and sincerity; they bound men in Conscience: they changed ancient readings and chants: they burdened the Church with a new yoke of servitude: they approved abuses long since overthrown: they permitted the Pope access to our Churches: they placed stumbling blocks before the weak: they handed over to the Antichrist authority over Christ, that is, over his spouse the Church: and to speak summarily, they strove to associate Christ and Belial, light and darkness, the temple of GOD and idols, believers and unbelievers, truth and falsehood, that is, to join two most diverse Religions into one body under a beautiful Concord. With what face, therefore, with what faith, with what Conscience, did those Theologians not fear to affirm that it was a matter of only a few adiaphora, and those indeed of no great moment? What of the fact that the yielding to the Romanists went so far that even in the very Articles of faith, those pusillanimous Theologians accommodated themselves to the style of the Roman curia, using phrases that utterly abhor the ὑποτυπώ- σει ὑγιαινόντων λόγων: Such as are:

1. Good works are necessary for salvation and righteousness before GOD.

2. It is impossible for anyone to be justified or saved without good works.

3. No one is ever justified without good works.

4. No one is saved without love and good works.

5. It is most true that these virtues, Faith, love, hope, and others are necessary for salvation: Or as the German Leipzig Conclusion has it: It is certainly true that these virtues, faith, love, and hope, and others, must be in us, and are necessary for salvation.

6. The dispute is not about the particle ALONE: but we say,

Latin:

Quæ certè necessitas Libertatem omnem Christianis eripit, & in tristissimam servitutem commutat. Tertiò Calendarij hujus promulgatio evertebat jura ac privilegia Transactionis Passaviensis,sive Sanctionis Pragmaticæ: quæ Pontifici Romano omnem jurisdictionem in causis Ecclesiasticis erga Ecclesias Protestantes, sive Augustanæ Confessioni addictas, simpliciter ademit: vel certè su spendit usque ad generalem in Religione Concordiam. Quartò: Omnium sapientum communis est sententia, Nullam in Repub. mutationem esse instituendam, nisi vel evidens ejus appareat utilitas, vel certè inevitabilis mali necessitas. Atqui neutrum ex Calendarij istius promulgatione erat sperandum; id quod eventus ipse, & experientia, Stultorum Magistra, satis, proh dolor, comprobavit: dum per violentam ejus incrustationem benè multæ florentissimæ Respub. graviter concussæ & turbatæ: non nullæ etiam ita disjectæ & distractæ fuerunt, ut civium animi vix unquam ampliùs in mutuum pacis ac amoris pristini vinculum sint coalituri. Et ex veteris Juliani Calendarij observatione, nihil prorsuspericuli erit metuendum. Etsi enim non omni anomaliâ sive errore illud caret: id quod, tacente etiam Pontifice, nostrates & Theologi, & Mathematici jamdudum observarunt, non tamen, uti B. LUTHERUS noster loquitur, Solæcis mus ille Astronomicus tanti est momenti, ut sine totius Imperij consensu & approbatione, Novum aliquod Calendarium, abrogatis per omnia veteribus, & vulgò receptis Ephemeridibus cudatur, & sub Anathematis fulmine ad observandum Ecclesiæ DEI obtrudatur.

Quintò hæc ipsa quoque Gregoriana, & novella Calendarij correctio, suis crassis erroribus non caret; id quod à nostris Mathematicis aliquoties evidenter, & ad oculum est demonstratum. Tandem, cùm secundum Calendarium hoc, omnia festa & sacra Synagogæ Romanæ propria, omnes Divorum fictitiorum cultus: Jejuniorum merita: Defunctorum invocationes, & cætera Idolomaniæ Pontificæ ἐθελύγματα peragantur: certè vel sola hæc Calendarij istius receptio, aliquam idolomaniæ hujus approbationem præ se ferre videtur.

Ergóne, quærat porrò aliquis, omnes illæ Ecclesiæ, & Respublicæ, quæ Calendarium Gregorianum sequuntur, participare de Idolomaniâ Pontificiâ censendæ sunt?

Minimè vero: Nam 1. Decisio nostra eas attinet Ecclesias, quæ libertate sua uti potuissent, sed ut palpum facerent Antichristo, in Calendarij hujus observationem, nulla cogente necessitate, consenserunt. Hæ certè peccatis alienis communicant, & de universâ Idolomaniâ Pontificia haud leviter participant Deinde de illis quoque censuram nostram superiorem intelligimus, qui usq; adeò Romano Pontifici adulantur, ut non in civilibus modò Calendarium hoc usurpent, sed & secundum illud festa Idololatrica, quale est Festum Corporis Christi: Nativitatis & Assumtionis Mariæ, Cathedræ Petri, Inventionis Crucis, Sebastiani, Fabiani, Vrbani, Kiliani, Margaretæ, Annæ, Exaltationis Crucis, Catharinæ, Cosmæ, Damiani, & similia celebrent, sub plau sibili schemate, se neglectis cultibus Idololatricis, textus alios biblicos, ædificationi plebis inservientes proponere. Quod quâ Conscientiâ fieri possit, & quomodo Libertatem Christianam labefactet, imò veritatem Evangelij prodat & prostituat hactenus sufficienter ostensum. Viderint autem Calviniæni nonnulli, quas aliquando justissimo mortalium judici reddituri sint rationes, quòd, modò impetum in Ecclesiam aliquam facere, vel feudo aliquo potiri possint, tùm in receptionem hujus Calendarij, tùm in ritus alios idololatricos laxâ nimis libertate consentiunc.

Quemadmodum ergô hos graviter peccare statuimus: ita mitiorem ferimus sententiam de illis Ecclesiis, quibus invitis & coactis à superiore Magistratu, cui immediatè sunt subjectæ, per manifestam vim talis observatio obtruditur. Hoc certè casu, uti Ecclesia jure & libertate sua uti non potest, externâ obstante Tyrannide: ita Conscientiæ rectius consulit, quando vim hanc à Magistratu illatam patienter ferat, quàm si contumaciôs reluctando, Obedientiæ & subjectionis leges violet, & Seditionis crimen incurrat: modò illud constitutum habeat, nullam sub hoc prætextu, Religionis purioris immutationem aut depravationem quæri; sed à Magistratu liberum ejus exercitium relinqui. Hoc casu sufficit Ecclesiam puriorem protestando publicè testatam esse. 1. de suo dissensu, 2. quòd non in gratiam Pontificis: sed Magistratus Ordinarij tandem in receptionem Calendarij consenserit. 3. quòd ne latum quidem pilum, in capitibus Religionis Christianæ immutatum velit: sed vitam ac sanguinem profundere malit, quàm permittere, ut sub hoc adiaphoro, Religioni damnum inferatur. Exemplo potest esse Ecclesia Judaica, sub captivitate Babylonicâ, quæ libertate & jure suo spoliata, ad Babyloniorum consuetudinem se accommodare, & multa ferre, ac omittere coacta fuit, quæ in libero suo statu nunquàm permisisset. Cumprimis autem Ministrorum Ecclesiæ fuerit, non tribunitijs cancionibus ad seditionem plebem concitare: nedum Magistratui politico hac in parte omnem simpliciter obedientiam denegare: minimè omnium hoc casu, oves suæ fidei commissas deserere, & agmine facto, hoc est, in societatem suam pertractis alis, erumpere, Lupo gregem invadendi occasionem præbe. re, & sub nescio quâ specie Juris Magistratui publicè dicam scribere: sed patienter potiùs hanc vim tolerare, & suos ad eandem virtutem incitare Auditores: operamq; dare, ut adversus Idolomaniam Pontificiam rectiùs illi informentur; imò ad preces instigentur, quibus & Magistratui mentem meliorem, sibi ipsis verò majorem libertatem impetrent: DEO interim omnem eventum committentes, & gratias agentes, quòd sub hac ipsâ externa vi, puriore tamen Religionis exercitio frui liceat.

His ita explicatis, perspicuè constat: Quisnam verus & genuinus usus sit Libertatis Christianæ. 2. Quomodo in defectu, & inexcessu hac in parte peccetur. Summatim loquendo: In defectu peccatur, quando rebus adiaphoris affuitur Opinione necessitatis, cultus, & meriti.

In excessu verò. 1. Temeritate, quando Libertas Christiana in vagam omnium scelerum licentiam convertitur: vel infirmorum ratio non habetur. Quo pacto hodie graviter peccant, qui in Hispania aut Italiâ interesse solent Sacris Pontificiorum Idololatricis: vel jejunia à Pontifice præscripta observant: vel in similibus, sub prætextu Libertatis Christianæ, Pontificiis se adsociant. Quibus plærunque usu venire solet, ut postmodùm judicio confirmatione præditi, per omnem vitam conscientiæ morsum sentiant: haud pauci in graviores tentationes abripiantur: aliqui planè etiam desperent. Deinde verò in excessu circa adiaphora peccatur nimio rigore & prophanitate, exemplo Sacramentariorum, qui nimirum rigidi Ceremoniarum Ecclesiasticarum censores, omnia fermè Adiaphora eliminanda esse judicant, adhibitâ etiam bipeani, ac securi: uti praxis Calviniana hactenus ostendit.

Tandem ex parte excesus peccatur etiam Remissione animi, sive nimiâ pusillanimitate, quâ Adversariis vel in recipiendis novis, vel in abrogandis usitatis adiaphoris, ceditur. Quo pacto cessum & peccatum fuit ante annos viginti ampliüs in hoc ipso Electoratu Saxonico à quibusdam Theologis, qui in gratiam Crypto-Calvinistarum maluerunt abrogationemExorcismi suo calculo approbare, quàm reluctando præbendarum & conditionum jacturam facere. Nam si transfuga, ac proditor patriæ haberi solet, qui in castris cum hoste occultè colludit & conspirat: certè multò magis veritatis Evangelicæ proditor haberi debet, qui quando contra hostes veritatis in acie maximè esse standum, cedendo cum iisdem colludit. Vir certè bonus nunquàm talem ferret uxorem, quæ fidem quidem marito se debere verbis profiteatur: sed interim Corpus suum alij etiam prostituat. Quid ergò judicabimus de illis Vertumnis, qui tempore perfecutionis, & edendæ Confessionis, hostibus veritatis, circa usum libertatis Evangelicæ, ex merâ pusillanimitate, cedere non verentur.

Hoc ipso pacto cessum & peccatum gravissimè fuit, tempore συμβάζεως Inter misticæ, ubi Theologi quidam in gratiam Episcoporum Romanensium, in Ecclesiam DEI eos introduci ritus permiserunt: qui Romanam Idololatriam haud obscurè sapieebent. Et profectò cessio hæc tantò majore cum incommodo & periculo Ecclesiæ Lutheranæ erat conjuncta: quantò gravior tùm imminebat ex parte Romanensium persecutio: imò quantò vehementiùs puritas doctrinæ cœlestis tùm periclitabatur. Nam 1. non, uti nonnullis falsò tùm persuasum erat, negocium erat de recipiendis quibusdam adiaphoris, verè ac propriè sic dictis: sed de ejusmodi rebus, quæ cum manifestâ superstitione erant conjunctæ: uti testantur Acta Synodica edita de consilio & sententiâ Philippi, & Collegarum, Anno 1559. typis Georgij Rhavv. Tales utique erant, Unctio extrema: Sal & Cereus in administratione Baptismi: Quatern. Tt. fac. 4. a. Forma Missæ integra: modò planè impia reijciantur. Tt. Quotidiana missarum celebratio, & ad populum communicatio: Quod si nulla sint, qui communicent, nihilominus tamen accinantur, quæ in Missâ piè cani solent, exceptâ consecratione: Item usus candelarum, tintinnabulorum increpatio, imaginum restauratio: inunctio Ordinandorum: Vigiliæ, & quidem post sepulturam modò superstitiosæ preces, & Ceremoniæ omittantur, & cantiones ac preces aliæ substituantur. ibid. Festum corporis Christi: modò omittatur theatrica processio cum Sacramento: Yy. fac. 3. Jejunium quintæ & sextæ diei, cujusvis septimanæ, & totius Quadragesimæ. Xx. fac. 3. & similes ritus impij & superstitiosi,qui tempore Reformationis saluberrimo consilio, tanquam idololatriæ ex Ecclesiâ DEI fuerunt explosi, & exauctorati. Hos ergò cum in gratiam Romanensium denuò in Ecclesiam recipiendos esse, suaderet Philippus, rectè ab Illyrico & aliis reprehensus, quòd recto pede ad veritatem Evangelij, & hujus individuam comitem, libertatem Christianam asserendam, non incedat. Deinde ceremoniæ jam enumeratæ non recipiebantur consensu totius Ecclesiæ, sed obtrudebantur per vim ac fraudes ab Antichristo Romano, & ab iis, qui illi palpum faciebant: quorum vestigiis insistebant juniores Theologi, Pytagoreorum more, præceptoris placita, tanquàm mera oracula, exosculati. Tertiò ceremoniæ illæ nihil faciebant πρός εὐταξίαν, sed hanc potiùs turbabant, & contradicentes in exilium pellebant. Quartò non inserviebant Decoro Ecclesiastico. Quæ enim, obsecro, ea est εὐχημοσύνη, quando Missaticæ gesticulationes in templis conspiciuntur: quando vexilla circumferuntur in cemiteriis, instar bacchantium: quando Crux lignea deponitur in sepulchrum: quando statua asino imposita circumvehitur: & alia hujus generis ludicra, & theatrum magis histrionicum, quàm Ecclesiasticum decentia, in usum revocantur? Tandem nihil conferebant πρός οἰκοδομὴν; sed potiùs omnem fidem, pietatem, & sinceritatem destruebant; obligabant homines in Conscientiâ: mutabant veteres lectiones & cantilenas: novo servitutis jugo Ecclesiam onerabant: approbabant abusus jampridem profligatos: aditum permittebant Pontifici ad nostras Ecclesias: scandala ponebant infirmis: Antichristo tradebant imperium super Christum, hoc est, super ejus sponsam Ecclesiam: & summatim loquendo, Christum & Belial, lucem & tenebras, templum DEI & idola, fideles & infideles, veritatem & mendacium consociare, hoc est, Religiones duas diversifsimas sub pulchrâ Concordiâ in unum corpus coagmentare studebat. Quâ ergo fronte,quâ fide,quâ Conscientiâ, de nonnullis tantùm, & quidem haud magni momenti adiaphoris negotium esse, Theologi isti assirmare non sunt veriti? Quid, quòd usque adeò cessum fuit Romanensibus, ut in ipsis etiam Articulis fidei, se accommodarent pusillanimes isti Theologi, ad stylum curiæ Romanæ, iis usi phrasibus,quæ ab ὑποτυπώσει ὑγιαινόντων λόγων penitùs abhorrent: Quales sunt:

1. Bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem & justitiam coram DEO.

2. Impossibile est absque bonis operibus quenquam justificari aut salvari.

3. Nemo est unquàm sine bonis operibus justificatus.

4. Nemo sine dilectione & bonis operibus salvatur.

5. Verissimum est, has virtutes, Fidem, dilectionem, spem & alias ad salutem esse necessarias: Vel ut habet Conclusio Lipsica Germanica: Es ist gewislich war/ dz diese Tugenden/ Glaube/ Lieb/ vnd Hoffnung/ vnd andere/ in vns seyn müssen/ vnd zur Seeligkeit nötig seyn.

6. Non pugnatur de particulâ SOLA: sed dicimus,


### Caput II. On the Right and Legitimate Use of Adiaphorous Things: On the Errors fighting with nature, and of the true use of adiaphoral matters

that it is necessary that both other virtues and a good purpose be begun and remain in us.

Concerning which excellent little flowers and emblems, let the Acta Synodica be seen, Quatern, Ff. Kk. 3. Oo. 2. T. 4. b. etc.

It is evident, indeed, from this, not only that those theologians deserve praise and commendation who, in the time of the Augsburg Sphinx, or the Interimistic period, preferred to suffer and undergo every extreme rather than consent to such a concession, or in any way approve the timidity of the theologians: but also that it is certainly joined with the greatest danger, and with the depravation and loss of the purer religion, as soon as one yields to the enemies of the truth, and for their sake anything is changed regarding the use of indifferent things, either in one direction or in both.

CHAPTER III. Concerning errors conflicting with the nature and true use of indifferent things.

It is evident from those things which have been discussed thus far concerning the nature and true use of indifferent things, by how many parasangs the Evangelical doctrine differs PRIMARILY from Popery in this chapter of Christian doctrine: How great, likewise, is the mass of abominations with which the Papal Lerna teems in this one chapter. For 1. It urges necessity in indifferent things: 2. It establishes divine worship in them. 3. It seeks merit. 4. It constitutes perfection. 5. It exceeds the measure, or moderation: 6. It labors under a Mosaic κακοζηλίᾳ, and sometimes even a theatrical levity. 7. It assumes authority over consciences for itself. 8. It instructs bishops with foreign power, and grants them dominion over the very souls of men. 9. For the sake of obtaining the yoke of ceremonies, it spares no cruelty and savagery. 10. Finally, it places the unity of the Catholic Church in the conformity of these things, against that canonical rule of antiquity: The dissonance of ceremonies does not destroy the consonance of faith.

Then, the Calvinists differ from the purity of Christian doctrine in this chapter, who reject things free by their nature and indifferent to observe, as impious, profane, and superstitious, without distinction, and proscribe them from the Church in such a way that they might seem to have sworn a war clearly ἀσπονδον against the entire class of indifferent things: so that they do not even spare the celebration of the more solemn festivals; but, as interpreted by Daneau, lib. 2. of Christian Ethics, page 166. b., they do not fear to write: The ancients, indeed, in order to show that all things which are narrated by the Evangelists concerning the birth, passion, resurrection, etc., of Christ are true, therefore piously observed the memory of that event and the time in which they had been performed. But for us today, it is not at all necessary to observe the same days, with whom there is no business with heathens, or those who deny that Christ suffered or was born. Therefore, it is neither necessary nor even worth the effort to honor or observe those days. And hence, indeed, in the churches of the Calvinists, those solemn festivals of the Conception,

of the Nativity, the Apparition, the Resurrection, the Ascension of Christ: Likewise: The solemnity of Pentecost, of the Trinity, and other festivals of that kind, have been entirely relegated, and indeed under that pretty scheme, that in ancient times they were celebrated only because of heathens or heretics who denied these histories. As if, indeed, greater consideration had not been taken, and should not still be taken, for the Christians and believers themselves, especially the simpler ones: so that from that more solemn meditation on the mysteries of the faith, they might be so much the more rightly instructed and confirmed in the business of faith and salvation. This practice of the Calvinist Church does not contain itself only within its own borders: but it does not hesitate to invade, disturb, and disrupt the boundaries of other churches. The twenty-fourth year is now passing since, in this our illustrious Saxon Electorate, certain Crypto-Calvinists, under the scheme of Exorcism, caused clearly schismatic disturbances. Now, the reason for that ceremony, hitherto used by the Reformed churches under the assessment of ἀδιαφορίας, is indeed very well known to us. This is what ecclesiastical practice itself teaches, while under the most beautiful consensus of doctrine and the purest consonance of faith, other churches, throughout upper Germany, have long since abolished that rite: but ours retain it. But it is evident under what pretext of necessity, by what snares for depraving the purer doctrine, by what feigned concord to be established in the most diverse doctrine, by what treachery of counsel for overturning the Lutheran churches, the act of that tragedy was undertaken, so that the necessity of fighting for our churches has weighed upon us not more for the rite of Exorcism than for hearth and home.

The neighboring Anhaltines played the same story in the rest of the class of indifferent things, the Hessians still play it, and certain new disturbers of the Brandenburg Electorate, the champions of the Libertine race, who, so that they might not seem to have accomplished nothing in reforming religion, thought that the Adiaphoristic war must be restored. Therefore, as if in a formed battle line, equipped with axes, hatchets, crowbars, and other weapons worthy of such a Reformation, they rushed into the temples, and with the greatest zeal demolished altars, crosses, painted and sculpted images, musical organs, figured chant, the entire use of the Latin language: the uncovering of the head at the name of Christ, as well as kneeling, the customary division of the Decalogue, the sign of the Cross, lights, the garment of the linen vestment, and detested them simply as impious rites. In the Lord’s Supper they have exterminated golden and silver chalices, the form and matter of the Eucharistic bread, the unbroken distribution, the presentation to the mouth of the communicants, and the private communion of the sick and prisoners. And to exercise this intemperance of theirs, they have disturbed Republics with a Carlostadian spirit, shaken most peaceful Churches, devastated Schools and Academies, and, to speak briefly, have at last brought the matter to such a point that it must be said of them what the Synod of Rimini once wrote to the Emperor Constantius concerning the Arians: That the things brought forward by these men are likely to bring incredulity to the faithful and cruelty to the infidels.

And yet these are those fine little brothers, who, having cast aside all ecclesiastical discord, desire that we coalesce with them into a bond of fraternity: I know not whether they are deluding themselves more than us, or rather, what seems more likely, mocking GOD himself in the Heavens. May GOD paternally grant this people a right mind, and when they have been converted, true fellowship with the Orthodox Church, and constant fraternity. This will come to pass if they cease to persistently pull the rope of contention in these adiaphora, following the footsteps of pious antiquity, from which Augustine wrote: In those matters about which the divine Scripture has established no certain prescription, the custom of the people of GOD or the institutions of the ancestors are to be held as law. If we wish to dispute about these things, and to disapprove of others based on the custom of others, an interminable struggle will arise, which, since it insinuates no certain proofs of truth, must be guarded against, lest the serenity of charity be clouded by the storm of contention. August. Epist. 86 to Casulanus. With which sense of modesty Jerome also wrote: In those things which the Greeks call ἀδιάφορα and we call avà μέσον, every province abounds in its own sense. Ambrose, as cited by Augustine in his Epistle to Januarius, explained his own sense of this matter thus: If you do not wish to err, do what I am accustomed to do. For to whatever Church I come, I accommodate myself to its ceremonies. Nor certainly should the Church be deprived of that liberty which Christ always intended to be intact for it: To which our only Savior and Liberator be glory and thanksgiving for infinite ages. AMEN.

disagree; as one may read in the Harmony of the Augsburg Confession by Andreas Fabricius of Liège, page 435. They have even progressed to such a point of impudence that they did not hesitate to smear our Churches with the heresy of the Jovinians by this name. From which heresy, however, Augustine easily frees us, who in his treatise on heresies to Quodvultdeus, ch. 82, reports that Jovinian taught that one should not fast at all, and indeed that fasts are of no benefit whatsoever. Which very thing Ambrose also confirms in Epistle 82 to the Vercellenses. But the Romanists will not demonstrate that this error was ever approved or defended by us until they have proven that twice two is eight. What? That there are not lacking Ecclesiastical writers who free the Jovinians from this heresy, and report that they taught only this: that between the abstinence from foods and the partaking of the same with thanksgiving, there is no difference: but that both are of the same merit, as witnessed by the Blessed Jerome, Tom. III of his Works: as also by Thomas Aquinas in the book which he published against those who disparage Religion, ch. 6. Which opinion, indeed, if it be taken in the sense which the words themselves reveal: namely, that neither abstinence from foods, nor the legitimate partaking of the same, merits anything before GOD, then indeed we readily subscribe to them: nor yet shall we be heretics, but rather they too, regarding this opinion, are to be absolved from all heresy. For Scripture teaches this very thing: Rom. 14:17. The kingdom of GOD is not food and drink; but righteousness and peace. 1 Cor. 8:8. Food does not commend us to GOD. 1 Tim. 4:8. Bodily exercise profits little: and in the preceding verse 3, it is said to be a doctrine of demons, which forbids abstaining from foods which GOD created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful, and those who have known the truth: because every creature of GOD is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving: but is sanctified by the word of GOD and prayer.

Latin:

oportere in nobis & alias virtutes, & bonam propositum inchoari, & manere.

De quibus egregijs flosculis & emblematis videantur Acta Synodica, Quatern, Ff. Kk. 3. Oo. 2. T. 4. b. &c.

Constat nimirùm hinc, non modò laudem & commendationem mereri illos Theologos, qui tempore Sphingis Augustana, sive Interimistica maluerunt extrema quæque pati ac subire, quam in talem cessionem consentire, vel Theologorum timiditatem ullo pacto approbare: sed & maximi periculi, & cum purioris Religionis depravatione, & jacturâ certò conjunctum, quam primùm hostibus veritatis ceditur, & in ipsorum gratiam quicquam circa usum rerum adiaphorarum, vel in alterutram, vel in utramque partem immutatur.

CAPUT III. De Erroribus pugnantibus cum naturâ, & vero usu rerum adiaphorarum.

COnstat ex iis, quæ hactenùs de naturâ, & vero usu rerum adiaphorarum sunt disputata, quantis in hoc capite doctrinæ Christianæ parasangis, doctrina Evangelica PRIMUM dissideat à Papismo: Quanta sit item abominationum moles, quibus scatet in hoc uno capite lerna Pontificia. Nam 1. Necessitatem urget in adiaphoris: 2. Cultum divinum in iisdem statuit. 3. Meritum quærit. 4. Perfectionem constituit. 5. Modum, sive mediocritatem excedit: 6. Κακοζηλίᾳ Mosaicâ, interdum etiam levitate Scenicâ laborat. 7. Imperium in conscientias sibi sumit. 8. Episcopos alienâ potestate instruit, & in ipsas animas hominum dominium concedit. 9. Pro obtinendo ceremoniarum jugo, sævitiæ & crudelitati nulli parcit. 10. Tandem in horum conformitate, Catholicæ Ecclesiæ Unitatem collocat, contra Canonican illam Antiquitatis regulam: Dissenantia Ceremoniarum non tollit consonantia fidei.

Deinde à puritate doctrinæ Christianæ hoc in capite dissident Calviniani, qui res naturâ suâ liberas & observatu indifferentes, tanquam impias, profanas, & superstitiosas, sine discrimine rejiciunt, & ex Ecclesia ita proscribunt, ut universo generi rerum adiaphorarum, bellum planè ἀσπονδον jurasse videri possint: ita ut ne quidem celebrationi solenniorum festorum ab istis precatur: sed interprete Danæo, lib. 2. Ethicæ Christianæ, pag. 166. b. scribere non vereantur: Veteres quidẽ, ut ostenderent, vera esse omnia, quæ de Christi nativitãte, passione, Resurrectione &c. Narrantur ab Evangelistis, ideo ejus rei & temporis, quo gesta fuerant, memoriam piè observabant. Nobis verò hodie eosdem dies observare nihil necesse est, quibus cum Ethnicis, aut Christum passum vel natum negantibus, res non est. Itaq; neq; dies istos colere aut observare necesse est, aut etiam operæ pretium. Et hinc quidem in Ecclesijs Calvinianorum jam pridem solennes illæ festivitates, Conceptionis,

Nativitatis, Apparitionis, Resurrectionis, Ascensionis Christi: Item: Solennitas Pentecoftes, Trinitatis, & id genus festa alia, prorsus sint relegata, & quidem sub pulchello illo Schemate, quòd antiquitùs tantùm propter Ethnicos aut hæreticos, historias hasce negantes, ea fuerint celebrata. Quasi verò non potior ipsorum Christianorum ac fidelium, rudiorum præsertim habita fuerit, ac habenda etiamnum sit ratio: ut ex solenniore illa mysteriorum fidei meditatione, tantò rectiùs in negocio fidei & salutis instruerentur & confirmarentur. Praxis hæc Calvinianæ Ecclesiæ non intra suos tantùm terminos se contitinet: sed & aliarum Ecclesiarum pomœria invadere, turbare & disjicere non dubitat. Annũs jam agitur vicesimus quartus, ex quo in inclyto hoc nostro Electoratu Saxonico, quidam Crypto-Cavlinistæ, sub Schemate Exorcismi, turbas planè Schismaticas dederunt. Jam nota quidem nobis rectissimè est ceremoniæ istius ratio, hactenus sub censu ἀδιαφορίας ab Ecclesijs reformatis usurpatæ, Id quod praxis ipsa docet Ecclesiastica, dum sub pulcherrimo doctrinæ consensu, & consonantiâ fidei purissimâ, Ecclesiæ aliæ, per superiorem comprimis Germaniam, ritum istum jam pridem antiquarunt: nostræ autem illum retinent. Verùm constat, quo necessitatis prætextu, quibus purioris doctrinæ depravandæ insidiis, quâ simulatæ one constituendæ in doctrinâ diversissimâ Concordiæ, quâ perfidiâ consilij de evertendis Lutheranis Ecclesijs, Tragœdiæ istius actus susceptus fuerit, ut non pro Exorcismi ritu magis quàm pro aris & focis pugnandi necessitas Ecclesijs nostris incubuerit.

Eandem in reliquo etiam Adiaphororum genere fabulam luserunt vicini Anhaldini, ludunt etiamnum Hassi, & novelli quidam Electoratus Brandenburgici turbatores, Libertinæ gentis Hyperaspistæ, qui ne nihil in Religione reformanda præstitisse videantur, bellum Adiaphoristicum restaurandum esse, arbitrati sunt. Ergò agminè quasi facto, bipenni, securi, vectibus, & armis instructi aliis, tali Reformatione dignis, in templa irruerunt, altaria, cruces, imagines pictas fictasq; organa Musica, Cantum figuralem, Latini sermonis usum omnem: capitis apertionem ad nomen Christi, ut & genuflexionem, Decalogi consuetam divisionem, signum Crucis, Lumina, Vestis lineæ amiculum, summo studio sunt demoliti, & tanquam ritus impios simpliciter detestati. In Cœnâ Dominicâ Calices aureos & argenteos, panis Euchariftici formam & materiam, infractam distributionem, exhibitionem ad os communicantium, privatam ægrotorum, captivorumq; communicationem exterminarunt. Et pro hâc intemperie suâ exercendâ, spiritu Carlostadiano Respublicas torbarunt, Ecclesias pacatissimas concusserunt, Scholas & Academias devastarunt, & ut compendio dicam, eò rem jam tandem redegerunt, ut de ipsis sit dicendum, quod Synodus Ariminenfis quondam Constantio Imp. scripsit de Arianis: Quæ ab istis afferuntur, fidelibus incredulitatem; infidelibus crudelitatem allatura esse.

Et hi tamen belli isti sunt sraterculi, qui dissidio Ecclesiastico omni abjecto, nos secum in fraternitatis vinculum coalescere cupiunt: nescio an sibi magis ipsis, quàm nobis illudentes, imò quod magis videtur verisimile, DEUM ipsum in Cœlis ridentes. DEUS isti genti rectam mentem, & ubi conversi fuerint, veram cum Orthodoxâ Ecclesiâ societatem, constantemq; fraternitatem paternè largiatur. Id quod tùm futurum est, si in istis adiaphoris Contentionis funiculum pertinaciter trahere desinent, antiquitatis piæ vestigia secuti, ex qua Augustinus scripsit; In iis rebus, de quibus nihil certi statuit divina Scriptura certa præscriptio: mos populi DEI, vel instituta majorum pro lege tenenda sunt. De quibus si disputare voluerimus, & ex aliorum consuetudine alios improbare; orietur interminata luctatio, quæ cùm certa documenta veritatis nulla insinuet, cavendum est, ne tempestate contentionis serenitas charitatis obnubiletur. August. Epist. 86 ad Casulanum. Quo modestiæ sensu Hieronymus etiam scripsit: In his, quæ Græci ἀδιάφορα, nos avà μέσον appellant, abundat quævis provincia suo sensu. Ambrosius citante Augustino Epist. ad Januarium, sic de hoc negocio animi sui sensum explicavit: Si non vultis errare, facite, quod ego soleo. Ego enim ad quamcunque Ecclesiam venio, ad ejus ceremonias me accommodo. Neque certè Ecclesia eâ libertate privari debet, quam illi Christus semper voluit esse integram: Cui Servatori ac Liberatori nostro unico sit gloria & gratiarum actio seculis infinitis. AMEN.

dissendant; uti legere licet in Harmonia Confessionis Augustana Andreæ Fabricij Leodij, pag. 435. Quin eò usque impudentiæ progressi sunt, ut Jovinianorum hæresin, hoc nomine nostris Ecclesiis affricare haud dubitarent. A quâ tamen hærefi facilè nos liberat Augustinus, qui tractatu de hærefibus ad Quod vult Deum, c. 82. refert, docuisse Joviniano s, prorsus non esse jejunandum, imò nihil prorsus prodesse jejunia. Quod ipsum confirmat etiam Ambrosius Epistola 82. ad Vercellenses. Hunc verò errorem à nobis unquàm vel approbatum, vel defensum fuisse, haud prius demonstrabunt Romanenses, quàm probatum dederint, bis duo esse octo. Quid? quòd non desunt, ex Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis, qui Jovianos ab hac hærefi liberant, eosq; id tantùm docuisse referunt, quòd inter abstinentiam ciborum, & eorundem perceptionem cum gratiarum actione, nulla sit differentia: sed utraque ejusdem meriti, teste B. Hieronymo, Tom. III. Operum: ut & Thomâ aquinate in libro, quem edidit contra detrahentes Religioni, cap. 6. Quæ fanè sententia, si eo accipiatur sensu, quem verba ipsa produnt: quòd nimirùm neque abstinentia à cibis, neque eorundem perceptio legitima, apud DEUM quicquam mereatur, tùm profectò illis ultrò subscribimus: neque tamen erimus hæretici, quin & illi, quoad hanc sententia ab omni hærefi absolvendi. Nam hoc ipsum docet Scriptura: Rom. 14, 17. Regnum DEI non est cibus & potus; sed justitia & Pax. 1. Cor. 8. 8. Esca non commendat nos DEO 1. Tim. 4. 8. Corporalis exercitatio parum prodest: & versu præcedente 3. Doctrina dæmoniorum esse dicitur, quæ prohibet abstinere à cibis, quos DEUS creavit, ad percipiendum cum gratiarum actione fidelibus, & iis, qui cognoverunt veritatem: propterea quòd omnis creatura DEI bona est, & nihil reijciendum, quod cum gratiarum actione percipitur: sed sanctificatur per verbum DEI, & orationem.


## 29 On the Mortification of the Flesh

There are two main causes for whose sake the Question concerning the Mortification of the Flesh deserves some consideration: The first is: that the Romanists have been accustomed to designate their impious and superstitious human traditions concerning fasts, pilgrimages to the chapels of deceased Saints, hair shirts, flagellations, and other afflictive satisfactions of that kind, with the beautiful title and scheme of Mortification of the Flesh. The latter is that wicked desire for calumny, by which the Romanists try to persuade the whole Christian world that in the Churches of the Lutherans all discipline and Mortification of the flesh is simply prohibited. To which opinion Johannes à Daventria, a most impudent Monk, in his annotations on the articles of the Augsburg Confession, did not shudder to write: that the Lutherans maintain that they are then finally using Christian Liberty correctly, if they never afflict the flesh, if they never fast, if they indulge themselves beyond measure and beyond the strength of Nature with every kind of luxury on feast days, and [stuff] the belly.

But, since there is usually great power in calumnies, according to that old saying: Calumniate boldly, something always sticks: our Author did nothing beyond his duty in that he wished to undertake some treatment of the Question concerning the Mortification of the Flesh. It is indeed very succinct, consisting of two hypotheses: the first of which is: That the Mortification of the Flesh in the Scriptures, and especially in the Pauline Epistles, does not signify human traditions proposed to the Church under absolute necessity to be observed: but Patience in true Repentance, under the cross and afflictions sent by GOD: as also temperance, curbing the wicked lusts of the Flesh. The latter is: That it is free for anyone to choose certain exercises for the temperance commanded in general: provided that opinions of merit, worship, and necessity are not added to these exercises.

Having regard to the present age, we establish two heads for our treatise: the first we shall then demonstrate from the Holy Scriptures, what true mortification of the flesh is and by what works it may be performed, and what its end is. The subsequent ἀντιθετικὸν (antithetical section) will propose the doctrine of the Romanists, and especially of the modern Esauvites, concerning this matter, and will refute their principal arguments.

Latin:

Duæ potissimùm sunt causæ, quarum gratiâ Quæstio de Mortificatione Carnis aliquam considerationẽ meretur: Prior est: quòd Romanenses impias suas, & superstitiosas traditiones humanas de jejuniis, de peregrinationibus ad sacella Sanctorum defunctorum, de chamisætis, de flagellationibus aliisq; id genus satisfactionibus afflictivis, pulchello titulo ac Schemate Mortificationis Carnis indigetare consueverunt. Posterior est malefariata illa calumniandi libido, quâ Romanenses toti orbi Christiano persuadere conantur, Lutheranorum in Ecclesiis simpliciter prohiberi omnem disciplinam & Mortificationem carnis, Quam in sententiam Johannes à Daventria, impudentissimus Monachus, in suis ad Confeßionis Augustanæ articulos annotationibus, fcribere non exhorruit: Lutheranos statuere, tùm demùm rectè se uti Libertate Christiana, si Carnem nunquàm affligant, si nunquàm jejunent, sisupra modum, & supra Naturæ vires, omni genere ubuentiæm diebus festis, se insericant, & ventrem

Sed, cùm magna vis esse soleat Calumniarum, secundum vetus illud: Calumniare audačter, semper aliquid hæret: nihil præter officium fecit Autor noster, quòd Quæstionis de Mortificatione Carnis tractationem alquam suscipere voluit. Est verò ea succincta admodum duabus constans hypothesibus: quarum Prior est: Quòd Mortificatio Carnis in Scripturis, & præsertim Epistolis Paulinis, non significet traditiones humanas, Ecclesiæ sub absolutâ necessitate ad observandum propositas: sed Patientiam in verâ Pœnitentiâ, sub cruce & afflictionibus à DEO immifsis: ut & temperantiam, frænantem pravas Carnis concupiscentiam, frænantem pravas Carnis concupiscentias Posterior est: Quòd liberum sit cuilibet, el gere certa exercitia ad temperantiam in genere præceptam: modò his exercitijs non affuantur opiniones meriti, cultus, necessitatis.

Nos præsentis seculi habitâ ratione, duo constituimus Tractationis nostræ capita: Priùs deinde ex Scripturis Sacris monstrabic, Quid sit vera carnis mortificatio quibus operibus peragatur, & Quis ejus finis. POSTERIUS ἀντιθετικὸν, Romanensium, & cùmprimis modernorum Esavvittarum doctrinam de hac materia proponet, & præcipua eorum argumenta refutabit.


### A purer Doctrine, on the Mortification of the Flesh

That the mortification of the flesh is required of Christians and the faithful in the Scriptures is placed beyond all doubt. But what it properly is, is not a matter of universal agreement. We, in order to arrive more conveniently at an inquiry into the truth, establish two species of mortification: the one Internal, the other External: the former of the Spirit, the latter of the Body. For one may read much about both, as much in the writings of the Holy Fathers as in the books of our adversaries.

The Apostle expressed that Internal and Spiritual Mortification in Rom. 8:13: Mortify the deeds of the Body, by the Spirit. And Coloss. 3:5: Mortify your members which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, softness, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry: Where the Apostle refers even the depraved affections and desires of the mind and will among the earthly members, because, clearly, they savor not the things which are above, which are heavenly, but those which are earthly: in the preceding verse 2. The Apostle wills, however, that this Internal Mortification be performed not by bodily exercises, but BY THE SPIRIT, which happens when the Reborn, through the Grace and Spirit of GOD dwelling within them, daily resist the depraved concupiscences of the flesh, and thus compel them into order, so that they acquire or obtain no kingdom or dominion. Which mortification the same Apostle defined in Rom. 6:6 through the crucifixion of the old Man. Knowing this, he says, that our old man is crucified together with Christ, that the body of sin might be destroyed. Which old man he calls Flesh in Galat. 5:17, for the reason that it resists the Spirit in all things: For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit: and the Spirit against the flesh: And these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. Therefore, under this Mortification of the Flesh falls whatever in the Reborn resists the Spirit in any way, and whatever can be called under the scope or complex of evil affections, and motions, and concupiscences: so that not only the locomotive, sensitive, and appetitive faculties, but even the mind itself or the rational faculty of the soul is compelled to obey the Spirit and the Word of GOD. Which being done, our Flesh is truly mortified, and as the Apostle speaks, the Body of sin is truly destroyed: that henceforth we should not serve sin. Rom. 6:6. And again Galat. 5:16. If ye walk in the Spirit, ye shall not fulfill the lusts of the flesh.

With this decision standing, we infer two corollaries: The first is: That in this dispute, by the epithet of Flesh, not in the Esauvitic sense, is to be understood not merely our external flesh, or only the crasser affections: But the very reason and will of man, insofar as it, even in a man who is Reborn, fights against the Spirit: and strives to lead the same captive under the law of sin. Rom. 7:23. The latter is: That true Mortification of the flesh does not consist in external and bodily exercises, or afflictions of the Flesh, which are done by prickings, flagellations, or beatings: but in that internal and perpetual struggle of the Spirit against the Flesh, by which the latter is compelled to obey the former. And such indeed is the Internal, and most principal, Mortification of the flesh.

External or Bodily Mortification is to us, and is called, that which is undertaken to this end, that we may patiently subject ourselves and all that is ours to the divine will: and that we may be able to devote ourselves to divine worship with greater devotion. However, three species of this Mortification can be established not inconveniently.

THE FIRST is that of the Cross and Calamities sent by GOD, whether public or private. This Mortification is performed through true Patience, and Hope sustaining itself by the beneficent will of GOD, which at length with the temptation will provide a salutary ἔκβασιν (way of escape), nay, will supply strength, so that we may be able to bear it, 1 Cor. 10:13. By which means every murmur against GOD is repressed in our flesh. To this some accommodate that Apostolic saying in 2 Cor. 4:10: Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body. And that in Galat. 2:19: I through the law am dead to the law, that I might live unto GOD, I am crucified with Christ.

THE SECOND species is assiduity in dispatching the labors of our calling: Which, that it may be rightly ordered, requires temperance and sobriety and continence: Which indeed takes care of the body, but not for wantonness: but which grants to the health and strength of the body its due, yet is free and exempt from all excess in food and drink, and other lusts of the flesh.

THE THIRD and final species regards a singular case of necessity, and therefore requires mortification that is not perpetual, but adapted to certain times. To this pertain public fasts and other exercises of penitence, which we are so far from condemning that, rather, when public calamities are impending, we demand them all the more from our own people, so that they may be all the more eager for prayers, though not that they may merit anything before GOD. We define such fasts, however, not as to be performed through abstinence from certain foods and on certain days: much less through all-encompassing abstinence from food and drink, which might inflict violence upon the body: but through true temperance and sobriety.

he will conceive a true fear of the true GOD, than which nothing can be more effective for curbing the lusts of the wanton flesh: so that there is no need at all for those penances and castigations of the flesh, whether voluntarily undertaken or imposed by a priest, about which the Romanists invent fables.

Whoever observes those three species of external Mortification, for him nothing is lacking for the true subjection or discipline of the Body, much less does he need any other afflictive exercises of the Body, or flagellations.

Orthodox Antiquity is clearly ὁμόψηφos [of one mind] with this purer doctrine of ours. For thus Cyprian, Serm. 2: Vices must be crushed, and carnal sins, and the baneful corruption of the earthly body must be trampled underfoot with spiritual vigor, lest, while we revolve back to the conversation of the old man, we be entangled in lethal snares.

However, we do not establish the END of either mortification as meritorious or satisfactory in any respect: but only pedagogical, so that, indeed, that Internal mortification may take away all dominion from sin: but that the External may render us more prepared and more eager, both for obeying GOD and for executing the labors of our vocation. Which diversity of the end of both shows that whatever salutary effect is assigned to it in the Scriptures is owed not to that external, but to that internal and Spiritual Mortification of the flesh.

Augustine, book on true innocence, chapter 18: There is no one whose soul the corruptible body and earthly habitation does not weigh down: but one must strive that the desire of the flesh be overcome by the vigor of the Spirit: And the interior man, who always feels that he is being resisted, should always expect to be helped by divine aid.

Whence also that internal struggle of Spirit and Flesh is called, κατ' ἐξοχὴν [by way of eminence], the Mortification of the Flesh in the Scriptures. But this external one consists in a far lower degree, and only obtains this appellation κατ' ἀναλογίαν [by a certain analogy]. The Apostle confirms this very thing, 1 Tim. 4:8, saying: Bodily exercise profits little, πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐστιν ὠφέλιμos [it is profitable for a little]: But godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. Which aphorism contains two things in itself, necessary to be observed. One: That bodily exercise, or as the Romanists are accustomed to speak, bodily affliction voluntarily undertaken, does indeed profit: but little: that is, it does not at all aspire to those degrees of utility which the promises of the present and future life confer. Which single note of observation utterly undermines and overturns the whole structure of the Jesuitical doctrine concerning the Mortification of the flesh. The other is that the Apostle manifestly opposes Godliness to bodily exercises or carnal discipline, and assigns the promises of this life and the future to this alone: thus irrefragably demonstrating that true Mortification of the Flesh does not consist in those external and afflictive castigations of the Body, but properly in true godliness, or that Spiritual worship of GOD, which is always joined with that internal struggle of Flesh and Spirit, as we showed above. Looking to which, Eusebius rightly defined godliness in this manner: ἐυσέβεια Θεῶ ἡ πρὸς τὸν ἕνα καὶ μόνον, ὡς ἀληθῶς ὁμολογουμένωντο, καὶ ὄντα Θεὸν ἀνάνεσις, καὶ ἡ κατ' τοῦτον ζωή: Godliness is a regard for the one only true GOD, and a manner of life instituted according to Him: book 1, Preparation for the Gospel, 52. And St. Augustine: Godliness is the true worship of the true GOD; whence all the duties of living rightly ought to be derived. Before all things, therefore, let the Word of GOD, and that indeed alone, be the norm and rule of all our actions, studies, and exercises: He who follows this, he

The same author treats in tract 17 on John: It is a great and general fast to abstain from iniquities and from the illicit pleasures of this world, which is the perfect fast, so that denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live justly, piously, and soberly in this world.

Jerome on Virginity: The best measure is in every thing, and a standard is praiseworthy everywhere. The body is not to be broken, but to be governed. Let fasts therefore be moderate and holy, in all humility of mind, which so attenuate the body that they do not puff up the soul; lest the matter of humility beget pride, and vices be born from virtue.

Ambrose, Sermon 17: The fasts of Christians are to be observed spiritually rather than carnally. Whence let us fast primarily from our sin. For what kind of fast is it, that someone—I know not who—should abstain from food which the LORD created, and grow fat on the blood of sins?

Cyril, book 9 on John, chapter 24: Since the whole number of virtues is contained and perfected in love, let no one think that he attains anything great by starvation and fasting, or by prostrating himself on the ground, or by other exercises of virtue.

Hilary on Psalm 118: We, if we fast once, think that we have satisfied [the requirement]: if we give something from our storehouse to the needy, we believe that we have fulfilled justice, fasting so that we may please men: and in the midst of these very fasts, thinking of adulteries, injuries, and hatreds: or while we pursue a reputation for goodness through the empty and idle opinion of men, we think it is owed to us that we should be heard. But the Prophet hopes for everything from GOD, and expects everything from His mercy.

Latin:

Carnis Mortificationem à Christianis & fidelibus in Scripturis requiri, extra omnem dubitationis aleam est positum. Quid verò ea propriè sit, non una omnium est sententia. Nos ut ad veritatis inquisitione commodiùs perveniamus, duas constituimus Mortificationis species: Unam Internam: Alteram Externam: Illam Spiritus: Hanc Corporis. De utraque enim multa legere licet, tum in scriptis S. Patrum, tùm in Adversariorum libris.

Internam & Spiritualem illam Mortificationem expressit Apostolus, Rom. 8 13. Mortificate actiones Corporis, Spiritu. Et Coloss. 3. 5. Mortificate membra vestra terrestria, Scortationem, impuritatem, mollitiem, cupiditatem malam, & avaritiam, quæ est Idololatria: Ubi Apostolus Affectus & cupiditates etiam pravas mentis & voluntatis, refert inter membra terrena, quia videlicet sapiunt, non quæ cœlestia sursum sunt, sed quæ terrestria: versu præced. 2. Vult autem Apostolus, Mortificationem hanc Internam peragi non exercitiis Corporeis: sed SPIRITU, id quod fit, quando Renati per Gratiam & Spiritum DEI, in ipsis habitantem, pravis Concupiscentiis carnis quotidie resistunt, easdemq; sic in ordinem cogunt, ut nullum regnum, sive dominium acquirant, aut obtineant. Quam mortifi cationem definivit idem Apostolus, Rom. 6.6. per crucifixionem veteris Hominis. Hoc scie entes, inquiens, quod vetus noster homo, crucifixus est unà cum Christo, ut aboleatur corpus peccati. Quem veterem hominem Galat. 5. 17. Carnem appellat, propterea quòd Spiritui per omnia repugnat: Caro enim concupiscit adversus Spiritum: Spiritus autem adversus carnem: Et hæc sibi invicem adversantur, ut non quæcunq; vultis, illa faciatis. Sub hanc Mortificationem Carnis ergo cadit, quicquid in Renatis Spiritui quovis modo reluctatur, & quicquid sub malorum affectuum, & motuum, & concupiscentiarum ambitum, sive complexum vocari potest: ita ut non modò locomotiva, sensitiva & appetitiva: sed etiam ipsa mens sive Rationalis facultas animæ cogatur parere Spiritui, ac Verbo DEI. Quo facto, Caro nostra verè est mortificata, & ut Apostolus loquitur, verè est destructum Corpus peccati: ut ne posthac serviamus peccato. Rom. 6. 6. Et rursus Galat. 5. 16. Si Spiritu ambulaveritis, desideria carnis non perficietis.

Stante hac decisione, duo inferimus πορίσματα: Prius est: Quòd hac in disputatione Carnis epitheto, non sensu Esauvitico, intelligenda sit tantùm Caro nostra externa: vel crassiores duntaxat affectus: Sed ipsa ratio & voluntas hominis, quatenus ea in homine etiam Renato, pugnat adversus Spiri tum: & captivum ducere studet eundem, sub lege peccati. Rom. 7. 23. Posterius est: Veram Mortificationem carnis, non consistere in externis & corporalibus exercitiis, sive afflictionibus Carnis, quæ fiat compunctionibus, flagellationibus, pugnis: sed in internâ illâ & perpetuâ lucta Spiritus adversus Car nem, quâ hæc illi obtemperare cogitur. Et talis quidem est Interna, & maximè principalis Mortificatio carnis.

Externa sive Corporalis Mortificatio, nobis est ac dicitur ea, quæ eum in finem suscipitur, ut voluntati divinæ nos nostraq; omnia patienter subjiciamus: & cultui divino majore cum devotione vacare queamus. Possunt autem Mortificationis hujus tres quasi Species haud incommodè constitui.

PRIMA est Crucis & Calamitatum à DEO immissarum, sive publicarum, sive privatarum. Fit hæc Mortificatio per veram Patientiam, & Spem sustentantem se beneficâ DEI voluntate, quæ tandem cum tentatione salutarem datura sit ἔκβασιν, imò vires subministratura, ut ferendo esse possimus 1. Cor. 10. 13. Quo pacto omne murmur adversus DEUM, in carne nostrâ reprimitur. Huc accommodant nonnulli illud Aposto licum in 2. Corint. 4. 10. Mortificationem Christi Jesu semper in carne circumferentes, ut & vita Jesu in Corpore nostro manifestetur. Et illud Galat. 2. 19. Ego per legem legi mortuus sum, ut DEO viverem, crucifixus cum Christo.

ALTERA Species est assiduitas in expediundis vocationis nostræ laboribus: Quæ ut rectè se habeat, opus est temperantia & sobrietate, & continentia: Quæ Corporis curam quidem habet, sed non ad lasciviem: verùm quæ valetudini & viribus corporis suum tribuat, ab omni autem excessu in cibo & potu, aliisq; carnis concupiscentiis libera sit, & immunis.

TERTIA & postrema Species respicit singularem casum necessitatis, ac proinde non perpetuam, sed certis temporibus accommodatam, mortificationem exigit. Quò pertinent Jejunia publica, & alia pœnitentiæ exercitia, quæ tantum abest, ut damnemus, ut potiùs ingruentibus publicis calamitatibus, ea à nostris vel maximè exigamus, ut tantò alacriores ad preces esse possint, non verò ut apud DEUM aliquid promereantur. Definimus autem hujusmodi Jejunia non per abstinentiam à certis cibis, & certis quidem diebus peragendam: multò nimis per omnimodam abstinentiam à cibo & potu, quæ Corpori vim inferat: sed per veram temperantiam & sobrietatem.

verum veri DEI timorem concipiet, quo nihil ad frenandas carnis lascivientis concupiscentias efficacius esse potest: ut nihil prorsus opus sit pœnitentiis illis & castigationibus carnis, sive sponte susceptis, sive à sacrificulo impositis, de quibus Romanenses fabulantur.

Tres istas Mortificationis externæ species qui observat, illi ad veram subactionem, sive disciplinam Corporis nihil deest, nedum ullis aliis afflictivis Corporis exercitiis, sive flagellationibus indiget.

Puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ planè ὁμόψηφos est Orthodoxa Antiquitas. Sic enim Cyprianus Serm. 2. Obterenda sunt vitia, & peccata carnalia, & terreni corporis infesta labes Spirituali vigore conculcanda, ne dum ad veteris hominis conversationem revolvimur, letaflibus laqueis implicemur.

FINEM autem mortificationis utriusque non statuimus ullâ ex parte meritorium, aut satisfactorium: sed tantùm pædagogicum, ut nimirùm Interna illa mortificatio, peccato dominium omne auferat: Externa verò tum ad obediendum DEO, tùm ad labores vocationis exequendo, nos reddat paratiores, alacrioresq́;. Quæ finis utriusque diversitas, oftendit, non externæ, sed internæ illi & Spirituali Mortificationi carnis deberi, quicquid effectus salutaris ei in Scripturis assignatur.

Augustin. lib. de verâ innocentiâ cap. 18. Nemo est, cujus animam corruptibile corpus, & inhabitatio terrena non aggravet: sed annitendum est, ut carnis cupiditas Spiritus vigore superentur: Et interior homo, qui semper sentit sibi resisti, semper de divino auxilio expectet adjuvari.

Unde etiam κατ' ἐξοχὴν Interna illa Spiritus & Carnis lucta, Mortificatio Carnis in Scripturis dicitur. Externa verò hæc in longè inferiore gradu consistit, & tantùm κατ' ἀναλογίαν quandam appellationē hanc sortitur. Confirmat hoc ipsum Apostolus, 1. Tim. 4. 18. Corporalis, inquiens exercitatio parum prodest, πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐστιν ὠφέλιμos: Pietas verò ad omnia utilis est, promissionem habens vitæ hujus & futuræ. Qui aphorismus duo in se comprehendit, observatu necessaria. Unum: Corporalēm exercitationem, vel ut Romanenses loqui consueverunt, Corporalem afflictionem sponte susceptam prodesse quidem: sed parùm: hoc est, ad eos utilitatis grad¹9, quos promissiones præsentis & futuræ vitæ conferunt neutiquam aspirare. Quæ vel una observationis nota, totam structuram doctrinæ Esavviticæ de Mortificatione carnis funditùs subruit & evertit. Alterum est, Quòd Apostolus Pietatem, exercitiis corporalibus, sive disciplinæ carnali manifestè opponit, & huic soli Promissiones hujus & futuræ vitæ adsignat: sic irrefragabiliter demonstrans, veram Mortificationem Carnis non in externis illis, & afflictivis Corporis castigationibus, sed in verâ pietate, sive Spirituali illo cultu DEI propriè consistere, qui cum internâ illâ luctâ Carnis & Spiritus semper est conjunctus, uti suprà ostendimus. Quò respiciens Eusebius, Pietatem rectè definivit hunc in modum: ἐυσέβεια Θεῶ ἡ πρὸς τὸν ἕνα καὶ μόνον, ὡς ἀληθῶς ὁμολογουμένωντο, καὶ ὄντα Θεὸν ἀνάνεσις, καὶ ἡ κατ' τοῦτον ζωή: Pietas est respectus ad unum solum verum DEUM, & secundùm hunc instituta vitæ ratio: lib. 1. de præparat. Evang. 52. Et D. Augustinus: Pietas est verus veri DEI cultus; unde omnia rectè vivendi duci oportet officia. Antè omnia igitur DEI Verbum, & id quidem solum, omnium nostrarum actionum, studiorum, exercitationum norma sit & regula: Hanc qui sequitur, ille

Idem tractat. 17. in Johannem: Magnum & generale jejunium est abstinere ab iniquitatibus, & ab illicitis voluptatibus hujus seculi, quod est perfectum jejunium, ut abnegantes impietatem, & seculares cupiditates, justè, piè & sobrie vivamus in hoc seculo.

Hieron. de Virginitate: Optimus est in omni re modus, & laudabilis ubique mensura, Corpus non frangendum, sed regendum est. Sint ergo moderata & sancta, in omni mentis humilitate jejunia, quæ ita attenuent corpus, ne animum elevent; ne res humilitatis gignat superbiam, & vitia de virtute nascantur.

Ambrof. Sermon. 17. Jejunia Christianorum Spirituliter potius, quàm carnaliter observanda sunt. Unde à peccato nostro principaliter jejunemus. Quale est enim jejunium, ut à cibo, quos DOMINUS creavit, nescio quis impostor abstineat, & à peccatorum sanguine pinguescat?

Cyrill. lib. 9. in Joh. cap. 24. Cùm omnis virtutum numerus in dilectione contineatur, ac perficiatur, nemo inediam, atq; jejunium, nemo quia humi se prosternat, nemo cæteris virtutum exercitationibus magnum quid se consequi putet.

Hilar. in Psal. 118. Nos, si semel jejunamus, satisfecisse nos arbitramur: Si aliquid ex horreo inopi damus, implevisse nos justitiam credimus, jejunantes ut placeamus hominibus: & inter ipsa jejunia, stupta, injurias, odia cogitantes: aut dum bonitatis famam inani & ociosa hominum opinione sectamur, existimamus deberi nobis, ut exaudiamur. Verùm Propheta totum de DEO sperat, totum ex misericordia ejus expectat.

### A purer Doctrine, on the Mortification of the Flesh: Chap. I

CHAP. I.

Latin:

CAP. I.


### Chapter Second

The Papal doctrine concerning the Mortification of the Flesh errs enormously in two respects. First, in defining this mortification; and secondly, in establishing its proper end.

Regarding the first head of error, they understand by the Mortification of the flesh, penances or afflictive castigations of the body, whether voluntarily assumed or imposed by priests or Bishops: such as they wish to be alms, fasts with a distinction of foods on set days and times; likewise scourges, with which they lacerate and tear the body even to the flowing of blood; also that they crawl up the steps of temples, that they travel many miles bareheaded, barefoot, with arms extended and spread out, thus making pilgrimages to the basilicas of the Blessed Mary, to the statues of the dead, to sepulchers, temples, and relics; that they walk about hooded or clothed in haircloth, that they use wooden clogs, that with bowed neck they look at the ground from time to time; that they are girded with knotted ropes: that they lie on the ground, and undertake other exercises of the body of this kind, which are partly ridiculous and partly impious, which they claim require discipline and mortification of the flesh. And to put a gloss upon this impiety, they establish the defense of their cause in that Apostolic passage, 1 Cor. 9:27: 'I buffet my body and bring it into bondage, lest by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.' Moved by this very Apostolic passage, some of the Fathers held to a more austere manner of life: so that Basil lived only on bread, salt, and water. Which we read that Gregory Nazianzen also did. But they have not sufficiently grasped the mind of the Apostle. For 1. by 'Body' he does not understand the external flesh, or as the Scholastics have explained, merely the coarser affections of the mind: but in the style customary both to himself and to the whole of Scripture, by the word 'Body' and 'flesh' he understands all the powers of the soul, especially the Heart, from which proceed wicked concupiscences, warring against the Spirit: or as he explains himself in Rom. 6:6: The whole old man, which ought to be crucified with Christ, lest it obtain any dominion in the regenerate man. Which crucifixion or mortification is not performed by that more austere discipline or afflictive castigation of the flesh: But by the Spirit of renewal, which dwells in the regenerate and always wars against the concupiscences of the flesh, and represses them, Gal. 5:17. For as Hilary rightly noted in Psalm 118, that bodily discipline does not prevent us from thinking of lewdness, injuries, hatreds, and other crimes and wickednesses in our heart. Then indeed the Fathers have shamefully lapsed, who interpreted the Greek word ὑποπιάζω τὸ σῶμά με: 'I subdue my body,' concerning external

and those carnal castigations and afflictions of the flesh: which it cannot even be shown to be probably plausible from his entire history that the Apostle ever undertook. Nay, rather, the Apostle himself gravely reproves that more austere manner of life by which violence is done to the body and health. Rom. 13:14: 'Make provision for the flesh, but not to fulfill the lusts thereof.' And 1 Tim. 4:8: 'Bodily exercise profiteth little.' If it profits little, how, I ask, would the Apostle in this place affirm that he therefore subdues his body, so that by preaching to others, he himself might not become a castaway? Thus certainly, it would not profit little, but much, nay, most of all, would carnal castigation profit: which, however, Paul expressly denies.

Most rightly, therefore, the Apostolic phrase is understood of that spiritual mortification of the evil concupiscences of the flesh, of which we spoke in the thesis. But to return to the Esauitic doctrine, let them explain, I pray, in what way they can, or wish to, reconcile their flagellations, for which they fight as for altars and hearths, with the fifth commandment of the Decalogue? Or whether perhaps the Apostle is to be established as having mitigated or abolished the rigor of the Decalogue: so that GOD indeed commands: 'Thou shalt not kill:' but Paul by his own example commands: 'Scourge thy body, even to the most abundant flowing of blood, nay, even to the very fainting of the soul and mind.' Now, such is the emphasis of the fifth commandment that it prohibits not only the violent killing of oneself: but also all those things which can do violence to nature, accelerate death, injure health, and render us more inept and languid for performing the duties of our calling. And just as GOD by this very commandment prohibits not only that you should not kill your neighbor, but also that you should not wound him: so, since Charity is ordered so that it begins from oneself, GOD prohibits by this very same pact not only that you should not kill yourself: but also that you should not wound yourself or beat yourself with scourges. For which reason GOD also in Lev. 19:28 and Deut. 14:1 most severely prohibits that anyone should lacerate or cut his own flesh. Furthermore, sacred history teaches that this is a property of Hypocrites, who lacerate themselves unto the flowing of blood with swords and lances in the death of the Baalites. 1 Kings 18:28. From whom our Esauites differ in nothing at all, except that instead of swords and lances, they are accustomed to use scourges.

As for the LATTER head of the error, the Romanists establish the end of that external and corporal castigation as Satisfactory and meritorious, contending that such Mortification, especially when assumed voluntarily, satisfies GOD for the guilt of temporal punishments: and as Bonaventure speaks, as a price sufficient to pay off the debt, to compensate, to expiate, to take away temporal punishments, and that indeed by Condignity. Whence the Jesuit Bellarmine did not hesitate to write that David fasted and wept for this reason, that he might satisfy divine justice with his own tears and prayers by condignity: in the treatise on Indulgences, page 154. This is a swamp of the grossest errors and most foul impieties. For whatever is done or undertaken under the notion of Satisfaction, however good and praiseworthy it may otherwise be, turns out to be idolatrous: which is so far from satisfying GOD for sin, that it rather heaps sins upon sins, and increases and exacerbates punishments, not only temporal, but also eternal.
