The reason is 1. because this opinion of personal merit and Satisfaction enervates the mercy of GOD, by which alone it is that we are not consumed by His wrath and fury: Lam. 3. 22. 2. It removes the virtue and efficacy of the death of Christ, who fully satisfied GOD the Father not only for faults, but also for punishments, and indeed for punishments both temporal and eternal: having blotted out the handwriting that was against us, which contained the debt not only of eternal, but also of temporal punishments. Col. 2. 14. 3. Those scourges, with which the Romanists lacerate their bodies like madmen, and to which they ascribe the power of satisfaction for temporal and eternal punishments, are manifestly impious and insulting to the scourges of Christ the Savior. For we are healed not by our own, but by the Son of GOD's scourges and stripes. Is. 53. 5. To which pertains that notable dialogism which is described in Is. 58. 3. and following. For to the hypocrites asking: Why have we fasted, and You have not looked? We have humbled our souls, and You have not known it? The LORD answers: Is it such a fast that I have chosen, for a man to afflict his soul for a day? Is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the LORD? Behold, you fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness. Do not fast until this day, that your cry may be heard on high, etc.

The arguments taken from the Scriptures, by which they attempt to bolster this impiety, are three. One is taken from the example of the Ninevites, who, through works of mortification of the flesh spontaneously undertaken, averted the hand of GOD and His scourge.

The second is from the example of David, who reports of himself that he washes his bed every night and waters his couch with tears.

The third and last they construct from the words of the Apostle, Rom. 8. 13. If you mortify the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, you shall live.

But these are very weak quibbles. For as regards the example of the Ninevites, a gross sophistry is committed, taking that which is not a cause for a cause. For GOD, in taking away the punishment which He had threatened, by no means looked at the fasts, sackcloth, and ashes: but, as the text expressly has it, at that serious and true repentance and contrition of heart for the sins committed, of which those public exercises were only external signs. What is more? The text expressly names the formal and principal cause, in respect of which that repentance was pleasing and acceptable to GOD, namely FAITH. For the men of Nineveh believed in GOD, Jonah 3. 7. and verse 10. They turned from their evil way, and GOD repented of the evil that He had said He would do to them, and He did it not. This serious conversion, therefore, constituted that true mortification of the flesh, not the fasting, not the sackcloth, not the ashes.

Furthermore, that fasting and the other exercises were imposed not by the priests, but by the King and political counselors: and they were imposed (which is well to be noted) not only on men, but also on beasts. Where surely the opinion of any merit and Satisfaction had no place, unless perhaps one wishes to assert that the fasting of beasts also merited the expiation of punishments before GOD. Finally, the Prophet Jonah, chap. 4. 2., ascribes the cause of the remission of the punishment entirely to the mercy and goodness of God: saying, I know that You are a gracious and merciful GOD, patient, and of great mercy, and You repent of the evil. Now if GOD, according to the Papist hypothesis, had remitted the punishment to the Ninevites because they had satisfied His justice by that external mortification of the flesh, and had worthily merited the removal of the punishment: certainly the mercy of GOD could have had no place. For where satisfaction has been made to divine justice, there is no need for mercy: since the debt has already been paid in full.

The other passage taken from Psalm 6 does nothing for the matter, and overturns the cause of the Papists more than it confirms it. For David rejects all hope of personal satisfaction and rests in the mercy of GOD alone: crying, Have mercy on me, O LORD: Heal me, O LORD: Turn, O LORD, and deliver my soul: save me, for Your mercy's sake: verses 3 and 5. And these very groans, these sighs, these tears were that water with which he washed his bed every night and watered his couch: of which tears the entire practice of the Roman Church knows nothing.

The third passage, as shown in the thesis above, indeed ascribes life to the mortification of the flesh, but not that which is done through flagellations and other afflictive exercises of the body: but rather that which is done by the Spirit, in the way that has been explained: so that this argument wanders clearly off the mark.

*****

Latin:

DOctrina Pontificia de Mortificatione Carnis, in duobus enormiter impingit. Primùm quidem in definiendâ hac mortificatione: deinde verò in recto ejus constituendo fine.

Quoad PRIUS erroris caput, intelligunt illi per Mortificationem carnis, pœnitentias, sive castigationes corporis afflictivas, vel sponte assumtas, vel à Sacrificulis aut Episcopis impositas: Quales esse volunt, Eleemosynas, jejunia sub discrimine ciborum, statis diebus ac temporibus: flagella item, quibus ad sanguinis usq; profluvium corpus lacerant & dilaniant: Item quòd perrepunt gradus templorum, quòd nudo capite, nudis pedibus, extensis & dispersis brachiis benè multa miliaria conficiunt, sic peregrinantes ad D. Mariæ basilicas, ad defunctorum statuas, sepulchra, templa, reliquias: quòd cucullati, aut cilicio induti incedunt, quòd ligneis claceis utuntur, quòd incurvi cervici terram subinde spectant: quòd funibus nodosis cinguntur: quòd humi cubant, & alia hujus generis ludicra partim, partim impia Corporis exercitia suscipiunt, quæ disciplinam & mortificationem carnis indigetant. Et ut impietati huic fucum faciant, præsidium causæ constituunt in illo Apostolico. 1. Cor. 9. 27. Contundo corpus meum, & in servitutem redigo, ne forte alijs prædicans, ipse reprobus fiam. Quo ipso loco Apostolico moti Patrum aliqui, austeriorem vitæ rationem tenebant: ita ut Basilius pane tantùm, sale & aquâ victitaret. Quod ipsum Gregorium etiam Nazianzenum factitasse legimus. Sed mentem Apostoli non satis sunt assecuti. Nam 1. per Corpus non intelligit Carnem externam, vel ut Scholastici exposuerunt, crassiores tantùm animi affectus: sed Stylo, tùm sibi & tùm universæ Scripturæ usitato, Corporis & carnis vocabulo intelligit omnes animæ potentias, Cor cumprimis, ex quo exeunt pravæ concupiscentiæ, pugnantes cum Spiritu: vel ut Rom. 6. 6. se explicat: Totum veterem hominem, qui cum Christo crucifigi debeat, ne dominum aliquod obtineat in homine renato. Quam crucifixionem aut mortificationem non præstat austerior illa disciplina, vel afflictiva carnis castigatio: Sed Spiritus renovationis, qui in renato habitat, & semper pugnat cum concupiscentiis carnis, easŅs reprimit, Galat. 5. 17. Nam uti Hilarius in Psal. 118. rectè anno tavit, Corporalis illa disciplina non prohibet, quo minus in corde cogitemus stupra, injurias, odia, aliaq; scelera & flagitia. Deinde verò turpiter lapsi sunt Patres, qui verbum græcum ὑποπιάζω τὸ σῶμά με: Subigo corpus meum, de externis

& carnalibus illis castigationibus, & afflictionibus carnis interpretati sunt: Quales Apostolum unquam suscepisse, ex universâ ipsius historiâ demonstrari ne quidem in speciem probabiliter potest. Quin potiùs ipse Apostolus austeriorem illam vitae rationem, quâ corpori & sanitati vis infertur, graviter reprehendit. Rom. 13. 14. Carnis curam habete, modò non ad carnis lasciviam. & 1. Tim. 4. 8. Corporalis exercitatio parùm prodest. Si parum prodest, quomodo quaeso Apostolus hoc loco affirmaret, se ideò subigere corpus suum, ut ne aliis praedicando, ipse reprobus fiat. Sic certè non parum, sed multum, imò plurimum prodesset carnalis castigatio: id quod tamen Paulus disertè negat.

Rectissimè ergo phrasis Apostolica intelligitur de Spirituali illâ mortificatione, malarum carnis concupiscentiarum, de quâ in thesi verba fecimus. Sed ut ad doctrinam Esaviticam redeamus, edisserant quaeso illi, quo pacto flagellationes suas, pro quibus tanquam pro aris & focis pugnant, conciliare possint, aut velint cum quinto Decalogi praecepto? aut num fortassis Apostolus Decalogi rigorem mitigasse, vel antiquasse statuendus sit: ita ut DEUS quidem praecipiat: Non occides: Paulus autem suo exemplo jubeat: Flagellato corpus tuum, usque ad largissimum sanguinis profluvium, imò ad ipsum animi, mentisque deliquium. Jam verò ea est praecepti quinti emphasis, ut non modò violentam sui ipsius occisionem: sed & ea omnia prohibeat, quae naturae vim inferre, mortem accelerare, valetudinem laedere, & ad obeunda vocationis munia ineptiores, languidioresque nos reddere possunt. Et quemadmodum DEUS hoc ipso praecepto prohibet, non modò ne proximum occidas, sed & ne ipsum vulneres: ita, cum Charitas sit ordinata, ut à semetipsâ incipiat, prohibet hoc ipso etiam pacto DEUS, non modò ut teipsum non occidas: sed & ne teipsum vulneres, aut flagris caedas. Quam ob causam DEUS etiam Levit. 19. 28. Deut. 14. 1. severissimè prohibet, ne quis propriam carnem sauciet, aut incidat. Praeterea docet historia sacra, Hypocritarum hoc esse proprium, qui in mortem Baalitarum frameis, ac lanceolis, ad sanguinis usque profluvium se lacerant. 1. Reg. 8. 28. A quibus nihil quicquam distant nostri Esavitae, quàm quòd pro frameis ac lanceolis, flagris uti solent.

Quoad POSTERIUS erroris caput, Externae & corporalis istius castigationis finem constituunt Romanenses Satisfactorium & meritorium contendentes talem Mortificationem, sponte cumprimis assumtam, satisfacere DEO pro reatu poenarum temporalium: & ut Bonaventura loquitur, tanquam pretium ad exolvendum debitum sufficiens, compensare, expiare, tollere poenas temporarias, & id quidem ex Condigno. Unde Esavvita Bellarminus scribere non dubitavit, Davidem ideò jejunasse ac flevisse, ut divinæ justitiæ suis lachrimis ac precibus ex condigno satisfaceret: in tractatu de Indulgent. pag. 154. Lerna hæc est craffissimorum errorum, fœdissimarumq; impietatum. Quicquid enim sub ratione Satisfactionis sit, aut suscipitur, illud quantumvis aliàs bonum, & laudabile, evadit idololatricum: quod tantum abest, ut pro peccato DEO satisfaciat, ut potiùs peccata peccatis cumulet, & pœnas non modò temporales, sed & æternas augeat & exasperet. Ratio est 1. quia hæc opinio proprii meriti & Satisfactionis, enervat misericordiam DEI, cujus solius est, quòd irâ furore ipsius non consumimur: Thren. 3. 22. 2. tollit virtutem & efficaciam mortis Christi, qui non pro culpis tantùm, sed & pro pœnis, & pœnis quidem tàm temporalibus, quàm æternis, DEO Patri ad plenum satisfecit: deleto chirographo, quod adversum nos erat: & quod non æternarum modò, sed & temporalium pœnarum reatum continebat. Coloss. 2. 14. 3. Sunt flagra illa, quibus furiosorum instar corpora sua lacerant Romanenses, & quibus satisfactionis vim pro pœnis temporalibus & æternis adscribunt, manifestè impia, & in flagra Christi Servatoris contumeliosa. Non enim nostris, sed Filii DEI flagris, & vibicibus sanati sumus. Jes. 53. 5. Quò pertinet insignis ille dialogismus, qui describitur. Jes. 58. 3. & seqq. Hypocritis enim quærentibus; Quare jejunavimus, & non aspexistis: humiliavimus animas nostras, & nescivisti? Respondet DOMINUS: Numquid tale est jejunium, quod elegi per diem affligere hominem animam suam? Num ut incurvet quasi juncetum caput suum & saccum sternat, & cinerem? Numquid istud vocabis jejunium, & diem acceptabilem DOMINO? Ecce ad lites & contentiones jejunatis, & percutitis vos pugno impiè. Nolite jejunare usq; ad hunc diem, ut audiatur in excelso clamor vester &c.

Argumenta ex Scripturis petita, quibus impietatem hanc fulcire conantur, tria sunt, Unum petitum ab exemplo Ninivitarum, qui per opera Mortificationis carnis spontè suscepta, manum DEI, ejusdemq; flagellum averterunt.

Alterum ab exemplo Davidis, qui de seipso refert, quòd per singulas noctes lavet lectum suum, & stratum suum riget lacrymis.

Tertium & postremum extruunt ex verbis Apostoli, Rom. 8. 13. Si Spiritu opera carnis mortificaveritis, vivetis.

Sed nimis elumbia hæc sunt cavilla. Nam quoad exemplum Ninivitarum, crassa committitur Sophisticatio non causæ ut causæ. Nequaquam enim DEUS auferens pœnam, quam comminatus fuerat, respexit jejunia, saccum & cinerem: sed uti textus disertè habet, seriam illam, ac veram cordis pœnitentiam & contritionem de admissis peccatis, cujus externa tantùm signa erant exercitia illa publica. Quid? quòd textus expressè nominat causam formalem & principem, respectu cuju s Pœnitentia illa grata & accepta fuerit DEO nempe FIDEM. Crediderunt enim viri Ninivitæ in DEUM Jonæ 3. 7. & versu. 10. Conversi sunt de viâ suâ malâ, & pœnituit DEUM super malum, quod locutus fuerat, ut faceret eis, & non fecit. Hæc ergò seria conversio, absolvebat veram illam Carnis mortificationem, non jejunium, non saccus, non cineres.

Deinde jejunium illud, & reliqua exercitia imponebantur non à Sacrificulis, sed à Rege & Consiliariis politicis: & imponebantur (quod probè notandum) non modò hominibus, sed & jumentis. Ubi profectò nullum locum habuit opinio meriti alicujus & Satisfactionis, nisi forte jumentorum etiam jejunium coram DEO expiationem pœnarum promereri statuere quis velit. Tandem Propheta Jonas cap. 4. 2. causam Remissionis pœnæ in solidum adscribit Misericordiæ & bonitati divinæ: Scio, inquiens, quia tu DEUS clemens & misericors es, patiens, & multæ misericordiæ, & pœnitet te mali. Jam si DEUS, secundum hypothesin Pontificiam ideò Ninivitis remisisset pœnam, quia externâ illâ mortificatione carnis, justitiæ ipsius satisfecissent, & ex condigno pœnæ ablationem promeruissent: certè misericordia DEI locum ampliùs habere non potuisset. Ubi enim fatisfactum justitiæ divinæ, ibi misericordia nulla opus est: Siquidem debitum jam ex asse est persolutum.

Alter locus ex Psalmo 6. petitus nihil quicquam ad rem facit, & causam Efavvitarum magis evertit, quàm confirmat. David enim omnem spem de propria satisfactione objicit, & in sola DEI misericordiâ acquiescit: clamans, Miserere mei DOMINE: Sana me DOMINE: Convertere DOMINE, & eripe animam meam: salvum me fac, propter misericordiam tuam: versu 3. & 5. Et hi ipsi gemitus, hæc suspiria, hæ lachrymæ fuerunt aqua illa, qua singulis noctibus lavit lectum suum, & rigavit stratum suum: de quibus lachrymis nihil quicquam novit universa praxis Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

Tertius locus, uti in thesi suprà oftensum, adscribit quidem vitam Mortificationi Carnis, sed non illi, quæ fit per flagellationes, & alia Corporis exercitia afflictiva: verùm quæ fit Spiritu, eo modo quo explicatum: ita ut hoc argumentum planè extra oleas vagetur.

*****


### Chapter Second: Place

PLACE

Latin:

LOCUS


## 30 Concerning Scandal


### A Threefold Division of Scandals

The controversy concerning Christian Liberty and the right use of Adiaphora is followed by that treatment which is undertaken concerning the nature of Scandal. For as soon as one stumbles even in the slightest regarding the use of Christian Liberty, it cannot be but that Scandals arise in the Church, especially among the weak. Furthermore, the world, placed in wickedness, is almost entirely teeming with Scandals, so that there seems to be almost no distinction left between good and evil: no choice of things: no regard for the fear of God: no care for one's own salvation, let alone another's. This most sad face of affairs strikes a kind of horror into the pious and faithful, and certainly expresses tears, groans, and sighs more often. But Christ the Savior himself, because of the license of Scandals, devotes the World to eternal destruction: Matt. 18. 7 Woe, saying, to the world because of Scandals. Therefore, for the sake of both the pious and the impious, the treatment of Scandals is necessary: for the latter, indeed, so that, terrified by the gravity of this sin, they may learn to be wise and repent: for the former, however, so that, even when established in the midst of these turmoils of scandals, they may nevertheless be able to rightly consult their own Conscience and the liberty of faith.

The treatment of this Topic, however, consists of and is completed by three questions. The first is concerning Pharisaical Scandal, or that which is taken, which is to be cared for least: but it is shown that even with Pharisees and the impious raging, right things must be said and done. The second deals with Scandal given, either through the falsity of doctrine or through the corruption of life and morals, where the Author rightly warns that this sin is by far the most grave and to be avoided with great care and diligence. The third and final one inquires into certain rules by which scandals can be avoided: when, namely, every abuse of adiaphorous and indifferent things is guarded against, and the rights of Christian Liberty are not extended to any license whatsoever: but what serves the edification of one's neighbor is looked to above all.

Our treatment, insisting on almost the same footsteps, will be monomeres, and in investigating the nature of Scandals, it will run through the whole theoretically and practically, as to parts, as to causes, as to effects, as to ends.

SCANDAL in origin or etymology is the Greek skandalon, derived from skazo, which is to limp, and in general it signifies any proskomma or stumbling-block, any delay and impediment: such as are wont to be in public and military roads, namely, protruding rocks or snares placed by treachery, into which those who stumble either fall completely or wander from the straight path. Hence, by Metaphor, this word is transferred to the mind, and indeed in the Church, it denotes everything by which someone can be offended, in whatever way that may happen: so that whether you say or do things that are false or evil, by which another can be corrupted: or whether you say or do what is by its nature true, good, and lawful, yet it can provide a stumbling-block to a brother, if not by itself, at least by accident: you may seem to have immediately placed a scandal. And thus, Scandal understood in general is commonly defined as every word, or deed, or example by which another is offended and rendered worse: or by which one is cast into error, or by which a preconceived error is confirmed, or by which a wicked example is drawn for imitation and rule: or by which flames of greater hatred against the Gospel are supplied. Or as the Greeks define it: skandalon esti exastrophe skazontos peri ten aletheian, Scandal is the perversity of one limping around the truth. Thus, therefore, Scandal behaves as a relative to its Correlate, namely, the stumbling-block: although sometimes it is taken indiscriminately for the offense itself.

There are several divisions of Scandals, which nevertheless can be conveniently reduced to a ternary:

THE FIRST division concerns the object or matter in which and about which an offense can be given. For this happens either by words or by deeds, or by manners or examples. Scandal in words occurs again in two ways: First, indeed, when someone in common life and conversation offends and disturbs the chaste ears and minds of honest men with obscene and illiberal jokes or speeches. The Apostle expressed this species, citing that of the poet Menander in Thais: 1 Cor. 15:33, "Evil communications corrupt good manners": Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαὶ. Then, truly, this scandal is committed in the doctrine of the Christian religion, when, namely, either plainly false dogmas are spread, or thorny and intricate, useless, and less necessary questions and disputes about theological matters are raised, which render the weaker in faith more doubtful and weave ropes of contention that can never be untied. The Apostle disapproved and prohibited such a method of teaching in 2 Tim. 2:23: "Foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes," or contentions. And Tit. 3:9: "Avoid foolish questions: for they are unprofitable and vain." Indeed, as the same Apostle gravely judges in 1 Tim. 1:4, they "minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith." In this way, the Scholastic Doctors sinned enormously and gravely offended the Church of God, who filled the pulpits of schools and temples with such useless and intricate questions: such as, Whether God can command hatred of Himself? Whether He could actually produce an infinite thing according to every dimension? Whether He could have made this world better from eternity than He did? Whether He can make what is done undone? Whether any divine person can assume any nature? Whether this proposition, "God is a beetle or a gourd," is as possible as this: "God is man"? Whether the soul of Christ could have lied? And infinite other questions of this kind occur among the Scholastics in individual articles.

Latin:

COntroverfiam de Libertate Christiana, & recto usu Adiaphororum, excipit ea Tractatio, quæ de naturâ Scandali fuscipitur. Quam primum enim circa usum Libertatis Christianæ vel in minimo impingitur, fieri nequit, quin Scandala oboriantur in Ecclesiâ præsertim apud infirmos. Accedit, quòd mundus in maligno positus, totus fermè scatet Scandalis, ut nullum penè bonorum & malorum discrimen videatur esse reliquum: nullus rerum delectus: nullus divini timoris respectus: nulla salutis propriæ, nedum alienæ cura. Quæ tristissima rerum facies piis ac fidelibus horrorem quasi incutit, lachrymas certè sæpiùs, gemitus ac suspiria exprimit. Christus autem Servator ipse, ob Scandalorum licentiam, Mundum æterno devovet exitio: Matth. 18. 7 Væ, inquiens, mundo propter Scandala. Utrorumque ergo, & piorum & impiorum causâ, Scandalorum Tractatio est necessaria: horum quidem ideò, ut peccati istius gravitate absterriti, sapere, & resipiscere discant: illorum verò, ut in mediis etiam istis scandalorum turbis constituti, Conscientiæ tamen suæ, & libertati fidei rectè consulere possint.

Tractatio autem Loci hujus Philippéatribus quæstionibus constat & absolvitur. Prima est de Scandalo Pharisaico, sive accepto, quod minimè curandum: sed frementibus etiam Pharisæis & impiis, recta dicenda & facienda esse, ostenditur. Altera agit de Scandalo dato, vel per doctrinæ falsitatem, vel per vitæ morumq; conscelerationem, Ubi rectè monet Autor, Peccatum hoc longè esse gravissimum & magnâ curâ ac diligentiâ vitandum. Tertia & postrema inquirit in certas regulas, quibus scandala vitari possint: quando nimirum omnis abusus rerum adiaphorarum, & indifferentium cavetur, & Libertatis Christianæ jura non ad quamlibet licentiam extenduntur: sed quid ædificationi proximi inserviat potissimùm spectatur.

Tractatio nostra iisdem fermè insistens vestigiis, erit μονομερὴς, & in naturâ Scandalorum investiganda, quâ partes, quâ causas, quâ effecta, quâ fines, theoreticè & practicè tota decurret.

SCANDALUM origine sive etymo Græcum est σκάνδαλον, deductum à σκάζω, quod est claudico, & in genere significat quodlibet πρόσκομμα sive offendiculum, quamlibet etiam remoram, & impedimentum: Qualia in viis publicis & militaribus solent esse saxa eminentia, vel pedicæ per insidias collocatæ, in quas qui impingunt, vel planè corruunt, vel à recto tramite aberrant. Hinc per Metaphoram vox hæc ad animum translata, & quidem in Ecclesiâ, notat omne id, quo aliquis offendi potest, quocunque etiam modo illud fiat: ita ut sive dicas aut facias falsa, aut mala, quibus alter corrumpi possit: sive dicas aut facias, quod licet natura sua verum, bonum ac licitum sit, fratri tamen offendiculum, si non per se, saltem per accidens præbere queat: mox scandalum posuisse, videri possis. Et sic in genere intellectum Scandalum, vulgo definitur omne vel dictum, vel factum, vel exemplum, quo alius offenditur, & redditur deterior: vel quod in errorem conjicitur, vel quod error præconceptus confirmatur, vel quod pravum exemplum ad imitationem & regulam trahitur: vel flammæ majoris odij adversus Evangelium subministrantur. Vel ut Græci definiunt: σκάνδαλον ἐστὶ ἐξαστροφὴ σκάζοντος περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν, Scandalum est perversitas claudicantis circa veritatem. Sic ergo Scandalum habet se ut relatum, ad suum Correlatum, nempe offendiculum: quanquam interdum promiscue pro ipsa etiam offensione capitur.

Divisiones Scandalorum plures dantur, quæ tamen ad ternarium commode revocari possunt:

PRIMA divisio respicit objectum sive materiam, in qua & circa quam offendiculum dari potest. Fit enim hoc vel dictis: vel factis, sive moribus aut exemplis. Scandalum in dictis sit rursum duobus modis: Uno quidem, quando quis in communi vita & conversatione, obscenis & illiberalibus jocis aut sermonibus, castas honestorum hominum aures animosq; offendit, & perturbat. Quam speciem expsessit Apostolus, citans illud Menandri Poetæ in Thalia: 1. Cor. 15. 33. Corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava: Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαὶ. Deinde vero committitur hoc scandalum, in doctrina Religionis Christianæ, quando nimirum vel plane falsa sparguntur dogmata: vel de rebus Theologicis spinosa & intricatæ, inutiles, ac minus necessariæ quæstiones & disputationes, quæ infirmiores in fide magis dubios reddunt, & contentionum funes nunquam dissolvendos nectunt. Qualem docendi rationem improbavit & prohibuit Apostolus 2. Tim. 2. 23. Stultas & ineruditas illas quæstiones reijce, sciens quod pariant pugnas sive contentiones. & Tit. 3. 9. Stultas quæstiones cohibe: Sunt enim inutiles & vanæ: imo ut idem 1. Tim. 1. 4. graviter censet, quæstiones præbent potius, quam ædificationem DEI, quæ est per fidem. Hoc pacto enormiter peccarunt, & DEI Ecclesiam graviter offenderunt Doctores Scholastici, qui ejusmodi quæstionibus inutilibus & intricatis Scholarum & templorum pulpita compleverunt: Quales sunt: An DEUS possit odium sui præcipere? An posset actu infinitum secundum omnem dimensionem producere? An potuerit hunc mundum ab æterno meliorem facere, quam fecit? An possit factum reddere infectum? An qualibet persona divina possit quamlibet naturam assumere? An hæc propositio, DEUS est Scarabæus aut Cucurbita, tam possibilis sit, quam hæc; DEUS est homo? An anima Christi potuerit mentiri? Et quæ hujus generis quæstiones infinitæ aliæ, in singulis articulis apud Scholasticos occurrunt.


### Another division of scandals

Let some disputants of this our age see whether they are immune and free from this first species of scandals, who imagine that theological controversies can be defined much more correctly and solidly from metaphysical principles than from the Holy Scriptures: and who boast themselves to be excellent theologians if they have collected a certain farrago of distinctions from the pools of the Scholastics, and have sometimes splendidly inculcated the same to their auditors in teaching and disputing: when even one saying of Scripture can satisfy, and remove every doubt, and wonderfully confirm the faith. Certainly, that auditors are offended in this way, experience itself, the mistress of fools, alas, testifies abundantly enough: for hence arises a loathing of Scripture, and an admiration of Metaphysics: hence the writings of the old theologians now grow sordid, while the patches of certain moderns and juveniles please, who rattle with new, insolent, and almost by the very sound of the words terrifying terms, questions, and answers, breathing mere quiddities, entities, actualities, powers, and such obsolete trifles of the Scholastics: hence the old and truly Lutheran theology and method of disputing grows obsolete: but that new one succeeds, utterly destitute of any foundation and certainty of faith: which could be demonstrated by the example of certain disputants of this kind, who in temptations and agonies of conscience could draw no protection, no πληροφοριαν of faith, no firm comfort of conscience from the entire Scholastic and Metaphysical theology: as Drusius truly wrote in his notes on the New Testament: The protections that are sought from Philosophy are uncertain in the business of faith, and produce no certainty. For whatever is built upon philosophical principles can be destroyed and overturned by the same from another. But these things, ἐν παρόδῳ.

THE OTHER division of scandals can be taken from the diversity of ends. For some are directed by a set purpose so that they may precipitate others into error: as when either impious laws are promulgated, or dogmas are proposed that are manifestly false and adverse to Evangelical doctrine. In both these ways the Anti-Christ and the entire Roman Clergy have filled the Church of GOD with scandals: who did not fear to release subjects by public laws from the oath of fidelity owed to the ordinary Magistrate: to release children from obedience toward Lutheran parents: spouses from the mutual bond of love: citizens of the same Republic from mutual faith and love: provided only that all Lutherans be deprived of both life and property in general. Again, that the same Roman Pontiff gave scandals in doctrine, with the end that he might ensnare as many as possible in the bonds of his idolomania, is better known than that there is any need for proof. In this same way, the Sacramentarians also place scandals, who have nothing more prior or ancient than that they may by any means, through right or wrong, drag others into their snares: so that there are not wanting those from their flock who in Spain and Italy do not hesitate to attend all the idolatrous rites of the Papists, nay, even under the person and names of others to make confession in different temples, so that they may thus obtain for their associates a safe-conduct, as it were, through this medium.

Then, however, there are other scandals, which are not directly designed with that end and purpose that the Gospel should be either hindered or corrupted, but only that the desires and pleasures of the flesh should be indulged, and no, or certainly very little, care for piety and Religion be taken, and one should live more licentiously according to the flesh. Which kind of scandal, as it is most frequent today, so it is by far the most effective for corrupting others.

THE THIRD and last division of scandals, taken from the Subject, is most customary in the Schools today: so that one scandal is called Given, but another Received and Pharisaical. A scandal is Given if, whether in doctrine or in conversation and morals, or by untimely softness, or by importunate levity, lasciviousness, or rashness, you teach, say, or do something not in order, nor in its own place and time, by which the unskilled and weak are offended. Or as others define it more briefly: A scandal given is that whose fault has proceeded from its author. And because the weak are offended most of all by this kind of scandal, hence it has usually been called the scandal of the weak. A scandal is Received when either a doctrine in itself good and true, or some thing lawful in itself and permitted, not wickedly nor importunately proposed and admitted, is snatched by another out of mere malevolence, or some sinister judgment, as an occasion of offense. For a scandal was not given here: since there was no sin on the part of the agent, neither by reason of the matter, nor with respect to the end: but those sinister and malevolent Censors and interpreters invent and receive a scandal for themselves. This scandal has its place especially in hypocrites and enemies of the truth, such as were the Pharisees, who, at the doctrine and rightly done deeds of Christ and the Apostles, [took] scandal, which is committed by deeds, or morals, or examples, happens even in daily conversation: when someone, by the corruption of life and morals, entices others to commit the same wicked deeds: Which example could be seen in that incestuous Corinthian, of whom the Apostle, in 1 Cor. 5:6, affirms that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump. Or it is committed regarding the business of Religion, when someone in the assertion of truth limps either to the right or to the left: that is, sins either in excess or in defect. Such a Scandal the Apostle noted in Peter, Galat. 2. 14, not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel: while, namely, in the absence of the other Apostles, he would familiarly converse with the Gentiles; but afterwards would withdraw himself from their company, upon the arrival of the Apostles. By which manner, indeed, he gravely offended the weaker ones from among the Gentiles, as if he who fears God and works righteousness were not accepted by GOD from every Nation. Which Scandal, although it principally concerned only external conduct, yet by consequence, and indeed directly, it impinged upon the twin Article of the Christian Religion, concerning the Calling of the Gentiles to the kingdom and fellowship of Christ, and concerning Christian Liberty. without cause and just reason. Whence this kind of scandal deserved to be called Pharisaical and Hypocritical. Thus the Pharisees were offended in John 6:52, hearing Christ call himself the heavenly bread, and promising the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood. Thus they were offended in Matt. 15:2, when they heard Christ reprove those frequent washings of the Jews: and in John 8:18 and 19, when he named himself the Son of God: and in Matt. 9:3, when Christ healed the paralytic. Thus Caiaphas was offended, hearing Christ speak words about his return in the clouds of heaven, Matt. 26:65. Thus today the Sacramentarians are offended by the ceremonies used in our churches: thus the Papists are offended by the doctrine of justification by faith alone: they are offended by the eating of meat in Lent, etc.

And such indeed is the nature and affection of scandals considered in themselves: Now the practice that ought to be observed regarding both, the given and the accepted scandal, must be examined more accurately.

And first indeed regarding the given scandal, which some more recent writers are accustomed to call active scandal, that must be avoided with the greatest zeal, nor in any way permitted, that any occasion of offense be given to the weak: First indeed because of the most severe prohibitions and threats of God, Matt. 18:6 and 7, Luke 17:1 and 2: Whoever shall offend one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that he were drowned in the depth of the sea with a millstone hung about his neck: Woe to the world because of offenses: for it is necessary that offenses come: But woe to that man by whom the offense comes. Rom. 14:1: Receive the weak in faith. And verse 13: Let us not judge one another anymore: but judge this rather, that you do not put a stumbling block or scandal before a brother. Then indeed, because Christian charity is enormously harmed by this pact, which seeks and promotes the salvation of another as much as one's own. Now indeed by the offenses given by us, a brother is harmed, polluted, rendered uncertain, and cannot so easily see what life he can or ought to enter safely: nay rather, as the Apostle testifies, 1 Cor. 8:11, such a one is involved in eternal destruction by us, for whom nevertheless Christ himself died. With this Apostolic decision standing, it becomes clear that the atrocity of the given scandal redounds to the most sacred passion of Christ himself, insofar as its saving efficacy is rendered void by our offense given to a neighbor. Therefore, so that we do not sin in this way, two precipices must be avoided: One is that more general one, which is and is called doxosophia, or a vain persuasion of I know not what wisdom and justice, which, out of admiration for itself, dreams that no sin or error can be committed by it. The other is contempt for one's neighbor, by whose care we are touched either not at all or very lightly. Now, however, the Apostle warning, Rom. 15:1, & 2: we who are stronger ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves: but let each one of us please his neighbor for edification, since Christ also did not please himself.

Thirdly, given scandals are to be avoided so that we do not abuse Christian liberty. But we will use it rightly if we look not only at what is permitted, but also at what is profitable and edifying: that is, if we do not only attend to what Christian liberty, simply and in itself considered and in respect of our individual self, permits: but rather, what the edification, conscience, and salvation of our neighbor can bear: so that according to the rule of the Apostle, if you see that you offend a weak brother by the eating of meat, it is more prudent and you use your liberty more rightly if you do not eat meat, until he himself aspires to perfection and learns to use Christian liberty rightly. Where, however, two cautions or exceptions are to be noted. The first: That which was said about the weak brother, and one not utterly abhorring our religion, ought in no way to be extended to the stubborn enemies of the truth. For these do not come under the title of weak brothers, but as the Apostle speaks, they are false brothers, that is, they only simulate brotherhood: and under this guise they tempt the liberty which we have in Christ: to whom we must not yield even for an hour, Gal. 2:4 and 5. And if it should happen that they are offended: yet it must be established that the scandal was not given by us, but accepted by them through malice. The latter caution or exception is this: Infirmity has little place in those locations where the Gospel has been preached for many years. Therefore, just as in Evangelical churches there is no infirmity on account of which those rites that have once been removed ought to be restored: so there is also none on account of which the ceremonies hitherto used ought to be abrogated and removed. Our decision, therefore, about avoiding scandals concerns only those weak in faith and teachable, whom there is hope we can win for Christ by both our doctrine and our conversation. And to this are to be referred the testimonies of Scripture, dealing with this matter expressly: 1 Cor. 8:9: See to it, lest by any means your liberty becomes a stumbling block to the weak. 1 Cor. 10:25 and following: Everything that is sold in the meat market, eat, asking no questions for conscience' sake: If any of the unbelievers calls you, and you wish to go: everything that is set before you, eat, asking no questions for conscience' sake: But if anyone says, this has been sacrificed to idols: do not eat for the sake of him who pointed it out, and for conscience' sake: But I mean conscience, not your own, but the other's: For why is my liberty judged by another's conscience? And verse 31 and 32: Whether you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Be without offense, both to the Jews, and to the Gentiles, and to the Church of God. Gal 5. 13. You have been called unto liberty, brethren: only do not give your liberty for an occasion to the flesh: but by charity serve one another. To speak summarily: Our liberty ought to be directed to this end, that having peace with GOD in our souls, we may yield to the ignorance of the weaker brethren. But since this matter is of great moment, someone might perhaps ask, When therefore, and in what cases ought our liberty to yield to the ignorance of the weak, so that no stumbling block may be offered to them on our part or by our fault? Although the definitive answer to this question can and ought to be sought from those things which were disputed in the immediately preceding place concerning the right use of indifferent things: yet in this place, and regarding the present practice, we determine that this must be well noted, that there are three kinds of actions, from which men can be offended, or scandalized. For there are in the first place actions that are in themselves evil and perverse, both in doctrine and in morals: which not only hypocrites.

Latin:

Viderint autem nostro hoc seculo nonnulli Disputatores, num à prima hac specie Scandalorum immunes sint, & liberi, qui autumant, Controversias Theologicas, multò rectiùs & solidiùs ex metaphysicis, quàm ex Scripturis Sacris definiri posse: quique præclaros se Theologos venditant, si ex Scholasticorum lacunis farraginem quandam distinctionum collegerunt, eandemq́; in docendo, ac disputando splendidè aliquoties suis inculcarunt Auditoribus: cùm vel unum Scripturæ dictum satisfacere, & dubitationem omnem tollere, & fidem mirificè confirmare possit. Certè Auditorès hoc pacto offendi, ipsa proh dolor experientia, stultorum magistra, satis abundè testatur: Hinc enim Scripturæ oritur fastidium, & Metaphysicæ admiratio: hinc veterum Theologorum scripta jam sordescunt, arrident contrà quorundam neotericorum & Juvenalium centones, qui terminis, quæstionibus, responsionibus crepant novis, insolentibus, & ipso penè verborum sono tremendis, meras quidditates, entitates, actualitates, potentias, & hujusmodi obsoletas Scholasticorum quisquilias spirantibus: hinc vetus, & verè Lutherana Theologia & disputandi ratio exolescit: succedit verò nova illa, omni fundamento, & fidei certitudine planè destituta: id quod exemplo quorundam hujusmodi Disputatorum demonstrari posset, qui in tentationibus, & angoribus Conscientiæ, nullum præsidium, nullam πληροφοριαν fidei, nullum firmum Conscientiæ solatium, ex universa Scholastica & Metaphysica Theologiâ haurire potuerunt: ut verè Drusius scripserit in suis ad Novum Testamentum notis: Ex Philosophia quæ petuntur præsidia, in negocio fidei incerta sunt, & nullam pariunt certitudinem. Nam quicquid Philosophicus principiis adstruitur: iisdem ab alio destrui & everti potest. Sed hæc, ἐν παρόδῳ.

ALTERA Scandalorum divisio à finium diversitate sumi potest. Quædam enim destinato consilio eo diriguntur, ut in errorem alios præcipitent: ut quando vel Leges promulgantur impiæ, vel dogmata proponuntur manifestè falsa, & doctrinæ Evangelicæ adversa. Utroque isto modo Ecclesiam DEI scandalis complevit Anti-Christus & Clerus Romanus universus: qui non veritus est, legibus publicis solvere subditos, à juramento fidelitatis Magistratui ordinario debito: liberos ab obedientia erga parentes Lutheranos: conjuges à mutuo amoris vinculo: cives ejusdem Reipub. à mutua fide & dilectione: modò Lutherani & vita & facultatibus priventur in universum omnes. Rursus idem Pontifex Romanus, quæ in doctrina dederit scandala, eò fine, ut quamplurimos Idolomaniæ suæ vinculis irretiret, notius est, quàm ut probatione ulla opus sit. Ultro isto modo, Scandala ponunt etiam Sacramentarij, qui nihil prius aut antiquius habent, quàm ut quovis modo per fas nefasq́; alios in suos casses pertrahere possint: ita ut non desint ex istorum grege qui in Hispanijs & Italia non dubitent omnibus Pontificiorum interesse sacris idololatricis, imò sub aliorum persona & nominibus Confessionem in diversis templis edere, ut sic sociis suis, falvum quasi conductum per hoc medium impetrent.

Deinde verò alia sunt Scandala, quæ non directè eo fine & consilio designantur, ut Evangelium vel impediatur, vel corrumpatur, sed tantùm carnis cupiditatibus & voluptatibus indulgeatur, & nulla, vel certè exigua pietatis & Religionis cura habita, secundum carnem licentiùs vivatur. Quod Scandalorum genus uti hodie est frequentissimum, ita ad corrumpendos alios longè est efficacissimum.

TERTIA & postrema Scandalorum divisio à Subjecto petita, in Scholis hodie est usitatissima: ita ut Scandalum aliud dicatur Datum aliud verò Acceptum & Pharisaicum Datum est, si vel in doctrina vel in conversatione ac moribus, vel intempestiva mollitie, vel importuna levitate, lascivia aut temeritate, non ordine, nec suo loco ac tempore aliquid doceas, dicas, faciasvè, quo imperiti ac infirmi offendantur Vel ut alij brevius definiunt: Scandalum datum est, cujus culpa ab autore ejus profecta est. Et quia hoc Scandali genere infirmi potissimum offenduntur, hinc Scandalum infirmorum plerumque appellari consuevit. Acceptum Scandalum est, quando vel doctrina in se bona, & vera, vel res aliqua licita per se, & concessa, non improbè, nec importunè proposita & admissa, ab alio ex mera malevolentia, aut sinistro quodam judicio, in offensionis occasionem rapitur. Non enim hic datum erat Scandalum: siquidem ab agente, neque ratione materiæ, neque respectu finis, ulla ex parte peccatum fuit: sed sinistri illi & malevoli Censores atque interpretes sibiipsis Scandalum fingunt & accipiunt. Habet locum hoc Scandalum præcipuè in Hypocritis & hostibus veritatis, quales erant Pharisæi, qui doctrina & rectè factis Christi ac Apostolorum, præScandalum, quod factis, sive moribus, aut exemplis committitur, contingit vel in quotidiana conversatione: quando quis vitæ, morumq́; confceleratione, alios ad eadé perpetranda flagitia allicit: Quale exemplum in Corinthio illo incestuoso videre licuit, de quo Apostolus, in 1. Cor. 5. 6. affirmat, quòd pauxillum fermenti tota massam corrumpat. Vel committitur circa Religionis negocium, quando quis in veritatis assertione vel in dextram, vel in sinistram claudicat: hoc est, vel in excessu, vel in defectu peccat. Quale Scandalum notavit Apostolus in Petro, Galat. 2. 14. non recto pede incedente ad veritatem Evangelij: dum nimirum absentibus reliquis Apostolis, familiariter conversaretur cum Gentibus; sed postmodùm ab istorum conversatione se subduceret, supervenientibus Apostolis. Quo sanè pacto infirmiores ex gentilibus graviter offendebat, quasi non ex omni Gente, qui timet Deum, & operatur justitiam, acceptus esset DEO. Quod Scandalum licet principaliter externa tantum spectaret conversationem, per Consequentiam tamen, & quidem directè impingebat in Articulum Religionis Christianæ geminum, de Vocatione Gentium ad regnum & societatem Christi, & de Libertate Christiana. ter causam ac rationem justam offendebantur. Unde hoc genus Scandali Pharisaicum & Hypocryticum dici meruit. Sic offendebantur Pharisæi Joh. 6 52. audientes Christum se appellare panem cœleste, suæq́; carnis manducationem, & sanguinis sui bibitionem promittere. Sic offendebantur Matt. 15. 2. cùm audirent, Christum frequentes illas Judæorū lotiones reprehendere: & Joh. 8. 18. & 19. Filium DEI se nominare: & Matth. 9. 3. cùm Christus sanaret Paralyticū. Sic offendebatur Caiphas, audiens Christum verba facere, de suo in nubibus cœli reditu. Matt. 26. 65. Sic hodiè offenduntur Sacramentarij Ceremonijs in Ecclesiis nostris usitatis: Sic Pontificij offenduntur doctrina de sola justitia fidei : offenduntur esu carnium in Quadragesima &c.

Et talis quidem est natura & affectio Scandalorū in se consideratorum: Nunc qua Praxis circa utrumque, & datum, & acceptum Scandalu observari debeat, accuratiùs dispiciēdū.

Ac primùm quidem quoad Scandalum datū, quod recentiores nonnulli Scandalum activum appellere solent, illud summo studio est cavēdū, neq; ullo pacto permittendum, ut infirmis offensionis occasio aliqua detur: Primùm qui dem propter severissimas DEI prohibitiones, & comminationes Matt. 18. 6. & 7. Luc 17. 1. & 2. Quisquis offenderit unū ex parvulis istis, qui in me credunt, præstaret ei, ut suspensus de mola asinaria in profundū maris demergeretur : Væ mundo ab offendiculis : necesse est enim, ut eveniant offendicula : Veruntamē væ homini illi, per quem venit offendiculū. Rom. 14. 1. Infirmum in fide assumite. Et versu. 13. Non ampliùs invicem (alius aliū ) judicemus: sed hoc judicate magis, ne ponatis offendiculū fratri, vel scādalum. Deinde verò, quia Charitas Christiana enormiter hoc pacto læditur, quæ tàm alteri9: quàm propriam suiipsius salutem quærit & promovet. Jam verò per offendicula à nobis data, frater læditur, polluitur, incertus redditur, & quamnám vitam tutò ingredi possit, aut debeat, non ita facilè videre queat : quin imò teste Apostolo, 1. Cor. 8. 11. talis æterno exitio per nos involvitur, pro quo tamē Christ9 ipse est mortuus. Qua Apostolica stante decisione, palàm fit Scandali dati atrocitate, in ipsi9 Christi sacratissima passionem redundare, quatenus ejus salutaris efficacia redditur irrita per nostram, proximo datam, offensionem. Ne ergò hoc pacto delinquamus, duo cavenda sunt præcipitia: Unum generalius illud, quod est, ac dicitur δοξοσοφία, sive inanis, nescio cujus sapientiæ & justitiæ persuasio, quæ ex suiipsius admiratione nihil à se peccati, auc errari posse, somniat. Alterum v. est comtemtus proximi, cujus cura vel planè nulla, vel levi admodum tangimur. Jam v. Apostolo monente, Rom. 15. 1. & 2. nos qui firmiores sumus, infirmiorum imbecillitatem sustinere debemus, nec nobis ipsis placere: sed unusquisque nostrum proximo suo placeat ad ædificationem, quoniam neq; Christus sibi placuit.

Tertiò vitanda sunt Scandala data, ut ne Libertate Christiana abutamur. Tùm verò ea rectè utemur, si non tantùm quid liceat, sed &, quid prosit, & ædificet, spectemus : hoc est, si non tantùm attendamus, quid Libertas Christiana simpliciter & in se considerata, & ratione nostri individui permittat: sed potiùs, quid proximi ædificatio, conscientia, & salus ferre possit: adeò ut secundum regulam Apostoli, si esu carnium fratrem infirmū offendi videas, consultius sit & Libertate tua rectiùs utaris, si carnibus nõ vescaris, donec ipse ad perfectionē adspiret, & Libertate Christiana rectè uti discat. Ubi tamen duæ cautioñes sive exceptiones sũt notãdæ. Prior: Quod de fratre infirmo, & à nostra Religione nõ penitùs abhorrente dictũ est, illud ad præfractos hostes veritatis extendi nullo modo debet. Hi enim nõ veniunt titulo fratrü infirmorũ, sed ut Apostolus loquitur, falsi sunt fratres, hoc est, fraternitatem tantùm simulãt: & sub hac specie tentant libertatẽ, quá habemus in Christo: quibus ne ad horam quidem est cedendũ, Gal. 2. 4. & 5. Et si maximè contingat, hos offendi: tamen non à nobis datum: sed ab ipsis per malitiam scandalum acceptũ esse statui debet. Posterior cautio sive exceptio est hæc: Infirmitas illis in locis vix locum habet, in quibus multis annis prædicatum est Evangelium. Quemadmodum ergo in Ecclesiis Evangelicis nulla infirmitas datur, propter quàm ritus illi qui semel sunt sublati, restitui debeant: ita nulla etiam datur, propter quam ceremoniæ hactenùs usitatæ, abrogari & tolli debeant. Nostra ergo decisio de vitandis Scandalis, respicit tantùm infirmos in fide, & dociles, quos spes est, nos nostra & doctrina & conversatione Christo posse lucrifacere. Et huc referenda sunt Scripturæ testimonia, hac de re ex professo agentia: 1. Cor. 8. 9. Videte, ne forte libertas vestra offendiculum fiat infirmis. 1. Cor. 10. 25. & seqq. Omne quod in macello venit, manducate: nihil interrogantes propter Conscientiã: Si quis vocat vos infidelium, & vultis ire: omne quod vobis apponitur, manducate, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiã: Si quis autẽ dixerit, hoc immolatum est idolis: nolite manducare propter illum, qui indicavit, & propter conscientiam: Conscientiã autem dico non tuam, sed alterius: Cur enim libertas mea judicetur ab alterius conscientiâ? Et vers. 31. & 32. Sive editis, sive bibitis, sive aliud quid facitis, omnia in gloriã Dei facite. Sine offensione estote, tùm Judæis, tùm Gentib9, tùm Ecclesiæ Dei. Gal 5. 13. In libertatem vocati estis fratres: tantùm ne libertatem vestram in licentiam detis carni: sed per charitatem servite vobis invicem. Summatim loquendo: Libertas nostra eò dirigi debet, ut pacem cũ DEO in animis nostris habentes, fratrum infirmorũ ignorantiæ cedamus. Cæterùm cùm hæc res magni sit mo menti, quærat fortè aliquis, Quando ergo, & in quibus casibus infirmorũ ignorantiæ Libertas nostra cedere debeat, ne ex nostrâ parte aut culpâ ullum illis præbeatur offendiculum? Quanquam v. Quæstionis hujus definitiva ex iis, quæ de recto usu rerum adiaphorarũ, præcedente loco proximo, disputata sunt, peti potest, & debet: hoc tamen loco, & quoad præsentem praxin, illud probè notandum esse statuimus, quòd tria sint actionum genera, ex quibus homines offendi, sive scandalizari possunt. Sunt enim initiò actiones per se Malæ & perversæ, qua doctrinam qua mores: quæ non modò hypocritas.


### Another division of scandals (continued)

and the Pharisees: not also only weak brothers: but also those most firm in faith they can offend; Such are, heresy, fornication, adultery, gluttony, blasphemy, and other crimes and scandals of this kind: which must never be committed: For woe to the man who has done such things. Matt. 18.7. Gal. 5. 19. & 21. 1. Cor. 6. 9. Next are actions in themselves good and necessary for salvation: such as the preaching of the Word of GOD, the use of the Sacraments, the confession of the truth of the Gospel, the pursuit of piety and good works. These must always be done, and never for the sake of anyone, in any way or respect, ever be interrupted: even if the whole world cries out and is scandalized. The reason is; Because just as it is necessary to obey GOD more than men: so it is also necessary to have greater regard for the sanctification of the divine name, and the truth of the Gospel, than for the whole world, or any man, whether firm or weak: provided the glory of GOD, and of Christ, and the truth of the Gospel remains safe, sound, and protected. Christ shows this practice, Matt. 10. 33. He who denies me before men, I will also deny him before my heavenly Father. Where at the same time consolation is added, so that, if because of this assertion of the truth, dissensions and contentions arise, we may not be broken in spirit: For I came, says the Savior, to separate a man from his father, and a daughter from her mother, etc. Matt. 10. 35. And Gal. 1. 8. If anyone has preached another Gospel, besides that which you have received, let him be anathema.

Thirdly, there are free and indifferent actions, both mostly natural; such as, to eat, to drink, this or that: and ecclesiastical, depending solely on Christian liberty. Regarding the use of these, one must always see what the love of GOD and neighbor permits. This, as an infallible rule and cynosure, will hold up a torch, as it were, as to how you ought to moderate your liberty, or abstain from it entirely for a time: so that whatever is undertaken by you in this kind of action, may be done without danger to the glory of GOD, without injury to the charity owed to one's neighbor (but the one weak in faith), without loss of the Gospel and faith: that which was demonstrated in the treatise on Adiaphora with certain rules and practical examples. In this kind of thing, therefore, as soon as you sin, you have immediately given scandal, the effects of which are wont to be most sad.

Perhaps someone might ask here, if scandals provide a handle and occasion for such great evils and inconveniences, in what sense then does the Savior assert, Matt. 18. 7. Luke 17. 1. That it is necessary that scandals come. But the answer is known, by which a distinction is made even in this place between necessity simple or absolute, and between necessity hypothetical, and by accident. Therefore, God does not will by any absolute will that scandals should happen, Ps. 5. 5. You are not a GOD willing iniquity, and 1 John 2. 16. The things that are in the world, such as the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, are not from GOD the Father: But the Savior wished to express and note, partly the tireless effort of the Devil in inciting men to scandals, and partly the perverse will of men, which, as it is always prone and inclined to evil, so by its own nature it is snatched away as if by a blind impulse to design scandals, unless it is ruled by the Holy Spirit. For the judgment of men, in spiritual matters, outside of regeneration is by far most corrupt, so that where that dominion obtains, it is impossible that offenses should not come: 1 Cor. 2. 14. Whence the Apostle formed a general aphorism: Φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός, ἔχθρα εἰς θεόν: the mind of the flesh is enmity against GOD Rom. 8. 6. And he testifies that the word of the Cross of Christ is foolishness to the Gentiles, but an offense to the Jews. 1 Cor. 1. 23. Added to this is temporal happiness, by which many are so captivated that they prefer to serve idolatrous cults, whether feignedly or seriously, than to profess the truth of the Gospel ingenuously and freely with any loss of their faculties: by the example of the Jews, Jer. 44. 16 & 17. As for the word which you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you: but we will certainly do every word that will go out of our mouth, to sacrifice to the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings to her, as we have done, we and our fathers, and we were filled with bread, and it was well with us, and we saw no evil. The Savior looked to these causes, bringing in a certain necessity of scandals. But just as GOD would never permit any evil, unless He could elicit some good from it: So some good end of scandals given also appears among the pious and the elect: namely, the testing of faith, patience, hope, and other virtues worthy of a Christian man. For just as, the Apostle being witness, there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest, so also scandals must happen, so that the pious and the elect may always resist them through the indwelling grace of the Holy Spirit: 1 Cor. 11. 19. Matt. 18. 7.

And such indeed is the nature of scandals given, such also is the practice to be studiously observed regarding them.

There remains another species of scandal; namely, that of the receiver, or of the Pharisees, which some more recent writers have been accustomed to call passive scandals. But we need not be anxious about the practice of these: Since they are conceived by none but the wicked and hypocrites, without any cause or fault of ours: According to that of Cyprian, Epist. 2. Whoever does not imitate the wicked, offends them, just as drunken men are wont to do, who consider it an injury if someone does not accommodate himself to their manners by joining in. Hence Jerome: It is a solace for the wicked to carp at the good, while by the multitude of those sinning, they think the guilt of their offenses is diminished.

Such scandals, therefore, are not to be cared for by the pious and the faithful: but piety is to be followed; truth is to be preached; our liberty is to be used as is fitting, even if all Pharisees, hypocrites, the impious, nay, the whole world be scandalized. The Savior himself shows this practice in Matt. 15. 14, where, when the disciples say, "Do you not know that when this word was heard the Pharisees were scandalized?" Christ answers: "Let them alone, they are blind, and leaders of the blind." And the Apostle in Rom. 12. 2: "Do not be conformed to the customs of this world." The reason: For the glory of GOD, the truth of the Gospel, the confession of Christ, the legitimate use of Christian liberty, the pursuit of piety, and the edification of the weak among the pious, are to be preferred in all ways to the corrupt judgment of all Pharisees, hypocrites, heretics, and the whole world. The end and effect of scandal taken is usually hardening. For because hypocrites, heretics, and the impious, who are offended by the sound words and deeds of others, sin out of a deliberate malice of mind and too stubbornly and obstinately despise the degrees of admonition; it happens afterwards by the just judgment of God that they are left to their own depraved judgments and counsels; and thus, left to themselves and deserted by God, they fall more and more into errors, and in them at last, blinded and hardened, they perish. The sadder this effect is, the more we must strive to put a bridle on the wisdom of our flesh, and to repress its untamed affections more and more, and to show ourselves docile and obedient to the Holy Spirit.

AMEN.

Latin:

& Pharifæos: non etiam tantùm infirmos fratres: sed & in fide firmissimos offendere possunt; Quales sunt, hæresis, fornicatio, adulterium, crapula, blasphemia, & hujus generis scelera atq; flagitia alia: quæ nunquam sunt facienda: Væ n. homini qui talia fecerit. Matt. 18.7. Gal. 5. 19. & 21. 1. Cor. 6. 9. Deinde sunt actiones per se bonæ & necessariæ ad salutem: ut prædicatio Verbi DEI, usus Sacramentorum, Confessio veritatis Evangelij, studium pietatis & bonorum operum. Hæ semper sunt faciendæ, neque in ullius gratiam, ullo modo aut respectu unquàm intermittendæ: si maximè totus Mundus reclamat, & scandalizetur. Ratio est; Quia sicut DEO plus oportet obtemperare, quàm hominibus: ita oportet etiam potiorem habere rationem Sanctificationis nominis divini, & veritatis Evangelicæ, quàm totius Mundi, vel ullius hominis, sive firmi, sive infirmi: modò Gloria DEI, & Christi, & veritas Evangelij salva, sarta tecta permaneat. Praxin hanc monstrat Christus, Matth. 10 33. Qui me negaverit coram hominibus, negabo & eum coram Patre meo cælesti. Ubi simul additur consolatio, ut, si propter hanc veritatis assertionem, dissidia & contentiones oboriantur, nô frangamur animo: Veni enim, inquit Servator, separare hominem à Patre suo, & filiam à matre, &c. Matth. 10. 35. Et Gal. 1. 8. Si quis Evangelizaverit aliud Evangelium, præter id, quod accepistis, anathema sit.

Tertiò sunt actiones liberæ & indifferentes, tum naturales pleræque; quales sunt, Edere, bibere, hoc vel illud: tum Ecclesiasticæ, à Libertate Christiana unicè dependentes. Circa istarum usu semper videndum, quid dilectio DEI & proximi permittat. Hæc, tanquàm infallibilis regula ac cynosura facem quasi præferet, quomôdo moderari debeas libertatem tuam, vel eâ ad tempus planè abstinere: ita ut quicquid in hoc genere actionum à te suscipitnr, fiat sine periculo gloriæ DEI, sine læsione charitatis proximo (sed infirmo in fide) debitæ, sine jactura Evangelij & fidei: id quod in tractatu de Adiaphoris certis & regulis & exemplis practicis demonstratum fuit. In hoc ergo genere rerum quamprimù peccas, statim dedisti scandalum, cujus tristissimi solent esse effectus.

Quærat fortassis hîc aliquis, si tantis malis atque incommodis ansam & occasionem præbent scandala, Quo sensu ergo Servator asserat, Matt. 18 7. Luc. 17 1. Necessum esse venire scandala. Sed nota est responsio, qua distinguitur hoc etiam loco inter Necessitatem simplicem sive absolutam, & inter Necessitatem hypotheticam, & ex accidenti. Non ergò Deus absoluta aliqua voluntate vult, ut eveniant scandala, Psal. 5.5. non DEUS volens iniquitatē, tu es, & 1. Joh. 2. 16. Quæ in mundo sunt, velut concupiscentia carnis, concupiscentia oculorū, & fastus vitæ, non sunt ex DEO Patre: Sed exprimere & notare voluit Servator, partim Diaboli indefessum studium, in instigandis hominibus ad scandala, partim verò perversam hominū voluntatē, quæ uti ad malum semper est prona ac proclivis, ita sua natura cœco quasi impetu ad designada scandala, nisi regatur à Spiritu Sancto, abripitur. Est enim hominum judicium, in Spiritualibus, extra regenerationē longè corruptissimum, ut ubi illud dominium obtinet, impossibile sit, non venire offendicula: 1. Cor. 2. 14. Unde Apostolus generalem formavit aphorismum: Φρόνημα τῆς σαρxòs, ἔχθρα εἰς θεὸν: prudentia carnis inimicitia est adversus DEUM Rom. 8 6. Et Sermonem Crucis Christi, gentilibus stultitiam, Judæis verò offendiculum esse testatur. 1. Cor. 1. 23. Accedit temporalis felicitas, qua multi ita perstringuntur, ut malint cultib9 idololatricis, sive simulaté, sive feriò servire, quàm cum jactura aliqua facultatum, Veritatem Evangelij ingenuè & liberè profiteri: exemplo Judæorum, Jere. 44. 16 & 17. sermonem, quem loquutus nos, in nomine Domini, non audiemus ex te: sed facientes faciemus omne verbū, quod egredietur de ore nostro, ut sacrificemus reginæ cœli, & libemus ei libamina, sicut fecimus nos & Patres nostri, & saturati sumus panibus, & benè nobis erāt, malumq; non vidimus. Has ad causas respexit Servator, necessitatē quandam scandalorum afferens. Quemadmodum verò DEUS nullum unquàm malum permitteret, nisi bonum aliquid ex eo elicere posset: Ita scandalorum etiam datorum finis aliquis bonus apud pios & electos se exerit: nempe Probatio fidei, patientiæ, spei, aliarumq; Christiano homine dignarum virtutum. Quemadmodum enim, Apostolo teste hæreses esse oportet, ut qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant, ita scandala etiam evenire oportet, ut pij & electi illis per inhabitantem gratiam Spiritus Sancti semper resistant: 1. Cor. 11. 19. Matth. 18. 7.

Et talis quidem est natura Scandalorum datorum, talis etiam praxis circa ea studiosè observanda.

Restat altera species scandalorum; nempè acceptoris, sive Pharisaœorum quæ nonnulli recentiores Scriptores scandala passiva nominare consveverunt. De horum autem praxi non est, ut simus solliciti: Siquidem ea non nisi à malis & hypocritis concipiuntur, sine ulla nostra vel causâ, vel culpa: Secundum illud Cypriani, Epist. 2. Malos quisquis non imitatur, offendit, quemadmodum vinolenti homines facere solent, qui injuriæ loco ducunt, si quis comportando ad ipsorum mores se non accommodet. E. Hieronymus: Solatium malorum est, bonos carpere, dum peccantium multitudine, culpam delictorum putant esse minuā.

Ejusmodi ergò scandala piis & fidelib9 nô sunt curanda: sed sequenda est pietas: prædicanda veritas; utendum libertate nostra prout decet, etiamsi omnes Pharisæi, hypocritæ, impii, imò totus mundus scandalizetur. Praxin hanc monstrat Servator ipse Matth. 15. 14. ubi Christus discipulis dicentibus; Nescis, quòd verbo hoc audito Pharisæi scandalizati sint; Respodet: Sinite illos, cæci sunt, & cæcorum duces. Et Apostolus Rom. 12. 2. Ne conformemini moribus seculi hujus. Ratio: Gloria enim DEI, veritas Evangelij, confessio Christi, legitimus usus libertatis Christianæ, studium pietatis, piorum informorum ædificatio, modis omnib9 anteferenda, omniū Pharisæorum, hypocritarum hæreticorū, & totius mūdi corrupto judicio. Finis a. & effectus Scandali accepti, plerunque solet esse Induratio. Quia enim Hypocritæ, hæretici, & impij, qui sanis aliorum & dictis, & factis offenduntur, ex destinata animi malitia peccant: & gradus admonitionum nimis præfractè & obstinatè contemnunt; sit postmodum justo DEI judicio, ut pravis suis judicijs & consilijs relinquantur; & sic sibi ipsis relicti, ac à DEO deserti, magis magisq́; in errores prolabantur, inq́; illis tandem excœcati & indurati pereant. Qui effectus quò tristior est, eò magis annitendum nobis, ut carnis nostræ sapientiæ frena iniciamus, ejusq́; indomitos affectus magis magisque reprimamus: & Spiritui Sancto dociles nos & obsequentes præbeamus.

AMEN.


## 31 Concerning Spirit and Letter


### Oikonomy The Oikonomia of the future treatment

Of the Spirit and the Letter

The OIKONOMIA of the future treatment.

The greater and more pressing the utility of this controversy concerning the Letter and the Spirit, when rightly explained, is—both for the refutation of various errors by which heavenly doctrine is contaminated, and for the acknowledgment of our most sad corruption, and for the celebration of the ineffable benefits of Christ our Savior—the more wonderful and almost insolent it seems that not only in ancient times but also in these more recent centuries and times, very few have existed who have devoted any study or effort to explaining it accurately and skillfully. From orthodox antiquity, Augustine alone stands out, who explained this matter quite prolixly and diligently in a special treatise to his son Marcellinus, which exists in Volume III of his Works. Among the more recent writers, besides Philip, hardly anyone else mentions this controversy, unless perhaps incidentally; but in such a way that a great variety and discrepancy of opinions exists among the interpreters, which makes the matter itself more obscure and difficult rather than explaining it, as will be evident from our exposition.

The treatment of our author Philip Melanchthon is very succinct and is completed in two parts: one didactic or instructional, the other refutatory or polemical. Regarding the thesis, soon after the commendation of Evangelical doctrine, he defines the Letter as any doctrine, thought, habit, discipline, and good intention without the Holy Spirit—that is, without true fear, and without true faith, without trust consoling the minds, and without the acknowledgment and invocation of Christ. Then, however, he says that the Spirit signifies the Holy Spirit beginning and perfecting in hearts a new light, wisdom, righteousness, and eternal life, pleasing to God, and burning with the motions of the Holy Spirit, namely Fear, Faith, Invocation, Love, and in eternal life enjoying the sight of God and celebrating God. Finally, it signifies the fellowship of the divine nature, etc. Finally, toward the end of his treatment, Philip adds that although the Letter, according to the opinion of the Apostle, does not give life, it is nevertheless not entirely devoid of utility, because all who are not yet reborn must be restrained and accustomed to virtue and piety through the more severe discipline of the Law, which discipline of the law is a schoolmaster unto CHRIST.

Regarding the other, refutatory part, the author first refutes the error of Origen, who was accustomed to interpret the literal sense of Scripture as the Letter that kills, but the Allegorical or Mystical sense as the Spirit that gives life. Then he rejects the dream of the Enthusiasts, who imagine that the Scriptures, insofar as they are written with ink, and insofar as they are also explained by the ministers of the Church with a living voice, are a useless and killing letter; but that secret raptures and heavenly revelations are the Spirit that gives life.

And such indeed is the Philippean Treatise, concerning which, especially regarding the proposed definitions of Letter and Spirit, we shall candidly show in the conclusion itself what is to be determined: which (following the footsteps of the Author) we have likewise established as bipartite; in the beginning indeed intending to investigate the true, proper, and genuine meaning of the Apostolic Opposition between the killing Letter and the life-giving Spirit: then indeed, having taken into account the Controversies of our century, intending to refute each and every error which has ever existed anywhere concerning this matter, and which are even today defended by Romanists, Calvinists, Schwenckfeldians, Anabaptists, and other fanatics.

Latin:

De Spiritu & Litera

OIKONOMIA Futuræ tractationis.

QUo major & angustior est, controversiæ hujus de Litera & Spiritu, ritè explicatæ, tum ad variorum errorum, quibus doctrina cœlestis contaminatur, refutationem: tum ad agnitionem tristissimæ corruptionis nostræ: tùm ad inenarrabilium Christi Servatoris nostri beneficiorum celebrationem, Utilitas: eo mirum magis ac insolens quasi videtur, quòd non priscis modò, sed & recentioribus hisce seculis, ac temporibus paucissimi extiterunt, qui in ea accuratè &, dextrè explicanda, studij aliquid, operæq; collocarunt. Ex orthodoxa Antiquitate unus fermè eminet Augustinus, qui materiam hanc satis prolixè & diligenter explicavit, peculiari tractatu ad Marcellinum filium: qui extat Tomo III. Operum. Ex recentioribus præter Philippum, vix ullus alius, nisi fortè incidenter, Controversiæ hujus meminit: sed ita, ut magna sententiarum varietas & discrepantia interpretibus invicem intercedat: quæ rem ipsam obscurioré magis difficilioréq́; reddit, quàm explicat: uti ex nostra patebit diexodo.

Autoris nostri Philippi Melanchonis tractatio admodùm succincta est, & duabus absolvitur partib9: Una θετικὴ sive διδασκαλικὴ: altera verò ἀντιθετικὴ sive πολεμικὴ. Quoad θέσιν, mox post commendationem doctrinæ Evangelicæ definit Literam, quod sit qualibet doctrina, cogitatio, assuefactio, disciplina & intentio bona sine Spiritu S.id est, sine vero timore, & sine verá fide, sine fiducia consolante mentes, agnitione & invocatione Christi. Deinde verò Spiritum dicit significare Spiritum S. inchoantem, & perficientem in cordibus novam lucem, sapientiam, justitiam, & vitam perpetuam, placentem DEO, & motibus Spiritus Sancti ardentem, videlicet Timore, Fide, Invocatione, Dilectione, & in vita æterna fruentem conspectu DEI, & celebrantem DEUM. Denique significat societatem divinæ naturæ &c. Tandem sub finem Tractationis suæ subjicit Philippus, licet Litera ex sententia Apostoli non vivificet, eam tamen non omni prorsus destitui utilitate, propterea quòd omnes nondum renati coërcendi, & ad virtutem ac pietatem affuefaciendi sint, per severiorem disciplinam Legis: quæ legis disciplina sit Pædagogus in CHRISTUM.

Quoad partem alteram ἀνασκευτικὴν refutat Autor primùm errorem Origenis, qui literalem Scripturæ sensum, per literam Occidentem: Allegoricum verò sive Mysticum, per Spiritum Vivificantem interpretari consuevit. Deinde reijcit Enthusiastarum somnium, qui fingunt, Scripturas, quatenus atramento sunt scriptæ, quatenus etiam viva voce à ministris Ecclesiæ explicantur, esse literam inutilem & occidentem: Raptus verò arcanos, & revelationes cœlestes, esse Spiritum vivificantem.

Et talis quidem est Tractatio Philippea, de qua cumprimis quoad propositas definitiones Literæ & Spiritus, quid sit statuendum, in ipsa diexodo candidè ostendemus: quam (secuti vestigia Autoris) constituimus itidem bipartitam; initiò quidem investigaturi veram, propriam, ac genuinam sententiam Oppositionis Apostolicæ inter Literam occidentem, & Spiritum Vivificantem: deinde verò Controversiarum nostri seculi habitâ ratione, refutaturi singulos & universos errores, qui quidem unquam uspiam de hac materia extiterunt, ac etiamnum hodiè à Romanensibus, Calvinianis, Schwenckfeldianis, Anabaptistis aliisq; fanaticis propugnantur.


### Oikonomy: The First Part Thetical, or didactic

THE FIRST PART Thetical, or didactic.

IF we examine the Scriptures of both Testaments more accurately, it is plain that the Opposition of Spirit and Letter, such as indeed comes under investigation in this place, is nowhere expressed in the Old Testament, κτ᾽ ῥῆμα, μὲ αὐτολεξεὶ: although the thing itself is not obscurely handed down and explained there: as will be shown below. In the New Testament, however: in three places especially, the Lord Apostle opposes the Letter and the Spirit to one another. THE first PLACE Rom. 2. 27. 28. & 29. has it thus: That which is by nature uncircumcision, if it shall keep the Law, shall judge thee, who by the Letter and Circumcision art a transgressor of the law. For he is not a Jew who is one in the manifest; nor that which is in the open, Circumcision, that is, in the flesh, is Circumcision: But he who is a Jew in secret; and the Circumcision of the heart, in the Spirit, not in the letter, whose praise is not from men, but from GOD. If these words are considered more closely, it becomes plain that the Apostle establishes a twofold Circumcision, just as he does a twofold Jew: The one, which is according to the letter, in the open, and in the flesh, whose praise is from men. The other, however, the Circumcision of the heart, in the Spirit, not the letter, whose praise is from GOD. And similarly, another Jew, who is such in the open: but another who is such in secret. Circumcision, therefore, of the letter, in the open, and in the flesh, whose praise is from men: was nothing other than that external work, of which the Jews boasted without true piety, and promised themselves the grace of GOD and eternal life, for this one reason, that they were born from the seed of Abraham, and were circumcised, clearly forgetting the promises concerning the Messiah, and his Spiritual promises, when yet Circumcision was instituted for this reason above all, that it might be σφραγὶς δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίστεως, a seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4. 11. that faith, namely, which would embrace the promise concerning the blessed seed, as a sign or infallible τεκμήριον, distinguishing the posterity of Abraham from all other nations, indeed even from those Jews who, although they were children of Abraham according to the flesh, were not so according to the promise: Rom. 9. 7. & 8.

The other, however, the Circumcision of the Heart in the Spirit, not in the letter, is nothing other than true Conversion to GOD, cutting off the foreskin of sin, that is, truly and seriously grieving that one has offended GOD, by Original and Actual sin: And undoubtedly believing that, on account of the promised seed, sins are remitted to him, and the Holy Spirit is given. Concerning which Circumcision of the Spirit, Moses himself says in Deuteronomy 30. 6. The Lord thy GOD will circumcise thy heart, and the heart of thy seed, that thou mayest love the Lord thy GOD, with all thy heart, &c. And the Apostle in Colossians 2. 11. In Christ you are circumcised, with a Circumcision not made by hand, in the putting off of the Body of the Flesh: but in the Circumcision of Christ, buried with him through Baptism, in which you also rose again through the faith of GOD who works effectively, who raised him from the dead: And you when you were dead in the sins of the foreskin of your flesh, he made alive together with him, having forgiven all sins.

And this is indeed the first Apostolic passage where the letter and the spirit are opposed to one another: in this sense: that Circumcision, which consists only in the external amputation of the foreskin, but is destitute of faith in Christ, is the letter: but the Circumcision of the Heart, done in the faith of Christ, is the Spirit; as has now been shown.

ANOTHER passage exists in Rom. 7.6: But now we are delivered from the law, that being dead wherein we were held; that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter. Where the Lord Apostle attributes oldness to the letter, but newness to the Spirit. Moreover, the coherence or συνάφεια, both of what precedes and what follows, convinces us that by the letter in this passage the Apostle understands the Law, but by the Spirit, grace or the Gospel. Therefore, by the oldness of the letter, he understands the doctrine of the law, insofar as it, being placed outside of Christ, continually urges man to perform that which it requires, but denies to man all strength and faculty for performing it: and consequently leaves him even in the will of the flesh and of sin. By the newness of the Spirit, however, he understands the Grace of GOD proposed in the Gospel, and acquired through Christ: therefore so called, because it instructs man by an internal and effective principle, by which he can perform duties pleasing to GOD, and walk not in the oldness of sin, but in the newness of life.

THE THIRD and last passage, in 2 Cor. 3. 6. is as follows: GOD has made us sufficient ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter, but of the Spirit. For the Letter kills: but the Spirit gives life. Where the Letter, and indeed the killing Letter, is most manifestly attributed to the Old Testament, and the Mosaic Law: but the life-giving Spirit is attributed to the New Testament or the Gospel.

With these three passages compared with one another, and properly weighed, a Question emerges; and indeed a twofold one. The former: What is to be understood properly and primarily by the Letter and the Spirit, when these two are opposed to one another by the Apostle? The latter: In what sense is the Letter said to kill, but the Spirit to give life?

Although the decision of both questions is sufficiently manifest, if only the Scope and intention of the Apostle's words are weighed: yet the diverse expositions and opinions of different interpreters have rendered a matter in itself manifest, far most obscure.

And so that we may say nothing now of those expositions which impinge quite enormously upon the purity of this doctrine: which we shall examine and refute in the other part: yet even the Orthodox interpreters themselves depart into diverse opinions: concerning which it is rightly doubted, whether they can be reconciled with the words of the Apostle?
