PHILIP certainly in this place defines the Letter as any doctrine whatsoever which is destitute of faith and the Holy Spirit. But the Spirit, through the Holy Spirit himself, as beginning and perfecting in us the newness of life. Then, however, he applies both to the actions of men, both reborn and not reborn: of which he thinks the former are, and are called, the Spirit; the latter, however, the Letter. For thus his own words sound: When the light (the true knowledge of GOD) is kindled in the mind of David, all his good actions, interior and exterior, moral, political, and ceremonial, are actions of the Holy Spirit, they are not letter or shadow. On the contrary, in the hypocrite Saul, who is without the light of the Holy Spirit, oppressed by hypocritical or academic doubts; all interior and exterior actions, good intentions, and works, whether moral, or political, or ceremonies, are dying letters and shadows. And this indeed is the opinion of Philip concerning the Letter and the Spirit: which, although it contains nothing of impiety or error, yet does not fully attain the mind of the Apostolic Opposition: but extends it too loosely to any doctrine whatsoever, and any actions whatsoever: which thing, with the words of the Apostle simply fights against the property and genuine scope: as will be shown a little later.

II. Furthermore, there are other interpreters who philosophize about this matter in this way: Just as the Law of the letter is the law written by letters on stone tablets or paper, having nothing else but the letter which indeed teaches and urges, but is weak and ineffective: so the Law of the Spirit is a Law, not engraved with ink and letters on stone tablets, but implanted by the Spirit of GOD in the hearts of the elect and believers. And this law written by the Holy Spirit is not a certain doctrine, teaching and commanding what ought to be believed, what ought to be worshipped and loved, and what ought to be done toward GOD and neighbor: but it is the very act and impulse of the mind toward believing in heavenly grace, toward loving, toward hoping, toward doing and bearing anything according to the will of God: in sum, toward living in Christ. And since this act is the work of the Holy Spirit, it is therefore called the Law of the Spirit, to distinguish it from the law of the letter, which is the law of Moses: For although it itself is also given by the Holy Spirit, and is spiritual: yet it is not written by the finger of GOD on the hearts of mortals, but on stone tablets. This opinion certainly has nothing of impiety in itself, nay, it is analogous to the faith: but it fails primarily in this, that it denies that the Law has been imprinted by the finger of GOD on the hearts of mortals. Certainly, if you look at the knowledge of the Law, which is not only inscribed by nature on the hearts of men, but also most deeply imprinted on them by frequent repetition: it is manifest that this negative assertion cannot stand. Furthermore, this opinion also does not yet fully express the mind and scope of the Apostolic opposition.

III. Most recent interpreters look to these two interpretations, and establish that the Letter is every doctrine or action which is proposed merely externally, consists in the writing of letters, and is without any serious movement of the heart that leads to Christ and to eternal life: but that the Spirit is every doctrine or act and impulse of the mind that tends toward Christ and spiritual righteousness. Hence, most furthermore differ concerning the nature of the Letter and the Spirit in such a way that they contend that both the Law and the Gospel can be called now Letter, now Spirit, in one sense or another: so that even to the Law, in a certain respect, its own Spirit belongs: and the Gospel likewise, in a certain respect, has its own Letter. And they call to their aid the Apostle, who confesses that the Law is spiritual, Rom. 7:14, and teaches that it is weakened by the flesh so that it cannot justify, Rom. 8:3. Therefore, they say, the Law is the Letter, when it demands from us what must be done, and urges us to do it, and thunders a curse upon those who do not do these things. Again, the same law is the Spirit, if anyone could perform perfect obedience, and were not weakened by the flesh. Thus, they say, the Gospel also is in itself a life-giving Spirit, that is, the power of GOD for salvation to everyone who believes: and yet that same Gospel, accepted carnally, or rather despised by the impious and unrepentant, becomes and remains a killing Letter. To which they accommodate that of the Apostle, who in 2 Cor. 2:15 and 16 defines the Gospel as being a good fragrance to GOD both in those who are being saved and in those who are perishing: to the latter indeed an odor of death unto death: but to the former an odor of life unto life. The sense of these interpreters therefore finally emerges as this, that both the Law and the Gospel have these diverse effects: so that at one time one or the other of them kills: at another time, however, it gives life: indeed so that, since the Law is the norm and rule of the eternal righteousness of GOD, it could justify and save those who perform perfect obedience to it: according to that of the Apostle, Gal. 3:21, If a law had been given which could justify, righteousness would truly be from it: But now it condemns and kills because it is weakened by the flesh: according to that of Rom. 7:11, sin, having taken occasion through the law, deceived me, and through it killed me. Similarly, the Gospel in itself is a life-giving Spirit; but by accident, a killing Letter.

Latin:

PARS PRIOR Θετικὴ, ἢ διδασκαλικὴ.

SI utriusq; Testamenti Scripturas accuratiùs evolvamus, planum sit, Oppositionem Spiritus & Literæ, qualis quidem hoc loco sub disquisitionem venit, in Veteri Testamento, κτ᾽ ῥῆμα, μὲ αὐτολεξεὶ nuspiam exprimi: licet res ipsa haud obscurè ibi tradatur & explicetur: uti infrà ostendetur. In Novo autem Testamento: tribus potissimùm locis, D. Apostolus Literam & Spiritum inter se opponit. LOCUS primus Rom. 2. 27. 28. & 29. sic habet: Quod ex naturâ præputium est, si Legem servaverit, damnabit te, qui per Literam & Circumcisionem trangressor es legis. Non enim qui in manifesto Judæus est; nec ea, quæ est in propatulo, Circumcisio, hoc est, in carne, Circumcisio est: Sed quæ in occulto Judæus; & Circumcisio cordis, in Spiritu, non in litera, cujus laus non ex hominibus est, sed ex DEO. Quæ verba si preffius confideretur, planum fit, Apostolum duplicē constituere Circumcisionem, ut & Judæos duplices: Unam, quæ sit secundum literam, in manifestoc, & in carne, cujus laus est ex hominibus. Alteram verò Circumcisionem cordis, in Spiritu, non litera, cujus laus est ex DEO. Et consimiliter, Judæum alium, qui in manifesto talis est: alium verò qui talis est in abscondito. Circumcisio igitur litera, in manifesto, & in carne, cujus laus ex hominibus est: nihil erat aliud, quàm externum illud opus, de quo Judæi sine vera pietate gloriabantur, & gratiam DEI, vitamque æternam sibi pollicebantur, hanc unam ob causam, quòd ex semine Abraham orti, & circumcisi essent, planè obliti pro missionum de Messia, & Spiritualibus ejus promissionibus, cùm tamen Circumcisio idco potissimum instituta fuerit, ut esset σφραγίς δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίστεως signaculum justitiæ fidei, Rom. 4. 11. illius nimirum fidei, quæ amplecteretur promissionem de semine benedicto, tanquàm signum sive τεκμήριον infallibile, discernens posteritatem Abrahæ à cæteris gentibus cunctis, imò ab illis quoque Judæis, qui licèt secundum carnem, non tamen secundum promissionem erant filij Abrahæ: Rom. 9. 7. & 8.

Altera verò Circumcisio Cordis in Spiritu, non in litera, nihil aliud est, quàm vera Conversio ad DEUM, amputans præputium peccati, hoc est, verè & seriò dolens se DEUM offendisse, peccato Originali, & Actualibus: Et indubitarò credens, sibi propter semen promissum remitti peccata, & donari Spiritum Sanctum. De qua Circumcisione Spiritus, Moses ipse Deuteron 30. 6. Circumcidet Dominus DEUS tuus Cor tuum, & Cor seminis tui, ut deligas Dominum DEUM tuum, ex toto corde, &c. Et Apostolus Coloss 2. 11. In Christo circumcisi estis, Circumcisione non manu factâ, in depositione Corporis Carnis: sed in Circumcisione Christi, consepulti cum eo per Baptismum, in quo & resurrexistis per fidem DEI efficaciter agentis, qui suscitavit illum è mortuis: Et vos cùm mortui essetis in peccatis præputio carnis vestræ, convivificavit cum illo, condonatis omnibus peccatis.

Et hic quidem primus est locus Apostolicus quo litera & spiritus sibi invicem opponuntur: hoc sensu: quòd Circumcisio, quæ constat solâ externâ amputatione præputij, fide verò in Christum destituitur, sit litera: Circumcisio autem Cordis, facta in fide Christi, sit Spiritus; uti jam ostensum.

ALTER locus extat Rom. 7.6. Nunc autem liberati sumus à lege, mortui ei, in quâ detinebamur, ut serviamus in novitate Spiritus, & non in vetustate litera. Ubi D. Apostolus Literæ Vetustatem, Spiritui autem novitatem tribuit. Evincit autem tùm præcedentium, tùm sequentium cohærentia sive συνάφεια, Literâ hoc loco ab Apostolo de Lege; Spiritû verò de gratia sive Evagelio accipi. Per Vetustatem ergo literæ, intelligit doctrinam legis, quatenus illa extra Christum posita, subinde instigat hominem ad præstandum id, quod requirit, sed præstandi vim atque facultatem omnem homini denegat: ac proindè ipsum etiam in voluntate carnis & peccati relinquit. Per novitatem autem Spiritus intelligit Gratiam DEI in Evangelio propositam, & per Christum acquisitam: ideò sic appellatam, quia interno atque efficace principio hominem instruit, quo à ditionibus DEO placentibus fungi, & non in vetustate peccati, sed in novitate vitæ ambulare possit.

TERTIUS & postremus locus, in 2. Cor. 3. 6. sic habet: Fecit nos DEUS idoneos ministros Novi Testamenti, non literæ, sed Spiritus. Nam Litera occidit: Spiritus autem vivificat. Ubi Litera, & Litera quidem occidens, manifestissimè V. Testamento, & Legi Mosaicæ: Spiritus verò vivificans Novo Testamento sive Evangelio attribuitur.

Tribus istis locis ad invicem collatis, & probè expensis, emergit Quæstio; & quidem gemina. Prior: Quidnam per Literam & Spiritum, quando hæc duo sibi invicem ab Apostolo opponuntur, propriè ac primò sit intelligendum? Posterior: Quo sensu Litera dicatur occidere, Spiritus autem vivificare?

Quanquam verò utriusque quæstionis decisio satis est manifesta, si modò Scopus ac intentio verborum Apostoli pensi habeatur: diversæ tamen diversorum interpretum expositiones & sententiæ, rem per se manifestam, reddiderunt longè obscurissimam.

Et ut de illis expositionibus nihil jam dicamus, quæ in puritatem hujus doctrinæ enormiter satis impingunt: quas parte altera examinabimus & refutabimus: ipsi tamen quoque Orthodoxi interpretes, in diversas abeunt sententias: de quibus meritò dubitatur, an cum verbis Apostoli conciliari queant?

PHILIPPUS certè hoc loco Literam definit per quamcunque doctrinam, quæ fide ac Spiritu Sancto destituitur. Spiritum verò per ipsum Spiritum Sanctum inchoantem & perficientem in nobis novitatem vitæ. Deinde verò accommodat utrumque ad actiones hominum renatorum, & non renatorum: quarum illas Spiritum; has verò Literam esse & appellari existimat. Sic enim sonant ipsius verba: Cum lux (vera agnitiohus DEI) in mente Davidis accensa est, omnes ejus bonæ actiones, interio res & exteriores, morales, politicæ & ceremoniæ, sunt actiones Spiritus Sancti, non sunt litera aut umbra. Econtrà in hypocrita Saule, qui est sine luce Spiritus Sancti, oppressus dubitationibus hypocriticis seu academicis; omnes actiones interiores & exteriores, bonæ intentiones, & Opera seu moralia, seu politica seu Ceremoniæ, sunt literæ & umbræ morientes. Et hæc quidem Philippi est sententia de Litera & Spiritu: quæ etsi impietatis aut erroris nihil contineat, mentem tamen Oppositionis Apostolicæ plenè non assequitur: sed nimis laxè eam ad quamlibet doctrinam, & quasvis actiones extendit: id quod cum verborum Apostoli proprietate & scopo genuino simpliciter pugnat: uti paulò pòst ostendetur.

II. Sunt porrò interpretes alij, qui hac de materia hunc in modum philosophantur: Quemadmodum Lex litera, est lex scripta per literas in tabulas lapideas, vel chartaceas, nihil habens aliud quàm literam docentem quidem, & urgentem; verùm infirmam & inefficacem: ita Lex Spiritus, Lex est, non atramento & literis in tabulas lapideas exarata, sed Spiritu DEI in cordibus electorum & credentium indita. Et hæc lex à Spiritu Sancto scripta, non est doctrina quædam, docens ac præcipiens, quid credi, quid coli ac diligi, quidƋ; fieri erga DEUM & proximum debeat: sed est ipse animi actus & impulsus, ad credendum cœlesti gratiæ, ad diligendum, ad sperandum ad faciendum & ferendum pro voluntate Dei quidvis: in summâ, ad vivendum in Christo. Et quoniam hic actus opus est Spiritus Sancti, ideò Lex Spiritus vocatur, ad discernendum à lege literæ, quæ est lex Mosis: Quanquam enim & ipsa est à Spiritu Sancto lata, & Spiritualis: tamen non est digito DEI in corda mortalium, sed in tabulas lapideas scripta. Habet sanè & hæc sententia per se nihil impietatis, quin analoga fidei est: verùm in eo primùm deficit, quòd negat, Legem digito DEI in corda mortalium impressam esse. Certè si notitiam Legis spectes, quæ non modò naturâ insculpta est in cordibus hominum, sed & ex crebra repetitione iisdem penitissimè impressa: manifestum sit, Negativam hanc assertionem subsistere non posse. Deinde & hæc sententia mentem & scopum oppositionis Apostolicæ nondum per omnia exprimit.

III. Ad duas has interpretationes pleriq; recentiores interpretes respiciunt, & statuunt, Literam esse omnem sive doctrinam, sive actionem, quæ exterius duntaxat proponitur, in literarum scriptura consistit, & sit sine ullo serio motu cordis, qui ad Christum, & ad vitam æternam ducat: Spiritum verò esse omnē vel doctrinam, vel animi actum & impulsum, qui in Christum, & Spiritualem justitiam tendat. Hinc plerique porrò de Natura Literæ & Spiritus sic differunt; ut & Legem & Evangelium, jam Literam, jam Spiritum, alio atq; alio sensu dici posse contendant: ita ut Legi etiam certo quodam respectu, suus competat Spiritus: & Evangelium certo itidem respectu suam habeat Literam. Et in subsidium vocant Apostolum, qui Legem spiritualem esse fatetur, Rom. 7. 14. eamq; quo minùs justificet, à carne infirmari docet, Rom. 8. 3. Ergo, inquiunt, Lex Litera est, cù quæ facienda sunt, à nobis exigit, & ut faciamus urget, & non facientibus ea, maledictionem intonat. Rursus eadē lex, Spiritus est, si quis perfectam præstare posset obedientiam, & non infirmaretur à carne. Sic Evangelium quoque per se, inquiunt, est Spiritus vivificans, hoc est, potentia DEI ad salutem omni credenti: & tamen idipsum Evangelium carnaliter acceptum, vel contemptum potiùs ab impiis & impœnitentibus, fit & manet Litera occidens. Quo accómodant illud Apostoli, qui in 2. Cor. 2. 15. & 16. definit Evangeliũ, quòd sit bonus fragrantia DEO & in his, qui salvi fiunt, & in his, qui pereunt: his quidem odor mortis ad mortem: illis verò odor vitæ ad vitam. Sensus ergò istorum interpretum tandem emergit iste, quòd diversos hos effectus habeat & Lex, & Evangelium: ut aliàs quidem alterutrum eorum occidat : aliàs verò vivificet : ita quidem, ut cùm Lex sit norma & regula æternæ justitiæ DEI, justificare possit, & salvare eos, qui perfectam ei præstant obedientiam : secundum illud Apostoli Galat. 3.21. Si data esset Lex, quæ posset justificare, verè ex eâ esset justitia : Jam verò damnet & occidat propterea, quòd infirmatur à carne : secundum illud Rom 7.11. peccatum occasione acceptâ per legem decepit me, & per eam occidit. Consimiliter Evangelium per se sit Spiritus vivificans; per accidens autem Litera occidens.


### Oikonomy: The First Part Thetical, or didactic (continued)

Moreover, although these things, proposed thus far concerning the Letter and the Spirit from the opinion of certain interpreters, as also of our Author, are sufficiently certain and true, and entirely congruent with the testimonies of Scripture which they bring forward: yet, we wish to say with all respect to them, they do not properly pertain to the Apostolic opposition of Letter and Spirit: nor do they sufficiently explain the mind of the Apostle: which can be demonstrated to the eye by these reasons.

First, therefore, these interpreters establish that both kinds of doctrine, Law and Gospel, although in a different respect and according to different subjects, at one time kill, at another time give life. But the Apostolic antithesis or comparison intends this, that the letter always kills, never gives life: the Spirit, on the contrary, always gives life, never kills, so that to each kind of doctrine, not two different effects in a different respect, but one certain effect, contrary to the other effect, is expressly attributed.

Then that hypothesis concerning the fulfillment of the law indeed has a place in Pauline disputations at other times: but in this opposition of Letter and Spirit, it is expressly excluded, which the nature of the Apostolic opposition clearly proves.

Finally, the true and genuine sense of this opposition of Letter and Spirit ought to be constructed not from other places, but only from those passages of Scripture which contain the foundation and proper seat of this matter: such as those three which we recited above immediately at the threshold of this treatise. If we examine these more accurately, it becomes manifest that both Letter and Spirit hold the place now of Predicate, now of Subject. They hold the place of Predicate indeed when Letter is predicated 1. of the circumcision of the flesh, Rom. 2. 27, then of the Law itself, Rom. 7. 6, and finally of the Old Testament, 2 Cor. 3. 6. Spirit, however, holds the place of predicate when in the same places it is predicated of the circumcision of the heart, of Grace or the Gospel, and of the New Testament. What the Apostle understands by the circumcision of the flesh can be most correctly perceived from the very doctrine of the false apostles, which is proposed in Acts 15. 1. in these words: Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved: but the circumcision of the Spirit, the Apostle himself defines thus: In Christ you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the sins of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried together with him through baptism, in which you also rose again with him through faith in the working of GOD, who raised him from the dead. Coloss. 2. 11. & 12.

They err, therefore, from the Pauline scope, who say that the circumcision of the flesh is the letter, for the reason that, understood according to the letter, it is done only through the amputation of the flesh: but the circumcision of the heart is therefore named the Spirit, because, understood spiritually, it is done through the amputation of vices. Now the Law, to which the Apostle attributes the oldness of the letter, comprises under its scope in this place not only the ceremonial, but also the Moral or Decalogue. This is what even the example of the precept concerning Concupiscence, which the Apostle uses immediately in the following verse 7 of the same chapter 7, evidently demonstrates. Grace, however, which in this very place is opposed to the Law, signifies not some infused habit, or some virtues, or our works: but the mercy of GOD promised in the Gospel: as the Apostle himself explains, Rom. 11, 6. If by grace, then it is no longer of works, since grace would not be grace: But if of works, then it is no longer of grace: since a work would no longer be a work.

Finally, regarding the third member of the Opposition, namely the Old Testament, that also signifies in this antithesis the Law, deformed in letters on stones 2. Cor. 3, 7. Concerning which matter Moses himself also, when he had read the volume of the covenant to the hearing of all the people, and had sprinkled the same with the blood of victims, thus preaches: This is the blood of the covenant, or Testament: which the Lord has made with you upon all these words. Exod. 24. 7 & 8. The New Testament, therefore, which the Apostle opposes to the Old, will denote the doctrine proper to the Gospel. Concerning which new covenant GOD himself once spoke thus through Jeremiah c. 31. 31. & following: Behold the days shall come, says the LORD, and I will make with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah a new covenant. 32. Not according to the pact which I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand, to lead them out of the land of Egypt: the pact which they made void, and I was a lord over them, says the Lord: 33. But this shall be the pact, which I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord; I will give my law in their bowels, and I will write it in their heart: and I will be to them a GOD, and they shall be to me a people: 34. And a man shall not teach further his neighbor, and a man his brother, saying, Know the Lord; For all shall know me from the least of them even to the greatest, says the Lord: because I will be propitious to their iniquity, and I will not remember their sin any more.

And this is the first Consideration of the Letter and the Spirit, from the nature of the Predicate. Whence it may shine forth more clearly than the midday light that the Apostle names, and understands by the Letter, nothing else than that pseudo-apostolic Circumcision, and thus the whole Law and the Old Testament: But by the Spirit he understands the Circumcision of the Heart, Grace, or the Gospel, and the New Testament.

This interpretation, indeed, sought from the very words of the Apostle, Augustine also held in his own time, in the book on the Spirit and the Letter, writing thus among other things in chapter 4. This precept (Thou shalt not covet) the Apostle therefore chose as something general, by which he has encompassed all things, as if this were the voice of the Law, prohibiting from every sin, which he says, Thou shalt not covet. For no sin is committed unless by coveting. And cap. 14. Although more evidently in that very place, where he says: The letter kills: but the Spirit gives life, he does not wish any other thing to be understood by the letter than the Decalogue itself, written on those two tablets. And a little later: You will attend to that whole passage, and you see that he does not say anything because of Circumcision or the Sabbath, or any other thing of a shadowy Sacrament, and not the whole because of this, that the Letter prohibiting sin does not justify, but rather kills, by increasing concupiscence and iniquity, by heaping up transgression, unless it is freed by grace through the Law of faith, which is in Christ Jesus.

And book 15 against Faustus the Manichaean, c. 8. The true Spouse of Christ understands what differs between the Letter and the Spirit: which two are said in another way, Law and Grace. And a little later: The Law without Grace commands, it does not help.

And this indeed is the prior consideration of the Letter and the Spirit, from the nature of the Predicate: which they perform in the Apostolic places. There remains the posterior consideration, which is of the most diverse effects. These, however, can easily be understood by the six Predicates, which are attributed to the Letter and the Spirit, as if to subjects. For thus the Apostle says of the Letter: The letter kills 2. Cor. 3, 6. and for that reason it is the ministry of death, and of condemnation, verses 7 and 9. and although it has glory, yet in Christ it is abolished, verse 11. and it finally has an end and a veil, ver. 13 and 14. But concerning the Spirit the same Apostle enunciates these predicates: The Spirit gives life, ver. 6. it is the administration of justice, ver. 9. it remains, v. 11. it takes away the veil of Moses, v. 16. it frees from the curse of the law, verse 17. finally, offering the glory of the Lord to be beheld with unveiled face, it transforms us into the same image, from glory to glory, as if from the Spirit of the Lord; ver. 18.

These things having been solidly demonstrated in this manner concerning the prior question: It is asked now in the second place. In what sense is the letter said to kill: but the Spirit to give life? To which question it is rightly answered that the Letter or the Law in this antithesis is considered according to its accidental effect: but the Gospel according to its proper and principal effect, for which it was promulgated and revealed. It is indeed the proper office of the Law, not only to command the good, and to prohibit the evil: but also to save eternally those who do the things which are written in the book of the law: Now, however, because the Law is weakened through the flesh, and no mortal can provide perfect obedience to it, it happens that it cannot execute this its proper end and office: but assumes the contrary, and pronounces transgressors cursed: and thus it kills. This, therefore, it does, not by its own fault, but by the fault of our flesh, which is so corrupted that it always strives for what is forbidden, and the more the Law prohibits sins, the more and more ardently it desires the depraved, and is delighted by it.

On the contrary, the Gospel is, and is called, the life-giving Spirit, from its own proper office: Because 1. it announces the free remission of sins, and eternal life through Christ, apprehended by faith. 2. It not only delivers this doctrine, but also actually provides and exhibits the faith which it demands, that is, the power of believing and of receiving the life offered in the Gospel, as an efficacious instrument of the Holy Spirit. 3. Because it comforts and raises up those prostrated by a sense of sins and divine wrath, and renders them most certain of eternal salvation.

Latin:

Cæterùm licèt hæc, ex quorundam interpretum, ut & Autoris nostri sententiâ hactenus de Litera & Spiritu proposita, satis sint certa & vera, & Scripturæ testimoniis, quæ adducunt, omninò congrua: tamen, quod bona ipsorum pace dictum volumus, ad Oppositionem Apostolicam Literæ & Spiritus propriè non pertinent : neque mentem Apostoli satis explicant : id quod his rationibus ad oculum demonstrari potest.

Primum igitur, Interpretes isti statuunt, utrumque doctrinæ genus, Legem & Evangelium, diverso licet respectu, & secundum diversa subjecta, aliàs quidem occidere, aliàs verò vivificare. Atqui Apostolica ἀντίθεσις sive comparatio hoc vult, quòd litera semper occidat, nunquàm vivificet: Spiritus contrà semper vivificet, nunquàm occidat, ita ut unicuique doctrinarum generi, non duo diversi, diverso respectu, sed unus certus effectus, alterius effectui contrarius, disertè attribuatur.

Deinde hypothesis illa, de Impletione legis, aliàs quidem in disputationibus Paulinis locum habet : in hac verò oppositione Literæ & Spiritus, disertè excluditur, id quod natura Oppositionis Apostolicæ luculenter evincit.

Tandem verus ac genuinus sensus Oppositionis hujus Literæ & Spiritus, non ex aliis, sed illis tantum Scripturæ locis extrui debet, qui fundamentum & sedem propriam hujus materiæ continent: Quales sunt tres illi, quos supra statim in limine hujus ttactationis recitavimus. Hos si accuratiùs evolvamus, manifestum sit, & Literam, & Spiritū, jam Prædicati, jam Subjecti locū obtinere. Prædicati quidem locū tùm, quando Litera prædicatur 1. de Circumcisione carnis, Rom. 2. 27. deinde de Lege ipsa Rom. 7. 6. & tandem de V. T. 2. Cor. 3. 6. Spiritus autem prædicati locum tenet, quando iisdem in locis prædicatur de Circumcisione cordis, de Gratia sive Evangelio, & de N. T. Per Circumcisionem a carnis, quid intelligat Apostolus: rectissimè ex ipsa Pseudoapostolorum doctrina perspici potest, quæ Actor. 15.1. his verbis proponitur : Nisi circumcidamini secundum morem Mosis, non potestis esse salvi: Circumcisionem verò Spiritus, isa definit Apostolus ipse: Per Christum circumcisi estis Circumcisione, quæ fit sine manibus, dum exuistis corpus peccatorum carnis, per Circumcisionem Christi, consepulti simul cum isto per Baptismum, in quo simul etiam cum illo resurrexistis, per fidem operationis DEI, qui excitavit illum è mortuis. Coloss. 2. 11. & 12.

Aberrant ergò à scopo Paulino, qui Circumcisionem carnis dicunt esse literæ ided, quia secundum literam intellecta fiat tantum per amputationem carnis: Circumcisio auté cordis ideò nominetur Spiritus, quia spiritualiter intellecta fiat per amputationem vitiorum. Jam Lex, cui Apostolus Vetustatem literæ tribuit, non ceremonialem tantùmmodò, sed & Moralem sive Decalogum, sub suo ambitu hoc etiam loco comprehendit. Id quod vel exemplum præcepti de Concupiscentia, quo Apostolus sequente statim vers. 7. ejusdem capitis 7. utitur, evidenter demonstrat. Gratia antem, quæ hoc ipso in loco Legi opponitur, non habitum aliquem infusum, aut virtutes aliquas, aut opera nostra: sed misericordiam DEI in Evangelio promissam, significat:sic explicante ipso Apostolo, Rom. 11, 6. Si per gratiam, jam non ex operibus, quandoquidem gratia non effet gratia: Sin ex operibus, jam non ex gratia: quandoquidem opus jam non esset opus.

Tandem, quoad tertium Oppositionis membrum, nempe Vetus Testamentum, illud quoq; in hac αντιθέσει Legem significat, in literis deformatam in saxis 2. Cor. 3, 7. Quà dere ipse quoq; Moses, cum volumen fœderis legiffet, audiente omni populo, eundemq; sanguine victimarum aspersisset, sic concionatur: Hæ est sanguis fœderis, sive Testamenti:quod pepigit Dominus vobiscum super cunctis sermonibus his. Exod. 24. 7 & 8. Novum ergò Testamentum, quod Apostolus Veteri opponit, notabit doctrinam Evangelij propriam. De quo novo fœdere sic olim DEUS ipse per Jeremiam c. 31. 31. & sequentibus: Ecce dies venient, dicit DOMINUS, & feriam domui Israel, & domui Juda fœdus novũ. 32. Non secundum pactum, quod pepigi cum patrib9 eorum, in die, qua apprehendi manum eorum, ut educerem eos de terra Ægypti: pactum, quod irritum fecerunt, & ego dominatus sum eis, dicit Dominus: 33. Sed hoc erit pactum, quod feriam cum domo Israel post dies illos, dicit Dominus; Dabo legem meam in visceribus eorum, & in corde eorum scribam eam: & ero eis in DEUM, & ipsi erunt mihi in populum : 34. Et non docebit ultrà vir proximum suum, & vir fratrem suum, dicens, Cognosce Dominum; Omnes enim cognoscent me à minimo eorum usque ad maxmum, ait Dominus: quia propitiabor iniquitati eorum, & peccati eorum non memorabor amplius.

Et hæc est prima Consideratio Literæ & Spiritus, ex naturâ Prædicati. Undè luce meridiana clariùs elucescat D. Apostolum nominare, & intelligere per Literam, nihil aliud, quàm Circumcisionem illam pseudoapostlolicam, atque adeò totam Legem & Vetus Testamentum: Per Spiritum autem intelligere, Circumcisionem Cordis, Gratiam, sive Evangelium, & Novum Testamentum..

Interpretationem hanc quippe ex ipsis Apostoli verbis petitam, suo etiam tempore tenuit Augustinus, lib. de Spiritu & Litera, sic inter reliqua scribens capite 4. Præceptum hoc (Non concupisces) ideò elegit Apostolo generale quiddam, quo cuncta complexo est, quasi hæc esset vox Legis, ab omni peccato prohibentis, quod ait, No concupisces. Neque enim ullum peccatum, nisi concupiscedo committitur. Et cap. 14. Quamvis evidentiùs eo ipso loco, ubi ait: Litera occidit: Spiritus autem vivificat, non aliam velit intelligi litera, quàm ipsum Decalogum, in illis duabus tabulis scriptum. Et paulò post: Quem totum locum attendes, & vides, utric quicquam propter Circumcisionẽ vel Sabbatum, vel quid aliud umbratilis Sacramenti, ac non totũ propter hoc dicat, quod Litera prohibens peccatum non justificat, sed potius occidit, augendo concupiscentiam & iniquitatem, prævaricationē cumulando, nisi liberet gratia perLegem fidei, quæ est in Christo Jesu.

Et lib. 15. contra Faustum Manichæum, c. 8. Vera Sponsa Christi intelligit, quid distet inter Literam & Spiritum: quæ duo dicuntur alio modo, Lex & Gratia. Et paulò póst: Lex sine Gratia jubet, non juvat.

Et hæc quidem prior est consideratio Literæ & Spiritus, ex naturâ Prædicati: quo in locisApostolicis funguntur. Restat posterior cõ sideratio, quæ est diversissimorũ effectuu. Hi autē facilè possunt intelligi sex Prædicatis, quæ Literæ & Spiritui, tanquà subjectis attribuuntur. Sic enim Apostolus de Literâ: Litera occidit 2. Cor. 3, 6. ac propterea mortis est ministerium, & condemnationis, versibus 7. &9. ac tametsi gloriam habet, in Christo tamen aboleturs vers: 11. ac is finem deniq; habet & velamen, ver. 13. & 14. De Spiritu verò idem Apostolo hæc prædicata enunciat: Spiritus vivificat, vers.6. est administratio justitiæ,ver. 9.manet,v.11. aufert velamen Mofis, v. 16. liberat à maledicto legis vers. 17. revelatâ deniq; facie conspiciendũ præbens gloriam Do mini, ad eandem imaginē nos transformat, à gloria in gloriam, tanquam à Domini Spiritu; vers. 18.

His de priore quæstione hunc in modum solidè demonstratis: Quæritur jà secundo loco. Quo sensu litera dicatur occidere: Spiritus autem vivificare? Ad quam quæstione recte respondetur Literam sive Legem in hac αντιθέσει considerari secundum effectum suũ accidentalem: Evangelium verò secundum effectum proprium, & principalem, propter quem promulgatum & revelatum est. Est quidem propriumLegis officium, non tantùm præcipere bonum, ac prohibere malum: sed & æternum salvare eos, qui faciunt ea, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis: Jam verò quia Lex infirmatur per carnem, eiq; nemo mortalium perfectam obedientiam præstare potest, sit, ut proprium hunc suum finem ac officium exequi non possit: sed contrariû assumat, & maledictos pronunciet transgresfores: & sic occidat. Hoc ergo facit, non suo, sed carnis nostræ vitio, quæ sic est corrupta,ut semper nitatur in vetitu, & quò magis Lex peccata prohibet, eò magis atq; ardentiùs pravũ appetat, eoq; delectetur.

Contrà verò Evangelium est, ac dicitur Spiritus vivificans, ex officio suo proprio: Quia 1. annunciat gratuitam peccatorum remissionem, & vitam æternam per Christum, fide apprehensum. 2. non solum hanc tradit doctrinam, verùm etiam fidem, quam exigit, hoc est, vim credendī, & vitam inEvangelio oblatam recipiendi, reipsâ præstat, & exhibet, tanquam efficax Spiritus Sancti organum. 3. Quia solatur & erigit sensu peccatorum & iræ divinæ prostratos, eos que de æterna salute reddit certissimos,


### Part II. Autostiche he palaike Greek: The ancient one is self-contained

All of which do not fall into the doctrine of the Law. For it is nowhere read: Faith is from the hearing of the law: just as it is written concerning the Gospel: Faith is from hearing; but hearing through the word of the Gospel: Rom 10. 17. Thus Scripture nowhere asserts that the Law, or the hearing of the Law, which demands obedience, is situated so as to confer the very power of obeying itself. Therefore, it cannot be affirmed of the Law either that it is a life-giving Spirit: but it is and remains the killing Letter.

But it is asked in this place, How and in whom is the Gospel a life-giving Spirit? Where it is most rightly answered, That the Gospel does not perform or effect this by itself, and from itself. For the doctrine of the Gospel also, when taken and considered by itself so nakedly, unless something else is added, only announces faith in Christ, and promises life to those who believe: and beyond that it effects nothing. Because thus nakedly, only by reason of doctrine and preaching, it neither bestows faith, nor life. Otherwise, all who hear the Gospel would receive faith, and through faith eternal life. Therefore, it is necessary that something else be added, namely the Holy Spirit, who uses the preaching and doctrine of the Gospel as an instrument, and as it were an ὄχηματι, in kindling faith, and effecting eternal life, in all those who do not contumaciously resist his operation: but show themselves teachable. In these, therefore, the Holy Spirit, through the preached and heard Gospel, first by his own power effects that it penetrates not only into their ears, but also into their minds and hearts: then, that it is received by Faith: and finally, that it vivifies what has been received. And this is why the Apostle did not wish to call the Gospel simply a life-giving doctrine: but a life-giving Spirit: Because, clearly, this doctrine has the Holy Spirit joined to itself, and through him is effective in believers and the Elect; not only unto faith, but also unto eternal life: according to that of the Apostle, Gal. 3. 2. You received the Spirit not from the works of the law, but from the hearing of faith.

These things having been thus explained in the thesis, it becomes plain, 1. What the Apostle properly understands in his opposition by the Letter and the Spirit. 2. In what sense he affirms the same, that the Law is the killing letter: but the Gospel the life-giving Spirit: ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι.

PART II. The Antithetical or Polemical.

The purer doctrine concerning the Spirit and the Letter was contradicted both in the ancient Church of the Holy Fathers: and is still contradicted today by various fanatics quite impiously.

Of those ancients, those easily hold the first place who understood by the killing Letter the literal sense of Scripture, which the letter itself, and the ῥητὸν of the individual words, offers and insinuates to those reading: But by the life-giving Spirit, the latent and mystical sense. Although indeed not a few places occur in the sacred writings in which the surface of the letter, or the propriety of the individual words, cannot or ought not to be attended to: but in which something mystical, regarding words and figurative phrases, lies hidden as if in a certain wrapping: nevertheless, the difference between the Letter and the Spirit, that is, of the Law and the Gospel, is not at all posited in this matter. For in the Gospel also, most things are said in such a way that they cannot be taken otherwise than according to their proper and literal sense: so much so, that if they were transformed into a foreign sense, different from the literal, it would be necessary that infinite absurdities follow, indeed that all certainty of the Scriptures be removed. What? That by this pact not only the Law, but also the Gospel, consisting as it does in a literal sense, would kill: which clashes diametrically with the opinion of Paul. And truly, by this device, all human εθελοθρησκειαι have been brought into the Church, and can be defended.

But the first in the Church of GOD was Origen Adamantius, who, having understood the opposition of the Letter and the Spirit less skillfully, publicly introduced into the Church a triple mode of interpreting the Holy Scriptures: Historical, Moral, and Mystical or Allegorical, in his fifth Homily on Leviticus, and often elsewhere. Of these, he indeed named the Historical the Literal or the killing Letter: but he named the Mystical the Spiritual or the life-giving Spirit. And although he sometimes acknowledged that historical sense, and did not wish for an Allegory to be sought when the Letter also edifies: although he also did not hesitate to write that there are some things in the sacred writings which ought not to be clearly transmuted into allegories, but must be understood in every way as the Letter has it: Homily 11 on Numbers: and book 4 περι αρχων chapter 2. In the very treatment of the Holy Scriptures, however, he almost always neglected the historical sense and overturned the true and simple meaning of the Scriptures with prodigious allegories: and he introduced into the Church dogmas conflicting with the analogy of faith. Nay, more, in his other writings he revealed his mind more fully: as when in book 6 against the philosopher Celsus he explains the letter that kills as the Scripture itself, when it is explained according to the proper and literal signification of the words: but the same to be the spirit that gives life, if it is explained mystically and spiritually, or allegorically: saying that the Apostle called it the letter that kills, when we accept the divine letters according to their sense: but the spirit that gives life, when according to the understanding. And more clearly in book 7, chapter 10, that the Law is twofold: the one, namely, according to the letter: the other according to the meaning: just as our ancestors also taught. Now that which is accepted as it is written, not so much we, as GOD through a certain Prophet (Ezek. 20) calls not a good law, and not good precepts. Whom our Paul imitated, and pronounced, The letter kills: which is just as if he had said the words kill. But the spirit, he says, gives life; as if he had written that we obtain life by the understanding of them (namely, the words). Thus far Origen, who for the sake of defending his error urged that especially, Rom. 7. 14, The Law is spiritual. For hence he gathered that, in order for the Law to maintain its spirituality, therefore the letter or the literal sense of all histories and phrases must be transformed into allegories. But our author responds most correctly that the Apostle speaks clearly and expressly about the moral Law, or Decalogue, which he calls Spiritual, not because he wishes it to be transformed into Allegories: but because through it the spiritual judgment of GOD is revealed, and furthermore because it requires spiritual Conformity or obedience, and spiritual movements of the soul: so that in the Origenian Collection a Sophism is committed, partly of non-cause, and partly of Figure of Speech.

interpreter who could render the mystical or allegorical sense of all words and sentences.

Rightly, however, Orthodox Antiquity long ago opposed this immoderate study of allegories: and faithfully and gravely admonished that one certain sense of the Scriptures, which the very propriety of speech produces in individual passages, should be retained. Whence arose the rule of Epiphanius, most worthy of observation by all interpreters of the Scriptures, especially preachers: πᾶνὰ τὰ θεῖα ῥήματα ἐκ ἀλληγορίας δεῖται, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἔχει: θεωρίας δὲ δεῖται καὶ αἰσθήσεως, εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ἑκάσης ὑποθέσεως την δύναμιν: that is: All divine sayings do not have need of allegory, but as they are: (namely, they are to be accepted) they do have need of speculation and sense, for knowing the power and faculty of each proposed argument. Book 2, Tome 1, heresy 61, among the Apostolic or Apotactic heretics. By θεωρίαν or speculation, Epiphanius seems to name the assiduous reading and collation of the Scriptures, for which a knowledge of Grammar and Dialectic is necessary. For just as Grammar weighs the kind of Speech and the weight of words: so Dialectic seeks the order of parts and members in divine texts; and employs a method which collects the sum of the whole Christian doctrine, and shows how errors can be learnedly and lucidly refuted by employing the defenses of the Scriptures. But αἴσθησιν or sense, Epiphanius calls the spiritual Experience of the pious, in terrors of conscience, in consolations, in daily invocation, in repentance, in all the dangers and miseries of life.

It pleases me, however, to demonstrate with one or two examples how he has depraved the Scriptures through Allegorical interpretations, and converted them into a sense that is entirely foreign, absurd, and impious. It is read in Genesis 25:1 that Abraham, now worn out by old age, had taken as a wife the concubine Keturah. This history, understood according to the letter, Origen said was the Letter that killeth: Therefore, the historical sense was transmuted into an Allegorical or Mystical one, and indeed such a one: Keturah was a foreigner and a Concubine. Allegorically, therefore, the liberal arts are denoted by concubines: which if we learn, and transfer to our own institutions: then we take either foreigners or concubines into marriage. Now if, relying on the defense of these arts, we discourse, dispute, and inform and educate others; then we beget sons from a foreigner and a Concubine. For such marriages, therefore, and for begetting sons of this kind, no one is excluded by old age: nay rather, this chaste progeny is more suitable to mature age; just as Abraham, advanced in years, took Keturah as his wife. Homily 11 on Genesis, page 39, Tome 1 of the Works, Basil Edition, A.D. 1571.

Thus in Genesis 20:2 it is read that Abimelech, King of the Philistines, wished to join Sarah, the wife of Abraham, to himself in marriage. Concerning this history, Origen says thus: If anyone wishes to hear and understand these things according to the letter: he will be more a Jew than a Christian. Therefore, an allegory must be sought. Sarah, therefore, represents the form of virtue: but Abimelech holds the form of the Student and Wise man of this age, who devotes effort to Philosophy. Abraham, therefore, desires to impart Sarah, that is, the gift of virtue, even to the Gentiles: but it was not yet the time to pass from the Jew to the Gentiles. Virtue, therefore, remains with Abraham until the time comes that the whole and perfect virtue may pass to the Church of the Gentiles. Then, therefore, the house of Abimelech and his handmaids give birth to the sons of the Church. For this will be the time in which the barren woman will give birth, and in which there will be more daughters of the desolate one than of her who had a husband. Pharaoh indeed once wished to take Sarah: but he could not: Abimelech, however, could. For Abimelech denotes the Philosopher and the Student: but Pharaoh denotes the unskilled and sordid man. Now, however, virtue cannot stand except with purity of Heart. Homily 6 on Genesis.

Latin:

Quæ omnia in doctrinam Legis non cadunt. Nusquam enim legitur: Fides est ex auditu legis: sicut de Evangelio scriptum est: Fides est ex auditu; auditus autem per verbum Evangelij: Rom 10. 17. Sic nuspiam asserit Scriptura, quòd Lex, vel auditus Legis, quæ obedientiam exigit, sita usim ipsam quoque vim obediendi conferat. Ergò de Lege etiam affirmari nequit, quòd sit Spiritus vivificans: sed est & manet Litera occidens.

Quæritur autem hoc loco, Quomodo & in quibus Evangelium sit Spiritus vivificans? Ubi rectissimè respondetur, Quod Evangelium hoc non præstet aut efficiat per se, & à se. Nam doctrina etiam Evangelij per se ita nudè accepta & considerata, nisi aliud accedat, tantùm annunciat fidem in Christum, & vitam pollicetur credentibus: & præterea nihil efficit. Quia sic nudè tantùm ratione doctrinæ & prædicationis, neque fidem largitur, neque vitam. Alioquin omnes, qui audiunt Evangelium, reciperent fidem, & per fidem vitam æternam. Ergò aliud accedat necesse est, nempe Spiritus Sanctus, qui prædicatione & doctrina Evangelij, tanquam organo, & quasi ὄχηματι utitur, in accendenda fide, & efficiendâ vitâ æternâ, in illis omnibus qui ipsius operationi non contumaciter resistunt: sed se dociles præbent. In his ergò Spiritus Sanctus per prædicatum, & auditum Evangelium, primò suâ virtute efficit, ut non tantùm in aures, sed etiam in animos & corda eorum penetret: deinde, ut Fide recipiatur: & tandem, ut receptum vivificet. Et hoc est, quòd Apostolus Evangelium non simpliciter voluit nominare doctrinam vivificantem: sed Spiritum vivificantem: Quia videlicet hæc doctrina Spiritũ Sanctum sibi habet adjunctum, & per hunc est efficax in credentibus & Electis; non modò ad fidem, sed etiam ad vitam æternam: secundum illud Apostoli, Gal. 3. 2. Spiritum accepistis non ex operibus legis, sed ex auditu fidei.

His ita in θέσει expeditis, planum fit, 1. Quid in oppositione suâ Apostolus propriè per Literam et Spiritum intelligat 2. Quo sensu idem affirmet, Legem esse literam occidentem: Evangelium verò Spiritum vivificantem: ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι.

PARS II. Ἀντιθετικὴ ἡ πολεμική.

Puriori doctrinæ de Spiritu & Literâ, tùm in antiquâ S. Patrum Ecclesia contradictum fuit: tùm etiamnum hodiè à variis fanaticis satis impiè contradicitur.

Ex antiquioribus illis primas facilè tenent illi, qui per Literam Occidentem intellexerunt sensum Scripturæ literalem, quem ipsa litera, & singulorum verborum ῥητὸν legētibus offert & insinuat: Per Spiritum verò vivificantem, sensum latentem & mysticum, Quanquam verò in sacris haud pauca occurrunt loca, in quibus non fupērficies literæ, sive proprietas singulorum verborum, attendi potest teft, aut debet: sed in quibus mysticum quid quoad verba ac phrases figuratas, tanquam in involucro quodam absconditum latet: minime tamen hac in re Litera & Spiritus hoc est, Legis & Evangelij posita est differentia. Nam in Evangelio quoque pleraque sic dicuntur, ut non possint aliter, quam secundum proprium ac literalem sensum accipi: usq; adeo, ut si in alienum, & a literali diversum sensum transformentur, infinitas absurditates sequi, imo omnem Scripturarum certitudinem tolli necesse sit. Quid? quod hoc pacto non Lex tantum, sed & Evangelium, quippe literali sensu constans, occideret: id quod cum sententia Pauli e diametro pugnat. Et sane hoc commeto omnes εθελοθρησκειαι humanæ invectæ sunt in Ecclesiam, & defendi possunt.

Primus autem in Ecclesia DEI fuit Origenes Adamantius, qui oppositione Literæ & Spiritus minus dextre intellecta, publice in Ecclesiam, triplicem Sacras Scripturas interpretandi modum introduxit: Historicum, Moralem & Mysticu sive Allegoricum, Homilia quinta in Leviticum, & alias sæpe. Ex his Historicum quide nominavit Literalem sive Literam Occidentem: Mysticum vero nominavit Spiritualem sive Spiritum vivificantem. Et quanquam Historicum illum sensum interdum agnovit, neque Allegoriam quæri voluit, tum, quando Litera etiam ædificat: quanquam etiam non dubitavit scribere, esse quædam in sacris, quæ in allegorias plane transmutari non debeant, sed omnimodo, uti Litera habet, intelligenda sint: Homil. 11. super Numeros: & lib. 4. περι αρχων cap. 2. In ipsa tamen Sacrarum literarum tractatione, Historicu sensum ferme semper neglexit & prodigiosis Allegoriis veram ac simplicem Scripturarum sententiam evertit: & dogmata cum fidei analogia pugnantia in Ecclesia introduxit. Quin imo in aliis suis scriptis animi sensa plenius aperuit: ut quando lib. 6. Contra Celsum Philosophum Literam Occidentem exponit Scriptura ipsam, quando ea juxta propriam ac literalem verborum significationem exponitur: Eande autem Spiritum esse vivificantem, si mystice & spiritualiter, sive Allegorice exponatur: Literam occidentem, inquiens nominavit Apostolus, quando divinas literas juxta sensum suum accipimus: Spiritum vero vivificantem, quando juxta intellectum Et clarius lib. 7. Decimus, Legem esse duplicem: illnam videlicet juxta literam: alteram juxta sententia: sicut & majores nostri docuerunt. Jam illam, quæ sicut scriptum est, accipitur, non tam nos, quam DEUS per quendam Prophetam (Jezech. 20.) jus non bonu nominat, & præcepta non bona. Quem imitatus Paulus noster, pronunciavit, Literam occidere: Quod perinde est, ac si verba occidere dixisset. Cæterum Spiritus, inquit, vivificat; ac si nos eorum (scilicet verborum) intellectu, vitam consequi scripsisset. Hactens Origenes, qui pro defendendo suo errore illud cumprimis Rom. 7. 14. urgebat, Lex Spiritualis est, Hinc enim colligebat, ut Legi sua constaret Spiritualitas, ideo Literam sive Literalem sensum omnium Historiarum & phrasin transformandum esse in Allegorias. Sed reriffimè respondet autor noster, Apostolum manifestè, & ex professo loqui de Lege morali, sive Decalogo, quem nominat Spiritualem, non quòd eum velit transformari in Allegorias: sed quòd per eum r. spirituale DEI judicium reveletur, deinde quòd spiritualem Conformitatê sive obedientiam, & motus animi spirituales requirat: ita ut in Collectione Origeniana committatur Sophisma partim non causæ, partim Figuræ Dictionis.

terpretem, qui omnium verborum & sententiarum sensum mysticum sive allegoricum reddere possit.

Rectè autem jam olim Orthodoxa Antiqui tas immodico huic allegoriarũ studio se oppo suit: & de uno certo Scripturarum sensu, quẽ ipsa sermonis proprietas singulis locis gignit, retinendo fideliter & graviter admonuit. Unde Epiphanio nata est regula, omnibus Scripturarũ interpretibus, concionatoribus præsertim, observatu dignissima: πᾶνὰ τὰ θεῖα ῥήματα ἐκ ἀλληγορίας δεῖται, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἔχει: θεωρίας δὲ δεῖται καὶ αἰσθήσεως, εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ἑκάσης ὑποθέσεως την δύναμιν: hoc est: Omnia divina dicta non opus habent allegoria, sed prout se habent: (scilicet accipienda sunt) Opus autem habent speculatione & sensu, ad cognoscendam uniuscujusq; propositi argumenti vim atq; facultatem. lib. 2. Tom. 1. hæresi 61. in Apostolicis sive Apotacticis hæreticis. θεωρίαν sive speculationem videtur nominare Epiphanius, assiduam lectionem, & collationem Scripturarum, ad quam necessaria est notitia Grammaticæ & Dialecticæ. Sicut enim Grammatica expendit genus Sermonis, & pondera verborum: Sic Dialectica quærit ordinem partium atq; membrorum in textibus divinis; & methodũ adhibet, quæ totius doctrinæ Christianæ summam colligit, & ostendit, quomodo errores adhibitis Scripturarum præsidiis eruditè & dilucidè refutari possint. αἴσθησιν verò sive sensum appellat Epiphanius Experientiam spiritualẽ piorũ,in pavoribus conscientiæ, in consolationib9,in quotidianâ invocatione, in poe nitẽtia, in omnibus vitæ periculis & ærumnis.

Placet autem uno atque altero exmplo demonstrare, quomodò Scripturas per Allegoricas interpretationes depravârit, & in sensum prorsus alienum, absurdum & impium converterit. Legitur Genes. 25, 1. Abrahamus senio jam confectus uxorem duxisse concubi nam Cethuram. Historiam hanc, secundum literam intellectam, dicebat Origenes, esse Literam Occidentem: Ergò sensum historicum esse transmutatũ, in Allegoricũ sive Mysticu, & quidem talem: Cethura fuit alienigena, & Concubina. Allegoricè ergò per Concubinas notãtur artes liberales: quas si addiscimus, & ad nostra instituta transferimus: tunc vel alienigenas, vel concubinas, in matrimonium sumimus. Jam si freti artium istarum præsidio, difserimus, disputamus, & alios informamus, ac erudimus; tùm ex alienigenâ & Concubinâ filios procreamus. Ad tales igitur nuptias, & ad hujusmodi filios procreandos, per senectutem nullus excluditur: imò potius casta hæc progenies maturæ ætati plus convenit; sicut & Abraham grandævus Cethuram duxit uxorem. Homil. 11. in Genesin, pag. 39. Tom. 1. Operum Edit. Basil. A. 1571.

Sic Genes. 20. 2. legitur Abimelech Rex Phillstinorum voluisse Saram uxorem Abrahæ sibi jungere in matrimonium. De hac historiâ sic Origenes: Si quis hæc secundum literam audire, & intelligere velit : magis Judæus, quàm Christianus erit. Proinde allegoria quærenda. Sara igitur virtutis formam repræsentat: Abimelech verò formam tenet Studiosi & Sapientis hujus seculi, qui Philosophiæ operã navat. Abraham ergò cupit Sarã,hoc est,donum virtutis impertire etiam Gentibus: sed nondum erat tempus transeundi à Judæo ad Gentes. Manet ergò apud Abrahã virtus,donec tempus veniat,ut integra & perfecta virtus ad Ecclesiam Gentium transeat. Tunc ergò domus Abimelech,& ancillæ ejus pariũt Ecclesiæ filios. Hoc enim tempus erit, quo sterilis pariet,& quo plures erunt filiæ desertæ,quàm illius, quæ habebat virum. Voluit quide aliquando etiam Pharao accipere saram:sed non poterat: Abimelech verò potuit. Abimelech enim Philosophum & Studiosum notat: Pharao verò imperitum & sordidum hominem. Jam verò virtus non nisi cum Cordis munditiâ stare potest. Homil. 6 in Genesin.


### Part II. Autostiche he palaike Greek: The ancient one is self-contained (continued)

This contemplation and sense, therefore, if it be employed in the interpretation of the Scriptures, there will be no need to invent inept and untimely allegories: and specifically in moral precepts, in divine promises, and in articles of faith, no place at all is left for Allegories: In deeds, however, and ceremonies, there is need of prudent circumspection, so that we may discern where an Allegory can have a place: and we must take the greatest care that nothing is brought forth against the perpetual analogy of faith: especially since Allegories have the power only of illustrating, not of proving or confirming, much less of deciding, controversies of faith.

To which opinion Blessed Jerome writes gravely in chapter 4 to the Galatians: Allegories are to be understood not from the will of the reader, but from the authority of the Writer. And Augustine, book 3 of Christian Doctrine, chapter 26: To explain one place of Holy Scripture by another clearer one of the same Scripture, he says, is the best interpretation.

Although, therefore, to construct allegories aptly and neatly, and to accommodate them to the text, is a matter of some erudition: yet they sin enormously who are so liberal in constructing them that there is almost no Biblical text which certain novel preachers and interpreters do not dare to convert into allegories: to such an extent that even the pericopes of the Sunday Gospels are not spared by some: but they are [torn away] from their own and native sense, which the Holy Spirit uniquely wished to be indicated and insinuated to the reader and hearer

Thus that passage in Leviticus 7:9: There are three things in which sacrifices ought to be prepared: in the oven, in the frying pan, and on the gridiron. The oven ought to be taken for the most profound and abstruse mystery of God, which are inexplicable. The frying pan, however, denotes those things which, if they are frequently and often agitated and considered, can be understood and explained. The gridiron, finally, signifies those things which are plain and are seen without any wrappings: Homily 5 on Leviticus.

Thus throughout the entire history and Holy Scripture Origen played in his allegories: and he considered him to be the most fortunate of the Scriptures in that they are transformed into something clearly foreign, although Orthodox, yet not pertaining to the proposed subject matter: as may be gathered from the Postils of certain moderns, especially the Jesuits. Let these men therefore remember that in this part they are proposing to their hearers not the Word of God, but the dreams and opinions of their own wit: and if they perceive no utility from such sermons, it should seem strange to no one. For how could the Holy Spirit be effective through such an interpretation of Scripture, by which He Himself, the author and sole Master of Scripture, did not wish to be so expounded and understood? It is therefore a matter of great wonder how such license undermines the authority of the Scriptures; since in this way the hearers may suspect that no certain and proper sense can be elicited from the letter and the τω ρητω of individual words. For this very reason Porphyry and Julian also falsely mocked the teachers of the Christian religion, and reproached them with the fact that they held such a Scripture as could assume any interpretation whatsoever.

Moreover, if it pleases an interpreter to extract allegories from Biblical texts, he should observe the following rules, provided he does not wish to stumble shamefully and present himself as more of a laughingstock to the learned than an object of admiration.

I. An allegory which does not have an express testimony elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures is not easily to be approved: but one which does injury to Scripture itself is simply to be exploded. Such an allegory was fabricated by the Synergists and Semi-Pelagians from the Gospel history of the man wounded by robbers and left half-dead; for because he was not killed outright, but left half-dead, they dared to gather from it that the powers of free will were not entirely extinguished by the fall of our first parents, but at least weakened and left half-alive. This allegory does injury to the parable. For the Savior by no means wished to show through it what or how much power remains to man in spiritual matters after the fall: but the parable aims solely at teaching who our neighbor is. Therefore, let allegories be accommodated only to those things which can be proven from other certain places of Scripture.

For allegories do not produce firm proofs: but only, like pictures, render more illustrious that which they are employed to explain.

II. In the Evangelical promises, and in explaining the Articles of the Christian faith, there is no more need for allegories than there is for a lantern in the midday sun. Rather, the τ' ρητόν and the literal sense of the individual words must be firmly retained there.

III. Allegories have a place only in deeds, or things done, and ceremonies: in which, however, the literal sense is by no means to be neglected for that reason: but it must be laid down as a foundation for the allegories themselves. Which Eusebius of Caesarea also seems to hint at in these words: καθ' όλης της ιεράς και θεοπνευς γραφης, ο προ- ηγούμενος της διανοίας σκοπος, μυσικώτερα και θεια βουλεται παιδευειν, κ' τ8 κ' την προ-

χείρονα διάνοιαν σώζεσθαι ἐν μέρει ἱστορικῶς πε- πραγμένων : that is: Throughout the whole Sacred and divinely inspired Scripture, the primary scope of the meaning wishes to teach certain things more mystical and divine: while preserving, however, in that part which commemorates deeds historically, the meaning that is at hand. Book 9 of the Evangelical Demonstration.

IV. In figurative phrases and promises of Scripture, allegory likewise has no place: but what is metaphorical and figurative must be reduced to the proper locution according to the analogy of faith. For example: That first Evangelical promise, Gen. 3:15, The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent: is figurative and metaphorical. Now if anyone wishes to urge an allegorical sense, neglecting the proper one, he will attempt to bring darkness into the light. Therefore, having explained the metaphor, let the sense of the promise be rendered as Scripture itself rendered it, Heb. 2:14: Christ through death destroyed him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil. That this explanation is Allegorical, no one will affirm, unless he who is ἀπαίδευτος too much confuses Metaphor with Allegory and is ignorant that every metaphor and figurative phrase can easily be reduced to its proper sense: On the contrary, however, that Allegory pretends one thing in words, and signifies another in sense, as Jerome speaks in chapter 4 to the Galatians: Or more properly and accurately speaking, that Allegory is such an interpretation of Scripture, which is sometimes sought from further away, and is removed from the meaning of the words: having only some likeness of the things which are compared with one another.

V. Every allegory, which does not fit aptly to all parts of the proposed text, ought to be seen as violent and twisted: and more to be laughed at than received or followed: since it reveals more of an empty game and display of wit than it attains the truth and substance of the matter, however much it may be polished with plausible words and phrases.

VI. The treatment of allegories ought to be brief, witty, and to touch upon the proposed matter with a certain pleasant sharpness rather than to treat it at length. By the example of the Apostle: 1 Cor. 9. 9. Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn: Doth GOD take care for oxen? Or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this is written: that he that ploweth should plow in hope; and that he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope. Such an Allegory is found in the Apostle again in Eph. 5. 25. concerning the spiritual marriage of Christ with the Church. Such as are also found in Gal. 4. 24. concerning Sarah and Hagar: and 2 Cor. 3. 14. concerning the veil of Moses, accommodated to the blindness of the Jews.

VII. Because one and the same place of Scripture can often be explained in diverse ways through Allegories, the faithful interpreter will diligently beware lest he recite or propose those many diverse Allegorical interpretations: but let him be content with one, namely that which approaches most closely to the text, and illustrates that common place which the literal sense most admits: so that the rectitude and conformity of the likeness may thus stand.

VIII. Allegories are to be handled and proposed very sparingly, soberly, and with prudent salt, so that careful consideration may be had for the hearers, not primarily the learned, but the weak: lest while the interpreter displays his erudition, the unlearned and weak hearer meanwhile perceives nothing beyond the external sound of the words. And as Flacius rightly warns, he who dares to forge allegories frequently, easily slips into error: and sometimes brings forth what the skilled and good despise: the unskilled and malevolent mock: by which finally the weak are offended: who, noticing that Scripture is exposed so variously almost in the manner of poetic fables, immediately think that there is little or no solid doctrine in it, and that it can be dragged into whatever direction one pleases, according to the inclination of the disputants: part 2. Clavv. page 48.

they transferred. Which kind of exposition should rather be called ethical: since rhetoricians use the name of tropology much otherwise; namely, for everything that is expressed figuratively. But they interpreted allegory, when they spoke of the Church, as they say, militant, or even of Christ the Savior, as the same place or text of Scripture which they had previously expounded according to the letter and tropology. Finally, anagogy (more correctly called Anagoge, since anagogia denotes petulance: from anagogos, that is, wild, petulant, intractable) when they adapted that same Biblical text to the Church Triumphant in Heaven, or to the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity. For example, wherever mention is made of Jerusalem in the Scriptures: there the Romanists interpret this word initially according to the letter, for the metropolis of Judea, Jerusalem: then tropologically, for any well-constituted Republic. 3. Allegorically, concerning the Church in this life, militant under the banner of the cross of Christ. 4. Anagogically, for the eternal blessedness of the Elect.

IX. And lastly: Allegories should be adapted principally to the institution or correction of life and morals: but not to prove dogmas of faith, or to decide sacred controversies: For as Augustine rightly warns, in his Epistle to Vincentius, necessary arguments are not drawn from allegories, but only probable ones, and those which persuade by verisimilitude. But if, however, it pleases anyone to seek proving arguments from allegories, it will be most advisable that he use them in the last place, and not before he has rendered the question about which there is doubt, settled and confirmed by certain and immovable arguments drawn from Scripture.

And these things, indeed, said on the occasion of the Origenian error concerning allegories and their right use, shall suffice.

Latin:

Hæc igitur θεωρία κὶ αἴσθησις contẽplatio & sensus, si in interpretatione Scripturarũ adhibeatur, nihil necesse fuerit,ineptas & intempestivas cõfingere allegorias: &nominatim in præceptis moralibus, in promissionibus divinis, & in articulis fidei, nullus prorsus loco relinquitur Allegoriis: In factis verò & ceremoniis prudenti circumspectione opus est,ut ubi nám locum habere possit Allegoria despiciamus: & maximoperè caveamus, ne quid contra fidei perpetuam analogiã proferatur:præsertim cùm Allegoriæ non probandi aut confirmandi,nedũ decidendi controversias fidei: sed illustrãdi tantùm vim& potestatẽ habeãt.

Quàm in sententiam graviter scribit B: Hieronymus, in cap.4 ad Galat. Sunt Allegoriæ non ex legentis volutate, sed ex Scribentis autoritate intelligendæ, Et August.lib 3. de doctr.Christ.c. 26. Unum, inquit, Sacræ Scripturæ locum exponere per alium ejusdem Scripturæ clariorem, optima est interpretatio

Quanquam igitur Allegorias aptè & concinnè extruere, & ad textum accommodare, alicujus est eruditionis:enormiter tamen peccant,qui in illis extruendis usque adeò sunt liberales, ut nullus fermè occurrat textus Bibli cus, quẽ Novelli quidã concionatores & interpretes in Allegorias convertere, non ausint: usq; adeo, ut ne quidem Evangelicorum Dominicalium pericopis à nonnullis parcatur: sed illæ à proprio & nativo suo sensu, quém Spiritus Sanctus unice etiam indigitatum, & Lectori ac Auditori insinuatum voluit

Sic illud Levit. 7.9.Tria sunt,in quib9 Sacrificia preparari debẽt,in clibano,in sartagine, in craticula. Clibanus accipi debet pro profũdissimo & abstrusißimo DEI mysterio, quæ inexplicabilia sunt.Sartago verò notat ea, quæ si frequenter ac sæpe agitẽtur, & considerentur, intelligi & explicari possunt. Craticula deniq; significat ea, quæ plana sunt, & absque ullis involucris cernuntur: Homil.5. in Levit.

Sic per universam historiam & Scripturam Sacram ludebat Origines in suis allegorijs: & eũ censebat esse fœlicissimũ Scripturarum in in alienum plane, licet Orthodoxum, ad propositam tamen materiam haud pertinentem, transformentur: uti ex Postillis quorundam Neotericorum, Esawitarum cumprimis, colligere licet. Hi ergo meminerint, se hac in parte non Verbum DEI, sed proprij ingenii somnia ac placita, suis Auditoribus proponere: qui si nihil utilitatis ex hujusmodi Concipnibus percipiant, mirum nemini videri debet. Quomodo enim Spiritus Sanctus per talem Scripturae interpretationem esset efficax, qua ipse, Scripturae autor & Magister unicus, sic exponi & intelligi noluit. Mirum ergo in modu ejusmodi licentia Scripturarum autoritatem labefactat; siquidem hoc pacto Auditores suspiciantur, nullum certum & proprium sensum ex litera, & τω ρητω singulorum verboru elici posse. Quam ipsam ob causam etiam Porphyrius, & Julianus, false irridebant Religionis Christianae Doctores, iisdemq; exprobrabant, quod Scripturam talem haberent, qua quamvis assumeret interpretationem.

Caeterum si interpreti placeat Allegorias ex textibus Biblicis eruere, is sequentes regulas observet, dummodo non turpiter impingere, & doctis ridendum magis, quam admirandum se praebere velit.

I. Allegoria, quae non alibi in Scripturis Sanctis expressum habet testimonium, non facile est probanda: quae autem ipsi Scripturae injuriam faciat, simpliciter explodenda. Talis allegoria fabricata est a Synergistis & Semi pelagianis, ex historia Evangelica, de Homine vulnerato a latronibus, & semivivo relicto; Quia enim ille non plane occisus, sed semimortuus relictus fuit, colligere inde ausi fuerunt, vires Liberi arbitrij non prorsus, per lapsum protoparentum, esse extinctas, sed saltem debilitatas, & semivivas relictas. Quae Allegoria injuriam facit parabolae. Siquidem Servator neutiquam per eam ostendere voluit, quid vel quantum virium in Spiritualibus homini post lapsum sit relictum: sed eo unice parabola collineat, ut doceat, quis sit proximus noster. Ergo ad ea saltem Allegoriae accommodentur, quae ex aliis certis Scripturae locis probari possunt.

Neque enim firmas probationes pariunt Allegoriae: sed tantum velut picturae illustrio reddunt id, ad quod explicandum adhibentur.

II. In promissionibus Evangelicis, inque Articulis fidei Christianae explicandis, haud magis Allegoriis opus est, atque Soli meridiano lucerna aliqua. Quin potius ibi τ' ρητόν, & literalis singulorum verborum sensus firmiter retinendus.

III. Allegoriae habent locum tantum in factis, sive rebus gestis & Ceremoniis: in quibus ipsis tamen literalis propterea sensus minime negligendus: sed fundamenti instar ipsis Allegoriis est substernendus. Quod & Eusebio Caesariensis innuere videtur his verbis: καθ' όλης της ιεράς και θεοπνευς γραφης, ο προηγούμενος της διανοίας σκοπος, μυσικώτερα και θεια βουλεται παιδευειν, κ' τ8 κ' την προ-

χείρονα διάνοιαν σώζεσθαι ἐν μέρει ἱστορικῶς πεπραγμένων : hoc est: Per totam Sacram, & divinitus inspiratam Scripturam, præcipuus quidem sententiæ scopus, quædam magis mystica & divina vult docere: servatâ tamen illâ in parte, quæ res gestas historicè commemorat, eâ, quæ præ manibus est, sententiâ. lib. 9. demonstr. Evangelicæ.

IV. In figuratis Scripturæ phrasibus & promissionibus, allegoria itidem locum non habet: Sed quæ Metahporica & figurata sunt ad locutionem propriam, secundum analogiam fidei reducenda. Exempli gratia: Promissio illa prima Evangelica, Gen. 3. 15. Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis : est figurata & Metaphorica. Jam si quis sensum Allegoricũ, neglecto proprio, urgere velit, is luci tenebras inferre conabitur. Explicatâ ergo saltem Metaphora, sensus promissionis reddatur is, quẽ reddidit Scriptura ipsa, Hebr. 2. 14. Christus per mortem destruxit eum, qui mortis habebat imperiũ, id est, Diabolum. Quam explicationem esse Allegoricam, nemo affirmabit, nisi qui ἀπαίδευτος nimis Metaphoram cum Allegoria cõfundit & ignorat metaphoram omné & figuratâ phrasin ad propriam facilè reduci posse: Contrà verò Allegoriam aliud prætendere in verbis, aliud significare in sensu, uti loquitur Hieronymus in cap. 4. ad Galatas : Vel magis propriè & accuratè loquendo, Allegoriam esse talem Scripturæ interpretationem, quæ aliquandò longiùs petita, & à verborum sententiâ remota est: similitudinem tantùm aliquam habens rerum, quæ invicem conferuntur.

V. Omnis allegoria, quæ non ad omnes textûs propositi partes appositè quadrat, violenta & contorta videri debet: & ridenda magis, quàm recipienda, aut sequenda: quippe quæ inanem magis ingenii ludum & ostentationem prodit, quàm ut rei veritatem & nervum assequatur, quantumvis etiam plausibilibus verbis & phrasibus ea sit expolita.

VI. Tractatio allegoriarum debet esse brevis, arguta, & suavi quâdam acrimonia perstringere magis, quàm pertractare materiam propositam. Exemplo Apostoli: 1. Cor. 9. 9. Non obligabis os bovi trituranti: Num boves curæ sunt DEO? an hoc propter nos omninò dicit? Propter nos hoc scriptum est, quod sub spe debeat is, qui arat, arare: & qui triturat sub spe, spei suæ particeps esse debeat. Talis Allegoria est apud Apostolum rursus Ephes. 5. 25. de spirituali connubio Christi cum Ecclesia. Quales etiam reperiuntur Galat. 4. 24. de Sarâ & Agar: & 2. Cor. 3. 14. de velamine Mosis, accommodato ad excæcationem Judæorum.

VII. Quia unus idemq́; Scripturæ locus, per Allegorias diversimodè explicari sæpiùs potest, sedulò cavebit fidelis interpres, ne plures illas diversas interpretationes Allegoricas recitet aut proponat: sed contentus sit unâ, eâ nimirùm, quæ ad textum quàm proximè accedit, & illum locum communem, quem literalis sensus maximè admittit, illustrat: ut sic similitudini sua constet rectitudo & conformitas.

VIII. Allegoriæ parcè admodùm, sobriè, & sali cum prudentiâ sunt tractandæ & proponendæ, ut Auditorum, non literatorum potissimùm sed infirmorum accurata habeatur ratio: ne dum interpres eruditionem oftentat, Auditor interim rudis & infirmus, præter externum verborum sonum, nihil percipiat. Et ut Flacius rectè admonet, qui allegorias crebrò audet cudere, facilè in errorem labitur:& nonnunquam profert, quod periti & boni contemnant: imperiti ac malevoli derideant: quo denique infirmi offendantur: qui animadvertentes Scripturam propemodùm fabularum poeticarum more adeò variè exponi, opinantur protinus, modicum aut nihil in eâ esse solidæ doctrinæ, eamque in quam partem libuerit, pro disceptantium affectu posse pertrahi: part. 2. Clavv. pag. 48.

transferebant. Quod expositionis genus ἠθικὸν potiùs dicendum esset: cùm τροπολογίας nomine multò aliter Rhetores utantur; pro omni videlicet, quod figuratè effertur. Allegoriam verò, cum de Ecclesiâ ut loquuntur, militante, aut etiam de Christo Servatore, eundem Scripturæ locum sive textum, quem secundum literam & Tropologiam priùs exposuerant, interpretabantur. Anagogiam denique (rectiùs ἀναγωγὴν Anagogen dictam: Siquidem ἀναγωγία petulantiam notat: ab ἀνάγωγος id est, ferus, petulans, intractabilis) cùm ad Triumphantem in Cœlis Ecclesiam, aut ad Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis mysterium, illum ipsum textum Biblicum accommodabant. Exempli gratia, Ubicunque in Scripturis mentio fit Hierosolymæ: ibi Romanenses vocem hanc initiò secundum literam interpretantur, pro metropoli Judææ Hierosolyma: deinde Tropologicè, pro quavis Republ. benè constituta. 3. Allegoricè de Ecclesia, hac in vitâ, sub vexillo crucis Christi militante. 4. Anagogicè, pro æternâ beatitudine Electorum.

IX. Et postrema: Allegoriæ principaliter ad vitæ, morumque institutionem sive correctionem: non autem ad dogmata fidei comprobanda, vel ad decidendas Controversias sacras accommodentur: Nam ut rectè monet Augustinus, in Epist. ad Vincentium, ex allegoriis non ducuntur argumentationes necessariæ, sed tantùm probabiles, atque verisimiliter suadentes. Quod si tamen argumenta probantia ex allegoriis petere cuipiam placeat, consultissimum fuerit, ut postremo ea loco, & non priùs adhibeat, quàm certis ac immotis argumentis è Scripturâ petitis, quæstionem de quâ dubitatur, expeditam, & confirmatam dederit.

Et hæc quidem, occasione erroris Origeniani, de Allegoriis, earumque recto usu dicta sufficiant.


### Part II. Autostiche he palaike Greek: II. Ancient & recent Romanists

II. ANCIENT & recent ROMANISTS.

To the class of those who err belong, in the second place, the Scholastic Doctors, and those who followed them, the more recent Romanists and Jesuits: who fostered, and still foster today, two gross errors concerning the Letter and the Spirit. For initially, deviating not far from the opinion of Origen, they interpreted the killing letter likewise as the literal sense of the Scriptures: but the life-giving Spirit as the mystical and spiritual sense, and therefore, beyond the literal sense of Scripture, which they nevertheless almost everywhere neglected following Origen's example, they sought and urged the Spirit, that is, the mystical sense of Scripture: and established three species of it: namely, Tropology, Allegory, and Anagogy. Which very opinion the Jesuits hold today, as one may read in Bellarmine, book 3, on the written and unwritten Word of God: chapter 3. They named it tropology, when they applied history, or any saying of Scripture, to the doctrine of morals

Moreover, this opinion of the Romanists labors under manifest falsehoods and absurdities. For 1. it is false and erroneous that they imagine that those four senses of Scripture can be adapted to each and every place or saying of Scripture. For if the literal sense, as Bellarmine defines it, is that which the words immediately convey: then certainly there will be clearly no literal sense for very many sayings of Scripture: as when it is read in the Psalms concerning Christ: Thou shalt rule them with a rod of iron: I am a worm, and no man: Many bulls have compassed me: fat bulls have beset me round: many dogs have compassed me: they have told all my bones: Save me from the lion's mouth: and from the horns of the unicorns my humility: Lift up your heads, O ye gates: and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors: Thou shalt walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shalt trample the lion and the Dragon: When likewise the Prophets predict concerning the Kingdom of Christ, that it shall be that the wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid, and the calf, and the lion, and the sheep shall dwell together, and the calf and the bear shall feed together, and other things of this kind: When finally Christ himself said: If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out and cast it from thee: If thy foot offend thee, cut it off. Here certainly, as in infinite other places, such a literal sense as the Jesuits imagine, and which the words themselves immediately convey, cannot simply have a place. We therefore reject this definition of the literal sense: since it is not, nor should it be called, such a sense as the words themselves immediately convey: but that which is born from the words themselves, whether understood properly or figuratively: or as Alphonsus de Castro, book 1, against heresies, chapter 3, not ineptly writes: which either the words themselves by themselves, or the things expressed and noted by the words, signify.
