Where at the same time it is also to be noted, that such figurative phrases and locutions do not, as the Romanists dream, produce some new sense: but they declare the same thing which elsewhere in the Scriptures is expressed by a proper mode of speech. For example: Gen. 3. 15. is a figurative expression: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the Serpent. Where the propriety of the words has no place: since neither the seed by itself performed this: nor does that Serpent, that is, the Devil, have a head. Therefore a figurative expression is admitted here, but such a one as provides that very literal sense which Scripture elsewhere expressed in proper words, as when by the Seed of the woman it understands Christ: by the Head of the Serpent it denotes the empire and power of the Devil and of hell over the human race: finally, by the crushing of this head, the breaking and removal of all Diabolical power. By which interpretation no new sense is introduced into the saying of Genesis: but the figurative signification of the words is merely reduced to the proper: so that now its sense is the same as if Moses had said: Christ born of a woman will break and crush the power of the Devil: as is explained in Heb. 2. 14.

Furthermore, it is false and erroneous to invent so many senses of Scripture, which the words themselves, according to the variety of interpreters, seem to admit. Because that mystical, and indeed triple, kind of exposition searches for and inquires into the true sense of Scripture, not through the words, whether placed properly or figuratively: but through certain things placed outside the complex of the words, and not so much (as they speak) signified: as rather fabricated by a certain luxury and pleasure of the mind; we certainly explode that varied and diverse itch for interpreting the Scriptures more rightly than we expound it: And we labor most for the literal sense, and that derived either from a proper or a figurative mode of speech: for these reasons especially. 1. Because this literal sense obtains the greatest weight and moment for the confirmation of faith, and the instruction of those things which must be believed by us, and the solid and firm refutation of those who contradict the truth. 2. Because every speech which does not have one and simple meaning, but can be transmuted into various forms, teaches nothing certain: but leaves the Reader and Hearer doubtful, and hanging in suspense. 3. Because all Metaphorical and Symbolical Theology is not argumentative: as Thomas long ago established, in the first part of the Summa: quest. 1. Art. 10. The reason is this: Because in order for an argument taken from the Scriptures to be firm and indubitable, it is necessary that it be certainly established that this is, and not another, the sense of the author of the Scriptures himself, namely the Holy Spirit. Now it is established that the sense of the Holy Spirit is always that which is elicited from the words themselves. But we cannot be certain concerning the tropological, allegorical, or anagogical sense that it is the sense of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, those three senses being neglected, the literal alone is most rightly urged and admitted: nor should any place be granted to them for the Confirmation of dogmas in the Church before the Holy Spirit himself explicitly insinuates in the Scriptures either all those three senses, or at least one or another of them. For example: Exod. 12. 46. it is written concerning the Paschal lamb: You shall not break a bone of it. We could understand this saying according to the letter and the sense of the Holy Spirit only concerning the paschal lamb: but because the Holy Spirit himself in John 19. 36. accommodates it to Christ: we certainly admit that anagogy or Typical interpretation. We conclude therefore with Andradius, from book 2 of the Defense of the Council of Trent: that the literal sense alone provides arguments to confirm the dogmas of religion.

Finally, it is erroneous and false that Allegory, Anagoge, and Tropology produce new and peculiar senses of Scripture. For 1. regarding Allegories, we have just noted above that the Literal sense of it is by no means to be neglected: but that this must always be placed under them as a foundation. Allegory therefore performs nothing else than that it accommodates the proper and literal sense of Scripture to various and diverse things: By the example of Paul, who does not distort the history of the two wives of Abraham, Sarah and Hagar; one free, the other a slave, into a double sense of history: but accommodates the literal sense of the history to the two Testaments, one of which begets children into slavery; the other, children into freedom. Galat. 4. 24. Where a Typical rather than an allegorical accommodation has place: however much the Apostle may use the word αλληγορίας there in a broad sense, and by a certain quasi-catachresis.

Thus Anagoge does not produce a new sense of Scripture: but only compares corporal things with spiritual and heavenly ones, with the literal, or historical, or Grammatical sense preserved, and that derived either from words taken properly, or from words understood figuratively; or from both at once. In which respect it approaches very closely to Allegory. Which is the very reason that most ancient and recent Orthodox Theologians have held Allegory and Anagoge to be the same: and have not distinguished them from each other: Just as therefore Allegory in histories, deeds, and ceremonies simply follows the literal sense: and only compares similar things to the literal sense, as if to an example or image: So Anagoge does exactly the same: as when Theologians, with the literal sense of the history retained, accommodate the leading out of the Israelite people from Egyptian captivity as a type to that spiritual liberation of the human race from Diabolical captivity, accomplished through Christ the Savior. Where no new sense, departing from the letter, is introduced into the Mosaic history; but it is only accommodated by a certain comparison to a similar one: so that what happened to the Israelites through Moses corporally: that is shown to have happened to the human race, through Christ, Spiritually.

There are indeed writers today of no mean standing who consider Allegories and Types to be the same; and where a Type presents itself in the Scriptures, they think it is an Allegory. But the opinion of other theologians, who establish the following differences between Allegory and Type, pleases us more.

I. First (let it be permitted to use their words), a Type or figure is when some deed is brought forward from the Old Testament, and it is shown to have prefigured or shadowed forth something done or to be done in the New Testament. An Allegory, however, is when something, whether from the Old or the New Testament, is expounded in a new sense and adapted to spiritual doctrine or to the instruction of life. For example: the Apostle, 1 Cor. 10, adapting the example of the Israelites struck down in the desert to the Christians of the New Testament, treats indeed of a Type, but not an Allegory.

Next, a Type consists in the comparison of deeds and is entirely historical; an Allegory, however, is occupied not so much with deeds as with the discourses themselves, from which it draws out doctrine and many things that are of a didactic nature.

Third: A Type in the Scriptures is for the most part adapted to Christ and the state of the New Testament; an Allegory, however, extends more widely and can be referred to almost anything. Whence it can happen that in one and the same history, on the one hand a type, on the other an allegory, or interpretations separated by a long interval, may be noted in a different way. For example: if someone says that the single combat of David with Goliath prefigured the single combat of Christ with the Devil, he interprets the history of David by a type; but if someone adapts that same combat of David to the spiritual struggle of the faithful with the flesh and the Devil, he interprets that same history allegorically.

Latin:

II. ROMANENSES VETERES & recentiores.

AD classem errantium pertinent secundo loco Doctores Scholastici, & hos secuti recentiores Romanenses ac Esawitæ: qui duos crassos errores de Litera & Spiritu foverūt, hodieque fovent. Nam initiò haud procul ab Origenis sententiâ deflectentes, Literam occidentem itidem de literali Scripturarum sensu: Spiritum verò vivificantem, de mystico & spirituali sunt interpretati, ac proindè præter Literale Scripturæ sensum, quem tamen Origenis exemplo fermè passim negligebãt, Spiritum, hoc est, Mysticum Scripturæ sensum quærebant & urgebant: ejusque tres constituebant species: Tropologiam nempè Allegoriam, & Anagogiam. Quam ipsam sententiam hodieque tenent Esawitæ, uti legere licet apud Bellarminum, lib. 3. de Verbo Dei scripto & non scripto: cap. 3. Tropologiam autem nominabant, cùm historiam, aut quodcunque Scripturæ dictum, ad doctrinam de moribus

Cæterùm laborat hæc Romanensium opinio manifestis falsitatibus & absurditatibus. Nam 1. falsum & erroneum est, quòd fingunt, quatuor istos Scripturæ sensus, ad singula & universa Scripturæ loca, sive dicta, posse accommodari. Nam si Literalis sensus, definiente Bellarmino, est ille, quem præ se ferunt verba immediatè: utique literalis sensus plurimorum Scripturæ dictorum dabitur planè nullus: ut quando in Psalmis legitur de Christo: Reges eos in virgâ ferreâ: Ego sum vermis, non homo: Circumdederunt me vituli multi: tauri pingues obsederunt me: circumdederunt me canes multi: dinumeraverunt omnia ossa mea: Salva me ex ore leonis: & à cornibus unicornium humilitatem meam: Attollite ò portæ capita vestra: & elevamini portæ mundi: Super aspidem & basiliscum ambulabis, & conculcabis leonem & Draconem: Quando item de Regno Christi prædicunt Prophetæ, fore, ut lupus cum agno habitet, & pardus cum hædo accubet, & vitulus, leo, & ovis simul morentur, & vitulus & ursus simul pascantur, & quæ sunt hujus generis alia: Quando denique Christo ipse dixit: Si oculus tuus dexter offenderit te, erue & abjice eum: Si pes tuus te offenderit, abscinde eū. Hic certè, ut & in infinitis locis aliis, talis literalis sensus, qualem Jesuvitæ fingunt, & quem verba ipsa immediatè præ se ferunt, locū simpliciter habere nequit. Reijcimus proinde definitionem hanc sensus Literalis: Siquidem non ille talis est, aut dici debet, quem verba ipsa immediatè præ se ferunt: sed qui ex ipsis verbis, sive propriè, sive figuratè, intellectis, nascitur: vel ut Alphonsus de Castro, lib. 1. contra hæreses, cap. 3. haud ineptè scribit: quem vel voces ipsæ per se, vel res vocibus expressæ & notatæ significant. Ubi simul & illud notandum, quòd ejusmodi figuratæ phrases, & locutiones non, uti Romanenses somniant, novum aliquem sensum pariunt: sed idem enunciant, quod alibi in Scripturis proprio dicendi genere est expressum. Exempli gratia: Genes. 3. 15. figurata est locutio: Semen mulieris caput conteret Serpentis. Ubi verborum proprietas locum non habet: siquidem neque semen per se hoc præstitit: neque Serpens ille, hoc est, Diabolus caput habet. Ergò figurata hîc admittitur locutio, sed talis, quæ literalem sensum præbeat illum ipsum, quem alibi Scriptura propriis verbis expressit, ut quando per Semen mulieris intelligit Christum: per Caput Serpentis notat imperium & potestatem Diaboli ac inferni in genus humanum: per contritionem denique capitis hujus, comminutionem, & ablationem omnis potestatis Diabolicæ. Quâ interpretatione non novus aliquis sensus dicto Geneseos infertur: sed figurata tantùm vocabulorum significatio reducitur ad propriam: ut jam idem ejus sit sensus, ac si dixisset Moses: Christus natus ex muliere, infringet & comminuet potestatem Diabolo: prout explicatur Heb. 2. 14.

Deinde falsum & erroneum est tot fingere Scripturæ sensus, quod verba ipsa secundum interpretum varietatem, admittere videntur. Quia enim mysticum illud, & quidem triplex expositionis genus, Sensum Scripturæ rimatur & inquirit verum, non per verba, sive propriè, sive figuratè posita: sed per res quasdam, extra verborum complexum positas, & non tam (ut illi loquuntur) significatas: quàm ingenij potiùs quadam luxuria & placito confictas; utiq; varium illud & diversum interpretandi Scripturas cacoëthes rectiùs explodimus, quàm exponimus: Et pro literali, eóque vel ex proprio, vel figurato orationis genere; petito sensu maximè laboramus: ob has potissimùm causas. 1. Quia literatis iste sensus ad fidei cofirmationem, & earum rerum, quæ sunt nobis credendæ, instructionem, & eorum, qui veritati contradicunt, refutationem solidam, firmamque, ponderis momentíq; plurimum obtinet. 2. Quia omnis oratio, quæ non habet unam & simplicem sententiam, sed in varias formas transmutari potest, nihil certi docet: sed Lectorem ac Auditorem relinquit dubium, & in suspenso hærentem. 3. Quia omnis Metaphorica & Symbolica Theologia non est argumentativa: uti jam olim statuit Thomas, prima parte Summæ: quæst. 1. Art. 10. Ratio est hæc: Quia ut argumentum ex Scripturis petitum sit firmum ac indubium, necessum est, ut certo constet, hunc esse, & non alium, ipsius Scripturarum autoris, nempe Spiritus Sancti sensũ. Jam verò cõstat, semper illũ esse Spiritẽ Sancti sensũ, qui ex verbis ipsis elicitur. Atqui de sẽsu tropologico, allegorico, anagogico certi esse non possumus, quod sit Spiritus Sancti sensus. Ergò sensibus istis tribus neglectis, solus literalis rectissimè urgetur, & admittitur: neque priùs illis locus aliquis pro Confirmatione dogmatum in Ecclesiâ concedi debet, quàm ipse Spiritus Sanctus, vel omnes illos tres sensus, vel unum saltem aut alterum illorum, diserte in Scripturis insinuet. Exempli gratia: Exod. 12. 46. scriptum est de agno Paschali: Os non confringetis ipsi. Hoc dictum secundum literam & sensum Spiritus Sancti tantum de paschali agno intelligere possemus: verum quia ipse Spiritus Sanctus Joh. 19. 36. illud ad Christum accommodat: utique anagogiam illam sive Typicam interpretationem admittimus. Concludimus ergo cum Andradio, ex lib. 2. Defens. Trid. Concilij: Sensum literalem solum suppeditare argumenta ad religionis dogmata confirmanda.

Tandem erroneum & falsum est, quod Allegoria, Anagoge, & Tropologia novos & peculiares Scripturae sensus pariat. Nam 1. quoad Allegorias, jam modo supra annotavimus, in illius Literalem sensum minime negligendum: sed hunc illis, fundamenti loco, semper substerneadum esse. Nihil ergo Allegoria praestat aliud, quam quod sensum Scripturae proprium & literalem ad res varias ac diversas accommodat: Exemplo Pauli qui historiam de duabus uxoribus Abrahae, Sara & Agar; una libera, altera serva, non in duplicem historiae sensum detorquet: sed literalem historiae sensum, ad duo Testamenta accommodat, quorum unum filios in servitutem; alterum filios in libertatem gignat. Galat. 4. 24. Ubi Typica magis, quam allegorica accommodatio locum habet: quantumvis etiam αλληγορίας voce Apostolus εν πλατει, & per quandam quasi κατάχρησιν, ibi utatur.

Sic Αναγωγή novum Scripturae sensum non parit: sed corporalia cum spiritualibus & coelestibus tantum confert, servato literali, sive historico, aut Grammatico sensu, eoq; vel ex verbis proprie sumtis, vel ex verbis figurate intellectis; vel ex utrisque simul petito. Quo respectu ad Allegoriam quam proxime accedit. Quae ipsa causa est, quod veteres & recentiores Theologi Orthodoxi plerique, Allegoriam & Anagogen pro iisdem habuerunt: neque a se mutuo distinxerunt: Quemadmodum ergo Allegoria in historiis, factis & ceremoniis, simpliciter sequitur sensum literalem: & tan tum res similes ad literalem sensum, velut ad exemplum aut imaginem comparat: Ita Anagoge idem omnino facit: ut quando eductionem populi Israelitici ex captivitate Egyptiaca, retento literali sensu historiae, tanquam typum accommodant Theologi, ad spiritualem illam liberationem generis humani ex captivitate Diabolica, per Christum Servatorem expedita. Ubi historiae Mosaicae non novus aliquis, & a litera discedens sensus infertur; sed ea tantum per comparationem quandam accommodatur ad similem: ita quod Israelitis obtigit per Mosen corporaliter: id ostendatur obtigisse generi humano, per Christum, Spiritualiter.

Sunt quidem hodie Scriptores haud ignobiles, qui Allegorias & Typos pro ijsdem habent: atq; ubi Typus in Scripturis se offert; ibi Allegoriam effe opinantur. Sed magis nobis arridet aliorum Theologorum sententia, qui inter Allegoriam & Typum sequentes differentias constituunt.

I. Primum (liceat ipsorum uti verbis) Typus seu figura est,cum factum aliquod accersitur e Veteri Testamento: idq; ostenditur præsignificasse, sive adumbrasse aliquid gestum, vel gerendem in Novo Testamento. Allegoria verò est cum aliquid sive ex Veteris sive ex Novo Testamento,novo sensu exponitur, atq; accommodatur ad Spiritualem doctrinam, sive ad vitæ in stitutionem. Exempli gratia: Apostolus 1, Cor 10. Exemplum Israelitarum in deserto prostratorum, ad Christianos Novi Testamenti accommodans, Typum quidem pertractat: sed non Allegoriam.

Deinde, Typus consistit in factorum collatione, & totus historicus est: Allegoria verò occupatur, non tam in factis, quam in ipsis Concionibus, è quibus doctrinam, & multa, quæ didactici sunt generis, depromit.

Tertio: Typus in Scripturis utplurimùm ad Christum, & statum Novi Testamenti accommodatur: Allegoria autem latiùs patet, & ad quævis ferme referri potest. Unde fieri potest, ut in una eademq; historia, hinc typus, inde allegoria, sive interpretationes longo intervallo dissitæ, diversâ ratione annotentur. Exempli gratia: Si quis dicat monomachiam Davidis cum Goliatho, præsignificasse monomachiam Christi cum Diabolo: is interpretatur historiam Davidis per typum: si verò eandem monomachiam Davidis aliquis accommodet ad priorum pugnam Spiritualem cum carne & Diabolo: is eandem historiam interpretatur allegoricè.


### Part II. Autostiche he palaike Greek: II. Ancient & recent Romanists (continued)

And let this suffice to have argued against the Romanists concerning the fourfold sense of the Scriptures, establishing that as the best and most certain interpretation which everywhere preserves and follows the literal sense in the way that has been shown hitherto. That this may be done more conveniently, a faithful interpreter must look back from time to time to these four rules, as to an infallible Cynosure of truth.

I. A faithful interpreter ought not to bring a meaning into the Scriptures, but to draw it out.

II. Scripture is to be interpreted by Scripture itself, since it is the best interpreter of itself. That, indeed, will be done, partly if the revelation and exposition of more obscure passages is sought from those which are placed most clearly elsewhere in these very Scriptures: as Augustine himself also advises, lib. 3 de doct. Christ. cap. 26, and Basil, lib. 2 de Bapt. quaest. 4; and partly if the circumstances of the Scriptures, if the antecedents and consequents, and thus the whole context

or coherence, are accurately considered.

III. The proper seat of every subject matter is to be well noted, and it must be observed that if any difficulty arises, the interpretation must always be made from a comparison of those places where the seat of that subject matter is, and in which that subject matter is expressly treated.

IV. Just as sailors have a polar star, by whose guidance they direct the whole course of their navigation: so in place of a polar star or Cynosure, for interpreters (as the Apostle advises, Rom. 12:6) there will be the analogy of faith, to which they will always precisely adapt themselves; since Scripture must be consistent with itself everywhere, and there is nothing in it that is contradictory, no more than the Holy Spirit himself can ever contradict himself.

Moreover, because a diligent, frequent, and accurate reading of Scripture ought to precede its interpretation, many anxiously inquire how this ought to be instituted rightly and in order. In which matter, so that we may not be wanting to students of theology with our counsel, we shall comprehend the whole matter in certain laws or rules.

I. Let the beginning of reading be made with ardent prayers, asking of GOD that He Himself may teach us His ways, give understanding that we may learn His commandments: that He may enlighten our eyes that we may learn His justifications: that He may direct us in the truth, lest we decline anywhere from His paths: that He may bind and seal His Word in our mind, that we may never forget it: finally, that He may sanctify us in His truth, which is His Word. In which sentiment we read that Tertullian had begun Biblical reading, and had thereupon exclaimed: Arise, truth: enlighten, and do you yourself interpret the Scriptures: etc.

II. The mind of one about to read the Scriptures should be humble and teachable: and let him enter this School of the Holy Spirit with an affection void of all pride, and of confidence in himself, and of all prejudices; and let him learn only those things which the Holy Spirit Himself teaches through the Scriptures: not those things which the notions of human wit fashion outside the Scriptures.

III. Let the Bibles be turned over by hand assiduously, diligently, and without intermission, by night and by day. For although you may not immediately understand everything, either the phrases or the things themselves: one must not therefore despair, and the reading of Scripture either be plainly abandoned, or exchanged for the reading of postillators or other interpreters: but it must be strenuously continued. For in this way it will finally come to pass, GOD hearing our prayers, that as we become accustomed to the phrases, histories, and doctrines of the Scriptures, nothing in them will be obscure to us: so that truly this common saying may have a place here: A reading read pleases, repeated ten times it will please.

IV. He who is about to read the Bibles with fruit, let him bring with him a knowledge of those languages in which the Holy Spirit Himself in them has written

he wished to use, namely Hebrew and Greek. For the meanings of words and the properties of expressions in any language are more correctly perceived by those who are skilled in it. And it is known what gross and absurd errors the ignorance of languages has given rise to. If, however, there are any—as there certainly are very many—who are skilled in neither language, I am their author and advisor that they should most diligently study the German version of Luther, which approaches the very sources as closely as possible: And if perhaps it should please them to read a Latin edition as well, let them choose one that most closely attains the propriety of the Hebrew and Greek language: such as the edition of Pagninus, Vatablus, and among the more recent ones, Osiander, both father and son, as far as the Latin version is concerned. For I do not yet pass judgment on the marginal annotations added by Vatablus and others.

V. Let there be added a diligent and accurate comparison of the Scriptures among themselves: this is done in two ways: 1. by examining everything according to the analogy of faith: Romans 12:6. Therefore, whatever in any way conflicts either with the Scriptures themselves, as the principles of faith, or with the Sum of Christian doctrine, which is comprised most briefly and most vigorously in the Apostles' Creed, or finally with Catechetical doctrine, as the most compendious rule of both what is to be believed and what is to be done: let us simply reject it.

Furthermore, this is done if those passages which deal with the same subject matter are diligently compared with one another. And the Apostle intends this when he writes to Timothy: 1 Tim. 4:13, give attention to reading. And Peter, chapter 1:19, we have the firm prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention προσέχοντες.

VI. Lest the reader be deceived regarding the true and genuine understanding of the Scriptures, let him keep himself within their boundaries, both real and verbal. This is done 1. if the τὸ ῥητόν of the words and phrases of Scripture is firmly retained, and one does not depart from it until that literal sense manifestly strikes against the analogy of faith: or implies a contradiction with respect to other passages of Scripture: or finally produces absurdities, not only of reason, but also of faith. Then: If philosophical speculations, empty subtleties, and carnal imaginations are removed from the eyes and minds. The Apostle hints at this, 1 Tim. 6:20, commanding that βεβήλες κενοφωνίας, καὶ ἀνθέσεις τῆς ψευδωνύμε γνώσεως be avoided: profane clamors about empty things, and oppositions of falsely named science: which some, boasting of, have wandered from the faith. Let the Papist idolomania concerning the Mass, Transubstantiation, and other similar things be an example: Likewise the κενοφωνίαι of the Sacramentarians concerning the Ascension of Christ to Heaven, concerning the substance of the Sacraments; concerning Predestination, and other articles, which have been born from the neglect of this rule.

VII. Let the reader of Scripture, having cast aside all ἀυθαδεια in rightly understanding the more obscure passages of Scripture, not indulge in his own speculations: but let him employ interpreters, not indeed just any, much less those suspected in matters of Religion: but sincere ones and those approved by the Orthodox Church. For such Doctors and interpreters are not born like mushrooms: but are specifically raised up by GOD for that purpose, and are instructed with the gift of prophecy, so that the truth may be known from them. For which reason this age of ours will suffer the more severe punishments: in that it has more excellent Doctors and interpreters of the Truth: whom it despises and harasses as if they were men from the street. We have the Apostle himself as the author of this rule, 1 Thess. 5:20, Do not despise prophecies. Moreover, there will be need for an accurate judgment in this part, so that we may apply the δοκιμασιαν, and not swear by the words of a Master: but test everything against the analogy of faith: which is what the Apostle intends, saying, Test all things, hold fast to what is good.

VIII. In order that the reader may infallibly attain the genuine sense of any Biblical text, let him diligently and above all inquire into the Scope, or argument, which the Holy Spirit has taken upon Himself to treat in that place, and at which He uniquely, or at least primarily, aims. Once this Scope is found, all the rest will be reasons, means, or arguments by which the Author either confirms or refutes that proposed theme. For example: the principal scope of the Epistle to the Romans is that he wishes to demonstrate that a man is justified before GOD by faith without the works of the law: Now if anyone substitutes another ὑπόθεσιν, or proposition, such as this: all have sinned and fall short of the glory of GOD: he will labor unhappily in the reading of this Epistle, and will never attain its true and genuine understanding. Moreover, in order for the reader to be able to accomplish this, he will have need of the aid of Dialectics and Rhetoric, by whose help he may be able to resolve a text or Biblical book into its parts and members, and to elicit the force and propriety of individual words and phrases.

IX. In order that we may fix the Scripture, now understood by the benefit of GOD, more and more into our memory, there will be need of assiduous meditation: For blessed, says David, is he who meditates on the law of the LORD day and night. Which meditation, if it be joined with constant invocation of the divine name, and with the exercise of Piety and faith, which B. Luther was accustomed to call Temptation: will certainly have a perfect knowledge of the Scriptures, as much as can indeed fall to mortals.

And let this suffice to have said concerning the first error of the Romanists, regarding the doctrine of the Spirit and the Letter.

ANOTHER error of the Romans is by far of all the most foul. For since the Apostle says that the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life, they try to elicit from this that there is no need for Scripture in the New Testament; and they repeatedly claim that it is done contrary to the character of the New Testament and beyond the mind of the Holy Spirit that the doctrine of the Gospel is comprised in written monuments, which ought not to have been written, but inscribed on the tablets of the heart by the work of ecclesiastical traditions; especially since the Apostle in this very place, 2 Cor. 3:2-3, affirms of the Corinthians that they are a letter of Christ, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of flesh of the heart. They also adapt to this that prophetic prediction by which a distinction is made between the Old and New Testaments, in that the Old was inscribed on tablets of stone, but the New, by reason of the Gospel, ought to be written on the hearts of men: The words of the Prophet are as follows: Jer. 31:34 and following. Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt: the covenant which they broke, and I became their Lord, says the Lord: But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart: and I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people.

Latin:

Et hæc quidem de quadruplici Scripturarum sensu contra Romanenses disputasse sufficiat: eam & optimam, & certissimam interpretationem statuentes, quæ sensum literalem, eo, quo hactenus ostensum est, modo, ubique servat & sequitur. Quod ut commodiùs fiat, fideli interpreti, ad quatuor hasce regulas, tanquàm ad Cynosuram veritatis infallibilem, subindè respiciendum.

I. Fidelis interpres sententiam in Scripturas non inferre, sed efferre debet.

II. Scriptura per Scripturam ipsam est interpretanda,quippe quæ est optimus sui interpres. Id verò fiet, partim, si obscuriorum locorum, ex his, quæ alibi in his ipsis Scripturis apertissimè sunt posita, petatur revelatio & expositio: sic ipso etiam monente Augustino, lib. 3. de doct. Christ. cap. 26. & Basilio lib. 2. de Bapt. quæst. 4. & partim si Circumstantia Scripturarum, si antecedentia, & consequentia, & sic tota contextus com-

pages, sive cohærentia, accuratè considerentur.

III. Sedes cujusque materiæ propria probè notanda est, observandumq;, si difficultas aliqua oboritur semper interpretationem esse faciendam ex collatione eorum locorum: ubi sedes est illius materiæ, & in quibus materiæ illa ex professo traditur.

IV. Quemadmodum Nautæ stellam habent polarem, ex cujus ductu totum navigationis cursum dirigunt: Ita stellæ polaris, sive Cynosuræ loco, interpretibus (monente Apostolo Rom. 12,6.) erit analogia fidei,ad quam se semper præcisè accommodabunt: Siquidem consentiens sibi undequaque Scriptura fit oportet, & nihilin eâ pugnans, nihilo magis, quam ipse Spiritus Sanctus nequit ipse sibi unquam contradicere.

Cæterùm, Quia interpretationem Scripturæ præcedere debet sedula, frequens, & accurata ejusdem Lectio: quomodo hæc ritè & ordine institui debeat, sollicitè à multis quæritur. Quâ in parte ut Studiosis Theologiæ nostro non desimus consilio, rem omnem certis quibusdam sive legibus, sive Regulis comprehendemus.

I. A precibus ardentibus fiat Lectionis initium, rogantibus à DEO, ut ipse doceat nos vias suas, det intellectum, ut discamus mantada ipsius: illuminet oculos nostros,ut discamus justificationes ipsius: dirigat nos in veritate, ne uspiam à semitis ipsius declinemus: Liget & obsignet Verbum suum in mente nostrâ, ut nunquam obliviscamur ejus: Sanctificet denique nos in veritate sua, quæ est Verbum ipsius. Quam in sententiam Tertullianus lectionem Biblicam exorsum fuisse, & subinde exclamasse legimus: Exurge veritas: illuminare, & tua ipsa Scripturas interpretare: &c.

II. Animus Scripturas lecturi sit humilis atq; docilis: & ingrediatur Scholam hanc Spiritus Sancti, affectu ab omni superbia, suique fiducia, atque ab omnibus præjudicijs vacuo? & ea tantùm, quæ Spiritus ipse Sanctus per Scripturas docet, discat: non quæ humani ingenij placita extra Scripturas confingunt.

III. Assiduè, diligenter, & sine intermissione nocturna, diurnaǫ; manu evolvantur Biblia. Nam licet non statim omnia in telligas, vel phrases, vel res ipsas: non ideô tamen desperandum, Scripturæq; lectio vel planè deserenda, vel cum Postillatorum aut aliorum interpretum lectione permutanda: sed strenuè continuanda. Hac enim ratione tandem fiet, DEO preces nostras exaudiente, ut nobis ad Scripturarum phrases, historias, doctrinas assuefactis, nihil in eis suturum ser obscurum: ut verè & hic locum habeat illud vulgatum: Lectio lecta placet, decies repetita placebit.

IV. Lecturus Biblia cum fructu, adferat secum cognitionem earum linguarum, quibus Spiritus Sanctus ipse in illis exaran-

dis uti voluit, Hebræa nimirum & Græca. Rectiùs enim significata verborum, & proprietates locutionum in quâvis linguâ percipiuntur ab illis, qui eam callent. Et notum est quàm crassis & absurdis erroribus, Linguarum ignoratio ansam præbuerit. Si qui tamen sunt, uti certè sunt quamplurimi, qui neutram calleant linguam, his autor, suasorque sum, ut Germanicam Lutheri versionem, ad fontes ipsos quàm proximè acceden tem, diligentissimè evolvant: Et si fortassis Latinam etiam editionem legere libeat, talem eligant, quæ proprietatem Hebræi & Græci Sermonis maximè assequatur: qualis est editio Pagnini, Vatabli, & ex recentioribus, Osiandri utriusq; Patris & filij: quoad versionem Latinam. Nam de adjectis à Vatablo & aliis marginalibus annotationibus jam judicium non fero.

V. Accedat Scripturarum inter se collatio diligens & accurata: id quod fit duobus modis: 1. examinando omnia secundum analogiam fidei: Roman. 12. 6. Quicquid ergò quovis modo pugnat, vel cum Scripturis ipsis, tanquam principijs fidei: vel cum Summa doctrinæ Christianæ, quæ in Symbolo Apostolico & brevissimè, & nervosissimè comprehensa est: vel denique cum doctrinâ Catechetica, tanquam compendiosissima, & credendorum, & agendorum regula: illud simpliciter rejiciamus.

Deinde verò fit hoc, si diligenter inter se conferantur ea loca, quæ de eadem materiâ agunt. Et hoc vult Apostolus, quando ad Thimotheum scribit: 1. Tim. 4. 13. attende lectioni. Et Petrus 2. cap. 1. 19. habemus firmum sermonem Propheticum, cui rectè facitis ei attendentes προσέχοντες.

VI. Ne decipiatur Lector circa veram & genuinam Scripturarum intelligentiam, contineat se intra ipsarum terminos tam reales, quàm verbales. Fit hoc 1. si τὸ ῥητόν verborum & phraseωn Scripturæ firmiter retinetur, neque prius inde disceditur, quàm literalis iste sensus manifestè impingat in analogiam fidei: vel contradictionem implicet, respectu aliorum Scripturæ locorum: vel denique absurditates pariat, non modò rationis, sed & fidei. Deinde: Si philosophicæ Speculationes, inanes subtilitates, & imaginationes carnales, ex oculis & animis removeantur. Innuit hoc Apostolus, 1. Tim. 6. 20. jubens vitari βεβήλες κενοφωνίας, καὶ ἀνθθέσεις τῆς ψευδωνύμε γνώσεως. profanos clamores de rebus inanibus, & oppositiones falsò nominatæ scientiæ: quam nonnulli jactitantes, circa fidem aberrarunt. Exemplo sit Idolomania Pon tificia de Missa, de Transsubstantiatione & aliæ consimiles: Item Sacramentariorum κενοφωνίαι de Ascensione Christi ad Cœlos, de substantiâ Sacramentorum; de Prædestinatione, & alijs articulis, qui ex neglectu hujus regulæ nati sunt.

VII. Lector Scripturæ abjectâ omni ἀυθαδεια in obscurioribus Scripturæ locis dextrè intelligendis, non proprijs indulgeat speculationibus : sed interpretes adhibeat, non quidem quosvis, multò minùs de Religione suspectos: sed sinceros & ab Ecclesiâ Orthodoxâ probatos. Nam tales Doctores & interpretes, non ceu fungi nascuntur: sed eo fine peculiariter à DEO excitantur, & prophetiæ dono instruuntur, ut veritas ex illis cognoscatur. Quam ob causam eò graviores pœnas luet nostra hæc ætas: quo ex cellentiores habet Doctores, & Veritatis in terpretes: quos tanquam homines de trivio contemnit & exagitat. Regulæ hujus autorem habemus ipsum Apostolum, 1. Thess. 5, 20. Prophetias nolite spernere. Cæterùm ac curato etiam judicio hac in parte opus fuerit, ut δοκιμασιαν adhibeamus, non juremus in verba Magistri: sed ad analogiam fidei omnia exigamus : id quod vult Apostolus, Omnia, inquiens, probate, quod bonum est, tenete.

VIII. Ut Lector genuinum sensum cujuslibet textus Biblici infallibiliter assequatur, diligenter & ante omnia inquirat Scopum, sive argumentum, quod eo loci Spiritus Sanctus tractandum sibi sumsit, & ad quod unicè, vel certè præcipuè collimat. Scopo hoc invento, reliqua omnia erunt rationes, media sive argumenta, quibus Autor propositum illud thema vel confirmat, vel refutat. Exempli gratiâ: Epistolæ ad Romanos scopus principalis est, quòd demonstrare vult, Hominem justificari coram DEO fide sine operibus legis : Jam si quis aliam substituat ὑπόθεσιν, sive propositionem. qualis est hæc; omnes peccaverunt, & destituuntur gloria DEI: is infeliciter versabitur in lectione hujus Epistolæ, & ejus verum ac genuinum intellectum nunquàm assequetur. Cæterùm ut Lector hoc præstare possit, opus habebit præsidio Dialectices & Rhetorices, cujus ope textum, vel librum Biblicum in suas partes, & membra resolvere, & singularum vocum ac phraseωn vim & proprietatem elicere possit.

IX. Ut Scripturam jam DEI beneficio intellectam, magis magisq; memoriæ infigamus, assiduâ meditatione opus fuerit: Beatus enim, inquit David, qui meditatur legem DOMINI die ac nocte. Quæ Meditatio si conjuncta sit cum jugi invocatione nominis divini, & cum exercitio Pietatis ac fidei, quod B. Lutherus Tentationem nominare consuevit: certè perfectam Scripturarum notitiam habebit, quanta quidem in mortales cadere potest.

Et hæc de primo Romanensium errore, circa doctrinam de Spiritu & Litera dixisse sufficiat.

ALTER Romanensium error longè omniũ est fœest foedissimus. Cùm enim Apostolus dicat Literam occidere: Spiritum vivificare: elicere inde conantur, Scripturâ non opus esse in No vo Testamento: quin & contra proprietatem Novi Testamenti, & præter mentem Spiritus Sancti factũ esse dictitant, quòd literarum monumentis doctrina Evangelij est comprehensa: quæ non scribi, sed in tabulis cordis, traditionum Ecclesiasticarum operâ, exarari debuerit: præsertim cùm Apostolus hoc ipso loco 2. Cor. 3, 2. & 3. de Corinthijs affirmet, quòd sint epistola Christi, scripta non atramento: sed Spiritu DEI vivi: non in tabulis lapideis, sed in carneis tabuleis còrdis. Accommodant huc etiam vaticinium illud Propheticum, quo inter Vetus & Novum Testamenta ita distinguitur, quòd Vetus tabulis lapideis inscriptum fuerit: Novum verò ratione Evangelij in cordibus hominum scribi debeat: Verba Prophetæ sic habent: Jerêm. 31. 34 & seqq. Ecce dies venient, dicit Dominus, & feriam domui Israels&domui Iuda fœdus novum,non secundum pactum,quod pepegi cum patribus eorum in die,quâ apprehendi manum eorum, ut educerem eos de terrâ Ægypti: Pactum,quod irritum fecerunt, & ego factus sum illorum Dominus: dicit Dominus: Sed hoc erit pactum,quod feriam cum domo Israels post dies illos;dicit DOMINVS: Dabo legem meam in visceribus eorum, & in corde eorum scribam eam: & ero eis in DEVM: & ipsi mihi erunt in populum.


### Part II. Autostiche he palaike Greek: II. Ancient & recent Romanists (continued)

Although, indeed, from those things which were discussed in the former positive part concerning the true and genuine sense of the Apostolic passage 2 Cor. 3:6, a most solid refutation of this error can be sought, nothing prevents us from reducing the weight of the arguments into a sort of compendium and opposing it to the impiety of the Romanists.

Three things, however, deserve observation in this place: 1. What is called the Letter and the Spirit. 2. Why the Letter is said to kill and the Spirit to give life. 3. Why the Letter is referred by the Apostle to the Old Testament, but the Spirit to the New. These three having been duly settled, the Papist sophistry will be satisfied.

First, therefore: It is undoubted from what was said above that the Law is understood by the Letter, but the Gospel by the Spirit. Now the Law, or the doctrine of commandments, is called the Letter because, written outside of man, it indeed teaches what God requires of us, but it does not provide the power to perform it. And although the work of the law, as far as knowledge is concerned, is written in the heart, the Law is nevertheless said to be written outwardly, because it does not renew the heart. The doctrine of the Gospel, however, is called the Spirit. For although it is also written outwardly on tablets, and even when preached it does not always change and renew the hearts of men, yet this doctrine is the vehicle and, as it were, the workshop of the Holy Spirit, through which He is accustomed to be effective in the hearts of men. Moses, therefore, when he brought the law to the people from the mountain, brought nothing besides the letters carved on tablets. Christ, however, although He neither wrote letters Himself nor brought them written by another, nevertheless bestowed the Spirit of grace, which cannot even be written, with great efficacy.

Regarding the second point, we have already examined above the false reasons of Origen and others for which the Letter is said to kill, but the Spirit to give life. There are others who think that killing is attributed to the Law because of the threats of punishment, but vivification to the Gospel because of the promises of life and grace. And yet, the Law also has a promise. Matt. 19:17, If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. Luke 10:28, Do this, and you will live. Rom. 7:10, The commandment was found by me, which was for life, to be for death. And the Gospel is said by some to be the odor of death unto death: 2 Cor. 2:16. Therefore, this answer also falters. It is therefore answered more correctly and truly from what was said above, that the Law is said to kill in the same sense in which it is also said to work, Rom. 4:15, and in which it is affirmed to increase concupiscence, Rom. 7:8, not, to be sure, by itself, but by accident: not effectively, but occasionally; and that by an occasion not given, but taken.

The third point in this question against the Romanists is the most important. For because in the Old Testament there was neither Law without grace, nor letter without Spirit (since the Fathers, who could not bear the yoke of the law, were saved in the same way by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ as we are, Acts 15:11), nor does the Spirit flourish in the New Testament without the letter, or grace without the law, it is not without reason asked: Why is the Spirit excluded by the Apostle from the Old Testament, and the Letter in turn from the New? This knot is solved by the distinction between propriety and impropriety; likewise by the distinction of that which is in itself and that which is for another; likewise by the distinction of that which is in a certain respect and that which is simply, or of things compared and things simple. For the Law pertains to the Old Testament in itself and properly, and in greater measure, while the Spirit and Grace pertain to the New. Whatever, however, was found in the Old Testament of Spirit and Grace, or is found in the New of Letter and Law, is not the property of that in which it is found, but of that by which one Testament is distinguished from the other as its proper end. Most viciously, therefore, do the Romanists distort the Apostle's passage against the written doctrine of the Gospel; especially since the Apostle wished that this very thing which he taught here should not only be handed down by word of mouth, but also written and comprised in ink and commended; and the Apostle did not say that the Corinthians were converted to God and gifted with true faith without writing, by tradition alone, but he proclaims with a figurative phrase only the truth of the renewal in them, which was brought about by the ministry of both the living voice and Scripture, the power of which, however, does not lie open outwardly on a tablet, but lies hidden inwardly in the breast; not by the power of men, but of the Spirit alone

Effected by the help and work of the Holy Spirit. The Romanists therefore confuse the Thing and the mode of the Thing, while they sophistically accept what the Apostle asserts about the thing itself as applying to the mode of the thing.

II. A manifold error is committed in the depravation of the Prophetic prophecy. 1. A vicious opposition. For the books of the Old and New Testament are not opposed in this place: But that old covenant on Mount Sinai is opposed to the covenant initiated by Christ in the New Testament with the faithful. This is proved from the fact that that old covenant is expressly predicted to be about to be abolished: which cannot be understood of the doctrine of the law. 2. σόφισμα ἀπὸ τὸ ἑπόμενον (a fallacy from the consequent). For it does not follow: GOD writes the Gospel in hearts: Therefore it ought not to have been written on tablets: or in this manner; The doctrine of the law was written on tablets: Therefore the Gospel ought not to have been written on tablets. Where the reason of the consequence appears no more than if someone were to argue: GOD writes the Gospel in hearts: Therefore it must not be preached to the ears of men. 3. ἀπὸ τὸ σχη̃μα τη̃ς λέξεως (from the figure of speech). For they confuse homonyms with synonyms. For to write on tablets is taken properly: But to write in hearts is taken improperly and figuratively: Therefore these two do not exclude each other: but can stand together. 4. A fallacy of definition occurs. For to write in hearts does not signify in the Elavvitic sense to hand down something by living voice without Scripture, for such a mode would better suit the Old Testament, whose doctrine was propagated for two thousand years by the tradition of the living voice, without writing. But to inscribe on the Heart does not signify merely to fix the doctrine of the Gospel, as far as naked knowledge is concerned, into hearts: In which sense the doctrine of the law was also inscribed on the heart: but that hearts may be renewed, receive the Holy Spirit, obtain faith, and from faith bring forth the fruits of New Obedience. In which way the Law was not inscribed in hearts, as that which did not renew hearts by the Holy Spirit: according to that Rom. 8, 15. You have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear: but the Spirit of adoption of sons, in whom we cry: Abba Father. 5. Contradictions are made from subordinate things, while the efficient and instrumental cause are opposed to each other. For the Apostles write on tablets what GOD nevertheless writes in hearts. 6. The Romanists are violently refuted. For if the Gospel must be ἄγραφος (unwritten), because GOD inscribes it on the hearts of men: for the same reason it must also be ἀναπόδοτος (not to be given back), and not proposed by the tradition of the living voice: especially since GOD immediately subjoins in the Prophet, verse 34. And man shall no longer teach his neighbor, and man his brother, saying: Know the Lord: For all shall know me from the least to the greatest, says the LORD. 7. They are refuted by the same ἀπίστω καὶ ἀ- δυνάτω (unbelieving and impossible). For if all Scripture is θεόπνευστος (God-breathed), which the Apostle expressly asserts, 2. Timoth. 3, 16: it certainly could not have been done against the mind and will of the Holy Spirit that the Gospel was recorded on tablets of letters. This manifold depravation of this prophecy must be corrected, as if the Scripture of the New Testament were in any way either denied or disapproved: or because the Evangelical promises were not likewise inscribed on the hearts of men in the Old Testament: but this whole Prophecy is to be understood only comparatively, namely, concerning the greater light and efficacy of the Holy Spirit, which was to be in the New Testament, than that which was in the Old.

But there remains the third and last error of the Romanists, who interpret the Apostolic passage, The letter kills, the Spirit gives life: 2 Cor. 3, 6. and especially the words immediately preceding: GOD has made us sufficient ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter, but of the Spirit: as if the Apostle understood by the Letter, doctrine expressed in letters and ink: but by the Spirit, doctrine proposed only by living voice and the Spirit: As if the Apostle had said, GOD has made us sufficient ministers of the New Testament, not that I may act with letters written in ink: but that I may preach the Gospel by living voice. However, this depravation collapses by its own futility. For if the Apostle had wished to say this, and thus to establish such a distinction between doctrine consisting of letters and ink, and that which is proposed only by living voice, as the Romanists imagine: certainly the Apostle himself would condemn all that part of his doctrine which he sent to various churches comprised in letters written in ink: the utility of which, however, was and is today no less than that of preaching handed down by living voice: and thus it proceeded no less from the Holy Spirit than the latter. Therefore this error is also corrected by a true exposition of the Apostolic passage, which consists in this, that the Apostle shows that he was constituted by GOD a minister of the New Testament, and indeed not of the letter, that is, of the law, but of the spirit, that is, of the Gospel; not that he ought not to have proposed the doctrine of the Law at all: but that the chief and primary part of his office was placed in preaching the Gospel concerning Christ: as was also shown above.

Since these things are so, Johannes Eckius betrayed huge stupidity joined with a gross ignorance of the Scriptures, who from the Apostolic antithesis between the Letter and the Spirit tries to elicit that the authority of the Roman Church is greater than that of Scripture, because Scripture consists of letters and ink: but the Church of living voice and the Spirit. Whence also among other axioms of the Church he refers to this one, that the Church is only in the Spirit: as can be seen in the Enchiridion of Eckius, Place 1, proposition 4, concerning the Church and its authority; page 17, edition of Paris, year 1559.

Latin:

Quanquam verò ex ijs, quæ in parte priore θετικῇ de vero ac genuino sensu loci Apostolici 2. Cor. 3, 6. disputata sunt, erroris hujus solidissima refutatio peti potest: nihil tamen obstat, quò minùs in Compendium quasi quoddam, argumentorum momenta redigamus, & Romanensium impietati opponamus.

Tria autem hoc loco observationem merentur: 1. Quid Litera & Spiritus vocetur. 2. Cur Litera occidere: Spiritus vivificare dicatur: 3. Cur Litera ab Apostolo referatur ad Vetus Testamentum: Spiritus Verò ad Novum: Tribus istis ritè expeditis, fatisfactum erit Sophisticationi Pontificiæ.

Prmùm igitur: Per Literam intelligi Legem per Spiritum verò Evangelium ex supra dictis indubium est. Lex autem, sive doctrina mandatorum,ideò appellatur Litera, quia extra hominem scripta docet quidem, quid à nobis requirat DEUS: at virtutem præstandi non subministrat. Et licet legis opus, quoad notitiam, scriptum sit in corde: dicitur tamen Lex foris scripta; qui corda non renovat. Evangelij autem doctrina dicitur Spiritus. Nam tametsi foris etiam scribatur in tabulis: &prædicata etiam non semper immutet, atque renovet Corda hominum: tamen hæc doctrina est ὄχημα, & officina quasi Spiritus Sancti, per quam incordibus hominum ille efficax esse consuevit. Moses ergò cùm legem afferret populo ex monte, præter literas tabulis incisas nihil attulit. Christus autem, quamvis literas neque ipse scripserit: nec ab alio scriptas attulerit : tamen Spiritum gratiæ, qui ne scribi quidem potest, magnâ efficacitate contulit.

Quoàd alterum, jam suprà Origenis & aliorum falsas rationes, propter quas Litera dicatur occidere, Spiritus autem vivificare examinavimus. Sunt alij, qui Legi occisionem tribui putant, propter comminationes pœnarum : Evangelio autem vivificationem propter promissiones vitæ & gratiæ. Atqui verò Promissionem etiam Lex habet. Matth. 19, 17. Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Luc. 10, 28. Fac hoc, & vives. Rom. 6, 10. Inventum est mihi mandatum; quod erat ad vitam, hoc esse ad mortem. Et Evangelium aliquibus dicitur esse odor mortis ad mortem: 2. Cor. 2, 16. Vacillat ergo hæc quoque responsio. Rectiùs ergo ac veriùs éx suprà dictis responderur, quòd Lex eo sensu dicatur occidere, quo etiam operari perhibetur : Rom. 4, 15. quo item concupiscentiam augete affirmatur, Rom. 7. 8. non videlicet per se, sed per accidens: non effectivè : sed occasionaliter: idque occasione non data : sed accepta.

Tertium in quæstione hac contra Romanenses est præcipuum. Nam quia in Veteri Testamento neque Lex fuit sine gratia, aut litera sine Spiritu (siquidem Patres, qui legis jugum portare non potuerunt, eodem modo per Gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi, sunt salvati, quo nos Act. 15, 11.) Neque in Novo Testamento Spiritus viget sine litera, aut Gratia sine lëge: haud immeritò quæritur, Cur Spiritus Veteri : & Litera vicissim a Novo Testamento per Apostolum excludatur? Solvitur autem nodus iste, distinctione proprietatis ab improprietate : item τοῦ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ καὶ τοῦ δι᾽ ἄλλο: item distinctione τοῦ κατὰ τὶ, καὶ τοῦ ἁπλῶς, sive Comparatorum & simplicium. Nam Lex ad Vetus Testamentum per se & propriè, καὶ κατὰ τὸ μᾶλλον pertinet, Spiritus & Gratia ad novum. Quicquid verò vel in Veteri Spiritus & Gratiæ repertum fuit : vel in Novo, Literæ & legis invenitur: non ëjus proprium est, in quo invenitur : sed ejus, quo unum Testamentum, ceu proprio fine, ab altero Testamento discernitur. Vitiosissimè ergò Romanenses locum Apostoli contra scriptam Evangelij doctrinam detorquent : præcipuè, cùm hoc ipsum, quod hic docuit, non ore tantùm traditum : sed atramento etiam scriptum & comprehensum, commendatumq́, Apostolus voluerit : & non hoc dixerit Apostolus, Corinthios sine scripto sola traditione esse ad Deum conversos, veraq́; fide donatos; sed phrasi figurata tantùm veritatem renovationis in ipsis prædicet, quæ tùm vivæ vocis, tùm Scripturæ ministerio facta sit : cujus vis tamen non foris pateat in tabula : sed intus lateat in pectore; non virtute hominum, sed solius

Spiritus Sancti ope atque operà effecta. Confundunt ergò Romanenses Rem, & modum Rei, dum quod Apostolus de reipsa asserit, illi de modo rei Sophisticè accipiunt.

II. In vaticinij Prophetici depravatione multiplex error committitur. 1. Vitiosa oppositionis. Non enim opponuntur hoc loco libri Veteris & Novi Testamenti: Sed pactum illud vetus in monte Sina, cum pacto à Christo in Novo Testamento cum fidelibus inito. Probatur hoc inde, quia vetus illud pactum expressè prædicitur antiquatum iri: id quod de doctrinâ legis intelligi non potest. 2. σόφισμα ἀπὸ τὸ ἑπόμενον Non enim sequitur: DEVS Evangelium scribit in cordibus: Ergo idem scribi non debuit in tabulis: vel in hunc modum; Doctrina legis fuit scripta in tabulis: Ergo Evangelium non debuit scribi in tabulis. Ubi ratio Consequentiâe haud magis ulla apparet, ac si quis argucret: DEVS Evangelium scribit in cordibus: Ergo auribus hominum illud non est prædicandum. 3. ἀπὸ τὸ σχη̃μα τη̃ς λέξεως. Confundunt enim ὁμώνυμα cum συνωνύμοις. Scribere enim in tabulis propriè sumitur: Scribere autem in cordibus, impropriè & figuratè accipitur: Ergo hæc duo se invicem non excludunt: sed simul stare possunt. 4. Occurrit Sophisma definitionis. Scribere enim in cordibus, non significat sensu Elavvitico, vivâ voce aliquid tradere absq́; Scriptura, Talis enim modus magis competeret Veteri Testamento, quippe cujus doctrina annis bis mille, vivâ vocis traditione, sine scripto, propagata fuit, Sed inscribere in Cor significat, non saltem doctrinam Evangelij, quoad notitiam nudam infigere cordibus: Quo sensu etiam doctrina legis cordi inscripta fuit: sed ut corda renoventur, Spiritum Sanctum accipiant, fidem consequantur, & ex fide fructus Novæ Obedientiæ proferant. Quo pacto Lex non erat inscripta in cordibus, ut quæ non renovabat corda Spiritu Sancto: secundum illud Rom. 8, 15. Non accepistis iterum Spiritum servitutis in timorem: sed Spiritum adoptionis filiorum, in quo clamamus: Abba Pater. 5. Ex subordinatis pugnantia fiunt, dum causa efficiens & instrumentalis invicem opponuntur. Scribunt enim Apostoli in tabulis, quod DEUS nihilominus scribit in cordibus. 6. βιαίως revincuntur Romanenses. Si enim ἄγραφος debet esse Evangelium, quia DEUS id cordibus hominum inscribit: eâdem etiam ratione debet esse ἀναπόδοτος, & vivæ vocis traditione non proponi: præsertim cùm DEUS apud Prophetam statim immediatè subjiciat, versu 34. Et non docebit ultra vir proximum suum, & vir fratrem suum, dicens: Cognosce Dominum: Omnes enim cognoscent me à minimo, usque ad maximum, ait DOMINVS. 7. ἀπίστω καὶ ἀ- δυνάτω ijdem refelluntur. Si enim omnis Scriptura est θεόπνευστος, quod disertè asserit Apostolus, 2. Timoth. 3, 16: præter mentem ac voluntatem Spiritus Sancti certè factum esse nequit, ut in literarum tabulis Evangelium relatum sit. Multiplex isthæc vaticinij hujus depravatio corrigenda est, ac siScriptura Novi Testamenti ullo pacto vel negetur, vel improbetur: vel quòd Evangelicæ promissiones in Veteri Testamento non itidem cordibus hominum inscriptæ fuerint: sed totum hoc Vaticinium Comparatè duntaxat est intelligendum, nempe de majori luce, & efficacitate Spiritus Sancti, quæ sit futura in Novo Testamento, quàm quæ fuerit in Veteri.

Sed superest Tertius & postremus error Romanensium, qui locum Apostolicum. Litera occidit, Spiritus vivificat: 2. Corin. 3, 6. & cumprimis verba immediatè præcedentia: DEVS nos fecit idoneos ministros Novi Testamenti, non literæ, sed Spiritus: sic interpretantur, ac si Apostolus intelligat per Literam, doctrinam literis & atramento expressam: per Spiritum verò doctrinam vivâ voce ac Spiritu tantùm propositam: Quasi dixerit Apostolus, DEUS nos fecit idoneos ministros Novi Testamenti, non ut literis agam atramento scriptis: sed ut vivâ voce prædicem Evangelium. Cæterùm propriâ futilitate depravatio hæc concidit. Si enim hoc dicere voluisset Apostolus, & sic inter doctrinam literis & atramento constantem, & inter eam, quæ vivâ tantùm voce proponitur, discrimen tale, quale fingunt Romanenses, constituere: certè ipse Apostolus omnem eam doctrinæ suæ partem damnaret, quam literis atramento scriptis comprehensam ad varias ecclesias misit: cujus tamen utilitas non minor fuit, & est hodie quoque quàm prædicationis vivâ voce traditæ: adeòque non minus ex Spiritu Sancto profecta, quàm hæc. Corrigitur ergò & iste error per veram expositionem loci Apostolici, quæ in eo consistit, quòd Apostolus ostendit, se esse â DEO constitutum ministrum Novi Testamenti, & quidem non literæ hoc est, legis, sed spiritus, hoc est, Evangelij; non quòd Legis doctrinam planè non proponere debuerit: sed quòd præcipua ac primaria muneris sui pars, posita sit in prædicando Evangelio de Christo: uti suprà etiam ostensum

Quæ cùm ita se habeant, ingentem stoliditatem cum crassâ Scripturarum ignorantiâ conjunctam prodidit Iohannes Eccius, qui ex antithesi Apostolicâ, inter Literam & Spiritum, elicere conatur, Majorem esse autoritatem Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quàm Scripturæ, propterea quòd Scriptura literis & atramento: Ecclesia verò vivâ voce ac Spiritu constet. Unde etiam inter alia axiomata Ecclesiæ istud quoque refert, quòd Ecclesia solùm sit in Spiritu: uti videre est in Enchiridio Eccij, Loco 1. proposit 4. de Ecclesia, ejusq; autoritate; pag. 17. edit. Paris. anno 1559.


### Part II. Autostiche he palaike Greek: III. Schvvenck- III. Schwenkfeldians & Enthusiasts

III. Schvvenck-

III. Schwenkfeldians & Enthusiasts

In the class of those who err concerning the Spirit and the Letter, the Schwenkfeldians hold a place that is by no means the last, named after a certain CASPAR SCHWENKFELD, a Silesian nobleman, the primary master and author of this error; who interpret the killing letter as the ministry of the Word and Sacraments: but they understand the life-giving Spirit as internal raptures, or Enthusiasms: contending meanwhile that the ministry of the Word and Sacraments is an empty sound and an idle ceremony: but on the contrary, ascribing all the power of regeneration, Spirit, and life to secret motions and Enthusiasms. Whence they also deserved to be called Enthusiasts: not indeed in the sense in which the ancient Messalians, or Euchites, were once also called enthusiasts, because, seized by an insane frenzy, they dreamed that they were anything, and when asked whether they were Prophets, or Abraham, or the Patriarchs, or Christ, they would profess that they were all these things, and the wretches would persuade themselves. Whence, rushing into the midst of a gathering of men, they would dance in various ridiculous ways and gesticulate, or snap their fingers, as if they were attacking demons with these gestures of theirs, and casting them out from themselves: dreaming that Satan is sensibly and visibly expelled by their prayers, and exits from their mouths in the form of a sow or a pig with piglets: and that in its place the Holy Spirit immediately succeeds and enters, also visibly and sensibly. This most foul heresy we certainly do not ascribe to the Schwenkfeldians, but we determine that they participate in the name of Enthusiasts only for this reason, that outside of and beyond the written, preached, and heard Word of GOD, they invent such a mode of regeneration and illumination, which consists of secret motions and raptures, which they observe and kiss as suggestions of the Holy Spirit.

However, the entire Holy Scripture, and the certainty of the infallible analogy of faith which depends upon it, most solidly refutes, nay, utterly overthrows this error. For first, this delirium fights against the true meaning of the Apostolic Opposition between the killing Letter and the life-giving Spirit, which ought to be sought from the preceding and referred to here.

Then it diametrically fights against the scope and intention of JEHOVAH, who for this reason willed that His Word be consigned to letters, and that the ministry of the Word and Sacraments be instituted, so that He might call men away from the dreams, speculations, and Enthusiasms of their own wit, and through this Word of His, written, read, preached, and heard, might work true conversion and faith in them, and consequently salvation and eternal life. For GOD Himself wills this, sending us by the Prophet to

the Law, and to the Testimony, with this express threat: Unless they were to speak according to these, they would not see the morning dawn. Isa. 8. 20. The Savior willed this, sending those who wish to obtain eternal life and avoid infernal torments to the Scriptures, to Moses and the Prophets, John 5. 39. Search the Scriptures: for you think that you have eternal life in them: and they are those which bear witness of me. Luke 16. 29. They have Moses and the Prophets, let them hear them: If they will not hear them, neither will they believe, even if someone should return to them from the dead, etc.

Thirdly, this delirium fights against the principal end, for the sake of which Scripture, with God as its author, was consigned to letters, which consists in this, that it might instruct us unto salvation through the faith which is in Christ Jesus. 1 Tim. 3. 15. that it might convert our souls, that it might provide wisdom to the simple: gladden the heart: enlighten the eyes: confer joy and firm consolation in affliction: provide a lamp to our feet, and a light to our paths: Ps. 119. 8. 9. 92. 105. show how we may have hope through patience and consolation Rom. 15. 4: that we may finally obtain eternal life. John 5. 39. Which ends, both individually and collectively, clearly prove that Holy Scripture is the medium or instrument through which He Himself wills to work all these Spiritual gifts, and thus salvation and eternal life in men, nay, indeed, truly and in the very act, does work them.

Fourthly, this delirium fights against that effect which GOD Himself, through the Holy Scripture read, preached, and heard, has certainly and infallibly, nay, holily promised that He would work in men. For the hearing of this Word, whether read or preached, effects faith in us: according to that of the Savior, John 17. 20. I do not pray for them only; but also for those who are to believe in me through their Word. And according to that of the Apostle, Rom. 10. 17. Faith comes from hearing: and hearing through the Word of GOD: but through the Word not secret and Enthusiastic: but which, as the Apostle defines, has been preached in the whole world: and which is near in our mouth, and in our heart, that is, the Word of faith, which is preached: ibid. verses 8 and 18. Whence the same Apostle here and there in his Epistles calls the foolishness of Evangelical preaching the power of GOD unto salvation to everyone who believes. Rom. 1. 16. Eph. 1. 13. 1 Cor. 1. 18. and 21. Hence in the Acts concerning Peter, the heavenly vision to Cornelius the Caesarean: Send to Joppa, and call Simon, who is surnamed Peter, who SHALL SPEAK to you words, in which you and your whole house shall be saved, Acts 11. 14. And this is that fulfillment of the divine promise, already long ago published by the Prophet concerning the efficacy of Evangelical preaching: Just as the rain and the snow descend from Heaven, and do not return thither, unless they have watered the earth, and made it fruitful, and caused it to germinate, and given seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: So shall my word be, that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void; but it shall do whatsoever I have willed, and shall prosper in those things, to which I sent it. Isa. 55, 10. & 11.

Finally, this delusion conflicts with those illustrious titles with which not only the Apostles, but also any sincere heralds and ministers of the Word are distinguished: namely, that they are stewards of the mysteries of GOD: fellow-workers of GOD: GOD's husbandry: GOD's building: 1 Cor. 3, 7. 9. & chap. 4, 1. that they give the knowledge of salvation to the people: Luke 1, 77. that they open and enlighten the eyes of the Gentiles, that they may be turned from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto GOD Eph. 3, 9. that they justify men, beget children of GOD, save themselves and others, etc. 1 Cor. 4, 15. Gal. 4, 19. 1 Tim. 4, 16. Which same thing Scripture affirms also concerning the use and administration of the Sacraments: that we are regenerated of water and the Spirit. John 3, 5. that we are saved by the washing of regeneration and renewing in the Holy Spirit. Tit. 3, 5. 1 Pet. 3, 21. that we are cleansed by the washing of water in the Word. Eph. 5, 26. that by the eating of bread we are made partakers of the very Body of Christ, by the drinking of wine, we are made partakers of the very Blood of Christ, in the use of the Eucharistic Sacrament: 1 Cor. 10, 16. and all these things come to us for the remission of sins. Matt. 26, 28.

These things being thus established, we deservedly cast out and proscribe from the field and borders of the Church this foul error of the Schwenkfeldians: how far Zwingli differs from it, let those see who have been accustomed to fight for his dogma even today, as if for hearth and home. Certainly, with Schwenkfeld he denied that the true body is distributed with the bread, and the true blood of Christ with the wine, in the Sacrament of the Supper: Thus he also denied that the use of the Sacraments is salutary: because GOD saves us without this instrument: Gott macht vns selig ohne diese geschirr. In Confession to Charles V, in the year 1530. Thus he denied with Schwenkfeld: That only those believing in Christ through the Word preached and heard are eternally saved: inasmuch as he associates Hercules, Numa Pompilius, Palamedes, Socrates, and any other wiser Gentiles, who never heard the Word of GOD, never read it, much less believed in Christ, in Heaven, and in eternal blessedness, with the faithful Elect. In his Confession to the King of France. But we have discussed this matter more fully elsewhere, and expressly. We proceed to the remaining errors, pronouncing anathema upon all this impiety, both Zwinglian and Schwenkfeldian: of which Hosius the Pole left behind a brief epitome, writing thus in his book on the express Word of GOD: We shall bid the Scriptures themselves to depart, and we shall rather hear GOD speaking, than that we should turn ourselves to these beggarly elements: It is not necessary to be skilled in the Law and Scripture; but to be taught by GOD: Vain is the labor which is spent on the Scriptures: for Scripture is created, and a certain beggarly element.

Nor does it carry any weight or moment that they clamor that GOD is afflicted with ignominy if it be established that He acts effectively for our salvation through these beggarly elements. For although the ministry of the Word and Sacraments, in itself, insofar as it is the work of man, can have no power or efficacy in the minds of the hearers: yet the efficacy which is everywhere in the sacred writings ascribed to this Ministry: is not attributed to it merely for the sake of an honorary title: but it has truly pleased GOD thus, through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe, 1 Cor. 1, 21. Thus therefore GOD is and remains the Principal efficient agent: but the Ministry of the Word and Sacraments is an Instrument only, through which GOD is ordinarily effective in men for salvation: yet so that these two actions, namely of GOD and of the ministers, do not concur to produce the salutary effect of Conversion and faith separately and apart: but conjointly and unitedly. By which way, indeed, neither is GOD afflicted with any ignominy; nor is more than is just attributed to man and his ministry, when it is indicated what GOD accomplishes through him. And thus also both remain most true: first this: Neither is he that planteth anything, neither he that watereth: but GOD that giveth the increase, 1 Cor. 3, 7. then also that which is immediately added: We are fellow-workers of GOD: you are GOD's husbandry: GOD's building, according to the grace of GOD.

Of the same vanity is it that the Schwenkfeldians, to weaken the efficacy of the Ministry, abuse the distinction of the External and Internal man: as if the Minister were occupied only about the External man, but the Lord only about the Internal. For the Apostle, in those places where he uses this distinction, Rom. 7, 22. 2 Cor. 4, 16. Eph. 3, 16. does not deal at all with the means or instruments of our salvation: but with the effects of our Restitution or Renovation. But let these suffice, we proceed to the remaining errors.

Latin:

III. Schvvenck-

III. Schvvenckfeldiani & Enthusiastæ

IN classe errantium de Spiritu & Litera, locum minimè postremum obtinent Schvvenckfeldiani, à quodam CASPARO Schvvenckfeldio, nobili Silesio, erroris hujus primario Magistro, & autore sic dicti; qui Literam occidentem exponunt de ministerio Verbi & Sacramentorum: Spiritum verò vivificantem intelligunt de internis raptibus, sive Enthusiasmis: contendentes interim, Ministerium Verbi & Sacramentorum esse inanem sonitum, & otiosam Ceremoniam: contrà verò arcanis motibus & Enthusiasmis, omnem regenerationis virtutem, Spiritum ac vitam adscribentes. Unde etiam Enthusiastæ dici meruerunt: non eo quidem sensu, quo Veteres Messaliani, sive Εὐχῆται olim etiam appellabantur ἐνθουσιασταὶ, eò quòd insano furore abrepti, se quidvis esse somniarent, & interrogati, an Prophetæ, an Abraham, an Patriarchæ, an Christus essent, omnia hæc se esse profiterentur, & miseri persuaderent. Unde in medium hominum cætum proruentcs, saltabant variè ridiculeque gesticulabantur, vel digitis crepabant, tanquàm his suis gestibus dæmonas impugnent, & à se ejiciant: somniantes, Satanam sensibiliter & visibiliter suis precibus expelli, & exire ex ore ipsorum in formâ porcæ sive scrofæ cum porcellis: inque hujus locum statim visibiliter quoq; & sensibiliter succedere ac ingredi Spiritum Sanctum. Quam sanè foedissimam hæresin nos Schvvenkfeldianis minimè adscribimus, sed Enthusiastarum nomine eos ob id tantùm participiare statuimus, quòd extra & præter verbum DEI scriptum, prædicatum, & auditum talem regenerationis & illuminationis modum fingunt, qui arcanis motibus, & raptibus constet, quos pro suggestionibus Spiritus Sancti observant, & deosculantur.

Errorem autem hunc solidissimè refutat, imò funditùs evertit universa Scriptura Sacra, & quæ ex eâ dependet, infallibilis analogiæ fidei certitudo. Nam primùm delirium hoc pugnat cum verâ sententiâ Oppositionis Apostolicæ inter Literam Occidentem, & Spiritum vivificantem, quæ ex superioribus peti, & huc referri debet.

Deinde diametraliter pugnat cum scopo atq; intentione JEHOVÆ, qui ideò Verbum suum literis consignari, & ministerium Verbi ac Sacramentorum institutùm voluit, ut homines à proprij ingenij somnijs, Speculationibus & Enthusiasmis avocaret, & per Verbum hoc suum scriptum, lectum, prædicatum & auditum, veram conversionem ac fidem in illis, & Consequenter salutem ac vitam æternam operaretur. Hoc enim vult DEUS ipse, per Prophetam nos ablegans ad

Legem, & ad Testimonium, cum expressa hac comminatione: Nisi dicturi essent secundum hæc, ipsos non visuros auroram matutinam. Esa. 8. 20. Hoc voluit Servator, ablegans eos, qui vitam æternam consequi, & infernales cruciatus evitare velint, ad Scripturas, ad Mosen & Prophetas, Joh. 5. 39. Scrutamini Scripturas: quia putatis vos ex ipsis vitam æternam habere: & illæ sunt, quæ testimonium perhibent de me. Luc, 16, 29. Habent Mosen & Prophetas, hos audiant: Hos si non audierint, neque credent, si maximè ex mortuis aliquis ad ipsos redeat &c.

Tertiò pugnat hoc delirium cum fine principali, cujus gratia Scriptura, autore Deo, literis est consignata, qui in eo consistit, ut erudiat nos ad salutem per fidem, quæ est in Christo Jesu. 1. Tim. 3. 15. ut convertat animas nostras, ut præstet sapientiam parvulis: lætificet cor: illuminet oculos: conferat gaudium & solatium firmum in afflictione: præferat lucernam pedibus nostris, & lumen semitis nostris: Psal. 119, 8. 9. 92. 105. monstret, quomodò per patientiam & consolationem spem habeamus Rom. 15, 4: ut tandem vitam æternam consequamur. Ioh 5, 39. Qui fines singuli & universi luculenter evincunt, Scripturam Sacram esse medium sive instrumentum, per quod ipse dona hæc Spiritualia omnia, & sic salutem ac vitam æternam in hominibus operari velit, imo reverà, & actu ipso operetur.

Quartò pugnat delirium hoc cum effectu illo, quem DEUS ipse per scripturam sacram lectam, prædicatam, auditam, se operaturum in hominibus, certò & infallibiliter, imò sanctè promisit. Nam auditus Vertibi hujus sive lecti, sive prædicati, efficit in nobis fidem: secundum illud Servatoris, Joh. 17. 20. Non pro eis tantùm, rogo; sed & pro illis, qui per Sermonem illorum credituri sunt in me Et secundum illud Apostoli, Rom. 10, 17. Fides ex auditu: Auditus autem per Verbum DEI: per Verbum autem non arcanum, & Enthusjasticum: sed quod, definiente Apostolo, prædicatum est in toto terrarum orbe: & quod propè est in ore nostro, & in corde nostro, hoc est, Verbum fidei, quod prædicatur: ibid. versu 8. & 18. Unde idem Apostolus passim in suis Epistolis, Stultitiam prædicationis Evangelicæ nominat potentiam DEI ad salutem omni credenti. Rom. 1, 16. Ephes. 1, 13. 1. Cor. 1, 18. & 21. Hinc in Actis de Petro Cœlestis visio ad Cornelium Cæsareensem: Mitte in Ioppen, & voca Simonem, qui cognominatur Petrus, qui LOQVETVR tibi verba, in quibus salvaberis tu, & universa domus tua, Actor. 11. 14. Et hoc est complementum illud promissionis divinæ, jam olim de efficacia prædicationis Evangelicæ per Prophetam editæ: Quemadmodum descendit imber, & nix de Cœlo, & illuc ultra non revertitur, nisi inebriaverit terram, & fœcundavit eam, & germinare fecerit, & dederit semen serenti, & panem comedenti: Sic erit Verbum meum, quod egreditur de ore meo: non revertetur ad me vacuum; sed faciet quacunq; volui, & prosperabitur in his, ad quæ misi illud. Esa. 55, 10. & 11.

Tandem pugnat hoc delirium cum præclaris illis elogijs, quibus non modò Apostoli, sed & quilibet sinceri præcones, & ministri Verbi insigniuntur: quòd nimitùm sint dispensatores mysteriorum DEI: Cooperarij DEI: DEI agricultura: DEI ædificatio: 1. Cor. 3, 7. 9. & cap. 4, 1. quòd dent scientiam salutis populo: Luc. 1, 77. quòd aperiant & illuminent oculos gentium, ut convertantur à tenebris ad lucem, & potestate Satanæ ad DEVM Ephes. 3, 9. quòd iustificent homines, DEI filios gignant, salvent seipsos & alios &c. 1. Corin. 4, 15. Gal. 4, 19. 1. Timoth. 4, 16. Quod ipsum de Sacramentorum etiam usu, & administratione affirmat Scriptura: quòd ex aquâ & Spiritu regeneremur. Iohan. 3, 5. quòd salvemur per lavacrum regenerationis & renovationis in Spiritu Sancto. Tit. 3, 5. 1 Pet. 3, 21. quòd mundemur lavacro aquæ in Verbo. Ephes. 5, 26. quòd per manducationem panis participes reddamur ipsius Corporis Christi, per bibitionem vini, reddamur participes ipsius Sanginis Christi, in usu Sacramenti Eucharistici: 1. Cor. 10. 16. & hæc omnia nobis obtingant in remissionem peccatorum. Matth. 29, 28.

Quibus ita constitutis, meritò ex agro & finibus Ecclesiæ ejicimus & proscribimus fœdum istum Schvvenckfeldianorum errorem: à quò num discrepet Zvvinglius, viderint illi, qui pro ipsius dogmatis, tanquam pro aris ac focis pugnare hodieq; consveverunt. Certè cum Schvvenckfeldio negavit, in Sacramento Cœnæ cum pane distribui verum corpus, & cum vino verum sanguinem Christi: Ita negavit etiam usum Sacramentorum esse salutiferum: quia DEUS absque eo nos salvet: Gott macht vns selig ohne diese geschirr. In Confess. ad Carolum V. anno 1530. Sic negavit cum Schvvenckfeldio: Tantum per Verbum prædicatum & auditum credentes in Christum, æternùm salvari: siquidem Herculem, Numam Pompilium, Palamedem, Socratem, & alios quosvis sapientiores Gentiles, qui Verbum DEI nunquàm audiverunt, nunquam legerunt, nedum in Christum crediderunt, in Cœlo, inq; æternâ beatitudine, Electis fidelibus consociat. In Confessione ad Regem Galliæ. Sed hac de re fusiùs alibi, & ex professo disseruimus. Pergimus ad errores reliquos, anathema dicentes universæ huic impietati tùm Zvvinglianæ, tùm Schvvenckfeltianæ: cujus brevem Epitomen, post se reliquit, Hosius Polonus, in libro de expresso DEI Verbo sic scribens: Nos ipsas Scripturas facessere iubebimus, & DEVM loquentem potiùs audiemus, quàm ut ad egena ista elementa nos convertamus: Non oportet Legis & Scripturæ peritum esse; sed à DEO doctum: Vanus est labor, qui Scripturis impenditur: Scriptura enim creata est, & egenum quoddam elementum.

Neque ponderis, momentić; aliquid obtinet, quòd DEUM ignominia affici clamitant, si statuatur ille per egena ista elementa, ad nostram salutem DEUM efficaciter agere. Quanquam enim ipsum per se ministerium, Verbi & Sacramentorum, quatenus opus est hominis, vim & efficaciam nullam habere potest in animis Auditorum: tamen quæ Ministerio huic passim in sacris literis efficacia adscribitur: ae non honorarij tantum modò cognomenti causa illi attribuitur: sed revera DEO sic placuit, per stultitiam prædicationis salvos facere credentes, 1. Cor. 1, 21.
