Sic ergo DEUS est & manet agens efficiens Principale: Ministerium verò Verbi & Sacramentorum est Organon tantùm per quòd DEUS ordinariè in hominibus ad salutem est efficax: ita tamen, ut duæ hæ actiones, DEI nimirùm, & ministrorum, ad producendum salutarem Conversionis & fidei effectum non διηρημένως divisim ac separatim: sed ήνωμένως conjunctim, & unitè concurrant. Quo sanè pacto, nec DEUS igominia aliquà afficitur; neque homini, ejusque ministerio, plus justo tribuitur, cùm quid DEUS per eum efficiat, indicatur. Atque ita etiam utrumque verissimum manet: primùm hoc: Neq; qui plantat est aliquid, neq; qui rigat: sed, qui dat incrementum, DEUS, 1. Cor. 3, 7. deinde & illud, quod immediatè subjicitur: DEI sumus cooperarij: DEI agricolario: DEI ædificatio estis, secundum gratiam DEI.

Ejusdem vanitatis est, quòd Schvvenckfeldiani, ad enervandam Ministerij efficaciam, distinctione Externi, & Interni hominis abutuntur: quasi circa Externum solummodò hominem Minister occupatus sit, Dominus verò circa Internum tantùm. Nam Apostolus illis in locis, in quibus distinctione hac utitur, Rom. 7, 22. 2. Cor. 4, 16. Ephes. 3. 16. de medijs sive instrumentis salutis nostræ nihil quicquam agit: sed de Restitutionis sive Renovationis nostræ effectis. Verùm hæc sufficiant, Pergimus ad errores reliquos.


### Part II. Autostiche he palaike Greek: IV. Anabaptists

IV. Anabaptists.

CIrca puriorem doctrinam de Spiritu & Litera turpiter & periculosè errant etiam Anabaptistæ, qui Literam Occidentem accipiebant de Libris Veteris Testamenti: vel quod eòdem recidit, de scriptis Mosis & Prophetarum: Spiritum verò vivificantem, de libris Novi Testamenti, sive de scriptis Evangelistarum & Apostolorum. Emersit error iste tandem in manifestum furorem, ut contenderent, Libros Veteris Testamenti, ut Mosis & Prophetarum, non modò imperfectos esse: sed & multa continere dogmata, cum libris Novi T. directè pugnantia: ac proinde Christianos relicto Mose & Regarding the purer doctrine of the Spirit and the Letter, the Anabaptists also err basely and dangerously, who took the killing Letter to refer to the books of the Old Testament: or, which amounts to the same thing, to the writings of Moses and the Prophets: but the life-giving Spirit, to the books of the New Testament, or to the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles. This error finally emerged into manifest madness, so that they contended that the books of the Old Testament, such as those of Moses and the Prophets, were not only imperfect: but also contained many dogmas directly conflicting with the books of the New T.: and consequently that Christians, having abandoned Moses and

To the Prophets, who delivered nothing but the killing letter, one ought to progress to Christ and his Gospel, as to the life-giving Spirit. This error was already committed long ago by the Simonians, Cerdonians, Marcionites, Tatianists, and Manichaeans: whose reasonings and ravings, rather than arguments, St. Augustine most solidly explains and refutes in almost the entire sixth volume of his Works: but especially in the thirty-three books against Faustus the Manichaean: and in the two books against the adversary of the Law and the Prophets. In this our century, and indeed, as Sleidan testifies in book 6, around the year of Christ 1527, the Anabaptists interpolated this foul error: and they undertook its defense both elsewhere and especially in the Electorate of the Palatinate publicly: for the sake of repressing which, a public Colloquy was also instituted at Frankenthal in the year 1571, under the auspices of the Elector Palatine Frederick III. In which part the Orthodox, and the theologians of our party, did not fail in their duty, but rather opposed themselves so manfully in public writings to the fury of the Anabaptists, both in this and in other articles of the Christian faith, that unless one be insane, one would hardly, nay, would never, assent to this insanity today.

The moral [law], which is a tutor to Christ, and leads to the acknowledgment of sin: Gal. 3:24, Rom. 3:20. Furthermore, there are contained in them, as also in the prophecies of the Prophets, very illustrious Evangelical promises: concerning the seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the serpent, and in whom all the nations of the earth are to be blessed: concerning the birth, person, and office of the Messiah: concerning the state of the Church of the New Testament: concerning the perpetual preservation of the Church, even under the most atrocious persecutions: concerning the furies of the Devil against the same: concerning the faith and constancy of the pious in defending the heavenly truth.

If all these things are compared with the New Testament, and transferred to a practice worthy of a Christian man: our faith will truly be wonderfully increased and confirmed. There are besides examples of most beautiful virtues, proper to the Church of God alone, and shining even amidst the very miseries themselves, and inviting to their imitation. 4. Christ himself sent us to Moses and the Prophets: Luke 16:29, and was accustomed to confirm his sermons from their writings: Whence he expressly asserts that those things which were written in Moses, in the Prophets, and in the Psalms were fulfilled in him, Luke 24:44. Which method of teaching the Apostles also held: as is to be seen, Rom. 3:21, and ch. 15:4, 1 Cor. 10:6, and 2 Tim. 3:15 and 16, 2 Pet. 1:19. Finally, that contradictory things are delivered in the Old Testament is manifestly false. For no article of faith can be given, no question concerning faith and morals, which has not been decided and defined with the same truth in the Old Testament as it is illustrated more fully and clearly in the New: which can be demonstrated to the eye by an induction of all the articles and controversies of the Christian Religion: nay, in this whole treatise it has been evidently demonstrated thus far.

Although we ourselves also willingly grant that the Ceremonial Law is clearly fulfilled in Christ, and therefore abrogated, and not necessary for a Christian to observe: and likewise that the forensic Law does not bind us in the least: yet what the Anabaptists wish to infer from that, namely that the Books of the Old Testament are the killing letter, and therefore to be shunned by Christians: that indeed can by no means be admitted, nor ought it to be. For 1. The consequence from a part to the whole is not valid. 2. From the sophistry of a statement in a certain respect to a statement simply, this most vicious collection emerges: Ceremonial and Forensic laws are abrogated for Christians as regards their observation: Therefore there can be no use at all for them in the Church of the New Testament. For just as there are usually several causes and ends for one thing: so there is another use for these laws, however abrogated, besides observation: namely, that by the example of the Epistle to the Hebrews, from the comparison of the Types to the thing signified; and especially of the Ceremonies and Sacrifices of the Old Testament to Christ, we may confirm our faith in the same: but from the consideration of the forensic laws, we may construct a sort of norm, according to which it may be permitted to examine modern civil laws: and especially to seek from thence the material for considering the divine justice and wisdom, which prescribed laws most accommodated to that people and to that region. 3. A sophism of ἑτεροζητήσεως (asking about a different thing) is committed: For it is one thing to inquire about the ceremonies themselves and the forensic laws, but another about the books themselves in which they are written. Where, from the abrogation of the former, the consequence to the annihilation of the latter is not valid. For there is contained in them, moreover, the doctrine of the Law

Latin:

IV. Anabaptistæ.

CIrca puriorem doctrinam de Spiritu & Litera turpiter & periculosè errant etiam Anabaptistæ, qui Literam Occidentem accipiebant de Libris Veteris Testamenti: vel quod eòdem recidit, de scriptis Mosis & Prophetarum: Spiritum verò vivificantem, de libris Novi Testamenti, sive de scriptis Evangelistarum & Apostolorum. Emersit error iste tandem in manifestum furorem, ut contenderent, Libros Veteris Testamenti, ut Mosis & Prophetarum, non modò imperfectos esse: sed & multa continere dogmata, cum libris Novi T. directè pugnantia: ac proinde Christianos relicto Mose &

Prophetis, nihil præter literam Occidentem tradentibus, progredi debere ad Christum, ejusq; Evangelium, tanquam ad Spiritum vivificantem. Errorem istum errarunt jam olim quoque Simoniani, Cerdoniani, Marcionitæ, Tatiani, Manichæi: quorum rationes & deliramenta potiùs, quàm argumenta D. Augustinus toto fermè tomo sexto Operum: præcipuè verò libro contra Faustum Manichæum triginta tribus: & libris duobus contra adversarium Legis & Prophetarum solidissimè explicat, & refutat. Hunc fœdum errorem nostro hoc seculo, & quidem, teste Sleidano lib. 6. circa annum Christi 1527. inter polarunt Anabaptistæ: ejusq; defensionem tum alibi, tùm inprimis in archipalatinatu susceperunt publicè: Cujus reprimendi gratiâ publicum etiam Colloquium, auspicijs Electoris Palatini Friderici III. Franckenthalæ anno 1571. institutum fuit. Quâ in parte Orthodoxi etiam, ac nostrarum partium Theologi suo officio non defuerunt, quin scriptis Publicis Anabaptistarum furori tùm in hoc, tùm in alijs fidei Christianæ articulis, ita masculè se opposuerunt, ut nisi qui insanus sit, insaniæ huic hodie vix, imò nunquàm adstipuetur.

Moralis, quæ pædagogus est ad Christum, & ad agnitionem peccati adducit: Gal. 3. 24. Rom. 3, 20. Deinde continentur in illis, ut & in vaticinijs Prophetarum, illustres admodum promissiones Evangelicæ, de semine mulieris, contrituro caput serpentis, & in quo benedicendæ sint omnes gentes terræ: de nativitate, personâ & officio Messiæ: de statu Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti: de perpetuâ Conservatione Ecclesiæ, sub atrocissimis etiam persecutionibus:de furoribus Diaboli adversus eandem: de fide & constantiâ piorum in defensa veritate cœlesti.

Quæ omnia si cum Novo Testam. conferantur, & ad praxin Christiano homine dignam transferantur: mirificè profectò fides nostra augebitur, & confirmabitur. Exempla præterea pulcherrimarum & solius Ecclesiæ DEI propriarum, ac inter ipsas plerumque ærumnas lucentium, & ad sui imitationem invitantium virtutum. 4. Christus ipse ad Mosen & Prophetas nos ablegavit: Luc. 16, 29. & ex istorum scriptis suas conciones confirmare consuevit: Unde disertè asserit, in se completa esse, quæ scripta sint in Mose, in Prophetis, & Psalmis, Luc. 24. 44. Quam docendi methodum tenuerunt etiam Apostoli: uti videre est, Rom. 3, 21. & cap. 15, 41, 1. Cor. 10, 6. & II. 2. Tim. 3, 15. & 16. 2. Pet. 1, 19. Tandem pugnantia in Veteri Testamento tradi, manifestè falsum est. Nam nullus dari potest articulus fidei, nulla quæstio, fidem moresq; concernens, quæ non eadem veritate in Veteri Testamento sit decisa, & definita, quâ in Novo fusius & dilucidiùs est illustrata: id quod per inductionem omnium articulorum, & Controversiarum Religionis Christianæ ad oculum demonstraria potest: imò in toto hoc tractatu evidenter hactenus demonstratum est.

Quanquam verò nos ipsi quoque ultrò largimur, Legem Ceremonialem in Christo planè esse completam, ac proinde abrogatam, neque Chrisstianus observatu necessariam: Legem item forensem nos minimè obligare: tamen quod inde inferre volunt Anabaptistæ, nempe Libros Veteris Testamenti, esse Literam Occidentem, ac proinde Christianis fugiendos: id verò admitti nullo pacto vel potest, vel debet. Nam 1. à parte ad totum non valet Consequentia. 2. Ex Sophisticatione à dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter, vitiosissima emergit collectio ist hæc: Leges Ceremoniales & Forenses sunt abrogatæ Christianis,quòad earum observationem: Ergo nullus pla né usus earum esse potest in Ecclesia Novi Testamenti. Quemadmodum enim aliàs Unius rei plures causæ & fines dari solent: ita Legum istarum, quantumvis abrogatarum, usus præter observationem datur alius: ut nimirum exemplo epistolæ ad Hebræos, ex collatione Typorum ad rem significatam; & cumprimus Ceremoniarum & Sacrificiorum Veteris Testamenti ad Chtistum, fidem nostram in eundem confirmemus: Ex consideratione verò legum forensium, normam quasi quandam extruamus, secundum quam leges civiles modernas examinare liceat: & potissimùm inde petere materiam confiderandæ justitiæ, & sapientiæ divinæ, quæ Leges illi populo, illiq; regioni accommodatissimas præscripsit. 3. Sophisma committitur ἑτεροζητήσεως : Aliud enim est, quærere de ceremonijs ipsis, & legibus forensibus,aliud verò de libris ipsis, quibus ea scripta continentur. Ubi ex illarum abrogatione, ad istorum etiam annihilationem non valet Consequentia. Continetur enim in illis insuper doctrina Legis


### Part II. Autostiche he palaike Greek: V. The Sacramentarians

V. The Sacramentarians

Into the purer doctrine concerning the Letter and the Spirit, the Sacramentarians also foully impinge, who explain the Letter, and indeed the killing Letter, as the external symbols or elements of the Sacraments: but the Spirit as the heavenly thing, signified only by the elements. Which theology Theodore Beza betrayed in his greater annotations on verse 27 of the second chapter to the Romans, in these words: Sometimes this antithesis of Letter and Spirit is viewed particularly in ceremonies, as in this place, and often elsewhere. Then therefore Paul calls the external sign, separated from the end or virtue of the sign itself, γράμμα or Letter: which he calls Spirit: Since an external ceremony is a thing dead and useless in itself, unless the truth is conjoined, as its life. Thus far Beza:

The interpretation of which suffers from manifest and very gross absurdities. For in the beginning, if the external symbols of the Sacraments, or Elements, are the Letter: it is necessary that they kill; since the Apostle expressly assigns this office to the Letter, when it is opposed to the spirit, that it kills. 2 Cor. 3:6. Furthermore, since by the Apostle's definition the Sacraments are seals of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4:11, and yet both the external elemental thing and the heavenly or spiritual thing pertain to the essence of a Sacrament: how, I ask, can the other part of them, namely the elemental, be said to kill? For these contrary effects, namely to kill and to be a seal of the righteousness of faith, cannot stand together at the same time and in the same subject. Finally, Holy Scripture ascribes the power and efficacy of cleansing from sins and of saving to the whole Sacrament of Baptism, not to one part of it only: Eph. 5:25, 1 Pet. 3:21. And although we also distinguish between the symbols or elements of the Sacraments and the heavenly thing itself: yet no reason at all militates for us to consider the elements on that account as the killing Letter. For although water is much inferior in dignity to the benefit of regeneration, if you look at this element by itself and in its own nature; yet because it pleased the Savior to regenerate us not by the Spirit alone, but by Water and the Spirit: it is necessary that we ascribe this spiritual effect of regeneration to both parts, as much to the elemental as to the heavenly. The same must be established concerning the other Sacrament also: so that just as the elements alone can neither be nor ought to be called Sacraments: so also the heavenly thing alone can by no means be held as a Sacrament. And again: Just as no spiritual power or efficacy is to be ascribed to the elements alone and by themselves: so neither should the heavenly thing be exhibited to us in the Sacrament without the external elements.

Furthermore, from this error results a horrendous profanation of the Ecclesiastical Ministry. For if the external elements of the Sacraments, which are dispensed here on earth, are the killing Letter: it necessarily follows that the Ecclesiastical Ministry, which likewise arises here on earth, is a ministry of the Letter and of Death. By which profanation indeed hardly a more atrocious one can be devised against the most holy Ministry, nay, hardly a greater blasphemy against this ordinance of GOD, by which He willed the Ministers of the Word to be dispensers of the mysteries of GOD: fellow-workers of GOD. 1 Cor. 3:7 and 9, and indeed such fellow-workers who perform a ministry of righteousness, and a ministry not of the Letter, but of the Spirit. 2 Cor. 3:6 and 9, and indeed for the salvation and justification of men: Eph. 3:9, 1 Cor. 4:14, Gal. 4:19, 1 Tim. 4:16.

Nor by this arrangement is the power and efficacy, which is due to the Holy Spirit alone in effecting the conversion and salvation of men, attributed to men through some kind of sacrilege. For although the Ministry by itself, insofar as it is the work of man, can have no spiritual power and efficacy in the souls of the hearers: yet because in the sacred writings such efficacy is expressly ascribed even to the Ministry: it follows necessarily that it has this efficacy, if not from itself, by itself, or in respect of the person ministering: yet it truly obtains it in another respect. Which respect is none other than that it pleased GOD, not without the ministry of men, but through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe, 1 Cor. 1:21. By which arrangement and respect GOD's glory is left untouched and entire: so indeed that He alone is, and remains, the Principal acting agent: but the Ministry of the Word and Sacraments is the medium and instrument through which GOD acts effectively, so that these two actions, namely of GOD and of the Ministers, concur to produce one single salutary effect, not διηρημένως, dividedly or separately: but ἡνωμένως, conjointly and unitedly.

But here we draw in the sails of the present discussion: and we determine that, besides the errors discussed thus far, a judgment can be made about other similar ones: such as that of certain Zwinglians and Papists, who have determined: that some men are justified by the Law of Nature: others by the Law of Moses: others finally by the Law of the Gospel. For since the Law of Moses, by reason of our corruption and infirmity, is the killing Letter, and no mortal can render full obedience to it: how, I ask, can salvation be obtained by anyone from it? Now if the power and efficacy of justification (in the sense already explained) is deservedly denied to the Law of Moses, as being more divine: how, I ask, can such an effect be ascribed to the Law of Nature, which is in every way inferior and more imperfect?

The other error of the Romanists also pertains here, who contend that the Gospel is a certain new law, properly so called, as one that commands certain singular works, which obtain the power of justifying: Nay, that even certain counsels of perfection are handed down in the Gospel, though not necessary for all. The shameful vanity of both these figments may be made clear from the fact that the Apostle denies the power of vivifying not to this or that law, but indefinitely to every Law: and ascribes it to the Gospel alone, insofar as it is opposed to the Law ἀντιδιῃρημένως, and is nothing else than a discourse concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, through and on account of Christ apprehended by faith.

Finally, from what has been discussed thus far, a judgment can be made concerning that error of the Sacramentarians, who contend that the Old and New Testament differ not according to the substance itself, but only according to the administration, or the mode of dispensation, and thus that they are not two distinct but only one Testament, although its tablets are diverse. Although we have expressly refuted this error in the Article concerning the distinction between the Old and New Testament, yet in this place these three observations alone are to be noted

I. If the Old Testament (as was evidently demonstrated above in the thesis), taken properly and specifically, and set in direct opposition to the New Testament, is, as the Apostle defines it, the Letter that kills: but the New Testament, taken in this same way, is the Spirit that gives life: Or as the Apostle speaks, Gal. 4:24, If the Old Testament begets children into slavery: but the New begets children into freedom: it will certainly be impossible for the substance of both to be one: unless someone wishes to contradict the Apostle to his face: and to establish that the New Testament, and its substance, is equally the Letter that kills, and begets children into slavery: which is manifestly absurd.

II. Although in the books of the Old Testament, promises also exist concerning the free remission of sins on account of the Messiah: yet these do not pertain to the Old Testament properly so called: but to the New.

III. On account of the promises, and the faith applied to them by the Church of the Old Testament, these two Testaments ought not to be confused with one another: but the New, rather, with respect to time, ought to be subdivided into the time before, and the time after the Messiah was exhibited: Because, namely, although the glory of the New Testament flourished only after the Messiah was exhibited, yet before he was exhibited, there was no other method of justification: as the Council of Jerusalem defines, Acts 15:10 and 11. This very thing we explain, by way of a conclusion, in the words of Augustine, who in book 1 against the adversary of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 17, has it thus: Although in the Old Testament, on account of the promise of temporal goods and the threatening of evils, the temporal Jerusalem begets servants: In the New, however, where faith obtains charity, by which the law can be fulfilled, not more by fear of punishment than by love of justice, the eternal Jerusalem begets free children: yet even in those times there were spiritual just men, whom the commanding Letter did not kill, but the helping Spirit made alive: Whence also the faith of the coming Christ dwelt indeed in the Prophets, who announced that Christ would come, etc.

Latin:

V. Sacramentarij

IN puriorem doctrinam de Literâ & Spiritu, turpiter etiam impingunt Sacramentarij, qui Literam, & Literam quidem Occidentem, de externis Sacramentorum Symbolis sive Elementis: Spiritum verò de re cœlesti, per Elementa tantùm significatâ exponunt. Quam Theologiam prodidit Theodorus Beza, in annotationibus majoribus ad versum 27. capitis secundi ad Romanos, his verbis: Interdum hæc Litera & Spiritus antithesis peculiariter spectatur in Ceremoniis, ut hoc loco, & alibi sæpe. Tunc igitur γράμμα sive Literam vocat Paulus, Externum Signum, ab ipsius Signi fine sive virtute sejunctum: quam vocat Spiritum: Quoniam externa cæremonia est res per se mortua, & inutilis, nisi conjungatur veritas, quasi illius vita. Hactenus Beza:

Cujus interpretatio manifestis ijsq; craffiffimis laborat abfurditatibus. Initio enim, si externa Sacramentorum Symbola, sive Elementa, sunt Litera: occidant utique necesse est: siquidem hoc officium diferte Apostolus Litera, quando spiritui opponitur, adsignat, quod occidat. 2. Cor 3, 6. Deinde cum definiente Apostolo Sacramenta sint signaculam justitiae fidei, Rom. 4, 11. ad Sacramenti vero essentiam tam externa Elementaris, quam coelestis sive Spiritualis res pertineat: quomodo quaeso altera eorum pars, nempe elementaris, dici queat occidere? Contrarij enim isti effectus: nempe occidere, & esse signaculum justitiae fidei, simul & in eodem subjecto, simul stare non possunt. Tandem Scriptura Sacra toti Sacramento Baptismi vim atque efficaciam mundandi a peccatis, & salvandi, non alteri tantum ejus parti adscribit: Ephes. 5, 25. 1. Pet. 3. 21. Et quanquam inter Sacramentorum Symbola, sive Elementa, & inter rem coelestem ipsi quoque distinguimus: ut tamen propterea Elementa habeamus pro Litera Occidente, ratio plane nulla militat. Nam licet Aqua, dignitate multo sit inferior Regenerationis beneficio, si elementum hoc per se, & in sua natura spectes; quia tamen Servatori placuit, non solo Spiritu, sed Aqua & Spiritu nos regenerare: utrique sane parti, tam Elementari, quam Coelesti, Spiritualem, hunc Regenerationis effectum ut adscribamus, necesse est. Quod ipsum de altero quoque Sacramento est statuendum: ita ut quemadmodum sola Elementa, neque possunt, neq; debent dici Sacramenta: Ita quoque Res Coelestis Sola pro Sacramento haberi neutiquam possit. Et rursus: Quemadmodum Elementis solis, & per se, vis aut efficacia Spiritualis nulla est adscribenda: ita neque Res Coelestis, sine Externis Elementis, nobis in Sacramento exhibeatur

Praeterea ex errore isto resultat horrenda prophanatio Ministerij Ecclesiastici. Sienim externa elementa Sacramentorum, quae in terris hisce dispensantur, sunt Litera occidens: necessario sequitur, Ministerium Ecclesiasticum, quod itidem in terris hisce oritur, esse ministerium Literae & Mortis. Qua sane prophanatione vix atrocior in Sacrosanctum Ministerium excogitari potest imo vix major blasphemia, in hanc DEI ordinationem, qua Ministros Verbi voluit esse dispensatores mysteriorum DEI: cooperarios DEI. 1. Corinth, 3, 7. & 9. & tales quidem cooperarios, qui obeant ministerium justitiae, & ministerium non literae, sed Spiritus. 2. Cor. 3. 6. & 9. & quidem in salutem & justificationem hominum: Ephes. 3, 9. 1. Cor. 4, 14. Gal. 4, 19. 1. Tim. 4, 16.

Neque hoc pacto virtus & efficacia, quae soli Spiritui Sancto in efficienda conversione & salute hominum debetur, hominibus per sacrilegium quoddam tribuitur. Etsi enim Ministerium per se, quatenus opus est hominis, vim & efficaciam spiritualem nullam habere potest in animis Auditorum: quia tamen in sacris disserè etiam Ministerio efficacia talis adscribitur: sequitur necessariò, quod illud efficaciam hanc habeat, si non ex se, per se, aut respectu personæ ministrantis: eam tamen alio respectu reverà obtineat. Qui respectus nullus alius est, quàm quòd DEO placuit, non sine ministerio hominum, sed per stultitiam prædicationis salvos facere credentes, 1. Cor. 1, 21. Quo pacto & respectu DEO gloria sua intacta atque integra relinquitur: ita quidem, ut ipse solus sit, & maneat agens, efficiens Principale: Ministerium verò Verbi & Sacramentorum, sit medium & organon, per quod DEUS efficaciter agit, ita, ut duæ hæ actiones DEI nimirùm, & Ministrorum, ad producendum unum numero salutarem effectum, concurrant non διηρημένως, divisim aut separatim: sed ἡνωμένως conjunctim & unitè.

Sed vela præsentis disputationis hîc contrahimus: & præter errores hactenus discussos, de alijs quoque consimilibus judicium fieri posse, statuimus: Qualis est ille quorundam Zvvinglianorum & Pontificiorum, qui statuerunt: Homines alios quidem per Legem Naturæ: alios per Legem Mosis: alios denique per Legem Evangelij justificari. Quia enim Lex Mosis, ratione nostræ corruptionis & infirmitatis est Litera occidens, neque mortalium quisque plenam ei obedientiam præstare potest: quomodo quæso ex ea Salus cuiquam obtingere possit. Jam si legi Mosis, tanquam diviniori Justificationis virtus & efficacia (sensu jam explicato) meritò derogatur: quomodo quæso Legi Naturæ quippe modis omnibus inferiori & imperfectiòri, talis effectus adscribi queat?

Pertinet huc & error alter Romanensium, qui contendunt, Evangelium esse novam quandam legem, propriè sic dictam, ut quæ singularia quædam præcipiat opera, vim justificandi obtinentia: Imò in Evangelio Consilia etiam quædam tradi perfectionis, non tamen omnibus necessaria. Utriusque hujus figmenti pudenda vanitas vel inde elucescat, quòd Apostolus Legi non huic, vel illi, sed indefinite omni Legi, vim vivificandi derogat: eamq́; soli Evangelio, quatenus illud Legi ἀντιδιῃρημένως opponitur, & nihil est aliud, quàm Concio de gratuitâ peccatorum remissione, per & propter Christum fide apprehensum.

Tandem ex hactenus disputatis judicium fieri potest de errore illo Sacramentariorum, qui contendunt, Vetus & Novum Testamentum non secundum substantiam ipsam: sed tantùm secundum admnistrationem, sive dispensationis modum differre: adeoque non duo distincta, sed unum tantummodò esse Testamentum : licet diversa sint ejus tabula. Quem errorem licèt ex professo protriverimus, in Articulo de discrimine Veteris & Novi Testamenti: Hoc tamen loco tres tantùm hæ observationes notandæ veniunt

I. Si Vetus Testamentum (uti supra in thesi evidenter demonstratum fuit) propriè ac specificè sumtum, & Novo Testamento contradistinctè oppositum, definiente Apostolo, est Litera Occidens : Novum verò Testamentum, hoc itidem modo acceptum, est Spiritus vivificans : Vel ut Apostolus loquitur, Gal. 4, 24, Si Vetus Testamentum filios generat in servitutem: Novum verò filios in libertatem: impossibile utique erit, ut una utriusque sit substantia: nisi quis Apostolo in faciem contradicere: & Novum Testamentum, ejusque substantiam æquè Literam esse Occidentem, & filios in servitutem generare, statuere velit: id quod manifeste absurdum.

II. Etsi in veteris Testamenti libris, promissiones etiam extant de gratuita peccatorum remissione propter Messiam: ea tamen non ad Vetus Testamentum propriè sic dictum: sed ad Novum pertinent.

III Propter promissiones, & fidem illis ab Ecclesia Vet. Test. adhibitam, non debent confundi duo hæc inter se Testamenta: sed Novum potiùs temporis respectu, debet subdividi, in tempus ante, & tempus post exhibitum Messiam: Quòd videlicet, licèt gloria Novi Testamenti, post exhibitum demùm Messiam effloruerit, ante exhibitum tamen eundem, non alia fuerit justificandi ratio: sic definiente Concilio Hierosolymitano, Actor. 15, 10. & 11. Quod ipsum Coronidis loco verbis Augustini explicamus, qui lib. 1. contra adversarium Legis & Prophetarum, cap. 17. sic habet: Quamvis in Veteri Testamento, propter temporalium bonorum promissionem, malorumq́; comminationem, servos pariat temporalis Ierusalem: In Novo autem, ubi fides impetrat charitatem, quâ lex possit impleri, non magis timore pœnæ, quam dilectione justitiæ, liberos pariat æterna Ierusalem: tamen & illis temporibus fuerunt justi spirituales, quos non occidebat Litera jubens, sed vivificabat Spiritus juvans: Vnde & fides venturi Christi habitabat utiq; in Prophetis, futurum pronuncientibus Christum &c.


### Part II. Autostiche he palaike Greek: To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 32 On the Cross and Calamities, or human afflictions

The arrangement of the following Treatise.

The treatment of this Article by Philippus consists of two general parts: namely, the preparation or preliminary therapy. This is a kind of preparation for the sounder doctrine of the Church concerning the Cross and Calamities: and then, indeed, the actual exposition or Treatise of this Article. The preparation differs partly concerning the magnitude of human miseries, which cannot be expressed by any abundance of speech, or indeed even comprehended by thinking: and partly concerning the blindness of the Gentile Philosophers or the wise men of this age, who sought and established the causes of evils partly in matter, partly in the position of the stars, and partly in a certain blind error of human counsels, thus wandering far and shamefully from the path of Truth.

The exposition itself, or Treatise, is fourfold. For in the beginning the Author discourses specifically concerning the afflictions of the pious, and submits their causes, both impelling and final, on account of which the Church is always subject to the Cross in this world. Then, indeed, he shows certain places of Consolation, by which the Pious may raise and sustain themselves in any afflictions whatsoever: And he shows how much Evangelical Consolation differs from Philosophical. Thirdly, he speaks concerning the salutary effect of Evangelical Consolations, which is True Patience, and shows that it is not a certain Stoic stupor, or insensibility: but an obedience acquiescing in the just and beneficent will of GOD, and suffering any adversities whatsoever, without indignation or murmuring against GOD. Fourthly and lastly, he establishes certain kinds of Calamities: namely, punishment; probation; the testimony of the Evangelical Truth sealed by the shedding of blood, or at least confirmed by true constancy; and finally, the price of Redemption for the sins of men.

And such indeed is the Philippean Treatise: following in the footsteps of which, we establish two members or chapters of the subsequent exposition: THE FIRST will investigate the Nature, Kinds, and causes of human afflictions.

The second part will be entirely practical, showing firm and immovable foundations of consolations, which must be opposed to any internal and external adversities of soul, body, and fortunes, both in general and in particular, and which can impart to the pious the spirit of true patience and strength.

Latin:

Οἰκονομία insequentis Tractationis.

Octi hujus Tractatio apud Philippum duabus constat partibus generalibus: nempe προ παρασκευῆ sive προθεραπείᾳ. Hoc est præparatione quasi quâdam, ad saniorem Ecclesiæ doctrinam de Cruce & Calamitatibus: deinde verò ipsâ Articuli hujus diexodo sive Tractatione, Προπαρασκευη differit partim de miseriarum humanarum magnitudine, quæ nullâ orationis copiâ exprimi, imò ne cogitando quidem comprehendi queat: partim verò de Philosophorum Gentilium sive Sapientum hujus seculi cæcitate, qui malorum causas partim in materia, partim in positu siderum, partim in cæco quodam consiliorum humanorum errore quæsiverint, & constituerint sic à Veritatis tramite plurimùm turpissimè aberrantes.

Diexodus ipsa, sive Tractio est quadrimembris. Initiò enim differit Autor in specie de piorum afflictionibus, causasque subjiciit tùm impellentes, tùm finales, propter quas Ecclesia hoc in mundo Cruci semper sit subjecta. Deinde verò certos quosdam monstrat Consolationum locos, quibus Pij in quibusvis afflictionibus se erigere & sustentare possint: Et quantum Consolatio Evangelica à Philosophicâ differat, ostendit. Tertiò de Consolationum Evangelicarum effectu salutari, qui sit Vera Patientia, verba facit, eamq́; ostendit, non esse Stoicum quemdam stuporem, sive ἀναλ θησίαν: sed obedientiam acquiescentem in justâ ac benefica DEI voluntate, & adversa quævis, sine indignatione, sive murmuratione adversus DEUM, sufferentem. Quartò & postremò certa constituit Calamitatum genera: videlicet τιμωρίαν sive pœnam: δοκιμασίαν sive probationem: μαρτύριον sive testimonim Veritatis Evangelicæ sanguinis profusione obsignatum, vel saltem verâ constantiâ confirmatum: λύτρον deniq; sive pretium Redemptionis pro peccatis hominum.

Et talis quidem est Tractatio Philippèa: cujus vestigiis nos insistentes, duo constituimus subsequentis diexodi membra sive capita: PRIMUM investigabit Naturam, Genera & causas afflictionum humanarum.

ALTERUM totum erit practicum, firma & immota Consolationum fundamenta monstrans, quæ quibusvis adversitatibus internis & externis, animæ, Corporis, fortunarum, tum in genere, tum in specie opponi debent, & pijs veræ patientiæ ac roboris Spiritum impertire possunt.


### Chapter I. On the Nature, genera and causes of human afflictions

On the nature, kinds, and causes of human afflictions.

Calamities or afflictions, by which the pious and the impious are exercised in this life, are sometimes indicated in the Holy Scriptures by the word Cross; sometimes, however, they are called Judgments of the LORD. The appellation of CROSS has a certain analogy and allusion to the Cross of Christ the Savior, whom it behooved to suffer and die: and thus to enter into his glory? Luke 24, 26. So it is right for all those also who wish to follow Christ to take up their cross, and to enter into the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations. Matt. 10, 38. and ch. 16, 24, Mark 8, 34. Luke 9, 23. Luke 14, 27. Acts 14, 21. But they are called Judgments of the Lord: not only because GOD, in sending them, is just and does injury to no one: but also because, before He sends them, He is accustomed to denounce them through His ministers, and as it were to pass sentence upon the accused and convicted men.

Afflictions or calamities are divided, first by reason of time, into eternal and temporal.

Eternal ones are named in the Scriptures as the worm that shall never die: the fire that is unquenchable: the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, Gehenna, etc. But concerning these, there will be a discussion for us not in this place, but below in the Article on Hell. They are called eternal, however, not by reason of their beginning, but of their end which shall never be finished.

Temporal are those which are called and are such that they are terminated by a certain interval of time, or even by the limits of this life and the corruption of our flesh. And these, by reason of their subject, are again twofold: For they are either Internal, and of the mind, such as blindness and madness of mind from GOD, by a just judgment deserted and hardened: and therefore gravely erring in all counsels, studies, and actions, and rushing as if with a blind impulse to one's own and others' destruction. The effect of this blindness is an Evil Conscience, arising from the thought of committed crimes and the sense of the wrath of GOD, joined with horrible

of afflictions.

dread, anxiety, trepidation, sorrow, and torture of heart, because of the fear of evils and punishments hanging over one at every moment. Or they are External and of the body: and these again are either private or public. Private ones are almost infinite, which either plainly take away or enormously harm the goods of the body and fortune, or diminish health: such as calumny and injury, by which our fame and reputation are hindered: loss of property: an unhappy marriage: disobedience of children: perfidy of friends: and other innumerable similar ones. Public ones are those which infest either an entire region, or at least a city and our Republic: such as are enumerated in the long series of divine curses in Leviticus 26, 14. and following, Deuteronomy 28, 15. and following: namely, various kinds of diseases: hostile incursions: sterility of the land: ravaging beasts: wars and sieges of cities: pestilence: horrible famine: devastations of cities: exile and dissipation of the people: servitude: fires and conflagrations of buildings: to which can be added the overthrows of Republics: changes of empires, and other infinite things of that kind. Although these public calamities also are so varied and manifold that they can scarcely be reduced to certain classes: yet the Holy Spirit, among the Prophets, especially Ezekiel ch. 14, 21, recalls individual and universal ones to four main kinds, as it were: namely, the Sword, Famine, Beasts, and Pestilence. Thus Jeremiah 15, 2. & 3. not only are the same kinds recited: but also certain species of a third kind are expressed, dogs, the birds of the air, and the beasts of the earth: For thus GOD himself to the Prophet: If they shall say to thee: Whither shall we go forth? thou shalt say to them: Thus saith the LORD: Such as are for death, to death: and such as for the sword, to the sword: and such as for famine, to famine: and such as for captivity, to captivity: And I will visit upon them four species, saith the LORD: The sword to slay; The dogs to tear; The birds of the air, and the beasts of the earth to devour; and to dissipate; and I will give them into a fury or commotion to all the kingdoms of the earth.

Furthermore, calamities or afflictions with respect to their ends, for the sake of which they are sent by GOD, are divided into four different species, for they are either τιμωρίαι punishments, or δοκιμασίαι explorations, or probations; or μαρτύρια; or λύτρον or the price of Redemption.

I. Τιμωρίαι or Punishments are afflictions either internal or external, which GOD sends to punish the sins of men, that he may partly declare his justice, partly correct the stubborn, and finally partly deter others, by their example, from sins. In the Schools of Theologians, this first kind of afflictions is usually called the Evil of punishment, or the evil of penalty. In the Scriptures, however, it is very often called Evil simply, without any added determination; likewise wrath & The fury of GOD: The indignation of GOD, or synecdochically, a Visitation. Jerem. 66.

GOD himself treats of this Evil, Isa. 45, 7. I am the LORD, and there is none else forming light, and creating darkness, making peace, and creating evil: I the LORD, doing all these things. And Amos 3, 6. Shall there be evil in a city, which the LORD hath not done? And Lam. Jer. 3, 37. & 38. Who is he that hath said, and it cometh to pass, when the LORD commandeth it not? Out of the mouth of the most High proceedeth not evil and good?

II. Δοκιμασία, or Exploration, or Probation, is an affliction, either of the mind, or of the body, or of both at once, which GOD inflicts upon his pious and elect, that he may prove their faith in divine promises, their patience in adversities, their obedience toward the Law of GOD, and exercise them in works of piety. In the Scriptures this kind of affliction is more often called divine Temptation: concerning which the Apostle to his Corinthians: There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but GOD is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able: but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it, 1. Cor. 10, 13. And James treats of this kind of affliction as a common place, saying, Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, δόκιμος γενόμενος, he shall receive the crown of life, which GOD hath promised to them that love him: Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of GOD: for GOD tempteth no man to evil. James 1, 12. & 13.

Nor do the pious pray against this Temptation or affliction in the Lord's Prayer: Lead us not into temptation: For they know that it is joined with great use and fruit: since Vexation giveth understanding: Isa. 28, 19. But they only pray that GOD may not permit them to be tempted above their strength, but may bestow strength and patience, by which, being sustained, they may be able to bear the temptation.

To this pertain those testimonies of Scripture which expressly mention the probation of the pious, as Gen. 22, 1. GOD did tempt Abraham, and said: Take thy son, thine only begotten, and offer him for a burnt offering. Deut. 8, 2. Thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy GOD led thee through the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, and to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no? Psal. 66, 10. Thou, O GOD, hast proved us: thou hast tried us with fire (of tribulation), as silver is tried. 1. Pet. 1, 6. & 7. Ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: that the trial of your faith, being much more precious than gold.

Concerning these afflictions of the pious, a Question was raised in previous years among Orthodox Theologians, whether they ought to be defined simply by δοκιμασία or probation: or whether they also take on the nature and respect of punishment? Where the Theologians went into different opinions: But this knot is most rightly solved if a response is not given in either direction, neither affirming nor denying, or a simple Categorical one: but certain respects, both on the part of GOD who sends them and on the part of the Elect who suffer such afflictions, are accurately considered. For there are afflictions of the pious which take on the definition of τιμωρίαι or punishments: there are also afflictions of the same which take on the nature of δοκιμασίαι or probations: finally, there are those which, in a different respect, can be called both punishments and probations. For although it can happen that things which are purely δοκιμασίαι not rarely befall the pious: in which category the Calamity of Job is especially held: yet it hardly ever happens that some respect cannot at the same time be given, even in the pious and Elect, by reason of which their calamities have a respect to some Punishment. Certainly our protoparents, after the fall, though greatly reconciled to GOD, nevertheless endured punishments, such as being cast out of Paradise. Thus David, after committing adultery, is indeed reconciled to GOD: but nonetheless he is bereaved of his firstborn son by Bathsheba: he is driven into exile by his son Absalom: he is forced to choose a three-day plague as a punishment for his pride: That all these obtained the nature of punishment is clearly evident from the Scriptures.

Most rightly, therefore, is it answered to the proposed Question, that the afflictions of the pious are neither punishments properly so called: nor purely and simply δοκιμασίαι. The former, because GOD punishes even in the elect wicked concupiscences, which often erupt into most sad acts; and thus he restrains their flesh. In which respect they obtain some nature of punishment, according to that of Micah 7, 9. I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned against him: But now, insofar as those very punishments do not proceed from an angry GOD, and are finally directed toward most useful ends: in this respect, certainly, those afflictions do not admit the definition of Punishments properly so called. They are therefore of a mixed kind; insofar as the causes and ends of one thing can be diverse: so that one and the same calamity in the Elect can be called, but in a loose sense, and as it were improperly, a Punishment for committed sins, and a remedy for future ones; but it ought properly to be called a trial, for the following reasons: 1. Because it is not sent by an angry GOD. 2. Because it does not lead to the destruction, but the salvation of the elect. 3. Because it lasts for a small interval of time, or at least is finished by the limits of this life: whereas a Punishment properly so called both has GOD as an angry judge, and is in this life the beginning of eternal punishments, never to be finished in hell. 4. Because in this case the justice of GOD always runs with mercy, as Lyra speaks, that is, just as a Father chastises his Sons, so GOD chastises the elect gently and moderately: but the wicked are forced to taste the dregs of the fury of the Lord.

III. Kind

Latin:

De Natura, generibus & causis afflictionum humanarum.

CAlamitâtes sive afflictiones, quibus pij & impij hâc in vitâ exercentur, in Scripturis sacris interdum Crucis vocabulo indigetantur; interdum verò Judicia DOMINI nominantur. CRUCIS appellatio analogiam quandam & allusionem habet ad Crucem Christi Servatoris, quem uti oportuit pati & mori: & ita intrare in gloriam suam Luc. 24, 26? Ita omnes etiam eos, qui Christum sequi volunt, Crucem suam tollere, & per multas tribulationes in regnum cœlorum ingredi par est. Math. 10. 38. & cap. 16, 24, Marci 8, 34. Luc. 9, 23. Luc. 14, 27. Actor. 14, 21. Judicia autem Domini appellantur: non modò, quia DEUS eas immittens, justus est: & nemini facit injuriam: sed etiam, quia priusquàm illas immittit, denunciaret eas per Ministros suos, & quasi sententiam de accusatis & convictis hominibus ferre solet.

Dividuntur autem Afflictiones sive Calamitates, primum ratione Temporis, in Æternas, & in Temporales.

Æternæ in Scripturis nominantur Vermis nunquàm moriturus: Ignis inextinguibilis: Tenebræ exteriores, ubi est fletus, & stridor dentium, Gehenna &c. De his autem non hoc loco, sed infrà in Articulo de Inferno futura nobis disputatio. Dicuntur autem hæ æternæ, non ratione principij, sed finis nunquam finiendi.

Temporales sunt & dicuntur, quæ certo temporis intervallo, vel etiam vitæ hujus terminis, carnisq; nostræ corruptione terminantur. Et hæ ratione subjecti, rursus sunt duplices: Vel enim sunt Internæ, & animi, Quales sunt, Cæcitas & furor mentis à DEO, justo judicio desertæ ac induratæ: & propterea in omnibus consilijs, studijs, & actionibus graviter errantis, inq; suum & aliorum exitium, cœco quasi impetu ruentis. Cœcitatis hujus effectus est, Mala Conscientia, orta ex cogitatione commissorum scelerum, & sensu iræ DEI, conjuncta cum horribili

bus afflictionum.

pavore, anxietate, trepidatione, dolore, & cruciatu cordis, propter metum malorum ac pœnarum singulis momentis impendentium. Vel sunt Externa & corpora: & hæ rursus vel privata, vel publica. Privata sunt fermè infinitæ, quæ bona Corporis & Fortunæ, vel plane tollunt, vel enormiter lædunt, aut salutem imminuunt: Quales sunt, Calumnia & injuria, quibus fama, & existimatio nostra impeditur: Amissio facultatum: in fœlix conjugium: Liberorum inobedientia: amicorum perfidia: & consimiles aliæ innumerabiles, Publica sunt, quæ vel integram regionem, vel civitatem saltem & Rempub, nostram infestant: Quales sunt in Catalogo Maledictionum divinarum Levit. 26, 14. & seqq. Deuter. 28. 15. & seqq. longâ serie enumerantur: Varia videlicet morborum genera: incursiones hostiles: sterilitas terræ: bestiæ grassantes: bella & obsidiones urbium: pestilentia: fames horrenda: vastationes urbium: exilium & dissipatio populi: Servitus: Incendia & conflagrationes ædium: Quibus addi possunt Eversiones Rerumpublicarum: mutationes imperiorum, & id genus aliæ infinitæ. Quanquam verò hæ quoq? publicæ calamitates usq; adeò sunt variæ & multiplices, ut in certas classes redigi vix possint: Spiritus Sanctus tamen apud Prophetas, Ezechielem cumprimis cap. 14, 21. ad quatuor summâ quasi genera, singulas & universas revocat: nempe, Gladium, Famem, Bestias & Pestilentiam. Sic Ieremiæ 15, 2. & 3. non modò eâdem genera recitantur: sed etiam tertij generis species quædam exprimuntur, canes, volatilia cæli, & bestiæ terræ: Sic enim DEUS ipse ad Prophetam: Si dixerint ad te: Quò egrediemur? dices ad eos: Hæc dicit DOMINVS: Qui ad mortem, ad mortem: & qui ad gladium, ad gladium: & qui ad famem, ad famem: & qui ad captivitatem, ad captivitatem: Et visitabo super eos quatuor species, dicit DOMINVS: Gladium ad occisionem; Canes ad lacerandum; Volatilia cæli, & bestias terræ ad devorandum; & dissipandum; & dabo eos in fervorem sivè commotionem universis regnis terræ.

Porrò Calamitates sive afflictiones respectu finium, quorum gratia illæ à DEO immittuntur, dividuntur in quatuor diversas species, vel enim sunt τιμωρίαι pœnæ, vel δοκιμασίαι explorationes, sive probationes; vel μαρτύρια; vel λύτρον sive Redemtionis precium.

I. Τιμωρίαι sive Pœnæ sunt afflictiones vel Internæ, vel externæ, quas DEUS immittit, ad puniendum peccata hominum, ut suam partim declaret justitiam, partim contumaces corrigat, partim deniq; alios, istorum exemplo, à peccatis deterreat. In Scholis Theologorum, primum hoc afflictionum genus usitatè vocatur Malum pœnæ, sive malum supplicij. In Scripturis autem sæpissimè Malum simpliciter, fine adjecta determinatione ullâ nominatur; item ira & furor DEI: Indignatio DEI, vel συνεκδοχικῶς Visitatio. Ierem. 66.

De hoc Malo agit DEUS ipse, Jesa. 45, 7. Ego DOMINUS, & non est alser formans lucem, & creans tenebras, faciens pacem, & creans malum: ego DOMINVS, faciens omnia hæc Et Amos 3, 6. Anne erit malum in civitate, quod non fecerit DOMINUS; Et Thren. Jerm. 3, 37. & 38. Quis est ille, qui dixit, aliquid fieri DOMINO non jubente: Ex ore altissimi annon egrediuntur & bona, & mala?

II. Δοκιμασία, sive Exploratio, aut Probatio, est afflictio, vel animi, vel corporis, vel utriusque simul, quam DEUS pijs & electis suis imperitit, ut eorum fidem in promissiones divinas, patientiam in adversis, obedientiam erga Legem DEI, probet, & in pietatis operibus exerceat. In Scripturis vocatur hoc afflictionis genus sæpiùs Tentatio divina: de quâ Apostolus ad Corinthios suos: Tentatio vos non apprehendit, nisi humana: Fidelis enim DEVS, qui non patitur vos tentari supra vires: sed largitur cum tentatione jalararem exitum, ut sufferre possitu, 1. Cor. 10, 13. Et Jacobus locum quasi communem integrum de hoc afflictionis genere pertractat, Beatus vir, inquiens, qui suffert tentationem: quoniam cum probatus fuerit, δόκιμος γενόμενος, accipiet coronam vitæ, quàm compromisit DEVS diligentibus se: Nemo cùm tentur, dicat, se tentari à DEO: quia DEVS neminem tentat ad malum. Jacob 1, 12. & 13.

Neq; hanc sive Tentationem, sive afflictionem deprecantur pij in precatione Dominicâ: Ne nos inducas in tentationem: Noverunt enim eam cum magno usu ac fructu esse conjunctam: siquidem Vexatio dat intellectum: Esa. 28, 19. Sed tantúm orant, ut ne DEUS supra vires permittat se tentari, sed robur ac patientiam largiatur, quâ sustentati, tentationi ferundæ parés esse possint.

Pertinent huc ea Scripturæ testimonia quæ ex professo probationis piorum meminerunt, ut Gen. 22, 1. Tentavit DEVS Abraham, & dixit: Tolle filium tuum unigenitum, & offer eum in holocaustum. Deut. 8, 2. Recordaberis itineris per desertum, per quod adduxit te DOMINVS DEVS tuus, ut affligeret te, atque tentaret, & nota fierent, quæ in tuo versabantur animo, utrum custodires mandata illius, annon? Psal 66, 10. Tu Demine probasti nos : & igni (tribulationis) nos examinasti, sicut examinatur argentum 1. Pet. 1, 6. & 7. Oportet modicum vos contristarem variis tentatio nibus: ut probatio vestræ fidei, multò preciosior inveniatur auro.

De his afflictionibus piorum mota fuit superioribus annis, inter Orthodoxos Theologos, Quæstio, An ea simpliciter per δοκιμασίαν sive probationem definiri debeant: an vero pœnæ etiam rationem & respectum fortiantur? Ubi in diversas sententias abierunt Theologi: Rectissimè autem nodus iste solvitur, si in neutram partem, neque affirmantem, neque negantem, sive simplex Categorica detur responsio: sed certi respectus tùm ex parte DEI immittentis, tùm ex parte Electorum sufferentium hujusmodi afflictiones, accuratè considerentur. Dantur enim afflictiones piorum, quæ τιμωριῶν sive pœnarum definitionem fortiuntur: dantur etiam afflictiones eorundem, quæ δοκιμασιῶν sive probationum naturam induunt: dantur denique, quæ diverso respectu, & pœnæ, & probationes dici possunt. Etsi enim fieri potest, ut haud rarò pijs obtingant, quæ purè sunt δοκιμασίαι: quo in genere præcipue habetur Calamitas Jobis: vix tamen unquam fit, ut non simul respectus aliquis dari possit, in pijs etiam & Electis, ratione cujus calamitates ipsorum Pœnæ alicujus respectum habeant. Certè protoparentes nostri, post lapsum maximè reconciliati DEO, pœnas tamen sustinuerunt, ut quòd ejecti sunt è Paradiso. Sic David post commissum adulterium, reconciliatur quidem DEO: sed nihilominus orbatur filio primogenito Bethsabæ: pellitur à filio Absolone in exilium: pestem triduanam, in pœnam superbiæ, expetiri cogitur: Quæ omnia pœnæ rationem obtinuisse, ex Scripturis liquidò constat.

Rectissimè ergò ad Quæstionem propositam respondetur, afflictiones piorum neque pœnas esse propriè sic dictas: neque purè ac simpliciter δοκιμασίας. Prius illud ideò, quia DEUS in electis quoque pravas concupiscentias, sæpiùs in actus tristissimos erumpentes, punit; & sic carnem ipsorum coërcet. Quo respectu pœnæ rationem aliquam obtinent, secundum illud Michææ 7, 9. Iram Domini portabo, qui peccavi ei: Jam verò quatenus illæ ipsæ pœnæ non ab irato DEO proveniunt, & ad fines utilissimos tandem diriguntur: hoc sanè respectu Pœnæ propriè sic dictæ definitionem, afflictiones illæ non, admittunt. Sunt ergò eæ mixti alicujus generis; quatenus unius rei causæ & fines possunt esse diversi: ita ut una eademq; calamitas in Electis dici possit, sed in laxa significatione, & quasi impropriè Pœna commissorum peccatorum, & remedium futurorum; Proprie autem dici debeat exploratio, propter sequentes causas: 1. Quia non ab irato DEO immittitur. 2. Quia non cedit ad de structionem, sed salutem electorum. 3. Quia exiguo temporis intervallo durat, vel certè vita hujus ter minis finitur: cum Pœna proprie sic dicta & DEUM iratum judicem habeat, & hac in vitâ sit initium æternarum pœnarum, in inferno nunquam finiendarum. 4. Quia hoc casu justitia DEI semper currit cum misericordia, uti Lyra loquitur, hoc est, quemadmodum Pater Filios, ita DEUS electos leniter & moderatè castigat: impij autem feces furoris Domini gustare coguntur.

III. Genus


### Chapter I. On the Nature, genera and causes of human afflictions: Difference of the species of Martyrdom

III. The kind of calamities of the elect is called μαρτύριον, which is nothing else than a singular gift of GOD, by which, on account of Christ, for the sake of bearing holy witness to the Evangelical truth, out of true faith, the elect patiently suffer any adversity whatsoever, or even pour out their very life and blood.

Moreover, μαρτύριον is defined as being a gift of GOD, as the Apostle teaches in Philip. chap. 1, 29: ἐχαρίσθη, it has been gifted, or it has been given freely to you, not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for him. The Apostle therefore expresses a singular kind of suffering, which is not a work of our own will and our own powers, but comes to us by the peculiar grace and gift of GOD. Otherwise, to suffer is common to all, good and bad: in this respect, therefore, it is not a singular gift of GOD; indeed, it is rather an evil by its own nature, because it is Φθαρτικὸν τῆς Φύσεως, a destruction or corruption: but all things seek their own preservation. Thus, to suffer for a bad cause, for committed crimes and wicked deeds, is not a gift, but rather the wrath and justice of GOD. But to suffer for a good cause, especially for Christ and the truth of the Gospel, is a singular gift of GOD, and it is an honorable thing, finally to be compensated in eternal life with an unfading crown of glory.

Then, in the place of specific differences, Martyrdom is defined as being a suffering for Christ and for the truth of the Gospel. In which part, so that we may nowhere stumble, but may be certain where and when it is permitted to glory in Martyrdom, two things must be well noted. One from the part of the acting subject, or of him who inflicts the suffering: as if it happens that you are oppressed by hatred and envy, that you are proscribed, cast into prison, driven into exile, afflicted with torments and death: I say, that all these things are committed against you, not because of your crimes and sins, but only because of Christ, and indeed not because of just any Christ: for the Romanists, and the Calvinists, and all heretics have a false and fictitious Christ: but because of that true Christ whom the Apostles preached. Thus, not because of any doctrine of Christ, but because of that which is handed down and revealed in the writings of the Apostles. For there is also given a true heresy, for which he who suffers is a martyr not of Christ, but of the Devil. Such as were the Donatists of old, from whom Augustine denies the eulogy of martyrs for the reason that they indeed suffered, but not for the true Christ and for his doctrine, but because of their crimes and contumacy against the Emperors. August. Epist. 61 to Dulcitius: and Tom. 7 against Cresconius the Donatist Grammarian. To which pertains that saying of Cyprian, frequently repeated by Augustine: It is not the punishment, but the cause that makes a true martyr. The other from the part of the suffering subject, or of him who endures the suffering, so that not only

those who persecute do so only because of Christ, whom you confess: but also that you do not suffer all things for any other cause than because of Christ and the truth, and not indeed because of a desire for fame and immortality, or because of other causes, bringing on a weariness of this life out of a certain impatience: and therefore, that you suffer all things out of true faith and love for Christ and his doctrine. Looking to which, Cyprian truly wrote: Where there is not charity, and the true love of Christ and the church, there true Martyrdom is not: and he cannot show himself a martyr who has not held brotherly charity. Cyprian, treatise 3 on the simplicity of prelates, page 108.

Two species of martyrdom are commonly established: one is Bloodless, which belongs to those confessors of Christ who indeed do not pour out their blood, but for Christ and the truth of the Gospel undergo and sustain many indignities, calumnies, ignominy, prisons, exiles, and infinite other dangers with a brave spirit: prepared also to undergo death itself, if GOD so wills and necessity brings it.

The other is Bloody, of those who so freely confess Christ before Tyrants that by that very act they not only neglect all good things, but also pour out their life and blood. And these, as Augustine teaches, and before him Cyprian, were held κατ' ἐξοχήν as martyrs only. For they are martyrs, says Augustine, who on account of the testimony of Christ have been weakened by various sufferings, and have struggled for the truth even unto death. Tom. 8 in Psalm 118. Although Cyprian does not exclude the former from the census of martyrs: For they, he says, did not lack torments, but torments lacked them. Epist. book 3, epist. 6.

The Fathers established the effect of Martyrdom as by far the greatest, so that Cyprian did not hesitate to write that Martyrdom is at once both baptism and a crown, because it both baptizes and crowns. Which opinion is easily admitted, if only it is understood of metaphorical baptism, of which the Savior speaks, Matth. 20. 22, Mark 10. 35, to the mother of the sons of Zebedee: Can you be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?

The Fathers added to the same, that the souls of the martyrs in heaven intercede with GOD for us: for they are not deprived in the heavens of either the memory of the Church, militant here on earth, or of brotherly charity; since, as the Apostle testifies, Charity never falls away or fails: 1 Cor. 13:8. We also add our vote to this opinion, if it is understood of that general affection of the Saints in heaven, by which in general they desire the well-being of their brothers still living in this age. But that from this any distinct or particular knowledge of all things which are done in this world can be assigned to them, and from that the invocation of the Saints can in any way be constructed or established, that indeed has no [basis] in the Scriptures clearly has a foundation, and is diametrically opposed to the analogy of faith. Augustine himself acknowledged this, writing that he did not know whether they pray in particular for this or that person in heaven: Vol. 4, On the care to be taken for the dead, ch. 15 and following. However, the ancient Church acted rightly, which held the memory of the martyrs in such high esteem that it diligently recorded their names and made a commemoration of them in the public assembly of the Church as often as the Lord's Supper was celebrated: with thanks solemnly given to God that He had bestowed such grace upon this or that brother, that he had constantly professed the name of Christ even unto death. Nor did it sin in this, that the bodies or corpses of the martyrs, which were left unburied by profane men, were collected by faithful brothers and buried in secret places, which are now called crypts: they also gathered in vain the ashes of those either torn apart by beasts or burned by fire, and buried them in a more sacred place. For all these things were done for the glory of God, and so that the remaining living brothers might be stirred up to constancy of faith. It was also a work of piety that the bodies, which had been temples of the Holy Spirit, should not be neglected or allowed to be trampled under the feet of beasts. But the Devil, the enemy of the Church, converted both of these efforts of the Church in honoring the martyrs into a most foul idolomania: the former indeed into the cult and adoration of the Saints: the latter, however, into that monstrous historical devotion and veneration which is still today, under the Papacy, solemnly offered to the relics, as they are called, of the martyrs and saints: as will be shown in the following article.

But just as these men sin enormously in excess, so in the old Church those heretics gravely stumbled on the side of defect, who, as Philastrius testifies, taught that it is foolish to suffer death for the confession of the name of Christ, since Christ and the Truth can be denied without crime. For it is written in Psalm 15 that he who speaks truth in his heart shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord and be blessed; it does not say, in his tongue, but in his heart: It is enough, therefore, if each person retains truth and faith in his heart. As if speaking truth in the heart did not presuppose confession of the mouth. David himself certainly says in Psalm 116: I believed, therefore I have spoken. And the Apostle in Romans 10: With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation; and the Savior Himself in Matthew 10: Whoever does not confess me before men, him I also will not confess before my heavenly Father. Therefore a gross sophistication of the phrase is committed. For to speak truth in one's heart is the same as to confess candidly, sincerely, and without deceit or hypocrisy, nay, as David has it, to speak the truth: that this is done with the mouth, no one is so dull as not to understand. Eusebius, in book 6, chapter 33 of his Ecclesiastical History, refutes this error of Basilides, the Helcesaites, and the Priscillianists with many arguments.

and Augustine, Vol. 4, Against Lying, to Consentius, ch. 2, and proves that martyrdom consists in confession, not in dissimulation: For from what is one called a martyr, if not from confession? But enough about martyrdom.

IV. A kind of calamity is the λύτρον or price of redemption for us: and it is that most bitter Passion which the Son of God alone, in our place, in His most holy soul and body, endured to satisfy the justice of God for us. The Son of God claims this kind of calamity as so proper to Himself that He admits no one among men as a partner or colleague: For He alone trod the winepress of divine wrath, and with Him there was no man from the peoples, Isaiah 63:3.

And thus far concerning the various kinds of calamities: It follows that we should investigate their true and proper causes.

Latin:

III. Genus Calamitatum Electorum dicitur μαρτύριον, quod nihil est aliud, quàm singulare DEI donum, quo propter Christum, ad perhibendum Sanctum Veritati Evangelicæ testimonium, ex vera fide, vel adversa quævis Electi patienter sufferunt, vel ipsam etiam vitam ac sanguinem profundunt.

Definitur autem μαρτύριον esse donum DEI, sic docente Apostolo Philip. cap. 1, 29. ἐχαρίσθη Donatum, sive gratis datum est vobis, non tantùm credere in Christum, sed etiam pro eo pati. Singulare ergo passionis genus exprimit Apostolus, quod non nostri arbitrij nostrarumque virium opus sit: sed peculiari gratia & dono DEI nobis obtingat. Aliàs Pati, commune est omnibus, bonis & malis: H oc ergò respectu non est singulare DEI donum: imò potius est malum suâ natura: quia est Φθαρτικὸν τῆς Φύσεως, destructio, sive corruptio: omnia autem appetunt sui conservationem. Sic pati pro malâ causa, pro admissis sceleribus & flagitijs, non est donum, sed ira potiùs & justitia DEI.Verùm pati prò causâ bonâ, præsertim pro Christo, & Veritate Evangelij, singulare DEI donum est, & res est honorifica, tandem iu æternâ vitâ immarcescibili gloriæ corona compensanda.

Deinde differentiæ specificæ loco definitur Martyrium, quod sit Passio pro Christo, & pro veritate Evangelij, Quâ in parte ut nuspiam impingamus: sed certi esse possimus, Ubi & quando de Martyrio gloria liceat, duo probè notanda veniunt. Vnum ex parte Subjecti agentis, sive illius, qui passionem infert: ut si contingat, te odio ac in vidiâ premi, te proscribi, in carcerem conjici, in exilium pelli, tormentis & morte affici: ut inquam hæc omnia in te committantur, non propter tua scelere & pecca ta: sed tantùm propter Christum, & quidem non propter quemcunque Christum: Habent enim & Romanenses, & Calviniani, & uulli non hæretici, sed falsum & fictitium Christum: Verùm propter Christum illum verum, quem Apostoli prædicarunt. Sic non propter quamcunque doctrinam Christi: sed propter e am, quæ in scriptis Apostolorum est tradita & revelata. Datur enim & vera hæresis, pro quâ qui patitur, non Christi, sed Diaboli Martyr est. Quales olim fuerunt Donatistæ, quibus Martyrum elogium ideò derogat Augustinus, quòd passi quidem sint, sed non pro Christo vero, proque doctrinâ; sed propter scelera &c contumaciam in Imperatores. August. Epist. 61. ad Dulcitium: & Tom. 7. contra Cresconium Grammaticum Donatistam. Quò pertinet illud Cypriani, frequenter ab Augustino repetitum: Non pœna: sed causa veram facit Martyrem. Alterum ex parte Subjecti patientis, sive illius, qui passionem perfert, ut non tantùm

"qui de persequuntur, id faciant propter Solum Christum, quem confiteris: sed &c, ut tu non aliam ob causam, quam propter "Christum & veritatem, non vero propter 'nominis gloriam, & immortalitatem, vel 'propter causas alias, vitae hujus taedium ex 'impatientia quadam adferentes: ac proin- 'de, ut ex vera fide & dilectione in Christum, ejusq; doctrinae omnia patiaris. Quo respiciens Cyprianus vere scripsit: Vbi non est caritas, veraq; Christi & ecclesiae dilectio, ibi verum Martyrium non est: & exhibere se non potest Martyrem, qui fraternam non tenuit charitatem. Cyprian. tractatu 3. de simplicitate praelatorum. pag. 108.

Martyrij duae vulgo constituuntur species: Unum Incruentum, quod eorum est confessorum Christi, qui sanguinem quidem non fundunt; sed pro Christo & veritate Evangelij multa indigna, calumnias, ignominiam, carceres, exilia, & infinita alia pericula forti subeunt & sustinent animo: parati, ipsam quoque subire mortem, si ita DEUS velit, & necessitas ferat.

Alterum est Cruentum, eorum, qui ita libere Christum coram Tyrannis profitentur, ut ipso actu non bona modo omnia negligant, sed & vitam ac sanguinem profundant. Et hi docente Augustino, ac ante ipsum Cypriano, κατ' ἐξοχήν pro Martyribus tantum habiti fuerunt. Martyres enim sunt, inquit Augustinus, qui propter testimonium Christi, diversis passionibus debilitati sunt, & usque ad mortem pro veritate decertarunt. Tom. 8. in Psal. 118. Quanquam Cyprianus priores illos ex censu Martyrum non eximit: Non enim, inquit, illi defuerunt tormentis: sed tormenta defuerunt illis. Epist. lib. 3. epist. 6.

Effectum Martyrij Patres constituerunt longe maximum, ita ut Cyprianus scribere non dubitaverit, Martyrium simul esse & baptismum, & coronam, quia & baptizet, & coronet. Quae sententia facile admittitur, si modo intelligatur de baptismo metaphorico, de quo Servator, Matth. 20. 22. Marc. 10. 35. ad matrem filiorum Zebedaei: Potestis baptizari baptismo, quo ego baptizor.

Addiderunt ijsdem Patres, animas Martyrum in coelo interpellare DEUM pro nobis: neque enim eos in coelis destitui vel memoria Ecclesiae, hisce in terris militantis, vel fraterna charitate; siquidem Apostolo teste, Charitas nunquam excidat aut deficiat: 1. Cor. 13, 8. Cui sententiae nostrum quoque calculum adjicimus, si de generali illo affectu Sanctorum in coelis accipiatur, quo in genere bene esse cupiunt fratribus suis, hoc in seculo adhuc viventibus. Verum ut inde vel discreta aliqua, sive particularis rerum omnium, quae hoc in mundo aguntur, notitia, illis assignari, indeque Sanctorum in vocatio quoque modo extrui aut stabiliri possit, id vero in Scripturis nullum planè habet fundamentum, & analogiæ fidei è diametro repugnat. Quod ipsum agnovit etiam Augustinus, scribens se nescire, utrum in particulari pro hoc, aut illo orent in cælis: Tom. 4. de curâ pro mortuis gerenda: cap. 15. & sequentibus. Rectè autem fecit antiqua Ecclesia, quæ Martyrum memoriam in tanto habuit pretio, ut eorum nomina diligenter annotaret, & eorum in publico Ecclesiæ cœtu faceret commemorationem, quoties Cœna Domini celebrabatur: gratijs solenniter actis Deo, quòd huic aut illi fratri tantam præstitisset gratiam, ut usque ad mortem constanter Christi nomen professus fuerit. Neque etiam in eo peccavit, quòd corpora sive cadavera Martyrum, quæ à profanis homininibus insepulta relinquebantur, per fideles fratres collegerunt, & in secretis locis, quæ nunc Cryptæ vocantur, sepelierunt: frustra etiam & cineres, vel à bestijs discerptorum, vel igni combustorum, comportarunt, & loco sacratiore condiderunt. Fiebant enim hæc omnia in gloriam DEI, & ut reliqui fratres viventes ad fidei constantiam excitarentur. Erat etiam pietatis opus, ut corpora, quæ fuiffent templa Spiritus Sancti, non negligerentur, vel bestiarum pedibus conculcanda permitterentur. Sed hostis Ecclesiæ Diabolus, utrumque istud Ecclesiæ studium in honorandis Martyribus, in fœdissimam idolomaniã convertit: prius quidem illud in cultum & adorationem Sanctorum: Posterius verò hoc in monstHistoricam illam devotionem, & venerationem quæ hodieq́; sub Papatu, Reliquiis, quas vocant, Martyrum, & Sanctorum solenniter defertur: uti sequenti articulo ostendetur.

QUemadmodum verò hi in excessu enormiter peccant, ita in veteri Ecclesia ex parte defectus graviter impingebant illi hæretici, qui teste Philastrio, docuerunt, Stultum esse, ferre mortem, propter confessionem nominis Christi, cùm citra crimen possit & Christus, & Veritas negari. Esse enim scriptum in Psalmo 15, illum ascensurum in montem Domini, & beatum fore, qui loquitur veritatem in corde suo, non ait, in linguâ, sed in corde: Satis igitur esse, si quisq; veritatem & fidem retineat in corde suo. Quasi verò loqui veritatem in corde, non præsupponat confessionem oris. Idem certè David, Psal. 116. Credidi, inquit, propterea locutus sum. Et Apostolus Rom. 10. Corde creditur ad justitiam, Ore autem fit confessio ad salutem; Et Servator ipse Matth. 10. Qui me non confessus fuerit coram hominibus, eundem neque ego confitebor coram Patre meo cœlesti. Committitur ergò crassa Sophisticatio phrasews. Loqui enim veritatem in corde suo, idem est, ac candidè, sincerè, & sine dolo ac hypocrisi, confiteri, imò, ut David habet, loqui veritatem: id quod Ore fieri, nemo tàm bardus est, quin intelligat. Errorem istum Basilidis Helcesuitarum, Priscillianistarum multis nervosè refutat Eusebius lib. 6. cap. 33. hist. eccl.

& Augustinus Tom. 4. contra mendacium ad Consentium, cap. 2. & probat Martyrium in confessione consistere, non in dissimulatione: Unde enim dicitur Martyr, nisi à Confessione? Sed de Martyrio satis.

IV. Genus Calamitatum est λύτρον sive pretium redemtionis pro nobis: & est acerbissima illa Passio, quam solus Filius DEI, loco nostri, in sanctissima animâ & corpore suo, ad satisfaciendum pro nobis justitiæ Dei sustinuit. Hoc calamitatis genus ita sibi proprium Filius DEI vendicat, ut neminem ex hominibus socium vel collegam admittat: Ipse enim solus torcular iræ divinæ calcavit, & cum ipso non fuit vir de hominibus Jesa. 63. v. 3.

Et hactenus quidem de variis calamitatum generibus: Sequitur: ut earũ causas veras ac proprias investigemus.


### Chapter I. On the Nature, genera and causes of human afflictions: Of the Causes of afflictions

On this question, it does not seem the same to everyone. Therefore, so that we may investigate the truth more correctly, we will proceed little by little by removal of false opinions, κατ᾽ ἄρσιν καὶ θέσιν, to the position of true doctrine.

And indeed, from the beginning, there have been found long ago, and are found today, ἐμπαĩκται, mockers, and swine from the herd of Epicurus, who ascribed afflictions, just as all other things, to blind chance and a certain volatility of Fortune, ἀπὸ τῆς ἐνοικόσης ἀυτῆς ἀθεότητος, through a certain indwelling impiety, as Basil says. But to the fury of these men, rather than to their error, we have opposed above in the Exegesis of the Article concerning the Providence of GOD a just and accurate Refutation. In this place, let it suffice that Holy Scripture expressly refers each and every thing that is done and carried out under the Sun to the providence of GOD: so much so that not even the steps of men, the flight of sparrows, the falling of hairs, nay, not even lots should be excluded from it: Jerem. 10. v. 23. Proverb. 5. v. 21. & cap. 16. v. 1, 2. & 9. & 33. Matth. 10. v. 29. & 30. Coloss. 1. v. 17. Hebr. 1. v. 3. Solomon, certainly the most wise king, expressly teaches that a happy and prosperous state of a kingdom, and fruitful successes in carrying out affairs, are to be hoped for and sought from GOD alone, 1. Kings 3. v. 9. The Prophet Amos writes that there is no evil or punishment in a city which the LORD has not done, chap. 3. v. 6. Jeremiah in the Lamentations, chap. 3. v. 37. Who is this, he says, who dares to say that anything happens without the LORD commanding it? That from the mouth of the Most High there do not proceed either good or evil: namely, the evils of punishments and afflictions. Therefore, let the profanity of these men depart.

II. There are, moreover, others who were in the habit of saying that all things happen by Fate, and they wove a certain everlasting series of immutable causes, included within the very nature of things and the world. This error was noted long ago in the Stoics by Augustine, saying: 'These men call things fatal which, apart from the will of God and men, happen by the necessity of some Order.' Book 5, On the City of God, chapter 1. For if they understood by Fate the very will and power of God, considered however without any coercion and Stoic violence: they would certainly hold the opinion, but ought to correct the language: as Augustine rightly adds in the same place. Now, however, what they understood by Fate is clear from this: 1. that they distinguished Fate from God: and contended that not only the will of men, but God himself also, is subject to it. 2. They attributed to secondary causes fixed in nature that power by which they could act of themselves and produce any effects whatsoever by their own strengths. 3. They established the series of those causes as absolutely immutable, and therefore they opined that all things happen and come to pass by an absolute and simple necessity, as Augustine reports, Book 5, On the City of God, chapters 8, 9, 10. Such a Fate, therefore, labors under stupendous profanity: so that Augustine did not judge badly that the Stoics would never have believed in such a fate, unless their own heart had been fatuous. We, however, oppose to this profanity, at the beginning, those very testimonies of Scripture by which we just now crushed the madness of the Epicureans. Then, the prophetic predictions of punishments: as also the events corresponding exactly to the predictions. For example: Jeroboam, the first king of Israel, when he was building two golden idolatrous calves: not only is the overthrow of that idolatry predicted by a prophet from the tribe of Judah; but King Josiah is even named, more than three hundred years before he was born, 1 Kings 13:2, 2 Kings 23:15. And Isaiah, chapter 44:28 and chapter 45:1, not only predicts the liberation of the Jewish people from the Babylonian captivity, to happen almost two hundred years later: but he even names the Persian King Cyrus, who was to grant the Jews a return to their homeland. Jeremiah likewise not only establishes a certain number of years during which the Babylonian captivity would last, Jer. 25:12 and chapter 29:10, but he even expressly predicts how many kings are to reign during the time of the captivity, Jer. 27:7. And Daniel not only preaches about the coming Messiah and his benefits: but he also establishes seventy weeks of years, within which Christ was to come, chapter 9:24. Truly, no fatal series of causes can be given or shown here. Away, therefore, with this impiety of the Stoics; to which is also most rightly opposed, in the third place, that condition added to the prophetic threats of punishments. 'If that nation against whom I have spoken turns from its evil, I will also repent of the evil that I thought to do to it.' Jer. 18:8.

which is most evidently demonstrated by the example of the Ninevites, who repented at the preaching of Jonah.
